title: Prevention: stopping disease before it starts
question: What can be prevented — heart attacks, strokes, diabetes, cancer, fractures, infections — and what does the evidence say actually works?
balance: Prevention is where this library’s evidence is strongest and strangest. Some of it is medicine’s greatest hits: folic acid prevents neural tube defects; statins and blood-pressure treatment prevent heart attacks and strokes; HPV vaccination prevents cervical cancer. Some of it failed its trials: vitamin E did not prevent prostate cancer, beta-carotene caused lung cancer in smokers, and annual vitamin D mega-doses caused falls. This shelf lists every prevention question in the library, grouped by what you are trying to prevent — the wins, the nulls, and the backfires alike — and points to the shelf where each one’s evidence lives.
citation: SourceMed Shelf #1, “Prevention: stopping disease before it starts”, sourcemed.io

title: Albumin in sepsis & critical illness Deposit #1 · Oct 23, 2026
question: Does giving albumin change survival — and what do the level, and its fall, tell you?
balance: Giving albumin as a fluid does not change overall survival (SAFE; ALBIOS), with a hypothesis-generating hint in severe sepsis. The level and its trajectory are strong prognostic signals — persistently low or falling is worse, rising is better — but nearly all trajectory evidence is retrospective, and this shelf grades it Low, honestly. The resuscitation trials match the measurement lesson: albumin as a drug shows no overall mortality advantage; albumin as a measurement predicts by its trajectory, not its door value.
citation: SourceMed Shelf #2, “Albumin in sepsis & critical illness Deposit #1 · Oct 23, 2026”, sourcemed.io

title: Albuminuria thresholds & progression to CKD stage 3 Deposit #2 · Oct 23, 2026
question: Where does albuminuria risk actually begin — and what drives progression?
balance: Risk begins well inside the “normal” range — progression risk roughly doubles above a urine albumin of ~ 8.4 mg/g in type 2 diabetes, far below the standard 30 mg/g boundary, which is a consensus classification line rather than a risk inflection. Over decades, blood pressure drives albuminuria up, while blood pressure, smoking, and cholesterol drive kidney function down — and falling kidney function mechanically raises measured albuminuria on its own.
citation: SourceMed Shelf #3, “Albuminuria thresholds & progression to CKD stage 3 Deposit #2 · Oct 23, 2026”, sourcemed.io

title: Vitamin D and respiratory infection in adults Deposit #3 · Oct 23, 2026
question: Does vitamin D prevent or soften infections in adults — respiratory, tuberculosis, COVID-19, critical illness?
balance: The newest and largest synthesis (Jolliffe 2025) finds vitamin D’s overall effect on acute respiratory infection borderline and not significant (OR 0.94, p=0.057), with a residual signal in daily dosing (0.84) — while the dramatic 2017 benefit in the severely deficient (aOR 0.30) did not survive as effect modification in the update. Tuberculosis prevention shows no benefit; a critical-illness mortality signal (RR 0.78) rests on small trials and a route subgroup. Correcting deficiency remains sensible care; vitamin D is not a proven shield against infection in adults. The children evidence now lives on its own shelf, #37.
citation: SourceMed Shelf #4, “Vitamin D and respiratory infection in adults Deposit #3 · Oct 23, 2026”, sourcemed.io

title: Low phosphate, breathing muscles and weaning Deposit #4 · Oct 23, 2026
question: What does low phosphate do to breathing muscles, ventilator weaning, and survival?
balance: Low phosphate travels with weak breathing muscles and harder ventilator weaning — the 1988 classic showed strength returning as phosphate was repleted, but nothing here is randomized, and the weaning data rest on handfuls of events.
citation: SourceMed Shelf #5, “Low phosphate, breathing muscles and weaning Deposit #4 · Oct 23, 2026”, sourcemed.io

title: The 365-day supply evidence base Deposit #5 · Oct 23, 2026
question: How big is the treatment gap, how many people have diabetes — and what happens when medicines are dispensed in longer supplies?
balance: The gap is measured: statin use after heart disease or stroke is 14.6% worldwide, and no low- or middle-income region reaches the WHO 50% target. The population is counted: 589 million adults with diabetes, 42.8% undiagnosed. Longer supplies travel with better continuation wherever observed — 90 vs 30 days after heart procedures, and a full year of contraception. What does not exist anywhere on this shelf is a randomized trial of a full year’s supply of chronic medicines — that empty space is the trial this project exists to run.
citation: SourceMed Shelf #6, “The 365-day supply evidence base Deposit #5 · Oct 23, 2026”, sourcemed.io

title: Albumin & coronary calcium Deposit #7 · Oct 23, 2026
question: Does a lower serum albumin go with more coronary calcium and faster progression — and does LDL matter only when coronary calcium is present?
balance: Within the normal range, lower albumin goes with more coronary calcium and faster progression (Korea, Taiwan) — but the link is fragile: in the Taiwan cohort the coronary-calcium association disappeared once age was accounted for, and nothing on this shelf is randomized. The shelf’s strongest card is about LDL, not albumin: in 23,132 Danish patients, LDL predicted heart attacks and strokes only when coronary calcium was already present. Albumin here behaves as a marker travelling with age and inflammation — not a proven lever.
mesh: Serum Albumin · Coronary Artery Disease · Vascular Calcification · Atherosclerosis · Hypercholesterolemia · Disease Progression · Risk Factors · Longitudinal Studies

title: Grip strength, mortality and weaning Deposit #6 · Oct 23, 2026
question: What does a squeeze of the hand predict — about dying, and about coming off a ventilator?
balance: In the community, weaker grip is one of the most consistent mortality signals in epidemiology — per 5 kg lower grip, death rates run about 16–20% higher in half a million UK Biobank participants, dose-responsive across 3.1 million people pooled — and an uneven grip between the hands adds a further ~12%. In the ICU the picture splits: grip tracks difficult and prolonged weaning, but the largest study found it did not predict extubation failure, and the pooled extubation difference was not significant. Grip is a strong risk marker; nothing on this shelf shows that strengthening it changes outcomes.
citation: SourceMed Shelf #9, “Grip strength, mortality and weaning Deposit #6 · Oct 23, 2026”, sourcemed.io

title: Zinc and wound healing Deposit #9 · Oct 23, 2026
question: Does zinc — in the blood, by mouth, or on the skin — change whether diabetic foot and leg ulcers heal?
balance: Low zinc is common where ulcers are — 26.9% deficient in a prospective foot-clinic cohort — and lower zinc travels with ulcer presence and slower early healing. But the one prospective healing cohort found baseline zinc did not predict who healed (HR 1.05), and giving zinc is unproven: the positive diabetic-ulcer trial carries a 2024 Expression of Concern, the combined-nutrient pilot was neutral at 12 weeks, and Cochrane’s pooled verdict for venous ulcers is no benefit. Topical zinc has older, small positive trials. On this shelf, association does most of the work.
citation: SourceMed Shelf #10, “Zinc and wound healing Deposit #9 · Oct 23, 2026”, sourcemed.io

title: BMI and ICU extubation
question: Does a patient’s weight — especially being underweight — change the odds the breathing tube has to go back in after extubation?
balance: Both fully-checked cohorts point the same way: being underweight when the tube comes out travels with higher odds of needing it back within 72 hours — adjusted OR 1.58 in a 41,016-patient Japanese registry and 3.80 in a small Taiwan cohort — while obesity sat below the mid-range reference (0.69) in the big registry. Both studies are observational and graded Low: thin ICU patients are often ill in ways a BMI number doesn’t capture, so this reads as an association to weigh at the bedside, not a cause.
citation: SourceMed Shelf #11, “BMI and ICU extubation”, sourcemed.io

title: Cancer cachexia Deposit #11 · Oct 23, 2026
question: What is cancer cachexia, how much does it shorten life, and can anything be done about it?
balance: The definition is settled (Fearon 2011: weight loss >5%, or >2% with BMI <20 or sarcopenia — three stages) and the prognosis is precisely grim: median survival falls stepwise from 20.9 months (grade 0) to 4.3 months (grade 4) in 8,160 patients, CT muscle measures predict survival far better than BMI alone (concordance 0.92 vs 0.73), and sarcopenic obesity carries a fourfold mortality hazard. The mechanisms are real biology — lipolysis switched on, tumor PTHrP browning fat, MIC-1 switching appetite off, tumor vesicles driving muscle wasting through TLR4, glucose recycling running fivefold through the Cori cycle while glycogen stores empty, and autophagy switched on in muscle with its cleanup stalled — but treatment remains the honest gap: anamorelin adds lean mass in two phase III trials yet did not improve grip strength, a multimodal program preserved weight only in a small feasibility trial, and nothing on the shelf reverses the syndrome.
citation: SourceMed Shelf #12, “Cancer cachexia Deposit #11 · Oct 23, 2026”, sourcemed.io

title: Statin compliance and continuation Deposit #12 · Oct 23, 2026
question: What actually works to keep patients on their statins?
balance: Intensity works, nudges barely do: pharmacist-led multifaceted care after a heart event lifted statin adherence to 93.2% vs 71.3%, while automated reminders bought only 2–3 points, decision support was borderline (OR 1.18), texts did nothing (RR 0.93), a reminder device and a risk mailer were both null — and pharmacist counseling’s early persistence benefit was gone by 12 months.
mesh: Medication Adherence · Hydroxymethylglutaryl-CoA Reductase Inhibitors · Acute Coronary Syndrome · Secondary Prevention · Reminder Systems · Humans
citation: SourceMed Shelf #13, “Statin compliance and continuation Deposit #12 · Oct 23, 2026”, sourcemed.io

title: ACTH response, cortisol binding, and survival in sepsis Deposit #13 · Oct 23, 2026
question: In sepsis and septic shock, do cortisol levels, the ACTH stimulation response, and cortisol’s binding protein predict who dies — and does treating a blunted response help?
balance: The ACTH test sorts septic-shock patients by risk (26/67/82%), and the shelf now anchors how common failure is — 9% of severe-sepsis patients fail the test, split between secondary adrenal insufficiency and adrenal dysfunction — and the mechanism underneath: cortisol alone raises glucose production entirely through gluconeogenesis, and growth hormone raises it by sustaining glycogenolysis. The treatment evidence is still one 43-patient pilot.
citation: SourceMed Shelf #14, “ACTH response, cortisol binding, and survival in sepsis Deposit #13 · Oct 23, 2026”, sourcemed.io

title: Feeding hospitalized patients Deposit #14 · Oct 23, 2026
question: Does feeding hospitalized patients — on the wards and around surgery — help them live longer?
balance: On the medical wards and around surgery, feeding works: individualized nutritional support cut 30-day mortality in EFFORT ( 7% vs 10% , aOR 0.65 ; card on Shelf #99), a specialized supplement halved 90-day mortality in NOURISH (RR 0.49 , a secondary endpoint; card on Shelf #99), and perioperative nutrition cut hospital deaths in malnourished GI-cancer patients (Wu 2006, 2.1% vs 6.0% ). The founding caution stands: the thin and recent-weight-loss subgroups are almost never reported separately.
citation: SourceMed Shelf #15, “Feeding hospitalized patients Deposit #14 · Oct 23, 2026”, sourcemed.io

title: Immune-modulating nutrition (the AIM shelf) Deposit #15 · Oct 23, 2026
question: Do immune-modulating feeds and nutrients — arginine, fish oil, RNA, antioxidants, vitamin A — change outcomes in critically ill and septic patients?
balance: Thirty years of immunonutrition in one shelf, and it argues with itself: the early surgical and trauma trials were positive (Kudsk — pneumonia 11.8% vs 31% with enteral feeding; Daly — complications 11% vs 37% ), and Galbán’s septic-patient trial cut mortality — yet the one severe-sepsis immunonutrition trial was stopped for harm (ICU mortality 44.4% vs 14.3% ), and the nitric-oxide lesson looms over the whole arginine idea (blocking NO in septic shock raised mortality, 59% vs 49% ). Fish oil pools positive (RR 0.74 ) but leans on small heterogeneous trials, the developer’s own vitamin A trial was negative, and two physiology cards explain why the field keeps trying: muscle ATP collapses within a week of critical illness, and septic hypoalbuminemia is a distribution problem, not a synthesis problem.
citation: SourceMed Shelf #16, “Immune-modulating nutrition (the AIM shelf) Deposit #15 · Oct 23, 2026”, sourcemed.io

title: Diabetes vs no diabetes — ICU mortality Deposit #16 · Oct 23, 2026 · Founding shelf
question: Does pre-existing diabetes change a critically ill patient’s chance of dying?
balance: The shelf now says something sharper: pre-existing diabetes does not raise sepsis mortality — in 16,497 Taiwanese ICU patients it was identical (22.6% vs 22.6%), and across nine studies known diabetics died at half the rate of patients with new-onset hyperglycemia (12.5% vs 26.7% in hospital) at similar glucose levels, as if prior exposure adapts the body to hyperglycemia. The metabolic parallel is real — diabetes shares cancer’s raised glucose production and leucine turnover — but the albumin card (54% higher death rate per 0.5 g/dL lower) is a different population, transplant-listed lung disease, and the shelf’s mechanism section (glucose variability) still awaits its papers.
citation: SourceMed Shelf #17, “Diabetes vs no diabetes — ICU mortality Deposit #16 · Oct 23, 2026 · Founding shelf”, sourcemed.io

title: Herbs and dietary supplements Deposit #17 · Oct 23, 2026
question: For the supplements patients actually take, what does the randomized evidence show about benefit?
balance: The shelf sorts into three piles: real but mostly modest benefits — potassium salt substitute cut stroke and death in a 21,000-person trial, vitamin E improved liver histology without improving fibrosis, and psyllium, creatine with training, melatonin, ginger, curcumin, and cranberry each show small, specific, replicated effects on surrogate or symptom endpoints — plus one lonely hard-outcome positive, CoQ10 in heart failure ( HR 0.50 ), unreplicated since 2014. And a harm pile every supplement conversation needs: vitamin E raised prostate cancer in SELECT ( HR 1.17 ), an annual mega-dose of vitamin D increased falls and fractures, and beta-carotene with vitamin A raised lung cancer in smokers (CARET, stopped early) — the pattern being that replacement-level uses behave, while pharmacologic mega-doses in healthy people are where the harm lives.
citation: SourceMed Shelf #18, “Herbs and dietary supplements Deposit #17 · Oct 23, 2026”, sourcemed.io

title: Low creatinine and mortality Deposit #18 · Oct 23, 2026 · Founding shelf
question: Is a LOW admission creatinine a danger signal for death — not just a high one?
balance: Low creatinine as a frailty signal gains its mechanism: in 118 hemodialysis patients the creatinine-based estimate of lean body mass matched DEXA with a mean difference of zero — but the authors present it as a hypothesis, and the shelf still has no study that measured muscle mass directly against mortality.
citation: SourceMed Shelf #19, “Low creatinine and mortality Deposit #18 · Oct 23, 2026 · Founding shelf”, sourcemed.io

title: A1C compliance
question: What actually moves A1c — and how many recommendations can a patient carry?
balance: Remote diabetes care works when it adjusts medicines: DiaTel −1.7 vs −0.8 points, comprehensive telehealth −0.61 against monitoring alone, pharmacist-coach mobile health −0.62, Thai tele-insulin titration −0.65 — but gains fade (EMPOWER-D’s advantage gone by 12 months) and teleconsultation is non-inferior to in-person care. Underneath all of it, the burden literature, shelved in full on Shelf #135: one ‘most important’ label doubled implementation, five or more recommendations cut action, and delayed recall collapses at 3–4 instructions — with one large dissent (Press) arguing the bottleneck is the patient’s memory, not the physician’s list.
citation: SourceMed Shelf #20, “A1C compliance”, sourcemed.io

title: Feeding more in the ICU
question: In the ICU, does feeding more — more energy, more protein, earlier — help patients live longer?
balance: In the ICU, every large trial of more is neutral: energy-dense formula (RR 1.05 ), higher protein (RR 1.08 ), augmented protein (RR 0.99 alive), full vs trophic feeding, permissive underfeeding (RR 0.94 ) and early restriction in shock all cross no-difference. Whether thin patients are the exception is untested — none of these trials isolated them.
citation: SourceMed Shelf #21, “Feeding more in the ICU”, sourcemed.io

title: Elevated phosphate on admission as a danger signal
question: Should elevated phosphate on admission be a danger signal?
balance: Developer’s verdict (Oct 29, 2026): POSSIBLE. Five cohorts, about 199,000 patients, and the pattern refuses to settle. Arrive with a high phosphate and you die more often — 10.7% vs 2.2% in the emergency department, adjusted odds of 3.89 at the Mayo Clinic for levels of 4.9 mg/dL or more, 16.4% vs 6.6% in-hospital mortality across 126,088 infection admissions, 25% vs 3% at 30 days in pancreatitis — and in three of those cohorts the association survives adjustment for kidney function. But the entanglement never goes away: the ED study’s high-phosphate patients had a median eGFR of 22 against 93, and the largest ICU cohort — 27,131 patients — lost the association entirely once severity and kidney function were adjusted for. Every study here is observational; nobody was randomized. A high phosphate on admission may be a danger signal in its own right, or it may be the sound of failing kidneys and severe illness. Posted as a possible, not a fact.
citation: SourceMed Shelf #22, “Elevated phosphate on admission as a danger signal”, sourcemed.io

title: Chlorthalidone vs hydrochlorothiazide
question: In adults with hypertension, does chlorthalidone (long half-life, roughly 60 hours) give better cardiovascular, stroke, or mortality outcomes than hydrochlorothiazide (short half-life, roughly 6 hours) — and at what cost in potassium, sodium, and kidney effects?
balance: The head-to-head trial found no cardiovascular advantage for chlorthalidone over hydrochlorothiazide (HR 1.04, null) — but chlorthalidone lowers ambulatory and nighttime pressure more in small comparisons, and costs more potassium wherever it is measured head-to-head or matched (HR 1.38 in the trial, 1.70 in Ontario, 2.72 in LEGEND). The longer half-life buys pressure control, not proven outcome benefit — which is exactly what the developer’s individual-data paper is designed to test.
mesh: Hypertension · Chlorthalidone · Hydrochlorothiazide · Diuretics · Sodium Chloride Symporter Inhibitors · Antihypertensive Agents · Hypokalemia · Humans

title: Diabetes control by race and ethnicity in US health centers
question: In US health centers, why do diabetes control rates differ by race and ethnicity — and what closes the gap?
balance: Black patients run a few points worse than White patients in every UDS era, and the gap survives access and adherence adjustment — it is not only a clinic-door problem. Asian patients run lowest on poor control even though they are tested least, which strengthens rather than weakens the finding — but ‘Asian’ aggregates subgroups that differ, and lumping Asian with NHPI hides the NHPI gap, where published control numbers barely exist.
citation: SourceMed Shelf #24, “Diabetes control by race and ethnicity in US health centers”, sourcemed.io

title: Potassium and blood pressure Deposit #23 · Oct 24, 2026
question: Does potassium — as tablets, or as potassium-enriched salt — lower blood pressure, and does it prevent strokes, heart attacks, and death?
balance: Potassium lowers pressure modestly — about 4–5 mmHg systolic in meta-analyses, near 7 in untreated hypertension — but the one trial in high-normal pressure faded by 6 months, and the only hard-outcome win combined sodium cutting with potassium enrichment, so it doesn’t prove potassium tablets prevent strokes. The mechanism is plausible; the tablet benefit is pressure, not proven outcomes.
citation: SourceMed Shelf #25, “Potassium and blood pressure Deposit #23 · Oct 24, 2026”, sourcemed.io

title: Vitamin E Deposit #23 · Oct 24, 2026
question: Does vitamin E help — liver, prostate, or anything else — and at what cost?
balance: Vitamin E improves liver histology in nondiabetic NASH/MASH ( 43% vs 19% in PIVENS; 29.3% vs 14.1% at 300 mg in MASH) without improving fibrosis — but the same vitamin, at 400 IU daily for prevention in healthy men, raised prostate cancer ( HR 1.17 ). Benefit is disease-specific and biopsy-deep; harm is prevention-dose-specific. Neither generalizes to the other. On dose, the 2026 VEDS trial found 200 IU/day matched 800 IU/day for ALT reduction over 24 weeks with no safety signal — if vitamin E is used, the lowest effective dose has the best-supported risk position.
citation: SourceMed Shelf #26, “Vitamin E Deposit #23 · Oct 24, 2026”, sourcemed.io

title: Psyllium Deposit #23 · Oct 24, 2026
question: Does psyllium supplementation improve lipid profiles in adults?
balance: Three LDL sources, one consistent direction — Gholami 2025 pooled LDL −8.55 mg/dL , Anderson 2000 pooled −7% vs placebo, and Anderson’s 26-week trial −6.7% — but heterogeneity is very high (I² 88% in Gholami), and lipid changes are not cardiovascular events: a surrogate win, not an outcome win. Bonus side fact: psyllium also lowered fasting glucose ( −37.0 mg/dL ) and HbA1c ( −0.97% ) in treated type 2 diabetes (Gibb 2015) — noted here only as a bonus; the full glycemic evidence is reserved for its own shelf.
citation: SourceMed Shelf #27, “Psyllium Deposit #23 · Oct 24, 2026”, sourcemed.io

title: ICU glucose variability and mortality
question: Does glucose variability predict ICU death — and does diabetes change that relationship?
balance: Variability tracks death in patients without diabetes in the two big cohorts (Sechterberger top quartile OR 1.69; Krinsley threefold crude gap at CV >40%) and in influenza (HR 1.34 per 10 points) — but the diabetes interaction is never significant (Fluit p=0.25; Krinsley’s adjusted association absent in diabetes), and hypoglycemia predicts death in both groups (ORs 2.5/4.2; NICE-SUGAR HRs 1.41/2.10). Variability is a risk marker, sharpest without diabetes; it is not shown to be a treatment target, and diabetes does not cleanly modify it.
citation: SourceMed Shelf #28, “ICU glucose variability and mortality”, sourcemed.io

title: Vitamin E and prostate cancer (SELECT)
question: Does vitamin E 400 IU/day raise prostate cancer risk in healthy men?
balance: SELECT’s harm arrived in two acts: the 2009 primary report showed no prevention benefit and a nonsignificant vitamin E trend (473 vs 416 cases, HR 1.13), and the supplements were stopped early for futility; extended follow-up made the harm significant — 620 vs 529 cases, HR 1.17, about 1.6 extra cancers per 1,000 person-years (Klein 2011). The harm is prevention-dose-specific: the same vitamin at treatment doses improves liver histology in MASH without this signal.
citation: SourceMed Shelf #29, “Vitamin E and prostate cancer (SELECT)”, sourcemed.io

title: Annual vitamin D mega-dose and falls/fractures (Sanders)
question: Does a single annual 500,000-IU vitamin D dose prevent falls and fractures — or cause them?
balance: It caused them: falls up 15%, fractures up 26% in 2,256 older women. The finding belongs to the annual mega-dose alone and says nothing about daily replacement for deficiency.
citation: SourceMed Shelf #30, “Annual vitamin D mega-dose and falls/fractures (Sanders)”, sourcemed.io

title: Beta-carotene, vitamin A, and lung cancer (CARET)
question: Does high-dose beta-carotene plus vitamin A prevent lung cancer in smokers?
balance: Twice tested, twice harmful: beta-carotene raised lung cancer 18% in 29,133 Finnish smokers (ATBC 1994), and the beta-carotene + vitamin A combination raised it 28% in 18,314 US smokers and asbestos-exposed workers (CARET 1996, stopped 21 months early). The harm belongs to high-dose supplements in high-risk lungs, not to carotenoids in food.
citation: SourceMed Shelf #31, “Beta-carotene, vitamin A, and lung cancer (CARET)”, sourcemed.io

title: Salt substitute and hyperkalemia (SSaSS)
question: Does potassium-enriched salt raise the risk of serious hyperkalemia?
balance: Checked in 20,995 people over 4.74 years and not found: serious hyperkalemia events 3.35 vs 3.30 per 1,000 person-years (RR 1.04), while the same trial cut stroke, major cardiovascular events, and death. A feared harm, looked for properly, that did not appear.
citation: SourceMed Shelf #32, “Salt substitute and hyperkalemia (SSaSS)”, sourcemed.io

title: Peppermint oil and adverse events (Ingrosso 2022)
question: Does peppermint oil cause adverse events in IBS — and do they outweigh the benefit?
balance: In 10 trials of 1,030 patients, peppermint oil helped global IBS symptoms (RR 0.65, NNT 4) and pain (RR 0.76, NNT 7) — but any adverse event was more common (RR 1.57: 17.1% vs 12.1%), driven partly by reflux symptoms (RR 1.67), on very-low-certainty evidence. A modest benefit with a real, if uncertain, adverse-event cost.
citation: SourceMed Shelf #33, “Peppermint oil and adverse events (Ingrosso 2022)”, sourcemed.io

title: Glucose production, recycling, and gluconeogenesis (Katz & Tayek)
question: How much of the glucose your liver makes comes from new synthesis versus recycling — and what changes it in fasting, diabetes, and cancer?
balance: Across five small physiology studies, the method holds up — a single isotope plus mass isotopomer analysis measures gluconeogenesis, and the corrected production rate matches the tritium gold standard (r=0.86). The biology: after 40 hours of fasting, gluconeogenesis is 92% of glucose production; in diabetes, production runs higher (2.8 vs 1.9) because gluconeogenesis runs higher; in one cancer subgroup, gluconeogenesis supplies most of the glucose and tracks cortisol (r=0.96). The doses matter too: low-dose glucagon raises production only through glycogen breakdown, high-dose through both routes. All of it is small-n physiology — the shelf is a methods story with biological payoffs, not clinical outcomes.
citation: SourceMed Shelf #34, “Glucose production, recycling, and gluconeogenesis (Katz & Tayek)”, sourcemed.io

title: Cancer metabolism: glucose production, anabolism, and the liver
question: In cancer, why does the body burn glucose differently — and can feeding or hormones reverse it?
balance: Across eight small Clinical Research Center studies, cancer raises hepatic glucose production and blunts insulin action — worst in the most malnourished, where production hits 2.98 and tracks growth hormone (r=0.71) — while five days of 5-FU nudges production higher still, and the liver’s TPN injury tracks duration of feeding more than the lipid itself (though early lipid drives the AST rise). Growth hormone raises IGF-I threefold but fails to build protein overall; it works only in patients who aren’t yet severely malnourished. And the one survival signal is thin: four metabolic numbers predict survival with 59% accuracy — barely above a coin toss.
citation: SourceMed Shelf #35, “Cancer metabolism: glucose production, anabolism, and the liver”, sourcemed.io

title: Diabetes drugs: sulfonylureas and the liver
question: Do sulfonylureas lower glucose by making the liver produce less — even before insulin rises?
balance: Three small studies, one thread: a very low dose of glyburide cuts fasting glucose by cutting hepatic glucose production — 16% in healthy volunteers with insulin unchanged, 19% in people with impaired fasting glucose — and a full-dose trial shows 2.5 mg of glipizide added to metformin moves A1c and fasting glucose significantly in 122 patients. The honest limit: the glipizide trial’s abstract prints p-values without effect sizes, so the card can say it worked, not by how much.
citation: SourceMed Shelf #36, “Diabetes drugs: sulfonylureas and the liver”, sourcemed.io

title: Vitamin D and respiratory infection in children
question: Does high-dose vitamin D prevent upper respiratory infection in children?
balance: The two child RCTs split — Urashima positive for influenza A specifically ( RR 0.58 ), Aglipay null for all viral upper respiratory infections when extra dose is added on top of standard intake in replete toddlers; the 2017 IPD child stratum was strongly positive ( OR 0.60 ) while the pooled children-only meta-analysis (Carboo) is null and imprecise. The signal may be real for influenza and for deficient children; it is not a general “vitamin D prevents colds in kids” result.
citation: SourceMed Shelf #37, “Vitamin D and respiratory infection in children”, sourcemed.io

title: Vitamin D and bladder infection in adults
question: Does vitamin D help adults fight bladder infection — and does supplementation prevent urinary infection?
balance: In adults, low vitamin D tracks with more urinary infection — a 2019 meta-analysis puts the odds at 3.01 — but the link is observational, and the one trial that cut UTIs (Jorde, 18 vs 34 over five years) used self-reported outcomes as a secondary endpoint. The bladder mechanism is real in tissue (Hertting): vitamin D primes bladder cells to make cathelicidin on bacterial contact. Correcting deficiency is sensible care; preventing infection with vitamin D is still open.
citation: SourceMed Shelf #38, “Vitamin D and bladder infection in adults”, sourcemed.io

title: Vitamin D and bladder infection in children
question: Does vitamin D help children fight bladder infection — and does supplementation prevent urinary infection in children?
balance: In children, low vitamin D tracks with more urinary infection — a 2023 meta-analysis of 13 studies finds levels about 8 ng/mL lower in children with UTI, and below 20 ng/mL the odds rise fivefold — but every study is observational, and the one small trial of supplementation found nothing. Correcting deficiency is sensible; preventing UTI with vitamin D is unproven in children.
citation: SourceMed Shelf #39, “Vitamin D and bladder infection in children”, sourcemed.io

title: Glipizide GITS: less hypoglycemia, no weight gain?
question: Does glipizide XL, through its delayed (GITS) delivery in the gut, prevent or reduce hypoglycemia and weight gain with sulfonylureas?
balance: Glipizide GITS (glipizide XL) lowers glucose without weight gain — two randomized trials in 347 patients and two combination trials found no weight change — and glipizide carries less hypoglycemia than glyburide (a 2007 meta-analysis: 83% higher risk with glyburide than with other sulfonylureas including glipizide). What is not shown: no trial compares GITS head-to-head against immediate-release glipizide on hypoglycemia, so the delayed-delivery advantage over its own immediate-release form is a mechanism — smoother levels, less between-meal insulin — not a measured outcome.
citation: SourceMed Shelf #40, “Glipizide GITS: less hypoglycemia, no weight gain?”, sourcemed.io

title: Fish oil and atrial fibrillation: a dose-dependent harm?
question: Does taking fish oil (omega-3) raise the rate of atrial fibrillation in humans?
balance: High-dose omega-3 raises AF risk — about 25% relatively across the trials, roughly 1 extra case per 70–125 people treated at 4 g a day — and the risk climbs with dose: 4 g clearly, 1.8 g borderline, 840 mg no signal. The same 4 g of icosapent ethyl that cut heart events 25% in REDUCE-IT raised AF hospitalization from 2.1% to 3.1% — yet stroke was still lower overall. EVAPORATE, the 80-patient plaque trial, reported no AFib signal because it was far too small to see one.
citation: SourceMed Shelf #41, “Fish oil and atrial fibrillation: a dose-dependent harm?”, sourcemed.io

title: Pegfilgrastim for alcohol-associated hepatitis: a negative phase II trial
question: Does adding pegfilgrastim (long-acting G-CSF) to standard care improve 90-day survival in severe alcohol-associated hepatitis?
balance: In the United States, adding pegfilgrastim to prednisolone did not improve 90-day survival — 73% vs 83% in a trial stopped early at 34 patients — and it moved nothing else either: kidney injury, encephalopathy, and infections were the same. That sits against a 2020 meta-analysis in which G-CSF looked life-saving in Asian trials (death OR 0.15) and possibly harmful in European ones (OR 1.89), with the authors refusing to recommend it anywhere. A negative trial, honestly reported, is still evidence — and this one is the developer's own.
citation: SourceMed Shelf #42, “Pegfilgrastim for alcohol-associated hepatitis: a negative phase II trial”, sourcemed.io

title: Oral arginine and blood pressure: a modest, temporary fall
question: Does oral L-arginine, taken in moderation, lower blood pressure in humans?
balance: Oral arginine lowers blood pressure — about 6 systolic and 3 diastolic across 22 trials — and the effect holds in healthy and hypertensive people alike. But it is modest, it needs at least 4 grams a day, it doesn't grow past 9 grams, and it fades: in the developer's own crossover, pressure fell within two hours and was back within an hour of stopping. The responder pattern runs through the whole story — only the people whose citrulline rose got the full metabolic effect — and the biggest drops of all came in a handful of dialysis patients starting at 171 systolic.
citation: SourceMed Shelf #43, “Oral arginine and blood pressure: a modest, temporary fall”, sourcemed.io

title: AIONID: anti-inflammatory nutrition in hypoalbuminemic dialysis patients
question: Can an anti-inflammatory, anti-oxidative oral nutrition supplement raise serum albumin in hypoalbuminemic maintenance hemodialysis patients?
balance: Supplements reliably raise albumin a little ( +0.19 to +0.23 g/dL across the syntheses; +0.21 in AIONID), an anti-inflammatory drug alone does the same with CRP falling (Pakfetrat), and the one large trial with a mortality endpoint (FINE) found no survival gain from intensifying nutrition — patients whose prealbumin rose did better, but raising the number has never been shown to be what saves them. Albumin here is a marker that moves, not yet a lever proven to change outcomes.
citation: SourceMed Shelf #44, “AIONID: anti-inflammatory nutrition in hypoalbuminemic dialysis patients”, sourcemed.io

title: Plaque in type 2 diabetes: how common, and can icosapent ethyl regress it?
question: In type 2 diabetes, how common is coronary plaque, and can icosapent ethyl regress it — or is the placebo doing the work?
balance: In type 2 diabetes, plaque is common but not universal — one in five screened patients had normal coronaries. On icosapent ethyl, plaque didn't just slow, it regressed and stabilized: low-attenuation plaque down 17% while placebo rose 109%, and the lipid-rich necrotic core shrank within 9 months. The open question is the placebo arm: the published comparison says mineral oil didn't drive the progression, but that comparison is post-hoc and small — which is why the developer is asking the author directly.
citation: SourceMed Shelf #45, “Plaque in type 2 diabetes: how common, and can icosapent ethyl regress it?”, sourcemed.io

title: The vitamin D guideline: who should get vitamin D, and who shouldn’t be tested.
question: What does the 2024 Endocrine Society guideline say about who should get vitamin D — and who shouldn’t be tested for it?
balance: Thirteen years of guidance trace one arc — aim high and test (Endocrine 2011: target above 30 ng/mL , 1,500–2,000 IU/day); the nutrition establishment demurring the same year (IOM: 20 ng/mL suffices, bone outcomes only); prevention policy unable to judge screening (USPSTF 2021: I statement); and the specialty society finally landing on empiric supplementation for four defined groups with no routine testing and no definable target level (Endocrine 2024). The shelf is the record of a field correcting itself.
citation: SourceMed Shelf #46, “The vitamin D guideline: who should get vitamin D, and who shouldn’t be tested.”, sourcemed.io

title: Insulin, not leptin, tracks growth-hormone pulses after weight loss.
question: After weight loss, what tracks growth-hormone pulse size — insulin or leptin?
balance: The energy-balance seesaw is consistent across three decades — fasting multiplies GH production fivefold in two days (Hartman) and triples integrated GH over five (Ho); visceral fat and fasting insulin predict blunted GH in larger samples (Clasey, Makimura); and in the developer’s own weight-loss study it was insulin, not the fat hormone leptin, that tracked the pulses’ recovery. None of these small physiology studies can say whether raising GH by lowering insulin changes outcomes — they map the signal, not its clinical use.
citation: SourceMed Shelf #47, “Insulin, not leptin, tracks growth-hormone pulses after weight loss.”, sourcemed.io

title: Folic acid and neural tube defects
question: Does periconceptional folic acid prevent neural tube defects?
balance: Two randomized trials, two populations: 4 mg a day cut recurrence by 72% in women with a previous affected pregnancy, and 0.8 mg in a multivitamin eliminated first occurrences in the trial (0 vs 6). The 400–800 mcg a day recommendation is the public-health dose between them — lower than either trial dose, anchored by these two trials.
citation: SourceMed Shelf #48, “Folic acid and neural tube defects”, sourcemed.io

title: AREDS2 formulation and macular degeneration
question: Does the AREDS2 formulation slow progression to advanced age-related macular degeneration?
balance: The original AREDS formula's 25% reduction in progression stands; nothing added on top in AREDS2 helped further. AREDS2's real contribution is subtraction — beta-carotene out, because it raised lung cancer in former smokers, and lutein with zeaxanthin in.
citation: SourceMed Shelf #49, “AREDS2 formulation and macular degeneration”, sourcemed.io

title: Cranberry for recurrent urinary tract infection
question: Does cranberry prevent recurrent urinary tract infection in women?
balance: A defined product at a defined dose — 500 mg a day of whole cranberry fruit powder — halved recurrence in one good trial. Across 50 trials of mixed products the average is about 30% fewer UTIs. Product and dose are the whole story: juice and mixed products vary, and the pooled number is an average over unlike products.
citation: SourceMed Shelf #50, “Cranberry for recurrent urinary tract infection”, sourcemed.io

title: Creatine monohydrate in older adults
question: Does creatine monohydrate help older adults — and what does it do to the creatinine?
balance: Creatine adds a small strength increment on top of resistance training in healthy older adults — g 0.31 — while muscle mass and physical function show no significant additional benefit. And it reliably raises serum creatinine while true kidney filtration stays put. Know both before you prescribe it or interpret the labs.
citation: SourceMed Shelf #51, “Creatine monohydrate in older adults”, sourcemed.io

title: Standardized red yeast rice
question: Does standardized red yeast rice prevent cardiovascular events?
balance: One hard-outcome trial in post-MI patients — 45% fewer coronary events — plus a modern LDL trial. But both are standardized products, and the supplement-market version is not the trial product: Xuezhikang is a prescription-grade extract in China, and over-the-counter red yeast rice varies in monacolin content.
citation: SourceMed Shelf #52, “Standardized red yeast rice”, sourcemed.io

title: Coenzyme Q10 in heart failure (Q-SYMBIO)
question: Does coenzyme Q10 improve outcomes in chronic heart failure?
balance: One trial says CoQ10 halves events in heart failure; everything around it says handle with care — the earlier literature was 395 patients of short-term surrogate data (ejection fraction +3.67% , Fotino 2013), and the pooled mortality benefit ( RR 0.69 , Lei & Liu 2017; Cochrane 2021: probably reduces mortality and hospitalisation) appears only when Q-SYMBIO is in the pool. The honest statement is not “CoQ10 works” but “one good trial, never replicated, carries the entire outcome claim.”
citation: SourceMed Shelf #53, “Coenzyme Q10 in heart failure (Q-SYMBIO)”, sourcemed.io

title: Oat beta-glucan and LDL cholesterol
question: Does oat beta-glucan lower LDL cholesterol?
balance: The pooled trials say about 10 mg/dL off LDL (0.25 mmol/L) at 3 grams a day or more; the newest feeding trial points the same way but doesn't reach significance on its own. A food, not a pill — the dose is a bowl of oats.
citation: SourceMed Shelf #54, “Oat beta-glucan and LDL cholesterol”, sourcemed.io

title: Alpha-lipoic acid in diabetic neuropathy
question: Does alpha-lipoic acid ease diabetic neuropathy?
balance: Alpha-lipoic acid 600 mg eases neuropathic symptoms in five weeks, and the 2026 pool agrees on symptoms while the objective nerve measures stay flat. Symptom relief, not disease modification — and 600 mg is the dose; higher doses add side effects without added benefit.
citation: SourceMed Shelf #55, “Alpha-lipoic acid in diabetic neuropathy”, sourcemed.io

title: Routine calcium plus vitamin D (fracture prevention)
question: Does routine calcium plus vitamin D prevent fractures in healthy adults?
balance: The biggest trial says no significant hip-fracture benefit and more kidney stones; the 69-trial pool says little to no clinically meaningful fracture effect. Routine calcium plus D for fracture prevention in healthy adults is a near-null with a real stone risk.
citation: SourceMed Shelf #56, “Routine calcium plus vitamin D (fracture prevention)”, sourcemed.io

title: High-dose zinc (copper depletion)
question: What happens when zinc is taken far above the recommended intake?
balance: The guidance threshold is real and the clinical harm is documented — NIH puts the upper limit at 40 mg/day and warns that 50 mg/day or more for weeks blocks copper absorption; the denture-cream case series (Nations 2008; Hedera 2009) show the neurologic syndrome at extreme exposure, with improvement only mild after the zinc stops; and routine prescribing itself often crosses the line without monitoring ( 62% of audited prescriptions at copper-depleting doses, copper checked in 2 of 70 — Duncan 2015). High-dose zinc’s main verifiable effect is copper deficiency, preventable and partly irreversible.
citation: SourceMed Shelf #57, “High-dose zinc (copper depletion)”, sourcemed.io

title: High-dose biotin (false laboratory results)
question: Can high-dose biotin falsify laboratory results?
balance: The FDA warning is not theoretical: a controlled human experiment shows a standard 10 mg/day supplement dose corrupts 39% of biotin-based assays within a week (TSH driven below range on one platform), and about 1 in 13 outpatients and emergency patients carry biotin at or above interference levels. The failure mode is a falsified result in a patient who never mentions the supplement.
citation: SourceMed Shelf #58, “High-dose biotin (false laboratory results)”, sourcemed.io

title: Selenium and prostate cancer (SELECT)
question: Does selenium prevent prostate cancer?
balance: Selenium doesn't prevent prostate cancer — and in men who already have enough, supplementing raises high-grade disease by about 90%. The supplement helps no one in SELECT and harms the replete. The vitamin E harm from the same trial lives on Shelf #29 (Klein 2011, HR 1.17).
citation: SourceMed Shelf #59, “Selenium and prostate cancer (SELECT)”, sourcemed.io

title: High-dose vitamin B6 (neuropathy)
question: Can high-dose vitamin B6 cause neuropathy?
balance: The story runs from gram-dose abuse in 1983 to a European limit of 12 mg a day in 2023. Dose and duration decide: grams injure in months, a few hundred milligrams over a year or two, and case reports reach toward 50 mg — and the mechanism is a paradox, the supplement form blocking the active form. No safe dose below 50 mg a day has been established by trial.
citation: SourceMed Shelf #60, “High-dose vitamin B6 (neuropathy)”, sourcemed.io

title: Pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy (antiquitin deficiency)
question: Why do some infants' seizures stop only with vitamin B6 — and what does treatment change?
balance: A blocked step in lysine breakdown floods the body with a compound that chemically switches off active vitamin B6, so the brain starves for B6 while the diet is normal. Large-dose pyridoxine overrides the block and stops seizures no standard drug touches — but it does not undo the metabolites' other damage: most patients still have intellectual disability, which is why treatment now adds lysine restriction and starts before birth when the risk is known.
citation: SourceMed Shelf #61, “Pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy (antiquitin deficiency)”, sourcemed.io

title: Vitamin B6 deficiency neuropathy
question: Can too little vitamin B6 damage peripheral nerves?
balance: Yes — and the proof is a drug: isoniazid switches B6 off, nerves fail, and pyridoxine switches it back on. On high-dose isoniazid without B6 protection about a third of patients developed neuropathy, and giving B6 reversed it; in dialysis patients today, isoniazid prevention still produces neuropathy in about 1 in 6, and raising the pyridoxine dose resolves most cases. The deficiency state is measurable and reversible — the failure mode is not checking the level.
citation: SourceMed Shelf #62, “Vitamin B6 deficiency neuropathy”, sourcemed.io

title: Beni-kōji (red yeast rice) supplement outbreak, Japan 2024 — a contamination event
question: What happened when a mold toxin contaminated beni-kōji supplements in Japan in 2024?
balance: This shelf documents a manufacturing contamination failure, not a pharmacological harm of red yeast rice — the deaths and kidney injuries trace to puberulic acid from mold contamination of specific 2023 batches, not to monacolin K or to beni-kōji as an ingredient. It sits next to Shelf #52 (red yeast rice LDL evidence) as the product-safety record for the same ingredient class, and as a case study in the risks of a lightly regulated supplement category (Japan’s “foods with function claims”).
citation: SourceMed Shelf #63, “Beni-kōji (red yeast rice) supplement outbreak, Japan 2024 — a contamination event”, sourcemed.io

title: Nigella sativa (black seed) — safety: no harm signal found
question: What harm, if any, does oral Nigella sativa (black seed) cause at the doses used in trials?
balance: Across two decades of reviews and the trial record, no severe harm signal for oral Nigella sativa at customary doses (1–3 g/day seeds, 5 mL/day oil) has been found — the documented items are minor gastrointestinal effects, rare skin reactions (mostly topical), a hypoglycemia note in hepatitis C patients, and a CYP-interaction flag at 5 g/day. This shelf exists so the negative is on the record: examined, not overlooked.
citation: SourceMed Shelf #64, “Nigella sativa (black seed) — safety: no harm signal found”, sourcemed.io

title: Glucosamine (± chondroitin) and warfarin — the INR interaction
question: Does glucosamine, with or without chondroitin, raise the INR in patients taking warfarin?
balance: In randomized trials glucosamine and chondroitin are as benign as placebo; the one consistent post-marketing signal is INR elevation in patients on warfarin — case-report grade and mechanism unknown, but noted by the FDA, WHO, and EFSA, and clinically actionable: a patient on warfarin who starts glucosamine needs INR monitoring. (Not carded: three liver-injury cases on multi-ingredient glucosamine products in the LiverTox record — the products contained other potentially hepatotoxic herbals and were never characterized, so attribution is not possible.)
citation: SourceMed Shelf #65, “Glucosamine (± chondroitin) and warfarin — the INR interaction”, sourcemed.io

title: Turmeric/curcumin liver injury — the bioavailability-enhanced product problem
question: Can turmeric or curcumin supplements injure the liver — and is the injury tied to the modern high-absorption formulations?
balance: Culinary turmeric and plain curcumin show a flat adverse-event record in trials (pooled RR ~1.03) — the liver injury belongs to bioavailability-enhanced products (piperine combinations, phytosome and similar formulations engineered to defeat curcumin’s poor absorption). Three independent literatures converge: US DILIN clinical cases (10, one fatal), Italian phytovigilance (7 cases plus 23 in review; mandatory warning labels followed), and a US pathology series (11 cases). The injury is hepatocellular, appears 1–4 months in, and concentrates in HLA-B*35:01 carriers; NIH LiverTox now rates turmeric/curcumin a well-documented cause of clinically apparent liver injury, and Australia’s TGA issued a 2023 alert (9 assessable reports, one death). Rare, idiosyncratic, occasionally fatal — and invisible to the trial adverse-event pooling.
citation: SourceMed Shelf #66, “Turmeric/curcumin liver injury — the bioavailability-enhanced product problem”, sourcemed.io

title: Selenium and type 2 diabetes — an unresolved signal
question: Does selenium supplementation cause type 2 diabetes?
balance: Two randomized trials disagree. In the NPC trial’s secondary analysis, selenium raised new diabetes (HR 1.55), and the risk climbed with baseline selenium — highest tertile HR 2.70. In SELECT, nearly thirty times larger, the same 200 µg/day dose showed no significant increase (RR 1.07; extended follow-up 1.04). If the harm is real, it likely sits in people already selenium-replete — but the biggest trial, run in exactly such men, is null. This shelf records a disagreement, not a verdict.
citation: SourceMed Shelf #67, “Selenium and type 2 diabetes — an unresolved signal”, sourcemed.io

title: SGLT2 inhibitors and cardiovascular outcomes in type 2 diabetes
question: In type 2 diabetes at high cardiovascular risk, do SGLT2 inhibitors prevent heart attacks, strokes, and cardiovascular death?
balance: Three large trials point the same way on the composite, but the wins differ: empagliflozin’s is mortality, dapagliflozin’s is heart-failure hospitalization with a null MACE result, and canagliflozin carries an amputation signal the others do not.
mesh: Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Cardiovascular Diseases · Sodium-Glucose Transporter 2 Inhibitors · Hypoglycemic Agents · Hospitalization · Humans
citation: SourceMed Shelf #68, “SGLT2 inhibitors and cardiovascular outcomes in type 2 diabetes”, sourcemed.io

title: SGLT2 inhibitors and kidney protection
question: Do SGLT2 inhibitors slow chronic kidney disease progression — in people with and without diabetes?
balance: Three dedicated kidney trials, three positive primary outcomes — the most consistent story in this drug class, and it holds in people without diabetes.
mesh: Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Diabetic Nephropathies · Renal Insufficiency, Chronic · Glomerular Filtration Rate · Sodium-Glucose Transporter 2 Inhibitors · Humans
citation: SourceMed Shelf #69, “SGLT2 inhibitors and kidney protection”, sourcemed.io

title: SGLT2 inhibitors in heart failure, across the ejection-fraction spectrum
question: Do SGLT2 inhibitors improve outcomes in established heart failure — reduced and preserved ejection fraction, with and without diabetes?
balance: Three positive trials spanning reduced to preserved ejection fraction. The hospitalization benefit is uniform; the mortality benefit is clear in reduced-ejection-fraction disease and fades as ejection fraction rises.
mesh: Heart Failure · Sodium-Glucose Transporter 2 Inhibitors · Benzhydryl Compounds · Glucosides · Hospitalization · Stroke Volume · Humans
citation: SourceMed Shelf #70, “SGLT2 inhibitors in heart failure, across the ejection-fraction spectrum”, sourcemed.io

title: GLP-1 receptor agonists and cardiovascular outcomes
question: Do GLP-1 receptor agonists prevent cardiovascular events in type 2 diabetes?
balance: Three positive outcome trials, three different drivers: liraglutide’s win is cardiovascular death, semaglutide’s is nonfatal MI and stroke with a retinopathy caution attached, and dulaglutide’s is stroke in the broadest, mostly primary-prevention population.
mesh: Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Cardiovascular Diseases · Glucagon-Like Peptides · Hypoglycemic Agents · Double-Blind Method · Humans
citation: SourceMed Shelf #71, “GLP-1 receptor agonists and cardiovascular outcomes”, sourcemed.io

title: GLP-1 receptor agonists with demonstrated cardiovascular benefit: the remaining Level A trials
question: Beyond the three trials on Shelf #71, which other GLP-1 receptor agonists have demonstrated cardiovascular benefit — and which did not clear that bar?
balance: Under the ADA’s own Level A wording, the GLP-1 benefit is agent-specific, not class-wide. Beyond the three trials on Shelf #71, three more agents cleared the superiority bar: albiglutide (HR 0.78, a drug no longer sold), efpeglenatide (HR 0.73, with a renal composite win), and oral semaglutide in SOUL (HR 0.86 over ~4 years). Lixisenatide and once-weekly exenatide did not clear it and are excluded from this shelf by the developer’s filter.
mesh: Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Cardiovascular Diseases · Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonists · Glucagon-Like Peptide 1 · Hypoglycemic Agents · Humans
citation: SourceMed Shelf #72, “GLP-1 receptor agonists with demonstrated cardiovascular benefit: the remaining Level A trials”, sourcemed.io

title: Finerenone (non-steroidal MRA) in diabetic kidney disease
question: Does finerenone — a non-steroidal mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist — slow diabetic kidney disease and prevent cardiovascular events, on top of RAS blockade?
balance: Two trials, one drug, complementary halves: in advanced diabetic kidney disease the kidney win leads (HR 0.82); in earlier disease the cardiovascular win leads (HR 0.87) and the kidney signal does not reach significance. Hyperkalemia is the recurring price in both — roughly double the placebo rate, though few patients had to stop.
mesh: Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Diabetic Nephropathies · Renal Insufficiency, Chronic · Naphthyridines · Albuminuria · Humans
citation: SourceMed Shelf #73, “Finerenone (non-steroidal MRA) in diabetic kidney disease”, sourcemed.io

title: Spironolactone (steroidal MRA) and albuminuria in diabetic kidney disease
question: Does adding spironolactone to maximal ACE inhibitor / ARB therapy lower albuminuria in diabetic kidney disease — and has that ever been shown to change outcomes?
balance: The albuminuria effect is real and reproducible — about a third lower, on top of maximal RAS blockade, within weeks, and not explained by blood pressure. But every positive trial is small, short, and surrogate-only; the one large hard-outcome trial, in mostly non-albuminuric stage 3b CKD, found no cardiovascular benefit and two of three patients stopped the drug inside six months. A marker that moves, at a tolerability price.
citation: SourceMed Shelf #74, “Spironolactone (steroidal MRA) and albuminuria in diabetic kidney disease”, sourcemed.io

title: GLP-1 receptor agonists and the kidney
question: Do GLP-1 receptor agonists protect the kidney in type 2 diabetes with chronic kidney disease?
balance: FLOW gives the class its dedicated kidney-outcome win — kidney failure, halved eGFR, and death in one composite, with cardiovascular and all-cause mortality benefits attached. AWARD-7 is the supporting act: against insulin in stage 3–4 CKD, dulaglutide matched glucose control, slowed eGFR decline, and caused far less hypoglycemia. Whether GLP-1 benefit adds to SGLT2 therapy is the open question FLOW could not answer.
citation: SourceMed Shelf #75, “GLP-1 receptor agonists and the kidney”, sourcemed.io

title: Pioglitazone and thiazolidinediones: albuminuria
question: Do thiazolidinediones lower albuminuria in diabetes — and on how much evidence?
balance: The albuminuria signal is consistent — roughly a fifth to a quarter lower — but it rests entirely on small, short trials and a surrogate endpoint. No thiazolidinedione has been tested in a kidney-outcome trial, and the class carries weight gain, fluid retention, and heart-failure baggage. This is the cluster’s thinnest shelf, and it says so.
citation: SourceMed Shelf #76, “Pioglitazone and thiazolidinediones: albuminuria”, sourcemed.io

title: When should parenteral nutrition start in the ICU?
question: In a critically ill patient whose gut cannot meet calorie targets, how early should intravenous feeding start — within two days, or not before day 8?
balance: Withholding parenteral nutrition for a week beat starting it early — fewer infections, faster recovery, same mortality — in 4,640 adults and again in 1,440 children. The exception-shaped counterweight: when enteral feeding is truly impossible, early PN at modest targets did no harm and spared some ventilator days. ‘Late by default, early only when the gut is closed’ is what the trials support. (Panel position, 2016 SCCM/ASPEN: withhold supplemental PN until day 7–8 in patients who are not malnourished — attributed, for developer verification.)
citation: SourceMed Shelf #77, “When should parenteral nutrition start in the ICU?”, sourcemed.io

title: Enteral or parenteral: does the route matter?
question: For early nutrition in critical illness, does feeding through the gut beat feeding through a vein — or the reverse?
balance: At trial scale, the route did not decide survival or infections — early parenteral nutrition was neither the villain of the old literature nor inferior in CALORIES. The one place route bit back: full-dose enteral feeding into a vasopressor-dependent gut caused more bowel ischemia. Route matters less than dose and timing; in shock, the gut sets the limit. (Panel position: enteral preferred over parenteral when the gut works — attributed, for developer verification.)
citation: SourceMed Shelf #78, “Enteral or parenteral: does the route matter?”, sourcemed.io

title: Glutamine and antioxidants in the ICU: the REDOXS reversal
question: Do high-dose glutamine and antioxidant supplements help critically ill patients with multiorgan failure?
balance: The supplement era’s flagship trial reversed the field: early high-dose glutamine in multiorgan failure did not just fail — mortality ran higher at every horizon. Antioxidants were simply null. What small positive trials had promised, one large blinded trial took away. (Panel position after REDOXS: parenteral glutamine not recommended for routine use in the critically ill — attributed, for developer verification.)
citation: SourceMed Shelf #79, “Glutamine and antioxidants in the ICU: the REDOXS reversal”, sourcemed.io

title: Gastric residual volume: a ritual on trial
question: Should gastric residuals keep being aspirated and measured in tube-fed patients — and at what volume should feeds be held?
balance: Checking gastric residuals did not prevent pneumonia, and loosening the limit from 200 to 500 mL changed nothing except the number of alarms. The monitored ritual mostly interrupted feeding. Two trials, one message: the stomach’s leftover volume is not the safety signal it was treated as. (Panel position, 2016: do not use gastric residual volumes in routine monitoring; if measured, do not hold feeds below 500 mL — attributed, for developer verification.)
citation: SourceMed Shelf #80, “Gastric residual volume: a ritual on trial”, sourcemed.io

title: Glucose control in the ICU: how tight is too tight?
question: In critically ill patients, should insulin drive blood glucose down to 80–110 mg/dL — or is that the range where tight control turns harmful?
balance: One single-center trial made tight control (80–110 mg/dL) look lifesaving; every large multicenter test after it found no benefit or harm, and hypoglycemia every time. The 140–180 target in the guidelines is not a compromise — it is where the trial record actually lands. (Panel position, SCCM/ASPEN 2016 H5, strong recommendation on moderate evidence — attributed, for developer verification.)
citation: SourceMed Shelf #81, “Glucose control in the ICU: how tight is too tight?”, sourcemed.io

title: Postpyloric or gastric feeding?
question: Should tube feeds be delivered past the pylorus, into the small bowel — or is the stomach good enough?
balance: Two independent meta-analyses say feeding past the pylorus cuts pneumonia by about a third; the largest single trial found nothing; mortality never moves either way. The honest reading: fewer pneumonias on paper, no survival gain, and a harder tube to place — which is why the guidelines aim it at high aspiration risk and gastric intolerance rather than everyone. (Panel positions: SCCM/ASPEN recommend, moderate-to-high quality; ESPEN Grade B — attributed, for developer verification.)
citation: SourceMed Shelf #82, “Postpyloric or gastric feeding?”, sourcemed.io

title: Early enteral nutrition: start within 24–48 hours?
question: Should enteral nutrition start within 24–48 hours of injury or ICU admission — or can it wait?
balance: Start the gut early and infections fall and hospital stay shortens. A survival benefit is suggested by small-trial meta-analyses but has not been confirmed at scale — the large dose trials (EDEN, TARGET) and the timing network meta-analysis are null on mortality, and in established shock the enteral route carries a small bowel-ischaemia signal.
citation: SourceMed Shelf #83, “Early enteral nutrition: start within 24–48 hours?”, sourcemed.io

title: Statins after ASCVD: the secondary-prevention trials
question: In patients with established ASCVD, does a statin — and driving LDL lower still — reduce deaths and further events?
balance: Four trials, three decades, one direction: after ASCVD, statins cut deaths (4S, HPS), and driving LDL lower with high-intensity therapy cuts events further (TNT, PROVE-IT). This is the trial record under the Class 1, Level A recommendation for high-intensity statin in secondary prevention. (Panel position: 2018 AHA/ACC cholesterol guideline — attributed, for developer verification.)
mesh: Coronary Disease · Myocardial Infarction · Anticholesteremic Agents · Hydroxymethylglutaryl-CoA Reductase Inhibitors · Cholesterol, LDL · Humans
citation: SourceMed Shelf #84, “Statins after ASCVD: the secondary-prevention trials”, sourcemed.io

title: A statin for diabetes, risk score or not
question: Should adults 40–75 with diabetes take a statin even when their LDL and their calculated risk look unremarkable?
balance: In diabetes, the benefit does not wait for a high LDL or a high risk score: CARDS enrolled patients with unremarkable cholesterol and still cut first events by more than a third, HPS found the same proportional gain with or without prior disease, and the trialists’ pooled analysis shows the per-mmol benefit in diabetes equals everyone else’s. That record is why the statin in diabetes 40–75 is Class 1, Level A regardless of calculated risk. (Panel position: 2018 AHA/ACC cholesterol guideline — attributed, for developer verification.)
mesh: Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Cardiovascular Diseases · Hydroxymethylglutaryl-CoA Reductase Inhibitors · Anticholesteremic Agents · Cholesterol, LDL · Humans
citation: SourceMed Shelf #85, “A statin for diabetes, risk score or not”, sourcemed.io

title: Primary prevention at intermediate and high risk
question: In people without prior cardiovascular disease, who gains from a statin — and how much does the choice of population change the size of the win?
balance: Primary prevention works, and the size of the win tracks how the patients were chosen: −31% in high-LDL men (WOSCOPS), −36% in hypertensive patients with risk factors (ASCOT-LLA), −44% in an inflammation-selected trial stopped early (JUPITER), −24% in unselected intermediate risk (HOPE-3). The relative benefit is consistent; the absolute benefit is the baseline risk — which is why the recommendation is written around risk, not cholesterol alone. (Panel position: 2018 cholesterol / 2019 primary prevention guidelines, COR 1 LOE A at intermediate risk — attributed, for developer verification.)
mesh: Hypercholesterolemia · Cardiovascular Diseases · Coronary Disease · Hydroxymethylglutaryl-CoA Reductase Inhibitors · Anticholesteremic Agents · Humans
citation: SourceMed Shelf #86, “Primary prevention at intermediate and high risk”, sourcemed.io

title: Blocking the renin-angiotensin system in HFrEF: ACE inhibitor, ARB, ARNI
question: Does blocking the renin-angiotensin system — ACE inhibitor, ARB, or ARNI — save lives in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction?
balance: Each generation of renin-angiotensin blockade beat the last standard: enalapril cut deaths in the sickest patients (CONSENSUS) and then in ordinary HFrEF (SOLVD), candesartan covered the ACE-intolerant (CHARM-Alternative), and adding neprilysin inhibition beat enalapril itself by a fifth (PARADIGM-HF). Four trials, four decades, same pathway — which is why an ARNI, ACE inhibitor, or ARB is Class 1, Level A for every patient with HFrEF. (Panel position: 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA heart failure guideline — attributed, for developer verification.)
mesh: Heart Failure · Enalapril · Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme Inhibitors · Angiotensin Receptor Antagonists · Neprilysin · Double-Blind Method · Humans

title: Beta-blockers in HFrEF: the drug class doctors feared
question: Do beta-blockers — once considered dangerous in heart failure — reduce mortality in HFrEF?
balance: Beta-blockers were once considered dangerous in heart failure; four randomized programs then showed the same ~35% mortality reduction, in mild disease and in the sickest patients, with three different molecules. When a feared drug class reproduces like that, it stops being controversial — bisoprolol, carvedilol, and metoprolol succinate are Class 1, Level A. (Panel position: 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA heart failure guideline — attributed, for developer verification.)

title: Mineralocorticoid antagonists: the third pillar, with a guardrail
question: Do mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists reduce mortality in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction — and what does the potassium guardrail cost?
balance: Three trials, three severity levels — post-MI, mild symptoms, severe disease — and the class cut deaths in all three, which is what Class 1, Level A means in practice. The guardrail is part of the evidence: every positive trial ran with potassium and renal monitoring and exclusions, and when real-world prescribing skipped the monitoring after RALES, hyperkalemia hospitalizations and deaths rose sharply (Juurlink 2004, observational — named in this note, not carded). The drug works; the surveillance is not optional. (Panel position: 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA heart failure guideline — attributed, for developer verification.)

title: The ICD shelf: who actually benefits
question: Does a prophylactic implantable cardioverter-defibrillator reduce total mortality — and in whom?
balance: The ICD story is two true halves. In post-MI and mixed populations the device cut total mortality by roughly a quarter (MADIT-II, SCD-HeFT), earning Class 1, Level A. In modern nonischemic disease on contemporary therapy it halved sudden death and still did not significantly move total mortality (DANISH) — because the deaths it prevents are a smaller share of a better-treated total. The device works; the question the shelf leaves open is which patient, on today’s drugs, still has enough arrhythmic risk to gain. (Panel position: 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA heart failure guideline — attributed, for developer verification.)
citation: SourceMed Shelf #90, “The ICD shelf: who actually benefits”, sourcemed.io

title: Antiresorptives for postmenopausal osteoporosis: bisphosphonates and denosumab
question: Do bisphosphonates and denosumab prevent fractures in postmenopausal osteoporosis — and how long should treatment continue?
balance: Three different antiresorptive strategies each cut vertebral fractures by half to two-thirds and hip fractures by about half (FIT, HORIZON, FREEDOM) — the fracture record is not in dispute. The live question FLEX answers is duration: after five years, women whose risk had fallen gained little from continuing except at the spine, which is why the guideline pairs a strong treat recommendation with reassessment and holidays rather than lifetime-by-default. (Panel position: Endocrine Society 2019/2020 — attributed, for developer verification.)
citation: SourceMed Shelf #91, “Antiresorptives for postmenopausal osteoporosis: bisphosphonates and denosumab”, sourcemed.io

title: Bone-building therapy for very high risk: teriparatide and romosozumab
question: For women at very high fracture risk, does building new bone beat slowing its loss — and at what cardiovascular price?
balance: For very high risk, building bone beats only slowing its loss: teriparatide cut vertebral fractures by two-thirds, and a year of romosozumab followed by an antiresorptive beat both placebo (FRAME) and alendronate itself (ARCH) — the only head-to-head anabolic win in the field. The same ARCH trial is why this shelf is not a simple endorsement: the cardiovascular imbalance, absent in FRAME’s placebo comparison, put a boxed warning on the drug and a risk screen in the guideline. Benefit and warning come from the same two trials, and the shelf keeps them together. (Panel position: Endocrine Society 2019 + 2020 update — attributed, for developer verification.)

title: How low? The intensive blood pressure trials
question: How far should systolic pressure be pushed — and in whom does pushing it prevent events rather than just add harm?
balance: Five large trials, one arc: SPRINT said lower is better but excluded diabetes and stroke; ACCORD-BP then missed in diabetes and froze the field for a decade; STEP, ESPRIT, and BPROAD — 33,000 patients, including the diabetics and stroke survivors SPRINT left out — all landed the same way. Intensive systolic control prevents events across every population actually tested; the price is hypotension, syncope, and electrolytes, paid openly on every card. (Panel position: ACC/AHA hypertension guideline — attributed, for developer verification.) The J-curve pair, 2002 and 2018: pushing systolic down has a diastolic floor — both analyses put the risk nadir at a diastolic of 70–84 mmHg and warn below 70 in coronary patients.

title: The foundation trials: treating hypertension at all, and with what first
question: Before asking how low to go — does treating blood pressure prevent events at all, does it still help past 80, and does the first drug chosen matter?
balance: Before targets came foundations: SHEP and Syst-Eur proved treating systolic pressure in older adults prevents strokes, HYVET proved it saves lives past 80, and ALLHAT — 33,000 patients — proved the first drug matters less than starting, with the thiazide never beaten. Every modern target argument, including Shelf #93’s, stands on these four. (Panel position: ACC/AHA hypertension guideline — attributed, for developer verification.)

title: After a stroke: preventing the second one
question: Once a first stroke or TIA has happened, which treatments actually prevent the second one — and what does each cost in bleeding?
balance: Six trials define life after a first stroke: an antiplatelet (clopidogrel at least matches aspirin — CAPRIE), a short burst of two antiplatelets when the event is minor and the clock is early (CHANCE and POINT — benefit front-loaded, bleeding the price of duration), a high-intensity statin even without coronary disease (SPARCL, with its small hemorrhagic excess shown), an LDL driven under 70 rather than merely treated (Treat Stroke to Target, HR 0.78), and blood-pressure lowering that prevents recurrence in normotensives too (PROGRESS). (Panel position: AHA/ASA stroke prevention guideline — attributed, for developer verification.)

title: The Mediterranean diet trials
question: Tested the way drugs are tested — randomised, with heart attacks, strokes, and deaths as the endpoints — does a Mediterranean dietary pattern actually prevent cardiovascular events, in people who have never had one and in people who already have?
balance: Three randomized trials, three decades: Lyon showed a Mediterranean-type diet could prevent second events after infarction but was small and pre-statin; PREDIMED tested the pattern at scale in primary prevention and cut major events by about 30% — and its retraction and republication over randomization lapses is stated on its card, because the shelf keeps the correction with the claim; CORDIOPREV then showed the pattern beats a low-fat diet in patients with established coronary disease (HR 0.73). No drug-style effect size is claimed: the pattern is the intervention. (Panel positions: AHA dietary guidance and ASN statements endorse Mediterranean-style patterns — attributed, for developer verification.)
citation: SourceMed Shelf #96, “The Mediterranean diet trials”, sourcemed.io

title: Salt substitution and sodium reduction: the outcome trials
question: Does changing the salt itself — swapping regular salt for a potassium-enriched substitute, or eating less sodium for a few years — actually prevent strokes, cardiovascular events, and deaths, or does it only move the blood-pressure number? And what price, if any, does the added potassium carry?
balance: The salt shaker, trialed: SSaSS — 21,000 villagers — shows swapping regular salt for a potassium-enriched substitute prevents strokes and saves lives, with no hyperkalemia price in a population screened for kidney risk; TOHP shows a few years of sodium reduction still paying off a decade later; DECIDE-Diet confirms the blood-pressure mechanism in institutional kitchens, and is labeled the surrogate of the three. Kinship: Shelf #25 covers potassium itself — this shelf covers the salt it replaces. (Panel positions: AHA and WHO sodium guidance — attributed, for developer verification.)
citation: SourceMed Shelf #97, “Salt substitution and sodium reduction: the outcome trials”, sourcemed.io

title: Feeding acute pancreatitis early
question: For decades the inflamed pancreas was “rested” by starvation. When should feeding start, by what route — and what happened the one time a trial added something extra?
balance: Feed early, by mouth when the patient can. The older pooled trials say starting enteral feeding early — within 24 hours where possible — beats feeding through a vein or waiting, on mortality, pancreatic infection, and organ failure (Reference 2); the newest network ranking puts early oral feeding first of all strategies (Reference 3). But the one large modern trial found that forcing a tube in within 24 hours did not beat simply offering food at 72 hours and tubing only those who could not eat (Reference 1) — and in mild disease, eating immediately was safe and sent patients home sooner (Reference 4). Timing matters more than the tube’s tip: a gastric tube performed like a jejunal one (Reference 5). And more intervention is not more care — the one attempt to add something extra to early feeding in this disease killed people (PROPATRIA, Card 6).
citation: SourceMed Shelf #98, “Feeding acute pancreatitis early”, sourcemed.io

title: Feeding the undernourished hospital patient
question: Does feeding hospital patients who are truly undernourished change survival — and how do you know which patients those are?
balance: Across five decades of trials, the pattern is consistent: feeding helps the genuinely undernourished and does nothing measurable for the well-nourished. One large modern RCT (EFFORT) and two meta-analyses put mortality roughly a quarter to a third lower with nutritional support in malnourished medical inpatients; the biggest null (FOOD) supplemented a population only 8% of whom were undernourished. Potter’s 2001 subgroup result — the shelf’s anchor — agrees with the Cochrane undernourished stratum, but on its own it is a subgroup of an overall-null trial that was powered for weight, not survival. Screen for undernutrition, feed the ones who have it, and deliver the supplement like a medicine — prescribed, scheduled, and observed.
citation: SourceMed Shelf #99, “Feeding the undernourished hospital patient”, sourcemed.io

title: Anticoagulation in atrial fibrillation: from warfarin to the DOACs
question: In atrial fibrillation at elevated risk of stroke, does anticoagulation actually prevent strokes and emboli — and can the direct oral anticoagulants match or beat warfarin, the drug that proved the principle, without its monitoring burden and its bleeding price?
balance: Warfarin proved the principle (EAFT: events halved after cerebral ischemia), then four trials in five years replaced it: dabigatran superior on strokes, rivaroxaban noninferior in the highest-risk cohort, apixaban superior on strokes, bleeding, and death together, edoxaban noninferior with less bleeding — every one of them kinder to the brain than warfarin on hemorrhagic stroke. (Panel position: ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS atrial fibrillation guideline — attributed, for developer verification.)
