title: Rate versus rhythm: the strategy trials
question: In atrial fibrillation, is it better to restore and keep sinus rhythm, or simply to control the heart rate and let the rhythm be — and does the answer change if rhythm control starts early, if the rhythm is restored by ablation rather than drugs, or if the heart is failing?
balance: For twenty years the strategy question had one answer: AFFIRM and RACE said rhythm control buys nothing and costs hospitalizations. EAST-AFNET 4 reframed it — rhythm control delivered EARLY, within a year of diagnosis, cuts events by a fifth. Ablation’s own record is two-sided: CABANA’s intention-to-treat was null, CASTLE-AF’s failing-heart population won clearly. Timing and substrate, not the strategy label, decide. (Panel position: ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS atrial fibrillation guideline — attributed, for developer verification.)
citation: SourceMed Shelf #101, “Rate versus rhythm: the strategy trials”, sourcemed.io

title: Peripheral artery disease: the antithrombotic trials
question: In peripheral artery disease, can antithrombotic therapy do better than a single antiplatelet drug — by blocking platelets harder, or by adding a small dose of anticoagulant alongside aspirin?
balance: PAD’s drug lesson comes in two parts: blocking platelets harder does nothing (EUCLID’s flat null), but blocking the clotting cascade a little — rivaroxaban 2.5 mg twice daily on top of aspirin — prevents heart attacks, strokes, acute limb ischemia, and amputations in stable disease (COMPASS) and after revascularization (VOYAGER), at a bleeding price both cards state. Dual pathway, not dual platelet. (Panel position: ACC/AHA peripheral artery disease guideline — attributed, for developer verification.)
citation: SourceMed Shelf #102, “Peripheral artery disease: the antithrombotic trials”, sourcemed.io

title: Stable coronary disease: open the artery, or not?
question: In stable coronary disease, does opening a narrowed artery with a stent prevent death or heart attack — or does it only relieve symptoms, and how much of that relief survives comparison with a placebo procedure?
balance: Four trials discipline the catheter in stable disease: opening the artery does not prevent death or heart attack (COURAGE, ISCHEMIA), a sham procedure nearly matches it on exercise time in fully medicated patients (ORBITA) — and yet symptoms genuinely improve when PCI is tested against placebo in unmedicated patients (ORBITA-2). The synthesis the four support together: drugs carry the prognosis; the stent is a symptom treatment, chosen with open eyes. (Panel position: AHA/ACC chest pain guideline — attributed, for developer verification.)

title: Blocking the renin-angiotensin system in diabetic kidney disease: the anchor trials
question: In diabetic kidney disease, does blocking the renin–angiotensin system protect the kidney beyond blood-pressure lowering — and is blocking it twice, with an ACE inhibitor and an ARB together, better than blocking it once?
balance: Three decades, one axis: captopril halved renal failure in type 1 nephropathy (Lewis), losartan and irbesartan repeated it in type 2 (RENAAL, IDNT — with amlodipine proving it was never just blood pressure), and ONTARGET drew the ceiling — doubling the blockade adds harm, not protection. Every proteinuria shelf that followed (#69 SGLT2, #73 finerenone, #74 spironolactone, #75 GLP-1, #76 pioglitazone) is measured against patients already standing on this foundation. (Panel position: ADA Standards of Care — attributed, for developer verification.)

title: Aspirin for primary prevention: the statin-era verdict
question: For a person who has never had a heart attack or stroke, does a daily aspirin still prevent more first events than the bleeding it causes — in diabetes, in healthy old age, and at moderate estimated risk?
balance: Three trials, 47,000 people, one verdict: in the statin era, aspirin’s primary-prevention benefit shrank to the size of its bleeding harm — in diabetes the two nearly cancel (ASCEND), in healthy elders there is no benefit and a mortality signal nobody has explained (ASPREE), and at moderate risk there is nothing to weigh at all (ARRIVE). Secondary prevention is a different shelf and a different answer; this one is only about starting aspirin in people who have never had an event. (Panel positions: ACC/AHA primary prevention guideline and USPSTF — attributed, for developer verification.)

title: Vitamin C in sepsis: the rise and fall
question: Does intravenous vitamin C — alone, or in the vitamin C–thiamine–hydrocortisone cocktail — improve outcomes in sepsis, as a widely adopted before-and-after study promised?
balance: A before-and-after study launched a thousand protocols (Marik 2017 — retrospective, not randomized, and not carded here). The randomized trials then answered in sequence: no primary benefit in CITRIS-ALI, whose celebrated mortality difference was one secondary endpoint among many; no benefit for the full cocktail in VICTAS; and in LOVIT, the largest and cleanest trial, a harm signal. The Surviving Sepsis Campaign now recommends against intravenous vitamin C. The shelf keeps the correction alongside the claim. (Panel position: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021 — attributed, for developer verification.)

title: Hormone therapy and stroke: the WHI verdict
question: Observational studies said hormone therapy protected women’s hearts. What did the randomized trials find — above all, about stroke?
balance: The observational claim that “hormones protect the heart” was refuted by randomization. HERS warned first, in 1998: no protection for women who already had coronary disease, more venous clots, and a pattern of early coronary harm. The Women’s Health Initiative then answered in healthy postmenopausal women — twice. Estrogen plus progestin increased stroke (HR 1.41) alongside coronary events, pulmonary embolism, and breast cancer, against fewer colorectal cancers and hip fractures, for a global index of net harm; and estrogen alone increased stroke too (HR 1.39), with no coronary benefit to set against it. Two randomized trials, two hormone regimens, one direction on stroke: up. The benefits that are real — hip fracture on both WHI cards, colorectal cancer on the combined card — are on the cards, at full weight. (Panel positions: Endocrine Society and NAMS statements — attributed, for developer verification.)

title: Supplemental parenteral nutrition: completing the calories early
question: Does completing calories and protein early with supplemental parenteral nutrition improve survival in critical illness?
balance: The two biggest nutrition trials of the last fifteen years both favor patience: delaying parenteral completion by a week sped recovery rather than slowing it, doubling the protein dose did nothing, and the feeding route itself is a tolerance question, not a survival one. More, earlier, is not better.

title: Methods to delay the formal diagnosis of diabetes: lifestyle
question: In people with prediabetes, can changing how they live — food, movement, weight — push back the day the diagnosis arrives, and by how long?
balance: Diabetes is progressive; nothing here cures or prevents it. What these trials show is delay, measured honestly: lifestyle pushed diagnosis back by the same ~58% on two continents (DPP, Finnish DPS), Da Qing timed the delay at about three and a half years and then watched it compound into fewer events and longer life over thirty years, and DPPOS shows the pushed-back clock keeps its lead even after the program ends. The developer’s arithmetic: roughly a pound lost, a point of glucose; ten pounds, ten points — and years. (Panel position: ADA Standards of Care — attributed, for developer verification.)
citation: SourceMed Shelf #111, “Methods to delay the formal diagnosis of diabetes: lifestyle”, sourcemed.io

title: Methods to delay the formal diagnosis of diabetes: medicines
question: Can a drug push back the day prediabetes becomes diabetes — and is the clock it moves the disease’s clock, or only the laboratory’s?
balance: Every glucose drug is also a clock drug. In ADOPT, rosiglitazone held monotherapy longest (15% failure at 5 years; the developer’s extrapolation reaches ~8 years to A1c 8%), canagliflozin’s slope runs to ~7, metformin’s to ~5, the DPP-4 agents and repaglinide to ~4 — a figure the developer himself questions — and glyburide, driving weight gain and insulin resistance, failed fastest: the clock can be wound forward as well as back. Durability is not destiny: rosiglitazone’s own harms are on its card. What none of these agents does is prevent diabetes — they delay its formal diagnosis, which is exactly what the developer’s decree says to call it. One caveat rides the whole shelf: a glucose-lowering drug can mask hyperglycemia rather than delay disease — hold the glucose down pharmacologically and the diagnosis is deferred whether or not the disease itself has slowed. Against pure masking stands the washout evidence: in TRIPOD (Reference 6), protection persisted eight months after the drug was stopped, which argues true delay for the thiazolidinedione class. That tension is stated here, not resolved.

title: Melatonin for sleep onset
question: Does melatonin improve sleep onset, total sleep time, or sleep quality in primary sleep disorders?
balance: Melatonin shortens the time to fall asleep by minutes, on average — a real, small, replicated effect on a symptom, not a treatment for any disease.

title: Ginger for nausea in pregnancy
question: Does oral ginger improve nausea or vomiting during pregnancy?
balance: Ginger eases nausea in pregnancy in the trial evidence; symptom relief is the whole claim — no outcome data beyond it.

title: Peppermint oil for irritable bowel syndrome
question: Does peppermint oil relieve the pain and global symptoms of irritable bowel syndrome — and does the answer survive a large, rigorous trial with regulator-defined endpoints?
balance: Peppermint oil is the supplement shelf’s small-trial parable: a dozen small trials pool into a large, tidy benefit (RR 2.39) — and then the largest, most rigorous trial (PERSUADE) misses its primary endpoint while its secondaries nod yes. The effect on IBS pain and global symptoms is probably real and probably smaller than the pooled number; formulation and release site may decide who gets it. Symptom relief is the entire claim — there are no disease outcomes in IBS to win.

title: Steroids in septic shock
question: In septic shock, do corticosteroids save lives — or only shorten the shock?
balance: Two mega-trials, one answer on speed, two answers on survival: hydrocortisone resolves shock faster in both; a mortality benefit appeared only when fludrocortisone was added in the sicker trial population.

title: The polypill: several proven medicines in one tablet
question: Cardiovascular prevention fails mostly at the pill bottle, not the prescription pad — what happens when the proven drugs are combined into a single tablet?
balance: Across three randomized trials on three continents, putting proven cardiovascular medicines into one tablet cut major events by roughly a quarter to a third — not because the drugs are new, but because people actually take one pill: adherence is the active ingredient. The evidence is strongest after a heart attack (SECURE) and in pragmatic primary prevention (PolyIran); in the blinded primary-prevention trial (TIPS-3), the polypill alone was borderline and needed aspirin added to reach significance.

title: Intravenous iron in heart failure: three trials, one direction, no clean win
question: Iron deficiency affects half of heart-failure patients. Does fixing it intravenously change outcomes — or only how patients feel?
balance: Three large trials, one direction, no clean win: intravenous iron in iron-deficient heart failure makes people feel and function better — that part is proven — and probably keeps some out of hospital, but every outcomes trial has narrowly missed its primary endpoint and none has shown a mortality benefit. The guidelines recommend it for symptoms and quality of life; read the hospitalization claim as likely, not established, and the mortality claim as absent.

title: Balanced crystalloids vs saline: the biggest fluid argument in critical care
question: Every ICU resuscitates with one of two fluids. Thirty years of habit says saline; physiology says balanced. What do 34,000 randomized patients say?
balance: One large single-center trial said balanced fluids win by a whisker on a kidney composite; the two big blinded multicentre trials found no mortality difference at all; pooling every patient suggests a small benefit — about one life per 250 treated, with roughly a 90% probability of being real — and a probable harm in traumatic brain injury, where saline remains the safer default. Balanced crystalloids are a reasonable default for most ICU patients; saline has not been convicted; and the size of the prize, if it exists, is small.

title: Transfusion thresholds: how low can hemoglobin go?
question: How low can hemoglobin fall before transfusion helps more than it harms — and is the infarcting heart different?
balance: For a quarter-century the answer was simple: transfusing at a hemoglobin of 7 ties transfusing higher in the ICU, in septic shock, after hip fracture, and in cardiac surgery — and uses half the blood. MINT is the one trial that leans the other way: in acute myocardial infarction, every component favored the liberal strategy without reaching significance. Seven remains the rule almost everywhere; the acutely ischemic heart is the unresolved exception, and MINT is a trend demanding a second trial, not a verdict.

title: MAP targets in shock: how high is high enough?
question: Once the fluids are in and the pressors are running, what number should the nurse be chasing — and what does chasing more cost?
balance: Aim at 65 and stop chasing more. Driving mean arterial pressure to 80–85 in septic shock saved no lives and bought atrial fibrillation; letting older patients run at 60–65 spent less vasopressor and killed no one extra — if anything, the adjusted analysis favored less drug. The Surviving Sepsis target of 65 is the rare guideline number attacked from both directions that held: higher does not help, lower does not hurt, and the kidney in chronic hypertension is the one voice still arguing for a little more.

title: Hyponatremia: how fast is too fast — and who says so?
question: The emergency treatment of low sodium turns on two numbers everyone quotes and almost nobody can source: the bolus, and the ceiling.
balance: The ceilings are real practice and the injury they guard against is real — but they were set by expert panels grading their own evidence D, and no randomized trial of correction speed has ever been run. The one trial we have says bolus and infusion are equally safe ways to give hypertonic saline. And across nearly 12,000 patients in the modern cohorts, the association runs against the fear: correcting slowly tracked with more deaths — about 32 extra per thousand versus rapid correction — while demyelination stayed rare at every speed. Treat the ceiling as a guardrail, not a cliff edge: below it, the documented danger is leaving a seizing, encephalopathic patient hyponatremic — and in concentrated-urine states, normal saline itself can push the sodium further down (Reference 5).

title: Hypernatremia: the speed limit that was never measured
question: Every trainee learns the speed limit for bringing high sodium down. Almost none learn that in adults, it was never measured.
balance: For high sodium, the famous limit — no faster than about ten points a day, lest the brain swell — has never been tested in an adult trial. It was borrowed from neonatal cases and expert opinion. In the two large modern adult cohorts, rapid correction produced not one attributed case of cerebral edema, while slow correction carried roughly double the adjusted odds of death. That gap is confounded — the sickest patients correct slowest — but the asymmetry is the finding: one side of the argument has more than 4,700 patients behind it; the other has a tradition.

title: VTE prophylaxis: preventing clots, buying bleeding
question: Hospital clot prevention is universal and automatic — what do the big trials actually buy, and what do they charge?
balance: Prophylaxis prevents clots — that part is not in doubt. Everything after it is margins. In the ICU, the better-marketed drug tied on the clots the trial was powered for and won on pulmonary embolism and HIT only as secondary findings its own authors tell us to hold loosely. In medical patients, extending prophylaxis past the standard course prevented mostly silent clots and paid for them in bleeding, and the largest extension trial missed its primary endpoint outright. No prophylaxis trial has ever moved mortality. Give it to patients whose clot risk is real, stop it when the stay stops, and do not mistake an ultrasound endpoint for a life saved.

title: Digoxin in heart failure: mortality neutral, fewer hospitalizations
balance: What an agent should take from this shelf: in the only large randomized trial, digoxin at a median 0.25 mg a day did not change mortality (RR 0.99) and cut heart-failure hospitalizations (RR 0.72); two randomized withdrawal trials agree from the other direction — stopping it made heart failure worse within weeks. There is no randomized evidence of toxicity at these doses; the harm signal lives in one post-hoc analysis at serum levels of 1.2 ng/mL or more, so the practical lesson is to aim low (0.5–0.8 ng/mL), not to avoid the drug. The Beers 0.125 mg ceiling rests on that post-hoc signal and pharmacology; the developer’s evidence revision records the toxicity claim as unproven — Level B — with benefit the better-supported reading.

title: Colorectal cancer screening: what the randomized trials actually showed
question: Does endoscopic screening prevent colorectal cancer deaths — and why did the biggest colonoscopy trial look weaker than the smaller sigmoidoscopy trials?
balance: The sigmoidoscopy trials — one look, or two — cut both incidence and mortality by a fifth to a third. The colonoscopy trial cut incidence by 18% but showed no significant mortality benefit at 10 years, in a trial where only 42% of the invited actually got scoped. Read together: screening works roughly in proportion to how much of it actually happens; intention-to-screen arithmetic punishes low uptake, and the per-protocol numbers in the older trials show the biological effect is real.

title: Steroids in severe community-acquired pneumonia
question: In severe community-acquired pneumonia, do corticosteroids save lives?
balance: The benefit tracks severity and inflammation. In the most inflamed severe patients, methylprednisolone cut treatment failure (Torres); in all-comer hospitalized pneumonia, prednisone bought faster stability, not survival, at a glucose price (STEP); the one big mortality result is in ICU-severe disease (CAPE COD) — hydrocortisone, started early, stopped early for benefit, cutting 28-day mortality nearly in half; and one underpowered trial in an older VA population (ESCAPe) found nothing. Different steroids, different populations, different power — CAPE COD is the strongest single signal steroids have produced outside septic shock, and it is one trial stopped early, which inflates effects.

title: Preventing falls in older adults: exercise works on falls, systems haven't proven it on injuries
question: What actually prevents falls — and fall injuries — in older adults at risk?
balance: Exercise in three delivery forms — class-based balance training (tai ji quan), a prescribed home program (Otago), training embedded in daily life (LiFE) — cuts falls by a third to a half, and multifactorial risk-factor treatment worked under efficacy conditions in 1994 (Tinetti). Falls prevented is a fact at trial scale; injuries prevented at system scale is not yet.

title: Sodium bicarbonate in CKD: the open-label win and the blinded null
question: Does treating metabolic acidosis with sodium bicarbonate slow kidney failure in chronic kidney disease?
balance: The two trials split exactly the way the library's evidence hierarchy predicts. UBI — open-label, no placebo — reported large wins on hard endpoints: less progression, less dialysis, fewer deaths. BiCARB — double-blind, placebo-controlled, in older patients with milder acidosis — found nothing: no functional benefit, no GFR benefit, higher costs, and slightly worse quality of life. And the mechanism is acid retention itself — retained acid drives compensatory ammonia production and endothelin-1 that injure the tubulointerstitium — which is why a diet can do what the pill does, and why the open-label/blinded split here is about proof, not plausibility. Correcting a low bicarbonate is cheap and reasonable; believing the mortality claim requires the blinded trial that hasn't confirmed it.

title: Temperature control after cardiac arrest: the cooling era, tested twice

title: Oxygen targets in critical illness: neither lower nor higher won
question: In ICU patients on oxygen, does targeting a lower (conservative) oxygen level improve outcomes — or does liberal oxygen do harm the trials should catch?
balance: Both directions were tested at scale and both came back null. HOT-ICU's low vs high PaO₂ targets in hypoxemic respiratory failure: identical mortality. ICU-ROX's conservative vs usual oxygen in ventilated patients: identical ventilator-free days and survival. The wide middle is safe; the trials retire the anxiety at both ends — extremes, not targets, are where the harm lives (neither trial tested extreme hyperoxia).

title: Albumin in cirrhosis: five trials, one pattern
question: When does infusing albumin actually help patients with cirrhosis — and when is it just chasing a number?
balance: The five trials sort cleanly by indication. Albumin works where there's a defined circulatory job: alongside antibiotics in spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (Sort: mortality cut by two-thirds), and covering large-volume paracentesis (Ginès 1988: no renal complications vs 11 without). It works given long-term to outpatients with ascites (ANSWER: survival 77% vs 66%). It fails as a short inpatient campaign to normalize the level (ATTIRE: null, more serious adverse events) and bundled with midodrine on the transplant waitlist (MACHT: null). The pattern: albumin is a drug for specific hemodynamic jobs, not a lab-value cosmetic.

title: Lowering urate to protect the kidney: three trials, no protection
question: Does lowering serum urate with allopurinol slow the progression of chronic kidney disease?
balance: A beautiful epidemiologic association — high urate, faster decline — taken to trial twice in the same journal issue, and both times the kidney slopes came out identical. CKD-FIX (advanced CKD, mean eGFR 32): −3.33 vs −3.23 ml/min/yr. PERL (type 1 diabetes, measured iohexol GFR): a between-group difference of 0.001 after washout — as null as null gets, with the urate separation fully achieved (6.1 → 3.9 mg/dL). Urate is a marker of kidney disease, not a driver of it. FEATHER (Reference 3) makes three: febuxostat in stage 3 CKD with asymptomatic hyperuricemia, eGFR slope difference 0.70 (−0.21 to 1.62), P=0.1 — the drug prevented gout (0.91% vs 5.86%) and did not protect the kidney. Closing line: the ACR 2020 guideline and KDIGO 2024 both advise against treating asymptomatic hyperuricemia to protect the kidney.

title: Early mobilization: up sooner isn't better — in the ICU it's neutral, after stroke it harmed
question: Does mobilizing critically ill patients as early and as much as possible improve recovery?
balance: The arc runs small-and-positive → large-and-neutral → large-and-harmful, ordered almost perfectly by trial size and by how much of the original bundle was stripped away. Schweickert's early PT/OT — bundled with daily sedation interruption — doubled independent recovery at discharge in 104 patients. TEAM tested mobilization alone at 750 patients and found nothing but more adverse events. AVERT pushed earliest-and-most after stroke in 2,104 patients and made outcomes worse. What survives: wake patients, sit them up, ambulate as tolerated. What doesn't: mobilization as a dosed, forced, earlier-is-always-better intervention.

title: C. difficile: the cure is easy — preventing the comeback is the contest
question: For C. difficile infection, standard antibiotics tie on initial cure — which strategies prevent the recurrence that causes the real toll?
balance: Standard antibiotics cure roughly 87–89% of first episodes no matter which you pick (Louie, Cornely). The disease's real toll is the ~1-in-4 who relapse — and three randomized strategies cut that: a narrow-spectrum drug that spares the flora (recurrence 15% vs 25%), the same drug stretched into a pulse in older patients (sustained cure 70% vs 59%), and an antibody that disarms the toxin while the gut recovers (recurrence ~17% vs ~27%, twice). What doesn't differ anywhere on this shelf: the initial cure.

title: Exercise in heart failure: fitter, not longer-lived
question: Does structured exercise training change outcomes in heart failure — or only how patients feel and move?
balance: Four exhibits, one shape. Training reliably makes heart-failure patients fitter and more functional — HF-ACTION's exercise-capacity gains, REHAB-HF's large SPPB jump in the frailest patients — and just as reliably fails to move death or hospitalization: HF-ACTION's unadjusted primary null, REHAB-HF's flat rehospitalization, SMARTEX's evaporating gains, and an 18-trial individual-patient pool with every hard-outcome estimate crossing 1. Prescribe exercise for what patients can do and how they feel. Don't promise it extends life — the trials haven't shown that.

title: Time-restricted eating: the clock adds nothing
question: Does confining eating to a daily window (16:8 or similar) cause weight loss beyond what eating less already does?
balance: Two randomized trials asked it cleanly and got the same answer. TREAT found the fasting window produced no between-group weight difference at all — and the small loss leaned toward lean mass. Liu added time restriction on top of calorie restriction for a full year and gained nothing: the calories did all the work in both arms. Time-restricted eating is a scheduling preference some people find easier to keep; as a metabolic intervention, the trials say the clock itself contributes nothing measurable.

title: Uncomplicated diverticulitis: leaving out the antibiotic.
question: In CT-proven uncomplicated diverticulitis, does treatment without antibiotics recover patients as safely as treatment with them?
balance: Two randomized trials, 1,151 patients. Omitting antibiotics did not significantly slow recovery, raise complications (AVOD 1.9% vs 1.0%; DIABOLO 3.8% vs 2.6% — both non-significant, both numerically favoring antibiotics), or raise recurrence; DIABOLO’s no-antibiotic group left hospital a day sooner. The boundary is the exclusions: sepsis, peritonitis, CT-complicated disease, and immune suppression were kept out of both trials.

title: Chasing hemoglobin with ESAs in kidney disease: the target was the harm.
question: In CKD patients not on dialysis, does using an erythropoiesis-stimulating agent to push hemoglobin to normal (13 g/dL or above) improve cardiovascular outcomes versus partial correction?
balance: CHOIR (targets 13.5 vs 11.3) — the high target caused MORE of the composite, 17.5% vs 13.5%, HR 1.34, and the trial stopped early. CREATE (13–15 vs 10.5–11.5) — no cardiovascular benefit, and more patients in the high group reached dialysis (127 vs 111). TREAT, the only placebo-controlled trial — no benefit on either primary composite, and stroke nearly doubled, 5.0% vs 2.6%, HR 1.92. What the drugs did deliver: fewer transfusions (TREAT 297 vs 496 patients) and modest quality-of-life gains (CREATE).

title: Early continuous neuromuscular blockade in severe ARDS: ACURASYS versus ROSE
question: In adults with early moderate-to-severe ARDS, does a 48-hour continuous cisatracurium infusion improve survival compared with usual care or placebo?
balance: ACURASYS found lower adjusted 90-day mortality with cisatracurium, although the crude mortality difference was not statistically significant. ROSE, a much larger trial using high PEEP and a lighter-sedation usual-care strategy, found virtually identical 90-day mortality. Taken together, these trials do not establish a consistent survival benefit from routine early continuous neuromuscular blockade in moderate-to-severe ARDS.

title: Niacin added to treated cholesterol: AIM-HIGH and HPS2-THRIVE
question: In patients with established vascular disease whose LDL cholesterol is already treated with statin-based therapy, does adding niacin reduce major cardiovascular events?
balance: No. AIM-HIGH found no incremental clinical benefit from adding extended-release niacin to intensive statin therapy. HPS2-THRIVE likewise found no significant reduction in major vascular events with niacin-laropiprant and reported more serious adverse events. Together, the trials do not support adding niacin to well-treated LDL cholesterol to improve cardiovascular outcomes.
citation: SourceMed Shelf #184, “Niacin added to treated cholesterol: AIM-HIGH and HPS2-THRIVE”, sourcemed.io

title: Dexamethasone in hospitalized COVID-19: mortality benefit depends on respiratory support
question: In hospitalized patients with COVID-19, does dexamethasone reduce 28-day mortality, and does benefit differ by respiratory support at randomization?
balance: Dexamethasone lowered 28-day mortality in patients receiving invasive mechanical ventilation (29.3% vs 41.4%) and in those receiving oxygen without invasive ventilation (23.3% vs 26.2%). It did not reduce mortality in patients receiving no respiratory support (17.8% vs 14.0%). Benefit was therefore concentrated in patients needing respiratory support.

title: Intracranial stenting for symptomatic stenosis: two trials, both stopped early, both against the stent
question: In patients with a recent stroke or TIA from 70–99% intracranial arterial stenosis, does adding a stent to aggressive medical therapy prevent further strokes?
balance: No — twice, with two different stents. In SAMMPRIS (451 patients), 30-day stroke or death was 14.7% with the Wingspan stent vs 5.8% on aggressive medical therapy alone, and the gap persisted at one year (20.0% vs 12.2%); enrollment was stopped for the early harm. VISSIT (112 patients), testing a balloon-expandable stent, was halted early after SAMMPRIS reported and pointed the same way — one-year stroke or hard TIA 36.2% vs 15.1%. The strokes the stent was meant to prevent happened around the procedure instead. Aggressive medical therapy — antiplatelet treatment, blood-pressure and risk-factor control — is the treatment.
citation: SourceMed Shelf #186, “Intracranial stenting for symptomatic stenosis: two trials, both stopped early, both against the stent”, sourcemed.io

title: Antibiotics vs appendectomy for appendicitis: a real alternative — with an appendicolith exception and a five-year tail
question: In uncomplicated acute appendicitis, can antibiotics replace appendectomy — and for whom does that trade fail?
balance: Mostly yes, with two carve-outs. CODA (1,552 adults) found antibiotics noninferior to appendectomy on 30-day health status, and 71% of the antibiotics group had avoided surgery at 90 days — but complications ran higher with antibiotics (8.1 vs 3.5 per 100 patients), driven entirely by patients with an appendicolith (20.2 vs 3.6 per 100; 41% of them came to surgery). APPAC (530 CT-proven uncomplicated cases) missed its strict noninferiority test, yet 72.7% avoided appendectomy at one year with no penalty for having waited; by five years 39.1% of the antibiotics group had had an appendectomy, while overall complications favored antibiotics (6.5% vs 24.4%). The honest offer: antibiotics first is reasonable for uncomplicated appendicitis without an appendicolith, accepting roughly a 3-in-10 chance of surgery within a year and 4-in-10 by five years.
citation: SourceMed Shelf #187, “Antibiotics vs appendectomy for appendicitis: a real alternative — with an appendicolith exception and a five-year tail”, sourcemed.io

title: Arthroscopic knee surgery vs sham: the scope adds nothing
question: For osteoarthritis of the knee and degenerative (wear-and-tear) meniscus tears — not a ruptured ligament or an acute injury — does arthroscopic surgery help more than a sham operation or physical therapy alone?
balance: Three NEJM trials, three nulls. Against a true placebo operation, arthroscopy never came out ahead at any point in two years; against sham surgery for a degenerative meniscus tear, removing meniscus tissue gained nothing at one year; and added to good physical and medical therapy, it added nothing. The relief patients report is real — it is the placebo effect and the knee’s natural course, not the scope. Scope: every patient on this shelf had a degenerative knee — arthritic pain or a wear-and-tear meniscus tear. Nobody had a torn ligament; for the ligament trials, see Shelf #193.
citation: SourceMed Shelf #188, “Arthroscopic knee surgery vs sham: the scope adds nothing”, sourcemed.io

title: Closing a patent foramen ovale after cryptogenic stroke
question: After a cryptogenic stroke in a patient with a patent foramen ovale, does device closure beat medical therapy at preventing another stroke?
balance: In selected patients — younger, with a moderate-to-large shunt or an atrial septal aneurysm — the three 2017 NEJM trials all favored closure: RESPECT’s long-term follow-up HR 0.55, REDUCE 1.4% vs 5.4%, CLOSE zero strokes vs 14. The price is real: more atrial fibrillation after the device (up to 6.6%), procedural complications (about 6% in CLOSE), and venous clots in RESPECT. Absolute gains are small because recurrence on medical therapy is already low — this is a carefully-selected-patient treatment, not a close-every-PFO answer. The earlier 2013 RESPECT primary report, at a median 2.1 years, had been null; the benefit emerged with longer follow-up.
citation: SourceMed Shelf #189, “Closing a patent foramen ovale after cryptogenic stroke”, sourcemed.io

title: Colchicine for pericarditis: the recurrence is the disease
question: Does adding colchicine to standard anti-inflammatory treatment prevent pericarditis from coming back?
balance: Two double-blind, placebo-controlled trials from the same Italian group — one in a first acute attack, one in patients with multiple recurrences — and both cut recurrence roughly in half, with numbers needed to treat of 4 and 5 and no serious-harm signal. The evidence is strong in effect and narrow in provenance: essentially one research group has run these trials, which is the honest caveat on the shelf. (Colchicine also lives on Shelf #120 for coronary disease — a different question, so no one-home conflict.)
citation: SourceMed Shelf #190, “Colchicine for pericarditis: the recurrence is the disease”, sourcemed.io

title: PCSK9 inhibitors and cardiovascular outcomes
question: In patients with established cardiovascular disease whose LDL cholesterol stays at or above 70 mg/dL on a statin, do PCSK9 inhibitor injections reduce cardiovascular events?
balance: Two large double-blind trials, 46,488 patients: adding a PCSK9 inhibitor to a statin cut the combined rate of heart attack, stroke, and related events by about 15% — roughly 1.5 fewer events per 100 patients treated over 2–3 years — and lowered LDL by about 60%. Neither trial showed fewer cardiovascular deaths; the lower all-cause mortality in ODYSSEY OUTCOMES was a secondary endpoint. Injection-site reactions were the main excess harm.
citation: SourceMed Shelf #191, “PCSK9 inhibitors and cardiovascular outcomes”, sourcemed.io

title: Intensive glucose control in type 2 diabetes
question: In people with long-standing type 2 diabetes, does pushing A1c toward normal with intensive therapy prevent heart attacks, strokes, and death?
balance: Three large randomized trials, 23,182 patients with long-standing diabetes: pushing A1c down to about 6.5–6.9% did not reduce heart attacks, strokes, or cardiovascular death in any of them. ACCORD — the most aggressive, targeting A1c below 6% — was stopped early because more patients died on intensive therapy (5.0% vs 4.0%). The one consistent gain was kidney protection: ADVANCE cut new or worsening nephropathy (4.1% vs 5.2%). Severe hypoglycemia rose in every trial. All three trials enrolled patients with roughly a decade of diabetes — they do not answer what early control does in the newly diagnosed.
citation: SourceMed Shelf #192, “Intensive glucose control in type 2 diabetes”, sourcemed.io

title: Ruptured ACL: reconstruct now, or rehabilitate first?
question: For a torn anterior cruciate ligament, does early surgical reconstruction give a better knee than structured rehabilitation first, with reconstruction reserved for knees that stay unstable?
balance: Three randomized trials, 604 patients — and the answer depends on which knee. For a fresh tear in a young, active patient, rehabilitation first matched early surgery at 2 and 5 years, and about half never needed the operation (KANON). For acute tears more broadly, early surgery finished modestly ahead on patient-reported function at 2 years — an edge the trial’s own authors call not clinically relevant — and half the rehabilitation group still avoided surgery (COMPARE). For an older, non-acute tear where the knee keeps giving way, surgery clearly won: better function at 18 months and cost-effective (ACL SNNAP), though 41% of the rehabilitation group crossed over to surgery anyway. So the contrast with Shelf #188 is real — a ruptured ligament is a structural injury with genuine instability, and reconstruction has randomized support, strongest exactly where instability persists. But ‘everyone with a torn ACL needs immediate surgery’ is not what these trials show: starting with rehabilitation cost the half who stabilize nothing, and the operation stayed available for the rest.
citation: SourceMed Shelf #193, “Ruptured ACL: reconstruct now, or rehabilitate first?”, sourcemed.io

title: DPP-4 inhibitors: cardiovascular safety without benefit
question: In type 2 diabetes at high cardiovascular risk, do DPP-4 inhibitors (the gliptins) prevent cardiovascular events — or at least do no cardiovascular harm?
balance: Five double-blind randomized trials, 49,564 patients: no DPP-4 inhibitor prevented cardiovascular events, and none increased the primary composite either — saxagliptin HR 1.00, alogliptin 0.96, sitagliptin 0.98, linagliptin 1.02 against placebo, and 0.98 against glimepiride. These were the FDA-era safety trials, and on ischemic events the class is acquitted. One genuine exception: saxagliptin increased hospitalization for heart failure (3.5% vs 2.8%; HR 1.27) — a signal strong enough to put a heart-failure warning on the saxagliptin and alogliptin labels, and not seen with sitagliptin (HR 1.00) or linagliptin. The glucose gains were modest throughout (A1c about 0.3 points below placebo). So the gliptins are safe, gentle glucose-lowering drugs that prevent nothing — a different species from the SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP-1 agents, which reduce events. Their clearest comparative win is against a sulfonylurea: in CAROLINA, linagliptin matched glimepiride event-for-event over 6.3 years with about a quarter of the hypoglycemia.
citation: SourceMed Shelf #194, “DPP-4 inhibitors: cardiovascular safety without benefit”, sourcemed.io

title: When to start dialysis in acute kidney injury
question: In critically ill patients with severe acute kidney injury and no emergency indication, does starting renal-replacement therapy early save lives — or is it better to wait?
balance: Five randomized trials, 4,636 patients with severe acute kidney injury in intensive care: in the three large multicenter trials, starting dialysis early saved no lives — 60-day mortality 48.5% vs 49.7% when the delayed strategy waited for a conventional trigger (AKIKI), 90-day mortality 58% vs 54% in septic shock (IDEAL-ICU, stopped early for futility), and 43.9% vs 43.7% with an accelerated strategy (STARRT-AKI). Waiting let about half of AKIKI's delayed-strategy patients — and 38% in STARRT-AKI's standard arm — recover without ever being dialyzed. The one positive trial, ELAIN, was small, single-center, and mostly surgical; no multicenter trial reproduced it. Early was not harmless: more catheter bloodstream infections in AKIKI (10% vs 5%) and more survivors still dependent on dialysis at 90 days in STARRT-AKI (10.4% vs 6.0%). And waiting has a limit — AKIKI-2 found that postponing beyond the usual triggers bought no extra dialysis-free days and carried higher adjusted 60-day mortality (HR 1.65). The practice these trials support: absent an emergency indication, wait and watch — but do not postpone indefinitely.
citation: SourceMed Shelf #195, “When to start dialysis in acute kidney injury”, sourcemed.io

title: Vitamin A toxicity: birth defects and fragile bone
question: Can too much preformed vitamin A (retinol) — from supplements and fortified food — cause birth defects, fractures, or liver damage?
balance: Four exhibits — three large cohorts (97,407 participants) and one biopsy series; no trials — this harm can never be randomized. The pregnancy signal is the strong one: vitamin A supplements above about 10,000 IU a day carried about 4.8 times the prevalence of cranial-neural-crest birth defects, with an apparent threshold near that dose, the risk concentrated in exposure before the seventh week — the finding the 3,000 µg/day upper limit for preformed vitamin A rests on. The bone signal is real but uneven against the developer's floor: hip fracture at the highest blood levels (2.47×) and the top 1% of blood levels (~7× any fracture) clear the 2.0 line, while the broad dietary estimates (1.5–1.9×) sit inside the band the developer calls not solid. Every signal names retinol — beta-carotene showed no association in any cohort. The liver story is the same shape: never measured in trials, but biopsy-proven and dose-graded at sustained intakes from 25,000 IU/day (Reference 4) — a poison's signature, not a population risk estimate. Posted as a possible: the birth-defect evidence is strong for observational data; the fracture evidence is moderate.
citation: SourceMed Shelf #196, “Vitamin A toxicity: birth defects and fragile bone”, sourcemed.io

title: Vitamin C and the common cold
question: Does vitamin C prevent the common cold, shorten it, or treat it once it starts?
balance: Seventy years of argument, and the pooled answer is narrow. Vitamin C taken every day does not stop ordinary people catching colds — across 29 trial comparisons and 11,306 participants the risk was essentially unchanged (RR 0.97), far inside the developer's not-solid band. What regular use does do, consistently, is shorten colds a little: about 8% in adults and 14% in children — roughly half a day on a week's cold. Starting vitamin C only after symptoms begin has no consistent effect. The one large effect is real but narrow: in five trials of 598 marathon runners, skiers, and soldiers under brief extreme physical stress, regular vitamin C halved cold incidence (RR 0.48) — the clearest exhibit is the Comrades ultramarathon trial, 33% vs 68%. And the shelf carries its own warning label: the famous 1975 NIH trial, whose apparent benefit dissolved once participants guessed their capsules by taste — the reason this literature is read with suspicion, though the reanalysis disputes how clean that lesson is. Routine prevention: no. A modest duration effect, and a genuine niche under extreme exertion: yes.
citation: SourceMed Shelf #197, “Vitamin C and the common cold”, sourcemed.io

title: Vitamin B12 replacement: pills or injections?
question: For vitamin B12 deficiency, does high-dose oral B12 work as well as intramuscular injections?
balance: Three randomized trials, 391 patients, one pooled review — and the needle mostly loses. High-dose oral B12 (1–2 mg a day) corrected deficiency as reliably as injections in every trial: blood counts and neurologic findings recovered the same (Bolaman), and in the most careful small trial the pill finished ahead on chemistry (B12 1,005 vs 325 pg/mL; methylmalonic acid 169 vs 265 nmol/L at four months) — because roughly 1% of a large oral dose crosses the gut by passive diffusion even when intrinsic factor is absent, pernicious anemia included. The 2018 Cochrane review of the small trials (3 trials, 153 patients) called the evidence low quality but found no difference in normalization, and lower cost by mouth. The caution comes from the largest and most pragmatic trial: in 283 primary-care patients over 65, oral matched injections at 8 weeks, but once-weekly oral maintenance had slipped behind monthly injections by week 52 (74% vs 80% still normal; non-inferiority not established) — even as 83% of patients preferred the pill. So: pills replace shots to correct deficiency, and for maintenance when the dose stays substantial or the level is rechecked; a token weekly tablet is where the route fails. Developer's verdict: POSSIBLE — consistent direction across three randomized trials, but small, open-label, and largely biochemical outcomes.
citation: SourceMed Shelf #198, “Vitamin B12 replacement: pills or injections?”, sourcemed.io

title: Vitamin A supplementation in deficient children: does it save lives?
question: In populations where vitamin A deficiency is common, does giving preschool children periodic vitamin A reduce deaths?
balance: Four positive trials and one enormous null — and the shelf's grade turns on how you weigh them. In the high-deficiency, high-mortality settings of the 1980s and early 1990s, vitamin A supplementation cut preschool deaths by 34% (Aceh, open), 54% (Tamil Nadu, masked, weekly small dose), 30% (Nepal, double-masked, placebo-controlled), and 19% (Ghana, double-blind) — four randomized designs, one direction, and the reason WHO built programs on it. Then DEVTA randomized about a million Indian children and found nothing: mortality ratio 0.96. DEVTA's authors, pooling their null with the eight earlier trials, put the overall effect at 11%; the Cochrane pool lands at 12% (RR 0.88). The reconciling read: the benefit is real where deficiency is severe and child mortality is high — the early trials' worlds — and shrinks toward zero as deficiency and mortality fall, which is the direction the world has moved. Developer's verdict: POSSIBLE — a mortality benefit in deficient populations, unproven in replete ones.
citation: SourceMed Shelf #199, “Vitamin A supplementation in deficient children: does it save lives?”, sourcemed.io

title: Vitamin K and fractures
question: Does vitamin K — K1, or high-dose K2 (MK-4) — prevent fractures in postmenopausal women?
balance: The most dramatic vitamin-K numbers in the library — and the least trustworthy address they live at. The fracture claim rests on Japanese trials of high-dose MK-4 (45 mg a day, a drug dose, not a supplement dose): pooled in 2006, they showed odds ratios of 0.40 for vertebral, 0.23 for hip, and 0.19 for nonvertebral fractures — far past the developer's 0.5 benefit line. But every one of those seven trials was small and most were open-label, and when the same York group updated the pool in 2019 — after the integrity of some earlier trials had been questioned — the vertebral-fracture effect vanished entirely (OR 0.98) and the remaining clinical-fracture signal (OR 0.74) lost significance when restricted to low-risk-of-bias trials (0.76; 0.58 to 1.01). The one large double-blind trial, ECKO, found no effect on bone density at all; its fewer fractures (9 vs 20) were a secondary endpoint in a trial not powered for them. Developer's verdict: MAYBE (weak evidence) — a claim whose size shrinks every time the methods improve.
citation: SourceMed Shelf #200, “Vitamin K and fractures”, sourcemed.io

title: Total diet replacement programmes for type 2 diabetes remission
question: Can supervised total diet replacement followed by food reintroduction and weight-maintenance support induce remission of recent type 2 diabetes, and how durable is remission?
balance: Two independent open-label randomized trials support remission with supervised diet-replacement programmes in recent type 2 diabetes: DiRECT 46% vs 4% and DIADEM-I 61% vs 12% at 12 months. Remission tracked weight loss. DiRECT remission was 36% vs 3% at 24 months; at 5 years, 11/85 (13%) observed extension participants were in remission. That selected extension percentage is not an intention-to-treat estimate. Long-term durability is limited. DiRECT follow-up reports are the same trial, not independent replications. A small randomized feasibility trial in UK South Asian adults (STANDby) pointed the same way: remission 5/13 versus 0/12.
citation: SourceMed Shelf #201, “Total diet replacement programmes for type 2 diabetes remission”, sourcemed.io

title: Low-FODMAP diet for irritable bowel syndrome: better than a usual diet, not better than good advice
question: In adults with irritable bowel syndrome, does a low-FODMAP diet improve symptoms compared with a usual diet or with standard dietary advice?
balance: A low-FODMAP diet clearly beat a typical diet in a controlled feeding study, but in two pragmatic trials it did no better than competent standard dietary advice. Reasonable to try; not proven superior to good standard advice. Developer’s verdict: POSSIBLE for symptom relief vs a usual diet · MAYBE (weak evidence) for superiority over standard dietary advice.
citation: SourceMed Shelf #202, “Low-FODMAP diet for irritable bowel syndrome: better than a usual diet, not better than good advice”, sourcemed.io

title: B vitamins and folic acid for stroke prevention: the population's folate status decides
question: Does lowering homocysteine with B vitamins or folic acid prevent stroke?
balance: Folic acid prevented first stroke in a large trial in a non-fortified, low-folate population. In folate-replete populations after stroke, B-vitamin lowering was null to borderline. The answer depends on the population's folate status. Developer’s verdict: POSSIBLE in low-folate, non-fortified settings · MAYBE (weak evidence) for general use.
citation: SourceMed Shelf #203, “B vitamins and folic acid for stroke prevention: the population's folate status decides”, sourcemed.io

title: Probiotics to prevent antibiotic-associated diarrhea in older inpatients: a small yes, a large no
question: In older inpatients receiving antibiotics, do probiotics prevent antibiotic-associated diarrhea or Clostridioides difficile diarrhea?
balance: One small trial showed a large benefit; the large, definitive multicentre trial that followed found none. Routine probiotics for this purpose are not supported by the best evidence. Developer’s verdict: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the small positive stands as the dissenting card; the shelf's weight rests on PLACIDE.

title: Replacing sugary drinks in children and teenagers: works while it lasts
question: Does replacing sugar-sweetened drinks with sugar-free drinks slow weight gain in children and teenagers?
balance: Replacing sugary drinks with sugar-free ones slowed weight gain while the substitution lasted; the effect faded once the intervention stopped. A maintenance problem, not a one-time fix. Developer’s verdict: POSSIBLE — modest and maintenance-dependent.

title: DASH diet and sodium reduction for blood pressure
question: Does the DASH eating pattern lower blood pressure, and does cutting sodium on top of it lower blood pressure further?
balance: The DASH eating pattern lowers blood pressure, and lowering sodium on top of it lowers it further — effects proven in controlled feeding trials. No trial has tested DASH itself against heart attacks or death; this shelf is about blood pressure, and says so. Developer’s verdict: LIKELY for blood-pressure lowering (surrogate endpoint; no event claim).

title: Zinc for acute diarrhea in young children
question: Does oral zinc shorten acute diarrhea in young children?
balance: Zinc shortens episodes and cuts prolonged diarrhea in young children in low-income settings — two double-blind trials and a very large community trial agree, and this is the basis of the WHO recommendation. But a hospital-based trial in India found no effect, so the benefit is not universal: it tracks with deficiency-prone, community populations. Developer’s verdict: POSSIBLE — consistent benefit in community, low-income settings; not shown in every setting.

title: Multiple micronutrients vs iron–folate in pregnancy: one positive, one null
question: In pregnancy, do multiple-micronutrient supplements improve fetal and infant outcomes compared with iron–folic acid alone?
balance: The Indonesian trial found fewer early infant deaths with multiple micronutrients than with iron–folate alone; the equally large Bangladeshi trial found no mortality difference, though babies were less often preterm or low birthweight. One positive against a large null — the mortality claim is a maybe. Developer’s verdict: MAYBE (weak evidence) for infant mortality · POSSIBLE for preterm birth and low birthweight.

title: Low-carb vs low-fat for weight loss: composition is not the active ingredient
question: For weight loss, does the macronutrient composition of the diet — low-carbohydrate vs low-fat — matter?
balance: Across the large modern trials, composition barely matters: low-fat and low-carb produce near-identical weight loss, and neither genotype nor insulin secretion predicts who does better on which. Adherence is the active ingredient. The A TO Z result stands as the earlier-era outlier the two larger trials supersede. Developer’s verdict: LIKELY that no composition is meaningfully superior.

title: Look AHEAD: intensive lifestyle in type 2 diabetes — remission without fewer heart attacks
question: In adults with established type 2 diabetes, does an intensive lifestyle intervention reduce cardiovascular events?
balance: Intensive lifestyle produced large weight loss and real but modest diabetes remission — and no reduction in cardiovascular events over nearly a decade. Weight loss alone did not buy event protection in established diabetes. Developer’s verdict: LIKELY — the null event result comes from a large, definitive trial.

title: Calcium in pregnancy: helps where intake is low
question: Does calcium supplementation in pregnancy prevent preeclampsia and hypertensive disorders?
balance: Calcium helps where dietary intake is low — fewer hypertensive disorders in Argentina, and in the WHO trial less severe disease even though preeclampsia itself was not significantly reduced. In a well-nourished US population it did nothing. The benefit follows the deficiency. Developer’s verdict: POSSIBLE in low-intake populations · the null in replete populations is solid.
citation: SourceMed Shelf #211, “Calcium in pregnancy: helps where intake is low”, sourcemed.io

title: PSA screening for prostate cancer: a small mortality benefit at a large overdiagnosis cost
question: Does PSA screening reduce deaths from prostate cancer?
balance: The European trial found a 20% lower prostate-cancer death rate with screening at 9 years, bought with heavy overdiagnosis — 1,410 men screened and 48 extra cases treated for each death prevented. The US trial found no benefit, but its control group was screened anyway at high rates (PSA use rose from 40% to 52% over the trial), which dilutes any difference. The two trials are not as contradictory as they look; the honest reading is a small benefit at a large overdiagnosis cost. Developer’s verdict: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the one positive mortality ratio (0.80) sits inside the house gray zone, and the second trial is null.

title: Mammography screening for breast cancer: the two longest trials disagree
question: Does mammography screening reduce deaths from breast cancer?
balance: The two longest trials point in opposite directions. The Swedish trial found about 30% fewer breast-cancer deaths over 29 years of follow-up. The Canadian trial found no mortality difference over 25 years and measured the overdiagnosis directly: about 22% of screen-detected invasive cancers — one excess diagnosis for every 424 women screened — would never have surfaced on their own. Both trials predate modern imaging and modern drug therapy, which shrinks the margin screening can add. Developer’s verdict: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the two best trials disagree; older technology in both.

title: Ovarian cancer screening with CA-125 and ultrasound: no lives saved
question: Does screening average-risk women with CA-125 and ultrasound reduce deaths from ovarian cancer?
balance: Two very large trials give one answer: screening average-risk women does not reduce ovarian cancer deaths. The UK trial's early, non-significant suggestion of benefit (15% at the primary analysis) disappeared with longer follow-up (HR 0.94). The US trial found no benefit and quantified the harm: of women with false-positive results who went to surgery, 15% suffered a serious complication. Developer’s verdict: LIKELY — no mortality benefit; a negative shelf resting on two huge, concordant trials.

title: HPV testing vs cytology for cervical cancer screening: less cancer at the second round
question: Does HPV-based cervical screening prevent more invasive cervical cancer than cytology alone?
balance: HPV-based screening catches more precancer at the first round and leaves less disease to find at the next. In the Italian trial, invasive cancers across two rounds numbered 7 with HPV testing vs 18 with cytology, and none appeared in the HPV arm in round 2; the Dutch trial showed the same pattern for high-grade lesions and for cancer (4 vs 14 cases). The trade-off is more positive tests and, in younger women, treatment of lesions that would have regressed on their own. Developer’s verdict: LIKELY for earlier detection of high-grade lesions · POSSIBLE for fewer invasive cancers — concordant, but the event counts are small.

title: HPV vaccination: near-complete protection against vaccine-type precancer when given before infection
question: Does HPV vaccination prevent high-grade cervical lesions?
balance: In young women not previously infected, both vaccines prevented nearly all high-grade cervical lesions caused by the vaccine HPV types (98% for the quadrivalent vaccine per-protocol; 93% for the bivalent vaccine). The protection is preventive, not treatment: counted across all randomized women regardless of prior infection, efficacy against vaccine-type lesions was 44%, and against high-grade lesions from all HPV types combined only 17–30%. Both trials measured precancer (CIN 2/3), not cancer itself — the cancer claim rests on the surrogate. Developer’s verdict: LIKELY — prevention of vaccine-type high-grade lesions in HPV-naive young women (surrogate endpoint; no cancer endpoint in either trial).

title: Tamoxifen and raloxifene to prevent breast cancer: fewer cancers, real harms, no mortality benefit
question: In women at increased risk, do tamoxifen or raloxifene prevent breast cancer, and at what cost?
balance: Tamoxifen cut invasive breast cancer by about half in high-risk women (cumulative incidence 43.4 vs 22.0 per 1,000 over about 6 years), entirely among estrogen-receptor-positive tumors, at the cost of more endometrial cancer (RR 2.53) and blood clots, partly offset by fewer fractures. In the head-to-head trial, raloxifene matched tamoxifen against invasive cancer with fewer clots and cataracts and a trend toward fewer uterine cancers, but was weaker against noninvasive cancer. Neither trial showed any mortality benefit — this shelf is about incidence and harm trade-offs, and says so. Developer’s verdict: LIKELY for incidence reduction (tamoxifen vs placebo) and for raloxifene's equivalence on invasive cancer — no mortality claim.

title: Finasteride and dutasteride to prevent prostate cancer: fewer diagnoses, mostly low-grade
question: Do 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors prevent prostate cancer?
balance: Both drugs cut the chance of a prostate-cancer diagnosis by about a quarter, and the reduction is concentrated in low-grade tumors — the kind most often overdiagnosed and overtreated. Both trials also produced a high-grade warning signal (more Gleason 7–10 tumors among cancers found in PCPT; a 12-vs-1 excess of Gleason 8–10 tumors late in REDUCE), partly explained by the drugs shrinking the prostate so biopsy samples it better. Long-term PCPT follow-up found no survival difference either way. Neither drug is approved for prevention; the shelf presents the trade-off, not a recommendation. Developer’s verdict: LIKELY for fewer diagnoses, mostly low-grade · MAYBE (weak evidence) for any effect on the cancers that matter.

title: Eradicating H. pylori to prevent gastric cancer: incidence halved in high-risk populations
question: Does eradicating Helicobacter pylori prevent gastric cancer?
balance: In a high-risk Chinese county, two weeks of antibiotics for H. pylori roughly halved gastric cancer incidence over 22 years (OR 0.48 — the one ratio on this slate that clears the house floor) and reduced gastric-cancer deaths (HR 0.62). In Korean patients who had already had an early gastric cancer removed endoscopically, eradication halved new cancers appearing elsewhere in the stomach (HR 0.50). Both trials come from high-incidence East Asian populations; benefit in low-incidence populations is unproven. The Shandong trial's vitamin arm also reduced incidence and mortality — reported on Card 1; the trial's one home is this shelf. Developer’s verdict: POSSIBLE — two randomized trials, concordant, large and long; one population type.

title: Aspirin in Lynch syndrome: one trial, a delayed and durable benefit
question: Does daily aspirin prevent colorectal cancer in carriers of Lynch syndrome?
balance: One trial, reported twice. At about 5 years the intention-to-treat analysis was not significant (HR 0.63) though the per-protocol analysis was (HR 0.41); at the planned 10-year follow-up both were significant (ITT HR 0.65; per-protocol HR 0.56), with protection appearing roughly 5 years after starting and persisting in registry follow-up to 20 years. The dose was high — 600 mg daily for about 2 years — and the follow-on trial testing lower doses (CaPP3) has not reported. Cancers outside the colon in Lynch syndrome were not reduced (36 vs 36 cases). Developer’s verdict: POSSIBLE — single randomized trial; delayed effect consistent across two reports and both analyses.

title: Daily sunscreen: fewer squamous-cell tumors; the melanoma signal is fragile
question: Does daily sunscreen use prevent skin cancer?
balance: One community trial in subtropical Australia. Daily sunscreen did not significantly reduce the rate of first basal-cell or squamous-cell cancers per person, but it did reduce the total number of squamous-cell tumors (rate ratio 0.61); beta-carotene had no effect on either cancer. Ten years after the trial ended, the daily-use group had half as many melanomas (11 vs 22) and fewer invasive melanomas (3 vs 11) — a result resting on only 33 melanomas, presented as fragile. Developer’s verdict: POSSIBLE for squamous-cell tumor burden · MAYBE (weak evidence) for melanoma (one trial, 33 events) · no effect on basal-cell carcinoma.

title: Clozapine: the one drug that works when others fail, and the suicide-risk trial
question: In schizophrenia that has failed other antipsychotics, does clozapine work — and does it reduce suicidal behavior?
balance: Clozapine remains the only drug ever shown to work in truly treatment-resistant schizophrenia — 30% responded vs 4% on a high-dose standard drug, in patients who had already failed at least three agents and then failed a prospective haloperidol trial. The suicide trial was open-label (patients and clinicians knew the drug; only the raters were masked), and its benefit was in suicidal behavior overall (HR 0.76); completed suicides were rare and did not differ (5 vs 3). Clozapine's costs are real — blood monitoring for agranulocytosis, metabolic effects, sedation — and are why it is reserved for this population. Developer’s verdict: LIKELY for response in treatment-resistant schizophrenia · MAYBE (weak evidence) for reducing suicidal behavior (one open-label trial, gray-zone ratio).

title: Ketamine and esketamine for treatment-resistant depression: fast, brief, and not the whole story
question: Do ketamine and its S-enantiomer esketamine lift treatment-resistant depression quickly?
balance: A single ketamine infusion beat an active placebo (midazolam, chosen so patients could not easily tell which drug they got) within 24 hours — 64% vs 28% response — but the separation was gone by day 7. Esketamine nasal spray, added to a newly started oral antidepressant, beat the oral drug plus placebo spray by 4 MADRS points at 4 weeks in one trial — while two sister trials (a fixed-dose study and a study in patients 65 and older) missed their primary endpoints. This is a fast, short-horizon effect on symptom scores, with dissociation and blood-pressure rises to manage; neither shelf card shows durability beyond weeks. Developer’s verdict: POSSIBLE — rapid short-term symptom improvement; durability unproven and two of three esketamine phase-3 trials missed.

title: Fluoxetine for depression in children and adolescents: works, best with therapy, warning attached
question: Does fluoxetine help depressed children and teenagers?
balance: Fluoxetine is the one antidepressant with two positive placebo-controlled trials in youth. The first, in 96 patients aged 7–17, found 56% improved on 20 mg vs 33% on placebo. The large NIMH trial found fluoxetine alone (60.6% response) beat placebo (34.8%), and fluoxetine plus cognitive-behavioral therapy did best of all (71.0%), while CBT alone (43.2%) did not separate from placebo. The safety shadow is printed on the shelf: 7 of 439 TADS patients (1.6%) attempted suicide during 12 weeks (none completed), suicidal thinking improved most in the combination arm, and fluoxetine carries the FDA's boxed warning for adolescents. Developer’s verdict: POSSIBLE — two positive placebo-controlled trials; combination with CBT was best in the big trial; the boxed warning stands.

title: Varenicline for quitting smoking: the best quit rates, and the big safety trial that cleared it
question: Does varenicline help smokers quit, and is it neuropsychiatrically safe?
balance: Varenicline roughly doubled-to-tripled quit rates in the pivotal trials: 44.0% abstinent at weeks 9–12 vs 29.5% on bupropion and 17.7% on placebo, with the advantage persisting, smaller, at one year (21.9% vs 16.1% vs 8.4%). The safety question that hung over the drug — reports of depression, agitation, and suicidality — was put to an 8,144-person trial enrolling smokers with and without psychiatric disorders: moderate-to-severe neuropsychiatric events did not differ significantly between varenicline, bupropion, patch, and placebo in either cohort, and varenicline again produced the highest abstinence. On this trial's evidence the FDA removed varenicline's boxed warning in 2016. Developer’s verdict: LIKELY — the highest quit rates of the first-line drugs, and no significant neuropsychiatric excess in the largest safety trial.

title: Naltrexone for alcohol dependence: fewer relapses to heavy drinking
question: Does oral naltrexone help people with alcohol dependence stay off heavy drinking?
balance: The small founding trial was strikingly positive: recently detoxified men on naltrexone relapsed to heavy drinking at less than half the placebo rate (23% vs 54%), and when they did drink, half as many progressed to a full relapse (50% vs 95%). The large pragmatic COMBINE trial found a smaller, real benefit when naltrexone was paired with structured medical management — 80.6% vs 75.1% of days abstinent, and a hazard ratio of 0.72 for a heavy-drinking day — while acamprosate showed no benefit alone or in combination, and the naltrexone advantage had faded a year after treatment ended. Expect a modest effect that needs the follow-up structure around it. Developer’s verdict: POSSIBLE — a large effect in the small early trial, a modest one in the big pragmatic trial, gone a year after treatment stopped.

title: Extended-release naltrexone vs buprenorphine for opioid dependence: the hard part is starting
question: How does monthly injected naltrexone compare with daily buprenorphine-naloxone for opioid use disorder?
balance: Both trials were open-label — patients knew whether they were getting a monthly injection or a daily film — and both tell the same story: once people are actually on the medication, the two work about the same; the difference is getting on. In the US trial, only 72% of patients assigned to the injection completed detox and received it, vs 94% started on buprenorphine, and that induction gap drove the overall relapse difference (65% vs 57%). Among those successfully inducted, relapse was 52% vs 56%. Fatal overdoses were few and similar (2 vs 3). The Norwegian trial found the injection noninferior on retention and opioid-negative tests over 12 weeks. Developer’s verdict: POSSIBLE — comparable outcomes once started; buprenorphine is far easier to start, and that difference dominates the intention-to-treat result.

title: After a first psychotic episode: staying on antipsychotics prevents relapse, but the 7-year recovery data point the other way
question: After remission of a first psychotic episode, is it better to stay on antipsychotic maintenance or to reduce and stop?
balance: The two trials answer two different questions and both answers stand. In the double-blind Hong Kong trial, stopping (switching to placebo) after a year of treatment nearly doubled relapse in the next year — 79% vs 41%. In the Dutch strategy trial, guided dose reduction or discontinuation also caused more early relapses (43% vs 21% by 2 years) — but at 7 years the reduction/discontinuation group had twice the full recovery rate (40.4% vs 17.6%; OR 3.49), driven by functional remission: holding a job, managing daily life. Symptomatic remission at 7 years was the same. Relapse prevention and long-run functioning pull in opposite directions, and the shelf says so rather than resolving it. Developer’s verdict: POSSIBLE — maintenance clearly prevents relapse in the first year; the single long follow-up found better functional recovery after early reduction/discontinuation. Two outcomes, two directions.

title: Brexanolone for postpartum depression: a 60-hour infusion with a fast, large effect
question: Does a single 60-hour brexanolone infusion relieve postpartum depression?
balance: All three placebo-controlled trials — one small phase-2 and two phase-3 studies run by the drug's sponsor — point the same way: depression scores fell much further on brexanolone within 60 hours, and the advantage held to day 30. Remission at the end of the infusion ran 51–70% on the effective doses vs 9–38% on placebo, depending on the trial and dose. The practical costs are printed on the shelf: the drug is given as a supervised 60-hour inpatient infusion, it carries a boxed warning for excessive sedation and sudden loss of consciousness, and breastfeeding is paused during treatment. Samples are small by the standards of this library, and there is no independent replication. Developer’s verdict: POSSIBLE — rapid, large, consistent symptom improvement across three trials from one development program; small samples, no independent replication, burdensome administration.

title: STAR*D: what actually happened when depression treatment was measured step by step
question: In real-world practice, how many patients remit on a first antidepressant — and what happens when the first one fails?
balance: STAR*D is the largest practical answer available: with careful measurement-based dosing, about 28% of patients remitted on citalopram alone (33% by self-report scale) and 47% responded. For those who did not remit, switching to any of three chemically different antidepressants remitted about one in five — 21.3%, 17.6%, and 24.8%, with no significant difference between them and no tolerability winner. Because there was no placebo and no blinding, some of these remissions are the natural course of the illness and expectation effects; the trial's value is the honest arithmetic of sequential treatment, not proof that any step beats doing nothing. Developer’s verdict: POSSIBLE — about a third remit at step 1 and about a quarter of the remainder remit after a switch; no switch drug beat another. Open-label throughout.

title: Suvorexant for insomnia: modest, consistent gains from blocking orexin
question: Does the orexin blocker suvorexant improve sleep onset and maintenance?
balance: Across two 3-month trials totaling 2,040 patients, the higher age-adjusted dose (40 mg under 65, 30 mg at 65+) beat placebo on nearly every subjective and polysomnography endpoint — about 30 more minutes of subjective total sleep time at month 3 — and the lower dose (20/15 mg) still won on the maintenance measures. A separate year-long trial found the advantage persisted (subjective total sleep time +38.7 vs +16.0 minutes at month 1) and that stopping abruptly after a year produced no rebound insomnia or withdrawal. Printed on the shelf: the trials excluded patients with other sleep disorders, including sleep apnea, and enrolled primary insomnia only; somnolence was the commonest adverse effect, and the doses tested were above the 20 mg maximum later approved in the US. Developer’s verdict: LIKELY for modest improvements in sleep onset and maintenance in primary insomnia — consistent across trials and a full year of use; effect sizes are minutes, not transformations.

title: Epinephrine in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest
question: In out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, does epinephrine improve survival — and survival with a good neurologic outcome?
balance: Epinephrine restarts hearts and raises 30-day survival — 3.2% vs 1.3% in the big trial — but has not been shown to raise survival with a good neurologic outcome, and more of its survivors live with severe impairment. Developer’s verdict: POSSIBLE for survival; the intact-survival claim is unproven.

question: After benzodiazepines fail in established status epilepticus, which second-line drug stops the seizure?

title: Dexamethasone in bacterial meningitis
question: Does dexamethasone improve outcomes in bacterial meningitis — and does the answer depend on where the patient is?
balance: Dexamethasone’s answer depends on where the patient is. It cut death and bad outcomes where patients arrive early with susceptible organisms (Europe 2002, Costa Rica 1991); it did nothing in Malawi adults and children, and pointed toward harm in a small Pakistan trial. Setting is part of the result. Developer’s verdict: POSSIBLE — setting-dependent; no global claim.

title: Thrombolysis and catheter treatment for intermediate-risk pulmonary embolism
question: In intermediate-risk pulmonary embolism, do thrombolysis or catheter treatments help more than they harm?
balance: Full-dose lysis prevents hemodynamic collapse (1.6% vs 5.0%) and buys it with major bleeding (6.3% vs 1.2%) and stroke (2.4% vs 0.2%); it has not been shown to save lives in this group. The alternatives — half-dose lysis, catheter techniques — rest on small trials, surrogate endpoints, or composites driven by ICU use. Developer’s verdict: POSSIBLE for decompensation prevention; the harm figures are part of the claim.

title: Magnesium in acute asthma
question: Does magnesium improve outcomes in acute asthma?
balance: The largest modern trial found nothing overall. The older, smaller trials consistently show benefit confined to the severest obstruction, and nebulized magnesium helped children in one good trial. A largely negative shelf with a severe-presentation signal. Developer’s verdict: MAYBE (weak evidence) overall; possible benefit in severe presentations.

question: Does dexamethasone improve outcomes in croup — and at what dose?
balance: The rare shelf where a cheap steroid works across the severity range: dexamethasone cut hospitalizations from 71% to 23% in moderately severe croup and roughly halved return visits in mild croup; 0.15 mg/kg does what 0.6 does, and prednisolone is not its equal. Developer’s verdict: LIKELY.

title: Restrictive transfusion thresholds in acute bleeding
question: In acute bleeding, is a restrictive transfusion threshold safer than a liberal one?
balance: In acute upper GI bleeding, transfusing at a hemoglobin of 7 rather than 9 g/dL lowered 45-day mortality (5% vs 9%) and rebleeding. The paired question in septic shock — where the restrictive threshold proved equally safe, with half the blood — is answered by TRISS, which lives on Shelf #124 (Reference 3) under the one-home rule and is not re-carded here. Developer’s verdict: LIKELY for GI bleeding; see Shelf #124 for septic shock.

title: Prehospital plasma in bleeding trauma
question: Does plasma given before hospital arrival improve survival in bleeding trauma?
balance: Plasma given in the air cut 30-day mortality by about 10 points; plasma given on the ground in a city with short transport times did nothing. Transport time may be the difference — or the positive trial is the outlier. One for, one against. Developer’s verdict: MAYBE (weak evidence) (house rule: one positive against one null).

title: Overactive bladder drugs: the anticholinergic head-to-head
question: Head to head, how do tolterodine and oxybutynin compare for overactive bladder — on symptoms, and on dry mouth?
balance: The mirabegron half of this topic is already home on Shelf #149 (SCORPIO and ARIES: modest gains over placebo, dry mouth at placebo rates) and is not re-carded here. This shelf adds the anticholinergic head-to-head, OBJECT — and it cuts against the usual summary: extended-release oxybutynin beat tolterodine on all three of the trial’s main diary outcomes, while dry mouth, the side effect that decides tolerability, was no less common on tolterodine (33.2% vs 28.1%, not significant). For refractory overactive bladder, the named next-step trials are BESIDE (mirabegron added to solifenacin) and ROSETTA (onabotulinumtoxinA vs sacral neuromodulation) — noted here, not carded.

title: Emergency contraception: the standard changed twice
question: After unprotected sex, which emergency-contraception pill works best — and how did the standard change twice?
balance: Two trials, two changes of standard. In 1998 the WHO Task Force trial showed levonorgestrel alone beat the Yuzpe combined regimen on pregnancies (1.1% vs 3.2%) with far less nausea and vomiting — and levonorgestrel became the standard. In 2010 ulipristal acetate was non-inferior to levonorgestrel within 72 hours (1.8% vs 2.6%), and in the 72–120-hour group every one of the three pregnancies was on levonorgestrel. For both regimens, earlier is better: efficacy fell the longer treatment was delayed.
