title: Ovulation induction in PCOS: letrozole, clomiphene, metformin
question: For infertility in the polycystic ovary syndrome, which first drug gives the most live births — letrozole, clomiphene, or metformin?
balance: Metformin alone lost clearly in 2007: live birth 7.2% against 22.5% on clomiphene, and adding metformin to clomiphene (26.8%) was not significantly better than clomiphene alone. In 2014 letrozole then beat clomiphene outright — live births 27.5% vs 19.1%, a higher ovulation rate, and fewer twin pregnancies (3.4% vs 7.4%). The popular drug order is not the order the trials support: on live births, it is letrozole first, clomiphene second, metformin a distant third.

title: Endometriosis pain: elagolix, the twin Elaris trials
question: Does elagolix, an oral GnRH antagonist, reduce endometriosis pain — and what does the estrogen suppression cost?
balance: The twin Elaris trials agree: both elagolix doses beat placebo on dysmenorrhea and nonmenstrual pelvic pain at 3 months, sustained at 6 months — and the higher dose (200 mg twice daily) roughly doubled the dysmenorrhea response of the lower dose. The cost is printed on both cards: dose-dependent loss of bone mineral density, more hot flushes, and higher serum lipids — the hypoestrogenic price of GnRH blockade, and the reason treatment duration is limited.

title: Uterine fibroids: relugolix combination therapy
question: Does once-daily relugolix combination therapy control fibroid bleeding — without costing bone?
balance: Two replicate trials, one answer: about 7 in 10 women on relugolix combination therapy met the response definition (menstrual blood loss under 80 mL and at least 50% down from baseline) against about 1 in 6 on placebo — with bone mineral density preserved, because the combination’s low-dose estradiol and norethindrone add back what the GnRH blockade takes away. The trial’s own delayed-treatment arm, which spent its first 12 weeks on relugolix alone, lost bone — the internal control that proves the add-back is doing the work. Adverse events overall were similar to placebo.

title: Heavy menstrual bleeding: the IUS, and surgery head-to-head
question: For heavy menstrual bleeding, what beats what — the hormonal IUS against usual medical therapy, and ablation against hysterectomy?
balance: ECLIPSE, in primary care: the levonorgestrel IUS beat usual medical therapy on bleeding-specific quality of life at 2 years (between-group difference 13.4 points on the Menorrhagia Multi-Attribute Scale), and more women were still using it (64% vs 38%). HEALTH, among women who had reached surgery: laparoscopic supracervical hysterectomy beat endometrial ablation on satisfaction at 15 months (97% vs 87%) and on best-possible quality-of-life scores — bought with a longer operation and a longer recovery, at a similar rate of serious complications. Both trials were open-label and their headline outcomes are patient-reported; the cards carry the label.

title: Stress incontinence surgery: slings, and tape vs colposuspension
question: For stress incontinence surgery, which sling route — and how does the tension-free tape compare with the older colposuspension?
balance: TOMUS found the two sling routes equivalent on objective success at 12 months (80.8% retropubic vs 77.7% transobturator, inside the pre-set ±12-point margin) — so the choice is made on complications, which differ: voiding dysfunction needing surgery 2.7% vs 0% with the retropubic route, neurologic symptoms 9.4% vs 4.0% with the transobturator route. Against the older open operation, tension-free vaginal tape at 2 years cured at least as many women (63% vs 51% on the strict count that treats missing data as failure; the authors’ own conclusion was “as effective as”). Both trials were open-label — surgery cannot be blinded — and the cards carry that label.

title: Hot flushes without hormones: fezolinetant
question: Without hormones, does the neurokinin-3 blocker fezolinetant reduce menopausal hot flushes — and what needs monitoring?
balance: The twin SKYLIGHT trials agree: fezolinetant 30 mg and 45 mg cut flush frequency by roughly 2 to 2.5 more flushes a day than placebo at weeks 4 and 12, with severity down as well, benefit visible by week 1 and maintained through the 40-week extension — a real but moderate effect, measured against a large placebo response. Liver monitoring is printed on this shelf as the desk required: enzyme elevations in the trials were uncommon and transient (in SKYLIGHT 2, ALT/AST rises above 3× the upper limit of normal occurred in 6 participants across all groups, with no Hy’s-law cases) — and liver-function monitoring is part of the drug’s labeled use.

title: Uncomplicated UTI in women: which short course cures?
question: For uncomplicated cystitis in women, which short course actually cures — and which convenient option underperforms?
balance: Huttner 2018 was the surprise: the single 3 g dose of fosfomycin — the most convenient regimen on this shelf — resolved fewer infections than 5 days of nitrofurantoin (clinical resolution 58% vs 70% through day 28). Gupta 2007 supplies the older comparison: 5 days of nitrofurantoin matched 3 days of trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (clinical cure 84% vs 79%) — except where the organism was TMP-SMX-resistant, when TMP-SMX cure fell to 41%. Both trials were open-label. For preventing recurrent UTI rather than treating it, methenamine (ALTAR 2022, non-inferior to daily antibiotic prophylaxis) is noted here without a card; cranberry and vaginal estriol already live on Shelves #50 and #150.

title: Acute otitis media: do antibiotics beat placebo in young children?

balance: In strictly diagnosed otitis media in children under 3, amoxicillin or amoxicillin-clavulanate roughly halves treatment failure; about 1 child in 5 treated gets diarrhea or rash. title: After a first febrile UTI: does antibiotic prophylaxis prevent recurrences?
question: After a first febrile urinary tract infection, does antibiotic prophylaxis prevent recurrences?
balance: Continuous low-dose prophylaxis halves recurrences while a child takes it — about 13% vs 24% in the largest trial — but has not been shown to prevent kidney scarring, and the recurrences that break through are far more often drug-resistant. Developer’s verdict: POSSIBLE–LIKELY — population-dependent.

question: Do monoclonal antibodies prevent RSV in infancy?

question: Do probiotics prevent necrotizing enterocolitis in preterm infants?

title: Febrile seizures: can medicine at fever onset stop the next one?
question: Can medicine at fever onset stop the next febrile seizure?

question: Does more time outdoors delay myopia in children?

title: PCSK9 inhibitors: long-term outcomes and the mortality signal
question: In patients already on a statin, does adding a PCSK9 inhibitor reduce cardiovascular events — and does it save lives?
balance: Two large double-blind trials (46,488 patients) cut combined cardiovascular events by about 15% relative on top of a statin. On mortality the two trials split: FOURIER showed no reduction in cardiovascular death (HR 1.05); ODYSSEY OUTCOMES showed fewer deaths from any cause (3.5% vs 4.1%) as a secondary endpoint. The open-label extension (Reference 3) is where a cardiovascular-death difference first appeared — with longer, earlier treatment. Developer-approved Nov 3, 2026.

title: Ezetimibe added to a statin after acute coronary syndrome
question: After an acute coronary syndrome, does adding ezetimibe to a statin prevent cardiovascular events — and how big is the gain, honestly?
balance: IMPROVE-IT answers yes — with a small absolute gain: 32.7% vs 34.7% on the primary composite at 7 years, a 2.0-percentage-point absolute difference (HR 0.936, a 6.4% relative reduction) for adding ezetimibe 10 mg to simvastatin 40 mg. RACING (Reference 2) answers the practical follow-up: a moderate-intensity statin plus ezetimibe matched high-intensity statin alone, with more patients at LDL goal and fewer intolerance dropouts. EWTOPIA 75 (Reference 3) extends the evidence to primary prevention at age 75 and older, without a statin. Developer-approved Nov 3, 2026.

title: Dual antiplatelet therapy after a stent: shorter vs longer
question: After a coronary stent, how long should two antiplatelet drugs continue — where does the bleeding cost overtake the ischemic gain?
balance: Duration is a trade, and the three trials price it from both ends. In high-bleeding-risk patients, stopping the second drug at 1 month cost nothing ischemic and cut bleeding (MASTER DAPT). Dropping aspirin instead — ticagrelor alone after 3 months — halved major bleeding with identical ischemic outcomes (TWILIGHT). Extending both drugs to 30 months prevented stent thrombosis and MI but raised bleeding, with a borderline excess of deaths (2.0% vs 1.5%) that has never been fully explained (DAPT Study). Shorter wins for high bleeding risk; longer buys ischemic protection only in patients who tolerate the first year cleanly. Developer's verdict: LIKELY.

title: CABG vs PCI in diabetes and multivessel disease
question: In a patient with diabetes and multivessel coronary disease, does bypass surgery beat stenting — and does either beat medicines alone?
balance: FREEDOM is the head-to-head answer: at 5 years the composite of death, MI, or stroke was 18.7% with CABG vs 26.6% with PCI — fewer deaths (10.9% vs 16.3% at five years, P=0.049) and far fewer MIs with surgery, paid for with more strokes (5.2% vs 2.4%). BARI-2D adds the humbler lesson that prompt revascularization of either kind did not beat intensive medical therapy overall in stable disease; the CABG stratum was the exception. SYNTAX's diabetes subgroup points the same way in complex disease, driven by repeat revascularization. Developer's verdict: LIKELY — and flagged: the balance line rests in part on FREEDOM's mortality difference (P=0.049).

title: TAVR vs surgical aortic valve replacement, by surgical risk
question: For severe aortic stenosis, when does a transcatheter valve (TAVR) match or beat surgical replacement — and what is not yet known?
balance: Across every surgical-risk stratum tested, TAVR was at least noninferior to surgery on death and stroke: high risk (PARTNER 1), intermediate risk (PARTNER 2), and low risk with either a balloon-expandable valve (PARTNER 3 — the 1-year composite actually favored TAVR) or a self-expanding valve (Evolut Low Risk). TAVR's consistent prices are paravalvular leak and, with the self-expanding valve, pacemakers (17.4% vs 6.1%); surgery's are bleeding, kidney injury, and new atrial fibrillation. The honest limit: these primary reports run 1–2 years. Valve durability over the 10–20 years a younger low-risk patient needs is not in this evidence. Developer-approved Nov 3, 2026.

title: Complete vs culprit-only revascularization in STEMI
question: In STEMI with multivessel disease, should the non-culprit lesions be opened too — or only the artery that caused the infarct?
balance: COMPLETE, the large trial, gives the hard-outcome answer: the composite of cardiovascular death or MI was 7.8% with complete revascularization vs 10.5% with culprit-only PCI over a median 3 years (HR 0.74, a 26% relative reduction) — but the gain was fewer heart attacks, not fewer deaths: cardiovascular death itself was unchanged, and with ischemia-driven revascularization added the gap widened (8.9% vs 16.7%, HR 0.51) on far fewer repeat procedures. No mortality benefit is claimed on this shelf. The two smaller earlier trials pointed the same way on their composites (CvLPRIT 10.0% vs 21.2%; DANAMI-3-PRIMULTI 13% vs 22%) but were driven by repeat revascularization and showed no death or MI difference on their own. Developer-approved Nov 3, 2026.

title: Bempedoic acid in statin-intolerant patients
question: In patients who cannot or will not take a statin, does bempedoic acid prevent cardiovascular events?
balance: One outcomes trial, honestly sized: in 13,970 statin-intolerant patients, bempedoic acid cut the primary composite from 13.3% to 11.7% (HR 0.87 — a 13% relative reduction; absolute difference 1.6 percentage points over a median 40.6 months), with fewer MIs and fewer revascularizations — and no effect on stroke or on death from any cause. Gout (3.1% vs 2.1%) and gallstones (2.2% vs 1.2%) were the price. Card 2 is the supporting LDL/safety trial in statin-treated patients. A single outcomes trial cannot carry a Level A verdict. title: Which P2Y12 inhibitor after PCI: ticagrelor, prasugrel, or clopidogrel
question: After PCI for an acute coronary syndrome, which P2Y12 inhibitor — ticagrelor, prasugrel, or clopidogrel — prevents the most events, and at what bleeding cost?
balance: Each potent agent beat clopidogrel in its own trial: ticagrelor in PLATO (9.8% vs 11.7%, with vascular death 4.0% vs 5.1% and all-cause death 4.5% vs 5.9% — a mortality finding flagged below) and prasugrel in TRITON-TIMI 38 (9.9% vs 12.1%), prasugrel paying with more major and fatal bleeding. Head-to-head, ISAR-REACT 5 favored prasugrel over ticagrelor (6.9% vs 9.3%) with similar major bleeding — in an open-label trial. Stronger platelet blockade prevents more ischemic events than clopidogrel; between the two potent agents the only direct trial favors prasugrel. Developer's verdict: LIKELY.

title: How low after a stroke: LDL target under 70 vs around 100 mg/dL

title: Catheter ablation for atrial fibrillation
question: Does catheter ablation for atrial fibrillation improve hard outcomes — death, stroke, hospitalization — or mainly symptoms and rhythm?
balance: The two landmark trials answer differently because they enrolled different hearts. In CABANA's broad symptomatic-AF population, ablation did not significantly reduce the primary composite in the intention-to-treat analysis (8.0% vs 9.2%; HR 0.86, P=0.30) — while clearly reducing AF recurrence and death-or-cardiovascular-hospitalization. In CASTLE-AF's failing hearts (LVEF ≤35%), ablation cut death or heart-failure hospitalization from 44.6% to 28.5%, with all-cause death 13.4% vs 25.0% — a mortality finding from one small, open-label trial, flagged below. Developer's verdict: POSSIBLE.

title: Left atrial appendage closure vs anticoagulation
question: In non-valvular atrial fibrillation, does closing the left atrial appendage prevent stroke as well as long-term anticoagulation — and at what procedural price?
balance: Three randomized trials, one consistent answer on efficacy and one consistent price. Against warfarin, Watchman closure was noninferior for the composite of stroke, systemic embolism, and cardiovascular death in PROTECT-AF and PREVAIL — with more early safety events, mostly periprocedural. Against a modern DOAC, PRAGUE-17 again met noninferiority for its broad net-benefit composite (sHR 0.84; P=0.004 for noninferiority) in high-risk patients, with major device complications in 4.5%. None of the three shows closure prevents strokes better than anticoagulation; the case for the device is avoiding lifelong blood thinners in selected patients, bought with an upfront procedural risk. The honest label is: LIKELY — for noninferiority, not superiority.

title: Early rhythm control in atrial fibrillation
question: Does starting rhythm control early — within a year of an atrial fibrillation diagnosis — prevent cardiovascular death, stroke, and hospitalization, where the older strategy trials found nothing?
balance: The old verdict — rhythm control buys nothing — came from trials that started late, in established AF, with older drugs. EAST-AFNET 4 asked the timing question and got a different answer: early rhythm control cut the cardiovascular composite (3.9 vs 5.0 events per 100 person-years; HR 0.79, a 21% relative reduction), at the cost of more therapy-related serious adverse events (4.9% vs 1.4%). ATHENA, the dronedarone outcomes trial, points the same way on its hospitalization-or-death composite (31.9% vs 39.4%; HR 0.76), though dronedarone did not significantly reduce death from any cause, and the drug later proved harmful in permanent AF and advanced heart failure — populations ATHENA did not enroll. The honest label is: POSSIBLE.

title: Cardiac resynchronization therapy in HFrEF
question: In heart failure with a wide QRS complex, does resynchronizing the ventricles keep people alive and out of hospital — and how far down the symptom scale does the benefit reach?
balance: The most consistent device story in heart failure. In severe symptoms, CRT cut the composite of death or major hospitalization by about a third in CARE-HF (39% vs 55%; HR 0.63) — with death itself down from 30% to 20% — and COMPANION's CRT-defibrillator arm reduced mortality by a 36% relative margin. The benefit follows the QRS down the symptom scale but changes character: RAFT (NYHA class II–III) reduced both death or heart-failure hospitalization (33.2% vs 40.3%; HR 0.75) and death alone (HR 0.75), while MADIT-CRT (NYHA I–II) prevented heart-failure events (17.2% vs 25.3%; HR 0.66) with no mortality difference at all. The price is procedural — RAFT saw roughly twice as many 30-day device adverse events with CRT. The honest label is: LIKELY.

title: Ivabradine in HFrEF
question: Does slowing the sinus rate with ivabradine, on top of standard therapy, improve outcomes in heart failure — or only in the trial built around a high heart rate?
balance: One trial says yes, inside its chosen boundaries; the other says no, outside them. SHIFT enrolled exactly the physiology the drug targets — sinus rhythm, resting heart rate 70 or above, LVEF 35% or less, a heart-failure hospitalization within the previous year — and ivabradine cut the composite of cardiovascular death or heart-failure hospitalization (24% vs 29%; HR 0.82), driven by hospitalizations (16% vs 21%), not by a demonstrated survival effect. BEAUTIFUL, in stable coronary disease with left-ventricular dysfunction but mostly no heart-failure syndrome, was flat on its primary composite (HR 1.00), including in its heart-rate-70-and-above subgroup. The claim that survives both trials: fewer heart-failure hospitalizations for SHIFT-shaped patients. The honest label is: POSSIBLE.

title: ARNI in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction
question: After sacubitril-valsartan's win in reduced-ejection-fraction heart failure, does neprilysin inhibition also help when the ejection fraction is preserved?
balance: The preserved-ejection-fraction sequel never matched the reduced-ejection-fraction original (carded on Shelf #87 ). PARAGON-HF, the 4,822-patient outcomes trial, missed its primary endpoint — total heart-failure hospitalizations and death from cardiovascular causes, rate ratio 0.87 with P=0.06 — and cardiovascular death itself was flat (8.5% vs 8.9%). The two companion trials explain how the field got there: PARAMOUNT and PARALLAX both lowered NT-proBNP significantly more than their comparators, and PARALLAX found no accompanying gain in walking distance, quality of life, or NYHA class. A surrogate that moves while outcomes do not is the whole lesson of this shelf. The honest label is: MAYBE (weak evidence) — benefit unproven.

title: Bedtime vs morning dosing of blood-pressure medicines
question: Should antihypertensive medicines be taken at bedtime rather than in the morning — and what should a patient actually do with the answer?
balance: One large independent trial says the clock does not matter; one research group's trials say it matters implausibly much. TIME randomized 21,104 UK patients to evening vs morning dosing of their usual medicines and found no difference in vascular death or hospitalization for nonfatal myocardial infarction or stroke (3.4% vs 3.7%; HR 0.95; P=0.53). The Hygia trial reported a 45% relative reduction in its cardiovascular composite with bedtime dosing (adjusted HR 0.55) — an effect size that timing alone cannot plausibly deliver, from a paper that has drawn sustained methodological criticism and an expression of concern from its journal. The teaching point of this shelf is adherence, not timing: blood-pressure medicines protect when they are taken, so take them at the time of day they will actually be taken, every day. The honest label is: MAYBE (weak evidence) — for any bedtime advantage; TIME's null is the reliable anchor.

title: The fourth drug for resistant hypertension
question: When blood pressure stays high on three medicines, which fourth drug actually works best?
balance: Two randomized trials, one answer: spironolactone. PATHWAY-2's crossover design — every patient tried every option — showed spironolactone lowered home systolic pressure by 8.70 mmHg against placebo, beat the average of bisoprolol and doxazosin by a further 4.26 mmHg, and beat each drug individually; its advantage was many-fold greater at low plasma renin, the fingerprint of the sodium retention the trial was designed to detect. ReHOT, testing spironolactone against clonidine head-to-head, found identical control rates (about 21% in both arms) but greater 24-hour pressure reductions with spironolactone and a simpler once-daily regimen. The honest label is: LIKELY.

title: Lipid lowering in kidney disease: SHARP vs the dialysis nulls
question: Does lowering LDL cholesterol prevent cardiovascular events in chronic kidney disease — and does the answer change once a patient is on dialysis?
balance: The kidney is where the LDL story splits in two. SHARP — 9,270 patients with chronic kidney disease, a third of them already on dialysis — found simvastatin plus ezetimibe cut major atherosclerotic events (11.3% vs 13.4%; rate ratio 0.83, a 17% relative reduction), and its prespecified analyses found no good evidence that the proportional effect differed between dialysis and non-dialysis patients. But the two trials confined to established dialysis populations both returned null primary endpoints: 4D, atorvastatin in diabetic hemodialysis patients (relative risk 0.92; P=0.37), and AURORA, rosuvastatin in hemodialysis (HR 0.96; P=0.59) — despite LDL falls of 42–43% in each. Why the broad-CKD trial benefited where the dialysis-only trials did not is genuinely unsettled: a different event mix on dialysis (more sudden death, heart failure, and infection; less plaque rupture), treatment started too late, and subgroup power all play a part. The honest label is: POSSIBLE.

title: Claudication: supervised exercise vs stenting
question: For intermittent claudication, what works better — supervised exercise, opening the narrowed artery with a stent, or the two combined?
balance: Exercise is the treatment to beat. CLEVER randomized aortoiliac claudication three ways, and at 6 months supervised exercise produced the largest gain in peak walking time (+5.8 minutes, vs +3.7 for stenting and +1.2 for medical care alone) — although patients reported better disease-specific quality of life with a stent. ERASE then showed the ceiling sits higher when the two are combined: endovascular revascularization plus supervised exercise beat exercise alone by 282 m of maximum walking distance at one year, with better disease-specific quality of life. Neither trial was powered for limb or cardiovascular events; these are walking and quality-of-life verdicts, and both depend on exercise programs patients actually attend. The honest label is: POSSIBLE.

title: Catheter-directed thrombolysis for deep-vein thrombosis
question: After an acute proximal deep-vein thrombosis, does dissolving the clot through a catheter prevent the post-thrombotic syndrome — or mainly add bleeding?
balance: The biggest trial says no, and the smaller trial that said yes explains why the question was worth asking. ATTRACT (692 patients with proximal DVT) found pharmacomechanical catheter-directed thrombolysis did not reduce the post-thrombotic syndrome at all (47% vs 48%; risk ratio 0.96) while causing more major bleeding (1.7% vs 0.3%) — though moderate-to-severe post-thrombotic syndrome was less frequent (18% vs 24%) and severity scores were lower. CaVenT, confined to iliofemoral DVT, had found fewer cases of post-thrombotic syndrome with additional catheter-directed thrombolysis (41.1% vs 55.6%; absolute reduction 14.4 percentage points, NNT 7), at the price of 20 bleeding complications. Read together: no routine role for thrombolysis to prevent the syndrome; the residual case is the selected patient with iliofemoral clot, severe symptoms, and low bleeding risk, where CaVenT's signal and ATTRACT's severity signal overlap. The honest label is: MAYBE (weak evidence).

title: Tirzepatide outcomes: heart failure, cardiovascular events, sleep apnea
question: In people with obesity-related HFpEF, type 2 diabetes with atherosclerotic disease, or obstructive sleep apnea with obesity, does tirzepatide improve clinical outcomes?
balance: Tirzepatide's outcome record is real but narrower than its weight-loss fame. In obesity-related HFpEF (SUMMIT), it cut the composite of cardiovascular death or worsening heart failure (9.9% vs 15.3%, HR 0.62) — an effect carried by fewer worsening-heart-failure events (8.0% vs 14.2%), while cardiovascular deaths were few and numerically higher on the drug (2.2% vs 1.4%, HR 1.58, 95% CI 0.52–4.83). In type 2 diabetes with established atherosclerotic disease (SURPASS-CVOT), tirzepatide was noninferior to dulaglutide for cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, or stroke (12.2% vs 13.1%, HR 0.92) — superiority was not shown (P = 0.09). In moderate-to-severe sleep apnea with obesity (SURMOUNT-OSA), it cut the apnea-hypopnea index by about 20–24 more events per hour than placebo over 52 weeks — a breathing measure, not a hard outcome. All three trials were funded by Eli Lilly.

title: Degludec vs glargine U100: hypoglycemia
question: At the same glycemic control, does basal insulin degludec cause less hypoglycemia than insulin glargine U100?
balance: At equal HbA1c — all three trials were treat-to-target — degludec causes less hypoglycemia than glargine U100 in both types of diabetes. Overall symptomatic episodes ran 11% relatively lower in type 1 (SWITCH 1, rate ratio 0.89) and 30% relatively lower in type 2 (SWITCH 2, rate ratio 0.70); nocturnal episodes ran 36–42% relatively lower (rate ratios 0.64 and 0.58). Severe hypoglycemia was clearly lower in the two larger datasets — DEVOTE: 4.9% vs 6.6% of patients (rate ratio 0.60, a prespecified superiority win) and SWITCH 1: 10.3% vs 17.1% of patients — but not significantly different in SWITCH 2 (1.6% vs 2.4%, P = 0.35), where severe events were few. Cardiovascular safety in DEVOTE: degludec noninferior to glargine for major cardiovascular events (HR 0.91, 0.78–1.06) — safety, not advantage. The comparison is against glargine U100 only; these trials say nothing about glargine U300 or once-weekly insulin. All three trials were funded by Novo Nordisk, degludec's maker.

title: How tight should glucose control be? Intensive control, timing, and the legacy effect
balance: Timing is the whole story. Start tight early — at diagnosis — and the payoff compounds: fewer microvascular events inside the trial, and a decade later fewer heart attacks and deaths, long after glucose levels have reconverged. Start late — older patients, a decade or more of diabetes, high cardiovascular risk — and pushing toward normal buys no cardiovascular benefit within five years, at two to three times the severe hypoglycemia; ACCORD's push below 6.0% increased mortality and was stopped for it. Glucose control is microvascular protection. In long-standing, high-risk diabetes, cardiovascular protection comes from treating the risk factors — statin, blood pressure, and the kidney- and heart-protecting diabetes medicines — not from a lower A1c.

title: Anti-VEGF injections vs laser for diabetic eye disease
balance: For proliferative diabetic retinopathy, anti-VEGF injections match laser on vision and beat it on the collateral damage. At 2 years in Protocol S, ranibizumab was noninferior to panretinal photocoagulation (PRP) for visual acuity (+2.8 vs +0.2 letters) with far less peripheral visual field loss, fewer vitrectomies (4% vs 15%), and less new diabetic macular edema (9% vs 28%); CLARITY found aflibercept noninferior and superior to PRP at 1 year (+3.9 letters difference). At 5 years the vision advantage had closed — acuity was identical (about 20/25 in both groups) — but the ranibizumab group still had less visual field loss and roughly half the cumulative rate of vision-impairing macular edema (22% vs 38%). The price is burden: about 19 injections over 5 years, and injections only work while the patient keeps coming — laser, once done, does not depend on the next appointment. For diabetic macular edema itself, monthly ranibizumab in RISE and RIDE roughly tripled the chance of gaining 15 or more letters versus sham (33.6–45.7% vs 12.3–18.1% across doses and trials) and cut the need for macular laser. Anti-VEGF is first-line where follow-up is reliable; PRP remains the durable choice when it is not.

title: Metformin in pregnancy: what it buys the mother, what it costs the baby in size
question: For women with type 2 diabetes or gestational diabetes in pregnancy, does metformin — added to insulin, started at diagnosis, or used instead of insulin — improve outcomes for mother and baby, and what are the trade-offs versus insulin?
balance: Across all three trials the maternal side of the ledger is consistent: metformin improves or matches glucose control while using less insulin (MiTy: 1.1 vs 1.5 units/kg/day added to insulin; EMERGE: insulin initiation 38.4% vs 51.1%; MiG: noninferior to insulin as the first treatment, with insulin added in 46.3%), about 1–2 kg less weight gain, fewer caesarean births in MiTy (53% vs 63%), and women prefer the tablet (MiG: 76.6% vs 27.2% would choose the same treatment again). The baby's side is a shift, not a clear win: no trial improved its primary neonatal composite (MiTy 40% vs 40%; MiG 32.0% vs 32.2%), but babies were consistently smaller — fewer very large infants (MiTy above the 97th centile 9% vs 15%; EMERGE large-for-gestational-age 6.5% vs 14.9%) set against more small ones (MiTy small-for-gestational-age 13% vs 7%, relative risk 1.96; EMERGE 5.7% vs 2.7%, not significant), and in MiG more preterm births offset less severe neonatal hypoglycaemia. Gastrointestinal effects are the everyday price (24.3% in EMERGE; about 5% of women stopped). The practical reading: metformin is a reasonable first or add-on treatment for diabetes in pregnancy when the alternative is more insulin, provided fetal growth is watched — it trades large-baby risk for small-baby risk, and whether that trade helps or harms the child in the long term is still being followed up.

title: GLP-1 receptor agonists added to insulin in type 1 diabetes: modest gains, real hypoglycemia and ketosis costs (off-label)
question: In adults with type 1 diabetes treated with insulin, does adding a GLP-1 receptor agonist (liraglutide) improve HbA1c, body weight, and insulin dose — and at what cost in hypoglycemia and ketosis?
balance: The two phase 3 trials are mirror images and they agree. When insulin was titrated to target in both groups (ADJUNCT ONE, 52 weeks), adding liraglutide bought a small extra HbA1c reduction (estimated treatment difference −0.20% at 1.8 mg, −0.15% at 1.2 mg), about 5–8% relatively less insulin (dose ratios 0.95 and 0.92), and real weight loss (−3.6 and −4.9 kg vs placebo). When insulin was capped instead (ADJUNCT TWO, 26 weeks), the same pattern showed as a −0.33% HbA1c change at 1.8 mg against +0.01% on placebo, with −5.1 kg of weight. The safety bill was the same in both trials: symptomatic hypoglycemia rose by roughly 30% relatively at the 1.2 and 1.8 mg doses (rate ratios 1.27 and 1.31 in ADJUNCT ONE; 21.3 vs 16.6 events per patient-year at 1.2 mg in ADJUNCT TWO), and hyperglycemia with ketosis roughly doubled at 1.8 mg (rate ratio 2.22 in ADJUNCT ONE; 0.5 vs 0.1 events per patient-year in ADJUNCT TWO) — a signal that matters in people with no insulin reserve of their own. The 0.6 mg dose did little for HbA1c. Neither trial measured hard outcomes, and the trialists concluded the adverse events limit clinical use. GLP-1 receptor agonists are not approved for type 1 diabetes, so this is off-label use. The practical reading: a niche option for selected adults with type 1 diabetes — above all those with overweight and high insulin requirements — who can check ketones and accept more hypoglycemia in exchange for less weight and slightly less insulin; not a general adjunct for the type 1 population.

title: Metabolic surgery for type 2 diabetes: big glycemic effects, small trials, an intention-to-treat caveat
question: In adults with type 2 diabetes and obesity, does metabolic (bariatric) surgery control blood glucose better than intensive medical therapy — and how solid is that answer?
balance: Across three randomized trials, metabolic surgery controls type 2 diabetes far more powerfully than intensive medical therapy — more remission (37.5% of surgical patients stayed in remission throughout 10 years in the longest trial), much larger A1c and weight falls. The fences: STAMPEDE’s intention-to-treat primary endpoint was not significant (P=0.08 and 0.17); the trials randomized 60–150 patients each; most remissions eventually relapse; and no trial shows fewer heart attacks, strokes, or deaths. The diet route to the same goal — total diet replacement (DiRECT) — lives on Shelf #201 and is not re-carded here. Developer-approved Nov 6, 2026.

title: Weekly insulin icodec: one basal injection a week instead of seven
question: In people with diabetes who need basal insulin, does once-weekly insulin icodec control blood glucose as well as once-daily basal insulin — and at what hypoglycemia cost?
balance: One injection a week does the basal-insulin job: in insulin-naive type 2 diabetes, icodec lowered A1c slightly more than daily glargine or degludec, with hypoglycemia rates under 1 event per patient-year in both arms — somewhat higher on icodec in relative terms. In type 1 diabetes the trade was starker: equal A1c, but a 1.9 relative rate of clinically significant or severe hypoglycemia. The US approval (FDA, March 26, 2026 — Awiqli) covers type 2 diabetes only. All three trials were funded by Novo Nordisk, icodec’s maker. Developer-approved Nov 6, 2026.

title: Thiazolidinedione harms: fractures, heart failure, the bladder-cancer signal
question: In type 2 diabetes, what harms do the thiazolidinediones (pioglitazone, rosiglitazone) cause?
balance: Thiazolidinediones make the body hold fluid, and in randomized trials they clearly increase heart-failure admissions — RECORD: heart-failure admission or death HR 2.10 (1.35–3.27); PROactive: 5.7% vs 4.1% admitted — while neither trial showed more heart-failure or cardiovascular deaths on the drug (PROactive: heart-failure mortality did not differ; RECORD: cardiovascular death HR 0.84, 0.59–1.18). In women, rosiglitazone roughly doubles limb fractures (ADOPT: 9.3% vs 5.1% on metformin and 3.5% on glyburide over about 4 years; men unaffected) — PPAR-γ activation shifts marrow stem cells toward fat and away from bone-forming cells, and lowers insulin/IGF-1 signaling to bone. The bladder-cancer question for pioglitazone stays MAYBE (weak evidence): two large cohorts found no clear overall increase (Kaiser ever-use HR 1.2, 0.9–1.5), with weak rises after more than 2 years of use (Kaiser HR 1.4; UK rate ratio 1.83 overall, 2.54 at the highest cumulative dose) — small absolute risks, causality unproven.

title: Diabetic foot ulcers: offloading heals, adjuncts add a little
question: In people with diabetic foot ulcers, what actually heals the wound — how much comes from taking pressure off it, and what do dressings and patches add?
balance: The ulcer heals when the pressure comes off and stays off: total contact casts and irremovable walkers beat removable devices in both offloading trials, largely because patients take removable devices off. On top of standard care, a sucrose octasulfate dressing (neuroischaemic ulcers) and the LeucoPatch (hard-to-heal ulcers) each added roughly 12–18 percentage points of healing at 20 weeks — real, modest, and adjunctive, not substitutes for offloading, debridement, vascular assessment, and infection control. title: Early vs late dialysis start: starting sooner did not help patients live longer
question: In adults with progressive stage 5 chronic kidney disease, does planning to start dialysis early (at eGFR 10–14) improve survival compared with waiting until eGFR falls to 5–7 or symptoms demand it?
balance: One trial is the whole shelf, and it is a good one: 828 patients randomized to start dialysis at eGFR 10–14 or to wait for 5–7. Starting early bought about 5.6 extra months on dialysis and no survival benefit (HR 1.04) — and three-quarters of the “late” group still started above their target eGFR when symptoms demanded it, which is the real-world lesson: start when the patient needs it, not when a number says so. No second randomized trial of dialysis timing exists. Developer-approved Nov 6, 2026.

title: Frequent hemodialysis: better intermediate outcomes, a mortality warning in follow-up
question: In patients on maintenance hemodialysis, does dialyzing six times a week instead of three improve outcomes — and what does the only long-term mortality follow-up show?
balance: Dialyzing six times a week instead of three clearly changes physiology — better blood-pressure and phosphate control in both FHN trials — and in the in-center Daily trial it improved composites of death-or-left-ventricular-mass and death-or-physical-health-score, in relative terms. The smaller Nocturnal trial found neither, and its extended follow-up produced the shelf’s warning: a mortality hazard ratio of 3.88 in the nocturnal arm, from tiny numbers with an implausibly healthy control group — carded as cautionary observational context, not proof of harm. More frequent dialysis also meant more vascular-access interventions. Developer-approved Nov 6, 2026.

title: Intravenous iron in kidney disease: dose and target matter
question: In patients with chronic kidney disease and iron-deficiency anemia, does intravenous iron — given proactively at higher doses, or targeting a higher ferritin — improve outcomes compared with reactive low-dose or oral iron?
balance: In dialysis patients, giving iron proactively at high dose (PIVOTAL) beat waiting for deficiency: fewer first cardiovascular events or deaths (HR 0.85), fewer recurrent events (rate ratio 0.77), and less erythropoiesis-stimulating agent needed — with death alone not significantly different (HR 0.84, P=0.054) and identical infection rates. Before dialysis (FIND-CKD), IV iron beat oral iron only when it targeted a high ferritin (400–600 µg/L); the low target was indistinguishable from pills. Dose and target, not the IV route alone, are the active ingredients. Developer-approved Nov 6, 2026.

title: Phosphate binders: calcium-free vs calcium-based — no proven outcome difference
question: In patients on dialysis with hyperphosphatemia, do non-calcium-based phosphate binders (sevelamer, lanthanum) reduce death or cardiovascular events compared with calcium-based binders?
balance: The binder wars end in a draw on outcomes. DCOR (sevelamer vs calcium-based binders, 2,103 patients) found no significant overall mortality difference; LANDMARK (lanthanum vs calcium carbonate, 2,309 randomized) found no difference in cardiovascular events and a higher cardiovascular-death rate on the non-calcium binder. The older meta-analytic claim of a 22% relative mortality advantage for non-calcium binders (Reference 3) is carded MAYBE (weak evidence): it predates LANDMARK and pools trials whose individual binder classes were each non-significant. Choose a binder on phosphate control, calcium load, pill burden, tolerance, and cost — not on a promised survival benefit. Developer-approved Nov 6, 2026.

title: Cinacalcet in dialysis (EVOLVE): the primary outcome was null
question: In patients on hemodialysis with moderate-to-severe secondary hyperparathyroidism, does the calcimimetic cinacalcet reduce death or major cardiovascular events?
balance: EVOLVE asked whether lowering parathyroid hormone with cinacalcet would prevent death and cardiovascular events in dialysis patients, and its primary answer was no: HR 0.93 (0.85–1.02), P=0.11 — printed first on the card, because everything favorable on this shelf (the adjusted HR 0.88, the lag-censored HR 0.85, the older-patient subgroup HR 0.74) was computed after that null, in a trial where about two-thirds of patients stopped their assigned drug. What cinacalcet demonstrably did was lower PTH and reduce parathyroidectomy (HR 0.44). For cardiovascular or mortality benefit, the verdict is MAYBE (weak evidence). Developer-approved Nov 6, 2026.

title: Tolvaptan in ADPKD: slower kidney growth, slower decline, a liver to watch
question: In autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease, does the vasopressin V2-receptor antagonist tolvaptan slow kidney growth and the loss of kidney function — in early and in later-stage disease?
balance: Tolvaptan is the first drug shown to slow ADPKD itself: kidney growth roughly halved over 3 years in early disease (TEMPO 3:4), and eGFR decline slowed by about 1.27 ml/min/1.73 m² per year in later disease (REPRISE) — in a trial that randomized only patients who had already tolerated the drug in a run-in. The benefits are slopes, not prevented kidney failure, and they are bought with aquaretic side effects (thirst, polyuria), a 23% discontinuation rate in TEMPO, and a liver-enzyme signal that requires regular monitoring. Developer-approved Nov 6, 2026.

title: Immunosuppression in IgA nephropathy: steroids work and harm; targeted budesonide and sparsentan
question: In patients with IgA nephropathy at high risk of progression despite optimized supportive care, does immunosuppression — systemic steroids, targeted-release budesonide, or the dual endothelin–angiotensin antagonist sparsentan — slow the loss of kidney function, and at what cost?
balance: High-risk IgA nephropathy is treatable, and every effective option charges for its benefit. Methylprednisolone cut the composite of kidney-function decline, kidney failure, or kidney death nearly in half in relative terms (TESTING, HR 0.53) while roughly quadrupling serious adverse events, concentrated in the abandoned full-dose era. STOP-IgAN’s null on eGFR loss — printed on its card — is the fence: older combination immunosuppression added to optimized supportive care did not slow decline, and about a third of its run-in patients remitted on supportive care alone. Targeted-release budesonide (NefIgArd) and the non-immunosuppressive sparsentan (PROTECT) preserved eGFR slope and cut proteinuria with gentler, though real, side-effect ledgers. title: Stopping ACE inhibitors and ARBs in advanced CKD: stopping did not slow the kidney decline
question: In patients with advanced, progressive chronic kidney disease (eGFR below 30), does stopping renin–angiotensin system inhibitors — ACE inhibitors and ARBs — slow the loss of kidney function, or is it safer to continue them?
balance: The randomized answer is no: in STOP-ACEi, stopping RAS inhibitors in advanced CKD did not slow the eGFR decline at 3 years (difference −0.7 ml/min/1.73 m², P=0.42), and kidney failure or dialysis started somewhat more often in the stopping group (62% vs 56%; HR 1.28, confidence interval crossing 1). The observational counterpoint (Fu 2021) cuts the other way on the outcomes patients fear most — stopping was associated with higher 5-year risks of death and major cardiovascular events, though a lower risk of starting kidney replacement therapy — but it is observational, and people who stop these drugs differ from people who continue them. Read together: there is no kidney case for routinely stopping, and a possible safety case against it. Developer-approved Nov 6, 2026.

title: Preventing contrast-associated kidney injury: neither bicarbonate nor acetylcysteine helped — and routine hydration went unproven
question: In patients at risk of kidney injury from iodinated contrast, do intravenous sodium bicarbonate, oral acetylcysteine, or routine prophylactic intravenous hydration prevent acute kidney injury and its consequences?
balance: Two widely used rituals failed their trials. PRESERVE (5,177 high-risk patients) found no benefit of bicarbonate over saline, and none of acetylcysteine over placebo, for death, dialysis, or persistent kidney damage at 90 days — or for contrast-associated kidney injury itself. AMACING went one step further and asked whether the saline ritual is needed at all in patients with eGFR 30–59: kidney injury occurred in 2.6% with no prophylaxis vs 2.7% with hydration, noninferior and cost-saving, while 5.5% of hydrated patients had a hydration complication. The honest fence: AMACING excluded eGFR below 30 and emergency cases, so its answer does not extend to the highest-risk patients. Developer-approved Nov 6, 2026.

title: Potassium binders to keep RAAS inhibitors going: enablement proven, outcomes not
question: In patients whose renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system inhibitors (RAASi) are limited by high potassium, do the newer potassium binders — patiromer and sodium zirconium cyclosilicate — control potassium well enough to keep patients on the RAASi doses that help them?
balance: The enablement claim is real. In OPAL-HK, patients who stayed on patiromer stayed on their RAAS inhibitors (94% vs 44% after withdrawal to placebo), and hyperkalemia recurred in 15% vs 60%. DIAMOND and REALIZE-K repeat the pattern in heart failure: fewer hyperkalemia events, fewer forced dose cuts. But the shelf’s framing is enablement, not outcomes — DIAMOND’s primary endpoint was switched during the trial from cardiovascular death or hospitalization to the change in serum potassium, so it cannot testify about outcomes at all; and REALIZE-K’s exploratory cardiovascular composite ran the wrong way (11% vs 3%), underpowered but printed here as a caution, not buried. Whether binder-enabled RAASi therapy saves lives remains untested. Developer-approved Nov 6, 2026.

title: CPAP for cardiovascular prevention in sleep apnea: the honest null
question: In patients with obstructive sleep apnea and established cardiovascular disease who are not very sleepy, does CPAP treatment prevent cardiovascular events — heart attack, stroke, cardiovascular death?
balance: This shelf exists to say the quiet part plainly: CPAP did not prevent cardiovascular events in the patients these trials enrolled. SAVE’s primary endpoint ran at 17.0% on CPAP vs 15.4% on usual care (HR 1.10, not significant); ISAACC’s ran at 16% vs 17% (HR 0.89, not significant). Both trials enrolled minimally sleepy patients — the people least driven to use the machine, with average use under 3.5 hours a night — so the null is a null for this population and this adherence, not a verdict on CPAP for sleepiness, which SAVE did improve. Symptom benefit is a different question, and it is not this shelf’s claim. Developer-approved Nov 6, 2026.

title: Triple therapy in COPD: fewer exacerbations than dual therapy, at a pneumonia price
question: In patients with COPD at risk of exacerbations, does single-inhaler triple therapy — an inhaled corticosteroid plus a long-acting muscarinic antagonist plus a long-acting beta-agonist — reduce exacerbations compared with dual therapy, and at what cost?
balance: Triple therapy beats dual therapy on exacerbations in both mega-trials: IMPACT’s rate ratios were 0.85 against ICS/LABA and 0.75 against LAMA/LABA; ETHOS’s were 0.76–0.87 depending on dose and comparator. The price is consistent too — more pneumonia in the corticosteroid-containing arms (IMPACT hazard ratio 1.53 vs LAMA/LABA). ETHOS also produced a mortality signal favoring its higher-dose triple therapy; because death was a secondary endpoint in a trial powered on exacerbations, that signal is graded POSSIBLE on the ETHOS card itself and deliberately kept off this shelf’s headline. Developer-approved Nov 6, 2026.

title: Pulmonary rehabilitation after a COPD exacerbation: start it after discharge — starting it in hospital harmed
question: After a hospitalization for a COPD exacerbation, does pulmonary rehabilitation reduce readmissions and deaths — and does it matter whether rehabilitation starts during the admission or after discharge?
balance: Timing is the whole shelf. Rehabilitation started after the exacerbation, in the Cochrane pool of 20 trials, cut hospital readmissions (odds ratio 0.44) and produced large gains in quality of life and walking distance — though the readmission result was heterogeneous and the pooled mortality result was not significant. The one large trial that started rehabilitation during the admission itself (Greening 2014) found no readmission benefit and significantly higher one-year mortality — the harm boundary: do not start progressive exercise rehab in the first days of the acute illness. The largest survival number (Lindenauer’s hazard ratio 0.63 in 197,376 Medicare patients) is observational and sits inside the 0.5–2.0 band this library does not treat as solid evidence; it is carded labeled as such. Developer-approved Nov 6, 2026.

title: Long-term oxygen therapy in COPD: lifesaving in severe resting hypoxemia — no benefit in moderate desaturation
question: In patients with COPD, does long-term supplemental oxygen prolong life — and how low does the oxygen level have to be before it helps?
balance: Oxygen is a drug with a threshold. In severe resting hypoxemia, the founding trials agree: NOTT found mortality nearly twice as high on 12-hour nocturnal oxygen as on continuous oxygen, and the MRC trial found 19 deaths among 42 oxygen-treated patients against 30 of 45 controls over five years. In moderate desaturation — resting saturation 89–93% or exercise-induced dips — LOTT’s 738 patients gained nothing: death or first hospitalization hazard ratio 0.94, with no benefit on any measured outcome. Prescribe it below the line; above the line it is burden without benefit. Developer-approved Nov 6, 2026.

title: Noninvasive ventilation in acute COPD exacerbation: fewer deaths, far fewer intubations
question: In adults admitted to hospital with acute hypercapnic respiratory failure from a COPD exacerbation, does noninvasive ventilation (BiPAP) added to usual care reduce death and the need for intubation?
balance: One of the clearest shelves in the library. Across 17 randomized trials in acute hypercapnic respiratory failure from COPD exacerbation, noninvasive ventilation cut the risk of death by 46% relative (risk ratio 0.54; number needed to treat 12) and the risk of intubation by 65% relative (risk ratio 0.36; number needed to treat 5), in Cochrane’s 2017 pool. The evidence is graded moderate quality — most trials could not be blinded — but the direction never wavers. Developer-approved Nov 6, 2026.

title: Thrombolysis for intermediate-risk pulmonary embolism: collapse prevented, paid for in bleeding
question: In normotensive patients with intermediate-risk pulmonary embolism — right-ventricular dysfunction plus myocardial injury — does thrombolysis with tenecteplase prevent death or hemodynamic collapse, and what does it cost in major bleeding and stroke?
balance: PEITHO is a trade, stated in one breath: tenecteplase halved the composite of death or hemodynamic collapse (2.6% vs 5.6%; odds ratio 0.44) — a benefit carried almost entirely by preventing collapse, since death itself did not differ (1.2% vs 1.8% at 7 days; 2.4% vs 3.2% at 30 days) — and paid for it with major extracranial bleeding (6.3% vs 1.2%) and hemorrhagic stroke in 2.0% of treated patients vs 0.2% on placebo. For roughly every 30 patients treated, one collapse is prevented and one serious bleed is caused. Whether that trade is worth making, and in which patient, is a bedside judgment — the shelf’s job is to print both sides at full size. Developer-approved Nov 6, 2026.

title: As-needed ICS-formoterol in mild asthma: exacerbation protection without a daily inhaler
question: In patients with mild asthma, does taking budesonide-formoterol only as needed — instead of a daily maintenance inhaler or a short-acting reliever alone — control symptoms and prevent severe exacerbations?
balance: For mild asthma, the reliever itself can carry the anti-inflammatory drug. SYGMA 1 showed as-needed budesonide-formoterol beat a short-acting reliever alone on symptom control and cut the severe exacerbation rate by nearly two-thirds relative (rate ratio 0.36), at 17% of the steroid dose of daily maintenance — though daily maintenance still controlled day-to-day symptoms best. PRACTICAL, the pragmatic open-label trial, then showed as-needed therapy beat maintenance head-to-head on the outcome that matters most: severe exacerbations, relative rate 0.69. The honest summary: you give up a little day-to-day symptom control and gain exacerbation protection without a daily inhaler most patients stop taking anyway. Developer-approved Nov 6, 2026.

title: Biologics for severe asthma: tezepelumab prevents exacerbations — and failed to spare steroids
question: In severe, uncontrolled asthma, do biologic medicines prevent exacerbations — and can they replace the daily oral steroids that do so much long-term harm?
balance: Tezepelumab, the TSLP-blocking biologic, cut severe-asthma exacerbations by more than half relative in NAVIGATOR (rate ratio 0.44) — and, unusually for this class, the benefit held at low eosinophil counts (0.59). But its dedicated steroid-sparing trial, SOURCE, failed its primary endpoint outright: patients on tezepelumab could not reduce their daily oral corticosteroid dose any more than patients on placebo (OR 1.28, P=0.43). Both halves belong on the label in the clinic: prescribe it to prevent exacerbations, not on a promise that the prednisone can stop. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: Varenicline safety and efficacy: the neuropsychiatric fear, tested in 8,144 smokers
question: Is varenicline — the most effective single quit-smoking medicine — safe for the brain, including in people with psychiatric disorders?
balance: For a decade varenicline carried a boxed warning for neuropsychiatric harm, built on case reports. EAGLES — 8,144 smokers, half with psychiatric disorders, randomized against bupropion, nicotine patch, and placebo — found no excess of moderate-to-severe neuropsychiatric events on varenicline in either cohort (1.3% vs 2.4% on placebo in the non-psychiatric cohort), and the FDA removed the boxed warning on the strength of it. The efficacy half of the same trial — varenicline quits more smokers than patch, bupropion, or placebo — is carded at its home on Shelf #225. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: Harms of inhaled corticosteroids: pneumonia (LIKELY) and bone (POSSIBLE)
question: What do inhaled corticosteroids cost the patients they help — in pneumonia, and in bone?
balance: The pneumonia harm is the solid half: in the Cochrane pooling of the COPD trials, fluticasone raised serious (hospitalized) pneumonia with an odds ratio of 1.78 — about 18 extra cases per 1,000 treated over 18 months — with no offsetting mortality change in either direction. The bone half is thinner: fractures ran modestly higher on inhaled steroids in both trial and observational poolings (OR 1.27 and 1.21, both inside the band this library will not call solid), with a dose gradient that keeps the question open rather than closed. Prescribe inhaled steroids in COPD for exacerbations, with the pneumonia price known and the bone price watched. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: Oral versus IV antibiotics for bone and joint infection: the line is not the therapy
question: For bone, joint, and heart-valve infections, does the antibiotic have to run through a vein for weeks — or can pills do the same job?
balance: Two large randomized trials say the vein is optional once the patient is stable and the organism is covered. OVIVA (1,054 bone and joint infections): oral step-down within a week was noninferior to six weeks of IV (failure 13.2% vs 14.6%), with a tenth of the catheter complications. POET (400 stable left-sided endocarditis patients): switching to oral after at least 10 IV days was noninferior at 6 months (9.0% vs 12.1%), and the long-term follow-up favored the oral group (HR 0.64) — carded as observational, noted, not sold. What the trials share: selected, stable patients, susceptible organisms, and an oral regimen that actually absorbs. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: Short-course antibiotics for pneumonia: 8 days tied 15 — with one organism-shaped exception
question: How short can pneumonia treatment safely go — in the ventilated patient, and on the ward?
balance: Shorter won or tied everywhere it was honestly tested — with the exception printed, not buried. PneumA randomized ventilator-associated pneumonia to 8 vs 15 days: no mortality difference, more antibiotic-free days — but recurrence in nonfermenting gram-negative infections (Pseudomonas and its kin) ran 40.6% vs 25.4%, so the short course is not one-size-fits-all. On the ward, Uranga showed a stability-based stop at day 5 matched physician-chosen durations for community-acquired pneumonia. The rule the evidence supports: stop early by stability and organism — not by habit, and not blindly by calendar. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: Procalcitonin-guided antibiotic decisions: fewer antibiotic days (LIKELY); a mortality claim graded POSSIBLE
question: Does a procalcitonin number help clinicians start fewer antibiotics and stop them sooner — and does anyone live longer because of it?
balance: Two claims live on this shelf and they do not share a grade. The stewardship claim — procalcitonin guidance cuts roughly 2–3 antibiotic days — replicated from PRORATA’s ICU to the Cochrane individual-patient pooling, and it is LIKELY. The mortality claim rests on that pooling’s adjusted OR 0.83, inside the not-solid band, against PRORATA’s day-60 wobble in the wrong direction and ProACT’s clean null in US emergency departments; it is POSSIBLE, and the null is printed on the shelf, not in a footnote. title: Don’t treat asymptomatic bacteriuria: the bacteria are not the disease
question: Bacteria in the urine, no symptoms: treat, or leave alone?
balance: Leave it alone. In diabetic women — the group most often treated — antibiotics cleared the urine and prevented nothing (symptomatic episodes 42% treated vs 40% untreated; Harding 2002). In young women with recurrent UTI, treating the quiet bacteriuria made things worse: recurrence 46.8% vs 13.1% untreated, an adjusted hazard ratio of 3.09, labeled observational on its card (Cai 2012). The IDSA exceptions are printed here because they are part of the rule: DO screen and treat in pregnancy, and before invasive urologic procedures. Everyone else’s positive culture without symptoms is colonization, not a diagnosis. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: Seven versus fourteen days for UTI: a week is enough
question: For urinary tract infection — kidney infection in women, UTI in men, and the bacteremia that so often starts in the urinary tract — does the second week of antibiotics buy anything?
balance: Three noninferiority trials, three populations, one answer. Women with acute pyelonephritis: 7 days of ciprofloxacin cured 97%, 14 days 96% (Sandberg). Afebrile men with UTI: symptom resolution 93.1% on 7 days vs 90.2% on 14 (Drekonja). And BALANCE — 3,608 bloodstream infections, the urinary tract their commonest source — found 90-day mortality of 14.5% on 7 days vs 16.1% on 14. The exclusions matter and are printed on the cards: febrile men, S. aureus bacteremia, deep foci, and severe immunosuppression were not in these trials. Within the studied ground, the second week is habit, not therapy. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis: pills work when taken — injections work when pills don’t get taken
question: In people at high risk of acquiring HIV, how well does pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) prevent infection — daily pills, long-acting injections, and twice-yearly lenacapavir?
balance: Every positive trial on this shelf carries the same asterisk: the drug works in proportion to its presence in the body. Daily oral tenofovir-based PrEP cut HIV incidence by 44% relative in iPrEx and by 67–75% relative in Partners PrEP — and by over 90% in participants with detectable drug levels — while the FEM-PrEP and VOICE trials in African women found no protection at all, because adherence was too low for drug to be present. The long-acting era is the adherence answer: injectable cabotegravir every 8 weeks beat daily pills head-to-head in HPTN 083 (hazard ratio 0.34) and HPTN 084 (hazard ratio 0.12), and twice-yearly lenacapavir recorded zero infections among 2,134 women in PURPOSE 1 and an incidence of 0.10 per 100 person-years in PURPOSE 2. All efficacy figures on this shelf are relative reductions; absolute incidences are printed on every card. Tier C — prevention-of-infection claims; developer verdict given personally. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: Early antiretroviral therapy: start at diagnosis — for the patient, and for the partner
question: In people with HIV who feel well and have high CD4 counts, does starting antiretroviral therapy immediately — rather than waiting for the CD4 count to fall — prevent illness, death, and transmission?
balance: START settled the timing question for the patient's own health: starting ART at a CD4 count above 500 rather than waiting for 350 cut the composite of serious AIDS events, serious non-AIDS events, and death by 57% relative (hazard ratio 0.43) — and the absolute difference is printed beside it on the card, because it is the honest size of the prize: 1.8% versus 4.1% over about 3 years, an absolute difference of about 2.3 percentage points, a number-needed-to-treat of about 43. TEMPRANO, run in Côte d'Ivoire, found the same direction independently for early ART (hazard ratio 0.56) and added a second, separate win for six months of isoniazid preventive therapy (0.65). HPTN 052 answers the second question — the partner's: early ART cut genetically linked transmission by 93% relative, and no linked infection occurred while the index partner's virus was stably suppressed. Tier C — mortality and transmission claims; developer verdict given personally. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: Four-month rifapentine-moxifloxacin for tuberculosis: two months back — from one pivotal trial
question: For drug-susceptible pulmonary tuberculosis, can a 4-month daily regimen — rifapentine in place of rifampin, moxifloxacin in place of ethambutol — cure as reliably as the standard 6 months?
balance: One trial carries this shelf, and the shelf says so. Study 31/A5349 randomized 2,516 people with drug-susceptible pulmonary TB: the 4-month rifapentine-moxifloxacin regimen was noninferior to the 6-month standard (unfavorable outcomes 11.6% vs 9.6% in the assessable population, inside the 6.6-point margin), with grade 3-or-higher adverse events no more frequent (18.8% vs 19.3%). The regimen's internal control is instructive — rifapentine WITHOUT moxifloxacin failed noninferiority in the same trial (14.2% vs 9.6%) — and the shelf's third card is the graveyard of earlier shortcuts: REMoxTB and OFLOTUB both tried to shorten therapy to 4 months with fluoroquinolones and both failed. The shortening is real, but it belongs to this specific regimen, not to the idea of shortening. Single pivotal trial — the flag stays on the shelf until a second trial confirms it. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: RSV vaccines in older adults: strong first-season protection that fades — and a rare Guillain-Barré warning on the label
question: In adults 60 and older, do respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) vaccines prevent RSV lower respiratory tract disease — how well, for how long, and at what risk?
balance: Two prefusion-F vaccines, two large trials, the same shape of answer. GSK's adjuvanted vaccine (AReSVi-006) prevented RSV lower respiratory tract disease with 82.6% relative efficacy in its first season — in absolute terms, 7 cases versus 40 (1.0 vs 5.8 per 1,000 participant-years), roughly one case averted per 380 vaccinated per season — and 94.1% relative efficacy against severe disease. Pfizer's bivalent vaccine (RENOIR) showed 66.7% relative efficacy against illness with at least two symptoms and 85.7% against illness with at least three. Protection then fades: over three seasons a single GSK dose cumulatively held 62.9% relative efficacy, and a second dose a year later added nothing measurable — revaccination is not (yet) the answer. The harm side is carded on the same shelf, as it should be: post-marketing surveillance found a small excess of Guillain-Barré syndrome, on the order of 1.8 cases per million doses, and in January 2025 the FDA required warnings on both vaccines' labels. Every efficacy figure on this shelf is a relative reduction; the absolute case counts are printed on the cards. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: High-dose influenza vaccine: better against flu itself — the big hospitalization trials split
question: In adults 65 and older, does high-dose influenza vaccine prevent more illness and hospitalization than the standard dose?
balance: DANFLU-2 comes first because it is the largest and the most sobering: 332,438 Danes randomized, and the primary end point — hospitalization for influenza or pneumonia — was NOT met (0.68% vs 0.73%; relative effectiveness 5.9%; P=0.14). What DANFLU-2 did show was a 43.6% relative reduction in hospitalization for influenza specifically, with pneumonia hospitalizations identical (0.63% vs 0.63%) — the composite was diluted by the outcome the vaccine cannot be expected to move much. GALFLU, the second mega-trial, met the same composite (relative effectiveness 23.7%) in a younger 65–79 population. The older evidence agrees on the narrower claim: FIM12 proved 24.2% relative efficacy against laboratory-confirmed influenza illness, and INVESTED — in post-MI and heart-failure patients — found no difference in death or cardiopulmonary hospitalization (HR 1.06). So: LIKELY that high-dose vaccine prevents more influenza and influenza hospitalization than standard dose; only POSSIBLE that it moves the broad hospitalization composites clinics actually feel. All effectiveness figures are relative; absolute risks are printed on every card. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: Eradicating H. pylori to prevent gastric cancer: the benefit is real where incidence is high — and unproven as a blanket policy where it is low
question: In people infected with Helicobacter pylori, does eradication treatment prevent gastric cancer — in healthy carriers, in those with a family history, and in stomachs that have already produced one cancer?
balance: The pooled randomized record (Ford, Cochrane 2020: 7 trials, 8,323 healthy infected adults, six of them Asian) says eradication prevents gastric cancer with a relative risk of 0.54 — labeled relative, as this library insists — with a number-needed-to-treat of 72, and gastric-cancer mortality at a relative risk of 0.61 (NNT 135), while all-cause mortality did not move (RR 0.97). The regional gradient is the shelf: the same relative effect buys an NNT of roughly 57 in East Asia and roughly 345 in North America, because the absolute risk underneath it differs six-fold. The targeted trials sharpen the point — in Koreans with an affected first-degree relative, eradication halved cancer incidence (1.2% vs 2.7%; HR 0.45), and after endoscopic resection of an early cancer it halved metachronous cancers (HR 0.50; the Ford neoplasia subgroup pooled at RR 0.49, NNT 21). Shandong's 22-year follow-up adds the timing lesson: benefit concentrates in stomachs treated before advanced precancerous change. Hence the split stamp: LIKELY where incidence is high or risk is individual and concrete; POSSIBLE as a blanket policy in low-incidence Western populations, where it has never been directly tested. Tier C — cancer-incidence claims; developer verdict given personally. Two cards on this shelf (Choi 2018; Shandong) are re-cards — their home is Shelf #219, and they are counted once, there. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: Drugs for MASH: three positive biopsy trials, two accelerated approvals — and no outcomes trial yet
question: In metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH, formerly NASH) with liver fibrosis, do resmetirom, semaglutide, or tirzepatide improve liver histology — and what remains unproven?
balance: Stamped LIKELY by the developer's explicit override (the evidence was proposed at POSSIBLE; the developer raised it Nov 6, 2026, and the stamp carries that decision openly). The record itself: resmetirom (MAESTRO-NASH) resolved steatohepatitis without worsening fibrosis in 25.9–29.9% versus 9.7% on placebo and improved fibrosis in 24.2–25.9% versus 14.2% — the first drug FDA-approved for MASH (accelerated approval, March 2024, for F2–F3 fibrosis). Semaglutide (ESSENCE, part 1) posted the largest resolution figure yet, 62.9% versus 34.3%, with fibrosis improvement of 36.8% versus 22.4%, and received accelerated approval in August 2025. Tirzepatide (SYNERGY-NASH, phase 2, n=190) resolved MASH in 44%, 56%, and 62% at ascending doses versus 10% — and is NOT FDA-approved for MASH; that is printed on its card, not implied away. Every endpoint on this shelf is a biopsy surrogate at about a year; no trial has yet shown fewer cases of cirrhosis decompensation, transplant, or death, and the cautionary card (REGENERATE's obeticholic acid — a fibrosis endpoint met, approval refused) is the standing reminder of what surrogate success does not guarantee. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: Early effective therapy in Crohn's disease: top-down beats step-up — decisively, in newly diagnosed disease
question: In Crohn's disease, does starting effective therapy early — combined immunosuppression or biomarker-guided tight control from diagnosis — produce better remission and endoscopic outcomes than the conventional step-up sequence?
balance: PROFILE is the strongest strategy trial this field has produced: in 386 patients randomized within days of diagnosis, top-down infliximab plus immunomodulator produced sustained steroid-free, surgery-free remission in 79% versus 15% on accelerated step-up — a 64-point absolute difference, with endoscopic remission 67% versus 44% and FEWER serious adverse events in the top-down group (15 vs 42). Two honest footnotes travel with it: the biomarker that was supposed to select who needs top-down therapy (PredictSURE) failed outright (interaction P=0.944) — everyone benefited, so the test adds nothing — and 'accelerated step-up' in PROFILE was still faster than real-world care usually is. CALM supplies the complementary lesson: managing to biomarkers plus symptoms (tight control) beat managing to symptoms alone on endoscopic remission (46% vs 30%). D'Haens 2008 and REACT show the same direction at longer horizons, with REACT's 24-month composite of surgery, hospitalization, and complications lower under early combined immunosuppression (HR 0.73). The boundary is printed plainly: all of this evidence is Crohn's disease — it does not card ulcerative colitis by analogy. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: Long-term PPI safety: the one large randomized trial acquits the class of nearly every accused harm — the real harms are smaller and specific
question: In people taking a proton pump inhibitor for years, which of the harms attributed to PPIs in observational studies — fractures, pneumonia, kidney disease, dementia, cancer, death — survive randomization, and which harms are real?
balance: COMPASS is the reassurance trial and this shelf's anchor: 17,598 patients randomized to pantoprazole or placebo for a median of three years, prespecifying the whole observational charge sheet — pneumonia, fracture, gastric atrophy, chronic kidney disease, diabetes, COPD, dementia, cardiovascular disease, cancer, hospitalization, death — and finding no significant difference in any of it. The single exception was enteric infections (1.4% vs 1.0%; OR 1.33), with C. difficile about twice as frequent on only 13 events, not significant. The observational edifice that COMPASS acquits deserves its own honest sentence: claims-database associations (for example, dementia hazard ratios around 1.44 in German claims data) repeatedly failed to replicate in prospective and randomized data — confounding by indication and frailty, not pharmacology. What IS real is smaller and specific, and it is carded: rebound acid hypersecretion producing symptoms on withdrawal (44% vs 15% in healthy volunteers — a dependency mechanism, demonstrated in a blinded trial), and the clopidogrel interaction scare, which COGENT's randomized test cleared for cardiovascular harm while confirming the GI protection. COMPASS is a re-card here — its home summary sits on Shelf #137 — counted once, there. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: Antivirals in chronic hepatitis B: suppressing the virus prevents progression and liver cancer — proven once against placebo, extended by histology and cohorts
question: In chronic hepatitis B, does long-term antiviral therapy prevent disease progression, cirrhosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma — or only normalize blood tests?
balance: Liaw 2004 is the one placebo-controlled hard-outcome trial this question will ever have — it was stopped early because withholding treatment had become untenable: in 651 patients with advanced fibrosis or cirrhosis, lamivudine cut disease progression from 17.7% to 7.8% (hazard ratio 0.45, labeled relative, with the absolute rates printed beside it) and hepatocellular carcinoma from 7.4% to 3.9% (HR 0.49). Its weakness is also carded: YMDD resistance mutations in 49% of treated patients eroded the benefit — the reason lamivudine itself is now a historical agent and entecavir and tenofovir, with high resistance barriers, carry the practice. What those drugs add is shown, not placebo-proven: five years of tenofovir regressed fibrosis in 51% of biopsied patients and left 74% of cirrhotics no longer cirrhotic on biopsy (Marcellin — an uncontrolled roll-over, labeled as such), and the Hosaka cohort found 5-year HCC incidence of 3.7% on entecavir versus 13.7% untreated after propensity matching (adjusted HR 0.37 — observational, and above this library's 0.5 observational floor it is supportive rather than decisive). The residual-risk sentence belongs on the shelf: suppression reduces but does not abolish HCC, HBsAg loss runs at only about 1% per year, and surveillance continues on treatment. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: Low-FODMAP diet for IBS: real relief against a usual diet — unproven against good dietary advice
question: In adults with irritable bowel syndrome, does eating low in FODMAPs — fermentable oligosaccharides, disaccharides, monosaccharides and polyols — improve symptoms, and at what cost?
balance: The honest summary is a split result. Against a typical diet, the effect is large (Halmos: symptom scores 22.8 vs 44.9 in a feeding study). Against a sham diet in the one placebo-controlled trial, low-FODMAP won clearly on symptom severity (IBS-SSS 173 vs 224) but its adequate-relief endpoint reached significance only per-protocol (61% vs 39%; intention-to-treat 57% vs 38%, P=0.051). Against competent traditional advice it tied twice (Böhn responders 50% vs 46%; Eswaran adequate relief 52% vs 41%, not significant, though pain responders favoured low-FODMAP 51% vs 23%). The trials are small and short — four weeks in the pragmatic studies — and the positive ones were dietitian-delivered. The costs are carded, not footnoted: fecal bifidobacteria fall on the diet, diet quality dips, and the reintroduction phase has no sham-controlled evidence. Three of the five cards are re-cards homed on Shelf #202, which holds the same trials under its own verdict (POSSIBLE vs a usual diet); each is counted once, at its home shelf. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: Surgery versus PPI for GERD: a near-tie in ordinary reflux — surgery wins only the truly refractory, carefully selected case
question: In chronic gastroesophageal reflux disease, how does laparoscopic antireflux surgery compare with long-term proton-pump inhibitor therapy — and in PPI-refractory heartburn, who actually benefits from an operation?
balance: Two trials, two different questions, one coherent answer. In ordinary PPI-responsive GERD (LOTUS, 554 patients), five-year remission was 92% on esomeprazole vs 85% after surgery (P=0.048) — and that slim medical edge disappeared under dropout modelling; what durably differed was the symptom trade: surgery nearly abolished regurgitation (2% vs 13%) at the cost of more dysphagia (11% vs 5%), bloating (40% vs 28%), and flatulence (57% vs 40%), with similar serious adverse events. In refractory heartburn (Spechler 2019), the fence must be printed with the result: of 366 referred veterans, 288 were excluded before randomization — 99 had functional heartburn, not reflux — and only among the 78 with proven reflux-related refractory heartburn did surgery win clearly (success 67% vs 28% active medical vs 12% control). Sweden’s unselected registry then prices durability: 17.7% recurrence by a median 5.6 years, most managed by restarting medication. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: Secretagogues for IBS-C and chronic constipation: about one patient in five responds durably — diarrhoea and nausea are the price
question: In chronic constipation and irritable bowel syndrome with constipation, do the gut secretagogues (linaclotide, plecanatide, lubiprostone) and the prokinetic prucalopride produce durable responders beyond placebo?
balance: The class pattern is consistent across four drugs and five trials: a durable-responder rate of roughly one in five on drug against roughly one in ten — or fewer — on placebo, a number needed to treat of about 6–8. Linaclotide’s two trials put durable responders at 16–21% vs 3–6%; plecanatide at 21.0%/19.5% vs 10.2%; prucalopride (a prokinetic shelved with the secretagogues because the clinic question groups them) reached three or more complete bowel movements weekly in 30.9%/28.4% vs 12.0%, with no cardiovascular signal in a trial that monitored for one. In IBS-C, linaclotide’s FDA composite responder rate was 33.7% vs 13.9% (NNT 5.1). Lubiprostone’s base is the thinnest — one 4-week trial — and its nausea rate (31.7%) is the class’s worst; the secretagogues’ tax is diarrhoea, stopping treatment in about 4–6%. Every pivotal trial ran 12 weeks (lubiprostone 4); durability beyond that rests on open-label extensions, and no trial compares these drugs head-to-head with polyethylene glycol. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.
