title: NSAID gastroprotection: celecoxib protected the whole gut better than diclofenac plus omeprazole — in patients not taking aspirin
question: In patients who need long-term NSAIDs, which strategy best prevents serious gastrointestinal harm — a COX-2-selective drug, a nonselective NSAID plus a proton-pump inhibitor, or misoprostol — and where does the evidence stop?
balance: The strategies separate by where in the gut you look. For the whole gastrointestinal tract, CONDOR (4,484 arthritis patients) found fewer clinically significant events on celecoxib alone than on diclofenac plus omeprazole (0.9% vs 3.8%; hazard ratio 4.3, a relative measure) — and the shelf prints CONDOR’s fence in its title and on its card: the trial excluded aspirin users, so it does not answer the aspirin question. For the upper gut alone, the shields tie (Chan 2002: recurrent bleeding 4.9% vs 6.4% after a healed bleed), yet about 1 in 20 of those highest-risk patients rebled within 6 months anyway. Misoprostol is the historical control on complacency: MUCOSA proved a hard-endpoint benefit against placebo (serious complications 0.57% vs 0.95%, a 40% relative reduction) and was abandoned anyway, because a fifth of patients quit it within a month, mostly with diarrhoea. Both Chan trials screened out or eradicated H. pylori first — eradication timing is part of the strategy, not an afterthought. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: Probiotics for IBS: strain-specific, heterogeneous, small trials — which strain, for whom, remains unclear
question: In irritable bowel syndrome, do probiotics improve global symptoms — and can the evidence name the strain, the dose, and the patient?
balance: The pooled number looks friendly — Ford 2018: relative risk of symptoms persisting 0.79 across 53 trials and 5,545 patients, a number needed to treat of about 7 — and the shelf still takes the library’s weakest stamp, because everything underneath that number is soft: dozens of different organisms and doses pooled together, heterogeneity and publication bias, and an update (Goodoory 2023: 82 trials, 10,332 patients) that found only 24 trials at low risk of bias and GRADE certainty low to very low for nearly every strain and outcome. The best single-strain trial (Whorwell) worked at exactly one of three doses, in women, for 4 weeks. The guidelines read the same record and split the difference the same way: ACG suggests against routine use; the AGA calls IBS probiotics a knowledge gap best used inside trials; British practice allows a time-limited trial of a named product. Adverse events in the trials tracked placebo; the rare harms (invasive infection in susceptible hosts, D-lactate case reports) are carded on Card 5. Strain-specific, heterogeneous, small trials — the framing is the finding. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: Multidomain lifestyle intervention for cognition (FINGER): one positive cognitive score — no trial has shown dementia prevention
question: In older people at risk, does a multidomain intervention — diet, exercise, cognitive training, and vascular-risk monitoring — preserve cognition, or prevent dementia?
balance: The split stamp is the shelf. For cognition: FINGER — the one large, well-run positive trial — improved its neuropsychological composite by 0.022 Z points per year over 2 years (P=0.030) in selected at-risk Finns, a small but real signal, graded POSSIBLE. For dementia prevention: no trial has shown it. PreDIVA, which actually measured dementia over 6 years in 3,526 people, found 7% vs 7% (HR 0.92); MAPT found no significant cognitive effect of the multidomain programme with or without omega-3. FINGER never measured dementia incidence at all. Printed plainly, as the shelf requires: a multidomain programme may modestly support cognition in at-risk older adults; that it prevents dementia is MAYBE (weak evidence) — an extrapolation the dementia-endpoint trials have so far failed to confirm. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: Anti-amyloid antibodies in Alzheimer’s disease: amyloid falls decisively; decline slows by less than patients can feel — and ARIA is the price
question: In early Alzheimer’s disease, do anti-amyloid monoclonal antibodies (lecanemab, donanemab) produce patient-important benefit — and at what risk?
balance: The two halves of this shelf must never be quoted separately. The biomarker half is strong: lecanemab cut brain amyloid by 59.1 centiloids against placebo, donanemab cleared plaque on a stop-when-clear schedule, and both slowed decline on the CDR-SB scale — biomarker and scale efficacy this shelf grades LIKELY. The patient-important half is weaker, and its numbers are printed with their yardstick: lecanemab’s CDR-SB difference was −0.45 and donanemab’s −0.67, against a minimal clinically important difference of about 1.0–1.6 points at this disease stage (Reference 3). The harms are neither rare nor theoretical: ARIA-E in 12.6% on lecanemab (about a third of ApoE ε4 homozygotes) and 24.0% on donanemab, ARIA-H in 17.3% and 31.4% respectively, and three treatment-related deaths in the donanemab trial. Net clinical benefit is therefore stamped POSSIBLE — real slowing, below the feel-able threshold, bought with brain-swelling and bleeding risk that demands MRI monitoring. The aducanumab arc (surrogate approval, discordant trials, withdrawal) is carded on Card 3 as the standing warning against upgrading this stamp on biomarker data alone. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: PFO closure after cryptogenic stroke: fewer second strokes in the young, high-risk-anatomy patient — bought with atrial fibrillation and a device
question: After a cryptogenic stroke in a patient with a patent foramen ovale, does device closure beat medical therapy at preventing another stroke?
balance: In selected patients — younger, with a moderate-to-large shunt or an atrial septal aneurysm — the three 2017 trials all favoured closure: CLOSE found zero strokes in 238 closure patients vs 14 of 235 on antiplatelets; REDUCE found 1.4% vs 5.4%; RESPECT’s long-term follow-up gave a hazard ratio of 0.55 (relative), with absolute rates of 0.58 vs 1.07 events per 100 patient-years. The selection card (Kent 2021) sharpens the fence: pooled across all six trials, benefit concentrated in PASCAL-’probable’ patients (HR 0.10) and vanished in ’unlikely’ ones (HR 1.14), while device atrial fibrillation rose most in the group that gained least. The price is real throughout: atrial fibrillation after the device in 4.6–6.6%, procedural complications in about 6% in CLOSE, and more venous thromboembolism in RESPECT. Absolute gains are small because recurrence on medical therapy is already low — a carefully-selected-patient treatment, not a close-every-PFO answer, and no mortality benefit is claimed. Cards 1–3 are re-cards homed on Shelf #189; each is counted once, at its home shelf. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: Carotid stenting versus endarterectomy: level at ten years in CREST, age decides in symptomatic disease — and a 2026 trial re-asks the question against modern medicine
question: In carotid stenosis, how do stenting and endarterectomy compare — in early hazard, in long-term protection, by age and symptoms — and against modern medical therapy alone?
balance: The through-line of six trials and one pooled analysis: after the periprocedural window, stenting and endarterectomy protect about equally for at least a decade (CREST at 10 years: 11.8% vs 9.9%, not significant). They differ in how they charge for that protection — periprocedural stroke 4.1% vs 2.3% with stenting, myocardial infarction 1.1% vs 2.3% with surgery (CREST) — and in symptomatic patients the early gap was wider and uglier (EVA-3S 9.6% vs 3.9%, stopped early; ICSS 8.5% vs 5.2%). Age is the strongest modifier: stenting’s periprocedural risk climbs steeply with age while surgery’s stays flat, making endarterectomy clearly superior at 70 and beyond (pooled hazard ratio 2.09 at 70–74). In asymptomatic disease, ACST-2 found both procedures down to about 1% procedural disabling stroke or death with 5-year stroke around 5% either way. And the newest evidence re-asks the founding question: in CREST-2 (reported 2026, and dated as such on its card), adding stenting to intensive medical therapy lowered 4-year events (2.8% vs 6.0%; P=0.02) while adding endarterectomy did not, significantly (3.7% vs 5.3%; P=0.24). Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: CGRP therapies for migraine prevention: roughly half of patients respond, versus a quarter on placebo — in trials that mostly ran twelve weeks
question: In episodic and chronic migraine, do CGRP-pathway therapies — the monoclonal antibodies and the oral gepants — prevent attacks better than placebo and better than older preventives, and what remains unknown?
balance: Printed the way this shelf insists — as absolute responder percentages, drug vs placebo: STRIVE (erenumab) 43.3% at 70 mg and 50.0% at 140 mg vs 26.6%; HALO episodic (fremanezumab) 47.7% vs 27.9%, and in chronic migraine 40.8% vs 18.1%; EVOLVE-1 (galcanezumab) 62.3% vs 38.6%; ADVANCE (atogepant, oral) about 61% at 60 mg. In monthly-migraine-day terms the antibodies and the gepant alike buy roughly 1.3–1.9 days a month beyond placebo. The one head-to-head trial (HER-MES) favoured erenumab over topiramate on both response (55.4% vs 31.2%; odds ratio 2.76, relative) and tolerability (discontinuation for adverse events 10.6% vs 38.9%). Now the two standing cautions. First, time: the pivotal trials behind these numbers ran a median of about 12 weeks (STRIVE and EVOLVE-1 ran 6 months) — durability and rare harms beyond that window rest on extension studies, not blinded trials. Second, biology: CGRP is a potent vasodilator, and long-term cardiovascular safety of blocking it for years remains open; the trial-era harms were mostly injection-site reactions, constipation, and nausea, with erenumab additionally carrying constipation and hypertension warnings on its label. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: First-line antiseizure medicines (SANAD II): lamotrigine holds focal epilepsy, valproate holds generalised — behind a teratogenicity fence
question: In newly diagnosed epilepsy, which antiseizure medicine should be started first — and where the winner is valproate, what does winning cost?
balance: Start where SANAD II landed. In focal epilepsy, levetiracetam — the modern default — FAILED noninferiority against lamotrigine for time to 12-month remission (HR 1.18, against a limit of 1.329), per-protocol analyses favoured lamotrigine outright (HR 1.32 and 1.37), lamotrigine caused fewer adverse reactions (33% vs 44% on levetiracetam and 45% on zonisamide), and lamotrigine was cost-dominant. In generalised or unclassifiable epilepsy, levetiracetam failed noninferiority against valproate the same way (HR 1.19), and valproate cut treatment failure (HR 0.65, relative). Now the asterisk, printed on the shelf rather than footnoted: valproate in pregnancy carries roughly a 10% risk of major congenital malformations and lowers the exposed child's IQ by about 7–10 points, and regulators fence it away from women and girls of childbearing potential unless alternatives have failed and a pregnancy-prevention programme is in place. Both things are true at once: valproate is the most effective first drug for generalised epilepsy, and a large group of patients must not take it. SANAD I (2007) is the anchor — it pointed the same way a trial generation earlier. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: Levodopa first in Parkinson's disease: the old drug wins on quality of life — and starting it early changes nothing long-term
question: In early Parkinson's disease, should treatment start with levodopa or with a levodopa-sparing drug — and does levodopa's timing change the disease?
balance: Levodopa-phobia — delaying the best drug for fear of spending it — is retired by this shelf. PD MED randomized 1,620 people to start on levodopa or to spare it (agonist or MAO-B inhibitor first): patient-rated mobility ran 1.8 points better on levodopa, sustained over 7 years, with no mortality penalty. Print the yardstick beside the effect, as this shelf insists: 1.8 points on the PDQ-39 mobility dimension is below the published minimal-important-difference estimates for that dimension (~3.2 points; the trial's own protocol used 6 points) — a real but modest edge, bought with the oldest, cheapest drug. LEAP then asked the timing question directly and answered it with a null: starting levodopa 40 weeks earlier changed nothing measurable at week 80, and five-year follow-up found no significant dyskinesia penalty for starting early (46/160 vs 62/161, P=0.06 — numerically favouring early, if anything). The agonists' price list is carded, not whispered: impulse-control disorders in 17.1% of agonist-treated patients vs 6.9% of those not taking one, in DOMINION's 3,090-patient cross-section. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: Middle meningeal artery embolization for chronic subdural hematoma: fewer reoperations in two trials — but one primary endpoint missed, one trial null, and the pooled estimate is not significant
question: In chronic subdural hematoma, does embolizing the middle meningeal artery — added to surgery or usual care — prevent the hematoma coming back?
balance: Three large randomized trials ran at once, and they do not agree cleanly — which is why this shelf is POSSIBLE, not more. EMBOLISE (surgical patients) cut reoperation from 11.3% to 4.1%. STEM (surgical or nonsurgical care) cut its treatment-failure composite from 36% to 16%. But MAGIC-MT, the largest trial, MISSED its primary endpoint (6.7% vs 9.9%, P=0.10) — printed on this shelf's face, not footnoted — and EMPROTECT, in high-risk post-surgical patients, missed too (14.8% vs 21.0%, P=0.13). Pool the three NEJM trials and the recurrence estimate is RR 0.50 with a confidence interval that crosses 1 (0.23–1.06, P=0.058): not significant overall, significant only in the nonsurgical subgroup, and with no effect on functional outcome (RR 1.01). The procedure's own harms are small but real — in EMBOLISE, 2.0% had a serious procedure-related event by 30 days, including disabling stroke in 2 patients. A promising adjunct whose best-supported use may be in patients managed without surgery; the developer ruled POSSIBLE on Nov 7, 2026. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: Preventing delirium: multicomponent bundles work — the founding trial was matched, not randomized, and prevention is the whole game
question: In hospitalized older patients, can delirium be prevented — and does anything here treat it once it starts?
balance: The design caveat comes first, in the shelf's first lines, because the founding trial is routinely misdescribed: Inouye 1999 was a controlled MATCHED study, not a randomized trial — 852 patients, delirium 9.9% on the intervention units vs 15.0% on usual care (matched OR 0.60). The randomized and meta-analytic evidence that followed points the same way: Hshieh's meta-analysis pooled OR 0.47 for incident delirium, and the Burton Cochrane review found multicomponent interventions reduced delirium incidence to 10.5% vs 18.4% (RR 0.57 — a 43% relative reduction, moderate-certainty evidence), with mortality and length-of-stay benefits unproven. Marcantonio's randomized geriatrics-consultation trial in hip fracture cut delirium from 50% to 32%. And the shelf's boundary is printed in its founding card: once delirium was established, severity and recurrence did not improve — these bundles prevent; they do not treat. Treatment is the next shelf's null. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: Antipsychotics do NOT treat delirium: the randomized trials are null — and in palliative care they made symptoms worse
question: In established delirium, do antipsychotic drugs shorten it, soften it, or save lives — in the ICU, as prophylaxis, or at the end of life?
balance: The null is the shelf, printed first. MIND-USA randomized 566 ICU patients with delirium to haloperidol, ziprasidone, or placebo: days alive without delirium or coma ran 8.5 on placebo vs 7.9 on haloperidol and 8.7 on ziprasidone (P=0.26) — every endpoint null. Prophylaxis failed too: REDUCE gave haloperidol to 1,789 high-risk ICU patients and moved neither survival nor delirium incidence. AID-ICU's primary outcome was null; its secondary mortality tilt (36.3% vs 43.3%) is printed on its card as a wrinkle, not a claim — one secondary endpoint does not repeal three null trials. In palliative care, Agar's trial found delirium symptom scores significantly WORSE on risperidone and haloperidol than on placebo. The contrast card is a different drug class: dexmedetomidine freed ventilator hours in agitated delirium (DahLIA). The PADIS guideline advises against routine antipsychotic use for delirium. What remains legitimate — a severely agitated patient endangering themselves or a lifeline — is symptom rescue, not delirium treatment, and no trial here licenses calling it therapy. title: Hip fracture: how fast to the operating room, and which anaesthetic? The randomized answers are 'no proven difference' — the observational ones carry labels
question: After a hip fracture, does accelerating surgery save lives, does the wait-time literature prove a deadline, does co-management help, and does spinal beat general anaesthesia?
balance: Split this shelf the way its evidence splits. Randomized: HIP ATTACK took 2,970 patients to surgery at a median of 6 hours vs 24 and found 90-day mortality of 9% vs 10% (HR 0.91 — not significant) and a composite of major complications at 22% vs 22% (HR 0.97), with less delirium, fewer urinary tract infections, and less pain on the accelerated side; REGAIN found spinal vs general anaesthesia statistically indistinguishable (18.5% vs 18.0% for death or inability to walk at 60 days), with delirium in about 20% of both arms. Observational, and labeled as such wherever it appears here: waits beyond 24 hours are associated with higher mortality in population data (Pincus: 6.5% vs 5.8% in matched patients), and orthogeriatric co-management is associated with lower mortality across non-randomized studies (Grigoryan) — associations that a sicker, slower-to-theatre patient mix can help manufacture. The honest practice line: fix the fracture promptly, co-manage the patient, choose the anaesthetic on the patient — and do not quote a mortality deadline the randomized trial did not find. Tier C — developer-ruled Nov 7, 2026.

title: Exercise to prevent mobility disability: structured activity delays it — protein alone does not carry the effect
question: In frail, sarcopenic older adults, does a structured exercise-led program prevent mobility disability — and can a protein supplement do the job instead?
balance: Two large trials, one European and one American, converge — and both are re-cards: SPRINTT and LIFE live on Shelf #130, where they are counted; they are re-asked here because this shelf's question adds the decomposition. In SPRINTT's prespecified primary population (SPPB 3–7), mobility disability ran 46.8% vs 52.7% (HR 0.78, a relative effect, with the absolute rates beside it); LIFE found 30.1% vs 35.5% (HR 0.82, relative). The benefit concentrates in people already impaired — SPRINTT's less-impaired stratum was null. Then the null this shelf exists to print: protein without training does not carry the effect. Fiatarone's factorial trial more than doubled strength with resistance training (+113%) while the supplement showed no independent effect on any primary outcome; PROVIDE's leucine-and-vitamin-D whey raised lean mass slightly and improved the chair-stand test, while its primary outcomes — grip strength and SPPB — were null between groups. title: Testosterone in older men: cardiovascularly noninferior in TRAVERSE — with the excesses on the same card, and benefit narrower than the marketing
question: In older men with confirmed hypogonadism, is testosterone replacement safe for the heart, does it fracture bones, and which symptoms does it actually improve?
balance: Split the verdict the way the evidence splits. Safety: TRAVERSE — 5,246 hypogonadal men at high cardiovascular risk — met noninferiority for major adverse cardiac events (7.0% vs 7.3%; HR 0.96), and in 2025 the FDA removed the boxed cardiovascular warning from testosterone labelling. The excesses are printed on the same card, not a different shelf: atrial fibrillation 3.5% vs 2.4%, acute kidney injury 2.3% vs 1.5%, pulmonary embolism 0.9% vs 0.5% — and the trial's own fracture study found MORE fractures on testosterone (3.50% vs 2.46%; HR 1.43) even as bone density improved. TRAVERSE and its fracture study appear as exhibits on Shelf #137 and are re-carded here, counted once at home. Benefit: the T Trials (790 men) improved sexual function and corrected anemia impressively (hemoglobin up at least 1 g/dL in 54% vs 15%), but their walking and vitality primaries were MISSED and cognition was null. Budoff's plaque substudy — more noncalcified coronary plaque growth on testosterone — stands as the caution that noninferiority on events is not the same as innocence. Tier C — developer-ruled Nov 7, 2026.

title: Gabapentinoids for chronic pain: real but modest in nerve pain, split by condition — null in sciatica, and prescribed far beyond the evidence
question: For which pains do pregabalin and gabapentin actually work, how many patients benefit per hundred treated — and what follows them off-label?
balance: This shelf splits because the evidence splits. Postherpetic neuralgia is the strong suit: pregabalin produced at least 50% pain relief in 32% vs 13% on placebo at 300 mg (NNT 5.3) and an NNT of 3.9 at 600 mg (Derry, Cochrane 2019) — real, and still leaving most patients without substantial relief. Diabetic neuropathy is thinner: 31% vs 24% at 300 mg, for an NNT of about 20. Fibromyalgia sits between (NNT roughly 11–12; pregabalin's fibromyalgia detail is cross-pointed to Shelf #391). Gabapentin's own Cochrane numbers are of the same modest family (postherpetic neuralgia NNT 6.7; diabetic neuropathy 5.9). Then the null, printed: in sciatica — one of the commonest reasons these drugs are started — pregabalin did nothing in a properly blinded trial (PRECISE). The harm ledger is carded too: the FDA's December 2019 warning on respiratory depression, the UK's 2019 scheduling of both drugs as controlled drugs, and an estimated 83% of gabapentinoid use that is off-label. title: Opioids versus non-opioids in chronic pain: no advantage on function — and worse symptoms on opioids
question: In chronic back and joint pain, does an opioid strategy beat a non-opioid strategy over a year — and what does the wider trial literature say?
balance: SPACE is the trial this question always needed: 240 VA patients with chronic back pain or hip/knee osteoarthritis pain, randomized to an opioid or a non-opioid medication strategy for 12 months. Pain-related function: 3.4 vs 3.3 (P=0.58) — no advantage. Pain intensity actually favoured the non-opioid arm (4.0 vs 3.5), and medication-related symptoms were twice as burdensome on opioids (1.8 vs 0.9). The standard critique is printed fairly on SPACE's own card: the opioid arm's mean dose was modest, about 21 morphine milligram equivalents a day, so the trial convicts a cautious opioid strategy rather than maximal dosing. Busse's 96-trial meta-analysis converges: opioids beat placebo by 0.69 cm on a 10-cm pain scale — under the 1-cm threshold for clinical importance — and showed no edge over non-opioid alternatives. OPAL extends the null to acute back and neck pain, the gateway prescription. The harm card is explicitly observational, and is labeled as such. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: Arthroscopy for degenerative knee disease: no benefit over sham — and at ten years, more arthritis progression in the operated knee
question: In a degenerative knee — osteoarthritis or a degenerative meniscus tear — does arthroscopic surgery beat sham surgery, therapy, or time?
balance: The sham trials anchor this shelf, and two of them are re-cards from Shelf #188, where they are counted. FIDELITY randomized 146 patients with a degenerative meniscus tear to partial meniscectomy or sham surgery: at 12 months the groups were indistinguishable. Its ten-year follow-up (Kalske, NEJM 2026 — dated 2026, as published) is the uncomfortable coda: radiographic osteoarthritis progression in 81% of the operated knees vs 70% of the sham knees, and knee replacement or osteotomy in 12% vs 4%. METEOR found surgery plus therapy no better than therapy alone — with 30% of the therapy group crossing over to surgery, printed on its card, where it cuts both ways. Moseley's 2002 placebo-surgery trial said it first. Cochrane's 2022 synthesis puts the average pain benefit at 2.4 mm on a 100-mm scale — printed with its scale, because 2.4 mm is what 'trivial' looks like numerically. The carve-outs are printed, not implied: a truly locked knee, traumatic tears in young patients, and meniscal root tears are different questions these trials did not ask. title: Imaging and injections for low back pain: routine imaging does not help, most scans of pain-free backs look 'abnormal', and epidural steroid added nothing to lidocaine
question: For low back pain and spinal stenosis, do routine imaging and epidural steroid injections improve outcomes — or mostly label normal aging as disease?
balance: Three different designs converge on restraint. Randomized trials pooled: imaging people sooner does not make them better (6 trials, 1,804 patients, no significant difference in pain or function at any horizon). Anatomy explains why: in people with NO pain at all, disc degeneration is present in 37% at age 20 and 96% at age 80 — a scan finding is usually a birthday, not a diagnosis. And the injection most often offered for spinal stenosis failed its best test: in the 400-patient LESS trial, adding glucocorticoid to epidural lidocaine improved 6-week disability by −1.0 points on a 24-point scale (P=0.07 — not significant, and below any plausible importance threshold), with adverse events numerically higher on the steroid arm (21.5% vs 15.5% in the trial report). What this shelf does not say: imaging for red flags — cancer, infection, cauda equina, fracture, progressive deficit — remains essential; these trials excluded suspected serious disease. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: Multivitamins and cognition: a small, replicated test-score benefit inside COSMOS — against a 12-year null in PHS II, and no dementia endpoint anywhere
question: Does a daily multivitamin slow cognitive aging in older adults — and has any trial ever tested the outcome people actually fear, dementia?
balance: Hold-boundary finding, printed first because it governed how this shelf was built: Shelves #48–#60 — the developer's dietary-supplements set — are held for new cards until his supplements paper publishes. The gate checked those shelves and the dataset before building: neither COSMOS nor PHS II is carded anywhere in #48–#60 (the word 'multivitamin' appears there only inside Shelf #48's folic-acid trial tablet), so this shelf is the trials' first and only home, and NOTHING was added to the held shelves. The evidence itself splits by trial generation. Inside COSMOS, three non-overlapping cognitive substudies point the same small way: global cognition +0.07 SD (COSMOS-Mind), memory-first benefit (COSMOS-Web), and a pooled +0.07 SD (P=0.0009) the authors equate to about 2 years less cognitive aging. Against that stands PHS II: 5,947 men followed for 12 years, difference −0.01 SD — null. And the fence around everything: NO trial on this shelf has a dementia endpoint; every number here is a test-score difference of 0.07 SD, whose real-world meaning is unproven. title: Hearing aids and cognitive decline: the trial's primary result was NULL — a prespecified higher-risk cohort analysis is the only positive signal
question: In older adults with hearing loss, does treating the hearing loss slow cognitive decline?
balance: The null prints first, because the null is the trial's primary result: in ACHIEVE's full cohort of 977 older adults, hearing intervention vs health-education control changed 3-year cognition by 0.002 SD (P=0.96) — as close to zero as trials get. The positive finding lives one level down, in a prespecified analysis by recruitment cohort: participants who came from the long-running ARIC cardiovascular cohort — older, with more risk factors and lower baseline cognition — declined 48% slower on the intervention (relative figure; absolute difference 0.191 SD, P=0.027), while de novo community volunteers showed no benefit; the interaction was significant (P=0.010). That pattern — help for the higher-risk, nothing for the healthy volunteer — is biologically coherent and prespecified, which earns POSSIBLE for the higher-risk group; it is still one subgroup of one trial, which is why it earns no more. No dementia endpoint; no significant adverse events attributed to either intervention. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: Bisphosphonate drug holidays: after 3–5 years, lower-risk patients lose little by stopping — vertebral fractures are the exception that stratifies the decision
question: After several years on a bisphosphonate, who can safely take a drug holiday — and who should keep taking it?
balance: One-home note: FLEX already lives on Shelf #91, where it is counted; its card here is a labeled re-card, and nothing on this shelf changes #91. The holiday evidence is two extension trials, and both tell the same two-part story. Stopping costs almost nothing on the outcomes patients fear most — in FLEX, nonvertebral fractures were identical after stopping alendronate (RR 1.00) — except at the spine, where continuing protected: clinical vertebral fractures 2.4% continuing vs 5.3% stopped in FLEX, and morphometric vertebral fractures roughly halved by continuing zoledronic acid in the HORIZON extension (14 vs 30 patients, OR ≈0.51, relative). Bone density drifts down off drug (hip −2.4% in FLEX) but stays above pretreatment levels for years — the drug lingers in bone, which is the whole pharmacologic basis of a holiday. The ASBMR rule that closes the shelf is therefore stratified, not universal: reassess after 5 years oral or 3 years IV; holiday for 2–3 years if risk is not high; continue up to 10/6 years if it is. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: Perioperative beta-blockade (POISE): starting metoprolol around surgery prevented heart attacks and caused deaths and strokes — continue chronic therapy, never start it on the day
question: Should a beta-blocker be started around noncardiac surgery to protect the heart — and what does the largest trial say about the trade?
balance: POISE is the cleanest benefit-harm trade in perioperative medicine, and both sides are printed on one card, as the ruling requires: starting extended-release metoprolol in 8,351 patients cut the primary composite (HR 0.84, relative) and myocardial infarction (HR 0.73, relative) — and increased death (HR 1.33, relative) and stroke (HR 2.17, relative). Per 1,000 patients treated: about 15 fewer MIs, bought with about 8 extra deaths and 5 extra strokes. The trials that had made perioperative beta-blockade look safe — the DECREASE family — were discredited for research misconduct and fabricated data; the meta-analysis of only the secure trials (Reference 2) finds starting beta-blockade raises 30-day mortality by 27% in relative terms. The guideline rule that survived (Reference 3): continue a chronic beta-blocker through surgery (Class 1); do not start one on the day of surgery (Class 3, Harm). Tier C — developer-ruled, harm-inclusive. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: POISE-2: perioperative aspirin did not prevent death or MI but caused bleeding; clonidine did not prevent events but caused hypotension and cardiac arrests
question: Around noncardiac surgery, do aspirin or clonidine prevent death and heart attack — the two cheap-drug hopes POISE left standing?
balance: One factorial trial of 10,010 patients answered both questions, and both answers are no-with-harm. Aspirin: primary outcome (death or nonfatal MI) HR 0.99 — a null — while major bleeding rose (HR 1.23, relative; 4.6% vs 3.8%). The eye-catching exception, a prior-PCI subgroup with HR 0.50, is carded as what it is: a hypothesis-grade subgroup finding inside a null trial, not a license. Clonidine: primary HR 1.08 — null leaning harmful — with clinically important hypotension in 47.6% vs 37.1% (HR 1.32, relative) and nonfatal cardiac arrest tripled in relative terms (HR 3.20; 0.3% vs 0.1%). The POISE programme's combined lesson with Shelf #352: around surgery, starting cardiovascular drugs on spec does not protect the heart — it destabilizes the circulation. title: Treating subclinical hypothyroidism: in the older adults actually studied, levothyroxine changed nothing — symptoms, tiredness, quality of life all null

balance: The trials asked the patients' own question — will I feel better? — and answered it with zeros. TRUST (737 patients, age ≥65, mean TSH 6.40): the levothyroxine-vs-placebo difference in hypothyroid symptoms was 0.0 points. The ≥80 trial (251 patients): differences of 1.3 and −0.1 points against a 9-point minimum important difference. Feller's meta-analysis of all 21 randomized trials (2,192 patients): no association with quality of life or thyroid-related symptoms. The BMJ Rapid Recommendation panel issued a strong recommendation against routine treatment. The boundaries are printed on the shelf's face, because the null has edges: TSH ≥10, genuinely symptomatic patients, younger patients, and pregnancy or trying to conceive are OUTSIDE the studied null — the trials enrolled mostly older adults with mild TSH elevations, and this shelf does not extend their answer past their populations. title: Inpatient insulin: basal-bolus beats sliding scale for glucose control — and in surgical patients cut complications, at a fivefold hypoglycemia cost printed on the same card
question: On the wards, should hyperglycemia in type 2 diabetes be managed with scheduled basal-bolus insulin or with sliding-scale insulin alone?
balance: The glucose-control verdict is consistent across three randomized trials: scheduled basal insulin (with bolus or correction doses) controls inpatient glucose better than sliding-scale regular insulin alone, which leaves a stubborn tail of patients above 240 mg/dL. The complications claim rests mainly on one surgical trial — RABBIT 2 Surgery's composite fell from 24.3% to 8.6% — and its price is printed on the same card, as the ruling requires: hypoglycemia below 70 mg/dL in 23.1% vs 4.7%. Severe hypoglycemia (below 40) did not differ significantly in any of the three trials. The ADA's position closes the shelf: sliding-scale insulin alone is strongly discouraged (its inpatient standard carries a Grade A recommendation for scheduled basal or basal-plus regimens in noncritically ill patients), with a glucose target of 140–180 mg/dL for most hospitalized patients. title: Semaglutide and cardiovascular outcomes — the five-trial family: benefit proven for the composite, with the hierarchy breaks and the retinopathy harm kept on the cards

balance: One-home discipline governs this shelf: SUSTAIN-6 is counted on Shelf #71 and SOUL on Shelf #72 — their cards here are labeled re-cards; FLOW's kidney primary is counted on Shelf #75 and appears here only as a pointer to its MACE strand; SELECT and PIONEER-6 are carded here for the first time. In PIONEER-6, superiority was NOT shown (HR 0.79 [0.57–1.11]); its striking death ratios (0.49, 0.51) rest on 15-vs-30 and 23-vs-45 events and are not mortality evidence. In SOUL, the confirmatory kidney secondary was NOT significant. And SUSTAIN-6 carries the family's harm on its face: retinopathy complications HR 1.76. title: What happens when GLP-1 therapy stops: about two-thirds of the weight returns within a year — and no randomized tapering strategy exists
question: When semaglutide or tirzepatide treatment stops, how much of the lost weight comes back — and is there a proven way to taper off?
balance: Three withdrawal datasets, one direction. In the STEP 1 extension, stopping semaglutide (and the lifestyle programme with it) returned 11.6 of the 17.3 percentage points lost — about two-thirds — within one year, and the cardiometabolic improvements reverted toward baseline with it. STEP 4 randomized the question directly: switch to placebo and weight rose 6.9% over 48 weeks while continuers lost a further 7.9% — a 14.8-point gap. SURMOUNT-4 shows the same physics for tirzepatide (labeled as such — a different molecule, carded as the class's withdrawal evidence): switchers regained 14.0% while continuers lost 5.5% more, and only 16.6% of switchers kept at least 80% of their loss versus 89.5% of continuers. Printed plainly, as the shelf requires: NO randomized trial of a tapering strategy exists — no dose-reduction schedule, no drug-holiday design, nothing. Everything known says these are chronic treatments for a chronic condition; the regain figures are the reason 'stop when you reach goal' is not an evidence-based plan. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: Intensive lifestyle intervention in type 2 diabetes (Look AHEAD): the cardiovascular result was NULL — stopped for futility

title: Stress-ulcer prophylaxis in the ICU: fewer bleeds, no mortality benefit — three trials, one pattern
question: In critically ill patients, does stress-ulcer prophylaxis prevent gastrointestinal bleeding — and does preventing it save lives?
balance: Three large trials draw the same two-line picture, and this shelf states both lines on every card. Bleeding: pantoprazole or a PPI strategy reduced clinically important gastrointestinal bleeding in relative terms (SUP-ICU 2.5% vs 4.2%, RR 0.58; REVISE 1.0% vs 3.5%, HR 0.30; PEPTIC, PPI vs H2-blocker, 1.3% vs 1.8%, RR 0.73). Mortality: unmoved everywhere it was measured — SUP-ICU RR 1.02, REVISE HR 0.94 (NS), PEPTIC RR 1.05 leaning the other way. The feared costs of acid suppression (pneumonia, C. difficile) did not materialize in REVISE. So prophylaxis is a bleeding decision for high-risk patients, not a survival intervention; the PEPTIC cardiac-surgery subgroup mortality signal (RR 1.27) is flagged as a subgroup on Card 2, beside the dedicated cardiac-surgery analysis that did not confirm it. title: Smoking cessation before surgery: intensive programmes cut complications — brief advice and late varenicline do not
question: Does helping smokers quit before surgery reduce postoperative complications — and how much intervention does it take?
balance: The dose makes the effect. Intensive programmes — weekly counselling plus nicotine replacement, started 4–8 weeks before surgery — produced the shelf's large numbers: cessation RR 10.76 and complication RR 0.42 in relative terms (Cochrane), complications 18% vs 52% (Møller) and 21% vs 41% (Lindström). Brief interventions raised quitting modestly (RR 1.30, relative) and did not reduce complications (RR 0.92, NS). Varenicline started a week before surgery improved quitting over the following year and did not reduce complications (RR 0.94, NS). Stated on the shelf, as required: the intensive-intervention pool behind the headline relative effects is only ~210 patients in 2 trials — the direction is consistent across every cut; the sizes are upper bounds until a larger trial exists. title: Three versus six months of adjuvant chemotherapy in colon cancer (IDEA): noninferiority NOT confirmed overall — the answer splits by regimen and by risk
question: In stage III colon cancer, can adjuvant chemotherapy stop at 3 months instead of 6 — and for whom?
balance: Stated first, because it is the headline the collaboration itself reported: in 12,834 patients, noninferiority of 3 months was NOT confirmed overall (HR 1.07 against a prespecified 1.12 margin). Inside that null, the split that governs practice: CAPOX 3 months was noninferior (HR 0.95), FOLFOX was not (HR 1.16); low-risk (T1–3N1) disease was noninferior (HR 1.01), high-risk was not (HR 1.12, 6 months superior). The reason the question was worth asking is toxicity: significant neuropathy roughly halves with the shorter course (SCOT: grade ≥2 in 25% vs 58%). With a decade of follow-up, SCOT's final analysis (J Clin Oncol 2026, Card 4) proved noninferiority for overall survival itself — 82.4% in both arms — with the same CAPOX/FOLFOX split. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: First-line immunotherapy in non-small-cell lung cancer: survival proven — with the benefit concentrated where PD-L1 is high
question: In advanced NSCLC without targetable mutations, does first-line immunotherapy prolong survival — and in whom?
balance: Three independent drug families won the same argument: adding a checkpoint inhibitor to first-line chemotherapy (or, at high PD-L1, giving it alone) prolongs survival in metastatic NSCLC — KEYNOTE-189 5-year survival 19.4% vs 11.3% (HR 0.60), KEYNOTE-407 in squamous disease (HR 0.64 at its primary report), KEYNOTE-024 monotherapy at PD-L1 ≥50% (5-year survival 31.9% vs 16.3%), CheckMate 9LA (HR 0.69), IMpower150 (HR 0.78). The survival gaps persisted despite 57–66% crossover from the control arms. The shelf's fence is Card 4: pembrolizumab monotherapy at PD-L1 1–49% produced HR 0.92 and no significant benefit — the class's benefits concentrate at high PD-L1, and below it the chemotherapy combinations carry the evidence. Every hazard ratio on this shelf is a relative measure, stated with its absolute rates. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: PARP inhibitor maintenance in ovarian cancer: the benefit follows the biomarker — BRCA, then HRD, then a survival null
question: In newly diagnosed advanced ovarian cancer, does PARP-inhibitor maintenance after platinum chemotherapy help — and in whom?
balance: The gradient is this shelf's point, and every card is placed on it. Top: BRCA-mutated disease, where olaparib produced the class's largest effects — PFS HR 0.30 and, at 7 years, 67.0% vs 46.5% alive (SOLO-1). Middle: HRD-positive disease, where niraparib's PFS HR was 0.43 and olaparib-plus-bevacizumab's survival HR 0.62 (PRIMA; PAOLA-1). Bottom: HRD-negative disease, where the PFS effect shrinks (HR 0.68) and no survival benefit has been shown — graded POSSIBLE/disfavored inside this shelf. Stated where it belongs, on Card 2: PRIMA's final overall survival was HR 1.01 — null , and the FDA restricted niraparib's first-line indication to HRD-positive tumors. PAOLA-1's overall survival was likewise null overall (HR 0.92, NS) — the survival claims on this shelf live inside the biomarker strata, labeled as such. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: CDK4/6 inhibitors in early breast cancer: abemaciclib and ribociclib work — palbociclib failed twice; an agent effect, not a class effect
question: In HR-positive, HER2-negative early breast cancer, does adding a CDK4/6 inhibitor to adjuvant endocrine therapy prevent recurrence?
balance: Four large trials, two answers, split cleanly by drug. Abemaciclib (monarchE, high-risk node-positive disease): 5-year iDFS HR 0.68, with the absolute benefit still deepening after treatment ends — and its harms on the same card (VTE 2.5% vs 0.6%). Ribociclib (NATALEE, broader stage II–III disease): iDFS HR 0.75 at 3 years, 0.72 at 4 years. In both positive trials overall survival remains immature and is stated as such. The fence, carded with equal weight: palbociclib failed twice — PALLAS (final HR 0.96) and PENELOPE-B (HR 0.93), the second in the highest-risk residual-disease population. Nothing on this shelf licenses 'CDK4/6 inhibitors prevent recurrence' as a class sentence; the evidence names two drugs, two regimens, and two populations. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: DOACs for cancer-associated VTE: the class is split by agent — apixaban without a bleeding excess, edoxaban and rivaroxaban with a gastrointestinal one
question: In cancer-associated venous thromboembolism, can a direct oral anticoagulant replace daily dalteparin injections — and which agent?
balance: All three trials beat or matched dalteparin on recurrence, and the shelf's split is the bleeding column. Apixaban (CARAVAGGIO): recurrence HR 0.63 — noninferior, and stated as NOT superior (P=0.09) — with major bleeding HR 0.82 and no gastrointestinal excess (1.9% vs 1.7%). Edoxaban (Hokusai-VTE Cancer): composite HR 0.97, a figure that pools fewer recurrences with more major bleeds (HR 1.77, GI-driven). Rivaroxaban (SELECT-D): recurrence HR 0.43, clinically relevant non-major bleeding 13% vs 4%, and a mid-trial protocol amendment excluding esophageal cancers, noted on its card. Stated across the shelf: no trial showed a mortality difference. All three cards are re-cards of trials whose home is Shelf #156; they are counted once, there. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: Early palliative care in advanced cancer: better quality of life, mood, and satisfaction — survival POSSIBLE, never proven
question: In advanced cancer, does introducing palliative care early — alongside oncology care — improve quality of life, mood, and end-of-life care?
balance: The honest summary of this literature is outcome-by-outcome. Quality of life, mood, and satisfaction: LIKELY better — Temel's trial improved quality of life and halved depressive symptoms (16% vs 38%), and Zimmermann's improved satisfaction with care, though Zimmermann missed its primary quality-of-life endpoint (P=0.07) and ENABLE III's patient-reported outcomes were null, both stated on their cards. Survival: POSSIBLE — Temel (11.6 vs 8.9 months) and ENABLE III (1-year survival 63% vs 48%) both found survival differences, and in both trials survival was a secondary outcome ; the label travels with the number everywhere on this shelf. Less aggressive end-of-life care: POSSIBLE (Temel 33% vs 54%; ENABLE III's resource use was null). And the boundary: RESPECT-Meso found no benefit of routine early referral in mesothelioma centers with good on-demand access — a null carded at full weight. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: Transfusion thresholds in acute myocardial infarction: the one place the restrictive rule may not travel
question: In acute myocardial infarction with anemia, is transfusing at a hemoglobin of 7–8 g/dL as safe as transfusing at 10?
balance: This shelf is deliberately narrow. The general restrictive-threshold evidence — ICU, septic shock, hip fracture, cardiac surgery, GI bleeding — lives on Shelf #124 and Shelf #240 and is pointed to here, not re-carded; outside acute MI, restriction remains LIKELY fine and uses half the blood. Inside acute MI the two trials lean opposite ways and both are inconclusive: REALITY (668 patients) met noninferiority for restriction while conceding its interval included important harm (MACE 11.0% vs 14.0%; death 5.6% vs 7.7%), and MINT (3,504 patients; Card 2, re-carded from its home on Shelf #124) found MI or death in 16.9% on restriction vs 14.5% on liberal transfusion (RR 1.15, P=0.07), with death 9.9% vs 8.3% — every component leaning liberal, none significant. The stamp follows that shape exactly: harm of restriction in acute MI is POSSIBLE, benefit of liberality is POSSIBLE, and certainty either way would be a fabrication. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: Intravenous iron for iron-deficiency anemia in non-dialysis CKD: faster repletion and fewer escalations — no event benefit shown
question: In non-dialysis chronic kidney disease with iron-deficiency anemia, does intravenous iron beat oral iron on anything beyond the blood count?
balance: The honest claim for IV iron before dialysis is narrow, and this shelf states it narrowly: ferritin-targeted IV ferric carboxymaltose repletes faster and delays the day a patient needs an ESA, other iron, or a transfusion (FIND-CKD, Card 1 — re-carded from its home on Shelf #294 , the kidney-iron dose-and-target shelf) — a treatment-trigger endpoint, not an event endpoint. No trial here shows a mortality or cardiovascular benefit , and the one trial that asked a harder question, REVOKE (Reference 2), found no difference in kidney-function decline and was stopped early over more serious cardiovascular and infectious events on IV iron. The heart-failure iron literature is a different population and lives on Shelf #122 — linked, not merged. POSSIBLE is the stamp because the repletion claim is real but the outcome claims are absent and the safety record is mixed. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: G-CSF primary prophylaxis in chemotherapy: febrile neutropenia roughly halved, early deaths fewer — inside the ≥20% risk fence
question: Does giving granulocyte colony-stimulating factor from the first chemotherapy cycle prevent febrile neutropenia and early death?
balance: Two independent meta-analyses agree: primary G-CSF prophylaxis roughly halves febrile neutropenia in relative terms (RR 0.54, Kuderer; RR 0.51, Cooper), and Kuderer's adds the outcome that earns this shelf its Tier C stamp — fewer infection-related deaths (RR 0.55, relative) and fewer early all-cause deaths during chemotherapy (RR 0.60, relative), printed beside the one absolute harm the source states, bone pain in 19.6% vs 10.4%. The fence prints on the shelf's face: primary prophylaxis is standard when a regimen's febrile-neutropenia risk is ≥20%; this shelf makes no claim below that threshold , where baseline risk is too low for a halving to buy much. Nor does the shelf claim any cancer-survival benefit — Kuderer states the data were insufficient for disease-free or overall survival. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: How long should androgen deprivation run with radiation for prostate cancer? Six months is too short; 18 may be enough for some; high risk earns the long course
question: With radiotherapy for localized prostate cancer, how much androgen deprivation is enough — and for whom?
balance: The gradient is the shelf. At the bottom, short courses fail where disease is locally advanced or high-risk: 6 months was inferior to 3 years (EORTC 22961 — 5-year mortality 19.0% vs 15.2%, prostate-cancer deaths 47 vs 29), and 4 months was inferior to 28 months with high-dose radiation (DART 01/05 — 5-year survival 86% vs 95%, the benefit concentrated in high-risk disease). At the top, the returns flatten: PCS IV found 36 months not superior to 18 in high-risk men (deaths 147 vs 143; quality of life clearly better at 18) — carded with its logic intact, as a failed superiority test rather than a proven equivalence. So the risk-stratified reading: high-risk disease earns a long course (roughly 18–36 months; 4–6 months is undertreatment), and for selected men 18 months is a defensible stop. This is the library's prostate ADT shelf; later urology topics are checked against it before they are proposed. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: Anti-VEGF for wet (neovascular) age-related macular degeneration: two drugs, equal vision — one safety signal left deliberately UNRESOLVED
question: For wet AMD, which anti-VEGF drug, on which schedule — and what should be made of the cheaper drug's serious-event excess?
balance: On vision, the question is settled twice over: bevacizumab and ranibizumab gain patients the same letters at 1 and 2 years (CATT, Cards 1–2), with IVAN (Reference 3) formally inconclusive on strict noninferiority but pointing the same way; monthly treatment protects a couple of letters that as-needed drift surrenders. On safety, this shelf follows the developer's ruling and prints the CATT finding as UNRESOLVED : serious systemic adverse events ran 24.1% vs 19.0% at year 1 and 39.9% vs 31.7% at year 2 on bevacizumab vs ranibizumab, while death, MI, stroke, and arteriothrombotic events never differed — an excess without a pattern, neither dismissed nor convicted. The diabetic macular edema comparison of the same drug family (DRCR Protocol T) has its home on Shelf #373 and is cross-linked, not duplicated, here. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: Treatment protocols for diabetic macular edema: the drug matters only when vision is already poor — and sometimes the right protocol is to wait
question: In center-involved diabetic macular edema, which anti-VEGF drug, when should laser join, and when is observation the treatment?
balance: Four protocols, four different answers, all carded at full weight. Drug choice (Protocol T, Cards 1–2 — this shelf is Protocol T's home; Shelf #372 cross-links here): all three anti-VEGF drugs work, aflibercept's advantage is real only in eyes starting 20/50 or worse, and by 2 years it had narrowed to the bevacizumab comparison alone. Laser timing (Protocol I, Card 3): deferring laser at least 24 weeks behind ranibizumab cost no vision versus prompt laser. Threshold to treat (Protocol V, Card 4): at 20/25 or better, monitored observation with rescue treatment matched immediate injections. And the burden is carded as a cost on Card 2, not footnoted: some fifteen injections over two years in Protocol T — the visit-and-needle load is part of every protocol's real effect size. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: Dupilumab for atopic dermatitis: clear or almost-clear skin for about a third of patients — sustained for a year, with conjunctivitis as the signature price
question: In moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis that topical treatment cannot control, does dupilumab clear the skin — and does the effect last?
balance: The evidence is three large placebo-controlled trials pointing one way: two 16-week monotherapy trials (SOLO 1 and 2, Card 1) put clear-or-almost-clear skin at 36–38% on dupilumab vs 8–10% on placebo, with weekly dosing adding nothing over every-other-week — and the 1-year CHRONOS trial (Reference 2) shows the benefit holding alongside topical steroids (EASI-75 64–69% vs 23%), with no accumulation of serious harm. The price is consistent and specific: injection-site reactions and conjunctivitis , the IL-4/IL-13 class's signature adverse effect, more frequent on dupilumab in every trial here. What the shelf does not claim: comparative standing against the newer oral and biologic rivals — those trials are not on this shelf, and no head-to-head claim is made. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: Biologics for chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps: a gradient — dupilumab largest, omalizumab real — as adjuncts for severe disease
question: In severe chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps that steroids and surgery have not controlled, do biologics shrink polyps and restore quality of life?
balance: Both biologics beat placebo in severe, refractory CRSwNP, and the shelf is organized by the size of what they did: dupilumab's polyp-score effect (about −2 points vs placebo at 24 weeks, with congestion and CT opacification moving in parallel, Card 1) is the largest; omalizumab's (about −1 point, with SNOT-22 gains of 15+ points over placebo, Card 2) is roughly half — a gradient read across separate placebo-controlled programmes, not a head-to-head trial, and labeled that way. The fence is the trials' entry gate: these are adjuncts for severe disease in patients already failing intranasal steroids, many post-surgery or steroid-dependent — surgery-sparing is a hope the trials gesture at through reduced need, not an outcome either programme proved as a primary claim, and this shelf cards it no more strongly than the trials state it. Asthma comorbidity runs through both populations (SINUS stratified by it) — for the many patients carrying both diseases, one drug treating two is part of the real-world calculus. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: Peanut oral immunotherapy: desensitization is LIKELY — net benefit only POSSIBLE, because the treatment itself causes the reactions it guards against
question: Does peanut oral immunotherapy protect children with peanut allergy — and what does the protection cost?
balance: This is the shelf Shelf #1's prevention index points to ('Food allergy — preventing reactions'), and its split stamp is the honest summary of a genuinely two-sided literature. Desensitization is LIKELY and large: two-thirds of 4–17-year-olds tolerated a 600 mg challenge after AR101 vs 4% on placebo (PALISADE, Card 1), and starting at age 1–3 produced desensitization in 71% and — uniquely — remission after avoidance in 21% (IMPACT, Card 2). Net benefit is only POSSIBLE, because the harm side is at full weight on Card 3: across 12 trials, OIT increased anaphylaxis (RR 3.12, relative; +15.1 points absolute) and epinephrine use, and did not improve quality of life. The therapy trades accidental-exposure risk for scheduled, treatment-caused reactions; whether that trade serves a given child depends on their exposure risk, reaction history, and family — which is why the stamp refuses to collapse the two halves into one word. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: Biologics for plaque psoriasis: the IL-23 and IL-17 classes clear skin the TNF era could not — PASI-90 is the new normal
question: For moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis, how completely do modern biologics clear skin — and what does each class cost in safety?
balance: A class-efficacy shelf, read against the adalimumab-era baseline: where TNF blockade cleared 90% of skin (PASI-90) in about half of patients, the IL-23 inhibitors put that figure at 73–75% at week 16 (guselkumab, Card 2; risankizumab, Card 1 — the latter also beating ustekinumab head-to-head), and dual IL-17A/F blockade with bimekizumab reached 85% (Reference 3). Safety is carded per class rather than averaged: screening for tuberculosis and hepatitis B precedes starting any of these immunosuppressants ; candidiasis is the IL-17 class's signature infection (Reference 3); and IL-17 agents carry an inflammatory-bowel-disease caution the IL-23 class does not share. Trial adverse-event rates were otherwise comparable to placebo or active comparators throughout. No mortality claims are made anywhere on this shelf — these are skin-clearance trials, and the stamp grades exactly that. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: Sudden sensorineural hearing loss: steroids are the standard treatment — the placebo evidence is thin, the route is settled, salvage is a maybe
question: A patient loses hearing in one ear overnight. Do steroids restore it — by mouth, by injection through the eardrum, or as salvage after the first treatment fails?
balance: Card the uncertainty honestly, because this shelf's foundation is unusually weak for such a universal practice: Cochrane (Reference 1) found three small placebo-controlled trials, all at high risk of bias, two of them null — so whether primary systemic steroids beat natural history at all is genuinely unsettled, and spontaneous recovery (32% of controls improved in the one positive trial) inflates every uncontrolled series. What is solid is the route comparison: Rauch's 250-patient noninferiority trial (Reference 2) showed intratympanic methylprednisolone recovering hearing within 2 dB of oral prednisone, inside its 10 dB margin — choose the route by the patient's systemic-steroid risks, not by expected hearing. For ears that fail systemic therapy, salvage intratympanic steroids (Reference 3) point the right way in 11 studies with no serious harms, at moderate-to-very-low certainty. The stamps follow that shape exactly: POSSIBLE that steroids work, LIKELY that the routes are equivalent, POSSIBLE for salvage. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: Allergen immunotherapy for allergic rhinitis: symptoms LIKELY controlled, the effect LIKELY outlasts treatment — asthma prevention only POSSIBLE, because GAP missed its primary
question: Does allergen immunotherapy — the SLIT tablet taken daily for years — actually change allergic disease, and can it stop hay fever from becoming asthma?
balance: Immunotherapy is the only hay-fever treatment whose benefit survives stopping it: three years of the grass SLIT tablet left symptom scores ~26% and medication scores ~29% relatively lower a full year after the last dose (Reference 1), an effect antihistamines and nasal steroids have never shown — LIKELY on both symptom control and sustained effect. The prevention claim is where discipline matters. GAP (Reference 2) randomized 812 asthmatic-free children for exactly this question and missed its primary endpoint : time to objectively defined asthma did not differ; only asthma symptoms and medication use favored treatment. That earns POSSIBLE, printed behind the null. Virchow (Reference 3) belongs to a different claim — treating established house-dust-mite asthma, where the tablet delayed exacerbations during steroid withdrawal (HR 0.69 relative; ~10-point absolute difference). Three claims, three grades, no borrowing between them. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: Topical ruxolitinib for vitiligo: the first drug that repigments — partially, slowly, and honestly short of a cure
question: Vitiligo had no approved repigmenting drug. Does the JAK-inhibitor cream change that?
balance: Two replicate phase 3 trials, one direction, one magnitude: about 30% of patients reached 75% facial repigmentation at 24 weeks against 7–11% on vehicle, with responses still deepening at a year and a harm profile of application-site acne and itch rather than systemic toxicity. That is a real first — vitiligo's first approved pharmacotherapy — and this shelf prints its limits in the same type size: most patients do not reach the endpoint, repigmentation is measured in months, the evidence covers limited (≤10% body-surface) nonsegmental disease with the face as the readout, and nothing here speaks to what happens after the cream stops. LIKELY for repigmentation as trialed; no cure is claimed anywhere on this shelf. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: Adalimumab for hidradenitis suppurativa: weekly dosing beats placebo in two phase 3 trials — response, not remission, and tunnels still belong to surgery
question: For moderate-to-severe hidradenitis suppurativa, does TNF blockade with adalimumab actually reduce lesions?
balance: Two replicate phase 3 trials agree that weekly adalimumab roughly doubles the 12-week HiSCR rate over a substantial placebo response — an absolute gain of about 16 points in PIONEER I and 31 points in PIONEER II — with serious adverse events no more frequent than on placebo. The shelf's honesty is in its definitions: a response is ≥50% fewer abscesses and nodules without new abscesses or draining fistulas, which leaves established tunnels and scarring untouched; those remain surgical disease. Approved-dose nuance worth printing: the trialed regimen is 40 mg weekly — the every-other-week schedule familiar from psoriasis is not what won here. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: Febuxostat cardiovascular safety: MACE noninferior in two big trials — CARES found more deaths, FAST found none, and the discordance is the finding
question: In gout, is febuxostat as cardiovascularly safe as allopurinol — and does the answer change when the patient already has cardiovascular disease?
balance: Two large trials agree on the composite and disagree on death. CARES (Reference 1), in gout with established cardiovascular disease, met MACE noninferiority (HR 1.03) while all-cause mortality ran HR 1.22 and cardiovascular death HR 1.34 against febuxostat — the result behind the FDA's 2019 boxed warning. FAST (Reference 2), in an older but lower-risk European population, found the primary endpoint at HR 0.85 and fewer deaths on febuxostat (7.2% vs 8.6%). This shelf does not average them into reassurance: populations differed exactly on the variable the mortality claim is about. Noninferiority for cardiovascular events: LIKELY. A mortality excess in patients with established cardiovascular disease: POSSIBLE — unrefuted by a trial that largely did not enroll them. Urate-lowering efficacy is not what this shelf grades; febuxostat's kidney claims live on Shelf #168 . Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: Treat-to-target in rheumatoid arthritis: the strategy is the treatment — measure on schedule, escalate to a target, and the drugs you already have work better
question: In rheumatoid arthritis, does managing to a measured disease-activity target — rather than treating by impression — improve outcomes, whichever drugs are used?
balance: Four strategy trials, one shared ingredient — a number, a schedule, and a rule that the number triggers action. TICORA (Reference 1) tripled-to-quadrupled remission over routine care (65% vs 16%); CAMERA (Reference 2) won with the same single drug in both arms, differing only in visit cadence and a computer enforcing the target; CAMERA-II (Reference 3) showed a defined steroid dose inside the strategy adds structural protection; BeSt (Reference 4) showed four different strategies converging clinically once all were aimed at the same target. The claim stamped LIKELY is the strategy itself — measured, protocolized escalation to a disease-activity target — and this shelf deliberately credits no molecule: the drug shelves are graded elsewhere, on their own trials. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: Tofacitinib safety after ORAL Surveillance: cancers LIKELY increased in older, cardiovascular-risk patients — MACE POSSIBLE, noninferiority missed for both
question: In older patients with rheumatoid arthritis and cardiovascular risk, is tofacitinib as safe as a TNF inhibitor for heart events and cancer?
balance: One large, purpose-built safety trial drives this shelf, and its two endpoints earn different grades. Malignancies excluding nonmelanoma skin cancer: HR 1.48 with an interval [1.04–2.09] that excludes no-effect, on absolute rates of 4.2% vs 2.9% over a median 4 years — LIKELY, in patients who look like ORAL's: 50 or older, cardiovascular-risk-bearing, methotrexate-experienced RA. MACE: HR 1.33 [0.91–1.94] — the point estimate leans against tofacitinib and noninferiority was missed, but the interval includes benefit, so increased cardiovascular events are POSSIBLE, not established. Both stamps are fenced to the studied population; the trial says nothing direct about younger, low-risk patients, and neither does this shelf. The class-wide boxed warnings that followed are regulatory prudence built on this single trial's shape — the shelf reports the trial, and grades only what the trial showed. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: Tocilizumab for giant cell arteritis: sustained remission quadrupled while the prednisone burden halved
question: Giant cell arteritis relapses as prednisone tapers, and prednisone itself maims. Does IL-6 blockade hold remission while the steroid falls away?
balance: GiACTA is the rare trial that wins on both axes of its disease: sustained glucocorticoid-free remission at one year in 56% vs 14% against the like-for-like taper, and a cumulative prednisone exposure cut from ~3,300 mg to ~1,860 mg — efficacy and steroid-sparing in the same result, with serious adverse events running lower on the drug than on placebo-plus-steroid. The fences are printed on the card: a one-year horizon, remission judged while IL-6 blockade suppresses the CRP clinicians usually watch, and no mortality claim of any kind. Within them, this is among the cleanest biologic verdicts in rheumatology. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: Rituximab for ANCA-associated vasculitis: cyclophosphamide's equal for induction, clearly better than azathioprine for maintenance
question: Can rituximab replace cyclophosphamide to induce remission in ANCA-associated vasculitis — and what holds the remission afterward?
balance: The induction claim rests on RAVE (Reference 1): noninferior remission at 6 months (64% vs 53%), superior in relapsing disease, with no early adverse-event separation — equal efficacy, with cyclophosphamide's cumulative toxicities avoided by substitution rather than measured head-to-head. RITUXVAS (Reference 2) sets the boundary in severe renal disease: a rituximab-based combination matched intravenous cyclophosphamide (76% vs 82% sustained remission; 18% mortality in both arms in a very sick cohort) without proving superiority. Maintenance is the decisive card: MAINRITSAN (Card 3, labeled annex) cut major relapse to 5% vs 29% against azathioprine at matched severe-event rates. Serious infection ran similar across arms wherever the records report it — the expectation that rituximab would prove dramatically gentler in the short run is not what these trials show, and this shelf does not claim it. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: Belimumab for lupus: a modest, twice-replicated responder gain in SLE — and a real renal gain in lupus nephritis
question: Does blocking B-lymphocyte stimulator with belimumab help systemic lupus — in the joints-and-rash disease, and in the kidney disease that decides its prognosis?
balance: Belimumab's case is accumulation, not drama: BLISS-52 (Reference 1) gained 14 SRI points over placebo, BLISS-76 (Reference 2) gained 10 and attenuated by week 76 — both printed at full size — and BLISS-LN (Reference 3) moved the outcome that matters most in lupus, renal response (43% vs 32%) with renal events or death at HR 0.51 relative. Safety across the program ran close to placebo for serious infection, with no malignancy signal in the trials; the monitored neuropsychiatric caution from labeling is stated on Card 1 and belongs in prescribing, not hidden from it. Modest absolute gains, consistently in one direction, across two organ systems: LIKELY. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: Anifrolumab for lupus: one phase 3 trial missed its primary, the other hit a different one — POSSIBLE
question: Does blocking the type I interferon receptor with anifrolumab reduce lupus activity — and why do its two phase 3 trials disagree?
balance: This shelf exists to teach discordance. TULIP-1 (Reference 1) prespecified SRI-4 and missed it outright — 36% vs 40% on placebo. TULIP-2 (Reference 2) prespecified BICLA instead, the endpoint that had leaned positive inside TULIP-1, and hit it cleanly: 47.8% vs 31.5%. Both facts are on the shelf at full size, in that order. The drug plausibly works — interferon biology, a consistent BICLA direction across both trials, steroid-sparing secondaries — but a library that demands two concordant trials cannot stamp LIKELY on a split pair, and the zoster cost (7.2%) plus a pneumonia death on the winning card argue against generosity. POSSIBLE: a real option for active SLE despite standard care, prescribed with the disagreement disclosed. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: Treating the acute gout flare: low-dose colchicine is the dose, steroids equal NSAIDs — and the practice points matter as much as the drugs
question: A joint is hot, red, and exquisitely painful at 2 a.m. Which treatment relieves an acute gout flare, at what dose, and what should not be done?
balance: Three interchangeable first moves, each with its trial: low-dose colchicine 1.8 mg early in the flare (Card 1 — equal to high-dose, placebo-like harms; the high-dose ritual survives only as this shelf's cautionary tale); an NSAID or a 5-day oral prednisolone course, proven equivalent head-to-head (Reference 2), chosen by the patient's kidneys, stomach, and anticoagulation rather than by efficacy. Canakinumab (Reference 3) wins on pain in patients who have failed or cannot take those — and stays fenced there by its phase II evidence, its immunosuppression, and its cost. Printed practice points: treat as early in the flare as possible — AGREE's window was the first 36 hours — and do not stop allopurinol during a flare : a flare is treated on top of urate lowering, never by interrupting it. Long-term flare prevention is a urate question, graded on Shelf #168 and Shelf #382 . Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: Fibromyalgia treatment: the drugs help about one patient in ten — exercise is the better bet, and neither is strong
question: Pain everywhere, exhaustion, no lesion to fix. What actually helps fibromyalgia — the licensed drugs, the old tricyclic, or exercise?
balance: Three Cochrane drug reviews agree on the shape: duloxetine, milnacipran, and pregabalin each give substantial pain relief to roughly one patient in ten beyond placebo (References 1–2) — a real effect, honestly small, with most patients getting nothing but the side effects. Amitriptyline, the oldest prescription in this clinic, has no first- or second-tier evidence at all; its reputation rests on small old trials (Reference 2). Exercise (Reference 3) buys a similar-sized benefit with low-certainty evidence and almost no harm, which is why it grades a step higher here. Nothing on this shelf modifies the disease, and nothing claims a mortality effect — fibromyalgia does not kill; it grinds. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: Milk oral immunotherapy: most children can be desensitized — remission is fragile, reactions are part of the treatment, and nature resolves many cases anyway
question: A child is allergic to cow's milk. Does feeding tiny, rising doses of milk under supervision free them — or just trade avoidance for a treatment that itself causes reactions?
balance: Milk OIT desensitizes: about six in ten treated children in the early trials could drink a full serving of milk, against fewer than one in ten controls (Reference 1) — graded POSSIBLE as a single grade. Three cautions ride on the same shelf. The protection is rented, not owned: two to eight weeks after stopping a successful course, only about a third of patients in the World Allergy Organization's synthesis still tolerated milk (Reference 2). The treatment causes the disease's own events — anaphylaxis and epinephrine use are far more frequent on OIT than on avoidance (Reference 2). And the comparison is never against nothing: in a large referral cohort, milk allergy resolved on its own in 19% of children by age 4 and 79% by age 16 (Reference 3), so some of every OIT cohort's 'successes' were going to happen anyway. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: Egg oral immunotherapy: desensitization is LIKELY — sustained unresponsiveness after stopping is only POSSIBLE, and the gap between the two is the shelf
question: Egg is in everything. Can oral immunotherapy free a child with egg allergy — and does the freedom survive stopping the treatment?
balance: The NEJM trial (Reference 1) draws the line this shelf is built on: after 22 months of egg OIT, 75% of children passed a 10 g egg-white challenge while on therapy — but after 4–6 weeks off it, only 28% still passed. Desensitization is common; remission is the minority outcome. Longer treatment buys more remission: by year 4 of the same program (Reference 2), 50% had achieved sustained unresponsiveness, and those who had were eating egg freely years later. The reactions along the way were mostly oral and gastrointestinal, with mild symptoms in over half of children still dosing in years 3–4. Quote the two numbers together — 75% and 28% — or do not quote either. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: Early introduction of allergenic foods: in high-risk infants, feeding peanut early prevents the allergy — for the general population the proof is thinner
question: For decades the advice was delay. Do the randomized trials say feeding allergenic foods early — peanut, egg — prevents food allergy instead?
balance: LEAP (Reference 1) is the strongest prevention result in this library's allergy wing: in infants with severe eczema or egg allergy, eating peanut from infancy cut peanut allergy at age 5 from 13.7% to 1.9% in the skin-test-negative stratum — and the protection persisted through a full year of complete avoidance (Reference 2). EAT (Reference 3) asked the general-population question and its intention-to-treat answer was null; early introduction worked only in the families who actually managed it, which in an unselected population was the minority. PETIT (Reference 4) extends the principle to heated egg in infants with eczema, at the price of more hospital admissions in the egg group. Prevention is the correct word on this shelf: these trials prevented allergy from developing; they treated nothing. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: Omalizumab for multiple food allergies: one pivotal trial raises the reaction threshold while dosing continues — it is not tolerance
question: For a patient allergic to peanut and at least two other foods, can an anti-IgE antibody — with no allergen ingestion at all — raise the dose it takes to trigger a reaction?
balance: One trial carries this shelf, and the shelf says so: OUtMATCH stage 1 (Reference 1) randomized 180 patients and showed that 16–20 weeks of omalizumab let 67% tolerate a 600 mg peanut challenge vs 7% on placebo, with concordant threshold-raising for cashew, milk, and egg. On that basis the FDA approved omalizumab for food allergy in February 2024. The fences are printed in the same size of type: the drug raises the reaction threshold only while dosing continues — it induces neither tolerance nor remission — and avoidance plus epinephrine carriage continue unchanged. What happens over years of dosing, or after stopping, this trial does not say. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: Dupilumab for eosinophilic esophagitis: weekly injections put about 60% into histologic remission vs about 5%
question: The esophagus is inflamed and narrowing, and swallowing is failing. Does blocking IL-4/IL-13 signaling with dupilumab clear the eosinophils and the dysphagia?
balance: LIBERTY EoE TREET (Reference 1) is a two-part phase 3 program with one consistent answer: weekly dupilumab 300 mg produced histologic remission (≤6 eosinophils per high-power field) in about 60% of patients vs about 5% on placebo, and — at the weekly dose — significantly improved dysphagia symptom scores in both parts. The dosing lesson is inside the same trial: every-2-week dosing matched the histology but did not significantly improve symptoms, which is why the approved EoE regimen is weekly. Serious adverse events were uncommon and split across the arms; the injection burden is weekly and indefinite. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: Venom immunotherapy: systemic reactions to a later sting fall from about 40% to about 3% — but preventing deaths has never been proven
question: After a systemic reaction to a bee or wasp sting, does a course of venom injections protect against the next sting — and what, exactly, has been proven?
balance: The efficacy core is old and small and consistent: in the 1978 controlled trial (Reference 1), sting challenge provoked systemic reactions in 1 of 18 venom-treated patients vs 7 of 12 on placebo — and the Cochrane pool (Reference 2) puts later systemic reactions at 2.7% on VIT vs 39.8% untreated. The fence is stated in Cochrane's own words: whether VIT prevents fatal reactions cannot be confirmed, because fatal stings are too rare for any trial to have counted them; the protection claim is about systemic reactions, full stop. Treatment itself carries risk (systemic reactions to the injections in ~9–14%), and the course runs 3–5 years; guidelines extend it indefinitely for mastocytosis or near-fatal index reactions — that extension is guideline-based, not trial-proven, and is labeled as such here. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.
