title: Omalizumab for chronic spontaneous urticaria: complete response (UAS7 = 0) in roughly a third vs under a tenth on placebo
question: Hives on most days for months, unmoved by antihistamines. Does the anti-IgE antibody omalizumab switch them off?
balance: Three phase 3 trials in antihistamine-refractory patients agree: monthly omalizumab 300 mg roughly quadruples complete response (UAS7 = 0: 35.8% vs 8.8% in ASTERIA I, Card 2), cuts itch scores by about twice the placebo change (Cards 1 and 3), and works even in patients already failing combination therapy (GLACIAL, Card 3). The population fence matters — everyone here had failed H1 antihistamines, many at up to four times the licensed dose; this is not first-line evidence. Omalizumab carries a boxed warning for anaphylaxis (the label puts its frequency at roughly 0.1–0.2% of patients); serious adverse events in these trials were uncommon and close to placebo. Symptoms return when treatment stops — this is control, not cure. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: Aspirin desensitization in AERD: symptoms and quality of life improve in small trials — at a real cost in gastritis, bleeding, and a 63% real-world dropout
question: Asthma, nasal polyps, and respiratory reactions to every NSAID. Does desensitizing to aspirin — then taking it daily, indefinitely — control the disease?
balance: The evidence shape is stated plainly because it decides the grade: five small randomized trials (233 patients in total), pooled in 2019 (Reference 1), show better sinonasal symptoms and quality of life on desensitization plus daily aspirin, with moderate-to-high certainty on those symptom outcomes — and significantly more treatment-stopping adverse events, including major bleeding and gastritis. The surgery literature (Reference 2) finds lower revision rates in patients maintained on aspirin after sinus surgery, but it is a review of uncontrolled series. And real-world follow-up (Reference 3) supplies the cold water: 63% of patients quit the daily aspirin, and those treated had no fewer revision surgeries than controls. No large trial with hard endpoints exists. That is a POSSIBLE shelf: a real option for a miserable disease, sold with its dropout rate attached. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: Prophylaxis for hereditary angioedema: targeted drugs cut attacks by half to nearly nine-tenths
question: Swelling attacks that can close an airway, several times a month. Can long-term prophylaxis — kallikrein blockade or C1-inhibitor replacement — prevent them?
balance: Three phase 3 programs, three attacks on the same pathway, one direction. Lanadelumab (Reference 1) cut attacks from 1.97 to 0.26 per month at the every-2-week dose — an 87% relative reduction with the absolute rates beside it. Oral berotralstat (Reference 2) achieved a smaller but real reduction (1.31 vs 2.35 per month) as a once-daily pill. Subcutaneous C1 inhibitor (Reference 3) reduced attacks by 2.4–3.5 per month against placebo in a crossover design, with ~90% responders at the higher dose. None of these trials was powered on laryngeal attacks or death — the endpoints are attack counts, and no mortality claim is made on this shelf. The access line is printed once, plainly: these are orphan drugs at orphan prices, and cost decides who receives them in most of the world. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: House-dust-mite SLIT tablets: rhinitis improves modestly — asthma exacerbations fall in established disease — asthma prevention has not been shown
question: A daily tablet of house-dust-mite allergen dissolved under the tongue. What does it do for rhinitis — and what, separately, does it do for asthma?
balance: The rhinitis claim rests on a 992-patient phase III trial (Reference 1): the combined symptom-and-medication score fell by ~1.2 points more than on placebo over a year of daily tablets — statistically solid, clinically modest, and the reason this grades LIKELY rather than enthusiastically. The asthma claim is a treatment claim, re-carded from its home on Shelf #379 (Reference 2): in established house-dust-mite asthma, the tablet delayed exacerbations during steroid withdrawal (HR 0.69, relative; ~10-point absolute difference). The fence is printed in the shelf's title and meant: asthma prevention has not been shown for this tablet — the grass-tablet prevention trial on Shelf #379 missed its primary endpoint — and the FDA indication for the HDM tablet is rhinitis, not asthma. title: Methadone vs buprenorphine for opioid use disorder: being in treatment — on either drug — is where the mortality difference lives
question: For opioid use disorder, what do methadone and buprenorphine each do to the risk of dying — and how do they compare with each other?
balance: The mortality evidence is observational — cohorts, not randomized mortality trials — and the stamp carries that on its face. Within that fence, the signal is large and consistent: pooled death rates in treatment run at roughly a third of the rates out of treatment for methadone and under half for buprenorphine, for overdose deaths as for all deaths, with the danger concentrated in methadone's first four weeks and in the weeks after leaving either drug. The between-drug question is narrower than it looks: flexible-dose methadone retains people better than flexible-dose buprenorphine (RR 0.83, relative), and at adequate fixed doses the retention gap closes — but no randomized trial compares the two drugs on mortality, and the cohort rates cannot be read as a head-to-head. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: Extended-release naltrexone vs buprenorphine (X:BOT): equivalent once started — harder to start
question: A monthly naltrexone injection against daily buprenorphine: which keeps people off opioids — and what does the answer depend on?
balance: One trial, two honest answers, and both are stamped. As offered (intention-to-treat), buprenorphine-naloxone produced fewer relapses over 24 weeks (57% vs 65%; HR 1.36, relative) — a difference manufactured almost entirely at the front door, where 94% of patients successfully started buprenorphine against 72% for the injection, which demands an opioid-free interval first. Once successfully inducted, relapse did not differ (per-protocol, P=0.44), and the Norwegian trial — where induction was inpatient and already complete — found XR-naltrexone noninferior on retention and urine tests over 12 weeks. Mortality in X:BOT was five fatal overdoses in total (2 XR-NTX, 3 BUP-NX); neither trial was powered for death. The practical reading: the choice between these drugs is mostly a choice about which induction problem your setting can solve. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: Medicines for alcohol use disorder: modest absolute effects — NNTs of 12 to 20 — and one drug that only works watched
question: Which medicines actually reduce drinking in alcohol use disorder, how large are the effects in absolute terms, and where does disulfiram fit?
balance: Two medicines have replicated, placebo-controlled support with small absolute effects: acamprosate (NNT 12 to prevent return to any drinking) and oral naltrexone 50 mg (NNT 20 for any drinking, NNT 12 for heavy drinking) — printed as NNTs because the percentages alone flatter them. The largest single trial complicates both stories: COMBINE found naltrexone plus simple medical management sufficient, intensive behavioral therapy and acamprosate adding nothing measurable, and its acamprosate arm flatly null against the meta-analysis's positive pool. Disulfiram is carded at its true grade: null for abstinence in the blinded VA trial, with any real benefit confined to supervised administration — a claim about watching, not about the molecule. None of these trials establishes a mortality benefit, and the shelf claims none. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: Contingency management for stimulant use disorder: the largest psychosocial effect during treatment — durability after the incentives stop is the open question
question: Paying people, in vouchers or prizes, for verified abstinence: does contingency management work for stimulant use disorder — and for how long?
balance: During treatment, the evidence is as strong as psychosocial evidence gets: across two independent syntheses, contingency management carries the largest effect sizes of any psychosocial approach (Dutra 2008), and in the 157-study cocaine network it was the only category of any kind — drug or therapy — significantly associated with drug-negative tests at end of treatment (OR 2.13, relative). The fence is printed in the title: both syntheses measure outcomes while the incentives are running. Abstinence commonly attenuates after incentives end, and neither card's record quantifies long-term post-incentive abstinence — so durability grades POSSIBLE, not LIKELY, and any program built on this shelf should be read as buying abstinence during the program, with the after-period unproven. The VA's national rollout of contingency management is implementation of this evidence, not additional evidence. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: Community naloxone distribution: stamped LIKELY by developer override, over observational evidence printed at its true grade
question: Does putting naloxone kits and overdose training into the hands of bystanders lower a community's overdose death rate?
balance: The evidence, graded on its own: one interrupted time-series study of 19 Massachusetts communities found overdose death rates lower where overdose-education-and-naloxone programs were implemented, with a dose-response by implementation intensity (adjusted rate ratios 0.73 low, 0.54 high, both relative and ecological) and 327 reported rescues by trained bystanders. That is the whole spine — no randomized trials exist, and the developer's own observational-evidence floor treats ratios between 0.5 and 2.0 as not solid, which covers the low-implementation estimate entirely. The LIKELY stamp is therefore explicitly the developer's judgment — weighing the dose-response, the rescues, the mechanism (naloxone reverses opioid overdose; that pharmacology is not in doubt), and the absence of a plausible harm — laid over evidence that on this library's usual rules would grade lower. Both facts stay printed. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: Esketamine for treatment-resistant depression: one pivotal trial met its primary, two missed — a modest effect with a clinic-visit burden
question: Does esketamine nasal spray, added to a new oral antidepressant, work for treatment-resistant depression — across the whole pivotal trial set, not just the winner?
balance: The short-term set, carded whole: TRANSFORM-2 (flexible dose) met its primary with a −4.0-point MADRS advantage at 4 weeks; TRANSFORM-1 (fixed dose) missed (P=0.088 at the gatekeeping dose) and TRANSFORM-3 (age 65+) missed (P=0.059). The point estimates barely move across the three — roughly −3 to −4 MADRS points — so the honest dispute is not direction but how much a modest average difference, measured on a subjective scale in trials where dissociation partly unblinds patients, is worth. SUSTAIN-1 shows continuing esketamine delays relapse in patients already selected for responding to it (NNT 4–6), which supports continuation decisions, not starting ones. Against the benefit: dissociation, vertigo, and transient blood-pressure effects around dosing, discontinuation for adverse events of 7% vs 0.9% in TRANSFORM-2, and administration only in a certified clinic under observation (REMS) — a real burden priced into every dose. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: Ketamine vs ECT for severe depression: noninferior where it was tested — untested where ECT is strongest
question: Head to head, is intravenous ketamine as good as electroconvulsive therapy for treatment-resistant depression — and in whom was that actually tested?
balance: ELEKT-D is the comparison the field waited for, done in ECT-referred patients: ketamine met noninferiority and numerically out-responded ECT (55.4% vs 41.2%), with ECT's cost showing up where it always has — memory, measurably worse at 3 weeks and recovering only gradually — and ketamine's showing up as dissociation. Quality of life ended equal. The boundary is printed, not buried: psychotic depression was excluded, and that is precisely the population where ECT's historical claim is strongest and where no modern randomized comparison exists — so the second half of the stamp grades ECT's continued primacy there as POSSIBLE, an extrapolation from older evidence, not a trial result. In the tested population, a patient who can avoid anesthesia and memory effects without giving up response has a real option. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: Psychedelic-assisted therapy: positive trials under a MAYBE (weak evidence) stamp — unblinding, a complete response letter, and 2024 retractions
question: Do psilocybin (for treatment-resistant depression) and MDMA-assisted therapy (for PTSD) work — and what do the blinding problem, the FDA's 2024 decision, and the retractions do to the grade?
balance: The trial results, stated fairly: a single 25-mg psilocybin dose beat a 1-mg control on depression scores at 3 weeks (−6.6 MADRS points), and two MDMA phase-3 trials beat placebo-plus-therapy on PTSD severity with large effect sizes. The grade is MAYBE (weak evidence) anyway, for reasons printed on the cards rather than whispered: functional unblinding is near-total for both drugs, so the double-blind design cannot do its usual work and expectancy is an unmeasured co-treatment; the psilocybin effect did not persist as sustained response at 12 weeks; and the MDMA program carries an FDA complete response letter (August 2024, declining approval and requesting a further trial) plus the 2024 retraction of three phase-2 pooled analyses over data-integrity and ethics violations. Positive p-values were never the whole of evidence; this shelf is where the library says so. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: Cytisine for smoking cessation: beats placebo and nicotine replacement — not yet shown varenicline's equal
question: Cytisine — a low-cost plant alkaloid used for decades in Eastern Europe — against placebo, against nicotine replacement, and against varenicline: where does it actually stand?
balance: Against placebo the case is consistent across eras and regimens: 8.4% vs 2.4% sustained abstinence at 12 months on the traditional 25-day course (West 2011), and 32.6% vs 7.0% at weeks 9–12 on ORCA-2's modern 12-week 3-mg regimen, with tolerability at least as good. Against nicotine replacement, the one pragmatic trial found superiority (40% vs 31% at 1 month). Against varenicline — the strongest standard — the single head-to-head trial failed to demonstrate noninferiority (11.7% vs 13.3%), which demotes 'varenicline alternative' to POSSIBLE without making cytisine a proven lesser drug. As of the sources checked for this shelf, cytisine/cytisinicline is not FDA-approved in the US; its affordability case belongs to the countries where it is licensed. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: Cannabis and cannabinoids for chronic pain: a small average effect, honestly sized — and harms that grow with duration
question: For chronic pain, how much do cannabis and cannabinoids actually help — in absolute terms patients can feel — and what do they cost?
balance: Sized honestly, the benefit is small: across 32 non-inhaled trials the average pain advantage is half a centimetre on a 10-cm scale, which translates to about 1 in 10 more patients reaching the smallest difference patients can feel — and no improvement at all in emotional, role, or social functioning (high certainty). The broadest review's responder statistic (37% vs 31%) carries a confidence interval that touches the null, and the most favorable result on the shelf — inhaled cannabis for neuropathic pain, NNT 5.6 — rests on 178 patients followed for days to weeks with unblinding built in. The harms are neither rare nor static: dizziness in 9 more patients per 100 in short trials and 28 more per 100 in trials of 3 months or longer, plus drowsiness, nausea, and cognitive effects. Follow-up across the whole literature is 1 to 5.5 months; nothing here speaks to years of use. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: Aspirin to prevent preeclampsia: the ASPRE strategy works — whether the 81 mg US dose does the same is unproven
question: Does aspirin prevent preeclampsia — and does the answer depend on the dose and the start date?
balance: In screened high-risk women, 150 mg nightly from the first trimester prevented about 1 case of preterm preeclampsia for every 37 treated (1.6% vs 4.3%), with no excess of adverse events — and preeclampsia is delayed/prevented disease where the word fits: this is true prevention of the preterm form, not the term form, which no dose has been shown to reduce. The dose-and-timing meta-analyses agree that dose and start date are the intervention: benefit is confined to ≥100 mg started at or before 16 weeks. The open wound is dose translation: the 81 mg dose US practice actually uses has never been shown to do the same job (Reference 3), and whether two 81 mg tablets equal the ASPRE regimen is inference, not trial evidence. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026 (Tier C — personal ruling).

title: Magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection: the flagship trial’s primary was null — the cerebral-palsy signal pooled true
question: When preterm birth is imminent, does giving the mother magnesium sulfate protect the baby’s brain?
balance: Five trials, one direction, a consistent relative effect on cerebral palsy in survivors (RR ≈0.68, labeled relative; NNT 46 in the patient-level pooling) on a devastating outcome, at an NNT in the 40s–60s depending on baseline risk — against a cheap drug with transient maternal side effects and no excess of serious maternal harm at these doses. The honest caveats are structural, not hidden: the flagship trial’s primary endpoint was null because mortality did not move (death 9.5% vs 8.5% on BEAM), and the cerebral-palsy claim rests on a prespecified secondary endpoint in BEAM that the pooled literature then confirmed as its primary question. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: Antenatal steroids beyond 34 weeks: a late-preterm benefit with a hypoglycemia bill — and a smaller trade before term cesarean
question: Steroids before 34 weeks are settled medicine. Does extending the window — late preterm, or before a planned term cesarean — help babies or just expose them?
balance: Two different trades. Late preterm (ALPS): a solid, blinded trial — one severe respiratory complication prevented per 25 treated, paid for with one extra case of neonatal hypoglycemia per ~11 babies exposed (24.0% vs 15.0%); whether that hypoglycemia has any lasting consequence is unproven either way, and the trial was not built to answer childhood outcomes. There were no deaths in the 72-hour window in either arm, so the composite is about respiratory support, not survival. Term cesarean (ASTECS): a real relative effect in one open-label trial, small absolute stakes (11 vs 24 babies), and a competing intervention — delaying the cesarean to 39 weeks — that the trial’s own authors conclude also reduces these admissions, with no drug at all. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: Delayed cord clamping and preterm survival: the biggest trial’s composite was null — the pooled deaths say wait
question: Does waiting at least a minute before clamping the cord save preterm babies’ lives?
balance: The pooled patient-level evidence says waiting a minute or more reduces preterm death before discharge by roughly a third in relative terms (OR 0.68, high-certainty in the authors’ grading), at zero cost and with no maternal harm signal — one of the cheapest mortality interventions in medicine. The counterweight is honest and specific: the one trial large enough to answer alone (APTS) hit its composite of death or major morbidity dead level (37.0% vs 37.2%), and its mortality gap (6.4% vs 9.0%) does not survive adjustment for the many secondary outcomes examined (P=0.39 adjusted vs P=0.03 unadjusted — both printed on Card 1). The claim stands on the consistency of 48 trials, not on any single one. Cord milking is not a substitute: it showed no clear difference from immediate clamping. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026 (Tier C — personal ruling).

title: Uterotonics compared: carbetocin is oxytocin’s equal where the fridge fails — combinations win at 500 mL, not at 1,000
question: Oxytocin is the standard for preventing postpartum hemorrhage — is anything better, and does heat-stable carbetocin earn its place where the cold chain fails?
balance: For routine prevention: oxytocin, or heat-stable carbetocin where the fridge can’t be trusted — a genuine equal at the ≥500 mL outcome (14.5% vs 14.4%), with the ≥1,000 mL proof incomplete (noninferiority not shown, on low event rates). For high-risk women, adding misoprostol to oxytocin prevents more moderate hemorrhages (RR 0.70, relative) and roughly halves additional-uterotonic use, but no regimen has beaten oxytocin at preventing severe hemorrhage, and the extra efficacy at ≥500 mL is bought with side effects — more nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and fever. Nobody should read the combination rankings as a severe-hemorrhage claim. Postpartum hemorrhage is the leading cause of maternal death worldwide (Card 2’s record); this shelf grades prevention regimens, and prints the severe-hemorrhage outcome beside every moderate-hemorrhage claim. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026 — single grade, LIKELY, by the developer’s ruling.

title: 17-OHPC to prevent preterm birth: the PROLONG reversal — accelerated approval is a loan, not a verdict
question: Does weekly 17-hydroxyprogesterone caproate (17-OHPC) prevent recurrent preterm birth?
balance: 17-OHPC did not prevent preterm birth in the trial built to confirm it, and the episode is this library’s cleanest lesson that accelerated approval is a loan, not a verdict. (Developer’s balance line, of record.) One trial, stopped early, with a large effect bought a decade of routine use; the confirmatory trial — larger, with the same indication — found preterm birth <35 weeks at 11.0% vs 11.5% and no difference in the neonatal composite or in fetal/early infant death (1.7% vs 1.9%). The honest complication stays printed: PROLONG’s women were lower-risk and mostly outside the US, with placebo event rates far below Meis’s, so the trials disagree partly about who was studied, not only about the drug. The fence: vaginal progesterone is a different drug by a different route for a different indication — that question lives on Shelf #418, and nothing on this shelf rules on it. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: Short cervix: vaginal progesterone vs cervical pessary — one pooled case, one unreplicated debut
question: An asymptomatic singleton pregnancy, cervix ≤25 mm at midtrimester — what actually prevents preterm birth?
balance: These are not two equivalent contenders, and the shelf keeps the tension printed under the developer’s single LIKELY stamp. Progesterone’s case is five trials pooled at the patient level (974 women) with concordant neonatal benefits — preterm birth <33 weeks RR 0.62 (relative), respiratory distress syndrome RR 0.47, composite neonatal morbidity/mortality RR 0.59 — against a neonatal-death estimate too small to call (1.4% vs 3.2%, RR 0.44, NS). The pessary’s case is one unblinded trial whose headline effect (6% vs 27%) no larger trial has reproduced: the 932-woman replication found 12.0% vs 10.8%, with perinatal death 3.2% vs 2.4%. There is still no adequate head-to-head trial of the two — every “versus” in this shelf’s title is an indirect comparison, and the shelf says so. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026 — LIKELY overall, both treatments, by the developer’s ruling, overriding the split stamp proposed at presentation.

title: Antibiotics for preterm rupture of membranes — and for preterm labor with intact membranes (ORACLE): one question where they help, one where the children paid
question: When labor threatens early, do broad-spectrum antibiotics help the baby — and does the answer flip when the membranes are still intact?
balance: These are two different clinical questions sharing one shelf, and the fence between them is the shelf’s whole point. With ruptured membranes (ORACLE I, Card 1), erythromycin prolonged pregnancy and improved a run of short-term neonatal outcomes — the primary composite reached significance in singletons (11.2% vs 14.4%, P=0.02) though not in all infants (12.7% vs 15.2%, P=0.08) — and the 7-year follow-up (Reference 2) found no childhood penalty. Co-amoxiclav bought no primary benefit in PPROM and significantly more necrotizing enterocolitis, so it is the drug to avoid. With intact membranes (ORACLE II, Card 3), the same drugs produced no short-term neonatal benefit at all — and at age 7 the children exposed to erythromycin carried more functional impairment and roughly double the cerebral palsy. In PPROM the trade favors a macrolide; with intact membranes there is no short-term benefit to weigh against the long-term signal. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026 — split stamp LIKELY (PPROM macrolide) / POSSIBLE (intact-membrane childhood harm), as ruled.

title: Immediate kangaroo care for low-birth-weight infants: start skin-to-skin at birth, not after stabilization
question: For a baby born at 1.0–1.8 kg, does skin-to-skin care started immediately — rather than after the baby stabilizes — save lives?
balance: Two independent evidence layers point the same way. The older trials — kangaroo care begun mostly after stabilization, pooled by Cochrane (Reference 2) — found mortality relative risks of 0.60 at discharge and 0.67 at latest follow-up. The one large trial of the immediate strategy (iKMC, Card 1) found death by 28 days at 12.0% vs 15.7% — RR 0.75 (relative), an absolute 3.7 points, NNT ≈27 — in the low-resource settings where most of these deaths occur. The discounts are printed, not hidden: iKMC was stopped early on its monitoring board’s recommendation, which can flatter an effect; care could not be blinded; and the control group was not “no kangaroo care” but delayed kangaroo care, which if anything biases the estimate down. The claim is fenced to the studied band: infants of 1.0–1.8 kg, in hospitals able to keep mothers resident in the unit (Reference 3). Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: CPAP first vs early surfactant in extremely preterm infants: start noninvasive, ventilate selectively
question: For a baby born at 24–28 weeks, should the default be a tube and surfactant in the first hour, or CPAP in the delivery room with surfactant only if needed?
balance: No individual trial won its primary endpoint — SUPPORT’s death-or-BPD composite was 47.8% vs 51.0% (RR 0.95, NS) and COIN’s was OR 0.80 (NS) — and this shelf prints those nulls first, because they are the honest headline. What CPAP-first bought, consistently, was exposure: fewer intubations, fewer ventilator days, roughly half the surfactant, and less postnatal steroid use, at no measured cost in death, BPD, or 18–22-month neurodevelopment (SUPPORT follow-up: death or impairment 27.9% vs 29.9%, NS). Pooled across the avoidance-of-ventilation trials, death or BPD does reach significance (OR 0.83, NNT 35 — Card 3, with the record’s own numbers). The price on the ledger is COIN’s pneumothorax signal (9% vs 3%), from the highest-pressure CPAP strategy in the set and not reproduced in SUPPORT. Nothing here says surfactant is obsolete — nearly half of CPAP-first babies receive it anyway; what changed is the default order. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: Plasma and platelet ratios in massive transfusion: 1:1:1 stops the bleeding sooner — overall mortality does not significantly move
question: In severe trauma with major bleeding, does transfusing plasma, platelets and red cells in a 1:1:1 ratio rather than 1:1:2 save lives?
balance: The only large randomized test missed both of its mortality endpoints — 24-hour mortality 12.7% vs 17.0% (P=.12) and 30-day 22.4% vs 26.1% (P=.26) for 1:1:1 vs 1:1:2 — and this shelf prints that null first, because it is the honest headline. What the higher ratio did deliver, in PROPPR itself, was hemostasis (86% vs 78% achieving it) and fewer deaths from exsanguination by 24 hours (9.2% vs 14.6%), at no measured cost across 23 prespecified complications. The observational PROMMTT cohort points the same way — early high ratios associated with lower 6-hour mortality — but it is association, and PROPPR is what the association survived when randomized: a bleeding-control benefit, not a proven overall-survival benefit. POSSIBLE. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: Prehospital plasma: why did the helicopter trial win and the city trial lose?
question: Does plasma given before hospital arrival save lives in bleeding trauma — and does the answer depend on how long the transport takes?
balance: The entire randomized record is two trials, and they disagree. PAMPer — plasma during air transport, where journeys are long — cut 30-day mortality from 33.0% to 23.2%. COMBAT — plasma during urban ground transport, median under 20 minutes — found 15% vs 10% against plasma and stopped for futility. Pooled, the pair shows a 24-hour mortality signal (RR 0.69) that dissolves by one month (RR 0.86, not significant). The transport-time explanation is coherent — plasma may need time at risk to pay — but it is an explanation fitted to two points, and by this library’s house rule for one positive against one null it would grade MAYBE (weak evidence) — the developer rules it POSSIBLE. Shelf #241 holds these trials’ home cards; this shelf asks the setting question they raise together. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: Early cryoprecipitate in major hemorrhage: CRYOSTAT-2 — empiric fibrinogen for everyone saves no one
question: In bleeding trauma patients activating a major hemorrhage protocol, does adding early, high-dose cryoprecipitate to standard care improve survival?
balance: CRYOSTAT-2 is a large, well-run, international trial with a flat answer: 28-day mortality 25.3% with early high-dose cryoprecipitate vs 26.1% without (OR 0.96 [0.75–1.23]), and identical thrombotic-event rates. Giving fibrinogen empirically to every major-hemorrhage activation — before any test shows a deficiency — does not improve survival, and the confidence interval excludes a large benefit. That earns LIKELY for the null, fenced to what was tested: empiric use in unselected protocol activations. Whether replacing fibrinogen helps at all is a different question — it has its own shelf (Shelf #523); which product to use is Shelf #426. Card 2 is CRYOSTAT-1, the small feasibility pilot that made this trial possible: early cryoprecipitate proved deliverable within 90 minutes, and CRYOSTAT-2 is what that deliverable intervention achieved when tested at scale. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: Viscoelastic testing (TEG/ROTEM) in trauma: iTACTIC — the assay did not beat the laboratory
question: In major trauma hemorrhage, does guiding a major hemorrhage protocol with viscoelastic assays (TEG/ROTEM) improve patient outcomes compared with conventional coagulation tests?
balance: The one purpose-built trauma trial is null on everything: iTACTIC’s primary outcome (alive and free of massive transfusion at 24 hours) was 67% vs 64%, and 28-day mortality 25% vs 28%, viscoelastic guidance vs conventional tests. The counterweight is a Cochrane pool suggesting lower mortality with TEG/ROTEM guidance (RR 0.76) — assembled mostly from elective cardiac surgery and graded very low certainty by its own reviewers. A single mid-sized trauma RCT with confidence intervals that still admit a moderate benefit earns POSSIBLE for the trauma null, not more: in trauma, viscoelastic guidance is unproven, and the burden of proof has not moved. title: Replacing fibrinogen: concentrate vs cryoprecipitate — interchangeable on everything measured; survival untested either way
question: When a bleeding patient needs fibrinogen replaced, is fibrinogen concentrate as good as cryoprecipitate?
balance: Eight randomised comparisons now answer the product question, and they answer it the same way in every setting: the two products are interchangeable on everything that has been measured. In cardiac surgery — the deepest evidence — FIBRES proved concentrate noninferior to cryoprecipitate on 24-hour transfusion (16.3 vs 17.0 units), and the pooled cardiac trials find no difference in mortality (RR 1.25 [0.79–1.96]), blood loss, transfusion or thrombosis. In trauma, FEISTY shows concentrate reaching the patient about twice as fast (29 vs 60 minutes) — a logistics result, not an outcome result — and RETIC supports concentrate-first hemostatic efficiency against plasma. The remaining trials repeat the pattern across abdominal, paediatric, neonatal and mixed surgery: equal hemostasis, occasional speed or cost advantages, no clinical-outcome separation. The fence is explicit: nearly every primary endpoint on this shelf is a process — units transfused, minutes to delivery, millilitres lost, a laboratory trace, a price — and no trial here is powered for mortality. Choosing between the products is therefore a decision about availability, speed, cost and product safety, not about demonstrated efficacy. Whether replacing fibrinogen improves outcomes at all is a different question — Shelf #523 — and empiric replacement in unselected trauma bleeding is answered, negatively, on Shelf #424. POSSIBLE. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: Whole blood, randomised at last: two prehospital trials, no benefit at 2 units — the dose question remains
question: In bleeding trauma, is resuscitation with whole blood better than giving the components separately?
balance: This shelf was rebuilt because its first claim died: the comparative evidence is no longer entirely observational. Two phase-3 prehospital trials, published back-to-back in the same NEJM issue in June 2026, each gave up to 2 units of whole blood against blood components — TOWAR (cluster-randomised across 44 North American air bases; 30-day mortality 25.9% vs 20.5%) and SWiFT (individually randomised across 10 English air ambulance services; death or massive transfusion at 24 hours, 48.7% vs 47.7%) — and neither found a benefit; pooled across the three randomised trials, the mortality odds ratios are 1.12 at 24 hours and 1.15 at 28–30 days with zero heterogeneity. The observational literature still points the other way — the largest pool (Ibrahim 2026) finds civilian 24-hour mortality OR 0.73 — but it prints its own caution beside the estimate: I² of 89%, a 95% prediction interval of 0.28–1.91, a null military subgroup, and a search that closed a year before the two big trials reported. Confounding by indication remains a standing explanation for the gap. What the trials did not test is dose: both capped whole blood at 2 units, while the observational signal concentrates where whole blood is a large share of everything transfused — the question the in-hospital trials (TROOP in adults, MATIC-2 in children) are now running to answer. Split stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for prehospital whole blood at up to 2 units; MAYBE (weak evidence) for higher-dose and in-hospital use. Proposed split stamp — proposed, pending the developer’s review. Tier C: mortality claims — the developer’s personal ruling governs this shelf.

title: REBOA for uncontrolled bleeding: UK-REBOA — the balloon may increase mortality [Tier C]
question: In trauma patients with exsanguinating hemorrhage, does adding REBOA to standard emergency department care reduce mortality?
balance: One randomized trial exists, and it points the wrong way: in UK-REBOA, 90-day mortality was 54% with a REBOA strategy vs 42% with standard care alone (OR 1.58 [95% credible interval 0.72–3.52]; 86.9% posterior probability of increased odds of death), with every earlier mortality endpoint leaning the same direction and more deaths from bleeding in the REBOA group. The trial is small and its interval includes no effect — a harm signal, stated as a signal. REBOA spread through trauma systems on registry data and mechanism; the first randomized test found no benefit to weigh against the signal. Tier C — mortality/harm claim: developer-approved Nov 7, 2026 (personal ruling).

title: Platelet transfusion before procedures: PACER — before a central line at counts of 10–50,000, give the unit
question: In patients with platelet counts of 10,000–50,000, can prophylactic platelet transfusion be safely withheld before ultrasound-guided central venous catheter placement?
balance: PACER asked whether the platelet unit could be skipped and got a clear no: withholding prophylaxis before ultrasound-guided CVC placement failed its noninferiority test, with grade 2–4 catheter-related bleeding at 11.9% without transfusion vs 4.8% with it (RR 2.45), and grade 3–4 bleeding at 4.9% vs 2.1%. The absolute rates are modest and the setting is fenced — counts of 10,000–50,000, ultrasound guidance, hematology and ICU patients — but within that fence the answer is as firm as single-trial answers get: LIKELY. title: Tranexamic acid in GI bleeding: HALT-IT — the indication that failed
question: Does tranexamic acid reduce death from acute gastrointestinal bleeding?
balance: HALT-IT is as definitive as nulls get: 12,009 patients, death due to bleeding within 5 days at 4% in both arms (RR 0.99 [0.82–1.18]), venous thromboembolism nearly doubled on tranexamic acid (0.8% vs 0.4%; RR 1.85), and an authors’ conclusion that the drug should not be used for GI bleeding outside a randomized trial. Before it, the randomized record in the highest-risk population — liver disease — was literally empty (Reference 2). The null earns LIKELY, and its contrast with trauma and childbirth on Shelf #138 is the most instructive comparison in the tranexamic acid literature: same drug, different bleeding biology. This shelf re-cards HALT-IT from its home on Shelf #138 to give the GI question its own hearing. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: Calcium in cardiac arrest: COCA — no ROSC benefit, a consistent harm lean, stopped early
question: Does giving calcium during adult out-of-hospital cardiac arrest improve return of spontaneous circulation or survival?
balance: COCA, the first placebo-controlled trial of calcium in unselected out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, was stopped early at a planned interim analysis because its own steering committee was worried about harm — and the finished numbers justify the worry without proving it: sustained ROSC 19% vs 27% (RR 0.72, P=.09), 30-day survival 5.2% vs 9.1%, favorable neurology 3.6% vs 7.6%, with the same leans at one year. No significant result, and no result in calcium’s favor: the grade is POSSIBLE for the null, fenced to routine administration — COCA says nothing about calcium for its classic specific indications (hyperkalemia, hypocalcemia, calcium-channel-blocker overdose), which were not its question. title: Autonomous AI for diabetic eye screening: two pivotal trials prove the grading — outcomes untested
question: Can an autonomous AI system, with no specialist reading the images, detect diabetic retinopathy accurately enough for primary-care screening?
balance: The diagnostic question is about as well answered as diagnostic questions get: two independent preregistered pivotal trials, against reading-center reference standards, put autonomous AI sensitivity for referable diabetic retinopathy at 87.2% (IDx-DR) and 95.5% (EyeArt), with specificities of 90.7% and 85.0%. The grade stops at POSSIBLE because of what the design cannot show: no trial here randomized a screening strategy or counted referrals completed, treatment delivered, or vision saved. Accuracy is proven; benefit is inferred. Proposed stamp POSSIBLE — proposed, pending the developer’s review.

title: AI-assisted colonoscopy: adenomas found, reliably — cancers prevented, unproven
question: Does computer-aided detection during colonoscopy find more adenomas — and does finding them prevent colorectal cancer?
balance: The detection claim earns LIKELY: randomized trials on three continents agree that computer-aided detection raises the adenoma detection rate (54.8% vs 40.4% in the GI-Genius trial; pooled RR 1.24, relative, across 21 trials and 18,232 patients) and roughly halves the adenoma miss rate in tandem studies. The fence is equally consistent: the extra lesions are overwhelmingly diminutive, advanced adenoma detection did not increase in the pooled analysis, nonneoplastic polypectomies rose, and no trial has measured cancer incidence or cancer death. Buy the detection claim at LIKELY; the cancer claim is not on this shelf because no one has earned it yet. Proposed stamp LIKELY — proposed, pending the developer’s review.

title: AI sepsis alerts: a mortality claim resting on 142 randomized patients [Tier C]
question: Do machine-learning sepsis alert systems make patients with sepsis less likely to die?
balance: Every sepsis-alert claim eventually becomes a mortality claim, so this shelf is Tier C and its proposed grade is MAYBE (weak evidence). The randomized record is a single open-label trial of 142 patients reporting a 58% relative mortality reduction — an implausibly large effect at that sample size. The two large deployments agree on direction and disagree on size: TREWS (6,877 sepsis patients; adjusted relative mortality reduction 18.7% when providers confirmed alerts within 3 hours — a comparison of provider behavior, not of the alert) and COMPOSER (6,217 patients; 1.9-point absolute reduction in a before-and-after design). Alerts plausibly speed recognition; whether they save lives is unproven at any grade this library can defend. Tier C — mortality claim: built Nov 7, 2026 and held for the developer’s personal verdict; no approval stamp is claimed for this shelf. Proposed grade: MAYBE (weak evidence).

title: An LLM at the doctor’s elbow: management scores up, diagnosis scores flat — in vignettes
question: Does giving physicians a large language model improve their clinical reasoning?
balance: Two randomized trials, one honest split result. For diagnosis, GPT-4 access did not significantly improve physicians’ reasoning scores (76% vs 74% per case). For management — choosing tests and treatments under uncertainty — it did (+6.5 points), at a cost of about two extra minutes per case. Both trials graded written vignettes against expert rubrics; neither touched a real patient, and in both, the LLM alone matched or beat the physicians who were given it. POSSIBLE for the vignette claim as fenced; no card here supports a claim about real-world diagnostic safety. title: Screening for silent atrial fibrillation: watches and patches find it — stroke prevention still unproven
question: Does screening people who feel well for atrial fibrillation with wearable or implantable devices prevent strokes?
balance: Split the claim. Detection: as strong as evidence gets — randomized and prospective studies at every intensity (watch, patch, handheld, implant) find more AF and start more anticoagulation. Outcomes: STROKESTOP’s invitation to screen produced a combined-endpoint HR of 0.96 [0.92–1.00] — inside the small-effect band, on a composite — and LOOP’s far more intensive monitoring produced a non-significant stroke HR of 0.80 with more bleeding. One stamp for the shelf as asked (does screening prevent strokes?): POSSIBLE, and the cards show exactly how much of that grade is detection wearing outcome’s clothes. title: Digital CBT for insomnia: Sleepio and its class — real effects, placebo-tested
question: Does cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia delivered by an app or website actually improve sleep?
balance: Digital CBT-I is the best-evidenced product on this slate: a placebo-controlled trial with large effects on sleep efficiency (Sleepio, d≈1.0 against an active placebo), the largest psychological-intervention trial of its era confirming a large insomnia effect at scale (OASIS, d=1.11), and a second program whose randomized gains persisted a full year (SHUTi). title: Hospital at home: cheaper and better liked — the mortality claim depends on which trials you pool [Tier C]
question: For acutely ill adults, is hospital-level care at home as safe and effective as care in a hospital building?
balance: The consistent findings are operational: in the one modern US randomized trial, home care cost 38% less, used far fewer tests, got patients moving, and readmitted fewer of them (7% vs 23%) — in 91 selected patients, most of whom had refused or been screened out of the alternative. The disputed finding is mortality, and it is why this shelf is Tier C: the broad 61-trial pool finds a mortality advantage (OR 0.81, relative; NNT 50), while the stricter Cochrane early-discharge pool finds little or no mortality difference (RR 1.07 in mixed conditions). Both pools are printed; the shelf takes no side. Proposed grade: POSSIBLE for the cost/readmission/satisfaction package, mortality unsettled. Tier C — mortality claim: built Nov 7, 2026 and held for the developer’s personal verdict; no approval stamp is claimed for this shelf. (No ICD-10 code is printed: hospital at home is a place of care across many principal conditions, and this library does not guess codes.)

title: Text-message programs: small nudges, honestly sized — adherence and risk factors improve a little
question: Do text-message programs improve medication adherence and the numbers adherence is meant to move?
balance: Three randomized trials, three diseases, one consistent size of effect: small. TEXT ME modestly improved LDL cholesterol and other risk factors at 6 months in coronary disease; StAR’s adherence texts bought about 2 mmHg of systolic pressure over a year; WelTel’s weekly nurse text — the most human and most interactive program here — produced the strongest yield, an NNT of 9 for adherence and 11 for viral suppression. No trial measured heart attacks, strokes, or deaths. POSSIBLE: texts are a cheap, safe nudge with real but modest effects on adherence-linked measures — an adjunct, never a treatment. title: Polygenic risk scores: real prediction, tiny increment, no outcome evidence
question: Do polygenic risk scores improve prediction or prevention enough to belong in clinical care?
balance: The three cards tell one story at three altitudes. The scores genuinely stratify: 8% of people carry a polygenic coronary risk above threefold (Reference 1). Added to the clinical equations already in use, that stratification buys almost nothing: a C-statistic gain of 0.02 and net reclassification of 4% (Reference 2). And the single randomized trial of actually using a score changed a process — more statins started, LDL 9.4 mg/dL lower at 6 months, n=203 — not an outcome (Reference 3). No trial shows a polygenic score preventing a heart attack, a stroke, or a death, and the scores transport poorly beyond the ancestries they were built in. MAYBE (weak evidence), as briefed. Proposed stamp MAYBE (weak evidence) — proposed, pending the developer’s review.

title: Multi-cancer blood tests: a signal in 1.4% of adults — benefit not yet tested in a randomized trial
question: Do multi-cancer early detection blood tests help asymptomatic people live longer or avoid advanced cancer?
balance: What is proven: the tests can be run at scale, a signal appears in about 1.4% of screened adults, 38% of signals in PATHFINDER were cancers, and the diagnostic cascade that follows is usually tolerable — a median 79 days to resolution, longer for the 62% whose signal was false. What is not proven is everything that makes screening worthwhile: no randomized comparison, no stage-shift or mortality result, no measure of overdiagnosis or of cancers falsely reassured. Both prospective studies are carded in full because they are honest feasibility work; the shelf’s grade is the library’s lowest, as briefed: MAYBE (weak evidence). title: Shingles vaccine and dementia: two birthday cut-offs, two falls in dementia diagnoses — for the old vaccine
question: Does herpes zoster (shingles) vaccination prevent or delay dementia?
balance: No randomised trial exists, but two countries accidentally ran the next best thing. In Wales, zoster-vaccine eligibility turned on an exact birthday; people a week younger were vaccinated at 47% and people a week older at 0.01%, and the vaccinated side accumulated 3.5 percentage points fewer dementia diagnoses over seven years — a 20% relative reduction [6.5–33.4]. In Australia, the same design on a different birthday line found the same direction (eligibility effect 1.8 percentage points [0.4–3.3]) with balanced comparison groups and quiet negative controls. POSSIBLE, capped by three fences: the designs are quasi-experimental, the outcomes are recorded diagnoses rather than adjudicated dementia, and the vaccine both experiments studied is the live-attenuated one most programmes have replaced with a recombinant vaccine whose dementia evidence is still ordinary observational data. Proposed stamp POSSIBLE — proposed, pending the developer’s review.

title: Influenza vaccine after a heart attack: one double-blind trial, fewer deaths — a Tier C claim
question: Does influenza vaccination given early after a myocardial infarction reduce death and further cardiovascular events?
balance: One trial carries this shelf: IAMI randomised 2,571 patients in hospital after myocardial infarction to influenza vaccine or saline placebo and found the 12-month composite of death, infarction or stent thrombosis lower on vaccine (5.3% vs 7.2%; HR 0.72 [0.52–0.99]), with all-cause death lower as well (2.9% vs 4.9%; HR 0.59 [0.39–0.89]). The fences are on the card: the trial stopped early in the COVID-19 pandemic, the composite interval ends at 0.99, and the mortality difference rests on small counts. Proposed grade: POSSIBLE. title: Pneumococcal vaccines in older adults: vaccine-type disease prevented — pneumonia overall, not shown
question: Do pneumococcal vaccines prevent pneumococcal pneumonia and invasive disease in older adults?
balance: One very large trial anchors the conjugate claim: in CAPiTA (84,496 adults ≥65), PCV13 prevented 45.6% of vaccine-type pneumococcal pneumonia and 75.0% of vaccine-type invasive disease — and 5.1% (not significant) of pneumonia from any cause, which is the number that keeps the shelf honest. The older polysaccharide vaccine’s pooled record (Cochrane) supports protection against invasive disease, largely on non-randomised evidence, with no shown effect on all-cause pneumonia or mortality. Split stamp: LIKELY for the conjugate vaccine against vaccine-type disease; POSSIBLE for the polysaccharide vaccine’s broader claim. Proposed split stamp — proposed, pending the developer’s review.

title: HPV vaccination and cervical cancer: the registries deliver the endpoint the trials could not wait for
question: Does HPV vaccination prevent invasive cervical cancer?
balance: The trials proved precancer prevention (Shelf #216); the cancer endpoint could only come from registries, and two of the world’s best now agree. In Sweden, invasive cervical cancer’s adjusted rate ratio for vaccinated women was 0.37 [0.21–0.57] — and 0.12 [0.00–0.34] when vaccination came before age 17. In England, cohorts offered the vaccine at 12–13 had 87% lower cervical cancer rates than unvaccinated cohorts, with a clean gradient by age at offer. Both effects sit far beyond this library’s 0.5 observational floor, with the age gradient confounding would struggle to fake. LIKELY rather than the top tier because the design is observational and the cohorts are still young: lifetime magnitude is not yet in any record. Proposed stamp LIKELY — proposed, pending the developer’s review.

title: Tdap in pregnancy: antibodies across the placenta, 91% programme effectiveness in the newborn’s first months
question: Does Tdap vaccination in pregnancy protect the newborn against pertussis?
balance: The mechanism is randomised and the outcome is measured where it matters. A small double-blind trial showed Tdap at 30–32 weeks puts high pertussis-antibody concentrations into the newborn (68.8 vs 14.0 EU/mL at birth), still present at two months, with no safety signal in 48 women. England’s national programme then measured the clinical claim: 91% effectiveness [84–95] against confirmed pertussis in infants under 3 months, with cases in that age group falling 78% in the programme’s first year. LIKELY, with the fence printed: the effectiveness is observational (screening method), and the trial’s size proves mechanism, not rare-event safety. Proposed stamp LIKELY — proposed, pending the developer’s review.

title: The dengue vaccine serostatus lesson: protection for the previously infected, harm for the never-infected
question: Does the dengue vaccine CYD-TDV (Dengvaxia) protect against dengue — and in whom can it cause harm?
balance: One reanalysis, two opposite truths. Pooling the CYD-TDV trials by baseline serostatus (Sridhar 2018): in previously infected children the vaccine cut hospitalisation for dengue by about two-thirds (HR 0.32 [0.23–0.45]) — and in never-infected children it raised hospitalisation risk (HR 1.75 [1.14–2.70]), the antibody-dependent-enhancement pattern made real. The trials’ original pooled efficacy was the average of a benefit and a harm. POSSIBLE grades the knowledge, not the product: the benefit and the harm are each credible within their subgroup, and the shelf’s claim is the split itself. Proposed stamp POSSIBLE — proposed, pending the developer’s review.

title: Malaria vaccines: R21 prevents most first-year episodes; RTS,S a third over four years — mortality untested

title: Hepatitis B vaccination in diabetes: the standard vaccine leaves a third unprotected — the 2-dose CpG vaccine leaves a tenth
question: In adults with diabetes, does the 2-dose CpG-adjuvanted hepatitis B vaccine protect more of them than the standard 3-dose vaccine?
balance: Diabetes blunts hepatitis B vaccine response so reliably that the pivotal phase 3 trial made diabetic seroprotection its primary endpoint — and the standard 3-dose alum vaccine protected only 65.1% of its diabetic participants (58.5% at ages 60–70). The 2-dose CpG-adjuvanted vaccine protected 90.0% (85.8% in the older subgroup), with one fewer visit. title: What moves vaccine uptake: reminders add ~8 points; a presumptive ‘announcement’ added 5.4
question: What actually moves vaccine uptake: patient reminders, and how clinicians offer?
balance: Two different levers, both randomised. Patient reminder and recall systems — letters, postcards, calls, texts — raise immunisation receipt by a pooled 8 percentage points across 55 trials and 138,625 participants (RR 1.28; Cochrane, moderate certainty). And how the clinician opens the conversation matters: training clinics to make a presumptive ‘announcement’ rather than open a discussion raised HPV vaccine initiation by 5.4 percentage points in a 30-clinic randomised trial, while conversation training did nothing. LIKELY for the uptake claim as asked — the reminder half rests on one of the largest randomised evidence bases in implementation science. title: Exercise dose for blood pressure: isometric training network meta-analysis
question: In adults, how do exercise modes — especially isometric training — compare for lowering resting blood pressure, and what dose maintains the benefit?

Effects are on a surrogate outcome (resting blood pressure), not on cardiovascular events, and the isometric estimate rests on far fewer trials than the aerobic estimate. title: Aerobic vs resistance vs combined training for A1c — DARE trial
question: In type 2 diabetes, how do aerobic training, resistance training and combined training compare for lowering hemoglobin A1c?
balance: LIKELY: Two large randomised trials point the same way — combined aerobic plus resistance training lowers hemoglobin A1c more than either mode alone. In DARE, combined training gave an additional -0.46 percentage point versus aerobic alone and -0.59 percentage point versus resistance alone; in HART-D only the combination group improved hemoglobin A1c versus control (-0.34%). A 47-trial meta-analysis found structured exercise overall lowered hemoglobin A1c by -0.67%, with larger falls above 150 minutes per week. balance: POSSIBLE: For young, active adults with an acute ACL tear, the KANON strategy trial found rehabilitation plus early reconstruction was not superior to rehabilitation with optional delayed reconstruction at 5 years (mean KOOS4 change 42.9 versus 44.9 points; between-group difference 2.0 points, 95% CI -8.5 to 4.5; P=0.54), and about half of the rehab-first group never needed surgery by 5 years (30 of 59, 51%, had delayed reconstruction). title: Cardiac rehab after MI: mortality evidence
question: Does exercise-based cardiac rehabilitation after myocardial infarction / coronary heart disease reduce mortality?
balance: POSSIBLE — Tier C (mortality claim; developer's personal ruling required). Pooled older trials show a relative reduction in cardiovascular mortality, but the largest single modern-era trial of rehabilitation as actually delivered (RAMIT) was null for mortality, and the 2021 Cochrane update's short-term estimates for all-cause and cardiovascular mortality both cross 1.0, with cardiovascular mortality benefit appearing only at medium/long-term follow-up in fewer trials. title: Exercise to prevent falls in older adults — Otago
question: Does exercise — including the Otago home strength-and-balance programme — prevent falls in community-dwelling older adults?
balance: LIKELY — exercise reduces falls in community-dwelling older adults: the founding Otago trial in women aged 80+ cut the fall rate from 1.34 to 0.87 falls per year, the Otago meta-analysis gives a relative fall rate ratio of 0.68, and the Cochrane synthesis (high-certainty) gives a relative rate ratio of 0.77, equivalent on its illustrative absolute risks to 195 fewer falls per 1,000 people over a year. Balance-and-functional and multiple-type programmes work; walking, dance or resistance training alone are uncertain. A mortality signal in the small Otago meta-analysis is not relied on for this stamp. Proposed stamp LIKELY — proposed, pending the developer’s review.

title: Tendinopathy: loading programmes vs injections
question: For tendinopathy, do loading (exercise) programmes beat, match or lose to injections — and which loading programme?
balance: POSSIBLE — the one direct head-to-head (LEAP, gluteal tendinopathy) found education plus exercise beat a corticosteroid injection on global improvement at both 8 weeks (absolute risk difference 19.9%) and 52 weeks (20.4%), while pain at 52 weeks no longer differed; the steroid's advantage is early and short-lived. Among loading programmes themselves, heavy slow resistance matched eccentric training for Achilles tendinopathy and progressive tendon-loading beat eccentric exercise for patellar tendinopathy — so loading works, the exact recipe matters less, and no loading-vs-injection trial exists for Achilles or patellar tendons in this pack. That single direct injection comparison is why the stamp is POSSIBLE, not higher. Proposed stamp POSSIBLE — proposed, pending the developer’s review.

title: Concussion: strict rest vs early activity
question: After concussion, does strict rest help recovery, or does early, graduated activity do better?
balance: LIKELY — strict rest does not help and may harm: prescribed 5-day strict rest produced more symptoms and slower resolution than usual care (Thomas 2015). Early activity helps when it is prescribed and dosed: subsymptom-threshold aerobic exercise sped median recovery from 17 to 13 days (Leddy 2019) and replicated with a relative 48% lower risk of persistent symptoms (Leddy 2021). Generic 'resume activity at 72 hours' advice was null on intention-to-treat in the larger PedCARE trial, with benefit only in adherent participants — so the claim is for prescribed, targeted early activity, not simply telling patients to push through. Evidence is in adolescents/young people; adults are extrapolation. Proposed stamp LIKELY — proposed, pending the developer’s review.

title: Periodontal treatment for glycemic control: meta-analyses vs the DPTT null

title: Antibiotic prophylaxis before dental work and endocarditis: no-trial guideline
question: In people at risk of infective endocarditis, does antibiotic prophylaxis before invasive dental procedures prevent endocarditis, serious illness or death compared with no prophylaxis — and what evidence, in the complete absence of randomized trials, supports current guideline recommendations?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — No randomized trial of dental antibiotic prophylaxis for endocarditis has ever been done, in any era: the Cochrane review found no RCTs, controlled trials or cohort studies, only one small case-control study with no significant effect. Guidelines still recommend prophylaxis for the highest-risk patients, resting on observational data — a US study linking invasive dental work to subsequent endocarditis in high-risk people and linking prophylaxis to lower incidence, against an English time-series in which endocarditis rose after prophylaxis was stopped, which cannot prove causation. Tier C: developer ruling — a guideline-only topic resting on observational data for a serious-outcome prevention claim. Proposed grade: MAYBE (weak evidence). title: Fluoride varnish and sealants in children
question: In children and adolescents, do fluoride varnish and pit-and-fissure sealants prevent dental caries compared with placebo, no treatment, or each other?
balance: POSSIBLE — Two Cochrane reviews of randomised trials, both rated moderate quality, support each intervention against doing nothing: fluoride varnish prevented 43% (relative) of the caries increment in permanent teeth and 37% (relative) in primary teeth, and resin-based sealants cut the relative odds of occlusal caries sharply at 2 years, with absolute benefits that grow with baseline caries risk. Head-to-head, which of the two is better is unresolved (very low certainty). Effects come mostly from older, higher-caries populations, so absolute benefit in a low-caries, fluoridated population will be smaller. title: Wisdom teeth: prophylactic removal vs watchful waiting
question: In adolescents and adults with asymptomatic, disease-free impacted wisdom teeth, does prophylactic surgical removal improve health-related quality of life, dental-arch outcomes, or long-term harm to neighbouring teeth compared with retention and watchful waiting?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — There is almost no comparative evidence to settle this common operation: the Cochrane review found exactly one small RCT (on incisor crowding after orthodontic treatment, which found no clinically significant benefit from removal) and one prospective cohort (very low certainty, suggesting retained impacted teeth may raise periodontitis risk for the neighbouring second molar). No included study measured quality of life, costs, or the harms on either side — pericoronitis and cysts if retained, nerve injury and dry socket if removed. Removal for crowding prevention is not justified by the one RCT; beyond that, shared decision-making with regular review of retained teeth is what the evidence supports. Proposed stamp MAYBE (weak evidence) — proposed, pending the developer’s review.

title: Implants vs dentures: eating and nutrition in older adults

title: Chlorhexidine oral care in the ICU: VAP benefit vs possible mortality signal
question: In mechanically ventilated ICU patients, does routine oral care with chlorhexidine reduce ventilator-associated pneumonia without increasing mortality, and does de-adopting it change ICU mortality?

title: Pre-emptive pharmacogenomic panels: test once, before the first prescription
question: Does pre-emptive testing with a multi-gene pharmacogenomic panel, applied before a first prescription, reduce clinically relevant adverse drug reactions compared with standard care?
balance: One large trial carries this shelf. PREPARE, a cluster-randomised crossover implementation study in seven European countries, tested a 12-gene panel before a first prescription and found clinically relevant adverse drug reactions in 21.0% vs 27.7% of patients with an actionable result (OR 0.70) and 21.5% vs 28.6% across all patients (OR 0.70) — about a 30% relative reduction, roughly 7 percentage points absolute in both analyses. The trial was open-label, the outcome was adverse reactions rather than death or hospitalisation, and 97.7% of participants reported European, Mediterranean, or Middle Eastern ethnicity, so the panel's yield in other ancestries is less certain. No second randomized trial of a pre-emptive panel exists yet; the single-gene questions PREPARE bundles are carded on their own shelves in this slate. Proposed stamp POSSIBLE — proposed, pending the developer's review.

title: CYP2C19 testing for clopidogrel after PCI: escalate carriers, or de-escalate everyone else?
question: After PCI, does CYP2C19 genotype-guided selection of P2Y12 inhibitor therapy improve ischemic outcomes or reduce bleeding compared with a single default strategy?
balance: The two trials test opposite directions of the same idea, and they land differently. TAILOR-PCI asked whether escalating CYP2C19 loss-of-function carriers from clopidogrel to ticagrelor prevents ischemic events: in carriers the primary endpoint was 4.0% vs 5.9% (HR 0.66 [95% CI 0.43–1.02]; P=.06) — a 34% relative reduction that did not reach significance, in a trial powered for an implausibly large HR of 0.50. POPular Genetics asked the reverse in primary PCI for STEMI — genotype-guided de-escalation, noncarriers to clopidogrel — and met noninferiority for the combined thrombotic outcome (5.1% vs 5.9%) with less bleeding (9.8% vs 12.5%; HR 0.78). Neither trial showed a mortality difference. Proposed split stamp: POSSIBLE for escalation of carriers, LIKELY for de-escalation in STEMI primary PCI — proposed, pending the developer's review.

title: Pharmacogenetic warfarin dosing: two trials in one journal issue disagreed
question: Does genotype-guided warfarin dosing (CYP2C9, VKORC1, CYP4F2) improve anticoagulation control or clinical outcomes compared with clinical dosing algorithms or standard loading?
balance: Three randomized trials, three different comparators, and no mortality answer anywhere. COAG (n=1,015), testing genotype-plus-clinical dosing against a clinical algorithm with blinded doses, found no difference in time in therapeutic range at 4 weeks (45.2% vs 45.4%) — and a significant race interaction, with black patients doing worse on genotype guidance (P=0.003 for interaction). EU-PACT (n=455), testing genotype-guided loading against a fixed 3-day loading regimen, found more time in range over 12 weeks (67.4% vs 60.3%) and faster time to a therapeutic INR (21 vs 29 days). GIFT (n=1,650, elective hip/knee arthroplasty, age ≥65) found fewer composite events on genotype guidance (10.8% vs 14.7%), driven by INR ≥4.0 (56 vs 77 events); major bleeding was 2 vs 8 events and there were no deaths in either group. The fairest reading: genotype guidance helps most where the comparator is weakest and the setting is initiation — a process benefit with an unproven clinical dividend, never a demonstrated survival or major-bleeding benefit. Developer's stamp (Nov 8, 2026): MAYBE (weak evidence).

title: DPYD testing before fluoropyrimidines: dose the carriers down, before the first cycle
question: Does prospective DPYD genotyping with genotype-guided dose reduction reduce severe fluoropyrimidine toxicity in patients starting fluorouracil or capecitabine?
balance: There is no randomized trial here, and there will not be one: randomising known DPYD variant carriers to full-dose fluoropyrimidine is not an ethical design. What exists is two large prospective safety studies pointing the same way. Screening for DPYD*2A alone and halving carriers' starting dose cut grade ≥3 toxicity in carriers from 73% in historical full-dose controls to 28%, and drug-induced death from 10% to 0% (Deenen). Screening for four variants and reducing dose cut carriers' relative risk of severe toxicity from 2.87 (historical, full dose) to 1.31 against wild-type patients for DPYD*2A, with the same direction for the other variants (Henricks) — though carriers on reduced doses still had more severe toxicity than wild-type patients (39% vs 23%), and two variants may need a 50% rather than 25% reduction. The comparison is prospective-versus-historical, not randomized, and that fence is on both cards; the size and consistency of the toxicity reduction is why the stamp is not lower. Proposed stamp LIKELY — proposed, pending the developer's review.

title: Cascade screening for familial hypercholesterolemia: finding relatives is proven — helping them live longer is not
question: Does cascade screening of relatives of people with familial hypercholesterolemia identify new cases — and does identifying them improve cardiovascular outcomes?
balance: Cascade screening does the first half of its job measurably well. Screening toddlers at immunisation visits found familial hypercholesterolemia in 0.4% of children — and, by testing the parents, one affected parent per affected child: 8 people identified per 1,000 children screened (Wald). A 2026 randomized trial of a web-based, patient-mediated cascade programme (CATCH) doubled relatives' testing uptake vs usual care (30.4% vs 16.7%; OR 2.18) and doubled new-case identification (17.0% vs 8.1%). But even the better arm left 70% of eligible relatives untested, and no trial — randomized or otherwise — has shown that cascade screening reduces heart attacks or deaths; the outcome benefit is inferred from the proven benefit of treating FH once found, not demonstrated for the screening strategy itself. Detection is LIKELY real; outcome benefit is unproven. Proposed stamp MAYBE (weak evidence) — proposed, pending the developer's review.

title: Aspirin dose in Lynch syndrome: CaPP3 asks whether 100 mg does what 600 mg did
question: In carriers of Lynch syndrome, are lower daily aspirin doses (100 mg or 300 mg) noninferior to 600 mg for preventing Lynch syndrome cancers — the dose question left open by CAPP2?
balance: This shelf does not re-ask whether aspirin works in Lynch syndrome: that question — CAPP2's 600 mg daily, with colorectal cancer protection emerging at 10 years (ITT HR 0.65) — is home on Shelf #220, and CAPP2 is not re-carded here under the one-home rule. This shelf asks the question CAPP2 left open and Shelf #220 flagged as unreported: the dose. CaPP3 (n=1,866) compared 100 mg and 300 mg against 600 mg and formally concluded noninferiority for NEITHER lower dose: for 100 mg the intention-to-treat estimates sat inside the 1.5 margin (HR 0.97 [95% CI 0.67–1.42]; IRR 0.94 [0.65–1.38]) but the per-protocol time-to-first-cancer analysis did not (HR 1.00 [0.61–1.63]); for 300 mg both analyses missed. What the lower dose clearly bought was safety: serious bleeding events over 5 years occurred in 0 patients on 100 mg, 3 (0.5%) on 300 mg, and 11 (1.5%) on 600 mg. The authors' own reading — 100 mg looked similar for cancer with fewer harms, without formal noninferiority — is the honest summary. Proposed stamp POSSIBLE — proposed, pending the developer's review.

title: Risk-reducing surgery in BRCA carriers: large observational benefits, no randomized trial
question: In women carrying BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutations, do risk-reducing mastectomy and risk-reducing salpingo-oophorectomy reduce cancer incidence and mortality?
balance: SLOW-LANE SHELF — flagged for the developer's personal ruling: every mortality figure on this shelf is observational, because randomising BRCA carriers to surgery or no surgery has never been done. The cohorts are large and consistent. In the prospective PROSE consortium cohort (n=2,482), no breast cancers occurred in 247 women after risk-reducing mastectomy vs 98 of 1,372 without it, and salpingo-oophorectomy was associated with lower ovarian cancer (HR 0.14–0.28 by prior-cancer status) and lower all-cause mortality (10% vs 3%; HR 0.40 [95% CI 0.26–0.61]). In an international registry cohort (n=5,783), oophorectomy was associated with an 80% relative reduction in ovarian/fallopian/peritoneal cancer (HR 0.20) and, in women cancer-free at baseline, a 77% relative reduction in all-cause mortality to age 70 (HR 0.23). The earliest matched study (Rebbeck 2002) found the same direction (coelomic cancer HR 0.04; breast cancer HR 0.47). A 2025 international cohort of 5,290 young carriers already diagnosed with breast cancer likewise associated both surgeries with better overall survival (adjusted HR 0.65 and 0.58). Consistency across four cohorts and two decades is real; so is the confounding — women who choose surgery differ from women who do not, and immortal-time and selection biases run in surgery's favour. Proposed grade: POSSIBLE. Tier C — built Nov 8, 2026 and held for the developer’s personal verdict; no approval stamp is claimed for this shelf.

title: Telling people their APOE result: the REVEAL trials found no psychological harm — in people who asked to know
question: Does disclosing APOE genotype for Alzheimer's disease risk cause psychological harm — and can disclosure be done safely with brief protocols?
balance: Two randomized trials from the REVEAL programme agree. In REVEAL I (n=162 asymptomatic adult children of Alzheimer's patients), disclosure of APOE genotype produced no significant differences vs nondisclosure in time-averaged anxiety (4.5 vs 4.4; P=0.84), depression (8.8 vs 8.7; P=0.98) or test-related distress (6.9 vs 7.5; P=0.61) over a year — including in the subgroup who learned they carried ε4; ε4-negative participants had less test-related distress than ε4-positive participants (P=0.01). In the REVEAL follow-on noninferiority trial (n=343), condensed disclosure protocols — by genetic counsellors or by physicians — were noninferior to standard multi-session genetic counselling on anxiety and depression at 12 months, with all mean scores well below clinical concern cut-offs. The fence is selection: participants actively sought testing, were screened, and people with high baseline distress fared worse afterwards regardless of result — baseline anxiety and depression strongly predicted post-disclosure scores. 'No measurable harm in trial volunteers' is the claim; it is LIKELY true there and unproven in unselected direct-to-consumer settings. Proposed stamp LIKELY — proposed, pending the developer's review.

title: Newborn genomic screening: it finds risk standard screening misses — outcome benefit untested
question: Should genome or exome sequencing be added to standard newborn screening — what does it find, what does it do to families, and does it improve children's outcomes?
balance: The yield is real and the outcome evidence is absent — the definition of this slate's second MAYBE (weak evidence) shelf. In the BabySeq randomized pilot, sequencing 159 newborns found a childhood-onset disease risk in 9.4% — none anticipated from clinical or family history — plus carrier status in 88% and pharmacogenomic findings reported in 5%. Its companion randomized analysis found no persistent negative psychosocial effect on families, even in parents whose infant received a monogenic risk finding. The GUARDIAN study showed the model scales: 4,000 diverse New York newborns screened for 156 early-onset actionable conditions (plus an optional 99 neurodevelopmental disorders), 72% of approached families consenting, 99.6% of tests completed, and a 3.7% screen-positive rate including treatable conditions current screening cannot detect. What no study shows is the step that matters: that sequencing newborns makes children healthier than standard screening does. GUARDIAN is a single-group feasibility study still enrolling toward 100,000; BabySeq was a pilot. Proposed stamp MAYBE (weak evidence) — proposed, pending the developer's review.

title: HLA-B*57:01 before abacavir: the pharmacogenetic test that eliminated its reaction
question: Does prospective HLA-B*57:01 screening before starting abacavir prevent abacavir hypersensitivity reactions in people with HIV-1?
balance: The cleanest result in pharmacogenetics. PREDICT-1 (n=1,956, double-blind, randomized) screened prospectively for HLA-B*57:01 and excluded carriers from abacavir: immunologically confirmed hypersensitivity fell to 0% with screening vs 2.7% without (P<0.001), clinically diagnosed hypersensitivity fell from 7.8% to 3.4% (P<0.001), and the test's negative predictive value was 100% (positive predictive value 47.9% — about half of carriers would have reacted). A prospective Western Australian cohort had already shown the same pattern in practice: no hypersensitivity cases among 148 allele-negative recipients after screening was introduced. The fence is ancestry and era: the trial population was 84% white, allele prevalence (5.6% here) and predictive values differ across populations, and abacavir is a smaller part of modern HIV therapy than in 2008. Within its question, though, the evidence is a definitive randomized elimination of the immunologically confirmed reaction. Proposed stamp LIKELY — proposed, pending the developer's review.

title: BPH combination therapy: an alpha-blocker plus a 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor beats either drug alone
question: In men with benign prostatic hyperplasia at risk of progression, does combination therapy (alpha-blocker plus 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor) prevent clinical progression, retention and surgery better than either drug alone?
balance: Two large, long, double-blind trials answer this the same way. In MTOPS (3,047 men, mean follow-up 4.5 years), overall clinical progression fell 39% relative on doxazosin and 34% relative on finasteride versus placebo, and 66% relative on the combination — significantly more than either drug alone; retention and invasive therapy fell on finasteride-containing arms, not on doxazosin alone. In CombAT (4,844 men with prostate volume ≥30 cm³), dutasteride plus tamsulosin beat tamsulosin on acute retention or BPH surgery over 4 years and beat both monotherapies on clinical progression and symptoms. The finasteride-alone anchor (PLESS, 3,040 men) shows where the retention/surgery benefit comes from: surgery 10% placebo vs 5% finasteride, retention 7% vs 3% over four years. The fence is selection: these were men with larger prostates and progression risk — the combination buys little for a small prostate or pure symptom relief, and it buys the side effects of both classes. Proposed stamp LIKELY — proposed, pending the developer's review.
