title: Thiazides to prevent kidney stone recurrence: the one large modern trial was null
question: Do thiazide diuretics prevent recurrence of calcium kidney stones?
balance: For decades thiazides were standard prevention on the strength of small old trials. The one large modern test removed the support: NOSTONE (416 patients with recurrent calcium stones, median follow-up 2.9 years) found recurrence in 59% on placebo, 59% on hydrochlorothiazide 12.5 mg, 56% on 25 mg and 49% on 50 mg — rate ratios 1.33, 1.24 and 0.92, no dose relation (P=0.66), with more hypokalemia, gout, new diabetes, skin allergy and creatinine rises on the drug. The older record is genuinely positive but small and soft: Laerum & Larsen's 50-patient general-practice trial (probability of staying stone-free 75% thiazide vs 45% placebo) and Ettinger's chlorthalidone trial, whose own authors warned that even placebo arms beat historical predictions. The syntheses split by era and population: the 2013 ACP review found thiazides halved recurrence (RR 0.52) in multiple-stone formers, and a 2025 updated meta-analysis still pools to RR 0.63 — but restricted to hypercalciuric patients and built from those same small trials. The honest summary: unselected recurrence prevention at modern doses is a null; a hypercalciuria-selected benefit remains possible and untested at NOSTONE's scale. Proposed stamp SPLIT: LIKELY null for hydrochlorothiazide at 12.5–50 mg in unselected recurrent calcium stone formers (NOSTONE) / POSSIBLE benefit in hypercalciuric patients, where the older small trials were done — proposed, pending the developer's review.

title: Medical expulsive therapy for ureteral stones: the large trials were null overall; a larger-stone signal survives in one subgroup
question: Do alpha-blockers (tamsulosin) or calcium-channel blockers (nifedipine), given as medical expulsive therapy, increase spontaneous passage of ureteral stones?
balance: Medical expulsive therapy was adopted on meta-analyses of small trials; the large trials then failed to confirm it. SUSPEND (1,167 patients, stones ≤10 mm, 24 UK hospitals) found no need for further intervention in 80% on placebo, 81% on tamsulosin and 80% on nifedipine — adjusted risk differences of 1.3 and 0.5 percentage points, both null, with no subgroup rescue by stone size or location in its full HTA analysis. The US STONE trial (512 emergency-department patients, stones <9 mm) found passage in 50% on tamsulosin vs 47% on placebo (RR 1.05, P=0.60). One signal survives, fenced where it belongs: in Furyk's distal-stone trial the overall result was null (87.0% vs 81.9%), but the prespecified subgroup with 5–10 mm stones passed in 83.3% on tamsulosin vs 61.0% on placebo (difference 22.4 percentage points, NNT 4.5) — a subgroup of 77 patients inside a null trial, hypothesis-grade, not a licence to treat every colic. Proposed stamp SPLIT: LIKELY no benefit for stones ≤5 mm or unselected ureteric colic / POSSIBLE for distal stones 5–10 mm — proposed, pending the developer's review.

title: Overactive bladder drugs compared: small symptom gains, traded against dry mouth — combination adds a little more
question: Head to head, how do overactive bladder drugs — antimuscarinics and the beta-3 agonist mirabegron, alone and combined — compare on symptoms and side effects?
balance: No overactive-bladder drug is a large-effect drug; the comparison is about small margins and which side effects a patient will accept. In STAR, flexible-dose solifenacin beat tolterodine ER on urgency episodes, incontinence, urge incontinence and pad use — with a dosing asymmetry fenced on its card. In BESIDE, patients still incontinent on solifenacin 5 mg gained more from adding mirabegron 50 mg than from staying on solifenacin 5 mg, and the combination matched solifenacin 10 mg on key endpoints while beating it on micturitions. The 64-trial network meta-analysis (46,666 patients) puts mirabegron 50 mg at efficacy comparable to most antimuscarinics, with significantly less dry mouth, constipation and urinary retention than most comparators, and the solifenacin-plus-mirabegron combination ahead of mirabegron alone on some outcomes. Mirabegron's own placebo-controlled trials live on Shelf #149 and the oxybutynin–tolterodine head-to-head on Shelf #243; this shelf is the comparison layer above them. Proposed stamp POSSIBLE — proposed, pending the developer's review.

title: Stress incontinence: pelvic floor training first, or straight to a midurethral sling?
question: In women with stress urinary incontinence, how does initial pelvic floor muscle training (physiotherapy) compare with initial midurethral-sling surgery?
balance: This is the rare shelf with a direct randomised answer. Labrie's multicentre trial (460 women) compared initial midurethral-sling surgery with initial physiotherapy, crossover allowed: at 12 months subjective improvement was 90.8% with surgery versus 64.4% with physiotherapy (absolute difference 26.4 percentage points), subjective cure 85.2% versus 53.4%, objective cure 76.5% versus 58.8% — while 49.0% of the physiotherapy group crossed over to surgery (and 11.2% of the surgery group crossed to physiotherapy). The 12-year follow-up (2025) found crossover from physiotherapy had reached 86.9% among responders, and women who had physiotherapy only remained about 50 percentage points behind on improvement — on a 47.7% questionnaire response, fenced on its card. Physiotherapy itself is not placebo: Cochrane's review of PFMT versus no or inactive treatment found women with stress incontinence eight times more likely to report cure (56% vs 6%). The sling-versus-sling and sling-versus-colposuspension record lives on Shelf #249 and is not repeated here. The choice the evidence frames: surgery wins on cure at one year and at twelve; training is non-invasive, helps about half, and half of its starters end up in theatre anyway. Proposed stamp LIKELY — proposed, pending the developer's review.

title: Desmopressin for nocturia: fewer night voids by a fraction, bought against hyponatremia
question: Does low-dose desmopressin reduce nocturnal voiding in adults with nocturia, and at what hyponatremia cost?
balance: Low-dose desmopressin orally disintegrating tablet works a little, measurably, in both sexes — and its risk is the kind that has to be managed, not merely disclosed. In men (Weiss 2013, 385 patients), 50 µg and 75 µg cut nocturnal voids by 0.37 and 0.41 more than placebo and doubled the odds of a ≥33% response (OR 1.98 and 2.04), delaying the first void by about 40 minutes. In women (Sand 2013, 261 patients), 25 µg cut voids by 0.22 versus placebo (P=0.028), raised ≥33%-responder odds (OR 1.85), and delayed the first void by 49 minutes. Sodium is the fence: in the men's trial, sodium <130 mmol/L occurred in 2 men on 50 µg but 9 on 75 µg; the pooled hyponatremia analysis (Juul 2017) shows risk rises with dose, age, low baseline sodium and reduced kidney function, and that sex-specific minimum dosing (25 µg women, 50 µg men) plus baseline and early sodium monitoring would have screened out every clinically significant case in the trial data. Fractions of a void a night, in exchange for a monitoring obligation. Proposed stamp POSSIBLE — proposed, pending the developer's review.

title: Antibiotic duration for UTI in men: 7 versus 14 days — afebrile men are settled; febrile men are not
question: In men with urinary tract infection, is 7 days of antibiotics enough compared with 14 days?
balance: The men's question splits on fever. For afebrile men, the one dedicated trial — Drekonja 2021, 272 VA patients on ciprofloxacin or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole — found 7 days noninferior to 14 for symptom resolution (93.1% vs 90.2% in the as-treated analysis); that trial's home is Shelf #316, where it sits with the women's pyelonephritis and bloodstream-infection duration trials, and it is pointed to here rather than re-carded. For febrile UTI, the only randomised duration evidence including men points the other way at short-term follow-up: van Nieuwkoop 2017 (200 randomised, ciprofloxacin 7 vs 14 days) confirmed noninferiority in women but found 7 days inferior in men at the 10–18-day visit (clinical cure 86% vs 98%; difference −11.2 percentage points), even though by 70–84 days the men's long-term cure met noninferiority. So: a week for the afebrile man rests on one good trial; a week for the febrile man rests on a subgroup that failed its short-term test and recovered later. Proposed stamp POSSIBLE — proposed, pending the developer's review.

title: Cranberry products for UTI prevention: the 2023 Cochrane reversal, and the primary trials that explain it
question: Do cranberry products prevent urinary tract infections — and in whom?
balance: The headline lives on Shelf #50 and is pointed to, not re-carded: the 2023 Cochrane update (Williams; 50 studies, 8,857 participants) reversed the review's earlier no-benefit position, finding cranberry products reduced symptomatic, culture-verified UTI (RR 0.70 [95% CI 0.58–0.84], moderate certainty) — with benefit concentrated in women with recurrent UTI (RR 0.74), children (RR 0.46) and people susceptible after an intervention (RR 0.47), and little or no benefit in elderly institutionalised people (RR 0.93), pregnant women (RR 1.06) or adults with neuromuscular bladder dysfunction (RR 0.97). This shelf cards the primary trials underneath that pattern: Kontiokari 2001 (open trial; first recurrence at 6 months 16% cranberry-lingonberry vs 36% control), Maki 2016 (clinical UTI episodes cut, IRR 0.61 — while culture-confirmed time-to-UTI was null, HR 0.97), Barbosa-Cesnik 2011 (blinded juice trial in college women: recurrence 20.0% cranberry vs 14.0% placebo — null, in the wrong direction), and Juthani-Mehta 2016 (nursing-home women: bacteriuria-plus-pyuria 29.1% vs 29.0%, OR 1.01 — null, matching Cochrane's elderly subgroup). Product, dose and population are the whole story, exactly as Shelf #50's balance warns. Proposed stamp POSSIBLE — proposed, pending the developer's review.

title: Finasteride and prostate cancer prevention (PCPT): fewer diagnoses, mostly low-grade — and no survival difference at 18 years
question: Does finasteride prevent prostate cancer, what did the high-grade signal amount to, and did prevention change survival?
balance: The PCPT itself — Thompson 2003: prostate cancer in 18.4% on finasteride vs 24.4% on placebo over 7 years, a 24.8% relative reduction in prevalence, with Gleason 7–10 tumours more common on finasteride (6.4% vs 5.1% of men analysed) — is carded on Shelf #218 (finasteride and dutasteride prevention), and the PSA-screening frame around it is Shelf #212; neither is re-carded here. This shelf adds what #218 does not carry: the long view. At up to 18 years (Thompson 2013), cancer had been diagnosed in 10.5% on finasteride vs 14.9% on placebo (relative risk 0.70), high-grade cancer in 3.5% vs 3.0% (relative risk 1.17, P=0.05) — and 15-year survival was 78.0% vs 78.2% (HR for death 1.02), with no survival difference after diagnosis in either grade group. A Medicare-claims extension (Unger 2018; median follow-up 16 years) found the diagnosis reduction persisted (HR 0.79) with no rebound after the drug stopped (HR 1.10 beyond 7.5 years) — observational linkage, corroborating the trial, and fenced as such. Prevention here means fewer diagnoses, concentrated in low-grade disease, with no demonstrated survival gain and a high-grade signal that shrank but never fully vanished. Proposed stamp SPLIT: LIKELY fewer prostate-cancer diagnoses, mostly low-grade / LIKELY no demonstrated survival benefit at 15–18 years — proposed, pending the developer's review.

title: Low-risk localised prostate cancer: monitoring vs surgery vs radiation (ProtecT) — cancer death ~3% at 15 years in all three arms
question: In men with PSA-detected localised prostate cancer, how do active monitoring, radical prostatectomy and radiotherapy compare on death, metastases and progression?
balance: ProtecT randomised 1,643 men with PSA-detected localised prostate cancer to active monitoring, prostatectomy or radiotherapy. At 15 years (Hamdy 2023), prostate-cancer death was 3.1% on monitoring, 2.2% on surgery and 2.9% on radiotherapy (P=0.53) — about 3% in every arm — and death from any cause was 21.7% overall, similar across arms. What radical treatment bought was not survival but spread: metastases developed in 9.4% on monitoring versus 4.7% (surgery) and 5.0% (radiotherapy); clinical progression in 25.9% versus 10.5% and 11.0%; long-term androgen deprivation in 12.7% versus 7.2% and 7.7%. And monitoring was often not treatment deferred forever but treatment chosen: 24.4% of the monitoring group were alive without any prostate-cancer treatment at 15 years. The harms are asymmetric and durable (Donovan 2016): prostatectomy worst for sexual function and continence throughout; radiotherapy worst early for bowel function, with bloody stools increasing over time. A 2025 secondary analysis adds a biological fence: cribriform-positive disease carried a much higher metastasis risk (HR 3.61), and cribriform-negative men did well on any strategy. TIER C — this shelf carries mortality claims and is flagged for the developer's personal ruling. Proposed grade: LIKELY. title: Melatonin: jet lag vs insomnia — strong for jet lag, small for insomnia
question: Does melatonin help jet lag after crossing time zones, and does it help ordinary insomnia — and are those the same claim?
balance: Two different questions share one bottle, and the evidence splits cleanly. For jet lag, the Cochrane review found 9 of 10 placebo-controlled trials positive when melatonin was taken close to the destination bedtime after flights crossing five or more time zones, with 0.5–5 mg similarly effective and a number needed to treat of 2 — a short-term circadian claim, graded LIKELY. For ordinary insomnia, the pooled effects are minutes, not hours: sleep onset latency fell by 4.0 minutes in the Brzezinski meta-analysis (17 studies, 284 subjects) and total sleep rose by 12.8 minutes; the later Auld review again found its most convincing signal in sleep-onset latency in primary insomnia (P=0.002) across only 12 randomised trials. The Ferracioli-Oda 2013 meta-analysis (sleep latency −7.06 minutes) is carded at its home on Shelf #116 and is not re-carded here. Split stamp: LIKELY for jet lag; POSSIBLE for insomnia sleep-onset. title: Sleep duration and health: the U-curve — an observational shelf
question: Are both short and long habitual sleep associated with higher mortality and cardiovascular events — and how solid is that association?
balance: Every number on this shelf is observational, and every pooled ratio sits between 1.05 and 1.47 — inside the 0.5–2.0 band this library does not treat as solid evidence. The shape is consistent across three large dose-response meta-analyses: risk is lowest at about 7 hours, short sleep carries a mortality relative risk of 1.12 (Cappuccio) rising 6% relative per hour below 7 (Yin), and long sleep carries the larger signal — relative risk 1.30 for death (Cappuccio), 1.39 in Jike's long-sleep pool, and 1.47 at 11 hours in Kwok's spline. Long sleep is also the arm most plausibly explained by reverse causation: sick people sleep longer. Association, consistently shaped, causality unproven. Proposed stamp MAYBE (weak evidence) — proposed, pending the developer's review.

title: Weekend catch-up sleep: the metabolic rescue that wasn't
question: Does sleeping longer on weekends undo the metabolic harm of weekday sleep restriction?
balance: The one randomised test says no. In Depner 2019, 36 healthy young adults lived through repeated 5-hour weekday nights with an ad libitum weekend: they slept only about 1.1 hours more than baseline across the weekend, ate more after dinner and gained weight during restriction, and — once restriction resumed — whole-body, hepatic and muscle insulin sensitivity fell by roughly 9–27% relative to baseline, with circadian phase delayed. The weekend did not protect them. The large observational counterweight (Chaput 2024, 73,513 UK Biobank adults with wrist accelerometry, 8 years) found weekend catch-up sleep was not associated with mortality (HR 1.17 [0.97–1.41] for ≥2 hours) or incident cardiovascular disease (HR 1.05 [0.94–1.18]) — a null that sits inside the not-solid band in any case. Catch-up sleep may feel restorative; as a metabolic strategy it is unproven and, in the laboratory, insufficient. Proposed stamp POSSIBLE — proposed, pending the developer's review.

title: Napping and cardiovascular events — long naps mark risk; short naps do not
question: Is daytime napping associated with cardiovascular disease and death — and does nap length change the answer?
balance: This shelf is one large dose-response pool and its limits. Across 11 prospective cohorts (151,588 participants, mean 11 years), naps of 60 minutes or more were associated with cardiovascular disease (rate ratio 1.82 [1.22–2.71]) and with all-cause mortality (rate ratio 1.27 [1.11–1.45]), while naps under 60 minutes were associated with neither. The dose-response was J-shaped for cardiovascular disease. Every figure is observational: the mortality ratio sits inside the 0.5–2.0 not-solid band, and even the 1.82 cardiovascular ratio — the shelf's largest — stays below the developer's 2.0 floor for solid observational harm. Long naps most plausibly mark poor night sleep, apnea and illness rather than causing events. Proposed stamp MAYBE (weak evidence) — proposed, pending the developer's review.

title: Shift-work disorder: wake agents work modestly; the sleepiness remains
question: In shift-work disorder, do wake-promoting agents (modafinil, armodafinil) improve night-shift sleepiness and performance — and what role does light have?
balance: Two large placebo-controlled trials, one honest message: the wake agents help, modestly, and leave the disorder standing. Modafinil 200 mg before night shifts (209 patients, 3 months) lengthened nighttime sleep latency by 1.7 vs 0.3 minutes, improved clinical symptoms in 74% vs 36%, and cut reported accidents or near-accidents on the commute home (29% vs 54%) — yet treated patients remained excessively sleepy with impaired performance. Armodafinil 150 mg (254 workers, 12 weeks) raised mean sleep latency from 2.3 to 5.3 minutes vs 2.4 to 2.8 on placebo and improved clinician ratings (79% vs 59%). Neither drug harmed daytime sleep. For bright light — part of this shelf's question — no pivotal randomised trial in shift-work disorder was verified for carding; light remains a guideline-supported adjunct with indirect evidence, and the shelf says so rather than borrowing strength from the depression shelves. Proposed stamp POSSIBLE — proposed, pending the developer's review.

title: Bright light therapy beyond seasonal depression: real in nonseasonal depression, unproven in dementia
question: Does bright light therapy help conditions other than seasonal affective disorder — nonseasonal depression, bipolar depression, dementia?
balance: Beyond winter depression, light's record divides by diagnosis. In nonseasonal major depression, the CAN-BIND trial (Lam 2016, 122 patients) found light monotherapy (effect size d=0.80) and light-plus-fluoxetine (d=1.11) beat sham-plus-placebo while fluoxetine alone did not (d=0.24) — a single well-built trial, graded POSSIBLE. In bipolar depression, one 46-patient trial (Sit 2018) found midday bright light produced remission in 68.2% vs 22.2% on dim red placebo (adjusted OR 12.6), with no polarity switches — promising, small, single-centre in spirit, also POSSIBLE. The older meta-analysis (Golden 2005) agrees in direction for nonseasonal depression (effect size 0.53 across 3 studies) but found adjunctive light added nothing (effect size −0.01). In dementia, the Cochrane pool found no effect on cognition, sleep or behaviour, and the one large factorial trial's light effects (0.9 MMSE points) came packaged with melatonin arms — MAYBE (weak evidence). Split stamp as proposed. Proposed split stamp — proposed, pending the developer's review.

title: Restless legs: iron first — and the augmentation price of dopamine agonists
question: In restless legs syndrome, does iron treatment (especially with low ferritin) improve symptoms, and how often do dopamine agonists cause augmentation over time?
balance: Iron first is a dose-and-status claim, not a slogan. The Cochrane pool (Trotti 2019; 10 studies, 428 participants) found iron beat placebo on restless-legs severity (IRLS mean difference −3.78 [95% CI −6.25 to −1.31], moderate-certainty). The dose story matters: 1,000 mg ferric carboxymaltose improved IRLS by 8.9 vs 4.0 points over placebo at day 28 (Allen 2011), while a single 500 mg dose did not separate from placebo at week 6 (Cho 2018) — under-dosing iron and declaring it failed is the trap this shelf exists to prevent. The harm half is the dopamine agonists: augmentation — symptoms starting earlier, spreading, intensifying on treatment — appeared in 42% of a long-term pramipexole cohort (mean onset 16.5 months) and in 20% with definite/highly-suggestive signs in a community dopamine-treated sample, accruing at roughly 8% per year. Split stamp: POSSIBLE for iron benefit; LIKELY for augmentation as a real long-term harm. Proposed split stamp — proposed, pending the developer's review.

title: CBT-I vs sleeping pills, long-term: the pills stop working when they stop; CBT-I doesn't
question: Head-to-head and long-term, how does cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia compare with hypnotic medication?
balance: Four randomised head-to-head trials, spanning three hypnotics and 24 months, tell one story with unusual consistency. Acutely, CBT-I and medication both work: in Morin 1999 (78 older adults), wake-after-sleep-onset fell 63.5% on combined therapy, 55% on CBT-I, 46.5% on temazepam, 16.9% on placebo. The separation is durability: CBT-I gains were sustained to 24 months while temazepam-alone gains were not; Sivertsen 2006 found CBT-I superior to zopiclone at 6 months (sleep efficiency 90.1% vs 81.9%) with zopiclone indistinguishable from placebo on most outcomes; Jacobs 2004 found CBT beat zolpidem, with drug gains returning toward baseline after discontinuation; and Morin 2009 showed the best long-term remission (68%) came from combined therapy followed by CBT-I alone — continued zolpidem did worse (42%). No card on this shelf duplicates Shelves #231 (suvorexant drug trials) or #437 (digital CBT-I vs placebo): this shelf's question is the comparison itself. title: Deprescribing benzodiazepines and Z-drugs in older adults: EMPOWER — ask the patient, with a taper in hand
question: Can direct patient education get long-term older benzodiazepine users to stop — safely and at scale?
balance: EMPOWER is the rare deprescribing trial that worked by mailing the patient, not lecturing the doctor. Among 303 long-term benzodiazepine users aged 65–95, a brochure describing harms plus a stepwise taper produced discontinuation at 6 months in 27% vs 5% on usual care (risk difference 23% [95% CI 14% to 32%]; number needed to treat 4), with a further 11% reducing dose — and 62% of recipients started the cessation conversation themselves. The programme's larger successor, D-PRESCRIBE (489 patients), replicated the model through pharmacists for inappropriate medicines overall (43% vs 12% discontinued) including sedative-hypnotic users specifically (43.2% vs 9.0%). The systematic-review context (Reeve 2017) shows education-plus-taper interventions yielding discontinuation between 27% and 80% across studies, with mostly no worsening of sleep or withdrawal outcomes. title: Later school start times and teen sleep: Seattle's natural experiment
question: When a school district delays start times, do teenagers actually sleep more — and does anything measurable improve?
balance: Seattle did the experiment policy usually only debates: the district delayed secondary start times by nearly an hour, and researchers measured students objectively before and after. Median daily sleep rose by 34 minutes — gained by waking later, not by going to bed earlier, exactly as circadian biology predicts — median grades rose 4.5%, and attendance improved (Dunster 2018). The wider literature agrees in direction: Bowers & Moyer's meta-analysis (5 longitudinal and 15 cross-sectional comparison studies) found later start times associated with longer sleep, less daytime sleepiness and less tardiness, while warning that longitudinal primary research is thin. This is a natural experiment, not a randomised trial: one district, one pre/post comparison, concurrent changes uncontrolled. Proposed stamp POSSIBLE — proposed, pending the developer's review.

title: Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia: switch to pills early in low-risk patients — and do not add a second drug for MRSA
question: In Staphylococcus aureus bloodstream infection, can carefully selected low-risk patients switch from intravenous to oral antibiotics after 5–7 days — and, in MRSA bacteremia, does adding an antistaphylococcal beta-lactam to vancomycin or daptomycin improve outcomes?
balance: The two halves of this shelf point in opposite directions, and both are printed. For the switch: SABATO randomized low-risk S. aureus bloodstream infection to oral switch after 5–7 days of IV therapy or continued IV, and the oral route was noninferior on SAB-related complications (13% vs 12%) — but the trial stopped at 213 of a planned 430 patients, used a wide 10-point noninferiority margin, and screened 5,063 patients to randomize 213, so it answers the question only for the carefully selected few. For the combination: a small pilot (CAMERA) hinted that adding flucloxacillin cleared MRSA bacteremia faster, but the adequately sized CAMERA2 trial found no benefit on its composite of death, persistence, relapse, or failure (35% vs 39%), a numerically higher 90-day mortality with combination therapy (21% vs 16%, not significant), and a clear kidney price — acute kidney injury in 23% vs 6% of patients not on dialysis at baseline. Faster blood-culture clearance did not translate into better outcomes, and the kidney harm was real. Proposed stamp: POSSIBLE for the early oral switch in low-risk SAB; LIKELY that adding an antistaphylococcal beta-lactam to standard MRSA therapy brings kidney harm without outcome benefit — proposed, pending the developer's review.

title: Gram-negative bacteremia: seven days is enough for uncomplicated infection
question: In hospitalized patients with uncomplicated gram-negative bacteremia who have achieved clinical stability, is 7 days of antibiotic therapy as good as 14 days?
balance: Two randomized trials asked this question specifically in gram-negative bacteremia and both found the short course noninferior. Yahav 2019 randomized 604 stable, afebrile inpatients: the 90-day composite of death, relapse, complications, or prolonged/readmission hospitalization occurred in 45.8% on 7 days vs 48.3% on 14 days. Von Dach 2020 randomized 504 patients three ways and found 30-day clinical failure of 6.6% on fixed 7 days vs 5.5% on 14 days, with CRP-guided stopping lower still at 2.4%. The honest limits: both trials were open-label, both used a wide 10-point noninferiority margin, von Dach's observed event rates were far below what its margin assumed, and both excluded uncontrolled foci and complicated infection. The largest supporting trial, BALANCE 2025 (3,608 patients with bloodstream infection of any source except S. aureus; 90-day mortality 14.5% on 7 days vs 16.1% on 14 days), is not re-carded here — its home is Shelf 316 — but its direction agrees. Proposed stamp LIKELY — proposed, pending the developer's review.

title: MRSA pneumonia: linezolid vs vancomycin — better clinical cure in the one prospective trial, the same survival
question: For nosocomial pneumonia caused by MRSA, is linezolid better than dose-optimized vancomycin — on clinical cure, and on survival?
balance: Linezolid's advantage is real but narrow. The one prospective double-blind trial designed for MRSA pneumonia (ZEPHyR, 1,184 treated) found higher clinical success with linezolid in the per-protocol population (57.6% vs 46.6%) and less nephrotoxicity (8.4% vs 18.2%), but 60-day mortality was essentially identical (15.7% vs 17.0%) — and the superiority signal did not come from the intention-to-treat population. The earlier randomized program (Rubinstein 2001) found linezolid and vancomycin equivalent in gram-positive nosocomial pneumonia overall. The striking survival gap sometimes quoted for linezolid (80.0% vs 63.5%) comes from a retrospective subset analysis of those earlier trials — hypothesis-generating, and its mortality claim is exactly what ZEPHyR's prospective test failed to confirm. Proposed stamp POSSIBLE — proposed, pending the developer's review.

title: Skin abscess: antibiotics after incision and drainage add a modest cure benefit — drainage is still the treatment
question: After a skin abscess has been incised and drained, do adjunctive antibiotics improve cure and prevent new lesions, compared with drainage alone?
balance: Two large double-blind NEJM trials say yes, modestly. Talan 2016 (1,247 in the modified intention-to-treat population) found cure of 80.5% with TMP-SMX vs 73.6% with placebo after drainage — a 6.9-percentage-point gain, with fewer subsequent drainage procedures, fewer new-site infections, and fewer infections in household members. Daum 2017 (786 patients, abscesses ≤5 cm) found cure of 83.1% with clindamycin and 81.7% with TMP-SMX vs 68.9% with placebo, with the benefit restricted to patients whose abscess grew S. aureus, and more adverse events with clindamycin (21.9%) than TMP-SMX (11.1%) or placebo (12.5%). The earlier, smaller Schmitz 2010 trial missed its primary endpoint (treatment failure 17% vs 26%, P=.12) while also showing fewer new lesions on antibiotics (9% vs 28%). The benefit is consistent in direction, real, and single-digit: most drained abscesses cure without antibiotics, so the drug is an adjunct, not the therapy. Proposed stamp LIKELY — proposed, pending the developer's review.

title: Cellulitis: how many days? Five is probably enough when it is uncomplicated and improving — severe cellulitis remains untested
question: For cellulitis, how short can antibiotic therapy safely be — five or six days instead of ten to twelve — and in which patients has that actually been tested?
balance: This is the thinnest shelf in the slate, and it says so. The affirmative evidence is one small double-blind trial: Hepburn 2004 randomized only patients whose uncomplicated cellulitis was already improving at day 5 — 87 of 121 enrolled — and found identical 98% success on 5 vs 10 days of levofloxacin. For severe, hospitalized cellulitis, the DANCE trial (151 randomized) could neither confirm nor refute noninferiority of 6 vs 12 days (cure 49.3% vs 50.0%, with a confidence interval spanning −15.0 to +16.3 points) and raised a warning: relapse by day 90 was 24% after 6 days vs 6% after 12 days among those initially cured without relapse. A third trial (Switch, 80 patients) asked about IV duration rather than total days and was too compromised by misdiagnosis and recruitment failure to answer anything. Proposed stamp POSSIBLE — proposed, pending the developer's review.

title: Invasive candidiasis: an echinocandin first
question: For invasive candidiasis, should an echinocandin be the first drug — ahead of fluconazole and ahead of amphotericin B?
balance: Two randomized trials, against two different comparators, point the same way. Against fluconazole (Reboli 2007), anidulafungin was noninferior and numerically superior on global response at the end of IV therapy (75.6% vs 60.2%), in a population that was 89% candidemia-only and 97% non-neutropenic; all-cause mortality was 23% vs 31%, a difference that was not significant (P=0.13) and is printed here as such — no mortality claim is made. Against amphotericin B deoxycholate (Mora-Duarte 2002), caspofungin was at least as effective (modified intention-to-treat success 73.4% vs 61.7%; in evaluable patients 80.7% vs 64.9%) with significantly fewer drug-related adverse events. No trial shows an echinocandin saving more lives; the case for 'echinocandin first' is response rates at least as good as either older drug, with amphotericin's toxicity avoided. Proposed stamp LIKELY — proposed, pending the developer's review.

title: Invasive aspergillosis: voriconazole beat amphotericin B on response and survival; isavuconazole matched voriconazole with fewer drug harms
question: For primary therapy of invasive aspergillosis, what replaced amphotericin B — and is the newer triazole, isavuconazole, as good as voriconazole?
balance: One unblinded trial moved the standard. Herbrecht 2002 randomized 277 patients with definite or probable invasive aspergillosis: successful outcomes at week 12 were 52.8% on voriconazole vs 31.6% on amphotericin B deoxycholate, and 12-week survival was 70.8% vs 57.9% — mortality 29.2% vs 42.1%, hazard ratio 0.59 (95% CI 0.40 to 0.88), a relative measure printed here beside the absolute rates; because this shelf carries a mortality claim it is Tier C and returns for the developer's personal verdict. Voriconazole's price was transient visual disturbances in 44.8% of patients, against fewer severe drug-related adverse events overall than amphotericin B. Fourteen years later, SECURE found isavuconazole noninferior to voriconazole on its primary endpoint of day-42 all-cause mortality (19% vs 20%) with fewer drug-related adverse events (42% vs 60%). Proposed grade: LIKELY. Tier C — built Nov 8, 2026 and held for the developer’s personal verdict; no approval stamp is claimed for this shelf.

title: Latent tuberculosis: short rifamycin regimens match nine months of isoniazid — and people actually finish them
question: For latent tuberculosis infection, can short rifamycin-based regimens — 3 months of weekly rifapentine plus isoniazid, 1 month of daily rifapentine plus isoniazid, or 4 months of daily rifampin — prevent active tuberculosis as well as 9 months of isoniazid, with better completion and safety?
balance: Three large randomized trials, in three populations, all found a short rifamycin regimen noninferior to 9 months of isoniazid for preventing active tuberculosis — with completion rates 7 to 15 percentage points higher and less hepatotoxicity. PREVENT TB (7,731 in the modified intention-to-treat analysis): tuberculosis in 0.19% on 3 months of weekly rifapentine–isoniazid vs 0.43% on 9 months of isoniazid; completion 82.1% vs 69.0%; hepatotoxicity 0.4% vs 2.7%, though permanent discontinuation for adverse events was slightly higher on the combination (4.9% vs 3.7%). BRIEF TB (3,000 people with HIV): the primary endpoint occurred in 2% in both arms on 1 month of daily rifapentine–isoniazid vs 9 months of isoniazid, with 97% vs 90% completion. Menzies 2018: 4 months of rifampin matched 9 months of isoniazid (confirmed tuberculosis 4 vs 4 cases) with fewer grade 3–5 and hepatotoxic adverse events. The event rates are low everywhere — prevention trials measure rare outcomes — so noninferiority is the honest verb. Proposed stamp LIKELY — proposed, pending the developer's review.

title: Severe malaria: artesunate saves more lives than quinine — in Asian adults and in African children
question: For severe falciparum malaria, does intravenous artesunate reduce mortality compared with intravenous quinine?
balance: Two large open-label randomized trials, on two continents and in two age groups, found the same thing. In Asian adults (SEAQUAMAT, 1,461 patients), mortality was 15% on artesunate vs 22% on quinine — an absolute difference of 7 percentage points, a relative reduction of about 35%. In African children (AQUAMAT, 5,425 children), mortality was 8.5% vs 10.9% — odds ratio 0.75, a relative reduction of 22.5% — with less coma, fewer convulsions, and less hypoglycemia on artesunate; quinine's hypoglycemia harm also appeared in SEAQUAMAT (relative risk 3.2). Neither trial was blinded, and the comparator is a drug much of the world has already replaced — but the consistency across age, continent, and baseline risk is what two-trial evidence looks like. Because this shelf claims a mortality benefit, it is Tier C and returns for the developer's personal verdict. Proposed grade: LIKELY. Tier C — built Nov 8, 2026 and held for the developer’s personal verdict; no approval stamp is claimed for this shelf.

title: Ventilator-associated pneumonia: stop early by response — REGARD-VAP confirms the short-course answer PneumA first gave
question: For ventilator-associated pneumonia, can antibiotics be stopped after a short, response-guided course (about a week or less) instead of a fixed long course — without costing lives or inviting recurrence?
balance: The founding trial of this question — PneumA (Chastre 2003), 8 vs 15 days in 401 patients with culture-proven VAP — is not re-carded here: its home is Shelf 313, where its result (no mortality difference; recurrence 40.6% vs 25.4% in nonfermenting gram-negative infections on the short course) is already carded, and that organism-shaped exception is part of this shelf's fence. What this shelf adds is the modern confirmation. REGARD-VAP (2024, 461 patients) tested an individualized short course — stop at 3–7 days once fever resolved and the patient was stable — against usual care (median 14 days): the 60-day composite of death or pneumonia recurrence was 41% vs 44%, meeting noninferiority, with far fewer antibiotic side effects (8% vs 38% per-protocol). Singh 2000 supplies the older, narrower lesson: in ICU patients whose pulmonary infiltrates scored as low-likelihood pneumonia, a 3-day stop was safe and halved resistance/superinfection. Proposed stamp LIKELY — proposed, pending the developer's review.

title: Levothyroxine in pregnancy: subclinical hypothyroidism and TPO-positive euthyroid women — two large RCTs, both null
question: Does levothyroxine treatment of subclinical hypothyroidism, hypothyroxinemia, or thyroid-peroxidase-antibody-positive euthyroid status in pregnancy improve offspring cognition, live birth, or pregnancy outcomes?
balance: Two large randomized trials point the same way: levothyroxine started in pregnancy for subclinical hypothyroidism or hypothyroxinemia did not improve children's IQ at 5 years (Casey 2017), and levothyroxine given before conception to euthyroid TPO-antibody-positive women did not raise live-birth rates (TABLET 2019). A 2024 meta-analysis of the RCTs agrees. This does not touch overt hypothyroidism in pregnancy, which is treated on other grounds and has never been placebo-tested. Proposed stamp: LIKELY — the null is strong and concordant across two large trials, but the label scale reserves higher certainty for Level A benefit claims and these are null results in defined sub-populations.

title: Levothyroxine + liothyronine combination vs levothyroxine alone: no consistent benefit in the trials
question: In adults with hypothyroidism who remain symptomatic on levothyroxine, does adding liothyronine (T3) improve symptoms, mood, quality of life, weight, or lipids compared with levothyroxine alone?
balance: Across 11 randomized trials and 1,216 patients, pooled symptom, mood, quality-of-life, weight, and lipid outcomes show no difference between combination T4+T3 and T4 alone (Grozinsky-Glasberg 2006). The honest complication is preference: about half of blinded trial participants say they prefer the combination, a signal one meta-analysis found indistinguishable from chance (2019) and a later one found positive but highly heterogeneous (2025). Preference is not measured symptom benefit. Proposed stamp: LIKELY — no consistent objective benefit across many trials; the preference-subgroup question remains open and is fenced as such.

title: Graves' orbitopathy: teprotumumab reverses proptosis; glucocorticoids mainly calm inflammation
question: In active, moderate-to-severe Graves' orbitopathy (thyroid eye disease), what do teprotumumab and intravenous glucocorticoids each achieve — proptosis reversal, activity-score improvement, diplopia, quality of life?
balance: Teprotumumab is the treatment that moves proptosis: in the phase 3 OPTIC trial 83% had a >=2 mm proptosis response vs 10% on placebo, with concordant phase 2 results. Intravenous glucocorticoids, in the EUGOGO-era randomized comparison, beat oral glucocorticoids on overall response (87.8% vs 63.4%) but reduced proptosis by only ~1.6 mm — they mainly suppress inflammation and activity scores. No head-to-head trial of teprotumumab vs IV glucocorticoids was verified. Proposed stamp: LIKELY.

title: Low-risk papillary thyroid cancer after surgery: radioactive iodine or not — two noninferiority trials say it can be omitted
question: After total thyroidectomy for low-risk differentiated thyroid cancer, does omitting postoperative radioactive iodine (ablation) worsen recurrence or event rates compared with routine ablation? What does active-surveillance cohort evidence add for microcarcinoma?
balance: Two phase 3 noninferiority trials now agree: in low-risk differentiated thyroid cancer after total thyroidectomy, a no-ablation follow-up strategy was noninferior to routine radioiodine — ESTIMABL2 at 3 and 5 years (event-free 95.6% vs 95.9% at 3 years; 93.2% vs 94.8% at 5 years) and the UK IoN trial at 5 years (recurrence-free 97.9% vs 96.3%). Active-surveillance cohorts for papillary microcarcinoma are supportive context only and are labeled observational. Proposed stamp: LIKELY.

title: Primary hyperparathyroidism: parathyroidectomy vs surveillance — one 10-year RCT (SIPH)
question: In mild primary hyperparathyroidism, does parathyroidectomy improve quality of life, bone density, or fracture outcomes compared with observation without treatment over 10 years?
balance: The entire randomized evidence base is one Scandinavian trial (SIPH, 191 patients, 10 years). Surgery improved bone density at every measured site versus observation (a surrogate) and produced one better SF-36 domain (vitality) of uncertain clinical significance; it did not reduce fractures, and psychiatric symptom scores improved equally in both groups. Observation was stable and safe over a decade in this mild-disease population. Single-trial shelf: stamp capped at POSSIBLE, and the topic file flags this shelf for the developer's personal verdict (slow lane). Proposed stamp: POSSIBLE.

title: Subclinical hyperthyroidism: treat or watch — associations are real but modest, and no trial shows treatment prevents events
question: In endogenous subclinical hyperthyroidism (low TSH, normal free T4, no symptoms), do the observed risks of atrial fibrillation, coronary events, mortality, and fracture justify treatment, and has any randomized trial shown treatment prevents those outcomes?
balance: Pooled prospective cohorts associate subclinical hyperthyroidism with more atrial fibrillation, coronary mortality, and hip fracture — but the hazard ratios (1.24-1.68 in the individual-participant analyses) sit inside the 0.5-2.0 band that this library does not count as solid evidence, rising above it only in the smallest TSH<0.10 subgroups with few events. The one randomized treatment trial (elderly, TSH<0.1) compared radioiodine with methimazole — both worked biochemically — but had no observation arm, so whether treating changes any clinical outcome is untested. Observational-dependent shelf, flagged for the developer's personal verdict. Proposed stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence).

title: Levothyroxine over-replacement: a suppressed TSH tracks with atrial fibrillation and fracture — observational harm evidence
question: In patients taking levothyroxine, is a suppressed (or low) TSH associated with atrial fibrillation, cardiovascular events, and fractures, and where does the risk begin — suppressed TSH only, or any low TSH?
balance: The classic signal is Sawin 1994 (Framingham): a TSH <=0.1 mU/L carried a relative risk of atrial fibrillation of 3.1 — the one estimate here that clearly crosses the library's 2.0 observational fence. In people actually taking thyroxine (Tayside cohort), a fully suppressed TSH (<=0.03) tracked with more cardiovascular disease (HR 1.37), dysrhythmia (HR 1.6), and fractures (HR 2.02), while a low-but-not-suppressed TSH showed no increased risk; a large case-control study adds a levothyroxine dose-response for fracture. All of it is observational — no trial has randomized patients to TSH targets and counted events. Harm/observational shelf, flagged for the developer's personal verdict. Proposed stamp: POSSIBLE.

title: Graves' disease: long-term low-dose methimazole vs radioiodine vs surgery — remission, relapse, and the hypothyroidism trade
question: For Graves' hyperthyroidism, how does long-term low-dose methimazole compare with conventional-duration antithyroid treatment, radioiodine, and surgery on remission/relapse, hypothyroidism, and safety?
balance: The strongest randomized finding is about duration: continuing low-dose methimazole for a total of 60-120 months instead of stopping at 18-24 months cut post-withdrawal relapse from 53% to 15% in adults (Azizi 2019), a result that held at 84 months of extended follow-up (56% vs 17% recurrence) and was echoed in a juvenile trial. Safety over up to a decade of low-dose therapy was reassuring in these trials (skin reactions and two liver-enzyme elevations, all early). Direct randomized comparisons against radioiodine are thin — the Cochrane review found only two small RCTs — and surgery has no randomized comparison here. The trade is stated plainly: radioiodine and surgery end hyperthyroidism definitively at the price of near-certain hypothyroidism; long-term methimazole preserves the gland but requires years of therapy. Proposed stamp: LIKELY (for the long-term methimazole remission benefit).

title: After total thyroidectomy: routine calcium + calcitriol vs symptom-guided replacement for transient hypocalcemia
question: After total thyroidectomy, does routinely giving oral calcium plus calcitriol to everyone prevent symptomatic transient hypocalcemia better than PTH- or symptom-guided selective supplementation?
balance: Routine prophylaxis works for symptoms: in the largest RCT, adding calcitriol 1 mcg twice daily to routine calcium cut tetany from 7.4% to 0% and severe day-3 hypocalcemia from 27.2% to 9.9%, and a meta-analysis of the RCTs found symptomatic hypocalcemia in 4% with calcitriol+calcium vs 19% with calcium alone and 31% with nothing (odds ratio ~0.31-0.32, a relative measure). A randomized PTH-guided strategy shows the selective alternative is also safe: patients with a day-1 PTH >=10 pg/mL were discharged without supplements and only 10% had transient symptoms. The question is symptoms and length of management, not permanent hypoparathyroidism — no card here touches that. Proposed stamp: LIKELY.

title: Benign thyroid nodules: radiofrequency ablation vs surgery — a young field with no adequate head-to-head trial
question: For symptomatic benign thyroid nodules, how does radiofrequency ablation compare with surgery on volume reduction, symptom relief, complications, and the loss of definitive histology?
balance: The topic file's flag is borne out: there is no adequately powered randomized trial of RFA against surgery. What exists: Italian RCTs of RFA against laser ablation (12-month volume reduction 70.9% vs 60.0% for laser), a Brazilian RFA-vs-thyroidectomy randomized comparison with only 5 patients per arm, and large observational series pooling to a 1.35% major-complication rate for RFA. RFA shrinks nodules by roughly two-thirds over a year and relieves pressure/cosmetic scores, but leaves tissue in place and yields no histology; surgery removes the nodule definitively. Certainty is capped accordingly. Proposed stamp: POSSIBLE at best, per the topic file's flag.

title: Baricitinib in hospitalized COVID-19: ACTT-2 and COV-BARRIER
question: In hospitalized patients with COVID-19, what does adding baricitinib — to remdesivir, or to standard care — actually buy?
balance: Baricitinib shortened recovery in ACTT-2; its mortality estimate was uncertain. COV-BARRIER reported lower mortality but did not meet its primary progression endpoint. ACTT-2 tested addition to remdesivir; COV-BARRIER tested addition to standard care, commonly including corticosteroids. COV-BARRIER mortality findings were secondary/exploratory, with nominal testing for day-28 mortality; its PubMed abstract does not report recovery time. title: Does replacing fibrinogen help at all? Concentrate vs placebo across cardiac, trauma, obstetric and liver bleeding
question: In bleeding patients, does replacing fibrinogen with fibrinogen concentrate improve outcomes — or only the fibrinogen level?
balance: Split the question. As biochemistry, replacement works every time: every trial on this shelf shows concentrate raising fibrinogen and clot firmness within the hour. As transfusion-sparing, it works sometimes, in one setting: two single-centre cardiac trials cut allogeneic transfusion (Rahe-Meyer 2013; Ranucci 2015), but the multicentre phase 3 in the same setting found the opposite (REPLACE: more units transfused, fewer patients avoiding transfusion), and a JAMA trial dosing to a target fibrinogen level found no reduction in blood loss (Bilecen). As patient benefit — survival, organ failure, complications — there is no positive randomised result anywhere on this shelf. In trauma the evidence is feasibility and laboratory studies, and the one large strategy trial (FiiRST-2 — a concentrate combination, not fibrinogen alone) stopped for futility. In obstetrics, three double-blind trials are null, but they treated women whose mean fibrinogen was 4.1–4.5 g/L; the single trigger-based trial randomised only 55 of 663 enrolled women, just 7 of them truly hypofibrinogenaemic. In liver transplantation, preemptive replacement and higher replacement targets are both null. The untested patient is the one the entire idea was built for: the actively bleeding patient whose fibrinogen is genuinely low. Which product to give that patient is Shelf #426; empiric cryoprecipitate for unselected trauma activations is Shelf #424. Grade: POSSIBLE for the narrow claim that replacement moves fibrinogen and, inconsistently, transfusion counts; for any claim of clinical benefit the evidence is MAYBE (weak evidence) at best, and this balance line says so. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

title: Zambia’s CHAP trial: a penny-a-day antibiotic that cut child HIV deaths by 43% (relative) — country 41
question: In HIV-infected children in a high-resistance, pre-ART-era setting, does daily co-trimoxazole prophylaxis reduce mortality?
balance: One trial carries this shelf, and it is a strong one: 541 Zambian children randomised double-blind, mortality 28% vs 42% (HR 0.57 [0.43–0.77]), consistent across ages and CD4 counts, stopped early by its safety board, in the very setting — high bacterial resistance, no ART — where sceptics expected the drug to fail. Zambia is a not-yet-covered country, so the developer’s country exception applies: one strong RCT may card. The grade is LIKELY, not the top tier, precisely because there is one trial: the benefit’s direction is secure, its size in an ART-era cohort is not something this trial can price. Proposed stamp LIKELY — proposed, pending the developer’s review.

title: Czechoslovakia’s shelf: the WHO clofibrate trial — fewer heart attacks, more deaths (Prague centre, 1978)
question: Does lowering cholesterol with clofibrate prevent ischaemic heart disease — and at what cost?
balance: The balance must carry both halves, because the trial did: clofibrate lowered cholesterol ~9% and cut major ischaemic heart disease by 20% relative (5.9 vs 7.4 per 1,000/year), driven by non-fatal infarction — and raised all-cause mortality during treatment (162 vs 127 deaths; 4.9 vs 3.8 per 1,000 person-years), an excess that vanished when exposure stopped. POSSIBLE grades the pair of claims together: the event benefit is real and randomised; so is the mortality signal, unexplained then and now. The Prague centre (IKEM) enrolled roughly a third of the 15,745 men — Czechoslovakia is this shelf’s country of evidence, flying its own flag by the developer’s ruling. Proposed stamp POSSIBLE — proposed, pending the developer’s review.

title: Cambodia’s CAMELIA trial: ART at 2 weeks, not 8, in HIV with tuberculosis — deaths 18% vs 27% (country 42)
question: In adults with HIV and newly diagnosed tuberculosis and CD4 counts of 200 or lower, does starting ART at 2 weeks rather than 8 weeks after TB treatment improve survival?
balance: One Cambodian trial, a mortality primary endpoint, and a result with no ambiguity of direction: deferring ART from week 2 to week 8 of TB treatment cost roughly one life in eleven among profoundly immunosuppressed patients (deaths 18% vs 27%; HR 0.62 [0.44–0.86]). The cost side is on the same record — TB-IRIS at 2.51 times the hazard with the early start — and the survival benefit survived it. Cambodia is a not-yet-covered country, so the country exception applies; LIKELY, not the top tier, because a single trial with a stavudine-era regimen and a median CD4 of 25 cannot price other strata. title: Sri Lanka’s antivenom trial: adrenaline before the drip prevents severe reactions — the steroid undoes it (country 43)
question: In snakebite patients about to receive antivenom, does premedication with adrenaline, promethazine, or hydrocortisone prevent severe acute reactions?
balance: A prevention-of-harm shelf from a single large, rigorous trial: 1,007 Sri Lankan snakebite patients, factorial and double-blind, in a setting where antivenom itself causes reactions in 75% of recipients. Low-dose adrenaline prevented severe reactions — 43% relative reduction at 1 hour, 38% through 48 hours; promethazine and hydrocortisone did nothing; hydrocortisone, added to adrenaline, negated its benefit. Sri Lanka is a not-yet-covered country, so the country exception applies; LIKELY, not the top tier, because one trial — however well built — prices its benefit against one region’s antivenom. Proposed stamp LIKELY — proposed, pending the developer’s review.

title: The fibrates after clofibrate: lipids improved, outcomes mostly didn’t
question: Do fibrates reduce cardiovascular events?
balance: Every fibrate trial moved the lipids it aimed at; the events followed only twice. Gemfibrozil, in the pre-statin era, cut coronary events by 34% relative in primary prevention (Helsinki, 4,081 men) and by 22% relative in secondary prevention (VA-HIT, 2,531 men) — with total mortality unchanged in both. Then the class’s modern record is a run of well-run nulls: bezafibrate’s primary endpoint missed, its benefit confined to a post hoc high-triglyceride subgroup (BIP); fenofibrate’s primary missed in 9,795 people with diabetes (FIELD, HR 0.89 [0.75–1.05]) and again when added to a statin (ACCORD-Lipid, HR 0.92 [0.79–1.08]); and pemafibrate — the most potent agent, tested in exactly the high-triglyceride, low-HDL phenotype the subgroups had pointed to — lowered triglycerides 26% and produced a hazard ratio of 1.03 (PROMINENT). Ciprofibrate has no outcome trial at all: unknown, not disproven. Split stamp: POSSIBLE for gemfibrozil’s pre-statin event benefit; LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for the statin-era fibrates. Proposed split stamp — proposed, pending the developer’s review.

title: Home blood-pressure self-monitoring, with self-titration or telemonitoring
question: Does home self-monitoring of blood pressure, used to titrate treatment, lower blood pressure more than clinic-based usual care?
balance: LIKELY: Self-monitoring used to titrate treatment lowered systolic blood pressure by about 3.5-5.4 mm Hg more than clinic-based usual care at 12 months in the TASMINH trials, and an individual-patient meta-analysis found the effect depends on co-interventions: self-monitoring alone had no effect (-1.0 mm Hg), while monitoring with systematic titration or support lowered systolic pressure by up to 6.1 mm Hg. All outcomes are blood pressure, a surrogate — no trial here reports cardiovascular events.
stamp: LIKELY

title: Screening for abdominal aortic aneurysm in older men
question: Does one-time ultrasound screening of older men reduce aneurysm-related death enough to justify a screening programme?
balance: Proposed LIKELY, pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C — aneurysm-mortality claim): In MASS, inviting men aged 65-74 to one ultrasound scan reduced aneurysm-related death from 0.33% to 0.19% over about 4 years (42% relative reduction, 95% CI 22 to 58), and the smaller Viborg trial found a 67% relative reduction (29 to 84) in aneurysm-specific mortality. The Cochrane synthesis of the four screening trials found reduced aneurysm mortality in men (OR 0.60, 0.47 to 0.78) but no significant difference in all-cause mortality at 3-5 years (OR 0.95, 0.85 to 1.07), and no demonstrated benefit in women. Screening roughly doubled aneurysm surgery in men. Tier C — built Nov 8, 2026 and held for the developer’s personal verdict; no approval stamp is claimed for this shelf.

title: E-cigarettes for smoking cessation
question: Do nicotine e-cigarettes help smokers quit more than nicotine replacement therapy or non-nicotine e-cigarettes?
balance: LIKELY: Nicotine e-cigarettes produced higher quit rates than nicotine replacement therapy in the largest head-to-head trial (1-year abstinence 18.0% vs 9.9%; relative risk 1.83, 95% CI 1.30 to 2.58) and in the Cochrane living review (relative risk 1.63, 1.30 to 2.04; an additional four quitters per 100), and higher quit rates than non-nicotine e-cigarettes (relative risk 1.94, 1.21 to 3.13). The earliest trial (Bullen 2013) was underpowered and inconclusive on its own. Most abstinent e-cigarette users were still vaping at one year (80%), and long-term safety data remain limited (longest follow-up two years in the review).
stamp: LIKELY

title: General health checks in primary care
question: Do routine general health checks reduce illness or death, or mainly find risk factors?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): Across 17 randomised trials (251,891 participants), general health checks had little or no effect on total mortality (risk ratio 1.00, 95% CI 0.97 to 1.03; high-certainty evidence), cancer mortality (1.01, 0.92 to 1.12) or ischaemic heart disease events (0.98, 0.94 to 1.03). The largest single trial, Inter99, likewise found no effect on ischaemic heart disease, stroke or total mortality at 10 years (hazard ratio 1.00, 0.91 to 1.09). Health checks do find risk factors and diagnoses — the trials say that finding them this way does not translate into fewer deaths or events.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference)

title: Collaborative care for depression and anxiety in primary care
question: Does collaborative (care-manager + specialist-supervised) care improve depression outcomes versus usual primary care?
balance: LIKELY: Collaborative care improved depression outcomes across 79 randomised trials (24,308 participants) in the Cochrane synthesis — short-term standardised mean difference -0.34 (95% CI -0.41 to -0.27) with response risk ratio 1.32 (1.22 to 1.43), sustained at long-term follow-up — and in the IMPACT trial 45% of older adults achieved at least a 50% symptom reduction at 12 months versus 19% on usual care. Anxiety outcomes improved similarly. Benefits were not demonstrated at very long-term follow-up in the synthesis.
stamp: LIKELY

title: HIV self-testing
question: Does making HIV self-tests available increase testing uptake and linkage versus facility-based testing alone?
balance: LIKELY (for uptake; linkage less certain): Facility-based self-testing in Malawi raised same-day testing among outpatients from 13% to 51% (adjusted odds ratio 8.52, 95% CI 3.98 to 18.24 versus standard provider-initiated testing), and the earlier randomised-trial synthesis found self-testing doubled testing uptake among men (risk ratio 2.12, 1.51 to 2.98). STAR-programme community distribution in Zimbabwe delivered tens of thousands of kits with about a quarter of surveyed participants linking to post-test services, and no social harms were reported in the Malawi or Zimbabwe trials. Evidence that self-testing increases linkage to treatment, rather than testing itself, is thinner — the synthesis explicitly calls for more research on supporting linkage.
stamp: LIKELY (for uptake; linkage less certain)

title: Brief alcohol interventions in primary care
question: Do brief alcohol interventions in primary care reduce drinking in hazardous and harmful drinkers?
balance: POSSIBLE: The Cochrane synthesis of 69 trials (33,642 participants) found moderate-quality evidence that brief intervention reduced drinking by 20 g of alcohol per week (95% CI -28 to -12) at one year versus minimal or no intervention — a small average effect with substantial heterogeneity (I2 = 73%). The large pragmatic SIPS trial, however, found no additional benefit from brief advice or lifestyle counselling beyond simple screening feedback and a leaflet. Longer (extended) interventions added nothing over brief ones.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Expedited partner therapy for sexually transmitted infections
question: Does giving patients antibiotics (or prescriptions) for their partners reduce reinfection and partner infection versus partner referral alone?
balance: POSSIBLE: In the largest trial (Golden 2005), expedited partner treatment reduced persistent or recurrent gonorrhoea or chlamydial infection from 13% to 10% (relative risk 0.76, 95% CI 0.59 to 0.98), driven by gonorrhoea (3% vs 11%) rather than chlamydia (11% vs 13%). The Cochrane synthesis found expedited therapy better than simple patient referral for reinfection (risk ratio 0.71, 0.56 to 0.89), but the effect attenuated when high-attrition trials were excluded (0.80, 0.62 to 1.04) and in chlamydia-only trials (0.90, 0.60 to 1.35), and it was not superior to enhanced patient referral. A trichomonas trial found patient-delivered treatment no better than referral for partner treatment or reinfection, though cheaper. All relative effects sit inside the 0.5-2.0 band and are graded accordingly.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Workplace wellness programmes
question: Do employer wellness programmes improve employee health, health-care use, or costs?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference on health and economic outcomes): Two large randomised trials agree. In the BJ's Wholesale Club trial (32,974 employees), a wellness programme improved two self-reported behaviours (regular exercise and actively managing weight) but had no significant effect on 10 clinical measures, 38 spending and utilisation measures, or employment outcomes at 18 months. In the Illinois Workplace Wellness Study (4,834 employees), the programme had no significant effects on biometrics, medical diagnoses or medical use at 12 or 24 months, though more treated employees reported having a primary care physician (92.2% vs 86.1% at 24 months) and health beliefs improved slightly. Neither trial found the cost savings employers typically expect, within its follow-up window.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference on health and economic outcomes)

title: Financial incentives for smoking cessation in pregnancy
question: Do financial incentives increase quit rates in pregnant smokers, during pregnancy and after delivery?
balance: LIKELY: Two randomised trials in different health systems agree. In the Scottish CPIT trial, offering up to £400 of vouchers on top of routine cessation services raised cotinine-verified cessation in late pregnancy from 8.6% to 22.5% (relative risk 2.63, 95% CI 1.73 to 4.01; absolute difference 14.0 percentage points; number needed to treat 7.2). In the French FISCP trial, abstinence-contingent vouchers raised continuous abstinence before delivery from 7% to 16% (odds ratio 2.45, 1.34 to 4.49). Birth weight did not differ significantly in CPIT (3,140 g vs 3,120 g); the French trial's neonatal findings were secondary and partly post hoc, and are fenced as such on its card.
stamp: LIKELY

title: Glucosamine ± chondroitin for knee osteoarthritis pain
question: Do glucosamine and chondroitin, alone or combined, relieve knee osteoarthritis pain more than placebo?
balance: LIKELY — the treatment made no difference is the finding for the overall population: in GAIT (1,583 patients) glucosamine, chondroitin and their combination were not significantly better than placebo on the primary pain response, and a network meta-analysis of 10 large trials (3,803 patients) found pain differences of only -0.3 to -0.5 cm on a 10 cm scale, none reaching the prespecified clinically important difference. MOVES found the combination non-inferior to celecoxib in severe pain, but with no placebo arm it cannot show the combination beats placebo. The one positive signal — GAIT's exploratory moderate-to-severe subgroup — is a subgroup finding, not the trial's primary result. The warfarin-interaction question for these products is a different question, home on Shelf #65, and is not re-carded here.

title: Saw palmetto for benign prostatic hyperplasia symptoms
question: Does saw palmetto extract improve urinary symptoms in BPH more than placebo, at standard or escalating doses?
balance: LIKELY — the treatment made no difference is the finding: two large, well-blinded placebo-controlled trials found no benefit at the standard dose for a year (STEP, n=225) or at up to three times the standard dose for 72 weeks (CAMUS, n=369, where placebo improved slightly more), and the Cochrane review of 32 trials (5,666 men) reaches the same conclusion on symptom scores, responder rates, flow and prostate size. title: Zinc lozenges for the common cold
question: Do zinc lozenges started at cold onset shorten how long a cold lasts?
balance: POSSIBLE: properly composed zinc lozenges at more than 75 mg/day of elemental zinc, started within 24 hours, shortened colds in the placebo-controlled trials — median resolution 4.4 vs 7.6 days in Mossad 1996, a recovery rate ratio of 3.1 in an individual-patient-data meta-analysis of three zinc acetate trials (199 patients), and a 33% relative reduction in mean duration across seven trials (575 participants). The ceiling is POSSIBLE, not higher: the trials are small, lozenge taste threatens blinding (bad-taste reactions 80% vs 30% in Mossad), formulations vary, and side effects are common (90% vs 62% in Mossad).
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: St John's wort for major depression
question: Does St John's wort (hypericum) treat major depression as well as standard antidepressants, and better than placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE: the Cochrane synthesis of 29 trials (5,489 patients) found hypericum extracts superior to placebo (response rate ratio 1.28 in the nine larger trials) and statistically similar to standard antidepressants (rate ratios 1.02 vs tricyclics and 1.00 vs SSRIs), with fewer dropouts for adverse effects — but placebo-controlled results were markedly heterogeneous, trials from German-speaking countries reported more favourable findings, and the largest US trial (n=340) found neither hypericum nor sertraline significantly better than placebo on its primary outcomes. Extracts differ between products, so a class-level POSSIBLE is the honest ceiling.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Echinacea for preventing and treating colds
question: Does echinacea prevent colds, or shorten them, versus placebo?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence): the largest rigorous treatment trial (Barrett 2010, n=719) found illness duration and severity not statistically significant versus placebo (a 0.53-day trend), the Cochrane review of 24 trials (4,631 participants) found no individual prevention comparison significant and only one of seven treatment trials significant for duration, and concluded echinacea products have not been shown to provide benefits for treating colds, with at most a possible weak benefit from some products. One large prevention trial (Jawad 2012, n=755) reported fewer episodes on a single extract, but its abstract reports no episode counts. Products differ appreciably in composition, which further weakens any class claim.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence)

title: Magnesium for nocturnal leg cramps
question: Does oral magnesium prevent night-time leg cramps, in older adults or in pregnancy?
balance: Split stamp. LIKELY the null in older adults: the Cochrane review (Garrison 2020) found, for idiopathic cramps in older adults (trial mean ages 61.6 to 69.3 years), differences versus placebo that were small, non-significant and homogeneous — cramps per week MD -0.18 (-0.84 to 0.49) and a ≥25% cramp-reduction responder rate ratio of 1.04 (0.84 to 1.29) on high-certainty evidence — and concludes clinically meaningful prophylaxis is unlikely. MAYBE (weak evidence) in pregnancy: the same review could not pool the five pregnancy trials (408 participants) because their results conflict, and the two primary trials carded here disagree — Dahle 1995 positive, Nygaard 2008 null — all judged at high risk of bias.

title: Coenzyme Q10 for statin-associated muscle symptoms
question: Does CoQ10 relieve muscle symptoms in people taking statins?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence): an updated meta-analysis of 12 small randomised trials (575 patients) found CoQ10 lowered symptom scores for pain, weakness, cramp and tiredness versus placebo, with no effect on creatine kinase — but the most rigorous primary trial, which first confirmed true statin myalgia by blinded statin-versus-placebo cross-over (only 36% of complainers reproduced symptoms), found CoQ10 600 mg/day did not reduce muscle pain at all. The positive pool rests on small, short trials like Caso 2007 (n=32, vitamin E comparator, 30 days). Q-SYMBIO, the heart-failure outcomes trial, is a different question and stays home on Shelf #53; it is not re-carded here.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence)

title: Vitamin D for preventing asthma exacerbations
question: Does vitamin D supplementation reduce asthma exacerbations in people with asthma?
balance: Split stamp. LIKELY the null overall: both large primary trials were null on their primary outcomes — VIDA (n=408; treatment failure 28% vs 29%, adjusted HR 0.9, 0.6-1.3) and ViDiAs (n=250; time to first severe exacerbation adjusted HR 1.02, 0.69-1.53) — and the 2023 Cochrane update (20 studies) found no effect on the proportion having an exacerbation treated with systemic corticosteroids (OR 1.04, 0.81-1.34; high-quality evidence). MAYBE (weak evidence) for profound deficiency: a 2017 individual-patient-data meta-analysis found a lower exacerbation rate overall (adjusted incidence rate ratio 0.74, 0.56-0.97), with the largest point estimate in participants below 25 nmol/L — but that subgroup held only 92 participants, the interaction test was not significant (p=0.25), and the Cochrane update found no effect modification by baseline vitamin D status, with profound deficiency poorly represented.

title: Dietary nitrate (beetroot) for blood pressure
question: Does dietary inorganic nitrate lower blood pressure in hypertensive patients?
balance: POSSIBLE: one phase-2 randomised trial in the target population (Kapil 2015, 68 hypertensive patients) found sustained 4-week reductions with daily beetroot juice versus nitrate-free juice on all three measurement methods — clinic -7.7/-2.4 mm Hg, 24-hour ambulatory -7.7/-5.2 mm Hg and home -8.1/-3.8 mm Hg — and meta-analyses of many very small, short cross-over trials find systolic falls of about -4 mm Hg. The ceiling is POSSIBLE: Kapil is a single small phase-2 trial, the pooled trials enrolled 7-65 participants each for days to weeks, and the medium-term meta-analysis found the effect significant in clinic measurements but not on 24-hour ambulatory or home monitoring. title: Berberine for blood glucose and lipids
question: Does berberine lower glucose or lipids in type 2 diabetes or dyslipidaemia?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence): the carded trials report large glucose and lipid falls — HbA1c from 7.5% to 6.6% versus placebo over 3 months in Zhang 2008 (n=116) and falls comparable to metformin in Yin 2008 — but the systematic review of the same programme (Dong 2012, 14 trials, 1,068 participants) states plainly that methodological quality was generally low, sample sizes small, trials few and risks of bias unidentified, and found berberine not significantly better than oral hypoglycaemic drugs for glycaemic control when used alone. Effects of this size from trials of this quality are exactly what MAYBE (weak evidence) is for; nothing here is placebo-controlled beyond 3 months or measures clinical outcomes.

title: Anticoagulation for device-detected subclinical atrial fibrillation: one positive trial, one stopped trial
question: In patients whose devices detect brief subclinical AF, does anticoagulation prevent stroke enough to justify the bleeding?
balance: Proposed stamp — SPLIT, pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, slow lane): ARTESiA POSSIBLE / NOAH-AFNET 6 MAYBE (weak evidence). The two trials point in different directions. Apixaban versus aspirin (ARTESiA) lowered stroke or systemic embolism from 1.24% to 0.78% per patient-year (hazard ratio 0.63) while raising major bleeding from 0.94% to 1.71% per patient-year (hazard ratio 1.80). Edoxaban versus placebo (NOAH-AFNET 6) did not significantly reduce its composite of cardiovascular death, stroke or systemic embolism (3.2% vs 4.0% per patient-year; hazard ratio 0.81, 95% CI 0.60 to 1.08) and increased the composite of death or major bleeding (hazard ratio 1.31); that trial was stopped early. Both hazard ratios for benefit sit inside the 0.5–2.0 band this library does not treat as solid on their own, so the absolute rates printed on the cards carry the argument. title: Mitral transcatheter edge-to-edge repair for secondary mitral regurgitation: COAPT vs MITRA-FR, the discordant pair
question: Does TEER (MitraClip) on top of medical therapy improve outcomes in heart failure with secondary mitral regurgitation?
balance: Proposed stamp POSSIBLE, pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, slow lane). The discordance is the finding and is not averaged away. In COAPT-selected patients, TEER plus medical therapy cut heart-failure hospitalisation (35.8% vs 67.9% per patient-year at 2 years) and all-cause mortality beside it (29.1% vs 46.1% at 2 years; 57.3% vs 67.2% at 5 years). In MITRA-FR, the same device strategy changed nothing at 1 year: death or unplanned heart-failure hospitalisation 54.6% vs 51.3%, with all-cause mortality 24.3% vs 22.4%. title: Left main coronary disease: PCI vs bypass surgery — EXCEL vs NOBLE, discordant composites, convergent mortality
question: For left main disease, is PCI with modern stents an acceptable alternative to CABG?
balance: Proposed stamp POSSIBLE, pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, slow lane). EXCEL and NOBLE are carded two-handed and not averaged away. EXCEL met noninferiority at 3 years for death, stroke or MI (15.4% PCI vs 14.7% CABG), but at 5 years all-cause death was higher with PCI (13.0% vs 9.9%) even though the composite did not differ significantly (22.0% vs 19.2%). NOBLE's wider composite (MACCE, including repeat revascularisation and non-procedural MI) favoured CABG at 5 years (29% vs 19%; hazard ratio 1.48) while all-cause mortality did not differ (12% vs 9%; hazard ratio 1.07) — and at 10 years mortality was 23% with PCI vs 25% with CABG (hazard ratio 0.93). Repeat revascularisation is consistently more frequent after PCI in both trials. Tier C — built Nov 8, 2026 and held for the developer’s personal verdict; no approval stamp is claimed for this shelf.

title: Endovascular (EVAR) vs open repair of abdominal aortic aneurysm: early gain, late loss, no durable survival winner
question: For patients fit for either, does EVAR beat open repair on early and late survival?
balance: Proposed stamp LIKELY, pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, slow lane). The pattern is consistent across three trials and is time-dependent, so it is stated as a pattern, not a single winner. EVAR wins early: aneurysm-related mortality was lower in the first months (EVAR trial 1 adjusted hazard ratio 0.47 for aneurysm-related death at 0–6 months; DREAM's 2-year aneurysm-related death 2.1% EVAR vs 5.7% open, a perioperative-period effect). The advantage then disappears (DREAM at 6 years: survival 68.9% EVAR vs 69.9% open) and in EVAR trial 1 reverses after 8 years (total mortality adjusted hazard ratio 1.25; aneurysm-related mortality 5.82, driven by secondary sac rupture). The US OVER trial found no significant survival difference at any epoch over up to 14 years (deaths 68.0% EVAR vs 70.0% open; hazard ratio 0.96). EVAR consistently requires more secondary procedures. Tier C — built Nov 8, 2026 and held for the developer’s personal verdict; no approval stamp is claimed for this shelf.

title: Ultrafiltration for acute decompensated heart failure: more fluid off in UNLOAD, worse kidneys in CARRESS-HF
question: Does ultrafiltration relieve congestion better than intravenous diuretics in acute heart failure with cardiorenal syndrome?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence): The three trials disagree by population, and none shows an outcome benefit that survives its own caveats. In broad decompensated heart failure (UNLOAD, 200 patients), ultrafiltration removed more weight and fluid than intravenous diuretics at 48 hours (5.0 vs 3.1 kg) and was followed by fewer 90-day heart-failure rehospitalisations (18% vs 32% of patients) — with deaths printed beside it, 9 vs 11, no difference. In the cardiorenal population the shelf question names (CARRESS-HF, 188 patients), ultrafiltration was worse: creatinine rose (+0.23 vs -0.04 mg/dL), weight loss was the same, and serious adverse events were more frequent (72% vs 57%). The third trial, AVOID-HF, was stopped by its sponsor at 224 of 810 planned patients and is inconclusive. Fluid removal is achievable; routine outcome benefit is unproven, and in cardiorenal syndrome the tested strategy harmed renal function.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence)

title: Treatment of varicose veins: laser vs surgery vs foam — laser and surgery ahead on disease-specific quality of life at 5 years
question: For primary varicose veins, how do endovenous laser ablation, surgery and ultrasound-guided foam sclerotherapy compare on symptoms, quality of life and recurrence?
balance: LIKELY: One large three-way randomised trial (CLASS, 798 participants) with its 5-year follow-up answers the comparison directly. At 6 months, generic quality of life did not differ between treatments; disease-specific quality of life was slightly worse after foam than after surgery, and similar after laser and surgery; procedural complications were least frequent after laser (1% vs 7% surgery, 6% foam), while successful ablation of the saphenous trunks was less common after foam. At 5 years, disease-specific quality of life was better after laser or surgery than after foam (adjusted differences -2.86 and -2.60 points on the Aberdeen questionnaire), and cost-effectiveness modelling favoured laser (77.2% of iterations at a £20,000-per-QALY threshold).
stamp: LIKELY
