title: Tafamidis for transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy: one pivotal trial — mortality 29.5% vs 42.9% at 30 months
question: Does tafamidis reduce death and cardiovascular hospitalisation in transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy?
balance: Proposed stamp POSSIBLE, pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, slow lane) — capped at POSSIBLE because the shelf rests on a single pivotal trial. In ATTR-ACT (441 patients, 30 months), all-cause mortality was 29.5% (78 of 264) on tafamidis vs 42.9% (76 of 177) on placebo (hazard ratio 0.70; 95% CI 0.51 to 0.96) — an absolute difference of 13.4 percentage points — printed beside the cardiovascular-hospitalisation result, as required: 0.48 vs 0.70 hospitalisations per year (relative risk ratio 0.68, a relative measure, with the absolute rates beside it). Decline in 6-minute walk distance and quality-of-life score was also slower on tafamidis. The long-term extension, in which placebo patients crossed to tafamidis, found better survival in those treated from the start (deaths 44.9% vs 62.7%; hazard ratio 0.59) — supportive, but no longer a placebo-controlled comparison. No second placebo-controlled trial exists. Tier C — built Nov 8, 2026 and held for the developer’s personal verdict; no approval stamp is claimed for this shelf.

title: Dietary sodium restriction in chronic heart failure: SODIUM-HF — a large trial, a null result
question: Does restricting dietary sodium to under 100 mmol/day improve outcomes in chronic heart failure?
balance: POSSIBLE (single-trial cap, for the null): In SODIUM-HF (806 patients), a dietary intervention targeting under 100 mmol of sodium per day did not reduce the composite of cardiovascular hospital admission, cardiovascular emergency-department visit or all-cause death at 12 months (15% low-sodium vs 17% usual care; hazard ratio 0.89; 95% CI 0.63 to 1.26; p=0.53), and all-cause death — printed beside the composite, as required — was numerically higher in the low-sodium group (6% vs 4%; hazard ratio 1.38; 95% CI 0.73 to 2.60; p=0.32), not significantly. Achieved intake separation was modest: median sodium fell to 1,658 mg/day in the intervention group vs 2,073 mg/day on usual care. One large trial, honestly null on its own terms; the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE because a single trial carries the shelf.

title: Self-monitoring of blood glucose in non-insulin-treated type 2 diabetes
question: Does routine fingerstick self-monitoring improve control or quality of life in type 2 diabetes not treated with insulin?

title: Lithium for relapse prevention and suicide in mood disorders

title: Prazosin for PTSD nightmares
question: Does prazosin reduce nightmares and improve sleep in PTSD?
balance: Split — POSSIBLE in the small early trials / MAYBE (weak evidence) overall after the large null VA trial: the early single-centre evidence was positive (a 40-veteran parallel trial reported prazosin significantly superior on nightmares, sleep quality and global status, with large effect sizes but no numeric scores in its record), while the large multicentre VA Cooperative Study of 304 veterans found no difference from placebo on nightmare, sleep-quality or global-change scores at 10 or 26 weeks. title: Acupuncture for chronic pain
question: Does acupuncture relieve chronic pain (back/neck, osteoarthritis, headache, shoulder) more than sham acupuncture and more than no treatment?
balance: POSSIBLE: In individual-patient-data meta-analyses pooling roughly 18,000-21,000 patients, acupuncture beat both sham and no-acupuncture controls for each chronic pain condition, but the specific effect over sham was small — about 0.15-0.23 standard deviations in the 2012 analysis, and close to 0.2 standard deviations in the 2018 update — versus about 0.5 standard deviations against no treatment. Most of the benefit over doing nothing is therefore not needle-specific, though the sham difference was statistically robust and the effect largely persisted at 1 year (about a 15% decrease).

title: Topical NSAIDs for chronic musculoskeletal pain
question: Do topical NSAIDs relieve osteoarthritis and other chronic musculoskeletal pain, and with what harm trade versus oral NSAIDs?
balance: LIKELY: The Cochrane synthesis found topical diclofenac and topical ketoprofen beat their carrier in 6-12-week osteoarthritis trials — numbers needed to treat for clinical success of 9.8 and 6.9, with about 60% of participants achieving much reduced pain against a carrier response of around half — on moderate-quality evidence. The few trials against oral NSAIDs showed similar efficacy (low-quality evidence). Local skin reactions increased with diclofenac but not ketoprofen; systemic adverse-event reporting was poor, so the harm advantage over oral NSAIDs is plausible and consistent with the pharmacology but thinly documented in these trials. The evidence is almost entirely knee osteoarthritis.
stamp: LIKELY

title: Lisdexamfetamine for binge-eating disorder
question: Does lisdexamfetamine reduce binge-eating days in adults with moderate-to-severe binge-eating disorder?
balance: LIKELY: Three placebo-controlled trials from one programme agree: the dose-ranging trial found 50 mg and 70 mg (not 30 mg) reduced binge-eating days and raised 4-week cessation rates (42.2% and 50.0% versus 21.3% on placebo), and the two pivotal trials found treatment differences of -1.35 and -1.66 binge-eating days per week. The harm side is stimulant-typical: any treatment-emergent adverse event in 84.7% on drug versus 58.7% on placebo in the dose trial, dry mouth, insomnia and headache most common in the pivotal trials, with small mean rises in pulse and blood pressure and weight loss of about 4-5 kg versus about 0 kg on placebo in the dose trial.

title: COVID-19 mRNA vaccines: the pivotal efficacy trials
question: Did the BNT162b2 and mRNA-1273 vaccines prevent symptomatic and severe COVID-19 in their pivotal trials?
balance: LIKELY — proposed pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, slow lane): In their pivotal placebo-controlled trials, two doses of BNT162b2 were 95% effective in relative terms against symptomatic COVID-19 (8 cases among 21,720 vaccine recipients, 0.04%, versus 162 among 21,728 placebo recipients, 0.75%) and two doses of mRNA-1273 were 94.1% effective in relative terms (11 cases among 15,210 vaccine recipients, 0.07%, versus 185 among 15,210 placebo recipients, 1.22%). Severe disease was uncommon and mostly in placebo groups (BNT162b2: 9 of 10 severe cases on placebo; mRNA-1273: all 30 severe cases on placebo, with the trial's one fatality in the placebo group) — the trials prove prevention of symptomatic and severe illness, not a measured reduction in death, for which events were too few. title: Nirmatrelvir-ritonavir for early outpatient COVID-19: benefit in high-risk, null in standard-risk

title: Insecticide-treated bed nets for malaria prevention
question: Do insecticide-treated nets reduce malaria illness and child death where malaria is endemic?
balance: LIKELY — proposed pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, slow lane): Across 23 randomised trials enrolling more than 275,793 adults and children, insecticide-treated nets reduced child mortality from all causes versus no nets by 17% in relative terms (rate ratio 0.83, 95% CI 0.77 to 0.89; 5 trials, 200,833 participants, high-certainty evidence) — an absolute saving of 5.6 lives (95% CI 3.6 to 7.6) each year for every 1,000 children protected. The mortality figure printed here is all-cause mortality, as the standing rule requires. Nets also reduced uncomplicated Plasmodium falciparum episodes by almost a half in relative terms (rate ratio 0.55) and severe malaria episodes by 44% in relative terms (rate ratio 0.56). The trials were conducted between 1987 and 2001, before widespread pyrethroid resistance — the review judged the resistance data insufficient to downgrade the mortality evidence, but present-day effect sizes may differ. title: Doxycycline post-exposure prophylaxis for bacterial STIs
question: Does doxycycline taken after sex prevent syphilis, chlamydia and gonorrhoea in high-risk groups?
balance: Split — LIKELY in men who have sex with men and transgender women: in the DoxyPEP trial, a bacterial STI was diagnosed at 10.7% of quarterly visits on doxycycline PEP versus 31.9% on standard care in the PrEP cohort (relative risk 0.34) and 11.8% versus 30.5% in the cohort living with HIV (relative risk 0.38), and the earlier IPERGAY substudy also found fewer first STIs (hazard ratio 0.53, a ratio inside the 0.5-2.0 band, carried by its chlamydia and syphilis components). MAYBE (weak evidence) in cisgender women: the Kenyan women's trial found no significant difference (relative risk 0.88, 95% CI 0.60 to 1.29), with doxycycline detected in only 29.0% of hair samples from the treatment group — a null that may reflect low use rather than no biological effect, and is printed as such. Gonorrhoea is the weakest component throughout, and tetracycline resistance is the standing watch-out.

title: Oseltamivir for treating and preventing influenza
question: Does oseltamivir shorten influenza illness or prevent complications and transmission, on the full trial record?
balance: POSSIBLE: Two independent syntheses of the same manufacturer trial programme agree that oseltamivir shortens illness modestly in adults — by 16.8 hours in the Cochrane review of full clinical study reports (from 7.0 to 6.3 days) and by a median 25.2 hours in the Dobson individual-participant-data meta-analysis (97.5 versus 122.7 hours). They disagree on complications: Dobson found fewer lower-respiratory complications requiring antibiotics (4.9% versus 8.7%) and fewer hospital admissions (0.6% versus 1.7%), while Cochrane, working from the full study reports, found no significant effect on hospitalisation (risk difference 0.15%, 95% CI -0.78 to 0.91) and no significant reduction in serious complications, with the apparent pneumonia effect confined to self-reported, unverified pneumonia. Both agree on harm: nausea and vomiting are increased (Dobson risk differences +3.7 and +4.7 percentage points). Prophylaxis reduced symptomatic influenza in Cochrane's analysis (risk difference 3.05% in individuals; 13.6% in households) but not asymptomatic infection. Influenza vaccines are a different intervention and live on their own shelves (#321, #443, #451); nothing vaccine is carded here.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Antibiotics for acute COPD exacerbations
question: Do antibiotics improve outcomes in acute COPD exacerbations, and in which severity strata?
balance: POSSIBLE: The Cochrane synthesis of 16 trials (2,068 participants) found antibiotics reduced treatment failure in inpatients with severe exacerbations (risk ratio 0.77, 95% CI 0.65 to 0.91) and in outpatients (risk ratio 0.75, 95% CI 0.60 to 0.94) — both ratios inside the 0.5-2.0 band and therefore not presented as solid evidence on their own — but the outpatient effect lost significance when restricted to currently available drugs (risk ratio 0.80, 95% CI 0.63 to 1.01). The single ICU trial (93 patients) showed a large effect on treatment failure (risk ratio 0.19) and on mortality (Peto odds ratio 0.21), while four inpatient trials showed no mortality effect (Peto odds ratio 1.02, 95% CI 0.37 to 2.79) — the mortality figures are printed together, as required, and no general mortality claim is made. The founding Anthonisen trial found success in 68% of exacerbations on antibiotic versus 55% on placebo. Adverse events, especially diarrhoea, were more common with antibiotics. Maintenance COPD therapy lives at #303-#306; only exacerbation antibiotics are carded here.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Antibiotics for acute sinusitis
question: Does amoxicillin beat placebo for acute uncomplicated rhinosinusitis in primary care?
balance: LIKELY (for the null-to-small verdict): In the Garbutt randomised trial, a 10-day course of amoxicillin did not improve disease-specific quality of life at day 3 (mean difference 0.03 on a 0-3 scale, 95% CI -0.12 to 0.19) or day 10, and symptom improvement did not differ at day 3 (37% versus 34%) or day 10 (78% versus 80%); only day 7 favoured amoxicillin. The Young individual-patient-data meta-analysis of 2,547 adults in 9 trials found 15 patients must be treated for one additional cure (NNT 15, with an interval running from NNT-benefit 7 to NNT-harm 190), and no clinical sign or symptom — not even symptoms lasting longer than 7-10 days — identified a subgroup in whom antibiotics were clearly justified; purulent discharge in the pharynx lowered the NNT to 8, with an interval still crossing into harm. The honest claim is that routine antibiotics for uncomplicated acute rhinosinusitis buy, at most, a small average benefit most patients will not notice.
stamp: LIKELY (for the null-to-small verdict)

title: Prolonged antibiotics for persistent symptoms attributed to Lyme disease
question: Do longer courses of antibiotics help patients with persistent symptoms after Lyme disease?
balance: LIKELY (for the null): Three randomised programmes converge. In PLEASE (281 patients), 12 weeks of doxycycline or clarithromycin-hydroxychloroquine after 2 weeks of open-label ceftriaxone gave SF-36 physical-component scores of 35.0 and 35.6 versus 34.8 on placebo (P=0.69). In the two Klempner trials (129 patients), 90 days of intravenous then oral antibiotics improved quality-of-life scores no more than placebo (among seropositive patients, improvement in 37% on antibiotics versus 40% on placebo). The one discordant note is Fallon's small trial (37 patients): 10 weeks of IV ceftriaxone gave a moderate cognitive improvement at week 12 that was not sustained to week 24, with adverse events in 26.1% on ceftriaxone versus 7.1% on placebo. The defensible claim is that longer antibiotic courses do not produce durable benefit for persistent symptoms attributed to Lyme disease, while carrying line and drug harms — not that patients' symptoms are unreal; baseline impairment in these trials was severe.
stamp: LIKELY (for the null)

title: Universal decolonization and chlorhexidine bathing in the ICU — and beyond it
question: Does universal (vs targeted) decolonization with chlorhexidine bathing ± nasal mupirocin reduce ICU infections and MRSA?
balance: Split — LIKELY in intensive care: in REDUCE MRSA (43 hospitals, 74,256 patients), universal decolonisation cut bloodstream infection from any pathogen more than targeted decolonisation or screening and isolation (hazard ratio 0.56 versus baseline, compared with 0.78 and 0.99; one bloodstream infection prevented per 54 patients decolonised), and in the Climo crossover trial daily chlorhexidine bathing lowered hospital-acquired bloodstream infections from 6.60 to 4.78 cases per 1,000 patient-days (a 28% relative reduction). MAYBE (weak evidence) outside intensive care: the ABATE Infection trial (53 hospitals, 339,902 patients in the intervention period) found no significant reduction in MRSA or VRE clinical cultures with universal chlorhexidine bathing plus targeted mupirocin in non-critical-care units (relative hazard ratios did not differ, p=0.17). This shelf is about skin bathing and nasal decolonisation only; chlorhexidine oral care for ventilated patients is a different intervention and lives at #469 — none of its trials is re-carded here.

title: Reduced-osmolarity oral rehydration solution
question: Does reduced-osmolarity ORS beat the standard WHO formulation for acute diarrhoea?
balance: LIKELY: In the Hahn systematic review of 15 randomised trials (2,397 children), reduced-osmolarity ORS was associated with fewer unscheduled intravenous infusions than standard WHO ORS (odds ratio 0.61, 95% CI 0.47 to 0.81 — a ratio inside the 0.5-2.0 band, printed with its absolute-outcome context: in three trials no child needed unscheduled infusion at all), with lower stool output and less vomiting (odds ratio 0.71, 95% CI 0.55 to 0.92) and no significant difference in hyponatraemia. A primary trial points the same way (treatment failure 1% versus 8% in the Santosham trial, as reported). The cholera-specific Cochrane review is the caution: in cholera, reduced-osmolarity ORS brought more biochemical hyponatraemia (risk ratio 1.67, 95% CI 1.09 to 2.57) with no significant difference in need for unscheduled intravenous infusion and no symptomatic hyponatraemia or deaths reported — in 718 participants, a small total experience. Zinc as an adjunct for childhood diarrhoea lives at #207 and probiotics at #141; neither is carded here.
stamp: LIKELY

title: Remote ischaemic preconditioning to prevent injury from cardiac surgery
question: Does remote ischaemic preconditioning protect the kidney and heart during cardiac surgery?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): Two large multicentre sham-controlled trials published back-to-back in 2015 found no benefit. RIPHeart (1,385 patients in the full analysis set) found the composite of death, myocardial infarction, stroke or acute renal failure in 14.3% with preconditioning versus 14.6% with sham (P=0.89), and ERICCA (1,612 patients) found its 12-month composite of cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, revascularisation or stroke in 26.5% versus 27.7% (hazard ratio 0.95, 95% CI 0.79 to 1.15; P=0.58). Acute kidney injury — the kidney component of this shelf's question — did not differ in either trial. Smaller earlier single-centre reports of kidney protection were not confirmed at scale.

title: Belatacept vs ciclosporin after kidney transplantation
question: Does belatacept-based immunosuppression preserve kidney function better than ciclosporin, and at what rejection cost?
balance: SPLIT: LIKELY better renal function / POSSIBLE overall. In the twin phase-3 BENEFIT trials, belatacept gave similar patient/graft survival to ciclosporin at 12 months (BENEFIT: 95% more-intensive, 97% less-intensive, 93% ciclosporin; BENEFIT-EXT: 86%, 89%, 85%) with better measured GFR (BENEFIT: 65, 63 versus 50 mL/min) and fewer patients reaching the composite renal impairment end point. The cost was more early acute rejection in BENEFIT (22% and 17% versus 7%; similar rates in BENEFIT-EXT: 18%, 18%, 14%) and more posttransplant lymphoproliferative disorder, concentrated in the central nervous system, on belatacept. Kidney function — a surrogate — favours belatacept; survival does not differ at 1 year, so the overall stamp cannot exceed POSSIBLE.
stamp: SPLIT

title: Early TIPS for high-risk variceal bleeding
question: Does early covered TIPS (within 72 hours) improve survival in high-risk cirrhosis patients bleeding from varices?
balance: Tier C — slow lane: this stamp is PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict, because the shelf carries a mortality claim. Two randomised trials agree on direction. García-Pagán 2010 (63 high-risk patients): 16 deaths in total — 12 of 31 on pharmacotherapy plus band ligation versus 4 of 32 on early TIPS (P=0.01); 1-year actuarial survival 61% versus 86% (an absolute difference of 25 percentage points). Lv 2019 (129 patients in the intention-to-treat population): 15 of 84 (18%) died on early TIPS versus 15 of 45 (33%) on standard treatment; transplantation-free survival hazard ratio 0.50 (95% CI 0.25 to 0.98; P=0.04), with 1-year transplantation-free survival 86% versus 73% (absolute difference 13 percentage points, 95% CI 2 to 28). All-cause mortality is stated on every card beside any relative measure. Both trials are small and enrolled selected high-risk patients (Child-Pugh C, or B with active bleeding), so LIKELY — not higher — is the honest ceiling, and it remains proposed until the developer rules. title: Ustekinumab for ulcerative colitis

title: Direct-acting antivirals for hepatitis C: cure rates and the outcome gap
question: Do direct-acting antivirals cure hepatitis C across genotypes — and what evidence links cure (SVR) to liver outcomes?
balance: LIKELY for the surrogate only — and this shelf makes NO hard-outcome claim. The randomised trials prove sustained virologic response (SVR, the cure surrogate): 90% SVR with sofosbuvir plus peginterferon-ribavirin in NEUTRINO, 99% SVR with sofosbuvir-velpatasvir versus 0% on placebo in ASTRAL-1, and 95–99% SVR in ASTRAL-2/3. title: High fluid intake to prevent kidney-stone recurrence
question: Does drinking enough water to produce over 2 litres of urine a day prevent stone recurrence?
balance: POSSIBLE — an honest single-flagship-trial ceiling. Borghi 1996, the one randomised trial of high water intake itself (199 first-episode idiopathic calcium stone formers, 5 years), found recurrence in 12 of 99 patients advised high water intake versus 27 of 100 with no treatment — 12.1% versus 27.0%, an absolute difference of about 15 percentage points. The 2026 PUSH trial (1,658 participants) tested something different — a behavioural programme to help people drink more, on top of guideline care advising high intake in both arms — and found symptomatic recurrence in 19% versus 20% (hazard ratio 0.96, 95% CI 0.77 to 1.20): the programme raised urine volume modestly but did not reduce events. So: drinking more water probably helps; programmes to make people drink more have not been shown to. title: Rifaximin to prevent hepatic encephalopathy recurrence
question: Does rifaximin prevent breakthrough hepatic encephalopathy episodes in cirrhosis patients already on lactulose?
balance: POSSIBLE — the honest ceiling for a single pivotal trial. Hospitalisation involving hepatic encephalopathy occurred in 13.6% versus 22.6% (hazard ratio 0.50, 95% CI 0.29 to 0.87; P=0.01). Adverse events were similar to placebo. title: Methenamine hippurate instead of prophylactic antibiotics for recurrent UTI
question: Is methenamine hippurate non-inferior to daily low-dose antibiotics for preventing recurrent UTI in women?
balance: POSSIBLE — an honest single-head-to-head-trial ceiling, now with a placebo-controlled companion. ALTAR (2022), the one non-inferiority trial against daily antibiotics (205 women in the modified intention-to-treat analysis), found 1.38 antibiotic-treated UTI episodes per person-year on methenamine versus 0.89 on antibiotics — an absolute difference of 0.49 episodes (90% CI 0.15 to 0.84), inside the predefined 1-episode margin, so non-inferiority was met while antibiotics remained numerically better. The 2025 ImpresU trial (281 women aged 70 or older) found fewer antibiotic treatments for UTI on methenamine than placebo during 6 months of treatment (incidence rate ratio 0.75, 95% CI 0.57 to 1.0; P=0.049) — a ratio inside the 0.5–2.0 band, so not solid evidence on its own — and a rebound after stopping (rate ratio 1.7 in the 6-month follow-up). Together: a reasonable non-antibiotic option, not a proven equal in every population.

title: Personalised cooler dialysate (MyTEMP)
question: Does dialysing at a personalised cooler temperature reduce cardiovascular death or hospitalisation in maintenance haemodialysis?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): MyTEMP, a single but very large pragmatic cluster-randomised trial (84 centres, 15,413 patients, about 4.3 million haemodialysis treatments), found the primary composite of cardiovascular death or hospital admission with myocardial infarction, ischaemic stroke or congestive heart failure in 21.4% of patients on personalised cooler dialysate versus 22.4% on standard 36.5°C dialysate (adjusted hazard ratio 1.00, 96% CI 0.89 to 1.11; P=0.93). The mean intradialytic systolic blood-pressure drop was also essentially identical (26.6 versus 27.1 mm Hg). The trial is null on its primary outcome and makes no benefit claim; its size earns the null a LIKELY stamp despite being a single trial.

title: How much fluid in acute pancreatitis: aggressive vs moderate resuscitation
question: Does aggressive early fluid resuscitation improve outcomes in acute pancreatitis, or cause overload?
balance: POSSIBLE — an honest single-trial ceiling, for harm from the aggressive strategy. WATERFALL (249 patients in the first interim analysis, of 744 planned) was halted early because aggressive resuscitation caused more fluid overload without improving outcomes: moderately severe or severe pancreatitis developed in 22.1% on aggressive versus 17.3% on moderate resuscitation (adjusted relative risk 1.30, 95% CI 0.78 to 2.18; P=0.32), while fluid overload developed in 20.5% versus 6.3% (adjusted relative risk 2.85, 95% CI 1.36 to 5.94; P=0.004) — an absolute overload excess of 14.2 percentage points. Early stopping and the single-trial base cap the stamp at POSSIBLE, but the direction is clear enough to retire routine aggressive resuscitation as the default.

title: Treating gestational diabetes
question: Does treating gestational diabetes (including mild GDM) improve pregnancy and neonatal outcomes?
balance: LIKELY: Treating gestational diabetes reduced serious perinatal complications in ACHOIS (1% vs 4%; adjusted relative risk 0.33, relative) and, in the mild-GDM Landon trial, treatment missed its primary composite (32.4% vs 37.0%, P=0.14) but reduced large-for-gestational-age babies (7.1% vs 14.5%), shoulder dystocia (1.5% vs 4.0%), caesarean delivery (26.9% vs 33.8%) and pre-eclampsia/gestational hypertension (8.6% vs 13.6%). Treatment buys these gains at the price of more inductions and more neonatal-nursery admissions in ACHOIS.
stamp: LIKELY

title: Progesterone for miscarriage: threatened and recurrent
question: Does progesterone prevent miscarriage in women with early-pregnancy bleeding, or with recurrent miscarriage?
balance: SPLIT — LIKELY the overall null; POSSIBLE for the prior-miscarriage subgroup: In women with early-pregnancy bleeding, PRISM found live births at 75% on progesterone vs 72% on placebo (relative rate 1.03, P=0.08) — no significant overall benefit — and in women with unexplained recurrent miscarriage, PROMISE found 65.8% vs 63.3% (relative risk 1.04, P=0.45), also null. The signal is confined to a prespecified PRISM subgroup, labelled as such throughout this shelf: among women with bleeding who had had three or more previous miscarriages, live births were 72% vs 57% (relative rate 1.28, relative) — a subgroup finding inside an overall-null trial, in a population PROMISE (recurrent miscarriage without the bleeding criterion) did not reproduce.

title: Treating hypertension in pregnancy: targets and thresholds
question: Should hypertension in pregnancy be treated tightly, and should mild chronic hypertension be treated to under 140/90?
balance: LIKELY: The two trials answer two halves of the question. CHIPS found tight diastolic control (target 85 mm Hg) no better than less-tight control (target 100 mm Hg) on pregnancy loss or high-level neonatal care (30.7% vs 31.4%), but less-tight control produced far more severe hypertension (40.6% vs 27.5%). CHAP then showed that actively treating mild chronic hypertension to under 140/90 lowered its primary composite (30.2% vs 37.0%; adjusted risk ratio 0.82, relative) with no increase in small-for-gestational-age births (11.2% vs 10.4%). Treating to under 140/90 in mild chronic hypertension is the supported strategy; pushing diastolic pressure to 85 rather than 100 added nothing on the baby outcomes CHIPS measured.
stamp: LIKELY

title: Magnesium sulfate for the mother: preventing and treating eclamptic seizures
question: Does magnesium sulfate prevent eclampsia in pre-eclampsia, and is it the best drug once seizures occur?
balance: LIKELY: Two large trial programmes answer the mother's seizure question directly. For prevention, the Magpie Trial found eclampsia in 0.8% of women with pre-eclampsia given magnesium sulfate versus 1.9% on placebo — a 58% lower risk (95% CI 40 to 71), a relative reduction with the absolute rates beside it — with maternal mortality lower but not significantly (relative risk 0.55, 95% CI 0.26 to 1.14) and no clear difference in baby deaths. For treatment once seizures have occurred, the Collaborative Eclampsia Trial found recurrent convulsions in 13.2% on magnesium versus 27.9% on diazepam, and 5.7% versus 17.1% on phenytoin. Side effects were commoner on magnesium in Magpie (24% vs 5%).
stamp: LIKELY

title: Adjuvant bisphosphonates in early breast cancer
question: Do adjuvant bisphosphonates reduce recurrence and breast-cancer death, and in whom?
balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED, pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, slow lane — breast-cancer mortality claim): The EBCTCG individual-patient-data meta-analysis found definite benefit only in women who were postmenopausal when treatment began: among 11,767 postmenopausal women, adjuvant bisphosphonates reduced recurrence (rate ratio 0.86), distant recurrence (0.82), bone recurrence (0.72) and breast-cancer mortality (rate ratio 0.82, 95% CI 0.73 to 0.93 — a relative reduction), with 10-year breast-cancer mortality of 14.7% on bisphosphonate versus 18.0% on control (a 3.3-percentage-point absolute reduction) and 10-year bone recurrence of 6.6% versus 8.8%. In premenopausal women there was no apparent effect on any outcome, and the overall results across all women were only of borderline significance. This stamp is proposed only and does not take effect without the developer's personal Tier C verdict. Tier C — built Nov 8, 2026 and held for the developer’s personal verdict; no approval stamp is claimed for this shelf.

title: Treating glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis
question: Which bone therapy best prevents fractures and bone loss in patients on long-term glucocorticoids?
balance: SPLIT — LIKELY for bone-density benefit; POSSIBLE for fracture prevention: Alendronate raised lumbar-spine bone density by 2.1% (5 mg) and 2.9% (10 mg) over 48 weeks while placebo lost 0.4% in Saag 1998, and in the head-to-head trial teriparatide raised spine density more than alendronate at 36 months (11.0% vs 5.3%) with fewer new vertebral fractures (1.7% vs 7.7%). The fracture evidence is thinner than the density evidence: Saag 1998's vertebral-fracture difference was not significant (2.3% vs 3.7%; relative risk 0.6, 95% CI 0.1 to 4.4) and the teriparatide fracture result comes from one active-comparison trial, so fracture prevention is stamped POSSIBLE while the density benefit is LIKELY.

title: Comprehensive geriatric assessment for older adults admitted to hospital
question: Does CGA on hospital wards increase the chance of older patients being alive and in their own homes later?
balance: LIKELY: The Ellis 2017 Cochrane synthesis of 29 trials (13,766 participants) found comprehensive geriatric assessment on hospital admission increased the chance of being alive and in one's own home at 3 to 12 months (risk ratio 1.06, 95% CI 1.01 to 1.10; high-certainty evidence) and reduced nursing-home admission (risk ratio 0.80, 95% CI 0.72 to 0.89; high-certainty evidence), with little or no difference in mortality itself (risk ratio 1.00, 95% CI 0.93 to 1.07) or dependence (0.97). The effect is small and it is an effect on where survivors live, not on survival — the stamp rests on the certainty and consistency of the evidence, not on a large ratio.
stamp: LIKELY

title: Hip protectors for fracture prevention
question: Do external hip protectors prevent hip fractures in older people at high risk?
balance: SPLIT — POSSIBLE in nursing or residential care; MAYBE (weak evidence) in the community: The arc of this literature runs from an early strikingly positive trial to later, larger nulls. Kannus 2000 found hip fractures at 21.3 vs 46.0 per 1000 person-years (relative hazard 0.4). The later individually randomised van Schoor trial found no difference (18 vs 20 fractures; hazard ratio 1.05). The Cochrane synthesis in its Parker 2005 form pooled a marginally significant reduction in nursing/residential care (relative risk 0.77, 95% CI 0.62 to 0.97, with significant heterogeneity) and no reduction in the community (1.16, 0.85 to 1.59); its 2014 update softened the care-setting estimate further (0.82, 0.67 to 1.00; absolute effect 11 fewer per 1000, CI from 20 fewer to 0) and confirmed little or no community effect (1.15, 0.84 to 1.58). Acceptance and long-term adherence were poor throughout. Both halves of the arc stay printed: the early positive result is not deleted, and it does not outrank the later nulls.

title: DHEA supplementation in older adults
question: Does DHEA improve body composition, strength, metabolism or wellbeing in older men and women?
balance: LIKELY the null: In the rigorous two-year Nair trial, DHEA had no significant effect on body composition, peak oxygen consumption, muscle strength, insulin sensitivity or quality of life in elderly men or women. The earlier one-year DHEAge study restored 'young' DHEAS concentrations and reported selective findings — improved bone turnover and most libido parameters in women over 70, and improved skin status particularly in women — without harmful accumulation of steroids. Those selective positives do not overturn the null on the outcomes this shelf's question asks about: composition, strength, metabolism and wellbeing.

title: Vaginal laser treatment for postmenopausal vaginal symptoms
question: Does fractional CO2 laser improve genitourinary syndrome of menopause symptoms more than sham treatment?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference, on one rigorous sham trial against an earlier positive small-trial pooling): The one large, double-blind, sham-controlled trial with 12-month follow-up (Li 2021, 85 women) found no significant difference between fractional CO2 laser and sham on symptom severity, quality of life, Vaginal Health Index or histology. A 2021 systematic review of the three earlier, much smaller sham-controlled trials (164 women in total) had pooled in laser's favour on symptom, sexual-function and urinary scores. The rigorous trial outranks the small-trial pooling, but with a single such trial the null is stamped POSSIBLE, not LIKELY.

title: Laser first for glaucoma: selective laser trabeculoplasty vs drops
question: In open-angle glaucoma and ocular hypertension, is first-line selective laser trabeculoplasty as good as — or better than — starting with IOP-lowering drops?
balance: LIKELY: Two randomised trials frame the choice. LiGHT (718 treatment-naive patients) found selective laser trabeculoplasty gave the same health-related quality of life as drops at 3 years, with 74.2% of laser-first patients still drop-free and fewer glaucoma operations (0 vs 11). UKGTS supplies the benchmark the drops arm rests on: latanoprost preserved the visual field versus placebo (adjusted hazard ratio 0.44), the first placebo-controlled proof that IOP lowering protects vision. Laser-first is therefore an equal-outcome, drop-sparing first line — not a claim that laser beats a working drop on pressure.
stamp: LIKELY

title: Chronic central serous chorioretinopathy: eplerenone failed, half-dose photodynamic therapy leads
question: In chronic central serous chorioretinopathy, does eplerenone help — and does half-dose photodynamic therapy beat micropulse laser or observation?
balance: Split: POSSIBLE — half-dose photodynamic therapy over micropulse laser · POSSIBLE — eplerenone ineffective (each on a single trial): VICI (114 patients) found eplerenone no better than placebo on visual acuity at 12 months (adjusted difference 1.73 letters, CI crossing zero), and its authors say prescribers should stop. PLACE (179 patients, open-label) found half-dose photodynamic therapy resolved subretinal fluid far more often than high-density subthreshold micropulse laser at first review (51.2% vs 13.8%) and at 7–8 months (67.2% vs 28.8%). One trial each way caps both halves at POSSIBLE.

title: Dry eye disease: omega-3 supplements and prescription drops
question: Do omega-3 supplements improve dry eye (DREAM) — and do lifitegrast or cyclosporine drops beat vehicle?
balance: Split: LIKELY — omega-3 ineffective · POSSIBLE — lifitegrast improves dryness symptoms: DREAM was a large multicentre trial (535 randomised) and its null was complete — symptom scores, staining, tear break-up time and Schirmer results all statistically indistinguishable from olive-oil placebo at 12 months — so the null carries LIKELY under this library's large-null rule. OPUS-3 (711 participants) found lifitegrast improved the eye-dryness symptom score versus vehicle at day 84 (treatment effect 7.16 points) but showed no difference on the ocular discomfort score or any objective sign, so the symptom claim is POSSIBLE on a single carded trial. title: Fenofibrate to slow diabetic retinopathy progression
question: In type 2 diabetes, does fenofibrate slow progression of diabetic retinopathy or reduce the need for laser treatment, beyond its lipid effects?
balance: LIKELY: Two large randomised programmes agree. In FIELD (9,795 patients with type 2 diabetes), fenofibrate cut first laser treatment for retinopathy from 4.9% to 3.4% (hazard ratio 0.69, a relative measure). In ACCORD-Eye (2,856 participants), fenofibrate plus simvastatin cut 4-year retinopathy progression from 10.2% to 6.5% (adjusted odds ratio 0.60, relative). Both relative ratios sit inside the 0.5–2.0 band this library treats as not solid on their own; the LIKELY rests on two concordant trials with absolute differences printed beside them, and the FIELD photography substudy's overall progression endpoint was itself null (p=0.19) — the benefit is clearest for laser need and for patients with pre-existing retinopathy.
stamp: LIKELY

title: Amblyopia in children: patching vs atropine penalisation
question: In moderate amblyopia in children under 7, is atropine penalisation of the sound eye as effective as patching — and how much patching is enough?
balance: LIKELY: Two PEDIG randomised trials settle both halves. Atropine and patching improved acuity by a similar amount at 6 months (3.16 vs 2.84 lines; mean difference 0.034 logMAR, clinically inconsequential), so either is an appropriate initial treatment for moderate amblyopia at age 3 to under 7. And 2 hours of daily patching matched 6 hours at 4 months (2.40 lines gained in each group) when combined with 1 hour of near activities — less patching is enough for moderate disease.

title: Low-dose atropine to slow childhood myopia
question: Does low-dose atropine (0.01–0.05%) slow myopia progression in children, at what concentration, and with what rebound on stopping?
balance: LIKELY: Atropine slows progression in a concentration-dependent way across two randomised programmes. LAMP (438 children, placebo-controlled) found 1-year spherical-equivalent change of -0.27 D on 0.05%, -0.46 D on 0.025%, -0.59 D on 0.01% and -0.81 D on placebo, with axial elongation ordered the same way. ATOM2 (400 children, no concurrent placebo arm) found 2-year progression of -0.30 D (0.5%), -0.38 D (0.1%) and -0.49 D (0.01%), with 0.01% nearly free of accommodation and pupil effects. Neither carded abstract reports what happens on stopping, so the drafted question's rebound half is not answered by the carded records and is not claimed.

title: Retinopathy of prematurity: anti-VEGF injection vs laser
question: For stage 3+ retinopathy of prematurity, does intravitreal bevacizumab (or ranibizumab) beat laser ablation, by zone of disease?
balance: Split: LIKELY — bevacizumab over laser for zone I recurrence · POSSIBLE — ranibizumab benefit: BEAT-ROP (150 infants) found recurrence requiring retreatment in 4% of bevacizumab eyes versus 22% of laser eyes (P=0.002), with the significant effect in zone I disease (P=0.003) and not zone II (P=0.27). title: Uveitis: fluocinolone implant vs systemic immunosuppression (MUST)
question: For non-infectious intermediate/posterior/pan-uveitis, does a sustained-release fluocinolone implant control inflammation and preserve vision as well as systemic therapy — and at what ocular price?

title: Glaucoma drainage surgery: tube shunt vs trabeculectomy
question: In eyes with prior surgery or high failure risk, does a tube shunt give better pressure control and fewer failures than trabeculectomy with mitomycin?
balance: LIKELY: In eyes with previous surgery, tube shunt surgery beat trabeculectomy with mitomycin C on the outcome that matters — failure over 5 years was 29.8% versus 46.9% in TVT (hazard ratio 2.15 for trabeculectomy versus tube, a relative measure), with reoperation in 9% versus 29%, while achieved pressure and medication counts were similar. The second carded programme refines the tube choice itself: pooled Ahmed–Baerveldt data (514 patients) found the Baerveldt implant failed less (37% vs 49% at 5 years) and reached lower pressure on fewer medications, at a higher hypotony risk (4.5% vs 0.4%).

title: Optical myopia control: multifocal and dual-focus contact lenses
question: Do multifocal or dual-focus soft contact lenses slow myopia progression and axial elongation in children versus single-vision lenses?
balance: LIKELY: Two double-masked randomised trials agree. BLINK (294 children) found high-add (+2.50 D) multifocal lenses slowed 3-year progression to -0.60 D versus -1.05 D on single-vision lenses (difference 0.46 D) and slowed eye growth (0.42 vs 0.66 mm), while medium-add lenses sat in between. title: Acne in adult women and adolescents: spironolactone and fixed-dose topical combinations

title: Preventing eczema in infancy: daily emollients from birth
question: Does applying emollient daily from birth prevent atopic eczema (and food allergy) in high-risk infants?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): Two large randomised trials, one in high-risk infants and one in the general population, both found that daily emollients from birth did not prevent eczema. BEEP (1,394 newborns) found eczema at age 2 in 23% on emollient versus 25% on standard care (adjusted relative risk 0.95, CI 0.78 to 1.16), with more skin infections in the emollient group. PreventADALL (2,397 infants) likewise found no reduction by 12 months. Families should not use daily emollients to try to prevent eczema. Neither carded abstract reports a food-allergy prevention result, so that half of the drafted question is not claimed here.

title: Scabies: permethrin vs oral ivermectin, and mass drug administration
question: For ordinary scabies, is oral ivermectin as effective as permethrin cream — and does community mass drug administration control endemic scabies and impetigo?
balance: LIKELY: For community control the evidence is strong: in the Fiji trial (2,051 participants), mass ivermectin administration cut scabies prevalence from 32.1% to 1.9% at 12 months (relative reduction 94%), far beyond standard care (36.6% to 18.8%) or mass permethrin (41.7% to 15.8%), and cut impetigo most as well. For individual treatment, the Cochrane synthesis of 20 small trials (2,392 people) found topical permethrin appeared more effective than oral ivermectin in the one small head-to-head trial (85 participants), so 'ivermectin is as effective as permethrin for an individual case' is NOT what this shelf claims — permethrin leads for individual treatment, ivermectin leads as a population tool.
stamp: LIKELY

title: Common warts: cryotherapy vs salicylic acid vs waiting
question: For cutaneous warts in primary care, does cryotherapy beat topical salicylic acid — and does either beat watchful waiting by much?
balance: Split: POSSIBLE — cryotherapy for common warts · MAYBE (weak evidence) — any treatment advantage for plantar warts: The one primary-care trial that tested all three strategies head-to-head (250 patients) found 13-week cure of 39% with cryotherapy, 24% with salicylic acid and 16% with waiting — but the cryotherapy advantage was confined to common warts (49% vs 15% vs 8%), with no significant difference for plantar warts. The Cochrane synthesis (85 trials, 8,815 participants) is more cautious still: salicylic acid beat placebo modestly (relative risk 1.56), cryotherapy did not beat placebo in pooled analysis, and cryotherapy did not beat salicylic acid (relative risk 1.23, interval crossing 1) — all relative measures inside the 0.5–2.0 caution band, which is why neither half rises above POSSIBLE.
stamp: Split

title: Androgenetic alopecia in men: finasteride and minoxidil
question: Do finasteride 1 mg and topical minoxidil 5% regrow or preserve hair in male pattern hair loss versus placebo?
balance: LIKELY: Both drugs beat placebo in double-blind trials. Finasteride 1 mg/day (1,553 men in two 1-year trials, with blinded extensions) produced clinically significant hair-count gains over placebo at 1 and 2 years (+107 and +138 hairs in the measured vertex circle versus placebo) and slowed progression, which continued on placebo. Minoxidil 5% foam (352 men) significantly increased hair counts and subjective improvement versus placebo at 16 weeks and was well tolerated over 52 weeks of open-label follow-up. Neither carded abstract prints its placebo arm's absolute counts, so the shelf claims direction and the finasteride differences, not invented percentages.
stamp: LIKELY

title: Papulopustular rosacea: ivermectin cream and comparators
question: Does ivermectin 1% cream clear inflammatory rosacea lesions better than vehicle, metronidazole, or azelaic acid?
balance: POSSIBLE: A network meta-analysis of the topical rosacea trials found ivermectin 1% cream once daily more likely to succeed than azelaic acid 15% gel (relative risk 1.25) or metronidazole 0.75% cream (relative risk 1.17) at 12 weeks, with larger inflammatory-lesion reductions — but both relative risks sit inside the 0.5–2.0 band this library treats as not solid on their own, and the comparison is indirect. Two 40-week extension trials found ivermectin safe and tolerable long-term with fewer related adverse events than azelaic acid gel. The underlying vehicle-controlled phase 3 trials are described inside these records but are not themselves carded, and no vehicle-comparison figures appear in the carded abstracts — hence POSSIBLE, and no vehicle claim is quantified.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Actinic keratosis: field-directed topical therapy compared (fluorouracil, imiquimod, photodynamic therapy, ingenol mebutate)
question: Among field treatments for actinic keratosis (5-fluorouracil, imiquimod, methyl aminolevulinate photodynamic therapy, ingenol mebutate), which keeps patients free from treatment failure most durably at 12 months?
balance: POSSIBLE (single pivotal trial): In Jansen 2019 (624 patients with five or more actinic keratosis lesions on the head), the cumulative probability of remaining free from treatment failure at 12 months was 74.7% with 5% fluorouracil cream, 53.9% with 5% imiquimod cream, 37.7% with methyl aminolevulinate photodynamic therapy and 28.9% with ingenol mebutate gel — fluorouracil clearly first, with hazard ratios for failure of 2.03 (imiquimod), 2.73 (MAL-PDT) and 3.33 (ingenol) against it, all relative measures. Conformed to the trial it rests on: the drafted question named diclofenac, which Jansen did not test, so the shelf question names the trial's four actual arms; diclofenac is not answered here. A single trial caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.
stamp: POSSIBLE (single pivotal trial)

title: Impetigo: topical vs oral antibiotics
question: For limited impetigo, are topical antibiotics (mupirocin/fusidic acid) as effective as oral antibiotics — and better than placebo or disinfection alone?
balance: LIKELY (on a 68-trial synthesis): The Cochrane review (68 trials, 5,578 participants) found topical antibiotics cured impetigo better than placebo (pooled relative risk 2.24, a relative measure beyond the 2.0 solidity threshold), that mupirocin and fusidic acid did not differ from each other (relative risk 1.03), and that topical mupirocin was slightly superior to oral erythromycin (relative risk 1.07, inside the caution band) with no significant difference against other oral antibiotics — so for limited impetigo, topical treatment is at least as effective as oral, with fewer side effects. There was no evidence supporting disinfectant solutions. The review could not settle extensive impetigo, where oral therapy may still be needed.
stamp: LIKELY (on a 68-trial synthesis)

title: Preventing recurrent leg cellulitis: prophylactic penicillin (PATCH)
question: In people with recurrent leg cellulitis, does low-dose prophylactic penicillin prevent the next episode — and for how long after stopping?
balance: LIKELY: PATCH I (274 patients with two or more prior episodes) found penicillin 250 mg twice daily for 12 months cut recurrence during prophylaxis from 37% to 22% (hazard ratio 0.55, a relative measure; number needed to treat 5), with fewer repeat episodes overall (119 vs 164), and no difference once treatment stopped (27% first recurrence in both groups during follow-up) — protection lasts only while taking it. PATCH II (123 patients after a first or subsequent episode; under-recruited at 31% of target) pointed the same way over 6 months of prophylaxis (20% vs 33% recurrence; hazard ratio 0.53, relative) without reaching significance. Antibiotic duration for an acute episode is Shelf #506 — a different question, not re-carded here.
stamp: LIKELY

title: Plaque psoriasis, topical therapy: vitamin D–steroid combination foam/gel
question: Does fixed calcipotriol–betamethasone combination (foam or gel) clear plaque psoriasis better than either component alone?
balance: LIKELY: The component question is answered directly by the 1,603-patient four-arm trial: mean PASI change at 4 weeks was -71.3% on the combination ointment versus -57.2% on betamethasone alone, -46.1% on calcipotriol alone and -22.7% on vehicle. The modern formulation evidence points the same way: in the PSO-ABLE subgroup with moderate-to-severe disease, the calcipotriol–betamethasone aerosol foam beat the same combination as a gel on mPASI75 at week 12 (57.1% vs 35.4%). Systemic biologics for moderate-to-severe psoriasis are Shelf #377 — a different treatment level, not re-carded here.

title: Tympanostomy tubes for recurrent acute otitis media and effusion
question: In children with recurrent acute otitis media, do tympanostomy tubes reduce further episodes versus medical management — and do grommets improve hearing in persistent effusion?
balance: Split: POSSIBLE — no reduction in otitis episodes · POSSIBLE — small, short-lived hearing gain in effusion: In the one large randomised trial of tubes versus medical management for recurrent acute otitis media (Hoberman 2021), the episode rate over two years was 1.48 versus 1.56 per child-year (P=0.66) — a null from a single trial, so POSSIBLE rather than LIKELY. For effusion, the Cochrane synthesis of 10 trials (1,728 children) found hearing about 12 dB better at three months and 4 dB better at six to nine months with grommets, with no difference by 12 to 18 months and no effect on language, behaviour or cognition — a real but transient gain as effusion resolves naturally.

title: Tonsillectomy for recurrent throat infection: children and adults
question: Does tonsillectomy reduce sore-throat episodes enough to justify surgery — in severely affected children (Paradise criteria) and in adults?
balance: LIKELY: Two randomised trials, one in each age group, point the same way. In severely affected children (Paradise 1984), throat-infection incidence was significantly lower in the surgical groups in each of the first two follow-up years, though many untreated children also improved and most of their episodes were mild. In adults (NATTINA 2023, 453 randomised), immediate tonsillectomy gave a median 23 versus 30 sore-throat days over 24 months (adjusted incident rate ratio 0.53, relative) and was cost-effective — against a 19% postoperative bleeding rate. The benefit is a reduction in episode burden, not elimination, and it is bought with surgical risk.
stamp: LIKELY

title: Adenotonsillectomy for childhood sleep-disordered breathing
question: In children with obstructive sleep apnea or mild sleep-disordered breathing, does early adenotonsillectomy improve behaviour, cognition, and breathing versus watchful waiting?
balance: Split: LIKELY — no gain in attention or executive function · LIKELY — symptom, behaviour and breathing gains: Two large randomised trials, in established obstructive sleep apnea (CHAT 2013) and in mild sleep-disordered breathing (PATS 2023), agree closely. Neither found a significant benefit on its primary cognitive outcome — attention/executive function improved 7.1 vs 5.1 points in CHAT (P=0.16) and executive-function and attention changes were non-significant in PATS. Both found surgery better on secondary outcomes: behaviour, symptoms, quality of life and polysomnography (breathing normalised in 79% vs 46% in CHAT; progression of the apnea-hypopnea index beyond 3 events/hour in 1.3% vs 13.2% in PATS). Operate for symptoms and breathing, not for cognition.
stamp: Split

title: Septoplasty for nasal obstruction (NAIROS)
question: In adults with a deviated septum and nasal obstruction, does septoplasty improve symptoms more than defined medical management?
balance: LIKELY: Two pragmatic randomised trials in two countries agree that septoplasty beats non-surgical management for nasal obstruction from a deviated septum. NAIROS (UK, 378 adults) found Sino-Nasal Outcome Test-22 scores 20.0 points lower (better) with septoplasty than with a defined nasal-steroid-and-saline regimen at six months, against a 9-point minimal clinically important difference. The Dutch trial (van Egmond 2019, 203 adults) found general health-related quality of life 8.3 points better at 12 months, sustained to 24 months. Harms were those of surgery: in NAIROS, 4% were readmitted with bleeding and 12% needed antibiotics for infection.
stamp: LIKELY

title: Ménière's disease: betahistine and intratympanic therapy
question: Does betahistine prevent Ménière's vertigo attacks — and for refractory disease, does intratympanic methylprednisolone match gentamicin with less hearing risk?
balance: Split: LIKELY — betahistine does not prevent attacks (the treatment made no difference) · POSSIBLE — methylprednisolone matches gentamicin for vertigo control: BEMED (221 adults, double-blind, nine months, two doses) found attack rate ratios of 1.036 and 1.012 versus placebo — as tight a null as this field has, and a very large single double-blind trial may carry LIKELY for the null, stated as such. Attacks fell by about a quarter over time in every arm, placebo included. For refractory disease, one double-blind trial (Patel 2016, 60 patients) found vertigo attacks fell 87% with gentamicin and 90% with methylprednisolone over two years (difference −0.9 attacks) — a single small trial, so POSSIBLE; more steroid patients needed repeat injections (15 vs 8).

title: Tinnitus: cognitive behavioural therapy and sound therapy
question: Does CBT reduce tinnitus distress and severity versus waiting list or usual care?
balance: LIKELY: Two randomised trials, seventeen years and two delivery models apart, agree that cognitive behavioural therapy reduces tinnitus distress. Cima 2012 (492 patients) found a stepped-care CBT programme (with sound-focused retraining therapy) beat usual care on health-related quality of life (difference 0.059; effect size d=0.24), tinnitus severity (d=0.43) and tinnitus impairment (d=0.45) over 12 months. Andersson 2002 found internet-delivered CBT beat a waiting list, with significantly more treated patients achieving at least a 50% improvement on the Tinnitus Reaction Questionnaire — though only 26 of about 59 treated participants completed all stages. Effects are modest, and CBT changes the reaction to tinnitus, not the sound itself.
stamp: LIKELY

title: Hypoglossal nerve stimulation for obstructive sleep apnea
question: In CPAP-intolerant moderate-to-severe OSA, does upper-airway (hypoglossal) stimulation reduce apnea events and sleepiness?
balance: POSSIBLE: The STAR study (126 implanted patients) is a single-group cohort, not a randomised comparison against no treatment: at 12 months the median apnea-hypopnea index fell 68% (29.3 to 9.0 events/hour) and the oxygen desaturation index fell 70% (25.4 to 7.4), with sleepiness and quality of life improved and a procedure-related serious adverse event rate under 2%. Its embedded randomised withdrawal sub-study is the controlled kernel: among responders, scores stayed flat with therapy maintained (AHI 8.9) and rebounded when therapy was switched off for a week (25.8 vs 7.6 events/hour, P<0.001), showing the measured effect belongs to the device. A single pivotal study with a one-week withdrawal test caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Vestibular rehabilitation for chronic dizziness
question: Does vestibular rehabilitation — clinic-based or internet-delivered — reduce dizziness handicap in adults with chronic vestibular symptoms?
balance: LIKELY: Two randomised trials of internet-delivered vestibular rehabilitation versus usual care, in Dutch and English primary care, agree. Van Vugt 2019 (322 adults aged 50+) found vertigo symptom scores 4.1 points lower with stand-alone online rehabilitation and 3.5 points lower with physiotherapy-supported rehabilitation than with usual care at six months, against a 3-point clinically relevant difference. Geraghty 2017 (296 patients aged 50+) found scores 2.75 points better at three months and 2.26 points at six months, with less dizziness-related disability. Adding physiotherapy support did not obviously add benefit. No serious adverse events related to online rehabilitation occurred in either trial.

title: Nasal saline irrigation for chronic rhinosinusitis and recurrent sinus symptoms
question: Does daily nasal saline irrigation improve symptoms in chronic or recurrent rhinosinusitis versus usual care?
balance: LIKELY (for a modest symptomatic benefit): Two randomised trials agree in direction across twenty years. STEAM (Little 2016; 871 patients analysed in UK primary care) found nasal irrigation improved Rhinosinusitis Disability Index scores more than no irrigation at three months (adjusted mean difference −2.51) and left more patients holding a 10-point clinically important improvement at six months (44.1% vs 36.6%), with less over-the-counter medication use. Rabago 2002 (76 patients) found larger quality-of-life and symptom gains with daily hypertonic irrigation and less antibiotic use. The large pragmatic trial's own authors note the benefit was smaller than earlier evidence suggested — the stamp is for a modest benefit, not a large one. Steam inhalation, tested alongside in STEAM, did not work.

title: Surgery for obstructive sleep apnea in adults: multilevel and pharyngoplasty techniques
question: In adults with OSA who cannot use CPAP, does multilevel upper-airway surgery reduce apnea severity and sleepiness versus continued medical management?
balance: POSSIBLE: One small open-label randomised trial and one selected single-centre surgical trial programme support multilevel/pharyngoplasty surgery in CPAP-failure patients, but neither is large or blinded. SAMS (MacKay 2020, 102 adults) found combined palatal and tongue surgery beat ongoing medical management at six months on the apnea-hypopnea index (baseline-adjusted difference −17.6 events/hour) and Epworth Sleepiness Scale (−6.7 points), with two serious adverse events in the surgery group, including a postoperative myocardial infarction. SKUP3's modified uvulopalatopharyngoplasty cohort, drawn from its earlier randomised trial, sustained an AHI fall from 52.9 to about 24 at both 6 and 24 months in patients selected by Friedman stage and tonsil size. title: Probiotics (L. reuteri) for infant colic
question: Does Lactobacillus reuteri DSM 17938 reduce crying time in breastfed infants with colic versus placebo?
balance: Split: POSSIBLE — breastfed infants · MAYBE (weak evidence) — formula-fed infants: The trials genuinely disagree, and feeding type explains most of it. Savino 2010 (50 exclusively breastfed infants) found crying fell to a median 35 versus 90 minutes/day by day 21. Sung 2014 (167 breastfed and formula-fed infants) found the probiotic group cried or fussed 49 minutes MORE than placebo at one month (P=0.02), driven by fussing in formula-fed infants. The individual-participant meta-analysis of all four double-blind trials (345 infants) found 25.4 minutes less crying/fussing at day 21 overall and treatment success almost twice as likely (incidence ratio 1.7, relative), with the effect dramatic in breastfed infants (number needed to treat 2.6) and insignificant in formula-fed infants, for whom the data were insufficient. Hence POSSIBLE for breastfed infants from a pooling anchored by one small positive trial against a larger null, and MAYBE (weak evidence) for formula-fed infants.

title: Acid suppression for infant reflux and irritability
question: Do proton-pump inhibitors improve crying/irritability attributed to gastro-oesophageal reflux in infants versus placebo?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): Two double-blind, placebo-controlled trials agree that proton-pump inhibitors do not reduce infant crying or irritability attributed to reflux. Orenstein 2009 (162 infants) found identical responder rates for lansoprazole and placebo (54% in each group) — and significantly more serious adverse events, particularly lower respiratory tract infections, with lansoprazole (10 vs 2 infants; P=0.032). Moore 2003 (30 infants, crossover) confirmed the mechanism and the disconnect: omeprazole cut oesophageal acid exposure (reflux index −8.9% vs −1.9%; P<0.001) yet irritability improved with time regardless of treatment, with no difference between omeprazole and placebo. The drug does what it is sold to do to acid; it does not do what it is prescribed to do to crying.

title: Bracing for adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (BrAIST)
question: Does rigid bracing prevent curve progression to the surgical threshold in adolescent idiopathic scoliosis — and is there a dose (hours worn) response?
balance: POSSIBLE: BrAIST is one trial programme — a randomised cohort nested in a larger preference cohort — and it was stopped early for efficacy. Across both cohorts, treatment success (reaching skeletal maturity without progression to 50 degrees) was 72% with bracing versus 48% with observation (propensity-adjusted odds ratio 1.93, relative — inside the 0.5–2.0 caution band); in the randomised intention-to-treat analysis alone, success was 75% versus 42% (odds ratio 4.11, relative). Hours worn mattered: success rose significantly with longer daily brace wear (P<0.001). A single trial programme, half of it non-randomised, caps the stamp at POSSIBLE despite the dose-response.

title: ADHD in children: stimulant medication and the MTA strategy trial
question: For childhood ADHD, how do stimulants compare with behavioural treatment and their combination — acutely (MTA) and in preschool children (PATS)?
balance: LIKELY: For core ADHD symptoms in school-age children, carefully managed medication beat intensive behavioural treatment and routine community care over 14 months in the MTA trial (579 children): the combined and medication-management groups improved significantly more than behavioural treatment and community care, and combined treatment did not significantly beat medication management alone on core symptoms — though it edged ahead on several non-core outcomes (oppositional symptoms, internalising symptoms, social skills, parent–child relations, reading). In preschoolers (PATS, Greenhill 2006), immediate-release methylphenidate given three times daily reduced symptoms significantly at 2.5, 5 and 7.5 mg doses versus placebo, with smaller effect sizes (0.4–0.8) than in school-age children and only 21% of preschoolers reaching the MTA remission criterion on their best dose. These are 14-month and short-term findings; neither trial answers what years of treatment do.

title: Early behavioural intervention for autism
question: Does intensive early behavioural intervention (Early Start Denver Model; parent-mediated communication therapy) improve cognition, language, or symptom severity in young autistic children?
balance: POSSIBLE: Two randomised trials of two different models both found gains, but each carries a ceiling. ESDM (Dawson 2010) randomised only 48 toddlers: after two years the ESDM group had improved 17.6 IQ standard-score points versus 7.0 in the community-intervention group, maintained adaptive-behaviour growth, and was more likely to shift diagnosis from autism to pervasive developmental disorder–not otherwise specified. PACT (Pickles 2016 long-term follow-up of 152 children) found a parent-mediated communication therapy reduced autism symptom severity across the trial and follow-up period (effect size 0.55, 95% CI 0.14 to 0.91; P=0.004), though the follow-up-only difference was not significant (0.70, −0.05 to 1.47) and there was no language-composite difference at follow-up (0.15, −0.23 to 0.53). Small numbers and one follow-up analysis keep the stamp at POSSIBLE.

title: Nocturnal enuresis: alarm therapy vs desmopressin
question: In childhood nocturnal enuresis, does an enuresis alarm produce more durable dryness than desmopressin — and what does each do while used?
balance: LIKELY: The Cochrane synthesis of alarm trials (55 trials, 3,152 children) and an 18-trial network meta-analysis (1,649 children) draw the same picture from opposite ends. While used, about two thirds of children become dry on an alarm (relative risk of failure 0.38 versus no treatment, relative); nearly half of those who persist remain dry after the alarm stops, versus almost none after no treatment. Desmopressin may act faster, but alarms were more effective by the end of a treatment course (relative risk 0.71, relative) and clearly more durable afterwards (failure or relapse 18% vs 67% in the limited head-to-head data; network analysis: relapse much lower with alarm monotherapy than desmopressin monotherapy). Combinations topped the network rankings for initial response, but the alarm is the durability play — at the price of weeks of family effort.
stamp: LIKELY

title: Kawasaki disease: IVIG, aspirin dose, and added steroids for high-risk children
question: Does adding corticosteroids to IVIG prevent coronary artery abnormalities in high-risk Kawasaki disease — and does IVIG regimen (single high dose) matter?
balance: PROPOSED stamp, pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C — coronary-outcome benefit claims): Split: POSSIBLE — single high-dose IVIG · POSSIBLE — added prednisolone in severe disease. Newburger 1991 (549 children) found a single 2 g/kg IVIG infusion beat four daily 400 mg/kg infusions on coronary abnormalities at two weeks (relative prevalence 1.94 for the four-day regimen versus single, relative; absolute rates not printed in the abstract) with faster fever resolution — though the seven-week comparison was not significant (1.84, 95% CI 0.89 to 3.82). RAISE (Kobayashi 2012; 248 children with severe Kawasaki disease in Japan) found adding prednisolone to IVIG cut coronary artery abnormalities from 23% to 3% (risk difference 0.20) during the study period. Each claim rests on a single trial — and RAISE enrolled risk-score-selected Japanese children in an open-label design — so both halves are POSSIBLE, and the shelf is Tier C because its claims are cardiovascular-outcome benefits.

title: Childhood functional constipation: polyethylene glycol vs lactulose
question: Is PEG more effective than lactulose (or other osmotic laxatives) for functional constipation in children?
balance: LIKELY: Two double-blind randomised trials support polyethylene glycol on both sides of the comparison. Against lactulose head-to-head (Voskuijl 2004, 100 children), treatment success at eight weeks was 56% with PEG 3350 versus 29% with lactulose, with less abdominal pain, straining and pain at defecation on PEG (though a worse taste). Against placebo (Nurko 2008, 103 children), PEG 3350 at 0.2–0.8 g/kg/day produced successful treatment in 73–77% versus 42% on placebo (P<0.04), with the authors recommending a starting dose of 0.4 g/kg/day; the highest dose brought more abdominal pain and faecal incontinence. Two blinded trials, two comparators, one direction — LIKELY.
stamp: LIKELY

title: Probiotics to prevent antibiotic-associated diarrhoea in children
question: Do probiotics given with antibiotics prevent antibiotic-associated diarrhoea in children — and does strain/dose decide it?
balance: LIKELY: The Cochrane prevention review (Guo 2019; 33 trials, 6,352 children) found antibiotic-associated diarrhoea in 8% of probiotic children versus 19% of controls (pooled risk ratio 0.45, relative — at or beyond the library's ≤0.5 solidity threshold — with a number needed to treat of 9), and the benefit survived an extreme-plausible intention-to-treat re-analysis (12% vs 19%; risk ratio 0.61, relative). Dose decided it: high-dose probiotics (≥5 billion CFU/day) performed better (number needed to treat 6), while low-dose studies were compatible with no effect in the intention-to-treat analysis. No serious adverse events were attributed to probiotics in the 24 reporting trials. The carded primary trial (Arvola 1999, Lactobacillus GG) matches the pooled pattern: diarrhoea in 5% versus 16% on placebo.
stamp: LIKELY

title: Inguinal hernia repair: mesh vs sutured repair, and laparoscopic vs open mesh
question: Does mesh repair reduce recurrence versus sutured repair — and does laparoscopic repair beat open mesh on pain and recovery at any recurrence cost?
balance: LIKELY: Open mesh repair reduces hernia recurrence compared with open non-mesh repair (Cochrane individual-patient-data review of 20 trials: Peto odds ratio 0.37, a relative figure), with quicker return to usual activities. For the approach question, the large VA trial found open mesh superior to laparoscopic mesh for primary hernias on recurrence (4.9% vs 10.1% at two years), while laparoscopy bought only modest early-pain and one-day-earlier-return advantages and more complications; for recurrent hernias the two approaches had similar recurrence. Mesh, placed open, is the evidence-backed default in this trial base.
stamp: LIKELY

title: Timing of cholecystectomy for acute cholecystitis: early vs delayed
question: Is early (same-admission, within days) laparoscopic cholecystectomy safer than delayed interval surgery for acute cholecystitis?
balance: LIKELY: Early laparoscopic cholecystectomy — within 24 hours of admission in ACDC, and on admission even after more than 72 hours of symptoms in the Roulin trial — produces substantially less overall morbidity than antibiotics-first delayed surgery (11.8% vs 34.4% in ACDC; 14% vs 39% in Roulin), with shorter total hospital stay and lower costs, and no significant difference in conversion to open surgery or mortality in ACDC. Two concordant randomised trials, one large and multicentre, support operating during the index admission in operable patients.
stamp: LIKELY

title: Incisional negative-pressure wound therapy: open fractures and closed incisions
question: Does incisional negative-pressure therapy reduce deep surgical-site infection after lower-limb fracture surgery or caesarean delivery versus standard dressings?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): Two large randomised trials found no significant reduction in surgical-site infection from incisional negative-pressure wound therapy over standard dressings — WHIST (1548 major-trauma lower-limb fracture patients: deep infection 5.84% vs 6.68% at 30 days) and Tuuli 2020 (1624 obese women after caesarean delivery: 3.6% vs 3.4%), with significantly more adverse skin reactions in the caesarean trial (7.0% vs 0.6%). title: Displaced femoral neck fracture: total hip arthroplasty vs hemiarthroplasty
question: In ambulatory older adults with a displaced femoral neck fracture, does total hip arthroplasty reduce secondary procedures or improve function versus hemiarthroplasty?
balance: POSSIBLE: In the large HEALTH trial (1495 independently ambulating patients), total hip arthroplasty did not significantly reduce secondary hip procedures within 24 months versus hemiarthroplasty (7.9% vs 8.3%), produced only a clinically unimportant improvement in function and quality of life, caused more hip instability/dislocation (4.7% vs 2.4%), and had similar mortality (14.3% vs 13.1% — reported alongside, with no mortality claim made). A smaller earlier trial in fitter elderly patients was concordant on similar final pain and function. A single pivotal trial caps the stamp at POSSIBLE. Mortality was a secondary outcome with no between-group difference; because this shelf makes no mortality or cardiovascular benefit claim, it is not flagged Tier C under the build rule (see summary.md).

title: Carpal tunnel syndrome: surgery vs splinting, and steroid injection
question: Does surgical release beat night splinting for carpal tunnel syndrome — and how durable is a corticosteroid injection?
balance: POSSIBLE: Surgery beat night splinting on every outcome in the one randomised head-to-head trial (success 80% vs 54% at 3 months; 90% vs 75% at 18 months, by which time 41% of the splint group had crossed to surgery). A methylprednisolone injection beat placebo on symptom severity at 10 weeks and delayed or reduced surgery at one year in the one placebo-controlled trial — yet about three of four injected patients still had surgery within a year. Each comparison rests on a single trial, which caps the stamp at POSSIBLE for both halves of the question.

title: Subacromial shoulder pain: decompression surgery vs sham and exercise
question: Does arthroscopic subacromial decompression improve pain and function more than sham (diagnostic arthroscopy) or exercise therapy?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): Two independent sham-controlled randomised trials — CSAW (313 patients, UK) and FIMPACT (210 patients, Finland) — found arthroscopic subacromial decompression no better than diagnostic arthroscopy alone on pain and function: CSAW's Oxford Shoulder Score difference was −1.3 points (95% CI −3.9 to 1.3) at 6 months, and FIMPACT's 24-month pain differences (−4.6 at rest, −9.0 on activity, on 0–100 scales) did not reach its 15-point minimal clinically important difference. Two concordant placebo-surgery trials justify LIKELY for the null; knee arthroscopy shelves (#188, #347) are different joints and operations and are not re-carded here.

title: Lumbar disc herniation with sciatica: early surgery vs prolonged conservative care
question: Does early discectomy relieve sciatica faster than conservative care with surgery if needed — and do outcomes converge by one year?
balance: LIKELY: Early surgery relieves sciatica faster, but outcomes converge. In the Peul trial (283 patients), early microdiscectomy and conservative care with surgery if needed produced no significant difference in disability over the first year, leg-pain relief and perceived recovery were faster with early surgery (recovery hazard ratio 1.97, a relative figure), and perceived recovery at one year was 95% in both groups — with 39% of the conservative group crossing to surgery. SPORT's randomised trial likewise found substantial improvement in both groups with small, non-significant intention-to-treat differences (its observational cohort, carded separately, favoured surgery but is confounded by self-selection). Gabapentinoid drugs for sciatica live on Shelf #345 and are not re-carded here.

title: Surgical-site infection prevention: skin antisepsis and suture choice
question: Does chlorhexidine–alcohol skin preparation prevent surgical-site infection better than povidone-iodine — and do triclosan-coated sutures add anything?
balance: Split: POSSIBLE — chlorhexidine–alcohol over povidone-iodine · LIKELY — triclosan-coated sutures do not reduce infection. Darouiche 2010 (849 patients) found overall surgical-site infection of 9.5% with chlorhexidine–alcohol vs 16.1% with povidone-iodine (relative risk 0.59) after clean-contaminated surgery — a single large trial, so that half caps at POSSIBLE. PROUD (1224 patients, 24 German hospitals) found triclosan-coated PDS Plus sutures did not reduce infection after elective midline laparotomy (14.8% vs 16.1%; odds ratio 0.91, 95% CI 0.66 to 1.25) — a very large single null trial, which under the library's rule may carry LIKELY for the null.

title: Perioperative fluids and haemodynamic therapy in major surgery
question: Does a restrictive fluid strategy harm kidneys compared with liberal fluids (RELIEF) — and does cardiac-output-guided haemodynamic therapy reduce complications (OPTIMISE)?
balance: Split: LIKELY — restrictive fluids give no survival advantage and more kidney injury · POSSIBLE — cardiac-output-guided therapy. RELIEF (3000 patients) found disability-free survival at 1 year was not higher with a restrictive regimen (81.9% vs 82.3%) while acute kidney injury was significantly more common (8.6% vs 5.0%) — a large pragmatic null-plus-harm result carrying LIKELY. OPTIMISE's own trial (734 patients) missed significance on its composite of complications and 30-day mortality (36.6% vs 43.4%; relative risk 0.84, 95% CI 0.71 to 1.01; P=0.07), and only its accompanying 38-trial meta-analysis favoured the intervention — so the guided-therapy claim rests substantially on pooled small trials and caps at POSSIBLE. Mortality was a secondary outcome in both trials and no mortality benefit is claimed for either strategy; perioperative drug questions (POISE programme) live on Shelves #352/#353.
stamp: Split

title: Postoperative nausea and vomiting: combination prophylaxis and aprepitant
question: Do antiemetic combinations outperform single agents for PONV prophylaxis — and where does aprepitant fit?
balance: LIKELY: In the IMPACT factorial trial (5199 high-risk patients), ondansetron, dexamethasone and droperidol each reduced postoperative nausea and vomiting by about 26% relative, propofol by 19% relative and nitrogen (avoiding nitrous oxide) by 12% relative — and all acted independently, so combined relative risks multiply while absolute benefit scales with the patient's baseline risk. Aprepitant fits as the strongest anti-vomiting component in its head-to-head trial: aprepitant plus dexamethasone halved 48-hour vomiting versus ondansetron plus dexamethasone after craniotomy (16% vs 38%), though nausea itself was unchanged. Reserve multi-drug prophylaxis for high-risk patients, as IMPACT's authors advise.
stamp: LIKELY

title: Long-acting reversible contraception: levonorgestrel intrauterine system vs copper IUD
question: How do the levonorgestrel intrauterine system and copper IUD compare on continuation, bleeding, and satisfaction in head-to-head randomised data?
balance: POSSIBLE: The one head-to-head randomised trial — 199 women living with HIV in Cape Town, South Africa (median age 31) — found the levonorgestrel intrauterine system did not increase genital or plasma HIV viral load versus the copper IUD over 24 months, while continuation favoured the levonorgestrel system (copper users had significantly more expulsions, 8% vs 1%, and far more elective discontinuations, adjusted hazard ratio 8.75, a relative figure) and haemoglobin rose more with the levonorgestrel system (+0.71 g/dL at 24 months). A single trial in a specific population caps the stamp at POSSIBLE, and its continuation and bleeding findings should not be generalised beyond that population without corroboration. A second implant-versus-IUD randomised anchor named in the topic file could not be pinned to a verified head-to-head record at build and was not carded (see summary.md). Emergency contraception lives on Shelf #244 and is not re-carded here.
