title: Early medical abortion at home and by telemedicine
question: Is home administration of misoprostol (and telemedicine-supported medical abortion) as effective and safe as clinic-based care?
balance: Split: POSSIBLE — home first misoprostol dose at 12–22 weeks · MAYBE (weak evidence) — telemedicine consultation for early abortion. PRIMA (457 participants, six Swedish hospitals) found taking the first misoprostol dose at home in medical abortion at 12–22 gestational weeks significantly increased day-care completion (71% vs 46%; difference 24.9 percentage points) with adverse events in 22% of the safety population and no signal that home dosing was unsafe — one large open-label trial, so POSSIBLE. The UTAH telemedicine trial was stopped by COVID-19 at about 10% of planned recruitment (125 women): efficacy looked similar (90.5% vs 77.4% complete abortion without surgery) but non-inferiority was formally not demonstrated, so the telemedicine half is MAYBE (weak evidence) — an underpowered pilot, not a verdict.

title: Preimplantation genetic testing for aneuploidy (PGT-A) in IVF
question: Does PGT-A with single embryo transfer improve live-birth rates per transfer or per started cycle versus morphology-based selection?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference on live birth per started cycle): In the Yan 2021 trial (1212 subfertile women with at least three good-quality blastocysts), cumulative live birth within a year was 77.2% with PGT-A vs 81.8% with conventional IVF — conventional IVF was noninferior (absolute difference −4.6 percentage points, 95% CI −9.2 to −0.0), though clinical pregnancy loss was less frequent with PGT-A (8.7% vs 12.6%). STAR likewise found no overall ongoing-pregnancy advantage per transfer (50% vs 46%) or per intention-to-treat (41.8% vs 43.5%), with a per-transfer subgroup signal at ages 35–40 that disappeared per intention-to-treat. Two concordant randomised trials justify LIKELY that PGT-A does not raise live-birth rates per started cycle in these populations.

title: Induction of labour: timing at 39 weeks, and Foley catheter vs prostaglandin
question: Does elective induction at 39 weeks in low-risk nulliparas change caesarean rates or perinatal outcomes (ARRIVE) — and is a Foley catheter as effective as prostaglandins?
balance: LIKELY: ARRIVE (6106 low-risk nulliparous women) found induction at 39 weeks did not significantly change the composite of perinatal death or severe neonatal complications (4.3% vs 5.4%; relative risk 0.80, 95% CI 0.64 to 1.00 — non-significant, and no perinatal-mortality benefit is claimed from it) but significantly lowered caesarean delivery (18.6% vs 22.2%; relative risk 0.84). In the PROBAAT programme, a Foley catheter matched vaginal prostaglandin E2 on caesarean rates (23% vs 20%; relative risk 1.13, interval spanning no effect), and oral misoprostol was noninferior to Foley on the composite of asphyxia or postpartum haemorrhage (12.2% vs 11.5%) — so the mechanical and pharmacological routes are equivalent for effectiveness in an unfavourable cervix, with the choice resting on safety profile and logistics.
stamp: LIKELY

title: Oral antihypertensives for severe hypertension in pregnancy
question: For acute severe hypertension in pregnancy, are oral nifedipine, labetalol, and methyldopa equally effective at reaching target blood pressure without caesarean or adverse effects?
balance: POSSIBLE: All three oral drugs controlled severe hypertension in pregnancy in most women in the Easterling trial (894 women, two Indian public hospitals): blood-pressure control within 6 hours without adverse outcomes in 84% on nifedipine retard, 77% on oral labetalol and 76% on methyldopa — nifedipine significantly beat methyldopa (p=0.03) but not labetalol (p=0.05). The smaller Shekhar trial points the same way on speed: oral nifedipine reached target faster than intravenous labetalol (median 40 vs 60 minutes). One large open-label trial plus one small single-centre trial caps the stamp at POSSIBLE. Magnesium for seizure prophylaxis is a different drug and question, home on Shelf #602, and is not re-carded here.

title: Planned caesarean vs planned vaginal birth for term breech
question: For a singleton breech at term, does planned caesarean reduce perinatal death or serious morbidity versus planned vaginal birth (Term Breech Trial) — and can external cephalic version avert the choice?
balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: perinatal mortality claim). The Term Breech Trial (2088 women, 121 centres in 26 countries) found the composite of perinatal mortality, neonatal mortality or serious neonatal morbidity was significantly lower with planned caesarean than planned vaginal birth (1.6% vs 5.0%; relative risk 0.33, 95% CI 0.19 to 0.56 — a relative figure, with the absolute rates beside it), while maternal mortality or serious maternal morbidity did not differ (3.9% vs 3.2%). External cephalic version can avert the choice for some women: the Cochrane review found starting ECV at 34–35 weeks rather than at term reduced non-cephalic presentation at birth (relative risk 0.81, high-quality evidence) at the cost of more late preterm labour (6.6% vs 4.3%). Because the headline claim includes perinatal death, this shelf is Tier C and its stamp is proposed only.

title: Breastfeeding promotion and support (PROBIT)
question: Does a Baby-Friendly-style breastfeeding promotion intervention increase duration and exclusivity of breastfeeding — and children's later health?
balance: LIKELY: PROBIT — a cluster-randomised trial of 17,046 mother–infant pairs in 31 Belarusian maternity hospitals and polyclinics — found a Baby-Friendly-style promotion intervention markedly increased exclusive breastfeeding at 3 months (43.3% vs 6.4%) and 6 months (7.9% vs 0.6%), any breastfeeding at 12 months (19.7% vs 11.4%), and reduced gastrointestinal infection (9.1% vs 13.2%; adjusted odds ratio 0.60, a relative figure) and atopic eczema (3.3% vs 6.3%; adjusted odds ratio 0.54) in the first year, with no reduction in respiratory infection. A smaller home-based peer-counselling trial (130 mothers, Mexico City) was strongly concordant on exclusivity (67% and 50% with six and three visits vs 12% control at 3 months). Promotion works on the behaviour; the infant-health effects carded here are the ones PROBIT actually measured.

title: Surgery for pelvic organ prolapse: mesh, graft, or native-tissue repair (PROSPECT)
question: For primary transvaginal prolapse repair, does mesh or biological graft beat native-tissue repair on symptoms and reoperation?
balance: Split: LIKELY — mesh/graft augmentation does not improve patient-reported outcomes (PROSPECT) · POSSIBLE — mesh improves 1-year anatomical success, with more complications (Altman). PROSPECT (1352 women, two parallel trials) found no difference in prolapse symptom scores or prolapse-related quality of life at 1 or 2 years between standard native-tissue repair and repair augmented with synthetic mesh or biological graft, while 12% of mesh-exposed women had a mesh complication within 2 years. Altman 2011 (389 women, anterior compartment only) found a trocar-guided mesh kit beat colporrhaphy on a 1-year composite dominated by anatomical staging (60.8% vs 34.5%) — with longer surgery, more haemorrhage, more new stress incontinence (12.3% vs 6.3%) and 3.2% needing reintervention for mesh exposure. The split is real: anatomy improves, symptoms do not, and the price is mesh-specific harm. Stress-incontinence surgery is Shelf #249 and is not re-carded here.

title: Non-hormonal drugs for menopausal hot flushes: SSRI/SNRI options
question: Do low-dose paroxetine or escitalopram reduce hot-flush frequency versus placebo in women who cannot or will not use hormones?
balance: LIKELY: Two double-blind, placebo-controlled randomised trials of different serotonin-reuptake inhibitors converge: escitalopram 10–20 mg reduced hot-flush frequency by 1.41 more flushes per day than placebo at 8 weeks (55% vs 36% achieving at least a 50% reduction), and paroxetine CR 12.5–25 mg reduced daily flush frequency by about 3.3 per day versus 1.8 on placebo at 6 weeks (median reductions 62–65% vs 38%). title: Cervical cerclage for short cervix
question: In singleton pregnancies with a short cervix, does cerclage prevent preterm birth — in women with and without prior spontaneous preterm birth?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — for women WITHOUT prior spontaneous preterm birth, the population both of this shelf's anchors study: the individual-patient meta-analysis of five trials (419 women with cervical length <25 mm) found no significant reduction in preterm birth <35 weeks with cerclage (21.9% vs 27.7%; relative risk 0.88, 95% CI 0.63 to 1.23) and graded the evidence low quality; the 2025 randomised trial of cerclage plus progesterone vs progesterone alone (90 women analysed, stopped early) likewise missed its primary outcome (preterm birth <35 weeks 16.3% vs 23.4%; relative risk 0.70, 0.30 to 1.63) while showing longer latency to delivery. title: Hydroxyurea in sickle cell disease: adults and infants
question: Does hydroxyurea reduce painful crises in adults with sickle cell anaemia (MSH) — and is it safe and spleen-protective in infants (BABY HUG)?
balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED only, pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: a mortality signal in long-term MSH follow-up was flagged at topic stage; neither carded abstract reports mortality, and no mortality figure is printed on this shelf). Two randomised trials, in different populations, agree that hydroxyurea cuts sickle pain: in adults with three or more crises a year (MSH, 299 patients) the median crisis rate fell from 4.5 to 2.5 per year, and in infants aged 9–18 months (BABY HUG, 193 randomised) pain events numbered 177 on hydroxycarbamide versus 375 on placebo. BABY HUG's primary organ endpoints were null — no significant difference in splenic function (p=0.21) or glomerular filtration rate (p=0.84) — so the spleen-protection half of the question is not answered yes; the infant claim carded is fewer pain and dactylitis events with only mild-to-moderate neutropenia over 2 years.

title: Preventing stroke in sickle cell disease: transfusion, and switching to hydroxyurea
question: In children with abnormal transcranial Doppler, does chronic transfusion prevent first stroke (STOP) — and can hydroxyurea replace transfusion for maintenance (TWiTCH)?
balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED only, pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: stroke-prevention claim). STOP (130 children with transcranial Doppler velocities ≥200 cm/s) was stopped early after 11 stroke events on standard care versus 1 on transfusion — a 92% relative difference in stroke risk, with absolute rates of 11 of 67 versus 1 of 63 over the trial period. TWiTCH then showed that, after at least a year of transfusions and in children without severe vasculopathy, switching to hydroxycarbamide kept 24-month Doppler velocities non-inferior to continued transfusion (138 vs 143 cm/s), with no strokes identified among 29 adjudicated neurological events. The carded claim is: transfusion prevents first stroke in high-velocity children; hydroxyurea is a maintenance alternative once velocities are controlled — not a first-line substitute tested from diagnosis.

title: Emicizumab prophylaxis in haemophilia A
question: Does emicizumab prophylaxis reduce bleeding versus no prophylaxis or prior factor therapy — in patients with and without inhibitors?
balance: LIKELY: Two phase 3 trials, one in each population, show very large reductions in treated bleeding versus no prophylaxis. Without inhibitors (HAVEN 3, 152 participants): annualised rates of 1.5 (weekly) and 1.3 (every 2 weeks) versus 38.2 events with no prophylaxis — 96–97% lower — and an intraindividual 68% lower rate than prior factor VIII prophylaxis. title: Intravenous iron for iron-deficiency anaemia in pregnancy
question: Does intravenous ferric carboxymaltose correct anaemia faster and more completely than oral iron in pregnant women with iron deficiency?
balance: Split: POSSIBLE — faster, more complete correction (FER-ASAP) · POSSIBLE — no difference in anaemia prevalence at 36 weeks (IVON). The two trials differ in population and timing and their headline results pull apart. FER-ASAP (252 women, haemoglobin entry at 16–33 weeks) found more women corrected to Hb ≥11.0 g/dL with ferric carboxymaltose than oral ferrous sulfate (84% vs 70%; odds ratio 2.06) and corrected faster (median 3.4 vs 4.3 weeks). IVON (1,056 Nigerian women with Hb <10 g/dL at 20–32 weeks) found no significant difference in anaemia at 36 weeks (58% vs 61%; risk ratio 0.95, 95% CI 0.85–1.06) or preterm birth, though iron deficiency itself was reduced more by intravenous iron. Both trials are open-label and single per half, so each half is capped at POSSIBLE. Intravenous iron in kidney disease is Shelf #294 and is not re-carded here.

title: Lenalidomide maintenance after autologous transplant in myeloma
question: Does lenalidomide maintenance after stem-cell transplantation prolong progression-free and overall survival — at what second-malignancy price?
balance: Split: LIKELY — longer time to progression · POSSIBLE — survival benefit — both PROPOSED only, pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: survival claim). Two placebo-controlled trials agree on progression: CALGB 100104 (460 patients) found median time to progression of 46 versus 27 months, and IFM 2005-02 (614 patients) found median progression-free survival of 41 versus 23 months (hazard ratio 0.50, a relative measure at the solidity threshold). They disagree on survival at the reported horizons: CALGB found fewer deaths on lenalidomide (15% vs 23%, P=0.03), while IFM found overall survival similar at 4 years (more than 70% alive in both groups). Both trials found more second primary cancers on lenalidomide (CALGB 8% vs 3%; IFM 3.1 vs 1.2 per 100 patient-years, P=0.002) and more grade 3–4 haematologic toxicity.

title: First-line therapy for chronic lymphocytic leukaemia: targeted agents vs chemoimmunotherapy
question: Does ibrutinib beat chlorambucil in older untreated CLL (RESONATE-2) — and does fixed-duration venetoclax–obinutuzumab beat chlorambucil–obinutuzumab (CLL14)?
balance: Split: LIKELY — progression-free survival · POSSIBLE — survival benefit — both PROPOSED only, pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C candidate at topic stage: survival/PFS claims in a cancer shelf; ruled Tier C at build under the brief's mortality-claim rule). Both trials beat their chlorambucil-based controls on progression by wide margins: RESONATE-2 (269 patients aged ≥65) found a hazard ratio of 0.16 for progression or death with ibrutinib, and CLL14 (432 patients with coexisting conditions) found a hazard ratio of 0.35 for venetoclax–obinutuzumab, with 24-month progression-free survival of 88.2% versus 64.1%. On survival they diverge: RESONATE-2 reported 24-month survival of 98% versus 85% (hazard ratio 0.16), while CLL14's all-cause mortality was 9.3% on venetoclax–obinutuzumab versus 7.9% on the control at a median 28.1 months — no survival advantage. Both controls are chlorambucil regimens, a weak comparator by current standards, which is why the survival half stays POSSIBLE.

title: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma: polatuzumab with R-CHP (POLARIX) and the R-CHOP benchmark
question: Does replacing vincristine with polatuzumab vedotin in first-line R-CHOP improve progression-free survival in DLBCL?
balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED only, pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C at build: the benchmark card carries the survival claim that established R-CHOP). title: Platelet transfusion strategy in haematologic malignancy: prophylaxis and dose
question: Does a no-prophylaxis (therapeutic-only) platelet strategy increase bleeding versus prophylaxis (TOPPS) — and does platelet dose matter (PLADO)?
balance: LIKELY: Two large randomised trials settle the two halves. TOPPS (600 patients) tested dropping prophylaxis and failed to show non-inferiority: WHO grade 2–4 bleeding occurred in 50% without prophylaxis versus 43% with it (adjusted difference 8.4 percentage points, 90% CI 1.7–15.2; P=0.06 for non-inferiority), with more bleeding days and shorter time to first bleed without prophylaxis — although a prespecified subgroup undergoing autologous transplantation showed similar rates. PLADO (1,272 transfused patients) found bleeding of grade 2 or higher in 71%, 69% and 70% at low, medium and high doses respectively — dose, across a fourfold range, did not change bleeding; the low dose simply used fewer platelets per patient (median 9.25×10¹¹) at the cost of more transfusion episodes (median 5 vs 3). Red-cell transfusion thresholds are Shelf #124 and are not re-carded here.

title: Psoriatic arthritis: IL-17 inhibition (secukinumab, ixekizumab)

balance: LIKELY: Two double-blind phase 3 trials of two IL-17A inhibitors agree on joint responses at 24 weeks. title: Gout: nurse-led treat-to-target urate lowering
question: Does a nurse-led, treat-to-target allopurinol strategy achieve target urate and fewer flares more often than GP usual care?
balance: POSSIBLE: One large randomised trial answers the question directly, and a single trial caps the stamp at POSSIBLE. title: Knee osteoarthritis: physical therapy vs glucocorticoid injection, and the cartilage question

balance: Split: POSSIBLE — physical therapy beats injection at 1 year · POSSIBLE — repeated triamcinolone loses cartilage without pain benefit. title: Exercise therapy for knee and hip osteoarthritis
question: Does land-based exercise therapy reduce pain and improve function in knee and hip osteoarthritis versus no exercise?
balance: LIKELY: Two Cochrane syntheses of randomised trials point the same way for both joints. For knee OA (Fransen 2015; 54 studies identified, 44 trials pooled), land-based exercise reduced pain by 12 points on a 100-point scale (95% CI 10–15) and improved physical function by 10 points (8–13) immediately after treatment, with smaller benefits sustained 2–6 months after formal treatment ended (pain 6 points, 3–9). For hip OA (Fransen 2014; 10 RCTs, with high-quality evidence from 9 trials and 549 participants), exercise reduced pain (standardised mean difference −0.38, −0.55 to −0.20) and improved function (SMD −0.38) immediately after treatment. The reviewers themselves flag vulnerability to selection, attrition and detection bias — exercise trials cannot blind participants — which is why the effect sizes, not just their significance, are printed on the cards. Exercise for other indications is carded across Shelves #452–#461 and is not re-carded here.
stamp: LIKELY

title: Lateral epicondylitis (tennis elbow): corticosteroid injection — short-term win, long-term loss
question: Does a corticosteroid injection for tennis elbow beat physiotherapy or wait-and-see at one year, despite winning at six weeks?
balance: LIKELY: Two randomised trials, in the same Brisbane research programme, show the same reversal. Coombes 2013 (165 patients, 2×2 factorial): corticosteroid injection produced lower complete recovery or much improvement at 1 year than placebo injection (83% vs 96%; relative risk 0.86, 99% CI 0.75–0.99) and far greater 1-year recurrence (54% vs 12%; recurrence relative risk for placebo vs steroid 0.23) — while physiotherapy made no significant 1-year difference (91% vs 88%). Bisset 2006 (198 patients): injections were significantly better at 6 weeks, but 47 of 65 early successes subsequently regressed, and injection outcomes were significantly poorer than physiotherapy in the long term; physiotherapy beat wait-and-see early, with no difference by 52 weeks. The relative risks sit inside the 0.5–2.0 caution band individually; the LIKELY rests on two concordant trials plus the large absolute recurrence split (54% vs 12%).

title: Dupuytren's contracture: collagenase injection vs surgery
question: Does collagenase clostridium histolyticum correct Dupuytren's contracture versus placebo — and how does it compare with limited fasciectomy on recurrence and recovery?
balance: Split: LIKELY — collagenase corrects contracture versus placebo · POSSIBLE — fasciectomy gives better 1-year hand-health scores. Against placebo (CORD, 308 patients), collagenase took 64.0% of treated cords to within 5 degrees of full extension versus 6.8% on placebo, and improved total range of motion from 43.9 to 80.7 degrees versus 45.3 to 49.5 — a large, blinded win. The head-to-head half is a single trial, hence POSSIBLE.

title: Frozen shoulder: capsular release, manipulation, or structured physiotherapy (UK FROST)
question: In primary frozen shoulder, do arthroscopic capsular release or manipulation under anaesthesia beat early structured physiotherapy on shoulder function?
balance: POSSIBLE: One large three-arm trial programme, reported at two horizons on this shelf, found no clinically superior option. title: Myasthenia gravis: thymectomy and complement inhibition
question: Does thymectomy improve outcomes in non-thymomatous acetylcholine-receptor-positive generalised myasthenia (MGTX) — and does eculizumab help refractory disease (REGAIN)?
balance: Split: POSSIBLE — thymectomy: in MGTX (126 patients), thymectomy plus prednisone beat prednisone alone over 3 years on both co-primary outcomes (time-weighted Quantitative Myasthenia Gravis score 6.15 vs 8.99; prednisone dose 44 mg vs 60 mg), a single randomised trial, so POSSIBLE. MAYBE (weak evidence) — eculizumab: REGAIN's pre-specified primary analysis MISSED (worst-rank MG-ADL difference −11.7, 95% CI −24.3 to 0.96; p=0.0698), and its authors state the secondary and sensitivity analyses were inconsistent with the primary result — a missed primary endpoint is weak evidence of benefit, printed as MAYBE (weak evidence), never as established efficacy.

title: Parkinson's disease with motor complications: deep brain stimulation
question: Does subthalamic DBS improve quality of life and motor function versus best medical therapy — in advanced disease, and earlier at first motor complications?
balance: LIKELY: Two randomised trials at two disease stages agree. In advanced disease (Deuschl 2006, 156 patients), subthalamic stimulation beat medication alone on quality of life and off-medication motor scores at 6 months. In earlier disease (EARLYSTIM, Schuepbach 2013, 251 patients, mean age 52), stimulation plus medical therapy improved the PDQ-39 by 7.8 points while medical therapy alone worsened by 0.2 (difference 8.0 points, P=0.002) over 2 years. The benefit carries a real surgical price — serious adverse events were more frequent with stimulation in both trials, including a fatal intracerebral haemorrhage in the 2006 trial — and the cards print that price beside the benefit.
stamp: LIKELY

title: Essential tremor: MR-guided focused ultrasound thalamotomy
question: Does unilateral focused-ultrasound thalamotomy reduce hand tremor versus sham in medication-refractory essential tremor?
balance: POSSIBLE: One sham-controlled randomised trial (Elias 2016, 76 patients) found hand tremor improved by 8.3 points more with focused ultrasound thalamotomy than with sham at 3 months (95% CI 5.9 to 10.7; P<0.001), and a 5-year follow-up of the same trial's cohort (Cosgrove 2023) shows the improvement largely held (combined hand tremor/motor scores still 40.4% better than baseline at 60 months). A follow-up cohort of the SAME trial is durability evidence, not a second trial — so under the single-trial ceiling the stamp is POSSIBLE. Gait disturbance (36%) and paraesthesias or numbness (38%), persisting at 12 months in 9% and 14%, are part of the claim.

title: Relapsing multiple sclerosis: fingolimod vs placebo and vs interferon
question: Does oral fingolimod reduce relapses and MRI activity versus placebo (FREEDOMS) and versus intramuscular interferon beta-1a (TRANSFORMS)?
balance: LIKELY: Two large double-blind trials agree. Against placebo (FREEDOMS, 1,272 patients, 24 months), fingolimod cut the annualised relapse rate to 0.18 (0.5 mg) and 0.16 (1.25 mg) versus 0.40. Against intramuscular interferon beta-1a (TRANSFORMS, 1,292 patients, 12 months), the rate was 0.16 (0.5 mg) versus 0.33. The disability-progression hazard ratios (0.70 and 0.68) sit inside this library's 0.5–2.0 caution band and were NOT significant against interferon, so the LIKELY stamp rests on relapse rates and MRI measures, not on a disability claim. Harms carded include bradycardia and AV block at initiation, macular oedema, and two fatal infections at the 1.25 mg dose in TRANSFORMS.
stamp: LIKELY

title: Painful diabetic neuropathy and postherpetic neuralgia: duloxetine and high-dose capsaicin
question: Does duloxetine relieve painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy — and does the 8% capsaicin patch relieve postherpetic neuralgia versus a low-dose control patch?
balance: POSSIBLE: Each treatment rests on a single randomised trial here. Duloxetine 60 mg and 120 mg/day beat placebo on the 24-hour Average Pain Score in a 12-week trial of 457 patients with painful diabetic neuropathy (Goldstein 2005) — though the abstract reports the pain separation without responder percentages, which the card states plainly. One 60-minute application of the 8% capsaicin patch reduced postherpetic neuralgia pain by −29.6% versus −19.9% on a low-dose control patch over weeks 2–8 (Backonja 2008, 402 patients), a difference of −9.7 percentage points, with a responder odds ratio of 1.56 that sits inside the 0.5–2.0 caution band. Two single trials, two different pains: POSSIBLE for each, claimed separately.

title: Bell's palsy: prednisolone, with or without an antiviral
question: Does early prednisolone increase full recovery from Bell's palsy — and does adding valaciclovir help?
balance: LIKELY: Two randomised trial programmes agree on both halves of the question. Prednisolone started within 72 hours raised recovery to 83.0% versus 63.6% without it at 3 months and 94.4% versus 81.6% at 9 months (Sullivan 2007, factorial, 551 randomised), and the Scandinavian trial programme (829 patients) found higher complete recovery with prednisolone at every baseline severity at 12 months (Axelsson 2012). Acyclovir/valaciclovir added nothing in either programme — no benefit alone and no added benefit combined. Steroid benefit and antiviral null each rest on two randomised datasets: LIKELY for both.

title: Fluoxetine for stroke recovery: FLAME's promise vs FOCUS/AFFINITY's nulls
question: Does fluoxetine started soon after stroke improve motor/functional recovery — the small positive FLAME trial against the large pragmatic FOCUS-family trials?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): The small, selected FLAME trial (118 patients with moderate-to-severe motor deficit) found fluoxetine improved Fugl-Meyer motor scores at 90 days (adjusted mean 34.0 vs 24.3 points, p=0.003). Two large pragmatic trials then tested the question at scale and both were null on functional outcome: FOCUS (3,127 patients; modified Rankin common odds ratio 0.951, 95% CI 0.839 to 1.079) and AFFINITY (1,280 patients; adjusted common odds ratio 0.94, 0.76 to 1.15), with more fractures — and in AFFINITY more falls and seizures — on fluoxetine. Over 4,400 patients in the large trials outweigh 118 in the small one: LIKELY that routine fluoxetine does not improve functional recovery after stroke. This is a functional-outcome shelf, not a mortality claim.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference)

title: Drug-resistant temporal lobe epilepsy: surgery vs continued medication
question: In temporal lobe epilepsy uncontrolled by medication, does surgery free patients from disabling seizures versus continued drug therapy?
balance: LIKELY: Both randomised trials point the same way with large absolute effects. In Wiebe 2001 (80 patients), 58% of surgical patients versus 8% on continued medication were free of seizures impairing awareness at 1 year (P<0.001). In ERSET (Engel 2012), surgery soon after two drug failures left 11 of 15 patients seizure-free in year 2 versus 0 of 23 on continued medication (P<.001) — a striking result in a trial stopped at 38 of a planned 200 patients, which is why the effect is carded with its small numbers printed rather than as a percentage triumph. Surgical adverse effects (10% in Wiebe) and memory decline after resection (ERSET) are on the cards.
stamp: LIKELY

title: Antipsychotic comparative effectiveness in chronic schizophrenia (CATIE & CUtLASS)
question: Do second-generation antipsychotics outperform first-generation drugs on effectiveness, discontinuation, and quality of life in chronic schizophrenia?
balance: LIKELY (no class advantage): Two large publicly funded pragmatic trials agree that second-generation antipsychotics (SGAs) as a class do not outperform first-generation drugs (FGAs). In CATIE (1,493 patients), 74% discontinued their assigned drug before 18 months; olanzapine lasted longest, but the first-generation perphenazine performed similarly to quetiapine, risperidone and ziprasidone — while olanzapine caused more weight gain and metabolic change, and perphenazine more extrapyramidal discontinuation. In CUtLASS (227 patients), the hypothesis that SGAs improve quality of life over a year was excluded, with a trend favouring FGAs. The claim carded is the class-level null, not that individual drugs are interchangeable in every patient.
stamp: LIKELY (no class advantage)

title: After ECT works: continuation therapy to prevent relapse
question: In patients who respond to ECT for major depression, does continuation pharmacotherapy (nortriptyline ± lithium) or continuation ECT prevent relapse?
balance: LIKELY: Without continuation treatment, relapse after successful ECT is near-universal — 84% within 24 weeks on placebo in Sackeim 2001. Nortriptyline plus lithium cut that to 39% (nortriptyline alone: 60%) in the same randomised trial. The CORE trial (Kellner 2006, 201 remitted patients) then found continuation ECT and the nortriptyline–lithium combination statistically indistinguishable (relapse 37.1% vs 31.6% over 6 months), both far below the historical placebo rate. Two randomised trials support the core claim — continuation treatment prevents most relapses and the two strategies are comparable — while both cards keep visible that even the best strategy still let roughly a third relapse.
stamp: LIKELY

title: Obsessive-compulsive disorder: exposure therapy, SSRIs, and their combination
question: In OCD, does exposure-and-response-prevention beat or augment SSRIs — in adults, and in children (POTS)?
balance: LIKELY: In children and adolescents (POTS, 112 patients), CBT, sertraline and their combination all beat placebo on symptom change, the combination beat either treatment alone, and remission was 53.6% combined, 39.3% CBT alone, 21.4% sertraline alone and 3.6% placebo. In adults still symptomatic on an SRI, adding exposure-and-response-prevention beat adding stress-management training (Simpson 2008, 108 patients). Two randomised trials at two ages agree that exposure-based CBT works, works added to an SRI, and that the combination is the strongest start in youth — LIKELY.
stamp: LIKELY

title: PTSD: trauma-focused psychotherapies head-to-head
question: Do prolonged exposure and cognitive processing therapy reduce PTSD symptoms versus present-centred or waitlist controls in veterans and assault survivors?
balance: POSSIBLE: Both anchor trials are positive but modest or small. Prolonged exposure beat present-centred therapy in 284 women veterans and active-duty personnel (Schnurr 2007) — but by an effect size of 0.27, with loss of PTSD diagnosis in 41.0% versus 27.8% (odds ratio 1.80, inside this library's 0.5–2.0 caution band). Cognitive processing therapy beat a waitlist in just 60 veterans (Monson 2006), 40% of the treated intention-to-treat sample no longer meeting PTSD criteria after treatment. Positive randomised evidence at two sites with two therapies, but small effects against active control and a tiny waitlist trial: POSSIBLE, not LIKELY.

title: Anorexia nervosa: family-based treatment, and olanzapine for weight restoration
question: Does family-based treatment beat individual therapy for adolescent anorexia (Lock) — and does olanzapine aid weight restoration in adults (Attia)?
balance: Split — POSSIBLE on both halves, one trial each. Family-based treatment (FBT) and adolescent-focused individual therapy produced equal full remission at end of treatment in Lock 2010 (121 adolescents), but FBT was significantly superior at 6- and 12-month follow-up — a durability advantage in a single trial. Olanzapine produced a statistically significant but modest extra weight gain in adults (Attia 2019, 152 outpatients: BMI rising 0.259 versus 0.095 points per month) with NO significant benefit on obsessionality. Neither result supports a stronger stamp: FBT's advantage is follow-up-only in one trial, and olanzapine's is a small effect on weight alone, not on the illness's psychology.

title: Bulimia nervosa: fluoxetine and cognitive behavioural therapy
question: Does fluoxetine 60 mg reduce binge–purge frequency versus placebo — and how does CBT compare with interpersonal psychotherapy?
balance: POSSIBLE: Two older randomised trials support their halves, neither with the precision this library would want for LIKELY. Fluoxetine 60 mg/day beat placebo on binge-eating and vomiting frequency in an 8-week trial of 387 women (1992) — but the record's abstract reports the superiority without printing the episode-frequency numbers, and the card says so. CBT beat interpersonal psychotherapy clearly at end of treatment (recovered 29% vs 6%; remitted 48% vs 28%) in Agras 2000 (220 patients) — but by 1-year follow-up the difference was no longer significant, because IPT caught up. A drug effect stated without abstract-level figures, and a therapy advantage that converges within a year: POSSIBLE.

title: Continuing antidepressants after recovery: maintenance vs discontinuation
question: In patients well on antidepressants in primary care, does continuing treatment prevent relapse versus tapering to placebo (ANTLER) — and what does the older maintenance trial base show?
balance: LIKELY: The modern primary-care trial and the older trial base agree. In ANTLER (478 patients in UK general practices, well and considering stopping), relapse by 52 weeks was 39% on maintenance versus 56% on tapering to placebo (hazard ratio 2.06, 95% CI 1.56 to 2.70 — just beyond this library's 2.0 solid-evidence line, with a 17-percentage-point absolute difference beside it). The Geddes 2003 synthesis of 31 maintenance trials (4,410 participants) found the same pattern at larger scale: relapse 18% on continued antidepressants versus 41% on discontinuation. Two independent evidence layers, one absolute difference of about 17–23 percentage points in each: LIKELY that continuing prevents relapse in patients like those enrolled — people with recurrent depression or long treatment histories, not everyone who has ever taken an antidepressant.
stamp: LIKELY

title: Bipolar depression: quetiapine and lurasidone
question: Do quetiapine and lurasidone treat acute bipolar depression versus placebo — the depressive pole that antimanic trials do not cover?
balance: Split: LIKELY — quetiapine: a pooled analysis of FOUR randomised placebo-controlled trials in bipolar II depression (Young 2013; 776 patients across the dose arms reported) found MADRS improvement of −15.58 (300 mg) and −14.88 (600 mg) versus −11.61 on placebo (both p<0.001), with significantly higher response and remission at week 8. title: ADHD in adults: stimulant and non-stimulant medications
question: In adults with ADHD, do methylphenidate, amphetamines, and atomoxetine improve core symptoms versus placebo — and how do they compare?
balance: LIKELY (short-term): The Cortese 2018 network meta-analysis of 133 double-blind randomised trials (51 in adults; efficacy analysis in 8,131 adults) found amphetamines (SMD −0.79), methylphenidate (−0.49), bupropion (−0.46) and atomoxetine (−0.45) all superior to placebo on clinician-rated core symptoms in adults at about 12 weeks, while modafinil was not (0.16). Head-to-head differences favoured amphetamines. The same analysis found these drugs less well tolerated than placebo in adults (dropout-for-adverse-event odds ratios 2.33–3.26), and data were insufficient at 26 and 52 weeks — so the LIKELY stamp is explicitly a SHORT-TERM stamp, which the balance and the card both state.

title: Borderline personality disorder: dialectical behaviour and mentalization-based therapy
question: Does dialectical behaviour therapy reduce parasuicidal behaviour versus treatment as usual (Linehan) — and does mentalization-based treatment beat structured clinical management (Bateman)?
balance: POSSIBLE: Linehan 1991 randomised chronically parasuicidal women with borderline personality disorder to a year of dialectical behaviour therapy (DBT) or community treatment as usual and found fewer and less medically severe parasuicide episodes, better therapy retention and fewer inpatient days on DBT — in a single small early trial whose abstract does not even state its sample size. Bateman 2009 (134 patients) found 18 months of mentalization-based treatment (MBT) produced a steeper decline in crisis events, suicide attempts and hospitalisation than structured clinical management — though both structured treatments improved substantially. Structured specialist therapy helping, with MBT ahead of a strong active control, is real but thin randomised evidence: POSSIBLE.

title: Telemedicine versus in-person care: what holds condition-by-condition, and the untested wholesale switch
question: Does delivering care by telemedicine (video/phone), as a substitute for in-person visits, improve or worsen clinical outcomes in primary care and urgent/emergency care — and has switching a practice to mostly-telemedicine ever been randomised?
balance: Split (PROPOSED, Tier C — the developer's personal verdict is required): POSSIBLE that telemedicine substituted condition-by-condition performs about as well as in-person care — 93 randomised trials in the Cochrane synthesis (heart-failure mortality relative risk 0.89, confidence interval crossing 1) and a 19-study primary-care review finding similar or lower service use and prescribing. MAYBE (weak evidence) for any claim that switching a practice wholesale to mostly-telemedicine improves outcomes: that switch has never been randomised; the one practice-cluster trial's mortality result (Whole System Demonstrator: 4.6% vs 8.3%) is implausibly large for remote monitoring and was flagged by its own team as a possible recruitment artefact; and commercial direct-to-consumer care carries a prescribing-quality cost (antibiotics at 52% of visits vs 31% in offices).

title: Subcutaneous vs transvenous ICD: trading lead complications for shocks?
question: In patients who need a defibrillator but not pacing, does a fully subcutaneous ICD match a transvenous ICD on complications and inappropriate shocks (PRAETORIAN, ATLAS)?
balance: LIKELY (the trade-off, not a winner): Two randomised trials and their individual-patient-data pooling agree on the shape of the exchange. The subcutaneous ICD avoids the vein and the lead: perioperative lead-related complications were 0.4% vs 4.8% in ATLAS, and device-related complications ran lower in PRAETORIAN (hazard ratio 0.69). In return it shocks inappropriately more often — the pooled first-inappropriate-shock rate was 2.5 vs 1.5 per 100 patient-years (hazard ratio 1.61, a relative figure inside the 0.5–2.0 band this library treats as not solid on its own, though here it is pooled randomised data, not an observational claim). PRAETORIAN's composite of complications plus inappropriate shocks was noninferior (hazard ratio 0.99). Who benefits from a prophylactic ICD at all is Shelf #90; this shelf is only about which box, once one is chosen.
stamp: LIKELY (the trade-off, not a winner)

title: Wearable cardioverter-defibrillator after myocardial infarction (VEST)

title: Ablation as first-line treatment for paroxysmal atrial fibrillation
question: In symptomatic paroxysmal AF, does first-line cryoballoon ablation prevent recurrence better than starting with antiarrhythmic drugs (EARLY-AF, STOP AF First)?
balance: LIKELY: Two randomised trials of first-line cryoballoon ablation in drug-naïve symptomatic paroxysmal AF agree. EARLY-AF (303 patients, continuous implantable monitoring) found recurrence of any atrial tachyarrhythmia in 42.9% with ablation vs 67.8% with drugs at 1 year (hazard ratio 0.48 — a relative figure at the edge of this library's 0.5 solidity threshold, with the absolute rates beside it). STOP AF First (203 patients) found 12-month treatment success of 74.6% vs 45.0% (P<0.001). Serious adverse events were uncommon and similar in both. The claim is recurrence and symptoms only: whether ablation improves hard outcomes in established AF is Shelf #271, and early rhythm control as a strategy is Shelf #273 — neither is re-carded here.

title: Catheter ablation for ventricular tachycardia in ischaemic cardiomyopathy
question: In patients with prior MI, an ICD, and recurrent VT, does catheter ablation beat escalating antiarrhythmic drugs — and does ablating after the first shock beat waiting (VANISH, PARTITA)?
balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: both anchors' composites include death): VANISH (259 patients) found ablation lowered a composite of death, VT storm or appropriate ICD shock vs escalating antiarrhythmic drugs (59.1% vs 68.5%; hazard ratio 0.72, 95% CI 0.53 to 0.98 — a relative figure inside the 0.5–2.0 band, not solid on its own) with no significant mortality difference on its own. PARTITA found ablating immediately after the first ICD shock markedly lowered a composite of death or heart-failure hospitalisation (4% vs 42%; hazard ratio 0.11) — but in only 47 randomised patients, in a trial stopped early at interim analysis, the exact setting in which effects inflate. title: Cardiac resynchronization in narrow QRS: the EchoCRT harm
question: In heart failure with a narrow QRS but echocardiographic dyssynchrony, does CRT help — or harm (EchoCRT)?
balance: LIKELY (harm / no benefit) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: mortality harm signal): EchoCRT (809 randomised patients with QRS <130 ms and echocardiographic dyssynchrony) was stopped for futility and found no reduction in death or heart-failure hospitalisation with CRT switched on (28.7% vs 25.2%; hazard ratio 1.20) and more deaths (11.1% vs 6.4%; hazard ratio 1.81, 95% CI 1.11 to 2.93 — a relative figure inside the 0.5–2.0 band, printed with its absolute rates). A large trial stopped early with a null primary and a mortality signal in the wrong direction carries LIKELY for 'do not do this'. title: Transcatheter tricuspid repair for severe tricuspid regurgitation (TRILUMINATE)
question: In severe symptomatic tricuspid regurgitation, does edge-to-edge repair improve quality of life versus medical therapy alone?
balance: POSSIBLE: A single pivotal trial, TRILUMINATE Pivotal (350 patients), found percutaneous tricuspid edge-to-edge repair beat medical therapy on a hierarchical composite (win ratio 1.48) — but the win was carried by quality of life: the Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire score rose 12.3 points with repair vs 0.6 with control (P<0.001), while death or tricuspid surgery and heart-failure hospitalisation did not differ between groups (the heart-failure figure printed with mortality beside it, per this library's rule — neither is carded as a benefit). Repair did reduce regurgitation severity (87.0% vs 4.8% at no more than moderate at 30 days) and was safe (98.3% free of major adverse events at 30 days). One trial caps the stamp at POSSIBLE, and the claim carded is quality of life, nothing harder. Mitral repair for secondary MR is Shelf #550 and is not re-carded here.

title: Mitral repair vs replacement surgery for primary (degenerative) mitral regurgitation (EVEREST II)
question: For severe degenerative mitral regurgitation, how does percutaneous edge-to-edge repair compare with surgery on effectiveness and safety?
balance: POSSIBLE: The single randomised comparison, EVEREST II (279 patients), found percutaneous clip repair less effective than surgery at 12 months on its efficacy composite (freedom from death, surgery for valve dysfunction, or grade 3+/4+ regurgitation: 55% vs 73%; P=0.007) — the gap driven by more patients needing surgery after the clip (20% vs 2%), with death identical (6% in each group; mortality printed beside every figure here per this library's rule) — but much safer at 30 days (major adverse events 15% vs 48%). title: Antithrombotic therapy after TAVR: when anticoagulation harmed (GALILEO, ATLANTIS)
question: After transcatheter aortic valve replacement, does routine anticoagulation (rivaroxaban, apixaban) beat antiplatelet-based standard care — or cause harm?
balance: LIKELY (routine anticoagulation does not help, and rivaroxaban harmed) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: GALILEO carries a mortality harm claim): GALILEO (1,644 patients without an anticoagulation indication) was stopped early for safety: rivaroxaban 10 mg produced more death or thromboembolic events than an antiplatelet strategy (9.8 vs 7.2 per 100 person-years; hazard ratio 1.35) and more deaths (5.8 vs 3.4 per 100 person-years; hazard ratio 1.69 — relative figures, absolute rates beside them). ATLANTIS (1,500 patients) found apixaban not superior to standard care on its primary composite (18.4% vs 20.1%; hazard ratio 0.92), with less obstructive valve thrombosis but a signal of higher non-cardiovascular mortality in the no-indication stratum. Two trials, no benefit, one clear harm: LIKELY, proposed in the Tier C lane. TAVR versus surgery is Shelf #266 and is not re-carded here.

title: Stent-grafting for uncomplicated type B aortic dissection (INSTEAD-XL)
question: In stable, uncomplicated type B dissection, does pre-emptive thoracic endovascular repair plus medical therapy beat medical therapy alone over five years?
balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C candidate: aorta-related mortality claim at 5 years): INSTEAD-XL's 5-year analysis of 140 randomised patients found aorta-specific mortality lower with stent-grafting plus medical therapy than with medical therapy alone (6.9% vs 19.3%; P=0.04), with all-cause mortality not significantly different (11.1% vs 19.3%; P=0.13) — mortality figures always printed in pairs on this shelf. But the long-term analysis rests on landmark analyses of a small trial, and the second randomised trial, ADSORB (61 patients), showed only a 1-year remodelling benefit with no deaths in either arm at 30 days and one death by 1 year in the stent group. title: Ablate-and-pace for permanent atrial fibrillation (APAF-CRT, PABA-CHF)
question: In permanent AF with heart failure, does AV-junction ablation plus resynchronization (or pulmonary-vein isolation) beat pharmacological rate control?
balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: APAF-CRT carries a mortality claim): APAF-CRT (133 patients with severely symptomatic permanent AF, narrow QRS and a recent heart-failure hospitalisation) was stopped early for efficacy: all-cause mortality was 11% with ablation plus CRT vs 29% with pharmacological rate control (hazard ratio 0.26; estimated 2-year death rates 5% vs 21%), and the composite of mortality or heart-failure hospitalisation was 29% vs 51% (hazard ratio 0.40) — heart-failure figures printed with mortality beside them throughout, per this library's rule. title: Cryptococcal meningitis in HIV: single-dose liposomal amphotericin and the ACTA combinations
question: In HIV-associated cryptococcal meningitis, is a single high dose of liposomal amphotericin (with flucytosine and fluconazole) as good as a week of amphotericin — and which oral partner regimen saves most lives (AMBITION-cm, ACTA)?
balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: mortality outcomes throughout): Two large African randomised trials settle the induction question. AMBITION-cm (844 randomised) found a single high dose of liposomal amphotericin B plus 14 days of flucytosine and fluconazole noninferior to the WHO-recommended week of amphotericin B deoxycholate for 10-week mortality (24.8% vs 28.7%), with fewer grade 3–4 adverse events (50.0% vs 62.3%). ACTA (721 patients) found 1 week of amphotericin and a fully oral fluconazole-plus-flucytosine regimen both noninferior to 2 weeks of amphotericin, flucytosine superior to fluconazole as the amphotericin partner (10-week mortality 31.1% vs 45.0%; hazard ratio 0.62 — a relative figure inside the 0.5–2.0 band, believed here as randomised data with absolute rates beside it), and the lowest mortality with 1 week of amphotericin plus flucytosine (24.2%). The stamp is LIKELY and proposed only, because every load-bearing figure is mortality.

title: Tecovirimat for mpox: the stockpiled drug meets its trials (PALM007, STOMP)
question: Does tecovirimat speed lesion resolution or improve outcomes in mpox — clade I in Congo (PALM007) and clade II (STOMP) — versus placebo?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): The stockpiled antiviral failed both of its placebo-controlled tests. PALM007 (597 patients with clade I mpox in the Democratic Republic of Congo) found lesion resolution at a median of 7 days on tecovirimat vs 8 days on placebo (competing-risks hazard ratio 1.13, 95% CI 0.97 to 1.31; P=0.14 — a relative figure inside the 0.5–2.0 band, with its absolute medians beside it), with similar PCR negativity at day 14 and no safety signal. The STOMP trial's virological analysis in clade II disease found tecovirimat did not reduce virus isolation from skin swabs (culture-positive at day 8 in 9% vs 12%), and its authors note all three phase 3 trials showed no substantial clinical benefit. Two randomised tests, two clades, one null: LIKELY. Supportive care in PALM007 held overall mortality to 1.7%, below the 4.6% case fatality reported in the DRC in 2023 — context, not a drug effect.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference)

title: Cytomegalovirus after transplant: letermovir prevention and maribavir rescue
question: Does letermovir prophylaxis prevent CMV infection after stem-cell transplant — and does maribavir clear refractory/resistant CMV better than investigator-assigned therapy (SOLSTICE)?
balance: Split: POSSIBLE — letermovir prophylaxis · POSSIBLE — maribavir rescue. Two different questions share this shelf, each resting on a single phase 3 trial, so each is capped at POSSIBLE. Letermovir through week 14 after stem-cell transplant cut clinically significant CMV infection by week 24 (37.5% vs 60.6% on placebo; P<0.001), with all-cause mortality at week 48 of 20.9% vs 25.5% printed beside it as the record states it — a difference the abstract does not test and this shelf does not claim. title: Long-acting injectable HIV treatment: cabotegravir–rilpivirine (ATLAS, FLAIR)
question: In people already suppressed on oral therapy (ATLAS) or starting treatment (FLAIR), is monthly injectable cabotegravir–rilpivirine non-inferior to staying on daily pills?
balance: LIKELY: Two phase 3 noninferiority trials of monthly injectable cabotegravir plus rilpivirine agree. ATLAS (616 patients already suppressed on oral therapy): HIV-1 RNA of 50 copies/mL or more at week 48 in 1.6% on injections vs 1.0% on pills (adjusted difference 0.6 percentage points, within the 6-point margin). FLAIR (566 patients after oral induction): 2.1% vs 2.5% (adjusted difference −0.4 points). Suppression below 50 copies was 92.5–93.6% on injections vs 93.3–95.5% on pills. The price is injection-site reactions (75–86% of recipients, mostly mild or moderate, median 3 days; about 1% withdrew for injection pain in ATLAS, 4 participants for injection-related reasons in FLAIR) and more grade 3-or-higher adverse events in FLAIR's injection arm (11% vs 4%). Noninferiority in two trials earns LIKELY; HIV prevention (PrEP) is Shelf #317 and is not re-carded here.

title: Two-drug HIV treatment: dolutegravir plus lamivudine (GEMINI)
question: Can initial HIV treatment drop to two drugs — dolutegravir plus lamivudine — without losing viral suppression versus a three-drug dolutegravir regimen?
balance: LIKELY: The twin GEMINI trials (1,441 antiretroviral-naive adults, identically designed, double-blind) found two-drug dolutegravir plus lamivudine noninferior to three-drug dolutegravir plus tenofovir/emtricitabine at week 48: suppression below 50 copies/mL in 91% vs 93% pooled (adjusted difference −1.7 percentage points, 95% CI −4.4 to 1.1, against a −10-point margin), with the result consistent in each trial separately (90% vs 93% in GEMINI-1; 93% vs 94% in GEMINI-2). Drug-related adverse events were numerically fewer on two drugs (18% vs 24%). Two blinded trials earn LIKELY — scoped to the enrolled population: screening viral load of 500,000 copies/mL or less, treatment-naive. title: Shorter all-oral regimens for rifampin-resistant tuberculosis (TB-PRACTECAL)
question: Does a 24-week all-oral BPaL-based regimen beat the long standard of care for rifampin-resistant TB on efficacy and safety?
balance: POSSIBLE: TB-PRACTECAL's stage-2 comparison found a 24-week all-oral BPaLM regimen (bedaquiline, pretomanid, linezolid, moxifloxacin) noninferior to a 9-to-20-month standard of care — and on the modified intention-to-treat numbers, far fewer unfavourable outcomes (11% vs 48%; risk difference −37 percentage points) — with fewer grade 3-or-higher or serious adverse events (19% vs 59%). But recruitment was terminated early, the evaluable populations shrink fast across analyses (301 enrolled in stage 2; 128 in the modified intention-to-treat set; the per-protocol difference was −9 points), and the trial was open-label — one trial, so POSSIBLE. STREAM supplies the supporting arc: an earlier 9-to-11-month regimen was noninferior to the 20-month standard (favourable status 78.8% vs 79.8%), showing 'shorter' itself was sound while its injectable-era regimen has been superseded by the all-oral one. Drug-susceptible TB is Shelf #319 and latent TB Shelf #509; neither is re-carded here.

title: Typhoid conjugate vaccine (TyVAC trials)
question: Does a single dose of typhoid conjugate vaccine protect children in endemic settings — efficacy in Nepal and four-year durability in Malawi?
balance: LIKELY: Two large phase 3 trials in endemic settings agree on a single dose of typhoid conjugate vaccine. In Nepal (20,019 children vaccinated), blood-culture-confirmed typhoid occurred at 79 vs 428 cases per 100,000 person-years against a meningococcal control vaccine (efficacy 81.6%, 95% CI 58.8 to 91.8 — a relative figure, absolute incidence beside it). In Malawi (28,130 children), the final 4-year analysis found efficacy of 78.3% (66.3 to 86.1), with protection in every age band including children under 2 years (70.6%, with a wide interval) and 163 children needing vaccination to prevent one case. Serious adverse events were similar between groups in Nepal (132 events in 6 months; one vaccine-related, pyrexia). Two large trials, consistent efficacy, proven durability: LIKELY.

title: Baloxavir for influenza: one dose against the virus and the oseltamivir benchmark
question: Does single-dose baloxavir shorten influenza illness versus placebo — and versus oseltamivir — in healthy and high-risk outpatients (CAPSTONE-1/-2)?
balance: LIKELY (for symptom shortening vs placebo; not for superiority over oseltamivir): CAPSTONE-1 (1,064 infected patients in its phase 3 intention-to-treat-infected population) found single-dose baloxavir shortened time to symptom alleviation vs placebo (median 53.7 vs 80.2 hours; P<0.001), with a similar time to alleviation as oseltamivir and a greater day-1 viral-load reduction than either comparator. CAPSTONE-2, in high-risk outpatients, repeated the placebo result (median time to improvement 73.2 vs 102.3 hours, difference 29.1 hours) and again did not separate from oseltamivir (73.2 vs 81.0 hours, difference 7.7 hours with an interval crossing zero). The counterweight sits on CAPSTONE-1's own card: viral variants with reduced baloxavir susceptibility emerged in 9.7% of phase 3 baloxavir recipients. Oseltamivir's own treatment/prevention evidence is Shelf #583 and is not re-carded here.

title: Molnupiravir for community COVID-19: two trials, two populations (PANORAMIC, MOVe-OUT)
question: Does molnupiravir help in COVID-19 — in unvaccinated high-risk adults (MOVe-OUT) and in a largely vaccinated community population (PANORAMIC)?
balance: Split: POSSIBLE — unvaccinated high-risk adults (MOVe-OUT era) · LIKELY — no benefit in a largely vaccinated community population (PANORAMIC) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C candidate: hospitalisation-or-death composite). title: Single-dose lipoglycopeptides for skin infection: dalbavancin and oritavancin
question: Is one dose of dalbavancin (DISCOVER) or oritavancin (SOLO) non-inferior to a full course of vancomycin for acute bacterial skin infection?
balance: LIKELY: Two drug programmes, both noninferior to vancomycin-based courses on early clinical response. Dalbavancin's twin DISCOVER trials (pooled 1,312 patients in the primary analysis) gave early response in 79.7% on two once-weekly doses vs 79.8% on vancomycin with optional oral linezolid (weighted difference −0.1 percentage points, 95% CI −4.5 to 4.2), with fewer adverse events on dalbavancin. The claim is noninferiority and convenience — one or two infusions instead of a course — not superiority. Antibiotics after abscess drainage (Shelf #505) and cellulitis duration (Shelf #506) are different questions and are not re-carded here.

title: Hemodiafiltration versus high-flux hemodialysis
question: In maintenance dialysis, does high-dose hemodiafiltration reduce mortality versus conventional high-flux hemodialysis?
balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: the primary claim is all-cause mortality). Two randomised trials point the same way: CONVINCE (1,360 patients, median 30 months) found death from any cause in 17.3% on high-dose hemodiafiltration versus 21.9% on high-flux hemodialysis (hazard ratio 0.77, 95% CI 0.65 to 0.93), and the earlier open-label ESHOL trial (906 patients) found a relative hazard of 0.70 (0.53 to 0.92) for all-cause mortality. title: Roxadustat and the HIF stabilizers for anaemia in chronic kidney disease

title: Membranous nephropathy: rituximab versus calcineurin inhibition
question: In primary membranous nephropathy, does rituximab beat cyclosporine for durable remission (MENTOR) — and a rituximab sequence versus cyclical steroids/cyclophosphamide (STARMEN)?
balance: LIKELY: Two randomised trials answer the two halves. MENTOR (130 patients) showed rituximab non-inferior to cyclosporine for remission at 12 months (60% vs 52%) and clearly superior at maintaining remission at 24 months (60% vs 20%; risk difference 40 percentage points). STARMEN (86 patients) then showed the older cyclical corticosteroid–cyclophosphamide regimen beating a sequential tacrolimus–rituximab regimen on the same 24-month remission outcome (83.7% vs 58.1%; relative risk 1.44 — a relative measure inside the 0.5–2.0 caution band, printed with its absolute rates). Rituximab's win is over a calcineurin inhibitor's durability, not over the cyclical alkylating regimen.

title: Lupus nephritis induction: mycophenolate versus cyclophosphamide
question: For induction in proliferative lupus nephritis, is mycophenolate non-inferior to IV cyclophosphamide — full-dose (ALMS) or low-dose “Euro-Lupus” — and what does long-term follow-up show?
balance: LIKELY (for comparability, not superiority): The international ALMS induction trial (370 patients, classes III–V) found nearly identical response rates for mycophenolate and IV cyclophosphamide (56.2% vs 53.0%) and explicitly did not meet its objective of showing mycophenolate superior. The Euro-Lupus trial (90 patients) separately showed a low-dose IV cyclophosphamide regimen (cumulative 3 g, followed by azathioprine) achieving results comparable to a high-dose regimen (treatment failure 16% vs 20%; renal remission 71% vs 54%, neither difference statistically significant). Two randomised trials thus support mycophenolate as a comparable induction option and low-dose cyclophosphamide as a comparable dose strategy — neither supports a superiority claim for any arm.

title: ANCA vasculitis with kidney failure: plasma exchange and steroid dose
question: In severe ANCA-associated vasculitis, does plasma exchange reduce death or end-stage kidney disease — and is a reduced-dose steroid regimen as safe (PEXIVAS; MEPEX as the earlier exchange trial)?
balance: Split, PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: the primary composite is death or end-stage kidney disease). LIKELY for the PEXIVAS null: in 704 patients followed up to 7 years, plasma exchange did not reduce death or ESKD (28.4% vs 31.0%; hazard ratio 0.86, 95% CI 0.65 to 1.13 — a relative measure inside the 0.5–2.0 caution band, with absolute rates beside it), a very large null that may carry LIKELY under the library's large-null rule; the same trial found a reduced-dose glucocorticoid regimen noninferior to standard dose on the same composite, with fewer serious infections. POSSIBLE for the older MEPEX signal: in 137 patients presenting with creatinine above 500 micromol/L, exchange beat IV methylprednisolone on dialysis independence at 3 months (69% vs 49%) — a smaller, earlier, severe-renal-only trial whose recovery endpoint PEXIVAS did not reproduce on death/ESKD.

title: Preventing AV fistula failure: clopidogrel and fish oil
question: After new fistula creation, does clopidogrel prevent early thrombosis (DAC) or fish oil prevent failure (FAVOURED) — and do either improve usability for dialysis?
balance: Split: LIKELY for the null on the outcome that matters — usability/failure — and POSSIBLE for clopidogrel's isolated thrombosis effect. In DAC (877 patients), clopidogrel cut fistula thrombosis at 6 weeks (12.2% vs 19.5%; relative risk 0.63 — a relative measure inside the 0.5–2.0 caution band, with absolute rates beside it) but did not increase the proportion of fistulas becoming suitable for dialysis (61.8% vs 59.5% unsuitable-failure rates as reported; relative risk for failure 1.05). In FAVOURED (567 randomised), neither fish oil (failure 47% vs 47%; relative risk 1.03) nor aspirin in its factorial subset (45% vs 43%; relative risk 1.05) reduced fistula failure at 12 months. Preventing a clot is not the same as producing a usable fistula, and the stamps keep those apart.

title: Difelikefalin for dialysis itch
question: Does the kappa-opioid agonist difelikefalin reduce uraemic pruritus in hemodialysis patients versus placebo?

title: Transplant immunosuppression: the low-dose tacrolimus standard
question: Which initial regimen after kidney transplant best balances rejection, graft function, and harm — the four-arm ELITE-Symphony comparison that set modern practice?
balance: POSSIBLE: A single landmark four-arm randomised trial (1,645 recipients) found the low-dose tacrolimus regimen (with daclizumab induction, mycophenolate and corticosteroids) giving the highest mean calculated GFR at 12 months (65.4 ml per minute vs 56.7 to 59.4 in the other arms), the lowest biopsy-proven acute rejection rate (12.3% vs 25.8% standard-dose cyclosporine, 24.0% low-dose cyclosporine, 37.2% low-dose sirolimus), and the highest allograft survival (94.2% vs 89.3% to 93.1%). One trial, however large and practice-setting, caps the stamp at POSSIBLE under the single-trial rule; the regimen question has not been re-randomised at this scale. Belatacept-versus-ciclosporin is a different comparison and stays home on Shelf #590.

title: Atrasentan for diabetic kidney disease
question: In type 2 diabetes with CKD already on maximum RAS blockade, does the endothelin antagonist atrasentan slow kidney progression in the enriched responder population SONAR selected — at what fluid-retention cost?
balance: POSSIBLE: One large double-blind trial with an enrichment design (SONAR: 2,648 randomised responders) found the primary renal composite — doubling of serum creatinine or end-stage kidney disease — in 6.0% on atrasentan versus 7.9% on placebo (hazard ratio 0.65, 95% CI 0.49 to 0.88 — a relative measure, printed with its absolute rates). A single trial caps the stamp at POSSIBLE, and the design caveat belongs on the shelf face: only patients who first responded to atrasentan in an enrichment period (albuminuria down at least 30% without substantial fluid retention) were randomised. The harm side is printed with the benefit: fluid retention and anaemia were more frequent, heart-failure hospital admission was 3.5% versus 2.6% (hazard ratio 1.33, 0.85 to 2.07 — not significant), and deaths were 4.4% versus 3.9% (hazard ratio 1.09, 0.75 to 1.59) — the heart-failure figures are always shown beside the mortality figures, and no heart-failure or mortality benefit is claimed.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Rituximab for childhood steroid-dependent nephrotic syndrome
question: In children with frequently relapsing/steroid-dependent nephrotic syndrome, does rituximab prolong relapse-free survival versus placebo (Iijima) or versus low-dose mycophenolate (RITURNS)?
balance: LIKELY: Two double-blind, placebo-controlled randomised trials, in complementary populations, both found rituximab prolonging relapse-free survival: Iijima 2014 in complicated frequently relapsing / steroid-dependent disease (median relapse-free period 267 vs 101 days; hazard ratio 0.27, 95% CI 0.14 to 0.53 — a relative measure at the strong end, outside the 0.5–2.0 caution band) and the 2025 JSKDC10 trial in uncomplicated disease (median 285 vs 81 days; 3-year cumulative relapse-free survival 38% vs 9% on follow-up). title: Hormone replacement for chronic hypoparathyroidism: rhPTH(1-84) and palopegteriparatide
question: Can parathyroid-hormone replacement free patients with chronic hypoparathyroidism from high-dose calcium and active vitamin D — REPLACE (rhPTH 1-84) and the PaTHway programme (palopegteriparatide)?
balance: LIKELY: Two separate phase 3, double-blind, placebo-controlled programmes reached the same endpoint family. title: Differentiated thyroid cancer: lenvatinib and sorafenib
question: In radioiodine-refractory differentiated thyroid cancer, do lenvatinib (SELECT) and sorafenib (DECISION) prolong progression-free survival versus placebo — at what toxicity cost?
balance: LIKELY (for progression-free survival; no overall-survival claim is made): Two double-blind phase 3 trials against placebo both prolonged progression-free survival — SELECT: median 18.3 vs 3.6 months on lenvatinib (hazard ratio for progression or death 0.21, 99% CI 0.14 to 0.31 — a relative measure well outside the 0.5–2.0 caution band) with a 64.8% response rate; DECISION: median 10.8 vs 5.8 months on sorafenib (hazard ratio 0.59, 95% CI 0.45 to 0.76 — a relative measure inside the caution band's lower half, printed with its absolute medians). title: Vaptans for SIADH: raising sodium with tolvaptan
question: In euvolemic/hypervolemic hyponatremia (SIADH and heart failure), does tolvaptan raise serum sodium versus placebo — and does faster correction translate into outcomes?

title: Acromegaly: pasireotide versus octreotide, and pegvisomant
question: In medically untreated acromegaly, does pasireotide beat octreotide on biochemical control (the PAOLA head-to-head) — and where does the growth-hormone-receptor antagonist pegvisomant fit?

title: The older anti-obesity drugs: phentermine–topiramate and naltrexone–bupropion
question: How much weight do the pre-GLP-1 oral agents lose versus placebo — and what did their safety programmes show (CONQUER/EQUIP; COR-I/LIGHT-era trials)?
balance: LIKELY (for weight loss versus placebo; no cardiovascular-benefit claim is made): Two large double-blind phase 3 trials anchor the shelf. question: Is phenoxybenzamine better than doxazosin for preoperative alpha blockade in pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma — the PRESCRIPT head-to-head?

title: SGLT2 inhibitors as add-on in type 1 diabetes
question: Does adding an SGLT2 inhibitor to insulin in type 1 diabetes improve HbA1c and weight — at what ketoacidosis cost (DEPICT-1 dapagliflozin; EASE empagliflozin)?
balance: Split, both halves LIKELY on concordant phase 3 programmes. title: Medical therapy for Cushing's disease: pasireotide and osilodrostat
question: In persistent/recurrent Cushing's disease, do pasireotide (phase II/III programme) and osilodrostat (LINC-3) normalize cortisol versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE: Two different mechanisms, each supported at phase 3 level but neither with a conventional placebo-controlled induction trial. Pasireotide's phase 3 trial (162 patients) randomised between two doses with no placebo arm: urinary free cortisol normalised at month 6 in 15% (600 μg twice daily) and 26% (900 μg) of patients, after a 15-day phase 2 proof-of-concept in which 76% reduced urinary cortisol and 17% normalised it — with hyperglycaemia-related adverse events in 118 of 162 phase 3 patients. Osilodrostat's LINC-3 used a randomised-withdrawal design: among responders randomised at week 26, 86% maintained a complete response on continued osilodrostat versus 29% switched to placebo at week 34 (odds ratio 13.7 — a relative measure well outside the 0.5–2.0 caution band, printed with its absolute rates), at the cost of hypocortisolism in 51% of all treated patients. title: High-flow oxygen and non-invasive ventilation in acute hypoxemic failure (FLORALI, HENIVOT)
question: In acute hypoxemic respiratory failure, does high-flow nasal oxygen (FLORALI) or helmet NIV (HENIVOT) beat standard oxygen or face-mask NIV on intubation and mortality?
balance: POSSIBLE — proposed pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C candidate, because FLORALI's mortality difference was a secondary endpoint and is a mortality claim): Neither anchor trial won its primary endpoint — FLORALI's intubation rates did not differ significantly (38% high-flow vs 47% standard vs 50% NIV), and HENIVOT's days free of respiratory support did not differ (median 20 vs 18 days; P=0.26). What favoured the newer devices was secondary: FLORALI's 90-day mortality hazard ratios (2.01 for standard oxygen vs high-flow; 2.50 for NIV vs high-flow — relative figures, absolute rates not stated in the abstract) and HENIVOT's lower intubation rate (30% vs 51%). The 2025 RENOVATE trial then showed high-flow nasal oxygen noninferior to NIV on intubation or death at 7 days in most acute-respiratory-failure groups (39% vs 38% overall; noninferiority not established in immunocompromised patients). Promising, largely secondary-endpoint and noninferiority evidence: POSSIBLE, not more.

title: Sedation strategy in the ICU: early dexmedetomidine and no sedation (SPICE III, NONSEDA)
question: Does sedation strategy change outcomes — early dexmedetomidine as the primary sedative (SPICE III), or a plan of no sedation versus light sedation with daily interruption (NONSEDA)?

title: How much renal replacement: intensity of CRRT and dialysis in ICU acute kidney injury (ATN, RENAL)
question: In ICU acute kidney injury, does more intensive renal replacement improve survival versus standard intensity?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): Two large trials, testing two different ways of intensifying renal replacement, agree exactly — ATN: 60-day mortality 53.6% with intensive therapy vs 51.5% with less-intensive (odds ratio 1.09; 95% CI 0.86 to 1.40); RENAL: 90-day mortality 44.7% in each arm (odds ratio 1.00; 0.81 to 1.23). title: Early versus late tracheostomy (TracMan, Terragni)
question: Does performing tracheostomy early in anticipated prolonged ventilation reduce mortality or pneumonia versus waiting?
balance: POSSIBLE: Early tracheostomy did not reduce mortality in either trial — TracMan: 30-day mortality 30.8% early vs 31.5% late (absolute difference 0.7 points in early's favour, 95% CI −5.4 to 6.7), 2-year mortality 51.0% vs 53.7% (P=0.74); Terragni: the hazard ratio for dying was 0.80 (95% CI 0.56 to 1.15), not significant. Terragni's primary endpoint also missed significance — ventilator-associated pneumonia 14% early vs 21% late (P=0.07) — although early patients left the ventilator and the ICU sooner (hazard ratios 0.70 and 0.73 for remaining connected/in the ICU). The honest summary is 'no mortality or pneumonia proof, some process gains, and clinicians predicted prolonged ventilation poorly' (in TracMan's late arm, only 44.9% ever received a tracheostomy): POSSIBLE for the modest process benefits, no benefit stamp for mortality or pneumonia. Tier C: no, as flagged in the topic file.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Decompressive craniectomy for traumatic brain injury (RESCUEicp, DECRA)
question: For refractory intracranial hypertension after TBI, does decompressive craniectomy save lives — and at what disability cost (RESCUEicp, last-tier; DECRA, early bifrontal)?
balance: Split, proposed pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C — a mortality-versus-disability trade-off): POSSIBLE that last-tier decompressive craniectomy for refractory intracranial hypertension lowers mortality while shifting survivors toward severe disability — RESCUEicp at 6 months: death 26.9% surgical vs 48.9% medical, but vegetative state 8.5% vs 2.1% and lower severe disability 21.9% vs 14.4%, with moderate disability and good recovery similar. POSSIBLE that the early, bifrontotemporoparietal operation in diffuse injury (DECRA) worsens outcome: worse Extended Glasgow Outcome Scale scores (odds ratio 1.84 for a worse score) and more unfavourable outcomes (odds ratio 2.21), with 6-month mortality similar (19% vs 18%). Same operation, different timing, population and technique — opposite lessons; neither result should be quoted without the other. Tier C.

title: Bicarbonate for severe metabolic acidemia (BICAR-ICU)
question: In ICU patients with severe metabolic acidemia, does sodium bicarbonate infusion improve survival overall — and in the pre-specified acute-kidney-injury subgroup?
balance: Split, proposed pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C — mortality claims): LIKELY the null on mortality. title: Securing the airway: video laryngoscopy, the bougie, and preoxygenation (DEVICE, BOUGIE, PREOXI, FELLOW)
question: Do video laryngoscopy (DEVICE) and routine bougie use (BOUGIE) improve first-attempt intubation success in critically ill adults — and do non-invasive-ventilation preoxygenation (PREOXI) and apneic oxygenation (FELLOW) prevent hypoxemia?
balance: Split: LIKELY that video laryngoscopy raises first-attempt success (DEVICE: 85.1% vs 70.8%; absolute difference 14.3 points) and that non-invasive-ventilation preoxygenation reduces hypoxemia during intubation (PREOXI: 9.1% vs 18.5%; difference −9.4 points) — two large multicentre trials with clear primary-endpoint wins on the process outcomes they tested. title: How long trastuzumab for early HER2-positive breast cancer: 12 months, 6 months, or shorter?
question: Is six months of adjuvant trastuzumab non-inferior to twelve (PERSEPHONE) — and what did six months versus twelve show in the French PHARE trial?
balance: Split: The two non-inferiority trials disagree because they set different margins and enrolled somewhat different patients. PERSEPHONE (4,089 patients; 3% absolute margin for 4-year disease-free survival) showed 6 months non-inferior: 4-year disease-free survival 89.4% vs 89.8% (hazard ratio 1.07; 90% CI 0.93 to 1.24; non-inferiority p=0.011), with fewer severe adverse events (19% vs 24%) and far fewer early stops for cardiotoxicity (3% vs 8%). PHARE (3,380 patients; hazard-ratio margin 1.15) failed to show non-inferiority: 2-year disease-free survival 91.1% vs 93.8% (hazard ratio 1.28; 95% CI 1.05 to 1.56), with fewer cardiac events on 6 months (1.9% vs 5.7%). A shorter course is a defensible, margin-dependent option for lower-risk patients — not a proven equal for everyone. Disease-free-survival claims only; no mortality claim is made. Tier C: no, after evaluating the topic file's candidacy against the brief's mortality/MI/stroke/CV-benefit rule.
stamp: Split

title: Adjuvant immunotherapy after resected melanoma: pembrolizumab and nivolumab
question: Does a year of adjuvant anti-PD-1 after resected stage III melanoma improve recurrence-free survival versus placebo (KEYNOTE-054) or versus ipilimumab (CheckMate 238)?
balance: LIKELY: Two large double-blind phase 3 trials agree that a year of adjuvant anti-PD-1 prolongs recurrence-free survival after resected high-risk melanoma — KEYNOTE-054 vs placebo: 1-year recurrence-free survival 75.4% vs 61.0% (hazard ratio for recurrence or death 0.57; 98.4% CI 0.43 to 0.74); CheckMate 238 vs high-dose ipilimumab: 12-month recurrence-free survival 70.5% vs 60.8% (hazard ratio 0.65; 97.56% CI 0.51 to 0.83), with far fewer grade 3–4 treatment-related adverse events than ipilimumab (14.4% vs 45.9%). title: First-line immunotherapy for metastatic melanoma: nivolumab–ipilimumab and nivolumab–relatlimab
question: Does dual checkpoint blockade beat nivolumab alone on survival in untreated metastatic melanoma (CheckMate 067) — and does adding relatlimab beat nivolumab alone on progression-free survival (RELATIVITY-047)?
balance: Split, proposed pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, for the overall-survival claim): POSSIBLE that nivolumab plus ipilimumab improves survival versus ipilimumab alone — CheckMate 067's 5-year overall survival was 52% with the combination, 44% with nivolumab alone and 26% with ipilimumab (hazard ratio for death, combination vs ipilimumab, 0.52); the trial was not powered for the combination-vs-nivolumab comparison, so 'the combination beats nivolumab alone on survival' is NOT established by this shelf. LIKELY that adding relatlimab to nivolumab improves progression-free survival versus nivolumab alone (RELATIVITY-047: median 10.1 vs 4.6 months; hazard ratio 0.75) — a direct randomised comparison on its primary endpoint. Toxicity is the price: grade 3–4 treatment-related adverse events were 55.0% with nivolumab–ipilimumab vs 16.3% with nivolumab (CheckMate 067 primary report) and 18.9% vs 9.7% with relatlimab–nivolumab (RELATIVITY-047).
