title: Beta blockade to prevent decompensation in compensated cirrhosis (PREDESCI)
question: In compensated cirrhosis with clinically significant portal hypertension, do beta blockers (propranolol in responders, carvedilol in non-responders) prevent first decompensation versus placebo?
balance: LIKELY (Tier C — the PREDESCI composite includes death): In PREDESCI — the single randomised trial of this question — beta blockade titrated by hepatic venous pressure gradient response (propranolol for responders, carvedilol for non-responders) reduced the composite of decompensation or death vs placebo (16% vs 27%; hazard ratio 0.51, 95% CI 0.26 to 0.97), driven by less ascites (hazard ratio 0.44). The individual-patient-data meta-analysis of carvedilol (Villanueva 2022, Card 2) corroborates it across four randomised trials (352 patients): carvedilol lowered decompensation (subdistribution hazard ratio 0.506, 95% CI 0.289 to 0.887), ascites (0.491, 0.247 to 0.974) and death (0.417, 0.194 to 0.896) — relative measures, with no heterogeneity (I² = 0%). Two independent randomised evidence bases pointing the same way carry the stamp to LIKELY; the strategy still requires HVPG measurement to replicate PREDESCI, and the meta-analysis tests carvedilol against mixed controls rather than the HVPG-guided strategy itself. Note the topic draft's shorthand: PREDESCI is a beta-blocker trial, not a carvedilol-only trial.
stamp: LIKELY (Tier C — the PREDESCI composite includes death)

title: Microscopic colitis: budesonide induction
question: Does budesonide induce remission in collagenous and lymphocytic colitis versus placebo — and in the incomplete microscopic colitis subtype?
balance: Split: POSSIBLE — budesonide induction in lymphocytic colitis: one small double-blind trial (57 patients) found clinical remission at week 8 in 79% on budesonide 9 mg vs 42% on placebo, with histological remission 68% vs 21%. MAYBE (weak evidence) — incomplete microscopic colitis: the one trial stopped early for poor recruitment (44 patients) and missed its primary endpoint (71.4% vs 43.5% remission, p=0.058), though secondary endpoints favoured budesonide. The topic draft promised maintenance data; both carded trials are 8-week induction studies, so this shelf makes no maintenance claim.
stamp: Split

title: Biosimilar switching: NOR-SWITCH and PLANETRA
question: Is switching from originator infliximab to its biosimilar (CT-P13) non-inferior to staying on originator — across immune-mediated diseases including IBD (NOR-SWITCH) and in rheumatoid arthritis (PLANETRA)?
balance: LIKELY: Switching from originator infliximab to biosimilar CT-P13 was non-inferior to continued originator treatment on disease worsening over 52 weeks in NOR-SWITCH (30% vs 26%; adjusted difference −4.4%, within the prespecified 15% margin), and CT-P13 was equivalent to originator on ACR20 response at week 30 in PLANETRA's rheumatoid arthritis population (60.9% vs 58.6%, confidence interval within ±15%), with near-identical immunogenicity (antidrug antibodies 48.4% vs 48.2%). NOR-SWITCH was not powered for non-inferiority within any single disease, including IBD — stated on its card.
stamp: LIKELY

title: Starting buprenorphine in the emergency department (D'Onofrio)
question: Does ED-initiated buprenorphine with primary-care referral engage more patients in addiction treatment at 30 days than referral or brief intervention alone?
balance: POSSIBLE: In the single randomised trial (329 ED patients), ED-initiated buprenorphine with 10 weeks of primary-care follow-up engaged 78% of patients in addiction treatment at 30 days, vs 37% with referral alone and 45% with brief intervention — a large effect on a process outcome (treatment engagement), with no significant difference in opioid-negative urine tests (57.6% vs 53.8% and 42.9%). The trial's own authors state the findings require replication in other centres, and a single trial caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Injectable opioid agonist treatment: hydromorphone and diacetylmorphine (SALOME, NAOMI)
question: For people with severe opioid use disorder unresponsive to oral therapy, is injectable hydromorphone non-inferior to injectable diacetylmorphine (SALOME) — and does diacetylmorphine beat oral methadone (NAOMI)?
balance: LIKELY: In treatment-refractory, long-term injecting opioid use disorder, supervised injectable diacetylmorphine beat oral methadone on retention in treatment (87.8% vs 54.1%; relative rate ratio 1.62) and on reduction in illicit-drug use or illegal activity (67.0% vs 47.7%) in NAOMI, and injectable hydromorphone was non-inferior to diacetylmorphine on street-heroin use in the double-blind SALOME trial — at the cost of overdose and seizure harms concentrated in the diacetylmorphine arms, which is why both programmes are supervised-injection programmes, not prescriptions.

title: Long-acting depot buprenorphine: weekly/monthly injections
question: Are weekly and monthly depot buprenorphine formulations non-inferior to daily sublingual buprenorphine–naloxone (the CAM2038 and Sublocade phase 3 trials)?
balance: LIKELY: Depot buprenorphine matched or beat the daily sublingual standard in two phase 3 trials — weekly-then-monthly CAM2038 was non-inferior to daily sublingual buprenorphine–naloxone on response rate (17.4% vs 14.4%) and opioid-negative urines (35.1% vs 28.4%), and monthly BUP-XR (Sublocade) beat placebo decisively on percentage abstinence (41.3% and 42.7% for the two dosing regimens vs 5.0%). Response rates on the stringent responder definition were low in every arm — that is a property of the definition, printed on the card.
stamp: LIKELY

title: Gabapentin for alcohol use disorder
question: Does gabapentin increase abstinence and reduce heavy drinking versus placebo — and does the enacarbil prodrug formulation replicate it?
balance: Split: POSSIBLE — immediate-release gabapentin: two single-programme placebo-controlled trials are positive, with a dose-response in Mason 2014 (abstinence 17.0% at 1800 mg/day vs 4.1% on placebo; no heavy drinking 44.7% vs 22.5%) and, in Anton 2020, benefit concentrated in patients with more alcohol-withdrawal symptoms (no heavy drinking 27% vs 9% overall). POSSIBLE the null — the enacarbil prodrug: the one large multisite trial of gabapentin enacarbil XR 1200 mg/day (Falk 2019, 346 patients) found no benefit on any drinking outcome (no heavy drinking days 28.3% vs 21.5%, p=0.157), with lower gabapentin exposure than the positive immediate-release trials. Topic-file correction: the enacarbil trial is Falk 2019, not Anton 2020 — Anton 2020 tested immediate-release gabapentin itself.

title: Yoga for chronic low back pain (Saper, Sherman)
question: Is a structured yoga programme non-inferior to physical therapy (Saper) or superior to education (Sherman) for chronic low back pain?
balance: LIKELY: A structured yoga programme was non-inferior to physical therapy for function and pain at 12 weeks in Saper 2017 (320 adults), and superior to a self-care book in Sherman 2011 (function mean difference −2.5 points at 12 weeks, maintained at 26 weeks) — but NOT superior to conventional stretching classes in Sherman, which bounds the claim: yoga works about as well as other structured exercise-based care, not better than all of it. Behavioural interventions are unblindable by nature; both trials are labelled as such.
stamp: LIKELY

title: Spinal manipulation for low back pain (UK BEAM and the chiropractic-care trials)
question: Does adding spinal manipulation to GP care (UK BEAM) or chiropractic care to usual medical care improve low-back-pain outcomes?
balance: POSSIBLE: Adding manipulation-based care to usual care produced small-to-moderate improvements in two large pragmatic trials — UK BEAM (manipulation followed by exercise improved disability scores by 1.9 points more than GP best care at 3 months and 1.3 at 12 months; manipulation alone 1.6 and 1.0) and Goertz 2018 in US service members (pain −1.1 points and disability −2.2 points at 6 weeks with chiropractic care added). The effects are real but small on 24-point disability scales, the interventions are unblindable by nature, and satisfaction effects (Goertz +2.5 points) run larger than pain effects — hence POSSIBLE, not LIKELY.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Muscle relaxants for acute low back pain: the null shelf
question: Do non-benzodiazepine muscle relaxants add anything to NSAIDs in acute low back pain — the pooled RCT answer (Cashin) and the ED head-to-heads (Friedman)?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): Adding a muscle relaxant to an NSAID does not produce a clinically important benefit in acute low back pain. The Cashin 2021 synthesis of 31 trials (6,505 participants) found very-low-certainty evidence of a small, not clinically important pain reduction (−7.7 points on a 0–100 scale at ≤2 weeks), no disability reduction, and a possible increase in adverse events (relative risk 1.6); the two Friedman ED trials then found cyclobenzaprine and diazepam each added nothing to naproxen on function at 1 week (between-group differences 0.3 and 0 points). A concordant null across a 31-trial synthesis and two direct trials carries LIKELY under the large-null rule.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference)

title: Ketamine infusions for chronic pain and complex regional pain
question: Do ketamine infusions produce durable relief in CRPS and other chronic pain states beyond the infusion window (the Schwartzman and Sigtermans RCTs)?
balance: POSSIBLE: Two small randomised placebo-controlled trials of multi-day ketamine infusion in complex regional pain syndrome type 1 found significant pain relief during and shortly after infusion — in Sigtermans 2009, pain scores over 12 weeks were significantly lower with ketamine (lowest at week 1: 2.68 vs 5.45), but the difference had lost significance by week 12 (P=0.07) and there was NO functional improvement; Schwartzman 2009 likewise reported significant reductions in many pain parameters over 3 months of follow-up. Psychomimetic side effects were common (76% vs 18% in Sigtermans). Durability beyond the infusion window is the unproven half of the claim, which caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Duloxetine for musculoskeletal pain: knee osteoarthritis and chronic low back pain
question: Does duloxetine reduce pain in knee osteoarthritis and chronic low back pain versus placebo (the Skljarevski and Chappell trial programmes) — and how large is the effect?
balance: LIKELY (a small effect): Duloxetine 60 mg daily beat placebo on 24-hour average pain in randomised trials in both target conditions — chronic low back pain (least-squares mean change −2.32 vs −1.50 at week 13, a difference of about 0.8 points on a 0–10 scale) and osteoarthritis pain (−2.23 vs −1.73, difference −0.50 points) — with significantly more discontinuations for adverse events in the back-pain trial (13.9% vs 5.8%). The stamp is LIKELY that the effect exists; its size is small, and both halves of that sentence belong on the shelf face. (Programme note: the CLBP anchor is first-authored by Skljarevski; the OA programme's Western pivotal trials could not be pinned to a single verified record in this pass, so the OA card uses the programme's verified phase 3 trial in Chinese patients — disclosed in summary.md.)
stamp: LIKELY (a small effect)

title: Psychological therapies for chronic pain: CBT and ACT (Cochrane)
question: How much do CBT and acceptance-and-commitment therapy improve pain, disability, and mood in chronic pain — the Cochrane synthesis of the RCT base?
balance: Split: LIKELY — CBT: across 59 randomised trials in the 2020 Cochrane synthesis (75 trials, 9,401 participants in total), CBT produced small benefits vs treatment-as-usual for pain (standardised mean difference −0.22), disability (−0.32) and distress (−0.34), and very small benefits vs active control (pain −0.09; disability −0.12; distress −0.09), on mostly moderate-quality evidence. MAYBE (weak evidence) — ACT and behavioural therapy: the ACT base is five trials (443 participants) and the behavioural-therapy base eight trials (647), with estimates rated very low quality throughout — the review's own caution is that these estimates are uncertain and could easily be overturned. Adverse events were inadequately recorded across the field.

title: Transitional care after hospital discharge in older adults
question: Do structured post-discharge interventions — Coleman's Care Transitions coaching and Naylor's APN-led transitional care — reduce readmissions in older adults?
balance: LIKELY: Three randomised trials of structured transitional care for older adults all reduced readmissions: Coleman's transition-coach model cut rehospitalisation at 30 days (8.3% vs 11.9%) and 90 days (16.7% vs 22.5%), Naylor's 1999 advanced-practice-nurse discharge-planning and home follow-up trial cut any readmission by 24 weeks (20.3% vs 37.1%), and Naylor's 2004 heart-failure trial delayed first readmission or death and nearly halved total costs. The interventions differ (coaching vs APN-led) and none could be blinded, but the direction is consistent across three trials and two decades.
stamp: LIKELY

title: Drug prophylaxis for postoperative delirium
question: Does prophylactic low-dose dexmedetomidine after surgery prevent delirium in older ICU patients (Su) — and does prophylactic haloperidol in at-risk older inpatients (Kalisvaart)?
balance: Split: LIKELY — prophylactic dexmedetomidine prevents postoperative delirium · LIKELY the null — haloperidol prophylaxis prevents it. Su 2016 (700 patients, double-blind) found delirium in 9% with overnight low-dose dexmedetomidine vs 23% with placebo (odds ratio 0.35, 95% CI 0.22-0.54 — a relative measure, with the absolute rates beside it on the card). Kalisvaart 2005 (430 hip-surgery patients, double-blind) found delirium in 15.1% on haloperidol vs 16.5% on placebo (relative risk 0.91, 0.6-1.3) — no prevention, though delirium that occurred was less severe and shorter. One positive and one null, each from a single rigorous trial — hence LIKELY on both halves rather than a pooled claim. Multicomponent NON-drug prevention (the HELP programme) is home on Shelf #340 and is not re-carded here.

title: Cataract surgery timing and falls and fractures
question: Does prompt first-eye cataract surgery reduce falls and fractures in older women (Harwood) — and expedited second-eye surgery (Foss)?
balance: Split: LIKELY — prompt first-eye cataract surgery reduces the rate of falling · POSSIBLE — prompt second-eye surgery does. Harwood 2005 (306 women over 70) found expedited first-eye surgery cut the fall rate by a relative 34% (rate ratio 0.66, 95% CI 0.45-0.96), with fewer fractures (3% vs 8%). Foss 2006 (239 women) found a similar-sized point estimate for second-eye surgery (rate ratio 0.68) but with a confidence interval crossing 1 (0.39-1.19; P=0.18), so the second-eye half is stamped POSSIBLE. Both trials compared expedited surgery (approximately 4 weeks) with a routine 12-month wait, so they test timing, not surgery versus never operating.

title: Orthogeriatric co-management after hip fracture
question: Does comprehensive geriatric assessment delivered as orthogeriatric co-management improve mobility and outcomes after hip fracture versus usual orthopaedic care?
balance: POSSIBLE — proposed pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C candidate: mortality claims appear in the co-management syntheses, which are home on another shelf and are not carded here). title: Advance care planning interventions
question: Do structured advance-care-planning interventions — the PREPARE web programme (Sudore) and facilitated ACP in elderly inpatients (Detering) — increase documentation and goal-concordant care?
balance: LIKELY: Two randomised trials in different settings both moved their primary outcomes by large margins. PREPARE (Sudore 2018; 986 primary-care patients aged 55 or older) raised new advance care planning documentation at 15 months versus an easy-to-read advance directive alone (43.0% vs 33.1% unadjusted; adjusted 43.0% vs 32.0%). Detering 2010 (309 inpatients aged 80 or older) found that among patients who died, end of life wishes were known and followed in 86% with facilitated planning vs 30% with usual care. Documentation and concordance are process outcomes — neither trial shows a survival effect, and none is claimed.

title: Supporting dementia caregivers
question: Do multicomponent caregiver interventions reduce burden and depression (REACH II) and delay nursing-home placement (Mittelman NYU)?
balance: LIKELY: Two large randomised trials of multicomponent caregiver support, in different designs and populations, both met their primary aims. REACH II (642 caregivers across three ethnic groups) improved a composite quality-of-life indicator versus control calls (P<0.001 in Hispanic or Latino caregivers and P=0.037 in white caregivers, with a significant effect also in Black or African-American spouse caregivers) and lowered clinical depression prevalence (12.6% vs 22.7%). The NYU intervention (406 spouse caregivers) reduced the rate of nursing-home placement by a relative 28.3% (adjusted hazard ratio 0.717), a model-predicted median delay of 557 days. Behavioural interventions cannot be blinded, but two independent trials with concordant benefit support LIKELY.
stamp: LIKELY

title: Preventing pressure injuries: repositioning and support surfaces
question: Can nursing-home residents at moderate/high risk be repositioned every 4 hours instead of 2 (TURN) — and do alternating-pressure mattresses beat overlays in hospital (PRESSURE 2)?
balance: Split: POSSIBLE — repositioning every 3–4 hours is as safe as every 2 hours on a high-density foam mattress · MAYBE (weak evidence) — alternating-pressure mattresses prevent pressure ulcers better than high-specification foam. TURN (942 nursing-home residents) found pressure-ulcer incidence of 2.5%, 0.6% and 3.1% on 2-, 3- and 4-hourly schedules with no significant difference (P=.68) — one large trial, hence POSSIBLE for the no-difference claim. PRESSURE 2 (2,029 hospital patients) found insufficient evidence of a difference in time to a new category 2 or worse ulcer (hazard ratio 0.76, 95% CI 0.56-1.04; P=0.089 — a relative measure inside the 0.5–2.0 caution band, non-significant on its primary analysis), with a small benefit only in a treatment-phase sensitivity analysis — hence MAYBE (weak evidence).

title: Screening for osteoporosis with FRAX
question: Does community screening with FRAX (with DXA for the high-risk band) reduce hip fractures versus usual care (SCOOP; ROSE)?
balance: Split: POSSIBLE — FRAX-based community screening reduces hip fractures (SCOOP) · POSSIBLE the null — two-step FRAX screening reduces fractures overall (ROSE). SCOOP (12,483 women aged 70-85) missed its primary outcome (all osteoporosis-related fractures: hazard ratio 0.94, 95% CI 0.85-1.03) but reduced hip fractures (HR 0.72, 0.59-0.89 — a relative measure; the abstract gives no absolute hip-fracture rates). ROSE (34,229 women aged 65-80) found no significant overall reduction in fractures on intention-to-treat analysis, with benefit only in per-protocol analyses of women who were FRAX-positive and accepted DXA (hip fracture adjusted subhazard ratio 0.741). Two large trials, discordant at the whole-population level — each half is stamped POSSIBLE. Treatment of established osteoporosis is a different question and is not re-carded here.

title: Preventing falls in care homes
question: Does a multifactorial falls-prevention programme (staff training, assessment, exercise components) reduce falls in care-home residents — the FinCH trial?
balance: Split: LIKELY — the GtACH programme reduced falls in UK care homes · POSSIBLE the null — care-facility falls interventions in general. FinCH (1,657 residents, 84 care homes, cluster randomised) found the Guide to Action for Care Homes programme cut the fall rate in its primary window (91-180 days after randomisation) to an unadjusted incidence rate ratio of 0.57 (95% CI 0.45-0.71 — a relative measure; rates were six falls per 1,000 residents vs 10 per 1,000). The wider trial base is weaker: the Cameron 2018 Cochrane review of 95 trials found multifactorial interventions in care facilities uncertain for rate of falls (rate ratio 0.88, 0.66-1.18, very low-quality evidence) and exercise uncertain (0.93, 0.72-1.20). One well-run large programme trial against an uncertain class literature — the programme earns LIKELY, the class only POSSIBLE the null. Community falls prevention is home on Shelf #161 and is not re-carded here.

title: Geriatric assessment before surgery
question: Does preoperative comprehensive geriatric assessment and optimization (POPS) reduce complications and length of stay in older patients undergoing elective surgery?

title: Supplemental MRI screening in extremely dense breasts
question: Does adding MRI to mammography in women with extremely dense breasts reduce interval cancers (DENSE) — and an abbreviated-MRI versus tomosynthesis comparison (EA1141)?
balance: LIKELY: In the randomised DENSE trial (40,373 women with extremely dense breasts and a normal mammogram), invitation to supplemental MRI halved the interval-cancer rate over a 2-year screening period (2.5 vs 5.0 per 1,000 screenings). title: MRI before prostate biopsy: the PRECISION pathway
question: Does an MRI-first pathway (biopsy only if MRI is suspicious, targeted cores) detect more significant cancer with fewer biopsies than systematic TRUS biopsy (PRECISION; PROMIS as the accuracy anchor)?
balance: LIKELY: The randomised PRECISION trial (500 biopsy-naïve men) found an MRI-first pathway — biopsy only if MRI is suspicious, targeted cores only — detected more clinically significant cancer than standard TRUS biopsy (38% vs 26%; adjusted difference 12 percentage points, 95% CI 4-20) and less clinically insignificant cancer (adjusted difference -13 points, -19 to -7), while 28% of the MRI group avoided biopsy altogether. The paired accuracy study PROMIS (576 men, all receiving MRI, TRUS biopsy and template mapping biopsy) explains why: MRI sensitivity for clinically significant cancer was 93% vs 48% for TRUS biopsy, at lower specificity (41% vs 96%). Detection endpoints only — no mortality claim. Whether to test at all (PSA screening) is home on Shelf #212.

title: Colonoscopy versus FIT as the screening invitation
question: Is inviting a population to once-only colonoscopy non-inferior to biennial FIT on colorectal-cancer mortality at 10 years (COLONPREV) — and what did the Swedish and US VA comparisons show (SCREESCO; CONFIRM)?
balance: POSSIBLE — proposed pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: colorectal cancer mortality is the primary outcome). COLONPREV's 10-year report (53,051 people in the intention-to-screen population) found biennial FIT non-inferior to one-time colonoscopy for colorectal cancer mortality: 0.24% (60 deaths) vs 0.22% (55 deaths); risk difference -0.02 percentage points (95% CI -0.10 to 0.06), against a prespecified non-inferiority margin of 0.16 percentage points — with higher participation for FIT (39.9% vs 31.8%). A single trial's non-inferiority finding on a mortality endpoint caps the stamp at POSSIBLE. SCREESCO's diagnostic-phase report (278,280 people) compares each strategy with usual care, not with each other, and shows early-detection gains (more stage I-II cancers) with slightly higher first-year gastrointestinal and cardiovascular event rates. The US CONFIRM trial's outcome report could not be pinned at build (see the slate summary); it is not carded.

title: AI-supported mammography screening (MASAI)
question: Does AI-supported screen reading match double human reading on interval cancers and workload (the MASAI randomised trial, interim and interval-cancer reports)?
balance: POSSIBLE: One large randomised trial (MASAI, Sweden) with two sequential reports, counted once as evidence. title: HPV self-sampling to reach screening non-attenders
question: Does offering self-sampling (mailed kits, or choice of self- vs clinician-sampling) raise cervical-screening participation among non-attenders versus repeat invitations?
balance: LIKELY: Two programmes in two countries agree that offering self-sampling raises participation among screening non-attenders, and that how it is offered matters. title: Natriuretic-peptide-guided heart-failure therapy
question: Does titrating heart-failure therapy to an NT-proBNP target beat usual care on outcomes (GUIDE-IT; TIME-CHF in older patients)?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): Two randomised trials, one in high-risk US/Canadian patients with reduced ejection fraction and one in older European patients, both found natriuretic-peptide-guided titration no better than good usual or symptom-guided care on their primary outcomes. GUIDE-IT was stopped for futility at 894 of 1,100 planned patients (primary composite of first heart-failure hospitalisation or cardiovascular mortality 37% vs 37%; adjusted hazard ratio 0.98, 95% CI 0.79-1.22; cardiovascular mortality itself 12% vs 13% — reported as a null component of the composite, not as a benefit claim). TIME-CHF (499 patients aged 60 or older) found survival free of all-cause hospitalisation in 41% vs 40% (HR 0.91, 0.72-1.14). Two concordant nulls of this size earn LIKELY the null under the library's large-null rule. Heart-failure hospitalisation figures are paired with mortality wherever they appear on this shelf, per the developer's rule.

title: Rapid rule-out pathways for chest pain
question: Do accelerated diagnostic pathways (high-sensitivity troponin 0/1-h algorithms; the HEART Pathway) safely increase early discharge in suspected ACS?
balance: Split: LIKELY — the HEART Pathway safely increases early discharge · LIKELY the null — implementing a high-sensitivity troponin 99th-centile threshold did not reduce later myocardial infarction or cardiovascular death. The HEART Pathway randomised trial (282 emergency-department patients; primary report Mahler 2015 with 1-year outcomes in Stopyra 2018 — one trial, counted once) cut objective cardiac testing at 30 days (56.7% vs 68.8%), shortened stay by 12 hours and raised early discharge (39.7% vs 18.4%), with no major adverse cardiac events in patients identified for early discharge at 30 days and a 100% negative predictive value among low-risk patients at 1 year (MACE 9.9% vs 11.3% overall). High-STEACS (48,282 patients, stepped-wedge cluster-randomised) reclassified 17% more patients with myocardial injury or infarction using the high-sensitivity assay, yet subsequent myocardial infarction or cardiovascular death at 1 year in reclassified patients did not fall (adjusted odds ratio 1.10, 95% CI 0.75-1.61) — a very large null, stamped LIKELY the null under the library's large-null rule. The High-STEACS endpoint is a null implementation result reported with its mortality component; no benefit claim is made from it.

title: Diagnostic algorithms for suspected pulmonary embolism
question: Do the YEARS algorithm and age-adjusted D-dimer cutoffs safely reduce CT imaging in suspected PE (YEARS; ADJUST-PE)?
balance: LIKELY: Two large prospective management-outcome studies — labelled honestly as management studies, not blinded randomised trials — show these algorithms safely cut imaging. YEARS (3,465 patients) excluded pulmonary embolism without CT pulmonary angiography in 48% of patients (vs 34% under Wells' rule plus a fixed D-dimer threshold), with a 3-month venous thromboembolism failure rate of 0.61% (95% CI 0.36-0.96) among untreated ruled-out patients. ADJUST-PE (3,346 patients) found a 3-month failure rate of 0.3% (0.1-1.7) in patients left untreated on an age-adjusted cutoff, and in patients aged 75 or older the cutoff raised D-dimer-only exclusion from 6.4% to 29.7% with no additional false-negative findings. Concordant prospective validation at this scale earns LIKELY for safe imaging reduction. Pulmonary embolism treatment after diagnosis is a different question and is not re-carded here.
stamp: LIKELY

title: Population BRCA testing in Ashkenazi Jewish populations
question: Does offering BRCA testing to an entire (unselected by family history) Ashkenazi Jewish population find more carriers cost-effectively versus family-history-based testing — the GCaPPS randomised trial?
balance: POSSIBLE: A single randomised trial (GCaPPS; 1,034 Ashkenazi Jewish adults in North London) with two reports — the primary psychological-outcomes report (Manchanda 2015) and the 3-year follow-up (Manchanda 2020) — counted once as evidence. title: Gestational diabetes screening: one-step versus two-step
question: Does the one-step (75-g, IADPSG criteria) screening approach diagnose more GDM and improve outcomes versus the two-step approach — or only label more women (Hillier 2021)?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference on clinical outcomes): One very large pragmatic randomised trial (23,792 women) found the one-step approach nearly doubled the diagnosis rate of gestational diabetes (16.5% vs 8.5%; unadjusted relative risk 1.94, 97.5% CI 1.79-2.11) while every clinical primary outcome was statistically indistinguishable: large-for-gestational-age infants 8.9% vs 9.2% (relative risk 0.95), the perinatal composite outcome 3.1% vs 3.0% (1.04), gestational hypertension or preeclampsia 13.6% vs 13.5% (1.00), and primary cesarean section 24.0% vs 24.6% (0.98) — relative measures with their absolute rates beside them. title: Antifibrotics for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis: nintedanib and pirfenidone
question: Do nintedanib (INPULSIS-1/-2) and pirfenidone (ASCEND) slow the decline in lung function in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis versus placebo — and what do they cost in gastrointestinal harm?
balance: LIKELY: Two independent antifibrotic programmes, each placebo-controlled and replicated, slow lung-function decline in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. Nintedanib cut the annual forced vital capacity (FVC) decline by 125.3 ml in INPULSIS-1 and 93.7 ml in INPULSIS-2; pirfenidone produced a 47.9% relative reduction in the proportion with a 10-point FVC decline or death in ASCEND. The price is gastrointestinal harm: diarrhoea in about 62% on nintedanib versus about 19% on placebo, and more gastrointestinal and skin events on pirfenidone. This shelf claims slowed decline only — ASCEND itself found no significant difference in death from any cause (P=0.10), and no mortality claim is made here.

title: Dupilumab for COPD with type 2 inflammation
question: In COPD with blood-eosinophil evidence of type 2 inflammation, does dupilumab reduce exacerbations versus placebo on top of inhaled triple therapy?

title: Pulmonary arterial hypertension: macitentan and selexipag on morbidity and mortality
question: Do macitentan (SERAPHIN) and selexipag (GRIPHON) reduce the composite of death and pulmonary-hypertension complications versus placebo, on top of background therapy?

title: Long-term macrolides to prevent bronchiectasis exacerbations
question: In non-cystic-fibrosis bronchiectasis, does long-term low-dose macrolide therapy (azithromycin in EMBRACE; erythromycin in BLESS) reduce exacerbations — and at what cost in resistance and cardiac effects?

title: Pleural procedures: intrapleural tPA-DNase for infection, and indwelling catheter vs talc for malignant effusion
question: Does intrapleural tPA plus DNase improve drainage and cut referrals for surgery in pleural infection (MIST2) — and does an indwelling pleural catheter relieve breathlessness and cut hospital days as well as talc pleurodesis in malignant effusion (TIME2, AMPLE)?
balance: Split: POSSIBLE — tPA-DNase for pleural infection · LIKELY — catheter equals talc on breathlessness with fewer hospital days. For pleural infection, one blinded factorial trial (MIST2, 210 patients) found combined tPA–DNase improved drainage, cut surgical referral (4% vs 16%) and shortened hospital stay by 6.7 days versus placebo, while either agent alone was ineffective and DNase alone increased surgical referral (39% vs 16%) — a single trial, so the benefit caps at POSSIBLE. title: Brensocatib for bronchiectasis
question: Does the DPP-1 inhibitor brensocatib prolong time to first exacerbation and reduce exacerbation rates in bronchiectasis — the phase 2 WILLOW signal tested at scale in the phase 3 ASPEN trial?

title: Oral JAK inhibitors for atopic dermatitis: upadacitinib and abrocitinib

title: Rituximab for pemphigus: first-line, and against mycophenolate
question: Does first-line rituximab with short-term prednisone beat prednisone alone for pemphigus (Ritux 3) — and does rituximab beat mycophenolate mofetil in pemphigus vulgaris (PEMPHIX)?
balance: LIKELY: Two randomised trials against two different standard comparators both favoured rituximab decisively in pemphigus. First-line rituximab plus short-term prednisone achieved complete remission off therapy at month 24 in 89% versus 34% on prednisone alone (Ritux 3, open-label), with fewer grade 3–4 adverse events (27 events in 16 patients vs 53 in 29). Against mycophenolate, rituximab achieved sustained complete remission at week 52 in 40% versus 10% (PEMPHIX), with less cumulative glucocorticoid (3545 mg vs 5140 mg) and far fewer disease flares (6 vs 44), but more serious adverse events (22% vs 15%). The open-label design of Ritux 3 is the shelf's main caveat; the effect sizes are large in both trials.

title: IL-17 blockade for hidradenitis suppurativa: bimekizumab and secukinumab
question: Do bimekizumab (BE HEARD I/II) and secukinumab (SUNSHINE/SUNRISE) improve lesion response in moderate-to-severe hidradenitis suppurativa versus placebo?

title: Molluscum contagiosum: cantharidin drug-device and berdazimer gel
question: Do cantharidin 0.7% applied in clinic (CAMP-1/-2) and home-applied berdazimer gel (B-SIMPLE4) clear molluscum lesions versus vehicle?
balance: LIKELY: Two treatment programmes cleared molluscum contagiosum in vehicle-controlled phase 3 trials, in a disease with high spontaneous resolution (vehicle clearance 13–20%). Cantharidin's adverse events were near-universal but expected, local and mostly mild-to-moderate (application-site vesicles, pain, pruritus); berdazimer's were few, mainly application-site pain and erythema.

title: Remibrutinib for chronic spontaneous urticaria
question: Does the oral BTK inhibitor remibrutinib reduce weekly urticaria activity versus placebo in chronic spontaneous urticaria inadequately controlled by antihistamines?
balance: LIKELY: Two identical phase 3 placebo-controlled trials (REMIX-1, 470 patients; REMIX-2, 455 patients) of remibrutinib 25 mg twice daily in chronic spontaneous urticaria symptomatic despite second-generation H1-antihistamines both met their primary endpoint: the weekly urticaria activity score (UAS7) fell by 20.0 versus 13.8 points (REMIX-1) and 19.4 versus 11.7 points (REMIX-2) at week 12 (P<0.001 for both), sustained through week 24. title: Uterine artery embolization vs surgery for symptomatic fibroids: FEMME and EMMY

title: Relugolix combination therapy for endometriosis pain (SPIRIT 1 and 2)
question: Does once-daily relugolix combination therapy (GnRH antagonist plus hormonal add-back) reduce dysmenorrhoea and non-menstrual pelvic pain in endometriosis versus placebo, without costing bone?
balance: LIKELY: Two replicate double-blind phase 3 trials (SPIRIT 1 and 2, 1,261 women randomised across the two) agree closely: dysmenorrhoea responder rates of about 75% on relugolix combination therapy vs 27–30% on placebo, and non-menstrual pelvic pain responder rates of 58–66% vs 40–43%. title: Mifepristone plus misoprostol for missed miscarriage (MifeMiso)
question: Does adding mifepristone to misoprostol improve complete expulsion in missed miscarriage versus misoprostol alone — in the blinded MifeMiso trial and in Schreiber's early-pregnancy-loss trial?

title: Tubal ectopic pregnancy: systemic methotrexate vs laparoscopic salpingostomy, fertility after treatment, and the GEM3 combination
question: In haemodynamically stable tubal ectopic pregnancy, does systemic methotrexate resolve the pregnancy as safely as laparoscopic salpingostomy — and what does each cost in subsequent fertility (the Hajenius trial; DEMETER/GEM3-era data)?
balance: Split: POSSIBLE — methotrexate matches salpingostomy on resolution and later fertility · POSSIBLE the null — adding gefitinib does not help: Hajenius 1997 (100 women) found similar treatment success and identical homolateral tubal patency (55% vs 59%) for systemic methotrexate vs laparoscopic salpingostomy, and DEMETER (406 women) found no significant difference in 2-year intrauterine pregnancy rates between medical treatment and conservative surgery (67% vs 71%). title: Freeze-all embryo transfer vs fresh transfer in IVF: PCOS and non-PCOS
question: Does freezing all embryos and transferring later improve live birth versus fresh transfer — in polycystic ovary syndrome (Chen), and in women without PCOS (Vuong)?
balance: Split: LIKELY — freeze-all improves live birth in PCOS · POSSIBLE the null — no benefit shown without PCOS: In PCOS, Chen 2016 (1,508 women) found frozen transfer raised live birth after the first transfer (49.3% vs 42.0%, relative rate ratio 1.17) and cut ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (1.3% vs 7.1%), at the cost of more pre-eclampsia (4.4% vs 1.4%). title: Ovulation induction for unexplained infertility: letrozole vs gonadotropins vs clomiphene (AMIGOS)
question: In unexplained infertility, which stimulation drug gives the most live births with the fewest multiple pregnancies — letrozole, clomiphene, or gonadotropins (AMIGOS)?
balance: POSSIBLE: One large three-arm trial (AMIGOS, 900 women) ranks the drugs: live birth was highest with gonadotropins (32.2%), then clomiphene (23.3%), then letrozole (18.7%) — but multiple gestation among ongoing pregnancies ran the other way for gonadotropins (32%, including 10 triplet gestations) vs 9% with clomiphene and 13% with letrozole. The older Bhattacharya trial (580 couples) adds the caution that empirical clomiphene did not beat expectant management on live birth (14% vs 17%). title: Preventing perineal trauma: antenatal massage and second-stage techniques
question: Does antenatal perineal massage reduce perineal trauma and episiotomy — and do second-stage techniques (warm compresses, massage, hands-on vs hands-poised) reduce severe tears?
balance: Split: POSSIBLE — antenatal massage reduces episiotomy and suturing in first births · POSSIBLE — warm compresses and second-stage massage reduce severe tears: The antenatal-massage Cochrane review (4 trials, 2,497 women) found less trauma requiring suturing (relative risk 0.91) and fewer episiotomies (relative risk 0.84), significant only in women without a previous vaginal birth, and no difference in third/fourth-degree tears. title: Ulipristal acetate for uterine fibroids: the PEARL trials, and the liver-safety ending
question: Does ulipristal acetate control fibroid bleeding and shrink fibroids before surgery versus placebo (PEARL I) — and how does it compare with monthly leuprolide (PEARL II), given the later hepatotoxicity restrictions that ended its use?

title: First-line therapy for chronic-phase CML: imatinib's benchmark and dasatinib's challenge (IRIS, DASISION)

title: Caplacizumab for acquired thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TITAN, HERCULES)
question: Does adding the von-Willebrand-factor inhibitor caplacizumab to plasma exchange and immunosuppression speed platelet recovery and cut exacerbations in acquired TTP?
balance: LIKELY: A phase 2 trial (TITAN, 75 patients) and a double-blind phase 3 trial (HERCULES, 145 patients) agree: caplacizumab shortened the time to platelet-count normalisation (39% reduction in median time in TITAN; median 2.69 vs 2.88 days and 1.55 times the likelihood of normalisation in HERCULES), cut exacerbations in TITAN (3 vs 11 patients) and, in HERCULES, reduced the composite of TTP-related death, recurrence or thromboembolism during treatment by a relative 74% (12% vs 49%) and recurrence at any time by a relative 67% (12% vs 38%). Mucocutaneous bleeding is the consistent cost (65% vs 48% in HERCULES). The shelf stamps faster recovery and fewer recurrences; deaths were few (all in the placebo arms during treatment) and no standalone mortality claim is made.
stamp: LIKELY

title: Newer disease-modifying drugs for sickle cell disease: voxelotor and crizanlizumab — and their reversals
question: Does voxelotor raise haemoglobin and reduce haemolysis in sickle cell disease (HOPE) — and did crizanlizumab reduce pain crises (SUSTAIN), given its confirmatory-trial failure and withdrawal that the shelf must carry?
balance: Split: POSSIBLE — voxelotor haemoglobin response (surrogate; drug later withdrawn) · MAYBE (weak evidence) — crizanlizumab for pain crises: HOPE (274 participants) found a haemoglobin response in 51% on voxelotor 1500 mg vs 7% on placebo, with reduced haemolysis markers — a surrogate-endpoint benefit, and voxelotor was later withdrawn from the market after post-approval safety findings, which this shelf carries on its face. Crizanlizumab's phase 2 SUSTAIN trial (198 patients) found a 45.3% relative lower annual crisis rate at the high dose, but the phase 3 STAND trial (252 patients, carded here from the currency sweep) found no significant difference from placebo (rate ratios 1.08 and 0.89) — a positive phase 2 followed by a null confirmatory phase 3 and withdrawal is the definition of MAYBE (weak evidence).
stamp: Split

title: Eltrombopag added to immunosuppression in severe aplastic anaemia (RACE)
question: Does adding eltrombopag to horse antithymocyte globulin plus ciclosporin improve haematologic response in treatment-naïve severe aplastic anaemia — the randomised RACE trial, on the earlier NIH cohort-randomised experience?
balance: POSSIBLE: One randomised trial plus one prospective cohort programme with a historical comparison — labelled as such, not double-Level-A. RACE (197 patients, open-label) found complete response at 3 months in 22% with eltrombopag added vs 10% without (odds ratio 3.2), and overall response at 6 months in 68% vs 41%, with faster time to first response (median 3.0 vs 8.8 months). The NIH Townsley programme (92 consecutive patients) found complete response at 6 months of 58% in its best-timing cohort vs 10% in its historical cohort. A single RCT, however consistent with the cohort experience, caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Reversing anticoagulants: andexanet for factor Xa inhibitor bleeding, and idarucizumab for dabigatran
question: Does andexanet alfa achieve haemostasis in factor-Xa-inhibitor intracerebral haemorrhage versus usual care (ANNEXA-I) — and does idarucizumab fully reverse dabigatran in bleeding or urgent surgery (RE-VERSE AD)?
balance: Tier C — PROPOSED only, pending the developer's personal verdict (thrombotic-harm signal, including ischaemic stroke): Split: POSSIBLE — andexanet haemostatic efficacy with a thrombotic-harm signal · POSSIBLE — idarucizumab reversal (single-arm evidence). ANNEXA-I (530 patients, randomised) found haemostatic efficacy in 67.0% on andexanet vs 53.1% on usual care (adjusted difference 13.4 percentage points), but thrombotic events in 10.3% vs 5.6% — including ischaemic stroke in 6.5% vs 1.5% — with no appreciable difference in modified Rankin score or death within 30 days; that harm signal is why this shelf is Tier C. RE-VERSE AD (503 patients) is a single-arm cohort: idarucizumab reversed dabigatran by a median maximum of 100% on clotting assays, with thrombotic events in 6.3–7.4% and mortality of about 19% at 90 days in a very sick population — reversal of a laboratory effect is well shown; comparative clinical benefit is not testable from this design, hence POSSIBLE.

title: First-line immunotherapy for advanced hepatocellular carcinoma: atezolizumab-bevacizumab and STRIDE
question: In unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma, does first-line atezolizumab plus bevacizumab (IMbrave150) — or single-dose tremelimumab plus durvalumab, the STRIDE regimen (HIMALAYA) — improve survival versus sorafenib?
balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, overall-survival claims): Two independent phase 3 trials beat sorafenib on overall survival. title: HER2-positive metastatic breast cancer: trastuzumab deruxtecan versus trastuzumab emtansine (DESTINY-Breast03)

title: Sleeve gastrectomy versus Roux-en-Y gastric bypass: SLEEVEPASS and SM-BOSS
question: In severe obesity, how do sleeve gastrectomy and Roux-en-Y gastric bypass compare on durable weight loss, diabetes remission, and reflux — at five years and at ten?
balance: Split: POSSIBLE — bypass gives modestly more durable weight loss · LIKELY — reflux is worse after sleeve. On weight: SM-BOSS at 5 years found excess BMI loss 61.1% (sleeve) versus 68.3% (bypass), a difference that was not significant after adjustment (P=.22); SLEEVEPASS at 10 years found percentage excess weight loss not equivalent and 8.4 points higher after bypass (median 43.5% vs 50.7%). Diabetes remission did not differ significantly in SLEEVEPASS at 10 years (26% vs 33%; P=.63); hypertension remission favoured bypass (8% vs 24%; P=.04). On reflux the trials agree and the differences are large: reflux remission 60.4% after bypass versus 25.0% after sleeve and worsening in 31.8% versus 6.3% (SM-BOSS); oesophagitis 31% versus 7% at 10 years (SLEEVEPASS). Metabolic surgery versus medical therapy is a different question and stays home on Shelf #288.
stamp: Split

title: Sentinel-node-positive melanoma: completion lymph-node dissection versus observation
question: After a positive sentinel-node biopsy in melanoma, does immediate completion dissection improve survival or regional control versus ultrasound observation (MSLT-II, DeCOG-SLT)?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference on survival): Two randomised trials agree that immediate completion dissection does not improve survival. MSLT-II (1934 evaluable patients): 3-year melanoma-specific survival 86% in both groups (P=0.42), with dissection improving regional nodal control (92% vs 77% at 3 years) at the cost of lymphoedema in 24.1% versus 6.3%. DeCOG-SLT (473 analysed): 3-year distant metastasis-free survival 77.0% on observation versus 74.9% with dissection. A null carried by two concordant trials, one very large, earns LIKELY; there is no survival-benefit claim, so the shelf is not Tier C.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference on survival)

title: Sentinel-node-positive breast cancer: axillary dissection versus radiotherapy or no further axillary treatment
question: In early breast cancer with one or two positive sentinel nodes, can axillary dissection be safely omitted (ACOSOG Z0011) or replaced by axillary radiotherapy (AMAROS)?
balance: LIKELY: Two randomised trials support de-escalation in their stated populations. Z0011: omitting axillary dissection in women with T1-T2 tumours, breast-conserving therapy and 1-2 positive sentinel nodes was noninferior on 10-year overall survival (86.3% without dissection vs 83.6% with; hazard ratio 0.85, relative). AMAROS: axillary radiotherapy matched dissection on axillary control (5-year recurrence 1.19% vs 0.43%, on very few events) with significantly less lymphoedema. Non-inferiority on survival with less harm is the claim — no survival-benefit claim is made, so the shelf is not Tier C.

title: Small peripheral lung cancer: segmentectomy versus lobectomy
question: For peripheral stage IA non-small-cell lung cancer 2 cm or smaller, is anatomical segmentectomy non-inferior to lobectomy on survival (JCOG0802) — and is sublobar resection non-inferior on disease-free survival (CALGB 140503)?
balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: overall survival is JCOG0802's primary endpoint and the trial claims a survival advantage, so under the brief's rule this candidate IS Tier C). The evidence: JCOG0802 found segmentectomy non-inferior and superior on 5-year overall survival (94.3% vs 91.1%; hazard ratio 0.663, relative) with identical relapse-free survival but more local relapse (10.5% vs 5.4%); CALGB 140503 found sublobar resection non-inferior on disease-free survival (hazard ratio 1.01) with similar overall survival (80.3% vs 78.9% at 5 years; hazard ratio 0.95, relative). title: Off-pump versus on-pump coronary-artery bypass grafting
question: Does avoiding cardiopulmonary bypass in CABG improve early outcomes or graft patency versus conventional on-pump surgery (ROOBY, CORONARY)?
balance: Split: LIKELY — no 30-day advantage for off-pump · POSSIBLE — worse 1-year composite and graft patency in ROOBY. CORONARY (4752 patients) found the 30-day composite of death, stroke, myocardial infarction or dialysis-requiring renal failure at 9.8% off-pump versus 10.3% on-pump (hazard ratio 0.95, relative, non-significant), with less transfusion, reoperation for bleeding, acute kidney injury and respiratory complications off-pump, but more early repeat revascularisation (0.7% vs 0.2%). ROOBY (2203 patients) found no 30-day difference (7.0% vs 5.6%; P=0.19) but a worse 1-year composite off-pump (9.9% vs 7.4%; P=0.04), fewer completed grafts (17.8% vs 11.1% incomplete) and lower graft patency (82.6% vs 87.8%). Mortality was a component of both composites and neither trial claims a mortality benefit, so the shelf is not Tier C.

title: Minimally invasive versus open oesophagectomy
question: Does minimally invasive (TIME) or hybrid minimally invasive (MIRO) oesophagectomy reduce pulmonary and major complications versus open resection for oesophageal cancer, without compromising oncological outcomes?
balance: LIKELY: Two randomised trials using different minimally invasive techniques agree on fewer pulmonary/major complications. TIME (totally minimally invasive): pulmonary infection in the first 2 weeks in 9% versus 29% (relative risk 0.30). MIRO (hybrid — laparoscopic abdomen, open chest): major complications in 36% versus 64% (odds ratio 0.31, a relative measure), major pulmonary complications 18% versus 30%, with 3-year overall survival 67% versus 55% and disease-free survival 57% versus 48% — reported as not compromising oncological outcomes, not as a survival benefit. Both relative effect measures are below the 0.5 solid-evidence threshold and the absolute differences are large.
stamp: LIKELY

title: Laparoscopic versus open resection for colon cancer: COLOR, COST, and CLASICC
question: Is laparoscopic colectomy for colon cancer oncologically equivalent to open surgery — the COLOR long-term results and the COST/CLASICC programmes that settled the question?
balance: LIKELY (oncological equivalence): Three randomised programmes converge. COST: 3-year recurrence 16% laparoscopically assisted versus 18% open (hazard ratio 0.86, relative, non-significant), 3-year survival 86% versus 85%. COLOR: 3-year disease-free survival 74.2% versus 76.2% and overall survival 81.8% versus 84.2% — COLOR could not formally rule out its 7% non-inferiority boundary (upper confidence limit 7.2%), and the card says so; the difference was small. CLASICC's short-term report showed similar margins, Dukes C2 proportions and in-hospital mortality (4% vs 5%). Equivalence with faster recovery (COST: hospital stay 5 vs 6 days) is the claim — no survival-benefit claim, so not Tier C.

title: Robotic versus laparoscopic rectal cancer resection (ROLARR and REAL)
question: Does robotic assistance lower conversion to open surgery or improve outcomes in rectal-cancer resection versus conventional laparoscopy?
balance: Split: POSSIBLE — no conversion advantage (ROLARR) · POSSIBLE — lower locoregional recurrence in middle/low rectal cancer (REAL). ROLARR (471 patients, international): conversion to open laparotomy 8.1% robotic versus 12.2% laparoscopic (adjusted odds ratio 0.61, relative, non-significant, P=.16), with no significant difference in margins, complications or dysfunction. REAL (1171 analysed, China, middle/low tumours only): 3-year locoregional recurrence 1.6% versus 4.0% (hazard ratio 0.45, relative) and disease-free survival 87.2% versus 83.4% (hazard ratio 0.74), with no significant difference in overall survival (94.7% vs 93.0%). Each half rests on a single trial, so each caps at POSSIBLE; overall survival did not differ in REAL, so no survival claim is made and the shelf is not Tier C.

title: Enhanced recovery after surgery (ERAS) pathways in colorectal surgery
question: Do ERAS pathways — the bundled perioperative package of early feeding, opioid-sparing analgesia, and early mobilisation — shorten hospital stay and reduce complications after colorectal resection versus traditional care?
balance: POSSIBLE (via synthesis — the certainty ceiling is stated on the shelf face): The randomised base is many small trials, not two large ones. Varadhan 2010 pooled six RCTs (452 patients, 4-12 ERAS elements per trial): hospital stay was 2.55 days shorter (weighted mean difference -2.55; 95% CI -3.24 to -1.85) and complications fewer (relative risk 0.53; 0.44 to 0.64 — a relative measure), with no significant difference in readmission or mortality. LAFA, a 400-patient factorial trial, found laparoscopy — not fast-track care — was the only independent factor reducing stay and morbidity in its regression, with the shortest stay (median total 5 days) in the laparoscopy-plus-fast-track group. That tension is why the stamp is POSSIBLE, not LIKELY. Perioperative fluid strategy alone is drafted Shelf #657 and perioperative drugs are Shelves #352/#353 — different interventions, not carded here.
stamp: POSSIBLE (via synthesis — the certainty ceiling is stated on the shelf face)

title: Obesity pharmacotherapy in adolescents: semaglutide and liraglutide
question: In adolescents with obesity, how much weight do once-weekly semaglutide and daily liraglutide lose versus placebo, on top of lifestyle therapy?
balance: LIKELY: Two double-blind, placebo-controlled trials in adolescents aged 12 to <18 years point the same way: once-weekly semaglutide 2.4 mg changed BMI by -16.1% versus +0.6% on placebo at 68 weeks (STEP TEENS), and daily liraglutide 3.0 mg beat placebo on BMI standard-deviation score by an estimated -0.22 at 56 weeks (Ellipse), with 43.3% versus 18.7% achieving at least 5% BMI reduction. Gastrointestinal adverse events were more common on both drugs (62% vs 42% semaglutide; 64.8% vs 36.5% liraglutide), and weight tended to return after liraglutide was stopped. No cardiovascular-outcome claim is made on this shelf.

question: In preterm infants on CPAP with respiratory distress, does giving surfactant through a thin catheter without intubation reduce death or bronchopulmonary dysplasia versus sham or standard intubation-based administration?

title: Step-up therapy for childhood asthma: BADGER and TREXA
question: In children whose asthma is uncontrolled on low-dose inhaled steroids, which step-up works best — and can rescue steroid replace daily control in mild persistent asthma?
balance: Split: LIKELY that, for children uncontrolled on low-dose inhaled corticosteroid (ICS), adding a long-acting beta-agonist (LABA) is the step-up most likely to give the best response (BADGER: relative probability 1.6 versus leukotriene-antagonist step-up and 1.7 versus ICS step-up, relative) — though nearly every child had a differential response and many did best on another option. title: Preventive drugs for paediatric migraine: the CHAMP trial
question: Do amitriptyline or topiramate prevent migraine in children and adolescents better than placebo?
balance: LIKELY the null: In CHAMP — a large double-blind, placebo-controlled trial stopped early for futility — neither amitriptyline (52% achieving at least a 50% relative reduction in headache days) nor topiramate (55%) beat placebo (61%) over 24 weeks, and both drugs caused more adverse events than placebo. title: Vitamin D in pregnancy to delay offspring asthma and wheeze: VDAART and COPSAC
question: Does high-dose vitamin D supplementation during pregnancy reduce asthma or recurrent or persistent wheeze in the child by age 3?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence): Each trial was null alone on its primary — VDAART: asthma or recurrent wheeze by age 3 in 24.3% versus 30.4% (hazard ratio 0.8, relative, 95% CI 0.6 to 1.0; P=.051); COPSAC: persistent wheeze in 16% versus 20%, not statistically significant. Any pooled positivity rests on combining two individually null trials, and the hazard ratio of 0.8 sits inside the 0.5–2.0 band that is not solid evidence on its own — so the shelf prints MAYBE (weak evidence) for any delay or reduction in offspring wheeze. title: Influenza vaccination in pregnancy: protection for mother and infant
question: Does vaccinating pregnant women against influenza protect their infants in the first months of life?
balance: LIKELY: Two randomised trials in different settings found maternal influenza vaccination protects young infants who are too young to be vaccinated themselves — Bangladesh (Zaman): laboratory-confirmed influenza in infants 6 versus 16 cases, vaccine effectiveness 63% (relative), with febrile respiratory illness reduced by 29% (relative) in infants and 36% (relative) in mothers; South Africa (Madhi): vaccine efficacy 48.8% (relative) in infants not exposed to HIV and 50.4% (relative) in HIV-uninfected mothers. Effects are partial, not complete, protection.

title: Short-course antibiotics for childhood urinary tract infection (SCOUT)
question: In children with UTI who have improved by day 5, is stopping at 5 days as good as continuing to 10?
balance: POSSIBLE: In SCOUT, the single large randomised trial, stopping antibiotics at 5 days in children who had already improved produced more treatment failures than continuing to 10 days (4.2% vs 0.6%; absolute difference 3.6%) and non-inferiority was not established — yet the absolute failure rate on the short course was low, which is why the trial's authors call 5 days a reasonable option for improvers. title: Donor human milk versus preterm formula when mother's own milk is unavailable
question: In extremely preterm infants fed no or insufficient mother's own milk, does donor human milk reduce necrotising enterocolitis versus preterm formula — and at what growth cost?
balance: POSSIBLE: The trial base is small and old. The largest single randomised trial (Schanler) found no difference between donor milk and preterm formula in late-onset sepsis and/or necrotising enterocolitis (NEC), with slower weight gain on donor milk; the Cochrane synthesis of 12 trials (1,879 infants) found formula feeding raised NEC risk versus donor milk (typical relative risk 1.87, relative; risk difference 0.03) while formula-fed infants grew faster in hospital, with no effect on all-cause mortality or neurodevelopment — moderate-certainty evidence, hence POSSIBLE. Mother's own milk outperformed both substitutes in Schanler.

title: Community health workers for hypertension control: COBRA-BPS and the Argentina trial
question: Do multicomponent interventions led by community health workers lower blood pressure in low- and middle-income settings?
balance: LIKELY: Two large cluster-randomised trials in low- and middle-income settings found concordant blood-pressure gains from community-health-worker-led multicomponent programmes — COBRA-BPS (rural Bangladesh, Pakistan, Sri Lanka): systolic BP fell 5.2 mm Hg more than usual care at 24 months, with control (<140/90) in 53.2% versus 43.7%; Argentina (He): systolic BP fell 6.6 mm Hg more at 18 months, with control rising to 72.9% versus 52.2%. The interventions are unblindable by nature and were bundles — home visits plus physician training and system supports — so the shelf credits the programme, not the home visit alone. No mortality claim is made: COBRA-BPS's mortality figures were a secondary, unpowered outcome and are reported on its card as such.

title: Remote monitoring and telemedical management in heart failure: TIM-HF2 versus BEAT-HF
question: Does structured remote patient management reduce hospitalisation and death in heart failure — the positive German TIM-HF2 system against the null Californian BEAT-HF programme?
balance: PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C — TIM-HF2's outcomes include all-cause mortality): POSSIBLE. The two large trials discord: TIM-HF2's intensive, physician-centre remote patient management reduced days lost to unplanned cardiovascular admission or all-cause death (4.88% vs 6.64% of days; ratio 0.80, relative; P=.046) and all-cause mortality (hazard ratio 0.70, relative; P=.028), with cardiovascular mortality not significant (hazard ratio 0.671, relative; P=.056) — mortality is printed beside the hospitalisation figures throughout this shelf. BEAT-HF's lighter post-discharge coaching-plus-telemonitoring changed nothing: 180-day readmission 50.8% versus 49.2% (adjusted hazard ratio 1.03, relative) and no mortality difference. Intensity and population, not the label 'telemonitoring', separate the two. FENCE: telemedicine as a substitute for in-person visits is drafted Shelf #709 — a visit-substitution question, not a monitoring-system question; no #709 material is carded here.

title: Early supported discharge after stroke
question: Do early supported discharge services reduce death or dependency and shorten hospital stay after acute stroke?
balance: LIKELY: The Cochrane synthesis of 17 randomised trials (2,422 participants) found early supported discharge (ESD) reduced death or long-term dependency (odds ratio 0.80, relative, 95% CI 0.67 to 0.95; about five fewer adverse outcomes per 100 patients) and shortened hospital stay by about 5.5 days, with death alone unchanged (odds ratio 1.04, relative) — the dependency benefit is printed beside the null mortality figure, and no standalone mortality-benefit claim is made. Benefits concentrated in trials with a co-ordinated multidisciplinary ESD team and in patients with mild-to-moderate disability; death or institutional care was also reduced (odds ratio 0.75, relative).

title: Audit and feedback to change professional practice
question: Does giving clinicians audit-and-feedback reports on their own performance improve the care they deliver — and what makes feedback work harder?
balance: Split: POSSIBLE that audit and feedback produces small improvements in professional practice — across 140 randomised trials the weighted median adjusted risk difference was a 4.3% absolute increase in compliance with desired practice (IQR 0.5% to 16%) — and MAYBE (weak evidence) that it improves patient outcomes, where the weighted median risk difference was -0.4% (IQR -1.3% to 1.6%) for dichotomous outcomes. Feedback appears more effective when baseline performance is low, it comes from a supervisor or colleague, is given more than once, is delivered in both verbal and written formats, and includes explicit targets and an action plan.

title: Group medical visits (shared medical appointments) for chronic conditions
question: Do group medical visits improve glycaemic and blood-pressure control in diabetes and other chronic conditions versus usual one-to-one care?
balance: POSSIBLE: The randomised evidence is thinner and more mixed than the model's popularity suggests. Adding intensive weight management to group medical visits was non-inferior to group visits alone for HbA1c at 48 weeks (8.2% vs 8.3%; difference -0.1%) and superior for weight (-3.7 kg), medication intensity and hypoglycaemic events (incidence rate ratio 0.49, relative) — a comparison of two group-visit variants, not of group visits versus usual care. title: Geographic atrophy: complement inhibition with pegcetacoplan and avacincaptad pegol
question: Do intravitreal complement inhibitors slow the growth of geographic atrophy lesions in age-related macular degeneration — and does slowing lesion growth preserve vision?
balance: Split: LIKELY — slowing of lesion growth · MAYBE (weak evidence) — preserving vision: Three phase 3 sham-controlled trials across two complement inhibitors (OAKS, DERBY, GATHER2) all slowed geographic-atrophy lesion growth, by 11–22% relative depending on trial, drug and time point, with DERBY's 12-month result not reaching significance before its 24-month result did. title: Faricimab for wet AMD and diabetic macular oedema: durability against aflibercept
question: Does faricimab dosed up to every 16 weeks match aflibercept every 8 weeks on vision — in neovascular AMD and in diabetic macular oedema?
balance: LIKELY: Four phase 3 double-masked non-inferiority trials (TENAYA, LUCERNE, YOSEMITE, RHINE; 3,220 patients randomised in total) each found faricimab — dosed every 8 weeks or by a personalised interval extending to every 16 weeks — non-inferior to aflibercept every 8 weeks on visual-acuity change, with treatment differences of −0.2 to +1.5 letters against a 4-letter margin and comparable ocular adverse-event rates. title: Adalimumab for non-infectious uveitis: active disease and flare prevention (VISUAL I and II)
question: Does adalimumab delay treatment failure in active non-infectious uveitis, and prevent flare in inactive steroid-controlled disease during steroid taper?

title: Brolucizumab for wet AMD: drying power against a retinal vasculitis signal (HAWK and HARRIER)
question: Does brolucizumab match aflibercept on vision with better retinal drying — and how large is the intraocular-inflammation and retinal-vasculitis harm signal that emerged after approval?

title: Preventing endophthalmitis after cataract surgery: intracameral cefuroxime (ESCRS)
question: Does intracameral cefuroxime at the end of cataract surgery prevent acute postoperative endophthalmitis?
balance: POSSIBLE: One very large randomised factorial trial (ESCRS, 16,603 patients, 29 endophthalmitis cases) found that omitting intracameral cefuroxime carried a 4.92-fold relative increase in total postoperative endophthalmitis (95% CI 1.87 to 12.9) — equivalently, cefuroxime's relative risk is about 0.20, outside the 0.5–2.0 caution band — and the Cochrane synthesis of the prophylaxis trials reports the same comparison at risk ratio 0.21 (0.06 to 0.74). title: Persistent throat symptoms: lansoprazole and the reflux hypothesis (TOPPITS)
question: In adults with persistent unexplained throat symptoms referred to ENT, does lansoprazole beat placebo?
balance: Split: LIKELY the null — unselected persistent throat symptoms · POSSIBLE — benefit in patients selected for laryngeal reflux signs. title: Cochlear implantation for single-sided deafness: the CINGLE randomised trial

title: Tonsillotomy vs tonsillectomy: partial against total removal
question: In children and adults undergoing tonsil surgery for obstruction or recurrent infection, does tonsillotomy (partial, intracapsular) match tonsillectomy on symptom control with less postoperative pain and bleeding — and at what regrowth or reoperation cost?
balance: Split: POSSIBLE — less early postoperative morbidity · MAYBE (weak evidence) — equal long-term symptom control. The carded evidence base is paediatric (the Cochrane review covers children aged 2–16 with obstructive sleep-disordered breathing): tonsillotomy probably speeds return to normal activity by about 4 days and probably lowers first-week complications requiring medical intervention (2.6% vs 4.9% — the review prints the pair with risk ratio 1.75 for tonsillectomy vs tonsillotomy), while pain scores barely differ and every longer-term outcome — symptom control, quality of life, recurrence, reoperation — is rated very low certainty. title: Chronic suppurative otitis media: topical antibiotics
question: Do topical quinolone antibiotics resolve discharge in chronic suppurative otitis media better than antiseptics, systemic antibiotics, or aural toilet alone?
balance: Split: POSSIBLE — topical quinolone beats antiseptic or placebo for discharge resolution · MAYBE (weak evidence) — quinolones vs other antibiotic classes. The 2025 Cochrane synthesis (18 studies, 1,783 participants) rates nearly everything low or very low certainty, but the direct randomised comparisons line up: topical ciprofloxacin resolved discharge in 59% vs 32% on boric-acid antiseptic in 427 Kenyan schoolchildren (relative risk 1.86), beat a framycetin–steroid combination 76.4% vs 51.8% in Aboriginal children, and the review's placebo comparison (84% vs 12%, very low certainty) and add-on-to-systemic comparison (88% vs 60%) point the same way. title: Prostatic artery embolization vs TURP for benign prostatic hyperplasia
question: Does prostatic artery embolization match transurethral resection of the prostate on symptom relief in benign prostatic hyperplasia — and what is the trade in functional outcomes, adverse events and reintervention (the Abt randomised non-inferiority trial, with the UK-ROPE comparison alongside)?
balance: POSSIBLE: In the one randomised trial (Abt 2018, 103 patients), embolization's symptom improvement at 12 weeks was close to resection's (IPSS reduction 9.23 vs 10.77 points) but non-inferiority was formally NOT shown (difference 1.54 points, 95% CI −1.45 to 4.52; p=0.17 for non-inferiority), and TURP was clearly better on flow, residual urine, prostate-volume reduction and desobstruction, while embolization caused fewer adverse events (36 vs 70). One randomised trial plus a concordant observational comparison caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.

title: Refractory overactive bladder: bladder botulinum toxin vs sacral neuromodulation (ROSETTA)
question: In women with refractory urgency incontinence, does onabotulinumtoxinA bladder injection beat sacral neuromodulation on leakage episodes — and what does each cost in urinary infection, retention and revision (ROSETTA), read against the botulinum toxin pivotal placebo trial?

title: Ureteric stones: shockwave lithotripsy vs ureteroscopy (TISU)
question: For adults with a ureteric stone needing intervention, is shockwave lithotripsy non-inferior to ureteroscopic treatment on stone clearance without further intervention — the TISU trial, against the earlier distal-stone randomised comparison?
balance: POSSIBLE: TISU (613 participants) found shockwave lithotripsy (SWL) non-inferior to ureteroscopy (URS) only against a generous prespecified 20% margin: 22.1% of the SWL group vs 10.3% of the URS group needed further treatment to clear the stone (absolute difference 11.7%, 95% CI 5.6% to 17.8%, in favour of URS) — so SWL met the letter of non-inferiority while URS was better on the trial's own primary outcome and, in the trialists' words, on overall clinical outcomes. title: Peyronie's disease: collagenase injections (IMPRESS I and II)

title: Male stress incontinence after prostate surgery: sling vs artificial urinary sphincter (MASTER)
question: In men with urodynamic stress incontinence after prostate surgery, is a synthetic male sling non-inferior to an artificial urinary sphincter on patient-reported incontinence — the MASTER non-inferiority trial, its health-technology-assessment report, and its 24-month outcomes?
balance: POSSIBLE: MASTER is ONE large randomised trial (380 men) with three reports — the 12-month primary report, the HTA monograph, and the 24-month outcomes found in the currency sweep and carded here — and a single trial caps at POSSIBLE however many reports it has. On its strict composite definition the sling was non-inferior to the artificial sphincter at both 12 months (incontinence rates 87.0% vs 84.2% still wet; non-inferiority p=0.003 against a 15% margin) and 24 months (difference −0.006, 95% CI −0.092 to 0.080), symptoms and quality of life improved substantially in both groups and satisfaction was high — yet nearly every secondary outcome favoured the sphincter, symptom scores were better with it (ICIQ-UI SF 7.5 vs 8.7 at 12 months), and by 24 months more sling patients had needed further surgery (11% vs 2%). Most men in both groups were still not completely dry: that is the honest headline. Female stress-incontinence shelves (#249, #486) are a different population and are not re-carded here.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Bladder pain syndrome / interstitial cystitis: amitriptyline and pentosan
question: Do the two long-standing oral drugs for bladder pain syndrome beat placebo — amitriptyline in treatment-naïve patients, and pentosan polysulfate in the Nickel randomised trial — and how thin is the benefit?
balance: Split — POSSIBLE for amitriptyline at adequate dose; LIKELY that pentosan does not work: Foster 2010 (271 treatment-naïve patients) missed its primary endpoint overall (response 55% vs 45% on placebo, p=0.12) and found benefit only in the subgroup that actually reached 50 mg or more (66% vs 47%, p=0.01) — a comparison the authors note was not specified in advance, which caps that half at POSSIBLE. Nickel 2015 (368 patients, 24 weeks, two pentosan doses against placebo, stopped early for futility at interim) found responder rates of 39.8% and 42.6% on pentosan vs 40.7% on placebo — a clean null in the largest test of the drug, carrying LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) under the library's large-null reasoning, tempered by its early termination. Both trials also show how large the placebo/context response is in this syndrome: 45% and 40.7% of placebo patients responded.

title: Non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer: maintenance BCG
question: Does maintenance bacillus Calmette-Guérin after induction reduce recurrence and progression in recurrent Ta/T1 and carcinoma-in-situ bladder cancer versus induction alone — the Southwest Oncology Group randomised trial, read against the EORTC dose-and-duration trial?
balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: this shelf carries progression and survival outcomes in a cancer population, so it returns for personal review, per the flag on the topic draft, which the builder upholds): Maintenance BCG doubled median recurrence-free survival in the SWOG trial (76.8 vs 35.7 months, p<0.0001) and lengthened worsening-free survival (p=0.04), with 5-year overall survival of 83% vs 78% as reported, no significance claimed for survival in the abstract. The EORTC trial (1,355 patients) then answered how much maintenance: full dose for 3 years beat one-third dose for 1 year on disease-free interval (HR 0.75, 95% CI 0.59 to 0.94), the extra years helped only high-risk patients and only at full dose, and there were NO differences in progression or survival in EORTC — so the recurrence benefit is LIKELY, while any progression or survival benefit remains unproven and is not claimed on this shelf. Newer BCG-combination trials from the currency sweep are fenced in the synthesis, not carded.

title: Single-dose gemcitabine after bladder tumour resection (SWOG S0337)
question: Does one intravesical dose of gemcitabine immediately after resection of suspected low-grade non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer reduce recurrence versus saline?
balance: POSSIBLE: One large, well-run double-blind trial (SWOG S0337, 406 patients) found a single post-resection gemcitabine instillation cut 4-year recurrence from a 47% Kaplan–Meier estimate on saline to 35% (hazard ratio 0.66, 95% CI 0.48 to 0.90 — a relative measure, printed with its absolute rates beside it), with a larger relative effect in the confirmed low-grade subgroup (HR 0.53; 34% vs 54%) and no grade 4 or 5 adverse events. A single pivotal trial caps at POSSIBLE under the library's rules, however clean the result. Progression (5 vs 10 patients) and deaths (17 vs 25) were not significantly different and no progression or survival claim is made. Maintenance BCG for higher-risk disease is Shelf #918 and is not re-carded here.

title: Narcolepsy wake promotion beyond modafinil: solriamfetol and pitolisant
question: Do the newer wake agents reduce excessive sleepiness in narcolepsy versus placebo — solriamfetol in its phase 3 trial, pitolisant (an H3 inverse agonist) against placebo and modafinil — and does pitolisant also cut cataplexy?
balance: LIKELY: Three double-blind randomised trials cover the two halves of the question. Solriamfetol (236 patients) beat placebo on both wakefulness (Maintenance of Wakefulness Test +9.8 and +12.3 minutes at 150 and 300 mg vs +2.1) and sleepiness (Epworth −5.4 and −6.4 vs −1.6). Pitolisant beat placebo on sleepiness in HARMONY (ESS difference −3.0, 95% CI −5.6 to −0.4) but did NOT show non-inferiority to modafinil in that 95-patient trial, and in the dedicated HARMONY-CTP trial it cut weekly cataplexy by 75% vs 38% on placebo (rate ratio 0.512, 0.43 to 0.60 — a relative measure, with the absolute weekly rates printed on its card). Three concordant blinded trials carry LIKELY; the honest limits are that pitolisant's sleepiness effect is smaller than solriamfetol's trial showed and its modafinil comparison is unresolved. Sodium oxybate for narcolepsy is Shelf #921 and is not re-carded here.
stamp: LIKELY

title: Sodium oxybate for narcolepsy: cataplexy and sleepiness
question: Does sodium oxybate reduce cataplexy attacks and excessive daytime sleepiness in narcolepsy versus placebo — the two blinded reports of the oxybate programme, with its controlled-substance burden on the shelf face?
balance: POSSIBLE: The two carded reports are two papers from ONE randomised programme — the same 228 patients with narcolepsy with cataplexy, analysed for cataplexy in one report and for sleepiness in the other — so this shelf has a single trial programme and caps at POSSIBLE however consistent the reports are. Within it, the results are strong and dose-related: median weekly cataplexy falls of 57.0%, 65.0% and 84.7% at 4.5, 6 and 9 g nightly, and at 9 g a median increase of over 10 minutes in wakefulness latency (p<.001) with significant sleepiness-score improvements at 6 and 9 g — on top of the stimulants most patients continued. Sodium oxybate is the sodium salt of gamma-hydroxybutyrate, a controlled substance with a tightly restricted distribution; that burden, and the twice-nightly dosing the drug's short action imposes, belong on the shelf face beside the efficacy. The lower-sodium formulation in a different disorder is Shelf #922 and is not re-carded here.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Idiopathic hypersomnia: lower-sodium oxybate
question: In idiopathic hypersomnia, does lower-sodium oxybate hold its benefit under randomised withdrawal — and does the parent compound, sodium oxybate, beat placebo in the same disorder?
balance: LIKELY: Two double-blind randomised trials of oxybate in idiopathic hypersomnia, of two formulations, now agree. The lower-sodium oxybate phase 3 trial (154 enrolled; 115 randomised into withdrawal) showed that switching to placebo for 2 weeks worsened Epworth scores while continuing the drug held them (least-squares mean difference −6.5, 95% CI −8.0 to −5.0), after open-label treatment had brought scores from 15.7 to 6.1. The 2025 sodium oxybate trial pinned from the currency sweep (45 patients, parallel placebo control) found an almost identical adjusted Epworth advantage (−6.86, −9.73 to −4.00) plus better severity scores and wakefulness latency. Two concordant blinded trials carry LIKELY for oxybate's effect on sleepiness in this disorder — with the caveats that one is a withdrawal design in open-label responders, the other is small and single-centre, and adverse events are frequent (nausea 22% in the large trial; any treatment-emergent event in 81.8% on sodium oxybate in the small one).
stamp: LIKELY
