title: Mandibular advancement devices vs CPAP for obstructive sleep apnea
question: In obstructive sleep apnea, does a mandibular advancement device match CPAP on sleepiness, blood pressure and health outcomes despite lowering the apnea–hypopnoea index less — the Phillips randomised crossover trial and the CRESCENT blood-pressure trial?
balance: LIKELY — for comparable health outcomes, not for equal apnea control, and with no cardiovascular-event claim made on this shelf: Phillips 2013 (126 patients, crossover) found CPAP lowered the apnea–hypopnoea index more (4.5 vs 11.1 events/hour) but patients wore the device longer (6.50 vs 5.20 hours/night), and sleepiness, driving performance and disease-specific quality of life improved similarly on both. CRESCENT (220 randomised patients with hypertension and increased cardiovascular risk) found the device non-inferior to CPAP on 24-hour mean arterial pressure at 6 months (between-group difference −1.6 mm Hg, non-inferiority p<0.001 against a 1.5 mm Hg margin), with the device group's pressure actually falling 2.5 mm Hg while CPAP's did not change. Two randomised trials carry LIKELY for outcome comparability in patients who use the device. Whether treating sleep apnea prevents cardiovascular EVENTS is Shelf #302's question and is not claimed here.

title: Positional therapy for positional obstructive sleep apnea
question: In patients whose apnea is predominantly supine, does a vibrotactile sleep-position trainer reduce supine sleep and the apnea–hypopnoea index — against no treatment, head-to-head against an oral appliance, and against sham?
balance: LIKELY: Three randomised trials now triangulate positional therapy. Laub 2017 (101 patients, open, against no treatment) halved supine sleep (47% to 17% of the night) and cut the total index from 18 to 10 events/hour while controls barely moved. Benoist 2017 (99 patients) found the trainer and an oral appliance equally effective head-to-head (median index 13.0 to 7.0 vs 11.7 to 9.1). And the sham-controlled, double-blind Thorax trial found in the currency sweep (120 patients, neck-worn device) beat sham by −4.41 events/hour (95% CI −7.77 to −1.06) over 3 months, improving sleep quality though not sleepiness. The honest price is persistence: discontinuation reached 28.8% by 2 months and 49.4% by 6 months in Laub's cohort. Three concordant randomised trials, one of them sham-blinded, carry LIKELY for patients whose apnea is genuinely positional.
stamp: LIKELY

title: Central sleep apnea: transvenous phrenic nerve stimulation
question: Does transvenous phrenic nerve stimulation reduce central apnea events and improve sleep quality and quality of life in moderate-to-severe central sleep apnea — the pivotal randomised trial and its five-year follow-up? (No mortality claim is made on this shelf.)
balance: POSSIBLE: One pivotal randomised trial (151 implanted patients, stimulation on vs off for 6 months) found 51% of the treatment group vs 11% of controls achieved at least a 50% reduction in the apnea–hypopnoea index (difference 41%, 95% CI 25 to 54; p<0.0001), with concordant improvements in oxygenation, sleep metrics and quality of life, and 91% of patients free of serious procedure-, system- or therapy-related adverse events at 12 months. The five-year report is a follow-up of the same trial's remnant (52 completers of the original 151), showing sustained index improvements (median apnea–hypopnoea index 46 to 17 events/hour; central-apnea index 23 to 1) — supportive durability, not a second trial, so the shelf caps at POSSIBLE. Seven deaths occurred during the trial's first year, all judged unrelated to implant, system or therapy; no mortality benefit or harm claim is made or implied on this shelf.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Pharmacotherapy for obstructive sleep apnea: atomoxetine plus oxybutynin
question: Can a noradrenergic–antimuscarinic combination taken at night reduce obstructive sleep apnea severity pharmacologically — atomoxetine plus oxybutynin in the Taranto-Montemurro crossover trial, the MARIPOSA trial of the fixed combination, and the phase 3 SynAIRgy trial?
balance: LIKELY — for reducing the apnea–hypopnoea index, with the effect shrinking as trials get longer and larger: the 1-night crossover (20 patients) cut the index by 63% (from a median 28.5 to 7.5 events/hour); the 4-week MARIPOSA trial (211 randomised) cut it by about 47% and 43% at the two fixed-combination doses against a smaller placebo fall; and the 26-week phase 3 SynAIRgy trial found in the currency sweep (646 patients unable to use PAP) showed a mean treatment difference of −4.0 events/hour (95% CI −6.4 to −1.6), a model-estimated 44.1% vs 17.6% fall from baseline (relative figures, with the absolute difference beside them). Three randomised blinded trials in sequence carry LIKELY for the index effect. The price also belongs on the face: in SynAIRgy 21.2% on the drug vs 3.1% on placebo stopped because of adverse events (dry mouth, nausea, insomnia, urinary hesitation the commonest), and no trial shows the combination improves sleepiness, fatigue (null in SynAIRgy) or any clinical outcome beyond the index and oxygenation.

title: Non-24-hour sleep-wake disorder in totally blind people: tasimelteon (SET and RESET)
question: Does tasimelteon entrain the circadian clock and improve night sleep in totally blind people with non-24-hour sleep-wake disorder — the SET entrainment trial and the RESET maintenance-withdrawal trial?
balance: LIKELY: The twin phase 3 programme (two trials in one paper) shows a coherent entrainment story. In SET (84 randomised), tasimelteon entrained 20% of patients by month 1 vs 3% on placebo (difference 17%, 95% CI 3.2 to 31.6) and produced a clinical response in 24% vs none on placebo. In RESET (20 entrained patients randomised to continue or withdraw), 90% who continued stayed entrained vs 20% withdrawn to placebo (difference 70%, 26.4 to 100) — the drug works and stopping it loses the effect, which is strong causal evidence in a rare disorder. Two concordant blinded trials carry LIKELY, with the absolute scale on the face: most treated patients in SET did not entrain by the trial's strict definition (20% did), so this is a real effect for a minority-to-substantial fraction, not a universal fix. Melatonin itself for jet lag and insomnia in sighted people is Shelves #492 and #116 and is not re-carded here.
stamp: LIKELY

title: Sleep problems in children with autism and neurodevelopmental disorders: melatonin
question: Does melatonin improve sleep onset and total sleep in children with autism spectrum disorder or neurodevelopmental disorders — prolonged-release melatonin in the Gringras autism trial, and immediate-release melatonin in the MENDS trial?
balance: LIKELY — for faster sleep onset and a modest gain in total sleep: Two double-blind placebo-controlled trials, of two formulations, agree on the shape of the effect. Prolonged-release melatonin in the Gringras autism trial (125 children whose sleep had failed behavioural intervention) lengthened night sleep (a 57.5-minute within-group rise vs 9.14 minutes on placebo; p=.034 on the adjusted primary analysis) and shortened sleep latency (falls of 39.6 vs 12.5 minutes; adjusted difference −25.30 minutes), with 68.9% vs 39.3% achieving a clinically meaningful response. Immediate-release melatonin in MENDS (146 children) added 22.4 minutes of diary-measured total sleep (95% CI 0.5 to 44.3) and cut sleep onset latency by 37.5 minutes — but children also woke 29.9 minutes earlier, and the actigraphy total-sleep estimate was not significant (13.3 minutes, −15.5 to 42.2). Two concordant randomised trials carry LIKELY for onset and a small total-sleep gain; neither shows significant behaviour or family-functioning improvement, and MENDS's authors call the added sleep 'little' — that sizing is part of the stamp. Adult melatonin shelves (#116, #492) are not re-carded here.

title: Restless legs syndrome: alpha-2-delta ligands against the dopamine standard
question: Do pregabalin and gabapentin enacarbil relieve restless legs symptoms without the augmentation that collects on dopamine agonists — pregabalin head-to-head against pramipexole over a year, and gabapentin enacarbil against placebo?
balance: LIKELY: Two double-blind randomised trials establish the non-dopaminergic class. Pregabalin beat placebo over 12 weeks in the year-long Allen trial (719 participants; symptom-score improvement greater by 4.5 points, responders 71.4% vs 46.8%) and — the shelf's key comparison — produced significantly less augmentation over 40–52 weeks than pramipexole 0.5 mg (2.1% vs 7.7%; p=0.001), though not significantly less than pramipexole 0.25 mg (2.1% vs 5.3%; p=0.08). Gabapentin enacarbil beat placebo in its own trial (222 patients; symptom change −13.2 vs −8.8, adjusted difference −4.0 [95% CI −6.2 to −1.9]; responders 76.1% vs 38.9%, adjusted odds ratio 5.1 — a relative measure, printed with the absolute responder rates beside it). The costs are sedation-class effects: somnolence 27% vs 7% and dizziness 20% vs 5% on gabapentin enacarbil, and six cases of suicidal ideation in the pregabalin arm of Allen's trial (vs three and two in the pramipexole arms) belong on the shelf face. Iron therapy and dopamine-agonist augmentation as a harm are home on Shelf #498 and are not re-carded here.
stamp: LIKELY

title: Structured medication review for older adults with polypharmacy (OPERAM and SPPiRE)
question: In multimorbid older adults taking many medicines, does a structured, team-based medication review reduce drug-related hospital admissions versus usual care — and what did the primary-care SPPiRE programme find on potentially inappropriate prescribing?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference on admissions, with only small prescribing effects): The large hospital-based OPERAM cluster trial (2,008 inpatients aged 70 or older) found no effect of structured pharmacotherapy optimisation on first drug-related hospital admission (21.9% vs 22.4%; hazard ratio 0.95, 95% CI 0.77 to 1.17), and no effect on falls or death. The primary-care SPPiRE cluster trial (404 patients on 15 or more medicines) trimmed the number of medicines slightly (incidence rate ratio 0.95) but showed no significant effect on having at least one potentially inappropriate prescription. Structured review tidies prescribing a little; on this evidence it does not keep people out of hospital.

title: Droxidopa for neurogenic orthostatic hypotension
question: Does droxidopa improve orthostatic symptoms and standing blood pressure in neurogenic orthostatic hypotension (Parkinson disease, autonomic failure) versus placebo — in the pivotal phase 3 trial and in the randomised withdrawal study of responders?
balance: POSSIBLE: In the pivotal phase 3 trial, patients who had already responded to open-label droxidopa improved more on droxidopa than placebo over seven days on the Orthostatic Hypotension Questionnaire composite (by 0.90 units, P=0.003), with standing systolic pressure up 11.2 vs 3.9 mm Hg. But the randomised withdrawal study in responders failed its primary endpoint — dizziness/lightheadedness worsened by 1.9 units on placebo vs 1.3 on continued droxidopa (P=0.509) — with only secondary and post-hoc composite scores favouring the drug. Short-term symptomatic benefit in selected responders is plausible; durability is unproven, which caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.

title: High-intensity resistance and impact training for bone in older adults (LIFTMOR and LIFTMOR-M)
question: Is supervised high-intensity resistance and impact training safe — and does it improve bone mineral density and function — in postmenopausal women with low bone mass (LIFTMOR) and in middle-aged and older men (LIFTMOR-M), against the long-standing fear that heavy loading fractures osteoporotic spines?
balance: POSSIBLE: Two randomised programmes — LIFTMOR in 101 postmenopausal women and LIFTMOR-M in 93 men — found that supervised twice-weekly high-intensity resistance and impact training improved lumbar spine bone mineral density by about 3–4 percentage points more than control over eight months, improved function, and produced only minor adverse events (one back spasm in the women's trial; five minor events in the men's). The stamp is POSSIBLE, not LIKELY, because both trials are small, bone density is a surrogate — neither trial measured fractures — and the safety record comes from closely supervised, screened volunteers.

title: Home-based dementia care: the COPE programme and the Tailored Activity Program
question: Do structured home-based programmes for people with dementia and their caregivers — occupational-therapy-led COPE, and the Tailored Activity Program (TAP) — improve patient function and behaviour and caregiver well-being versus control?
balance: POSSIBLE: COPE (237 randomised dementia–caregiver dyads) produced small improvements at four months in patient functional dependence and engagement and in caregiver well-being and confidence, which were no longer present for patients at nine months. TAP (250 dyads) missed its primary outcome — agitation/aggression did not improve (P=0.43) — but reduced the help patients needed with daily activities, improved caregiver well-being and confidence, and was followed by fewer health-related events at six months (15 vs 28 dyads). Real but small, partly secondary-outcome benefits from two single trials: POSSIBLE.

title: Stopping antipsychotics in dementia: the DART-AD withdrawal trial
question: In people with Alzheimer's disease already taking antipsychotics, does continuing them beat switching to placebo — acutely, and on survival and cognition over long-term follow-up (DART-AD)?
balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: the long-term report carries a survival difference). Stopping antipsychotics had no overall detrimental effect on cognition or neuropsychiatric symptoms at 6–12 months in DART-AD (165 randomised; differences −0.4 points on the Severe Impairment Battery and −2.4 on the Neuropsychiatric Inventory, both non-significant). On long-term follow-up, survival was lower in patients who continued antipsychotics (24-month survival 46% vs 71%; hazard ratio for death 0.58 favouring the switch-to-placebo group) — a mortality claim from a single small trial programme, which is why this stamp is proposed, not settled, and sits in the Tier C slow lane.

title: Protein supplementation in frail older adults: the Tieland programme
question: Does protein supplementation improve physical performance and muscle mass in frail older people — alone, and added to resistance-type exercise training?
balance: POSSIBLE: One small Dutch trial programme, two reports. Protein supplementation alone (15 g twice daily, 24 weeks; 65 frail older people) improved short physical performance battery scores (8.9 to 10.0 points vs 7.8 to 7.9 on placebo; interaction P=.02) but did not increase muscle mass or fibre size. Added to twice-weekly resistance training (62 frail older people), protein did allow lean mass to rise (47.2 to 48.5 kg vs no change on placebo; interaction P=.006), while strength and performance improved with training in both groups. Single-programme, small-n evidence for a performance effect and a training-dependent mass effect: POSSIBLE.

title: Prehabilitation for frail patients before colorectal surgery
question: In frail patients awaiting colorectal cancer resection, does multimodal prehabilitation (exercise, nutrition, anxiety reduction) cut postoperative complications versus starting rehabilitation after surgery — and does the larger PREHAB trial in a broader surgical population agree?
balance: Split: POSSIBLE — prehabilitation reduces severe complications in the broader colorectal-surgery population (PREHAB) · MAYBE (weak evidence) — benefit in frail patients specifically, where the one frail-only trial was null. In PREHAB (251 adults with colorectal cancer, not selected for frailty), severe complications (Comprehensive Complication Index above 20) occurred in 17.1% with prehabilitation vs 29.7% with standard care (odds ratio 0.47). In the frail-only trial (110 frail patients), starting the same kind of programme before rather than after surgery changed nothing (Complication Index difference −3.2, P=.45). The frail-specific claim the shelf was drafted for is the weaker half.

title: Vaccinating care-home staff against influenza to protect residents
question: Does vaccinating health-care workers in long-term care against influenza reduce deaths and influenza-like illness among the residents they care for — the Potter trial and the Hayward cluster trial?
balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C ruled at build: the claimed beneficiary outcome is resident mortality). Two cluster trials from the 1990s–2000s found lower resident mortality where staff were vaccinated: Potter 1997 (total patient mortality 10% vs 17%; odds ratio 0.56) and Hayward 2006 (five fewer deaths per 100 residents during the 2003–4 influenza-activity period — but no significant difference in the low-influenza 2004–5 season or outside influenza-activity periods). A mortality benefit that appears only in influenza-active periods, from two older cluster trials with staff uptake under two-thirds, is a Tier C claim: proposed, not settled.

title: Preventive home visits for community-dwelling older people
question: Do regular preventive home visits (geriatric assessment and follow-up in the home) delay functional decline, nursing-home admission, or death in community-dwelling older people — the Elkan and Stuck syntheses of the randomised trials?
balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C ruled at build: the shelf carries a mortality claim resting on two syntheses and subgroup meta-regression). The Elkan synthesis (15 studies) pooled a mortality odds ratio of 0.76 (0.64 to 0.89) in general elderly populations and 0.72 in frail at-risk groups, with fewer admissions to long-term institutional care (odds ratio 0.65) — but no effect on hospital admissions, health status or daily-living activities. The Stuck synthesis (18 trials, 13,447 people) found benefits only under conditions: many visits, multidimensional assessment with follow-up, and younger-old, lower-risk populations; mortality benefit appeared at ages 72.7–77.5 (relative risk 0.76) but not at 80.2–81.6 (1.09). Conditional, synthesis-level evidence: proposed POSSIBLE, Tier C.

title: Exercise rehabilitation after hip fracture: extended and home-based programmes
question: After hip-fracture rehabilitation ends, does more exercise — extended outpatient rehabilitation (Binder), or a home-based programme after discharge from rehab (Latham) — improve physical function versus usual care?
balance: POSSIBLE: Two randomised trials of different 'more exercise after hip fracture' programmes each found modest functional gains. Extended supervised outpatient rehabilitation with progressive resistance training (Binder 2004, 90 patients) beat low-intensity home exercise on physical performance (+6.5 vs +2.5 points) and function scores. A minimally supervised home-based programme (Latham 2014, 232 patients) beat an attention control on the Short Physical Performance Battery by 0.8 points (0.4 to 1.2) at six months, with differences persisting at nine months — its authors state the clinical importance remains to be determined. Two positive but modest, non-replicating programmes: POSSIBLE.

title: Breast screening with tomosynthesis (TOSYMA)
question: Does digital breast tomosynthesis plus synthesised mammography detect more invasive cancers than digital mammography alone in population screening — and at what recall and interval-cancer cost (TOSYMA; the TMIST trial in North America)?
balance: POSSIBLE: One very large randomised screening trial programme. TOSYMA (99,689 women) found tomosynthesis plus synthesised mammography detected more invasive cancers than digital mammography alone (7.1 vs 4.8 per 1,000 screened; odds ratio 1.48, a relative figure). Its 24-month follow-up found fewer invasive interval cancers with tomosynthesis (14.2 vs 18.6 per 10,000 screen-negative women), but that second primary endpoint did not reach significance (adjusted odds ratio 0.76, 95% CI 0.55 to 1.06; P=0.11). Detection is a surrogate for benefit, there is no mortality endpoint, and a single trial programme caps the stamp at POSSIBLE. The North American TMIST trial has published no main-results report, so it cannot be carded.

title: Ovarian suppression in premenopausal breast cancer: SOFT and TEXT
question: In premenopausal women with hormone-receptor-positive early breast cancer, does adding ovarian suppression to tamoxifen — or using exemestane with ovarian suppression — improve disease-free survival, and in whom (SOFT; TEXT)?
balance: Split: LIKELY — exemestane plus ovarian suppression beats tamoxifen plus ovarian suppression for recurrence · POSSIBLE — adding ovarian suppression to tamoxifen, where benefit concentrates in women at high enough risk to have had chemotherapy. In the joint TEXT/SOFT primary analysis (4,690 women), five-year disease-free survival was 91.1% with exemestane plus suppression vs 87.3% with tamoxifen plus suppression (hazard ratio 0.72). In SOFT alone, adding suppression to tamoxifen did not significantly improve disease-free survival overall (hazard ratio 0.83, P=0.10 at first report; 15-year breast cancer-free interval hazard ratio 0.82 in the final report), and the 15-year final outcomes confine meaningful survival benefit to high-risk subgroups, with overall survival in the combined HER2-negative analysis at hazard ratio 0.89 (0.74 to 1.06) — no standalone mortality claim is made.

title: Extending adjuvant endocrine therapy to ten years: ATLAS and MA.17R
question: Does extending adjuvant endocrine therapy beyond five years — tamoxifen to ten years (ATLAS), or letrozole after five years of aromatase-inhibitor-based therapy (MA.17R) — reduce recurrence and breast-cancer death enough to justify the extra years of harm?
balance: Split, PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: ATLAS carries a breast-cancer mortality claim): LIKELY — continuing tamoxifen to ten years reduces recurrence and breast-cancer mortality in ER-positive disease (ATLAS: recurrence 21.4% vs 25.1% and breast-cancer mortality 12.2% vs 15.0% over years 5–14, an absolute mortality reduction of 2.8%, bought with more endometrial cancer, 3.1% vs 1.6%, and more pulmonary embolism) · POSSIBLE — extending an aromatase inhibitor with five more years of letrozole (MA.17R: disease-free survival hazard ratio 0.66 and fewer contralateral cancers, but overall survival 93% vs 94%, hazard ratio 0.97, and more bone pain, fractures and new osteoporosis).

title: Ductal carcinoma in situ: radiotherapy after lumpectomy, and tamoxifen
question: For DCIS treated with breast-conserving surgery, how much does radiotherapy cut ipsilateral recurrence in good-risk disease (RTOG 9804) — and what did the long-term NSABP B-17/B-24 programme show for radiotherapy and tamoxifen on invasive recurrence?
balance: LIKELY: Radiotherapy after lumpectomy for DCIS roughly halves invasive ipsilateral recurrence over 15 years in the NSABP programme (15-year cumulative incidence 8.9% with radiotherapy vs 19.4% with lumpectomy alone; hazard ratio 0.48), and in good-risk DCIS the RTOG 9804 trial found a seven-year local failure rate of 0.9% with radiotherapy vs 6.7% with observation (hazard ratio 0.11) — a large relative effect on a low absolute risk. Adding tamoxifen to radiotherapy reduced invasive recurrence further (hazard ratio 0.68; 15-year incidence 8.5% vs 10.0%). Neither programme showed a survival difference, and none is claimed: the 15-year breast-cancer death incidence stayed between 2.3% and 4.7% across all arms.
stamp: LIKELY

title: Vulvovaginal symptoms after menopause: vaginal estradiol, moisturiser, or placebo (MsFLASH)
question: For postmenopausal vulvovaginal symptoms, do a low-dose vaginal estradiol tablet or a vaginal moisturiser actually beat a dual placebo — the MsFLASH three-arm trial whose result surprised prescribers?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): In the one large, rigorous three-arm trial (MsFLASH, 302 postmenopausal women with moderate-to-severe symptoms), neither low-dose vaginal estradiol (most-bothersome-symptom severity reduction −1.4) nor a vaginal moisturiser (−1.2) beat dual placebo (−1.3) over 12 weeks — P=.25 and P=.31 — and sexual-function scores improved similarly in all arms. title: Non-oestrogen options for dyspareunia: ospemifene and prasterone
question: Do ospemifene (an oral SERM) and intravaginal prasterone (DHEA) improve dyspareunia and vulvovaginal atrophy versus placebo in postmenopausal women who avoid or cannot use oestrogen?
balance: POSSIBLE: Two non-oestrogen options each beat placebo on dyspareunia and on the tissue signs of vulvovaginal atrophy over 12 weeks. Ospemifene's pivotal trial (605 women) was significant on all co-primary endpoints including dyspareunia severity (P=0.0001), though its abstract reports significance rather than effect sizes, with hot flushes the commonest treatment-related adverse event (6.6% vs 3.6%). Prasterone's pooled three-trial data (436 treated, 260 placebo) show a 0.46-unit greater reduction in dyspareunia severity over placebo (P<0.0001). Symptom-scale benefits of modest, partly unquantified size from short trials: POSSIBLE.

title: Drugs for hypoactive sexual desire disorder: flibanserin and bremelanotide
question: Do flibanserin (nightly, premenopausal women — pooled pivotal trials) and bremelanotide (on-demand injection, RECONNECT) improve satisfying sexual events and desire versus placebo, and at what cost in dizziness, nausea, and hypotension?
balance: POSSIBLE: Both approved drugs beat placebo on desire and distress scores, by small amounts. Flibanserin's pooled pivotal trials (2,465 premenopausal women) found about one extra satisfying sexual event per 28 days over placebo (change 2.1 vs 1.2) and small gains on desire and distress scales, with dizziness and somnolence in at least 10% of patients. Bremelanotide's twin RECONNECT trials (1,202 in the efficacy population) found integrated gains of 0.35 points on the desire domain and −0.33 on the distress item versus placebo, with nausea, flushing and headache in at least 10%. Statistically consistent, clinically modest: POSSIBLE.

title: Preventing recurrent bacterial vaginosis: Lactin-V and suppressive metronidazole
question: After standard treatment clears bacterial vaginosis, can recurrence be held off — by a live Lactobacillus crispatus biotherapeutic (Lactin-V) or by twice-weekly suppressive metronidazole gel?
balance: POSSIBLE: Two single randomised trials of two different hold-off strategies each reduced recurrence while they were used. Lactin-V after metronidazole gel (228 women) cut 12-week recurrence from 45% to 30% (risk ratio 0.66, a relative figure). Twice-weekly suppressive metronidazole gel (112 randomised women) cut recurrence during suppression from 59.1% to 25.5% (relative risk 0.43), an effect that faded once therapy stopped (51.0% vs 75.0% over 28 weeks), with more vaginal candidiasis. One trial per strategy caps the stamp at POSSIBLE. A 2025 trial of treating the male partner (StepUp) is fenced in the synthesis — it changes the question, and its result is strong enough that this shelf should not be read as the whole recurrence story.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Trichomoniasis in women: single-dose secnidazole, and how much metronidazole is enough
question: Does single-dose oral secnidazole cure trichomoniasis in women versus placebo — and does the older standard, metronidazole, work better as a seven-day course than as the traditional single 2 g dose (the Kissinger trial)?
balance: POSSIBLE: Single-dose oral secnidazole cured trichomoniasis microbiologically in 92.2% of women versus 1.5% on placebo in its phase 3 trial (131 women in the modified intention-to-treat population) — a large effect from a single small trial against placebo, with no comparison against metronidazole. The older standard itself was then beaten by its longer course: in the Kissinger trial (623 HIV-uninfected, non-pregnant women), seven days of metronidazole left fewer women test-positive at four weeks than a single 2 g dose (11% vs 19%; relative risk 0.55). One trial per half, so POSSIBLE — and the practical headline is that the single-dose habit is the weaker half of this shelf.

title: Elinzanetant for menopausal vasomotor symptoms (OASIS 1, 2 and 3)
question: Does the dual neurokinin-1/3 antagonist elinzanetant reduce the frequency and severity of menopausal hot flushes versus placebo — in the twin OASIS 1/2 trials and the longer OASIS 3?
balance: LIKELY: Three double-blind phase 3 trials of the same drug and dose agree. In the twin OASIS 1 and 2 trials (about 800 postmenopausal women with moderate-to-severe vasomotor symptoms), elinzanetant 120 mg daily reduced daily hot-flush frequency by about 3.2–3.3 more flushes than placebo at weeks 4 and 12, and reduced severity by 0.2–0.4 points, with better sleep and quality-of-life scores. OASIS 3 (628 women, 52 weeks) confirmed the week-12 frequency effect (difference −1.6 flushes per day) with no hepatotoxicity, endometrial hyperplasia or meaningful bone-density change, though treatment-related adverse events were commoner on drug (30.4% vs 14.6% — somnolence, fatigue, headache). Two-plus blinded trials with consistent effects support LIKELY.
stamp: LIKELY

title: Continuous glucose monitoring in insulin-treated type 2 diabetes
question: In type 2 diabetes treated with insulin — basal insulin in primary care, or multiple daily injections — does continuous glucose monitoring improve A1c versus finger-stick monitoring?
balance: LIKELY: Three randomised trials in three insulin-treated type 2 diabetes populations point the same way. MOBILE (basal insulin, primary care) found A1c 0.4 percentage points lower with CGM at 8 months; the DIAMOND type 2 study (multiple daily injections) found 0.3 points lower at 24 weeks; and the 2026 FreeDM2 trial (basal insulin plus modern agents, UK primary and secondary care) found 0.6 points lower at 16 weeks, sustained at 32 weeks. The gains are modest and consistent, bought with a device patients must wear — the trials agree on direction and rough size, which is what carries the stamp.

title: Oral semaglutide: the PIONEER glycaemic trials
question: Does once-daily oral semaglutide lower A1c versus sitagliptin (PIONEER 3) and versus injectable liraglutide (PIONEER 4) in type 2 diabetes?
balance: LIKELY: Two double-blind phase 3 trials show once-daily oral semaglutide is a real glycaemic drug, not a convenience formulation. PIONEER 3: the 7 mg and 14 mg doses beat sitagliptin on A1c at 26 weeks (−0.3 and −0.5 percentage points) with more weight loss; the 3 mg dose did not reach noninferiority. PIONEER 4: oral semaglutide 14 mg was noninferior to injectable liraglutide 1.8 mg on A1c and superior on weight. title: Tirzepatide versus semaglutide, head to head
question: In direct head-to-head trials, how much more do patients gain — on A1c in type 2 diabetes (SURPASS-2, vs semaglutide 1 mg) and on weight in obesity without diabetes (SURMOUNT-5, vs semaglutide 2.4 mg) — with tirzepatide than with semaglutide?
balance: LIKELY: In the only two direct head-to-head randomised trials, tirzepatide beat semaglutide in both populations tested. In type 2 diabetes (SURPASS-2, against semaglutide 1 mg weekly), tirzepatide lowered A1c by a further 0.15–0.45 percentage points across its dose range and took off 1.9–5.5 kg more weight. In obesity without diabetes (SURMOUNT-5, against semaglutide up to 2.4 mg), weight loss at 72 weeks was −20.2% versus −13.7%. Both trials were open-label — patients knew which drug they were on — and gastrointestinal adverse events were common on both drugs; neither caveat reverses differences of this size.

title: Insulin glargine 300 U/mL versus glargine 100 U/mL (EDITION 1 and 2)

title: Nasal glucagon for severe hypoglycaemia
question: Does glucagon given as a nasal powder rescue insulin-induced hypoglycaemia as reliably as intramuscular glucagon — in adults, and in children and adolescents with type 1 diabetes?
balance: POSSIBLE: One randomised crossover trial in adults found nasal glucagon 3 mg non-inferior to intramuscular glucagon 1 mg for reversing insulin-induced hypoglycaemia — every participant in the efficacy analysis succeeded on both routes. title: Closed-loop insulin delivery for type 2 diabetes: hospital and home
question: In type 2 diabetes, does fully closed-loop insulin delivery keep glucose in range better than conventional insulin therapy — in hospital inpatients on general wards, and in outpatients at home?
balance: POSSIBLE: In hospital, one open-label randomised trial (Bally 2018, 136 inpatients on general wards) found fully closed-loop delivery put sensor glucose in range 65.8% of the time versus 41.5% on conventional subcutaneous therapy, with no difference in hypoglycaemia exposure. title: Structured education at diagnosis of type 2 diabetes (DESMOND)
question: Does a single structured group education programme for people newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes (DESMOND) improve biomedical outcomes, illness beliefs, and lifestyle at one year — and do the effects persist at three years?
balance: Split: LIKELY — no A1c benefit (the treatment made no difference) · POSSIBLE — short-term weight, smoking and illness-belief gains. DESMOND, a single six-hour structured group education course for people newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes, was tested in one large cluster trial (824 adults, 207 practices) with a three-year follow-up. It did not improve HbA1c at 12 months (adjusted difference 0.05%, CI spanning zero) or at three years (−0.02), and by three years the groups did not differ on any biomedical or lifestyle outcome. At 12 months the education group had lost more weight (−2.98 vs −1.86 kg), had higher odds of not smoking, and held better illness beliefs — beliefs that were still better at three years. A large, well-run null on the biomedical primary carries LIKELY (the treatment made no difference); the secondary gains are POSSIBLE.

title: Continuous glucose monitoring in pregnancy with type 1 diabetes (CONCEPTT)
question: In pregnant women with type 1 diabetes, does continuous glucose monitoring improve glycaemic control and neonatal outcomes versus capillary monitoring alone (CONCEPTT)?
balance: POSSIBLE: One large multicentre randomised trial (CONCEPTT, 325 women) found CGM in pregnancy with type 1 diabetes produced a small HbA1c advantage (−0.19 percentage points at 34 weeks) and better neonatal outcomes: fewer large-for-gestational-age babies (odds ratio 0.51), fewer neonatal intensive care admissions over 24 hours (0.48), fewer neonatal hypoglycaemia episodes (0.45), and one day shorter neonatal hospital stay — with comparable severe hypoglycaemia in mothers. title: Blood-pressure control in Black barbershops
question: Does pharmacist-led blood-pressure care delivered through Black-owned barbershops, with barber encouragement, lower systolic pressure far more than barber health promotion alone — and what did the programme's earlier barber-monitoring trial find?
balance: LIKELY: Two cluster-randomised trials from the same research programme, a decade apart, show venue-based barbershop care works — and that what the barber hands the patron to matters enormously. BARBER-1 (17 Dallas barbershops): barbers checking blood pressure and promoting physician follow-up raised hypertension control rates by 8.8 percentage points versus pamphlets, with only a marginal systolic effect (−2.5 mm Hg, non-significant). The 2018 Los Angeles trial (52 barbershops, 319 men): barber encouragement coupled with pharmacists prescribing in the shop under collaborative agreements cut systolic pressure 21.6 mm Hg more than health promotion alone, and 63.6% versus 11.7% reached below 130/80 mm Hg. Blood-pressure endpoints only — no event outcomes — so the stamp rests on trial count and effect size, not on outcomes beyond pressure.
stamp: LIKELY

title: Pedometers and exercise referral in primary care: PACE-UP and e-coachER
question: Do primary-care activity interventions work at scale — a pedometer programme with and without nurse support (PACE-UP), and an exercise-referral scheme augmented with web-based support (e-coachER) — on objectively measured activity a year later?
balance: Split: LIKELY — pedometer programmes raise activity · POSSIBLE — web support added to exercise referral does not (the treatment made no difference). One positive trial carries the pedometer claim to LIKELY under this library's behavioural-trial convention (unblindable by nature, judged on trial count and rigour); the web-augmentation null rests on one trial and is POSSIBLE.

title: School-based childhood obesity prevention: WAVES and IDEFICS
question: Do school-delivered obesity-prevention programmes change children's weight — the UK WAVES trial (null on its BMI primary) and the eight-country European IDEFICS intervention?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): Two very large school-based cluster trials found these programmes did not change children's weight trajectory. WAVES (54 UK primary schools, 1467 pupils aged 5–6) found no significant effect on BMI z score at 15 months (−0.075, CI including zero) or 30 months (−0.027), and no significant effects on diet, activity or psychological measures. IDEFICS (more than 16,000 children aged 2–9.9 years in eight European countries) found no intervention effects on parent-reported diet, sedentary behaviour or physical activity overall. Two large independent nulls, on the outcomes the programmes themselves chose, carry LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — for programmes of this intensity, delivered through schools alone.

title: Screening for oral cancer by visual inspection (the Kerala trial)

title: Treating insomnia to delay depression: digital CBT-I
question: In people with insomnia but no current depression, does digital CBT-I reduce depression symptoms and new depressive episodes over the following year — the SHUTi GoodNight Study, and Cheng's digital CBT-I prevention trial?
balance: Split: LIKELY — fewer depression symptoms · POSSIBLE — fewer new depressive episodes. Two randomised trials of fully automated digital CBT-I agree that treating insomnia lowers depression symptoms over the following 6–12 months (GoodNight/SHUTi: significantly lower PHQ-9 scores at 6 weeks and 6 months; Cheng: significantly lower depression severity at 1 year). The episode-prevention claim is thinner: GoodNight found no significant difference in major depressive disorder diagnoses at 6 months (9 vs 13 cases, p=0.32), while Cheng found the incidence of moderate-to-severe depression at 1 year was roughly halved in the subgroup with minimal-to-no baseline depression — a relative claim from one trial's subgroup. title: Text-message support for smoking cessation: txt2stop and Text2Quit
question: Do automated text-message programmes double quit rates versus control messages — txt2stop in the UK, Text2Quit in the US?
balance: LIKELY: Two randomised trials on two continents found automated text-message programmes roughly doubled biochemically verified quit rates at 6 months. txt2stop (UK, 5800 smokers): continuous abstinence 10.7% versus 4.9% (relative risk 2.20). Text2Quit (US, 503 smokers recruited online): repeated point-prevalence abstinence 11.1% versus 5.0% (relative risk 2.22). The relative doubling is real; the absolute quit rates (~11% vs ~5%) are the figures to quote — most smokers in both arms were still smoking at 6 months.

title: Financial incentives for smoking cessation in the general population
question: Do employer-offered financial incentives raise long-term quit rates — alone against information (Volpp), and combined with workplace group training in a European cluster trial (van den Brand)?
balance: LIKELY: Two randomised trials in working populations found financial incentives roughly tripled long-term quit rates. Volpp 2009 (878 employees of one US multinational; up to $750 in staged incentives): cessation at 9–12 months was 14.7% versus 5.0% on information alone, and the advantage persisted at 15–18 months (9.4% vs 3.6%) after the money stopped. Van den Brand 2018 (61 Dutch companies, 604 smokers): adding up to €350 in vouchers to workplace group training raised 12-month continuous abstinence to 41% versus 26% (adjusted odds ratio 1.93 — inside the 0.5–2.0 caution band on its own, but printed beside absolute rates and consistent with Volpp). The claim is about quitting while incentives run and shortly after; neither trial shows lifetime abstinence.

title: Single-dose HPV vaccination: KEN SHE, DoRIS and ESCUDDO
question: Is one dose of HPV vaccine enough — the KEN SHE randomised efficacy trial in Kenyan women, the DoRIS immunobridging trial in Tanzanian girls, and the ESCUDDO one-versus-two-dose noninferiority trial?
balance: LIKELY: Three randomised data sets now support one dose. KEN SHE (2275 Kenyan women aged 15–20) found single-dose vaccine efficacy against persistent HPV16/18 infection of 97.5% (bivalent) and 98.8% (nonavalent) at 3 years. DoRIS immunobridging showed antibody responses in girls aged 9–14 — the actual target age — were non-inferior to those in the KEN SHE women in whom efficacy was proven. And the ESCUDDO trial (20,330 girls aged 12–16), found by this shelf's currency sweep, showed one dose was noninferior to two doses against HPV16/18 infection for both vaccines, with vaccine effectiveness of at least 97% in every group. What one dose has not yet shown in a trial is prevention of cervical cancer itself — that endpoint belongs to the multi-dose registry evidence on Shelves #216 and #446.
stamp: LIKELY

title: Seasonal malaria chemoprevention in children: combinations and additions
question: In the Sahel's rainy season, does seasonal malaria chemoprevention still add protection when combined with RTS,S vaccination — and does adding azithromycin to chemoprevention reduce deaths or admissions?
balance: Split: LIKELY — vaccine + chemoprevention beats either alone · LIKELY — adding azithromycin does not reduce death or admission (the treatment made no difference). title: Water, sanitation and handwashing for child diarrhoea and growth: WASH Benefits
question: Do household water-quality, sanitation, and handwashing interventions — alone or combined with nutrition — reduce diarrhoea and improve linear growth in young children, in the twin WASH Benefits cluster trials in Bangladesh and Kenya?
balance: Split: POSSIBLE — WASH reduces diarrhoea in Bangladesh · LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — WASH alone does not improve growth, and Kenya found no diarrhoea benefit either. The twin WASH Benefits cluster trials (Bangladesh: 5551 pregnant women, 720 clusters; Kenya: 8246 women, 702 clusters) tested water quality, sanitation and handwashing, alone and combined with nutrition. In Bangladesh, sanitation, handwashing, combined WASH and the nutrition-containing arms each cut 7-day diarrhoea prevalence to about 3.5% versus 5.7% in controls (prevalence ratios 0.60–0.69), while water treatment alone did not (0.89). In Kenya, no intervention reduced diarrhoea. In both trials, only the nutrition arms (counselling plus lipid-based supplements) improved length-for-age — WASH itself never did, in either country, at high measured adherence in Bangladesh.

title: Vericiguat after a worsening heart-failure event (VICTORIA), and in stable HFrEF (VICTOR)

title: Maternal RSV vaccination to protect infants (MATISSE)
question: Does bivalent RSV prefusion F vaccination in pregnancy prevent medically attended RSV lower-respiratory illness in infants through their first months — and what is the preterm-birth balance?
balance: POSSIBLE: One pivotal trial, MATISSE (7,358 pregnant women), met its success criterion for severe disease: vaccine efficacy against medically attended severe RSV lower-respiratory illness was 81.8% within 90 days of birth (6 vs 33 cases) and 69.4% within 180 days, while efficacy against all medically attended RSV illness at 90 days (57.1%) did not meet the statistical success criterion. The phase 2b trial showed efficient transplacental antibody transfer (ratios 1.41–2.10) without evident safety concerns. The caution on this shelf is preterm birth: MATISSE's own dedicated analysis found 5.7% vs 4.7% (relative risk 1.20, 95% CI 0.98 to 1.46), concentrated in non-high-income settings, and the rival GSK maternal vaccine's phase 3 trial was stopped for a significant preterm excess (6.8% vs 4.9%; RR 1.37) and its development terminated — the signal that shaped the licensed gestational window for the Pfizer vaccine. A single pivotal trial caps the stamp at POSSIBLE. Older-adult RSV vaccination (Shelf #320) and infant monoclonal prophylaxis (Shelf #255) are different questions and are not re-carded here.

title: The second dengue vaccine: TAK-003 (Qdenga) in the TIDES trial
question: Does the live attenuated tetravalent TAK-003 vaccine prevent virologically confirmed dengue and dengue hospitalisation in children and adolescents — including in baseline-seronegative children?
balance: POSSIBLE: One large phase 3 programme (TIDES, ~20,000 children and adolescents in endemic countries). Efficacy against virologically confirmed dengue was 80.9% in the first year (0.5 vs 2.5 cases per 100 person-years), with 95.4% efficacy against dengue leading to hospitalisation; by 4.5 years the cumulative efficacy had waned to 61.2% against confirmed dengue and 84.1% against hospitalised dengue. In baseline-seronegative participants, cumulative efficacy was 53.5% against confirmed dengue and 79.3% against hospitalised dengue, with efficacy shown against DENV-1 and DENV-2 but NOT observed against DENV-3 (and too few DENV-4 cases to judge) — a narrower seronegative profile than its predecessor's harm pattern, but not a clean all-serotype bill. Serious adverse events were similar (3.1% vs 3.8% initially; 5.0% vs 5.9% in the long-term phase) and no death was judged vaccine-related. One programme caps the stamp at POSSIBLE. The first dengue vaccine (CYD-TDV/Dengvaxia) and its serostatus lesson live on Shelf #448 and are not re-carded here.

title: A tuberculosis vaccine that half-worked: M72/AS01E
question: Does M72/AS01E vaccination prevent progression to active pulmonary tuberculosis in already-infected (IGRA-positive) adults?
balance: POSSIBLE: One phase 2b trial in IGRA-positive, HIV-negative adults in Kenya, South Africa and Zambia, reported at two pre-specified horizons: vaccine efficacy against bacteriologically confirmed active pulmonary tuberculosis was 54.0% at the primary analysis (10 vs 22 cases; incidence 0.3 vs 0.6 per 100 person-years) and 49.7% in the final 3-year analysis (13 vs 26 cases) — roughly halving progression, with wide confidence intervals (final 95% CI 2.1 to 74.2) built on only 39 cases in total. Injection-site and influenza-like reactions were more common on vaccine (67.4% vs 45.4% reported unsolicited adverse events); serious adverse events, potential immune-mediated diseases and deaths were similar. A single trial with a surrogate-adjacent endpoint (progression in already-infected adults) and few events caps the stamp at POSSIBLE; the phase 3 test is the missing rung.

title: Microbiome therapy for recurrent C. difficile: donor faeces, then a defined product (SER-109)
question: Does restoring the gut microbiome stop recurrent C. difficile infection — by donor-faeces infusion, and by the defined oral spore product SER-109?
balance: POSSIBLE: Two randomised trials, a decade and a technology apart, point the same way. Van Nood 2013 (43 randomised patients analysed): donor-faeces infusion resolved recurrent C. difficile diarrhoea in 81% after one infusion (15 of 16 ultimately, 94%, after a second donor infusion) vs 31% on vancomycin alone and 23% on vancomycin with lavage — but the trial was small, open-label and stopped early. ECOSPOR III 2022 (182 patients, double-blind): the defined spore product SER-109 cut recurrence by 8 weeks to 12% vs 40% on placebo (relative risk 0.32, 95% CI 0.18 to 0.58 — beyond the 0.5 threshold this library treats as solid). Adverse events were mostly mild-to-moderate gastrointestinal in both programmes and similar to controls. Two trials, but one is small/open/stopped-early and the products differ, so the stamp is POSSIBLE, not LIKELY. The drug contest for C. difficile (fidaxomicin, bezlotoxumab, vancomycin regimens) lives on Shelf #170 and is not re-carded here.

title: BCG revaccination to prevent tuberculosis infection
question: Does revaccinating BCG in adolescents prevent sustained M. tuberculosis infection?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference, on the larger trial's primary endpoint): The 2025 phase 2b trial (1,836 QFT-negative adolescents) tested exactly the endpoint the earlier trial had suggested — sustained QuantiFERON conversion — as its PRIMARY endpoint, and found no protection: sustained conversion in 62 of 871 BCG-revaccinated vs 59 of 849 placebo participants (hazard ratio 1.04, 95% CI 0.73 to 1.48; vaccine efficacy −3.8%). The 2018 trial (990 adolescents) had found revaccination did not prevent initial QFT conversion (efficacy 20.1%, P=0.29) but reduced sustained conversion on a SECONDARY endpoint (efficacy 45.4%, P=0.03). When the definitive test of a secondary-endpoint signal returns a null on that very endpoint, the signal is read as refuted; the stamp is POSSIBLE for the null rather than LIKELY because both trials are modest in size and the endpoint is a laboratory definition of infection, not disease. Injection-site reactions were more common with revaccination in both trials. Distinct from Shelf #982 (M72/AS01E against progression to disease in already-infected adults).
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference, on the larger trial's primary endpoint)

title: Hepatitis E vaccine (HEV 239): efficacy and its long tail
question: Does the recombinant hepatitis E vaccine prevent hepatitis E in healthy adults in an endemic setting — in the phase 3 trial, and in long-term follow-up?
balance: POSSIBLE: One very large phase 3 trial in Jiangsu, China (112,604 randomised adults aged 16–65): after three doses, vaccine efficacy against hepatitis E in the 12 months from a month after the third dose was 100.0% (95% CI 72.1 to 100.0) — 15 cases in the placebo group, none in the vaccine group. In the extended, still double-blind follow-up of the same trial, 4.5-year efficacy was 86.8% (95% CI 71 to 94), with 7 cases on vaccine (0.3 per 10,000 person-years) vs 53 on the hepatitis-B-vaccine control (2.1 per 10,000 person-years), and 87% of baseline-seronegative three-dose recipients maintaining antibody at 4.5 years. Adverse events were few, mild and similar between groups. One trial programme (however large) in one endemic province, with hepatitis B vaccine as the control, caps the stamp at POSSIBLE; durability beyond 4.5 years rests on immunogenicity, not case counts. Hepatitis B vaccine material (Shelf #450) is a different virus and is not re-carded here.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Ring vaccination for Ebola: the Guinea Ebola Ça Suffit trial
question: Does immediate ring vaccination with single-dose rVSV-ZEBOV prevent Ebola virus disease in contacts and contacts-of-contacts versus delayed vaccination?
balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C candidate ruled Tier C at build; a prevention claim against a usually fatal disease, from a single open-label cluster trial conducted inside an epidemic): In the randomised rings, no Ebola cases with onset 10 days or more after randomisation occurred among immediately vaccinated contacts and contacts-of-contacts, vs 16 cases among eligible individuals in delayed-vaccination rings — a vaccine efficacy estimate of 100% (95% CI 68.9 to 100.0; p=0.0045); across all 117 clusters (including non-randomised rings) the estimate was likewise 100% (79.3 to 100.0), with 23 cases in the comparison groups. Of 5,837 vaccinees, 53.9% reported at least one adverse event in 14 days (mostly mild; headache 25.4%, fatigue 18.9%, muscle pain 13.1% of events); 80 serious adverse events included two judged vaccine-related and one possibly related, all recovering. The Liberian PREVAIL I cluster-vaccination experience (650 contacts identified, only 32% consenting) is carded as the implementation companion: the strategy's weak point is uptake, not the point estimate. A single epidemic-era cluster trial caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.

title: Yaws: single-dose azithromycin against benzathine penicillin, and mass treatment
question: Is single-dose oral azithromycin non-inferior to benzathine benzylpenicillin injection for yaws in children — and do repeated mass rounds beat one round plus targeted treatment for eradication?
balance: POSSIBLE: Mitjà 2012 (250 children in Papua New Guinea, open-label) showed a single 30 mg/kg oral dose of azithromycin non-inferior to benzathine benzylpenicillin injection for serological cure at 6 months (96% vs 93%; difference −3.4%, 95% CI −9.3 to 2.4, within the 10% margin) — the result that made mass treatment thinkable. The 2022 cluster trial (38 wards, ~57,000 people) then found three rounds of mass azithromycin reduced active yaws prevalence further than one mass round plus targeted treatment (0.04% vs 0.16% at 18 months; adjusted relative risk 4.08 for the control strategy's higher prevalence), and latent yaws prevalence was 3.28% vs 6.54% — but three cases of macrolide-resistant yaws were found in the three-round group, the resistance shadow the topic asks about. Each claim rests on a single trial, so the stamp is POSSIBLE.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Mass azithromycin and child mortality in Africa (MORDOR)
question: Does biannual mass distribution of azithromycin reduce mortality in preschool children in high-mortality settings?
balance: Split stamp — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C; the claim is child mortality itself): POSSIBLE for the MORDOR claim — in 1,533 communities across Niger, Malawi and Tanzania, biannual azithromycin to children 1–59 months gave an annual mortality of 14.6 vs 16.5 deaths per 1,000 person-years, 13.5% lower in relative terms (95% CI 6.7 to 19.8) — a relative effect inside this library's 0.5–2.0 caution band, heterogeneous by country (Niger 18.1% lower; Malawi 5.7% and Tanzania 3.4%, both non-significant) and largest at 1–5 months of age (24.9% lower). The PRET secondary analysis points the same way but weakly (biannual vs annual distribution: mortality rate ratio 0.81, 0.66 to 1.00; P=0.07 — not significant, and not a placebo comparison). MAYBE (weak evidence) for the narrowed infant strategy — the MIRAMA trial in Burkina Faso (302,668 children reached, ages 1–11 months only) found NO mortality difference (2.6 vs 2.5 per 1,000 person-years; incidence rate ratio 1.04, 0.75 to 1.46). Antibiotic resistance is the standing cost: MORDOR's own abstract defers the resistance evaluation, and any implementation claim must carry it.

title: Shorter rabies post-exposure prophylaxis: one-week intradermal regimens
question: Do abbreviated (one-week) intradermal rabies PEP regimens produce antibody responses non-inferior to standard regimens?
balance: POSSIBLE: The immunogenicity evidence is consistent that one-week regimens seroconvert everyone, and mixed on whether they match standard regimens titre-for-titre. Quiambao 2019 (600 exposed patients, Philippines): the one-week 4-site intradermal regimen, with or without rabies immunoglobulin, was non-inferior to the updated Thai Red Cross 28-day regimen for day-14 seroconversion (100% and 99.4% vs 98.8%), with higher geometric mean titres (11.3 and 9.89 vs 6.15 IU/mL) and better one-year persistence (97.6% and 89% vs 79.8% still ≥0.5 IU/mL). The 2026 Indian equivalence trial (400 healthy volunteers) found the one-week IPC regimen did NOT meet its prespecified day-42 titre-equivalence criterion against the updated Thai Red Cross regimen (geometric mean concentration ratios 0.59 for PCECV and 0.76 for PVRV, against a 0.72–1.04 window) — although every participant in every group was at or above 0.5 IU/mL from day 14 to one year. All of this is surrogate (antibody) evidence: no trial on this shelf measures rabies cases prevented, and none should be read as doing so. Rabies appears elsewhere in the index only inside vaccine-survey material (Shelf #449), which is not re-carded here.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Memantine in moderate-to-severe Alzheimer's disease, and whether to continue donepezil (DOMINO)
question: Does memantine improve cognition and function in moderate-to-severe Alzheimer's disease — and, once patients reach that stage, does continuing donepezil (with or without adding memantine) beat stopping it?
balance: Split: LIKELY — continuing donepezil · POSSIBLE — memantine. Continuing donepezil past the moderate-to-severe threshold beat stopping it on cognition by more than the trial's own minimum clinically important difference (DOMINO: SMMSE +1.9 points against a 1.4-point MCID), with a significant functional benefit beside it. Memantine's case is thinner: positive on function and global impression in Reisberg 2003, but in DOMINO its average gains (+1.2 SMMSE points; −1.5 BADLS points) fell below both of that trial's pre-set clinically important differences, and adding it to donepezil gave no extra benefit over donepezil alone. Both drugs' effects are symptomatic and modest; neither trial speaks to disease modification.

title: Cannabidiol for severe childhood epilepsy syndromes (Dravet and Lennox–Gastaut)
question: Does pharmaceutical cannabidiol, added to standard therapy, reduce convulsive seizures in Dravet syndrome and drop seizures in Lennox–Gastaut syndrome versus placebo?
balance: LIKELY: Two double-blind, placebo-controlled trials of the same pharmaceutical cannabidiol solution — one in Dravet syndrome (Devinsky 2017, n=120) and one in Lennox–Gastaut syndrome (Devinsky 2018, n=225, two doses) — both met their primary seizure-frequency endpoints, with median reductions roughly two to two-and-a-half times the placebo response. The benefit is a reduction in seizure frequency, not seizure freedom (5% vs 0% seizure-free in Dravet, not significant), and it comes with somnolence, gastrointestinal effects and liver-enzyme elevations that caused withdrawals. Neither trial addresses mortality, development, or long-term outcomes.
stamp: LIKELY

title: Fenfluramine for Dravet and Lennox–Gastaut syndromes
question: Does low-dose fenfluramine — the withdrawn appetite suppressant, repurposed — reduce seizures in Dravet syndrome and in Lennox–Gastaut syndrome versus placebo, and what cardiac safety did the trials show?
balance: LIKELY: Two double-blind, placebo-controlled trials — Lagae 2019 in Dravet syndrome (n=119) and Knupp 2022 in Lennox–Gastaut syndrome (n=263) — both met their primary endpoints at the 0.7 mg/kg/day dose, with a clear dose gradient beneath them. The Dravet effect is large (a 62.3% greater reduction in mean monthly convulsive seizure frequency than placebo); the Lennox–Gastaut effect is smaller (an estimated median difference of −19.9 percentage points in drop-seizure frequency). On the drug's defining historical risk: echocardiography in the Dravet trial found valve function within the normal physiological range in all patients, and neither trial observed valvular heart disease or pulmonary arterial hypertension — over trial durations of 14–20 weeks, which is reassurance about the trials, not a lifetime guarantee.
stamp: LIKELY

title: Non-invasive brain stimulation for treatment-resistant depression: iTBS and tDCS
question: Is intermittent theta-burst stimulation non-inferior to conventional high-frequency rTMS for treatment-resistant depression — and does transcranial direct-current stimulation beat placebo, measured against escitalopram?
balance: Split: POSSIBLE — iTBS non-inferior to standard rTMS · POSSIBLE — tDCS beats placebo but was not shown non-inferior to escitalopram. THREE-D (414 patients) showed iTBS non-inferior to 10 Hz rTMS on depression scores, delivered in 3 minutes against 37.5 — a logistics advance on a single large trial, hence POSSIBLE rather than LIKELY. ELECT-TDCS (245 patients) is two-handed: tDCS beat placebo (difference 3.2 HDRS-17 points), but non-inferiority to escitalopram could not be claimed — escitalopram beat placebo by more (5.5 points) and the tDCS-versus-drug confidence interval crossed the pre-set margin. Anyone citing tDCS as 'as good as an antidepressant' is citing half of that trial.

title: Long-acting injectable antipsychotics for relapse prevention in schizophrenia
question: Do depot antipsychotics prevent relapse versus placebo in stabilised schizophrenia — aripiprazole once-monthly in its pivotal maintenance trial, and paliperidone palmitate in its relapse-prevention trial?
balance: LIKELY: Two double-blind, placebo-controlled maintenance trials of once-monthly depot antipsychotics in patients first stabilised on the same drug both showed large delays to relapse: impending relapse 10.0% versus 39.6% on placebo in the aripiprazole depot trial (relative hazard for placebo versus depot 5.03), and a relative hazard of 3.60 for placebo versus paliperidone palmitate. Both trials share the design caveat that defines this literature: only patients who had already stabilised on the drug were randomised, so the estimates describe continuing a tolerated depot, not starting one in an unselected patient. The aripiprazole trial was also stopped early at a pre-planned interim analysis, which tends to flatter effect sizes.
stamp: LIKELY

title: Exercise training for people with dementia: the DAPA trial's null
question: Does a moderate-to-high-intensity aerobic and strength programme improve cognition in people with mild-to-moderate dementia — or slow its decline by any measure that matters?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): The DAPA trial (494 people with mild-to-moderate dementia, 12-month primary outcome) found that a well-delivered, well-attended moderate-to-high-intensity exercise programme did not slow cognitive impairment — the exercise group's ADAS-cog score was statistically slightly worse (adjusted difference −1.4 points, P=0.03), a difference the investigators describe as small with uncertain clinical relevance — and no secondary outcome (daily living, neuropsychiatric symptoms, quality of life, carer outcomes) differed. A single very large, pragmatic, investigator-masked trial with a null this complete may carry LIKELY for the null, per the library's large-single-trial-null rule; fitness genuinely improved (6-minute walk +18.1 m), which is what makes the cognitive null informative rather than a delivery failure. The shelf's question is established dementia: trials in mild cognitive impairment are a different question and are fenced, not carded.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference)

title: Spinal cord stimulation for chronic back and leg pain: HF10 and closed-loop
question: Does 10-kHz high-frequency spinal cord stimulation relieve chronic back and leg pain better than traditional low-frequency stimulation — and does ECAP-controlled closed-loop stimulation beat open-loop on pain and function?
balance: POSSIBLE: Two randomised trials, each against an active stimulation comparator rather than sham, favoured the newer technology on responder rates: HF10 (10-kHz) beat traditional low-frequency stimulation in SENZA-RCT (back-pain responders 84.5% vs 43.8% at 3 months, sustained to 12 months), and ECAP-controlled closed-loop beat fixed-output open-loop in the double-blind Evoke trial (≥50% pain reduction 82.3% vs 60.3% at 3 months; 83.1% vs 61.0% at 12 months). The grade stops at POSSIBLE because both trials are industry-run device comparisons with a subjective responder endpoint, SENZA was unblinded (HF10 produces no paraesthesias, so patients could tell), and neither trial compares stimulation with no stimulation — the absolute value of any spinal cord stimulation is a different shelf's question.

title: The buprenorphine implant for opioid dependence (Probuphine)
question: In adults already stable on sublingual buprenorphine, does a six-month buprenorphine implant keep them opioid-negative as reliably as continuing sublingual therapy — and did the implant beat placebo in untreated dependence?
balance: LIKELY: The implant works in both populations in which it was tested. In untreated opioid dependence, Ling 2010 (n=163) showed more opioid-negative urine samples than placebo implants over weeks 1–16 (mean 40.4% vs 28.3%) with far better completion (65.7% vs 30.9%). In patients already stable and abstinent on low-dose sublingual buprenorphine, Rosenthal 2016 (n=177) showed the implant non-inferior to continuing sublingual therapy on responder rates (96.4% vs 87.6%). The two trials answer different questions — starting treatment versus maintaining stability — and the shelf claims each only for its own population. title: Exercise as a treatment for major depression: SMILE and TREAD
question: Does aerobic exercise treat major depression as well as sertraline in older adults — and does simply facilitating more physical activity help depressed adults in primary care?
balance: Split: POSSIBLE — exercise comparable to sertraline at 16 weeks in older adults (SMILE) · LIKELY — facilitated physical activity does not improve depression in primary care (TREAD, the null). The discordance is the shelf. SMILE (156 older adults) found 16 weeks of aerobic exercise statistically indistinguishable from sertraline on depression scores — but it was small, had no placebo arm, and medication worked faster. TREAD (361 primary-care adults) tested the weaker real-world offer — a facilitator encouraging activity — and found no improvement in mood at 4, 8 or 12 months and no reduction in antidepressant use, even though activity itself rose. Structured, supervised exercise as treatment and being encouraged to be more active are different interventions; this shelf refuses to merge them.

title: Goal-oriented cognitive rehabilitation in early dementia (GREAT)
question: Does individual, goal-oriented cognitive rehabilitation improve everyday functioning — attainment of the person's own goals — in early-stage Alzheimer's and related dementias, even though it does not move global cognition scores?
balance: POSSIBLE: The GREAT trial (475 people with early-stage dementia) found large, durable effects on its chosen primary outcome — attainment of the individual's own functional goals (standardised effect d=0.97 by self-rating and d=1.11 by informant rating at 3 months, maintained at 9 months) — and no significant differences on any secondary outcome, including global cognition, quality of life and mood. That pattern is the intervention working as designed: rehabilitation targeted the goals, and only the goals moved. title: Behavioural nudges against inappropriate antibiotic prescribing (Meeker; stewardship by audit)
question: Do behavioural interventions in primary care — accountable justification and suggested alternatives in the record, and peer comparison against top performers — cut inappropriate antibiotic prescribing for respiratory infections, and does a paediatric outpatient stewardship programme with audit-and-feedback do the same?
balance: LIKELY: Two cluster-randomised trials in US primary care networks both cut inappropriate antibiotic prescribing. In Meeker 2016 (47 practices, 248 clinicians), accountable justification (difference-in-differences −7.0 percentage points, P<0.001) and peer comparison (−5.2 points, P<0.001) worked; suggested alternatives did not reach significance (P=0.66 for trajectories) — the shelf credits only the two interventions that worked. title: Patient decision aids: what the Cochrane evidence actually shows
question: Do patient decision aids improve knowledge, risk perception and decisional conflict — and change uptake of screening and surgery — across the Cochrane review's hundred-plus trials, in its 2017 analysis and its 2024 update?
balance: LIKELY: The Cochrane review of patient decision aids — 105 trials and 31,043 participants in 2017, growing to 209 trials and 107,698 participants in the 2024 update — consistently finds that decision aids increase knowledge (mean difference about 12–13 points on a 100-point scale, high-certainty), improve accuracy of risk perceptions, and reduce decisional conflict about feeling uninformed and unclear about values, with more people making choices congruent with their informed values. Effects on what people actually choose are decision-specific and smaller: fewer chose major elective surgery (relative risk 0.86) and PSA screening (relative risk 0.88) in 2017, more started diabetes medication (relative risk 1.65), and most other choices did not change. There was no difference in decision regret (2024). The two editions are one living review, carded as versions — the update confirms and enlarges the 2017 findings rather than independently replicating them.
stamp: LIKELY

title: Mailed faecal testing outreach for colorectal cancer screening (STOP CRC)
question: Does mailing FIT kits to patients due for colorectal screening raise completion — in community health clinics in the STOP CRC cluster trial, and in the Systems of Support programme whose economic evaluation priced the strategy?
balance: POSSIBLE: Mailed FIT outreach works, modestly and unevenly. STOP CRC (26 federally qualified health centre clinics, 41,193 adults) raised FIT completion by 3.4 percentage points over usual care (13.9% vs 10.4%) and any screening by 3.8 points — a real gain on a low base, but with clinic-level effects ranging from −7.4 to +17.6 percentage points and implementation (proportion actually mailed a FIT) ranging from 6.5% to 68.2%: the mailing is easy to prescribe and hard to deliver well. The Systems of Support economic evaluation (Meenan 2015, of the Green programme's stepped EHR-linked mailings trial) supplies the price side: delivery cost $21–$27 per participant brought up to date on screening, with the automated and assisted arms cost-saving once induced testing costs were counted. One effectiveness trial plus one programme's economic evaluation is a POSSIBLE base, not LIKELY.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Point-of-care C-reactive protein testing to guide antibiotics
question: Does CRP point-of-care testing safely reduce antibiotic prescribing — for COPD exacerbations in Butler's NEJM trial, and for respiratory infections when paired with communication-skills training in Cals's factorial trial?
balance: LIKELY: Two randomised trials in primary care, a decade apart and in different clinical problems, both found large reductions in antibiotic prescribing with no signal of harm. Butler 2019 (653 patients with COPD exacerbations, 86 practices) cut patient-reported antibiotic use from 77.4% to 57.0% (adjusted relative odds 0.31) while meeting non-inferiority on COPD health status. Cals 2009 (431 patients with lower respiratory tract infection, factorial design) cut prescribing at the index consultation from 53% to 31% with CRP testing, and communication-skills training independently did as well or better (54% to 27%), with recovery and satisfaction unchanged. Safety here means 'no evidence of harm' on symptom and health-status outcomes in these trials — neither was powered for rare complications, and Butler recorded two deaths in the usual-care group, judged unrelated to participation.
stamp: LIKELY

title: Delayed antibiotic prescribing as a safety-net strategy
question: For respiratory infections, does a delayed-prescription strategy (collect later if not improving) cut antibiotic use without worsening symptoms or complications versus immediate or no antibiotics?
balance: LIKELY: The Cochrane individual-study evidence (Spurling 2023: 12 trials, 3,968 participants) and the large pragmatic Little 2014 factorial trial (889 patients) agree: delayed prescribing slashes antibiotic use compared with immediate prescribing (Cochrane relative odds 0.03 — an extreme ratio from few studies, printed with its caution on the card; in Little, 33–39% used antibiotics across delayed strategies versus 97% with immediate prescriptions), symptom severity and duration are broadly similar, satisfaction is preserved, and complication rates do not differ. The honest edges: delayed beats no-prescription on satisfaction but not on use (more delayed patients end up taking antibiotics than no-prescription patients — relative odds 2.52), and for sore throat and acute otitis media some symptom outcomes modestly favour immediate antibiotics. Delayed prescribing is a safety-net for the uncertain middle, not a universal default.
stamp: LIKELY

title: Making professionals change: educational outreach visits and local opinion leaders
question: Do educational outreach visits (academic detailing) change prescribing and practice — and do local opinion leaders change compliance with desired practice — across the two Cochrane syntheses of randomised trials?
balance: POSSIBLE: Two Cochrane reviews of randomised trials find small, real improvements in professional compliance with desired practice. Educational outreach visits (O'Brien 2007: 69 studies, over 15,000 health professionals) produced a median adjusted risk difference of +5.6 percentage points in compliance (interquartile range 3.0% to 9.0%), most consistent for prescribing (+4.8%). Local opinion leaders (Flodgren 2019 update: 24 studies) produced a median adjusted risk difference of +10.8 percentage points (interquartile range 3.5% to 14.6%; moderate-certainty evidence), with patient-outcome effects uncertain (very low certainty). The grade is POSSIBLE rather than LIKELY because the outreach-visits review is old (2007), effects are heterogeneous and unexplained in both reviews, and neither base shows what these strategies do to patient outcomes or costs. Small absolute gains, reliably in the right direction, at unknown price.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Comprehensive medication review in hospital, with post-discharge follow-up
question: Does a hospital-based comprehensive medication review — pharmacist-led, with post-discharge follow-up — reduce readmissions and emergency visits in older, polymedicated patients?
balance: Split: POSSIBLE — the single-centre ward-pharmacist model (Gillespie) · LIKELY — hospital CMR with post-discharge follow-up does not reduce unplanned hospital visits (MedRev, the null). The two trials disagree in an instructive way. Gillespie 2009 (400 patients aged 80+, one Swedish hospital, ward-based pharmacists embedded in the team) cut all hospital visits by a relative 16% and drug-related readmissions by a relative 80%, and saved money. The MedRev trial (Kempen 2021: 2,637 patients, 8 wards, 4 hospitals, cluster crossover) tested the exportable version — comprehensive medication review in hospital, with or without structured post-discharge follow-up — and found no reduction in unplanned hospital visits (adjusted rate ratios 1.04 and 1.15), with emergency department visits actually higher in the follow-up arm (1.29). The modern multicentre null governs the general claim; Gillespie stands as evidence that an intensive, single-centre, pharmacist-in-the-team model can differ — a POSSIBLE, not a transferable promise. OPERAM (structured review aimed at drug-related admissions) is drafted at Shelf #930 and is a different service design, not re-carded here.
stamp: Split

title: Nurses as substitutes for doctors in primary care (Laurant; Mundinger)
question: Can trained nurses deliver primary care with outcomes, satisfaction and resource use comparable to doctors — across the Cochrane substitution review, anchored on Mundinger's randomised trial of nurse-practitioner versus physician panels?
balance: LIKELY: Across 18 randomised trials (Cochrane review, Laurant 2018), trained nurses substituting for doctors in primary care probably achieve similar or better health outcomes for a broad range of conditions (low- to moderate-certainty evidence), probably slightly higher patient satisfaction, and probably slightly better blood-pressure outcomes — at the price of probably longer consultations and slightly more return visits, with little or no difference in prescriptions or emergency attendance (high-certainty) and uncertain effects on costs and process of care. The anchor trial, Mundinger 2000 (1,316 patients randomised to nurse practitioners with physician-equivalent independence or to physicians), found no differences in health status, diabetes or asthma measures, or utilisation at 6 months and 1 year. The review's mortality signal is low-certainty and inconsistent (nurse-led care 'may lead to slightly fewer deaths among certain groups' but may make little or no difference) — this shelf makes no mortality claim on it, and it is reported on the card as the uncertainty it is.
stamp: LIKELY

title: Financial incentives for weight loss: lotteries, deposits and groups
question: Do lottery-based and deposit-contract incentives produce more weight loss than control — and do group-based incentives beat individual incentives at the same expected value?
balance: POSSIBLE: Two small randomised trials show financial incentives increase weight loss while the money is live. Volpp 2008 (57 participants) found lottery and deposit-contract groups lost about 13–14 lb in 16 weeks against 3.9 lb in controls, with about half the incentive participants hitting a 16-lb target versus 10.5% of controls — but by 7 months, three months after incentives ended, the between-group differences were no longer statistically significant. Kullgren 2013 (105 employees) found group incentives beat both control (by 4.4 kg) and individual incentives (by 3.2 kg) at 24 weeks, with the group advantage over control partly maintained 12 weeks after incentives ended (2.9 kg). POSSIBLE, not LIKELY: two small, single-employer/single-centre trials, short horizons, and Volpp's regain pattern is the central unanswered question for this whole strategy. Financial incentives for smoking cessation are drafted at Shelf #966 and workplace wellness programmes at Shelf #537 — different questions, not re-carded here.
stamp: POSSIBLE
