title: Pharmacist prescribing for hypertension and cardiovascular risk (RxACTION, RxEACH)
question: Does pharmacist prescribing — assessing, prescribing and following up — lower blood pressure in community patients (RxACTION) and reduce cardiovascular risk in high-risk patients (RxEACH) versus usual care?
balance: LIKELY (for blood pressure and risk-factor improvement; not for cardiovascular events): Two randomised trials from the same Alberta programme show community pharmacists with prescribing authority improving the numbers they targeted. RxACTION (248 patients with above-target blood pressure) found an extra 6.6 mm Hg systolic reduction at 6 months versus usual care (adjusted difference; P=0.0006) and higher odds of reaching target. RxEACH (723 high-risk patients) found greater improvement in estimated cardiovascular risk over 3 months, with systolic pressure down 9.37 mm Hg more, LDL cholesterol 0.2 mmol/L (≈8 mg/dL) lower, HbA1c 0.92% lower and more smoking cessation in the intervention group. The boundary is explicit: RxEACH's primary outcome is a change in a risk score (the greater of Framingham, International or UKPDS estimates), not observed heart attacks or strokes, and neither trial reports event outcomes — this shelf claims risk-factor control only. Home blood-pressure self-monitoring with self-titration (drafted/built Shelf #529) is patient-led and is not re-carded here.
stamp: LIKELY (for blood pressure and risk-factor improvement; not for cardiovascular events)

title: Prehospital airway strategy in cardiac arrest: supraglottic device vs intubation, laryngeal tube vs intubation (AIRWAYS-2, PART)
question: In out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, does an initial supraglottic airway strategy give better functional outcome than tracheal intubation — and does an initial laryngeal-tube strategy give better 72-hour survival than intubation?
balance: Split: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for the i-gel question — in AIRWAYS-2 (9,296 patients), a supraglottic-airway-first strategy was no better than tracheal intubation on good functional outcome at 30 days (6.4% vs 6.8%) despite much better initial ventilation success (87.4% vs 79.0%). POSSIBLE for the laryngeal-tube question — in PART (3,004 patients), a laryngeal-tube-first strategy gave higher 72-hour survival than intubation (18.3% vs 15.4%, adjusted difference 2.9%), with hospital survival and good neurological status also higher, but this is a single pragmatic cluster-crossover trial in which first-attempt intubation success was unusually low (51.6%), so the benefit may belong to the setting as much as to the device. The two trials test different supraglottic devices and are not interchangeable evidence. Tier C ruled no at drafting (a resuscitation-strategy question, no drug-benefit claim).
stamp: Split

title: Defibrillation strategies for refractory ventricular fibrillation: double sequential and vector change (DOSE VF)
question: In refractory VF after three failed standard shocks, does double sequential external defibrillation or vector-change defibrillation improve survival to discharge and good neurological outcome versus continuing standard defibrillation?
balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: the headline outcomes are survival to discharge and neurological outcome after cardiac arrest). One cluster-randomised trial with crossover (DOSE VF, 405 patients, stopped early when COVID-19 disrupted the trial) found survival to hospital discharge of 30.4% with double sequential defibrillation and 21.7% with vector-change defibrillation vs 13.3% with standard defibrillation (relative risks 2.21 and 1.71 respectively, printed as relative with the absolute rates beside them), and good neurological outcome higher with double sequential (relative risk 2.21) but not significantly with vector change (1.48, CI crossing 1). A single, small, early-stopped trial caps a survival-benefit claim at POSSIBLE; the currency sweep found no confirmatory randomised trial.

title: Extracorporeal CPR for refractory out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (ARREST, Prague OHCA)
question: Does extracorporeal CPR improve survival with good function in refractory out-of-hospital cardiac arrest — in the single-centre ARREST trial and in the Prague trial of intra-arrest transport to an ECPR/invasive strategy?
balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: a survival claim in refractory arrest). The two randomised trials point in different directions. ARREST (30 patients, single centre, stopped at its first interim analysis for superiority) found survival to discharge of 43% with early ECMO-facilitated resuscitation vs 7% with standard ACLS. The larger Prague trial (256 patients) of a bundled invasive strategy (intra-arrest transport, ECPR, immediate invasive assessment) missed its primary outcome — survival with good neurological outcome at 180 days 31.5% vs 22.0% (odds ratio 1.63, 95% CI 0.93 to 2.85; P=.09) — and was stopped for futility, with more bleeding in the invasive group (31% vs 15%). A tiny stopped-early positive trial against a larger neutral-primary trial is the definition of POSSIBLE.

title: Vasopressin plus methylprednisolone for in-hospital cardiac arrest (VAM)
question: In in-hospital cardiac arrest, does vasopressin plus methylprednisolone added to standard resuscitation improve return of spontaneous circulation — and does any ROSC gain translate into survival or good neurological outcome?
balance: Split, PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C ruled YES at build: the shelf carries a survival-to-discharge-with-good-neurology benefit claim from the Mentzelopoulos trial, a mortality-adjacent endpoint in the composite). On the process outcome both randomised trials agree: the vasopressin–steroid combination raises ROSC — VAM: 42% vs 33% (risk ratio 1.30); Mentzelopoulos VSE programme: ROSC ≥20 minutes 83.9% vs 65.9% (odds ratio 2.98) — LIKELY for ROSC. On survival the trials disagree: VAM found 30-day survival numerically lower with the combination (9.7% vs 12%; risk ratio 0.83, not significant) and identical favourable neurological outcome (7.6% vs 7.6%), while the smaller Greek programme found survival to discharge with CPC 1–2 of 13.9% vs 5.1% (odds ratio 3.28) — a single-trial claim, capped at POSSIBLE.

title: Mechanical versus manual chest compressions (PARAMEDIC, LINC)
question: Does a mechanical piston compression device improve survival or neurological outcome versus high-quality manual CPR in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C ruled YES at build: survival was the primary outcome in both trials, and both were null). PARAMEDIC (4,471 patients, LUCAS-2 vs manual CPR) found 30-day survival of 6% vs 7% (adjusted odds ratio 0.86, 95% CI 0.64–1.15). LINC (2,589 patients, mechanical compressions with simultaneous defibrillation vs guideline manual CPR) found 4-hour survival of 23.6% vs 23.7% and no significant difference in survival with good neurological outcome at any point to 6 months (8.5% vs 7.6%). Two large concordant randomised nulls on survival carry LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): routine mechanical CPR does not improve survival over good manual CPR.

title: Vasopressin versus epinephrine for out-of-hospital cardiac arrest
question: Does vasopressin beat, match, or lose to epinephrine as the first vasopressor in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest?
balance: Split, PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C ruled YES at build: the shelf carries a survival-to-discharge benefit claim in the asystole subgroup of the Wenzel trial). Overall equivalence is LIKELY: two randomised head-to-head trials found no significant overall difference in survival to hospital discharge between vasopressin and epinephrine (Wenzel: no difference in VF or PEA admission rates; Ong: discharge survival 2.9% vs 2.3%, relative risk 1.72 with a confidence interval of 0.65–4.51, inside the caution band and not significant). title: Oxygen therapy in suspected acute myocardial infarction (DETO2X)
question: In normoxaemic patients with suspected MI, does routine supplemental oxygen change death or rehospitalisation with MI at one year — and what did the smaller STEMI trial's infarct-size signal mean beside it?
balance: Split, PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: all-cause mortality was DETO2X's primary outcome). LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) on benefit: DETO2X (6,629 patients, registry-based randomised trial) found 1-year mortality of 5.0% on routine oxygen vs 5.1% on ambient air (hazard ratio 0.97, 95% CI 0.79–1.21) and no reduction in rehospitalisation with MI (3.8% vs 3.3%; hazard ratio 1.13) — a very large null that excludes a meaningful mortality benefit in normoxaemic suspected MI. POSSIBLE on harm: the smaller AVOID trial in confirmed STEMI found signals of greater myocardial injury with oxygen (higher peak creatine kinase, more recurrent MI, larger infarct size on 6-month MRI) on surrogate and secondary measures — enough to argue against routine oxygen, not enough to prove it harms.

title: A single dose of dexamethasone for acute sore throat (TOAST)
question: In adults presenting to primary care with acute sore throat not given immediate antibiotics, does one dose of oral dexamethasone speed complete symptom resolution at 24 and 48 hours?
balance: POSSIBLE: TOAST (576 adults, double-blind) missed its primary outcome — complete resolution at 24 hours was 22.6% on dexamethasone vs 17.7% on placebo (relative risk 1.28, 95% CI 0.92–1.78; P=.14) — but met the 48-hour outcome (35.4% vs 27.1%; relative risk 1.31, 1.02–1.68). The accompanying systematic review of 10 trials (1,426 participants) found single low-dose corticosteroids roughly doubled the chance of pain relief at 24 hours (relative risk 2.2, moderate-quality evidence) and brought complete pain resolution about 11 hours earlier (low-quality evidence). A real but modest, delayed symptom benefit from one trial plus a supportive pooling — with the primary outcome of the best trial null — is POSSIBLE, not LIKELY. This is symptom relief only; no claim about complications is made.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Drug route in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest: intraosseous first vs intravenous first (PARAMEDIC-3, IVIO)
question: In out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, does an intraosseous-first vascular-access strategy improve survival at 30 days versus an intravenous-first strategy — and how does the Danish IVIO trial read beside it?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C ruled YES at build: 30-day survival was PARAMEDIC-3's primary outcome, and both trials were null on survival). Two large randomised trials agree: PARAMEDIC-3 (6,082 patients, UK) found 30-day survival of 4.5% with intraosseous-first vs 5.1% with intravenous-first access (adjusted odds ratio 0.94, 95% CI 0.68–1.32), with return of spontaneous circulation actually lower in the intraosseous group (36.0% vs 39.1%; adjusted odds ratio 0.86, 0.76–0.97); IVIO (1,479 analysed patients, Denmark) found sustained ROSC of 30% vs 29% (risk ratio 1.06) and 30-day survival of 12% vs 10% (risk ratio 1.16, CI crossing 1), and its long-term follow-up found 1-year survival of 11% vs 9% (risk ratio 1.24, CI crossing 1). Faster, easier access (92% vs 80% success within two attempts in IVIO) did not buy survival.

title: Routine low-dose oxygen after acute stroke: the Stroke Oxygen Study (SO2S)
question: In adults with acute stroke who are not hypoxaemic, does routine low-dose oxygen supplementation for the first three days reduce death or disability at 90 days?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: death or disability at 90 days was the primary outcome). SO2S randomised 8,003 non-hypoxaemic adults with acute stroke to continuous oxygen for 72 hours, nocturnal oxygen for 3 nights, or control (oxygen only if clinically indicated): the common odds ratio for a better 90-day modified Rankin outcome was 0.97 (95% CI 0.89 to 1.05; P=.47) for oxygen vs control and 1.03 (0.93 to 1.13) for continuous vs nocturnal oxygen, and no subgroup benefited. No confirmatory or contradicting large trial exists; the currency sweep found none.

title: Rotator cuff tears: tendon repair versus physiotherapy (Moosmayer; Kukkonen)
question: For small-to-medium rotator cuff tears, does surgical repair beat physiotherapy — in traumatic tears, and in non-traumatic tears in older patients?
balance: Split: POSSIBLE both ways, because the two trials ask different questions. In Moosmayer's trial of tears up to 3 cm (many traumatic; repair vs physiotherapy with optional secondary repair), primary repair was statistically better at 5 years — Constant score by 5.3 points (P=0.05), ASES by 9.0 points, pain by 1.1 cm — but the authors themselves state the differences were small and may be below clinical importance, and 12 of 51 physiotherapy patients crossed to repair. In Kukkonen's trial of non-traumatic supraspinatus tears in older patients, repair, acromioplasty and physiotherapy alone did not differ on the Constant score at 2 years (changes 22.6 vs 20.5 vs 18.4 points; P=0.38), while repair cost significantly more. One trial per sub-question caps both halves at POSSIBLE.

title: Acute Achilles tendon rupture: surgery versus non-operative treatment (Myhrvold; Willits; CARTA)
question: Does operative repair of an acute Achilles rupture improve function or reduce re-rupture versus non-operative treatment with functional rehabilitation?
balance: LIKELY: Surgery does not improve function, and it trades one complication profile for another. Myhrvold (554 randomised) found no difference in Achilles tendon Total Rupture Score change at 12 months between non-operative treatment, open repair and minimally invasive surgery (−17.0 vs −16.0 vs −14.7 points; P=0.57), but re-rupture was higher without surgery (6.2% vs 0.6% in each surgical group) while nerve injuries clustered in the surgical groups (5.2% minimally invasive, 2.8% open, 0.6% non-operative). Willits (144 patients, both arms on accelerated functional rehabilitation) likewise found no clinically important difference in strength, motion or scores, with re-rupture in 2 operative vs 3 non-operative patients and more soft-tissue complications with surgery. The newer CARTA trial (300 patients) found an ultrasound-guided individualised algorithm did not improve heel-rise work at 12 months, but cut re-rupture versus default non-operative care (3% vs 11%) while operating on 36% fewer patients than routine surgery. Function: no surgical advantage, across three concordant trials. Re-rupture: surgery (or selecting for it) prevents most re-ruptures, at the price of surgical complications.
stamp: LIKELY

title: Femoroacetabular impingement: hip arthroscopy versus conservative care (FASHIoN, FAIT)
question: In symptomatic femoroacetabular impingement, does hip arthroscopy improve hip-related quality of life more than personalised hip therapy / physiotherapy with activity modification?
balance: LIKELY: Two multicentre randomised trials — unblindable by nature, assessor-blinded — agree that arthroscopy beats good conservative care by a modest, clinically relevant margin. UK FASHIoN (348 participants): iHOT-33 improved to 58.8 with arthroscopy vs 49.7 with personalised hip therapy at 12 months (adjusted mean difference 6.8 points, 95% CI 1.7–12.0), just exceeding the 6.1-point minimum clinically important difference. FAIT (222 participants): Hip Outcome Score ADL at 8 months was 10.0 points higher with arthroscopy (95% CI 6.4–13.6), above its 9-point clinically important difference. The price in FASHIoN was more patient-reported adverse events (147 vs 102 events) including one post-operative hip joint infection; FAIT reported no serious adverse events. Benefit is real but single-digit-to-10 points on 100-point scales — an average gain, not a transformation.
stamp: LIKELY

title: Unstable ankle fracture in older adults: close contact casting versus surgery (Willett; CROSSBAT)
question: In adults over 60 with an unstable ankle fracture, does close contact casting give equivalent ankle function to surgery, with fewer complications — and what does the younger-adult CROSSBAT trial add?
balance: POSSIBLE: The older-adult question rests on one large equivalence trial. Willett (620 adults over 60) found close contact casting equivalent to surgery on the Olerud-Molander Ankle Score at 6 months (64.5 vs 66.0; mean difference −0.6, 95% CI −3.9 to 2.6, inside the ±6-point equivalence margin; P for equivalence=.001), with far fewer infections and wound breakdowns (1% vs 10%; odds ratio 7.3) and fewer additional operations (1% vs 6%), but more radiological malunion (15% vs 3%; odds ratio 6.0) and a 19% conversion rate from casting to surgery. CROSSBAT, in younger adults (18–65) with a less severe fracture pattern, independently found surgery not superior to non-surgical care (function scores 49.8 vs 53.0) with more adverse events after surgery (32% vs 14%) — supportive, but a different population and fracture, so the older-adult equivalence claim stays at POSSIBLE.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Chronic plantar heel pain: plantar fascia–specific stretching (DiGiovanni)
question: Does a programme of plantar fascia–specific stretching relieve chronic plantar heel pain and keep patients off surgery versus standard Achilles stretching — and what does the shock-wave trial add?
balance: POSSIBLE: One pivotal randomised trial and its own two-year follow-up support plantar fascia–specific stretching: DiGiovanni randomised 101 patients with plantar fasciitis of at least 10 months' duration and found the fascia-specific programme superior to standard Achilles stretching at 8 weeks on worst pain (P=0.02) and first-step morning pain (P=0.006), with better satisfaction; at two years, after all patients had been taught the fascia programme, 92% of respondents reported total satisfaction or satisfaction with minor reservations and 94% reported decreased pain. The confirmatory trial carded here tests a different intervention — Gerdesmeyer's radial shock-wave therapy beat placebo at 12 weeks (VAS composite reduction 72.1% vs 44.7%; overall success 61.0% vs 42.2%) — which supports 'mechanical loading/stimulation treatments can beat controls in recalcitrant heel pain' without confirming stretching itself. One trial for the shelf's own question caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.

title: Total knee replacement versus non-surgical treatment for knee osteoarthritis (Skou / MEDIC)
question: In moderate-to-severe knee osteoarthritis eligible for replacement, does total knee replacement beat a supervised non-surgical programme on pain and function at one year — and at what serious-adverse-event price?
balance: POSSIBLE: A single randomised trial (Skou / MEDIC, 100 patients) found total knee replacement followed by 12 weeks of non-surgical care improved the KOOS4 score more than the same non-surgical programme alone at 12 months (improvement 32.5 vs 16.0 points; adjusted mean difference 15.8, 95% CI 10.0–21.5), but the replacement group had more serious adverse events (24 vs 6; P=0.005). Notably, 26% of the non-surgical group crossed over to replacement within the year while most did not — the authors' own framing is that replacement works better on average and that most patients assigned to non-surgical care still avoided it at one year. No second randomised trial of replacement versus conservative care was found (the currency sweep confirms the gap), so a single 100-patient unblindable trial caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.

title: Preventing hamstring injuries in football: Nordic eccentric training (Petersen)
question: Does a progressive Nordic hamstring eccentric programme reduce overall, new and recurrent hamstring injuries in male footballers?
balance: LIKELY: Petersen's cluster-randomised trial (54 teams, 942 players) found overall hamstring injury rates of 3.8 vs 13.1 per 100 player seasons with the Nordic programme (adjusted rate ratio 0.293, 95% CI 0.150–0.572), with new injuries at 3.1 vs 8.1 (rate ratio 0.410) and recurrent injuries at 7.1 vs 45.8 per 100 player seasons (rate ratio 0.137); the number needed to treat was 13 players to prevent one injury. The Al Attar meta-analysis of programmes including the Nordic exercise (5 studies) independently pooled an injury risk ratio of 0.490 (0.291–0.827), described as up to a 51% relative reduction. Two concordant sources with large relative effects and absolute rates printed beside them earn LIKELY. ('Preventing' here is ordinary sports-injury language for a training programme, not a diabetes-onset claim.)

title: Trigger finger: ultrasound-guided versus blind corticosteroid injection
question: Does ultrasound guidance improve the success of a first corticosteroid injection for trigger finger versus landmark-guided ('blind') injection, measured by symptom resolution and need for surgery?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence): The two randomised comparisons of ultrasound-guided versus blind injection disagree, and both are small. Tunçez 2023 (66 patients) found faster triggering resolution, earlier return to work and better QDASH/VAS scores at weeks 1 and 4 with ultrasound guidance, but no significant difference at 12 or 24 weeks. Cecen 2015 (74 patients) found both groups improved significantly with no significant difference between them at 6 weeks or 6 months, and second injections were needed by 6 blind-group vs 3 ultrasound-group patients (all of those needing a second injection had diabetes). Durability data come from a different comparison: Hansen's trial of open surgery versus ultrasound-guided injection found success falling from 86% at 3 months to 49% at 12 months after injection, versus 99% and 99% after surgery. Whether guidance improves injection success at all is genuinely unsettled — MAYBE (weak evidence). A related ultrasound-versus-landmark randomised paper in this field was retracted (PMID 30947606); it is not carded and its existence is disclosed in the summary.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence)

title: Patellar tendinopathy: heavy slow resistance versus corticosteroid injection versus eccentric training (Kongsgaard)
question: In patellar tendinopathy, how do heavy slow resistance training, eccentric decline-squat training and corticosteroid injection compare at 12 weeks and beyond?
balance: POSSIBLE: One small randomised trial (Kongsgaard, 39 men) carries the whole three-way comparison. All three treatments improved VISA-p function scores and activity pain (VAS) at 12 weeks; by the half-year follow-up, the corticosteroid group's gains had deteriorated while the eccentric and heavy-slow-resistance groups maintained theirs, and treatment satisfaction was highest with heavy slow resistance. Tendon swelling fell in the corticosteroid (−13%) and heavy-slow-resistance (−12%) groups at 12 weeks, and vascularisation fell in both (−52% and −45%), while tendon mechanical properties were unchanged by any treatment. The pattern — injection wins early, training wins late — is clinically coherent and matches wider tendinopathy experience, but 39 patients in one trial is POSSIBLE, never LIKELY. The heavy-slow-resistance trial in Achilles tendinopathy (Beyer) is already carded on Shelf #460 and is fenced here, not re-carded.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Lumbar spinal stenosis: surgery versus non-surgical treatment (Delitto; SPORT)
question: In symptomatic lumbar spinal stenosis, does surgical decompression improve physical function more than a structured physical-therapy programme at two years — against the SPORT programme's as-treated signal?
balance: POSSIBLE: The randomised (intention-to-treat) evidence is close to null, and the pro-surgery signal lives in analyses that crossover contaminates. Delitto (169 surgical candidates) found mean physical-function improvement at 2 years of 22.4 points with surgery vs 19.2 with physical therapy (intention-to-treat difference 0.9 points, 95% CI −7.9 to 9.6), with 57% of the therapy group crossing to surgery — and causal-effects sensitivity analyses accounting for crossover still showed no significant difference. SPORT's randomised cohort (289 patients) found a significant intention-to-treat advantage for surgery only on bodily pain (mean difference 7.8, 1.5–14.1), not on physical function or the Oswestry Disability Index; its combined as-treated analysis (randomised plus observational cohorts, 654 patients) favoured surgery on all primary outcomes by 3 months, sustained at 2 years — but as-treated comparisons after 43–67% treatment switching are observational in effect. Honest stamp: POSSIBLE that surgery helps some patients more than therapy; the randomised comparisons do not prove a functional advantage.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Albuterol–budesonide rescue inhaler for asthma (MANDALA, BATURA)
question: In asthma, does as-needed albuterol–budesonide fixed-dose rescue reduce severe exacerbations versus as-needed albuterol alone — in moderate-to-severe disease (MANDALA) and in mild disease (BATURA)?
balance: LIKELY: Two large double-blind event-driven trials agree across severity. In uncontrolled moderate-to-severe asthma (MANDALA, 3,132 patients), the higher-dose combination (albuterol 180 µg / budesonide 160 µg) lowered the risk of a first severe exacerbation versus albuterol alone (hazard ratio 0.74, 95% CI 0.62 to 0.89 — a relative measure; the abstract reports no absolute event rates for MANDALA); the lower-dose combination did not reach significance (HR 0.84, 0.71 to 1.00; P=0.052). In mild asthma (BATURA, 2,516 participants), a severe exacerbation occurred in 5.1% on the combination versus 9.1% on albuterol alone in the on-treatment population (HR 0.53, 0.39 to 0.73, relative). Both headline hazard ratios sit inside the 0.5–2.0 band this library treats cautiously on its own; the stamp rests on two concordant randomised trials, not on either ratio alone.
stamp: LIKELY

title: Dupilumab in uncontrolled asthma: exacerbations (QUEST) and steroid dependence (VENTURE)
question: Does dupilumab reduce severe exacerbations in moderate-to-severe uncontrolled asthma (LIBERTY ASTHMA QUEST) — and can it let glucocorticoid-dependent patients cut their oral steroid dose without losing control (VENTURE)?
balance: LIKELY: Two double-blind placebo-controlled trials answer the two halves of the question. title: Omalizumab for severe allergic asthma (Busse; INNOVATE)
question: Does anti-IgE omalizumab reduce exacerbations and steroid use in severe allergic asthma inadequately controlled on inhaled therapy — in Busse's pivotal trial and in the INNOVATE programme in the most severe patients?
balance: LIKELY: Two double-blind placebo-controlled trials, in progressively more severe populations, agree. Busse 2001 (525 patients with inhaled-corticosteroid-dependent severe allergic asthma) found fewer exacerbations per subject on omalizumab than placebo in both the stable-steroid phase (0.28 versus 0.54) and the steroid-reduction phase (0.39 versus 0.66), with greater inhaled-steroid reduction (median 75% versus 50%). INNOVATE (419 patients inadequately controlled despite high-dose ICS-LABA) found an adjusted clinically significant exacerbation rate of 0.68 versus 0.91 (a 26% relative reduction; P=0.042) and a severe-exacerbation rate of 0.24 versus 0.48 (P=0.002). Effects are modest in relative terms and sit inside the 0.5–2.0 band; the stamp rests on two concordant randomised trials. title: Single-inhaler triple therapy in uncontrolled asthma (TRIMARAN, TRIGGER, IRIDIUM)
question: In asthma uncontrolled on medium- or high-dose ICS-LABA, does adding a long-acting muscarinic antagonist in the same inhaler improve lung function and exacerbations — in the beclometasone–formoterol–glycopyrronium trials (TRIMARAN, TRIGGER) and the indacaterol-based IRIDIUM trial?
balance: Split: LIKELY for lung-function benefit; POSSIBLE for exacerbation reduction. Three large double-blind trials consistently improved pre-dose/trough FEV1 when a LAMA was added in the same inhaler: by 57 mL (TRIMARAN) and 73 mL (TRIGGER) versus beclometasone–formoterol, and by 65–76 mL (IRIDIUM) versus matched mometasone–indacaterol. The exacerbation evidence is thinner: moderate/severe exacerbation rates fell by 15% in relative terms in TRIMARAN (rate ratio 0.85, 95% CI 0.73 to 0.99) but by a non-significant 12% in TRIGGER (0.88, 0.75 to 1.03), and IRIDIUM's primary endpoint was lung function, not exacerbations. Relative ratios of 0.85–0.88 sit well inside the 0.5–2.0 band this library does not treat as solid on their own — hence POSSIBLE for that half of the claim.

title: Peanut epicutaneous immunotherapy: the Viaskin patch (PEPITES, EPITOPE)
question: Does a daily peanut patch (250 µg) raise the reaction threshold in peanut-allergic children — in school-age children (PEPITES, which missed its pre-set clinical bar) and in toddlers (EPITOPE)?

title: Icatibant and C1-inhibitor for acute hereditary angioedema attacks (FAST-3, IMPACT)
question: For an acute hereditary angioedema attack, does on-demand treatment shorten time to symptom relief — icatibant, a bradykinin B2-receptor antagonist (FAST-3), and plasma-derived C1-inhibitor concentrate (IMPACT)?
balance: LIKELY: Two double-blind placebo-controlled trials of two different on-demand drugs agree that treatment shortens time to relief. IMPACT (125 patients) found a median time to onset of relief of 0.5 hours on C1-inhibitor concentrate 20 U/kg versus 1.5 hours on placebo (P=.0025), with the 10 U/kg dose not significantly better than placebo. title: Bronchial thermoplasty for severe asthma (AIR2, RISA)
question: In severe asthma uncontrolled on ICS-LABA, does bronchial thermoplasty reduce severe exacerbations and emergency visits versus a sham bronchoscopy procedure (AIR2) — at what cost in peri-procedure hospitalisations?
balance: POSSIBLE: One sham-controlled trial with a modest quality-of-life primary, one small unblinded safety trial. AIR2 (288 adults) found a superior improvement in integrated Asthma Quality of Life Questionnaire score with thermoplasty versus sham (1.35 versus 1.16; posterior probability of superiority 96.0% in the intention-to-treat analysis), with fewer severe exacerbations, emergency department visits and days missed in the post-treatment period — but 6% more thermoplasty subjects were hospitalised during the treatment period (up to 6 weeks after the procedure). RISA (32 subjects) likewise found transient worsening and 7 hospitalisations in 4 of 15 treated subjects during treatment, against later improvements in rescue-medication use and asthma control. A single sham-controlled trial with Bayesian analysis and a peri-procedure harm signal caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.

title: Benralizumab for eosinophilic COPD exacerbations (GALATHEA, TERRANOVA, ABRA)
question: In COPD with eosinophilic inflammation and frequent exacerbations, does benralizumab prevent COPD exacerbations (the twin GALATHEA and TERRANOVA trials, both null) — and does a single dose help during an acute eosinophilic exacerbation (ABRA)?
balance: Split: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for maintenance prevention; POSSIBLE for acute treatment. title: Ligelizumab for chronic spontaneous urticaria (phase 2b, PEARL 1 & 2)
question: Does the high-affinity anti-IgE antibody ligelizumab control hives better than placebo — and better than omalizumab — in chronic spontaneous urticaria inadequately controlled by antihistamines (Maurer's phase 2b dose-finding trial and the PEARL phase 3 programme)?

title: The VITAL factorial: vitamin D and marine omega-3 for cancer and cardiovascular outcomes
question: In generally healthy adults, does vitamin D3 (2,000 IU/day), marine omega-3 (1 g/day), both, or neither lower the incidence of invasive cancer or major cardiovascular events (VITAL, n=25,871, two-by-two factorial design)?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C; the outcomes tested are invasive cancer and major cardiovascular events): In VITAL's 25,871 participants (median follow-up 5.3 years), vitamin D did not lower invasive cancer (793 versus 824 cases; hazard ratio 0.96, 95% CI 0.88 to 1.06 — relative) or major cardiovascular events (396 versus 409; HR 0.97, 0.85 to 1.12), and marine omega-3 did not lower major cardiovascular events (386 versus 419; HR 0.92, 0.80 to 1.06) or invasive cancer (820 versus 797; HR 1.03, 0.93 to 1.13). All-cause mortality was also null for both (vitamin D HR 0.99; omega-3 HR 1.02). This is one very large factorial trial answering two intervention questions in one cohort — not two independent trials — and the word 'prevention' appears on this shelf only because it is the trial's own stated question; the answer the trial returned was no. The omega-3 secondary finding of fewer total myocardial infarctions (HR 0.72, 0.59 to 0.90) is a secondary endpoint inside a null-primary trial and is not a benefit claim. Fish oil and atrial fibrillation (a harm question) lives on Shelf #41 and is not re-carded here.

title: Alternate-day oral iron absorption (Stoffel programme)
question: In iron-depleted and iron-deficiency-anaemic women, is fractional iron absorption from oral supplements higher when doses are given on alternate days as single morning doses than on consecutive days or split twice daily (Stoffel's randomised absorption trials)?
balance: POSSIBLE: The absorption physiology is consistent across the programme, but every endpoint on this shelf is absorption, not a clinical outcome. In iron-depleted women (Stoffel 2017, two trials in one report), cumulative fractional absorption was 21.8% on alternate-day dosing versus 16.3% on consecutive-day dosing (p=0.0013), with total absorbed iron 175.3 versus 131.0 mg (p=0.0010); splitting the daily dose in two did not help (fractional absorption 11.8% once daily versus 13.1% twice daily; p=0.33). In women with iron-deficiency anaemia (Stoffel 2020, crossover), fractional absorption on the alternate-spaced day was 40–50% higher than on the second consecutive day (P<0.001) for both 100 and 200 mg doses. Dosing raises hepcidin for about 24 hours, and the next day's dose pays for it. Whether the absorption gain converts into faster anaemia correction in routine care is not tested here — hence POSSIBLE, on absorption endpoints alone. Intravenous iron shelves (#122, #294, #369, #673) are different questions and are not re-carded.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Alternate-day fasting versus daily calorie restriction (Trepanowski, HELENA)
question: Does alternate-day fasting (or 5:2 intermittent restriction) produce more weight loss, better weight maintenance, or better cardiometabolic risk markers than daily calorie restriction at one year (Trepanowski; HELENA)?
balance: LIKELY (equivalence, not superiority): Two randomised trials with matched energy deficits agree that intermittent schedules lose no more weight than daily restriction. Trepanowski (100 metabolically healthy obese adults, 1 year) found identical month-6 weight loss (−6.8% in both the alternate-day-fasting and daily-restriction groups) and similar month-12 loss (−6.0% versus −5.3%), with the highest dropout in the fasting group (38% versus 29%) and LDL cholesterol significantly higher on fasting by month 12 (between-group difference 11.5 mg/dL, 95% CI 1.9 to 21.1). HELENA (150 overweight/obese adults, 50 weeks) found week-50 weight loss of −5.2% (intermittent 5:2) versus −4.9% (continuous) (P for the comparison = 0.89) and no differences in adipose-tissue gene expression or circulating metabolic biomarkers. The claim stamped LIKELY is the negative one: intermittent fasting is not superior to the daily restriction it replaces.
stamp: LIKELY (equivalence, not superiority)

title: Early high-dose vitamin D in critically ill vitamin-D-deficient patients (VIOLET, VITdAL-ICU)
question: In critically ill patients with vitamin D deficiency, does a single early high dose of vitamin D3 (540,000 IU) reduce mortality versus placebo (VIOLET, stopped for futility) — and what did the earlier VITdAL-ICU trial show?

title: Honey for acute cough in children (Cochrane evidence)

title: Gluten restriction in self-reported non-coeliac gluten sensitivity (Biesiekierski)
question: In patients with IBS-type symptoms who believe gluten harms them, does gluten itself reproduce symptoms once fermentable carbohydrates (FODMAPs) are controlled (Biesiekierski's double-blind crossover trial) — and how does that sit beside the same group's earlier positive challenge trial?
balance: POSSIBLE (gluten-specific effects not reproduced once FODMAPs are controlled): The 2011 trial (34 patients, symptoms controlled on a gluten-free diet, no FODMAP control) found gluten worsened symptoms — 13 of 19 (68%) on gluten reported inadequately controlled symptoms versus 6 of 15 (40%) on placebo. The same group's 2013 crossover trial (37 subjects) first put everyone on a reduced-FODMAP diet — symptoms improved consistently — and then challenged with high-gluten (16 g/day), low-gluten or whey-control diets: symptoms worsened to a similar degree on gluten and on whey, gluten-specific effects appeared in only 8% of participants, no biomarker changed, and a 3-day rechallenge in 22 participants reproduced no gluten-specific effect. One small positive trial superseded in design by one small rigorous negative trial from the same investigators: POSSIBLE that the culprit in most self-reported gluten sensitivity is not gluten itself. The low-FODMAP diet shelf itself is already built elsewhere; this shelf asks only the gluten-specific question and does not re-card it.
stamp: POSSIBLE (gluten-specific effects not reproduced once FODMAPs are controlled)

title: Omega-3 fatty acids in pregnancy and preterm birth (ORIP)
question: Does prenatal omega-3 long-chain fatty-acid supplementation reduce early preterm birth in an unselected obstetric population (ORIP, n≈5,500) — against the pooled signal from the earlier, smaller trials in the Cochrane review?
balance: Split: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) in an unselected population; POSSIBLE for the pooled earlier-trial signal. ORIP (5,486 pregnancies in the primary analysis) found early preterm delivery (before 34 weeks) in 2.2% on n-3 supplements versus 2.0% on control (adjusted relative risk 1.13, 95% CI 0.79 to 1.63; P=0.50) — no reduction, in the largest single trial. The Cochrane review (70 trials, 19,927 women) pooled a lower risk of preterm birth before 37 weeks (risk ratio 0.89, 0.81 to 0.97 — relative; high-quality evidence) and of early preterm birth before 34 weeks (RR 0.58, 0.44 to 0.77; 9 trials, 5,204 participants; high-quality evidence), alongside more prolonged gestation beyond 42 weeks (RR 1.61, 1.11 to 2.33) — a pooling dominated by smaller, often higher-risk-population trials that ORIP does not reproduce in an unselected population. Neither half is strong enough to erase the other: both are stamped POSSIBLE. (In the Cochrane abstract the comparison percentages are printed control-first; they are presented that way, and flagged, on the card.)

title: Ascorbic acid, corticosteroids and thiamine in septic shock (ACTS, VITAMINS)
question: In septic shock, does the combination of ascorbic acid, hydrocortisone and thiamine reduce organ injury (SOFA change) versus placebo (ACTS) — and does it beat hydrocortisone alone on time alive and free of vasopressors (VITAMINS)?

title: Enteral glutamine for major burn injury (RE-ENERGIZE)
question: In patients with severe burns, does enteral glutamine supplementation reduce time to discharge alive, infections, or mortality versus placebo (RE-ENERGIZE)?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): A single very large double-blind trial is enough, under this library's rule for a very large null, to carry the null at LIKELY. RE-ENERGIZE (1,200 patients analysed with severe burns, mean burn size 33% of total body surface area) found a median time to discharge alive of 40 days on enteral glutamine (0.5 g/kg/day) versus 38 days on placebo (subdistribution hazard ratio for discharge alive 0.91, 95% CI 0.80 to 1.04; P=0.17 — a relative measure, with death handled as a competing risk), and 6-month mortality of 17.2% versus 16.2% (HR 1.06, 0.80 to 1.41 — relative, printed beside the discharge outcome per this library's rule for any composite-adjacent endpoint). No substantial differences in serious adverse events were observed. TIER C note: mortality was a secondary outcome and no benefit claim is made, so the shelf is not flagged Tier C; if the developer reads the discharge-alive composite as Tier C territory, it returns for his verdict — that choice is his, and it is recorded in summary.md. The general-critical-illness glutamine trial (REDOXS) is already carded elsewhere and is fenced, not re-carded, here; the general ICU-nutrition shelves (#16, #21, #110) test different questions.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference)

title: Restrictive versus liberal intravenous fluid in septic shock (CLASSIC, CLOVERS, ARISE FLUIDS)
question: In patients with septic shock or sepsis-induced hypotension, does a restrictive intravenous fluid strategy (with earlier vasopressors) change mortality versus standard or liberal fluid therapy?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, mortality primary outcome): Three large randomised trials now agree. CLASSIC (1,554 ICU patients with septic shock) found 90-day mortality of 42.3% with fluid restriction versus 42.1% with standard therapy. CLOVERS (1,563 patients with sepsis-induced hypotension) found mortality before discharge home by day 90 of 14.0% with a restrictive, vasopressor-early strategy versus 14.9% with a liberal strategy. The currency sweep added a third, concordant trial, ARISE FLUIDS (1,000 emergency-department patients, 2026), whose primary outcome — days alive and out of hospital at day 90 — was identical at a median of 76 days in both groups. Restricting fluid (within the ranges these trials achieved, roughly 1.1–2.1 litres less) does not save lives; neither, on this evidence, does giving more.

title: Fractional-dose yellow fever vaccination: one-fifth of a dose, the same antibodies?
question: Do fractional (one-fifth) doses of 17D yellow fever vaccines produce seroconversion non-inferior to full doses, in adults and in young children?
balance: LIKELY: In adults, a randomised double-blind non-inferiority trial of all four WHO-prequalified vaccines (960 enrolled; 900 in the per-protocol analysis) found fractional doses met non-inferiority for day-28 seroconversion for every vaccine (absolute differences from −0.90% to +1.82%). In young children, the YEFE substudy of the same programme (420 children aged 9–59 months) also met non-inferiority at day 28 (97% vs 100% seroconversion; difference −2 percentage points, 95% CI −5 to 1), although fewer children had seroconverted by day 10. These are immunogenicity endpoints for an outbreak dose-sparing strategy — labelled as such — and the consistency across products, substrains and ages supports LIKELY.
stamp: LIKELY

title: BCG vaccination against COVID-19 in healthcare workers (BRACE)
question: Does BCG vaccination reduce symptomatic and severe COVID-19 in healthcare workers — the largest randomised test of the trained-immunity hypothesis — and what did its 12-month outcomes show?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): BRACE randomised 3,988 healthcare workers to BCG-Denmark or saline placebo. At 6 months, symptomatic COVID-19 was 14.7% on BCG versus 12.3% on placebo (risk difference +2.4 points, 95% CI −0.7 to 5.5) and severe COVID-19 was 7.6% versus 6.5% — numerically worse, not better. The 12-month report of the same trial (counted once) found symptomatic COVID-19 significantly HIGHER with BCG (22.6% vs 19.6%; adjusted difference +3.0 points, 95% CI 0.2 to 5.8; p=0.04), with hospitalisations 11 versus 7. A large blinded trial whose follow-up moves against the hypothesis carries LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for BCG as COVID-19 protection.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference)

title: Cefiderocol for Gram-negative infection (APEKS-NP and CREDIBLE-CR)
question: Is cefiderocol non-inferior to high-dose extended-infusion meropenem for Gram-negative nosocomial pneumonia — and how does its mortality record in the CREDIBLE-CR trial of carbapenem-resistant infections read beside it?
balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, mortality outcomes on both cards): In APEKS-NP (300 randomised patients with Gram-negative nosocomial pneumonia), cefiderocol was non-inferior to high-dose extended-infusion meropenem on day-14 all-cause mortality (12.4% vs 11.6%; adjusted difference 0.8%, 95% CI −6.6 to 8.2, against a 12.5% margin). In CREDIBLE-CR — a descriptive, non-powered randomised trial in carbapenem-resistant infections — clinical cure was similar to best available therapy, but more patients died on cefiderocol (34% vs 18% by end of study), driven by the Acinetobacter subset, as the record itself reports. One non-inferiority trial plus an unresolved mortality imbalance caps at POSSIBLE, and the imbalance is why this shelf is Tier C.

title: Ensitrelvir for mild-to-moderate COVID-19 (SCORPIO-SR, SCORPIO-HR)
question: Does the oral 3CL-protease inhibitor ensitrelvir shorten symptom resolution in mild-to-moderate COVID-19 versus placebo — in the Japanese SCORPIO-SR trial and in the global SCORPIO-HR trial?
balance: Split: POSSIBLE — symptom shortening in SCORPIO-SR · POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) in SCORPIO-HR. SCORPIO-SR (1,030 patients in the primary analysis population, treated within 72 hours of onset in Japan, Vietnam and South Korea) found 125-mg ensitrelvir shortened time to resolution of five characteristic Omicron symptoms by about 1 day of median time (167.9 vs 192.2 hours; P=0.04). SCORPIO-HR (2,093 non-hospitalised adults globally; 1,888 treated within 3 days) found NO significant difference in time to sustained resolution of 15 symptoms (12.5 vs 13.1 days; difference −0.6 days, 95% CI −1.38 to 0.19; P=0.14), despite clear antiviral activity (day-4 viral RNA reduced by 0.72 log10 more; negative cultures 95.5% vs 75.0%). Symptom-resolution outcomes only — no mortality claim, not Tier C. The split is the honest summary: a modest symptom benefit in one population and endpoint definition, not reproduced in the other.
stamp: Split

title: Retatrutide, the triple-hormone agonist: phase 2 in obesity and in type 2 diabetes
question: Does once-weekly retatrutide (GIP/GLP-1/glucagon triple agonist) produce weight loss in adults with obesity (phase 2) — and glycaemic control and weight loss in type 2 diabetes against dulaglutide and placebo (phase 2) — at what gastrointestinal price, ahead of any outcomes trial?
balance: LIKELY: The phase 2 signal has been confirmed at phase 3 scale for weight. TRIUMPH-1 (2,339 adults with obesity without diabetes) found −25.0% body weight at 80 weeks on 12 mg versus −3.9% on placebo, extending the phase 2 obesity result (−24.2% at 48 weeks; Jastreboff 2023). In type 2 diabetes, the phase 2 trial (Rosenstock 2023: HbA1c −2.02% on 12 mg at 24 weeks versus −0.01% on placebo and −1.41% on dulaglutide 1.5 mg) is backed by two phase 3 reports fenced in the synthesis (TRIUMPH-2 and TRANSCEND-T2D-1). Randomised blinded trials at both stages earn LIKELY for the weight and glycaemic claims. There is still no cardiovascular-outcomes trial, the gastrointestinal price and the dose-dependent heart-rate signal from phase 2 stand, and no event claim is made on this shelf.
stamp: LIKELY

title: Orforglipron, the daily oral small-molecule GLP-1 agonist: phase 2 in obesity and type 2 diabetes
question: Does daily oral orforglipron — a non-peptide GLP-1 receptor agonist needing no food or water restrictions — produce weight loss in obesity (phase 2) and A1c and weight reductions in type 2 diabetes (phase 2 dose-response)?
balance: LIKELY: A daily oral small-molecule GLP-1 agonist, taken with no food or water restrictions, now has concordant randomised evidence at both stages — phase 2 in obesity (Wharton 2023, 272 adults: −9.4% to −14.7% at 36 weeks versus −2.3% on placebo) and in type 2 diabetes (Frias 2023, 383 adults: HbA1c up to −2.10% at 26 weeks versus −0.43% on placebo), and phase 3 in obesity (ATTAIN-1, 3,127 patients: −11.2% at the 36 mg dose versus −2.1% at 72 weeks). The ACHIEVE phase 3 diabetes programme is fenced in the synthesis. The gastrointestinal price is the class's own (discontinuation 5.3 to 10.3% in ATTAIN-1). No cardiovascular-outcomes claim is made on this shelf.

title: Cagrilintide plus semaglutide (CagriSema): the REDEFINE phase 3 pair
question: Does co-administered once-weekly cagrilintide (amylin analogue) with semaglutide beat either component's expected effect on weight — in obesity without diabetes (REDEFINE 1) and in type 2 diabetes (REDEFINE 2)?
balance: LIKELY: Two parallel phase 3 randomised, double-blind trials of the same combination — REDEFINE 1 (3,417 adults without diabetes: −20.4% body weight at 68 weeks versus −3.0% on placebo) and REDEFINE 2 (1,206 adults with type 2 diabetes: −13.7% versus −3.4%, with 73.5% versus 15.9% reaching an HbA1c of 6.5% or less) — agree that co-administered cagrilintide plus semaglutide produces weight loss beyond either component's established effect, at a gastrointestinal price paid by roughly three quarters of treated participants (79.6% and 72.5%, versus 39.9% and 34.4% on placebo). Two large blinded phase 3 trials earn LIKELY for the weight and glycaemic outcomes; there is no cardiovascular-outcomes trial of the combination, and no event claim is made.
stamp: LIKELY

title: Setmelanotide for melanocortin-4-receptor pathway obesity: POMC/LEPR deficiency and Bardet–Biedl syndrome
question: Does the MC4R agonist setmelanotide produce weight loss and hunger reduction in severe obesity due to POMC, PCSK1 or LEPR deficiency (single-arm phase 3 trials, judged against a pre-set responder bar) — and in Bardet–Biedl and Alström syndromes, where a randomised placebo-controlled phase 3 trial exists?
balance: Split: POSSIBLE — POMC/LEPR deficiency · POSSIBLE — Bardet–Biedl syndrome (Alström inconclusive). In ultra-rare MC4R-pathway disease the evidence cannot take the usual shape: the POMC/LEPR programme (Clément 2020) is two single-arm, open-label phase 3 trials in 21 people, judged against a prespecified responder bar — 8 of 10 (80%) with POMC deficiency and 5 of 11 (45%) with LEPR deficiency reached at least 10% weight loss at about one year, with hunger scores falling 27.1% and 43.7%. The Bardet–Biedl programme (Haqq 2022) has the randomised design — 38 patients, 14 weeks blinded then open-label — with 32.3% of patients aged 12 or older with Bardet–Biedl syndrome reaching at least 10% weight loss after 52 weeks of setmelanotide; the Alström results were inconclusive. Dramatic responses in diseases with no alternative therapy earn POSSIBLE on both halves, not more: there is no blinded placebo-controlled weight comparison in either programme.
stamp: Split

title: Survodutide, the glucagon/GLP-1 dual agonist, for obesity
question: Does once-weekly survodutide (glucagon/GLP-1 dual agonist) produce dose-dependent weight loss in adults with obesity in its phase 2 dose-finding trial — and how do its gastrointestinal discontinuation rates read against the class?
balance: LIKELY (weight loss in obesity) — with the MASH claim at phase 2 only. The obesity question now has two randomised, double-blind trials at two stages: phase 2 dose-finding (le Roux 2024, 386 treated: −14.9% at the 4.8 mg dose versus −2.8% on placebo at 46 weeks) and phase 3 (SYNCHRONIZE-1, 725 adults: −13.0% at 6.0 mg versus −5.4% on placebo at 76 weeks). The liver claim rests on a single phase 2 biopsy trial (Sanyal 2024: histologic improvement in 47–62% across doses versus 14% on placebo) and is fenced at that strength in the synthesis. Across all three trials the price is gastrointestinal — events in 75% of treated participants in the phase 2 obesity trial and up to 89.7% in phase 3.

title: Bimagrumab in type 2 diabetes with obesity: fat mass down, lean mass up?
question: Does the activin type II receptor antibody bimagrumab reduce body fat mass while preserving or increasing lean mass versus placebo in adults with type 2 diabetes and obesity (phase 2) — the body-composition claim no incretin drug makes?
balance: POSSIBLE: Bimagrumab makes the body-composition claim no incretin drug makes — fat mass down, lean mass up — and two phase 2 randomised, double-blind trials support its direction: in type 2 diabetes with obesity (Heymsfield 2021, 75 patients), fat mass fell 20.5% while lean mass rose 3.6% over 48 weeks against placebo's −0.5% and −0.8%; in obesity without diabetes (Heymsfield 2026, 507 adults), high-dose bimagrumab alone lowered body weight by 9.3 kg and its combination with semaglutide 2.4 mg by 17.8 kg versus 3.3 kg on placebo at 48 weeks. The stamp is POSSIBLE: the diabetes trial randomised only 75 patients and analysed completers, the obesity trial's primary end point is weight rather than composition, and neither trial measures function, strength outcomes or clinical events.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Verapamil to preserve beta-cell function in newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes
question: In children and adolescents with newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes, does daily oral verapamil preserve stimulated C-peptide at 52 weeks versus placebo — the randomised test of the thioredoxin-interacting-protein (TXNIP) hypothesis?
balance: POSSIBLE: Two randomised, double-blind trials at two ages point the same way on the same surrogate: in children and adolescents (Forlenza 2023, 88 participants), verapamil held stimulated C-peptide essentially flat over 52 weeks (0.66 to 0.65 pmol/mL) while placebo fell (0.60 to 0.44 pmol/mL; adjusted difference 0.14 pmol/mL, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.27) — a 30% higher C-peptide level at one year; in adults (Ovalle 2018), the trial reports improved mixed-meal-stimulated C-peptide at 3 and 12 months with lower insulin requirements and fewer hypoglycaemic events, though its abstract prints no figures. The stamp is POSSIBLE: C-peptide is a surrogate for beta-cell function, both trials are small, and neither shows durability beyond a year or a clinical-outcome benefit. This is preservation after diagnosis, not delay of onset — teplizumab's delay question is home on Shelf #567 and is not re-opened here.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Dorzagliatin, the glucokinase activator: the SEED and DAWN phase 3 pair
question: Does the dual-acting glucokinase activator dorzagliatin lower A1c in drug-naïve type 2 diabetes (SEED) and as add-on to metformin (DAWN) versus placebo — the first phase 3 programme of a class three decades in development?
balance: LIKELY: Two parallel phase 3 randomised, double-blind trials in the same journal issue — SEED (463 drug-naïve patients: HbA1c −1.07% on dorzagliatin versus −0.50% on placebo at 24 weeks; estimated treatment difference −0.57%) and DAWN (767 patients on metformin: −1.02% versus −0.36%; difference −0.66%) — agree that the first glucokinase activator lowers HbA1c by a modest, consistent margin, with adverse-event rates similar to placebo and no severe hypoglycaemia or drug-related serious adverse events in either trial. Two concordant blinded phase 3 trials earn LIKELY for the glycaemic claim. The caveats are scope, not consistency: a single-country (China) programme, 24 weeks of controlled treatment, and no cardiovascular-outcomes data for a class whose predecessors failed on durability and hypoglycaemia.
stamp: LIKELY

title: Imeglimin in type 2 diabetes: the TIMES programme
question: Does imeglimin — the first glimin, targeting mitochondrial bioenergetics — lower A1c as add-on to insulin (TIMES 3) and across its Japanese dose-ranging phase 2b trial, in a development programme run almost entirely in one country?
balance: POSSIBLE: The TIMES programme shows a consistent, modest glycaemic effect in Japanese patients — TIMES 3 (215 patients on insulin: placebo-adjusted HbA1c difference −0.60% at 16 weeks, sustained to 52 weeks in open-label extension) and the phase 2b dose-ranging trial (299 patients: placebo-adjusted differences of −0.52%, −0.94% and −1.00% across the 500, 1000 and 1500 mg twice-daily doses at 24 weeks) — with hypoglycaemia balanced against placebo in both. The stamp is POSSIBLE, not LIKELY, because the entire controlled programme was run in one country (Japan), the phase 3 primary period is 16 weeks, and there are no data in other populations or on any outcome beyond HbA1c.

title: Tesamorelin for HIV-associated visceral adiposity
question: In people with HIV and excess abdominal fat on antiretroviral therapy, does the growth-hormone-releasing-factor analogue tesamorelin reduce visceral adipose tissue versus placebo — and what does it do to glucose, the metabolic price of pushing the GH axis?
balance: LIKELY: Two parallel phase 3 randomised, placebo-controlled trials agree that daily tesamorelin selectively shrinks visceral fat in people with HIV and abdominal fat accumulation on antiretroviral therapy — Falutz 2007 (412 patients: visceral adipose tissue −15.2% versus +5.0% on placebo at 26 weeks) and Falutz 2010 (404 patients: −10.9% versus −0.6% at 6 months, deepening to about −18% in those continuing to 12 months and rapidly lost in those switched to placebo) — with triglyceride and cholesterol-ratio improvements in both and, on the shelf's key safety question, no significant differences in glycaemic measures in either trial. Two concordant blinded phase 3 trials earn LIKELY for the visceral-fat claim. The outcome is imaging-measured fat, not cardiovascular events: the metabolic rationale is plausible, the event benefit unproven.
stamp: LIKELY

title: Aprocitentan for resistant hypertension (PRECISION)
question: In resistant hypertension confirmed on standardised triple background therapy, does the dual endothelin antagonist aprocitentan lower office and ambulatory blood pressure through its randomised withdrawal phase (PRECISION) — and at what fluid-retention price?
balance: LIKELY: A phase 3 trial with a built-in randomised withdrawal (PRECISION, 730 patients on standardised triple therapy: office systolic pressure −3.8 and −3.7 mm Hg versus placebo at 4 weeks for the 12.5 mg and 25 mg doses, with pressure rising again by 5.8 mm Hg when treatment was withdrawn) plus an earlier dose-finding trial (Verweij 2020, 490 patients: placebo-corrected office systolic/diastolic decreases of 7.05/4.93, 9.90/6.99 and 7.58/4.95 mm Hg at 10, 25 and 50 mg) establish that the endothelin pathway lowers blood pressure when finally targeted — modestly in resistant hypertension, at a fluid-retention price (oedema or fluid retention in 9% and 18% on drug versus 2% on placebo in PRECISION's blinded part). LIKELY for the blood-pressure claim; there is no outcomes trial, and no event claim is made.
stamp: LIKELY

title: Zilebesiran, the twice-yearly RNA-interference antihypertensive: KARDIA-1 and KARDIA-2
question: Does a single subcutaneous dose of zilebesiran (RNA interference against hepatic angiotensinogen) lower ambulatory blood pressure for up to six months — alone in mild-to-moderate hypertension (KARDIA-1) and added to a standard first-line drug in inadequately controlled hypertension (KARDIA-2)?
balance: POSSIBLE: Two phase 2 randomised, double-blind trials — KARDIA-1 (394 patients, monotherapy after washout: least-squares mean differences versus placebo in 24-hour ambulatory systolic pressure at 3 months of −14.1 to −16.7 mm Hg across regimens) and KARDIA-2 (663 randomised patients, add-on to indapamide, amlodipine or olmesartan: differences of −12.1, −9.7 and −4.5 mm Hg by background-drug cohort) — show that silencing hepatic angiotensinogen lowers pressure for months after a single injection. The stamp is POSSIBLE: both trials are phase 2 with a 3-month primary end point, the placebo group's pressure rose 6.8 mm Hg in KARDIA-1 (inflating the between-group difference), hyperkalaemia, hypotension and acute kidney failure were all numerically commoner on zilebesiran in KARDIA-2, and no trial yet tests repeated dosing over years or any clinical outcome.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Sotatercept for pulmonary arterial hypertension: PULSAR and STELLAR
question: Does the activin-signalling inhibitor sotatercept, added to background PAH therapy, improve exercise capacity and pulmonary vascular resistance (PULSAR, phase 2) and six-minute walk distance with a favourable clinical-worsening composite (STELLAR, phase 3)?
balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: this shelf carries death-containing composites, so it was ruled Tier C at build by the mortality-in-composite test). Three randomised, double-blind trials: PULSAR (phase 2, 106 adults: pulmonary vascular resistance −239.5 dyn·sec·cm-5 versus placebo at the target dose), STELLAR (phase 3, 323 adults: 6-minute walk difference 40.8 m at 24 weeks, with time to death or clinical worsening among its significantly improved secondary end points — its abstract prints no figure for that end point, and none is printed here), and ZENITH (phase 3, 172 high-risk patients, stopped early: the composite of death, transplant or hospitalisation occurred in 17.4% versus 54.7%, relative hazard ratio 0.24, with death itself in 8.1% versus 15.1%). The exercise-capacity and haemodynamic claims earn LIKELY; the event claims are printed with their components and remain PROPOSED at the Tier C gate. The haematologic and bleeding-adjacent prices (thrombocytopenia, raised haemoglobin, epistaxis, telangiectasia) recur across the programme.

title: Inclisiran, the twice-yearly PCSK9 siRNA: ORION-10, ORION-11 and ORION-9
question: Does inclisiran — small interfering RNA against PCSK9, dosed twice a year after loading — lower LDL cholesterol by about half versus placebo in atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease and risk equivalents (ORION-10/11) and in heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia (ORION-9), with the cardiovascular OUTCOMES trial still pending?
balance: LIKELY: Three phase 3 randomised, double-blind trials across two reports — ORION-10 (1,561 patients with ASCVD: LDL cholesterol −52.3% placebo-corrected at day 510) and ORION-11 (1,617 patients with ASCVD or risk equivalents: −49.9%), and ORION-9 in heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia (482 patients: between-group difference −47.9 percentage points) — agree that twice-yearly inclisiran lowers LDL cholesterol by about half, sustained between doses (time-adjusted reductions of 53.8%, 49.2% and −44.3 percentage points), with injection-site reactions the only clearly excess adverse event. Two reports and three trials earn LIKELY — for the LDL claim only, stated on the shelf face: the cardiovascular OUTCOMES trial is still pending, and no event claim is made or implied.

title: Lipoprotein(a) lowering with RNA therapies: pelacarsen and olpasiran phase 2
question: Do hepatocyte-targeted RNA therapies lower lipoprotein(a) by 80–98% — the antisense oligonucleotide pelacarsen in its phase 2 dose-ranging trial, and the siRNA olpasiran in OCEAN(a)-DOSE — with both programmes' cardiovascular OUTCOMES trials still running and no event claim yet earned?
balance: POSSIBLE: Two phase 2 randomised, double-blind dose-ranging trials of two different hepatocyte-targeted RNA molecules agree that lipoprotein(a) can be lowered by magnitudes no previous drug approached — pelacarsen (Tsimikas 2020, 286 patients with cardiovascular disease: mean decreases of 35% to 80% across dosing regimens versus 6% on placebo) and olpasiran (OCEAN(a)-DOSE, 281 patients: placebo-adjusted mean changes of −70.5% to −101.1% at 36 weeks). The stamp is POSSIBLE, and the shelf face carries the limit in plain words: lipoprotein(a) is a surrogate, both trials are phase 2, and both programmes' cardiovascular OUTCOMES trials are still running — no event claim has been earned by any Lp(a)-lowering drug, and none is made here.

title: Olezarsen for apolipoprotein C-III: familial chylomicronaemia and high-risk hypertriglyceridaemia
question: Does the antisense oligonucleotide olezarsen lower triglycerides and apolipoprotein C-III and reduce acute pancreatitis events in familial chylomicronaemia syndrome (Balance) — and lower triglycerides in high-cardiovascular-risk hypertriglyceridaemia (Bridge–TIMI 73a)?
balance: LIKELY: Randomised, double-blind trials now cover the apoC-III question at every severity: Balance (phase 3, 66 patients with familial chylomicronaemia: triglycerides −43.5 percentage points versus placebo at 80 mg, with 11 adjudicated pancreatitis episodes on placebo versus 1 in each olezarsen group), Bridge–TIMI 73a (phase 2b, 154 patients: −49.3 and −53.1 percentage points), ESSENCE-TIMI 73b (phase 3, 1,349 patients with mainly moderate hypertriglyceridaemia: −58.4 and −60.6 percentage points) and the fenced CORE pair in severe hypertriglyceridaemia (synthesis), which adds a pancreatitis rate ratio of 0.15 (relative; 95% CI 0.05 to 0.40). LIKELY for the triglyceride and apoC-III claims. title: Preoperative intravenous iron for anaemia before major abdominal surgery (PREVENTT)
question: In patients with anaemia undergoing major open abdominal surgery, does a single preoperative dose of intravenous iron reduce blood transfusion, complications or death versus placebo (PREVENTT) — given two to six weeks before surgery, as guidelines assumed it would?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C ruling at build: death is a component of PREVENTT's coprimary composite of transfusion or death, so by the mortality-in-composite test the shelf goes to the developer personally). PREVENTT (487 randomised) gave a single 1,000 mg ferric carboxymaltose dose 10–42 days before surgery and found the coprimary composite of death or transfusion in 29% on iron versus 28% on placebo (risk ratio 1.03, 95% CI 0.78 to 1.37), with transfusion counts no different (105 versus 111; rate ratio 0.98). A single moderately sized trial supports POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) rather than the large-null LIKELY: the interval still admits a transfusion benefit or harm of about a fifth either way, and no confirmatory placebo-controlled trial in abdominal surgery was pinned at build. title: Aspirin versus anticoagulants after hip or knee arthroplasty: CRISTAL and EPCAT II
question: After hip or knee arthroplasty, is aspirin enough? Does aspirin beat enoxaparin on symptomatic venous thromboembolism (CRISTAL), and is aspirin non-inferior to rivaroxaban for extended prophylaxis after an initial rivaroxaban run-in (EPCAT II)?
balance: Split: LIKELY on both halves, because the two large trials answer two different questions and both answers are firm. Used from the start as monotherapy, aspirin was worse: CRISTAL (9,711 patients, cluster-randomised across 31 Australian hospitals, stopped early) found symptomatic VTE within 90 days in 3.45% on aspirin versus 1.82% on enoxaparin — non-inferiority failed and enoxaparin was significantly superior (p=0.007). Used as the extended phase after 5 days of rivaroxaban for everyone, aspirin was non-inferior: EPCAT II (3,424 patients) found VTE in 0.64% on aspirin versus 0.70% on continued rivaroxaban (difference 0.06 percentage points; p<0.001 for non-inferiority), with major bleeding in 0.47% versus 0.29%. The discordance is the shelf: timing and run-in, not the molecule, explain it. Mortality was a secondary outcome in CRISTAL, reported among six secondary outcomes with none significantly better in the enoxaparin group; no mortality claim is made on this shelf.
stamp: Split

title: Intraoperative ketamine to prevent postoperative delirium and pain in older adults (PODCAST)

title: Speeding gastrointestinal recovery after bowel surgery: alvimopan, and chewing gum

balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): In the single randomised trial (HEADS; 84 infants aged 5–6 months with moderate-to-severe positional skull deformation), six months of helmet therapy changed head shape no more than the natural course — plagiocephaly change-score difference −0.2 (95% CI −1.6 to 1.2; P=0.80) and brachycephaly 0.2 (−1.7 to 2.2; P=0.81) at 24 months, with full recovery in 26% versus 23% (odds ratio 1.2). A single small trial caps the null at POSSIBLE, but its intervals are narrow enough to exclude a large shape benefit, and the authors discourage helmets as standard treatment for healthy infants.

title: Pilocarpine drops for presbyopia: GEMINI 1
question: Does pilocarpine 1.25% eye drops, dosed daily, improve mesopic near visual acuity without losing distance vision in presbyopia — and at what price in adverse effects?
balance: POSSIBLE: In the single standalone phase 3 report (GEMINI 1; 323 participants aged 40–55), pilocarpine 1.25% once daily beat vehicle on the primary endpoint — gaining ≥3 lines of mesopic near visual acuity at hour 3 on day 30 in 30.7% versus 8.1% (difference 22.5 percentage points) — with a smaller margin at hour 6 (18.4% vs 8.8%) and no participant with a near gain losing more than 5 letters of distance acuity. The twin trial, GEMINI 2, has no standalone report — only a pooled analysis exists, which the library does not card as an anchor — so this remains a single-report shelf and caps at POSSIBLE. title: Lotilaner for Demodex blepharitis: Saturn-1 and Saturn-2
question: Does lotilaner 0.25% ophthalmic solution eradicate Demodex mites and clear collarettes versus vehicle in Demodex blepharitis?

title: SMILE versus LASIK for myopia
question: Does small-incision lenticule extraction (SMILE) match femtosecond LASIK on visual quality and patient experience in myopia?
balance: POSSIBLE: The randomised evidence is two small trials with equivalence-shaped results. In the paired-eye trial (70 patients, one eye SMILE and one LASIK), subjective visual symptoms did not differ at 3 months, though SMILE caused more intraoperative discomfort during tissue manipulation and more blurring at 1 month. In the parallel trial (SMILE 113 eyes, FS-LASIK 84 eyes), uncorrected acuity was worse with SMILE on day 1 but identical by 6 months, with less induced spherical aberration after SMILE. The wider SMILE literature is dominated by cohort series and meta-analyses of them, which is itself stated here: two small RCTs with short follow-up earn POSSIBLE, not more.

title: Antibiotics for acute infective conjunctivitis
question: Do topical antibiotics actually shorten acute infective conjunctivitis — fusidic acid versus placebo in adults, and chloramphenicol versus placebo in children — or does a self-limiting illness mostly need time?
balance: LIKELY (antibiotics add little): Two placebo-controlled trials in primary care, one in adults and one in children, point the same way. Fusidic acid in adults: recovery at 7 days differed by an adjusted 5.3 percentage points (95% CI −11 to 18) despite bacterial eradication of 76% versus 41%. Chloramphenicol in children: clinical cure by day 7 was 86% versus 83% (risk difference 3.8%, −4.1% to 11.8%). Most acute infective conjunctivitis resolves by itself; the antibiotic reliably kills bacteria on the swab without reliably speeding the patient's recovery. Two blinded placebo trials carrying the same message earn LIKELY.
stamp: LIKELY (antibiotics add little)

title: Lebrikizumab for moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis: ADvocate 1 and 2, and ADhere
question: Does the IL-13 antibody lebrikizumab clear skin and itch versus placebo — as monotherapy in adolescents and adults (ADvocate 1 and 2), and combined with topical corticosteroids (ADhere)?
balance: LIKELY: Two identically designed phase 3 monotherapy trials (ADvocate 1: 424 patients; ADvocate 2: 427) both met their primary endpoint at week 16 — clear or almost clear skin with ≥2-point improvement in 43.1% and 33.2% on lebrikizumab versus 12.7% and 10.8% on placebo, with EASI-75 in 58.8% and 52.1% versus 16.2% and 18.1%. The combination trial (ADhere, with topical corticosteroids) found the same direction (EASI-75 69.5% vs 42.2%). Conjunctivitis was the consistent excess adverse event. Two blinded trials plus a concordant combination trial carry LIKELY. Dupilumab (Shelf #374) and the oral JAK inhibitors (Shelf #820) are different mechanisms and are not re-carded here.

title: Continuous terbinafine versus pulse itraconazole for toenail onychomycosis: the LION study
question: For toenail onychomycosis, does continuous terbinafine cure more nails than intermittent (pulse) itraconazole — and does the advantage persist at five-year blinded follow-up?
balance: LIKELY: In the LION study (496 patients, double-blind, double-dummy), mycological cure at week 72 was 75.7–80.8% in the continuous terbinafine groups versus 38.3–49.1% in the pulse itraconazole groups (all comparisons P<0.0001). The programme's 5-year blinded follow-up (151 patients) found the gap persisted — mycological cure without second intervention in 46% versus 13%, with relapse roughly twice as common after itraconazole. One randomised programme plus its pre-planned long-term follow-up, with very large and durable differences, carries LIKELY; there were no differences in adverse events between the strategies in LION.

title: Head lice without the comb-out battle: spinosad, and ivermectin lotion
question: Do modern pediculicides clear head lice in one or two applications without nit combing — spinosad versus permethrin creme rinse, and single-application 0.5% ivermectin lotion versus vehicle?
balance: LIKELY: Two product programmes answer the same practical question. title: An oral pill for hereditary angioedema attacks: sebetralstat (KONFIDENT)

title: Oral acyclovir for herpes simplex eye disease: the Herpetic Eye Disease Study
question: Does oral acyclovir help herpes simplex stromal keratitis heal when added to topical steroids — and does a year of suppressive acyclovir after an episode reduce recurrences of ocular herpes?
balance: Split: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for acute stromal treatment — in the HEDS stromal trial (104 patients, all on topical steroids and trifluridine), adding oral acyclovir changed nothing that mattered: median time to treatment failure 84 versus 62 days (not significant), failure by 16 weeks 75% versus 74%, resolution 18% versus 19%. POSSIBLE for recurrence prevention — in the HEDS prevention trial (703 patients), a year of oral acyclovir 400 mg twice daily cut any ocular recurrence from 32% to 19% (P<0.001) and recurrent stromal keratitis from 28% to 14% (P=0.005) in those with prior stromal disease; a single trial, however definitive it became in practice, caps at POSSIBLE under the library's rules. title: Screening for type 2 diabetes, then treating hard: ADDITION-Europe and the Danish screening comparison
question: In people whose diabetes is found by screening, does early intensive multifactorial treatment reduce cardiovascular events versus routine care — and does the screening invitation itself change population mortality?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — Tier C, developer’s personal verdict (the treatment trial’s primary composite includes cardiovascular death and the screening question is a mortality question): ADDITION-Europe (3,055 screen-detected patients, cluster-randomised) found first cardiovascular events in 7.2% versus 8.5% with intensive versus routine treatment (hazard ratio 0.83, 95% CI 0.65 to 1.05 — a relative figure whose interval includes no effect) and all-cause mortality of 6.2% versus 6.7% (hazard ratio 0.91). The Danish population comparison (1,912,392 adults) found screening invitation associated with no reduction in mortality (hazard ratio 0.99) or cardiovascular events (0.99). This shelf is about screen-detected diabetes and earlier treatment; it makes no claim about delaying diabetes onset, and the word for onset is not used here. Delaying the formal diagnosis in prediabetes lives on Shelves #111/#112 and is not re-carded here.

title: Universal HIV testing and treatment for a whole population: PopART and SEARCH
question: Does a community-wide package of home-based HIV testing, linkage support and immediate antiretroviral therapy for all who test positive reduce population HIV incidence versus standard care?
balance: POSSIBLE: Two giant community-randomised trials point in different directions on incidence. PopART (21 communities, about 1 million people) found incidence 30% lower in relative terms where the prevention package was paired with ART per local guidelines (adjusted rate ratio 0.70, 95% CI 0.55 to 0.88) but not where it was paired with universal ART from the start (0.93, 0.74 to 1.18) — an internal inconsistency the authors call unanticipated. SEARCH (32 communities, 150,395 people) raised viral suppression (79% vs 68%) yet found 3-year cumulative incidence essentially identical (0.77% vs 0.81%; relative risk 0.95), while death among HIV-infected persons was lower with the intervention (relative risk 0.77) — a mortality-adjacent finding reported here for context, with no mortality claim built on it. Cluster-randomised by community and unblindable by nature. Mixed incidence evidence across two mega-trials earns POSSIBLE.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Masks as a community intervention: the Bangladesh promotion trial, and DANMASK-19
question: Does promoting surgical masks at village scale reduce symptomatic COVID-19 — and how does that sit beside DANMASK-19, the individually randomised trial of a mask recommendation, which was inconclusive?
balance: POSSIBLE: The Bangladesh cluster-randomised promotion trial (600 villages, 342,183 adults) tripled proper mask-wearing (13.3% to 42.3%) and reduced symptomatic seroprevalence modestly (adjusted prevalence ratio 0.91, 95% CI 0.82 to 1.00 — a relative figure inside the 0.5–2.0 caution band), with a larger effect in surgical-mask villages among adults over 60 (0.65, 0.45 to 0.85, a subgroup). DANMASK-19 (6,024 adults individually randomised to a mask recommendation plus supply, in a low-incidence, masks-uncommon setting) found infection in 1.8% versus 2.1% (odds ratio 0.82, CI includes 1) and was explicitly inconclusive. The design difference is the lesson: promoting masks to a community and recommending them to individuals are different interventions. Both trials are unblindable by nature.

title: A community package for cardiovascular risk: HOPE-4
