title: Deworming a million preschool children: DEVTA
question: Does deworming every six months with albendazole, given to a whole population of preschool children, reduce mortality or improve growth?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, ruled at build: mortality was the programme's headline outcome and was not reduced): DEVTA (about 1 million preschool children in 72 administrative blocks in north India, 5 years) found deaths per child-care centre of 3.00 versus 3.16 (mortality ratio 0.95, 95% CI 0.89 to 1.02 — a relative figure inside the caution band, consistent with no effect), absolute risks of dying between ages 1 and 6 of roughly 2.5% versus 2.6%, and no weight effect (difference 0.04 kg) despite halving worm-egg prevalence (16% vs 36%). The Cochrane synthesis of 51 trials concurs: no effect on mortality (low certainty), height, haemoglobin, cognition or school performance, with any weight effect confined to two decades-old study areas. A mega-trial null plus a concordant synthesis carries LIKELY (the treatment made no difference). DEVTA's companion vitamin A report (PMID 23498849) is already carded on the vitamin A shelves and is fenced here as background, not re-carded.

title: Monthly vitamin D and mortality in older adults: the D-Health trial, with ViDA
question: Does monthly high-dose vitamin D reduce all-cause mortality in older adults, most of whom are not vitamin-D-deficient?

title: Finding domestic violence in primary care, and having somewhere to send her: IRIS and WEAVE
question: Does a primary-care training and support programme with a referral pathway to advocacy (IRIS) increase identification of women experiencing domestic violence and referrals to specialist support — and does screening plus brief counselling (WEAVE) improve women's outcomes?
balance: LIKELY for identification and referral: In IRIS (48 UK general practices, cluster-randomised), a training-and-support programme with a named advocate pathway produced 223 recorded referrals to advocacy versus 12 in control practices over a year (adjusted intervention rate ratio 22.1, a relative figure) and recorded disclosures of 641 versus 236 (rate ratio 3.1). WEAVE (52 Australian doctors, 272 women screening positive) is the necessary counterweight: screening plus brief counselling improved no primary outcome — quality of life, safety planning, or mental health at 12 months — though depression caseness fell (odds ratio 0.3). The shelf's claim is a service claim: training plus a pathway finds women and refers them; it makes no claim that identification alone reduces violence or mortality. title: HPV vaccination in males: the quadrivalent efficacy trial and its long-term extension
question: Does quadrivalent HPV vaccination prevent external genital lesions and vaccine-type HPV infection in young men — and does the protection last?
balance: POSSIBLE: In the single pivotal placebo-controlled trial (4,065 boys and men aged 16–26 from 18 countries), quadrivalent HPV vaccine efficacy against external genital lesions related to HPV 6, 11, 16 or 18 was 65.5% in relative terms in the intention-to-treat population and 90.4% per protocol, with intention-to-treat efficacy of 60.2% against all external genital lesions. title: Defibrillators where the public can reach them: the Public Access Defibrillation trial
question: Does training and equipping lay community volunteers to use automated external defibrillators, alongside CPR, increase survival to discharge after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest versus CPR alone?

title: Cerebral embolic protection in TAVR: PROTECTED TAVR and BHF PROTECT-TAVI

title: Bardoxolone methyl in diabetic kidney disease: BEACON's cardiovascular harm and the TSUBAKI shadow
question: Did bardoxolone methyl, an Nrf2 activator that raised measured eGFR, help or harm patients with type 2 diabetes and stage 4 chronic kidney disease, and what do the later Japanese trials' eGFR rises mean under that shadow?
balance: LIKELY (the harm, and no benefit on the primary outcome) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: this shelf IS a cardiovascular-harm claim from a trial stopped for harm). BEACON (2,185 patients) was terminated early: its primary composite of ESRD or cardiovascular death was identical (6% vs 6%; relative hazard ratio 0.98), while hospitalisation for heart failure or heart-failure death was higher on bardoxolone (96 vs 55 patients; relative hazard ratio 1.83; absolute 8.8% vs 5.0%). The later phase 2 TSUBAKI trial showed a genuine measured-GFR rise (+6.64 ml/min/1.73 m2 vs placebo) in patients screened to exclude heart-failure risk — a surrogate result that cannot launder BEACON's outcome harm, and the shelf presents bardoxolone as a cautionary exhibit, not an option. Nothing on this shelf re-sequences diabetes therapy.

title: Etelcalcetide, an intravenous calcimimetic at dialysis: twin placebo trials and the cinacalcet head-to-head
question: Does intravenous etelcalcetide, given thrice weekly at dialysis, lower parathyroid hormone in secondary hyperparathyroidism more than placebo, and how does it compare with oral cinacalcet — at what cost in hypocalcaemia and gut symptoms?
balance: LIKELY (for PTH lowering — a surrogate): Two parallel placebo-controlled trials in one report (1,023 patients) each found >30% PTH reduction in about three-quarters on etelcalcetide vs under 10% on placebo, and a randomised head-to-head (683 patients) found etelcalcetide noninferior — indeed superior on the primary comparison — to cinacalcet (68.2% vs 57.7% achieving >30% reduction), with more decreased blood calcium (68.9% vs 59.8%). All are PTH-surrogate trials, stated on the shelf face; no calcimimetic trial of this generation showed a mortality benefit, no outcome claim is made, and EVOLVE's null stays home on Shelf #296.
stamp: LIKELY (for PTH lowering — a surrogate)

title: Zibotentan on top of dapagliflozin in chronic kidney disease (ZENITH-CKD)
question: Does adding low-dose zibotentan, a selective endothelin-A antagonist, to dapagliflozin reduce albuminuria more than dapagliflozin alone in chronic kidney disease, and can the SGLT2 inhibitor contain the fluid retention that sank earlier endothelin blockers?
balance: POSSIBLE: One phase 2b trial (ZENITH-CKD, 447 treated patients, 12 weeks) found zibotentan 1.5 mg plus dapagliflozin reduced urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio by -33.7% relative to dapagliflozin alone, and the 0.25 mg dose by -27.0% (both relative measures) — with fluid-retention events in 18% on the higher dose vs 8% on dapagliflozin alone. An albuminuria-surrogate trial; no outcome trial exists yet and the shelf says so. Albuminuria here is a kidney-damage marker and trial surrogate; no claim connects it to diet. No kidney-survival or cardiovascular claim is made.

title: Baricitinib to preserve beta cells in new-onset type 1 diabetes (BANDIT)
question: Does daily baricitinib preserve stimulated C-peptide over 48 weeks in children and young adults with newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes?
balance: POSSIBLE: One phase 2 trial (BANDIT, 91 patients diagnosed within the previous 100 days) found higher mixed-meal-stimulated C-peptide at week 48 on baricitinib than placebo (median 0.65 vs 0.43 nmol/litre/min, P=0.001) and a lower daily insulin dose (0.41 vs 0.52 U/kg/day), with similar glycaemic levels. A C-peptide-surrogate trial; no claim about insulin independence or complications is made. BANDIT is post-diagnosis preservation — this library says DELAY, never prevention, for diabetes onset, and teplizumab's pre-diagnosis delay is home on Shelf #567.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Screening everything at once in men 65-74: DANCAVAS
question: Does inviting men aged 65 to 74 to a single bundled cardiovascular screen — coronary calcium, aneurysm and peripheral-artery imaging, blood pressure, rhythm, cholesterol and diabetes testing, with treatment of what is found — reduce all-cause mortality?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: all-cause mortality was the primary outcome). One very large population-based trial (DANCAVAS, 46,526 men analysed, median follow-up 5.6 years) found death from any cause in 12.6% of the invited group vs 13.1% of controls (relative hazard ratio 0.95; 95% CI 0.90 to 1.00; P=0.06) — not significant. A single very large null trial may carry LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) under the library's rule, stated as the reasoning. Stroke was lower (hazard ratio 0.93, CI 0.86 to 0.99) as a secondary outcome and is labelled secondary. The companion Danish programme, VIVA, is deliberately NOT an anchor here: its primary report is already cited inside built Shelf #530's synthesis card and is fenced against that home, not re-carded. The topic file's note of a signal in the youngest age band is not in the trial abstract, so no subgroup figure is printed.

title: A medical emergency team for the deteriorating ward patient (MERIT)
question: Does introducing a medical emergency team, summoned by calling criteria before arrest, reduce cardiac arrests, unexpected deaths or unplanned ICU admissions across a hospital?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C candidate ruled YES at build: unexpected death is a named component of the primary composite, so the mortality surface returns to the developer; the trial's result was null and no mortality-benefit claim is made). One pivotal cluster-randomised trial (MERIT, 23 Australian hospitals) found the system greatly increased emergency calling (8.7 vs 3.1 per 1000 admissions) without reducing the composite of cardiac arrest, unexpected death or unplanned ICU admission (5.31 vs 5.86 per 1000, p=0.640). A single cluster trial caps the null at POSSIBLE. (The record carries a published erratum, PMID 17470891; not a retraction.)

title: Coaching the WHO Safe Childbirth Checklist into use (BetterBirth)
question: Does a coaching-based implementation programme for the WHO Safe Childbirth Checklist improve maternal and neonatal outcomes, or only the practices on the list?
balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C candidate ruled YES at build: maternal and perinatal mortality sit inside the primary composite; no mortality benefit was shown and none is claimed). One large cluster-randomised trial (BetterBirth, 120 facilities in Uttar Pradesh, 157,689 enrolled women) found the programme substantially improved adherence to 18 essential birth practices (72.8% vs 41.7% at 2 months) but did not improve the composite of perinatal death, maternal death or severe maternal complications (15.1% vs 15.3%; relative risk 0.99). title: Making the serious-illness conversation happen: the Serious Illness Care Program trials
question: Does a system intervention — clinician training, a structured conversation guide, and prompts — produce earlier, better-documented serious-illness conversations and less patient anxiety in advanced cancer?
balance: POSSIBLE: One programme tested in cluster-randomised trials at a single cancer centre, reported in two companion papers (counted as one programme): the communication-outcomes report found documented conversations in 96% of intervention patients vs 79% of controls, a median 2.4 months earlier (143 vs 71 days before death), more comprehensive and far more accessible in the record (61% vs 11%); the patient-outcomes report found its coprimary outcomes (goal-concordant care, peacefulness) null, but significantly fewer patients with moderate-to-severe anxiety (5.0% vs 10.2% at 14 weeks) and depression (10.6% vs 20.8%). Conversation, documentation and mood outcomes; no mortality claim is made — survival did not differ.

title: ICU diaries and post-traumatic stress: Jones 2010 and the French ICU-diary trial
question: Does keeping a diary of a patient's ICU stay, written by staff and family and given to the patient afterwards, prevent post-traumatic stress after critical illness?
balance: Split: POSSIBLE — the treatment made no difference in the larger 2019 trial · MAYBE (weak evidence) — benefit in Jones 2010. Two randomised trials of the same intervention disagree: Jones 2010 (352 randomised) found new-onset PTSD in 5% with a diary vs 13% without (P=0.02), while the larger, assessor-blinded French trial (657 randomised, 339 assessed) found significant PTSD symptoms in 29.9% vs 34.3% (risk difference -4%, CI -15 to 6; P=0.39). The discordance is the shelf: the later, larger, blinded-assessment trial outranks the earlier positive one, and the benefit claim is stamped MAYBE (weak evidence). Psychiatric-symptom outcomes; no mortality claim is made.
stamp: Split

title: An intensivist in the building all night: the nighttime-staffing trial
question: Does adding an in-house nighttime intensivist to a daytime-staffed ICU that already has residents improve mortality or length of stay?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference, in the studied setting): One randomised trial (Kerlin 2013, 1,598 patients, one academic ICU, nights randomised in 7-night blocks) found nighttime in-hospital intensivist staffing did not improve ICU length of stay (rate ratio for discharge 0.98, CI 0.88 to 1.09), ICU mortality (relative risk 1.07, CI 0.90 to 1.28), hospital stay, discharge disposition or readmission. A single-centre trial caps the stamp at POSSIBLE, and its resident-present setting bounds the claim — stated on the shelf face. Mortality was measured and was null; no benefit claim is made, and the topic is not Tier C.

title: Rapid multiplex PCR for bloodstream infection, with a steward at the elbow (Banerjee)
question: Does rapid multiplex PCR identification of blood-culture organisms, reported with antimicrobial-stewardship review, shorten time to effective and optimal therapy versus conventional identification?
balance: POSSIBLE: One randomised trial (Banerjee 2015, 617 patients with positive blood cultures) in a three-arm design showed the test alone cut identification time (1.3 vs 22.3 hours) and reduced contaminant treatment, but the stewardship-paired arm — not the test alone — was fastest to antimicrobial de-escalation (21 vs 34 hours for control and 38 for test alone). Mortality, length of stay and cost did not differ, and none is claimed. The confirmatory rapid-diagnostic randomised report sought at build could not be pinned to a verified record, so the shelf rests on Banerjee alone (see summary). Process and antibiotic-use outcomes only.

title: Housing First for homeless adults with mental illness (At Home/Chez Soi, Stergiopoulos)
question: For homeless adults with mental illness and moderate support needs, does scattered-site housing with rent supplements and intensive case management — offered without treatment preconditions — produce more stable housing than treatment as usual?

title: Nurses initiating and managing HIV treatment: STRETCH and CIPRA-SA
question: Can primary-care nurses initiate and manage antiretroviral therapy as safely as doctors, on mortality and viral suppression, in South African primary care?
balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C candidate ruled YES at build: mortality sits inside both trials' outcome frames — STRETCH's cohort-1 primary outcome was time to death and CIPRA-SA's composite includes mortality; the claims are equivalence of a delivery model, not superiority of a treatment). Two randomised trials agree: STRETCH (16,481 patients in two cohorts, cluster design) found time to death did not differ (hazard ratio 0.94) and viral suppression was equivalent (71% vs 70%); CIPRA-SA (812 patients) found nurse-monitored care noninferior on its composite of treatment-limiting events (hazard ratio 1.09, CI within the 1.40 margin), with deaths 10 vs 11. Unblindable by nature, as care-delivery trials are.

title: Group antenatal care (CenteringPregnancy): the Ickovics trials
question: Does group prenatal care improve perinatal outcomes versus individual care, in Ickovics's first randomised trial and in the New York City cluster-randomised trial in adolescents?
balance: POSSIBLE: Two randomised trials of the same care model in different young populations each found a benefit — on different outcomes: the 2007 trial reduced preterm birth (9.8% vs 13.8%; relative odds ratio 0.67), stronger in African-American women (10.0% vs 15.8%), while the 2016 New York City cluster trial reduced small-for-gestational-age infants (11.0% vs 15.8%; relative odds ratio 0.66) without reporting a preterm-birth effect in its abstract. Each outcome rests on a single trial, and the model is unblindable by nature — POSSIBLE. Preterm-birth and process outcomes; no mortality claim is made. title: Acetazolamide to stop mountain sickness before it starts: the Himalayan trials and the dose question
question: Does acetazolamide prevent acute mountain sickness in travellers ascending fast to high altitude, and is the low 125 mg twice-daily dose as good as 375 mg twice daily?
balance: LIKELY: Three randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials agree that acetazolamide prevents acute mountain sickness on rapid ascent: AMS incidence 12% on acetazolamide versus 34% on placebo in Gertsch's Himalayan factorial trial, 21-24% on either dose versus 51% on placebo in Basnyat's dose-comparison trial (no significant difference between 125 mg and 375 mg twice daily, with more paraesthesia at the higher dose), and 36.9% versus 55.9% with a once-daily extended-release 500 mg preparation in a 2026 Chinese phase III trial. The low dose is the tolerable one and the trials give no reason to prefer the high dose. Ginkgo biloba, tested in the same factorial trial, was no better than placebo. Cross-reference: dexamethasone for mountain sickness is Shelf #1217; high-altitude pulmonary oedema prophylaxis is Shelf #1211.
stamp: LIKELY

title: Stopping high-altitude pulmonary oedema in people who have had it before: nifedipine, and tadalafil or dexamethasone
question: In climbers known to be susceptible to high-altitude pulmonary oedema, does prophylaxis — slow-release nifedipine, or tadalafil or dexamethasone — stop it recurring on rapid re-ascent?
balance: POSSIBLE: Two small randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials in HAPE-susceptible climbers re-ascending rapidly to 4,559 m point the same way — pulmonary oedema in 7 of 11 on placebo versus 1 of 10 on slow-release nifedipine (Bärtsch 1991), and in 7 of 9 on placebo versus 1 of 8 on tadalafil and 0 of 10 on dexamethasone (Maggiorini 2006). The relative effects are very large, but each drug rests on a single trial of 21-29 highly selected susceptible climbers, so under the single-trial ceiling each drug's claim caps at POSSIBLE; neither trial was powered for death and this shelf makes no mortality claim. Acute mountain sickness, the cerebral syndrome, is Shelf #1210 (acetazolamide) and Shelf #1217 (dexamethasone).
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Rewarming is not enough for deep frostbite: iloprost and thrombolysis (the Cauchy trial)
question: After rapid rewarming of severe frostbite, does adding a prostacyclin (iloprost), thrombolysis, or both reduce amputation compared with older vasodilator-based care?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: the primary outcome is amputation, a major-harm outcome). The only randomised trial ever run on medical therapy for severe frostbite, Cauchy 2011, was published by the New England Journal of Medicine as correspondence: its PubMed record (PMID 21226604) carries publication types 'Letter; Randomized Controlled Trial' and contains NO abstract in PubMed or in Europe PMC, so under this library's gate no figure from it can be carded and it is NOT carded here as a trial report — it is fenced in the synthesis, exactly as earlier letter-format records were rejected or fenced rather than silently carded. What can be carded is the 2023 systematic review of 71 reports (978 cases, only one RCT among them), which reports that the single RCT found iloprost beneficial in severe frostbite given within 48 hours and that its meta-analyses of non-randomised data favoured thrombolytics given within 24 hours. That is hypothesis-grade evidence resting on one abstract-less trial report and observational series: MAYBE (weak evidence).

title: One dose of antibiotic for travellers' diarrhoea: azithromycin in Thailand, and the TrEAT TD three-way trial
question: Can a single dose cure travellers' diarrhoea — single-dose azithromycin against longer regimens in Thailand, and three single-dose regimens head-to-head in the military TrEAT TD trial?
balance: LIKELY: Two randomised, double-blind trials a decade apart support single-dose treatment. In Thailand, where Campylobacter predominated and half the isolates were levofloxacin-resistant, single-dose azithromycin cured 96% by 72 hours against 85% for 3-day azithromycin and 71% for 3-day levofloxacin, with the shortest time to last unformed stool. In TrEAT TD, single-dose azithromycin (500 mg) was non-inferior to single-dose levofloxacin for 24-hour clinical cure (78.3% vs 81.4%), with all three single-dose regimens reaching about 96% cure by 72 hours; rifaximin's non-inferiority could not be shown (P=0.07), so the single-dose claim is LIKELY for azithromycin and levofloxacin where susceptibility holds, and unproven for rifaximin. Prevention with rifaximin is a different question — Shelf #1214.
stamp: LIKELY

title: Rifaximin before the trip: chemoprophylaxis of travellers' diarrhoea
question: Does daily rifaximin — a non-absorbed antibiotic that stays in the gut — prevent travellers' diarrhoea in travellers to Mexico versus placebo?
balance: LIKELY: Two randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials in US travellers to Mexico agree: travellers' diarrhoea in 14.74% on rifaximin versus 53.70% on placebo in DuPont 2005 (rate ratio 0.27, a relative figure, with the absolute rates beside it on the card; 72% protection, all three doses superior), and in 20% versus 48% in Martinez-Sandoval 2010 at 600 mg/day (a stated 58% protection rate), with minimal changes in coliform flora in the first trial and fewer adverse events than placebo in the second. title: Which malaria pill for the traveller: atovaquone-proguanil against mefloquine, and against chloroquine-proguanil
question: For non-immune travellers, does atovaquone-proguanil protect against malaria as well as the older standards, with fewer neuropsychiatric and other adverse effects?
balance: POSSIBLE: Two large randomised, double-blind trials in non-immune travellers found atovaquone-proguanil similarly tolerated overall and better tolerated where it matters for adherence — fewer treatment-related neuropsychiatric adverse events than mefloquine (14% vs 29%), fewer moderate/severe events and far fewer discontinuations (1.2% vs 5.0%), and fewer gastrointestinal events than chloroquine-proguanil (12% vs 20%). The efficacy half of the claim is weaker than the tolerability half: no confirmed malaria occurred in either arm of the mefloquine trial, and the chloroquine-proguanil trial's abstract reports adverse events rather than malaria counts, so protection in travellers rests on these equivalence designs plus the endemic-resident efficacy data the abstracts cite — hence POSSIBLE, not LIKELY, and no mortality claim is made (neither trial was powered for malaria death). The Schlagenhauf four-arm mood-profile RCT (PMID 19192127) was verified at drafting and is fenced as background, not carded: it profiles mood effects, not prophylactic efficacy.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Stockings against the flight clot: Scurr's long-haul trial and LONFLIT 4
question: Do graduated compression stockings prevent the symptomless deep-vein thrombosis found by ultrasound after long-haul flights, and what does a benefit confined to ultrasound findings buy?
balance: POSSIBLE: Two randomised trials agree on the surrogate: symptomless calf DVT in 12 of 116 passengers without stockings versus 0 of 115 with class-I stockings in Scurr 2001 (10% vs 0%), and thrombotic events in 6 of 179 controls versus 0 of 179 with flight socks in part I of LONFLIT 4 (and 6 of 143 versus 0 of 142 in part II), with markedly less leg oedema on stockings in both LONFLIT parts. Every event in both trials was asymptomatic and ultrasound-detected; neither trial measured symptomatic venous thromboembolism, pulmonary embolism or death, and this shelf claims none — a real reduction in a silent surrogate, in passengers over 50 or at low-medium risk, is POSSIBLE-grade evidence for the stocking, not proof of prevented clinical events.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Dexamethasone for mountain sickness when acetazolamide is not enough, or not tolerated (Hackett)
question: Does dexamethasone prevent and treat acute mountain sickness, and how should a drug that masks the syndrome without acclimatising the traveller be fenced?
balance: Split: MAYBE (weak evidence) — prevention · POSSIBLE — treatment. The evidence is two small, old reports. In Hackett's Denali field trial, dexamethasone 2 mg every 6 hours did NOT prevent AMS in soldiers flown to 4,400 m (the whole placebo group and 5 of 7 on dexamethasone became ill within 5 hours), so the prevention claim at that dose is MAYBE (weak evidence) and leans null. For treatment, Hackett's open treatment phase (11 men with moderate-to-severe AMS) improved markedly on 4 mg every 6 hours (symptom score 4.5 to 1.0 at 12 hours) with symptoms recurring after abrupt discontinuation (2.4), and Levine's randomised double-blind crossover chamber study (6 men) found dexamethasone reduced symptoms by 63% versus 23% on placebo — real but tiny numbers, capping treatment at POSSIBLE. The fence stands regardless of stamp: dexamethasone suppresses symptoms without acclimatisation, so it is a rescue-and-descent adjunct, never a substitute for going down. Acetazolamide prophylaxis is Shelf #1210; dexamethasone's HAPE-prophylaxis arm sits on Shelf #1211.
stamp: Split

title: Rabies vaccine into the skin, not the muscle: intradermal pre-exposure in children, and the one-week post-exposure regimen
question: Can intradermal dosing — a fraction of the intramuscular dose — immunise reliably enough to stretch scarce rabies vaccine, before exposure in children and after exposure in adults?
balance: LIKELY (for the immunogenicity claim as framed): Two randomised trials of intradermal delivery met their antibody endpoints cleanly. In 703 Thai schoolchildren, 3 intradermal doses of purified chick embryo cell vaccine gave rabies virus-neutralising antibody titres ≥0.5 IU/mL in every subject, with a rapid anamnestic rise after simulated post-exposure boosters a year later and no serious adverse drug reactions (Kamoltham 2007). In 80 healthy Indian adults, the one-week 4-4-4 intradermal post-exposure regimen with either of two vaccines kept every subject ≥0.5 IU/mL from day 14 to day 180, with a successful anamnestic response to a day-365 booster in those who needed it (Sudarshan 2012). Both are antibody-endpoint trials — no trial randomises anyone to forgo prophylaxis after exposure, and none ever will — so the LIKELY stamp covers immunogenicity and safety, not clinical rabies prevented, and the shelf says so.
stamp: LIKELY (for the immunogenicity claim as framed)

title: Scopolamine for seasickness: the naval trial, and the patch question
question: Does scopolamine prevent seasickness — oral scopolamine, alone or with ephedrine, in a naval trial at sea, and the transdermal patch travellers actually use?
balance: POSSIBLE: Two small, old randomised trials support scopolamine at sea. Laitinen 1981 (30 naval cadets, double-blind, placebo-controlled) confirmed the superiority of oral scopolamine 0.3 mg — alone or combined with ephedrine 25 mg — over placebo, with ephedrine adding no clear benefit. Price 1981 found transdermal scopolamine (applied 4 to 16 hours before motion) protective against motion sickness at sea versus placebo (P=0.0001), with oral dimenhydrinate also better than placebo (P=0.05) and minimal dry mouth, drowsiness and blurred vision on the patch. That is the whole randomised patch evidence this gate could pin in English: two trials from 1981 with small numbers, which caps the shelf at POSSIBLE exactly as the topic drafting anticipated. The German-language transdermal report (Becker 1984, PMID 6499689) was verified at drafting and is fenced as background, not carded.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Fix the vein early and the leg ulcer heals: EVRA and ESCHAR
question: In venous leg ulceration, does treating the refluxing vein change healing, or only recurrence — early endovenous ablation (EVRA) against surgery added to compression (ESCHAR)?
balance: LIKELY, with the healing/recurrence split the two trials draw: early endovenous ablation hastened healing in EVRA (median 56 vs 82 days; hazard ratio for healing 1.38, relative, with the absolute medians and 24-week healing rates — 85.6% vs 76.3% — on the card), while ESCHAR's older open surgery did not improve healing at all (89% vs 93% healed at 3 years, P=0.73) but cut recurrence over 4 years (31% vs 56%) and increased ulcer-free time. Together: treat the vein early for healing (modern ablation), and expect the recurrence dividend over years either way. Which compression delivers the pressure while the ulcer heals is Shelf #1221; diabetic foot ulcers are Shelf #291, a different disease.

title: Hosiery or bandages to heal the venous ulcer: VenUS IV
question: Does two-layer compression hosiery heal venous leg ulcers as fast as the four-layer bandage, and do the programme's trials — VenUS I, VenUS IV and VenUS 6 — agree on which compression system to use?
balance: LIKELY: Three randomised trials from one programme converge. VenUS I (2004) found the four-layer bandage more clinically and cost-effective than the short-stretch bandage after adjustment. VenUS IV (2014) found two-layer hosiery healed as fast as the four-layer bandage (median 99 vs 98 days; healed 70.9% vs 70.4%) — but more hosiery patients changed treatment (38.3% vs 27.0%), so hosiery suits many, not all. VenUS 6 (2026) found two-layer bandage non-inferior to evidence-based compression (four-layer bandage or two-layer hosiery) on its treatment-policy analysis (hazard ratio 1.01) while compression wraps healed more slowly (HR 0.78 vs evidence-based compression). The system matters less than sustained, correctly applied compression — and vein ablation timing is Shelf #1220.
stamp: LIKELY

title: Maggots to clean the wound: larval therapy in VenUS II
question: Do sterile larvae debride venous and mixed leg ulcers faster than hydrogel — and does faster debridement buy faster healing, or only a cleaner wound and more pain?
balance: Split: LIKELY — faster debridement · POSSIBLE — no faster healing. Two randomised trials agree that larvae clean the wound faster: VenUS II's hazard ratio for debridement was 2.31 (a relative measure, absolute times not stated in the abstract) and Mudge 2014 debrided 67.4% of larvae-treated ulcers within 21 days versus 26.2% on hydrogel. But VenUS II, the large trial, found no healing advantage (hazard ratio for healing 1.13, 95% CI 0.76 to 1.68) and no reduction in bacterial load — while ulcer pain was substantially higher with larvae (mean differences of 46.74 and 38.58 points on a 150 mm scale for loose and bagged larvae). The debridement effect is consistent across two trials (LIKELY); the healing null rests on the one large trial (POSSIBLE, per the single-trial ceiling). Larvae are a debridement tool with a pain cost, not a healing therapy.
stamp: Split

title: Feeding the pressure ulcer shut: arginine-enriched nutrition (Cereda; van Anholt)
question: Does a nutritional formula enriched with arginine, zinc and antioxidants heal established pressure ulcers faster than standard nutrition — in malnourished patients, and in patients who are not malnourished?
balance: POSSIBLE: Two randomised trials of arginine-, zinc- and antioxidant-enriched formulas point the same way but are small and surrogate-ended. Cereda 2015 (200 malnourished patients, blinded, isocaloric/isonitrogenous control) found a greater reduction in ulcer area at 8 weeks on the enriched formula (60.9% vs 45.2%; adjusted difference 18.7%), with complete healing — the outcome patients care about — among secondary endpoints that did not differ. Van Anholt 2010 (43 non-malnourished patients, double-blind) found faster ulcer-size decrease and severity-score improvement with fewer dressings. Two small trials, one shared sponsor-era formula concept, no demonstrated complete-healing benefit: POSSIBLE. Wording note, per the library's standing rule: this shelf presents the formula as a pharmacologic-dose supplement tested as a drug; nothing here attributes ulcer healing, or any albumin change, to diet correcting a deficiency — albumin in this library reflects inflammation or injury, never diet. Pressure-injury PREVENTION (repositioning, support surfaces) is Shelf #796 and is not re-carded here.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Oxygen under pressure for the diabetic foot: DAMO2CLES and Löndahl
question: Does hyperbaric oxygen therapy heal ischaemic diabetic foot ulcers and save legs — DAMO2CLES, which did not significantly improve its primary limb outcomes, against Löndahl, where healing improved?
balance: Split: POSSIBLE — healing · MAYBE (weak evidence) — limb salvage — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: major amputation and amputation-free survival sit inside DAMO2CLES's outcome frame). The two randomised trials disagree in a way that tracks their populations. DAMO2CLES (120 patients with diabetes and ischaemic ulcers, intention-to-treat) found no significant benefit on limb salvage (risk difference 10%, 95% CI −4 to 23), healing (RD 3%, −14 to 21) or amputation-free survival (RD 13%, −2 to 28); its better outcomes in the 65% who completed the chamber protocol are a completer analysis, not randomised evidence. Löndahl (94 patients with chronic ulcers >3 months, double-blind against hyperbaric air) found healing of 52% versus 29% at 1 year (P=0.03). Healing in selected chronic ulcers: POSSIBLE. Limb salvage: only the null DAMO2CLES answers it directly, its intervals are wide, and the completer signal is exactly the bias randomisation exists to remove — MAYBE (weak evidence). No mortality benefit is claimed anywhere on this shelf: DAMO2CLES reports amputation-free survival, printed on its card with its interval, and Löndahl's abstract reports no mortality figures. Offloading and dressings for diabetic foot ulcers are Shelf #291, fenced, not re-carded.

title: Suction on the open wound: negative-pressure therapy for open fractures (WOLLF) and after diabetic foot amputation (Armstrong)
question: Does negative-pressure wound therapy on the open wound itself help — in severe open fractures of the lower limb (WOLLF), and after partial diabetic foot amputation (Armstrong)?
balance: Split: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — open fractures · POSSIBLE — post-amputation diabetic foot wounds. WOLLF (460 patients, multicentre) is a large, well-powered null: disability at 12 months did not improve with negative-pressure therapy (Disability Rating Index 45.5 vs 42.4; difference −3.9, 95% CI −8.9 to 1.2, against a minimal important difference of 8), nor did deep infection (7.1% vs 8.1%) or quality of life — a single very large null trial may carry LIKELY (the treatment made no difference), and this one does. Armstrong (162 patients, multicentre) found more post-amputation diabetic foot wounds healed on NPWT (56% vs 39%; P=0.040) and healed faster — a single positive trial, capped at POSSIBLE. Same suction, different wounds: the split is the shelf. Incisional NPWT over CLOSED incisions is Shelf #651 and is not re-carded here.

title: Blunting the burn's hypermetabolism with propranolol: the Galveston children's programme
question: Does long-term propranolol reduce cardiac work and preserve lean mass in severely burned children, and did the programme's safety analysis find a cost in inflammation or infection?
balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: mortality is tracked and reported across this single programme's reports in a population where burns kill — 6% control versus 5% propranolol in the safety analysis, printed on its card — and any shelf carrying mortality figures from one centre's programme takes the developer's eye; no survival benefit is claimed). The randomised efficacy report (Herndon 2012, 179 children with >30% TBSA burns, propranolol 4 mg/kg/day for 12 months) found significantly reduced predicted heart rate and resting energy expenditure, less central mass and fat accumulation, prevented bone loss and improved lean-body-mass accretion, with very few adverse effects. The programme's prospective safety analysis (Jeschke 2007, 245 children) found no increase in infection (21% vs 30%), sepsis (7% vs 10%) or mortality, with resting energy expenditure significantly decreased. One centre, one programme, surrogate and body-composition endpoints: POSSIBLE. The opposite pharmacological direction against the same catabolic state — oxandrolone — is Shelf #1227.

title: Oxandrolone to keep the burned child's muscle: the Wolf trial
question: Does oxandrolone improve net protein balance, lean mass and long-term bone outcomes in severely burned children versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE: Two randomised reports from the same single-centre programme support benefit on body-composition and bone surrogates, and no carded trial shows a survival or functional benefit. Wolf 2003 (32 severely burned children) found oxandrolone improved net protein balance over one week while placebo did not change, preserved body weight and fat-free mass that placebo lost, and shifted muscle gene expression toward functional muscle proteins. The programme's 5-year randomised trial (Reeves/Herndon 2016; oxandrolone for up to 24 months) found significantly greater whole-body and lumbar-spine bone mineral content, higher adjusted lumbar BMD, fewer children meeting paediatric osteoporosis criteria and greater height velocity, with no attributed adverse effects. Surrogate and growth endpoints from one centre: POSSIBLE. Beta-BLOCKADE against the same catabolic state is Shelf #1226 — the opposite pharmacological direction, cross-referenced, not re-carded.

title: Cutting the burn off early: early excision versus conservative care (Herndon 1989)
question: Does early tangential excision and grafting beat conservative care with late grafting in severely burned patients — including Herndon 1989's subgroup mortality report, and a 2026 randomised replication of the hospital-stay question?
balance: Split: POSSIBLE — shorter hospital stay · MAYBE (weak evidence) — mortality benefit (subgroup only) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C firm: this shelf carries a mortality report). Herndon 1989 (85 adults with >30% TBSA burns, randomised) found mortality without inhalation injury significantly lower with early excision in patients aged 17 to 30 (9% vs 45%; P<0.025) — a subgroup of a small, old trial, with no mortality difference demonstrable over age 30 or with inhalation injury, and a separate paediatric series in the same report in which mortality rose with burn size and inhalation injury. A subgroup mortality finding from 1989 is MAYBE (weak evidence) by this library's rules and is printed only as a subgroup, on the card and here. The modern, modest claim is better supported: survivors' hospital stay was under one day per percent TBSA in Herndon's series, and the 2026 North India RCT (36 adults) found early excision halved median stay (13.5 vs 28.5 days; P=0.009) with no significant difference in organ dysfunction, transfusion or mortality — POSSIBLE for the stay benefit, and a second randomised 'no mortality difference' datapoint that further fences the 1989 subgroup claim.

title: Manufactured healing for the diabetic foot: Dermagraft, and becaplermin gel
question: Do manufactured biological adjuncts — Dermagraft living dermal substitute and becaplermin growth-factor gel — close chronic diabetic foot ulcers that standard care has not, and does the modern comparative trial (DOLCE) still find a benefit?
balance: POSSIBLE: The two registration-era trials were positive but modest against good standard care: Dermagraft closed 30.0% of ulcers by 12 weeks versus 18.3% on conventional therapy (Marston 2003), and becaplermin 100 µg/g closed 50% versus 35% on placebo gel (a 43% relative increase, with the absolute rates beside it on the card; Wieman 1998). But the modern head-to-head trial, DOLCE 2025, found no difference at all between cellular matrix (Dermagraft), acellular matrix and standard care alone (healing by 12 weeks 49% vs 69% vs 57%; P=0.16 — with standard care matching the products). Two older positives against a null modern comparative trial, all in pre-modern-offloading eras for the positives: POSSIBLE, and falling. Shelf #291 (offloading, dressings, LeucoPatch) is the diabetic-foot home for standard care and is fenced, not re-carded; the Integra dermal template was excluded at drafting as a non-randomised postapproval report and is not carded here.

title: Rocuronium versus succinylcholine for rapid-sequence intubation
question: In adults undergoing emergency rapid-sequence induction, does rocuronium produce first-pass intubating conditions and safety equivalent to succinylcholine?
balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED: Two small randomised blinded comparisons in different populations point the same way: in patients aged 80 or over (Vested 2025, 90 patients), excellent intubating conditions at 60 seconds were 73% on rocuronium 1.0 mg/kg versus 75% on suxamethonium 1.0 mg/kg (95% CI for the difference -16 to 20), with first-pass success 98% in both groups and a slower onset for rocuronium (131 vs 99 seconds); in children (Kumar 2023, 200 patients), excellent conditions were 65% on rocuronium 1.2 mg/kg versus 60% on succinylcholine 2 mg/kg. The endpoint is intubating conditions — a surrogate — and neither trial was powered for patient-important harm, so the stamp caps at POSSIBLE.

title: Cricoid pressure during rapid-sequence induction (IRIS)
question: In patients undergoing rapid-sequence induction, does cricoid pressure prevent pulmonary aspiration compared with a sham procedure, without worsening laryngoscopic view?
balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED: The one large randomised test (IRIS, 3,472 patients) could not settle the question either way: pulmonary aspiration was rare and nearly identical (0.6% with cricoid pressure versus 0.5% with a sham procedure; risk difference -0.06%, 95% CI -0.57 to 0.42), but the sham procedure FAILED its prespecified noninferiority test (upper limit of the one-sided 95% CI for relative risk 2.00, above the 1.50 margin; P=.14), so omitting cricoid pressure was not proven safe. Cricoid pressure did make intubation harder: Cormack-Lehane grade 3-4 views in 10% versus 5% (P<.001) and intubation over 30 seconds in 47% versus 40% (P<.001). A single trial with a failed noninferiority design and a very low event rate caps at POSSIBLE.

title: Prehospital benzodiazepine route for status epilepticus (RAMPART)
question: In prehospital convulsive status epilepticus, is intramuscular midazolam at least as effective as intravenous lorazepam at stopping seizures before ED arrival?
balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED: The one large double-blind randomised test (RAMPART, 893 subjects in the primary analysis) found seizures absent on ED arrival without rescue therapy in 73.4% with intramuscular midazolam versus 63.4% with intravenous lorazepam (absolute difference 10 percentage points, 95% CI 4.0 to 16.1; P<0.001 for both noninferiority and superiority), with similar intubation rates (14.1% vs 14.4%) and seizure recurrence (11.4% vs 10.6%). The win was logistical as much as pharmacological: median time to active treatment was 1.2 minutes intramuscularly versus 4.8 minutes intravenously, partly offset by a slower time from treatment to cessation (3.3 vs 1.6 minutes). One very large blinded trial with a decisive primary result carries LIKELY under the library's large-trial rule.

title: Droperidol for sedation of acute behavioural disturbance in the ED
question: In ED patients with acute behavioural disturbance, is droperidol as effective and safe as other parenteral sedatives (midazolam, olanzapine) for rapid sedation?
balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED: The randomised leg is one blinded trial (DORM, 91 patients): median duration of violent behaviour was 20 minutes on intramuscular droperidol 10 mg versus 24 minutes on midazolam 10 mg and 25 minutes on the combination, but additional sedation was needed less often with droperidol (33% vs 62% vs 41%; hazard ratio for midazolam versus droperidol 2.31 relative, 95% credible interval 1.01 to 4.71) and adverse effects were fewer (6% vs 28% vs 7%). The large safety cohort the topic file anchors on (Calver 2015, 1,403 sedated patients) is a prospective OBSERVATIONAL study, not a trial: median time to sedation 20 minutes, abnormal QT in 1.3% of those with an ECG (half attributable to other causes), no torsades. Randomised efficacy from one small trial plus observational safety caps at POSSIBLE.

title: Ketamine versus haloperidol for acute agitation in the ED
question: In adults with severe acute agitation in the ED, does ketamine achieve faster, safer sedation than haloperidol?
balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED: A single small randomised trial (Sadrzadeh 2025, 120 patients) compared intravenous ketamine 2 mg/kg with intravenous haloperidol 5 mg: admission Richmond Agitation-Sedation Scale (RASS) scores were 1.73 on haloperidol and 1.58 on ketamine, falling after treatment to 0.07 (SD 1.25) versus -0.92 (SD 1.19) — deeper sedation with ketamine — and the authors report a faster onset of action for ketamine. title: Greater occipital nerve block versus intravenous metoclopramide for ED migraine
question: In adults presenting to the ED with acute migraine, does greater occipital nerve block with bupivacaine relieve headache as durably as intravenous metoclopramide?
balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED (favouring metoclopramide): The one direct randomised test (Friedman 2020, 99 patients, double-dummy noninferiority design) found greater occipital nerve block was NOT as efficacious as intravenous metoclopramide: mean 1-hour pain improvement was 5.0 points on a 0-10 scale with the block versus 6.1 with metoclopramide (between-group difference -1.1, 95% CI -2.3 to 0.1 — the lower limit crossed the -1.3 noninferiority margin), sustained 48-hour relief was 22% versus 38%, and rescue medication was needed by 33% versus 17%. A single modest-sized trial caps the verdict at POSSIBLE.

title: Adding ipratropium to salbutamol in acute asthma in the ED
question: In children and adults with acute asthma in the ED, does adding nebulised ipratropium bromide to salbutamol reduce hospital admission versus salbutamol alone?
balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED: Two double-blind randomised trials, one in each age group, agree. In children (Qureshi 1998, 434 patients, all also given corticosteroid), hospitalisation was 27.4% with ipratropium added versus 36.5% with salbutamol alone (P=0.05), driven by the severe subgroup (37.5% vs 52.6%; P=0.02), with no benefit in moderate exacerbations (10.1% vs 10.7%). In adults with peak flow under 200 L/min (Lin 1998, 55 patients), airflow improved significantly faster with the combination (P<=.001) and admissions were 3 of 27 versus 10 of 28 (absolute difference 25%, 95% CI 3 to 46; P=.03). Two concordant blinded trials earn LIKELY, scoped to severe exacerbations.

title: Single-dose dexamethasone versus multi-day prednisone after asthma exacerbation
question: In adults discharged after an acute asthma exacerbation, is a single dose of oral dexamethasone non-inferior to 5 days of prednisone for preventing relapse?
balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED: The one randomised test (Rehrer 2016, 376 patients completing follow-up) came within a whisker of the line and fell the wrong side of it: relapse within 14 days was 12.1% after a single 12 mg dose of dexamethasone plus 4 days of placebo versus 9.8% on 5 days of prednisone 60 mg (difference 2.3%, 95% CI -4.1 to 8.6) — the upper confidence limit exceeded the prespecified 8% noninferiority margin, so noninferiority was NOT demonstrated, by a very small margin (the topic file's summary said it was met; the record says it was not, and the record governs). title: Ketorolac versus morphine for renal colic
question: In adults with acute renal colic in the ED, does intravenous ketorolac relieve pain as effectively as intravenous morphine, with fewer adverse effects?
balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED: Two small randomised comparisons support comparable analgesia. In the head-to-head trial (Pourafzali 2023, 272 patients), pain scores fell by about 9 points in both groups over 90 minutes with no significant between-group difference, and nausea (5.1%) and reduced oxygen saturation (1.5%) occurred only with morphine, while dizziness was similar (2.9% vs 2.2%). In a double-blind three-arm trial (Safaie 2022, 195 patients), adding ketorolac (or ibuprofen) to morphine beat morphine alone from 15 minutes (120-minute pain scores 2.9 vs 7.0), with the lowest rescue-analgesia use in the ketorolac combination arm. title: Intravenous lidocaine versus ketorolac for renal colic
question: In adults with suspected renal colic in the ED, does intravenous lidocaine relieve pain as effectively as ketorolac?

title: Regional anaesthesia with propofol versus volatile general anaesthesia for breast-cancer recurrence
question: In women having potentially curative breast-cancer surgery, does paravertebral regional anaesthesia with propofol reduce cancer recurrence versus sevoflurane general anaesthesia with opioids?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED: The one large randomised test (Sessler 2019, 2,108 women analysed, 13 hospitals) found breast-cancer recurrence essentially identical between techniques: 102 of 1,043 (10%) with paravertebral regional anaesthesia plus propofol versus 111 of 1,065 (10%) with sevoflurane general anaesthesia and opioids (hazard ratio 0.97 relative, 95% CI 0.74 to 1.28; P=0.84), at a median follow-up of 36 months; the trial was stopped at a prespecified futility boundary. Persistent incisional pain also did not differ (52% vs 52% at 6 months). A single very large trial with a tight result around no effect carries LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) under the library's large-null rule. Cancer recurrence sits outside this library's Tier C definition (mortality/MI/stroke/CV events), so the stamp is proposed ordinarily.

title: Volatile versus total intravenous anaesthesia in cardiac surgery (MYRIAD)
question: In patients undergoing coronary-artery bypass grafting, does volatile anaesthesia reduce one-year mortality versus total intravenous anaesthesia?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, one-year mortality primary outcome): The one large randomised test (MYRIAD, 5,400 patients, 36 centres in 13 countries) found death from any cause at 1 year in 2.8% with a volatile-based regimen versus 3.0% with total intravenous anaesthesia (relative risk 0.94 relative, 95% CI 0.69 to 1.29; P=0.71), and at 30 days 1.4% versus 1.3% (relative risk 1.11 relative, 0.70 to 1.76), with no secondary outcome or prespecified adverse event — including myocardial infarction — significantly different. The trial was stopped for futility at the second interim analysis. A very large blinded-assessment trial null on mortality carries LIKELY (the treatment made no difference).

title: Phenylephrine versus ephedrine for spinal hypotension at caesarean delivery
question: In women having caesarean delivery under spinal anaesthesia, does phenylephrine maintain maternal blood pressure with better fetal acid–base status than ephedrine?
balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED, split by outcome: the two blinded trials trade blows. For TREATING established hypotension in non-elective caesarean section (Ngan Kee 2008, 204 women), umbilical arterial and venous pH and base excess were similar between phenylephrine 100-microgram and ephedrine 10-mg boluses, but fetal lactate was higher with ephedrine (umbilical arterial median 2.6 vs 2.4 mmol/L; P=0.002) and maternal nausea/vomiting more frequent (12.7% vs 3.9%; P=0.02). For PREVENTION (Magalhães 2009, 60 women), ephedrine prevented hypotension better (incidence 70% vs 93%; P<0.05) yet umbilical arterial pH and 1-minute Apgar were lower with ephedrine. The consistent thread is a slightly worse fetal acid–base profile with ephedrine; the blood-pressure thread favours whichever drug the protocol used first. Surrogate endpoints (cord pH, lactate) and small trials cap at POSSIBLE.

title: Quadratus lumborum block for pain after caesarean delivery
question: In women after caesarean delivery, does quadratus lumborum block reduce postoperative opioid use and pain versus sham or transversus abdominis plane block?
balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED: Two small double-blind trials from the same group support an opioid-sparing effect. Against sham block (Blanco 2015, 50 women), quadratus lumborum block (QLB) with bupivacaine significantly reduced morphine consumption at 6 and 12 hours (not 24-48) and morphine demands through 48 hours (all P<0.001), with lower pain scores at rest and on movement at nearly all time points. Against transversus abdominis plane (TAP) block (Blanco 2016, 76 women), QLB used significantly less morphine at 12, 24 and 48 hours (P<0.05) with similar pain scores. Small, single-group trials with an opioid-consumption surrogate cap at POSSIBLE.

title: Perioperative intravenous lidocaine infusion for postoperative pain and recovery
question: In adults having abdominal/colorectal surgery, does a perioperative intravenous lidocaine infusion shorten hospital stay and reduce postoperative pain versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED: The anchor trial (Herroeder 2007, 60 colorectal patients) found intravenous lidocaine shortened hospital stay by one day and sped return of bowel function, with no difference in daily pain ratings. The Cochrane synthesis (Weibel 2018, 68 trials, 4,525 participants) is much more cautious: it is UNCERTAIN whether lidocaine improves early pain (standardised mean difference -0.50 relative, 95% CI -0.72 to -0.28; very low-quality evidence), it probably has no clinically relevant effect on pain at 24 hours (SMD -0.14 relative) or 48 hours, while estimates for ileus (risk ratio 0.37 relative, 0.15 to 0.87), time to first bowel movement (-7.92 hours) and opioid consumption (-4.52 mg morphine equivalents) were all very low quality. One small positive trial against a very-low-certainty review caps at POSSIBLE.

title: Dexmedetomidine to prevent emergence agitation after sevoflurane in children
question: In children recovering from sevoflurane anaesthesia, does a single dose of dexmedetomidine reduce emergence agitation versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED: Two small double-blind trials agree on direction. Ibacache 2004 (90 children aged 1-10): emergence agitation occurred in 37% on saline versus 17% on dexmedetomidine 0.15 micrograms/kg and 10% on 0.30 micrograms/kg (P<0.05), with no difference in eye-opening time or PACU discharge and no adverse effects. Guler 2005 (60 children aged 3-7, adenotonsillectomy): agitation and pain scores were significantly better with dexmedetomidine 0.5 micrograms/kg (P<0.05), severe agitation and severe pain were significantly less frequent, and severe coughing was reduced — but emergence and extubation times were significantly longer. Consistent small trials on a behaviour-score endpoint, with a real trade-off against recovery time, cap at POSSIBLE.

title: Tranexamic acid in coronary-artery surgery (ATACAS)
question: In patients undergoing coronary-artery surgery, does tranexamic acid reduce transfusion and major haemorrhage without increasing death or thrombotic complications?
balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, the primary outcome is a death/thrombotic composite): In the one large blinded trial (ATACAS, 4,631 patients analysed), tranexamic acid did not increase the composite of death and thrombotic complications within 30 days (16.7% vs 18.1% on placebo; relative risk 0.92 relative, 95% CI 0.81 to 1.05; P=0.22), while total blood-product transfusion fell from 7,994 to 4,331 units (P<0.001) and major haemorrhage or tamponade requiring reoperation halved (1.4% vs 2.8%; P=0.001). The price was seizures: 0.7% versus 0.1% (P=0.002). This shelf covers coronary surgery only; the general perioperative TXA question is home on Shelf #138 and POISE-3 on Shelf #1124.

title: Aprotinin versus lysine analogues in high-risk cardiac surgery (BART)
question: In high-risk cardiac surgery, how do aprotinin, tranexamic acid and aminocaproic acid compare on major bleeding and mortality?
balance: LIKELY (harm) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, mortality harm): The one head-to-head blinded trial (BART, 2,331 high-risk cardiac-surgery patients) was terminated early because of higher mortality with aprotinin. Massive postoperative bleeding was modestly less frequent with aprotinin (9.5% vs 12.1% on tranexamic acid and 12.1% on aminocaproic acid; relative risk 0.79 relative, 95% CI 0.59 to 1.05 for both comparisons), but 30-day death was 6.0% on aprotinin versus 3.9% on tranexamic acid (relative risk 1.55 relative, 0.99 to 2.42) and 4.0% on aminocaproic acid (relative risk 1.52 relative, 0.98 to 2.36); against both lysine analogues combined the relative risk of death was 1.53 relative (1.06 to 2.22). A large blinded trial stopped for a consistent mortality trend carries LIKELY (harm).

title: Intraoperative methadone versus morphine for postoperative analgesia
question: In patients having cardiac or major surgery, does a single intraoperative dose of methadone reduce postoperative pain and opioid requirements versus morphine?
balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED: Two small double-blind cardiac-surgery trials lean the same way. Udelsmann 2011 (55 patients, three arms including placebo) reports the first rescue analgesic came later, fewer doses were needed, analgesia quality was better and nausea/vomiting less frequent with a single 20 mg induction dose of methadone than 20 mg morphine — but prints no numbers. Carvalho 2018 (100 patients, off-pump CABG) found lower pain scores at 24 hours with methadone (1.9 [SD 2.2] vs 2.9 [SD 2.6]; P=0.029) and fewer patients requiring rescue morphine (29% vs 43%; P=0.002) — yet, inconsistently, a SHORTER time to first analgesic request in the methadone group (145.9 vs 269.4 minutes; P=0.005), an internal contradiction in the record that is flagged on the card. Small trials, an analgesic-consumption surrogate and one inconsistent record cap at POSSIBLE.

title: Perioperative gabapentin for postoperative pain and opioid sparing
question: In adults having surgery, does perioperative gabapentin reduce postoperative opioid requirements and pain versus placebo?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — PROPOSED: The two carded records barely test the shelf's question. The topic file's anchor (Guanzon 2026, 114 prolapse-surgery patients) does not compare gabapentin with placebo at all — it compares preoperative-only gabapentin (with postoperative placebo) against pre- plus postoperative gabapentin, and could NOT conclude the shorter course was noninferior for opioid prescription at discharge (27.0% vs 32.0%; absolute difference 5.0%, 95% CI -12 to 21, crossing the 20% margin). The one placebo-controlled trial carded (Lerner 2024, 35 sinus-surgery patients) found no significant difference in pain (P=0.18) or opioid consumption (2.3 vs 4.8 oxycodone tablets; P=0.18) — numerically FEWER tablets on placebo, in an operation where 15 of 35 patients needed no opioid at all. As carded, the placebo-controlled evidence is one tiny null trial: MAYBE (weak evidence). A large older RCT literature exists per the topic file but was not verified for this pack and is not carded.

title: Multiple-dose activated charcoal in yellow oleander poisoning
question: In patients with yellow oleander poisoning, does multiple-dose activated charcoal reduce mortality versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, mortality primary outcome): The one randomised test (de Silva 2003, 401 patients in Sri Lanka, single-blind) found death in 5 of 201 patients (2.5%) given multiple-dose activated charcoal versus 16 of 200 (8%) on placebo (percentage difference 5.5%, 95% CI 0.6 to 10.3; P=0.025), with secondary endpoints (life-threatening arrhythmias, atropine dose, pacing, ICU admission) also favouring charcoal. A single single-blind, single-country trial carries POSSIBLE. Note the tension with Shelf #1251: in the much larger unselected self-poisoning trial — over a third of whose patients had taken oleander — multiple-dose charcoal showed no mortality benefit overall; the two shelves answer different questions (oleander-specific protocol versus routine use) and both records stand.

title: Activated charcoal dosing strategy in acute self-poisoning
question: In adults presenting after acute self-poisoning, does single-dose or multiple-dose activated charcoal reduce mortality versus no charcoal?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, mortality primary outcome): The one large randomised test (Eddleston 2008, 4,632 patients in three Sri Lankan hospitals, open-label) found mortality of 6.3% with six doses of activated charcoal versus 6.8% with no charcoal (adjusted odds ratio 0.96 — a relative measure — 95% CI 0.70 to 1.33), with no differences in subgroups by poison type, severity on admission or early presentation; the single-dose arm was randomised alongside (1,545 patients) and the report's headline comparison is multiple-dose versus none. The confidence interval still admits a worthwhile benefit or harm, and the design was open-label — so the null is stamped POSSIBLE, not LIKELY. The oleander-specific trial (Shelf #1250) found a benefit in its narrower population; both records stand.

title: Shortened acetylcysteine regimens for paracetamol poisoning
question: In patients treated for paracetamol overdose, can acetylcysteine be stopped early or given in a two-bag regimen without loss of protection, and with fewer adverse reactions, versus the standard three-bag regimen?
balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED: Two randomised trials support shorter, gentler acetylcysteine in selected patients. NACSTOP 2 (Wong 2026, 186 low-risk patients): stopping the two-bag regimen at about 13 hours was non-inferior to the full 20 hours on the prespecified liver-enzyme endpoint (difference in median ALT change -1 IU/L, 95% CI -2 to 1, against a 3 IU/L margin), and no patient in either group developed hepatic injury — but entry required a normal ALT both at presentation and after 12 hours of treatment, so this is a low-risk subgroup result. SNAP (Bateman 2014, 222 patients): a 12-hour modified regimen halved vomiting/retching/rescue-antiemetic use at 2 hours (39 of 108 vs 71 of 109; adjusted odds ratio 0.26 relative, 97.5% CI 0.13 to 0.52) and cut severe anaphylactoid reactions (5 vs 31; adjusted common odds ratio 0.23 relative), with no difference in ALT rise — though SNAP was explicitly not powered to prove the shorter regimen equally protective. Supportive but bounded evidence: POSSIBLE.

title: Physostigmine versus lorazepam for anticholinergic toxidrome
question: In patients with antimuscarinic (anticholinergic) delirium, does physostigmine resolve delirium more effectively than lorazepam?
balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED: The one blinded randomised trial (Wang 2021) is tiny — 19 adolescents — but the separation is large: delirium persisted after the initial bolus in 44% on physostigmine versus 100% on lorazepam (P=0.01), and at the 4th hour of infusion in 22% versus 100% (P<0.001); agitation scores improved significantly more often after the physostigmine bolus (89% vs 30%; P=0.02), with no seizures, bradycardia, bronchorrhoea, bronchospasm, intubation or dysrhythmias in either arm. A single very small trial in adolescents (84% diphenhydramine ingestions) caps at POSSIBLE. The older Burns trial named in the topic file could not be verified from the fetched records and is not carded.

title: Octreotide for sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycaemia
question: In patients with sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycaemia, does adding octreotide to dextrose reduce recurrent hypoglycaemia versus dextrose alone?
balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED: The one verified double-blind randomised trial (Fasano 2008, 40 ED patients) found that a single 75-microgram subcutaneous dose of octreotide added to standard dextrose therapy kept serum glucose consistently higher over the first 8 hours (differences significant from 4 to 8 hours, approaching significance at 1 to 3 hours), with no difference in later hours, and the authors report recurrent hypoglycaemic episodes occurred less frequently with octreotide — without printing the episode counts. A single 40-patient trial on a glucose surrogate caps at POSSIBLE. The older Boyle trial named in the topic file could not be verified from the fetched records and is not carded.

title: Pralidoxime infusion versus bolus in organophosphate poisoning
question: In patients with organophosphorus pesticide poisoning, does continuous pralidoxime infusion improve outcomes (mortality, ventilation duration) versus repeated bolus dosing?
balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, mortality in the outcome set): The balance is genuinely contested. Pawar 2006 (200 patients, open trial, India) found a high-dose constant infusion (1 g/hour for 48 hours after a 2 g load) beat repeated bolus dosing on every reported measure: median atropine need in 24 hours 6 mg versus 30 mg (P<0.0001), intubation 64% versus 88% (relative risk 0.72 relative, 95% CI 0.62 to 0.86), and ventilation 5 versus 10 days (P<0.0001); its abstract asserts a mortality benefit in its interpretation but prints no mortality figures. Eddleston 2009 (235 patients, double-blind, Sri Lanka) asked the prior question — pralidoxime versus NO pralidoxime at a lower infusion dose — and found mortality nonsignificantly HIGHER with pralidoxime (24.8% vs 15.8%; adjusted hazard ratio 1.69 relative, 95% CI 0.88 to 3.26; P=0.12) despite clear acetylcholinesterase reactivation. A positive open regimen trial against a null double-blind placebo trial caps at POSSIBLE.

title: Magnesium sulfate as an adjuvant in organophosphate poisoning
question: In acute organophosphate pesticide poisoning, does adding intravenous magnesium sulfate to standard atropine/oxime therapy improve outcomes?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — PROPOSED: The only carded record is a phase II dose-finding safety study (Basher 2013, 50 patients): magnesium was well tolerated with no adverse reactions at total doses of 4 to 16 g, and deaths were distributed 6 of 10 in the small placebo group versus 3 of 16, 2 of 8, 1 of 8 and 0 of 8 across the ascending dose groups. Those mortality counts come from sequential dose-escalation groups of 8-16 patients with a 1-to-4 allocation ratio — the study was designed to test tolerability and magnesium handling, not efficacy, and its own conclusion is that larger studies are required. On this library's scale that is MAYBE (weak evidence): we don't know.

title: Antivenom for scorpion envenomation in children (Boyer)
question: In critically ill children with neurotoxic scorpion envenomation, does scorpion-specific antivenom (F(ab')2) resolve the clinical syndrome faster than placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED: The one randomised test (Boyer 2009) is tiny (15 children) but the effect is categorical: the clinical syndrome resolved within 4 hours in all 8 antivenom recipients versus 1 of 7 on placebo (P=0.001), cumulative midazolam sedation was far lower with antivenom (0.07 vs 4.61 mg/kg; P=0.01), and plasma venom was undetectable 1 hour after treatment in all 8 treated children versus 1 on placebo (P=0.001). A double-blind trial with a near-deterministic result earns POSSIBLE despite n=15 — the stamp reflects the sample size, not doubt about direction.

title: Antivenom for redback spider envenomation (RAVE programme)
question: In patients with latrodectism from redback spider bite, does antivenom (intravenous or intramuscular) relieve pain better than placebo or standard analgesia?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED: The placebo-controlled test (RAVE-II, 224 patients) found antivenom added to standardised analgesia did NOT significantly improve pain at 2 hours (clinically significant improvement in 34% on antivenom vs 23% on placebo; difference 10.7%, 95% CI -1.1 to 22.6; P=.10) or resolution of systemic effects (26% vs 22%; difference 3.8%, -15 to 23; P=.79), with no secondary outcome significant and acute hypersensitivity reactions in 3.6% of antivenom recipients. The route trial (RAVE, 126 patients, all receiving antivenom) found intravenous barely ahead of intramuscular administration (pain improved 62% vs 53%; +9%, 95% credible interval -8 to +26) — a comparison the authors note is moot if the drug itself adds nothing over placebo. One well-run 224-patient null carries POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): the interval still admits a pain benefit of up to ~23 points.

title: Low-dose versus high-dose antivenom for snakebite in India
question: In patients with haemotoxic/neurotoxic snake envenomation, is a low-dose polyvalent antivenom regimen as effective as high-dose, with fewer reactions and lower cost?
balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED: The randomised record (Sagar 2020, 140 patients with haemotoxic bite, open-label) compared the Indian national protocol (100 mL initial dose, then 100 mL six-hourly, capped at 300 mL) with the local institutional protocol (70 mL, then 30 mL six-hourly): total antivenom required did not differ significantly between protocols, neither did mortality or acute kidney injury reach significance (both numerically higher in the national-protocol group, in patients the authors note were sicker), and no patient in either group relapsed with clotting abnormality. The neurotoxic-bite comparison (Sarin 2017, 51 patients) was NOT randomised — a prospective comparison whose authors call for a randomised trial: the national (lower-dose) protocol used far less antivenom (224 vs 982 mL per patient) with shorter ventilation (24 vs 43.5 hours) and no difference in recovery, reactions or mortality (there were no deaths in either group). Lower-dose regimens look adequate in both records, but the randomised trial is open-label and confounded, and the cleaner dose contrast is observational: POSSIBLE.

title: Corticosteroids after significant head injury (CRASH)
question: In adults with clinically significant head injury, does intravenous methylprednisolone reduce death within 14 days versus placebo?
balance: LIKELY (harm) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, mortality harm): The one large randomised test (CRASH, 10,008 adults with head injury and Glasgow Coma Scale score of 14 or less) found corticosteroids INCREASED death: within 14 days, 21.1% died on methylprednisolone versus 17.9% on placebo (relative risk 1.18 relative, 95% CI 1.09 to 1.27; P=0.0001), and the 6-month report of the same trial (counted once) found death in 25.7% versus 22.3% (relative risk 1.15 relative, 1.07 to 1.24; P=0.0001), with no subgroup — by injury severity or time since injury — escaping the harm. Recruitment was stopped early by the data monitoring committee when the harm emerged. This is the library's clearest harm verdict in brain injury: steroids after head injury kill more people than they save, and no benefit claim of any kind survives this record.

title: Hypertonic saline versus mannitol for raised intracranial pressure in traumatic brain injury
question: In patients with traumatic brain injury and raised intracranial pressure, does hypertonic saline control ICP and improve outcomes better than mannitol?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED: Disclosure first: the anchor pinned in the topic file for this shelf (PMID 40067302) is, on verification, a prospective multicentre COHORT study of children — not the randomised comparison the topic file described — so it is carded below labelled as observational, and the shelf's randomised anchor is the small adult trial pinned by title search instead. That trial (Jagannatha 2016, 38 adults with severe TBI and refractory intracranial hypertension) found hypertonic saline lowered ICP faster per bolus than equiosmolar mannitol (slope of ICP fall, P=0.0001) and avoided the progressive ICP rise seen with mannitol, but 6-month mortality (6 vs 10 deaths; P=0.41) and dichotomised Glasgow Outcome Scale scores (P=0.21) did not differ. The paediatric cohort (445 children) likewise found no adjusted difference in mortality (7.1% hypertonic saline vs 11.0% mannitol; P=.34) or functional outcomes. Faster ICP physiology, no demonstrated outcome advantage: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) on outcomes.

title: Seizure prophylaxis after traumatic brain injury: phenytoin and levetiracetam
question: In patients with severe head injury, does prophylactic phenytoin prevent early post-traumatic seizures, and how does levetiracetam compare?
balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED, for the first-week claim, with the levetiracetam comparison at POSSIBLE: The one large double-blind trial (Temkin 1990, 404 patients with serious head trauma) found phenytoin cut seizures in the first week from 14.2% on placebo to 3.6% (risk ratio 0.27 relative, 95% CI 0.12 to 0.62; P<0.001) — and did nothing thereafter: seizures between day 8 and one year were 21.5% versus 15.7%, and by two years 27.5% versus 21.1%. So prophylaxis prevents early seizures only, and does not prevent later epilepsy. The head-to-head levetiracetam trial (Szaflarski 2010, 52 patients, single-blind) found no difference in seizure occurrence (5 of 34 vs 3 of 18 during continuous EEG; P=1.0), with better adjusted long-term functional scores on levetiracetam in a very small sample — an alternative at POSSIBLE, not a proven equal.

title: Erythropoietin in traumatic brain injury (EPO-TBI)
question: In patients with moderate-to-severe TBI, does epoetin alfa improve neurological outcome at 6 months or reduce mortality versus placebo?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, neurological outcome with mortality co-reported): The one large double-blind trial (EPO-TBI, 606 patients with moderate-to-severe TBI in 29 centres across seven countries) found erythropoietin did not reduce severe neurological dysfunction at 6 months: an Extended Glasgow Outcome Scale level of 1–4 in 44% on erythropoietin versus 45% on placebo (relative risk 0.99 relative, 95% CI 0.83 to 1.18; P=0.90). Six-month mortality was 11% versus 16% (relative risk 0.68 relative, 0.44 to 1.03; P=0.07) — not significant, and the trial's own interpretation is that the effect on mortality remains uncertain; no mortality benefit is claimed on this shelf. Lower-limb deep venous thrombosis was not increased (16% vs 18%).

title: Progesterone for acute traumatic brain injury (ProTECT III and SYNAPSE)
question: In patients with moderate-to-severe acute TBI, does early intravenous progesterone improve functional outcome versus placebo?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, functional outcome with mortality as a component/secondary outcome): Two large phase 3 double-blind trials, run in parallel and published side by side, are concordantly null. ProTECT III (882 patients randomised before stopping for futility) found no difference in favourable outcome at 6 months (relative benefit 0.95 relative, 95% CI 0.85 to 1.06; P=0.35), with more phlebitis/thrombophlebitis on progesterone (relative risk 3.03 relative, 1.96 to 4.66). SYNAPSE (1,195 patients with severe TBI) found favourable outcome in 50.4% on progesterone versus 50.5% on placebo (adjusted odds ratio 0.96 relative, 0.77 to 1.18), with mortality similar in the two groups. Two thousand randomised patients across two trials, both null: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference).

title: Prophylactic hypothermia in severe traumatic brain injury (POLAR)
question: In patients with severe TBI, does early sustained prophylactic hypothermia (33–35 °C) improve neurological outcome at 6 months versus normothermia?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, functional outcome with mortality embedded): For PROPHYLACTIC hypothermia — cooling before pressure rises — POLAR (511 patients with severe TBI) found favourable neurologic outcome at 6 months in 48.8% on early sustained hypothermia (33–35 °C) versus 49.1% on normothermia (relative risk 0.99 relative, 95% CI 0.82 to 1.19; P=.94). For THERAPEUTIC hypothermia — cooling to treat established intracranial hypertension — the neighbouring Eurotherm3235 trial (387 patients) found WORSE outcomes with hypothermia: favourable outcome 26% versus 37% (adjusted common odds ratio for a worse GOS-E distribution 1.53 relative, 1.02 to 2.30; P=0.04), and recruitment was suspended over safety concerns. Neither use is supported; the therapeutic use leans harmful.

title: Amantadine for disorders of consciousness after traumatic brain injury
question: In patients with traumatic disorders of consciousness in rehabilitation, does amantadine accelerate functional recovery versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED: The one randomised trial (Giacino 2012, 184 patients in a vegetative or minimally conscious state 4–16 weeks after TBI, in inpatient rehabilitation) found amantadine accelerated functional recovery DURING the 4-week treatment period — the Disability Rating Scale improved faster by 0.24 points per week (P=0.007) — but the advantage did not persist: during the 2-week washout, improvement in the amantadine group slowed significantly (slope difference 0.30 points per week; P=0.02), and overall improvement from baseline to week 6 was similar in the two groups. A real but treatment-bound acceleration on a recovery-rate surrogate, from a single trial: POSSIBLE.

title: Citicoline for traumatic brain injury (COBRIT)
question: In patients with complicated mild-to-severe TBI, does citicoline improve functional and cognitive status at 90 days versus placebo?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED: The one large double-blind phase 3 trial (COBRIT, 1,213 patients with complicated mild, moderate or severe TBI at 8 US level 1 trauma centres) found citicoline for 90 days did not improve functional or cognitive status: favourable improvement on the Glasgow Outcome Scale-Extended was 35.4% on citicoline versus 35.6% on placebo, the global test across the 9-scale core battery gave an odds ratio of 0.98 relative (95% CI 0.83 to 1.15) at 90 days, neither severity subgroup showed a treatment effect, and at 180 days the groups still did not differ (global odds ratio 0.87 relative, 0.72 to 1.04). A large blinded null with tight intervals, on a drug approved for TBI in 59 countries: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference).
