title: Surgical stabilisation of rib fractures (flail chest and displaced fractures)
question: In patients with flail chest or multiple displaced rib fractures, does operative rib fixation improve pain, ventilation duration and recovery versus conservative management?
balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED, split by population: The three randomised trials answer three different versions of the question. In VENTILATED flail chest (Marasco 2013), operative fixation shortened ICU stay after randomisation (285 vs 359 hours; P=0.03) and nearly eliminated post-extubation noninvasive ventilation (3 vs 50 hours; P=0.01), with no difference in 3-month spirometry or 6-month quality of life. In NON-ventilated patients with displaced fractures (Marasco 2022, 124 patients), fixation produced no improvement in pain or quality of life at 3 or 6 months. In the broadest population (SOFRIB 2026, 236 patients), fixation did not reduce ICU stay (mean difference 1.8 days, 95% CI −0.8 to 4.4; P=0.17), lengthened hospital stay (+3.3 days; P=0.01) and raised pneumonia rates (11.4% vs 3.3%; risk ratio 3.45 relative; P=0.02), while improving several quality-of-life and pain-impact scores beyond their minimal clinically important differences. Process gains in the ventilated flail subgroup; null-to-mixed elsewhere: POSSIBLE, and selective rather than routine.

title: Immediate total-body CT in severe trauma (REACT-2)
question: In patients with severe trauma, does immediate total-body CT scanning reduce mortality versus conventional imaging with selective CT?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, in-hospital mortality primary outcome): The one randomised trial (REACT-2, 1,403 patients randomised at four Dutch hospitals and one in Switzerland) found in-hospital mortality identical between immediate total-body CT and the standard work-up with selective CT: 86 of 541 (16%) versus 85 of 542 (16%) (P=0.92). The prespecified subgroups agreed — polytrauma 22% versus 25% (P=0.46) and traumatic brain injury 38% versus 44% (P=0.31). With no mortality benefit and a higher radiation dose, the trial's own reading is that future work should target patient selection, not routine total-body scanning: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference).

title: Bromelain-based enzymatic debridement of burns (NexoBrid)
question: In patients with deep partial- or full-thickness burns, does bromelain-based enzymatic debridement remove eschar faster and reduce surgical excision versus standard care?
balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED: Two open-label randomised trials, in children and in adults, agree on large effects. In children (Shoham 2025, 145 patients), bromelain-based debridement completed eschar removal in a median of 1 day versus 6 days for standard care (P<0.001) and cut the wound area needing surgical excision from 48.1% to 1.5% (P<0.001), with 12-month scar scores non-inferior (Modified Vancouver Scar Scale 3.8 vs 4.9). In adults (DETECT, 175 patients), complete eschar removal was 93% on NexoBrid versus 4% on gel vehicle (P<.001), surgical excision was 4% versus 72% against standard care (P<.001), median time to removal was 1.0 versus 3.8 days, and debridement blood loss was 14 mL versus 814 mL (P<.0001), again with non-inferior scar scores at 12 and 24 months. The endpoints are process and surgical-burden outcomes rather than survival, and neither trial could be blinded — but the effect sizes are large, mechanistic, and concordant across age groups: LIKELY.

title: Honey versus silver sulfadiazine for partial-thickness burns
question: In superficial partial-thickness burns, does honey dressing heal faster than silver sulfadiazine?
balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED: Two small randomised comparisons from South Asia, a quarter-century apart, both favour honey. Malik 2010 (150 patients, each contributing two comparable burn sites randomised within-patient) found re-epithelialisation faster with honey (13.47 ± 4.06 versus 15.62 ± 4.40 days; P<0.0001) and fewer Pseudomonas-positive cultures (6 versus 27 patients). Subrahmanyam 1998 (50 patients) found satisfactory epithelialisation by day 7 in 84% of honey-treated wounds versus 72% with silver sulfadiazine, and 100% versus 84% by day 21, with earlier histological reparative activity under honey. Small, single-centre, unblinded dressing trials with a healing-time surrogate: POSSIBLE.

title: Biobrane versus silver sulfadiazine in paediatric burns
question: In children with second-degree burns, does the biosynthetic dressing Biobrane shorten healing time and pain versus 1% silver sulfadiazine?
balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED: The anchor trial (Barret 2000, 20 children with second-degree burns) reports Biobrane superior to 1% silver sulfadiazine on pain, pain-medication requirements, wound healing time and length of hospital stay — but its abstract prints no figures for any of those outcomes, so the size of the advantage cannot be verified from the record. The second trial (Cassidy 2005) compared Biobrane with another modern dressing, Duoderm, and found no significant difference in time to healing or pain scores, with Biobrane statistically more expensive. Biobrane probably beats daily silver-cream tubbing on comfort and speed; against other coverings its edge is unproven: POSSIBLE.

title: High-dose vitamin C in burn resuscitation
question: In severely burned patients, does adjuvant high-dose ascorbic acid reduce resuscitation fluid volumes and oedema versus standard resuscitation?
balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED: The one randomised trial (Tanaka 2000, 37 patients with burns over 30% of body surface area at a single Japanese centre) found high-dose ascorbic acid (66 mg/kg per hour for the first 24 hours) roughly halved 24-hour resuscitation fluid requirements (3.0 ± 1.7 versus 5.5 ± 3.1 mL/kg per percentage of burn area; P<.01), reduced first-day weight gain (9.2% ± 8.2% versus 17.8% ± 6.9%) and burned-tissue water content, and shortened mechanical ventilation (12.1 ± 8.8 versus 21.3 ± 15.6 days; P<.05), with haemodynamics and urine output equivalent between groups. A single small trial whose primary measures are fluid volumes and oedema — surrogates — carries POSSIBLE, and no mortality result is reported in its abstract.

title: Hypertonic fluids for burn shock resuscitation
question: In severely burned patients, does hypertonic (sodium lactate or saline) resuscitation reduce total fluid volume and complications versus isotonic lactated Ringer's?
balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED, split between the two records: The older randomised trial (Gunn 1989, 51 adults with burns of at least 20% of body surface area) found NO advantage for hypertonic sodium lactate over lactated Ringer's — the authors were not able to demonstrate decreased fluid requirements, improved tolerance of feedings, or decreased weight gain. The larger later comparison (Belba 2009, 110 patients) found higher first-hour fluid and sodium loads with hypertonic lactate saline but lower net fluid accumulation (P=.0025), concluding 24-hour fluid requirements fell — though its abstract describes group allocation loosely and reports P values without the underlying volumes. One null RCT and one positive, loosely reported comparison on a volume surrogate: POSSIBLE, unproven either way.

title: Early enteral nutrition in major burns
question: In patients with major burns, does enteral nutrition started within 24 hours improve metabolic response, infection and healing versus delayed feeding?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED: The one randomised trial (Peck 2004) tested the metabolic claim directly: enteral feeding started within 24 hours did NOT decrease post-burn hypermetabolism — after adjustment for burn size, inhalation injury and age, average daily energy expenditure was if anything higher in the early group (mean difference 0.17 in the REE/BEE ratio; P=0.07). Mortality was similar (early 28%; late 38%) and infections and length of stay were reported as similar between groups, without figures. The trial's record does not state how many patients were randomised, and its measured question is metabolic; the infection and healing outcomes named in this shelf's question were not its endpoints. One small trial, a surrogate primary, an honest null: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference).

title: Silver foam and biosynthetic dressings for partial-thickness burns and scalds
question: In children and adults with partial-thickness burns/scalds, do modern silver-foam or biosynthetic (Suprathel) dressings heal as fast as standard care with less pain and fewer dressing changes?
balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED, split by comparison: Suprathel versus Mepilex Ag (Hundeshagen 2018, 62 outpatients with partial-thickness burns): healing time identical (12 days in both groups; P=0.75), but pain ratings were significantly lower with Suprathel over the first 5 days (P=0.03; paediatric subgroup P<0.001) and patients reported better overall scar quality (2 versus 4.5; P<0.001) — at considerably higher cost per cm² than Mepilex Ag. Silver foam versus porcine xenograft (Karlsson 2019, 58 children with scalds): silver foam healed significantly faster (median time to 97% healing 9 versus 15 days; P=0.004) with fewer and quicker dressing changes, and similar pain, infection and hospital stay. Modern dressings trade blows by endpoint: POSSIBLE.

title: Negative-pressure therapy over skin grafts in burns
question: In burn patients treated with (Meek) skin grafting, does negative-pressure wound therapy improve graft take/survival versus conventional dressing?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — PROPOSED: The entire randomised record for this question is one single-centre study of 13 burn patients (Zhang 2026), using each patient's two limbs as the comparison — Meek grafting under negative-pressure wound therapy on one side, traditional dressing on the other — and its abstract reports the direction of the results only: polyamide gauze adherence rate and skin survival rate were higher with negative pressure. No rates, no differences and no P values appear in the record, so the size of any benefit cannot be stated, let alone weighed. Thirteen patients, within-patient allocation, and a results-free abstract define weak evidence on this library's scale: MAYBE (weak evidence). Negative-pressure therapy for open wounds generally is home elsewhere (Shelf #1225) and is not re-carded here.

title: Gabapentin for pain after burn-wound debridement
question: In patients undergoing surgical debridement of burn wounds, does perioperative gabapentin reduce morphine consumption and pain versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED: The one double-blind trial (Rimaz 2012, 50 burn patients undergoing surgical debridement/resection of burn wounds) found a single oral dose of gabapentin 1200 mg, given 2 hours before surgery, significantly reduced 24-hour patient-controlled morphine consumption and visual analogue pain scores at rest and on movement at every measured time point (1, 4, 8, 12, 16, 20 and 24 hours after the operation; P<0.05), with sedation scores similar and no differences in adverse effects. The abstract reports significance without effect sizes, so the saving cannot be quantified from the record. A single small trial on an opioid-consumption surrogate: POSSIBLE. Perioperative gabapentin across surgery generally is a different, larger question (Shelf #1249) and is not re-carded here.

title: Dermal regeneration templates versus split-thickness grafts for full-thickness burns
question: In acute full-thickness burns, do dermal regeneration templates (e.g. Integra) improve scar quality and function versus split-thickness skin grafting alone?
balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED: Disclosure first: the anchor pinned in the topic file for this shelf (PMID 38313591) is, on verification, a systematic review and meta-analysis — not the comparative primary study the topic file described — so it is fenced in the synthesis, and the shelf's randomised anchor is the programme's founding trial pinned by title search instead. That trial (Heimbach 1988, 11 centres, 106 patients with life-threatening burns, 139 sites randomised within-patient) found median artificial-dermis take of 80% versus 95% for all comparative sites — equivalent to non-autograft control materials, below autograft-containing controls — while donor grafts for template sites were half as thick (.006 vs .013 inches; P<.0001) and donor sites healed 4 days sooner (10 ± 6 vs 14 ± 8 days; P<.0001); as wounds matured over a year there was less hypertrophic scarring at template sites and more patients preferred them. One old within-patient trial, take slightly worse, donor and scar outcomes better: POSSIBLE. A later randomised report in this field (PMID 33124156) is a retracted publication and is not evidence; it is named in the synthesis so no agent mistakes it for support.

title: Irrigation of open fractures: solution and pressure (FLOW)
question: In patients with open fractures, does irrigating the wound with castile soap versus saline, or at high versus low pressure, change reoperation rates?
balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED: The definitive factorial trial (FLOW, 2,447 eligible patients at 41 centres) answers both halves. Pressure does not matter: reoperation within 12 months occurred in 13.2% with high pressure, 12.7% with low pressure and 13.7% with very low pressure (hazard ratios for the pairwise comparisons 0.92 to 1.02 relative, all confidence intervals crossing 1) — very low pressure is an acceptable, low-cost alternative. Solution does matter, against soap: reoperation occurred in 14.8% with castile soap versus 11.6% with normal saline (hazard ratio 1.32 relative, 95% CI 1.06 to 1.66; P=0.01). One large trial settles the pressure question (LIKELY (the treatment made no difference)) and convicts soap in the same randomisation.

title: Silver dressings for venous leg ulcers (VULCAN)
question: In patients with venous leg ulcers, do silver-donating antimicrobial dressings heal ulcers faster than non-adherent non-antimicrobial dressings?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED: Disclosure first: the PMID pinned in the topic file for this shelf (20140943) is, on verification, a comment letter about the trial with no abstract — not the trial report; the shelf is built on the trial's full report pinned from the record the topic file cross-referenced (PMID 19939335). In VULCAN (213 patients randomised), silver-donating dressings did not beat simple low-adherent dressings under compression on any endpoint: complete healing at 12 weeks was 59.6% with silver versus 56.7% with control (not significant), median time to healing did not differ (P=0.408), recurrence at 1 year was 11.6% versus 14.4%, quality-of-life measures showed no differences at any time point — and silver cost more, with an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio of £489,250 per QALY, leading the investigators to conclude the dressings were not cost-effective. A concordant null on every measured outcome, at higher cost: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference).

title: Honey-impregnated dressings for venous leg ulcers
question: In patients with venous leg ulcers receiving compression, do honey-impregnated dressings improve healing versus usual care dressings?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED: The one large trial (Jull 2008, 368 participants with venous ulcers, all receiving compression bandaging) found honey-impregnated calcium alginate dressings did not significantly improve healing: at 12 weeks, 55.6% had healed on honey versus 49.7% on usual care (absolute increase 5.9 percentage points, 95% CI −4.3 to 15.7; P=0.258), with no significant differences in time to healing, change in ulcer area, infection incidence, or quality of life — while honey was probably more expensive and was associated with more adverse events (relative risk 1.3 relative, 95% CI 1.1 to 1.6; P=0.013). The confidence interval cannot exclude a modest benefit, which is why this is POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) rather than LIKELY — and the adverse-event excess runs against honey. Honey for burns (Shelf #1271) is a different wound with positive small trials; the two must not be merged.

title: Pentoxifylline for venous leg ulcers
question: In patients with venous leg ulcers, does oral pentoxifylline (with or without compression) increase healing versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED: Two double-blind placebo-controlled trials point the same way but only one reaches significance. Colgan 1990 (80 patients, six months) found complete healing of the reference ulcer in 23 of 38 on pentoxifylline versus 12 of 42 on placebo, with life-table healing proportions at six months of 64% versus 34% (log rank P=0.03). Dale 1999 (200 patients, factorial design) found complete healing in 64% on pentoxifylline versus 53% on placebo — and its authors state plainly that the difference did NOT reach statistical significance, a qualification the topic file's one-line summary omitted; the record governs, and it is printed on the card below. Two concordant moderate signals, one significant and one not, on top of compression in both: POSSIBLE.

title: Prophylactic silicone foam dressings to prevent hospital pressure injuries
question: In high-risk hospital/aged-care patients, do prophylactic multi-layer silicone foam dressings on sacrum and heels reduce pressure-injury incidence versus standard prevention alone?
balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED: Two randomised trials of the same dressing family in two high-risk settings agree. In aged care (Border III, 288 residents in 40 Australian nursing homes), pressure injuries developed in 16 residents on standard prevention versus 3 with prophylactic sacrum and heel dressings added (P=0.004) — an 80% relative risk reduction, with one injury prevented for every 12 residents treated. In critically ill hospital patients (the Border Trial, 440 patients), sacral and heel pressure-ulcer incidence was also significantly reduced with dressings (P=0.001), and the within-trial economic analysis found the intervention cost-saving overall (net AU$70.82 versus AU$144.56 per person). Concordant randomised evidence in hospital and residential care: LIKELY — with the standing caveat that a dressing trial cannot be blinded.

title: Support surfaces for pressure-ulcer prevention (PRESSURE programme)
question: In patients at risk of pressure ulcers, do alternating-pressure mattresses/systems prevent ulceration better than standard or overlay surfaces?
balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED: The PRESSURE programme's two large trials are more equivocal than the topic file's summary suggests, and the records govern. PRESSURE 2 (2,029 high-risk inpatients) compared alternating-pressure mattresses with high-specification foam: at the primary 30-day post-treatment follow-up there was INSUFFICIENT evidence of a difference in time to a new category ≥2 pressure ulcer (hazard ratio 0.76 relative, 95% CI 0.56 to 1.04; P=0.089; absolute difference 2%); only the treatment-phase sensitivity analysis reached significance (hazard ratio 0.66 relative, 0.46 to 0.93; P=0.0176; absolute difference 2.6%). PRESSURE 1 (1,972 patients) compared alternating-pressure mattresses with alternating-pressure overlays and found no difference at all (new grade ≥2 ulcers in 10.3% versus 10.7%; difference 0.4%, −2.3 to 3.1; P=0.75). Small, time-limited advantages over foam at best: POSSIBLE.

title: Repositioning frequency for pressure-injury prevention (TEAM-UP and TURN)
question: In nursing-home residents at risk, can repositioning every 3–4 hours (on high-density foam) replace 2-hourly turning without increasing pressure injuries?
balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED: Two large nursing-home trials on modern high-density foam mattresses found no penalty for longer intervals. TURN (942 residents at moderate or high risk, 27 nursing homes) found pressure-ulcer incidence of 2.5% with 2-hourly, 0.6% with 3-hourly and 3.1% with 4-hourly repositioning over 3 weeks — no significant difference (P=.68). TEAM-UP (992 residents analysed, nine nursing homes cluster-randomised to 2-, 3- or 4-hour protocols with sensor-cued staff) recorded ZERO pressure injuries in any arm during the 4-week intervention (versus 5.24% in the baseline period), with compliance best at 4 hours (95% vs 80% at 2 hours) — and its authors state explicitly that a causal link between interval and outcome was not established. Very low event rates throughout mean equivalence is suggested, not proven: POSSIBLE.

title: Topical wound oxygen therapy for diabetic foot ulcers (TWO2)
question: In patients with chronic diabetic foot ulcers, does cyclical pressurised topical wound oxygen increase complete healing versus standard care with sham?
balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED: The one double-blind, sham-controlled trial (TWO2) reported a large healing advantage for cyclical pressurised topical wound oxygen added to optimal standard care — complete closure at 12 weeks in 41.7% versus 13.5% (odds ratio 4.57 relative, 97.8% CI 1.19 to 17.57; P=0.010; adjusted odds ratio 6.00 relative), with 56% versus 27% still closed at 12 months (P=0.013). But the trial was STOPPED AT ITS FIRST predetermined interim analysis — after only 73 of a planned 220 patients completed the treatment phase — and trials stopped this early for benefit are known to overestimate effects; the confidence interval (odds ratios from 1.19 to 17.57 relative) is correspondingly wide. A real blinded signal at a fragile scale: POSSIBLE. Hyperbaric (systemic) oxygen is a different intervention, home on Shelf #1224.

title: Sucrose octasulfate (TLC-NOSF) dressings for diabetic foot ulcers (Explorer)
question: In patients with neuroischaemic diabetic foot ulcers, does a sucrose octasulfate dressing increase wound closure versus a control dressing?
balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED: The one double-blind trial (Explorer, 240 patients with non-infected neuroischaemic diabetic foot ulcers in five European countries) found wound closure at 20 weeks in 48% on the sucrose octasulfate dressing versus 30% on an identical dressing without it — an 18-percentage-point difference (95% CI 5 to 30; adjusted odds ratio 2.60 relative, 1.43 to 4.73; P=0.002) — with target-wound infections actually somewhat fewer on the active dressing (25 of 126 patients (20%) versus 32 of 114 (28%)), minor amputations in 1 versus 2 patients, and deaths in 3 (2%) versus 4 (4%) patients, none related to treatment. title: Tap water versus sterile saline for wound cleansing
question: In patients with acute wounds/lacerations, does cleansing or irrigating with tap water result in infection rates no higher than sterile saline?
balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED: The human randomised evidence is one multicentre trial (Moscati 2007, 715 adults enrolled with acute simple lacerations requiring sutures or staples; follow-up on 634): wound infection occurred in 12 of 300 (4%) irrigated with tap water versus 11 of 334 (3.3%) with sterile saline (relative risk 1.21 relative, 95% CI 0.5 to 2.7), and the authors conclude the rates were equivalent, agreeing with previous single-institution trials. Disclosure: the second PMID pinned in the topic file for this shelf (9835469) is a laboratory RAT study — animal data, which this library does not card — so it is fenced in the synthesis and the shelf rests on the human trial alone. Infection is a hard endpoint and the rates are low and close, but the interval reaches a 2.7-fold relative risk: POSSIBLE.

title: Age of transfused red blood cells (ABLE and the storage-age trials)
question: In critically ill adults, does transfusion of fresh (short-storage) red cells reduce 90-day mortality versus standard-issue (older) red cells?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, 90-day mortality primary outcome in both trials): Two large randomised, blinded trials agree. ABLE (2,430 critically ill adults; mean storage 6.1 days fresh versus 22.0 days standard-issue) found 90-day mortality of 37.0% versus 35.3% (absolute difference 1.7 percentage points, 95% CI −2.1 to 5.5; hazard ratio 1.1 relative, 0.9 to 1.2). TRANSFUSE (4,919 patients analysed; mean storage 11.8 versus 22.4 days) found 90-day mortality of 24.8% versus 24.1% (absolute difference 0.7 points, −1.7 to 3.1; P=0.57). Fresh blood does not save lives in the ICU; the storage-age question is settled at this scale, and the stamp is proposed pending the developer's personal verdict because the outcome is mortality (Tier C).

title: Prothrombin complex concentrate versus plasma for warfarin-related intracerebral haemorrhage (INCH)
question: In patients with vitamin-K-antagonist-related intracerebral haemorrhage, does 4-factor PCC normalise INR faster and limit haematoma expansion versus fresh frozen plasma?
balance: POSSIBLE: The single randomised test (INCH, 50 patients treated) found 4-factor PCC normalised the INR far faster than fresh frozen plasma — INR of 1.2 or lower within 3 hours in 67% on PCC versus 9% on plasma (adjusted odds ratio 30.6 relative, 95% CI 4.7 to 197.9; P=0.0003) — and the trial was stopped early after a safety analysis because of harm signals in the plasma arm: 8 of 23 plasma patients (35%) died, five of them from haematoma expansion within 48 hours, versus 5 of 27 (19%) on PCC, none from haematoma expansion. A small, stopped-early, open-label trial caps the stamp at POSSIBLE; the primary claim is reversal speed and haematoma behaviour, so the shelf is not Tier C, with the mortality figures printed on the card.

title: Desmopressin for intracerebral haemorrhage on antiplatelet drugs (DASH)
question: In patients with spontaneous intracerebral haemorrhage taking antiplatelet drugs, does desmopressin improve functional outcome?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, death-or-dependency outcome): DASH is explicitly a phase 2 feasibility trial, not an efficacy trial: 54 patients were randomised (27 desmopressin, 27 placebo) of 1,380 screened, and recruitment itself was the primary outcome. The outcome figures are hypothesis-generating only — death or dependency at day 90 (modified Rankin Scale score above 4) in 22% on desmopressin versus 37% on placebo, with serious adverse events in 44% versus 48% — in a sample far too small to support any efficacy reading. The honest stamp for whether desmopressin improves outcome is MAYBE (weak evidence): feasibility was shown, benefit was not tested at scale, and a definitive trial is what the record calls for.

title: Intraoperative cell salvage
question: In patients having surgery with expected blood loss, does intraoperative cell salvage reduce allogeneic transfusion versus standard care?
balance: POSSIBLE: The carded randomised test is small and single-specialty: 61 patients having off-pump coronary bypass were randomised to washed salvaged-blood autotransfusion or homologous blood only; the salvage group had a higher 24-hour haemoglobin (11.9 vs 10.5 g/dL; P=0.0007) and a lower frequency of homologous blood product use (5 of 30 versus 11 of 31) that did not reach significance (P=0.095), with no derangement of clotting measures, no excess bleeding or adverse events, and no significant cost difference. The direction favours salvage for transfusion sparing, but the carded evidence is one 61-patient trial with a transfusion-exposure surrogate, so the stamp is POSSIBLE and the shelf says so.

title: Granulocyte transfusion for neutropenic infection (RING)
question: In neutropenic patients with bacterial or fungal infection, do transfused granulocytes from G-CSF/dexamethasone-stimulated donors improve infection response and survival?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): The definitive randomised test (RING, 114 patients randomised) found no overall effect: the composite of survival plus microbial response at 42 days succeeded in 42% with granulocyte transfusion versus 43% with standard antimicrobial therapy alone (P>0.99), and 49% versus 41% among patients who received their assigned treatments (P=0.64), with no difference in any infection-type subgroup. But RING enrolled only half its planned sample, so its power to detect a true benefit was low, and a post hoc analysis hinted that patients receiving higher granulocyte doses (at least 0.6×10^9 per kilogram per transfusion) fared better. An underpowered null caps at POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): no demonstrated benefit, with the dose question honestly left open.

title: Erythropoietin in critically ill and trauma patients
question: In critically ill patients, does epoetin alfa reduce transfusion or mortality versus placebo — and does any mortality benefit concentrate in trauma patients?
balance: Split: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — transfusion sparing in critical illness overall · POSSIBLE — a mortality benefit confined to trauma patients — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, mortality claim): In the 1,460-patient trial (Corwin 2007), epoetin alfa did NOT reduce transfusion (relative risk 0.95 relative, 95% CI 0.85 to 1.06) and overall mortality was not significantly lower (day-29 adjusted hazard ratio 0.79 relative, 0.56 to 1.10) — while thrombotic events increased (hazard ratio 1.41 relative, 1.06 to 1.86). The trauma signal is a prespecified subgroup finding repeated across the programme: day-29 mortality hazard ratio 0.37 relative (0.19 to 0.72) in Corwin's trauma patients, and the pooled trauma-cohort analysis of the two large trials (EPO-2 and EPO-3) found day-29 mortality of 4.1% versus 8.9% and 3.5% versus 6.7% (hazard ratios 0.46 and 0.51 relative). A subgroup-replicated mortality signal without an overall effect is POSSIBLE, not more — the trauma analysis authors themselves call for a definitive trauma trial.

title: Leukocyte depletion of transfused blood
question: In patients undergoing cardiac surgery, does leukocyte-depleted transfusion reduce postoperative complications and mortality versus standard transfusion?
balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, mortality claim): One randomised trial (van de Watering 1998, 914 cardiac-surgery patients in three arms) found 60-day postoperative mortality of 7.8% with buffy-coat-reduced (non-filtered) packed cells versus 3.6% with fresh-filtered and 3.3% with stored-filtered leukocyte-depleted units (P=0.015), while infection rates (23.0% versus 16.9% and 17.9%) did not differ significantly (P=0.13) and hospital and ICU stay were unchanged. A single 1998 three-arm trial, with the mortality difference only partly explained by infections and later leukoreduction literature mixed, supports POSSIBLE — not more — and the mortality claim makes it Tier C.

title: Pathogen-reduced platelets (SPRINT and successors)
question: In patients receiving platelet transfusions for thrombocytopenia, do pathogen-reduced (amotosalen/UVA) platelets prevent bleeding as effectively as conventional platelets?
balance: POSSIBLE: The pivotal randomised trial (SPRINT, 645 thrombocytopenic patients) met its non-inferiority test on the bleeding endpoint: WHO grade 2 bleeding occurred in 58.5% on amotosalen/UVA pathogen-inactivated platelets versus 57.5% on conventional platelets, and grade 3 or 4 bleeding in 4.1% versus 6.1% (non-inferiority P=0.001), with fewer transfusion reactions (3.0% vs 4.4%; P=0.02). The price was platelet quality: 1-hour corrected count increments were lower (11.1 versus 16.0 ×10^3), the interval to the next transfusion shorter (1.9 versus 2.4 days), and more platelet transfusions were needed (8.4 versus 6.2). Bleeding-grade endpoints are surrogates for the outcomes that matter most, and a single pivotal trial caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.

title: Cold-stored platelets for surgical bleeding (CHIPS)
question: In patients undergoing cardiac surgery at risk of bleeding, are cold-stored platelets non-inferior to room-temperature platelets for postoperative bleeding?
balance: POSSIBLE: One phase 3 trial (CHIPS, 989 patients analysed — children and adults undergoing cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass at 27 sites) found cold-stored platelets (stored up to 21 days) non-inferior to room-temperature platelets (up to 7 days) on the primary haemostatic efficacy score, with a posterior probability of non-inferiority above 99.9% for every cold-storage duration tested (pooled mean difference 0.09 points on a 1–5 scale where higher means more bleeding, 95% credible interval −0.06 to 0.23, against a 1-point margin) and no significant difference in 24-hour chest-tube output. A single — albeit large and adaptive — trial on a haemostatic-score surrogate, in a mixed paediatric-adult population, caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.

title: Liberal versus restrictive transfusion in traumatic brain injury (HEMOTION)
question: In adults with moderate-to-severe TBI and anaemia, does a liberal transfusion threshold (Hb ≤100 g/L) improve 6-month neurological outcome versus a restrictive threshold (≤70 g/L)?

title: Stress-ulcer prophylaxis with pantoprazole (SUP-ICU)
question: In ICU patients at risk of gastrointestinal bleeding, does prophylactic pantoprazole reduce clinically important bleeding without increasing mortality or infection?
balance: Split: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — mortality · LIKELY — less clinically important bleeding — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, mortality co-reported): SUP-ICU (3,298 ICU patients at bleeding risk) found 90-day mortality identical on pantoprazole versus placebo (31.1% vs 30.4%; relative risk 1.02 relative, 95% CI 0.91 to 1.13; P=0.76) and a composite of clinically important events no different (21.9% vs 22.6%), while clinically important gastrointestinal bleeding was lower on pantoprazole (2.5% vs 4.2%). title: Permissive underfeeding versus standard enteral feeding (PermiT)
question: In critically ill adults, does permissive underfeeding (40–60% of caloric goal, full protein) improve 90-day mortality versus standard feeding (70–100%)?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, mortality primary/co-reported): PermiT (894 critically ill adults; permissive underfeeding at 40–60% of caloric goal with full protein versus standard feeding at 70–100%) found 90-day mortality of 27.2% versus 28.9% (relative risk 0.94 relative, 95% CI 0.76 to 1.16; P=0.58), with no differences in intolerance, infections or length of stay. title: Higher protein dosing in critical illness (EFFORT Protein)
question: In mechanically ventilated patients at nutritional risk, does high-dose protein (≥2.2 g/kg/day) improve time to discharge alive versus usual dose (≤1.2 g/kg/day)?

A single trial with a harm-leaning subgroup pattern supports POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) and no use of high-dose protein as a default.

title: Early active mobilisation during mechanical ventilation (TEAM)
question: In ICU patients on mechanical ventilation, does protocolised early active mobilisation improve days alive and out of ICU (and mortality) versus usual-care mobilisation?
balance: Split: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — at TEAM scale · POSSIBLE — functional benefit in the earlier small trial — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, mortality co-reported): TEAM (750 ventilated adults; protocolised early active mobilisation with sedation minimisation versus usual care) found no difference in days alive and out of hospital at 180 days (median 143 versus 145; difference −2.0 days, 95% CI −10 to 6; P=0.62), death by day 180 in 22.5% versus 19.5% (odds ratio 1.15 relative, 0.81 to 1.65), and significantly more mobilisation-related adverse events (9.2% vs 4.1%; P=0.005). title: Flexible family visitation in the ICU (ICU Visits)
question: In ICU patients, does a flexible family-visitation policy (up to 12 h/day) reduce delirium incidence versus restricted visitation?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): The one large randomised test (ICU Visits, 1,685 patients in 36 Brazilian ICUs, cluster-crossover) found delirium incidence of 18.9% with flexible visitation (up to 12 hours/day, with family education; actual visits averaged 4.8 hours) versus 20.1% with restricted visitation (median 1.5 hours/day) — an adjusted difference of −1.7 percentage points (95% CI −6.1 to 2.7; P=0.44). ICU-acquired infections and staff burnout also did not differ. What did improve was the family: anxiety (adjusted difference −1.6 points) and depression (−1.2 points) scores were significantly better with flexible visitation. A large null on the patient outcome with a real family benefit carries LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for the delirium claim. title: Subglottic secretion drainage to prevent ventilator-associated pneumonia
question: In intubated patients expected to be ventilated >48–72 hours, does subglottic secretion drainage reduce ventilator-associated pneumonia versus a standard endotracheal tube?
balance: POSSIBLE: The patient-level randomised trial of the drainage itself (Lacherade 2010, 333 patients ventilated at least 48 hours) found microbiologically confirmed VAP in 14.8% with intermittent subglottic secretion drainage versus 25.6% without (P=0.02; a 42.2% relative risk reduction, relative), with no difference in ventilation duration or hospital mortality. The newer automation trial (MICROINHALO 2026, 250 patients analysed, cluster-randomised) tested automatic cuff-pressure management plus automatic drainage against manual management of both — and MISSED its primary endpoint: day-3 tracheal colonisation was 37% versus 41.5% (difference −4%, 95% CI −16 to 8; P=0.52), although its secondary VAP rates were lower (clinical VAP 12.6% vs 24.4%, P=0.016; microbiologically confirmed 10.2% vs 19.5%, P=0.039). One positive mid-size trial of drainage plus a null-primary automation trial supports POSSIBLE — and the shelf discloses on its face that MICROINHALO's primary endpoint was colonisation, not VAP, contrary to how the topic draft framed it.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Lung recruitment manoeuvres with titrated PEEP in ARDS (ART)
question: In moderate-to-severe ARDS, does an aggressive lung-recruitment strategy with PEEP titration reduce 28-day mortality versus a low-PEEP strategy?
balance: LIKELY (harm) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, mortality harm): The one large randomised test (ART, 1,010 patients with moderate-to-severe ARDS in 120 ICUs) found an aggressive lung-recruitment manoeuvre with PEEP titrated to best respiratory-system compliance INCREASED 28-day all-cause mortality: 55.3% versus 49.3% on a low-PEEP strategy (hazard ratio 1.20 relative, 95% CI 1.01 to 1.42; P=0.041). Six-month mortality was also higher (65.3% vs 59.9%; hazard ratio 1.18 relative, 1.01 to 1.38), ventilator-free days fewer (5.3 vs 6.4), and barotrauma more frequent (5.6% vs 1.6%; P=0.001), as was pneumothorax requiring drainage (3.2% vs 1.2%). A 1,010-patient trial with concordant harm across mortality, barotrauma and ventilator-free days carries LIKELY (harm): the ART strategy should not be used routinely.

title: Oesophageal-pressure-guided PEEP in ARDS (EPVent)
question: In moderate-to-severe ARDS, does titrating PEEP to oesophageal pressure improve the composite of death and ventilator-free days versus an empirical high-PEEP/FiO2 table?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, death within the primary composite): The phase 2 trial (EPVent-2, 200 patients with moderate-to-severe ARDS) found no difference on its ranked composite of death and ventilator-free days (probability of a more favourable outcome with oesophageal-pressure-guided PEEP 49.6%, 95% CI 41.7 to 57.5; P=0.92), with 28-day mortality of 32.4% versus 30.6% on an empirical high-PEEP/FiO2 strategy and no difference in ventilator-free days among survivors — although rescue therapy was needed less often (3.9% vs 12.2%; P=0.04). The earlier pilot (EPVent-1, 61 patients) had shown better oxygenation (PaO2/FiO2 88 mm Hg higher at 72 hours) and compliance, a physiology result the larger trial did not convert into outcome benefit. A single 200-patient phase 2 trial supports POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference).

title: Corticosteroids before extubation to prevent laryngeal oedema
question: In ICU patients at high risk of post-extubation laryngeal oedema, does pre-extubation methylprednisolone reduce laryngeal oedema and reintubation?
balance: LIKELY: One large double-blind multicentre trial (François 2007, 698 patients analysed of 761 randomised, all ventilated more than 36 hours before a planned extubation) found 12-hour methylprednisolone pretreatment (20 mg starting 12 hours before extubation, then every 4 hours until tube removal) cut postextubation laryngeal oedema from 22% to 3% (P<0.0001) and overall reintubation from 8% to 4% (P=0.02); reintubations caused by laryngeal oedema fell from 54% to 8% of reintubations (P=0.005). A single trial with effects this large on both the mechanism endpoint and the clinical endpoint it feeds supports LIKELY for patients like those enrolled — ventilated more than 36 hours, planned extubation. The paediatric companion question is separate and is not carded here.
stamp: LIKELY

title: Post-extubation high-flow oxygen with noninvasive ventilation in high-risk patients
question: In patients at high risk of extubation failure, does alternating high-flow nasal oxygen with NIV after extubation reduce reintubation versus high-flow oxygen alone?
balance: LIKELY: Two randomised trials support active post-extubation support in high-risk patients. Thille 2019 (641 patients at high risk of extubation failure — over 65 or with cardiac/respiratory disease) found reintubation by day 7 in 11.8% with high-flow nasal oxygen alternating with NIV versus 18.2% with high-flow oxygen alone (difference −6.4 percentage points, 95% CI −12.0 to −0.9; P=0.02), with postextubation respiratory failure also lower (21% vs 29%) and ICU mortality not significantly different (6% vs 9%). Hernández 2016 (604 high-risk patients) found high-flow oxygen non-inferior to NIV for reintubation (22.8% vs 19.1%, within the 10-point margin) with less postextubation respiratory failure (26.9% vs 39.8%). Together: in high-risk patients, high-flow oxygen is at least NIV's equal, and alternating the two beats high-flow alone — LIKELY.
stamp: LIKELY

title: Conservative versus interventional treatment of primary spontaneous pneumothorax
question: In haemodynamically stable patients with moderate-to-large primary spontaneous pneumothorax, is conservative management non-inferior to chest-drain intervention for lung re-expansion?
balance: POSSIBLE: One open-label non-inferiority trial (PSP, 316 patients aged 14–50 with a first moderate-to-large primary spontaneous pneumothorax) found lung re-expansion within 8 weeks in 94.4% with conservative management versus 98.5% with intervention in the complete-case analysis (risk difference −4.1 percentage points, 95% CI −8.6 to 0.5; P=0.02 for non-inferiority against a −9-point margin) — but in the sensitivity analysis treating all missing data as failure, the difference was −11.0 points (−18.4 to −3.5), OUTSIDE the margin, so the authors themselves call the evidence 'modest'. Conservative care (which still intervened in 15.4% of patients under protocol rules) carried a lower risk of serious adverse events and recurrence. A single trial whose primary result is not robust to missing-data assumptions caps at POSSIBLE.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Ambulatory management of primary spontaneous pneumothorax (RAMPP)
question: In stable primary spontaneous pneumothorax needing intervention, does ambulatory management with a pleural vent reduce total hospital stay versus standard chest-drain care?
balance: POSSIBLE: The single randomised trial (RAMPP, 236 patients aged 16–55 with symptomatic primary spontaneous pneumothorax) found ambulatory management with a pleural vent significantly shortened total hospital stay to day 30 — median 0 days (IQR 0–3) versus 4 days (0–8) on standard care (P<0.0001; median difference 2 days, 95% CI 1 to 3) — at the cost of more adverse events: 55% of the ambulatory group versus 39% of standard care had adverse events, and all 14 serious adverse events occurred in the ambulatory arm, eight of them related to the intervention (enlarging pneumothorax, asymptomatic pulmonary oedema, device malfunction, leak or dislodgement). One open-label trial with a clear stay benefit and a clear adverse-event price supports POSSIBLE. (Anchor pins, as flagged at drafting: the results report is pinned here as Hallifax et al., Lancet 2020, PMID 32622394 — the topic draft cited the journal as Lancet Respiratory Medicine, which the record corrects to The Lancet; the draft's verified programme record, PMID 31179004, is the trial PROTOCOL and is not carded.)
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Pigtail catheter versus chest tube for traumatic pneumothorax
question: In injured patients with uncomplicated traumatic pneumothorax, is a small-bore pigtail catheter as effective as a chest tube, with less pain?
balance: POSSIBLE: One small single-centre randomised trial (40 injured patients with uncomplicated traumatic pneumothorax; 20 per arm) found 14-Fr pigtail catheters resolved the pneumothorax as successfully as 28-Fr chest tubes, with similar duration of tube placement and insertion-related complications, while tube-site pain was substantially lower with the pigtail at every measurement — after insertion 3.2 versus 7.7, day 1 1.9 versus 6.2, day 2 2.1 versus 5.5 (all significant) — although total pain-medication use did not differ significantly and chest-wall trauma pain was similar in both groups. Forty patients and a pain-score primary endpoint cap the stamp at POSSIBLE.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Epidural analgesia for traumatic rib fractures
question: In patients with multiple traumatic rib fractures, does thoracic epidural analgesia improve pain, pulmonary complications and mortality versus systemic/parenteral analgesia?
balance: POSSIBLE: The largest primary randomised trial pinned at build (Bulger 2004) enrolled only 46 patients — of 408 admitted with more than three rib fractures, 282 met exclusion criteria and 80 could not be consented — and found, despite the epidural group having MORE direct pulmonary injury (more flail segments, contusions and chest tubes), a pneumonia rate of 18% on epidural versus 38% on intravenous opioids (adjusted odds ratio 6.0 relative for pneumonia with opioids, 95% CI 1.0 to 35; P=0.05) and, in patients with pulmonary contusion, twice the ventilator days on opioids (incidence rate ratio 2.0 relative, 1.6 to 2.6). A 46-patient trial from 2004 with a barely-significant adjusted estimate is POSSIBLE and no more — this is the weakest pack in its slate, and the shelf says so. (Anchor note: the topic draft anchored this shelf to a systematic review/meta-analysis, PMID 25683770; per build rules the meta-analysis is fenced and the largest primary RCT — Bulger 2004, PMID 15300210 — is carded instead.)
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Ketamine versus morphine for traumatic pain (prehospital and ED)
question: In patients with acute traumatic pain, does (low-dose) ketamine provide analgesia non-inferior to morphine, with an acceptable adverse-effect profile?
balance: POSSIBLE: One multicentre single-blind non-inferiority trial (KETAMORPH, 251 patients with out-of-hospital traumatic pain and a verbal pain score of at least 5) found intravenous ketamine non-inferior to morphine for pain reduction at 30 minutes — mean pain-score change −3.7 versus −3.8 (difference 0.1 points, 95% CI −0.7 to 0.9, against a non-inferiority margin of 1.3) — with no clinically meaningful vital-sign differences, but with adverse effects in 40.8% on ketamine versus 16.8% on morphine, most commonly emergence phenomena (20.0% of ketamine patients) versus nausea (10.6% of morphine patients); no adverse event required intervention. A single trial on a pain-score endpoint supports POSSIBLE: ketamine is a legitimate morphine alternative prehospital, with a different and busier minor-adverse-effect profile.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Intranasal ketamine versus intranasal fentanyl for children's limb-injury pain (PICHFORK)
question: In children with moderate-to-severe limb-injury pain, is intranasal ketamine non-inferior to intranasal fentanyl for pain relief?
balance: POSSIBLE: One double-blind randomised trial (PICHFORK, 80 children enrolled, 73 analysed, aged 3–13 with isolated limb injury and pain above 6 of 10, all co-administered oral ibuprofen) found intranasal ketamine 1 mg/kg and intranasal fentanyl 1.5 μg/kg produced similar pain reduction at 30 minutes — median reductions of 45 mm versus 40 mm (difference 5 mm, 95% CI −10 to 20 mm) — maintained to 60 minutes, with reductions above 20 mm in 82% versus 79% and satisfaction in 83% versus 72%. Adverse events, mainly mild, were more frequent with ketamine (78% versus 40%), including moderate sedation in three ketamine patients. A single small trial supports POSSIBLE: comparable analgesia, more minor ketamine effects.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Perioperative rosuvastatin in cardiac surgery (STICS)
question: In patients undergoing elective cardiac surgery, does perioperative rosuvastatin prevent postoperative atrial fibrillation or acute kidney injury?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference, with kidney harm): One large randomised trial (STICS, 1,922 patients in sinus rhythm scheduled for elective cardiac surgery in China) found perioperative rosuvastatin 20 mg daily did NOT prevent postoperative atrial fibrillation (21.1% versus 20.5% on placebo; odds ratio 1.04 relative, 95% CI 0.84 to 1.30; P=0.72) and did not reduce perioperative myocardial injury (troponin I release area under the curve essentially identical; between-group difference 1%, −9 to 13; P=0.80), with no benefit in any subgroup or secondary outcome — while significantly increasing postoperative acute kidney injury by an absolute 5.4 (SE 1.9) percentage points (P=0.005), despite lower LDL cholesterol and C-reactive protein after surgery. A large, internally consistent null with a harm signal carries LIKELY (the treatment made no difference).
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference, with kidney harm)

title: Opioid-free anaesthesia (POFA)
question: In patients having major or intermediate noncardiac surgery, does dexmedetomidine-based opioid-free anaesthesia reduce postoperative opioid-related adverse events versus remifentanil-based anaesthesia?
balance: POSSIBLE (harm-leaning; the treatment made no difference): The single randomised test (POFA, 312 patients analysed having major or intermediate noncardiac surgery) REFUTED its hypothesis: the composite of postoperative opioid-related adverse events (hypoxaemia, ileus or cognitive dysfunction within 48 hours) occurred MORE often with dexmedetomidine-based opioid-free anaesthesia than with remifentanil-based anaesthesia — 78% versus 67% (relative risk 1.16 relative, 95% CI 1.01 to 1.33; P=0.031) — driven by hypoxaemia (72% vs 61%; relative risk 1.19 relative, 1.02 to 1.40), and the trial was stopped prematurely because of five cases of severe bradycardia in the dexmedetomidine group. Opioid-free patients did use less postoperative morphine and had less nausea and vomiting, with similar analgesia, but had more delayed extubation and longer recovery-room stays. A stopped-early single trial supports POSSIBLE against the opioid-free strategy as tested. (Journal correction: the topic draft cited this trial as JAMA 2021; the verified record is Beloeil et al., Anesthesiology 2021.)
stamp: POSSIBLE (harm-leaning; the treatment made no difference)

title: Desflurane versus sevoflurane for recovery from anaesthesia
question: In ambulatory/minor-to-moderate surgery, does desflurane produce faster emergence and recovery than sevoflurane, and at what cost in adverse respiratory events?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): The carded randomised test in the population where the question matters most (Taschner 2024, 190 patients aged 65 or older having minor-to-moderate-risk noncardiac surgery with same-day discharge intent) found NO significant difference in postoperative recovery time between desflurane and sevoflurane: median time from PACU arrival to reaching discharge criteria (modified Aldrete score at least 12) was 0 minutes in both groups (P=0.245), because most patients already met criteria on arrival (81.1% desflurane versus 88.4% sevoflurane; P=0.277). Postoperative nausea and vomiting, PACU bispectral index values and maximum S100B concentrations also did not differ. One single-centre trial with a ceiling-limited endpoint supports POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): in older day-case patients, the classic 'desflurane wakes you faster' claim did not survive measurement.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference)

title: Total intravenous versus volatile anaesthesia for major noncardiac surgery
question: In adults having major noncardiac surgery, does total intravenous anaesthesia with propofol improve postoperative outcomes versus volatile inhalational anaesthesia?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): One large pragmatic randomised trial (2,508 patients aged 50 or older having elective major noncardiac surgery at 49 UK hospitals) found total intravenous anaesthesia with propofol and volatile inhalational anaesthesia produced essentially identical recovery: days alive and at home at 30 days were 22.5 (SD 6.8) versus 22.4 (SD 6.6) (incidence rate ratio 1.00 relative, 95% CI 0.99 to 1.02; adjusted P=0.68), with no differences in days alive and at home at 90 days, mortality at 30 days, 90 days or 6 months, Quality of Recovery-15 score at day 3, delirium, or major complications (12.4% overall). TIVA patients reported less thirst, hoarseness and nausea/vomiting; the trial's only two cases of certain or probable unintentional awareness both occurred in the TIVA group. A 2,508-patient trial with a dead-centre primary estimate carries LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for the recovery claim.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference)

title: Dexamethasone to prevent post-extubation airway obstruction in children
question: In mechanically ventilated children at risk of post-extubation airway obstruction, does intravenous dexamethasone before extubation reduce obstruction/stridor and reintubation?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence): The only placebo-controlled randomised trial in children (Varghese 2024, 70 children in one Indian PICU) found no significant difference in its primary outcome — clinically significant stridor (Westley score at least 3) occurred in 25.7% on dexamethasone versus 31.4% on placebo (P=0.79), and reintubation was 11.4% versus 17.1% (P=0.73). The second randomised trial (Parajuli 2021, 287 children) compares low-dose with high-dose dexamethasone with no placebo arm, and its PubMed record's abstract states the design and the 12% non-inferiority margin but prints no results, so it cannot be weighted. A single small null trial plus an unweightable dose comparison is weak evidence in both directions: MAYBE (weak evidence). The adult pre-extubation steroid evidence is a different population and a different shelf (#1308) and is not imported here.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence)

title: Pressure-support versus T-piece spontaneous breathing trials (Subirà)
question: In patients receiving mechanical ventilation, does a pressure-support spontaneous breathing trial produce more successful extubations than a T-piece trial?
balance: LIKELY: One large randomised trial (Subirà 2019, 1,153 patients in 18 Spanish ICUs) found that a 30-minute pressure-support spontaneous breathing trial (8 cm H2O) produced significantly more successful extubations than a 2-hour T-piece trial — 82.3% versus 74.0% (difference 8.2 percentage points, 95% CI 3.4 to 13.0; P=.001) — with no difference in reintubation (11.1% vs 11.9%). Hospital mortality was also lower with pressure support (10.4% vs 14.9%; P=.02) and 90-day mortality lower (13.2% vs 17.3%), but those are secondary outcomes of a single trial and are not the shelf's claim. A single large, well-run trial with a clear primary-endpoint result carries LIKELY for the extubation question.
stamp: LIKELY

title: Statins in ARDS (HARP-2 and SAILS)
question: In patients with ARDS, does enteral simvastatin (HARP-2) — or rosuvastatin in sepsis-associated ARDS (SAILS) — improve ventilator-free days or mortality?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, mortality co-reported in both trials): Two large double-blind trials of two different statins agree. HARP-2 (540 patients with ARDS of any cause; enteral simvastatin 80 mg) found ventilator-free days of 12.6 versus 11.5 (P=0.21) and 28-day mortality of 22.0% versus 26.8% (P=0.23). SAILS (745 patients with sepsis-associated ARDS; enteral rosuvastatin, stopped early for futility) found 60-day in-hospital mortality of 28.5% versus 24.9% (P=0.21), identical ventilator-free days (15.1 vs 15.1), and fewer renal-failure-free and hepatic-failure-free days on rosuvastatin. Neither statin improved any clinical outcome; the stamp is proposed pending the developer's personal verdict because mortality is co-reported (Tier C).

title: Inhaled nitric oxide in acute lung injury / ARDS
question: In adults with acute lung injury/ARDS, does low-dose inhaled nitric oxide improve oxygenation, ventilator-free days or mortality?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): Inhaled nitric oxide improves oxygenation briefly and does not improve any clinical outcome. The large triple-blind trial (Taylor 2004, 385 patients with moderately severe acute lung injury not due to sepsis) found days alive and off assisted breathing of 10.7 on nitric oxide versus 10.6 on placebo (P=.97), with mortality 23% versus 20% (P=.54), despite a statistically significant PaO2 rise that resolved by 48 hours. The earlier phase II dose-ranging trial (Dellinger 1998, 177 patients with ARDS) found the same pattern: an acute oxygenation response in 60% of treated patients, and no difference in mortality or days alive off mechanical ventilation. The claim tested is oxygenation; mortality was null in both trials and no survival benefit is claimed or implied.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference)

title: Surfactant therapy for adult ARDS
question: In adults with ARDS, does exogenous (recombinant surfactant protein-C-based) surfactant improve oxygenation or mortality versus standard care?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): Recombinant surfactant protein C-based surfactant improves early gas exchange and does not improve survival or free patients from ventilation in adult ARDS. The phase 3 programme (Spragg 2004, two multicentre double-blind trials, 448 patients) found 28-day survival of 66% overall with no significant difference between surfactant and standard care in mortality or need for mechanical ventilation (median ventilator-free days 0), despite significantly greater improvement in blood oxygenation over the first 24 hours. The earlier North American phase I/II trial (Spragg 2003) likewise found no significant treatment benefit. A treatment that works dramatically in neonatal respiratory distress does not transfer to the adult syndrome on this evidence.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference)

title: Nebulised heparin for acute lung injury and inhalation injury
question: In ventilated patients with acute lung injury (including smoke-inhalation injury), does nebulised unfractionated heparin improve ventilator-free days or prevent intubation/death?
balance: Split: POSSIBLE — smoke-inhalation injury · POSSIBLE — COVID-19 (meta-trial). Two different populations, two different evidence shapes, neither strong enough for more than POSSIBLE. In smoke-inhalation injury, one small trial (Hakim 2025, 88 adults) found inhaled heparin associated with more ventilator-free days at 28 days after adjustment (P=.046) and faster weaning, with 28-day mortality comparable between groups (P=.596) — the abstract reports P values without the underlying day counts. In hospitalised, non-intubated COVID-19, a prospective meta-trial of six randomised studies (478 patients) found lower odds of intubation or death with nebulised unfractionated heparin (odds ratio 0.43 relative, 95% CI 0.26 to 0.73) and lower in-hospital mortality (odds ratio 0.26 relative, 0.13 to 0.54) — relative measures whose abstract prints no absolute event rates. Neither population's result should be read onto the other.
stamp: Split

title: Conservative versus liberal fluid management in acute lung injury (FACTT)
question: In patients with acute lung injury, does a conservative fluid strategy improve ventilator-free days and mortality versus a liberal strategy?
balance: Split: LIKELY — more ventilator-free days · LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — 60-day mortality — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, mortality was the primary end point). FACTT (1,000 patients with acute lung injury, ARDS Network) compared protocolised conservative versus liberal fluid management for 7 days: cumulative 7-day fluid balance was -136 mL versus +6,992 mL. Death at 60 days (the primary end point) was 25.5% conservative versus 28.4% liberal (P=0.30; 95% CI for the difference -2.6 to 8.4 percentage points) — no significant mortality difference. Ventilator-free days were 14.6 versus 12.1 (P<0.001) and ICU-free days 13.4 versus 11.2 (P<0.001), with improved oxygenation index and lung injury score and no increase in shock or nonpulmonary organ failure (dialysis 10% vs 14%; P=0.06). The fluid question in sepsis resuscitation (#1070) and balanced-crystalloid choice (#123) are different shelves' questions.
stamp: Split

title: Dalteparin versus unfractionated heparin for ICU thromboprophylaxis (PROTECT)
question: In critically ill patients, does once-daily dalteparin reduce proximal deep-vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism versus twice-daily unfractionated heparin, without more bleeding?
balance: Split: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — proximal deep-vein thrombosis · LIKELY — fewer pulmonary emboli, no extra bleeding. PROTECT (3,764 critically ill patients) tested superiority of once-daily dalteparin 5,000 IU over twice-daily unfractionated heparin 5,000 IU and did not find it on the primary outcome: proximal leg DVT occurred in 5.1% versus 5.8% (hazard ratio 0.92 relative, 95% CI 0.68 to 1.23; P=0.57). Pulmonary embolism was significantly less frequent with dalteparin (1.3% vs 2.3%; hazard ratio 0.51 relative, 0.30 to 0.88; P=0.01), major bleeding was identical (hazard ratio 1.00 relative, 0.75 to 1.34) and hospital death did not differ (hazard ratio 0.92 relative, 0.80 to 1.05). The PE finding is a secondary outcome of a trial whose primary outcome was null — real, but graded accordingly.

title: Earplugs and eye masks to protect sleep and prevent delirium in the ICU
question: In ICU patients, does night-time use of earplugs and eye masks improve sleep quality and reduce delirium versus usual care?
balance: POSSIBLE: Three small single-blind randomised trials (60, 84 and 114 patients, all single-centre) point the same way: night-time earplugs plus eye masks improved measured sleep quality in every trial, and delirium measures favoured the intervention — delirium development differed significantly at several time points in the 60-patient trial (Kiliç 2023), delirium screening scores were lower by the second night in the 84-patient coronary-ICU trial (Akpinar 2022), and delirium severity scores were significantly lower on postoperative days 2-4 after cardiac surgery in the 114-patient trial (Shorofi 2024). The stamp is POSSIBLE, not more: the patients cannot be blinded to wearing the devices, the delirium outcomes are scores and time-point comparisons rather than pooled incidence figures (none of the three records prints a delirium incidence rate for both arms), and every trial is small and single-centre.

title: Neuromuscular electrical stimulation for ICU-acquired weakness
question: In mechanically ventilated critically ill patients, does neuromuscular electrical stimulation (alone or with early activity) preserve muscle mass/strength and improve functional outcomes versus usual care?
balance: POSSIBLE: Two small single-centre randomised trials found better strength and functional measures when neuromuscular electrical stimulation (NMES) was added to early activity. In a four-arm Egyptian trial (Othman 2024, 124 patients), day-7 MRC strength scores were highest with combined range-of-motion exercise plus NMES (50.37) and NMES alone (49.77) versus exercise alone (44.97) and conventional care (41.10), with ICU-acquired weakness in 0% of the combined group versus 100% of controls — a separation so complete it should itself invite caution. In a Brazilian trial (Campos 2022, 139 patients), adding NMES to early mobilisation produced significantly higher Functional Status Score for the ICU at first awakening and at ICU and hospital discharge, fewer days to stand, shorter hospital stay and less ICU-acquired weakness — reported qualitatively in the record's abstract without arm-specific figures. Small samples, strength and function surrogates, and one implausibly perfect result cap the stamp at POSSIBLE. Protocolised early active mobilisation itself (TEAM) is Shelf #1303 and is not re-carded here.

title: Tubal flushing: oil-based vs water-based contrast at hysterosalpingography (H2Oil)
question: In infertile women undergoing HSG, does oil-based contrast vs water-based contrast increase ongoing pregnancy within 6 months?
balance: LIKELY: One large multicentre randomised trial (H2Oil, 1,119 infertile women in 27 Dutch hospitals) found that hysterosalpingography with oil-based contrast produced more ongoing pregnancies within 6 months than the same procedure with water-based contrast — 39.7% versus 29.1% (rate ratio 1.37 relative, 95% CI 1.16 to 1.61; P<0.001) — and more live births (38.8% vs 28.1%; rate ratio 1.38 relative, 1.17 to 1.64; P<0.001), with low and similar adverse-event rates. A single very large trial with a hard outcome (live birth) and a precise estimate carries LIKELY; the mechanism (tubal flushing) is inseparable from the diagnostic procedure itself, which is exactly the comparison women face.

title: ICSI vs conventional IVF when the male partner has normal sperm parameters
question: In couples with non-male-factor infertility, does ICSI vs conventional IVF improve live birth after the first embryo transfer?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): Two randomised trials, twenty years apart, agree that ICSI adds nothing when sperm parameters are normal. INVICSI (Dang 2021, 1,064 couples in Vietnam, male partner with normal total sperm count and motility) found live birth after the first embryo transfer in 35% with ICSI versus 31% with conventional IVF (absolute difference 3.4 percentage points, 95% CI -2.4 to 9.2; risk ratio 1.11 relative, 0.93 to 1.32; P=0.27), with no difference in fertilisation failure (5% vs 6%). The earlier UK trial (Bhattacharya 2001, 415 couples with non-male-factor infertility) found implantation actually higher with conventional IVF (30% vs 22%; relative risk 1.35 relative, 1.04 to 1.76) at a fraction of the laboratory time. Routine ICSI for non-male-factor infertility is an expense without a randomised benefit.

title: Time-lapse embryo imaging/incubation vs standard care in IVF/ICSI
question: In women undergoing IVF/ICSI, does time-lapse imaging (undisturbed culture ± embryo selection) vs standard incubation increase live birth?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): Two large, multicentre, double-blind randomised trials — together over 3,300 couples — found no benefit from time-lapse imaging, whether used for embryo selection, for undisturbed culture, or both. TILT (Bhide 2024, 1,575 participants, three arms) found live birth in 33.7% with time-lapse selection and 36.6% with undisturbed culture alone versus 33.0% with standard care (adjusted odds ratios 1.04 relative, 97.5% CI 0.73 to 1.47, and 1.20 relative, 0.85 to 1.70). SelecTIMO (Kieslinger 2023, 1,731 couples, three arms) found 12-month cumulative ongoing pregnancy of 50.8% (time-lapse selection), 50.9% (undisturbed culture) and 49.4% (control) (P=0.85). The systems cost money and are marketed on improved results; the randomised results do not support the promise.

title: Metformin vs placebo during pregnancy in women with PCOS (PregMet programme)
question: In pregnant women with PCOS, does metformin from the first trimester to delivery vs placebo reduce late miscarriage and preterm birth?
balance: POSSIBLE: The two randomised trials do not individually show a significant benefit, and the encouraging signal lives in a post-hoc pooled analysis. PregMet2 (Løvvik 2019, 487 women) found its primary composite — late miscarriage or preterm birth — in 5% on metformin versus 10% on placebo (odds ratio 0.50 relative, 95% CI 0.22 to 1.08; P=0.08 — not significant); only the post-hoc individual-participant pooled analysis of all three programme trials reached significance (5% vs 10%; odds ratio 0.43 relative, 0.23 to 0.79; P=0.004). PregMet (Vanky 2010, 274 pregnancies) found no reduction in its composite of preeclampsia, gestational diabetes and preterm delivery (25.9% vs 24.4%; P=0.78). Neither trial reduced gestational diabetes. A real but unproven-in-trial benefit for late miscarriage/preterm birth is POSSIBLE; a claim of prevention would overstate the record. Metformin in pregnancy for glycaemia and baby size is Shelf #286's different question.

title: Oral dydrogesterone vs vaginal micronised progesterone for luteal-phase support in IVF (Lotus I & II)
question: In women undergoing IVF, is oral dydrogesterone non-inferior to micronised vaginal progesterone for pregnancy at 12 weeks' gestation?
balance: LIKELY: Two industry-sponsored phase 3 non-inferiority trials (Lotus I, 1,031 women, blinded, versus vaginal progesterone capsules 600 mg/day; Lotus II, 1,034 women, open-label, versus 8% vaginal progesterone gel 90 mg/day) both demonstrated non-inferiority of oral dydrogesterone 30 mg/day for the primary endpoint of pregnancy with fetal heartbeat at 12 weeks — 37.6% versus 33.1% (difference 4.7 percentage points, 95% CI -1.2 to 10.6) and 38.7% versus 35.0% (adjusted difference 3.7 points, -2.3 to 9.7) — with live birth rates in the same direction (34.6% vs 29.8%; 34.4% vs 32.5%). The endpoint caveat stands: both trials were powered on the 12-week pregnancy rate, a surrogate for live birth, as both papers themselves state; the live-birth figures are consistent but were not the powered comparison.

title: GnRH antagonist vs long GnRH agonist protocol for ovarian stimulation in IVF
question: In women undergoing ovarian stimulation with recombinant FSH, does a ganirelix (GnRH antagonist) protocol vs a long agonist protocol give comparable pregnancy outcomes with shorter, simpler treatment?
balance: POSSIBLE: Two large randomised trials from the ganirelix development programme show the antagonist protocol is dramatically shorter and simpler, with pregnancy rates close to — but numerically below — the long agonist protocol in both. Against long intranasal buserelin (730 women), ongoing pregnancy per attempt was 20.3% on ganirelix versus 25.7% on the agonist, with median GnRH-analogue treatment of 5 versus 26 days, less recombinant FSH (1,500 vs 1,800 IU) and less ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (2.4% vs 5.9%). Against long triptorelin (355 women), ongoing pregnancy was 31.0% versus 33.9% with an identical implantation rate (22.9%), a regimen on average 17 days shorter, and fewer local skin reactions (11.9% vs 24.1%). Neither trial was reported against a modern prespecified non-inferiority margin for pregnancy, so 'proven equivalent' overstates them; 'comparable outcomes with a much shorter, better-tolerated protocol' is POSSIBLE-to-fair — graded POSSIBLE on the pregnancy question specifically.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Levonorgestrel 52 mg IUD vs copper IUD for emergency contraception
question: In women seeking emergency contraception who want an IUD, is the levonorgestrel 52 mg IUD non-inferior to the copper T380A IUD for pregnancy at 1 month?
balance: LIKELY: One randomised non-inferiority trial (Turok 2021, 711 women randomised at six Utah clinics; participants unaware of their assignment) found the levonorgestrel 52 mg IUD non-inferior to the copper T380A IUD for emergency contraception: pregnancy at 1 month was 1 in 317 (0.3%) with levonorgestrel versus 0 in 321 (0%) with copper — an absolute difference of 0.3 percentage points (95% CI -0.9 to 1.8), inside the prespecified 2.5-point non-inferiority margin, in both modified intention-to-treat and per-protocol analyses. Adverse events prompting medical care in the first month were similar (5.2% vs 4.9%). A single large trial with a near-zero event rate in both arms and a prespecified margin carries LIKELY for the non-inferiority claim. Ongoing contraceptive use of these devices is Shelf #659's different question.

title: Etonogestrel implant vs low-dose levonorgestrel IUS: continuation and bleeding
question: In women aged 18–35 choosing long-acting contraception, how do the etonogestrel implant and the 13.5 mg LNG-IUS compare on 12-month discontinuation and bleeding-related discontinuation?
balance: POSSIBLE: One open-label randomised trial (Apter 2016, 766 women aged 18-35 at 38 European centres) found the low-dose 13.5 mg levonorgestrel intrauterine system (LNG-IUS 8, releasing about 8 µg/day) had a lower 12-month discontinuation rate than the etonogestrel implant — 19.6% versus 26.8% (difference -7.2 percentage points, 95% CI -13.2 to -1.2) — driven mainly by bleeding-related discontinuation (3.2% vs 11.3%) and fewer adverse-event discontinuations (14.3% vs 21.8%); satisfaction with the bleeding pattern (60.9% vs 33.6%) and preference to continue the method (70.1% vs 58.5%) also favoured the IUS. title: Elective single-embryo transfer (eSET) vs double-embryo transfer in IVF
question: In women under 36 with at least two good-quality embryos, does an eSET strategy (fresh single transfer plus frozen single transfer if needed) vs double-embryo transfer achieve equivalent live birth with fewer multiple pregnancies?
balance: LIKELY: One multicentre randomised equivalence trial (Thurin 2004, 661 women under 36 with at least two good-quality embryos, Scandinavia) found the elective single-embryo-transfer strategy — one fresh single transfer, then one frozen single transfer if needed — produced live-birth pregnancies in 38.8% versus 42.9% with double-embryo transfer (difference 4.1 percentage points, 95% CI -3.4 to 11.6), while multiple births collapsed from 33.1% to 0.8% (P<0.001). Two honest qualifications, both printed in the record: the trial did NOT formally demonstrate equivalence (its margin was 10 points and the interval reached 11.6), so a live-birth cost of up to about 11 points cannot be excluded; and the strategy comparison includes the frozen transfer, so this is not a fresh-transfer-only comparison. The multiple-birth effect is so large and the live-birth difference so bounded that the strategy claim carries LIKELY. Distinct from Shelf #834 (freeze-all vs fresh transfer).

title: Laparoscopic ovarian drilling vs gonadotropin ovulation induction in clomiphene-resistant PCOS
question: In women with clomiphene-resistant PCOS, does laparoscopic ovarian electrocautery vs ovulation induction with recombinant FSH give comparable long-term pregnancy outcomes and costs?
balance: POSSIBLE: One randomised programme (168 women with clomiphene-citrate-resistant PCOS in the Netherlands, randomised 1998-2001) compared a strategy of laparoscopic electrocautery of the ovaries (followed by clomiphene and then gonadotrophins if anovulation persisted) against ovulation induction with recombinant FSH. At 8-12 years of follow-up, at least one live birth had occurred in 86% of the electrocautery-strategy group (71 of 83) versus 81% of the gonadotrophin group (69 of 85), and the programme's reports describe the surgical strategy as at least comparable for a first live birth, with increased chances of a second live birth, a reduced need for further ovulation induction or assisted reproduction, and significantly lower mean costs per first live birth (€11,176 versus €14,423; difference €3,247, 95% CI €650 to €5,814; P<0.05). The stamp is POSSIBLE: a single trial programme whose carded record is its long-term economic evaluation, with live-birth results reported alongside the cost analysis rather than as a powered primary comparison, in one country's practice.

title: Transdermal testosterone for low libido in postmenopausal women
question: In postmenopausal women with hypoactive sexual desire disorder, does a testosterone patch (300 µg/day) vs placebo improve satisfying sexual activity and desire?
balance: POSSIBLE: Two double-blind placebo-controlled trials of the 300 µg/day testosterone patch found modest improvements in sexual function. APHRODITE (Davis 2008, 814 postmenopausal women NOT taking estrogen) found the 4-week frequency of satisfying sexual episodes rose by 2.1 on 300 µg/day versus 0.7 on placebo (P<0.001), with significant increases in desire and decreases in distress at both doses; the 150 µg/day dose did not beat placebo on the primary endpoint (1.2 episodes; P=0.11). The earlier surgical-menopause trial (Braunstein 2005, 447 women on oral estrogen) found the same pattern at 300 µg/day (desire +67% vs +48%, P=.05; satisfying activity +79% vs +43%, P=.049). The harms are part of the claim: unwanted hair growth was more frequent at 300 µg/day (30.0% vs 23.1% in APHRODITE), and four breast cancers were diagnosed in testosterone-treated women versus none on placebo in APHRODITE (one diagnosed within 4 months, one with symptoms predating randomisation) — long-term breast safety is unresolved, which is why the stamp is POSSIBLE and the balance carries the safety signal, not just the benefit.

title: Bazedoxifene/conjugated estrogens (tissue-selective estrogen complex) for vasomotor symptoms (SMART)
question: In postmenopausal women, does bazedoxifene 20 mg + conjugated estrogens 0.45/0.625 mg (no progestogen) vs placebo reduce hot flushes while protecting the endometrium?
balance: LIKELY: The phase 3 SMART programme shows bazedoxifene 20 mg combined with conjugated estrogens 0.45 or 0.625 mg (no progestogen) substantially reduces hot flushes versus placebo. The dedicated vasomotor trial (SMART-2; Pinkerton 2009, 332 women with at least 7 moderate-to-severe flushes/day) found flush frequency fell 74% (0.45 mg CE) and 80% (0.625 mg CE) versus 51% on placebo by week 12, with at least 75% reduction achieved by 61% and 73% versus 27% (P<0.001). The larger 2-year SMART-1 trial (Lobo 2009, 3,397 women with an intact uterus) found the same direction — week-12 flush reductions of 51.7% to 85.7% across BZA/CE doses versus 17.1% on placebo — with improved vaginal atrophy measures, improved lipid parameters, and breast-pain and adverse-event rates similar to placebo. Two concordant blinded trials earn LIKELY for symptom relief; neither trial was powered for long-term cardiovascular, breast or endometrial outcomes, and no such claim is made on this shelf.
