title: Cognitive behavioural therapy for problematic hot flushes and night sweats (MENOS 1 & 2)
question: In menopausal women with problematic hot flushes/night sweats, does CBT (group or self-help) vs no-treatment control reduce how problematic the symptoms are?
balance: LIKELY: Two randomised trials from the MENOS programme found that CBT — delivered in groups or as guided self-help — significantly reduced how problematic hot flushes and night sweats were rated, with effects maintained at 26 weeks. MENOS 2 (Ayers 2012, 140 women with at least 10 problematic episodes/week) found problem-rating reductions versus no-treatment control of 2.12 points (95% CI 1.36 to 2.88) for group CBT and 2.08 points (1.29 to 2.86) for self-help CBT at 6 weeks on a 1-10 scale, still significant at 26 weeks (1.33 and 1.19 points), with reduced night-sweat frequency and improved mood and quality of life. MENOS 1 (Mann 2012, 96 women after breast-cancer treatment) found group CBT reduced problem rating by 1.67 points versus usual care at 9 weeks (-2.43 to -0.91; P<0.0001), maintained at 26 weeks (-1.76), with no CBT-related adverse events. The honest framing is in both trials' design: CBT targets how problematic symptoms feel and how women manage them — the primary outcome is a problem rating, not flush counts — and participants cannot be blinded. That is the claim, and on that claim the evidence is consistent and sustained. SSRI/SNRI drugs for the same symptoms are Shelf #667.

title: Gabapentin vs placebo for menopausal hot flushes
question: In postmenopausal women with hot flushes, does gabapentin vs placebo reduce hot-flush frequency and severity?
balance: POSSIBLE: Three small double-blind placebo-controlled trials agree that gabapentin reduces hot flushes more than placebo, but the trials are small (59, 200 and 60 women) and short (4-12 weeks). Guttuso 2003 (59 women, gabapentin 900 mg/day) found 12-week reductions of 45% in flush frequency and 54% in composite score versus 29% (P=.02) and 31% (P=.01) on placebo. Butt 2008 (200 women, 900 mg/day for 4 weeks) found hot-flush scores fell 51% versus 26% (P<0.001). Reddy 2006 (60 women) found gabapentin titrated to 2,400 mg/day reduced the composite score by 71% versus 54% on placebo (P=.004) — statistically indistinguishable from estrogen's 72% in the same trial (P=.63 between them). The harms are consistent too: dizziness, unsteadiness and drowsiness, with Reddy estimating the headache/dizziness/disorientation cluster may occur in about every fourth treated patient. Three concordant trials with one mid-sized study and surrogate symptom scores: POSSIBLE, leaning favourable. Distinct from the SSRI/SNRI shelf #667.

title: Tibolone in older postmenopausal women with osteoporosis: fractures vs stroke (LIFT)
question: In older postmenopausal women with osteoporosis, does tibolone 1.25 mg vs placebo reduce fractures, and at what cost in stroke and other events?
balance: Split: LIKELY — fracture reduction · LIKELY — increased stroke — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, stroke in the balance). The LIFT trial (4,538 women aged 60-85 with osteoporosis, median 34 months of treatment) found tibolone 1.25 mg daily reduced vertebral fracture (70 versus 126 cases per 1,000 person-years; relative hazard 0.55 relative, 95% CI 0.41 to 0.74; P<0.001) and nonvertebral fracture (122 versus 166 per 1,000 person-years; relative hazard 0.74 relative, 0.58 to 0.93; P=0.01), and reduced invasive breast cancer (relative hazard 0.32 relative, 0.13 to 0.80) and colon cancer (relative hazard 0.31 relative, 0.10 to 0.96). But stroke risk was increased (relative hazard 2.19 relative, 1.14 to 4.23; P=0.02) — a harm large enough that the data and safety monitoring board stopped the trial in February 2006. There were no significant differences in coronary heart disease or venous thromboembolism. In women of this age the stroke harm is the governing fact of the shelf; the stamp is proposed pending the developer's personal verdict because the balance turns on stroke (Tier C).

title: Dienogest vs placebo for endometriosis-associated pelvic pain

title: Route of hysterectomy for benign disease: laparoscopic vs abdominal and vs vaginal (eVALuate)
question: In women needing hysterectomy for benign disease, how do laparoscopic, abdominal, and vaginal routes compare on major complications, pain, and recovery?
balance: LIKELY: The eVALuate programme ran two parallel multicentre randomised trials (1,380 women recruited; 1,346 had surgery). In the abdominal trial, laparoscopic hysterectomy caused MORE major complications than abdominal hysterectomy (11.1% versus 6.2%; P=0.02; difference 4.9 percentage points, 95% CI 0.9 to 9.1; number needed to treat to harm 20) and took longer (84 versus 50 minutes), but was less painful (VAS 3.51 versus 3.88; P=0.01), shortened hospital stay (3 versus 4 days), and gave less pain and better quality of life at six weeks. In the vaginal trial, major complications did not differ between laparoscopic and vaginal hysterectomy (9.8% versus 9.5%; P=0.92) — but that trial was underpowered and is inconclusive on complications; vaginal hysterectomy was much quicker (39 versus 72 minutes). The record's own conclusion is the balance: laparoscopy versus abdomen trades a higher major-complication rate for a faster, less painful recovery; against the vaginal route it showed no advantage and took twice as long.

title: Systematic pelvic lymphadenectomy vs no lymphadenectomy in early endometrial cancer (ASTEC)
question: In women with endometrial cancer apparently confined to the uterus, does adding systematic pelvic lymphadenectomy to hysterectomy/BSO improve overall or recurrence-free survival?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, the primary claim is survival): Two randomised trials agree that adding systematic pelvic lymphadenectomy to hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy does not improve survival in early endometrial cancer. MRC ASTEC (Kitchener 2009, 1,408 women) found adjusted hazard ratios of 1.04 relative (95% CI 0.74 to 1.45) for overall survival and 1.25 relative (0.93 to 1.66) for recurrence-free survival — the unadjusted analyses leaned against lymphadenectomy (overall survival HR 1.16; recurrence-free survival HR 1.35, P=0.017). The Italian trial (Benedetti Panici 2008, 514 women) found 5-year disease-free survival of 81.0% with lymphadenectomy versus 81.7% without, and overall survival of 85.9% versus 90.0%, while lymphadenectomy found more node metastases (13.3% vs 3.2%) — better staging information — and caused significantly more early and late postoperative complications (81 versus 34 patients with complications; P=.001). More surgery, more staging information, more complications, no survival gain. The stamp is proposed pending the developer's personal verdict because the outcome is survival (Tier C).

title: Primary HPV testing vs cytology for cervical cancer screening (HPV FOCAL)
question: In women in an organised screening programme, does primary HPV testing vs liquid-based cytology reduce high-grade cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN3+) detected by 48 months?
balance: POSSIBLE: One large randomised trial inside an organised screening programme (HPV FOCAL, Ogilvie 2018, 19,009 women aged 25-65 in Canada; 16,374 completed) found that primary HPV testing was followed by significantly less high-grade disease detected at the 48-month exit screen than cytology-based screening: CIN3+ incidence 2.3 per 1,000 versus 5.5 per 1,000 (risk ratio 0.42 relative, 95% CI 0.25 to 0.69) and CIN2+ incidence 5.0 per 1,000 versus 10.6 per 1,000 (risk ratio 0.47 relative, 0.34 to 0.67). Women negative on HPV at baseline also had lower subsequent CIN3+ incidence than cytology-negative women (1.4 per 1,000; risk ratio 0.25 relative, 0.13 to 0.48). The stamp is POSSIBLE: a single (very large) trial, and the outcome is detection of CIN3+ — a surrogate for cervical cancer incidence and mortality, which the trial did not measure; fewer lesions at exit is the expected signature of earlier detection and clearance in the HPV arm, and its translation into fewer cancers requires the longer evidence this one trial does not contain.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Hysteroscopic morcellation vs electrosurgical resection for endometrial polyps
question: In women undergoing office hysteroscopic polypectomy, is morcellation vs bipolar electrosurgical resection faster, less painful, and more complete?
balance: POSSIBLE: Two small randomised trials agree that hysteroscopic morcellation is faster and at least as complete as electrosurgical resection for endometrial polyps. Smith 2014 (121 women, office setting, multicentre, single-blind) found morcellation quicker (median 5 minutes 28 seconds versus 10 minutes 12 seconds; P<.001), less painful (mean pain 35.9 versus 52.0 on a 100-mm scale; difference -16.1 points, 95% CI -24.7 to -7.6; P<.001) and more often complete (61 of 62, 98%, versus 49 of 59, 83%; odds ratio 12.5 relative, 95% CI 1.5 to 100.6; P=.02), with 99% of women finding office polypectomy acceptable. RESMO (Stoll 2021, 90 women, single centre, reusable morcellator) found the same direction on Bayesian analysis — shorter morcellation (6.1 vs 9 minutes) and total operating time (12.7 vs 15.6 minutes), fewer device insertions (1.5 vs 6), less fluid used and smaller fluid deficit, and better operator comfort — with no difference in pain or hospital stay. The stamp is POSSIBLE: the outcomes are procedural (time, pain, completeness), both trials are small, and RESMO's analysis is Bayesian with probability statements rather than conventional confidence intervals.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Planned delivery vs expectant management for late-preterm pre-eclampsia (PHOENIX)
question: In women with pre-eclampsia at 34–37 weeks, does planned delivery vs expectant management reduce maternal severe morbidity without unacceptable neonatal harm?
balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, severe maternal morbidity composite): One large multicentre randomised trial (PHOENIX, 901 women in 46 UK maternity units) found planned delivery reduced the co-primary maternal outcome (maternal morbidity composite or systolic blood pressure ≥160 mm Hg) from 75% to 65% (adjusted relative risk 0.86 relative, 95% CI 0.79 to 0.94; P=0.0005). The trade-off is real and is printed on the card: the co-primary perinatal outcome (perinatal death or neonatal unit admission) was significantly HIGHER with planned delivery (42% vs 34% of infants; adjusted relative risk 1.26 relative, 1.08 to 1.47; P=0.0034) — the trial's perinatal non-inferiority hypothesis was not met — although indicators of neonatal morbidity itself were similar, and 2-year neurodevelopment scores were within the normal range in both groups (PARCA-R 89.5 vs 91.9; adjusted difference −2.4 points, −5.4 to 0.5). Planned delivery was also cost-saving in the trial's health-technology assessment. The topic file anchored this shelf to the HTA full report (PMID 36547875); the primary trial report is the Lancet 2019 paper (PMID 31472930), which is carded first here, with the HTA report and the 2-year follow-up fenced as reports of the same single trial, not as independent evidence.

title: Planned caesarean vs planned vaginal birth for twin pregnancy (Twin Birth Study)
question: In women with a twin pregnancy and a cephalic first twin at 32–38 weeks, does planned caesarean vs planned vaginal birth reduce perinatal death or serious neonatal morbidity?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, perinatal death inside the primary composite): One very large international randomised trial (Twin Birth Study, 2,804 women, 5,607 fetuses) found no significant difference in the composite of fetal or neonatal death or serious neonatal morbidity between planned caesarean and planned vaginal delivery (2.2% vs 1.9% of fetuses/infants; odds ratio 1.16 relative, 95% CI 0.77 to 1.74; P=0.49). A single trial, however large, caps at POSSIBLE on this library's scale. Two features qualify the null: 43.8% of the planned-vaginal group ultimately delivered by caesarean, and the trial required a cephalic first twin and centres able to offer intrapartum caesarean.

title: Antenatal betamethasone for women at risk of late preterm delivery (ALPS)
question: In singleton pregnancies at 34+0 to 36+5 weeks at high risk of late preterm delivery, does betamethasone vs placebo reduce neonatal respiratory complications?
balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, precautionary — stillbirth/neonatal death inside the primary composite; the claim itself is respiratory): One large multicentre double-blind trial (ALPS, 2,827 infants) found betamethasone reduced the primary neonatal composite (respiratory treatment in the first 72 hours, or stillbirth/neonatal death within 72 hours) from 14.4% to 11.6% (relative risk 0.80 relative, 95% CI 0.66 to 0.97; P=0.02), with severe respiratory complications, transient tachypnoea, surfactant use and bronchopulmonary dysplasia also significantly less frequent. The price was neonatal hypoglycaemia: 24.0% vs 15.0% (relative risk 1.60 relative, 1.37 to 1.87; P<0.001). A single trial earns POSSIBLE; the long-term neurodevelopmental follow-up of steroid exposure at this gestation is not part of this record. This shelf is the late-preterm population only — early-preterm antenatal corticosteroids are a different shelf (#1132).

title: Nifedipine vs atosiban tocolysis for threatened preterm birth (APOSTEL III)
question: In women with threatened preterm birth at 25–34 weeks, does nifedipine vs atosiban improve perinatal outcome?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, perinatal death inside the composite): One multicentre open-label randomised trial (APOSTEL III, 510 women, 591 babies with outcome data) found no significant difference in the composite adverse perinatal outcome between 48 hours of oral nifedipine and intravenous atosiban (14% vs 15% of babies; relative risk 0.91 relative, 95% CI 0.61 to 1.37). The figure that keeps this shelf honest is printed on the card: perinatal deaths were numerically more frequent with nifedipine (16 babies, 5%, vs 7, 2%; relative risk 2.20 relative, 0.91 to 5.33) — not significant, all deaths judged unlikely to be drug-related, and the trial was not powered for mortality — but the direction is against nifedipine and no summary may omit it. Maternal adverse events did not differ. A single trial caps at POSSIBLE; the authors themselves call for large placebo-controlled trials, because neither drug has beaten placebo on perinatal outcomes in a trial of this design.

title: Immersion in water during the first stage of labour
question: In low-risk women in labour, does immersion in water during the first stage vs standard care reduce use of epidural/spinal analgesia and other interventions?
balance: POSSIBLE: The pooled randomised evidence (Cochrane review, Cluett 2018: 15 trials, 3,663 women) finds first-stage water immersion probably has little or no effect on mode of birth or perineal trauma, but modestly reduces use of regional analgesia — from 43% to 39% of women (relative risk 0.91 relative, 95% CI 0.83 to 0.99; 5 trials, 2,439 women; moderate-quality evidence) — with no evidence of increased adverse effects for woman or baby, though neonatal outcomes were imprecisely estimated. The one primary trial carded here (Cluett 2004, 99 nulliparous women with dystocia) points the same way on epidural use (47% vs 66%; relative risk 0.71 relative, 0.49 to 1.01) but is a dystocia-management trial, not a low-risk first-stage trial, and it recorded more neonatal unit admissions in the water group (6 vs 0; P=0.013) — printed on its card. Unblindable intervention, small absolute analgesia effect, and a review-level anchor cap the stamp at POSSIBLE. The Cochrane review is carded as what it is — a systematic review of the primary trials — because no single trial answers this question at scale.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Antenatal dietary and lifestyle intervention in overweight and obese pregnancy (LIMIT & UPBEAT)
question: In pregnant women who are overweight or obese, does structured dietary/lifestyle advice vs routine care reduce large-for-gestational-age infants or gestational diabetes?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): Two large unblinded randomised trials agree. LIMIT (Dodd 2014, 2,212 women with BMI ≥25 in South Australia) found no significant reduction in large-for-gestational-age infants (19% vs 21%; adjusted relative risk 0.90 relative, 95% CI 0.77 to 1.07; P=0.24) and no differences in maternal pregnancy and birth outcomes; birth weight over 4,000 g was lower (15% vs 19%; relative risk 0.82 relative, 0.68 to 0.99) — a secondary outcome. UPBEAT (Poston 2015, 1,555 women with BMI ≥30 in the UK) found neither co-primary outcome moved: gestational diabetes 25% vs 26% (relative risk 0.96 relative, 0.79 to 1.16) and large-for-gestational-age infants 9% vs 8% (relative risk 1.15 relative, 0.83 to 1.59), despite improvements in dietary glycaemic load, gestational weight gain and physical activity. Advice-based programmes of this intensity do not deliver the birth outcomes they aim at — LIKELY (the treatment made no difference). Neither trial was powered for, or showed, hard maternal or perinatal event benefits; the topic file's 'prevention' framing is the trials' own, and the claim tested is risk-factor modification in women without diabetes, distinct from gestational-diabetes treatment (#599).
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference)

title: Nicotine replacement therapy for smoking cessation in pregnancy (SNAP)
question: In pregnant smokers, do nicotine patches vs placebo patches increase validated cessation by delivery without harming birth outcomes?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): One large double-blind trial (SNAP, 1,050 pregnant smokers in England) found no significant increase in validated abstinence from quit date until delivery with a 15 mg/16-hour nicotine patch added to behavioural support (9.4% vs 7.6%; odds ratio 1.26 relative, 95% CI 0.82 to 1.96), although abstinence at 1 month was higher (21.3% vs 11.7%). Rates of adverse pregnancy and birth outcomes were similar between groups. The decisive caveat is printed on the card: compliance was very low — only 7.2% of the nicotine group used patches for more than a month — so the trial tests offering patches more than it tests sustained nicotine replacement, and its safety assessment is limited by the same low exposure, as the authors state. A single trial caps at POSSIBLE.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference)

title: Intermittent preventive treatment of malaria in pregnancy: dihydroartemisinin–piperaquine vs sulfadoxine–pyrimethamine
question: In pregnant women in sub-Saharan Africa with high sulfadoxine–pyrimethamine resistance, does IPTp with dihydroartemisinin–piperaquine vs sulfadoxine–pyrimethamine reduce placental malaria and adverse birth outcomes?
balance: LIKELY: Two randomised trials in high-resistance East African settings agree that preventive dihydroartemisinin–piperaquine (DP) beats sulfadoxine–pyrimethamine (SP) on malaria endpoints. In Uganda (Kakuru 2016, 300 women, double-blind), histopathologically confirmed placental malaria was 50.0% on SP versus 34.1% on three-dose DP (P=0.03) and 27.1% on monthly DP (P=0.001), symptomatic malaria episodes were far fewer on DP, and the composite adverse birth outcome was lower with monthly DP (9.2%) than with SP (18.6%; P=0.05) or three-dose DP (21.3%; P=0.02). In western Kenya (Desai 2015, 1,546 women, open-label), malaria infection at delivery was 10% on SP versus 3% on preventive DP (relative risk 0.32 relative, 95% CI 0.18 to 0.56), while the screening-and-treatment DP strategy failed (13%; relative risk 1.23 relative) — only preventive DP works. Two concordant trials earn LIKELY for the malaria endpoints; the birth-outcome benefit rests mainly on one trial's composite and is stated at that strength. The primary placental endpoint is a histopathological measure, as the topic file flagged.
stamp: LIKELY

title: Membrane sweeping at term to prevent post-term pregnancy
question: In low-risk women at term, does membrane sweeping vs no sweeping reduce post-term pregnancy and the need for formal induction?
balance: POSSIBLE: The carded anchor is one multicentre randomised trial (de Miranda 2006, 742 low-risk Dutch women at 41 weeks): serial membrane sweeping every 48 hours reduced post-term pregnancy (≥42 weeks) from 41% to 23% (relative risk 0.57 relative, 95% CI 0.46 to 0.71; number needed to treat 6, 4 to 9), with consistent effects in nulliparous (29% vs 46%) and parous (17% vs 34%) women, similar adverse effects except more uncomplicated bleeding with sweeping, and similar other obstetric and neonatal outcomes (two perinatal deaths in each group). The wider literature of smaller sweeping trials is Cochrane-summarised in the same direction, but no pooled record was verified for this shelf, so the stamp rests on the single large trial plus that qualitative concordance: POSSIBLE. The wording on this shelf is the trial's own ('reduce post-term pregnancy'); this is an obstetric timing intervention, not a diabetes-onset claim.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Immediate vs delayed pushing in the second stage with neuraxial analgesia
question: In nulliparous women receiving neuraxial analgesia, does delayed pushing vs immediate pushing at full dilatation increase spontaneous vaginal delivery?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): One large pragmatic multicentre trial (Cahill 2018, 2,414 nulliparous women at six US centres; stopped early for futility at 2,414 of 3,184 planned) found spontaneous vaginal delivery rates essentially identical with immediate versus delayed pushing (85.9% vs 86.5%; absolute difference −0.6 percentage points, 95% CI −3.4 to 2.1; relative risk 0.99 relative, 0.96 to 1.03). Delayed pushing lengthened the second stage overall (134.2 vs 102.4 minutes) despite shorter active pushing, and was associated with more chorioamnionitis (9.1% vs 6.7%; P=0.005) and more postpartum haemorrhage (4.0% vs 2.3%; P=0.03); the neonatal morbidity composite did not differ significantly (8.9% vs 7.3%). The topic file attributed this trial to 'Tuuli et al.' — the record's first author is Cahill AG (JAMA 2018), and the card is corrected to the record. A single very large trial with a tight interval around no difference carries LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) under the library's large-null rule.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference)

title: Therapeutic hypothermia after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest in children (THAPCA-OH)
question: In comatose children after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, does therapeutic hypothermia (33.0 °C) vs therapeutic normothermia (36.8 °C) improve survival with good neurobehavioural outcome at 12 months?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, survival is the primary claim): One multicentre randomised trial (THAPCA-OH, 295 children randomised at 38 children's hospitals) found no significant benefit of hypothermia at 33.0 °C over normothermia at 36.8 °C: survival with a good neurobehavioural outcome (Vineland VABS-II ≥70) at 12 months was 20% versus 12% among the 260 evaluable children with good baseline function (relative likelihood 1.54 relative, 95% CI 0.86 to 2.76; P=0.14), change in VABS-II did not differ significantly (P=0.13), and 1-year survival was 38% versus 29% (relative likelihood 1.29 relative, 0.93 to 1.79; P=0.13), with similar infection, serious arrhythmia, blood-product use and 28-day mortality. The point estimates lean toward hypothermia but the intervals are wide and cross no-effect in both directions — this is an imprecise null, which is why the stamp is POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) rather than LIKELY, and why the card prints the favourable point estimates rather than burying them. This shelf is out-of-hospital arrest only; the in-hospital companion trial is a different population and is not carded here.

title: Racecadotril for acute watery diarrhoea in children
question: In young children with acute watery diarrhoea, does racecadotril vs placebo, both with oral rehydration, reduce stool output and diarrhoea duration?
balance: POSSIBLE: One double-blind placebo-controlled trial (Salazar-Lindo 2000, 135 hospitalised boys aged 3–35 months in Peru) found racecadotril added to oral rehydration reduced 48-hour stool output by 46% relative (92±12 vs 170±15 g/kg; P<0.001), total stool output (157±27 vs 331±39 g/kg; P<0.001), and median diarrhoea duration (28 hours versus 72 hours in rotavirus-positive and 52 hours in rotavirus-negative placebo patients; P<0.001), with lower oral rehydration intake and only mild transient adverse effects in seven treated children. The relative reduction is labelled relative; the absolute outputs are printed beside it. A single trial, in boys only, in one country, nearly three decades old, caps at POSSIBLE however clean its result.

title: Oral prednisolone for preschool children with acute virus-induced wheeze
question: In preschool children admitted with acute virus-induced wheezing, does a short course of oral prednisolone vs placebo shorten hospital stay?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): One large double-blind placebo-controlled trial (Panickar 2009, 700 children aged 10–60 months presenting to three English hospitals with viral wheeze) found no benefit from a 5-day course of oral prednisolone on the primary outcome — duration of hospitalisation 11.0 hours on prednisolone versus 13.9 hours on placebo (ratio of geometric means 0.90 relative, 95% CI 0.77 to 1.05) — nor on time to physician sign-off for discharge, Preschool Respiratory Assessment Measure scores, albuterol use, 7-day symptom scores, or adverse events. A large, clean null in exactly the population where the practice was widespread carries LIKELY (the treatment made no difference). title: Oral propranolol for infantile haemangioma
question: In infants with infantile haemangioma requiring treatment, does oral propranolol vs placebo achieve complete or near-complete resolution?
balance: LIKELY: Two double-blind placebo-controlled randomised trials agree. The large adaptive phase 2–3 trial (Léauté-Labrèze 2015, 460 infants aged 1–5 months with proliferating haemangioma requiring systemic therapy) selected 3 mg/kg/day for 6 months at interim analysis and found successful treatment (complete or near-complete resolution at week 24, blinded central photographic assessment) in 60% on that regimen versus 4% on placebo (P<0.001), with 88% of the selected-regimen group improved by week 5 versus 5% on placebo; known propranolol adverse events (hypoglycaemia, hypotension, bradycardia, bronchospasm) occurred infrequently without significant difference from placebo, and 10% of successes needed systemic retreatment in follow-up. The smaller earlier trial (Hogeling 2011, 40 children aged 9 weeks to 5 years, 2 mg/kg/day) found growth stopped by week 4 and significantly greater reductions in volume, redness and elevation. Two blinded trials, a very large effect on the large trial's primary endpoint, earn LIKELY.
stamp: LIKELY

title: Extending initial prednisolone treatment in childhood nephrotic syndrome
question: In children with a first episode of steroid-sensitive nephrotic syndrome, does extending initial prednisolone beyond the standard course vs standard duration reduce relapses?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): One double-blind placebo-controlled randomised trial designed to separate duration from dose (Teeninga 2013, 150 children in 69 Dutch hospitals) gave both groups the same cumulative prednisolone dose (approximately 3,360 mg/m²) over either 3 months of prednisolone followed by 3 months of placebo, or 6 months of prednisolone. With median follow-up of 47 months, relapses occurred in 77% of the 3-month group and 80% of the 6-month group; frequent relapses (45% vs 50%), eventual maintenance or other immunosuppression (50% vs 59%), steroid dependence and adverse effects did not differ significantly. The trial's own interpretation — earlier apparent benefits of longer regimens most likely reflected higher cumulative dose, not duration — is the shelf's balance point. One well-designed trial carrying the exact comparison earns LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for duration extension at equal dose; it does not test higher cumulative doses. Distinct from #739 (rituximab for established steroid-dependent disease).
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference)

title: Adenotonsillectomy vs watchful waiting for childhood obstructive sleep apnoea (CHAT)
question: In children aged 5–9 with obstructive sleep apnoea, does early adenotonsillectomy vs watchful waiting improve neurobehavioural outcomes and polysomnography?
balance: SPLIT — POSSIBLE for polysomnographic and symptom benefit / LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for the primary neuropsychological outcome: One large randomised trial (CHAT, Marcus 2013, 464 children aged 5–9 years) split cleanly by outcome type. The primary outcome — change in attention and executive function (Developmental Neuropsychological Assessment) — did not differ significantly (mean improvement 7.1±13.9 with early adenotonsillectomy vs 5.1±13.4 with watchful waiting; P=0.16), from baselines already close to the population mean of 100. Secondary outcomes favoured surgery: significantly greater improvements in behaviour, quality of life and symptoms, and normalisation of polysomnographic findings in 79% versus 46%. A single trial with a null primary endpoint and positive secondary endpoints is exactly a split stamp: the operation demonstrably fixes the sleep study and symptoms, and demonstrably did not fix the cognitive measure the trial was powered on.

title: Vitamin A supplementation for morbidity and mortality in children 6 months–5 years
question: In children aged 6 months to 5 years in low-income settings, does periodic high-dose vitamin A vs placebo reduce all-cause mortality?
balance: SPLIT — POSSIBLE for a mortality benefit in vitamin-A-deficient populations / LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for the largest trial — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, mortality is the primary claim): The randomised record genuinely conflicts. DEVTA (Awasthi 2013, cluster-randomised, about 1 million preschool children in north India) found no significant mortality reduction from 6-monthly retinol (mortality ratio 0.96 relative, 95% CI 0.89 to 1.03; P=0.22; absolute risks about 2.5% vs 2.6% between ages 1 and 6 years), despite halving severe deficiency. The earlier Nepal trial (West 1991, 28,630 children, double-masked, placebo-controlled) found a 30% relative mortality reduction (relative risk 0.70 relative, 0.56 to 0.88). DEVTA's own interpretation threads the needle: pooling DEVTA with eight previous randomised trials gives a weighted average mortality reduction of 11% relative (95% CI 5 to 16) — reliably contradicting no-effect, and reliably contradicting the 20–30% reductions once expected. Any single-grade stamp would misrepresent this record; the split, with the pooled 11% relative figure and its absolute context, is the honest balance. Distinct from #1164 (the DEVTA deworming question).

title: Buccal dextrose gel for neonatal hypoglycaemia (Sugar Babies)
question: In at-risk newborn infants with hypoglycaemia, does buccal 40% dextrose gel plus feeding vs placebo gel plus feeding reduce treatment failure and NICU admission?
balance: POSSIBLE: One double-blind placebo-controlled trial (Sugar Babies, Harris 2013, single tertiary centre in New Zealand) found buccal 40% dextrose gel 200 mg/kg plus feeding reduced treatment failure (blood glucose under 2.6 mmol/L (≈47 mg/dL) after two treatment attempts) from 24% to 14% (relative risk 0.57 relative, 95% CI 0.33 to 0.98; P=0.04) in 237 analysed at-risk babies who became hypoglycaemic, with no serious adverse events. A single-centre, single-trial result on a biochemical-process endpoint (treatment failure, not brain injury or NICU admission as a powered outcome) caps at POSSIBLE; the topic question's NICU-admission limb is not answered by this record and the balance does not claim it.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Daily emollient from birth to prevent eczema in high-risk infants (BEEP)
question: In newborn infants at high risk of eczema, does daily whole-body emollient for the first year vs standard skin care prevent eczema by age 2?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): One large pragmatic multicentre randomised trial (BEEP, Chalmers 2020, 1,394 term newborns at high risk of eczema in the UK) found no evidence that daily emollient for the first year prevented eczema at age 2 (23% vs 25%; adjusted relative risk 0.95 relative, 95% CI 0.78 to 1.16; P=0.61; adjusted risk difference −1.2 percentage points, −5.9 to 3.6), with other eczema definitions supporting the primary analysis — and a harm signal in the other direction: more skin infections per child in year 1 in the emollient group (mean 0.23 vs 0.15; adjusted incidence rate ratio 1.55 relative, 1.15 to 2.09). Adherence was good (74–88% across the year), so this is a genuine null, not a compliance failure. A large clean null carries LIKELY (the treatment made no difference). The question's 'prevent' wording is the trial's own framing for eczema onset; no diabetes-onset claim is involved.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference)

title: Antibiotics-first vs appendicectomy for uncomplicated acute appendicitis in children
question: In children with acute non-perforated appendicitis, does non-operative antibiotic treatment vs appendicectomy avoid surgery without increasing perforation or complications?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence): The paediatric randomised record is one pilot trial (Svensson 2015, 50 children at a Swedish centre, 1-year follow-up) designed to test feasibility and safety, not efficacy. Of 24 children randomised to antibiotics, 22 (92%) had initial resolution of symptoms; two had appendicectomy during primary treatment and one more at 9 months for recurrent appendicitis, while six further children had appendicectomies for recurrent abdominal pain (five) or parental wish (one) — none of those six specimens showed appendicitis. Overall 62% of the antibiotic group had not had an appendicectomy at follow-up; all 26 surgical children had histopathologically confirmed appendicitis with no significant complications in the surgery group. A 50-child pilot can show a strategy is feasible; it cannot show it is equivalent, safer, or perforation-neutral — hence MAYBE (weak evidence), the weakest stamp in this batch. Adult APPAC and CODA evidence must not be imported as paediatric evidence, and this shelf does not do so.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence)

title: Internet-based CBT for adolescents with chronic fatigue syndrome (FITNET)
question: In adolescents with chronic fatigue syndrome, does internet-based cognitive behavioural treatment vs care as usual increase recovery (school attendance and fatigue) at 6 months?
balance: POSSIBLE: One open-label randomised trial (FITNET, Nijhof 2012, 135 adolescents aged 12–18 at one Dutch tertiary centre) found internet-based CBT markedly superior to usual care on all three dichotomised primary outcomes at 6 months: full school attendance 75% versus 16% (relative risk 4.8 relative, 95% CI 2.7 to 8.9), absence of severe fatigue 85% versus 27% (relative risk 3.2 relative, 2.1 to 4.9), and normal physical functioning 78% versus 20% (relative risk 3.8 relative, 2.3 to 6.3), all P<0.0001, with no serious adverse events reported. The effects are very large — which, in a single unblinded trial with self-reported outcomes and a heterogeneous 'usual care' comparator, is itself a reason for caution rather than a higher stamp: expectation and engagement effects cannot be separated from treatment effects in this design. One trial, one country, one centre: POSSIBLE.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Family-based treatment vs adolescent-focused therapy for anorexia nervosa
question: In adolescents with anorexia nervosa, does family-based treatment vs individual adolescent-focused therapy improve remission?
balance: POSSIBLE: One randomised trial (Lock 2010, 121 adolescents aged 12–18 at Stanford and the University of Chicago) comparing 24 outpatient hours over 12 months of family-based treatment (FBT) with adolescent-focused therapy (AFT) found no difference in full remission at end of treatment, but FBT significantly superior on full remission at both 6- and 12-month post-treatment follow-up; FBT was also superior for partial remission and BMI percentile at end of treatment, though not at follow-up, and for Eating Disorder Examination change at end of treatment only. The trial's abstract reports these findings without printing the remission percentages, and none are supplied here from outside the record — the card states the pattern exactly as the record gives it. A single trial whose advantage appears after treatment ends, on a categorical outcome whose rates the abstract does not quantify, earns POSSIBLE.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: CBT, sertraline, and combination for paediatric OCD (POTS I & POTS II)
question: In children/adolescents with OCD, does CBT, sertraline, or their combination vs placebo reduce OCD severity?
balance: LIKELY: Two linked randomised trials from the same programme answer the initial-treatment and the augmentation questions. POTS I (2004, 112 patients aged 7–17, masked, three US academic centres) found combined CBT plus sertraline, CBT alone and sertraline alone all superior to pill placebo on CY-BOCS change (P=.001, .003 and .007 respectively); combined treatment was superior to each monotherapy on the continuous outcome (P=.008 vs CBT; P=.006 vs sertraline) while remission rates (CY-BOCS ≤10) were 53.6% combined, 39.3% CBT alone, 21.4% sertraline alone and 3.6% placebo — with the combined-versus-CBT remission difference itself not significant (P=.42) and sertraline alone not significantly different from placebo on remission (P=.10), both printed on the card because they qualify the headline. POTS II (2011, 124 SRI partial responders) found adding full CBT to medication management produced a 68.6% response rate versus 30.0% for medication management alone and 34.0% for medication management plus brief CBT instructions (which did not beat medication alone, P=.72). Two trials, concordant that CBT is the active ingredient and combination is the strongest start, earn LIKELY. Distinct from #877 (CAMS anxiety disorders).
stamp: LIKELY

title: Advance provision of emergency contraception for adolescents
question: In adolescent women, does advance provision of emergency contraception vs standard access change EC use, unprotected sex, or pregnancy/STI risk behaviour?
balance: POSSIBLE: One randomised trial (Gold 2004, 301 sexually active young women aged 15–20 at an urban Pittsburgh adolescent clinic — note the record's age range extends beyond adolescence, printed on the card) found advance provision of emergency contraception (EC) was not associated with more unprotected intercourse or less condom or hormonal contraception use over 6 months; at 1 month the advance group reported nearly twice as much EC use (15% vs 8%; P=0.05) and began EC significantly sooner after unprotected intercourse (11.4 vs 21.8 hours; P=0.005), though EC use no longer differed at 6 months (8% vs 6%; P=0.54). Condom use in the past month at 6 months was actually higher in the advance group (77% vs 62%; P=0.02), while use at last intercourse did not differ. The reassurance claim (no risk compensation) rests on self-reported behaviour in one trial from 1997–2002, before modern EC formulations and access routes: POSSIBLE. This is an access/behaviour question, distinct from #244 (EC drug efficacy).
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: First- vs second-generation antipsychotics in early-onset schizophrenia (TEOSS)
question: In adolescents with early-onset schizophrenia/schizoaffective disorder, do risperidone or olanzapine vs molindone improve response?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): One double-blind multisite randomised trial (TEOSS, Sikich 2008, 119 youth randomised, 116 treated) found no significant efficacy difference over 8 weeks between the first-generation agent molindone and the second-generation agents risperidone and olanzapine in early-onset schizophrenia and schizoaffective disorder: response rates were 50% (molindone), 46% (risperidone) and 34% (olanzapine), with no significant difference in the magnitude of symptom reduction. The harms differed by drug and are part of the claim: olanzapine and risperidone produced significantly greater weight gain; olanzapine showed the greatest weight-gain risk plus significant increases in fasting cholesterol, LDL, insulin and liver transaminases; molindone produced more self-reported akathisia. A single trial with response-rate intervals too wide to prove equivalence caps at POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the correct claim is 'no demonstrated superiority', not 'proven equal'.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference)

title: Text-message vaping-cessation programme for adolescents
question: In adolescent e-cigarette users, does a tailored text-message quit programme vs assessment-only control increase abstinence?
balance: POSSIBLE: One double-blind randomised trial (Graham 2024, 1,503 US adolescents aged 13–17 who vaped and wanted to quit, recruited via social media) found self-reported 30-day point-prevalence abstinence at 7 months of 37.8% with the interactive text programme versus 28.0% with assessment-only control (relative risk 1.35 relative, 95% CI 1.17 to 1.57; P<0.001), with missing responses coded as vaping, a 70.8% follow-up rate, and no evidence that quitters switched to combustible tobacco. The topic file quoted abstinence of '~24% vs ~19%' for this shelf — those are the figures of the companion YOUNG-ADULT trial (Graham 2021, PMID 33999133: 24.1% vs 18.6%), not of the adolescent trial; the card prints the adolescent trial's own 37.8% vs 28.0%, and the young-adult trial is fenced in the synthesis as a different age group. One trial, self-reported abstinence without biochemical verification, in motivated volunteers: POSSIBLE.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Dating Matters: comprehensive teen dating-violence prevention
question: In middle-school students, does the multi-component Dating Matters programme vs standard health education reduce dating-violence perpetration and victimisation?
balance: POSSIBLE: One longitudinal cluster-randomised trial (Niolon 2019, 46 middle schools in high-risk urban neighbourhoods in four US cities; analysis sample 2,349 students who had dated) found the multi-component Dating Matters model outperformed the standard-of-care curriculum (Safe Dates, itself an evidence-based programme) on three of four self-reported outcomes, averaged across sixth-to-eighth grade: teen dating-violence perpetration 8.43% lower, victimisation 9.78% lower, and use of negative conflict-resolution strategies 5.52% lower (all relative differences as the record reports them), with no significant effect on positive relationship behaviours. Effects of this size on self-reported behaviour, from one cluster trial whose schools had 71% retention (lost schools were replaced and independently re-randomised — a design awkwardness printed on the card), support POSSIBLE. The comparator was an active evidence-based curriculum, not nothing, which strengthens the comparative claim while shrinking its expected size. Note the programme's own 'prevention' framing is retained from the record; no diabetes-onset claim is involved.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: CBT for insomnia (internet and group formats) in adolescents
question: In adolescents with insomnia, does CBT-I (internet or group) vs waiting list improve sleep?
balance: POSSIBLE: One randomised trial (de Bruin 2015, 116 adolescents meeting DSM-IV insomnia criteria, mean age 15.6 years, in the Netherlands) found both guided internet CBT-I and group CBT-I (six weekly sessions each) significantly improved sleep efficiency, sleep onset latency, wake after sleep onset and total sleep time versus waiting list at post-treatment, on both actigraphy and sleep logs, with improvements maintained at 2-month follow-up, medium-to-large effect sizes, and significantly decreased insomnia complaints and chronic sleep-reduction symptoms. The record's abstract reports significance and effect-size ranges without printing the group means, and none are invented here. A waiting-list comparator (which controls for time but not attention or expectation), one trial, and a 2-month horizon cap the stamp at POSSIBLE.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Interpersonal Psychotherapy–Adolescent Skills Training (IPT-AST) for depressive symptoms in school adolescents
question: In school adolescents with subthreshold depressive symptoms, does IPT-AST vs group counselling prevent or reduce depressive symptoms?
balance: SPLIT — POSSIBLE for symptom reduction / LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for onset of depression diagnoses: One randomised trial (Young 2016, 186 adolescents with elevated depressive symptoms in schools) found IPT-AST delivered by research staff produced significantly greater improvements in self-reported depressive symptoms and evaluator-rated overall functioning than group counselling delivered by school counsellors, from baseline to 6-month follow-up — but NO significant difference between the conditions in onset of depression diagnoses, the outcome the word 'prevention' actually refers to. The balance therefore splits: a modest symptom benefit over an active, session-matched comparator (POSSIBLE, one trial, and confounded by deliverer — research staff versus school counsellors — as the card notes), and no demonstrated prevention of depressive disorder (the treatment made no difference on diagnoses, in a trial with limited power for that outcome). This is a subthreshold-symptom programme, distinct from depression treatment (#1145).

title: Telephone reminder/recall to raise adolescent immunisation
question: In adolescents due immunisations or preventive visits, does telephone reminder/recall vs usual care increase uptake?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence): One randomised trial (Szilagyi 2006, 3,006 adolescents aged 11–14 in four urban US primary care practices, 18 months) found an intensive audiotaped telephone reminder/recall system largely ineffective: at study end the intervention group had slightly higher completed hepatitis B coverage (62% vs 57.8%; P=.02), well-child visit rates were identical (53% vs 54%), and impact on other vaccinations was minimal. The authors' own analysis locates the failure: contact information — 71% of study subjects with a single stable telephone number had a well-child visit, versus 25% of those with multiple or changed numbers. A process intervention whose single trial shows one significant vaccine among several, null visits, and a mechanism defeated by phone-number churn earns MAYBE (weak evidence) that telephone reminder/recall, as implemented here, raises adolescent uptake. Modern text/electronic reminder systems are a different intervention and are not covered by this record.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence)

title: Early nasal CPAP vs intubation at birth in very preterm infants
question: In very preterm infants, does starting nasal CPAP vs intubation/ventilation in the delivery room reduce death or bronchopulmonary dysplasia?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, death in the primary composite): Two large randomised trials agree that early CPAP does not significantly reduce death or bronchopulmonary dysplasia. COIN (Morley 2008, 610 infants born at 25–28 weeks) found death or BPD at 36 weeks in 33.9% on CPAP versus 38.9% with intubation (odds ratio 0.80 relative, 95% CI 0.58 to 1.12; P=0.19). SUPPORT (Finer 2010, 1,316 infants born at 24–27 weeks) found death or BPD in 47.8% with CPAP versus 51.0% with intubation/surfactant (relative risk 0.95 relative, 0.85 to 1.05). CPAP did reduce intubation (46% intubated in the first 5 days in COIN), halved surfactant use, and reduced ventilation days and postnatal steroid use — real process gains — at a cost of more pneumothorax in COIN (9% vs 3%; P<0.001). The composite-outcome claim is a LIKELY null; the strategy's value is avoiding intubation, not preventing death or BPD.

title: Oxygen-saturation target range in extremely preterm infants (SUPPORT)
question: In extremely preterm infants, does a lower SpO2 target (85–89%) vs higher target (91–95%) affect death, retinopathy of prematurity, or BPD?
balance: Split: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for the composite · LIKELY for the trade-off — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, mortality): In SUPPORT's oximetry comparison (Carlo 2010, 1,316 infants born at 24–27 weeks), the composite of severe retinopathy of prematurity or death before discharge did not differ significantly between the lower (85–89%) and higher (91–95%) saturation targets (28.3% vs 32.1%; relative risk 0.90 relative, 95% CI 0.76 to 1.06; P=0.21) — but the components moved in opposite directions: death before discharge was HIGHER with the lower target (19.9% vs 16.2%; relative risk 1.27 relative, 1.01 to 1.60; P=0.04) while severe retinopathy among survivors was substantially LOWER (8.6% vs 17.9%; relative risk 0.52 relative, 0.37 to 0.73; P<0.001). A composite that hides a mortality increase behind a retinopathy decrease must not be stamped as a simple null: the trade-off itself is the finding. The wider BOOST/NeOProM family is named in the topic file as supporting this direction but was not pinned trial-by-trial at build, so this shelf rests on SUPPORT alone and says so.
stamp: Split

title: Prophylactic indomethacin in extremely-low-birth-weight infants (TIPP)
question: In extremely-low-birth-weight infants, does prophylactic indomethacin vs placebo improve survival without neurodevelopmental impairment, despite reducing severe intracranial haemorrhage?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, death/impairment composite): The single large trial (TIPP, Schmidt 2001, 1,202 infants with birth weights 500–999 g) found prophylactic indomethacin did NOT improve the primary long-term outcome: death or survival with impairment at a corrected age of 18 months occurred in 47% on indomethacin versus 46% on placebo (odds ratio 1.1 relative, 95% CI 0.8 to 1.4; P=0.61). The short-term pharmacology worked exactly as expected — patent ductus arteriosus fell from 50% to 24% (odds ratio 0.3 relative; P<0.001) and severe periventricular/intraventricular haemorrhage from 13% to 9% (odds ratio 0.6 relative; P=0.02) — and none of it converted into better survival without impairment. A 1,200-infant blinded trial whose long-term confidence interval centres on no effect carries LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for the outcome that matters, and this shelf is the library's cleanest neonatal example of a surrogate win that is not a patient win.

title: Systemic hydrocortisone to prevent BPD in preterm infants (PREMILOC vs SToP-BPD)
question: In extremely/very preterm ventilated infants, does low-dose hydrocortisone vs placebo improve survival without BPD?
balance: Split: POSSIBLE (early start) · POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) (later start) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, survival in the composite): The two trials differ mainly in TIMING, and their results differ with it. PREMILOC (Baud 2016, 523 infants born before 28 weeks, hydrocortisone started within 24 hours of birth for 10 days) found survival without BPD at 36 weeks in 60% on hydrocortisone versus 51% on placebo (adjusted odds ratio 1.48 relative, 95% CI 1.02 to 2.16; P=0.04; number needed to treat 12, with a very wide interval of 6 to 200) — with a sepsis signal in the 24–25-week subgroup (40% vs 23%). SToP-BPD (Onland 2019, 372 ventilator-dependent infants, hydrocortisone started at 7–14 days for a 22-day course) found death or BPD in 70.7% versus 73.7% (adjusted risk difference −3.6%, −12.7% to 5.4%; P=0.54) — no composite benefit, though death at 36 weeks alone was lower (15.5% vs 23.7%; P=0.048) among 29 secondary outcomes, and hyperglycaemia requiring insulin was more common (18.2% vs 7.9%). Discordant trials on different schedules get a split stamp keyed to timing, not an average.
stamp: Split

title: Erythropoietin for neuroprotection in extremely preterm infants (PENUT)
question: In extremely preterm infants, does high-dose erythropoietin vs placebo reduce death or severe neurodevelopmental impairment?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, death in the primary composite): The single large trial (PENUT, Juul 2020, 941 infants born at 24–27 weeks) found high-dose erythropoietin, started within 24 hours of birth and continued through 32 weeks of postmenstrual age, did not reduce death or severe neurodevelopmental impairment at 2 years: 26% versus 26% (relative risk 1.03 relative, 95% CI 0.81 to 1.32; P=0.80). There were no significant differences in retinopathy, intracranial haemorrhage, sepsis, necrotising enterocolitis, BPD, death, or serious adverse events. A near-1,000-infant double-blind trial with a point estimate of 1.03 is a definitive test of the regimen as given, and the preclinical/phase-2 promise behind it does not survive it: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference).

title: Sustained lung inflation vs standard positive-pressure ventilation at preterm birth (SAIL)
question: In extremely preterm infants needing resuscitation at birth, does sustained inflation vs intermittent positive-pressure ventilation reduce bronchopulmonary dysplasia or death?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference, with an early-harm signal) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, death in the primary composite plus an early-mortality signal): The single trial (SAIL, Kirpalani 2019) was stopped early after enrolling 426 of a planned 600 infants, following a prespecified review of adverse outcomes. Sustained inflation did not reduce BPD or death at 36 weeks (63.7% vs 59.2%; adjusted risk difference +4.7%, 95% CI −3.8% to 13.1%; P=0.29) — and death within the first 48 hours was significantly HIGHER with sustained inflation (7.4% vs 1.4%; adjusted risk difference +5.6%, 2.1% to 9.1%; P=0.002), with blinded adjudication judging most of the excess early deaths possibly attributable to the resuscitation. Early stopping truncates the evidence, capping the null at POSSIBLE; the harm signal is part of the stamp, not an aside.

title: Aggressive vs conservative phototherapy in extremely-low-birth-weight infants
question: In ELBW infants, does aggressive vs conservative phototherapy reduce neurodevelopmental impairment without increasing mortality?
balance: Split: POSSIBLE (less impairment) · POSSIBLE (unresolved mortality concern in the smallest infants) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, mortality signal): The single large trial (Morris 2008, 1,974 infants with birth weight ≤1,000 g) found aggressive phototherapy lowered peak bilirubin (7.0 vs 9.8 mg/dL) but did NOT significantly reduce the primary composite of death or neurodevelopmental impairment (52% vs 55%; relative risk 0.94 relative, 95% CI 0.87 to 1.02; P=0.15). The impairment component alone was significantly lower (26% vs 30%; relative risk 0.86 relative, 0.74 to 0.99), while death was numerically higher overall (24% vs 23%; relative risk 1.05 relative, 0.90 to 1.22) and, in the preplanned 501–750 g subgroup, 39% versus 34% (relative risk 1.13 relative, 0.96 to 1.34) — a subgroup signal whose interval includes no effect, set against 13% versus 14% in the 751–1,000 g subgroup. Neither half of this split may be quoted without the other.

title: Early inhaled budesonide to prevent BPD (NEuroSIS)
question: In extremely preterm infants, does early inhaled budesonide vs placebo prevent bronchopulmonary dysplasia?
balance: Split: POSSIBLE (BPD reduction) · POSSIBLE (unresolved mortality concern) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, mortality signal): The single trial (NEuroSIS, Bassler 2015, 863 infants born at 23–27 weeks) found early inhaled budesonide reduced bronchopulmonary dysplasia (27.8% vs 38.0%; relative risk 0.74 relative, 95% CI 0.60 to 0.91; P=0.004), while the primary composite of death or BPD only bordered on significance (40.0% vs 46.3%; relative risk 0.86 relative, 0.75 to 1.00; P=0.05) because death was numerically HIGHER with budesonide (16.9% vs 13.6%; relative risk 1.24 relative, 0.91 to 1.69; P=0.17). The trial's own conclusion states the BPD advantage may have been gained at the expense of increased mortality. A BPD-only headline for this shelf would misstate the trial; the split is the record.

title: Buprenorphine vs morphine for neonatal abstinence syndrome (BBORN)
question: In infants with neonatal abstinence syndrome needing pharmacotherapy, does sublingual buprenorphine vs oral morphine shorten treatment?

title: Oral sucrose analgesia for neonatal procedural pain
question: In newborns undergoing heel lance/venepuncture, does oral sucrose vs water/placebo reduce validated pain scores?
balance: POSSIBLE: The evidence is many small blinded randomised trials, summarised in the Cochrane review carded here (Stevens 2016; 74 studies, 7,049 infants) — carded explicitly AS a systematic review, because no single primary trial anchors this question and the gate permits a labelled review card only with that status disclosed. Pooled results consistently favoured sucrose on validated pain scores: for heel lance, the Premature Infant Pain Profile (PIPP) was lower with sucrose plus non-nutritive sucking at 30 seconds (weighted mean difference −1.70, 95% CI −2.13 to −1.26; 3 studies, 278 infants; graded high-quality evidence by the review) and at 60 seconds (−2.14, −3.34 to −0.94); for venipuncture, 2 mL of 24% sucrose gave a PIPP weighted mean difference of −2.79 (−3.76 to −1.83). Most other analyses were graded low- or moderate-quality, and every endpoint is a pain score or crying measure — a surrogate with no demonstrated downstream outcome benefit: POSSIBLE, surrogate-only, as flagged in the topic file.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Risperidone for irritability in autism

title: Parent-mediated communication intervention (PACT) in preschool autism
question: In preschool children with autism, does parent-mediated communication-focused therapy vs treatment as usual improve child social-communication outcomes?
balance: Split: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) on the child outcome the question asks about · POSSIBLE on dyadic interaction: The question asks whether the intervention improves CHILD social-communication outcomes, and the pivotal trial's answer on its own primary outcome is no. PACT (Green 2010, 152 children aged 2 years to 4 years 11 months) found autism symptom severity at 13 months reduced by 3.9 points on PACT versus 2.9 on treatment as usual — a between-group effect size of −0.24 (95% CI −0.59 to 0.11), not significant — and the authors state they cannot recommend adding PACT to treatment as usual for reducing autism symptoms. What DID improve, significantly, were measures of the interaction itself: parental synchronous response (effect 1.22, 0.85 to 1.59), child initiations with the parent (0.41, 0.08 to 0.74), with shared attention borderline (0.33, −0.02 to 0.68). The South Asian adaptation (PASS, Rahman 2016, 65 children aged 2–9) replicated the dyadic pattern delivered by non-specialist workers — parental synchrony effect size 1.61 and child initiation 0.99 — while mutual shared attention was REDUCED (−0.70), a negative effect not seen in PACT. Interventions that change how parents and children interact without demonstrably changing the child's measured symptoms earn exactly this split.
stamp: Split

title: Community speech and language therapy for preschool speech/language delay
question: In preschool children with primary speech/language delay, does community speech and language therapy vs watchful waiting/deferred therapy improve language outcomes?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): The single trial (Glogowska 2000, 159 preschool children in 16 Bristol community clinics) compared routine community speech and language therapy with 12 months of watchful waiting and found little evidence of benefit: of four quantitative language measures, only auditory comprehension significantly favoured therapy (adjusted difference in means 4.1, 95% CI 0.5 to 7.6; P=0.025), while expressive language (1.4, −2.1 to 4.8), phonology error rate (−4.4, −12.0 to 3.3), language development (0.1, −0.4 to 0.6) and improvement on the trial entry criterion (odds ratio 1.3 relative, 0.67 to 2.4) were all non-significant. At the end of the trial 70% of ALL children still had substantial speech and language deficits. One positive secondary measure among five, in one community trial of therapy as routinely delivered, supports POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for routine provision as tested — and the authors' own call to reconsider the timing, nature and intensity of such therapy is printed on the card.

title: Intensive remedial reading instruction for severe reading disability / dyslexia
question: In children with severe reading disability, does intensive phonologically-based remedial instruction improve reading achievement vs standard provision?
balance: POSSIBLE — with a correction to the topic file on the card's face: the question as drafted asks about intensive instruction VERSUS STANDARD PROVISION, but the pinned trial (Torgesen et al.) contains NO standard-provision or untreated control arm. Sixty children with severe reading disabilities were randomised between TWO intensive instructional programmes (differing in depth of phonemic-awareness and phonemic-decoding instruction), each delivering 67.5 hours of one-to-one tuition over 8 weeks. Both programmes produced very large gains in generalised reading skills (growth effect sizes of 4.4 and 3.9 relative to the children's previous 16 months in learning-disability resource rooms — a within-child historical comparison, not a randomised contrast), stable over 2 years, with accuracy and comprehension reaching the average range while reading RATE remained severely impaired for most children; 40% no longer needed special-education services within a year. The two approaches were not differentially effective. So the record supports: intensive one-to-one phonologically based instruction is followed by large, durable gains — POSSIBLE, on an uncontrolled-for-this-question design. It does not randomise the 'versus standard provision' comparison. CORRECTION: the topic file dates this paper 2004; the record is the Journal of Learning Disabilities, 2001 (the study's later reports are separate publications).

title: Botulinum toxin A for lower-limb spasticity in cerebral palsy
question: In children with spastic cerebral palsy, does botulinum toxin A injection vs placebo/usual care reduce spasticity and improve function?
balance: POSSIBLE: The pinned anchor (Bjornson 2007, 33 children with spastic diplegia, mean age 5.5 years, Gross Motor Function Classification System levels I–III) is a randomised, double-masked, placebo-controlled trial of botulinum toxin A 12 U/kg into both gastrocnemius muscles, evaluated across all five rehabilitation domains. The topic file's balance line is exactly right and is adopted: benefit is proven mainly on tone and physiology, with functional gains limited and inconsistent: POSSIBLE. title: Maternal choline supplementation in pregnancies with heavy alcohol exposure (fetal alcohol spectrum)
question: In heavy-drinking pregnant women, does choline supplementation vs placebo mitigate prenatal alcohol effects on infant growth and cognition?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence): The single trial (Jacobson 2018, 69 heavy-drinking pregnant women in Cape Town, South Africa, randomised in mid-pregnancy to 2 g/day choline or placebo until delivery) is described by its own authors as exploratory, and its abstract reports directions rather than figures: infants of choline-treated mothers were more likely to meet the criterion for eyeblink conditioning at 6.5 months (the primary outcome), showed considerable catch-up growth in weight and head circumference at 6.5 and 12 months after both groups were small at birth, and had higher novelty-preference scores (better visual recognition memory) at 12 months; within the choline arm, maternal adherence strongly predicted eyeblink performance. No percentages, effect sizes or P values appear in the record's abstract, so none are printed on the card. Sixty-nine mothers, one population, an adherence-dependent signal and no quantified effects: MAYBE (weak evidence). Nothing on this shelf should be read as making continued heavy drinking safe — the intervention was tested as mitigation alongside ongoing exposure, in women who continued to drink.

title: Memantine for dementia/cognition in adults with Down syndrome (MEADOWS)
question: In adults over 40 with Down syndrome, does memantine vs placebo improve cognition or function?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): The single trial (MEADOWS, Hanney 2012, 173 adults over 40 with Down syndrome, with and without dementia) found memantine did not improve cognition or function over 52 weeks: both groups declined, and adjusted differences numerically favoured PLACEBO on all three outcomes — DAMES score difference −4.1 (95% CI −13.1 to 4.8), adaptive behaviour scale part I −8.5 (−20.1 to 3.1), part II 2.0 (−7.2 to 11.3), all non-significant. Serious adverse events occurred in 11% on memantine versus 7% on placebo (P=0.33), and deaths from serious adverse events in 5 versus 4 participants (P=0.77). The intervals are wide enough that a modest benefit is not excluded, capping the null at POSSIBLE; the authors' conclusion — memantine is not an effective treatment in this group, and Alzheimer's-drug efficacy does not transfer by assumption — is the shelf's position.

title: Pegvaliase for phenylketonuria (PKU) with uncontrolled phenylalanine
question: In adults with PKU and blood phenylalanine above target despite prior management, does pegvaliase vs control lower blood phenylalanine?
balance: POSSIBLE — with two corrections to the topic file on the card's face. First, attribution: the pinned record (PMID 29653686) is Thomas et al., Molecular Genetics and Metabolism 2018, reporting the PRISM programme — not 'Harding et al., Genet Med 2018' as the topic file states. Second, design: although the question asks 'versus control', the carded report is a long-term phase 3 programme summary (PRISM-1 randomised patients between two pegvaliase maintenance doses, 20 vs 40 mg/day — not drug vs placebo — and PRISM-2 was largely open-label extension); there is no placebo-controlled comparison in this record. Among 261 treated adults with baseline blood phenylalanine 1,232.7 µmol/L, mean Phe fell to 564.5 µmol/L at 12 months (−51.1%) and 311.4 µmol/L at 24 months (−68.7%); within 24 months, 68.4% reached Phe ≤600 µmol/L, 60.7% ≤360 µmol/L and 51.2% ≤120 µmol/L. Falls of this size in patients uncontrolled on prior management are unlikely to be spontaneous, which earns POSSIBLE despite the uncontrolled design; the price is immunogenicity — arthralgia 70.5%, injection-site reaction 62.1%, headache 47.1%, and acute systemic hypersensitivity events meeting anaphylaxis criteria in 12 participants (17 events), all resolving without sequelae. Phe is a surrogate endpoint, as the topic file flags.

title: Sapropterin (BH4) for phenylketonuria

title: Eliglustat (substrate reduction) for Gaucher disease type 1
question: In treatment-naïve adults with Gaucher disease type 1, does oral eliglustat vs placebo reduce splenomegaly and improve haematological measures?
balance: POSSIBLE: The pinned trial (ENGAGE, Mistry 2015, 40 previously untreated adults with Gaucher disease type 1) found nine months of oral eliglustat significantly improved every measured disease parameter versus placebo: spleen volume changed by −27.77% versus +2.26% (absolute treatment difference −30.03%, 95% CI −36.82% to −23.24%; P<0.001), haemoglobin rose by an adjusted 1.22 g/dL (P<0.001), liver volume fell by 6.64% (P=0.007) and platelet count rose by 41.06% (P<0.001), with no serious adverse events and one non-treatment-related withdrawal. title: Migalastat (pharmacological chaperone) for Fabry disease with amenable GLA variants
question: In patients with Fabry disease and amenable mutations, does migalastat vs placebo (FACETS) or vs enzyme replacement (ATTRACT) reduce substrate deposition?
balance: POSSIBLE — with the primary-result correction stated plainly: the topic file says FACETS showed migalastat 'reduced kidney capillary GL-3 inclusions and plasma lyso-Gb3 vs placebo in the amenable-mutation subgroup'. The record's primary analysis says more and less than that: in ALL randomised patients, the proportion achieving a ≥50% reduction in kidney interstitial-capillary GL-3 inclusions at 6 months was 41% on migalastat versus 28% on placebo — NOT significant (P=0.30). The amenable-mutation framing rests on a validated assay substituted before unblinding, which reclassified the population (50 of 67 randomised patients had suitable mutant forms); among suitable patients treated up to 24 months, renal function was essentially stable and left-ventricular-mass index fell (−7.7 g/m², 95% CI −15.4 to −0.01). ATTRACT (Hughes 2017, 57 adults previously on enzyme replacement) found migalastat and continued ERT had similar effects on renal function over 18 months in an open-label switch design, with left-ventricular-mass index decreasing significantly on migalastat (−6.6 g/m², −11.0 to −2.2) and plasma lyso-Gb3 remaining low and stable after switching. Two trials, a missed primary endpoint in the placebo trial, an open-label active-comparator trial, and surrogate substrate/organ-mass endpoints: POSSIBLE, and the FACETS primary miss must travel with any citation of this shelf.

title: Glycerol phenylbutyrate for urea cycle disorders
question: In patients with urea cycle disorders, does glycerol phenylbutyrate vs sodium phenylbutyrate provide equivalent ammonia control?
balance: POSSIBLE: The pivotal evidence is a randomised, double-blind, crossover phase 3 trial in adults (reported within Diaz 2013) in which glycerol phenylbutyrate was non-inferior to sodium phenylbutyrate for ammonia control: mean 24-hour ammonia AUC was 866 (SD 661) versus 977 (SD 865) µmol·h/L. Across 65 adult and paediatric patients completing three similarly designed short-term comparisons, ammonia AUC was directionally lower on glycerol phenylbutyrate in each study and significantly lower in the pooled analysis, as was plasma glutamine; 12 months of open-label treatment kept average ammonia in the normal range. The paediatric card requires a correction to the topic file: the under-6 study (Smith 2013, 15 children aged 2 months to under 6 years) was an OPEN-LABEL switch-over study, not the randomised trial the topic file describes — it met predefined non-inferiority criteria for daily ammonia exposure (ratio of means 0.79, 95% CI 0.593 to 1.055) after switching from sodium phenylbutyrate. Ammonia is a surrogate endpoint, the samples are small rare-disease samples, and 'equivalent control with a better-behaving formulation' is the claim: POSSIBLE.

title: Velmanase alfa for alpha-mannosidosis
question: In patients with alpha-mannosidosis, does velmanase alfa (enzyme replacement) vs placebo improve serum oligosaccharides, motor function, and immunoglobulin levels?
balance: Split: POSSIBLE (biochemical) · MAYBE (weak evidence) (functional) — with a correction to the topic file, which states velmanase 'improved the trial's biochemical and functional measures'. The record (Borgwardt/Lund 2018, 25 patients randomised to weekly velmanase alfa 1 mg/kg or placebo for 52 weeks) supports only half of that: the biochemical co-primary endpoint moved strongly (serum oligosaccharide mean relative change −77.6% on velmanase versus −24.1% on placebo at week 52), but the functional co-primary endpoint did NOT — the 3-minute stair-climb test changed by −1.1% on velmanase at week 52, versus a placebo figure the record prints incompletely ('− %', 95% CI −13.4 to 6.5), i.e. no separation. After placebo patients switched to active treatment in the extension, their oligosaccharides also fell (−55.7% at last observation) while stair-climb changes remained small and imprecise in both groups (3.9% and 9.0%, intervals spanning zero). A 25-patient rare-disease trial with a strong biomarker result and a null functional co-primary earns a split stamp, and the incomplete placebo stair-climb figure is printed as it appears in the record rather than repaired.
stamp: Split

title: Nusinersen for spinal muscular atrophy (ENDEAR & CHERISH)
question: In infants with SMA type 1 (ENDEAR) and children with later-onset SMA (CHERISH), does intrathecal nusinersen vs sham control improve motor milestones and motor function?
balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: ENDEAR's co-primary endpoint is event-free survival — time to death or permanent assisted ventilation — and its overall-survival result is part of the claim set; the topic file ruled this shelf Tier C No on the grounds that the primary claims are motor outcomes, but the survival endpoint is a prespecified co-primary, so the Tier C flag is applied here and the discrepancy is disclosed). Two randomised, double-blind, sham-controlled phase 3 trials agree. In ENDEAR (infantile-onset SMA), a motor-milestone response occurred in 51% of nusinersen infants versus 0% on sham in the final analysis, event-free survival favoured nusinersen (hazard ratio 0.53 relative for death or permanent assisted ventilation), and overall survival favoured nusinersen (hazard ratio 0.37 relative for death). In CHERISH (later-onset SMA, 126 children), the HFMSE motor score rose by 4.0 points on nusinersen while falling 1.9 points on sham (least-squares mean difference 5.9 points, 95% CI 3.7 to 8.1), and 57% versus 26% gained at least 3 HFMSE points. Both trials were stopped early after positive prespecified interim analyses. Adverse-event incidence and severity were similar to sham in both trials.

title: Patisiran for hereditary transthyretin amyloidosis with polyneuropathy (APOLLO)
question: In adults with hereditary transthyretin amyloidosis and polyneuropathy, does patisiran vs placebo improve neuropathy impairment scores?
balance: LIKELY: One large randomised, double-blind phase 3 trial (APOLLO, 225 patients) found patisiran not merely slowed but on average reversed neuropathy impairment over 18 months: the modified Neuropathy Impairment Score+7 changed by −6.0 points on patisiran versus +28.0 points on placebo (least-squares mean difference −34.0 points; P<0.001), with quality of life moving the same way (Norfolk QOL-DN difference −21.1 points; P<0.001), gait speed better by 0.31 m per second, and modified BMI better preserved. A single trial, but large for this rare disease, double-blind, and consistent across every prespecified clinical measure. Mild or moderate infusion-related reactions occurred in about 20% on patisiran versus 10% on placebo. The ATTR cardiomyopathy questions (tafamidis, acoramidis, vutrisiran) are homed on Shelves #556/#1170 and are not re-opened here.
stamp: LIKELY

title: Vosoritide for achondroplasia
question: In children with achondroplasia, does daily subcutaneous vosoritide vs placebo increase annualised growth velocity?
balance: POSSIBLE: One randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (121 children aged 5 to under 18 years) found daily subcutaneous vosoritide increased annualised growth velocity by an adjusted mean of 1.57 cm/year versus placebo over 52 weeks (95% CI 1.22 to 1.93; p<0.0001). Adverse events occurred in 98% of both groups, none of the serious adverse events were judged treatment-related, and no deaths occurred. The stamp is POSSIBLE rather than LIKELY because growth velocity over one year is a surrogate: the trialists themselves state it is not known whether final adult height will be increased, or what the harms of long-term therapy might be, and there is a single trial.

title: Luspatercept for β-thalassaemia (BELIEVE & BEYOND)
question: In adults with transfusion-dependent β-thalassaemia (BELIEVE) and non-transfusion-dependent β-thalassaemia (BEYOND), does luspatercept vs placebo reduce transfusion burden / raise haemoglobin?
balance: LIKELY: Two randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials in the two β-thalassaemia populations agree. In transfusion-dependent disease (BELIEVE, 336 adults), 21.4% on luspatercept versus 4.5% on placebo achieved the primary endpoint of at least a 33% reduction in transfusion burden plus at least 2 fewer red-cell units during weeks 13–24 (P<0.001), and 70.5% versus 29.5% achieved a ≥33% reduction during any 12-week interval. In non-transfusion-dependent disease (BEYOND, phase 2, 145 adults), 77% on luspatercept versus 0% on placebo achieved a ≥1.0 g/dL rise in mean haemoglobin over weeks 13–24 without transfusions (p<0.0001). The price is transient bone pain, arthralgia, dizziness, hypertension and hyperuricemia, each more common on luspatercept. Luspatercept in myelodysplastic syndromes is Shelf #674 — a different disease, not re-carded here.
stamp: LIKELY

title: Emicizumab prophylaxis for haemophilia A (HAVEN 1 & HAVEN 3)
question: In people with haemophilia A with inhibitors (HAVEN 1) and without inhibitors (HAVEN 3), does subcutaneous emicizumab prophylaxis vs no prophylaxis / prior factor prophylaxis reduce treated bleeding episodes?
balance: LIKELY: Two randomised phase 3 trials in the two haemophilia A populations show very large reductions in treated bleeding. In patients with factor VIII inhibitors previously on episodic bypassing-agent treatment (HAVEN 1), the annualised bleeding rate was 2.9 events on emicizumab prophylaxis versus 23.3 on no prophylaxis — 87% lower (relative) — with 63% versus 6% having zero bleeds. In patients without inhibitors previously on episodic factor VIII (HAVEN 3), annualised treated bleeding rates were 1.5 (weekly) and 1.3 (every 2 weeks) versus 38.2 on no prophylaxis — 96–97% lower (relative) — and an intraindividual comparison showed a 68% lower rate than previous factor VIII prophylaxis. The safety flag is real: in HAVEN 1, thrombotic microangiopathy and thrombosis were each reported in 2 participants who had received multiple infusions of activated prothrombin complex concentrate for breakthrough bleeding; HAVEN 3 reported no thrombotic or microangiopathy events. Injection-site reactions were the most frequent adverse event in both trials (15% in HAVEN 1).
stamp: LIKELY
