title: Evolocumab for paediatric heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia (HAUSER-RCT)
question: In children and adolescents with heterozygous FH on standard therapy, does evolocumab vs placebo lower LDL cholesterol?
balance: POSSIBLE: One randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (HAUSER-RCT, 157 patients aged 10–17 years with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia on stable lipid-lowering therapy) found monthly evolocumab 420 mg lowered LDL cholesterol by 44.5% at 24 weeks versus 6.2% on placebo (difference −38.3 percentage points; P<0.001), an absolute difference of −68.6 mg per deciliter (−1.8 mmol per liter). title: Everolimus for tuberous sclerosis complex tumours (EXIST-1 & EXIST-2)
question: In patients with tuberous sclerosis complex, does everolimus vs placebo shrink subependymal giant cell astrocytomas (EXIST-1) and renal angiomyolipomas (EXIST-2)?
balance: LIKELY: Two randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trials of everolimus in tuberous sclerosis complex both met their primary tumour-response endpoints. In EXIST-1 (117 patients with subependymal giant cell astrocytoma), 35% on everolimus versus 0% on placebo achieved at least a 50% reduction in target SEGA volume (difference 35 percentage points, 95% CI 15 to 52; p<0.0001). In EXIST-2 (118 adults with renal angiomyolipoma), the response rate (≥50% volume reduction) was 42% on everolimus versus 0% on placebo. The price is mTOR-inhibitor toxicity — mouth ulceration and stomatitis prominent in EXIST-1 (32% and 31%) — with adverse events mostly grade 1–2 and no discontinuations for adverse events in EXIST-1. Endpoints are tumour-volume responses, not survival or surgery avoidance, though those are the clinical reasons the responses matter.

title: Losartan vs atenolol / control for aortic dilatation in Marfan syndrome
question: In children, young adults, and adults with Marfan syndrome, does losartan vs atenolol (or control) slow aortic-root dilatation?
balance: POSSIBLE: Two randomised trials answer two different halves of the question, and they do not add up to superiority over standard care. In adults (COMPARE, 233 participants, open-label with blinded assessment), losartan versus no additional treatment slowed aortic-root dilatation over about 3 years (0.77±1.36 mm vs 1.35±1.55 mm; P=0.014), and slowed aortic-arch dilatation after prior root replacement (0.50±1.26 vs 1.01±1.31 mm; P=0.033), but dilatation beyond the root was not significantly reduced and no difference in the clinical composite (aortic dissection, elective aortic surgery, cardiovascular death) could be demonstrated. In children and young adults (Pediatric Heart Network, 608 participants aged 6 months–25 years), losartan was NOT superior to atenolol: aortic-root z-score change was −0.107±0.013 versus −0.139±0.013 SD units per year (P=0.08), with no difference in surgery, dissection or death over 3 years. The endpoint throughout is a dilatation-rate surrogate; no trial shows losartan reduces dissection or death, and no event claim is made. Losartan is an ARB: nothing on this shelf supports its initiation in pregnancy, where ARBs are fetotoxic.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Trofinetide for Rett syndrome (LAVENDER)
question: In girls and young women with Rett syndrome, does trofinetide vs placebo improve co-primary Rett Syndrome Behaviour Questionnaire and clinician global-impression scores?

title: Burosumab vs conventional therapy for X-linked hypophosphataemia in children
question: In children with X-linked hypophosphataemia, does burosumab vs continued conventional therapy (phosphate/active vitamin D) improve rickets severity and growth?
balance: POSSIBLE: One randomised, active-controlled, open-label phase 3 trial (61 children aged 1–12 years with X-linked hypophosphataemia already on conventional therapy) found switching to burosumab improved rickets severity at week 40 substantially more than continuing conventional therapy: the Radiographic Global Impression of Change global score rose by a least-squares mean of +1.9 versus +0.8 (difference 1.1, 95% CI 0.8 to 1.5; p<0.0001), with the trial also reporting greater improvements in growth and biochemistries. Treatment-related adverse events were more frequent on burosumab (59% vs 22%); three serious adverse events occurred in each group, all judged unrelated to treatment and all resolved. The stamp is POSSIBLE: a single, small, open-label trial with a radiographic primary endpoint, albeit against the active standard of care rather than placebo.

title: Vamorolone for Duchenne muscular dystrophy
question: In boys with Duchenne muscular dystrophy, is vamorolone non-inferior in efficacy to prednisone with a better bone-safety profile?
balance: POSSIBLE — with a correction to the topic file on the card's face: the topic file frames the question as vamorolone's non-inferiority to prednisone, but VBP15-004 was not a non-inferiority trial against prednisone. Its primary endpoint was vamorolone 6 mg/kg/day versus PLACEBO on time-to-stand velocity at 24 weeks, which it met (least-squares mean velocity 0.05 vs −0.01 m/s; 95% CI for the difference 0.02 to 0.10; P=.002), along with its first four sequential secondary endpoints. Prednisone was a parallel control arm, not a non-inferiority comparator. The bone-safety contrast was supportive: height percentile declined on prednisone (−1.88) but not on vamorolone 6 mg/kg (+3.86; P=.02), and bone turnover markers declined with prednisone but not vamorolone — but boys with DMD already had low ACTH-stimulated cortisol and a high incidence of adrenal insufficiency at baseline, and all three treatment groups led to increased adrenal insufficiency. One 24-week trial earns POSSIBLE.

title: Corticosteroid dosing regimens in Duchenne muscular dystrophy (FOR-DMD)
question: In boys with DMD, do daily prednisone or daily deflazacort vs intermittent prednisone (10 days on/10 days off) improve motor and pulmonary outcomes over 3 years?
balance: LIKELY: One large double-blind randomised trial (FOR-DMD, 196 steroid-naïve boys aged 4–7, followed for 3 years) settled the regimen question: both daily prednisone 0.75 mg/kg and daily deflazacort 0.90 mg/kg were superior to intermittent prednisone (10 days on/10 days off) on the global primary outcome combining rise-from-floor velocity, forced vital capacity, and treatment satisfaction (P<.001 and P=.017 respectively, Bonferroni-adjusted threshold .017), and the two daily regimens did not differ significantly from each other (P=.38). The differences were driven principally by rise-from-floor velocity (0.06 rise/s for each daily regimen vs intermittent); the pairwise comparisons for forced vital capacity and satisfaction were not statistically significant. The commonest adverse events — abnormal behaviour (34–38%), upper respiratory infection (29–37%) and vomiting (23–29%) — were similar across regimens. Vamorolone is Shelf #1420.
stamp: LIKELY

title: Growth hormone therapy for Turner syndrome
question: In girls with Turner syndrome, does growth hormone therapy vs no treatment increase adult height?
balance: POSSIBLE — with the design disclosed on the card's face: this was a randomised trial only in its initial 12–24-month phase (70 karyotype-verified girls assigned to observation, oxandrolone, GH, or GH plus oxandrolone); after that phase, girls in the GH-alone group continued GH and ALL other subjects were switched to GH plus oxandrolone, so the adult-height results are not a randomised comparison. The 17 girls who received GH alone throughout reached a mean adult height of 150.4±5.5 cm — 8.4±4.5 cm above their mean projected adult height (95% CI 6.3 to 10.6 cm) — and the 43 who received GH plus oxandrolone reached 152.1±5.9 cm, 10.3±4.7 cm above projected (95% CI 8.9 to 11.7). A comparison group of 25 never-treated historical American subjects reached 144.2±6.0 cm, exactly matching their projected height, which supports (but does not prove, being historical) that the gains are treatment effects rather than projection error. An older programme, a projection-based endpoint and a non-randomised long-term phase hold the stamp at POSSIBLE.

title: Low-dose vs high-dose calcium supplementation in pregnancy (India & Tanzania trials)
question: In pregnant women in low-calcium-intake populations, is 500 mg/day calcium non-inferior to 1,500 mg/day for preventing pre-eclampsia and preterm birth?
balance: SPLIT — LIKELY for the pre-eclampsia non-inferiority claim · SPLIT on preterm birth (non-inferior in India, NOT non-inferior in Tanzania). Two independent randomised trials, each enrolling 11,000 nulliparous pregnant women in low-calcium-intake populations (India and Tanzania), compared 500 mg/day calcium with the WHO-recommended 1,500 mg/day. For pre-eclampsia, the low dose was non-inferior in both trials (India: cumulative incidence 3.0% vs 3.6%, relative risk 0.84 — a relative measure — 95% CI 0.68 to 1.03; Tanzania: 3.0% vs 2.7%, RR 1.10 relative, 0.88 to 1.36; non-inferiority margin RR 1.54). For preterm live birth, non-inferiority (margin RR 1.16) was met in India (11.4% vs 12.8%; RR 0.89 relative, 0.80 to 0.98) but NOT in Tanzania (10.4% vs 9.7%; RR 1.07 relative, 0.95 to 1.21, which exceeded the margin). This is a dose-comparison shelf: it shows the lower dose is not unacceptably worse than the higher dose; it is not a trial of calcium versus no calcium (that question is Shelf #211).

title: Induction of labour at 41 weeks vs expectant management to 42 weeks (SWEPIS & INDEX)
question: In low-risk women with uncomplicated pregnancy, does induction at 41 weeks vs expectant management with induction at 42 weeks reduce perinatal mortality and morbidity?
balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: perinatal mortality is central to the claim). Two large open-label randomised trials point the same way on mortality but neither is clean. SWEPIS (2,760 women, Sweden) was STOPPED EARLY because perinatal mortality was higher in the expectant group: 0 deaths with induction at 41 weeks versus 6 (five stillbirths, one early neonatal death) with expectant management to 42 weeks (P=0.03) — yet its primary composite perinatal outcome did NOT differ (2.4% vs 2.2%; relative risk 1.06 relative, 95% CI 0.65 to 1.73; P=0.90), and caesarean, instrumental delivery and major maternal morbidity did not differ. INDEX (1,801 women, Netherlands) found its adverse perinatal composite lower with induction (1.7% vs 3.1%; absolute difference −1.4 percentage points, 95% CI −2.9 to 0.0) but could NOT demonstrate non-inferiority of expectant management (P=0.22 for non-inferiority); fetal deaths were 1 versus 2 and there were no neonatal deaths. A mortality signal carried by a secondary outcome in a stopped-early trial, supported directionally by a second trial's composite, earns POSSIBLE, not more. Correction on the card's face: the topic file pinned SWEPIS at PMID 34911689, a duplicate record carrying no abstract or data; the primary report (PMID 31748223, BMJ 2019) is the record carded here.

title: Intermittent montelukast for episodic viral wheeze in preschool children (WAIT)
question: In children aged 10 months to 5 years with episodic viral wheeze, does parent-initiated intermittent montelukast vs placebo reduce unscheduled medical attendances for wheeze?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): One large multicentre randomised, placebo-controlled trial (WAIT, 1,358 children aged 10 months to 5 years with at least two wheeze episodes) found no significant overall difference in unscheduled medical attendances for wheeze over 12 months with parent-initiated intermittent montelukast versus placebo (mean 2.0 vs 2.3 attendances; incidence rate ratio 0.88 relative, 95% CI 0.77 to 1.01; p=0.06). A prespecified genotype stratum (ALOX5 promoter 5/5) showed a significant reduction (IRR 0.80 relative, 0.68 to 0.95; p=0.01) while the other stratum showed none (IRR 1.03 relative), but the interaction test was not significant (p=0.08) — so the genotype result is a subgroup signal inside an overall null trial, not a demonstrated responder group, and it is not promoted to the headline. One serious adverse event was recorded (a skin reaction, in a child on placebo).
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference)

title: Dialectical behaviour therapy for adolescents with repeated suicidal and self-harming behaviour

title: Oral dexamethasone vs oral prednisone for acute paediatric asthma in the emergency department
question: In children presenting to the emergency department with acute asthma, is a short course of oral dexamethasone vs oral prednisone non-inferior for relapse and admission outcomes?
balance: POSSIBLE — with a design caveat disclosed on the card's face: the record describes allocation by calendar day (prednisone on odd days, dexamethasone on even days), which is a quasi-random, predictable scheme despite the paper's 'randomized' label, so allocation concealment was not protected. Within that limit, the trial (533 children aged 2–18 years presenting to an emergency department with acute asthma) found 2 days of oral dexamethasone (0.6 mg/kg) gave outcomes similar to 5 days of oral prednisone/prednisolone: relapse within 10 days 7.4% vs 6.9%, hospitalisation from the ED 11% vs 12%, symptom persistence at 10 days 22% vs 21%. Dexamethasone had practical advantages: fewer children excluded for vomiting in the ED (0.3% vs 3%; P=.008), fewer noncompliant parents (0.4% vs 4%; P=.004), and fewer children missing at least 2 days of school (13.2% vs 19.5%; P=.05). The topic file notes later confirmatory RCTs exist; only this anchor is carded here. Long-term controller step-up therapy is Shelf #872.

title: Combined oral contraceptive pill for primary dysmenorrhoea
question: In women with primary dysmenorrhoea, does the combined oral contraceptive pill vs placebo or no treatment reduce menstrual pain?
balance: POSSIBLE: The Cochrane review (Schroll 2023; 21 RCTs, 3,723 women) found combined oral contraceptives reduce dysmenorrhoea pain versus placebo or no treatment — a moderate standardised effect (SMD −0.58, 95% CI −0.74 to −0.41; 6 RCTs, 588 women; the review rates this evidence high-quality) — and improve the chance of pain improvement (risk ratio 1.65 relative, 1.29 to 2.10; 6 RCTs, 717 women; low-quality evidence), corresponding to improvement in 37–60% of treated women versus 28% on placebo. The largest single placebo-controlled trial carded beside the review (Davis 2005, 76 adolescents) agrees: Moos Menstrual Distress Questionnaire pain score 3.1 vs 5.8 at the third cycle (P=.004). The harms are real and quantified by the review: any adverse events RR 1.31 relative (1.20 to 1.43), irregular bleeding RR 2.63 relative (2.11 to 3.28; absolute risk 39–60% vs 18% on placebo), headache RR 1.51 relative and nausea RR 1.64 relative. Pain-score outcomes, mostly older small trials, and the review's mixed certainty ratings (high for the pooled pain score, low for improvement) hold the stamp at POSSIBLE. Long-term effects were not covered by the review.

title: Cariprazine for acute schizophrenia
question: In adults with an acute exacerbation of schizophrenia, does cariprazine (1.5–6 mg/day) reduce total PANSS score versus placebo over 6 weeks?
balance: LIKELY: Two independent randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trials in acute exacerbation of schizophrenia both found cariprazine superior to placebo on PANSS total score at 6 weeks. In the fixed-dose trial (Durgam 2015, 617 patients, with an aripiprazole active-control arm), the least-squares mean differences versus placebo were −6.0 points at 3 mg/day (95% CI −10.1 to −1.9; adjusted P=.0044) and −8.8 points at 6 mg/day (−12.9 to −4.7; P<.0001), with CGI-S differences of −0.4 and −0.5. In the international flexible-dose trial (Kane 2015, 446 patients in the safety population), the differences were −6.8 points at 3–6 mg/day (P=0.003) and −9.9 points at 6–9 mg/day (P<0.001). The consistent harms are akathisia, extrapyramidal symptoms and tremor (each ≥5% and twice the placebo rate in Kane), and insomnia; metabolic changes were small and prolactin fell in all groups in Kane. Effect sizes are in the usual antipsychotic range.

title: Adjunctive brexpiprazole for major depressive disorder
question: In adults with major depression responding inadequately to an antidepressant, does adjunctive brexpiprazole (2–3 mg/day) improve MADRS score versus adjunctive placebo?
balance: LIKELY — with the analysis population disclosed on the cards: both phase 3 trials' headline results come from the 'efficacy population per final protocol' (patients meeting amended criteria for inadequate response throughout an 8-week prospective antidepressant run-in), not the full randomised set. Within that population, adjunctive brexpiprazole 2 mg reduced MADRS by −8.36 versus −5.15 on placebo at 6 weeks (P=.0002; Thase 2015a), and in the twin trial brexpiprazole 3 mg reduced MADRS by −8.29 versus −6.33 (P=.0079) while 1 mg did NOT separate (−7.64 vs −6.33; P=.0737; Thase 2015b). So the supported doses are 2–3 mg/day; the 1 mg dose failed its primary test. Harms: akathisia (7.4% at 2 mg vs 1.0% placebo; 13.5% at 3 mg vs 2.3%) and weight gain (8.0% vs 3.1% at 2 mg). Absolute MADRS advantages are about 2–3 points over an already-treated baseline.

title: Vortioxetine for major depressive disorder
question: In adults with major depressive disorder, does vortioxetine (5–20 mg/day) improve MADRS score versus placebo over 8 weeks?
balance: SPLIT — one negative trial, one positive only at the higher dose — with a correction to the topic file on the cards' faces: the topic file describes its pinned anchor (Mahableshwarkar 2015, PMID 26035186) as showing that 'vortioxetine improved depression scores versus placebo with a dose-related signal'. The record shows the opposite: that trial's own conclusion is that vortioxetine 10 mg and 15 mg 'did not differ significantly from placebo on MADRS total score after 8 weeks' (469 randomised). The second trial (Jacobsen 2015, 462 randomised) found vortioxetine 20 mg significantly reduced MADRS versus placebo (−14.41 vs −10.77 mean change; P=.002), while 10 mg missed significance (P=.058). So the honest record is: of the two carded trials, one is null at 10/15 mg and one is positive only at 20 mg. Nausea is the characteristic adverse event across the programme. title: Zuranolone for major depressive disorder (non-postpartum)
question: In adults with major depressive disorder, does a 14-day course of zuranolone 50 mg/day reduce HAM-D score versus placebo by day 15?
balance: POSSIBLE — with two scope corrections on the card's face. First, dose: the topic question asks about a 50 mg/day course, but the carded phase 2 trial used SAGE-217 (zuranolone) 30 mg/day for 14 days; the 50 mg dose belongs to the later phase 3 programme, which is not carded here. Second, size: the trial randomised only 89 patients. title: Dextromethorphan–bupropion (AXS-05) for major depressive disorder

title: Lamotrigine for maintenance treatment of bipolar I disorder
question: In adults with bipolar I disorder recently recovered from a mood episode, does lamotrigine maintenance prolong time to intervention for a new mood episode versus placebo (and how does it compare with lithium)?
balance: LIKELY — with the enrichment design disclosed on both cards: in each trial, patients were first stabilised on OPEN-LABEL lamotrigine (other drugs withdrawn) and only those who stabilised were randomised, a design that selects lamotrigine tolerators/responders and must temper any lamotrigine-versus-lithium reading. Two 18-month randomised, double-blind maintenance trials, one in recently depressed patients (Calabrese 2003) and one in recently manic/hypomanic patients (Bowden 2003), found both lamotrigine and lithium superior to placebo at prolonging time to intervention for any mood episode. The polarity split is consistent: lamotrigine was superior to placebo against DEPRESSIVE episodes (Calabrese: time to intervention for depression, p=.047; 57% intervention-free for depression at 1 year vs 45% placebo; median survival 200 days on lamotrigine vs 93 on placebo for any episode), while lithium's clearest strength was against MANIC episodes (Calabrese: p=.026; Bowden: p=.006). Headache was the commonest adverse event. Lamotrigine for epilepsy is Shelf #337 — a different question.

title: Acamprosate for alcohol dependence
question: In adults with alcohol dependence who have completed detoxification, does acamprosate increase continuous abstinence over 6–12 months versus placebo?
balance: SPLIT — positive in the European trials, null in the US COMBINE trial, and the shelf carries both. In the anchor European trial (Whitworth 1996, 455 patients, 360 days), acamprosate roughly doubled continuous abstinence at the end of treatment (18.3% vs 7.1%; p=0.007), with mean cumulative abstinence duration 138.8 vs 103.8 days (p=0.012) and a higher proportion without treatment failure throughout (p<0.001); at 27 months, 11.9% vs 4.9% remained continuously abstinent. In COMBINE (Anton 2006, 1,383 recently abstinent US volunteers, 16 weeks), by contrast, acamprosate showed NO significant effect on drinking versus placebo, either alone or combined with naltrexone and/or behavioural intervention — while naltrexone and the behavioural intervention did show effects. The transatlantic disagreement is unresolved by these records (differences in populations, abstinence requirements at entry, and concurrent care are the usual explanations offered, none proven); the stamp is a split, and quoting only the European result would misstate the library's evidence.

title: Bupropion sustained-release for smoking cessation
question: In adult smokers, does bupropion SR (150–300 mg/day) increase prolonged abstinence at 12 months versus placebo?
balance: LIKELY: Two randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials agree that bupropion sustained-release roughly doubles one-year abstinence. In the dose-ranging trial (Hurt 1997, 615 smokers, 7 weeks of treatment), carbon-monoxide-confirmed cessation at end of treatment rose with dose (19.0% placebo, 28.8% at 100 mg, 38.6% at 150 mg, 44.2% at 300 mg; P<0.001), and at one year the rates were 12.4%, 19.6%, 22.9% and 23.1% — significant for the 150 mg (P=0.02) and 300 mg (P=0.01) doses but not 100 mg (P=0.09). In Jorenby 1999 (893 smokers), 12-month abstinence was 30.3% on bupropion versus 15.6% on placebo (P<0.001), 16.4% on nicotine patch alone (not meaningfully above placebo), and 35.5% on bupropion plus patch (higher than bupropion alone but not significantly). Bupropion also blunted post-cessation weight gain in both trials. Insomnia and headache were the commonest adverse events; discontinuation for adverse events was 11.9% on bupropion versus 3.8% on placebo in Jorenby. Varenicline is homed on Shelves #225/#310 — a different drug — and bupropion within AXS-05 for depression is Shelf #1435.

title: Behavioural activation for depression
question: In adults with major depression, is behavioural activation delivered by junior psychological workers non-inferior to full cognitive behavioural therapy for depressive symptoms at 12 months?
balance: POSSIBLE: One large randomised non-inferiority trial (COBRA, 440 adults with major depressive disorder recruited from primary care and psychological therapy services in England) found behavioural activation delivered by junior mental health workers non-inferior to cognitive behavioural therapy delivered by psychological therapists on PHQ-9 at 12 months: in the modified intention-to-treat population both groups averaged 8.4 points (mean difference 0.1; 95% CI −1.3 to 1.5; p=0.89) against a non-inferiority margin of 1.9 points, and the per-protocol analysis agreed (difference 0.0; −1.5 to 1.6). The trial's cost analysis favoured behavioural activation (the authors' conclusion is that it can be delivered with less intensive and costly training 'with no lesser effect than CBT'), though the abstract as fetched does not print a specific cost figure, so none is printed on the card. Treatment was open-label (outcome assessors masked), and 21% of the behavioural-activation group versus 14% of the CBT group were not assessable for the primary outcome in the modified ITT population. A single — albeit large and well-designed — non-inferiority trial earns POSSIBLE.

title: Riluzole for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
question: In adults with ALS, does riluzole 100 mg/day prolong tracheostomy-free survival versus placebo?
balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, survival is the primary claim): Two double-blind placebo-controlled trials agree. In Bensimon 1994 (155 outpatients), 12-month survival was 74% on riluzole 100 mg/day versus 58% on placebo (P=0.014), with the advantage concentrated in bulbar-onset disease (73% vs 35%) and a smaller but still significant advantage at the end of the placebo-controlled period (49% vs 37%; P=0.046); muscle-strength deterioration was slower (P=0.028). In the confirmatory dose-ranging trial (Lacomblez 1996, 959 outpatients, 50/100/200 mg/day for up to 18 months), tracheostomy-free survival rose dose-dependently (50.4% placebo; 55.3%, 56.8% and 57.8% across doses) with a significant dose-related decrease in the risk of death or tracheostomy (P=0.04) and, after adjustment for prognostic factors, a 35% relative decrease in the risk of death at the 100-mg dose (P=0.002). The benefit is a survival extension measured in proportions alive, not a functional cure: the dose-ranging trial found no significant treatment effect on functional measures.

title: Edaravone for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis

title: Atogepant for preventive treatment of migraine
question: In adults with episodic migraine, does daily oral atogepant reduce mean monthly migraine days versus placebo over 12 weeks?
balance: LIKELY: The episodic-migraine anchor trial (ADVANCE, Ailani 2021; 873 patients in the efficacy analysis) found all three atogepant doses beat placebo on the change in mean monthly migraine days across 12 weeks: −3.7 (10 mg), −3.9 (30 mg) and −4.2 days (60 mg) versus −2.5 days on placebo (mean differences −1.2, −1.4 and −1.7 days; all P<0.001). The programme's chronic-migraine trial (PROGRESS, 755 in the modified intention-to-treat population) pointed the same way in that harder population (−7.5 and −6.9 versus −5.1 days; differences −2.4 and −1.8; adjusted P<0.0001 and P=0.0009) and is carded as programme support, not as episodic-migraine evidence. title: Intravenous immunoglobulin versus plasma exchange for Guillain–Barré syndrome
question: In adults with Guillain–Barré syndrome unable to walk unaided, is intravenous immunoglobulin at least as effective as plasma exchange for recovery of walking and disability at 4 weeks and beyond?
balance: LIKELY: Two randomised trials agree that IVIg is at least as effective as plasma exchange. In the Dutch trial (van der Meché 1992, 150 patients), improvement by at least one motor grade at 4 weeks occurred in 53% on IVIg versus 34% on plasma exchange (difference 19 percentage points, 95% CI 3 to 34; P=0.024), the median time to improvement by one grade was 27 versus 41 days (P=0.05), and the IVIg group had significantly fewer complications and less need for artificial ventilation. In the international Plasma Exchange/Sandoglobulin trial (1997, 379 assessed), mean improvement on the disability scale at 4 weeks was 0.8 grades on IVIg versus 0.9 on plasma exchange and 1.1 on the combination — no significant differences, with the IVIg-versus-exchange difference small enough to exclude a 0.5-grade difference at the 95% confidence level, and no differences in time to unaided walking or ventilation discontinuation up to 48 weeks. One trial leans IVIg-superior, the larger one says equivalent: the honest joint reading is at-least-as-effective, with no gain from combining both.
stamp: LIKELY

title: Radiofrequency denervation for facet-joint and sacroiliac chronic low back pain (MINT)
question: In adults with chronic low back pain attributed to the facet joints or sacroiliac joint, does radiofrequency denervation added to a standardised exercise programme improve pain intensity at 3 months versus exercise alone?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): The three MINT trials (Juch 2017, 681 randomised patients with block-positive facet-joint, sacroiliac or combination pain) found that adding radiofrequency denervation to a standardised exercise programme produced mean pain-intensity differences at 3 months of −0.18 points (facet joint; 95% CI −0.76 to 0.40), −0.71 (sacroiliac; −1.35 to −0.06) and −0.99 (combination; −1.73 to −0.25) on a 0–10 scale — all far below the trials' prespecified minimal clinically important difference of 2 points. The sacroiliac and combination differences are statistically significant but clinically trivial by the trials' own threshold, and the topic file's summary — no clinically important pain benefit in any of the three trials — is what the record shows. Three parallel pragmatic trials earn LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for a clinically important effect.

title: Cooled radiofrequency ablation of the genicular nerves for knee osteoarthritis pain
question: In adults with chronic knee osteoarthritis pain refractory to conservative care, does cooled radiofrequency ablation of the genicular nerves relieve pain more than intra-articular corticosteroid injection over 6 months?
balance: POSSIBLE: One multicentre randomised trial (Davis 2018, 151 subjects) found cooled radiofrequency ablation (CRFA) of the genicular nerves clearly superior to a single intra-articular corticosteroid injection at 6 months: ≥50% pain reduction in 74.1% versus 16.2% (P<0.0001), mean numeric rating scale reduction 4.9 versus 1.3 points (P<0.0001), mean Oxford Knee Score 35.7 versus 22.4 (P<0.0001), and improved Global Perceived Effect in 91.4% versus 23.9%, with no procedure-related serious adverse events. The comparator is the catch: a single steroid injection's effect wanes within weeks, so beating it at 6 months is a low bar, the trial was unblinded, and no sham-controlled trial is carded here — a single open trial against a short-lived comparator caps at POSSIBLE.

title: Dorsal root ganglion stimulation for complex regional pain syndrome (ACCURATE)
question: In adults with CRPS or causalgia of the lower limb, does dorsal root ganglion stimulation achieve higher treatment success (≥50% pain relief) than conventional tonic spinal cord stimulation at 12 months?
balance: POSSIBLE: One randomised comparative trial (ACCURATE, Deer 2017, 152 subjects with lower-limb CRPS or causalgia) found the composite primary endpoint of treatment success — ≥50% pain relief with no stimulation-related neurological deficit — was achieved by significantly more patients with dorsal root ganglion (DRG) stimulation than with tonic spinal cord stimulation (SCS): 81.2% versus 55.7% at 3 months (P<0.001), with the trial reporting the advantage maintained through the 12-month assessments and no stimulation-related neurological deficits in either arm; device-related and serious adverse events did not differ between groups. A single industry pivotal trial, unblinded by the nature of the devices, caps at POSSIBLE. Benefit at 12 months is as the report's headline states; the abstract prints the exact percentages for the 3-month endpoint, and those are the figures carded.

title: Mirror therapy for phantom limb pain
question: In adults with unilateral lower-limb amputation and phantom limb pain, does mirror therapy reduce phantom pain versus covered-mirror or mental-visualisation control over 4 weeks?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence): The only randomised anchor is a very small trial (Chan 2007) published as a brief report (N Engl J Med 2007, pages 2206–2207) whose PubMed record carries NO abstract — so no effect sizes, denominators or confidence intervals could be re-derived from the source record at build time, and none are printed on the card. title: Mindfulness-based stress reduction for chronic low back pain
question: In adults with chronic low back pain, does mindfulness-based stress reduction improve back-related function and pain bothersomeness versus usual care (and how does it compare with CBT) at 26 weeks?
balance: POSSIBLE: One large interviewer-blind trial (Cherkin 2016, 342 adults) found mindfulness-based stress reduction (MBSR) and cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) both beat usual care on the coprimary outcomes at 26 weeks: clinically meaningful (≥30%) functional improvement in 60.5% (MBSR), 57.7% (CBT) and 44.1% (usual care) (relative risk for MBSR vs usual care 1.37 relative, 95% CI 1.06 to 1.77; MBSR vs CBT RR 0.95 relative — no difference), and clinically meaningful improvement in pain bothersomeness in 43.6%, 44.9% and 26.6% (RR 1.64 relative, 1.15 to 2.34, for MBSR vs usual care), with MBSR's findings persisting with little change at 52 weeks. A single trial, however well run, caps at POSSIBLE; the comparative message is that MBSR matched CBT, and both beat usual care.

title: Low-dose naltrexone for fibromyalgia
question: In women with fibromyalgia, does low-dose naltrexone (4.5 mg/day) reduce daily pain versus placebo?

title: Lidocaine 5% medicated plaster for postherpetic neuralgia
question: In adults with postherpetic neuralgia, does the lidocaine 5% topical patch relieve pain versus a vehicle patch?
balance: POSSIBLE: Two small, old double-blind vehicle-controlled trials agree. In the enriched-enrolment trial (Galer 1999, 32 subjects, all prior regular lidocaine-patch responders continuing treatment for at least a month), the median time to exit for loss of pain relief was greater than 14 days on the lidocaine patch versus 3.8 days on vehicle (P<0.001), and 78.1% of subjects preferred the lidocaine phase versus 9.4% the vehicle phase. In Rowbotham 1996 (35 subjects completing a four-session random-order double-blind study), lidocaine patches significantly reduced pain intensity at all time points from 30 minutes to 12 hours versus no-treatment observation, and from 4 to 12 hours versus vehicle patches, with maximal blood lidocaine of 0.1 micrograms/mL and no systemic side effects. The enrichment design of the larger claim — testing withdrawal in known responders — inflates the apparent effect for treatment-naive patients, and the trials' size and age cap the stamp at POSSIBLE.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Radiofrequency denervation of the sacroiliac joint (lateral branch cooled RF)
question: In adults with sacroiliac-joint pain confirmed by diagnostic blocks, does cooled radiofrequency lateral-branch denervation achieve ≥50% pain relief at 3 months versus placebo denervation?
balance: POSSIBLE: Two small sham-controlled trials in block-confirmed sacroiliac-joint pain agree. In Cohen 2008 (28 patients), ≥50% pain relief with significant functional improvement occurred in 79% (11 of 14) of the cooled-RF group versus 14% (2 of 14) on placebo denervation at 1 month, 64% versus 0% at 3 months, and 57% at 6 months in the RF group — though only 2 patients (14%) retained relief at 1 year. title: Balloon kyphoplasty versus non-surgical care for vertebral compression fracture
question: In adults with painful osteoporotic vertebral compression fractures, does balloon kyphoplasty improve quality of life (SF-36 physical component) versus non-surgical care at 1 and 12 months?

title: Constraint-induced movement therapy after stroke (EXCITE)
question: In adults 3–9 months after stroke with preserved wrist/finger extension, does constraint-induced movement therapy improve upper-limb function versus usual care, sustained to 12 months?
balance: LIKELY: One large multisite single-blind randomised trial (EXCITE, Wolf 2006, 222 patients 3–9 months after a first stroke) found a 2-week programme of constraint-induced movement therapy (CIMT) produced greater improvements than usual and customary care from baseline to 12 months on both primaries: Wolf Motor Function Test Performance Time fell 52% in the CIMT group versus 26% in controls (between-group difference 34%, 95% CI 12% to 51%; P<0.001), Motor Activity Log Amount of Use rose from 1.21 to 2.13 versus 1.15 to 1.65 (difference 0.43, 0.05 to 0.80; P<0.001) and Quality of Movement from 1.26 to 2.23 versus 1.18 to 1.66 (difference 0.48, 0.13 to 0.84; P<0.001); self-perceived hand function difficulty (Stroke Impact Scale hand domain) also improved more (−19.5 vs −10.1; P=0.05). A single large, durable, assessor-blinded result of this size, consistent with the smaller CIMT trial literature fenced in the synthesis, earns LIKELY — in the narrow population with preserved wrist and finger extension.

title: Locomotor training after stroke (LEAPS)
question: In adults with residual gait impairment after stroke, does body-weight-supported treadmill locomotor training improve the proportion achieving functional walking recovery at 1 year versus a home exercise programme?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): One large definitive trial (LEAPS, Duncan 2011, 408 participants) found body-weight-supported treadmill locomotor training was NOT superior to a structured home exercise programme managed by a physical therapist: at 1 year, 52.0% of all participants had improved functional walking ability, with no significant difference for early locomotor training versus home exercise (adjusted odds ratio 0.83 relative, 95% CI 0.50 to 1.39) or for late locomotor training versus home exercise (adjusted OR 1.19 relative, 0.72 to 1.99), and all groups had similar improvements in walking speed. The confidence intervals are wide enough that a modest benefit is not excluded, which keeps the null at POSSIBLE rather than LIKELY; but nothing in the trial supports the treadmill programme over the cheaper home programme, which is the decision-relevant reading.

title: Very early mobilisation after stroke (AVERT)
question: In adults with acute stroke, does very early, frequent, short mobilisation begun within 24 hours improve the odds of a favourable outcome (mRS 0–2) at 3 months versus usual stroke-unit care?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference, harm-leaning) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: the favourable-outcome scale includes death). One very large trial (AVERT, 2,104 randomised at 56 stroke units in five countries) found very early, frequent, higher-dose mobilisation begun within 24 hours REDUCED the odds of a favourable outcome (modified Rankin Scale 0–2) at 3 months: 46% (480 patients) versus 50% (525) with usual care (adjusted odds ratio 0.73 relative, 95% CI 0.59 to 0.90; P=0.004). Deaths were numerically higher with very early mobilisation (88 [8%] vs 72 [7%]; OR 1.34 relative, 0.93 to 1.93; P=0.113) and non-fatal serious adverse events were similar (19% vs 20%), with no reduction in immobility-related complications. A single very large trial whose primary result is a significant harm-direction finding earns LIKELY for the proposition that this protocol does not help and may hurt; the mortality difference itself is not significant and no mortality claim is made.

title: Cognitive functional therapy for chronic disabling low back pain (RESTORE)
question: In adults with chronic, disabling low back pain, does cognitive functional therapy (with or without movement-sensor biofeedback) reduce activity limitation (Roland Morris) versus usual care at 13 weeks and 52 weeks?
balance: LIKELY: Two randomised trials at two scales agree. In RESTORE (Kent 2023, 492 participants), cognitive functional therapy (CFT) reduced activity limitation (Roland Morris Disability Questionnaire) versus usual care at 13 weeks by −4.6 points whether delivered alone (95% CI −5.9 to −3.4) or with movement-sensor biofeedback (−4.6; −5.8 to −3.3), with similar effect sizes at 52 weeks, better quality-adjusted life-years, and far lower societal costs (−AU$5,276 and −AU$8,211). In the earlier classification-based CFT trial (Vibe Fersum 2013, 121 patients), CFT improved the Oswestry Disability Index by 13.7 points versus 5.5 points with manual therapy and exercise, and pain intensity by 3.2 versus 1.5 points (both P<0.001), at 12-month follow-up. Two concordant randomised trials earn LIKELY.

title: Therapies for chronic fatigue syndrome: CBT, graded exercise, adaptive pacing (PACE)
question: In adults with chronic fatigue syndrome, do cognitive behaviour therapy or graded exercise therapy added to specialist medical care improve fatigue and physical function versus specialist medical care alone — and does adaptive pacing therapy help?
balance: POSSIBLE: One large trial (PACE, White 2011, 641 patients meeting Oxford criteria) found that adding cognitive behaviour therapy (CBT) or graded exercise therapy (GET) to specialist medical care (SMC) moderately improved both primary outcomes at 52 weeks — fatigue scores 3.4 (95% CI 1.8 to 5.0; P=0.0001) and 3.2 points (1.7 to 4.8; P=0.0003) lower than SMC alone, and physical function scores 7.1 (2.0 to 12.1; P=0.0068) and 9.4 points (4.4 to 14.4; P=0.0005) higher — while adaptive pacing therapy (APT) did not differ from SMC alone on either outcome (fatigue 0.7 points lower, P=0.38; physical function 3.4 points lower, P=0.18). Serious adverse reactions were uncommon and similar across groups (1–2%). The stamp is POSSIBLE, and the shelf face carries the contest: PACE's reanalyses and its recovery definitions have been heavily disputed by patient organisations and later commentators, outcomes were self-rated by necessarily unmasked participants, and no second trial of this size exists — the trial's own numbers are carded as printed and the dispute is disclosed, not adjudicated.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Early physical and occupational therapy in mechanically ventilated patients
question: In adults receiving mechanical ventilation in intensive care, does early exercise and mobilisation with daily sedation interruption increase the proportion returning to independent functional status by hospital discharge versus usual care?
balance: Split: POSSIBLE — functional benefit in Schweickert · POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) in TEAM. PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C — ruled Tier C at build, contrary to the topic file's flag: the TEAM trial carded here has a mortality-bearing primary outcome, days alive and out of hospital). In Schweickert 2009 (104 patients at two university hospitals), early exercise and mobilisation during daily sedation interruption nearly doubled return to independent functional status at hospital discharge (59% [29 patients] vs 35% [19]; odds ratio 2.7 relative, 95% CI 1.2 to 6.1; P=0.02), shortened delirium (median 2.0 vs 4.0 days; P=0.02) and increased ventilator-free days (23.5 vs 21.1; P=0.05). In TEAM 2022 (750 patients), increased early mobilisation did NOT increase days alive and out of hospital at 180 days (median 143 vs 145 days; absolute difference −2.0 days, 95% CI −10 to 6; P=0.62), death by day 180 was 22.5% versus 19.5% (OR 1.15 relative, 0.81 to 1.65), and adverse events potentially due to mobilisation were more frequent (9.2% vs 4.1%; P=0.005). A small single-centre positive and a large multicentre null do not average into a claim: the split is the record.
stamp: Split

title: Mirror therapy for upper-limb recovery after stroke
question: In patients with subacute stroke and severe arm paresis, does mirror therapy added to conventional rehabilitation improve hand function and self-care versus sham mirror treatment?
balance: POSSIBLE: One small assessor-blinded randomised trial (Yavuzer 2008, 40 inpatients with subacute stroke) found that 30 minutes of mirror therapy daily (wrist and finger flexion/extension) added to a conventional rehabilitation programme for 4 weeks improved Brunnstrom stages for the hand (by 0.83 more than control) and upper extremity (by 0.89) and FIM self-care scores (by 4.10) more than sham mirror treatment (all P<0.01), with smaller advantages persisting at 6-month follow-up (0.16, 0.43 and 2.34 respectively; all P<0.05), and no significant difference in spasticity (Modified Ashworth Scale). A single 40-patient trial caps at POSSIBLE; the wider mirror-therapy trial literature is small-trial throughout and is fenced in the synthesis. The phantom-limb mirror question is a different population and outcome (#1453).
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Accelerated rehabilitation for acute lateral ankle sprain
question: In adults with acute grade I–II lateral ankle sprain, does an accelerated rehabilitation programme with early therapeutic exercises improve ankle function in the first 2 weeks versus standard protection, rest, ice, compression and elevation?
balance: POSSIBLE: One assessor-blinded randomised trial (Bleakley 2010, 101 patients with acute grade 1 or 2 ankle sprain) found an accelerated intervention with early therapeutic exercise improved subjective ankle function versus standard protection, rest, ice, compression and elevation at week 1 (baseline-adjusted difference 5.28 points on the Lower Extremity Functional Scale, 98.75% CI 0.31 to 10.26; P=0.008) and week 2 (4.92, 0.27 to 9.57; P=0.0083), with no differences at weeks 3–4 or in pain or swelling at any point, and an identical reinjury rate (4%, two in each group) at 16 weeks. A single small trial with an early, transient functional advantage earns POSSIBLE. The CAST trial of mechanical supports after severe sprain is a different intervention and is fenced in the synthesis, not counted as a second rehabilitation trial.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Neuromuscular warm-up programmes to prevent football injuries (FIFA 11 / 11+)
question: In young footballers, does a structured neuromuscular warm-up programme reduce the rate of severe and overall injuries versus a usual warm-up over one season?
balance: POSSIBLE: Two cluster-randomised trials point the same way but neither is clean. In young female players (Soligard 2008, 1,892 players in 125 Norwegian clubs), the comprehensive warm-up's PRIMARY outcome — lower-extremity injury rate — did NOT reach significance (rate ratio 0.71 relative, 95% CI 0.49 to 1.03); significant reductions appeared in secondary categories: injuries overall (0.68 relative, 0.48 to 0.98), overuse injuries (0.47 relative, 0.26 to 0.85) and severe injuries (0.55 relative, 0.36 to 0.83). In male youth players (Owoeye 2014, 414 players, Lagos), FIFA 11+ reduced overall injury rate by 41% relative (RR 0.59 relative, 0.40 to 0.86; p=0.006) and lower-extremity injuries by 48% relative (RR 0.52 relative, 0.34 to 0.82; p=0.004). A non-significant primary in the larger trial caps the pair at POSSIBLE.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Early targeted aerobic exercise after sport-related concussion
question: In adolescents with sport-related concussion, does early prescribed aerobic exercise at a sub-symptom heart-rate threshold shorten time to recovery versus a placebo stretching programme?
balance: LIKELY: Two randomised trials from the same programme, in the same population, agree. The pilot (Leddy 2019, 103 adolescents) found recovery in a median of 13 days (IQR 10–18.5) on subsymptom-threshold aerobic exercise versus 17 days (IQR 13–23) on placebo-like stretching (P=.009). The multicentre replication (Leddy 2021, 118 adolescents) found aerobic-exercise patients more likely to recover within 4 weeks, with a 48% relative reduction in the risk of persistent post-concussive symptoms (hazard ratio for stretching vs aerobic exercise 0.52 relative, 95% CI 0.28 to 0.97; p=0.039), and no adverse events in either trial. Two concordant randomised trials with a placebo-like control earn LIKELY — for adolescents seen within 10 days of injury. Note: the topic draft's '≈14 vs ≈19 days' median figures appear in NEITHER abstract; the carded figures are the records' own (13 vs 17 days in the pilot; the replication reports the hazard ratio, not medians).
stamp: LIKELY

title: Radial extracorporeal shock-wave therapy for chronic plantar fasciitis
question: In adults with chronic recalcitrant plantar fasciitis, does radial extracorporeal shock-wave therapy improve heel-pain treatment success at 12 weeks versus placebo shock-wave?
balance: POSSIBLE: One multicentre randomised placebo-controlled trial (Gerdesmeyer 2008, 245 patients with chronic plantar fasciitis) found three sessions of radial shock-wave therapy beat placebo at 12 weeks on the visual analogue scale composite score (reduction 72.1% vs 44.7%; P=.0220) and on overall treatment success (61.0% vs 42.2%; P=.0020), with superiority more pronounced at 12 months and no relevant side effects. A single positive trial — with percentage reductions printed without the underlying absolute scores — earns POSSIBLE. Plantar fascia–specific stretching is a different intervention, homed elsewhere.

title: External ankle bracing to prevent recurrent ankle sprain
question: In athletes recovering from a lateral ankle sprain, does wearing an ankle brace during sport reduce recurrent sprains over 12 months versus neuromuscular training or their combination?
balance: POSSIBLE: One three-arm randomised trial (Janssen 2014, 384 athletes aged 18–70 after a lateral ankle sprain) found self-reported recurrence over 1 year in 27% with neuromuscular training, 15% with bracing, and 19% with the combination; bracing beat training (relative risk 0.53 relative, 95% CI 0.29 to 0.97), while the combination was not significantly better than either and no group differed on time loss or costs. A single trial with a self-reported primary outcome earns POSSIBLE.

title: Pre-exercise static stretching to prevent lower-limb injury
question: In military recruits, does a pre-exercise static stretching programme reduce the risk of lower-limb injury over a 12-week training period versus no stretching?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): One large randomised trial (Pope 2000, 1,538 male army recruits) found pre-exercise static stretching did not reduce injury risk over 12 weeks of training: all-injuries hazard ratio 0.95 relative (95% CI 0.77 to 1.18), soft-tissue injury 0.83 relative (0.63 to 1.09), bone injury 1.22 relative (0.86 to 1.76) — 158 injuries in the stretch group and 175 in controls. A second recruit trial (Herbert & Gabriel) is reported in the topic literature as agreeing with the null and is fenced in the synthesis without carded figures. A large, precise null earns LIKELY (the treatment made no difference).
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference)

title: Cold-water immersion for post-exercise recovery
question: In athletes, does post-exercise cold-water immersion improve recovery of sprint performance and reduce muscle soreness versus passive recovery?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence): The carded recovery trial is very small (Leeder 2019, 21 trained male games players in a simulated tournament): cold-water immersion was associated with improved recovery of sprint speed 24 hours after the final match simulation (effect size 0.83 ± 0.59; p=.034) and attenuated creatine kinase efflux, while the authors themselves conclude immersion was 'in the main ineffective' at managing the tournament's physiological stress and provides only limited benefits. Set against it, a randomised strength-training study (Roberts 2015) found regular post-exercise cold-water immersion blunted anabolic signalling, satellite-cell responses and long-term strength and hypertrophy gains. One tiny, mixed recovery trial plus a real adaptation cost is MAYBE (weak evidence) for any net benefit.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence)

title: Arthroscopic stabilisation versus non-operative care for first-time traumatic shoulder dislocation in young active patients
question: In young active patients with a first-time traumatic anterior shoulder dislocation, does early arthroscopic stabilisation reduce recurrence versus non-operative treatment over 2–3 years?
balance: POSSIBLE: One small prospective randomised trial (Bottoni 2002, military patients with acute traumatic first-time dislocation) found recurrent instability in 1 of 9 followed patients (11.1%) after arthroscopic Bankart repair versus 9 of 12 (75%) after immobilisation and rehabilitation over an average 36 months; six of the nine non-operative recurrences went on to open Bankart repair. The effect is very large, but the trial randomised only 24 patients and lost 3 to follow-up — POSSIBLE, not more. A second randomised trial reported in the topic literature (Jakobsen) could not be pinned to a verified record at build and is fenced in the synthesis.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Blood-flow-restriction training in post-surgical musculoskeletal rehabilitation
question: In patients rehabilitating after ACL reconstruction, does low-load blood-flow-restriction resistance training produce strength and hypertrophy gains comparable with conventional heavy-load training, with less joint pain?
balance: POSSIBLE: One small single-assessor-blinded randomised trial (Hughes 2019, 28 ACL-reconstruction patients; 24 completed) found 8 weeks of low-load blood-flow-restriction training (30% of 1-repetition maximum) produced strength and muscle-thickness gains statistically indistinguishable from heavy-load training (70% 1RM) — scaled 10RM strength rose 104 ± 30% versus 106 ± 43% in the injured limb, muscle thickness 5.8 ± 0.2% versus 6.7 ± 0.3% — with greater reductions in knee joint pain (67 ± 15% vs 39 ± 12%) and effusion and larger self-reported function gains. A single 28-patient trial earns POSSIBLE.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Active training for long-standing adductor-related groin pain in athletes
question: In athletes with long-standing adductor-related groin pain, does an active physical training programme (strengthening, coordination, core) increase the proportion returning to sport without pain versus conventional physiotherapy?
balance: POSSIBLE: One randomised trial (Hölmich 1999, 68 athletes with median 40 weeks of adductor-related groin pain) found 23 of the active-training group versus 4 of the conventional-physiotherapy group returned to sport at the same level without groin pain (odds ratio 12.7 relative, 95% CI 3.4 to 47.2, multiple-logistic-regression). The second carded trial (Weir 2011) complicates the exercise story: a multimodal manual-therapy programme returned athletes to sport faster than exercise therapy (12.8 vs 17.3 weeks; p=0.043), with only 50–55% in either group fully returned — exercise helps, but slowly and incompletely, and manual multimodal care beat exercise alone on speed. Two small trials, one dramatic and one sobering, earn POSSIBLE.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Intra-articular hyaluronic acid for knee osteoarthritis
question: In adults with symptomatic knee osteoarthritis, do intra-articular hyaluronic acid injections reduce pain versus intra-articular placebo at 3–6 months?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence): The carded primary trial (Chevalier 2010, 253 patients) found a single 6 ml hylan G-F 20 injection beat placebo on WOMAC pain over 26 weeks by −0.15 points (SE 0.076; p=0.047) — statistically significant and described by the authors as 'clinically relevant', a characterisation the margin does not obviously support. The explicitly labelled review card beside it (Rutjes 2012, systematic review and meta-analysis of 89 trials, 12,667 adults) found that in the 18 large trials with blinded outcome assessment (5,094 patients) the effect size was −0.11 (95% CI −0.18 to −0.04) — clinically irrelevant — with an increased risk of serious adverse events (relative risk 1.41 relative, 1.02 to 1.97). A borderline small positive trial plus a large-trial literature at clinically irrelevant size is MAYBE (weak evidence) for any meaningful benefit.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence)

title: Repeated intra-articular triamcinolone for knee osteoarthritis: cartilage and pain
question: In adults with symptomatic knee osteoarthritis, does intra-articular triamcinolone 40 mg every 3 months for 2 years reduce knee pain versus saline — and what does it do to cartilage volume?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): One definitive 2-year double-blind randomised trial (McAlindon 2017, 140 patients with symptomatic knee OA and ultrasound synovitis) found intra-articular triamcinolone 40 mg every 3 months caused significantly GREATER cartilage volume loss than saline (index-compartment cartilage thickness change −0.21 mm vs −0.10 mm; between-group difference −0.11 mm, 95% CI −0.20 to −0.03) and NO significant pain difference (−1.2 vs −1.9 on the WOMAC Likert pain subscale; between-group difference −0.6, −1.6 to 0.3), against a minimal clinically important pain improvement of 3.94 points that neither group approached. Repeated scheduled steroid injection, as tested, loses cartilage and does not relieve pain: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) on benefit, with structural harm. Single as-needed injections are a different question, homed elsewhere.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference)

title: Sprifermin for knee osteoarthritis (structure modification)
question: In adults with symptomatic knee osteoarthritis, does intra-articular sprifermin (recombinant FGF-18) increase femorotibial cartilage thickness on MRI versus placebo at 2 years?
balance: Split: POSSIBLE (cartilage thickness) · LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) (symptoms) — PROPOSED: The FORWARD trial (Hochberg 2019, 549 participants with symptomatic radiographic knee OA) found intra-articular sprifermin 100 µg increased total femorotibial cartilage thickness versus placebo at 2 years (+0.05 mm, 95% CI 0.03 to 0.07, every 6 months; +0.04 mm, 0.02 to 0.06, every 12 months), with the 30 µg doses non-significant — a statistically real MRI effect whose clinical importance the authors themselves call uncertain, with the minimal clinically important difference for the primary outcome unknown. On symptoms there was NO significant difference in total WOMAC score change for any dose — a clean null. One trial, a surrogate structural endpoint, and a symptom null: the split is the honest stamp. Neither half is Tier C (no mortality or event claim).
stamp: Split

title: Tanezumab (anti-nerve growth factor) for osteoarthritis pain
question: In adults with knee osteoarthritis pain inadequately controlled by standard analgesics, does tanezumab reduce pain and improve function versus placebo — and what joint and sensory harms accompany it?
balance: POSSIBLE: Two randomised double-blind trials agree the anti-NGF antibody reduces OA pain: the proof-of-concept trial (Lane 2010, 450 patients with knee OA) found mean reductions in knee pain while walking of 45–62% across tanezumab doses versus 22% on placebo (P<0.001), with OMERACT-OARSI response rates of 74–93% versus 44% and paresthesia in 7%; and the phase 3 trial (Schnitzer 2019, 698 patients with hip or knee OA) found statistically significant but MODEST advantages on all three co-primaries at 16 weeks (WOMAC Pain least-squares mean differences −0.60 and −0.73 on a 0–10 scale), alongside rapidly progressive osteoarthritis only in tanezumab patients (2.2% and 0.4%) and more total joint replacements (3.5% and 6.9% vs 1.7%). Real analgesia, small phase-3 margins, and a joint-safety problem that shadows the class: POSSIBLE. Joint and sensory harms are not cardiovascular events, so the shelf is not Tier C.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Gluteal tendinopathy: education plus exercise versus corticosteroid injection versus wait-and-see (LEAP)
question: In adults with gluteal tendinopathy (greater trochanteric pain syndrome), does education plus exercise improve global outcome and pain versus corticosteroid injection or a wait-and-see approach at 8 weeks and 12 months?
balance: LIKELY: One large, well-run three-arm single-blinded randomised trial (LEAP, Mellor 2018, 204 participants with MRI-confirmed gluteal tendinopathy) found education plus exercise (EDX) beat both alternatives on global improvement at 8 weeks (success 51/66 EDX vs 38/65 corticosteroid injection vs 20/68 wait-and-see; EDX vs wait-and-see risk difference 49.1%, 95% CI 34.6% to 63.5%; EDX vs injection 19.9%, 4.7% to 35.0%) and remained better than injection at 52 weeks (success 51/65 vs 36/63; difference 20.4%, 4.9% to 35.9%), while pain at 52 weeks no longer differed between EDX and injection (mean difference −0.26, −1.06 to 0.55). A single trial, but large, pragmatic and decisive on its primary outcome: LIKELY.
stamp: LIKELY

title: Partial versus total knee replacement for medial compartment osteoarthritis (TOPKAT)
question: In adults with isolated medial compartment knee osteoarthritis suitable for either procedure, does partial (unicompartmental) knee replacement match total knee replacement on patient-reported outcome (Oxford Knee Score) at 5 years, and how do costs and reoperations compare?
balance: LIKELY: One large multicentre pragmatic randomised trial (TOPKAT, Beard 2019, 528 patients with isolated medial compartment knee OA suitable for either operation) found no difference in Oxford Knee Score at 5 years between partial and total knee replacement (mean difference 1.04, 95% CI −0.42 to 2.50; p=0.159), a similar incidence of reoperations and complications, and better cost-effectiveness for partial replacement (0.240 additional quality-adjusted life-years, 0.046 to 0.434; £910 less expensive, −1503 to −317, in UK 2017 prices). A single large trial with 94% five-year follow-up earns LIKELY for equivalence of patient-reported outcome in the eligible population.

title: Spinal manipulation, medication, or home exercise for neck pain
question: In adults with acute or subacute mechanical neck pain, does spinal manipulation or home exercise with advice relieve pain more than medication over 12 weeks?
balance: POSSIBLE: One randomised trial (Bronfort 2012, 272 adults with nonspecific neck pain of 2–12 weeks) found spinal manipulation had a statistically significant pain advantage over medication after 8, 12, 26 and 52 weeks (P≤0.010 at each), home exercise with advice was superior to medication at 26 weeks (P=0.02), and manipulation and home exercise did not differ importantly at any time point. The abstract prints P values without pain-score effect sizes, participants and providers could not be blinded, and no clinically-important-difference criteria were prespecified — a single unblindable trial with incompletely printed figures earns POSSIBLE.

title: Ultrasound-guided needling and lavage (barbotage) for rotator-cuff calcific tendinitis
question: In adults with rotator-cuff calcific tendinitis, does ultrasound-guided percutaneous needling and lavage improve shoulder function versus subacromial corticosteroid injection at 1 year?
balance: POSSIBLE: One small randomised trial (de Witte 2013, 48 patients) found ultrasound-guided needling and lavage combined with subacromial corticosteroid injection produced significantly better shoulder function at 1 year than subacromial corticosteroid injection alone — mean Constant score 86.0 (95% CI 80.3 to 91.6) versus 73.9 (67.7 to 80.1); P=.005 — with greater calcification shrinkage (−11.6 ± 6.4 mm vs −5.1 ± 5.7 mm; P=.001) and a baseline-adjusted treatment effect of 20.5 points in favour of barbotage (P=.05). NOTE — topic-file correction: the draft described this trial as 'not superior'; the record shows it WAS superior on its primary outcome at 1 year, and the card follows the record. One small trial earns POSSIBLE.

title: Mesenchymal stem-cell injections for knee osteoarthritis
question: In adults with knee osteoarthritis, does an intra-articular injection of adipose-derived mesenchymal stem cells improve pain and function versus conservative care at 12 months?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence): The carded randomised trial (Freitag 2019) randomised only 30 participants into three groups (single injection, two injections, or conservative-care control) and its abstract prints NO numerical results at all — it states that both treatment groups showed 'clinically significant pain and functional improvement' at 12 months and that MRI scoring 'indicated modification of disease progression', without effect sizes, confidence intervals or P values. A conclusion of 'safe and effective… may prevent disease progression' drawn on unprinted numbers in 30 patients is the definition of MAYBE (weak evidence) on this library's scale, and the gap between the abstract's claims and its printed data is flagged on the card face. No serious adverse events were observed.

title: Intensive diet and exercise for knee osteoarthritis in overweight older adults (IDEA)
question: In overweight or obese older adults with knee osteoarthritis, does intensive dietary weight loss combined with exercise reduce knee joint loads, inflammation (IL-6) and pain versus exercise alone over 18 months?
balance: LIKELY: The IDEA trial (Messier 2013, 454 overweight and obese older adults with knee OA) found diet plus exercise produced 11.4% weight loss versus 2.0% with exercise alone over 18 months, with less pain (3.6 vs 4.7 on a 0–20 scale; P=.004 for the exercise comparison), better function (14.1 vs 18.4; P<.001), lower IL-6 (2.7 vs 3.1 pg/mL) and lower knee compressive force in the diet groups (2487 N diet vs 2687 N exercise; pairwise difference 200 N, 95% CI 55 to 345; P=.007). The programme's earlier ADAPT trial (316 participants) agrees: diet plus exercise beat the healthy-lifestyle control on function, pain and mobility. Two concordant randomised trials from one programme earn LIKELY.
stamp: LIKELY

title: Withdrawal of psychotropic medicines to prevent falls
question: In older adults taking psychotropic medicines, does gradual withdrawal of those medicines reduce the rate of falls over the following year versus continuation?
balance: POSSIBLE: One small double-blind randomised trial (Campbell 1999, 93 older adults taking psychotropic medication, 2×2 factorial with a home exercise programme) found gradual psychotropic withdrawal reduced the relative hazard of falls over 44 weeks to 0.34 relative (95% CI 0.16 to 0.74) versus continuing medication — while the exercise programme did not significantly reduce falling — and the authors stress that permanent withdrawal proved very difficult to achieve. A single small trial with a large relative effect and a hard-to-sustain intervention earns POSSIBLE. The topic draft's second 'nursing-home withdrawal trial' could not be pinned to a verified record at build and is fenced without figures.

title: Daily-dose vitamin D for fall prevention
question: In older adults, does daily vitamin D (700–1,000 IU), with or without calcium, reduce falls versus placebo?
balance: Split: POSSIBLE (institutionalised, vitamin-D-deficient older women, short term) · LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) (community-dwelling older adults) — PROPOSED: The carded positive trial is small, short and set in long-stay geriatric care (Bischoff 2003, 122 elderly women, mean age 85.3): calcium plus 800 IU cholecalciferol for 12 weeks reduced falls by 49% relative (95% CI 14% to 71%; p<0.01) versus calcium alone, with improved musculoskeletal function. The era split is the shelf's core fact: the later, much larger trials in community-dwelling older adults — DO-HEALTH and the VITAL programme, fenced in the synthesis without carded falls figures — did not reproduce fall or related benefits, so for the general older population the honest stamp is LIKELY (the treatment made no difference). The harmful annual mega-dose regimen is a separate shelf and is not re-opened here. No mortality or fracture claim is made, so the shelf is not Tier C.
stamp: Split

title: Testosterone for frail older men with mobility limitations (TOM)
question: In older men with low testosterone and mobility limitations, does testosterone gel improve leg-press strength and physical function versus placebo — and at what cardiovascular cost?
balance: POSSIBLE (harm-leaning) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: cardiovascular events are central to the record): The TOM trial (Basaria 2010, 209 community-dwelling men aged 65+ with mobility limitations and low testosterone) was STOPPED EARLY on data-safety-monitoring advice because cardiovascular-related adverse events occurred in 23 men in the testosterone group versus 5 in the placebo group, with higher rates of cardiac, respiratory and dermatologic events on testosterone, even as leg-press and chest-press strength and loaded stair climbing improved significantly more on testosterone. A single small trial, stopped early on a harm signal it was not powered to characterise, earns POSSIBLE (harm-leaning) for this frail population — the strength benefit is real on the record and cannot be separated from the risk that stopped the trial. The later TRAVERSE trial addresses a different, lower-risk population and is fenced in the synthesis.

title: Leucine-enriched whey protein plus vitamin D for sarcopenia (PROVIDE)
question: In sarcopenic older adults, does a leucine- and vitamin-D-enriched whey protein supplement improve appendicular muscle mass and chair-stand performance versus an isocaloric control over 13 weeks?
balance: POSSIBLE: One multicentre double-blind randomised trial (PROVIDE, Bauer 2015, 380 sarcopenic older adults) found, over 13 weeks, that the enriched supplement beat an isocaloric control on two secondary outcomes — chair-stand test (between-group effect −1.01 seconds, 95% CI −1.77 to −0.19; P=.018) and appendicular muscle mass (+0.17 kg, 0.004 to 0.338; P=.045) — while BOTH primary outcomes, handgrip strength and Short Physical Performance Battery score, improved in both groups WITHOUT significant between-group differences. The authors' conclusion ('improvements in muscle mass and lower-extremity function') is accurate for the secondaries but silent about the null primaries — flagged on the card face. Null primaries plus positive secondaries in a single 13-week trial earn POSSIBLE. Plain protein supplementation in frailty is homed elsewhere.

title: Treadmill training plus virtual reality to prevent falls (V-TIME)
question: In older adults at risk of falls (including subgroups with mild cognitive impairment or Parkinson's disease), does treadmill training augmented with non-immersive virtual reality reduce fall rates over 6 months versus treadmill training alone?
balance: POSSIBLE: One multicentre randomised trial (V-TIME, Mirelman 2016, 302 adults aged 60–90 at high fall risk across five countries) found that 6 weeks of treadmill training plus non-immersive virtual reality reduced the incident fall rate over the following 6 months versus treadmill training alone (incident rate ratio 0.58 relative, 95% CI 0.36 to 0.96; p=0.033), with no serious training-related adverse events. A single trial with a confidence interval ending at 0.96 earns POSSIBLE — promising, and one replication away from more.

title: Occupational-therapist home-hazard assessment and modification to prevent falls
question: In older people living at home, does a structured OT home visit assessing and modifying environmental hazards reduce falls over 12 months versus no visit?
balance: POSSIBLE: One randomised trial (Cumming 1999, 530 community-dwelling older people, mean age 77) found the OT home-hazard intervention's overall effect was borderline — at least one fall during 12 months in 36% of the intervention group versus 45% of controls (P=.050) — with the clear effect concentrated in the prespecified-relevant subgroup who had fallen in the year before recruitment (n=206; relative risk of at least one fall 0.64 relative, 95% CI 0.50 to 0.83), and only about 50% of recommended modifications actually in place at 12 months. title: Personalised physiotherapy falls prevention in Parkinson's disease (PDSAFE)
question: In people with Parkinson's disease and a history of falls, does a personalised, physiotherapist-delivered home exercise and strategy programme reduce repeat falls over 6 months versus usual care?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): The largest randomised trial of falls management in Parkinson's disease (PDSAFE, Ashburn 2019, 474 participants with Hoehn and Yahr stages 1–4 and at least one prior fall) found NO difference in repeat falling within 6 months (PDSAFE vs control odds ratio 1.21 relative, 95% CI 0.74 to 1.98; p=0.447), although near-falling fell (OR 0.67 relative, 0.53 to 0.86; p=0.001) and balance, functional strength and falls efficacy improved. A prespecified subgroup analysis suggested possible benefit in moderate disease but a possible INCREASE in falls in more severe disease, especially with freezing of gait. A large, well-conducted null on the primary outcome — with a harm-leaning severe-subgroup signal — earns LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for the population as randomised.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference)

title: Zoledronic acid after hip fracture (HORIZON Recurrent Fracture Trial)
question: In patients who have undergone repair of a recent hip fracture, does once-yearly intravenous zoledronic acid reduce new clinical fractures and all-cause mortality versus placebo?
balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: all-cause mortality is a headline outcome): In the single large definitive trial (HORIZON Recurrent Fracture Trial, Lyles 2007, 2,127 patients after surgical repair of a low-trauma hip fracture, all receiving vitamin D and calcium, median follow-up 1.9 years), yearly intravenous zoledronic acid 5 mg reduced any new clinical fracture (8.6% vs 13.9%; a 35% relative risk reduction; P=0.001), new clinical vertebral fracture (1.7% vs 3.8%; P=0.02) and nonvertebral fracture (7.6% vs 10.7%; P=0.03), and reduced deaths from any cause (101 of 1054 [9.6%] vs 141 of 1057 [13.3%]; a 28% relative reduction; P=0.01). Rates of renal and cardiovascular adverse events, including atrial fibrillation and stroke, were similar between groups, and no osteonecrosis of the jaw was reported. One large trial with concordant fracture and mortality benefits earns LIKELY, Tier C by its mortality claim. Postmenopausal osteoporosis antiresorptives generally are homed elsewhere.

title: Calcium plus vitamin D in care-home residents for fracture prevention (Decalyos)
question: In elderly women living in nursing homes, does daily calcium (1,200 mg) plus vitamin D3 (800 IU) reduce hip and other non-vertebral fractures versus placebo over 18 months?
balance: LIKELY: One large double-blind placebo-controlled trial (Decalyos, Chapuy 1992, 3,270 healthy ambulatory women in nursing homes, mean age 84 ± 6 years) found 18 months of daily tricalcium phosphate (1.2 g elemental calcium) plus 800 IU vitamin D3 reduced hip fractures by 43% relative (P=0.043) and total nonvertebral fractures by 32% relative (P=0.015) versus double placebo among women completing the study, with intention-to-treat analyses similar; proximal femur bone density rose 2.7% on treatment and fell 4.6% on placebo (P<0.001). The population — institutionalised, elderly, and by the trial's own biochemical account vitamin-D-insufficient — is the point: routine supplementation in healthy community adults is a different shelf and is not re-carded here. Fracture outcomes without a mortality claim keep this shelf out of Tier C.
stamp: LIKELY

title: Lifestyle-integrated functional exercise to prevent falls (LiFE)
question: In older people at risk of falls living at home, does embedding balance and strength activities into daily routines (LiFE) reduce the rate of falls versus a sham gentle-exercise control over 12 months?
balance: POSSIBLE: One three-arm randomised trial (LiFE study, Clemson 2012, 317 adults aged 70+ at high fall risk in Sydney) found embedding balance and strength training into daily routines reduced the fall rate over 12 months by 31% relative versus a sham gentle-exercise control (incidence rate ratio 0.69 relative, 95% CI 0.48 to 0.99), while the conventional structured exercise programme did not significantly differ from control (0.81 relative, 0.56 to 1.17). title: Ramelteon for chronic insomnia
question: In adults with chronic primary insomnia, does ramelteon (4–16 mg) reduce latency to persistent sleep and improve total sleep time versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE: One randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled five-period crossover trial (Erman 2006, 107 adults with chronic primary insomnia, each patient receiving placebo and ramelteon 4, 8, 16 and 32 mg in sequence) found every tested dose significantly reduced latency to persistent sleep and significantly increased total sleep time versus placebo, with no next-day residual effects and no excess adverse events. The stamp is POSSIBLE, not higher: this is a single crossover trial, the abstract prints no effect sizes in minutes for either outcome, and the topic question's dose range (4–16 mg) understates the range actually tested (4–32 mg) — the discrepancy is disclosed on the card. The Roth et al. ramelteon trials named in the topic draft were not pinned to verified records at build and are fenced without figures.

title: Low-dose doxepin for insomnia
question: In adults with chronic primary insomnia, does low-dose doxepin (3–6 mg) improve sleep maintenance (wake after sleep onset) versus placebo without next-day sedation?
balance: POSSIBLE: One randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled 35-day sleep-laboratory trial (Krystal 2011, 221 adults with chronic primary insomnia) found doxepin 3 mg and 6 mg significantly improved wake after sleep onset on nights 1, 15 and 29, latency to persistent sleep on night 1, and total sleep time across the study, with no significant next-day residual effects, no rebound insomnia on discontinuation, and safety comparable to placebo. A single (well-conducted) trial earns POSSIBLE. The topic draft attributed this trial to Scharf et al.; the record's first author is Krystal AD — corrected on the card. title: Aerobic exercise for chronic primary insomnia
question: In adults with chronic primary insomnia, does a programme of moderate aerobic exercise improve sleep quality (PSQI), sleep latency and sleep efficiency versus a non-exercise control?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence): The pinned trial (Passos 2011) randomised only 19 sedentary adults with chronic primary insomnia — and it randomised them to morning versus late-afternoon exercise, NOT to exercise versus a non-exercise control; every sleep figure on the card is a before-and-after change pooled across the two timing groups. Polysomnography showed sleep onset latency falling from 17.1 to 8.7 minutes, wake after sleep onset from 63.2 to 40.1 minutes, and sleep efficiency rising from 79.8% to 87.2% after 6 months of moderate aerobic exercise, with no difference by time of day. A 19-person pre–post comparison inside a timing trial cannot answer the question as posed (exercise versus no exercise) at better than MAYBE (weak evidence). The Reid et al. 2010 trial named in the topic draft was not pinned to a verified record at build and is fenced without figures.

title: Valerian for insomnia
question: In adults with insomnia, does valerian extract improve self-rated sleep quality versus placebo?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence): One internet-based randomised double-blind trial (Oxman 2007, 405 adults with insomnia in Norway) MISSED its primary outcome: a minimally important improvement in self-reported sleep quality occurred in 29% on valerian versus 21% on placebo (difference 7.5%, 95% CI −0.9 to 15.9; P=0.08 — not significant). A secondary global self-assessment favoured valerian by 5.5 percentage points (P=0.04), with similar non-significant trends for night awakenings and sleep duration, and no important adverse-event differences. The topic draft's 'modest improvement' framing rests on the secondary outcomes; the primary-outcome null governs the stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence).
