title: Weighted blankets for insomnia
question: In adults with insomnia and psychiatric disorders, do weighted chain blankets improve insomnia severity (ISI) versus light control blankets over 4 weeks?
balance: POSSIBLE: One randomised controlled trial (Ekholm 2020, 120 outpatients with major depressive disorder, bipolar disorder, generalised anxiety disorder or ADHD and insomnia) found a significant advantage for weighted metal chain blankets over light plastic chain blankets on the Insomnia Severity Index at 4 weeks (P<.001; large effect size, Cohen d 1.90), with better sleep maintenance, higher daytime activity, and reduced fatigue, depression and anxiety symptoms, and no serious adverse events. A single 4-week trial earns POSSIBLE. title: Adjunctive armodafinil/modafinil for residual sleepiness in CPAP-treated obstructive sleep apnea
question: In adults with obstructive sleep apnea who remain excessively sleepy despite adherent CPAP, does adjunctive armodafinil improve objective wakefulness (Maintenance of Wakefulness Test) versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE: One 12-week multicentre double-blind randomised trial (Roth 2006, 395 enrolled patients with residual excessive sleepiness despite adherent nCPAP) found adjunctive armodafinil 150 or 250 mg significantly improved Maintenance of Wakefulness Test sleep latency at the final visit versus placebo, with more patients at least minimally improved on the Clinical Global Impression of Change (72% vs 37%), and larger improvements in Epworth Sleepiness Scale (−5.5 vs −3.3) and fatigue scores, with no effect on nighttime sleep or nCPAP use. A single trial earns POSSIBLE; the modafinil adjunct trials named in the topic draft were not pinned to verified records at build and are fenced without figures. title: CPAP for blood pressure in resistant hypertension with obstructive sleep apnea (HIPARCO)
question: In patients with resistant hypertension and obstructive sleep apnea, does CPAP reduce 24-hour mean blood pressure versus no CPAP over 12 weeks?
balance: POSSIBLE: One open-label randomised trial with blinded endpoint assessment (HIPARCO, Martínez-García 2013, 194 patients with resistant hypertension and an apnea–hypopnea index of at least 15) found CPAP lowered 24-hour mean blood pressure by 3.1 mm Hg (95% CI 0.6 to 5.6; P=.02) and 24-hour diastolic pressure by 3.2 mm Hg (1.0 to 5.4; P=.005) more than control at 12 weeks, but NOT 24-hour systolic pressure (3.1 mm Hg, −0.6 to 6.7; P=.10), and increased the proportion with a nocturnal dipper pattern (35.9% vs 21.6%; adjusted odds ratio 2.4 relative, 1.2 to 5.1). This is a blood-pressure surrogate shelf over 12 weeks — it is not Tier C and borrows no cardiovascular-events claim (the events question is homed on Shelf #302). title: Oropharyngeal (myofunctional) exercises for obstructive sleep apnea
question: In adults with moderate obstructive sleep apnea, does a daily programme of oropharyngeal exercises reduce the apnea–hypopnoea index and neck circumference versus a control programme over 3 months?
balance: POSSIBLE: One small randomised trial (Guimarães 2009, 31 patients with moderate obstructive sleep apnea) found 3 months of daily oropharyngeal exercises reduced the apnea–hypopnea index within the exercise group from 22.4 to 13.7 events/h and neck circumference from 39.6 to 38.5 cm, with significant improvements in snoring, daytime sleepiness and sleep quality, while the sham-therapy control group showed no significant change in any variable. title: Nasal expiratory positive airway pressure (EPAP) for obstructive sleep apnea
question: In adults with obstructive sleep apnea, does a nasal EPAP device worn nightly reduce the apnea–hypopnoea index versus a sham device over 3 months?
balance: POSSIBLE: One prospective multicentre sham-controlled double-blind randomised trial (Berry 2011, 250 randomised patients with obstructive sleep apnea and a pre-study AHI of at least 10/hour) found the nasal EPAP device reduced AHI far more than sham — median AHI on versus off device 5.0 versus 13.8 events/h at week 1, and a 42.7% median AHI decrease at month 3 versus 10.1% on sham (P<0.0001) — with Epworth Sleepiness Scale improving from 9.9 to 7.2 and median reported whole-night use on 88.2% of nights. title: Melatonin for REM sleep behaviour disorder
question: In adults with REM sleep behaviour disorder, does melatonin (3–12 mg at bedtime) improve clinical global impression of RBD severity versus placebo?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence): The entire randomised record pinned at build is one two-part double-blind placebo-controlled crossover study in EIGHT men (Kunz & Mahlberg 2010), using melatonin 3 mg only — not the 3–12 mg range in the shelf question, which no pinned trial tested. Melatonin significantly reduced the percentage of 30-second REM sleep epochs without muscle atonia (39% at baseline versus 27%; P=0.012) and improved clinical global impression (6.1 versus 4.6; P=0.024), with a carry-over pattern suggesting effects persisted into a subsequent placebo phase. Eight participants and a single low dose: MAYBE (weak evidence), and most clinical melatonin use in RBD rests on open-label experience outside this record.

title: L-methylfolate as adjunctive therapy for SSRI-resistant depression
question: In adults with major depression responding inadequately to an SSRI, does adjunctive L-methylfolate 15 mg/day improve response and remission versus adjunctive placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE — split by trial, as the programme was designed: Papakostas 2012 reports TWO sequential parallel comparison design trials in one paper. The first (148 outpatients with SSRI-resistant major depression; L-methylfolate 7.5 mg/day rising to 15 mg/day) found NO significant difference between treatment groups. The second (75 patients; L-methylfolate 15 mg/day throughout) found significantly greater efficacy than continued SSRI plus placebo on both primary outcome measures (response rate and change in depression symptom score) and two secondary severity measures, with a number needed to treat for response of approximately 6 and adverse-event rates no different from placebo. One positive small trial at the 15 mg dose after one null trial earns POSSIBLE for the 15 mg strategy — and the shelf carries the null first trial on its face, not underneath it.

title: N-acetylcysteine as adjunctive treatment for schizophrenia
question: In adults with chronic schizophrenia on stable antipsychotics, does adjunctive N-acetylcysteine (1 g twice daily) improve negative symptoms and overall psychopathology versus placebo over 24 weeks?

title: Swallowing strategies for aspiration in dementia or Parkinson's disease
question: In patients with dementia or Parkinson's disease who aspirate thin liquids on videofluoroscopy, does a chin-down posture or nectar/honey-thickened liquids reduce the 3-month incidence of pneumonia?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): One large randomised trial (Robbins 2008, 515 patients aged 50 or older with dementia or Parkinson disease who aspirated thin liquids on videofluoroscopy; 504 followed) found NO significant difference in 3-month pneumonia incidence between chin-down posture (9.8%) and thickened liquids (11.6%; hazard ratio 0.84 relative, 95% CI 0.49 to 1.45; P=0.53), and no significant difference between nectar-thick (8.4%) and honey-thick (15.0%; HR 0.50 relative, 0.23 to 1.09; P=0.083) — with more dehydration (6% vs 2%), urinary tract infection (6% vs 3%) and fever (4% vs 2%) on thickened liquids. The authors state no definitive conclusions about superiority can be made, and there was no untreated control group, so the null is a null between strategies, not proof that all strategies are useless. The companion videofluoroscopy study (Logemann 2008, 711 patients) found honey-thick liquids most often eliminated aspiration immediately, then nectar-thick, then chin-down. The topic draft attributed the pneumonia trial to Logemann; its first author is Robbins J — corrected on the card. One trial programme: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference). Pneumonia incidence is the primary outcome; it is not a mortality/CV claim, so this shelf is not Tier C.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference)

title: Radial versus femoral access for coronary angiography and intervention in ACS (RIVAL and MATRIX)
question: In patients with acute coronary syndromes undergoing angiography with possible PCI, does radial access, compared with femoral access, reduce the composite of death, MI, stroke, and non-CABG major bleeding?
balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, the composites include death, MI and stroke): Two large randomised trials point the same way on net clinical events but not identically. RIVAL (7,021 ACS patients) found no difference in its primary composite of death, MI, stroke or non-CABG major bleeding at 30 days (3.7% radial vs 4.0% femoral; HR 0.92 relative, 95% CI 0.72 to 1.17; P=0.50), with death/MI/stroke identical (3.2% vs 3.2%) and major bleeding itself not significantly different (0.7% vs 0.9%) — the clear RIVAL gains were local vascular complications (large haematoma 42 vs 106 patients; pseudoaneurysm needing closure 7 vs 23). MATRIX (8,404 ACS patients) met its net adverse clinical events co-primary outcome (9.8% vs 11.7%; rate ratio 0.83 relative, 0.73 to 0.96; P=0.0092), driven by BARC major bleeding (1.6% vs 2.3%) and all-cause mortality (1.6% vs 2.2%; rate ratio 0.72 relative, 0.53 to 0.99) — while its MACE co-primary (8.8% vs 10.3%; P=0.0307) did NOT reach significance at the prespecified split alpha of 0.025. Two large trials with a consistent bleeding and net-event advantage, one mortality component significant in one trial, support LIKELY for the net-benefit claim; the topic draft's framing of RIVAL as showing a mortality signal is corrected on the card — RIVAL's death/MI/stroke rates were identical, and its significant interactions were for the primary composite in STEMI and in high-radial-volume centres.

title: Bivalirudin versus heparin monotherapy in myocardial infarction treated with PCI (VALIDATE-SWEDEHEART)
question: In patients with STEMI or NSTEMI undergoing PCI, does bivalirudin, compared with heparin monotherapy, reduce the composite of death, MI, and major bleeding at 180 days?

title: Routine manual thrombus aspiration in STEMI (TASTE and TOTAL)
question: In patients with STEMI undergoing primary PCI, does routine manual thrombus aspiration before PCI, compared with PCI alone, reduce cardiovascular death and related hard outcomes?

title: Culprit-lesion-only versus multivessel PCI in cardiogenic shock with multivessel disease (CULPRIT-SHOCK)

title: Intra-aortic balloon pump in MI complicated by cardiogenic shock (IABP-SHOCK II)
question: In patients with acute MI and cardiogenic shock undergoing early revascularisation, does intra-aortic balloon counterpulsation, compared with no balloon pump, reduce 30-day all-cause mortality?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, mortality primary outcome): IABP-SHOCK II (600 patients with MI and cardiogenic shock, all planned for early revascularisation) found 30-day all-cause mortality of 39.7% with intra-aortic balloon counterpulsation versus 41.3% without (RR 0.96 relative, 95% CI 0.79 to 1.17; P=0.69), with no differences in haemodynamic stabilisation, ICU stay, lactate, catecholamine dose or renal function, and no safety penalty or benefit. The companion programme trial CRISP-AMI — a different population (anterior STEMI WITHOUT shock) and a surrogate primary outcome (MRI infarct size) — was likewise null (infarct size 42.1% vs 37.5% of LV mass). The mortality null in shock rests on IABP-SHOCK II; CRISP-AMI is carded as programme support and labelled by its own population. The topic draft's claim of 'none at 6-year follow-up' refers to a later report not pinned at build and is fenced in the synthesis.

title: Early routine VA-ECMO in infarct-related cardiogenic shock (ECLS-SHOCK and ECMO-CS)
question: In patients with acute MI and cardiogenic shock planned for revascularisation, does early extracorporeal life support (VA-ECMO), compared with usual care without routine ECLS, reduce 30-day all-cause mortality?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, mortality outcome): Two randomised trials of early routine VA-ECMO in cardiogenic shock are concordantly null on mortality. ECLS-SHOCK (420 patients with acute MI and shock planned for early revascularisation) found 30-day all-cause mortality of 47.8% with early ECLS versus 49.0% without (RR 0.98 relative, 95% CI 0.80 to 1.19; P=0.81), with more moderate/severe bleeding (23.4% vs 9.6%; RR 2.44 relative) and more peripheral vascular complications (11.0% vs 3.8%). ECMO-CS (117 patients analysed, severe or rapidly deteriorating cardiogenic shock of mixed cause) found its composite primary end point not significantly different (63.8% vs 71.2%; HR 0.72 relative, 0.46 to 1.12) and 30-day mortality 50.0% versus 47.5%, with 39% of the conservative group crossing over to downstream VA-ECMO. Routine early VA-ECMO, as tested, does not reduce mortality and adds bleeding: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference).

title: Microaxial flow pump (Impella CP) in STEMI-related cardiogenic shock (DanGer Shock)
question: In patients with STEMI and cardiogenic shock, does a microaxial flow pump (Impella CP) plus standard care, compared with standard care alone, reduce all-cause mortality at 180 days?
balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, mortality benefit claim): DanGer Shock (360 randomised; 355 analysed) is the first randomised trial of a mechanical support device to show a mortality benefit in infarct shock: death from any cause at 180 days occurred in 45.8% with the microaxial flow pump versus 58.5% with standard care (HR 0.74 relative, 95% CI 0.55 to 0.99; P=0.04) — an absolute difference of 12.7 percentage points. The price was substantial: the composite safety end point (severe bleeding, limb ischaemia, haemolysis, device failure, or worsening aortic regurgitation) occurred in 24.0% versus 6.2% (RR 4.74 relative), and renal-replacement therapy in 41.9% versus 26.7%. One trial of 355 analysed patients, with a P value of 0.04 and heavy harms, earns POSSIBLE — a real but fragile and costly benefit claim after the null device trials on Shelves #1534 and #1535.

title: FFR-guided complete revascularisation in STEMI with multivessel disease (DANAMI-3-PRIMULTI and Compare-Acute)
question: In patients with STEMI and multivessel disease after successful culprit PCI, does FFR-guided complete revascularisation, compared with culprit-lesion-only treatment, reduce major adverse cardiovascular events?
balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, the composites include death and MI): Two randomised trials of FFR-guided complete revascularisation after culprit PCI in STEMI both reduced their composites — DANAMI-3-PRIMULTI (627 patients: 13% vs 22%; HR 0.56 relative, 95% CI 0.38 to 0.83; P=0.004) and Compare-Acute (885 patients: 8 vs 21 events per 100 patients at 12 months; HR 0.35 relative, 0.22 to 0.55) — and in both the benefit was driven by fewer repeat revascularisations, with no significant difference in death or MI (Compare-Acute: death 1.4% vs 1.7%; MI 2.4% vs 4.7%, HR 0.50 relative, CI crossing 1). A revascularisation-driven composite earns POSSIBLE, not more. Build correction: the topic draft anchored this shelf on FAME (Tonino 2009, PMID 19144937), but FAME enrolled stable multivessel disease and tested FFR-guided lesion selection against angiography-guided PCI — it does not test this shelf's question and is fenced, not carded. The DANAMI-3 programme design paper (PMID 25965708) is likewise fenced; the carded report is the PRIMULTI primary publication. Angiography-guided complete revascularisation (COMPLETE) is a separate strategy and is not folded in.

title: Early versus delayed invasive strategy in NSTE-ACS (TIMACS and VERDICT)
question: In patients with non-ST-elevation acute coronary syndromes, does an early invasive strategy (angiography within 24 hours), compared with a delayed strategy (after 36 hours), reduce the composite of death, MI, and stroke at 6 months?
balance: SPLIT — LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) overall / POSSIBLE benefit in highest-risk patients — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, the composites include death, MI and stroke): TIMACS (3,031 NSTE-ACS patients; angiography at a median of 14 vs 50 hours) found no significant difference in death, MI or stroke at 6 months (9.6% early vs 11.3% delayed; HR 0.85 relative, 95% CI 0.68 to 1.06; P=0.15), while its secondary composite including refractory ischaemia favoured early intervention (9.5% vs 12.9%; HR 0.72 relative) and a prespecified analysis showed benefit confined to the highest-risk third (HR 0.65 relative, 0.48 to 0.89; P=0.01 for heterogeneity). VERDICT (2,147 patients; angiography at 4.7 vs 61.6 hours; median follow-up 4.3 years) was likewise null overall (27.5% vs 29.5%; HR 0.92 relative, 0.78 to 1.08) with a significant interaction favouring very early treatment at GRACE score >140 (HR 0.81 relative, 0.67 to 1.01; interaction P=0.023). Two trials, the same shape: no overall benefit, a high-risk subgroup signal in both. Note VERDICT's primary composite differs from the shelf question's — it adds admissions for refractory ischaemia and heart failure and does not include stroke — disclosed on its card.

title: Deferred stenting after initial reperfusion in STEMI (DANAMI-3-DEFER)
question: In patients with STEMI and restored flow after initial intervention, does deferred stent implantation (48 hours later), compared with conventional immediate stenting, improve clinical outcomes?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, the composite includes death and MI): DANAMI-3-DEFER (1,215 STEMI patients with stabilised flow in the infarct artery) found its primary composite — all-cause mortality, heart-failure admission, recurrent infarction, or unplanned target-vessel revascularisation over a median 42 months — in 17% with deferred stenting versus 18% with conventional immediate stenting (HR 0.99 relative, 95% CI 0.76 to 1.29; P=0.92), with no difference in procedure-related complications (4% vs 5%). A completed trial with the point estimate dead on the null carries LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for routine deferral. The smaller earlier trials named in the topic draft (DEFER-STEMI, INNOVATION) tested microvascular surrogates and are fenced in the synthesis, not carded.

title: Antithrombotic strategy after PCI in atrial fibrillation (AUGUSTUS)
question: In patients with atrial fibrillation who have had an ACS or PCI and are taking a P2Y12 inhibitor, does apixaban (versus warfarin) and aspirin versus placebo change bleeding and ischaemic outcomes — i.e., is dual therapy without aspirin safer than triple therapy?
balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, ischaemic outcomes include death, MI and stroke): AUGUSTUS (4,614 patients with AF and recent ACS or PCI, all on a P2Y12 inhibitor, 2×2 factorial, 6 months) answered both halves of the question. Apixaban caused less major or clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding than a vitamin K antagonist (10.5% vs 14.7%; HR 0.69 relative, 95% CI 0.58 to 0.81) and less death or hospitalisation (23.5% vs 27.4%; HR 0.83 relative). Aspirin caused much more bleeding than placebo (16.1% vs 9.0%; HR 1.89 relative, 1.59 to 2.24) with no difference in death/hospitalisation or ischaemic events. Dual therapy with apixaban plus a P2Y12 inhibitor, without aspirin, is the trial's supported regimen — LIKELY, concordant with the wider four-trial programme fenced in the synthesis. This shelf is the post-PCI combination question, distinct from Shelf #719 (apixaban vs warfarin for AF generally).

title: Clopidogrel versus aspirin as long-term monotherapy after PCI (HOST-EXAM)
question: In patients who have completed 6–18 months of dual antiplatelet therapy after PCI without events, does clopidogrel monotherapy, compared with aspirin monotherapy, reduce the composite of death, MI, stroke, readmission for ACS, and major bleeding?
balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, the composite includes death, MI and stroke): HOST-EXAM (5,438 patients randomised in South Korea after 6–18 event-free months of dual antiplatelet therapy following drug-eluting stent PCI) found the composite of all-cause death, nonfatal MI, stroke, readmission for ACS, and BARC type ≥3 bleeding lower on clopidogrel monotherapy than aspirin monotherapy at 24 months (5.7% vs 7.7%; HR 0.73 relative, 95% CI 0.59 to 0.90; P=0.0035). A single trial — open-label, single-country, in event-free survivors of the DAPT period — caps at POSSIBLE; the topic draft's 'borderline THIN' flag is answered by the stamp rather than a thin label, since the trial is large and its end point clinical. The record's abstract prints only the composite, so no claim is made here about which components drove it.

title: Gastroprotection with a PPI during dual antiplatelet therapy (COGENT)
question: In patients taking clopidogrel plus aspirin who are at risk of gastrointestinal complications, does adding omeprazole, compared with clopidogrel plus aspirin alone, reduce gastrointestinal events without increasing cardiovascular events?
balance: SPLIT — POSSIBLE for gastrointestinal protection / MAYBE (weak evidence) for cardiovascular safety — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: cardiovascular events — death from cardiovascular causes, nonfatal MI, revascularisation, or stroke — were a primary end point of this trial, so the shelf carries an event claim): COGENT (3,873 randomised; 3,761 analysed; terminated prematurely when the sponsor lost financing, against ~5,000 planned) found gastrointestinal events at 180 days markedly lower with omeprazole (1.1% vs 2.9%; HR 0.34 relative, 95% CI 0.18 to 0.63) and overt upper GI bleeding lower still (HR 0.13 relative). The cardiovascular end point did not differ (4.9% vs 5.7%; HR 0.99 relative, 0.68 to 1.44) — but the authors themselves state the results 'do not rule out a clinically meaningful difference in cardiovascular events', and with only 109 cardiovascular events in a stopped-early trial, they cannot. Hence the split: GI protection POSSIBLE (one trial, stopped early, but a large effect on its primary end point); cardiovascular safety only MAYBE (weak evidence).

title: Platelet-function-guided escalation of antiplatelet therapy after PCI (GRAVITAS and ARCTIC)
question: In patients with high on-treatment platelet reactivity after PCI, does high-dose clopidogrel guided by platelet-function testing, compared with standard-dose clopidogrel, reduce cardiovascular death, MI, and stent thrombosis?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, the composites include cardiovascular death and MI): Two randomised trials of test-guided antiplatelet adjustment are concordantly null. GRAVITAS (2,214 patients with high on-treatment platelet reactivity after drug-eluting stent PCI) found doubling clopidogrel (150 mg daily) produced an identical primary event rate to standard dosing (2.3% vs 2.3% at 6 months; HR 1.01 relative, 95% CI 0.58 to 1.76) despite a real pharmacodynamic effect (persistently high reactivity at 30 days 40% vs 62%). ARCTIC (2,440 patients scheduled for coronary stenting) found a monitoring-and-adjustment strategy no better than conventional care — primary composite 34.6% vs 31.1% at 1 year (HR 1.13 relative, 0.98 to 1.29), numerically worse. The biomarker predicts events; acting on it does not prevent them: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference). The wider programme (ANTARCTIC, TAILOR-PCI) is fenced in the synthesis.

title: Vorapaxar for secondary prevention after MI (TRA 2°P–TIMI 50 and TRACER)
question: In patients with prior MI or peripheral artery disease on standard antiplatelet therapy, does adding the PAR-1 antagonist vorapaxar, compared with placebo, reduce cardiovascular death, MI, and stroke, and at what bleeding cost?
balance: SPLIT — LIKELY benefit-with-harm in stable secondary prevention / POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference, with harm) in ACS — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, benefit and harm both on death/MI/stroke territory): TRA 2°P–TIMI 50 (26,449 patients with prior MI, ischaemic stroke, or PAD) found vorapaxar reduced cardiovascular death, MI or stroke at 3 years (9.3% vs 10.5%; HR 0.87 relative, 95% CI 0.80 to 0.94) — an absolute reduction of 1.2 points — while increasing moderate or severe bleeding (4.2% vs 2.5%; HR 1.66 relative) and intracranial haemorrhage (1.0% vs 0.5%); the data and safety monitoring board stopped treatment in the prior-stroke subgroup for ICH risk. TRACER (12,944 patients with NSTE-ACS, follow-up terminated early after a safety review) found no significant reduction in its primary composite (2-year rates 18.5% vs 19.9%; HR 0.92 relative, 0.85 to 1.01; P=0.07) with more major bleeding (7.2% vs 5.2%) and a threefold ICH excess (1.1% vs 0.2%; HR 3.39 relative). The shelf question names prior MI or PAD; the trial's stroke-history stratum is disclosed on the card, since its early discontinuation is part of the record.

title: Fondaparinux versus enoxaparin in acute coronary syndromes (OASIS-5 and OASIS-6)
question: In patients with non-ST-elevation ACS, does fondaparinux, compared with enoxaparin, achieve similar protection against death, MI, and refractory ischaemia with less major bleeding?
balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, the composites include death and MI): OASIS-5 (20,078 patients with ACS) found fondaparinux noninferior to enoxaparin on death, MI or refractory ischaemia at 9 days (5.8% vs 5.7%; HR 1.01 relative, 95% CI 0.90 to 1.13) with less than half the major bleeding (2.2% vs 4.1%; HR 0.52 relative; P<0.001) and significantly fewer deaths at 30 days (295 vs 352 patients; P=0.02) and 180 days (574 vs 638; P=0.05). The companion OASIS-6 trial — a different question, STEMI patients randomised against placebo/UFH usual care — found death or reinfarction reduced (9.7% vs 11.2% at 30 days; HR 0.86 relative), with the explicit exception of patients undergoing primary PCI, in whom there was no benefit. Equal ischaemic protection with half the bleeding in the head-to-head trial earns LIKELY.

title: Bridging anticoagulation in atrial fibrillation patients interrupting warfarin for a procedure (BRIDGE and PERIOP2)
question: In patients with atrial fibrillation who need to interrupt warfarin for an elective procedure, does forgoing bridging anticoagulation, compared with low-molecular-weight heparin bridging, prevent arterial thromboembolism as well while causing less bleeding?
balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, the thromboembolism outcomes include stroke): BRIDGE (1,884 patients with AF interrupting warfarin for an elective procedure, double-blind) found forgoing bridging noninferior for arterial thromboembolism (0.4% no-bridging vs 0.3% bridging; risk difference 0.1 points, 95% CI −0.6 to 0.8) and superior for major bleeding (1.3% vs 3.2%; RR 0.41 relative, 0.20 to 0.78). PERIOP2 (1,471 patients with AF or mechanical heart valves) tested the postoperative half of bridging and likewise found no thromboembolism benefit (1.0% dalteparin vs 1.2% placebo) and no significant bleeding difference (1.3% vs 2.0%). Two double-blind trials agree there is nothing to buy with bridging in these populations: LIKELY.

title: Continuing versus interrupting oral anticoagulation for cardiac device surgery (BRUISE CONTROL programme)
question: In patients on warfarin or a direct oral anticoagulant undergoing pacemaker or defibrillator surgery, does continuing the anticoagulant, compared with interruption (with heparin bridging for warfarin), reduce clinically significant device-pocket haematoma?
balance: SPLIT — LIKELY that continued warfarin beats heparin bridging / LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for continued versus interrupted DOAC: The two programme trials answer different halves of peri-device anticoagulation. title: Rivaroxaban versus warfarin in high-risk triple-positive antiphospholipid syndrome (TRAPS)
question: In patients with high-risk (triple-positive) antiphospholipid syndrome, is rivaroxaban, compared with warfarin, noninferior for preventing thromboembolic events, major bleeding, and vascular death?
balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, thromboembolism and vascular death outcomes): TRAPS was a small open-label noninferiority trial (120 triple-positive APS patients, Italy) terminated prematurely because of excess events on rivaroxaban: the composite of thromboembolic events, major bleeding and vascular death occurred in 11 of 59 (19%) rivaroxaban patients versus 2 of 61 (3%) on warfarin over a mean follow-up of 569 days; thromboembolic events were 7 (12%) versus 0 — four ischaemic strokes and three MIs, all arterial, all on rivaroxaban — and major bleeding 4 (7%) versus 2 (3%); no deaths occurred. One small stopped trial earns POSSIBLE (harm) — directionally stark, numerically fragile. title: Prasugrel pretreatment before angiography in NSTE-ACS (ACCOAST)
question: In patients with non-ST-elevation ACS scheduled for angiography, does prasugrel pretreatment before the anatomy is known, compared with prasugrel given only after angiography confirms PCI, reduce ischaemic events without increasing bleeding?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference, with bleeding harm) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, the composite includes death, MI and stroke): ACCOAST (4,033 troponin-positive NSTE-ACS patients scheduled for angiography within 2 to 48 hours) found prasugrel pretreatment (30 mg before angiography) did not reduce its primary efficacy composite through day 7 versus deferred dosing (HR 1.02 relative, 95% CI 0.84 to 1.25; P=0.81) — including among the 69% who proceeded to PCI — while significantly increasing TIMI major bleeding (HR 1.90 relative, 1.19 to 3.02; P=0.006), with non-CABG major bleeding increased threefold and life-threatening bleeding sixfold (relative factors as printed in the record). One large trial with a dead-null efficacy result and a significant harm result carries LIKELY (the treatment made no difference, with harm). The record's abstract does not print the absolute primary event rates, and none are supplied here.

title: Chlorthalidone versus placebo for hypertension in advanced CKD (CLICK)
question: In patients with stage 4 chronic kidney disease and poorly controlled hypertension, does chlorthalidone, compared with placebo on top of existing therapy, lower 24-hour ambulatory systolic blood pressure?
balance: POSSIBLE: CLICK (160 patients with stage 4 CKD — mean eGFR 23.2 ml/min/1.73 m² — and poorly controlled hypertension on a mean of 3.4 antihypertensive drugs) found chlorthalidone (12.5 mg titrated to 50 mg) lowered 24-hour ambulatory systolic BP by 11.0 mm Hg versus 0.5 mm Hg on placebo at 12 weeks (between-group difference −10.5 mm Hg, 95% CI −14.6 to −6.4; P<0.001), with the urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio falling 50 percentage points more than placebo. Harms were the class's own: hypokalaemia, reversible creatinine increases, hyperglycaemia, dizziness and hyperuricaemia all occurred more frequently with chlorthalidone (the abstract does not print their rates). One small, single, 12-week trial with a blood-pressure (surrogate) end point caps at POSSIBLE. Not Tier C: the claim is blood pressure. title: Quadruple single-pill combination as initial therapy for hypertension (QUARTET)
question: In adults with hypertension starting or on monotherapy, does initial treatment with a single pill containing quarter-doses of four antihypertensive classes, compared with standard-dose monotherapy, achieve better blood-pressure control?
balance: POSSIBLE: QUARTET (591 Australian adults with hypertension, untreated or on monotherapy; mean age 59 years, 60% men) found starting treatment with a quarter-dose quadpill (irbesartan 37.5 mg, amlodipine 1.25 mg, indapamide 0.625 mg, bisoprolol 2.5 mg) beat starting with standard-dose irbesartan monotherapy: unattended office systolic BP lower by 6.9 mm Hg (95% CI 4.9 to 8.9) and control (<140/90) in 76% versus 58% at 12 weeks (RR 1.30 relative, 1.15 to 1.47), with the advantage maintained at 52 weeks in the continuation subgroup (−7.7 mm Hg; control 81% vs 62%) and far fewer add-on medications needed (15% vs 40% by 12 weeks). Serious adverse events up to 12 weeks were 7 (3%) on quadpill versus 3 (1%) on control, with no difference in withdrawals for adverse events. One double-blind trial with a blood-pressure (surrogate) end point: POSSIBLE. Not Tier C: the claim is BP control.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Low-dose triple-pill combination versus usual care for hypertension (TRIUMPH)
question: In adults with mild-to-moderate hypertension needing treatment, does a fixed low-dose triple combination pill, compared with usual care, increase the proportion reaching target blood pressure?
balance: POSSIBLE: TRIUMPH (700 patients with mild-to-moderate hypertension in Sri Lanka; mean age 56 years, 58% women) found a fixed low-dose triple pill (telmisartan 20 mg, amlodipine 2.5 mg, chlorthalidone 12.5 mg) increased the proportion reaching target BP at 6 months versus usual care (70% vs 55%; risk difference 12.7 percentage points, 95% CI 3.2 to 22.0), with mean BP 125/76 versus 134/81 mm Hg (adjusted systolic difference −9.8 mm Hg over follow-up) and no excess withdrawals for adverse events (6.6% vs 6.8%). One open-label, single-country trial with a blood-pressure (surrogate) end point: POSSIBLE. Not Tier C: the claim is BP control.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Initial antihypertensive combinations in Black African patients (CREOLE)
question: In Black patients with hypertension in sub-Saharan Africa, does initial combination therapy with amlodipine plus hydrochlorothiazide or amlodipine plus perindopril, compared with perindopril plus hydrochlorothiazide, lower ambulatory blood pressure more?
balance: POSSIBLE: CREOLE (728 Black patients with uncontrolled hypertension in six sub-Saharan African countries; mean age 51 years, 63% women) found both amlodipine-containing combinations lowered 24-hour ambulatory systolic BP more at 6 months than perindopril plus HCTZ — by 3.14 mm Hg (95% CI −5.90 to −0.38; P=0.03) for amlodipine+HCTZ and 3.00 mm Hg (−5.8 to −0.20; P=0.04) for amlodipine+perindopril — while the two amlodipine combinations did not differ from each other (−0.14 mm Hg; P=0.92). One single-blind regional trial with a blood-pressure (surrogate) end point: POSSIBLE. Not Tier C: the claim is BP lowering.

title: Community-based intensive BP management by non-physician providers in rural populations (CRHCP)
question: In rural adults with hypertension, does a village-doctor-led multifaceted intervention (protocol-based treatment, coaching, monitoring), compared with usual care, reduce cardiovascular events and death?
balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, cardiovascular events and death are the primary outcomes of the effectiveness report): The China Rural Hypertension Control Project randomised 326 villages (33,995 hypertensive adults aged ≥40). Its 36-month effectiveness report found the primary composite (MI, stroke, heart failure hospitalisation, or cardiovascular death) lower with the village-doctor-led intervention (1.62% vs 2.40% per year; HR 0.67 relative, 95% CI 0.61 to 0.73), with every component and all-cause death also reduced (all-cause death HR 0.85 relative, 0.76 to 0.95), at the cost of more hypotension (1.75% vs 0.89%). The trial's earlier primary report showed the mechanism: BP <130/80 at 18 months in 57.0% versus 19.9%, with systolic BP 14.5 mm Hg lower. Both cards are reports of ONE cluster trial (counted once): a single-country, open-label, cluster-randomised delivery-model trial caps at POSSIBLE. Build correction: the topic draft attributed the event outcomes to the 2022 anchor record; that record (PMID 35500594) reports the 18-month BP outcomes only — the events live in the trial's 2023 effectiveness report (PMID 36871573), pinned at build and carded here.

title: Self-monitoring of blood pressure in pregnancy with hypertension (BUMP 1 and BUMP 2)
question: In pregnant individuals with chronic or gestational hypertension, does self-monitoring of blood pressure (with telemonitoring in BUMP 2), compared with usual clinic-based monitoring, improve blood-pressure control or detect pre-eclampsia sooner?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): The BUMP programme's two randomised trials (one programme, one registry number, two populations and two questions) are both null on their primary outcomes. BUMP 2 (850 pregnant individuals with chronic or gestational hypertension) found self-monitoring with telemonitoring did not improve clinic systolic BP before birth in either cohort (chronic: 133.8 vs 133.6 mm Hg, adjusted difference 0.03 mm Hg; gestational: 137.6 vs 137.2 mm Hg, difference −0.03 mm Hg). BUMP 1 (2,441 pregnant individuals at higher risk of pre-eclampsia, without diagnosed hypertension at entry) found self-monitoring did not detect hypertension sooner (time to clinic-recorded hypertension 104.3 vs 106.2 days; difference −1.6 days, 95% CI −8.1 to 4.9). Build correction: the topic draft describes BUMP 1 as the gestational-hypertension trial — it is not; BUMP 2 itself contains both the chronic and gestational cohorts, and BUMP 1 answers the detection question in higher-risk pregnancy. Not Tier C: process/BP outcomes, no drug-initiation claim (self-monitoring only).
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference)

title: Endothelin-receptor antagonism with darusentan in resistant hypertension (DORADO)
question: In patients with resistant hypertension on at least three drugs including a diuretic, does the endothelin-receptor antagonist darusentan, compared with placebo, lower blood pressure?
balance: LIKELY: Two double-blind, placebo-controlled randomised trials of darusentan in resistant hypertension agree on blood-pressure lowering. DORADO (379 patients on at least three drugs including a diuretic at full or maximally tolerated doses) found clinic systolic/diastolic reductions at 14 weeks of 17/10, 18/10 and 18/11 mm Hg at 50, 100 and 300 mg versus 9/5 mm Hg on placebo (P<0.0001 for all dose effects), with oedema or fluid retention in 27% on darusentan versus 14% on placebo. The earlier forced-titration dose-ranging trial (Black 2007, 115 patients) likewise found dose-dependent reductions, largest at 300 mg (−11.5/−6.3 mm Hg at week 10 as printed). The stamp is LIKELY for the BP-lowering claim only: the end points are blood pressure (surrogate), the harm is fluid retention, and the programme was abandoned before marketing — no outcome claim is made. Distinct from Shelf #743 (the aprocitentan/baxdrostat era). Not Tier C.
stamp: LIKELY

title: Midodrine for prevention of recurrent vasovagal syncope
question: In patients with recurrent vasovagal syncope, does midodrine, compared with placebo, reduce the recurrence of syncope?
balance: POSSIBLE: One double-blind randomised trial (Sheldon 2021, 133 patients with recurrent vasovagal syncope — median 6 episodes in the prior year, median age 32 years, 73% female) found fewer patients on midodrine had at least one syncope episode over 12 months (42% [28 of 66] vs 61% [41 of 67]; RR 0.69 relative, 95% CI 0.49 to 0.97; P=0.035), an absolute reduction of 19 percentage points (number needed to treat 5.3), with time to first syncope also longer (HR 0.59 relative, 0.37 to 0.96) and adverse effects similar between groups. A single small trial in young, healthy, high-burden patients caps at POSSIBLE, matching the authors' own stated limitations. Not Tier C: syncope recurrence, not a mortality/event claim. (This is a blood-pressure-regulation disorder shelf, adjacent to the hypertension slate.)
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Droxidopa for symptomatic neurogenic orthostatic hypotension
question: In patients with neurogenic orthostatic hypotension from Parkinson disease, multiple system atrophy, or autonomic failure, does droxidopa, compared with placebo, improve orthostatic symptoms and standing blood pressure?
balance: POSSIBLE: The droxidopa programme is two short, responder-enriched phase 3 trials with mixed primary results. Kaufmann 2014 (162 responders randomised after open-label titration) found droxidopa improved the Orthostatic Hypotension Questionnaire composite over a 7-day double-blind phase (between-group improvement 0.90 units; P=0.003) and raised standing systolic BP more (11.2 vs 3.9 mm Hg; P<0.001) — with supine systolic BP also higher (7.6 vs 0.8 mm Hg) and supine systolic >180 mm Hg in 4.9% versus 2.5%. The randomised-withdrawal trial (Biaggioni 2015, 101 responders) FAILED its primary end point (worsening of dizziness/lightheadedness 1.3 vs 1.9 units favouring continued droxidopa; P=0.509 — not significant), with significance only in secondary and post hoc composite analyses. Build correction: the topic draft describes the Biaggioni trial as 'positive on falls/symptoms' — the record shows a missed primary end point and no falls outcome. One positive 7-day trial and one primary-null withdrawal trial, both enriched for responders, earn POSSIBLE. Not Tier C: symptom claim.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Spironolactone versus clonidine as fourth-line therapy for resistant hypertension (ReHOT)
question: In patients with true resistant hypertension on a three-drug regimen including a diuretic, does spironolactone, compared with clonidine, achieve better 24-hour blood-pressure control as the fourth drug?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference for clonidine superiority): ReHOT (187 patients with true resistant hypertension — uncontrolled on office and ambulatory measurement despite three drugs including a diuretic for 12 weeks, adherence checked by pill counting; Brazil) found the primary end point (combined office <140/90 and 24-hour ambulatory <130/80 control after 12 weeks as fourth drug) nearly identical: 20.8% on spironolactone versus 20.5% on clonidine (RR 1.01 relative, 95% CI 0.55 to 1.88; P=1.00). Secondary readings were also similar for control (office 33.3% vs 29.3%; ambulatory 44% vs 46.2%), though spironolactone produced greater decreases in 24-hour systolic and diastolic BP (magnitudes not printed in the abstract). The dominant finding is that only about one in five truly resistant patients reached combined control on either drug. One small single-country trial: POSSIBLE. Build note: the topic draft's 'n=159' misreads the record — 1,597 patients were recruited, of whom 187 met the resistant-hypertension criteria and were randomised. Not Tier C: BP-control claim. PATHWAY-2 (spironolactone vs alternatives including placebo) is a different comparison, housed in the main hypertension shelves.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference for clonidine superiority)

title: Icosapent ethyl for cardiovascular risk reduction in statin-treated patients with raised triglycerides (REDUCE-IT)
question: In statin-treated patients with established cardiovascular disease or diabetes plus risk factors and triglycerides 135–499 mg/dL, does icosapent ethyl 4 g daily, compared with placebo, reduce major adverse cardiovascular events?
balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, cardiovascular death/MI/stroke benefit claim): REDUCE-IT (8,179 statin-treated patients, 70.7% secondary prevention, median follow-up 4.9 years) found icosapent ethyl 4 g daily cut the primary composite (cardiovascular death, nonfatal MI, nonfatal stroke, coronary revascularisation, unstable angina) from 22.0% to 17.2% (HR 0.75 relative), the key secondary composite from 14.8% to 11.2% (HR 0.74 relative), and cardiovascular death from 5.2% to 4.3% (HR 0.80 relative), offset by more hospitalisations for atrial fibrillation or flutter (3.1% vs 2.1%) and a small, non-significant excess of serious bleeding (2.7% vs 2.1%). The one discordant note is the comparator trial of a different agent: STRENGTH's mixed EPA/DHA carboxylic acids were null against corn oil (HR 0.99), and REDUCE-IT's placebo was mineral oil, which critics argue may have raised LDL cholesterol and inflammatory markers in the control group and inflated the relative benefit — that controversy is unresolved and sits on the card. One large positive trial of this agent, with no second outcomes trial, carries LIKELY rather than a stronger stamp.

title: Pemafibrate for cardiovascular risk reduction in diabetes with hypertriglyceridaemia (PROMINENT)
question: In patients with type 2 diabetes, triglycerides 200–499 mg/dL, and low HDL on statins, does pemafibrate, compared with placebo, reduce major adverse cardiovascular events?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, cardiovascular events claim): PROMINENT (10,497 patients with type 2 diabetes, hypertriglyceridaemia and low HDL, median follow-up 3.4 years) lowered triglycerides by 26.2% relative to placebo, along with VLDL cholesterol, remnant cholesterol and apolipoprotein C-III — and changed cardiovascular outcomes not at all: 572 primary events on pemafibrate versus 560 on placebo (HR 1.03 relative, 95% CI 0.91 to 1.15), with no subgroup signal. Pemafibrate was associated with more adverse renal events and more venous thromboembolism, and less nonalcoholic fatty liver disease. A single very large, well-powered null on the exact question, with the lipid hypothesis cleanly falsified (the drug did lower triglycerides), carries LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): in the statin era, triglyceride lowering by this mechanism does not buy events. It complements Shelf #528 (fibrates).

title: CETP inhibition with anacetrapib in atherosclerotic vascular disease (REVEAL)
question: In patients with atherosclerotic vascular disease on intensive atorvastatin, does anacetrapib, compared with placebo, reduce major coronary events?
balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, coronary events benefit claim): REVEAL (30,449 patients with atherosclerotic vascular disease on intensive atorvastatin, median follow-up 4.1 years) found anacetrapib 100 mg daily reduced major coronary events from 11.8% to 10.8% (rate ratio 0.91 relative, 95% CI 0.85 to 0.97; P=0.004) — a real but modest 1.0-percentage-point absolute benefit over about four years, with no difference in death or cancer. Anacetrapib raised HDL cholesterol by 43 mg/dL and lowered non-HDL cholesterol by 17 mg/dL at the trial midpoint; the benefit is generally attributed to the non-HDL/LDL lowering, not the HDL rise. The drug was never marketed — it accumulates in adipose tissue — so the shelf is a class-evidence shelf: it shows CETP inhibition can reduce events modestly, against a class history in which torcetrapib harmed and dalcetrapib and evacetrapib were null (named here without figures; those trials are fenced, not carded). One very large positive trial carries LIKELY.

title: Pitavastatin for cardiovascular prevention in people with HIV (REPRIEVE)
question: In people with HIV on antiretroviral therapy at low-to-moderate traditional cardiovascular risk, does pitavastatin, compared with placebo, reduce major adverse cardiovascular events?
balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, cardiovascular events benefit claim): REPRIEVE (7,769 people with HIV on antiretroviral therapy at low-to-moderate traditional risk, median age 50) was stopped early for efficacy after a median follow-up of 5.1 years, with major adverse cardiovascular events at 4.81 versus 7.32 per 1,000 person-years on pitavastatin 4 mg versus placebo (HR 0.65 relative, 95% CI 0.48 to 0.90; P=0.002). The offsets: muscle-related symptoms in 2.3% versus 1.4%, and new diabetes in 5.3% versus 4.0%. Two cautions temper the stamp: trials stopped early tend to overestimate benefit, and the absolute event rates were low (about 2.5 events per 1,000 person-years difference), so the absolute gain in this risk stratum is small even if the relative effect is real. One large trial, stopped early, in a population no other outcomes trial covers: LIKELY.

title: Pravastatin in older adults at risk of vascular disease (PROSPER)
question: In adults aged 70–82 with a history of, or risk factors for, vascular disease, does pravastatin 40 mg, compared with placebo, reduce the composite of coronary death, nonfatal MI, and stroke?
balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, coronary death/MI/stroke claim): PROSPER (5,804 men and women aged 70–82 with vascular disease or risk factors, mean follow-up 3.2 years) found pravastatin 40 mg reduced the primary composite (coronary death, nonfatal MI, fatal or nonfatal stroke) with 408 events versus 473 on placebo (HR 0.85 relative, 95% CI 0.74 to 0.97; P=0.014), driven by coronary events (HR 0.81 relative); coronary mortality fell 24% in relative terms (P=0.043). Stroke was unaffected (HR 1.03 relative). The debated signal: new cancer diagnoses were more frequent on pravastatin (HR 1.25 relative, 95% CI 1.04 to 1.51; P=0.020) — the record itself notes that pooling with all other pravastatin and statin trials showed no overall increase, and no outcomes trial since has reproduced a statin–cancer effect. The abstract prints event counts and hazard ratios rather than percentages, and the card follows the record. LIKELY for coronary prevention in this age band; the stroke and cancer lines are stated as printed.

title: Ezetimibe for primary prevention in adults aged 75 and older (EWTOPIA 75)
question: In adults aged 75 or older with raised LDL and no history of coronary disease, does ezetimibe, compared with dietary counselling alone, prevent atherosclerotic cardiovascular events?
balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, cardiovascular events benefit claim): EWTOPIA 75 (3,796 Japanese patients aged ≥75 with raised LDL and no coronary history, open-label with blinded end-point evaluation, median follow-up 4.1 years) found ezetimibe reduced the primary composite (sudden cardiac death, MI, coronary revascularisation, or stroke) with a hazard ratio of 0.66 relative (95% CI 0.50 to 0.86; P=0.002), and the composite of cardiac events at HR 0.60 relative — note the topic draft assigned the 0.66 figure to the cardiac composite; the record assigns 0.66 to the primary composite and 0.60 to cardiac events, and the card follows the record. There was no difference in stroke, all-cause mortality, or adverse events. The discounts are substantial: open-label treatment, premature termination, and 385 randomised patients (about 10%) excluded from the primary analysis over consent and protocol issues, with high discontinuation — the authors themselves say the magnitude should be interpreted with caution. A single open-label trial with those caveats caps at POSSIBLE. Cross-reference: the staged Shelf #263 carries an EWTOPIA note; this shelf is the trial's home and the pointer should be reconciled at insert.

title: ApoA1 infusion (CSL112) after acute myocardial infarction (AEGIS-II)
question: In patients with acute MI, multivessel coronary disease, and additional risk factors, do four weekly infusions of the apoA1 preparation CSL112, compared with placebo, reduce cardiovascular death, MI, and stroke at 90 days?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, cardiovascular death/MI/stroke claim): AEGIS-II (18,219 patients with acute MI, multivessel disease and additional risk factors) gave four weekly infusions of CSL112 6 g or placebo, first dose within 5 days, and found no significant difference in the primary composite (MI, stroke, or cardiovascular death) at 90 days — 4.8% versus 5.2% (HR 0.93 relative, 95% CI 0.81 to 1.05; P=0.24) — nor at 180 days (HR 0.91 relative) or 365 days (HR 0.93 relative). The confidence interval at 90 days excludes a relative benefit larger than about 19%, and the trial is by far the largest test of the cholesterol-efflux hypothesis: raising efflux capacity pharmacologically after MI does not translate into fewer events. More hypersensitivity events were reported with CSL112; other adverse events were similar. One very large definitive null: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference).

title: Lp-PLA2 inhibition with darapladib in stable coronary disease and after ACS (STABILITY; SOLID-TIMI 52)
question: In patients with stable chronic coronary heart disease on guideline therapy — and, in the companion trial, after an acute coronary syndrome — does the Lp-PLA2 inhibitor darapladib, compared with placebo, reduce cardiovascular death, MI, and stroke?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, cardiovascular death/MI/stroke claim): two large outcomes trials of darapladib 160 mg, in complementary populations, both missed. STABILITY (15,828 patients with stable coronary disease, median follow-up 3.7 years): primary composite (cardiovascular death, MI, stroke) 9.7% versus 10.4% (HR 0.94 relative, 95% CI 0.85 to 1.03; P=0.20), with no difference in any component or in all-cause mortality; secondary coronary composites were nominally lower (major coronary events HR 0.90 relative, P=0.045) — secondary findings under a null primary, carded as such. SOLID-TIMI 52 (13,026 patients within 30 days of an ACS, median follow-up 2.5 years): primary coronary composite HR 1.00 relative (P=0.93), cardiovascular death/MI/stroke identical at 15.0% versus 15.0%, all-cause mortality HR 0.94 relative — null across the board, with more odour-related complaints (11.5% vs 2.5%) and diarrhoea (10.6% vs 5.6%). Two concordant large nulls (a DOUBLE-A pair): LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for Lp-PLA2 inhibition as an event-prevention strategy.

title: Lomitapide (MTP inhibition) in homozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia
question: In patients with homozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia on standard lipid-lowering therapy, does the microsomal triglyceride transfer protein inhibitor lomitapide, compared with baseline on continued standard therapy, lower LDL cholesterol, and at what hepatic cost?
balance: POSSIBLE: the entire clinical evidence for lomitapide in homozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia is one single-arm, open-label phase 3 study of 29 patients, with no comparator group: LDL cholesterol fell 50% in relative terms from baseline (8.7 to 4.3 mmol/L (≈337 to 166 mg/dL)) at 26 weeks and remained 38% lower at 78 weeks, on a median dose of 40 mg/day. The hepatic cost is real: gastrointestinal symptoms were the most common adverse event, and 4 patients had aminotransferase levels above five times the upper limit of normal (resolving with dose reduction or interruption; no one discontinued permanently for liver abnormalities). A within-patient change of this size in a disease this severe is unlikely to be artefact, but with no control group, 29 patients, and a surrogate end point, the record earns no more than MAYBE (weak evidence). Not Tier C: the claim is LDL lowering; there are no outcomes data. Flagged for the developer: this is a two-trial-gate exception candidate — no randomised trial exists or is likely in this ultra-rare disease — as with other rare-disease shelves.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: CETP inhibition with obicetrapib for LDL lowering in high-risk patients (BROADWAY; BROOKLYN)
question: In patients with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia or atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease whose LDL remains raised on maximally tolerated therapy, does obicetrapib, compared with placebo, lower LDL cholesterol?
balance: LIKELY (for LDL lowering only): two concordant phase 3 placebo-controlled trials. BROADWAY (2,530 patients with HeFH or ASCVD on maximally tolerated therapy) found obicetrapib 10 mg lowered LDL cholesterol by 29.9% while placebo rose 2.7% — a between-group difference of −32.6 percentage points at day 84 (P<0.001). BROOKLYN (354 patients with HeFH) found a placebo-adjusted LDL change of −36.3% at day 84, with placebo-adjusted reductions in apolipoprotein B (−24.4%), non-HDL cholesterol (−34.5%) and lipoprotein(a) (−45.9%). Adverse events appeared similar to placebo in BROADWAY and the drug was reported well tolerated in BROOKLYN. Not Tier C, deliberately: this shelf claims LDL lowering only. A pooled cardiovascular-events analysis of the phase 3 programme (2025) exists but is hypothesis-generating and is fenced, not carded; the dedicated cardiovascular-outcomes trial (PREVAIL) is still in flight and is named on the closing card — any events language must wait for it. Contrast Shelf #1562 (REVEAL): anacetrapib showed that a CETP inhibitor can reduce events modestly, which raises — but does not answer — the outcomes question for this agent.

title: Darbepoetin alfa for anaemia in systolic heart failure (RED-HF)
question: In patients with systolic heart failure and mild-to-moderate anaemia, does darbepoetin alfa titrated to haemoglobin 13 g/dL, compared with placebo, reduce the composite of death and hospitalisation for worsening heart failure?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, death claim): RED-HF (2,278 patients with systolic heart failure and haemoglobin 9.0–12.0 g/dL) titrated darbepoetin alfa to a haemoglobin target of 13 g/dL and found the primary composite (death from any cause or hospitalisation for worsening heart failure) in 50.7% on darbepoetin versus 49.5% on placebo (HR 1.01 relative, 95% CI 0.90 to 1.13; P=0.87) — no benefit in any secondary outcome or prespecified subgroup. The topic draft's figures (49.6% vs 50.1%) are not the proportions this record prints (50.7% vs 49.5%); the card follows the record. Harm ran the other way: thromboembolic adverse events in 13.5% versus 10.0% (P=0.01), with fatal or nonfatal stroke numerically higher (3.7% vs 2.7%, P=0.23). Correcting anaemia with an erythropoiesis-stimulating agent in heart failure does not improve outcomes and adds thromboembolic risk: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference), with harm. Distinct from the intravenous-iron shelves — different mechanism, different claim.

title: Patiromer to enable RAAS-inhibitor therapy in HFrEF with hyperkalaemia risk (DIAMOND; PEARL-HF)
question: In patients with HFrEF and current or previous hyperkalaemia on RAAS inhibitors, does patiromer, compared with placebo after a run-in, maintain potassium control and allow continued guideline-directed RAAS-inhibitor dosing?
balance: POSSIBLE: DIAMOND randomised 878 patients with HFrEF and current or previous RAAS-inhibitor-related hyperkalaemia — but only after a patiromer run-in in which 84.6% achieved the specified target RAAS-inhibitor doses, so the randomised population is enriched for people who tolerate the strategy. Over a median 27 weeks, patiromer's adjusted mean potassium change was 0.10 mmol/L lower than placebo's, with fewer hyperkalaemia episodes above 5.5 mmol/L (HR 0.63 relative), fewer MRA dose reductions (HR 0.62 relative), and fewer total hyperkalaemia events (77.7 vs 118.2 per 100 person-years). The predecessor trial PEARL-HF (105 patients, 4 weeks) points the same way: potassium 0.45 mEq/L lower, hyperkalaemia 7.3% versus 24.5%, and more patients titrated to spironolactone 50 mg (91% vs 74%). The claim is enablement — a potassium and dosing outcome, not an events outcome — and no trial shows the strategy improves death or hospitalisation. Run-in enrichment, a surrogate primary end point, and modest effect sizes cap the stamp at POSSIBLE. Not Tier C: no mortality or events claim is made.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Sacubitril–valsartan versus ramipril after acute myocardial infarction (PARADISE-MI)
question: In patients with acute MI complicated by left-ventricular dysfunction, pulmonary congestion, or both, does sacubitril–valsartan, compared with ramipril, reduce cardiovascular death and heart-failure events?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, cardiovascular death and heart-failure events claim): the PARADISE-MI primary report (NEJM 2021; 5,661 patients with MI complicated by reduced ejection fraction, pulmonary congestion, or both; median follow-up 22 months) found the primary outcome — cardiovascular death or incident heart failure — in 11.9% on sacubitril–valsartan versus 13.2% on ramipril (HR 0.90 relative, 95% CI 0.78 to 1.04; P=0.17): not significant, with cardiovascular death (5.9% vs 6.7%; HR 0.87 relative) and all-cause death (7.5% vs 8.5%; HR 0.88 relative) also non-significant — per the developer's rule, the heart-failure figures are printed with mortality beside them. Build note: the topic draft anchored this shelf on the trial's win-ratio analysis because the primary report could not be pinned in the drafting pass; the primary report has now been pinned (PMID 34758252) and leads the shelf. The win-ratio paper is carded second, with its status disclosed: it is a post-hoc analysis (Berwanger et al., European Journal of Heart Failure 2022 — the draft said European Heart Journal and Pfeffer as first author; the record says otherwise), it reaches significance (win ratio 1.17) only when investigator-identified events without committee confirmation are included, and its own committee-confirmed sensitivity analysis is null (win ratio 1.11, 0.96 to 1.30; P=0.16). A post-hoc re-analysis cannot overturn the primary report of the same trial: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for superiority over ramipril post-MI.

title: Eplerenone in left-ventricular dysfunction after myocardial infarction (EPHESUS)
question: In patients with acute MI complicated by left-ventricular systolic dysfunction and heart failure (or diabetes), does adding eplerenone to standard therapy, compared with placebo, reduce all-cause mortality?
balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, mortality benefit claim): EPHESUS (6,632 patients with MI complicated by left-ventricular dysfunction and heart failure, or diabetes; mean follow-up 16 months) found 478 deaths on eplerenone versus 554 on placebo (relative risk 0.85 relative, 95% CI 0.75 to 0.96; P=0.008), with cardiovascular death (RR 0.83 relative), sudden cardiac death (RR 0.79 relative), and the co-primary composite of cardiovascular death or hospitalisation for cardiovascular events (RR 0.87 relative) all reduced — the record prints death counts and relative risks rather than mortality percentages, and the card follows the record (the topic draft's 14.4% vs 16.7% come from the full text's denominators). The cost is potassium: serious hyperkalaemia in 5.5% versus 3.9% (P=0.002), partly offset by less hypokalaemia (8.4% vs 13.1%). One large definitive trial, concordant with the mineralocorticoid-antagonist class in chronic HFrEF (RALES, EMPHASIS-HF, housed in the main HF shelves): LIKELY.

title: Empagliflozin in patients hospitalised with acute heart failure (EMPULSE)
question: In patients hospitalised for acute heart failure, does empagliflozin started once stabilised, compared with placebo, improve the hierarchical composite of death, heart-failure events, and symptoms at 90 days?
balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, the hierarchical composite includes death): EMPULSE (530 patients hospitalised with acute de novo or decompensated chronic heart failure, randomised a median of 3 days after admission once stable, treated for 90 days) met its primary end point: clinical benefit — a hierarchical composite of death from any cause, heart-failure events, and a ≥5-point difference in KCCQ symptom-score change — by a stratified win ratio of 1.36 (95% CI 1.09 to 1.68; P=0.0054), consistent across ejection fraction and diabetes status, with fewer serious adverse events on empagliflozin (32.3% vs 43.6%). The restraint: 530 patients and 90 days, a win ratio whose component numbers (deaths and heart-failure events separately) the abstract does not print — so neither the mortality nor the hospitalisation contribution can be quantified from this record — and a composite in which symptom scores do much of the work. A positive, well-conducted but small and short trial with an opaque composite: POSSIBLE. Distinct from Shelf #70 (SGLT2 inhibitors in chronic established HF) and from Shelf #978 (sotagliflozin in worsening HF).

title: SGLT2 inhibition after acute myocardial infarction at risk of heart failure (EMPACT-MI; DAPA-MI)
question: In patients with acute MI and newly reduced ejection fraction or congestion, plus an additional risk factor, does empagliflozin — and, in the companion trial, dapagliflozin in patients without diabetes or prior heart failure — compared with placebo, reduce first heart-failure hospitalisation or death?
balance: SPLIT — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, death/heart-failure-hospitalisation claims): on the hard outcomes, both post-MI SGLT2 trials are null. EMPACT-MI (6,522 patients at risk of heart failure after acute MI, median follow-up 17.9 months): the primary composite of first heart-failure hospitalisation or all-cause death occurred in 8.2% on empagliflozin versus 9.1% on placebo (HR 0.90 relative, 95% CI 0.76 to 1.06; P=0.21); first heart-failure hospitalisation alone was lower (3.6% vs 4.7%; HR 0.77 relative, 0.60 to 0.98) while death was not (5.2% vs 5.5%; HR 0.96 relative) — the hospitalisation and mortality figures are printed together here, as they must be. DAPA-MI (4,017 post-MI patients without diabetes or prior heart failure): the cardiovascular death/heart-failure-hospitalisation composite occurred in 2.5% versus 2.6% (HR 0.95 relative, 0.64 to 1.40) — null, in a low-event population. The other half of the split: DAPA-MI's primary hierarchical win-ratio outcome was positive (1.34, 1.20 to 1.50), driven by its cardiometabolic components (new diabetes, weight, functional class) — after the analysis method was changed mid-trial because event accrual was low, a change the card discloses. So: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for preventing death or heart-failure hospitalisation after MI; POSSIBLE for a cardiometabolic composite benefit whose event core is null. Neither trial supports starting an SGLT2 inhibitor after MI to prevent heart-failure events on current evidence.

title: Fully magnetically levitated centrifugal LVAD (HeartMate 3) in advanced heart failure (MOMENTUM 3)
question: In patients with advanced heart failure eligible for a durable LVAD, does the fully magnetically levitated centrifugal-flow pump, compared with the axial-flow pump, improve survival free of disabling stroke or reoperation for pump malfunction?
balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, survival and stroke claims): MOMENTUM 3's final report (1,028 patients with advanced heart failure, randomised irrespective of bridge-to-transplant or destination-therapy intent) found the centrifugal-flow HeartMate 3 superior on the primary composite — alive at 2 years free of disabling stroke or reoperation to replace or remove a malfunctioning device — in 76.9% versus 64.8% on the axial-flow HeartMate II (P<0.001 for superiority), driven above all by pump replacement (2.3% vs 11.3%; RR 0.21 relative): the magnetically levitated rotor nearly abolishes pump thrombosis. The 5-year extended-phase follow-up of the same trial (an observational, per-protocol analysis of patients still on support at 2 years — carded as a follow-up report, not a second trial) found the composite at 54.0% versus 29.7% (HR 0.55 relative) and overall survival 58.4% versus 43.7% (HR 0.72 relative; P=0.003). One trial programme, randomised once against the incumbent device: the device comparison carries LIKELY; the 5-year survival figures carry the observational-extension caveat on their card. The topic draft pinned the trial's 2018 interim report (first 366 patients); the final report leads this shelf and the interim report is fenced as superseded.

title: Withdrawal of heart-failure therapy in recovered dilated cardiomyopathy (TRED-HF)
question: In patients with dilated cardiomyopathy whose ejection fraction, volumes, and biomarkers have normalised on therapy, does phased withdrawal of heart-failure treatment, compared with continuation, lead to relapse of cardiomyopathy?
balance: POSSIBLE: TRED-HF (51 patients whose dilated cardiomyopathy had apparently recovered — asymptomatic, ejection fraction improved from below 40% to 50% or more, normalised volumes, NT-pro-BNP below 250 ng/L) randomised patients to phased treatment withdrawal or continuation. Within 6 months, 11 of 25 (44%) in the withdrawal group met the prespecified relapse definition versus none continuing treatment (Kaplan-Meier estimate 45.7%; P=0.0001); when the continuation group then withdrew, 9 more relapsed (36.0%). No deaths occurred; three serious adverse events (non-cardiac admissions) were reported in the withdrawal group. The effect is dramatic and the relapse definition is objective-leaning (imaging, biomarker, or clinical criteria), but this is a single, small, open-label pilot with a 6-month horizon — POSSIBLE, and enough to ground the counselling message: recovered dilated cardiomyopathy is usually remission on treatment, not cure. Not Tier C: the claim is relapse of ventricular dysfunction; no mortality claim is made (there were no deaths).
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Aficamten for symptomatic obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (SEQUOIA-HCM)
question: In patients with symptomatic obstructive HCM on background therapy, does the cardiac myosin inhibitor aficamten, compared with placebo, improve exercise capacity and symptoms over 24 weeks?
balance: POSSIBLE: SEQUOIA-HCM (282 patients with symptomatic obstructive HCM; mean age 59.1 years; 59.2% men; mean resting gradient 55.1 mm Hg) found aficamten improved the primary end point — change in peak oxygen uptake at 24 weeks — by 1.8 versus 0.0 mL/kg/min (least-squares mean difference 1.7, 95% CI 1.0 to 2.4; P<0.001), with all 10 prespecified secondary end points (symptoms by KCCQ, NYHA class, post-Valsalva gradient, septal-reduction-therapy eligibility, workload) also significantly improved, and adverse events similar to placebo. The restraints are the class's usual ones: 24 weeks, 282 patients, and surrogate/functional end points — no outcome data on death, arrhythmia, or progression, and long-term safety is still accruing. One positive pivotal trial on functional end points: POSSIBLE. Not Tier C: an exercise-capacity and symptom claim. The class's first agent, mavacamten (EXPLORER-HCM), is housed on its own shelf under the one-home rule and is not duplicated here.

title: Influenza vaccination to reduce vascular events in heart failure (IVVE)
question: In patients with heart failure in low- and middle-income settings, does annual influenza vaccination, compared with placebo, reduce the composite of cardiovascular death, nonfatal MI, nonfatal stroke, and heart-failure hospitalisation?
balance: SPLIT — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, cardiovascular death/MI/stroke claim): IVVE (5,129 heart-failure patients in ten countries in Asia, the Middle East, and Africa, vaccinated annually for up to 3 years) missed both co-primary outcomes over the full observation period: the first-event composite (cardiovascular death, nonfatal MI, nonfatal stroke) at 14.8% versus 16.0% (HR 0.93 relative, 95% CI 0.81 to 1.07; P=0.30), and the recurrent-events composite including heart-failure hospitalisation (HR 0.92 relative, 0.84 to 1.02; P=0.12); all-cause death, cardiovascular death, MI, stroke, and heart-failure hospitalisation individually did not differ. The other half of the split: pneumonia was clearly reduced (HR 0.58 relative; P=0.0006), all-cause hospitalisation modestly so (HR 0.84 relative; P=0.013), and in the prespecified analysis restricted to periods of peak influenza circulation, the first co-primary outcome and all-cause and cardiovascular death were significantly lower with vaccination. The authors' interpretation — that a clinical benefit is likely — leans on that period-restricted analysis; this shelf presents the full-period null first and the peak-season result as the secondary, prespecified-but-conditional finding it is. Split verdict: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for year-round event prevention; POSSIBLE for benefit concentrated in influenza season. Adjacent and distinct: IAMI (vaccination after MI) is housed with the vaccine shelves (#442–#451 family).

title: Apixaban for treatment and extended treatment of acute venous thromboembolism (AMPLIFY; AMPLIFY-EXT)
question: In patients with acute symptomatic proximal DVT or pulmonary embolism, is oral apixaban (without initial parenteral therapy), compared with enoxaparin followed by warfarin, noninferior for recurrent VTE and superior for major bleeding — and, after 6–12 months of anticoagulation, does extended apixaban beat placebo?
balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C — a deviation from the topic draft's flag, disclosed here: AMPLIFY's primary efficacy outcome is recurrent symptomatic VTE or death related to VTE, a mortality-bearing composite, so by the build gate's Tier C discipline the shelf comes to the developer personally; no mortality claim is made or supported by the record). AMPLIFY (5,395 patients with acute VTE): apixaban alone was noninferior to enoxaparin-then-warfarin for recurrent VTE or VTE-related death (2.3% vs 2.7%; RR 0.84 relative) and clearly safer — major bleeding 0.6% versus 1.8% (RR 0.31 relative) and major plus clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding 4.3% versus 9.7% (RR 0.44 relative). AMPLIFY-EXT (2,486 patients in equipoise after 6–12 months of anticoagulation) then showed both apixaban doses (2.5 mg and 5 mg twice daily) cut recurrence from 8.8% on placebo to 1.7%, without increasing major bleeding (0.2% and 0.1% vs 0.5%), with all-cause death numerically lower (0.8% and 0.5% vs 1.7% — printed here beside the recurrence figures, and not a powered mortality finding). Two large, concordant, double-blind trials (a DOUBLE-A pair): LIKELY.

title: Rivaroxaban versus aspirin for extended secondary prevention after VTE (EINSTEIN CHOICE)
question: In patients who have completed 6–12 months of anticoagulation for VTE and in whom there is equipoise about continuing, does rivaroxaban 20 mg or 10 mg daily, compared with aspirin, prevent recurrent VTE without excess major bleeding?
balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C — a deviation from the topic draft's flag, disclosed here for the same reason as Shelf #1580: the primary outcome is symptomatic recurrent fatal or nonfatal VTE, a mortality-bearing composite; no mortality claim is made or supported). EINSTEIN CHOICE (3,396 patients in equipoise after 6–12 months of anticoagulation, treated for up to 12 months) found recurrent VTE in 1.5% on rivaroxaban 20 mg (HR 0.34 relative) and 1.2% on rivaroxaban 10 mg (HR 0.26 relative) versus 4.4% on aspirin — relative reductions of two-thirds to three-quarters — with major bleeding statistically indistinguishable (0.5%, 0.4%, and 0.3% respectively) and clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding modestly higher on rivaroxaban (2.7%, 2.0%, 1.8%). Aspirin is therefore not an adequate substitute for continued anticoagulation in this population, and the 10 mg dose performed as well as 20 mg. One large trial, consistent with AMPLIFY-EXT across the class (Shelf #1580): LIKELY.

title: Aspirin versus rivaroxaban for extended prophylaxis after hip or knee arthroplasty (EPCAT II)
question: In patients undergoing total hip or knee arthroplasty who have received 5 days of rivaroxaban, is switching to aspirin, compared with continuing rivaroxaban, noninferior for preventing symptomatic VTE and as safe for major bleeding?
balance: LIKELY: EPCAT II (3,424 arthroplasty patients, all given rivaroxaban 10 mg for the first 5 postoperative days, then randomised) found symptomatic VTE in 0.64% after switching to aspirin 81 mg versus 0.70% on continued rivaroxaban (difference 0.06 percentage points; P<0.001 for noninferiority), over an additional 9 days (knee) or 30 days (hip) of prophylaxis with 90-day follow-up. Major bleeding was 0.47% on aspirin versus 0.29% on rivaroxaban (P=0.42), and clinically important bleeding 1.29% versus 0.99% — no significant differences, with point estimates marginally favouring rivaroxaban on safety even as efficacy was identical. One large, well-conducted trial with a clear-cut result: after a 5-day rivaroxaban lead-in, aspirin is an equally effective, cheaper completion strategy. LIKELY. Not Tier C: symptomatic VTE and bleeding claims only.

title: Fondaparinux for superficial-vein thrombosis of the legs (CALISTO)
question: In patients with acute symptomatic superficial-vein thrombosis of the lower limbs at least 5 cm long, does fondaparinux 2.5 mg for 45 days, compared with placebo, reduce the composite of death, symptomatic VTE, and extension or recurrence of superficial thrombosis?
balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C — a deviation from the topic draft's flag, disclosed here: the primary composite leads with death from any cause among its components, so by the build gate's Tier C discipline the shelf comes to the developer personally; deaths were identical at 0.1% in both groups and no mortality claim is made). CALISTO (3,002 patients with acute symptomatic superficial-vein thrombosis at least 5 cm long, without concomitant DVT or PE) found 45 days of fondaparinux 2.5 mg cut the primary composite (death, symptomatic PE or DVT, extension to the saphenofemoral junction, or recurrence) from 5.9% to 0.9% at day 47 — an 85% relative risk reduction as printed in the record — with PE or DVT specifically at 0.2% versus 1.3% (88 patients needed to treat to prevent one), death identical (0.1% both groups), and major bleeding in one patient per group. One large trial with a big effect on a clinically meaningful composite and a clean safety record: LIKELY, with the caveat that most prevented events were extension and recurrence of superficial thrombosis rather than embolism.
