title: Graduated compression stockings to prevent post-thrombotic syndrome (SOX)
question: In patients with a first proximal DVT, do graduated compression stockings worn for two years, compared with placebo (sham) stockings, prevent post-thrombotic syndrome?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): SOX (806 patients with a first symptomatic proximal DVT in Canada and the USA) is the trial that reversed a decades-old practice by finally using a sham control: post-thrombotic syndrome by Ginsberg's criteria occurred in 14.2% with active graduated compression stockings versus 12.7% with placebo stockings worn for 2 years (HR 1.13 relative, 95% CI 0.73 to 1.76; P=0.58) — a point estimate on the harm side of null — and the prespecified per-protocol analysis of frequent wearers was the same. The older positive trials (Brandjes, Prandoni) were small, single-centre and open-label without sham stockings, which is why this blinded trial governs the shelf. One well-designed trial against weak contrary evidence: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for routine stockings to prevent post-thrombotic syndrome. Not Tier C: a symptom-syndrome claim only.

title: Large-bore mechanical thrombectomy versus catheter-directed thrombolysis for intermediate-risk pulmonary embolism (PEERLESS)
question: In patients with intermediate-risk pulmonary embolism, does large-bore mechanical thrombectomy, compared with catheter-directed thrombolysis, improve the hierarchical composite of death, intracranial haemorrhage, major bleeding, clinical deterioration, and ICU use?
balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, the composite includes death and intracranial haemorrhage): PEERLESS (550 patients with intermediate-risk PE, right-ventricular dilatation and additional risk factors) met its primary end point for large-bore mechanical thrombectomy over catheter-directed thrombolysis (win ratio 5.01, 95% CI 3.68 to 6.97; P<0.001) — but the win is carried by the softest components: post-procedural ICU admission (41.6% vs 98.6%) and ICU stay over 24 hours (19.3% vs 64.5%), in a comparison where the thrombolysis pathway conventionally mandates ICU care, plus less clinical deterioration or bailout (1.8% vs 5.4%; P=0.04). On the hard components there was no difference: the secondary win ratio excluding ICU use was 1.34 (0.78 to 2.35; P=0.30), and 30-day mortality was 0.4% versus 0.8% (P=0.62) — mortality is printed here beside the composite, as it must be. Hospital stay was shorter (4.5 vs 5.3 nights) and readmissions fewer (3.2% vs 7.9%). A first-of-kind, open-label device trial whose headline number overstates its hard-outcome content: POSSIBLE for the procedural-strategy claim, with the composition of the win stated plainly. The follow-on trial against anticoagulation alone (PEERLESS II) is in flight and is named on the closing card.

title: Cilostazol for intermittent claudication
question: In patients with intermittent claudication from peripheral artery disease, does cilostazol, compared with placebo, increase maximal walking distance?
balance: POSSIBLE: the pivotal trial (Beebe et al., 1999; 516 patients with moderately severe stable claudication, 24 weeks) found cilostazol 100 mg twice daily produced a 51% geometric-mean improvement in maximal walking distance and 50 mg a 38% improvement (both P<0.001 versus placebo; the record does not print the placebo group's geometric-mean change, so no placebo-adjusted percentage is stated), with maximal distance rising in absolute terms from 129.7 m to 258.8 m on the 100 mg dose, corroborated by pain-free distance, quality-of-life and global assessments. Headache, diarrhoea, dizziness and palpitations were the common adverse effects; withdrawals for adverse events were 14.5% overall, evenly spread; there was no difference in cardiovascular morbidity or all-cause mortality. Two corrections to the topic draft: the anchor's first author is Beebe HG (Dawson DL is second author), and the draft's '~25% over placebo' figure is not what this record prints — the card follows the record. The pentoxifylline-comparator trial in the programme (Dawson 2000) could not be pinned to a verified record at build and is fenced, not carded. Old, smallish trials, a surrogate end point, and an agent contraindicated in heart failure: POSSIBLE for a modest walking-distance benefit. Not Tier C: no events claim (the mortality line is a safety observation, printed as such).
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Renal-artery stenting versus medical therapy for atherosclerotic renal-artery stenosis (CORAL; ASTRAL)
question: In patients with atherosclerotic renal-artery stenosis and hypertension or chronic kidney disease, does renal-artery stenting plus medical therapy, compared with medical therapy alone, reduce cardiovascular and renal events?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, the composite includes cardiovascular/renal death, MI, and stroke): two large trials agree. CORAL (947 patients with renal-artery stenosis and hypertension on two or more drugs or CKD; median follow-up 43 months) found the composite of cardiovascular or renal death, MI, stroke, heart-failure hospitalisation, progressive renal insufficiency, or dialysis in 35.1% with stenting versus 35.8% without (HR 0.94 relative, 95% CI 0.76 to 1.17; P=0.58), no component differences, and no all-cause-mortality difference — only a 2.3 mm Hg systolic advantage. ASTRAL (806 patients, unblinded; median follow-up 34 months) found no worthwhile difference in renal-function trajectory (P=0.06), renal events (HR 0.97 relative), major cardiovascular events (HR 0.94 relative), or death (HR 0.90 relative), while revascularisation itself caused serious complications in 23 patients, including 2 deaths and 3 amputations. Two concordant large nulls (a DOUBLE-A pair) with procedural harm on the record: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for routine stenting in atherosclerotic renal-artery stenosis.

title: Doxycycline to slow growth of small abdominal aortic aneurysms (N-TA3CT)
question: In patients with small (3.5–5.0 cm) infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysms, does doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for two years, compared with placebo, slow aneurysm growth?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): N-TA3CT (261 patients aged 50 or older with small infrarenal aneurysms — 3.5–5.0 cm in men, 3.5–4.5 cm in women; mean age 71.0 years; 14% women) found no effect of doxycycline 100 mg twice daily on aneurysm growth over 2 years: the primary rank-based analysis was null (one-sided P=0.71), and the directly measured change in maximum transverse diameter was identical — 0.36 cm in both groups (difference 0.0 cm, 95% CI −0.07 to 0.07; two-sided P=0.93). One definitive trial with a precisely estimated zero: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference). Not Tier C: an aneurysm-growth claim.

title: Endovascular repair versus no intervention in patients unfit for open AAA repair (EVAR-2)
question: In patients with abdominal aortic aneurysm of at least 5.5 cm who are physically ineligible for open repair, does endovascular aneurysm repair, compared with no intervention, reduce all-cause mortality?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, all-cause mortality claim): EVAR-2 (338 patients aged 60 or older with aneurysms of at least 5.5 cm judged unfit for open repair, at 31 UK hospitals) found no survival benefit from endovascular repair: all-cause mortality did not differ (HR 1.21 relative, 95% CI 0.87 to 1.69; P=0.25 — the point estimate runs against EVAR), aneurysm-related mortality did not differ in this report, overall mortality reached 64% by 4 years, and EVAR carried a 9% 30-day operative mortality in this frail group plus substantially higher costs (£13,632 vs £4,983 per patient over 4 years) with no quality-of-life gain. Crossover was substantial (47 patients assigned no intervention underwent repair; adherence 80%), which biases toward null — one reason the stamp is POSSIBLE rather than LIKELY. The topic draft's 'fewer aneurysm-related deaths later' belongs to the trial's long-term follow-up report, not this record, whose abstract reports no difference in aneurysm-related mortality; it is fenced here. EVAR-1 and OVER address fit patients and are separate questions.

title: Bosentan to prevent new digital ulcers in systemic sclerosis (RAPIDS-1 and RAPIDS-2)
question: In patients with systemic sclerosis and a history of digital ulcers, does bosentan, compared with placebo, reduce the number of new digital ulcers over 16–24 weeks?
balance: POSSIBLE. Two randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials from the same programme point the same way on the same surrogate-style count endpoint: RAPIDS-1 (122 patients, 16 weeks) found 48% fewer new ulcers on bosentan (mean 1.4 vs 2.7; P=0.0083), and RAPIDS-2 (188 patients, 24 weeks) found a 30% reduction (mean 1.9 vs 2.7 new ulcers; P=0.04) — both figures are relative reductions in ulcer counts, and neither trial showed any benefit on healing of existing ulcers, pain, or disability. The effect is consistent but rests on ulcer counts in a single sponsor programme in a restricted population, with the class's known hepatic signal (aminotransferase elevations in RAPIDS-2; transaminases >3× the upper limit of normal in RAPIDS-1) and no patient-centred outcome gain. Two concordant RCTs on a count endpoint with null secondary clinical outcomes: POSSIBLE.

title: Dabigatran versus warfarin for cerebral venous thrombosis (RE-SPECT CVT), with the SECRET rivaroxaban feasibility trial
question: In patients with cerebral venous thrombosis stabilised after initial parenteral anticoagulation, is dabigatran, compared with dose-adjusted warfarin, similarly safe and effective over 24 weeks?
balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C — a deviation from the topic draft's flag, disclosed here: the second carded trial, SECRET, has a primary safety composite that includes mortality at 180 days, so by the build gate's Tier C discipline the shelf comes to the developer personally; no mortality claim is made or supported — the only primary-outcome event in SECRET was a haemorrhage, and RE-SPECT CVT recorded no deaths as an endpoint). RE-SPECT CVT (120 patients, exploratory, open-label with blinded adjudication) found no recurrent VTE in either arm over 24 weeks, one major bleed on dabigatran (intestinal, 1.7%) versus two on warfarin (both intracranial, 3.3%) — reassuring but far too small to establish efficacy, with zero events in both arms. SECRET (55 patients, rivaroxaban vs standard care) was a feasibility trial: its single primary safety event, and all its bleeding and recurrence events, fell in the rivaroxaban arm, at rates the authors describe as low overall. Two small trials, no efficacy events between them, directionally reassuring safety: POSSIBLE.

title: D-dimer-guided duration of anticoagulation after a first unprovoked VTE (PROLONG; DULCIS)
question: In patients who have completed anticoagulation for a first unprovoked VTE, does a D-dimer-guided strategy (stopping if normal, resuming if abnormal), compared with stopping in everyone, reduce recurrent VTE without excess bleeding?
balance: POSSIBLE. PROLONG (2006) randomised only the patients whose D-dimer was abnormal one month after stopping anticoagulation: recurrence was 15.0% in those who stayed off treatment versus 2.9% in those who resumed (adjusted HR 4.26 for stopping); patients with a normal D-dimer, who were not randomised, recurred at 6.2%. The DULCIS management study (2014) then applied serial D-dimer testing in practice: patients who stopped on persistently negative D-dimers recurred at 3.0% per patient-year, versus 0.7% per patient-year in those who resumed and 8.8% per patient-year in the self-selected group who refused to resume, at a cost of major bleeding of 2.3% per patient-year in those who resumed. The randomised core is a single trial of a single assay strategy, and the confirmatory study's key comparison is not randomised: POSSIBLE.

title: Anticoagulation for symptomatic calf deep-vein thrombosis (CACTUS)
question: In low-risk outpatients with a first symptomatic calf (distal) deep-vein thrombosis, does therapeutic-dose nadroparin for six weeks, compared with placebo, reduce proximal extension or pulmonary embolism without excess bleeding?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference). CACTUS is the only randomised trial of anticoagulation for isolated calf DVT, and it was stopped early — at 259 of a planned ~520 patients, because of slow recruitment and expiry of the study drug. The composite of proximal extension, contralateral proximal DVT, and symptomatic pulmonary embolism occurred in 3% on nadroparin versus 5% on placebo (risk difference −2.1%, 95% CI −7.8 to 3.5; P=0.54), while bleeding occurred in 4% versus 0% (risk difference 4.1%, 95% CI 0.4 to 9.2; P=0.0255). A single, underpowered, stopped-early trial whose point estimate mildly favours treatment on efficacy and clearly disfavours it on bleeding: the null on net benefit is POSSIBLE, not proven.

title: Drug-coated balloon for dysfunctional dialysis arteriovenous fistulas (IN.PACT AV; Lutonix AV)
question: In patients with dysfunctional native arteriovenous fistulas for haemodialysis, does a paclitaxel drug-coated balloon, compared with standard balloon angioplasty, improve target-lesion primary patency at six months?
balance: LIKELY. IN.PACT AV (330 patients) showed target-lesion primary patency at 6 months of 82.2% with the drug-coated balloon versus 59.5% with standard angioplasty (difference 22.8 percentage points; P<0.001), with the 30-day access-circuit safety endpoint noninferior. The second randomised trial, Lutonix AV (285 patients), points the same way in its final 2-year report: target-lesion primary patency favoured the coated balloon at 9 months (58% vs 46%; P=0.02) and 12 months (44% vs 36%; P=0.04), attenuating by 18–24 months, with mortality not different between groups. Two concordant RCTs on a patency endpoint: LIKELY for patency — a surrogate; neither trial was designed or powered for mortality, and none is claimed. title: Bypass surgery versus endovascular therapy for chronic limb-threatening ischaemia (BEST-CLI; BASIL-2)
question: In patients with chronic limb-threatening ischaemia suitable for both strategies, does surgical bypass, compared with endovascular therapy, reduce the composite of major adverse limb events and death — and does the answer depend on having a good single-segment saphenous vein?
balance: SPLIT — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: both primary outcomes embed death). The two trials pull in opposite directions in different anatomies. BEST-CLI (1,830 patients): in cohort 1 — patients with an adequate single-segment great saphenous vein — surgery beat endovascular therapy on the composite of major adverse limb events or death (42.6% vs 57.4%; HR 0.68); in cohort 2 (alternative conduit needed) there was no significant difference (42.8% vs 47.7%; HR 0.79). BASIL-2 (345 patients, infrapopliteal disease with or without more proximal work): a vein-bypass-first strategy was worse on amputation-free survival (major amputation or death 63% vs 53%; adjusted HR 1.35), driven mainly by more deaths in the bypass group (53% vs 45%; adjusted HR 1.37). The honest synthesis is anatomical: vein-available, largely infrainguinal disease favours surgery in BEST-CLI; infrapopliteal disease favours endovascular-first in BASIL-2. Neither verdict can be generalised over the other: SPLIT, both sides POSSIBLE.

title: Andexanet alfa for factor Xa inhibitor–associated intracerebral haemorrhage (ANNEXA-I)
question: In patients with intracerebral haemorrhage within 15 hours of taking a factor Xa inhibitor, does andexanet alfa, compared with usual care (predominantly prothrombin complex concentrate), improve haemostatic efficacy without excess thrombotic harm?
balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: thrombotic events including ischaemic stroke are a headline safety outcome, and 30-day death is reported). ANNEXA-I is the only randomised trial of andexanet in intracerebral haemorrhage: haemostatic efficacy was better with andexanet (67.0% vs 53.1%; adjusted difference 13.4 percentage points; P=0.003), but thrombotic events were more frequent (10.3% vs 5.6%; P=0.048), including ischaemic stroke (6.5% vs 1.5%), and there were no appreciable differences in modified Rankin scale scores or death within 30 days. The primary endpoint is itself a composite surrogate (haematoma expansion, NIHSS change, and rescue-therapy use), efficacy was assessed in an interim-analysis population, and the trial's functional outcome was neutral. A real benefit on bleeding control, a real thrombotic cost, no functional gain: POSSIBLE.

title: Sulodexide for secondary prevention of recurrent VTE (SURVET)
question: In patients who have completed oral anticoagulation for a first unprovoked deep-vein thrombosis, does sulodexide, compared with placebo, reduce recurrent venous thromboembolism without increasing bleeding?
balance: POSSIBLE. SURVET is a single double-blind trial of 615 patients: recurrent VTE occurred in 15 of 307 on sulodexide versus 30 of 308 on placebo over 2 years (hazard ratio 0.49 relative; 95% CI 0.27–0.92; P=0.02), with no major bleeding in either arm and two clinically relevant bleeds in each. title: Naftidrofuryl for intermittent claudication (Cochrane individual-patient-data meta-analysis)
question: In patients with intermittent claudication, does naftidrofuryl oxalate, compared with placebo, improve pain-free and maximal walking distance?
balance: POSSIBLE. FORMAT EXCEPTION, flagged for the developer as the topic draft itself requests: this shelf's anchor is a systematic review, not a trial, because no single naftidrofuryl trial is cardable on its own — the randomised programme is a set of old, small, heterogeneously reported trials whose usable evidence exists only as an individual-patient-data (IPD) meta-analysis. title: Early intensive blood-pressure lowering in acute intracerebral haemorrhage (INTERACT2; ATACH-2; INTERACT3)
question: In patients with acute spontaneous intracerebral haemorrhage within six hours, does intensive systolic BP lowering (target <140 mm Hg within one hour), compared with guideline-recommended lowering (<180 mm Hg), reduce death and major disability at 90 days?
balance: SPLIT — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: death and disability are the primary outcomes). The answer depends on how low and in what package. INTERACT2 (2,839 patients, target <140 within 1 hour vs <180) narrowly missed its primary outcome — death or major disability 52.0% vs 55.6% (OR 0.87; P=0.06) — while its prespecified ordinal analysis favoured intensive lowering (OR 0.87 for greater disability; P=0.04), with identical mortality (11.9% vs 12.0%). ATACH-2 (1,000 patients, nicardipine to 110–139 vs 140–179 mm Hg, stopped for futility) was cleanly null on death or disability (38.7% vs 37.7%; RR 1.04) with more renal adverse events on intensive treatment (9.0% vs 4.0%; P=0.002). Gentle early lowering toward <140: POSSIBLE. Pushing to 110–139: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference).

title: Early minimally invasive evacuation of supratentorial intracerebral haemorrhage (ENRICH; MISTIE III)
question: In patients with acute supratentorial intracerebral haemorrhage of 30–80 mL treated within 24 hours, does early minimally invasive trans-sulcal parafascicular evacuation, compared with guideline-based medical management, improve utility-weighted functional outcome at 180 days?
balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: mortality is a headline result). question: In patients aged 60 or younger with malignant MCA infarction treated within 48 hours, does decompressive craniectomy, compared with conservative care, reduce mortality and change the distribution of disability?
balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: this is a mortality claim, the clearest in the stroke library). The pooled individual-patient analysis of DECIMAL, DESTINY, and HAMLET (93 patients aged 18–60, treated within 48 hours, pooled prospectively while the trials were still recruiting) found survival of 78% with decompressive surgery versus 29% with conservative care — mortality 22% versus 71%, an absolute reduction of about 50 points (NNT 2) — with more survivors at modified Rankin ≤4 (75% vs 24%) and ≤3 (43% vs 21%). DESTINY II then extended the question to patients over 60 (112 patients): survival without severe disability was 38% versus 18% (OR 2.91), mortality 33% versus 70% — but no survivor in either group achieved a Rankin score of 0–2, and most survivors needed assistance with most bodily needs. The mortality effect is large, consistent, and replicated across the age boundary; what surgery buys is survival, much of it with substantial disability: LIKELY.

title: Endovascular thrombectomy for acute basilar-artery occlusion (ATTENTION; BAOCHE; BEST; BASICS)
question: In patients with acute basilar-artery occlusion, does endovascular thrombectomy plus best medical care, compared with best medical care alone, improve functional outcome at 90 days?
balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: mortality and stroke outcomes). Four randomised trials in two generations. The first generation was neutral: BEST (131 patients, stopped early for crossover and poor recruitment) found no intention-to-treat difference in Rankin 0–3 at 90 days (42% vs 32%; adjusted OR 1.74, non-significant), and BASICS (300 patients, ~79% receiving intravenous thrombolysis) found 44.2% vs 37.7% (RR 1.18; 95% CI 0.92–1.50). The second generation, both from China, was clearly positive: ATTENTION (340 patients, within 12 hours) found Rankin 0–3 in 46% vs 23% (adjusted rate ratio 2.06) with mortality 37% vs 55%, and BAOCHE (217 patients, 6–24 hours, stopped early for superiority) found 46% vs 24% (adjusted rate ratio 1.81) with mortality 31% vs 42%. Symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage ran higher with thrombectomy throughout (5–6% vs 0–1% in the positive trials). Two large, concordant, positive trials on top of two explicable neutral ones: LIKELY — with the generalisability caveat that both positive trials are single-country (China) with lower background thrombolysis rates than BASICS.

title: MRI-guided intravenous thrombolysis for stroke of unknown onset (WAKE-UP; EXTEND)
question: In patients with ischaemic stroke of unknown time of onset and an MRI diffusion–FLAIR mismatch, does alteplase, compared with placebo, improve functional outcome at 90 days?
balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: death and haemorrhage are reported outcomes). WAKE-UP (503 patients, stopped early when funding ended, at 503 of a planned 800) found a favourable outcome (Rankin 0–1 at 90 days) in 53.3% on alteplase versus 41.8% on placebo (adjusted OR 1.61; P=0.02), with numerically more deaths (4.1% vs 1.2%; OR 3.38; P=0.07) and symptomatic haemorrhage (2.0% vs 0.4%). EXTEND (225 patients, also terminated early) asked an adjacent question — perfusion-imaging selection at 4.5–9 hours or on awakening — and also found more Rankin 0–1 outcomes with alteplase (35.4% vs 29.5%; adjusted RR 1.44; P=0.04) with more symptomatic haemorrhage (6.2% vs 0.9%), though its ordinal analysis was not significant. Two positive but prematurely stopped trials using different imaging selection, with a consistent haemorrhage cost and a worrying, non-significant mortality imbalance in WAKE-UP: POSSIBLE.

title: Intensive blood-pressure lowering after successful thrombectomy (ENCHANTED2/MT; BP-TARGET; BEST-II)
question: In patients with acute ischaemic stroke and successful reperfusion after thrombectomy with sustained hypertension, does intensive systolic lowering (target <120 mm Hg), compared with standard management (140–180 mm Hg), improve functional outcome?
balance: LIKELY (harm) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: functional outcome after stroke, with mortality reported). ENCHANTED2/MT (821 patients, target <120 vs 140–180 mm Hg after successful reperfusion) was stopped early because of persistent efficacy and safety concerns: intensive lowering worsened functional outcome (common OR 1.37 for a poorer Rankin distribution), increased early neurological deterioration (OR 1.53) and major disability (OR 2.07), with no difference in symptomatic haemorrhage or mortality. BP-TARGET (324 patients, target 100–129 vs 130–185) found no reduction in its primary outcome of radiographic intraparenchymal haemorrhage (42% vs 43%; adjusted OR 0.96). BEST-II (120 patients, a phase 2 futility trial of <140 and <160 targets vs ≤180) did not meet its futility boundaries but estimated only a 25% and 14% predicted probability that a future trial of the lower targets would succeed. The largest trial shows harm, the mechanistic trial shows no haemorrhage benefit, and the pilot shows low promise: intensive lowering after successful thrombectomy should be avoided — LIKELY (harm).

title: Intensive versus standard insulin therapy for hyperglycaemia in acute ischaemic stroke (SHINE; GIST-UK)
question: In hyperglycaemic patients with acute ischaemic stroke, does intensive intravenous insulin targeting glucose 80–130 mg/dL, compared with standard subcutaneous insulin targeting 80–179 mg/dL, improve 90-day functional outcome?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: functional outcome after stroke; mortality was GIST-UK's primary endpoint). SHINE (1,151 patients, stopped for futility) achieved clean glucose separation (mean 118 vs 179 mg/dL during treatment) and found no difference in favourable 90-day outcome (20.5% vs 21.6%; adjusted relative risk 0.97; P=0.55), with severe hypoglycaemia occurring only in the intensive group (2.6% vs 0%). GIST-UK (933 patients, stopped early for slow enrolment against a planned 2,355) tested glucose-potassium-insulin infusion against saline and found no reduction in its primary outcome of 90-day death (odds ratio 1.14; 95% CI 0.86–1.51). Two null trials of two different intensive-glucose strategies, one definitive in size and separation: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference).

title: Head positioning in acute stroke (HeadPoST)
question: In patients with acute stroke, does lying flat (0°) for the first 24 hours, compared with sitting up at ≥30°, improve disability outcomes at 90 days?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: disability and mortality outcomes after stroke). HeadPoST is a single but definitive trial: 11,093 patients with acute stroke (85% ischaemic) in a pragmatic cluster-randomised crossover design across nine countries, comparing lying flat with sitting up at ≥30° for the first 24 hours. There was no shift in 90-day disability (unadjusted odds ratio 1.01; 95% CI 0.92 to 1.10; P=0.84), mortality was identical (7.3% vs 7.4%), and there were no differences in serious adverse events including pneumonia. A very large, precise null from one well-executed trial: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — head position in the first day can be chosen for comfort and nursing care, not outcome.

title: Nerinetide for acute ischaemic stroke treated with thrombectomy (ESCAPE-NA1; ESCAPE-NEXT)
question: In patients with large-vessel occlusion stroke undergoing endovascular thrombectomy, does the neuroprotectant nerinetide, compared with placebo, improve functional outcome at 90 days?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: functional outcome after stroke, with mortality a secondary outcome in both trials). ESCAPE-NA1 (1,105 thrombectomy patients) found no overall benefit (Rankin 0–2 at 90 days: 61.4% vs 59.2%; adjusted risk ratio 1.04; P=0.35), with a prespecified interaction suggesting benefit only in patients not receiving alteplase — plausibly because alteplase-generated plasmin cleaves the peptide. The topic draft asked for ESCAPE-NEXT's status to be checked at build: it has now reported (Lancet 2025), and in exactly the population the interaction nominated — thrombectomy without prior thrombolysis, 850 patients — nerinetide again showed no benefit (Rankin 0–2: 45% vs 46%; odds ratio 0.97; P=0.82). A subgroup hypothesis that was tested head-on and failed to confirm is stronger evidence of the null than the original trial alone: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference).

title: Anticoagulation versus aspirin for embolic stroke of undetermined source (NAVIGATE ESUS; RE-SPECT ESUS)
question: In patients with recent embolic stroke of undetermined source, does rivaroxaban 15 mg daily, compared with aspirin, prevent recurrent stroke without excess major bleeding?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: recurrent stroke is the primary outcome). Two large trials tested empirical anticoagulation for ESUS against aspirin, with two different drugs, and both failed. NAVIGATE ESUS (7,213 patients, rivaroxaban 15 mg) was terminated early: recurrent stroke or systemic embolism occurred at 5.1% per year on rivaroxaban versus 4.8% on aspirin (HR 1.07; P=0.52), while major bleeding was higher on rivaroxaban (1.8% vs 0.7% per year; HR 2.72; P<0.001). RE-SPECT ESUS (5,390 patients, dabigatran) completed: recurrent stroke 4.1% versus 4.8% per year (HR 0.85; 95% CI 0.69 to 1.03; P=0.10), with major bleeding not significantly different (1.7% vs 1.4% per year) but more clinically relevant non-major bleeding on dabigatran. Empirical anticoagulation for unselected ESUS is closed by 12,603 randomised patients: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference), with bleeding harm demonstrated for rivaroxaban.

title: Antiplatelet versus anticoagulant therapy for cervical artery dissection (CADISS; TREAT-CAD)
question: In patients with acute extracranial carotid or vertebral artery dissection, does anticoagulation, compared with antiplatelet therapy, prevent ipsilateral stroke or death in the first three months?
balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: the endpoint is stroke or death). Genuine equipoise survives both trials, and the shelf should say so plainly. CADISS final results (250 patients, antiplatelet vs heparin-then-warfarin): recurrent stroke at 1 year was low overall — 6 of 250 (2.4%) on intention-to-treat — with no significant difference between groups for any outcome. (The topic draft's 'ipsilateral stroke ≈2% vs 1%' comes from the earlier 3-month CADISS report; the pinned final-results record does not print per-arm event counts in its abstract, and none are carded.) TREAT-CAD (194 patients, aspirin 300 mg vs vitamin K antagonist) failed to show aspirin non-inferior on its per-protocol composite of clinical and MRI outcomes (23% vs 15%; absolute difference 8%, 95% CI −4 to 21; non-inferiority P=0.55), with all seven ischaemic strokes in the aspirin group and no deaths. One trial says 'no detectable difference at very low event rates'; the other says 'aspirin not proven non-inferior, with a stroke imbalance against it'. Neither licenses certainty: POSSIBLE, unresolved.

title: Early versus delayed DOAC initiation after AF-related ischaemic stroke (ELAN; TIMING; OPTIMAS)
question: In patients with acute ischaemic stroke and atrial fibrillation, does early initiation of a direct oral anticoagulant (within 48 hours for minor/moderate stroke, day 6–7 for major stroke), compared with later guideline-based initiation, reduce recurrent ischaemic events without increasing symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage?
balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: recurrent stroke and intracranial haemorrhage are the primary outcomes). Three randomised trials now triangulate the timing question. ELAN (2,013 patients, severity-stratified early vs later start) estimated the 30-day composite of recurrent ischaemic stroke, systemic embolism, major extracranial bleeding, symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage, or vascular death at 2.9% early versus 4.1% later (risk difference −1.18 points; 95% CI −2.84 to 0.47), with symptomatic haemorrhage at 0.2% in both groups — an estimation design, not a superiority proof. TIMING (888 patients) found early initiation (≤4 days) non-inferior to delayed (5–10 days) on its 90-day composite (6.89% vs 8.68%), with no symptomatic haemorrhage in either arm. OPTIMAS (3,621 patients analysed, the largest) found early initiation (≤4 days) non-inferior to delayed (7–14 days) on its 90-day composite — 3.3% in both groups — with symptomatic haemorrhage at 0.6% versus 0.7%. Early initiation is safe and non-inferior across 6,522 randomised patients, with point estimates consistently favouring earlier treatment: LIKELY.

title: Colchicine for secondary prevention after non-cardioembolic ischaemic stroke or high-risk TIA (CONVINCE)
question: In patients with non-cardioembolic ischaemic stroke or high-risk TIA, does long-term colchicine 0.5 mg daily added to standard care, compared with standard care alone, reduce major adverse cardiovascular events?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: the primary outcome is a cardiovascular-event composite). CONVINCE (3,144 patients in the intention-to-treat analysis) found its primary composite — first fatal or non-fatal recurrent ischaemic stroke, myocardial infarction, cardiac arrest, or hospitalisation for unstable angina — in 9.8% on colchicine versus 11.7% on usual care (hazard ratio 0.84 relative; 95% CI 0.68 to 1.05; P=0.12, against a prespecified significance threshold of 0.048). The trial finished early, before its planned 367 outcomes accrued, because of COVID-era budget constraints. One correction to the topic draft: it places CONVINCE in The Lancet Neurology; the record's journal is The Lancet (vol 404, pp 125–133), and the card follows the record. A single, under-accrued, open-label trial with a point estimate favouring treatment and an interval crossing 1: the ITT null stands at POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — benefit is neither shown nor excluded. The coronary colchicine trials are a different population and are not imported here.

title: Prehospital glyceryl trinitrate in ultra-acute presumed stroke (RIGHT-2)
question: In patients with presumed stroke within four hours, treated by paramedics before hospital arrival, does a transdermal glyceryl trinitrate patch, compared with sham, improve functional outcome at 90 days?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: functional outcome and death after stroke). RIGHT-2 (1,149 patients randomised by paramedics at a median of 71 minutes from onset) found no difference in 90-day modified Rankin scores in patients with confirmed stroke or TIA (adjusted common odds ratio 1.25 for a poorer outcome; 95% CI 0.97 to 1.60; P=0.083) or in the full intention-to-treat cohort (OR 1.04; P=0.69), despite lowering systolic pressure by 5.8 mm Hg. The point estimate in the confirmed-stroke cohort leans toward harm, not benefit. One disclosure: the topic draft reports a harm signal in the intracerebral-haemorrhage subgroup (worse outcomes, more early deaths); the record's abstract does not print subgroup results, so no subgroup figures are carded and the claim is neither confirmed nor denied here. A single large, well-conducted, sham-controlled trial with a null-to-harm-leaning result: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for prehospital GTN as tested.

title: Remote ischaemic conditioning for acute ischaemic stroke (RICAMIS; RESIST)
question: In patients with acute moderate ischaemic stroke ineligible for reperfusion therapy, does twice-daily remote ischaemic conditioning for 10–14 days, compared with usual care alone, improve excellent functional outcome at 90 days?
balance: SPLIT — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: functional outcome after stroke). Two large trials of the same intervention family disagree. RICAMIS (1,893 patients with acute moderate ischaemic stroke in China, open-label with blinded endpoint assessment) found excellent outcome (Rankin 0–1 at 90 days) in 67.4% with twice-daily bilateral arm conditioning for 10–14 days versus 62.0% with usual care (risk difference 5.4%; odds ratio 1.27; P=0.02). RESIST (1,500 patients in Denmark, sham-controlled, conditioning started prehospital) found no improvement in 90-day Rankin distribution in its target stroke population (odds ratio 0.95; 95% CI 0.75 to 1.20; P=0.67) — with the sham group's median Rankin score (1) numerically better than the conditioning group's (2). The designs differ (in-hospital confirmed moderate stroke, open-label, versus prehospital all-comers including haemorrhage, TIA, and mimics, sham-controlled), which may explain the divergence without resolving it. One correction to the topic draft: it describes RICAMIS's population as 'ineligible for reperfusion therapy'; the RICAMIS record's abstract describes acute moderate ischaemic stroke randomised within 48 hours and does not state reperfusion ineligibility, so the card follows the record. Genuine two-trial tension: SPLIT.

title: Bypass surgery for haemorrhagic moyamoya disease (Japan Adult Moyamoya Trial)
question: In adults with haemorrhagic moyamoya disease, does extracranial–intracranial bypass surgery plus medical care, compared with medical care alone, reduce rebleeding, death, and disability?
balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: the composite includes death and disability; also flagged here as a TWO-TRIAL-GATE EXCEPTION CANDIDATE — this is the only randomised trial in moyamoya disease, and none other exists to pair with it). The Japan Adult Moyamoya Trial (80 patients, 5 years of follow-up) found its primary composite of all adverse events in 6 of 42 surgical patients (14.3%) versus 13 of 38 non-surgical patients (34.2%) (annual rates 3.2% vs 8.2%/year; P=0.048 by Kaplan–Meier analysis), and rebleeding in 5 (11.9%) versus 12 (31.6%) (2.7% vs 7.6%/year; P=0.042) — while the Cox hazard ratios' confidence intervals both cross 1 (0.391 [0.148–1.029] for the composite; 0.355 [0.125–1.009] for rebleeding), and the authors themselves call the difference 'statistically marginal'. A correction to the topic draft: its '5-year rebleed risk roughly 12% vs 42%' is not what the record prints — the record gives crude proportions of 11.9% vs 31.6% and the annual rates above; the card follows the record. One small single-country trial in a rare disease, with a real but fragile signal: POSSIBLE.

title: Stenting versus medical therapy for symptomatic vertebral artery stenosis (VIST; VAST)
question: In patients with recently symptomatic vertebral artery stenosis of at least 50%, does vertebral artery stenting plus best medical therapy, compared with best medical therapy alone, prevent subsequent stroke?
balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: the primary outcome is fatal or non-fatal stroke). Both trials stopped short of answering the question. VIST (179 patients analysed, reported as a full Health Technology Assessment monograph rather than a journal paper) found its primary endpoint — fatal or non-fatal stroke in any territory — in 5 patients in the stent group versus 12 in the medical group (hazard ratio 0.40; 95% CI 0.14 to 1.13; P=0.08), was underpowered after failing its recruitment target, and could stent only 61 of the 91 patients assigned to stenting because stenosis was not confirmed in many; extracranial stenting caused no perioperative complications, while two strokes occurred during intracranial stenting. VAST (115 patients, phase 2, stopped early for regulatory and funding reasons) found a 30-day composite of vascular death, myocardial infarction, or stroke in 5% with stenting versus 2% with medical treatment, and territory stroke over a median 3 years in 12% versus 7%. A favourable point estimate from an underpowered trial against a periprocedural-harm signal from a small one: the question is unresolved — POSSIBLE.

title: Clazosentan to prevent vasospasm-related morbidity after aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage (CONSCIOUS programme)
question: In patients with aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage secured by clipping or coiling, does the endothelin-receptor antagonist clazosentan, compared with placebo, reduce vasospasm-related morbidity and mortality?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: the phase 3 primary composites include all-cause mortality). This shelf is the library's cleanest surrogate-versus-outcome arc. CONSCIOUS-1 (413 patients, phase 2 dose-finding) did exactly what the pharmacology promised: moderate or severe angiographic vasospasm fell dose-dependently from 66% on placebo to 23% at clazosentan 15 mg/h (65% relative reduction; P<0.0001), with no significant effect on its morbidity/mortality endpoints. The phase 3 trials then failed to convert the surrogate: CONSCIOUS-2 (clipping; 1,157 randomised) found the primary composite in 21% on clazosentan 5 mg/h versus 25% on placebo (relative risk reduction 17%; 95% CI −4 to 33; P=0.10), with poor functional outcome numerically worse on clazosentan (29% vs 25%) and mortality 6% in both groups. CONSCIOUS-3 (coiling) was halted after CONSCIOUS-2 at 577 of 1,500 planned patients: its 15 mg/h arm did significantly reduce the primary composite (15% vs 27%; OR 0.47; P=0.007) — a correction to the topic draft's blanket statement that both phase 3 trials 'failed their composites' — but neither dose improved functional outcome (poor outcome 24% placebo, 25% at 5 mg/h, 28% at 15 mg/h), and mortality was 6%, 4%, and 6%. A drug that abolishes the angiographic lesion without improving how patients do, across two phase 3 trials: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for clinical benefit. The later Japanese REACT programme is fenced in the synthesis, not carded.

title: Ultra-early tranexamic acid after aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage (ULTRA)
question: In patients with CT-confirmed aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage, does ultra-early short-course tranexamic acid started in the emergency department, compared with standard care, improve functional outcome at six months?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: functional outcome after subarachnoid haemorrhage). ULTRA (955 patients) tested the strongest version of the antifibrinolytic idea: tranexamic acid started immediately on CT diagnosis — 1 g bolus then 1 g every 8 hours until aneurysm treatment or 24 hours. Good clinical outcome (modified Rankin 0–3) at 6 months occurred in 60% on tranexamic acid versus 64% on usual care (adjusted odds ratio 0.86; 95% CI 0.66 to 1.12), and rebleeding before aneurysm treatment, though numerically lower (10% vs 14%; odds ratio 0.71; 95% CI 0.48 to 1.04), was not significantly reduced either. A single large, well-conducted trial whose point estimates lean against the intervention on outcome: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for ultra-early tranexamic acid as tested.

title: Off-pump versus on-pump coronary artery bypass grafting (CORONARY, ROOBY, GOPCABE)
question: In patients undergoing CABG, does off-pump surgery, compared with on-pump surgery, reduce the composite of death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke, and renal failure requiring dialysis?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: the composite includes death, myocardial infarction, and stroke). Three large randomised trials, in three different populations, found no reduction in the death/MI/stroke/dialysis composite with off-pump CABG. CORONARY (4,752 patients): 9.8% versus 10.3% at 30 days (HR 0.95; P=0.59) and 23.1% versus 23.6% at five years. ROOBY (2,203 US veterans): no 30-day difference, a worse 1-year composite off-pump (9.9% vs 7.4%; P=0.04) and lower graft patency (82.6% vs 87.8%). GOPCABE (2,539 patients aged 75 or older): 7.8% versus 8.2% at 30 days and 13.1% versus 14.0% at 12 months. Off-pump surgery buys fewer transfusions, less acute kidney injury, and fewer respiratory complications, at the price of more early repeat revascularisation; it does not buy fewer deaths, infarctions, or strokes: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference).

title: Radial artery versus saphenous vein and right internal thoracic artery as the second bypass conduit (RAPCO)
question: In patients undergoing CABG, does using the radial artery as the second conduit, compared with saphenous vein (older patients) or the right internal thoracic artery (younger patients), improve long-term patency and clinical outcomes?
balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: long-term mortality is reported on the shelf). The RAPCO programme (one centre, two randomised comparisons, 619 patients) found better 10-year graft patency for the radial artery than for the free right internal thoracic artery (89% vs 80%; hazard ratio for graft failure 0.45 relative) and than for saphenous vein (85% vs 71%; HR 0.40 relative, with a confidence interval touching 1.00). Ten-year survival estimates favoured the radial artery over the right internal thoracic artery (90.9% vs 83.7%; HR for mortality 0.53 relative) but not significantly over saphenous vein (72.6% vs 65.2%; HR 0.76, CI 0.47 to 1.22) — and mortality was a nonpowered coprimary end point in a single-centre programme, so those survival figures are hypothesis-generating, not a mortality claim. The drafting note for this shelf said clinical event rates did not differ significantly; the record prints a nominally significant survival difference against the right internal thoracic artery, and the card follows the record. title: Perioperative corticosteroids for cardiac surgery (DECS dexamethasone; SIRS methylprednisolone)
question: In adults undergoing cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass, does a prophylactic high-dose corticosteroid (dexamethasone 1 mg/kg in DECS; methylprednisolone in SIRS), compared with placebo, reduce the composite of death, myocardial infarction, stroke, renal or respiratory failure, and infection within 30 days?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: the composites include death, myocardial infarction, and stroke). Two large double-blind trials, testing two different steroids, both failed. DECS (4,494 patients, single 1 mg/kg dexamethasone dose): primary composite 7.0% versus 8.5% (relative risk 0.83; 95% CI 0.67 to 1.01; P=0.07). SIRS (7,507 high-risk patients, methylprednisolone 250 mg twice): 30-day mortality 4% versus 5% (RR 0.87; P=0.19) and death-or-major-morbidity 24% versus 24% (RR 1.03; P=0.52). title: Perioperative levosimendan in cardiac surgery with low ejection fraction (LEVO-CTS, LICORN, CHEETAH)
question: In patients with reduced ejection fraction undergoing cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass, or who need haemodynamic support after cardiac surgery, does levosimendan, compared with placebo, reduce death and major postoperative complications?

title: Posterior left pericardiotomy to prevent atrial fibrillation after cardiac surgery (PALACS)
question: In patients undergoing elective cardiac surgery, does posterior left pericardiotomy (draining the pericardium into the left pleural space), compared with no pericardiotomy, reduce postoperative atrial fibrillation?
balance: POSSIBLE — a single-centre, single-trial result awaiting multicentre confirmation. In PALACS (420 patients undergoing elective coronary, aortic-valve, or ascending-aorta surgery at one centre), postoperative atrial fibrillation occurred in 17% (37 of 212) with posterior left pericardiotomy versus 32% (66 of 208) without (adjusted odds ratio 0.44 relative; 95% CI 0.27 to 0.70; P=0.0005), and pericardial effusion was also less frequent (12% vs 21%; relative risk 0.58). No intervention-related complications were seen, and 30-day deaths were 2 versus 1. The effect is large and mechanistically direct, but one centre's surgeons and one trial are all the evidence there is: POSSIBLE. Note for the developer: the drafting figures for this shelf (11.9% vs 25.9%, OR 0.40) do not match the trial record; the record's figures (17% vs 32%, adjusted OR 0.44) are what is carded.

title: Mitral-valve repair versus replacement for severe ischaemic mitral regurgitation (CTSN)
question: In patients with severe ischaemic mitral regurgitation, does mitral-valve repair, compared with chordal-sparing replacement, improve left-ventricular reverse remodelling, survival, and valve durability?
balance: SPLIT — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: mortality is reported throughout). LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for remodelling and survival: in the CTSN trial (251 patients), left-ventricular end-systolic volume index at 12 months and at 2 years did not differ between repair and replacement, and neither did mortality (14.3% vs 17.6% at 1 year, HR 0.79, P=0.45; 19.0% vs 23.2% at 2 years, HR 0.79, P=0.39). LIKELY for the durability advantage of replacement: recurrent moderate or severe regurgitation was far more common after repair — 32.6% versus 2.3% at 1 year and 58.8% versus 3.8% over 2 years (both P<0.001) — and by 2 years the repair group had more heart-failure-related serious adverse events and cardiovascular readmissions. Repair and replacement remodel the ventricle and keep patients alive at the same rate; replacement corrects the valve far more durably. The smaller RIME trial asked a different question (repair plus CABG versus CABG alone) and is fenced, not carded.

title: Concomitant tricuspid annuloplasty at mitral surgery for degenerative regurgitation (CTSN)
question: In patients undergoing mitral-valve surgery for degenerative regurgitation who have moderate tricuspid regurgitation or annular dilatation, does concomitant tricuspid annuloplasty, compared with mitral surgery alone, reduce progression of tricuspid regurgitation and reoperation at two years, and at what cost in permanent pacemakers?
balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: the primary composite includes death). One definitive trial (CTSN, 401 patients): the two-year composite of death, tricuspid reoperation, or tricuspid-regurgitation progression was lower with concomitant annuloplasty (3.9% vs 10.2%; relative risk 0.37 relative), driven almost entirely by less progression to severe regurgitation (0.6% vs 6.1%). The price was permanent pacemaker implantation: 14.1% versus 2.5% (rate ratio 5.75 relative) — roughly one extra pacemaker for every nine concomitant repairs. Whether preventing an echocardiographic progression endpoint converts into long-term clinical benefit is unproven; the trial's own authors say only longer follow-up can tell. A real benefit on a surrogate-heavy composite, bought with a real harm: POSSIBLE.

title: Early surgery versus conventional treatment for infective endocarditis with large vegetations (EASE)
question: In patients with left-sided infective endocarditis, severe valve dysfunction, and vegetations larger than 10 mm, does early valve surgery (within 48 hours), compared with conventional treatment, reduce the composite of in-hospital death and embolic events?
balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: the composite includes death). One small trial (EASE, 76 patients at one Korean centre, all at low predicted surgical risk): the primary composite of in-hospital death and embolic events within 6 weeks occurred in 1 patient (3%) with early surgery versus 9 (23%) with conventional treatment (hazard ratio 0.10 relative; 95% CI 0.01 to 0.82; P=0.03), driven almost entirely by embolism — there were no embolic events after early surgery. Six-month all-cause mortality did not differ significantly (3% vs 5%; HR 0.51, CI 0.05 to 5.66) — no mortality claim is made or supported. Two structural caveats cap the stamp: 77% of the conventional group underwent surgery anyway during the same admission, so the trial tests timing more than surgery itself; and the population was young and low-risk, unlike the older, comorbid endocarditis population in most Western series. A strong embolism signal in a narrow population: POSSIBLE.

title: Partial oral versus intravenous antibiotic therapy for left-sided endocarditis (POET)
question: In stabilised patients with left-sided infective endocarditis who have completed at least 10 days of intravenous therapy, is switching to oral antibiotics noninferior to continuing intravenous therapy for the composite of mortality, unplanned surgery, embolism, and relapse?

title: Early valve intervention for asymptomatic severe aortic stenosis (EARLY TAVR; EVOLVED)
question: In patients with asymptomatic severe aortic stenosis, does early transcatheter aortic-valve replacement (EARLY TAVR), or fibrosis-guided early valve intervention (EVOLVED), compared with clinical surveillance or guideline-directed management, reduce the composite of death, stroke, and unplanned cardiovascular hospitalisation?
balance: SPLIT — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: both composites include death; EARLY TAVR's includes stroke). EARLY TAVR (901 patients, transfemoral TAVR versus surveillance): the composite of death, stroke, or unplanned cardiovascular hospitalisation occurred in 26.8% versus 45.3% (hazard ratio 0.50 relative; P<0.001) over a median 3.8 years — but the components show what drove it: death 8.4% versus 9.2% and stroke 4.2% versus 6.7% did not differ significantly, while unplanned hospitalisation did (20.9% vs 41.7%); 87.0% of the surveillance group crossed over to valve replacement during follow-up, so the trial compares early with eventually — POSSIBLE for the composite, with no death or stroke claim made or supported. EVOLVED (224 patients selected for myocardial fibrosis, early surgical or transcatheter intervention versus guideline-directed care): the primary composite of all-cause death or unplanned aortic-stenosis hospitalisation was neutral (18% vs 23%; HR 0.79; 95% CI 0.44 to 1.43; P=0.44), in a trial that enrolled 224 of a planned 356 patients; deaths were 14% versus 13%. The divergence is real and is stated, not averaged away: an unselected echocardiographic population with a hospitalisation endpoint benefited; a smaller fibrosis-selected trial did not show it.

title: Baloxavir post-exposure prophylaxis in household contacts of influenza patients (BLOCKSTONE)
question: In household contacts of patients with influenza, does a single dose of baloxavir prevent clinical influenza confirmed by RT-PCR testing, compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE — one pivotal trial. title: Posaconazole prophylaxis against invasive fungal infection in neutropenia and graft-versus-host disease
question: In patients with prolonged neutropenia from chemotherapy, or with graft-versus-host disease on immunosuppression, does posaconazole prophylaxis prevent invasive fungal infection, compared with fluconazole or itraconazole?
balance: LIKELY — two randomised trials in two high-risk populations agree on the outcome that matters most, invasive aspergillosis. In neutropenic patients (Cornely 2007, 602 patients), proven or probable invasive fungal infections occurred in 2% on posaconazole versus 8% on fluconazole or itraconazole (P<0.001), invasive aspergillosis in 1% versus 7% (P<0.001), and overall survival was significantly longer on posaconazole (P=0.04), with more treatment-related serious adverse events (6% vs 2%). In severe graft-versus-host disease (Ullmann 2007, 600 patients), posaconazole was superior for invasive aspergillosis (2.3% vs 7.0%; P=0.006) and fungal-infection deaths were fewer (1% vs 4%; P=0.046), although the primary all-fungal-infection end point was not significant (5.3% vs 9.0%; P=0.07) and overall mortality was similar — both facts are printed on the card, not smoothed over. The primary outcome in both trials is infection, not a mortality or cardiovascular event, so this shelf is not Tier C; survival figures are printed beside the infection figures wherever the records give them.

title: Empiric micafungin in ICU patients at risk of invasive candidiasis (EMPIRICUS)
question: In non-neutropenic ICU patients with ICU-acquired sepsis, multiple Candida colonisation, and multiorgan failure, does empiric micafungin improve survival free of invasive fungal infection at day 28, compared with placebo?

title: Inhaled amikacin to prevent ventilator-associated pneumonia (AMIKINHAL)

title: Valganciclovir 200 versus 100 days for CMV prophylaxis in high-risk kidney transplant (IMPACT)

title: Gepotidacin for uncomplicated urogenital gonorrhoea (EAGLE-1)
question: In adolescents and adults with uncomplicated urogenital gonorrhoea, is oral gepotidacin non-inferior to ceftriaxone plus azithromycin for microbiological cure?
balance: POSSIBLE — one pivotal trial, a noninferiority design. In EAGLE-1 (628 randomised; 406 in the microbiological intention-to-treat population), microbiological success at test-of-cure (days 4–8) was 92.6% on gepotidacin (two 3000 mg oral doses 10–12 hours apart) versus 91.2% on intramuscular ceftriaxone plus oral azithromycin (adjusted difference −0.1%; 95% CI −5.6 to 5.5), inside the prespecified −10% noninferiority margin. No bacterial persistence was observed in either group. Gepotidacin caused more adverse events, mainly gastrointestinal, almost all mild or moderate, with no treatment-related severe or serious events in either group. The primary population was restricted to participants with ceftriaxone-susceptible isolates at baseline — so the trial shows gepotidacin matches standard therapy where standard therapy works; it does not test the ceftriaxone-resistant scenario that motivates new gonorrhoea drugs. title: Dalbavancin step-down for complicated Staphylococcus aureus bacteraemia (DOTS)
question: In patients with complicated Staphylococcus aureus bacteraemia who have cleared blood cultures, is a two-dose dalbavancin course non-inferior to standard intravenous therapy on a desirability-of-outcome ranking at day 70?

title: Rifampin combination therapy for staphylococcal prosthetic-device infection (Zimmerli)
question: In staphylococcal infections of stable orthopaedic implants managed with debridement and implant retention, does ciprofloxacin plus rifampin cure more infections than ciprofloxacin alone?
balance: POSSIBLE — a single small pre-registration-era trial, flagged for the developer as a two-trial-gate exception candidate: it remains, decades later, the only randomised trial of rifampin combination therapy for staphylococcal implant infection, and no second trial exists to satisfy the gate. In the Zimmerli trial (33 randomised patients with culture-proven staphylococcal infection of stable orthopaedic implants and short symptom duration), among the 24 patients who completed the trial, cure at a median of roughly 3 years was 12 of 12 (100%) with ciprofloxacin–rifampin versus 7 of 12 (58%) with ciprofloxacin–placebo (P=0.02). Nine of 33 patients dropped out (adverse events, noncompliance, protocol violations); 7 of the dropouts were later treated with rifampin combinations and 5 were cured without device removal. title: Three versus six weeks of antibiotics after debridement for diabetic foot osteomyelitis
question: In patients with diabetic foot osteomyelitis treated with surgical debridement, is 3 weeks of antibiotic therapy non-inferior to 6 weeks for remission?
balance: POSSIBLE — one randomised pilot trial, and the pilot status matters. In the Gariani trial (93 patients with diabetic foot osteomyelitis after surgical debridement), remission in the intention-to-treat population was 84% (37 of 44) with 3 weeks of antibiotics versus 73% (36 of 49) with 6 weeks (P=0.21), and per-protocol results were similar (33 of 39 vs 32 of 43); adverse events were similar (17 of 44 vs 16 of 49). The authors declared noninferiority against a 25% margin — a wide margin that a 93-patient pilot cannot narrow. Note for the developer: the drafting note describes this anchor as a full trial backed by 'a supportive randomised pilot'; the record shows the anchor itself is the pilot (its own title says so), and the companion pilot from the same programme (Pham 2022) asked a different question — 10 versus 20 days for soft-tissue diabetic foot infection without osteomyelitis — so it is fenced in the synthesis, not carded as support. Direction reassuring, precision low: POSSIBLE.

title: Upfront ambrisentan plus tadalafil in pulmonary arterial hypertension (AMBITION)
question: In treatment-naive pulmonary arterial hypertension, does initial combination therapy with ambrisentan plus tadalafil reduce clinical-failure events, compared with initial monotherapy with either agent?

title: Dupilumab for COPD with type 2 inflammation (BOREAS and NOTUS)
question: In COPD with type 2 inflammation (blood eosinophils at least 300 per microlitre) on standard inhaled therapy, does dupilumab reduce annualised moderate or severe exacerbations, compared with placebo?
balance: LIKELY — two phase 3 trials replicate the result. In BOREAS (939 patients on triple therapy), the annualised rate of moderate or severe exacerbations was 0.78 on dupilumab versus 1.10 on placebo (rate ratio 0.70 relative; 95% CI 0.58 to 0.86; P<0.001), with an 83 ml greater FEV1 improvement at week 12, sustained to week 52. NOTUS (935 patients) confirmed it: 0.86 versus 1.30 exacerbations per year (rate ratio 0.66 relative; 95% CI 0.54 to 0.82; P<0.001). The claim is bounded by the trials' borders: eosinophils at least 300 per microlitre, elevated exacerbation risk, background inhaled therapy. The primary outcome is exacerbation rate — not a mortality, infarction, or stroke claim — so this shelf is not Tier C, and no mortality claim is made. (Benralizumab in COPD is a separate question, homed on Shelf #1037.)

title: Ensifentrine, dual PDE3/4 inhibitor, for COPD maintenance (ENHANCE-1 and ENHANCE-2)
question: In symptomatic moderate-to-severe COPD, does nebulised ensifentrine improve lung function (FEV1 area under the curve over 12 hours) and symptoms, compared with placebo, over 24 weeks?
balance: POSSIBLE — twin phase 3 trials, surrogate-led. The single programme report covers ENHANCE-1 (760 patients) and ENHANCE-2 (789): ensifentrine improved the primary lung-function end point in both (average FEV1 AUC over 12 hours: +87 ml [95% CI 55 to 119] and +94 ml [65 to 124] versus placebo; both P<0.001). Symptoms and quality of life improved significantly in ENHANCE-1 but NOT in ENHANCE-2 — a divergence printed on the card, not averaged away. Moderate or severe exacerbation rates over 24 weeks were lower (rate ratios 0.64 [P=0.050] and 0.57 [P=0.009]) as secondary end points. Most patients were on a background LAMA or LABA. title: Withdrawing inhaled corticosteroids in severe COPD on triple therapy (WISDOM)
question: In patients with severe COPD on triple therapy, does stepwise withdrawal of the inhaled glucocorticoid increase exacerbations, compared with continued triple therapy?
balance: POSSIBLE — one pivotal trial, a noninferiority result with a measurable lung-function cost. In WISDOM (2,485 patients with severe COPD and an exacerbation history, all run in on tiotropium plus salmeterol plus fluticasone), stepwise glucocorticoid withdrawal over 12 weeks met the prespecified noninferiority criterion for time to first moderate or severe exacerbation (hazard ratio 1.06 relative; 95% CI 0.94 to 1.19; prespecified criterion: upper limit under 1.20). The cost was trough FEV1: a 38 ml greater reduction from baseline at week 18 and 43 ml at week 52 in the withdrawal group (both significant), with no change in dyspnoea and minor health-status changes. So: withdrawal did not significantly increase exacerbations in this population, and it did give back some lung function. The population boundary matters — SUNSET later studied de-escalation in non-frequent exacerbators and is fenced in the synthesis as a different question. POSSIBLE, on one trial.

title: Indacaterol–glycopyrronium versus salmeterol–fluticasone in COPD (FLAME)
question: In patients with COPD and a history of exacerbations, does once-daily LAMA/LABA (indacaterol–glycopyrronium) prevent exacerbations better than LABA/ICS (salmeterol–fluticasone)?
balance: POSSIBLE — one pivotal head-to-head trial. In FLAME (3,362 patients with COPD and at least one exacerbation in the previous year, 52 weeks), indacaterol–glycopyrronium was superior to salmeterol–fluticasone on the primary outcome, the annual rate of all exacerbations (3.59 vs 4.03; rate ratio 0.89 relative; 95% CI 0.83 to 0.96; P=0.003), and on moderate or severe exacerbations (0.98 vs 1.19; rate ratio 0.83 relative; P<0.001); time to first exacerbation was longer (hazard ratio 0.84 relative). Pneumonia was less frequent on the steroid-free regimen (3.2% vs 4.8%; P=0.02). The abstract states that adverse events and deaths were similar in the two groups without printing death rates, so no mortality claim is made or supported. The comparison is regimen against regimen — it does not isolate what dropping the steroid alone does (that is WISDOM's question, Shelf #1643). One large trial: POSSIBLE.

title: Home non-invasive ventilation after hypercapnic COPD exacerbation (HOT-HMV)
question: In patients with persistent hypercapnia after an acute COPD exacerbation requiring non-invasive ventilation, does home mechanical ventilation plus oxygen prolong admission-free survival, compared with home oxygen alone?
balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: the primary composite is time to readmission or death). One small, heavily screened trial (HOT-HMV, 116 randomised of 2,021 screened patients with persistent hypercapnia, PaCO2 over 53 mm Hg, 2–4 weeks after an exacerbation): median time to readmission or death was 4.3 months with home ventilation plus oxygen versus 1.4 months with oxygen alone (adjusted hazard ratio 0.49 relative; 95% CI 0.31 to 0.77; P=0.002), and the 12-month readmission-or-death risk was 63.4% versus 80.4% (absolute reduction 17.0%). The composite was driven by readmission: deaths at 12 months were 16 versus 19 — no mortality claim is made or supported, and the balance says so explicitly. The eligible population is a narrow slice of post-exacerbation patients (obesity over BMI 35, obstructive sleep apnoea, and other respiratory-failure causes were excluded), and only 64 patients completed 12 months. A strong time-to-event signal in a small selected trial: POSSIBLE. (Non-invasive ventilation during the acute exacerbation itself is homed on Shelf #306; this shelf is the home-ventilation question.)

title: Endobronchial valves for severe emphysema (LIBERATE; EMPROVE)
question: In severe emphysema with heterogeneous disease and little or no collateral ventilation, do endobronchial valves improve FEV1 responder rates, compared with standard care, at one year — and at what pneumothorax cost?
balance: LIKELY — two randomised programmes, two different valve systems, the same direction. LIBERATE (Zephyr valve, 190 patients): at 12 months, 47.7% of valve patients versus 16.8% of controls achieved at least a 15% FEV1 improvement (P<0.001), with between-group differences of +0.106 L in FEV1, +39.31 m in 6-minute walk distance, and −7.05 points in St. George's Respiratory Questionnaire score; the price was pneumothorax in 26.6% of valve patients in the treatment period, and four deaths occurred in the valve group during that phase (plus one in each group later) — printed here beside the benefit, as the record gives them. EMPROVE (Spiration valve) corroborates: its 24-month follow-up report (147 patients) found the FEV1 and quality-of-life advantages maintained with significantly less dyspnoea, though that record's abstract states significance without printing FEV1 effect sizes, and none are supplied here. Benefit is real, mechanical, and bought with a one-in-four early pneumothorax rate in the pivotal Zephyr trial: LIKELY, in carefully selected patients with absent collateral ventilation. No mortality claim is made or supported.

title: Higher versus lower PEEP in ARDS (ALVEOLI, LOVS, EXPRESS)
question: In moderate-to-severe ARDS, does a higher-PEEP ventilation strategy reduce mortality, compared with a lower-PEEP strategy?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: mortality is the primary outcome of all three trials). Three randomised trials tested higher-PEEP strategies against lower-PEEP strategies on a background of low-tidal-volume ventilation, and none reduced mortality. ALVEOLI (549 patients): death before discharge 27.5% with higher PEEP versus 24.9% with lower PEEP (P=0.48). LOVS (983 patients; higher PEEP plus recruitment manoeuvres): hospital mortality 36.4% versus 40.4% (relative risk 0.90 relative; P=0.19). EXPRESS (767 patients; PEEP set to a plateau-pressure target): 28-day mortality 27.8% versus 31.2% (P=0.31), with more ventilator-free and organ-failure-free days in the higher-PEEP group. Higher PEEP reliably improves oxygenation; across 2,299 patients it did not reliably keep anyone alive: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for an across-the-board higher-PEEP strategy. (Whether an individualised, recruitability-guided approach differs is a separate question, not tested by these three.)

title: High-frequency oscillatory ventilation in early severe ARDS (OSCILLATE and OSCAR)
question: In adults with early moderate-to-severe ARDS, does high-frequency oscillatory ventilation reduce mortality, compared with conventional lung-protective ventilation?
balance: SPLIT — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: mortality is the primary outcome of both trials). The two 2013 trials diverge and the split is the honest summary. OSCILLATE (548 patients randomised of 1,200 planned; stopped early on the data monitoring committee's recommendation): in-hospital mortality was 47% on HFOV versus 35% on a control strategy of low tidal volumes with high PEEP (relative risk of death 1.33 relative; 95% CI 1.09 to 1.64; P=0.005), with more sedation, more neuromuscular blockade, and more vasoactive-drug exposure on HFOV — LIKELY (harm) for that aggressive recruitment-oriented HFOV protocol. OSCAR (795 patients): 30-day mortality was 41.7% versus 41.1% (P=0.85) — LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for HFOV as practised in UK centres against usual care. Together they closed routine early HFOV in adult ARDS: no benefit anywhere, harm in the trial that pushed pressures hardest. Note for the developer: the drafting note pins PMID 23339638 as 'OSCILLATE (Ferguson)' — that record is in fact OSCAR (Young); OSCILLATE is PMID 23339639. Both trials are carded under their correct identities.

title: Tiotropium in early-stage COPD (Tie-COPD)
question: In patients with mild-to-moderate (GOLD 1–2) COPD, does daily tiotropium improve FEV1 and slow its decline, compared with placebo, over two years?
balance: POSSIBLE — one pivotal trial, single-country (China). In Tie-COPD (841 patients with GOLD stage 1 or 2 COPD), tiotropium kept FEV1 higher than placebo throughout 2 years (mean differences of 127 to 169 ml before bronchodilator use, 71 to 133 ml after; all P<0.001). The decline story is split, and the card prints both halves: the annual decline in FEV1 BEFORE bronchodilator use was not significantly slowed (38 vs 53 ml per year; difference 15 ml per year; 95% CI −1 to 31; P=0.06), while the decline AFTER bronchodilator use was significantly less (29 vs 51 ml per year; difference 22 ml per year; P=0.006). The authors' conclusion — that tiotropium 'ameliorated the annual decline' — leans on the post-bronchodilator measure and is flagged on the card as an overstatement of the primary-frame result. The drafting note also says tiotropium 'reduced exacerbations'; the record's abstract prints no exacerbation rates, so none are carded. A real level effect on lung function, an unproven effect on pre-bronchodilator decline, one country: POSSIBLE.

title: Tralokinumab monotherapy for moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis (ECZTRA 1 and 2)
question: In adults with moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis, does the IL-13 antibody tralokinumab achieve clear/almost-clear skin (IGA 0/1) versus placebo at 16 weeks?
balance: LIKELY. Two identically designed phase 3 trials, one direction on both co-primary endpoints. At week 16, an IGA score of 0 or 1 was achieved by 15.8% versus 7.1% in ECZTRA 1 (difference 8.6 percentage points) and 22.2% versus 10.9% in ECZTRA 2 (difference 11.1 points); EASI-75 responses were 25.0% versus 12.7% and 33.2% versus 11.4%. The absolute gains are modest — most patients on tralokinumab did not reach clear or almost-clear skin — but they are consistent across two independent trials, and most week-16 responders who continued tralokinumab maintained their response to week 52 without rescue medication. Adverse-event rates over the first 16 weeks were similar to placebo. Two concordant randomised trials meeting both primary endpoints: LIKELY.

title: Anti-IL-5 therapy for eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (MIRRA and MANDARA)
question: In relapsing or refractory EGPA, does anti-IL-5 therapy induce remission and spare glucocorticoids versus placebo (mepolizumab) or versus mepolizumab (benralizumab)?
balance: LIKELY. MIRRA showed mepolizumab clearly superior to placebo on both co-primary endpoints — accrued remission of at least 24 weeks in 28% versus 3%, and remission at both weeks 36 and 48 in 32% versus 3% — with the annualised relapse rate halved (rate ratio 0.50 relative) and 44% versus 7% of patients tapered to 4 mg/day or less of prednisolone. MANDARA then showed benralizumab non-inferior to mepolizumab head-to-head (remission at weeks 36 and 48 in 59% versus 56%), with more patients withdrawing oral glucocorticoids completely (41% versus 26%). Two randomised trials, concordant: anti-IL-5 therapy induces remission and spares steroids in EGPA. The honest limit, printed on the MIRRA card: even on mepolizumab, only about half of patients achieved protocol-defined remission.

title: Hydrolysed infant formula and later allergic disease (GINI)
question: In infants at high hereditary risk of atopy who are not exclusively breastfed, does feeding a hydrolysed formula instead of conventional cow's-milk formula reduce the incidence of allergic disease through childhood?
balance: POSSIBLE. One large randomised programme (GINI, 2,252 infants) with three hydrolysed formulas tested against cow's-milk formula: by age 6, the incidence of any allergic manifestation was lower with partially hydrolysed whey (relative risk 0.82) and extensively hydrolysed casein (relative risk 0.80) but not significantly with extensively hydrolysed whey (0.90; 95% CI 0.78 to 1.04); for atopic eczema the figures were 0.79, 0.92 (not significant), and 0.71. title: Perinatal probiotics to prevent atopic eczema (Kalliomäki; Wickens)
question: In families with atopic disease, does giving Lactobacillus GG to mothers prenatally and to infants postnatally prevent atopic eczema in the first two years of life?

title: Fish-oil supplementation in pregnancy and offspring allergic disease (Palmer / DOMInO)
question: In pregnant women whose offspring are at high risk of allergy, does n-3 long-chain polyunsaturated fatty-acid supplementation reduce infant allergic disease (eczema, food allergy) in the first year?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference). title: Myotomy strategies for achalasia: pneumatic dilation versus Heller, and POEM (European Achalasia Trial; Werner; Ponds)
question: In treatment-naive achalasia, how do pneumatic dilation and laparoscopic Heller myotomy compare on treatment success at two years — and does peroral endoscopic myotomy (POEM) beat pneumatic dilation?
balance: SPLIT. LIKELY that pneumatic dilation and laparoscopic Heller myotomy are equivalent at 2 years: the European Achalasia Trial found therapeutic success in 86% versus 90% (P=0.46), with different harms (perforation 4% with dilation; mucosal tears 12% with myotomy). LIKELY that POEM is non-inferior to Heller myotomy (Werner: success 83.0% versus 81.7%, meeting the non-inferiority margin) and superior to pneumatic dilation (Ponds: success 92% versus 54% at 2 years, and 81% versus 40% at 5 years) — at a consistent price: reflux oesophagitis in 41–57% after POEM versus 7–20% after the alternatives in the early assessments. title: Vonoprazan for erosive oesophagitis (Laine; Ashida)
question: In adults with erosive oesophagitis, is the potassium-competitive acid blocker vonoprazan non-inferior to lansoprazole for healing at eight weeks and for maintenance of healing?
balance: LIKELY. Two independent phase 3 programmes agree. In the US/European trial (Laine), healing by week 8 was 92.9% on vonoprazan versus 84.6% on lansoprazole — non-inferior in the primary analysis and higher on the exploratory analysis, with superiority concentrated in severe (LA grade C/D) disease — and maintenance of healing at 24 weeks was also non-inferior and higher on the secondary analysis (differences 8.7 and 7.2 points for the 20 mg and 10 mg doses). title: Telephone and web cognitive-behavioural therapy for refractory IBS (ACTIB)

title: Endoscopic versus surgical drainage for painful chronic pancreatitis (Cahen; ESCAPE)
question: In patients with painful chronic pancreatitis and an obstructed, dilated pancreatic duct, does surgical drainage relieve pain more durably than endoscopic drainage?
balance: POSSIBLE. Two small, necessarily unblinded Dutch trials point the same way on pain scores. Cahen (39 patients): surgical drainage produced lower Izbicki pain scores over 24 months (25 versus 51; P<0.001) and more complete or partial pain relief at the end of follow-up (75% versus 32%; P=0.007), with a median of 3 procedures versus 8. ESCAPE (88 patients) compared timing strategies — early surgery versus an endoscopy-first step-up: the integrated 18-month Izbicki score was lower with early surgery (37 versus 49; P=0.02), though end-of-follow-up pain relief was not significantly different (58% versus 39%; P=0.10) and mortality was 0% in both groups. Subjective endpoints, no blinding, and small samples cap this at POSSIBLE; the two trials also ask related but distinct questions (modality in Cahen; timing/strategy in ESCAPE), and the cards keep them distinct.

title: Ursodeoxycholic acid to prevent gallstones after bariatric surgery (UPGRADE)
question: In patients undergoing bariatric surgery, does six months of ursodeoxycholic acid reduce symptomatic gallstone disease versus placebo?

title: ZED1227, a transglutaminase-2 inhibitor, for coeliac disease
question: In adults with coeliac disease on a gluten-free diet, does oral ZED1227 prevent gluten-challenge-induced duodenal mucosal injury versus placebo?
