title: Tenofovir in pregnancy to prevent mother-to-child hepatitis B transmission (Pan; Jourdain)
question: In pregnant women with chronic hepatitis B and high viral load (HBV DNA >200,000 IU/mL), does tenofovir disoproxil from weeks 30–32 of gestation reduce mother-to-child transmission versus no antiviral therapy?
balance: SPLIT — the two trials differ in context, and the cards do not average them. Pan (China; HBeAg-positive mothers, HBV DNA >200,000 IU/mL; tenofovir versus usual care without antiviral therapy): mother-to-child transmission at postpartum week 28 was 5% versus 18% by intention to treat (P=0.007) and 0% versus 7% per protocol. Jourdain (Thailand; double-blind, placebo-controlled; infants received hepatitis B immune globulin and vaccine within a median of about 1.2–1.3 hours of birth): transmission was 0% (0 of 147) versus 2% (3 of 147) — not significant (P=0.12) — because transmission with vigorous immunoprophylaxis alone was already low. Both findings stand: tenofovir clearly reduces transmission where background transmission is high; its added value where immunoprophylaxis is prompt and complete is unproven on these numbers.

title: Obeticholic acid for primary biliary cholangitis (POISE)

title: Norfloxacin primary prophylaxis in advanced cirrhosis (Fernández; NORFLOCIR)
question: In patients with advanced cirrhosis (Child-Pugh ≥9) and low ascitic protein, does long-term norfloxacin prevent spontaneous bacterial peritonitis and improve survival versus placebo?

title: Simvastatin after variceal bleeding in cirrhosis (BLEPS)
question: In patients surviving a variceal bleed on standard secondary prophylaxis, does adding simvastatin reduce rebleeding or death versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: mortality is a headline outcome). One trial (BLEPS): the primary endpoint — the composite of rebleeding and death — was NOT reduced (22 of 69 on simvastatin versus 30 of 78 on placebo; P=0.423), and rebleeding alone was unchanged (25% versus 28%; P=0.583). Death, a secondary endpoint, was lower: 6 of 69 (9%) versus 17 of 78 (22%) (hazard ratio 0.39 relative; 95% CI 0.15 to 0.99; P=0.030), with no survival benefit in Child-Pugh class C. The trial's own authors state that survival was not the primary endpoint and the result requires validation — the card adopts their caution verbatim in substance. A survival signal on a secondary endpoint of a single trial whose primary was null: POSSIBLE, Tier C.

title: Lanifibranor, a pan-PPAR agonist, in MASH (NATIVE)
question: In patients with active, non-cirrhotic MASH, does the pan-PPAR agonist lanifibranor reduce the SAF activity score without worsening fibrosis versus placebo at 24 weeks?
balance: POSSIBLE — a single phase 2b trial on histological surrogate endpoints, flagged on its face as a two-trial-gate exception candidate for the developer. In NATIVE (247 patients), the primary endpoint — a decrease of at least 2 points in the SAF activity score without worsening of fibrosis at 24 weeks — was met at the 1200 mg dose (55% versus 33% on placebo; P=0.007) but not at 800 mg (48% versus 33%; P=0.07). Secondary histology favoured both doses: MASH resolution without fibrosis worsening in 49% and 39% versus 22%, and fibrosis improvement of at least one stage without MASH worsening in 48% and 34% versus 29%. Diarrhoea, nausea, peripheral oedema, anaemia, and weight gain were more frequent on lanifibranor. Histology at 24 weeks is not a clinical outcome; the topic file notes a phase 3 trial in progress, whose results are not carded here. This shelf is lanifibranor; resmetirom, semaglutide and tirzepatide in MASH are Shelf #323.

title: Fexinidazole for late-stage gambiense sleeping sickness (Mesu)
question: In patients aged 15 and older with late-stage Trypanosoma brucei gambiense infection, is oral fexinidazole non-inferior to nifurtimox–eflornithine combination therapy for treatment success at 18 months?
balance: PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C). Tier C deviation, disclosed: the topic file flags this shelf not Tier C, but the trial's primary success endpoint is a composite whose first component is being alive at 18 months, so it is ruled Tier C at build under the gate rule; no mortality claim is made or supported — deaths were 3% on fexinidazole versus 2% on NECT and the trial was not powered for mortality. On the record: in the single pivotal randomised non-inferiority trial (394 patients, DRC and Central African Republic), success at 18 months was 91% (239 of 264) on fexinidazole versus 98% (124 of 130) on NECT — a difference of −6.4% (97.06% CI −11.2 to −1.6), inside the prespecified 13% margin, so non-inferiority was met on the trial's own terms while the point estimate favours NECT. Treatment-related adverse events were similar (81% versus 79%). This shelf rests on one pivotal trial and is flagged as a two-trial-gate exception candidate: it should be withdrawn or re-scoped if the developer rejects the exception. PROPOSED stamp: POSSIBLE.

title: Single-dose acoziborole for gambiense sleeping sickness (Betu Kumeso)
question: In adults and adolescents with gambiense human African trypanosomiasis, what treatment success does a single oral dose of acoziborole achieve at 18 months, judged against historical standard-of-care rates (no concurrent control)?
balance: In the single pivotal study — a multicentre, open-label, SINGLE-ARM phase 2/3 trial with no concurrent control group — a single 960 mg dose of acoziborole gave an 18-month treatment success rate of 95.2% (159 of 167) in late-stage gambiense disease (98.1%, 159 of 162, in the evaluable population), and all 41 early/intermediate-stage patients completed follow-up; a post-hoc comparison put this beside a historical NECT success estimate of 94%. Four deaths occurred, none judged treatment-related; drug-related adverse events occurred in 14% and were mild or moderate. A single-arm study cannot separate the drug's effect from case mix and secular change, so the record earns no more than MAYBE (weak evidence). This shelf is flagged as a two-trial-gate exception candidate — indeed a no-randomised-trial candidate, the field being ethically constrained — and should be withdrawn or re-scoped if the developer rejects the exception.

title: Wolbachia mosquito deployments to control dengue: the AWED trial (Yogyakarta)
question: In a dengue-endemic city, does releasing wMel Wolbachia-infected Aedes aegypti mosquitoes reduce the incidence of virologically confirmed dengue in residents versus no deployment?
balance: In the single cluster-randomised trial (24 geographic clusters in Yogyakarta, Indonesia; 8,144 febrile patients assessed by a test-negative design), virologically confirmed dengue occurred in 2.3% of participants in intervention clusters versus 9.4% in control clusters — a protective efficacy of 77.1% (95% CI 65.3–84.9), similar across all four serotypes — and hospitalisation for dengue was reduced by a protective efficacy of 86.2% (0.4% versus 3.0%). The effect is large, precise, and measured on clinical disease rather than a surrogate. The bounds are scope, not signal: one city, one Wolbachia strain (wMel), and one trial — this shelf is adjacent to but distinct from the dengue vaccine shelves (#448, #981), which ask about immunisation, not vector deployment. PROPOSED stamp: LIKELY.

title: Ebola virus disease therapeutics: the PALM trial (REGN-EB3 and mAb114)
question: In patients with Ebola virus disease, do the monoclonal antibody therapies REGN-EB3 or mAb114 reduce 28-day mortality compared with ZMapp or remdesivir?
balance: PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C) — mortality is the primary endpoint. In the single randomised trial conducted during the 2018–20 Democratic Republic of the Congo outbreak (681 patients), 28-day mortality was 33.5% with REGN-EB3 versus 51.3% in the contemporaneous ZMapp subgroup (P=0.002) and 35.1% with mAb114 versus 49.7% with ZMapp (P=0.007); the data and safety monitoring board stopped assignment to ZMapp and remdesivir early on the strength of an interim analysis. The abstract does not print a mortality figure for the remdesivir arm, so none is carded — comparisons against remdesivir rest on the trial's interim decision, not on a printed number here. Two independent monoclonal products beating the same control in one trial is mutually reinforcing, but it remains one trial from one outbreak. PROPOSED stamp: LIKELY.

title: Fully oral rifampicin–clarithromycin for limited Buruli ulcer (Phillips)
question: In limited Buruli ulcer (single lesion ≤10 cm), is eight weeks of oral rifampicin plus extended-release clarithromycin non-inferior to rifampicin plus intramuscular streptomycin for lesion healing without recurrence at 52 weeks?
balance: In the single pivotal phase 3 trial (310 recruited in Ghana and Benin; 297 with PCR-confirmed disease analysed), lesions healed without recurrence in 96% (140 of 146) on the fully oral rifampicin–clarithromycin regimen versus 95% (144 of 151) on rifampicin–streptomycin — a difference of −0.5 percentage points (95% CI −5.2 to 4.2), comfortably inside the 12% non-inferiority margin — with fewer treatment-related adverse events on the oral regimen (7% versus 13%) and the one serious ototoxicity case in the streptomycin arm. Healing rates are near-identical and the interval is narrow; the limits are a single trial, an open-label design, and a population of early, limited lesions only. PROPOSED stamp: POSSIBLE.

title: Melioidosis eradication therapy: TMP-SMX alone versus TMP-SMX plus doxycycline (MERTH)
question: In melioidosis after intensive-phase therapy, is trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole alone non-inferior to TMP-SMX plus doxycycline for preventing culture-confirmed relapse?
balance: In the single pivotal trial (626 patients, northeast Thailand; double-blind), culture-confirmed recurrent melioidosis occurred in 5% (16 of 311) on TMP-SMX plus placebo versus 7% (21 of 315) on TMP-SMX plus doxycycline — hazard ratio 0.81 relative (95% CI 0.42–1.55) — meeting the prespecified non-inferiority criterion (margin HR 1.7; P=0.01 for non-inferiority), with fewer adverse drug reactions on monotherapy (39% versus 53%). The confidence interval is wide in relative terms, but the absolute recurrence rates are low and close, and the simpler regimen is the safer one. Single-country programme evidence. PROPOSED stamp: POSSIBLE.

title: Magnesium sulphate for severe tetanus (Thwaites)
question: In adults with severe tetanus, does a magnesium sulphate infusion reduce the need for mechanical ventilation versus standard spasm control?
balance: SPLIT — the trial answers its primary question in the negative and its secondary questions positively, and the cards do not average them. In the single pivotal trial (Vietnam; double-blind), magnesium did not reduce the requirement for mechanical ventilation (odds ratio 0.71 relative, 95% CI 0.36–1.40; P=0.324), and survival was much the same in the two groups (no figures printed). What magnesium did do was reduce the need for other drugs: less midazolam and pipecuronium to control spasms (P=0.026 and P=0.005) and substantially less verapamil for cardiovascular instability (patients on magnesium were 4.7 times less likely to require it; 95% CI 1.4–15.9). One internal inconsistency is flagged on the card, not repaired: the abstract describes a trial of 256 patients but prints arm sizes of 97 and 98 (195 in total). PROPOSED stamp: SPLIT as above.

title: Single-dose liposomal amphotericin B for visceral leishmaniasis in India (Sundar)
question: In visceral leishmaniasis in Bihar, India, is a single 10 mg/kg infusion of liposomal amphotericin B non-inferior to conventional amphotericin B deoxycholate given on alternate days for 30 days?
balance: Two randomised trials from the same Bihar programme agree. In the anchor trial (412 patients), cure at 6 months was 95.7% after a single 10 mg/kg liposomal amphotericin B infusion versus 96.3% with 15 alternate-day deoxycholate infusions — non-inferior, with less fever/rigor (40% versus 64%) and less anaemia (2% versus 19%). In the second trial (634 patients), three short-course combinations built on the single-dose liposomal platform (with 7 days of miltefosine, with paromomycin, or miltefosine plus paromomycin) were each non-inferior to standard amphotericin B, with cure rates of 97.5–98.7% versus 93.0% and fewer adverse events. The evidence is geographically narrow — Bihar's anthroponotic transmission — and East African disease may behave differently; within its setting it is consistent and precise. PROPOSED stamp: LIKELY.

title: Pyronaridine–artesunate for uncomplicated falciparum malaria (WANECAM and the phase 3 programme)
question: In patients with repeated episodes of uncomplicated falciparum malaria, is pyronaridine–artesunate as effective and safe over two years of repeated use as artemether–lumefantrine or dihydroartemisinin–piperaquine?
balance: Two randomised programmes agree. In WANECAM (4,710 participants in Burkina Faso, Guinea, and Mali, treated and retreated over 2 years), the 2-year malaria incidence rate on pyronaridine–artesunate was non-inferior to artemether–lumefantrine and to artesunate–amodiaquine (rate ratios 1.05 and 0.97 relative), and PCR-adjusted cure exceeded 99.5% at day 28 for all regimens; unadjusted cure favoured pyronaridine–artesunate. In the earlier phase 3 trial (1,271 patients, Asia and Africa), pyronaridine–artesunate was non-inferior to mefloquine plus artesunate (per-protocol day-28 cure 99.2% versus 97.8%). The standing caveat in both records is hepatic: transient transaminase elevations were more frequent with pyronaridine–artesunate, and WANECAM excluded patients with baseline ALT above twice the upper limit of normal. Nine deaths occurred in WANECAM, none treatment-related. PROPOSED stamp: LIKELY.

title: Molecular point-of-care respiratory virus testing in hospital (ResPOC)
question: In adults hospitalised with acute respiratory illness, does routine molecular point-of-care testing for respiratory viruses shorten antibiotic courses and length of stay versus routine clinical care?
balance: SPLIT — the trial's primary outcome was null and its secondary outcomes were positive, and the cards do not average them. In the single pivotal trial (720 patients, one UK hospital, two winter seasons), the proportion of patients who received antibiotics while hospitalised was 84% with point-of-care testing versus 83% with routine care (difference 0.6%, 95% CI −4.9 to 6.0; P=0.84), and mean antibiotic duration did not differ (7.2 versus 7.7 days; P=0.32). What improved: single-dose or brief (<48 h) courses among treated patients (17% versus 9%; P=0.0047; number needed to test 13), mean length of stay (5.7 versus 6.8 days; P=0.0443), and appropriate antiviral treatment of influenza-positive patients (91% versus 65%). A provenance correction is printed on the card: the topic file's anchor PMID is the trial's protocol paper, not its results; the results report is carded instead. PROPOSED stamp: SPLIT as above.

title: Direct oral penicillin challenge in low-risk penicillin allergy (PALACE)
question: In outpatients with a low-risk penicillin allergy label, is direct oral penicillin challenge non-inferior to skin testing followed by oral challenge for delabelling safely?
balance: In the single pivotal randomised trial (377 adults analysed, six specialist centres in North America and Australia, all with PEN-FAST scores below 3), a physician-verified positive immune-mediated reaction within 1 hour of challenge occurred in 0.5% (1 of 187) after direct oral challenge versus 0.5% (1 of 190) after skin testing followed by challenge — a risk difference of 0.0084 percentage points (90% CI −1.22 to 1.24), far inside the 5-percentage-point non-inferiority margin — with no serious adverse events and similar 5-day immune-mediated event counts (9 versus 10). A provenance correction is printed on the card: the topic file's anchor PMID is a secondary summary record, not the trial; the carded record is the trial itself, which the file described as merely the decision-rule paper. The result applies only to decision-rule-defined low-risk labels. PROPOSED stamp: LIKELY.

title: Diagnostic algorithm for suspected UTI in nursing-home residents (Loeb minimum criteria)
question: In nursing-home residents, does implementing minimum criteria for initiating antibiotics for suspected urinary tract infection reduce antimicrobial prescriptions without increasing hospitalisation or death?
balance: In the single cluster-randomised trial (24 nursing homes in Ontario and Idaho; outcomes in 4,217 residents), a multifaceted intervention built around a diagnostic and treatment algorithm reduced antimicrobial courses for suspected urinary tract infection from 1.59 to 1.17 courses per 1,000 resident days (weighted mean difference −0.49, 95% CI −0.93 to −0.06) — about a 26% relative reduction — and cut the share of all antimicrobial courses attributable to suspected UTI from 38.6% to 28.4%. Total antimicrobial use did not differ significantly (3.52 versus 3.93 per 1,000 resident days), and there was no significant difference in hospital admissions or mortality. The benefit is specific to UTI prescribing, delivered by a bundle (algorithm plus education and outreach), in one trial. PROPOSED stamp: POSSIBLE.

title: Prewritten stop orders for urinary catheters (Loeb)
question: In hospitalised patients with urinary catheters, do prewritten stop orders (automatic removal prompts at a set interval) reduce catheter duration and inappropriate catheterisation versus usual care?
balance: In the single randomised trial (692 hospitalised patients in three Ontario tertiary-care hospitals), prewritten stop orders reduced inappropriate catheter days by 1.69 days and total catheter days by 1.34 days versus usual care (both P<0.001), without increasing catheter reinsertion (8.6% versus 7.0%; P=0.45) — but urinary tract infections were essentially unchanged (19.0% versus 20.2%; relative risk 0.94, 95% CI 0.66–1.33; P=0.71). A citation correction is printed on the card: the topic file gives this trial as BMJ 2008; the record's journal is the Journal of General Internal Medicine. The intervention reliably shortens catheterisation; an infection benefit is unproven on this record. PROPOSED stamp: POSSIBLE.

title: The Antibiotic Review Kit for hospitals (ARK-Hospital)
question: In acute medical patients started on intravenous antibiotics, does a hospital-wide antibiotic review kit (a structured review-and-decide tool) reduce total antibiotic use versus usual stewardship?
balance: PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C). Tier C deviation, disclosed: the topic file flags this shelf not Tier C, but 30-day all-cause mortality was a patient-level co-primary outcome (a non-inferiority safety endpoint), so it is ruled Tier C at build under the gate rule; no mortality claim — benefit or harm — is made or supported by this shelf. On the record: in the stepped-wedge cluster trial (39 UK hospital sites followed for at least 14 months; 7,160,421 acute general medical admissions), the review kit reduced total antibiotic defined daily doses per admission by 4.8% per year (95% CI −9.1 to −0.2) on adjusted analysis. title: Faecal microbiota transplantation to eradicate multidrug-resistant organism carriage (Huttner)
question: In patients carrying multidrug-resistant Enterobacterales, does a short oral antibiotic course followed by faecal transplantation eradicate carriage versus no intervention, at the trial's 35–48-day primary assessment?
balance: An endpoint correction first: the topic file frames this shelf around eradication at six months, but the trial's primary outcome in the record is detectable carriage at 35–48 days after randomisation, and the abstract prints no six-month eradication figures — the shelf question follows the record and no six-month numbers are carded. On the record: in the single small randomised trial (39 patients, four European centres), decolonisation at 35–48 days was 41% (9 of 22) after 5 days of oral colistin plus neomycin followed by frozen FMT versus 29% (5 of 17) with no intervention — odds ratio 1.7 relative (95% CI 0.4–6.4), not significant — in a trial the authors note was terminated early and underpowered. Three intervention patients stopped the antibiotics for diarrhoea but received FMT. MAYBE (weak evidence) is all this record earns. This shelf is flagged as a two-trial-gate exception candidate (single small trial): it should be withdrawn or re-scoped if the developer rejects the exception.

title: Bacteriophage cocktail for Pseudomonas burn wounds (PhagoBurn)
question: In burn wounds infected with Pseudomonas aeruginosa, does a cocktail of lytic bacteriophages reduce bacterial burden as effectively as standard sulfadiazine silver cream?
balance: In the single small phase 1/2 trial (27 patients randomised; 25 in the efficacy population), the phage cocktail reduced bacterial burden significantly more slowly than standard care: median time to sustained ≥2-quadrant burden reduction was 144 hours on phages versus 47 hours on sulfadiazine silver cream (hazard ratio 0.29 relative, 95% CI 0.10–0.79; P=0.018), and the trial was stopped for insufficient phage efficacy. The decisive caveat is printed on the record: the manufactured cocktail's titre decayed, and patients actually received about 1×10² PFU/mL per dose instead of the planned 1×10⁶ — so the trial tests a failed dose, not the phage concept at specification. Adverse events were fewer on phages (23% versus 54%); one death occurred in each group after follow-up, neither treatment-related. PROPOSED stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for the question as posed — as delivered, phages were not as effective as standard care. This shelf is flagged as a two-trial-gate exception candidate (single small trial) and should be withdrawn or re-scoped if the developer rejects the exception.

title: Audit and feedback for dental antibiotic prescribing (RAPID)
question: In general dental practice, does individualised audit and feedback reduce antibiotic prescribing rates versus no feedback?
balance: Scope boundary, stated on the shelf face: Shelf #884 covers audit and feedback to change professional practice generally, and Shelf #463 covers antibiotic prophylaxis before dental work; this shelf is the dental-prescribing setting alone, with prescribing rate as the sole target. In the single cluster trial (all 795 antibiotic-prescribing NHS general dental practices in Scotland; outcome data for 761 practices), individualised audit and feedback reduced dentists' antibiotic prescribing rate by 5.7% relative (95% CI −10.2% to −1.1%; P=0.01) versus control over 12 months — from baselines of 8.5 versus 8.3 items per 100 treatment claims, follow-up falls were 1.0 versus 0.4 items. A written behaviour-change message added benefit (−6.1% relative for recipients versus non-recipients); a health-board comparator line and a third feedback round did not significantly add. The trial could not assess appropriateness, only volume. PROPOSED stamp: POSSIBLE.

title: Web-based prescriber training for respiratory infections (GRACE INTRO)
question: In European primary care, does internet-based training in communication skills (with or without point-of-care CRP) reduce antibiotic prescribing for lower respiratory tract infection versus usual care?

title: Oral step-down therapy for low-risk febrile neutropenia (Freifeld; Kern)
question: In low-risk febrile neutropenic patients, is oral ciprofloxacin plus amoxicillin–clavulanate as effective as intravenous therapy for empirical treatment?
balance: Two randomised trials published back-to-back in 1999 agree. In Freifeld (double-blind; 232 episodes), treatment succeeded without modification in 71% of oral-therapy episodes versus 67% of intravenous episodes (difference 3%, 95% CI −8 to 15; P=0.48), with no deaths in either group; oral therapy failed more often through intolerance (16% versus 1%) and intravenous therapy more often through regimen modification (32% versus 13%). In Kern (open-label, multicentre; 353 enrolled, equivalence margin 10%), success was 86% versus 84% in the per-protocol analysis and 80% versus 77% by intention to treat, meeting the trial's equivalence definition. Both trials treated patients in hospital until fever resolved — this is oral-versus-intravenous route evidence in monitored low-risk patients, not evidence for unsupervised outpatient care. Neither record carries a registry ID (1999, pre-registration era). PROPOSED stamp: LIKELY.

title: Triple artemisinin-based combination therapies for resistant malaria (TRACII)
question: In uncomplicated falciparum malaria in the Greater Mekong Subregion and Africa, are triple ACTs (adding mefloquine to dihydroartemisinin–piperaquine, or amodiaquine to artemether–lumefantrine) as effective and safe as standard ACTs where artemisinin resistance is spreading?
balance: SPLIT — the two triple regimens answer differently in different resistance settings, and the cards do not average them. In TRACII (1,100 patients, eight countries), where dihydroartemisinin–piperaquine was failing in Cambodia, Thailand, and Vietnam, adding mefloquine restored 42-day PCR-corrected efficacy to 98% versus 48% on the dual therapy (risk difference 51%, 95% CI 42–59) — LIKELY for that rescue question. Artemether–lumefantrine plus amodiaquine performed similarly to artemether–lumefantrine alone where the dual therapy still works (98% versus 97%), and in the confirmatory Mekong trial (310 patients) the triple regimen's 42-day efficacy was 97% versus 95% (hazard ratio for recrudescence 0.6 relative, 0.2–1.9; P=0.38), including in kelch13-mutant infections (96% versus 90%; P=0.17) — supportive but not decisive: POSSIBLE. A geography correction is printed on the card: the topic file describes the confirmatory trial as African; its record places it in Cambodia and Vietnam. Both triple regimens were generally well tolerated, with more early vomiting (and, in the confirmatory trial, more bradycardia) on the amodiaquine-containing regimen.

title: Four artemisinin-based treatments for malaria in pregnancy (PREGACT)
question: In African women in the second or third trimester with falciparum malaria, how do four artemisinin-based combinations compare with each other on cure and birth outcomes?
balance: In the single pivotal trial (3,428 pregnant women in four African countries; open-label), PCR-adjusted cure rates at day 63 (per protocol) were 94.8% on artemether–lumefantrine, 98.5% on artesunate–amodiaquine, 99.2% on dihydroartemisinin–piperaquine, and 96.8% on mefloquine–artesunate; intention-to-treat rates were 94.2%, 96.9%, 98.0%, and 95.5%. Artemether–lumefantrine's cure rate was significantly lower than the other three, although within the trial's 5-percentage-point equivalence margin, and its post-treatment prophylactic effect was clearly shortest (unadjusted cure 52.5% versus 73.8–86.9%). The record reports no significant difference among groups in serious adverse events or birth outcomes — but prints no birth-outcome figures, so none are carded. Drug-related adverse events were most frequent on mefloquine–artesunate (50.6%) and artesunate–amodiaquine (48.5%) and least on artemether–lumefantrine (11.5%). PROPOSED stamp: POSSIBLE — one large trial, comparative rather than placebo-anchored.

title: Intermittent preventive treatment of malaria in schoolchildren (Clarke)
question: In schoolchildren in an area of high perennial transmission, does intermittent preventive treatment with sulfadoxine–pyrimethamine plus amodiaquine reduce malaria parasitaemia and anaemia and improve classroom attention?
balance: Two corrections from the topic file are carried on the card: the record describes an area of high PERENNIAL transmission (western Kenya), not seasonal; and the file's claim that IPT cut parasitaemia by about 88% does not appear in the trial's abstract — no parasitaemia rates are printed there, so none are carded. On the record: in the single cluster-randomised, double-blind trial (30 primary schools; 6,758 children received allocated treatment), anaemia prevalence at 12 months was 6.3% on IPT versus 12.6% on placebo (adjusted risk ratio 0.52 relative, 95% CI 0.29–0.93; P=0.028), and two of the class-based sustained-attention tests improved significantly (code transmission +6.05 points, P=0.0007; counting sounds +1.80, P=0.03), with no effect on inattentive or hyperactive-compulsive behaviours or on educational achievement. Serious adverse events within 28 days of treatment were more frequent on IPT (19 versus 4), mainly transient balance, dizziness, faintness, nausea, and vomiting shortly after dosing. Scope boundary: distinct from Shelf #968 (seasonal chemoprevention in under-fives) and from pregnancy IPT topics. PROPOSED stamp: POSSIBLE.

title: Single low-dose primaquine to block falciparum transmission (Eziefula; Gonçalves)
question: In children with uncomplicated falciparum malaria treated with an ACT, does adding a single low dose of primaquine clear gametocytes and reduce mosquito infectivity versus ACT alone?
balance: Scope boundary, stated on the shelf face: Shelf #1182 covers radical cure of vivax malaria with tafenoquine and primaquine; this shelf is falciparum gametocyte clearance in children. Two randomised, double-blind trials agree. In Eziefula (468 Ugandan children with normal G6PD function, all on artemether–lumefantrine), mean gametocyte carriage was 12.4 days on placebo versus 6.6 days at the 0.75 mg/kg reference dose and 6.3 days at 0.4 mg/kg (non-inferior to reference), with 0.1 mg/kg inconclusive (8.0 days); no treatment-related haemolysis occurred and haemoglobin falls did not differ by dose. In Gonçalves (360 asymptomatic Burkinabè children), 0.25 and 0.40 mg/kg cleared gametocytes in 7.7 and 8.2 days versus 19.7 days on placebo, and after treatment only one participant — in the placebo group — infected mosquitoes. A topic-file correction is printed on the second card: the file describes that record as an individual-participant pooled analysis; it is a standalone randomised trial, and is carded as one. Both trials measure gametocyte carriage and mosquito infectivity — surrogates for community transmission, which neither measured. PROPOSED stamp: LIKELY for the gametocyte/infectivity endpoints as scoped.

title: Priming after a fractional dose of inactivated poliovirus vaccine (Resik)
question: In infants, does a single fractional (one-fifth) dose of inactivated poliovirus vaccine prime immunological memory as effectively as a full dose, measured by the response to a later full-dose challenge?
balance: SPLIT — the two trials test different schedules and point different ways, and the cards do not average them. In Resik (320 Cuban infants, doses at 4 and 8 months), a single fractional dose primed 89.6–94.0% of infants across the three poliovirus types versus 97.6–98.3% after a full dose — close, though single-dose seroconversion was much lower with the fractional dose (for example type 1: 16.6% versus 46.6%) and cumulative two-dose seroconversion remained a few points lower (93.6–98.1% versus 99.4–100%). In Anand (975 Bangladeshi infants, doses from 6 weeks), intradermal fractional IPV FAILED its non-inferiority tests against full-dose IPV for seroconversion after one or two doses and for priming after one dose. The endpoint throughout is immunogenicity — a surrogate for protection against paralysis, which no trial here measured. The topic file's summary figures (about 95% versus 98%) match neither record exactly; the cards print the records' own type-specific rates. PROPOSED stamp: SPLIT as above.

title: Prednisone for paradoxical tuberculosis-associated IRIS (Meintjes)
question: In HIV-infected patients who develop paradoxical TB-IRIS after starting antiretroviral therapy, does a tapering course of prednisone reduce a composite of hospitalisation, procedures and symptom burden versus placebo?
balance: In the single pivotal trial (110 patients in South Africa; double-blind), prednisone (1.5 mg/kg/day for 2 weeks, then 0.75 mg/kg/day for 2 weeks) reduced the primary composite of hospital days plus outpatient therapeutic procedures: median 0 days (IQR 0–3) on prednisone versus 3 days (IQR 0–9) on placebo (P=0.04). Symptoms, Karnofsky score, and quality of life improved significantly more on prednisone at 2 and 4 weeks but not later, and chest radiographs improved more at weeks 2 and 4. Infections on study medication were more frequent on prednisone (27 versus 17 participants; P=0.05), though severe infections were not (2 versus 4). Patients with immediately life-threatening IRIS were excluded. The related NEJM 2018 trial of prednisone to PREVENT TB-IRIS in high-risk ART starters (Meintjes et al., PMID 30428290) asks a different question and is fenced in the synthesis, not carded. PROPOSED stamp: POSSIBLE.

title: Dexamethasone in tuberculous meningitis (Thwaites)
question: In adolescents and adults with tuberculous meningitis, does adjunctive dexamethasone reduce death versus placebo?
balance: PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C) — death is the outcome at issue. In the single pivotal trial (545 patients over 14 years of age in Vietnam; double-blind), adjunctive dexamethasone was associated with a reduced risk of death: relative risk 0.69 relative (95% CI 0.52–0.92; P=0.01), consistent across disease-severity grades (stratified RR 0.68) and in the HIV-infected subgroup (stratified RR 0.78, 0.59–1.04). The abstract prints no absolute mortality rates, so none are carded — the shelf carries the relative effect and says so. Dexamethasone did NOT significantly reduce severe disability among survivors (18.2% versus 13.8%; P=0.27), and the combined outcome of death or severe disability was not significant (odds ratio 0.81, 0.58–1.13; P=0.22): this is a survival benefit without a demonstrated disability benefit. Serious adverse events were fewer on dexamethasone (26 of 274 versus 45 of 271). Scope boundary: bacterial meningitis dexamethasone is Shelf #236; this shelf is tuberculous meningitis only. PROPOSED stamp: LIKELY.

title: Intensified antituberculosis therapy in tuberculous meningitis (Heemskerk)
question: In adults with tuberculous meningitis, does intensified therapy — higher-dose rifampin (15 mg/kg) plus levofloxacin for the first eight weeks — reduce mortality versus the standard regimen?
balance: PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C) — mortality is the primary outcome, and the result is a null. In the single pivotal trial (817 adults in Vietnam; double-blind; 349 HIV-infected), death by 9 months occurred in 113 of 408 patients on intensified therapy versus 114 of 409 on the standard regimen: hazard ratio 0.94 relative (95% CI 0.73–1.22; P=0.66), with no significant difference in any subgroup (the possible exception of isoniazid-resistant disease is hypothesis-generating only) and no significant differences in secondary outcomes. A correction is printed on the card: the topic file gives the hazard ratio as about 1.1; the record prints 0.94. Adverse events leading to treatment interruption were numerically more frequent on intensified therapy (95 versus 64 events; P=0.08). PROPOSED stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference).

title: Vitamin A in children with severe measles (Hussey; Coutsoudis)
question: In children hospitalised with severe measles, does high-dose vitamin A reduce mortality and pneumonia morbidity versus placebo?
balance: PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C) — mortality in children is at issue. Two South African randomised trials agree in direction. In Hussey (189 hospitalised children with measles complicated by pneumonia, diarrhoea, or croup; median age 10 months), 12 children died — 10 on placebo and 2 on vitamin A (P=0.05) — and the risk of death or a major complication was halved on vitamin A (relative risk 0.51 relative, 95% CI 0.35–0.74); recovery from pneumonia (6.3 versus 12.4 days) and diarrhoea (5.6 versus 8.5 days) was faster, croup less frequent (13 versus 27 cases), and hospital stay shorter (10.6 versus 14.8 days). A precision correction is printed on the card: the topic file's 'cut mortality by more than half' belongs to the death-or-major-complication composite (RR 0.51); the mortality counts themselves are 2 versus 10 — a large relative difference on very few events, at P=0.05. In Coutsoudis (60 hospitalised children), integrated morbidity scores were reduced by 82%, 61%, and 85% at day 8, 6 weeks, and 6 months, mainly through respiratory infection; one death occurred, on placebo. Both trials predate modern measles epidemiology and neither record carries a registry ID. PROPOSED stamp: LIKELY. Scope boundary: distinct from population vitamin A supplementation for prevention (wave-1 topic #1366).

title: Shorter and combination benznidazole regimens for chronic Chagas disease (BENDITA)
question: In adults with chronic indeterminate Chagas disease, do shorter benznidazole courses (two weeks) or benznidazole combined with fosravuconazole achieve sustained parasitological clearance non-inferior to the standard eight-week course, with fewer adverse events?
balance: In the single phase 2 trial (210 adults in Bolivia; double-blind, seven arms including placebo), sustained parasitological clearance at 6 months (the record's primary efficacy endpoint — the topic file's 12-month framing reflects the follow-up period, not the printed primary analysis) was 83–89% across all benznidazole arms versus 3% (1 of 30) on placebo: 89% for the standard 300 mg 8-week course, 89% for 4 weeks, 83% for 2 weeks, 83% for 150 mg for 4 weeks, and 83–85% for the fosravuconazole combinations (all P<0.0001 versus placebo). Adverse events leading to discontinuation (15 patients, 7%) clustered in the 8-week and combination arms; none occurred in the 2-week arm or on placebo. Six patients had serious adverse events (including leukopenia and neutropenia); there were no treatment-related deaths. The endpoint is PCR clearance — a surrogate; no cardiac or clinical outcome was measured. This shelf is flagged as a two-trial-gate exception candidate (single phase 2 trial, surrogate endpoint) and should be withdrawn or re-scoped if the developer rejects the exception. PROPOSED stamp: POSSIBLE.

title: Efruxifermin, an FGF21 analogue, in MASH (HARMONY)
question: In patients with biopsy-confirmed MASH and stage F2–F3 fibrosis, does once-weekly efruxifermin improve fibrosis by at least one stage without worsening MASH versus placebo at 24 weeks?
balance: Scope boundary, stated on the shelf face: Shelf #323 covers resmetirom, semaglutide, and tirzepatide in MASH, and Shelf #1679 covers the pan-PPAR agonist lanifibranor; this shelf is the FGF21 analogue efruxifermin alone. (The carded record uses the era's term NASH for the same condition the question calls MASH.) In the single phase 2b trial (128 patients in the USA), fibrosis improvement of at least one stage without worsening of steatohepatitis at 24 weeks occurred in 39% (15 of 38) on efruxifermin 28 mg and 41% (14 of 34) on 50 mg versus 20% (8 of 41) on placebo in the biopsy analysis set (risk ratios 2.3 and 2.2 relative; P=0.025 and P=0.036); in the full analysis set the 50 mg comparison was not significant (33% versus 19%; P=0.123). Diarrhoea (≈40% versus 19%) and nausea were the commonest drug-related events; no deaths occurred. An author overclaim is flagged on the card: the record's interpretation claims the drug 'resolved NASH', but the printed primary endpoint was fibrosis improvement without worsening — resolution was not the primary measure. PROPOSED stamp: POSSIBLE. title: Obeticholic acid for MASH fibrosis (REGENERATE)
question: In patients with MASH and stage F2–F3 fibrosis, does obeticholic acid 25 mg improve fibrosis by at least one stage without worsening MASH versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE — the claim rests on a single phase 3 trial, carded in two reports of the same patients (counted once). At the planned 18-month interim analysis, fibrosis improvement with no worsening of NASH occurred in 23% on obeticholic acid 25 mg versus 12% on placebo (p=0.0002), while the NASH-resolution co-endpoint was not met (12% versus 8%; p=0.13). A 2023 consensus-panel re-read of the same biopsies confirmed the fibrosis result (22.4% versus 9.6%; p<0.0001) and again missed resolution (6.5% versus 3.5%; p=0.093). Histology is a surrogate: no clinical-outcomes benefit is shown in these records, pruritus affected about half of patients on 25 mg, and the drug was not ultimately approved for this indication. Flagged on its face as a two-trial-gate exception candidate — if the developer rejects the exception, this shelf should be withdrawn or re-scoped. Distinct from Shelf #1671 (obeticholic acid for primary biliary cholangitis, POISE) and adjacent to Shelf #1710 (efruxifermin) and Shelf #323 (other MASH drugs).

title: Stopping nucleos(t)ide therapy in chronic hepatitis B (FINITE; Toronto STOP)
question: In patients with chronic hepatitis B who have long-term viral suppression on nucleos(t)ide analogues, does stopping therapy (with close monitoring and retreatment rules) lead to durable off-treatment response or HBsAg loss versus continuing therapy?
balance: SPLIT — the two randomised stop trials answer in different registers, and the cards do not average them. FINITE (n=42, HBeAg-negative patients suppressed on tenofovir for years) found 62% of stoppers still off therapy at 144 weeks, with 43% achieving HBsAg loss or HBV DNA below 2,000 IU/mL and 19% losing HBsAg outright — POSSIBLE for that tightly selected population. The Toronto STOP study (n=67, broader population and agents) found sustained disease remission in only 29% of stoppers versus 82% of continuers at 72 weeks, HBsAg loss in a single stopper, a third relapsing and 38% retreated, and its authors conclude the benefit of stopping is limited — POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for any general expectation of durable remission. The shelf question was re-scoped from the topic file's tenofovir-only wording to nucleos(t)ide therapy generally, because the second trial tests the broader question; the correction is disclosed here. Stopping is a monitored strategy with flares, not a cure pathway, on either record.

title: Tenofovir alafenamide versus tenofovir disoproxil for chronic hepatitis B
question: In HBeAg-positive and HBeAg-negative chronic hepatitis B, is tenofovir alafenamide non-inferior to tenofovir disoproxil fumarate for viral suppression at 48 weeks, with less bone and renal toxicity?
balance: LIKELY — two twin phase 3 non-inferiority trials, one in each HBeAg population, agree. In HBeAg-negative patients, HBV DNA below 29 IU/mL at week 48 occurred in 94% on tenofovir alafenamide versus 93% on tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (difference 1.8%, 95% CI −3.6 to 7.2), inside the 10% non-inferiority margin. In HBeAg-positive patients, suppression was 64% versus 67% (adjusted difference −3.6%, −9.8 to 2.6), also non-inferior. In both trials, alafenamide caused significantly smaller declines in hip and spine bone mineral density and smaller worsening of renal measures. The separation is on viral suppression plus bone and renal safety markers at 48 weeks; no record here shows a difference in clinical outcomes such as cirrhosis or liver cancer.

title: Mycophenolate versus azathioprine as first-line therapy in autoimmune hepatitis (CAMARO)
question: In treatment-naive autoimmune hepatitis, does mycophenolate mofetil induce biochemical remission more often than azathioprine (each with prednisolone) at six months?
balance: POSSIBLE — one open-label randomised trial (n=70) with its own 3-year follow-up (same patients, counted once). At 24 weeks, biochemical remission was achieved by 56.4% on mycophenolate plus prednisolone versus 29.0% on azathioprine plus prednisolone (difference 27.4 percentage points, 95% CI 4.0 to 46.7; p=0.022), with no serious adverse events on mycophenolate versus 12.9% on azathioprine and fewer discontinuations (5.1% versus 25.8%). At 3 years, time to biochemical response remained faster on mycophenolate (median 16 versus 64 weeks; adjusted HR 2.74 relative), but the difference in patients still on their assigned treatment with normalised ALT was no longer significant (76% versus 57%; p=0.099). Flagged on its face as a two-trial-gate exception candidate — a single randomised trial supports the shelf; withdraw or re-scope it if the developer rejects the exception. The topic file's pinned anchor (PMID 36514163) is the CAMARO protocol paper, not a results report; it is fenced by name and this shelf is built on the trial's primary report (PMID 38101756), pinned at build, with the 3-year follow-up (PMID 42880409) as the second card.

title: Guselkumab for Crohn's disease (GRAVITI; GALAXI)
question: In moderately to severely active Crohn's disease, does guselkumab — subcutaneous induction in GRAVITI, intravenous induction in GALAXI 2 and 3 — achieve clinical remission and endoscopic response versus placebo, and versus ustekinumab?
balance: LIKELY — three phase 3 trials agree. GRAVITI (subcutaneous induction and maintenance): clinical remission at week 12 in 56.1% versus 21.4% on placebo and endoscopic response in 41.3% versus 21.4%, with week-48 remission of 60.0–66.1% versus 17.1%. GALAXI-2 and GALAXI-3 (intravenous induction, reported together): both guselkumab regimens beat placebo on both composite co-primary endpoints in both trials (remission composite 47–55% versus 12–13%; endoscopic composite 34–39% versus 5–6%). The GALAXI report's interpretation claims superiority over ustekinumab at week 48 across multiple endpoints, but the abstract does not print the ustekinumab arm's endpoint rates, so that comparison is noted as the authors' claim and not carded with figures. Journal correction: GRAVITI's record is Gastroenterology 2025, not Lancet Gastroenterology & Hepatology as the topic file states.

title: Guselkumab for ulcerative colitis (QUASAR)
question: In moderately to severely active ulcerative colitis, does guselkumab induction followed by subcutaneous maintenance achieve clinical remission at week 44 versus placebo?
balance: LIKELY — a phase 3 programme whose parts agree, preceded by a concordant phase 2b induction study (same programme, same registry number). Phase 3 induction: clinical remission at week 12 in 23% on intravenous guselkumab versus 8% on placebo. Phase 3 maintenance: remission at week 44 in 50% (200 mg subcutaneously every 4 weeks) and 45% (100 mg every 8 weeks) versus 19% on placebo (withdrawal). The phase 2b study had already shown week-12 clinical response in about 61% on either intravenous dose versus 27.6% on placebo. Safety was favourable and consistent across the programme, with adverse-event rates in induction identical between groups (49%). Journal correction: the phase 3 record is The Lancet 2025, not Lancet Gastroenterology & Hepatology as the topic file states.

title: Lirentelimab for eosinophilic gastritis and duodenitis (ENIGMA)
question: In patients with eosinophilic gastritis or duodenitis, does the anti-Siglec-8 antibody lirentelimab reduce tissue eosinophils and total symptom scores versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE — a single small phase 2 trial (n=65) with large effects on its endpoints: gastrointestinal eosinophil counts fell by a mean of 86% on lirentelimab versus a 9% rise on placebo, the composite treatment response occurred in 63% versus 5%, and total symptom scores fell by 48% versus 22%. Infusion-related reactions were more frequent on the drug (60% versus 23%), otherwise adverse events were similar. The shelf must also carry what the trial cannot: the follow-on phase 3 development programme was discontinued, so no confirmatory trial exists or is coming from this programme. Flagged on its face as a two-trial-gate exception candidate — if the developer rejects the exception, this shelf should be withdrawn or re-scoped.

title: Pitavastatin to prevent cardiovascular disease in HIV (REPRIEVE)
question: In people with HIV at low-to-moderate cardiovascular risk on antiretroviral therapy, does pitavastatin 4 mg daily reduce major adverse cardiovascular events versus placebo?
balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C), because the primary outcome is a cardiovascular-event composite. In REPRIEVE (7,769 people with HIV at low-to-moderate predicted risk), the incidence of major adverse cardiovascular events was 4.81 per 1,000 person-years on pitavastatin versus 7.32 on placebo (HR 0.65 relative, 95% CI 0.48 to 0.90; P=0.002) over a median 5.1 years — an absolute difference of about 2.5 events per 1,000 person-years. The trial was stopped early for efficacy, which can exaggerate effect sizes, and it is a single trial. Muscle-related symptoms (2.3% versus 1.4%) and incident diabetes (5.3% versus 4.0%) were more frequent on pitavastatin. Correction printed on the card: the topic file gives the pitavastatin rate as 5.10 per 1,000 person-years; the record prints 4.81.

title: Dolutegravir-based first-line therapy versus efavirenz (ADVANCE; NAMSAL)
question: In treatment-naive people with HIV, is dolutegravir-based first-line therapy non-inferior to efavirenz-based therapy for viral suppression at 48 weeks — and what does it cost in weight gain?
balance: LIKELY — two phase 3 trials in African populations agree on non-inferiority and on the weight signal. ADVANCE (South Africa, n=1,053): HIV-1 RNA below 50 copies/mL at week 48 in 84% (dolutegravir with tenofovir alafenamide) and 85% (dolutegravir with tenofovir disoproxil) versus 79% on efavirenz standard care, non-inferior against a −10-point margin. NAMSAL (Cameroon, n=613): 74.5% on dolutegravir versus 69.0% on low-dose efavirenz 400 mg (difference 5.5 points, 95% CI −1.6 to 12.7; P<0.001 for non-inferiority). Weight gain was consistently greater on dolutegravir regimens — in ADVANCE a mean of 6.4 kg on the alafenamide combination (most in women) versus 1.7 kg on efavirenz; in NAMSAL a median of 5.0 versus 3.0 kg, with obesity in 12.3% versus 5.4%. Correction printed on the ADVANCE card: the trial enrolled patients from age 12, so the topic file's 'adults' framing is wider than the record.

title: Letermovir versus valganciclovir for CMV prophylaxis in high-risk kidney transplant
question: In donor-positive/recipient-negative kidney transplant recipients, is letermovir non-inferior to valganciclovir for preventing CMV disease through week 52, with less myelosuppression?
balance: POSSIBLE — a single phase 3 non-inferiority trial (601 randomised). Committee-confirmed CMV disease through week 52 occurred in 10.4% on letermovir versus 11.8% on valganciclovir (stratum-adjusted difference −1.4%, 95% CI −6.5 to 3.8), inside the prespecified 10% non-inferiority margin; no letermovir patient developed CMV disease by week 28, versus five (1.7%) on valganciclovir. The safety separation is large: leukopenia or neutropenia through week 28 in 26% versus 64% (P<.001), and discontinuation for adverse events in 4.1% versus 13.5%. Flagged on its face as a two-trial-gate exception candidate — a single pivotal trial supports the shelf; withdraw or re-scope it if the developer rejects the exception. Distinct from Shelf #722 (letermovir prophylaxis in stem-cell transplant recipients, and maribavir rescue) by population, and from Shelf #1634 (valganciclovir duration in kidney transplant) by question — drug choice here, duration there.

title: Nirmatrelvir–ritonavir as post-exposure prophylaxis for COVID-19 (EPIC-PEP)
question: In adults exposed to COVID-19 in the household, does a 5- or 10-day course of nirmatrelvir–ritonavir prevent symptomatic, confirmed infection versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — one large placebo-controlled trial (n=2,736) found no significant reduction in symptomatic, confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection by day 14 with either a 5-day course (2.6% versus 3.9% on placebo; relative risk reduction 29.8%, 95% CI −16.7 to 57.8; P=0.17) or a 10-day course (2.4% versus 3.9%; relative reduction 35.5%, −11.5 to 62.7; P=0.12). The stamp is POSSIBLE rather than LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) because the intervals are wide: a relative benefit approaching 60% is not excluded by this record, so the honest statement is 'no benefit shown', not 'no benefit exists'. Dysgeusia was the commonest adverse event (5.9% and 6.8% versus 0.7%). Distinct from Shelf #580 (nirmatrelvir–ritonavir as treatment of early infection) — this shelf is prophylaxis after exposure, in people not yet infected.

title: Male-partner treatment to prevent recurrent bacterial vaginosis (StepUp)
question: In women with bacterial vaginosis whose male partners are treated concurrently (oral metronidazole plus penile clindamycin cream) versus the woman treated alone, does partner treatment reduce recurrence within 12 weeks?
balance: POSSIBLE — a single open-label randomised trial (164 couples), stopped early by its data and safety monitoring board because woman-only treatment was inferior. Recurrence within 12 weeks occurred in 35% of women whose partners were also treated versus 63% under standard care (recurrence rate 1.6 versus 4.2 per person-year; absolute difference −2.6 per person-year, 95% CI −4.0 to −1.2; P<0.001). Early stopping for efficacy tends to inflate effect sizes, and there is no second trial, so the stamp is POSSIBLE despite the large point estimate. Flagged on its face as a two-trial-gate exception candidate — if the developer rejects the exception, this shelf should be withdrawn or re-scoped. Distinct from Shelf #947 (strategies directed at the woman — Lactin-V and suppressive metronidazole): this shelf's intervention treats the male partner.

title: Sublingual MV140 bacterial vaccine for recurrent urinary tract infection
question: In women with recurrent urinary tract infection, does daily sublingual MV140 (a whole-cell bacterial preparation) for three months reduce the proportion experiencing UTI episodes over the following nine months versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE — a single randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (240 women). Over the 9-month efficacy period after treatment, the median number of UTI episodes was 0.0 in both MV140 groups versus 3.0 on placebo (P<0.001), and 56% (3-month course) and 58% (6-month course) of MV140 recipients stayed UTI-free versus 25% on placebo. The trial was industry-funded and its own authors describe it as of 'modest size and duration'; the 3- and 6-month courses performed alike, so no duration advantage is shown. Flagged on its face as a two-trial-gate exception candidate — a single trial supports the shelf; withdraw or re-scope it if the developer rejects the exception. Distinct from Shelf #596 (methenamine hippurate as antibiotic-sparing prophylaxis) and Shelf #489 (cranberry products): a bacterial vaccine preparation is a different intervention aimed at the same condition.

title: Long-term inhaled hypertonic saline in cystic fibrosis (Elkins)
question: In patients with cystic fibrosis aged six years and older, does twice-daily inhaled hypertonic saline (7%) improve lung function and reduce pulmonary exacerbations over 48 weeks versus isotonic saline?
balance: POSSIBLE — a single long-term double-blind trial (n=164) whose own primary endpoint was null: the rate of change (slope) in lung function over 48 weeks did not differ between groups (P=0.79). The positive findings are secondary framings of the same data — averaged across all post-randomisation visits, FEV1 was 68 mL higher (95% CI 3 to 132) and FVC 82 mL higher on hypertonic saline — plus fewer pulmonary exacerbations (a 56% relative reduction, P=0.02, labelled relative) and more exacerbation-free patients (76% versus 62%; P=0.03). The card leads with the null primary, as the record requires; the topic file's summary ('modestly improved FEV1 and cut exacerbation frequency') quotes only the favourable half. Flagged on its face as a two-trial-gate exception candidate for the long-term question in this age group. Adjacent to Shelf #811 (CFTR modulators) without overlap — a different therapy class.

title: Azithromycin for persistent uncontrolled asthma (AMAZES; AZISAST)
question: In adults with persistent uncontrolled asthma despite inhaled therapy, does azithromycin three times weekly for 48 weeks reduce severe exacerbations versus placebo?
balance: SPLIT — the two asthma macrolide trials answer differently in different populations, and the cards do not average them. AMAZES (n=420, persistent symptomatic asthma on inhaled corticosteroids plus a long-acting bronchodilator): azithromycin 500 mg three times weekly for 48 weeks reduced total exacerbations to 1.07 versus 1.86 per patient-year (IRR 0.59 relative, 95% CI 0.47 to 0.74) and improved quality of life, at the price of more diarrhoea (34% versus 19%) — LIKELY. AZISAST (n=109, severe exacerbation-prone asthma, 6 months): the primary endpoint rate was not significantly different overall (0.75 versus 0.81 per subject; p=0.682); a predefined subgroup analysis found benefit only in non-eosinophilic severe asthma (0.44 versus 1.03; p=0.013) — POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) overall with a phenotype-specific signal. Correction: the topic file says AZISAST 'agrees in the eosinophilic subgroup' — the record shows the NON-eosinophilic subgroup; the card follows the record. Distinct from Shelf #817 (azithromycin in COPD) and Shelf #815 (macrolides in bronchiectasis) by disease.

title: FeNO-guided asthma management in adolescents and young adults
question: In adolescents and young adults with asthma, does adding exhaled nitric oxide (FeNO) measurements to guideline-based treatment decisions reduce exacerbations versus guideline-based care alone?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — one large randomised trial (546 patients aged 12–20) found that adding FeNO measurements to guideline-based management changed nothing clinical over 46 weeks: symptom days 1.93 versus 1.89 (difference 0.04, 95% CI −0.22 to 0.29; p=0.78), with no differences in other symptoms, pulmonary function, or exacerbations — while the FeNO group received significantly higher inhaled corticosteroid doses (+119 µg/day; p=0.001) to achieve the same control. The wider FeNO literature is fenced in the synthesis rather than carded: a pregnancy-population trial (a different question) and a 2016 Cochrane review of FeNO-guided treatment in children, which is a review and is named without figures. A single large, well-conducted null trial in exactly this population carries the stamp.

title: Antibiotic treatment strategies for community-acquired pneumonia (CAP-START)
question: In adults hospitalised with community-acquired pneumonia on non-ICU wards, is a default strategy of beta-lactam monotherapy non-inferior to beta-lactam plus macrolide, or to fluoroquinolone monotherapy, for 90-day mortality?
balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C), because the primary outcome is 90-day mortality. In CAP-START (2,283 patients on Dutch non-ICU wards, cluster-randomised crossover), crude 90-day mortality was 9.0% under the beta-lactam strategy, 11.1% under beta-lactam plus macrolide, and 8.8% under fluoroquinolone monotherapy; the authors concluded the beta-lactam strategy was non-inferior against a 3-percentage-point margin. The caveat printed on the card: in the intention-to-treat analysis as the abstract reports it, the risk difference for the combination strategy versus beta-lactam alone was +1.9 points with a 90% CI up to +4.4 — beyond the 3-point margin — so the non-inferiority conclusion rests on the trial's adjusted analyses rather than on the crude interval printed in the record. Single trial; hospital stay was a median of 6 days under all strategies.

title: Exercise training in haemodialysis patients (EXCITE; CYCLE-HD)
question: In adults on maintenance haemodialysis, does a personalised low-intensity exercise programme improve physical performance (six-minute walk distance) versus usual care?
balance: SPLIT — the two dialysis exercise trials test different deliveries against different primary endpoints, and the cards do not average them. EXCITE (n=296): a personalised, low-intensity home walking programme improved six-minute walk distance (328 to 367 m) versus usual care (321 to 324 m; P<0.001 between groups) and sit-to-stand time at 6 months — LIKELY for walk performance. CYCLE-HD (n=130): six months of intradialytic cycling significantly reduced left ventricular mass (−11.1 g between groups) — a cardiac surrogate — but had no significant effect on physical function or quality of life, its secondary outcomes — POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for the functional question this shelf asks. Neither trial reports clinical-event outcomes, and neither shelf claim touches mortality, so the shelf is not Tier C. Attrition was material in both (EXCITE: 227 of 296 repeated the 6-month evaluations; CYCLE-HD: 101 of 130 completed).

title: Ferric pyrophosphate citrate in dialysate (CRUISE 1 and 2)
question: In iron-deficient adults on haemodialysis, does ferric pyrophosphate citrate delivered via the dialysate maintain haemoglobin and reduce intravenous iron and ESA requirements versus placebo dialysate?
balance: LIKELY — two identical phase 3, randomised, placebo-controlled trials reported together (599 iron-replete chronic haemodialysis patients). Haemoglobin was maintained from baseline to end of treatment on ferric pyrophosphate citrate (FPC) dialysate but fell by 0.4 g/dL on placebo (P<0.001, combined results); reticulocyte haemoglobin and ferritin also fell less on FPC, and adverse and serious adverse event proportions were similar between groups. The outcomes are haemoglobin and iron indices — maintenance-of-iron-balance surrogates — not transfusion or clinical-event outcomes, and the shelf claims nothing beyond them. Correction printed on the card: the topic file's pinned anchor (PMID 28371161) is a narrative review of FPC by two authors, not the trials' results report; it is fenced by name, and this shelf cards the CRUISE trials' combined report (PMID 26175145), pinned at build.

title: Incremental twice-weekly haemodialysis start (TWOPLUS)
question: In patients starting dialysis with residual kidney function, does a twice-weekly haemodialysis start with adjuvant pharmacotherapy and planned transition to thrice-weekly treatment match conventional thrice-weekly start on patient-reported outcomes and safety?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — a single small pilot trial whose carded report (patient-reported outcomes) prints no between-group comparisons at all. Both arms' symptom scores improved over the first 6 weeks (Dialysis Symptom Index change −9.7 in the incremental group versus −13.8 in the conventional group; PHQ-9 −2.5 versus −3.5; GAD-7 −1.9 versus −1.5), with the P values in the record being within-group, and week-6-to-12 changes small and non-significant in both arms. The authors' conclusion of a 'possible mitigating effect' of the incremental start on anxiety and depression is flagged on the card: no between-group estimate in the abstract supports it, and on the printed changes the conventional arm improved at least as much on most measures. This was a feasibility and safety pilot (about 20 patients per group in the outcome analyses); it generates the hypothesis for a definitive trial and answers nothing yet. Flagged on its face as a two-trial-gate exception candidate — if the developer rejects the exception, this shelf should be withdrawn or re-scoped.

title: Buttonhole versus stepladder cannulation (MacRae)
question: In conventional (in-centre) haemodialysis patients with an arteriovenous fistula, does buttonhole cannulation reduce pain and complications versus standard (rope-ladder) cannulation?
balance: LIKELY (harm) — a single randomised trial (n=140) found no pain benefit and a clear infection cost. Pain at 8 weeks was similar (median VAS 1.5 on buttonhole versus 1.2 on standard needling; P=0.57). Buttonhole produced fewer haematomas (295 versus 436 per 1,000 sessions; P=0.03) but more localised infection signs (50 versus 22.4 per 1,000 sessions; P=0.003), one Staphylococcus aureus bacteraemia during the 8-week trial versus none, and — within 12 months of follow-up — two further buttonhole bacteraemias and nine needling-site abscesses requiring intravenous antibiotics versus zero in the standard group (P=0.003). Question re-scoped to the record and disclosed here: the topic file frames the population as home haemodialysis patients, but the trial enrolled conventional in-centre haemodialysis patients. The shelf's claim is a harm/null claim resting on one trial; it is stated as such on the face.

title: Gentamicin–citrate catheter lock (Moran; Dogra)
question: In haemodialysis patients with tunneled central venous catheters, does a gentamicin–citrate lock reduce catheter-related bloodstream infection versus a heparin lock?
balance: LIKELY — two randomised trials, a decade apart, agree strongly. Moran 2012 (n=303): catheter-related bloodstream infection at 0.28 episodes per 1,000 catheter-days on gentamicin 320 µg/mL in 4% citrate versus 0.91 on heparin (P=0.003), with thrombolytic use no different. Dogra 2002 (112 catheters in 83 patients): infection at 0.03 versus 0.42 per 100 catheter-days (P=0.003) with gentamicin–citrate filling. The caution travels with the benefit and is printed on the Dogra card: the concentrations differ about a hundredfold between the trials (40 mg/mL versus 320 µg/mL), and Dogra's record itself shows measurable predialysis gentamicin levels and warns of aminoglycoside exposure and ototoxicity risk — these records establish that gentamicin–citrate locks prevent bacteraemia, not which concentration is safe for long-term use.

title: Depression treatment in dialysis: sertraline versus CBT (ASCEND)
question: In patients on maintenance dialysis with depression, is chairside cognitive behavioural therapy as effective as sertraline for depressive symptoms?
balance: POSSIBLE — a single open-label randomised trial (120 patients in the treatment phase) found sertraline modestly superior to chairside CBT on the primary symptom measure: QIDS-C scores at 12 weeks favoured sertraline by 1.84 points (95% CI −3.54 to −0.13; P=0.035), with adverse events more frequent on sertraline. Correction printed on the card: the topic file states symptoms improved 'with no significant difference between CBT and sertraline' — the record shows a statistically significant difference, and the card follows the record. Two bounds on the claim: the 1.84-point difference is below the 2-point minimal clinically important difference used for this scale in the CAST trial (Shelf #1736), and ASCEND had no untreated control group, so neither arm's absolute efficacy — only their comparison — is established here. The trial's phase 1 found an engagement interview did not increase treatment acceptance (66% versus 64%).

title: Sertraline for depression in non-dialysis CKD (CAST)
question: In patients with non-dialysis chronic kidney disease and major depression, does sertraline improve depressive symptoms versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — a single double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (n=201) found no improvement: QIDS-C16 scores changed by −4.1 on sertraline versus −4.2 on placebo over 12 weeks (between-group difference 0.1, 95% CI −1.1 to 1.3; P=0.82). The interval is informative — it excludes the 2-point minimal clinically important difference the trial prespecified — so this is a measured null, not an absence of data. Gastrointestinal adverse events were more frequent on sertraline (nausea or vomiting 22.7% versus 10.4%; diarrhoea 13.4% versus 3.1%). The stamp is POSSIBLE rather than LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) because the shelf rests on this one trial. Read beside Shelf #1735 (ASCEND), where sertraline modestly beat CBT in dialysis patients without a placebo arm — the two records together do not establish that sertraline works in kidney disease at all.

title: Antibiotic exit-site cream in peritoneal dialysis (Bernardini)
question: In peritoneal dialysis patients, does daily gentamicin cream at the catheter exit site prevent exit-site infection and peritonitis compared with mupirocin cream?
balance: POSSIBLE — a single double-blind randomised trial (n=133) with consistent, organism-specific advantages for gentamicin cream: catheter infection rates 0.23 versus 0.54 episodes per dialysis-year (P=0.005), peritonitis 0.34 versus 0.52 per year (P=0.03), no Pseudomonas catheter infections on gentamicin versus 0.11 per year on mupirocin (P<0.003), and Gram-negative peritonitis 0.02 versus 0.15 per year (P=0.003), while Staphylococcus aureus exit-site infections were equally infrequent in both groups (0.06 versus 0.08 per year). The comparison is against mupirocin — an active prophylactic — not against no prophylaxis. The topic file's wider double-A framing rests on other mupirocin-prophylaxis randomised trials that were not separately pinned in this build; the stamp therefore rests on this trial alone, and that is stated here rather than borrowed.

title: Neutral-pH low-GDP peritoneal dialysis fluid (balANZ)

title: Icodextrin for the long dwell in peritoneal dialysis
question: In peritoneal dialysis patients, does icodextrin for the long dwell improve ultrafiltration and fluid status versus glucose-based solutions?
balance: POSSIBLE — the quantitative case rests on the classic MIDAS report (Wolfson 2002; two randomised double-blind studies reported together): net ultrafiltration on the long dwell was 587 versus 346 mL per exchange versus 2.5% dextrose (P<0.001), with higher urea and creatinine clearances, no weight gain over 52 weeks versus about 2 kg gained on dextrose, and less oedema (6.3% versus 17.9%). The recent trial the topic file pins (Li 2025, n=40, 4 months) points the same way — greater nighttime ultrafiltration, P<0.05 — but its abstract prints no effect sizes at all, so no figures from it are carded; that absence is flagged on its card. Two randomised comparisons in the same direction, one of them small and numberless: POSSIBLE. Outcomes are ultrafiltration and fluid-status surrogates; neither record reports mortality or technique-survival endpoints.

title: Paricalcitol and cardiac structure in CKD (OPERA; PRIMO)
question: In patients with chronic kidney disease and left ventricular hypertrophy, does paricalcitol reduce left ventricular mass versus placebo?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — two double-blind, placebo-controlled trials with the same primary endpoint agree. PRIMO (n=227, 48 weeks): change in left ventricular mass index was +0.34 g/m^2.7 on paricalcitol versus −0.07 on placebo — no difference, and diastolic measures likewise. OPERA (n=60, 52 weeks): LV mass index changed by −2.59 on paricalcitol versus −4.85 g/m² on placebo — again no significant difference, numerically favouring placebo. Both trials confirm paricalcitol suppresses parathyroid hormone; PRIMO found more hypercalcaemia on the drug. Question re-scoped to the records and disclosed here: the topic file also asks about left atrial volume, but neither carded record's abstract reports a left-atrial-volume result — OPERA's record in particular does not support the file's statement that it 'reduced left atrial volume index'; a separate small vitamin-D trial reports an LA-volume finding and is fenced in the synthesis, not carded. OPERA's fewer cardiovascular-related hospitalisations on paricalcitol are a secondary observation printed without figures in its abstract and carry no stamp weight.

title: Pentoxifylline in diabetic kidney disease (PREDIAN)
question: In patients with type 2 diabetes and diabetic kidney disease on RAAS blockade, does pentoxifylline slow eGFR decline and reduce albuminuria versus control?
balance: POSSIBLE — two randomised trials point the same way on surrogate outcomes, and neither reports a hard kidney outcome. PREDIAN (open-label, n=169, 2 years): eGFR fell by 2.1 ml/min/1.73 m² on pentoxifylline versus 6.5 on control (between-group difference 4.3, 95% CI 3.1 to 5.5; P<0.001), with albuminuria falling 14.9% against a 5.7% rise. Han 2015 (double-blind, placebo-controlled, n=174, 6 months): proteinuria fell 23% versus 4% (P=0.012). Both trials were add-ons to RAAS blockade; dialysis, kidney failure and death were not endpoints in either record, so no progression-to-ESRD claim is made. Surrogate endpoints in modest-sized trials cap the stamp at POSSIBLE.

title: Sparsentan in paediatric focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (DUPLEX subgroup)
question: In children and adolescents with focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, does sparsentan reduce proteinuria versus irbesartan?
balance: POSSIBLE — with two disclosures on the face of the shelf. First, the paediatric evidence is a POST HOC subgroup analysis of the DUPLEX trial (35 children), not a standalone paediatric randomised trial as the topic draft implied. Second, the parent DUPLEX trial (n=371, ages 8–75) MISSED its primary endpoint: eGFR slope at 108 weeks did not differ significantly between sparsentan and irbesartan (total-slope difference 0.3 ml/min/1.73 m²/year, 95% CI −1.7 to 2.4), even though the proteinuria surrogate favoured sparsentan (partial remission 42.0% vs 26.0% at 36 weeks, P=0.009). In the paediatric subgroup, proteinuria fell more on sparsentan (mean UPCR reduction 39.5% vs 24.9% at 108 weeks; partial remission endpoint 56.3% vs 36.8%), consistent with the parent trial's surrogate result; no paediatric kidney-function outcome is reported. PROPOSED as a two-trial-gate exception candidate: the whole shelf rests on one trial programme, and the paediatric claim on a 35-patient post hoc subgroup — it should be withdrawn or re-scoped if the developer rejects the exception.

title: Apixaban versus phenprocoumon in haemodialysis patients with atrial fibrillation (AXADIA–AFNET 8)
question: In patients with atrial fibrillation on chronic haemodialysis, is apixaban as safe and effective as the vitamin K antagonist phenprocoumon for bleeding and thromboembolic outcomes?
balance: PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C). Both of the trial's primary composites embed all-cause death — the safety composite (major bleeding, clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding, or all-cause death) and the efficacy composite (ischaemic stroke, all-cause death, myocardial infarction, deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism) — so the shelf is Tier C even though no mortality claim is made or supported by the data. AXADIA–AFNET 8 randomised only 97 patients and stopped early: the safety composite occurred in 45.8% on apixaban versus 51.0% on phenprocoumon (HR 0.93, 95% CI 0.53 to 1.65) and noninferiority was NOT established (P for noninferiority = 0.157); the efficacy composite occurred in 20.8% versus 30.6% (P=0.51), with all-cause mortality 18.8% versus 24.5%. The confidence intervals are wide enough to include important benefit and important harm, so the record earns MAYBE (weak evidence): an underpowered trial cannot settle anticoagulant choice in dialysis.

title: Hydroxychloroquine in IgA nephropathy
question: In patients with IgA nephropathy and persistent proteinuria despite supportive care, does hydroxychloroquine reduce proteinuria versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE — one small double-blind phase 2 trial with a large surrogate effect and no hard outcome. In 60 patients with IgA nephropathy on optimised RAAS inhibition, hydroxychloroquine changed proteinuria by −48.4% at 6 months against +10.0% on placebo (P<0.001), with no serious adverse events recorded. Six months, 60 patients, a single centre, and a proteinuria endpoint — with no eGFR or kidney-failure data — cap the stamp at POSSIBLE. PROPOSED as a two-trial-gate exception candidate: a single small trial with no second randomised test; it should be withdrawn or re-scoped if the developer rejects the exception. title: Low-dose ('renal-dose') dopamine in early renal dysfunction (ANZICS)

title: Ferric citrate in non-dialysis CKD: iron indices and haemoglobin

title: Nicotinamide-based phosphate lowering in CKD (COMBINE)

title: Sodium bicarbonate after kidney transplantation (PRESERVE-TRANSPLANT)
question: In kidney transplant recipients with metabolic acidosis, does sodium bicarbonate preserve graft function (eGFR trajectory) versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — a single well-run phase 3 trial with a precise null: in 242 transplant recipients with metabolic acidosis treated for 2 years, the eGFR slope difference between sodium bicarbonate and placebo was 0.032 ml/min/1.73 m²/year (95% CI −1.644 to 1.707), even though bicarbonate corrected the acidosis itself (serum bicarbonate 21.3 to 23.0 mmol/L). title: DHEA replacement in adrenal insufficiency
question: In adults with adrenal insufficiency, does dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA) replacement improve psychological well-being and sexual function versus placebo?
balance: SPLIT — the two crossover trials agree on well-being and disagree, by population, on sexuality. Arlt 1999 (24 WOMEN with adrenal insufficiency): DHEA 50 mg/day improved overall well-being (global severity index change −0.18 vs +0.03 on placebo; P=0.02), depression and anxiety scores, and sexual thoughts, interest and satisfaction (P=0.002 to 0.02) — the topic draft's question said 'adults', but this record is women only, and the shelf is scoped accordingly. Hunt 2000 (39 patients with Addison's disease, both sexes): DHEA improved self-esteem, mood and fatigue, but had NO effect on sexual function. So: POSSIBLE for psychological well-being and mood (two small trials, same direction); the sexuality claim rests on one 24-woman trial and was not reproduced in the mixed-sex trial — it is not confirmed. Scope boundary: DHEA supplementation in older adults without adrenal insufficiency is a different question, homed on its own shelf.

title: Growth hormone replacement in adult growth hormone deficiency
question: In adults with growth hormone deficiency, does GH replacement improve body composition and quality of life versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE — the body-composition claim is supported by the trial that actually measured it; the topic draft's pinned anchor did not. The draft anchored this shelf on PMID 8231841 (Fowelin 1993) described as a body-composition trial; that record is a 9-patient clamp study of insulin sensitivity with no body-composition results, so it is demoted to a second card and the shelf is re-anchored on Salomon 1989 (n=24): lean body mass rose 5.5 kg and fat mass fell 5.7 kg on GH over 6 months (both P<0.0001), with no weight change. title: Levoketoconazole in Cushing's syndrome (LOGICS randomised withdrawal)
question: In patients with Cushing's syndrome responding to levoketoconazole, does continuing the drug maintain urinary free cortisol normalisation versus switching to placebo (randomised withdrawal)?
