title: Relacorilant in endogenous Cushing's syndrome (GRACE)
question: In patients with endogenous Cushing's syndrome and diabetes or hypertension, does the glucocorticoid-receptor antagonist relacorilant improve glycaemic and blood-pressure control versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE — for blood-pressure control only, on this record; with a flagged gap on the glycaemic half of the question. GRACE is a randomised-withdrawal trial: 62 responders to open-label relacorilant were randomised to continue the drug or switch to placebo, and loss of hypertension response was significantly more frequent on placebo (proportion difference 34%; OR 0.17, 95% CI 0.04 to 0.77; p=0.022 — a relative measure, printed beside the proportion difference). The record's abstract prints NO glycaemic outcome figures, so the draft question's glycaemic claim cannot be carded and is flagged rather than filled. The withdrawal design in enriched responders proves maintenance of effect, not efficacy in untreated patients. PROPOSED as a two-trial-gate exception candidate: a single trial.

title: Adrenalectomy for subclinical Cushing's syndrome (Toniato)
question: In patients with adrenal incidentaloma and subclinical Cushing's syndrome, does adrenalectomy improve metabolic abnormalities (diabetes, hypertension, obesity) versus conservative management?
balance: POSSIBLE — one small randomised surgical trial with very long follow-up and very small denominators. In 45 patients followed for a mean of 7.7 years, adrenalectomy normalised or improved diabetes in 5 of 8 affected patients (62.5%), hypertension in 12 of 18 (67%), hyperlipidaemia in 3 of 8 (37.5%) and obesity in 3 of 6 (50%), while the conservative arm is described only as showing 'some worsening' — the record prints no figures or P values for the conservative arm's outcomes, so no comparative effect size can be carded. Direction favours surgery in patients meeting the trial's selection criteria; precision is minimal. PROPOSED as a two-trial-gate exception candidate: a single small trial; it should be withdrawn or re-scoped if the developer rejects the exception.

title: Flash glucose monitoring in type 1 diabetes on multiple daily injections (IMPACT)
question: In adults with type 1 diabetes on multiple daily injections, does flash glucose monitoring reduce time in hypoglycaemia versus self-monitoring of blood glucose?
balance: LIKELY — one large multicentre trial, carded in its primary report and in the pre-specified MDI subgroup report that answers this shelf's question (counted once: they are the same trial). In IMPACT (n=241, well-controlled type 1 diabetes, HbA1c ≤7.5%), flash monitoring cut time in hypoglycaemia by 1.24 h/day versus SMBG overall (P<0.0001; a 38% relative reduction), and by 1.65 h/day (95% CI −2.21 to −1.09; P<0.0001) in the MDI subgroup of 163 patients — without deterioration in HbA1c. The population was well controlled at baseline, so the result addresses hypoglycaemia avoidance in people already at target, not glucose lowering in poorly controlled diabetes. Single trial, stated on the face of the shelf (two-trial-gate exception candidate in form), but a large, consistent, precisely estimated one. Scope boundary: flash (intermittently scanned) monitoring is a distinct device class from the real-time CGM questions homed on Shelves #560/#561 and from the older-adult CGM question on Shelf #1762.

title: Flash glucose monitoring in type 2 diabetes on intensive insulin (REPLACE)
question: In adults with type 2 diabetes on intensive insulin therapy, does flash glucose monitoring improve HbA1c and reduce hypoglycaemia versus self-monitoring of blood glucose?
balance: SPLIT — REPLACE's randomised phase separates the two halves of the question cleanly. HbA1c at 6 months: no difference (−0.29% flash versus −0.31% SMBG; p=0.8222) — LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for the HbA1c claim overall, with a nominally positive under-65 subgroup (p=0.0301) disclosed as a subgroup finding, not the trial's answer. Hypoglycaemia: time below 3.9 mmol/L (≈70 mg/dL) fell by 0.47 h/day versus control (P=0.0006; 43% relative) — POSSIBLE. The trial's 12-month report is demoted to a second card with its status disclosed: after month 6 the control group disappears into an open-access phase, so its 12-month figures are within-group changes against baseline, not randomised evidence. Single trial, stated on the face of the shelf.

title: Continuous glucose monitoring in older adults with type 1 diabetes (WISDM)
question: In adults aged 60 and older with type 1 diabetes, does continuous glucose monitoring reduce time in hypoglycaemia versus blood glucose monitoring?
balance: LIKELY — one well-designed multicentre trial directly in the population the question names, with the hypoglycaemia benefit visible in both continuous and event terms: median time below 70 mg/dl fell from 5.1% at baseline to 2.7% during follow-up on CGM versus 4.7% to 4.9% on BGM (adjusted difference −1.9% of the day, 95% CI −2.8% to −1.1%; P<0.001), and severe hypoglycaemic events numbered 1 on CGM versus 10 on BGM — the last being the more clinically important signal, though with counts too small for a rate ratio. HbA1c fell slightly more on CGM (adjusted difference −0.3%, P<0.001). Single trial, stated on the face of the shelf (two-trial-gate exception candidate in form). Scope boundary: this is real-time CGM in older adults with type 1 diabetes; flash monitoring in younger MDI users is Shelf #1760, and hybrid closed loop is shelf #561.

title: Insulin pump (CSII) versus multiple daily injections in type 2 diabetes failing MDI (OpT2mise)
question: In adults with type 2 diabetes poorly controlled on high-dose multiple daily injections, does continuous subcutaneous insulin infusion improve HbA1c versus continuing MDI?
balance: LIKELY — a large multicentre randomised trial in exactly the population the question names: patients selected for failure on high-dose MDI. At 6 months HbA1c fell by 1.1% on pump versus 0.4% on continued MDI (between-group difference −0.7%, 95% CI −0.9 to −0.4; p<0.0001), with total daily insulin dose ending lower on pump (97 versus 122 units; p<0.0001) and no significant difference in bodyweight change between groups. Screening context matters: 590 patients were screened and 331 randomised, so the result applies to the subset meeting the trial's run-in criteria, not to all MDI-failing patients. Single trial, stated on the face of the shelf (two-trial-gate exception candidate in form).

title: Open-source automated insulin delivery versus sensor-augmented pump in type 1 diabetes (CREATE)
question: In children and adults with type 1 diabetes, does open-source automated insulin delivery increase time in range versus sensor-augmented pump therapy?
balance: LIKELY — a clean randomised result for a community-built system: time in range (3.9–10.0 mmol/L (≈70–180 mg/dL)) during the final 2 weeks was 71.2% on open-source AID versus 54.5% on sensor-augmented pump, an adjusted between-group difference of 14 percentage points (95% CI 9.2 to 18.8; P<0.001), with no severe hypoglycaemia or diabetic ketoacidosis in either group over 24 weeks. Caveats on the face: 97 patients, an open-label trial of a highly motivated population willing to run open-source software, and a 24-week horizon — safety beyond that rests on community experience, not randomised data. Single trial (two-trial-gate exception candidate in form). Scope boundary: commercial hybrid closed-loop systems are Shelf #561; CREATE is specifically the open-source question.

title: Suspend-before-low and threshold-suspend insulin pumps in type 1 diabetes (PROLOG, ASPIRE)
question: In patients with type 1 diabetes at risk of hypoglycaemia, do automated insulin-suspension pump features reduce hypoglycaemic events versus sensor-augmented pump therapy without suspension?
balance: LIKELY — two randomised trials of successive generations of the same idea agree. PROLOG (predictive low-glucose suspend, n=103, 6 weeks): median sensor time below 70 mg/dl was 2.6% with suspend-before-low versus 3.2% on sensor-augmented pump (difference −0.8 percentage points; P<0.001), a 31% relative reduction in mean time below range, with no increase in mean glucose. ASPIRE (threshold suspend, n=247, 3 months): the area-under-curve rate of nocturnal hypoglycaemic events was 37.5% lower (a relative measure; P<0.001), the event rate was 31.8% lower (also relative), with nocturnal events at 1.5 versus 2.2 per patient-week — the absolute rates are printed beside the relative ones. PROLOG recorded one severe hypoglycaemic event, in the sensor-augmented-pump period; ASPIRE recorded four patients with severe events, all in the control group, and no DKA in either. Mean glucose did not rise in PROLOG and HbA1c did not differ in ASPIRE — suspension is a hypoglycaemia-safety feature, not a glucose-lowering one. Generation boundary stated: threshold-suspend reacts at a threshold; suspend-before-low predicts; full hybrid closed loop is Shelf #560/#561 territory and is not claimed here.

title: Community health workers plus peer leaders in diabetes self-management (Latino adults)
question: In Latino adults with type 2 diabetes, does a diabetes self-management programme combining community health workers and peer leaders improve HbA1c versus enhanced usual care?
balance: POSSIBLE — a single two-stage randomised trial in Latino adults with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes. A CHW-led 6-month self-management programme lowered HbA1c more than enhanced usual care at 6 months (between-group difference −0.45%; 95% CI −0.87 to −0.03; P<0.05), and participants stepped into a peer-leader maintenance phase maintained their HbA1c improvements at 12 and 18 months on the record’s reporting, while CHW-only telephone follow-up maintained diabetes-distress improvements. One trial, 222 randomised patients, single programme; the peer-leader companion literature (Heisler 2010, reciprocal peer support by telephone) is a different design and is fenced rather than carded. Nothing here supports claims for non-Latino populations.

title: Structured self-monitoring of blood glucose in non-insulin-treated type 2 diabetes (STeP)
question: In patients with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes not treated with insulin, does structured self-monitoring of blood glucose improve HbA1c versus active usual care?
balance: POSSIBLE — the STeP trial is positive but modest, and its two reports must not be confused. The primary report (carded first) randomised 483 patients: structured SMBG lowered HbA1c by 0.3% more than an active control at 12 months (−1.2% vs −0.9%; P=0.04) in the intention-to-treat analysis. The primary report’s per-protocol difference was larger (−0.5%; P<0.003), and the companion report — the record pinned in the topic draft — found the benefit concentrated in patients who received treatment-change recommendations (−1.2% versus −0.8% among those with at least one recommendation; P<0.03): a physician-behaviour analysis, not the trial’s answer, and it is demoted to a second card with that status stated. Scope boundary within the library: the DiGEM trial of SMBG strategies in non-insulin-treated type 2 diabetes is carded on Shelf #559 (a different, largely null trial of monitoring intensity without STeP's structured-profile protocol); STeP's distinct angle — a defined 7-point-profile structure reviewed at each visit — is what this shelf answers, and DiGEM is fenced here rather than re-carded.

title: Pharmacist prescribing for cardiovascular risk in chronic kidney disease (RxEACH-CKD)
question: In patients with chronic kidney disease at high cardiovascular risk, does pharmacist-led assessment and prescribing reduce estimated cardiovascular risk versus usual care?
balance: POSSIBLE — a positive secondary analysis of a parent trial, on an estimated-risk endpoint, stated as such. RxEACH-CKD (n=290, CKD patients at high cardiovascular risk) found the estimated 10-year cardiovascular risk fell by 20% more in relative terms with pharmacist assessment, prescribing and follow-up than with usual care (difference in change in estimated risk, P<0.001), with significant improvements in systolic blood pressure (P<0.001), A1c (P<0.001), LDL cholesterol (P=0.004) and smoking cessation (P=0.04). The '20%' is a relative difference in the change of a risk estimate — not a reduction in events; the parent RxEACH trial (Al Hamarneh 2017), which randomised diabetics broadly and is carded on Shelf #1009, found the same direction of effect. This shelf's distinct angle is the CKD population; it is NOT Tier C: the primary endpoint is estimated risk, and no mortality or event claim is made or supported.

title: Subcutaneous rapid-acting insulin for uncomplicated diabetic ketoacidosis
question: In patients with uncomplicated diabetic ketoacidosis, does subcutaneous rapid-acting insulin achieve resolution comparable to intravenous insulin infusion?
balance: POSSIBLE — two small single-centre randomised trials of two different analogues point the same way. Umpierrez 2004 (insulin lispro hourly subcutaneously, n=40): time to resolution of ketoacidosis (10 vs 11 h) and of hyperglycaemia (7 vs 7 h) did not differ significantly from IV regular insulin; hospital stay did not differ; no deaths occurred. Umpierrez 2004 (insulin aspart every 1–2 h, n=45): time to hyperglycaemia correction (6.9 and 6.1 h for hourly and 2-hourly aspart versus 7.1 h) and to DKA resolution (10 and 10.7 versus 11 h) were comparable; length of stay did not differ; there were no deaths in any group — mortality is printed beside the resolution outcomes, as required, and shows only that these small uncomplicated-DKA cohorts had no signal either way. Both trials are small (40 and 45 patients) and explicitly excluded complicated DKA (severe acidosis, altered mentation, hypotension and comorbidity exclusions vary slightly between them) — the shelf's claim does not extend to severe or complicated DKA, children, or pregnancy.

title: Balanced crystalloids versus saline for fluid resuscitation in diabetic ketoacidosis
question: In adults with diabetic ketoacidosis, do balanced crystalloids shorten time to DKA resolution versus 0.9% sodium chloride?
balance: POSSIBLE — a single DKA-specific randomised comparison, a secondary (subgroup) analysis of two companion cluster trials, answers the DKA question directly. In the Self 2020 analysis of the SALT-ED and SMART trials (n=172 DKA patients), balanced crystalloids shortened median time to DKA resolution (13.0 vs 16.9 h; adjusted HR 1.68, 95% CI 1.18 to 2.38; P=.004) and time to insulin-infusion discontinuation (9.8 vs 13.4 h; aHR 1.45, 1.03 to 2.03) versus saline — the hazard ratios are relative measures, printed beside the absolute medians they summarise. The parent fluid shelves answer the general critical-care question (Shelf #123, SALT-ED/SMART-era evidence in acutely ill adults); this shelf's distinct angle is the DKA population and its resolution endpoint, and the parent trials are not re-carded here. One trial subgroup (two-trial-gate exception candidate in form); the SCOPE-DKA randomised trial is the in-flight confirmatory test named on the closing card.

title: Liraglutide versus sulfonylurea during Ramadan fasting in type 2 diabetes (LIRA-Ramadan)
question: In patients with type 2 diabetes who fast during Ramadan, does liraglutide maintain glycaemic control as well as sulfonylurea, with less weight gain and hypoglycaemia?
balance: POSSIBLE — one open-label randomised trial in a specific and clinically distinct setting: patients switched from metformin plus sulfonylurea to metformin plus liraglutide before Ramadan, then compared through the fast. The primary outcome — change in fructosamine during Ramadan — was similar between groups (estimated treatment difference +3.51 µmol/L, 95% CI −5.26 to 12.28; p=0.43): sulfonylurea's within-Ramadan fall was slightly larger, but the liraglutide arm entered Ramadan with lower fructosamine because the switch had already improved control, and HbA1c fell more on liraglutide overall (ETD −0.59%; p<0.0001) — a design feature disclosed on the card, since the comparison bundles the switch with the drug. Body weight decreased more on liraglutide during Ramadan (ETD −0.54 kg; p=0.0091), and documented symptomatic hypoglycaemic episodes were reported by 2% of liraglutide patients (3 subjects) versus 11% on sulfonylurea (18 subjects), with no severe episodes in either arm. Single trial, open-label (two-trial-gate exception candidate in form), in adults with HbA1c 7–10% who intended to fast — the result does not extend to patients advised not to fast, or to insulin-treated patients.

title: Collaborative care for depression with diabetes and/or coronary disease (TEAMcare)
question: In adults with depression and poorly controlled diabetes, coronary heart disease, or both, does nurse-led collaborative care improve depression scores and cardiometabolic control (HbA1c, LDL cholesterol, systolic blood pressure) versus usual care?
balance: POSSIBLE — one randomised trial, so this shelf is a two-trial-gate exception candidate for the developer. TEAMcare (n=214) randomised patients with depression and poorly controlled diabetes, coronary heart disease, or both — the topic file's question said diabetes alone; the question is re-scoped to the record, which enrolled the mixed population and cannot be read as a diabetes-only result. The intervention improved all four modelled outcomes together at 12 months (between-group differences: HbA1c 0.58%, LDL cholesterol 6.9 mg/dL, systolic blood pressure 5.1 mm Hg, depression score 0.40 points; combined primary model P<0.001), with more medication adjustment in the intervention arm. title: Sitagliptin-based therapy for inpatient hyperglycaemia
question: In hospitalised adults with type 2 diabetes on general medicine and surgery wards, does sitagliptin alone or combined with basal insulin achieve glycaemic control similar to basal-bolus insulin?
balance: LIKELY — a single 90-patient open-label pilot trial, flagged here as a two-trial-gate exception candidate. The topic file asked whether sitagliptin is 'non-inferior' to basal-bolus insulin; the record is a pilot randomised study with no non-inferiority design or margin, so the question is re-scoped to the similarity the pilot actually observed, and the correction is disclosed here. Mean daily glucose, readings in target, readings above 200 mg/dL, treatment failures, length of stay and hypoglycaemic events did not differ between sitagliptin alone, sitagliptin plus glargine, and basal-bolus insulin, while total insulin dose and injection count were significantly lower in the sitagliptin arms. The abstract prints P values without the groups' absolute glucose values, so no absolute control figures are carded. The authors' conclusion that sitagliptin is 'safe and effective' overstates what a 90-patient open-label pilot can establish; the card records the data, not the claim. If the developer rejects the exception, this shelf should be withdrawn.

title: Abatacept in new-onset type 1 diabetes
question: In patients with newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes, does co-stimulation blockade with abatacept preserve stimulated C-peptide versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE — one randomised trial with a surrogate endpoint, flagged here as a two-trial-gate exception candidate. In 112 patients aged 6–45 with recent-onset type 1 diabetes, two years of abatacept left stimulated C-peptide AUC 59% higher in relative terms (95% CI 6.1–112) than placebo — absolute values 0.378 versus 0.238 nmol/L (P=0.0029) — an estimated 9.6-month delay in C-peptide decline. The trial's own interpretation notes that after month 6 the decline ran parallel to placebo despite continued infusions, so the drug bought time rather than changing the trajectory's slope. C-peptide preservation is a surrogate: this record shows no clinical-outcome benefit (no hypoglycaemia, HbA1c or complication outcomes are claimed), and no mortality claim is made or supported. If the developer rejects the single-trial exception, this shelf should be withdrawn.

title: Dasiglucagon for severe hypoglycaemia
question: In people with type 1 diabetes and insulin-induced severe hypoglycaemia, does ready-to-use dasiglucagon restore plasma glucose faster than placebo, and how does its speed compare with reconstituted glucagon?
balance: LIKELY — three randomised double-blind phase 3 trials (two adult, one paediatric) agree. A correction to the topic file is disclosed here: the file pinned the paediatric trial (PMID 33934456) as the anchor and quoted '10 versus 12 minutes' against reconstituted glucagon; those figures are from the adult trial (Pieber 2021), and the adult trial's primary comparison was against placebo, with reconstituted glucagon as a reference arm — no formal non-inferiority test is printed in the record. In adults, dasiglucagon restored glucose in a median 10 minutes versus 40 minutes on placebo (P<0.001), essentially matching reconstituted glucagon's 12 minutes while removing the reconstitution step; an autoinjector trial and the paediatric trial (ages 6–17) show the same 10-minute median. Recovery within 15 minutes: 99% of adults on dasiglucagon versus 2% on placebo. Nausea and vomiting were the common adverse effects, as expected for glucagon-class drugs.

title: Metformin in type 1 diabetes (REMOVAL)
question: In adults with type 1 diabetes aged 40 and over with cardiovascular risk factors, does metformin slow carotid intima-media thickness progression versus placebo?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — one large trial, stated on the face of the shelf. REMOVAL (428 patients, 3 years) missed its primary outcome: progression of mean carotid intima-media thickness was −0.005 mm/year on metformin (95% CI −0.012 to 0.002; P=0.1664), not significant. A prespecified tertiary outcome (maximal cIMT) did fall significantly (−0.013 mm/year; P=0.0093), and metformin produced small sustained reductions in weight (−1.17 kg) and LDL cholesterol (−0.13 mmol/L (≈-5 mg/dL)) with a rise in eGFR (+4.0 mL/min/1.73m²); the average HbA1c reduction (−0.13%) was driven by a 3-month effect that was not sustained. Gastrointestinal intolerance drove discontinuation in 27% versus 12%. Tier C is ruled NOT applicable, with the deviation logic stated explicitly: the topic file said no, and the record agrees — the primary outcome is a surrogate, and the five versus two deaths were a safety count judged unrelated to study medication; no cardiovascular-event or mortality claim is made or supported by this shelf. Single trial: if the developer wants a second randomised test before any stamp, this shelf should be held rather than upgraded.

title: Pramlintide as adjunct insulin therapy in type 1 diabetes
question: In adults with type 1 diabetes, does adjunctive pramlintide improve HbA1c and body weight versus insulin alone?
balance: POSSIBLE — two randomised double-blind trials, with an honest inconsistency between them on HbA1c. In the 52-week trial (Whitehouse 2002, n=480), pramlintide cut HbA1c by −0.67% versus −0.16% on placebo at week 13 (P<0.0001), the placebo-corrected difference was sustained through week 52 (P=0.0071, magnitude not printed in the abstract), and patients lost weight rather than gaining, without an increase in overall severe hypoglycaemia. In the 29-week trial run with proactive mealtime-insulin reduction and re-optimisation (Edelman 2006, n=296), HbA1c fell identically in both groups (−0.5%), while postprandial excursions and weight clearly favoured pramlintide (weight −1.3 kg versus +1.2 kg; P<0.0001) and the severe hypoglycaemia rate was higher on pramlintide (0.57 versus 0.30 events/patient-year; P<0.05). Read together: the weight and postprandial effects are consistent; the HbA1c advantage depends on how insulin is managed around it; nausea is frequent (63% versus 36% in Edelman). POSSIBLE, not LIKELY, because the headline glycaemic claim is design-dependent.

title: Scalp cooling to prevent chemotherapy-induced alopecia (SCALP)
question: In women receiving taxane/anthracycline chemotherapy for breast cancer, does scalp cooling prevent hair loss versus no cooling?
balance: LIKELY — one randomised trial plus a large prospective cohort, with a correction to the topic file disclosed here: the file named the Rugo 2017 JAMA paper as 'the SCALP randomised clinical trial'; Rugo is a prospective cohort study, not a randomised trial. The randomised SCALP trial is Nangia 2017, and it leads this shelf: hair preservation (less than 50% hair loss) in 50.5% of cooled women versus 0% of controls at the end of four cycles. The Rugo cohort, carded second and labelled as a cohort, found Dean-scale success in 66.3% versus 0% on non-anthracycline regimens. The two studies use different success scales (CTCAE grade 0–1 versus Dean 0–2), so their percentages are not interchangeable. The randomised trial was stopped early at a planned interim analysis for efficacy, which tends to flatter effect sizes; even allowing for that, a 0% control rate makes the direction secure. LIKELY.

title: Palifermin for oral mucositis in transplant conditioning
question: In patients undergoing haematopoietic stem-cell transplantation, does palifermin reduce severe oral mucositis versus placebo — and does the answer depend on the conditioning regimen?
balance: SPLIT — LIKELY in total-body-irradiation conditioning / MAYBE (weak evidence) in melphalan-only conditioning. The question is widened from the topic file's TBI-only framing to cover both randomised settings, with the split stated on the face of the shelf. In the TBI-plus-high-dose-chemotherapy trial (Spielberger 2004, n=212), palifermin cut WHO grade 3–4 mucositis from 98% to 63% and grade 4 from 62% to 20% (both P<0.001), with less opioid use and less total parenteral nutrition. In the chemotherapy-only high-dose melphalan setting (Blijlevens 2013, n=281), palifermin showed no significant effect on maximum mucositis severity (severe mucositis 37% placebo, 38% pre/post-transplant dosing, 24% pre-transplant-only dosing) and more infections and fever in the pre/post arm. The topic file's 'DOUBLE-A' label is therefore misleading as filed: the second trial does not confirm the first — it bounds it to the irradiation setting. Quote the split, never a single pooled claim.

title: Oral cryotherapy for chemotherapy-induced mucositis
question: In patients receiving bolus fluorouracil or high-dose melphalan, does oral cryotherapy (ice chips) during infusion prevent oral mucositis versus standard care?
balance: POSSIBLE — two small randomised trials in different regimens, both positive, each with reporting limits stated on its card. In high-dose melphalan transplant conditioning (Lilleby 2006, n=40), cryotherapy cut grade 3–4 mucositis from 74% to 14% (P=0.0005). In bolus fluorouracil-plus-leucovorin (Mahood 1991, n=95), mucositis was significantly reduced by both physician (P=.0002) and patient (P=.0001) assessment — but that abstract prints no event rates at all, so the size of the 5-FU effect cannot be carded, only its significance. Small samples, an unblindable intervention, and one rate-free record cap the stamp at POSSIBLE despite the dramatic melphalan figures.

title: Oral versus intravenous antibiotics for low-risk febrile neutropenia
question: In low-risk patients with febrile neutropenia, is oral antibiotic therapy as effective as intravenous therapy?
balance: LIKELY — two randomised trials published back-to-back in 1999 (one double-blind, one open-label equivalence trial) agree that, in carefully defined low-risk patients treated in hospital, oral ciprofloxacin plus amoxicillin-clavulanate performs equivalently to intravenous regimens. Success without regimen modification was 71% versus 67% in the double-blind trial (difference 3%, 95% CI −8 to 15) and 86% versus 84% per-protocol in the equivalence trial, whose ≤10% equivalence margin was met. The trade-off is tolerability: oral therapy failed more often through intolerance (16% versus 1% in Freifeld) and intravenous therapy more often through regimen modification. There were no deaths in the double-blind trial. Both trials kept patients hospitalised until fever and neutropenia resolved — the outpatient step-down use this evidence is often cited for is an extrapolation beyond these records, stated plainly on the cards.

title: Levofloxacin prophylaxis in neutropenia (Bucaneve; Cullen)
question: In patients expected to have prolonged chemotherapy-induced neutropenia, does levofloxacin prophylaxis reduce febrile episodes and documented infection versus placebo?
balance: LIKELY — two large double-blind placebo-controlled trials (NEJM 2005) agree. In patients facing more than seven days of neutropenia, including acute leukaemia (Bucaneve, n=760), levofloxacin cut febrile episodes from 85% to 65% (relative risk 0.76; absolute difference −20 percentage points) and microbiologically documented infections by 17 points. In solid-tumour and lymphoma patients on cyclic chemotherapy (Cullen, n=1565), febrile episodes fell from 15.2% to 10.8% across the course (cycle 1: 7.9% to 3.5%) and infection-related hospitalisation from 21.6% to 15.7%. The populations differ — deep, prolonged neutropenia versus shorter cyclic neutropenia — and the question's 'prolonged' framing fits Bucaneve most directly; Cullen is carded as the same-intervention trial in the adjacent population, and the difference is disclosed rather than smoothed over. Neither trial showed a mortality benefit (mortality similar in Bucaneve; four infection-related deaths in each arm in Cullen), and no mortality claim is made. Both trials leave the resistance cost unmeasured — Bucaneve's authors state it explicitly — which is the standing caveat on this shelf.

title: Direct oral anticoagulant prophylaxis in ambulatory cancer patients (AVERT; CASSINI)
question: In ambulatory patients with cancer starting chemotherapy at high venous-thromboembolism risk (Khorana score ≥2), does prophylaxis with a direct oral anticoagulant (apixaban or rivaroxaban) prevent VTE versus placebo, and at what bleeding cost?
balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: the primary outcome is a venous-thromboembolism event composite that includes death from VTE). Two placebo-controlled trials of factor Xa prophylaxis in Khorana score ≥2 ambulatory patients starting chemotherapy point the same way on treatment but differ over the full follow-up. AVERT (apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily, n=563 analysed) reduced VTE over 180 days from 10.2% to 4.2% (hazard ratio 0.41 in relative terms; P<0.001), with major bleeding higher on apixaban over the same window (3.5% versus 1.8%; HR 2.00). CASSINI (rivaroxaban 10 mg daily, n=841) missed its primary 180-day analysis (6.0% versus 8.8%; HR 0.66; P=0.10) but its prespecified on-treatment analysis was clearly positive (2.6% versus 6.4%; HR 0.40), with major bleeding 2.0% versus 1.0%. The question is widened from the topic file's apixaban-only framing to the class question the two trials jointly answer, and the widening is disclosed here. Net reading: prophylaxis prevents VTE while the drug is being taken, at roughly double the major-bleeding rate; no mortality benefit is shown or claimed — all-cause mortality is not an endpoint of either record, and the death component of the composites is death from VTE only. POSSIBLE rather than LIKELY because one of the two primary analyses is null.

title: Progressive resistance training in breast-cancer lymphoedema (PAL)
question: In breast-cancer survivors with stable arm lymphoedema, does progressive weight lifting worsen lymphoedema — or improve symptoms — versus no exercise?
balance: LIKELY — the large definitive trial (PAL, n=141) answered the safety question the field had feared: slowly progressive weight lifting did not increase arm swelling over one year (≥5% swelling increase in 11% versus 12%; cumulative incidence ratio 1.00, 95% CI 0.88–1.13), and it reduced specialist-assessed exacerbations (14% versus 29%; P=0.04) and symptom severity while increasing strength. The earlier pilot (Ahmed 2006, n=45 — the topic file calls it 'the Schmitz pilot'; first author is Ahmed, with Schmitz a co-author, corrected here) points the same way. A condition of the PAL result belongs on the face of the shelf: participants wore a well-fitted compression garment while lifting, and progression was slow and supervised. The claim is 'does not worsen, and helps symptoms' — not that exercise treats lymphoedema as a decongestive therapy.

title: Acupuncture for aromatase-inhibitor joint pain (SWOG S1200)
question: In postmenopausal women with aromatase-inhibitor-related arthralgia, does true acupuncture reduce joint pain versus sham acupuncture or waitlist control?
balance: POSSIBLE — a downgrade from the strength the topic file implies, for a reason printed on the trial's own card: SWOG S1200 (n=226) prespecified 2 points on the Brief Pain Inventory worst-pain scale as the clinically meaningful difference, and true acupuncture beat sham by 0.92 points at 6 weeks (P=.01) and by 1.08 points at 52 weeks — statistically significant, durable, and below the trial's own meaningfulness threshold, which the authors themselves flag ('uncertain clinical importance'). The smaller Crew 2010 trial (38 evaluable) showed a much larger separation (worst pain 3.0 versus 5.5 at 6 weeks), larger than the definitive trial supports. The 52-week report carded here is a follow-up report of S1200, not a second trial — the trial is counted once; Crew is the independent second trial. Real but small average benefit, honestly labelled: POSSIBLE.

title: Venlafaxine for hot flashes (Loprinzi)
question: In women with bothersome hot flashes (including breast-cancer survivors), does venlafaxine reduce hot-flash scores versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE — one placebo-controlled randomised trial, flagged here as a two-trial-gate exception candidate. The topic file claimed a second trial (venlafaxine against clonidine) as the shelf's second leg; no such record could be pinned in PubMed searches for this build, so the claim is treated as unverified and the shelf is built honestly on the single trial. In 221 women (191 evaluable) with a history of breast cancer or reluctance to use hormones, four weeks of venlafaxine reduced median hot-flash scores by 61% at both 75 mg and 150 mg daily versus 27% on placebo, with a dose gradient at 37.5 mg (37%). The cost is side effects — dry mouth, appetite loss, nausea and constipation were significantly more frequent at 75–150 mg. Four weeks is the whole of the evidence horizon. If the developer rejects the exception, this shelf should be withdrawn or held until a second placebo-controlled trial is pinned.

title: Olanzapine for breakthrough chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting (Navari)

title: Megestrol acetate for cancer anorexia–cachexia
question: In patients with advanced cancer and anorexia/cachexia, does megestrol acetate improve appetite and weight versus placebo — and is there a dose–response?
balance: POSSIBLE — the two carded trials pull in different directions on the placebo question, and the balance shows both. The 1994 NCCTG dose-ranging trial (342 evaluable patients, no placebo arm) found a significant dose–response for appetite stimulation (P=0.02) across 160–1280 mg/day, with only a trend for nonfluid weight gain and 800 mg/day judged optimal. The one modern placebo-controlled trial pinned for this build (Currow 2021, n=190) missed its primary endpoint: day-7 appetite responders were 79.3% on megestrol 480 mg versus 58.5% on placebo (P=0.067), with no quality-of-life or performance differences. Older placebo-controlled trials exist — the dose trial's own abstract references them — but their records were not pinned in this build and they are not carded. The topic file's paediatric megestrol RCT is a different population and is not imported. Net: a real dose-related appetite signal that the best modern placebo test could not confirm at conventional significance, and no carded trial demonstrating significant weight gain with figures. POSSIBLE, and one of the weaker shelves in this batch.

title: Celecoxib to prevent capecitabine hand–foot syndrome
question: In patients receiving capecitabine, does celecoxib prevent grade ≥2 hand–foot syndrome versus capecitabine alone?
balance: POSSIBLE — a single randomised trial, flagged here as a two-trial-gate exception candidate, with two corrections to the topic file disclosed. Second, the record's abstract does not print the number of patients randomised at all, an unusual reporting gap flagged on the card. Within those limits, the trial (stage II–III colorectal cancer, single centre) found grade 2 hand–foot syndrome in 14.7% with celecoxib versus 29.6% without (P=0.035), grade 1 in 57.4% versus 74.6% (P=0.034), and hazard ratios in relative terms of 0.414 for grade ≥2 (P=0.005) and 0.556 for grade ≥1 (P=0.001), with celecoxib the only significant factor in the multivariable model. title: Mometasone cream for acute radiation dermatitis
question: In women receiving breast radiotherapy, does prophylactic mometasone cream reduce acute radiation dermatitis versus placebo or emollient?
balance: LIKELY — two double-blind randomised trials in different breast-radiotherapy settings, both positive on clinician-assessed dermatitis. The topic file pinned a single trial; a second (Ho 2018, postmastectomy) was pinned in this build and is carded. In breast-conserving radiotherapy (Hindley 2014), mometasone beat an emollient comparator on mean and maximum RTOG scores and erythema, with better dermatology quality-of-life scores — but that abstract prints neither its sample size nor any effect sizes, only P values, a gap flagged on its card. title: Palonosetron for chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting
question: In patients receiving highly emetogenic chemotherapy, is palonosetron superior to first-generation 5-HT3 antagonists for delayed-phase emesis control?
balance: LIKELY — two large phase III double-blind trials, with two corrections to the topic file disclosed. First, the comparator: the Aapro trial compared palonosetron with ONDANSETRON, not dolasetron as the file states; the second trial (Saito 2009) used granisetron — the question's 'first-generation 5-HT3 antagonists' framing covers both and is retained. Second, in Aapro the whole-population delayed-phase advantage was numerical, and the statistically significant delayed-phase superiority was demonstrated in the dexamethasone-pretreated stratum; Saito, in which everyone received dexamethasone, showed delayed-phase superiority outright (56.8% versus 44.5% complete response; P<0.0001) with acute-phase non-inferiority. The shelf's claim is therefore precise: with dexamethasone co-treatment, palonosetron is at least as good acutely and better in the delayed phase than a first-generation comparator. Doses differ between the trials (0.25 mg in Aapro's licensed-dose arm; 0.75 mg in Saito's Japanese programme) and are printed on the cards.

title: Pilocarpine for Sjögren's-related dry mouth
question: In patients with Sjögren's syndrome, does oral pilocarpine improve salivary flow and dry-mouth symptoms versus placebo?
balance: LIKELY — two placebo-controlled randomised trials agree, with an anchor correction disclosed here: the topic file pinned Johnson 1993 (PMID 8326972) as the Sjögren's trial, but that record is post-IRRADIATION xerostomia in head-and-neck cancer patients — a different population answering a different question — so it is not carded on this shelf. LIKELY on direction and consistency; the absence of printed responder rates in both abstracts is stated plainly.

title: Methylnaltrexone for opioid-induced constipation in advanced illness (Thomas)
question: In patients with advanced illness and opioid-induced constipation unresponsive to laxatives, does subcutaneous methylnaltrexone induce laxation versus placebo?
balance: LIKELY — one fully reported phase III trial (Thomas 2008, n=133) plus the pooled responder analysis of both phase III trials, carded second and labelled post hoc. In Thomas, laxation within 4 hours of the first dose occurred in 48% on methylnaltrexone versus 15% on placebo, and after at least two of the first four doses in 52% versus 8% (P<0.001 for both co-primary outcomes), with no evidence of central opioid withdrawal or loss of analgesia. The pooled analysis of Studies 301 and 302 (the second trial is represented through this pooled report; its standalone primary report was not pinned in this build, and the structure is disclosed rather than hidden) found rescue-free bowel movements within 4 hours in more than 50% on methylnaltrexone versus 14.6% on placebo (P<0.0001). No mortality claim is made or supported by this shelf: post hoc survival analyses of these pooled data exist in the literature but are not randomised mortality evidence and are not carded.

title: Octreotide for malignant bowel obstruction
question: In patients with inoperable malignant bowel obstruction, does octreotide reduce vomiting versus placebo (with standard co-therapy)?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — one randomised trial whose primary endpoint was null. The topic file anchored this shelf on the trial's quality-of-life secondary report and spoke of the parent trial as a separate source; there is one trial, reported twice, and it is counted once here, with the primary report (Currow 2015 — the file's 'Curley' attribution is also corrected) leading the shelf. On the primary outcome, days free of vomiting at 72 hours, octreotide did not beat placebo (17 versus 14 patients completely free of vomiting, P=0.67; mean days free 1.87 versus 1.69, P=0.47). An adjusted secondary analysis found fewer vomiting episodes on octreotide (incidence rate ratio 0.40 in relative terms, 95% CI 0.19–0.86; P=0.019), but octreotide patients were also twice as likely to receive hyoscine butylbromide (P=0.004), a confounder the authors themselves raise; and the quality-of-life report found no between-group difference. A null primary with a confounded adjusted secondary signal earns MAYBE (weak evidence) — enough to justify the further study the authors call for, not enough to claim benefit.

title: Cannabis extract for refractory chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting (Grimison)
question: In patients with refractory CINV despite guideline prophylaxis, does an oral THC:CBD cannabis extract improve complete response versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE — one randomised placebo-controlled trial, flagged here as a two-trial-gate exception candidate. The topic file offered older dronabinol and nabilone trials as the second leg; those are different agents tested before modern prophylaxis existed — a different question — and they are not imported. In the carded trial, an oral THC:CBD extract (2.5 mg/2.5 mg three times daily) added to guideline-consistent prophylaxis raised complete response (no vomiting or retching and no rescue medication, hours 0–120) from 8% to 24% (absolute difference 16 points, 95% CI 4–28; P=.01) in patients whose nausea or vomiting was already refractory. Two qualifications belong on the face of the shelf: the trial recruited 147 evaluable patients against a planned 250, so it is smaller than designed; and the benefit came with more sedation (18% versus 7%), dizziness (10% versus 0%) and transient anxiety (4% versus 1%). If the developer rejects the exception, withdraw the shelf.

title: Fostamatinib for chronic immune thrombocytopenia (FIT-1 & FIT-2)
question: In adults with persistent or chronic ITP and an insufficient response to prior therapy, does fostamatinib achieve stable platelet responses versus placebo?
balance: LIKELY — two parallel phase III randomised trials (FIT-1 and FIT-2), reported together in a single publication and carded as what they are: two trials in one report, with the pooled denominators the report itself uses. A correction to the topic file: stable response was 18% on fostamatinib versus 2% on placebo (P=.0003), not 0% as filed. Responses were achieved in a heavily pretreated population (median ITP duration 8.5 years; baseline median platelet count 16,000/µL; many had failed splenectomy, thrombopoietin agents and/or rituximab). The 'overall response' figure (43% versus 14%) was defined retrospectively in the report and is flagged as such on the card; the prespecified stable-response endpoint carries the stamp. Costs: diarrhoea (31% versus 15%), hypertension (28% versus 13%), nausea and transaminase rises. The trials' registry IDs do not appear in the record's databank fields and are stated as absent rather than supplied from elsewhere.

title: Platelet transfusion thresholds in preterm infants (PlaNeT-2)
question: In preterm infants born before 34 weeks' gestation who develop severe thrombocytopenia, does a higher platelet-transfusion threshold (50 × 10⁹/L) versus a lower threshold (25 × 10⁹/L) change the rate of death or major bleeding?
balance: LIKELY (harm) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: death is a component of the primary outcome). One large multicentre randomised trial, reported in its primary paper and a prespecified 2-year follow-up — one trial, counted once, stated on the face of the shelf. The question is corrected from the topic file, which described the population by birth weight (under 1500 g); the record enrolled infants born before 34 weeks' gestation with severe thrombocytopenia (platelets <50 × 10⁹/L; median birth weight 740 g). The liberal threshold caused harm: death or new major bleeding within 28 days occurred in 26% at the 50 × 10⁹/L threshold versus 19% at 25 × 10⁹/L (odds ratio 1.57 in relative terms, 95% CI 1.06–2.32; P=0.02), and at 2 years death or neurodevelopmental impairment remained higher (50% versus 39%; OR 1.54; P=0.017). The liberal arm was also transfused far more (90% versus 53% received at least one transfusion) — more product, more harm. Single trial, but large, multicentre and internally consistent across two timepoints; if the developer wants a second trial before any stamp, this shelf should be held rather than softened.

title: Luspatercept in transfusion-dependent beta-thalassaemia (BELIEVE)
question: In adults with transfusion-dependent beta-thalassaemia, does luspatercept reduce red-cell transfusion burden versus placebo?
balance: LIKELY — one phase III trial, flagged here as a two-trial-gate exception candidate, reported in its primary paper and a long-term final report (one trial, counted once). The topic file anchored the shelf on the final-results paper and described sustained benefit 'versus placebo over long-term follow-up'; the record is more precise — placebo-controlled comparison ends at unblinding, and the final report explicitly performs no comparative analyses after week 96 because of crossover. The randomised result stands on the primary report: a ≥33% transfusion-burden reduction with ≥2 fewer units during weeks 13–24 in 21.4% on luspatercept versus 4.5% on placebo (P<0.001), with 70.5% versus 29.5% achieving ≥33% reduction over any 12-week interval. Long-term follow-up shows the effect is durable on treatment (77% achieved a ≥33% reduction over some 12-week interval across follow-up) with no treatment-related deaths. If the developer rejects the single-trial exception, this shelf should be withdrawn.

title: Mitapivat in pyruvate kinase deficiency (ACTIVATE)
question: In adults with pyruvate kinase deficiency who are not regularly transfused, does mitapivat raise haemoglobin versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE — one phase III randomised trial in a rare disease, flagged here as a two-trial-gate exception candidate. In ACTIVATE (n=80, patients not regularly transfused), a sustained haemoglobin response (rise ≥1.5 g/dL at two or more of the week 16/20/24 assessments) occurred in 16 of 40 patients (40%) on mitapivat versus none of 40 on placebo (adjusted difference 39.3 percentage points, 95% CI 24.1–54.6; two-sided P<0.001), with all secondary endpoints favouring mitapivat; the abstract asserts the average haemoglobin change favoured mitapivat without printing its size, and none is supplied here. A correction to the topic file's 'DOUBLE-A' label: the companion ACTIVATE-T study is an open-label, SINGLE-ARM trial in regularly transfused patients — a different population and no control group — so it cannot serve as this shelf's second randomised trial; it is fenced in the synthesis card, not carded as evidence. Grade ≥3 adverse events were more frequent on mitapivat (25% versus 13%). If the developer rejects the rare-disease exception, this shelf should be withdrawn.

title: Ravulizumab versus eculizumab in paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria (Studies 301 and 302)
question: In adults with paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria, is the long-acting C5 inhibitor ravulizumab (every 8 weeks) non-inferior to eculizumab (every 2 weeks) — in patients new to complement inhibition, and in patients already stable on eculizumab?
balance: LIKELY — two parallel phase 3 randomised trials, one in complement-inhibitor-naive patients (Study 301) and one in patients stable on eculizumab (Study 302), each found ravulizumab non-inferior to eculizumab on every prespecified endpoint, with a similar safety profile; the practical gain is dosing every 8 weeks instead of every 2. Both trials were open-label (the infusion schedules cannot be blinded) and both were non-inferiority designs against an active standard, not placebo tests of efficacy. Scope boundary: this shelf is the terminal-C5 head-to-head; proximal complement inhibition (pegcetacoplan and its class) is a different question, homed on Shelf #845. PROPOSED: LIKELY.

title: Platelet transfusion after antiplatelet-associated intracerebral haemorrhage (PATCH)
question: In patients with spontaneous intracerebral haemorrhage who were taking antiplatelet therapy, does platelet transfusion improve functional outcome versus standard care alone?
balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — a single randomised trial found platelet transfusion made things worse: the odds of death or dependence at 3 months were about doubled. title: Abelacimab versus rivaroxaban in atrial fibrillation (AZALEA-TIMI 71)
question: In patients with atrial fibrillation at moderate-to-high stroke risk, does the factor XI inhibitor abelacimab reduce major or clinically relevant bleeding versus rivaroxaban?
balance: POSSIBLE — the trial was stopped early because bleeding on monthly abelacimab injections was far lower than on rivaroxaban (hazard ratios 0.38 and 0.31 for the two doses). Two cautions define this shelf. First, the primary endpoint is bleeding, a safety outcome: the record reports no stroke or systemic-embolism efficacy results, and no claim that abelacimab prevents stroke as effectively as rivaroxaban can be made or supported from this record. Second, early stopping for a larger-than-expected benefit tends to inflate the estimated effect. PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C): an anticoagulant comparison in atrial fibrillation, where any benefit claim is framed against stroke-prevention therapy. PROPOSED as a two-trial-gate exception candidate: a single trial, stopped early; the shelf should be withdrawn or re-scoped if the developer rejects the exception.

title: Voclosporin in active lupus nephritis (AURORA 1)

title: Upadacitinib in giant cell arteritis (SELECT-GCA)

title: Tapering low-dose glucocorticoids in senior rheumatoid arthritis (the GLORIA programme)
question: In patients aged 65 and over with rheumatoid arthritis who have taken low-dose prednisolone for two years in the GLORIA trial, can the glucocorticoid be tapered and stopped over three months without loss of disease control — and what did the two years of treatment itself achieve?
balance: POSSIBLE — the GLORIA trial showed two years of add-on prednisolone 5 mg/day modestly improved disease activity and joint damage in patients aged 65+, at the cost of more (mostly non-severe) adverse events; its blinded tapering study then showed that stopping over three months returned disease activity to placebo-group levels, with a numerical (not significant) excess of flares and no evidence of adrenal insufficiency. The tapering study is a post-trial withdrawal phase in trial completers, not a fresh randomisation, and is carded as such. PROPOSED: POSSIBLE.

title: Methotrexate for painful knee osteoarthritis (PROMOTE)
question: In adults with painful knee osteoarthritis, does weekly oral methotrexate added to usual analgesia reduce knee pain versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE — a single multicentre double-blind trial found a statistically significant but small average pain benefit at 6 months: 0.79 points on a 0-to-10 scale, with a confidence interval (0.08 to 1.51) that reaches from negligible to worthwhile. Stiffness and function also favoured methotrexate, and an adherence analysis suggested a dose-response. The card prints the effect's size plainly; whether an average gain under one point justifies weekly methotrexate's monitoring burden is a clinical judgement this record informs but does not settle. PROPOSED as a two-trial-gate exception candidate: a single trial; the shelf should be withdrawn or re-scoped if the developer rejects the exception. A later biomarker substudy of PROMOTE (PMID 42413648) reports the pain response concentrated in participants with elevated baseline hs-CRP — a subgroup finding, fenced in the synthesis card, not carded as evidence.

title: Hydroxychloroquine withdrawal in stable systemic lupus erythematosus
question: In patients with clinically stable systemic lupus erythematosus, does withdrawing hydroxychloroquine increase the risk of disease flare versus continuing it?
balance: POSSIBLE — the only randomised withdrawal trial (47 patients, 1991) found that switching stable patients to placebo roughly doubled-to-tripled flare risk over 24 weeks (relative risk 2.5, 95% CI 1.08 to 5.58; flares in 16 of 22 versus 9 of 25). The direction has never been contradicted and underlies the modern practice of continuing hydroxychloroquine indefinitely, but the evidence is one small trial from before modern background therapy. title: Mycophenolate versus cyclophosphamide in scleroderma lung disease (SLS I and SLS II)
question: In patients with systemic-sclerosis interstitial lung disease, does immunosuppression improve forced vital capacity — cyclophosphamide versus placebo, and two years of mycophenolate mofetil versus one year of oral cyclophosphamide?
balance: LIKELY — the programme's two randomised trials together support both drugs. SLS I showed one year of oral cyclophosphamide beat placebo on forced vital capacity by 2.53 percentage points of predicted value. SLS II then compared the two active strategies head-to-head: its prespecified primary analysis was negative for the hypothesis that mycophenolate would prove superior at 24 months (p=0.24), with FVC improving within both groups (2.19 and 2.88 points) and mycophenolate clearly better tolerated (leucopenia in 4 versus 30 patients; premature withdrawal 20 versus 32). Deaths over 24 months in SLS II were 5 (7%) on mycophenolate versus 11 (15%) on cyclophosphamide, mostly from progressive lung disease — printed beside the primary results as the record reports them; SLS II was not powered for mortality. Scope boundary: nintedanib and tocilizumab in systemic-sclerosis ILD are a different question, homed on Shelf #688. PROPOSED: LIKELY.

title: Autologous stem-cell transplantation in severe systemic sclerosis (ASTIS and SCOT)
question: In patients with severe early diffuse systemic sclerosis, does autologous haematopoietic stem-cell transplantation improve event-free and overall survival versus monthly cyclophosphamide — and at what early cost?
balance: LIKELY — two randomised trials in different health systems point the same way: an early hazard from transplant-related deaths, then a widening long-term survival advantage over cyclophosphamide. In ASTIS, 8 treatment-related deaths occurred in the first year in the transplant arm versus none on cyclophosphamide, yet by 2 to 4 years the hazard of death or major organ failure was about a third (time-varying HR 0.35 and 0.34). In SCOT, overall survival at 72 months was 86% versus 51% in the per-protocol population, with treatment-related mortality of 6% by 72 months versus 0%. PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C): overall survival is a headline outcome. Both trials are small (156 and 75 patients) and enrolled a selected, severely affected population treated at expert centres.

title: Abaloparatide in postmenopausal osteoporosis (ACTIVE)
question: In postmenopausal women with osteoporosis, does abaloparatide reduce new vertebral fractures versus placebo — and how does it compare with teriparatide on fractures and hypercalcaemia?
balance: POSSIBLE — ACTIVE is a large (2463 women), double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial in which abaloparatide reduced new vertebral and nonvertebral fractures over 18 months and raised BMD more than placebo, with less hypercalcaemia than the open-label teriparatide arm (3.4% versus 6.4%). One verification limit must be stated plainly: the record's abstract reports the fracture results qualitatively ('occurred less frequently'; a lower Kaplan-Meier nonvertebral event rate) and does NOT print the arm-level fracture rates, which appear only in the paper's tables — so no fracture percentages are carded on this shelf, and the exact size of the fracture benefit cannot be quoted from the verified record. PROPOSED as a two-trial-gate exception candidate: a single trial; the shelf should be withdrawn or re-scoped if the developer rejects the exception. Distinct angle versus Shelf #92: that shelf asks the class question (bone-building versus antiresorptive therapy at very high risk, with ACTIVE as one of several carded trials); this shelf is the dedicated ACTIVE record — the placebo-controlled fracture outcomes and the prespecified hypercalcaemia comparison with teriparatide. title: Zoledronic acid after denosumab-teriparatide combination therapy (DATA-HD extension)
question: In postmenopausal women who have completed combined high-dose denosumab and teriparatide (DATA-HD), does a single zoledronic acid infusion preserve the bone microarchitecture and strength gains after the combination stops?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — this is a single-arm extension, not a randomised comparison: all 53 participants received zoledronic acid, so nothing here estimates zoledronic acid's effect against not giving it. The answer the record gives is largely negative for peripheral bone: despite zoledronic acid, volumetric BMD at the radius drifted back to baseline values over 27 months and estimated stiffness and failure load fell progressively (remaining above baseline only at the tibia). A correction to the topic file, which described zoledronic acid as having 'largely maintained the microarchitecture and strength gains': that maintenance claim belongs to DXA-measured spine and hip BMD in the parent DATA-HD report (as summarised in this record's introduction); for the HR-pQCT microarchitecture and strength outcomes this extension actually measured, the authors conclude a single dose was NOT as effective at maintaining the gains. The question has been kept as filed because the record answers it — mostly in the negative. PROPOSED: MAYBE (weak evidence).

title: Zoledronic acid versus risedronate in Paget's disease of bone
question: In patients with Paget's disease of bone, is a single zoledronic acid infusion superior to a course of oral risedronate for biochemical response, and is the response more durable?
balance: LIKELY — two identical randomised double-blind trials, pooled in a single report (as with FIT-1 and FIT-2 on Shelf #1800, they are carded as what they are: two trials in one publication), found a single zoledronic acid infusion clearly superior to 60 days of risedronate: therapeutic response 96.0% versus 74.3% at six months, faster normalisation of alkaline phosphatase, and far more durable responses in post-trial follow-up (loss of response 1 of 113 versus 21 of 82). The endpoints are biochemical (alkaline phosphatase), which is the accepted activity measure in Paget's disease, not a fracture or pain outcome — pain scores improved in both groups without a reported between-group difference. The record carries no registry ID (a 2005 report). PROPOSED: LIKELY.

title: Strontium ranelate in postmenopausal osteoporosis (SOTI and TROPOS)
question: In postmenopausal women with osteoporosis, does strontium ranelate reduce vertebral fractures (SOTI) and nonvertebral fractures (TROPOS) versus placebo?
balance: LIKELY — two large double-blind placebo-controlled trials, each powered for its own fracture family: SOTI (1649 women with prevalent vertebral fracture) reduced new vertebral fractures (relative risk 0.59 over three years), and TROPOS (5091 women) reduced nonvertebral fractures by a relative 16%, with a relative 36% hip-fracture reduction confined to a prespecified-age-and-BMD high-risk subgroup (flagged as a subgroup on the card). Both abstracts report relative measures without arm-level absolute fracture rates, so the cards print relative effects only and flag the missing absolutes — the absolute gains are smaller than the relative ones suggest. Adverse-event incidence was similar to placebo in both trials. Neither record carries a registry ID (2004-2005 reports). PROPOSED: LIKELY.

title: Zoledronic acid in men with osteoporosis
question: In men with osteoporosis, does annual zoledronic acid reduce vertebral fractures versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE — a single large double-blind trial (1199 men) found two annual zoledronic acid infusions cut new morphometric vertebral fractures over 24 months from 4.9% to 1.6% (relative risk 0.33). Clinical vertebral and nonvertebral fractures were also fewer but not significantly so (few events). Deaths (2.6% versus 2.9%) and serious adverse events (25.3% versus 25.2%) did not differ — printed beside the fracture results, as safety counts in a trial not powered for mortality. PROPOSED as a two-trial-gate exception candidate: a single trial; the shelf should be withdrawn or re-scoped if the developer rejects the exception.

title: Fluoride therapy in postmenopausal osteoporosis (the Riggs programme)
question: In postmenopausal women with osteoporosis, does high-dose sodium fluoride increase bone mineral density — and does it reduce vertebral fractures or increase nonvertebral fractures?
balance: POSSIBLE (no benefit, with harm) — the Riggs randomised trial (202 women, 4 years) is the definitive test of high-dose fluoride: lumbar spine BMD rose by a median 35%, yet new vertebral fractures were not reduced (163 versus 136 fractures) and nonvertebral fractures were significantly MORE frequent on fluoride (72 versus 24; P<0.01), with dose reductions for side effects in 54 versus 24 women. The 1994 extended observations (a single-arm follow-up of 50 treated women) found spine BMD kept rising for 6 years and speculated that lower doses might thread the needle — an authors' hypothesis from uncontrolled data, flagged as such on its card, not a finding. One trial programme: the shelf stands as a two-trial-gate exception candidate, kept because the harm answer is clinically important and unlikely ever to be re-tested at this dose. PROPOSED: POSSIBLE (no benefit, with harm), as a two-trial-gate exception candidate.

title: High-dose versus standard-dose teriparatide, each combined with denosumab (DATA-HD)
question: In postmenopausal women with osteoporosis, does doubling the teriparatide dose within denosumab combination therapy (40 versus 20 micrograms daily) increase spine and hip BMD more over 15 months?
balance: POSSIBLE — with a correction to the topic file, disclosed here: the filed question asked whether the combination beats 'either agent alone'. That is the parent DATA study's question, not DATA-HD's. The verified DATA-HD record randomised women between two doses of teriparatide (40 versus 20 micrograms), with denosumab added in BOTH arms — there is no monotherapy arm — and the shelf's question has been re-scoped to the comparison the trial actually made. title: Romosozumab versus teriparatide after oral bisphosphonates (STRUCTURE)
question: In postmenopausal women with osteoporosis transitioning from oral bisphosphonate therapy, does romosozumab increase total-hip BMD more than teriparatide over 12 months?
balance: POSSIBLE — a single open-label phase 3 trial (436 women, all previously on oral bisphosphonates) found total-hip BMD rose 2.6% over 12 months on romosozumab while falling 0.6% on teriparatide (difference 3.2 percentage points). Hypercalcaemia was much less frequent on romosozumab (under 1% versus 10%). title: Nasal salmon calcitonin in established osteoporosis (PROOF)
question: In postmenopausal women with established osteoporosis, does nasal salmon calcitonin reduce new vertebral fractures versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE — the single large trial (PROOF, 1255 women, 5 years) found a significant vertebral-fracture reduction at exactly one of its three doses: 200 IU daily (relative risk 0.67; 51 of 287 versus 70 of 270), while 100 IU (RR 0.85) and 400 IU (RR 0.84) were not significant. A benefit confined to the middle dose, with no dose-response, is a fragile pattern that multiplicity can manufacture, and the cards flag it as such; the 200 IU result is nonetheless the trial's prespecified primary comparison. Attrition was heavy (only 511 of 1255 women completed 5 years). PROPOSED as a two-trial-gate exception candidate: a single trial; the shelf should be withdrawn or re-scoped if the developer rejects the exception.

title: Perioperative and neoadjuvant immunotherapy in resectable NSCLC (CheckMate 816, KEYNOTE-671, AEGEAN)
question: In resectable stage II-III non-small-cell lung cancer, does adding PD-(L)1 blockade to platinum chemotherapy around surgery — neoadjuvant or perioperative — improve event-free survival versus chemotherapy alone?
balance: LIKELY for event-free survival — three large randomised trials with three different antibodies converge: event-free survival hazard ratios of 0.63 (CheckMate 816, neoadjuvant nivolumab), 0.58 (KEYNOTE-671, perioperative pembrolizumab) and 0.68 (AEGEAN, perioperative durvalumab), with pathological complete response rates roughly five-to-ten-fold higher than chemotherapy alone. The survival ledger is younger: in the reports carded here, overall survival had NOT reached significance in either trial that reported it (CheckMate 816 first interim HR 0.57, confidence interval crossing 1; KEYNOTE-671 24-month survival 80.9% versus 77.6%, P=0.02 against a stricter prespecified criterion) — so no mortality claim is made on this shelf, and the stamp covers event-free survival and pathological response. PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C): a class whose rationale is an eventual survival benefit. Later overall-survival reports should be swept and carded as updates to these trials, not as new shelves.

title: Adjuvant immunotherapy after resection and chemotherapy in NSCLC (IMpower010, KEYNOTE-091)
question: In completely resected stage IB-IIIA non-small-cell lung cancer, does one year of adjuvant PD-(L)1 blockade after resection (with adjuvant chemotherapy in most patients) improve disease-free survival versus observation or placebo — and does PD-L1 expression identify who benefits?
balance: SPLIT — LIKELY that adjuvant immunotherapy improves disease-free survival in the overall resected population: two large trials agree (IMpower010 DFS HR 0.81 in the intention-to-treat population; KEYNOTE-091 median DFS 53.6 versus 42.0 months, HR 0.76). title: First-line alectinib versus crizotinib in ALK-positive NSCLC (ALEX and ALESIA)
question: In untreated ALK-positive advanced non-small-cell lung cancer, does alectinib improve progression-free survival and CNS control versus crizotinib?

title: Prophylactic cranial irradiation in extensive-stage small-cell lung cancer: two eras, two answers
question: In extensive-stage small-cell lung cancer responding to chemotherapy, does prophylactic cranial irradiation improve overall survival — in the era before routine brain MRI, and in the era of MRI staging and surveillance?
balance: SPLIT — the two randomised trials disagree because their worlds differ, and the balance is the shelf. The EORTC trial (Slotman 2007), conducted without baseline brain imaging or MRI surveillance, found prophylactic cranial irradiation cut symptomatic brain metastases (hazard ratio 0.27; 1-year cumulative incidence 14.6% versus 40.4%) and improved 1-year survival (27.1% versus 13.3%). The Japanese trial (Takahashi 2017), which required MRI-confirmed absence of brain metastases at entry and MRI surveillance every 3 months, found no survival benefit (hazard ratio 1.27, favouring observation numerically) and was stopped early for futility. The honest reading: where MRI surveillance is practised, Slotman's survival benefit has not been reproduced; where it is not, the older result may still hold. PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C): survival claims in both directions.

title: Postoperative radiotherapy after complete resection of stage IIIA-N2 non-small-cell lung cancer (Lung ART; PORT-C)
question: In completely resected stage IIIA N2 NSCLC after (neo)adjuvant chemotherapy, does modern postoperative radiotherapy improve disease-free or overall survival versus no PORT?
balance: Two large phase 3 trials asked whether modern mediastinal postoperative radiotherapy (PORT) helps after complete resection of stage IIIA-N2 non-small-cell lung cancer, and both missed their primary endpoint. In Lung ART (n=501), 3-year disease-free survival was 47% with PORT versus 44% without (HR 0.86, 95% CI 0.68–1.08, p=0.18). In PORT-C (n=364 eligible), 3-year disease-free survival was 40.5% versus 32.7% (HR 0.84, 95% CI 0.65–1.09, P=.20 unadjusted), and 3-year overall survival was 78.3% with PORT versus 82.8% without (HR 1.02) — no survival gain in either direction of the comparison. PORT did improve locoregional control in PORT-C (locoregional recurrence-free survival HR 0.71), but at a toxicity price: in Lung ART, late grade 3–4 cardiopulmonary toxicity was 11% with PORT versus 5% without, and all three treatment-related deaths (two from pneumonitis, one from chemotherapy sepsis) occurred in the PORT arm. The exploratory and per-protocol analyses suggesting a DFS signal in PORT-C were pre-planned as exploratory or post-randomisation subsets and do not overturn the intention-to-treat nulls. Balance: routine mediastinal PORT after complete resection of IIIA-N2 disease does not improve disease-free or overall survival and adds cardiopulmonary harm; it is not standard care. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).

title: ctDNA-guided adjuvant therapy in stage II colon cancer (DYNAMIC)
question: In resected stage II colon cancer, does a ctDNA-guided strategy (chemotherapy only if ctDNA-positive) safely reduce chemotherapy use without compromising recurrence-free survival versus standard clinicopathological management?
balance: One strategy trial answers this question. In DYNAMIC (n=455), management guided by circulating tumour DNA results roughly halved adjuvant chemotherapy use (15% vs 28%) while 2-year recurrence-free survival was noninferior to standard clinicopathological management (93.5% vs 92.4%; absolute difference +1.1 percentage points, 95% CI −4.1 to 6.2, against a noninferiority margin of −8.5 points). At 3 years, recurrence-free survival was 86.4% in ctDNA-positive patients who received chemotherapy and 92.5% in ctDNA-negative patients who did not. Two cautions keep the stamp moderate: this is a single trial with a wide noninferiority margin, and the record does not show that chemotherapy actually improves outcomes for ctDNA-positive patients — DYNAMIC tested the strategy, not the treatment; the confirmatory trials (COBRA, CIRCULATE and others) were still in flight when this record was published. No survival (mortality) claim is made or supported by this record. PROPOSED POSSIBLE.

title: Trifluridine/tipiracil (TAS-102) in refractory metastatic colorectal cancer (RECOURSE; TERRA)
question: In metastatic colorectal cancer refractory to fluoropyrimidine, oxaliplatin, irinotecan and biologics, does trifluridine/tipiracil improve overall survival versus placebo?
balance: Two double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trials in chemotherapy-refractory metastatic colorectal cancer agree. In the global RECOURSE trial (n=800), trifluridine/tipiracil (TAS-102) improved median overall survival from 5.3 to 7.1 months (HR for death 0.68, 95% CI 0.58–0.81, P<0.001) and delayed worsening of performance status. In the Asian TERRA trial (n=406), the survival benefit replicated: median overall survival 7.8 versus 7.1 months (HR 0.79, 95% CI 0.62–0.99, P=.035). The absolute gains are modest — roughly one to two months of median survival in a population with no remaining standard options — and the price is myelosuppression: neutropenia in 38% and febrile neutropenia in 4% in RECOURSE, with one treatment-related death; TERRA reported no treatment-related deaths and serious adverse-event rates similar to placebo (23.2% vs 23.7%). Balance: a real, replicated survival benefit of modest absolute size in refractory disease. PROPOSED LIKELY pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).

title: Regorafenib in treatment-refractory metastatic colorectal cancer (CORRECT; CONCUR)
question: In metastatic colorectal cancer after all standard therapies, does regorafenib improve overall survival versus placebo?
balance: Regorafenib was the first agent to prolong survival in treatment-refractory metastatic colorectal cancer — flagged OUTSTANDING-SINGLE for CORRECT in the topic plan — and the benefit was then confirmed by a second double-blind trial, so the shelf stands on two trials. In CORRECT (n=760, global), median overall survival was 6.4 months on regorafenib versus 5.0 on placebo (HR 0.77, 95% CI 0.64–0.94); in CONCUR (n=204, Asian patients), median overall survival was 8.8 versus 6.3 months (HR 0.55, 95% CI 0.40–0.77). Both trials report one-sided P values (CORRECT one-sided p=0.0052, endpoint met at a pre-planned interim analysis; CONCUR one-sided p=0.00016), which are flagged as one-sided on the cards. The absolute gain is modest — about 1.4 months of median survival in CORRECT — and toxicity is substantial: treatment-related adverse events in 93% on regorafenib in CORRECT, with grade ≥3 hand-foot skin reaction in 17%, fatigue 10%, diarrhoea 7% and hypertension 7%. Balance: a real, replicated survival benefit of small absolute size, bought with considerable skin and constitutional toxicity in patients without other options. PROPOSED LIKELY pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).

title: Triplet FOLFOXIRI plus bevacizumab versus doublet chemotherapy plus bevacizumab in metastatic colorectal cancer (TRIBE; TRIBE2)
question: In untreated metastatic colorectal cancer fit for intensive therapy, does triplet FOLFOXIRI plus bevacizumab improve outcomes versus a doublet plus bevacizumab?
balance: Upfront triplet chemotherapy improves progression outcomes but has not, on the carded primary records, been shown to extend life. In TRIBE (n=508), FOLFOXIRI plus bevacizumab beat FOLFIRI plus bevacizumab on the primary endpoint of progression-free survival (12.1 vs 9.7 months; HR 0.75, 95% CI 0.62–0.90, P=0.003) and response rate (65% vs 53%), but overall survival — 31.0 versus 25.8 months, HR 0.79 (95% CI 0.63–1.00), P=0.054 — did NOT reach significance in the primary report; the drafting topic file's implication of an overall-survival benefit is not supported by the record and is corrected here. In TRIBE2 (n=679), an upfront-triplet strategy with reintroduction beat a pre-planned doublet sequence on its primary endpoint, progression-free survival 2 (19.2 vs 16.4 months; HR 0.74, 95% CI 0.63–0.88, p=0.0005); the TRIBE2 record prints no overall-survival figures, so none are carded. The cost is real toxicity: in TRIBE2's first-line phase, grade 3–4 neutropenia occurred in 50% versus 21% and diarrhoea in 17% versus 5%, with eight treatment-related deaths in the triplet-strategy arm versus four in the control arm. Balance: for fit patients the triplet buys response and progression control, not proven survival. PROPOSED POSSIBLE pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).

title: Adding bevacizumab to first-line chemotherapy in metastatic colorectal cancer (AVF2107g; NO16966)
question: In untreated metastatic colorectal cancer, does adding bevacizumab to chemotherapy improve overall survival?
balance: The answer depends on the chemotherapy backbone. With the irinotecan–bolus-fluorouracil regimen (IFL) used in the 2004 pivotal trial AVF2107g (n=813), adding bevacizumab produced a clear survival benefit: median overall survival 20.3 versus 15.6 months (HR for death 0.66, P<0.001), with progression-free survival 10.6 versus 6.2 months (HR 0.54) and response 44.8% versus 34.8%. With the oxaliplatin doublets that later became standard, the much larger NO16966 trial (n=1,401) found a significant progression-free-survival gain (9.4 vs 8.0 months; HR 0.83, P=.0023) but overall survival of 21.3 versus 19.9 months (HR 0.89; 97.5% CI 0.76–1.03; P=.077) — not significant — and no response-rate improvement; the trial's own analysis noted that few patients were actually treated until progression (29% of the bevacizumab group), which may have diluted the survival effect. The consistent harm is hypertension (grade 3 hypertension 11.0% vs 2.3% in AVF2107g). Balance: bevacizumab prolongs progression-free survival across backbones; a survival benefit is proven with IFL and attenuated, not excluded, with modern oxaliplatin doublets. PROPOSED POSSIBLE pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).

title: Total neoadjuvant therapy with watch-and-wait organ preservation in locally advanced rectal cancer (OPRA)
question: In locally advanced rectal cancer, does total neoadjuvant therapy with a watch-and-wait option for clinical complete responders achieve organ preservation without compromising disease-free survival versus chemoradiotherapy, total mesorectal excision and adjuvant chemotherapy?
balance: One randomised phase 2 trial supports the strategy, with an important design caveat. In OPRA (n=324 with stage II–III rectal adenocarcinoma), total neoadjuvant therapy — induction chemotherapy then chemoradiotherapy, or chemoradiotherapy then consolidation chemotherapy — followed by total mesorectal excision or watch-and-wait according to response achieved 3-year disease-free survival of 76% in both sequence groups, matching the 75% rate of the historical controls the trial was designed against. Organ preservation differed by sequence: 3-year TME-free survival was 53% with chemoradiotherapy-then-consolidation and 41% with induction-then-chemoradiotherapy (the drafting topic file's figure of 47% does not appear in the record and is corrected here — no overall-survival claim is made or supported). No differences were found between the groups in local recurrence-free, distant metastasis-free, or overall survival, and patients salvaged with TME after tumour regrowth had similar disease-free survival to those taken straight to TME. The caveat: OPRA was designed as two stand-alone studies benchmarked against historical data, not as a randomised comparison against the standard chemoradiotherapy–TME–adjuvant-chemotherapy pathway, so 'without detriment' rests partly on that historical benchmark. PROPOSED POSSIBLE.
