title: Oxaliplatin HIPEC added to cytoreductive surgery for colorectal peritoneal metastases (PRODIGE 7)
question: In colorectal peritoneal metastases undergoing complete cytoreductive surgery, does adding oxaliplatin HIPEC improve overall survival versus cytoreductive surgery alone?
balance: A single phase 3 trial overturned an entrenched practice. In PRODIGE 7 (n=265 patients with colorectal peritoneal metastases in whom complete or near-complete cytoreduction was achieved), adding oxaliplatin HIPEC to cytoreductive surgery produced median overall survival of 41.7 months versus 41.2 months with surgery alone — a hazard ratio of 1.00 (95.37% CI 0.63–1.58; p=0.99), as flat a null as a trial prints. Treatment-related deaths at 30 days were 2% in each group, but by 60 days grade 3 or worse adverse events were more frequent with HIPEC (26% vs 15%; p=0.035). The confidence interval is wide — the trial cannot exclude a moderate benefit or harm — which is why the stamp is POSSIBLE rather than LIKELY: the point estimate is exactly null and the practice-changing weight of the trial is high, but it is one trial of 265 patients. Balance: oxaliplatin HIPEC as delivered in PRODIGE 7 adds late morbidity and no survival; cytoreductive surgery alone is the cornerstone. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).

title: Perioperative FOLFOX for resectable colorectal liver metastases (EORTC 40983): a progression-free-survival gain that did not become a survival gain
question: In resectable colorectal liver metastases, does perioperative FOLFOX improve progression-free survival versus surgery alone, and does the benefit persist as overall survival?
balance: One trial answers both halves of the question, and the two halves diverge. In EORTC 40983 (n=364 with up to four resectable liver metastases), perioperative FOLFOX4 (six cycles before and six after surgery) raised 3-year progression-free survival from 28.1% to 35.4% in the intention-to-treat analysis — an absolute gain of 7.3 points that narrowly missed significance (HR 0.79, 95% CI 0.62–1.02, p=0.058) and was significant in the eligible (HR 0.77, p=0.041) and resected (HR 0.73, p=0.025) populations. With 8.5 years of median follow-up, however, overall survival showed no difference: median 61.3 versus 54.3 months (HR 0.88, 95% CI 0.68–1.14, p=0.34), 5-year survival 51.2% versus 47.8%, deaths 59% versus 63%. Postoperative complications were more frequent after chemotherapy (25% vs 16%; p=0.04). No mortality claim is made or supported by this shelf: overall survival was not the trial's primary endpoint, the comparison was underpowered for it, and the honest summary is a progression-free-survival benefit that did not persist as a survival benefit. PROPOSED POSSIBLE.

title: First-line cetuximab versus bevacizumab with chemotherapy in RAS wild-type metastatic colorectal cancer (FIRE-3; CALGB/SWOG 80405)
question: In KRAS/RAS wild-type metastatic colorectal cancer, is FOLFIRI plus cetuximab superior to FOLFIRI plus bevacizumab as first-line therapy?
balance: The two head-to-head trials disagree, and the disagreement is the answer. FIRE-3 (n=592, Germany/Austria, FOLFIRI backbone) MISSED its primary endpoint — objective response 62.0% on cetuximab versus 58.0% on bevacizumab (OR 1.18, p=0.18) — with no progression-free-survival difference (10.0 vs 10.3 months; HR 1.06), yet reported longer overall survival with cetuximab (28.7 vs 25.0 months; HR 0.77, 95% CI 0.62–0.96, p=0.017), an advantage that grew in the post-hoc extended-RAS wild-type subgroup (33.1 vs 25.0 months; HR 0.70) — a subgroup analysis, labelled as such on the card, not the randomised primary population. CALGB/SWOG 80405 (n=1,137, North America, physician-choice FOLFOX or FOLFIRI backbone, overall survival as the PRIMARY endpoint) found no significant difference: median overall survival 30.0 versus 29.0 months (HR 0.88, 95% CI 0.77–1.01, P=.08), progression-free survival HR 0.95, response 59.6% versus 55.2% (P=.13). The trials differ in backbone, geography and era, and neither carded record provides the tumour-sidedness analysis that later came to dominate this choice, so no sidedness figures are carded here. Balance: cetuximab-first is not proven superior; FIRE-3's survival signal is real but rests on a secondary endpoint and a post-hoc subgroup against a larger trial whose primary survival analysis was null. PROPOSED POSSIBLE pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).

title: Adjuvant low-dose aspirin in PI3K-altered localised colorectal cancer (ALASCCA) — OUTSTANDING-SINGLE
question: In resected stage I–III colorectal cancer with PI3K-pathway alterations (PIK3CA / PIK3R1 / PTEN), does low-dose aspirin reduce recurrence versus placebo?
balance: OUTSTANDING-SINGLE: one double-blind, placebo-controlled trial with a recurrence risk roughly halved in a biomarker-defined population, flagged under the developer's standing rule for outstanding single trials. In ALASCCA (626 patients randomised from 2,980 genotyped; PI3K-pathway alterations found in 37.0%), aspirin 160 mg daily for 3 years cut the estimated 3-year recurrence incidence from 14.1% to 7.7% in the pre-specified primary group with PIK3CA exon 9/20 hotspot mutations (HR 0.49, 95% CI 0.24–0.98, P=0.04) and from 16.8% to 7.7% in the broader group with other PIK3CA/PIK3R1/PTEN alterations (HR 0.42, 95% CI 0.21–0.83). Disease-free survival favoured aspirin in both groups (HR 0.61 in group A, not significant; HR 0.51 in group B), and severe adverse events were more frequent on aspirin (16.8% vs 11.6%). The cautious points: the confidence intervals are wide, the group A result rests on P=0.04, and this is a recurrence endpoint — the record makes NO mortality claim, and none is carded. Until a second trial or a survival analysis appears, this stays a single-trial shelf the developer may card as OUTSTANDING-SINGLE. PROPOSED POSSIBLE.

title: Trastuzumab deruxtecan in HER2-low metastatic breast cancer (DESTINY-Breast04) — OUTSTANDING-SINGLE
question: In previously treated HER2-low (IHC 1+ or 2+/ISH−) metastatic breast cancer, does trastuzumab deruxtecan improve progression-free and overall survival versus physician's-choice chemotherapy?
balance: OUTSTANDING-SINGLE: one open-label trial that created a new treatment category and showed a survival benefit in it. In DESTINY-Breast04 (n=557 with HER2-low metastatic breast cancer after one or two lines of chemotherapy), trastuzumab deruxtecan beat physician's-choice chemotherapy on every pre-specified endpoint: in the hormone-receptor-positive cohort (494 patients), median progression-free survival was 10.1 versus 5.4 months (HR 0.51) and overall survival 23.9 versus 17.5 months (HR 0.64, P=0.003); among all patients, overall survival was 23.4 versus 16.8 months (HR 0.64, P=0.001). Grade ≥3 adverse events were actually less frequent on the conjugate (52.6% vs 67.4%), but its signature harm is interstitial lung disease: adjudicated drug-related ILD or pneumonitis in 12.1%, with grade 5 events in 0.8%. The stamp is POSSIBLE, not LIKELY, because the result stands on a single — albeit large and internally consistent — open-label trial; distinct from the HER2-positive comparison on Shelf #856 (trastuzumab deruxtecan versus T-DM1), this shelf's question is the HER2-low population. PROPOSED POSSIBLE pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).

title: PD-(L)1 blockade plus chemotherapy in advanced triple-negative breast cancer (KEYNOTE-355; IMpassion130)
question: In untreated PD-L1-positive (CPS ≥10) advanced triple-negative breast cancer, does pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy improve overall survival versus chemotherapy?
balance: For the question as posed — pembrolizumab in CPS ≥10 disease — a double-blind trial answers yes. In KEYNOTE-355 (n=847), pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy improved median overall survival in the CPS ≥10 subgroup from 16.1 to 23.0 months (HR for death 0.73, 95% CI 0.55–0.95; two-sided P=0.0185, the pre-set significance criterion met), while the broader CPS ≥1 subgroup was not significant (HR 0.86; P=0.1125) and the intention-to-treat analysis (HR 0.89) was not formally tested — the benefit is bounded by the CPS ≥10 biomarker gate, and grade 3–5 regimen-related adverse events were similar (68.1% vs 66.9%). The class contrast is sobering: IMpassion130 (n=902), testing atezolizumab plus nab-paclitaxel, improved progression-free survival (ITT HR 0.80) but its intention-to-treat overall survival was not significant (21.3 vs 17.6 months; HR 0.84; P=0.08), which stopped the hierarchical testing — so its striking PD-L1-positive survival figures (25.0 vs 15.5 months; HR 0.62) are descriptive only, never formally tested, and its PD-L1-positive definition differs from KEYNOTE-355's combined positive score. Balance: pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy prolongs survival in CPS ≥10 triple-negative disease; the atezolizumab experience shows the class effect cannot be assumed across agents and assays. PROPOSED LIKELY pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).

title: Sacituzumab govitecan in heavily pretreated metastatic triple-negative breast cancer (ASCENT) — OUTSTANDING-SINGLE
question: In metastatic triple-negative breast cancer after ≥2 prior lines, does sacituzumab govitecan improve progression-free and overall survival versus single-agent chemotherapy?
balance: OUTSTANDING-SINGLE: one open-label trial with an unusually large effect in refractory disease. In ASCENT's primary population (468 patients without brain metastases, all previously treated with taxanes), sacituzumab govitecan tripled median progression-free survival (5.6 vs 1.7 months; HR 0.41, 95% CI 0.32–0.52) and nearly doubled median overall survival (12.1 vs 6.7 months; HR for death 0.48, 95% CI 0.38–0.59), with response in 35% versus 5%. The harms are myelosuppression and gastrointestinal toxicity: grade ≥3 neutropenia 51% versus 33%, diarrhoea 10% versus <1%, febrile neutropenia 6% versus 2%; three adverse-event deaths occurred in each group, none attributed to sacituzumab. The stamp is POSSIBLE, not LIKELY, because this remains a single trial — but its effect size (a death hazard ratio of 0.48 in a population with a 6.7-month median survival on standard chemotherapy) is exactly the outstanding hard-endpoint result the developer's standing rule wants surfaced on one trial. PROPOSED POSSIBLE pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).

title: Ribociclib plus endocrine therapy and overall survival in HR-positive/HER2-negative advanced breast cancer (MONALEESA-2; MONALEESA-3)
question: In postmenopausal HR-positive/HER2-negative advanced breast cancer, does adding ribociclib to letrozole improve overall survival versus letrozole alone?
balance: Two double-blind trials of ribociclib plus endocrine therapy show significant overall-survival benefits. In MONALEESA-2 (n=668, first-line letrozole in postmenopausal patients), the protocol-specified final survival analysis after a median 6.6 years of follow-up showed median overall survival of 63.9 months with ribociclib versus 51.4 months with placebo — more than a year longer (HR for death 0.76, 95% CI 0.63–0.93, P=0.008; deaths 54.2% vs 65.6%). In MONALEESA-3 (n=726, ribociclib plus fulvestrant as first- or second-line therapy), the protocol-specified survival analysis likewise favoured ribociclib (HR 0.72, 95% CI 0.57–0.92, P=0.00455; estimated 42-month survival 57.8% vs 45.9%). Neither record reports new safety signals in these analyses. Two boundaries: the shelf answers the ribociclib question — whether the other CDK4/6 inhibitors share the survival benefit is a separate question whose trials are not carded here — and the adjuvant/early-breast-cancer CDK4/6 question is homed on Shelf #365, not here. PROPOSED LIKELY pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).

title: Adjuvant olaparib in germline BRCA1/2-mutated high-risk early breast cancer (OlympiA) — OUTSTANDING-SINGLE
question: In germline BRCA1/2-mutated, HER2-negative early breast cancer at high recurrence risk after chemotherapy, does one year of adjuvant olaparib improve invasive disease-free and overall survival versus placebo?
balance: OUTSTANDING-SINGLE: one double-blind trial, and the first to show a survival benefit from adjuvant PARP inhibition. In OlympiA (n=1,836 patients with germline BRCA1/2 pathogenic variants and high-risk HER2-negative early breast cancer after local treatment and (neo)adjuvant chemotherapy), one year of olaparib improved 3-year invasive disease-free survival from 77.1% to 85.9% (HR 0.58; 99.5% CI 0.41–0.82) at the first interim analysis; deaths were fewer on olaparib (59 vs 86; HR 0.68) but that difference did NOT cross the strict interim significance boundary (P<0.01 required; P=0.02 observed) — a boundary detail earlier summaries often drop, kept on the card here. At the pre-specified second interim analysis (median follow-up 3.5 years), overall survival did cross its boundary: HR 0.68 (98.5% CI 0.47–0.97; P=0.009 against a required P<0.015), with 4-year overall survival 89.8% versus 86.4% and 4-year invasive disease-free survival 82.7% versus 75.4%; no new safety signals and no new cases of acute myeloid leukaemia or myelodysplastic syndrome. The ovarian-cancer PARP-inhibitor questions are a different diagnosis and are homed on Shelf #364, not here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).

title: Omitting adjuvant chemotherapy guided by the 21-gene recurrence score in HR-positive/HER2-negative early breast cancer (TAILORx; RxPONDER)
question: In HR-positive/HER2-negative node-negative (and 1–3-node) early breast cancer with intermediate genomic risk, can adjuvant chemotherapy be omitted without compromising invasive disease-free survival?
balance: Two large prospective randomised trials answer this with an age/menopause boundary, not a blanket yes. In TAILORx (6,711 randomised patients with node-negative disease and recurrence scores of 11–25), endocrine therapy alone was noninferior to chemoendocrine therapy for invasive disease-free survival (HR 1.08, 95% CI 0.94–1.24), with 9-year invasive disease-free survival of 83.3% versus 84.3% and overall survival of 93.9% versus 93.8% — but the treatment effect varied with age and score (interaction P=0.004), with some chemotherapy benefit in women aged 50 or younger with scores of 16–25. In RxPONDER (5,083 patients with 1–3 positive nodes and scores of 25 or lower), postmenopausal women gained nothing from chemotherapy (5-year invasive disease-free survival 91.9% endocrine-only vs 91.3% chemoendocrine; HR 1.02, P=0.89), while premenopausal women clearly benefited (89.0% vs 93.9%; HR 0.60, P=0.002; interaction P=0.008). No mortality claim is made or supported by this shelf — the carded endpoints are invasive disease-free survival, and the survival rates printed (TAILORx 9-year overall survival ~94% in both arms) show no difference. Balance: chemotherapy can be omitted in postmenopausal patients within these score ranges, node-negative or 1–3-node; younger and premenopausal patients are the exception, not the rule. PROPOSED LIKELY.

title: Adjuvant T-DM1 for residual invasive disease after neoadjuvant therapy in HER2-positive early breast cancer (KATHERINE) — OUTSTANDING-SINGLE
question: In HER2-positive early breast cancer with residual invasive disease after neoadjuvant therapy, does adjuvant T-DM1 improve invasive disease-free and overall survival versus trastuzumab?
balance: OUTSTANDING-SINGLE: one open-label trial in the highest-risk early-disease setting, with benefits that grew at final analysis. In KATHERINE (n=1,486 patients with residual invasive disease in breast or axilla after neoadjuvant taxane-plus-trastuzumab therapy), switching adjuvant treatment to T-DM1 halved invasive disease events at the primary analysis (events in 12.2% vs 22.2%; 3-year invasive disease-free survival 88.3% vs 77.0%; HR 0.50, 95% CI 0.39–0.64). At the pre-specified final analysis (median follow-up 8.4 years), the invasive disease-free-survival advantage was sustained (HR 0.54; 7-year rates 80.8% vs 67.1%) and overall survival was significantly better with T-DM1 (HR for death 0.66, 95% CI 0.51–0.87, P=0.003; 7-year overall survival 89.1% vs 84.4%). Grade ≥3 adverse events were more frequent on T-DM1 (26.1% vs 15.7%). The stamp is POSSIBLE because a single trial carries the shelf; its size, consistency and hard-endpoint final analysis are why it is flagged OUTSTANDING-SINGLE rather than treated as a reluctant exception. PROPOSED POSSIBLE pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).

title: One-week (26 Gy in 5 fractions) versus three-week radiotherapy after surgery for early breast cancer (FAST-Forward)
question: In early breast cancer after breast-conserving surgery, is 26 Gy in 5 fractions over 1 week noninferior for local control and late toxicity versus 40 Gy in 15 fractions over 3 weeks?
balance: One very large noninferiority trial settles the 26 Gy schedule, and separates it from the 27 Gy schedule that shares its card. In FAST-Forward (n=4,096 after breast conservation surgery or mastectomy), 5-year ipsilateral breast tumour relapse was 2.1% with the standard 40 Gy in 15 fractions; the five-fraction schedules were noninferior, with absolute differences of −0.7 percentage points for 26 Gy (HR 0.67) and −0.3 points for 27 Gy (HR 0.86) against a pre-set noninferiority margin of 1.6 points of excess relapse. Late normal-tissue effects split the two experimental arms: moderate or marked clinician-assessed effects at 5 years occurred in 9.9% (40 Gy), 11.9% (26 Gy — not significantly different across 1–5 years, odds ratio 1.12, p=0.20) and 15.4% (27 Gy — significantly worse, odds ratio 1.55, p<0.0001). So the one-week answer is specifically 26 Gy in 5 fractions: equal local control, equal late toxicity, one week instead of three. The wider fractionation family (the FAST and START trials) is concordant background, named here but not carded; this shelf stands on FAST-Forward, whose size and directness carry the stamp. PROPOSED LIKELY.

title: Adjuvant capecitabine in HER2-negative/triple-negative breast cancer (CREATE-X; CIBOMA): benefit tracks the residual-disease population
question: In triple-negative (and HER2-negative) breast cancer with residual disease after neoadjuvant chemotherapy, does adjuvant capecitabine improve disease-free and overall survival versus observation?
balance: Two randomised trials of adjuvant capecitabine after standard chemotherapy point in different directions, and the population difference explains much of it. CREATE-X (n=910) enrolled the shelf's exact population — HER2-negative breast cancer with RESIDUAL invasive disease after neoadjuvant chemotherapy — and was stopped early at a pre-specified interim analysis that met its primary endpoint: 5-year disease-free survival 74.1% versus 67.6% (HR 0.70, 95% CI 0.53–0.92) and overall survival 89.2% versus 83.6% (HR for death 0.59, 95% CI 0.39–0.90), with the triple-negative subgroup showing the largest gains (disease-free survival HR 0.58; overall survival HR 0.52) and hand-foot syndrome in 73.4% of capecitabine patients. CIBOMA (n=876) enrolled early triple-negative patients after standard neo-/adjuvant chemotherapy WITHOUT requiring residual disease, and its primary analysis was null: disease-free survival HR 0.82 (95% CI 0.63–1.06; P=.136). CIBOMA's pre-planned phenotype analysis suggested benefit confined to the nonbasal subgroup (disease-free survival HR 0.53 vs 0.94 in basal; overall-survival HR 0.42 vs 1.23; interaction P=.0052) — hypothesis-generating by the authors' own statement, and flagged as such here. Balance: adjuvant capecitabine improves disease-free and overall survival where the trial question was residual disease after neoadjuvant therapy; it is not supported as blanket extended therapy after standard chemotherapy in unselected early TNBC. PROPOSED POSSIBLE pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).

title: Tucatinib plus trastuzumab and capecitabine in previously treated HER2-positive metastatic breast cancer (HER2CLIMB)
question: In HER2-positive metastatic breast cancer previously treated with trastuzumab, pertuzumab and T-DM1, does tucatinib plus trastuzumab and capecitabine improve progression-free and overall survival versus trastuzumab and capecitabine — including in patients with brain metastases?
balance: One double-blind trial answers the question, including its brain-metastases clause. In HER2CLIMB (612 patients previously treated with trastuzumab, pertuzumab and T-DM1), adding tucatinib to trastuzumab plus capecitabine improved progression-free survival in the primary population (1-year PFS 33.1% vs 12.3%; HR 0.54, 95% CI 0.42–0.71 — note the drafting topic file's 'PFS HR 0.66' is wrong; 0.66 is the overall-survival hazard ratio, and the record governs) and improved overall survival (2-year 44.9% vs 26.6%; HR for death 0.66, 95% CI 0.50–0.88, P=0.005; median 21.9 vs 17.4 months). Uniquely, the trial enrolled patients with brain metastases, in whom 1-year progression-free survival was 24.9% versus 0% (HR 0.48, 95% CI 0.34–0.69). Diarrhoea and grade ≥3 aminotransferase elevations were more common with tucatinib (the abstract does not print the percentages). The topic file called this shelf DOUBLE-A on the strength of HER2CLIMB-02, a trial of a DIFFERENT combination (tucatinib with T-DM1) that is not carded here; as built, the shelf rests on HER2CLIMB alone and is flagged as a two-trial-gate exception candidate — if the developer rejects single-trial shelves it should be withdrawn or re-scoped, though the double-blind design, the survival benefit and the brain-metastases population make it a strong candidate for his OUTSTANDING-SINGLE pathway. PROPOSED POSSIBLE pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).

title: Adding abiraterone (± enzalutamide) to ADT in high-risk non-metastatic prostate cancer (STAMPEDE platform trials)
question: In high-risk non-metastatic prostate cancer treated with ADT and radiotherapy, does adding abiraterone (± enzalutamide) for 2 years improve metastasis-free and overall survival?
balance: Two randomised phase 3 trials within the STAMPEDE platform, pooled in a pre-planned meta-analysis of their primary results (the publication form is disclosed on the card), give a clear answer. Among 1,974 men with high-risk non-metastatic prostate cancer on 3 years of ADT (radiotherapy mandated or encouraged; 85% planned to receive it), adding 2 years of abiraterone-based combination therapy improved metastasis-free survival (HR 0.53, 95% CI 0.44–0.64; 6-year metastasis-free survival 82% vs 69%) and overall survival (HR 0.60, 95% CI 0.48–0.73), with prostate-cancer-specific survival HR 0.49. Adding enzalutamide to abiraterone gave no additional metastasis-free-survival benefit (interaction HR 1.02, p=0.91) but substantially more grade ≥3 toxicity (58% vs 37% for the abiraterone-only combination in the respective trials), and all seven grade 5 adverse events occurred in the combination arms. The platform's design used a one-sided type-1 error of 1.25% for power calculations, flagged on the card. Balance: two years of abiraterone on top of ADT improves metastasis-free and overall survival in high-risk non-metastatic disease; the enzalutamide addition adds harm without benefit. PROPOSED LIKELY pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).

title: Enzalutamide (± leuprolide) in high-risk biochemical recurrence after definitive therapy (EMBARK)
question: In high-risk biochemical recurrence after prostatectomy/radiotherapy without metastases on conventional imaging, does enzalutamide (with or without leuprolide) delay metastasis versus leuprolide alone?
balance: One phase 3 trial, on a surrogate primary endpoint, with survival data not yet in the record. In EMBARK (n=1,068 patients with high-risk biochemical recurrence — PSA doubling time ≤9 months — and no metastases on conventional imaging), 5-year metastasis-free survival was 87.3% with enzalutamide plus leuprolide versus 71.4% with leuprolide alone (HR for metastasis or death 0.42, 95% CI 0.30–0.61, P<0.001 — note the drafting topic file's hazard ratio of 0.58 does not appear in the record; 0.42 governs), and 80.0% with enzalutamide monotherapy (HR 0.63, 95% CI 0.46–0.87, P=0.005). No new safety signals were observed and quality-of-life measures showed no substantial between-group differences. The record reports NO overall-survival results, so no mortality claim is made or supported by this shelf: metastasis-free survival is a surrogate here, and whether delaying metastasis in a population defined by PSA kinetics translates into longer life is precisely what longer follow-up must show. The shelf is flagged as a two-trial-gate exception candidate for the developer (single trial, surrogate primary). PROPOSED POSSIBLE.

title: 177Lu-PSMA-617 radioligand therapy in PSMA-positive metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (VISION) — OUTSTANDING-SINGLE
question: In PSMA-positive metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer after AR-pathway inhibition and taxane chemotherapy, does 177Lu-PSMA-617 plus standard care improve overall survival versus standard care?
balance: OUTSTANDING-SINGLE: one open-label trial establishing a new drug class in this disease, with benefits on both of its alternate primary endpoints. In VISION (831 of 1,179 screened patients randomised, all with PSMA-positive scans after at least one AR-pathway inhibitor and one or two taxane regimens), adding 177Lu-PSMA-617 to protocol-permitted standard care prolonged imaging-based progression-free survival (median 8.7 vs 3.4 months; HR 0.40, 99.2% CI 0.29–0.57) and overall survival (median 15.3 vs 11.3 months; HR for death 0.62, 95% CI 0.52–0.74), with all key secondary endpoints also favouring the radioligand. Grade ≥3 adverse events were more frequent with 177Lu-PSMA-617 (52.7% vs 38.0%), but quality of life was not adversely affected. Two scope notes: the standard-care control excluded chemotherapy, immunotherapy, radium-223 and investigational drugs by protocol, so the comparison is against a deliberately restricted standard; and the population is gated by PSMA-PET positivity (348 of the 1,179 screened patients were not randomised). The lutetium-PSMA question in neuroendocrine tumours is a different diagnosis, homed on Shelf #742, not here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).

title: PARP inhibition in HRR-altered metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (PROfound; TRITON3)
question: In metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer with homologous-recombination-repair gene alterations progressing on an AR-pathway inhibitor, does olaparib improve progression-free and overall survival versus physician's-choice AR switch?
balance: Two open-label phase 3 trials of PARP inhibition in biomarker-selected mCRPC agree on progression, and one shows a survival benefit despite heavy crossover. In PROfound (cohort A: 245 men with BRCA1, BRCA2 or ATM alterations progressing on a next-generation hormonal agent), olaparib improved imaging-based progression-free survival (median 7.4 vs 3.6 months; HR 0.34, 95% CI 0.25–0.47) versus physician's choice of the other AR agent, and the final analysis showed longer overall survival (median 19.1 vs 14.7 months; HR for death 0.69, 95% CI 0.50–0.97, P=0.02) even though 66% of control patients crossed over to olaparib (crossover-adjusted cohort A hazard ratio 0.42, with wide confidence intervals). In TRITON3, rucaparib improved imaging-based progression-free survival in the BRCA subgroup (11.2 vs 6.4 months; HR 0.50, 95% CI 0.36–0.69) and in the intention-to-treat population (HR 0.61) versus physician's choice of docetaxel or an AR switch; its record reports no overall-survival analysis. The honest caveat is ATM: PROfound's cohort A bundled ATM with BRCA1/2, while TRITON3's exploratory ATM analysis showed no progression benefit (HR 0.95, 95% CI 0.59–1.52) — the class benefit is BRCA-driven, and ATM-only disease should not be assumed to share it. Anaemia and nausea were olaparib's main toxic effects; fatigue and nausea were rucaparib's most frequent. PROPOSED LIKELY pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).

title: Adjuvant versus early-salvage radiotherapy after radical prostatectomy (RADICALS-RT; RAVES; GETUG-AFU 17)
question: After radical prostatectomy with adverse pathology or detectable PSA, does adjuvant radiotherapy improve outcomes versus observation with early-salvage radiotherapy at PSA recurrence?
balance: Three randomised trials converge: irradiating everyone up front buys no biochemical-control advantage over watching PSA and irradiating early at recurrence — it only irradiates many men who never need it and adds urinary and sexual morbidity. In RADICALS-RT (n=1,396), 5-year biochemical progression-free survival was 85% with adjuvant radiotherapy versus 88% under an observation-with-salvage policy (HR 1.10, 95% CI 0.81–1.49, p=0.56), while only 33% of the salvage-policy group ever received radiotherapy by 8 years; grade 3–4 urethral stricture was 6% versus 4% and self-reported incontinence was worse at 1 year with adjuvant treatment. In RAVES (n=333), 5-year freedom from biochemical progression was 86% versus 87% (HR 1.12) — its formal noninferiority criterion was not met (p for noninferiority = 0.15), disclosed on the card, though control was near-identical and grade ≥2 genitourinary toxicity was lower with salvage (54% vs 70%). In GETUG-AFU 17 (n=424, all patients also receiving 6 months of hormonal therapy), 5-year event-free survival was 92% versus 90% (HR 0.81, p=0.42), with more late genitourinary toxicity and erectile dysfunction in the adjuvant arm. Two caveats are printed on the cards: RADICALS-RT's primary endpoint (10-year freedom from distant metastases) is not yet reported in its record, so the shelf's endpoints are biochemical; and GETUG-AFU 17's abstract prints two irreconcilable pairs of late genitourinary toxicity figures, flagged rather than repaired. Balance: an early-salvage policy is the standard these trials support. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference for adjuvant superiority).

title: Moderately hypofractionated radiotherapy (60 Gy in 20 fractions) versus conventional fractionation in localised prostate cancer (CHHiP; PROFIT)
question: In localized prostate cancer, is moderately hypofractionated radiotherapy (60 Gy in 20 fractions) noninferior to conventional fractionation (74 Gy in 37 fractions) for biochemical/clinical failure?
balance: Two large noninferiority trials say yes for the 60 Gy in 20 fractions schedule. In CHHiP (n=3,216, localised prostate cancer, most receiving 3–6 months of androgen suppression), the proportion free of biochemical or clinical failure at 5 years was 90.6% with 60 Gy in 20 fractions versus 88.3% with 74 Gy in 37 fractions — noninferior (HR 0.84, 90% CI 0.68–1.03; p for noninferiority = 0.0018 against a critical HR of 1.208) — with similar long-term side-effects and 5-year cumulative grade ≥2 bowel/bladder adverse events of 11.9%/11.7% (60 Gy) versus 13.7%/9.1% (74 Gy). CHHiP's more aggressive 57 Gy in 19 fractions schedule did NOT establish noninferiority (HR 1.20; pNI=0.48), a boundary printed on the card: the answer licenses 60/20, not every shorter schedule. In PROFIT (n=1,206, intermediate-risk disease, no androgen deprivation permitted, and a 78 Gy in 39 fractions control), 5-year biochemical-clinical failure-free survival was 85% in both arms (HR 0.96, 90% CI 0.77–1.2), again noninferior, with prostate-cancer deaths of 10 versus 12 and no significant difference in late grade ≥3 genitourinary or gastrointestinal toxicity. Balance: 60 Gy in 20 fractions over 4 weeks is a standard-equivalent, more convenient schedule. PROPOSED LIKELY.

title: Second-generation androgen-receptor inhibitors in non-metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (SPARTAN; PROSPER; ARAMIS)
question: In non-metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer with rapid PSA doubling, does adding apalutamide to ADT improve metastasis-free and overall survival versus ADT alone?
balance: Three double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trials — one per drug — answer the question for the class, with the apalutamide trial leading. In SPARTAN (n=1,207, PSA doubling time ≤10 months), apalutamide more than doubled median metastasis-free survival (40.5 vs 16.2 months; HR for metastasis or death 0.28, 95% CI 0.23–0.35) and, at the pre-specified final analysis (median follow-up 52 months), significantly improved overall survival (median 73.9 vs 59.9 months; HR 0.78, 95% CI 0.64–0.96, p=0.016) despite 19% of placebo patients crossing over to apalutamide; its characteristic harms were rash (23.8% vs 5.5%), hypothyroidism (8.1% vs 2.0%) and fracture (11.7% vs 6.5%). PROSPER (enzalutamide, n=1,401) and ARAMIS (darolutamide, n=1,509) replicate the pattern: metastasis-free-survival hazard ratios of 0.29 and 0.41, and final overall-survival hazard ratios of 0.73 (median 67.0 vs 56.3 months) and 0.69 (3-year survival 83% vs 77%) respectively — each trial counted once across its two reports on its card. Darolutamide's adverse-event profile was closest to placebo (discontinuation 8.9% vs 8.7%). A provenance note for the developer: the drafting topic file pinned SPARTAN to a citation that proved to be a letter commenting on the trial; the carded anchor is the recovered primary report (Smith et al., NEJM 2018, PMID 29420164), as detailed in the first card's watch-out. PROPOSED LIKELY pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).

title: Metastasis-directed therapy for oligometastatic prostate cancer recurrence (STOMP; ORIOLE)
question: In oligometastatic prostate cancer (≤3–5 lesions), does metastasis-directed SBRT delay progression and defer ADT versus surveillance?
balance: Two small randomised phase 2 trials give a consistent but fragile signal, and the fragility must be stated plainly. In STOMP (n=62 men with choline-PET-detected oligorecurrent prostate cancer, ≤3 extracranial lesions), metastasis-directed therapy (surgery or stereotactic radiotherapy to all lesions) lengthened median ADT-free survival from 13 to 21 months — but the comparison did NOT reach significance (HR 0.60 with an 80% confidence interval of 0.40–0.90; log-rank P=.11), a detail the drafting topic file omitted and this shelf restores: with 80% intervals and P=.11, STOMP is a hypothesis-raising result, not a demonstrated one. In ORIOLE (n=54 men with 1–3 metastases on conventional imaging), stereotactic ablative radiotherapy reduced progression at 6 months from 61% on observation to 19% (P=.005) and improved median progression-free survival (not reached vs 5.8 months; HR 0.30, 95% CI 0.11–0.81, P=.002), with no grade ≥3 toxicity; STOMP likewise saw no grade 2–5 toxicity. Neither trial reports overall survival, and both endpoints — ADT deferral and 6-month progression — are surrogates whose link to longer life is unproven. The shelf is flagged as a two-trial-gate exception candidate in spirit (two trials, but small phase 2s with surrogate endpoints). PROPOSED POSSIBLE.

title: Triplet therapy in metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer: an AR inhibitor added to ADT plus docetaxel (ARASENS; PEACE-1)
question: In metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer, does adding darolutamide to ADT plus docetaxel improve overall survival versus ADT plus docetaxel?
balance: This shelf asks the TRIPLET question — an androgen-receptor agent added on top of ADT plus docetaxel — which is distinct from the doublet-intensification question (ADT plus docetaxel, or ADT plus an AR agent) homed on Shelf #767; the angle is named here so the two shelves do not duplicate. Two phase 3 trials support the triplet, with different agents. In ARASENS (n=1,306; 86.1% with de novo metastatic disease), adding darolutamide to ADT plus docetaxel significantly reduced the risk of death (HR 0.68, 95% CI 0.57–0.80, P<0.001 — described in the record as a 32.5% lower relative risk; the abstract prints no median survivals, so none are carded, and the drafting topic file's 'not reached vs 48.9 months' figures do not appear in the record), with grade 3/4 adverse events similar between arms (66.1% vs 63.5%; neutropenia 33.7% vs 34.2%). In PEACE-1 (n=1,172 analysed; 2×2 factorial, open-label), adding abiraterone to standard care improved overall survival in the pre-specified ADT-plus-docetaxel population (HR 0.75, 95.1% CI 0.59–0.95, p=0.017) and in the overall population (HR 0.82, 95.1% CI 0.69–0.98, p=0.030) — note the topic file attached the 0.82 figure to the docetaxel stratum; the record assigns 0.75 to that stratum and 0.82 overall, and the record governs. In PEACE-1's docetaxel population, grade ≥3 adverse events were 63% with abiraterone versus 52% without, driven mainly by hypertension (22% vs 13%), without increased neutropenia or febrile neutropenia. PROPOSED LIKELY pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).

title: Radium-223 in symptomatic bone-metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (ALSYMPCA)
question: In symptomatic bone-predominant metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer without visceral disease, does radium-223 improve overall survival versus placebo?
balance: One large double-blind placebo-controlled trial answers this question, and it is an outstanding single: in ALSYMPCA, 921 men with castration-resistant prostate cancer and bone metastases (post-docetaxel, ineligible, or declining) received six injections of radium-223 or placebo on top of best standard care, and overall survival improved (updated analysis: median 14.9 vs 11.3 months; HR 0.70, 95% CI 0.58–0.83), with low rates of myelosuppression and fewer adverse events than placebo. No second randomised trial asks the same question. The one combination trial is fenced as a warning: adding radium-223 to abiraterone/prednisone (ERA-223) gave no symptomatic-skeletal-event benefit and nearly tripled fractures (29% vs 11%), so the survival claim belongs to radium-223 as used in ALSYMPCA — bone-targeted therapy added to standard care, not layered onto abiraterone. PROPOSED LIKELY pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).

title: Neoadjuvant cisplatin-based chemotherapy before cystectomy in muscle-invasive bladder cancer (SWOG 8710; BA06 3081)
question: In muscle-invasive bladder cancer, does neoadjuvant cisplatin-based combination chemotherapy before radical cystectomy improve overall survival versus cystectomy alone?
balance: Two randomised trials of two different cisplatin triplets give the same answer. SWOG 8710 (307 eligible patients) found median survival of 77 months with three cycles of MVAC before cystectomy versus 46 months with cystectomy alone, and no residual cancer in the specimen in 38% vs 15% — though the survival comparison itself sat at P=0.06. The larger BA06 trial (976 patients, median follow-up 8 years) found a statistically significant 16% relative reduction in the risk of death with neoadjuvant CMV (HR 0.84, 95% CI 0.72–0.99), raising 10-year survival from 30% to 36%. Neither trial alone is overwhelming — one is large but modest in effect, the other striking in its medians but not conventionally significant — but they are independent, randomised, and concordant, and together they are the evidence base for the neoadjuvant standard. PROPOSED LIKELY pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).

title: Adjuvant nivolumab after resection of high-risk urothelial carcinoma (CheckMate 274; AMBASSADOR)
question: In high-risk muscle-invasive urothelial carcinoma after radical surgery, does one year of adjuvant PD-1 blockade improve disease-free survival versus no adjuvant therapy?
balance: Two phase 3 trials of one year of adjuvant PD-1 blockade after radical surgery for high-risk muscle-invasive urothelial carcinoma agree closely. CheckMate 274 (709 patients, double-blind, nivolumab vs placebo) doubled median disease-free survival (20.8 vs 10.8 months; HR 0.70), with a larger effect in PD-L1-positive tumours (HR 0.55). AMBASSADOR (702 patients, open-label, pembrolizumab vs observation) found the same class effect with a different antibody and a no-treatment comparator (median disease-free survival 29.6 vs 14.2 months; HR 0.73). Neither carded record establishes an overall-survival benefit — CheckMate 274's primary report is a disease-free-survival analysis and AMBASSADOR's abstract reports its disease-free-survival co-primary end point as met without a survival claim — so this shelf claims delayed recurrence, not longer life. Toxicity is real: grade 3 or higher treatment-related events in 17.9% on nivolumab (including two pneumonitis deaths) and grade 3 or higher events of any attribution in 50.6% on pembrolizumab. PROPOSED LIKELY.

title: Avelumab maintenance after first-line chemotherapy in advanced urothelial cancer (JAVELIN Bladder 100)
question: In advanced urothelial cancer without progression after first-line platinum chemotherapy, does switch-maintenance avelumab plus best supportive care improve overall survival versus best supportive care alone?
balance: A single large randomised trial created this standard, and it is an outstanding single. In JAVELIN Bladder 100, 700 patients whose advanced urothelial cancer had not progressed on four to six cycles of gemcitabine plus cisplatin or carboplatin were randomised to maintenance avelumab plus best supportive care or best supportive care alone; overall survival improved (median 21.4 vs 14.3 months; HR 0.69, 95% CI 0.56–0.86), with 1-year survival of 71.3% vs 58.4% and a larger effect in PD-L1-positive tumours (HR 0.56). The trial was open-label — survival is a hard end point, but adverse-event comparisons (grade 3 or higher: 47.4% vs 25.2%) carry that caveat. No second trial asks the switch-maintenance question. PROPOSED LIKELY pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).

title: Chemoradiotherapy for bladder preservation in muscle-invasive bladder cancer (BC2001; BCON)
question: In muscle-invasive bladder cancer managed with radical radiotherapy, does adding a concurrent radiosensitiser improve locoregional control versus radiotherapy alone?
balance: Two randomised trials of two different radiosensitising strategies on a radical-radiotherapy backbone both favour adding treatment. BC2001 (360 patients) added synchronous fluorouracil/mitomycin to radiotherapy and improved 2-year locoregional disease-free survival from 54% to 67% (HR 0.68, 95% CI 0.48–0.96), with no significant increase in late toxicity; its overall-survival difference was not significant (HR 0.82; 95% CI 0.63–1.09) — the treatment made no established difference to survival in that trial. BCON (333 patients) added carbogen breathing and nicotinamide to radiotherapy: its primary end point, cystoscopic control at 6 months, was not significantly improved (81% vs 76%), but 3-year overall survival was 59% vs 46% (P=.04). Read together: concurrent sensitisation improves control of the bladder primary (LIKELY), while the survival picture rests on one trial's secondary end point and is stated here as reported, not claimed. PROPOSED LIKELY.

title: Adjuvant pembrolizumab after nephrectomy in high-risk clear-cell renal cell carcinoma (KEYNOTE-564)
question: In clear-cell renal cell carcinoma at high recurrence risk after nephrectomy (± metastasectomy), does one year of adjuvant pembrolizumab improve disease-free and overall survival versus placebo?
balance: One double-blind placebo-controlled trial carries this shelf, and it is an outstanding single. In KEYNOTE-564, 994 patients with clear-cell renal cell carcinoma at high risk of recurrence after nephrectomy (with or without metastasectomy) received pembrolizumab or placebo for about a year: disease-free survival at 24 months was 77.3% vs 68.1% (HR 0.68, 95% CI 0.53–0.87), and the interim overall-survival estimate also favoured pembrolizumab (96.6% vs 93.5% alive at 24 months; HR 0.54, 95% CI 0.30–0.96) — the first adjuvant therapy in this disease to show such a signal, though survival data were immature at this prespecified interim analysis and the confidence interval is wide. The class context cuts the other way and is fenced on the card: other adjuvant checkpoint-inhibitor trials in renal cancer did not meet their end points, so this is a pembrolizumab result, not a class effect. Grade 3 or higher adverse events occurred in 32.4% vs 17.7%, with no treatment-related deaths. PROPOSED LIKELY pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).

title: Adjuvant VEGF-targeted therapy after nephrectomy in high-risk renal cell carcinoma (S-TRAC versus ASSURE and PROTECT)
question: In high-risk localized renal cell carcinoma after nephrectomy, does adjuvant VEGF-targeted therapy improve disease-free survival, and at what toxicity cost?
balance: This is a discordance shelf: four randomised reads of adjuvant VEGF inhibition after nephrectomy, one positive and three negative. S-TRAC (615 patients, double-blind) found one year of sunitinib lengthened median disease-free survival on blinded central review (6.8 vs 5.6 years; HR 0.76, 95% CI 0.59–0.98). But ASSURE (1,943 patients) found no disease-free-survival difference for sunitinib (HR 1.02) or sorafenib (HR 0.97) against placebo — median disease-free survival was numerically longest on placebo — and PROTECT's primary analysis of pazopanib 600 mg was likewise negative (HR 0.86; 95% CI 0.70–1.06), with only its 800-mg secondary cohort positive. No trial shows an overall-survival benefit. The toxicity, by contrast, is consistent everywhere: roughly a third to nearly half of patients needed dose reductions or stopped treatment (ASSURE recorded five deaths related to treatment or within 30 days of it). Balance: a sunitinib disease-free-survival effect may exist (POSSIBLE, one trial), but as a class strategy adjuvant VEGF therapy made no established difference, at substantial cost in tolerability. PROPOSED SPLIT.

title: Carboplatin versus radiotherapy in stage I seminoma (MRC TE19 / EORTC 30982)
question: In stage I seminoma after orchidectomy, is one cycle of carboplatin noninferior to adjuvant para-aortic radiotherapy for relapse-free survival?
balance: One large randomised trial answers this, with mature follow-up. TE19 randomised 1,447 men with stage I seminoma after orchidectomy to a single infusion of carboplatin (AUC 7) or para-aortic radiotherapy: 5-year relapse-free rates were 94.7% vs 96.0%, meeting the trial's noninferiority design, and carboplatin clearly reduced contralateral germ-cell tumours (2 vs 15; HR 0.22). Relapse in this disease is highly salvageable — only one seminoma death occurred, in the radiotherapy arm — so the real choice the trial informs is between two effective adjuvant strategies with different late-effect profiles, not between treatment and danger. The modern third option, active surveillance, was not an arm of this trial and is fenced. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: a single trial, however large and mature, on a relapse end point.

title: Second-line therapy after antiangiogenic treatment in advanced renal cell carcinoma: nivolumab and cabozantinib versus everolimus (CheckMate 025; METEOR)
question: In advanced clear-cell renal cell carcinoma after antiangiogenic therapy, does nivolumab improve overall survival versus everolimus — and what does the shared-comparator cabozantinib trial show?
balance: Everolimus is the shared comparator of the two pivotal second-line trials, and both beat it on survival. CheckMate 025 (821 patients after one or two antiangiogenic regimens) found nivolumab prolonged overall survival versus everolimus (median 25.0 vs 19.6 months; HR 0.73, 98.5% CI 0.57–0.93) with fewer grade 3–4 treatment-related events (19% vs 37%) — despite no progression-free-survival difference (HR 0.88), a dissociation worth teaching. METEOR (658 patients after VEGFR-TKI therapy) found cabozantinib likewise superior to everolimus on survival (median 21.4 vs 16.5 months; HR 0.66), with progression-free survival (HR 0.51) and response (17% vs 3%) also in its favour, at the price of more hypertension and diarrhoea. The third member of the era's family, axitinib (AXIS), showed a progression-free but not survival benefit and is fenced as framing. PROPOSED LIKELY pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).

title: Pembrolizumab in platinum-refractory advanced urothelial cancer (KEYNOTE-045; the IMvigor211 contrast)
question: In advanced urothelial cancer progressing after platinum chemotherapy, does pembrolizumab improve overall survival versus investigator-choice chemotherapy?
balance: One positive trial and one instructive failure define this shelf. KEYNOTE-045 (542 patients) found pembrolizumab prolonged overall survival versus investigator-choice chemotherapy after platinum failure (median 10.3 vs 7.4 months; HR 0.73, 95% CI 0.59–0.91), with far fewer severe treatment-related events (15.0% vs 49.4%) — despite no progression-free-survival difference (HR 0.98). The discordant sibling matters: IMvigor211 (931 patients) tested the PD-L1 antibody atezolizumab in the same setting and missed its primary end point — in the PD-L1-high (IC2/3) population survival was 11.1 vs 10.6 months (HR 0.87; 95% CI 0.63–1.21), and the hierarchical design precluded formal testing beyond that. So checkpoint blockade after platinum is not an automatic class effect: the survival claim belongs to pembrolizumab on KEYNOTE-045's evidence. PROPOSED LIKELY pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).

title: Erdafitinib in FGFR-altered advanced urothelial cancer (THOR, cohort 1)
question: In advanced urothelial cancer with susceptible FGFR3/2 alterations after platinum chemotherapy and PD-(L)1 therapy, does erdafitinib improve overall survival versus chemotherapy?
balance: One randomised trial answers this, in a biomarker-selected population, and it is an outstanding single. In THOR cohort 1, 266 patients with metastatic urothelial carcinoma bearing susceptible FGFR3/2 alterations, all previously treated with platinum chemotherapy and an anti-PD-1/PD-L1 agent, were randomised to erdafitinib or investigator-choice chemotherapy: overall survival improved (median 12.1 vs 7.8 months; HR 0.64, 95% CI 0.47–0.88), as did progression-free survival (5.6 vs 2.7 months; HR 0.58). Severe toxicity was comparable (grade 3–4 treatment-related events 45.9% vs 46.4%), with fewer treatment-related deaths on erdafitinib (0.7% vs 5.4%). The trial was open-label and the eligible population is the FGFR-altered minority; no second randomised trial of the question exists (the earlier BLC2001 study was single-arm). PROPOSED LIKELY pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).

title: Perioperative FLOT in resectable gastric and gastro-oesophageal junction adenocarcinoma (FLOT4; the MAGIC lineage)
question: In locally advanced resectable gastric/GEJ adenocarcinoma, does perioperative FLOT improve overall survival versus perioperative epirubicin-based chemotherapy (ECF/ECX)?
balance: FLOT4 is the trial that matters here, with MAGIC as its historical pillar. FLOT4 (716 patients with locally advanced resectable gastric/GEJ adenocarcinoma) randomised perioperative FLOT against the epirubicin-based standard ECF/ECX and improved overall survival (HR 0.77, 95% CI 0.63–0.94; median 50 vs 35 months), with similar rates of serious adverse events (27% in both arms) and toxic deaths (2 in each). MAGIC (503 patients) is the trial that created the comparator: perioperative ECF beat surgery alone (HR 0.75; 5-year survival 36% vs 23%), establishing that perioperative chemotherapy helps at all. The two-trial lineage reads: chemotherapy around surgery works (MAGIC), and FLOT is the better chemotherapy (FLOT4). PROPOSED LIKELY pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).

title: Neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy in oesophageal and junctional cancer (CROSS; NEOCRTEC5010)
question: In resectable oesophageal or oesophagogastric-junction cancer, does neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy plus surgery improve overall survival versus surgery alone?
balance: Two randomised trials, in different populations with different chemotherapy backbones, give the same answer. CROSS (366 patients, 75% adenocarcinoma) added weekly carboplatin/paclitaxel with 41.4 Gy before surgery and improved overall survival (median 49.4 vs 24.0 months; HR 0.657, 95% CI 0.495–0.871), with R0 resection in 92% vs 69% and no increase in in-hospital mortality (4% in both arms). NEOCRTEC5010 (451 patients, all squamous-cell carcinoma, China) used cisplatin/vinorelbine with 40 Gy and likewise improved survival (median 100.1 vs 66.5 months; HR 0.71), with a pathological complete response rate of 43.2% and R0 resection in 98.4% vs 91.2%. The principle — chemoradiotherapy before surgery — replicates across histology and regimen; the absolute numbers differ with the populations and should not be averaged. PROPOSED LIKELY pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).

title: Perioperative FLOT versus CROSS chemoradiotherapy in oesophageal adenocarcinoma (ESOPEC)
question: In resectable locally advanced oesophageal adenocarcinoma, is perioperative FLOT chemotherapy superior to CROSS-regimen neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy for overall survival?
balance: The first direct head-to-head of the two curative-intent standards favours chemotherapy — on one trial. ESOPEC randomised 438 patients with resectable oesophageal adenocarcinoma to perioperative FLOT plus surgery or CROSS-regimen chemoradiotherapy (41.4 Gy with carboplatin/paclitaxel) plus surgery: at a median follow-up of 55 months, 3-year overall survival was 57.4% vs 50.7% (HR 0.70, 95% CI 0.53–0.92) and 3-year progression-free survival 51.6% vs 35.0% (HR 0.66). FLOT carried somewhat more grade 3 or higher toxicity (58.0% vs 50.0% of patients starting treatment) but lower 90-day postoperative mortality (3.1% vs 5.6%). There is no second head-to-head trial, and the comparison applies to adenocarcinoma only — squamous disease was not studied here. A single-trial survival claim is capped at POSSIBLE. PROPOSED POSSIBLE pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).

title: FOLFIRINOX in metastatic pancreatic cancer (PRODIGE 4 / ACCORD 11)
question: In metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma with good performance status, does FOLFIRINOX improve overall survival versus gemcitabine?
balance: One trial redefined first-line treatment for fit patients with metastatic pancreatic cancer, and it is an outstanding single. PRODIGE 4/ACCORD 11 randomised 342 patients with ECOG performance status 0–1 to FOLFIRINOX or gemcitabine: overall survival improved by the largest relative margin of the gemcitabine era (median 11.1 vs 6.8 months; HR 0.57, 95% CI 0.45–0.73), with progression-free survival (6.4 vs 3.3 months; HR 0.47) and response rate (31.6% vs 9.4%) also strongly in FOLFIRINOX's favour — and, notably, slower quality-of-life deterioration despite more toxicity (febrile neutropenia in 5.4%). The price is real and the population was selected for fitness; the trial says nothing about patients with performance status 2 or worse. No second trial of the same regimen exists; the later NALIRIFOX regimen is a different question and is fenced. PROPOSED LIKELY pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).

title: Maintenance olaparib in germline BRCA-mutated metastatic pancreatic cancer (POLO)
question: In germline BRCA1/2-mutated metastatic pancreatic cancer without progression on platinum chemotherapy, does maintenance olaparib improve progression-free survival versus placebo — and does it extend survival?
balance: POLO is the library's cleanest lesson in surrogate dissociation. Of 3,315 patients screened, 154 with a germline BRCA1/2 mutation and metastatic pancreatic cancer that had not progressed on first-line platinum chemotherapy were randomised to maintenance olaparib or placebo in a double-blind trial. Progression-free survival (blinded central review) was clearly longer on olaparib (median 7.4 vs 3.8 months; HR 0.53, 95% CI 0.35–0.82). But overall survival showed no difference at the carded interim analysis (median 18.9 vs 18.1 months; HR 0.91; 95% CI 0.56–1.46, at 46% data maturity), and health-related quality of life did not differ either. Grade 3 or higher adverse events were 40% vs 23%. So: maintenance olaparib delays scans turning positive in this small molecular subgroup (POSSIBLE), without demonstrated survival or quality-of-life benefit (POSSIBLE that the treatment made no difference to survival, on interim data). The split is the shelf. PROPOSED SPLIT.

title: Second-line FOLFOX in advanced biliary tract cancer (ABC-06)
question: In advanced biliary tract cancer progressing after gemcitabine–cisplatin, does second-line FOLFOX plus active symptom control improve overall survival versus active symptom control alone?
balance: One modest-sized trial is the entire randomised evidence for second-line chemotherapy in this disease. ABC-06 randomised 162 patients with advanced biliary tract cancer progressing after cisplatin–gemcitabine (ECOG 0–1) to active symptom control with or without FOLFOX (up to 12 cycles): overall survival improved (median 6.2 vs 5.3 months; adjusted HR 0.69, 95% CI 0.50–0.97). The median gain of 0.9 months understates the tail: 6-month survival was 50.6% vs 35.5% and 12-month survival 25.9% vs 11.4%. The cost was grade 3–5 adverse events in 69% vs 52%, including three chemotherapy-related deaths. An honest small win in a disease with few options — and a single open-label trial, so the survival claim is stamped POSSIBLE. PROPOSED POSSIBLE pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).

title: Ramucirumab in previously treated gastric/GEJ adenocarcinoma (RAINBOW; REGARD)
question: In advanced gastric or GEJ adenocarcinoma progressing on first-line chemotherapy, does ramucirumab — with paclitaxel, or alone — improve overall survival versus control?
balance: Two double-blind, placebo-controlled trials of the same VEGFR-2 antibody make this a clean two-trial shelf. RAINBOW (665 patients) added ramucirumab to paclitaxel in the second line and improved overall survival (median 9.6 vs 7.4 months; HR 0.807, 95% CI 0.678–0.962), at the cost of more neutropenia (grade ≥3: 41% vs 19%), hypertension (14% vs 2%) and fatigue (12% vs 5%). REGARD (355 patients) tested ramucirumab alone against placebo plus best supportive care and also improved survival (median 5.2 vs 3.8 months; HR 0.776, 95% CI 0.603–0.998), with hypertension the main excess (16% vs 8%). The effects are moderate, the design quality is the best on this slate (both randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled), and the two questions — combination and monotherapy — are kept distinct on their cards. PROPOSED LIKELY pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).

title: Trastuzumab in HER2-positive advanced gastric cancer (ToGA)
question: In HER2-positive advanced gastric or GEJ adenocarcinoma, does adding trastuzumab to cisplatin–fluoropyrimidine chemotherapy improve overall survival?
balance: One trial established HER2 as the first actionable target in gastric cancer, and it is an outstanding single. ToGA randomised 594 patients with HER2-positive advanced gastric or GEJ adenocarcinoma (overexpression by immunohistochemistry or amplification by FISH) to cisplatin plus a fluoropyrimidine with or without trastuzumab: overall survival improved (median 13.8 vs 11.1 months; HR 0.74, 95% CI 0.60–0.91), with no excess in overall grade 3–4 adverse events (68% in both groups) or cardiac adverse events (6% in both). The trial was open-label and has no randomised replication for this exact question; its population is defined by the HER2 testing of its era. PROPOSED LIKELY pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).

title: Adjuvant nivolumab after chemoradiotherapy and resection in oesophageal cancer (CheckMate 577)
question: In resected oesophageal/GEJ cancer with residual pathological disease after neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy, does adjuvant nivolumab improve disease-free and overall survival versus placebo?
balance: One double-blind placebo-controlled trial created the adjuvant standard for this high-risk residue, and it is an outstanding single. CheckMate 577 randomised 794 patients with R0-resected stage II–III oesophageal or GEJ cancer who had residual pathological disease after neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy to up to a year of nivolumab or placebo: disease-free survival doubled at the median (22.4 vs 11.0 months; HR 0.69, 96.4% CI 0.56–0.86), with grade 3–4 treatment-related events in 13% vs 6% and discontinuation for related events in 9% vs 3%. The carded primary record reports disease-free survival; no overall-survival claim is taken from it, and the Tier C flag reflects the shelf's survival question and the developer's designation. The population is precisely fenced: complete responders to chemoradiotherapy were not eligible — this is a treatment for proven residual disease. PROPOSED LIKELY pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).

title: Adjuvant atezolizumab + bevacizumab after resection or ablation of high-risk hepatocellular carcinoma (IMbrave050)
question: In hepatocellular carcinoma at high recurrence risk after curative resection or ablation, does adjuvant atezolizumab plus bevacizumab improve recurrence-free survival versus active surveillance?
balance: One randomised phase 3 trial, read twice. At its prespecified interim analysis (median follow-up 17.4 months), IMbrave050 met its primary endpoint: adjuvant atezolizumab plus bevacizumab improved recurrence-free survival versus active surveillance (HR 0.72, adjusted 95% CI 0.53–0.98; p=0.012), at the cost of grade 3–4 adverse events in 41% versus 13%. In the trial's updated analysis, that benefit was not sustained — the recurrence-free-survival hazard ratio attenuated to 0.90 (95% CI 0.72–1.12) — and overall survival remained immature with a point estimate against the treatment (HR 1.26, 95% CI 0.85–1.87); the investigators concluded the benefit–risk profile does not support adjuvant use. The class warning stands behind it: adjuvant sorafenib (STORM) was also negative, and the first-line atezolizumab–bevacizumab question in advanced disease is homed on Shelf #850. Balance: an early recurrence delay that faded with follow-up; on the mature data, no sustained difference. Single trial — THIN. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference).

title: Bevacizumab added to first-line chemotherapy in advanced ovarian cancer (GOG-0218; ICON7)
question: In newly diagnosed advanced ovarian cancer, does adding bevacizumab to carboplatin–paclitaxel (with maintenance) improve progression-free survival, and in whom does it affect overall survival?
balance: Two randomised phase 3 trials agree on the shape of the effect. GOG-0218 (double-blind, placebo-controlled, n=1,873) found bevacizumab given throughout — during chemotherapy and as maintenance — prolonged median progression-free survival from 10.3 to 14.1 months (HR 0.717), while bevacizumab only during chemotherapy did not (HR 0.908); there was no overall-survival difference. ICON7 (open-label, n=1,528, half the bevacizumab dose) confirmed a smaller progression-free-survival benefit (HR 0.81) that peaked while bevacizumab was being given and waned after it stopped, with an overall-survival difference confined to the subgroup at high risk of progression (median 36.6 vs 28.8 months). Toxicity is real but bounded: hypertension requiring treatment in 23% versus 7% (GOG-0218 throughout arm) and gastrointestinal-wall disruption in about 2.6% versus 1.2%. Balance: bevacizumab throughout first-line therapy delays progression by roughly 2–4 months with no overall survival gain; the only survival signal sits in ICON7's high-risk subgroup. PROPOSED LIKELY.

title: Intraperitoneal chemotherapy after optimal debulking in stage III ovarian cancer (GOG-172; GOG-252)
question: In optimally debulked stage III ovarian cancer, does intraperitoneal cisplatin-based chemotherapy improve overall survival versus intravenous chemotherapy?
balance: The two eras of this question disagree, and the shelf's work is the disagreement. GOG-172 (2006, n=415 eligible) gave the largest survival gain of its era: adding intraperitoneal cisplatin and paclitaxel to intravenous paclitaxel extended median overall survival from 49.7 to 65.6 months (P=0.03) and progression-free survival from 18.3 to 23.8 months — but only 42% of patients completed six intraperitoneal cycles, grade 3–4 toxicity was substantially higher, and quality of life was worse during and shortly after treatment (though not at one year). GOG-252 (2019, n=1,560), run a generation later with dose-dense weekly paclitaxel and bevacizumab in every arm, found no significant progression-free-survival advantage for either intraperitoneal regimen (medians 24.9 months intravenous carboplatin, 27.4 intraperitoneal carboplatin, 26.2 intraperitoneal cisplatin). Whether the difference is the modern backbone (weekly paclitaxel, bevacizumab), the lower intraperitoneal cisplatin dose in GOG-252, or the old result itself is unresolved. Balance: a real survival benefit in the trial that asked the question plainly, not reproduced when the regimen was modernised. PROPOSED POSSIBLE pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).

title: HIPEC at interval cytoreductive surgery in stage III ovarian cancer (OVHIPEC; KOV-HIPEC-01)
question: In stage III ovarian cancer responding to neoadjuvant chemotherapy, does adding hyperthermic intraperitoneal chemotherapy to interval cytoreductive surgery improve recurrence-free and overall survival versus surgery alone?
balance: Two randomised trials converge on the interval-surgery setting and diverge outside it. OVHIPEC (n=245, all interval surgery after neoadjuvant chemotherapy) found hyperthermic intraperitoneal cisplatin improved recurrence-free survival (14.2 vs 10.7 months; HR 0.66) and overall survival (45.7 vs 33.9 months; HR 0.67), with grade 3–4 adverse events no higher than surgery alone (27% vs 25%). KOV-HIPEC-01 (n=184, mixed primary and interval surgery) was null on its primary population (progression-free survival P=0.43; overall survival P=0.52) — but in its prespecified interval-surgery subgroup the effects matched OVHIPEC (progression-free-survival HR 0.60; overall-survival HR 0.53), while its primary-surgery subgroup showed nothing. Balance: at interval cytoreduction after neoadjuvant chemotherapy, one dedicated trial plus a concordant subgroup support a survival benefit; at primary surgery, there is none. The single-trial flag (OUTSTANDING-SINGLE for the interval question's dedicated trial) is carried on the cards. PROPOSED LIKELY pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).

title: Dose-dense weekly paclitaxel in advanced ovarian cancer (JGOG 3016; GOG-262; MITO-7)
question: In advanced ovarian cancer, does dose-dense weekly paclitaxel with 3-weekly carboplatin improve progression-free and overall survival versus conventional 3-weekly therapy?
balance: One positive Japanese trial and two Western trials that could not repeat it. JGOG 3016 (n=631 eligible) found dose-dense weekly paclitaxel with 3-weekly carboplatin improved progression-free survival (28.0 vs 17.2 months; HR 0.71) and 3-year overall survival (72.1% vs 65.1%; HR 0.75), with more early discontinuation for toxicity and much more grade 3–4 anaemia (69% vs 44%). GOG-262 (n=692, 84% receiving bevacizumab) found no overall progression-free-survival benefit (HR 0.89; P=0.18), with a significant interaction: benefit in patients not receiving bevacizumab (HR 0.62) and none in those who did (HR 0.99). MITO-7 (n=810) tested a different weekly regimen (weekly carboplatin as well) and found no progression-free-survival difference (HR 0.96), though quality of life and several toxicities favoured the weekly schedule. Balance: the dose-dense advantage was real in the population and regimen in which it was discovered, and has not generalised — whether the gap is pharmacogenomic, regimen design, or the bevacizumab backbone remains unsettled. PROPOSED POSSIBLE pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).

title: Mirvetuximab soravtansine in platinum-resistant, FRα-positive ovarian cancer (MIRASOL)
question: In folate-receptor-alpha-positive, platinum-resistant ovarian cancer, does mirvetuximab soravtansine improve progression-free and overall survival versus investigator-choice chemotherapy?
balance: A single randomised phase 3 trial, and the first to show an overall-survival benefit in platinum-resistant ovarian cancer. In 453 patients with high folate-receptor-α expression (≥75% of tumour cells with ≥2+ staining) and one to three prior lines, mirvetuximab soravtansine beat investigator-choice chemotherapy on every endpoint: progression-free survival 5.62 versus 3.98 months, objective response 42.3% versus 15.9%, and overall survival 16.46 versus 12.75 months (HR 0.67; 95% CI 0.50–0.89) — while causing fewer grade ≥3 adverse events (41.7% vs 54.1%), fewer serious adverse events and fewer discontinuations. The earlier SORAYA study was single-arm and cannot substitute for a second randomised trial, so the OUTSTANDING-SINGLE flag stands: an open-label trial whose survival result is strong, internally consistent and unmatched by any comparator-era result in this disease, but unreplicated. Balance: for FRα-high platinum-resistant disease, this is the new reference treatment on one trial's evidence. PROPOSED LIKELY pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).

title: Pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy in persistent, recurrent or metastatic cervical cancer (KEYNOTE-826; BEATcc)
question: In persistent, recurrent or metastatic cervical cancer, does adding pembrolizumab to platinum chemotherapy (± bevacizumab) improve overall survival?
balance: Two randomised phase 3 trials, two different checkpoint inhibitors, the same answer. KEYNOTE-826 (double-blind, n=617) added pembrolizumab to platinum chemotherapy with or without bevacizumab: in PD-L1 CPS ≥1 disease, progression-free survival improved (10.4 vs 8.2 months; HR 0.62) and 24-month overall survival was 53.0% versus 41.7% (HR 0.64), with consistent effects in the intention-to-treat and CPS ≥10 populations. BEATcc (open-label, n=410) added atezolizumab to a fixed bevacizumab-plus-platinum backbone: progression-free survival 13.7 versus 10.4 months (HR 0.62) and interim overall survival 32.1 versus 22.8 months (HR 0.68). The regimens differ (pembrolizumab with optional bevacizumab versus atezolizumab with mandatory bevacizumab), so this is class replication rather than a duplicate trial — and it is why the stamp is LIKELY rather than a single-trial flag. Toxicity is additive but familiar: anaemia and neutropenia dominate in KEYNOTE-826; BEATcc's grade ≥3 rates were 79% versus 75%. The locally advanced (chemoradiation) setting is a different question, homed on Shelf #854. PROPOSED LIKELY pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).

title: Bevacizumab added to chemotherapy in advanced cervical cancer (GOG-240)
question: In metastatic, persistent or recurrent cervical cancer, does adding bevacizumab to chemotherapy doublets improve overall survival?
balance: One randomised trial broke a decades-long survival plateau in this disease, and none has repeated the experiment. GOG-240 (n=452, 2×2 factorial) found that adding bevacizumab 15 mg/kg to chemotherapy doublets improved overall survival from 13.3 to 17.0 months (HR 0.71; 98% CI 0.54–0.95) and response rates from 36% to 48%; the trial's other question — topotecan–paclitaxel versus cisplatin–paclitaxel — was answered in the negative (HR for death 1.20). The harms are specific and must ride with the benefit: grade ≥2 hypertension 25% versus 2%, grade ≥3 thromboembolism 8% versus 1%, and grade ≥3 gastrointestinal fistula 3% versus 0% — in a population many of whose members had received prior pelvic radiation. Flagged OUTSTANDING-SINGLE (open-label). The bevacizumab backbone this trial established is the platform onto which checkpoint inhibitors were later added (Shelf #1895). PROPOSED LIKELY pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).

title: Adjuvant chemoradiotherapy versus radiotherapy alone in high-risk endometrial cancer (PORTEC-3)
question: In high-risk endometrial cancer after surgery, does adjuvant chemoradiotherapy improve overall and failure-free survival versus radiotherapy alone?
balance: One large randomised trial with a split answer. In PORTEC-3's final analysis (n=660, median follow-up 60.2 months), adding chemotherapy during and after pelvic radiotherapy improved 5-year failure-free survival (75.5% vs 68.6%; HR 0.71; 95% CI 0.53–0.95; p=0.022) but did not significantly improve 5-year overall survival (81.8% vs 76.7%; adjusted HR 0.76; 95% CI 0.54–1.06; p=0.11). The cost was steep: grade ≥3 adverse events during treatment in 60% versus 12%, and grade ≥2 neuropathy persisting at 3 years in 8% versus 1%. Trial-level subgroup reporting (outside this record) suggests the benefit concentrates in stage III and serous/p53-abnormal disease, which is how the trial is usually applied — but on the carded record the population-level claim is a failure-free-survival benefit without a proven overall-survival benefit. THIN: single trial, survival claim subgroup-dependent. PROPOSED POSSIBLE pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).

title: Adjuvant chemotherapy after chemoradiotherapy in locally advanced cervical cancer (OUTBACK)
question: In locally advanced cervical cancer treated with chemoradiotherapy, does additional adjuvant (outback) chemotherapy improve overall survival versus chemoradiotherapy alone?
balance: A large, clean negative trial. OUTBACK (n=919 eligible, median follow-up 60 months) added four cycles of carboplatin–paclitaxel after standard cisplatin-based chemoradiotherapy in locally advanced cervical cancer and found 5-year overall survival of 72% versus 71% (HR 0.90; 95% CI 0.70–1.17; p=0.81) — no benefit, with more grade 3–4 toxicity (decreased neutrophils 20% vs 8%; anaemia 18% vs 8%) and more serious adverse events (30% vs 22%). The investigators' conclusion was unambiguous: adjuvant chemotherapy after chemoradiotherapy should not be given in this setting. Do not confuse the timing: chemotherapy given BEFORE chemoradiotherapy (induction, INTERLACE) is a different strategy with positive results, homed on Shelf #854. Balance: on a survival primary endpoint, in an adequately sized trial, additional post-chemoradiation chemotherapy made no difference and added harm. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).

title: Carboplatin–paclitaxel versus cisplatin–paclitaxel–doxorubicin (TAP) in advanced endometrial cancer (GOG-0209)
question: In advanced or recurrent endometrial cancer, is carboplatin–paclitaxel noninferior to cisplatin–paclitaxel–doxorubicin (TAP) for overall survival, with less toxicity?
balance: One very large noninferiority trial settled the practical question. GOG-0209 (n=1,381) compared carboplatin–paclitaxel (TC) with the three-drug TAP regimen and concluded noninferiority for overall survival (median 37 vs 41 months; HR 1.002; 90% CI 0.90–1.12) and progression-free survival (median 13 vs 14 months; HR 1.032; 90% CI 0.93–1.15). The median-survival gap favouring TAP is the nuance that belongs on the card face: the point estimates lean slightly toward the triplet, and noninferiority was established against the trial's prespecified margin, not by equality of medians. What tipped practice was deliverability and harm: TAP caused more grade ≥3 thrombocytopenia (23% vs 12%), vomiting (7% vs 4%), diarrhoea (6% vs 2%) and metabolic toxicity (14% vs 8%), while TC caused more neutropenia (80% vs 52%); febrile neutropenia was similar (6% vs 7%), grade >2 sensory neuropathy was recorded in 20% (TC) versus 26% (TAP), and small quality-of-life differences favoured TC. Balance: equivalent-enough survival with a simpler, better-tolerated doublet — the basis on which TC became the global first-line standard. THIN in form (a single trial carries an equivalence claim), large in size. PROPOSED LIKELY pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).

title: Neoadjuvant-plus-adjuvant versus adjuvant-only pembrolizumab in resectable stage IIIB–IV melanoma (SWOG S1801)
question: In resectable stage IIIB–IV melanoma, does starting pembrolizumab before surgery (3 doses) and continuing afterwards improve event-free survival versus the same total therapy given entirely after surgery?
balance: One randomised trial asked a timing question, not a drug question — both arms received 18 doses of pembrolizumab; only the placement of the first three (before versus after surgery) differed. SWOG S1801 (phase 2, n=313) found event-free survival at 2 years of 72% with neoadjuvant-plus-adjuvant therapy versus 49% with adjuvant-only therapy (P=0.004 by log-rank), at a median follow-up of 14.7 months, with grade ≥3 treatment-related adverse events no higher in the neoadjuvant arm (12% vs 14%). The event-free-survival endpoint includes failure to reach or complete surgery, which is part of the strategy being tested, not a flaw in it. Overall survival was not yet reported — this shelf claims an event-free-survival benefit only. NADINA (neoadjuvant ipilimumab–nivolumab) answers the adjacent question with a different, more intense regimen and is fenced, not merged; adjuvant-only pembrolizumab and nivolumab are homed on Shelf #761. Flagged OUTSTANDING-SINGLE. PROPOSED LIKELY.

title: Adjuvant dabrafenib + trametinib in resected BRAF-mutated stage III melanoma (COMBI-AD)
question: In resected stage III BRAF V600-mutated melanoma, does 12 months of adjuvant dabrafenib plus trametinib improve relapse-free survival versus placebo, and does it extend survival?
balance: A double-blind, placebo-controlled trial whose two answers must not be fused. COMBI-AD (n=870) showed 12 months of adjuvant dabrafenib plus trametinib substantially improves relapse-free survival — 3-year 58% versus 39% at the primary analysis (HR 0.47) and HR 0.52 in the final analysis after nearly a decade of follow-up, with distant metastasis-free survival HR 0.56. But the final overall-survival analysis was not significant (HR 0.80; 95% CI 0.62–1.01; P=0.06), despite an early interim estimate (HR 0.57) that had not crossed its prespecified boundary; the prespecified BRAF V600E subgroup showed HR 0.75 (0.58–0.96). The dissociation — durable relapse prevention without a proven survival extension — is the balance of this shelf, and any summary that sells the combination as life-extending overstates the record. The adjuvant alternatives (pembrolizumab, nivolumab) are homed on Shelf #761; no randomised trial compares the targeted and immune adjuvant strategies head-to-head. PROPOSED LIKELY (for relapse-free survival; no survival claim).
