title: Combined BRAF + MEK inhibition versus BRAF inhibition alone in metastatic BRAF-mutated melanoma (COMBI-d; COMBI-v)
question: In untreated BRAF V600-mutated metastatic melanoma, does dabrafenib plus trametinib improve overall survival versus BRAF inhibition alone?
balance: Two randomised phase 3 trials, each against a different single-agent BRAF inhibitor, plus their pooled 5-year follow-up. COMBI-v (n=704, versus vemurafenib) crossed its prespecified interim stopping boundary for overall survival: 12-month survival 72% versus 65% (HR 0.69; P=0.005), with progression-free survival 11.4 versus 7.3 months (HR 0.56) and far fewer cutaneous squamous-cell cancers (1% vs 18%). COMBI-d (n=423, double-blind versus dabrafenib alone) improved progression-free survival (9.3 vs 8.8 months; HR 0.75) and response (67% vs 51%); its interim survival estimate favoured the combination (HR 0.63) without crossing its stringent stopping boundary. The pooled 5-year analysis of both trials (n=563 on the combination) gives the durable picture: overall survival 34% at 5 years, and 71% at 5 years among the 19% who achieved a complete response. Pyrexia is the combination's signature toxicity (51% vs 28% in COMBI-d). Balance: adding MEK inhibition to BRAF inhibition improves survival over BRAF inhibition alone — the question that defined an era of melanoma therapy, now largely superseded by immunotherapy-first sequencing (Shelf #1905) but not by any failure of these trials. PROPOSED LIKELY pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).

title: Tebentafusp in HLA-A*02:01-positive metastatic uveal melanoma
question: In HLA-A*02:01-positive metastatic uveal melanoma, does tebentafusp improve overall survival versus investigator-choice therapy?
balance: A single randomised phase 3 trial that produced the first overall-survival benefit ever shown in metastatic uveal melanoma — a disease where, as the trial record puts it, 1-year survival was approximately 50% and no systemic treatment had proven a survival benefit. In 378 previously untreated HLA-A*02:01-positive patients, tebentafusp (a bispecific gp100-targeting T-cell engager) improved 1-year overall survival to 73% versus 59% (HR 0.51; 95% CI 0.37–0.71) against investigator's choice of pembrolizumab, ipilimumab or dacarbazine, with progression-free survival also favouring tebentafusp (6-month 31% vs 19%; HR 0.73). The toxicity is front-loaded and mechanism-typical: rash 83%, pyrexia 76%, pruritus 69%, mostly in the first doses, with only 2% discontinuing for treatment-related events and no treatment-related deaths. Two fences: the benefit applies only to HLA-A*02:01-positive patients (roughly half of populations of European ancestry, fewer in others), and there is no second trial — flagged OUTSTANDING-SINGLE. PROPOSED LIKELY pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).

title: Tumour-infiltrating lymphocyte therapy versus ipilimumab in advanced melanoma
question: In advanced melanoma progressing on/after anti-PD-1 (mostly), does tumour-infiltrating lymphocyte therapy improve progression-free survival versus ipilimumab?
balance: The first randomised trial of adoptive cell therapy in a solid tumour, and it won its primary endpoint. In 168 patients with unresectable stage IIIC/IV melanoma — 86% of them refractory to anti-PD-1 therapy — tumour-infiltrating lymphocyte (TIL) therapy after lymphodepleting chemotherapy, followed by high-dose interleukin-2, doubled median progression-free survival versus ipilimumab (7.2 vs 3.1 months; HR 0.50; 95% CI 0.35–0.72) and more than doubled the response rate (49% vs 21%). Median overall survival was numerically longer with TIL therapy (25.8 vs 18.9 months), but the record reports no hazard ratio and the trial was not powered to settle survival — this shelf claims the progression-free-survival result only. The price is the platform: grade ≥3 treatment-related adverse events in 100% of TIL patients (mainly chemotherapy-related myelosuppression) versus 57% with ipilimumab, plus the manufacturing and centre requirements of a bespoke cell product. Flagged OUTSTANDING-SINGLE (open-label; landmark first randomised cell-therapy win). PROPOSED LIKELY.

title: Immunotherapy-first versus targeted-therapy-first sequencing in BRAF-mutated metastatic melanoma (DREAMseq; SECOMBIT)
question: In untreated BRAF V600-mutated metastatic melanoma, does starting with nivolumab + ipilimumab (switching to dabrafenib + trametinib at progression) improve overall survival versus the reverse sequence?
balance: Two randomised sequencing trials point the same way: in BRAF-mutated metastatic melanoma, immunotherapy first, targeted therapy in reserve, beats the reverse order. DREAMseq (phase 3, n=265) was stopped early by its data safety monitoring committee because the primary endpoint had been reached: 2-year overall survival was 71.8% for patients starting on nivolumab–ipilimumab versus 51.5% for those starting on dabrafenib–trametinib, with crossover to the alternate therapy at progression built into both strategies; second-line response was asymmetric (47.8% for targeted therapy after immunotherapy versus 29.6% for immunotherapy after targeted therapy), and response duration favoured immunotherapy first (not reached vs 12.7 months). SECOMBIT (randomised phase 2, three arms, n=209, using encorafenib–binimetinib) was directionally concordant: 2-year overall survival 73% for immunotherapy-first versus 65% for targeted-first, with a sandwich arm between them (69%). Only 52% of DREAMseq patients with documented progression actually crossed over, which is itself part of the finding — a strategy that depends on reaching second line fails the patients who never get there. Balance: sequence matters, and the immune-first sequence is the one to default to. PROPOSED LIKELY pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).

title: Adding concurrent chemotherapy to postoperative radiotherapy in high-risk cutaneous squamous-cell carcinoma of the head and neck (TROG 05.01)
question: In high-risk cutaneous squamous-cell carcinoma of the head and neck after surgery, does postoperative chemoradiotherapy improve disease-free survival versus postoperative radiotherapy alone?
balance: One randomised phase 3 trial, and it was negative. In TROG 05.01 (n=321 randomised), adding weekly carboplatin to postoperative radiotherapy (60–66 Gy) after resection of high-risk cutaneous squamous-cell carcinoma of the head and neck did not improve freedom from locoregional relapse — the primary endpoint (hazard ratio 0.84; 95% CI 0.46–1.55; P=0.58; 5-year rates 87% versus 83%) — and there were no significant differences in disease-free or overall survival. Surgery plus radiotherapy alone already achieved excellent locoregional control (5-year freedom from locoregional relapse 83%), locoregional failure remained the dominant first failure site, and 84% of the chemoradiotherapy arm completed six carboplatin cycles, so the null is not explained by under-delivery. Chemotherapy also did not measurably worsen radiotherapy toxicity — the addition was, in effect, all cost and no gain, though the cost too was modest. THIN: a single trial with a wide confidence interval that cannot exclude a moderate locoregional benefit; the stamp is therefore POSSIBLE rather than LIKELY for the no-difference reading. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference).

title: Nivolumab + ipilimumab versus nivolumab alone for melanoma brain metastases (ABC trial)
question: In melanoma brain metastases (asymptomatic, untreated), does nivolumab plus ipilimumab achieve better intracranial control than nivolumab alone?
balance: One small randomised phase 2 — the only randomised comparison in this setting — favours the combination for intracranial control. In the ABC trial's randomised cohorts (asymptomatic, previously untreated brain metastases), intracranial responses occurred in 46% of patients on nivolumab plus ipilimumab versus 20% on nivolumab alone, with complete intracranial responses in 17% versus 12%; median follow-up was 17 months at the primary report. The non-randomised third cohort — patients with failed local therapy, neurological symptoms, or leptomeningeal disease — responded at only 6% on nivolumab, marking how different the favourable randomised population is from the patients clinicians worry about most. The combination cost substantially more high-grade toxicity (grade 3–4 treatment-related adverse events 54% versus 16%). Survival was not a randomised endpoint of this report, so the shelf claims intracranial response only; CheckMate 204, the larger combination cohort, was single-arm and is fenced. THIN: 60 treated patients in the randomised comparison and a response endpoint. PROPOSED POSSIBLE.

title: Adjuvant cemiplimab in high-risk cutaneous squamous-cell carcinoma after surgery and radiotherapy (C-POST)
question: After surgery and radiotherapy for high-risk cutaneous squamous-cell carcinoma, does adjuvant cemiplimab improve disease-free survival versus placebo?
balance: One recent randomised, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial with a large effect on its primary endpoint. In C-POST (n=415), patients with cutaneous squamous-cell carcinoma at high risk of recurrence after surgical resection and postoperative radiotherapy received up to 48 weeks of adjuvant cemiplimab or placebo: disease-free survival strongly favoured cemiplimab (24 versus 65 recurrence-or-death events; HR 0.32; 95% CI 0.20–0.51), with estimated 24-month disease-free survival of 87.1% versus 64.1%, locoregional recurrence HR 0.20 and distant recurrence HR 0.35, at a median follow-up of 24 months. Grade ≥3 adverse events were more frequent with cemiplimab (23.9% vs 14.2%), as were discontinuations for adverse events (9.8% vs 1.5%). Overall survival was not yet reported — this shelf claims disease-free survival only, and the effect, though large, rests on 89 total events in a single trial (THIN in form). The contrast with Shelf #1906 is instructive: in the same broad disease, adding carboplatin chemotherapy to radiotherapy did nothing, while adjuvant PD-1 blockade after radiotherapy substantially delayed recurrence. PROPOSED LIKELY.

title: Individualised neoantigen vaccine (mRNA-4157/V940) plus pembrolizumab in resected high-risk melanoma (KEYNOTE-942)
question: In resected high-risk melanoma, does adding an individualised neoantigen mRNA vaccine to pembrolizumab improve recurrence-free survival versus pembrolizumab alone?
balance: One small open-label phase 2b trial (n=157) found fewer recurrences when a personalised neoantigen mRNA vaccine was added to adjuvant pembrolizumab: recurrence or death in 22% versus 40%, hazard ratio 0.56 — but the 95% confidence interval (0.31 to 1.02) crosses 1.0 and the two-sided P value was 0.053, so the primary comparison did not reach conventional significance. Eighteen-month recurrence-free survival was 79% versus 62%. Grade 3 or worse treatment-related adverse events were somewhat more frequent with the combination (25% vs 18%), with no vaccine-related grade 4–5 events. This is a promising, unconfirmed signal: recurrence-free survival is a surrogate, overall survival is unreported, and the phase 3 trial (V940-001) is still in flight. Adjuvant pembrolizumab or nivolumab versus placebo is homed on Shelf #761; this shelf asks only what the vaccine adds. PROPOSED POSSIBLE.

title: First-line pembrolizumab in recurrent or metastatic head and neck squamous-cell carcinoma (KEYNOTE-048; CheckMate 651; KESTREL)
question: In recurrent or metastatic HNSCC, does first-line pembrolizumab (alone or with chemotherapy) improve overall survival versus the EXTREME regimen — and did the other checkpoint programmes beat the same comparator?
balance: Three phase 3 trials tested checkpoint blockade against the same EXTREME comparator (cetuximab plus platinum and 5-fluorouracil), and only the pembrolizumab programme won. In KEYNOTE-048 (n=882), pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy improved overall survival in the total population (median 13.0 vs 10.7 months; HR 0.77), and pembrolizumab alone improved survival in PD-L1 CPS ≥20 (HR 0.61) and CPS ≥1 (HR 0.78) disease while proving non-inferior overall. But nivolumab plus ipilimumab (CheckMate 651, n=947) did not significantly improve survival in the total or CPS ≥20 populations, and durvalumab with or without tremelimumab (KESTREL) was not superior in PD-L1-high disease. The shelf's claim is therefore agent-specific, not a class effect: pembrolizumab-based first-line therapy prolongs survival; dual-checkpoint and durvalumab-based strategies did not beat EXTREME on survival despite gentler toxicity. PROPOSED LIKELY, Tier C (overall-survival claims — the developer rules personally).

title: Nivolumab in platinum-refractory recurrent or metastatic HNSCC (CheckMate 141; KEYNOTE-040)
question: In recurrent or metastatic HNSCC progressing during or within 6 months of platinum therapy, does PD-1 blockade improve overall survival versus investigator-choice single-agent therapy?
balance: Two phase 3 trials asked the same salvage question and both answered yes. CheckMate 141 (n=361) found nivolumab prolonged overall survival versus methotrexate, docetaxel, or cetuximab (median 7.5 vs 5.1 months; HR 0.70), nearly doubling 1-year survival (36.0% vs 16.6%) with a third of the grade 3–4 treatment-related toxicity (13.1% vs 35.1%). KEYNOTE-040 (n=495) replicated the class effect with pembrolizumab (median 8.4 vs 6.9 months; HR 0.80). Neither drug improved median progression-free survival — the benefit is a long survival tail, not slower average progression. PROPOSED LIKELY, Tier C (overall-survival benefit — the developer rules personally).

title: Cetuximab versus cisplatin with radiotherapy in HPV-positive oropharyngeal cancer (RTOG 1016; De-ESCALaTE)
question: In HPV-positive oropharyngeal squamous-cell carcinoma, can cetuximab replace cisplatin alongside radiotherapy without losing overall survival (de-escalation)?
balance: Two randomised trials tested the same de-escalation idea and both found the substitution costs lives. In RTOG 1016 (n=849), cetuximab failed non-inferiority for overall survival — 5-year survival 77.9% versus 84.6% with cisplatin (HR 1.45), with significantly more locoregional failure (5-year 17.3% vs 9.9%). In De-ESCALaTE (n=334, low-risk patients — the population with most to gain from gentler treatment), cetuximab again lost: 2-year survival 89.4% versus 97.5% (HR 5.0) and 2-year recurrence 16.1% versus 6.0%. Decisively, neither trial found the toxicity advantage that justified the swap — severe toxicity was essentially identical. The verdict is unusually clean: do not substitute cetuximab for cisplatin in cisplatin-eligible HPV-positive oropharyngeal cancer. PROPOSED LIKELY (harm), Tier C (mortality harm from substitution — the developer rules personally).

title: Postoperative chemoradiotherapy in high-risk resected HNSCC (EORTC 22931; RTOG 9501)
question: In resected HNSCC with high-risk features, does adding concurrent cisplatin to postoperative radiotherapy improve disease-free and overall survival?
balance: Two 2004 phase 3 trials, published back to back, tested postoperative cisplatin chemoradiation against radiotherapy alone. EORTC 22931 (n=334) found significant gains in progression-free survival (HR 0.75; 5-year 47% vs 36%) and overall survival (HR 0.70; 5-year 53% vs 40%), with locoregional relapse nearly halved. RTOG 9501 (n=459) found significantly better local-regional control (HR 0.61) and disease-free survival (HR 0.78) but no significant survival difference (HR 0.84, 95% CI 0.65–1.09). Both trials roughly doubled severe acute toxicity (grade ≥3: 41% vs 21% and 77% vs 34%), and RTOG 9501 recorded four treatment deaths on the combined arm. Later pooled analyses localise the clearest benefit to positive margins and extracapsular extension. PROPOSED LIKELY, Tier C (overall-survival claim — the developer rules personally). CORRECTION: the topic file quoted EORTC 22931's overall-survival HR as 0.84; the fetched record gives HR 0.70 (0.84 is RTOG 9501's survival HR).

title: Induction docetaxel chemotherapy (TPF) versus PF in locally advanced HNSCC (TAX 324; TAX 323)
question: In unresectable locally advanced HNSCC, does induction TPF (docetaxel/cisplatin/5-fluorouracil) improve overall survival compared with PF (cisplatin/5-fluorouracil) induction?
balance: Two phase 3 trials compared docetaxel-containing induction (TPF) with the older PF doublet, and both favoured TPF. TAX 324 (n=501, induction followed by chemoradiotherapy) found overall survival HR 0.70, with median survival 71 versus 30 months and 3-year survival 62% versus 48%. TAX 323 (n=358, induction followed by radiotherapy) found progression-free survival HR 0.72 and a 27% relative reduction in the risk of death (median survival 18.8 vs 14.5 months). The claim this shelf supports is narrow: TPF is the better induction regimen. Whether induction chemotherapy at all beats proceeding directly to chemoradiotherapy is a different question — the later PARADIGM and DeCIDE trials of induction followed by chemoradiation versus chemoradiation alone were null and are fenced here, not carded. PROPOSED LIKELY, Tier C (overall-survival benefit — the developer rules personally).

title: Induction chemotherapy before chemoradiotherapy in locoregionally advanced nasopharyngeal carcinoma (gemcitabine–cisplatin; TPF)
question: In locoregionally advanced nasopharyngeal carcinoma, does induction chemotherapy (gemcitabine–cisplatin or TPF) before concurrent chemoradiotherapy improve recurrence-free and overall survival versus chemoradiotherapy alone?
balance: Two Chinese phase 3 trials, testing two different induction regimens before the same chemoradiotherapy backbone, both improved failure-free outcomes. Induction gemcitabine–cisplatin (Zhang 2019, n=480) raised 3-year recurrence-free survival from 76.5% to 85.3% (HR 0.51) and 3-year overall survival from 90.3% to 94.6% (HR 0.43). Induction TPF (Sun 2016, n=480) raised 3-year failure-free survival from 72% to 80% (HR 0.68). The cost is upfront toxicity: grade 3–4 acute adverse events in 75.7% versus 55.7% in the gemcitabine–cisplatin trial, with no excess of late toxicity. Two concordant trials with different regimens support the induction strategy itself in this disease — unusually, the opposite pattern to HNSCC induction (Shelf #1914). PROPOSED LIKELY, Tier C (overall-survival claim — the developer rules personally).

title: Cetuximab plus radiotherapy in locally advanced HNSCC (Bonner trial)
question: In locally advanced HNSCC treated with definitive radiotherapy, does adding cetuximab improve locoregional control and overall survival versus radiotherapy alone?
balance: A single multinational randomised trial (n=424) — never replicated head-to-head — found that adding weekly cetuximab to high-dose radiotherapy improved locoregional control (median 24.4 vs 14.9 months; HR 0.68) and overall survival (median 49.0 vs 29.3 months; HR 0.74), and the mature 5-year analysis confirmed the survival benefit (HR 0.73; 5-year survival 45.6% vs 36.4%). The stamp follows the mature data, per house rule. Toxicity beyond acneiform rash and infusion reactions was not increased — the fact that later made cetuximab the default partner for cisplatin-ineligible patients, and the result that made its failure as a cisplatin substitute (Shelf #1912) so surprising. Flagged OUTSTANDING-SINGLE: one open-label trial that carried a standard of care for two decades. PROPOSED LIKELY, Tier C (overall-survival benefit — the developer rules personally).

title: PD-1 blockade plus chemotherapy in recurrent or metastatic nasopharyngeal carcinoma (JUPITER-02; RATIONALE-309; CAPTAIN-1st)
question: In recurrent or metastatic nasopharyngeal carcinoma, does adding a PD-1 inhibitor to gemcitabine–cisplatin improve progression-free and overall survival versus chemotherapy alone?
balance: Three double-blind phase 3 trials in endemic-region populations added three different PD-1 inhibitors to the same gemcitabine–cisplatin backbone, and all three improved progression-free survival with near-identical hazard ratios: toripalimab (JUPITER-02) PFS HR 0.52 (median 21.4 vs 8.2 months), tislelizumab (RATIONALE-309) HR 0.52, and camrelizumab (CAPTAIN-1st) HR 0.54 (median 9.7 vs 6.9 months). Overall survival is mature only for toripalimab: HR 0.63 at a median 36 months of follow-up (median not reached vs 33.7 months). The class claim — PD-1 blockade added to first-line chemotherapy prolongs progression-free survival in recurrent/metastatic nasopharyngeal carcinoma — rests on three concordant blinded trials; the survival claim currently rests on one. PROPOSED LIKELY, Tier C (overall-survival benefit — the developer rules personally).

title: Perioperative pembrolizumab in resectable locally advanced HNSCC (KEYNOTE-689)
question: In resectable locally advanced HNSCC, does neoadjuvant plus adjuvant pembrolizumab added to surgery and postoperative radiotherapy (± cisplatin) improve event-free survival versus standard care?
balance: A single phase 3 trial (n=714) found that adding two neoadjuvant cycles and fifteen adjuvant cycles of pembrolizumab to standard care — surgery then postoperative radiotherapy with or without cisplatin — significantly improved event-free survival in every prespecified population: hazard ratio 0.66 in PD-L1 CPS ≥10, 0.70 in CPS ≥1, and 0.73 in the total population, with 36-month event-free survival of 57.6% versus 46.4% overall. Neoadjuvant pembrolizumab did not compromise surgery (completion ~88% in both arms), and grade ≥3 treatment-related adverse events were similar (44.6% vs 42.9%). Overall survival was immature at this first interim analysis, so this shelf claims an event-free-survival benefit only — no survival claim, hence not Tier C. Single recent trial; the stamp is LIKELY on the strength of a large, consistently positive phase 3 result, pending survival data and any replication. PROPOSED LIKELY.

title: Larynx preservation in advanced laryngeal cancer (VA Laryngeal Cancer trial; RTOG 91-11)
question: In advanced laryngeal squamous-cell carcinoma, do non-surgical strategies (induction chemotherapy plus radiotherapy, or concurrent chemoradiotherapy) preserve the larynx without compromising overall survival, compared with laryngectomy-based or radiotherapy-only treatment?
balance: Two landmark randomised programmes built larynx preservation. The VA Laryngeal Cancer trial (n=332) showed induction chemotherapy followed by definitive radiotherapy preserved the larynx in 64% of patients with 2-year survival identical to laryngectomy plus postoperative radiotherapy (68% in both groups). RTOG 91-11 (n=520, 10-year follow-up) then separated the non-surgical strategies: both induction PF followed by radiotherapy and concomitant cisplatin-radiotherapy improved laryngectomy-free survival versus radiotherapy alone (HR 0.75 and 0.78), and concomitant chemoradiation gave the best larynx preservation (HR 0.58 versus the induction arm). Overall survival did not differ significantly between any of RTOG 91-11's arms — but deaths not attributed to larynx cancer or treatment were higher with concomitant chemotherapy (30.8% vs 20.8% and 16.9%), and the concomitant-versus-induction survival hazard ratio was 1.25 (P=0.08). The balance: organ preservation is real and survival-equivalent on the trials' own terms, bought with more late non-cancer deaths in the most intensive arm. PROPOSED LIKELY, Tier C (survival-equivalence balance — the developer rules personally).

title: Temozolomide with radiotherapy in newly diagnosed glioblastoma (Stupp regimen; EORTC-NCIC 26981)
question: In newly diagnosed glioblastoma, does adding concomitant and adjuvant temozolomide to radiotherapy improve overall survival versus radiotherapy alone?

Never replicated because it never needed to be: the control arm became unethical once reported. Flagged OUTSTANDING-SINGLE (open-label). PROPOSED LIKELY, Tier C (overall-survival benefit — the developer rules personally).

title: Short-course radiotherapy plus temozolomide in elderly glioblastoma (NCIC CE.3)
question: In patients aged 65 or older with newly diagnosed glioblastoma, does adding temozolomide to short-course radiotherapy (40 Gy in 15 fractions) improve overall survival versus short-course radiotherapy alone?

title: Tumour Treating Fields plus maintenance temozolomide in newly diagnosed glioblastoma (EF-14)
question: After chemoradiotherapy for newly diagnosed glioblastoma, does adding Tumour Treating Fields to maintenance temozolomide improve progression-free and overall survival versus temozolomide alone?

Systemic adverse events were similar (48% vs 44%); the device's signature toxicity is mild-to-moderate skin injury under the arrays (52%). Two structural caveats ride the shelf: randomisation occurred after patients had completed chemoradiotherapy without progression, so survival is counted from a post-treatment landmark, not from diagnosis; and the trial is unblinded with no sham device. The recurrent-disease trial (EF-11) was not positive on survival and is fenced. Flagged OUTSTANDING-SINGLE (open-label device trial; hard-endpoint result). title: Vorasidenib in IDH-mutant grade 2 glioma (INDIGO)
question: In residual or recurrent IDH-mutant grade 2 glioma treated with surgery only, does vorasidenib delay progression and time to next intervention versus placebo?
balance: One double-blind phase 3 trial (n=331) in patients with residual or recurrent grade 2 IDH-mutant glioma whose only prior treatment was surgery: the oral mutant-IDH inhibitor vorasidenib more than doubled median progression-free survival (27.7 vs 11.1 months; HR 0.39) and markedly delayed the time to next anticancer intervention (HR 0.26) — the endpoint that matters in a young population for whom delaying radiation and chemotherapy is the therapeutic goal. Grade ≥3 adverse events were more frequent on vorasidenib (22.8% vs 13.5%), driven by liver-enzyme elevation (grade ≥3 ALT increase 9.6% vs 0%). Follow-up was short (median 14.2 months), overall survival is immature, and placebo patients could cross over at progression — so this shelf claims delayed progression and deferred intervention, not longer life. PROPOSED LIKELY.

title: Pazopanib in pretreated non-adipocytic soft-tissue sarcoma (PALETTE)
question: In advanced non-adipocytic soft-tissue sarcoma after chemotherapy, does pazopanib improve progression-free survival versus placebo?
balance: One double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (n=369) in metastatic non-adipocytic soft-tissue sarcoma progressing after standard chemotherapy: pazopanib tripled median progression-free survival (4.6 vs 1.6 months; HR 0.31) without improving overall survival (12.5 vs 10.7 months; HR 0.86, P=0.25) — and with no crossover permitted, that survival null is a clean one. The price is a heavy low-grade toxicity load: fatigue 65%, diarrhoea 58%, nausea 54%, weight loss 48%, and hypertension 41% on pazopanib. This shelf claims a progression benefit only, with the survival result printed beside it so the two are never separated. PROPOSED LIKELY.

title: Eribulin versus dacarbazine in pretreated liposarcoma or leiomyosarcoma
question: In advanced liposarcoma or leiomyosarcoma after at least two prior regimens, does eribulin improve overall survival versus dacarbazine?
balance: One open-label phase 3 trial (n=452) against an active comparator found eribulin improved overall survival versus dacarbazine (median 13.5 vs 11.5 months; HR 0.77, P=0.0169) in patients with advanced liposarcoma or leiomyosarcoma after at least two prior regimens. The gain is modest — 2.0 months of median survival — and the harm side is not trivial: grade 3 or worse adverse events in 67% versus 56%, and deaths in 4% versus 1% (one death judged treatment-related, on eribulin). The trial pooled two histologies stratified at randomisation; the primary record reports the pooled result, and claims that the benefit is concentrated in liposarcoma rest on subgroup analyses not carded here. A single trial with a modest effect and a real toxicity increment carries POSSIBLE, not LIKELY. PROPOSED POSSIBLE, Tier C (overall-survival benefit — the developer rules personally).

title: Three years versus one year of adjuvant imatinib in high-risk GIST (SSGXVIII/AIO)
question: In resected high-risk gastrointestinal stromal tumour, does 3 years of adjuvant imatinib improve recurrence-free and overall survival versus 1 year?
balance: One open-label randomised trial (n=400) settled GIST adjuvant duration: 36 months of imatinib 400 mg/day beat 12 months on recurrence-free survival (HR 0.46; 5-year 65.6% vs 47.9%) and overall survival (HR 0.45; 5-year 92.0% vs 81.7%) in patients at high risk of recurrence after resection. The cost of the longer course is attrition: 25.8% of the 36-month group discontinued imatinib for reasons other than recurrence, versus 12.6% of the 12-month group. ACOSOG Z9001 (1 year versus placebo) answers the prior question — whether any adjuvant imatinib helps — and is fenced, not merged. Flagged OUTSTANDING-SINGLE (open-label; duration-defining survival benefit). PROPOSED LIKELY, Tier C (overall-survival benefit — the developer rules personally).

title: Ripretinib in fourth-line advanced GIST (INVICTUS)
question: In advanced GIST progressing on or after imatinib, sunitinib, and regorafenib, does ripretinib improve progression-free survival versus placebo?
balance: One double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (n=129) in patients whose GIST had progressed on at least three prior kinase inhibitors: ripretinib, a switch-control KIT/PDGFRA inhibitor, improved median progression-free survival from 1.0 to 6.3 months (HR 0.15) — one of the largest progression effects recorded in a refractory solid tumour. Placebo patients were permitted to cross over to ripretinib at progression, which was ethically necessary and makes any survival comparison uninterpretable by design; this record's carded content claims the progression benefit only. The population is heavily pretreated with no remaining standard options, which is the context for the effect size. PROPOSED LIKELY.

title: Interval-compressed chemotherapy in localized Ewing sarcoma (AEWS0031)
question: In newly diagnosed localized Ewing sarcoma, does interval-compressed VDC/IE chemotherapy (every 2 weeks) improve event-free survival versus standard 3-weekly scheduling?
balance: One large cooperative-group randomised trial (n=568 eligible) in patients under 50 with newly diagnosed localized Ewing sarcoma: giving the same VDC/IE chemotherapy every 2 weeks instead of every 3 improved 5-year event-free survival from 65% to 73% (P=0.048), with similar toxicity — the gain bought purely by schedule compression, enabled by filgrastim support, with no new drug. The delivered compression was partial: median achieved cycle interval was 15 days (mean 17.3) versus 21 days (mean 22.5), because cycles waited on count recovery. The abstract reports event rates and the P value without a hazard ratio; none is printed on these cards. A single-trial result at P=0.048 is real but not lavish — the stamp reflects a large, well-run, practice-defining trial whose effect, while modest, costs no extra toxicity. PROPOSED LIKELY.

title: Nirogacestat in progressing desmoid tumours (DeFi)
question: In adults with progressing desmoid tumours, does nirogacestat improve progression-free survival and symptom burden versus placebo?
balance: The DeFi trial is the first positive randomised trial in desmoid tumours — a phase 3, double-blind, placebo-controlled study of the γ-secretase inhibitor nirogacestat in 142 adults whose tumours were progressing. Progression-free survival strongly favoured the drug (hazard ratio 0.29, 95% CI 0.15 to 0.55; P<0.001), with an estimated 76% versus 44% of patients event-free at 2 years — a 32-percentage-point absolute difference — and objective responses in 41% versus 8% (complete responses 7% versus 0%). Patient-reported pain, symptom burden, functioning and quality of life all improved significantly more on nirogacestat (P≤0.01). The price is real but mostly low-grade toxicity: diarrhoea in 84%, nausea 54%, fatigue 51%, hypophosphataemia 42% and rash 32%, with 95% of adverse events grade 1 or 2 — plus ovarian dysfunction in 27 of 36 (75%) women of childbearing potential, which resolved in 74% of those affected and must be counselled before treatment. There is no second trial and no survival claim; this shelf rests on progression and symptom endpoints in a rare tumour with no previously approved therapy. Flagged OUTSTANDING-SINGLE. PROPOSED LIKELY.

title: GP referral to commercial and total-diet-replacement weight programmes (WRAP; DROPLET)
question: In adults with overweight or obesity in primary care, does referral to a commercial open-group weight-management programme produce more weight loss than brief GP intervention or written information, and does the benefit persist?
balance: Two UK primary-care trials answer two strengths of the same idea. WRAP (1,267 adults with BMI ≥28) randomised patients to brief advice with self-help materials, a 12-week commercial open-group programme (Weight Watchers), or the same programme for 52 weeks: at 1 year the programmes beat brief intervention by an adjusted 2.71 kg, and 52 weeks beat 12 weeks by a further 2.14 kg. But the mature data discipline the claim — at 5 years mean losses were −0.46 kg (brief), −1.95 kg (12-week) and −2.67 kg (52-week), and the adjusted 52-week-versus-brief difference of −1.76 kg was no longer statistically significant (95% CI −3.68 to 0.17). DROPLET tested the intensive end of referral: GP referral to a total-diet-replacement programme (810 kcal/day for 8 weeks with behavioural support) produced −10.7 kg versus −3.1 kg with nurse-led usual care at 12 months, an adjusted difference of −7.2 kg. So referral beats brief advice at one year in both trials, longer beats shorter, intensity buys more loss — and most of the advantage attenuates by five years. Cost-effectiveness modelling in WRAP favours referral despite that fade. Both trials were necessarily open-label. PROPOSED LIKELY.

title: Screening and brief alcohol intervention in primary care (SIPS)
question: In primary-care patients who screen positive for hazardous or harmful drinking, does screening plus structured brief intervention reduce alcohol consumption more than screening with simple feedback and a leaflet?
balance: SIPS was built to find the extra value of doing more: 3,562 primary-care patients were screened, 900 screened positive for hazardous or harmful drinking, and practices were cluster-randomised to hand over a patient information leaflet, add five minutes of structured brief advice, or add twenty minutes of brief lifestyle counselling — with every participant first receiving simple feedback on their screening result. At 6 months there were no significant differences in the proportion no longer drinking hazardously (AUDIT-negative): versus the leaflet group, the odds ratio was 0.85 (95% CI 0.52 to 1.39) for brief advice and 0.78 (0.48 to 1.25) for lifestyle counselling, with the same picture at 12 months and in per-protocol analysis. All three groups drank less than at baseline — screening and feedback happened to everyone, and that shared ingredient is the plausible active one. Smaller earlier brief-intervention trials sit behind SIPS, but a pragmatic cluster trial of this size, null on its own primary outcome with point estimates leaning the wrong way, sets the shelf: brief advice and counselling add nothing measurable on top of feedback plus a leaflet. The shelf says nothing about screening versus no screening, which SIPS did not test. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference).

title: Amoxicillin for acute lower-respiratory-tract infection when pneumonia is not suspected (GRACE)
question: In adults presenting to primary care with acute cough and lower-respiratory-tract infection where pneumonia is not suspected, does amoxicillin speed recovery or reduce symptom severity versus placebo?
balance: The GRACE trial randomised 2,061 adults with acute cough and lower-respiratory-tract infection — pneumonia not suspected — across 12 European countries to amoxicillin 1 g three times daily for 7 days or placebo, double-blind. On the outcomes patients care about, the antibiotic did nothing significant: duration of 'moderately bad or worse' symptoms (hazard ratio 1.06, 95% CI 0.96 to 1.18) and symptom severity on days 2–4 (difference −0.07 points, p=0.074). The one significant secondary result — fewer new or worsening symptoms, 15.9% versus 19.3% (number needed to treat 30) — is smaller than the harm flowing the other way: nausea, rash or diarrhoea significantly more common (number needed to harm 21), plus one anaphylaxis on amoxicillin. The prespecified older subgroup (age ≥60, n=595) showed no selective benefit either, answering the 'older patients are different' argument directly. Hospitalisations were 1 versus 2 and there were no study-related deaths. A large, blinded, placebo-controlled trial with a null primary endpoint and harms exceeding the one positive secondary: the stamp follows. The same research programme's prescriber-training question (GRACE INTRO) is a different shelf (pack #1698); this shelf is the drug question. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference).

title: Oral prednisolone for acute lower-respiratory-tract infection in non-asthmatic adults (OSAC)
question: In non-asthmatic adults with acute lower-respiratory-tract infection, does a short course of oral prednisolone shorten the duration of moderately severe symptoms versus placebo?
balance: OSAC randomised 401 adults with acute cough and at least one lower-respiratory symptom — no asthma, no chronic lung disease, no immediate need for antibiotics — in 54 English family practices to prednisolone 40 mg daily for 5 days or placebo. The primary outcome, duration of moderately bad or worse cough, was identical at the median: 5 days in both groups (adjusted hazard ratio 1.11, 95% CI 0.89 to 1.39; P=.36). The co-primary symptom-severity score was 1.99 versus 2.16 points (adjusted difference −0.20, 95% CI −0.40 to 0.00), which at P=.05 against the trial's prespecified α of 0.001 is a null, not a near-miss. Nothing else moved either — not other symptom durations, peak flow, or antibiotic use — and there were no serious adverse events. Why only POSSIBLE where the companion antibiotic trial (GRACE, shelf #1932) earns LIKELY: OSAC is a single trial a fifth of GRACE's size, and its duration interval (0.89–1.39) cannot exclude a modest severity benefit. One good trial, a clean primary null, some residual imprecision. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference).

title: Fluvoxamine for early COVID-19 in high-risk outpatients (TOGETHER; ACTIV-6)
question: In symptomatic high-risk adults with early COVID-19 managed in the community, does fluvoxamine reduce emergency care retention or hospitalisation versus placebo?
balance: Two platform trials, two answers — and the disagreement is structured, not random. TOGETHER randomised high-risk, largely unvaccinated Brazilian outpatients early in the pandemic to fluvoxamine 100 mg twice daily for 10 days or placebo: the composite of retention in a COVID-19 emergency setting or transfer to hospital occurred in 11% versus 16% (relative risk 0.68, 95% Bayesian credible interval 0.52 to 0.88; absolute difference 5.0 percentage points), and the arm was stopped for superiority. Deaths (17 versus 25; OR 0.68, 95% CI 0.36–1.27) were not significantly different and are not claimed. ACTIV-6, in the United States, used HALF the dose (50 mg twice daily) in a mostly vaccinated, lower-risk population with a recovery-time primary outcome and found nothing: median sustained recovery 12 versus 13 days (hazard ratio 0.96), with hospital-level events at 3.9% versus 3.8%. ACTIV-6 does not refute TOGETHER on TOGETHER's terms — different dose, population, era and endpoint — but it removes any presumption that the effect generalises, and a single positive platform result contradicted in a second setting is exactly what POSSIBLE is for. PROPOSED POSSIBLE.

title: Metformin for early COVID-19 and post-COVID condition (COVID-OUT)
question: In adults with overweight or obesity and early COVID-19, does immediate metformin reduce severe acute outcomes — and does it reduce the incidence of post-COVID condition over 10 months?
balance: COVID-OUT randomised 1,431 adults aged 30–85 with overweight or obesity, within days of a positive test, in a quadruple-blind 2×3 factorial of metformin, ivermectin and fluvoxamine against concurrent controls. The acute story is a null: the primary composite (hypoxaemia, emergency visit, hospitalisation or death) gave an adjusted odds ratio of 0.84 for metformin (95% CI 0.66 to 1.09; P=0.19), and the hospitalisation-or-death composite also crossed 1 (OR 0.47, 0.20–1.11); only a prespecified secondary composite of ED visit, hospitalisation or death was nominally positive (OR 0.58, 0.35–0.94). The long-term story is the interesting one: over 10 months, in the 1,126 participants followed for it, provider-diagnosed post-COVID condition occurred in 6.3% on metformin versus 10.4% on placebo (hazard ratio 0.59, 95% CI 0.39–0.89; p=0.012) — a 4.1-percentage-point absolute reduction, about 41% in relative terms, with a stronger estimate when treatment started within 3 days of symptoms (HR 0.37). Ivermectin (HR 0.99) and fluvoxamine (HR 1.36) showed no long-COVID effect. One trial, and the positive outcome is a prespecified but secondary endpoint ascertained by survey report of a provider diagnosis: that combination is POSSIBLE, and this shelf makes no acute-treatment claim. PROPOSED POSSIBLE.

title: N-of-1 statin rechallenge for muscle symptoms (StatinWISE; SAMSON)
question: In patients who stopped or are considering stopping a statin because of muscle symptoms, do symptom scores differ between statin and placebo periods in a series of randomised double-blind n-of-1 trials?
balance: Two independent research groups asked patients who blamed a statin for their muscle symptoms to test themselves, blinded. StatinWISE ran 200 patients through six randomised 2-month periods of atorvastatin 20 mg or placebo: symptom scores did not differ (mean difference −0.11 on a 0–10 scale, 95% CI −0.36 to 0.14; P=0.40), withdrawals for intolerable symptoms were 9% in statin periods and 7% in placebo periods, and two thirds of completers planned to restart statins. SAMSON was smaller and more granular — 60 patients, monthly bottles of statin, placebo or nothing, daily symptom scores by app: symptoms were 8.0 in no-tablet months, 16.3 in statin months and 15.4 in placebo months, with no statin-versus-placebo difference (P=0.388) and a nocebo ratio of 0.90, meaning 90% of the symptom burden provoked by a statin tablet was also provoked by an identical dummy tablet; half the participants were back on statins 6 months later. Same drug, same dose, same design family, same answer: in this population the symptoms are real, but they are not, in aggregate, pharmacologically caused by atorvastatin 20 mg — they are triggered by taking a tablet believed to cause them. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference).

title: Gabapentin for chronic pelvic pain in women (GaPP2)
question: In women with chronic pelvic pain and no identified pathology, does gabapentin reduce pelvic pain versus placebo?
balance: GaPP2 was designed to settle a widespread off-label habit: 306 women with chronic pelvic pain of at least 3 months and no obvious pathology at laparoscopy, in 39 UK centres, randomised double-blind to gabapentin titrated to a maximum of 2,700 mg daily or placebo for 16 weeks. Both co-primary outcomes were null. Worst pain scores at weeks 13–16 were 7.1 versus 7.4 (adjusted mean difference −0.20, 97.5% CI −0.81 to 0.42; p=0.47) and average pain 4.3 versus 4.5 (adjusted difference −0.18, −0.71 to 0.35; p=0.45), with intervals that exclude a one-point benefit on a 0–10 scale. The harm side was not symmetrical: serious adverse events occurred in 10 women (7%) on gabapentin versus 3 (2%) on placebo (p=0.04), and dizziness, drowsiness and visual disturbances were all more common on the drug. An adequately powered, double-blind, single trial with a null primary and a significant harm excess earns the definitive-negative stamp; the population boundary — pain without identified pathology — is on the card's face. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference).

title: Haemorrhoidal artery ligation versus rubber band ligation (HubBLe)
question: In symptomatic grade II–III haemorrhoids, does haemorrhoidal artery ligation (HAL) reduce recurrence at one year versus rubber band ligation (RBL)?
balance: Correction first, because the topic draft had the headline backwards: the fetched record shows recurrence at 1 year was LOWER after haemorrhoidal artery ligation than after rubber band ligation — 30% (48/161) versus 49% (87/176), adjusted odds ratio 2.23 (95% CI 1.42–3.51; p=0.0005) for recurrence with banding versus ligation. What complicates the verdict is everything around that number. The difference was driven by repeat procedures: 32% of banded patients needed a subsequent haemorrhoid procedure versus 14% after ligation — and repeat banding is an accepted part of an RBL course, so HubBLe effectively compared one operation against one banding, not against a banding strategy. Ligation also hurt more (day-1 pain 4.6 versus 3.4; day-7 pain 3.1 versus 1.6) and produced more serious adverse events requiring admission (12 events, ~7%, versus 2, ~1%), which is why the trialists themselves concluded that patients and commissioners might prefer a course of RBL despite the recurrence figures. A single open-label trial whose own conclusion cuts against its primary outcome, with the comparison structurally favouring the operation: POSSIBLE for the narrow claim that HAL reduces 1-year recurrence after a single procedure, at a pain and safety cost. PROPOSED POSSIBLE.

title: Behavioural weight-loss treatment delivered in primary care practice (POWER)
question: In obese adults with cardiovascular risk factors, do remote (telephone/web) or in-person behavioural weight-loss interventions delivered through primary care produce more weight loss at two years than a self-directed control?
balance: POWER randomised 415 obese adults (mean BMI 36.6) with at least one cardiovascular risk factor, recruited from six primary care practices, to self-directed weight loss or to a behavioural programme delivered remotely (telephone, website, email) or in person (group and individual sessions plus the remote tools), with primary care providers reinforcing participation at routine visits. At 24 months both supported programmes clearly beat control: −4.6 kg (remote) and −5.1 kg (in-person) versus −0.8 kg, both P<0.001 against control, with 38.2% and 41.4% losing at least 5% of body weight versus 18.8% of controls. The comparison that gives this shelf its practical payload — remote versus in-person — showed no significant difference: travelling to sessions bought nothing measurable over the phone and the website. A single trial, and unblinded as behavioural trials must be; it is flagged as such. Its direction agrees with the referral trials on shelf #1930, but this shelf stands on POWER alone: supported behavioural treatment, however delivered, produces ~4–5 kg more loss than going it alone, sustained to two years. PROPOSED LIKELY (single trial).

title: A re-engineered hospital discharge programme (Project RED)
question: In medical inpatients, does a re-engineered discharge — nurse discharge advocate, tailored after-hospital care plan, and pharmacist follow-up call — reduce hospital utilisation (readmission plus emergency visits) at 30 days versus usual discharge?
balance: Project RED tested a package, not a pill: a nurse discharge advocate who arranged follow-up appointments, confirmed medication reconciliation and taught from an individualised instruction booklet (copied to the primary care provider), plus a clinical pharmacist telephone call 2–4 days after discharge to reinforce the plan and review medications. In 749 medical inpatients at a single urban US safety-net hospital, the intervention group used significantly less hospital care in the 30 days after discharge — 0.314 versus 0.451 visits per person per month, an incidence rate ratio of 0.695 (95% CI 0.515 to 0.937; P=0.009), roughly a 30% relative reduction — with the effect concentrated in patients who had used hospital care in the previous 6 months. The limits define the stamp: one centre, one trial, no blinding of participants or providers (follow-up assessors were blinded), outcome assessment partly by participant report, and adverse events were collected but not assessed in this report. A promising, widely imitated single-centre result that has not been re-run at this rigour on this card. PROPOSED POSSIBLE.

title: Extended thromboprophylaxis after hospitalisation for medical illness (MARINER; EXCLAIM; APEX)
question: In medically ill patients discharged from hospital at raised VTE risk, does 45 days of rivaroxaban reduce symptomatic VTE and VTE-related death versus placebo without excess major bleeding?
balance: Three large trials of extended post-discharge prophylaxis tell one consistent, uncomfortable story. MARINER — the only trial powered on symptomatic outcomes — randomised 12,024 discharged medically ill patients at raised VTE risk to rivaroxaban 10 mg daily or placebo for 45 days: its primary composite of symptomatic VTE or VTE-related death was NOT significantly reduced (0.83% vs 1.10%; hazard ratio 0.76, 95% CI 0.52 to 1.09; P=0.14), although the symptomatic nonfatal VTE component was lower (0.18% vs 0.42%; HR 0.44, 0.22–0.89), and major bleeding was numerically higher (0.28% vs 0.15%; HR 1.88, 0.84–4.23). EXCLAIM found extended enoxaparin cut a VTE endpoint dominated by screening-detected clots (2.5% vs 4.0%; absolute difference −1.53 points) at the cost of significantly more major bleeding (0.8% vs 0.3%), with benefit concentrated in women, patients over 75 and the most immobile. APEX missed its prespecified primary cohort analysis (6.9% vs 8.5%; relative risk 0.81, 95% CI 0.65 to 1.00; P=0.054); its positive broader-cohort results are formally exploratory under the trial's own gatekeeping plan. Net: extended prophylaxis prevents some, mostly asymptomatic, clots; a symptomatic or survival benefit is unproven where it was tested head-on, and bleeding tilts against treatment. Tier C because the question includes VTE-related death. PROPOSED POSSIBLE.

title: Oral midodrine to wean intravenous vasopressors in the ICU (MIDAS)
question: In ICU patients with persistent hypotension on a single intravenous vasopressor, does oral midodrine shorten time to vasopressor discontinuation versus placebo?
balance: MIDAS asked a practical ICU question — can an oral α1-agonist get stable patients off the drip that is keeping them in the unit? In 132 analysed patients on a single intravenous vasopressor for at least 24 hours across three US and Australian tertiary centres, midodrine 20 mg every 8 hours did not shorten time to vasopressor discontinuation: median 23.5 hours versus 22.5 hours on placebo (difference 1 hour, 95% CI −10.4 to 12.3; p=0.62). No secondary endpoint moved — not ICU-discharge readiness, lengths of stay or readmission — and the trial's one clear between-group difference was harm-shaped: bradycardia in 5 patients (7.6%) on midodrine versus none on placebo (p=0.02). The stamp stops at POSSIBLE because a single 132-patient trial whose interval still admits roughly ten hours' faster weaning shows 'no demonstrated benefit', not proof of none. Midodrine's other common question — preventing vasovagal syncope — is a different shelf (pack #1557). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference).

title: Patient education to prevent falls among older hospital inpatients (Haines; Hill)
question: In older hospital inpatients, does individualised patient education (with written and video materials and follow-up) reduce falls and fall-related injuries versus usual care?
balance: Two Australian trials converge on the same qualifier: education works in patients who can act on it. Haines (2011) randomised 1,206 older inpatients to usual care, multimedia materials alone, or materials plus trained-professional follow-up: overall fall rates did not differ significantly (9.27, 8.61 and 7.63 per 1,000 patient-days), but there was a significant interaction with cognitive status — among cognitively intact patients the complete programme nearly halved falls versus control (4.01 vs 8.72 per 1,000 patient-days; adjusted hazard ratio 0.43, 95% CI 0.24 to 0.78) and beat materials alone (HR 0.51). Hill (2015) then tested individualised education plus staff training and feedback in eight rehabilitation units, enrolling only patients with MMSE above 23 — that is, the cognitively intact population Haines pointed to — and found falls cut from 13.78 to 7.80 per 1,000 patient-days (adjusted rate ratio 0.60, 95% CI 0.42–0.94) with injurious falls also reduced (rate ratio 0.65). The shelf's claim is therefore scoped: individualised education with professional follow-up reduces falls in cognitively intact older inpatients, best evidenced in rehabilitation settings. Materials alone did nothing measurable; the human follow-up is part of the treatment. PROPOSED LIKELY.

title: Multifaceted clinical pharmacist intervention in hospital (OPTIMIST)
question: In acutely admitted medical patients, does a multifaceted clinical-pharmacist intervention (medication review, discharge planning, and post-discharge follow-up) reduce readmissions versus usual care?
balance: The OPTIMIST trial (reported by Ravn-Nielsen and colleagues) randomised 1,499 acutely admitted Danish medical patients taking at least five medications to usual care, a basic intervention (medication review alone), or an extended intervention (medication review, three motivational interviews, and structured follow-up with the primary care physician, pharmacy and nursing home). The extended package worked on the outcomes it aimed at: versus usual care it reduced readmission within 30 days (hazard ratio 0.62, 95% CI 0.46 to 0.84) and within 180 days (HR 0.75, 0.62–0.90), and the primary composite of readmission or emergency visit within 180 days (HR 0.77, 0.64–0.93), with a number needed to treat of 12. Drug-related readmissions and deaths were numerically lower but not significant (deaths HR 0.83, 0.22–3.11) — no mortality claim is made. Crucially, the record reports no significant effect for the basic review-only arm: the benefit belongs to the extended, follow-up-heavy package, not to 'a pharmacist looked at the chart'. Single trial, one country's system, and the stamp prices that in. PROPOSED POSSIBLE.

title: Automated electronic alerts for acute kidney injury (Wilson 2015; Wilson 2021)
question: In hospitalised patients who develop acute kidney injury, does an automated electronic alert to the treating team improve kidney recovery and reduce dialysis or death versus usual care without alerts?
balance: The same investigative group tested AKI alerting twice, at two scales, and got the same answer with a warning attached. The 2015 single-centre trial randomised 2,393 inpatients with stage 1 or greater AKI to a text alert to the covering provider and unit pharmacist or usual care: the primary composite of creatinine change, dialysis and death at 7 days did not differ (p=0.88), with dialysis (7.2% vs 5.9%; OR 1.25) and death (5.9% vs 5.1%; OR 1.16) both numerically higher in the alert arm. The 2021 multicentre trial randomised 6,030 patients across six hospitals to an EHR pop-up alert with an AKI order set or usual care: the primary composite of AKI progression, dialysis or death within 14 days was 21.3% versus 20.9% (relative risk 1.02, 95% CI 0.93 to 1.13; P=0.67) — and at the two non-teaching hospitals alerts were associated with significantly WORSE outcomes (relative risk 1.49, 1.12–1.98), including more deaths (15.6% vs 8.6%). Alerts did increase some AKI care practices without those changes mediating outcomes. Two randomised trials, over 8,400 patients, no benefit on any primary outcome: telling clinicians louder that AKI has happened does not, by itself, change what happens next. (Correction: the topic draft cited the 2021 trial as N Engl J Med; the fetched record is BMJ 2021.) PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference).

title: Ramelteon and melatonin to prevent delirium in hospital (Hatta; Al-Aama)
question: In older hospitalised or ICU patients at risk of delirium, does nightly ramelteon (or melatonin) reduce incident delirium versus placebo?
balance: Two small placebo-controlled trials of melatonin-pathway agents point the same way, with effect sizes large enough to demand a discount. Hatta randomised just 67 patients aged 65–89 admitted with serious medical problems to ramelteon 8 mg nightly or placebo for 7 days: delirium occurred in 3% versus 32% (relative risk 0.09, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.69; adjusted odds ratio 0.07). Al-Aama randomised 145 patients aged 65 or over on a medical unit to melatonin 0.5 mg nightly or placebo: delirium in 12.0% versus 31.0% (adjusted odds ratio 0.19, 95% CI 0.06–0.62). Put together, that is about 210 patients, two different agents, two countries — and relative reductions of 70–90%, exactly the profile (tiny samples, huge effects) that most often shrinks on replication. Al-Aama also carries an honesty flag on its own record: loss to follow-up made an intention-to-treat analysis impossible. The signal is worth a larger trial and worth this shelf; it is not yet worth more than POSSIBLE. No mortality or length-of-stay claim is made. PROPOSED POSSIBLE.

title: Sustained care intervention for hospitalised smokers (Rigotti 2014; Helping HAND 2)
question: In smokers hospitalised for any cause who want to quit, does a sustained care intervention — free cessation medication plus automated calls and counsellor contact after discharge — increase biochemically confirmed abstinence versus standard post-discharge advice?
balance: This shelf's second card reverses its first impression, so the correction leads. The topic draft promised an earlier, concordant JAMA 2012 trial by the same group; no such trial exists in the record (the group's 2012 JAMA item is a clinical review, not a trial). The real second trial is the later, larger replication — Helping HAND 2 (2016) — and it failed on its primary outcome. The sequence in full: Rigotti 2014, a single-centre trial of 397 hospitalised smokers who wanted to quit, found sustained care (free cessation medication for up to 90 days plus automated interactive-voice-response calls with counsellor triage) beat standard care on biochemically confirmed 7-day abstinence at 6 months, 26% versus 15% (relative risk 1.71, 95% CI 1.14 to 2.56; NNT 9.4). HAND 2 then ran the same model across three hospitals in 1,357 smokers, with quitline linkage added for scalability: confirmed abstinence at 6 months was 17% versus 16% (p=0.58) — no difference — although self-reported abstinence was higher during the 3 treatment months (overall self-reported relative risk 1.25) and treatment use was greater. A positive single-centre result that its own scale-up could not confirm on the outcome that counts earns POSSIBLE, scoped to the original model and setting. PROPOSED POSSIBLE.

title: Symptom-triggered versus fixed-schedule benzodiazepines for alcohol withdrawal (Saitz; Daeppen)
question: In hospitalised patients treated for alcohol withdrawal, does symptom-triggered dosing (CIWA-guided) achieve safe withdrawal with less benzodiazepine and shorter treatment than a fixed tapering schedule?
balance: Two double-blind randomised trials, on two continents, with two different benzodiazepines, found the same thing. Saitz (1994) randomised 101 patients on a VA detoxification unit to fixed-schedule chlordiazepoxide four times daily (plus as-needed doses) or to symptom-triggered dosing guided by a validated withdrawal-severity scale: the symptom-triggered group was treated for a median of 9 hours instead of 68, and received 100 mg of chlordiazepoxide instead of 425 mg (both P<.001), with no significant differences in withdrawal severity during treatment or in seizures or delirium tremens. Daeppen (2002) repeated the experiment in 117 patients at two Swiss university hospitals with oxazepam: only 39% of the symptom-triggered group needed any benzodiazepine at all (versus 100%), the mean dose was 37.5 mg versus 231.4 mg, mean duration 20.0 versus 62.7 hours (all P<.001), comfort did not differ, and complications were limited to a single seizure in the symptom-triggered group. Symptom-triggered dosing individualises treatment, cuts drug exposure roughly four- to six-fold and treatment time roughly three- to seven-fold, with no observed safety penalty — provided the structured scale and monitoring that both trials used are actually in place. Both trials predate routine registration. PROPOSED LIKELY.

title: Oral versus intravenous prednisolone for hospitalised COPD exacerbation (de Jong)
question: In patients hospitalised with an acute COPD exacerbation, is oral prednisolone non-inferior to intravenous prednisolone for treatment failure over 90 days?
balance: One double-blind, double-dummy randomised trial (210 patients hospitalised with COPD exacerbation) found oral prednisolone 60 mg daily for 5 days not inferior to the same dose intravenously: 90-day treatment failure was 56.3% on oral versus 61.7% on IV therapy, with the one-sided lower confidence bound (−5.8%) inside the non-inferiority margin, and no differences in early failure, length of stay, spirometry recovery, or quality of life. Treatment failure was common in both arms — this trial answers the route question, not whether steroids help (that is settled elsewhere). Single trial, modest size, so the stamp is POSSIBLE: the oral route is a reasonable default for patients who can swallow and absorb, sparing a cannula, but one 210-patient trial cannot exclude a small penalty. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (single trial, THIN).

title: High perioperative oxygen fraction and surgical-site infection (PROXI vs Belda)
question: In patients having abdominal surgery, does 80% inspired oxygen during and shortly after surgery reduce surgical-site infection versus 30% oxygen?
balance: Two randomised trials of the same contrast disagree, and the larger one is null. Belda (2005, 300 colorectal patients, double-blind) found fewer infections with 80% oxygen — 14.9% versus 24.4% (relative risk 0.61, 95% CI 0.38–0.98). PROXI (2009, 1,400 laparotomy patients, blinded) found no difference — 19.1% versus 20.1% (odds ratio 0.94, 95% CI 0.72–1.22) — and no difference in pneumonia, atelectasis, or respiratory failure; 30-day mortality was numerically higher with high oxygen (4.4% vs 2.9%; OR 1.56, CI 0.88–2.77, not significant). A third trial in an open-lung ventilation strategy (iPROVE-O2, 2020) also found no infection benefit (8.9% vs 9.4%). Two of three trials, including by far the largest, show no effect, and Belda's confidence interval only just excludes 1.0 — so the disagreement caps the stamp at POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): on current evidence, 80% oxygen should not be given to prevent wound infection. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference).

title: Continuing versus stopping renin–angiotensin inhibitors before major surgery (STOP-or-NOT; SPACE)
question: In patients on renin–angiotensin system inhibitors having major noncardiac surgery, does continuing the drug through surgery versus stopping it 48 hours before change postoperative complications?
balance: Two randomised trials agree that the continue-versus-stop decision does not move hard outcomes. STOP-or-NOT (2024, 2,222 patients, major noncardiac surgery) found the composite of death and major postoperative complications identical at 22% in both strategies (risk ratio 1.02, 95% CI 0.87–1.19); continuing caused more intraoperative hypotension (54% vs 41%; RR 1.31, CI 1.19–1.44) without any downstream outcome penalty. The smaller UK SPACE trial (262 patients) found myocardial injury no less frequent when the drug was stopped (48.3% vs 41.3% continuing; OR for continuing 0.77, CI 0.45–1.31, crossing 1.0) and more acute hypertensive episodes when it was stopped. The physiological trade-off is real in both directions — more hypotension if you continue, more hypertension if you stop — but neither trial shows a difference in complications, myocardial injury, or death. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference), Tier C (the composite includes mortality — the developer rules personally).

title: Liberal versus restrictive transfusion after hip fracture surgery (FOCUS)
question: In older patients with cardiovascular risk after hip fracture surgery, does a liberal transfusion threshold (haemoglobin 100 g/L) improve death or functional recovery versus a restrictive threshold (80 g/L or symptoms)?
balance: One large definitive trial: FOCUS randomised 2,016 patients aged 50+ with cardiovascular disease or risk factors whose haemoglobin fell below 10 g/dL after hip fracture surgery, to transfusion at a 10 g/dL threshold (median 2 units given) or a restrictive strategy (symptoms, or haemoglobin below 8 g/dL; median 0 units). The primary outcome — death or inability to walk across a room unaided at 60 days — was 35.2% liberal versus 34.7% restrictive (OR 1.01, 95% CI 0.84–1.22; absolute difference 0.5 points, CI −3.7 to 4.7), and 60-day mortality was 7.6% versus 6.6%. Restrictive transfusion was as safe as liberal in exactly the population clinicians most feared under-transfusing, while using far less blood. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference), Tier C (mortality is in the primary composite — the developer rules personally). The general threshold question across critical care is homed on Shelf #124; this shelf is the hip-fracture surgical anchor, with a functional endpoint that shelf does not carry.

title: Nitrous oxide in major noncardiac surgery (ENIGMA-II)
question: In at-risk patients having major noncardiac surgery, does adding nitrous oxide to general anaesthesia increase death or cardiovascular complications versus nitrous-free anaesthesia?
balance: One very large trial settles the safety question that the smaller ENIGMA-I era left open. ENIGMA-II randomised 7,112 patients aged 45+ with known or suspected coronary disease having major noncardiac surgery to anaesthesia with or without nitrous oxide. The composite of death and cardiovascular complications at 30 days occurred in 8% in both groups (283 vs 296 patients; relative risk 0.96, 95% CI 0.83–1.12), and surgical-site infection did not differ (9% vs 9%). The one clear penalty was emetogenic: severe nausea and vomiting in 15% versus 11%, manageable with antiemetic prophylaxis. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for the harm question asked — nitrous oxide did not increase death or cardiovascular complications. Tier C (mortality/cardiovascular composite — the developer rules personally).

title: Epidural anaesthesia and analgesia for major abdominal surgery (MASTER)
question: In high-risk patients having major abdominal surgery, does adding epidural anaesthesia and analgesia to general anaesthesia improve survival or major complications versus general anaesthesia with systemic opioids?
balance: The MASTER trial (915 high-risk patients having major abdominal surgery) found that adding intraoperative epidural anaesthesia and 72 hours of postoperative epidural analgesia to general anaesthesia did not reduce its primary endpoint: death at 30 days or major morbidity occurred in 57.1% with epidural versus 60.7% with control (P=0.29), and 30-day mortality was 5.1% versus 4.3% (P=0.67). Of eight morbidity categories, only respiratory failure was less frequent with epidural (23% vs 30%; P=0.02), and pain scores were lower over the first 3 days. Catheter insertion caused no major adverse consequences in the trial. So the split is the story: epidurals buy better analgesia and fewer respiratory failures in this population, not survival. PROPOSED SPLIT stamp as above, Tier C (mortality in the primary endpoint — the developer rules personally).

title: Preoperative oral carbohydrate loading
question: In patients having elective surgery, does a preoperative carbohydrate drink (versus fasting or placebo) reduce preoperative discomfort and postoperative insulin resistance, nausea, and length of stay?
balance: Two small double-blind trials from the group that pioneered preoperative carbohydrate loading support a comfort benefit, not a hard-outcome one. Hausel 2001 (252 elective abdominal surgery patients) found a 12.5% carbohydrate drink (800 mL the evening before, 400 mL on the morning of surgery) left patients less hungry and less anxious than both placebo (flavoured water) and overnight fasting while waiting for surgery, and reduced thirst as effectively as placebo — without increasing gastric fluid volumes or acidity and with no adverse events. Hausel 2005 (172 laparoscopic cholecystectomy patients) found less postoperative nausea and vomiting with carbohydrate than with fasting in the 12–24-hour window (P=0.039), with no difference in pain scores. Neither trial measured length of stay or insulin resistance as a clinical endpoint, and both are small, single-group-of-investigators studies of surrogate and symptom outcomes — hence POSSIBLE, and the shelf makes no claim on complications or stay. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (THIN — symptom endpoints only).

title: Dexmedetomidine after cardiac surgery (DECADE)
question: In patients having cardiac surgery, does prophylactic dexmedetomidine reduce postoperative atrial fibrillation and delirium versus placebo?
balance: One well-blinded placebo-controlled trial says no — with a lean toward harm on one coprimary outcome. DECADE randomised 798 cardiac surgery patients (with cardiopulmonary bypass) to dexmedetomidine infusion from before incision through 24 hours postoperatively or saline placebo. Atrial fibrillation occurred in 30% on dexmedetomidine versus 34% on placebo (relative risk 0.90, 97.8% CI 0.72–1.15; P=.34), and delirium in 17% versus 12% (RR 1.48, 97.8% CI 0.99–2.23) — a non-significant increase whose interval starts at 0.99. Serious adverse events were more frequent with dexmedetomidine (5% vs 2%), with hypotension the recognised mechanism. The trial's own conclusion is that dexmedetomidine should not be infused to prevent atrial fibrillation or delirium after cardiac surgery. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — a single trial, and the delirium point estimate points the wrong way, so this is not a reassurance shelf. Distinct from Shelf #791, which homes low-dose dexmedetomidine for delirium prevention after non-cardiac surgery (Su 2016) — a different population and dose strategy.

title: High versus low PEEP during open abdominal surgery (PROVHILO; iPROVE)
question: In patients having open abdominal surgery under general anaesthesia, does a high-PEEP, recruitment-manoeuvre ventilation strategy reduce postoperative pulmonary complications versus low PEEP without recruitment?
balance: Two multicentre randomised trials agree that aggressive open-lung ventilation does not protect the lungs after abdominal surgery. PROVHILO (900 patients at risk, open abdominal surgery) compared PEEP 12 cmH2O with recruitment manoeuvres against PEEP ≤2 without: postoperative pulmonary complications were 40% versus 39% (relative risk 1.01, 95% CI 0.86–1.20), and the high-PEEP group needed more vasoactive drugs for intraoperative hypotension. iPROVE (1,012 patients, four arms) tested individualised PEEP after recruitment, with or without postoperative CPAP, against standard protective ventilation: the composite of pulmonary and systemic complications was 46–48% in the three intervention arms versus 51% on standard care, every relative risk crossing 1.0. Simpler ventilation — low tidal volume, low PEEP, no routine recruitment — is the strategy the evidence leaves standing. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference).

title: Screening by clinical breast examination in Mumbai (Mittra)
question: In women aged 35–64 in a low-resource setting without mammography, does screening by clinical breast examination every two years reduce breast cancer mortality over 20 years versus no screening?
balance: One very large, very long cluster-randomised trial (151,538 women in Mumbai, 20 clusters, 20 years, four biennial rounds of clinical breast examination by trained primary health workers). Screening clearly downstaged disease: stage III/IV cancers were 37% of diagnoses in the screening arm versus 47% in controls (P=0.001), and cancers were detected about 1.3 years younger. The mortality result is split by age and by analysis: overall, breast cancer mortality was 15% lower in relative terms (rate ratio 0.85, 95% CI 0.71–1.01; P=0.07) — a confidence interval crossing 1.0, so the overall claim is not significant. In a post hoc subgroup of women aged 50 and over the relative reduction was nearly 30% (rate ratio 0.71, 95% CI 0.54–0.94; P=0.02), while women under 50 showed none (0.93, CI 0.79–1.09). PROPOSED POSSIBLE — a single programme, a non-significant primary mortality result, and a significant subgroup that was post hoc; Tier C because the claim is about cancer mortality (the developer rules personally).

title: Screening older people for impaired vision in primary care (Smeeth)
question: In people aged 75 and over in primary care, does screening for impaired vision (with referral) improve visual function and quality of life versus usual care?
balance: One cluster-randomised trial nested in the MRC trial of assessment and management of older people. Important design correction to the naive version of this question: Smeeth 2003 did not compare screening with no screening — it compared universal visual-acuity screening (everyone aged 75+ assessed and tested, with referral for impairment) against targeted screening (acuity testing offered only to those with health problems), both inside a multidimensional assessment programme. Three to five years later there was no difference: the relative risk of visual acuity worse than 6/18 in either eye was 1.07 (95% CI 0.84–1.36) for universal versus targeted, and visual-function questionnaire scores were essentially identical (86.0 vs 85.6; difference 0.4, CI −1.7 to 2.5). Adding a nurse-led vision check for everyone did not improve eyesight outcomes over checking those who already had problems. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — one trial, and its contrast is intensity of screening, not screening versus none.

title: Routine opt-out rapid HIV screening in the emergency department (Haukoos)
question: In emergency department patients, does nontargeted opt-out rapid HIV screening identify more new HIV infections than diagnostic (clinician-initiated) testing?
balance: One large single-centre study — and a design correction matters here: despite sometimes being cited as a trial, Haukoos 2010 used a quasi-experimental equivalent time-samples design, alternating 4-month blocks of nontargeted opt-out screening and physician-directed diagnostic testing over two years in a Denver safety-net ED; patients were not individually randomised. Opt-out screening found more new infections: 15 new diagnoses among 28,043 eligible patients (0.05%) versus 4 among 29,925 (0.01%) in the diagnostic phase, an adjusted risk ratio of 3.6 (95% CI 1.2–10.8) in relative terms — but in absolute terms that is 11 extra diagnoses per roughly 58,000 eligible patients, only 25% of eligible patients completed testing during the opt-out phase, and most new diagnoses were still late (median CD4 count 69/µL in the opt-out phase). PROPOSED POSSIBLE — a real relative increase in detection, a tiny absolute yield, and non-randomised evidence.

title: Screening for hearing loss in older adults (Yueh; SAI-WHAT)
question: In older adults, does screening for hearing impairment (otoscopy, questionnaire, or both) increase hearing-aid use versus no screening?
balance: One four-arm randomised trial (the SAI-WHAT study, 2,305 older US veterans, mean age 61) compared screening by otoscopy (a hand-held audioscope), by the Hearing Handicap Inventory for the Elderly questionnaire, by both, or no screening, with screen-positive participants invited to audiology. Screening moved behaviour, modestly: audiology attendance was 14.7% (otoscopy), 23.0% (questionnaire), and 26.6% (both) versus 10.8% unscreened, and hearing-aid use at 1 year was 6.3%, 4.1%, and 7.4% respectively versus 3.3% in controls (P<.01). The questionnaire-based strategies found far more candidates (59–64% screening positive) than otoscopy alone (19%). The absolute gains in aid use — roughly 1 to 4 extra users per 100 people screened — are small, most screen-detected impairment still went untreated, and the setting (VA, minimal cost barriers) flatters uptake. PROPOSED POSSIBLE. This shelf is about detecting hearing loss; the separate question of whether hearing treatment protects cognition is homed on Shelf #350 (ACHIEVE).

title: Population mass H. pylori eradication on the Matsu Islands (Chiang)
question: In a high-incidence population, does mass Helicobacter pylori screening and eradication reduce gastric cancer incidence and mortality?
balance: One long-running population programme in a genuinely high-incidence setting — but read its design before its numbers. Chiang 2021 reports the Matsu Islands (Taiwan) mass eradication programme: six screening rounds between 2004 and 2018 in residents aged 30+, 85.5% coverage of 7,616 eligible people, cut H. pylori prevalence from 64.2% to 15.0%, with reinfection under 1% per person-year. Against the programme's own historical control period (1995–2003, before eradication), gastric cancer incidence was 53% lower in relative terms (95% CI 30–69%; P<0.001), while gastric cancer mortality was 25% lower in relative terms with an interval crossing no effect (95% CI −14% to 51%; P=0.18) — not significant. Two corrections to the topic draft stand on this shelf: the design is a long-term cohort study with historical controls, not a randomised trial (so the OUTSTANDING-SINGLE framing does not apply), and the eligible population was about 7,600 residents, not the draft's larger figure. PROPOSED POSSIBLE, Tier C (cancer mortality claimed — the developer rules personally). Individual-patient eradication evidence is homed on Shelves #219 and #322; this shelf is the population-programme question.
