title: Screening for cognitive impairment in primary care — patient and family outcomes (Fowler; IU CHOICE)
question: In primary care patients aged 65 and over, does systematic screening for cognitive impairment (versus no screening) improve health-related quality of life, depression, or anxiety for patients or their care partners?
balance: Two randomised trials, a quarter-century of screening enthusiasm apart, give the same answer: none. IU CHOICE (4,005 patients aged 65+ in Indiana safety-net and university clinics) found no effect of cognitive screening on health-related quality of life at 12 months (effect size 0.009, 95% CI −0.063 to 0.080) and depression and anxiety differences inside prespecified equivalency margins. Fowler 2026 (29 clinics, 1,808 patient–family dyads) extended the question to families and to a screening-plus-collaborative-care arm: only 5.1% of screened patients tested positive, over a third of positives offered diagnostic work-up in the intensive arm declined it, and at 24 months family members' physical and mental quality-of-life scores did not differ between arms (differences −0.21 and 0.58, both intervals crossing zero), nor did depression, anxiety, or caregiver outcomes. Screening finds cases; it does not, by itself or with collaborative care attached, make patients or families measurably better or worse off. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference).

title: Postnatal depression screening with psychological therapy (PoNDER; Morrell)
question: In postnatal women, does health-visitor screening for depression with referral to psychological therapy (listening visits or CBT) reduce depression at 6 months versus usual care?
balance: One large cluster-randomised trial from UK primary care. PoNDER trained health visitors to identify postnatal depression (Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale at 6–8 weeks and again at 8 months) and to deliver psychological support — nondirective listening visits (counselling) or cognitive-behavioural therapy — in home visits, versus usual primary care. Among women identified as at risk at 6 weeks (EPDS ≥12), 33.9% in intervention clusters still scored EPDS ≥12 at 6 months versus 45.6% in control clusters (P=0.036), and mean EPDS scores were lower (9.2 vs 11.3; adjusted P=0.001); across all women the figures were 11.7% versus 16.4% (P=0.003). Listening visits and CBT did not differ from each other (P=0.74). The absolute benefit is meaningful (about 12 points in the at-risk group) and the intervention was cost-effective at NICE thresholds in the trial's analysis — but the trial's own authors warn the estimate is imprecise and 'the true effect may be small'; a single cluster trial with a wide interval keeps this at POSSIBLE. Benefit persisted to 12 months and faded by 18.

title: Treating microalbuminuria to prevent cardiovascular events (PREVEND IT)
question: In people with microalbuminuria but no hypertension or hypercholesterolaemia, does fosinopril (or pravastatin) prevent cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, stroke, or heart failure?
balance: PREVEND IT is the cautionary tale for treating a screening marker: a 2×2 factorial trial that randomised 864 microalbuminuric people drawn from a city-wide screening programme (28,256 urine samples screened to find them) to fosinopril 20 mg or placebo, and pravastatin 40 mg or placebo, for four years. Fosinopril did exactly what the surrogate promised — urinary albumin excretion fell 26% (P<0.001) — but the clinical endpoint did not follow: the composite of cardiovascular mortality and hospitalisation for myocardial infarction, heart failure, stroke, end-stage renal disease, or vascular intervention occurred in 45 patients overall (5.2%), with a hazard ratio for fosinopril of 0.60 whose confidence interval crosses 1.0 (95% CI 0.33–1.10; P=0.098) — not significant. Pravastatin showed even less (HR 0.87, CI 0.49–1.57; P=0.649). With only 45 events the trial was underpowered for the question it asked, and two decades on it remains essentially the only randomised test of treating isolated microalbuminuria. The topic draft's wording that fosinopril 'reduced the composite' overstates a non-significant trend; this shelf corrects it. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence), Tier C (cardiovascular mortality in the composite — the developer rules personally).

title: Single low-dose CT screen for lung cancer in high-risk people (UKLS)
question: In high-risk ever-smokers aged 50–75 selected by a validated risk model, does a single low-dose CT screen reduce lung cancer mortality versus usual care?
balance: UKLS is the small, single-screen sibling of the repeated-screening trials. It randomised 4,055 people aged 50–75 at high risk by the LLPv2 model (5-year lung cancer risk ≥4.5%) to one low-dose CT screen or usual care, and followed them a median of 7.3 years. Lung cancers numbered 86 in the screened group versus 75 in controls; lung cancer deaths were 30 versus 46 — a relative rate of 0.65 (95% CI 0.41–1.02), an absolute difference of roughly 1.5% versus 2.3% of participants, with P=0.062: suggestive, not significant, in a trial the authors describe as underpowered alone. The same paper's meta-analysis of nine screening trials (NLST, NELSON, and others) found a pooled relative risk of lung cancer death of 0.84 (95% CI 0.76–0.92) for CT screening — so the modality works on the pooled evidence; what UKLS itself adds is that risk-model selection concentrates yield and that even one screen may carry much of the benefit. PROPOSED POSSIBLE for this shelf's single-screen question (the repeated-screening mortality claim lives on Shelf #164), Tier C (cancer mortality — the developer rules personally).

title: Screening for chlamydia to prevent pelvic inflammatory disease (POPI)
question: In sexually active young women, does a single chlamydia screening test (with treatment of positives) reduce the incidence of pelvic inflammatory disease over 12 months versus deferred screening?
balance: POPI randomised 2,529 sexually active female students in London to immediate chlamydia testing and treatment or to deferred testing a year later. Clinical pelvic inflammatory disease over 12 months occurred in 1.3% of the screened group versus 1.9% of controls — a relative risk of 0.65, but the 95% confidence interval (0.34 to 1.22) crosses 1.0, so the trial's primary comparison is a favourable trend, not a demonstrated reduction. The benefit was concentrated where biology predicts it: among women who tested positive at baseline, pelvic inflammatory disease developed in 1.6% of the screened versus 9.5% of controls (relative risk 0.17, 95% CI 0.03 to 1.01). But 79% of all pelvic inflammatory disease episodes occurred in women who tested negative at baseline, which caps what a single screen can achieve, and 22% of controls obtained testing independently, diluting the contrast. One trial, a non-significant primary result, and a strong subgroup signal: PROPOSED POSSIBLE.

title: The dietary portfolio of cholesterol-lowering foods (Jenkins)
question: In people with hyperlipidaemia, does a dietary portfolio (plant sterols, soy protein, viscous fibres, nuts) lower LDL cholesterol versus a low-saturated-fat control diet?
balance: Two randomised trials from the same Toronto programme point the same way. In the definitive self-selected-diet trial (351 adults with hyperlipidaemia, 6 months), the portfolio lowered LDL cholesterol by 13.8% with intensive counselling and 13.1% with routine counselling, versus 3.0% on a low-saturated-fat therapeutic diet (P<.001 for each portfolio arm versus control). A decade earlier, under fully controlled feeding for one month, the portfolio lowered LDL by 28.6% — statistically indistinguishable from lovastatin 20 mg (−30.9%) and far more than the control diet (−8.0%). The claim carded here is narrow and is the question asked: the portfolio lowers LDL cholesterol more than standard low-saturated-fat advice. Both trials are unblinded (diet trials cannot be blinded), the endpoint is a surrogate, and no trial tests clinical events. PROPOSED LIKELY for LDL lowering.

title: Daily walnuts for two years in healthy elders (WAHA)
question: In healthy older adults, does eating walnuts daily for two years improve the lipoprotein profile versus a walnut-free control diet?
balance: The Walnuts and Healthy Aging (WAHA) trial randomised healthy elders to a walnut-supplemented diet (about 15% of daily energy, roughly 30–60 g/day) or to walnut abstinence for two years. The trial's designated two-year lipoprotein-subclass report (Rajaram et al., Circulation 2021) is named in the topic file, but its PubMed record carries no abstract, so no figures can be verified from that record — this shelf cards it for provenance and takes no numbers from it. The figures that can be gate-verified come from a WAHA sub-study with an abstract: at one year, in 330 participants, LDL cholesterol had fallen by 9.07 mg/dL in the walnut group (95% CI −12.87 to −5.73), a change reported as significant versus the control group (p=0.010). A modest, real LDL reduction in a single trial, resting on surrogate endpoints and a sub-study for its verifiable numbers. PROPOSED POSSIBLE.

title: Cocoa flavanol extract for cardiovascular prevention (COSMOS)
question: In older adults, does daily cocoa flavanol extract reduce total cardiovascular events versus placebo?
balance: COSMOS randomised 21,442 older US adults (women ≥65, men ≥60, free of major cardiovascular disease and recent cancer) in a 2×2 factorial trial of cocoa extract (500 mg flavanols/day, including 80 mg (−)-epicatechin) and a multivitamin. Over a median 3.6 years, the primary outcome — a composite of total cardiovascular events — occurred in 410 participants on cocoa extract versus 456 on placebo: hazard ratio 0.90 (95% CI 0.78 to 1.02; P=0.11), not statistically significant. Cardiovascular death, a secondary endpoint, was lower (hazard ratio 0.73, 95% CI 0.54 to 0.98), and a per-protocol analysis censoring at non-adherence gave 0.85 (0.72 to 0.99) for total events — hypothesis-generating signals inside a null primary result, with no safety concerns. The shelf question is the primary composite: PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference). Tier C: the shelf concerns cardiovascular-event claims, and the cardiovascular-death secondary result must not be promoted past the null primary.

title: Two years of calorie restriction in non-obese adults (CALERIE)
question: In healthy non-obese adults, does sustained calorie restriction (target 25%, achieved ~12%) improve cardiometabolic risk factors versus ad libitum eating over two years?
balance: CALERIE phase 2 randomised 218 healthy non-obese adults (BMI 22.0–27.9, aged 21–50) 2:1 to a prescribed 25% calorie restriction or ad libitum eating for two years. The restriction group achieved an 11.9% reduction in calorie intake (versus 0.8% in controls) and sustained weight loss of 7.5 kg (versus a 0.1 kg gain), 71% of it fat mass. On exploratory cardiometabolic outcomes, calorie restriction produced persistent, significant improvements versus control in LDL cholesterol, the total-to-HDL cholesterol ratio, systolic and diastolic blood pressure, C-reactive protein, insulin sensitivity and metabolic syndrome score — improvements the authors report as robust after controlling for the weight loss itself. One trial, surrogate endpoints, exploratory analysis set. PROPOSED POSSIBLE.

title: Ultra-processed versus unprocessed diets, fed ad libitum (Hall)
question: In adults fed inpatient diets matched for presented calories, macronutrients, fibre, sugar and sodium, does an ultra-processed diet cause greater ad libitum energy intake and weight gain than an unprocessed diet over two weeks?
balance: In the only inpatient randomised crossover test of the question, 20 weight-stable adults lived at the NIH Clinical Center and received ultra-processed and unprocessed diets for two weeks each, in random order, with meals matched for presented calories, energy density, macronutrients, sugar, sodium and fibre, and instructions to eat as much or as little as they wished. On the ultra-processed diet they ate 508 kcal/day more (p=0.0001) — the excess coming from carbohydrate and fat, not protein — gained 0.9 kg, and on the unprocessed diet lost 0.9 kg, with weight change tightly correlated with intake (r=0.8). A large, mechanistically clean effect in a very small, very short, single trial: it shows ultra-processing can drive intake under matched presentation, not what years of free-living eating do. PROPOSED POSSIBLE.

title: Eating breakfast versus fasting until noon (Bath Breakfast Project)
question: In lean adults, does eating breakfast daily for six weeks change body weight, energy intake, and physical-activity energy expenditure versus morning fasting?
balance: The Bath Breakfast Project ran the same six-week randomised experiment twice — in lean adults and in adults with obesity — allocating participants to a daily breakfast (≥700 kcal before 11:00) or extended morning fasting (nothing until noon). In neither trial did body weight or adiposity differ between groups, and resting metabolic rate was essentially unchanged in both. What breakfast did change was movement: physical-activity thermogenesis was markedly higher in the morning in both trials (by 442 kcal/day in lean adults; by 188 kcal/day for morning activity in adults with obesity), while energy intake rose in lean adults (+539 kcal/day) and was not significantly different in adults with obesity (+338 kcal/day, 95% CI −313 to 988), who partly compensated later in the day. Breakfast is not a weight lever in these trials — for the weight question, PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference), on two concordant trials from one programme.

title: Low free-sugar diet in adolescents with fatty liver (Schwimmer)
question: In adolescent boys with nonalcoholic fatty liver disease, does a diet low in free sugars reduce hepatic steatosis versus a usual diet over eight weeks?
balance: Forty adolescent boys (aged 11–16) with histologically diagnosed nonalcoholic fatty liver disease and active disease were randomised to eight weeks of a diet restricting free sugars to under 3% of daily calories — with individualised menu planning and study meals provided for the whole household — or to their usual diet. Liver fat fell from 25% to 17% on the low-sugar diet versus 21% to 20% on usual diet (adjusted difference −6.23 percentage points, 95% CI −9.45 to −3.02; P<.001), and alanine aminotransferase improved (adjusted ratio of geometric means 0.65, 95% CI 0.53 to 0.81; P<.001); adherence was high (18 of 20 hit the sugar target). A clear short-term surrogate result in one small, open-label trial whose intervention included feeding the entire household — promising, preliminary, and labelled as such by its own authors. PROPOSED POSSIBLE.

title: Mediterranean-style diet in pregnancy with metabolic risk factors (ESTEEM)
question: In pregnant women with metabolic risk factors, does a Mediterranean-style diet reduce gestational diabetes and gestational weight gain versus usual antenatal care?
balance: ESTEEM randomised 1,252 inner-city pregnant women with metabolic risk factors (obesity, chronic hypertension or hypertriglyceridaemia) at five UK maternity units to individualised Mediterranean-style dietary advice or usual care. Both primary composites missed significance: maternal composite (gestational diabetes or pre-eclampsia) 22.8% versus 28.6% (adjusted odds ratio 0.76, 95% CI 0.56 to 1.03; p=0.08) and offspring composite 17.3% versus 20.9% (adjusted odds ratio 0.79, 0.58 to 1.08; p=0.14). Inside those composites, gestational diabetes alone was reduced (adjusted odds ratio 0.65, 95% CI 0.47 to 0.91; p=0.01), and mothers gained less weight (6.8 versus 8.3 kg; adjusted difference −1.2 kg, p=0.03). So the honest reading is narrower than the shelf question's framing: the diet did not significantly reduce the trial's primary maternal or offspring composites, but it did reduce gestational diabetes as an individual component and modestly limited weight gain. PROPOSED POSSIBLE.

title: Dietary protein restriction in chronic kidney disease (MDRD)
question: In patients with chronic kidney disease, does dietary protein restriction (with usual- versus low-dose blood-pressure control) slow the decline in glomerular filtration rate versus usual protein intake?
balance: The Modification of Diet in Renal Disease (MDRD) study remains the definitive randomised test of protein restriction: 840 patients in two studies, each crossing diet with blood-pressure target. In Study 1 (585 patients, GFR 25–55), the projected three-year GFR decline did not differ significantly between usual-protein (1.3 g/kg/day) and low-protein (0.58 g/kg/day) diets, or between usual and low blood-pressure targets; the low-protein group declined faster in the first four months (a haemodynamic effect of eating less protein) and slower thereafter, a pattern the authors read as suggesting at most a small benefit. In Study 2 (255 patients, GFR 13–24), a very-low-protein diet (0.28 g/kg/day with keto-acid supplements) was only marginally slower than low protein (P=0.07), and in neither study was there any delay in end-stage renal disease or death. The one positive interaction: patients with heavier baseline proteinuria declined significantly more slowly in the low-blood-pressure group. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for protein restriction as a progression-slowing strategy.

title: Brief intervention for drug use in primary care (ASPIRE)
question: In primary-care patients who screen positive for illicit drug use, does a brief intervention (with or without a booster) reduce drug use versus screening with information only?
balance: ASPIRE randomised 528 primary-care patients who screened positive for drug use (main drug marijuana in 63%, cocaine in 19%, opioids in 17%) to a 10–15 minute brief negotiated interview, a 30–45 minute motivational-interviewing intervention with a booster, or no brief intervention (all groups received a written list of treatment and mutual-help resources). At six months, days of use of the main drug were 12 in the control group, 11 with the brief negotiated interview (incidence rate ratio 0.97, 95% CI 0.77 to 1.22) and 12 with motivational interviewing (incidence rate ratio 1.05, 0.84 to 1.32; P=.81 for both comparisons) — and there were no significant effects on any secondary outcome, hair testing included, or in any severity subgroup. A large, complete (98% follow-up), unambiguous null for the alcohol-derived brief-intervention model applied to drug use. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference).

title: Nabiximols (cannabis extract) for cannabis dependence (Lintzeris)
question: In people seeking treatment for cannabis dependence, does nabiximols oromucosal spray reduce cannabis use versus placebo over 12 weeks?
balance: Two Australian randomised trials of the cannabinoid agonist nabiximols (THC:cannabidiol oromucosal spray) support a during-treatment benefit. In the outpatient dependence trial (Lintzeris 2019; 128 treatment-seeking adults who had not responded to prior treatment), nabiximols recipients reported using cannabis on 35.0 days over 12 weeks versus 53.1 days on placebo — an estimated difference of 18.6 days (95% CI 3.5 to 33.7; P=.02) — with comparable retention and tolerability. In the inpatient withdrawal trial (Allsop 2014; 51 patients), a six-day nabiximols course significantly reduced withdrawal severity (P=.01) and more than tripled treatment retention (hazard ratio 3.66, 95% CI 1.18 to 11.37) — but after medication stopped, post-withdrawal cannabis use fell equally in both groups (P=.75). The pattern is consistent: an agonist that works while taken, with no demonstrated carry-over after it stops. PROPOSED LIKELY for reducing use during treatment.

title: N-acetylcysteine for cannabis dependence (Gray)
question: In adolescents with cannabis dependence, does N-acetylcysteine increase abstinence versus placebo when both groups receive contingency management and cessation counselling?
balance: The same investigative group ran the same trial design — N-acetylcysteine 1200 mg twice daily plus contingency management and counselling — in two age groups and got opposite answers, and this shelf keeps them separate rather than pooling them away. In 116 cannabis-dependent adolescents (ages 15–21), N-acetylcysteine more than doubled the odds of negative urine cannabinoid tests during eight weeks of treatment (odds ratio 2.4, 95% CI 1.1 to 5.2). In 302 adults (ages 18–50) over twelve weeks, the odds ratio was 1.00 (95% CI 0.63 to 1.59; p=0.984), with 22.3% versus 22.4% of urine tests negative. PROPOSED SPLIT: POSSIBLE benefit in adolescents (a single small trial), LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) in adults (a larger, precise null).

title: As-needed nalmefene for alcohol dependence (ESENSE)
question: In adults with alcohol dependence at high drinking risk, does as-needed nalmefene reduce heavy drinking days and total consumption versus placebo over six months?
balance: The ESENSE programme tested a different treatment model: nalmefene 18 mg taken only on days the patient felt at risk of drinking, aiming at reduced drinking rather than abstinence, with all patients receiving a motivational adherence intervention. In ESENSE 2 (718 patients), nalmefene beat placebo on heavy drinking days (−1.7 days/month, 95% CI −3.1 to −0.4; p=0.012) at six months, while total alcohol consumption fell by a non-significant −5.0 g/day (p=0.088). In the pooled subgroup of patients from ESENSE 1 and ESENSE 2 who remained at high drinking risk after initial assessment (667 patients), both co-primary outcomes were clearly positive: −3.2 heavy drinking days (95% CI −4.8 to −1.6; P<0.0001) and −14.3 g/day total consumption (−20.8 to −7.8; P<0.0001). Adverse events were more frequent on nalmefene, with similar dropout rates. Two concordant trials with the clearest effect in persistent high-risk drinkers: PROPOSED LIKELY for a modest reduction in heavy drinking.

title: Topiramate for alcohol dependence (Johnson)
question: In adults with alcohol dependence, does topiramate reduce heavy drinking versus placebo over 14 weeks?
balance: Two double-blind randomised trials from the same programme, four years apart, agree. The 2007 JAMA trial (371 adults with alcohol dependence, topiramate titrated to up to 300 mg/day over 14 weeks with weekly compliance enhancement) found topiramate reduced the percentage of heavy drinking days versus placebo — by 8.44 percentage points (95% CI 3.07 to 13.80; P=.002) in the conservative analysis treating all dropouts as relapsed, and by 16.19 points in the prespecified mixed-model analysis — with all other drinking outcomes also favouring topiramate (P<.001). The group's earlier Lancet trial (150 patients, 12 weeks) had found the same pattern: 27.6% fewer heavy drinking days and 26.2% more abstinent days (both p=0.0003), corroborated by gamma-glutamyl transferase. The cost is tolerability: paraesthesia in 50.8% versus 10.6%, taste perversion, anorexia and concentration difficulty all clearly more common on topiramate. PROPOSED LIKELY.

title: Supervised injectable heroin versus optimised oral methadone (RIOTT)
question: In people with chronic heroin addiction who have not responded to optimised oral methadone, does supervised injectable heroin (or injectable methadone) reduce regular street-heroin use versus continuing optimised oral methadone?
balance: RIOTT randomised 127 chronic heroin users in England who had been on conventional oral treatment for at least six months yet still injected street heroin on at least half of days, to supervised injectable heroin, supervised injectable methadone, or continued optimised oral methadone, for 26 weeks in supervised injecting clinics. On the primary outcome — at least half of weekly urine specimens negative for street heroin during weeks 14–26 — injectable heroin produced 72% responders versus 27% on oral methadone (odds ratio 7.42, 95% CI 2.69 to 20.46; p<0.0001; number needed to treat about 2.2), with the difference evident within six weeks. Injectable methadone sat between (39%) and was not significantly different from oral methadone (odds ratio 1.74, 0.66 to 4.60). A single, necessarily open-label trial with an objective urine endpoint and a very large effect in a narrowly defined, treatment-refractory population: PROPOSED POSSIBLE, held below LIKELY by the single-trial, single-country-programme base. (The neighbouring Canadian SALOME question is homed on Shelf #781 and is not duplicated here.)

title: Cognitive and exposure therapies for problem gambling
question: In adults with problem gambling, do cognitive therapy or exposure therapy reduce gambling severity versus waitlist, and how do the two compare?
balance: The anchor trial behind this shelf does not contain the waitlist comparison the question asks about: Smith and colleagues randomised 87 problem gamblers to cognitive therapy (44) or exposure therapy (43) with no untreated control arm, so the trial can compare the two therapies but cannot by itself show either beats nothing. Within that limit, gambling severity (Victorian Gambling Screen) improved in both groups, and the therapies were statistically indistinguishable — mean difference −0.18 points at 12 weeks (95% CI −4.48 to 4.11) and 1.47 points at six months (−4.46 to 7.39) — intervals too wide to declare equivalence either. Only 59% completed treatment, which is itself a finding about this field. The supporting CBT programmes of Petry and Ladouceur are literature context, not a second carded trial. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — both therapies improved symptoms in the only head-to-head randomised test, with efficacy against no treatment untested on this shelf.

title: Mirtazapine for methamphetamine use disorder (Colfax)
question: In people who use methamphetamine, does mirtazapine reduce methamphetamine use versus placebo?
balance: Two double-blind placebo-controlled trials from the same San Francisco programme, a decade apart and in overlapping populations, both found mirtazapine 30 mg daily reduced methamphetamine-positive urine tests when added to counselling. Colfax 2011 (60 methamphetamine-dependent, sexually active men who have sex with men, 12 weeks): relative risk of a positive urine test 0.57 (95% CI 0.35 to 0.93; P=.02), with positivity falling from 73% to 44% on mirtazapine versus 67% to 63% on placebo, and parallel reductions in sexual risk behaviour. Coffin 2020 (120 cisgender men and transgender women who have sex with men, 24 weeks of treatment plus 12 weeks follow-up): risk ratio 0.67 (0.51 to 0.87) at week 12, 0.75 (0.56 to 1.00) at week 24 and 0.73 (0.57 to 0.96) at week 36, despite medication adherence under 40%. One caution: both trials come from a single programme and a specific population. PROPOSED LIKELY.

title: Bupropion plus naltrexone for methamphetamine use disorder (ADAPT-2)
question: In adults with moderate or severe methamphetamine use disorder, does the combination of extended-release bupropion and injectable naltrexone increase treatment response versus placebo?
balance: ADAPT-2 was a multisite, double-blind trial using a two-stage sequential parallel comparison design (403 participants in stage 1, 225 re-randomised in stage 2) of extended-release injectable naltrexone 380 mg every three weeks plus oral extended-release bupropion 450 mg/day. Response — at least three of four urine samples methamphetamine-negative at the end of a stage — was higher on the combination in both stages (16.5% versus 3.4%; 11.4% versus 1.8%), giving a weighted average response of 13.6% versus 2.5% on placebo, a treatment effect of 11.1 percentage points (P<0.001). Statistically robust, but the absolute terms matter: even on active treatment, about six of seven participants did not meet the response definition over 12 weeks. One trial, a demanding two-drug regimen, serious adverse events in 3.6% of the combination group. PROPOSED POSSIBLE.

title: Buprenorphine–naloxone: brief taper versus extended maintenance in prescription opioid dependence (POATS)
question: In people dependent on prescription opioids, does extended buprenorphine–naloxone maintenance outperform a brief taper — and does adjunctive drug counselling add benefit?
balance: One large two-phase randomised trial (POATS, 653 outpatients dependent on prescription opioids, 10 US sites). Brief treatment failed almost everyone: after a 2-week stabilisation and 2-week taper, only 6.6% had a successful outcome. Patients who did not succeed entered extended treatment, and while taking buprenorphine–naloxone for 12 weeks 49.2% had successful outcomes — but 8 weeks after that taper ended, success had fallen back to 8.6%. The drug works while it is taken; stopping it, even after 12 weeks, returns most patients to opioid use. Adjunctive opioid-dependence counselling added nothing to standard medical management in either phase. PROPOSED LIKELY — a single trial, but large, multisite, and internally decisive: the contrast between on-treatment and post-taper outcomes is the finding, and it is stark. No mortality claim is made.

title: Interdisciplinary palliative care in advanced heart failure (PAL-HF)
question: In patients with advanced heart failure, does an interdisciplinary palliative care intervention improve quality of life versus usual care?
balance: One single-centre randomised trial (PAL-HF, 150 patients with advanced heart failure). Adding an interdisciplinary palliative care intervention to usual care improved both primary quality-of-life measures at 6 months by clinically significant margins: Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire by 9.49 points (95% CI 0.94–18.05, P=0.030) and FACIT-Pal by 11.77 points (CI 0.84–22.71, P=0.035). Depression, anxiety, and spiritual well-being also improved. Rehospitalisation and mortality were not affected. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — a single small single-centre trial with subjective endpoints and intervals that only just exclude no effect; the direction is consistent across every patient-reported measure, which keeps it above MAYBE (weak evidence).

title: Palliative oxygen versus room air for refractory breathlessness (Abernethy)
question: In patients with life-limiting illness and refractory dyspnoea who are not hypoxaemic, does oxygen relieve breathlessness more than room air delivered the same way?
balance: One large double-blind randomised trial (Abernethy 2010, 239 patients with life-limiting illness, refractory dyspnoea, and PaO2 above 7.3 kPa — i.e., not qualifying for long-term oxygen therapy). Oxygen and room air were delivered identically by concentrator and nasal cannula at 2 L/min for 7 days. Both groups' breathlessness improved; oxygen was not better: morning breathlessness changed by −0.9 points on oxygen versus −0.7 on room air (P=0.504), and evening scores likewise did not differ (P=0.554). Side-effect frequency was similar. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — the definitive double-blind trial for this exact question; smaller blinded trials in palliative and COPD populations exist but none approaches this rigour, and none is carded here.

title: Parenteral hydration in advanced cancer at the end of life (Bruera)
question: In patients with advanced cancer receiving hospice care, does parenteral hydration (1 L/day) improve dehydration symptoms, quality of life, or survival versus placebo?
balance: One multicentre double-blind placebo-controlled randomised trial (Bruera 2013, 129 patients with advanced cancer in six hospices): 1 L/day of normal saline versus 100 mL/day placebo, each over 4 hours daily. The primary outcome — change in the sum of four dehydration symptoms (fatigue, myoclonus, sedation, hallucinations) by day 4 — did not differ (−3.3 vs −2.8, P=.77), nor did symptom scales, delirium measures, or quality-of-life measures at day 4 or day 7. Overall survival did not differ either (median 21 vs 15 days, P=.83) — a null on survival in a small trial, not evidence of harm or benefit. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for symptoms and quality of life at this dose and duration; not Tier C, because no benefit on survival is claimed — the survival result is reported as the null it is.

title: Dignity therapy at the end of life (Chochinov)
question: In terminally ill patients, does dignity therapy improve sense of dignity, quality of life, and end-of-life experience versus standard palliative care or client-centred care?
balance: One randomised trial (Chochinov 2011, 441 patients with a life expectancy of 6 months or less in Canada, the USA, and Australia) comparing dignity therapy with client-centred care and standard palliative care. Read primary-first: the trial's primary outcomes — dimensions of distress measured on validated scales before and after the intervention — showed NO significant differences between the three groups. The positive findings are all in the secondary, self-reported end-of-life experience survey: patients who received dignity therapy were significantly more likely to say it had been helpful, improved their quality of life, increased their sense of dignity, and helped their family (all P≤.002). PROPOSED POSSIBLE — the experience outcomes are consistent and strongly significant, but they are unblinded self-reports in a trial whose prespecified distress outcomes were null; the topic draft's summary ('improved quality of life') repeats the secondary claim without the null primary, and the card corrects that order.

title: CALM therapy for depression in advanced cancer (Rodin)
question: In patients with advanced cancer, does CALM (Managing Cancer and Living Meaningfully), a brief individual psychotherapy, reduce depressive symptoms versus usual care?
balance: One randomised trial (Rodin 2018, 305 patients with advanced cancer at a single comprehensive cancer centre). CALM — a brief, manualised individual psychotherapy — reduced depressive symptoms (the primary outcome) versus usual care at 3 months (difference 1.09 points, P=.04, Cohen's d 0.23) and at 6 months (difference 1.29 points, P=.02, d 0.29), with greater end-of-life preparation at 6 months and no adverse effects identified. The effects are statistically significant but small — effect sizes of roughly a quarter of a standard deviation. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — a single unblinded trial with a small effect on a self-reported outcome; consistent and prespecified, which keeps it above MAYBE (weak evidence).

title: Meaning-centred psychotherapy in advanced cancer (Breitbart)
question: In patients with advanced cancer, does meaning-centred psychotherapy (group or individual format) improve spiritual well-being and reduce depression versus supportive group therapy or therapeutic massage?
balance: Two randomised trials of meaning-centred psychotherapy from the same programme, in two formats. The group trial (Breitbart 2015, 253 patients) found meaning-centred group psychotherapy superior to supportive group psychotherapy on spiritual well-being and quality of life, with greater reductions in depression, hopelessness, desire for hastened death, and physical symptom distress; intention-to-treat analyses retained significant effects for quality of life, depression, and hopelessness. The individual-format trial (Breitbart 2018, 321 patients, published in Cancer — the topic draft's 'J Clin Oncol 2018' attribution is wrong) found small-to-medium effects versus enhanced usual care on five of seven outcomes, with a smaller margin over supportive psychotherapy (significant for quality of life and sense of meaning only). PROPOSED LIKELY — two concordant randomised trials against active comparators; the effects are modest and shrink against the strongest comparator, which the cards state.

title: Prophylactic scopolamine butylbromide for death rattle (SILENCE)
question: In dying patients recognised as entering the dying phase, does prophylactic subcutaneous scopolamine butylbromide prevent death rattle versus placebo?
balance: One multicentre double-blind placebo-controlled randomised trial (SILENCE, van Esch 2021, six Dutch hospices). Among 157 patients analysed, a grade ≥2 death rattle occurred in 13% on prophylactic subcutaneous scopolamine butylbromide (20 mg four times daily, started when the dying phase was recognised) versus 27% on placebo — an absolute difference of 14 percentage points (95% CI 2%–27%, P=.02), i.e. about a halving in relative terms; time to death rattle also favoured scopolamine (subdistribution hazard ratio 0.44, CI 0.20–0.92). Anticholinergic adverse events (restlessness, dry mouth, urinary retention) were not clearly worse. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — a single well-designed trial of modest size for a prophylactic intervention given to all dying patients to prevent a sign that troubles witnesses more than patients; replication is lacking.

title: Regular low-dose extended-release morphine for chronic breathlessness in COPD (BEAMS)
question: In people with COPD and severe chronic breathlessness despite optimal treatment, does regular low-dose extended-release morphine improve worst breathlessness versus placebo?
balance: The largest trial answers the question directly and negatively. BEAMS (Ekström 2022, 160 people with COPD and severe chronic breathlessness, double-blind) found no significant difference in worst breathlessness at 1 week for 8 mg/day (−0.3 points, 95% CI −0.9 to 0.4) or 16 mg/day (−0.3, CI −1.0 to 0.4) extended-release morphine versus placebo, and no difference in daily step count at week 3 at any dose. The smaller MORDYC trial (2020) complicates the picture only at the edges: its primary outcome was health status, which improved modestly (CAT score −2.18 points, P=.03), while breathlessness in the previous 24 hours was unchanged overall and worst breathlessness improved only in the prespecified severe (mMRC 3–4) subgroup. Read together: for worst breathlessness — the outcome this shelf asks about — the treatment made no difference at the doses tested (PROPOSED LIKELY, the treatment made no difference); a small health-status signal in MORDYC is a different question and is carded as such.

title: The handheld fan for chronic breathlessness (Galbraith)
question: In patients with chronic breathlessness at rest, does directing a handheld fan at the face relieve breathlessness versus the fan directed at the legs?
balance: One small randomised crossover trial (Galbraith 2010, 50 patients with advanced disease and chronic breathlessness). Each participant used a handheld fan for five minutes directed at the face and five minutes at the legs, in randomised order. Breathlessness on a 10 cm visual analogue scale improved significantly more with the fan to the face (P=0.003); the trial's responder definition was a fall of more than 1 cm. The abstract does not report the size of the mean difference, so the card does not invent one. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — a single tiny unblinded crossover trial, but the intervention is free, harmless, and mechanistically plausible (facial cooling), and later fan studies are feasibility work pointing the same way rather than contradicting it.

title: Dexamethasone for cancer-related fatigue (Yennurajalingam)
question: In patients with advanced cancer, does dexamethasone 4 mg twice daily for 14 days improve cancer-related fatigue versus placebo?
balance: One small double-blind placebo-controlled randomised trial (Yennurajalingam 2013, 84 evaluable patients with advanced cancer and multiple fatigue-related symptoms). Dexamethasone 4 mg twice daily for 14 days improved the FACIT-F fatigue subscale at day 15 significantly more than placebo (mean improvement 9 [SD 10.3] vs 3.1 [SD 9.59], P=.008), with better FACIT-F total quality-of-life scores (P=.03) and physical distress scores (P=.013), but no difference in overall symptom distress (P=.22) or psychological distress (P=.76), and no significant difference in adverse-effect frequency. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — a single small trial with a short 14-day horizon; the fatigue-specific benefit is real on its own measure, but durability, and the balance against steroid harms beyond two weeks, are untested. The trial record carries no registry ID.

title: Multicomponent communication and pain intervention in nursing homes with dementia (COSMOS)
question: In nursing-home residents with dementia, does a multicomponent intervention (staff education in communication, pain assessment and treatment, medication review, and activities) reduce neuropsychiatric symptoms and psychotropic use versus usual care?
balance: The anchored report of the COSMOS cluster-randomised trial (Habiger 2021; 67 units in 33 Norwegian nursing homes, 723 residents) does not show what the topic draft claims. Read from the record: pain was associated with psychosis symptoms over time (odds ratio 2.03 for psychosis symptoms as a group, P=.009; delusion OR 2.12, P=.007), but NO significant intervention effect on psychosis symptoms was observed, analgesic prescription was not affected, and the one positive intervention finding was less musculoskeletal pain in residents with dementia (β −0.47, P=.047). Psychotropic use as such is not reported as improved in this record. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for the neuropsychiatric-symptom and medication questions as asked, with the pain signal carded honestly. This card follows the anchored 2021 report; other COSMOS reports (e.g. on quality of life) are not adjudicated here. The trial record carries no registry ID.

title: Guided Care teams for multimorbid older adults (Boult)
question: In multimorbid older adults at high risk of hospitalisation, does a nurse-led Guided Care team embedded in primary care reduce use of health services and improve quality of care versus usual care?
balance: One cluster-randomised trial (Boult 2011, 850 older patients at high predicted risk of heavy health-care use, three systems in the Baltimore–Washington area, 20 months). Guided Care — a nurse embedded with primary care physicians providing assessment, care planning, monitoring, transitional care, coordination, self-management and caregiver support, and community-service access — produced exactly one statistically significant overall effect: fewer episodes of home health care (odds ratio 0.70, 95% CI 0.53–0.93). Hospital admissions and other service use were not significantly reduced overall; in a preplanned subgroup analysis, Kaiser Permanente patients also had fewer skilled-nursing-facility admissions (OR 0.53, CI 0.31–0.89) and days (OR 0.48, CI 0.28–0.84). PROPOSED POSSIBLE — for the narrow home-health effect; the broader hope of cutting hospital use was not realised in the whole sample. Quality-of-care ratings were addressed in a companion report and are not carded here.

title: Community health worker support in primary care: the IMPaCT model (Kangovi)
question: In low-income patients with chronic conditions, does a standardised community-health-worker intervention improve chronic disease control, mental health, and hospital use versus usual care?
balance: Split by outcome, because the trials split. In the multicentre primary-care trial (Kangovi 2018, 592 low-income patients with ≥2 chronic diseases), the PRIMARY outcome — change in self-rated physical health — did not differ (P=.89), and the record does not support the topic draft's claim of improved chronic disease control and mental health as headline findings. What did improve was patient-perceived quality of primary care (odds ratio 1.8, CI 1.4–2.4) and hospital use: total hospital days were 155 versus 345 at 6 months and 300 versus 471 at 9 months, with lower odds of repeat hospitalisation (OR 0.4, CI 0.2–0.9) and 30-day readmission (OR 0.3, CI 0.1–0.9). A pooled analysis of all three IMPaCT randomised trials (1,340 patients, including the programme's post-discharge trial) confirms the utilisation result: hospital days per patient were 66% of control (incidence rate ratio 0.66, P<.0001; 849 vs 1258 days), driven by fewer hospitalisations (0.27 vs 0.34 per patient) and shorter stays. PROPOSED SPLIT — LIKELY for fewer hospital days; POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for self-rated health.

title: Person-centred care, activities, and antipsychotic review in dementia care homes (WHELD)
question: In people with dementia living in care homes, do person-centred care training, person-centred activities, and structured antipsychotic review improve quality of life and reduce antipsychotic use and agitation versus usual care?
balance: Split by outcome inside one programme. The large WHELD trial (Ballard 2018, 69 UK nursing homes, 847 residents) found person-centred care training plus social interaction, with antipsychotic review built in, improved quality of life (DEMQOL-Proxy mean difference 2.54, P=.0042, effect size 0.24), agitation (effect size 0.23), and overall neuropsychiatric symptoms (effect size 0.30) — statistically significant but small effects. Antipsychotic use, however, was NOT reduced: it sat at a low stable level in both arms — the topic draft's claim that the 2018 report 'quantifies the antipsychotic reduction' is wrong; there was none. The programme's earlier factorial report (2017, 16 homes) adds a caution: antipsychotic review alone worsened two quality-of-life domains, social interaction improved quality of life, and the combination caused no deterioration. An independent earlier trial (Fossey 2006) shows staff training and support CAN cut neuroleptic use (23.0% vs 42.1% of residents) without worsening agitation — so the drug-reduction claim belongs to that design, not to WHELD. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — real but small quality-of-life and agitation benefits from one programme; the antipsychotic-sparing claim is not WHELD's to make.

title: Case management after wrist fracture to start osteoporosis care (Majumdar)
question: In patients who have had a fragility (wrist) fracture, does a case-manager or multifaceted intervention increase osteoporosis assessment and treatment initiation versus usual care?
balance: Process outcomes, dramatically improved, in small Alberta trials from one research group. The anchored pilot (Majumdar 2011) randomised 46 patients still untreated a year after a wrist fracture: a nurse case-manager (counselling, arranging bone-density tests, prescribing treatment) versus the group's multifaceted intervention (patient education plus physician guidelines and reminders). At 6 months, bisphosphonate treatment was 43% versus 12% (relative risk 3.6, 95% CI 1.1–11.5 — a relative measure; the absolute rates are 43% and 12%), bone-density testing 81% versus 52%, and appropriate care 57% versus 28%. The same record reports the group's earlier controlled trial, in which the multifaceted intervention itself tripled treatment versus controls in relative terms (22% vs 7% absolute). PROPOSED POSSIBLE — pilot-scale numbers (46 patients) and process outcomes only; nothing here shows fracture prevention, only that the care gap after fracture can be closed, best by a case-manager. Case management cost $44 (Canadian) per patient versus $12 for the multifaceted intervention.

title: GRACE geriatric care management for low-income seniors (Counsell)
question: In low-income older adults, does GRACE team care (geriatrician-led interdisciplinary team with an advanced practice nurse and social worker) improve quality of care and reduce acute service use versus usual primary care?
balance: One randomised trial (GRACE, Counsell 2007, 951 low-income adults aged 65+, income below 200% of the federal poverty level, two years of home-based care management by a nurse practitioner and social worker working with the primary care physician and a geriatrics team under 12 condition protocols). Quality-of-life results were mixed: at 24 months, four of eight SF-36 scales (general health, vitality, social functioning, mental health) and the Mental Component Summary improved significantly, but physical function and ADLs did not differ, and neither did death. Emergency department visits not resulting in admission were lower over two years (1,445 vs 1,748 per 1,000; P=.03), while hospital admissions overall were not (700 vs 740 per 1,000; P=.66); in the predefined high-risk subgroup, both ED visits and admissions were lower in the second year. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — a large, long trial with genuine but partial gains: mental-health-related quality and emergency use improved; physical function and overall admissions did not.

title: Advance care planning in dialysis: the SPIRIT intervention (Song)
question: In adults receiving dialysis and their surrogates, does a structured advance-care-planning intervention improve surrogate readiness, patient–surrogate congruence, and bereavement outcomes versus usual care?
balance: One cluster-randomised trial (SPIRIT, Song 2024, 42 dialysis clinics in five US states, 426 patient–surrogate dyads). Trained clinic staff held a 45–60 minute structured discussion with each dyad (remote after March 2020), with a summary in the record. The two-week preparedness outcomes improved: dyad congruence on goals of care (odds ratio 1.61, 95% CI 1.12–2.31, P=.001), decisional conflict (β −0.10, P<.001), and the congruence-plus-confidence composite (OR 1.57, CI 1.06–2.34, P=.03); surrogate decision-making confidence alone did not differ (P=.12). Bereavement outcomes, in only 77 bereaved surrogates, were mixed: anxiety was lower (β −1.55, CI −3.08 to −0.01, P=.05 — a borderline result whose interval nearly touches zero), while depression (P=.84) and posttraumatic distress (P=.75) were similar. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — preparation for decision-making clearly improved; the bereavement claim rests on a small subsample and one borderline outcome, and the topic draft's broader 'surrogate outcomes improved' needs that qualification.

title: Tai chi for fibromyalgia (Wang)
question: In adults with fibromyalgia, does tai chi improve symptoms and function versus aerobic exercise (and versus wellness education with stretching)?
balance: Two randomised trials, both from one research group, both single-blind, both positive on symptom scores. The larger comparative-effectiveness trial (226 patients, BMJ 2018) found tai chi improved the revised Fibromyalgia Impact Questionnaire 5.5 points more than aerobic exercise at 24 weeks (95% CI 0.6 to 10.4, P=0.03) — a modest edge, and larger (16.2 points) when the dose and duration were matched. The earlier trial (66 patients, NEJM 2010) found a much larger difference against wellness education and stretching (FIQ change −18.4 points, P<0.001). Participants cannot be blinded to exercise, the outcomes are symptom scores, and no independent group has replicated the comparison — so the evidence is moderate, not strong. PROPOSED POSSIBLE.

title: Bed rest for acute sciatica and low back pain (Vroomen; Malmivaara)
question: In patients with acute sciatica (or acute low back pain), does prescribed bed rest speed recovery versus watchful waiting and staying active?
balance: Two randomised trials in the New England Journal of Medicine, consistent. In sciatica (183 patients), bed rest for two weeks produced improvement in 70% versus 65% with watchful waiting (adjusted odds ratio 1.2, 95% CI 0.6 to 2.3), and by 12 weeks 87% of both groups had improved, with no differences in pain, function, absenteeism or surgery. In acute low back pain (186 patients), bed rest was the slowest of three strategies — continuing ordinary activities as tolerated recovered significantly faster than either bed rest or exercises on pain duration and intensity, disability and days absent from work. Bed rest does not speed recovery, and in back pain it delayed it. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference).

title: Antibiotics for chronic low back pain with Modic changes (Albert; AIM)
question: In patients with chronic low back pain and Modic type 1 changes after a disc herniation, does a 100-day course of amoxicillin (± clavulanate) reduce pain and disability versus placebo?
balance: The classic shrinkage, carded in full. Albert 2013 (162 patients, single centre) reported dramatic gains from 100 days of amoxicillin–clavulanate in Modic type 1 disease — disability (RMDQ) fell from 15 to 5.7 at one year against 15 to 14 on placebo. The larger AIM trial (180 patients, six Norwegian centres, BMJ 2019) found a between-group RMDQ difference of −1.6 points (−3.1 to 0.0, P=0.04) — statistically significant but well below its own predefined clinically important difference of 4 points; in type 1 changes the difference was −2.3, in type 2 it was −0.1. Drug-related adverse events: 56% on amoxicillin versus 34% on placebo. The stamp follows the mature multicentre data: at most a small benefit of doubtful clinical importance, bought with three months of antibiotics. PROPOSED POSSIBLE.

title: Colchicine for knee osteoarthritis (COLKOA)
question: In patients with knee osteoarthritis, does low-dose colchicine reduce pain and inflammation versus placebo?
balance: One double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (COLKOA, 109 patients, 16 weeks of colchicine 0.5 mg twice daily). The primary endpoint — at least 30% improvement in total WOMAC score at week 16 — was met by 39% of the colchicine group and 49% of the placebo group (P=0.284; odds ratio 0.66, 95% CI 0.31 to 1.41), and no clinical secondary endpoint differed. Colchicine did reduce inflammatory and bone-turnover biomarkers (serum hs-CRP and synovial-fluid CTX I fell significantly), so the drug engaged its targets without relieving symptoms. A single small trial cannot make this LIKELY, but a blinded trial with no symptom signal in any endpoint justifies the no-difference lean. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference).

title: Methotrexate for hand osteoarthritis (Ferrero; HERO as companion)
question: In patients with hand osteoarthritis refractory to usual treatment, does weekly methotrexate reduce pain versus placebo — and what did hydroxychloroquine do in the parallel question?
balance: CORRECTION to the topic draft: the draft's claim that methotrexate reduced pain is not what the trial found. In Ferrero 2021 (64 patients with erosive hand osteoarthritis), the decrease in pain VAS at three months was 21.1 mm on methotrexate versus 11.7 mm on placebo (p=0.2), and the authors' own conclusion is that weekly 10 mg methotrexate showed no superiority over placebo for pain relief at 3 or 12 months; the only significant signal was structural (more eroded joints progressing to a remodelling phase, 27% vs 15%, p=0.03). The companion hydroxychloroquine trial, HERO (248 patients), was a firm null: hand pain at six months 5.66 on hydroxychloroquine versus 5.49 on placebo, difference −0.16 (−0.73 to 0.40, P=0.57). Two anti-rheumatic drugs, no analgesic benefit. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference).

title: Emergency-department care and physiotherapy for acute whiplash (MINT)
question: In patients presenting to emergency departments with acute whiplash, does a physiotherapy package (or active management advice) improve recovery versus usual-care advice alone?
balance: One large two-step pragmatic trial (MINT, ISRCTN33302125). Step 1 (cluster-randomised, 3,851 patients in 15 emergency departments): training staff to give active-management consultations made no difference to the Neck Disability Index at 12 months versus usual consultations (difference 0.5, 95% CI −1.5 to 2.5). Step 2 (599 patients with persisting symptoms): a package of up to six physiotherapy sessions gave a modest benefit at 4 months versus a single advice session (NDI difference −3.7, −6.1 to −1.3) that was gone by 8 and 12 months, and the package was not cost-effective. The trial's own recommendation — usual consultations plus a single advice session — is what the evidence supports. PROPOSED POSSIBLE.

title: Paracetamol for acute low back pain (PACE)
question: In patients with acute low back pain, does regular or as-needed paracetamol speed recovery versus placebo?
balance: One large, rigorous double-blind trial (PACE, 1,652 patients) with a precise result. Median time to recovery was 17 days with regular paracetamol, 17 days with as-needed paracetamol and 16 days with placebo (regular vs placebo hazard ratio 0.99, 95% CI 0.87 to 1.14; as-needed vs placebo 1.05, 0.92 to 1.19), with no differences on secondary outcomes and identical adverse-event rates (about 18.5% in every group). Paracetamol was the recommended first-line analgesic for acute low back pain when the trial ran; this is the trial that removed its evidence base. Correction to the topic draft: the placebo group's median recovery was 16 days, not 17. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference).

title: Motor control exercise for chronic low back pain (Costa)
question: In patients with chronic non-specific low back pain, does motor control (specific stabilisation) exercise improve activity limitation and pain versus placebo (detuned ultrasound and diathermy)?
balance: Two Australian randomised trials that answer two halves of the question. Against placebo (detuned ultrasound and diathermy), Costa 2009 (154 patients) found motor control exercise improved activity by 1.1 points (95% CI 0.3 to 1.8) and global impression of recovery by 1.5 points (0.4 to 2.5) at two months — but the effect on pain itself was 0.9 points (−0.01 to 1.8), not significant. Against another active exercise, Macedo 2012 (172 patients) found no significant difference between motor control exercise and graded activity at any time point for any outcome (pain effect at 2 months 0.0, −0.7 to 0.8). So: exercise of this kind gives small short-term functional gains over doing nothing real, but there is nothing specifically superior about the motor control approach. PROPOSED POSSIBLE.

title: Canakinumab for secondary prevention after myocardial infarction (CANTOS) ⚠ OUTSTANDING-SINGLE
question: In patients with previous myocardial infarction and residual inflammatory risk (hsCRP ≥2 mg/L), does interleukin-1β inhibition with canakinumab reduce recurrent major cardiovascular events versus placebo?
balance: OUTSTANDING-SINGLE (flagged for the developer under the Nov 8 rule): one large double-blind trial, and the trial that proved the inflammatory hypothesis of atherothrombosis. In 10,061 patients with previous myocardial infarction and hsCRP ≥2 mg/L, canakinumab 150 mg every three months reduced the primary composite (nonfatal MI, nonfatal stroke or cardiovascular death) from 4.50 to 3.86 events per 100 person-years — a 15% relative reduction (hazard ratio 0.85, 95% CI 0.74 to 0.98, P=0.021) — without lowering lipids at all. Only the 150 mg dose met the prespecified multiplicity-adjusted significance threshold (50 mg: HR 0.93, P=0.30; 300 mg: HR 0.86, P=0.031). All-cause mortality was not significantly reduced (HR 0.94, 0.83 to 1.06) and fatal infection was more frequent on canakinumab. A real, hard-endpoint benefit from a single trial — LIKELY, Tier C, and not to be read as an instruction to prescribe a drug that was never adopted for this indication.

title: Low-dose methotrexate for cardiovascular prevention (CIRT)
question: In patients with previous myocardial infarction or multivessel coronary disease plus diabetes or metabolic syndrome, does low-dose methotrexate reduce major cardiovascular events versus placebo?
balance: The deliberate negative control to CANTOS, from the same investigators. CIRT randomised 4,786 patients with stable atherosclerosis (previous MI or multivessel coronary disease, plus type 2 diabetes or metabolic syndrome) to low-dose methotrexate (target 15–20 mg weekly) or placebo. Methotrexate did not lower interleukin-1β, interleukin-6 or CRP at all — and it did not reduce events: the final primary endpoint occurred at 4.13 versus 4.31 events per 100 person-years (hazard ratio 0.96, 95% CI 0.79 to 1.16); the original primary endpoint gave HR 1.01 (0.82 to 1.25). The trial was stopped after a median 2.3 years. Methotrexate brought more liver-enzyme elevations, cytopenias and non-basal-cell skin cancers. The inflammation hypothesis survived CANTOS; this particular drug simply never engaged the pathway. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference), Tier C.

title: Metformin as adjuvant therapy in early breast cancer (MA.32)
question: In patients with high-risk operable breast cancer without diabetes, does adding metformin to standard therapy improve invasive disease-free survival versus placebo?
balance: A single large phase 3 trial (MA.32, 3,649 patients) with an unambiguous answer in both hormone-receptor strata. In ER/PgR-positive disease (the primary analysis population), invasive disease-free survival events occurred at 2.78 versus 2.74 per 100 patient-years on metformin versus placebo (hazard ratio 1.01, 95% CI 0.84 to 1.21, P=.93), and deaths at 1.46 versus 1.32 (HR 1.10, 0.86 to 1.41). In ER/PgR-negative disease, futility was declared at the second interim analysis (IDFS HR 1.01, 0.79 to 1.30). Grade 3 non-haematological toxicity was commoner on metformin (21.5% vs 17.5%, P=.003). The observational and preclinical promise did not survive the randomised test. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference), Tier C.

title: B vitamins and brain atrophy in mild cognitive impairment (VITACOG)
question: In older adults with mild cognitive impairment, does high-dose B-vitamin treatment (folic acid, B12, B6) slow the rate of brain atrophy and cognitive decline versus placebo?
balance: One small single-centre trial (VITACOG, 271 randomised; 168 with before-and-after MRI scans) with a clear effect on an imaging surrogate: brain atrophy proceeded at 0.76% per year on high-dose B vitamins versus 1.08% per year on placebo (P=0.001), with the largest effect in participants whose baseline homocysteine was above 13 µmol/L (53% lower rate — a relative figure). The trial did not test cognition as its primary outcome — it reports only that faster atrophy was associated with lower final cognitive scores — and the authors themselves state that trials are needed to see whether the treatment delays Alzheimer's disease. A surrogate-endpoint, single-trial benefit: POSSIBLE, and no higher.

title: Omega-3 and vitamin D to prevent depression (VITAL-DEP)
question: In adults aged 50 and over without depression at baseline, do long-term marine omega-3 or vitamin D3 supplements prevent incident depression versus placebo?
balance: Two huge prespecified reports from one factorial trial (VITAL-DEP, 18,353 adults aged 50+, median treatment 5.3 years). Correction to the topic draft, which said both agents reached 'the same null': vitamin D3 did — depression or clinically relevant symptoms occurred at 12.9 versus 13.3 per 1,000 person-years (hazard ratio 0.97, 95% CI 0.87 to 1.09, P=.62), with no difference in mood scores. Omega-3 did not reach a clean null: depression risk was significantly HIGHER on omega-3 — 651 events (13.9 per 1,000 person-years) versus 583 (12.3 per 1,000) on placebo, hazard ratio 1.13 (1.01 to 1.26, P=.03) — while mood scores were again identical (difference 0.03 points). Neither supplement prevents depression; for vitamin D the null is clean, and for omega-3 the endpoint result leans the wrong way, modestly. PROPOSED SPLIT — LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for vitamin D / POSSIBLE (harm) for omega-3.

title: Aspirin to prevent colorectal adenoma recurrence (Baron; Sandler)
question: In patients with a recent colorectal adenoma (or previous colorectal cancer), does daily aspirin reduce adenoma recurrence versus placebo?
balance: Two double-blind randomised trials from the same 2003 NEJM issue, in adjacent populations, pointing the same way. In patients with a recent adenoma (Baron, 1,121 patients), at least one adenoma was found at follow-up colonoscopy in 47% on placebo, 38% on aspirin 81 mg and 45% on aspirin 325 mg (relative risk 0.81, 95% CI 0.69 to 0.96 for 81 mg; 0.96, 0.81 to 1.13 for 325 mg), with advanced neoplasms reduced at 81 mg (RR 0.59, 0.38 to 0.92). In patients with previous colorectal cancer (Sandler, 635 patients), adenomas were found in 17% on aspirin 325 mg versus 27% on placebo (adjusted RR 0.65, 0.46 to 0.91). A modest absolute benefit — roughly 9–10 fewer patients with recurrence per 100 — with an odd dose picture (low dose better in Baron, only 325 mg tested in Sandler). The endpoint is adenoma recurrence, a surrogate: these trials did not measure colorectal cancer or death. PROPOSED LIKELY.

title: Calcium and vitamin D for colorectal adenoma prevention (Baron 2015)
question: In patients with a recently removed colorectal adenoma, do calcium, vitamin D, or both reduce adenoma recurrence over three to five years versus placebo?
balance: One large double-blind factorial trial (Baron 2015, 2,259 participants) with tight confidence intervals and no effect anywhere: over 3–5 years, 43% of participants had at least one recurrent adenoma regardless of assignment. Adjusted risk ratios for recurrent adenomas were 0.99 (95% CI 0.89 to 1.09) for vitamin D versus no vitamin D, 0.95 (0.85 to 1.06) for calcium versus no calcium and 0.93 (0.80 to 1.08) for both versus neither; advanced adenomas behaved the same way. title: Calcium supplements and myocardial infarction (Bolland)
question: In older adults (mostly women) not taking vitamin D co-supplements, do calcium supplements increase myocardial infarction and cardiovascular events?
balance: This shelf's evidence is deliberately trial-level synthesis — no single trial was powered for the question — and it is contested, which is why the stamp is POSSIBLE (harm) and Tier C. Bolland 2010 (patient-level data from five trials, 8,151 participants) found myocardial infarction in 143 patients on calcium versus 111 on placebo (hazard ratio 1.31, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.67, P=0.035) — about a 30% relative increase, on small absolute numbers; stroke (HR 1.20, 0.96 to 1.50), the composite (1.18, 1.00 to 1.39) and death (1.09, 0.96 to 1.23) were not individually significant. The 2011 re-analysis of the Women's Health Initiative found the signal concentrated in women NOT already taking personal calcium supplements (hazard ratios 1.13–1.22 for cardiovascular events on calcium plus vitamin D), with nothing in women who were. The original WHI publication reported no overall increase; the re-analysis argues widespread personal supplement use diluted it. That argument is clever, post hoc, and unresolved — the balance of the randomised evidence leans to a modest real increase in myocardial infarction, of a size that matters mainly because calcium supplements are so widely taken.

title: Folic acid for colorectal adenoma prevention (Cole): no reduction — and a late signal of more advanced lesions
question: In patients with a history of colorectal adenomas, does folic acid 1 mg/day prevent new adenomas versus placebo?
balance: One large double-blind trial, and it answers no. In 1,021 patients with a recent colorectal adenoma, folic acid 1 mg/day did not reduce recurrence at the first surveillance colonoscopy (44.1% vs 42.4% on placebo) — and at the second surveillance cycle the folic acid group had more advanced lesions (11.6% vs 6.9%; relative risk 1.67, 95% CI 1.00 to 2.80), a borderline signal toward harm rather than benefit, alongside more multiple adenomas. A nutrient with a plausible protective story that, tested properly, does not prevent adenomas and may do the opposite in people who already form them. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for the prevention claim, with the advanced-lesion signal kept on the face of the shelf.

title: 10-kHz spinal cord stimulation for painful diabetic neuropathy (SENZA-PDN): large relief in an open-label trial
question: In adults with painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy refractory to gabapentinoids and at least one other analgesic class, does adding 10-kHz spinal cord stimulation to conventional medical management produce ≥50% pain relief without neurological worsening, compared with medical management alone?
balance: A dramatic result from an unblinded trial. In SENZA-PDN, 216 patients with painful diabetic neuropathy refractory to gabapentinoids and at least one other analgesic class were randomised to conventional medical management alone or with an implanted 10-kHz spinal cord stimulator. At 3 months, 79% of the stimulation group had at least 50% pain relief without neurological worsening, versus 5% on medical management alone; mean pain scores at 6 months were 1.7 versus 6.9 on a 10-cm scale. The catch is structural: patients knew whether they had an implant (open-label, no sham), pain is the most expectation-sensitive endpoint there is, and the 24-month durability figures come from follow-up after most controls crossed over to the device, so there is no long-term comparator. Real relief, quite possibly large — but the design cannot separate device effect from expectation effect. PROPOSED POSSIBLE, Tier C: no.

title: Mirogabalin for diabetic peripheral neuropathic pain: small, replicated pain-score gains in Asian trials
question: In adults with diabetic peripheral neuropathic pain, does mirogabalin (a gabapentinoid licensed in parts of Asia) reduce average daily pain scores compared with placebo over 14 weeks?
balance: A real but small effect, replicated in the same direction. Mirogabalin, a gabapentinoid licensed in parts of Asia, beat placebo on average daily pain scores in a Chinese phase 3 trial (difference −0.39 points on a 0–10 scale, 95% CI −0.74 to −0.04) and in the pooled Japanese pivotal programme (−0.31 and −0.63 points at the two twice-daily doses) — statistically significant, consistently, and clinically modest: fractions of one point on a ten-point scale, over 14 weeks, against a large placebo response. Somnolence and dizziness rise steeply with dose (up to 19% and 13%). PROPOSED POSSIBLE: the drug works a little, in Asian populations, over three months; durability and comparative value against pregabalin or duloxetine are not established by these records.

title: Home foot temperature monitoring to prevent ulcer recurrence: early win, larger trial missed its primary endpoint
question: In people with diabetes at high risk of foot ulceration (previous ulcer or amputation), does daily home infrared temperature monitoring of the feet, with activity reduction and nurse contact when a hot spot appears, prevent ulcer recurrence compared with standard preventive care?
balance: The first trial said yes clearly; the bigger, later trial could not confirm it on its own primary endpoint. Armstrong 2007 (225 patients, physician-blinded): ulceration 4.7% with home thermometry versus 12.2% with standard therapy over 18 months. DIATEMP (304 patients, multicentre, assessor-blinded): recurrence at the measured sites 29.1% versus 37.3% — relative risk 0.78, confidence interval crossing 1, p=0.133 — though recurrence at any foot site was significantly lower (relative risk 0.76), and the benefit concentrated in patients who actually reduced activity when a hotspot appeared. The intervention is really a behaviour loop — measure, spot asymmetry, rest the foot — and it works only when the loop is completed. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: promising, cheap, harmless, and not yet proven at the standard the largest trial set.

title: Bilayered living skin equivalent (Graftskin/Apligraf) for diabetic foot ulcers (Veves): faster, fuller closure in a single pivotal trial
question: In noninfected, non-ischaemic chronic plantar diabetic foot ulcers, does a bilayered living skin equivalent added to debridement and off-loading achieve complete wound closure by 12 weeks more often than saline-moistened gauze with the same adjunctive care?
balance: One pivotal trial, a clean result, and no replication on this shelf. In 208 patients with noninfected, non-ischaemic chronic plantar diabetic foot ulcers, adding the bilayered living skin equivalent Graftskin (Apligraf) — up to five weekly applications — to debridement and off-loading produced complete healing at 12 weeks in 56% versus 38% with saline-moistened gauze (odds ratio 2.14 relative), and cut median time to closure from 90 to 65 days. Osteomyelitis and amputations were also less frequent in the treatment group, though the record gives no figures for those. An 18-percentage-point absolute gain in closure from a single 2001 manufacturer-era trial, unblinded by necessity. PROPOSED POSSIBLE.

title: Autologous platelet-rich plasma gel for diabetic foot ulcers: consistent direction, fragile anchor trial
question: In nonhealing diabetic foot ulcers, does autologous platelet-rich plasma gel added to standard care increase complete healing over 12 weeks compared with standard care with a saline gel dressing?
balance: The direction is consistent and the foundations are shaky. The named pivotal trial (Driver 2006) found significance only after an independent audit excluded 32 of its 72 randomised patients from the per-protocol analysis and five wound-size outliers were set aside: 81.3% versus 42.1% healed in the adjusted per-protocol set. A 2024 systematic review pooling 8 small randomised trials (598 patients) found healing improved overall (relative risk 1.32 relative) and healing time shortened by about 17 days. Many small trials, varying preparations, one fragile anchor: the sum is a probable benefit of uncertain size on top of good standard care. PROPOSED POSSIBLE.

title: Alendronate for acute Charcot neuro-arthropathy: the placebo-controlled trial's record carries no abstract
question: In acute Charcot neuro-arthropathy of the foot in diabetes, does six months of alendronate, added to off-loading, reduce disease activity (foot temperature, pain, bone-turnover markers) compared with off-loading alone?
balance: The honest answer is that the abstract-bearing record cannot settle this question. A randomised controlled trial of six months of alendronate in acute Charcot neuro-arthropathy exists (Pitocco 2005) — but its PubMed record carries no abstract, so under this library's rule no figures may be carded from it, and the drug-versus-off-loading effect cannot be verified from the record. The one comparative trial with an abstract (Bharath 2013) randomised patients between zoledronic acid and weekly alendronate, both with total contact casting: 75% reached complete clinical resolution in about 122 days on average, with no significant difference between the two drugs — but there was no cast-only arm, so it cannot show that either drug beats casting alone. Bisphosphonate treatment of acute Charcot remains a practice resting on an unverifiable-here trial and clinical habit. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).

title: Relamorelin for diabetic gastroparesis: composite symptoms improved in phase 2 — vomiting did not beat placebo
question: In diabetic patients with moderate-to-severe gastroparesis symptoms and objectively delayed gastric emptying, does the ghrelin agonist relamorelin improve cardinal symptoms and accelerate gastric emptying compared with placebo over 12 weeks?
balance: A phase 2 trial with a split personality. Relamorelin, a ghrelin agonist, significantly reduced the composite of cardinal gastroparesis symptoms (nausea, abdominal pain, postprandial fullness, bloating) versus placebo across all three doses over 12 weeks, and accelerated gastric emptying by about 12% — but vomiting, the symptom patients rank worst and the one most improved from baseline (down 75%), was NOT significantly better than placebo. It also worsened glycaemic control in 14.5% of patients who received it — a serious asterisk in a diabetes drug. The phase 3 programme was never completed and the drug remains unapproved. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: a genuine symptom signal in a single phase 2 trial of a drug that does not exist on the market.

title: Metformin causes vitamin B12 deficiency (HOME substudy): a 4.3-year placebo-controlled trial
question: In insulin-treated type 2 diabetes, does long-term metformin treatment cause vitamin B12 deficiency — the trial basis for monitoring B12 in metformin users?
balance: Settled by a proper trial: yes, metformin causes vitamin B12 deficiency, gradually and measurably. In 390 insulin-treated patients with type 2 diabetes randomised to metformin or placebo for 4.3 years (the HOME trial's B12 substudy), B12 concentrations fell 19% on metformin relative to placebo, and the absolute risk of frank deficiency (<150 pmol/L) was 7.2 percentage points higher — one extra case of deficiency for roughly every 14 patients treated for 4.3 years. The trial measured blood levels, not clinical outcomes like anaemia or neuropathy, but deficiency of this size is exactly what monitoring exists to catch, and it is preventable and treatable once seen. PROPOSED LIKELY (harm) — a harm claim on a biochemical endpoint, supported by one long, clean, placebo-controlled trial.

title: Starting finerenone and empagliflozin together lowers albuminuria more than either alone (CONFIDENCE)
question: In type 2 diabetes with CKD and albuminuria on a renin-angiotensin inhibitor, does simultaneous initiation of finerenone plus empagliflozin lower albuminuria more than starting either drug alone?
balance: A clean answer to a narrow, practical question — on a surrogate endpoint, over six months. In CONFIDENCE, patients with type 2 diabetes, CKD and albuminuria, all on a renin-angiotensin system inhibitor, were randomised to finerenone alone, empagliflozin alone, or both started together. At 180 days the combination reduced the urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio 29% more in relative terms than finerenone alone and 32% more in relative terms than empagliflozin alone, with no unexpected adverse events; symptomatic hypotension, acute kidney injury and hyperkalaemia leading to discontinuation were uncommon. Albuminuria is a well-worn surrogate, not kidney failure or death, and 180 days cannot show whether starting both together changes hard outcomes or simply reaches the same place faster. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — a real, additive effect on albuminuria from one well-run trial; whether it converts into fewer kidney failures is not yet shown (THIN: surrogate endpoint, 6 months).

title: Second-line drugs on metformin compared head-to-head (GRADE): glargine and liraglutide held A1c best
question: In type 2 diabetes of under 10 years' duration on metformin with A1c 6.8-8.5%, which added drug — insulin glargine, glimepiride, liraglutide, or sitagliptin — best maintains A1c below 7.0% over years of follow-up, and at what hypoglycaemia and weight cost?
balance: The fairest comparison the field has: one large, publicly funded, five-year head-to-head trial of the four commonest second-line choices added to metformin. All four lowered A1c, but insulin glargine and liraglutide held the A1c target modestly better — confirmed A1c at or above 7.0% occurred at 26.5 and 26.1 per 100 participant-years respectively, against 30.4 for glimepiride and 38.1 for sitagliptin. Severe hypoglycaemia was uncommon but most frequent with glimepiride (2.2% of participants, versus 1.3% glargine, 1.0% liraglutide, 0.7% sitagliptin), and liraglutide caused more gastrointestinal side effects and the most weight loss. The companion GRADE outcomes paper found no material differences between the four groups in microvascular complications or death over the same five years, so the ranking is about durability of glucose control, not about preventing complications. PROPOSED LIKELY — one pivotal-grade comparative-effectiveness trial, internally consistent across its glycaemic and outcomes papers.
