title: Acarbose in coronary disease with impaired glucose tolerance (ACE): no cardiovascular benefit; diabetes onset delayed
question: In patients with established coronary heart disease and impaired glucose tolerance, does acarbose reduce cardiovascular events — and does it delay the onset of type 2 diabetes?
balance: A split result, and the stamp is split to match. On the question the trial was built to answer — cardiovascular events — acarbose did nothing: the five-point composite occurred in 14% on acarbose versus 15% on placebo in absolute terms over a median 5.0 years (HR 0.98; p=0.73), with no difference in the three-point composite, death, or any component. On the secondary question, diabetes onset was delayed: diabetes developed in 13% on acarbose versus 16% on placebo in absolute terms (rate ratio 0.82, an 18% lower relative rate; p=0.005) — delay, not prevention: acarbose lowers post-meal glucose while it is taken, which postpones crossing the diagnostic threshold. Gastrointestinal disorders were the commonest reason for discontinuation or dose change (7% vs 5%). The population was entirely Chinese patients with coronary disease, which bounds how far the result travels. PROPOSED SPLIT — (the treatment made no difference) for cardiovascular events; POSSIBLE for delaying diabetes onset (Tier C).

title: Intensive insulin after myocardial infarction in diabetes (DIGAMI 1 and 2): the two trials disagree
question: In type 2 diabetes (DIGAMI 1: diabetes broadly) after acute myocardial infarction, does an insulin-glucose infusion followed by long-term multidose insulin reduce mortality compared with conventional glucose management?
balance: The two trials of the same strategy point in opposite directions, so the stamp is split. DIGAMI 1 (620 patients, 1995) found that an insulin-glucose infusion followed by at least 3 months of multidose insulin cut 1-year mortality to 18.6% versus 26.1% on conventional care in absolute terms — a 29% lower relative mortality (p=0.027), with the largest absolute gain in the low-risk, previously insulin-naive subgroup (8.6% vs 18.0%). DIGAMI 2 (1,253 patients, 2005), designed to confirm it, found no mortality difference at all: 23.4% with infusion plus long-term insulin-based control versus 22.6% with infusion plus standard control (HR 1.03), and 19.3% with routine management. DIGAMI 2 never achieved the glucose separation it planned (HbA1c converged to about 6.8% in all groups), which its authors note as a caveat — but a strategy that cannot be separated in practice cannot claim the benefit either. PROPOSED SPLIT — DIGAMI 1 alone would merit POSSIBLE; DIGAMI 2 showed (the treatment made no difference); taken together the claim rests at MAYBE (weak evidence) (Tier C).

title: Intensive glucose control after coronary bypass surgery (GLUCO-CABG): no fewer complications in patients with diabetes
question: In patients with hyperglycaemia after coronary artery bypass graft surgery, does an intensive insulin target of 100-140 mg/dL reduce perioperative complications compared with a conservative target of 141-180 mg/dL — in patients with and without diabetes?
balance: One randomised trial, and for patients with diabetes — the population this library serves — the answer is plainly no difference. In GLUCO-CABG, 302 patients with hyperglycaemia after coronary bypass surgery (152 with diabetes, 150 without) were randomised to intensive insulin targeting 100-140 mg/dL or conservative targeting 141-180 mg/dL; achieved ICU glucose was 132 vs 154 mg/dL. Overall, the composite of complications was 42% vs 52% in absolute terms (P=0.08, not significant). Split by diabetes status, there was heterogeneity: among patients with diabetes, complications were identical (49% vs 48%; P=0.87), while the apparent benefit was confined to patients without diabetes (34% vs 55%; P=0.008) — a subgroup finding in the group this shelf is not about. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for patients with diabetes after CABG (THIN: single trial; the diabetes answer rests on its diabetes stratum).

title: Paricalcitol for albuminuria in diabetic kidney disease (VITAL): a near-miss on its primary endpoint
question: In type 2 diabetes with albuminuria already treated with an ACE inhibitor or ARB, does adding the vitamin D analogue paricalcitol reduce albuminuria?
balance: A well-run trial that missed its own finish line. In VITAL, 281 patients with type 2 diabetes and albuminuria on ACE inhibitor or ARB therapy received placebo or paricalcitol 1 or 2 micrograms daily for 24 weeks. The primary endpoint — percentage change in urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio for the combined paricalcitol groups versus placebo — came out at a between-group difference of −15% in relative terms (95% CI −28 to 1; p=0.071): not statistically significant. The 2-microgram dose alone gave −18% (−32 to 0; p=0.053), and a longitudinal look at that dose showed sustained reductions of −18% to −28% (p=0.014 vs placebo in that analysis) — suggestive, but secondary. Hypercalcaemia and adverse events were similar across groups. A surrogate endpoint, six months, and a primary result on the wrong side of significance cannot carry more than a maybe. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (THIN: surrogate endpoint, primary endpoint formally non-significant).

title: Dietary protein restriction in type 1 diabetic nephropathy (Hansen): GFR decline unchanged, fewer reached ESRD or death
question: In type 1 diabetes with progressive diabetic nephropathy, does a low-protein diet (0.6 g/kg/day prescribed) slow GFR decline or reduce end-stage renal disease or death compared with a usual-protein diet?
balance: Two answers in one small trial, and they do not agree — so the stamp is split. On the direct measure of kidney function, protein restriction did nothing: GFR declined at 3.8 ml/min/year on the low-protein diet versus 3.9 on usual protein, identical over four years, and the achieved separation in intake was modest (0.89 vs 1.02 g/kg/day against a 0.6 g/kg/day prescription). On the clinical endpoint, end-stage renal disease or death occurred in 10% on low protein versus 27% on usual protein in absolute terms (log-rank P=0.042; adjusted relative risk 0.23, 95% CI 0.07 to 0.72) — but in 82 patients that is roughly 4 versus 11 events, a handful of events carrying a large claim, with blood pressure and glycaemic control comparable between groups. PROPOSED SPLIT — (the treatment made no difference) for rate of GFR decline; MAYBE (weak evidence) for fewer ESRD or death events (THIN: 82 patients, few events, incomplete dietary separation).

title: Pirfenidone for diabetic nephropathy (Sharma): eGFR rose at the lower dose in one small trial
question: In diabetic nephropathy with reduced eGFR and albuminuria, does the antifibrotic pirfenidone (1200 or 2400 mg/day) improve the one-year change in eGFR compared with placebo?
balance: One small, fragile trial. In 77 patients with diabetic nephropathy, eGFR 20-75 and albuminuria, one year of pirfenidone 1200 mg/day was followed by a mean eGFR rise of +3.3 ml/min/1.73 m2 versus a fall of −2.2 on placebo (P=0.026) among the 52 patients who completed the study. The higher dose showed no such effect (−1.9, not significantly different from placebo) and lost 11 of its 25 patients to dropout — so the dose-response runs the wrong way, and the positive arm is the one with tolerability on its side rather than a stronger pharmacological push. Dialysis initiation (4 on placebo, 1 on 2400 mg, 0 on 1200 mg) did not differ significantly (P=0.25). Pirfenidone is named here as the specific tested antifibrotic product under study for this use. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (THIN: 77 randomised, 52 completers, inverted dose-response, surrogate endpoint).

title: Faster-acting insulin aspart (onset 1 programme): noninferior A1c, better post-meal glucose in type 1 diabetes
question: In adults with type 1 diabetes on basal-bolus therapy, does fast-acting insulin aspart (faster aspart) control HbA1c and postprandial glucose at least as well as conventional insulin aspart, at 26 and 52 weeks?
balance: One large phase 3 trial programme (the onset 1 trial, reported at 26 and 52 weeks) gives a consistent answer: faster aspart is noninferior to conventional insulin aspart for HbA1c and slightly better, with clearly better post-meal glucose. At 26 weeks, mealtime faster aspart beat aspart on HbA1c by an estimated −0.15 percentage points (statistically superior, P=0.0003, on top of confirmed noninferiority), and postmeal dosing was also noninferior (+0.04 points) — so the faster formulation can be given after the meal without losing control. At 52 weeks the HbA1c advantage persisted (−0.10 points; P=0.0424) and the 1-hour postprandial glucose increment remained lower (−0.91 mmol/L (≈-16 mg/dL); P=0.0002), with no difference in severe or blood-glucose-confirmed hypoglycaemia. The gains are real but small — fractions of a percent of A1c and better meal spikes, not a step change. PROPOSED LIKELY for noninferiority with modest postprandial superiority.

title: Inhaled technosphere insulin for type 1 diabetes: noninferior A1c, less hypoglycaemia, much more cough
question: In type 1 diabetes on basal insulin, does prandial inhaled technosphere insulin control HbA1c as well as injected rapid-acting insulin analogues (aspart, lispro), and how do hypoglycaemia, weight and cough compare?
balance: Two independent randomised trials agree that inhaled technosphere insulin — the specific tested inhaled insulin product — lowers HbA1c about as much as injected mealtime analogues, with less hypoglycaemia, less weight gain, and a lot more cough. In the larger trial (345 patients, 24 weeks, open-label), HbA1c fell −0.21% on inhaled insulin versus −0.40% on insulin aspart — a between-group difference of 0.19 points that met the 0.4-point noninferiority margin, though fewer inhaled-insulin patients reached HbA1c below 7.0% (18.3% vs 30.7%); hypoglycaemia was lower (9.8 vs 14.0 events per patient-month) and weight fell slightly (−0.4 kg vs +0.9 kg), but cough affected 31.6% versus 2.3% and drove 5.7% to stop treatment. The second trial (138 patients, stopped early against a planned 230) likewise found comparable HbA1c against insulin lispro, lower early post-meal glucose, and fewer mild-to-moderate hypoglycaemic events (5.97 vs 8.01; P=0.0269), with cough again the commonest adverse event. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — consistent noninferiority across two trials, but open-label, marginal, and with the second trial under-enrolled (THIN elements).

title: Quick-release bromocriptine safety (Cycloset Safety Trial): serious adverse events no higher; a small cardiovascular signal
question: In type 2 diabetes on usual therapy, is quick-release bromocriptine safe overall — serious adverse events and cardiovascular events — compared with placebo over 52 weeks?
balance: One large safety trial. The Cycloset Safety Trial randomised 3,095 patients with type 2 diabetes 2:1 to quick-release bromocriptine or placebo on top of usual therapy for 52 weeks. It met its purpose: serious adverse events occurred in 8.6% on bromocriptine versus 9.6% on placebo in absolute terms (HR 1.02, with the upper bound of the 96% one-sided CI at 1.27, inside the prespecified 1.5 noninferiority margin). A prespecified cardiovascular composite (MI, stroke, revascularisation, hospitalisation for angina or heart failure) occurred less often on bromocriptine — 1.8% versus 3.2% in absolute terms (HR 0.60; 95% CI 0.35 to 0.96) — but that is 37 versus 32 events in a trial designed and powered for safety, not efficacy, so it is a signal to test, not a benefit shown. Nausea was the commonest adverse event. Note on sources: the trial's design paper (Scranton 2007) describes this same trial and registry number; it is not a second trial, so this shelf honestly rests on one randomised trial. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — safety established to the trial's standard; the cardiovascular signal is hypothesis-grade (Tier C).

title: Colesevelam added to insulin or sulfonylurea therapy: A1c down about half a point, LDL down too
question: In type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled on insulin-based or sulfonylurea-based therapy, does adding the bile acid sequestrant colesevelam improve HbA1c and LDL cholesterol compared with placebo?
balance: Two modest, consistent, industry-era trials from the drug's diabetes development programme. Added to insulin-based therapy (Goldberg 2008, 287 patients, 16 weeks), colesevelam lowered A1c by a treatment difference of −0.50 percentage points versus placebo (−0.41% vs +0.09%; P<0.001) and lowered LDL cholesterol by 12.8% relative to placebo. Added to sulfonylurea-based therapy (Fonseca 2008, 461 patients, 26 weeks), the A1c difference was −0.54 points (−0.32% vs +0.23%; P<0.001) and the LDL difference was −16.7% in relative terms. The effect is real but small, the endpoints are surrogates, the trials ran 16-26 weeks, and the drug's pill burden and gastrointestinal effects sit outside these abstracts. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (THIN: small, short trials; surrogate endpoints; a half-point A1c effect).

title: Once-weekly insulin efsitora (QWINT programme): noninferior A1c to daily basal insulin in three settings
question: In type 2 diabetes — insulin-naive, on basal insulin, or on basal-bolus therapy — does once-weekly insulin efsitora control HbA1c noninferiorly to once-daily basal insulin (glargine or degludec), and how does hypoglycaemia compare?
balance: Three large phase 3 trials, one in each starting situation, all open-label treat-to-target, and all telling the same story: once-weekly efsitora is noninferior to daily basal insulin for HbA1c. In insulin-naive patients (QWINT-1, 795 patients, vs daily glargine) the A1c difference was −0.03 points, and clinically significant or severe hypoglycaemia was actually less frequent on the weekly insulin (0.50 vs 0.88 events per participant-year; rate ratio 0.57). In patients switching from daily basal insulin (QWINT-3, 986 patients, vs degludec) the difference was −0.09 points with similar hypoglycaemia (0.84 vs 0.74 events per patient-year). In basal-bolus patients (QWINT-4, 730 patients, vs glargine, both with mealtime lispro) A1c fell −1.01 vs −1.00 points, hypoglycaemia 6.6 vs 5.9 events per patient-year. What weekly dosing buys is convenience — 52 injections a year instead of 365, and in QWINT-1 a median of 2 dose adjustments versus 8 — not better glucose control. PROPOSED LIKELY for noninferiority across the programme (DOUBLE-A: three independent trials).

title: Early vildagliptin plus metformin in newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes (VERIFY): treatment failure halved over five years
question: In newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes, does starting vildagliptin plus metformin together from diagnosis delay initial treatment failure (confirmed HbA1c at or above 7.0%) compared with the standard stepwise approach of starting metformin alone?
balance: One large, long, double-blind trial with a striking result on a process endpoint. In VERIFY, 2,001 people with newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes were randomised to start vildagliptin plus metformin immediately or to start metformin alone, with vildagliptin added only after confirmed failure — the standard stepwise strategy. Over five years, initial treatment failure occurred in 43.6% on early combination versus 62.1% on the stepwise approach in absolute terms (HR 0.51, a 49% lower relative hazard; p<0.0001); median time to failure was 36.1 months on monotherapy and beyond the study's 61.9 months on combination. Both approaches were safe and well tolerated, with no treatment-related deaths. Two cautions cap the stamp: this is a single trial, and 'treatment failure' is crossing an A1c threshold — a durability-of-control endpoint, not a complication, event or mortality endpoint; whether starting two drugs at diagnosis changes what happens to eyes, kidneys or hearts is not shown here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (THIN: single trial, glycaemic process endpoint).

title: Fixed-ratio insulin/GLP-1 combinations beat their own components (DUAL I and LixiLan-O)
question: In type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled on oral therapy, does a once-daily fixed-ratio combination of basal insulin plus a GLP-1 receptor agonist lower HbA1c more than either component given alone?
balance: Two independent development programmes, testing two different fixed-ratio products, asked the same question against the same comparators — each combination against its own two components — and got the same answer. In DUAL I (1,663 insulin-naive patients), insulin degludec/liraglutide lowered A1c by −1.9% versus −1.4% on degludec alone and −1.3% on liraglutide alone (differences −0.47 and −0.64 points, both p<0.0001), with nausea in 8.8% (versus 19.7% on liraglutide alone) and confirmed hypoglycaemia at 1.8 events per patient-year (versus 2.6 on degludec, 0.2 on liraglutide). In LixiLan-O (1,170 patients), insulin glargine/lixisenatide lowered A1c by −1.6% versus −1.3% on glargine and −0.9% on lixisenatide (both P<0.0001), with 74% reaching A1c below 7% versus 59% and 33%, weight essentially neutral (−0.3 kg versus +1.1 kg on glargine), and nausea 9.6% versus 24% on lixisenatide alone. The combination predictably sits between its components on both gastrointestinal effects and hypoglycaemia, and above both on A1c. PROPOSED LIKELY (DOUBLE-A: two independent randomised programmes).

title: Concentrated U-500 insulin for severe insulin resistance: twice- or thrice-daily dosing equivalent; pump delivery slightly better
question: In type 2 diabetes requiring more than 200 units of insulin a day, how should concentrated regular U-500 insulin be given — twice-daily versus thrice-daily injections, and pump (CSII) versus multiple daily injections?
balance: Two open-label strategy trials in the small, highly insulin-resistant population that needs U-500 regular insulin (500 units/mL) — named here as the specific concentrated product these trials tested. On scheduling, Hood 2015 randomised 325 patients previously on a mean 287.5 units/day of U-100 insulin to thrice-daily or twice-daily U-500: A1c fell −1.12% and −1.22% respectively, a difference of −0.10 points (95% CI −0.33 to 0.12) meeting the 0.4-point clinical-equivalence margin, with documented symptomatic hypoglycaemia less frequent on thrice-daily dosing and weight gain similar (5.4 vs 4.9 kg). On delivery method, the VIVID study randomised 420 patients to U-500 by pump or by injections: the pump group achieved a larger A1c fall (−1.27% vs −0.85%; difference −0.42; P<0.001) with almost no dose increase (+2.8 U vs +51.3 U), at the cost of a higher rate of nocturnal hypoglycaemia. Both trials are open-label dosing-strategy studies over 24 weeks with glycaemic endpoints — enough for practical guidance, not for hard outcomes. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (DOUBLE-A: two independent randomised trials; THIN: open-label, strategy comparisons).

title: Switching to biosimilar insulin glargine LY2963016 (ELEMENT 1 and 2): same control, same safety as originator glargine
question: In type 1 and type 2 diabetes already treated with insulin glargine, does switching to the biosimilar insulin glargine LY2963016 at the same dose maintain glycaemic control and safety compared with staying on originator insulin glargine?
balance: For a biosimilar, 'no difference' is the success criterion, and that is what the randomised evidence shows. The carded report pools the prespecified subgroups of patients in the two ELEMENT trials who were already on originator insulin glargine before randomisation — 452 with type 1 diabetes in the 52-week open-label ELEMENT-1 and 299 with type 2 diabetes in the 24-week double-blind ELEMENT-2 — and who switched at equivalent doses either to the biosimilar LY2963016 insulin glargine (the specific tested product, named because identifying the exact biosimilar is the question) or stayed on originator glargine. No statistically significant treatment differences were found in efficacy or safety outcomes, apart from three isolated findings — weight change in type 1 diabetes, overall incidence of detectable insulin antibodies in type 2 diabetes, and serious adverse events in type 2 diabetes — which were not consistent across both studies or in the total populations and were judged not clinically meaningful. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — read here as demonstrated similarity, the intended result for a biosimilar switch (DOUBLE-A: the anchor report covers both randomised trials).

title: Teriparatide versus risedronate in severe osteoporosis (VERO): fewer vertebral and clinical fractures on the anabolic
question: In postmenopausal women with severe osteoporosis and prevalent vertebral fractures, does daily teriparatide prevent new fractures better than weekly risedronate — the rare head-to-head fracture trial between an anabolic and an antiresorptive?
balance: In the only large head-to-head fracture trial between an anabolic and an antiresorptive, teriparatide beat risedronate. In 1,360 postmenopausal women with severe osteoporosis and prevalent vertebral fractures (VERO, 24 months), new radiographic vertebral fractures occurred in 5.4% on teriparatide versus 12.0% on risedronate (risk ratio 0.44 — a 56% relative reduction, 6.6 percentage points absolute), and clinical fractures in 4.8% versus 9.8% (hazard ratio 0.48). Non-vertebral fragility fractures did not differ significantly (4.0% versus 6.1%; HR 0.66, p=0.10). The benefit was consistent across subgroups in the prespecified subgroup report. This is a single trial, industry-funded, in a high-risk population — the comparison is against an active drug, not placebo, so both drugs work; teriparatide worked better on vertebral and clinical fractures. PROPOSED LIKELY — one large, double-blind, fracture-endpoint head-to-head trial with a clear result on its primary outcome.

title: Zoledronate after stopping denosumab: partial protection against rebound bone loss, no winning timing
question: In patients discontinuing denosumab, does a zoledronate infusion (and at what timing) prevent the rapid rebound bone loss and vertebral fracture risk that follow denosumab cessation?
balance: Stopping denosumab without follow-on treatment causes rapid rebound bone loss; zoledronate softens that loss but does not prevent it. In a Taiwanese randomised trial of 101 patients who had taken denosumab for at least 2 years, one zoledronate infusion lost lumbar spine BMD in year 1 (median −0.68%) while continued denosumab gained (+1.30%; p=.03), though hip BMD was preserved in both groups; loss was worse after 3 or more years of denosumab (−3.20%). In a Danish randomised timing study of 61 patients stopping after a mean 4.6 years, spine BMD fell about 4% by 24 months whichever timing was used (6 months, 9 months, or turnover-guided), with BMD then maintained during year 2. Neither trial tested fractures. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — two small randomised trials agree zoledronate only partially protects, BMD endpoints only, and no timing strategy has been shown superior.

title: Benign thyroid nodules: microwave versus radiofrequency ablation — equal shrinkage in one randomised trial
question: In predominantly solid, nonfunctioning benign thyroid nodules, how do microwave ablation and radiofrequency ablation compare for nodule volume reduction, complications, and durability over two years?
balance: One prospective randomised multicentre trial (152 patients, five Chinese institutions, follow-up at least 2 years) found microwave ablation (MWA) noninferior to radiofrequency ablation (RFA) for shrinking predominantly solid, nonfunctioning benign thyroid nodules: the volume reduction rate differed by −5.6% at 6 months and −2.4% at 2 years (noninferiority met at both), technique efficacy (≥50% volume reduction) was 91% versus 86% (p=.40), and volume change over time did not differ. Safety is the open part: the commonest major complication, voice change, occurred in 6.6% on MWA versus 1.3% on RFA (p=.21) — not statistically different in a trial this size, and the authors state a larger sample is needed to show safety is comparable. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — a single open-label trial, a volume (not symptom or cancer) endpoint, and an underpowered safety comparison. Cross-point: Shelf #521 covers RFA versus surgery, a different comparison.

title: Desiccated thyroid extract versus levothyroxine: no symptom or cognition difference; preference split between trials
question: In primary hypothyroidism stable on levothyroxine, does desiccated thyroid extract differ from levothyroxine in symptoms, neurocognitive function, or patient preference?
balance: Two randomised double-blind crossover trials agree on the main question and disagree on preference. In 70 patients stable on levothyroxine (Hoang 2013, 16 weeks per treatment), desiccated thyroid extract (DTE) produced no differences in symptoms or neurocognitive measures versus levothyroxine, with about 3 lb lower weight on DTE; yet 48.6% preferred DTE, 18.6% preferred levothyroxine, and 32.9% had no preference. In a 75-patient three-arm crossover (Shakir 2021, 22 weeks per arm: levothyroxine, levothyroxine + liothyronine, DTE), there were again no differences in primary or secondary outcomes as a group and preference did not differ — except that the third of patients most symptomatic on levothyroxine preferred and responded to T3-containing treatment. SPLIT: (the treatment made no difference) for symptoms, cognition, and quality of life in the whole groups, in both trials; patient preference favoured DTE in one trial and not the other, with a symptomatic-subgroup signal that is hypothesis-generating, not proven. DTE preparations are animal-derived, fixed-ratio T4/T3 products that are not FDA-approved as safe and effective in the modern sense and vary by maker — a reason the generic claim cannot be stretched product to product.

title: Bedtime versus morning levothyroxine: better blood levels at night, no difference in quality of life
question: In primary hypothyroidism, does taking levothyroxine at bedtime improve thyroid hormone levels and quality of life compared with the conventional morning fasting dose?
balance: One randomised double-blind crossover trial (105 patients with primary hypothyroidism; 90 completed) compared the same levothyroxine dose taken at bedtime versus in the morning, 3 months each. Bedtime intake lowered TSH by 1.25 mIU/L (95% CI 0.60–1.89; P<.001) and raised free T4 by 0.07 ng/dL (P=.01) and total T3 by 6.5 ng/dL (P=.02) relative to morning intake. But quality of life, fatigue, anxiety/depression, symptoms, lipids, BMI, and heart rate did not differ between timings. SPLIT: POSSIBLE for a modest biochemical advantage to bedtime dosing; (the treatment made no difference) for how patients felt or for lipid levels. The practical reading is that bedtime dosing is a legitimate alternative for patients who cannot manage the morning fast — with levels rechecked after any switch — not that everyone should move their dose.

title: Selenium in Hashimoto thyroiditis: antibodies fell in one small trial; thyroid function did not change
question: In autoimmune thyroiditis with high thyroid-peroxidase antibody concentrations, does selenium supplementation lower antibody levels or change thyroid function?
balance: The evidence is a single small trial measuring antibodies, not illness. In 70 women with autoimmune thyroiditis and high antibody levels (Gärtner 2002, blinded and placebo-controlled, 3 months), selenium as sodium selenite 200 μg daily (the specific tested preparation — selenium supplements are not well regulated and forms differ by maker) lowered thyroid peroxidase antibody concentrations to 63.6% of baseline versus 88% on placebo, with complete antibody normalisation in 9 of 36 on selenium versus 2 of 34 on placebo (P=0.01). TSH and free thyroid hormone levels did not change in either group, and no clinical outcome — symptoms, progression to hypothyroidism, or levothyroxine need — was shown to improve. The topic draft could not pin a results record for the large CATALYST trial (protocol only at drafting), so this shelf rests on the 2002 trial alone and must be re-checked for CATALYST results at review. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — an antibody surrogate moving in a small, short trial, with thyroid function unchanged.

title: Iodine in pregnancy and child neurodevelopment: no IQ benefit in mild deficiency (a large null trial)
question: In mildly iodine-deficient pregnant women, does daily iodine supplementation (200 μg) until delivery improve their children's IQ and executive function?
balance: Tested properly, in the population where benefit was most plausible, iodine did not help. In a randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial in Bangalore, India, and Bangkok, Thailand, 832 mildly iodine-deficient pregnant women (median urinary iodine 131 μg/L) took iodine 200 μg daily or placebo until delivery; 313 children were tested at age 5–6 years. Verbal IQ was 89.5 on iodine versus 90.2 on placebo (difference −0.7, 95% CI −2.9 to 1.5; p=0.77), performance IQ 97.5 versus 99.1 (difference −1.6; p=0.44), and the executive-function composite 90.6 versus 91.5 (difference −0.9; p=0.74) — every point estimate slightly favoured placebo, and adverse events in pregnancy did not differ (24 vs 28 women). This answers mild deficiency in areas where schoolchildren were iodine sufficient; it does not address severe deficiency, where iodine's role is established by other evidence. PROPOSED (the treatment made no difference) — one large trial with clinical (neurodevelopmental) endpoints and confidence intervals that exclude a meaningful IQ gain.

title: Levothyroxine after myocardial infarction with subclinical hypothyroidism (ThyrAMI): no ejection-fraction benefit in a small trial
question: In patients with acute myocardial infarction and subclinical hypothyroidism, does levothyroxine titrated to TSH 0.4–2.5 mU/L improve left ventricular ejection fraction at 52 weeks compared with placebo?
balance: A plausible idea, tested once, in a trial too small to settle it. In ThyrAMI (95 patients with acute myocardial infarction and subclinical hypothyroidism, 6 UK hospitals), levothyroxine starting at 25 μg and titrated to a TSH of 0.4–2.5 mU/L for 52 weeks did not improve left ventricular ejection fraction versus placebo: LVEF rose from 51.3% to 53.8% on levothyroxine and from 54.0% to 56.1% on placebo (adjusted difference +0.76%, 95% CI −0.93% to 2.46%; p=0.37). None of the six secondary outcomes — ventricular volumes, infarct size, vascular measures, or patient-reported outcomes — differed, and cardiovascular adverse events were similar (33.3% vs 36.7%). The authors call the study preliminary. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — a null result, but from a single 95-patient trial whose confidence interval still allows a small LVEF benefit; it argues against routine treatment, it does not prove none can exist.

title: Zoledronic acid versus pamidronate for hypercalcaemia of malignancy: higher, faster, longer responses
question: In moderate-to-severe hypercalcaemia of malignancy, is a single dose of zoledronic acid superior to pamidronate for complete response (normalised corrected calcium) by day 10 and duration of response?
balance: Two identical randomised double-blind trials, pooled as the protocol specified, give a clear answer. In 275 patients evaluable for efficacy with moderate-to-severe hypercalcaemia of malignancy (corrected calcium ≥3.00 mmol/L), a single dose of zoledronic acid produced complete response (normalised corrected calcium) by day 10 in 88.4% at 4 mg and 86.7% at 8 mg, versus 69.7% on pamidronate 90 mg (P=.002 and P=.015) — absolute advantages of about 19 and 17 percentage points. Calcium normalised by day 4 in roughly 50% on zoledronic acid versus 33.3% on pamidronate, and complete responses lasted a median of 32 days (4 mg) and 43 days (8 mg) versus 18 days. The recommended initial dose from the trials is 4 mg. PROPOSED LIKELY — two concurrent identical double-blind trials with concordant, clinically large differences on the defining endpoint of the condition.

title: Cabergoline versus bromocriptine in hyperprolactinaemia: more effective and better tolerated
question: In women with hyperprolactinaemic amenorrhoea (mostly microprolactinoma or idiopathic), is cabergoline more effective and better tolerated than bromocriptine for restoring normoprolactinaemia and ovulatory cycles?
balance: One landmark double-blind trial settled the comparison for women with hyperprolactinaemic amenorrhoea. In 459 women (Webster 1994; 279 with microprolactinomas, 167 with idiopathic hyperprolactinaemia), stable normoprolactinaemia was achieved in 83% on cabergoline (0.5–1.0 mg twice weekly) versus 59% on bromocriptine (2.5–5.0 mg twice daily) — a 24-percentage-point absolute advantage (P<0.001). Ovulatory cycles or pregnancy occurred in 72% versus 52%, amenorrhoea persisted in 7% versus 16%, adverse effects were recorded in 68% versus 78% (P=0.03), and discontinuation for intolerance was 3% versus 12% (P<0.001), with gastrointestinal symptoms less frequent, less severe, and shorter-lived on cabergoline. PROPOSED LIKELY — a single large trial, but double-blind for its first phase, with large concordant advantages on efficacy and tolerability; only the first 8 weeks were double-blind, the following 16 weeks open with dose adjustment.

title: Withdrawing cabergoline in prolactinoma: about two-thirds stay in remission; an MRI remnant predicts relapse
question: In nontumoral hyperprolactinaemia, microprolactinoma, and macroprolactinoma with normalised prolactin and major tumour shrinkage on long-term cabergoline, what happens after withdrawal — recurrence rates, tumour regrowth, and predictors?
balance: This shelf is observational by design — a prospective withdrawal cohort, not a randomised trial — and is stamped accordingly. In 200 carefully selected patients whose prolactin had normalised on long-term cabergoline and whose MRI showed no tumour or at least 50% shrinkage (Colao 2003), hyperprolactinaemia recurred within 2–5 years of withdrawal in 24% of nontumoral cases, 31% of microprolactinomas, and 36% of macroprolactinomas — so roughly two in three stayed in remission. No patient had renewed tumour growth, though gonadal dysfunction redeveloped in 22% of women and 39% of men whose hyperprolactinaemia recurred. A visible tumour remnant on MRI at withdrawal predicted recurrence: estimated 5-year recurrence was 78% versus 33% in macroprolactinomas with versus without a remnant, and 42% versus 26% in microprolactinomas. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — large, prospective, and directly on-question, but a single selected cohort with no randomised continue-versus-stop comparison; the rates apply only to patients meeting the study's strict withdrawal criteria.

title: Enclomiphene citrate for secondary male hypogonadism: testosterone rises and sperm are preserved in one phase II trial
question: In men with secondary hypogonadism, does oral enclomiphene citrate raise testosterone and gonadotropins while preserving sperm production, compared with topical testosterone gel (which suppresses spermatogenesis)?
balance: One small phase II randomised trial supports the mechanism, and nothing more can honestly be claimed. In men with secondary hypogonadism, oral enclomiphene citrate (the specific tested product — an investigational selective estrogen receptor modulator that is not FDA-approved for this or any use, named here for clarification) raised morning testosterone, estradiol, and LH to levels similar to those on topical testosterone gel, while — unlike the gel — it also raised FSH and sperm counts were conserved (Wiehle 2014). The abstract reports directions of effect, not magnitudes or group sizes, and the outcomes are hormones and semen parameters over a short phase II horizon: no symptom, fertility (pregnancy), fracture, or safety outcomes are established. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — a single small phase II trial with laboratory endpoints, for a product without regulatory approval.

title: Liraglutide before IVF in PCOS: a large pregnancy-rate signal in a 28-woman pilot
question: In obese women with PCOS and poor response to first-line reproductive treatment, does preconception liraglutide added to metformin improve IVF pregnancy rates and weight compared with metformin alone?
balance: A striking result in a trial far too small to trust at face value. In a pilot randomised open-label study of just 28 infertile obese women with PCOS who had responded poorly to first-line reproductive treatment (Salamun 2018), 12 weeks of liraglutide 1.2 mg daily added to metformin — followed by a 4-week medication-free period before IVF — gave a pregnancy rate per embryo transfer of 85.7% versus 28.6% on metformin alone (P=0.03), and a 12-month cumulative pregnancy rate of 69.2% versus 35.7%, despite nearly identical weight loss (7.5 kg vs 7.0 kg). With 28 patients, a handful of pregnancies moving between groups would erase the difference, there was no blinding, and live birth was not the endpoint. A second small randomised study from the same centre (Jensterle 2016, 44 women) supports only the weight part of the story: metformin plus low-dose liraglutide lost 6.2 kg versus 3.8 kg on liraglutide alone over 12 weeks — it tested weight, not pregnancy, and its comparison differs. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — pilot-size, open-label, single-centre evidence for a large claimed fertility effect that needs a proper confirmatory trial.

title: Modified-release hydrocortisone in congenital adrenal hyperplasia (Chronocort): the phase 3 primary endpoint failed
question: In adults with classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia, does modified-release hydrocortisone (designed to mimic the circadian cortisol profile) control androgen excess better than standard glucocorticoid therapy without increasing total exposure?
balance: The trial's own primary endpoint failed, and the honest shelf is that failure plus what was found underneath it. In the 6-month randomised phase 3 trial of the specific tested modified-release hydrocortisone programme (Chronocort; 122 adults with classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia), the primary outcome — change in 24-hour 17-hydroxyprogesterone SD score — was not met at 6 months. Secondary measures favoured modified-release hydrocortisone: lower 17OHP SDS at 4 weeks (P=.007) and 12 weeks (P=.019) and between 07:00 and 15:00 at 6 months (P=.044), with controlled 09:00 17OHP in 91% versus 71% on standard therapy (P=.002); in the single-arm extension, control was 80% at 18 months and the median daily hydrocortisone dose fell from 25 mg at baseline to 20 mg. Patient-reported benefits included menses restoration in 8 patients (1 on standard therapy) and 3 patient and 4 partner pregnancies (none on standard therapy); three adrenal crises occurred in phase 3, none on modified-release hydrocortisone, and 4 in the extension. SPLIT: (the treatment made no difference) on the prespecified primary outcome; POSSIBLE for better morning biochemical control — secondary and extension-phase findings that a failed-primary trial cannot promote to proven benefit.

title: Empagliflozin for SIAD: raises sodium modestly in two small randomised trials
question: In patients with the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis (SIAD), does empagliflozin raise plasma sodium compared with placebo, in hospitalised hyponatraemia and in chronic outpatient SIAD?
balance: Two small randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials from one research group point the same way, in two different settings. In hospitalised patients with SIAD-induced hyponatraemia on fluid restriction, 4 days of empagliflozin raised plasma sodium by a median 10 mmol/L versus 7 mmol/L on placebo (P=0.04) — a modest 3 mmol/L advantage on top of restriction (Refardt 2020, 88 patients). In outpatients with chronic SIAD, a crossover trial of empagliflozin 25 mg/day for 4 weeks raised median sodium from 131 to 134 mmol/L while placebo left it at 130 mmol/L, a treatment difference of 4.1 mmol/L (95% CI 1.7 to 6.5; P=0.004), with an exploratory 1.16-point MoCA improvement (Refardt 2023, only 14 patients completing). The endpoint in both trials is the sodium number, not symptoms, falls, or hospitalisation; treatment was well tolerated with no hypoglycaemia or hypotension reported in the hospital trial and no serious adverse events in the crossover. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — concordant randomised evidence for a real but modest sodium-raising effect, with clinical-outcome benefit unproven and independent replication still needed.

title: Preoperative octreotide in acromegaly (POTA): a short-term macroadenoma advantage that faded by 5 years
question: In newly diagnosed acromegaly, does 6 months of preoperative octreotide improve transsphenoidal surgical cure rates compared with direct surgery — overall, in macroadenomas, and at long-term follow-up?
balance: The randomised evidence splits by tumour size and by time. In the Norwegian POTA trial (Carlsen 2008; 62 newly diagnosed patients randomised to 6 months of octreotide LAR 20 mg every 28 days or direct transsphenoidal surgery), overall cure by IGF-1 criteria at 3 months was 45% with pretreatment versus 23% with direct surgery — not statistically significant (P=0.11). The significant finding sat in macroadenomas: 50% cured (13/26) versus 16% (4/25) (P=0.017); in microadenomas pretreatment did worse numerically (1/5 vs 3/5; P=0.52), on tiny numbers. The same trial's long-term follow-up (Fougner 2014), using stricter combined cure criteria, found the macroadenoma gap narrowed and lost significance: 38% versus 24% at 1 year (P=0.27) and 41% versus 27% at 5 years (P=0.34); pooling with the one other long-term randomised study gave 37% versus 19% long-term (P=0.08). SPLIT: POSSIBLE for a short-term surgical-cure advantage confined to macroadenomas; (the treatment made no difference) proven for overall cure or for durable long-term cure — a single small national trial, whose own authors say the results need confirmation.

title: Antiandrogens for hirsutism: spironolactone, flutamide, and finasteride all beat placebo and looked similar in one small trial
question: In women with hirsutism, how do spironolactone, flutamide, and finasteride compare with each other and with placebo for reducing hair growth over 6 months?
balance: One small but well-measured trial answers the head-to-head question: at the doses tested, the three drugs look alike. In Moghetti 2000, 40 hirsute women were randomised double-blind to spironolactone 100 mg/day, flutamide 250 mg/day, finasteride 5 mg/day, or placebo for 6 months, with hair growth measured objectively — mean hair-shaft diameter by blinded computer-assisted microscopy — as well as by Ferriman-Gallwey score. Hair diameter fell 11.7% on spironolactone, 18.0% on flutamide, and 12.6% on finasteride, with no statistically significant differences among the active drugs; Ferriman-Gallwey scores fell 41.0%, 38.9%, and 31.6% respectively, again without differences among groups. Placebo changed nothing (hair diameter −1.4%; Ferriman-Gallwey +5.4%). With only 10 women per arm, 'no difference among drugs' is a weak claim — the trial could not have detected moderate differences — and 6 months is short for a hair-cycle outcome. Choice among these drugs in practice is therefore driven by safety and patient factors, not proven superiority: flutamide carries a recognised risk of serious liver injury, finasteride is teratogenic to a male fetus, and spironolactone requires contraception and potassium/blood-pressure awareness. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — a single small trial supports that all three work modestly versus placebo; it does not establish that they are truly equal.

title: Biomarker-guided KDIGO bundle after cardiac surgery (PrevAKI): fewer severe injuries, overall AKI unchanged in the multicentre trial
question: In cardiac-surgery patients identified as high-risk by urinary [TIMP-2]·[IGFBP7], does implementing the KDIGO care bundle (haemodynamic optimisation, nephrotoxin avoidance, glycaemic control) reduce AKI within 72 hours compared with standard care?
balance: The two trials of the same idea point in different directions depending on which outcome you read, so this stamp is split. In the single-centre PrevAKI trial, cardiac-surgery patients flagged high-risk by urinary [TIMP-2]·[IGFBP7] who received the KDIGO bundle developed AKI within 72 hours in 55.1% of cases versus 71.7% with standard care (absolute reduction 16.6 percentage points). In the multicentre PrevAKI trial (278 patients), overall AKI did not differ (46.3% bundle versus 41.5% control), but moderate-to-severe AKI was less frequent with the bundle (14.0% versus 23.9%; absolute reduction 10.0 points), and the trial's primary purpose was feasibility — bundle adherence was 65.4% versus 4.2%. The specific tested programme is the KDIGO care bundle (haemodynamic optimisation, nephrotoxin avoidance, glycaemic control) triggered by the [TIMP-2]·[IGFBP7] biomarker test. PROPOSED SPLIT — POSSIBLE benefit for moderate-to-severe AKI; (the treatment made no difference) for overall AKI in the multicentre trial.

title: Continuous versus intermittent dialysis in ICU AKI (Hemodiafe): survival was the same either way
question: In critically ill patients with AKI as part of multiple-organ dysfunction, does continuous venovenous haemodiafiltration improve survival compared with intermittent haemodialysis delivered to the same tolerance and metabolic-control standards?
balance: One multicentre randomised trial, now two decades old, found no survival advantage for the continuous mode when both modes were delivered carefully. In 360 critically ill patients with AKI as part of multiple-organ dysfunction in 21 French ICUs, 60-day survival was 32% with intermittent haemodialysis versus 33% with continuous venovenous haemodiafiltration — essentially identical, and the same at every other time point. The trial's own interpretation was narrower than 'mode does not matter': with strict guidelines to improve tolerance and metabolic control, almost all such patients could be treated intermittently. THIN: a single trial from 1999–2003, before modern membranes, dosing, and hybrid modes. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — one well-run multicentre trial, but old and unconfirmed by a second modality trial.

title: Far-infrared therapy for arteriovenous fistula maturation: one small positive trial, effects unquantified
question: In haemodialysis patients with a new arteriovenous fistula, does far-infrared therapy improve fistula maturation, blood flow, and 12-month patency compared with usual care?
balance: The evidence here is small and fragile, and this stamp stays weak. In one single-centre randomised trial of 80 haemodialysis patients (40 per group), adding far-infrared therapy to mucopolysaccharide polysulfonate cream for 3 months was followed by significantly larger vein diameter, higher pump-controlled and brachial-artery blood flow, shorter maturation time, lower pain scores, fewer fistula complications, and a higher primary patency rate than cream alone — but the PubMed abstract reports these only as statistically significant (P<0.05), without the actual values, so no effect size can be quoted or checked from the record. A second randomised trial named in the drafting notes (PMID 35887935) could not be gate-verified in this build session and is therefore not carded. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — one small single-centre trial, qualitative reporting only.

title: Intradialytic parenteral nutrition for protein-energy wasting: albumin up in one small trial, primary endpoint null in another
question: In maintenance haemodialysis patients with protein-energy wasting who cannot tolerate oral supplements, does intradialytic parenteral nutrition improve nutritional status compared with intensive dietary counselling alone?
balance: Two small randomised trials of intradialytic parenteral nutrition (IDPN) disagree on their primary nutritional markers, so this stamp is split and weak. In a Thai trial of 38 haemodialysis patients with protein-energy wasting who could not tolerate oral supplements, 3 months of fish-oil-based IDPN raised serum albumin (3.5 to 3.8 g/dL) while intensive dietary counselling did not (3.6 to 3.5 g/dL; p=0.01 between patterns as reported), with improved dietary intake, body weight, and malnutrition-inflammation score in the IDPN group only. In the multicentre ENEFLUID study — the specific tested product is named here for clarification, as it is a single proprietary formulation (ENEFLUID) — 39 analysed patients showed no difference in the primary endpoint, change in serum transthyretin at 12 weeks (difference 1.3 mg/dL; 95% CI −1.7 to 4.3; P=0.41), although protein intake fell less with IDPN. Neither trial measured survival or hospitalisation. PROPOSED SPLIT — POSSIBLE for short-term nutritional markers in supplement-intolerant patients; (the treatment made no difference) on the ENEFLUID trial's transthyretin primary endpoint. THIN: 38 and 39 patients.

title: Blood-volume-monitoring-guided ultrafiltration for intradialytic hypotension: no reduction in the crossover trial
question: In haemodialysis patients whose sessions are frequently complicated by symptomatic intradialytic hypotension, does blood-volume-monitoring-guided ultrafiltration biofeedback reduce hypotensive episodes compared with best clinical practice alone?
balance: One small crossover trial in exactly the patients the technology is meant for found no benefit — if anything, the point estimate ran the wrong way. In 32 randomised haemodialysis patients whose sessions were frequently complicated by symptomatic intradialytic hypotension, the rate of symptomatic hypotension was 0.10 episodes per hour with blood-volume-monitoring-guided ultrafiltration biofeedback versus 0.07 per hour with best clinical practice alone (P=0.29), with no differences in asymptomatic episodes, symptoms alone, weight gain, cardiac biomarkers, or recovery time. THIN: 26 patients completed the study, from a single programme in Calgary. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — a properly randomised test in the right population, but small enough that a modest effect in either direction cannot be excluded.

title: Machine perfusion versus cold storage for deceased-donor kidneys: hypothermic perfusion helps, a 1-hour normothermic add-on does not
question: In deceased-donor kidney transplantation, does hypothermic machine perfusion of the graft reduce delayed graft function compared with static cold storage?
balance: The answer depends on which machine perfusion is meant. In the international paired trial (Moers 2009), one kidney from each of 336 deceased donors was randomised to hypothermic machine perfusion and the other to static cold storage: delayed graft function occurred in 70 recipients on machine perfusion versus 89 on cold storage (20.8% versus 26.5%; adjusted odds ratio 0.57, a relative effect), and 1-year graft survival was 94% versus 90%. In the later DCD trial (Hosgood 2023), adding just 1 hour of normothermic machine perfusion at the end of cold storage made no difference: delayed graft function was 60.7% with normothermic perfusion versus 58.5% with cold storage alone (adjusted odds ratio 1.13). So sustained hypothermic perfusion reduced delayed graft function, while a brief normothermic perfusion period after cold storage did not. PROPOSED SPLIT — LIKELY for hypothermic machine perfusion reducing delayed graft function / POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for 1-hour normothermic perfusion added to cold storage — two large randomised trials, but testing two different perfusion strategies, so the verdict is split by technique rather than pooled.

title: Donor hypothermia for delayed graft function: helps without machine perfusion, adds nothing to it, loses to it head-to-head
question: In deceased (brain-dead) kidney donors, does therapeutic hypothermia (34–35°C) reduce delayed graft function in recipients — and how does it compare with hypothermic machine perfusion?
balance: Three randomised trials give a context-dependent answer. Where kidneys were not routinely machine-perfused, donor hypothermia helped: Niemann 2015 (370 donors, 572 recipients) found delayed graft function in 28% of recipients of hypothermia-donor kidneys versus 39% with normothermia (odds ratio 0.62; 95% CI 0.43 to 0.92; P=0.02) — though that trial was stopped early for efficacy, which tends to inflate effects. Where machine perfusion was routine, hypothermia added nothing detectable: HYPOREME (Canet 2024; 526 recipients of expanded-criteria donor kidneys, all machine-perfused) found delayed graft function in 16% versus 21% (odds ratio 0.71; 95% CI 0.44 to 1.13; P=0.14), with 1-year creatinine slightly favouring hypothermia. And head-to-head, hypothermia lost: Malinoski 2023 (1,349 kidneys) found delayed graft function in 30% with donor hypothermia versus 19% with machine perfusion (adjusted risk ratio 1.72; 95% CI 1.35 to 2.17 — a relative measure, against absolute rates of 30% and 19%), with the combination (22%) no better than machine perfusion alone, and 1-year graft survival similar in all groups. PROPOSED SPLIT — POSSIBLE for hypothermia reducing delayed graft function when machine perfusion is not used / POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) when added to routine machine perfusion, and inferior to machine perfusion in direct comparison.

title: Early corticosteroid cessation after kidney transplantation: matched graft outcomes, more mild rejection (Woodle trial, 5- and ~16-year results)
question: In kidney transplant recipients without delayed graft function, does stopping corticosteroids at day 7 match long-term low-dose prednisone (5 mg/day) on the 5-year composite of death, graft loss, and moderate/severe acute rejection?
balance: One double-blind programme answers this, followed for a very long time. In 386 kidney transplant recipients without delayed graft function, randomised to stop corticosteroids at day 7 or continue low-dose prednisone (5 mg/day), the 5-year composite of death, graft loss, or moderate/severe acute rejection was 15.7% with early cessation versus 14.4% with continued steroids — no difference (Woodle 2008). Registry-linked follow-up to a median of 15.8 years still showed no difference in allograft failure (adjusted hazard ratio 0.83, relative; 95% CI 0.62 to 1.10). The trade-off was rejection: biopsy-confirmed acute rejection was more frequent after early cessation (17.8% versus 10.8% at 5 years), but the extra episodes were mainly mild, steroid-sensitive Banff 1A rejections, while metabolic markers (triglycerides, weight gain, diabetes needing insulin) favoured stopping. PROPOSED SPLIT — POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for the death/graft-loss composite / POSSIBLE (harm) for biopsy-confirmed acute rejection — a single (THIN) double-blind programme, so the stamp stays at POSSIBLE despite the long follow-up.

title: Everolimus with calcineurin-inhibitor elimination after kidney transplantation (ZEUS): better GFR, more early rejection
question: In de novo kidney transplant recipients, does converting at 4.5 months from ciclosporin to an everolimus-based, calcineurin-inhibitor-free regimen improve renal function without losing efficacy (biopsy-proven rejection, graft loss, death)?
balance: In the single ZEUS trial, 503 de novo kidney transplant recipients were started on ciclosporin-based therapy and 300 were randomised at 4.5 months to eliminate the calcineurin inhibitor (everolimus-based regimen) or continue ciclosporin (Budde 2011). At 12 months, estimated GFR was clearly better after conversion (71.8 versus 61.9 mL/min/1.73 m², mean difference 9.8), and a living-donor subgroup report found the gap persisted at 5 years (67.2 versus 60.8; Sommerer 2016). The cost was rejection and tolerability: biopsy-proven acute rejection after randomisation was 10% versus 3% (full-period rates were equal at 15%), and everolimus brought more lipid elevation, proteinuria, low haemoglobin, thrombocytopenia, mouth ulcers, and diarrhoea. Patient and graft survival did not differ. This is one trial programme (THIN), with a surrogate renal-function primary end point. PROPOSED SPLIT — POSSIBLE for improved renal function / POSSIBLE (harm) for post-conversion rejection and adverse effects — the function benefit and the rejection/tolerability cost come from the same single programme and should not be merged into one stamp.

title: Switching to sirolimus to prevent further skin cancers after kidney transplantation (TUMORAPA, 5-year results)
question: In kidney transplant recipients on a calcineurin inhibitor who have had at least one cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma, does switching to sirolimus prolong skin-cancer-free survival compared with maintaining calcineurin-inhibitor therapy?
balance: In the single TUMORAPA randomised trial, kidney transplant recipients who had already had at least one cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma were switched from a calcineurin inhibitor to sirolimus (n=64) or kept on the calcineurin inhibitor (n=56). At 5 years, survival free of squamous cell carcinoma was significantly longer with sirolimus (P=.007), and far fewer switched patients had developed new skin cancers: 22% versus 59% for squamous cell carcinoma, 34% versus 66% for other skin cancers, and 20% versus 37.5% for basal cell carcinoma (absolute rates). Kidney function and patient and graft survival were similar. This is one small trial (THIN) in a rare, high-risk population, which is why the stamp stays at POSSIBLE despite the large absolute differences. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — a benefit claim resting on a single small randomised trial with 5-year follow-up.

title: High-dose versus low-dose vitamin D after kidney transplantation (VITALE): no extraskeletal benefit; fewer fractures
question: In non-diabetic kidney transplant recipients with low vitamin D levels, does high-dose cholecalciferol (100,000 IU) versus low-dose (12,000 IU) reduce diabetes, major cardiovascular events, cancer, or death — and does it prevent fractures?
balance: VITALE (Courbebaisse 2023) randomised 536 non-diabetic kidney transplant recipients with 25-hydroxyvitamin D below 30 ng/mL to high-dose cholecalciferol (100,000 IU) or low-dose (12,000 IU), given every 2 weeks for 2 months then monthly for 22 months. Levels rose much more on high dose (+23 versus +6 ng/mL), but the primary composite — diabetes, major cardiovascular events, cancer, and death — occurred in 15% versus 16% (hazard ratio 0.94; 95% CI 0.60 to 1.48; P=.78): no difference. The one positive finding was secondary: incident symptomatic fractures in 1% versus 4% (odds ratio 0.24; 95% CI 0.07 to 0.86; P=.03), an absolute difference of about 3 percentage points on small event numbers. Adverse-event incidence was similar. This is a dose-comparison trial with no placebo or untreated arm (THIN for the broader 'does vitamin D help' question). PROPOSED SPLIT — POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for the extraskeletal composite / POSSIBLE for fewer symptomatic fractures. This shelf does not add references to the held dietary-supplements shelves (#48–#60); it is the transplant-specific dose question only.

title: Early basal insulin after kidney transplantation: pilot promised less post-transplant diabetes; the multicentre trial found none
question: In kidney transplant recipients without prior diabetes, does early postoperative basal insulin (treating glucose from 140 mg/dL) reduce post-transplant diabetes compared with standard threshold-based care?
balance: A promising pilot did not hold up at scale. The single-centre proof-of-concept trial (Hecking 2012; 50 recipients) randomised patients to immediate postoperative basal (isophane) insulin whenever evening glucose reached 140 mg/dL, versus standard care treating at 180–250 mg/dL, and reported 73% lower odds of new-onset diabetes after transplantation with the early-insulin strategy (odds ratio 0.27 — a relative odds measure; the abstract reports no absolute diabetes rates), HbA1c on average 0.38% lower, and no treatment-group patient needing antidiabetic agents at 12 months versus 7 of 25 controls (28%). The multicentre trial designed to confirm it (Schwaiger 2021, ITP-NODAT; 263 recipients) found post-transplant diabetes at 12 months in 12.2% versus 14.7% on intention-to-treat (odds ratio 0.82; 95% CI 0.39 to 1.76) and 13.4% versus 17.4% at 24 months (odds ratio 0.71; 95% CI 0.34 to 1.49) — no significant difference — with a lower odds only in per-protocol and adjusted analyses (adjusted odds ratio 0.21; 95% CI 0.07 to 0.62), and more hypoglycaemia (mostly asymptomatic or mild) on early insulin. Per-protocol findings cannot rescue a null intention-to-treat result. PROPOSED SPLIT — POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) on the multicentre intention-to-treat analysis / MAYBE (weak evidence) for the pilot's suggested benefit. Wording note: this is post-transplant diabetes arising in people without prior diabetes, not prediabetes; the outcome is described as its occurrence, per the trials.

title: CMV prevention after kidney transplant: prophylaxis suppresses the virus better than preemptive therapy, without a rejection or graft advantage
question: In cytomegalovirus-seropositive kidney transplant recipients, does universal valganciclovir prophylaxis beat preemptive therapy (treatment triggered by DNAemia) on acute rejection, CMV disease, and long-term graft outcomes?
balance: Two independent randomised trials point the same way on CMV itself but not on rejection or graft survival. In VIPP (Witzke 2018, 7-year results), valganciclovir prophylaxis in CMV-positive recipients cut CMV infection to 11.5% versus 39.7% and CMV disease to 4.7% versus 15.9% compared with preemptive therapy, while graft loss (7.4% versus 8.6%), death (9.5% versus 11.3%), and rejection (29.1% versus 28.5%) did not differ. In the OVERT trial (Reischig 2023), acute rejection at 12 months — its primary outcome — was 13% on prophylaxis versus 23% on preemptive therapy, a difference that was not statistically significant; subclinical rejection was less frequent with prophylaxis (13% versus 29%), DNAemia was much more frequent under preemptive therapy (75% versus 44%), CMV disease was 4% in both groups, and preemptive therapy meant less drug exposure and less neutropenia. PROPOSED SPLIT — LIKELY for prophylaxis preventing CMV infection and disease / POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for acute rejection and long-term graft outcomes — two independent trials (DOUBLE-A) agree that prophylaxis suppresses the virus better, and neither shows a rejection or graft-survival advantage.

title: LCP-tacrolimus once daily versus immediate-release tacrolimus twice daily: noninferior, no outcome advantage
question: In kidney transplant recipients, does once-daily LCP-tacrolimus (extended-release formulation) prevent rejection and preserve graft function as well as twice-daily immediate-release tacrolimus — de novo and after conversion in stable patients?
balance: The honest answer from the trials is equivalence, not advantage. In the primary de novo phase 3 trial (Budde 2014; 543 recipients), once-daily LCP-tacrolimus — the specific extended-release MeltDose formulation tested, named here because the question is about that formulation — met its noninferiority margin against twice-daily tacrolimus: treatment failure at 12 months was 18.3% versus 19.6%, with the upper 95% confidence limit of the difference (+5.27%) below the predefined +10% margin, and no significant differences in individual efficacy events or adverse events. Target troughs were reached faster and at a 14% lower cumulative dose. In stable recipients converting from immediate-release tacrolimus, the carded evidence is thinner: a post hoc Hispanic subgroup analysis of the conversion phase 3 trial (Faravardeh 2021; only 55 patients) found composite treatment failure in 4% versus 3%, with similar kidney function, troughs, and adverse events; a post hoc metaboliser analysis of the de novo trial (Suwelack 2020) likewise found no outcome differences in any metaboliser stratum. So there is no outcome the once-daily formulation improves — the case for it is convenience and pharmacokinetics, not better graft outcomes (THIN on the conversion side, where only subgroup analyses are carded). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — for clinical outcomes in both settings, with noninferiority formally shown de novo.

title: Bortezomib for late antibody-mediated rejection after kidney transplantation (BORTEJECT): no benefit, real toxicity
question: In kidney transplant recipients with late donor-specific-antibody-positive antibody-mediated rejection, do two cycles of the proteasome inhibitor bortezomib halt GFR decline compared with placebo?
balance: The only randomised trial in late antibody-mediated rejection is a clean negative. In BORTEJECT (Eskandary 2018), 44 kidney transplant recipients with donor-specific-antibody-positive late antibody-mediated rejection (median 5 years after transplant) received two cycles of bortezomib or placebo. The primary end point — the slope of eGFR decline — differed by 0.5 mL/min/1.73 m² per year (95% CI −4.8 to 5.8; P=0.86), and nothing else separated the groups: measured GFR at 24 months, 2-year graft survival (81% versus 96%, not significant), proteinuria, donor-specific antibody levels, and biopsy morphology or molecular phenotypes were all similar. Bortezomib did cause gastrointestinal and haematologic toxicity. This is a single small trial (THIN), but it is placebo-controlled and internally consistent across every end point, and its confidence interval centres on no effect. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — a null verdict on one small but rigorous trial, with documented toxicity on the harm side of the ledger.

title: Bepirovirsen for chronic hepatitis B (B-Clear): sustained HBsAg loss in about 1 in 10 (phase 2b)
question: In chronic hepatitis B (on or off nucleos(t)ide therapy), does 24 weeks of the antisense oligonucleotide bepirovirsen 300 mg weekly produce sustained HBsAg and HBV DNA loss after treatment ends — a step toward functional cure?
balance: In the single phase 2b B-Clear trial (Yuen 2022), 457 people with chronic hepatitis B — about half on nucleos(t)ide therapy, half not — were randomised to several bepirovirsen regimens or a placebo-first control. The primary outcome (HBsAg and HBV DNA both undetectable, sustained for 24 weeks after treatment ended, with no new antiviral therapy) was met by 9% of participants on nucleos(t)ide therapy and 10% not on it who received bepirovirsen 300 mg weekly for 24 weeks — roughly 1 in 10, with very wide credible intervals (0 to 31 and 0 to 38 respectively) — versus 0% in the control groups. Shorter or dose-reduced regimens did less (1–9%). Injection-site reactions, fever, fatigue, and alanine aminotransferase rises were more common on bepirovirsen. This is a genuine step toward finite therapy, but it is one phase 2 trial (THIN) in which the endpoint was met by a minority. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — a benefit claim for a minority endpoint on a single phase 2b trial, with phase 3 confirmation still pending.

title: Pegozafermin for MASH with F2–F3 fibrosis (ENLIVEN): fibrosis improvement in about 1 in 4 (phase 2b)
question: In biopsy-proven metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) with stage F2–F3 fibrosis, does the FGF21 analogue pegozafermin improve fibrosis by at least one stage without worsening steatohepatitis at 24 weeks, versus placebo?
balance: In the single phase 2b ENLIVEN trial (Loomba 2023), 222 adults with biopsy-proven noncirrhotic steatohepatitis and stage F2–F3 fibrosis received subcutaneous pegozafermin (15 mg or 30 mg weekly, or 44 mg every 2 weeks) or placebo for 24 weeks. Fibrosis improvement by at least one stage without worsening of steatohepatitis occurred in 22%, 26%, and 27% on pegozafermin versus 7% on placebo — absolute differences of 14 percentage points (95% CI −9 to 38; not significant for the 15 mg dose), 19 points (5 to 32; P=0.009), and 20 points (5 to 35; P=0.008). Steatohepatitis resolution without worsening fibrosis occurred in 37%, 23%, and 26% versus 2% on placebo. Nausea and diarrhoea were the most common adverse events. Both primary end points are 24-week biopsy surrogates from one phase 2b trial (THIN), and the lowest dose's fibrosis result was not significant. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — a genuine phase 2b histology signal at the two higher regimens, awaiting phase 3 confirmation on longer, harder outcomes.

title: Peginterferon add-on or switch after entecavir suppression in hepatitis B: seroconversion benefit only in suppressed patients
question: In HBeAg-positive chronic hepatitis B suppressed on long-term entecavir, does adding on or switching to peginterferon improve HBeAg seroconversion and HBsAg decline versus continuing entecavir alone?
balance: The answer depends on where the patient starts, and the two randomised trials genuinely diverge. In patients already suppressed on long-term entecavir (Hu 2022; 153 HBeAg-positive patients with low HBsAg and undetectable DNA), adding on or switching to peginterferon alfa-2b for 48 weeks gave HBeAg seroconversion in 18.0% and 19.2% versus 2.0% on continued entecavir (absolute gains of about 16–17 percentage points), with HBsAg below 100 IU/mL in 30.0% and 34.6% versus 0%. In treatment-naïve patients, however, adding peginterferon to entecavir made no difference to seroconversion (Yang 2020; HBsAg seroconversion 4.1% versus 1.8%, P=0.809; HBeAg conversion 11.0% versus 12.5%, P=0.787), though elastography values improved slightly more with the combination. Both trials are small, open-label, single-country (China), and use serological surrogates (THIN); interferon adverse effects are the price of the strategy. PROPOSED SPLIT — POSSIBLE for seroconversion benefit in entecavir-suppressed patients / POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for seroconversion when peginterferon is added in treatment-naïve patients.

title: Peginterferon for hepatitis delta (HIDIT-I): HDV RNA clearance in about 1 in 4; adefovir ineffective
question: In chronic hepatitis delta, does 48 weeks of peginterferon alfa-2a — alone or combined with adefovir — clear HDV RNA versus adefovir alone?
balance: HIDIT-I (Wedemeyer 2011) remains the anchor randomised trial in hepatitis delta, and it is small (90 patients, THIN). Forty-eight weeks of peginterferon alfa-2a cleared HDV RNA at week 48 in 23% of patients when combined with adefovir and 24% with peginterferon alone, versus 0% on adefovir alone (P=0.006 and P=0.004) — so adefovir added nothing virologically, and adefovir alone was ineffective. The combined primary end point (HDV RNA clearance plus ALT normalisation) was met by only 2 patients in each peginterferon arm and none on adefovir. Twenty-four weeks after treatment, 28% of peginterferon-treated patients remained HDV RNA-negative. The combination did produce more large HBsAg declines (>1 log10 in 10 patients versus 2 and 0). Ten-year follow-up of the same trial (Wranke 2020; follow-up data in 60 patients) found liver-related complications in 17 patients, concentrated in non-responders and those with baseline cirrhosis, consistent with — but not proof of — a long-term payoff from off-treatment response; 19 patients were retreated, which clouds attribution. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — a real but minority virological response to peginterferon on a single small trial, with adefovir's contribution null.

title: Pioglitazone for MASH in prediabetes or type 2 diabetes: histology improves in two trials; weight gain is the trade-off
question: In adults with prediabetes or type 2 diabetes and biopsy-proven metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH), does pioglitazone 45 mg daily improve liver histology versus placebo?
balance: Two randomised trials from the same research group point the same way. Belfort 2006 (55 patients with impaired glucose tolerance or type 2 diabetes and biopsy-proven steatohepatitis; 6 months of pioglitazone 45 mg plus diet versus diet plus placebo) improved steatosis, ballooning, and inflammation, with necroinflammation reduced in 85% versus 38%, though the fibrosis difference was not significant (P=0.08). Cusi 2016 (101 patients with prediabetes or type 2 diabetes; 18 months) met its primary histological outcome in 58% on pioglitazone — an absolute treatment difference of 41 percentage points (95% CI 23 to 59) — with steatohepatitis resolution in 51% (difference 32 points; 95% CI 13 to 51) and a modest fibrosis-score improvement (−0.5; P=0.039). The costs: weight gain 2.5 kg greater than placebo in Cusi 2016, plus the class cautions carried on the separate pioglitazone harms shelf (#290) — this shelf is the liver-histology question only, distinct from the vitamin E question on Shelf #26. Both trials are single-group, single-centre, biopsy-surrogate studies (THIN in breadth, consistent in direction). PROPOSED LIKELY — consistent histological benefit across two randomised trials in the diabetes/prediabetes population, with weight gain as the quantified trade-off.

title: Efinopegdutide versus semaglutide 1 mg for fatty liver: greater relative liver-fat reduction in one phase IIa trial
question: In adults with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (fatty liver), does efinopegdutide (a GLP-1/glucagon co-agonist) 10 mg weekly reduce liver fat more than semaglutide 1 mg weekly over 24 weeks?
balance: In the single phase IIa trial (Romero-Gómez 2023), 145 adults with fatty liver disease and MRI liver fat of at least 10% were randomised open-label to efinopegdutide 10 mg weekly or semaglutide 1 mg weekly for 24 weeks. The primary end point — the relative reduction in liver fat content — was larger with efinopegdutide: a least-squares mean relative reduction of 72.7% (90% CI 66.8 to 78.7) versus 42.3% (90% CI 36.5 to 48.1) with semaglutide (P<0.001). Those are relative reductions in an imaging measure, not proportions of patients cured, and not histology. Weight loss was similar (8.5% versus 7.1% of body weight; P=0.085), and gastrointestinal adverse events were somewhat more frequent with efinopegdutide. The comparison is against semaglutide 1 mg — a low dose by current standards — in an open-label, industry-run phase IIa study with no biopsy or clinical outcomes (THIN). PROPOSED POSSIBLE — a clear imaging-surrogate win over a low-dose comparator in one small open-label trial; whether it means better liver outcomes is untested.

title: Entecavir versus lamivudine prophylaxis during R-CHOP: hepatitis 0% versus 13.3% in one trial
question: In HBsAg-positive patients with diffuse large B-cell lymphoma receiving R-CHOP chemotherapy, does entecavir prophylaxis prevent hepatitis B reactivation and HBV-related hepatitis better than lamivudine?
balance: In the single randomised trial (Huang 2014), 121 HBsAg-positive patients with untreated diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, normal liver function, and HBV DNA below 10³ copies/mL received entecavir 0.5 mg daily or lamivudine 100 mg daily from 1 week before R-CHOP chemotherapy until 6 months after it ended. Entecavir was better on every efficacy outcome: HBV-related hepatitis (the primary end point) occurred in 0% versus 13.3% (absolute difference 13.3 percentage points; 95% CI 4.7 to 21.9; P=.003), HBV reactivation in 6.6% versus 30% (difference 23.4 points; 95% CI 10.2 to 36.6; P=.001), and chemotherapy disruption in 1.6% versus 18.3% (difference 16.7 points; 95% CI 6.4 to 27.0; P=.002). Treatment-related adverse events were similar (24.6% versus 30%; P=.50). The effects are large and internally consistent, but this is one open-label trial from 10 centres in a single country, in patients with low baseline viral load (THIN). PROPOSED POSSIBLE — a strong single-trial result that guidelines have since broadly followed, held at POSSIBLE because the pack rests on that one trial.

title: Elebsiran (VIR-2218) with or without peginterferon in chronic hepatitis B: deep HBsAg falls, seroclearance uncontrolled (phase 2)
question: In chronic hepatitis B on nucleos(t)ide therapy, does the siRNA elebsiran (VIR-2218), with or without pegylated interferon-alfa-2a, lower HBsAg and produce HBsAg seroclearance?
balance: This is early, uncontrolled evidence and the stamp says so. In an open-label phase 2 study (Yuen 2024), 84 adults with chronic hepatitis B on nucleos(t)ide therapy (HBV DNA below 90 IU/mL, no cirrhosis) were enrolled — not randomised — into six cohorts receiving the siRNA elebsiran (VIR-2218) 200 mg every 4 weeks, alone or with pegylated interferon-alfa-2a for varying durations. Elebsiran lowered HBsAg substantially in every cohort (mean maximum reductions of −1.7 to −3.0 log10 IU/mL). HBsAg seroclearance occurred in 11 participants, all in the longer interferon-combination cohorts, and 6 of them remained clear 24 weeks after treatment ended; no one on elebsiran alone (cohort 1) or the shortest combination (cohort 6) cleared HBsAg. Alanine aminotransferase elevations were common in the interferon cohorts (60–94%) but uncommon on elebsiran alone (13%), and most adverse events were grade 1–2. Without randomisation or a control arm there is no counterfactual: how many of these patients would have cleared HBsAg anyway, and how much is elebsiran versus interferon, cannot be separated (THIN). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — promising pharmacology and a minority seroclearance signal in longer combination cohorts, from a single uncontrolled phase 2 study.

title: Bariatric-metabolic surgery for MASH (BRAVES): resolution in 56–57% versus 16% with lifestyle care at 1 year
question: In adults with obesity and biopsy-proven metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH), does bariatric-metabolic surgery (Roux-en-Y gastric bypass or sleeve gastrectomy) resolve steatohepatitis without worsening fibrosis at 1 year, compared with lifestyle intervention plus best medical care?
balance: BRAVES (Verrastro 2023) is the first randomised trial of metabolic surgery for steatohepatitis. In 288 adults with obesity (body mass index 30–55 kg/m²) and biopsy-confirmed steatohepatitis, with or without type 2 diabetes, histological resolution of steatohepatitis without worsening of fibrosis at 1 year occurred in 56% after Roux-en-Y gastric bypass and 57% after sleeve gastrectomy, versus 16% with lifestyle modification plus best medical care (P<0.0001) — absolute gains of about 40 percentage points; expressed relatively, the probability of resolution was 3.60 times (95% CI 2.19 to 5.92) and 3.67 times (2.23 to 6.02) higher with surgery. Per-protocol rates were 70%, 70%, and 19%. There were no deaths or life-threatening complications; severe adverse events occurred in 10 surgical participants (6%) and were managed without re-operation. This remains a single, open-label trial from one city (Rome) with a 1-year histological endpoint (THIN for durability and hard outcomes). PROPOSED POSSIBLE — a large, decisive effect on the histological endpoint in one trial, distinct from Shelf #288, which asks whether metabolic surgery induces diabetes remission; this shelf's question is liver histology. (For prediabetes material the standing wording is 'delay', not prevention; this trial enrolled established steatohepatitis, with or without diabetes.)
