title: Tetrathiomolybdate versus trientine in neurological Wilson disease: less early deterioration in one small trial; drug never marketed
question: In patients presenting with neurological Wilson disease, does initial treatment with tetrathiomolybdate preserve neurological function better than trientine?
balance: One small double-blind trial is the whole randomised evidence base (Brewer 2006; 48 patients, THIN). In patients presenting with neurological Wilson disease, mostly newly diagnosed, initial treatment for 8 weeks with ammonium tetrathiomolybdate (the specific salt tested — named because tetrathiomolybdate is not a marketed, regulated product and preparations differ) caused less early neurological deterioration than trientine: 1 of 25 patients (4%) worsened on tetrathiomolybdate versus 6 of 23 (26%) on trientine (P<.05), an absolute difference of about 22 percentage points. Four trientine patients died during follow-up, 3 of whom had shown initial deterioration; no deaths were reported in the tetrathiomolybdate arm in the record. The trade-off was haematological and hepatic laboratory effects: anaemia and/or leukopenia in 3 tetrathiomolybdate patients and further transaminase elevations in 4, versus anaemia in 1 trientine patient. Neurological and speech recovery over 3 years was good in both arms. The access caveat is part of the answer: tetrathiomolybdate has never been marketed, so this is evidence about a drug most patients cannot obtain, from a single 48-patient trial run by its developer's group. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — less early neurological worsening than trientine in one small trial, with more laboratory adverse effects and a major availability caveat.

title: Machine perfusion versus cold storage in liver transplantation (Nasralla 2018; DHOPE-DCD 2021)
question: In liver transplantation, does machine perfusion of the donor liver reduce graft injury and organ discard compared with conventional static cold storage?
balance: Two randomised trials, two perfusion strategies, one direction. In 220 liver transplantations, normothermic machine perfusion halved graft injury (a 50% relative reduction in hepatocellular enzyme release) and halved the organ discard rate versus static cold storage, while allowing 54% longer mean preservation — but it did not significantly change bile duct complications, graft survival, or patient survival. In livers donated after circulatory death, dual hypothermic oxygenated perfusion cut symptomatic nonanastomotic biliary strictures — a clinical endpoint, not a surrogate — from 18% to 6%, and also reduced postreperfusion syndrome and early allograft dysfunction. The normothermic trial's headline endpoints are injury markers and utilisation; the hypothermic trial supplies the patient-level outcome. Neither trial shows a survival difference, and the two machines are not interchangeable — but machine perfusion, in one form or another, beats the ice box on every endpoint actually measured. PROPOSED LIKELY — two independent randomised trials with concordant benefit, tempered by a surrogate primary endpoint in one and no demonstrated survival gain in either.

title: Everolimus with reduced tacrolimus after liver transplantation (H2304)
question: In de novo liver transplant recipients, does introducing everolimus at day 30 with reduced-exposure (or eliminated) tacrolimus preserve renal function without losing efficacy (treated biopsy-proven rejection, graft loss, death) at 12 months?
balance: One large trial, a split answer. In H2304, 719 de novo liver recipients were randomised a month after transplant to everolimus with reduced tacrolimus, standard tacrolimus, or tacrolimus elimination. Everolimus plus reduced tacrolimus was noninferior on the composite of treated rejection, graft loss, or death (6.7% vs 9.7%), with significantly less treated rejection (2.9% vs 7.0%) and a significantly better adjusted change in kidney function (a difference of 8.50 mL/min/1.73 m² in eGFR change). But the tacrolimus-elimination arm was stopped early for excess rejection, and the everolimus arm paid for its gains with more discontinuations for adverse events (25.7% vs 14.1%) and more serious infections. So the strategy works on paper at 12 months for patients who tolerate it — roughly one in four did not. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — a single trial (THIN), noninferiority on a composite, a renal-function surrogate rather than hard kidney outcomes, and a real tolerability cost.

title: Bezafibrate for primary biliary cholangitis with incomplete response to ursodeoxycholic acid (BEZURSO)
question: In primary biliary cholangitis with an inadequate response to ursodeoxycholic acid (Paris-2 criteria), does adding bezafibrate 400 mg/day achieve a complete biochemical response over 24 months compared with placebo?
balance: A small trial with a lopsided biochemical result. In BEZURSO, 100 patients with primary biliary cholangitis responding inadequately to ursodeoxycholic acid were randomised to add bezafibrate 400 mg/day or placebo for 24 months. A complete biochemical response occurred in 31% on bezafibrate versus 0% on placebo, and alkaline phosphatase normalised in 67% versus 2%. But the outcomes that matter most did not separate: end-stage liver complications occurred in 2 patients in each group, and the trial was far too small and short to detect differences in transplant or death. Bezafibrate also raised creatinine slightly (+5% vs −3%) and caused more myalgia (20% vs 10%). Biochemical response is the accepted working endpoint in PBC and correlates with prognosis in cohort data, but it is still a surrogate. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — one trial of 100 patients (THIN), decisive on blood tests, silent on clinical outcomes. Shelf #1062 homes the other second-line PBC therapies; this shelf is the fibrate-specific trial.

title: Treating minimal hepatic encephalopathy with lactulose: cognition and quality of life (Prasad 2007)
question: In cirrhosis with minimal hepatic encephalopathy, does 3 months of lactulose improve cognitive function and health-related quality of life compared with no treatment?
balance: One small, open trial. Of 90 patients with cirrhosis screened, 61 had minimal hepatic encephalopathy and were randomised to lactulose or no treatment for 3 months. On lactulose, the mean number of abnormal neuropsychological tests fell from 2.74 to 0.75, while the untreated group barely moved (2.47 to 2.55); total Sickness Impact Profile scores — a quality-of-life measure — improved from 10.39 to 3.77 on lactulose and did not change without it (10.36 to 10.39). The direction is consistent and the effect sizes are not trivial, but the trial is tiny, unblinded (patients and testers knew who was treated), and short; practice effects on repeated cognitive testing and expectation effects on quality-of-life scores can both imitate benefit in exactly this design. No outcomes like overt encephalopathy episodes, falls, driving safety, or hospitalisation were measured. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — a plausible, cheap, low-risk intervention resting on one small nonblinded trial (THIN). One harm belongs on the record even though this trial did not show it: the AASLD/EASL guideline warns that overuse of lactulose can cause dehydration, hypernatraemia and electrolyte loss, and can itself precipitate or worsen hepatic encephalopathy — the opposite of the intent. That is a dosing harm, and it matters most in exactly this population, where a slide from minimal to overt encephalopathy is the outcome everyone is trying to prevent. The dose must be titrated to soft stools, not pushed.

title: Which plasma expander after large-volume paracentesis: albumin versus dextran 70 or polygeline (Ginès 1996)
question: In cirrhotic ascites treated by total paracentesis, does albumin prevent post-paracentesis circulatory dysfunction better than synthetic expanders (dextran 70, polygeline)?
balance: One randomised trial from 1996, and it favours albumin clearly on its chosen endpoint. In 289 patients undergoing total paracentesis, post-paracentesis circulatory dysfunction — defined by a rise in plasma renin activity at day 6 — occurred in 18.5% with albumin, 34.4% with dextran 70 (P=0.018), and 37.8% with polygeline (P=0.004). Two cautions keep the stamp modest. First, circulatory dysfunction is a renin-based surrogate: patients who developed it did worse afterwards (shorter time to readmission and shorter survival), but the trial did not show that the choice of expander itself changed readmission or survival — those follow-up comparisons were between patients with and without dysfunction, not between treatment arms. Second, it is a single trial (THIN), and polygeline is no longer widely used. Albumin is the expander with the evidence; the synthetics are not equivalent substitutes on the surrogate that predicts trouble. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — one trial, a surrogate endpoint, but a large and consistent separation. The separate 1988 question of expansion versus no expansion lives on Shelf #167.

title: Simvastatin plus rifaximin in decompensated cirrhosis (LIVERHOPE)
question: In decompensated cirrhosis (Child-Pugh B or C), does simvastatin 20 mg/day plus rifaximin 1200 mg/day for 12 months prevent acute-on-chronic liver failure and other severe complications compared with placebo?
balance: A properly done phase 3 trial with a null answer. LIVERHOPE randomised 237 patients with decompensated cirrhosis (Child-Pugh B or C) in 14 European hospitals to simvastatin 20 mg/day plus rifaximin 1200 mg/day or placebo for 12 months. Acute-on-chronic liver failure — the primary endpoint — developed in 17.9% on treatment versus 14.2% on placebo (HR 1.23, 95% CI 0.65 to 2.34; P=.52); if anything the point estimate leans the wrong way. Transplant or death occurred in 18.8% versus 24.2% (HR 0.75, 0.43 to 1.32; P=.32) and overall cirrhosis complications in 42.7% versus 45.8% (HR 0.93; P=.70) — neither significant, and the confidence intervals are too wide to claim the combination was proven useless for those endpoints, only that no benefit was shown. Adverse events were evenly matched (426 vs 419 events), but 3 patients (2.6%) on simvastatin developed rhabdomyolysis — the known statin hazard in advanced liver disease, and the reason statin enthusiasm in decompensated cirrhosis needs this trial in view. Tier C: death is part of the headline outcomes, so this shelf goes to the developer personally. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — a single trial (THIN) whose primary endpoint clearly failed, with secondary-endpoint intervals too wide for a stronger null stamp.

title: Cilofexor in non-cirrhotic primary sclerosing cholangitis (PRIMIS)
question: In non-cirrhotic large-duct primary sclerosing cholangitis, does the FXR agonist cilofexor 100 mg daily improve liver fibrosis over 96 weeks compared with placebo?
balance: The first phase 3 trial in primary sclerosing cholangitis, stopped early because it was going nowhere. PRIMIS randomised 419 adults with non-cirrhotic (F0–F3) large-duct PSC at 205 sites in 16 countries to cilofexor 100 mg daily or placebo for 96 weeks; 416 were analysed. A planned interim futility analysis put the probability of eventual success at 6.8% (futility boundary ≤10%), and the trial was terminated. In patients with paired biopsies, fibrosis progressed in 31% on cilofexor versus 33% on placebo (difference −1.4 percentage points, 95% CI −15.2 to 12.3; P=0.42). Itching — the class side effect — was more common on cilofexor (49% vs 36%). The early stop and the wide interval mean a modest benefit is not formally excluded, but a futility-stopped trial with a point estimate of essentially zero is not a maybe in any practical sense: there is no current reason to give this drug for PSC. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — a single trial (THIN), stopped for futility, so the null carries the wider uncertainty of an incomplete trial.

title: Switching suppressed patients to dolutegravir plus boosted darunavir (DUALIS)
question: In virologically suppressed adults on two NRTIs plus boosted darunavir, can the NRTI backbone be dropped — switching to dolutegravir + boosted darunavir — without losing suppression at 48 weeks?
balance: Yes for suppression, at a small tolerability cost — on one open-label trial. DUALIS randomised 263 virologically suppressed adults already taking two NRTIs plus boosted darunavir to switch to dolutegravir + boosted darunavir or to continue the three-drug regimen. At week 48, HIV RNA was below 50 copies/mL in 86.3% of switchers versus 87.9% of continuers (difference −1.6%, 95.48% CI −9.9 to +6.7), meeting the prespecified −10% noninferiority margin, and no treatment-emergent resistance developed in either arm. The trade-off: discontinuations for adverse events were 4.6% (6 patients) on the two-drug regimen versus 0.8% (1 patient) on the three-drug regimen. The interval's lower bound sits close to the margin, the trial is open-label, and everyone entered already suppressed on a darunavir-based regimen — a selected, adherent population. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — a single trial (THIN) on a virologic surrogate endpoint, adequate to support the switch in similar patients but not stronger.

title: Long-acting cabotegravir–rilpivirine every 8 weeks versus every 4 weeks (ATLAS-2M)
question: In suppressed adults on long-acting cabotegravir + rilpivirine maintenance, is dosing every 8 weeks as effective as every 4 weeks?
balance: A large, definitive noninferiority trial: every-8-week injections hold suppression as well as every-4-week injections. ATLAS-2M randomised 1,045 suppressed adults on long-acting cabotegravir + rilpivirine to continue every 4 weeks or stretch to every 8 weeks. At week 48, HIV-1 RNA ≥50 copies/mL — the nonresponse endpoint — occurred in 2% on 8-weekly versus 1% on 4-weekly dosing (adjusted difference 0.8 percentage points, 95% CI −0.6 to 2.2), comfortably inside the 4% noninferiority margin. Confirmed virological failure was uncommon in both arms but numerically higher with the longer interval (8 patients, 2%, vs 2, under 1%) — the one number to keep in view, because failures on long-acting therapy can select resistance to two drug classes at once. Adverse events other than injection-site reactions were reported by 81% of participants, with no treatment-related deaths. PROPOSED LIKELY — one large trial that settles the interval question for patients already stable on this regimen. Distinct from Shelf #723, which cards the original monthly-versus-oral question (ATLAS/FLAIR).

title: Lenacapavir for multidrug-resistant HIV-1 (CAPELLA)
question: In people with multidrug-resistant HIV-1 and few remaining options, does adding the capsid inhibitor lenacapavir to an optimised background regimen suppress the virus?
balance: For patients with almost no options left, lenacapavir plainly does something: in CAPELLA's randomised lead-in, 88% of patients given oral lenacapavir on top of their failing regimen achieved at least a 0.5 log₁₀ viral-load drop by day 15, versus 17% on placebo — proof the drug itself is active, not just the optimised background built around it. By week 26, with subcutaneous lenacapavir every 6 months plus that optimised background, 81–83% had viral loads below 50 copies/mL, with mean CD4 gains of 75–104 cells/mm³. The cautions are structural: only 72 patients, one cohort randomised only for the 14-day lead-in, no long-term comparator, and capsid resistance substitutions emerged in 8 patients (6 with M66I) — the drug's Achilles heel when the background regimen is weak. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — a single small trial (THIN) in a population with no alternatives; the randomised lead-in makes the activity claim solid, the durability claim less so. Distinct from Shelf #317, which covers lenacapavir as pre-exposure prophylaxis.

title: Dolutegravir-based therapy in children and adolescents (ODYSSEY)
question: In children and adolescents (≥14 kg) starting first- or second-line ART, is dolutegravir-based therapy better than standard non-dolutegravir care?
balance: The trial that settled paediatric first- and second-line policy, and it did more than show noninferiority — it showed superiority. ODYSSEY randomised 707 children and adolescents weighing at least 14 kg (median age 12.2 years; 44% starting first-line, 56% second-line) to dolutegravir-based therapy or standard care (mostly efavirenz-based first-line, protease-inhibitor-based second-line). By 96 weeks, treatment failure — a composite of virologic and clinical failure — had occurred in 47 children on dolutegravir versus 75 on standard care (estimated probabilities 0.14 vs 0.22; difference −0.08, 95% CI −0.14 to −0.03; P=0.004). Safety was at least as good: fewer children on dolutegravir had adverse events that forced a change of therapy (5 vs 17; P=0.01), with similar serious adverse event counts (35 vs 40). Open-label design and a composite endpoint keep this at LIKELY rather than beyond, but the effect is consistent across first- and second-line strata. PROPOSED LIKELY — one large randomised trial with a superiority result on a clinically meaningful composite.

title: Dolutegravir when ART starts in late pregnancy (DolPHIN-2)
question: In women who start ART in the third trimester (≥28 weeks), does dolutegravir suppress viral load by delivery more reliably than efavirenz?
balance: When treatment starts at 28 weeks or later, speed is the whole question — every unsuppressed week is transmission risk — and dolutegravir is much faster. DolPHIN-2 randomised 268 women in South Africa and Uganda starting ART in the third trimester (median time on therapy before birth: 55 days) to dolutegravir- or efavirenz-based regimens. By the post-partum visit, viral load was below 50 copies/mL in 74% on dolutegravir versus 43% on efavirenz (risk ratio 1.64, 95% CI 1.31 to 2.06 — a relative effect; the absolute gap is 31 percentage points). The safety ledger needs stating plainly: more maternal serious adverse events were reported on dolutegravir (30 vs 14 reports; P=0.013), though these clustered around pregnancy and the puerperium and were not judged drug-caused; stillbirths were 3 versus 1, judged unrelated; and all 3 infant HIV infections occurred in the dolutegravir group but were judged likely acquired in utero before suppression could be achieved — a marker of how late these women presented, not of drug failure. PROPOSED LIKELY — a single randomised trial with a large effect on the outcome that drives transmission risk, with the adverse-event imbalance disclosed on the face of the shelf.

title: Dolutegravir with rifampicin-based tuberculosis therapy (INSPIRING)
question: In ART-naive adults being treated for drug-susceptible tuberculosis with rifampicin, can dolutegravir (dose-doubled during TB therapy) hold HIV suppression as well as efavirenz?
balance: Encouraging, but the study was not built to prove the comparison its question implies. INSPIRING randomised 113 ART-naive adults on rifampicin-based TB therapy to dolutegravir 50 mg twice daily (the dose doubled to offset rifampicin's enzyme induction) or efavirenz. At week 48, HIV RNA was below 50 copies/mL in 75% (52/69) on dolutegravir versus 82% (36/44) on efavirenz — numerically lower on dolutegravir, with wide, overlapping intervals. The dolutegravir shortfall was driven by non-treatment-related discontinuations (10 patients lost to follow-up), not by virologic failure or resistance, and TB-associated immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome occurred in 4 patients per arm with no IRIS discontinuations. In other words: no signal that dose-doubled dolutegravir fails during rifampicin therapy, and a clean interaction story — but a small, open-label study whose primary endpoint was noncomparative cannot establish 'as good as efavirenz'. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — single study (THIN), underpowered for the comparison, reassuring on feasibility and safety.

title: Enhanced antimicrobial prophylaxis when starting ART in advanced HIV (REALITY) ⭐ OUTSTANDING-SINGLE
question: In adults and children (CD4 <100) starting ART in Africa, does an enhanced prophylaxis package (co-trimoxazole + isoniazid, 12 weeks fluconazole, 5 days azithromycin, single-dose albendazole) reduce early death versus standard prophylaxis?
balance: OUTSTANDING-SINGLE — flagged under the Nov 8, 2026 rule: one randomised trial, a hard mortality endpoint, a decisive result; the developer's personal verdict is required and Tier C applies (death is the primary endpoint). REALITY randomised 1,805 patients with CD4 counts under 100 starting ART in Uganda, Zimbabwe, Malawi, and Kenya to an enhanced prophylaxis package — the REALITY package: continuous trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole plus at least 12 weeks of isoniazid–pyridoxine, 12 weeks of fluconazole, 5 days of azithromycin, and a single dose of albendazole — versus standard prophylaxis (trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole alone). Death at 24 weeks was 8.9% with enhanced prophylaxis versus 12.2% with standard care (HR 0.73, 95% CI 0.55 to 0.98; P=0.03 — a relative effect; absolute difference 3.3 percentage points), and the benefit persisted at 48 weeks (11.0% vs 14.4%; HR 0.76; P=0.04). Rates of tuberculosis, cryptococcal infection, oral or oesophageal candidiasis, death of unknown cause, and new hospitalisation were all significantly lower, without compromised viral suppression. One trial is one trial — but 1,805 patients, a mortality endpoint, and concordant cause-specific effects are as strong as single-trial evidence gets. PROPOSED LIKELY, held at that level — not higher — precisely because it stands alone.

title: Cryptococcal-antigen screening plus community adherence support when starting ART (REMSTART) ⭐ OUTSTANDING-SINGLE
question: In adults with advanced HIV (CD4 <200) starting ART, does serum cryptococcal-antigen screening with pre-emptive antifungal treatment, plus four weeks of lay-worker home adherence visits, reduce mortality versus standard clinic care?
balance: OUTSTANDING-SINGLE — flagged under the Nov 8, 2026 rule: one randomised trial, a mortality endpoint, a decisive result; the developer's personal verdict is required and Tier C applies. REMSTART randomised 1,999 adults with CD4 counts under 200 starting ART in Tanzania and Zambia to standard clinic care or the REMSTART programme: serum cryptococcal-antigen screening with pre-emptive antifungal therapy for those testing positive, plus weekly home visits by lay workers for the first 4 weeks of treatment (with TB re-screening at 6–8 weeks in Tanzania only). Mortality at 12 months was 13% (134/1,001) with the programme versus 18% (180/998) with standard care — a 28% relative reduction (95% CI 10 to 43; P=0.004) and a 5-percentage-point absolute difference. The bundle design is the honest caveat: screening and home visits were delivered together, so the trial cannot apportion credit between finding cryptococcus early and keeping people in care. It is also a service-delivery intervention, whose effect depends on the clinics and lay-worker systems delivering it. PROPOSED LIKELY, held there because a single trial of a programme — however large — is still a single trial.

title: Same-day ART initiation at the first clinic visit (RapIT)
question: In newly diagnosed, treatment-eligible adults, does offering ART dispensing at the very first clinic visit improve uptake and viral suppression versus the standard multi-visit initiation process?
balance: One unblinded trial of a process, and the process won on its combined endpoint. RapIT randomised 377 newly diagnosed, treatment-eligible adults at two South African clinics (median CD4 210) to the RapIT rapid-initiation algorithm — point-of-care testing and ART dispensed at the first visit — or the standard multi-visit pathway. At 10 months, 64% of the rapid group had both started ART and achieved viral suppression, versus 51% of the standard group (relative risk 1.26, 95% CI 1.05 to 1.50 — a relative effect; absolute rates 64% vs 51%). Initiation itself within 90 days was near-universal with rapid initiation (97% vs 72%; RR 1.36). The reassuring harm check: among patients who did start, attrition was no worse (HR 1.06, 0.61 to 1.84) — rushing the start did not obviously push people out of care. The limits are those of any workflow trial: two clinics, one country's staffing and testing platforms, an unblinded design, and an endpoint that mixes starting with suppressing. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — a single trial (THIN) of a site-specific care pathway, with a clinically meaningful combined outcome.

title: Bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide as initial HIV therapy (studies 1489 and 1490)
question: In treatment-naive adults, is the single-tablet bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide regimen non-inferior to dolutegravir-based initial therapy?
balance: Two independent double-blind phase 3 trials (DOUBLE-A) against two different dolutegravir-based comparators, same answer. In study 1489, bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide (B/F/TAF) was noninferior to dolutegravir/abacavir/lamivudine: week-48 suppression 92.4% versus 93.0% (difference −0.6%, 95.002% CI −4.8 to 3.6). In study 1490, B/F/TAF was noninferior to dolutegravir plus emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide: 89% versus 93% (difference −3.5%, 95.002% CI −7.9 to 1.0) — met its margin, though the point estimate and interval lean slightly toward the dolutegravir arm. No treatment-emergent resistance emerged in either trial. Tolerability favoured B/F/TAF: drug-related adverse events 26% versus 40% in 1489 (nausea 10% vs 23%) and 18% versus 26% in 1490, though adverse-event discontinuations in 1490 were 5 versus 1 the other way. Noninferiority on a virologic endpoint in two blinded trials is the strongest evidence class this library asks for on a regimen question. PROPOSED LIKELY — DOUBLE-A, both double-blind, no resistance signal; superiority over dolutegravir is not claimed by either trial.

title: Dapivirine vaginal ring (ASPIRE + Ring Study): about a 27–31% relative reduction in HIV acquisition across two phase 3 trials
question: In women at risk in sub-Saharan Africa, does a monthly vaginal ring releasing dapivirine reduce HIV-1 acquisition versus a placebo ring?
balance: Two independent phase 3 placebo-controlled trials point the same way, with a modest effect that depends on the ring actually being worn. In ASPIRE (2,629 women in Malawi, South Africa, Uganda and Zimbabwe), HIV incidence was 3.3 versus 4.5 per 100 person-years — 27% relatively lower on the dapivirine ring (95% CI 1 to 46; P=0.046), rising to 56% relative protection in women over 21 and disappearing in younger women, tracking measured adherence. In the Ring Study (1,959 women in South Africa and Uganda), incidence was 4.1 versus 6.1 per 100 person-years — 31% relatively lower (hazard ratio 0.69; 95% CI 0.49 to 0.99; P=0.04). Neither trial found a safety signal of concern. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — two concordant randomised trials, but the protection is partial, borderline in precision, and adherence-dependent. Note: the topic draft cited the Ring Study as PMID 26900911; that number resolves to an unrelated pre-eclampsia review. The Ring Study was gate-verified and is carded under its correct PubMed record, PMID 27959766.

title: On-demand (2-1-1) PrEP in MSM (IPERGAY): 86% relative reduction in HIV acquisition in one double-blind trial
question: In men who have sex with men at high risk, does pericoital ("2-1-1") tenofovir/emtricitabine taken around sex prevent HIV acquisition versus placebo?
balance: One double-blind trial, stopped early because the answer was already clear: in 400 high-risk men who have sex with men in France and Canada, taking tenofovir/emtricitabine only around sex (two tablets 2–24 hours before, one at 24 hours, one at 48 hours) cut HIV acquisition from 6.60 to 0.91 infections per 100 person-years — an 86% relative reduction (95% CI 40 to 98) on absolute rates of 14 infections in the placebo group versus 2 on treatment. Gastrointestinal adverse events (14% vs 5%) and renal adverse events (18% vs 10%) were more common on treatment. OUTSTANDING-SINGLE: this shelf rests on a single double-blind randomised trial, but the effect is large, the endpoint is HIV acquisition itself, and the regimen it created is now guideline-endorsed — so it is carded on that one trial and flagged here. PROPOSED LIKELY — a single trial, but a double-blind one with an outstanding hard-endpoint result.

title: VRC01 antibody prevention (AMP trials): no overall protection in two randomised trials — proof of concept against sensitive viruses only
question: In at-risk adults, do 8-weekly infusions of the broadly neutralising antibody VRC01 prevent HIV-1 acquisition versus placebo?
balance: Two large randomised trials, one clear overall answer and one important proof of concept. Across ~4,600 at-risk adults, 8-weekly infusions of the broadly neutralising antibody VRC01 (10 or 30 mg/kg) did NOT prevent HIV-1 acquisition overall: prevention efficacy was 26.6% (95% CI −11.7 to 51.8; P=0.15) in the Americas/Europe trial and 8.8% (−45.1 to 42.6; P=0.70) in the African women's trial, on absolute incidences of 2.35 vs 2.98 and 2.49 vs 3.10 per 100 person-years. But against viruses highly sensitive to VRC01, efficacy was 75.4% (45.5 to 88.9) — the antibody worked exactly where the virus let it, which is the proof of concept for antibody prevention, not a usable prevention method in itself. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — two independent randomised trials agree on the overall null; the sensitive-virus finding is a subgroup mechanism result, not overall protection.

title: Daily tenofovir PrEP in people who inject drugs (Bangkok Tenofovir Study): HIV incidence roughly halved
question: In people who inject drugs, does daily oral tenofovir reduce HIV acquisition versus placebo?
balance: One large double-blind trial in the population where sexual-transmission PrEP data do not reach: among 2,413 HIV-negative people who injected drugs, attending Bangkok drug-treatment clinics, daily oral tenofovir cut HIV incidence from 0.68 to 0.35 per 100 person-years — 17 infections versus 33 — a 48.9% relative reduction (95% CI 9.6 to 72.2; P=0.01). The confidence interval is wide, the absolute incidence was low, and nausea was more common on tenofovir, but serious adverse events were similar. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — a single large, clean, placebo-controlled trial with a significant hard endpoint, held at POSSIBLE because it stands alone in this population and the effect estimate is imprecise.

title: Tenofovir vaginal gel (CAPRISA 004): 39% relative reduction in one trial — not replicated (THIN)
question: In women at risk, does pericoital 1% tenofovir vaginal gel reduce HIV acquisition versus placebo gel?
balance: One positive trial that the field could not repeat. In CAPRISA 004, 889 women in KwaZulu-Natal using 1% tenofovir gel before and after sex had an HIV incidence of 5.6 per 100 women-years versus 9.1 on placebo gel — incidence rate ratio 0.61, a 39% relative reduction (P=0.017), and 54% relatively lower in high adherers. But this is a single trial, and the later FACTS 001 trial of the same strategy did not replicate the result — which is why this shelf is flagged THIN. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — a real randomised signal that failed confirmation; it should not be quoted as established protection.

title: RV144 prime-boost HIV vaccine (Thai trial): 31.2% efficacy in one of three analyses — a borderline, unreproduced signal (THIN)
question: In a general-population cohort at heterosexual risk, does the ALVAC prime / AIDSVAX gp120 boost regimen prevent HIV-1 infection versus placebo?
balance: The only HIV vaccine regimen ever to show any efficacy signal — and the signal is fragile. In RV144, 16,402 Thai adults received four ALVAC-HIV primes plus two AIDSVAX B/E gp120 boosts or placebo. Vaccine efficacy was 31.2% in the modified intention-to-treat analysis (95% CI 1.1 to 52.1; P=0.04) but only 26.4% and not significant in the full intention-to-treat analysis (95% CI −4.0 to 47.9; P=0.08) and 26.2% per-protocol (P=0.16); vaccination did not affect viral load or CD4 counts in those infected. The regimen was never reproduced at scale, and its clade-C rebuild failed in HVTN 702 (Shelf #2149). THIN. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — historically important, evidentially borderline: one of three prespecified analyses crossed significance, by a hair.

title: Male circumcision to prevent HIV acquisition: three randomised trials agree — risk roughly halved
question: In uncircumcised men in high-incidence settings, does medical male circumcision reduce HIV acquisition versus deferred circumcision?
balance: As settled as prevention evidence gets: three independent randomised trials in South Africa, Kenya and Uganda, all stopped early for efficacy, all finding roughly the same protection. HIV incidence was 0.85 versus 2.1 per 100 person-years in South Africa (60% relative protection, 95% CI 32 to 76), 2-year incidence 2.1% versus 4.2% in Kenya (53% relative reduction, 95% CI 22 to 72), and 0.66 versus 1.33 per 100 person-years in Uganda (51% efficacy, 95% CI 16 to 72). No trial found behavioural risk compensation of consequence; surgical adverse events were uncommon and resolved. PROPOSED LIKELY — three concordant randomised trials with a hard endpoint; the stamp stops short of the top grade only because all three trials were open (circumcision cannot be blinded) and stopped early, which can inflate estimates.

title: Daily oral PrEP in heterosexual adults in Botswana (TDF2): 62.2% relative efficacy in one early-closed trial
question: In HIV-negative heterosexual men and women, does daily tenofovir/emtricitabine prevent acquisition versus placebo?
balance: One double-blind trial in a general heterosexual population — the population Shelf #317's serodiscordant-couples trial does not cover. In TDF2, 1,219 HIV-negative men and women in Botswana (45.7% women) took daily tenofovir/emtricitabine or placebo: 9 infections on treatment versus 24 on placebo, at 1.2 versus 3.1 per 100 person-years — efficacy 62.2% relative (95% CI 21.5 to 83.4; P=0.03). The trial closed early because of low retention and logistics, only 33 infections drive the estimate, and treatment caused significantly more nausea, vomiting and dizziness plus a significant decline in bone mineral density, whose long-term meaning the authors state is unknown. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — a single, significant, double-blind trial, held at POSSIBLE by its early closure, wide interval, and the open bone-safety question.

title: Oral and vaginal PrEP in African women (VOICE): none of three strategies worked — adherence too low to deliver protection
question: In reproductive-age African women, do daily oral tenofovir, daily oral tenofovir/emtricitabine, or daily tenofovir vaginal gel prevent HIV acquisition versus placebo?
balance: A large, definitive null — with the reason measured, not guessed. In VOICE, 5,029 women in South Africa, Uganda and Zimbabwe were randomised to daily oral tenofovir, daily oral tenofovir/emtricitabine, daily 1% tenofovir vaginal gel, or matching placebos. None reduced HIV acquisition: hazard ratios were 1.49 (95% CI 0.97 to 2.29) for tenofovir, 1.04 (0.73 to 1.49) for tenofovir/emtricitabine, and 0.85 (0.61 to 1.21) for the gel, against an overall incidence of 5.7 per 100 person-years. Blood testing showed why: tenofovir was detected in only 30%, 29% and 25% of samples in the three active groups — the products were largely not being used, so the trial tested a delivery strategy, and the strategy failed. Serum creatinine elevations were more frequent on oral tenofovir/emtricitabine (1.3% vs 0.2%, P=0.004). PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — as randomised and as actually delivered, in 5,029 women; the null is about use, not proof the drug cannot work when taken (see Shelves #2140, #2147).

title: Subtype-C ALVAC/gp120 vaccine in South Africa (HVTN 702): stopped for non-efficacy — the RV144 signal did not transfer
question: In South African adults, does the subtype-C-adapted ALVAC-HIV plus bivalent gp120/MF59 regimen prevent HIV-1 acquisition versus placebo?
balance: A clean, large, definitive negative. HVTN 702 rebuilt the RV144 concept for subtype C — ALVAC-HIV primes plus bivalent subtype C gp120 in MF59 (the specific tested programme) — and randomised 5,404 South African adults. Vaccinations were halted when prespecified non-efficacy criteria were met: over 24 months, HIV-1 infection was diagnosed in 138 vaccine recipients and 133 placebo recipients (hazard ratio 1.02; 95% CI 0.81 to 1.30; P=0.84), with similar adverse-event incidence. The RV144 signal did not transfer. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — one large trial, stopped by its own futility rule, with an estimate centred on zero.

title: Four-month treatment for nonsevere childhood TB (SHINE): non-inferior to 6 months [Tier C]
question: In children with nonsevere, smear-negative, drug-susceptible tuberculosis, is 4 months of first-line therapy non-inferior to the standard 6 months?
balance: Tier C shelf (the primary composite includes death; presented for the developer's personal verdict). In SHINE, 1,204 children under 16 with nonsevere, smear-negative, presumably drug-susceptible tuberculosis in Uganda, Zambia, South Africa and India were randomised to 4 or 6 months of standard first-line treatment. Unfavourable status by 72 weeks occurred in 16 children (3%) on 4 months versus 18 (3%) on 6 months — adjusted difference −0.4 percentage points (95% CI −2.2 to 1.5), comfortably inside the 6-point non-inferiority margin and consistent across intention-to-treat, per-protocol and adjudicated-TB analyses. Grade 3-or-higher adverse events occurred in 8% overall, with 15 adverse drug reactions, mostly hepatic and mostly in the first 8 weeks when both groups received identical treatment. PROPOSED LIKELY — 4 months is non-inferior for this defined nonsevere population; the claim is about duration, not about a new drug.

title: Bedaquiline-containing short regimens for rifampicin-resistant TB (STREAM stage 2): superior to the injectable control, with less hearing loss [Tier C]
question: In rifampicin-resistant TB without fluoroquinolone or injectable resistance, do a 9-month all-oral bedaquiline regimen or a 6-month bedaquiline-plus-injectable regimen beat the 9-month injectable-containing STREAM control?
balance: Tier C shelf (the favourable-status outcome embeds death; mortality figures are printed on the card; presented for the developer's personal verdict). In STREAM stage 2, 588 people aged 15 or older with rifampicin-resistant tuberculosis (without fluoroquinolone or aminoglycoside resistance) in seven countries were randomised to bedaquiline-containing regimens or the 9-month injectable-containing control. The 9-month all-oral bedaquiline regimen gave favourable outcomes in 83% versus 71% on control (adjusted difference 11.0 percentage points; 95% CI 2.9 to 19.0), and the 6-month bedaquiline-plus-8-weeks-injectable regimen in 91% versus 69% of concurrently randomised controls (difference 22.2 points; 95% CI 13.1 to 31.2) — both superior, not merely non-inferior. Grade 3–4 hearing loss was far less frequent without the prolonged injectable (2% oral vs 9% control; 4% on the 6-month regimen). Deaths by 76 weeks were 3% on the oral regimen and 2% on control. PROPOSED LIKELY — a phase 3 randomised trial showing superiority of the bedaquiline regimens on the composite, with a clear toxicity dividend.

title: Optimising linezolid dose and duration in BPaL (ZeNix): 600 mg for 26 weeks kept efficacy with much less toxicity [Tier C]
question: In XDR, pre-XDR, or treatment-intolerant rifampicin-resistant TB, which linezolid dose/duration within bedaquiline–pretomanid–linezolid preserves efficacy with least toxicity?
balance: Tier C shelf (the favourable-outcome composite includes death; presented for the developer's personal verdict). ZeNix randomised 181 people with XDR, pre-XDR, or treatment-intolerant rifampicin-resistant tuberculosis to bedaquiline–pretomanid with linezolid at 1200 mg for 26 or 9 weeks, or 600 mg for 26 or 9 weeks. Favourable outcomes were 93%, 89%, 91% and 84% respectively — efficacy held up at 600 mg — while toxicity fell steeply with dose: peripheral neuropathy in 38% (1200 mg/26 weeks) versus 24% (600 mg/26 weeks) and 13% (600 mg/9 weeks); myelosuppression in 22% versus 2% at 600 mg/26 weeks; linezolid dose modifications in 51% versus 13%. Optic neuropathy occurred in 4 participants (9%), all on 1200 mg for 26 weeks, and resolved. Six of the seven unfavourable microbiologic outcomes occurred in the 9-week linezolid groups, which is why the authors favoured 600 mg for the full 26 weeks. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — one modest-sized randomised dose-finding trial (about 45 participants per arm, no non-BPaL control); the dose ranking is clear, the absolute numbers are small.

title: Nine-month all-oral regimens for rifampin-resistant TB (endTB): three regimens non-inferior to standard therapy [Tier C]
question: In fluoroquinolone-susceptible, rifampin-resistant TB, are experimental 9-month all-oral bedaquiline-based regimens non-inferior to standard longer therapy?
balance: Tier C shelf (the favourable-outcome definition embeds unfavourable outcomes including death; presented for the developer's personal verdict). In endTB, 754 participants with fluoroquinolone-susceptible, rifampin-resistant tuberculosis were randomised (Bayesian response-adaptive) to standard longer therapy or one of five experimental 9-month all-oral bedaquiline-based regimens (the specific tested programmes: BCLLfxZ, BLMZ, BDLLfxZ, DCLLfxZ and DCMZ, built from bedaquiline, delamanid, linezolid, levofloxacin or moxifloxacin, clofazimine and pyrazinamide). Favourable outcome at week 73 occurred in 80.7% on standard therapy in the modified intention-to-treat analysis; four regimens were non-inferior in that population, with risk differences favouring the experimental regimens of 9.8 points (BCLLfxZ; 95% CI 0.9 to 18.7), 8.3 (BLMZ; −0.8 to 17.4), 4.6 (BDLLfxZ; −4.9 to 14.1) and 2.5 (DCMZ; −7.5 to 12.5) against a −12-point margin — but DCMZ was not non-inferior per-protocol, and the authors' conclusion supports three regimens. Grade 3-or-higher adverse events were similar across regimens; grade 3-or-higher hepatotoxicity occurred in 11.7% overall versus 7.1% on standard therapy. PROPOSED LIKELY — a phase 3 multinational trial; non-inferiority of shortened all-oral treatment is consistent across analyses for three regimens.

title: Urine LAM-guided TB treatment in HIV inpatients (STAMP): 8-week mortality 21% vs 25% [Tier C · OUTSTANDING-SINGLE]
question: In hospitalised HIV-positive adults with suspected TB, does adding point-of-care urine lipoarabinomannan testing to routine diagnostics to guide treatment initiation reduce mortality?
balance: Tier C shelf (mortality is the primary endpoint; presented for the developer's personal verdict) and OUTSTANDING-SINGLE: one pragmatic randomised trial with a significant mortality benefit. In STAMP, 2,659 HIV-positive hospital inpatients with suspected tuberculosis in ten African hospitals were randomised to routine diagnostics plus bedside urine lipoarabinomannan testing (the specific tested product: the Alere Determine tuberculosis LAM Ag lateral-flow strip) with nurse recommendations to start treatment on a positive result, versus routine diagnostics alone. Eight-week all-cause mortality was 21% with LAM guidance versus 25% without — an absolute reduction of 4 percentage points (95% CI 1 to 7); adjusted risk ratio 0.83 (0.73 to 0.96; P=0.012), a 17% relative risk reduction, and an adjusted hazard ratio of 0.82 (0.70 to 0.96). No adverse events were associated with LAM testing. PROPOSED LIKELY — a single trial, but a large multicountry pragmatic one whose endpoint is death itself; flagged OUTSTANDING-SINGLE because it stands alone.

title: Empiric TB therapy versus isoniazid in advanced HIV (REMEMBER): no mortality benefit — 5% vs 5% [Tier C]
question: In outpatients with CD4 <50 starting ART in high-burden settings, does empiric four-drug TB treatment reduce early mortality versus isoniazid preventive therapy after TB screening?
balance: Tier C shelf (mortality was the primary endpoint, and the result is null — this shelf must not be read as implying any mortality benefit; presented for the developer's personal verdict). In REMEMBER, 850 outpatients with CD4 counts under 50 cells/μL (median 18) starting antiretroviral therapy at 18 clinics in ten countries — all screened for tuberculosis first, with confirmed or suspected TB excluded — were randomised to empiric four-drug tuberculosis therapy or to isoniazid preventive therapy. At 24 weeks, 22 participants (5%) in each group had died or were of unknown status — absolute risk difference −0.06 percentage points (95% CI −3.05 to 2.94). Grade 3 or 4 signs, symptoms and laboratory abnormalities were similar between groups. The authors' reading: systematic TB screening plus isoniazid preventive therapy is the strategy the data support; blanket empiric treatment adds nothing after screening. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — a multicountry randomised trial with an estimate centred on zero.

title: Adjunctive prednisolone in tuberculous pericarditis (IMPI): primary composite null, less constriction, more HIV-associated cancer [Tier C · SPLIT]
question: In adults with definite or probable tuberculous pericarditis, do adjunctive prednisolone or Mycobacterium indicus pranii immunotherapy reduce death, tamponade, or constriction?
balance: Tier C shelf (death is a headline component of the primary composite; presented for the developer's personal verdict), with a SPLIT verdict because the outcomes genuinely diverge. In IMPI, 1,400 adults with definite or probable tuberculous pericarditis (two-thirds HIV-positive) were randomised in a 2×2 factorial design to prednisolone or placebo for 6 weeks and to Mycobacterium indicus pranii immunotherapy (the specific tested product) or placebo. Neither intervention moved the primary composite of death, tamponade requiring pericardiocentesis, or constrictive pericarditis: 23.8% versus 24.5% for prednisolone (hazard ratio 0.95; 95% CI 0.77 to 1.18; P=0.66) and 25.0% versus 24.3% for immunotherapy (hazard ratio 1.03; 0.82 to 1.29; P=0.81). The split: prednisolone did reduce constrictive pericarditis (4.4% vs 7.8%; hazard ratio 0.56; 0.36 to 0.87; P=0.009) and hospitalisation (20.7% vs 25.2%; hazard ratio 0.79; P=0.04) — but both prednisolone and immunotherapy were associated with significantly more cancer, mainly HIV-associated (1.8% vs 0.6%, hazard ratio 3.27; and 1.8% vs 0.5%, hazard ratio 3.69). PROPOSED SPLIT — LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for the primary composite for both interventions; prednisolone carries a real secondary benefit on constriction and a real harm signal on cancer, so no single stamp is honest.

title: Point-of-care Xpert MTB/RIF in primary care (TB-NEAT): faster, more accurate decisions — no reduction in TB morbidity [THIN · SPLIT]
question: In adults with suspected TB at primary-care clinics, does nurse-performed point-of-care Xpert MTB/RIF improve same-day treatment decisions and TB-related morbidity versus sputum smear microscopy?
balance: A SPLIT result, and the split is the lesson. In this pragmatic randomised trial (TB-NEAT), 1,502 adults with suspected tuberculosis at five primary-care facilities in South Africa, Zimbabwe, Zambia and Tanzania were assigned to nurse-performed point-of-care Xpert MTB/RIF (the specific tested product) or sputum smear microscopy. The test itself performed: sensitivity 83% versus 50% for microscopy at similar specificity (95% vs 96%), and accuracy matched laboratory-based Xpert. Decisions sped up: same-day diagnosis in 24% versus 13% and same-day treatment initiation in 23% versus 15%, and fewer culture-positive patients never started treatment (8% vs 15% untreated). But the primary outcome did not move: tuberculosis-related morbidity (TBscore and Karnofsky score) in treated culture-positive patients was identical at 2 and 6 months — partly, the authors note, because smear-negative patients in the microscopy arm were widely treated empirically anyway. THIN: a single pragmatic trial with a morbidity-score endpoint. PROPOSED SPLIT — POSSIBLE for faster, more accurate same-day decisions; (the treatment made no difference) for patient morbidity as measured.

title: Digital adherence technologies for TB in China: no effect on unfavourable outcomes in a 24-cluster trial (THIN)
question: In patients with drug-sensitive pulmonary TB, does a medication-monitor package (daily reminders, monthly provider adherence review, differentiated care for poor adherence) improve treatment outcomes versus standard care?
balance: One large cluster-randomised trial in one health system, with a clear null on outcomes and a candid explanation. Across 24 counties/districts in four Chinese prefectures, 2,686 patients with drug-sensitive pulmonary tuberculosis were in clusters assigned to a medication-monitor package (the specific tested programme: a monitor giving daily dosing reminders, monthly provider review of adherence data, and differentiated care for poor adherence) or to routine care with silent-mode monitors. By 18 months, the composite unfavourable outcome (death, loss to follow-up, treatment failure, switch to multidrug-resistant treatment, or recurrence) occurred in 16% of each group — adjusted risk ratio 1.01 (95% CI 0.73 to 1.40). Loss to follow-up made up 62% of events. The authors' own diagnosis: identifying non-adherence at monthly reviews failed to change patient management. THIN: a single cluster trial in a single system, and the interval still allows meaningful benefit or harm. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — no effect was shown, but one trial in one system cannot close the question for better-implemented versions.

title: Four-drug fixed-dose combinations versus separate drugs (Study C): non-inferiority met in 2 of 3 analyses — not fully demonstrated
question: In adults with newly diagnosed smear-positive pulmonary TB, is the 4-drug fixed-dose combination non-inferior to the same drugs given separately during the intensive phase?
balance: The honest answer is 'almost, and the shortfall is in the analysis rules, not in a visible efficacy gap'. In Study C, 1,585 adults with newly diagnosed smear-positive pulmonary tuberculosis at 11 sites in Africa, Asia and Latin America received rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol as a 4-drug fixed-dose combination or as separate drugs during the 8-week intensive phase. Favourable outcome at 18 months was 93.9% versus 94.6% per-protocol (risk difference −0.7 percentage points; 90% CI −3.0 to 1.5) — inside the 4% non-inferiority margin — but the strictest modified intention-to-treat model (every treatment change counted unfavourable) gave −1.5 points (90% CI −4.7 to 1.8), crossing the margin, so prespecified non-inferiority was met in only 2 of 3 analyses. A post hoc model gave −1.2 points (−3.9 to 1.5). Adverse events related to trial drugs were similarly distributed. The authors still preferred fixed-dose combinations for their administration advantages. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — outcomes are clinically near-identical, but the trial did not demonstrate full non-inferiority by its own strict definition, and every point estimate leaned slightly toward separate drugs.

title: Xalnesiran with or without an immunomodulator in chronic hepatitis B (Piranga): HBsAg loss in a minority, most often with peginterferon added
question: In nucleos(t)ide-suppressed chronic hepatitis B, does the siRNA xalnesiran — alone, with the TLR7 agonist ruzotolimod, or with pegylated interferon — produce HBsAg loss after treatment ends?
balance: Early, promising, and small. In the phase 2 Piranga platform trial, 159 people with chronic hepatitis B who were virologically suppressed on a nucleos(t)ide analogue received 48 weeks of xalnesiran alone or with an immunomodulator. HBsAg loss 24 weeks after treatment ended occurred only in xalnesiran arms: 7% on xalnesiran 100 mg, 3% on 200 mg, 12% with the TLR7 agonist ruzotolimod added, 23% with pegylated interferon alfa-2a added, and 0% on nucleos(t)ide analogue alone. Every case of HBsAg loss was in a participant whose screening HBsAg was below 1000 IU/mL, and grade 3 or 4 adverse events were common — 50% in the peginterferon arm, mostly raised alanine aminotransferase. The arms held about 30 people each, the trial was open-label with no formal between-group comparison, and HBsAg loss is a surrogate for functional cure rather than a clinical outcome. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — a real off-treatment HBsAg-loss signal from one small phase 2 platform trial, strongest when peginterferon is added, in a selected low-HBsAg population.

title: REEF-1: JNJ-3989 siRNA moved 16–19% to stopping criteria; adding bersacapavir made it worse, not better
question: In chronic hepatitis B, does the siRNA JNJ-3989 (ARO-HBV) — with or without the capsid assembly modulator bersacapavir (JNJ-6379) — get patients to nucleos(t)ide-stopping criteria on a nucleos(t)ide backbone?
balance: The components pull in opposite directions, so this stamp is split. REEF-1 randomised 470 patients with chronic hepatitis B across 108 sites in 19 countries, all on nucleos(t)ide analogues (NA), to NA plus placebo (control, n=45), bersacapavir (JNJ-6379) dual therapy (n=48), JNJ-3989 (ARO-HBV) dual therapy at 40 mg (n=93), 100 mg (n=93), or 200 mg (n=96), or triple therapy with bersacapavir plus JNJ-3989 100 mg (n=95). The siRNA alone worked dose-dependently: the primary end point — meeting NA-stopping criteria at week 48 — was reached by 19% (18 of 94) at 200 mg and 16% (15 of 92) at 100 mg versus 2% (1 of 45) on control, with mean HBsAg declines of 2.6 and 2.1 log10 IU/mL at end of treatment, and 3 patients achieved HBsAg seroclearance 24 weeks after end of treatment. The capsid inhibitor subtracted value: bersacapavir dual therapy met stopping criteria in 0% of patients, and the triple combination (9%, 8 of 94; HBsAg decline 1.8 log) did worse than the matched siRNA-alone arm. Serious adverse events occurred in 10 of 470 patients (2%), with no deaths. PROPOSED SPLIT: POSSIBLE — the JNJ-3989 siRNA component moves patients toward finite therapy; the bersacapavir component contributed nothing and diluted the combination. Read as one stamp it would mislead in both directions.

title: REEF-2: siRNA plus capsid modulator with NUC cessation in suppressed chronic hepatitis B — no functional cure in anyone
question: In NUC-suppressed, HBeAg-negative chronic hepatitis B, can 48 weeks of JNJ-3989 + bersacapavir + NUC lead to off-treatment functional cure after stopping all therapy?
balance: A cleanly negative answer on the question that matters. In REEF-2, 130 nucleos(t)ide analogue (NA)-suppressed, HBeAg-negative patients received 48 weeks of the siRNA JNJ-73763989 plus the capsid assembly modulator bersacapavir plus NA, or placebos plus NA, then stopped all treatment and were followed for 48 weeks. On treatment, HBsAg fell by a mean of 1.89 log10 IU/mL in the active arm versus 0.06 with control — but at follow-up week 24, no patient in either arm had achieved the primary end point of off-treatment HBsAg seroclearance (functional cure), and none had by week 48 either. The combination did soften what happened after stopping — fewer and less severe HBV DNA rises and alanine aminotransferase flares, and more patients kept HBV DNA suppressed off treatment — but softening relapse is not cure. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the stamp grades the functional-cure claim, which a well-run double-blind phase 2b trial tested directly and found in zero patients; the secondary off-treatment signals are noted, not upgraded.

title: GS-4774 therapeutic vaccine in suppressed chronic hepatitis B: well tolerated, no HBsAg decline at any dose
question: In virally suppressed chronic hepatitis B, does the yeast-based T-cell vaccine GS-4774 lower HBsAg versus continuing oral antivirals alone?
balance: A well-tolerated vaccine that did not move its target. In this randomised phase 2 trial, 178 patients with chronic hepatitis B, no cirrhosis, and at least a year of viral suppression on an oral antiviral were assigned to continue the antiviral alone or to add GS-4774 — a heat-inactivated, yeast-based T-cell vaccine — at 2, 10, or 40 yeast units every 4 weeks until week 20. There were no significant differences between groups in mean HBsAg decline at week 24 or week 48, and no patient in any group lost serum HBsAg. The only favourable crumbs were five cases of HBeAg loss among GS-4774 recipients versus none on control, and three patients on the highest dose with HBsAg declines of at least 0.5 log10 IU/mL — far too few to grade as benefit. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — a direct, adequately sized phase 2 test of the vaccine's stated purpose, negative at every dose.

title: Selgantolimod (TLR8 agonist) in suppressed chronic hepatitis B: primary end point met by one patient of 48
question: In virally suppressed chronic hepatitis B, does weekly oral selgantolimod (GS-9688) produce clinically meaningful HBsAg declines versus placebo?
balance: Immune activation, yes; meaningful antigen decline, barely. In this randomised, placebo-controlled phase 2 trial, 48 virally suppressed patients with chronic hepatitis B (24 HBeAg-positive, 24 HBeAg-negative) received weekly oral selgantolimod 3 mg or 1.5 mg, or placebo, for 24 weeks while continuing oral antivirals. The primary end point — an HBsAg decline of at least 1 log10 IU/mL by week 24 — was reached by exactly one participant. Against placebo (n=9), only selgantolimod-treated patients (n=39) had HBsAg declines greater than 0.1 log10 IU/mL (18% at week 24, 26% at week 48), HBsAg loss (5%, 2 of 39 through week 48), or HBeAg loss (16%, 3 of 19) — real pharmacology at a scale far below clinical usefulness, in a trial too small to weigh two HBsAg losses. Nausea (46%) and vomiting (23%) were common. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — a phase 2 signal of serologic movement in a handful of patients, with the pre-specified primary end point met by one person.

title: BRII-179 therapeutic vaccine after siRNA HBsAg lowering: immune responses restored on paper, HBsAg not cleared
question: In chronic hepatitis B, does lowering HBsAg with the siRNA elebsiran (BRII-835) restore HBV-specific immunity, and does adding the therapeutic vaccine BRII-179 (± interferon) amplify it?
balance: An immunology study with an immunology answer — and no clinical one. In this phase 2a study, 90 participants with chronic hepatitis B received nine 4-weekly doses of the siRNA elebsiran (BRII-835), alone (n=10) or with the virus-like-particle therapeutic vaccine BRII-179, co-administered with interferon alfa (n=39) or without it (n=41), and were analysed over 72 weeks. Lowering HBsAg with the siRNA alone produced minimal recovery of HBV-specific immunity; adding BRII-179 changed the immune picture — anti-HBs antibody production and an expansion of interleukin-2-producing helper T cells specific for the Pre-S1/Pre-S2 antigens — and anti-HBs antibodies persisted at ≥100 IU/L in about 40% of combination participants for at least 32 weeks. But there was no sustained HBsAg seroclearance and no notable difference in mean HBsAg reduction at group level. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — immune-response endpoints only, in a small phase 2a analysis; whether this immune 'restoration' ever converts into functional cure is exactly what it does not show. Distinct from topic #2117 (elebsiran plus peginterferon as antiviral therapy): this shelf is the vaccine-immunogenicity question.

title: Bulevirtide plus pegylated interferon for hepatitis D (MYR204): 46% undetectable HDV RNA after treatment ended
question: In chronic hepatitis D, does combining bulevirtide with pegylated interferon alfa-2a produce more durable off-treatment HDV RNA undetectability than peginterferon alone?
balance: The strongest off-treatment result yet for a finite hepatitis D regimen — from one open-label phase 2b trial. In MYR204, patients received peginterferon alfa-2a alone for 48 weeks, bulevirtide 2 mg or 10 mg plus peginterferon for 48 weeks followed by bulevirtide alone for 48 weeks, or bulevirtide 10 mg alone for 96 weeks. Twenty-four weeks after all treatment ended, HDV RNA was undetectable in 46% of the 10-mg combination group versus 17% on peginterferon alone and 12% on bulevirtide alone — a 34-percentage-point advantage over bulevirtide monotherapy (95% CI 15 to 50; P<0.001) for the primary comparison — and the 46% figure held at 48 weeks after treatment. The end point is virologic, not clinical; the trial was open-label; and the winning regimen still left most patients detectable. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — one phase 2b trial with a durable off-treatment virologic benefit for the 10-mg combination. Cross-point: bulevirtide monotherapy versus delayed treatment is Shelf #1063; this shelf is only the combination question.

title: Tobevibart plus elebsiran for hepatitis D (SOLSTICE): the combined end point favoured the antibody alone, the deep virologic end points favoured the pair
question: In chronic hepatitis D, does monthly tobevibart (anti-HBsAg monoclonal antibody) plus elebsiran (siRNA) beat tobevibart alone on combined virologic-plus-ALT response at 24 weeks?
balance: A genuinely split result, and the split is the story. In the ongoing phase 2 SOLSTICE trial, 65 participants with chronic hepatitis D were randomised to tobevibart plus elebsiran every 4 weeks or tobevibart monotherapy every 2 weeks. On the pre-specified combined end point (virologic response plus alanine aminotransferase normalisation) at week 24, the combination did worse: 47% (15 of 32) versus 70% (23 of 33) on tobevibart alone. Yet on the deeper virologic measures the combination pulled ahead by week 48: undetectable HDV RNA in 66% (21 of 32) versus 48% (16 of 33), and HBsAg below 10 IU/mL in 91% (29 of 32) versus 21% (7 of 33), while combined response converged (56% versus 61%). With 32–33 people per arm, no pre-specified hypothesis test, and an ongoing trial, neither half of the split can carry a strong stamp. SPLIT PROPOSED STAMP: MAYBE (weak evidence) — adding elebsiran improves the combined response (the week-24 primary comparison went the other way); POSSIBLE — adding elebsiran deepens HDV RNA undetectability and HBsAg decline by week 48.

title: HERO: patient navigation versus modified DOT for hepatitis C in people who inject drugs — equal cures either way
question: For people who inject drugs with hepatitis C, does modified directly observed therapy (mDOT) beat patient navigation for achieving cure (SVR)?
balance: Two good models, no winner. In the HERO study — a pragmatic randomised trial at eight US cities (eight opioid treatment programmes and 15 community health centres) — 755 people actively injecting drugs received 12 weeks of sofosbuvir/velpatasvir and were randomised to peer patient navigation (n=379) or modified directly observed therapy, mDOT (n=376). Sustained virologic response in the modified intention-to-treat population was 74% (226 of 306) with mDOT versus 76% (236 of 317) with navigation (adjusted odds ratio 0.97, 95% CI 0.66 to 1.42; p=0.35); intention-to-treat SVR was 60% versus 62%, and per-protocol SVR among those who completed treatment and assessment was 91% versus 93% — no significant difference in any analysis. Treatment initiation (81% versus 84%) and completion (82% versus 83%) were also similar; mean adherence was higher with mDOT (78% versus 73%; difference 4.7%; p=0.0010) without translating into more cures. There were 421 serious adverse events, reflecting this population's burden of illness rather than the antivirals. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — a large pragmatic trial shows the delivery model is not the bottleneck: with either organised support model, about three in four treated patients who inject drugs are cured, and programmes can choose on cost and fit.

title: Six weeks is too short for recently acquired hepatitis C (REACT): more relapses, non-inferiority not met, trial stopped early
question: In recently acquired hepatitis C, is 6 weeks of sofosbuvir/velpatasvir non-inferior to the standard 12 weeks?
balance: The short course fell short, and the trial was stopped early because of it. REACT randomised 188 people with recently acquired hepatitis C (infection within the previous 12 months; 97% male, 69% HIV-positive) to sofosbuvir/velpatasvir for 6 weeks (n=93) or 12 weeks (n=95); the data safety monitoring board advised stopping enrolment early after a higher relapse rate in the short arm. Intention-to-treat SVR12 was 81.7% (76 of 93; 95% CI 72.4 to 89.0) with 6 weeks versus 90.5% (86 of 95; 82.7 to 95.6) with 12 weeks — an absolute shortfall of about 9 fewer cures per 100 patients — and non-inferiority against the 12% margin was not established in either the ITT or per-protocol analysis (per-protocol SVR12 89.4% versus 97.7%; difference −8.3%; p=0.025). Relapses: 9 in the short arm versus 2 in the standard arm. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm) — for the 6-week strategy in recently acquired HCV: a randomised comparison shows materially more relapses and fewer cures, so the saving of six weeks of drug is bought with retreatment.

title: Oral fexinidazole for rhodesiense sleeping sickness: a single-arm benchmark study met its fatality target
question: In stage 1 and stage 2 Trypanosoma brucei rhodesiense human African trypanosomiasis, is oral fexinidazole an effective alternative to suramin and melarsoprol?
balance: The only modern treatment study for this rapidly lethal infection, and deliberately not a randomised one — a randomised comparison against melarsoprol, an arsenical that kills a measurable share of the people who receive it, is not a trial anyone can run. In a prospective, open-label, single-arm phase 2–3 study in Uganda and Malawi, 45 patients with parasitologically confirmed rhodesiense human African trypanosomiasis (35 stage 2, 10 stage 1) received 10 days of oral fexinidazole. The primary end point — fatality at end of hospital admission in stage 2 disease, counting only deaths possibly related to the disease or the drug — was 0 of 34 (0%; 90% CI 0 to 8.43), below the predefined 8.5% benchmark drawn from melarsoprol-era literature (p=0.0488, just under the line). One stage 2 patient relapsed at week 9; there were no stage 1 failures and no unexpected safety signals. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — the benchmark was met in a small single-arm study of a disease that is fatal untreated; the evidence is thin by design and by necessity, and the margin over the benchmark was narrow.

title: Paromomycin + miltefosine for East African visceral leishmaniasis: 91% cured, non-inferiority narrowly missed in mITT, met per-protocol
question: In East African visceral leishmaniasis, is 14 days of paromomycin + miltefosine non-inferior to 17 days of SSG + paromomycin?
balance: Statistically a near-miss, clinically a strong candidate. In this open-label phase 3 trial at seven East African sites, 439 patients were randomised to paromomycin (20 mg/kg/day) plus miltefosine (allometric dosing) for 14 days, or SSG plus paromomycin for 17 days; 424 completed the trial. Definitive cure at 6 months in the modified intention-to-treat population was 91.2% (155 of 170) on PM/MF versus 91.8% (156 of 170) on SSG/PM — a difference of 0.6% whose 97.5% confidence interval (−6.2 to 7.4) crossed the 7% non-inferiority margin, so non-inferiority narrowly failed in mITT; in the per-protocol population it was met (92% versus 91.7%; difference −0.3%, 97.5% CI −7.0 to 6.5). The challenger regimen removes SSG entirely — no antimonial cardiotoxicity risk — needs one less injection per day, and is 3 days shorter. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — one well-run phase 3 trial with cure rates above 91% in both arms and a borderline formal non-inferiority result; the evidence supports PM/MF as a comparable alternative, not yet a proven-equal replacement.

title: Whipworm combinations (Pemba 2015): albendazole + oxantel pamoate cured 68.5%; albendazole + mebendazole no better than mebendazole alone
question: For Trichuris (whipworm) infection in children, which single-dose combination works — albendazole + oxantel pamoate, albendazole + ivermectin, or albendazole + mebendazole?
balance: One combination clearly worked against whipworm; one helped somewhat; one added nothing. In this four-arm randomised trial, 440 children aged 6–14 infected with Trichuris trichiura on Pemba Island, Tanzania (110 per arm; 431 analysed) received a single dose of albendazole plus oxantel pamoate, albendazole plus ivermectin, albendazole plus mebendazole, or mebendazole alone. Trichuris cure: 68.5% (74 of 108; 95% CI 59.6 to 77.4) with albendazole–oxantel pamoate, with a 99.2% egg-reduction rate; 27.5% (30 of 109) with albendazole–ivermectin (egg reduction 94.5%); and just 8.4% (9 of 107) for both albendazole–mebendazole and mebendazole alone — adding a second benzimidazole to mebendazole bought nothing. Adverse events were mostly mild (abdominal cramps in 9–18% across arms). PROPOSED POSSIBLE — one randomised four-arm trial with a large, internally consistent gradient; oxantel pamoate is the component that changes whipworm outcomes, and later combination work builds on exactly this result.

title: Arpraziquantel for preschool schistosomiasis: cure 87.8% versus 81.3% for the standard tablet, in a formulation young children can take
question: Is the child-friendly dispersible tablet arpraziquantel (L-praziquantel) as effective as standard praziquantel for schistosomiasis in preschool children?
balance: The paediatric formulation did what it was designed to do. Arpraziquantel is the levorotatory enantiomer of praziquantel, developed as a smaller, dispersible, better-tasting tablet for children too young to swallow the standard 600 mg tablet. In this phase 3 trial in Côte d'Ivoire and Kenya, 2,663 preschool children were prescreened and 326 were diagnosed with Schistosoma mansoni or S. haematobium infection; the efficacy population was 280 children (median age 5.1 years; 47% female). In the randomised cohort of 4–6-year-olds with S. mansoni, cure rates were numerically higher on arpraziquantel than on standard praziquantel — 87.8% (95% CI 79.6 to 93.5) versus 81.3% (67.4 to 91.1) — and the formulation was well tolerated: the commonest drug-related events were abdominal pain (14% of 288 treated children), diarrhoea (9%), somnolence (7%), and vomiting (6%). PROPOSED POSSIBLE — one open-label partly randomised phase 3 trial supporting comparable efficacy with a formulation advantage in exactly the age group the standard tablet fails.

title: Doxycycline anti-Wolbachia therapy for lymphatic filariasis: microfilariae nearly eliminated, adult worms gone in most at 14 months
question: In lymphatic filariasis, does 8 weeks of doxycycline (anti-Wolbachia) sterilise and kill adult Wuchereria bancrofti worms?
balance: A small trial with a striking biological result. Doxycycline does not attack the filarial worm directly; it depletes Wolbachia, the bacterial endosymbionts the worm needs to reproduce and survive. In this double-blind, placebo-controlled field trial in Tanzania, 72 people infected with Wuchereria bancrofti received doxycycline 200 mg/day for 8 weeks (n=34) or placebo (n=38), with follow-up at 5, 8, 11, and 14 months. Microfilaraemia was almost completely eliminated at 8–14 months in the doxycycline group (p<0.001 at all timepoints); at 14 months, adult worms were detectable by ultrasonography in only 22% (6 of 27) of the doxycycline group versus 88% (24 of 27) on placebo (p<0.0001) — evidence of a macrofilaricidal effect no single-dose antifilarial then offered — and circulating filarial antigen fell to about half its baseline (p=0.015). One death (HIV-related) occurred in the doxycycline group; other adverse events were few and mild. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — a single small per-protocol field trial, but with large, coherent effects across microfilariae, adult worms, and antigen; the 8-week daily course is the practical barrier to mass use.

title: Uniform six-month multidrug therapy for leprosy (U-MDT/CT-BR): matched 12 months on reactions and disability; relapse still the open question
question: In multibacillary leprosy, is a uniform 6-month regimen (the paucibacillary regimen given to everyone) as safe and effective as the standard 12-month multibacillary MDT?
balance: Six months looked as safe as twelve on everything measured during the trial — with the decisive outcome, relapse, still thinly counted when the trial reported. In U-MDT/CT-BR, 613 newly diagnosed multibacillary patients in Brazil were randomised to the uniform regimen (dapsone, rifampicin, and clofazimine for 6 months) or regular MDT (the same three drugs for 12 months). There was no statistically significant difference between groups in the Kaplan-Meier survival functions for leprosy reactions or for disability progression, and bacilloscopic index trends were compared as a main outcome. During active follow-up, four patients in the uniform group relapsed — a rate of 2.6 per 1000 patients per year (95% CI 0.81 to 6.2) — and during passive follow-up three more relapsed in the uniform group and one in the regular group: small numbers, wide intervals, and exactly the outcome a shortened regimen must be judged on over a decade, not a trial period. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — one open-label randomised trial supporting the uniform regimen on reactions and disability, with relapse ascertainment still limited at report.

title: Thermotherapy for cutaneous leishmaniasis (Kabul): one heat treatment matched intralesional antimony, beat intramuscular antimony
question: For a single cutaneous leishmaniasis lesion from L. tropica, does local thermotherapy cure as well as antimonial injections?
balance: Heat beat the systemic drug and matched the injected-into-the-lesion drug — in one Afghan trial of single L. tropica lesions. Four hundred one patients with a single lesion were randomised to thermotherapy (localised current applied at 50°C for 30 seconds), intralesional sodium stibogluconate (SSG), or intramuscular SSG. Complete reepithelialisation at 100 days: 69.4% (75 of 108) with thermotherapy, 75.3% (70 of 93) with intralesional SSG, and 44.8% (26 of 58) with intramuscular SSG; the odds ratio for cure with thermotherapy versus intramuscular SSG was 2.80 (95% CI 1.45 to 5.41; P=.002), and median time to cure was 53 days versus 75 days (intralesional) versus more than 100 days (intramuscular) (P=.003). For programmes, the practical point is large: one heat application, no cardiotoxic systemic antimony, no weeks of painful injections. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — a single randomised trial, in a single-species, single-lesion population, with the analysed set smaller than the enrolled 401; generalisation to other species, multiple lesions, or mucosal risk is untested here.

title: SSG + paromomycin for East African visceral leishmaniasis (LEAP 2012): 17-day combination matched 30-day SSG; paromomycin alone was worse
question: In East African visceral leishmaniasis, does 17 days of SSG + paromomycin match 30 days of SSG alone — and is paromomycin alone enough?
balance: The combination matched the standard; paromomycin alone did not — a clean geographic lesson. In this multicentre East African trial (the LEAP study), patients aged 4–60 with parasitologically confirmed visceral leishmaniasis were randomised in two comparisons. Paromomycin alone (20 mg/kg/day for 21 days) was significantly worse than SSG alone (20 mg/kg/day for 30 days): efficacy at 6 months 84.3% versus 94.1% (difference 9.7%, 95% CI 3.6 to 15.7; p=0.002) — the regimen registered in India underperformed in East Africa. The SSG-plus-paromomycin combination (17 days) was comparable to 30-day SSG: 91.4% versus 93.9% (difference 2.5%, 95% CI −1.3 to 6.3; p=0.198), with no apparent safety differences, nearly halving the treatment course and the antimony exposure. A WHO Expert Committee recommended SSG-plus-paromomycin as first-line for East Africa in March 2010. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — one large randomised trial supports the combination as equivalent-in-effect to standard SSG; the stamp is a single verdict on the combination question, with paromomycin-alone inferiority recorded in the card rather than split, because the shelf's question is the combination.

title: Weekly doxycycline prophylaxis against leptospirosis (Panama trial): 20 cases on placebo versus 1 on doxycycline
question: In soldiers training in a leptospirosis-endemic jungle environment, does weekly doxycycline 200 mg prevent clinical leptospirosis versus placebo?
balance: One old, large, well-run trial with a dramatic result that has never been replicated at scale. In the autumn of 1982, 940 US Army volunteers training in the Panamanian jungle were randomised, double-blind, to weekly doxycycline 200 mg or placebo for about three weeks of training plus a dose at completion. Leptospirosis struck 20 soldiers on placebo (attack rate 4.2%) versus 1 on doxycycline (attack rate 0.2%; P<0.001) — a 95.0% protective efficacy, an absolute reduction of about 4 cases per 100 soldiers over three weeks. The setting is narrow: healthy young soldiers, one jungle, one short exposure window, one season. Later evidence in civilian and flood-exposure settings is observational and mixed (named, not carded). PROPOSED POSSIBLE — a single 1982 field trial, large and blinded, with an effect too big to be noise but confined to its setting; Prevention hub cross-point: Shelf #1.

title: Two antivenoms for carpet viper envenoming (Nigeria): EchiTAb Plus-ICP slightly more effective, EchiTAb-G slightly safer
question: For Echis ocellatus envenoming, is the polyspecific antivenom EchiTAb Plus-ICP non-inferior to the monospecific EchiTAb-G for restoring blood clotting?
balance: Both antivenoms worked; the polyspecific one worked slightly better and reacted slightly more. In this randomised, double-blind non-inferiority trial at Kaltungo, Nigeria, patients with Echis ocellatus envenoming and incoagulable blood received either EchiTAb Plus-ICP (a polyspecific equine antivenom; initial dose 3 vials) or EchiTAb-G (a monospecific ovine antivenom; initial dose 1 vial), with additional doses as needed. Permanent restoration of blood coagulability 6 hours after the initial dose was achieved by 83.0% (161 of 194) with EchiTAb Plus-ICP versus 75.7% (156 of 206) with EchiTAb-G — a relative risk of 1.10 (one-sided 95% CI lower limit 1.01; P=0.05), meeting the non-inferiority criterion with a small superiority trend: an absolute difference of about 7 more patients per 100 restored by 6 hours. Early (anaphylactoid) reactions were more frequent with EchiTAb Plus-ICP: 25.8% (50 of 194) versus 18.9% (39 of 206) (relative risk 1.36, one-sided 95% CI upper limit 1.86; P=0.06). PROPOSED POSSIBLE — a single randomised head-to-head trial; the authors' own summary is the fair one: EchiTAb Plus-ICP slightly more effective, EchiTAb-G slightly safer, both recommended for West African Echis envenoming.
