title: Micafungin vs fluconazole prophylaxis after stem cell transplant: success 80.0% vs 73.5% in 882 patients
question: In patients undergoing haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, is micafungin superior to fluconazole for preventing invasive fungal infection during neutropenia?
balance: One large, clean head-to-head answers this: in 882 adults and children undergoing haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, overall prophylaxis success during the neutropenic phase was higher with micafungin than with fluconazole — 80.0% versus 73.5%, an absolute difference of 6.5 percentage points (95% CI 0.9 to 12; P=.03). Success was a composite (no suspected, proven or probable invasive fungal infection through treatment and no proven/probable infection in the 4 weeks after). It is a single phase 3 trial, but it is large, double-blind and multicentre, and the comparator is the standard drug rather than placebo. PROPOSED LIKELY — one large double-blind randomised trial showing a modest absolute advantage for micafungin on a composite prophylaxis-success endpoint.

title: Fluconazole prophylaxis in very-low-birth-weight infants
question: In preterm infants with birth weight under 1500 g, does prophylactic fluconazole prevent invasive fungal infection compared with placebo?
balance: Two double-blind, placebo-controlled randomised trials in preterm infants agree. In the single-centre trial of infants under 1000 g, invasive fungal infection occurred in 0% on fluconazole versus 20% on placebo over six weeks. In the larger eight-centre Italian trial of infants under 1500 g, invasive fungal infection occurred in 2.7% (6 mg/kg) and 3.8% (3 mg/kg) versus 13.2% on placebo, with colonisation roughly a third of the placebo rate, and no difference in mortality or other neonatal outcomes. A later trial in infants under 750 g confirmed fewer invasive candidiasis cases without a significant difference in the combined death-or-infection outcome. The proposed stamp is LIKELY: two independent double-blind randomised trials show a consistent, large reduction in invasive fungal infection, though neither showed a mortality benefit and routine use must be weighed against local infection rates and resistance selection.

title: Micafungin prophylaxis in high-risk liver transplantation: non-inferior to standard care in one open-label trial (TENPIN)
question: In liver transplant recipients at high risk of invasive fungal infection, is micafungin non-inferior to centre standard care (fluconazole, liposomal amphotericin B, or caspofungin)?
balance: Micafungin met non-inferiority against a bundle of centre standard-care regimens — but that is all this single open-label trial can show. In 344 high-risk liver transplant recipients, clinical success at end of prophylaxis was 98.6% with micafungin versus 99.3% with standard care in the per-protocol set (difference 0.7 points; 95% CI −2.7 to 4.4) and 96.5% versus 93.6% in the full analysis set, within the 10% non-inferiority margin; kidney function was better with micafungin and drug-related adverse events were fewer (11.6% vs 16.3%). The comparator was three different drugs across centres, success rates were near the ceiling in both arms, and there is no placebo or single-drug comparison. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — a single open-label non-inferiority trial against heterogeneous standard care (THIN).

title: Caspofungin prophylaxis in high-risk ICU patients (MSG-01): fewer candida infections, but not significantly
question: In high-risk ICU patients without invasive candidiasis at baseline, does caspofungin prophylaxis (with biomarker-triggered preemptive therapy) reduce proven/probable invasive candidiasis versus placebo?
balance: The prophylaxis question was not answered affirmatively: in MSG-01, 222 ventilated high-risk ICU patients were randomised double-blind to caspofungin or placebo, and proven/probable invasive candidiasis in patients without baseline disease occurred in 9.8% (10/102) on caspofungin versus 16.7% (14/84) on placebo — an absolute difference of about 7 points that was not statistically significant (P=.14). A secondary 'preemptive approach' analysis that included patients with baseline disease gave 18.8% versus 30.4% (P=.04), but that analysis mixes patients who already had candidiasis at entry, so it cannot rescue the prophylaxis claim. Mortality, antifungal use and length of stay did not differ, and there were no safety differences. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — a single underpowered trial whose primary prophylaxis comparison did not reach significance (THIN).

title: Empirical vs preemptive antifungal therapy in febrile neutropenia: similar survival, more fungal infections when treatment waits
question: In high-risk neutropenic patients with persistent fever on broad-spectrum antibacterials, does a preemptive strategy (treat on clinical/imaging/galactomannan evidence) match empirical antifungal therapy on survival while reducing antifungal exposure?
balance: The two halves of this strategy trial point different ways, so the stamp is split. In 293 high-risk neutropenic patients with persistent fever, survival 14 days after neutropenia recovery was similar with a preemptive strategy (treat only on clinical, imaging or galactomannan evidence) and with empirical treatment for everyone still febrile — 95.1% versus 97.3%, and the lower 95% confidence limit for the mortality difference (−5.9%) sat inside the −8% non-inferiority margin; antifungal drug costs fell 35% with preemptive care and nephrotoxicity was not reduced. But proven/probable invasive fungal infections were more common under the preemptive strategy — 13 of 143 versus 4 of 150 (P<.05), concentrated during induction chemotherapy (12/73 vs 3/78; P<.01) — and the authors cautioned that empirical treatment may give better survival for induction patients. PROPOSED SPLIT: POSSIBLE for preemptive care preserving survival overall with less antifungal exposure, but LIKELY (harm) on invasive fungal infection incidence, especially during induction — one open-label strategy trial, so neither half is settled.

title: Voriconazole therapeutic drug monitoring: fewer drug stoppages and better response in the only randomised trial (n=110)
question: In patients treated with voriconazole for invasive fungal infection, does routine concentration-guided dose adjustment improve treatment response and reduce drug-related adverse events versus fixed dosing?
balance: The only randomised trial of voriconazole therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM) found a real but narrow benefit, in a small single-centre study. In 110 adults with invasive fungal infection, dose adjustment to a trough of 1.0–5.5 mg/L did not change the overall incidence of adverse events (42% in both groups; P=.97), but far fewer TDM patients stopped voriconazole because of adverse events (4% vs 17%; P=.02), and complete or partial response at 3 months was higher with TDM (81%, 30/37, vs 57%, 20/34; P=.04) among those assessed for response. The response denominators (71 of 110) and single-centre design keep this from being stronger. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — one small single-centre randomised trial (THIN), with benefit on discontinuation and response but not on overall adverse-event rates.

title: Adjunctive dexamethasone in HIV cryptococcal meningitis (CryptoDex): stopped for safety — more disability, no survival benefit
question: In HIV-associated cryptococcal meningitis treated with amphotericin B plus fluconazole, does adjunctive dexamethasone improve survival?
balance: Adjunctive dexamethasone harmed patients in the CryptoDex trial, and the trial was stopped early for safety. In 451 adults with HIV-associated cryptococcal meningitis in Asia and Africa, all receiving amphotericin B plus fluconazole, mortality at 10 weeks was 47% with dexamethasone versus 41% with placebo (hazard ratio 1.11, a relative effect; 95% CI 0.84 to 1.47; P=0.45) and 57% versus 49% by 6 months (HR 1.18; 0.91 to 1.53; P=0.20) — the mortality differences themselves were not statistically significant, but everything else pointed the same harmful way: fewer patients had a good outcome at 10 weeks (13% vs 25%; odds ratio 0.42, a relative effect; 0.25 to 0.69; P<0.001), clinical adverse events were more common (667 vs 494 events; P=0.01), grade 3/4 infections, renal and cardiac events were more frequent, and fungal clearance from cerebrospinal fluid was slower. Tier C: this is a mortality-outcome harm shelf for the developer to rule on personally. PROPOSED LIKELY (harm) — a large double-blind trial stopped for safety, with disability and adverse-event harm shown clearly and mortality numerically higher.

title: Adjunctive sertraline in HIV cryptococcal meningitis (ASTRO-CM): no survival benefit — 52% vs 46% mortality, stopped for futility
question: In HIV-associated cryptococcal meningitis on standard amphotericin/fluconazole therapy, does adjunctive sertraline improve 18-week survival?
balance: No: despite anticryptococcal activity in the laboratory, adjunctive sertraline did not improve survival in the ASTRO-CM phase 3 trial, which was stopped for futility. In 460 HIV-positive adults with cryptococcal meningitis in Uganda receiving amphotericin B and fluconazole, 18-week mortality was 52% (120/229) with sertraline versus 46% (106/231) with placebo (hazard ratio 1.21, a relative effect; 95% CI 0.93 to 1.57; P=0.15), fungal clearance from cerebrospinal fluid was similar (0.43 vs 0.47 −log10 CFU/mL per day; P=0.59), and grade 4/5 adverse events were similar (31% vs 32%). Tier C applies because survival was the primary endpoint — this shelf makes no mortality claim for sertraline; the result is a null on a mortality endpoint. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — a large double-blind phase 3 trial, stopped for futility, with mortality numerically higher on sertraline.

title: Adjunctive interferon-γ1b in AIDS cryptococcal meningitis: faster CSF culture conversion in a 75-patient phase 2 trial
question: In AIDS-related cryptococcal meningitis on amphotericin-based therapy, does adjunctive recombinant interferon-γ1b speed CSF fungal clearance?
balance: A promising surrogate signal, nothing more. In this phase 2 double-blind trial of 75 patients with AIDS-related acute cryptococcal meningitis, all on amphotericin B-based therapy, cerebrospinal fluid cultures had converted to negative at 2 weeks in 36% of patients receiving interferon-γ1b 100 µg and 32% receiving 200 µg, versus 13% on placebo; combined mycologic and clinical success trended the same way (26% vs 8%; P=.078). Treatment was well tolerated, with no apparent effect on CD4 counts or HIV load. But 75 patients cannot answer survival, culture conversion is a surrogate, and the combined-success comparison did not reach significance. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — a small phase 2 trial on a surrogate endpoint (THIN); 'holds promise, warrants further study' is exactly where the evidence stops.

title: Isavuconazole for mucormycosis (VITAL study)
question: In patients with invasive mucormycosis, does isavuconazole treatment produce outcomes comparable to amphotericin B-based therapy?
balance: There is no randomised trial of isavuconazole for mucormycosis. The VITAL study was a single-arm, open-label trial: 37 patients with mucormycosis were treated with isavuconazole, and by day 42, 35% had died, 11% had a partial response and 43% had stable disease. Among patients receiving it as primary treatment, day-42 crude mortality was 33% (7/21), compared with 39% (13/33) in matched amphotericin B controls from a registry (weighted comparison 33% versus 41%, p=0.595 — not significant). The proposed stamp is MAYBE (weak evidence): the numbers are in the same range as historical amphotericin B outcomes and isavuconazole gives an oral option where amphotericin B is impossible or failing, but a single-arm study with matched controls cannot show that it works as well, and this shelf must never be read as randomised-trial evidence.

title: Zoliflodacin single-dose oral treatment for uncomplicated gonorrhoea
question: In adolescents and adults with uncomplicated urogenital gonorrhoea, is a single 3 g oral dose of zoliflodacin non-inferior to ceftriaxone injection plus azithromycin for microbiological cure?
balance: One large phase 3 trial (930 randomised, 17 clinics in five countries) tested a single 3 g oral dose of zoliflodacin — a first-in-class spiropyrimidinetrione antibiotic — against ceftriaxone 500 mg intramuscularly plus azithromycin 1 g orally. Urogenital microbiological cure in the microbiological intention-to-treat population was 90.9% (460/506) with zoliflodacin versus 96.2% (229/238) with the comparator; the difference of 5.3 percentage points (95% CI 1.4 to 8.6) fell within the prespecified 12% non-inferiority margin. Side effects were similar overall. The proposed stamp is POSSIBLE: a single large trial met its non-inferiority criterion, but the margin was wide, the trial was open-label, cure was numerically lower than with ceftriaxone, and zoliflodacin is a new, not yet widely available agent whose real-world performance and resistance behaviour are untested.

title: Gentamicin plus azithromycin as an alternative to ceftriaxone for gonorrhoea (G-ToG)
question: In people with uncomplicated gonorrhoea, is gentamicin 240 mg intramuscularly plus azithromycin as effective as ceftriaxone plus azithromycin at clearing infection?
balance: The pragmatic G-ToG trial randomised 720 people in English sexual-health clinics to gentamicin 240 mg intramuscularly or ceftriaxone 500 mg intramuscularly, both with azithromycin 1 g. Clearance of infection at two weeks was 91% (267/292) with gentamicin versus 98% (299/306) with ceftriaxone — an adjusted risk difference of −6.4 percentage points (95% CI −10.4 to −2.4) — so non-inferiority was NOT established, and the gap was largest in the throat (clearance about 80% versus 96%). The proposed stamp is LIKELY (harm): on the best randomised evidence, swapping ceftriaxone for gentamicin leaves roughly 7 more infections uncured per 100 treated. Gentamicin remains a fallback when ceftriaxone truly cannot be used, but it is not an equal substitute, particularly for pharyngeal infection.

title: Single-dose azithromycin versus benzathine penicillin for early syphilis
question: In people with early syphilis, is a single 2 g oral dose of azithromycin as effective as benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units intramuscularly for serological cure?
balance: Two randomised equivalence trials agree that a single 2 g oral dose of azithromycin cures early syphilis about as often as a benzathine penicillin injection: in Tanzania, cure was 97.7% versus 95.0% (difference confidence interval −1.7 to 7.1, meeting equivalence criteria), and in a multinational phase 3 trial in HIV-negative patients, serological cure at six months was 77.6% (180/232) versus 78.5% (186/237). The proposed stamp is LIKELY for the narrow trial question — the equivalence finding is consistent across two independent trials. The crucial limit is outside the trials: macrolide resistance in Treponema pallidum (23S rRNA mutations) is widespread in many regions, so azithromycin should not be used where resistance is prevalent, and penicillin remains the standard — it is also the only recommended treatment in pregnancy. Nonserious side effects, mostly gastrointestinal, were more common with azithromycin (61.5% versus 46.3% in the phase 3 trial).

title: Oral cefixime plus doxycycline as a needle-free regimen for gonorrhoea
question: In people with gonorrhoea, is an all-oral regimen of cefixime 800 mg single dose plus doxycycline for seven days non-inferior to ceftriaxone injection plus azithromycin?
balance: One small open-label non-inferiority trial (161 randomised, 152 per-protocol, Prague) compared cefixime 800 mg as a single oral dose plus doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for seven days against ceftriaxone 1 g intramuscularly plus azithromycin 2 g. In the per-protocol analysis, 86% (65/76) of the oral-regimen group were both culture- and NAAT-negative at week three versus 100% of the comparator group — a risk difference of 14.5 percentage points (95% CI 6.56 to 22.38), so non-inferiority was NOT achieved overall. Crucially, every failure in the oral arm was a pharyngeal infection; efficacy was high at urogenital and rectal sites. The proposed stamp is therefore SPLIT: POSSIBLE that the all-oral regimen works well for urogenital and rectal gonorrhoea, but MAYBE (weak evidence) — effectively a warning — for pharyngeal infection, where it failed in this trial. This corrects any impression that the oral regimen was shown broadly comparable to the injection.

title: Doxycycline versus azithromycin for rectal chlamydia in men who have sex with men
question: In men who have sex with men with rectal Chlamydia trachomatis infection, is doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for seven days more effective than a single 1 g dose of azithromycin?
balance: A double-blind, placebo-controlled randomised trial in 177 men who have sex with men with rectal chlamydia (Seattle and Boston) compared doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for seven days with azithromycin 1 g as a single dose. Among participants who completed the study, cure was 100% (70/70) with doxycycline versus 74% (48/65) with azithromycin — a difference of 26 percentage points (95% CI 16 to 36; P<0.001); in the intention-to-treat analysis cure was 91% (80/88) versus 71% (63/89), a difference of 20 points (95% CI 9 to 31; P<0.001). The proposed stamp is LIKELY: this is a well-designed double-blind trial with a large, consistent effect in both analyses — single-dose azithromycin leaves roughly one in four rectal infections uncured, which is why doxycycline is the preferred treatment for rectal chlamydia.

title: Azithromycin versus doxycycline for urogenital chlamydia
question: In adolescents and adults with uncomplicated urogenital Chlamydia trachomatis infection, is a single 1 g dose of azithromycin non-inferior to doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for seven days?
balance: Two randomised trials give slightly different answers. The older multicentre trial (457 patients, antigen-test diagnosis) found non-response in 4% on azithromycin versus 2% on doxycycline (difference 2 points; 95% CI 0 to 6) and concluded the single dose was as effective. The modern trial — 567 adolescents in youth correctional facilities, all treatment directly observed, failure judged by nucleic acid testing with genotyping — found zero failures on doxycycline and five failures (3.2%) on azithromycin; the upper bound of the 90% confidence interval for the difference (5.9 points) exceeded the prespecified 5-point non-inferiority cutoff, so azithromycin's non-inferiority was NOT established. The proposed stamp is POSSIBLE: both drugs cure the great majority (97–100%), and any true difference is small, but on the most rigorous trial azithromycin may be a few percentage points worse, and doxycycline is now generally preferred — especially since the same drug is clearly better for rectal infection.

title: Suppressive acyclovir to prevent HIV transmission in HSV-2/HIV-coinfected couples (Partners in Prevention)
question: In HIV-1/HSV-2 serodiscordant couples, does suppressive acyclovir 400 mg twice daily in the coinfected partner reduce transmission of HIV-1 to the uninfected partner?
balance: The Partners in Prevention trial randomised 3,408 HIV-1/HSV-2 serodiscordant couples at 14 African sites to acyclovir 400 mg twice daily or placebo for the coinfected partner. Despite acyclovir lowering plasma HIV-1 RNA by 0.25 log10 copies/mL (P<0.001) and reducing HSV-2-positive genital ulcers by 73% (relative risk 0.27; 95% CI 0.20 to 0.36), genetically linked HIV transmissions were 41 in the acyclovir group versus 43 on placebo (hazard ratio 0.92; 95% CI 0.60 to 1.41; P=0.69) — no reduction. The proposed stamp is LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): a large, well-conducted trial shows suppressing HSV-2 improves herpes outcomes and modestly lowers viral load but does not prevent HIV transmission to partners. (Note: this shelf is anchored on Partners in Prevention; HPTN 039 was a separate trial of HSV suppression and HIV acquisition, not transmission.)

title: Single-dose secnidazole for bacterial vaginosis
question: In women with bacterial vaginosis, does a single oral dose of secnidazole (1 g or 2 g granules) produce higher clinical cure rates than placebo?
balance: A phase 2 double-blind, dose-ranging randomised trial enrolled 215 women meeting all Amsel criteria for bacterial vaginosis at 24 US centres; 188 were in the modified intention-to-treat population. A single dose of secnidazole oral granules beat placebo clearly: clinical cure at 21–30 days in the intention-to-treat analysis was 65.3% with 2 g and 49.3% with 1 g versus 19.4% on placebo, and in the modified intention-to-treat analysis the 2 g dose gave clinical cure 67.7%, microbiological cure 40.3% and therapeutic cure 40.3%, versus 17.7%, 6.5% and 6.5% on placebo (all P<0.05; the authors' conclusion cites P<0.001 for both doses). Both doses were well tolerated. The proposed stamp is POSSIBLE: the placebo-controlled effect is large and dose-ordered, but this is a single phase 2 trial (THIN), cure was judged at three to four weeks, and it does not address BV recurrence, which is the harder clinical problem (covered separately on the BV recurrence shelf). This shelf is about treating an acute episode; single-dose secnidazole for trichomoniasis is a different question, covered on its own shelf.

title: Imiquimod cream versus podophyllotoxin solution for anogenital warts
question: In adults with anogenital warts, is self-applied imiquimod 5% cream as effective as podophyllotoxin 0.5% solution for complete clearance of warts?
balance: The only head-to-head randomised trial is small and open-label: 45 evaluable patients in Graz, Austria. Complete clearance of baseline warts was 72% (95% CI 52 to 86) with podophyllotoxin 0.5% solution at the end of its four-week course, and 75% (95% CI 53 to 98) with imiquimod 5% cream at the end of its sixteen-week course (P=1, identical); side-effect frequency did not differ significantly (P=0.24). The proposed stamp is MAYBE (weak evidence): with only 45 patients and very wide confidence intervals, identical point estimates cannot establish that the two treatments are equivalent — the trial could not rule out large differences either way — and the comparison is uneven, since one treatment was assessed after four weeks and the other after sixteen. Choice in practice turns on treatment duration, tolerability, and patient preference rather than proven superiority.

title: Resistance-guided sequential therapy for Mycoplasma genitalium
question: In people with Mycoplasma genitalium infection, does a resistance-guided sequential programme — doxycycline first, then azithromycin if macrolide-susceptible or sitafloxacin if macrolide-resistant — achieve high cure rates?
balance: This is a prospective programme evaluation, not a randomised trial. At Melbourne Sexual Health Centre, patients with Mycoplasma genitalium first received doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for seven days (which cut organism load by a mean of 2.60 log10), then a macrolide-resistance-mutation test directed the second drug: azithromycin 2.5 g in divided doses if no resistance mutation was found, or sitafloxacin 100 mg twice daily for seven days if one was. Resistance mutations were present in 167 of 244 evaluable infections (68.4%). Cure was 94.8% (73/77) in the macrolide-susceptible group and 92.2% (154/167) in the resistant group treated with sitafloxacin, and new macrolide resistance was selected in only 2 of 76 (2.6%). The proposed stamp is POSSIBLE: a single-centre prospective evaluation (THIN, no randomised comparison) shows very high cure in both resistance strata, supporting the resistance-guided sequential programme as tested — but sitafloxacin, the fluoroquinolone used for resistant cases in this programme, is not approved in the United States, so the exact programme cannot simply be copied everywhere.

title: VGX-3100 therapeutic DNA vaccine for HPV-16/18 CIN2/3: regression in one phase 2b trial, not cleanly replicated in phase 3
question: In women with HPV-16/18-associated CIN2/3, does the DNA vaccine VGX-3100 (E6/E7 plasmids delivered by electroporation) cause histopathologic regression versus placebo, sparing ablative surgery?
balance: One properly randomised phase 2b trial says this therapeutic DNA vaccine can push high-grade cervical lesions backwards, but the evidence is thin. In 167 women with HPV-16/18-positive CIN2/3, histopathologic regression to CIN1 or normal occurred in 49.5% on VGX-3100 versus 30.6% on placebo in the per-protocol analysis — an absolute difference of 19.0 percentage points, but with a wide confidence interval (1.4 to 36.6) whose lower end is close to no effect, from a small placebo group. The modified intention-to-treat analysis agreed (48.2% vs 30.0%). The only clearly more common side effect was injection-site redness. This is a single phase 2b trial, and the later phase 3 programme did not cleanly replicate the result, so the finding stays fragile. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — one clean, positive, placebo-controlled trial on a real tissue endpoint, held back by its size, its wide interval, and the failure of phase 3 to confirm it cleanly.

title: Vacc-4x therapeutic HIV vaccine: coprimary endpoints null in an underpowered phase 2 treatment-interruption trial
question: In ART-suppressed adults with HIV-1, does the p24 peptide vaccine Vacc-4x reduce viral load after analytic treatment interruption versus placebo?
balance: Judged by the endpoints it set for itself, this trial did not work. Vacc-4x, a p24 peptide therapeutic vaccine, was tested in ART-suppressed adults who then interrupted treatment. Enrolment stopped early — only 136 of a planned 345 participants were randomised — and BOTH coprimary endpoints were negative: the proportions resuming combination ART were 34% on vaccine versus 29% on placebo, and the change in CD4 percentage did not differ between groups (difference −5.71, 95% CI −13.01 to 1.59). Viral load was lower in the vaccine group at weeks 48 and 52 of the interruption follow-up, a secondary finding in an underpowered trial, and one possibly related serious adverse event (an exacerbation of multiple sclerosis) occurred on vaccine. A lower viral-load set-point in secondary analyses is a hypothesis, not a demonstrated benefit. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — an underpowered phase 2 trial whose coprimary endpoints were both null; the viral-load signal is hypothesis-generating only.

title: CMV glycoprotein B/MF59 vaccine in postpartum women: 50% efficacy in one phase 2 trial, never taken to phase 3
question: In CMV-seronegative women within a year of giving birth, does recombinant glycoprotein B vaccine with MF59 adjuvant prevent primary CMV infection versus placebo?
balance: A single phase 2 trial found that a recombinant cytomegalovirus glycoprotein B vaccine with MF59 adjuvant roughly halved primary CMV infection in seronegative women in the year after childbirth: vaccine efficacy 50% (95% CI 7 to 73) per 100 person-years, with 18 infections on vaccine versus 31 on placebo over 42 months. The confidence interval is wide — the true efficacy could be as low as 7% — the trial was stopped at an interim efficacy analysis, and no phase 3 trial ever followed to confirm it. Congenital infections in subsequent pregnancies were too few to judge (1 vs 3). Local and systemic reactions were more common on vaccine. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — a genuine randomised signal on the infection endpoint itself, but from one phase 2 trial stopped early and never confirmed.

title: Intranasal norovirus VLP vaccine: prevented illness in a human challenge trial; field efficacy untested
question: In healthy adults, does an intranasal norovirus virus-like-particle vaccine prevent gastroenteritis after experimental Norwalk virus (GI.1) challenge versus placebo?
balance: Inside a human challenge model, this intranasal norovirus virus-like-particle vaccine worked: after volunteers were deliberately infected with the homologous Norwalk virus (GI.1) strain, gastroenteritis occurred in 37% of vaccinees versus 69% on placebo (P=0.006), and infection itself was less frequent (61% vs 82%, P=0.05). But this is a small challenge study — 77 people in the per-protocol analysis — using one laboratory strain matched to the vaccine, in healthy adults. It shows the vaccine can protect against an artificial exposure to its own strain; it does not show protection against the varied norovirus strains people meet in the community. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — a clear positive result on the exact question the challenge model asks, with field efficacy untested for this formulation.

title: C. difficile toxoid vaccine (CLOVER): phase 3 trial of 17,535 adults did not prevent first CDI
question: In adults aged 50 years or older at increased risk of Clostridioides difficile infection, does the detoxified toxin-A/B vaccine PF-06425090 prevent a first CDI episode versus placebo?
balance: The definitive trial was negative. CLOVER randomised 17,535 adults aged 50 or older at increased risk of C. difficile infection to the detoxified toxin A/B vaccine PF-06425090 (the specific tested product, an investigational vaccine that is not FDA-approved) or placebo. The primary endpoint was not met: first CDI at least 14 days after dose 3 occurred in 17 vaccine versus 25 placebo recipients, a vaccine efficacy of 31.0% relative whose 96.4% confidence interval (−38.7 to 66.6) crosses zero widely; the post-dose-2 analysis was the same story (24 vs 34; efficacy 28.6%, CI −28.4 to 61.0). Two softer signals appeared — CDI episodes were shorter on vaccine (median 1 vs 4 days, nominal P=0.02) and in a post hoc analysis no vaccinee versus 11 placebo recipients sought medical attention for CDI — but neither rescues a missed primary endpoint. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — a very large phase 3 trial that did not prevent first CDI as tested; the duration and care-seeking findings are nominal and post hoc, not evidence of protection.

title: V710 S. aureus vaccine before cardiothoracic surgery: no protection, and higher mortality in vaccinees who became infected (Tier C)
question: In adults scheduled for cardiothoracic surgery with median sternotomy, does preoperative V710 (IsdB) vaccination prevent serious postoperative Staphylococcus aureus infection versus placebo?
balance: This vaccine failed on benefit and raised a harm flag: a SPLIT verdict. On prevention, V710 (an IsdB staphylococcus aureus vaccine given before cardiothoracic surgery) made no difference: the primary outcome of S. aureus bacteraemia or deep sternal wound infection occurred at 2.6 versus 3.2 per 100 person-years (relative risk 0.81, 95% CI 0.44 to 1.48; P=0.58). On harm, among the minority who did develop S. aureus infection, mortality was far higher in vaccinees than in placebo recipients — 23.0 versus 4.2 deaths per 100 person-years, a difference of 18.8 (95% CI 8.0 to 34.1) — and multiorgan failure was also more frequent on vaccine (31 vs 17 events, P=0.04), while all-cause mortality overall did not differ significantly (5.7 vs 5.0 per 100 person-years, P=0.20). The trial was terminated after its second interim analysis for safety and low efficacy. PROPOSED SPLIT — (the treatment made no difference) for prevention; POSSIBLE (harm) for death once S. aureus infection occurred. Tier C: the developer reviews this shelf personally because of the mortality signal.

title: Recombinant zoster vaccine after autologous stem cell transplant (ZOE-HSCT): confirmed zoster cut by about two-thirds
question: In adults who have just undergone autologous haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, do two doses of adjuvanted recombinant zoster vaccine prevent herpes zoster versus placebo?
balance: In one of the most immunosuppressed populations ever vaccinated in a trial, the adjuvanted recombinant zoster vaccine worked clearly. ZOE-HSCT randomised 1,846 adults within 50–70 days of autologous stem cell transplantation: confirmed herpes zoster occurred in 49 vaccine versus 135 placebo recipients — incidence 30 versus 94 cases per 1,000 person-years, an incidence rate ratio of 0.32 (95% CI 0.22 to 0.44), i.e. vaccine efficacy of 68.2% in relative terms, over a median 21 months of follow-up. This is a single phase 3 trial, but it is large, placebo-controlled, in exactly the population the question asks about, and the effect is big with a tight interval. It answers a different question from the older-adult zoster trials: protection in the early post-transplant window. PROPOSED LIKELY — one large, definitive phase 3 trial with a two-thirds relative reduction in confirmed zoster and absolute rates printed alongside.

title: High-dose vs standard-dose influenza vaccine in transplant recipients: better antibody responses, clinical benefit untested
question: In adult solid-organ transplant recipients, does high-dose influenza vaccine improve immunogenicity versus standard-dose vaccine?
balance: High-dose influenza vaccine produced clearly stronger antibody responses than standard-dose vaccine in transplant recipients — on the only kind of endpoint this trial measured. In 172 solid-organ transplant recipients in the 2016–17 season, seroconversion to at least one vaccine antigen occurred in 78.6% with high-dose versus 55.8% with standard-dose vaccine (P<0.001), with the advantage present for every strain (A/H1N1 40.5% vs 20.5%; A/H3N2 57.1% vs 32.5%; B 58.3% vs 41.6%); the adjusted odds ratio for seroconversion was 3.23 (95% CI 1.56 to 6.67). But seroconversion is an immunogenicity surrogate: the trial was a single season, 161 analysed patients, and measured no clinical outcomes — not influenza illness, hospitalisation, or rejection. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — a clean randomised immunogenicity result, capped by the surrogate endpoint and the small, single-season design (THIN).

title: Pneumococcal conjugate vaccine in HIV-infected adults (Malawi): one trial, 74% efficacy against recurrent invasive disease — OUTSTANDING-SINGLE
question: In predominantly HIV-infected adolescents and adults who have recovered from invasive pneumococcal disease, does 7-valent pneumococcal conjugate vaccine prevent further vaccine-serotype invasive disease versus placebo?
balance: OUTSTANDING-SINGLE: this shelf rests on one randomised trial, and it is flagged as such. In Malawi, 496 adolescents and adults who had recovered from invasive pneumococcal disease — 88% of them HIV-positive — were randomised to 7-valent pneumococcal conjugate vaccine or placebo. Vaccine-serotype or serotype 6A invasive episodes occurred in 5 vaccine versus 19 placebo recipients: vaccine efficacy 74% in relative terms (95% CI 30 to 90) over 798 person-years of follow-up. That is a large effect on a hard clinical endpoint in a population with no other proven option, and it is the trial that established conjugate (not just polysaccharide) vaccination for HIV-infected adults. The honest limits: a single trial, and no mortality benefit — deaths were 73 on vaccine versus 63 on placebo (HR 1.18, 95% CI 0.84 to 1.66). Serious adverse events within 14 days were fewer on vaccine (3 vs 17, P=0.002); minor reactions were more common (41 vs 13, P=0.003). PROPOSED LIKELY — a single double-blind trial with a large, significant effect on invasive disease itself; the OUTSTANDING-SINGLE flag stays on the shelf because there is no second trial.

title: ExPEC9V vaccine in older adults (E.mbrace): no protection against invasive E. coli disease; stopped for futility
question: In adults aged 60 years or older with a recent UTI history, does the nine-valent ExPEC conjugate vaccine (ExPEC9V) prevent invasive E. coli disease caused by vaccine O-serotypes versus placebo?
balance: The definitive trial showed no protection. E.mbrace randomised over 17,600 adults aged 60 or older with a urinary tract infection in the previous 2 years to the nine-valent extraintestinal pathogenic E. coli vaccine ExPEC9V (the specific tested product) or placebo. Invasive E. coli disease caused by vaccine O-serotypes occurred in 11 vaccine versus 13 placebo recipients — vaccine efficacy 14.63% in relative terms with a 95% confidence interval from −106.57 to 65.38, squarely consistent with no effect. The trial was stopped at its prespecified futility analysis despite the vaccine producing robust antibody responses, and development of the vaccine was discontinued. Antibodies rose; disease did not fall. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — a very large phase 3 trial, stopped for futility, with a point estimate near zero.

title: IL-6 receptor antagonists for hospitalised COVID-19: RECOVERY and REMAP-CAP agree on a survival benefit (Tier C)
question: In patients admitted to hospital with hypoxic COVID-19 and systemic inflammation, do IL-6 receptor antagonists (tocilizumab, sarilumab) reduce 28-day mortality?
balance: Two large platform trials point the same way: IL-6 receptor antagonists reduce mortality in hospitalised patients with hypoxic, inflamed COVID-19, most of whom were also receiving corticosteroids. In RECOVERY, 28-day mortality was 31% with tocilizumab versus 35% with usual care — an absolute reduction of 4 percentage points, a rate ratio of 0.85 (95% CI 0.76 to 0.94), i.e. a 15% relative reduction — and more patients were discharged alive (57% vs 50%). In REMAP-CAP's critically ill population, tocilizumab and sarilumab both improved organ-support-free days (median 10 and 11 vs 0 days; adjusted OR 1.64 and 1.76) with a pooled 90-day survival hazard ratio of 1.61 (95% credible interval 1.25 to 2.08). The benefit belongs to the population studied: patients sick enough to need oxygen with CRP at least 75 mg/L, on background steroids. PROPOSED LIKELY — two independent platform trials (DOUBLE-A), concordant on survival-relevant endpoints. Tier C: a mortality claim, so the developer reviews this shelf personally.

title: Early outpatient remdesivir (PINETREE): hospitalisation cut from 5.3% to 0.7% in high-risk patients (Tier C)
question: In non-hospitalised patients with COVID-19 within 7 days of symptom onset and at least one risk factor, does a 3-day course of intravenous remdesivir prevent hospitalisation or death versus placebo?
balance: One well-run trial with a large effect. PINETREE randomised 562 non-hospitalised patients with COVID-19, symptom onset within 7 days, and at least one risk factor for progression, to 3 days of intravenous remdesivir or placebo. The composite of COVID-19-related hospitalisation or death by day 28 occurred in 0.7% (2 patients) on remdesivir versus 5.3% (15) on placebo — hazard ratio 0.13 (95% CI 0.03 to 0.59), an 87% relative reduction and a 4.6-percentage-point absolute reduction; there were no deaths in either group by day 28, so the composite is driven by hospitalisations. Medically attended visits were also fewer (1.6% vs 8.3%; HR 0.19, 95% CI 0.07 to 0.56), and adverse events were similar (42.3% vs 46.3%). The event count is small (17 events total) and the trial predates widespread vaccination and later variants, which limits how far the absolute benefit travels. PROPOSED LIKELY — a single double-blind placebo-controlled trial with a big, significant effect on hospitalisation. Tier C: death is part of the composite claim, so the developer reviews this shelf personally.

title: Early convalescent plasma for outpatients (CSSC-004): hospitalisation 2.9% vs 6.3% when given early and high-titre
question: In symptomatic outpatients treated within 8 days of onset, does early high-titre COVID-19 convalescent plasma prevent hospitalisation versus control plasma?
balance: Timing and titre were the whole story. CSSC-004 randomised 1,225 symptomatic outpatients within 8 days of symptom onset to high-titre COVID-19 convalescent plasma or control plasma, transfused within a day of randomisation. Hospitalisation within 28 days occurred in 2.9% (17/592) on convalescent plasma versus 6.3% (37/589) on control plasma — an absolute reduction of 3.4 percentage points (95% CI 1.0 to 5.8), a 54% relative reduction. Nearly everyone hospitalised was unvaccinated (53 of 54; one was partially vaccinated), so the trial speaks to an unvaccinated population treated early with potent product. This does not rehabilitate convalescent plasma given late to hospitalised patients, where the big trials were negative — a different question with its own shelf logic. PROPOSED LIKELY — one large double-blind randomised trial with a clear absolute benefit on hospitalisation, in the population and window it studied.

title: Inhaled budesonide in community COVID-19: faster recovery in PRINCIPLE and STOIC; admission/death benefit not proven (Tier C)
question: In older or comorbid adults with suspected COVID-19 in the community (up to 14 days unwell), does inhaled budesonide speed recovery and reduce hospital admission or death versus usual care?
balance: Two randomised trials agree that inhaled budesonide speeds recovery from community COVID-19; neither proves it prevents admission or death. In PRINCIPLE (older or comorbid UK adults, unwell up to 14 days), budesonide shortened time to first self-reported recovery by an estimated 2.94 days (median 11.8 vs 14.7 days; HR 1.21, 95% BCI 1.08 to 1.36; probability of superiority >0.999, meeting its threshold). The hospital admission or death outcome favoured budesonide — estimated 6.8% vs 8.8%, OR 0.75 (95% BCI 0.55 to 1.03) — but its probability of superiority, 0.963, fell short of the prespecified 0.975 threshold, so that claim is unproven. The smaller double-blind STOIC trial was concordant on early deterioration: COVID-19-related urgent care visits in 1 of 69 (1%) on budesonide versus 10 of 70 (14%) on usual care per-protocol. PROPOSED LIKELY — for faster recovery (DOUBLE-A: PRINCIPLE + STOIC); the admission/death benefit is a favourable trend only, and the balance says so plainly. Tier C: the composite includes death, so the developer reviews this shelf personally.

title: Vilobelimab in ventilated COVID-19 (PANAMO): mortality signal whose primary analysis missed significance — OUTSTANDING-SINGLE (Tier C)
question: In invasively ventilated patients with severe COVID-19, does the anti-C5a antibody vilobelimab improve survival versus placebo, each on standard care?
balance: OUTSTANDING-SINGLE, and a borderline one: this shelf rests on a single phase 3 trial whose prespecified primary analysis did not reach significance. In PANAMO, 368 invasively ventilated patients with severe COVID-19 were randomised to the anti-C5a antibody vilobelimab or placebo, each on standard care. Deaths by day 28 were 31% (54/177) on vilobelimab versus 40% (77/191) on placebo (Kaplan–Meier estimates 32% vs 42%), but the primary site-stratified analysis gave a hazard ratio of 0.73 (95% CI 0.50 to 1.06) with p=0.094 — not significant. A predefined unstratified analysis was significant (HR 0.67, 95% CI 0.48 to 0.96; p=0.027). Serious treatment-emergent adverse events were similar (59% vs 63%). A possible ~9–10 point absolute mortality advantage that depends on which prespecified analysis you read is a genuine signal, not a settled benefit. (Desk note: the topic draft quoted mortality of 31.9% vs 41.6%; those figures do not appear in the published abstract and are not used here.) PROPOSED POSSIBLE — single trial, primary analysis formally negative, supportive secondary analysis positive. Tier C: a mortality claim, so the developer reviews this shelf personally, and the OUTSTANDING-SINGLE flag stays on it.

title: Ivermectin for early COVID-19: no benefit in TOGETHER or COVID-OUT — two large trials agree
question: In symptomatic high-risk outpatients within 7 days of onset, does ivermectin 400 µg/kg daily for 3 days reduce hospitalisation or extended emergency observation versus placebo?
balance: Two large placebo-controlled platform trials, run independently on different continents, agree: ivermectin did not help. In TOGETHER (Brazil), the composite of hospitalisation or extended emergency observation occurred in 14.7% on ivermectin versus 16.3% on placebo (relative risk 0.90, 95% Bayesian credible interval 0.70 to 1.16), with the modified intention-to-treat and per-protocol analyses the same (RR 0.89 and 0.94) and no significant effects on secondary outcomes or adverse events. In COVID-OUT (USA), the ivermectin arm's adjusted odds ratio for the primary composite of hypoxemia, emergency visit, hospitalisation, or death was 1.05 (95% CI 0.76 to 1.45; P=0.78) — the point estimate on the wrong side of 1. When two adequately sized double-blind trials both land on no effect, the question is settled for this dose and population. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — DOUBLE-A concordant nulls.

title: Colchicine for community COVID-19: COLCORONA missed its primary endpoint overall; PRINCIPLE stopped for futility (Tier C)
question: In non-hospitalised patients aged 40 years or older with COVID-19 and at least one risk factor, does colchicine reduce the composite of death or hospital admission versus placebo?
balance: Read whole, the randomised evidence does not show that colchicine helps community COVID-19. COLCORONA, the big double-blind trial, missed its primary endpoint in the full population: death or hospital admission occurred in 4.7% on colchicine versus 5.8% on placebo (OR 0.79, 95.1% CI 0.61 to 1.03; p=0.081). Only inside the prespecified PCR-confirmed subset did the difference reach significance (4.6% vs 6.0%; OR 0.75, 95% CI 0.57 to 0.99; p=0.042) — a subset of a negative trial, not a positive trial. The second randomised evaluation, PRINCIPLE's colchicine arm, was stopped for futility on recovery time (HR 0.92, 95% credible interval 0.72 to 1.16; probability of a meaningful benefit 1.8%), with hospital admission or death also null (OR 0.76, 95% CrI 0.28 to 1.89). Colchicine also caused more diarrhoea (13.7% vs 7.3% in COLCORONA), though serious adverse events were slightly fewer (4.9% vs 6.3%). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the headline result of the only adequately sized trial is null and the platform arm was futile; the PCR-confirmed subset keeps this from a stronger null stamp, and the balance gives it its exact weight: a subset finding, nothing more. Tier C: the composite includes death, so the developer reviews this shelf personally.

title: suPAR-guided anakinra for COVID-19 pneumonia (SAVE-MORE): better day-28 status and lower mortality in one biomarker-guided trial (Tier C)
question: In hospitalised patients with COVID-19 pneumonia selected by plasma suPAR of at least 6 ng/mL (risk of respiratory failure), does early anakinra improve day-28 clinical status versus placebo?
balance: A biomarker-guided strategy with a strong single-trial result. SAVE-MORE randomised 594 hospitalised patients with COVID-19 pneumonia whose plasma suPAR was at least 6 ng/mL — a marker of risk of respiratory failure — to anakinra (interleukin-1 receptor antagonist) or placebo; 85.9% were also receiving dexamethasone. By day 28, patients on anakinra had substantially better clinical status on the WHO Clinical Progression Scale (adjusted proportional odds ratio 0.36, 95% CI 0.26 to 0.50, for a worse outcome), with a greater median improvement (decrease of 4 vs 3 points; OR 0.40), less progression in organ dysfunction (day-7 SOFA odds ratio 0.63, P=0.004), shorter hospital stay, and lower 28-day mortality (HR 0.45, P=0.045). It is one trial, and the mortality result is a secondary endpoint with a p-value just under 0.05; the strategy also depends on suPAR testing being available and applied with the same threshold. PROPOSED LIKELY — a well-powered double-blind trial hitting its ordinal primary endpoint decisively, with a concordant mortality signal. Tier C: a mortality benefit will print on this shelf, so the developer reviews it personally.

title: Therapeutic-dose heparin in noncritically ill COVID-19: more organ-support-free days in the multiplatform trial and HEP-COVID (Tier C)
question: In hospitalised patients with COVID-19 who are not critically ill, does therapeutic-dose heparin increase organ-support-free days versus usual-care thromboprophylaxis?
balance: For patients on the ward — explicitly not the critically ill — therapeutic-dose heparin improved outcomes in two randomised evaluations. The combined ATTACC / ACTIV-4a / REMAP-CAP multiplatform trial (2,219 noncritically ill patients) found a 98.6% probability that therapeutic-dose heparin increased organ-support-free days versus usual-care thromboprophylaxis (adjusted OR 1.27, 95% credible interval 1.03 to 1.58), with an adjusted absolute increase of 4.0 percentage points (95% CrI 0.5 to 7.2) in survival to discharge without organ support; results held across d-dimer subgroups. HEP-COVID, which enrolled patients with very high d-dimer or sepsis-induced coagulopathy, found the primary composite of thromboembolism or death in 28.7% on therapeutic versus 41.9% on standard dosing (RR 0.68, 95% CI 0.49 to 0.96) — with the benefit concentrated in non-ICU patients (RR 0.46) and absent in ICU patients (RR 0.92). The cost is bleeding: major bleeding 1.9% versus 0.9% in the multiplatform trial and 4.7% versus 1.6% in HEP-COVID (not significant there). PROPOSED LIKELY — DOUBLE-A concordance in noncritically ill patients, with the bleeding trade-off printed, not buried. Tier C: death is embedded in the primary ordinal outcome, so the developer reviews this shelf personally. The companion critically-ill multiplatform report is a separate question and is not this shelf.

title: After source control for intra-abdominal infection, about 4 days of antibiotics is enough (STOP-IT)
question: In complicated intra-abdominal infection with adequate source control, is a fixed course of about 4 days of antibiotics as safe as continuing until 2 days after fever, leukocytosis and ileus resolve (up to 10 days)?
balance: One large randomised trial answers this cleanly. In STOP-IT, 518 patients with complicated intra-abdominal infection and adequate source control were randomised to a fixed course of 4±1 days or to antibiotics continued until 2 days after fever, leukocytosis and ileus resolved (median 8 days). The composite of surgical-site infection, recurrent intra-abdominal infection or death within 30 days was 21.8% on the short course versus 22.3% on the longer course (absolute difference −0.5 percentage points; 95% CI −7.0 to 8.0; P=0.92), with no significant difference in any component. The lesson is conditional: the clock starts at adequate source control, and the trial says nothing about patients whose source was not controlled. PROPOSED LIKELY — the fixed short course is as safe as the longer course once source control is adequate (Tier C: death is a component of the primary composite).

title: Prosthetic joint infection: 6 weeks of antibiotics is not enough — 12 weeks won (DATIPO)
question: In microbiologically confirmed prosthetic joint infection managed with appropriate surgery, is 6 weeks of antibiotic therapy non-inferior to 12 weeks?
balance: This duration trial's answer is 'longer'. In DATIPO, 410 patients with microbiologically confirmed prosthetic joint infection managed with an appropriate surgical procedure were randomised to 6 or 12 weeks of antibiotics. Persistent infection within 2 years occurred in 18.1% on 6 weeks versus 9.4% on 12 weeks — an absolute risk difference of 8.7 percentage points (95% CI 1.8 to 15.6) — and non-inferiority of the shorter course was not shown. Halving therapy roughly doubled the failure rate in absolute terms. PROPOSED LIKELY (harm) — the harm belongs to the 6-week course; 12 weeks remains the course this trial supports.

title: De-escalating antibiotics in severe sepsis: the one randomised trial found no ICU-stay benefit and more superinfections
question: In ICU patients with severe sepsis on appropriate empiric therapy, does protocolised de-escalation to the narrowest effective regimen match continuation of the empiric regimen on ICU stay and outcomes?
balance: THIN — a single small trial, and its abstract does not say what stewardship advocates might expect. Leone and colleagues randomised 116 patients with severe sepsis in nine French ICUs to de-escalation or continuation of empiric therapy, with ICU length of stay as the primary outcome and a 2-day non-inferiority margin. Median ICU stay was 9 days with de-escalation versus 8 days with continuation (mean difference 3.4 days; 95% CI −1.7 to 8.5; P=0.71) — the authors' own conclusion was that de-escalation resulted in a prolonged ICU stay, and non-inferiority was not demonstrated. Superinfection occurred in 27% versus 11% (P=0.03) and antibiotic days were higher, not lower, with de-escalation; mortality was similar in a trial far too small to judge it. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — the randomised evidence neither confirms de-escalation's safety on patient outcomes nor proves harm; it is one small open-label trial powered on ICU stay.

title: After discharge, repeated MRSA decolonisation cut infections by about a third (CLEAR)
question: In hospitalised MRSA carriers after discharge, does repeated decolonisation (chlorhexidine body wash and mouthwash plus nasal mupirocin, 5 days twice monthly for 6 months) reduce MRSA infection and infection-related hospitalisation versus hygiene education alone?
balance: A large, clean randomised trial. In CLEAR, 2,121 MRSA carriers were randomised after discharge to hygiene education alone or education plus decolonisation (chlorhexidine mouthwash, chlorhexidine baths or showers, and nasal mupirocin, 5 days twice monthly for 6 months) and followed for 1 year. MRSA infection occurred in 9.2% with education alone versus 6.3% with decolonisation — a hazard ratio of 0.70 (95% CI 0.52 to 0.96; P=0.03), i.e. a 30% relative reduction, with a number needed to treat of 30 to prevent one infection; infection-related hospitalisation was also lower (HR 0.76; 95% CI 0.62 to 0.93). Side effects were all mild and occurred in 4.2%. PROPOSED LIKELY — one large trial with a patient-important outcome and absolute rates that make the benefit's size plain.

title: Gloves and gowns for every ICU contact: no effect on combined MRSA/VRE acquisition (BUGG)
question: In medical and surgical ICUs, does requiring gloves and gowns for all patient contact reduce acquisition of MRSA or VRE versus usual care?
balance: A 20-ICU cluster-randomised trial with a split answer. In BUGG, universal glove-and-gown use for all patient contact did not change the primary outcome — combined MRSA or VRE acquisition (difference in change −1.71 acquisitions per 1,000 patient-days; 95% CI −6.15 to 2.73; P=.57) — and did not change VRE acquisition. MRSA acquisition alone, a secondary outcome, fell more in intervention ICUs (difference −2.98 per 1,000 patient-days; 95% CI −5.58 to −0.38; P=.046), alongside fewer room entries and better room-exit hand hygiene; the authors themselves say the secondary findings require replication. There was no significant difference in adverse events. PROPOSED SPLIT — LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for the combined primary outcome; POSSIBLE for MRSA acquisition alone.

title: Enhanced terminal room disinfection: adding UV-C helped; bleach strategies did not clearly (BETR Disinfection)
question: In hospital rooms vacated by patients infected or colonised with target organisms, do enhanced terminal disinfection strategies (ultraviolet light, bleach, or both) reduce acquisition and infection in the next occupant versus standard quaternary-ammonium disinfection?
balance: One large pragmatic cluster-randomised crossover trial, nine hospitals, with different answers by strategy. Adding UV-C to standard disinfection reduced the incidence of target-organism infection or colonisation in the next room occupant (33.9 vs 51.3 cases per 10,000 exposure days; relative risk 0.70; 95% CI 0.50 to 0.98; p=0.036). Bleach alone (RR 0.85; 95% CI 0.69 to 1.04; p=0.116) and bleach plus UV-C (RR 0.91; 95% CI 0.76 to 1.09; p=0.303) were not significantly lower, and adding UV to bleach did not change C. difficile infection (RR 1.0; 95% CI 0.57 to 1.75). The UV result is a single significant comparison among several, on a composite dominated by colonisation. PROPOSED SPLIT — POSSIBLE for adding UV-C to standard cleaning; MAYBE (weak evidence) for bleach-based strategies.

title: Surveillance plus expanded barrier precautions in the ICU did not reduce MRSA/VRE (STAR*ICU)
question: In adult ICUs, does active surveillance for MRSA/VRE with expanded barrier precautions reduce colonisation or infection versus existing practice?
balance: A landmark negative cluster-randomised trial. In STAR*ICU, 18 adult ICUs were randomised to surveillance for MRSA/VRE colonisation with results reported and expanded barrier precautions for carriers, or to existing practice (surveillance cultures taken but results not reported). The intervention was delivered — carriers spent a median of 92% of ICU days under barrier precautions versus 38% in control ICUs (P<0.001) — yet the adjusted incidence of MRSA or VRE colonisation or infection was 40.4 versus 35.6 events per 1,000 patient-days at risk (P=0.35), numerically higher in the intervention group. The authors note actual use of precautions by providers was less than required, which is the standing caveat; but as a strategy as implemented, it did not work. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference).

title: Copper alloy surfaces in ICU rooms: fewer infections and colonisation in one small trial
question: In ICU patients, does placement in rooms fitted with copper alloy surfaces on high-touch objects reduce healthcare-acquired infection and MRSA/VRE colonisation versus standard rooms?
balance: THIN — one small randomised trial in the ICUs of three hospitals. Patients placed in rooms with copper alloy surfaces on high-touch objects had a lower rate of the composite of healthcare-acquired infection and/or MRSA or VRE colonisation than patients in standard rooms (7.1% vs 12.3% in absolute proportions; P=.020), and a lower rate of healthcare-acquired infection alone (3.4% vs 8.1%; P=.013). The direction is consistent and the mechanism (continuous antimicrobial activity of copper) is plausible, but this is a single trial, in 16 rooms, unblinded by the nature of the intervention, with a composite that includes colonisation. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — promising, not proven; replication in more settings is exactly what the authors called for.

title: Coronary disease: treating to an LDL target of 50–70 mg/dL matched fixed high-intensity statin (LODESTAR)
question: In patients with coronary artery disease, does treating to an LDL cholesterol target of 50–70 mg/dL with titrated statin therapy prevent major cardiovascular events as well as a fixed high-intensity statin strategy?
balance: One large strategy trial, and the two strategies landed in the same place — partly because they produced nearly identical LDL levels. In LODESTAR, 4,400 patients with coronary artery disease in South Korea were randomised to treat-to-target (LDL 50–70 mg/dL, titrated) or fixed high-intensity statin (rosuvastatin 20 mg or atorvastatin 40 mg). Mean LDL over 3 years was 69.1 versus 68.4 mg/dL. The 3-year composite of death, myocardial infarction, stroke or coronary revascularisation occurred in 8.1% versus 8.7% (absolute difference −0.6 percentage points; upper boundary of the one-sided 97.5% CI 1.1 points; P<.001 for non-inferiority, against a 3.0-point margin). In the target arm, 43% ended on moderate-intensity dosing — the practical dividend is dose flexibility, not better outcomes. PROPOSED LIKELY — non-inferiority of treat-to-target is established by this trial (Tier C: the composite includes death, MI and stroke).

title: Torcetrapib raised HDL by 72% — and increased deaths and cardiovascular events (ILLUMINATE)
question: In high-risk patients, does adding torcetrapib to atorvastatin — raising HDL cholesterol substantially — reduce cardiovascular events, or cause harm?
balance: The canonical warning against treating a surrogate. In ILLUMINATE, 15,067 high-risk patients were randomised to torcetrapib plus atorvastatin or atorvastatin alone. At 12 months the torcetrapib group had HDL cholesterol up 72.1% and LDL cholesterol down 24.9% in relative terms — and systolic blood pressure up 5.4 mm Hg, with lower potassium and higher sodium, bicarbonate and aldosterone, an off-target pattern. Cardiovascular events were increased (hazard ratio 1.25 — a 25% relative increase; 95% CI 1.09 to 1.44; P=0.001) and death from any cause was increased (HR 1.58 — a 58% relative increase; 95% CI 1.14 to 2.19; P=0.006); the trial was terminated prematurely. The authors could not rule out an adverse effect of CETP inhibition itself, but the blood-pressure and aldosterone signals point at this molecule. PROPOSED LIKELY (harm) — for torcetrapib specifically (Tier C: a mortality claim).

title: Heart failure: rosuvastatin did not reduce death or major events in two large trials (CORONA and GISSI-HF)
question: In patients with chronic heart failure, does rosuvastatin reduce mortality and major cardiovascular events compared with placebo?
balance: DOUBLE-A: two large, independent, placebo-controlled trials of the same drug in heart failure, and both are null on the outcomes that matter. In CORONA (5,011 older patients with ischaemic systolic heart failure), rosuvastatin 10 mg did not reduce the composite of cardiovascular death, nonfatal myocardial infarction or nonfatal stroke (hazard ratio 0.92; 95% CI 0.83 to 1.02; P=0.12) or all-cause mortality (HR 0.95; 95% CI 0.86 to 1.05; P=0.31). In GISSI-HF (4,574 patients with heart failure of any cause), rosuvastatin did not reduce death (29% vs 28%; adjusted HR 1.00; 95.5% CI 0.898 to 1.122; p=0.943) or death-or-cardiovascular-admission (adjusted HR 1.01; 99% CI 0.908 to 1.112). CORONA did show fewer cardiovascular hospitalisations on rosuvastatin (a prespecified secondary count of hospitalisations) — but hospitalisation benefit without a mortality or primary-endpoint benefit is exactly the pattern this library does not oversell, and GISSI-HF's admission composite was null. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) (Tier C: a mortality question).

title: Fish oil (n-3 PUFA) after a heart attack: benefit in 1999, none on modern therapy (GISSI-Prevenzione, OMEGA, Alpha Omega)
question: In patients after myocardial infarction, does n-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid supplementation (about 1 g daily) reduce death and major cardiovascular events?
balance: DOUBLE-A with an era split — this is the honest way to read three large trials. GISSI-Prevenzione (1999; 11,324 patients soon after myocardial infarction, in an era before routine statins and modern antiplatelet therapy) found n-3 PUFA 1 g daily lowered the composite of death, nonfatal myocardial infarction and stroke by a relative 10% (two-way analysis; 95% CI 1 to 18) to 15% (four-way), driven by fewer deaths. A decade later, on guideline-directed therapy, both OMEGA (3,851 patients; sudden cardiac death 1.5% vs 1.5%) and Alpha Omega (4,837 patients; EPA-DHA hazard ratio 1.01; 95% CI 0.87 to 1.17 for major cardiovascular events) found nothing. The 1999 result may have been real for its era — an untreated-baseline effect that modern therapy now covers — but for a patient on today's post-MI treatment, the randomised evidence says fish oil capsules add nothing measurable. PROPOSED SPLIT — POSSIBLE benefit in the pre-modern-therapy era / LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) on modern therapy (Tier C: a mortality claim).
stamp: SPLIT — POSSIBLE benefit in the pre-modern-therapy era (GISSI-Prevenzione) / LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) on top of modern post-MI therapy (OMEGA and Alpha Omega)

title: Kidney transplant recipients: fluvastatin missed its primary endpoint but cut cardiac death and MI (ALERT)
question: In renal transplant recipients, does fluvastatin versus placebo reduce major adverse cardiac events?
balance: THIN — a single trial, and its two layers point different ways, so this shelf splits. In ALERT, 2,102 renal transplant recipients were randomised to fluvastatin or placebo for a mean of 5.1 years; LDL cholesterol fell 32% relative on fluvastatin. The primary endpoint — cardiac death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, or coronary intervention — was not significantly reduced (risk ratio 0.83; 95% CI 0.64 to 1.06; p=0.139). But the prespecified secondary composite of cardiac death or nonfatal myocardial infarction did differ: 70 versus 104 events (6.7% versus 9.9% in absolute terms; RR 0.65; 95% CI 0.48 to 0.88; p=0.005). Other secondary endpoints, including overall mortality and graft outcomes, did not differ significantly. The coronary-intervention component counted in the primary endpoint but not the secondary one is the most likely reason the two disagree. PROPOSED SPLIT — MAYBE (weak evidence) on the trial's own primary question; POSSIBLE for cardiac death or nonfatal myocardial infarction (Tier C: a mortality-containing endpoint).
stamp: SPLIT — MAYBE (weak evidence) for the primary composite endpoint (not significant) / POSSIBLE reduction in cardiac death or non-fatal myocardial infarction (prespecified secondary)

title: After acute coronary syndrome, adding ezetimibe to pitavastatin and driving LDL below 70 did not significantly cut events (HIJ-PROPER)
question: In patients with acute coronary syndrome and dyslipidaemia, does pitavastatin plus ezetimibe targeting LDL cholesterol below 70 mg/dL reduce cardiovascular events versus pitavastatin alone targeting below 100 mg/dL?
balance: THIN — one open-label Japanese trial, underpowered beside the ezetimibe outcome trials in broader populations, and formally negative. In HIJ-PROPER, 1,734 patients with acute coronary syndrome and dyslipidaemia were randomised to pitavastatin plus ezetimibe targeting LDL below 70 mg/dL or pitavastatin alone targeting below 100 mg/dL; achieved LDL was 65.1 versus 84.6 mg/dL. The primary composite (death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke, unstable angina or ischaemia-driven revascularisation) occurred in 32.8% versus 36.9% (hazard ratio 0.89; 95% CI 0.76 to 1.04; P=0.152) — a point estimate favouring combination therapy whose confidence interval includes both a 24% relative benefit and a small harm, so the trial settles nothing by itself. A prespecified subgroup with high sitosterol (cholesterol-absorption markers) showed HR 0.71 (95% CI 0.56 to 0.91), a hypothesis about who benefits from absorption blockade, not a trial-level result. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (Tier C: the composite includes death, MI and stroke).
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence)

title: Diabetes with retinopathy: intensive LDL lowering to below 70 mg/dL did not significantly cut cardiovascular events (EMPATHY)
question: In patients with type 2 diabetes, hypercholesterolaemia and diabetic retinopathy but no prior cardiovascular disease, does intensive lipid lowering targeting LDL cholesterol below 70 mg/dL reduce cardiovascular events versus standard targeting of 100 to under 120 mg/dL?
balance: THIN — one large Japanese trial that missed its target separation and its primary endpoint. EMPATHY randomised 5,144 patients with type 2 diabetes, hypercholesterolaemia and diabetic retinopathy, without prior cardiovascular disease, to intensive therapy targeting LDL below 70 mg/dL or standard therapy targeting 100 to under 120 mg/dL. The primary endpoint of cardiovascular events or cardiovascular death gave a hazard ratio of 0.84 (95% CI 0.67 to 1.07; P=0.15) — not significant. The achieved LDL gap was small (about 28 mg/dL), and fewer than half of either group reached their target, so the trial tested a strategy that was only weakly delivered; a retinopathy substudy (157 patients with fundus photographs) likewise found no significant difference in retinopathy progression. One correction to this shelf's originating draft: the standard-care target was 100 to under 120 mg/dL, not 70–100, and the trial's primary endpoint was cardiovascular, not eye progression. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — intensive targeting may help, but this trial does not show it.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence)

title: Hypertension: pravastatin versus usual care did not reduce mortality in ALLHAT's lipid trial
question: In older hypertensive patients with moderately elevated LDL cholesterol, does open-label pravastatin 40 mg reduce all-cause mortality and coronary events versus usual care?
balance: A very large pragmatic trial with a null result — and a built-in explanation. In the ALLHAT lipid-lowering trial, 10,355 hypertensive patients aged 55 or older with LDL cholesterol 120–189 mg/dL were randomised to pravastatin 40 mg or usual care and followed a mean of 4.8 years. All-cause mortality was essentially identical (relative risk 0.99; 95% CI 0.89 to 1.11; P=.88; 6-year rates 14.9% vs 15.3%), and coronary heart disease events were not significantly reduced (RR 0.91; 95% CI 0.79 to 1.04; P=.16; 6-year rates 9.3% vs 10.4%). The catch is contrast: by year 4, about a third of the usual-care group had started lipid-lowering drugs themselves, so total cholesterol fell 17% relative on pravastatin versus 8% on usual care — a much smaller lipid gap than in blinded placebo trials. The trial shows that offering pravastatin into a usual-care system that adopts statins anyway changes outcomes little; it does not overturn the blinded-trial evidence that statins lower events versus no statin. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — for pravastatin versus usual care as delivered (Tier C: a mortality question).
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference)

title: Familial chylomicronaemia: volanesorsen cut triglycerides sharply but lowered platelets (APPROACH)
question: In familial chylomicronaemia syndrome, does volanesorsen (an apolipoprotein C-III antisense oligonucleotide) lower triglycerides versus placebo, and at what cost?
balance: THIN — one small phase 3 trial in a rare disease, with a dramatic surrogate benefit and a real harm, so this shelf splits. In APPROACH, 66 patients with familial chylomicronaemia syndrome received volanesorsen (named specifically because, as of the trial era, it was not FDA-approved; it is an apolipoprotein C-III antisense oligonucleotide) or placebo for 52 weeks. At 3 months, triglycerides had fallen 77% relative on volanesorsen (mean decrease 1,712 mg/dL) versus an 18% relative increase on placebo; 77% of volanesorsen patients reached triglycerides below 750 mg/dL versus 10% on placebo. Against that: injection-site reactions in 20 of 33 treated patients versus none on placebo, and platelet counts below 100,000 per microlitre in 15 of 33 versus none — including two patients below 25,000; no patient fell below 50,000 after enhanced platelet monitoring began. The trial reports the triglyceride endpoint, not a demonstrated reduction in pancreatitis. PROPOSED SPLIT — POSSIBLE for triglyceride lowering (a surrogate, from one 66-patient trial) / LIKELY (harm) for thrombocytopenia and injection-site reactions.
stamp: SPLIT — POSSIBLE triglyceride lowering (surrogate endpoint, single small trial) / LIKELY (harm) thrombocytopenia and injection-site reactions

title: Advanced medullary thyroid cancer: vandetanib and cabozantinib each roughly halve-to-quarter the progression hazard vs placebo — progression-free survival, not overall survival
question: In locally advanced or metastatic medullary thyroid cancer, do the multikinase inhibitors vandetanib or cabozantinib improve outcomes compared with placebo?
balance: LIKELY: two independent double-blind phase 3 trials, each against placebo, show large progression-free survival gains. In ZETA (331 patients), vandetanib 300 mg/day gave a progression-free survival hazard ratio of 0.46 (95% CI 0.31 to 0.69) — a 54% relative reduction in the progression hazard — with higher objective response and disease control rates. In EXAM (330 patients with documented radiographic progression), cabozantinib 140 mg/day gave a median progression-free survival of 11.2 months vs 4.0 months on placebo (hazard ratio 0.28; 95% CI 0.19 to 0.40 — a 72% relative reduction), with responses in 28% vs 0%. Neither trial demonstrated an overall-survival benefit in its primary report (ZETA survival was immature, hazard ratio 0.89 with a wide interval; EXAM's survival analysis is not reported in the primary paper). Toxicity is substantial: diarrhoea, rash, nausea and hypertension with vandetanib; with cabozantinib, dose reductions in 79% and discontinuation for adverse events in 16%. The benefit claim is delay of progression, not longer life.
stamp: LIKELY

title: RET-mutant medullary thyroid cancer: selpercatinib beats cabozantinib/vandetanib head-to-head — progression-free survival HR 0.28, and far better tolerated
question: In advanced RET-mutant medullary thyroid cancer, is the selective RET inhibitor selpercatinib better than the multikinase inhibitors cabozantinib or vandetanib as first-line treatment?
balance: LIKELY (single trial — developer's personal ruling requested under the outstanding-single rule): in the one randomised phase 3 trial (LIBRETTO-531, 291 patients with progressive RET-mutant medullary thyroid cancer), first-line selpercatinib beat physician's choice of cabozantinib or vandetanib on progression-free survival — hazard ratio 0.28 (95% CI 0.16 to 0.48), a 72% relative reduction in the hazard of progression or death; median not reached vs 16.8 months at a median follow-up of only 12 months, with 12-month progression-free survival 86.8% vs 65.7% in absolute terms. Overall response was 69.4% vs 38.8%. Selpercatinib was also easier to stay on: dose reductions 38.9% vs 77.3% and discontinuation for adverse events 4.7% vs 26.8%. Overall survival cannot be judged yet — follow-up is short and control patients could cross over to selpercatinib at progression. One trial only, an industry-funded interim analysis: the effect is large and the comparison is against active drugs, not placebo, but replication does not exist.
stamp: LIKELY (single trial — developer's personal ruling requested under the outstanding-single rule)

title: Radioiodine-refractory differentiated thyroid cancer after lenvatinib/sorafenib: cabozantinib prolongs progression-free survival (HR 0.22) — one interim trial analysis
question: In radioiodine-refractory differentiated thyroid cancer that has progressed after lenvatinib or sorafenib, does cabozantinib improve outcomes compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (single trial — developer's personal ruling requested): in the one randomised trial (COSMIC-311, 187 patients with radioiodine-refractory differentiated thyroid cancer who had progressed on lenvatinib and/or sorafenib, a population with no standard option), cabozantinib 60 mg/day prolonged progression-free survival vs placebo — hazard ratio 0.22 (96% CI 0.13 to 0.36), a 78% relative reduction in the progression hazard; median not reached vs 1.9 months at a preplanned INTERIM analysis with median follow-up of 6.2 months. The co-primary objective-response end point formally missed its prespecified significance level (15% vs 0%; P = 0.028 against a required alpha of 0.01). Toxicity was heavy: grade 3-4 adverse events in 57% vs 26%, and serious treatment-related events in 16% vs 2%, though no treatment-related deaths. Placebo patients could cross over at progression, so overall survival will be hard to read. One interim analysis of one trial, against placebo, in a no-option population: a real progression benefit is probable, its size and durability not yet settled.
stamp: POSSIBLE (single trial — developer's personal ruling requested)

title: BRAF V600E anaplastic thyroid cancer: dabrafenib + trametinib responded in 69% (11 of 16) — single-arm evidence in a near-uniformly fatal cancer
question: In BRAF V600E-mutated anaplastic thyroid cancer, does dabrafenib plus trametinib produce meaningful tumour responses?
balance: POSSIBLE (single-arm evidence — Tier C, developer's personal ruling required): anaplastic thyroid cancer is among the most lethal solid tumours, historically killing most patients within months, and the BRAF V600E-mutant subset is the one place targeted therapy has changed the picture. In the ROAR basket trial's anaplastic cohort — 16 evaluable patients, all previously treated with radiation and/or surgery and six with prior systemic therapy — dabrafenib plus trametinib produced a confirmed overall response rate of 69% (11 of 16; 95% CI 41% to 89%), with seven responses ongoing at the report; 12-month estimates were 79% for progression-free survival and 80% for overall survival, against a historical expectation of roughly 20-40% alive at one year with conventional care. There is NO control group, the cohort is 16 patients, and response rate is the primary evidence — this is dramatic-signal evidence in an orphan disease, not proof of the size a randomised trial would give. Common adverse events across the basket's safety population were fatigue (38%), fever (37%) and nausea (35%). Benefit, if real at this scale, applies only to the BRAF V600E-mutant minority (about a quarter to a half of anaplastic cancers) — mutation testing is the gate.
stamp: POSSIBLE (single-arm evidence — Tier C, developer's personal ruling required)
