title: Heart failure: fat-soluble (lipophilic) statins — atorvastatin and pitavastatin — as a contrast to the water-soluble rosuvastatin trials
question: In patients with chronic heart failure, do fat-soluble (lipophilic) statins such as atorvastatin or pitavastatin improve clinical outcomes, in contrast to the water-soluble (hydrophilic) rosuvastatin that was null in CORONA and GISSI-HF?
balance: This shelf exists as the contrast to Shelf #2232, where two large trials of rosuvastatin — a water-soluble (hydrophilic) statin — found no benefit in heart failure. The hypothesis behind it (argued in an editorial by this library's developer at the time) is that the null belonged to the molecule's solubility class: a fat-soluble (lipophilic) statin, which penetrates cell membranes including myocardium, might behave differently. The direct randomised evidence for fat-soluble statins in heart failure is much thinner than the rosuvastatin evidence, and it does not confirm the hypothesis on clinical outcomes. PEARL randomised 574 Japanese patients with chronic heart failure to pitavastatin (lipophilic) or control: the primary composite of cardiac death or hospitalisation for worsening heart failure did not differ (adjusted HR 0.922; 95% CI 0.632 to 1.345; P=0.672). There was a significant interaction with ejection fraction (P=0.004): in patients with LVEF at least 30%, the composite was lower on pitavastatin (adjusted HR 0.525; 95% CI 0.308 to 0.896; P=0.018), while below 30% the point estimate ran the other way (adjusted HR 1.582; 95% CI 0.890 to 2.813) — a subgroup pattern, not an overall benefit. The one placebo-controlled atorvastatin trial (Sola 2006, 108 patients with non-ischaemic heart failure and LVEF at most 35%) improved ejection fraction (0.33 to 0.37 on atorvastatin while placebo declined; P=0.01), reduced ventricular dimensions, and lowered inflammatory markers over 12 months — surrogate and imaging endpoints only, with no power for death or hospitalisation. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): the fat-soluble hypothesis remains biologically coherent and was exactly what PEARL set out to test (its abstract opens by contrasting lipophilic pitavastatin with the negative hydrophilic rosuvastatin trials), but on hard outcomes the lipophilic evidence is one null-primary trial with a subgroup signal plus one small surrogate-endpoint trial. Nothing here overturns #2232; it records that the contrast was tested and not confirmed. Tier C: heart-failure mortality and hospitalisation claims, so the developer reviews this shelf personally.

title: Frail elderly patients stable on a vitamin K antagonist: switching to a DOAC caused more bleeding (FRAIL-AF)
question: In frail patients aged 75 or older with atrial fibrillation already stable on a vitamin K antagonist, does switching to a direct oral anticoagulant reduce bleeding compared with continuing the VKA?
balance: A large pragmatic trial whose result ran against its hypothesis. FRAIL-AF randomised 1,330 frail patients (age 75 or older, Groningen Frailty Indicator score at least 3; mean age 83) with atrial fibrillation who were managed on a vitamin K antagonist, to switch to a non-vitamin-K oral anticoagulant (NOAC/DOAC) or to continue INR-guided VKA treatment, followed for 12 months. The primary outcome — major or clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding — occurred more often after switching: 101 events in the switch arm versus 62 in the continuation arm, hazard ratio 1.69 (95% CI 1.23 to 2.32), and the trial was stopped early for futility. Thromboembolic events were not reduced (HR 1.26; 95% CI 0.60 to 2.61). PROPOSED LIKELY (harm): in frail elderly patients already stable on a VKA, switching to a DOAC increases bleeding without a thromboembolism advantage. This is a verdict about switching stable patients, not about starting anticoagulation: in the untreated very elderly, low-dose edoxaban helped (ELDERCARE-AF, drafted topic #2244) — the pair is the balance.

title: Where dronedarone harms: permanent AF with risk factors, and severe heart failure (PALLAS + ANDROMEDA)
question: In permanent atrial fibrillation with cardiovascular risk factors, and in recently decompensated severe heart failure, does dronedarone reduce events — or increase death and hospitalisation?
balance: DOUBLE-A harm: two double-blind placebo-controlled trials, in two different populations, both stopped early because dronedarone hurt people. In PALLAS (permanent AF in patients 65 or older with risk factors for major vascular events; 3,236 enrolled), dronedarone roughly doubled the first coprimary outcome of stroke, myocardial infarction, systemic embolism or cardiovascular death (43 vs 19 events; hazard ratio 2.29 — a 129% relative increase; 95% CI 1.34 to 3.94; P=0.002), doubled cardiovascular death (HR 2.11; 95% CI 1.00 to 4.49), more than doubled stroke (HR 2.32), and increased heart-failure hospitalisation (HR 1.81). In ANDROMEDA (627 patients hospitalised with symptomatic heart failure and severe LV systolic dysfunction), dronedarone doubled early mortality — 8.1% versus 3.8% died over a median of 2 months (HR 2.13; 95% CI 1.07 to 4.25; P=0.03) — the excess predominantly from worsening heart failure. The positive sibling trial (ATHENA, non-permanent AF) is carded elsewhere in this library; this shelf is the harm boundary. PROPOSED LIKELY (harm), Tier C: mortality claims, developer's personal-approval territory.

title: Adding vein-of-Marshall ethanol infusion to ablation for persistent AF: a modest gain in freedom from AF (VENUS)
question: In persistent atrial fibrillation, does vein-of-Marshall ethanol infusion plus catheter ablation improve freedom from AF or atrial tachycardia versus ablation alone?
balance: THIN — one randomised trial, a real but modest gain. VENUS randomised 350 patients with persistent AF referred for first ablation (343 analysed) to catheter ablation alone or ablation plus retrograde ethanol infusion into the vein of Marshall. Freedom from AF or atrial tachycardia after a single procedure, off antiarrhythmic drugs, at both 6 and 12 months was 49.2% with the ethanol addition versus 38.0% with ablation alone — an absolute difference of 11.2 percentage points (95% CI 0.8 to 21.7; P=.04). Ethanol delivery succeeded in 155 of 185 assigned patients; AF burden and perimitral block success also favoured the combined approach, and adverse events were similar. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: a single trial, a borderline P value on the primary outcome, and success still under half — promising adjunct, not a new standard on this evidence alone.

title: After successful AF ablation, rivaroxaban versus aspirin: event rates too low to separate (OCEAN)
question: In patients free of recurrence at least a year after successful AF ablation and at moderate stroke risk, is rivaroxaban superior to aspirin for preventing stroke, systemic embolism, or covert embolic stroke on MRI?
balance: THIN on events, whatever its size. OCEAN randomised 1,284 patients who had undergone successful catheter ablation at least a year earlier and had a CHA2DS2-VASc score of at least 1, to rivaroxaban 15 mg daily or aspirin, followed for 3 years with MRI after enrolment and at 3 years. The primary composite — stroke, systemic embolism, or new covert embolic stroke (a new infarct at least 15 mm on MRI) — occurred in just 5 patients on rivaroxaban (0.31 events per 100 patient-years) versus 9 on aspirin (0.66 per 100 patient-years): relative risk 0.56, but with a 95% confidence interval of 0.19 to 1.65 (P=0.28) — the data are compatible with rivaroxaban being much better, no better, or somewhat worse. Fatal or major bleeding was numerically more frequent with rivaroxaban (1.6% vs 0.6%; HR 2.51; 95% CI 0.79 to 7.95). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): what the trial actually establishes is that event rates after successful ablation are very low; it does not establish that stopping anticoagulation is safe, nor that continuing it helps. Tier C: a stroke claim, so the developer reviews it personally.

title: After AF ablation, left atrial appendage closure matched anticoagulation on events with less bleeding (OPTION)
question: In patients undergoing AF ablation at moderate-to-high stroke risk, is left atrial appendage closure with Watchman FLX noninferior to continued oral anticoagulation for death, stroke or systemic embolism, with less bleeding?
balance: A large randomised trial that met both of its tests. OPTION randomised 1,600 patients with AF undergoing catheter ablation and an elevated CHA2DS2-VASc score (at least 2 in men, at least 3 in women; mean 3.5) to left atrial appendage closure or continued oral anticoagulation. At 36 months, the primary safety endpoint — non-procedure-related major or clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding — occurred in 8.5% with closure versus 18.1% with anticoagulation (P<0.001 for superiority): an absolute reduction of about 10 percentage points. The primary efficacy composite of death from any cause, stroke, or systemic embolism was 5.3% versus 5.8% (P<0.001 for noninferiority), and major bleeding including procedure-related bleeding was also noninferior (3.9% vs 5.0%). Device- or procedure-related complications occurred in 23 patients. PROPOSED LIKELY: closure after ablation is noninferior for events and clearly gentler on bleeding — in patients already undergoing ablation. Distinct from Shelf #272 (occlusion versus anticoagulation outside the ablation setting).

title: Severe tricuspid regurgitation: transcatheter valve replacement beat medical therapy on a hierarchical composite, driven by symptoms (TRISCEND II)
question: In symptomatic severe tricuspid regurgitation, does transfemoral tricuspid valve replacement (EVOQUE) improve the hierarchical composite of survival, heart-failure events, and patient-reported health status versus medical therapy?
balance: One randomised trial, a positive composite whose weight sits in how patients feel, not in whether they live or stay out of hospital. TRISCEND II randomised 400 patients with severe symptomatic tricuspid regurgitation 2:1 to transcatheter tricuspid-valve replacement plus medical therapy or medical therapy alone. The hierarchical primary outcome (death, RVAD or transplant, postindex tricuspid intervention, heart-failure hospitalisation, then KCCQ improvement of at least 10 points, NYHA class, and 6-minute walk) favoured replacement with a win ratio of 2.02 (95% CI 1.56 to 2.62; P<0.001). But the pair comparisons show where the wins came from: quality-of-life improvement (23.1% vs 6.0% of pairs) and NYHA class (10.2% vs 0.8%), while heart-failure hospitalisation pairs slightly favoured control (9.7% vs 10.0%) and the death comparison was close (14.8% vs 12.5%). The costs were real: severe bleeding 15.4% versus 5.3% (P=0.003) and new permanent pacemakers 17.4% versus 2.3% (P<0.001). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (Tier C: the composite embeds death, so the developer reviews it personally) — symptoms and quality of life improve, at a procedural price, with no demonstrated survival or hospitalisation benefit at one year.

title: Severe mitral annular calcification: transcatheter mitral replacement met its performance goal in a single-arm study (SUMMIT-MAC)
question: In patients with severe mitral disease and severe annular calcification at high surgical risk, what are the outcomes of Tendyne transcatheter mitral valve replacement against prespecified performance goals?
balance: THIN by construction — a single-arm pivotal study with no comparator, carded as an explicit exception to the two-trial gate and labelled as such on its face. SUMMIT-MAC treated 103 patients (mean age 78; 55% women) with severe mitral annular calcification and significant mitral disease (regurgitation in nearly all) at high surgical risk with the Tendyne transcatheter mitral valve. Technical success was 94.2% and 30-day mortality 6.8%. The prespecified primary endpoint — freedom from all-cause mortality and heart-failure hospitalisation at 12 months — was 60.4%, against a performance goal of 43% (P=0.0002), so the goal was met. Symptoms improved markedly among survivors assessed (NYHA class I/II from 30.6% at baseline to 87.5% at 12 months; KCCQ overall summary up 18.7 points on average). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): the study shows the procedure can be done in this anatomy with outcomes better than a prespecified floor; without a control group it cannot show the valve caused the difference, and 12-month freedom from death or HF hospitalisation of 60.4% also states how sick this population is.

title: Degenerative mitral regurgitation: PASCAL edge-to-edge repair noninferior to MitraClip at one year (CLASP IID)
question: In prohibitive-surgical-risk degenerative mitral regurgitation, is the PASCAL edge-to-edge repair system noninferior to MitraClip for major adverse events and mitral regurgitation reduction at one year?
balance: THIN — a single randomised device-comparison trial, and a clean one. CLASP IID randomised 300 prohibitive-risk patients with significant symptomatic degenerative mitral regurgitation 2:1 to the PASCAL system or MitraClip. Noninferiority held on both primary endpoints in the full cohort: 30-day major adverse events 4.6% versus 5.4% (rate difference −0.8 points, upper 95% confidence bound 4.6%), and mitral regurgitation of 2+ or less at 6 months in 97.9% versus 95.7% (difference 2.2 points, lower bound −2.5%). At one year, MR 2+ or less was 95.8% versus 93.8% and MR 1+ or less 77.1% versus 71.3%; differences in survival, freedom from heart-failure hospitalisation, and major adverse events were not significant, and functional and quality-of-life gains were sustained in both groups. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: PASCAL is a noninferior alternative device — an equivalence result from one trial at one year, in prohibitive-risk patients only. (Desk note: this record carries no MeSH terms and no registry ID in the PubMed record — checked at the desk pass, never invented.)

title: After TAVR, dapagliflozin reduced death or worsening heart failure (DapaTAVI)
question: In older patients after successful TAVR who have heart failure plus diabetes, kidney disease, or reduced ejection fraction, does dapagliflozin reduce all-cause death or worsening heart failure?
balance: An OUTSTANDING-SINGLE candidate by this library's rule: one randomised trial with a hard-endpoint composite in a population the big SGLT2 trials excluded. DapaTAVI randomised 1,257 older patients with aortic stenosis undergoing TAVI — all with a history of heart failure plus renal insufficiency, diabetes, or LV systolic dysfunction — to dapagliflozin 10 mg daily or standard care alone after TAVI; 1,222 were analysed. At one year the primary composite of death from any cause or worsening heart failure (hospitalisation or urgent visit) occurred in 15.0% on dapagliflozin versus 20.1% on standard care (hazard ratio 0.72 — a 28% relative reduction; 95% CI 0.55 to 0.95; P=0.02). The components: death 7.8% versus 8.9% (HR 0.87; 95% CI 0.59 to 1.28 — not significant on its own) and worsening heart failure 9.4% versus 14.4% (subhazard ratio 0.63; 95% CI 0.45 to 0.88), so the composite win is carried by heart-failure events. Genital infection and hypotension were significantly more common on dapagliflozin. PROPOSED LIKELY (Tier C: a mortality-embedding composite — the developer's personal approval, sought here). Single trial, open-label, one country (Spain); the stamp reflects a large, well-sized effect on a hard composite, and the shelf says 'one trial' on its face.

title: Aortic stenosis: intensive lipid lowering did not slow the valve (SEAS + SALTIRE)
question: In aortic stenosis, does intensive lipid lowering slow valve progression or reduce valve-related events?
balance: DOUBLE-A null on the valve: two double-blind placebo-controlled trials, two different regimens, the same answer. SEAS randomised 1,873 patients with mild-to-moderate asymptomatic aortic stenosis to simvastatin 40 mg plus ezetimibe 10 mg or placebo for a median of 52.2 months: the primary composite (cardiovascular death, valve replacement, MI, unstable-angina hospitalisation, heart failure, bypass surgery, PCI, non-haemorrhagic stroke) occurred in 35.3% versus 38.2% (hazard ratio 0.96; 95% CI 0.83 to 1.12; P=0.59), and valve replacement itself was identical (28.3% vs 29.9%; HR 1.00). SALTIRE randomised 155 patients with calcific aortic stenosis to atorvastatin 80 mg or placebo: despite LDL falling to 63 versus 130 mg/dL, aortic-jet velocity progressed identically (0.199 vs 0.203 m/s per year; P=0.95) and valve calcium progressed identically (22.3% vs 21.7% per year; P=0.93). SEAS did show fewer ischaemic cardiovascular events on treatment (HR 0.78; 95% CI 0.63 to 0.97) — an atherosclerosis effect, not a valve effect — and a cancer excess (105 vs 70 cases; P=0.01) that later pooled analyses of the statin-ezetimibe programme did not confirm. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for valve progression and valve events (Tier C: the composite embeds cardiovascular death). Lipid lowering treats these patients' arteries; it does not treat their valve.

title: Asymptomatic severe aortic stenosis: early surgery won on a composite in AVATAR; imaging-selected early intervention was null in EVOLVED
question: In truly asymptomatic severe aortic stenosis with normal ejection fraction and negative exercise test, does early surgical AVR reduce death, MI, stroke, or heart-failure hospitalisation versus conservative care — and does selecting patients by myocardial fibrosis change the answer?
balance: Two small randomised trials of early intervention in asymptomatic severe aortic stenosis that do not agree, because they asked different questions. AVATAR randomised 157 patients with severe AS, normal LV function and a mandatory negative exercise test to early surgical AVR or conservative care: the primary composite (all-cause death, MI, stroke, or unplanned HF hospitalisation) occurred in 13 patients on early surgery versus 26 on conservative care (hazard ratio 0.46; 95% CI 0.23 to 0.90; P=0.02), with operative mortality 1.4% among the 92.3% who underwent surgery; no secondary endpoint, including mortality alone, differed significantly at this size. EVOLVED randomised 224 asymptomatic patients selected for myocardial fibrosis on cardiac MRI (of 356 planned — the trial under-enrolled) to early valve intervention or guideline-directed conservative care: the primary composite (death or unplanned AS-related hospitalisation) was 18% versus 23% (HR 0.79; 95% CI 0.44 to 1.43; P=.44), death was 14% versus 13%, while AS-related hospitalisation (6% vs 17%; HR 0.37) and 12-month symptoms favoured early intervention. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (Tier C): early surgery plausibly reduces the composite in carefully tested asymptomatic patients (AVATAR), but the effect rests on 39 events in one small trial, and fibrosis-based selection did not reproduce it (EVOLVED). How patients are chosen matters more than the blanket question suggests.

title: AF with a bioprosthetic mitral valve: rivaroxaban noninferior to warfarin (RIVER)
question: In patients with atrial fibrillation and a bioprosthetic mitral valve, is rivaroxaban noninferior to warfarin for death, major cardiovascular events, or major bleeding?
balance: THIN in setting (one trial, one country, open-label warfarin management) but large and internally consistent. RIVER randomised 1,005 patients with AF and a bioprosthetic mitral valve at 49 Brazilian sites to rivaroxaban 20 mg daily or dose-adjusted warfarin (INR 2.0–3.0). The primary outcome — death, major cardiovascular events (stroke, TIA, systemic embolism, valve thrombosis, HF hospitalisation), or major bleeding at 12 months — occurred at a mean of 347.5 days on rivaroxaban versus 340.1 days on warfarin (restricted mean survival time difference 7.4 days; 95% CI −1.4 to 16.3; P<0.001 for noninferiority). The components leaned toward rivaroxaban: cardiovascular death or thromboembolic events 3.4% versus 5.1% (HR 0.65; 95% CI 0.35 to 1.20), stroke 0.6% versus 2.4% (HR 0.25; 95% CI 0.07 to 0.88), major bleeding 1.4% versus 2.6% (HR 0.54; 95% CI 0.21 to 1.35). PROPOSED LIKELY (Tier C: the composite embeds death and stroke): rivaroxaban is a legitimate alternative to warfarin in this specific valve population — bioprosthetic mitral valves only; mechanical valves are the opposite story (Shelf #2257).

title: Mechanical heart valves: dabigatran caused more clots and more bleeding than warfarin (RE-ALIGN)
question: In patients with mechanical aortic or mitral valves, does dabigatran prevent valve thrombosis and embolism as safely as warfarin?
balance: A definitive harm result from a trial stopped early. RE-ALIGN was a phase 2 dose-validation study randomising patients with mechanical aortic or mitral valves — either within a week of surgery or at least 3 months after — 2:1 to dabigatran (dose by kidney function, adjusted to a trough level of at least 50 ng/mL) or warfarin. After 252 patients the trial was terminated prematurely because of excess thromboembolic AND bleeding events on dabigatran: ischaemic or unspecified stroke occurred in 9 patients (5%) on dabigatran versus none on warfarin, and major bleeding in 7 (4%) versus 2 (2%) — all of it pericardial. Nearly a third of dabigatran patients (32%) needed dose adjustment or discontinuation. Direct thrombin inhibition fails where valve-surface thrombin generation dominates, and no dosing strategy in the trial fixed it. PROPOSED LIKELY (harm) (Tier C): mechanical valves mean warfarin; this is the trial that settled it.

title: Amulet or Watchman for left atrial appendage occlusion: noninferior, with better sealing (Amulet IDE)
question: In nonvalvular atrial fibrillation at stroke risk, is the dual-seal Amulet occluder noninferior to Watchman for occlusion success, safety, and stroke prevention?
balance: A large device-versus-device trial with a split practical answer: the same protection, a better seal, a rockier procedure. Amulet IDE randomised 1,878 patients with nonvalvular AF at increased stroke risk to the Amulet dual-seal occluder or Watchman. Amulet was noninferior on the primary safety composite (14.5% vs 14.7% at 12 months) and on effectiveness — ischaemic stroke or systemic embolism 2.8% versus 2.8% at 18 months — and the composite of stroke, systemic embolism or cardiovascular/unexplained death was 5.6% versus 7.7% (noninferior). Complete occlusion at 45 days was higher with Amulet (98.9% vs 96.8% with residual jet at most 5 mm; P=0.003 for superiority). The trade: procedure-related complications were higher with Amulet (4.5% vs 2.5%), mainly more pericardial effusions and device embolisations, falling with operator experience; major bleeding and death were similar. PROPOSED LIKELY: device choice can rest on anatomy and operator experience; neither device prevents stroke better at 18 months. (Desk note: this record's MeSH is sparse as published — copied verbatim, not supplemented.)

title: Rheumatic mitral stenosis: balloon valvotomy matched closed surgical commissurotomy over long follow-up — in one very small trial
question: In rheumatic mitral stenosis, does percutaneous balloon mitral valvotomy give better long-term event-free survival than closed mitral commissurotomy?
balance: THIN — a genuinely randomised comparison, but only 40 patients, from the era before trial registration, and its abstract reports comparability rather than the superiority sometimes claimed for it. Rifaie and colleagues randomised 40 consecutive patients with moderate-to-severe rheumatic mitral stenosis (valve area under 1.5 cm²) to percutaneous mitral valvotomy by the double-balloon technique (20) or closed surgical commissurotomy (20), with echocardiographic follow-up yearly for up to 15 years (mean follow-up 99 ± 12 months). Immediate results did not differ: final valve area 1.8 cm² in both groups and similar mean gradients. Restenosis occurred in 5 of 19 followed patients after valvotomy (26.3%) versus 5 of 18 after commissurotomy (27.8%), and restenosis-free survival curves did not differ. The authors' conclusion is that balloon valvotomy achieves comparable results to closed commissurotomy in the short and long term. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): randomised long-term data this old and this small can support 'no large difference was seen' — nothing stronger, in either direction.

title: Stable chest pain: adding coronary CT angiography to standard care cut coronary death and MI at five years (SCOT-HEART)
question: In patients with suspected stable angina, does CTCA-guided management reduce coronary heart disease death or nonfatal myocardial infarction at five years versus standard care alone?
balance: A large open-label strategy trial with a hard-outcome win, achieved without more procedures at five years. SCOT-HEART randomised 4,146 patients with stable chest pain referred to cardiology clinics to standard care plus coronary CT angiography or standard care alone, followed a median of 4.8 years. Death from coronary heart disease or nonfatal MI occurred in 2.3% with CTA versus 3.9% without (hazard ratio 0.59 — a 41% relative reduction; 95% CI 0.41 to 0.84; P=0.004). Invasive angiography and revascularisation were more frequent early in the CTA group but identical overall at 5 years (angiography HR 1.00; revascularisation HR 1.07). The plausible mechanism is on the face of the trial: more preventive therapies were started in the CTA group (odds ratio 1.40) — a clearer diagnosis led to better-targeted prevention. There were no significant differences in cardiovascular, noncardiovascular, or all-cause death individually. PROPOSED LIKELY (Tier C: an MI/mortality composite — the developer's personal approval territory). Pairs with PROMISE (Shelf #2261) as designed: positive in a UK secondary-care population, neutral in a lower-risk US one.

title: Suspected coronary disease: anatomic (CTA) versus functional first testing — no outcome difference (PROMISE)
question: In symptomatic patients with suspected coronary artery disease, does an initial coronary CT angiography strategy improve outcomes versus initial functional testing (stress ECG, echo, or nuclear)?
balance: The necessary counterweight to SCOT-HEART, and the pair is the balance. PROMISE randomised 10,003 symptomatic patients with suspected CAD (mean age 60.8; 52.7% women; mean pretest likelihood of obstructive CAD 53.3%) to initial anatomical testing with coronary CTA or initial functional testing. Over a median of 25 months the primary composite (death, MI, hospitalisation for unstable angina, or major procedural complication) occurred in 3.3% with CTA versus 3.0% with functional testing (adjusted hazard ratio 1.04; 95% CI 0.83 to 1.29; P=0.75). CTA led to more catheterisation within 90 days (12.2% vs 8.1%) but fewer catheterisations showing no obstructive disease (3.4% vs 4.3%; P=0.02); median radiation exposure per patient was lower with CTA, though overall exposure was higher because a third of the functional group had none. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment — the testing strategy — made no difference to outcomes) (Tier C). Read with Shelf #2260: in a UK secondary-care population with five years of follow-up, adding CTA to standard care prevented infarctions; in this broader, lower-event-rate US population over two years, choosing CTA first did not.

title: Referred for invasive angiography: a CT-first strategy matched catheterisation on events with far fewer procedural complications (DISCHARGE)
question: In patients with stable chest pain and intermediate pretest probability referred for invasive angiography, does a CT-first strategy match catheterisation on major adverse cardiovascular events with fewer procedural complications?
balance: A pragmatic trial in the exact population where the question bites: patients already referred for the catheter lab. DISCHARGE randomised 3,561 patients with stable chest pain and intermediate pretest probability of obstructive CAD at 26 European centres to initial CT or initial invasive coronary angiography. Over 3.5 years, major adverse cardiovascular events (cardiovascular death, nonfatal MI, nonfatal stroke) occurred in 2.1% with CT versus 3.0% with invasive angiography (hazard ratio 0.70; 95% CI 0.46 to 1.07; P=0.10) — similar, and numerically lower with CT. Major procedure-related complications were fourfold lower with the CT-first strategy (0.5% vs 1.9%; HR 0.26; 95% CI 0.13 to 0.55). Angina in the final follow-up weeks did not differ significantly (8.8% vs 7.5%). PROPOSED LIKELY (Tier C): CT first is at least as safe on events and clearly gentler in this referred population. (Desk note: the record's MeSH is brief as published — copied verbatim.)

title: FFRCT-guided care in stable chest pain: no cost saving and no outcome difference, fewer invasive angiograms (FORECAST)
question: In stable chest pain, does a CT angiography plus selective FFRCT strategy reduce total cardiac costs or improve outcomes versus standard care?
balance: THIN — one trial, recruited through the COVID period, with a null primary endpoint whose confidence interval still spans meaningful savings and meaningful extra cost. FORECAST randomised 1,400 patients with stable chest pain at 11 UK centres to CTCA with selective FFRCT or standard clinical care pathways. Total cardiac costs at 9 months were £114 higher (8%) in the FFRCT group — not significant (95% CI −£112 to +£337; P=0.10). Major adverse cardiac and cerebrovascular events did not differ (10.2% vs 10.6%), and angina and quality of life improved similarly in both groups. The strategy did reshape downstream testing: invasive coronary angiography fell (19% vs 25%; P=0.01). In the experimental group 96% had initial CTCA and 38% of those underwent FFRCT. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): FFRCT-guided care demonstrably reduces invasive angiography; whether it saves money or changes outcomes is unproven on this trial. (Registry ID: none printed in the fetched record — flagged, not invented.)

title: Suspected acute coronary syndrome: early CT coronary angiography did not improve one-year outcomes (RAPID-CTCA)
question: In intermediate-risk suspected acute coronary syndrome presenting to emergency care, does early CT coronary angiography reduce death or subsequent type 1 myocardial infarction, or shorten stay?
balance: A large, well-run negative trial of a plausible idea. RAPID-CTCA randomised 1,748 adults with suspected or provisionally diagnosed ACS at intermediate risk (prior coronary disease, raised troponin, or abnormal ECG; mean GRACE score 115) at 37 UK hospitals to early CTCA plus standard care or standard care alone; scans happened a median of 4.2 hours after randomisation. The primary endpoint — all-cause death or subsequent type 1 or 4b MI at one year — occurred in 5.8% with early CTCA versus 6.1% with standard care (adjusted hazard ratio 0.91; 95% CI 0.62 to 1.35; P=0.65). There were no overall differences in revascularisation, ACS drug treatment, or later preventive therapy. Early CTCA did reduce invasive coronary angiography (54.0% vs 60.8%; adjusted HR 0.81; P=0.001) but slightly lengthened hospital stay (median increase 0.21 days). The authors conclude the findings do not support routine early CTCA in intermediate-risk acute chest pain. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment — the early-scan strategy — made no difference to outcomes) (Tier C).

title: Catheter ablation versus drug therapy in AF: no hard-endpoint win overall (CABANA), a large one in heart failure (CASTLE-AF)
question: Does catheter ablation reduce death, stroke, bleeding, or cardiac arrest versus drug therapy in symptomatic AF overall — and in AF with reduced-ejection-fraction heart failure?
balance: The pair is the balance: the same intervention, a null result in the broad population and a large benefit in the sickest subgroup. CABANA randomised 2,204 symptomatic AF patients (median age 68; ≥65, or younger with stroke risk factors) to ablation or drug therapy (rhythm and/or rate control): over a median 48.5 months the primary composite (death, disabling stroke, serious bleeding, cardiac arrest) was 8.0% versus 9.2% (hazard ratio 0.86; 95% CI 0.65 to 1.15; P=.30) and mortality 5.2% versus 6.1% (HR 0.85, not significant), while death or cardiovascular hospitalisation (51.7% vs 58.1%; HR 0.83; P=.001) and AF recurrence (49.9% vs 69.5%; HR 0.52) clearly favoured ablation; 27.5% of the drug group crossed over to ablation, diluting the intention-to-treat contrast. CASTLE-AF randomised 363 patients with AF, EF at most 35%, NYHA class II–IV and an implanted defibrillator, who had failed, not tolerated, or declined antiarrhythmic drugs: the composite of death or worsening-HF hospitalisation was 28.5% with ablation versus 44.6% with medical therapy (HR 0.62; 95% CI 0.43 to 0.87; P=0.007), and death alone was 13.4% versus 25.0% (HR 0.53; 95% CI 0.32 to 0.86; P=0.01). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (Tier C): ablation's hard-endpoint case is strong in HFrEF and unproven in the general symptomatic population — population, not procedure, is the difference.

title: Cryoballoon versus contact-force radiofrequency ablation: identical rhythm outcomes under continuous monitoring (CIRCA-DOSE)
question: In drug-refractory paroxysmal AF, do cryoballoon (4-minute or 2-minute freezes) and contact-force radiofrequency ablation differ in one-year arrhythmia recurrence measured by an implanted loop recorder?
balance: A three-way randomised comparison with the most honest rhythm ascertainment in the ablation literature — every patient carried an implantable loop recorder — and a flat result. CIRCA-DOSE randomised 346 patients with drug-refractory paroxysmal AF to contact-force radiofrequency (115), 4-minute cryoballoon (115), or 2-minute cryoballoon (116) ablation. One-year freedom from any atrial tachyarrhythmia (days 91–365) was 53.9%, 52.2%, and 51.7% respectively (P=0.87); freedom from symptomatic arrhythmia was 79.1%, 78.2%, and 73.3% (P=0.26); AF burden fell by a median of about 99% in all three groups (P=0.36). Serious adverse events did not differ significantly (2.6%, 5.3%, 6.0%; P=0.24). Radiofrequency took longer but used less fluoroscopy. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment — the energy source and freeze duration — made no difference): operator and anatomy, not energy, should drive the choice; and the 53% freedom figure under continuous monitoring is the honest benchmark against which intermittently monitored trials' higher success rates should be read.

title: Surgical ablation added to mitral valve surgery: far more sinus rhythm, no mortality or stroke difference in the randomised trials, more pacemakers
question: In patients with AF undergoing mitral valve surgery, does concomitant surgical ablation improve sinus rhythm, mortality, stroke, and pacemaker rates in randomised trials?
balance: THIN for hard outcomes, strong for rhythm: a randomised-trials-only meta-analysis separates what surgical ablation proves from what it merely suggests. Pooling 13 randomised trials (1,089 patients) of concomitant surgical ablation during mitral valve replacement or repair, sinus rhythm was far more frequent with ablation at discharge (odds ratio 9.62; 95% CI 4.87 to 19.02), 6 months (OR 7.21), and 1 year (OR 8.41; 95% CI 5.14 to 13.77). But all-cause mortality did not differ, stroke and thromboembolic events did not differ, and permanent pacemaker implantation was more likely with ablation (OR 1.87; 95% CI 1.11 to 3.17). A larger 2025 meta-analysis including observational studies (38 studies; 24 analysed for mortality, 41,678 patients) did find lower long-term mortality (HR 0.78) and stroke (HR 0.60) with ablation — while stating in its own abstract that the survival benefits were predominantly observed in the observational studies, which is exactly why this shelf rests on the randomised pool. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: rhythm benefit is real and large; hard-outcome benefit is unproven in randomised data; the pacemaker cost is real.

title: Early rhythm control works: EAST-AFNET 4 for outcomes, EARLY-AF for first-line ablation
question: In recently diagnosed AF, does early rhythm control — drugs or ablation — reduce cardiovascular outcomes versus usual care, and is first-line cryoablation better than first-line drugs at preventing recurrence?
balance: DOUBLE-A support for acting early, from two directions. EAST-AFNET 4 randomised 2,789 patients with early AF (diagnosed within a year; median 36 days) and cardiovascular conditions to early rhythm control (antiarrhythmic drugs or ablation) or usual care, and was stopped for efficacy after a median 5.1 years: the first primary outcome (cardiovascular death, stroke, or hospitalisation for worsening heart failure or acute coronary syndrome) occurred at 3.9 versus 5.0 per 100 person-years (hazard ratio 0.79; 96% CI 0.66 to 0.94; P=0.005), with no significant difference in nights in hospital or in the primary safety composite — though serious adverse events related to rhythm-control therapy were more frequent with early rhythm control (4.9% vs 1.4%). EARLY-AF randomised 303 patients with symptomatic paroxysmal AF, untreated, to first-line cryoballoon ablation or antiarrhythmic drugs, with implantable monitors in everyone: recurrence of atrial tachyarrhythmia at 1 year was 42.9% with ablation versus 67.8% with drugs (HR 0.48; 95% CI 0.35 to 0.66; P<0.001), symptomatic recurrence 11.0% versus 26.2% (HR 0.39), and serious adverse events were similar (3.2% vs 4.0%). A second first-line cryoballoon trial (STOP AF First) points the same way (treatment success 74.6% vs 45.0%). PROPOSED LIKELY (Tier C: EAST's composite embeds cardiovascular death).

title: Persistent AF: adding MRI-guided fibrosis ablation to pulmonary vein isolation did not reduce recurrence — and caused strokes (DECAAF II)
question: In persistent AF, does ablating MRI-detected left atrial fibrosis in addition to pulmonary vein isolation reduce atrial arrhythmia recurrence versus isolation alone?
balance: A well-powered negative trial with a harm signal — the combination that should change practice. DECAAF II randomised 843 patients with persistent AF at 44 centres in 10 countries to pulmonary vein isolation plus MRI-guided fibrosis ablation (421) or isolation alone (422); 815 contributed to efficacy analyses. Atrial arrhythmia recurrence after the 90-day blanking period did not differ: 43.0% versus 46.1% (hazard ratio 0.95; 95% CI 0.77 to 1.17; P=.63). The safety composite (stroke, pulmonary vein stenosis, bleeding, heart failure, or death within 30 days) occurred in 9 patients (2.2%) in the fibrosis-guided group versus none with isolation alone (P=.001) — including 6 ischaemic strokes (1.5%) versus none, and 2 deaths in the fibrosis-guided group, the first possibly procedure-related. The authors' conclusion: findings do not support MRI-guided fibrosis ablation for persistent AF. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) on efficacy, with the early safety excess stated on the shelf's face — more ablation was worse, not merely useless.

title: Device-detected subclinical AF: apixaban beat aspirin for stroke (ARTESiA); edoxaban did not beat placebo (NOAH-AFNET 6)
question: In patients with device-detected subclinical AF or atrial high-rate episodes (6 minutes to 24 hours) and stroke risk factors, does anticoagulation reduce stroke and systemic embolism enough to justify its bleeding cost?
balance: DOUBLE-A trials that point in the same direction with different comparators — and the comparator is the lesson. ARTESiA randomised 4,012 patients with device-detected subclinical AF lasting 6 minutes to 24 hours (mean age 76.8; mean CHA2DS2-VASc 3.9) double-blind to apixaban or aspirin 81 mg: stroke or systemic embolism occurred at 0.78% per patient-year on apixaban versus 1.24% on aspirin (hazard ratio 0.63; 95% CI 0.45 to 0.88; P=0.007), while major bleeding was higher on apixaban (1.71% vs 0.94% per patient-year; HR 1.80; 95% CI 1.26 to 2.57; P=0.001), with fatal bleeding numerically lower on apixaban (5 vs 8 patients). NOAH-AFNET 6 randomised 2,536 patients aged 65 or older with atrial high-rate episodes of at least 6 minutes plus a stroke risk factor to edoxaban or placebo, and was terminated early (median follow-up 21 months) for safety concerns and informal futility: the efficacy composite (cardiovascular death, stroke, systemic embolism) was 3.2% versus 4.0% per patient-year (HR 0.81; 95% CI 0.60 to 1.08; P=0.15), stroke itself ran at about 1% per patient-year in both groups, and the safety composite (death or major bleeding) was higher on edoxaban (HR 1.31; 95% CI 1.02 to 1.67; P=0.03). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (Tier C): against aspirin there is a real relative stroke reduction bought with more major bleeding; against placebo the event rates are so low that no benefit could be shown — the absolute gains are small either way, and the decision is genuinely individual. A study-level meta-analysis of the two trials exists (PMID 37952187) and is consistent with this reading.

title: Pulsed field ablation versus thermal ablation for paroxysmal AF: noninferior at one year (ADVENT)
question: In drug-refractory paroxysmal AF, is pulsed field ablation noninferior to conventional thermal ablation (radiofrequency or cryoballoon) for effectiveness and safety at one year?
balance: THIN — one randomised trial, a clean noninferiority result, at one year. ADVENT randomised 607 patients with drug-refractory paroxysmal AF to pulsed field ablation (305) or conventional thermal ablation (302; radiofrequency or cryoballoon). The primary efficacy endpoint — freedom from initial procedural failure, documented atrial tachyarrhythmia after a 3-month blanking period, antiarrhythmic drug use, cardioversion, or repeat ablation — was met in an estimated 73.3% with pulsed field versus 71.3% with thermal (difference 2.0 points; 95% Bayesian credible interval −5.2 to 9.2; posterior probability of noninferiority >0.999). Primary safety events were 2.1% versus 1.5% (difference 0.6 points; credible interval −1.5 to 2.8; noninferiority >0.999). PROPOSED LIKELY: pulsed field ablation is a noninferior alternative energy at one year in paroxysmal AF, from a single trial using Bayesian noninferiority analysis; claims of superiority — for safety rarities like oesophageal or phrenic injury, or for durability — are not established by this trial, whose event counts for such harms are far too small. (Desk note: the trial's sample size appears as 607 randomised in the record; some summaries cite 687 enrolled — the record governs.)

title: At cardiac surgery, occluding the left atrial appendage cut stroke or systemic embolism — on top of anticoagulation (LAAOS III)
question: In patients with AF and elevated stroke risk undergoing cardiac surgery for another indication, does concomitant surgical left atrial appendage occlusion reduce ischaemic stroke or systemic embolism versus no occlusion, when most patients continue anticoagulation?
balance: A large, well-blinded surgical trial with a clear hard-outcome win — and an important framing: the benefit came on top of anticoagulation, not instead of it. LAAOS III randomised 4,811 patients with AF and a CHA2DS2-VASc score of at least 2 who were undergoing cardiac surgery for another indication to appendage occlusion or no occlusion (4,770 in the primary analysis; mean age 71; mean score 4.2); surgeons aside, everyone was blinded. Over a mean 3.8 years, ischaemic stroke or systemic embolism occurred in 4.8% with occlusion versus 7.0% without (hazard ratio 0.67; 95% CI 0.53 to 0.85; P=0.001). At 3 years, 76.8% of participants were still receiving oral anticoagulation. Perioperative bleeding, heart failure, and death did not differ significantly. PROPOSED LIKELY (Tier C: a stroke-embedding composite reviewed personally). The shelf must not be read as permission to stop anticoagulation after surgical occlusion — most of the trial's benefit accrued in patients who stayed on it.

title: Adding surgical ventricular reconstruction to bypass surgery shrank the ventricle but changed nothing that matters (STICH Hypothesis 2)
question: In ischaemic cardiomyopathy with dominant anterior left ventricular dysfunction, does adding surgical ventricular reconstruction to CABG reduce death or cardiac hospitalisation versus CABG alone?
balance: A clean anatomical-success/clinical-null trial: the operation did exactly what it was designed to do to the ventricle and none of what it was meant to do for the patient. STICH Hypothesis 2 randomised 1,000 patients with EF at most 35%, coronary disease amenable to CABG, and dominant anterior LV dysfunction amenable to reconstruction, to CABG alone (499) or CABG plus surgical ventricular reconstruction (501); median follow-up 48 months. Reconstruction reduced end-systolic volume index by 19% versus 6% with CABG alone — the anatomical goal achieved. But the primary outcome (death from any cause or hospitalisation for cardiac causes) occurred in 59% with CABG alone and 58% with the combined approach (hazard ratio 0.99; 95% CI 0.84 to 1.17; P=0.90), and cardiac symptoms and exercise tolerance improved to a similar degree in both groups. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) (Tier C). A smaller ventricle is not the same thing as a better outcome — the shelf is the library's standing example of that distinction.

title: Advanced heart failure: sacubitril/valsartan showed no advantage over valsartan alone (LIFE)
question: In advanced HFrEF with recent NYHA class IV symptoms, does sacubitril/valsartan reduce NT-proBNP and improve clinical outcomes versus valsartan alone?
balance: The PARADIGM-HF result does not extend to the sickest patients, and LIFE is the trial that drew that boundary. LIFE randomised patients with advanced HFrEF and recent NYHA class IV symptoms to sacubitril/valsartan (target 200 mg twice daily — the trial-size dose designation) or valsartan alone (target 160 mg twice daily) on top of recommended therapy; 335 patients entered the analysis after a run-in that itself excluded 72 eligible patients (18%) who could not tolerate even 100 mg/day of sacubitril/valsartan, and 29% of those assigned to it discontinued during the 24 weeks. The primary endpoint — the area under the curve for NT-proBNP ratio to baseline through 24 weeks — did not differ: estimated ratio of change 0.95 (95% CI 0.84 to 1.08; P=.45). Nor did the clinical composite of days alive, out of hospital, and free from heart-failure events improve. Non-life-threatening hyperkalaemia was more frequent on sacubitril/valsartan (17% vs 9%; P=.04). The trial was stopped early (March 2020) because of COVID-19 risk, which limits its size — but nothing in it trends toward the benefit seen in less advanced disease. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) (Tier C: the clinical composite embeds survival) in this advanced population; the shelf governs advanced/NYHA IV disease only and does not touch the PARADIGM-HF population.

title: Suspected angina: imaging-guided care (CMR or perfusion scintigraphy) cut unnecessary angiography fourfold versus guideline-directed care (CE-MARC 2)
question: In suspected coronary heart disease, does care guided by cardiovascular magnetic resonance or myocardial perfusion scintigraphy reduce unnecessary invasive angiography versus NICE-guideline-directed care?
balance: A pragmatic three-arm strategy trial whose endpoint is the angiograms that should not have happened. CE-MARC 2 randomised 1,202 symptomatic patients with suspected coronary disease (pretest likelihood 10–90%; mean 49.5%) at 6 UK hospitals to NICE-guideline-directed care (240), CMR-guided care (481), or perfusion-scintigraphy-guided care (481). Protocol-defined unnecessary angiography within 12 months (angiography showing no significant disease by FFR or quantitative criteria) occurred in 28.8% under guideline care versus 7.5% with CMR guidance and 7.1% with scintigraphy guidance — adjusted odds ratio 0.21 for CMR versus guidelines (95% CI 0.12 to 0.34; P<.001), with no significant difference between CMR and scintigraphy (OR 1.27; P=.32). Positive angiography rates were similar (12.1%, 9.8%, 8.7%), and major adverse cardiovascular events did not differ (1.7% guideline, 2.5% CMR, 2.5% scintigraphy) — this is a pathway-efficiency result, not an outcome result. PROPOSED LIKELY: gatekeeping the cath lab with imaging works; which of the two imaging tests is a local-resources question.

title: Stable angina: a perfusion-CMR strategy matched an FFR strategy on events with fewer revascularisations (MR-INFORM)
question: In stable angina with risk factors, does management guided by stress-perfusion CMR match FFR-guided invasive management on major adverse cardiac events, with less revascularisation?
balance: A strategy noninferiority trial that met its margin with room to spare. MR-INFORM randomised 918 patients with typical angina plus at least two risk factors or a positive exercise test to a perfusion-CMR strategy (revascularise if ischaemia in at least 6% of myocardium) or an invasive FFR strategy (revascularise if FFR at most 0.8). The primary outcome (death, nonfatal MI, or target-vessel revascularisation at 1 year) occurred in 3.6% with the CMR strategy versus 3.7% with FFR (risk difference −0.2 points; 95% CI −2.7 to 2.4; noninferiority margin 6 points — met). Fewer CMR-strategy patients met criteria for revascularisation (40.5% vs 45.9%) and fewer actually underwent index revascularisation (35.7% vs 45.0%; P=0.005). Freedom from angina at 12 months did not differ significantly (49.2% vs 43.8%; P=0.21). PROPOSED LIKELY (Tier C: the composite embeds death and MI): a noninvasive-first strategy is a legitimate equal in stable angina — with fewer procedures. Note Shelf #2263 (FORECAST): adding FFRCT on top of CTCA did not show the same economy — different strategy, different answer.

title: After STEMI: FFR guidance of complete revascularisation showed no advantage over angiography guidance (FLOWER-MI)
question: In STEMI with multivessel disease undergoing complete revascularisation, does FFR guidance beat angiography guidance on death, MI, or urgent revascularisation at one year?
balance: THIN on conclusion despite a thousand patients — the trial's own authors decline to interpret it definitively, and this shelf follows them. FLOWER-MI randomised 1,171 patients with STEMI and multivessel disease, after successful culprit PCI, to complete revascularisation guided by FFR or by angiography alone (1,163 analysed). The primary outcome (death, nonfatal MI, or unplanned hospitalisation leading to urgent revascularisation at 1 year) occurred in 5.5% with FFR guidance versus 4.2% with angiography guidance (hazard ratio 1.32; 95% CI 0.78 to 2.23; P=0.31). Components: death 1.5% versus 1.7%; nonfatal MI 3.1% versus 1.7%; urgent revascularisation 2.6% versus 1.9%. FFR guidance used fewer nonculprit stents (1.01 vs 1.50 per patient). The point estimate leans against FFR guidance, the interval spans meaningful effects in both directions, and the authors state the findings do not allow a conclusive interpretation. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (Tier C): no advantage was shown for adding FFR in this setting; harm is not established either. Distinct from Shelf #267 (complete versus culprit-only revascularisation — a settled benefit); this shelf is about guidance within complete revascularisation.

title: Angina with non-obstructive arteries: stratified therapy guided by invasive coronary function testing improved angina (CorMicA)
question: In ischaemia with non-obstructive coronary arteries (INOCA), does disclosing invasive coronary function test results and stratifying therapy (vasospasm, microvascular angina, noncardiac) improve angina and quality of life?
balance: THIN — one small trial, but randomised with a blinded control and a patient-reported primary endpoint that matters in a population medicine usually sends home unexplained. CorMicA enrolled 391 patients with angina referred for angiography; 206 (53.7%) had obstructive disease, and the 151 without obstruction were randomised to an interventional diagnostic procedure (guidewire coronary flow reserve, microcirculatory resistance, FFR, then acetylcholine vasoreactivity testing) with results disclosed and therapy stratified, or to a sham procedure with standard care. At 6 months the Seattle Angina Questionnaire summary score improved by a mean of 11.7 points more with stratified therapy (95% CI 5.0 to 18.4; p=0.001), with quality of life also better (EQ-5D index +0.10; p=0.024; visual analogue score +14.5; p<0.001). Major adverse cardiac events did not differ (2.6% in both groups). PROPOSED POSSIBLE: knowing the mechanism — vasospasm, microvascular dysfunction, or neither — and treating accordingly makes these patients feel better; event effects are unknown at this size.

title: Before cardioversion for AF: a TEE-guided strategy matched conventional anticoagulation-first on embolic events, with less bleeding and cardioversion a month sooner (ACUTE)
question: In AF of more than 48 hours, does a transoesophageal-echo-guided strategy (cardiovert if no thrombus, with short anticoagulation) match the conventional three-weeks-of-anticoagulation-first strategy on embolic events and bleeding?
balance: THIN — a single trial, but a large one for its question, and its answer has aged well. ACUTE randomised 1,222 patients with AF of more than two days' duration awaiting elective cardioversion to a TEE-guided strategy (anticoagulate, image, cardiovert promptly if no thrombus) or conventional care (warfarin for three weeks first). The primary composite (stroke, TIA, or peripheral embolism within 8 weeks) did not differ significantly: 5 events (0.8%) with TEE guidance versus 3 (0.5%) conventionally (P=0.50) — absolute rates tiny in both arms, and the trial cannot exclude a small difference in either direction. Haemorrhagic events were significantly fewer with the TEE strategy (2.9% vs 5.5%; P=0.03), cardioversion came a month sooner (mean 3.0 vs 30.6 days; P<0.001), and sinus rhythm was restored more often (71.1% vs 65.2%; P=0.03); death, maintenance of sinus rhythm, and functional status did not differ at 8 weeks. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: TEE guidance is a clinically effective alternative when cardioversion should not wait — warfarin-era logistics, but the comparison (image now versus anticoagulate blindly for weeks) is unchanged by direct-acting agents.

title: Cardiac rehabilitation by phone matches the rehab centre for exercise capacity — at a third of the delivery cost (REMOTE-CR + Telerehab III)
question: After a cardiac event, does remotely monitored home-based telerehabilitation match centre-based rehabilitation for exercise capacity, risk factors, and durability of benefit?
balance: DOUBLE-A for the delivery question. REMOTE-CR randomised 162 adults with coronary heart disease to 12 weeks of real-time smartphone-monitored telerehabilitation or centre-based rehabilitation: peak oxygen uptake was comparable and telerehabilitation was noninferior (adjusted mean difference +0.51 mL/kg/min; 95% CI −0.97 to 1.98; prespecified inferiority margin −1.25). Telerehabilitation participants were less sedentary at 24 weeks; waist and hip measures slightly favoured the centre group at 12 weeks; no other differences were detected. Costs clearly favoured telerehabilitation: programme delivery NZD 1,130 versus 3,466 per participant (about £573 vs £1,758) and medication costs were lower; hospital-utilisation costs did not differ significantly. Telerehab III's two-year follow-up (126 patients) found the telerehabilitation group's exercise capacity had declined after the programme ended (peak VO2 24 to 22 mL/kg/min) yet remained better than the no-telerehabilitation group (P=0.032), with quality-of-life gains and an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio of −€3,993 per QALY — better outcomes at lower cost. PROPOSED LIKELY: the centre is a delivery vehicle, not the active ingredient; monitored home rehabilitation reaches the same capacity for less money, with partial decay once supervision stops.

title: HFpEF exercise training: interval and continuous training both nudged peak VO2 at 3 months — below the meaningful threshold, gone by 12 (OptimEx-Clin)
question: In heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, do high-intensity interval training or moderate continuous training beat guideline activity advice on peak oxygen consumption — and does intensity matter?
balance: THIN — one well-run three-arm trial whose honest headline is how small the differences are. OptimEx-Clin randomised 180 sedentary patients with chronic stable HFpEF at 5 European sites to high-intensity interval training (3 sessions/week), moderate continuous training (5 sessions/week), or one-time guideline activity advice, for 12 months (3 months supervised, then telemonitored home training). At 3 months, peak VO2 rose 1.1 mL/kg/min with interval training and 1.6 with continuous training against a 0.6 fall with advice (differences 1.5 [95% CI 0.4 to 2.7] and 2.0 [0.9 to 3.1]) — but neither difference met the prespecified minimal clinically important difference of 2.5 mL/kg/min, interval versus continuous did not differ (−0.4; 95% CI −1.4 to 0.6), and no comparison was significant at 12 months. Diastolic function and natriuretic peptides did not change. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: supervised training of either intensity gives a modest early capacity gain over advice alone; intensity does not matter; without continued structure the gain does not persist. Distinct from Shelf #171 (exercise in HFrEF).

title: After AF ablation: comprehensive rehabilitation improved physical capacity, not mental health (CopenHeartRFA)
question: In patients treated with ablation for AF, does a comprehensive rehabilitation programme (exercise plus psychoeducation) improve physical capacity and mental health versus usual care?
balance: THIN — one trial, a clear physical result and a clean mental-health null. CopenHeartRFA randomised 210 patients treated with catheter ablation for AF (mean age 59; 74% men; 72% paroxysmal) to 12 weeks of exercise training plus four psychoeducational consultations, or usual care. Peak VO2 at 4 months was higher with rehabilitation (24.3 vs 20.7 mL/kg/min; main effect P=0.003; time-by-intervention interaction P=0.020). Self-rated mental health (SF-36) did not differ (53.8 vs 51.9 points; P=.20). Serious adverse events were 2 versus 1 (including one death unrelated to rehabilitation in each group pattern) — no significant difference (P=.56); non-serious adverse events were reported more often with rehabilitation (16 vs 7 patients; P=.047). PROPOSED POSSIBLE: rehabilitation after ablation buys fitness, not measurable mental-health improvement, in this population — a narrower claim than rehabilitation advocates usually make, and the trial's own.

title: After heart valve surgery: rehabilitation improved physical capacity, not mental health (CopenHeartVR)
question: After heart valve surgery, does comprehensive cardiac rehabilitation improve physical capacity and mental health versus usual care?
balance: THIN — one small trial, the same shape as its post-ablation sibling. CopenHeartVR randomised 147 patients after heart valve surgery (aortic 62%, mitral 36%; mean age 62; 76% men) to 12 weeks of exercise training plus monthly psychoeducational consultations, or usual care without structured exercise. Peak VO2 at 4 months was higher with rehabilitation (24.8 vs 22.5 mL/kg/min; P=0.045) — a smaller, borderline effect than in CopenHeartRFA. The SF-36 Mental Component Scale at 6 months did not differ (53.7 vs 55.2 points; P=0.40), and other exercise-capacity and self-reported outcomes were not improved. Self-reported non-serious adverse events were more frequent with rehabilitation (11 of 72 vs 3 of 75; P=0.02). The authors state further research is needed to justify rehabilitation in this group. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: a modest fitness gain is the demonstrated benefit; recommendations for post-valve rehabilitation currently rest on extrapolation from ischaemic-heart-disease populations, as the trial's introduction notes.

title: Varenicline started in hospital after acute coronary syndrome improved smoking abstinence (EVITA)
question: In patients hospitalised with acute coronary syndrome who smoke, does varenicline started in hospital improve abstinence at 24 weeks, and is it safe in this setting?
balance: THIN — one trial, but double-blind and placebo-controlled with biochemically validated abstinence, in exactly the teachable-moment population. EVITA randomised 302 smokers hospitalised with ACS (mean age 55; 75% men; 56% STEMI; mean 21 cigarettes/day for 36 years) to varenicline or placebo for 12 weeks, started in hospital, with low-intensity counselling for all. At 24 weeks, point-prevalence abstinence (7-day recall plus expired carbon monoxide validation) was 47.3% on varenicline versus 32.5% on placebo (P=0.012; number needed to treat 6.8). Continuous abstinence was 35.8% versus 25.8% (P=0.081) and at least halving daily consumption 67.4% versus 55.6% (P=0.05). Safety within 30 days of drug discontinuation was similar: serious adverse events 11.9% versus 11.3%; major adverse cardiovascular events 4.0% versus 4.6%. The authors note future studies are needed to establish safety in this population — the trial is far too small for rare-harm questions, which sit in the broader varenicline safety literature. PROPOSED LIKELY for the abstinence claim, which is the claim the trial was powered for.

title: After MI: treating depression and low social support improved mood and support — but not survival or reinfarction (ENRICHD)
question: In patients after myocardial infarction who are depressed or socially isolated, does cognitive behaviour therapy (with an SSRI when needed) reduce death or recurrent MI?
balance: The definitive trial of a beloved hypothesis — and the hypothesis lost. ENRICHD randomised 2,481 patients within 28 days of MI who had depression, low perceived social support, or both, at 8 centres to usual care or a cognitive behaviour therapy programme (median 11 individual sessions over 6 months, group therapy when feasible, plus an SSRI for severe or non-responding depression). The psychosocial targets moved: depression scores improved more with intervention (Hamilton change −10.1 vs −8.4; P<.001) and social support improved more (+5.1 vs +3.4; P<.001) — though usual-care patients also improved substantially, narrowing the gap. The clinical endpoint did not move at all: event-free survival (death or recurrent MI) over an average 29 months was 75.8% with intervention versus 75.9% with usual care, with no difference in any of the three risk groups. PROPOSED LIKELY (no difference) (Tier C): treat post-MI depression because depression is worth treating — Shelves #2289 covers the drug evidence — but do not promise patients it will keep them alive or out of hospital. Depression after MI remains a risk marker; ENRICHD shows it is not, via this route, a modifiable cause of events.

title: Depression in coronary disease: sertraline and citalopram are effective and cardiac-safe; adding interpersonal psychotherapy was not (SADHART + CREATE)
question: In patients with coronary disease and major depression, do SSRIs relieve depression without cardiac harm — and does short-term psychotherapy add anything?
balance: The two foundational randomised trials answer the safety question first, the efficacy question second. SADHART (369 patients hospitalised with MI or unstable angina and major depression; sertraline 50–200 mg/day versus placebo for 24 weeks) was designed as a safety trial: left ventricular ejection fraction did not change (54% to 54% on sertraline; 52% to 53% on placebo), and ventricular ectopy runs, QTc prolongation, and other cardiac measures did not differ; severe cardiovascular adverse events were numerically fewer on sertraline (14.5% vs 22.4%, not significant). Efficacy favoured sertraline on the global-impression measure (responders 67% vs 53%; P=.01), decisively in patients with recurrent or more severe depression (78% vs 45%; P=.001), while the overall Hamilton difference was not significant (P=.14). CREATE (284 patients with coronary disease and major depression, 2×2 factorial) found citalopram superior to placebo on depression scores (Hamilton difference 3.3 points; P=.005; response 52.8% vs 40.1%; remission 35.9% vs 22.5%), while interpersonal psychotherapy added nothing over clinical management alone — the difference numerically favoured management alone (−2.26 points; P=.06). PROPOSED LIKELY: in coronary patients, treat major depression with an SSRI (sertraline or citalopram) plus good clinical management; expect symptom relief, not event reduction (Shelf #2288), and do not count on a brief psychotherapy add-on.

title: Tai chi in systolic heart failure: quality of life, mood, and confidence improved — exercise capacity did not, in the larger trial (Yeh trials)
question: In chronic systolic heart failure, does a 12-week tai chi programme improve quality of life and exercise capacity compared with education or usual care?
balance: Two trials from the same programme, and their disagreement is the lesson. The small first trial (30 patients, ejection fraction 40% or less, tai chi twice weekly for 12 weeks added to usual care) reported large gains: quality-of-life scores improved by a mean between-group difference of −25 points (P=0.001), 6-minute walk distance by 135 metres (P=0.001), and B-type natriuretic peptide fell (−138 pg/mL; P=0.03). The larger, multisite, single-blind trial (100 outpatients, NYHA class I–III, ejection fraction 40% or less; group tai chi versus time-matched education) did NOT replicate the capacity findings: change in 6-minute walk distance (median +35 vs +2 metres; P=.95) and peak oxygen uptake (+1.1 vs −0.5 mL/kg/min; P=.81) were not significantly different. But the patient-reported benefits held up: Minnesota Living With Heart Failure scores improved more with tai chi (median change −19 vs +1; P=.02), as did exercise self-efficacy (P<.001) and mood (P=.01). PROPOSED POSSIBLE: offer tai chi to heart-failure patients for how they feel and function day to day — quality of life, mood, confidence to exercise — not as a proven way to raise walk distance or peak VO2; the big trial's null governs the capacity claim, and small-trial effect sizes should be discounted accordingly.

title: After TAVR: an early home-based exercise programme was feasible and improved physical function at 8 weeks in a pilot trial (REHAB-TAVR)
question: In older adults after transcatheter aortic valve replacement, does an early home-based exercise programme (with or without a cognitive-behavioural intervention) improve disability and physical function versus telephone education?
balance: THIN — a 51-patient pilot whose primary purpose was feasibility, and the shelf credits it for exactly what a pilot can show. REHAB-TAVR randomised 51 patients after TAVR (mean age 83.9 years) to home-based exercise with a cognitive-behavioural intervention (18), home exercise alone (15), or telephone education (18). The exercise programme (balance, flexibility, strength, endurance) began within 7 days of discharge, delivered weekly by a physical therapist for 8 weeks; the behavioural arm added goal-setting, planning, and a weekly cash adherence incentive. Completion of at least 5 of 8 sessions: 83.3% with the behavioural package, 58.8% exercise alone, 52.6% education (P=0.196). At 8 weeks the combined exercise groups had lower disability scores than education (2.6 vs 4.5 on a 0–22 scale; P=0.042) and better Short Physical Performance Battery scores (9.5 vs 6.5; P=0.003); the behavioural arm's disability score was lower than exercise alone (2.1 vs 3.4; P=0.047). PROPOSED POSSIBLE: early home rehabilitation after TAVR is feasible in octogenarians and points toward preserved function; a powered trial is still owed before stronger language.

title: Waiting for bypass surgery: a prehabilitation programme shortened hospital stay by a day and improved quality of life (Arthur trial)
question: In low-risk patients waiting at least 10 weeks for elective CABG, does a multidimensional preoperative programme (exercise, education, nurse support) improve postoperative length of stay and recovery?
balance: THIN — one randomised trial, a quarter-century old, in a health system whose waiting lists made the experiment possible. Arthur and colleagues randomised 249 low-risk patients awaiting elective CABG (surgery at least 10 weeks away) at an Ontario centre to a preoperative intervention — exercise training twice weekly, education and reinforcement, and monthly nurse-initiated telephone support during the wait — or usual waiting-list care; all patients were offered cardiac rehabilitation after surgery. The intervention group spent 1 less day in hospital overall (P=0.002) and less time in intensive care (P=0.001), had better quality of life during the waiting period, and the quality-of-life advantage persisted to 6 months after surgery. Mortality did not differ (the trial was far too small to test it). PROPOSED POSSIBLE: the waiting period is usable time — structured prehabilitation bought a shorter stay and better recovery experience in the one trial that tested it. Modern fast-track pathways may compress the room for this gain; the trial's population was explicitly low-risk.

title: ICD programming: higher rate thresholds and longer delays cut inappropriate therapy by about 80% — and mortality in MADIT-RIT (MADIT-RIT + ADVANCE III)
question: In patients with an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator, does programming therapy to higher heart rates or longer detection times reduce inappropriate pacing and shocks without costing safety?
balance: Two large randomised programming trials with the same message: most ICD therapy treats rhythms that would have stopped on their own, and patience is therapeutic. MADIT-RIT randomised 1,500 primary-prevention patients to conventional programming, high-rate therapy (treat only at 200 beats/min or above, after a 2.5-second delay), or delayed therapy (long delays at lower rates). Over an average 1.4 years, first inappropriate therapy fell by roughly four-fifths with either strategy (hazard ratio 0.21 for high-rate, 0.24 for delayed, versus conventional) — and all-cause mortality fell too: hazard ratio 0.45 (95% CI 0.24 to 0.85; P=0.01) for high-rate and 0.56 (0.30 to 1.02; P=0.06) for delayed, with no difference in procedure-related adverse events. ADVANCE III (1,902 primary and secondary prevention patients) tested a long detection interval (30 of 40 beats versus 18 of 24): total delivered therapies fell from 67 to 42 per 100 person-years (incident rate ratio 0.63; P<.001), inappropriate shocks fell (first occurrence 5.1 vs 11.6 per 100 patient-years; IRR 0.55; P=.008), while mortality (HR 0.87; P=.50) and arrhythmic syncope (IRR 1.60; P=.22) did not differ significantly. PROPOSED LIKELY (Tier C): conservative programming — treat fast, or treat late — is one of the few device decisions with randomised mortality support; the absence of a syncope penalty in ADVANCE III answers the obvious safety worry.

title: Remote monitoring of implanted devices: faster evaluation and fewer visits — outcome benefits inconsistent (IN-TIME + TRUST + REM-HF)
question: In patients with heart failure and an implanted defibrillator or resynchronisation device, does automatic remote monitoring improve clinical outcomes, or mainly logistics?
balance: Three randomised trials, three different answers — because they tested three different intensities of monitoring. TRUST (1,339 ICD patients) tested logistics and won clearly: automatic daily home monitoring cut in-hospital device evaluations by 45%, handled 85.8% of mid-year follow-ups remotely, and cut median time from an arrhythmic event to physician evaluation from 36 days to under 2 days (P<0.001), with no morbidity penalty. IN-TIME (664 heart-failure patients, ejection fraction at most 35%, recent ICD or CRT-D) tested one manufacturer's daily multiparameter telemonitoring with a clinical response pathway: the composite clinical score (death, heart-failure hospitalisation, NYHA change, patient self-assessment) worsened in fewer monitored patients (18.9% vs 27.2%; odds ratio 0.63; 95% CI 0.43 to 0.90; P=0.013), and deaths were 10 versus 27 — a striking secondary split the trial was not powered to confirm. REM-HF (1,650 heart-failure patients with devices in England; weekly downloads with formalised follow-up) then found nothing: death or unplanned cardiovascular hospitalisation 42.4% versus 40.8% (hazard ratio 1.01; 95% CI 0.87 to 1.18; P=0.87), and no secondary endpoint differed. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (Tier C): adopt remote monitoring for what is proven — faster event detection, fewer routine visits — and treat outcome benefit as possible but unestablished, likely dependent on what the monitoring centre does with the data.

title: AV block with a weak ventricle: biventricular pacing beat right-ventricular pacing on death, heart-failure care, and remodelling (BLOCK HF)
question: In patients with atrioventricular block, heart failure (NYHA I–III), and ejection fraction of 50% or less who need pacing, does biventricular pacing beat standard right-ventricular pacing?
balance: The trial that extended resynchronisation beyond wide-QRS heart failure to the pacing population itself. BLOCK HF enrolled patients with AV block and an indication for pacing, NYHA class I–III heart failure, and ejection fraction of 50% or less; all received a CRT pacemaker or defibrillator and were randomised to biventricular or standard right-ventricular pacing (691 randomised of 918 enrolled; average follow-up 37 months). The primary outcome — death from any cause, an urgent-care heart-failure visit requiring intravenous therapy, or a 15% or greater increase in left ventricular end-systolic volume index — occurred in 45.8% with biventricular pacing versus 55.6% with right-ventricular pacing (hazard ratio 0.74; 95% credible interval 0.60 to 0.90), with consistent results in the pacemaker and defibrillator subgroups. Left-ventricular lead complications occurred in 6.4% — the price of the extra lead. PROPOSED LIKELY (Tier C): when a patient with AV block and a reduced ejection fraction needs a device, pace both ventricles from the start rather than creating the dyssynchrony that heavy right-ventricular pacing causes. Note the composite leans partly on the remodelling component — the shelf reports the components' nature honestly rather than claiming a pure mortality result.

title: Failing on right-ventricular pacing: upgrading to CRT-D cut death or heart-failure hospitalisation from 32% to 10% (BUDAPEST-CRT Upgrade)
question: In heart-failure patients with reduced ejection fraction, a high right-ventricular pacing burden, and a wide paced QRS, does upgrading to cardiac resynchronisation therapy with defibrillator beat continuing with an ICD?
balance: The largest effect size in the devices literature this year — read it with its composite in view. BUDAPEST-CRT Upgrade randomised 360 symptomatic HFrEF patients (NYHA class II–IVa) with an existing pacemaker or ICD, right-ventricular pacing burden of at least 20%, and paced QRS of at least 150 ms, to CRT-D upgrade (215) or ICD (145). The primary outcome — all-cause mortality, heart-failure hospitalisation, or failure to reduce left ventricular end-systolic volume by at least 15% at 12 months — occurred in 32.4% of the CRT-D group versus 78.9% of the ICD group (odds ratio 0.11; 95% CI 0.06 to 0.19; P<.001). That composite is dominated by the remodelling term (most unchanged ventricles 'fail' it), so the clinically decisive figure is the hard secondary: death or heart-failure hospitalisation occurred in 10% versus 32% (hazard ratio 0.27; 95% CI 0.16 to 0.47; P<.001). Procedure- or device-related complications were similar (12.3% vs 7.8%). PROPOSED LIKELY (Tier C): in a paced patient whose ventricle has failed under a heavy right-ventricular burden, upgrade to resynchronisation — the hard-endpoint separation is too large to be a remodelling artefact. The shelf quotes both numbers so readers can weight them.

title: Dual-chamber versus single-chamber pacing: no survival or stroke advantage across three large trials — atrial fibrillation modestly reduced (MOST + UKPACE + CTOPP)
question: Does dual-chamber (physiological) pacing beat single-chamber ventricular pacing on death and stroke in sinus-node dysfunction and AV block?
balance: Six and a half thousand randomised patients across three trials, one consistent answer: the 'physiological' device does not keep people alive or prevent strokes. MOST (2,010 patients with sinus-node dysfunction; median 33.1 months) found death or nonfatal stroke in 21.5% with dual-chamber versus 23.0% with ventricular pacing (P=0.48), while atrial fibrillation was less frequent with dual-chamber pacing (hazard ratio 0.79; 95% CI 0.66 to 0.94; P=0.008), heart-failure scores were better, and quality of life slightly higher. UKPACE (2,021 patients aged 70 or older with high-grade AV block; median 4.6 years for mortality) found annual mortality of 7.4% versus 7.2% (hazard ratio 0.96; 95% CI 0.83 to 1.11) and no differences in atrial fibrillation, heart failure, or thromboembolism — notably, the AF advantage did not replicate in this AV-block population. CTOPP's extended follow-up (2,568 patients; mean 6.4 years) closed the 'delayed benefit' question: no difference in cardiovascular death or stroke, total mortality, or stroke, while the reduction in new atrial fibrillation with physiological pacing persisted (relative risk reduction 20.1%; 95% CI 5.4 to 32.5; P=0.009). PROPOSED LIKELY (no difference) (Tier C): choose pacing mode for symptoms, pacemaker syndrome, and patient preference — not for survival. Where dual-chamber pacing earns its keep on symptoms sits in the individual trials above; the AF reduction is real but has never converted into fewer strokes.

title: Tinnitus: cognitive behavioural therapy eases the distress it causes — no drug or supplement has been shown to quiet it
question: What is tinnitus, and does any treatment help it?
balance: Tinnitus is the perception of sound with no external source; 10–15% of adults report it and an estimated 1–3% are severely troubled by it. No treatment has been shown to remove the sound itself. What the trial literature does support is treating the distress the sound causes. The Cochrane review of cognitive behavioural therapy (28 randomised trials, 2,733 adults with tinnitus of at least three months) found CBT reduced the impact of tinnitus on quality of life versus waiting list (standardised mean difference −0.56; 95% CI −0.83 to −0.30 — about 11 points on the 0–100 Tinnitus Handicap Inventory, against a minimal clinically important difference of 7; low-certainty evidence), probably reduced it versus audiological care (mean difference −5.65 points; moderate certainty, below that 7-point threshold), and may reduce it versus other active treatments (SMD −0.30; low certainty). Depression scores improved slightly; anxiety and general quality-of-life effects were uncertain; serious adverse effects were not increased. The American Academy of Otolaryngology—Head and Neck Surgery guideline reaches the matching practical conclusions: recommend CBT and a hearing-aid evaluation when hearing loss is documented, and recommend AGAINST antidepressants, anticonvulsants, anxiolytics, intratympanic medications, ginkgo biloba, melatonin, zinc, and other dietary supplements as routine tinnitus treatment. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: the honest offer to a patient with bothersome tinnitus is help coping measurably better — not silence, and not a pill.
