title: ICD patients who don't need pacing: routine dual-chamber pacing at 70/min caused harm versus backup pacing at 40/min (DAVID)
question: In ICD recipients with ejection fraction of 40% or less and no pacing indication, does dual-chamber rate-responsive pacing at 70/min beat minimal ventricular backup pacing at 40/min on death or heart-failure hospitalisation?
balance: The trial that taught device medicine that pacing itself is a drug with side effects. DAVID randomised 506 patients with standard ICD indications, ejection fraction of 40% or less, no indication for antibradycardia pacing, and no persistent atrial arrhythmias to have their dual-chamber devices programmed to dual-chamber rate-responsive pacing at 70/min (DDDR-70) or to ventricular backup pacing at 40/min (VVI-40). The trial was stopped early: one-year survival free of death or first heart-failure hospitalisation was 83.9% with backup pacing versus 73.3% with dual-chamber pacing (relative hazard 1.61; 95% CI 1.06 to 2.44). The components pointed the same way without individually reaching significance — mortality 6.5% versus 10.1% (relative hazard 1.61; 95% CI 0.84 to 3.09) and heart-failure hospitalisation 13.3% versus 22.6% (relative hazard 1.54; 95% CI 0.97 to 2.46). The mechanism is the unnecessary right-ventricular pacing that an active dual-chamber programme delivers to a ventricle that did not need it — dyssynchrony as iatrogenesis. PROPOSED LIKELY (harm) (Tier C): in ICD patients without a pacing indication, program minimal ventricular pacing. The shelf closes the loop with MOST/UKPACE/CTOPP (Shelf #2297 — mode choice is neutral when pacing is needed) and with MADIT-RIT (Shelf #2293 — restraint in therapy programming): across all three, less unnecessary device activity is better.

title: Resynchronisation by the conduction system: left-bundle-branch pacing beat biventricular pacing on death or heart-failure hospitalisation in one randomised trial (HeartSync-LBBP)
question: In heart failure with reduced ejection fraction and left bundle-branch block, does left-bundle-branch pacing achieve better long-term outcomes than conventional biventricular pacing for cardiac resynchronisation?
balance: One randomised trial with a startlingly large effect — carded with its size and setting in plain view. HeartSync-LBBP randomised 200 patients with ejection fraction of 35% or less and left bundle-branch block at six centres in China to left-bundle-branch pacing (LBBP) or biventricular pacing (BiVP), with a median follow-up of 36 months. The primary endpoint (death from any cause or heart-failure hospitalisation) occurred in 8% with LBBP versus 28% with BiVP (hazard ratio 0.26; 95% CI 0.12 to 0.57; P<.001), driven by hospitalisation (7.0% vs 28.0%; HR 0.23) — mortality alone did not differ significantly (2.0% vs 5.0%; HR 0.40; 95% CI 0.08 to 2.04). Implant success was 98% versus 94%; echocardiographic response rates were similar (86% vs 81%), while super-response was more frequent with LBBP (55% vs 36%; P=.007). The earlier pilot, His-SYNC (41 patients, His-bundle pacing versus BiVP), is named here but NOT carded: its PubMed record is a two-page report carrying no abstract, so no figures from it are quoted anywhere on this shelf. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (Tier C): conduction-system pacing is the most promising challenger biventricular pacing has had — one 200-patient, single-country trial with an effect this size needs independent replication before stronger language; the authors themselves conclude that further trials are warranted.

title: Recurrent reflex syncope with a cardioinhibitory response: closed-loop-stimulation pacing cut recurrences in two blinded trials (SPAIN + BIOSync CLS)
question: In patients aged 40 or older with recurrent reflex (vasovagal) syncope and documented cardioinhibition or tilt-induced asystole, does dual-chamber pacing with closed-loop stimulation reduce syncope recurrence versus sham or switched-off pacing?
balance: Pacing for vasovagal syncope failed for decades in unselected patients; these two trials show what changed — selecting the cardioinhibitory phenotype and using a sensor that reacts to the faint itself. Closed-loop stimulation (CLS) adjusts rate from intracardiac impedance, rising as the vasovagal cascade begins. SPAIN (46 patients aged at least 40 with high-burden syncope and a cardioinhibitory tilt test; randomised crossover between CLS pacing and sham pacing) found at least a 50% reduction in syncope episodes in 72% of patients during CLS periods versus 28% during sham (P=0.017); events occurred in 4 patients (8.7%) on CLS versus 21 (45.7%) on sham. BIOSync CLS (127 patients aged at least 40 with severe recurrent reflex syncope and tilt-induced asystole over 3 seconds; pacing ON versus OFF, double-blind) found syncope recurrence in 16% versus 53% over a median 11.2 months (hazard ratio 0.23; P=0.00005), with estimated 2-year recurrence 22% versus 68%, and minor device-related adverse events in 4%. PROPOSED LIKELY: in this narrow, test-selected phenotype — recurrent, severe, cardioinhibitory — CLS pacing works. The shelf's boundary is the phenotype: these results say nothing about pacing unselected fainters, the population in which pacing earned its poor reputation.

title: Neurally mediated syncope with loop-recorder-documented asystole: pacing halved recurrence (ISSUE-3)
question: In patients aged 40 or older with recurrent neurally mediated syncope and implantable-loop-recorder documentation of asystole, does dual-chamber pacing reduce syncope recurrence versus sensing only?
balance: THIN — one trial, and its statistics sit exactly at the threshold, but the selection strategy it validated changed practice. ISSUE-3 gave implantable loop recorders to 511 patients aged at least 40 with at least three syncopes in two years; 89 documented syncope with asystole of at least 3 seconds (or at least 6 seconds without syncope), and 77 were randomised double-blind to dual-chamber pacing with rate-drop response switched ON or to sensing only (OFF). Over two years the estimated syncope recurrence was 25% with pacing ON versus 57% OFF (log-rank P=0.039, against a prespecified significance threshold of 0.04) — a 57% relative reduction (95% CI 4 to 81) and a 32-point absolute reduction. Procedural complications occurred in five patients (four lead dislodgements requiring correction, one subclavian vein thrombosis). PROPOSED POSSIBLE: document the asystole first, then pace — the loop recorder, not the tilt table, is this trial's selection tool (compare Shelf #2301, where tilt selection plus closed-loop stimulation produced larger effects). A P value at the boundary in 77 randomised patients earns POSSIBLE, not more.

title: Cardioinhibitory vasovagal syncope: cardioneuroablation kept 92% free of syncope at 2 years versus 46% with non-pharmacological care (Piotrowski RCT)
question: In patients with documented cardioinhibitory or mixed vasovagal syncope, does cardioneuroablation (ablation of the atrial ganglionated plexi) improve freedom from syncope versus optimal non-pharmacological management?
balance: THIN — the first randomised trial of a procedure that deletes part of the vagus nerve's cardiac wiring, in 48 patients. Piotrowski and colleagues randomised patients with documented symptomatic cardioinhibitory or mixed vasovagal syncope and a positive atropine test to cardioneuroablation (radiofrequency ablation of ganglionated plexi from both atria) or optimal non-pharmacological therapy, with two years of follow-up. The primary endpoint — first syncope recurrence — occurred in 2 of 24 ablation patients (8%) versus 13 of 24 controls (54%) (P=0.0004). After ablation, resting sinus rate was faster and heart-rate-variability measures shifted toward parasympathetic withdrawal, confirming the intended denervation physiology; quality of life improved significantly in the ablation group and was stable in controls. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: a dramatic result in a small, open-label, single-programme trial — the effect size invites belief and the design demands replication, particularly on durability (do the plexi regrow function?) and on the long-term cost of vagal denervation in patients whose mean age was 38. The control was non-pharmacological care, not sham ablation, so expectation effects are unconstrained.

title: Recurrent pericarditis that keeps coming back: continuing the IL-1 trap rilonacept prevented nearly all recurrences (RHAPSODY)
question: In colchicine-resistant, corticosteroid-dependent recurrent pericarditis with systemic inflammation, does continued rilonacept prevent recurrence versus withdrawal to placebo?
balance: A randomised-withdrawal trial — the standard architecture for a relapsing disease, and it should be read as one: everyone first had to respond to the drug. RHAPSODY enrolled 86 patients presenting with a pericarditis recurrence (pain plus elevated CRP) on standard therapy into a 12-week open run-in on rilonacept, an interleukin-1α/β trap, during which background medicines were stopped; pain resolved or nearly resolved in a median of 5 days and CRP normalised in a median of 7 days. The 61 responders were randomised to continue weekly rilonacept or switch to placebo. During withdrawal, recurrence occurred in 2 of 30 patients (7%) continuing rilonacept versus 23 of 31 (74%) on placebo (hazard ratio 0.04; 95% CI 0.01 to 0.18; P<.001); median time to recurrence on placebo was 8.6 weeks, while too few events occurred on rilonacept to estimate its median. The commonest adverse events were injection-site reactions and upper respiratory infections; four patients discontinued during the run-in for adverse events. PROPOSED LIKELY: in IL-1-driven recurrent pericarditis that has already declared itself steroid-dependent, blocking IL-1 keeps the disease off. Distinct from Shelf #190 (colchicine for pericarditis episodes) — this is the next line, for the patients colchicine and steroids fail.

title: Colchicine-resistant, steroid-dependent recurrent pericarditis: continuing anakinra prevented most recurrences (AIRTRIP)
question: In recurrent pericarditis with colchicine resistance and corticosteroid dependence, does continued anakinra (interleukin-1 receptor antagonist) prevent recurrence versus withdrawal to placebo?
balance: THIN — 21 patients, and the whole effect rests on 11 versus 10 randomised patients, but the separation is near-total and it anticipated the larger rilonacept trial (Shelf #2304). AIRTRIP enrolled patients with recurrent pericarditis (at least three prior recurrences), elevated CRP, colchicine resistance, and corticosteroid dependence at three Italian centres; all received open-label anakinra (2 mg/kg/day, up to 100 mg) for two months, and responders were randomised to continue anakinra (11) or switch to placebo (10). Over a median 14 months of follow-up, recurrence occurred in 2 of 11 patients (18.2%) continuing anakinra versus 9 of 10 (90%) withdrawn to placebo; median flare-free survival on placebo was 72 days and was not reached on anakinra (P<.001). Transient local skin reactions occurred in 20 of 21 patients (95.2%) during anakinra treatment; one patient each had herpes zoster, transaminase elevation, and ischaemic optic neuropathy; no patient permanently discontinued the drug. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: daily-injection IL-1 blockade works in this phenotype; the trial's size, not its direction, is the limitation. One records note: this article's PubMed record carries plainly mis-indexed MeSH terms (infant-nutrition descriptors that belong to a different article); per library policy the terms are copied verbatim from the record and flagged here rather than silently corrected.

title: Idiopathic recurrent pericarditis: goflikicept prevented every recurrence in a small withdrawal trial
question: In idiopathic recurrent pericarditis, does the interleukin-1 inhibitor goflikicept maintain remission versus withdrawal to placebo after an open-label response?
balance: THIN — the third IL-1 agent to clear the same bar, in the smallest and most geographically concentrated trial of the three. This phase II/III study at two centres enrolled 22 patients with idiopathic recurrent pericarditis into an open-label goflikicept run-in; CRP, chest pain, and pericardial effusion all improved from baseline, and the 20 responders were randomised to continue goflikicept or switch to placebo for a 24-week withdrawal period. Recurrence occurred in 9 of 10 patients on placebo and in none on goflikicept (P<0.001). A total of 122 adverse events were reported in 21 of 22 patients (95.5%) — a high count that reflects event-by-event reporting in a small cohort; there were no deaths and no new safety signals identified. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: directionally identical to rilonacept (Shelf #2304) and anakinra (Shelf #2305) — IL-1 blockade as a class holds remission in this disease — but goflikicept's own evidence base is 20 randomised patients from two centres in one region, and availability outside its home market is limited; the shelf claims class concordance, not a standalone verdict.

title: After cardiac surgery: colchicine prevents the post-pericardiotomy syndrome in two trials — but not postoperative AF (COPPS + COPPS-2)
question: In patients undergoing cardiac surgery, does perioperative colchicine prevent the post-pericardiotomy syndrome, postoperative atrial fibrillation, and effusions?
balance: Two multicentre double-blind trials from the same Italian programme, concordant on the syndrome and honestly split on the rhythm. COPPS (360 patients; colchicine started on postoperative day 3 for one month) cut the post-pericardiotomy syndrome at 12 months from 21.1% to 8.9% (P=0.002; number needed to treat 8) and reduced the composite of disease-related hospitalisation, tamponade, constriction, and relapses (0.6% vs 5.0%; P=0.024), with similar side-effect rates (8.9% vs 5.0%; P=0.212). COPPS-2 (360 patients; colchicine started 48–72 hours before surgery and continued one month) again cut the syndrome (19.4% vs 29.4%; absolute difference 10.0%; NNT 10) — but on intention-to-treat it did NOT significantly reduce postoperative atrial fibrillation (33.9% vs 41.7%; absolute difference 7.8%, CI crossing zero) or pericardial/pleural effusions (57.2% vs 58.9%), though a prespecified on-treatment analysis did show less AF (27.0% vs 41.2%). Gastrointestinal adverse events were more frequent with colchicine in COPPS-2 (20.0% vs 11.7%; number needed to harm 12), with similar discontinuation rates and no serious adverse events. PROPOSED LIKELY: a month of colchicine around cardiac surgery prevents roughly one post-pericardiotomy syndrome per ten patients treated; do not prescribe it for the AF — the larger perioperative trial's primary analysis says no.

title: Tuberculous pericarditis: steroids and immunotherapy did not move the composite of death, tamponade, or constriction — constriction fell, cancers rose (IMPI)
question: In tuberculous pericarditis, mostly in people with HIV, does adjunctive prednisolone or Mycobacterium indicus pranii immunotherapy reduce death, cardiac tamponade, or constrictive pericarditis?
balance: A 1,400-patient factorial trial that answered a decades-old practice question with a split verdict — and the split is the shelf. IMPI randomised adults with definite or probable tuberculous pericarditis (two-thirds with HIV infection) to prednisolone or placebo for six weeks and, independently, to Mycobacterium indicus pranii immunotherapy or placebo, on top of antituberculosis therapy. The primary composite (death, cardiac tamponade requiring pericardiocentesis, or constrictive pericarditis) did not differ for either intervention: 23.8% versus 24.5% for prednisolone (hazard ratio 0.95; 95% CI 0.77 to 1.18; P=0.66) and 25.0% versus 24.3% for immunotherapy (HR 1.03; P=0.81). Inside the composite, prednisolone did reduce constriction (4.4% vs 7.8%; HR 0.56; 95% CI 0.36 to 0.87; P=0.009) and hospitalisation (20.7% vs 25.2%; HR 0.79; P=0.04). Against that, both interventions increased cancer incidence (prednisolone 1.8% vs 0.6%, HR 3.27; immunotherapy 1.8% vs 0.5%, HR 3.69), owing mainly to HIV-associated cancers. PROPOSED LIKELY (no difference) (Tier C) on the question as posed: neither adjunct improves the composite outcome that matters most. The constriction finding keeps a narrower, judgement-level case for steroids alive in selected patients — and the cancer signal, in an HIV-prevalent population, is the price that has to be weighed against it; the shelf presents both rather than resolving that bedside trade.

title: Exudative pericarditis: intrapericardial urokinase prevented constriction in one randomised study — the wider literature is case reports
question: In large exudative (especially tuberculous or purulent) pericardial effusion, does intrapericardial fibrinolysis prevent constrictive pericarditis and drainage failure versus drainage alone?
balance: One randomised study with a large effect, surrounded by a literature of anecdotes — the shelf holds both facts at once. Cui and colleagues randomised 94 patients with infectious exudative pericarditis (60 tuberculous, 34 purulent; disease course under one month) to pericardiocentesis and drainage with or without intrapericardial urokinase irrigation (200,000–600,000 units). Over a mean follow-up of about 57 months, constriction developed in 9 of 47 patients (19.1%) with urokinase versus 27 of 47 (57.4%) with drainage alone (Cox relative hazard coefficient 0.185; P<0.0001); pericardial thickness fell from 3.1 to 1.6 mm in the urokinase group and was unchanged in controls; intrapericardial bleeding occurred in 6 of 47 patients with non-bloody effusion, with no systemic bleeding, no severe puncture complications, and no cardiac deaths. The systematic review alongside it is the cold water: across the whole published literature, Wiyeh and colleagues found 29 reports totalling just 109 patients — 17 case reports, 11 case series, and that single randomised trial — all at high risk of bias, with non-fatal procedure complications in 19.2% and, in the reviewers' words, very low certainty of efficacy and safety. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (Tier C — the trial's endpoint is a serious structural outcome and the shelf is graded for its evidence structure, not its topic): lysing the fibrin while the effusion is drained is biologically coherent and the one trial is strongly positive; a literature this thin cannot carry more.

title: Malignant pericardial effusion: prolonged catheter drainage matched surgical window on recurrence, with far fewer complications (retrospective)
question: In malignant pericardial effusion with tamponade, does percutaneous prolonged drainage match surgical pericardiotomy for recurrence, complications, and diagnostic yield?
balance: THIN — a single retrospective comparison, and the shelf says so up front; but it is the direct head-to-head for a decision made weekly on oncology wards, and its three answers are clean. Patel and colleagues reviewed 88 patients presenting with tamponade associated with malignancy: 43 treated with pericardiocentesis and extended catheter drainage, 45 with surgical pericardiotomy. Recurrence did not differ (12% with drainage versus 13% with surgery; P=0.78), and neither did diagnostic yield (44% versus 53%; P=0.39) — the surgical biopsy added no significant diagnostic value beyond the cytology available from the tap. Complications did differ, substantially: 2% overall with prolonged drainage versus 20% with surgery (P=0.007), with serious complications in none of the drainage patients versus 9% of the surgical group. Survival in this population is driven by the underlying malignancy, not by the drainage route — which is precisely why the less invasive route's equal efficacy matters. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: retrospective treatment selection (sicker patients may have been routed either way) caps the stamp; within that limit, prolonged drainage is the defensible default and surgery the exception for specific indications.

title: Constrictive pericarditis: survival after pericardiectomy is set by the cause — idiopathic best, post-radiation worst (Bertog cohort)
question: In chronic constrictive pericarditis, how do survival after pericardiectomy and its predictors differ by aetiology — idiopathic, post-surgical, or post-radiation?
balance: No randomised trial of pericardiectomy exists or will — this 163-patient surgical cohort is the evidence, presented as prognosis rather than as a treatment comparison. Bertog and colleagues followed 163 patients who underwent pericardiectomy for constrictive pericarditis over 24 years at a single surgical centre (perioperative mortality 6%; 61 deaths over a median 6.9 years of follow-up among survivors). Cause-specific seven-year survival diverged sharply: idiopathic constriction fared best (88%; 95% CI 76 to 94), post-surgical constriction next (66%; 95% CI 52 to 78), and post-radiation constriction worst by far (27%; 95% CI 9 to 58). In bootstrap-validated proportional-hazards analyses, predictors of poor overall survival were prior radiation, worse renal function, higher pulmonary artery systolic pressure, abnormal left ventricular systolic function, lower serum sodium, and older age; pericardial calcification had no impact on survival. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (Tier C — mortality is the outcome throughout): the numbers to bring to the consent conversation are these aetiology-stratified ones, and the relatively good survival after idiopathic pericardiectomy is itself an argument that the operation, in that subgroup, is safe and durable. The shelf makes no claim that surgery beats medical management in any subgroup — no such comparison exists in the record.

title: Autoreactive pericardial effusion: intrapericardial triamcinolone prevented most recurrences in an uncontrolled series — at the lower dose, with less Cushing syndrome
question: In autoreactive (non-infectious, non-malignant) pericardial effusion, does intrapericardial triamcinolone achieve remission while sparing systemic corticosteroid toxicity?
balance: Hypothesis-grade evidence, stamped as such. Maisch and colleagues worked up 260 consecutive patients with pericarditis/myopericarditis by pericardiocentesis, pericardioscopy, and epicardial biopsy with viral PCR and immunohistochemistry; 84 classified as autoreactive received intrapericardial triamcinolone — 54 at 600 mg/m² over 24 hours and 30 at 300 mg/m² (dose cohorts, not a randomised comparison). Symptomatic improvement with no effusion recurrence was seen in 92.6% (high dose) versus 86.7% (low dose) at 3 months and 86.0% versus 82.1% at one year (no significant difference between doses). There were no treatment-related acute complications; transient iatrogenic Cushing syndrome developed in 29.6% of the high-dose group versus 13.3% of the low-dose group (P<0.05) — the systemic spill was reduced, not abolished. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): there is no untreated or systemically treated control group, so the recurrence rates cannot be credited to the drug against the disease's natural history; what the series genuinely supports is feasibility, the lower dose's equal performance, and a smaller — real, but partial — steroid-sparing effect. The diagnostic pathway it depends on (pericardioscopy and epicardial biopsy for every effusion) is itself a specialised-centre undertaking.

title: Acute pericarditis: CRP is up in three of four patients, settles within four weeks — and a still-high CRP at week 1 flags recurrence risk (Imazio cohort)
question: In a first episode of acute pericarditis, how often is C-reactive protein elevated, how fast does it normalise on treatment, and does persistent elevation identify patients at risk of recurrence?
balance: A prognostic cohort, carded as prognosis — it describes the disease's inflammatory signature and the company recurrence keeps. Imazio and colleagues followed 200 consecutive patients with viral or idiopathic acute pericarditis at two Italian referral centres, measuring high-sensitivity CRP at presentation and weekly until normalisation. CRP was elevated in 156 of 200 patients (78%) at presentation; among the 44 without elevation, the recognised explanations were very early assessment (34%) and anti-inflammatory therapy already started (50%) — so a normal CRP does not exclude the diagnosis. On treatment, CRP normalised in 60% by week 1, 85% by week 2, 95% by week 3, and 100% by week 4. In multivariable analysis, three features independently predicted recurrence: incomplete response to empirical anti-inflammatory therapy at week 1 (hazard ratio 2.98; 95% CI 1.80 to 4.94), corticosteroid therapy (HR 2.80; 95% CI 1.59 to 4.95), and elevated hs-CRP still present at week 1 (HR 2.36; 95% CI 1.32 to 4.21). PROPOSED POSSIBLE: this is the observational basis for CRP-guided treatment duration — a strategy that has itself never been randomised, and the shelf says so; the steroid association, in particular, is the familiar confounding-by-severity pattern (steroids go to the worst cases) and should not be quoted as proof that steroids cause recurrences.

title: Eisenmenger syndrome: bosentan improved walk distance and haemodynamics without worsening oxygen saturation (BREATHE-5)
question: In Eisenmenger syndrome (WHO functional class III), does bosentan improve exercise capacity and haemodynamics without worsening systemic oxygen saturation?
balance: THIN — 54 patients and surrogate endpoints, but it was the first placebo-controlled trial in this disease and it answered the safety fear that had kept the drug class away. BREATHE-5 randomised patients with WHO class III Eisenmenger syndrome 2:1 to bosentan (37) or placebo (17) for 16 weeks, with haemodynamics by right- and left-heart catheterisation. The primary safety endpoint cleared: the placebo-corrected effect on systemic pulse oximetry was +1.0% (95% CI −0.7 to 2.8) — bosentan did not worsen oxygen saturation by shunting more blood right-to-left. The primary efficacy endpoint also moved: pulmonary vascular resistance index fell by 472 dyne·s·cm⁻⁵ versus placebo (P=0.0383), mean pulmonary artery pressure fell by 5.5 mm Hg (P=0.0363), and 6-minute walk distance rose by 53.1 m (P=0.0079). Four patients discontinued for adverse events (2 on bosentan, 5%; 2 on placebo, 12%). PROPOSED POSSIBLE: a small, short, surrogate-endpoint trial whose lasting contribution is permission — endothelin blockade does not desaturate Eisenmenger patients. Its class sibling's larger failure sits on the next shelf (MAESTRO, #2315), and the pair should be read together.

title: Eisenmenger syndrome: macitentan did not improve walk distance in the larger phase 3 trial (MAESTRO)
question: In Eisenmenger syndrome (WHO functional class II–III), does macitentan improve 6-minute walk distance versus placebo over 16 weeks?
balance: The larger, better-powered test of the endothelin hypothesis in Eisenmenger syndrome — and the primary endpoint missed cleanly, in the wrong direction by a whisker. MAESTRO randomised 226 patients aged at least 12 in WHO class II–III (60% in class II; 27% already on a PDE5 inhibitor; complex defects and Down syndrome eligible) to macitentan 10 mg daily (114) or placebo (112) for 16 weeks. Walk distance improved by 18.3 m on macitentan and 19.7 m on placebo (least-squares mean difference −4.7 m; 95% confidence limits −22.8 to 13.5; P=0.612); functional class improved in fewer macitentan patients (8.8% vs 14.3%; odds ratio 0.53). Two secondary signals favoured the drug — NT-proBNP fell relative to placebo (geometric-mean ratio 0.80; 95% CL 0.68 to 0.94) and, in the 39-patient haemodynamic substudy, pulmonary vascular resistance index fell (ratio 0.87; 95% CL 0.73 to 1.03) — biomarkers moving while the patient-centred endpoint did not. A haemoglobin fall of at least 2 g/dL occurred in 36.0% on macitentan versus 8.9% on placebo; headache was commoner (11.4% vs 4.5%); one patient died, in the macitentan group. PROPOSED LIKELY (no difference) on the primary question as posed. Placed beside BREATHE-5 (Shelf #2314) by design: small positive predecessor, larger null successor — the standard correction pattern of this literature, and a standing warning about class-level inference from pilot trials.

title: Fontan circulation: udenafil missed its peak-exercise primary endpoint but improved submaximal exercise measures (FUEL)
question: In adolescents with Fontan physiology, does the PDE5 inhibitor udenafil improve peak oxygen consumption and submaximal exercise performance versus placebo?
balance: A genuinely split result, and the shelf keeps it split. FUEL randomised 400 adolescents with Fontan physiology (mean age 15.5) at 30 centres to udenafil 87.5 mg twice daily or placebo for 26 weeks. The primary outcome — change in peak oxygen consumption — missed: peak VO2 rose 44 ± 245 mL/min (2.8%) on udenafil and fell 3.7 ± 228 mL/min (−0.2%) on placebo (P=0.071). At the ventilatory anaerobic threshold, however, three prespecified exercise measures all improved significantly with udenafil: oxygen consumption (+33 ± 185 [3.2%] vs −9 ± 193 [−0.9%] mL/min; P=0.012), ventilatory equivalents for carbon dioxide (−0.8 vs −0.06; P=0.014), and work rate (+3.8 vs +0.34 W; P=0.021). There was no difference in myocardial performance index, reactive hyperaemia index, or BNP. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: the honest summary is that submaximal exercise — the intensity at which Fontan patients actually live their days — improved, while the maximal-effort primary did not reach significance; whether the submaximal gains are worth a twice-daily drug in an adolescent is a judgement the trial informs but cannot settle. The shelf resists both available spins: it is not a positive trial, and it is not a nothing-happened trial.

title: Fontan circulation: bosentan improved peak oxygen uptake and functional class over 14 weeks (TEMPO)
question: In adolescents and adults after the Fontan operation, does bosentan improve peak oxygen uptake, exercise time, and functional class versus placebo?
balance: THIN — small and short, but randomised, double-blind, and positive on its primary where its larger macitentan successor (RUBATO, Shelf #2318) was not. TEMPO randomised 75 adolescents and adults after Fontan palliation 1:1 to bosentan or placebo for 14 weeks; 69 (92%) completed. Peak oxygen consumption rose 2.0 mL/kg/min (28.7 to 30.7) on bosentan versus 0.6 (28.4 to 29.0) on placebo (P=0.02); exercise test time rose 0.48 versus 0.08 minutes (P=0.04); nine bosentan patients improved one functional class and no placebo patient did (P=0.0085). Side effects were mild and equally frequent in both groups; no serious adverse effects occurred and no patient's liver enzymes exceeded three times the upper limit — notable for a bosentan trial. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: a 14-week, 75-patient trial can show that exercise capacity moves; it cannot show durability, and the Fontan literature's pattern (promising small trial, null large trial — BREATHE-5 into MAESTRO, this trial into RUBATO) is itself part of the evidence. The shelf is deliberately shelved adjacent to RUBATO so the pair is read together.

title: Fontan circulation: macitentan did not improve exercise capacity over 52 weeks in the phase 3 trial (RUBATO)
question: In Fontan-palliated adolescents and adults (NYHA class II–III), does macitentan improve peak oxygen consumption versus placebo?
balance: The definitive-sized endothelin trial in Fontan physiology, and it closed the question its pilot literature had opened. RUBATO randomised 137 Fontan-palliated patients aged at least 12 (NYHA class II–III, total cavopulmonary connection more than a year earlier, no signs of Fontan failure) to macitentan 10 mg (68) or placebo (69); 92.7% completed 52 weeks of double-blind treatment. The primary endpoint — change in peak oxygen consumption at week 16 — was not met: −0.16 ± 2.86 mL/kg/min on macitentan versus −0.67 ± 2.66 on placebo (treatment difference estimate 0.62; 99% CI −0.62 to 1.85; P=.19), and no treatment effect appeared in either secondary endpoint (peak VO2 change over 52 weeks; accelerometer-measured daily activity at week 16). Macitentan was generally well tolerated — headache, nasopharyngitis, and pyrexia were the commonest events in the double-blind phase — and the open-label extension was discontinued early precisely because the double-blind trial had missed. PROPOSED LIKELY (no difference): in stable Fontan patients without failure, macitentan does not improve exercise capacity. Beside TEMPO's small positive bosentan result (Shelf #2317), this completes the slate's repeated lesson — in congenital-heart physiology, the bigger trial is the one to believe.

title: Fontan circulation: sildenafil improved ventilatory efficiency but not peak oxygen uptake in the STEP crossover trial
question: In children and young adults after the Fontan operation, does oral sildenafil improve exercise performance?
balance: The mechanistic hope in Fontan physiology is that lowering pulmonary vascular resistance improves cardiac filling, and this small crossover trial (STEP) is the cleanest test of sildenafil against it. Twenty-eight children and young adults after Fontan were randomised to sildenafil 20 mg three times daily or placebo for 6 weeks, washed out for 6 weeks, then crossed over, with exercise testing at the start and end of each phase. Peak oxygen consumption did not change on sildenafil. What did improve was ventilatory efficiency: respiratory rate and minute ventilation at peak exercise fell significantly, and at the anaerobic threshold the ventilatory equivalents of carbon dioxide fell significantly. A suggestion of improved oxygen consumption at the anaerobic threshold was confined to two subgroups — single left or mixed ventricular morphology, and baseline BNP at least 100 pg/mL. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: sildenafil measurably improves ventilatory efficiency during peak and submaximal exercise after Fontan, but the headline exercise measure — peak oxygen uptake — did not move, and the trial is 28 patients. Read beside FUEL (Shelf #2316, udenafil: peak VO2 also missed) and RUBATO (Shelf #2318), the Fontan pharmacotherapy pattern is consistent: submaximal signals recur, peak capacity does not.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit on ventilatory efficiency only)

title: Fontan thromboprophylaxis in children: rivaroxaban looked comparable to aspirin in the descriptive UNIVERSE study
question: In children after the Fontan procedure, is weight-adjusted rivaroxaban an acceptable alternative to aspirin for thromboprophylaxis?
balance: UNIVERSE is the only randomised evidence for an everyday Fontan question, and it was designed to describe, not to prove. In part B, 100 children post-Fontan were randomised 2:1 to open-label body-weight-adjusted liquid rivaroxaban or aspirin for 12 months (112 enrolled overall including the 12-patient pharmacokinetic part A). Thrombotic events were few in both arms: one pulmonary embolism on rivaroxaban (2% overall event rate) versus one ischaemic stroke and two venous thromboses on aspirin (9% overall event rate) — fewer on rivaroxaban, not statistically significant. Bleeding: one major bleed on rivaroxaban (epistaxis requiring transfusion); clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding 6% on rivaroxaban versus 9% on aspirin; trivial bleeding 33% versus 35%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: rivaroxaban's safety profile looked similar to aspirin's and no efficacy signal ran against it, but with event counts of 1 versus 3 the study cannot establish equivalence — it establishes that the question is answerable and that neither arm misbehaved in a year of use.
stamp: POSSIBLE (comparable safety; efficacy descriptive only)

title: Systemic right ventricle: valsartan did not preserve ventricular function over 3 years in the van der Bom trial
question: In adults with a systemic right ventricle, does valsartan preserve right ventricular ejection fraction versus placebo?
balance: The systemic right ventricle — after atrial switch for transposition, or in congenitally corrected transposition — fails late, and whether renin–angiotensin blockade slows that failure was extrapolated for years from left-ventricular practice. The van der Bom trial is the direct test: 88 adults with a systemic right ventricle randomised double-blind to valsartan 160 mg twice daily or placebo for 3 years, with ejection fraction measured by cardiac magnetic resonance (or CT where MRI was contraindicated). The primary endpoint was null: the treatment effect on systemic RV ejection fraction was 1.3% (95% CI −1.3 to 3.9; P=0.34), and there was no significant effect on maximum exercise capacity, quality of life, or the frequency of significant clinical events; no serious adverse effects occurred in either group. The one asymmetry ran the other way from harm: right ventricular end-diastolic volume and mass rose more on placebo (by 15 mL and 8 g more) — remodelling markers favouring valsartan without a functional dividend. PROPOSED LIKELY (no difference): three years of valsartan does not preserve systemic RV function in this population, and the confidence interval excludes a large ejection-fraction benefit.
stamp: LIKELY (no difference)

title: Systemic right ventricular dysfunction: dapagliflozin was followed by better walk distance and function in a small uncontrolled study (DAPA-SRV)
question: In symptomatic patients with systemic right ventricular dysfunction, is starting dapagliflozin safe, and what happens to functional status and ventricular measures?
balance: Read this shelf for what the study is, because the gap between its design and its promise is the whole story. DAPA-SRV is NOT a randomised trial: it is a prospective, observational, single-centre before-and-after study of 32 symptomatic patients (NYHA class at least 2) with systemic right ventricular dysfunction — 62% transposition with atrial switch, 38% congenitally corrected transposition — assessed before and 3 and 6 months after dapagliflozin was started, on background therapy including sacubitril/valsartan. At 6 months, 6-minute walk distance had improved (585 m versus 558 m at baseline; P=0.04), as had quality of life (KCCQ-12 score 91.5 versus 80.5; P<0.001) and systemic RV function (fractional area change 33% versus 28%; P=0.02; global longitudinal strain −13.1% versus −11.2%; P=0.04), and no significant side effects were observed. Every one of those numbers comes from an uncontrolled comparison in which expectation, regression to the mean, and co-interventions all push the same direction. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): dapagliflozin appeared safe and well tolerated in 32 systemic-RV patients and the within-patient changes are encouraging — this is a reason to run the randomised trial the authors themselves call for, not a reason to treat the benefit as shown.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence)

title: Fontan circulation: resistance training raised cardiac output and exercise capacity in an 11-patient controlled study (Cordina)
question: In adults with a Fontan circulation, does lower-limb resistance training improve cardiac output, exercise capacity, and tolerance of positive airway pressure?
balance: The Fontan circulation has no subpulmonary ventricle, so cardiac filling leans on the respiratory bellows and the peripheral muscle pump — which makes this the rare exercise study with a direct haemodynamic hypothesis. Cordina and colleagues studied 11 adults with Fontan-type circulation; 6 underwent 20 weeks of high-intensity resistance training and the rest were non-exercising controls, with cardiac magnetic resonance flow measurement and exercise testing. In the trained state, muscle strength rose 43% (P=0.002), total muscle mass rose 1.94 kg (P=0.003), and peak oxygen uptake rose 183 mL/min (P=0.02). The detraining phase is what makes the physiology persuasive: after 12 months detrained, peak VO2 fell (2.72 versus 2.18 L/min; P<0.001), stroke volume fell at rest (by 11 mL; P=0.01) and during moderate exercise (by 16 mL; P=0.04), inspiratory-dependent inferior vena cava return during exercise rose 40% (P=0.02), and cardiac output on continuous positive airway pressure was lower than in the trained state (77 versus 101 mL/s; P=0.03). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): the within-person training–detraining pattern fits the muscle-pump mechanism beautifully, but this is 11 patients, six of them trained, in a non-randomised comparison — a mechanism demonstrated, not a therapy established.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence)

title: Anthracycline cardiotoxicity: dexrazoxane roughly halved cardiac events in two blinded trials (Swain)
question: In patients receiving doxorubicin-based chemotherapy, does dexrazoxane reduce cardiac events without compromising antitumour effect?
balance: Dexrazoxane is the one cardioprotectant whose evidence predates the imaging-surrogate era: two multicentre double-blind trials (088001 and 088006) randomised 534 women with advanced breast cancer receiving fluorouracil, doxorubicin, and cyclophosphamide to dexrazoxane (10:1 ratio to doxorubicin) or placebo, with serial MUGA monitoring and a cardiac-event endpoint of predefined ejection-fraction change or clinical heart failure. Placebo patients carried markedly higher cardiac-event hazard: hazard ratio for placebo versus dexrazoxane 2.63 (95% CI 1.61 to 4.27; P<.001) in 088001 and 2.00 (95% CI 1.01 to 3.96; P=.038) in 088006 — i.e., dexrazoxane cut the cardiac-event hazard by roughly 60% and 50% relative, respectively. The honest complication is antitumour effect: objective response rate was lower with dexrazoxane in 088001 (46.8% versus 60.5%, a 14-point difference; P=.019) but not in 088006 (53.7% versus 49.3%), and time to progression and survival did not differ significantly in either study. Toxicity traded mildly: lower granulocyte and platelet nadirs and more injection pain on dexrazoxane, no difference in fever, infection, or haemorrhage. PROPOSED LIKELY: dexrazoxane genuinely prevents doxorubicin cardiac events — the first agent shown to do so — while the single-study response-rate dip is why its use settled into high-cumulative-dose and metastatic settings rather than routine adjuvant care.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: Anthracycline therapy in breast cancer: candesartan slightly attenuated LVEF decline, metoprolol did not (PRADA)
question: In early breast cancer receiving anthracycline-based adjuvant therapy, do candesartan or metoprolol prevent decline in left ventricular ejection fraction?
balance: PRADA asked whether the two cheapest neurohormonal drugs could blunt the ejection-fraction decline of adjuvant breast-cancer therapy, and it answered differently for each. In a 2×2 factorial double-blind trial, 130 women with early breast cancer receiving anthracycline-containing regimens (with or without trastuzumab and radiation) were randomised to candesartan, metoprolol, both, or matching placebos, with LVEF measured by cardiac magnetic resonance (a 5-point change was prespecified as clinically important). The overall LVEF decline was 2.6 percentage points (95% CI 1.5 to 3.8) in the placebo group versus 0.8 points (95% CI −0.4 to 1.9) in the candesartan group — a between-group difference significant at P=0.026, but a fraction of the trial's own 5-point importance threshold. Metoprolol had no observed effect on LVEF decline, and there was no interaction between the two treatments (P=0.530). PROPOSED POSSIBLE: candesartan softens the early LVEF drift of anthracycline therapy by roughly 2 points on average — a real pharmacological signal on a surrogate, at a magnitude whose clinical meaning (events, later dysfunction) this trial could not show.
stamp: POSSIBLE (small surrogate benefit — candesartan only)

title: Intensive chemotherapy for blood cancers: enalapril plus carvedilol preserved LVEF and cut death or heart failure in a small trial (OVERCOME)
question: In patients with haematological malignancies receiving intensive anthracycline chemotherapy, does combined enalapril plus carvedilol prevent LV systolic dysfunction and the composite of death or heart failure?
balance: OVERCOME is the most clinically suggestive of the small cardioprotection trials — and the one whose control arm should make a careful reader pause. Ninety patients with haematological malignancies receiving intensive anthracycline chemotherapy (36 with acute leukaemia, 54 undergoing autologous stem-cell transplantation) and no baseline LV dysfunction were randomised to enalapril plus carvedilol or to control. At 6 months, LVEF was unchanged in the intervention group and fell significantly in controls — an absolute difference of −3.1% by echocardiography (P=0.035) and −3.4% by cardiac magnetic resonance (P=0.09). The clinical composite ran the same way: death or heart failure occurred in 6.7% on intervention versus 22.2% on control (P=0.036), and death, heart failure, or a final LVEF under 45% in 6.7% versus 24.4% (P=0.02). Those are large absolute differences from a 90-patient single-centre trial in which the untreated arm fared strikingly badly — contemporary anthracycline cohorts (see ICOS-ONE, Shelf #2328) usually show far less damage. PROPOSED POSSIBLE, and flagged Tier C because the composite embeds death: the direction is coherent and the LVEF preservation is real within the trial; the size of the clinical benefit is the part not to swallow whole.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Anthracycline cardiotoxicity: carvedilol did not prevent LVEF decline in the largest beta-blocker trial (CECCY)
question: In HER2-negative breast cancer receiving anthracyclines, does carvedilol prevent LVEF decline?
balance: CECCY is the largest beta-blocker prevention trial in this literature, and its primary answer is no. Two hundred patients with HER2-negative breast cancer and normal LVEF receiving anthracyclines (240 mg/m²) were randomised double-blind to carvedilol or placebo until chemotherapy completion. The primary endpoint — a reduction in LVEF of at least 10% at 6 months — occurred in 14.5% on carvedilol and 13.5% on placebo (P=1.0), and there were no differences in change in LVEF or in B-type natriuretic peptide between groups. Two secondary measures favoured carvedilol: troponin I levels over time were significantly lower (P=0.003), and the incidence of diastolic dysfunction was lower (P=0.039). PROPOSED LIKELY (no difference) on the question the trial was powered for: carvedilol does not prevent early LVEF-defined cardiotoxicity at contemporary anthracycline doses. The troponin and diastolic signals are the familiar secondary-endpoint residue — worth a hypothesis, not a prescription — and they sit beside PRADA's null metoprolol arm (Shelf #2325) as the beta-blocker half of the cardioprotection story.
stamp: LIKELY (no difference)

title: Anthracycline cardioprotection strategy: troponin-triggered enalapril matched universal enalapril in a low-event trial (ICOS-ONE)
question: In patients receiving anthracyclines, is enalapril given only when troponin rises as good as enalapril given to everyone from the start at preventing cardiotoxicity?
balance: ICOS-ONE compared two philosophies of enalapril prevention — give it to everyone before chemotherapy, or give it only to patients whose troponin rises — and the trial's real finding is how little cardiotoxicity there was to prevent. In this multicentre open-label trial, 273 patients receiving anthracyclines (76% breast cancer; median cumulative epirubicin 360 mg/m², doxorubicin 240 mg/m²; low cardiovascular risk) were randomised to universal pre-chemotherapy enalapril ('prevention') or troponin-triggered enalapril. The primary outcome, incidence of troponin elevation, was 23% in the prevention arm and 26% in the troponin-triggered arm (P=0.50). Cardiotoxicity — a 10-point LVEF reduction to below 50% — developed in just 3 patients (1.1%): two on prevention, one on triggered treatment. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (no difference): the strategies did not differ on the troponin endpoint, and with three outcome events in 273 patients the trial cannot rank them on the endpoint patients care about. The authors' own reading — that in low-risk patients at these cumulative doses a troponin-triggered strategy may be the more convenient way to capture enalapril's benefit — is a reasonable inference and an unproven one.
stamp: POSSIBLE (no difference)

title: Anthracycline therapy in lymphoma: atorvastatin cut EF-defined cardiac dysfunction from 22% to 9% (STOP-CA)
question: In patients with lymphoma receiving anthracycline-based chemotherapy, does atorvastatin 40 mg prevent significant LVEF decline?
balance: STOP-CA is the cleanest positive prevention trial in the cardio-oncology slate — with the discipline that its endpoint is an ejection-fraction definition, not heart failure. Three hundred patients with lymphoma receiving anthracycline-based chemotherapy at nine US and Canadian centres were randomised double-blind to atorvastatin 40 mg daily or placebo for 12 months. The primary endpoint — an absolute LVEF decline of at least 10 points to a final value below 55% — occurred in 9% (13/150) on atorvastatin versus 22% (33/150) on placebo (P=.002): an absolute difference of 13 points, about a 59% relative reduction (the odds of the endpoint were roughly 3 times higher on placebo; odds ratio 2.9, 95% CI 1.4 to 6.4). The secondary endpoint (decline of at least 5 points to below 55%) also favoured atorvastatin (13% versus 29%; P=.001). Clinical heart failure, printed here as the charter requires beside any dysfunction claim, did not differ: 13 adjudicated events (4%) over 24 months, 3% on atorvastatin versus 6% on placebo (P=.26). PROPOSED POSSIBLE: one well-executed blinded trial shows atorvastatin substantially reduces EF-defined cardiac dysfunction during lymphoma chemotherapy; whether that converts into fewer heart-failure events is untested at this size and horizon.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Cardiotoxicity surveillance: strain-guided cardioprotection halved cardiotoxicity-criteria events but not overall EF decline (SUCCOUR)
question: In patients at risk of anthracycline cardiotoxicity, does starting cardioprotection on a global-longitudinal-strain trigger beat waiting for an ejection-fraction trigger?
balance: SUCCOUR tested a surveillance philosophy: act on the sensitive early signal (global longitudinal strain) or wait for the established one (ejection fraction)? Three hundred thirty-one anthracycline-treated patients with another heart-failure risk factor were randomised internationally to start cardioprotective therapy on a relative GLS reduction of at least 12% or on an absolute LVEF reduction over 10%. At 1 year, the primary outcome — change in LVEF across the whole arms — was not significantly different between strategies. Beneath that null, the strain-guided arm used more cardioprotective therapy and fewer of its patients met the trial's cardiotoxicity (CTRCD) criteria: 5.8% versus 13.7% (P=0.02); 1-year EF was 57±6% versus 55±7% (P=0.05). Among patients who actually received cardioprotection, the EF-guided group's LVEF fell further by follow-up (9.1±10.9% versus 2.9±7.4%; P=0.03) — consistent with treatment starting later in the EF pathway. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: strain-guided surveillance plausibly catches injury earlier and halves the proportion crossing the cardiotoxicity definition, but the whole-population EF trajectory — the outcome least gamed by definitions — did not significantly separate, so the strategy's net clinical value remains an open question rather than a settled upgrade.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit of strain-guided strategy)

title: Trastuzumab cardiotoxicity: neither perindopril nor bisoprolol prevented LV remodelling in a small three-arm trial (MANTICORE)
question: In HER2-positive early breast cancer receiving trastuzumab, do perindopril or bisoprolol prevent LV remodelling or LVEF decline?
balance: MANTICORE is the trastuzumab counterpart to the anthracycline prevention trials, and it splits the same way they do: remodelling no, ejection fraction maybe. Ninety-four patients with HER2-positive early breast cancer receiving adjuvant trastuzumab were randomised double-blind to perindopril, bisoprolol, or placebo for the duration of therapy, with cardiac magnetic resonance at baseline and after cycle 17. The primary outcome — trastuzumab-mediated left ventricular remodelling, measured as indexed LV end-diastolic volume — was not prevented by either drug: LVEDV index rose +7±14 mL/m² on perindopril, +8±9 on bisoprolol, and +4±11 on placebo (P=.36). In secondary analyses, the LVEF decline was attenuated in the bisoprolol group (−1±5%) relative to perindopril (−3±4%) and placebo (−5±5%) (P=.001), and both drugs independently predicted maintained LVEF on multivariable analysis. Both drugs were well tolerated with no serious adverse events. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (no difference on the primary endpoint): with under 100 patients split three ways and a null primary, the LVEF attenuation is a secondary signal — interesting beside PRADA's candesartan result (Shelf #2325), not a stand-alone reason to pre-treat.
stamp: POSSIBLE (no difference on the primary endpoint)

title: Metastatic breast cancer: liposomal doxorubicin cut cardiotoxicity by about two-thirds relative at comparable efficacy (O'Brien)
question: In first-line metastatic breast cancer, do liposomal doxorubicin formulations reduce cardiotoxicity while preserving efficacy compared with conventional doxorubicin?
balance: Instead of protecting the heart from doxorubicin, liposomal formulations keep the drug away from it — and the randomised evidence says the trade works on the heart without costing antitumour effect. The anchor is O'Brien's phase III trial: 509 women with metastatic breast cancer and normal cardiac function randomised to pegylated liposomal doxorubicin (Caelyx/Doxil, 50 mg/m² every 4 weeks) or conventional doxorubicin (60 mg/m² every 3 weeks). Efficacy was comparable (progression-free survival 6.9 versus 7.8 months; hazard ratio 1.00, 95% CI 0.82 to 1.22; overall survival 21 versus 22 months), while the risk of cardiotoxicity was significantly higher on conventional doxorubicin (hazard ratio 3.16; 95% CI 1.58 to 6.31; P<0.001) — i.e., the liposomal formulation cut the cardiotoxicity hazard by roughly two-thirds relative. Toxicity moved rather than vanished: less alopecia, nausea, vomiting, and neutropenia with the liposomal drug; more palmar-plantar erythrodysesthesia (48% versus 2%), stomatitis, and mucositis. The supporting citation (Batist) is a retrospective pooled analysis of prior-adjuvant-doxorubicin patients from two earlier phase III trials of the non-pegylated liposomal formulation — cardiac events 22% versus 39% favouring liposomal — and is graded as supportive, not co-equal, evidence. PROPOSED LIKELY: a formulation change with randomised proof of less cardiotoxicity at comparable efficacy.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: Anthracycline cardiotoxicity: spironolactone preserved LVEF in a small trial with an unusually steep control-arm fall (Akpek)
question: In breast-cancer patients receiving anthracyclines, does spironolactone prevent LVEF decline?
balance: Akpek's trial is the mineralocorticoid chapter of the cardioprotection story, and it carries the largest ejection-fraction contrast in the whole slate — which is precisely why it should be read slowly. Eighty-three women with breast cancer were randomised to spironolactone 25 mg daily or control alongside anthracycline chemotherapy. LVEF was essentially preserved on spironolactone (67.0±6.1% to 65.7±7.4%; P=0.094 for the within-group change) while the control group's LVEF fell from 67.7±6.3% to 53.6±6.8% (P<0.001), with the between-group interaction significant at P<0.001; diastolic function grade was likewise protected on spironolactone and deteriorated in controls. A 14-point mean LVEF collapse in an untreated anthracycline arm is far outside what CECCY, PRADA, or ICOS-ONE saw in their control groups at comparable eras and doses — either this population was unusually vulnerable or something in the single-centre conduct amplified the contrast. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: the direction matches the rest of the neurohormonal literature and the drug was well tolerated, but an effect size this large from 83 patients in one centre is a finding to replicate, not to bank.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Pulmonary arterial hypertension: sildenafil improved walk distance by 45–50 m at every dose in SUPER-1
question: In symptomatic pulmonary arterial hypertension, does sildenafil improve exercise capacity and haemodynamics versus placebo?
balance: SUPER-1 is the pivotal trial that opened the PDE5 era in pulmonary arterial hypertension, and its most instructive feature is the flat dose-response. Two hundred seventy-eight patients with symptomatic PAH (idiopathic, connective-tissue-disease-associated, or after repaired congenital shunts) were randomised double-blind to placebo or sildenafil 20, 40, or 80 mg three times daily for 12 weeks. Six-minute walk distance rose in every sildenafil arm, with mean placebo-corrected effects of 45 m (+13.0%), 46 m (+13.3%), and 50 m (+14.7%) for 20, 40, and 80 mg respectively — all P<0.001, and all essentially the same, which is why 20 mg three times daily became the licensed dose. All doses reduced mean pulmonary artery pressure and improved WHO functional class; the incidence of clinical worsening did not differ significantly, and the trial was not powered for mortality (stated on its face). Among 222 patients completing one year of sildenafil monotherapy in the extension, the walk improvement from baseline was 51 m. Side effects were the class's familiar flushing, dyspepsia, and diarrhoea. PROPOSED LIKELY: sildenafil improves exercise capacity, functional class, and haemodynamics in PAH — a surrogate-primary claim, and the shelf claims nothing further.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: Pulmonary arterial hypertension: only the 40 mg tadalafil dose met its walk-distance endpoint in PHIRST
question: In pulmonary arterial hypertension, does once-daily tadalafil improve exercise capacity and delay clinical worsening?
balance: PHIRST gave the PDE5 class its once-daily member and a dose-finding lesson in the opposite direction from SUPER-1: here, only the top dose cleared the bar. Four hundred five PAH patients — treatment-naïve or on background bosentan — were randomised double-blind to placebo or tadalafil 2.5, 10, 20, or 40 mg once daily for 16 weeks. Six-minute walk rose dose-dependently, but only 40 mg met the prespecified significance level (P<0.01): the mean placebo-corrected effect was 33 m (95% CI 15 to 50), larger in bosentan-naïve patients (44 m; 95% CI 20 to 69) than in those on background bosentan (23 m; 95% CI −2 to 48). Tadalafil 40 mg also improved time to clinical worsening (P=0.041) and reduced the incidence of clinical worsening by 68% relative (P=0.038) — a relative figure; the fetched record does not report the absolute worsening rates — and improved health-related quality of life, while WHO functional class change was not statistically significant. Headache, myalgia, and flushing were the common treatment-related adverse events. PROPOSED LIKELY: tadalafil 40 mg daily improves exercise capacity in PAH and delays clinical worsening over 16 weeks; the lower doses are licensed-dose archaeology, not options.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: Pulmonary arterial hypertension: ambrisentan improved walk distance in both ARIES trials, with no liver-enzyme signal
question: In pulmonary arterial hypertension, does ambrisentan improve exercise capacity, and what is its hepatic safety profile?
balance: The ARIES programme answered two questions at once: whether the endothelin pathway's walk benefit survived a second drug, and whether an endothelin antagonist could escape the class's hepatic shadow. ARIES-1 (202 patients; ambrisentan 5 or 10 mg) and ARIES-2 (192 patients; 2.5 or 5 mg) were concurrent 12-week double-blind placebo-controlled trials in PAH. Walk distance improved at every dose: placebo-corrected effects of 31 m (P=0.008) and 51 m (P<0.001) in ARIES-1, and 32 m (P=0.022) and 59 m (P<0.001) in ARIES-2, with improvements in subsets of the secondary measures (time to clinical worsening in ARIES-2, functional class in ARIES-1, dyspnoea score and BNP in both). On safety, the distinguishing result: no patient treated with ambrisentan developed aminotransferase concentrations above 3 times the upper limit of normal — against the background of bosentan-era liver monitoring, that was a genuine product-level difference. In the extension, 280 patients completing 48 weeks of ambrisentan monotherapy held a 39 m improvement from baseline. PROPOSED LIKELY: ambrisentan improves exercise capacity in PAH with a hepatic profile cleaner than its class predecessor — two concordant trials, surrogate primary endpoints, no mortality claim attempted or made.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: Early pulmonary arterial hypertension: bosentan improved pulmonary vascular resistance but missed its walk-distance coprimary (EARLY)
question: In WHO functional class II pulmonary arterial hypertension, does bosentan improve haemodynamics and exercise capacity versus placebo?
balance: EARLY asked whether PAH treatment should start while patients are still mildly symptomatic — WHO functional class II — and its two coprimary endpoints split the answer down the middle. One hundred eighty-five class II patients with walk distance below 80% of predicted (or under 500 m with a Borg dyspnoea index of at least 2) were randomised double-blind to bosentan or placebo for 6 months. The haemodynamic coprimary was met decisively: pulmonary vascular resistance at month 6 was 83.2% of baseline on bosentan versus 107.5% on placebo (treatment effect −22.6%; 95% CI −33.5 to −10.0; P<0.0001). The walk coprimary was not: 6-minute walk rose 11.2 m on bosentan and fell 7.9 m on placebo, a treatment effect of 19.1 m (95% CI 3.6 to 41.8) that did not reach significance (P=0.0758). Serious adverse events occurred in 13% on bosentan and 9% on placebo — syncope the commonest on bosentan, right ventricular failure on placebo. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: bosentan clearly moves pulmonary haemodynamics in early PAH and probably slows the walk decline, but the trial's own functional coprimary missed, so 'treat early' rests on physiology and trajectory, not on a demonstrated symptomatic win at 6 months. Distinct from BREATHE-5 (Shelf #2314, Eisenmenger syndrome) — this is the early-disease question.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Pulmonary arterial hypertension: adding oral treprostinil to monotherapy reduced clinical worsening (FREEDOM-EV)
question: In pulmonary arterial hypertension on a single background oral therapy, does adding oral treprostinil reduce clinical worsening?
balance: FREEDOM-EV is the PAH slate's event-driven trial — the one that asked whether a prostacyclin-pathway drug added to a single background oral therapy changes clinical course, not just walk distance. Six hundred ninety patients with PAH who had recently begun one approved oral monotherapy were randomised double-blind to oral treprostinil extended-release three times daily or placebo, in an event-driven design whose primary endpoint was time to first adjudicated clinical worsening (death, hospitalisation for worsening PAH, initiation of inhaled or parenteral prostacyclin, disease progression, or unsatisfactory long-term response). Clinical worsening occurred in 26% on oral treprostinil versus 36% on placebo (hazard ratio 0.74; 95% CI 0.56 to 0.97; P=0.028) — a 10-percentage-point absolute reduction, about 26% relative. Functional class, Borg dyspnoea score, and NT-proBNP all favoured treprostinil from week 24 onward. The fetched record does not report mortality separately from the worsening composite, so no mortality claim is made here — the composite embeds death, which is why this shelf is Tier C. The price was tolerability: headache, diarrhoea, flushing, nausea, and vomiting were the commonest adverse events — the prostacyclin class burden that the earlier add-on trial (FREEDOM-C, against dual background therapy) could not get past. PROPOSED LIKELY: adding oral treprostinil to monotherapy genuinely delays clinical worsening; the absolute gain over the trial's horizon is about one worsening event avoided per ten patients treated.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: Agitation in Alzheimer's disease: citalopram reduced agitation (CitAD) but escitalopram failed its trial (S-CitAD)
question: In people with Alzheimer's disease and clinically significant agitation, does a citalopram-class SSRI reduce agitation compared with placebo, and at what cost in QT prolongation and cognition?
balance: This is the dementia slate's cleanest class-balance shelf: the same question asked twice, with two near-identical drugs, and answered two different ways. In CitAD (186 outpatients with probable Alzheimer's disease and clinically significant agitation, all receiving a psychosocial intervention), citalopram titrated to 30 mg/day beat placebo on both primary outcomes at 9 weeks — the agitation subscale difference was -0.93 points (95% CI -1.80 to -0.06), and 40% of citalopram patients versus 26% on placebo had moderate or marked global improvement. The costs were measured, not theoretical: MMSE scores fell an extra 1.05 points and the QT interval lengthened by 18.1 ms. The replication attempt then failed: in S-CitAD (173 patients who had not responded to a psychosocial intervention), escitalopram up to 15 mg/day did not significantly improve agitation at 12 weeks, and drug-related QT prolongation appeared again. So the class claim does not survive its own replication — what survives is a drug- and dose-specific signal for citalopram 30 mg, bought with cognitive and cardiac effects in exactly the population least able to afford either. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit for citalopram; escitalopram ineffective): citalopram probably reduces agitation modestly; escitalopram should not be substituted on a class assumption.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit for citalopram; escitalopram ineffective)

title: Agitation in Alzheimer's dementia: brexpiprazole 2 mg reduced agitation modestly across a four-trial programme
question: In people with Alzheimer's dementia and agitation, does brexpiprazole reduce agitation (CMAI total score) compared with placebo over 12 weeks?
balance: Brexpiprazole is the one antipsychotic with a regulatory approval for agitation in Alzheimer's dementia, and its programme is consistent in direction but modest in size. The confirmatory trial (345 patients) found a least-squares mean CMAI advantage of -5.32 points over placebo at 12 weeks for the pooled 2-3 mg doses (95% CI -8.77 to -1.87; P=.003; Cohen d 0.35). The two earlier trials were less tidy: in the first (433 randomised), only the 2 mg fixed dose separated from placebo (-3.77; P=.040) while 1 mg did nothing; in the second (270 randomised), flexible 0.5-2 mg dosing missed its primary endpoint (-2.34; P=.15), with benefit appearing only in a post-hoc maximum-dose subgroup. A Japanese phase 2/3 trial then confirmed both 1 mg (-3.7) and 2 mg (-7.2) over 10 weeks. Read together: a real but small effect at about 2 mg/day. The counterweight is class, not data from these trials: brexpiprazole is an atypical antipsychotic, and the class carries a boxed warning for increased mortality in older adults with dementia-related psychosis, which any prescribing decision has to weigh against a five-point CMAI gain. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: brexpiprazole probably reduces agitation modestly at 2 mg/day; the effect size, not the p-value, is the story.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Agitation in Alzheimer's disease: dextromethorphan-quinidine reduced agitation in a single phase 2 trial
question: In people with Alzheimer's disease and agitation, does dextromethorphan-quinidine reduce agitation (CMAI / NPI agitation) compared with placebo?
balance: Dextromethorphan-quinidine — the combination marketed for pseudobulbar affect — was tested for Alzheimer agitation in a single phase 2 trial using a sequential parallel comparison design, an enrichment design built to extract signal from small samples. Across its two consecutive 5-week stages the combination beat placebo on the NPI Agitation/Aggression domain (combined analysis P<.001); in stage 1, scores fell from 7.1 to 3.8 on drug versus 7.0 to 5.3 on placebo (least-squares mean difference -1.5; 95% CI -2.3 to -0.7; P<.001). Falls were more common on drug (8.6% vs 3.9%), as were serious adverse events (7.9% vs 4.7%); there was no signal for sedation, cognitive worsening, or clinically significant QTc prolongation over 10 weeks. The design caveat matters: stage 2 re-randomised only placebo non-responders, so the combined estimate is not a plain parallel-group estimate, and no confirmatory trial of this combination for this indication could be pinned at build time — the related dextromethorphan-bupropion programme is a different product and is not carded here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: a promising, unreplicated result — enough to justify the confirmatory trial, not enough to treat the benefit as established.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Agitation in dementia: mirtazapine did not reduce agitation (SYMBAD) — and more patients died on it
question: In people with dementia and agitation, does mirtazapine reduce agitation compared with placebo — and is it safe in this population?
balance: SYMBAD asked whether mirtazapine — widely prescribed for agitation in dementia precisely because it is perceived as the safer alternative to antipsychotics — actually works. In 204 people with probable or possible Alzheimer's disease and agitation unresponsive to non-drug treatment (CMAI score 45 or more) at 26 UK centres, mirtazapine titrated to 45 mg made no difference to agitation at 12 weeks: adjusted mean difference -1.74 CMAI points (95% CI -7.17 to 3.69; P=.53). Adverse events were as common on mirtazapine as on placebo (66% vs 64%). The balance line, though, is mortality: by week 16, 7 patients in the mirtazapine group had died versus 1 in the control group — a post-hoc difference of marginal statistical significance (P=.065) in a trial not powered for mortality. That is a possible harm signal, not a demonstrated one; but a drug with no shown benefit does not need a proven harm to fail its risk-benefit test, and the trial's own conclusion is that the data do not support mirtazapine for agitation in dementia. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (no difference; possible harm): mirtazapine probably does not reduce agitation in dementia, and SYMBAD's mortality imbalance is a standing reason for caution. Tier C: the shelf carries a mortality imbalance in its balance.
stamp: POSSIBLE (no difference; possible harm)

title: Depression in dementia: neither sertraline nor mirtazapine beat placebo (HTA-SADD)
question: In people with dementia and depression, do sertraline or mirtazapine improve depressive symptoms compared with placebo?
balance: HTA-SADD is the definitive pragmatic test of the two antidepressants most commonly prescribed for depression in dementia. In 326 people with probable or possible Alzheimer's disease and depression (Cornell Scale score 8 or more), neither sertraline (target 150 mg/day) nor mirtazapine (45 mg/day) reduced depression scores versus placebo at 13 weeks — mean differences of 1.17 (95% CI -0.23 to 2.58; P=.10) and 0.01 (95% CI -1.37 to 1.38; P=.99) respectively — and the null persisted unchanged to 39 weeks. What the drugs did add was adverse reactions: 43% of sertraline and 41% of mirtazapine participants versus 26% on placebo, with more severe serious adverse events on drug. Deaths were equal — 5 patients in every group by week 39 — so this is not a mortality shelf; it is a clean efficacy null with a tolerability cost, in the exact population and care setting where these drugs are prescribed first-line. The authors' conclusion, that the present practice of using these antidepressants first-line for depression in Alzheimer's disease should be reconsidered, is the one the data support. PROPOSED LIKELY (no difference): sertraline and mirtazapine do not improve depression in dementia beyond placebo with usual care.
stamp: LIKELY (no difference)

title: Dementia: 7-week cognitive stimulation therapy improved cognition (Spector 2003); weekly maintenance did not improve cognition further (Orrell 2014)
question: In people with mild-to-moderate dementia, does group cognitive stimulation therapy improve cognition and quality of life compared with usual care — and do maintenance sessions sustain any gain?
balance: Cognitive stimulation therapy is the dementia shelf where the induction works and the top-up does not — on cognition, at least. In Spector's single-blind multicentre trial, 201 people with dementia randomised to twice-weekly group CST for 7 weeks improved significantly more than usual-care controls on the MMSE (P=.044), on ADAS-Cog (P=.014), and on quality of life (P=.028); the number needed to treat for an improvement of 4 or more ADAS-Cog points was 6 — a showing the authors noted compares favourably with trials of drugs for dementia. A decade later, Orrell's maintenance trial first gave all 236 participants that same 7-week programme, then randomised them to weekly maintenance CST for 24 weeks or usual care: the primary cognition outcome did not significantly improve, although self-rated quality of life at 6 months (P=.03), proxy-rated quality of life and activities of daily living at 3 months, and — in the subgroup taking cholinesterase inhibitors — MMSE scores did. PROPOSED SPLIT: POSSIBLE (benefit) for the standard 7-week CST course on cognition and quality of life; POSSIBLE (no difference) for weekly maintenance on cognition, with the quality-of-life gains the maintenance trial did show carried on the face.
stamp: SPLIT — POSSIBLE (benefit) for induction CST / POSSIBLE (no difference) for maintenance CST on cognition

title: Alzheimer's disease: vitamin E slowed functional decline but memantine did not (TEAM-AD)
question: In people with mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's disease already on a cholinesterase inhibitor, do high-dose vitamin E, memantine, or their combination slow functional decline compared with placebo?
balance: TEAM-AD, the VA cooperative study, randomised 613 patients with mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's disease — all already taking a cholinesterase inhibitor — to vitamin E (alpha tocopherol) 2000 IU/day, memantine 20 mg/day, both, or placebo, and followed them for a mean of 2.27 years. Vitamin E slowed functional decline: ADCS-ADL scores fell 3.15 units less than on placebo (95% CI 0.92 to 5.39; adjusted P=.03), which the investigators translate as a delay in clinical progression of about 19% per year relative to placebo, roughly 6.2 months over the follow-up period, with the least increase in caregiver time. Memantine did not significantly slow decline (1.98 units less; 95% CI -0.24 to 4.20; adjusted P=.40) — the treatment made no difference — and neither did the combination, so adding memantine appeared to erase the vitamin E advantage, though the trial cannot say why. Serious adverse events classed as infections or infestations were more frequent in the memantine (31 events) and combination (44 events) groups than on placebo (13 events). The population was drawn from Veterans Affairs medical centres and was predominantly male, which bounds generalisation. PROPOSED SPLIT: POSSIBLE (benefit) for high-dose vitamin E on functional decline; LIKELY (no difference) for memantine in cholinesterase-inhibitor-treated mild-to-moderate disease.
stamp: SPLIT — POSSIBLE (benefit) for vitamin E / LIKELY (no difference) for memantine

title: Amnestic mild cognitive impairment: donepezil and vitamin E did not delay progression to Alzheimer's disease over 3 years (Petersen 2005)
question: In amnestic mild cognitive impairment, do donepezil or vitamin E delay progression to Alzheimer's disease over three years compared with placebo?
balance: The Alzheimer's Disease Cooperative Study trial randomised 769 people with amnestic mild cognitive impairment to donepezil 10 mg/day, vitamin E 2000 IU/day, or placebo for three years, with progression to possible or probable Alzheimer's disease as the primary outcome (overall progression rate about 16% per year; 212 progressions). At three years, neither drug delayed progression: hazard ratio 0.80 for donepezil (95% CI 0.57 to 1.13; P=.42) and 1.02 for vitamin E (95% CI 0.74 to 1.41; P=.91) — the treatment made no difference to the primary outcome. Two honest qualifications belong on the face: prespecified 6-month-interval analyses showed donepezil lowered the likelihood of progression during the first 12 months (P=.04), supported by secondary outcomes, and among carriers of one or more APOE epsilon4 alleles the donepezil benefit was evident throughout the three years — subgroup findings that generated hypotheses no dedicated trial has since confirmed. Vitamin E showed no benefit at any point, in any subgroup. The other cholinesterase-inhibitor programmes in MCI (rivastigmine, galantamine) were likewise null for progression, so this shelf is the class answer for MCI — distinct from cholinesterase inhibitors' symptomatic use in established dementia. PROPOSED LIKELY (no difference): for the question asked — delaying progression over three years — neither donepezil nor vitamin E works.
stamp: LIKELY (no difference)

title: Apathy in Alzheimer's disease: methylphenidate reduced apathy scores over 6 months (ADMET 2)
question: In people with Alzheimer's disease and apathy, does methylphenidate reduce apathy compared with placebo over six months?
balance: ADMET 2 randomised 200 people with Alzheimer's disease, mild-to-moderate cognitive impairment, and frequent or severe apathy to methylphenidate 10 mg twice daily or placebo for 6 months, with two coprimary outcomes. The symptom outcome was met: NPI apathy scores fell 1.25 points more on methylphenidate than placebo (95% CI -2.03 to -0.47; P=.002), the largest separation arriving in the first 100 days, and the hazard ratio for reaching no apathy symptoms was 2.16 (95% CI 1.19 to 3.91; P=.01). The global-impression coprimary outcome was not significant (odds ratio 1.90 for an improved rating; 95% CI 0.95 to 3.84; P=.07). Cognition and quality of life did not differ significantly between groups; 17 serious adverse events occurred, none judged related to the study drug, and the overall safety profiles were similar. So: a real but modest score benefit from the one adequately sized trial, on a symptom scale whose global counterpart just missed significance — the earlier, smaller ADMET pilot programme points the same way but is not carded here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: methylphenidate probably reduces measured apathy in Alzheimer's disease; whether patients or caregivers feel a difference of this size is less certain.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)
