title: Amnestic mild cognitive impairment: aerobic exercise did not beat stretching-and-balance exercise on cognition (EXERT)
question: In sedentary older adults with amnestic MCI, does 18 months of moderate-to-high-intensity aerobic exercise preserve cognition compared with low-intensity stretching, balance and range-of-motion exercise?
balance: EXERT, the phase 3 trial of exercise in sedentary older adults with amnestic mild cognitive impairment, randomised 296 participants to moderate-to-high-intensity aerobic training or to low-intensity stretching, balance, and range-of-motion exercise — an active control, not a sedentary one — with the first 12 months supervised and adherence high (81% of aerobic sessions and 87% of stretching sessions attended). The primary cognitive outcome (a global composite built on ADAS-Cog-Exec) did not differ between intensities (p=0.3) — the treatment made no difference between the two exercise prescriptions. The arresting finding is what did not happen in either arm: cognition did not decline over 12 months, and mean hippocampal volume loss was low at 0.51% for both groups. That stability is exactly what this design cannot explain: with no non-exercise control group, it may reflect the stretching programme itself, the supervision and social contact both arms received, practice effects, or volunteer selection. The record carries no registry identifier. Exercise in established dementia is a different question, answered elsewhere in the library. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (no difference): aerobic intensity confers no shown cognitive advantage over low-intensity structured exercise in amnestic MCI; whether exercise itself preserves cognition is a question EXERT's design cannot answer.
stamp: POSSIBLE (no difference)

title: Focal seizures: adjunctive perampanel reduced seizure frequency across three phase 3 trials (Studies 304, 305, 306)
question: In adults with refractory focal (partial-onset) seizures, does adjunctive perampanel increase responder rates and reduce seizure frequency compared with placebo?
balance: Perampanel's pivotal programme is three double-blind placebo-controlled trials in patients aged 12 and over with refractory partial-onset seizures on 1-3 antiseizure medicines, and the direction is consistent. Study 306 (706 patients) showed a dose-ordered median seizure-frequency change: -23.3% on 4 mg and -30.8% on 8 mg versus -10.7% on placebo (P=.0026 and P<.0001), with 50% responder rates of 28.5% and 34.9% versus 17.9% — absolute gains of about 11 and 17 points. Study 305 (386 patients) found responder rates of 33.3% (8 mg) and 33.9% (12 mg) versus 14.7% on placebo, both significant. Study 304 (388 patients) was positive on its median-frequency endpoint (-26.3% and -34.5% vs -21.0%) but its responder endpoint did not reach significance — the honest weak joint in the programme, carried on this shelf's face. The minimum effective dose is 4 mg/day (Study 306); dizziness is the dose-related price, with somnolence, irritability, headache, falls, and ataxia behind it. Absolute gains are moderate — roughly one additional responder per six to nine patients treated at effective doses. PROPOSED LIKELY: adjunctive perampanel at 4-12 mg/day reduces focal seizure frequency.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: Focal seizures: adjunctive brivaracetam — significant only at 50 mg in one trial and at 100 mg in another that missed its primary testing strategy
question: In adults with uncontrolled focal seizures, does adjunctive brivaracetam reduce seizure frequency compared with placebo?
balance: A correction first, on the face: the drafting sketch for this shelf described the anchor trial as showing significant effects at 50 mg and 100 mg. The fetched records say otherwise, and this pack follows the records. In Biton 2014 (N01253; 400 patients; fixed doses of 5, 20, or 50 mg/day given without titration), only 50 mg/day beat placebo on the primary endpoint — a 12.8% reduction in partial-onset seizure frequency over placebo (P=.025) — with a 50% responder rate of 32.7% versus 16.7% (P=.008); the 5 mg and 20 mg doses did not separate at all (reductions over placebo of -0.9% and 4.1%). In Ryvlin 2014 (N01252; 399 patients; doses 20, 50, or 100 mg/day), the trial formally missed its primary endpoint, because its sequential testing strategy required significance at 50 mg first and 50 mg was not significant (6.5%; P=.261); the 100 mg dose was significant (11.7% over placebo; P=.037; responders 36.0% vs 20.0%; P=.023). So the programme supports a real but small effect at the top of the tested dose range, with the two trials disagreeing about which dose that is. Somnolence, dizziness, and fatigue were the common adverse events, mostly mild to moderate. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: brivaracetam probably reduces focal seizure frequency modestly at 50-100 mg/day; effects at 20 mg/day and below were not shown.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Focal seizures: adjunctive lacosamide 400 mg/day increased responder rates in two randomised trials
question: In adults with partial-onset seizures uncontrolled on 1-3 antiseizure medicines, does adjunctive lacosamide reduce seizure frequency compared with placebo?
balance: Two double-blind placebo-controlled trials anchor lacosamide, and they agree. In Ben-Menachem 2007 (418 patients on 1-2 antiseizure medicines), median seizure-frequency reduction rose with dose — 10% on placebo, 26% on 200 mg/day, 39% on 400 mg/day, and 40% on 600 mg/day — with the reductions over placebo significant at 400 mg (P=.0023) and 600 mg (P=.0084); 50% responder rates were 22%, 33%, 41%, and 38% respectively, and the 200 mg dose did not separate. Chung 2010 (405 patients, mostly on 2-3 medicines) confirmed the pattern against a higher placebo response: median reductions of 37.3% (400 mg; P=.008) and 37.8% (600 mg; P=.006) versus 20.8% on placebo, with responder rates of 38.3% and 41.2% versus 18.3% (P<.001) — absolute responder gains of about 20 points at 400 mg/day. The dose lesson is the same in both trials: 400 mg/day captures the benefit, while 600 mg/day adds dose-related dizziness, nausea, diplopia, ataxia, and nystagmus without adding efficacy. Neither record carries a registry identifier. PROPOSED LIKELY: adjunctive lacosamide at 400 mg/day reduces focal seizure frequency and roughly doubles the odds of a 50% response over placebo.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: Infantile spasms: adding vigabatrin to hormonal therapy stopped spasms more often — without better development at 18 months (ICISS)
question: In infants with infantile spasms, does combining vigabatrin with hormonal treatment (prednisolone or tetracosactide) stop spasms more reliably than hormonal treatment alone?
balance: ICISS randomised 377 infants with infantile spasms and a hypsarrhythmic (or similar) EEG at 102 hospitals to hormonal therapy (prednisolone or tetracosactide) plus vigabatrin, or hormonal therapy alone — open-label treatment with masked electro-clinical outcome assessment. The combination won the primary outcome clearly: no witnessed spasms on and between days 14 and 42 in 72% of the combination group versus 57% on hormonal therapy alone (difference 15.0%; 95% CI 5.1 to 24.9; P=.002), with serious adverse reactions necessitating hospitalisation in 17 versus 16 infants and no deaths attributable to treatment. The planned 18-month follow-up is the necessary cold water: development (Vineland composite scores 73.9 vs 72.7; P=.55) and the presence of epilepsy at 18 months (30.0% vs 29.2%) did not differ between arms — the treatment made no difference to the outcomes families ultimately care most about. What did predict better development was achieving early spasm cessation by any route (Vineland 79.1 vs 63.2) and shorter lead-time to treatment. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit — spasm cessation): combination therapy probably stops spasms more reliably; a developmental dividend from the combination itself was not shown.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit — spasm cessation; no developmental advantage shown)

title: Drug-resistant childhood epilepsy: the ketogenic diet beat no dietary change in children (Neal 2008) but not a further antiseizure medicine in infants (KIWE)
question: In children with drug-resistant epilepsy, does a ketogenic diet reduce seizure frequency compared with no dietary change (and, in infants, compared with a further antiseizure medicine)?
balance: Two randomised trials ask two different versions of this question and answer them differently. Neal 2008 randomised 145 children aged 2-16 with drug-resistant epilepsy (daily seizures, at least two medicines failed) to start the ketogenic diet immediately or after a 3-month delay with no other treatment change: at 3 months, mean seizure count stood at 62.0% of baseline in the diet group versus 136.9% in controls (a 75% relative difference; 95% CI 42.4 to 107.4; P<.0001), and more than 50% seizure reduction occurred in 38% versus 6% — a 32-percentage-point absolute gap — in an unblinded trial where only 103 of 145 children contributed data. KIWE (2023) asked the harder, more clinical question in 136 infants: the classic ketogenic diet versus simply trying a further antiseizure medicine. At weeks 6-8, median seizures per day were 5 on the diet versus 3 on medicine (incidence rate ratio 1.33; 95% CI 0.84 to 2.11) — no difference shown; serious adverse events were similar (51% vs 45%), and three deaths in the diet arm were judged unrelated to treatment by the investigators and the safety committee. KIWE stopped early for slow recruitment and end of funding. PROPOSED SPLIT: in children, the diet probably beats changing nothing; in infants, it has not beaten the simpler option of another medicine.
stamp: SPLIT — POSSIBLE (benefit) vs no dietary change in children / POSSIBLE (no difference) vs further medication in infants

title: Drug-resistant focal epilepsy: vagus nerve stimulation beat low-stimulation control modestly in two randomised trials (E03, E05)
question: In people with medically intractable partial-onset seizures, does vagus nerve stimulation reduce seizure frequency compared with low-stimulation control?
balance: Vagus nerve stimulation was established the hard way: both pivotal trials implanted the device in everyone and randomised high (presumed therapeutic) versus low (presumed subtherapeutic) stimulation — an active control that shrinks the visible separation and caps the certainty any shelf can claim. E05 (196 patients) found an average seizure-frequency reduction of 28% on high stimulation versus 15% on low (P=.04). E03 (114 patients) found mean reductions of 24.5% versus 6.1% (P=.01), with 50% or greater reductions in 31% versus 13% (P=.02). The absolute separation is therefore about 13-18 percentage points of seizure frequency over 3 months — real, but modest, and measured against a control stimulation that may not be wholly inert. Voice alteration and dyspnoea (E05) and transient hoarseness during stimulation trains (E03) were the characteristic adverse effects; one E03 patient with no previous cardiac history had a myocardial infarction during the third month of stimulation — recorded here because the record reports it, without an attribution claim. Both trials predate trial-registration norms and neither record carries a registry identifier. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: VNS probably reduces focal seizure frequency modestly beyond low-level stimulation, in patients who have failed medicines and are not optimal surgical candidates.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Refractory focal epilepsy: anterior thalamic deep brain stimulation reduced seizures in the blinded phase (SANTE)
question: In adults with refractory focal epilepsy, does bilateral deep brain stimulation of the anterior nucleus of the thalamus reduce seizure frequency compared with sham stimulation?
balance: SANTE randomised 110 adults with medically refractory partial seizures (median baseline 19.5 seizures per month) to bilateral stimulation of the anterior nuclei of the thalamus or to no stimulation for a 3-month blinded phase, after which everyone received stimulation. In the last month of the blinded phase the stimulated group had a 29% greater reduction in seizures than the control group on the model-based estimate (P=.002); the unadjusted median declines were 40.4% versus 14.5%. Complex partial and 'most severe' seizures were significantly reduced. In the open phase that followed, benefit persisted — a 56% median reduction in seizure frequency and a 54% responder rate at 2 years, with 14 patients seizure-free for at least 6 months — but uncontrolled follow-up cannot separate device effect from time, expectation, and medication changes. Harms were modest but real: five deaths occurred, none attributed to implantation or stimulation; no participant had symptomatic haemorrhage or brain infection; two had acute transient stimulation-associated seizures; and stimulated participants were more likely to report depression or memory problems as adverse events even though formal cognition and mood testing showed no group differences. The record carries no registry identifier. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: anterior thalamic DBS probably reduces refractory focal seizures; the blinded separation is one trial deep.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Dravet syndrome: stiripentol cut convulsive seizures sharply in a small syndrome-dedicated trial (STICLO)
question: In children with Dravet syndrome (severe myoclonic epilepsy in infancy) whose seizures persist on valproate and clobazam, does adjunctive stiripentol reduce convulsive seizures compared with placebo?
balance: STICLO is the oldest leg of the Dravet tripod — cannabidiol and fenfluramine for Dravet syndrome live elsewhere in this library — and it remains the most dramatic. Forty-one children with severe myoclonic epilepsy in infancy whose seizures persisted on valproate plus clobazam were randomised to add stiripentol or placebo for a 2-month double-blind period. Responders (more than 50% reduction in clonic or tonic-clonic seizure frequency) were 71% on stiripentol (15 of 21 — nine of them free of clonic or tonic-clonic seizures) versus 5% on placebo (1 of 20, none seizure-free); the 95% confidence interval for the difference runs from 42.2 to 85.7 percentage points, and mean seizure frequency changed by -69% on stiripentol versus +7% on placebo (P<.0001). Moderate side effects (drowsiness, loss of appetite) occurred in 21 children on stiripentol versus 8 on placebo, and mostly disappeared when the dose of the companion medicines was reduced — stiripentol inhibits the metabolism of clobazam and valproate, which is part of how the combination works and part of its management burden. The sample is tiny and the blinded period short; the effect, as far as it goes, is not small. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: stiripentol probably produces large short-term reductions in Dravet convulsive seizures when added to valproate and clobazam; a single 41-child trial caps the stamp despite the effect size.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Tuberous sclerosis focal seizures: everolimus increased response rates dose-dependently (EXIST-3)
question: In people with tuberous sclerosis complex and treatment-resistant focal seizures, does adjunctive everolimus increase seizure response compared with placebo?
balance: EXIST-3 randomised 366 patients aged 2-65 with tuberous sclerosis complex and treatment-resistant focal-onset seizures (at least 16 seizures in the 8-week baseline) to placebo or everolimus titrated to a low (3-7 ng/mL) or high (9-15 ng/mL) trough exposure, added to 1-3 antiseizure medicines across 99 centres. Response — at least a 50% reduction in seizure frequency during the maintenance period — was 15.1% on placebo, 28.2% on low exposure (P=.0077), and 40.0% on high exposure (P<.0001): absolute gains of about 13 and 25 percentage points. Median percentage reductions in seizure frequency were 14.9%, 29.3% (P=.0028), and 39.6% (P<.0001), the same dose-ordered pattern. That gradient across two independently randomised exposure arms strengthens the causal reading of what is still a single trial. The price was graded too: grade 3 or 4 adverse events in 11% on placebo, 18% on low exposure, and 24% on high exposure, and serious adverse events in 3% versus 14% in both everolimus arms — an imbalance in serious events that belongs on the face of any benefit claim. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: adjunctive everolimus probably reduces TSC-associated focal seizures, with high exposure more effective and less well tolerated; one trial, however large and internally consistent, is one trial.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Medically intractable focal epilepsy: responsive neurostimulation reduced seizures versus sham in the blinded period (RNS pivotal trial)
question: In adults with medically intractable focal seizures from 1-2 foci, does responsive cortical neurostimulation reduce seizure frequency compared with sham stimulation?
balance: The RNS pivotal trial implanted 191 adults with medically intractable partial seizures arising from 1 or 2 predetermined foci with a responsive neurostimulator, then randomised them 1:1 to stimulation delivered in response to detected abnormal electrocorticographic activity or to no stimulation for a 12-week blinded period. Seizures fell 37.9% in the treatment group versus 17.3% in the sham group (P=.012) — an absolute separation of about 21 percentage points against an implanted, device-carrying control, which is the honest comparison for an implanted therapy. There was no difference between groups in adverse events during the blinded period. In the 84-week open-label period that followed, the reduction was sustained in the treatment group and emerged in the sham group once stimulation began; overall quality of life improved significantly (P<.02), with no deterioration in mood or neuropsychological function. The open-label accrual cannot be separated from expectation and time, so the blinded 12 weeks carry the claim. The record carries no registry identifier. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: responsive neurostimulation probably reduces disabling focal seizures in the narrow population trialled — adults who have failed at least two antiseizure medicines, with 3 or more seizures per month and 1-2 localisable foci.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis: dimethyl fumarate roughly halved relapse rates versus placebo in two phase 3 trials, with disability progression reduced in DEFINE (DEFINE; CONFIRM)
question: In relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis, does oral dimethyl fumarate reduce relapses and disability progression compared with placebo?
balance: Two phase 3 placebo-controlled trials of oral dimethyl fumarate (BG-12) in relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis agree. In DEFINE, the proportion of patients relapsing by 2 years was 27% on twice-daily BG-12 and 26% on thrice-daily dosing versus 46% on placebo, and the annualized relapse rate was 0.17 and 0.19 versus 0.36 — relative reductions of 53% and 48%. Confirmed disability progression was 16% and 18% versus 27% on placebo (relative reductions 38% and 34%). CONFIRM repeated the relapse result against placebo (annualized relapse rate 0.22 and 0.20 versus 0.40; relative reductions 44% and 51%), with a glatiramer acetate reference arm at 0.29, but its disability-progression reductions (21% and 24%) were not significant — the trial was not designed to compare BG-12 with glatiramer, and any head-to-head reading is post hoc. The consistent harms are flushing and gastrointestinal events, with falls in lymphocyte counts. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): two large randomised trials show an approximate halving of relapse activity; the disability claim rests on DEFINE alone.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: Relapsing multiple sclerosis: natalizumab cut relapses by about two-thirds and progression risk by 42% relative versus placebo — with progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy appearing in the add-on trial (AFFIRM; SENTINEL)
question: In relapsing multiple sclerosis, does natalizumab reduce relapses and sustained disability progression compared with placebo?
balance: Natalizumab is among the most effective relapse-suppressing treatments tested in relapsing multiple sclerosis, and its two phase 3 trials define both halves of the answer. In AFFIRM, natalizumab monotherapy reduced the risk of sustained disability progression by 42% relative over 2 years (hazard ratio 0.58; cumulative probability 17% versus 29% on placebo) and the clinical relapse rate at 1 year by 68% relative. In SENTINEL, adding natalizumab to interferon beta-1a in patients still relapsing on interferon cut the annualized relapse rate to 0.34 versus 0.75 and reduced the relative risk of sustained progression by 24% (hazard ratio 0.76; cumulative probability 23% versus 29%). The counterweight is in SENTINEL itself: two cases of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy, one fatal, occurred in natalizumab-treated patients — the opportunistic brain infection that has governed this drug's use and monitoring ever since. Hypersensitivity reactions occurred in 4% in AFFIRM, serious in 1%. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): large, consistent randomised effects on relapses and progression, with a rare but potentially fatal harm that post-dates the monotherapy trial and must travel with the claim.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: Relapsing multiple sclerosis: teriflunomide cut relapse rates by about a third relative in two phase 3 trials, with disability benefit only at the 14 mg dose (TEMSO; TOWER)
question: In relapsing multiple sclerosis, does oral teriflunomide reduce relapses compared with placebo?
balance: Oral teriflunomide gives a modest, consistent reduction in relapse activity in relapsing multiple sclerosis — about a third — in two phase 3 placebo-controlled trials. In TEMSO, the annualized relapse rate was 0.37 on either 7 mg or 14 mg versus 0.54 on placebo (relative reductions 31.2% and 31.5%), and confirmed disability progression was 20.2% on 14 mg versus 27.3% on placebo (P=0.03), with the 7 mg dose not significant on progression (21.7%, P=0.08). TOWER confirmed the relapse effect (0.32 on 14 mg and 0.39 on 7 mg versus 0.50 on placebo) and again found the progression benefit only at 14 mg (hazard ratio 0.68; the 7 mg hazard ratio was 0.95). The price is hepatic and cosmetic: alanine aminotransferase at or above the upper limit of normal in 54-57% on teriflunomide versus 35.9% on placebo in TEMSO (levels at least 3 times the limit were similar, about 6-7% in all groups), plus diarrhoea, nausea and hair thinning. TOWER recorded four deaths, none judged related to study drug, including one suicide in the 14 mg group. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): the effect is real but smaller than the fumarate and monoclonal shelves beside it, and the licensed 14 mg dose is the one with progression evidence.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: Relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis: alemtuzumab halved relapse rates versus interferon beta-1a in two phase 3 trials, with disability benefit only in previously treated patients — and delayed autoimmunity in up to a fifth (CARE-MS I & II)
question: In relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis, does alemtuzumab reduce relapses and disability progression compared with subcutaneous interferon beta-1a?
balance: Against an active comparator — high-dose subcutaneous interferon beta-1a — alemtuzumab roughly halved relapse rates in both of its phase 3 trials. In CARE-MS II (patients who had relapsed on prior therapy), the relapse rate ratio was 0.51 (a 49.4% relative improvement; 35% of alemtuzumab patients relapsed versus 51% on interferon) and sustained accumulation of disability was 13% versus 20% (hazard ratio 0.58, a 42% relative improvement). In CARE-MS I (treatment-naïve patients), the relapse rate ratio was 0.45 (54.9% relative improvement; relapse-free at 2 years 78% versus 59%), but the disability endpoint was not met (8% versus 11%; hazard ratio 0.70, P=0.22). The harm profile is the other half of this shelf and is unlike any neighbour: infusion reactions in about 90%, infections in 67-77%, and delayed secondary autoimmunity — thyroid disorders in 16-18% by 2 years and immune thrombocytopenia in about 1% in both trials, with two cases of thyroid papillary carcinoma in CARE-MS I. These harms, not the relapse numbers, are why the drug sits behind monitoring programmes. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): two randomised active-comparator trials agree on relapses; the disability claim holds only in the previously treated population.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: Relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis: short-course cladribine cut relapse rates by over half versus placebo in its single pivotal trial, with dose-dependent lymphopenia (CLARITY)
question: In relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis, do short courses of oral cladribine reduce relapses compared with placebo over two years?
balance: CLARITY is the single pivotal placebo-controlled trial of short-course oral cladribine in relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis, and its effects were large: the annualized relapse rate at 96 weeks was 0.14 on the 3.5 mg/kg cumulative dose and 0.15 on 5.25 mg/kg versus 0.33 on placebo (relative reductions of about 58% and 55%), relapse-free rates were 79.7% and 78.9% versus 60.9%, and the risk of 3-month sustained disability progression fell by about a third (hazard ratios 0.67 and 0.69). The treatment is given as a few short courses totalling 8-20 days per year, which makes the harm ledger specific: lymphocytopenia in 21.6% (3.5 mg/kg) and 31.5% (5.25 mg/kg) versus 1.8% on placebo, and herpes zoster in 8 and 12 patients versus none. The higher dose bought no extra efficacy, so the lower cumulative dose is the one the evidence favours. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) — flagged for the developer's personal verdict as a single-trial shelf: one trial, however large and clean, carries the whole claim, and questions the trial cannot answer (long-horizon malignancy and infection risk after immune reconstitution) sit outside its 96 weeks.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: Vitamin D in multiple sclerosis: high-dose cholecalciferol reduced disease activity in clinically isolated syndrome (D-Lay MS), but made no difference added to interferon in established relapsing-remitting disease (SOLAR; CHOLINE)
question: In clinically isolated syndrome or early relapsing MS, does high-dose vitamin D reduce disease activity (relapses and MRI lesions) compared with placebo?
balance: Vitamin D in multiple sclerosis splits cleanly by setting. As monotherapy at the very start of the disease, it worked: in D-Lay MS, untreated patients with clinically isolated syndrome and low vitamin D randomised to cholecalciferol 100,000 IU every 2 weeks had less disease activity over 24 months than on placebo (60.3% versus 74.1%; hazard ratio 0.66), with all MRI secondary outcomes favouring vitamin D — though relapse itself, the clinical component, was not significantly reduced (17.9% versus 21.8%; hazard ratio 0.69, P=0.16). As an add-on to interferon beta-1a in established relapsing-remitting disease, it did not: SOLAR missed its primary endpoint (no-evidence-of-disease-activity in 36.3% versus 35.3%; odds ratio 0.93, P=0.80 — the treatment made no difference), with only exploratory MRI lesion outcomes favouring vitamin D, and CHOLINE likewise missed its primary annualized-relapse-rate endpoint, its favourable results confined to the completer subset. Severe adverse events in D-Lay MS were 17 versus 13, none attributed to cholecalciferol. PROPOSED SPLIT: POSSIBLE (benefit) for high-dose vitamin D monotherapy in clinically isolated syndrome, on a single trial whose significant endpoint is MRI-driven; POSSIBLE (no difference) for vitamin D added to interferon in established relapsing-remitting MS, on two trials that both missed their primary endpoints. Flagged for the developer's personal verdict (SPLIT stamp).
stamp: SPLIT — POSSIBLE (benefit) in clinically isolated syndrome / POSSIBLE (no difference) as add-on to interferon in established relapsing-remitting MS

title: Relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis failing therapy: stem cell transplantation nearly abolished confirmed disability progression versus switching drugs in a single randomised trial (3 vs 34 progressors; MIST)
question: In relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis with breakthrough activity on disease-modifying therapy, does non-myeloablative autologous HSCT prevent disability progression compared with switching to another disease-modifying therapy?
balance: MIST produced the largest treatment separation ever recorded in a multiple sclerosis trial, and it did so on the hard endpoint. In 110 patients with relapsing-remitting MS who had relapsed at least twice in the prior year despite disease-modifying therapy, non-myeloablative autologous haematopoietic stem cell transplantation (cyclophosphamide plus antithymocyte globulin conditioning) was compared with switching to a different or higher-efficacy disease-modifying therapy. Disease progression — an EDSS rise of at least 1.0 point sustained on two evaluations 6 months apart after year 1 — occurred in 3 transplanted patients versus 34 on continued therapy (hazard ratio 0.07, 95% CI 0.02-0.24). Mean EDSS improved in the transplant group during the first year (3.38 to 2.36) while worsening on therapy (3.31 to 3.98), a between-group difference of -1.7 points. There were no deaths and no non-haematopoietic grade 4 toxicities in the transplant group. The caveats are structural, and they are on the face: a single trial of 110 patients, open-label treatment (EDSS was assessed blinded), median follow-up of 2 years, and a highly selected, young, actively relapsing population at four expert centres. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) — flagged for the developer's personal verdict as an OUTSTANDING-SINGLE: a landmark single randomised trial on a hard disease-progression endpoint, per the Nov 8, 2026 rule.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: Multiple sclerosis walking impairment: dalfampridine produced timed-walk responders in 35-43% versus 8-9% on placebo across two phase 3 trials, with responders walking about 25% faster
question: In people with multiple sclerosis and walking impairment, does extended-release dalfampridine (fampridine) increase walking speed compared with placebo?
balance: Extended-release dalfampridine (fampridine) is a responder drug: in two phase 3 placebo-controlled trials it made a consistent minority of people with multiple sclerosis walk measurably faster, and did nothing detectable for the rest. In the 2010 confirmatory trial, timed-walk responders — patients with consistent improvement on the Timed 25-Foot Walk — were 42.9% on dalfampridine 10 mg twice daily versus 9.3% on placebo over 9 weeks; the earlier 2009 phase 3 trial found the near-identical separation of 35% versus 8% over 14 weeks. Responders' walking speed improved by about 25% in both trials (24.7% and 25.2%), and the effect was maintained across the dosing interval. There is no claim here about relapses, progression or disability accumulation — the drug treats a symptom, in the subset who respond, and the responder definition was built into both trials' primary endpoints. Seizure risk at higher-than-licensed doses is the class warning from the wider record; within these trials the records report no new safety findings. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): two consistent randomised trials on a pre-specified responder endpoint, for walking speed only.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: Aquaporin-4-positive NMOSD: eculizumab cut adjudicated relapses to 3% versus 43% on placebo in a single trial stopped early for effect — disability unchanged within the trial, one death on treatment (PREVENT)
question: In aquaporin-4-IgG-positive neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder, does eculizumab prevent relapses compared with placebo?
balance: PREVENT nearly abolished relapses in aquaporin-4-IgG-positive neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder — a disease where each relapse can take sight or the ability to walk, and recovery is poor. In 143 adults (pre-treatment annualized relapse rate about 2.0; 76% continuing background immunosuppression), adjudicated relapses occurred in 3 of 96 patients on eculizumab versus 20 of 47 (43%) on placebo (hazard ratio 0.06, 95% CI 0.02-0.20), and the adjudicated annualized relapse rate was 0.02 versus 0.35 (rate ratio 0.04). The trial was stopped after 23 of the 24 prespecified relapses because the timing of the final event could not be estimated. Two qualifications belong on the face: disability scores did not differ significantly between groups over the trial's course (EDSS change -0.18 versus +0.12; least-squares mean difference -0.29, 95% CI -0.59 to 0.01) — the benefit is relapse prevention, not measured disability gain — and there was one death from pulmonary empyema in the eculizumab group, alongside more upper respiratory infections and headaches. Terminal complement blockade also carries the meningococcal risk that governs vaccination practice around this drug class. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) — flagged for the developer's personal verdict as an OUTSTANDING-SINGLE (landmark single randomised blinded trial; relapse is the disease's major-complication endpoint) and because the balance carries a death in the treatment arm.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: CIDP: intravenous immunoglobulin improved disability in 54% versus 21% on placebo (ICE), and weekly subcutaneous immunoglobulin prevented relapse in maintenance — 33-39% versus 63% relapsing or withdrawn (PATH)
question: In chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy, does immunoglobulin — intravenous for induction, subcutaneous for maintenance — improve disability and prevent relapse compared with placebo?
balance: Immunoglobulin works at both ends of CIDP care, and each route has its own randomised proof. For induction, ICE randomised 117 patients to intravenous immunoglobulin (a 10% caprylate-chromatography purified preparation, given every 3 weeks) or placebo: 54% improved by at least 1 INCAT disability point and sustained the improvement to week 24, versus 21% on placebo — an absolute difference of 33.5 percentage points — with grip strength also improved and, in the blinded extension, a longer time to relapse for those who stayed on immunoglobulin (P=0.011). For maintenance, PATH took 172 patients already known to respond to intravenous immunoglobulin and randomised them to weekly subcutaneous immunoglobulin at 0.2 or 0.4 g/kg or placebo for 24 weeks: relapse or withdrawal occurred in 63% on placebo versus 39% (low dose) and 33% (high dose) — absolute risk reductions of 25 and 30 percentage points, with no significant difference between the two subcutaneous doses. Serious adverse events were uncommon in both trials (in ICE, 0.8% of immunoglobulin infusions versus 1.9% of placebo infusions). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): two randomised trials answer the induction and maintenance questions separately and consistently.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: Parkinson's motor fluctuations: opicapone 50 mg once daily cut OFF time by about an hour a day versus placebo in two phase 3 trials — lower doses failed (BIPARK I & II)
question: In Parkinson's disease with end-of-dose motor fluctuations on levodopa, does once-daily opicapone reduce daily OFF time compared with placebo?
balance: Once-daily opicapone 50 mg, added to levodopa, buys about an hour of OFF time a day — and two phase 3 trials put the number in the same place. In BIPARK I, the change in absolute OFF time was -116.8 minutes on opicapone 50 mg versus -56.0 minutes on placebo (difference -60.8 minutes; P=0.0015), and opicapone was non-inferior to entacapone given with every levodopa dose (-96.3 minutes); the 5 mg and 25 mg doses were not significantly different from placebo. BIPARK II repeated the design without the entacapone arm: OFF time fell by 118.8 minutes on 50 mg versus 64.5 minutes on placebo (adjusted difference -54.3 minutes; P=0.008), again with 25 mg not significant (-37.2 minutes; P=0.11), and the reduction persisted through a 1-year open-label phase. The excess harm is the expected dopaminergic one — dyskinesia was the commonest adverse event on opicapone in BIPARK I (18 of 115 patients at 50 mg versus 5 of 121 on placebo). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): consistent, dose-specific effects in two randomised trials — for the 50 mg dose only.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: Parkinson's OFF episodes: istradefylline cut OFF time by roughly 0.7-1 hour a day versus placebo across three randomised trials — a real but small diary-measured effect
question: In Parkinson's disease treated with levodopa, does the adenosine A2A antagonist istradefylline reduce OFF time compared with placebo?
balance: Istradefylline, the adenosine A2A antagonist, reduces OFF time by a modest amount — somewhere under an hour to about an hour a day — and the record behind it is uneven in design even where it agrees in direction. The first randomised trial (2003, n=83) was explicitly exploratory, with no prespecified primary outcome among 19 analysed variables: OFF time fell by 1.2 hours on istradefylline while rising 0.5 hours on placebo (P=0.004), and ON time with dyskinesia increased even though dyskinesia severity did not. A 231-patient phase 3 trial in 2008 found a placebo-corrected OFF-time reduction of 0.7 hours at 20 mg/day (P=0.03), with no significant change in ON time with troublesome dyskinesia. A 373-patient Japanese trial in 2013 found OFF-time reductions of about 1 hour at both 20 mg and 40 mg versus 0.23 hours on placebo (P=0.003 for both), with dyskinesia the commonest adverse event (about 12-13% versus 4%). None of the trials shows an effect on UPDRS motor scores or global impression beyond the diary endpoints. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): three randomised trials point the same way, but the effect is small, diary-measured, and the founding trial was exploratory — enough for moderate confidence, not more.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Parkinson's motor fluctuations: apomorphine infusion cut OFF time by 2.47 hours a day versus 0.58 on saline in the first double-blind trial of the therapy (TOLEDO)
question: In Parkinson's disease with motor fluctuations uncontrolled by oral therapy, does continuous subcutaneous apomorphine infusion reduce OFF time compared with saline infusion?
balance: Apomorphine infusion was used for decades on open-label evidence; TOLEDO is its first double-blind trial, and it confirms the clinical impression at meaningful size. In 106 patients with Parkinson's disease for more than 3 years and motor fluctuations uncontrolled despite optimised oral or transdermal therapy, waking-hours subcutaneous infusion of apomorphine (mean final dose 4.68 mg/h) reduced daily OFF time by 2.47 hours over 12 weeks, versus 0.58 hours on saline placebo infusion — a difference of -1.89 hours per day (95% CI -3.16 to -0.62; P=0.0025). The infusion was well tolerated with no unexpected safety signals in the trial, though 6 apomorphine patients withdrew because of treatment-related adverse events. What the trial does not give is duration or comparison: 12 blinded weeks, no head-to-head against deep brain stimulation or intestinal levodopa gel, and an open-label extension that cannot separate drug effect from expectation. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — flagged for the developer's personal verdict as a single-trial shelf: one well-conducted randomised trial, a large symptomatic effect, and nothing behind it if the estimate is optimistic.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Levodopa-induced dyskinesia: extended-release amantadine reduced dyskinesia scores and OFF time in two randomised trials — with hallucinations in up to a quarter of patients (EASE LID; EASE LID 3)
question: In Parkinson's disease with levodopa-induced dyskinesia, does extended-release amantadine reduce dyskinesia and OFF time compared with placebo?
balance: Extended-release amantadine (274 mg at bedtime) is the first drug shown in randomised trials to reduce levodopa-induced dyskinesia — and it trims OFF time at the same time, which no antidyskinetic before it had done. In EASE LID, the Unified Dyskinesia Rating Scale total score fell by 15.9 points on amantadine ER versus 8.0 on placebo at week 12 (difference -7.9; P<0.001), and OFF time fell 0.6 hours while rising 0.3 hours on placebo (difference -0.9 hours; P=0.02). EASE LID 3, a smaller trial of identical design, found the same pattern larger: dyskinesia score change -20.7 versus -6.3 (difference -14.4; P<0.0001) and an OFF-time difference of -1.1 hours (P=0.0199). The harm side is substantial and consistent: in EASE LID, visual hallucinations in 23.8% versus 1.7%, peripheral oedema 23.8% versus 0, dizziness 22.2% versus 0, and adverse-event discontinuation in 20.6% versus 6.9%; EASE LID 3 discontinuations were 19% versus 8%. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): two concordant randomised trials on both endpoints, with a tolerability price that belongs in the same sentence.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: Parkinson's disease modification: rasagiline's delayed-start signature appeared at 1 mg in ADAGIO and at both doses in TEMPO but failed outright at 2 mg in ADAGIO — the claim remains unproven
question: In early Parkinson's disease, does starting rasagiline immediately rather than 9 months later leave patients ahead — the delayed-start test of disease modification?
balance: This shelf grades one claim only: that starting rasagiline early changes the disease's course, as tested by the delayed-start design. The design's logic is that if early starters remain ahead after everyone is on the drug, the head start cannot be a mere symptomatic effect. TEMPO (404 patients) found exactly that pattern over 12 months: patients on rasagiline 2 mg/day for the full year had a 2.29-unit smaller increase in total UPDRS than patients switched from placebo to rasagiline 2 mg at 6 months (P=0.01), with the 1 mg group also ahead (-1.82 units; P=0.05). ADAGIO (1,176 patients, 72 weeks) then split by dose: early-start 1 mg met all three prespecified hierarchical endpoints (baseline-to-week-72 change 2.82 versus 4.52 points; P=0.02), but early-start 2 mg failed the same endpoint outright (3.47 versus 3.11 points; P=0.60 — the delayed group nominally ahead). A disease-modifying drug should not lose its signature when the dose doubles, and regulators declined the claim; the ADAGIO authors themselves wrote that the results 'must be interpreted with caution'. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) for the disease-modification claim: the design produced its predicted pattern in three of four dose-arms across two trials and failed in the fourth, which is precisely the shape of an unproven claim. Rasagiline's symptomatic benefit is a separate question and is not graded here. Flagged for the developer's personal verdict: this is a claim-interpretation shelf where reasonable readers split.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence)

title: Parkinson's disease: exenatide's 3.5-point phase 2 motor advantage vanished in the 194-patient phase 3 trial — no evidence of disease modification (Exenatide-PD3)
question: In Parkinson's disease, does once-weekly exenatide slow motor progression compared with placebo?
balance: Exenatide in Parkinson's disease is the clearest small-positive, large-null sequence in this slate, and the two trials are carded in that order on purpose. The 2017 single-centre phase 2 trial (62 patients) found that after 48 weeks of weekly exenatide and a 12-week washout, off-medication motor scores had improved 1.0 points on exenatide while worsening 2.1 points on placebo — an adjusted difference of -3.5 points (P=0.0318) that persisted beyond exposure and launched the disease-modification hypothesis. The 2025 phase 3 Exenatide-PD3 trial (194 patients, six UK centres, 96 weeks) tested the same regimen against the same off-medication motor endpoint and found nothing: scores worsened by 5.7 points on exenatide and 4.5 points on placebo (adjusted coefficient 0.92, 95% CI -1.56 to 3.39; P=0.47 — the treatment made no difference), and the authors concluded there is no evidence to support exenatide as a disease-modifying treatment. Serious adverse events were similar (9% versus 11% in phase 3; 6 versus 2 in phase 2, none judged treatment-related). PROPOSED SPLIT: POSSIBLE (benefit) on the phase 2 record alone, superseded by POSSIBLE (no difference) on the phase 3 record — the shelf's operative answer is the phase 3 null. Flagged for the developer's personal verdict (SPLIT stamp).
stamp: SPLIT — POSSIBLE (benefit) in the phase 2 trial / POSSIBLE (no difference) in the phase 3 trial

title: Huntington's chorea: tetrabenazine cut chorea by 5.0 units versus 1.5 on placebo in its single trial — with a suicide and suicidal ideation among its serious adverse events (TETRA-HD)
question: In Huntington's disease, does tetrabenazine reduce chorea compared with placebo?
balance: TETRA-HD is the single randomised trial of tetrabenazine for Huntington's chorea, and both its benefit and its danger are in the same record. In 84 ambulatory patients titrated over 7 weeks to a maximum of 100 mg/day, the UHDRS chorea score fell by 5.0 units on tetrabenazine versus 1.5 units on placebo over 12 weeks (adjusted mean effect -3.5 units, 95% CI -5.2 to -1.9; P<0.0001), with a significant benefit on clinical global improvement as well. Against that: five withdrawals in the tetrabenazine group versus one on placebo, and five serious adverse events in four tetrabenazine subjects — a drowning suicide, a complicated fall, restlessness with suicidal ideation, and a breast cancer — versus none on placebo. The suicide and suicidal ideation in a drug that depletes monoamines, in a disease with elevated baseline suicide risk, are why this drug carries its depression and suicidality warnings; they are printed here, in the balance, not buried. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — flagged for the developer's personal verdict as a single-trial shelf whose balance carries a treatment-group suicide.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Huntington's chorea: valbenazine cut maximal chorea scores by 4.6 points versus 1.4 on placebo in a single phase 3 trial, with somnolence the commonest adverse event (KINECT-HD)
question: In Huntington's disease, does valbenazine reduce chorea compared with placebo?
balance: KINECT-HD is the single phase 3 trial of valbenazine — a selective VMAT2 inhibitor taken once daily — for Huntington's chorea. In 125 analysed adults with genetically confirmed disease and a Total Maximal Chorea score of at least 8, the least-squares mean change in chorea score from baseline to the week 10-12 maintenance period was -4.6 on valbenazine (up to 80 mg/day) versus -1.4 on placebo (difference -3.2, 95% CI -4.4 to -2.0; P<0.0001). Tolerability over the 12 weeks was comparatively clean: the commonest adverse event was somnolence (16% versus 3%), serious treatment-emergent events were single cases in each arm (angioedema from a shellfish allergy on valbenazine; colon cancer and psychosis on placebo), and — in explicit contrast to the older VMAT2 shelf beside this one — no suicidal behaviour or worsening of suicidal ideation was reported on valbenazine. Twelve weeks in one trial cannot exclude the class's depression risk over years, and the record says so in its own interpretation. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — flagged for the developer's personal verdict as a single-trial shelf.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Primary dystonia: pallidal deep brain stimulation beat sham in two small trials — movement scores improved 15.8 versus 1.4 points in generalized/segmental dystonia, severity 5.1 versus 1.3 in cervical dystonia
question: In medically refractory primary dystonia, does pallidal deep brain stimulation improve movement scores compared with sham stimulation?
balance: Pallidal deep brain stimulation for medically refractory primary dystonia rests on two small sham-controlled trials — every patient implanted, half switched on — and both are positive at 3 months. In Kupsch's trial of generalized or segmental dystonia (40 patients), the Burke-Fahn-Marsden movement score improved by 15.8 points on active stimulation versus 1.4 points on sham (P<0.001); when the sham group crossed to active treatment, it gained a similar benefit, and the whole cohort's improvement was sustained at 6 months. In Volkmann's cervical dystonia trial (62 patients), the TWSTRS severity score fell 5.1 points on active stimulation versus 1.3 points on sham (between-group difference 3.8 points; P=0.0024). The harms are the surgery's, and both trials report them plainly: in Kupsch, 22 adverse events in 19 patients including 4 stimulator-site infections and a lead dislodgment, with dysarthria the most frequent event; in Volkmann, adverse events in about a third of each group, the serious ones typically related to the implant procedure or device. The blinded phases are only 3 months long, the samples are 40 and 62, and treating physicians were unmasked in Volkmann (outcome videos were scored by masked experts). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): two concordant sham-controlled trials with large score differences, graded moderate rather than strong because of size and the short blinded window.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Tourette's disorder in youth: aripiprazole reduced tic scores versus placebo in two randomised trials — adults have no randomised record in this build
question: In children, adolescents and adults with Tourette's disorder, does aripiprazole reduce tic severity (YGTSS) compared with placebo?
balance: Aripiprazole reduces tics in children and adolescents with Tourette's disorder in two randomised trials, and that population limit belongs in the first sentence: no adult trial is carded here, because the randomised record is paediatric. In Yoo's 10-week trial (61 patients aged 6-18), the Yale Global Tic Severity Scale total tic score fell 15.0 points on aripiprazole versus 9.6 on placebo (P=0.0196), with global-improvement response in 66% versus 45%. In Sallee's 8-week phase 3 trial (133 patients aged 7-17), least-squares mean differences versus placebo were -6.3 points at low dose and -9.9 points at high dose (both significant), with 69% and 74% rated much or very much improved versus 38% on placebo. The metabolic ledger in Yoo is the caution: body weight, body mass index and waist circumference all increased significantly on aripiprazole (prolactin fell); in Sallee the commonest adverse events were sedation (up to 18.2%), somnolence (up to 15.6%) and fatigue, with no serious adverse events or deaths. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) for children and adolescents over 8-10 weeks; the adult half of the drafted question has no randomised record in this build and is not graded.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: Acute migraine in the emergency department: a single dose of dexamethasone probably reduces headache recurrence (pooled relative risk 0.74, NNT 9) — though the largest trial was null
question: In patients treated in the emergency department for acute migraine, does a dose of dexamethasone reduce headache recurrence within 24–72 hours compared with placebo?
balance: A single dose of parenteral dexamethasone added to standard emergency department migraine treatment probably reduces headache recurrence within 72 hours — but the trial record is small and mixed, and the pooled estimate does the heavy lifting. The largest single trial (Rowe 2008, 126 patients analysed) missed: relapse at 48-72 hours was 22% on dexamethasone versus 32% on placebo (odds ratio 0.6, 95% CI 0.3-1.3). An earlier, smaller trial (Innes 1999, 98 patients) was clearly positive for severe recurrence (18% versus 45%; odds ratio 0.28). The 2008 BMJ meta-analysis of all seven randomised trials found recurrence reduced by 26% relative (relative risk 0.74, 95% CI 0.60-0.90; number needed to treat 9), with no effect on pain relief for the index headache itself and no excess of side effects. Correction made on the face of this pack: the drafting slate named this shelf's anchor as 'Singh, Headache 2008' at PMID 18047499 — that record is in fact the Rowe 2008 trial, and the Singh 2008 paper (PMID 18976336) is a meta-analysis, not a trial. The shelf is built on the records as fetched. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a modest relative reduction in recurrence, resting on a pooled analysis of small trials whose largest member was null.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Menstrual migraine: six days of perimenstrual frovatriptan cut attack incidence from 67% to 41-52% in two randomised trials
question: In women with predictable menstrual migraine, does short-course frovatriptan taken across the perimenstrual window reduce menstrual migraine incidence compared with placebo?
balance: Six days of frovatriptan across the perimenstrual window clearly reduces menstrual migraine in two randomised trials, with a dose gradient. In the 546-woman crossover trial (Silberstein 2004), a menstrual migraine occurred in 67% of placebo periods versus 52% on frovatriptan 2.5 mg once daily and 41% on twice daily (both P<0.0001; twice daily beat once daily, P<0.001). In women whose menstrual migraine had already proved difficult to treat (Brandes 2009, 410 women), headache-free perimenstrual periods averaged 0.92 of 3 on twice-daily frovatriptan and 0.69 on once daily versus 0.42 on placebo (P<0.001 and P<0.02). Severity fell too, and adverse events resembled placebo in both trials. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): two consistent randomised trials, a within-trial dose response, and absolute incidence reductions of 15-26 percentage points per treated cycle.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: Medication-overuse headache: withdrawal plus a preventive from the start probably beats either alone at curing the overuse — though headache days fell equally on all three strategies (Carlsen 2020)
question: In medication-overuse headache, which strategy works best — abrupt withdrawal plus preventive medication, preventive medication alone, or withdrawal alone?
balance: One open-label randomised trial has compared the three strategies clinicians actually argue about in medication-overuse headache, and its answer needs care: on the primary outcome — reduction in headache days per month at 6 months — the three strategies did NOT differ significantly (reductions of 12.3 days for withdrawal plus preventive from the start, 9.9 for preventive alone, and 8.5 for withdrawal alone; P=.20 — the treatments made no difference on that endpoint). The combined strategy won on the secondary outcomes that arguably matter more: 74.2% reverted to episodic headache versus 60.0% (preventive alone) and 41.7% (withdrawal alone) (P=.03), and 96.8% were cured of medication overuse versus 74.3% and 88.9% (P=.03). The drafting slate described the combined strategy as producing 'the largest reduction in headache days' — numerically true, but that comparison was not significant, and the pack grades the shelf on the secondary endpoints with the primary null stated first. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for withdrawal plus preventive from the start — flagged for the developer's personal verdict as a single-trial shelf whose primary endpoint was null.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Trigeminal neuralgia: botulinum toxin type A injections probably reduce pain — responders 68-86% versus 15-32% on placebo in two small trials, with no advantage for the higher dose
question: In trigeminal neuralgia inadequately controlled or intolerant of standard drugs, do botulinum toxin type A injections reduce pain intensity and attack frequency compared with placebo?
balance: Two small randomised double-blind trials from the same research group agree that intradermal/submucosal botulinum toxin type A injections reduce trigeminal neuralgia pain for at least 8-12 weeks. In Wu 2012 (42 patients, 75 U versus saline), responders (at least 50% reduction in mean pain score at week 12) were 68.2% versus 15.0%, with pain intensity separating from week 2 and attack frequency from week 1. In Zhang 2014 (84 patients), response at week 8 was 70.4% on 25 U and 86.2% on 75 U versus 32.1% on placebo — with no significant difference between the two doses, so the lower dose carries the same evidence with less exposure. Adverse events were few and mild to moderate in both trials. The limits are structural: 126 patients in total, one centre and one group, 8-12 week horizons, and no comparison against carbamazepine or surgery. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): consistent, sizeable responder separations in two small trials — moderate confidence, not more.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension: acetazolamide added to diet probably improves visual fields modestly — a 0.71 dB advantage in the single trial, with clearer gains in papilloedema and quality of life (IIHTT)
question: In idiopathic intracranial hypertension with mild visual loss, does acetazolamide plus a weight-reduction diet improve visual field function compared with diet alone?
balance: The Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension Treatment Trial is the only randomised trial of acetazolamide in this disease, and its headline effect is modest and borderline: on top of the same low-sodium weight-reduction diet, acetazolamide (titrated to a maximum tolerated dose up to 4 g/day) improved perimetric mean deviation by 1.43 dB at 6 months versus 0.71 dB on placebo — a treatment difference of 0.71 dB whose 95% confidence interval runs from 0 to 1.43 (P=.050). The supporting outcomes were stronger: papilloedema grade improved by an extra 0.70 (P<.001) and vision-related quality of life by 6.35 points (P=.003). One confound travels with the result: the acetazolamide group also lost more weight (-7.50 kg versus -3.45 kg; difference -4.05 kg), and weight loss itself treats this disease, so the trial cannot fully separate the drug's effect from the extra weight loss it caused (largely through taste and appetite effects). The authors themselves left 'the clinical importance of this improvement' undetermined. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — flagged for the developer's personal verdict as a single-trial shelf with a borderline primary endpoint.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension in women with obesity: bariatric surgery lowered intracranial pressure far more than community weight management over two years in a single small trial (IIH:WT)
question: In women with idiopathic intracranial hypertension and obesity, does bariatric surgery lower intracranial pressure more than a community weight-management intervention?
balance: In women with active idiopathic intracranial hypertension and a body mass index of at least 35, bariatric surgery lowered intracranial pressure substantially more than a community weight-management programme, and the gap widened over two years: adjusted differences of -6.0 cm of cerebrospinal fluid at 12 months (P=.001) and -8.2 cm at 24 months (P<.001), driven by much larger weight loss (-21.4 kg at 12 months, -26.6 kg at 24 months). Quality of life also improved more after surgery. The trial is small and specific: 66 women randomised, 54 in the primary analysis; the comparator was a named community programme (Weight Watchers), not usual care; and surgery's risks, though not the trial's focus, are permanent in a way a diet programme's are not. Visual outcomes were secondary and the trial was not powered for blindness prevention. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — flagged for the developer's personal verdict as a single-trial shelf in women only.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Cluster headache: non-invasive vagus nerve stimulation probably aborts episodic attacks (34-48% vs 6-11% on sham) but made no difference in chronic cluster headache in either ACT trial
question: In cluster headache, does non-invasive cervical vagus nerve stimulation abort attacks compared with sham stimulation?
balance: Non-invasive cervical vagus nerve stimulation for acute cluster headache splits cleanly by subtype, and the split was seen twice. In ACT1 (133 patients in the intent-to-treat population), the primary endpoint — pain relief at 15 minutes for the first attack — was NOT met overall (26.7% on active stimulation versus 15.1% on sham; P=.1); in the prespecified episodic cluster subgroup it was clearly positive (34.2% versus 10.6%; P=.008), while chronic cluster went the other way numerically (13.6% versus 23.1%). ACT2 (92 patients) repeated the pattern: overall 14% versus 12% pain-free at 15 minutes (no difference), but in episodic cluster 48% versus 6% (P<0.01), and in chronic cluster 5% versus 13%. Two trials whose overall primaries were null and whose episodic subgroups agree are evidence for the episodic claim and against the chronic one — this shelf is stamped accordingly. PROPOSED SPLIT: POSSIBLE (benefit) for acute treatment of episodic cluster headache; POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for chronic cluster headache. Flagged for the developer's personal verdict (SPLIT stamp).
stamp: SPLIT — POSSIBLE (benefit) in episodic cluster headache / POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) in chronic cluster headache

title: Migraine with aura: single-pulse transcranial magnetic stimulation during the aura probably increases pain freedom at 2 hours (39% vs 22% on sham) — one trial (Lipton 2010)
question: In migraine with aura, does single-pulse transcranial magnetic stimulation applied during the aura increase pain freedom at 2 hours compared with sham?
balance: A single sham-controlled trial supports single-pulse transcranial magnetic stimulation, applied during the aura, as an acute treatment for migraine with aura: pain-free at 2 hours in 39% on active stimulation versus 22% on sham (therapeutic gain 17 percentage points, 95% CI 3-31; P=.0179), with sustained pain freedom at 24 and 48 hours also favouring the device and no device-related serious adverse events. The caveats are the usual single-trial ones, plus attrition built into the design: of 267 enrolled, only 164 treated an attack and entered the outcome analysis, and the population was narrowly defined (aura preceding at least 30% of attacks, headache following more than 90% of auras). Later studies of the device were open-label and are not carded. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — flagged for the developer's personal verdict as a single-trial shelf.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Acute migraine: remote electrical neuromodulation of the upper arm probably relieves pain (relief 66.7% vs 38.8% on sham) — a single large trial (Yarnitsky 2019)
question: In acute migraine, does smartphone-controlled remote electrical neuromodulation of the upper arm relieve pain at 2 hours compared with sham stimulation?
balance: Remote electrical neuromodulation — a smartphone-controlled device stimulating the upper arm to trigger conditioned pain modulation — beat sham clearly in its single large sham-controlled trial (Yarnitsky 2019, 252 randomised): pain relief at 2 hours in 66.7% versus 38.8% (therapeutic gain 27.9 points; P<.0001) and pain freedom in 37.4% versus 18.4% (P=.003), sustained at 48 hours, with device-related adverse events in 4.8% versus 2.4%. Correction made on the face of this pack: the drafting slate claimed a second consistent sham-controlled trial in adolescents/adults. No such record could be resolved this run — the only other randomised REN record found is a 19-patient paediatric emergency-department feasibility pilot (PMID 39290050), which was not powered for efficacy and is not carded. The shelf therefore rests on one trial, however clean, and is stamped and flagged accordingly. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — flagged for the developer's personal verdict as a single-trial shelf.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Migraine prevention: daily supraorbital trigeminal stimulation probably reduces migraine days — responders 38.1% vs 12.1% on sham in the single small PREMICE trial
question: In episodic migraine, does daily supraorbital external trigeminal nerve stimulation reduce monthly migraine days compared with sham stimulation?
balance: The PREMICE trial randomised 67 patients with episodic migraine to daily 20-minute supraorbital external trigeminal nerve stimulation with the tested device (named in the record as the Cefaly device) or sham for 3 months. Migraine days fell significantly in the active group (6.94 to 4.88 per month; P=.023) and not on sham (6.54 to 6.22), and the 50% responder rate was 38.1% versus 12.1% (P=.023) — a therapeutic gain of 26 points. Migraine attacks, headache days, and acute drug intake also fell on active treatment only. No adverse events occurred in either group. The record itself classifies the evidence as Class III, the trial is small and 3 months long, and the sham's credibility (verum stimulation is perceptible) is the standing question for this device class. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — flagged for the developer's personal verdict as a single small trial.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Ruptured aneurysm: coiling cut death or dependence at 1 year (23.5% vs 30.9%) in ISAT's both-treatments-suitable population — BRAT's all-comers found no overall difference and far more retreatment after coiling
question: In subarachnoid haemorrhage from a ruptured intracranial aneurysm suitable for either treatment, does endovascular coiling reduce death or dependency compared with neurosurgical clipping?
balance: For a ruptured aneurysm suitable for either treatment, the two randomised trials point in related but not identical directions, and the difference is the population. ISAT (2,143 patients, mostly good-grade with anterior-circulation aneurysms that both teams accepted as suitable for either approach) found death or dependence at 1 year in 23.5% after coiling versus 30.9% after clipping — an absolute reduction of 7.4 percentage points (P=.0001) — with the survival advantage significant out to 7 years, less epilepsy after coiling, but a higher late rebleeding risk. BRAT (500 enrolled at a single centre, all-comers) found no significant overall difference in poor outcome at 6 years (P=.24) — a trial heavily diluted by crossover, since 38% of patients assigned to coiling were actually clipped, against 1.9% the other way; coiled aneurysms were completely obliterated far less often (48% versus 96%) and retreated more often (16.4% versus 4.6%), yet posterior-circulation aneurysms favoured coiling in BRAT too, and no recurrent haemorrhage occurred in coiled patients followed to 6 years. BRAT is carded from its 6-year results paper; the 3-year record (PMID 23991842) carries no abstract data in PubMed, so no figures are taken from it. PROPOSED SPLIT: POSSIBLE (benefit) for coiling in ISAT-type patients — good-grade, aneurysm judged suitable for either treatment; POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for functional outcome across BRAT's all-comer population, with coiling's durability costs (obliteration, retreatment) stated on the face. Tier C: the primary outcome is death or dependency. Flagged for the developer's personal verdict.
stamp: SPLIT — POSSIBLE (benefit) for coiling when the aneurysm is suitable for either treatment / POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for functional outcome in an all-comer population

title: Aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage: oral nimodipine reduced cerebral infarction (22% vs 33%) and poor outcome (20% vs 33%) in the British trial, with the earlier Allen trial in support
question: After aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage, does oral nimodipine reduce cerebral infarction and poor outcome compared with placebo?
balance: Oral nimodipine is one of the few drug treatments in aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage backed by two positive placebo-controlled trials from the pre-registration era — the reason it became and remains standard care. The British aneurysm nimodipine trial (Pickard 1989, 554 patients) gave nimodipine 60 mg every 4 hours for 21 days: cerebral infarction occurred in 22% versus 33% on placebo (a 34% relative reduction), and poor outcome (death or severe disability) in 20% versus 33% — 55/278 versus 91/278 — a 40% relative reduction, an absolute difference of about 13 percentage points. The earlier American trial (Allen 1983, 125 neurologically normal patients after haemorrhage) used intravenous then oral nimodipine against a narrower endpoint: a severe persistent deficit or death from arterial spasm in 1/56 on nimodipine versus 8/60 on placebo (P=.03). Both trials predate modern trial registration and modern SAH care (most patients today also have their aneurysm secured early), so the absolute gains belong to their era; the direction has never been reversed by a later trial. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit). Tier C: the British trial's poor-outcome endpoint embeds death.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: Chronic subdural haematoma: dexamethasone made functional outcomes worse (favourable outcome 83.9% vs 90.3% on placebo) and caused more adverse events in the 748-patient Dex-CSDH trial
question: In symptomatic chronic subdural haematoma, does a tapering course of dexamethasone improve functional outcome compared with placebo?
balance: Dexamethasone for symptomatic chronic subdural haematoma was widely used on the theory that it would calm the haematoma's inflammatory membranes; the one large randomised trial showed the opposite. Dex-CSDH randomised 748 adults (mean age 74; 94% underwent surgical evacuation during the admission) to a 2-week tapering course of oral dexamethasone or placebo alongside standard care. At 6 months, a favourable outcome (modified Rankin scale 0-3) occurred in 83.9% on dexamethasone versus 90.3% on placebo — an absolute reduction of 6.4 percentage points in favour of placebo (P=.01) — and more adverse events occurred on dexamethasone (the trial's full funder report records serious adverse events in 16.0% versus 6.4%). The one endpoint favouring the drug was repeat surgery for recurrence: 1.7% versus 7.1%. Correction made on the face of this pack: the drafting slate described the 2024 Health Technology Assessment report (PMID 38512045) as 'a second UK placebo-controlled trial' — it is the same Dex-CSDH trial's monograph report (same 748 patients, same ISRCTN80782810), not a second trial, and it is not carded as one. PROPOSED LIKELY (harm) on the primary functional outcome — flagged for the developer's personal verdict as a single (large, definitive) trial, Tier C because the Rankin scale embeds death.
stamp: LIKELY (harm)

title: Critically ill adults: continuous EEG found far more seizures than routine EEG but made no difference to 6-month mortality (49% vs 48%) in the CERTA trial
question: In critically ill adults with altered consciousness and no recent seizure, does continuous EEG reduce 6-month mortality compared with routine (repeated spot) EEG?
balance: Continuous EEG in critically ill adults with altered consciousness does what it is supposed to do diagnostically — and, in the only randomised trial, none of it changed who lived. CERTA randomised 364 patients (Glasgow Coma Scale 11 or less or equivalent, no recent seizure) to 30-48 hours of continuous EEG or two 20-minute routine EEGs. Six-month mortality — the primary outcome — was 89/182 versus 88/182 (adjusted relative risk 1.02, 95% CI 0.83-1.26; P=.85 — the treatment made no difference). Continuous monitoring detected more interictal features (adjusted RR 1.26) and far more seizures (adjusted RR 3.37), and antiseizure therapy was changed more often (RR 1.84) — a clean demonstration that better detection plus more treatment changes did not translate into survival in this population. No subgroup showed an effect. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — flagged for the developer's personal verdict: a single trial with a mortality primary endpoint, Tier C.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference)

title: Intraventricular haemorrhage: alteplase through the drain made no difference to good functional outcome (48% vs 45%) but cut mortality (18% vs 29%) — while doubling survival with severe disability (CLEAR III)
question: In intracerebral haemorrhage with intraventricular extension obstructing the third or fourth ventricle, does intraventricular alteplase through an external ventricular drain improve functional outcome compared with saline irrigation?
balance: CLEAR III is the library's clearest mortality-disability trade-off, and both sides of it belong in the first paragraph. In 500 patients with intracerebral haemorrhage under 30 mL and intraventricular blood obstructing the third or fourth ventricle, irrigating the external ventricular drain with alteplase (1 mg up to every 8 hours, up to 12 doses) versus saline did NOT improve the primary outcome: good functional outcome (modified Rankin scale 0-3) at 180 days in 48% versus 45% (risk ratio 1.06, 95% CI 0.88-1.28; P=.554). But mortality at 180 days was significantly lower with alteplase (18% versus 29%; hazard ratio 0.60; P=.006) — and the proportion surviving with severe disability (Rankin 5) was higher (17% versus 9%; risk ratio 1.99). Ventriculitis (7% versus 12%) and overall serious adverse events (46% versus 60%) were less frequent with alteplase, and symptomatic bleeding did not differ (2% versus 2%). Whether trading deaths for severely disabled survivors is a benefit is a values question the trial cannot answer; this shelf reports the exchange rate and stamps the two endpoints separately. PROPOSED SPLIT: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for functional outcome; POSSIBLE (benefit) for mortality, with the severe-disability increase printed beside it. Tier C. Flagged for the developer's personal verdict.
stamp: SPLIT — POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for functional outcome / POSSIBLE (benefit) for mortality, with more survivors severely disabled

title: Acute vascular brain injury: device-based fever prevention halved fever burden but made no difference to functional recovery in the futility-stopped INTREPID trial
question: In critically ill patients with acute vascular brain injury (ischaemic stroke, ICH or SAH), does proactive device-based fever prevention improve functional outcome compared with standard fever treatment?
balance: INTREPID tested whether preventing fever, rather than treating it when it appears, improves recovery after acute vascular brain injury — and answered the mechanism question yes and the outcome question no. In 686 enrolled critically ill patients with ischaemic stroke, intracerebral haemorrhage, or subarachnoid haemorrhage, an automated surface device targeting 37.0 °C for up to 14 days roughly halved daily fever burden versus standard tiered fever treatment (0.37 versus 0.73 °C-hour; P<.001). Three-month functional recovery did not differ (median modified Rankin score 4.0 in both groups; odds ratio for a favourable shift 1.09, 95% CI 0.81-1.46; P=.54 — the treatment made no difference), and major adverse events were at least as frequent with prevention (82.2% versus 75.9%). Enrolment was stopped at a planned interim analysis for futility after 686 of 1,176 planned patients, so the null is a futility-stopped null: it excludes the effect the trial was powered for, not every conceivable small benefit. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — flagged for the developer's personal verdict: a single trial, stopped early, with an outcome scale that embeds death. Tier C.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference)

title: Severe traumatic brain injury: ICP-monitor-guided care made no difference to outcome or 6-month mortality versus imaging-and-examination-guided care in the BEST TRIP trial
question: In severe traumatic brain injury, does management guided by an intracranial-pressure monitor improve outcome compared with management guided by imaging and clinical examination?
balance: BEST TRIP is the only randomised trial of intracranial-pressure monitoring itself, and it found that care built around the monitor was not superior to care built around imaging and clinical examination. In 324 patients aged 13 or older with severe traumatic brain injury in Bolivia and Ecuador, the composite primary outcome (survival, consciousness, functional and neuropsychological status across 21 measures) scored at the 56th percentile with pressure-guided care versus the 53rd with imaging/clinical care (P=.49 — the treatment made no difference). Six-month mortality was 39% versus 41% (P=.60). One finding cuts against any reading of the imaging-based protocol as 'doing less': brain-specific treatments (hyperosmolar fluids, hyperventilation) were used on MORE days in the imaging/clinical group (4.8 versus 3.4 days; P=.002) — the trial compared two active management protocols, not monitoring versus neglect, and it was conducted in a pre-hospital and ICU system quite different from North American or European trauma care. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — flagged for the developer's personal verdict: a single trial, single-region, with a composite embedding mortality. Tier C.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference)

title: Aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage: early prophylactic lumbar drainage probably improves outcome — unfavourable outcome 32.6% vs 44.8% in the single EARLYDRAIN trial
question: After aneurysm treatment for subarachnoid haemorrhage, does early prophylactic lumbar CSF drainage improve outcome compared with standard care?
balance: EARLYDRAIN randomised 287 patients after aneurysm treatment for subarachnoid haemorrhage (all clinical grades; clipping or coiling within 48 hours) to an early prophylactic lumbar drain (5 mL/hour, started within 72 hours) plus standard care, or standard care alone, at 19 centres in Germany, Switzerland, and Canada. Unfavourable outcome (modified Rankin scale 3-6) at 6 months occurred in 32.6% with drainage versus 44.8% without — a risk ratio of 0.73 (95% CI 0.52-0.98) and an absolute difference of 12 percentage points (P=.04) — and secondary infarctions at discharge were fewer (28.5% versus 39.9%; risk ratio 0.71). The result is promising and fragile in the usual single-trial ways: open-label treatment (though outcome assessors were masked), a primary P value of .04, and a recruitment history spanning 2011-2016 with 20 invalid randomisations excluded before the intention-to-treat set. It also tests prophylactic drainage added to standard care — not drainage as rescue therapy for established delayed cerebral ischaemia. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — flagged for the developer's personal verdict as a single-trial shelf, Tier C because the outcome scale embeds death.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)
