title: Aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage: intravenous magnesium made no difference to outcome in two phase 3 trials (MASH-2; IMASH) — the question is closed
question: After aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage, does intravenous magnesium sulphate improve functional outcome compared with placebo?
balance: Intravenous magnesium after aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage is a closed question: two phase 3 placebo-controlled trials, run independently on different continents, both found nothing. MASH-2 (1,204 patients in Europe and South America; magnesium sulphate 64 mmol/day) found poor outcome at 3 months in 26.2% on magnesium versus 25.3% on placebo (risk ratio 1.03, 95% CI 0.85-1.25), and its updated meta-analysis of seven randomised trials (2,047 patients) gave a pooled risk ratio of 0.96 (0.86-1.08). IMASH (327 patients in Hong Kong and China; infusion titrated to double the serum level) found favourable outcome at 6 months in 64% versus 63% (odds ratio 1.0, 95% CI 0.7-1.6), with no subgroup — grade, age, hypertension, haematoma, aneurysm site or size, treatment mode — showing benefit. The pilot-era promise did not survive either definitive trial. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference). Tier C: poor outcome embeds death. Contrast nimodipine (Shelf #2390): same disease, same era of enthusiasm — opposite verdict, because its trials were positive.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference)

title: Depression after one failed antidepressant: augmenting with aripiprazole probably beats switching — remission 28.9% vs 22.3% in the single large VAST-D trial of veterans
question: In major depression unresponsive to one adequate antidepressant course, is it better to switch to bupropion, augment with bupropion, or augment with aripiprazole?
balance: VAST-D is the single large trial of the second-step choice in major depression that has not responded to one adequate antidepressant course, and its answer is a modest ranking, not a breakthrough. In 1,522 patients (85.2% men; US veterans) randomised to switch to bupropion, augment with bupropion, or augment with aripiprazole, 12-week remission was 22.3% (switch), 26.9% (augment-bupropion), and 28.9% (augment-aripiprazole). Only the aripiprazole-augmentation versus switch comparison was significant (relative risk 1.30, 95% CI 1.05-1.60; P=.02) — an absolute gain of 6.6 percentage points — and response rates also favoured aripiprazole augmentation (74.3% versus 62.4% and 65.6%). Relapse did not differ. The costs were asymmetric, as expected: anxiety was more frequent in both bupropion groups (24.3% and 22.5% versus 16.6%), while somnolence, akathisia, and weight gain were more frequent on aripiprazole. The authors themselves call the effect modest and ask for cost-effectiveness analysis before net utility can be judged. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for aripiprazole augmentation over switching — flagged for the developer's personal verdict as a single-trial shelf in a predominantly male veteran population.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Major depression: pharmacogenomic guidance steered prescribing away from drug–gene interactions and produced a small, nonpersistent remission gain in the single large PRIME Care trial
question: In major depressive disorder starting or switching antidepressant treatment, does providing pharmacogenomic drug–gene interaction results to clinicians improve remission compared with usual care?
balance: PRIME Care is the largest randomised trial of pharmacogenomic-guided antidepressant prescribing, and its two answers point in different strengths of direction. Giving clinicians commercial drug–gene interaction results at the point of prescribing changed what they prescribed, decisively: within 30 days, an estimated 59.3% of guided patients received an antidepressant with no predicted drug–gene interaction versus 25.7% under usual care (odds ratio 4.32 for no versus moderate/substantial interaction). The clinical dividend was small and not durable at the final time point: remission across the 24 weeks favoured guided care (odds ratio 1.28; risk difference 2.8 percentage points, 95% CI 0.6 to 5.1), but remission at week 24 itself did not differ significantly (estimated risk difference 1.5 points, 95% CI -2.4 to 5.3; P=.45), with 130 versus 126 patients in remission. The population was 75% male US veterans starting or switching a single antidepressant. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): testing reliably steers prescribing away from predicted interactions, and probably buys a small, early remission advantage — an absolute effect of about 3 points at its best estimate, in a single trial. Flagged for the developer's personal verdict as a single-trial shelf. (The pre-emptive panel-testing question lives at Shelf #472; this shelf is testing at the point of an antidepressant start or switch.)
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Recurrent depression: mindfulness-based cognitive therapy with taper support performed comparably to maintenance antidepressants over two years in PREVENT — no superiority, a real alternative
question: In people with recurrent depression in remission on maintenance antidepressants, is mindfulness-based cognitive therapy with tapering support as effective as continuing maintenance antidepressants for preventing relapse over two years?
balance: For people with recurrent depression who want an alternative to staying on antidepressants, PREVENT is the definitive head-to-head: 424 patients with three or more previous episodes, all on maintenance antidepressants, were randomised to mindfulness-based cognitive therapy with support to taper or stop the drug (MBCT-TS) or to continue maintenance antidepressants for 24 months. Time to relapse or recurrence did not differ (hazard ratio 0.89, 95% CI 0.67 to 1.18; P=.43) — the trial was designed to test superiority and found none, so the honest reading is comparability, not proven equivalence, though both groups had enduring positive outcomes on relapse, residual symptoms, and quality of life. The wider evidence leans the same way with more optimism: the individual-patient-data meta-analysis of 9 trials (1,258 patients) found MBCT reduced relapse risk versus non-MBCT controls over 60 weeks (hazard ratio 0.69) and versus active treatments (hazard ratio 0.79), with larger effects in patients with more residual symptoms. Serious adverse events in PREVENT were balanced (five in each group, including two deaths in each, none attributable). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference — MBCT with taper support performed comparably to maintenance antidepressants in the one head-to-head trial): an alternative for patients who prefer it, not a superior one.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference)

title: Major depression after an inadequate antidepressant response: adjunctive aripiprazole improved scores and remission in two concordant pivotal trials — with akathisia in about a quarter
question: In major depression with inadequate response to an antidepressant, does adjunctive aripiprazole increase response and remission compared with adjunctive placebo?
balance: Adding aripiprazole to an antidepressant that has already failed is supported by the twin pivotal trials that founded atypical-antipsychotic augmentation. Both used the same enrichment design — a prospective antidepressant course, then randomisation of inadequate responders to adjunctive aripiprazole or placebo for 6 weeks. Berman 2007 (362 randomised): depression scores fell 8.8 points on aripiprazole versus 5.8 on placebo (P<.001). Marcus 2008 (381 randomised): the same separation (8.5 versus 5.7 points; P=.001), with remission in 25.4% versus 15.2% (P=.016) and response in 32.4% versus 17.4% (P<.001) — absolute gains of about 10 and 15 percentage points. The price is consistent and characteristic: akathisia in roughly a quarter of aripiprazole patients (23.1% and 25.9% versus about 4% on placebo) and restlessness in about 14%, though discontinuations for adverse events stayed low (2-4%). The trials were 6 weeks long and industry-run; durability and the metabolic ledger of longer use sit outside them. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): two concordant randomised trials with the same design and the same result — the strategy VAST-D later ranked against switching (Shelf #2398).
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: Treatment-resistant depression in primary care: adding mirtazapine to an SSRI or SNRI made no clinically important difference in the 480-patient MIR trial
question: In treatment-resistant depression in primary care, does adding mirtazapine to an SSRI or SNRI improve depressive symptoms compared with adding placebo?
balance: Adding mirtazapine to an SSRI or SNRI is one of the commonest combination moves in primary-care depression — and the one large trial of it found no clinically important benefit. MIR randomised 480 primary-care patients whose depression had not responded adequately to at least 6 weeks of an SSRI or SNRI to add mirtazapine or placebo for 12 weeks, with follow-up to a year. Depression scores at 12 weeks were lower on mirtazapine, but the adjusted difference (-1.83 BDI-II points, 95% CI -3.92 to 0.27; P=.09) included the null and sat below the threshold of clinical importance the trial was designed around; adverse effects were more common on mirtazapine and more often stopped the drug. A single trial, however large and well-placed, leaves the confidence interval admitting a small benefit — which is why the stamp is POSSIBLE rather than LIKELY. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): the routine combination, directly tested in the population that receives it, did not deliver a clinically important effect. Flagged for the developer's personal verdict as a single-trial shelf.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference)

title: Bipolar I depression: cariprazine 1.5 mg/day improved depression scores in two phase 3 trials — the 3.0 mg dose failed in both
question: In bipolar I depression, does cariprazine improve depressive symptoms (MADRS) compared with placebo?
balance: Cariprazine for bipolar I depression has a consistent programme answer, and it is dose-specific: 1.5 mg/day works, 3.0 mg/day does not clearly. In Durgam 2016 (571 patients in the intent-to-treat population), the 1.5 mg dose beat placebo on depression scores by 4.0 points (significant after multiplicity adjustment), the 3.0 mg dose's 2.5-point advantage was not significant after adjustment, and 0.75 mg was indistinguishable from placebo. The second phase 3 trial (493 patients) repeated the pattern almost exactly: 1.5 mg significant on both the primary depression score (difference -2.5; adjusted P=.0417) and global severity, 3.0 mg not significant. Akathisia and insomnia were the commonest adverse events in the first trial; in the second, akathisia, restlessness, nausea, and fatigue — with mean weight gains of half a kilogram or less and small metabolic changes in both. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) for cariprazine 1.5 mg/day: two concordant phase 3 trials, the same dose winning twice and the higher dose failing twice — a shelf whose dose ceiling is part of the answer.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: Bipolar depression: lumateperone 42 mg improved depression scores as monotherapy and added to lithium or valproate in two randomised trials, with minimal extrapyramidal or metabolic signal
question: In major depressive episodes of bipolar I or II disorder, does lumateperone improve depressive symptoms compared with placebo?
balance: Lumateperone 42 mg improves bipolar depression in two settings, with an unusually quiet side-effect profile for its class. As monotherapy (Calabrese 2021, 377 patients with bipolar I or II depression), it beat placebo on depression scores by 4.6 points at day 43 (effect size -0.56), with superiority in both bipolar I and bipolar II subgroups; somnolence and nausea were the only adverse events meaningfully above placebo, extrapyramidal events were at placebo rates, and weight and metabolic measures barely moved. Added to lithium or valproate in inadequate responders (Suppes 2023, 529 patients), the 42 mg dose again separated (difference -2.4 points; P=.02) while the 28 mg dose did not reach significance on the primary endpoint (P=.10). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) for lumateperone 42 mg: two positive randomised trials — monotherapy and adjunctive — with the lower adjunctive dose failing, which sharpens rather than blurs the dose answer.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: Depression after acute coronary syndrome: escitalopram cut major adverse cardiac events over eight years (40.9% vs 53.6%) in the single EsDEPACS trial — with mortality itself unchanged
question: In patients with depression after acute coronary syndrome, does 24 weeks of escitalopram reduce long-term major adverse cardiac events compared with placebo?
balance: EsDEPACS is the first antidepressant trial to separate on hard cardiac outcomes, and it did so in a single Korean centre. Three hundred patients with depression after a recent acute coronary syndrome were randomised to 24 weeks of escitalopram or placebo and followed for a median of 8.1 years. Major adverse cardiac events — the composite of all-cause death, myocardial infarction, and percutaneous coronary intervention — occurred in 40.9% on escitalopram versus 53.6% on placebo (hazard ratio 0.69, 95% CI 0.49 to 0.96; P=.03): an absolute difference of 12.7 percentage points over eight years. The components must be read with the composite: myocardial infarction was significantly reduced (8.7% versus 15.2%; hazard ratio 0.54; P=.04), intervention trended the same way (P=.07), but all-cause mortality (20.8% versus 24.5%; hazard ratio 0.82; P=.43) and cardiac death (P=.48) did not differ significantly — the mortality claim is not established by this trial, and this shelf does not make it. Earlier post-MI antidepressant trials (SADHART, ENRICHD — Shelves #2289 and #2288) showed safety and symptom effects, not event reduction. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) — flagged for the developer's personal verdict as an OUTSTANDING-SINGLE under the Nov 8, 2026 rule (landmark single randomised blinded trial, hard MACE endpoint), Tier C because the balance carries a cardiovascular-event claim whose mortality component is null.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: Premenstrual dysphoric disorder: sertraline works on continuous dosing (62% vs 34% much improved), and symptom-onset dosing is probably effective — its trial's primary scale just missed
question: In premenstrual dysphoric disorder, does sertraline — continuous or symptom-onset dosing — improve symptoms compared with placebo?
balance: Sertraline treats premenstrual dysphoric disorder, and the dosing can probably be shortened to the symptomatic window — though the trial of that shorter strategy was mixed on its own primary scale. Continuous flexible-dose sertraline (Yonkers 1997, 243 randomised) beat placebo clearly: daily symptom scores fell from 64 to 44 versus 62 to 54 (P<.001), depression-scale scores fell 44% versus 29% (P<.002), and 62% versus 34% were rated much or very much improved (P<.001), with parallel gains in functioning. The 2015 symptom-onset trial (252 women, dosing from symptom onset to the first days of menses over 6 cycles) missed its primary outcome narrowly — the Premenstrual Tension Scale difference was 1.88 points (95% CI 0.01 to 3.75; P=.06) — while its secondary measures favoured sertraline (depressive-symptom difference 5.14 points, P=.02; response 67.0% versus 52.4%, P=.02) and abrupt monthly cessation produced no discontinuation symptoms. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): the drug's efficacy is established by the continuous-dosing trial; symptom-onset dosing is supported on secondary outcomes with a missed primary, and the pack grades it as probably effective rather than proven.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: Treatment-resistant depression: inhaled nitrous oxide improved depression scores within hours in two very small crossover trials — 44 patients in total
question: In treatment-resistant major depression, does inhaled nitrous oxide produce rapid antidepressant effects compared with placebo gas?
balance: Inhaled nitrous oxide produces rapid antidepressant effects in treatment-resistant depression — in two crossover trials so small that the whole evidence base is 44 patients. The proof-of-concept trial (Nagele 2015, 20 patients) found a single 1-hour inhalation of 50% nitrous oxide improved depression scores versus placebo gas at 2 hours (difference -4.8 points) and 24 hours (-5.5 points; P<.001), with response in 20% versus 5% and remission in 15% versus 0% — differences whose confidence intervals are very wide. The phase 2 trial (24 patients, three-way crossover) found nitrous oxide superior to placebo overall (P=.01), no difference between 25% and 50% concentrations (P=.58), effects that were individually non-significant at 2 and 24 hours but significant by week 2 (-5.19 points at 25%, P=.02; -7.00 at 50%, P=.001), and adverse events that declined substantially with the lower dose (P<.001). Three patients stopped nitrous oxide in the first trial; no serious adverse events occurred in either. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a real rapid signal, replicated in design if not in size — hours-to-two-weeks endpoints in two dozen-patient crossovers cap the stamp.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: PTSD: EMDR and fluoxetine both beat placebo over 8 weeks, but EMDR's gains persisted at 6 months while the stopped drug's did not — one trial, benefit concentrated in adult-onset trauma
question: In posttraumatic stress disorder, is eye movement desensitization and reprocessing (EMDR) as effective as an established antidepressant, and do its gains persist after treatment ends?
balance: This shelf answers the head-to-head and durability question, and the one randomised trial of it found a split verdict by trauma timing. Van der Kolk 2007 randomised 88 adults with PTSD to 8 weeks of EMDR, fluoxetine, or pill placebo, with blinded ratings after treatment and at 6-month follow-up. Both active treatments beat placebo acutely in the trial's reporting; the separation came after treatment stopped: the EMDR group maintained its gains at 6 months while the fluoxetine group's gains largely eroded after discontinuation — and the benefit accrued primarily to adult-onset trauma survivors, among whom 75.0% of the EMDR group achieved asymptomatic end-state functioning at follow-up versus none in the fluoxetine group (child-onset: 33.3% on EMDR, and for most childhood-onset patients neither treatment produced complete remission). The record's abstract reports the follow-up contrast in detail but gives no acute-phase effect sizes, and none are claimed here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for EMDR's durability advantage — flagged for the developer's personal verdict: a single 88-patient trial carries the head-to-head claim, and trauma-focused therapy as a class (prolonged exposure, cognitive processing therapy) lives at Shelf #702.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: PTSD prevention: early hydrocortisone looked promising in a 25-patient pilot but made no difference in the 118-patient emergency-department trial — only a night-time subgroup signal remains
question: In patients exposed to severe trauma, does a single high dose of hydrocortisone given within hours reduce later PTSD compared with placebo?
balance: A single high dose of hydrocortisone within hours of trauma was one of prevention psychiatry's most attractive ideas — and the larger, later trial did not confirm it. The 2011 pilot (Zohar; 25 patients with acute stress symptoms given intravenous hydrocortisone 100-140 mg or placebo within 6 hours of trauma) reported favourable changes in the trajectory of acute stress and later PTSD symptoms, a qualitative result the record states without event rates. The definitive emergency-department trial (118 patients, same strategy, 13-month follow-up) found no difference between hydrocortisone and placebo in PTSD prevalence or symptom severity — the treatment made no difference — with one subgroup signal: a significant interaction with time of trauma, and lower PTSD prevalence at 13 months in patients treated at night, when endogenous cortisol is low. Both records carry the same registry identifier (NCT00855270), indicating one research programme. PROPOSED SPLIT: POSSIBLE (benefit) on the pilot record alone, superseded by POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) in the larger trial — the shelf's operative answer is the null, with the nocturnal subgroup left as a research lead, not a claim. title: Chronic PTSD: SSRIs improve core symptoms — sertraline responders 53% vs 32%, paroxetine effective at both doses in a 551-patient trial
question: In chronic posttraumatic stress disorder, do SSRIs improve core PTSD symptoms compared with placebo?
balance: SSRIs were the first drug class proven for chronic PTSD, and the two pivotal trials here agree on a modest, real effect. Brady 2000 (187 outpatients, mean illness duration 12 years) found sertraline superior to placebo on three of four primary measures over 12 weeks — symptom scores fell 33.0 versus 23.2 points (P=.02) — with a responder rate of 53% versus 32% (P=.008); the intrusion/re-experiencing cluster, notably, did not separate (P=.14), while avoidance/numbing and arousal did. The paroxetine fixed-dose trial (551 patients) found both 20 mg and 40 mg significantly better than placebo on the primary symptom measure, on all three symptom clusters, and on social and occupational impairment and comorbid depression, in men and women and across trauma types; its record reports significance without effect sizes, and none are invented here. Insomnia was sertraline's only clearly excess adverse effect (16.0% versus 4.3%). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): two concordant pivotal trials — symptom relief of moderate size, not remission for most, and the drug half of a field where trauma-focused therapy (Shelf #702) carries the larger effects.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: Panic disorder: CBT and imipramine each beat placebo, the combination's advantage appeared only in maintenance — and after stopping, CBT's benefit endured while the drug's faded
question: In panic disorder, how do cognitive-behavioural therapy, imipramine, and their combination compare acutely, in maintenance, and after treatment is stopped?
balance: The landmark four-clinic trial (Barlow 2000, 312 patients) answers three questions at once, and the answer changes with time. Acutely (3 months), cognitive-behavioural therapy and imipramine each beat placebo on the Panic Disorder Severity Scale (response 48.7% and 45.8% versus 21.7%), and the combination (60.3%) was not significantly better than either alone. In the 6-month maintenance phase the combination did pull ahead (response 57.1%, significantly above either monotherapy), and among responders imipramine's responses were of higher quality. After all treatment stopped, the picture inverted: at 6-month post-discontinuation follow-up, response was highest for CBT plus placebo (41.0%) and CBT alone (31.9%), lower for the combination (26.3%), and lowest for imipramine alone (19.7%) — the drug's gains depended on staying on it, while CBT's persisted. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — one large trial carries all three comparisons, flagged for the developer's personal verdict as a single-trial shelf.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Body dysmorphic disorder: fluoxetine beat placebo (response 53% vs 18%), and continuing escitalopram after response halved 6-month relapse (18% vs 40%)
question: In body dysmorphic disorder, do serotonin reuptake inhibitors improve symptoms compared with placebo, and does continuing them after response prevent relapse?
balance: Body dysmorphic disorder has a thin pharmacotherapy record, but its two placebo-controlled trials point the same way. Phillips 2002 — the first placebo-controlled study in the disorder — randomised 67 patients to 12 weeks of fluoxetine or placebo: response in 53% on fluoxetine versus 18% on placebo (P=.003), with benefit from week 8; notably, patients with the delusional variant responded as often as non-delusional patients, and no delusional patient responded to placebo. The relapse-prevention trial answered the next question: after 14 weeks of open-label escitalopram (67.0% responded), the 58 responders randomised to continue escitalopram or switch to placebo for 6 months relapsed at 18% versus 40%, with time to relapse significantly longer on continued drug (hazard ratio 2.72, 95% CI 1.01 to 8.57 — an interval wide enough to include a small effect), and a third of continued patients improved further. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): concordant acute and continuation evidence, but from two small specialist-centre trials totalling 125 randomised patients.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Trichotillomania: N-acetylcysteine helped adults (56% vs 16% much improved) but made no difference in children — a clean age split across two trials
question: In trichotillomania (hair-pulling disorder), does N-acetylcysteine reduce hair pulling compared with placebo — in adults, and in children?
balance: A SPLIT shelf, split by age. In adults, Grant 2009 (50 patients, 12 weeks of N-acetylcysteine 1200-2400 mg/day versus placebo) found significantly greater reductions on both hair-pulling scales (P<.001 and P=.001), with 56% much or very much improved versus 16% on placebo (P=.003), improvement first appearing after 9 weeks, and no adverse events in the N-acetylcysteine group. In children and adolescents, the identically designed trial (Bloch 2013, 39 patients aged 8-17) found no difference between N-acetylcysteine and placebo on any primary or secondary measure — responders 25% versus 21% — with both groups improving over time regardless of assignment. The paediatric authors state the contrast plainly: adult efficacy cannot be assumed in children, and behavioural therapy (which has evidence in both age groups) should precede pharmacotherapy in children. PROPOSED SPLIT: POSSIBLE (benefit) in adults / POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) in children — flagged for the developer's personal verdict (SPLIT stamp; two small trials, opposite results).
stamp: SPLIT — POSSIBLE (benefit) in adults / POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) in children

title: Generalised anxiety disorder: duloxetine beat placebo by 3.1 anxiety-scale points across three trials — with 14% stopping for adverse events
question: In generalised anxiety disorder, does duloxetine improve anxiety symptoms and functioning compared with placebo?
balance: Duloxetine's generalised anxiety record is a standard regulatory package: three placebo-controlled trials, a consistent moderate effect on anxiety scores, and a tolerability cost paid mainly in nausea and early discontinuation. The pooled analysis of the three trials (1,163 patients) found anxiety scores fell 11.1 points on duloxetine versus 8.0 on placebo (P≤.001) — a 3.1-point advantage on the Hamilton Anxiety Scale — with global functioning improving 46% versus 25% (P≤.001). In the active-controlled trial (487 patients), duloxetine 60-120 mg and venlafaxine extended-release each beat placebo (P=.007 and P<.001), with no claim of difference between the two drugs; discontinuation for adverse events was 14.2% on duloxetine and 11.0% on venlafaxine versus 1.9% on placebo, and nausea was the commonest adverse event in the pooled data. The pooled trials ran 9-10 weeks and excluded comorbid psychiatric conditions. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): three concordant trials — a real but modest average effect, bought with a one-in-seven early dropout rate for adverse events.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: Generalised anxiety disorder: hydroxyzine beat placebo in two older trials (-12.2 vs -9.6 anxiety points at 12 weeks) and matched bromazepam — sedation is the price
question: In generalised anxiety disorder, does hydroxyzine reduce anxiety symptoms compared with placebo?
balance: Hydroxyzine is the shelf's curiosity: a sedating antihistamine with two positive placebo-controlled trials in generalised anxiety disorder, both from the 1990s-2000s French literature. The larger (Llorca 2002, 334 randomised outpatients, 12 weeks) found anxiety scores fell 12.16 points on hydroxyzine 50 mg/day versus 9.64 on placebo (P=.019), with responder (P=.003) and remission (P=.028) advantages, maintained efficacy, and no statistically significant difference from the bromazepam 6 mg/day active comparator; drowsiness was actually more frequent with bromazepam. The earlier 4-week trial (Ferreri 1994, 133 patients) found significant superiority from week 1, persisting a week after abrupt discontinuation without rebound — at the price of more side effects overall (52% versus 35%), led by transient sleepiness (28% versus 14%). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a real, modest anxiolytic effect in two trials of their era — no comparison with modern first-line agents exists, and current labelling cautions (not addressed in these records) should be checked before use.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: PTSD: five-session written exposure therapy was noninferior to prolonged exposure and to cognitive processing therapy — and patients actually finished it (dropout 12.5% vs 35.6%)
question: In posttraumatic stress disorder, is brief written exposure therapy (five sessions) as effective as prolonged exposure or cognitive processing therapy, with better completion?
balance: Written exposure therapy (WET) — five sessions built around 30 minutes of in-session writing about the trauma, with no homework — has now been tested head-to-head against the two flagship trauma-focused therapies in randomised noninferiority trials, and met noninferiority in both. Against prolonged exposure in 178 veterans (Sloan 2023), symptom change on the CAPS-5 was noninferior at every assessment (noninferiority margin 10 points), and dropout was a third of the longer therapy's: 12.5% versus 35.6%. Against cognitive processing therapy in 169 active-duty service members, WET was likewise noninferior (largest between-group difference 3.96 points, upper confidence bound below the 10-point margin at all timepoints), with session completion 76.5% versus 54.8% for the 12-session therapy. Two cautions temper the stamp: a 10-point CAPS-5 margin is generous, and 'noninferior for symptom change' says nothing about which patients need the fuller treatments. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the efficiency claim — comparable outcomes in five sessions with far less attrition — is the shelf's real finding, and attrition is a hard behavioural outcome, not a rating-scale artefact.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: PTSD: propranolol before memory-reactivation sessions added an 11.5-point CAPS advantage over reactivation alone — one 60-patient trial of reconsolidation blockade
question: In chronic posttraumatic stress disorder, does propranolol given before trauma-memory reactivation sessions reduce PTSD symptoms more than placebo with the same reactivation?
balance: Reconsolidation blockade is psychiatry's most theory-driven PTSD treatment: reactivate the trauma memory while beta-blockade blunts its re-storage, and the memory should lose emotional force. Brunet 2018 tested it properly — 60 adults with long-standing PTSD, propranolol or placebo 90 minutes before a brief weekly memory-reactivation session for 6 weeks, double-blind — and the drug added a real increment over reactivation alone: an adjusted post-treatment CAPS advantage of 11.50 points and a patient-rated advantage growing to 14.58 points by week 6. But read the within-group effect sizes before celebrating: reactivation with placebo alone produced a CAPS effect size of 1.25 — the ritual itself did much of the work — and there is no long-term follow-up in this record, so durability, the theory's core promise, is untested here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), flagged for the developer's personal verdict: a single 60-patient trial of a novel mechanism, however elegant.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Severe mental illness: Individual Placement and Support beat usual vocational rehabilitation on all vocational outcomes in the six-centre European trial — fidelity to the model was what made it work
question: In severe mental illness, does Individual Placement and Support (IPS) supported employment improve vocational outcomes compared with usual vocational rehabilitation?
balance: Individual Placement and Support (IPS) — rapid placement into ordinary competitive jobs with integrated clinical support, rather than train-then-place rehabilitation — is the best-evidenced vocational intervention in severe mental illness, and the European EQOLISE trial is its international anchor. The record carded on this shelf is the trial's predictors report, which states the trial's verdict directly: across six European centres, IPS was more effective than usual vocational rehabilitation for all vocational outcomes. The same report identifies who benefits and what makes it work: previous work history, fewer unmet social needs, better relationships with vocational workers, remission, and swifter service uptake predicted employment and longer work; and the only service characteristic associated with greater IPS effectiveness was closeness to the original IPS model — fidelity. One honesty note, printed here on the shelf's face: the employment rates themselves (the figures most often quoted from EQOLISE) sit in the trial's main outcome report, a separate publication not carded on this shelf, so this shelf claims the direction and the predictors, not rates it cannot show. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the direction is stated by the trial's own indexed report and concordant with the wider IPS literature, but the shelf's citable record carries no effect sizes.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Early-phase schizophrenia: long-acting injectables delayed first hospitalisation in the US PRELAPSE trial (hazard ratio 0.56) — but Europe's EULAST trial found no advantage over oral treatment at keeping patients on medication
question: In early-phase schizophrenia, do long-acting injectable antipsychotics delay first hospitalisation compared with usual-care oral treatment?
balance: Two large randomised trials in early-phase schizophrenia point in different directions, and they asked slightly different questions. PRELAPSE (489 patients; 39 US clinics cluster-randomised to encourage long-acting injectable aripiprazole once-monthly versus clinician's-choice usual care) found first hospitalisation significantly delayed: 22% versus 36% hospitalised over two years, hazard ratio 0.56 (95% CI 0.34–0.92), number needed to treat 7. EULAST (511 patients individually randomised in Europe and Israel to long-acting injectable versus oral paliperidone or aripiprazole, open-label) found no difference in its primary endpoint, time to all-cause discontinuation (hazard ratio 1.16, 95% CI 0.94–1.43). The designs differ in ways that matter: PRELAPSE tested a clinic-level policy of encouraging one injectable against unrestricted usual care (which could itself include injectables), while EULAST tested the formulations head-to-head and counted discontinuation for any reason, not hospitalisation. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a real hospitalisation signal from one trial, unconfirmed — and partly undercut on a neighbouring endpoint — by the other.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Primary insomnia: eszopiclone improved sleep onset, maintenance and total sleep time — objectively in elderly patients and sustained over 6 months in adults, with no tolerance
question: In adults and older adults with primary insomnia, does eszopiclone improve sleep onset and maintenance (polysomnographic and patient-reported) compared with placebo?
balance: Two double-blind, placebo-controlled trials from eszopiclone's development programme support the claim. In 264 elderly patients (aged 64–86) studied with polysomnography, two weeks of eszopiclone 2 mg significantly shortened sleep onset, reduced wake after sleep onset, and increased sleep efficiency and total sleep time versus placebo, with unpleasant taste the commonest adverse effect (12.5% versus 0%). In 788 adults, six months of nightly eszopiclone 3 mg produced significant, sustained improvements in sleep latency, wake time after sleep onset, awakenings, total sleep time and sleep quality, with better next-day function ratings and no evidence of tolerance. Both trials come from the manufacturer's programme, and both measured sleep parameters and ratings rather than downstream health outcomes. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit).
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: Insomnia in Alzheimer's dementia: suvorexant added about half an hour of sleep a night versus placebo over 4 weeks — one trial
question: In people with probable Alzheimer's dementia and insomnia, does suvorexant improve total sleep time compared with placebo?
balance: One phase 3 randomised trial answers this directly. In 285 people with mild-to-moderate probable Alzheimer's dementia and insomnia, four weeks of suvorexant (10 mg, increasable to 20 mg) improved polysomnographic total sleep time by 73 minutes from baseline versus 45 minutes on placebo — a treatment difference of 28 minutes (95% CI 11–45; p < 0.01). Somnolence was reported in 4.2% on suvorexant versus 1.4% on placebo. The trial measured sleep over four weeks only; it does not show longer-term safety in dementia, or effects on cognition, behaviour or falls. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a single well-conducted trial with a modest gain. Flagged Tier C as a single-trial benefit shelf.

title: Multiple sclerosis fatigue: amantadine, modafinil and methylphenidate all failed to beat placebo in one head-to-head crossover trial — and caused more side effects
question: In multiple sclerosis-related fatigue, do amantadine, modafinil or methylphenidate reduce fatigue compared with placebo?
balance: TRIUMPHANT-MS is the one properly powered test of the three drugs most prescribed for multiple sclerosis fatigue. In a four-period crossover trial, 141 patients each took amantadine, modafinil, methylphenidate and placebo in turn; fatigue scores (Modified Fatigue Impact Scale) improved by roughly 11–13 points on every arm including placebo, and no drug beat placebo (overall medication effect p = 0.20). Adverse events were commoner on each drug (39–40% of participants) than on placebo (31%), and the three serious adverse events occurred on active treatment. Older, smaller trials of amantadine and modafinil were mixed and underpowered; none outweighs this trial. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference).

title: Obstructive sleep apnoea with residual sleepiness: solriamfetol improved wakefulness dose-dependently — and blinded withdrawal lost the benefit within two weeks
question: In obstructive sleep apnoea with residual excessive daytime sleepiness, does solriamfetol improve wakefulness (maintenance of wakefulness test and Epworth score) compared with placebo?
balance: Two randomised trials from the TONES programme support solriamfetol for excessive sleepiness in obstructive sleep apnoea despite current or prior sleep-apnoea treatment. In TONES 3 (476 participants, 12 weeks), solriamfetol 37.5–300 mg met both coprimary endpoints — maintenance of wakefulness test latency and Epworth score — at every dose, with dose-dependent effects from week 1; adverse events were commoner than on placebo (67.9% vs 47.9%), headache (10.1%) and nausea (7.9%) the most frequent. In TONES 4, responders stabilised on solriamfetol were re-randomised: those switched to placebo worsened sharply over two weeks (wakefulness −12.1 minutes; Epworth +4.5 points) while those continuing held their gains — between-group differences of 11.2 minutes and −4.6 points. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) for wakefulness and sleepiness scores; the trials measured sleepiness, not accidents or cardiovascular outcomes.

title: Obstructive sleep apnoea with daytime sleepiness: pitolisant cut Epworth scores by about 2.6–2.8 points versus placebo — in patients refusing CPAP and in patients still sleepy on it
question: In obstructive sleep apnoea with excessive daytime sleepiness — in patients refusing CPAP or still sleepy on it — does pitolisant reduce sleepiness compared with placebo?
balance: The HAROSA programme ran the same 12-week design in the two populations that need an adjunct: patients refusing continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP), and patients adherent to CPAP with residual sleepiness. In CPAP-refusers (268 randomised), pitolisant titrated to 20 mg daily reduced Epworth Sleepiness Scale scores by 2.8 points more than placebo (95% CI −4.0 to −1.5; P < 0.001), though objective wake-maintenance testing did not improve; adverse events were similar to placebo (29.5% vs 25.4%). In CPAP-adherent patients (244 randomised), the advantage was 2.6 points (95% CI −3.9 to −1.4; P < .001), with responder rates 71.0% versus 54.1% and adverse events commoner on pitolisant (47.0% vs 32.8%). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): consistent across two trials, but the effect is a few points on a self-reported sleepiness scale, with objective wakefulness unproven in the trial that measured it head-on.

title: Parkinson's disease with poor early-morning control: overnight rotigotine patch improved early-morning motor scores and nocturnal sleep scores versus placebo (RECOVER) — one trial
question: In Parkinson's disease with unsatisfactory early-morning motor control, does overnight rotigotine patch improve early-morning function and sleep compared with placebo?
balance: RECOVER is the single randomised trial built for this question. In 287 patients with unsatisfactory early-morning motor control, rotigotine (2–16 mg/24 h transdermal patch) beat placebo on both coprimary endpoints at the end of maintenance: early-morning motor examination (UPDRS Part III) improved by 7.0 points versus 3.9 (treatment difference −3.55, 95% CI −5.37 to −1.73; P = 0.0002), and nocturnal sleep disturbance (PDSS-2) improved by 5.9 points versus 1.9 (difference −4.26, 95% CI −6.08 to −2.45; P < 0.0001). Nausea (21% vs 9%), application-site reactions (15% vs 4%) and dizziness (10% vs 6%) were the commonest costs. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): one trial, moderate gains on rating scales over roughly three months. Flagged Tier C as a single-trial benefit shelf.

title: Major depression: wake therapy plus bright light and sleep stabilisation (added to duloxetine) produced faster, higher remission than daily exercise — and the lead held at 29 weeks
question: In major depression, does a chronotherapeutic intervention — wake therapy combined with bright light and sleep-phase stabilisation — speed and sustain antidepressant response compared with an exercise control?
balance: One Danish trial programme: 75 patients, all started on duloxetine, randomised to a chronotherapeutic package (three wake-therapy nights in one week, then daily morning bright light and sleep-time stabilisation) versus daily exercise. The chronotherapy group responded within two weeks (response 41.4% vs 12.8%; odds ratio 4.8) and stayed ahead at week 9 (response 71.4% vs 47.3%, odds ratio 2.8; remission 45.6% vs 23.1%). In the 20-week follow-up report, remission at week 29 was 61.9% versus 37.9% (odds ratio 2.6; P = 0.01), with lower endpoint depression scores (7.5 vs 10.1). The caveats are structural: a single-centre programme, 75 patients, an active exercise comparator that itself helped, and assessor-blinded (not double-blind) delivery of a conspicuous intervention. title: Older adults with osteoarthritis pain and insomnia: CBT-I improved sleep in two trials — insomnia severity down 3.5 points versus control in the 327-patient COPE trial; pain relief was smaller and less durable
question: In older adults with osteoarthritis pain and insomnia, does cognitive-behavioural therapy for insomnia improve sleep — and does pain improve with it?
balance: Two randomised trials say CBT-I improves sleep in this population, with pain a secondary and less certain winner. The small first trial (51 patients; a secondary analysis) found self-reported sleep improved and pain reduced after CBT-I but not after an attention control, with gains maintained at one year — though its abstract reports directions rather than effect sizes. The definitive COPE trial (327 older adults with osteoarthritis pain; telephone CBT-I versus education-only control) cut Insomnia Severity Index scores by 3.5 points more than control at 2 months (95% CI −4.4 to −2.6; P < .001), sustained at 12 months (−3.0 points), with 56.3% versus 25.8% in insomnia remission at one year and significantly reduced fatigue; the pain advantage seen after treatment was not sustained at 12 months. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) for sleep, with the pain claim kept modest on the shelf's face.

title: Menopausal insomnia: telephone CBT-I beat menopause education — insomnia severity down 5.2 points more, with 70% versus 24% in the no-insomnia range at 8 weeks (MsFLASH) — one trial
question: In perimenopausal and postmenopausal women with vasomotor symptoms and insomnia, does telephone-delivered CBT-I improve insomnia severity compared with menopause education control?
balance: One well-run trial answers this. In the MsFLASH trial, 106 perimenopausal and postmenopausal women with moderate insomnia (Insomnia Severity Index ≥ 12) and at least two hot flashes daily received six telephone sessions of CBT-I or menopause education control over 8 weeks. Insomnia severity fell 9.9 points with CBT-I versus 4.7 with education (between-group difference 5.2 points; P < .001), sleep quality on the Pittsburgh index improved 2.7 points more, and at 8 weeks 70% of the CBT-I group versus 24% of controls scored in the no-insomnia range — differences sustained at 24 weeks. Hot-flash frequency did not differ between groups; hot-flash interference fell more with CBT-I. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a single trial, but randomised with blinded assessment and a durable effect. Flagged Tier C as a single-trial benefit shelf.

title: Delayed sleep-wake phase disorder: melatonin 0.5 mg an hour before the desired bedtime, plus scheduled sleep-wake times, advanced sleep onset by 34 minutes versus placebo — one trial
question: In delayed sleep-wake phase disorder, does low-dose melatonin timed before the desired bedtime, combined with behavioural sleep-wake scheduling, advance sleep and improve daytime function compared with placebo?
balance: One double-blind randomised trial — the first for this disorder on this record. In 116 clinically diagnosed patients whose endogenous melatonin rhythm was delayed relative to their desired bedtime, four weeks of fast-release melatonin 0.5 mg taken one hour before the desired bedtime, combined with behavioural sleep-wake scheduling (the placebo group received the scheduling too), brought actigraphic sleep onset 34 minutes earlier than placebo (95% CI −60 to −8). Sleep-related daytime impairment, sleep disturbance and insomnia severity also improved, and 52.8% versus 24.0% achieved more than minimal clinician-rated improvement; adverse events (light-headedness, daytime sleepiness, decreased libido) occurred at similar rates in both groups. Notably, melatonin onset time itself (DLMO) did not shift significantly in the subset tested — in this trial the benefit looks sleep-promoting rather than phase-shifting. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a single trial, 4 weeks. Flagged Tier C as a single-trial benefit shelf.

title: The enzyme humans don't make: alpha-galactosidase (Beano) for bean-and-vegetable gas
question: Does alpha-galactosidase (Beano), taken with a meal, prevent the gas produced by beans, lentils and cruciferous vegetables — and does it help people with IBS?
balance: Split: POSSIBLE — preventing meal-challenge gas · MAYBE (weak evidence) — routine use in IBS. Humans make no alpha-galactosidase, so the raffinose and stachyose in beans, lentils and cruciferous vegetables reach the colon intact and are fermented into gas. Supplying the enzyme by mouth works in challenge tests: it cut flatulence after a meatless-chili meal in a double-blind crossover trial (Ganiats 1994), reduced breath hydrogen and flatulence severity after a 420 g bean meal (Di Stefano 2007), reduced gas-related distress in children over 2 weeks (Di Nardo 2013), and relieved symptoms in the galacto-oligosaccharide-sensitive subgroup of IBS patients on a GOS challenge (Tuck 2018). Given as routine treatment to unselected IBS patients it did not beat placebo — a 12-week trial of 125 patients found no evidence for routine use and more withdrawals on the enzyme (Hillilä 2016), and a 20-patient crossover pilot found no difference in symptoms or breath gases (Böhn 2021). One caution with a diabetes edge: in patients taking acarbose, Beano reduced acarbose flatulence but partly blunted acarbose's glucose-lowering (Lettieri 1998). Shelf #1 (the Prevention hub) gains a pointer to this shelf at next deploy. Alpha-galactosidase to clear bowel gas before ultrasound is an imaging-preparation question (PMID 23730387), fenced, not carded. Drafted Nov 9, 2026 at the developer's request (practical over-the-counter questions series, with Shelf #2431).
stamp: SPLIT — POSSIBLE (meal-challenge gas) · MAYBE (weak evidence) (routine IBS use)

title: Does Gas-X work? Simethicone for gas and bloating
question: Does simethicone (Gas-X) relieve intestinal gas and bloating — and what did the placebo-controlled trials actually find?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence): Simethicone is a defoaming agent — it coalesces small gas bubbles into larger ones — that is not absorbed and does not reduce how much gas the gut produces. The clean placebo tests of simethicone alone are null: in a double-blind crossover challenge, 600 mg simethicone changed neither breath hydrogen nor symptom scores after a lactulose load (Friis 1991), and in the largest standalone test, a multicentre double-blind trial in infant colic, simethicone was no more effective than placebo, including in the subgroup whose parents reported gas-related symptoms (Metcalf 1994). In acute-diarrhoea trials, gas-related discomfort was relieved fastest by loperamide PLUS simethicone, beating either agent alone and placebo (Kaplan 1999; Hanauer 2007) — but neither abstract reports simethicone alone beating placebo on the gas endpoint. Simethicone's well-proven role is a different one — clearing bubbles so endoscopists and sonographers can see — fenced in the synthesis, not carded. For the enzyme that prevents bean-and-vegetable gas, see Shelf #2430 (draft). Drafted Nov 9, 2026 at the developer's request (practical over-the-counter questions series, with Shelf #2430).
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence)

title: Ginkgo biloba to prevent dementia: two large, long trials — GEM and GuidAge — both found no protection
question: In older adults with normal cognition, mild cognitive impairment, or memory complaints, does standardised ginkgo biloba extract (EGb 761, 240 mg/day) prevent dementia or Alzheimer's disease compared with placebo?
balance: Ginkgo biloba extract is one of the most widely bought supplements for memory, and it is one of the few ever tested at the scale the question deserves. Two large, long, double-blind trials asked whether 240 mg/day of the standardised extract EGb 761 prevents dementia. In the US GEM study (3,069 volunteers aged 75 and over, median 6.1 years), dementia developed at 3.3 per 100 person-years on ginkgo versus 2.9 on placebo (hazard ratio 1.12, 95% CI 0.94–1.33) — no protection in people with normal cognition and none in the subgroup with mild cognitive impairment. In the French GuidAge trial (2,854 adults aged 70 and over with memory complaints, 5 years), Alzheimer's disease was diagnosed in 61 people on ginkgo versus 73 on placebo (HR 0.84, 0.60–1.18; p=0.306). Neither trial showed an effect on stroke or other cardiovascular events, and adverse effects were similar. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): two adequately powered prevention trials, one answer — taking ginkgo to ward off dementia does not work.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference)

title: Nicotinamide to prevent skin cancer: fewer new cancers in high-risk immunocompetent adults (ONTRAC) — none in transplant recipients (ONTRANS)
question: In adults at high risk of keratinocyte cancer, does oral nicotinamide 500 mg twice daily for 12 months reduce new basal-cell and squamous-cell cancers — and does the answer change in organ-transplant recipients?
balance: Nicotinamide (the amide form of vitamin B3) repairs ultraviolet DNA damage in experimental work, and the ONTRAC trial tested whether that translates into fewer skin cancers. In 386 immunocompetent adults who had had at least two nonmelanoma skin cancers in the previous five years, 500 mg twice daily for 12 months lowered the rate of new nonmelanoma skin cancers by 23% relative to placebo (95% CI 4–38) and cut actinic keratoses by 11–20% at successive visits; the benefit vanished within months of stopping. The companion question — transplant recipients, whose skin-cancer risk is far higher — was answered by ONTRANS: 158 recipients, 207 new keratinocyte cancers on nicotinamide versus 210 on placebo (rate ratio 1.0, 0.8–1.3). Same drug, same dose, opposite answer by population. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), for immunocompetent high-risk adults only, and only while it is taken. Tier C: the benefit rests on a single positive trial.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Vitamin D to delay type 2 diabetes in prediabetes: D2d and the Tromsø trial both missed — supplementation does not hold back the diagnosis
question: In adults with prediabetes, does vitamin D3 supplementation delay progression to type 2 diabetes compared with placebo?
balance: Low blood vitamin D tracks with higher diabetes risk in observational studies, which made supplementation an attractive candidate for delaying diabetes. The two randomised tests agree that it does not delay onset in people who are not frankly deficient. In D2d (2,423 adults meeting at least two of three prediabetes criteria), vitamin D3 4,000 IU/day produced diabetes in 293 participants versus 323 on placebo over a median 2.5 years — 9.39 vs 10.66 events per 100 person-years, HR 0.88 (95% CI 0.75–1.04; p=0.12). In the Tromsø trial (511 people with prediabetes), five years of 20,000 IU/week gave progression in 103 versus 112 (HR 0.90, 0.69–1.18). Both point estimates lean the same way and neither is significant; a small effect is not excluded, but no trial shows supplementation delays the formal diagnosis. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference). This shelf is about vitamin D only; lifestyle and medicines to delay diagnosis live on Shelves #111 and #112.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference)

title: Coffee and the heart (CRAVE): no significant rise in atrial ectopy — more ventricular ectopy, about 1,000 extra steps, 36 minutes less sleep
question: In ambulatory adults, does drinking caffeinated coffee on randomly assigned days change atrial or ventricular ectopy, daily steps, sleep, or glucose compared with avoiding caffeine?
balance: Patients ask whether coffee is bad for palpitations, and CRAVE is the rare trial that randomised the beverage itself: 100 ambulatory adults wore a continuous ECG patch, an accelerometer and a glucose monitor for 14 days, receiving daily text instructions to drink caffeinated coffee or avoid caffeine. On coffee days, premature atrial contractions — the primary outcome — averaged 58 versus 53 per day (rate ratio 1.09, 95% CI 0.98–1.20; p=0.10): no significant difference, and no signal for sustained arrhythmia. Premature ventricular contractions were higher on coffee days (154 vs 102 per day; rate ratio 1.51, 1.18–1.94). Coffee days also brought about 1,058 more steps and 36 fewer minutes of sleep; glucose was unchanged. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — for the atrial-ectopy question patients actually ask about; the ventricular-ectopy increase is a count of extra beats, not a clinical-event finding, and rides in the balance rather than the stamp. THIN: one trial, surrogate counts.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference)

title: Alcohol abstinence in atrial fibrillation: recurrence 53% vs 73% over six months in the one randomised trial
question: In regular drinkers (10 or more standard drinks per week) with paroxysmal or persistent atrial fibrillation, does abstaining from alcohol reduce AF recurrence and AF burden compared with continuing usual drinking?
balance: Alcohol is the modifiable exposure patients with atrial fibrillation most often ask about, and one open-label randomised trial has tested abstinence itself. In 140 Australian patients drinking at least 10 standard drinks a week (abstinence group cut from 16.8 to 2.1 drinks/week; controls from 16.4 to 13.2), AF recurred over 6 months in 53% of the abstinence group versus 73% of controls — an absolute difference of 20 percentage points — with a hazard ratio of 0.55 (95% CI 0.36–0.84) for time to recurrence and a lower AF burden (0.5% vs 1.2% of time in AF). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit). Tier C: a single trial, open-label, in mostly male volunteers willing to attempt abstinence — the developer rules personally.

title: Chamomile extract for generalised anxiety: a modest benefit in the first controlled trial; continuation kept symptoms lower, relapse difference not significant
question: In adults with generalised anxiety disorder, does pharmaceutical-grade chamomile extract reduce anxiety symptoms compared with placebo — and does continuing it keep responders well?
balance: Chamomile tea is a folk anxiolytic; the extract has been through two randomised tests from one research group. In the first controlled trial (57 outpatients with mild-to-moderate generalised anxiety disorder, 8 weeks), chamomile extract produced a significantly greater reduction in Hamilton Anxiety scores than placebo (p=0.047), with tolerability no worse than placebo. In the continuation study, responders with moderate-to-severe GAD who kept taking chamomile for 26 weeks relapsed less often than those switched to placebo (15.2% vs 25.5%; HR 0.52, 95% CI 0.20–1.33 — not significant), while maintaining significantly lower symptom scores. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a real but modest effect in small single-centre trials, awaiting independent replication.

title: Lavender oil (Silexan) for anxiety: beat placebo in a 539-patient GAD trial, in the same range as paroxetine in that trial
question: In adults with anxiety disorders, does the oral lavender-oil preparation Silexan reduce anxiety compared with placebo — and how does it compare with standard anxiolytics?
balance: Silexan is a standardised oral lavender-oil preparation (named here because lavender products are not interchangeable, and only this preparation has this trial record). Its largest trial randomised 539 adults with generalised anxiety disorder to Silexan 160 mg, Silexan 80 mg, paroxetine 20 mg, or placebo for 10 weeks: Hamilton Anxiety scores fell 14.1 and 12.8 points on Silexan versus 9.5 on placebo (both doses p<0.01), while paroxetine's 11.3-point fall was only a trend in the full analysis set (p=0.10). Response rates were 60.3% and 51.9% on Silexan versus 37.8% on placebo, and adverse-event rates were comparable to placebo. The earlier programme — subsyndromal anxiety versus placebo, GAD versus lorazepam (comparable score reductions), restlessness versus placebo — is summarised in the 2010 review carded beside it, labelled as the review it is. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).

title: Black cohosh for hot flushes: the large year-long HALT trial found less than one symptom a day versus placebo — the positive trial's own effect size was tiny
question: In menopausal women, does black cohosh extract relieve climacteric symptoms and vasomotor symptoms compared with placebo?
balance: Black cohosh is among the most bought menopause supplements, and its two best trials bracket the answer. The larger and longer one, HALT (351 women aged 45–55 with at least two vasomotor symptoms a day, followed for a year), found that black cohosh alone or inside a multibotanical differed from placebo by less than one vasomotor symptom per day at 3, 6 and 12 months — while hormone therapy in the same trial differed by −4.06 symptoms per day. The smaller positive trial (Osmers; 304 patients, 12 weeks, an isopropanolic extract) reached statistical significance on the Menopause Rating Scale, but its own reported effect size was 0.03–0.05 scale units, and the benefit concentrated in women early in the climacteric. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): read together, if black cohosh does anything for hot flushes it is below what these trials could call important.

title: Ashwagandha for stress and anxiety: two small, short trials of two different extracts, both positive — weak evidence
question: In adults under stress, do standardised ashwagandha root extracts reduce stress and anxiety scores compared with placebo?
balance: Ashwagandha is marketed as an adaptogen for stress, and the randomised record is two small, short, single-centre trials — each of a different proprietary extract. Chandrasekhar (64 adults with chronic stress, 60 days) gave a high-concentration full-spectrum root extract 300 mg twice daily and reported significant reductions on all stress-assessment scales and in serum cortisol versus placebo. Lopresti (60 stressed adults, 60 days) gave a different extract (Shoden, 240 mg/day) and found a significant Hamilton Anxiety reduction (p=0.040), a near-significant DASS-21 result (p=0.096), and greater falls in morning cortisol. Effects of this size from trials of this size are exactly what MAYBE (weak evidence) is for — and 'ashwagandha' on a shop shelf is not one standardised thing, so the tested extracts are named. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).

title: Saffron for depression: matched fluoxetine in one small pilot and beat placebo in diabetic patients' comorbid symptoms — small, short trials only
question: In adults with mild-to-moderate major depression, does saffron (Crocus sativus) extract improve depressive symptoms compared with placebo or a standard antidepressant?
balance: Saffron has a traditional reputation in Persian medicine as a mood treatment, and its modern trial record is small, short and single-country. Noorbala randomised 40 outpatients with mild-to-moderate depression to saffron 30 mg/day or fluoxetine 20 mg/day for 6 weeks and found the two statistically indistinguishable (p=0.71 for the group comparison) — but with no placebo arm, 'as good as fluoxetine in a pilot' cannot show either drug worked. Milajerdi's placebo-controlled trial (54 patients with type 2 diabetes and comorbid mild-to-moderate depression–anxiety) found saffron significantly relieved the combined symptom measure, anxiety and sleep disturbance, though not depression alone. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): the signal is consistent, the trials are tiny, and nothing here supports saffron as a substitute for standard care.

title: Migraine prevention from the supplement shelf: riboflavin, magnesium and butterbur each beat placebo in one small trial — butterbur carries a liver warning
question: In people with migraine, do the supplement preventives patients buy for themselves — high-dose riboflavin, oral magnesium, or butterbur root extract — reduce attack frequency compared with placebo?
balance: Before (and alongside) prescription preventives, three supplements have each passed one proper placebo-controlled test for migraine prevention. Riboflavin 400 mg/day (55 patients): 59% achieved at least a halving of attacks versus 15% on placebo (p=0.002). Magnesium 600 mg/day (81 patients): attack frequency fell 41.6% versus 15.8% in weeks 9–12 (p<0.05), at the cost of diarrhoea in about one in five. Butterbur root extract 75 mg twice daily (245 patients): attack frequency fell 48% versus 26% on placebo over 4 months, with 68% versus 49% reaching a ≥50% reduction. Each result rests on a single small trial from the 1990s–2000s with no modern replication — and butterbur is the special case: the trials used a specific pyrrolizidine-alkaloid-free extract, because raw butterbur contains liver-toxic alkaloids; unprocessed products are not what was tested and are not safe to substitute. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), with the butterbur caution on the shelf's face.

title: UC-II collagen for knee osteoarthritis: one 191-patient trial beat placebo and glucosamine–chondroitin on WOMAC — a single manufacturer's programme
question: In adults with knee osteoarthritis, does undenatured type II collagen (UC-II, 40 mg/day) improve pain and function compared with placebo or with glucosamine plus chondroitin?
balance: Collagen powders and capsules are sold for joint pain in many forms; the one with a real osteoarthritis trial behind it is UC-II, a specific undenatured type II collagen preparation (named because the evidence belongs to this preparation, not to collagen in general). In its 191-patient, 180-day trial, UC-II improved total WOMAC scores significantly more than placebo (p=0.002) and more than glucosamine hydrochloride plus chondroitin sulfate (p=0.04), with pain, stiffness and function subscales all concordant and no safety separation. The programme's earlier trial was in 55 healthy volunteers with exercise-induced knee discomfort — knee extension and time to pain on exertion improved — which supports plausibility but is not osteoarthritis evidence. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): one adequate trial, from a manufacturer-linked programme, awaiting independent replication.

title: Lactase enzyme drops for lactose intolerance: one small 1992 crossover — less breath hydrogen, fewer symptoms
question: In adults with lactose malabsorption and intolerance, does adding lactase (beta-galactosidase) enzyme to milk reduce malabsorption and symptoms compared with placebo-treated milk?
balance: Lactase tablets and drops are a staple over-the-counter purchase for people who cannot digest milk sugar, and the randomised evidence behind them is remarkably thin: one small double-blind crossover from 1992. In 16 adults with lactose malabsorption and intolerance, milk pre-treated with beta-galactosidase from Aspergillus niger produced significantly lower breath-hydrogen measures (peak p<0.01; cumulative excretion p<0.005) and a significantly lower cumulative gastrointestinal intolerance index (p<0.005) than placebo-treated milk, using a 400 mL milk challenge. The direction is exactly what the enzyme's mechanism predicts, and the outcome combines a malabsorption marker with symptoms — but one 16-person crossover is the whole pinned record. title: Milk thistle (silymarin): the modern JAMA trial was null on every measure — against a 1989 trial claiming a survival benefit in cirrhosis
question: In chronic liver disease, does silymarin (milk-thistle extract) improve liver biochemistry, viral measures, or survival compared with placebo?
balance: Milk thistle is the liver supplement patients reach for most, and its record contains the starkest disagreement in this slate. The rigorous modern trial (SyNCH; 154 patients with chronic hepatitis C who had failed interferon therapy) tested silymarin at two and three times customary doses for 24 weeks: the primary ALT outcome was met by about 4% of patients in every arm including placebo, and ALT decline, HCV RNA and quality of life did not differ. Against that stands a 1989 trial in 170 patients with cirrhosis reporting 4-year survival of 58% on silymarin versus 39% on placebo (p=0.036), driven by alcoholic cirrhosis and Child A subgroups — a mortality claim this shelf prints plainly rather than burying. Tier C, because a survival claim sits in the balance. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): the large blinded trial's null across every measured outcome outweighs a smaller older trial's subgroup-driven survival signal, but the disagreement belongs to the developer's judgement, not the shelf's silence.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference)

title: Oral mucolytics in COPD: twice-daily N-acetylcysteine and carbocisteine cut exacerbations by about a quarter in Chinese trials — the older 600 mg once-daily European trial found nothing
question: In people with COPD, do oral mucolytic antioxidants — N-acetylcysteine or carbocisteine — reduce exacerbations compared with placebo?
balance: Mucolytic antioxidants are cheap, oral and widely used in COPD outside the English-speaking world, and the trial record splits by dose and place. PANTHEON (1,006 Chinese patients with moderate-to-severe COPD) found N-acetylcysteine 600 mg twice daily cut exacerbations from 1.49 to 1.16 per patient-year (risk ratio 0.78, 95% CI 0.67–0.90). PEACE (709 Chinese patients) found carbocisteine 1,500 mg/day cut exacerbations from 1.35 to 1.01 per year (risk ratio 0.75, 0.62–0.92). The older European BRONCUS trial (523 patients, three years) used half the NAC dose — 600 mg once daily — and found nothing: 1.25 vs 1.29 exacerbations per year (HR 0.99) and no effect on lung-function decline. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a real, modest effect at the higher dose in the populations studied, with the dose caveat on the shelf's face.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Blood thinners after TAVI when anticoagulation is needed: edoxaban matched warfarin on the composite but bled more; adding clopidogrel only added bleeding
question: In patients with atrial fibrillation who need oral anticoagulation after successful TAVI, does edoxaban match a vitamin K antagonist — and does adding clopidogrel to anticoagulation help or harm?
balance: This shelf covers patients who already have an indication for anticoagulation after TAVI — a different question from Shelf #717 (routine anticoagulation in patients without an indication, where anticoagulation harmed). Two trials draw the map. ENVISAGE-TAVI AF (1,426 patients, mean age 82) found edoxaban noninferior to a vitamin K antagonist on the composite of death, myocardial infarction, ischaemic stroke, systemic embolism, valve thrombosis or major bleeding (17.3 vs 16.5 per 100 person-years; HR 1.05) — but major bleeding was significantly higher on edoxaban (9.7 vs 7.0 per 100 person-years; HR 1.40, 95% CI 1.03–1.91), driven by gastrointestinal bleeding. POPular TAVI cohort B (313 patients) tested the add-on question: three months of clopidogrel on top of anticoagulation raised all bleeding from 21.7% to 34.6% over a year, while the ischaemic composite was noninferior without it. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm) — the harms are the actionable findings: extra antiplatelet therapy adds bleeding without shown benefit, and edoxaban's convenience costs gastrointestinal bleeds. Tier C: harm shelf.
stamp: POSSIBLE (harm)

title: Semaglutide for knee osteoarthritis (STEP 9): weight −13.7% vs −3.2% and WOMAC pain −41.7 vs −27.5 points at 68 weeks
question: In people with obesity and moderate knee osteoarthritis with at least moderate pain, does once-weekly semaglutide 2.4 mg reduce knee pain and body weight compared with placebo, on top of lifestyle counselling?
balance: Weight loss relieves knee osteoarthritis pain, and STEP 9 is the first large trial of a GLP-1 drug aimed at the knee itself. In 407 people with obesity (mean BMI 40.3) and moderate knee osteoarthritis with at least moderate pain, once-weekly semaglutide 2.4 mg for 68 weeks — with physical-activity and reduced-calorie counselling in both arms — produced weight loss of −13.7% versus −3.2% on placebo, and a WOMAC pain improvement of −41.7 versus −27.5 points (both p<0.001), with physical function also better (+12.0 vs +6.5 SF-36 points). Serious adverse events were similar; discontinuations for adverse events were 6.7% vs 3.0%, mostly gastrointestinal. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit). Tier C: a single trial carries the claim, and how much of the pain effect is weight loss itself — versus any joint-specific action — the trial cannot separate.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Metformin added to insulin in type 1 diabetes: no sustained HbA1c benefit and no slowing of carotid thickening (REMOVAL) — weight and insulin dose moved, stomachs objected
question: In people with type 1 diabetes, does adding metformin to insulin improve glycaemic control, weight, or atherosclerosis progression compared with placebo?
balance: Metformin is often added to insulin in type 1 diabetes to fight weight gain and insulin resistance, and two randomised trials bound what it actually does. REMOVAL (428 adults aged 40+ with type 1 diabetes and cardiovascular risk factors, 3 years) found no significant slowing of carotid intima-media thickness progression, its primary outcome (−0.005 mm/year; p=0.1664); HbA1c fell by an average 0.13%, an effect carried by the first 3 months and not sustained, while weight (−1.17 kg) and LDL cholesterol (−0.13 mmol/L (≈-5 mg/dL)) did improve and 27% stopped metformin versus 12% on placebo, mainly for gastrointestinal effects. In adolescents (140 overweight teenagers), an early HbA1c advantage at 13 weeks (−0.3%) had vanished by 26 weeks (0.0%), though insulin dose and adiposity measures favoured metformin and gastrointestinal events were far commoner. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — for glycaemic control and atherosclerosis; the modest weight effect is real and is recorded as such, not upgraded into the stamp.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference)

title: Fampridine for walking in MS: a consistent responder subgroup — about 35–43% walk meaningfully faster, versus 8–9% on placebo
question: In people with multiple sclerosis and walking impairment, does fampridine (dalfampridine, 4-aminopyridine) 10 mg twice daily improve walking speed compared with placebo?
balance: Fampridine is the one symptomatic MS drug aimed squarely at walking, and its two phase 3 trials tell an unusually consistent story — with a catch built into the design. Both trials defined response as consistent improvement on the timed 25-foot walk across visits. In MS-F203 (301 patients, 14 weeks), 35% on fampridine were responders versus 8% on placebo (p<0.0001); in MS-F204 (239 patients, 9 weeks), 42.9% versus 9.3% (p<0.0001). Responders walked about 25% faster, an effect maintained between doses, and reported less ambulatory disability on the MS Walking Scale. The catch: the majority do not respond, and the drug does nothing measurable for them — this is a try-it-and-stop-if-no-response medicine, and both trials were short. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): two concordant large trials with a validated, clinically meaningful responder definition — strong evidence, short of a Level A stamp on this library's scale.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: High-dose biotin in progressive MS: the small first trial was positive, the 642-patient replication was null — 'cannot be recommended'
question: In people with progressive multiple sclerosis, does high-dose biotin (MD1003, 100 mg three times daily) reverse or slow disability compared with placebo?
balance: High-dose pharmaceutical biotin (MD1003) was proposed to support neuronal and oligodendrocyte energetics in progressive MS, a field with almost no options — which is why its rise and fall is worth a shelf. The first randomised trial (MS-SPI; 154 patients) reported disability reversal in 12.6% on biotin versus 0% on placebo (p=0.005) over 12 months. The replication, SPI2 (642 patients across 13 countries, designed to confirm), found improvement in 12% versus 9% (odds ratio 1.35, 95% CI 0.81–2.26 — not significant), and its authors concluded MD1003 'cannot be recommended' — adding a practical harm that has nothing to do with MS: high-dose biotin distorts laboratory tests that use biotinylated antibodies (the subject of Shelf #58, cross-pointed, not duplicated here). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): the large, well-run replication outweighs the small positive first trial.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference)

title: Souvenaid (Fortasyn Connect) in prodromal Alzheimer's: the 24-month primary outcome was null; a 36-month analysis on a much-reduced set turned positive
question: In people with prodromal Alzheimer's disease, does a daily multinutrient drink (Fortasyn Connect, marketed as Souvenaid) slow cognitive decline compared with a control drink?
balance: Souvenaid is a medical-food drink (the Fortasyn Connect multinutrient combination: omega-3s, uridine, choline, phospholipids, B vitamins and antioxidants — named because only this formulation has been trialled) sold for early Alzheimer's disease. The LipiDiDiet trial randomised 311 people with prodromal Alzheimer's to the active drink or an isocaloric control for 24 months: the primary neuropsychological composite did not differ (treatment difference 0.098, 95% CI −0.041 to 0.237; p=0.166), partly because the control group declined far less than expected. A 36-month continuation analysis reported significant slowing on the 5-item composite, dementia-rating and memory measures — but on a much-reduced dataset (162 of 311 completed; 81 had data eligible for the efficacy analysis after censoring at open-label product or Alzheimer's medication). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): a null primary endpoint followed by a positive long-term analysis in a minority of the original cohort is a hypothesis, not a demonstration.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence)

title: Aripiprazole added to an antidepressant in treatment-resistant depression: remission roughly doubled in midlife adults, and rose from 29% to 44% over age 60 — at the price of akathisia
question: In adults — including older adults — with major depression that has not responded adequately to an antidepressant, does adding aripiprazole improve remission compared with adding placebo?
balance: When a first antidepressant fails, adding low-dose aripiprazole is one of the best-tested augmentation strategies. In the confirmatory midlife trial (349 patients who had prospectively failed an 8-week antidepressant course), adding aripiprazole (2–20 mg/day) cut MADRS scores by −10.1 versus −6.4 on added placebo and doubled remission (36.8% vs 18.9%; p<0.001) over 6 weeks. The older-adult trial matters most for this library's readers: in 181 patients over 60 who had not remitted on venlafaxine, adding aripiprazole produced remission in 44% versus 29% (OR 2.0, 95% CI 1.1–3.7; NNT 6.6) over 12 weeks — but akathisia affected 26% (vs 12%) and drug-induced parkinsonism 17% (vs 2%). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): real, replicated remission gains, with a movement-side-effect price that is highest in exactly the older patients the second trial studied.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)
