title: Agomelatine for major depression: the 50 mg dose beat placebo acutely (the 25 mg dose did not), and continuing it halved relapse — with liver-enzyme elevations to watch
question: In adults with major depressive disorder, does agomelatine treat acute depression and prevent relapse after response compared with placebo?
balance: Agomelatine — a melatonin-receptor agonist and 5-HT2C antagonist, marketed in Europe and elsewhere but not approved in the United States — has a two-part placebo-controlled record. Acutely, in 511 patients with moderate-to-severe depression, the 50 mg dose improved Hamilton scores significantly more than placebo at 8 weeks (treatment difference 2.5 points; p=0.004) while the 25 mg dose did not (p=0.505); sleep measures improved on 50 mg, and clinically notable transient transaminase elevations occurred in 4.5% of the 50 mg group. For continuation, patients who had responded to agomelatine were randomised to continue or switch to placebo: relapse over 6 months was 21.7% versus 46.6% (p=0.0001), with no discontinuation-syndrome pattern after abrupt switching. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a real but dose-specific acute effect and a strong relapse-prevention result, bounded by the failed 25 mg dose and the liver monitoring the drug requires.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Omega-3 as a treatment for major depression: two small 8-week trials — an add-on benefit in 28 patients, EPA matching fluoxetine in 60 — not the prevention question
question: In adults with major depressive disorder, do omega-3 fatty acids (EPA/DHA) improve depressive symptoms as a treatment — added to usual care or compared with an antidepressant?
balance: Fish oil for depression is asked about constantly, and this shelf answers the treatment question only — omega-3 for preventing depression is a separate shelf (#2024) and is not duplicated here. The treatment record pinned is two small, short trials. Su (28 patients with major depression) added omega-3 (6.6 g/day) to usual treatment for 8 weeks and found a significantly greater fall in Hamilton scores than added placebo (p<0.001). Jazayeri (60 outpatients) compared EPA 1,000 mg/day, fluoxetine 20 mg/day, and the combination for 8 weeks: response rates were 56%, 50% and 81% respectively, with EPA statistically comparable to fluoxetine and the combination superior to either alone from week 4. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): the direction is consistent, but 88 patients across two 8-week trials — one without a placebo-only arm — cannot carry more than that.

title: Gut-directed hypnotherapy for IBS in adults: benefits in ordinary clinics as well as in the founding unit, sustained to one year
question: In adults with irritable bowel syndrome that has not responded to standard management, does gut-directed hypnotherapy improve bowel symptoms compared with supportive therapy, waiting list, or psychotherapy?
balance: Gut-directed hypnotherapy is the best-known psychological treatment for IBS, and unusually for this slate it has both a founding trial and a pragmatic replication. Whorwell's 1984 Lancet trial randomised 30 patients with severe refractory IBS to hypnotherapy or psychotherapy-plus-placebo: the hypnotherapy group improved dramatically on all features — pain, distension, bowel habit and well-being — with no relapses over 3 months. Lindfors moved the question out of the specialist unit: 138 patients with refractory IBS were randomised in two studies (hypnotherapy in private psychology practices versus supportive therapy; hypnotherapy in a small county hospital versus waiting list). Symptoms improved significantly at 3 months in the hypnotherapy groups in both settings, significantly more than controls in the first study with a trend in the second (p=0.17), and the gains held at 1 year — though the authors note effectiveness is lower outside highly specialised centres. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), flagged THIN on trial count: two randomised studies, concordant, in exactly the refractory population that asks about it. (Paediatric hypnotherapy is Shelf #1142's question and is not duplicated.)
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Antispasmodics for IBS: pinaverium beat placebo clearly in a 427-patient trial; otilonium showed a dose-dependent effect in a small dose-ranging study
question: In adults with irritable bowel syndrome, do antispasmodic drugs — pinaverium bromide or otilonium bromide — relieve abdominal pain and global symptoms compared with placebo?
balance: Antispasmodics are first-line IBS prescriptions in much of the world yet are often dismissed as untested; two placebo-controlled trials of the two most studied agents say otherwise, at different strengths. Pinaverium bromide 50 mg three times daily, in 427 Rome III IBS patients across four Chinese hospitals, met its primary endpoints (pain reduction and stool-score improvement) in significantly more patients than placebo — 77.5% met a primary endpoint by week 4 (p<0.001) — and 60% versus 34% rated their symptoms globally improved, with mild side effects (nausea 3.7%, dizziness 3.2%). Otilonium bromide's evidence is a 93-patient dose-ranging study: individual symptoms mostly did not separate from placebo, but evacuation frequency fell significantly at 80 mg (−41.9% vs −8.36%; p<0.01) and a global discomfort index improved dose-dependently, significantly at 40 mg (p=0.013) and 80 mg (p=0.001). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): one solid trial for pinaverium, a supportive small one for otilonium.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Iron for tired, non-anaemic women with low ferritin: fatigue fell about 19 percentage points more than placebo — benefit confined to ferritin at or below 50 µg/L
question: In non-anaemic women with unexplained fatigue and low ferritin, does oral iron reduce fatigue compared with placebo?
balance: Tiredness with a normal blood count and a lowish ferritin is one of the commonest presentations in primary care, and iron is often given on instinct; two randomised trials from French and Swiss primary care test the instinct directly. Vaucher (198 non-anaemic women, ferritin <50 µg/L, haemoglobin >12.0 g/dL) found 12 weeks of oral ferrous sulfate (80 mg elemental iron daily) reduced fatigue scores by 47.7% versus 28.8% on placebo (difference −18.9 percentage points, 95% CI −34.5 to −3.2; p=0.02) — with no significant effect on quality of life, depression or anxiety. Verdon (144 women, 4 weeks, same dose) found fatigue fell 29% versus 13% on placebo (p=0.004), and the subgroup analysis in both eras agrees on the boundary: benefit appears confined to women with ferritin ≤50 µg/L. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a symptomatic benefit in a defined biochemical niche — not a licence to treat tiredness with iron when ferritin is normal.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Domperidone to boost milk supply after preterm birth: about 40 mL/day more in the one small placebo trial; most EMPOWER completers gained at least 50%
question: In mothers of preterm infants whose milk supply is low, does domperidone increase expressed breast-milk volume compared with placebo?
balance: When mothers of very preterm infants cannot produce enough milk, domperidone is the galactagogue most often reached for, and its randomised record is one small placebo trial plus a large trial known through a secondary analysis. Da Silva randomised 20 mothers of premature newborns to domperidone or placebo for 7 days: milk production rose by 49.5 mL/day versus 8.0 mL/day on placebo (p<0.05) in the 16 analysed, with prolactin rising on domperidone and only trace drug levels in milk. The EMPOWER trial's per-protocol analysis — carded as exactly that, a secondary analysis, not the trial's primary report — found that among 83 mothers of infants ≤29 weeks who completed a 14-day course (10 mg three times daily), the proportion achieving a ≥50% rise in milk volume was high whether treatment started early (77.8%) or after a placebo fortnight (65.8%), with timing itself not significant (OR 1.96, 95% CI 0.72–5.32; p=0.19). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), flagged THIN: the direction is consistent and the mechanism (prolactin) is demonstrated, but the placebo-controlled base is 16 analysed mothers, and domperidone carries cardiac cautions that sit outside these small short trials.

title: Berberine after polypectomy: adenomas recurred in 36% on berberine vs 47% on placebo over up to 2 years — one large trial, no cancers in either arm
question: In adults who have had colorectal adenomas completely removed, does berberine (0.3 g twice daily) prevent adenoma recurrence at follow-up colonoscopy compared with placebo?
balance: Berberine, a plant alkaloid long used in Chinese medicine and now sold widely as a supplement, has one genuinely large chemoprevention trial. In seven Chinese centres, 1,108 adults aged 18–75 who had one to six histologically confirmed adenomas completely removed within the previous 6 months were randomised to berberine 0.3 g twice daily or placebo, with colonoscopy at 1 year and again at 2 years if clear. In the full analysis set (891 participants), adenomas recurred in 155 of 429 (36%) on berberine versus 216 of 462 (47%) on placebo — an unadjusted relative risk of 0.77 (95% CI 0.66–0.91; p=0.001): a 23% relative reduction, 11 percentage points absolute. No colorectal cancers were detected in either arm, and the commonest adverse event was constipation (1% vs <0.5%), with no serious adverse events reported. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit). Tier C: a single trial carries a cancer-prevention-adjacent claim — and the claim is adenoma recurrence only, since no cancers occurred to be prevented. (Berberine for blood glucose and lipids is Shelf #548's question and is not duplicated.)

title: Sudafed PE doesn't work: oral phenylephrine was no better than placebo
question: In adults with nasal congestion (allergic rhinitis or the common cold), does oral phenylephrine at the sold 10 mg dose — the decongestant in 'PE' cold remedies — relieve congestion compared with placebo?
balance: No — at the 10 mg dose sold in 'PE' cold remedies, oral phenylephrine has not beaten placebo in any modern, adequately powered test. In the FDA-requested dose-ranging trial, 539 adults with seasonal allergic rhinitis took 10, 20, 30 or 40 mg or placebo for 7 days, and no dose separated from placebo on reflective or instantaneous congestion scores (Meltzer 2015). In the Vienna Challenge Chamber, a single 12 mg dose was indistinguishable from placebo (P=.56) while pseudoephedrine 60 mg beat both (Horak 2009). The only positive signal is old and small: a meta-analysis of 8 single-dose cold trials totalling 163 subjects found an objective nasal-airway-resistance advantage of 6.0 to 16.6 percentage points over placebo between 30 and 90 minutes — below the 20% the field calls clinically meaningful (Kollar 2007). As context, in 2023 an FDA advisory committee unanimously judged oral phenylephrine ineffective as a nasal decongestant. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): the large modern trials are null at and above the sold dose, and the one positive meta-analysis is tiny, old and below its own meaningfulness threshold.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference)

title: Colace doesn't soften much: docusate never beat placebo and lost to psyllium
question: In people with constipation, does docusate sodium — the 'stool softener' in Colace — soften stools or increase bowel movements compared with placebo or standard laxatives?
balance: Docusate sodium — the 'stool softener' sold as Colace — has never beaten placebo, because the only placebo-controlled test is an add-on trial and it was null: in 74 hospice patients, docusate plus sennosides produced no difference from placebo plus sennosides in stool frequency, volume, consistency, difficulty or completeness of evacuation over 10 days (Tarumi 2013). There is no clean trial of docusate alone versus placebo. Head-to-head, it lost to a fibre laxative on its own home ground: in 170 people with chronic constipation, stool water content rose 2.33% on psyllium versus 0.01% on docusate (P=.007), and bowel movements in week 2 were 3.5 versus 2.9 per week (P=.02) (McRorie 1998). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): the one placebo-controlled test is null and the one head-to-head is a clear loss, though a solo placebo trial was never run.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference)

title: Does Mucinex thin mucus? Guaifenesin's own trials mostly say no
question: In adolescents and adults with an acute respiratory infection and productive cough, does guaifenesin — the expectorant in Mucinex and Robitussin — thin mucus or relieve chest congestion compared with placebo?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence): Guaifenesin — the expectorant in Mucinex and Robitussin — is supposed to thin mucus, and on the direct tests of that claim it does not: in the main trial (NCT01046136; 378 randomised, 295 completed), extended-release guaifenesin for 7 days changed neither sputum volume (P=.41) nor any sputum property (percent solids, tension, elasticity, viscosity, impedance; P=.45–.88) (Hoffer-Schaefer 2014), and a single 1,200 mg dose of Mucinex changed neither mucociliary nor cough clearance nor sputum properties in 38 adults (Bennett 2015). The one favourable signal comes from the same main trial's patient-reported report: the SUM8 diary score separated most at day 4 in favour of guaifenesin — in a pilot study whose stated purpose was validating that diary instrument (Albrecht 2012). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): the objective expectorant claim fails its own trials, and the residual symptom signal is a single unvalidated-at-the-time diary score from a single trial counted once.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence)

title: Cold-sore creams work a little: about half a day to a day faster healing
question: In immunocompetent people with recurrent cold sores (herpes labialis), do antiviral creams — docosanol (Abreva), penciclovir, acyclovir, and acyclovir plus hydrocortisone — shorten healing or prevent the blister compared with vehicle or placebo?
balance: Yes, a little — consistently, across four product programmes, by about half a day to a day. Docosanol 10% cream healed cold sores a median of 18 hours sooner than placebo (4.1 days; P=.008) in 737 treated patients (Sacks 2001). Penciclovir 1% cream lost classical lesions 31% faster in relative terms (hazard ratio 1.31) with pain resolution at a relative hazard ratio of 1.28, in 3,057 treated patients (Raborn 2002). Acyclovir 5% cream shortened episodes from 4.8 to 4.3 days and from 5.2 to 4.6 days in its two trials, but did not prevent classical lesions forming (Spruance 2002). The combination ME-609 (acyclovir 5% plus hydrocortisone 1%) did prevent the ulcerative lesion in 42% of episodes versus 35% on acyclovir alone and 26% on placebo, in 1,443 treated patients (Hull 2011). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): multiple large double-blind trials agree the creams work, but the absolute gain is roughly half a day to a day of a self-limiting episode, earned only with treatment started at the first sign.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Pelargonium extract (EPs 7630) eased bronchitis in its maker's trials
question: In adults with acute bronchitis, does the Pelargonium sidoides root extract EPs 7630 shorten or soften the illness compared with placebo?
balance: In its own trials, yes: the Pelargonium sidoides root extract EPs 7630 beat placebo on bronchitis symptom scores in three randomised, double-blind trials totalling 998 adults. The Bronchitis Severity Score fell by 5.9 versus 3.2 points over 7 days in 468 patients, with 16% versus 43% still unable to work at day 7 (Matthys 2003); by 7.2 versus 4.9 points in 124 patients (Chuchalin 2005); and in dose-finding, by 4.3, 6.1 and 6.3 points at 30, 60 and 90 mg/day versus 2.7 on placebo in 406 patients — a dose-response (Matthys 2010). The tested product is named for clarification: EPs 7630, a registered trademark of Dr. Willmar Schwabe GmbH & Co. KG, Karlsruhe, Germany. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the results are consistent and dose-responsive, but every trial is the single manufacturer's programme, the endpoint is a symptom score in a self-limiting illness, and there is no independent replication.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Elderberry for flu: early small trials said yes, the best trial said no
question: In people with influenza or the common cold, does black elderberry extract shorten the illness or soften symptoms compared with placebo?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence): Two early trials pointed to benefit — symptoms relieved on average 4 days earlier in a 60-patient influenza trial (Zakay-Rones 2004), and fewer cold-episode days (57 versus 117, p = 0.02) in 312 air travellers (Tiralongo 2016), though cold episodes themselves were not significantly fewer there (12 versus 17, p = 0.4). The most rigorous test went the other way: in 87 emergency-department patients with PCR-confirmed influenza, elderberry was no better than placebo on the primary outcome (5.3 versus 4.9 days, p = 0.57), in a trial reported as powered over 0.90 to detect a 2-day benefit (Macknin 2020). Small early positive trials plus one well-powered null do not add up to proof. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): the early small trials said yes, but the best trial said no, so any benefit remains unproven.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence)

title: Cinnamon for blood sugar: small trials, mixed answers, one flagged paper
question: In people with type 2 diabetes, does cinnamon (powder or extract) lower fasting glucose or HbA1c compared with placebo?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence): Four small placebo-controlled trials give mixed answers. Khan 2003 reported large falls — fasting glucose −18–29%, triglycerides −23–30%, LDL cholesterol −7–27% and total cholesterol −12–26% after 1, 3 or 6 g per day for 40 days, with no changes on placebo — but in 2025 the American Diabetes Association issued an Expression of Concern about that paper, so its numbers cannot be taken at face value. Mang 2006 found fasting glucose fell more on an aqueous extract (−10.3% versus −3.4%, P = .046) with no significant HbA1c or lipid effect. Akilen 2010 found a small HbA1c fall (8.22% to 7.86% on cinnamon versus 8.55% to 8.68% on placebo, p < .005). Lu 2012 reported significant HbA1c and fasting-glucose reductions in both extract arms but published no effect sizes in its abstract. The preparations — powder and different extracts, at doses from 120 mg to 6 g per day — are not interchangeable, and none of the trials names a retail brand. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): small, inconsistent trials of differing preparations, with the largest reported effects in a paper now under an Expression of Concern.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence)

title: The MIND diet didn't beat a control diet in its one randomised trial
question: In cognitively unimpaired older adults with a family history of dementia, does the MIND diet slow cognitive decline compared with a control diet when both groups receive the same mild caloric restriction?
balance: Among 604 cognitively unimpaired older adults with a family history of dementia, a body-mass index over 25 and a suboptimal diet, three years on the MIND diet did not slow cognitive decline any more than a control diet when both groups received the same mild caloric restriction, counselling and weight-loss support. Global cognition improved slightly in both groups (+0.205 versus +0.170 standardised units); the between-group difference was 0.035 (95% CI −0.022 to 0.092), P = 0.23, and MRI measures of brain structure changed similarly in the two groups. The observational studies that linked MIND-style eating to less dementia show an association, not trial proof — people who eat that way differ in many other ways — and this trial is the randomised test of the diet itself, fenced here as observational background rather than evidence of effect. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): one large, long randomised trial with a null primary outcome and null imaging outcomes.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference)

title: Vitamin C after a wrist fracture: two positive trials, one null replication
question: In adults with a wrist (distal radius) fracture, does vitamin C 500 mg daily for about 50 days prevent complex regional pain syndrome (CRPS) compared with placebo?
balance: Two randomised trials from one Dutch group found vitamin C after a wrist fracture cut complex regional pain syndrome (CRPS, formerly reflex sympathetic dystrophy): 7% versus 22% in Zollinger 1999 — an absolute difference of 15 percentage points (95% CI 2–26) — and, in the 2007 dose-response trial, 2.4% on pooled vitamin C versus 10.1% on placebo, with the 500 mg dose at a relative risk of 0.17 relative to placebo and no extra gain at 1,500 mg. The independent replication went the other way: Ekrol 2014 (Edinburgh, n = 336) made function its primary outcome and found no benefit on the DASH score at any point, no overall difference in CRPS, and a few early secondary outcomes favouring placebo. Both positive trials come from a single research group and the one independent test was null on function and on CRPS overall; the pill is cheap and, at 500 mg daily for about 50 days, low-risk, but the evidence is split. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a plausible, inexpensive prophylactic backed by two positive trials from one group and contradicted by one independent null replication.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Low-dose atropine slows children's myopia: a clear dose-response
question: In children with progressing myopia (shortsightedness), do nightly low-dose atropine eye drops slow progression — prescription change and eye lengthening — compared with placebo?
balance: Nightly low-dose atropine slows myopia progression in children, with a clear dose-response in the LAMP trial. In LAMP (438 children aged 4–12, 1 year), spherical-equivalent change was −0.27 D on 0.05%, −0.46 D on 0.025% and −0.59 D on 0.01%, versus −0.81 D on placebo, and axial length grew by 0.20, 0.29 and 0.36 mm versus 0.41 mm. The older ATOM1 trial of the much stronger 1% dose in one eye found progression of −0.28 versus −1.20 D over 2 years. In the phase 3 CHAMP trial (576 children, 3 years) of NVK002 (Vyluma), the 0.02% dose missed its primary responder endpoint (odds ratio 1.77, P = .37), while 0.01% met all its main endpoints: responder odds ratio 4.54 (a relative measure; the abstract does not report the responder proportions themselves), a spherical-equivalent difference of +0.24 D and axial length −0.13 mm relative to placebo. The endpoints throughout are progression and eye lengthening during childhood, not adult eye disease. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): consistent slowing across three randomised trials, with a concentration-dependent effect in LAMP and a 3-year phase 3 confirmation at the 0.01% dose.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: Chronic cough that won't quit: gabapentin and gefapixant help some
question: In adults with refractory or unexplained chronic cough, do neuromodulators (gabapentin, pregabalin) or the P2X3 antagonist gefapixant reduce cough compared with placebo?
balance: For a cough that has lasted years and resisted standard treatment, neuromodulators and the P2X3 antagonist gefapixant each beat placebo — modestly, and at a tolerability price. Gabapentin (maximum 1,800 mg/day for 10 weeks) improved cough-specific quality of life by 1.80 Leicester Cough Questionnaire points over placebo (95% CI 0.56–3.04; number needed to treat 3.58) in 62 patients, with side-effects in 31% versus 10%. Pregabalin 300 mg/day added to speech pathology improved LCQ by a further 3.5 points (95% CI 1.1–5.8) in 40 patients, though objective cough frequency did not differ. Gefapixant 45 mg twice daily reduced 24-hour cough frequency by a relative 18.5% in COUGH-1 and 14.6% in COUGH-2 beyond placebo, in over 2,000 participants whose cough had lasted on average more than 11 years; the 15 mg dose did not work, and taste disturbance was common (dysgeusia 16.2% and 21.1%). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): placebo-controlled benefit is consistent across three agents, but the neuromodulator trials are small and the gefapixant effect is a modest relative reduction bought with taste side-effects.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Anal fissure: creams heal many, surgery heals more and lasts
question: In adults with chronic anal fissure, do glyceryl trinitrate (GTN) ointment or botulinum toxin injection heal the fissure, and how do they compare with lateral internal sphincterotomy (surgery)?
balance: A chronic anal fissure can often be healed without surgery — but surgery heals more, and keeps it healed. Glyceryl trinitrate (GTN) 0.2% ointment healed 26 of 38 fissures (68%) versus 3 of 39 (8%) on placebo over 8 weeks (Lund 1997), and botulinum toxin 20 U injected into the internal anal sphincter healed 11 of 15 versus 2 of 15 on saline at 2 months (Maria 1998). In the one head-to-head trial, lateral internal sphincterotomy beat GTN on pain relief at 6 months (93.6% versus 57.44%) and on healing (89.36% versus 68.08%), because GTN's gains were eroded by recurrence in 34.04% (Mustafa 2022). The trade-off runs the other way on continence and side-effects: transient flatus incontinence (8.51%) and liquid incontinence (6.4%) occurred only after surgery in that trial, while headache affected 61.7% on GTN. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): two placebo-controlled wins establish that medical therapy heals most fissures short-term, with surgery the more durable option when it fails or recurs.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Premature ejaculation: dapoxetine triples latency time, from a low base
question: In men with premature ejaculation, do on-demand dapoxetine or the lidocaine–prilocaine metered spray (TEMPE) lengthen intravaginal ejaculatory latency time (IELT) compared with placebo?
balance: Two on-demand treatments lengthen the time to ejaculation in men with premature ejaculation — from a very low base, and only to a few minutes. In an integrated analysis of two phase 3 trials in 2,614 men, mean baseline intravaginal ejaculatory latency time (IELT) was about 0.90 minutes; at endpoint it was 1.75 minutes on placebo, 2.78 minutes on dapoxetine 30 mg, and 3.32 minutes on dapoxetine 60 mg (both p<0.0001 versus placebo). Nausea was dose-related: 8.7% at 30 mg and 20.1% at 60 mg. In a small phase 2 trial of 54 men, the TEMPE lidocaine–prilocaine metered spray increased IELT by 3.8 minutes versus 0.7 minutes on placebo — an adjusted ratio of 2.4 times, a relative measure. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a large, internally consistent dapoxetine programme plus a small supportive spray trial, with benefit best described honestly in absolute minutes.

title: Steroid cream loosens a tight foreskin in most boys — no surgery
question: In boys with phimosis where treatment is wanted, does topical corticosteroid cream make the foreskin retractile and avoid circumcision, compared with placebo?
balance: When a boy's tight foreskin needs treatment, a course of topical corticosteroid cream usually makes it retractile and avoids circumcision. Betamethasone cream twice daily for 4 weeks cured 74% of boys versus 44% on placebo (Lund 2005) — the high placebo figure stated plainly, because the gentle retraction that goes with applying any cream itself loosens many foreskins — and with a second course for non-responders, surgery was avoided in about 85% of cases; at 18 months, 79 of 92 boys re-examined were still cured and 13 had relapsed. Three betamethasone valerate formulations (0.1%, 0.2%, and 0.2% plus hyaluronidase) each beat placebo over 60 days, with total plus partial response of about 95% versus a 29% placebo success rate (Nascimento 2011). Potency is not the lever: high-potency betamethasone valerate 0.06% and moderate-potency clobetasone butyrate 0.05% produced near-identical responses (81.3% versus 77.4%, not significant; Yang 2005). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): two placebo-controlled trials agree, the effect is durable at 18 months, and no side-effects were reported in these trials.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Daily antibiotics halve reflux children's UTIs — but scars were not prevented
question: In children with vesicoureteral reflux after a urinary tract infection, does daily low-dose antibiotic prophylaxis prevent further UTIs — and does it prevent kidney scarring?
balance: Daily low-dose antibiotic prophylaxis prevents further urinary tract infections in children with vesicoureteral reflux — but in the best trial it did not prevent kidney scarring, and it bred resistant bacteria. In RIVUR (607 children with reflux after a first or second UTI, treated for 2 years), recurrence occurred in 39 of 302 children on trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis (12.9%) versus 72 of 305 on placebo (23.6%): hazard ratio 0.50, a 50% relative reduction, on those absolute rates of about 13% versus 24%. Renal scarring was 11.9% on prophylaxis versus 10.2% on placebo, not significantly different, and among breakthrough E. coli recurrences, 63% of isolates were resistant to the drug versus 19% on placebo. PRIVENT (576 children after at least one symptomatic UTI, 42% with known reflux) pointed the same way over 12 months: UTI in 13% versus 19%, hazard ratio 0.61 (a 39% relative reduction), an absolute reduction of 6 percentage points. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): two large placebo-controlled trials agree that infections are prevented; scarring — the outcome prophylaxis ultimately aims at — was not shown to improve, and resistance is the price.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Sweaty armpits: Botox injections and a medicated cloth both work
question: In people with primary axillary hyperhidrosis, do botulinum toxin injections (Botox) or the topical anticholinergic glycopyrronium tosylate cloth reduce sweat production compared with placebo or vehicle?
balance: Both treatments beat their controls in randomised, double-blind trials. In Naumann 2001, 320 people with bilateral primary axillary hyperhidrosis received botulinum toxin type A (Botox) 50 U per axilla or placebo injections: responders (at least a 50% reduction in sweat production) at week 4 were 94% on Botox versus 36% on placebo, and at week 16 the rates were still 82% versus 21%, with much higher patient satisfaction on Botox. In the pooled ATMOS-1 and ATMOS-2 trials, a glycopyrronium tosylate 3.75% cloth used once daily for 4 weeks produced a responder rate (at least a 4-point improvement on the Axillary Sweating Daily Diary item 2) of 59.5% versus 27.6% on vehicle — although the measured sweat reduction was modest beside vehicle: −107.6 versus −92.1 mg/5 min. The Botox effect is large and durable to 16 weeks; the cloth works on patient-reported severity but its gravimetric margin is small and the trials lasted only 4 weeks. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): each treatment has randomised placebo- or vehicle-controlled support, but the cloth's objective sweat margin is modest and neither evidence base is large or long.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Stimulant laxatives work: bisacodyl and picosulfate beat placebo clearly
question: In adults with chronic constipation, do stimulant laxatives — bisacodyl tablets or sodium picosulfate drops — increase complete spontaneous bowel movements compared with placebo?
balance: Yes — in two large, modern, placebo-controlled trials the stimulant laxatives clearly increased complete spontaneous bowel movements (CSBMs). With bisacodyl 10 mg/day for 4 weeks in 368 adults with Rome III chronic constipation, CSBMs per week rose from 1.1 to 5.2 on bisacodyl versus 1.1 to 1.9 on placebo (p<.0001), with spontaneous bowel movements 7.9 versus 3.2 per week and concordant quality-of-life gains. With sodium picosulfate drops for 4 weeks in 367 patients, CSBMs per week rose from 0.9 to 3.4 versus 1.1 to 1.7 on placebo (p<.0001), and 51.1% versus 18.0% reached at least 3 CSBMs per week. An older, small trial in geriatric long-stay inpatients found a senna-plus-bulk combination (Agiolax) produced more bowel actions than lactulose, but it had no placebo arm. Both big trials lasted only 4 weeks and were manufacturer-funded, so they settle short-term efficacy, not long-term safety. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): two large concordant placebo-controlled trials with large absolute gains, held at POSSIBLE by short duration and manufacturer funding.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Loperamide shortens acute diarrhoea by about a day
question: In adults with acute (non-bloody) diarrhoea, does loperamide shorten the illness compared with placebo, and how does it compare with racecadotril and with antibiotics in travellers' diarrhoea?
balance: Loperamide shortens acute non-bloody diarrhoea by about a day in the placebo test: in Hughes 1995, a UK general-practice trial of loperamide oxide 1 mg, loperamide oxide 2 mg and loperamide 2 mg against placebo in acute non-dysenteric diarrhoea, every active preparation was significantly superior to placebo, cutting the time to complete relief to about 24 hours versus 45 hours on placebo. Against another antidiarrhoeal it has no edge: in Vetel 1999 (n=157), diarrhoea duration was 14.9 hours on racecadotril versus 13.7 hours on loperamide (not significant), with more rebound constipation on loperamide (18.7% versus 9.8%). And in travellers' diarrhoea (DuPont 2007, n=310), loperamide alone was the slowest arm — time to last unformed stool 69 hours, versus 32.5 hours on the antibiotic rifaximin and 27.3 hours on the combination — because it slows the gut without treating the infection. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a real, roughly one-day shortening against placebo in ordinary acute diarrhoea, with clear limits in infectious travellers' diarrhoea.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Athlete's foot: one week of terbinafine beat four weeks of clotrimazole
question: In people with athlete's foot (interdigital tinea pedis), does terbinafine 1% cream clear the fungus — and does one week of it beat four weeks of clotrimazole?
balance: Yes — and the short course beat the long one. In Evans 1994, 211 people with mycologically proven tinea pedis received terbinafine 1% cream twice daily for 1 week (followed by 3 weeks of placebo cream) or clotrimazole 1% cream twice daily for 4 weeks; at week 4, mycological cure was 93.5% on terbinafine versus 73.1% on clotrimazole (p=.0001), and effective treatment (cure with no or minimal signs and symptoms) was 89.7% versus 58.7%. Against its own vehicle, terbinafine 1% cream once daily for 1 week gave a mycological cure of 91.4% versus 37.1% (p<.001), maintained 7 weeks after treatment ended (Korting 2001). One week of terbinafine therefore clears the fungus in about nine of ten patients — better than four weeks of the older azole cream and far better than vehicle. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): two concordant double-blind trials with large absolute cure differences, held at POSSIBLE because both are older industry-era trials and one lacks a stated sample size in its abstract.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Period pain: NSAIDs beat placebo, and beat aspirin and paracetamol too
question: In women and adolescents with primary dysmenorrhoea, do NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen) relieve period pain compared with placebo — and how do they compare with acetaminophen (paracetamol) and aspirin?
balance: NSAIDs relieve period pain better than placebo — and, at the doses tested, better than aspirin or acetaminophen (paracetamol). In a small double-blind crossover (Dawood 2007; 12 women, 10 completed), both ibuprofen 400 mg and acetaminophen 1,000 mg, each taken four times daily for 3 days of one cycle, beat placebo on pain (ibuprofen p=.002; acetaminophen p=.022), and both cut menstrual-fluid prostaglandin F2α — from 36.2 µg on placebo to 14.8 µg on ibuprofen (p=.001) and 21.4 µg on acetaminophen (p=.008). In a 32-woman crossover (Rosenwaks 1981), naproxen sodium beat both aspirin (p=.02) and placebo (p=.002), while aspirin was not superior to placebo (p=.05). In a pooled analysis of five trials in 443 women at over-the-counter doses (Milsom 2002), naproxen 400 mg beat acetaminophen and placebo within 30 minutes, and at 6 hours both naproxen doses beat acetaminophen and ibuprofen 200 mg, with similar adverse-event rates. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): consistent wins across small crossovers and a 443-woman pooled analysis, held at POSSIBLE by the tiny size of the individual placebo-controlled trials.

title: Plant sterol and stanol spreads for cholesterol: two blinded trials show real LDL lowering — with no trial of heart attacks or strokes
question: In adults with normal or mildly raised cholesterol, do margarines enriched with plant sterols or stanols (about 2 g/day) lower LDL cholesterol compared with ordinary margarine?
balance: Plant sterols and stanols are sold in margarines and drinks on the claim that they lower cholesterol, and unusually for a supermarket health claim, the randomised evidence is real. In the Finnish trial (153 adults with mildly raised cholesterol, 12 months), margarine carrying sitostanol ester lowered LDL cholesterol by 14.1% while the control margarine lowered it by 1.1%. In a second double-blind trial (100 adults), margarines enriched with soy sterol esters or sitostanol esters lowered total and LDL cholesterol by 8–13% (0.37–0.44 mmol/L (≈14–17 mg/dL)), with no effect on HDL. The honest limits: these are cholesterol numbers, not heart attacks — no trial of a sterol spread has ever been powered for clinical events — the effect needs roughly 2 g of sterols a day eaten as part of a fat spread, and sterols also lower blood levels of some fat-soluble vitamins and carotenoids. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): consistent LDL lowering in two blinded trials; an add-on to, not a substitute for, proven lipid therapy.

title: Aged garlic extract for blood pressure: two positive trials of one product from one research group — promising, not yet independently confirmed
question: In adults with hypertension, does aged garlic extract (the Kyolic preparation) lower blood pressure compared with placebo?
balance: Garlic is one of the most-bought supplements for blood pressure, and the trial evidence comes almost entirely from one Australian research group testing one product — Kyolic aged garlic extract. In a dose-response trial (79 hypertensive patients, 12 weeks), 480 mg/day lowered systolic pressure by 11.8 mmHg against placebo (p=0.006); the higher 960 mg dose looked borderline at 8 weeks. In the group's AGE at Heart trial (88 completers, 1.2 g/day, 12 weeks), systolic pressure fell 5.0 mmHg on average (p=0.016), and the half of patients who responded fell by 11.5/6.3 mmHg. A 5 mmHg average systolic fall is clinically worthwhile if real — but two trials from a single programme, on a surrogate endpoint, with no independent replication, is exactly the profile that earns a moderate stamp rather than a strong one. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a genuine-looking blood-pressure effect for the tested aged garlic extract, awaiting confirmation by independent groups.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Shingrix for shingles prevention: 97% efficacy at 50+, about 90% at 70+ — with a genuinely rough two days after each dose
question: In adults aged 50 and over, does the adjuvanted recombinant zoster vaccine (Shingrix) prevent shingles and postherpetic neuralgia compared with placebo?
balance: The recombinant zoster vaccine (Shingrix) is one of the most effective vaccines ever tested in older adults — a population in which vaccines usually work least well. In ZOE-50 (15,411 adults aged 50 and over evaluated), shingles occurred in 6 people on vaccine versus 210 on placebo — 0.3 versus 9.1 cases per 1,000 person-years, a vaccine efficacy of 97.2% (95% CI 93.7–99.0). In ZOE-70 (13,900 adults aged 70 and over), efficacy was 89.8% (84.2–93.7), and pooled efficacy against postherpetic neuralgia in the over-70s was 88.8%. The price is reactogenicity: grade-3 symptoms (severe enough to stop normal activity) occurred in 17.0% of vaccinees versus 3.2% on placebo in ZOE-50 — a sore, rough two days is common, and worth warning about. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): two very large trials with near-total protection against a disease whose main burden is chronic nerve pain.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: Quinine for night leg cramps: it does work, modestly, in two small blinded trials — its problem is safety and licensing, not efficacy
question: In adults with nocturnal leg cramps, does quinine (or its relative hydroquinine) reduce cramp frequency compared with placebo?
balance: Quinine for night cramps is an old remedy that regulators have pushed off the market in several countries over rare but serious blood side effects — which makes the actual efficacy evidence worth stating precisely. Two small double-blind trials found a real effect. In a crossover trial of 27 men, quinine cut cramp frequency and the sleep disturbance cramps cause (13 of 27 had at least half their cramps abolished), while vitamin E, the comparison remedy, did nothing. In a Dutch trial (112 enrolled, 102 analysed), hydroquinine — quinine's close chemical relative — reduced cramps by a median of 8 attacks over the treatment period versus 3 on placebo, with 65% of the hydroquinine group achieving at least a 50% reduction in cramp frequency. So the efficacy answer is yes, modestly; the reason quinine is nonetheless hard to obtain is safety, not inefficacy, and this shelf grades the efficacy question only. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): two small blinded trials agree that quinine-class drugs reduce nocturnal cramps.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Vitex (chasteberry) for PMS: one proper randomised trial of the Ze 440 extract, responders 52% versus 24% — and a long tail of uncontrolled use
question: In women with premenstrual syndrome, does Vitex agnus-castus extract (the standardised preparation Ze 440) reduce premenstrual symptoms compared with placebo?
balance: Vitex (chasteberry) is the standard herbal answer to premenstrual syndrome, and it rests on one genuine randomised trial. In the Schellenberg trial (170 women evaluated over three cycles), the standardised extract Ze 440 was significantly better than placebo on the main symptom outcome (p<0.001), with 52% of women responding on the extract versus 24% on placebo, and only mild adverse events. An earlier prospective series of the same extract (43 completers) found a 42.5% fall in symptom scores — consistent, but with no comparison group it cannot separate the extract from the substantial placebo response PMS trials always show. One randomised trial, a named standardised extract, a plausible effect: that is a developer-verdict shelf, and the stamp stays moderate. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).

title: Calcium for PMS: one large trial found a 48% symptom fall against 30% on placebo — a good result that nobody has repeated
question: In women with premenstrual syndrome, does calcium carbonate (1,200 mg/day elemental calcium) reduce premenstrual symptoms compared with placebo?
balance: Calcium for PMS is an old hypothesis — that premenstrual symptoms reflect disturbed calcium regulation — tested once, properly, at scale. In the Thys-Jacobs multicentre trial (497 women enrolled, 466 analysed), calcium carbonate supplying 1,200 mg of elemental calcium a day, taken for three menstrual cycles, reduced total symptom scores by 48% from baseline against 30% on placebo; all four symptom factors (negative affect, water retention, food cravings, pain) were significantly reduced by the third cycle, and luteal-phase scores were already significantly lower by the second cycle. Thirty percent on placebo is a reminder of how much of PMS treatment response is non-specific — but the 18-point gap over placebo in a 466-woman double-blind trial is a real result. It has simply never been repeated. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): one large, well-run trial; a single-trial shelf for the developer's verdict.

title: SSRIs for premenstrual dysphoric disorder: fluoxetine and sertraline both clearly beat placebo — 62% much improved on sertraline versus 34%
question: In women with premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD), do SSRIs (fluoxetine, sertraline) reduce premenstrual symptoms and functional impairment compared with placebo?
balance: Premenstrual dysphoric disorder — the severe, function-wrecking end of premenstrual symptoms — is one of the clearest SSRI successes outside depression itself. In the Canadian fluoxetine trial (313 women randomised after a placebo washout), both 20 mg and 60 mg daily beat placebo on tension, irritability and dysphoria (p<0.001); 60 mg brought significantly more side effects, and the authors settled on 20 mg as the dose. In the sertraline trial (243 randomised, 200 completed), daily symptom scores fell from 64 to 44 on sertraline against 62 to 54 on placebo (p<0.001), depression ratings fell 44% versus 29% (p<0.002), and 62% of women were much or very much improved against 34% on placebo. Two drugs of the same class, two multicentre trials, the same answer. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): consistent class evidence for a disabling condition, on symptom and functioning outcomes rather than hard endpoints.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Evening primrose oil for breast pain: two blinded trials say no — pain fell just as much on dummy oils, with a 40% placebo response
question: In women with mastalgia (breast pain), does evening primrose oil / gamolenic acid reduce breast pain compared with placebo?
balance: Evening primrose oil has been the default recommendation for cyclical breast pain for decades — and the two proper trials of its active ingredient, gamolenic acid (GLA), both say it does not work. In a 120-woman factorial trial, days with pain fell 12.3% on evening primrose oil and 13.8% on its control oil (p=0.73); fish oil, tested alongside, was likewise indistinguishable from its control. In the much larger Efamast trial (555 women), breast pain improved substantially in every group — the placebo fatty-acid groups responded at 40% — with no significant difference for GLA in any comparison, with or without antioxidant vitamins. Mastalgia improves on its own and responds strongly to reassurance and placebo; the oil adds nothing measurable. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): two double-blind trials, one of them large, both null.

title: Treating a urine infection with ibuprofen first: two-thirds of women never needed an antibiotic — but symptoms lasted longer and kidney infections were commoner
question: In women with uncomplicated urinary tract infection, does starting with ibuprofen (symptomatic treatment, antibiotics held in reserve) safely reduce antibiotic use compared with an immediate antibiotic?
balance: Most uncomplicated urinary infections settle without antibiotics, and two German trials asked whether treating symptoms with ibuprofen first could spare antibiotics safely. The large trial (494 women) found the strategy works in the narrow sense: women on ibuprofen used significantly fewer antibiotic courses over 28 days, and two-thirds recovered with no antibiotic at all. But they paid for it — a significantly higher burden of symptoms over the first week, and more cases of pyelonephritis (kidney infection) in the ibuprofen group; four serious adverse events led to hospital referral, one possibly drug-related. The smaller pilot (80 women) had found day-4 symptom freedom at least as good on ibuprofen as on ciprofloxacin (58.3% versus 51.5%). Read together: an ibuprofen-first approach is a legitimate option for a woman with mild-to-moderate symptoms who wants to avoid antibiotics and accepts slower relief with a small risk of the infection climbing — it is not an equivalent treatment. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for antibiotic sparing, Tier C for the harm trade-off: the developer rules personally.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Tranexamic acid for heavy periods: measured blood loss fell about 40–45% in two trials — a real, non-hormonal option
question: In women with heavy menstrual bleeding, does oral tranexamic acid reduce menstrual blood loss compared with placebo or hormonal treatment?
balance: Tranexamic acid is the non-hormonal tablet option for heavy periods, and it has the trial record to back the claim. In the pivotal US trial (187 women with objectively heavy loss), tranexamic acid 3.9 g/day for up to five days per cycle cut menstrual blood loss by 69.6 mL (40.4%) against 12.6 mL (8.2%) on placebo (p<0.001), meeting all three pre-specified efficacy criteria, with quality-of-life gains to match and a side-effect profile comparable to placebo. An earlier Cambridge trial, using the objective alkaline-haematin measurement, found tranexamic acid reduced loss by 45% (175 to 97 mL), while the hormonal comparator norethisterone actually increased loss by 20%; 56% of tranexamic-acid cycles normalised (under 80 mL) versus 9.5% on norethisterone. Two trials, an objective endpoint, a consistent 40–45% relative reduction in measured blood loss. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).

title: Beta-sitosterol for prostate symptoms: two blinded trials show about a 5-point IPSS advantage and better flow — symptoms improve, the gland does not shrink
question: In men with benign prostatic hyperplasia, does beta-sitosterol improve urinary symptoms and flow compared with placebo?
balance: Beta-sitosterol, the plant sterol sold for prostate symptoms, is a useful contrast with its food-spread cousins on shelf #2481: there, sterols lower cholesterol; here, the question is urinary symptoms. Two German double-blind trials from the 1990s found genuine symptom benefit. In Berges (200 patients, 20 mg three times daily, 6 months), the modified Boyarsky symptom score fell 6.7 points against 2.1 on placebo (p<0.01), IPSS fell 7.4 versus 2.1 points, peak flow rose from 9.9 to 15.2 mL/s, and residual urine volume halved — with no change in prostate volume. In Klippel (177 men, the named preparation Azuprostat, 130 mg/day), the adjusted IPSS advantage over placebo was 5.4 points (p<0.01), with quality of life, flow rate and residual volume all moving the same way. Symptom relief without shrinkage is a coherent profile — think of it as a mild symptomatic drug, not a disease modifier — but both trials are old, short, and predate modern reporting standards. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).

title: Tea tree oil for acne: one 1990 trial found it about as good as benzoyl peroxide, slower, and gentler — and nobody has tested it properly since
question: In people with mild-to-moderate acne, does 5% tea-tree oil gel improve acne compared with standard topical treatment (benzoyl peroxide)?
balance: Tea tree oil is the natural-remedy answer to acne, and it has exactly one randomised trial — a 1990 Australian single-blind comparison (124 patients) against 5% benzoyl peroxide lotion, the standard of the day. Both treatments significantly reduced inflamed and non-inflamed lesion counts; the tea tree gel (5%) was slower to start working, and noticeably fewer patients reported side effects on it. That is the whole record: no placebo arm, no double blinding, no modern trial in the three decades since, and no named product — the publication describes a 5% tea-tree oil gel without a brand. A gentler-but-slower alternative to benzoyl peroxide is a fair reading; anything stronger is not. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence), Tier C as a single-trial benefit shelf for the developer's verdict.

title: Aloe vera for psoriasis: one trial claims an impossible 83% cure rate; a better trial shows it roughly matching a mild steroid — believe the second
question: In people with plaque psoriasis, does topical aloe vera improve psoriasis severity compared with placebo or a topical steroid?
balance: Aloe vera for psoriasis carries one of the most implausible result patterns in the supplement literature, which is why this shelf shows its working. The placebo-controlled trial (60 patients) reported that a 0.5% aloe vera extract cream 'cured' 25 of 30 patients (83.3%) against 2 of 30 (6.6%) on placebo over a 16-week study — a cure rate no psoriasis therapy, including modern biologics, approaches in this disease. The second trial is more believable: against 0.1% triamcinolone cream in 80 patients, aloe vera reduced PASI slightly more (−7.7 versus −6.6 points over 8 weeks, p=0.0237), with quality-of-life gains identical between groups. Two positive trials say aloe cream is not inert; the first trial's numbers say its report should be read with real scepticism. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — positive twice, discounted for the implausible anchor.

title: Ketoconazole shampoo for dandruff: 88% responded, and weekly use cut relapse from 47% to 19% — the rare OTC claim with a real trial behind it
question: In people with dandruff and scalp seborrhoeic dermatitis, does ketoconazole 2% shampoo clear the condition and prevent relapse compared with placebo shampoo?
balance: Ketoconazole 2% shampoo is the pharmacy-shelf treatment for dandruff and scalp seborrhoeic dermatitis, and its evidence is an old, large, well-shaped trial. In Peter 1995, 575 patients with moderate-to-severe scalp seborrhoeic dermatitis and dandruff responded to twice-weekly ketoconazole shampoo in 88% of cases over 2–4 weeks; 312 responders then entered a 6-month double-blind prophylaxis phase, in which relapse struck 47% on placebo shampoo against 19% on once-weekly ketoconazole (31% on an alternating regimen) — treatment and prevention in one design. The second card is a different kind of evidence: in a 40-woman crossover, a 1% pyrithione zinc conditioning shampoo was preferred over the 2% ketoconazole shampoo by 75% of users on overall performance and scored better on combing ease, smoothness and frizz — cosmetic acceptance, not efficacy, but the thing that decides whether anyone keeps using an anti-dandruff shampoo. title: Bath additives for childhood eczema: a 483-child trial found no benefit on any measure — the money is better spent on the creams that stay on
question: In children with eczema, do emollient bath additives added to standard care (leave-on emollients and topical treatments) improve eczema control compared with standard care alone?
balance: Emollient bath additives — the oils and dispersants poured into the bath for children with eczema — cost families and health services real money, and the BATHE trial tested them the way the question deserves: 483 children aged 1–11 in 96 UK general practices, randomised to prescribed bath additives or none for 12 months, with both groups continuing ordinary leave-on emollients and standard care. The answer was no. Weekly POEM eczema scores over the first 16 weeks did not differ significantly; the adjusted difference was 0.41 points (95% CI −0.27 to 1.10) — a fraction of the 3-point difference considered the smallest that matters — and there were no differences in severity over the year, flare consultations, quality of life, or costs. Leave-on emollients remain standard; the bath additive adds nothing measurable. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): one large, pragmatic, decisive null.

title: Steroids for glue ear: the 389-child OSTRICH trial found hearing recovered in 40% versus 33% on placebo — not a real difference
question: In children with persistent otitis media with effusion (glue ear) and hearing loss, does a short course of oral steroids restore acceptable hearing compared with placebo?
balance: Glue ear — otitis media with effusion — is one of the commonest reasons children undergo surgery, so a cheap steroid course that restored hearing would change practice. Older small trials hinted at short-term benefit but were underpowered and poor quality. The OSTRICH trial did the question properly: 389 children aged 2–8 with at least three months of effusion symptoms and confirmed bilateral hearing loss, randomised double-blind to a short course of oral prednisolone or placebo across 20 UK centres. At five weeks, acceptable hearing was found in 40% on steroids versus 33% on placebo — an absolute difference of 7% (95% CI −3 to 17), an adjusted odds ratio of 1.36 (0.88–2.11), p=0.16 — with no differences in adverse events or quality of life. A point estimate that leans the right way, a confidence interval that comfortably includes nothing: not a treatment. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference).

title: Glaucoma drops really do save sight: visual-field loss delayed (HR 0.44) in glaucoma, and onset cut from 9.5% to 4.4% in high eye pressure
question: In people with open-angle glaucoma or ocular hypertension, do pressure-lowering eye drops preserve vision and prevent glaucoma compared with placebo or observation?
balance: Glaucoma drops are prescribed for decades on a chain of reasoning — drops lower eye pressure, pressure damages the optic nerve, so drops must save sight — that long rested on the pressure number alone. Two landmark trials closed the loop. UKGTS randomised 516 people with newly diagnosed open-angle glaucoma to latanoprost or placebo drops: pressure fell 3.8 versus 0.9 mmHg, and visual-field deterioration was delayed with a hazard ratio of 0.44 (0.28–0.69; p=0.0003) — the first placebo-controlled proof that a drop preserves visual function, strong enough that the safety committee stopped the trial early. OHTS asked the earlier question in 1,636 people with high eye pressure but no glaucoma: treatment cut the 5-year probability of developing glaucoma from 9.5% to 4.4% (HR 0.40, 0.27–0.59) — about five cases prevented per hundred people treated for five years. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): sight itself, not just pressure, in two large randomised trials.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: Midodrine for orthostatic hypotension: standing pressure up 22 mmHg at the top dose and symptoms improved in two trials — with supine hypertension as the price
question: In patients with neurogenic orthostatic hypotension (autonomic failure), does midodrine improve standing blood pressure and orthostatic symptoms compared with placebo?
balance: Neurogenic orthostatic hypotension — the blood pressure collapse on standing that comes with autonomic failure — has few drug options, and midodrine, a vasoconstrictor prodrug, is the standard one. Two double-blind trials from the 1990s support it. In the multicentre trial (171 patients), midodrine 10 mg three times daily improved standing systolic pressure at every visit (p<0.001), lightheadedness by the second week (p=0.001), and global symptom relief as rated by both patients (p=0.03) and investigators (p<0.001). In the dose-ranging trial (97 patients), the 10 mg dose raised standing systolic pressure by 22 mmHg (28%; p<0.001 versus placebo) and improved dizziness, weakness, syncope, energy and ability to stand. The costs are intrinsic to a pressor drug: tingling scalp, urinary urgency or retention, and supine hypertension — lying-down blood pressure must be watched. Standing pressure is a surrogate, but here the symptoms moved with it, which is more than most surrogate stories offer. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).

title: Feverfew for migraine prevention: one trial marginally positive, one null overall — the honest verdict is maybe
question: In people with migraine, does feverfew (the standardised CO2 extract MIG-99) reduce migraine frequency compared with placebo?
balance: Feverfew is the classic herbal migraine preventive, and its modern evidence is two trials of one standardised CO2 extract, MIG-99 — which between them give a genuinely mixed answer. The larger trial (170 patients, 6.25 mg three times daily, 16 weeks) found attacks fell by 1.9 per month on MIG-99 versus 1.3 on placebo (p=0.0456), with a responder odds ratio of 3.4 (p=0.0049) and adverse events no commoner than placebo. The earlier dose-ranging trial (147 patients, three doses) found no significant difference on its primary endpoint in either the full or the confirmatory analysis — the dose-dependent signal appeared only in the pre-defined subgroup of patients with at least four attacks a month at baseline (n=49; p=0.001). A marginal positive and a primary-endpoint null is the profile of a weak-evidence stamp. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).

title: Collagen peptides for skin: two small trials from one group show device-measured improvements — a maybe, not the marketing
question: In middle-aged women, do oral collagen peptide supplements improve skin wrinkles and elasticity compared with placebo?
balance: Collagen drinks and powders are a large market built on a small evidence base: two little double-blind trials from one research group, both of the same kind of specific bioactive collagen peptides. In the wrinkle trial (114 women aged 45–65), 2.5 g/day of the named peptide product Verisol cut eye-wrinkle volume by about 20% relative to placebo after 8 weeks (p<0.05), with skin procollagen up 65% and elastin up 18% in a biopsy subgroup; the wrinkle effect persisted four weeks after stopping. In the elasticity trial (69 women aged 35–55), 2.5 g or 5 g of collagen peptides improved measured skin elasticity significantly against placebo over 8 weeks, while moisture and water-loss outcomes reached significance only in subgroups. Objective instruments, tiny samples, surrogate cosmetic endpoints, one group, one product family, and no independent replication: the profile of a weak-evidence stamp. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).

title: Aged garlic extract vs coronary calcium: slower progression in four small trials — one of them independent — but calcium is a surrogate and no trial counted heart attacks
question: In adults with subclinical coronary atherosclerosis, does aged garlic extract slow the progression of coronary artery calcium (CAC) compared with placebo?
balance: Four small randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials — each 1 year long, with 19 to 104 participants — have tested aged garlic extract (AGE) against placebo on coronary artery calcium progression, and all four found slower progression on treatment. In the Harbor-UCLA pilot (Budoff 2004), patients on statins gained a mean of 7.5% in calcium score on AGE versus 22.2% on placebo (relative percentage changes, P=0.046). In firefighters (Zeb 2012), CAC rose 32 versus 58 Agatston units on a combined AGE + coenzyme Q10 capsule. The one independent trial — Lund, Sweden (Wlosinska 2020), testing AGE alone as Kyolic Reserve 2,400 mg/day — found the adjusted odds of the lowest CAC progression were 2.95 times higher on AGE (95% CI 1.05–8.27). A 2023 systematic review of 49 calcification trials found AGE (6 trials) the one intervention that consistently attenuated calcification. Read the confounds on the face of the cards: two of the four trials tested combinations (AGE + B vitamins/folate/L-arginine in Budoff 2009; AGE + CoQ10 in Zeb 2012) from which garlic's own contribution cannot be separated; three of the four trials come from a single centre (Harbor-UCLA); and the manufacturer, Wakunaga, funded or supplied product for trials on both sides of the Atlantic. Above all: no trial measured heart attacks or deaths — CAC progression is a surrogate endpoint, and these trials were neither large enough nor long enough to test outcomes. For the separate question of AGE and blood pressure, see Shelf #2482. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a consistent direction of effect across four randomised trials, one of them independent and testing AGE alone, backed by a systematic review — held at POSSIBLE by the surrogate endpoint, small samples, single-centre predominance, combination confounding, and manufacturer involvement.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Hospitalist vs traditional attending care: stay about half a day shorter and cheaper — a mortality benefit showed only in one trial's second year
question: For general medical inpatients, does care led by a hospitalist rather than a traditional attending physician or the patient's own primary care physician improve mortality, length of stay and cost?
balance: Hospitalist care reliably shortens the stay and cuts hospital cost; whether it saves lives is unproven. In the one allocated comparison (Meltzer 2002, 6,511 patients), the hospitalist advantage appeared only in the service's second year: stay 0.49 day shorter, costs $782 lower, and 30-day mortality 4.2% versus 6.0% (adjusted relative risk 0.65 — a relative measure from a single centre's second year; with years 1 and 2 combined, mortality was not significantly different). The two systematic reviews agree on efficiency and not on outcomes: Peterson 2009 (33 reports) found general agreement on shorter stay and lower cost, with outcome gains only in pockets — orthopaedic co-management, pneumonia and heart-failure quality markers; White & Glazier 2011 (65 evaluations) found stay reduced in 69% of studies and costs in 70%, clinical quality comparable to traditional attendings, and the underlying studies methodologically weak. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the efficiency benefit is consistent; the mortality signal rests on one centre's experienced second year — which is why the experience question gets its own shelf (#2544). Tier C: this shelf carries a mortality claim.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Hospitalist experience and continuity: first-year hospitalists' patients die more often, and fragmented schedules track with more deaths and readmissions
question: Among hospitalists, do years of experience and more continuous work schedules change their patients' mortality, readmission and discharge outcomes?
balance: Within hospitalist care, who the hospitalist is and how they work appears to matter. In national Medicare data (Goodwin 2018; 21,612 hospitalists), patients of first-year hospitalists had higher mortality than patients of hospitalists a year further on: observed 30-day mortality 10.50% in a hospitalist's first year versus 9.97% in the second year (mortality odds ratio 0.90 for year 2 versus year 1 — a relative measure), with hospital mortality 3.33% versus 2.96% (odds ratio 0.84) and little further change after year 2. In Texas Medicare data (Goodwin 2020; 114,777 admissions), care from hospitalists in the most continuous schedule quartile was associated with lower mortality in the 30 days after discharge (adjusted odds ratio 0.88), fewer readmissions (0.94), more discharges home (1.08) and $223 lower 30-day post-discharge costs than the least continuous quartile. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): two large observational datasets with coherent dose patterns — but every ratio sits between 0.5 and 2.0, inside the library's weak-association band, and no trial has randomised experience or rosters. Tier C: this shelf carries mortality associations.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Hospitalist care after discharge: the in-hospital saving reverses — more ED visits, readmissions and Medicare cost in the 30 days after going home
question: After discharge, how do medical utilization, readmissions and total Medicare costs compare for medical inpatients cared for by hospitalists versus by their own primary care physicians?
balance: The hospitalist saving is partly a cost shift. In a national 5% Medicare sample (Kuo & Goodwin 2011), enrollees who had a primary care physician were compared according to who actually cared for them in hospital: those cared for by hospitalists stayed 0.64 day less and generated $282 lower hospital charges — but Medicare costs in the 30 days after discharge were $332 higher (P < 0.001 for both differences), more than wiping out the in-hospital saving. Hospitalist patients were also less likely to be discharged home (odds ratio 0.82) and more likely to have an emergency department visit (odds ratio 1.18) or a readmission (odds ratio 1.08) after discharge — relative measures, all inside the library's weak-association band — and they had fewer visits with their own primary care physician and more nursing facility visits. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm): the post-discharge pattern comes from a single large propensity-analysed observational study, so it is credible but not proven. The abstract reports no mortality outcome, so this shelf makes no mortality claim and is not Tier C.
stamp: POSSIBLE (harm)

title: Hospitalist co-management of surgical patients: fewer minor complications in the one trial — pooled stay and mortality gains only for team-based models
question: For surgical patients — older patients with hip fracture and patients having joint replacement in particular — does hospitalist (internal medicine) co-management improve complications, length of stay and mortality compared with surgeon-led care with consultation on request?
balance: Co-management works best as a team sport. The one randomised trial (Huddleston 2004; 526 higher-risk patients having elective hip or knee replacement) found a hospitalist–orthopaedic team discharged more patients with no complications (61.6% versus 49.8%) and fewer minor complications (30.2% versus 44.3%), with no significant difference in observed length of stay or total cost; adjusted for discharge delays, stay was 0.5 day shorter. In hip fracture specifically, a before-and-after cohort (Phy 2005; 466 patients aged 65 and over) found a hospitalist service cut time to surgery (38 to 25 hours), time from surgery to dismissal (9 to 7 days) and stay (10.6 to 8.4 days), with no difference in inpatient deaths or 30-day readmission rates. The meta-analysis (Shaw 2020; 14 studies, 35,800 patients, only one a randomised trial) found no significant overall association with stay (mean difference −1.02 days, 95% CI −2.09 to 0.04) or mortality (odds ratio 0.79, CI 0.56 to 1.11 — a relative measure), but multidisciplinary-team co-management was associated with shorter stay (−2.03 days) and lower mortality (odds ratio 0.67, CI 0.51 to 0.88); risk of bias was serious in 10 of the 14 studies. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a real complication benefit in one trial, process gains in hip fracture, and pooled hard-outcome signals only for team-based models in low-quality evidence. Tier C: this shelf carries mortality content.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Hospitalist burnout: over half report high depersonalisation or lost accomplishment in the quantifying survey — workload is the recurring driver
question: How common is burnout among hospitalists, and which features of the hospitalist job — workload, hours, control, support — drive it or protect against it?
balance: Burnout is common among hospitalists in every survey that has looked, and workload is the driver that recurs in all of them. The only survey here reporting percentages (Park 2025, Korea) found high-grade depersonalisation in 50.6% of respondents and reduced personal accomplishment in 57%, with excessive workload, long working hours and conflicts with caregivers as the shared risk factors — and a cap on daily inpatient load, the availability of a research mentor, and satisfaction with nonclinical work as the protective factors. A British Columbia workforce survey (Yousefi 2025) likewise found high rates of burnout, with workload the important associated factor in regression and many hospitalists planning to reduce or stop their acute-care work, though its abstract reports no prevalence figure and no respondent count. A small US survey (Warner 2025, 88 hospitalists) ties burnout to how safe the workload feels, frustration at work, and lack of control over the working day. All three are cross-sectional surveys: they show association, not causation, and none of them tested an intervention. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: prevalence and the workload story point the same way in three countries, but the hard percentages rest on one small survey with a 24.1% response rate. Tier C: survey-based workforce topic, taken to the developer personally.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Emergency physician burnout: front-line specialties rank highest in US national surveys, and 43% of ED staff meet burnout criteria across 29 studies
question: Is emergency medicine the highest-burnout specialty — how do emergency physicians compare with other physicians and with the wider emergency department workforce?
balance: Emergency physicians sit in the highest-burnout group in every source here, though no abstract publishes an emergency-medicine-only percentage or a numeric league table of specialties. In the US national survey (Shanafelt 2012), 45.8% of all physicians reported at least one burnout symptom, with the highest rates among the front-line specialties — family medicine, general internal medicine and emergency medicine; by 2014 the all-physician figure had risen to 54.4% (Shanafelt 2015). Pooling 29 studies of emergency department staff (Alanazy 2023), 43% met overall burnout criteria, with nurses the most affected group and physicians next. The emergency-physician-specific review (Somville 2024, 35 papers) found emergency physicians scoring higher than other healthcare professions on every burnout dimension, with critical incidents, aggression from patients, and organisational factors as the determinants. A caution the developer should see plainly: the often-quoted 'about 65% of emergency physicians' figure is NOT in the Shanafelt 2012 abstract and is not carded anywhere on this shelf. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: 'highest-burnout specialty' is supported as a front-line grouping, not as a proven solo ranking. Tier C: survey-based workforce topic, taken to the developer personally.

title: Geriatric care in hospital: the proven benefit sits in dedicated wards and units — the mobile consult team is the unproven model
question: For older hospital inpatients, does it matter how geriatric expertise is delivered — on a dedicated geriatric ward or Acute Care for Elders unit, or by a mobile consultation team visiting general wards?
balance: Whether geriatric assessment helps older inpatients at all is answered on shelf #605 (the Cochrane review: more patients alive and at home, risk ratio 1.06 — a relative measure; fewer nursing-home admissions, 0.80; no mortality difference, 1.00). This shelf asks the delivery question the Cochrane review left open: ward or team? The earlier meta-analysis of the same trial programme (Ellis 2011, 22 trials) found the same overall pattern — alive and at home, odds ratio 1.16 at a median 12 months — and a subgroup interaction suggesting the benefit belongs to designated wards rather than mobile teams; its abstract reports no subgroup effect sizes, and the 2017 Cochrane update judged the ward-versus-team analysis underpowered and uncertain. The named unit model has its own randomised trial: the Acute Care for Elders unit (Counsell 2000) did not improve its primary functional outcome but did reduce the composite of functional decline or nursing-home placement (34% vs 40% at discharge, sustained over the following year) at no extra length of stay or cost. No card on this shelf supports a roving consultation team improving outcomes — the one randomised proactive geriatrics consultation trial (hip fracture, Marcantonio 2001) and the Hospital Elder Life Program delirium-prevention evidence live on shelf #340. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the benefit concentrates in ward- and unit-based models; the consult-team model is the unproven one. Tier C: care-model topic with a composite touching death, taken to the developer personally. This shelf makes no mortality claim of its own.

title: Inpatient palliative care: quality of life improves modestly (the pooled effect halves in low-bias trials), symptoms ease, survival unchanged
question: For hospital inpatients with life-limiting illness, does involving a palliative care team improve quality of life and symptom burden — and does it change survival or cost?
balance: Yes for quality of life — with the size of the benefit honestly in doubt. Across 43 randomised trials in life-limiting illness (Kavalieratos 2016), palliative care improved quality of life at 1–3 months by a standardised mean difference of 0.46, translating to 11.36 points on the FACIT-Pal scale against a minimal clinically important difference of 9; but restricted to the five trials at low risk of bias the effect more than halved (0.20; 4.94 points, below the clinically important threshold) and the symptom-burden benefit (−0.66 overall) lost significance (−0.21, confidence interval reaching 0.00). There was no association with survival (hazard ratio 0.90, 95% CI 0.69 to 1.17 — a relative measure whose interval spans no effect). The inpatient model specifically has two randomised trials in stem-cell transplant patients (El-Jawahri 2016 and the 2025 multisite replication): quality of life fell less at the week-2 nadir, with less depression, anxiety and symptom burden, and a post-traumatic stress benefit still separating the groups at six months in 2025. An observational cost study (Morrison 2008) found palliative consultation associated with lower hospital costs, but it is propensity-matched administrative data, not a trial. The early-outpatient palliative care question (Temel 2010 and successors) is a different model and lives on shelf #367. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): direction consistent, magnitude bias-sensitive, no survival claim. Tier C: quality-of-life benefit claim in serious illness, taken to the developer personally.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Nicotine vaccines for smoking cessation: no trial beat placebo — the two phase III NicVAX trials quit at about 11% in both arms
question: Can a vaccine against nicotine help smokers quit — or stop recent quitters from relapsing?
balance: No. Every nicotine vaccine tested in a randomised trial failed to beat placebo on long-term abstinence. The Cochrane review (Hartmann-Boyce 2012) found four eligible trials covering 2,642 smokers and no statistically significant cessation benefit for any vaccine; the two phase III NicVAX trials, reported only in summary form, quit at approximately 11% in both the vaccine and placebo arms. The best individual results are no better: NicVAX added to varenicline and counselling quit at 27.7% versus 30.0% on placebo (Hoogsteder 2014), and the Niccine vaccine, tested for relapse prevention, left fewer people relapse-free than placebo at one year (43.3% versus 51.1%; Tonstad 2013). The one positive signal in the whole record is a subgroup: in the phase II Nicotine-Qbeta trial (Cornuz 2008), the third of vaccinees with the highest antibody levels had higher continuous abstinence than placebo (56.6% versus 31.3%) — but the trial's intention-to-treat result was null, and no later trial turned that subgroup signal into a treatment effect, including in pre-planned top-responder analyses. No nicotine vaccine is licensed. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): the null is consistent across three vaccine products, four-plus trials and a Cochrane review; what remains unproven is not whether these vaccines worked — they did not — but whether any future vaccine achieving much higher antibody levels could.
