title: GLP-1 drugs for alcohol use disorder: the largest trial cut heavy drinking days by 13.7 points more than placebo — smaller trials are mixed, and the biggest numbers are observational
question: In alcohol use disorder, do GLP-1 receptor agonists (semaglutide, exenatide) reduce heavy drinking and craving?
balance: Probably — with the evidence still young and concentrated. The strongest card is a 26-week Danish randomised trial in treatment-seeking patients with alcohol use disorder and obesity (Klausen 2026): once-weekly semaglutide 2.4 mg reduced heavy drinking days by 41.1 percentage points from baseline against 26.4 points on placebo, an estimated treatment difference of −13.7 points (95% CI −22.0 to −5.4; P = 0.0015). Two small phase 2 trials point the same way on some outcomes and not others: low-dose semaglutide reduced laboratory alcohol self-administration and drinks per drinking day but not drinking days (Hendershot 2025, n = 48), and oral semaglutide missed its primary craving endpoint while reducing heavy drinking days (Schacht 2026, n = 50). The class's other full-size trial is a caution: weekly exenatide for 26 weeks did not significantly reduce heavy drinking days overall (Klausen 2022, n = 127), though it blunted brain alcohol-cue reactivity and helped the obese subgroup in exploratory analysis. The very large numbers — a 50–56% lower risk of alcohol use disorder incidence and recurrence with semaglutide in electronic health records (Wang 2024) — are relative measures from observational data and cannot separate the drug from the kind of patient who receives it. No trial has yet tested hard outcomes (hospitalisation, liver events, mortality), follow-up is at most 26 weeks, and adverse events are the familiar gastrointestinal ones. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): one solid positive trial, two supportive small ones, one null — a real but unconfirmed effect. Tier C: early, small, mostly single-centre evidence for a new indication, taken to the developer personally.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Gene therapy for sickle cell disease: exa-cel freed 97% of evaluable patients from severe crises for at least a year; lovo-cel resolved severe events in all 25 evaluable patients
question: In severe sickle cell disease, does one-time gene therapy — CRISPR-edited exagamglogene autotemcel (exa-cel) or lentiviral lovotibeglogene autotemcel (lovo-cel) — eliminate vaso-occlusive crises?
balance: In the two pivotal single-arm studies, yes — for at least the first one to three years. In the phase 3 CLIMB SCD-121 study of the CRISPR-edited therapy exa-cel (Frangoul 2024), 44 patients aged 12–35 with at least two severe vaso-occlusive crises a year received the one-time treatment after busulfan myeloablation; of the 30 with enough follow-up to judge, 29 (97%) stayed free of severe crises for at least 12 consecutive months and all 30 stayed out of hospital for crises. The lentiviral therapy lovo-cel (Kanter 2022, HGB-206) reached the same place by a different route: all 25 evaluable patients had complete resolution of severe vaso-occlusive events, against a median of 3.5 events a year before treatment, with haemoglobin rising from 8.5 to at least 11 g/dL. The founding report (Frangoul 2021) is the first two patients ever treated this way — one with sickle cell disease, one with thalassaemia. What tempers the stamp: no randomised or controlled comparison exists for either product; median follow-up is 19.3 and 17.3 months in the pivotal cohorts; every patient first undergoes myeloablative busulfan conditioning with its own infertility and malignancy risks; and durability beyond about four years, and lifetime surveillance for late effects, are still unknown. The drug-therapy shelves are separate homes: hydroxyurea is #669, transfusion for stroke prevention #670, and voxelotor/crizanlizumab and their withdrawals #847. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): near-complete elimination of the disease's defining events in two independent single-arm programmes — short of LIKELY only because nothing here is controlled and the follow-up is short against a lifetime disease. Tier C: one-time irreversible therapy on single-arm evidence, taken to the developer personally.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Gene therapy for transfusion-dependent β-thalassaemia: transfusion independence in 91% with exa-cel and 89–91% with beti-cel, including the severe β0/β0 genotypes
question: In transfusion-dependent β-thalassaemia, does one-time gene therapy (exagamglogene autotemcel, exa-cel, or betibeglogene autotemcel, beti-cel) free patients from regular transfusions?
balance: In three phase 3 single-arm studies, about nine in ten patients stopped transfusing altogether. The CRISPR-edited therapy exa-cel (Locatelli 2024, CLIMB THAL-111) produced transfusion independence — a weighted average haemoglobin of at least 9 g/dL with no red-cell transfusion for at least 12 consecutive months — in 32 of 35 evaluable patients (91%), with mean haemoglobin 13.1 g/dL during independence. The lentiviral therapy beti-cel reached 20 of 22 evaluable patients (91%) in genotypes with some residual β-globin production (Locatelli 2022, HGB-207) and 16 of 18 (89%) in the severe β0/β0-type genotypes that make no β-globin at all (Kwiatkowski 2024, HGB-212), the latter with the longest follow-up here (median 47.9 months). No deaths and no cancers were reported in any of the three studies. The caveats mirror the sickle-cell shelf (#2553): no controlled comparison, busulfan myeloablation as the price of admission, evaluable-patient denominators smaller than the treated numbers, and durability proven only to about four years so far. The two-patient first-in-human CRISPR report (Frangoul 2021), which included the first thalassaemia patient treated, is homed on #2553. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit). Tier C: one-time irreversible therapy on single-arm evidence, taken to the developer personally.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Gene therapy for haemophilia: bleeding rates fell 64–84% (relative) against each cohort's own prophylaxis baseline in three phase 3 studies — liver enzyme rises were the tax
question: In severe haemophilia A and moderate-to-severe haemophilia B, does a single gene-therapy infusion replace regular factor prophylaxis and cut bleeding?
balance: One infusion of an AAV vector carrying the factor gene cut bleeding substantially in all three phase 3 programmes — each compared against the patients' own prophylaxis lead-in period, not against a randomised control. For severe haemophilia A, valoctocogene roxaparvovec (Ozelo 2022, GENEr8-1, 134 men) raised factor VIII activity by a mean of 41.9 IU/dL at one year and reduced treated bleeding by 83.8% relative and factor concentrate use by 98.6% relative in the rollover cohort. For haemophilia B, etranacogene dezaparvovec (Pipe 2023, HOPE-B, 54 men) cut the annualised bleeding rate from 4.19 to 1.51 (rate ratio 0.36 — a 64% relative reduction, with the absolute rates printed here), and fidanacogene elaparvovec (Cuker 2024, BENEGENE-2, 45 men) cut it from 4.42 to 1.28 (a 71% relative reduction). The price is hepatic: alanine aminotransferase rose in 85.8% of valoctocogene recipients, and 62% of fidanacogene recipients needed glucocorticoids for enzyme rises or falling factor levels — the immune response against the vector capsid is the therapy's running battle, and it is why factor VIII expression after valoctocogene is known to wane over the years after infusion (the carded record reports the first year). Pre-existing anti-AAV antibodies excluded most screened men from BENEGENE-2 (59.5% of those ineligible). No inhibitors and no thrombosis in any of the three studies. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit). Tier C: single-arm evidence with durability unresolved, taken to the developer personally. Emicizumab prophylaxis — the non-gene-therapy comparator most patients now use — is on shelves #671 and #1414.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Mepolizumab in eosinophilic COPD: exacerbations 0.80 vs 1.01 a year in MATINEE (rate ratio 0.79) — a real but modest effect, with no gain in symptoms or quality of life
question: In COPD with an eosinophilic phenotype despite triple inhaled therapy, does adding mepolizumab prevent exacerbations?
balance: Yes, modestly, and only in the eosinophil-high phenotype. In MATINEE (Sciurba 2025), 804 patients with COPD, previous exacerbations and blood eosinophils of at least 300 cells/µL on triple inhaled therapy had an annualised rate of moderate or severe exacerbations of 0.80 on monthly mepolizumab versus 1.01 on placebo (rate ratio 0.79, 95% CI 0.66 to 0.94; P = 0.01) — a 21% relative reduction, worth about one-fifth of an exacerbation per patient-year in absolute terms — and a longer time to first exacerbation (median 419 versus 321 days; hazard ratio 0.77, a relative measure). Quality of life and symptom scores did not differ, so patients had fewer events without feeling measurably better. The earlier METREX and METREO trials (Pavord 2017) point the same way at the higher eosinophil counts (rate ratio 0.82 in METREX's eosinophilic population) but were null in unselected patients (rate ratio 0.98) and not significant after multiplicity adjustment in METREO. Adverse events matched placebo in both programmes. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a replicated, phenotype-bound, clinically modest effect. Dupilumab in type-2 COPD — the neighbouring biologic question — is on shelves #812 and #1641.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Avacopan in ANCA-associated vasculitis: remission matched high-dose prednisone at 26 weeks and beat it on sustained remission at 52 (65.7% vs 54.9%)
question: In ANCA-associated vasculitis (granulomatosis with polyangiitis or microscopic polyangiitis), can avacopan replace most of the glucocorticoid taper without losing remission?
balance: In the phase 3 ADVOCATE trial (Jayne 2021), yes on both counts that matter. Avacopan — an oral complement C5a-receptor blocker, added to cyclophosphamide or rituximab induction with only a short low-dose steroid lead-in — matched a standard 20-week prednisone taper for remission at week 26 (72.3% versus 70.1%; noninferior, not superior) and beat it for sustained remission at week 52 (65.7% versus 54.9%; difference 12.5 percentage points, 95% CI 2.6 to 22.3; P = 0.007 for superiority). Serious adverse events were slightly less frequent on avacopan (37.3% versus 39.0%), and glucocorticoid-related toxicity — the harm the drug exists to avoid — accumulates on the steroid side of the ledger. The phase 2 trial (Jayne 2017) had shown the same shape: faster, at-least-as-good early response (86.4% and 81.0% versus 70.0% at week 12) with reduced-dose or no prednisone. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): one phase 3 trial with a superiority win on the endpoint that counts, supported by its phase 2 — short of LIKELY because the phase 3 evidence base is a single trial and remission was not superior at the primary timepoint. The vasculitis shelf's other disease-modifying questions (rituximab, plasma exchange, reduced-dose glucocorticoids) are on shelf #386.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Tarlatamab in previously treated small-cell lung cancer: overall survival 13.6 vs 8.3 months (hazard ratio 0.60) in the phase 3 DeLLphi-304 trial
question: In extensive-stage small-cell lung cancer that has progressed on or after platinum chemotherapy, does tarlatamab improve survival?
balance: Yes — tarlatamab, a bispecific T-cell engager aimed at DLL3, is the first agent in years to move survival in this setting. In the phase 3 DeLLphi-304 trial (Mountzios 2025), 509 patients whose small-cell lung cancer had progressed on or after platinum chemotherapy lived a median of 13.6 months on tarlatamab versus 8.3 months on the investigator's choice of standard second-line chemotherapy (topotecan, lurbinectedin or amrubicin) — hazard ratio 0.60 (95% CI 0.47 to 0.77; P < 0.001), a relative measure that here translates to 5.3 months of median survival — with fewer grade 3-or-worse adverse events than chemotherapy (54% versus 80%) and fewer discontinuations (5% versus 12%). The phase 2 DeLLphi-301 study (Ahn 2023) had set the stage with objective responses in 40% at the 10 mg dose (32% at 100 mg) in a heavily pretreated population, and the phase 1 study (Paz-Ares 2023) first showed the responses could last (median duration 12.3 months). The drug's signature toxicity is cytokine-release syndrome — about half of patients, mostly grade 1–2 and early — plus neurologic events, managed with step-up dosing and monitoring. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): a positive phase 3 survival trial in a disease with almost no wins, consistent with its phase 2. Flagged for the developer's eye: the phase 3 result is a prespecified interim analysis, so the stamp leans on one randomised trial rather than two. A different question — tarlatamab with durvalumab as first-line maintenance (DeLLphi-305) — is not carded here.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: Belzutifan in kidney cancer: progression-free survival advantage and 21.9% vs 3.5% response after immunotherapy in LITESPARK-005; 49% response in von Hippel–Lindau kidney tumours
question: In advanced clear-cell renal cell carcinoma after immunotherapy and anti-angiogenic treatment, does belzutifan (a HIF-2α inhibitor) help — and does it work in von Hippel–Lindau disease?
balance: For pretreated clear-cell kidney cancer, belzutifan beat everolimus on the measures that show a drug is active, but not yet on survival. In LITESPARK-005 (Choueiri 2024), 746 patients whose cancer had advanced after both checkpoint immunotherapy and anti-angiogenic therapy had identical median progression-free survival in the two arms (5.6 months each) yet clearly better progression-free rates at 18 months on belzutifan (24.0% versus 8.3%; P = 0.002) — the curves separate late, so the median hides the benefit — and a far higher objective response rate (21.9% versus 3.5%; P < 0.001). Overall survival was 21.4 versus 18.1 months (hazard ratio 0.88; 95% CI 0.73 to 1.07; P = 0.20 — not significant). Grade 3-or-worse adverse events were similar (61.8% versus 62.5%), with fewer discontinuations on belzutifan (5.9% versus 14.7%). In von Hippel–Lindau disease (Jonasch 2021), where HIF-2α accumulation is the disease mechanism itself, single-arm belzutifan produced responses in 49% of kidney tumours, 77% of pancreatic lesions and 30% of CNS haemangioblastomas, with every evaluable retinal eye improving; anaemia (90%) is the on-target cost. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): progression and response gains without a survival win in the randomised trial, plus mechanism-perfect but uncontrolled evidence in VHL.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: CAR T cells for severe autoimmune disease: all 15 patients in the founding series improved and stopped immunosuppression — uncontrolled evidence only, now with a 24-patient basket trial behind it
question: In severe refractory autoimmune disease (lupus, inflammatory myositis, systemic sclerosis), can CD19 CAR T-cell therapy induce drug-free remission?
balance: The results are dramatic and the evidence is weak — both halves of that sentence matter. In the founding Erlangen series (Müller 2024), 15 patients with severe, treatment-refractory disease — 8 with lupus, 3 with inflammatory myositis, 4 with systemic sclerosis — received CD19 CAR T cells after fludarabine–cyclophosphamide lymphodepletion: every lupus patient reached DORIS remission, every myositis patient had a major clinical response, every sclerosis patient improved on the EUSTAR activity index, and all 15 stopped immunosuppression entirely, over a median follow-up of 15 months. The CASTLE basket trial (Müller 2026) extends this to 24 patients with the engineered product zorpocabtagene autoleucel: 22 of 24 met their disease-specific efficacy endpoints at 24 weeks, including DORIS remission in 9 of 10 lupus patients, again with everyone off glucocorticoids and immunosuppression. Toxicity so far is milder than in oncology use — cytokine-release syndrome grade 1 in most, no ICANS in CASTLE, one pneumonia hospitalisation in the first series. What is missing is everything that makes evidence strong: no control group, no randomisation, no blinding, 39 patients in total worldwide in these reports, follow-up measured in months for diseases that relapse over years, and the near-certainty that the most spectacular responders are the ones written up. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — the display label for exactly this situation: a possibly transformative therapy whose evidence is two uncontrolled series from one research network. Tier C: taken to the developer personally. Rituximab and conventional immunosuppression shelves (for example lupus nephritis #1413) carry the controlled evidence for these diseases.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence)

title: Influenza vaccination in COPD: fewer influenza illnesses and fewer exacerbations in the randomised trials — but no trial shows fewer hospital admissions or deaths
question: In adults with COPD, does influenza vaccination reduce exacerbations and hospitalisation?
balance: The randomised evidence says influenza vaccination protects people with COPD against influenza itself, and probably against exacerbations — but it has never been shown to keep them out of hospital or alive longer. In the only placebo-controlled trial in COPD (Wongsurakiat 2004, PMID: 15189916), influenza-related respiratory illness occurred at 6.8 versus 28.1 episodes per 100 person-years (relative risk 0.24 — a 76% relative reduction), while overall respiratory illness did not differ. The Cochrane pooling of the COPD trials (Kopsaftis 2018, PMID: 29943802) found inactivated vaccine reduced exacerbations by a mean of 0.37 per vaccinated person per season (95% CI −0.64 to −0.11), an estimate the reviewers graded low quality and based on just 180 participants; the mortality data were too small to show any effect. The hospitalisation half of the question is unanswered by vaccine-versus-placebo trials, and the one large dose-comparison trial (DANFLU-1 chronic lung disease analysis, Duus 2025, PMID: 41177098) found no extra benefit from high-dose over standard-dose vaccine in lung-disease patients (hazard ratio 0.95, 95% CI 0.28 to 3.30, for pneumonia or influenza hospitalisation). Local reactions are commoner with vaccine (27% versus 6%) but mild, and vaccination did not provoke early exacerbations. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — real protection against influenza illness, probable protection against exacerbations, unproven against hospitalisation and death. Tier C: taken to the developer personally, because the COPD-specific clinical benefit rests substantially on one small trial.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Pegloticase for refractory gout: urate normalised in 42% on the drug alone and 60% with methotrexate cover, tophi completely resolved in about half — in the minority who keep responding
question: In adults with refractory chronic gout, does pegloticase lower serum urate and resolve tophi versus placebo?
balance: In gout that has failed or cannot tolerate conventional urate lowering, pegloticase does what no oral drug in these patients could: in the twin placebo-controlled trials (Sundy 2011, PMID: 21846852), sustained urate below 6.0 mg/dL was achieved by 42% of patients on biweekly pegloticase and 35% on monthly dosing, against 0 of 43 on placebo. Tophi — the visible burden of the disease — completely resolved in at least one tophus in 45% of biweekly patients versus 8% on placebo at six months (Baraf 2013, PMID: 24286509). The catch is immunogenicity: most patients eventually make anti-drug antibodies, lose the urate response and face infusion reactions, which is why covering pegloticase with methotrexate raised the 12-month responder rate to 60.0% versus 30.8% with placebo cover in the MIRROR randomised trial (Botson 2023, PMID: 37385296), with complete resolution of at least one tophus in 53.8% versus 31.0%. Deaths in the phase 3 trials were 4 on pegloticase and 3 on placebo among 225 patients. PROPOSED LIKELY — strong, replicated randomised evidence for urate lowering and tophus resolution in a population with no working alternative, with the responder minority and the infusion-reaction risk stated on the face of the shelf. Tier C: taken to the developer personally (harm profile and a surrogate primary endpoint).
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: Spironolactone on dialysis: two large blinded trials found no cardiovascular benefit — overturning a small open-label trial that had claimed mortality was cut by two thirds
question: In patients receiving maintenance dialysis for kidney failure, does spironolactone reduce cardiovascular death and hospitalisation for heart failure?
balance: This shelf replaces the assigned allopurinol-in-CKD question, which the library already covers on shelf #168 (CKD-FIX and PERL). For a decade the case for spironolactone on dialysis rested on one small open-label trial (Matsumoto 2014, PMID: 24184249) reporting cardiovascular death or hospitalisation in 5.7% versus 12.5% of patients and all-cause mortality of 6.4% versus 19.7%. The two large double-blind trials reported in 2025 did not reproduce any of it: in ACHIEVE (Walsh 2025, PMID: 40818850; 2,538 randomised patients), the composite of cardiovascular death or heart-failure hospitalisation occurred at 10.46 versus 11.33 events per 100 patient-years (hazard ratio 0.92, 95% CI 0.78 to 1.09), all-cause mortality was similar (hazard ratio 0.95, 95% CI 0.83 to 1.09), and the trial was stopped early for futility; in ALCHEMIST (Rossignol 2025, PMID: 40818851; 644 high-risk haemodialysis patients), major cardiovascular events occurred in 24% of both groups (hazard ratio 1.00, 95% CI 0.73 to 1.36), and potassium above 6 mmol/L was as common on placebo as on spironolactone (41% versus 42%) in this run-in-selected population. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — two adequately sized blinded trials agree on no benefit. Tier C: taken to the developer personally (a cardiovascular-event and mortality question).
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference)

title: Pneumococcal vaccination in COPD: fewer pneumonias and fewer exacerbations in the pooled trials — no difference in admissions or deaths
question: In adults with COPD, does pneumococcal vaccination reduce pneumonia and exacerbations?
balance: The randomised trials in COPD point the same way for infection outcomes and nowhere for survival. The Cochrane pooling (Walters 2017, PMID: 28116747) found vaccination reduced community-acquired pneumonia (odds ratio 0.62, 95% CI 0.43 to 0.89; six studies, 1,372 participants; moderate-quality evidence; number needed to vaccinate 21) and acute COPD exacerbations (odds ratio 0.60, 95% CI 0.39 to 0.93; four studies, 446 participants; number needed to vaccinate 8), with no difference in hospital admissions, all-cause mortality (odds ratio 1.00) or cardiorespiratory mortality (1.07). The largest single trial (Alfageme 2006, PMID: 16227328) was null on its primary analysis (24% efficacy against pneumonia, 95% CI −24 to 54; p = 0.333) with benefit concentrated in patients under 65 and those with severe obstruction, and the oldest trial (Leech 1987, PMID: 3545418) found no difference in deaths, admissions or emergency visits despite a two- to three-fold antibody rise. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — moderate-quality pooled evidence for fewer pneumonias and exacerbations, no evidence for fewer admissions or deaths. Pneumococcal vaccination in older adults generally is covered on shelf #444; this shelf is the COPD-specific record.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Capsaicin for postherpetic neuralgia: the clinic-applied 8% patch beats its control patch by a modest margin; the old 0.075% creams were never shown to do much beyond placebo
question: In adults with postherpetic neuralgia, does capsaicin — the clinic-applied 8% patch or low-concentration creams — reduce pain versus control?
balance: The two forms of capsaicin have very different evidence. For the clinic-applied 8% patch, the randomised trial carded here (Irving 2011, PMID: 21087403) found mean pain fell by 32.0% with the patch versus 24.4% with a low-dose control patch over weeks 2–8 (both figures are relative reductions from baseline), with at least 30% pain relief in 46% versus 34% of patients; the Cochrane pooling of high-concentration capsaicin in postherpetic neuralgia (Derry 2017, PMID: 28085183; four studies, 1,272 participants) found about 10% more patients much or very much improved than with control, a number needed to treat of 8.8. The patch's first large trial (Backonja 2008) is already carded on shelf #695 and is not re-carded here. For the home-applied 0.075% creams, the two small double-blind trials from 1989–1993 (Watson 1993, PMID: 8364943; Bernstein 1989, PMID: 2768576) reported statistically significant pain relief but published few responder numbers, and the Cochrane review of low-concentration capsaicin (Derry 2012, PMID: 22972149) concluded there were insufficient data to conclude it works, with a suggestion of no meaningful effect beyond placebo and local skin reactions at a number needed to harm of 2.5. PROPOSED SPLIT — POSSIBLE for the clinic-applied 8% patch; MAYBE (weak evidence) for low-concentration creams. Tier C: taken to the developer personally, because within this shelf the patch's benefit rests on one carded trial plus a pooled analysis that includes the trial held on shelf #695.
stamp: SPLIT — POSSIBLE for the clinic-applied 8% patch / MAYBE (weak evidence) for low-concentration (0.075%) creams

title: Benzonatate for cough: never shown to relieve cough in a clinical trial — its one controlled test measured a reflex and benzonatate alone failed it, while overdose data show real harm
question: In adults with acute or subacute cough, does benzonatate reduce cough versus placebo or other antitussives?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence): Benzonatate is one of the most prescribed cough suppressants in the United States, and there is no modern randomised trial showing it relieves anyone's cough. The only controlled trial of the drug itself (Dicpinigaitis 2009, PMID: 19121573) was a 30-person crossover study that measured capsaicin cough-reflex sensitivity — a laboratory reflex, not cough relief — in adults with acute viral cough: benzonatate 200 mg alone did not significantly suppress the reflex versus placebo, guaifenesin did, and only the benzonatate–guaifenesin combination beat either drug alone. The remaining efficacy record is a 3-patient case series in opioid-resistant cancer cough (Doona 1998, PMID: 9616460) and uncontrolled 1950s-era reports with no abstracted data. The harm record, by contrast, is modern and concrete: 4,689 paediatric exposure cases reported to US poison centres in 2010–2018, most of them unintentional ingestions by children aged 0–5 (Kim 2022, PMID: 36377394), and in a 20-year single-centre poison series, serious toxicity — seizures, ECG changes, coma — in 22% of intentional exposures, with 2 deaths among 265 exposures (Cicci 2025, PMID: 40511470). A drug can be widely used, genuinely unproven, and dangerous to toddlers who mistake the capsules for sweets; benzonatate is all three. The library's guaifenesin shelf (#2463) covers the expectorant tested alongside it. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (Tier C: a harm-bearing shelf resting on a single small surrogate-endpoint trial).
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence)

title: Topical diclofenac for knee and hand osteoarthritis: beats its vehicle in six double-blind trials and matches oral diclofenac for pain — the trade is skin irritation instead of stomach and blood-test harms
question: In adults with knee or hand osteoarthritis, does topical diclofenac reduce pain versus placebo or oral NSAIDs?
balance: LIKELY: Topical diclofenac is one of the better-tested rub-on treatments in the library. Against vehicle or placebo it won in every large double-blind trial carded here: the 1.5% solution in knee osteoarthritis (Roth 2004, PMID: 15477437, n = 326; Bookman 2004, PMID: 15313991, n = 248 — WOMAC pain change −3.9 versus −2.5 on both control solutions), the same solution in a 775-patient five-arm trial (Simon 2009, PMID: 19380203), the 1% gel in knee osteoarthritis (Barthel 2009, PMID: 19932833, n = 492) and in hand osteoarthritis (Altman 2009, PMID: 19648310, n = 385, NCT00171665). Against oral diclofenac it was not beaten: a 622-patient double-dummy equivalence trial (Tugwell 2004, PMID: 15468367) and Simon 2009 both found no significant efficacy difference, while gastrointestinal adverse events and abnormal liver-function, haemoglobin and creatinine-clearance results were significantly fewer with the topical route. The price is local: application-site dryness, rash or irritation in roughly a fifth to two-fifths of users depending on formulation, leading few to stop. The effect sizes are modest — these are symptom scores moving a few points further than vehicle, not joints restored — and almost all trials were industry-run and short (4–12 weeks). The class-level Cochrane synthesis, covering ketoprofen as well, is homed at shelf #577; shelf #330 covers diclofenac only as the oral comparator in gastroprotection strategies. PROPOSED LIKELY (not Tier C: a symptom claim with no mortality or cardiovascular benefit asserted).
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: Milnacipran for fibromyalgia: three positive phase 3 trials, but a small benefit — and one in five patients stopped the drug for side effects in the largest trial
question: In adults with fibromyalgia, does milnacipran improve pain and global status versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE: Milnacipran passed its pivotal trials — three large double-blind phase 3 studies (Clauw 2008, PMID: 19108787, n = 1,196, NCT00098124; Mease 2009, PMID: 19132781, n = 888; Branco 2010, PMID: 20156949, n = 884, NCT00436033) each found significantly more composite responders — patients simultaneously achieving at least 30% pain improvement, a global rating of much or very much improved, and in two trials a physical-function gain — on milnacipran 100 or 200 mg/day than on placebo, with a smaller phase 2 trial (Vitton 2004, PMID: 15378666) showing at least 50% pain reduction in 37% on twice-daily milnacipran versus 14% on placebo. The catch is size and price: the phase 3 abstracts report significance without printing the responder percentages, the Cochrane synthesis homed at shelf #391 puts substantial pain relief at roughly one patient in ten beyond placebo for this drug class, and adverse events drove 19.5–23.7% of milnacipran patients out of Clauw 2008 versus 9.5% on placebo, with nausea in about a third. Benefit persisted to a year in extension studies (Goldenberg 2010, PMID: 20002596), but extensions keep the patients who already tolerated and responded to the drug. Three positive industry-run pivotal trials clear the two-trial gate; the small absolute benefit and the dropout burden keep the stamp at moderate. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (not Tier C: no mortality or cardiovascular claim; benefit rests on multiple randomised trials, not a single trial or observational data).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Pseudoephedrine for a blocked nose: it does open the nose on objective testing — one positive trial, one missed endpoint, and about +1 mmHg and +3 beats/min as the average price
question: In adults with nasal congestion from the common cold, does oral pseudoephedrine relieve congestion versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE: Pseudoephedrine is the decongestant that survived the phenylephrine reckoning (shelf #2461) — and unlike phenylephrine, it has objective evidence behind it, though less than its reputation suggests. In the cleanest trial (Eccles 2005, PMID: 15794071), 238 adults with cold-related congestion took 60 mg or placebo: nasal airway resistance area-under-curve was significantly lower on pseudoephedrine after a single dose (p = 0.006) and after 3 days of dosing (p < 0.001), with subjective congestion scores significantly better on day 1 but not on the day-3 visual analogue scores. The second repeated-dose trial was cooler: in 216 subjects taking 60 mg four times daily for 3 days, the prespecified primary outcome — day-1 nasal airway resistance AUC — was not significantly different from placebo, with only small objective gains (total nasal volume +5.5% relative, p = 0.031) and a non-significant 7.0% relative fall in congestion VAS (p = 0.072) (Latte 2007, PMID: 17882915). The physiological price is real but small at standard doses: across 24 randomised trials (1,285 patients), pseudoephedrine raised systolic blood pressure by a mean of 0.99 mmHg (95% CI 0.08 to 1.90) and heart rate by 2.83 beats/min (2.0 to 3.6), with no diastolic effect; higher and immediate-release doses raised pressure more (Salerno 2005, PMID: 16087815). A real decongestant effect on objective testing, inconsistently felt by patients, bought with a small pressor effect — that is the whole of it. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (not Tier C: a symptom claim; the blood-pressure data are carded as context, not as a benefit claim).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Antihistamines for the common cold: a small benefit on the first day or two in adults, nothing after that and nothing in children — paid for in sedation
question: In adults with the common cold, do oral antihistamines (first-generation, sedating) reduce symptom severity versus placebo?
balance: SPLIT — a small, brief benefit in adults, then nothing. The Cochrane synthesis (De Sutter 2015, PMID: 26615034) pooled 18 randomised trials with 4,342 participants: in adults, antihistamines improved overall symptom severity on day 1 or 2 — 45% had a beneficial effect versus 38% on placebo (odds ratio 0.74, 95% CI 0.60 to 0.92) — but there was no difference from day 3 onward, and the statistically detectable gains on single symptoms (rhinorrhoea mean difference −0.23 and sneezing −0.35 on 4–5-point scales at day 3) were judged clinically non-significant; there was no clinically significant effect on nasal obstruction. The best individual trials show the same shape at symptom level: clemastine cut rhinorrhoea severity on day 3 (1.02 versus 1.39, P < .001) in 403 adults with natural colds, while sedation hit 14% versus 1.5% on placebo (Turner 1997, PMID: 9356796); in experimental rhinovirus colds, clemastine reduced sneeze scores by 50% relative and secretion weights by 35% relative (Gwaltney 1996, PMID: 8729205). In children the two trials conflict and Cochrane concludes there is no evidence of effectiveness. So the honest answer to 'do antihistamines help a cold?' is: in adults, slightly, for the first day or two, mostly by drying and sedating — and the sedation is not a side issue, since for many combination cold remedies it is most of what the buyer feels. PROPOSED SPLIT — POSSIBLE small benefit on overall symptoms in adults on days 1–2 / LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) from day 3 onward and for individual symptoms at any point; no evidence in children (not Tier C: symptom claims only). Children's cough-and-cold treatment, including the diphenhydramine comparison, is homed at shelf #1045.
stamp: SPLIT — POSSIBLE small benefit on overall symptoms in adults on days 1–2 / LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) from day 3 onward and for individual symptoms; no evidence of benefit in children

title: Allopurinol versus febuxostat, both titrated to target: the older, cheaper drug was noninferior for flares in STOP Gout — and numerically ahead
question: In adults with gout, when allopurinol and febuxostat are each titrated to a serum urate target, how do they compare on gout flares and safety?
balance: One large double-blind trial answers this directly, and its answer is unfashionable: titrated to the same urate target, allopurinol was noninferior to febuxostat for the outcome patients feel — flares. In STOP Gout (O'Dell 2022, PMID: 35434725; 940 participants, at least a third with stage 3 chronic kidney disease), 36.5% of allopurinol patients had one or more flares in the observation phase versus 43.5% on febuxostat (P<0.001 for noninferiority against an 8-percentage-point margin); 80% of both groups reached target urate, and serious adverse events, including cardiovascular events, did not differ. The trial's prespecified kidney subgroup (Helget 2024, PMID: 38906504) found the same shape in stage 3 CKD — flares 32% versus 45% (P=0.02) at equal urate control — with one caution: acute kidney injury was more common on allopurinol in that subgroup. A post-hoc look at the initiation phase (Barry 2024, PMID: 38925627) found starting and escalating either drug carried similar flare risk when prophylaxis (90% colchicine) was given. This shelf is about flare control under treat-to-target dosing; it is distinct from shelf #382, which asks the separate cardiovascular-safety question (CARES and FAST), and from shelf #681 (nurse-led treat-to-target care versus usual GP care). PROPOSED LIKELY (no meaningful difference — allopurinol noninferior) (Tier C: the comparison rests on a single trial and its own sub-analyses).
stamp: LIKELY (no meaningful difference — allopurinol noninferior to febuxostat for flare control)

title: INVICTUS: in rheumatic heart disease with atrial fibrillation, rivaroxaban was worse than a vitamin K antagonist — more cardiovascular events and more deaths, with no bleeding advantage
question: In patients with atrial fibrillation due to rheumatic heart disease, is rivaroxaban as good as a vitamin K antagonist at preventing stroke, systemic embolism, myocardial infarction and death?
balance: The direct-oral-anticoagulant trials that changed practice excluded rheumatic heart disease, and INVICTUS shows why that exclusion mattered. In 4,531 analysed patients with atrial fibrillation and echocardiographically documented rheumatic heart disease (Connolly 2022, PMID: 36036525), the composite of stroke, systemic embolism, myocardial infarction or death occurred in 560 patients on rivaroxaban versus 446 on a dose-adjusted vitamin K antagonist; restricted mean survival time was 1599 versus 1675 days (difference −76 days, 95% CI −121 to −31, P<0.001), and the mortality component alone favoured the vitamin K antagonist by 72 days of restricted mean survival. Major bleeding did not differ significantly — rivaroxaban bought its worse efficacy with no safety gain. Permanent discontinuation of trial medication was more common on rivaroxaban at every visit, a real-world weakness of a fixed-dose drug in this population. The result does not touch ordinary non-valvular atrial fibrillation, where the DOAC evidence stands on its own trials; it closes the door on extrapolating that evidence to rheumatic mitral disease. PROPOSED LIKELY (harm — rivaroxaban inferior) (Tier C: a mortality-bearing cardiovascular-outcome shelf resting on one trial).
stamp: LIKELY (harm — rivaroxaban inferior to vitamin K antagonist therapy)

title: GOAL: four-weekly benzathine penicillin injections for two years cut echocardiographic progression of latent rheumatic heart disease from 8.2% to 0.8%
question: In children and adolescents found by echocardiographic screening to have latent rheumatic heart disease, does secondary antibiotic prophylaxis with four-weekly benzathine penicillin G prevent progression of the valve lesions?
balance: Echocardiographic screening finds rheumatic heart disease years before symptoms, but until GOAL nobody had shown that treating the screen-detected, latent stage changes anything. In the GOAL trial (Beaton 2022, PMID: 34767321), Ugandan children and adolescents aged 5–17 with latent rheumatic heart disease were randomised to benzathine penicillin G injections every 4 weeks for 2 years or to no prophylaxis; at 2 years, echocardiographic progression had occurred in 3 participants (0.8%) on prophylaxis versus 33 (8.2%) without (risk difference −7.5 percentage points, 95% CI −10.2 to −4.7; P<0.001) — roughly 13 children treated for two years to prevent one progression. Harms were small: two serious adverse events attributable to prophylaxis, including one mild anaphylactic reaction (under 0.1% of all doses given). The caveats are structural, not statistical: the outcome is echocardiographic progression, not clinical heart failure or death; the trial sits in one high-burden country; and the screening funnel was enormous — 102,200 children screened to find 926 eligible — which is why the authors themselves say further research is needed before population-level screening can be recommended. Treating latent disease once found is supported; building the screening programme to find it is a separate, unproven step. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (Tier C: single-trial benefit on an imaging outcome).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Treating the soil, not just the rhythm: sustained weight loss, aggressive risk-factor management and exercise each reduced atrial fibrillation — but only one of the three tests was randomised
question: In people with atrial fibrillation, does structured management of weight and cardiovascular risk factors — sustained weight loss, exercise, blood pressure, lipids, glycaemia, alcohol and sleep apnoea — reduce atrial fibrillation burden and recurrence?
balance: Three Adelaide programmes make the same point at three levels of rigour. LEGACY (Pathak 2015, PMID: 25792361) followed 355 patients with atrial fibrillation and BMI ≥27 who had been offered goal-directed weight management: those who lost ≥10% of body weight had a 6-fold greater probability of arrhythmia-free survival than those who lost less (95% CI 3.4 to 10.3, a relative measure), while weight fluctuation over 5% doubled recurrence risk — but patients chose their own effort, so motivation is entangled with the weight loss itself. ARREST-AF (Pathak 2014, PMID: 25456757) applied aggressive risk-factor management after ablation in patients who opted in: arrhythmia-free survival was markedly better than in matched controls (multivariate hazard ratio 4.8, 95% CI 2.04 to 11.4, relative), with only 16% of the managed group still using antiarrhythmic drugs after multiple procedures versus 42.4% of controls. The one randomised test is of exercise rather than weight: ACTIVE-AF (Elliott 2023, PMID: 36752479) randomised 120 patients to a 6-month supervised-plus-home exercise programme and found freedom from AF at 12 months in 40% versus 20% (HR 0.50, 95% CI 0.33 to 0.78), with less severe symptoms — without any between-group difference in weight or blood pressure. Nothing here shows a mortality benefit, and none of it replaces anticoagulation or rate/rhythm therapy; it says the substrate responds to treatment. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (Tier C: the weight and risk-factor claims rest on self-selected cohorts; the single randomised trial is small).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: I-PASS: a structured handoff bundle cut medical errors by about a quarter and preventable adverse events by about a third in its first multicentre test — and the harm reduction held up when the programme spread and when families were brought into it
question: Does implementing the I-PASS structured handoff programme — a standardised mnemonic, training, and faculty observation — reduce medical errors and preventable adverse events in hospital care?
balance: I-PASS is a named programme (like the MENOS CBT protocol, it is identified by its programme name because that is what was tested): a mnemonic structuring oral and written handoffs — Illness severity, Patient summary, Action list, Situation awareness and contingency planning, Synthesis by receiver — bundled with communication training, faculty development and observation, and a sustainability campaign. In the original nine-hospital study (Starmer 2014, PMID: 25372088), across 10,740 admissions the medical-error rate fell from 24.5 to 18.8 per 100 admissions (a 23% relative reduction) and preventable adverse events from 4.7 to 3.3 per 100 admissions (a 30% relative reduction), while nonpreventable adverse events did not change — the internal control that makes the before–after design believable — and handoffs took no longer (2.4 vs 2.5 minutes per patient). When the programme was implemented across 32 hospitals in multiple specialties (Starmer 2023, PMID: 36326255), resident-reported major handoff-related adverse events fell from 1.7 to 0.9 per person-year (47% relative) and minor events from 17.5 to 9.3. The family-centred version (Khan 2018, PMID: 30518517) is the honest complication: overall medical errors did not fall significantly (41.2 vs 35.8 per 1,000 patient-days, P=0.21), though harmful errors fell 37.9% in relative terms (20.7 to 12.9 per 1,000 patient-days, P=0.01) — and non-preventable events fell too, which warns that some of the improvement may be secular trend rather than programme. No study randomised hospitals. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (Tier C: all evidence is before–after).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: FIRST and iCOMPARE: letting residency programmes flex shift-length rules did not worsen patient outcomes — death and serious complications in surgery, 30-day mortality in internal medicine — and interns slept no less
question: For resident physicians, do flexible duty-hour policies — no limits on shift length or on time off between shifts, within the 80-hour week — worsen patient outcomes or resident sleep, compared with the standard ACGME duty-hour rules?
balance: Two national cluster-randomised noninferiority trials asked whether the specific 2011 ACGME limits on shift length and time between shifts are load-bearing for safety. In surgery (FIRST; Bilimoria 2016, PMID: 26836220), 117 programmes were randomised to standard or flexible policies; among 138,691 patients, the 30-day rate of death or serious complications was 9.1% under flexible policies versus 9.0% under standard policies (P=0.92), with noninferiority satisfied, and residents in flexible programmes reported leaving operations (7.0% vs 13.2%) and handing off active issues (32.0% vs 46.3%) less often, with no significant difference in satisfaction with education or well-being. In internal medicine (iCOMPARE; Silber 2019, PMID: 30855740), 63 programmes were randomised; the change in 30-day mortality was noninferior under flexible rules (the upper limit of the one-sided 95% CI for the difference in change, 0.93 percentage points, sat below the 1-point margin), though noninferiority was not met for 30-day readmissions or prolonged stay. The companion sleep study (Basner 2019, PMID: 30855741) measured what the rules are supposed to protect: interns in flexible programmes slept 6.85 versus 7.03 hours per 24 hours — noninferior, as was morning sleepiness — but noninferiority was not established for objective alertness on psychomotor vigilance testing. The fair reading: the shift-length rules, specifically, are not what stands between patients and harm in these systems; the trials do not test abolishing the 80-hour week, which both kept. PROPOSED LIKELY (no difference to patient outcomes) (Tier C: mortality is a primary outcome of both trials).
stamp: LIKELY (the flexible policies made no difference to patient outcomes)

title: Etripamil nasal spray: the first trial missed its 5-hour primary endpoint, but the repeat-dose RAPID trial converted 64% versus 31% within 30 minutes — a self-treatment for PSVT that works in minutes, with a stuffy nose as the price
question: In adults with paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia, does self-administered etripamil nasal spray convert an acute episode to sinus rhythm faster than placebo?
balance: Etripamil is a fast-acting L-type calcium-channel blocker given as a nasal spray, designed — in the trials' own framing — as an investigational self-treatment for paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia (PSVT) outside a medical setting. The programme's two randomised parts tell a before-and-after story about endpoints. NODE-301 part 1 (Stambler 2022, PMID: 36441560) tested a single 70 mg dose against placebo with a 5-hour primary endpoint and missed it: hazard ratio for time to conversion 1.086 (95% CI 0.726 to 1.623, P=0.12) across 156 adjudicated events — although conversions in the first 30 minutes already favoured etripamil (53.7% vs 34.7%, HR 1.87, P=0.02). RAPID (Stambler 2023, PMID: 37331368), part 2 of the same study programme and registry number, added a symptom-prompted repeat dose at 10 minutes and a 30-minute primary endpoint, and hit it clearly: conversion by 30 minutes in 64% on etripamil versus 31% on placebo (HR 2.62, 95% CI 1.66 to 4.15, p<0.0001), median time to conversion 17.2 versus 53.5 minutes. The open-label extension (Ip 2023, PMID: 37753718) found a consistent 60.2% conversion within 30 minutes across 188 self-treated episodes, with repeat episodes in the same patient tending to respond the same way. Adverse effects are dominated by the nose: discomfort in about a quarter, congestion and rhinorrhoea in about a tenth, transient and mild-to-moderate, with no serious drug-related events reported in RAPID. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (Tier C: one positive randomised trial for the regimen that works, from a single development programme).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Non-sugar sweeteners: swapping them for sugar trims about a kilogram in trials; against water the advantage is unproven; the harm signals come from cohort studies that cannot separate the sweetener from the reasons people choose it
question: Do non-sugar sweeteners (aspartame, sucralose, stevia and similar) help with weight and metabolic health when they replace sugar — and is there evidence they cause harm?
balance: The answer depends entirely on the comparison, and the literature's three big syntheses disagree mainly because they weight the comparisons differently. Against sugar, the randomised evidence is consistent and modest: Rogers 2016 (PMID: 26365102) pooled the sustained intervention trials and found low-energy sweeteners reduced body weight by 1.35 kg relative to sugar (95% CI −2.28 to −0.42), with short-term energy intake 94 kcal lower than after sugar and no different from water (−2 kcal). Against nothing in particular, the Cochrane-methodology review for the WHO (Toews 2019, PMID: 30602577) found the cupboard nearly bare: a small BMI advantage in adults (−0.6, from two studies totalling 174 people, low certainty), a smaller BMI z-score rise in children versus sugar (−0.15, moderate certainty), and no detectable effect on any other outcome — including no effect in adults or children actively trying to lose weight. The one head-to-head trial inside a weight-loss programme cuts the other way on water: Peters 2014 (PMID: 24862170) randomised 303 adults to sweetened beverages or water and the sweetener group lost more at 12 weeks (5.95 vs 4.09 kg). The harm story is observational: Azad 2017 (PMID: 28716847) found the randomised trials null on BMI (mean difference −0.37, 95% CI −1.10 to 0.36) while 30 cohort studies linked routine sweetener use to higher weight, waist circumference, obesity, hypertension, metabolic syndrome, type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular events — associations fully compatible with reverse causation, since people gaining weight or developing diabetes are exactly the people who switch to sweeteners. The individual beverage-substitution trials in children and adults are homed at shelves #205 and #565; this shelf judges the sweeteners themselves. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (small benefit when replacing sugar).
stamp: POSSIBLE (small benefit when replacing sugar)

title: The J-curve is an artefact: when abstainer bias is removed and genes do the randomising, moderate drinking shows no protection — risk rises with dose for stroke, heart failure and blood pressure, and total mortality is lowest at or below about 100 g a week
question: Is moderate alcohol drinking actually protective against death and cardiovascular disease, as the J-shaped curve from observational studies suggests?
balance: For decades the observational J-curve — moderate drinkers outliving abstainers — was quoted as settled. Four analyses dismantle it from four directions. Wood 2018 (PMID: 29676281) pooled individual data on 599,912 current drinkers: all-cause mortality was lowest at or below about 100 g of alcohol per week (roughly five to six standard drinks), and above that, life expectancy at age 40 fell by about 6 months at 100–200 g/week, 1–2 years at 200–350 g/week and 4–5 years above 350 g/week; per additional 100 g/week, risk rose for stroke (HR 1.14), heart failure (1.09), fatal hypertensive disease (1.24) and coronary disease excluding myocardial infarction (1.06) — only myocardial infarction itself ran the other way (HR 0.94, all hazard ratios relative measures). Millwood 2019 (PMID: 30955975) used alcohol-metabolism genotypes in 512,715 Chinese adults as nature's randomisation: the conventional analysis reproduced the U-shape, but genotype-predicted intake showed a continuous, positive association with stroke (relative risk per 280 g/week 1.27 for ischaemic stroke, 1.58 for intracerebral haemorrhage) and no association with myocardial infarction (0.96) — the 'protection' did not survive the genetic test. Zhao 2023 (PMID: 37000449) re-ran the mortality meta-analysis across 107 cohorts (4.8 million participants) while modelling former-drinker and other abstainer biases: occasional drinkers (RR 0.96, P=.41) and low-volume drinkers (RR 0.93, P=.07) had no significant mortality advantage over lifetime nondrinkers, while risk became significant at 45–64 g/day (RR 1.19) and ≥65 g/day (RR 1.35), and appeared at lower intakes in women (RR 1.22). The Global Burden of Disease 2020 analysis (PMID: 35843246) lands in between: the theoretical minimum-risk exposure was effectively zero for ages 15–39, with a shallow J only in older adults. Nobody has randomised alcohol, and nobody will; this is as close to causal as the question gets. PROPOSED LIKELY (no protective effect) (Tier C: entirely observational and genetic-epidemiological evidence).
stamp: LIKELY (no protective effect — the apparent benefit of moderate drinking is an artefact of bias)

title: VILPA: in device-measured cohorts of non-exercisers, three or four minutes a day of vigorous everyday movement was associated with roughly a quarter to a half lower mortality — striking numbers from a single observational cohort, with no trial yet
question: In adults who do no formal exercise, do brief vigorous bursts of everyday activity — a minute or two of fast walking, stairs or carrying, a few times a day — reduce the risks of death, cardiovascular disease and cancer?
balance: Wearable accelerometers made a previously invisible exposure measurable: vigorous intermittent lifestyle physical activity (VILPA) — the 1–2 minute bursts of fast walking, stair climbing and load-carrying embedded in ordinary days, done by people who never 'exercise'. In the UK Biobank accelerometry cohort of 25,241 self-reported non-exercisers (Stamatakis 2022, PMID: 36482104), participants accruing the median frequency of 3 length-standardised bouts a day showed 38–40% lower all-cause and cancer mortality risk and 48–49% lower cardiovascular mortality risk than those with no VILPA (relative reductions as reported); the median total duration of 4.4 minutes a day was associated with 26–30% lower all-cause and cancer mortality and 32–34% lower cardiovascular mortality. The companion cancer-incidence analysis (Stamatakis 2023, PMID: 37498576) found 4.5 minutes a day associated with a hazard ratio of 0.80 for total cancer and 0.69 for the composite of physical-activity-related cancers, with a minimal dose around 3.4–3.7 minutes a day. And in the joint sedentary-behaviour analysis (Koemel 2025, PMID: 39325719), high sedentary time carried no excess major cardiovascular event risk in participants with medium-to-high incidental vigorous activity — about 4.1 minutes a day appeared to offset it. Now the discipline: all three papers draw on the same UK Biobank accelerometry subsample with overlapping participants, the design is observational, and the obvious confounder runs hard — people who are already ill move less, so some of the gradient is sickness causing stillness rather than stillness causing sickness. No randomised trial of VILPA exists. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (Tier C: observational, single-cohort).
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence)

title: JYNNEOS vaccine against mpox: two doses protect substantially, one dose less — and all the evidence is observational
question: In adults at risk during the 2022–2023 outbreak, how well did the JYNNEOS (MVA-BN) vaccine prevent mpox — one dose versus two?
balance: POSSIBLE — consistent observational protection, no trial. Three case-control studies from the 2022–2023 United States outbreak point the same way: adjusted effectiveness of two JYNNEOS doses against diagnosed mpox was 66.0% (95% CI 47.4 to 78.1) in a national electronic-health-record study (Deputy 2023, PMID: 37199451), 85.9% (73.8 to 92.4) in a 12-jurisdiction matched study (Dalton 2023, PMID: 37200229), and 88.5% in New York State (Rosenberg 2023, PMID: 37339074). One dose was consistently weaker and far less precise (35.8%, 75.2% and 68.1%). The dose-sparing intradermal route performed similarly to subcutaneous injection where both were measured. What this literature does not establish matters as much: there is no randomised trial, protection in immunocompromised patients is essentially unmeasured (70.2%, CI −37.9 to 93.6), and none of the studies could address severe disease, death, duration of protection, or other mpox clades. Tier C: the shelf rests entirely on observational evidence for a preventive claim, so it is flagged for the developer's personal verdict.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Daily toothbrushing in hospital: about a one-third relative reduction in hospital-acquired pneumonia across randomised trials
question: In hospitalised adults, does daily toothbrushing reduce hospital-acquired pneumonia?
balance: POSSIBLE — a consistent, moderate pooled effect for an intervention with no plausible downside at this scale. The 2024 synthesis of 15 randomised trials in 10,742 hospitalised adults found daily toothbrushing associated with lower hospital-acquired pneumonia (RR 0.67, 95% CI 0.56 to 0.81 — a 33% relative reduction), with the effect clear in ventilated patients (RR 0.68) and imprecise outside the ICU (RR 0.32, CI 0.05 to 2.02); ICU mortality was also lower (RR 0.81, 0.69 to 0.95), with fewer ventilation and ICU days (Ehrenzeller 2024, PMID: 38109100). The Cochrane oral-care review's toothbrushing comparison agrees (VAP RR 0.61, 0.41 to 0.91; low-certainty, 5 trials, 910 patients; Zhao 2020, PMID: 33368159). Brushing cannot be blinded and pneumonia ascertainment is soft, which is why this is POSSIBLE rather than LIKELY; the ICU mortality figure is a pooled secondary outcome and is flagged in the notes. Chlorhexidine oral care is a separate question, homed at shelf #469. Not Tier C: the claim rests on two concordant syntheses of randomised trials and is a pneumonia-prevention claim, not a mortality claim.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Cleaner cookstoves in pregnancy (HAPIN): pollution exposure fell by two-thirds, and birth weight, fetal growth and infant pneumonia did not change
question: In pregnant women who cook with biomass fuel, does switching to a liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) cookstove improve birth weight, fetal growth, or infant pneumonia?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — a large, well-delivered randomised programme with three concordant nulls. In HAPIN, 3,200 pregnant women in Guatemala, India, Peru and Rwanda were randomised to LPG stoves with free fuel or continued biomass cooking; measured particulate exposure fell by about two-thirds (median PM2.5 23.9 vs 70.7 µg/m³). Birth weight differed by 19.6 g (95% CI −10.1 to 49.2; Clasen 2022, PMID: 36214599), severe infant pneumonia occurred at 5.67 vs 6.06 per 100 child-years (IRR 0.96, 98.75% CI 0.64 to 1.44; McCollum 2024, PMID: 38169488), and ultrasound fetal growth was identical (Z-scores −0.13 vs −0.12; Checkley 2024, PMID: 38614630). The three papers are one trial, not three — the shelf says so on every card. The null is scoped: intervention began in mid-pregnancy, and residual exposure stayed above clean-air targets. Tier C: a single trial programme carrying infant-outcome claims, flagged for the developer's personal verdict.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference)

title: Over-the-counter cough suppressants in adults: codeine matched placebo exactly; dextromethorphan's pooled signal is small and contested
question: In adults with acute cough from a cold, do over-the-counter antitussives (dextromethorphan, codeine) reduce cough versus placebo?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the honest summary is that the standard suppressants have never clearly beaten placebo in the condition they are sold for. The Cochrane review of over-the-counter cough medicines (29 trials, 4,835 people) found the six adult antitussive trials variable and concluded there is no good evidence for or against these medicines (Smith 2014, PMID: 25420096). The direct tests explain why: codeine 50 mg was indistinguishable from placebo on sound-meter, frequency and subjective measures in 82 adults, while both groups improved dramatically on their own (Freestone 1997, PMID: 9364418); a single 30 mg dose of dextromethorphan gave 'very little if any support' for a clinically significant effect in 43 adults (Lee 2000, PMID: 11045895); yet pooling six single-dose dextromethorphan trials (710 patients) from the same measurement programme did find statistically significant reductions in sound-derived cough measures over 3 hours (Pavesi 2001, PMID: 11591548). A small, short-window, contested statistical signal is exactly what MAYBE (weak evidence) is for. Guaifenesin is homed at shelf #2463, sedating antihistamines at #2570, and benzonatate at #2566. Not Tier C: symptom claims only, resting on a Cochrane synthesis plus individual trials.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence)

title: Prophylactic antibiotics in necrotising pancreatitis: decades of trials, no demonstrated benefit — the largest blinded trial leaned the wrong way
question: In severe acute (necrotising) pancreatitis, do prophylactic antibiotics prevent infected pancreatic necrosis and death?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the pooled point estimates lean slightly toward antibiotics, but nothing reaches significance and the best trial is flat. The Cochrane review (7 trials, 404 patients with CT-proven necrosis) found mortality 8.4% versus 14.4% and infected necrosis 19.7% versus 24.4%, neither significant; its one significant subgroup — imipenem alone for pancreatic infection (RR 0.34) — was never confirmed (Villatoro 2010, PMID: 20464721). The largest double-blind trial, meropenem versus placebo in 100 patients, found infection in 18% versus 12% and mortality 20% versus 18%, both numerically favouring placebo (Dellinger 2007, PMID: 17457158). A 14-trial meta-analysis (841 patients) found mortality RR 0.74 (0.50 to 1.07) and infected necrosis RR 0.78 (0.60 to 1.02) and concluded no evidence supports routine prophylaxis (Wittau 2011, PMID: 21067283). The stamp stops at POSSIBLE rather than LIKELY because the syntheses' intervals still admit a modest benefit and the underlying trials are small and old. Tier C: the shelf turns on mortality in a lethal disease, so it is flagged for the developer's personal verdict. Probiotics in pancreatitis (PROPATRIA) are homed at shelf #98.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference)

title: Ginger for postoperative nausea: nausea eased modestly across 14 trials; vomiting not demonstrably reduced — and no tested product is named
question: In adults having surgery, does ginger reduce postoperative nausea and vomiting versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE — a consistent, modest effect on nausea, none demonstrated on vomiting. The meta-analysis of 14 randomised trials (1,417 participants) found ginger, versus placebo, lowered nausea severity (mean difference −0.71), cut nausea incidence in the first 6 hours (RR 0.68, 95% CI 0.55 to 0.85 — a 32% relative reduction) and reduced rescue antiemetic use (RR 0.71, 0.62 to 0.82), while vomiting was not significantly reduced (RR 0.78, 0.42 to 1.44) (Zhu 2021, PMID: 34312974). The classic trial found combined nausea-and-vomiting in 21% on powdered ginger root versus 41% on placebo in 120 women (Phillips 1993, PMID: 8214465), and a 150-woman trial of 500 mg ginger capsules found lower nausea severity but no difference in vomiting (Bameshki 2018, PMID: 29629059). Product naming, per the supplement rule: none of the carded publications names a specific product, brand or manufacturer — the trials used powdered root or locally prepared capsules — so no purchasable product can be identified from this record, and today's ginger products may differ in safety and effectiveness; that statement is carried on the cards. Not Tier C: the claim rests on a 14-trial synthesis and is symptom-only.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Hydroxyethyl starch for resuscitation: more kidney failure and dialysis in every large test, and more deaths in sepsis — LIKELY (harm)
question: In critically ill patients needing fluid resuscitation, does hydroxyethyl starch (HES) increase death or kidney failure versus crystalloid?
balance: LIKELY (harm) — two large trials and a 38-trial synthesis converge, and no outcome favours the starch. In severe sepsis, 6% HES 130/0.42 raised 90-day mortality to 51% versus 43% on Ringer's acetate (RR 1.17, 95% CI 1.01 to 1.36) and renal-replacement therapy to 22% versus 16% (Perner 2012, PMID: 22738085). In 7,000 general ICU patients, HES 130/0.4 did not significantly change mortality (18.0% vs 17.0%, RR 1.06, 0.96 to 1.18) but increased renal-replacement therapy (7.0% vs 5.8%, RR 1.21) and adverse events (5.3% vs 2.8%) (Myburgh 2012, PMID: 23075127). Pooling 38 trials, and excluding seven retracted trials whose fraud had flattered HES, mortality RR was 1.09 (1.02 to 1.17), renal failure RR 1.27 (1.09 to 1.47) and renal replacement RR 1.32 (1.15 to 1.50) (Zarychanski 2013, PMID: 23423413). Tier C: a harm shelf turning on mortality and kidney outcomes, flagged for the developer's personal verdict.
stamp: LIKELY (harm)

title: Bowel preparation plus oral antibiotics: the pooled record says infections halve; the largest modern trial found no difference — SPLIT
question: In elective colorectal surgery, does mechanical bowel preparation plus oral antibiotics reduce surgical site infection versus no preparation or mechanical preparation alone?
balance: SPLIT — the answer depends on which evidence you weight. The pooled randomised record favours the combination: a network meta-analysis of 46 trials (12,690 patients) found mechanical preparation plus oral antibiotics roughly halved the odds of surgical site infection versus preparation alone (OR 0.55, 95% CrI 0.39 to 0.76) and versus no preparation (OR 0.52, 0.32 to 0.84) (Koo 2023, PMID: 37256453). The largest modern direct trial disagrees: in MOBILE, 396 patients having colon resection had infection rates of 7% with the full package (polyethylene glycol plus oral neomycin and metronidazole) versus 11% with no preparation — not significant (p = 0.17) — with identical 4% dehiscence rates (Koskenvuo 2019, PMID: 31402112). The likely reconciliation is era: older trials ran against higher baseline infection rates and less modern background care. The shelf presents both without forcing a verdict the record does not contain. Not Tier C: a surgical-site-infection claim with no mortality claim, resting on a large pooled record plus a direct modern trial.
stamp: SPLIT — POSSIBLE on the pooled trial record / the largest modern randomised trial found no significant difference

title: Prophylactic mesh at laparotomy closure (PRIMA): hernias cut from 30% to 13% with onlay mesh in high-risk patients — one trial
question: In high-risk patients having elective midline laparotomy, does prophylactic mesh reinforcement reduce incisional hernia versus suture closure alone?
balance: POSSIBLE — a large effect in a single trial, in the population that has most to gain. In PRIMA, 480 patients having elective midline laparotomy with an abdominal aortic aneurysm or BMI ≥27 were randomised to suture closure, onlay mesh or sublay mesh: incisional hernia at 2 years occurred in 30% with suture, 13% with onlay mesh (OR 0.37, 95% CI 0.20 to 0.69) and 18% with sublay mesh (OR 0.55, 0.30 to 1.00), while seroma was more frequent with onlay mesh and wound infection did not differ (Jairam 2017, PMID: 28641875). Long-term follow-up found mesh explantation for complications in 3.1% of onlay and 0% of retrorectus patients among those with reoperation data — serious mesh-specific morbidity was uncommon (van den Berg 2026, PMID: 39239718). The absolute benefit (about 17 fewer hernias per 100 closures) is a high-risk-stratum number; it will be smaller where baseline hernia risk is lower. Tier C: benefit rests on a single randomised trial, flagged for the developer's personal verdict.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Omitting radiotherapy in low-risk older breast cancer: local recurrence rises to 9.5% at 10 years, survival unchanged — a trade-off, not a free pass
question: In older women with low-risk, hormone-receptor-positive early breast cancer treated with breast-conserving surgery and endocrine therapy, can radiotherapy be omitted without harming survival?
balance: LIKELY — the trial evidence is strong, and what it shows is a trade-off, not a verdict. In PRIME II, 1,326 women aged 65 or older with hormone-receptor-positive, node-negative tumours up to 3 cm, clear margins and adjuvant endocrine therapy were randomised to whole-breast radiotherapy or none: at 10 years, local recurrence was 9.5% without radiotherapy versus 0.9% with it (HR 10.4), yet distant recurrence was not higher (1.6% vs 3.0%) and overall survival was identical (80.8% vs 80.7%) (Kunkler 2023, PMID: 36791159; 5-year report Kunkler 2015, PMID: 25637340, carded as a companion, not independent evidence). The LUMINA cohort shows biomarker selection can find women whose 5-year recurrence risk without radiotherapy is lower still (2.3% in Ki67-defined luminal A disease; Whelan 2023, PMID: 37585627) — with PRIME II's warning attached: recurrence without radiotherapy keeps accruing through year 10. So omission is a legitimate, evidence-framed choice for women who fit these criteria and accept roughly 9 extra local recurrences per 100 over a decade in exchange for avoiding radiotherapy; it is not evidence that radiotherapy does nothing. Tier C: the shelf turns on cancer recurrence and survival outcomes from essentially one randomised trial, flagged for the developer's personal verdict. Radiotherapy for DCIS is homed at shelf #943.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: MenACWY in adolescents: programme data show group W and Y disease falling fast after vaccination, and a randomised trial shows carriage of vaccine serogroups cut by about a third
question: In adolescents, does quadrivalent meningococcal conjugate vaccine (MenACWY) prevent invasive meningococcal disease and reduce nasopharyngeal carriage?
balance: POSSIBLE — the disease evidence is observational and the carriage evidence is a randomised trial of a surrogate. No trial of MenACWY has invasive disease as an endpoint, and none is now feasible. What exists: in a phase 3 observer-blind randomised trial of 2,954 English university students, one dose of MenACWY-CRM reduced carriage of capsular group CWY meningococci by 36.2% relative and of serogroup Y by 39.0% relative versus control over 12 months, though there was no difference at 1 month (Read 2014, PMID: 25145775). England's emergency adolescent MenACWY programme, introduced in 2015 against a group W outbreak, was followed by incidence rate ratios of 0.35 for MenW and 0.21 for MenY disease in 14–18-year-olds, with an estimated overall vaccine effectiveness of 94% (95% CI 80 to 99) against MenCWY disease and most prevented cases attributed to indirect (herd) effects (Campbell 2022, PMID: 34883094). The mechanism is not speculative: when the serogroup C conjugate vaccine was introduced in the UK, serogroup C carriage fell by 81% relative (rate ratio 0.19), vaccine efficacy against carriage was 75%, and there was no serogroup replacement (Maiden 2008, PMID: 18271745). The honest limits: the disease numbers come from surveillance and modelling of an outbreak that might have waned anyway — the estimate of MenW cases prevented through herd effects ranges from 205 to 1,193 depending on the assumed counterfactual — and the carriage trial enrolled 18–24-year-olds, not the 13–18-year-olds programmes target. Whether the 4CMenB vaccine reduces carriage is a separate question, answered at shelf #2593; the recombinant and live zoster vaccines sit at shelves #2483 and #2596.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: 4CMenB in infants: England's programme was followed by group B disease falling by half, then by three quarters, in eligible cohorts — though the per-child effectiveness estimate is imprecise
question: In infants, does the 4CMenB meningococcal B vaccine prevent invasive meningococcal disease?
balance: POSSIBLE — a large, consistent programme effect, but every number is observational and the direct effectiveness estimate is imprecise. England introduced 4CMenB (Bexsero) in September 2015 at a reduced two-dose infant priming schedule (2 and 4 months) with a 12-month booster. In the first 10 months, two-dose vaccine effectiveness against all MenB cases was 82.9% (95% CI 24.1 to 95.2) by the screening method, and MenB cases in vaccine-eligible infants halved compared with the previous 4 years (37 versus an average of 74; incidence rate ratio 0.50, 95% CI 0.36 to 0.71), regardless of each infant's own vaccination status (Parikh 2016, PMID: 28100432). Over the first 3 years, 63 cases were observed in eligible cohorts versus 253 expected (incidence rate ratio 0.25, 95% CI 0.19 to 0.36) — a 75% relative reduction in fully eligible age groups — with an estimated 277 cases prevented (Ladhani 2020, PMID: 31971676). The tension a reader should see: in that 3-year analysis the adjusted per-child effectiveness was 52.7% for the two-dose schedule and 59.1% with the booster, but both confidence intervals cross zero (−33.5 to 83.2 and −31.1 to 87.2), because disease became so rare that the screening method lost precision. The programme-level fall is the stronger evidence; the per-child number is the weaker one. There is no randomised trial with a disease endpoint, and none is feasible at this incidence. Whether 4CMenB reduces adolescent carriage — the herd-protection question — is answered separately at shelf #2593, and its cross-protection against gonorrhoea at shelf #2594.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: 4CMenB does not stop adolescents carrying meningococci: in a 24,000-student cluster trial, carriage of disease-causing strains was 2.55% in vaccinated schools and 2.52% in controls
question: In adolescents and young adults, does MenB vaccination (4CMenB) reduce meningococcal carriage?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — for the outcome that matters, carriage of disease-causing meningococci. The definitive test is the South Australian 'B Part of It' cluster-randomised trial: 237 schools, 24,269 students aged 15–18, randomised by school to 4CMenB at baseline or at 12 months. At 12 months, carriage of disease-causing Neisseria meningitidis was 2.55% in the vaccination group and 2.52% in controls (adjusted odds ratio 1.02, 95% CI 0.80 to 1.31; P = 0.85), with no significant differences in any secondary carriage outcome (Marshall 2020, PMID: 31971677). A substudy of the same trial found no difference in carriage density either (3.80 versus 3.73 log CFU/mL, P = 0.51), although students who were already carriers at baseline were less likely to still be carrying at 12 months if vaccinated (31% versus 43%; odds ratio 0.60, 95% CI 0.40 to 0.90) — a clearance signal that did not translate into lower carriage prevalence (McMillan 2021, PMID: 32447370). One tension to state plainly: the smaller English student trial (Read 2014, homed at shelf #2591) found 4CMenB reduced carriage of capsular groups BCWY by 26.6% relative from 3 months — but its outcome counted all capsular-group carriage, not specifically disease-causing genogroups, in a population with much higher baseline carriage. The practical consequence: unlike the conjugate vaccines (shelf #2591), 4CMenB should not be expected to generate herd protection; its value is direct protection of the vaccinated person (shelves #2592 and #2594).
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference)

title: An accidental gonorrhoea vaccine: meningococcal B vaccination is associated with roughly a quarter to two fifths fewer gonorrhoea infections across three observational studies
question: In adults, does MenB vaccination protect against gonorrhoea?
balance: POSSIBLE — three observational studies, two related vaccines, a consistent direction, and no randomised trial. The signal first came from New Zealand's MeNZB campaign vaccine (an outer-membrane-vesicle MenB vaccine, later withdrawn): in a retrospective case-control study of 14,730 sexual-health clinic attendees aged 15–30, vaccinated people were less likely to have gonorrhoea than chlamydia-only controls, giving an adjusted effectiveness of 31% (95% CI 21 to 39) against gonorrhoea diagnosis (Petousis-Harris 2017, PMID: 28705462). A New Zealand cohort study of 935,496 people estimated effectiveness of 24% (95% CI 1 to 42) against hospitalisation from gonorrhoea (Paynter 2019, PMID: 30621260). With the current 4CMenB vaccine, a US study linking STI surveillance to immunisation registries in New York City and Philadelphia found complete two-dose vaccination 40% effective (95% CI 23 to 53) and a single dose 26% effective (12 to 37) against gonorrhoea in 16–23-year-olds (Abara 2022, PMID: 35427490). The biology is plausible — the gonococcus and meningococcus are close relatives and share outer-membrane antigens — but every estimate is vulnerable to confounding: people who got these vaccines differ from those who did not in healthcare contact and sexual-health service use, and the 'healthy vaccinee' problem has been raised specifically for this literature. Effect sizes of 24–40% relative are worth having for a disease with rising antibiotic resistance, but they are not trial-grade numbers, and no guideline should quote them as if they were. Trials of 4CMenB for gonorrhoea prevention are the missing evidence. Treatment of gonorrhoea itself is homed at shelves #1635 and #2190–#2193; post-exposure doxycycline at shelf #582.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)
