title: Two doses beat one: over ten years the varicella vaccine was 98.3% effective with two doses versus 94.4% with one, and breakthrough disease climbs steeply as the years since a single dose pass
question: In children, do two doses of varicella vaccine prevent chickenpox and breakthrough disease better than one dose?
balance: LIKELY — three different designs point the same way. In the randomised comparison with 10-year active follow-up of about 2,000 children, estimated efficacy of varicella vaccine (Oka/Merck, VARIVAX) was 94.4% for one injection and 98.3% for two (P < 0.001); the cumulative risk of varicella was 7.3% after one dose versus 2.2% after two — a 3.3-fold lower risk with two doses — and most breakthrough cases in both groups were mild (Kuter 2004, PMID: 14872179). The reason a second dose matters is visible in US surveillance: among one-dose recipients, the annual breakthrough rate rose from 1.6 per 1,000 person-years in the first year after vaccination to 9.0 at 5 years and 58.2 at 9 years, and children vaccinated 5 or more years earlier were more likely to have moderate or severe breakthrough disease (risk ratio 2.6, 95% CI 1.2 to 5.8) (Chaves 2007, PMID: 17360990). After the routine second dose was introduced, a matched case-control study with PCR-confirmed cases found 2-dose effectiveness of 98.3% (95% CI 83.5 to 100) and odds of varicella 95% lower with two doses than with one (odds ratio 0.053, 95% CI 0.002 to 0.320) (Shapiro 2011, PMID: 21208922). The residual questions are about the second dose's own durability — the case-control data cover only the first 2.5 years after the recommendation — and about herpes zoster in vaccinated cohorts as they age, which none of these studies answers. This shelf is about dose number; the live attenuated zoster vaccine given to older adults is shelf #2596.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: The live zoster vaccine halved shingles in its one big trial — but protection faded to about a fifth by years 7–11, which is why the recombinant vaccine has replaced it
question: In adults aged 60 and over, does the live attenuated zoster vaccine prevent shingles, and how fast does protection wane?
balance: LIKELY — one very large randomised trial, a consistent field cohort, and a clear waning curve. In the Shingles Prevention Study, 38,546 adults aged 60 and over were randomised to live attenuated Oka/Merck zoster vaccine or placebo: over a median 3.12 years there were 315 confirmed herpes zoster cases in vaccine recipients versus 642 in placebo recipients — efficacy 51.3% against incidence, 66.5% against postherpetic neuralgia (27 versus 80 cases), and 61.1% against the burden-of-illness measure (Oxman 2005, PMID: 15930418). In routine practice (Kaiser Permanente Southern California), vaccinated adults had a zoster incidence of 6.4 versus 13.0 per 1,000 person-years in matched unvaccinated adults (adjusted hazard ratio 0.45, 95% CI 0.42 to 0.48) (Tseng 2011, PMID: 21224457). The catch is durability: in the long-term persistence substudy, which followed 6,867 original vaccine recipients for up to 11 years against modelled placebo rates, estimated efficacy against zoster incidence fell from 51.3% to 21.1%, remained significantly above zero only through year 8 for incidence (year 10 for burden of illness), and declined across every outcome from years 7 to 11 (Morrison 2015, PMID: 25416754). So the live vaccine worked, briefly by vaccine standards — a profile that explains why the adjuvanted recombinant vaccine, with higher and more durable efficacy, has displaced it where available (that vaccine is shelf #2483; whether zoster vaccination affects dementia risk is a different question, at shelf #442). Being live, this vaccine was also contraindicated in significant immunosuppression, a restriction the recombinant product does not share.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: Tick-borne encephalitis vaccination in Austria: field effectiveness of about 99% in people vaccinated on schedule, and national incidence down to roughly a sixth of the pre-vaccine era
question: In endemic regions, does tick-borne encephalitis vaccination prevent TBE at population level?
balance: POSSIBLE — the effect size is very large and internally consistent, but the evidence is field epidemiology from essentially one country's programme and one research group, with no randomised trial. Austria is the natural experiment: by the 2000s, 88% of its population had a history of TBE vaccination and 58% were vaccinated within the recommended schedule. Comparing hospitalised cases in vaccinated and unvaccinated people against population denominators for 2000–2006, field effectiveness in regularly vaccinated persons was about 99%, with no significant difference between age groups; it was at least as high after the first two doses, but significantly lower — about 95% — in people with irregular vaccination histories. An estimated 2,800 cases were prevented in 2000–2006 (Heinz 2007, PMID: 17869389). Over 40 years, Austrian TBE incidence fell to about 16% of the prevaccination era while incidence in the unvaccinated population remained high, and incidence stayed high in the Czech Republic and Slovenia, where coverage was lower; about 4,000 cases were estimated prevented in Austria in 2000–2011 (Heinz 2013, PMID: 23259984). The caveats are structural: TBE incidence fluctuates strongly year to year with tick ecology and human exposure, case ascertainment and denominators come from surveys, and the comparison between countries is ecological. Even so, a fall confined to the vaccinated population, sustained over decades, at 99% estimated effectiveness, is not plausibly an artefact of weather. Both cards come from the Austrian reference-laboratory group that also advises the programme — independent replication in other high-coverage settings would strengthen this shelf.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Japanese encephalitis vaccines work: 91% efficacy in a 65,000-child randomised trial of the inactivated vaccine, and 97.5% effectiveness for two doses of the live SA14-14-2 vaccine
question: In children and travellers in endemic Asia, do Japanese encephalitis vaccines prevent JE?
balance: LIKELY — a large randomised trial with a clinical endpoint for one vaccine, a strong case-control estimate for the other, and an immunogenicity bridge to the modern product. In northern Thailand, 65,224 children were randomised to two doses of inactivated mouse-brain-derived JE vaccine (monovalent or bivalent) or tetanus toxoid placebo: the cumulative attack rate for JE was 51 per 100,000 on placebo versus 5 per 100,000 in each vaccine group — efficacy 91% (95% CI 70 to 97) (Hoke 1988, PMID: 2842677). For the inexpensive live attenuated SA14-14-2 vaccine used across China, a case-control study in Sichuan (56 serologically confirmed cases, 1,299 matched controls) estimated effectiveness of 80% (95% CI 44 to 93) for one dose and 97.5% (86 to 99.6) for two doses given a year apart (Hennessy 1996, PMID: 8667866). The modern Vero-cell inactivated vaccine (Ixiaro) was never trialled against disease; its licence rests on a non-inferiority immunogenicity trial in 867 adults, in which seroconversion was 98% versus 95% for the older mouse-brain vaccine and geometric mean titres were 2.3-fold higher (Tauber 2007, PMID: 18061060). That bridge is reasonable — neutralising antibody is the accepted correlate — but it is a bridge: the 91% figure belongs to a discontinued mouse-brain product, and travellers receiving the Vero-cell vaccine are protected by inference from antibody levels, not by a disease-endpoint trial of their vaccine. (The slate that proposed this shelf described the Hoke trial as a live SA14-14-2 trial; the fetched record shows it tested inactivated vaccines — the live vaccine's evidence is Hennessy 1996.)
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: Hepatitis A vaccine after exposure: it prevented secondary cases in a randomised household trial and met non-inferiority against immune globulin — with a hint it may be slightly less effective
question: After exposure to hepatitis A, does hepatitis A vaccine prevent illness as well as immune globulin?
balance: POSSIBLE — one head-to-head trial that met its non-inferiority criterion while pointing slightly the wrong way, plus one randomised trial showing the vaccine works as post-exposure prophylaxis at all. In Almaty, Kazakhstan, 1,090 susceptible household and day-care contacts aged 2–40 were randomised within 14 days of exposure to one dose of hepatitis A vaccine or to immune globulin: symptomatic laboratory-confirmed hepatitis A occurred in 4.4% of vaccine recipients (25 of 568) versus 3.3% of immune globulin recipients (17 of 522) — relative risk 1.35 (95% CI 0.70 to 2.67). The prespecified non-inferiority criterion was met, and both groups' rates were low, but the point estimate favours immune globulin and the authors themselves note the difference might be clinically meaningful in some settings (Victor 2007, PMID: 17947390). That the vaccine is active after exposure is independently supported by an Italian randomised trial in household contacts of sporadic cases: secondary infection occurred in 1.0% of vaccinated contacts (2 of 197) versus 5.8% of unvaccinated contacts (12 of 207) — protective efficacy 79% (95% CI 7 to 95), with 18 contacts needing vaccination to prevent one secondary infection (Sagliocca 1999, PMID: 10209977). The vaccine's practical advantages are real: it also confers long-term protection, is more available than immune globulin, and avoids a blood product. The honest summary for a clinician choosing today: vaccine is a reasonable, evidence-backed alternative to immune globulin for post-exposure prophylaxis in healthy younger contacts; where the exposure is high-risk or the contact is older or immunocompromised, the trial evidence does not exclude a modest advantage for immune globulin, and this shelf takes no position beyond the data.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Hepatitis B vaccination in dialysis patients: adjuvanted vaccines and intradermal rescue raise seroprotection in individual trials, but the pooled adjuvant advantage is not significant
question: In patients on dialysis, do intensified hepatitis B vaccine regimens (high-dose, four-dose, or adjuvanted) achieve seroprotection?
balance: POSSIBLE — intensified regimens beat the standard schedule in individual trials on the seroprotection surrogate, but the pooled evidence is equivocal and no trial measures clinical hepatitis B. The reference intensified regimen is four double doses of standard vaccine; against that benchmark, the AS04-adjuvanted vaccine (HBV-AS04) produced an earlier antibody response, higher titres and significantly higher seroprotection rates throughout 42 months of follow-up in pre-dialysis and haemodialysis patients, with slower decline and fewer boosters needed (Kong 2008, PMID: 18160963). A TLR9-agonist-adjuvanted vaccine (HBsAg-1018, the vaccine later licensed as Heplisav-B) given as 3 single doses achieved a seroprotection rate of 89.9% at week 28 versus 81.8% for four double doses of standard vaccine in 467 evaluable patients with chronic kidney disease — meeting both non-inferiority and superiority — with geometric mean antibody concentrations of 587.1 versus 156.5 mIU/mL (Janssen 2013, PMID: 23727422). For patients who have already failed a primary course, route matters: in 59 haemodialysis nonresponders, intradermal revaccination (10 µg weekly for 8 weeks) produced seroconversion in 79% versus 40% with intramuscular revaccination (odds ratio 5.5, 95% CI 1.6 to 18.4), with higher peak titres (Barraclough 2009, PMID: 19481320). Against all this stands the meta-analysis of adjuvanted hepatitis B vaccines in chronic kidney disease: across 10 randomised trials with 1,228 patients, the pooled odds ratio for seroprotection with adjuvants was 1.47 (95% CI 0.88 to 2.46) — not significant, including in the AS04/AS02 subgroup (Fabrizi 2012, PMID: 22285268). The fair reading: seroprotection is achievable in most dialysis patients with intensified schedules; adjuvanted products won their own trials but not the pooled analysis, possibly because trials differed in populations and comparators; and seroprotection (anti-HBs ≥10 mIU/mL) is a surrogate whose durability on dialysis is itself imperfect. Hepatitis B vaccination of healthcare workers who fail a first series is a different population, held as a separate question in the slate.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Tai chi and falls: fall rates fell by roughly two-fifths in the first year in pooled trials — the protection fades with time, and the evidence on injuries is thin
question: In community-dwelling older adults, does tai chi reduce falls and fall injuries?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — two meta-analyses of randomised trials and the best single trial agree that tai chi reduces falls in older adults, with the effect strongest in the first year. Lomas-Vega 2017 (PMID: 28736853) pooled 10 RCTs: fall incidence IRR 0.57 (95% CI 0.46 to 0.70) short term — a 43% relative reduction — attenuating to 0.87 (0.77 to 0.98) beyond 12 months; injurious falls IRR 0.50 short term on very low-quality evidence; time to first fall unchanged (HR 0.98). Del-Pino-Casado 2016 (PMID: 27430918), pooling 13 controlled trials as absolute risk reduction, found the same direction with low heterogeneity. In the landmark single trial, Li 2005 (PMID: 15814861), 256 inactive adults aged 70–92 randomised to thrice-weekly tai chi for 6 months had 38 falls versus 73 on stretching, with injurious falls in 7% versus 18%. The general falls-prevention shelf (#161) homes the later Li 2018 trial of Tai Ji Quan against multimodal exercise; this shelf answers the tai-chi-specific question and does not re-card it. What the evidence does not show: fewer fractures, a delay in the first fall, or protection that survives stopping practice.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: Yoga for blood pressure: pooled trials suggest about 5–10 mm Hg systolic — but the trials are small, unblinded and wildly inconsistent, and yoga did not beat ordinary exercise
question: In adults with hypertension, does yoga lower blood pressure?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the direction is consistent across three syntheses and the size is clinically meaningful if real, but the underlying trials are small, unblindable and extremely heterogeneous. In hypertension-specific trials, Cramer 2014 (PMID: 24795403) found −9.65 mm Hg systolic versus usual care on very low-quality evidence (I² = 90%), and no effect versus exercise. Wu 2019 (PMID: 30792067), pooling 49 controlled trials and 3,517 participants, found average reductions of 5.0/3.9 mm Hg, with the largest modelled effects (11/6 mm Hg) when breathing and meditation were included and practice was three times a week in hypertensive samples. Cramer 2014 (PMID: 24636547), across 44 RCTs in broader populations, found −5.85/−4.12 mm Hg versus usual care. Read together: yoga probably lowers blood pressure by roughly 4–6 mm Hg on average against doing nothing — comparable to other lifestyle measures — but no trial shows it lowers pressure more than ordinary exercise, and none measures cardiovascular events. It is an adjunct, not a substitute for drug treatment.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Wearable trackers and weight: pooled short trials say devices help a little; the one large two-year trial found the tracker group lost LESS weight
question: In adults with overweight, does adding a wearable activity tracker to a weight-loss programme help weight loss, or hinder it?
balance: SPLIT — the answer depends on the time horizon. In pooled short-term trials in overweight adults with chronic conditions, wearable-based strategies ranked best for weight reduction (McDonough 2021, PMID: 33731385), and trackers reliably raise physical activity. But the only large long-term randomised test, IDEA (Jakicic 2016, PMID: 27654602), found the opposite of the marketing claim: over 24 months, adding a wearable to a behavioural programme produced 3.5 kg of weight loss versus 5.9 kg without it. The long-term systematic review (Fawcett 2020, PMID: 32154788) found five studies of a year or more and no advantage over comparators in any of them. PROPOSED SPLIT — POSSIBLE small benefit in short pooled trials / LIKELY (no advantage over standard programmes long term — in the largest trial, less weight loss). A tracker is a reasonable activity prompt; as a weight-loss intervention in its own right it has failed its biggest test.
stamp: SPLIT — POSSIBLE small benefit in short pooled trials / LIKELY (no advantage over standard programmes long term — in the largest trial, less weight loss)

title: Produce prescriptions: vouchers are redeemed and produce intake rises, and HbA1c fell within groups in small studies — but the one pilot randomised trial found no significant advantage over control
question: In adults with food insecurity and diet-related disease, do produce prescriptions improve diet, glucose control and food security?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the programmes do what they mechanically promise: people redeem the vouchers and eat more produce. But the health-outcome evidence is one small pilot trial and uncontrolled before-and-after studies. The pilot RCT (Bryce 2021, PMID: 34150472; n = 112) found no significant between-group difference in HbA1c, blood pressure or BMI, though HbA1c fell within the intervention group (9.64% to 9.14%). The uncontrolled Detroit evaluation (Bryce 2017, PMID: 28702315) reported HbA1c falling from 9.54% to 8.83% in 65 patients — a fall of the size regression to the mean alone could produce in patients recruited for poor control. In food-insecure hypertensive patients, Trapl 2018 (PMID: 30447106) documented voucher redemption by 86% of participants and significantly improved self-reported fruit and vegetable intake, with no health outcomes measured. Food security itself was not an endpoint in any of the three studies. Tier C: a shelf resting on a pilot trial and observational programme evaluations, flagged for the developer's personal verdict.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence)

title: Medically tailored meals: an instrumental-variable cohort links them to half the admission rate, a small crossover trial shows diet quality transformed — and no trial has yet tested admissions or HbA1c
question: In patients with diabetes or heart failure, do medically tailored meals reduce admissions and improve control?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the direction is consistent and the mechanism is proven, but the headline outcome has never been randomised. The admissions claim comes from a single instrumental-variable cohort (Berkowitz 2019, PMID: 31009050): IRR 0.51 (95% CI 0.22 to 0.80) for inpatient admissions — a 49% relative reduction — in recipients far sicker than their matched comparators, a design whose answer depends on an unverifiable instrument. The randomised evidence is a 44-patient crossover trial (Berkowitz 2019, PMID: 30421335) showing diet quality transformed while meals were delivered (Healthy Eating Index 71.3 vs 39.9) with less food insecurity and less hypoglycaemia, but no HbA1c or admissions endpoint. Pooling the wider food-is-medicine literature in diabetes (Gao 2023, PMID: 36470724), five RCTs gave HbA1c 0.47 percentage points lower, with I² = 88% and half the literature at high risk of bias. Tier C: the shelf's main claim is observational-dependent, flagged for the developer's personal verdict. A definitive admissions trial remains the missing study.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Very-low-nicotine cigarettes: smokers given them smoked fewer cigarettes, took in less nicotine and showed no sign of smoking harder to compensate — and immediate reduction beat gradual
question: In smokers, do very-low-nicotine cigarettes reduce smoking and dependence without compensatory smoking?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — for the question asked, two large double-blind randomised trials agree. Donny 2015 (PMID: 26422724; n = 840) found smokers randomised to cigarettes at or below 2.4 mg nicotine per gram smoked about 5–7 fewer cigarettes a day at 6 weeks than controls (14.9 vs 21.3–22.2 per day at 0.4 mg/g), with lower nicotine exposure and dependence and no significant rise in expired carbon monoxide or total puff volume — minimal compensatory smoking. Hatsukami 2018 (PMID: 30193275; n = 1,250) showed immediate reduction to 0.4 mg/g beat both gradual reduction and continued normal nicotine on all three toxicant-exposure biomarkers over 20 weeks, while gradual reduction was indistinguishable from control — the policy-relevant finding that a standard must bite at once. The boundary of the claim: outcomes are cigarettes smoked and exposure biomarkers over weeks, in smokers not seeking treatment; biomarkers of biological harm did not consistently improve over 20 weeks (Hatsukami 2019, PMID: 31140663), and no trial measures disease outcomes or population-level quitting.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: Quitline counselling: multiple proactive calls raise quit rates by about a quarter to two-fifths relative — worth roughly 2–3 extra quitters per 100 callers at a year
question: In smokers trying to quit, does telephone quitline counselling increase abstinence?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — a large, consistent randomised literature with a real-world confirmation. The Cochrane synthesis (Matkin 2019, PMID: 31045250) pooled 104 trials and 111,653 smokers: multiple sessions of proactive counselling for helpline callers raised long-term abstinence with RR 1.38 (95% CI 1.19 to 1.61) relative, and telephone counselling offered to recruited smokers gave RR 1.25 (1.15 to 1.35) — both graded moderate certainty after downgrading for heterogeneity. In absolute terms the effect is modest: in the randomised trial embedded in the operating California Smokers' Helpline (Zhu 2002, PMID: 12362011), 12-month abstinence was 9.1% with the counselling protocol versus 6.9% in controls. Quitlines are cheap, scalable and genuinely effective — and even with them about 9 in 10 callers are smoking at a year, which is why counselling is normally paired with pharmacotherapy (shelves #2608, #225).
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: Combination NRT: patch plus a fast-acting form beats either alone — quit rates about 27% higher relative, the one high-certainty dosing answer in the NRT literature
question: In smokers, does combination nicotine replacement (patch plus a fast-acting form) beat single-form NRT?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — unusually for a dosing question, the evidence is high-certainty. The Cochrane review of NRT forms, doses, durations and schedules (Theodoulou 2023, PMID: 37335995) found combination NRT — a patch plus a fast-acting form — beat single-form NRT for abstinence at six months or longer with RR 1.27 (95% CI 1.17 to 1.37) relative, I² = 12%, across 16 studies and 12,169 smokers, while patch and fast-acting forms used alone produced similar quit rates (RR 0.90). The largest head-to-head pharmacotherapy trial (Piper 2009, PMID: 19884613; n = 1,504) fits the same pattern: patch plus lozenge was the only one of five regimens significantly better than placebo at 6 months after correction for multiple comparisons (OR 2.34). In absolute terms the combination advantage is a few additional quitters per 100 smokers treated — real, cheap and safe, and the default way NRT should be prescribed. Starting NRT before quit day (preloading) is covered by the same Cochrane review's comparisons and is homed on shelf #2609 with its dedicated trial.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: Pre-loading and reduce-to-quit: the pooled preloading signal is positive but the largest trial missed its primary endpoint; NRT-assisted gradual reduction roughly doubles eventual quitting in smokers not ready to stop
question: In smokers, does starting NRT before quit day (pre-loading) or reducing-to-quit with NRT improve success?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two strategies for smokers who cannot or will not stop abruptly, each with a real but insecure signal. For pre-loading, the dedicated pragmatic trial (Preloading Investigators 2018, PMID: 29899061; n = 1,792) missed its primary endpoint unadjusted (17.5% vs 14.4% abstinent at 6 months; OR 1.25, 95% CI 0.97 to 1.62) and reached significance only after adjustment for reduced varenicline use in the preloading arm (OR 1.34, 1.03 to 1.73). The Cochrane NRT review homed on shelf #2608 pooled 9 preloading studies (4,395 participants) at RR 1.25 (1.08 to 1.44) relative, moderate certainty — but the effect did not survive restriction to studies at low or unclear risk of bias. For reduce-to-quit, the harm-reduction Cochrane review (Lindson-Hawley 2016, PMID: 27734465) found NRT-assisted reduction in smokers not ready to quit raised both cutting down by at least half (RR 1.75, 1.44 to 2.13) and eventual quitting (RR 1.87, 1.43 to 2.44) versus placebo, on low-quality evidence, with biomarker falls smaller than the falls in cigarette counts. Neither strategy has evidence on health outcomes; both are reasonable offers to smokers who would otherwise do nothing.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Heated tobacco: switching lowers several toxicant biomarkers toward abstinence levels in industry-run trials — and there is no randomised evidence at all that it helps anyone quit
question: In adults who smoke, do heated tobacco products reduce exposure to toxicants compared with cigarettes — and compared with quitting?
balance: SPLIT — the exposure half of the industry claim is supported by randomised data; the cessation half has never been tested. Switching from cigarettes to heated tobacco lowered biomarkers of exposure — in one 180-day trial (Gale 2021, PMID: 34196886) to levels similar to those in smokers who abstained entirely — and improved 5 of 8 pre-specified biomarkers of biological effect over 6 months (Lüdicke 2019, PMID: 31270101). But the Cochrane review (Tattan-Birch 2022, PMID: 34988969) found 13 studies in which not one reported smoking-cessation outcomes; adverse events were no different from continued smoking (RR 1.03, 95% CI 0.92 to 1.15); follow-up was a median of 13 weeks; and every randomised trial was funded by a tobacco company. Compared with quitting, there is no comparison to make: no trial measures disease outcomes, and dual use — the common real-world pattern — sits outside the trials' exclusive-use designs. PROPOSED SPLIT — POSSIBLE (lower toxicant exposure than continued smoking) / no evidence of a cessation benefit. Tier C: surrogate-outcome evidence from a single interested source, flagged for the developer's personal verdict.
stamp: SPLIT — POSSIBLE (lower toxicant exposure than continued smoking) / no evidence of a cessation benefit

title: REACH-HF: a facilitated home-based rehabilitation programme improved quality of life in heart failure — tested against usual care, not against centre-based rehab
question: In patients with heart failure, does home-based cardiac rehabilitation work as well as centre-based programmes?
balance: The honest starting point is that the head-to-head question — home-based versus centre-based rehabilitation in heart failure — has never been randomised. What has been tested is a specific facilitated home programme, REACH-HF (Rehabilitation EnAblement in CHronic Heart Failure), against usual care, in a health system where usual care for most heart-failure patients meant no rehabilitation at all. In the main trial (Dalal 2019, PMID: 30304644), 216 patients with HFrEF (mean ejection fraction 34%) gained a clinically meaningful improvement in disease-specific quality of life at 12 months — Minnesota Living with Heart Failure score 5.7 points better than usual care (95% CI −10.6 to −0.7) — with no significant difference in clinical events, in a trial far too small to judge them. A 50-patient pilot extended the same programme to HFpEF with a favourable but imprecise signal (Lang 2018, PMID: 29632081), and UK modelling put the programme at £1,720 per quality-adjusted life-year (Taylor 2019, PMID: 30884975). So home-based rehabilitation is a reasonable, cheap way to deliver a benefit that exercise-based rehabilitation itself carries (homed at shelf #171); whether it matches a good centre-based programme patient-for-patient is unknown, and centre-based telerehabilitation after cardiac events is a separate question (shelf #2283), as is rehabilitation after myocardial infarction (shelf #458). Tier C: the shelf rests on a single trial programme, flagged for the developer's personal verdict.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: THEMIS: ticagrelor added to aspirin cut ischaemic events by a tenth relative and doubled major bleeding — the net gain sat in patients with a previous stent
question: In patients with stable coronary disease and type 2 diabetes, does adding ticagrelor to aspirin reduce cardiovascular events, and at what bleeding cost?
balance: THEMIS randomised 19,220 patients aged 50 or over with stable coronary disease and type 2 diabetes — none with previous myocardial infarction or stroke — to ticagrelor plus aspirin or aspirin alone (Steg 2019, PMID: 31475798). Over a median 39.9 months the primary ischaemic composite fell from 8.5% to 7.7% (hazard ratio 0.90, 95% CI 0.81 to 0.99): a 10% relative reduction worth 0.8 percentage points absolute. The price was TIMI major bleeding more than doubled in relative terms, 2.2% versus 1.0% (HR 2.32) — 1.2 percentage points absolute, more harm events added than ischaemic events removed — plus more intracranial haemorrhage (0.7% versus 0.5%). The trial's own irreversible-harm composite (death, myocardial infarction, stroke, fatal bleeding, intracranial haemorrhage) was statistically unchanged: 10.1% versus 10.8% (HR 0.93, 95% CI 0.86 to 1.02). The prespecified THEMIS-PCI analysis (Bhatt 2019, PMID: 31484629) locates the favourable trade: in the 11,154 patients with previous PCI, the composite fell 8.6% to 7.3% (HR 0.85) and net clinical benefit was positive (9.3% versus 11.0%, HR 0.85), while in patients without previous PCI it was not (interaction p = 0.012). A third of patients stopped ticagrelor early (34.5% versus 25.4%), which blunts any real-world gain further. Tier C: one trial and its own subgroup analysis, flagged for the developer's personal verdict.
stamp: SPLIT — POSSIBLE net benefit in patients with previous PCI / LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) to irreversible harm in the overall population

title: Anticoagulation in sinus-rhythm heart failure: warfarin halved ischaemic stroke in relative terms and doubled major bleeding — three trials found no net winner
question: In patients with HFrEF in sinus rhythm, does warfarin anticoagulation prevent stroke without unacceptable bleeding?
balance: Three randomised trials have asked whether anticoagulating heart-failure patients who are in sinus rhythm pays. WARCEF (Homma 2012, PMID: 22551105), the definitive warfarin-versus-aspirin test in 2,305 patients with reduced ejection fraction, found no difference in its primary composite of ischaemic stroke, intracerebral haemorrhage or death: 7.47 versus 7.93 events per 100 patient-years (HR 0.93, 95% CI 0.79 to 1.10). Inside that null, warfarin did exactly what anticoagulation promises and threatens: ischaemic stroke fell from 1.36 to 0.72 per 100 patient-years (HR 0.52 — a 48% relative reduction) while major haemorrhage rose from 0.87 to 1.78 per 100 patient-years. The earlier WATCH trial (Massie 2009, PMID: 19289640), stopped early at 1,587 of a planned 4,500 patients, found the same pattern — no difference between warfarin, aspirin and clopidogrel on death, infarction or stroke, with fewer nonfatal strokes on warfarin. COMMANDER HF (Zannad 2018, PMID: 30146935) then tested the modern version of the idea — low-dose rivaroxaban 2.5 mg twice daily in 5,022 patients with worsening heart failure and coronary disease — and its primary composite of death, infarction or stroke was likewise unchanged (25.0% versus 26.2%, HR 0.94). The answer to the question as posed is therefore no: strokes are prevented, but not 'without unacceptable bleeding', and no trial shows a net outcome gain. This shelf does not cover atrial fibrillation, where anticoagulation is a different and settled question.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference)

title: Physical counterpressure manoeuvres: leg-crossing and muscle-tensing cut recurrence from about a half to about a third in the one randomised trial — free, safe, and impossible to blind
question: In recurrent vasovagal syncope, do physical counterpressure manoeuvres prevent syncope?
balance: Physical counterpressure manoeuvres — crossing the legs and tensing the muscles, tensing the arms, handgrip, squatting — are the one syncope treatment that costs nothing and can do no direct harm. The evidence is a single randomised trial, the PC-Trial (van Dijk 2006, PMID: 17045903): 223 patients with recurrent vasovagal syncope and recognisable warning symptoms were randomised to conventional advice alone or conventional advice plus manoeuvre training; over a mean 14 months, syncope recurred in 31.6% of the trained group versus 50.9% of controls — a 39% relative risk reduction (95% CI 11% to 53%), about 19 percentage points absolute — with no adverse events. A prospective Dutch cohort of 100 frequent fainters given the full non-pharmacological package (fluids, salt, exercise and manoeuvres) points the same way, though without a control group: median recurrences fell from 3 in the prior year to 0, yet 49% still fainted at least once (Romme 2010, PMID: 20047924). Two cautions keep this at POSSIBLE: the manoeuvres cannot be blinded, and a 2024 meta-analysis of syncope trials found unblinded trials systematically report larger benefits than blinded ones (Kaza 2024, PMID: 38890128, carded at shelf #2615); and the treatment only exists for patients who get a prodrome long enough to use it. Drug and device options for the same condition are homed separately — midodrine at shelf #1557, fludrocortisone at shelf #2615, pacing and cardioneuroablation at shelves #2301–#2303. Tier C: a single unblinded randomised trial plus uncontrolled data, flagged for the developer's personal verdict.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: POST 2: fludrocortisone missed its primary endpoint (p = 0.069) — a possible benefit only after the dose settled, and blinded-trial syntheses call it neutral
question: In recurrent vasovagal syncope, does fludrocortisone prevent recurrence?
balance: POST 2 (Sheldon 2016, PMID: 27364043) is the only adequately designed test: 210 patients with recurrent vasovagal syncope (median 15 lifetime spells) randomised double-blind to fludrocortisone, titrated to the highest tolerated dose between 0.05 and 0.2 mg daily, or placebo for a year. It missed its prespecified target — the primary analysis gave a hazard ratio of 0.69 for first recurrence (95% CI 0.46 to 1.03, p = 0.069), short of both significance and the 40% relative reduction the trial was built to detect. The supportive findings are all secondary or post hoc: a multivariable model (HR 0.63, 95% CI 0.42 to 0.94) and an analysis restricted to the period after a 2-week dose-stabilisation phase (HR 0.51, 95% CI 0.28 to 0.89). Against even that charitable reading, the 2024 meta-analysis of syncope trials (Kaza 2024, PMID: 38890128) found that under blinded conditions fludrocortisone was neutral — the favourable syncope literature for several treatments shrinks or vanishes when blinding is enforced. The honest summary is MAYBE: a small benefit is not excluded, the point estimates lean favourable, but the one good trial did not prove it. Non-drug treatment is homed at shelf #2614 and midodrine at shelf #1557. Tier C: a single trial that missed its primary endpoint, flagged for the developer's personal verdict.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence)

title: Beta-blockers in HFmrEF: in the individual-patient pooling, deaths at ejection fraction 40–49% ran 7.2% versus 12.4% — on only 575 patients, with the interval touching no effect
question: In heart failure with mildly reduced ejection fraction, do beta-blockers reduce death and hospitalisation?
balance: No trial has ever randomised 'HFmrEF' as an entry criterion — the category (ejection fraction 40–49%) was named after the trials were done. The best evidence is the Beta-Blockers in Heart Failure Collaborative Group's individual-patient meta-analysis of 11 double-blind placebo-controlled trials (Cleland 2018, PMID: 29040525). Among 14,262 patients in sinus rhythm, the mortality benefit of beta-blockers was consistent across ejection-fraction strata below 50%. In the 40–49% stratum itself — only 575 patients — all-cause death occurred in 7.2% on beta-blockers versus 12.4% on placebo (adjusted HR 0.59, 95% CI 0.34 to 1.03): a large point estimate whose interval just touches no effect, while cardiovascular death was significantly lower (4.5% versus 9.2%, adjusted HR 0.48, 95% CI 0.24 to 0.97). Two qualifiers matter. First, rhythm: in the 3,050 patients in atrial fibrillation, beta-blockers raised ejection fraction but did not improve prognosis at any level below 50% — this shelf's answer is a sinus-rhythm answer. Second, the hospitalisation half of the question is not reported for the 40–49% stratum in this analysis. SENIORS (Flather 2005, PMID: 15642700) is consistent background: nebivolol in 2,128 patients aged 70 or over across a broad ejection-fraction range reduced death or cardiovascular admission (31.1% versus 35.3%, HR 0.86) with no interaction by ejection fraction — but only 35% of its patients had an ejection fraction above 35%, so it supports a class effect in older patients rather than proving the HFmrEF case. The HFrEF mortality evidence itself is homed at shelf #88.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: COSIRA: the coronary sinus Reducer doubled the chance of a two-class angina improvement over a sham procedure (35% versus 15%) — in 104 patients, with no gain in exercise time
question: In refractory angina, does a coronary sinus reducer improve symptoms?
balance: The coronary sinus Reducer (Neovasc) is a balloon-expandable, hourglass-shaped implant that narrows the coronary sinus, intended to redistribute blood toward ischaemic myocardium in patients with refractory angina who have no revascularisation option. Its evidence turns on one small sham-controlled trial, COSIRA (Verheye 2015, PMID: 25651246): 104 patients with class III–IV angina and myocardial ischaemia, not candidates for revascularisation, were randomised to the device or a sham procedure. At 6 months, 35% of the device group versus 15% of the sham group had improved by at least two angina classes (p = 0.02), and 71% versus 42% by at least one class (p = 0.003); quality-of-life scores also favoured the device (Seattle Angina Questionnaire improvement 17.6 versus 7.6 points). But the objective measures did not move — no significant difference in exercise time or in dobutamine-echocardiography wall-motion index — and a sham arm in which 42% of patients improve by a class or more is a standing warning about expectation effects in angina. The wider literature pooled by Hochstadt (2022, PMID: 34968714) — 9 prospective studies, 846 patients, all but one uncontrolled — reports 76% improving by at least one class with 98% procedural success and 3% non-major complications; consistent with COSIRA, but uncontrolled series cannot separate device effect from placebo effect and natural history. Tier C: a single small trial for a symptom endpoint, flagged for the developer's personal verdict.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: SIGNIFY: ivabradine slowed the heart and changed nothing — 19,102 patients, a null primary endpoint, and more events in patients with limiting angina
question: In patients with stable coronary artery disease and resting heart rate at least 70, does ivabradine reduce cardiovascular events?
balance: SIGNIFY (Fox 2014, PMID: 25176136) tested the pure heart-rate hypothesis in stable coronary disease: 19,102 patients without clinical heart failure and with a resting heart rate of at least 70 beats per minute received ivabradine (up to 10 mg twice daily, titrated to a heart rate of 55–60) or placebo on top of standard therapy. The drug did its pharmacological job — at 3 months heart rate averaged 60.7 versus 70.6 beats per minute — and it changed no outcomes. After a median 27.8 months, the primary composite of cardiovascular death or nonfatal myocardial infarction occurred in 6.8% on ivabradine versus 6.4% on placebo (HR 1.08, 95% CI 0.96 to 1.20, p = 0.20), with neither component significantly different. Worse, among the 12,049 patients with activity-limiting angina — the subgroup with the most symptomatic reason to take the drug — ivabradine was associated with an increase in the primary endpoint (p = 0.02 for interaction). Bradycardia was common: 18.0% versus 2.3%. The contrast with heart failure is the point of the cross-reference: in HFrEF, ivabradine reduced heart-failure hospitalisation in SHIFT (homed at shelf #275) — a different population, a different substrate, and no licence to extrapolate the benefit to stable coronary disease without heart failure. Tier C: a single (very large) trial shelf, flagged for the developer's personal verdict.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference)

title: Statin loading before PCI: small trials cut biomarker-defined injury; the one large clinical-outcome trial, SECURE-PCI, found nothing
question: In patients undergoing PCI, does high-dose statin loading (or reloading) beforehand reduce periprocedural myocardial infarction and later events?
balance: The statin-loading literature is a study in what endpoints do to conclusions. The ARMYDA programme randomised small numbers of patients to atorvastatin pretreatment and measured myocardial injury with cardiac biomarkers. In the original trial (Pasceri 2004, PMID: 15277322), 153 statin-naïve patients with stable angina given atorvastatin 40 mg daily for 7 days before elective intervention had less biomarker injury on every measure, and periprocedural myocardial infarction by creatine-kinase-MB criteria in 5% versus 18% on placebo. ARMYDA-RECAPTURE (Di Sciascio 2009, PMID: 19643320) extended the idea to reloading patients already on chronic statins (383 patients): the 30-day composite of cardiac death, myocardial infarction or unplanned revascularisation fell from 9.4% to 3.7% (p = 0.037), driven by periprocedural infarction. Then SECURE-PCI (Berwanger 2018, PMID: 29525821) tested loading properly: 4,191 patients with acute coronary syndrome and planned invasive management received two 80 mg atorvastatin loads or placebo, and 30-day major adverse cardiovascular events were 6.2% versus 7.1% (HR 0.88, 95% CI 0.69 to 1.11, p = 0.27) — no significant difference, in a trial where only 64.7% of patients actually proceeded to PCI. The reconciliation is that loading probably does blunt the small enzyme leaks that follow stenting — a surrogate whose link to prognosis is contested — while no trial shows it prevents death, spontaneous infarction, or other events patients feel. Nearly all these patients should be on a high-intensity statin anyway; the shelf answers only the narrower question of whether the extra pre-procedure load itself earns its keep.
stamp: SPLIT — POSSIBLE reduction in biomarker-defined periprocedural injury in small trials / LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) to clinical events in the large trial

title: AFIRE: rivaroxaban alone was noninferior for efficacy and superior for bleeding — the combination arm's excess deaths stopped the trial early
question: In patients with atrial fibrillation and stable coronary disease more than a year after stenting, is rivaroxaban alone as safe and effective as rivaroxaban plus an antiplatelet drug?
balance: AFIRE (Yasuda 2019, PMID: 31475793) randomised 2,236 Japanese patients with atrial fibrillation and stable coronary disease — PCI or bypass surgery more than a year earlier, or angiographic disease not requiring revascularisation — to rivaroxaban alone or rivaroxaban plus a single antiplatelet agent. The trial was stopped early because mortality was higher in the combination group. Rivaroxaban monotherapy was noninferior for the primary efficacy composite (stroke, systemic embolism, myocardial infarction, unstable angina requiring revascularisation, or death from any cause): 4.14% versus 5.75% per patient-year (HR 0.72, 95% CI 0.55 to 0.95, against a noninferiority margin of 1.46) — the point estimate favours dropping the antiplatelet, though a noninferiority design should not be read as proving superiority. On safety it was superior outright: major bleeding by ISTH criteria 1.62% versus 2.76% per patient-year (HR 0.59, 95% CI 0.39 to 0.89, p = 0.01). The answer to the question is therefore yes on both halves — as effective, and safer — within the limits of a single open-label trial stopped early in one country's population. Tier C: a single trial, flagged for the developer's personal verdict.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: A blood test for colorectal cancer screening: about four in five cancers found, but only one in eight advanced adenomas — a detection net, not a prevention tool
question: In asymptomatic adults, how accurately does a blood-based cell-free DNA test detect colorectal cancer and advanced adenomas?
balance: Two large prospective accuracy studies with colonoscopy as the reference standard point the same way. In ECLIPSE (Chung 2024, PMID: 38477985), a cell-free DNA blood test detected 83.1% of colorectal cancers (95% CI 72.2 to 90.3) with 89.6% specificity for advanced neoplasia — but only 13.2% of advanced precancerous lesions. In PREEMPT CRC (Shaukat 2025, PMID: 40455622), a second blood test in 27,010 evaluable adults detected 79.2% of cancers with 91.5% specificity, and its 12.5% sensitivity for advanced precancerous lesions fell below the study's own prespecified acceptance criterion. So the honest answer is: a blood test finds about four in five cancers that are already present, at the price of a false-positive rate near 1 in 10 — but it is nearly blind to the advanced adenomas whose removal is what makes screening prevent cancer rather than merely detect it. Its plausible role is reaching the large minority who refuse every stool and endoscopic test; whether that trade reduces incidence or mortality is unproven. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (Tier C: two prospective accuracy studies, no outcomes trial). The multitarget stool DNA comparison is at shelf #2622.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Multitarget stool DNA versus FIT: about 93% of cancers and 43% of advanced adenomas detected, against FIT's 67–74% and 23% — paid for with roughly double the false positives
question: In screening-age adults, does multitarget stool DNA testing detect more cancers and advanced adenomas than FIT, and at what false-positive cost?
balance: Three prospective studies against a colonoscopy reference standard give a consistent exchange. The multitarget stool DNA test detects more disease than a single FIT: in DeeP-C (Imperiale 2014, PMID: 24645800), 92.3% of cancers versus 73.8% and 42.4% of advanced precancerous lesions versus 23.8%; in BLUE-C (Imperiale 2024, PMID: 38477986), the next-generation test detected 93.9% of cancers versus 67.3% and 43.4% of advanced precancerous lesions versus 23.3%. The same direction held in Alaska Native people (Redwood 2016, PMID: 26520415). The cost is specificity: 86.6% (first generation) and 90.6% (next generation) versus about 95% for FIT — in absolute terms roughly 9–13 false positives per 100 people without advanced neoplasia, against about 5, each buying a colonoscopy. What no study here shows is a programme outcome: FIT is meant to be repeated annually, stool DNA three-yearly, and neither mortality nor cumulative programme detection is measured. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (Tier C: prospective accuracy studies, two manufacturer-funded, no outcomes trial). The blood-based test comparison is at shelf #2621.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: CT colonography versus colonoscopy: 90% of large lesions found, and in a randomised trial its higher uptake made the population yield equal — with a third of scanned patients still needing further investigation
question: In asymptomatic adults invited to colorectal screening, does CT colonography find as many cancers and large polyps as colonoscopy?
balance: CT colonography finds most of what matters and trades accuracy for acceptability. Against colonoscopy in 2,531 asymptomatic adults (Johnson 2008, PMID: 18799557), it identified 90% of people with adenomas or cancers ≥10 mm, but only 78% of those with lesions ≥6 mm, with a positive predictive value of 0.23. In the randomised COCOS invitation trial (Stoop 2012, PMID: 22088831), participation was higher for CT colonography than colonoscopy (34% versus 22% relative; relative risk 1.56), which exactly offset colonoscopy's higher per-participant yield: advanced neoplasia found per 100 invitees was 2.1 versus 1.9. In symptomatic patients (Atkin 2013, PMID: 23414650 — a different population, flagged on its card), detection was equal at 11%, but 30.0% of the CT group needed further colonic investigation versus 8.2%. So: as a programme, CT colonography can find as many cancers and large polyps per person invited; as a test, it misses about 1 in 10 large lesions and sends a substantial minority on to colonoscopy anyway. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (not Tier C: two randomised trials plus a large accuracy study).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: MRI-based prostate screening: insignificant-cancer diagnoses roughly halved in two population trials, significant-cancer detection held or improved — the overdiagnosis half of the bargain, proven; the mortality half, not yet
question: In men invited to prostate screening, does an MRI-based pathway reduce unnecessary biopsies and overdiagnosis versus PSA-only screening?
balance: The randomised evidence says the MRI pathway buys the trade screening has always wanted. In GÖTEBORG-2 (Hugosson 2024, PMID: 39321360), omitting biopsy after a negative MRI cut diagnoses of clinically insignificant cancer by more than half in relative terms (relative risk 0.43, 95% CI 0.32 to 0.57; overall detection 2.8% versus 4.5%), with no significant difference in significant-cancer detection (relative risk 0.84, 0.66 to 1.07) and fewer advanced cancers (15 versus 23). In STHLM3-MRI (Nordström 2021, PMID: 34391509), a risk-model-plus-MRI strategy detected more significant cancers (relative proportion 1.44) and fewer low-grade ones (0.46) than PSA plus systematic biopsy, with fewer biopsies and fewer biopsy infections. PROSTAGRAM (Eldred-Evans 2021, PMID: 33570542) points the same way in a paired comparison. What is not yet shown — anywhere — is a mortality benefit, and the significant-cancer estimate in GÖTEBORG-2 is compatible with a small loss. PROPOSED LIKELY (not Tier C: two population randomised trials plus a paired cohort, consistent direction). The MRI-first pathway in men already referred for suspected cancer is homed at shelf #801.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: Supplemental ultrasound after mammography: about 4 extra cancers per 1,000 screens, mostly small and node-negative, and interval cancers halved in the randomised trial — bought with a biopsy yield of only about 1 in 10
question: In women with dense breasts and a negative mammogram, does supplemental ultrasound screening find additional cancers?
balance: Yes, it finds more cancers — the question is the exchange rate. In the J-START randomised trial (Ohuchi 2016, PMID: 26547101), adding ultrasound to mammography in women aged 40–49 raised sensitivity from 77.0% to 91.1%, detection from 0.32% to 0.50%, and halved interval cancers (0.05% versus 0.10%), while specificity fell from 91.4% to 87.7%. In ACRIN 6666 (Berg 2008, PMID: 18477782; Berg 2012, PMID: 22474203), in elevated-risk women with dense tissue, the supplemental yield was 4.2 cancers per 1,000 women at the first screen and 3.7 per 1,000 at incidence screens — mostly small, invasive, node-negative cancers — while the positive predictive value of an ultrasound-prompted biopsy was only about 9–16%. Neither study measures mortality, and J-START's extra stage 0 disease warns that some of the gain is overdiagnosis. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (not Tier C: a large randomised trial plus a three-round prospective cohort). The MRI comparison for high-risk women is homed at shelf #800.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Lengthening lung screening intervals: two years after a negative round looks safe in the one randomised test — 2.5 years in NELSON let interval cancers and late stages climb
question: After a negative lung-cancer screening round, can screening intervals be safely lengthened beyond one year?
balance: The evidence supports one careful step, not two. MILD randomised smokers with negative screens to annual or biennial low-dose CT (Pastorino 2019, PMID: 31336289): at 10 years, lung-cancer mortality on biennial screening was HR 1.10 versus annual — statistically indistinguishable, but with a confidence interval (0.59 to 2.05) too wide to prove equivalence — while saving 44% of follow-up scans in baseline-negative participants and showing no increase in interval or advanced-stage cancers. NELSON's experience warns against going further: after a 2.5-year interval, interval cancers rose (28, versus 5 and 19 after shorter gaps) and the advanced-stage share of screen-detected cancers rose to 17.3% from 6.8% (Yousaf-Khan 2017, PMID: 27364640), against a background sensitivity of 84.6% (Horeweg 2014, PMID: 25282284). So: lengthening to two years after a negative round is a reasonable, evidence-backed economy; beyond that, the one large dataset shows the benefit leaking away. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (Tier C: a single small randomised interval comparison plus within-trial analyses). Whether screening itself reduces lung-cancer deaths is homed at shelf #164.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: The EarlyCDT autoantibody test shifted lung cancers to earlier stages in one randomised trial — against no screening at all, not against the CT screening it is meant to triage
question: In smokers eligible for lung screening, does a blood autoantibody test triage who benefits from low-dose CT?
balance: One trial, carefully read, supports a narrower claim than its headline. In ECLS (Sullivan 2021, PMID: 32732334), 12,208 high-risk Scots were randomised to the EarlyCDT-Lung autoantibody test — with CT follow-up only if positive — or to standard care. At 2 years, cancers in the intervention arm were less often diagnosed at stage III/IV: 58.9% versus 73.2% (hazard ratio 0.64, 95% CI 0.41 to 0.99). But mortality did not differ significantly, and the control arm received no CT screening at all — so the trial shows a test-plus-CT package beats symptomatic presentation, which was never in doubt, and says nothing about whether the blood test improves on the low-dose CT screening it would actually be triaging. The test-negative arm also went unimaged, a withholding whose cost is folded invisibly into the results. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (Tier C: a single randomised trial, surrogate stage outcome, no mortality signal). The mortality evidence for low-dose CT itself is homed at shelf #164; screening intervals are at shelf #2626.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Newborn pulse-oximetry screening: catches about three-quarters to five-sixths of critical heart defects before discharge at a false-positive rate near 1 in 700 — and cannot see aortic arch obstruction
question: In newborns, does universal pulse-oximetry screening detect critical congenital heart disease before collapse?
balance: Yes — with a defined blind spot. The meta-analysis of 13 studies (Thangaratinam 2012, PMID: 22554860; 229,421 babies) gives pulse oximetry a sensitivity of 76.5% and a specificity of 99.9% for critical congenital heart defects, with a false-positive rate of just 0.14% — and only 0.05% when screening is done after 24 hours of age. The Swedish prospective study (de-Wahl Granelli 2009, PMID: 19131383; 39,821 babies) found that oximetry plus examination detected 82.8% of duct-dependent circulation before discharge, and that babies in unscreened regions were far more likely to leave hospital undiagnosed (28% versus 8%; relative risk 3.36) — five died of undiagnosed lesions, versus none in the screened region. The lesions it misses are concentrated in aortic arch obstruction, where saturations can stay normal while the ductus is open. PROPOSED LIKELY (Tier C: observational evidence only — no randomised trial exists — but large, consistent, and mechanistically coherent).
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: Pancreatic surveillance in high-risk people: most cancers found at stage I and a large survival gap against cancers found outside — with lead-time bias entitled to much of the credit, and the yield concentrated in CDKN2A carriers
question: In adults at high inherited or familial risk of pancreatic cancer, does regular MRI/EUS surveillance find cancer earlier and improve survival?
balance: Surveillance does find pancreatic cancer earlier — that much the cohorts establish. In CAPS5 (Dbouk 2022, PMID: 35704792), seven of nine cancers diagnosed during surveillance were stage I, and screen-detected patients had a median survival of 9.8 years versus 1.5 years for cancers diagnosed outside surveillance (hazard ratio 0.13) — a contrast that lead-time and length bias guarantee is flattered, by an amount no observational design can remove. The European experience (Vasen 2016, PMID: 27114589) adds the crucial qualifier: the yield concentrates in CDKN2A mutation carriers (7.3% developed cancer; 75% resected; five-year survival 24%), while in familial kindreds without a known mutation only 0.9% developed a tumour and resections for ultimately low-risk precursor lesions outnumbered cancers found. There is no randomised trial and no unscreened control group. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (Tier C: prospective cohorts only, survival comparisons bias-exposed).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Combined first-trimester screening for pre-eclampsia: detects about 77–82% of preterm cases versus about 41% for the risk-factor checklist — better selection, proven; delivery of the aspirin it selects for, not
question: In pregnant women, does first-trimester combined screening for preterm pre-eclampsia (maternal factors, mean arterial pressure, uterine artery Doppler, placental growth factor) select aspirin prophylaxis better than risk-factor checklists?
balance: On accuracy, it is not close. The Fetal Medicine Foundation combined algorithm — maternal factors, mean arterial pressure, uterine artery Doppler, PAPP-A and placental growth factor at 11–13 weeks — detected 76.7% of preterm pre-eclampsia at a 10.5% screen-positive rate in ASPRE's screened population (Rolnik 2017, PMID: 28741785). In SPREE's head-to-head (Tan 2018, PMID: 29536574), the full combined test detected 82.4% of preterm pre-eclampsia versus 40.8% for the NICE risk-factor checklist at the same screen-positive rate; even the mini-combined test beat the checklist on all pre-eclampsia (42.5% versus 30.4%). Two qualifications keep this at POSSIBLE rather than higher: no trial randomises screening strategies to clinical outcomes — the benefit chain runs through the ASPRE aspirin trial (homed at shelves #151 and #412), whose 62% relative reduction in preterm pre-eclampsia applies only if the right women are actually given aspirin, and SPREE found checklist-era compliance of just 23%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (Tier C: prospective accuracy studies; the linked treatment trial is homed elsewhere).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Inhaled insulin (Exubera): glucose control matched injected insulin in both types of diabetes — the lungs lost a little FEV1 early, reversibly, and a third of patients coughed
question: In adults with type 1 or type 2 diabetes, does inhaled insulin control glucose as well as injected mealtime insulin, and what does it do to the lungs?
balance: The Exubera programme answered both halves of the question in randomised trials. For glucose: in type 2 diabetes, inhaled insulin matched injected insulin at 6 months (HbA1c −0.7% vs −0.6%; adjusted difference −0.07%, 95% CI −0.32 to 0.17; Hollander 2004, PMID: 15451900) with more patients reaching HbA1c <7% (46.9% vs 31.7%); in type 1 diabetes over 2 years it ran slightly behind (adjusted HbA1c difference 0.25% favouring injections; Skyler 2007, PMID: 17327324), while causing fewer severe hypoglycaemic events (risk ratio 0.67) and about 1.3 kg less weight gain in both types. For the lungs: FEV1 fell a little faster on inhaled insulin — in type 1, an extra −0.017 L/year averaged over 2 years — but the gap opened in the first 3 months and did not widen from month 3 to 24 in either type (Rosenstock 2008, PMID: 18535196, difference 0.000 L/year over months 3–24), diffusing capacity never differed, and the type 1 extension showed the difference vanishing on a 6-month washout and returning at the same size on restarting (Skyler 2008, PMID: 18824271) — a reversible functional effect, not progressive damage. The everyday cost was cough (37.6% vs 13.1% initially in type 1). All trials excluded smokers and people with lung disease, and all tested the one product, Exubera, since withdrawn from the market; the technosphere inhaled insulin record in type 1 diabetes is homed separately at shelf #2051. PROPOSED LIKELY (not Tier C: three randomised programmes, consistent results; the stamp carries the lung and cough qualifications on its face).
stamp: LIKELY (glycaemic control comparable to injected insulin; a small, early, non-progressive and reversible fall in FEV1, and much more cough)

title: Preventing the next diabetic foot ulcer: pressure-designed insoles and custom footwear work in high-risk patients who wear them — ordinary therapeutic shoes, and unworn prescriptions, do not
question: In people with diabetes and a healed foot ulcer, do therapeutic shoes and custom insoles prevent ulcer recurrence?
balance: Three randomised trials divide cleanly by risk and by whether the device was actually pressure-targeted and worn. In high-risk neuropathic patients with a prior ulcer, insoles designed from foot shape and barefoot plantar pressure cut submetatarsal ulcer recurrence (hazard ratio 3.4, 95% CI 1.3 to 8.7, for standard insoles versus pressure-based; Ulbrecht 2014, PMID: 24760263), and custom footwear with improved offloading cut recurrence from 47.8% to 25.7% in the patients who wore it for at least 80% of steps (Bus 2013, PMID: 24130357). But the same trial's intention-to-treat result was null (38.8% vs 44.2%; odds ratio 0.80, 0.44 to 1.47) because fewer than half the patients wore the footwear enough, and in lower-risk patients who did not need custom shoes, therapeutic shoes with either cork or prefabricated inserts showed no benefit at all over 2 years (15% and 14% vs 17%; Reiber 2002, PMID: 12020336). The honest summary: the prescription that prevents recurrence is pressure measurement plus custom manufacture plus adherence — footwear dispensed generically, or dispensed and not worn, has no demonstrated effect. Healing of active ulcers and offloading during treatment are a different question, homed at shelf #291. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (not Tier C: three randomised trials; the benefit is real but conditional, which the stamp grade reflects).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Closed loop in type 1 diabetes pregnancy (AiDAPT): time in the pregnancy target range rose by about 10 points and HbA1c fell — from one trial, on glucose endpoints
question: In pregnant women with type 1 diabetes, does automated insulin delivery (hybrid closed loop) improve glucose control versus standard pump or injection therapy with continuous glucose monitoring?
balance: One randomised programme answers the glucose question convincingly. In AiDAPT, 124 pregnant women with type 1 diabetes using the CamAPS FX hybrid closed-loop system spent 68.2% of time in the pregnancy target range (63–140 mg/dL) versus 55.6% with standard insulin therapy — an adjusted difference of 10.5 percentage points (95% CI 7.0 to 14.0) — with HbA1c 0.31 points lower and no excess of severe hypoglycaemia or ketoacidosis, both groups using CGM throughout (Lee 2023, PMID: 37796241). The prespecified postpartum extension found the advantage held for 6 months after delivery (time in range 72% vs 54%; Lee 2025, PMID: 39884300). What the evidence does not show is equally important: the trial was powered for glucose metrics, not for pre-eclampsia, caesarean delivery or neonatal outcomes, and it tested one system in UK clinics. CGM in pregnancy is homed at shelf #959 (CONCEPTT) and closed-loop therapy outside pregnancy at shelf #561; this shelf is the pregnancy-specific automated-delivery question. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (Tier C: a single trial programme — one randomised trial plus its extension — however clean the result).

title: CPAP for sleep apnoea in type 2 diabetes: sleepiness improves, HbA1c does not — the pooled trial difference is −0.10 points with a confidence interval that excludes a useful effect
question: In type 2 diabetes with obstructive sleep apnoea, does CPAP improve HbA1c?
balance: The pooled randomised record is a clean null. Across six trials with 581 patients, CPAP changed HbA1c by −0.10 percentage points (95% CI −0.25 to 0.04) at 12–24 weeks, moderate-certainty evidence, with no effect in either adherence stratum (Labarca 2018, PMID: 30073792). The best-designed individual trial agrees: double-blind therapeutic versus sham CPAP for 3 months moved HbA1c by −0.02% versus +0.1% (P = 0.7), even as sleepiness and wakefulness improved significantly — proof the treatment was working on the apnoea while doing nothing for glucose (West 2007, PMID: 17557769). The one positive trial (Martínez-Cerón 2016, PMID: 26910598) was small (n = 50), open-label and reports no HbA1c effect size in its abstract; it does not outweigh the sham-controlled and pooled results. CPAP should be prescribed for the apnoea — symptoms and sleep — not as a diabetes treatment, and an HbA1c that fails to fall on CPAP is the expected result, not non-adherence. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) (not Tier C: a meta-analysis of six randomised trials plus a sham-controlled trial, consistently null).

title: Preserving beta cells in new-onset type 1 diabetes: alefacept and low-dose ATG each slowed C-peptide decline for two years — in phase 2 trials of 49 and 89 patients
question: In newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes, do alefacept or low-dose anti-thymocyte globulin preserve beta-cell function?
balance: Two small randomised programmes, testing different immune strategies in patients within 100 days of diagnosis, converge on the same answer: beta-cell decline can be slowed, not stopped. Alefacept (T1DAL, 49 patients) missed its 12-month primary endpoint (2-hour C-peptide, P = 0.065) but preserved 4-hour C-peptide (P = 0.019), cut insulin use and roughly halved hypoglycaemic events; by 24 months both C-peptide measures were significantly preserved (Rigby 2013, PMID: 24622414; Rigby 2015, PMID: 26193635). Low-dose ATG (TrialNet, 89 patients) preserved C-peptide at 1 year (AUC 0.646 vs 0.406 nmol/L, P = 0.0003) and at 2 years (P = 0.00005), with lower HbA1c; adding G-CSF never improved on ATG alone (Haller 2018, PMID: 30012675; Haller 2019, PMID: 30967424). The qualifications are structural: phase 2 sample sizes, a surrogate primary endpoint, and neither agent available as routine treatment — alefacept was withdrawn from its psoriasis market, and ATG is unapproved for diabetes. Abatacept's new-onset record is homed at shelf #1776. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (Tier C: two small single-programme phase 2 records resting on a surrogate endpoint).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Islet transplantation for type 1 diabetes with dangerous hypoglycaemia: severe episodes are abolished in most recipients and awareness returns — insulin independence usually lasts about 15 months, and immunosuppression is forever
question: In type 1 diabetes with recurrent severe hypoglycaemia and impaired awareness, does islet transplantation restore awareness and prevent severe episodes?
balance: No randomised trial exists in this population, and the observational record is unusually coherent. In the single-arm phase 3 CIT-07 study, 48 adults whose severe hypoglycaemia persisted despite expert care met the composite endpoint (HbA1c <7.0% and no severe hypoglycaemic events) at a rate of 87.5% at 1 year and 71% at 2 years, with median HbA1c 5.6% and awareness restored (Hering 2016, PMID: 27208344). The registry's 677 recipients show steady improvement by era — 3-year insulin independence 27% rising to 44% — with enduring resolution of severe hypoglycaemia (Barton 2012, PMID: 22723582). The Edmonton 5-year view supplies the necessary cold water: about 80% still secreted C-peptide at 5 years but only about 10% stayed insulin-free, and median insulin independence was 15 months (Ryan 2005, PMID: 15983207). The price is procedural (bleeding requiring transfusion in about 1 in 10) and permanent (immunosuppression, with measurably falling GFR). Judged against its actual indication — abolishing life-threatening hypoglycaemia in the few who fail everything else — the benefit is real; judged as a cure for diabetes, it is not one. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (Tier C: single-arm and registry evidence only, by the nature of the question).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Glyburide for gestational diabetes: glucose control equals insulin, but babies are heavier, with more macrosomia and neonatal hypoglycaemia — and perinatal noninferiority was never proven
question: In gestational diabetes needing drug treatment, is glyburide as safe and effective as insulin or metformin?
balance: Split the question in two. Effective? Yes: the founding randomised trial found glyburide and insulin indistinguishable for glucose control (mean glucose 105 vs 105 mg/dL; 4% of the glyburide group needed insulin added; Langer 2000, PMID: 11036118). As safe? The record says no. Pooling 15 randomised comparisons, glyburide versus insulin produced heavier babies (+109 g), more macrosomia (risk ratio 2.62, 95% CI 1.35 to 5.08) and more neonatal hypoglycaemia (risk ratio 2.04, 1.30 to 3.20) — the reviewers' verdict was 'clearly inferior' (Balsells 2015, PMID: 25609400; glyburide and glibenclamide are the same drug). And the large French INDAO trial, designed specifically to prove perinatal noninferiority within a 7% margin, failed to do so: composite complications 27.6% versus 23.4%, with the confidence interval reaching +10.5% (Sénat 2018, PMID: 29715355). Where metformin is an option it beat glyburide on the same outcomes; the metformin-in-pregnancy record is homed at shelf #286. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm) (not Tier C: multiple randomised trials plus a meta-analysis; graded POSSIBLE rather than LIKELY because the harm rests on pooled small trials and a failed noninferiority test rather than a single decisive harm trial).
stamp: POSSIBLE (harm)

title: DAFNE education in type 1 diabetes: quality of life and dietary freedom improve durably, HbA1c improves modestly and fades — one 5-day course, no extra severe hypoglycaemia
question: In type 1 diabetes, does dose-adjustment education (DAFNE) improve quality of life and glycaemic control versus standard education?
balance: The trial evidence supports both halves of the claim, with different durability. In the DAFNE randomised trial (169 adults with type 1 diabetes and suboptimal control), a 5-day course in flexible intensive insulin management produced HbA1c of 8.4% versus 9.4% on the waiting-list control at 6 months, with significant improvements in dietary freedom, overall quality-of-life impact, wellbeing and treatment satisfaction — and no change in severe hypoglycaemia, weight or lipids (DAFNE Study Group 2002, PMID: 12364302). At a mean of 44 months, the quality-of-life gains were fully maintained, but the HbA1c advantage over baseline had shrunk to 0.36 points and was decaying (Speight 2010, PMID: 20399523). The REPOSE trial (homed at shelf #564) later delivered DAFNE-style education to both arms and found pumps added nothing to injections — evidence that the education itself is the active ingredient. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (Tier C: one randomised trial with a waiting-list control, plus an uncontrolled cohort follow-up; the quality-of-life outcomes are unblindable by design).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Diabetes distress in type 2 diabetes (REDEEM): distress falls with any structured support — the distress-specific programme adds value only in the most distressed — and HbA1c does not move
question: In adults with type 2 diabetes and high diabetes distress, does a distress-focused self-management intervention improve distress and HbA1c?
balance: REDEEM randomised 392 adults with type 2 diabetes and elevated distress to computer-assisted self-management, the same plus distress-specific problem-solving (CAPS), or minimal computer support. Distress fell significantly and clinically meaningfully in all three arms (P < 0.001) with no overall between-group difference; the distress-specific content earned its keep only in the subgroup with high baseline regimen distress (interaction P < 0.02). Self-management behaviours — eating, activity, medication adherence — improved alongside distress. HbA1c did not change in any arm (Fisher 2013, PMID: 23735726). So the intervention family does what its name promises for distress, non-specifically, and does nothing measurable for glucose; the trial had no untreated control, so some of the universal improvement may be time and regression to the mean in a group recruited at peak distress. Treating depression in diabetes is a different question with a different record. PROPOSED SPLIT — POSSIBLE for reducing diabetes distress / no improvement in HbA1c (Tier C: a single pragmatic trial, no untreated comparator).
stamp: SPLIT — POSSIBLE for reducing diabetes distress / no improvement in HbA1c

title: Starting insulin in type 2 diabetes (4T): begin with basal — control converges by 3 years, hypoglycaemia and weight gain stay lowest, and a premixed start reaches target least often
question: In type 2 diabetes starting insulin on top of oral therapy, which initiation strategy — basal alone, premixed (biphasic), or prandial — controls glucose best with least hypoglycaemia?
balance: The 4T trial (708 patients on metformin plus a sulfonylurea) is the one direct randomised comparison of the three ways to start insulin, and its two reports must be read together. At 1 year, meal-covering regimens looked better (HbA1c 7.3% biphasic, 7.2% prandial, 7.6% basal) — but that compared one insulin against two meal-covering regimens, and the basal arm paid far less for its result: 2.3 hypoglycaemic events per patient-year versus 5.7 and 12.0, and 1.9 kg weight gain versus 4.7 and 5.7 kg (Holman 2007, PMID: 17890232). By 3 years, once a second insulin was added when needed (as happened in 68–82% of patients), HbA1c converged (medians 7.1%, 6.8%, 6.9%; P = 0.28), the basal start kept the least hypoglycaemia (1.7 vs 3.0 and 5.7 events/year) and the biphasic start reached HbA1c at most 6.5% least often (31.9% vs 44.7% and 43.2%) (Holman 2009, PMID: 19850703). Strategy verdict: start basal, intensify by adding prandial insulin when required, and do not start with a premixed insulin. PROPOSED LIKELY (Tier C: a single trial — two reports of one experiment — however large and well conducted).
stamp: LIKELY (basal-first start: equal control by 3 years with the least hypoglycaemia and weight gain; a biphasic start reached target least often)

title: Sucroferric oxyhydroxide: the same phosphate control as sevelamer on roughly a third of the tablets — paid for with more diarrhoea and more early withdrawals
question: In haemodialysis patients with hyperphosphataemia, does sucroferric oxyhydroxide control phosphate with fewer pills than sevelamer?
balance: Yes — on the evidence of two randomised phase 3 trials, sucroferric oxyhydroxide (PA21 in the trial reports) lowers serum phosphate as effectively as sevelamer, and the tablet count is not close. In the global trial (Floege 2014, PMID: 24646861), phosphate fell −0.71 versus −0.79 mmol/L at 12 weeks, meeting non-inferiority, on an average of about 3 tablets a day against 8; in the Japanese trial (Koiwa 2017, PMID: 27496336) end-of-treatment phosphate was 1.62 versus 1.72 mmol/L on 5.6 versus 18.7 tablets a day. Recorded non-adherence was lower on sucroferric oxyhydroxide (15.1% vs 21.3%) — but so was tolerability at the margin: more patients withdrew for adverse events (15.7% vs 6.6%), with diarrhoea and discoloured faeces the typical price, against nausea and constipation on sevelamer. The 1-year post hoc analysis of the same global programme (Ketteler 2019, PMID: 29846719 — a repeat report of the Floege trial, flagged on its card) found phosphate down 30% relative and FGF-23 down a median 64% relative across both binders pooled; that is a class effect of phosphate lowering, not an advantage of one drug. What none of this answers is whether any binder changes death, cardiovascular events or fractures — the hard-outcome comparison of non-calcium versus calcium binders is shelf #295, and no sucroferric-versus-sevelamer trial has tested clinical endpoints.
stamp: LIKELY (sucroferric oxyhydroxide matches sevelamer for phosphate control with a much lower pill burden)

title: Vadadustat in non-dialysis CKD: the haemoglobin matched darbepoetin exactly, the cardiovascular safety did not — MACE hazard ratio 1.17 against a 1.25 non-inferiority margin
question: In non-dialysis CKD anaemia, does vadadustat match darbepoetin for haemoglobin control and cardiovascular safety?
balance: Half of the question gets a clean yes, and the other half gets a clean no. In the two PRO2TECT trials (Chertow 2021, PMID: 33913637; 3,476 patients with non-dialysis CKD), vadadustat's haemoglobin control was non-inferior to darbepoetin alfa in both the ESA-untreated and ESA-treated trials, with mean differences of +0.05 and −0.01 g/dL against a −0.75 g/dL margin. But the pooled primary safety analysis gave a hazard ratio for major adverse cardiovascular events of 1.17 (95% CI 1.01 to 1.36), failing the prespecified 1.25 non-inferiority margin — and because the interval excludes 1.0, it reads as a harm signal in this population, not just an unmet formality. The contrast with the companion dialysis programme is part of the evidence and is cross-referenced, not carded, here: in INNO2VATE (Eckardt 2021, PMID: 33913638), vadadustat in dialysis patients was non-inferior to darbepoetin for cardiovascular safety (MACE hazard ratio 0.96, 95% CI 0.83 to 1.11) as well as for haemoglobin. So the class story is population-specific: the safety failure belongs to the non-dialysis trials. The wider HIF-stabiliser class shelf, led by the roxadustat trials, is #731.
stamp: SPLIT — LIKELY (noninferior to darbepoetin for haemoglobin) / POSSIBLE (harm: cardiovascular noninferiority not met in non-dialysis CKD)
