title: Ferric maltol in stage 3–4 CKD: haemoglobin 0.5 g/dL higher than placebo at 16 weeks — a single trial, a modest gain, and a gastrointestinal price
question: In non-dialysis CKD with iron deficiency, does oral ferric maltol raise haemoglobin versus placebo?
balance: On the one placebo-controlled trial that exists, yes — modestly. In AEGIS-CKD (Pergola 2021, PMID: 34029682; 167 patients with stage 3–4 CKD and iron-deficiency anaemia), ferric maltol 30 mg twice daily raised haemoglobin by 0.5 g/dL more than placebo at 16 weeks (95% CI 0.1 to 0.9), with ferritin, transferrin saturation and serum iron all rising on the drug while they fell on placebo. The cost was gastrointestinal: adverse events in 41% versus 30% during the blinded phase, though withdrawals for adverse events were no higher than on placebo (6% vs 9%). The open-label extension suggests the gain persists to a year, but with no comparator that part is description, not proof. This shelf is deliberately narrow — ferric maltol against placebo. The neighbouring questions live elsewhere: whether intravenous iron given proactively or at higher ferritin targets improves outcomes in CKD and dialysis is shelf #294, and IV versus oral iron beyond the blood count in non-dialysis CKD is shelf #369.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Conservative kidney management after 75: dialysis buys about 1–2 years for the average patient, almost nothing for the highly comorbid — and quality of life holds steady without it
question: In older patients with kidney failure, does conservative kidney management give survival and quality of life comparable to dialysis?
balance: The honest answer splits in two. On survival, conservative management is not comparable for the average older patient: across four UK cohorts, dialysis patients lived longer — median survival 67.1 versus 21.2 months in the largest cohort (Chandna 2011, PMID: 21098012) and 37.8 versus 13.9 months in Carson 2009 (PMID: 19808244), a gain the authors put at about 2 years. But the margin collapses exactly where the question is hardest: in Murtagh 2007 (PMID: 17412702) the dialysis advantage was lost in patients with high comorbidity, especially ischaemic heart disease, and in Chandna's over-75s, adjusted for age, comorbidity and diabetes, the advantage was about 4 months and not statistically significant. On quality of life, the one prospective study (Da Silva-Gane 2012, PMID: 22956262) found conservative patients maintained their quality of life, while life satisfaction fell after starting dialysis; Carson's conservative patients also spent fewer of their remaining days in hospital (0.043 vs 0.069 hospital days per day survived) and were four times as likely to die at home or in a hospice. Every study here is observational and the conservative groups were older and sicker in all of them — adjustment shrinks the survival gap but cannot prove what remains is causal. There is no randomised trial, and there is unlikely ever to be one.
stamp: POSSIBLE (dialysis prolongs survival on average, but the advantage nearly vanishes in patients over 75 with high comorbidity, and quality of life is maintained on conservative care)

title: Potassium citrate for recurrent calcium stones: new stones cut by about three quarters relative in the pooled trials — small old studies, and four times the dropouts from gut side effects
question: In adults with recurrent calcium kidney stones, does potassium citrate reduce stone recurrence?
balance: Yes, on consistent randomised evidence — with a tolerability asterisk. In the two double-blind trials, potassium citrate cut stone formation from 1.2 to 0.1 per patient-year in hypocitraturic patients while placebo was unchanged (Barcelo 1993, PMID: 8230497; remission 72% vs 20%), and potassium-magnesium citrate cut new stone formation from 63.6% to 12.9% over up to 3 years (Ettinger 1997, PMID: 9366314; relative risk 0.16, an 84% relative reduction). The Cochrane synthesis of all citrate salts (Phillips 2015, PMID: 26439475; 7 trials, 477 participants) gives a pooled risk ratio for new stone formation of 0.26 (95% CI 0.10 to 0.68) — about a 74% relative reduction — with less retreatment (risk ratio 0.22). The same review is the source of the caution: the trials are small, old and moderately-to-poorly reported, and dropouts due to adverse events were significantly commoner on citrate (risk ratio 4.45, 95% CI 1.28 to 15.50), mostly gastrointestinal. Citrate is one leg of stone prevention, not the whole strategy: thiazides for hypercalciuric recurrence are shelf #483, and high urine volume is shelf #594.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: Veverimer: bicarbonate corrected and chair-stands faster in the small parent trial — but in 1,480 patients it did not slow kidney progression at all (hazard ratio 0.99)
question: In patients with chronic kidney disease and metabolic acidosis, does veverimer raise serum bicarbonate and improve physical function — and does it slow kidney progression?
balance: The two halves of this question have opposite answers, and the shelf keeps them separate. On bicarbonate and function: in TRCA-301 (Wesson 2019, PMID: 30857647; 217 patients), veverimer produced a bicarbonate response in 59% versus 22% on placebo at 12 weeks, and in its blinded 40-week extension (Wesson 2019, PMID: 31248662 — the same patients, flagged on its card) the response held at week 52 (63% vs 38%) alongside better patient-reported physical function (+12.1 points versus placebo) and a faster chair-stand. On the outcome that matters most, the answer is no: VALOR-CKD (Tangri 2024, PMID: 38261535; 1,480 patients) found no slowing of CKD progression — primary composite events 149/741 versus 148/739, hazard ratio 0.99 (95% CI 0.8 to 1.2). VALOR's randomised-withdrawal design left only about 1 mEq/L of bicarbonate separation between arms, which may have under-tested the hypothesis; but a clinician prescribing veverimer today has biochemical correction and small-trial function gains to offer, and a large negative outcomes trial to disclose. (This shelf also answers the slate's duplicate veverimer topic, which asked the same bicarbonate-and-function question of the same trials.)
stamp: SPLIT — LIKELY (raises bicarbonate and improved physical-function measures in the parent trial programme) / LIKELY (the treatment made no difference to CKD progression in VALOR-CKD)

title: Oral urea for chronic SIADH: sodium normalised in every series — and matched vaptans for a year in the only head-to-head — but there is no randomised trial
question: In SIADH with hyponatraemia, does oral urea work as well as fluid restriction or vaptans?
balance: Probably — and 'probably' is the strongest word this evidence base earns. There is no randomised trial of urea in SIADH. What exists is unusually consistent observational evidence: in the only direct comparison (Soupart 2012, PMID: 22403276), 12 patients held a serum sodium of 135 mEq/L for a year on vaptans and then the same 135 mEq/L for a year on urea, within-patient. In Decaux 2018 (PMID: 29017746), mild water restriction alone sufficed for about 30% of chronic SIADH patients — identifiable by a urine osmolality under 400 mOsm/kg — and adding 15–30 g of urea normalised sodium in the remainder. In the largest series (Perelló-Camacho 2022, PMID: 35715573; 48 patients), sodium rose from 125.6 to 134.4 mmol/L with only mild digestive symptoms, two refusals for taste, and a reported cost 87.9% below tolvaptan. A systematic review of urea in hospital hyponatraemia (Schwartz 2023, PMID: 35512769) found the same direction in all 8 studies and graded the evidence low. Every endpoint is the sodium level itself; nobody has shown urea changes symptoms, falls or survival. Emergency correction of severe symptomatic hyponatraemia — bolus versus infusion — is a different question, homed at shelf #126.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: ANDROMEDA: adding daratumumab tripled complete haematologic responses (53% vs 18%) and doubled cardiac and kidney responses at 6 months
question: In patients with newly diagnosed AL amyloidosis, does adding daratumumab to bortezomib, cyclophosphamide and dexamethasone deepen haematologic, cardiac and kidney responses?
balance: Yes — decisively on response, not yet on survival. In ANDROMEDA (Kastritis 2021, PMID: 34192431; 388 patients with newly diagnosed AL amyloidosis), adding subcutaneous daratumumab to CyBorD nearly tripled the haematologic complete-response rate (53.3% vs 18.1%; relative risk 2.9, 95% CI 2.1 to 4.1) and improved survival free from major organ deterioration or haematologic progression (hazard ratio 0.58, 95% CI 0.36 to 0.93). The organ responses that determine prognosis followed the blood responses: at 6 months, cardiac responses were 41.5% versus 22.2% and kidney responses 53.0% versus 23.9% — the kidney figure being why this shelf sits with the kidney tranche, although the trial enrolled AL amyloidosis overall rather than a kidney-selected population. Deaths within the short median follow-up of 11.4 months were equal (27 vs 29, mostly amyloid cardiomyopathy), so the survival dividend of deeper responses is, within this record, still a projection. Added toxicity was modest: more lymphopenia, pneumonia, cardiac failure and diarrhoea at grade 3–4, and administration reactions in 7.3%.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: Immunonutrition around GI cancer surgery: infections cut by roughly a third relative in the largest synthesis — consistently, across 48 trials — with no mortality benefit and timing that matters
question: Before major gastrointestinal cancer surgery, does perioperative immunonutrition reduce infectious complications?
balance: Yes for infections and complications; no for mortality — and the effect is clearest when the formula is given around and after surgery rather than only before it. The founding double-blind phase 3 trial (Braga 1999, PMID: 10199318; 206 GI cancer patients) found postoperative infections in 14% on an arginine-, RNA- and omega-3-enriched formula versus 30% on the identical unenriched feed. The pooled estimates have moderated as the literature grew: Zhang 2012 (PMID: 22317969; 19 trials) gives an infectious-complication risk ratio of 0.44, while the largest and most recent synthesis (Matsui 2024, PMID: 37882375; 48 trials, 4,825 patients, high-certainty) gives 0.71 for infections and 0.78 for total complications — roughly a 29% relative reduction in infections. Osland 2014 (PMID: 23411423) adds the timing lesson: perioperative and postoperative administration carried the benefit, preoperative-only administration showed none, and no timing stratum reduced mortality. Two cautions travel with the stamp: the formulas differ between trials and the records name enrichments rather than brands, so no specific commercial product is endorsed by this shelf; and immunonutrition for the critically ill — a different question with a different and contested record — is shelf #16.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: Aspirin after hip fracture (PEP): pulmonary embolism cut 43% relative and fatal PE 58% relative versus placebo — but the aspirin-versus-heparin trial has never been done
question: After hip fracture, is aspirin as effective as heparin for preventing venous thromboembolism?
balance: The question as posed has never been tested — and the shelf says so on its face, because the nearest evidence is routinely misquoted as if it had been. The PEP trial (PMID: 10776741; 13,356 hip-fracture patients) randomised aspirin 160 mg daily against placebo, layered on whatever other prophylaxis clinicians chose. Aspirin reduced pulmonary embolism by 43% relative (95% CI 18 to 60) and symptomatic DVT by 29% relative; confirmed PE or DVT occurred in 1.6% versus 2.5% (9 fewer events per 1,000 treated), and fatal PE fell by 58% relative (18 vs 43 deaths). There was no effect on other causes of death, and the price was bleeding: 6 extra transfused postoperative bleeds per 1,000, though bleeding deaths were equal (13 vs 15). Because some PEP patients also received heparin and aspirin's effect looked similar in that subgroup, PEP is consistent with aspirin adding benefit alongside heparin — it cannot rank aspirin against heparin. So: aspirin after hip fracture is better than no aspirin (POSSIBLE, one trial, Tier C); whether it is as effective as heparin is unknown. Prophylaxis after elective arthroplasty — where head-to-head evidence does exist — is shelf #1127, and the wider hip-fracture care bundle is shelf #342.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit versus no aspirin; equivalence to heparin is untested — the two have never been randomised head-to-head after hip fracture)

title: Stepwise prandial insulin in type 2 diabetes: one injection at the largest meal matched three on average HbA1c in both randomised tests — with less hypoglycaemia, but fewer patients reaching target
question: In type 2 diabetes not at target on basal insulin, does adding prandial insulin stepwise — starting with one daily injection at the largest meal — achieve glycaemic control comparable to immediate full basal-bolus (three daily injections), and with what hypoglycaemia and burden trade-offs?
balance: Two randomised trials have tested the stepwise idea directly, and they agree. In Davidson 2011 (PMID: 21324825), 631 adults with type 2 diabetes and A1C of 8.0% or more on oral agents entered a 14-week insulin glargine run-in; the 343 (54%) still above 7.0% were randomised to insulin glulisine once, twice, or three times daily for 24 weeks. A1C reductions with one or two injections were noninferior to three (95% CIs for the differences −0.39 to 0.36 and −0.30 to 0.43) — but the share reaching A1C below 7.0% was lower with fewer injections (30% with one, 33% with two, 46% with three), while severe hypoglycaemia ran the other way (7%, 8%, and 16% respectively; the differences were not statistically significant). In FullSTEP (Rodbard 2014, PMID: 24622667), 401 patients uncontrolled on basal insulin were randomised to stepwise addition of insulin aspart — one bolus at the largest meal, with further mealtime doses added at weeks 11 and 22 only if HbA1c remained at or above 7% — or to full basal-bolus from the start: HbA1c fell 0.98% versus 1.12% over 32 weeks (difference 0.14%, 95% CI −0.02 to 0.30; noninferior), and hypoglycaemic episodes were significantly fewer with the stepwise approach (rate ratio 0.58, 95% CI 0.45 to 0.75 — a relative rate). So on average glucose control, starting with one prandial injection at the largest meal and adding more only if needed gives up nothing measurable against routine three-injection basal-bolus; what it buys is fewer injections, fewer glucose checks, and less hypoglycaemia. What it may cost is the top end: in Davidson, more patients crossed below 7.0% when all three meals were covered from the outset. A third randomised comparison, Riddle 2014 (PMID: 24118931), which initiated and advanced insulin over one year, found the same shape — basal plus a single prandial injection noninferior to premixed insulin, with full basal-bolus only slightly ahead on target attainment — and is cross-referenced here rather than carded, because its question spans initiation (shelf #2640's home). Initiation strategy itself is shelf #2640; the self-monitoring burden each extra injection drags with it is shelves #559 and #1768; adding a GLP-1 agonist instead of prandial insulin is shelf #2653.
stamp: LIKELY (stepwise basal-plus matches full basal-bolus on average HbA1c reduction, with less hypoglycaemia; fewer patients reach an HbA1c below 7% than with three injections from the start)

title: De-intensifying basal-bolus insulin: three randomised trials kept HbA1c level when mealtime insulin was swapped for a GLP-1 agonist or an SGLT2 inhibitor — on a fraction of the insulin dose and with less hypoglycaemia
question: In type 2 diabetes already on a basal-bolus regimen, does de-intensification — dropping the prandial doses for basal insulin plus a GLP-1 receptor agonist (or fixed-ratio combination) or an SGLT2 inhibitor — maintain glycaemic control with less hypoglycaemia, weight gain, and injection burden?
balance: Three randomised trials have now tested deliberate de-intensification of basal-bolus insulin, and in all three glycaemic control held. In BEYOND (Giugliano 2021, PMID: 33883195), 305 patients with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled on basal-bolus (mean HbA1c 8.6%) were randomised to intensifying the basal-bolus regimen, switching to a once-daily fixed-ratio basal insulin/GLP-1 receptor agonist combination, or switching to basal insulin plus an SGLT2 inhibitor. At 6 months HbA1c had fallen equally (−0.6%, −0.6%, and −0.7%; noninferiority P < 0.001), but total insulin dose moved in opposite directions — up to 62 units/day on intensified basal-bolus versus down to 27 and 21 units/day in the switch arms — and hypoglycaemia was less frequent after switching (17.8% of patients versus 7.8% and 5.9%; P = 0.015). In the IDEAL trial (Novodvorský 2026, PMID: 41395661), 90 patients on multiple daily injections (HbA1c at most 9%, total dose at most 0.8 IU/kg, preserved fasting C-peptide) were randomised to once-daily iGlarLixi or continued injections: the HbA1c difference was −0.12% (95% CI −0.48 to 0.23), with weight 4.19 kg lower and insulin dose 28.6 IU/day lower on the simplified regimen. In a smaller Japanese trial (Ando 2021, PMID: 33650779), 40 patients well controlled on multiple daily injections had all bolus insulin replaced by canagliflozin or liraglutide: HbA1c and glucose variability were maintained for 24 weeks, insulin dose fell, quality-of-life scores rose, and there was no severe hypoglycaemia. The consistent picture: in patients with residual beta-cell function, much of the prandial insulin in a basal-bolus regimen is replaceable — control is kept while injections, dose, hypoglycaemia, and, where measured, weight all fall. The limits are equally consistent: every trial is open-label, none exceeds 6 months, the two smaller trials enrolled selected patients (well controlled, or dose-capped with measurable C-peptide), and BEYOND's switch arms lost 9–12 patients to dropout against none on continued basal-bolus — de-intensification suits many, not all. A 4-year follow-up of the BEYOND cohort has been reported (PMID: 40877579); its PubMed record carries no abstract data, so no figures are taken from it here. The mirror-image question — whether prandial insulin should be added stepwise in the first place — is shelf #2651; adding a GLP-1 agonist instead of prandial insulin when basal alone fails is shelf #2653.
stamp: POSSIBLE (de-intensification to basal insulin plus a GLP-1 receptor agonist or an SGLT2 inhibitor maintains HbA1c with less hypoglycaemia and far less insulin across three randomised trials — but all are open-label, none exceeds six months, and the two smaller ones enrolled selected patients)

title: Adding a GLP-1 agonist versus adding mealtime insulin to basal insulin: equal HbA1c in the head-to-head trial and across 13 pooled trials — with about half the hypoglycaemia, weight loss instead of gain, and 30 fewer units of insulin a day
question: In type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled on basal insulin, does adding a GLP-1 receptor agonist control glucose as well as adding prandial insulin — and how do hypoglycaemia, weight, and insulin dose compare?
balance: The direct head-to-head exists. In GetGoal Duo-2 (Rosenstock 2016, PMID: 27222510), patients whose HbA1c remained 7–9% after a 12-week glargine optimisation run-in were randomised to add lixisenatide once daily, insulin glulisine once daily, or glulisine three times daily: HbA1c ended at 7.2%, 7.2%, and 7.0% respectively — lixisenatide met its noninferiority endpoints against both prandial strategies — while symptomatic hypoglycaemia and body weight were lower with lixisenatide, at the price of more gastrointestinal events. A propensity-matched pooling of five randomised trials (Raccah 2014, PMID: 24246441) found basal insulin plus lixisenatide about twice as likely as basal insulin plus once-daily rapid-acting insulin to reach HbA1c below 7% without symptomatic hypoglycaemia (odds ratio 1.90, 95% CI 1.01 to 3.55 — a relative, odds-based measure) and without weight gain (OR 2.58, 1.23 to 5.40). Across the class, a meta-analysis of 13 randomised trials (Castellana 2019, PMID: 30270567) found GLP-1 agonist/insulin combinations and basal-plus/basal-bolus statistically indistinguishable on HbA1c (difference −0.06%, 95% CI −0.14 to 0.02), with 3.72 kg greater weight loss, roughly half the risk of hypoglycaemic events (relative risk 0.46, 0.38 to 0.55), and 30.3 IU/day less insulin. So for the average patient failing basal insulin, the prandial effect does not require prandial insulin: a GLP-1 agonist buys the same average control with less hypoglycaemia, no mealtime injections, and weight moving the other way. The caveats: the direct trial evidence rests largely on one short-acting agent (lixisenatide) over 26 weeks; gastrointestinal intolerance is the GLP-1 class's own burden; and patients with very high HbA1c, catabolic symptoms, or little residual beta-cell function were not these trials' population — prandial insulin keeps that territory. Fixed-ratio combinations as an initiation strategy are shelf #2056; switching an established basal-bolus regimen down to basal insulin plus a GLP-1 agonist is shelf #2652; adding prandial insulin stepwise is shelf #2651.
stamp: LIKELY (a GLP-1 receptor agonist added to basal insulin matches prandial insulin on HbA1c, with less hypoglycaemia, weight loss rather than gain, and a lower total insulin dose)

title: H2 blockers genuinely work for reflux — famotidine healed about 7 in 10 patients by 12 weeks against 3 in 10 on placebo — but PPIs heal roughly twice as fast and far more completely
question: In adults with reflux symptoms or erosive oesophagitis, do H2-receptor blockers (such as famotidine) relieve heartburn and heal the oesophagus versus placebo — and how do they compare with proton-pump inhibitors?
balance: LIKELY benefit versus placebo; LIKELY inferior to PPIs. The Cochrane review (Khan 2007, PMID: 17443524) pooled 134 trials with 35,978 oesophagitis patients: H2-receptor antagonists reduced the risk of remaining unhealed versus placebo (RR 0.74, 95% CI 0.66 to 0.84 — a relative effect), while PPIs beat H2RA-based therapy clearly (RR 0.51, 0.44 to 0.59). The class-level meta-analysis (Chiba 1997, PMID: 9178669) puts average healing at 51.9% for H2 blockers against 83.6% for PPIs and 28.2% for placebo, with heartburn freedom at 47.6% versus 77.4%. The famotidine trials themselves agree: 40 mg twice daily healed 69% of erosive oesophagitis by 12 weeks versus 29% on placebo (Simon 1994, PMID: 8186349), and both famotidine regimens beat placebo on symptoms and healing in the 338-patient US multicentre trial (PMID: 1746996). So the answer is two-part: for healing and symptom relief, H2 blockers are a real treatment, not a placebo with branding — and they are not interchangeable with PPIs, healing about three-fifths as many patients at about half the speed. PROPOSED SPLIT — LIKELY (benefit) versus placebo / LIKELY (less effective than proton-pump inhibitors) (not Tier C: multiple placebo-controlled trials plus two syntheses). Sucralfate, the other pre-PPI alternative, is at shelf #2656; vonoprazan versus lansoprazole at #1661.
stamp: SPLIT — LIKELY (benefit) versus placebo / LIKELY (less effective than proton-pump inhibitors)

title: Alginate–antacid (the tested product is Gaviscon Double Action) beats placebo for reflux symptoms — about 48% responders versus 33% — but it does not beat acid suppression, and adding it to a PPI failed its confirmatory trial
question: In adults with heartburn and reflux symptoms, do alginate–antacid combinations relieve symptoms better than placebo, antacids alone, or acid suppression?
balance: POSSIBLE — a real but modest symptom benefit against placebo or antacid alone, unproven against or on top of acid suppression. The meta-analysis (Leiman 2017, PMID: 28375448) pooled 14 trials (2,095 patients): alginates increased the odds of GERD symptom resolution versus placebo or antacids (OR 4.42, 95% CI 2.45 to 7.97, a relative odds measure), and appeared less effective than PPIs or H2 blockers without reaching significance (OR 0.58, 0.27 to 1.22). The largest single trial, of the branded alginate–antacid Gaviscon Double Action (Reckitt Benckiser), found 47.8% responders versus 33.2% on placebo at 7 days (Wilkinson 2019, PMID: 30272584) — about 15 extra responders per 100 treated — with a concordant pilot (Thomas 2014, PMID: 24471505). But when the same product was added to a PPI for breakthrough symptoms, the 262-patient confirmatory trial found 51% versus 48% response (Coyle 2017, PMID: 28464343). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit versus placebo/antacid; no proven added benefit on top of a PPI) (not Tier C: multiple randomised trials and a meta-analysis, all short-term and symptom-based).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit versus placebo or antacid alone; no proven added benefit on top of a PPI)

title: Sucralfate healed reflux oesophagitis about as often as cimetidine in three small pre-PPI trials — and matched it in duodenal ulcer (72% versus 71%, against 35% on placebo) — but the trials are tiny, old and mostly single-blind
question: In reflux oesophagitis and peptic ulcer, does sucralfate heal and relieve as well as H2-receptor blockade?
balance: POSSIBLE — sucralfate looks like an H2 blocker, on H2-blocker-era evidence. In the only double-blind reflux trial, healing at 12 weeks was 62% on sucralfate versus 59% on cimetidine (Elsborg 1991, PMID: 2011701); the two single-blind trials found 31% versus 14% (Hameeteman 1987, PMID: 3655273) and 48% versus 55% (Ros 1991, PMID: 1882895) at 8 weeks, none significantly different. The placebo anchor comes from duodenal ulcer: healing 71.8% on sucralfate versus 71.4% on cimetidine and 35% on placebo at 4 weeks (Khanna 1989, PMID: 2695513). No trial compares sucralfate with a PPI, and the trials are small enough that 'no significant difference' cannot exclude a real gap in either direction. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit — comparable to H2 blockers in small pre-PPI trials; never tested against PPIs) (not Tier C: four randomised trials, though all small and old). H2 blockers themselves are at shelf #2654.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit — comparable to H2 blockers in small pre-PPI trials; never tested against PPIs)

title: Baclofen measurably cuts reflux episodes, but symptom relief in PPI-refractory patients appeared only in the subgroup whose symptoms were proven to track reflux — and about 1 in 6 stopped it for side effects
question: In adults whose reflux symptoms persist despite a proton-pump inhibitor, does adding baclofen reduce reflux episodes and improve symptoms?
balance: POSSIBLE, narrowly. Baclofen reduces reflux events themselves — acid and non-acid — in every study that counts them: median combined episodes fell from 23 to 8 after a single dose in heartburn patients (Vela 2003, PMID: 12534409), and a meta-analysis of 9 trials (283 participants) found consistent short-term reductions in episodes and transient sphincter relaxations (Li 2014, PMID: 25389436). The symptom evidence is thinner. In the one trial of the actual clinical question — add-on therapy for symptoms persisting on twice-daily PPI — overall wellbeing only trended better (P = 0.06), and significant benefit was confined to the 25 patients whose symptoms were proven to associate with reflux events (Pauwels 2022, PMID: 35665521); in an earlier 2-week trial, no between-group difference reached significance (Cossentino 2012, PMID: 22428773). Five of 31 baclofen patients in the refractory trial stopped for side effects. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit — in patients with a proven symptom–reflux association) (Tier C: small trials, a subgroup-dependent main result, and a physiology-led evidence base). Baclofen for alcohol dependence in cirrhosis is a different question, homed at shelf #1677.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit — in patients with a proven symptom–reflux association)

title: FMT for IBS splits by delivery route: donor stool by colonoscope or gastroscope beat placebo clearly in two trials, while FMT capsules were no better than placebo — and in one trial worse
question: In adults with irritable bowel syndrome, does faecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) improve symptoms versus placebo?
balance: SPLIT — the route and donor seem to decide the answer. Donor FMT delivered endoscopically beat autologous placebo twice: 65% versus 43% response by colonoscope (Johnsen 2018, PMID: 29100842) and 76.9% (30 g) to 89.1% (60 g) versus 23.6% by gastroscope using one screened donor (El-Salhy 2020, PMID: 31852769). Capsule FMT failed twice: placebo produced significantly greater symptom improvement at 3 months in Halkjær 2018 (PMID: 29980607), and Aroniadis 2019 (PMID: 31326345) found no difference (IBS-SSS 221 versus 236) before stopping for futility. Placebo responses were large everywhere (24–43%), all trials were single-centre or small, and no trial compares routes directly. PROPOSED SPLIT — POSSIBLE (benefit) for endoscopically delivered donor FMT / LIKELY (no benefit) for oral capsule FMT as tested (not Tier C: four randomised placebo-controlled trials). Other IBS treatments are homed separately (peppermint oil #118, low-FODMAP diet #202, probiotics #331, amitriptyline #1662, rifaximin and eluxadoline #772).
stamp: SPLIT — POSSIBLE (benefit) for endoscopically delivered donor FMT / LIKELY (no benefit) for oral capsule FMT as tested

title: Sacral nerve stimulation cut incontinent episodes from 9.5 to 3.1 a week where optimal medical therapy changed nothing — with perfect continence in 47% of implanted patients — but only test responders are implanted, and the trial base is small
question: In adults with severe faecal incontinence that has not responded to conservative care, does sacral nerve stimulation improve continence versus continued conservative management?
balance: POSSIBLE — a big effect, a small and selected evidence base. In the only randomised trial against conservative care, sacral nerve stimulation reduced incontinent episodes from 9.5 to 3.1 per week over 12 months while optimal medical therapy (pelvic floor exercises, bulking agents, diet) produced no significant improvement, and 47.2% of implanted patients achieved perfect continence (Tjandra 2008, PMID: 18278532; Cochrane mean difference −6.30 episodes/week, 95% CI −10.34 to −2.26). A pilot trial found marginally larger short-term effects than percutaneous tibial nerve stimulation (Thin 2015, PMID: 25644291), and the Cochrane reviewers conclude there is limited evidence that SNS improves continence in a proportion of patients, with device adverse events — site pain, seroma, lead problems, occasional removal — throughout (Thaha 2015, PMID: 26299888). The caveats are structural: the trial was unblinded, and only patients who respond to a test phase (90% in Tjandra) receive implants, so the estimates describe the test-then-implant pathway rather than all-comers. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) (Tier C: the comparison with conservative care rests on a single randomised trial).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Diosmectite shortens acute diarrhoea by roughly a day in children (about 24 hours in pooled trials) and by about 15 hours in the one adult trial — a modest adjunct to rehydration, not a substitute for it
question: In acute diarrhoea, does diosmectite (smectite) shorten the illness in children or adults, as an adjunct to rehydration?
balance: POSSIBLE — a consistent, modest shortening of the illness. In children, the meta-analysis of 9 randomised trials (1,238 participants) found diarrhoea shortened by about 24 hours (random-effects pooled difference −24.4 h, 95% CI −29.8 to −19.1) with more children cured by day 3 (RR 1.64, 1.36 to 1.98; NNT 4) and adverse effects similar to placebo (Szajewska 2006, PMID: 16393300). The largest paediatric trials confirm a real, if small, physiological effect — stool output 94.5 versus 104.1 g/kg (Dupont 2009, PMID: 19268266, two trials reported together). In adults, a single trial found median recovery at 53.8 versus 69.0 hours (Khediri 2011, PMID: 21760777). The paediatric trials have quality limitations their own reviewers flag, and no trial shows an effect on dehydration or hospitalisation. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) (not Tier C: a multi-trial base, though the adult claim rests on one trial).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Naloxegol worked in both of its identical phase-3 trials — response in about 44% and 40% versus 29% on placebo at the 25 mg dose — with pain scores and opioid doses unchanged; the price is gastrointestinal side effects
question: In adults taking opioids for chronic non-cancer pain who have opioid-induced constipation, does naloxegol restore bowel function without reversing pain relief?
balance: LIKELY — the rare clean replication. Two identical phase-3 trials found naloxegol 25 mg beat placebo on a strict responder definition in both (44.4% versus 29.4% and 39.7% versus 29.3%; absolute gains of about 15 and 10 percentage points), with the same result in patients who had already failed laxatives; the 12.5 mg dose succeeded in only one of the two (Chey 2014, PMID: 24896818). The analgesia question is answered by the trials' own pain data: scores and opioid doses tracked placebo exactly (Webster 2018, PMID: 28898536 — a flagged secondary report of the same trials). Over 52 weeks against usual laxative care, naloxegol produced more gastrointestinal adverse events (abdominal pain 17.8% versus 3.3%; diarrhoea 12.9% versus 5.9%) but no withdrawal events and no bowel perforations (Webster 2014, PMID: 25112584). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) (not Tier C: two large replicated randomised trials plus a 52-week safety study).
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: Mesalazine does not prevent recurrent diverticulitis: in two phase-3 trials the placebo groups did numerically best, and no dose of mesalamine beat placebo at two years
question: In adults who have had acute diverticulitis, does mesalazine (mesalamine) prevent recurrence?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference). The two PREVENT trials randomised 1,182 patients with prior diverticulitis to mesalamine 1.2–4.8 g daily or placebo for two years: recurrence-free proportions were 53–63% on mesalamine versus 65% on placebo in PREVENT-1 and 59–69% versus 68% in PREVENT-2 — placebo numerically ahead at every dose (Raskin 2014, PMID: 25038431). The DIVA trial found no significant difference on its primary symptom score after an acute episode, with recurrence low and comparable across groups (Stollman 2013, PMID: 23426454), and the Cochrane review of 7 trials (1,805 patients) found no evidence of a preventive effect (Carter 2017, PMID: 28973845). PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) (not Tier C: two large phase-3 trials). Treating acute uncomplicated diverticulitis — antibiotics or not — is shelf #178.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference)

title: Alosetron relieves IBS-D symptoms in women (adequate relief 41% versus 29% sustained over 3 months) — and carries a real, uncommon serious harm: ischaemic colitis in roughly 1 per 1,000 patient-years, the risk that withdrew it from the market
question: In women with diarrhoea-predominant irritable bowel syndrome, does alosetron relieve symptoms — and how large is the risk of ischaemic colitis and serious constipation complications?
balance: SPLIT — a genuine benefit bought with a genuine, uncommon, serious harm. Efficacy is consistent: adequate relief sustained across 3 months in 41% versus 29% (Camilleri 2000, PMID: 10744088), urgency controlled on 73% versus 57% of days (Lembo 2001, PMID: 11569692), and pooled global improvement RR 1.60 across 8 trials (Rahimi 2008, PMID: 18555935) — relative measures sitting on an absolute gain of roughly 12 responders per 100 women. The everyday harm is constipation (30% versus 3%). The decisive harm is rare: ischaemic colitis in 0.15% of trial patients versus none on placebo, and about 1.1 per 1,000 patient-years post-marketing (Chang 2006, PMID: 16606352), running at 0.95 per 1,000 patient-years even under the restricted risk-management programme, though without deaths or surgeries in that series (Chang 2010, PMID: 20197759). That risk withdrew the drug in 2000; it returned in 2002 restricted to women with severe IBS-D who have failed conventional therapy. PROPOSED SPLIT — POSSIBLE (benefit) for symptom relief / POSSIBLE (harm): ischaemic colitis and serious constipation complications (Tier C: the serious-harm quantification rests on post-marketing and observational data).
stamp: SPLIT — POSSIBLE (benefit) for symptom relief / POSSIBLE (harm): ischaemic colitis and serious constipation complications

title: Oral versus intravenous steroids in acute asthma: every head-to-head trial found the drip added nothing for patients who can swallow
question: In acute asthma exacerbations, are oral corticosteroids as effective as intravenous corticosteroids?
balance: Three small head-to-head randomised trials spanning 25 years, in genuinely sick patients, all point the same way. Ratto 1988 randomised 77 patients with status asthmaticus (mean presenting FEV1 26% of predicted) to oral or intravenous methylprednisolone and found no difference in respiratory failure, FEV1, hospital days, speed of improvement or side effects (PMID: 3385910). Harrison 1986 asked the additive version — intravenous hydrocortisone on top of high-dose oral prednisolone in 52 admitted patients — and peak flow at 24 hours was identical (PMID: 2868207). Dembla 2011 randomised 65 admitted adults to oral prednisolone 100 mg daily or intravenous hydrocortisone for 72 hours: peak flow reached 53.2% versus 55.9% of predicted (p = 0.28) (PMID: 22479740). The neighbouring relapse question tells the same story: Rowe's 2017 network meta-analysis of steroids given at emergency-department discharge found no route clearly superior, with intramuscular ranking first only on a probability analysis with wide credible intervals (PMID: 27664401). The pharmacology agrees — oral prednisolone is almost completely absorbed — so the intravenous route's real indications are the patient who cannot swallow, is vomiting, or is ventilated, none of whom populated these trials. None of the three trials was a formal noninferiority study and all are small, so a modest difference cannot be excluded; but in four decades no trial has ever shown the drip to be better. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference — oral corticosteroids are as effective as intravenous in acute asthma) (not Tier C: three concordant RCTs plus a network meta-analysis, though the trials are small and old). Magnesium as an adjunct in acute asthma is a different question, homed at shelf #238.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference — oral corticosteroids are as effective as intravenous in acute asthma)

title: One inhaler for both jobs: maintenance-and-reliever therapy cut severe exacerbations by about a third relative versus fixed maintenance plus a separate reliever
question: In asthma, does single-inhaler maintenance-and-reliever therapy (MART) beat conventional maintenance plus a short-acting reliever?
balance: The pooled evidence is consistent and clinically meaningful. Sobieraj's 2018 JAMA systematic review and meta-analysis of 16 randomised trials (22,748 patients) found that in patients aged 12 and over, single maintenance-and-reliever therapy (SMART/MART) with budesonide–formoterol reduced exacerbations versus the same dose of inhaled corticosteroid/LABA maintenance plus a short-acting reliever (risk ratio 0.68, 95% CI 0.58 to 0.80; absolute risk difference −6.4 percentage points, 95% CI −10.2 to −2.6) and versus a higher maintenance dose (RR 0.77, 0.60 to 0.98) (PMID: 29554195). The largest constituent trial, Kuna 2007 (3,335 patients, 6 months), recorded severe exacerbation rates of 12 per 100 patients on MART versus 16 on fixed-dose budesonide–formoterol and 19 on salmeterol–fluticasone, both with terbutaline relief — rate ratios 0.72 and 0.61 — while MART patients used less inhaled corticosteroid overall (PMID: 17362472). The mechanism shows up in Buhl's 2012 pooled exploratory analysis: after a day of high reliever use, exacerbation treatment was needed within 21 days on only 2.5–3.4% of days with MART versus 6.0–10.1% with fixed-dose regimens — the extra reliever puffs deliver anti-inflammatory drug at exactly the moment of deterioration (PMID: 22816878). Caveats: every trial used budesonide–formoterol, because formoterol's rapid onset makes it usable as a reliever; the strategy cannot be assumed for salmeterol combinations. Data in children aged 4–11 rest on only 341 patients. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) (not Tier C: 16-trial meta-analysis with consistent direction). This is not shelf #308 — that asks about as-needed-only budesonide–formoterol in mild asthma with no daily maintenance; this shelf is for patients on daily maintenance treatment. Adding a long-acting muscarinic antagonist instead is shelf #1033.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: Montelukast for allergic rhinitis: better than placebo by a whisker, no better than an antihistamine, clearly beaten by a steroid spray — and it carries a boxed warning
question: In adults with allergic rhinitis, does montelukast relieve symptoms as well as oral antihistamines or intranasal corticosteroids?
balance: Montelukast works, but by margins that struggle to justify its risk frame. The 2020 systematic review and meta-analysis by Krishnamoorthy (15 studies, 10,387 participants) found montelukast beat placebo on daytime nasal symptoms by a mean difference of −0.12 points on a symptom scale — statistically firm, clinically tiny (PMID: 32915441). Against the standard treatments it loses or ties: oral antihistamines were superior to montelukast for daytime nasal symptoms (mean difference 0.08 in the antihistamine's favour, p = 0.002), and intranasal fluticasone was superior by a wide margin (daytime symptoms mean difference 0.71, night-time 0.63, both p < 0.001). The big placebo-controlled trials agree on the shape: in Nayak 2002 (907 patients), montelukast and loratadine each beat placebo, but adding montelukast to loratadine — the primary comparison — was not significantly better than loratadine alone (PMID: 12086367); Meltzer 2000 (460 patients) found each drug alone gave only 'modest improvements', with the combination better than either (PMID: 10808172). Against this small benefit sits a harm no comparator carries: in 2020 the US FDA required a boxed warning on montelukast for serious neuropsychiatric events (including suicidal thoughts and actions) and advised reserving it in allergic rhinitis for patients who do not respond to or cannot tolerate alternatives. PROPOSED SPLIT — POSSIBLE (small benefit versus placebo) / LIKELY (less effective than intranasal corticosteroids, and no better than oral antihistamines) (not Tier C: 15-study meta-analysis plus two large RCTs). The combined intranasal azelastine–fluticasone spray question is homed at shelf #907.
stamp: SPLIT — POSSIBLE (small benefit versus placebo) / LIKELY (less effective than intranasal corticosteroids, and no better than oral antihistamines)

title: Pulmonary rehabilitation in stable COPD: breathlessness, quality of life and walking distance all improve beyond the clinically important margin — hospital days halve, though no fewer patients are admitted
question: In stable COPD, does pulmonary rehabilitation improve breathlessness, exercise capacity and hospital admissions?
balance: For breathlessness, quality of life and exercise capacity this is among the best-supported interventions in COPD. McCarthy's 2015 Cochrane review pooled 65 randomised trials with 3,822 participants in stable disease: every Chronic Respiratory Questionnaire domain improved by more than its 0.5-unit minimal clinically important difference (dyspnoea mean difference 0.79, 95% CI 0.56 to 1.03; fatigue 0.68; emotional function 0.56; mastery 0.71), the St George's Respiratory Questionnaire total improved by −6.89 points (MCID 4), six-minute walk distance by 43.93 metres, and maximal exercise capacity by 6.77 watts (PMID: 25705944). The admissions part of the question needs care: the Cochrane review did not pool admission outcomes in stable COPD, and the largest single trial, Griffiths 2000 (200 patients followed for a year), found no difference in how many patients were admitted (40 versus 41) but half as many days in hospital among those admitted (10.4 versus 21.0 days, p = 0.022), alongside better walking ability and health status (PMID: 10665556). So: admissions prevented — not shown in stable disease; hospital burden reduced — suggested by one large trial. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) (not Tier C: 65-trial Cochrane synthesis). Rehabilitation started after a hospitalised exacerbation is a different question with its own readmission and mortality data — shelf #304; this shelf is the stable-disease programme.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: Airway clearance in bronchiectasis: one small year-long placebo-controlled trial found fewer exacerbations and better quality of life — the rest of the evidence is short, tiny crossover studies
question: In bronchiectasis, do airway-clearance techniques (oscillatory PEP, ELTGOL) reduce exacerbations and improve quality of life?
balance: Airway clearance is prescribed to almost everyone with bronchiectasis and chronic expectoration, yet the trial base is remarkably thin. The single long-term placebo-controlled trial, Muñoz 2018, randomised just 44 patients with chronic expectoration to twice-daily ELTGOL (slow expiration with the glottis open, in lateral posture) or placebo exercises for a year: the ELTGOL group cleared more sputum, had fewer exacerbations (p = 0.042) and clinically significant improvements in St George's Respiratory Questionnaire and Leicester Cough Questionnaire scores (both p < 0.001) (PMID: 29326318). Everything else is smaller and shorter: Lee's 2015 Cochrane review found only seven studies with 105 participants in total, six of them crossover designs, several testing a single treatment session; one oscillatory-device study (20 adults) found no significant difference in exacerbations at 12 weeks but a 7.5-unit SGRQ improvement, and short-term sputum expectoration rose by about 8.4 mL with oscillatory devices (PMID: 26591003). Heterogeneity precluded any meta-analysis. So the honest position: a plausible, low-harm intervention with one positive small trial on the outcomes that matter and a surrounding literature too small to confirm or refute it. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) (Tier C: the exacerbation claim rests on a single 44-patient trial; the rest of the base is tiny short crossover studies). Drug treatments for bronchiectasis exacerbations (macrolides, brensocatib) are separate questions, homed elsewhere in this area.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: A suppository before the journey: rectal artesunate halved death or disability when referral took more than six hours — and showed nothing when care was quick, or when the referral chain broke down in routine practice
question: In young children with severe malaria who cannot reach hospital quickly, does pre-referral rectal artesunate reduce death and disability?
balance: One very large trial, one crucial subgroup, and one sobering implementation lesson. Gomes 2009 randomised 17,826 patients with suspected severe malaria who could not be treated orally in Bangladesh, Ghana and Tanzania to a single rectal artesunate suppository or placebo before referral (12,068 analysed after exclusions). Overall, mortality was 2.5% versus 3.0% (p = 0.1 — not significant on its own), permanent disability was much rarer with artesunate (2 versus 13 patients), and the composite of death or permanent disability was significantly reduced: 2.6% versus 3.2% (p = 0.0484) (PMID: 19059639). The benefit was concentrated where the logic of the intervention says it should be: in patients who reached a clinic within about 6 hours there was no significant effect (death or disability 1.6% versus 1.9%, risk ratio 0.86), while in those still not in clinic after more than 6 hours — half of them still travelling after 15 hours — death or disability was halved, 1.9% versus 3.8% (risk ratio 0.49, 95% CI 0.32 to 0.77). There was no reduction in deaths within the first 6 hours: the suppository buys time, it does not rescue the already-moribund. The trial population was mostly young children, and guidelines subsequently adopted the intervention for young children facing long referral delays. But the CARAMAL roll-out across DR Congo, Nigeria and Uganda, following more than 6,200 severely ill children in routine practice, found no survival advantage — most likely, its investigators concluded, because referral was often incomplete and post-referral treatment inadequate: a suppository cannot compensate for a broken chain of care (PMID: 36549311). PROPOSED SPLIT — LIKELY (benefit when referral to injectable treatment takes many hours) / LIKELY (the treatment made no difference when patients reached care within about 6 hours, or in routine-practice roll-out with incomplete follow-up care) (Tier C: the efficacy claim rests on a single trial and its delay subgroup, and the real-world evidence is observational). Treatment of severe malaria once in hospital — intravenous artesunate — is a different question, homed at shelf #510.
stamp: SPLIT — LIKELY (benefit when referral to injectable treatment takes many hours) / LIKELY (the treatment made no difference when patients reached care within about 6 hours, or in routine-practice roll-out with incomplete follow-up care)

title: Oxygen at night for COPD patients who desaturate only in sleep: the one trial stopped at 243 of 600 planned patients and found nothing — too small to close the question
question: In COPD with isolated nocturnal desaturation, does nocturnal oxygen improve survival?
balance: Long-term oxygen prolongs life in COPD with severe daytime hypoxaemia — that is shelf #305 and is not in doubt. This shelf asks the harder question: the patient whose oxygen saturation is acceptable by day but falls at night (below 90% for at least 30% of the recording time) and who therefore does not qualify for long-term oxygen. The only randomised trial, INOX (Lacasse 2020), was double-blind and placebo-controlled — nocturnal oxygen versus ambient air from a sham concentrator — over 3 to 4 years, with a primary composite of death or progression to meeting long-term oxygen criteria. It stopped early for recruitment and retention difficulties after randomising 243 of a projected 600 patients. At 3 years, 39.0% of the nocturnal-oxygen group and 42.0% of the placebo group had died or met the criteria (difference −3.0 percentage points, 95% CI −15.1 to 9.1) (PMID: 32937046). That interval is wide enough to contain a clinically important benefit and a clinically important harm; the authors' own conclusion is that the underpowered trial 'provides no indication' of effect in either direction. The honest stamp is therefore a weak no-difference: nothing here justifies prescribing nocturnal oxygen for isolated nocturnal desaturation, and nothing here proves it useless. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference — but the single trial was stopped early and underpowered, so a modest benefit or harm is not excluded) (Tier C: single trial, stopped early).
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference — but the single trial was stopped early and underpowered, so a modest benefit or harm is not excluded)

title: Oxygen for exertion in COPD: small gains in breathlessness scores straight after exercise in short studies, but the largest blinded trial found no benefit in daily breathlessness, quality of life or function
question: In COPD with exertional desaturation only, does ambulatory oxygen improve breathlessness and activity?
balance: The evidence splits cleanly by what is measured and when. Moore 2011, the largest and most rigorous trial — 143 breathless COPD patients without severe resting hypoxaemia, double-blind, randomised to domiciliary ambulatory oxygen or cylinder air at 6 L/min for any breathlessness-provoking activity over 12 weeks — found no significant difference in dyspnoea, health-related quality of life, mood or functional status, and exertional desaturation (present in 50 patients, to 88% or below) did not predict who benefited; both groups improved slightly, suggesting the gas flow itself, or trial participation, carries a placebo effect (PMID: 20880870). The Cochrane review by Ameer 2014 pooled four studies (331 participants) and did find statistically significant benefits in breathlessness measured immediately after exercise in two studies, and in the dyspnoea (mean difference 0.28, 95% CI 0.10 to 0.45) and fatigue (0.17, 0.04 to 0.31) domains of quality of life — while finding no evidence of effect on survival and limited, mostly null effects on exercise capacity (PMID: 24957353). Reconciling the two: oxygen can ease breathlessness during or just after a laboratory exercise test, in small short studies; prescribed for everyday use in the best blinded trial, it did not improve how patients felt or functioned day to day. PROPOSED SPLIT — POSSIBLE (small benefit on breathlessness measured immediately after exercise in short studies) / LIKELY (the treatment made no difference to day-to-day breathlessness, quality of life or function in the largest trial) (not Tier C: multiple RCTs and a Cochrane synthesis, though all trials are small). Oxygen for resting hypoxaemia is shelf #305; oxygen at night only is shelf #2670.
stamp: SPLIT — POSSIBLE (small benefit on breathlessness measured immediately after exercise in short studies) / LIKELY (the treatment made no difference to day-to-day breathlessness, quality of life or function in the largest trial)

title: Eight weeks to cure hepatitis C: glecaprevir–pibrentasvir cleared the virus in 93–99% across genotypes 1–6, with or without compensated cirrhosis
question: In adults with chronic hepatitis C, does an 8-week course of glecaprevir–pibrentasvir cure infection across genotypes?
balance: The phase 3 programme answers the question directly, genotype by genotype. In patients without cirrhosis, ENDURANCE-1 and ENDURANCE-3 (Zeuzem 2018, 1,208 treated) found sustained virological response 12 weeks after treatment (SVR12 — the accepted definition of cure) of 99.1% with 8 weeks versus 99.7% with 12 weeks in genotype 1, and 95% in genotype 3 on either duration (the 12-week genotype-3 arm matched sofosbuvir–daclatasvir's 97%) (PMID: 29365309). For genotypes 2, 4, 5 and 6 without cirrhosis, Asselah 2018 pooled three phase 3 trials: 8-week SVR12 was 98% in genotype 2 and 93% in genotypes 4/5/6, against 99.5% and 99% at 12 weeks, with virological failure under 1% (PMID: 28951228). Cirrhosis was initially a 12-week population — EXPEDITION-1 (Forns 2017) achieved 99% SVR12 (145 of 146) with 12 weeks in compensated cirrhosis (PMID: 28818546) — until EXPEDITION-8 (Brown 2020) showed 8 weeks did the same in treatment-naïve compensated cirrhosis: SVR12 97.7% by intention to treat (335 of 343) and 99.7% per protocol, with one relapse (PMID: 31682879). Tolerability was benign throughout: adverse events resembled placebo in the blinded trial, and discontinuations for adverse events were at most 1%. The soft spots are genotype 3 (95%, and its 8-week cohort was a non-randomised add-on), the single-arm design of the cirrhosis and rarer-genotype trials, and populations these trials did not enrol — decompensated cirrhosis and patients who had already failed an NS5A-containing regimen. The programme was manufacturer-funded (AbbVie), stated on the cards where the record states it. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) (not Tier C: a multi-trial phase 3 programme with more than 2,000 patients across the carded studies).
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: Inhaled liposomal amikacin for refractory MAC lung disease: culture conversion 29% versus 9% — real, but most patients still did not convert, and nearly nine in ten had respiratory side effects
question: In refractory Mycobacterium avium complex lung disease, does adding inhaled liposomal amikacin to guideline-based therapy improve culture conversion?
balance: CONVERT (Griffith 2018) is the pivotal trial: 336 adults with amikacin-susceptible MAC lung disease whose sputum remained culture-positive despite at least 6 months of guideline-based therapy were randomised 2:1 to add daily amikacin liposome inhalation suspension (ALIS, 590 mg by nebuliser) to their regimen or continue guideline therapy alone. Culture conversion by month 6 — three consecutive monthly negative cultures — was achieved by 29.0% with ALIS versus 8.9% without (odds ratio 4.22, 95% CI 2.08 to 8.57; p < 0.001), an absolute gain of about 20 percentage points (PMID: 30216086). The follow-up report of the same trial (Griffith 2021) shows the conversions were meaningful: sustained and durable conversion (negative cultures through 12 months of further treatment and 3 months off it) in 16.1% of the ALIS group versus 0% on guideline therapy alone, intention to treat (PMID: 33887244). The price is tolerability: respiratory adverse events — mainly dysphonia, cough and dyspnoea — in 87.4% on ALIS versus 50.0% on guideline therapy alone, though serious treatment-emergent adverse events were comparable (20.2% versus 17.9%). Two framing points matter. First, 29% is a tripling of a low base: seven in ten patients on ALIS still had not converted by month 6, in a population defined by treatment failure. Second, the tested intervention is a specific manufactured liposomal formulation in 590 mg single-use vials; the record names the formulation and dose but no manufacturer, and nebulised intravenous amikacin or compounded preparations are not the tested intervention and may differ in delivery, safety and effect. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) (Tier C: a single randomised trial and its own follow-up report). Whether intermittent versus daily background regimens differ in nodular-bronchiectatic MAC is a separate question (slate topic 2962, not built in this batch).
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: Cluster headache: sumatriptan aborts three attacks in four within 15 minutes — verapamil prevention rests on a single 30-patient trial
question: In cluster headache, does subcutaneous sumatriptan abort attacks, and does verapamil prevent them?
balance: SPLIT — the abortive half of this shelf is solidly evidenced and the preventive half is not. In the randomised crossover trial (Sumatriptan Cluster Headache Study Group 1991, PMID: 1647496), 6 mg of subcutaneous sumatriptan relieved 74% of attacks to no or mild pain within 15 minutes versus 26% on placebo, left 46% completely pain-free at 15 minutes versus 10%, and cut the need for rescue oxygen from 49% to 13%. The dose-comparison trial (Ekbom 1993, PMID: 8396833) confirms the size of the effect in 134 patients — relief at 15 minutes in 35% on placebo, 75% on 6 mg and 80% on 12 mg — and shows the higher dose buys nothing but adverse events, so 6 mg is the dose. Prevention is a different evidential world: the only placebo-controlled trial of verapamil, the standard preventive, randomised 30 patients for 14 days and reported a significant reduction in attack frequency and abortive-medication use (Leone 2000, PMID: 10746617) — but its abstract prints no effect sizes at all, so the shelf can say verapamil beat placebo in a small short trial and nothing more precise. Galcanezumab prevention and high-flow oxygen are homed at shelf #690, and vagus nerve stimulation at #2385. PROPOSED SPLIT — LIKELY (benefit: subcutaneous sumatriptan aborts attacks) / POSSIBLE (benefit: verapamil prevention, on one 30-patient trial) (Tier C: the verapamil claim rests on a single small trial whose abstract reports no effect sizes).
stamp: SPLIT — LIKELY (benefit: subcutaneous sumatriptan aborts attacks) / POSSIBLE (benefit: verapamil prevention, on one 30-patient trial)

title: Topiramate versus botulinum toxin in chronic migraine: two small pilot trials found no difference in efficacy — and far more adverse events on topiramate
question: In chronic migraine, does topiramate prevent attacks as well as botulinum toxin (onabotulinumtoxinA)?
balance: Two small double-blind pilot trials have randomised chronic-migraine patients directly between the two standard preventives, and neither found an efficacy difference. Mathew 2009 (PMID: 19912346, n = 60) reported improvement in 68–83% of patients in both groups, a ≥50% reduction in headache/migraine days at month 9 in 40.9% on onabotulinumtoxinA and 42.9% on topiramate, and no significant between-group differences except one secondary measure at month 9. Cady 2011 (PMID: 21070228, n = 59) likewise found statistically significant improvement within both groups but not between them. What did differ was tolerability: in Mathew, 24.1% of topiramate patients discontinued for treatment-related adverse events versus 7.7% on onabotulinumtoxinA, with 87 treatment-related adverse events in 25 topiramate patients versus 41 in 18 onabotulinumtoxinA patients. Neither trial was powered as an equivalence or non-inferiority study, so the honest reading is "no difference demonstrated in two small pilots", not "proven equal". Each drug against placebo is homed elsewhere: onabotulinumtoxinA at shelf #571 (PREEMPT) and topiramate at shelf #2677. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (no difference demonstrated between the two treatments — similar efficacy in two small pilot trials; topiramate caused more adverse events and discontinuations) (not Tier C: two concordant randomised trials, though both are pilots).
stamp: POSSIBLE (no difference demonstrated between the two treatments — similar efficacy in two small pilot trials; topiramate caused more adverse events and discontinuations)

title: Malformation risk in pregnancy differs fivefold between antiseizure medicines: valproate about 1 in 10, lamotrigine and levetiracetam about 2–3 in 100 — and the risk climbs with dose
question: In women taking antiseizure medicines in pregnancy, how do malformation risks compare between drugs?
balance: Two large prospective pregnancy registries, on different continents with different methods, give the same ordering at the extremes. In EURAP (Tomson 2018, PMID: 29680205), major congenital malformations followed 10.3% of valproate-exposed pregnancies, 6.5% phenobarbital, 6.4% phenytoin, 5.5% carbamazepine, 3.9% topiramate, 3.0% oxcarbazepine, 2.9% lamotrigine and 2.8% levetiracetam — and risk rose with dose at conception for carbamazepine, lamotrigine, phenobarbital and valproate. The North American registry (Hernández-Díaz 2012, PMID: 22551726) found 9.3% for valproate, 5.5% phenobarbital, 4.2% topiramate, 3.0% carbamazepine, 2.9% phenytoin, 2.4% levetiracetam and 2.0% lamotrigine, with risk ratios versus lamotrigine of 5.1 for valproate, 2.9 for phenobarbital and 2.2 for topiramate. The registries disagree in the middle of the table (carbamazepine 5.5% versus 3.0%; phenytoin 6.4% versus 2.9%, on small exposure numbers) but agree on what matters most for drug choice: valproate is in a class of its own, and lamotrigine and levetiracetam sit at the bottom, within the range reported for unexposed pregnancies. These are observational data — women are not randomised to drugs, and dose and indication confound — but the size, the dose-response and the cross-registry agreement make the ordering secure. Neurodevelopmental outcomes after exposure (the NEAD question) are a different question and are not covered by this shelf. PROPOSED LIKELY (malformation risk differs substantially between antiseizure medicines — valproate highest at about 1 in 10, lamotrigine and levetiracetam lowest at about 2–3 in 100 — and rises with dose) (Tier C: prospective observational registries; randomisation is impossible, so this evidence type is the ceiling for the question).
stamp: LIKELY (malformation risk differs substantially between antiseizure medicines — valproate highest at about 1 in 10 exposed pregnancies, lamotrigine and levetiracetam lowest at about 2–3 in 100 — and rises with dose for several drugs)

title: Topiramate in chronic migraine: about 1.5–3 more headache-free days a month than placebo — a real but modest gain, with paraesthesia in up to half of patients
question: In adults with chronic migraine, does topiramate reduce monthly headache days?
balance: Two randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials of topiramate 100 mg/day in chronic migraine agree on a real, modest effect. The larger (Silberstein 2007, PMID: 17300356; 306 patients in the efficacy population) reduced migraine/migrainous days by 6.4 per month versus 4.7 on placebo (P = .010) and migraine days by 5.6 versus 4.1 (P = .032) — a placebo-subtracted gain of roughly 1.5–1.7 days a month. The smaller European trial (Diener 2007, PMID: 17441971; 59 patients, 78% with acute-medication overuse at baseline) found a larger separation: migraine days fell 3.5 ± 6.3 on topiramate versus 0.2 ± 4.7 on placebo (P < 0.05). The price is tolerability: paraesthesia in 28.8% (Silberstein) and 53% (Diener) of topiramate patients, with adverse-event discontinuation of 10.9% versus 6.1% in the larger trial, and only about 55% of patients completing either arm there. Head-to-head against onabotulinumtoxinA is shelf #2675; onabotulinumtoxinA against placebo (PREEMPT) is shelf #571. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) (not Tier C: two concordant randomised trials, one of 306 patients).
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: Childhood absence epilepsy: ethosuximide matches valproate on seizures and beats it on attention; lamotrigine is clearly the weakest of the three
question: In childhood absence epilepsy, which first drug — ethosuximide, valproate or lamotrigine — controls seizures with least attentional harm?
balance: One large double-blind randomised trial has compared the three standard first drugs head-to-head in 453 children with newly diagnosed childhood absence epilepsy, and its two reports (16 weeks and 12 months, both carded here and flagged as the same trial) give a clean answer. Freedom from treatment failure at 16 weeks was 53% on ethosuximide and 58% on valproic acid — statistically indistinguishable (OR 1.26, 95% CI 0.80–1.98) — and both were far above lamotrigine at 29% (Glauser 2010, PMID: 20200383). At 12 months the pattern held: 45%, 44% and 21% (Glauser 2013, PMID: 23167925). The tiebreaker is attention: attentional dysfunction affected 49% of children on valproic acid versus 33% on ethosuximide at 16 weeks (OR 1.95, 95% CI 1.12–3.41), and the difference persisted at 12 months, when valproate also produced the largest share of adverse-event discontinuations. Ethosuximide is therefore the trial's own conclusion as optimal initial monotherapy: equal seizure control to valproate, less cognitive cost, and lamotrigine relegated by a two-to-threefold efficacy gap. PROPOSED LIKELY (ethosuximide is the optimal first drug) (Tier C: a single trial programme — both cards are reports of the one randomised trial, NCT00088452).
stamp: LIKELY (ethosuximide is the optimal first drug — seizure control equal to valproate and clearly better than lamotrigine, with fewer attentional adverse effects than valproate)

title: Ocrelizumab in primary progressive MS: the first drug to beat placebo — confirmed progression in 32.9% versus 39.3% over at least two years
question: In adults with primary progressive multiple sclerosis, does ocrelizumab slow disability progression?
balance: ORATORIO (Montalban 2017, PMID: 28002688) is the single randomised trial behind ocrelizumab in primary progressive multiple sclerosis: 732 patients randomised 2:1 to intravenous ocrelizumab 600 mg or placebo every 24 weeks for at least 120 weeks. Confirmed disability progression at 12 weeks occurred in 32.9% on ocrelizumab versus 39.3% on placebo (hazard ratio 0.76, 95% CI 0.59–0.98; P = 0.03) — a relative reduction of about a quarter, and an absolute difference of 6.4 percentage points. The 24-week confirmed progression result was nearly identical (29.6% versus 35.7%; HR 0.75), timed 25-foot walk worsened less (38.9% versus 55.1% by week 120), T2 lesion volume fell on ocrelizumab and rose on placebo (−3.4% versus +7.4%), and brain-volume loss was slightly smaller (0.90% versus 1.09%). Against that: neoplasms occurred in 2.3% of ocrelizumab patients versus 0.8% on placebo, and infusion reactions, upper respiratory infections and oral herpes were commoner, with no significant difference in serious adverse events or serious infections. The effect is real but modest, it comes from one trial, and the neoplasm imbalance needs the long-term observation the authors themselves call for. Ocrelizumab in relapsing MS is a different question, homed at shelf #570. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) (Tier C: a single randomised trial, with a modest absolute effect and an unresolved neoplasm signal).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Nabiximols for MS spasticity: two positive but borderline trials — the clearest signal is that about 40% of patients get a worthwhile response
question: In multiple sclerosis spasticity, does nabiximols (THC:CBD oromucosal spray) reduce spasticity versus placebo?
balance: Two randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials of the THC:CBD oromucosal spray nabiximols (Sativex) as add-on treatment for multiple sclerosis spasticity both reached statistical significance on their primary endpoints — narrowly. Collin 2007 (PMID: 17355549) randomised 189 patients for 6 weeks: the spasticity numerical rating scale improved significantly more on active treatment (P = 0.048, intention-to-treat), the objective Ashworth score did not reach significance, and 40% of treated patients achieved a >30% improvement (P = 0.014). Novotna 2011 (PMID: 21362108) used an enriched design: of 572 patients given single-blind nabiximols for 4 weeks, the 272 who improved by ≥20% were the pool from which 241 were randomised to continue nabiximols or switch to placebo for 12 weeks; the spasticity score difference favoured nabiximols (P = 0.0002) — but the abstract prints no effect size, and by design the randomised phase can only speak about patients who already responded and tolerated the drug. Neither abstract names a manufacturer; Novotna's record names the tested product as nabiximols (Sativex®). The fair summary is a real symptomatic benefit concentrated in a responder minority, demonstrated with borderline statistics in unenriched patients. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) (not Tier C: two concordant randomised trials, though one is enriched and neither abstract reports a mean effect size).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Phenylbutyrate–taurursodiol in ALS: one small phase 2 trial showed slower decline and longer survival — the phase 3 trial did not confirm it, and the product was withdrawn
question: In adults with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, does sodium phenylbutyrate–taurursodiol slow functional decline or prolong survival?
balance: The randomised evidence for the fixed-dose coformulation of sodium phenylbutyrate and taurursodiol (developed by Amylyx Pharmaceuticals, named as the trial funder in the record) is a single phase 2 trial, CENTAUR (Paganoni 2020, PMID: 32877582): 137 patients with definite ALS within 18 months of symptom onset, randomised 2:1, declined on the ALSFRS-R at −1.24 points per month on the drug versus −1.66 on placebo over 24 weeks (difference 0.42 points per month, 95% CI 0.03–0.81; P = 0.03), with no significant differences in any secondary outcome and mainly gastrointestinal adverse events. A long-term analysis of the same trial (Paganoni 2021, PMID: 33063909 — a second report of CENTAUR, flagged as such on its card) found median survival of 25.0 months in those originally randomised to the drug versus 18.5 months on placebo (HR 0.56, 95% CI 0.34–0.92), in a design where most placebo patients crossed to the drug in the open-label extension. Regulatory context, not from a carded record: the sponsor subsequently ran the larger phase 3 PHOENIX trial, announced in 2024 that it had not met its endpoints, and withdrew the product from the market; no peer-reviewed PHOENIX results paper was found in PubMed when this shelf was built, so no PHOENIX figures are printed here. The shelf therefore preserves what the phase 2 record actually showed, and its non-confirmation, side by side. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit in one small phase 2 trial — not confirmed by the phase 3 trial, after which the product was withdrawn) (Tier C: a single small phase 2 programme; the survival analysis is an open-label-extension follow-up of the same patients).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit in one small phase 2 trial — not confirmed by the phase 3 trial, after which the product was withdrawn)

title: Non-invasive ventilation in ALS: in patients without severe bulbar dysfunction it prolongs survival by months with quality of life maintained — the largest survival effect of any ALS intervention trialled
question: In amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, does non-invasive ventilation prolong survival and improve quality of life?
balance: SPLIT — the answer turns on bulbar function. The single randomised trial (Bourke 2006, PMID: 16426990) enrolled 92 patients and randomised 41 of them when they developed orthopnoea with weak inspiratory muscles or symptomatic hypercapnia: non-invasive ventilation (NIV) versus standard care. In the subgroup with better bulbar function (n = 20), NIV conferred a median survival benefit of 205 days (P = 0.006) with quality of life maintained or improved for most of that period; in patients with poor bulbar function, NIV improved some sleep-related quality-of-life measures (P = 0.018) but conferred no survival benefit. The Cochrane synthesis (Radunovic 2017, PMID: 28982219) — carded here as the field's synthesis, with the explicit caveat that its conclusions rest on this same single 41-patient trial — quantifies the overall effect as median survival 219 versus 171 days (+48 days, 95% CI 12–91; P = 0.0062), and +205 days in the better-bulbar subgroup (216 versus 11 days). The review notes further placebo-controlled trials are no longer ethically feasible, so this one small trial is likely to remain the evidence ceiling. PROPOSED SPLIT — LIKELY (benefit in patients without severe bulbar dysfunction) / POSSIBLE (sleep-symptom relief only in severe bulbar dysfunction) (Tier C: the entire randomised base is one 41-patient trial).
stamp: SPLIT — LIKELY (benefit: longer survival with maintained quality of life in patients without severe bulbar dysfunction) / POSSIBLE (sleep-symptom relief only, without survival benefit, in severe bulbar dysfunction)

title: A second IVIG course in poor-prognosis Guillain–Barré syndrome: no improvement in disability — and more serious adverse events, including thromboembolism
question: In Guillain–Barré syndrome predicted to recover poorly after one course of IVIG, does a second course improve outcome?
balance: Worldwide, about a quarter of severely affected Guillain–Barré patients are given a second course of intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) when the prognosis looks poor — a practice SID-GBS (Walgaard 2021, PMID: 33743237) tested directly and found wanting. Patients with a poor prognosis (modified Erasmus GBS Outcome Score ≥6) on their first standard IVIG course were randomised to a second 2 g/kg course or placebo: 93 patients in the modified intention-to-treat analysis (49 second-dose, 44 placebo). The adjusted common odds ratio for improvement on the GBS disability score at 4 weeks was 1.4 (95% CI 0.6–3.3; P = 0.45) — no demonstrated benefit, in a trial whose point estimate, if anything, is too imprecise to exclude a moderate effect in either direction. The harm side is not ambiguous in direction: serious adverse events in the first 30 days occurred in 35% of the second-dose group versus 16% on placebo, including thromboembolic events, and four patients in the intervention group died 13–24 weeks after randomisation. The authors' conclusion — a second IVIG course should not be considered for poor prognosis — is the shelf's conclusion. First-course IVIG versus plasma exchange is a different question, homed at shelf #1449. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference — and caused more serious adverse events) (Tier C: a single randomised trial).
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference — and caused more serious adverse events)

title: CBT for schizophrenia: a real but small symptom effect that shrinks towards zero in blinded trials — and no proven edge over other talking therapies
question: In schizophrenia, does adding cognitive behavioural therapy to antipsychotics improve symptoms and functioning?
balance: A small effect, honestly measured. The bias-conscious synthesis (Jauhar 2014, PMID: 24385461) pooled 34 randomised trials of CBT added to standard care (including antipsychotics): overall symptoms improved with an effect size of −0.33 (95% CI −0.47 to −0.19), positive symptoms −0.25 and negative symptoms −0.13. But masking mattered enormously: in trials where outcome assessors were blinded, the overall effect fell to −0.15 (95% CI −0.27 to −0.03) and the positive-symptom effect to −0.08, no longer significant — against −0.62 and −0.57 in unblinded trials. The Cochrane head-to-head review (Jones 2018, PMID: 30480760) then asked the sharper question — CBT versus OTHER psychosocial therapies, 36 trials, 3,542 participants — and found no clear advantage on relapse (RR 1.05), rehospitalisation (RR 0.96), mental state, social functioning or quality of life, on mostly low-quality evidence; the one consistent edge was satisfaction, measured as fewer people leaving the study early (RR 0.86). So the answer is: yes, CBT helps symptoms a little on top of medication; no, it has not been shown to beat cheaper, simpler supportive therapies; and functioning outcomes are essentially unproven rather than disproven. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — small average symptom benefit, bias-sensitive, not Tier C (multi-trial symptom shelf).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Family intervention in schizophrenia: relapse roughly halved in the trial literature (RR 0.55, NNT 7) — one of the strongest psychosocial effects in psychiatry, with a quality caveat
question: In schizophrenia, do family interventions reduce relapse and readmission?
balance: Yes — and the size of the effect is unusual for a psychosocial treatment. The Cochrane review (Pharoah 2010, PMID: 21154340) pooled 53 randomised trials of community family intervention versus standard care: relapse fell with a relative risk of 0.55 (95% CI 0.5 to 0.6) — a 45% relative reduction — with a number needed to treat of 7 (95% CI 6 to 8); hospital admission fell too (RR 0.78, NNT 8), and medication compliance improved (RR 0.60 for non-compliance outcomes as reported, NNT 6). The earlier independent meta-analysis (Pitschel-Walz 2001, PMID: 11215551), 25 studies, found the relapse rate reduced by about 20 percentage points as the authors report it, with effects particularly marked when intervention continued beyond 3 months. Both syntheses carry the same warning: many trials were small and poorly reported, blinding of assessors was uncommon, and effects may be overestimated. Even discounted for that, a halving of relapse replicated across two decades of trials is not plausibly all bias. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) — large, consistent relative effect on the outcome that matters most to families; not Tier C.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)
