title: Early-intervention services in first-episode psychosis: better symptoms, fewer admissions and more work or study while the service lasts — gains that fade once it ends
question: In first-episode psychosis, do early-intervention services improve recovery versus standard care?
balance: While the service is running, yes, across the board. The meta-analysis of the randomised trials (Correll 2018, PMID: 29800949; 10 trials, 2,176 patients) found early-intervention services superior to treatment as usual on all 13 analysable outcomes: treatment discontinuation RR 0.70, at least one psychiatric hospitalisation RR 0.74 (a 26% relative reduction), involvement in school or work RR 1.13, and total symptom severity SMD −0.32. The two flagship trials agree: RAISE/NAVIGATE (Kane 2016, PMID: 26481174; 404 participants, 34 US clinics) produced greater improvement in quality of life and psychopathology and more work/school involvement over 2 years, with the largest gains in those whose untreated psychosis had lasted under 74 weeks; OPUS (Bertelsen 2008, PMID: 18606949; 547 patients) improved symptoms at 2 years. The catch is durability: at OPUS's 5-year follow-up, three years after the intensive service ended, the symptom advantages had equalised — only fewer days in hospital (149 vs 193) and less supported housing (4% vs 10%) persisted. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) — for outcomes during and shortly after the intervention; the honest rider is that nobody has shown the clinical gains survive discharge from the service. Not Tier C.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: Levodopa–carbidopa intestinal gel: off-time cut by about 4 hours a day, roughly 1.9 hours more than optimised oral therapy — at the price of a jejunal tube and its complications
question: In advanced Parkinson's disease with motor fluctuations despite oral therapy, does levodopa–carbidopa intestinal gel increase on-time without troublesome dyskinesia?
balance: The one double-blind trial says yes, clearly. Olanow 2014 (PMID: 24361112) randomised 66 analysable patients with advanced Parkinson's and motor complications, all with a percutaneous gastrojejunostomy tube, to intestinal-gel levodopa–carbidopa plus oral placebo or oral immediate-release levodopa–carbidopa plus placebo gel: over 12 weeks off-time fell by 4.04 hours on gel versus 2.14 hours on oral therapy (difference −1.91 hours, 95% CI −3.05 to −0.76), and on-time without troublesome dyskinesia rose by 4.11 versus 2.24 hours (difference 1.86 hours). The large open-label programme (Fernandez 2013, PMID: 23287001; 192 patients) found almost the same diary numbers at 12 weeks (off-time −3.9 hours, good on-time +4.6 hours) — and showed the cost side plainly: 87.5% reported an adverse event, abdominal pain in 30.7%, device-insertion complications in 21.4%, serious events in 31.3%, and 12.5% discontinued. The trial records name the formulation and the sponsor (AbbVie, as funder in the record) but no brand name. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C — a single small double-blind trial, however clean, plus open-label support; the benefit is real but the intervention is a device-drug package whose harms are procedural. The apomorphine-infusion comparison (TOLEDO) is homed at #2371 and is cross-referenced, not re-carded.

title: D-cycloserine augmentation of exposure therapy: a small benefit at the end of treatment in the individual-patient analysis (d ≈ 0.25) that fades by follow-up — and vanishes in the conventional meta-analysis
question: In anxiety disorders treated with exposure therapy, does D-cycloserine augmentation improve outcomes?
balance: At most a small, short-lived nudge. The strongest analysis — individual participant data from 21 of 22 eligible double-blind trials, 1,047 participants (Mataix-Cols 2017, PMID: 28122091) — found D-cycloserine superior to placebo augmentation from pre-treatment to post-treatment (mean difference −3.62 points on a standardised 0–100 metric; d = −0.25), but not to mid-treatment, and the pre-to-follow-up contrast just missed significance (P = .05; d = −0.19). The conventional aggregate meta-analysis (McGuire 2017, PMID: 27314661; 20 RCTs, 957 participants) found smaller, non-significant effects overall (g = 0.15; response RR 1.08; remission RR 1.11), with a nominally significant effect only in the anxiety-disorders subgroup (g = 0.33) and not for OCD or PTSD separately. Antidepressant co-treatment did not moderate the effect, and no patient- or study-level moderator reliably identified responders. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — two syntheses agree the ceiling is 'small'; they disagree on whether the average clears zero, which is exactly what POSSIBLE is for. Not Tier C: multi-trial, symptom outcomes only.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Acute vertigo: a single dose of an antihistamine relieves vertigo more than a benzodiazepine at 2 hours (16 points on a 100-point scale) — and neither class beat placebo at a week
question: In acute vertigo in the emergency department, do antihistamines beat benzodiazepines for vertigo relief?
balance: For the first two hours, yes; beyond that, neither drug class earns its keep. The systematic review and meta-analysis (Hunter 2022, PMID: 35849408) pooled the randomised trials of vestibular suppressants in acute vertigo of ≤2 weeks' duration: 27 trials identified, 17 (1,586 participants) in the quantitative analysis. On the primary outcome — change in 100-point vertigo VAS at 2 hours, 7 trials, 802 participants — single-dose antihistamines improved scores by 16.1 points more than single-dose benzodiazepines (95% CI 7.2 to 25.0), but by only a non-significant 2.7 points more than other active comparators such as metoclopramide or droperidol. At 1 week and 1 month, neither daily benzodiazepines nor antihistamines were superior to placebo, and the reviewers found no outcome on which benzodiazepine use was associated with improvement at all. The slate for this shelf named a 'Gerlier randomised trial'; no such head-to-head trial exists in the record — the 2022 JAMA Neurology evidence is this meta-analysis, whose head-to-head stratum rests on three older trials — and the shelf is built on the record as fetched. PROPOSED SPLIT — LIKELY (antihistamine superiority at 2 hours) / LIKELY (no difference from placebo at 1 week or 1 month for either class); not Tier C. Vestibular rehabilitation for ongoing dizziness is a different question, homed at #636 and #1465.
stamp: SPLIT — LIKELY (benefit: single-dose antihistamines relieve vertigo at 2 hours more than benzodiazepines) / LIKELY (the treatment made no difference: neither class beat placebo at 1 week or 1 month, and benzodiazepines showed no benefit on any outcome)

title: Surgery for drug-resistant trigeminal neuralgia: microvascular decompression leaves 70% pain-free off medication at 10 years; Gamma Knife leaves about 45% — with far fewer serious complications and a 1-in-5 numbness rate
question: In trigeminal neuralgia failing carbamazepine, do surgical options (microvascular decompression, radiosurgery) give durable relief?
balance: Durable relief is real for both operations — but no randomised trial has ever compared them, so every number here is a within-series rate, and the two flagship series differ in era, case mix and follow-up method. Microvascular decompression (Barker 1996, PMID: 8598865): 1,185 patients operated for medically intractable trigeminal neuralgia, median follow-up 6.2 years; at 10 years 70% were free of pain without medication and a further 4% had only occasional pain not needing long-term medication, with recurrences concentrated in the first 2 years and an annual recurrence rate under 1% after year 10 — at a cost of 2 operative deaths (0.2%), 1 brain-stem infarction (0.1%) and ipsilateral hearing loss in 1%. Gamma Knife radiosurgery (Régis 2016, PMID: 26339857): 497 patients with medically refractory classical trigeminal neuralgia, median follow-up 43.8 months; 91.75% became pain-free initially (median 10 days), but the actuarial probability of remaining pain-free without medication fell to 64.9% at 5 years and 45.3% at 10 years (67.8% maintained relief without further surgery at 10 years); facial hypesthesia reached an actuarial 21.1% at 7 years, though very bothersome numbness occurred in only 0.6%, and there were no operative deaths. The authors of the radiosurgery series themselves state that a randomised or case-matched comparison with decompression would be required to rank them. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C — observational series only, presented side by side without a fabricated head-to-head. Drug treatment, including botulinum toxin for refractory cases, is homed elsewhere (#2382).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Pyridostigmine in neurogenic orthostatic hypotension: standing diastolic fall cut from 34 to about 28 mm Hg with no rise in supine pressure — a modest, physiologically tidy effect
question: In patients with neurogenic orthostatic hypotension, does pyridostigmine raise standing blood pressure without worsening supine hypertension?
balance: Yes on the blood-pressure mechanics, modestly. The rationale is elegant: pyridostigmine amplifies sympathetic ganglionic transmission, which is quiet lying down and active standing — so it should lift standing pressure without the supine hypertension that limits midodrine. The double-blind 4-way crossover trial (Singer 2006, PMID: 16476804; 58 patients with neurogenic orthostatic hypotension, single 60 mg doses) found exactly that pattern: supine systolic and diastolic pressures did not differ from placebo (P = .36 and .85), while the fall in standing diastolic pressure was significantly blunted — 27.6 mm Hg on pyridostigmine versus 34.0 mm Hg on placebo (P = .04), and 27.2 mm Hg when 5 mg midodrine was added (P = .002) — and standing-pressure improvement tracked symptom improvement. The longer randomised evidence is weaker in design: Byun 2017 (PMID: 28794253; 87 patients, open-label, 3 months) found orthostatic drops improved in all three arms (midodrine, pyridostigmine, both) and symptoms improved least on pyridostigmine alone; the authors grade their own study Class IV. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C — one small single-dose crossover trial plus open-label follow-up; the standing-pressure claim is supported, the symptom claim only partly. Droxidopa and the midodrine/fludrocortisone comparisons are homed at #931 and #1558.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: High-dose methylprednisolone after spinal cord injury: a benefit that exists only inside the 8-hour, post-hoc window of NASCIS II — bought, when the infusion runs to 48 hours, with more sepsis and pneumonia
question: In acute traumatic spinal cord injury, does high-dose methylprednisolone improve neurological recovery, and at what cost?
balance: This is the most contested shelf in the batch, and the cards show why. NASCIS II (Bracken 1990, PMID: 2278545; 487 patients) was negative overall: the claimed benefit appears only in the subgroup treated within 8 hours of injury, where methylprednisolone (30 mg/kg bolus, then 5.4 mg/kg/h for 23 hours) improved 6-month motor change scores (16.0 vs 11.2; P = 0.03) and pinprick and touch sensation versus placebo; treatment after 8 hours, and naloxone at any time, did nothing. NASCIS III (Bracken 1997, PMID: 9168289; 499 patients, all given the bolus) had no placebo arm: extending the infusion to 48 hours helped only the subgroup started 3–8 hours after injury (motor recovery P = .01 at 6 months in that stratum) and that same group had more severe sepsis and severe pneumonia, with mortality unchanged (P = .97). The Cochrane synthesis (Bracken 2012, PMID: 22258943) concludes the within-8-hours regimen improves motor recovery — noting the result was replicated in a Japanese trial but not in the French one — and that complications and mortality were not significantly increased overall. Guideline bodies have famously split over whether a post-hoc subgroup of one trial should drive practice; this shelf takes no side beyond its stamp. PROPOSED SPLIT — POSSIBLE (benefit, within-8-hours subgroup only) / POSSIBLE (harm, 48-hour extension), Tier C: subgroup-dependent, single-programme evidence with a live methodological controversy stated on its face.
stamp: SPLIT — POSSIBLE (benefit when started within 8 hours of injury) / POSSIBLE (harm: more severe sepsis and severe pneumonia when treatment is extended to 48 hours)

title: Aspirin + paracetamol + caffeine for acute migraine: pain-free at 2 hours in 19.6% versus 9.0% on placebo, and superior to each of its components alone in the head-to-head trial
question: In migraine, does the combination of aspirin, paracetamol and caffeine beat single analgesics for acute attacks?
balance: Yes — the combination beats placebo clearly and beats its own ingredients head-to-head. The placebo-controlled meta-analysis (Diener 2022, PMID: 34519136; 7 randomised trials, 3,306 participants) found pain freedom at 2 hours in 19.6% on the fixed combination versus 9.0% on placebo (rate ratio 2.2, 95% CI 1.4 to 3.3 — a relative measure; the absolute gain is about 11 percentage points) and pain relief at 2 hours in 54.3% versus 31.2% (RR 1.7), with adverse events more frequent on the combination (10.9% vs 7.8%; RR 1.7). The pivotal six-arm trial behind the 'beats single analgesics' claim (Diener 2005, PMID: 16162254; 1,743 patients treating migraine or tension-type headache attacks) found the triple combination — two tablets of aspirin 250 mg + paracetamol 200 mg + caffeine 50 mg, a formulation the abstract names as Thomapyrin — significantly superior on time to 50% pain relief to the same doses without caffeine (P = 0.0181), to aspirin alone (P = 0.0398), to paracetamol alone (P = 0.0016), to caffeine alone and to placebo (both P < 0.0001). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) — consistent randomised evidence for an over-the-counter question; not Tier C. Triptan comparisons are a different shelf question and are not claimed here.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: Intratympanic gentamicin for refractory Ménière disease: the strongest vertigo control of the intratympanic options, bought with hearing — and the dosing schedule sets the price
question: In refractory Ménière disease, does intratympanic gentamicin control vertigo, and at what cost to hearing?
balance: SPLIT — the vertigo control is real, and so is the hearing bill; the schedule decides how big each is. The only double-blind placebo-controlled trial (Postema 2008, PMID: 18607963) found intratympanic gentamicin significantly reduced vertigo-complaint scores and aural fullness over one year in unilateral Ménière disease, at a mean hearing cost of about 8 dB in the treated ear (its abstract reports no sample size and no effect sizes — the shelf states the finding unquantified rather than inventing numbers). The pooled uncontrolled literature (Chia 2004, PMID: 15241234; 27 series) puts complete vertigo control between roughly two-thirds and four-fifths of patients depending on technique — titration dosing best at 81.7% complete and 96.3% complete-or-substantial control, low-dose worst at 66.7% complete — while overall hearing loss ranged from 13.1% with weekly dosing to 34.7% with multiple daily dosing, with no significant difference between techniques in profound hearing loss. The network meta-analysis of the randomised literature (Ahmadzai 2020, PMID: 32870918; 18 RCTs, 1,231 patients) ranked intratympanic gentamicin highest for complete vertigo control against placebo and worse than intratympanic steroid for hearing change, on an evidence base the reviewers rated mostly unclear or high risk of bias. So for the patient whose vertigo remains disabling despite conservative treatment, gentamicin is the most effective intratympanic option for stopping attacks — bought with a real, dose- and schedule-dependent risk to the hearing of an ear that may already be the patient's worse one. The head-to-head against intratympanic methylprednisolone (Patel 2016) is homed at shelf #633, where steroid matched gentamicin's vertigo control; this shelf answers the prior question — gentamicin against placebo and against its own dosing schedules. PROPOSED SPLIT — POSSIBLE (benefit: vertigo control) / POSSIBLE (harm: hearing loss, schedule-dependent); Tier C (one small placebo-controlled trial whose abstract reports no numbers, resting on uncontrolled series for the rates).
stamp: SPLIT — POSSIBLE (benefit: vertigo control in refractory Ménière disease) / POSSIBLE (harm: hearing loss, dose- and schedule-dependent)

title: Statins after aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage: the small trials' vasospasm promise, answered by STASH — 803 patients, no improvement in outcome and no harm either
question: After aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage, does acute statin treatment improve long-term functional outcome?
balance: The small trials promised; the big trial answered no. Two early phase II trials reported striking relative reductions on vasospasm physiology: pravastatin 40 mg in 80 patients cut vasospasm incidence by 32% relative and vasospasm-related delayed ischaemic deficits by 83% relative (Tseng 2005, PMID: 16049199 — relative measures as reported; the abstract does not give the absolute event rates), and a 39-patient simvastatin 80 mg pilot found the drug safe and feasible with numerically less vasospasm and infarction (Chou 2008, PMID: 18658043). STASH then randomised 803 patients to simvastatin 40 mg or placebo for up to 21 days (PMID: 24837690): favourable outcome (modified Rankin 0–2) at 6 months in 271 of 391 on simvastatin versus 289 of 412 on placebo, adjusted common odds ratio 0.97 (95% CI 0.75 to 1.25), deaths 10% versus 9%, serious adverse events 18% in both groups — no benefit on long-term or short-term outcome, and no safety concern either. The pattern is the familiar one: a surrogate (vasospasm on Doppler and angiography) improved in small single-centre trials while the patient-centred outcome did not move in the adequately powered multicentre trial. Routine acute statin treatment after aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage is therefore not supported; this is a 'does not work for this purpose' answer, not a safety warning. The magnesium half of the slate question is homed at shelf #2397 (MASH-2) and nimodipine at #2390; neither is re-carded here. Tseng 2007 (PMID: 17413047) is a second report of the same 80-patient pravastatin trial (rescue therapy and 6-month outcome) and is not carded separately. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference); Tier C (the verdict rests on one definitive outcome trial against small positive pilots — a mortality/functional-outcome shelf).
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference)

title: Tramadol for osteoarthritis and chronic musculoskeletal pain: a pain benefit too small to feel, bought with more adverse events, more dropouts and a mortality signal
question: In chronic musculoskeletal and osteoarthritic pain, does tramadol help enough to justify its dependence and harm risks?
balance: The benefit is real but smaller than the threshold patients can feel. The Cochrane synthesis (Toupin April 2019, PMID: 31132298) pooled 22 randomised trials in osteoarthritis: tramadol, alone or with acetaminophen, improved pain by 4% absolute over placebo — judged no important benefit — although slightly more people achieved a 20% improvement (15 of 100 versus 10 of 100). Function showed the same 4% pattern. The harms are not symmetrical with that small gain: adverse events were a third more common (risk ratio 1.34; a 17% absolute increase), nausea, dizziness and tiredness leading; withdrawal because of adverse events was 2.6 times as common (a 12% absolute increase); and serious adverse events were more frequent (110/2459 versus 22/1153; risk ratio 1.78). The trials averaged about two months, so they cannot measure dependence, falls in older users, or long-term outcomes at all. The one large long-horizon dataset is observational and points the wrong way: in 88,902 propensity-matched UK patients aged 50 and over with osteoarthritis (Zeng 2019, PMID: 30860559), starting tramadol was followed by higher one-year mortality than starting naproxen (23.5 versus 13.8 deaths per 1,000 person-years; hazard ratio 1.71), diclofenac, celecoxib or etoricoxib — though not codeine — and the authors themselves warn that confounding by indication (tramadol is prescribed to frailer patients) may explain it. The class-level opioid synthesis (Busse 2018, PMID: 30561481) is homed at shelf #346 and is not re-carded here; its pooled opioid effect was likewise below the minimally important difference. PROPOSED SPLIT — POSSIBLE (small benefit) / POSSIBLE (harm): a drug whose average benefit sits below what patients can feel, whose trial harms are certain, and whose dependence and mortality questions the trials never ran long enough to answer (Tier C: the mortality claim rests on observational data).
stamp: SPLIT — POSSIBLE (small benefit on pain) / POSSIBLE (harm: more adverse events and withdrawals in trials, and higher mortality than NSAIDs in a large observational cohort)

title: Capsaicin 8% patch for painful diabetic neuropathy: a modest, local pain reduction from a single clinic application — relief without systemic drug exposure
question: In painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy, does the capsaicin 8% patch relieve pain?
balance: One placebo-controlled trial carries the efficacy claim. In 369 patients with painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy, a single 30-minute application of the capsaicin 8% patch reduced average daily pain by 27.4% versus 20.9% on a placebo patch between weeks 2 and 8 (P = .025) (Simpson 2017, PMID: 27746370) — a modest absolute separation of about 6.5 percentage points on percentage pain reduction, with a faster median time to response (19 versus 72 days) and small improvements in sleep interference. The safety half of the question is better populated: in a 52-week open-label randomised study of 468 patients, repeated patch treatments (up to seven, at least eight weeks apart) plus standard care produced no deterioration in sensory perception or reflexes and no negative signal on neuropathy scales versus standard care alone, at the price of application-site pain in 28–29% (Vinik 2016, PMID: 27919222). The patch's appeal is what it does not do: no systemic exposure, no drug interactions, no sedation — in a population usually offered sedating systemic drugs. Its limits are equally plain: one efficacy trial, and a placebo problem (the active patch burns on application, the placebo patch much less, so blinding is fragile). The postherpetic-neuralgia evidence for the same patch is homed at shelf #2565, and the duloxetine comparison at #695; neither is re-carded here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) (Tier C: a single placebo-controlled efficacy trial).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Cyclobenzaprine in fibromyalgia: patients feel better overall and sleep better, pain improves early — fatigue and tender points do not move
question: In fibromyalgia and chronic back spasm, does cyclobenzaprine improve sleep and pain?
balance: The fibromyalgia evidence is old, small and consistent in shape. Pooling five randomised placebo-controlled trials, Tofferi 2004 (PMID: 14872449) found patients on cyclobenzaprine three times as likely to report global improvement (odds ratio 3.0, 95% CI 1.6 to 5.6; risk difference 0.21, so about five patients treated for one to improve), with pain better early and sleep the symptom that improved most — but no improvement in fatigue or tender points at any time point. A later mechanistic trial using very low bedtime doses (1–4 mg) in 36 patients (Moldofsky 2011, PMID: 21885490) found the same pattern over eight weeks — pain, tenderness, fatigue and depression scores improved versus placebo — and tied it to sleep physiology: nights of restorative, normalised cyclic-alternating-pattern sleep increased on the drug and correlated with the symptom gains. For the back-spasm half of the question, the muscle-relaxant class synthesis (Cashin 2021, PMID: 34233900) is homed at shelf #786 and is not re-carded here: it found small, not clinically important pain reductions in acute low back pain on very-low-to-low certainty evidence, and considerable uncertainty for chronic use. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a real but symptomatic effect, strongest on sleep and global impression, in trials too small and short to define its place against modern fibromyalgia therapy.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Spa therapy and hydrotherapy: a three-week spa course left half of knee osteoarthritis patients improved at six months, and warm-water therapy eases fibromyalgia pain a little
question: In knee osteoarthritis and fibromyalgia, does balneotherapy or hydrotherapy improve pain and function?
balance: Two different water-based interventions share this shelf, and the evidence differs by disease. For knee osteoarthritis, the load-bearing trial is large: 382 patients randomised (by a Zelen design, so patients did not know an alternative existed) to 18 days of spa therapy — massage, showers, mud and pool sessions — plus home exercise and usual care, or to exercise and usual care alone; at six months, 50.8% of the spa group versus 36.4% of controls had achieved a minimal clinically important improvement in pain or function (P = 0.005), though quality of life and patient-acceptable symptom state did not differ (Forestier 2010, PMID: 19734131). For fibromyalgia, the pooled hydrotherapy trials show a small pain reduction (standardised mean difference −0.42, 95% CI −0.61 to −0.24; eight studies, 462 participants) and a small quality-of-life gain, with no effect on depressive symptoms or tender point count; the reviewers graded the evidence moderate-to-strong but called for larger trials with long-term follow-up (Naumann 2014, PMID: 25000940). Neither literature can blind its participants — you know whether you have been sent to a spa — so expectation and the holiday itself are unmeasured co-interventions in every estimate. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a genuine but modest symptomatic gain, inseparable from context, with durability shown to six months only in the knee trial.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Abatacept in early rheumatoid arthritis: adding it to methotrexate roughly doubles early remission and slows damage — and a small group stay in remission after everything is stopped
question: In early rheumatoid arthritis, does abatacept with methotrexate induce remission and halt joint damage versus methotrexate alone?
balance: Two phase 3 trials in early, seropositive disease point the same way. In methotrexate-naive patients with poor prognostic factors (AGREE; Westhovens 2009, PMID: 19124524), abatacept plus methotrexate put 41.4% into DAS28 remission at one year versus 23.3% on methotrexate alone (P < 0.001) and slowed radiographic progression (mean Genant–Sharp change 0.63 versus 1.06; P = 0.040), with adverse events, serious infections and malignancies no more frequent than on methotrexate alone. In AVERT (Emery 2015, PMID: 25367713), subcutaneous abatacept plus methotrexate achieved DAS28 remission at 12 months in 60.9% versus 45.2% (P = 0.010); after all treatment was then withdrawn in patients with low disease activity, 14.8% versus 7.8% remained in remission at both 12 and 18 months (P = 0.045) — the drug-free-remission signal that makes this shelf more than a 'stronger suppression' story, though it applies to a small minority. Abatacept monotherapy (42.5% remission at 12 months) sat between the combination and methotrexate alone. The head-to-head AMPLE trial against adalimumab was in established, methotrexate-inadequate disease — a different question — and is not carded here. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): consistent randomised evidence in early disease for more remission and less damage, with a safety profile in these trials indistinguishable from methotrexate alone.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: Zoledronic acid for knee osteoarthritis with bone-marrow lesions: a promising six-month signal in 59 patients, extinguished by a 223-patient two-year trial
question: In knee osteoarthritis with bone-marrow lesions, does zoledronic acid reduce pain or lesion size?
balance: The two trials disagree in proportion to their size. The small one came first: in 59 patients with knee osteoarthritis and MRI bone-marrow lesions, a single zoledronic acid infusion reduced pain at six months (−14.5 mm on a visual analogue scale, 95% CI −28.1 to −0.9) and shrank total lesion area more than placebo (−175.7 mm², −327.2 to −24.3), with 39% versus 18% achieving a clinically significant lesion reduction — but the pain effect was absent at 3 and 12 months and function scores never separated (Laslett 2012, PMID: 22355040). The definitive test, ZAP, randomised 223 similar patients to yearly infusions for two years and found nothing: cartilage volume loss was identical (−878 versus −919 mm³; difference 41, −79 to 161; P = .50), pain scores numerically favoured placebo, lesion size did not differ, and adverse events were more common on zoledronic acid (96% versus 83%), driven by acute post-infusion reactions (87% versus 56%) (Cai 2020, PMID: 32315057). The authors' conclusion — these findings do not support the use of zoledronic acid in the treatment of knee osteoarthritis — is the one the larger trial earns. PROPOSED SPLIT: the small-trial six-month signal is on the record and was honestly generated, but a treatment decision today rests on ZAP.
stamp: SPLIT — POSSIBLE (short-term pain and lesion benefit in one small trial) / LIKELY (the treatment made no difference in the larger two-year trial)

title: Calcium and vitamin D in female Navy recruits: 2,000 mg calcium with 800 IU vitamin D cut stress fractures from 6.6% to 5.3% over eight weeks of basic training
question: In military recruits, do calcium and vitamin D supplementation prevent stress fractures?
balance: A single large trial answers this question, and it has never been repeated at scale. Lappe 2008 (PMID: 18433305) randomised 5,201 female US Navy recruits, double-blind, to 2,000 mg calcium plus 800 IU vitamin D daily or placebo through eight weeks of basic training — a population with a high, uniform mechanical load and a baseline stress-fracture incidence of about 6–7%. Supplementation reduced stress fractures by a fifth relative: 5.3% versus 6.6% on intention-to-treat (P = 0.0026), an absolute reduction of 1.3 percentage points — roughly one fracture prevented for every 77 recruits supplemented — and 6.8% versus 8.6% in the per-protocol analysis of the 3,700 who completed. The authors estimate that supplementing an entire intake cohort of 14,416 women would have prevented about 187 fractures. What the trial cannot say: whether the effect holds in men (none enrolled), in less extreme training loads, at lower doses, or whether calcium, vitamin D, or only the combination does the work. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) (Tier C: one trial, one sex, one training system).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Low-intensity pulsed ultrasound for fresh fractures: the large sham-controlled TRUST trial and the low-bias trial set both say no
question: In fresh fractures, does low-intensity pulsed ultrasound (LIPUS) speed healing?
balance: This is a literature whose answer flips with trial quality, and the high-quality end is unambiguous. TRUST randomised 501 patients with operatively fixed tibial fractures to daily self-administered LIPUS or an identical sham device for a year: functional recovery (SF-36 physical component) differed by 0.55 points (95% CI −0.75 to 1.84) against a minimally important difference of 3–5, and time to radiographic healing did not differ (hazard ratio 1.07, 0.86 to 1.34) (Busse 2016, PMID: 27797787). The accompanying systematic review of 26 randomised trials found the same split personality — trials at high risk of bias suggested benefit, trials at low risk of bias showed none, for return to work, reoperation, weight bearing, pain and radiographic healing alike (interaction P < 0.001) (Schandelmaier 2017, PMID: 28348110). Earlier positive small trials are the high-bias tail of that distribution. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): for fresh fractures, the trustworthy trials show LIPUS neither heals bone faster nor returns function sooner. Established nonunion, a different question, is not what these trials studied.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference)

title: Triple therapy in rheumatoid arthritis: three cheap oral drugs matched etanercept plus methotrexate on disease activity — in early disease and after methotrexate failure alike
question: In adults with rheumatoid arthritis responding inadequately to methotrexate, does triple therapy (methotrexate, sulfasalazine and hydroxychloroquine) match a tumour-necrosis-factor inhibitor plus methotrexate?
balance: Two blinded randomised trials, in the two populations where the question arises, give the same answer on disease activity. After methotrexate failure, RACAT randomised 353 patients to triple therapy (methotrexate + sulfasalazine + hydroxychloroquine) or etanercept + methotrexate, with a blinded switch to the other strategy at 24 weeks for non-responders: DAS28 improvement at 48 weeks was −2.1 versus −2.3 (P = 0.26), formally noninferior (upper confidence limit 0.41 against a 0.6 margin; P = 0.002), with no differences in radiographic progression, pain, quality of life or major adverse events, and 27% of each group needing the switch (O'Dell 2013, PMID: 23755969). In early aggressive disease, TEAR's factorial design compared immediate triple therapy, immediate etanercept + methotrexate, and step-up from methotrexate to either: over weeks 48–102 there was no DAS28 difference between the oral triple and the biologic combination, whichever way patients reached them — though etanercept + methotrexate did win the secondary radiographic comparison at 102 weeks (Moreland 2012, PMID: 22508468). PROPOSED LIKELY (no difference in disease activity): an oral regimen costing a small fraction of a biologic performs equivalently on the outcome patients feel, with radiographic protection the one place the biologic kept an edge in early disease.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference — triple therapy matched TNF-inhibitor combination on disease activity)

title: Denosumab versus zoledronic acid for bone metastases: superior in breast and prostate cancer, noninferior in other tumours — with hypocalcaemia traded for renal harm
question: In patients with advanced cancer at risk of skeletal complications, does denosumab prevent skeletal-related events better than zoledronic acid?
balance: Three identically designed phase 3 trials — same doses (denosumab 120 mg subcutaneously versus zoledronic acid 4 mg intravenously, every four weeks), same primary endpoint (time to first skeletal-related event: fracture, radiation or surgery to bone, or spinal cord compression) — cover the solid-tumour spectrum. In breast cancer (2,046 patients), denosumab was superior: hazard ratio 0.82 (95% CI 0.71 to 0.95) for first events and rate ratio 0.77 for first-and-subsequent events (Stopeck 2010, PMID: 21060033). In castration-resistant prostate cancer (1,904 patients), likewise superior: median time to first event 20.7 versus 17.1 months, hazard ratio 0.82 (0.71 to 0.95) (Fizazi 2011, PMID: 21353695). In other solid tumours and myeloma (1,776 patients), denosumab was noninferior (hazard ratio 0.84, 0.71 to 0.98) but superiority was not significant after multiplicity adjustment (Henry 2011, PMID: 21343556). Overall survival and disease progression never differed — this is complication prevention, not cancer treatment. The harm profiles trade places: hypocalcaemia is commoner on denosumab (13% versus 6% in the prostate trial), renal adverse events and acute-phase reactions commoner on zoledronic acid, and osteonecrosis of the jaw is infrequent and similar (about 1–2%) on both. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): a consistent relative reduction of about a fifth in first skeletal events (labelled relative) — in the prostate trial that is a 3.6-month delay in the median time to a first event.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: Oral versus intravenous methylprednisolone for MS relapses: the large double-blind COPOUSEP trial found oral treatment non-inferior at 28 days (81% vs 80% improved), and the earlier small-trial synthesis agrees
question: In adults having a multiple sclerosis relapse, is oral high-dose methylprednisolone as effective as intravenous methylprednisolone?
balance: LIKELY (no difference): One large double-blind non-inferiority trial and an earlier Cochrane synthesis of five small trials point the same way. In COPOUSEP (199 patients with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis treated within 15 days of a relapse), oral methylprednisolone 1,000 mg daily for 3 days was non-inferior to the same dose given intravenously: 81% of the oral group and 80% of the intravenous group had improved by day 28 without retreatment (absolute difference 0.5 percentage points, 90% CI −9.5 to 10.4, against a pre-set 15% non-inferiority margin) (Le Page E et al., PMID: 26135706). The Cochrane review (Burton JM et al., PMID: 23235634) pooled five older trials (215 patients) and likewise found no significant difference in disability recovery at four weeks (mean EDSS difference −0.22, P = 0.20) or in MRI activity — though only two of its five trials used modern methods, which is why COPOUSEP carries the weight. Adverse events in COPOUSEP were similar by route; insomnia was reported more often with oral treatment (77% vs 64%). A cost-utility analysis of the same COPOUSEP trial (Michel M et al., PMID: 34598781 — a secondary report of the carded trial, not carded separately) found oral treatment cost-effective, with larger savings if relapses are treated at home. The practical conclusion: the route is a logistics, comfort and cost decision, not an efficacy one. Tier C is set because the non-inferiority claim rests on one pivotal trial.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference — oral methylprednisolone was non-inferior to intravenous)

title: HLA-B*58:01 screening before allopurinol: in Taiwan's national prospective cohort, no screened-negative patient treated with allopurinol developed a severe cutaneous reaction — against seven expected
question: In patients about to start allopurinol, does HLA-B*58:01 screening prevent severe cutaneous adverse reactions?
balance: POSSIBLE: The genetic association is among the strongest in pharmacogenomics, and the one national implementation cohort found the screening strategy worked as designed. In Taiwan, all 51 patients with allopurinol-induced severe cutaneous adverse reactions (SCARs) carried HLA-B*58:01, versus 15% of allopurinol-tolerant controls (odds ratio 580.3, 95% CI 34.4 to 9780.9 — a relative figure with a very wide interval) (Hung SI et al., PMID: 15743917). When Taiwan screened prospectively (Ko TM et al., PMID: 26399967), 571 of 2,910 genotyped patients (19.6%) were carriers and were advised to avoid allopurinol; among the 2,339 screened-negative patients who took allopurinol, no SCAR occurred, against seven cases expected from the historical national incidence of 0.30% per year (P = 0.0026); mild transient rash occurred in 3%. The CPIC guideline on HLA-B genotype and allopurinol dosing was reviewed for its 2015 update and its recommendations left unchanged (Saito Y et al., PMID: 26094938). What is missing is any randomised or concurrently controlled comparison — the cohort's control is historical, the outcome is rare, and carrier frequency (and therefore screening yield) is far lower in most European-ancestry populations than the ~20% seen in this Han Chinese cohort. Tier C: observational-dependent. HLA-B*57:01 screening before abacavir — the pharmacogenetic test with a randomised trial behind it — is shelf #481.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Lumbar fusion versus cognitive intervention and exercise for chronic low back pain: three randomised trials and their pooled 11-year follow-up show no advantage for surgery
question: In chronic degenerative low back pain, does lumbar fusion beat structured exercise and cognitive rehabilitation?
balance: LIKELY (no difference): Every randomised comparison of lumbar fusion with a structured cognitive-and-exercise programme for chronic degenerative low back pain has found the same thing — both groups improve, and surgery does not beat rehabilitation. In the Norwegian trial, Oswestry disability fell from 41 to 26 after fusion and from 42 to 30 after cognitive intervention and exercises at one year (between-group difference 2.3 points, 95% CI −6.7 to 11.4; P = 0.33), with an 18% early complication rate in the surgical group (Brox JI et al., PMID: 12973134). The UK MRC trial (349 patients) found a marginal 2-year Oswestry difference of −4.1 points (95% CI −8.1 to −0.1; P = 0.045) favouring surgery — a difference its own authors called marginal, just reaching the predefined minimal clinical difference, with no difference in walking capacity or any other outcome (Fairbank J et al., PMID: 15911537). At four years in the merged Norwegian trials, 24% of the rehabilitation group had crossed over to surgery and 23% of the fusion group had undergone re-operation, with no difference in disability or return to work (Brox JI et al., PMID: 19635718). The pooled long-term follow-up of all three trials (473 patients; mean 11.4 years) found an adjusted Oswestry difference of −0.7 points (95% CI −5.5 to 4.2) (Mannion AF et al., PMID: 24200413). Two boundaries: the Swedish Lumbar Spine Study (Fritzell P et al., PMID: 11725230) compared fusion with unstructured usual care rather than a structured programme and is cross-referenced here, not carded; and fusion added to decompression for spinal stenosis is a different question, not answered by this shelf.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference)

title: Short antibiotics and early oral switch in childhood bone and joint infection: 10 days cured septic arthritis and 20 days cured osteomyelitis in the Finnish randomised trials, with intravenous treatment only for the first 2–4 days
question: In children with septic arthritis or acute osteomyelitis, are short antibiotic courses with an early switch from intravenous to oral treatment safe?
balance: LIKELY (no difference, within the studied conditions): Two randomised trials from one Finnish programme tested shorter against conventional durations, with antibiotics stopped on clinical response plus a falling C-reactive protein (CRP). For septic arthritis, 130 culture-positive children received 10 or 30 days of clindamycin or a first-generation cephalosporin, intravenous for only the first 2–4 days; every child recovered without sequelae (Peltola H et al., PMID: 19323633). For acute haematogenous osteomyelitis, 131 culture-positive children received 20 or 30 days on the same template; all but one child in each group recovered entirely, the exceptions being one mild sequela in each group (Peltola H et al., PMID: 20842069). The programme's prospective cohort of 265 cases (1983–2005) shows the same approach in routine practice: mean intravenous duration 4 days, hospital stay falling from 13 to 9 days, and sequelae rates unchanged (Pääkkönen M et al., PMID: 22568753). The conditions matter: these were culture-positive infections in a setting where Staphylococcus aureus was overwhelmingly methicillin-susceptible (89% of the osteomyelitis cases, all MSSA), surgery was kept to a minimum, and stopping was CRP-guided — the results cannot simply be assumed for MRSA, neonates, immunocompromised children, or infections responding slowly. Tier C: a single research programme in one low-resistance setting.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference — short courses with early oral switch recovered children as completely as 30-day courses)

title: IL-1 blockade for difficult gout flares: canakinumab beat an injected steroid on pain and cut new-flare risk by more than half; anakinra matched usual care and triamcinolone in two trials — at the price of more infections
question: In gout flares in patients who cannot take NSAIDs or colchicine, do IL-1 blockers (anakinra, canakinumab) relieve the flare?
balance: POSSIBLE: In patients whose flares cannot be treated with NSAIDs or colchicine, IL-1 blockade works about as well as — and for canakinumab somewhat better than — the steroid injection it replaces. In the two β-RELIEVED trials (456 patients with frequent flares in whom NSAIDs and/or colchicine were contraindicated, not tolerated or unresponsive), a single 150 mg dose of canakinumab gave lower pain at 72 hours than 40 mg intramuscular triamcinolone (25.0 vs 35.7 mm on a 100-mm scale; difference −10.7 mm, 95% CI −15.4 to −6.0) and reduced the risk of a new flare by 62% relative over the core studies (hazard ratio 0.38, 95% CI 0.26 to 0.57) and by 56% relative over the full 24 weeks (HR 0.44, 0.32 to 0.60) — but with more adverse events (66.2% vs 52.8%), more serious adverse events (8.0% vs 3.5%), and more infections, neutropenia and thrombocytopenia (Schlesinger N et al., PMID: 22586173). Anakinra was non-inferior to a clinician's choice of colchicine, naproxen or prednisone in a small double-blind trial of 88 patients with crystal-proven flares (Janssen CA et al., PMID: 30602035), and matched triamcinolone for pain relief in a 165-patient phase II trial restricted to patients for whom NSAIDs and colchicine were unsuitable (pain reduction −41.2 vs −39.4 points; P = 0.688) (Saag KG et al., PMID: 33605029). The earlier phase II canakinumab dose-ranging study (So A et al., PMID: 20533546) is carded at shelf #390 and is cross-referenced here, not re-carded. No placebo-controlled trial exists in this population — every comparison is against an active steroid — and canakinumab's infection signal is a large part of why these drugs sit behind steroids in practice despite the trial results.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Cherries and gout: eating cherries was associated with 35% fewer attacks in a case-crossover study — but the only randomised trial found cherry concentrate did not lower urate at all
question: In gout, do cherries or cherry concentrate prevent flares?
balance: POSSIBLE: The flare claim rests on a single observational study — a well-designed one, but one. In a case-crossover study of 633 gout patients followed online for a year, with each patient serving as their own control, cherry intake in the 2 days before a hazard period was associated with a 35% lower risk of a gout attack than no intake (odds ratio 0.65, 95% CI 0.50 to 0.85 — a relative figure); cherry extract showed a similar association (OR 0.55, 0.30 to 0.98), and cherry intake combined with allopurinol use was associated with an attack risk 75% lower than periods with neither exposure (OR 0.25, 0.15 to 0.42) (Zhang Y et al., PMID: 23023818). The proposed mechanism — urate lowering — failed its randomised test: in 50 gout patients given placebo or one of four doses of tart cherry concentrate for 28 days, the concentrate had no effect on serum urate, urinary urate excretion or flare frequency (P = 0.76) (Stamp LK et al., PMID: 31891407). A systematic review found six small studies pointing in the same direction as Zhang but too heterogeneous to pool (Chen PE et al., PMID: 31885677). So: a consistent association with fewer attacks, no demonstrated urate mechanism, and no randomised flare trial — a large tart-cherry flare trial exists only as a registered protocol. Tier C: observational-dependent.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Vitamin C for gout: the only trial in gout patients found a trivial 0.23 mg/dL urate fall against allopurinol's 1.9 mg/dL — and flares have never been tested
question: In gout, does vitamin C lower serum urate or prevent flares?
balance: POSSIBLE (no difference that matters): Vitamin C does lower urate slightly in the general population — a meta-analysis of 13 randomised trials (556 participants, mostly people without gout) found a mean reduction of −0.35 mg/dL (95% CI −0.66 to −0.03) at a median dose of 500 mg/day (Juraschek SP et al., PMID: 21671418). But in the only randomised trial in patients with gout, vitamin C 500 mg/day for 8 weeks lowered serum urate by just 0.014 mmol/L (0.23 mg/dL), against 0.118 mmol/L (1.9 mg/dL) in patients starting or increasing allopurinol (P < 0.001) (Stamp LK et al., PMID: 23681955). No trial in any population has measured gout flares as an outcome of vitamin C. An effect roughly an eighth the size of a low allopurinol dose, from a pilot of 40 patients, is the whole gout-specific evidence base: enough to say vitamin C is not a urate-lowering treatment for gout, not enough to exclude a trivial physiological effect. Tier C: the gout claim rests on a single small pilot trial.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference — no clinically significant urate lowering in gout, and flares untested)

title: Colchicine prophylaxis in pseudogout: a 10-patient before-and-after series from 1986 is nearly the whole evidence base — attacks fell from 3.2 to 1 per patient-year, and no randomised trial has ever tested it
question: In calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease, does colchicine prevent recurrent pseudogout flares?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence): Prophylactic colchicine for recurrent pseudogout is widespread practice built on almost no evidence. The only primary study with numbers is a 1986 before-and-after series: 10 patients with recurrent attacks recorded 32 attacks in the year before starting colchicine 0.6 mg twice daily (3.2 per patient-year) and 10 attacks in the year taking it (1 per patient-year; P < 0.001), with 90% of patients judged to benefit (Alvarellos A et al., PMID: 3772928). A second 1987 report (González T et al., PMID: 3625651) reaches the same conclusion in its title, but its PubMed record carries no abstract, so no figures from it are printed on this shelf. The systematic review of all CPPD management (Parperis K et al., PMID: 33360232) found 22 studies and 403 patients across every treatment for the disease, only three randomised trials in total (of methotrexate, hydroxychloroquine and magnesium carbonate — not colchicine), and states plainly that colchicine, NSAIDs and corticosteroids have not been evaluated by randomised trials in CPPD. Regression to the mean — patients start prophylaxis after a bad year — can manufacture exactly the pattern the 1986 series reports. Tier C: a single tiny uncontrolled series.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence)

title: Methotrexate in polymyalgia rheumatica: the 10 mg weekly trial got patients off prednisone sooner with fewer flares; the 7.5 mg trial found nothing — dose may be the difference
question: In polymyalgia rheumatica, does adding methotrexate allow faster steroid tapering without more relapses?
balance: POSSIBLE: Two small double-blind trials disagree, and the clearest difference between them is the dose. Caporali's multicentre trial (72 patients with newly diagnosed polymyalgia rheumatica) added methotrexate 10 mg weekly to a 24-week prednisone taper: by 76 weeks, 28 of 32 methotrexate patients versus 16 of 30 placebo patients were no longer taking prednisone (risk difference 34 percentage points, 95% CI 11 to 53; P = 0.003), fewer methotrexate patients had flared (15 of 32 vs 22 of 30; P = 0.04), and the median cumulative prednisone dose was 2.1 g versus 2.97 g (P = 0.03), with similar adverse events (Caporali R et al., PMID: 15466766). The earlier Dutch trial used methotrexate 7.5 mg weekly in 40 patients (six of whom also had giant cell arteritis) and found no difference in time to remission, relapses or cumulative prednisone dose (van der Veen MJ et al., PMID: 8733437). The Caporali cohort's follow-up at about six years found the steroid-sparing advantage had narrowed to non-significance (cumulative prednisone 2.6 g vs 3.2 g, P = 0.6; still taking steroids 31% vs 39.3%), while a third of all patients still needed steroids beyond six years (Cimmino MA et al., PMID: 18578959). IL-6 blockade for polymyalgia rheumatica is a separate question, at shelf #687.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Abatacept in giant cell arteritis: in the single randomised trial, continuing abatacept after a shared 12-week induction kept 48% of patients relapse-free at 12 months versus 31% on placebo, with remission lasting 9.9 versus 3.9 months
question: In adults with giant cell arteritis, does abatacept increase relapse-free remission?
balance: POSSIBLE: One small randomised-withdrawal trial supports abatacept in giant cell arteritis. All 49 enrolled patients (newly diagnosed or relapsing GCA) received abatacept 10 mg/kg intravenously plus prednisone for 12 weeks; the 41 who were in remission at week 12 were then randomised double-blind to continue monthly abatacept or switch to placebo, with prednisone tapered on a standardised schedule and discontinued in all patients at week 28. Relapse-free survival at 12 months was 48% for those continuing abatacept and 31% for those switched to placebo (P = 0.049), and median duration of remission was 9.9 versus 3.9 months (P = 0.023), with no difference in the frequency or severity of adverse events, including infection (Langford CA et al., PMID: 28133925). The design flatters the drug in one specific way: only patients who had already responded to 12 weeks of abatacept were randomised, so the trial estimates the value of continuing it, not of starting it — and with 41 randomised patients, the headline P value of 0.049 rests on a handful of events. IL-6 blockade with tocilizumab in GCA is shelf #385 and upadacitinib is shelf #1812; no head-to-head comparison among these agents exists. Tier C: single small trial.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Hydroxychloroquine and rituximab in primary Sjögren syndrome: three placebo-controlled trials, three negative primary endpoints — the two most-used systemic treatments do not improve dryness, pain or fatigue
question: In primary Sjögren syndrome, do hydroxychloroquine or rituximab improve systemic disease and dryness?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): The two systemic treatments most used in primary Sjögren syndrome have each failed their primary endpoint in placebo-controlled trials. Hydroxychloroquine 400 mg/day in JOQUER (120 patients): 17.9% versus 17.2% met the responder endpoint at 24 weeks (odds ratio 1.01) (Gottenberg JE et al., PMID: 25027140). Rituximab in TEARS (120 patients): no difference at week 24 (difference 1.0 percentage point), with transient early gains in fatigue that did not persist (Devauchelle-Pensec V et al., PMID: 24727841). Rituximab again in TRACTISS (133 patients, two courses): response 39.8% versus 36.8% after imputation (adjusted odds ratio 1.13), no improvement in any outcome except unstimulated salivary flow, and not cost-effective at £10,752 versus £2,672 per patient (Bowman SJ et al., PMID: 28296257). What does help dry mouth symptomatically — pilocarpine — is shelf #1796.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference)

title: Rituximab in refractory myositis: in the RIM trial 83% of patients improved — but with no placebo-only arm, the trial cannot show the drug caused it
question: In adults with inflammatory myopathies, does rituximab improve strength and disease activity?
balance: POSSIBLE: The RIM trial randomised 200 adults and children with refractory polymyositis, dermatomyositis or juvenile dermatomyositis to rituximab early or about 8 weeks late — everyone received the drug, so there was no placebo-only comparison. The early and late groups reached the definition of improvement at the same speed (median 20.0 vs 20.2 weeks; P = 0.74), yet 83% of all patients met the improvement definition over 44 weeks on background glucocorticoids and immunosuppressants (Oddis CV et al., PMID: 23124935). A post-hoc biomarker analysis of the same trial found improvement concentrated in patients with anti-synthetase, Mi-2 or non-myositis-associated antibodies and high interferon-regulated chemokine scores (Reed AM et al., PMID: 26382217) — hypothesis-generating only. For dermatomyositis specifically, intravenous immunoglobulin has the cleaner placebo-controlled evidence (shelf #2718). Tier C: a single trial whose placebo-phase design cannot isolate the drug's effect.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Intravenous immunoglobulin in dermatomyositis: 79% versus 44% responded at 16 weeks in ProDERM — with thromboembolism among the harms
question: In dermatomyositis, does intravenous immunoglobulin improve strength and function?
balance: LIKELY: Two placebo-controlled trials, 29 years apart, point the same way. ProDERM randomised 95 adults with active dermatomyositis to IVIG 2.0 g/kg every 4 weeks or placebo: at 16 weeks, 79% versus 44% achieved at least minimal improvement on the Total Improvement Score (difference 35 percentage points, 95% CI 17 to 53; P < 0.001), with at least moderate and major improvement also favouring IVIG (Aggarwal R et al., PMID: 36198179). The small 1993 crossover trial (15 patients with treatment-resistant disease) found significant gains in muscle strength scores on IVIG, and major improvement in 9 of the 12 patients who received it, versus none of 11 on placebo (Dalakas MC et al., PMID: 8247075). The price is real: in ProDERM, 9 serious adverse events were considered related to IVIG, including 6 thromboembolic events, and headache affected 42% of patients.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: Apremilast for Behçet oral ulcers: fewer ulcers and less pain in two placebo-controlled trials — the phase 3 ulcer-burden AUC was 129.5 versus 222.1
question: In Behçet disease with recurrent oral ulcers, does apremilast reduce ulcer number and pain?
balance: LIKELY: Apremilast 30 mg twice daily beat placebo for the cardinal manifestation of Behçet syndrome in two randomised trials. In the phase 3 RELIEF trial (207 patients with active oral ulcers and no major organ involvement), the area under the curve for the total number of oral ulcers over the 12-week placebo-controlled period was 129.5 on apremilast versus 222.1 on placebo (least-squares mean difference −92.6, 95% CI −130.6 to −54.6; P < 0.001), and the Behçet's Disease Quality of Life score improved more (−4.3 vs −1.2 points) (Hatemi G et al., PMID: 31722152). The earlier phase 2 trial (111 patients) found 0.5 versus 2.1 oral ulcers per patient at week 12 and a greater fall in ulcer pain (−44.7 vs −16.0 mm on a 100-mm scale) (Hatemi G et al., PMID: 25875256). The adverse-event pattern is gastrointestinal — diarrhoea, nausea and headache — and neither trial speaks to eye, vascular or neurological Behçet, whose patients were excluded or absent.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: IL-1 blockade in colchicine-resistant familial Mediterranean fever: canakinumab produced complete responses in 61% versus 6% — and anakinra halved attack rates in its small trial
question: In colchicine-resistant familial Mediterranean fever, do interleukin-1 inhibitors control attacks?
balance: LIKELY: Two randomised placebo-controlled trials support interleukin-1 blockade when colchicine fails. In CLUSTER, patients with genetically confirmed colchicine-resistant familial Mediterranean fever randomised at the time of a flare to canakinumab 150 mg subcutaneously every 4 weeks or placebo achieved a complete response — resolution of the flare and no new flare until week 16 — in 61% versus 6% (P < 0.001), rising to 71% when patients whose dose was increased to 300 mg are included (De Benedetti F et al., PMID: 29768139). In the smaller anakinra trial (25 patients), attacks per month were 1.7 ± 1.7 on anakinra versus 3.5 ± 1.9 on placebo (P = 0.037), and 6 of 12 anakinra patients versus 0 of 13 on placebo averaged less than one attack per month (Ben-Zvi I et al., PMID: 27860460). Infections are the main harm signal with canakinumab (173.3 events per 100 patient-years in the FMF cohort; serious infections 6.6 per 100 patient-years).
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: Methotrexate alone is not enough in psoriatic arthritis: etanercept beat it on ACR20 (60.9% vs 50.7%) and minimal disease activity — and adding methotrexate to etanercept added nothing
question: In psoriatic arthritis, is methotrexate alone enough, or does early TNF inhibition beat it?
balance: LIKELY: SEAM-PsA randomised 851 patients with psoriatic arthritis, double-blind, to methotrexate monotherapy, etanercept monotherapy, or the combination. At week 24, ACR20 response rates were significantly greater with etanercept monotherapy than with methotrexate monotherapy (60.9% versus 50.7%; P = 0.029), and with combination therapy than with methotrexate (65.0% versus 50.7%; P = 0.005); minimal disease activity was achieved by 35.9% and 35.7% versus 22.9% respectively (both P = 0.005). Outcomes were similar in the combination and etanercept monotherapy groups, except for some skin endpoints — combining methotrexate and etanercept did not improve the efficacy of etanercept — and both etanercept arms showed less radiographic progression at week 48 than methotrexate alone (Mease PJ et al., PMID: 30747501). Methotrexate still worked for half the patients: the trial demotes it from default monotherapy, it does not make it useless.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit — etanercept, alone or combined with methotrexate, beat methotrexate alone; the combination added nothing over etanercept alone)

title: Cancer-related fatigue: exercise is the treatment that works — ginseng helped at 8 weeks in one trial; methylphenidate did not beat placebo
question: In cancer-related fatigue, do exercise programmes, ginseng or methylphenidate help?
balance: SPLIT: The three proposed remedies have three different answers. Exercise: in a meta-analysis of 113 randomised trials (11,525 unique participants), exercise improved cancer-related fatigue with a weighted effect size of 0.30 (95% CI 0.25 to 0.36), psychological interventions 0.27 and the two combined 0.26 — while pharmaceutical interventions as a class did not (0.09, 95% CI 0.00 to 0.19) (Mustian KM et al., PMID: 28253393). Ginseng: American (Wisconsin) ginseng 2000 mg/day missed its 4-week primary endpoint (P = .07) but separated at 8 weeks (change in fatigue score 20 vs 10.3 points; P = .003) in one 364-patient trial (Barton DL et al., PMID: 23853057). Methylphenidate: the 148-patient NCCTG trial of the long-acting preparation found no benefit on its primary endpoint (P = .35), with a hypothesis-generating signal only in the most fatigued, most advanced subgroup (Moraska AR et al., PMID: 20625123). Prescribe exercise first; the pills are, at best, adjuncts.
stamp: SPLIT — exercise LIKELY (benefit) / ginseng POSSIBLE (benefit) / methylphenidate LIKELY (the treatment made no difference overall)

title: Methotrexate for pseudogout: the only randomised trial (26 patients, crossover) found nothing — a 10-patient refractory series is the entire case for it
question: In adults with calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease (pseudogout), does methotrexate reduce flare frequency or joint damage?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence): The randomised evidence is a single small crossover trial: 26 patients with chronic or recurrent calcium pyrophosphate deposition arthropathy received weekly subcutaneous methotrexate 15 mg or placebo for 3 months per period; the disease activity score (DAS44) changed by −0.08 on methotrexate versus −0.13 on placebo (P = 0.44), pain levels remained stable, and the trial's only serious adverse event (bicytopenia) occurred on methotrexate (Finckh A et al., PMID: 25315665). Against that, a retrospective series of 10 patients with refractory disease — persistent polyarthritis, persistent oligoarthritis or very frequently recurring monoarthritis — rated methotrexate a median 7.4 of 10, with physicians judging the response excellent in 2, good in 5 and medium in 3; 2 patients stopped for toxicity, including transient bone marrow aplasia (Andres M et al., PMID: 22832286). Neither study measured flare frequency as its primary outcome, and neither measured joint damage at all — those outcomes in the question are, strictly, untested. Colchicine prophylaxis for the same disease is shelf #2713. Tier C: one tiny trial plus a case series.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence)

title: One 8 Gy fraction relieves bone-metastasis pain as well as a multi-fraction course — the trade is a fourfold higher retreatment rate (25% vs 7%)
question: In metastatic cancer with bone pain, does single-fraction radiotherapy relieve pain as well as multi-fraction courses?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): The Dutch Bone Metastasis Study randomised 1,171 patients with painful bone metastases to a single 8 Gy fraction or 4 Gy in six fractions: a pain response — a decrease of at least two points on a 0–10 scale — occurred in 71% of patients at some time during the first year, the difference between the groups was not significant and stayed well within the 10% margin, and repeated-measures analysis confirmed the two schedules were equivalent in palliation; pain medication, quality of life and side effects also did not differ (Steenland E et al., PMID: 10577695). A cumulative meta-analysis of 29 randomised studies found that the meta-conclusion — single-fraction radiotherapy is equally efficacious — has remained consistent as trials accumulated (Chow R et al., PMID: 31445837). The honest caveats are retreatment (25% after the single fraction versus 7% after six fractions in the Dutch study, partly because doctors were more willing to retreat single-fraction patients) and more pathological fractures after the single fraction, though the absolute percentage was low. Treatment costs were €1,734 versus €2,305, the 25% saving narrowing to 8% once retreatment costs were included.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference — a single 8 Gy fraction relieves pain as well as multi-fraction courses; retreatment is more often needed after the single fraction)

title: Metastatic spinal cord compression: surgery plus radiotherapy beat radiotherapy alone — 84% versus 57% of patients walked after treatment
question: In metastatic spinal cord compression, does decompressive surgery plus radiotherapy beat radiotherapy alone?
balance: LIKELY: In the only randomised trial, 101 patients with spinal cord compression caused by metastatic cancer were assigned to direct decompressive surgical resection followed by radiotherapy (ten 3 Gy fractions) or to the same radiotherapy alone. Significantly more patients in the surgery group were able to walk after treatment (42 of 50, 84%, versus 29 of 51, 57%; odds ratio 6.2, 95% CI 2.0 to 19.8; P = 0.001); surgical patients retained the ability to walk much longer (median 122 versus 13 days; P = 0.003); and of the 32 patients who entered the study unable to walk, significantly more regained walking with surgery (10 of 16, 62%, versus 3 of 16, 19%; P = 0.01). The need for corticosteroids and opioid analgesics was significantly reduced in the surgical group (Patchell RA et al., PMID: 16112300). The trial was stopped early because a predetermined stopping rule was met at interim analysis — early stopping tends to exaggerate effect sizes — and its patients were selected for single-site compression and fitness for surgery, so the size of the advantage should be read down even though its direction has never been contradicted by a second trial. Tier C: a single trial, stopped early and non-blinded.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: Brain metastases: hippocampal-avoidance whole-brain radiotherapy plus memantine delays cognitive failure versus conventional whole-brain treatment — with no survival cost
question: In brain metastases, does hippocampal-avoidance whole-brain radiotherapy plus memantine preserve cognition versus conventional whole-brain radiotherapy?
balance: LIKELY: Two large randomised trials answer the two halves of this question. Adding memantine to conventional whole-brain radiotherapy (WBRT) delayed cognitive decline: in RTOG 0614 (554 patients accrued, 508 eligible), time to cognitive decline was longer on memantine (hazard ratio 0.78, 95% CI 0.62 to 0.99; P = .01), and the probability of cognitive failure at 24 weeks was 53.8% versus 64.9% on placebo — although the trial's primary endpoint, delayed recall at 24 weeks, narrowly missed significance (P = .059) after heavy patient loss left only 149 analysable patients and 35% power (Brown PD et al., PMID: 23956241). Sparing the hippocampi on top of memantine helped further: in NRG Oncology CC001 (518 patients), hippocampal-avoidance WBRT plus memantine cut the risk of cognitive failure versus WBRT plus memantine (adjusted hazard ratio 0.74, 95% CI 0.58 to 0.95; P = .02), with less deterioration in executive function at 4 months (23.3% vs 40.4%) and in learning and memory at 6 months, and no difference in overall survival, intracranial progression-free survival or toxicity (Brown PD et al., PMID: 32058845). The combined package has never been randomised against plain WBRT without memantine, so its total advantage over the old standard is a two-step inference from two trials sharing an investigator group and a control-arm design — but each step is a properly powered randomised comparison in the same direction, and neither step cost survival or tumour control. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) — not Tier C: two phase III randomised trials.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: Tumour lysis syndrome: rasburicase normalises uric acid far faster and deeper than allopurinol — but no study has shown fewer clinical tumour-lysis events, kidney failures or deaths
question: In patients at risk of tumour lysis syndrome, does rasburicase control uric acid better than allopurinol, and does it change clinical outcomes?
balance: SPLIT — the laboratory answer and the clinical answer point in different directions. On uric acid, rasburicase wins decisively in randomised trials: in children at high risk, uric-acid exposure over 96 hours was 2.6-fold lower on rasburicase than allopurinol (relative measure; AUC 128 vs 329 mg/dL·hour; P < .0001), with an 86% versus 12% fall in plasma uric acid within 4 hours of the first dose (Goldman SC et al., PMID: 11342423); in adults, uric-acid response rates were 87% on rasburicase versus 66% on allopurinol (P = .001), 90% versus 53% in patients already hyperuricaemic, with control reached in 4 hours versus 27 hours (Cortes J et al., PMID: 20713865). On clinical outcomes, there is no comparable win: the adult systematic review and meta-analysis (21 studies, 1,261 patients) found no statistically significant difference in clinical tumour-lysis development between rasburicase and control groups in the controlled trials, and concluded that evidence is lacking that rasburicase improves clinical outcomes compared with alternatives — at significant cost (Lopez-Olivo MA et al., PMID: 23684124). The trials were powered on a blood level, not on dialysis, kidney failure or death, and those events are uncommon enough that the observational literature cannot settle them either. PROPOSED SPLIT — LIKELY (faster, deeper uric-acid control) / LIKELY (no difference shown in clinical outcomes). Tier C: the clinical-outcome leg rests on observational and meta-analytic data, and the only adult randomised trial used a laboratory endpoint.
stamp: SPLIT — LIKELY (faster, deeper uric-acid control) / LIKELY (no difference shown in clinical tumour-lysis outcomes, acute kidney injury or death)

title: Plantar fasciitis: a corticosteroid injection buys about a month of modest pain relief and nothing beyond it — fascia rupture and infection are rare but real
question: In adults with plantar fasciitis, does a corticosteroid injection give more than short-term relief, and what harms follow?
balance: SPLIT — by time. The one well-blinded placebo-controlled trial found a real but brief effect: in 82 patients, a single ultrasound-guided dexamethasone injection beat saline by 10.9 points on a 0–100 pain scale at 4 weeks (95% CI 1.4 to 20.4; P = .03), with no significant pain difference at 8 or 12 weeks, though fascia thickness stayed lower for three months (McMillan AM et al., PMID: 22619193). The Cochrane synthesis of 39 trials (2,492 adults) agrees and adds the scale of the benefit: versus placebo or no treatment, heel pain was lower by a mean of 6.38 points on a 0–100 scale in the first month (low-quality evidence; the confidence interval includes only a marginal clinical benefit against a minimal important difference of 8), and there was no difference at 1–6 months (mean difference −3.47; 95% CI −8.43 to 1.48) (David JA et al., PMID: 28602048). Harms are uncommon but not zero: pooling 21 trials that reported adverse events, there were two plantar fascia ruptures and three injection-site infections among 699 participants in steroid arms, plus 27 less serious short-term events — and the reviewers warn that harms were under-reported, so a higher risk cannot be ruled out; the case-report harms patients ask about (fat-pad atrophy) were not quantified in any trial. PROPOSED SPLIT — POSSIBLE (small benefit in the first month) / LIKELY (no difference beyond the short term). Tier C: the pooled evidence is rated low to very low quality and the harm estimates rest on incomplete reporting.
stamp: SPLIT — POSSIBLE (small benefit in the first month) / LIKELY (the treatment made no difference beyond the short term)

title: Unexplained infertility: insemination with ovarian stimulation triples live births when the natural prognosis is poor — and adds nothing when the prognosis is intermediate
question: In couples with unexplained infertility, does intrauterine insemination with ovarian stimulation improve live birth rates over expectant management?
balance: SPLIT — the answer turns on the couple's prognosis for conceiving naturally, and the two direct randomised trials enrolled opposite ends of it. In couples with an unfavourable prognosis, the TUI trial (201 couples) found three cycles of intrauterine insemination (IUI) with ovarian stimulation produced a cumulative live birth rate of 31% versus 9% with expectant management (risk ratio 3.41, 95% CI 1.71 to 6.79; P = .0003) (Farquhar CM et al., PMID: 29174128). In couples with an intermediate prognosis (30–40% predicted chance of spontaneous ongoing pregnancy within 12 months), the earlier Dutch trial (253 couples) found ongoing pregnancy in 23% after six months of IUI with controlled ovarian hyperstimulation versus 27% with expectant management (relative risk 0.85, 95% CI 0.63 to 1.1) — a large benefit excluded (Steures P et al., PMID: 16844491). The INeS trial adds the comparison couples actually face next: six cycles of IUI with ovarian hyperstimulation gave a 47% healthy-child rate, statistically non-inferior to IVF with single embryo transfer (52%), with multiple pregnancy rates of 7% per ongoing pregnancy (Bensdorp AJ et al., PMID: 25576320). The multiple-pregnancy hazard of stimulation is real but was small in these oral-agent and carefully monitored trials (two twin sets in TUI, both in the IUI arm; one triplet in Steures). PROPOSED SPLIT — LIKELY (benefit when prognosis is unfavourable) / LIKELY (no difference when prognosis is intermediate). Not Tier C: three randomised trials, two of them asking this exact question. Which stimulation drug to use with IUI is a separate question, homed at shelf #835.
stamp: SPLIT — LIKELY (benefit when the prognosis for natural conception is unfavourable) / LIKELY (the treatment made no difference when the prognosis is intermediate)

title: Gestational diabetes found before 20 weeks: treating it straight away modestly reduced a composite of adverse neonatal outcomes — with no effect on pregnancy hypertension or neonatal lean mass (TOBOGM)
question: In pregnant women, does screening for and treating gestational diabetes early (before 20 weeks) improve outcomes compared with standard diagnosis at 24–28 weeks?
balance: POSSIBLE: One large randomised trial has asked this question. In TOBOGM, 802 women who had a risk factor for hyperglycaemia and met World Health Organization 2013 criteria for gestational diabetes before 20 weeks (mean gestation at testing 15.6 weeks) were randomised to immediate treatment or to deferred or no treatment depending on a repeat glucose-tolerance test at 24–28 weeks. Immediate treatment modestly reduced the composite of adverse neonatal outcomes — birth before 37 weeks, birth trauma, birth weight ≥ 4500 g, respiratory distress, phototherapy, stillbirth or neonatal death, or shoulder dystocia — which occurred in 24.9% versus 30.5% (adjusted risk difference −5.6 percentage points, 95% CI −10.1 to −1.2). The trial's other two primary outcomes did not move: pregnancy-related hypertension occurred in 10.6% versus 9.9%, and neonatal lean body mass was essentially identical (adjusted mean difference −0.04 kg), and there were no between-group differences in serious adverse events (Simmons D et al., PMID: 37144983). A 5.6-point absolute reduction in a broad composite, from a single trial, in women selected for having a risk factor and meeting one-step early criteria — many of whose early hyperglycaemia would not persist to 24–28 weeks — is a real but modest and not yet replicated finding. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit). Tier C: a single trial. The separate question of one-step versus two-step screening at the standard timepoint is homed at shelf #809.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Nitrous oxide in labour: used for over a century and liked by many women — but the evidence base is so poor that how much pain it relieves cannot honestly be stated
question: In women in labour, does inhaled nitrous oxide provide worthwhile pain relief compared with other options?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence): This is a shelf about the state of the evidence as much as about the gas. The definitive systematic review (Likis FE et al., PMID: 24356165) found 58 publications covering 59 study populations, of which only 2 were rated good quality, 11 fair and 46 poor. What can be said: inhaled nitrous oxide provided less effective pain relief than epidural analgesia — in studies that were predominantly poor quality; the outcomes used to assess women's satisfaction with the birth experience were so heterogeneous that no synthesis was possible; the commonest maternal effects were unpleasant tolerability effects — nausea, vomiting, dizziness and drowsiness; and Apgar scores in newborns of mothers using nitrous oxide were not significantly different from those with other methods or no analgesia. Evidence on occupational exposure harms for staff was limited. So the honest answer to 'does it provide worthwhile pain relief?' is that worthwhile relief is plausible and consistent with widespread continued use and women's reported satisfaction in individual studies, but no adequate trial quantifies the analgesic effect against placebo or modern comparators, and any shelf claiming a number would be inventing it. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence). Tier C: the evidence base is dominated by poor-quality studies. Water immersion in the first stage of labour — the non-drug comparison with better trial data — is homed at shelf #1354.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence)
