title: Episiotomy: cutting routinely prevents nothing — a selective policy leaves about 30% fewer women with severe perineal trauma, with no clear harm to mother or baby
question: Compared with selective use, does routine episiotomy prevent severe tears and pelvic-floor harm?
balance: LIKELY: The belief that a routine surgical cut prevents worse spontaneous tearing has been randomised and has failed. The Cochrane review of selective ('only if needed') versus routine episiotomy policies (12 trials, 6,177 women) found that where an unassisted vaginal birth was anticipated, a selective policy resulted in about 30% fewer women experiencing severe perineal/vaginal trauma (relative measure: risk ratio 0.70, 95% CI 0.52 to 0.94; 5,375 women, 8 trials; low-certainty evidence) (Jiang H et al., PMID: 28176333). No compensating harm from selectivity appeared: blood loss differences were unclear and small (an average of 27 mL less with selective), babies with Apgar score below seven at five minutes did not differ (no events in 3,908 women), perineal infection did not clearly differ (risk ratio 0.90, 95% CI 0.45 to 1.82), and at six months or more there was probably little or no difference in dyspareunia (risk ratio 1.14, 95% CI 0.84 to 1.53) and little or no difference in urinary incontinence (risk ratio 0.98, 95% CI 0.67 to 1.44). The one trial in women where an operative vaginal delivery was intended (175 women) was underpowered and showed no clear difference, so the instrumental-delivery setting remains genuinely open. Routine episiotomy also guarantees what it claims to prevent — perineal trauma requiring sutures — in every woman cut. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) for a selective policy in unassisted vaginal birth. Not Tier C: 12 randomised trials. Antenatal perineal massage and second-stage perineal techniques are a different question, homed at shelf #837.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: Where oxytocin cannot be relied on, oral misoprostol after delivery cuts postpartum haemorrhage — by about half in India and a quarter in Pakistan in community placebo-controlled trials
question: In settings where oxytocin is unavailable or unreliable, does oral misoprostol prevent postpartum haemorrhage?
balance: LIKELY: Two community-based, placebo-controlled randomised trials in exactly the settings the question specifies — births at home or in low-resource communities where oxytocin's cold chain and injection requirements fail. In rural India, 1,620 women attended by auxiliary nurse midwives received oral misoprostol or placebo after delivery: acute postpartum haemorrhage (≥ 500 mL within 2 hours) fell from 12.0% to 6.4% (relative risk 0.53, 95% CI 0.39 to 0.74; P < .0001) — one haemorrhage prevented for every 18 women treated — severe haemorrhage fell from 1.2% to 0.2% (relative risk 0.20, 95% CI 0.04 to 0.91), and mean blood loss fell from 262 mL to 214 mL (Derman RJ et al., PMID: 17027730). In Pakistan, 1,119 women giving birth at home received 600 micrograms of oral misoprostol or placebo from trained traditional birth attendants: haemorrhage ≥ 500 mL occurred in 16.5% versus 21.9% (relative risk 0.76, 95% CI 0.59 to 0.97 — a 24% relative reduction), and a haemoglobin drop of more than 3 g/dL occurred in 5.1% versus 9.6% (relative risk 0.53, 95% CI 0.34 to 0.83), with no maternal deaths in either arm (Mobeen N et al., PMID: 21176086). In both trials shivering, chills and transient fever were more common with misoprostol — the drug's signature, unpleasant but self-limiting. Neither trial compares misoprostol with oxytocin: where oxytocin is available and reliably cold-chained it remains the standard (see shelf #416 on oxytocin and heat-stable carbetocin); this shelf answers the fallback question, and the answer is yes. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit). Not Tier C: two placebo-controlled randomised trials with consistent direction.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: Balloon tamponade for refractory postpartum haemorrhage: believed in everywhere, shown to help nowhere — and the largest trial found more surgery and death after the device was introduced
question: In women with postpartum haemorrhage not responding to uterotonics, does intrauterine balloon tamponade control bleeding and avoid hysterectomy?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence): Balloon tamponade is standard rescue practice for haemorrhage that uterotonics fail to stop, supported by decades of enthusiastic case series — but comparative evidence, when finally gathered, did not confirm it. The largest evaluation, a stepped-wedge cluster-randomised trial introducing condom-catheter uterine balloon tamponade (UBT) into 18 secondary-level hospitals in Uganda, Egypt and Senegal (60,111 deliveries), found the combined incidence of postpartum-haemorrhage-related invasive surgery or maternal death was higher after introduction than before (11.6 vs 6.7 per 10,000 deliveries; adjusted incidence rate ratio 4.08, 95% CI 1.07 to 15.58) — though the device was actually used in only 55 of 1,037 diagnosed haemorrhage cases in the intervention period, so the signal may reflect detection, selection or system effects rather than device harm (Anger HA et al., PMID: 31410966). The systematic review of tamponade devices for refractory atonic haemorrhage after vaginal birth rated every included study at high risk of bias and the certainty of evidence very low to low: the one randomised comparison of a condom-catheter balloon against standard care gave unclear results for the composite of surgery or death (risk ratio 2.33, 95% CI 0.76 to 7.14) and for hysterectomy (risk ratio 4.14, 95% CI 0.48 to 35.93), and protocol-inclusion studies of Bakri and other devices were likewise unclear (Pingray V et al., PMID: 34165867). The fair summary is not that balloons harm — the data are too weak and confounded for that — but that the benefit generations of case series asserted has never been demonstrated against any comparator, and hysterectomy avoidance, the outcome that matters, is unproven. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence). Tier C: all comparative evidence is at high risk of bias with very low certainty.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence)

title: Contraception before discharge after birth: immediate IUD or implant placement gets far more women started — but pooled continuation at 6–12 months is unproven, and immediate IUDs are expelled far more often
question: Immediately after delivery, does placing an IUD or implant increase continuation and prevent rapid repeat pregnancy versus delayed placement?
balance: SPLIT — the strategy clearly wins on starting and is unproven on lasting. The Cochrane review of immediate versus delayed postpartum insertion (16 randomised trials; 5 implant studies with 715 participants and 11 IUD studies with 1,894) found immediate insertion probably improves initiation for implants (risk ratio 1.48, 95% CI 1.11 to 1.98; moderate-certainty) and for IUDs (risk ratio 1.27, 95% CI 1.07 to 1.51; moderate-certainty) — many women randomised to delayed insertion never return to get the method (Sothornwit J et al., PMID: 36302159). But pooled utilisation at 6 and 12 months was uncertain for both methods (implant use at 6 months risk ratio 1.16, 95% CI 0.90 to 1.50, very low certainty; IUD use at 6 months 1.02 and at 12 months 0.86, very low certainty), and immediate IUD insertion carried a clearly higher expulsion rate at 6 months (risk ratio 4.55, 95% CI 2.52 to 8.19). The best single trial cuts the other way on continuation: in Uganda, women randomised to immediate levonorgestrel implant insertion were using implants at 6 months at 97% versus 68% for delayed insertion (P < .001) (Averbach S et al., PMID: 28610898) — one of the trials inside the heterogeneous pooled estimate. Pregnancy prevention, the outcome that ultimately matters, is thin: one study of 1,000 women found fewer unintended pregnancies at 12 months with immediate IUD insertion (risk ratio 0.26, 95% CI 0.17 to 0.41; low-certainty). Breastfeeding was little affected by immediate progestin-releasing methods. PROPOSED SPLIT — LIKELY (benefit on initiation) / LIKELY (no difference demonstrated in pooled continuation; more expulsions). Not Tier C: 16 randomised trials, though several pooled outcomes are very low certainty.
stamp: SPLIT — LIKELY (benefit: more women start a method) / LIKELY (no difference demonstrated in pooled use at 6–12 months; IUD expulsion is more common)

title: Vaginal oestrogen after breast cancer: no overall increase in recurrence or breast-cancer death in the large cohorts — but a recurrence signal in women taking aromatase inhibitors
question: In breast cancer survivors with genitourinary symptoms of menopause, does low-dose vaginal oestrogen increase the risk of recurrence or breast-cancer death?
balance: SPLIT — the answer splits by the endocrine therapy a woman is taking alongside. In the Danish national cohort of 8,461 postmenopausal women treated for early oestrogen-receptor-positive breast cancer, vaginal oestrogen therapy (VET) was not associated with recurrence overall (adjusted relative risk 1.08, 95% CI 0.89 to 1.32) or with higher mortality (adjusted HR 0.78, 0.71 to 0.87) — but in the subgroup taking adjuvant aromatase inhibitors, recurrence was higher on VET (adjusted RR 1.39, 1.04 to 1.85), with no mortality increase (Cold S et al., PMID: 35854422). The Scottish and Welsh cohorts (49,237 women) found no higher breast-cancer-specific mortality in vaginal-oestrogen users (pooled adjusted HR 0.77, 0.63 to 0.94) (McVicker L et al., PMID: 37917089). A 2025 meta-analysis of six observational studies in women on endocrine therapy sharpened the same split: topical oestrogen during aromatase-inhibitor treatment was associated with increased recurrence (RR 2.51, 1.10 to 5.72, low-certainty evidence) but not mortality, while during tamoxifen it was associated with neither (Kastora SL et al., PMID: 39854791). No randomised trial exists and none is likely: every number here is observational, so residual confounding runs in both directions — women prescribed vaginal oestrogen may differ from non-users in symptom burden, endocrine-therapy adherence and surveillance. PROPOSED SPLIT — POSSIBLE (no increase in recurrence or mortality overall) / POSSIBLE (increased recurrence in women also taking aromatase inhibitors); Tier C: observational evidence only, on a harm question. Non-hormonal and non-oestrogen options for the same symptoms are homed at shelf #945.
stamp: SPLIT — POSSIBLE (no increase in recurrence or mortality overall) / POSSIBLE (increased recurrence in women also taking aromatase inhibitors)

title: Myo-inositol in pregnancy: gestational diabetes roughly halved in three Italian trials — all open-label, all from one research group
question: In pregnant women at increased risk of gestational diabetes, does myo-inositol supplementation from early pregnancy prevent gestational diabetes?
balance: POSSIBLE: Three randomised trials, all from the same Italian research group, point the same way. In women with a parent with type 2 diabetes, myo-inositol 2 g twice daily (with folic acid) from the end of the first trimester cut gestational diabetes (GDM) from 15.3% to 6.0% (odds ratio 0.35) and reduced fetal macrosomia (D'Anna R et al., PMID: 23340885). In obese women (BMI ≥ 30), GDM fell from 33.6% to 14.0% (OR 0.34, 95% CI 0.17 to 0.68) (D'Anna R et al., PMID: 26241420). In overweight non-obese women, GDM fell from 27.4% to 11.6% (OR 0.33, 0.15 to 0.70) (Santamaria A et al., PMID: 26698911). The consistency is striking — relative reductions of about two-thirds in three different risk groups — but so is the limitation: every trial is open-label, every trial comes from one collaborating group in two Italian university hospitals, and no independent group has replicated the finding at this size. Open-label conduct matters less for a laboratory diagnosis like GDM than for symptom outcomes, but co-interventions and OGTT scheduling were not blinded. No trial was powered for neonatal or maternal clinical outcomes beyond macrosomia. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — Tier C: a single research group's open-label trials of an unregulated supplement. The records name no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Duloxetine for stress urinary incontinence: leakage episodes roughly halved versus a quarter on placebo — with one in four women stopping for side effects
question: In women with stress urinary incontinence, does duloxetine improve continence versus placebo?
balance: LIKELY: Duloxetine 40 mg twice daily reduces stress incontinence episodes by about half, against about a quarter on placebo. In the first phase 3 trial (683 North American women), median incontinence episode frequency fell 50% versus 27% (P < .001), 51% of women on duloxetine achieved at least a halving of episodes versus 34% on placebo, and quality-of-life scores improved more (11.0 vs 6.8 points) (Dmochowski RR et al., PMID: 14501737). In women with severe incontinence already scheduled for surgery, episodes fell 60% versus 27%, the responder relative risk was 4.68 (2.27 to 9.66), and 20% of duloxetine responders no longer wanted their operation (Cardozo L et al., PMID: 15339761). The Cochrane synthesis of nine trials (3,327 adults) confirmed better quality of life (weighted mean difference 5.26 points) and subjective improvement, but found no demonstrated benefit on objective pad-test cure and only a small subjective-cure effect (~3%) (Mariappan P et al., PMID: 16034945). The price is tolerability: nausea is common (usually transient), about one in three women report a treatment-related adverse effect, and in the phase 3 trial 24% stopped duloxetine for adverse events versus 4% on placebo. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) — a real, moderate symptom benefit for women who can stay on the drug; it is not a cure, and objective dryness was never shown.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: POPPY: one-to-one pelvic-floor muscle training eased prolapse symptoms at 12 months versus a lifestyle leaflet — a modest average gain in the one large trial
question: In women with symptomatic pelvic organ prolapse, does individualised pelvic-floor muscle training improve symptoms versus lifestyle advice alone?
balance: LIKELY — on one large trial. In POPPY, 447 women with newly diagnosed symptomatic stage I–III prolapse were randomised to an individualised one-to-one pelvic-floor muscle training programme or to a prolapse lifestyle-advice leaflet alone. At 12 months, women in the training group reported fewer prolapse symptoms: the pelvic organ prolapse symptom score (POP-SS) fell by 3.77 points versus 2.09 on advice alone — an adjusted difference of 1.52 points (95% CI 0.46 to 2.59; P = .0053) (Hagen S et al., PMID: 24290404). The effect is real but modest on a symptom scale, both groups improved, and the trial measures symptoms, not anatomy: it does not show that training reverses prolapse stage or prevents eventual surgery. Adverse events were few and judged unrelated. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) — Tier C: a single (large, well-conducted, multicentre) trial, so the finding has no independent replication yet. Pelvic-floor training for urinary incontinence is a different question, homed elsewhere in the library.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: Continuous glucose monitoring in gestational diabetes: no shown improvement in neonatal outcomes — one small trial found less excessive weight gain
question: In women with gestational diabetes, does continuous glucose monitoring improve glucose control and neonatal outcomes compared with finger-prick self-monitoring?
balance: SPLIT — no outcome benefit shown, one possible maternal benefit. The only GDM-only randomised trial (106 women) found no significant differences between continuous glucose monitoring and self-monitoring in caesarean delivery, Apgar scores, macrosomia or neonatal hypoglycaemia, and a non-significant HbA1c difference — but fewer women on CGM gained excessive weight (33.3% vs 56.4%; P = .039) (Wei Q et al., PMID: 26814139). The larger GlucoMOMS trial (300 women with type 1, type 2 or gestational diabetes on insulin) found intermittent retrospective CGM did not reduce macrosomia (31.0% vs 28.4%; relative risk 1.06, 95% CI 0.83 to 1.37) and did not improve HbA1c (Voormolen DN et al., PMID: 29603547). So the devices reveal glucose patterns without, so far, changing the outcomes those patterns predict — in GDM specifically the randomised base is one small trial plus a mixed-diabetes trial in which GDM was a minority subgroup (109 of 300). PROPOSED SPLIT — LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for neonatal and obstetric outcomes / POSSIBLE (less excessive gestational weight gain); Tier C: small, indirect evidence base. CGM in type 1 diabetes in pregnancy (CONCEPTT) is a different question, homed at shelf #959.
stamp: SPLIT — LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for neonatal and obstetric outcomes / POSSIBLE (less excessive gestational weight gain)

title: Lichen sclerosus: clobetasol beat pimecrolimus on inflammation and appearance in the one head-to-head trial — symptoms improved equally on both
question: In lichen sclerosus, does ultrapotent topical corticosteroid beat topical calcineurin inhibitors for disease control?
balance: LIKELY — for clobetasol over the calcineurin inhibitors, on the outcomes that distinguish them. The systematic review of all seven randomised trials in genital lichen sclerosus (249 participants) found clobetasol propionate 0.05% clearly better than placebo (participant-rated improvement/remission relative risk 2.85, 95% CI 1.45 to 5.61), while head-to-head there was no difference between pimecrolimus and clobetasol in relieving pruritus (standardised mean difference −0.33, −0.99 to 0.33) or burning/pain (0.03, −0.62 to 0.69) — but pimecrolimus was clearly less effective on investigator-rated global improvement (−1.64, −2.40 to −0.87) (Chi CC et al., PMID: 22483994). The one direct double-blind trial (38 women with biopsy-proven vulvar disease) found the same pattern: clobetasol was superior to pimecrolimus at reducing biopsy-measured inflammation (P = .015), while itch and burning/pain improved in both groups without a significant difference (Goldstein AT et al., PMID: 21353334). The review also found no evidence supporting topical androgens or progesterone. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) for ultrapotent steroid over calcineurin inhibitor on inflammation and appearance — Tier C: the whole randomised base is 249 patients, and the head-to-head trial has 38.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: Emergency contraception and weight: pregnancy risk after the pills is over threefold higher in obese women — worst for levonorgestrel — while the copper IUD fails about 1 time in 1,000 at any weight
question: In women with higher body weight, do oral emergency contraceptives lose effectiveness, and does the copper IUD avoid the problem?
balance: SPLIT — the pills fade with weight; the device does not. Pooling the two randomised trials of ulipristal acetate versus levonorgestrel, the risk of pregnancy after oral emergency contraception was more than threefold higher in obese women than in women with normal BMI (odds ratio 3.60, 95% CI 1.96 to 6.53), whichever pill was taken — and the increase was larger for levonorgestrel (OR 4.41, 2.05 to 9.44) than for ulipristal (OR 2.62, 0.89 to 7.00, not significant) (Glasier A et al., PMID: 21920190). The copper IUD shows no such gradient in the data available: across 42 studies and 7,034 women over 35 years, the pregnancy rate after IUD insertion for emergency contraception was 0.09% — about 1 in 1,100 — and the review identified no weight-related loss of effect (Cleland K et al., PMID: 22570193). Two cautions: the weight analysis is a pooled secondary analysis of trial data, not a trial randomised by weight, and absolute failure rates remain low for all methods (the trials' overall pregnancy rates were around 1–2%); and intercourse near ovulation raised failure risk as much as obesity did (OR 4.42) for both pills. PROPOSED SPLIT — LIKELY (effectiveness falls with weight, most for levonorgestrel) / LIKELY (copper IUD unaffected); Tier C: pooled observational analysis plus case-series review. Which pill works best head-to-head is homed at shelf #244; the 2010 Glasier trial is carded there and is not re-carded here — this shelf cards the separate 2011 pooled risk-factor analysis.
stamp: SPLIT — LIKELY (oral emergency contraception loses effectiveness as weight rises, most for levonorgestrel) / LIKELY (the copper IUD remains highly effective)

title: ROSE: a four-session interpersonal-therapy programme in pregnancy cut postpartum major depression from 20–33% to 0–4% in two small trials — in low-income women, from one research group
question: In pregnant women at high risk of postpartum depression, does a preventive interpersonal-therapy programme (ROSE) prevent postpartum depression?
balance: POSSIBLE: The programme later manualised as ROSE (Reach Out, Stand Strong: Essentials for new mothers) — four antenatal group sessions based on interpersonal psychotherapy, aimed at the role transition to motherhood and at building support — was tested in two small randomised trials in pregnant women on public assistance who had at least one risk factor for postpartum depression. In the pilot (37 women), postpartum major depression occurred in 0 of 17 women in the intervention group versus 6 of 18 (33%) on treatment as usual within 3 months of delivery (Zlotnick C et al., PMID: 11282702). In the larger trial (99 women), postpartum major depressive disorder occurred in 4% on the intervention versus 20% on standard antenatal care at 3 months (Zlotnick C et al., PMID: 16877662). A later adaptation for low-income women with recent intimate partner violence (54 women) did not significantly reduce major depressive episodes, PTSD or further violence, though symptom scores moved in the programme's favour (Zlotnick C et al., PMID: 21153559). The effects in the main trials are large but the samples are tiny — 2 versus 8 cases decides the larger trial — follow-up stops at 3 months, and all trials come from one research group in one population (financially disadvantaged US women). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — Tier C: small single-group trials. A secondary analysis of the 99-woman trial (Kao 2015, PMID: 26076207) reported longer breastfeeding in the ROSE group; as a repeat report of the same trial it is noted here, not carded separately.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Self-managed medication abortion: 95–99% completed without surgery in the telemedicine and accompaniment cohorts, with serious adverse events under 1% — observational evidence only
question: Where clinic access is limited, is self-managed medication abortion with remote or accompaniment support as safe and effective as clinic-based care?
balance: POSSIBLE: Two large prospective cohorts describe self-managed medication abortion with structured remote support. Through Women on Web, 1,000 women in Ireland and Northern Ireland who self-sourced mifepristone and misoprostol reported 94.7% (95% CI 93.1 to 96.0) completing abortion without surgical intervention; 0.7% received a blood transfusion, 2.6% received antibiotics, and no deaths were reported (Aiken ARA et al., PMID: 28512085). In the SAFE study — 1,051 callers to accompaniment groups in Argentina and Nigeria, supported by phone through self-management — complete abortion without surgery was reported by 99% of misoprostol-alone users and 94% of combined-regimen users, and for pregnancies under 9 weeks both regimens were non-inferior to the completion rates of clinician-managed abortion in historical clinical trials (Moseson H et al., PMID: 34801131). There is no randomised comparison and there cannot realistically be one where clinic care is legally restricted; the comparisons are against historical clinic benchmarks, outcomes are self-reported, and roughly a quarter to a third of women in these programmes are lost to follow-up — the women not heard from may fare worse. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit — effectiveness and safety comparable to clinic-based care) — Tier C: observational evidence on a question where randomisation is not feasible. Telemedicine consultation inside a formal clinic service is a different model, homed at shelf #660.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Antioxidants for male infertility: the one rigorous placebo-controlled trial (MOXI) found nothing — live birth 15% vs 24% on placebo — against a positive but very-low-certainty pooled literature
question: In male infertility with abnormal semen parameters, do antioxidant supplements improve pregnancy and live-birth rates?
balance: SPLIT — the best trial and the pooled literature disagree, and the disagreement tracks trial quality. MOXI, the one large multicentre double-blind placebo-controlled trial (174 men with abnormal semen parameters or high DNA fragmentation), found antioxidants did not improve sperm concentration, motility, morphology or DNA fragmentation at 3 months, and cumulative live birth at 6 months was 15% on antioxidants versus 24% on placebo — numerically favouring placebo, not significantly (Steiner AZ et al., PMID: 32111479). The Cochrane review of 90 trials (10,303 men) pooled a benefit: live birth odds ratio 1.43 (95% CI 1.07 to 1.91) across 12 small trials with 246 live births, rated very-low-certainty — and when high-risk-of-bias studies were removed, the live-birth benefit disappeared (Peto OR 1.22, 0.85 to 1.75) (de Ligny W et al., PMID: 35506389). Clinical pregnancy was higher in the pooled analysis (OR 1.89, low certainty), and mild gastrointestinal discomfort was more common on antioxidants (OR 2.70). PROPOSED SPLIT — LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) in the rigorous trial / POSSIBLE (benefit) in the pooled low-certainty literature; Tier C: supplement evidence with a quality-dependent answer. The MOXI formulation's ingredients and doses are named in its record (vitamin C 500 mg, vitamin E 400 mg, selenium 0.20 mg, L-carnitine 1,000 mg, zinc 20 mg, folic acid 1,000 µg, lycopene 10 mg daily) but no brand or company is named — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
stamp: SPLIT — LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) in the rigorous placebo-controlled trial / POSSIBLE (benefit) in the pooled low-certainty literature

title: Parent training in ADHD: parenting and conduct problems clearly improve — the effect on core symptoms fades when the raters are blinded
question: In children with ADHD, does parent behaviour training improve symptoms and parenting versus usual care?
balance: SPLIT — what parent training changes depends on who is rating, and on what is being rated. The broadest synthesis (Sonuga-Barke EJ et al., PMID: 23360949) found psychological treatments, behavioural interventions among them, produced significant effects on ADHD symptoms when rated by those closest to treatment (standardised mean differences 0.40 to 0.64), but the effects attenuated to non-significance when the best probably blinded assessments were used. Daley D et al. (PMID: 25062591) show where the blinded evidence does hold: across 32 randomised trials, probably blinded ratings still showed improved positive parenting (SMD 0.63), less negative parenting (SMD 0.43) and fewer conduct problems (SMD 0.31), while the core-symptom effect did not persist. The Cochrane review of parent training specifically (Zwi M et al., PMID: 22161373) is the cautionary base: only five trials and 284 children, unclear-to-high risk of bias, a non-significant pooled effect on externalising behaviour (SMD −0.32, 95% CI −0.83 to 0.18) and a significant one on internalising behaviour (SMD −0.48, −0.84 to −0.13). PROPOSED SPLIT — LIKELY (benefit) for parenting quality and conduct problems, which survive blinding / MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) for core ADHD symptoms, where the blinded evidence is null. Stimulant-versus-behavioural treatment comparisons are homed at shelf #643.
stamp: SPLIT — LIKELY (benefit) for parenting quality and conduct problems / MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) for core ADHD symptoms, where blinded ratings show no clear effect

title: Neurofeedback for ADHD: parent ratings improve, blinded ratings and sham controls say no — the effect lives where blinding doesn't
question: In ADHD, does neurofeedback improve core symptoms versus sham or medication?
balance: SPLIT — neurofeedback's evidence divides cleanly along the blinding line. Cortese S et al. (PMID: 27238063), pooling 13 trials and 520 participants, found significant effects on ADHD symptoms only on the least blinded ratings — total symptoms SMD 0.35 (95% CI 0.11 to 0.59) — with no significant effect on probably blinded ratings and none in trials with active or sham controls; laboratory measures of attention and inhibition were also null, and only 4 studies checked that children had actually learned the EEG skill. Micoulaud-Franchi JA et al. (PMID: 25431555) found the same shape in 5 trials: parent (probably unblinded) ratings improved across all domains (overall SMD −0.49), while teacher (probably blinded) ratings improved only for inattention (−0.30). The one double-blind placebo-controlled trial, Vollebregt MA et al. (PMID: 24168522; 41 children, 30 sessions), found no effect on any neurocognitive measure. PROPOSED SPLIT — POSSIBLE (benefit) on unblinded parent ratings / LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) on blinded ratings, against sham, and for neurocognitive outcomes. No carded trial compares neurofeedback with medication head-to-head, so the 'versus medication' half of the question has no direct evidence.
stamp: SPLIT — POSSIBLE (benefit) on unblinded parent ratings / LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) on blinded ratings, against sham controls, and for neurocognitive outcomes

title: Tiotropium add-on in paediatric asthma: lung function improves by roughly 90–175 mL across four placebo-controlled trials — symptom-control gains are trends, not proof
question: In children and adolescents with asthma not controlled on standard inhalers, does tiotropium add-on improve lung function and control?
balance: The paediatric tiotropium programme is unusually complete: four double-blind placebo-controlled trials spanning ages 1 to 17, all as add-on to inhaled corticosteroids with or without other controllers. In adolescents with moderate asthma, peak FEV1 improved by 174 mL on 5 µg and 134 mL on 2.5 µg over placebo at 24 weeks (Hamelmann E et al., PMID: 26960245). In adolescents with severe asthma the primary endpoint was missed at 5 µg (90 mL, p = 0.104) and met at 2.5 µg (111 mL, p = 0.046), with numerical trough and control gains (Hamelmann E et al., PMID: 27811070). In children aged 6–11 with severe asthma, 5 µg improved peak FEV1 by 139 mL and trough FEV1 by 87 mL, while 2.5 µg did neither (Szefler SJ et al., PMID: 28189771). In children aged 1–5, an exploratory 102-child trial found symptom scores no different from placebo, with tolerability comparable to placebo (Vrijlandt EJLE et al., PMID: 29361462). PROPOSED LIKELY — benefit for lung function as add-on therapy in children aged 6–17; asthma-control effects are trends rather than demonstrated benefits, and efficacy under age 6 is unproven. The adult triple-therapy question is homed at shelf #1033.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — improved lung function as add-on therapy in children aged 6–17; asthma-control effects are smaller and less certain

title: Metabolic surgery in adolescents with severe obesity: about a quarter of body weight lost and most diabetes remitted at 3–5 years — observational evidence, with real nutritional and reoperation costs
question: In adolescents with severe obesity, does metabolic surgery improve weight and comorbidities versus lifestyle care?
balance: No randomised trial exists; the evidence is two prospective programmes followed 3–5 years. In Teen-LABS, 242 US adolescents (mean BMI 53) lost 27% of body weight by 3 years, with remission of type 2 diabetes in 95% of those affected, of prediabetes in 76%, of elevated blood pressure in 74% and of dyslipidaemia in 66% (Inge TH et al., PMID: 26544725). The same cohort at 5 years — a repeat report, not a second study — had kept off 26%, with diabetes remission of 86% against 53% in adults (Inge TH et al., PMID: 31116917). Sweden's AMOS study, prospective and controlled but NOT randomised despite sometimes being described that way, found BMI fell 13.1 kg/m² after bypass while rising 3.3 kg/m² in matched conservatively treated controls (Olbers T et al., PMID: 28065734). The costs are consistent across both programmes: nutritional deficiency in 57–72% (hypoferritinaemia 57% in Teen-LABS), additional abdominal surgery in 13–25%, and 3 deaths among 161 Teen-LABS adolescents over 5 years. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit); Tier C: the balance rests entirely on observational comparisons, and the intervention's consequences are lifelong.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — large, durable weight loss and comorbidity remission in prospective cohorts; no randomised trial exists

title: Growth hormone for idiopathic short stature: about 4 cm of extra adult height on average — real, modest, and highly variable between children
question: In idiopathic short stature, does growth hormone increase adult height, and by how much?
balance: The randomised evidence is consistent and the effect is quantified. Deodati A et al. (PMID: 21398350), pooling the three randomised trials with adult-height outcomes (115 children), found treated children ended 0.65 SD score — about 4 cm — taller than controls, with a mean height gain of 1.2 SD against 0.34 SD untreated; seven non-randomised trials gave a smaller 0.45 SD (about 3 cm). The one double-blind placebo-controlled trial (Leschek EW et al., PMID: 15240584) found adult height 0.51 SD (3.7 cm; 95% CI 0.10 to 0.92 SD) greater on growth hormone after a mean 4.4 years of treatment. Dahlgren J (PMID: 21912164), reviewing six long-term studies narratively, reports gains of 0.5 to 1.3 SD, largest in younger children furthest below their parental height, with a dose-dependent pattern but only about 1.2 cm between the dose regimens in the randomised pool. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): roughly 4 cm of adult height on average — an average that conceals wide individual variation, which the reviewers themselves emphasise. Growth hormone in Turner syndrome is homed at shelf #1422.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — adult height increased by roughly 0.65 SD (about 4 cm) in randomised trials

title: Prophylactic paracetamol at vaccination: fevers fall by about a quarter — and antibody levels fall too, though immunological memory survives
question: In infants, does prophylactic paracetamol given around vaccination reduce antibody responses to the vaccines?
balance: SPLIT — the same intervention wins on the outcome parents see and loses on the outcome the vaccine is for. In two consecutive randomised trials in 459 infants, three prophylactic paracetamol doses in the first 24 hours cut fever of 38.0 °C or more after at least one dose from 66% to 42% after primary vaccination and from 58% to 36% after the booster — absolute reductions of about 24 and 22 percentage points — while fever above 39.5 °C was uncommon in both groups (Prymula R et al., PMID: 19837254). Antibody concentrations, however, were significantly lower with paracetamol for all ten pneumococcal serotypes and several other antigens after priming, and for most serotypes after boosting. The follow-up of the same children at age 4 (Prymula R et al., PMID: 23391599 — a repeat report of the same cohort, flagged on its card) found immunological memory intact and functional antibody titres not significantly different, and the authors judge the reduction transient. PROPOSED SPLIT — LIKELY (benefit) fewer febrile reactions / POSSIBLE (harm) lower antibody responses, apparently transient; Tier C: the harm judgement rests on a surrogate outcome from a single trial programme. The trialists' own conclusion stands as the practical summary: prophylactic antipyretics at vaccination should not be routinely recommended.
stamp: SPLIT — LIKELY (benefit) fewer febrile reactions / POSSIBLE (harm) lower antibody responses after primary and booster doses, apparently transient

title: Exclusive enteral nutrition in paediatric Crohn's disease: remission matches corticosteroids in children — and the one trial that scoped the bowel found the mucosa heals better
question: In children with Crohn's disease, does exclusive enteral nutrition induce remission as well as corticosteroids, with better growth and mucosal healing?
balance: SPLIT by outcome, and the paediatric answer differs from the adult one. In children, enteral nutrition (EN) and corticosteroids have never been separated on clinical remission: the paediatric meta-analysis pooled a relative risk of 0.97 (95% CI 0.7 to 1.4) (Dziechciarz P et al., PMID: 17767463), and the Cochrane child subgroup pointed, if anything, toward EN (83% versus 61% remission; RR 1.35, 0.92 to 1.97), even though Cochrane's adult-dominated overall pool favoured steroids (Narula N et al., PMID: 29607496). On mucosal healing, the only randomised trial that scoped the bowel found healing in 74% on a polymeric diet versus 33% on corticosteroids, with remission rates the same (79% versus 67%) (Borrelli O et al., PMID: 16682258). On growth — the third limb of the question — the carded syntheses could not pool growth data at all, so a growth advantage is not demonstrated by this evidence. PROPOSED SPLIT — LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for clinical remission versus corticosteroids / POSSIBLE (benefit) for mucosal healing; Tier C: the healing claim rests on one small open-label trial and the remission evidence is graded very low quality.
stamp: SPLIT — LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for clinical remission versus corticosteroids / POSSIBLE (benefit) for mucosal healing

title: Infliximab for IVIG-resistant Kawasaki disease: fever breaks faster than with a second IVIG course in two small trials — coronary outcomes are untested at this size
question: In children with Kawasaki disease resistant to IVIG, does infliximab shorten fever and inflammation compared with a second IVIG course?
balance: Two small randomised trials in the target population point the same way on fever. In the phase 3 Japanese trial, defervescence within 48 hours occurred in 76.7% on infliximab versus 37.0% on a second IVIG course (p = 0.023), with earlier resolution overall (Mori M et al., PMID: 29386515). In the US pharmacokinetic trial, fever ceased within 24 hours in 11 of 12 children on infliximab versus 8 of 12 retreated with IVIG, with no significant differences in inflammatory markers or coronary echocardiography (Burns JC et al., PMID: 18672254). The largest infliximab trial in the disease (Tremoulet AH et al., PMID: 24572997) answers a different question — adding infliximab to FIRST treatment did not reduce IVIG resistance (11.2% versus 11.3%) — and is carded here as flagged context only; it does corroborate faster fever resolution (median 1 versus 2 days) under double-blind conditions. Coronary artery outcomes, the outcome that matters most, rest on 4 events across the refractory trials and are effectively untested. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit); Tier C: 55 randomised children in the target population, one trial open-label, no trial powered for coronary outcomes. Corticosteroids in high-risk primary Kawasaki treatment are homed at shelf #646.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — faster defervescence than a second IVIG course in small randomised trials; too few children to judge coronary outcomes

title: Xylitol to prevent ear infections: episodes fall by about a quarter in healthy daycare children — but not in the otitis-prone children this question asks about
question: In children prone to recurrent otitis media, does xylitol syrup or gum prevent acute otitis media episodes?
balance: SPLIT by population, and the split runs against the question as posed. The Cochrane synthesis (Azarpazhooh A et al., PMID: 27486835) pooled three trials of 1,826 healthy Finnish children attending daycare: xylitol in any form reduced acute otitis media from 30% to around 22% (relative risk 0.75, 95% CI 0.65 to 0.88 — a 25% relative reduction, about 8 percentage points absolute). The largest trial shows the same shape by formulation: at least one episode in 41% on control syrup versus 29% on xylitol syrup, with chewing gum effective and lozenges not significantly so (Uhari M et al., PMID: 9755259). But in otitis-prone children — the population named in this shelf's question — the pooled estimate is null (RR 0.90, 0.67 to 1.21), as it is when xylitol is given during a respiratory infection (RR 1.13, 0.83 to 1.53). PROPOSED SPLIT — LIKELY (benefit) in healthy daycare children / MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) in otitis-prone children; Tier C: the evidence is concentrated in a small number of trials from largely one research group, using dosing regimens of 8.4–10 g a day in divided doses. Tympanostomy tubes for established recurrent otitis media are homed at shelf #629.
stamp: SPLIT — LIKELY (benefit) in healthy children attending daycare / MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) in otitis-prone children and during respiratory infections, where trials show no effect

title: Omega-3 supplements in ADHD: a small symptom effect in pooled trials (g ≈ 0.38) that the Cochrane review could not find in parent or teacher ratings
question: In children with ADHD, do omega-3 fatty acid supplements improve core symptoms?
balance: The meta-analyses disagree in a way that tracks their methods. Bloch MH et al. (PMID: 21961774), pooling 10 placebo-controlled trials (699 children), found a small but significant effect on ADHD symptoms, with efficacy correlated with the EPA dose in the supplement. Chang JP et al. (PMID: 28741625) found the same direction with a number attached: symptom scores improved by g = 0.38 across 7 trials (534 youths), with attention-related cognitive measures improving more (g = 1.09) in only 3 small trials. The Cochrane review (Gillies D et al., PMID: 22786509), analysing parent and teacher ratings separately across 13 trials (1,011 participants), found no significant difference on any rated outcome — parent-rated symptoms SMD −0.17 (95% CI −0.38 to 0.03) — and concluded there is little evidence of benefit. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a small average improvement on pooled global scores, inconsistently found when outcomes are split by rater, and far smaller than the effect of stimulant medication. The trials' records name no specific product, brand or company — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — small average symptom improvement on pooled scores; individual rating-scale analyses are inconsistent

title: Oral vs IV rehydration for moderately dehydrated children: oral therapy rehydrates just as reliably, fails in about 1 child in 25, and gets children home sooner
question: In children with moderate dehydration from gastroenteritis, is oral rehydration as effective as intravenous fluids?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for successful rehydration — and the surrounding outcomes mostly favour the oral route. The one trial designed exactly on this question (Spandorfer PR et al., PMID: 15687435) randomised 73 moderately dehydrated children in an emergency department and found oral rehydration noninferior: half of each group was successfully rehydrated at 4 hours (difference −1.2%, 95% CI −24.0 to 21.6), treatment started about 21 minutes sooner by mouth, and fewer oral-therapy children were admitted (30.6% vs 48.7%). The two syntheses agree on the shape of the trade. Fonseca BK et al. (PMID: 15123483), pooling 16 trials and 1,545 children, found enteral therapy carried fewer major adverse events than IV (relative risk 0.36, 95% CI 0.14 to 0.89) and a hospital stay about 21 hours shorter, with an overall enteral failure rate of 4.0%. The Cochrane review (Hartling L et al., PMID: 16856044), 17 trials and 1,811 children, puts the failure excess precisely: 4 more failures per 100 children treated orally (risk difference 4%, 95% CI 1 to 7; one extra failure for every 25 treated), balanced against a stay 1.2 days shorter, more phlebitis with IV lines, more paralytic ileus with oral therapy, and no difference in the subgroup given modern low-osmolarity solution. Nasogastric infusion performs like IV too (Nager AL et al., PMID: 11927697). PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): oral rehydration is the equal of IV fluids for moderate dehydration, with a small, plannable failure rate rather than a hidden one.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — oral rehydration succeeds as often as IV fluids in moderate dehydration; about 4% of children started on oral therapy still need IV rescue

title: Gluten-free, casein-free diets in autism: the one positive trial had no placebo and parents who knew the diet — both double-blind tests found nothing
question: In children with autism spectrum disorder, does a gluten-free, casein-free diet improve behaviour or cognition?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the benefit claim rests on the weakest design in the set. The ScanBrit trial (Whiteley P et al., PMID: 20406576) randomised 72 Danish children and reported significant improvement on some ADOS, GARS and ADHD-IV sub-domains by 12 months — but it was single-blind with no placebo diet, analysed per protocol (26 diet vs 29 control children at 12 months), and its adaptive 'catch-up' design then moved the control group onto the diet, dissolving the comparison for the 24-month data. The two double-blind studies found nothing: Hyman SL et al. (PMID: 26343026) kept 14 children on the diet and challenged them blind with gluten, casein, both, or placebo snacks — no significant effect on behaviour problems or autism symptoms; Elder JH et al. (PMID: 16555138), in a double-blind crossover of 15 children, likewise found no statistically significant effect, even though several parents reported improvement. The Cochrane review (Millward C et al., PMID: 18425890) had only two small trials (n = 35) to work with and concluded the evidence for efficacy is poor. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): where the raters cannot know the diet, the effect disappears; where they can, it appears — the signature of expectation, not of gluten or casein.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — benefit unproven; the positive signal comes from a single-blind trial without a placebo, and the double-blind studies found no effect

title: Treating pain stepwise in nursing-home dementia: agitation fell by about a sixth in the one large cluster trial — untreated pain, not the dementia itself, was driving part of the behaviour
question: In nursing-home residents with dementia, does structured stepwise pain treatment reduce agitation?
balance: LIKELY (benefit). The anchor trial (Husebo BS et al., PMID: 21765198) cluster-randomised 60 nursing-home units and 352 residents with moderate-to-severe dementia and significant behavioural disturbance: eight weeks of an individual stepwise pain protocol — paracetamol first, then morphine, transdermal buprenorphine, or pregabalin — reduced agitation by 17% against usual care (treatment effect −7.0 points on the Cohen-Mansfield agitation inventory, 95% CI −10.3 to −3.7), with parallel gains in overall neuropsychiatric symptoms (−9.0) and measured pain (−1.3), and no difference in daily function or cognition. The second trial of a stepwise approach, STA OP! (Pieper MJ et al., PMID: 26804064), trained staff in a broader stepwise multidisciplinary method in 288 residents with advanced dementia and also reduced agitation (mean difference −4.07 points, 95% CI −7.90 to −0.24) and neuropsychiatric symptoms, with antidepressant use falling (odds ratio 0.32) — though its intervention reached well beyond analgesia and its control arm also received training, which dilutes the contrast. A related multicomponent programme that includes pain assessment and treatment among several components is homed at shelf #2001 (COSMOS); this shelf is the pain-protocol question specifically. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): before reaching for an antipsychotic in a resident who cannot report pain, a structured trial of analgesia is one of the few interventions with randomised evidence behind it.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — a systematic stepwise pain protocol reduced agitation in moderate-to-severe dementia, in one large cluster-randomised trial with a smaller stepwise trial pointing the same way

title: Stopping a long-term PPI: symptoms do return for some — on-demand use left more people with uncontrolled symptoms — but the pill burden falls by about four tablets a week and no serious harm from stopping has been shown
question: In long-term PPI users without an ongoing indication, does deprescribing cause unacceptable symptom relapse?
balance: SPLIT — deprescribing trades a real, modest symptom cost for a real reduction in drug burden, and the feared catastrophe is not in the data. The Cochrane review of deprescribing versus continuation (Boghossian TA et al., PMID: 28301676) pooled six trials and 1,758 chronic users: switching to on-demand use increased 'lack of symptom control' (risk ratio 1.71, 95% CI 1.31 to 2.21, low-quality evidence) and lowered satisfaction, but cut consumption by about 3.8 tablets a week (moderate-quality evidence), and the review found insufficient data to conclude anything about long-term benefits or harms of stopping — no serious harm signal appeared. The mechanism behind early relapse is rebound acid hypersecretion, demonstrated in volunteers and homed with the PPI harms evidence at shelf #325 (Reimer 2009): after eight weeks of therapy, 44% of healthy volunteers reported clinically relevant acid symptoms in the month after withdrawal versus 15% on placebo — real symptoms, but in people who never needed the drug, and time-limited. In the population this question is actually about — users whose indication does not survive scrutiny — a patient-centred deprescribing process judged 44% of verified indications potentially inappropriate, and every patient who attempted withdrawal in that small feasibility study ceased or reduced the drug (Reeve E et al., PMID: 25385826). PROPOSED SPLIT — POSSIBLE (harm) on symptoms, POSSIBLE (benefit) on burden; 'unacceptable' relapse is not what the trials show, but a symptom-free stop is not what they promise either. The harms of continuing PPIs are weighed at shelf #325.
stamp: SPLIT — POSSIBLE (harm: replacing daily therapy with on-demand use increased lack of symptom control, RR 1.71) / POSSIBLE (benefit: about 4 fewer tablets a week, and no demonstrated serious harm from deprescribing)

title: Cutting anticholinergic burden to protect the brain: three small trials and very low certainty — in the largest analysis the burden did not even fall, so cognition had nothing to respond to
question: In older adults, does reducing anticholinergic burden improve cognition?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — an important distinction runs through this shelf: the observational association between anticholinergic burden and dementia is not the question here. The question is whether intervening to reduce the burden improves cognition, and on that the randomised record is three trials and 299 people. The Cochrane review (Taylor-Rowan M et al., PMID: 38063254) found very low certainty evidence throughout: one trial improved Digit Symbol Substitution performance (treatment difference 0.70, 95% CI 0.11 to 1.30) without reducing burden at all; of the two trials that did reduce burden, one found no cognitive difference on any CERAD measure or the MMSE, and the other reported a correlation with one working-memory test amid multiple null measures. No trial reported safety outcomes, and none measured mortality, falls, function, or quality of life with any difference. The largest single analysis since (Nishtala PS et al., PMID: 37339754), a post hoc look at a New Zealand pharmacist deprescribing trial, shows the practical problem underneath: the intervention did not reduce anticholinergic burden overall (standardised effect −0.04, 95% CI −0.26 to 0.19) — a cognition benefit cannot appear if the exposure does not move. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): reducing burden remains sensible prescribing hygiene for other reasons, but improved cognition is a hope the trials have not yet earned. The Beers-list evidence base is re-graded at shelf #137.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the randomised evidence is insufficient to conclude that reducing anticholinergic burden improves cognition

title: Fludrocortisone vs midodrine in neurogenic orthostatic hypotension: never compared for benefit in any trial — and on the one head-to-head safety study, fludrocortisone users were hospitalised more
question: In neurogenic orthostatic hypotension, does fludrocortisone help as much as midodrine?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — because the honest headline is an absence: no trial has ever randomised fludrocortisone against midodrine for efficacy in neurogenic orthostatic hypotension, and the one attempt to build that trial (Mossop H et al., PMID: 41217271, the CONFORM-OH pilot) recruited 13 patients in ten months and was judged not feasible in its current design. What direct comparative evidence exists is about safety, and it favours midodrine: in a Tennessee Medicaid cohort of 1,324 fludrocortisone initiators and 797 midodrine initiators (Grijalva CG et al., PMID: 29025750), all-cause hospitalisation rates were higher with fludrocortisone (adjusted incidence rate ratio 1.20, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.40), the gap widened in patients with prior heart failure (1.42, 1.07 to 1.90), and heart-failure hospitalisations specifically did not differ significantly (1.33, 0.79 to 2.56) — despite midodrine users carrying more cardiovascular disease at baseline. Uncontrolled before-and-after ambulatory monitoring series (de Lange FJ et al., PMID: 39718670) report both drugs raise 24-hour pressures and reduce systolic drops, fludrocortisone perhaps more so, but with no control group and a mostly syncope population that is hypothesis, not comparison. Each drug's placebo-controlled evidence is homed separately — midodrine at shelf #2498, droxidopa at shelves #931 and #1558, pyridostigmine at shelf #2691 — and fludrocortisone's own randomised data are in vasovagal syncope (shelf #2615), not neurogenic hypotension. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): 'helps as much' is unknown for benefit and doubtful on hospitalisations; the choice between them today rests on mechanism, comorbidity (especially heart failure), and habit, not on comparative trials.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — comparative efficacy is unknown (no trial has ever randomised the two against each other); the only direct comparison, a safety cohort, favours midodrine

title: Tube feeding in advanced dementia: no survival benefit in any controlled study ever done, comfort never measured at all — and pressure ulcers were more likely, not less, after tube placement
question: In advanced dementia, does tube feeding prolong survival or improve comfort versus careful hand feeding?
balance: LIKELY (no difference) for survival — the rare case where a null result is consistent across every controlled comparison that exists, while the intervention is used on a third of the relevant population. The Cochrane review (Sampson EL et al., PMID: 19370678) found no randomised trials at all and seven observational controlled studies: no evidence of increased survival with enteral tube feeding, no evidence of benefit for nutritional status or pressure ulcers, and not one study that measured quality of life or comfort — the outcome families are usually told the tube will serve. The largest direct test of the pressure-ulcer rationale (Teno JM et al., PMID: 22782196), a propensity-matched national cohort, found the opposite of the intention: residents who received a PEG tube were more than twice as likely to develop a new stage 2+ pressure ulcer (odds ratio 2.27, 95% CI 1.95 to 2.65), and existing ulcers were less likely to heal (odds ratio 0.70, 95% CI 0.55 to 0.89). Survival data point the same way: in a matched Medicare cohort (Hwang D et al., PMID: 24112820), 180-day mortality was 51.9% with a tube versus 49.8% without (P = 0.11), while the tube group cost $2,224 more in hospital care over the following year and spent more days in intensive care. PROPOSED LIKELY (no difference) — no study has ever shown tube feeding prolongs life or improves comfort in advanced dementia; careful hand feeding remains the default the evidence supports, and the burden of proof sits on the tube. Because no randomised trial exists or is now likely to be done, this verdict rests on observational evidence and is marked Tier C.
stamp: LIKELY (no difference) — tube feeding has never been shown to prolong survival in advanced dementia; on pressure ulcers the observational signal is harm, and comfort has never been measured

title: Cold vs hot snare for small colorectal polyps: complete resection 98.2% vs 97.4% in CRESCENT, and the bleeding that needed treatment happened only with the hot snare
question: In adults with small (4–9 mm) colorectal polyps, does cold snare polypectomy achieve complete resection as often as hot snare polypectomy, with fewer adverse events?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for 4–9 mm adenomatous polyps the randomised record says cold snare removes the polyp completely about as often as hot snare, without the cautery-related bleeding seen in the hot arm. In CRESCENT (Kawamura T et al., PMID: 28970290) complete resection was 98.2% with cold snare versus 97.4% with hot snare (difference +0.8%, 90% CI −1.0 to 2.7; non-inferiority p<0.0001), and post-operative bleeding requiring endoscopic haemostasis occurred only with hot snare (0.5%, 2 of 402 polyps). A later meta-analysis of 19 trials (Cavassola PRP et al., PMID: 38511795) found a small edge in complete resection for hot snare (risk difference 0.02) offset by more delayed bleeding and longer procedure times with hot snare. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): cold snare is a reasonable standard technique for these small polyps — completeness is essentially preserved and the cautery harm is avoided.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — cold snare achieves complete resection about as often as hot snare for 4–9 mm polyps, with less cautery bleeding

title: Underwater EMR for 10–20 mm sessile polyps: R0 resection 69% vs 50% and en bloc 89% vs 75% against conventional EMR, with no extra time or harm
question: In adults with intermediate-to-large sessile colorectal polyps, does underwater endoscopic mucosal resection achieve en-bloc and complete resection more often than conventional EMR?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — underwater EMR removed intermediate-size sessile polyps in one piece with clear margins more often than conventional EMR, at no cost in time or safety. In the anchor RCT (Yamashina T et al., PMID: 30981791) R0 resection was 69% underwater versus 50% conventional (p=0.011) and en bloc resection 89% versus 75% (p=0.007), with adverse events 2.8% versus 2.0% and median procedure times 165 versus 175 seconds. A 2024 meta-analysis of nine studies (Wang X et al., PMID: 38451998) points the same way for en bloc, R0 and complete resection, with fewer recurrences after underwater resection. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the technique advantage is consistent, but it rests on one randomised trial plus pooled mostly non-randomised comparisons, and recurrence — not margin status — is the outcome patients ultimately care about.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — underwater EMR achieves en bloc and R0 resection more often than conventional EMR for 10–20 mm sessile polyps

title: Water-exchange colonoscopy: adenoma detection relative risk 1.28, pain about 2 points lower and less sedation requested — for about 90 seconds more insertion time
question: In adults undergoing colonoscopy, does water-exchange insertion improve adenoma detection and reduce insertion pain versus standard air insufflation?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — across 13 randomised trials and 7,056 patients, water-exchange colonoscopy found more adenomas and polyps, hurt less, and needed less sedation and fewer helping manoeuvres than air insufflation; its only cost was about a minute and a half more to reach the caecum. In the meta-analysis (Liu Y et al., PMID: 30226480) the adenoma detection rate was higher with water exchange (relative risk 1.28, 95% CI 1.18–1.38 — a relative measure; the record does not print the pooled absolute rates beside it) and the polyp detection rate likewise (relative risk 1.30, 95% CI 1.21–1.39), maximum pain was lower (weighted mean difference −1.99) and on-demand sedation was requested less often (relative risk 0.58, 95% CI 0.44–0.77). Caecal intubation success was the same (relative risk 1.01). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): this is a technique change with consistent randomised support on detection and comfort alike.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — water exchange raises adenoma and polyp detection and reduces pain and sedation versus air insufflation

title: CO2 instead of air at colonoscopy: pain 2.6 vs 3.4 during the procedure and still lower six hours later, less bloating — and identical detection, time and completion
question: In adults undergoing colonoscopy, does carbon dioxide insufflation reduce post-procedure pain and bloating versus room-air insufflation, without compromising performance indicators?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — carbon dioxide is absorbed from the bowel far faster than room air, and the pooled trial record shows the comfort benefit that physiology predicts, without any loss of colonoscopy quality. In the meta-analysis of 23 studies and 3,217 patients (Rogers AC et al., PMID: 31900583), pain scores were lower with CO2 during the procedure (visual analogue scale 2.6 vs 3.4 with air; mean difference −0.7) and remained lower at 30 minutes, 1–2 hours and 6 hours after it, with less distension, bloating and flatulence — while sedation required, procedure time, caecal intubation and polyp detection did not differ. The benefit is real but modest in size: fractions of a point on a pain scale, not a transformation. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a low-risk comfort improvement with no performance penalty, limited mainly by the small absolute size of the pain difference.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — CO2 insufflation reduces post-colonoscopy pain and bloating versus room air, without compromising performance indicators

title: Acotiamide for functional dyspepsia: global response 52.2% vs 34.8% — but the pooled benefit is all postprandial distress (RR 1.29), with epigastric pain at 0.92
question: In adults with functional dyspepsia, does acotiamide improve meal-related postprandial-distress symptoms versus placebo?
balance: SPLIT — the benefit is confined to meal-related, postprandial-distress symptoms. In the phase III trial (Matsueda K et al., PMID: 22157329), 52.2% on acotiamide 100 mg three times daily were global responders versus 34.8% on placebo (p<0.001; number needed to treat 6), but complete elimination of all three meal-related symptoms was uncommon on either arm — 15.3% versus 9.0% (p=0.004; NNT 16). The earlier meta-analysis (Xiao G et al., PMID: 25197703) found overall improvement (relative risk 1.29, 95% CI 1.19–1.40 — a relative measure) driven by postprandial distress syndrome (relative risk 1.29, 95% CI 1.09–1.53), with no benefit in epigastric pain syndrome (relative risk 0.92, 95% CI 0.76–1.11). PROPOSED SPLIT: worth considering where it is licensed for fullness, bloating and early satiation after meals; the record gives no reason to expect it to help epigastric pain or burning.
stamp: SPLIT — acotiamide improves meal-related postprandial-distress symptoms, with no shown benefit for epigastric pain syndrome

title: Diet in eosinophilic oesophagitis: remission 90.8% elemental, 72.1% six-food elimination — and only 45.5% for the allergy-test-directed diets families expect to work best
question: In children and adults with eosinophilic oesophagitis, do food-elimination diets induce histologic remission, and how do empiric elimination diets compare with allergy-test-directed diets?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — dietary therapy does induce histologic remission in eosinophilic oesophagitis, and the more the diet removes, the higher the remission rate — at a steep cost in burden. In the systematic review and meta-analysis (Arias A et al., PMID: 24534634), covering 33 studies and 1,317 patients, elemental (amino-acid formula) diets achieved remission in 90.8% of cases, six-food elimination in 72.1%, and allergy-test-directed elimination in only 45.5% — test-directed diets, the intuitively attractive option, performed worst. Children and adults responded similarly (63.3% vs 67.2% overall). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): empiric elimination — six-food, or elemental where feasible — is a genuine drug-free route to remission; test-directed elimination is not supported by its own numbers, and every diet here demands dietitian support and repeat endoscopy to prove it worked.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — empiric food-elimination diets induce histologic remission in eosinophilic oesophagitis, with elemental and six-food diets ahead of allergy-test-directed diets

title: Gastric electrical stimulation: vomiting scores better ON than OFF in the big crossover trial — yet no quality-of-life or emptying gain, and the earlier controlled pool was null
question: In adults with refractory gastroparesis vomiting despite dietary and drug therapy, does gastric electrical stimulation reduce vomiting frequency versus sham stimulation?
balance: SPLIT — gastric electrical stimulation reduced vomiting in the largest blinded trial, but it did not improve quality of life or speed gastric emptying, and the earlier controlled literature pooled to no symptom benefit at all. In the multicentre crossover RCT (Ducrotte P et al., PMID: 31647902), vomiting scores were better with the device ON than OFF (median 2 vs 1 on a 0–4 scale, p<0.001) in patients with and without diabetes and with delayed or normal emptying — yet quality of life did not increase and emptying was not accelerated. The earlier systematic review (Levinthal DJ et al., PMID: 27085627) found total symptom scores did not differ between ON and OFF periods across five controlled studies (difference 0.17, 95% CI −0.06 to 0.4), while open-label studies showed large apparent benefits the authors attribute substantially to regression to the mean. PROPOSED SPLIT: a vomiting-frequency benefit in the best single trial, against null pooled symptom, quality-of-life and emptying outcomes — an implanted device with surgical risk earns a cautious, outcome-specific reading.
stamp: SPLIT — gastric electrical stimulation reduced vomiting in one large crossover trial, but pooled controlled data show no overall symptom benefit and quality of life and gastric emptying did not improve

title: Prucalopride in gastroparesis: symptom index 1.65 vs 2.28 and emptying half-time 98 vs 143 minutes — one coherent but small 34-patient crossover trial
question: In adults with gastroparesis, does prucalopride accelerate gastric emptying and improve gastroparesis symptom scores versus placebo?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — one small crossover trial found prucalopride improved gastroparesis symptoms, quality of life and gastric emptying all at once, which is exactly the pattern a prokinetic should produce — but it is 34 patients, four weeks per period, and three patients dropped out with adverse events on the drug. In that trial (Carbone F et al., PMID: 31295161) the total Gastroparesis Cardinal Symptom Index was 1.65 on prucalopride 2 mg daily versus 2.28 on placebo (p<0.0001), and gastric half-emptying time was 98 minutes versus 143 on placebo (p=0.005). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): a promising, coherent single-trial result that needs a larger parallel-group trial before it can carry more weight — and a reminder that prucalopride's gastroparesis use sits outside its constipation licence in most places.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — one small crossover trial showed prucalopride improved gastroparesis symptoms, quality of life and gastric emptying versus placebo

title: Elobixibat for chronic constipation: 6.4 vs 1.7 spontaneous bowel movements in week 1 — a large effect on two weeks of controlled evidence, with a year of open-label safety behind it
question: In adults with chronic constipation, does the ileal bile-acid transporter inhibitor elobixibat increase spontaneous bowel movements versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — elobixibat produced a large short-term increase in spontaneous bowel movements in its phase 3 placebo-controlled trial, with mostly mild gut side effects, and a year of open-label treatment did not surface a new safety problem. In the 2-week randomised trial (Nakajima A et al., PMID: 29805116), spontaneous bowel movements in week 1 were 6.4 per week on elobixibat 10 mg daily versus 1.7 on placebo (p<0.0001). In the 52-week open-label study of 341 patients, 48% had an adverse drug reaction, most commonly mild abdominal pain (24%) and diarrhoea (15%). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the short-term efficacy signal is strong, but the controlled evidence is two weeks long, from one country, and the long-term data have no comparator — durability and comparative place among constipation drugs remain open.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — elobixibat increased spontaneous bowel movements versus placebo in a phase 3 trial, with mostly mild gastrointestinal side effects

title: Ondansetron for IBS-D: stools firmer by 0.9 points, urgency and frequency down, relief relative risk 4.7 — with pain unchanged and constipation the class price
question: In adults with diarrhoea-predominant irritable bowel syndrome, does ondansetron improve stool consistency and global symptoms versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — ondansetron, borrowed from antiemetic practice, firmed stools and cut urgency and frequency in a crossover trial in IBS-D, without improving pain — a pattern that fits its gut-slowing pharmacology. In that trial (Garsed K et al., PMID: 24334242), stool form improved versus placebo (mean difference −0.9, 95% CI −1.1 to −0.6), symptom severity fell further (83 vs 37 points), and 65% reported adequate relief on ondansetron but not placebo versus 14% the other way round (relative risk 4.7, 95% CI 2.6–8.5 — a relative measure). The class meta-analysis (Zheng Y et al., PMID: 28291778) supports 5-HT3 antagonists in IBS-D while flagging their price: constipation (pooled relative risk 3.71). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a useful off-label option for the stool-and-urgency burden of IBS-D, prescribed knowing pain is not its target and constipation is its trade-off.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — ondansetron improves stool consistency, urgency and frequency in IBS-D versus placebo, without improving pain

title: Colesevelam in bile-acid diarrhoea: every biomarker moved (p<0.001) and no blinded symptom did — mechanism proven, clinical benefit still waiting on a larger trial
question: In adults with bile-acid diarrhoea (including diarrhoea-predominant IBS with bile-acid malabsorption), does colesevelam improve stool consistency and bowel symptoms versus placebo?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the biology moves exactly as predicted and the symptoms, in the one placebo-controlled trial, do not. In that trial (Vijayvargiya P et al., PMID: 32088296), colesevelam significantly changed sequestered faecal bile-acid excretion and the synthesis markers C4 and FGF19 (all p<0.001) in 30 patients with bile-acid diarrhoea in IBS-D — yet stool frequency and consistency, colonic transit and permeability did not differ significantly from placebo. An earlier open-label study (Camilleri M et al., PMID: 25594801) did see firmer stools on colesevelam, and a meta-analysis of bile-acid sequestrants as a class (Soares GAR et al., PMID: 39428959) found more diarrhoea cessation (relative risk 3.27) across seven small trials. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): mechanism proven, clinical benefit unproven in the only blinded test of this drug — larger trials are needed, as that trial's own authors conclude.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — colesevelam changes bile-acid biomarkers as predicted, but the one placebo-controlled trial showed no significant improvement in stool frequency or consistency

title: CDED plus partial formula in children's Crohn's: tolerated by 97.5% vs 73.6% for all-formula feeding, and week-12 remission 75.6% vs 45.1%
question: In children with Crohn's disease, does the Crohn's disease exclusion diet plus partial enteral nutrition induce and sustain remission more often than exclusive enteral nutrition?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the Crohn's disease exclusion diet plus partial enteral nutrition was far better tolerated than exclusive enteral nutrition and, by week 12, kept significantly more children in corticosteroid-free remission. In the randomised trial (Levine A et al., PMID: 31170412), tolerance was 97.5% with CDED plus partial enteral nutrition versus 73.6% with exclusive enteral nutrition (p=0.002), week-6 remission was similar (75% vs 59%, p=0.38), and week-12 sustained corticosteroid-free remission favoured the exclusion diet (75.6% vs 45.1%, p=0.01; odds ratio 3.77). A 2024 network meta-analysis (Ma J et al., PMID: 39686992) ranked partial enteral nutrition plus CDED first among dietary strategies for both remission and tolerance. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): for a child with mild-to-moderate Crohn's, this is a real-food alternative to the all-formula diet with a randomised trial behind it — delivered, as in the trial, with formula providing half then a quarter of calories and dietitian supervision.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — Crohn's disease exclusion diet plus partial enteral nutrition induces and sustains remission in children at least as well as exclusive enteral nutrition, with better tolerance

title: FMT for ulcerative colitis: remission 24% vs 5% in the first placebo-controlled trial and a pooled odds ratio of 2.65 across 15 trials — with one donor behind most early remissions
question: In adults with active ulcerative colitis, does faecal microbiota transplantation induce clinical remission versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — faecal microbiota transplantation induced remission in active ulcerative colitis more often than placebo in its first rigorous trial, and the pooled randomised record since has kept the same direction. In that trial (Moayyedi P et al., PMID: 25857665), remission at week 7 was 24% with weekly donor-stool enemas versus 5% with water-enema placebo (risk difference 17%, 95% CI 2%–33%), with no difference in adverse events — though the trial was stopped early for futility at an interim look, and seven of the nine remitters had received stool from a single donor. A later meta-analysis of 15 randomised trials (Doukas PG et al., PMID: 41078065) found clinical remission in 62% on FMT versus 50.5% in controls (odds ratio 2.65, 95% CI 1.76–4.00) and endoscopic response in 42% versus 22% (odds ratio 2.00). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a real effect, of uncertain size, whose donor-dependence and delivery variability keep it a trial-and-specialist treatment rather than a standard one.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — faecal microbiota transplantation induces clinical remission in active ulcerative colitis more often than placebo, with donor-dependent effects

title: Probiotic maintenance in chronic pouchitis: relapse 15% on the tested VSL#3 preparation vs 100% on placebo — a dramatic result from one small trial of one specific product
question: In adults with chronic pouchitis after ileal pouch–anal anastomosis for ulcerative colitis, does oral multi-strain probiotic bacteriotherapy maintain remission versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in the only dedicated maintenance trial, the multi-strain probiotic preparation tested kept chronic pouchitis in remission in 85% of patients over nine months, while every patient on placebo relapsed. In that trial (Gionchetti P et al., PMID: 10930365), relapse was 15% (3 patients) on the preparation versus 100% (20 patients) on placebo (p<0.001). The Cochrane review of pouchitis treatment (Holubar SD et al., PMID: 20556748) reached the same conclusion for this preparation in maintaining remission of chronic pouchitis. Two cautions define the stamp: the trial is 40 patients from the year 2000, and the publication names the tested product as VSL#3 but gives no company name in the record — probiotic products sold under similar descriptions today are not necessarily the formulation tested, and current products may differ in safety and effectiveness. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a striking result for the specific tested preparation, in a single small trial, that should not be read across to probiotics generally.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the tested multi-strain probiotic preparation (VSL#3) maintained remission of chronic pouchitis versus placebo in a small double-blind trial

title: Curcumin added to mesalamine in UC: remission 53.8% vs 0% in a 50-patient trial and pooled relative risk 2.33 — big numbers on a small, heterogeneous base, with no named tested product
question: In adults with mild-to-moderate ulcerative colitis on mesalamine, does adding curcumin induce clinical remission versus placebo?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — one small trial produced remission numbers too large to take at face value, and the pooled literature since is positive but highly heterogeneous. In the anchor trial (Lang A et al., PMID: 25724700), clinical remission at 4 weeks was 53.8% with curcumin 3 g/day added to mesalamine versus 0% with placebo added (p=0.01; odds ratio 42, 95% CI 2.3–760 — an interval that itself announces how few patients drive the result). The updated meta-analysis (Peng Z et al., PMID: 39612780) pooled eight trials and 482 patients: clinical remission favoured adjunctive curcumin (relative risk 2.33, 95% CI 1.25–4.34 — a relative measure) with substantial heterogeneity (I²=80%), and endoscopic remission was not significant. The trial record names no brand or company for the curcumin capsules used — it says only curcumin capsules, 3 g/day — so no current product can be identified as the tested one, and current products may differ in safety and effectiveness. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): an inexpensive, apparently safe adjunct with a promising but fragile record, awaiting a large trial.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — adding curcumin to mesalamine showed high remission rates in one small trial and a positive but heterogeneous pooled record; no tested brand or company is named in the record
