title: Terlipressin versus noradrenaline in hepatorenal AKI: a clear terlipressin win in the one ACLF trial, a statistical dead heat in the pooled trials — which population is yours?
question: In patients with acute-on-chronic liver failure and hepatorenal-type acute kidney injury, is noradrenaline (norepinephrine) as effective as terlipressin for AKI reversal and survival?
balance: SPLIT — the answer depends on which population you mean, and the two records on this shelf genuinely disagree in emphasis. In the population the question names — acute-on-chronic liver failure with hepatorenal-type AKI — the one head-to-head randomised trial (Arora V et al., PMID: 30076614; 120 patients, open-label) found terlipressin clearly ahead: response by day 7 in 41.7% versus 20% on noradrenaline, HRS reversal 40% versus 16.7%, less renal replacement therapy (56.6% versus 80%), and better 28-day survival (48.3% versus 20%); noradrenaline carried a mortality hazard ratio of 2.08 (95% CI 1.32 to 3.30) against terlipressin. But the pooled record across the broader hepatorenal syndrome–AKI population (Olson JC et al., PMID: 38285703; 7 trials, 376 patients) shows only a non-significant numerical edge for terlipressin on reversal (OR 1.33, 95% CI 0.80 to 2.22) and short-term survival (OR 1.50, 95% CI 0.64 to 3.53), with more drug-limiting adverse events on terlipressin in the ACLF trial (23.3% versus 8.3%). PROPOSED SPLIT: in ACLF the single trial says terlipressin is superior and noradrenaline is not 'as effective'; across HRS-AKI generally the pooled trials cannot separate the two. Terlipressin against albumin alone is a different question, at shelf #1060.
stamp: SPLIT — in acute-on-chronic liver failure the one head-to-head trial found terlipressin superior (reversal 40% vs 16.7%; 28-day survival 48.3% vs 20%), while pooled HRS-AKI trials show no significant difference between the two vasopressors

title: Covered-stent TIPS for recurrent ascites: 93% versus 52% alive without transplant at one year — one small trial carrying a big claim, with the bare-stent era's encephalopathy warning behind it
question: In patients with cirrhosis and refractory ascites, does covered-stent TIPS improve transplant-free survival versus repeated large-volume paracentesis with albumin?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the modern covered-stent trial is small but its primary outcome is hard and the gap is wide. Bureau C et al. (PMID: 27663604) randomised 62 patients with cirrhosis and recurrent ascites (at least two large-volume paracenteses within three weeks) to polytetrafluoroethylene-covered TIPS or continued large-volume paracentesis with albumin: one-year transplant-free survival was 93% with TIPS versus 52% with paracentesis, hospital days were halved (17 versus 35), and portal-hypertension bleeding and hernia complications occurred only in the paracentesis group (18% each versus 0%) — while the one-year probability of remaining free of encephalopathy was identical at 65% in both groups. The older Cochrane synthesis (Saab S et al., PMID: 17054221; 5 trials, 330 patients, largely uncovered-stent era) found no mortality difference (24-month OR 1.29, 95% CI 0.65 to 2.56) and significantly more encephalopathy with TIPS (OR 2.24, 95% CI 1.39 to 3.6), though ascites control was far better. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): covered-stent TIPS probably improves transplant-free survival in recurrent ascites, but the survival claim rests on one 62-patient trial and the bare-stent literature warns that encephalopathy is the price when stents fail or patients are poorly selected. Early TIPS for variceal bleeding is a different question, at shelf #591.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — covered-stent TIPS improved one-year transplant-free survival versus repeated paracentesis with albumin (93% vs 52%) in the one randomised trial, against an older bare-stent literature showing better ascites control but no survival gain and more encephalopathy

title: L-ornithine L-aspartate for hepatic encephalopathy: consistently favourable small trials, a doubled relative chance of reversing minimal HE — and quality caveats that cap the claim
question: In patients with cirrhosis and hepatic encephalopathy, does L-ornithine L-aspartate improve encephalopathy grade and recovery versus placebo or standard care?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the direction of the randomised record is consistently favourable, but its foundations are soft. The appraisal by Butterworth RF et al. (PMID: 30706425) reports that meta-analyses of randomised trials over two decades generally find benefit for L-ornithine L-aspartate across presentations — better mental-state grade in overt encephalopathy, better psychometric performance in minimal encephalopathy (oral formulation particularly), and lower fasting blood ammonia in every trial that measured it — while noting that one meta-analysis raised study-quality concerns; network meta-analyses place LOLA comparable or superior to non-absorbable disaccharides and probiotics. The one pooled analysis with hard numbers on this shelf (He Q et al., PMID: 38403493; 6 trials, 292 patients, minimal encephalopathy) found LOLA more than doubled the relative chance of reversing minimal encephalopathy (RR 2.264, 95% CI 1.528 to 3.352) and reduced progression to overt encephalopathy (RR 0.220, 95% CI 0.076 to 0.637), with no mortality or ammonia difference in that subset. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): LOLA probably improves encephalopathy measures and minimal-HE reversal, but small trials, quality concerns, and no demonstrated mortality effect keep it short of LIKELY. The established HE shelves — rifaximin #595, PEG versus lactulose #1676, lactulose for minimal HE #2126 — ask different questions.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — LOLA improves encephalopathy grade and reverses minimal hepatic encephalopathy in pooled randomised trials (reversal RR 2.264), with no demonstrated mortality benefit and study-quality concerns in the underlying trials

title: High-dose ursodeoxycholic acid in PSC: the liver tests improved, the patients did worse — endpoints 39% versus 26%, serious adverse events 63% versus 37%
question: In adults with primary sclerosing cholangitis, does high-dose ursodeoxycholic acid improve liver biochemistry, histology or survival — or cause harm — versus placebo?
balance: LIKELY (harm) — this is the shelf where better blood tests hid a worse outcome. Lindor KD et al. (PMID: 19585548) randomised 150 adults with primary sclerosing cholangitis to high-dose ursodeoxycholic acid (28–30 mg/kg/day) or placebo for up to six years: liver enzymes fell significantly more on UDCA, yet 39% of the UDCA group reached a clinical endpoint (cirrhosis, varices, cholangiocarcinoma, transplantation or death) versus 26% on placebo, the adjusted risk of a primary endpoint was 2.3 times higher on UDCA (P < 0.01), the risk of death, transplantation or minimal listing criteria was 2.1 times higher (P = 0.038), and serious adverse events were far commoner (63% versus 37%; P < 0.01); the trial was stopped for futility. The wider meta-analysis (Othman MO et al., PMID: 23122450; 7 trials, 553 patients) found UDCA at any dose did not reduce mortality (RR 1.04, 95% CI 0.46 to 2.35) or transplantation (RR 1.22, 95% CI 0.7 to 2.12) despite improving liver tests, and noted the increased mortality signal came from the high-dose trial. PROPOSED LIKELY (harm): high-dose UDCA in PSC improves biochemistry while increasing serious adverse events and clinical endpoints — it should not be used at these doses, and no dose of UDCA has shown a survival benefit in PSC. Cilofexor for PSC is a different drug and question, at shelf #2129.
stamp: LIKELY (harm) — high-dose ursodeoxycholic acid in primary sclerosing cholangitis improved liver biochemistry but increased clinical endpoints (adjusted risk 2.3×) and serious adverse events (63% vs 37%) in the one long-term trial, and no UDCA dose has shown a survival benefit

title: Nintedanib for progressive fibrosing lung disease beyond IPF: decline slowed from 188 to 81 ml a year — a real surrogate win, bought with diarrhoea in two of three patients
question: In adults with progressive fibrosing interstitial lung diseases other than idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, does nintedanib slow the annual decline in forced vital capacity versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — INBUILD is a well-run phase 3 trial with a clear result on its chosen outcome, and the outcome is a surrogate. Flaherty KR et al. (PMID: 31566307) randomised 663 patients with progressive fibrosing interstitial lung diseases other than IPF — fibrosing disease over more than 10% of lung volume, progression within 24 months despite treatment — to nintedanib 150 mg twice daily or placebo: over 52 weeks the adjusted annual FVC decline was −80.8 ml/year on nintedanib versus −187.8 ml/year on placebo, a difference of 107.0 ml/year (95% CI 65.4 to 148.5; P < 0.001), and in the UIP-like pattern subgroup the difference was 128.2 ml/year (95% CI 70.8 to 185.6). The cost is gastrointestinal: diarrhoea in 66.9% versus 23.9%, and more liver-function-test abnormalities. What the trial does not show is equally important: no mortality, exacerbation or quality-of-life benefit is reported in the record — the claim is slower loss of lung volume, extrapolated from the IPF experience where the same drug class earned its place on the same endpoint. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): nintedanib probably slows FVC decline across the progressive fibrosing phenotype, with diarrhoea in two of three patients as the standing price. Nintedanib in IPF itself is at shelf #810 and in systemic-sclerosis ILD at shelf #688; this shelf is the cross-diagnosis phenotype question.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — nintedanib slowed the annual FVC decline in progressive fibrosing ILD (difference 107.0 ml/year versus placebo) in one phase 3 trial, at the cost of diarrhoea in two-thirds of patients, with no mortality or quality-of-life outcome reported

title: Inhaled antibiotics for bronchiectasis: one RESPIRE trial positive, its twin negative, a pooled 19% relative cut in exacerbations — and resistance emerging at twice the rate
question: In adults with non-cystic-fibrosis bronchiectasis and frequent exacerbations, do inhaled antibiotics (ciprofloxacin dry-powder; inhaled colistin in chronic Pseudomonas infection) reduce exacerbations versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the pooled record says a small real effect; the individual phase 3 record says it is fragile. The largest meta-analysis (Laska IF et al., PMID: 31405826; 16 trials, 2,597 patients) found inhaled antibiotics reduced exacerbation frequency (rate ratio 0.81, 95% CI 0.67 to 0.97 — a 19% relative reduction), prolonged time to first exacerbation (HR 0.83, 95% CI 0.69 to 0.99), cut severe exacerbations (rate ratio 0.43, 95% CI 0.24 to 0.78), and increased bacterial eradication (OR 3.36, 95% CI 1.63 to 6.91), without improving quality of life beyond the minimal important difference and with emergent bacterial resistance nearly doubled (risk ratio 1.91, 95% CI 1.46 to 2.49). The two RESPIRE trials of ciprofloxacin dry powder show why the pooled effect is modest: RESPIRE 1 (PMID: 29371383) met its endpoints on the 14-day on/off regimen (HR 0.53 for time to first exacerbation; 39% relative reduction in exacerbation frequency, from 1.0 to 0.6 mean exacerbations) but not the 28-day regimen, while RESPIRE 2 (PMID: 29371384) missed both primary endpoints. The colistin trial (Haworth CS et al., PMID: 24625200) likewise missed its primary endpoint overall (median time to exacerbation 165 versus 111 days; P = 0.11), reaching significance only in adherent patients. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): inhaled antibiotics probably reduce exacerbations modestly in frequently exacerbating bronchiectasis, with resistance emergence as the standing long-term concern. Macrolides for bronchiectasis are at shelf #815 and brensocatib at #818.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — inhaled antibiotics modestly reduce exacerbation frequency in non-CF bronchiectasis (pooled rate ratio 0.81), but the two largest ciprofloxacin trials disagree, the colistin trial missed its primary endpoint, and emergent bacterial resistance nearly doubles

title: Dornase alfa in non-CF bronchiectasis: the CF mucolytic that backfired — more exacerbations and faster FEV1 decline than placebo in the only trial
question: In adults with non-cystic-fibrosis bronchiectasis, does aerosolised recombinant human DNase (dornase alfa) improve lung function or reduce exacerbations — or cause harm?
balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — a cautionary shelf about borrowing a drug across diseases. Dornase alfa is established therapy in cystic fibrosis, but the one randomised trial in non-CF bronchiectasis (O'Donnell AE et al., PMID: 9596315; 349 stable adult outpatients with idiopathic bronchiectasis, aerosolised recombinant human DNase I twice daily versus placebo for 24 weeks) found the treatment worse on both primary endpoints: pulmonary exacerbations were more frequent and FEV1 decline was greater in the rhDNase group than on placebo, leading the investigators to conclude the drug was 'ineffective and potentially harmful' in this population. The record reports the direction of both effects without publishing the magnitudes in its abstract, so this shelf can state the harm direction but not size it — a real limitation, though for a harm verdict the direction plus a stopped-in-practice intervention is what matters. No later trial has rehabilitated the drug in non-CF bronchiectasis. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm): aerosolised DNase should not be used for non-cystic-fibrosis bronchiectasis; its cystic fibrosis benefit does not transfer, and the one direct test pointed the other way.
stamp: POSSIBLE (harm) — aerosolised recombinant human DNase increased exacerbations and accelerated FEV1 decline versus placebo in the one trial in non-CF bronchiectasis; its cystic fibrosis benefit does not transfer

title: Inhaled mannitol for bronchiectasis: safe, plausible, and twice short of its primary endpoint — exacerbations not reduced, quality of life not clearly better
question: In adults with non-cystic-fibrosis bronchiectasis, does inhaled dry-powder mannitol improve quality of life and reduce exacerbations versus placebo?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — two trials of inhaled mannitol in non-CF bronchiectasis, and the endpoints that matter most did not move in either. In the 12-week phase 3 trial (Bilton D et al., PMID: 23429964; 343 patients), the primary quality-of-life endpoint was null — St George's Respiratory Questionnaire total score −3.4 points on mannitol versus −2.1 on placebo (P = 0.304) — and the significant sputum-weight difference (4.3 g; P = 0.002) was driven largely by a fall in the placebo group's sputum weight alongside its higher antibiotic use (45% versus 37%). In the 52-week trial (Bilton D et al., PMID: 25246664; 461 patients, against a low-dose mannitol control rather than true placebo), the exacerbation rate was not significantly reduced (rate ratio 0.92; P = 0.31), though time to first exacerbation lengthened (HR 0.78; P = 0.022) and SGRQ improved by −2.4 units (P = 0.046) — a difference below the instrument's usual clinically important threshold. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): mannitol is safe and may delay a first exacerbation, but neither trial showed it reduces exacerbation rates or delivers a clearly felt quality-of-life benefit. Airway clearance techniques for bronchiectasis are at shelf #2668.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — inhaled mannitol missed its primary endpoints in both bronchiectasis trials (exacerbation rate ratio 0.92, NS; quality of life null at 12 weeks), leaving only secondary signals and a good safety record

title: Breathing exercises for asthma: quality of life up a little, hyperventilation symptoms down — asthma control itself unmoved in 22 trials
question: In adults with asthma, do breathing exercises (including physiotherapist-led and Buteyko-style programmes) improve quality of life and asthma control versus usual care?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a real but narrow benefit, on how patients feel rather than on the disease measures clinicians usually chase. The Cochrane review (Santino TA et al., PMID: 32212422; 22 studies, 2,880 participants with mostly mild-to-moderate asthma) found breathing exercises improved quality of life at three months versus inactive control (Asthma Quality of Life Questionnaire mean difference 0.42, 95% CI 0.17 to 0.68; moderate-certainty evidence) and reduced hyperventilation symptoms at four to six months (Nijmegen Questionnaire mean difference −3.22, 95% CI −6.31 to −0.13; moderate certainty), with FEV1 percent predicted higher (mean difference 6.88%, 95% CI 5.03 to 8.73) but absolute FEV1 inconclusive. Against that: asthma control scores were inconclusive at three months and essentially null at six months (ACQ mean difference −0.08, 95% CI −0.22 to 0.07), the AQLQ gain of 0.42 sits just below the 0.5-point change usually taken as the smallest patients notice, and certainty across outcomes ranged from moderate to very low with poor methods reporting in many trials — fourteen of the 22 studies were yoga trials, so 'breathing exercises' here is a bundle of unlike interventions. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): breathing retraining probably improves quality of life and breathlessness-pattern symptoms modestly as an adjunct; it is not a treatment for asthma control and must never displace inhaled therapy.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — breathing exercises improve asthma quality-of-life scores modestly at three months (AQLQ +0.42, moderate-certainty) and hyperventilation symptoms, with no demonstrated effect on asthma control

title: Montelukast for exercise-induced bronchoconstriction: the post-exercise lung-function fall cut nearly in half for a full 12 weeks — in one launch-era trial of mild asthma
question: In patients with exercise-induced bronchoconstriction, does daily montelukast attenuate the fall in FEV1 after exercise versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one well-designed trial, a physiological endpoint, and a clear result. Leff JA et al. (PMID: 9664090) randomised 110 patients aged 15–45 with mild asthma and documented exercise-induced bronchoconstriction (FEV1 fall of at least 20% after exercise on two run-in occasions) to montelukast 10 mg at bedtime or placebo for 12 weeks: montelukast inhibited the post-exercise FEV1 area-under-the-curve endpoint by 47.4% relative to placebo (P = 0.002) — the protection was present at weeks 4, 8 and 12 with no sign of tolerance, the maximal post-exercise FEV1 fall was significantly smaller (P = 0.003), recovery to within 5% of pre-exercise values was faster (P = 0.04), and there was no rebound worsening during the two-week washout. Adverse event rates were similar. The discounts: the endpoint is a laboratory exercise challenge, not exacerbations or symptoms in daily life (though patients on montelukast did rate their asthma control better and used less rescue beta-agonist around challenges); the population had mild asthma; and a single 110-patient trial from the drug's launch era is the whole direct record for this exact question. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): daily montelukast probably attenuates exercise-induced bronchoconstriction substantially in mild asthma. Montelukast's other shelves — preschool viral wheeze #1426 and allergic rhinitis #2666 — are different questions, and its neuropsychiatric boxed warning belongs in any real prescribing conversation even though it postdates this trial.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — daily montelukast attenuated the post-exercise FEV1 fall by 47.4% relative to placebo over 12 weeks in the one trial in mild asthma with exercise-induced bronchoconstriction, with no tolerance or rebound

title: Erdosteine in COPD: fewer and shorter exacerbations overall — but read by severity, the benefit is mild events only and the serious ones did not budge
question: In adults with COPD and chronic bronchitis, does erdosteine reduce the rate and duration of exacerbations versus placebo on top of usual inhaled therapy?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — with the benefit located precisely where it matters least. The RESTORE trial (Dal Negro RW et al., PMID: 29025888; 445 patients with GOLD stage II/III COPD on usual inhaled therapy) found erdosteine 300 mg twice daily for 12 months reduced the overall exacerbation rate by 19.4% in relative terms — 0.91 versus 1.13 exacerbations per patient-year (P = 0.01) — and shortened exacerbation duration by 24.6% in relative terms (9.55 versus 12.63 days; P = 0.023). But the rate reduction was driven entirely by mild events (0.23 versus 0.54 per patient-year; a 57.1% relative reduction; P = 0.002), while moderate and severe exacerbations — the ones that hospitalise and kill — were numerically more frequent on erdosteine (0.68 versus 0.59 per patient-year; P = 0.054), and neither quality of life (SGRQ) nor time to first exacerbation improved. The Cochrane mucolytic synthesis (Poole P et al., PMID: 31107966; 38 trials, 10,377 participants, erdosteine among the agents) supports a small class effect — mucolytic patients were more likely to stay exacerbation-free (Peto OR 1.73, 95% CI 1.56 to 1.91; number needed to treat 8 over about nine months) with 0.43 fewer disability days per month — while warning that recent trials show smaller effects than early ones and heterogeneity is high. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): erdosteine probably trims mild exacerbations and shortens episodes, with no demonstrated effect on the moderate-to-severe events that drive COPD outcomes. The N-acetylcysteine/carbocisteine mucolytic shelf is #2446; this is the erdosteine-specific question.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — erdosteine reduced overall COPD exacerbation rate (0.91 vs 1.13 per patient-year) and duration in one trial, but the reduction was confined to mild exacerbations, with moderate/severe events numerically higher and no quality-of-life gain

title: Vitamin D and COPD exacerbations: nothing for the average patient, a 45% relative rate cut for the profoundly deficient — the subgroup is the story
question: In adults with COPD, does vitamin D supplementation prevent moderate-to-severe exacerbations, particularly in those with baseline vitamin D deficiency?
balance: SPLIT — by baseline vitamin D level, and the split is the whole finding. The individual-participant-data meta-analysis (Jolliffe DA et al., PMID: 30630893) pooled the randomised trials of vitamin D for COPD exacerbation prevention (4 eligible trials, 560 participants; individual data for 469 of 472 participants in three trials) and found no overall effect on moderate/severe exacerbations (adjusted incidence rate ratio 0.94, 95% CI 0.78 to 1.13). But the pre-specified subgroup analysis separated cleanly: in participants with baseline 25-hydroxyvitamin D below 25 nmol/L, supplementation reduced the moderate/severe exacerbation rate (aIRR 0.55, 95% CI 0.36 to 0.84 — a 45% relative reduction), while in those at or above 25 nmol/L it did nothing (aIRR 1.04, 95% CI 0.85 to 1.27), with a significant interaction (P = 0.015). Serious adverse events did not differ (adjusted OR 1.16, 95% CI 0.76 to 1.75). PROPOSED SPLIT: vitamin D probably prevents COPD exacerbations only in patients with profound baseline deficiency (<25 nmol/L); supplementing the non-deficient is treating a number, not a risk. This is a different question from vitamin D for respiratory infection (shelf #4) and for asthma exacerbations (shelf #546).
stamp: SPLIT — vitamin D supplementation reduced moderate/severe COPD exacerbations only in patients with baseline 25-hydroxyvitamin D below 25 nmol/L (aIRR 0.55), with no effect at higher baseline levels (aIRR 1.04) and none overall (0.94)

title: Lung rehab by screen matches the rehab centre on walking distance — and far more people finish it (93% versus 70%)
question: In adults with chronic respiratory disease (mainly COPD), does telerehabilitation achieve exercise capacity and quality-of-life outcomes comparable to centre-based pulmonary rehabilitation?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for the outcome that matters most in pulmonary rehabilitation, getting people to finish a programme, telerehabilitation looks at least as good as the centre: in the Cochrane review (Cox NS et al., PMID: 33511633) 15 studies and 1,904 participants (99% with COPD) found probably little or no difference in 6-minute walk distance between telerehabilitation and in-person rehabilitation (mean difference 0.06 m, 95% CI −10.82 to 10.94; moderate-certainty evidence), little or no difference in quality of life or breathlessness, and a higher completion rate for telerehabilitation (93%, 95% CI 90% to 96%, versus 70% for in-person programmes). Against no rehabilitation, telerehabilitation may improve walk distance, and no safety signal appeared. The limits are real: five different telerehabilitation models, few participants per comparison, low certainty for several outcomes, and almost no evidence in chronic respiratory diseases other than COPD or beyond the programme period. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): telerehabilitation is a reasonable way to deliver pulmonary rehabilitation when travel or capacity blocks centre-based care — comparable outcomes, better completion — not a proven upgrade on the exercise benefit itself.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — telerehabilitation achieves exercise-capacity and quality-of-life outcomes comparable to centre-based pulmonary rehabilitation, with higher completion

title: Breathing-muscle training strengthens the in-breath and eases breathlessness in COPD — but adds nothing on top of a full rehab programme
question: In adults with COPD, does inspiratory muscle training improve inspiratory muscle strength, dyspnoea and exercise capacity versus sham or no training?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — inspiratory muscle training with threshold devices does what it mechanically promises in COPD: the systematic review and meta-analysis (Beaumont M et al., PMID: 29665262) pooled 43 studies (37 in the meta-analysis, 642 patients in the treatment groups) and found inspiratory muscle strength, exercise capacity, and quality of life increased and dyspnoea decreased after training. The important qualification sits in the same record: when inspiratory muscle training was added to a pulmonary rehabilitation programme, it produced no added effect on dyspnoea compared with pulmonary rehabilitation alone — so the benefit is clearest as a standalone intervention, not as an add-on to a programme that already trains the whole patient. The abstract reports directions of effect rather than pooled effect sizes, so the size of the gains cannot be graded from this record. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a reasonable standalone option for people with COPD who cannot access or complete full pulmonary rehabilitation; inside a rehabilitation programme, expect no extra breathlessness benefit.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — inspiratory muscle training improves inspiratory strength, exercise capacity and quality of life and reduces dyspnoea in COPD, with no added dyspnoea benefit when combined with pulmonary rehabilitation

title: Oxygen at night is not CPAP: in HeartBEAT only CPAP lowered blood pressure — oxygen was no better than sleep-hygiene advice
question: In adults with obstructive sleep apnoea, how does nocturnal supplemental oxygen compare with CPAP for blood-pressure lowering and sleepiness?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for CPAP, not for oxygen: the HeartBEAT trial (Gottlieb DJ et al., PMID: 24918372) randomised 318 patients with obstructive sleep apnoea and cardiovascular disease or multiple risk factors, and after 12 weeks CPAP lowered 24-hour mean arterial pressure versus control (−2.4 mm Hg, 95% CI −4.7 to −0.1) and versus supplemental oxygen (−2.8 mm Hg, 95% CI −5.1 to −0.5), while oxygen did not differ significantly from education alone. Correcting the low oxygen at night, by itself, did not reproduce CPAP's blood-pressure effect — the pressure problem in apnoea is apparently not only the oxygen dips. A 49-trial network meta-analysis of apnoea treatments and blood pressure (Kou C et al., PMID: 35703874) is consistent in kind: CPAP showed modest, stable blood-pressure lowering, while nocturnal supplemental oxygen was not among the treatments the authors identified as effective. Neither record reports a sleepiness advantage for oxygen. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): CPAP lowers blood pressure where nocturnal oxygen does not, so oxygen should not be substituted for CPAP when blood-pressure lowering is the goal.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — CPAP lowers 24-hour blood pressure in obstructive sleep apnoea where nocturnal supplemental oxygen does not; oxygen is not a substitute for CPAP for blood-pressure lowering

title: Servo-ventilation for central sleep apnoea in heart failure: the breathing normalised, and mortality rose by about a third
question: In patients with central sleep apnoea and heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, does adaptive servo-ventilation improve survival or cardiovascular outcomes — or increase mortality?
balance: LIKELY (harm) — adaptive servo-ventilation suppresses central sleep apnoea beautifully and harms the patients it was meant to save: in SERVE-HF (Cowie MR et al., PMID: 26323938), 1,325 patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (≤45%) and predominantly central sleep apnoea had their apnoea–hypopnoea index driven down to a mean of 6.6 events per hour at 12 months, yet the primary composite endpoint did not improve (54.1% versus 50.8%; HR 1.13, 95% CI 0.97 to 1.31) and both all-cause mortality (HR 1.28, 95% CI 1.06 to 1.55) and cardiovascular mortality (HR 1.34, 95% CI 1.09 to 1.65) were significantly higher with the device. A later systematic review and meta-analysis (Wang J et al., PMID: 33524864) found no significant reduction in all-cause or cardiovascular mortality across eight studies, while reporting subgroup signals of fewer major adverse cardiovascular events in patients with less severe heart failure or profound nocturnal desaturation — signals built partly on observational studies that cannot overturn a large randomised mortality result in the population SERVE-HF actually studied. PROPOSED LIKELY (harm): in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction and central sleep apnoea, adaptive servo-ventilation increases mortality and should not be used to improve survival in that population.
stamp: LIKELY (harm) — in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction and central sleep apnoea, adaptive servo-ventilation increased all-cause and cardiovascular mortality in SERVE-HF despite controlling the apnoea

title: The old IPF triple therapy harmed: 8 deaths versus 1 on placebo before the safety board stopped it (PANTHER-IPF)
question: In adults with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, does combination prednisone plus azathioprine plus N-acetylcysteine improve outcomes versus placebo — or increase death and hospitalisation?
balance: LIKELY (harm) — the long-standard triple therapy for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis was worse than doing nothing: in PANTHER-IPF (Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis Clinical Research Network, PMID: 22607134), patients with mild-to-moderate lung-function impairment randomised to prednisone plus azathioprine plus N-acetylcysteine had, at a planned interim analysis, eight deaths versus one on placebo (P=0.01) and 23 hospitalisations versus seven (P<0.001), with no evidence of physiological or clinical benefit — the data and safety monitoring board stopped the combination arm at a mean follow-up of 32 weeks. The wider drug-treatment landscape points the same way: a systematic review and network meta-analysis of 30 studies and 16 treatments (Canestaro WJ et al., PMID: 26836914) found no treatment better than placebo for respiratory-specific mortality, a reminder that for decades IPF pharmacotherapy produced activity without survival benefit — and in this case produced the opposite. PROPOSED LIKELY (harm): the prednisone–azathioprine–N-acetylcysteine combination should not be used in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis; this shelf answers the combination question only and does not judge N-acetylcysteine alone, whose separate comparison the trial continued.
stamp: LIKELY (harm) — prednisone plus azathioprine plus N-acetylcysteine increased death and hospitalisation versus placebo in PANTHER-IPF and showed no benefit

title: Rehab works in lung scarring too: 44 extra metres on the walk test and less breathlessness — durability beyond the programme unproven
question: In adults with interstitial lung disease, does pulmonary rehabilitation improve exercise capacity, dyspnoea and quality of life versus usual care?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — pulmonary rehabilitation, proven in COPD, also works in interstitial lung disease on the outcomes measured immediately after the programme: the Cochrane review (Dowman L et al., PMID: 25284270) included nine studies and meta-analysed five (86 rehabilitation and 82 control participants), finding six-minute walk distance improved by a weighted mean difference of 44.34 m (95% CI 26.04 to 62.64) and peak oxygen consumption by 1.24 mL/kg/min (95% CI 0.46 to 2.03), with quality of life improved (standardised mean difference 0.59, 95% CI 0.20 to 0.98) and no adverse effects reported. The idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis subgroup showed the same pattern — walk distance up 35.63 m (95% CI 16.02 to 55.23) and dyspnoea reduced (standardised mean difference −0.68, 95% CI −1.12 to −0.25). What the record cannot show is durability: the only two studies with longer follow-up found no significant effects on clinical variables or survival at three or six months, and the reviewers graded the evidence low to moderate quality because six of nine studies existed only as abstracts. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): offer pulmonary rehabilitation in interstitial lung disease for near-term function, breathlessness, and quality of life — with honest uncertainty about how long the gains persist.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — pulmonary rehabilitation improves exercise capacity, dyspnoea and quality of life immediately after the programme in interstitial lung disease, including IPF; longer-term benefit is unproven

title: Infliximab for pulmonary sarcoidosis: a statistically real 2.5% FVC gain that patients could not feel on any other measure
question: In patients with chronic pulmonary sarcoidosis and disabling symptoms despite corticosteroids, does infliximab improve forced vital capacity versus placebo?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the only randomised trial of infliximab in chronic pulmonary sarcoidosis (Baughman RP et al., PMID: 16840744) hit its primary endpoint narrowly and nothing else: in 138 patients, combined infliximab (3 or 5 mg/kg) produced a mean increase of 2.5% in percent of predicted forced vital capacity at week 24 versus no change on placebo (P=0.038), while every major secondary endpoint — St George's Respiratory Questionnaire, 6-minute walk distance, and Borg dyspnoea score — showed no significant difference, and the authors themselves state that the clinical importance of the lung-function finding is not clear. Post hoc analyses suggested patients with more severe disease tended to benefit more, which is a hypothesis, not a result. A 2.5% predicted FVC shift that patients cannot feel on any symptom or walk measure, from a single phase 2 trial, is a signal worth the further evaluation the authors call for — not an established treatment effect. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): infliximab may nudge lung function in chronic pulmonary sarcoidosis, but symptomatic benefit is unproven and the case rests on one small trial.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — a single phase 2 trial found a small FVC improvement of unclear clinical importance, with no benefit on symptoms, walk distance, or quality of life

title: High-flow oxygen at home for high-CO2 COPD: exacerbations probably fall and CO2 holds steady — survival unproven
question: In patients with COPD and chronic hypercapnic respiratory failure, does long-term domiciliary high-flow nasal cannula therapy reduce exacerbations and improve carbon dioxide control versus long-term oxygen therapy alone?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — domiciliary high-flow nasal cannula therapy in COPD with persistent hypercapnic failure stabilised patients who otherwise deteriorated: in the 12-month randomised-trial cohort analysis (Storgaard LH et al., PMID: 33208303), 74 long-term-oxygen-treated patients completing the study (31 on high-flow, 43 controls) showed PaCO2 falling 1.3% on high-flow while rising 7% in controls (P=0.003), exacerbations rising by 2.2 per year in controls but only 0.15 per year on high-flow, and hospital admissions falling by 0.67 per year on high-flow (P=0.013) while rising in controls. The systematic review and meta-analysis (Pitre T et al., PMID: 37804997) — four randomised trials, 440 patients — found high-flow probably reduces acute exacerbations (relative risk 0.77, 95% CI 0.66 to 0.89; 69 fewer exacerbations per 1,000 patients; moderate certainty), may reduce hospital admissions (relative risk 0.87, 95% CI 0.69 to 1.09; low certainty) and quality-of-life scores, but may have no effect on mortality (relative risk 1.22, 95% CI 0.64 to 2.35; low certainty). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): home high-flow therapy probably cuts exacerbations in chronic hypercapnic COPD; a survival benefit is unproven and the trial base is still small.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — home high-flow nasal cannula probably reduces exacerbations and stabilises PaCO2 in COPD with chronic hypercapnic failure; no mortality benefit has been shown

title: Varenicline plus bupropion quits more smokers at 3 and 6 months — by 12 months the edge is no longer significant
question: In cigarette smokers, does combining varenicline with bupropion increase prolonged abstinence versus varenicline alone?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — adding bupropion sustained-release to varenicline helped smokers stay quit through the treatment period and six months, but the advantage had faded into non-significance by one year: in the randomised, blinded, placebo-controlled trial (Ebbert JO et al., PMID: 24399554), 506 cigarette smokers achieved prolonged abstinence at 12 weeks in 53.0% on combination therapy versus 43.2% on varenicline alone (odds ratio 1.49, 95% CI 1.05 to 2.12) and at 26 weeks in 36.6% versus 27.6% (odds ratio 1.52, 95% CI 1.04 to 2.22), while 7-day point-prevalence abstinence never differed significantly and at 52 weeks neither outcome did (prolonged abstinence 30.9% versus 24.5%; odds ratio 1.39, 95% CI 0.93 to 2.07). The combination also cost more anxiety (7.2% versus 3.1%) and depressive symptoms (3.6% versus 0.8%). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a real but possibly temporary boost to quitting while both drugs are taken and shortly after — not a demonstrated improvement in one-year abstinence, and bought with more mood symptoms.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — combining varenicline with bupropion increased prolonged abstinence at 12 and 26 weeks versus varenicline alone, but the difference was not significant at 52 weeks

title: Warfarin for pulmonary fibrosis increased deaths 14 to 3 — ACE-IPF was stopped early, closing the anticoagulation hypothesis
question: In adults with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, does anticoagulation with warfarin improve survival or slow progression versus placebo — or increase mortality?
balance: LIKELY (harm) — anticoagulating the lung's clotting cascade was a biologically plausible idea that its randomised test refuted in the worst direction: in ACE-IPF (Noth I et al., PMID: 22561965), patients with progressive idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and no other indication for anticoagulation were randomised to warfarin (target INR 2.0 to 3.0) or placebo, and the data and safety monitoring board stopped the trial after 145 of the planned 256 subjects were enrolled because of low probability of benefit and an increase in mortality on warfarin — 14 deaths versus 3 on placebo (P=0.005) at a mean follow-up of 28 weeks. The primary composite of death, hospitalisation, or a ≥10% absolute decline in forced vital capacity showed no benefit. Together with PANTHER-IPF (shelf #2796), this closes the era in which plausible non-antifibrotic pharmacology was given to IPF patients untested: both landmark attempts increased mortality. PROPOSED LIKELY (harm): warfarin should not be used to treat idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis in patients who lack another indication for anticoagulation.
stamp: LIKELY (harm) — warfarin increased mortality in progressive idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (14 versus 3 deaths) in ACE-IPF, which was stopped early; it should not be used for IPF itself

title: Oxybutynin cools hot flushes: scores fell two to three times more than on placebo in six weeks — dry mouth included
question: In women with or without breast cancer who have bothersome hot flushes, does oxybutynin reduce hot-flush frequency and scores versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — oxybutynin, an anticholinergic bladder drug, reduced hot flushes more than placebo at both doses tested in the ACCRU SC-1603 trial (Leon-Ferre RA et al., PMID: 32337497): among 150 women with or without breast cancer who had at least 28 hot flushes per week and were not candidates for estrogen-based therapy, six weeks of oxybutynin cut the weekly hot-flush score by 16.9 points at 5 mg twice daily and 10.6 points at 2.5 mg twice daily versus 5.7 on placebo (P<.005 for both), and weekly frequency fell by 7.5 and 4.8 flushes versus 2.6 on placebo (P<.003 for both), with improvements in most daily-interference measures and overall quality of life. The price is the anticholinergic profile: more dry mouth, difficulty urinating, and abdominal pain than placebo, mostly grade 1 or 2, with no difference in discontinuation for adverse effects. Six weeks in 150 women establishes short-term efficacy, not long-term safety of daily anticholinergic exposure in this population. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): an effective nonhormonal option for bothersome hot flushes, with dose-dependent anticholinergic side effects and no long-term data.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — oxybutynin reduced hot-flush scores and frequency versus placebo over six weeks in women ineligible for estrogen therapy, with mostly mild anticholinergic side effects

title: Ginger for chemo nausea: day-1 severity fell at every dose in a 576-patient trial — best at half a gram, and no brand was tested
question: In patients receiving chemotherapy, does ginger reduce acute chemotherapy-induced nausea versus placebo on top of standard antiemetics?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — ginger added to a standard 5-HT3 antagonist antiemetic reduced the severity of acute chemotherapy-induced nausea in the largest trial of the question (Ryan JL et al., PMID: 21818642): 744 patients were randomised to placebo or 0.5 g, 1.0 g, or 1.5 g of ginger daily, and in the 576 analysed, all ginger doses significantly reduced acute nausea severity versus placebo on day 1 of chemotherapy (P=0.003), with the largest reductions at 0.5 g and 1.0 g (P=0.017 and P=0.036) — more ginger was not better. A systematic review and meta-analysis in breast cancer (Kim SD et al., PMID: 36232567) found the same direction across five randomised trials, for both acute and delayed nausea and vomiting severity, with no serious side effects. Two cautions discipline the claim: the Ryan record reports significance without a printed effect size on its 7-point nausea scale, so the size of the relief cannot be stated from the record, and the proven outcome is nausea severity on day 1 — not vomiting abolished, and not a substitute for guideline antiemetics, which every patient received. The trial report names no branded ginger product, so no specific commercial preparation is endorsed by this evidence, and current products may differ in safety and effectiveness. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a modest, inexpensive adjunct for acute nausea on top of standard antiemetics, at 0.5–1.0 g daily.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — ginger 0.5–1.0 g daily reduced acute chemotherapy-induced nausea severity versus placebo on top of standard antiemetics; no branded product was tested

title: Laser light before the sores start: severe mucositis fell from 40.5% to 6.4% in head and neck chemoradiation
question: In patients receiving radiotherapy (with or without chemotherapy) for head and neck cancer, does low-level laser therapy / photobiomodulation prevent severe oral mucositis versus sham?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — preventive low-level laser therapy (photobiomodulation) produced one of the largest supportive-care effects in this library: in the phase III trial (Antunes HS et al., PMID: 24044799), 94 patients receiving concurrent chemoradiation for head and neck squamous cell carcinoma had severe (grade 3–4) oral mucositis in 6.4% of the laser group versus 40.5% of the sham group — a relative risk of 0.158 (95% CI 0.050 to 0.498), an 84% relative reduction with the absolute rates printed here — alongside quality-of-life advantages in pain, swallowing, fatigue, and social eating. The MASCC/ISOO systematic review and guideline update (Zadik Y et al., PMID: 31286228) independently recommends photobiomodulation for prevention of oral mucositis in exactly these settings — head and neck radiotherapy with or without chemotherapy, and stem-cell transplantation — provided the clinician adheres to all parameters of one of the validated protocols. The discipline in that proviso is the catch: effects are protocol-specific (wavelength, dose, schedule), the flagship trial is a single centre's 94 patients, and the guideline finds evidence inadequate for treating established mucositis or for chemotherapy-only settings. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): preventive photobiomodulation, delivered to a validated protocol, substantially reduces severe oral mucositis in head and neck chemoradiation.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — preventive photobiomodulation substantially reduced severe oral mucositis in head and neck chemoradiation (6.4% versus 40.5%) and carries a MASCC/ISOO recommendation when a validated protocol is followed

title: A quarter-tablet appetite drug: 60% on low-dose olanzapine gained over 5% of their weight versus 9% on placebo
question: In patients with advanced cancer and chemotherapy-related anorexia, does low-dose olanzapine improve appetite and weight versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — low-dose olanzapine produced a strikingly large appetite and weight effect in a single randomised trial (Sandhya L et al., PMID: 36977285): among 124 patients with untreated locally advanced or metastatic gastric, hepatopancreaticobiliary, or lung cancer starting chemotherapy, 2.5 mg of olanzapine daily for 12 weeks gave weight gain of more than 5% in 60% of analysable patients (35 of 58) versus 9% on placebo (5 of 54; P<.001), appetite improvement on a visual analogue scale in 43% versus 13% (P<.001), and appetite improvement on the FAACT anorexia–cachexia subscale in 22% versus 4% (P=.004), with better quality of life and nutritional status, lesser chemotherapy toxicity, and minimal attributable side effects. The size of the effect is exactly why the stamp stops at POSSIBLE: one trial, 124 patients from a single programme, 80% metastatic disease across three tumour types, and 12 weeks of follow-up cannot establish durability, survival impact, or the longer-term metabolic and sedative profile of daily olanzapine in this population. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a simple, inexpensive, well-tolerated intervention that significantly improved appetite and weight in this trial — pending confirmation.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — low-dose olanzapine (2.5 mg daily) significantly improved appetite and weight gain versus placebo in advanced cancer patients on chemotherapy in a single randomised trial

title: Mirtazapine for cancer appetite: appetite rose in both arms of the one blinded trial — the placebo patients improved just as much
question: In patients with cancer-associated anorexia and cachexia, does mirtazapine improve appetite and weight versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the single double-blind trial behind this question (Hunter CN et al., PMID: 34051293) randomised 120 patients with incurable solid tumours, cancer-associated anorexia and cachexia to mirtazapine 15 mg at night or placebo for eight weeks. Appetite improved significantly in both arms (P < 0.0001 in each) and the improvement did not differ between arms in either the per-protocol (P = 0.472) or intention-to-treat (P = 0.462) analysis; weight, lean body mass, handgrip strength, quality of life, fatigue, inflammatory markers and survival likewise did not differ. Mirtazapine did blunt the rise in depressive symptoms and caused more somnolence — real drug effects, but not appetite effects. A placebo-arm improvement this large is itself the lesson: appetite in this setting fluctuates and responds to attention, so uncontrolled experience with mirtazapine will keep looking better than the drug is. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): on the one randomised test, mirtazapine is no better than placebo for appetite in cancer-associated anorexia and cachexia.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — in the one double-blind trial, mirtazapine improved appetite no more than placebo in cancer-associated anorexia and cachexia

title: Frozen gloves and socks against paclitaxel neuropathy: the cooled hand lost touch sensation a third as often — in a small trial where each patient was her own control
question: In patients receiving paclitaxel, does local cryotherapy (frozen gloves/socks during infusion) prevent or reduce peripheral neuropathy versus no cooling?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the anchor trial (Hanai A et al., PMID: 29924336) used each patient as her own control: 36 women wore frozen gloves and socks on the dominant side during weekly paclitaxel, and objective tactile-sensitivity loss at a cumulative 960 mg/m² was 27.8% on the cooled hand versus 80.6% on the uncooled hand (odds ratio 20.00), with subjective neuropathy symptoms of 2.8% versus 41.7% and a hazard ratio of 0.13 for symptom onset; nobody dropped out for cold intolerance. The wider record points the same way: a meta-analysis of 9 trials and 2,250 patients (Jia J et al., PMID: 34912720) found grade ≥2 sensory neuropathy at a relative risk of 0.65 (95% CI 0.56 to 0.75) with cryotherapy — a 35% relative reduction — and fewer taxane dose reductions (RR 0.48). The evidence is promising rather than settled: the anchor is small, unblinded by nature and self-controlled, and the meta-analysis pools small heterogeneous trials. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): cooling the hands and feet during paclitaxel probably reduces neuropathy, at the price of 90 minutes of cold discomfort per infusion.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — frozen gloves and socks during paclitaxel reduced objective and subjective neuropathy in a self-controlled trial, with a concordant meta-analysis

title: Acetyl-L-carnitine backfired: the supplement taken to prevent taxane neuropathy significantly increased it by 24 weeks (SWOG S0715)
question: In women receiving taxane chemotherapy for breast cancer, does acetyl-L-carnitine prevent chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy — or worsen it?
balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — this shelf exists because the answer reversed the expectation. Acetyl-L-carnitine was biologically plausible and supported by small earlier studies, so SWOG S0715 (Hershman DL et al., PMID: 23733756) randomised 409 women receiving adjuvant taxane chemotherapy to acetyl-L-carnitine 3,000 mg/day or placebo for 24 weeks. At the 12-week primary endpoint there was no protection (neurotoxicity scores 0.9 points worse on acetyl-L-carnitine, 95% CI −2.2 to 0.4, P = .17), and by 24 weeks the supplement arm had significantly MORE neuropathy: scores 1.8 points worse (95% CI −3.2 to −0.4, P = .01), more patients with a >5-point deterioration (38% vs 28%, P = .05), worse functional status scores, and grade 3–4 neurotoxicity in eight patients versus one on placebo. The authors' conclusion is blunt — patients should be discouraged from using supplements without proven efficacy. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm): a supplement taken to prevent chemotherapy neuropathy made the neuropathy worse in the only large blinded test. Established-neuropathy treatment with duloxetine is a different question, shelved at #1456.
stamp: POSSIBLE (harm) — acetyl-L-carnitine did not prevent taxane neuropathy and significantly worsened it by 24 weeks in SWOG S0715

title: Duloxetine for aromatase-inhibitor joint pain: a real but sub-one-point average advantage in SWOG S1202 — worth it for responders, not a transformation
question: In postmenopausal women with early breast cancer and aromatase-inhibitor arthralgia, does duloxetine reduce joint pain versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — SWOG S1202 (Henry NL et al., PMID: 29136387) randomised 299 postmenopausal women with early-stage breast cancer whose aromatase-inhibitor joint pain scored at least 4 of 10 to duloxetine or placebo for 13 weeks. Average joint pain at 12 weeks was 0.82 points lower on duloxetine (95% CI −1.24 to −0.40, P = .0002), with the same direction for worst pain, stiffness, pain interference and functioning. Two cautions keep the stamp at POSSIBLE: the average advantage (0.82 points) is well under the 2-point drop the trial itself defined as clinically significant for an individual patient, so the benefit is real on average but modest per person; and low-grade adverse events were much commoner on duloxetine (78% vs 50% any grade, though grade 3 rates were similar). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): duloxetine eases aromatase-inhibitor arthralgia by a modest average amount, bought with frequent low-grade side effects. The acupuncture trial for the same syndrome (SWOG S1200) is shelved at #1787; duloxetine for established chemotherapy neuropathy is #1456.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — duloxetine reduced aromatase-inhibitor joint pain by an average 0.82 points versus placebo in SWOG S1202, with more low-grade adverse events

title: NEPA versus palonosetron alone: one capsule containing both antiemetic pathways raised delayed complete response from 69.5% to 76.9%
question: In patients receiving moderately emetogenic chemotherapy (anthracycline–cyclophosphamide), does the fixed combination netupitant–palonosetron (NEPA) improve complete response versus palonosetron alone?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — in the phase 3 anchor trial (Aapro M et al., PMID: 24603643), 1,455 chemotherapy-naïve patients receiving anthracycline–cyclophosphamide chemotherapy (classified moderately emetogenic in the trial) took a single oral dose of the fixed netupitant 300 mg–palonosetron 0.50 mg combination (NEPA) or palonosetron 0.50 mg alone, each with day-1 dexamethasone. Complete response (no vomiting, no rescue medication) in the delayed phase (25–120 hours) — the primary endpoint — was 76.9% on NEPA versus 69.5% on palonosetron, an absolute gain of 7.4 percentage points (P = 0.001), with concordant gains overall (74.3% vs 66.6%) and in the acute phase (88.4% vs 85.0%), and a similar safety profile. A 2025 meta-analysis of 7 randomised trials (Luo WT et al., PMID: 39284781) found NEPA plus dexamethasone also beat aprepitant-based NK1 regimens on complete response (overall-phase relative risk 1.15, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.30), with the largest subgroup effect in moderately emetogenic chemotherapy (RR 1.31). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): adding netupitant to palonosetron in one capsule genuinely improves complete response, most clearly in the delayed phase where patients suffer longest. Note the trial's dexamethasone doses differed between arms (12 mg with NEPA, 20 mg with palonosetron), which if anything handicapped the combination.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — NEPA improved delayed-phase complete response over palonosetron alone (76.9% vs 69.5%) in a 1,455-patient phase 3 trial, with a concordant meta-analysis

title: Levofloxacin for the first 12 weeks of myeloma therapy (TEAMM): febrile episodes or death cut from 27% to 19%, with no resistance penalty detected
question: In patients with newly diagnosed multiple myeloma starting therapy, does levofloxacin prophylaxis for the first 12 weeks reduce febrile episodes and death versus placebo?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — TEAMM (Drayson MT et al., PMID: 31668592) is a large, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial: 977 patients with newly diagnosed myeloma in 93 UK hospitals received levofloxacin 500 mg daily or placebo for the first 12 weeks of anti-myeloma therapy. The primary outcome — first febrile episode or death within 12 weeks — occurred in 95 of 489 patients (19%) on levofloxacin versus 134 of 488 (27%) on placebo (hazard ratio 0.66, 95% CI 0.51 to 0.86, P = 0.0018), an absolute difference of about 8 percentage points. Serious adverse events were similar between arms (the exception was five episodes of mostly reversible tendonitis on levofloxacin), and the trial found no increase in health-care-associated infections or resistant-organism carriage — the harms that usually argue against prophylaxis. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): twelve weeks of levofloxacin at myeloma diagnosis prevents roughly one febrile episode or death for every 12–13 patients treated. This shelf is distinct from shelf #1784, which covers levofloxacin prophylaxis during prolonged chemotherapy-induced neutropenia (Bucaneve; Cullen) — a different population and treatment phase.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — 12 weeks of levofloxacin at myeloma diagnosis reduced first febrile episode or death from 27% to 19% in the 977-patient TEAMM trial

title: Imetelstat in ESA-failed lower-risk MDS (IMerge): 40% freed from transfusions for at least 8 weeks versus 15% on placebo — with grade 3–4 cytopenias in most
question: In adults with lower-risk myelodysplastic syndromes relapsed or refractory to erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, does imetelstat achieve red-cell transfusion independence versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — IMerge (Platzbecker U et al., PMID: 38048786) randomised 178 heavily transfused patients with lower-risk myelodysplastic syndromes who had relapsed on, were refractory to, or were ineligible for erythropoiesis-stimulating agents to imetelstat 7.5 mg/kg intravenously every 4 weeks or placebo. The primary endpoint — at least 8 consecutive weeks free of red-cell transfusion — was reached by 40% on imetelstat versus 15% on placebo (rate difference 25 percentage points, 95% CI 9.9 to 36.9, P = 0.0008), and the authors describe transfusion independence lasting approximately a year in responders, with disease-modifying activity. The price is myelosuppression: grade 3–4 treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 91% on imetelstat versus 47% on placebo, driven by neutropenia (68% vs 3%) and thrombocytopenia (62% vs 8%), though no treatment-related deaths were reported. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a real, clinically meaningful chance of transfusion independence for patients with no ESA option left, bought with substantial cytopenias that need monitoring. The stamp stops at POSSIBLE because this is a single trial and the benefit is concentrated in a responder minority.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — imetelstat achieved 8-week transfusion independence in 40% versus 15% on placebo in ESA-failed lower-risk MDS (IMerge), at the cost of frequent grade 3–4 cytopenias

title: Deferasirox versus deferoxamine: the once-daily tablet matched the overnight infusion on liver iron where doses were adequate — and patients much preferred it
question: In patients with transfusion-dependent beta-thalassaemia and iron overload, does the oral chelator deferasirox reduce liver iron concentration comparably to deferoxamine, with acceptable safety?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the pivotal phase 3 trial (Cappellini MD et al., PMID: 16352812) randomised 586 regularly transfused patients with beta-thalassaemia to once-daily oral deferasirox or deferoxamine, dosed according to baseline liver iron concentration (LIC). In patients with LIC ≥7 mg Fe/g dry weight, the two drugs produced significant and similar dose-dependent reductions in LIC and serum ferritin; the trial's primary endpoint (maintenance or reduction of LIC) was not met in the overall population, apparently because patients with LIC <7 received proportionally lower deferasirox doses relative to deferoxamine. The Cochrane review (Bollig C et al., PMID: 28809446; 16 studies, 1,807 participants) reaches the matching conclusion: similar efficacy is achievable depending on the dose ratio (about 1 mg deferasirox to 1.8–2 mg deferoxamine), pooled intermediate markers favoured deferoxamine at the ratios actually compared (LIC mean difference 2.37 mg Fe/g dry weight, 95% CI 1.68 to 3.07), patient satisfaction was clearly better with the oral drug (RR 2.20), and mortality and long-term safety data remain limited. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): deferasirox is a legitimate once-daily oral alternative that controls liver iron comparably when dosed adequately — its advantage is a life without nightly infusions, not superior iron removal.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — deferasirox controls liver iron comparably to deferoxamine at adequate dose ratios, with better patient satisfaction, in transfusion-dependent beta-thalassaemia

title: Ruxolitinib for steroid-refractory acute GVHD (REACH2): response in 62% versus 39% on best available therapy — and responses lasted
question: In patients with glucocorticoid-refractory acute graft-versus-host disease after allogeneic stem-cell transplantation, does ruxolitinib improve day-28 overall response versus best available therapy?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — REACH2 (Zeiser R et al., PMID: 32320566) randomised 309 patients aged 12 or older with glucocorticoid-refractory acute graft-versus-host disease after allogeneic stem-cell transplantation to ruxolitinib 10 mg twice daily or the investigator's choice from nine commonly used second-line therapies. Overall response at day 28 — the primary endpoint — was 62% on ruxolitinib versus 39% on control (odds ratio 2.64, 95% CI 1.65 to 4.22, P < 0.001), and responses were more durable: day-56 durable response 40% vs 22%, estimated loss of response by 6 months 10% vs 39%, and median failure-free survival 5.0 vs 1.0 months (HR 0.46). Overall survival leaned the same way without reaching significance (median 11.1 vs 6.5 months; HR 0.83, 95% CI 0.60 to 1.15). Thrombocytopenia was commoner on ruxolitinib (33% vs 18%), with anaemia and cytomegalovirus infection frequent in both arms. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): ruxolitinib is the first second-line therapy for steroid-refractory acute GVHD to beat best available therapy in a randomised trial — held at POSSIBLE because the trial was open-label and the survival difference is unproven.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — ruxolitinib beat best available therapy on day-28 response (62% vs 39%) in glucocorticoid-refractory acute GVHD (REACH2), with survival benefit unproven

title: L-glutamine in sickle cell disease: one fewer pain crisis and one fewer hospitalisation at the median over 48 weeks — a modest gain from a pharmaceutical-grade powder
question: In patients with sickle cell disease, does oral L-glutamine reduce pain crises and hospitalisations versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the single phase 3 trial (Niihara Y et al., PMID: 30021096) randomised 230 patients aged 5 to 58 with sickle cell anaemia or sickle β0-thalassaemia and at least two pain crises in the previous year to pharmaceutical-grade L-glutamine powder (0.3 g/kg twice daily, the tested product in this trial, funded by Emmaus Medical) or placebo for 48 weeks; about two thirds in both arms also took hydroxyurea. The glutamine group had fewer pain crises (median 3.0 vs 4.0, P = 0.005) and fewer hospitalisations (median 2.0 vs 3.0, P = 0.005). Low-grade nausea, non-cardiac chest pain, fatigue and musculoskeletal pain were commoner on glutamine. Two cautions define the stamp: the absolute gain is one fewer crisis and one fewer hospitalisation at the median over a year, and the result rests on medians from a single trial — the record does not report mean crisis rates or a rate ratio. Note also that the tested product was a pharmaceutical-grade L-glutamine powder; the publication names no consumer supplement brand, and current supplement products may differ in safety and effectiveness. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a modest, real reduction in crises for a disease with few oral options. Hydroxyurea is shelved at #669, transfusion at #670, and voxelotor/crizanlizumab (with their reversals) at #847.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — pharmaceutical-grade L-glutamine reduced median pain crises (3.0 vs 4.0) and hospitalisations (2.0 vs 3.0) over 48 weeks in one phase 3 sickle-cell trial

title: Argatroban for heparin-induced thrombocytopenia: fewer deaths, amputations and new clots than historical controls — the only kind of evidence this question has
question: In patients with heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, does argatroban anticoagulation prevent the composite of death, amputation and new thrombosis compared with historical controls?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — there is no randomised trial of argatroban in heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, and there is unlikely ever to be one: the anchor evidence (Lewis BE et al., PMID: 11294800) is a prospective multicentre study comparing 304 argatroban-treated patients with 193 historical controls. The composite of death, amputation or new thrombosis occurred in 25.6% of argatroban patients with isolated HIT versus 38.8% of historical controls (P = 0.014); in HIT with thrombosis syndrome the figures were 43.8% versus 56.5% (P = 0.13), with time-to-event analyses favouring argatroban in both groups (P = 0.010 and P = 0.014) and no increase in bleeding. Historical controls are the weakest comparator in routine use — supportive care, diagnosis speed and case mix all drift over time, and every one of those drifts tends to flatter the newer treatment. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): argatroban is a reasonable, widely used anticoagulant for HIT on the strength of this historically controlled evidence and its pharmacology, but the size of its benefit over simply stopping heparin has never been measured against a concurrent control.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — argatroban's advantage in HIT rests on one prospective study against historical controls; no randomised trial exists

title: Tranexamic acid to prevent bleeding in thrombocytopenic haematology patients: two blinded trials, two nulls — no routine role
question: In patients with haematological malignancies and severe thrombocytopenia, does prophylactic tranexamic acid prevent clinically significant bleeding versus placebo?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — two placebo-controlled randomised trials, in two countries and two eras, asked whether prophylactic tranexamic acid prevents bleeding in patients with haematological malignancies and severe thrombocytopenia, and both answered no. A-TREAT (Gernsheimer TB et al., PMID: 35667085) found WHO grade ≥2 bleeding in 50.3% on tranexamic acid versus 54.2% on placebo (adjusted odds ratio 0.83, 95% CI 0.50 to 1.34, P = .44), with no difference in platelet transfusions. TREATT (TREATT Trial Investigators, PMID: 39642900), the larger trial with 616 randomised patients, found death or grade ≥2 bleeding in 31.7% versus 34.2% (hazard ratio 0.92, 95% CI 0.67 to 1.27, P = 0.62), again with no difference in thrombotic events. Reassuringly, neither trial showed a thrombosis penalty — but a drug that neither helps nor measurably harms has no routine role. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): prophylactic tranexamic acid should not be used routinely to prevent bleeding in thrombocytopenic haematology patients. Tranexamic acid's life-saving roles in trauma, postpartum and surgical bleeding are different questions, shelved elsewhere (e.g., #138, #1246).
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — prophylactic tranexamic acid did not reduce grade ≥2 bleeding in either of two placebo-controlled trials (A-TREAT; TREATT) in haematological malignancy

title: Avatrombopag for chemotherapy-induced thrombocytopenia: 70% versus 73% met the endpoint — the placebo arm did just as well in a first-episode population
question: In patients with non-haematological malignancies and chemotherapy-induced thrombocytopenia, does avatrombopag raise platelet counts enough to avoid platelet transfusion and chemotherapy dose delays versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the phase 3 trial (Al-Samkari H et al., PMID: 35240074) randomised 122 patients with ovarian, bladder or lung cancer and platelet counts below 50 × 10⁹/L to oral avatrombopag 60 mg daily or placebo, given for 5 days before and after chemotherapy. The composite primary endpoint — avoiding platelet transfusion, a ≥15% chemotherapy dose reduction and a ≥4-day delay — was met by 70% (57/82) on avatrombopag and 73% (29/40) on placebo (difference −3.0%, 95% CI −21.6 to 15.6; P = 0.72), with the same picture per protocol (85% vs 84%). The investigators note the placebo group did surprisingly well: these were relatively chemotherapy-naïve patients (no previous chemotherapy-induced thrombocytopenia, at most two prior lines), whose counts may recover spontaneously, leaving little room for any drug to show benefit. Safety was acceptable (serious adverse events 18% vs 20%; no treatment-related deaths), and the drug does raise platelet counts in other settings — so the authors argue for testing in more persistent thrombocytopenia rather than abandoning the approach. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): in this population, avatrombopag did not keep chemotherapy on schedule any better than placebo.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — avatrombopag did not improve the composite of transfusion avoidance and on-schedule chemotherapy versus placebo in its single phase 3 trial

title: Intravenous iron for chemotherapy-induced anaemia: one transfusion spared for roughly every 20 patients treated instead of oral iron — a modest, clean effect
question: In patients with chemotherapy-induced anaemia, does intravenous iron (alone or with erythropoiesis-stimulating agents) raise haemoglobin and reduce transfusion versus oral iron or no iron?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the evidence here is a systematic review and meta-analysis (Buchrits S et al., PMID: 35887920) of 8 randomised trials totalling 1,015 patients with chemotherapy-induced anaemia, comparing intravenous iron with oral iron (271 patients) or no iron (191 patients), and excluding trials that used erythropoiesis-stimulating agents — so this shelf isolates iron's own effect. Intravenous iron reduced the proportion of patients needing a red-cell transfusion compared with oral iron (relative risk 0.72, 95% CI 0.55 to 0.95 — a 28% relative reduction — with a number needed to treat of 20, 95% CI 11 to 100) and increased the haematopoietic response, defined as a haemoglobin rise above 1 g/dL or above 11 g/dL (RR 1.23, 95% CI 1.01 to 1.5, a relative measure). Adverse events overall (RR 0.97, 95% CI 0.88 to 1.07) and severe adverse events (RR 1.09, 95% CI 0.76 to 1.57) did not differ. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): intravenous iron spares roughly one transfusion for every 20 patients treated compared with oral iron, without a safety penalty in these trials — a useful, modest effect, held at POSSIBLE because the underlying trials are few, small and span three decades of changing practice. Intravenous iron in kidney disease and pregnancy are different questions, shelved at #294/#369 and #673.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — intravenous iron reduced transfusion need versus oral iron (RR 0.72; NNT 20) across 8 randomised trials in chemotherapy-induced anaemia, with no excess adverse events

title: Ganaxolone for CDKL5 deficiency disorder: the first controlled trial in the syndrome cut major motor seizures by a median 30.7% versus 6.9% on placebo — real, modest, and so far only 17 weeks deep
question: In children and adults with CDKL5 deficiency disorder, does ganaxolone reduce convulsive seizure frequency versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one phase 3 randomised trial (Marigold, Knight EMP et al., PMID: 35429480) in 101 children and young people aged 2–21 years with CDKL5 deficiency disorder and refractory major motor seizures found a median percentage change in 28-day major motor seizure frequency of −30.7% on ganaxolone versus −6.9% on placebo over 17 weeks (p=0.0036; Hodges–Lehmann median difference −27.1%, 95% CI −47.9 to −9.6). Tolerability was broadly similar between arms (treatment-emergent adverse events 86% vs 88%; serious adverse events 12% vs 10%), with somnolence, pyrexia and upper respiratory infections commoner on ganaxolone, and no deaths in the double-blind phase. A 2025 systematic review of antiseizure medications in CDKL5 encephalopathy (Kalinowska-Doman A et al., PMID: 40834685) independently describes ganaxolone's effect as a modest reduction of approximately 30% in seizure frequency, in a field where most evidence is small and uncontrolled. This is a single trial in a rare syndrome, with a surrogate frequency outcome over 17 weeks and no long-term controlled data yet. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): ganaxolone modestly reduces major motor seizure frequency in CDKL5 deficiency disorder over the short term; durability and developmental benefit are unproven.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — ganaxolone modestly reduces major motor seizure frequency in CDKL5 deficiency disorder over 17 weeks in a single phase 3 trial

title: Rufinamide for Lennox–Gastaut syndrome: drop attacks fell by a median 42.5% versus a 1.4% rise on placebo in the pivotal trial, and the pooled studies agree
question: In patients with Lennox–Gastaut syndrome, does adjunctive rufinamide reduce drop seizures versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the pivotal trial (Glauser T et al., PMID: 18401024) randomised 138 patients aged 4–30 years with Lennox–Gastaut syndrome and found a median percentage reduction in total seizure frequency of 32.7% on adjunctive rufinamide versus 11.7% on placebo (p=0.0015), with tonic–atonic ('drop attack') seizures reduced by a median 42.5% on rufinamide versus a 1.4% increase on placebo (p<0.0001) and higher 50% responder rates for both total and tonic–atonic seizures. A 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis specific to Lennox–Gastaut syndrome (Sharawat IK et al., PMID: 34273668) pooled five placebo-controlled studies (265 rufinamide, 203 placebo patients) and found an average percentage reduction in total seizure frequency per 28 days of 29.3% versus 8.3% (difference 20.9%, 95% CI 14.4% to 27.3% as printed in the record; p<0.00001), at the cost of more treatment-emergent adverse events (60.2% vs 50.7%; RR 1.24 relative, 95% CI 1.03 to 1.51). Somnolence (24.3% vs 12.5%) and vomiting (21.6% vs 6.3%) were the commonest harms in the pivotal trial. The evidence is one pivotal trial plus small pooled studies, all short-term, in a syndrome where complete seizure freedom is rare. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): rufinamide reduces total and drop-attack seizures in Lennox–Gastaut syndrome by a clinically useful margin, with mild-to-moderate tolerability costs.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — adjunctive rufinamide reduces total and drop-attack seizures in Lennox–Gastaut syndrome versus placebo

title: Cannabidiol for tuberous sclerosis seizures: 48.6% fewer seizures at 25 mg/kg/day versus 26.5% on placebo — and 50 mg added diarrhoea and liver-enzyme rises, not benefit
question: In patients with tuberous sclerosis complex and drug-resistant seizures, does adjunctive cannabidiol reduce seizure frequency versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the GWPCARE6 trial (Thiele EA et al., PMID: 33346789) randomised 224 patients aged 1–65 years with tuberous sclerosis complex and medication-resistant epilepsy to cannabidiol 25 mg/kg/day, cannabidiol 50 mg/kg/day, or placebo for 16 weeks. Seizures fell by 48.6% (95% CI 40.4% to 55.8%) on the 25 mg dose and 47.5% (39.0% to 54.8%) on the 50 mg dose versus 26.5% (14.9% to 36.5%) on placebo — a percentage reduction from placebo of 30.1% (95% CI 13.9% to 43.3%; P<.001) and 28.5% (11.9% to 42.0%; nominal P=.002) respectively, i.e. the higher dose added nothing on efficacy. It did add harm: diarrhoea in 31% (25 mg) and 56% (50 mg) versus 25% on placebo, somnolence in 13% and 26% versus 9%, discontinuations for adverse events in 8, 10 and 2 patients respectively, and elevated liver transaminases in 28 cannabidiol patients (18.9%) versus none on placebo. A meta-analysis across the Dravet, Lennox–Gastaut and tuberous sclerosis randomised trials (Talwar A et al., PMID: 36206805) found the same pattern for tuberous sclerosis specifically (odds of a ≥50% seizure reduction OR 1.99 relative, 95% CI 1.06 to 3.76) alongside more adverse and serious adverse events overall. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): cannabidiol reduces tuberous sclerosis seizures versus placebo, the 25 mg/kg/day dose carries the better safety profile, and liver-enzyme and interaction monitoring are part of the treatment, not an afterthought.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — adjunctive cannabidiol reduces TSC-associated seizures versus placebo, with the 25 mg/kg/day dose offering the better safety profile

title: Eslicarbazepine acetate as a focal-seizure adjunct: responders 34% at 800 mg and 43% at 1200 mg versus 20% on placebo — efficacy climbs with dose, and so do dropouts
question: In adults with refractory focal seizures, does adjunctive eslicarbazepine acetate reduce seizure frequency versus placebo?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — in the pivotal phase III trial (Elger C et al., PMID: 19243424), 402 adults with refractory partial-onset seizures on one to two antiepileptic drugs had responder rates of 20% on placebo versus 23% on eslicarbazepine acetate 400 mg, 34% on 800 mg and 43% on 1200 mg once daily, with median relative reductions in seizure frequency of 16%, 26%, 36% and 45% respectively (seizure frequency significantly lower than placebo at 1200 mg, p=0.0003, and 800 mg, p=0.0028). A 2022 meta-analysis of ten randomised trials (2,565 people; Fei Y et al., PMID: 35911890) found the same dose pattern: in adults, 400 mg/day did not improve response, 800 mg/day improved the response rate (OR 2.16 relative, 95% CI 1.65 to 2.83) without significantly increasing severe adverse events, and 1200 mg/day improved response (OR 2.49 relative) but significantly increased severe adverse events (OR 3.72 relative). In the pivotal trial, discontinuation for adverse events rose with dose — 3.9% on placebo, 4% at 400 mg, 8.2% at 800 mg and 19.6% at 1200 mg — with dizziness, headache and diplopia the commonest effects. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): adjunctive eslicarbazepine acetate at 800–1200 mg once daily reduces refractory focal seizures, with 800 mg the better-tolerated effective dose and the benefit in children not established by the pooled record.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — adjunctive eslicarbazepine acetate 800–1200 mg once daily reduces refractory focal seizures versus placebo, with 800 mg the better-tolerated effective dose
