title: Zonisamide for refractory focal seizures: Cochrane's pool says one extra patient halves their seizures for every six treated — with one extra withdrawal for every fifteen
question: In adults with refractory focal seizures, does adjunctive zonisamide reduce seizure frequency versus placebo?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — in the pivotal dose-ranging trial (Brodie MJ et al., PMID: 15660766), 351 patients with refractory partial seizures on one to three antiepileptic drugs had a 51.2% decrease in complex partial seizure frequency on zonisamide 500 mg/day versus 16.3% on placebo (p<0.0001), with complex partial responder rates of 52.3% versus 21.3% (p<0.001) and a significant dose-response for all seizures. A contemporary review of the four randomised trials (848 patients; Brodie MJ, PMID: 16316744) found the same pattern at doses of at least 300 mg/day. The updated Cochrane review (Brigo F et al., PMID: 32715463) pooled eight studies (1,636 participants) and found, on moderate-certainty evidence, that zonisamide 300–500 mg/day raised the chance of at least a 50% relative reduction in seizure frequency versus placebo (RR 1.90 relative, 95% CI 1.63 to 2.22; number needed to treat 6), while also raising treatment withdrawal (RR 1.59 relative, 95% CI 1.18 to 2.13; number needed to harm 15) and specific harms including ataxia (RR 3.85 relative), somnolence (RR 1.52 relative), agitation (RR 2.35 relative) and anorexia (RR 2.74 relative). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): adjunctive zonisamide at 300–500 mg/day is an effective option for refractory focal seizures, with roughly one extra responder for every six treated and one extra withdrawal for every fifteen.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — adjunctive zonisamide 300–500 mg/day increases ≥50% responder rates in refractory focal epilepsy versus placebo (RR 1.90 relative, NNT 6)

title: Levetiracetam for juvenile myoclonic epilepsy: in the only randomised trial, 58.3% halved their myoclonic days versus 23.3% on placebo — a big effect resting on 120 patients
question: In patients with juvenile myoclonic epilepsy, does adjunctive levetiracetam reduce myoclonic seizure days versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the only randomised trial in this population (Noachtar S et al., PMID: 18285535) randomised 122 adolescents and adults with idiopathic generalised epilepsy with myoclonic seizures — 93.4% of them juvenile myoclonic epilepsy — who were still having myoclonic seizures on monotherapy, to adjunctive levetiracetam 3000 mg/day or placebo. A reduction of at least 50% in days per week with myoclonic seizures occurred in 58.3% on levetiracetam versus 23.3% on placebo (p<0.001; OR 4.77 relative, 95% CI 2.12 to 10.77), freedom from myoclonic seizures during the evaluation period in 25.0% versus 5.0% (p=0.004), and freedom from all seizure types in 21.7% versus 1.7% (p<0.001). The only adverse events more frequent with levetiracetam were somnolence and neck pain. The effect size is large and internally consistent, but it rests on a single trial of 120 evaluable patients with a 12-week evaluation period, in a condition treated for decades. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): adjunctive levetiracetam substantially reduces myoclonic seizure days in juvenile myoclonic epilepsy over the short term; long-term and comparative evidence is absent from the randomised record.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — adjunctive levetiracetam reduces myoclonic seizure days in juvenile myoclonic epilepsy versus placebo in a single randomised trial

title: Stopping epilepsy medicine after remission: the MRC trial says 41% recur within 2 years of withdrawal versus 22% who continue — a real, front-loaded risk that does not appear to ruin long-term prognosis
question: In people with epilepsy in sustained remission, does withdrawing antiseizure medication increase seizure recurrence versus continuing treatment?
balance: LIKELY (harm) — on the recurrence question the randomised record is unusually direct: the MRC Antiepileptic Drug Withdrawal Study (PMID: 1673736) randomised 1,013 patients who had been seizure-free for at least 2 years to continued treatment or slow withdrawal, and by 2 years after randomisation 78% of those who continued treatment remained seizure-free versus 59% of those who withdrew — i.e. recurrence in 22% versus 41% over the first 2 years — although thereafter the difference between the groups diminished. The study's prognostic index (PMID: 8518603) identifies who carries the risk: age 16 or older, taking more than one antiepileptic drug, seizures after starting treatment, a history of primary or secondarily generalised tonic-clonic seizures, a history of myoclonic seizures, and an abnormal EEG all increased recurrence risk, while longer seizure-free time reduced it. The long-term follow-up of patients who did recur (Chadwick D et al., PMID: 8917053) adds the balancing fact: by 3 years after a recurrence 95% had experienced a further 1-year remission and by 5 years 90% a further 2-year remission, with no evidence that having discontinued treatment before the recurrence worsened the outcome — withdrawal raises the short-term chance of a seizure without demonstrably worsening the long-term prognosis of the epilepsy. PROPOSED LIKELY (harm): withdrawing antiseizure medication after at least 2 years' remission roughly doubles 2-year recurrence (41% vs 22%), a harm that is front-loaded and individually predictable in part, but not shown to damage long-term remission prospects.
stamp: LIKELY (harm) — withdrawing antiseizure medication after ≥2 years' remission increases seizure recurrence over the next 1–2 years (41% vs 22%), without demonstrated long-term prognostic harm

title: First epilepsy medicine after 65: lamotrigine, gabapentin and carbamazepine controlled seizures equally in 593 older patients — but only 35.5% stayed on carbamazepine for a year, versus 55.8% on lamotrigine
question: In older adults with new-onset epilepsy, how do lamotrigine, gabapentin and carbamazepine compare on seizure control and tolerability?
balance: SPLIT — seizure control did not separate the three drugs, but tolerability did, decisively. In the VA Cooperative trial (Rowan AJ et al., PMID: 15955935), 593 elderly patients with newly diagnosed seizures (mean age 72 years, most commonly after cerebral infarction, taking an average of seven comedications) were randomised to gabapentin 1500 mg/day, lamotrigine 150 mg/day or carbamazepine 600 mg/day for 12 months, with retention in the trial as the primary outcome. Early terminations were 44.2% on lamotrigine, 51% on gabapentin and 64.5% on carbamazepine (p=0.0002), and terminations for adverse events were 12.1%, 21.6% and 31% respectively (p=0.001) — lamotrigine significantly better than carbamazepine (p<0.0001) and gabapentin (p=0.015) on adverse-event termination, and gabapentin significantly better than carbamazepine (p=0.008) on retention. There were no significant differences in seizure-free rate at 12 months. PROPOSED SPLIT: for an older adult starting treatment, the record supports choosing on tolerability — lamotrigine first, gabapentin second, carbamazepine last — while expecting similar seizure control from all three.
stamp: SPLIT — seizure control similar for lamotrigine, gabapentin and carbamazepine in older adults, but retention and tolerability favour lamotrigine, then gabapentin, over carbamazepine

title: Asenapine for acute schizophrenia: better than placebo across its four-trial programme (−3.6 PANSS points, responder OR 1.9 relative) — effective, and honestly average for its class
question: In adults with acute schizophrenia, does asenapine improve symptoms versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in the pivotal placebo- and risperidone-controlled trial (Potkin SG et al., PMID: 17960962), 174 patients with acute schizophrenia received sublingual asenapine 5 mg twice daily, placebo, or risperidone 3 mg twice daily for 6 weeks; asenapine beat placebo significantly on PANSS total score (p<.005), the negative subscale (p=.01), the general psychopathology subscale (p<.005), the positive subscale (p=.01) and CGI-S (p<.01), with overall adverse-event incidence comparable to placebo, whereas risperidone was associated with substantial weight gain and prolactin elevation. A meta-analysis pooling the four asenapine development-programme trials (Szegedi A et al., PMID: 23290326) confirmed superiority over placebo on PANSS total change (−3.6 points by LOCF, p=.002; −4.1 by MMRM, p=.001) with responder odds of OR 1.9 relative (p<.001), an effect comparable to the active controls in the same trials but somewhat lower than effect sizes reported in the literature for other second-generation antipsychotics. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): asenapine is an effective acute-schizophrenia treatment of modest average effect size — real, replicated across its development programme, and not a standout among its class.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — asenapine improves acute schizophrenia symptoms versus placebo by a modest average margin, comparable to active controls

title: Paliperidone ER for acute schizophrenia: −6.01 PANSS points versus placebo across 13 studies — effective at all three doses, with harms under-reported in the published versions
question: In adults with acute schizophrenia, does paliperidone extended-release improve symptoms versus placebo?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — in the pivotal 6-week trial (Kane J et al., PMID: 17092691), 628 patients with acute schizophrenia received paliperidone extended-release 6, 9 or 12 mg once daily or placebo (with an olanzapine arm for assay sensitivity); all three paliperidone doses significantly improved PANSS total score, all PANSS Marder factor scores (p<0.001) and personal and social functioning (p<0.001) versus placebo, with significantly more patients achieving at least a 30% relative reduction in PANSS total score (p<0.001), mean weight change under 1 kg, and movement-disorder adverse events similar to placebo at 6 mg but higher at 9 and 12 mg. An individual-participant-data meta-analysis (Hodkinson A et al., PMID: 34429113) pooling 13 paliperidone studies (3,821 participants) found a PANSS advantage of −6.01 points versus placebo (95% CI −8.7 to −3.32), with low heterogeneity (I²=4.3%) — while also showing that clinical study reports recorded nearly twice as many adverse events (relative difference 1.93) and almost eight times as many serious adverse events (relative difference 7.93) as the journal publications of the same trials. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): paliperidone extended-release is an effective acute-schizophrenia treatment with a consistent moderate effect; its published tolerability picture is rosier than the underlying study reports justify.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — paliperidone extended-release improves acute schizophrenia symptoms versus placebo (pooled PANSS −6.01 points) across a consistent trial programme

title: Amisulpride for acute schizophrenia: 400–800 mg/day topped the dose-response curve and beat haloperidol on parkinsonism — but the anchor trials never included a true placebo
question: In adults with acute schizophrenia, does amisulpride improve symptoms versus placebo and versus haloperidol?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the anchor evidence is comparative rather than placebo-controlled, and this shelf says so plainly. In the dose-ranging trial (Puech A et al., PMID: 9696517), 319 patients with acute exacerbation of schizophrenia received fixed doses of amisulpride 400, 800 or 1200 mg/day, haloperidol 16 mg/day, or amisulpride 100 mg/day as a potentially subtherapeutic comparator for 4 weeks: efficacy on BPRS total score and the PANSS positive subscale followed a bell-shaped dose-response curve, with 400 and 800 mg/day the most effective treatments for positive symptoms, and parkinsonism did not increase significantly at 400–1200 mg/day versus the 100 mg group, whereas the increase was significant for haloperidol (p<0.05). A pooled analysis of three studies (612 patients; Peuskens J et al., PMID: 12126869) found amisulpride 400–800 mg/day improved the BPRS anxiety/depression subscore more than haloperidol 15–20 mg/day and risperidone 8 mg/day combined comparators (mean improvement 5.6 ± 6.1 versus 4.4 ± 5.5 and 3.7 ± 4.7; p=0.011), with a larger advantage in more severely depressed patients (p=0.001) visible from the second week. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): amisulpride at 400–800 mg/day treats acute positive symptoms at least as well as haloperidol with less parkinsonism, and helps depressive symptoms in acute episodes — but no true placebo arm exists in the anchor record, which caps the stamp.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — amisulpride 400–800 mg/day treats acute positive symptoms with less parkinsonism than haloperidol, on comparative (not placebo-controlled) anchor evidence

title: Adding lurasidone to lithium or valproate for bipolar I depression: −17.1 versus −13.5 on the MADRS at 6 weeks — a modest, real add-on effect from one trial
question: In adults with bipolar I depression already taking lithium or valproate, does adjunctive lurasidone improve depression versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — this shelf asks the adjunctive question only: in PREVAIL 1 (Loebel A et al., PMID: 24170221), 348 patients with bipolar I depression who had had an insufficient response to mood-stabiliser monotherapy were randomised to 6 weeks of adjunctive lurasidone or placebo, each added to therapeutic levels of lithium or valproate. Lurasidone reduced the MADRS total score significantly more than placebo at week 6 (−17.1 versus −13.5; effect size 0.34), with parallel advantages on CGI-BP depression severity (−1.96 versus −1.51; effect size 0.36), anxiety symptoms, quality of life and functional impairment. Discontinuation for adverse events was actually lower on lurasidone than placebo (6.0% vs 7.9%); the commonest lurasidone adverse events were nausea, somnolence, tremor, akathisia and insomnia, and changes in weight, lipids and glycaemic measures were minimal over 6 weeks. The margin over placebo is modest — about 3.6 MADRS points on top of a large placebo-plus-mood-stabiliser response — and it rests on this single adjunctive trial. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): adding lurasidone to lithium or valproate improves bipolar I depression modestly over 6 weeks. The lurasidone monotherapy question is a different shelf's business (#706) and is not re-carded here.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — adjunctive lurasidone improves bipolar I depression versus placebo in patients already taking lithium or valproate, by a modest margin in a single trial

title: Cognitive remediation for schizophrenia: 40 studies and 2,104 participants show durable gains in cognition — and in daily functioning when rehabilitation comes with it
question: In people with schizophrenia, does cognitive remediation improve cognition and functioning versus control interventions?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the anchor for this shelf is itself the field's reference meta-analysis (Wykes T et al., PMID: 21406461): 40 studies (109 reports) with 2,104 participants, at least 70% diagnosed with schizophrenia and all receiving standard care, comparing cognitive remediation against control interventions. The pooled effects on global cognition and functioning were durable at follow-up and were described by the authors as small-to-moderate; the effect on symptoms was small and disappeared at follow-up. No treatment element — remediation approach, duration, or computer use — was associated with cognitive outcome, methodological rigour did not moderate any effect (even the most rigorous studies showed similar small-to-moderate effects), and remediation worked better in clinically stable patients. Functioning effects were significantly stronger when cognitive remediation was delivered together with other psychiatric rehabilitation, and much larger when a strategic (transfer-focused) approach was combined with adjunctive rehabilitation. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): cognitive remediation produces durable small-to-moderate gains in cognition and, especially when paired with rehabilitation, in everyday functioning — the record's own abstract reports no pooled point estimates, which is why this shelf grades the consistency and durability of the finding rather than a number it does not print.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — cognitive remediation produces durable small-to-moderate improvements in cognition and, with adjunctive rehabilitation, functioning in schizophrenia

title: Vilazodone for major depression: one 8-week trial beat placebo on the MADRS by 2.5 points, with response 44% versus 30% — and diarrhoea in nearly a third
question: In adults with major depressive disorder, does vilazodone improve depression versus placebo?
balance: One phase 3 trial (Khan A et al., PMID: 21527122) randomised 481 adults with major depressive disorder to vilazodone titrated to 40 mg/day or placebo for 8 weeks. Vilazodone improved the primary outcome — least-squares mean MADRS change −13.3 versus −10.8 on placebo (p=.009) — and the response rate was 44% versus 30% (p=.002), but remission did not separate significantly on either the MADRS (27.3% vs 20.3%, p=.066) or the HDRS-17 (24.2% vs 17.7%, p=.088). The benefit is therefore real but modest: a roughly 2.5-point extra MADRS fall and about one extra responder in seven, bought with diarrhoea in 31% versus 11%, nausea in 26% versus 6%, and discontinuation for adverse events in 5.1% versus 1.7%. Sexual function and weight were no different from placebo in this trial. This shelf rests on a single short trial with no active comparator, so how vilazodone compares with established antidepressants is not answered here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a genuine but modest short-term antidepressant effect, with tolerability — not efficacy — the main practical limit.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — vilazodone 40 mg/day modestly improves depression scores and response rates versus placebo over 8 weeks, at the cost of prominent gastrointestinal side effects

title: Levomilnacipran ER for major depression: all three doses beat placebo on the MADRS, with a dose gradient from −3.2 to −4.9 points
question: In adults with major depressive disorder, does levomilnacipran extended-release improve depression versus placebo?
balance: One phase 3 trial (Asnis GM et al., PMID: 23561229) randomised 724 outpatients with major depressive disorder to placebo or fixed-dose levomilnacipran sustained release 40, 80 or 120 mg once daily for 8 weeks. Every dose beat placebo on the primary MADRS change, with a clear dose gradient in the least-squares mean difference: −3.23 (p=.0186), −3.99 (p=.0038) and −4.86 (p=.0005). The 80 mg and 120 mg doses also separated on disability (Sheehan Disability Scale), HDRS-17 and global impression measures; the 40 mg dose separated only on the primary scale. The common adverse events — headache, nausea, constipation, dry mouth, increased heart rate and hyperhidrosis — are the expected noradrenergic profile of a serotonin-noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor, and the record reports the drug as generally well tolerated. The evidence is a single short fixed-dose trial: no active comparator, no maintenance phase, and no remission rates in the record. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a consistent, dose-ordered short-term effect on depression scores, with comparative and long-term questions unanswered.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — levomilnacipran ER 40–120 mg/day improves depression scores versus placebo over 8 weeks, with noradrenergic-type side effects

title: Transdermal selegiline for major depression: one small 6-week outpatient trial found greater improvement on every scale — but its record reports no effect sizes
question: In adults with major depressive disorder, does transdermal selegiline improve depression versus placebo?
balance: The randomised record carded here is one trial (Bodkin JA et al., PMID: 12411221): 177 adult outpatients with major depressive disorder received a transdermal selegiline patch (20 mg over a 20-cm² patch, once daily) or placebo for 6 weeks, on a tyramine-restricted diet. The record reports greater improvement with selegiline on all measures used — the 17- and 28-item Hamilton scales, the Montgomery–Åsberg scale and Clinical Global Impression severity and improvement — with separation on the Hamilton and Montgomery–Åsberg scores as early as week 1. Critically, the record reports no numeric effect sizes, response rates or remission rates, so the size of the benefit cannot be stated from the evidence in hand. Tolerability in the trial was close to placebo apart from application-site reactions, with no orthostatic hypotensive or hypertensive reactions observed. One small, short trial with qualitative reporting is the definition of a weak base. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): transdermal selegiline may improve major depression over 6 weeks, but the magnitude is unquantified in this record and replication at this dose and diet condition is not carded here.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — a single small short trial reports greater improvement with transdermal selegiline on all depression measures, but the record gives no numeric effect sizes

title: SWITCH: decompressive craniectomy for severe deep brain haemorrhage — unfavourable outcome 44% versus 58%, a difference that just missed significance in a trial stopped early for funding
question: In patients with severe deep supratentorial intracerebral haemorrhage, does decompressive craniectomy plus medical treatment improve survival and function versus medical treatment alone?
balance: SWITCH (Beck J et al., PMID: 38761811) randomised 201 adults aged 18–75 with severe deep (basal ganglia or thalamus) intracerebral haemorrhage in 42 European stroke centres to decompressive craniectomy plus best medical treatment or best medical treatment alone; 197 gave delayed consent and the trial was stopped early for lack of funding. The primary outcome — modified Rankin Scale 5–6 (severe disability or death) at 180 days — occurred in 42 of 95 (44%) surgical patients versus 55 (58%) medical patients (adjusted risk ratio 0.77, 95% CI 0.59 to 1.01; adjusted risk difference −13%, 95% CI −26 to 0; p=0.057). The per-protocol analysis leaned the same way (47% vs 60%; aRR 0.76, 0.58 to 1.00). Severe adverse events were similar (41% vs 44%). The authors themselves call this weak evidence, and the record is explicit that survival in both groups is associated with severe disability and that the results do not apply to haemorrhages in other locations. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): the point estimate favours surgery by a clinically large margin, but an underpowered, early-stopped trial whose confidence interval touches no-effect cannot carry a stronger stamp.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — decompressive craniectomy may reduce death or severe disability after severe deep intracerebral haemorrhage, but the one trial stopped early and its primary result was not significant

title: CHANCE-2: in CYP2C19 loss-of-function carriers after minor stroke or TIA, ticagrelor cut 90-day stroke to 6.0% versus 7.6% on clopidogrel — with more total bleeding but no more severe bleeding
question: In CYP2C19 loss-of-function carriers with minor stroke or high-risk TIA, does ticagrelor plus aspirin prevent recurrent stroke better than clopidogrel plus aspirin?
balance: CHANCE-2 (Wang Y et al., PMID: 34708996) randomised 6,412 Chinese patients with minor ischaemic stroke or TIA who carried CYP2C19 loss-of-function alleles, within 24 hours of onset, to ticagrelor (180 mg load, then 90 mg twice daily) or clopidogrel (300 mg load, then 75 mg daily) for 90 days, both with aspirin for the first 21 days. Stroke within 90 days occurred in 191 patients (6.0%) on ticagrelor versus 243 (7.6%) on clopidogrel — hazard ratio 0.77 (95% CI 0.64 to 0.94; p=0.008), a 23% relative risk reduction with absolute rates of 6.0% versus 7.6% printed beside it. Severe or moderate bleeding did not differ (0.3% in both groups), but any bleeding was more common on ticagrelor (5.3% vs 2.5%). The gain is real but modest in absolute terms — about 1.6 fewer strokes per 100 patients treated — and it is proven only in a genotype-selected, almost entirely Han Chinese population treated within 24 hours. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a genotype-guided switch that helps the subgroup in whom clopidogrel activation is impaired, not a general reason to prefer ticagrelor after stroke.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in CYP2C19 loss-of-function carriers, ticagrelor plus short-course aspirin modestly lowers 90-day stroke risk versus clopidogrel plus aspirin, with more minor bleeding

title: SPS3: adding clopidogrel to aspirin after lacunar stroke did not prevent recurrence — it doubled major haemorrhage and raised mortality; a lower blood-pressure target only trended to benefit
question: In patients with recent lacunar stroke, does adding clopidogrel to aspirin prevent recurrent stroke versus aspirin alone, and at what bleeding cost?
balance: SPS3 tested two questions in 3,020 patients with recent MRI-defined lacunar stroke. The antiplatelet comparison (PMID: 22931315) was double-blind: clopidogrel 75 mg plus aspirin 325 mg versus aspirin alone over a mean 3.4 years. Recurrent stroke was not significantly reduced (2.5% versus 2.7% per year; HR 0.92, 95% CI 0.72 to 1.16), nor was recurrent ischaemic stroke (HR 0.82, 0.63 to 1.09) or disabling/fatal stroke (HR 1.06). Major haemorrhage almost doubled (2.1% versus 1.1% per year; HR 1.97, 1.41 to 2.71; p<0.001) and all-cause mortality rose (113 versus 77 deaths; HR 1.52, 1.14 to 2.04; p=0.004), a difference not explained by fatal haemorrhage. The blood-pressure comparison (PMID: 23726159), in the same factorial cohort, achieved systolic pressures of 127 versus 138 mm Hg and found non-significant reductions in all stroke (HR 0.81, 0.64 to 1.03; p=0.08) with a significant reduction in intracerebral haemorrhage (HR 0.37, 0.15 to 0.95; p=0.03). PROPOSED LIKELY (harm): for the shelf's question the answer is unusually clear — long-term dual antiplatelet therapy after lacunar stroke buys bleeding and death, not protection; the gentler blood-pressure signal is hypothesis-supporting, not proven.
stamp: LIKELY (harm) — long-term clopidogrel added to aspirin after lacunar stroke increases major bleeding and death without reducing recurrent stroke

title: VNS-REHAB: implanted vagus nerve stimulation paired with rehab improved arm scores by 2.6 extra points, with 47% versus 24% achieving a meaningful response at 90 days
question: In patients with upper-limb weakness after ischaemic stroke, does vagus nerve stimulation paired with rehabilitation improve arm function versus rehabilitation with sham stimulation?
balance: VNS-REHAB (Dawson J et al., PMID: 33894832) randomised 108 patients with moderate-to-severe arm weakness at least 9 months after ischaemic stroke, in 19 UK and US services, to rehabilitation paired with active implanted vagus nerve stimulation or with sham (0 mA) stimulation; everyone received the implant, and patients, therapists and assessors were masked. After 6 weeks of in-clinic therapy, Fugl-Meyer Upper Extremity scores rose 5.0 points (SD 4.4) with active stimulation versus 2.4 (3.8) with sham — a between-group difference of 2.6 points (95% CI 1.0 to 4.2; p=0.0014). At 90 days a clinically meaningful response was achieved by 23 of 53 (47%) versus 13 of 55 (24%) — a difference of 24 percentage points (95% CI 6 to 41; p=0.0098) alongside the absolute rates of 47% and 24%. One surgery-related serious adverse event (vocal cord paresis) occurred, in the control group. The effect is statistically solid but modest in size, from a single industry pivotal trial, in a chronic population with an implanted device and its surgical burden. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a real incremental gain over intensive rehabilitation alone, to be weighed against implantation and cost.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — vagus nerve stimulation paired with rehabilitation modestly improves arm impairment in chronic ischaemic stroke, in one pivotal sham-controlled trial

title: RATULS: robot-assisted arm training did not improve arm function (44% success versus 42% on usual care) in the largest trial — while pooled smaller trials in Cochrane show small gains
question: In patients with upper-limb impairment after stroke, does robot-assisted training improve arm function versus usual care or matched therapy?
balance: The evidence genuinely splits by trial size. RATULS (Rodgers H et al., PMID: 31128926), a pragmatic UK trial of 770 stroke patients with moderate-to-severe upper-limb limitation, found Action Research Arm Test success at 3 months in 103 of 232 (44%) with robot-assisted training, 118 of 234 (50%) with an enhanced upper-limb therapy programme, and 85 of 203 (42%) with usual care — robot training did not improve function versus usual care (adjusted OR 1.17, 98.3% CI 0.70 to 1.96) or versus matched therapy (aOR 0.78, 0.48 to 1.27). The Cochrane review (Mehrholz J et al., PMID: 30175845), pooling 45 trials and 1,619 participants — mostly far smaller than RATULS — found electromechanical and robot-assisted training improved activities of daily living (SMD 0.31, 95% CI 0.09 to 0.52), arm function (SMD 0.32, 0.18 to 0.46) and arm strength (SMD 0.46, 0.16 to 0.77), on high-quality-rated evidence but with wide variation in dose, device and patients. PROPOSED SPLIT: small pooled trials say a small benefit exists; the one large pragmatic trial, testing the intervention as actually deliverable, says it does not beat usual care — routine adoption is not supported by RATULS, and any real effect is likely small and dose- or device-dependent.
stamp: SPLIT — the largest pragmatic trial found no benefit over usual care, while a Cochrane pool of smaller trials found small improvements in arm function and daily activities

title: DARS: adding co-careldopa to stroke rehabilitation did not improve walking — 41% walked independently at 8 weeks versus 45% on placebo
question: In patients recovering from stroke, does adding co-careldopa (levodopa) to occupational and physical therapy improve walking and arm function versus therapy alone?
balance: DARS (Ford GA et al., PMID: 31122493) randomised 593 patients, on average 18 days after ischaemic or haemorrhagic stroke and unable to walk 10 metres, at 51 UK stroke rehabilitation services to 6 weeks of co-careldopa or matched placebo taken 45–60 minutes before routine occupational and physical therapy sessions. The primary outcome — walking independently (Rivermead Mobility Index ≥7) at 8 weeks — was reached by 125 of 308 (41%) on co-careldopa versus 127 of 285 (45%) on placebo (OR 0.78, 95% CI 0.53 to 1.15): no evidence of benefit, with the point estimate favouring placebo. Mortality at 12 months did not differ (7% vs 6%), serious adverse events were largely similar, and vomiting during therapy was more frequent on the drug (6.2% vs 3.2%). This is a large, double-blind, pragmatic trial that directly tests the dopaminergic-enhancement hypothesis at a deliverable dose and timing, and it fails it. PROPOSED LIKELY (no benefit): co-careldopa as given in DARS should not be added to routine stroke rehabilitation to improve walking; different doses, timings or subgroups remain speculation the authors raise but this trial does not support.
stamp: LIKELY (no benefit) — co-careldopa added to routine rehabilitation does not improve walking independence after stroke in a large blinded trial

title: Perampanel for generalised tonic-clonic seizures: 64% achieved at least a halving of seizures versus 40% on placebo, and 31% were seizure-free during maintenance versus 12%
question: In adults with idiopathic generalised epilepsy and primary generalised tonic-clonic seizures, does adjunctive perampanel reduce seizure frequency versus placebo?
balance: Study 332 (French JA et al., PMID: 26296511) randomised 164 patients aged 12 and over with drug-resistant primary generalised tonic-clonic (PGTC) seizures in idiopathic generalised epilepsy to adjunctive perampanel (titrated from 2 mg to 8 mg/day) or placebo over 4 weeks of titration and 13 weeks of maintenance. Perampanel produced a greater median percent reduction in PGTC seizure frequency per 28 days and a higher 50% responder rate — 64.2% versus 39.5% (p=0.0019). During maintenance, 30.9% of perampanel patients achieved PGTC seizure freedom versus 12.3% on placebo. The most frequent adverse events were dizziness (32.1%) and fatigue (14.8%). The trial is a single, short, industry-funded study of 164 patients, and its abstract as indexed reports the median-change figures in garbled form; the responder and seizure-freedom proportions are the cleanest numbers in the record. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a large relative effect on a resistant population, held at POSSIBLE because one 17-week trial cannot speak to long-term control, behaviour effects, or comparison with other adjuncts. This shelf is the generalised-epilepsy question only; adjunctive perampanel in focal seizures is shelf #2349.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — adjunctive perampanel substantially reduces primary generalised tonic-clonic seizure frequency versus placebo in one randomised trial

title: MycarinG: rozanolixizumab lowered MG-ADL by about 3.4 points versus 0.8 on placebo at day 43 — headache in over a third was the price
question: In patients with generalised myasthenia gravis, does rozanolixizumab improve myasthenia activities-of-daily-living scores versus placebo?
balance: MycarinG (Bril V et al., PMID: 37059507) randomised 200 adults with acetylcholine-receptor or MuSK autoantibody-positive generalised myasthenia gravis (MGFA class II–IVa, MG-ADL at least 3, quantitative MG score at least 11) at 81 centres to weekly subcutaneous infusions for 6 weeks of rozanolixizumab 7 mg/kg, 10 mg/kg, or placebo. By day 43 the MG-ADL score had fallen by a least-squares mean of −3.37 (7 mg/kg) and −3.40 (10 mg/kg) versus −0.78 on placebo — differences of −2.59 (95% CI −4.09 to −1.25) and −2.62 (−3.99 to −1.16), both p<0.0001, a clinically meaningful margin on this scale with no advantage for the higher dose. Treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 81–83% on rozanolixizumab versus 67% on placebo, led by headache (45% and 38% versus 19%), diarrhoea and pyrexia; serious events were similar (8%, 10%, 9%) and there were no deaths. One 6-week phase 3 trial of an FcRn blocker: durability, retreatment cycles and infection risk over years are not in this record. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a clear short-term functional gain in antibody-positive disease, including the MuSK subgroup other agents often miss.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — rozanolixizumab improves MG-ADL scores versus placebo at 6 weeks in AChR- or MuSK-positive generalised myasthenia gravis

title: RAISE: daily self-injected zilucoplan lowered MG-ADL by 4.4 points versus 2.3 on placebo at 12 weeks in AChR-positive myasthenia
question: In patients with generalised myasthenia gravis, does zilucoplan improve myasthenia activities-of-daily-living scores versus placebo?
balance: RAISE (Howard JF et al., PMID: 37059508) randomised 174 adults with acetylcholine-receptor-positive generalised myasthenia gravis (MGFA class II–IV, MG-ADL at least 6, quantitative MG score at least 12) at 75 sites to daily self-injected subcutaneous zilucoplan 0.3 mg/kg or matched placebo for 12 weeks. The primary outcome — MG-ADL change at week 12 — was −4.39 (95% CI −5.28 to −3.50) on zilucoplan versus −2.30 (−3.17 to −1.43) on placebo, a least-squares mean difference of −2.09 (−3.24 to −0.95; p=0.0004), a clinically meaningful margin. Treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 77% versus 70%, most commonly injection-site bruising (16% vs 9%); serious events and serious infections were similar, and one death in each group (COVID-19 on zilucoplan, cerebral haemorrhage on placebo) was judged unrelated to study drug. As a complement C5 inhibitor, zilucoplan joins the mechanism tested for eculizumab on shelf #691, but in a self-administered daily peptide form and a broader AChR-positive population. One 12-week trial: long-term meningococcal and infection risk management and durability sit outside this record. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — zilucoplan improves MG-ADL scores versus placebo at 12 weeks in AChR-positive generalised myasthenia gravis

title: HERCULES: tolebrutinib cut 6-month confirmed disability progression to 22.6% versus 30.7% on placebo in non-relapsing secondary progressive MS — with more liver-enzyme elevations
question: In patients with non-relapsing secondary progressive multiple sclerosis, does tolebrutinib slow disability progression versus placebo?
balance: HERCULES (Fox RJ et al., PMID: 40202696) randomised 1,131 patients with non-relapsing secondary progressive multiple sclerosis — a population with no approved treatment — 2:1 to tolebrutinib 60 mg daily or placebo in an event-driven, double-blind trial with median follow-up of 133 weeks. Confirmed disability progression sustained at least 6 months occurred in 22.6% on tolebrutinib versus 30.7% on placebo (HR 0.69, 95% CI 0.55 to 0.88; p=0.003) — a 31% relative risk reduction with the absolute rates of 22.6% and 30.7% printed beside it, roughly 8 fewer progressors per 100 treated over the trial's follow-up. Serious adverse events were more common on tolebrutinib (15.0% vs 10.4%), and alanine aminotransferase rose above 3 times the upper limit of normal in 4.0% versus 1.6% — the liver signal that has shadowed this drug class. One large well-conducted trial in an untreated niche earns more than MAYBE, but a single trial with a hepatic warning and no approved status keeps it below LIKELY. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the first randomised evidence that progression independent of relapses can be slowed in this population, pending replication and liver-safety clarification.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — tolebrutinib lowers the risk of confirmed disability progression versus placebo in non-relapsing secondary progressive MS, with a liver-enzyme safety signal

title: Rivastigmine in dementia with Lewy bodies: 63% improved by at least 30% on neuropsychiatric measures versus 30% on placebo over 20 weeks — benefits faded after stopping
question: In people with dementia with Lewy bodies, does rivastigmine improve cognition, apathy and hallucinations versus placebo?
balance: The single randomised trial (McKeith I et al., PMID: 11145488) enrolled 120 patients with dementia with Lewy bodies in the UK, Spain and Italy, giving rivastigmine up to 12 mg daily or placebo for 20 weeks, followed by a 3-week washout. On treatment, rivastigmine patients were significantly less apathetic and anxious and had fewer delusions and hallucinations than controls; 37 patients (63%) on rivastigmine versus 18 (30%) on placebo showed at least 30% improvement from baseline on the neuropsychiatric assessment — both pre-defined primary efficacy measures differed significantly. Computerised and neuropsychological testing favoured rivastigmine, particularly on tasks with a substantial attentional component. After discontinuation the differences tended to disappear, marking this as a symptomatic, on-treatment effect. Nausea, vomiting and anorexia — the known cholinesterase-inhibitor effects — were more frequent on rivastigmine, though tolerability was judged acceptable in this multimorbid group. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a coherent behavioural and attentional benefit in a condition with few options, from one small 20-week trial conducted before modern diagnostic criteria settled. Rivastigmine for Parkinson's disease dementia is a different population, shelved at #1446.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — rivastigmine improves neuropsychiatric features and attention in dementia with Lewy bodies versus placebo over 20 weeks, in one small trial

title: Nabilone for agitation in Alzheimer's dementia: one 39-person crossover trial shows less agitation — and sedation in 45% of treatment phases
question: In people with moderate-to-severe Alzheimer's dementia and agitation, does nabilone reduce agitation versus placebo?
balance: The entire randomised case for nabilone in Alzheimer's agitation rests on one small trial: Herrmann 2019 (PMID: 31182351), a 14-week double-blind crossover in 39 people with moderate-to-severe Alzheimer's disease, found agitation lower on nabilone than placebo (Cohen Mansfield Agitation Inventory treatment difference −4.0, 95% CI −6.5 to −1.5), with total neuropsychiatric symptoms and caregiver distress also favouring nabilone — but sedation was far commoner on nabilone (45% versus 16%), and in the 25 participants who completed the Severe Impairment Battery, cognition favoured placebo (−4.6 points). The wider cannabinoid literature points the same way on symptoms and the same way on weakness of evidence: Bahji 2020 (PMID: 31835954) pooled nine trials and 205 participants across all cannabinoids (only one trial used nabilone) and found improvement on agitation and neuropsychiatric measures, rated low quality overall. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): a real but preliminary signal from very few patients, bought with substantial sedation, in a population where sedating drugs carry their own harms.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — one small crossover trial suggests nabilone reduces agitation in Alzheimer's disease, with frequent sedation and very low certainty

title: SENATOR: computer-generated prescribing advice changed almost nothing — ADRs 24.5% versus 24.8%, because clinicians acted on only ~15% of it
question: In hospitalised multimorbid older adults, does software-generated STOPP/START medication optimisation (SENATOR) reduce adverse drug reactions versus usual care?
balance: SENATOR asked whether software can do what medication-review teams do: generate STOPP/START-based optimisation advice for older, multimorbid hospital patients and thereby prevent adverse drug reactions (ADRs). The results paper (O'Mahony D et al., PMID: 32484850) randomised 1,537 patients at six European centres and found no difference at all in the primary outcome — probable or certain ADRs within 14 days occurred in 24.5% of the intervention group versus 24.8% of controls (odds ratio 0.98, 95% CI 0.77 to 1.24) — and no differences in mortality, rehospitalisation or quality of life. The trial's own explanation is in the same record: attending clinicians implemented only about 15% of the software-generated advice points, so SENATOR tested advice that was mostly never acted on. The protocol paper (Lavan AH et al., PMID: 30760204) shows the design was sound — blinded endpoint adjudication, a defined primary outcome — which makes the null a finding about implementation, not about whether optimising these prescriptions would help if actually done. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): as delivered, software-generated advice did not reduce ADRs; whether the same advice, implemented, would work remains untested by this trial.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — software-generated STOPP/START advice did not reduce adverse drug reactions in the SENATOR trial, with only about 15% of advice implemented

title: VISIBLE: swapping multifocals for single-lens glasses outdoors cut falls in active wearers (rate ratio 0.60) — and raised them in the least active
question: In older multifocal-glasses wearers who take part in regular outdoor activities, does switching to single-lens distance glasses reduce falls versus continuing multifocals?
balance: The VISIBLE trial (Haran MJ et al., PMID: 20501583) randomised 606 regular multifocal-glasses wearers (mean age 80, all at increased falls risk) to receive single-lens distance glasses with advice to wear them for walking and outdoor activities, or usual care. Overall, the result was null: an 8% relative reduction in falls that was not significant (incidence rate ratio 0.92, 95% CI 0.73 to 1.16), with the absolute fall counts not printed in the record. The pre-planned subgroup analyses split cleanly by behaviour: in people who regularly took part in outside activities, the intervention significantly reduced all falls (incidence rate ratio 0.60, 0.42 to 0.87), outside falls and injurious falls; in people with little outdoor activity, outside falls significantly increased. Only 54% of the intervention group used the distance glasses satisfactorily for at least seven of twelve months, so even the positive subgroup result was achieved with partial adherence. PROPOSED SPLIT: single-lens distance glasses for outdoor use help active multifocal wearers and may harm inactive ones — the right prescription depends on how much the person actually goes out.
stamp: SPLIT — single-lens distance glasses reduced falls in multifocal wearers who regularly go outdoors (rate ratio 0.60) but increased outside falls in the least active

title: Podiatry against falls: a multifaceted foot intervention cut the fall rate by a relative 36% in older people with disabling foot pain
question: In community-dwelling older people with foot pain/disability, does a multifaceted podiatry intervention prevent falls versus routine podiatry care?
balance: Spink 2011 (PMID: 21680622) randomised 305 community-dwelling older people with disabling foot pain and increased falls risk to a multifaceted podiatry intervention or routine podiatry care for twelve months. The intervention group had a 36% relative reduction in the rate of falls (incidence rate ratio 0.64, 95% CI 0.45 to 0.91; p=0.01), with the record printing 264 falls in total across both groups rather than arm-specific counts. The proportion of people who fell did not differ significantly (relative risk 0.85, 0.66 to 1.08), nor did multiple fallers (0.63, 0.38 to 1.04), and fractures were too few to judge (one versus seven; 0.14, 0.02 to 1.15). Strength, ankle range of motion and balance measures improved. Adherence was moderate: about half completed at least three-quarters of the requested exercise sessions. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a single, well-conducted trial shows fewer falls per person-year from a cheap, low-risk podiatry package in people whose feet hurt — without yet showing fewer people falling or fewer fractures.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a multifaceted podiatry intervention reduced the rate of falls in older people with disabling foot pain (rate ratio 0.64)

title: Home intervention teams against falls: 163 versus 204 falls in frail elders — and Cochrane agrees, but only for people selected as high-risk
question: In community-dwelling frail older people, does a home intervention team assessment and intervention programme prevent falls versus usual care?
balance: Two layers of evidence agree, with the same condition attached: home intervention works in people selected for high falls risk. The Falls-HIT trial (Nikolaus T et al., PMID: 12588572) randomised 360 frail older people (mean age 81.5) discharged from a geriatric hospital to a home intervention team — diagnostic home visit, hazard assessment, facilitated modifications, training in technical and mobility aids, and a reinforcement visit — versus assessment with recommendations and usual care. Over one year there were 163 falls in the intervention group versus 204 in controls, a 31% relative reduction (incidence rate ratio 0.69, 95% CI 0.51 to 0.97), concentrated in those with two or more falls in the prior year (rate ratio 0.63, 0.43 to 0.94). The Cochrane review of environmental interventions (Clemson L et al., PMID: 36893804) generalises the pattern across 22 studies: home fall-hazard interventions reduced the fall rate by a relative 26% overall (rate ratio 0.74, 0.61 to 0.91) and by a relative 38% in higher-risk selected populations (0.62, 0.56 to 0.70, high-certainty evidence), with no effect in unselected populations (1.05, 0.96 to 1.16). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): targeted home assessment and modification reduces falls in frail, high-risk older people; offered indiscriminately, it does not.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a home intervention team assessment and modification programme reduced falls in frail older people, with benefit concentrated in those at higher risk

title: HALT: a person-centred deprescribing programme cut regular antipsychotic use by 81.7% over 12 months with no rise in behavioural symptoms — in a single-arm study with no control group
question: In long-term aged-care residents prescribed antipsychotics, does a person-centred deprescribing intervention (HALT) achieve sustained antipsychotic reduction without worsening behavioural symptoms?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — HALT is a single-arm longitudinal programme, and everything on this shelf must be read with that limit in front. In the main outcome report (Brodaty H et al., PMID: 29941156), 139 residents of 23 nursing homes who had taken a regular antipsychotic for at least 3 months, without a primary psychotic illness or severe behavioural symptoms, went through a deprescribing protocol with education of general practitioners, pharmacists and nurses in non-pharmacological management: the number on regular antipsychotics fell by 81.7% (95% CI 72.4 to 89.0) over 12 months, without drug substitution and without a significant increase in as-needed antipsychotic or benzodiazepine use, and with no change in behavioural symptoms or in adverse outcomes including falls and hospitalisations. The companion analyses show both the mechanism and the leak: person-centred care training was what champions credited for the change (Chenoweth L et al., PMID: 30069476, the protocol and context paper for the programme; Jessop T et al., PMID: 28266282), and in Aerts L et al. (PMID: 31276255) 39 of 133 participants never ceased or were represcribed, most often at nurses' request (63.2%) for perceived — but not objectively measured — worsening agitation. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): sustained antipsychotic reduction of this size is clearly feasible in selected residents, but a single-arm study cannot show the programme caused it, nor exclude harm in the residents who were excluded or represcribed. The placebo-controlled withdrawal evidence is shelved separately at DART-AD #934.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — a single-arm programme achieved large sustained reductions, but without a comparator the effect cannot be separated from selection and secular change

title: Percutaneous tibial nerve stimulation for overactive bladder: 54.5% reported moderate or marked improvement versus 20.9% on sham in the SUmiT trial
question: In adults with overactive bladder, does percutaneous tibial nerve stimulation improve symptoms versus sham stimulation?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the anchor is a properly sham-controlled trial (Peters KM et al., PMID: 20171677): 220 adults with overactive bladder symptoms randomised 1:1 to 12 weekly percutaneous tibial nerve stimulation sessions or sham, with 54.5% of the stimulation group reporting moderately or markedly improved overall bladder symptoms at week 13 versus 20.9% on sham (p<0.001), statistically significant improvements in voiding-diary frequency, nighttime voids, moderate-to-severe urgency voids and urge incontinence episodes, and no serious device-related adverse events. The wider stimulation literature is supportive but less decisive: a systematic review and meta-analysis of electrical nerve stimulation protocols (Zomkowski K et al., PMID: 35119495) found tibial neurostimulation better than sacral neurostimulation for urge incontinence (mean difference 1.25 episodes, 95% CI 0.12 to 2.38, in 73 participants) but no superiority of any one stimulation protocol over others on frequency, nocturia, urgency or quality of life, with low-to-moderate effect sizes overall. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): twelve weeks of tibial nerve stimulation beats sham on symptoms in the short term; durability, maintenance schedules and standing against drug therapy are not settled by this record. Sacral neuromodulation is shelved separately at #912 and mirabegron at #149.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Functional incidental training in VA nursing homes: prompted voiding plus exercise improved incontinence, endurance and strength in a crossover trial — delivered by research staff, four times a day
question: In nursing-home residents with urinary incontinence, does functional incidental training (prompted voiding combined with exercise) reduce wet episodes versus usual care?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — functional incidental training (FIT) was tested in one randomised crossover trial in four Veterans Affairs nursing homes (Ouslander JG et al., PMID: 16108924): prompted voiding combined with individualised endurance and strength exercises, offered four times a day, five days a week, for eight weeks, delivered by trained research staff. Of 528 residents screened, 178 were eligible and 107 randomised (52 immediate, 55 delayed intervention); only 64 completed the intervention phase. The record reports a significant effect of FIT on virtually all measures of endurance, strength and urinary incontinence — but not on Functional Independence Measure scores for locomotion or toileting — with effects seen both against the control period and when the delayed group crossed over, deterioration when the first group crossed back to no intervention, and 43 of 64 completers (67%) classified as responders on at least one measure across endurance, strength and incontinence; no FIT-related adverse events occurred. Because the record gives no numeric effect size for wet episodes, and because delivery depended on research staff at an intensity ordinary nursing-home staffing rarely matches, the honest grade is feasibility-plus-signal rather than proven benefit. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence). Community pelvic-floor training is shelved separately at #486.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — one crossover trial with research-staff delivery and substantial attrition, and no numeric incontinence effect size in the record

title: Atomoxetine for neurogenic orthostatic hypotension: acute single-dose studies raised standing pressure, but the 4-week placebo-controlled trial found no symptom benefit
question: In adults with neurogenic orthostatic hypotension, does atomoxetine raise standing blood pressure and improve symptoms versus placebo?
balance: SPLIT — the evidence divides by treatment duration. The one trial of sustained treatment (Mwesigwa N et al., PMID: 39294522), a randomised double-blind placebo-controlled crossover study of 4-week atomoxetine periods in neurogenic orthostatic hypotension, found no difference on its primary symptom endpoint: orthostatic hypotension questionnaire composite scores of −0.3 ± 1.7 on atomoxetine versus −0.4 ± 1.5 on placebo at 2 weeks (P=0.806) and −0.6 ± 2.4 versus −0.5 ± 1.6 at 4 weeks (P=0.251), with no significant differences on the symptom or daily-activity subscales either; the drug was well tolerated. Set against that, a systematic review of the randomised literature (Jung YJ et al., PMID: 36647224) found only four randomised trials, mostly acute-dose, in which atomoxetine effectively increased systolic blood pressure and improved orthostatic symptoms, with effects most pronounced in central autonomic failure such as multiple system atrophy. PROPOSED SPLIT: a single dose can raise standing pressure in the laboratory; four weeks of treatment did not improve symptoms more than placebo in the trial designed to test exactly that. Droxidopa is shelved at #931/#1558 and pyridostigmine at #2691.
stamp: SPLIT — acute-dose trials show blood-pressure and symptom signals, but the only sustained-treatment trial found no benefit over placebo

title: Abdominal compression for orthostatic hypotension: a mild 10 mmHg binder applied before rising blunted the standing pressure drop in 13 patients — more compression added nothing
question: In adults with neurogenic orthostatic hypotension, does patient-controlled abdominal compression improve standing blood pressure versus sham compression?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the entire record for patient-controlled abdominal compression is one randomised crossover laboratory study of 13 adults with neurogenic orthostatic hypotension (Figueroa JJ et al., PMID: 25448247). Standing without a binder dropped systolic pressure by a median 57 mmHg; applying a mild 10 mmHg compression before rising blunted that drop to 50 mmHg with a conventional binder (P=.03) and 46 mmHg with an adjustable binder (P=.01). But squeezing harder did not help: subject-selected maximal tolerable compression while standing was associated with drops of 53 and 59 mmHg (both non-significant versus no binder), and easing back to a 'tolerable for prolonged use' level tended to worsen the drop (61 and 67 mmHg). Participants reported no difference between binders in preference or ease of use. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): a mild binder put on before standing probably takes a small edge off the postural drop — roughly 7 to 11 mmHg of a 57 mmHg fall — but this is 13 people, one laboratory, and surrogate blood-pressure readings rather than symptoms, falls or syncope. Atomoxetine in the same condition is shelved at #2870 and the fludrocortisone-versus-midodrine comparison at #2761.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — a 13-patient laboratory crossover study with a modest effect at one compression level

title: ACTIVE: cognitive training durably improved the trained ability in 2,832 older adults — speed and reasoning most, memory least — but everyday functioning did not improve at 2 years
question: In cognitively intact older adults, does cognitive training (memory, reasoning or speed of processing) improve trained cognitive abilities and everyday function versus control?
balance: SPLIT — ACTIVE (Ball K et al., PMID: 12425704) randomised 2,832 volunteers aged 65 to 94 to 10 sessions of memory, reasoning or speed-of-processing training or a no-contact control, and the answer depends entirely on which outcome you ask about. On the trained abilities, training worked and lasted: each intervention improved its targeted ability versus baseline, durable to 2 years (P<.001 for all), with reliable improvement immediately after training in 87% of speed-trained, 74% of reasoning-trained and only 26% of memory-trained participants; booster sessions in a 60% subsample enhanced and maintained speed and reasoning gains (speed booster 92% versus 68% without; reasoning 72% versus 49%). The gains were of a magnitude equivalent to the decline expected over 7 to 14 years without dementia. On everyday functioning — the outcome that would justify the effort clinically — no training effects were detected at 2 years, in a cohort that declined minimally in any arm. PROPOSED SPLIT: cognitive training is a reliable way to get better at the kind of task trained, for at least two years; whether that transfers to daily life was not shown here. The multidomain lifestyle approach (FINGER) is shelved separately at #332.
stamp: SPLIT — trained cognitive abilities improve durably, but everyday functioning did not improve at 2 years

title: Community occupational therapy in dementia: ten sessions produced very large gains in patients' daily functioning and caregivers' competence in one 135-person trial, still present at three months
question: In people with dementia and their caregivers, does community occupational therapy improve daily functioning and caregiver sense of competence versus usual care?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one single-blind randomised trial (Graff MJ et al., PMID: 17114212) of 135 community-living patients aged 65 or older with mild-to-moderate dementia and their primary caregivers: ten occupational-therapy sessions over five weeks, training patients to use aids compensating for cognitive decline and caregivers in coping and supervision. At six weeks the intervention group had improved far more than controls on every primary measure — process skills by 1.5 points (95% CI 1.3 to 1.7), daily-activity performance by −11.7 points (95% CI −13.6 to −9.7, lower is better), and caregiver sense of competence by 11.0 points (95% CI 9.2 to 12.8) — with effect sizes of 2.5, 2.3 and 1.2 respectively, a number needed to treat of 1.3 (95% CI 1.2 to 1.4) for clinically relevant improvement in motor and process skills, and benefits still significant at three months (effect sizes 2.7, 2.4 and 0.8). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the effects are implausibly large for a psychosocial intervention, which is exactly why the grade stops at possible — one trial, one Dutch memory-clinic setting, outcomes rated on scales the intervention explicitly trained toward. Cognitive stimulation therapy is shelved separately at #2344.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: FINALEX: a year of twice-weekly exercise — at home or in groups — slowed functional decline in Alzheimer's disease, with fewer falls and no increase in total care costs
question: In people with Alzheimer's disease living at home, does a structured home exercise programme slow functional decline versus usual care?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — FINALEX (Pitkälä KH et al., PMID: 23589097) randomised 210 home-dwelling patients with Alzheimer's disease, each living with a spousal caregiver, to group-based exercise, tailored home-based exercise, or usual community care, with both exercise arms training twice weekly for a full year. Everyone deteriorated, but deterioration on the Functional Independence Measure was significantly slower in both exercise groups at 6 months (P=.003) and 12 months (P=.015): 12-month FIM changes were −7.1 (95% CI −3.7 to −10.5) for home exercise, −10.3 (95% CI −6.7 to −13.9) for group exercise and −14.4 (95% CI −10.9 to −18.0) for controls. The exercise groups also had significantly fewer falls during the follow-up year, and total health and social service costs per dyad were not increased — $25,112 for home exercise (P=.13 versus control), $22,066 for group exercise (P=.03 versus control) and $34,121 for controls. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a sustained, intensive exercise programme slows — it does not stop — functional decline in home-dwelling Alzheimer's disease, from one Finnish trial of spousal-caregiver households. Exercise in dementia more broadly was dropped from this mining round where trials were already carded (DAPA); this shelf is the FINALEX question only.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: A five-day multicomponent programme — daylight, out of bed, activity, bedtime routine, quiet nights — strengthened rest/activity rhythms in nursing-home residents; sleep itself was not the measured outcome
question: In nursing-home residents with disrupted sleep and activity rhythms, does a multicomponent non-pharmacological intervention improve activity rhythms and sleep versus usual care?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the anchor trial (Martin JL et al., PMID: 17301040) randomised nursing-home residents with disrupted sleep/wake patterns to five days of a multicomponent intervention — increased outdoor bright light, efforts to keep residents out of bed during the day, structured physical activity, a bedtime routine, and reduced nighttime noise and light — or usual care. In the 100 residents with baseline and follow-up wrist actigraphy (mean age 87, 76% women), the intervention increased the duration of the active portion of the 24-hour rest/activity rhythm, primarily by shifting the rhythm's rise to an earlier time, and the findings persisted after adjustment for age, cognitive functioning, medical comorbidities and behavioural disturbances. That is a rhythm result, not a sleep result: the record reports modelled rhythm parameters, not hours slept or sleep quality. The surrounding literature is encouraging but thin — a systematic review of non-pharmacological sleep interventions in nursing homes (Shang B et al., PMID: 30795838) found 28 eligible studies across physical activity, light therapy, mind-body practices, complementary therapies and seven multicomponent programmes, with positive and promising signals but small trial numbers that 'should be interpreted cautiously'. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence). CBT-I basics are shelved elsewhere; this shelf is the institutional, non-CBT-I programme.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — one small trial measuring actigraphic rhythms over days, with sleep outcomes indirect

title: Sunbeam: progressive resistance and balance training cut the rate of falls by 55% relative in long-term aged care — one cluster trial of 16 facilities and 221 residents
question: In residents of long-term aged care, does progressive resistance and balance training (Sunbeam programme) prevent falls versus usual care?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the Sunbeam programme was tested in a cluster randomised trial of 16 residential aged-care facilities and 221 permanent residents (Hewitt J et al., PMID: 29402651): individually prescribed progressive resistance training plus balance exercise in a group setting, 50 hours over 25 weeks followed by a 6-month maintenance period, versus usual care. The rate of falls was reduced by 55% relative in the exercise group (incidence rate ratio 0.45, 95% CI 0.17 to 0.74) — the record does not print the absolute fall rates, so no absolute reduction can be quoted — and physical performance on the Short Physical Performance Battery also improved (P=.02), with no serious adverse events. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): this is the setting where falls trials have most often disappointed, and a single cluster trial with a wide confidence interval (the data are compatible with anything from an 83% to a 26% relative reduction) should not be upgraded beyond possible until replicated. The community Otago programme is shelved at #459 and the multifaceted care-home intervention of Becker at the companion falls shelves.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Deprescribing and mortality: the pooled randomised result is null (odds ratio 0.82) — but patient-specific deprescribing reduced mortality (0.62) while generalised education programmes did not (1.21)
question: In older adults, do deprescribing interventions reduce mortality and improve health outcomes versus usual care?
balance: SPLIT — Page AT et al. (PMID: 27077231) pooled 132 papers and 34,143 participants (mean age 73.8 ± 5.4 years) in which older adults had at least one medication deprescribed, and the answer splits cleanly by study design and by intervention type. In non-randomised studies deprescribing was associated with significantly lower mortality (odds ratio 0.32, 95% CI 0.17 to 0.60) — the design most exposed to confounding by who gets deprescribed. In randomised studies the pooled result was not significant (odds ratio 0.82, 95% CI 0.61 to 1.11). Within the randomised evidence, patient-specific deprescribing interventions significantly reduced mortality (odds ratio 0.62, 95% CI 0.43 to 0.88), while generalised educational programmes did not change it (odds ratio 1.21, 95% CI 0.86 to 1.69). PROPOSED SPLIT: 'deprescribing' is not one intervention — tailoring the withdrawal to the individual patient is the version with a randomised mortality signal; mailing education to prescribers is not. This cross-class synthesis complements, and does not duplicate, the drug-specific deprescribing shelves (#132, #500, #2759) and the medication-review shelf #930.
stamp: SPLIT — patient-specific deprescribing reduced mortality in randomised subgroup analysis; generalised educational programmes did not, and the overall randomised pool was null

title: Steroid-induced hyperglycaemia in hospital: the randomised record is scarce and mostly negative — the one strategy that helped was adding NPH insulin to a basal-bolus regimen
question: In hospitalised patients with glucocorticoid-induced hyperglycaemia, does scheduled insulin (basal or basal-bolus regimens adapted to the steroid dose) control glucose better than correction-only or oral-agent strategies, and at what hypoglycaemia cost?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the honest summary of this shelf is how little randomised evidence exists for a problem every hospital ward meets daily. The systematic review (Brooks D et al., PMID: 35940469) screened 1,230 references on non-COVID glucocorticoid-induced hyperglycaemia and included 33 articles, plus 7 studies of dexamethasone-associated hyperglycaemia in COVID-19, and found the randomised trials scarce, inconsistent in their definitions of hyperglycaemia, varied in strategy and endpoint, and generally not effective — the single exception being neutral protamine Hagedorn (NPH) insulin added to basal-bolus regimens. That means the common contest — scheduled basal or basal-bolus insulin versus correction-only sliding scale or oral agents — has never been settled by an adequate trial, and the review establishes no pooled hypoglycaemia price for any strategy. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): scheduled insulin for steroid-induced hyperglycaemia rests on physiology and practice habit rather than trial proof; the one randomised signal favours adding NPH insulin to a basal-bolus regimen, and the hypoglycaemia cost of any approach remains unquantified in the trial record.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — randomised evidence for scheduled insulin in glucocorticoid-induced hyperglycaemia is scarce and mostly null; only adding NPH insulin to basal-bolus showed benefit, and no hypoglycaemia price is established

title: Insulin for early cystic fibrosis diabetes: weight loss reversed in the one purpose-built trial, lungs unchanged — and the Cochrane pool still calls it unproven
question: In cystic fibrosis-related diabetes without fasting hyperglycaemia, does insulin therapy improve body mass index and lung function compared with an oral hypoglycaemic agent or no therapy?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the one multicentre randomised trial built for this question (Moran A et al., PMID: 19592632; 100 adults, 81 completing) found that a year of premeal insulin reversed the pre-treatment slide in body mass index in cystic fibrosis-related diabetes without fasting hyperglycaemia — from losing 0.30 BMI units in the year before therapy to gaining 0.39 units on therapy (P = 0.02) — while repaglinide's early gain (0.53 units, P = 0.01) was not sustained to 12 months and placebo changed nothing. No group differed in lung-function decline or hospitalisations. The Cochrane review (Onady GM et al., PMID: 33075159) is more guarded: across its included comparisons it found no conclusive between-group differences in blood glucose, lung function or nutritional status, on low to very low quality evidence, and no mortality data anywhere. So insulin's weight benefit rests on one trial's within-patient reversal pattern rather than a robust pooled between-group effect, and a lung benefit is unproven. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): insulin probably helps weight in CFRD without fasting hyperglycaemia; whether it protects the lungs is unknown.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — insulin reversed BMI decline in the one multicentre trial, but pooled between-group evidence is inconclusive and no lung-function benefit has been shown

title: Botox into the pylorus for gastroparesis: two controlled trials, no win over saline — the placebo injection did just as well
question: In diabetic gastroparesis with delayed gastric emptying, does intrapyloric botulinum toxin injection improve gastric emptying and symptoms compared with placebo injection?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the open-label literature promised a great deal for intrapyloric botulinum toxin, and the two controlled trials delivered none of it. In the placebo-controlled trial (Friedenberg FK et al., PMID: 18070232; 32 patients with idiopathic or diabetic gastroparesis), the response rate at one month was actually lower with botulinum toxin than with saline placebo — 37.5% versus 56.3% achieving the study's improvement definition — and although gastric emptying improved within the toxin group, it was not superior to placebo. The double-blind cross-over trial (Arts J et al., PMID: 17944739; 23 patients, 19 of them idiopathic) found the same pattern: symptoms and emptying improved after the first injection whichever fluid it was, with no significant difference between toxin and saline on solid or liquid emptying half-times, meal-related symptoms or the Gastroparesis Cardinal Symptom Index. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): intrapyloric botulinum toxin has not beaten placebo on symptoms or emptying in controlled trials; the apparent benefits in uncontrolled series are what a strong placebo and procedure effect looks like. Diabetic-specific controlled data are thinner still — most cross-over participants were idiopathic.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — intrapyloric botulinum toxin has not beaten placebo on symptoms or gastric emptying in the controlled trials

title: Setmelanotide for hypothalamic obesity: 89% lost at least 5% of BMI in 16 open-label weeks — a dramatic signal awaiting a randomised trial
question: In acquired hypothalamic obesity, does setmelanotide reduce body mass index and hunger compared with baseline in an open-label trial, ahead of any randomised outcomes data?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the effect size in this small open-label trial is far beyond what placebo or natural history produces in hypothalamic obesity, but the design still caps the stamp. In the phase 2 trial (Roth CL et al., PMID: 38697184), 16 of 18 patients (89%) met the primary endpoint of at least a 5% body mass index reduction at 16 weeks, against a prespecified historic control rate of under 5% (p<0.0001); mean BMI fell 15% (SD 10), and patients aged 12 or older reported a mean 45% reduction in hunger score. Twelve of 14 patients who rolled into the long-term extension and completed at least 12 months had a mean BMI change of −26% (SD 12) from index-trial baseline. The price was tolerability: nausea in 61%, vomiting in 33%, skin hyperpigmentation in 33% and diarrhoea in 22%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): setmelanotide produces large, durable BMI reductions in acquired hypothalamic obesity in open-label treatment; a randomised trial is still owed before the stamp can rise, and nausea and pigmentation are part of the deal.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Metreleptin in lipodystrophy: insulin sensitivity swings 32–41% within two weeks of starting or stopping — with food intake held constant
question: In generalised and partial lipodystrophy, does metreleptin improve insulin sensitivity, triglycerides and glycaemic control in open-label long-term treatment?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — lipodystrophy is the human model of leptin deficiency, and the mechanistic trial on this shelf isolates the drug's effect from its appetite effect: with food intake held constant on a metabolic ward (Brown RJ et al., PMID: 29723161), stopping metreleptin for 14 days cut peripheral insulin sensitivity by 41%, while starting it raised sensitivity by 32% in 14 days; in the initiation cohort fasting glucose fell 11%, triglycerides fell 41%, hepatic insulin sensitivity rose and liver fat fell from 21.8% to 18.7%. After 6 months of open treatment, lipolysis fell 30–35%. The systematic review of genotype-stratified treatment in monogenic insulin resistance (Semple RK et al., PMID: 37794082) concurs at lower resolution: metreleptin is associated with lower triglycerides and HbA1c across generalised and partial lipodystrophy (n = 111), while rating every included study at moderate or serious risk of bias. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): metreleptin genuinely improves insulin sensitivity, triglycerides and glycaemia in lipodystrophy — an open-label, small-numbers certainty, in a rare disease where randomised trials are barely feasible.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Growth hormone in Prader–Willi infants: lean mass up, fat down, motor gains doubled in six months — and the 36-study pool agrees
question: In infants and young children with Prader–Willi syndrome, does growth hormone treatment improve body composition and motor development compared with no treatment?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in the infant randomised trial (Whitman B et al., PMID: 15198290; 25 infants, mean age 15.5 months), six months of growth hormone significantly increased lean body mass (6.4 ± 2.4 kg to 8.9 ± 2.7 kg) and decreased body fat (27.6 ± 9.9% to 22.4 ± 10.3%), and age-equivalent motor scores improved by 4 months in the treated group against 2 months in controls (p < 0.01). The systematic review and meta-analysis across infancy, childhood and adolescence (Passone CGB et al., PMID: 32411831; 16 randomised and 20 non-randomised controlled trials) points the same way at larger scale: height improved by 1.67 standard deviation scores (95% CI 1.54 to 1.81), body mass index z-score fell 0.67 SD (−0.87 to −0.47) and fat mass proportion fell 6.5% (−8.46 to −4.54) versus controls, on evidence the reviewers call high quality for those outcomes; cognition data could not be aggregated. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): growth hormone in Prader–Willi syndrome improves body composition and stature and, started in infancy, motor development — the open questions are cognitive benefit and very long-term outcomes, not whether the body-composition effect is real.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Meglitinides for type 2 diabetes: HbA1c lowering on par with metformin — paid for in weight gain and mild hypos, with zero outcomes trials
question: In type 2 diabetes, do meglitinides (repaglinide, nateglinide) improve HbA1c compared with placebo or other oral agents, and how does hypoglycaemia compare?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the Cochrane review (Black C et al., PMID: 17443551; 15 trials, 3,781 participants) finds meglitinides genuinely lower HbA1c: against placebo, reductions ran 0.1% to 2.1% for repaglinide and 0.2% to 0.6% for nateglinide, and in head-to-head data repaglinide matched metformin's glucose-lowering (three trials, 248 participants) while nateglinide was similar or slightly weaker than metformin (one study, 355 participants); in the two trials comparing the two meglitinides directly (342 participants), repaglinide reduced HbA1c more. The costs: weight gain was generally greater than with metformin (up to 3 kg in three months), diarrhoea was less frequent, and hypoglycaemia was more frequent though rarely severe enough to require assistance. No study reported mortality or morbidity outcomes at all. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): meglitinides are a metformin-strength glucose-lowering option — reasonable where metformin is intolerable or contraindicated — bought with more weight and more, usually mild, hypoglycaemia, and with long-term outcome benefit entirely unproven.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)
