title: Alpha-glucosidase inhibitors: HbA1c down 0.8 points on acarbose — a real effect with a hard dose ceiling and a gastrointestinal bill
question: In type 2 diabetes, do alpha-glucosidase inhibitors (acarbose, miglitol, voglibose) improve HbA1c compared with placebo, and what gastrointestinal price do patients pay?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the Cochrane meta-analysis (Van de Laar FA et al., PMID: 15846673; 41 trials, 8,130 participants) gives acarbose a clear, quantified glycaemic effect against placebo: HbA1c −0.8% (95% CI −0.9 to −0.7), fasting glucose −1.1 mmol/L (≈-20 mg/dL) (−1.4 to −0.9) and post-load glucose −2.3 mmol/L (≈-41 mg/dL) (−2.7 to −1.9), with a dose ceiling — above 50 mg three times daily there was no additional HbA1c effect, only more adverse effects. The gastrointestinal price is the class's signature: adverse effects were mostly gastrointestinal in origin and dose-dependent, and against sulfonylureas acarbose caused more adverse effects while delivering inferior glycaemic control, though it lowered fasting and post-load insulin levels. There were no clinically relevant effects on lipids or body weight, and the reviewers found only few data on mortality, morbidity and quality of life — whether the class changes any hard outcome remains unclear. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): alpha-glucosidase inhibitors lower HbA1c by about 0.8 percentage points, a real but modest gain that patients pay for in dose-dependent gut symptoms.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Liraglutide on dialysis: blood levels run 49% higher, glucose still improves — one 12-week trial says start low and titrate slowly
question: In type 2 diabetes with end-stage kidney disease on dialysis, does liraglutide achieve glycaemic control safely compared with placebo, given altered drug exposure in uraemia?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — this shelf rests on a single small investigator-initiated trial (Idorn T et al., PMID: 26283739): 24 patients with type 2 diabetes and dialysis-dependent end-stage kidney disease plus 23 diabetic controls with normal kidney function, of whom 20 and 20 completed 12 weeks. Its primary outcome was pharmacokinetic, and it answered that question clearly: dose-corrected plasma trough liraglutide concentration was 49% higher (95% CI 6 to 109; P = 0.02) in the kidney-disease group — exposure really does rise in uraemia. Glycaemic control tended to improve in both liraglutide groups on daily glucose measurements (P < 0.01) with parallel reductions in baseline insulin dose (P < 0.04), and weight fell in both (−2.4 ± 0.8 kg in the kidney group, not significant at P = 0.22; −2.9 ± 1.0 kg in controls, P = 0.03). The cost was gastrointestinal: initial, temporary nausea and vomiting occurred more frequently in liraglutide-treated patients with kidney failure than in controls (P < 0.04). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): liraglutide can be used in dialysis patients with glycaemic effect, but exposure is roughly half again as high, so the trialists advise reduced doses and slower titration — a dosing caution, on 20 completing patients, not a settled safety profile.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — one small trial: liraglutide exposure rises 49% in dialysis patients, glycaemia tends to improve, gastrointestinal effects increase; reduced dose and slower titration advised

title: Glargine alongside the DKA insulin drip: resolution about four hours faster in the pooled small trials — stay and hypoglycaemia unchanged
question: In diabetic ketoacidosis, does adding subcutaneous insulin glargine to intravenous insulin infusion shorten time to resolution and hospital stay compared with intravenous insulin alone?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the meta-analysis (Andrade-Castellanos CA et al., PMID: 27861474) pooled just four randomised trials and 135 patients, and on low-quality evidence found that subcutaneous insulin glargine co-administered with standard intravenous insulin shortened time to resolution of diabetic ketoacidosis by a mean of 4.19 hours (95% CI −7.81 to 0.57 as printed in the record; p = 0.02), with neutral differences in length of hospital stay and hypoglycaemic episodes. Four hours faster biochemical resolution, if real, is clinically convenient — less infusion time, earlier step-down — but the evidence carrying it is thin: three of the four trials contributed to the resolution estimate, the printed confidence interval crosses zero despite the reported p-value, and no effect on stay or any harder outcome was shown. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): adding glargine early in DKA may shave about four hours off time to resolution without extra hypoglycaemia, but the pooled base is 135 patients and the finding needs a properly sized trial before it changes protocol by itself.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — adding subcutaneous glargine to IV insulin may shorten DKA resolution by about 4 hours, on low-quality evidence from 135 patients, with no change in stay or hypoglycaemia

title: HypoAware for lost hypo awareness: impaired-awareness odds significantly lower (OR 0.38), distress down, severe events leaning lower — at €2,233 per event prevented
question: In type 1 diabetes with impaired awareness of hypoglycaemia, does the HypoAware psychoeducational programme restore awareness and reduce severe hypoglycaemia compared with usual care?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the cluster-randomised trial (Rondags SM et al., PMID: 27797931; 137 participants with type 1 or insulin-treated type 2 diabetes and problematic hypoglycaemia, eight Dutch clinics, 6 months) found HypoAware significantly reduced the odds of impaired hypoglycaemia awareness (odds ratio 0.38, 95% CI 0.15 to 0.95; P = 0.038) and hypo-distress (relative risk 0.70, 0.56 to 0.88; P = 0.002 — a 30% relative reduction), with median severe hypoglycaemic events of 1 (IQR 0–6.5) in the HypoAware group versus 2.5 (IQR 1–10) on usual care over 6 months (P = 0.030); the adjusted episode-rate estimate, a 33% relative reduction (relative risk 0.67, 0.39 to 1.16), was not significant (P = 0.150), and HbA1c did not change. The economic evaluation (de Wit M et al., PMID: 29150861) puts the proportion with at least one severe event 0.22 lower and impaired awareness 0.16 lower on HypoAware, at €2,233 per severe event prevented and €708 higher mean societal costs, concluding the programme was not cost-effective on quality-adjusted life-years (€119,360 per QALY). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): HypoAware restores awareness and cuts distress and severe-event burden modestly — a clinical benefit whose cost-effectiveness, on QALY terms, its own evaluators dispute.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Diabetes-specific tube feeds: fasting glucose and HbA1c lower than standard formula in the pooled trials — lipids essentially unmoved
question: In patients with diabetes receiving enteral nutrition, does a diabetes-specific formula improve glycaemic and cardiometabolic measures compared with a standard formula?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the systematic review and meta-analysis (Ojo O et al., PMID: 31443185; 14 studies reviewed, 5 pooled) found every included study reporting lower blood glucose parameters on diabetes-specific formula than on standard formula, and the pooled analysis confirmed significantly lower fasting blood glucose (mean difference −1.15, 95% CI −2.07 to −0.23; p = 0.01) and significantly lower glycated haemoglobin (p = 0.005 after sensitivity analysis). The lipid story is thinner: no significant differences in total cholesterol, LDL cholesterol or triglycerides, and HDL cholesterol was higher by a mean of 0.09 (95% CI 0.00 to 0.18; p = 0.04) — a result the authors note was not consistent on sensitivity analysis, as the fasting-glucose result also lost significance when some studies were removed. The formulas differ from standard feeds in several ways at once (low-glycaemic-index carbohydrate, less carbohydrate, more protein, monounsaturated fats, different fibre), so no single ingredient can take the credit. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): diabetes-specific enteral formula improves fasting glucose and HbA1c modestly in type 2 diabetes; claims beyond glycaemia — lipids, outcomes — are not supported by the pooled record.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Insulin for TPN: in-the-bag regular insulin and half-and-half glargine tie during the infusion — glargine wins the two days after, with more mild hypos
question: In non-critically ill hospitalised patients with diabetes receiving total parenteral nutrition, does subcutaneous glargine control glucose as well as regular insulin added to the nutrition bag, and with how much hypoglycaemia?
balance: SPLIT — the one randomised trial built for this question (Olveira G et al., PMID: 30930133; INSUPAR, 161 non-critically ill inpatients with type 2 diabetes on total parenteral nutrition) found the two strategies glycaemically equivalent during the infusion: mean capillary glucose 165.3 ± 35.4 mg/dL with 100% regular insulin in the bag versus 172.5 ± 43.6 mg/dL with half the regular insulin in the bag and half as subcutaneous glargine (p = 0.25), on similar total insulin doses, with similar proportions of readings above 180 mg/dL and no differences in length of stay, infectious complications or hospital mortality. The split comes at the edges: in the two days after parenteral nutrition stopped, glucose ran significantly lower on the glargine strategy (141.7 ± 43.8 versus 160.3 ± 45.1 mg/dL; p = 0.024) — but the glargine group also had significantly more capillary readings at or below 70 mg/dL, more hypoglycaemic episodes per 100 days of nutrition, and more patients with non-severe hypoglycaemia, though no severe hypoglycaemia occurred in either arm. The systematic review of glucose management on parenteral and enteral nutrition (Laesser CI et al., PMID: 31261760; 15 studies, 1,170 patients) found the underlying study base generally of limited quality and no consensus regimen. PROPOSED SPLIT: on the nutrition bag the routes tie; glargine buys better post-infusion control at the price of more non-severe hypoglycaemia.
stamp: SPLIT — glucose control is equivalent during TPN either way; the glargine strategy controls glucose better after TPN stops but causes more non-severe hypoglycaemia

title: Metformin in kidney disease: lactic acidosis at 3–10 per 100,000 person-years, no different from background — a reassurance built entirely without randomised trials
question: In type 2 diabetes with chronic kidney disease, does continuing metformin increase the risk of lactic acidosis or other serious adverse events compared with other glucose-lowering therapy?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — this is a harm question answered without a single randomised trial: the systematic review (Inzucchi SE et al., PMID: 25536258) assembled 65 articles — pharmacokinetic studies, large case series, retrospective studies, meta-analyses and one clinical trial — and found that in mild to moderate chronic kidney disease (estimated glomerular filtration rate 30–60 mL/min/1.73 m2) metformin levels generally remain within the therapeutic range and lactate concentrations are not substantially increased. The overall incidence of lactic acidosis in metformin users across studies ran from approximately 3 to 10 per 100,000 person-years and was generally indistinguishable from the background rate in the overall diabetes population; data suggesting increased risk in kidney disease were limited, and population studies found metformin prescribed against prevailing renal guidelines in up to 1 in 4 patients with type 2 diabetes without, in most reports, increased lactic acidosis rates. The reviewers support cautious expansion of metformin use in mild to moderate kidney disease with dose reduction and kidney-function monitoring — while being explicit that no randomised trial has tested safety in significantly impaired kidney function. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): continuing metformin at eGFR 30–60 has not been shown to raise lactic acidosis above background rates, but the reassurance is observational, and below that range the record is silent rather than reassuring.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — no randomised safety trial exists, but assembled observational data show lactic acidosis on metformin in mild-to-moderate CKD at rates indistinguishable from background

title: Gliclazide MR versus glimepiride: same HbA1c, fewer lows — 3.7% versus 8.9% confirmed hypoglycaemia in the one large head-to-head trial
question: In type 2 diabetes, does once-daily gliclazide modified-release cause less hypoglycaemia than glimepiride at equivalent glycaemic control?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the head-to-head randomised record points one way. In GUIDE (Schernthaner G et al., PMID: 15305887), 845 patients achieved identical control on both drugs (HbA1c 7.2% in both arms; final difference −0.06%, noninferiority P < 0.0001), yet confirmed hypoglycaemia below 3 mmol/L (≈54 mg/dL) occurred in 3.7% on gliclazide modified-release versus 8.9% on glimepiride (P = 0.003) — an absolute difference of 5.2 percentage points — and no episode in either arm required external assistance. A network meta-analysis of sulfonylureas added to metformin (Andersen SE et al., PMID: 27426428) ranked gliclazide lowest for hypoglycaemia, with an odds ratio of 0.40 versus glimepiride, although its 95% credible interval (0.13 to 1.27) crosses 1, so the pooled estimate alone is not conclusive. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): at equal glycaemic control, gliclazide modified-release probably causes less hypoglycaemia than glimepiride, on one large direct trial backed by a consistent but imprecise network estimate.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — gliclazide modified-release causes less hypoglycaemia than glimepiride at equivalent glycaemic control

title: Glycated albumin in dialysis diabetes: it predicts death (HR 1.02 per unit across 25,932 patients) where A1C is distorted — but no trial shows managing to it helps
question: In diabetes treated with dialysis, does glycated albumin reflect glycaemic control and predict mortality better than HbA1c, which is distorted by anaemia and uraemia?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — as a prognostic marker, not as proven better day-to-day control guidance. The anchor record (Freedman BI, PMID: 22723586) is a point-counterpoint narrative, not a cohort study: it argues that HbA1c is distorted in end-stage kidney disease — where dialysis mortality is about 20% per year and both high and low A1C levels have been associated with mortality in large diabetic dialysis cohorts — and proposes glycated albumin as the preferred marker, a position the paired counterpoint disputes. The pooled data come from a meta-analysis of 12 studies and 25,932 dialysis patients with diabetes (Copur S et al., PMID: 32862262): higher glycated albumin was associated with all-cause mortality (hazard ratio 1.02 per unit, 95% CI 1.01 to 1.03; P < 0.001) irrespective of dialysis type, but not significantly with cardiovascular mortality (HR 1.03, 95% CI 0.99 to 1.06) or cardiovascular events (HR 1.03, 95% CI 0.97 to 1.09). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): glycated albumin carries real prognostic signal in diabetic dialysis patients where HbA1c is distorted, but the per-unit effect is small and no trial shows that managing to glycated albumin improves outcomes.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — glycated albumin predicts all-cause mortality in diabetic dialysis patients where HbA1c is distorted, as a prognostic marker only

title: Subacute thyroiditis: one week of prednisone did the work of six — same efficacy and recurrence, lower blood pressure and parathyroid hormone at withdrawal
question: In subacute (de Quervain) thyroiditis, does a short prednisone course relieve pain and inflammation as durably as a conventional six-week taper, with fewer steroid adverse effects?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for the short course. In the only randomised trial of treatment duration (Duan L et al., PMID: 33471681), 50 patients with moderate-to-severe subacute thyroiditis completed either 30 mg/day prednisone for 1 week followed by a week of a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug, or a conventional 6-week prednisone course: efficacy and recurrence rates did not differ significantly between groups at withdrawal (P = .65), thyroid function did not differ at weeks 6, 12 or 24, and the short-course group had lower parathyroid hormone (28.8 versus 38.9 pg/mL; P = .011) and lower systolic blood pressure (113.9 versus 122.4 mm Hg; P = .023) at discontinuation, consistent with less steroid exposure. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): one week of prednisone appears to relieve moderate-to-severe subacute thyroiditis as durably as six weeks, with fewer steroid effects — on a single small single-blind trial.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a 1-week prednisone course relieves subacute thyroiditis as durably as a 6-week taper, with fewer steroid effects

title: Amiodarone thyrotoxicosis type 2: prednisone worked in 100% — perchlorate alone failed in 29% until prednisone was added, and amiodarone could continue
question: In amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis type 2, does prednisone restore euthyroidism faster than methimazole or combination therapy?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for prednisone as the preferred treatment. In the randomised multicentre trial (Eskes SA et al., PMID: 22130792), 36 patients with amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis type 2 all continued amiodarone and received methimazole, and were randomised to prednisone alone, perchlorate alone, or both: initial therapy restored euthyroidism (thyroid-stimulating hormone at least 0.4 mU/liter) in 100% on prednisone, 71% on perchlorate alone and 100% on the combination (P = 0.03), and the 29% who failed on perchlorate alone became euthyroid only after prednisone was added. Times to euthyroidism did not differ significantly between groups, recurrent thyrotoxicosis occurred in 8.3%, and euthyroidism was ultimately reached in all patients despite continuing amiodarone. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): prednisone restores euthyroidism reliably in type 2 disease; perchlorate adds nothing and fails alone in nearly a third — but note every patient also received methimazole, so this is not prednisone versus methimazole as the question's wording might suggest.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — prednisone is the preferred treatment for amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis type 2; perchlorate alone fails in nearly a third

title: Thyroid cancer ablation: low-dose radioiodine with thyrotropin alfa matched high-dose treatment — 85.0% versus 88.9% success, with fewer harms and shorter stays
question: In low-risk differentiated thyroid cancer after thyroidectomy, does low-dose radioiodine ablation with thyrotropin alfa achieve remnant ablation as reliably as high-dose radioiodine or hormone withdrawal?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — for the low-dose, thyrotropin alfa strategy. In HiLo (Mallick U et al., PMID: 22551128), 438 patients with differentiated thyroid cancer were randomised in a two-by-two design to low-dose (1.1 GBq) or high-dose (3.7 GBq) radioiodine, each after thyrotropin alfa or thyroid hormone withdrawal: ablation success at 6–9 months was 85.0% with low dose versus 88.9% with high dose, and 87.1% with thyrotropin alfa versus 86.7% with withdrawal, with all 95% confidence intervals for the differences within the ±10 percentage point noninferiority margin; low-dose plus thyrotropin alfa succeeded in 84.3% versus 87.6% for high-dose plus withdrawal. The low-dose strategy cost less harm: adverse events in 21% versus 33% (P = 0.007) and hospitalisation for at least 3 days in 13.0% versus 36.3% (P < 0.001). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): low-dose radioiodine with thyrotropin alfa ablates the remnant as reliably as high-dose treatment, with fewer adverse events and shorter stays.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — low-dose radioiodine with thyrotropin alfa achieves remnant ablation as reliably as high-dose radioiodine or hormone withdrawal, with fewer adverse events

title: Watching a tiny thyroid cancer: 1,235 patients observed, no distant spread and no cancer deaths — growth in about 5% and nodal spread in about 2% by five years
question: In papillary thyroid microcarcinoma, does active surveillance avoid surgery without excess progression or metastasis compared with immediate surgery, in long-term cohort follow-up?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for active surveillance in selected low-risk patients, with an age gradient. In the long-term Kuma Hospital cohort (Ito Y et al., PMID: 24001104), 1,235 patients with low-risk papillary microcarcinoma chose observation without immediate surgery and were followed for a mean 75 months: none developed distant metastasis and none died of thyroid cancer, progression was least frequent in patients aged 60 and over and most frequent in those under 40 (young age an independent predictor on multivariate analysis), and of 191 patients who later had surgery, none died of the cancer and only one recurred, in the residual thyroid. A systematic review and meta-analysis of active surveillance for small papillary thyroid cancer (Cho SJ et al., PMID: 31368412) pooled a 5-year size-enlargement proportion of 5.3% (95% CI 4.4% to 6.4%) and 5-year lymph-node metastasis of 1.6% (1.1% to 2.4%). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): surveillance avoids surgery in most patients without excess metastasis or death in these cohorts — but there is no randomised comparison with immediate surgery, so the counterfactual rests on the cancers' indolent behaviour.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — active surveillance avoids surgery in most low-risk papillary microcarcinomas without distant metastasis or cancer death in long-term cohorts, with progression commonest in the young

title: Asymptomatic hyperparathyroidism: surgery builds bone (+3.5% at the spine) but randomised trials show no gain in how patients feel, fractures or stones
question: In asymptomatic primary hyperparathyroidism, does parathyroidectomy improve bone density and quality of life compared with medical observation?
balance: SPLIT — the evidence splits by outcome. For bone: in the randomised trial (Bollerslev J et al., PMID: 17284629), areal bone mineral density increased in the 191 patients randomised to parathyroidectomy while it remained stable on medical observation, with calcium and parathyroid hormone normalising after surgery; a meta-analysis of four randomised trials (Anagnostis P et al., PMID: 33074457) quantified gains of 3.55% at the lumbar spine (95% CI 1.81% to 5.29%) and 3.44% at the total hip (1.39% to 5.49%) versus surveillance. For how patients feel and fare: the same trial found no clinically significant change in quality of life (SF-36) or psychological symptoms in either group despite patients starting below healthy controls, and no change in kidney function or blood pressure; the meta-analysis found no difference in fracture risk, nephrolithiasis or quality-of-life indices except general health. PROPOSED SPLIT: parathyroidectomy improves bone density and normalises calcium, but randomised evidence does not show it improves quality of life, fractures, kidney stones or kidney function in asymptomatic patients.
stamp: SPLIT — parathyroidectomy improves bone density and normalises calcium, but does not improve quality of life, fractures, stones or kidney function in asymptomatic primary hyperparathyroidism

title: Cancer hypercalcaemia that bisphosphonates could not move: denosumab responded in 64% by day 10, with responses lasting a median 104 days
question: In hypercalcaemia of malignancy refractory to bisphosphonates, does denosumab lower corrected serum calcium compared with continuing standard care?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in the single-arm international study (Hu MI et al., PMID: 24915117), 33 patients whose albumin-corrected serum calcium remained above 12.5 mg/dL despite intravenous bisphosphonates given 7–30 days before screening received denosumab 120 mg on days 1, 8, 15 and 29 and then every 4 weeks: by day 10, 64% (21 patients) had responded (corrected calcium at most 11.5 mg/dL) and 12 patients (reported as 33% in the record) reached at most 10.8 mg/dL; over the study, 70% responded and 64% reached at most 10.8 mg/dL, with an estimated median response duration of 104 days. The commonest serious adverse events were worsening hypercalcaemia (15%) and dyspnoea (9%). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): denosumab lowers calcium in about two thirds of bisphosphonate-refractory hypercalcaemia of malignancy, with responses lasting a median of about three months — on uncontrolled single-arm evidence.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — denosumab lowers corrected serum calcium in about two thirds of bisphosphonate-refractory hypercalcaemia of malignancy

title: Inoperable parathyroid carcinoma: cinacalcet cut calcium by at least 1 mg/dL in 62% — responders from 15.0 down to 11.2 mg/dL
question: In inoperable parathyroid carcinoma, does cinacalcet reduce serum calcium compared with pretreatment values in open-label treatment?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in the open-label single-arm study (Silverberg SJ et al., PMID: 17666472), 29 patients with inoperable parathyroid carcinoma, mean baseline calcium 14.1 ± 0.4 mg/dL and parathyroid hormone 697 ± 94 pg/mL, had cinacalcet titrated from 30 mg twice daily up to 90 mg four times daily over 16 weeks: 62% achieved the endpoint of at least a 1 mg/dL fall in serum calcium (mean decline to 12.4 ± 0.5 mg/dL), and among the 18 responders calcium fell from 15.0 ± 0.5 to 11.2 ± 0.3 mg/dL (P < 0.001), with the greatest reductions in those with the highest baseline values. Parathyroid hormone fell only 4.6%, not significantly, and adverse events included nausea, vomiting, headache and fracture. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): cinacalcet lowers calcium in about two thirds of inoperable parathyroid carcinoma — meaningful palliation of the hypercalcaemia that drives this disease's morbidity, on uncontrolled evidence.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — cinacalcet reduces serum calcium in about two thirds of patients with inoperable parathyroid carcinoma

title: Desmopressin in central diabetes insipidus: action lasts 4 hours at low dose, 11 hours at the top dose — a 13-patient pharmacology study, not a regimen trial
question: In central diabetes insipidus, how long does the antidiuretic action of desmopressin last by formulation and dose, and does that duration support overnight control without hyponatraemia?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the pharmacology is clear and the clinical inference is thin. In the crossover dose study (Juul KV et al., PMID: 21626284), 13 patients with central diabetes insipidus received intravenous desmopressin in two three-way crossover designs: the duration of antidiuretic action was 4 hours at 125 ng, 8 hours at 250 ng and 11 hours at 500 ng, while the other dynamic measures showed no difference between 250 and 500 ng, indicating the upper plateau of the dose-response curve had been reached; no serious adverse events occurred and all treatment-emergent events were classified as unrelated or unlikely related. The authors calculate that 500 ng intravenously, corresponding to 160 μg orodispersible tablets twice daily, could achieve antidiuretic control. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): duration is dose-dependent and an 11-hour action at the top dose is long enough on paper to cover a night, but this 13-patient pharmacodynamic study measured urine output and osmolality — it did not measure overnight symptom control or hyponatraemia on any twice-daily regimen, so that part of the question is unanswered by the record.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — desmopressin's antidiuretic action lasts 4 to 11 hours by dose, but overnight control without hyponatraemia on twice-daily dosing was not tested

title: Late-blooming boys: letrozole and testosterone both induced puberty without psychosocial harm — sociability edged to letrozole, and waiting itself was never the comparator
question: In boys with constitutional delay of growth and puberty, does puberty-promoting treatment with letrozole or testosterone improve growth, psychosocial well-being and quality of life compared with watchful waiting?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — and note first what the trials do not contain: no watchful-waiting arm. Both reports come from one randomised open-label trial comparing letrozole 2.5 mg/day with intramuscular testosterone 1 mg/kg monthly for 6 months in boys with constitutional delay of growth and puberty. On psychosocial outcomes (Kariola L et al., PMID: 41054004; 30 boys), boys with the condition were more withdrawn than local peers at baseline (p = 0.02), sociability was higher in the letrozole group than the testosterone group after treatment (−0.48, 95% CI −0.89 to −0.08; p = 0.019) and at 12 months (−0.72, 95% CI −1.12 to −0.32; p = 0.001), and neither treatment caused adverse psychosocial effects on the temperament measures assessed. On growth (Huttunen H et al., PMID: 34596269; 28 boys), serum testosterone best predicted growth velocity in both groups, and a meta-analysis of letrozole in this condition (Dutta D et al., PMID: 34477355; 7 trials) found predicted adult height improved versus placebo (mean difference 4.63 cm, 95% CI 3.90 to 5.36) but not versus testosterone (2.21 cm, −1.71 to 6.16). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): both treatments promote puberty without psychosocial harm in these small studies, letrozole may edge testosterone on sociability and testicular volume, and neither has been shown better than watchful waiting for well-being in a randomised comparison.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — letrozole and testosterone both promote puberty without psychosocial harm, but neither has been randomised against watchful waiting for well-being

title: Turner syndrome: low-dose oxandrolone added 2.3 cm of adult height — the conventional double dose added virilisation and bone-age acceleration instead
question: In girls with Turner syndrome already treated with growth hormone, does adding oxandrolone increase adult height compared with growth hormone alone, and at what virilisation cost?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for the low dose only. In the Dutch dose-response trial (Menke LA et al., PMID: 20061421), 133 growth-hormone-treated girls with Turner syndrome received placebo or oxandrolone from age 8: adult height gain was 9.5 ± 4.7 cm on oxandrolone 0.03 mg/kg/day versus 7.2 ± 4.0 cm on placebo (P = 0.02), while the conventional 0.06 mg/kg/day dose gained 8.3 ± 4.7 cm, not significantly different from placebo (P = 0.3), partly because of accelerated bone maturation (P < 0.001). The Cochrane review (Mohamed S et al., PMID: 31684688; 6 trials, 498 participants) found adult height a mean 2.7 cm greater with oxandrolone plus growth hormone (95% CI 1.3 to 4.1; moderate-quality evidence). The costs are dose-dependent: breast development was slower on both oxandrolone doses, and virilisation was significantly more reported on 0.06 mg/kg/day than placebo (P < 0.001), which is why the trial authors discourage the conventional dose. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): low-dose oxandrolone adds roughly 2–3 cm of adult height, at the price of slower breast development and a virilisation risk that makes the higher dose a poor bargain.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — low-dose oxandrolone adds about 2–3 cm of adult height in growth-hormone-treated Turner syndrome, with slower breast development and dose-dependent virilisation

title: Mifepristone in Cushing's syndrome: HbA1c fell 7.43% to 6.29% and 60% met the glucose response in SEISMIC — but the trial had no control group, so the effect size is a before-and-after number
question: In Cushing's syndrome with diabetes or hypertension, does the glucocorticoid-receptor antagonist mifepristone improve glycaemic control and blood pressure in open-label treatment?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the entire evidence base for this shelf is one open-label, uncontrolled trial of 50 patients (Fleseriu M et al., SEISMIC, PMID: 22466348). In the diabetes/impaired-glucose-tolerance cohort, 60% met the glucose-area-under-the-curve response definition, HbA1c fell from 7.43% to 6.29%, and fasting glucose fell from 149.0 to 104.7 mg/dl; in the hypertension-only cohort, 38% met the diastolic blood-pressure response definition; weight fell by a mean 5.7% and 87% of patients were judged clinically improved overall. Those are large before-and-after changes in a disease where spontaneous improvement is uncommon, which is why the signal is credible — but with no control group, regression to the mean, co-interventions and assessor expectation cannot be separated from drug effect, and the adverse-effect list (fatigue, nausea, headache, low potassium, oedema, endometrial thickening in women) comes from the same uncontrolled exposure. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): mifepristone probably improves glycaemic control and blood pressure in Cushing's syndrome with diabetes or hypertension, but a single open-label trial cannot size the effect or the harm balance.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — mifepristone improved glucose and blood pressure in one open-label trial, but without a control group the size of the true effect is unknown

title: Amino acids for kidney protection in cardiac surgery: AKI in 26.9% versus 31.7% in the 3,511-patient PROTECTION trial — a real reduction, concentrated in milder injury, with dialysis rates unchanged
question: In patients undergoing cardiac surgery at risk of acute kidney injury, does perioperative intravenous amino acid infusion reduce the occurrence of acute kidney injury compared with placebo?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — one large, multinational, double-blind randomised trial answers this question directly (Landoni G et al., PROTECTION, PMID: 38865168): among 3,511 adults undergoing cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass, acute kidney injury occurred in 26.9% on amino acids versus 31.7% on placebo — a relative risk of 0.85 (95% CI 0.77 to 0.94), i.e. a 15% relative reduction alongside the absolute rates of 26.9% and 31.7% (about 5 fewer cases per 100 patients treated). Stage 3 injury was also less frequent (1.6% versus 3.0%; relative risk 0.56, 95% CI 0.35 to 0.87), while kidney-replacement therapy (1.4% versus 1.9%), other secondary outcomes and adverse events did not differ substantially. The benefit is therefore real but concentrated in milder, creatinine-defined injury; the trial does not show fewer patients reaching dialysis or death. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): perioperative intravenous amino acids reduce the occurrence of acute kidney injury after cardiac surgery, with the clearest effect on less severe stages.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: Fenoldopam in cardiac surgery: pooled trials show less acute kidney injury (odds ratio 0.41) — but only 440 patients, no effect on dialysis or survival, and more hypotension
question: In cardiac surgery, does fenoldopam prevent or treat acute kidney injury and reduce dialysis or death, in the pooled randomised trials?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the pooled randomised, placebo-controlled record is small but directionally consistent (Zangrillo A et al., PMID: 22459931): across 6 trials and 440 patients undergoing cardiac surgery, fenoldopam reduced the risk of acute kidney injury (odds ratio 0.41; 95% CI 0.23 to 0.74; p = 0.003). What it did not do is just as important: there was no effect on renal replacement therapy, survival, or intensive care or hospital length of stay, and hypotensive episodes and/or vasopressor use were more frequent on fenoldopam (27.5% versus 18.8%; odds ratio 2.09; 95% CI 0.98 to 4.47; p = 0.06). A drug that moves a creatinine-based endpoint in 440 patients without moving dialysis or death has shown a promising surrogate effect, not a proven patient-important one — exactly the gap the reviewers themselves flag in calling for a large, appropriately powered trial. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): fenoldopam reduces acute kidney injury after cardiac surgery in the pooled small trials, with a hypotension price and no demonstrated effect on dialysis or survival.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Furosemide for acute kidney injury: nine trials and 849 patients with no benefit on mortality, dialysis or recovery — and more deafness and tinnitus at high doses
question: In established acute kidney injury, does furosemide improve survival or kidney recovery compared with no diuretic therapy, in the pooled randomised trials?
balance: POSSIBLE (no benefit) — the pooled randomised record does not show furosemide helping the injured kidney (Ho KM & Sheridan DJ, PMID: 16861256): across 9 randomised trials and 849 adults with or at risk of acute renal failure, in-hospital mortality (relative risk 1.11, 95% CI 0.92 to 1.33), the risk of requiring renal replacement therapy or dialysis (0.99, 0.80 to 1.22), the number of dialysis sessions (weighted mean difference −0.48 sessions, −1.45 to 0.50) and persistent oliguria (0.54, 0.18 to 1.61) were all non-significantly different with furosemide, and splitting prevention from treatment trials did not change the mortality or dialysis results. The one clear signal was harm at high doses: temporary deafness and tinnitus were more frequent (relative risk 3.97, 95% CI 1.00 to 15.78). Furosemide can still make urine and manage fluid overload — that is a symptom indication, not kidney recovery. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (no benefit): furosemide has not been shown to improve survival or kidney recovery in acute kidney injury, and high doses carry an ototoxicity risk.
stamp: POSSIBLE (no benefit) — pooled randomised trials show no survival or kidney-recovery benefit from furosemide in acute kidney injury

title: Less salt in CKD: blood pressure down 10/4 mm Hg in the LowSALT trial and albuminuria down 36% relative in the Cochrane pool — consistent short-term gains, with hard outcomes never tested
question: In chronic kidney disease, does lowering salt intake reduce ambulatory blood pressure and proteinuria compared with usual salt intake?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the miner anchor for this candidate (PMID: 23082956) is the LowSALT CKD protocol paper, which reports no results; the results of that same trial were published by the same group (McMahon EJ et al., PMID: 24204003) and are carded here as the anchor evidence. In that double-blind crossover trial of 20 patients with hypertensive stage 3–4 chronic kidney disease, salt restriction lowered ambulatory systolic/diastolic blood pressure by 10/4 mm Hg (95% CI 5 to 15 / 1 to 6) and reduced extracellular fluid volume, albuminuria and proteinuria. The Cochrane review update (McMahon EJ & Campbell KL, PMID: 34164803; 21 studies, 1,197 participants) found the same pattern at scale: reducing salt by a mean 73.51 mmol/day lowered systolic/diastolic pressure by 6.91/3.91 mm Hg (high certainty evidence) and reduced albuminuria by 36% relative (95% CI 26 to 44) in earlier-stage disease, at the price of more symptomatic hypotension (relative risk 6.70, 95% CI 2.40 to 18.69). All of this is short-term surrogate evidence — no trial is long enough to test death, cardiovascular events or progression to dialysis. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): lowering salt intake reduces blood pressure and proteinuria in chronic kidney disease over weeks, with long-term outcome benefit plausible but untested.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Drinking more water for stage 3 CKD: patients drank more and copeptin fell, but eGFR declined identically in CKD WIT — the advice is unproven, not disproven
question: In adults with stage 3 chronic kidney disease, does coaching to increase water intake slow kidney function decline over one year compared with usual intake?
balance: POSSIBLE (no benefit) — the one randomised trial of this advice found the behaviour changed and the kidney outcome did not (Clark WF et al., CKD WIT, PMID: 29801012): among 631 adults with stage 3 chronic kidney disease, coaching to drink more water raised 24-hour urine volume by 0.6 L per day (95% CI 0.5 to 0.7) and lowered plasma copeptin (−2.2 pmol/L, 95% CI −3.9 to −0.5), so the intervention demonstrably engaged its target — yet the 12-month change in eGFR was −2.2 mL/min/1.73 m² in the hydration group versus −1.9 in controls (adjusted difference −0.3, 95% CI −1.8 to 1.2; P = .74), with no significant difference in urine albumin or self-rated health. The authors note the study may have been underpowered for a clinically important difference, and one year is short for kidney decline — but as the record stands, 'drink more water' is unproven advice for stage 3 disease, distinct from the separate ADPKD water question. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (no benefit): coaching to increase water intake did not significantly slow kidney function decline over one year in stage 3 chronic kidney disease.
stamp: POSSIBLE (no benefit) — coaching to increase water intake did not significantly slow kidney function decline over one year in stage 3 chronic kidney disease

title: Ketoanalogue-supplemented very-low-protein diet in advanced CKD: NNT 4.4 to avoid dialysis or halved eGFR in Garneata — in the 14% of screened patients compliant enough to be randomised
question: In advanced chronic kidney disease, does a very-low-protein vegetarian diet supplemented with ketoanalogues delay dialysis initiation compared with a conventional low-protein diet?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the anchor randomised trial is strikingly positive but heavily selected (Garneata L et al., PMID: 26823552): in nondiabetic adults with eGFR under 30 ml/min/1.73 m² who had already proven good diet compliance in a 3-month run-in — only 14% of screened patients were randomised — a ketoanalogue-supplemented vegetarian very-low-protein diet (0.3 g/kg/day) versus a conventional low-protein diet (0.6 g/kg/day) gave an adjusted number needed to treat of 4.4 (95% CI 4.2 to 5.1) to avoid the composite of dialysis initiation or halving of eGFR, and 2.7 (2.6 to 3.1) to avoid dialysis in those with eGFR under 20, with metabolic abnormalities correcting only on the supplemented diet and no nutritional deterioration. The 2024 meta-analysis (Chen CH et al., PMID: 39340710; 16 trials, 1,344 participants) points the same way more modestly: higher GFR, lower urea nitrogen and phosphorus, higher calcium, a marginally lower risk of end-stage kidney disease in participants without diabetes, and no differences in mortality, albumin or nutritional measures. The direction is consistent; the trial effect size comes from the most compliant sliver of patients. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a ketoanalogue-supplemented very-low-protein diet can defer dialysis in selected, compliant patients with advanced chronic kidney disease.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Treating PD peritonitis: intraperitoneal antibiotics beat intravenous in the one small head-to-head study and glycopeptides cured more completely — across 42 studies the Cochrane verdict is still low-quality evidence
question: In peritoneal dialysis-associated peritonitis, do intraperitoneal antibiotics achieve cure as reliably as intravenous or oral routes, in the pooled randomised trials?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the Cochrane record on treating peritoneal dialysis peritonitis is broad but shallow (Ballinger AE et al., PMID: 24771351): 42 studies in 2,433 participants, yet most comparisons rest on one or a few small trials with generally high risk of bias and inconsistent outcome definitions. The two positive findings are narrow: intraperitoneal glycopeptide regimens were more likely to achieve complete cure than first-generation cephalosporins (3 studies, 370 episodes: relative risk 1.66, 95% CI 1.01 to 2.72) with uncertain effects on response, relapse and catheter removal, and intraperitoneal antibiotics were superior to intravenous antibiotics for treatment failure in a single small study (relative risk 3.52, 95% CI 1.26 to 9.81, favouring the intraperitoneal route). Continuous and intermittent intraperitoneal dosing performed similarly; for relapsing or persistent peritonitis, simultaneous catheter removal and replacement beat urokinase in one small study. No optimal agent, combination or duration was identified. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): intraperitoneal administration and glycopeptide regimens have the best — still low-quality — support for treating peritoneal dialysis peritonitis.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — intraperitoneal administration and glycopeptide regimens have the best support for treating peritoneal dialysis peritonitis, but the underlying trials are few, small and low quality

title: Dialysate sodium in haemodialysis: 23 studies show a trade — higher sodium, more fluid gained between sessions; lower sodium, more hypotension during them — and no winner on blood pressure or survival
question: In maintenance haemodialysis, does a lower dialysate sodium concentration reduce interdialytic weight gain and blood pressure compared with standard or higher dialysate sodium, in the pooled trials?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — this literature cannot currently crown either prescription (Basile C et al., PMID: 25843783): 23 studies and 76,635 subjects sounds substantial, but the studies were highly heterogeneous in size, quality, follow-up, dialysate sodium levels and even in what counted as 'high' or 'low'. The only three mortality studies were observational, and the apparent relation between death and the plasma-to-dialysate sodium gradient was confounded by indication — sicker patients get different prescriptions. Blood pressure was not markedly affected by higher or lower dialysate sodium; interdialytic weight gain was overall higher with higher dialysate sodium; and three studies reported significantly more intradialytic hypotensive episodes with low dialysate sodium — the physiological trade at the heart of the question. Data on hospitalisations and antihypertensive use were sparse and inconclusive. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): lower dialysate sodium reduces interdialytic weight gain but may provoke intradialytic hypotension, and no definite evidence shows superiority of either uniform prescription on outcomes patients feel.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — lower dialysate sodium reduces interdialytic weight gain but increases intradialytic hypotension, with no definite evidence of superiority on blood pressure or survival

title: Medium cut-off dialysers: quality of life up 16.7 points and recovery time down 420 minutes in the pooled record, fewer infections in the pilot — paid for with albumin leak and no survival difference
question: In maintenance haemodialysis, does a medium cut-off dialyser improve clearance of large middle molecules and patient-reported outcomes compared with a high-flux dialyser?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two complementary records support the medium cut-off membrane. The anchor pilot crossover (Cozzolino M et al., PMID: 33564442) randomised the order of treatment in 20 prevalent haemodialysis patients for 3 months on each membrane: the medium cut-off dialyser (the tested product was the Theranova 400 membrane, named in the record) was associated with fewer infections (7 of 19 patients versus 14 of 20 on conventional high-flux haemodialysis; P = 0.03) and lower interleukin-1β and interleukin-6 levels, at the cost of a significant fall in serum albumin (median reduction −0.45 g/dL; P = 0.025), though median albumin stayed at or above 3.5 g/dL and no patient developed symptoms of hypoalbuminaemia or needed intravenous albumin. The systematic review and meta-analysis (Kandi M et al., PMID: 35083060; 22 studies, 1,811 patients) found moderate-certainty improvements in quality of life (mean difference 16.7 of 100 points), pruritus and restless legs syndrome, and a high-certainty reduction in post-dialysis recovery time (−420 minutes), with little to no difference in all-cause mortality (−0.4%, 95% CI −2.8 to 2.1). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): medium cut-off dialysers improve several patient-reported outcomes and recovery time versus high-flux membranes, with albumin leak the measurable price and no mortality difference shown.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Midodrine for dialysis hypotension: pressures up about 12 mmHg and symptoms better in six of ten small studies — coherent, but built on the weakest designs in the library
question: In haemodialysis patients with dialysis-induced hypotension, does prophylactic midodrine reduce intradialytic hypotensive episodes, in the pooled small trials?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the pooled record is a systematic review of small studies, and its numbers favour midodrine (Prakash S et al., PMID: 15280522): across 10 studies (9 published, 1 unpublished) of haemodialysis patients with dialysis-induced hypotension, midodrine 2.5 to 10 mg given 15–30 minutes before dialysis was associated with post-dialysis systolic pressure higher by 12.4 mmHg (95% CI 7.5 to 17.7), diastolic higher by 7.3 mmHg (3.7 to 10.9), nadir systolic higher by 13.3 mmHg (8.6 to 18.0) and nadir diastolic higher by 5.9 mmHg (2.7 to 9.1); six of 10 studies reported improvement in hypotensive symptoms, and no serious adverse events were ascribed to midodrine. Those are surrogate pressure outcomes from observational, crossover and pre–post designs as well as small trials — the review itself warns its conclusion must be viewed with caution given the quality and sample size of the included studies. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): prophylactic midodrine raises intra- and post-dialysis blood pressure and probably reduces hypotensive symptoms, on low-quality small-study evidence.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Gabapentin versus levodopa for restless legs on dialysis: scores improved about 17 versus 13 points in four weeks — one small trial, no placebo, and augmentation never measured
question: In haemodialysis patients with restless legs syndrome, does gabapentin improve symptoms compared with levodopa?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — one small, single-centre randomised trial is the whole comparative record in dialysis patients (Razazian N et al., PMID: 25758874): over four weeks, both gabapentin 200 mg and levodopa-carbidopa 110 mg improved restless legs symptoms and sleep in haemodialysis patients, with gabapentin improving the International Restless Legs Study Group score more (change from baseline approximately −17 versus approximately −13; P = 0.016); both drugs improved sleep parameters (P < 0.0001 within groups). A four-point difference on the symptom scale, in a trial whose record does not even state its sample size, over four weeks, with no placebo arm and no augmentation follow-up, is a hint rather than an answer — augmentation on dopaminergic therapy is precisely the long-term harm a four-week trial cannot see, and it is the main clinical reason to prefer a non-dopaminergic drug in this population. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): gabapentin improved restless legs scores slightly more than levodopa-carbidopa over four weeks in one small dialysis trial.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — gabapentin improved restless legs scores slightly more than levodopa-carbidopa over four weeks in one small dialysis trial

title: Citrate versus heparin catheter locks: the infection win belongs to citrate locks carrying an antimicrobial — plain citrate's proven prize is less bleeding
question: In haemodialysis patients with tunnelled catheters, does a citrate lock reduce catheter-related bloodstream infection and dysfunction compared with a heparin lock, in the pooled trials?
balance: The pooled randomised record separates into two different products wearing one name. Where the citrate lock contained an antimicrobial, catheter-related bloodstream infection fell sharply against heparin (relative risk 0.34, 95% CI 0.24 to 0.49, in Mai H et al., PMID: 31012037), and tunnelled cuffed catheters showed the clearest benefit (RR 0.42, 95% CI 0.25 to 0.69); citrate in non-tunnelled catheters cut exit-site infection (RR 0.48, 95% CI 0.31 to 0.75), and bleeding episodes were lower with citrate in tunnelled catheters (RR 0.53, 95% CI 0.32 to 0.86) and with citrate alone (RR 0.51, 95% CI 0.30 to 0.85). What did not move: catheter removal for poor flow, thrombolytic use, thrombocytopenia, access-related admission, or mortality. So the infection headline belongs largely to antimicrobial-containing locks, while plain citrate's own clearest gain is less bleeding — a heparin-sparing effect, not proof that citrate alone prevents bloodstream infection. PROPOSED SPLIT: antimicrobial-containing citrate locks likely prevent catheter-related bloodstream infection and citrate locks bleed less than heparin, but citrate alone has not been shown to deliver the infection benefit, and no lock strategy changed mortality or catheter survival for flow.
stamp: SPLIT — antimicrobial-containing citrate locks reduce catheter-related bloodstream infection and citrate locks bleed less than heparin, but citrate alone is unproven for infection and nothing changed mortality

title: Stent graft versus balloon for a failing dialysis graft: patency doubled at six months in REVISE and the pooled trials agree — the access still fails eventually, just later and with fewer redos
question: In failing dialysis arteriovenous grafts, does a stent graft improve patency compared with balloon angioplasty alone?
balance: For a failing prosthetic dialysis graft narrowed at the venous anastomosis, adding an expanded polytetrafluoroethylene stent graft to balloon angioplasty roughly doubled six-month patency in the REVISE trial (Haskal ZJ et al., PMID: 20147715): treatment-area patency 51% versus 23% and access-circuit patency 38% versus 20%, with binary restenosis in 28% versus 78%. The pooled record since (Ng B et al., PMID: 34108161; seven studies, 1,147 patients, 867 with grafts) points the same way, with covered stents associated with lower loss of patency at 6, 12, and 24 months and better access-circuit primary patency at 6 and 12 months — but no significant difference in loss of secondary patency at 12 or 24 months, meaning the graft is not ultimately saved more often, it is kept primarily patent longer with fewer repeat procedures (freedom from subsequent intervention at six months 32% versus 16% in REVISE). Adverse events in REVISE were equivalent apart from restenosis itself. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): for venous anastomotic stenosis in a failing prosthetic graft, a stent graft is the better revision — expect longer primary patency and fewer re-interventions, not a longer-lived access in the end. Drug-coated balloons in native fistulas are a different question (shelf #1594).
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — a stent graft gives longer primary patency and fewer re-interventions than balloon angioplasty alone for failing prosthetic dialysis grafts

title: Antithymocyte globulin versus basiliximab for transplant induction: rejection 15.6% versus 25.5%, infections 85.8% versus 75.2% — a trade that turns on how high-risk the recipient is
question: In kidney transplantation, does rabbit antithymocyte globulin induction reduce acute rejection compared with basiliximab induction, and at what infection cost?
balance: In the head-to-head randomised trial in high-risk deceased-donor recipients (Brennan DC et al., PMID: 17093248; 278 patients on ciclosporin, mycophenolate, and prednisone), rabbit antithymocyte globulin beat basiliximab on the outcome induction exists for: acute rejection 15.6% versus 25.5% (P=0.02), and rejection severe enough to need antibody treatment 1.4% versus 8.0% (P=0.005) — while the composite of rejection, delayed graft function, graft loss, and death did not differ (P=0.34), nor did graft loss (9.2% versus 10.2%), delayed graft function (40.4% versus 44.5%), or death (4.3% versus 4.4%). The price was infection overall: 85.8% versus 75.2% (P=0.03) — though cytomegalovirus disease ran the other way, 7.8% versus 17.5% (P=0.02), under the prophylaxis used. Pooled patient-level reanalysis of two international trials (Alloway RR et al., PMID: 30838775; 508 recipients) found treatment failure 25.1% with antithymocyte globulin versus 36.0% with interleukin-2 receptor antagonists (absolute difference −10.9%, 95% CI −18.8 to −2.9). PROPOSED SPLIT: in high-risk recipients antithymocyte globulin prevents more — and more severe — rejection than basiliximab, at the cost of more infections overall, with no demonstrated survival or graft-survival advantage at one year.
stamp: SPLIT — antithymocyte globulin prevents more and more severe rejection than basiliximab in high-risk recipients, but causes more infections overall, with no survival or graft-survival difference at one year

title: Skipping or stopping steroids after kidney transplant: rejection rises by half to three-quarters in relative terms across 48 trials — graft loss and death have not followed, within follow-up that ends too soon to be sure
question: After kidney transplantation, does steroid avoidance or early withdrawal increase rejection or graft loss compared with maintenance steroids, in the pooled randomised trials?
balance: Across 48 randomised studies and 7,803 kidney transplant recipients, the Cochrane review (Haller MC et al., PMID: 27546100) gives steroid avoidance or withdrawal a consistent signature: acute rejection rises — relative risk 1.58 (95% CI 1.08 to 2.30) when steroids were given for less than 14 days, and relative risk 1.77 (95% CI 1.20 to 2.61) when steroids were withdrawn later — while patient mortality and graft loss show no significant difference out to the follow-up available: death at one year, relative risk 0.68 (95% CI 0.36 to 1.30) for withdrawal versus maintenance and 0.96 (0.52 to 1.80) for avoidance versus maintenance; graft loss excluding death with a functioning graft, relative risk 1.17 (0.72 to 1.92) and 1.09 (0.64 to 1.86) respectively. There was also no evidence of a difference in infection or malignancy in adults, and the effect in children (three studies, 346 participants) is unclear. So the rejection harm is real and measured; the feared downstream cost in lost grafts has not appeared within five years — but the reviewers stress that no prospective long-term studies exist, so 'not yet seen' is not 'never'. PROPOSED SPLIT: steroid avoidance or withdrawal buys freedom from long-term steroids at a proven price in acute rejection, with graft loss and mortality unchanged so far — the split is between a certain early harm and an unproven late one, in both directions.
stamp: SPLIT — steroid avoidance or withdrawal significantly increases acute rejection, while mortality and graft loss show no difference within available follow-up; long-term consequences are unstudied

title: Mannitol around kidney transplantation: less delayed graft function in the pooled trials (RR as low as 0.25) — from eight small, dated studies the reviewers themselves grade cautiously
question: In deceased-donor kidney transplantation, does donor or recipient mannitol improve early graft function and reduce delayed graft function, in the pooled trials?
balance: The pooled record is small, old, and pointed in a friendly direction. Van de Laar SCV et al. (PMID: 34412911) found eight eligible studies among 3,570 references — one examining mannitol during kidney donation and seven during transplantation, six of them meta-analysable, totalling 1,143 patients — and reported significantly less acute renal failure with mannitol (relative risk 0.45, 95% CI 0.26 to 0.79; P<0.01) and less delayed graft function in the analyses reported (RR 0.25, 95% CI 0.08 to 0.77; and RR 0.69, 95% CI 0.51 to 0.94), while graft survival, rejection, renal failure, creatinine clearance, diuresis, and serum creatinine showed no significant differences. The authors themselves close with the caveats that decide the stamp: the quality of the underlying evidence must temper interpretation, only one study addresses donor-side administration, and more up-to-date research is needed. A cheap, familiar osmotic diuretic with pooled relative risks like these would normally earn more — but the trials predate modern donor, preservation, and recipient practice. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): mannitol around transplantation is associated with less delayed graft function in the pooled older trials, and that is all the record can honestly carry.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — pooled older trials associate mannitol with less delayed graft function and acute renal failure, but study quality is low and no hard outcome improved

title: Eculizumab in atypical HUS: platelets up 73×10⁹/L, 80% event-free, four of five dialysis patients off dialysis — prospective evidence with no control arm, in a disease that rarely allows one
question: In atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome, does terminal complement blockade with eculizumab improve kidney function and haematological remission in open-label prospective trials?
balance: There is no randomised trial of eculizumab in atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome, and there is unlikely ever to be one: the disease is rare, genetic, and life-threatening, and plasma therapy does not treat its underlying complement-driven microangiopathy. What exists is two prospective open-label phase 2 trials totalling 37 patients aged 12 and over (Legendre CM et al., PMID: 23738544). In trial 1 — patients with low platelets and renal damage — the platelet count rose by a mean of 73×10⁹ per litre by week 26 (P<0.001) and dialysis was discontinued in four of five patients on it. In trial 2 — patients with renal damage progressing despite at least eight weeks of plasma exchange or infusion — 80% achieved thrombotic microangiopathy event-free status. Estimated GFR improved continuously and in a time-dependent way in both trials, earlier treatment was associated with significantly greater GFR improvement, health-related quality of life improved, and through median exposures of 64 and 62 weeks there was no cumulative toxicity and no meningococcal or other serious infection-related adverse event. Before-and-after evidence in a disease this stereotyped carries real weight, but it cannot quantify the effect the way a control arm would, and spontaneous or plasma-related improvement cannot be fully excluded. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): terminal complement blockade reverses the haematology and improves kidney function in most treated patients — start early — on prospective but uncontrolled evidence.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — eculizumab normalised haematology and improved kidney function in two small prospective open-label trials, with earlier treatment recovering more GFR

title: Iptacopan in C3 glomerulopathy: proteinuria down by a third against placebo in the first phase 3 trial — six months, 74 patients, and no kidney-function result yet
question: In C3 glomerulopathy, does oral factor B inhibition with iptacopan reduce proteinuria and stabilise kidney function compared with placebo?
balance: APPEAR-C3G (Kavanagh D et al., PMID: 41016405) is the first placebo-controlled phase 3 trial in C3 glomerulopathy, and on its chosen ground it succeeded clearly: in 74 randomised adults with biopsy-confirmed disease, low serum C3, and proteinuria of at least 1 g/g, six months of oral iptacopan 200 mg twice daily — on top of renin–angiotensin blockade and immunosuppression — changed 24-hour urine protein-to-creatinine ratio by −30.2% against +7.6% on placebo, a 35.1% relative reduction (95% CI 13.8 to 51.1; P=0.0014) in the between-group comparison. Tolerability in this small sample was reassuring: treatment-emergent adverse events in 79% versus 67%, mostly mild or moderate; serious adverse events in three participants (8%) versus one (3%); no deaths, no discontinuations for adverse events, and no meningococcal infections in a vaccinated population. What the record does not yet contain is the kidney-function half of the question: the published primary analysis reports proteinuria, not an eGFR benefit, and six months in 74 patients cannot show slowed progression in an ultra-rare disease whose harm accrues over years. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): iptacopan reduces proteinuria meaningfully at six months; whether that becomes preserved kidney function is the open-label and longer-term question still running. Iptacopan in IgA nephropathy is a different shelf (#1056).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — iptacopan reduced proteinuria by a 35.1% relative reduction versus placebo at six months; an effect on kidney-function decline is not yet demonstrated

title: Atrasentan in IgA nephropathy: proteinuria −38.1% versus −3.1% at the ALIGN interim — a big surrogate win with the 132-week kidney verdict still outstanding
question: In IgA nephropathy at risk of progression despite supportive care, does the endothelin antagonist atrasentan reduce proteinuria and slow kidney-function decline compared with placebo?
balance: The ALIGN trial's prespecified interim analysis (Heerspink HJL et al., PMID: 39460694) answers the proteinuria half of the question decisively and the kidney-protection half not at all — yet. Among the first 270 patients with biopsy-proven IgA nephropathy, at least 1 g/day of proteinuria, and eGFR at least 30, atrasentan 0.75 mg daily changed the 24-hour urine protein-to-creatinine ratio by −38.1% at week 36 against −3.1% on placebo, a between-group difference of −36.1 percentage points (95% CI −44.6 to −26.4; P<0.001). The class-level pooled record (Tian Z et al., PMID: 40130231; four randomised trials, 1,346 patients with endothelin A receptor antagonists) agrees on proteinuria (mean difference −31.89 in urine protein-to-creatinine ratio) but adds the price list ALIGN's interim was too small to itemise: higher odds of anaemia (OR 2.38), fluid retention (OR 1.46), hypotension (OR 2.39), dizziness (OR 2.37), cough (OR 2.27), and acute kidney injury (OR 3.12), with the pooled eGFR difference (mean difference 4.10, 95% CI −0.76 to 8.96) not significant. In ALIGN itself fluid retention was reported in 11.2% versus 8.2% and led to no discontinuations, with no apparent cardiac failure or severe oedema. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): atrasentan is a potent proteinuria-lowering drug in IgA nephropathy whose defining trial has not yet reported whether kidneys are saved — that answer is scheduled at 132 weeks, and the endothelin class history in diabetic kidney disease (shelf #738) is exactly why it must be awaited rather than assumed.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — atrasentan reduced proteinuria by about a third beyond placebo at week 36, but no effect on kidney-function decline has been shown yet and the class carries fluid-retention and hypotension costs

title: Rigorous blood pressure in early ADPKD: kidney growth slowed from 6.6% to 5.6% a year in HALT-PKD — eGFR unmoved, dizziness up, and a second blocker proven useless alongside
question: In early autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease, does rigorous blood-pressure control slow total kidney volume growth and kidney-function decline compared with standard control?
balance: HALT-PKD Study A (Schrier RW et al., PMID: 25399733) randomised 558 hypertensive patients aged 15–49 with early autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (eGFR above 60) in a two-by-two design: a low blood-pressure target (95/60 to 110/75 mm Hg) versus a standard target (120/70 to 130/80), crossed with lisinopril plus telmisartan versus lisinopril plus placebo. Rigorous control slowed the primary outcome — total kidney volume grew 5.6% per year versus 6.6% (P=0.006) — and improved two secondary measures: left-ventricular-mass index fell faster (−1.17 versus −0.57 g/m² per year; P<0.001) and urinary albumin excretion fell 3.77% where it rose 2.43% on standard control (P<0.001). But the outcome patients feel, eGFR, showed no overall benefit — a negative short-term slope difference (P<0.001) and only a marginally positive long-term one (P=0.05) — and dizziness and light-headedness were commoner on the low target (80.7% versus 69.4%; P=0.002). Adding telmisartan to lisinopril changed nothing in Study A, and the companion Study B in later disease (Torres VE et al., PMID: 25399731; 486 patients, eGFR 25–60, followed five to eight years) found dual blockade identical to lisinopril alone on the composite of death, end-stage kidney disease, or halving of eGFR (hazard ratio 1.08, 95% CI 0.82 to 1.42). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): in young patients with early ADPKD and preserved function, aiming low slows kidney growth and helps the heart and albuminuria — a real but surrogate-level gain, bought with more dizziness, and not a licence to add a second renin–angiotensin blocker.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — rigorous blood-pressure control slowed total kidney volume growth and improved cardiac and albuminuria measures in early ADPKD, without an overall eGFR benefit and with more dizziness; dual renin–angiotensin blockade added nothing

title: Extended-release calcifediol in stage 3–4 CKD: vitamin D normalised in over 95% and parathyroid hormone down by a third in 40% at six months — all biochemistry, no outcomes trial
question: In stage 3–4 chronic kidney disease with secondary hyperparathyroidism, does extended-release calcifediol raise 25-hydroxyvitamin D and lower parathyroid hormone compared with placebo?
balance: The evidence here is two identical placebo-controlled trials wearing one publication. Sprague SM et al. (PMID: 27676085) randomised 429 adults with stage 3–4 chronic kidney disease, secondary hyperparathyroidism, and vitamin D insufficiency, 2:1 to extended-release calcifediol 30 or 60 µg at bedtime or placebo for 26 weeks across 89 United States sites: the drug normalised serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D (above 30 ng/ml) in over 95% of per-protocol participants, reduced intact parathyroid hormone by at least 10% in 72%, and produced parathyroid hormone reductions of at least 30% in a proportion that climbed with time on treatment — 22% at 12 weeks, 40% at 26 weeks, and 50% at 52 weeks in the open-label extension — with lowering significantly greater than placebo and independent of CKD stage, and with what the authors call an inconsequential impact on serum calcium, phosphorus, fibroblast growth factor 23, and adverse events. The anchor review (Sprague SM et al., PMID: 30058895) frames why the formulation matters: ordinary nutritional vitamin D has proven ineffective for secondary hyperparathyroidism, and active vitamin D receptor activators suppress parathyroid hormone at the price of hypercalcaemia and hyperphosphataemia risk, whereas gradual-release calcifediol corrected the hormone without meaningfully raising calcium or phosphorus in its trials. Every outcome here is a laboratory value — no trial shows fewer fractures, less cardiovascular disease, or slower dialysis onset. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): extended-release calcifediol reliably repletes 25-hydroxyvitamin D and lowers parathyroid hormone in stage 3–4 CKD without disturbing calcium or phosphate — a biochemical benefit, honestly labelled. Active vitamin D analogues such as paricalcitol are carded at shelves #1740 and #2047.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — extended-release calcifediol normalises 25-hydroxyvitamin D and lowers parathyroid hormone versus placebo in stage 3–4 CKD without raising calcium or phosphorus; no clinical outcome has been tested

title: Five units instead of ten for hyperkalaemia: hypoglycaemia odds nearly halved and potassium fell just as far — in ten retrospective studies and not one randomised trial
question: In acute hyperkalaemia, does a reduced insulin dose (5 units, or weight-based) lower potassium as effectively as the standard 10 units, with less hypoglycaemia, in the pooled studies?
balance: Everyone who treats acute hyperkalaemia knows the standard 10 units of intravenous insulin is a hypoglycaemia machine; the question is whether halving the dose surrenders potassium control. The pooled answer (Moussavi K et al., PMID: 33993515) comes from ten retrospective cohort studies and 3,437 patients — no randomised trials — comparing 10 units against alternatives of 5 units, 0.1 units/kg, or anything under 10 units. The reduced strategies were associated with lower pooled odds of hypoglycaemia (odds ratio 0.55, 95% CI 0.43 to 0.69; I²=8%) and of severe hypoglycaemia (OR 0.41, 95% CI 0.27 to 0.64; I²=0%), and potassium reduction was indistinguishable: mean difference −0.02 mmol/L (95% CI −0.11 to 0.07), albeit with moderate heterogeneity (I²=53%). Included studies carried low or moderate risk of bias on the scales used. That is a reassuring pattern — less of the harm, none of the efficacy lost — resting entirely on retrospective comparisons in which clinicians may have chosen smaller doses for patients they judged frailer or more hypoglycaemia-prone, a confounding direction that would actually work against the reduced dose on potassium and for it on hypoglycaemia, and which only a prospective trial can untangle; the authors say exactly that. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): reduced insulin dosing for hyperkalaemia appears to halve the odds of hypoglycaemia without compromising potassium lowering, on retrospective evidence that prospective studies have yet to confirm.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — reduced insulin dosing was associated with less hypoglycaemia and no loss of potassium lowering, but every pooled study was retrospective

title: Drinking more water for polycystic kidneys: PREVENT-ADPKD's three-year answer is no — urine diluted, copeptin unmoved, kidneys grew 6.8% versus 7.8% a year
question: In autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease, does prescribed increased water intake slow kidney growth and function decline compared with usual intake over three years?
balance: The logic was impeccable — vasopressin drives cyst growth, water suppresses vasopressin — and PREVENT-ADPKD (Rangan GK et al., PMID: 38319283) tested it properly: 184 adults with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease in Mayo imaging subclasses 1B–1E and eGFR at least 30, randomised for three years to water prescribed to drive 24-hour urine osmolality to 270 mOsmol/kg or below, or to drinking ad libitum. The intervention did dilute the urine (between-group difference in mean 24-hour urine osmolality −91 mOsmol/kg, 95% CI −127 to −54), yet kidney growth did not slow: height-corrected total kidney volume grew 6.8% per year on prescribed water versus 7.8% ad libitum, a mean difference of −0.97% per year (95% CI −2.37 to 0.44; P=0.18). Two internal findings explain the miss: only 52.3% of the prescribed group actually achieved the target urine osmolality, and serum copeptin — the vasopressin surrogate the whole strategy aimed to suppress — did not fall over three years. Adverse events were similar between groups, so the prescription is safe; it is the efficacy that failed. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): prescribed high water intake, as actually achieved in this trial, does not slow kidney growth in ADPKD — reasonable hydration advice, not a treatment, and no substitute for therapies with positive trials. Water coaching in non-ADPKD stage 3 CKD is a different population and question (a separate candidate in this programme); tolvaptan in ADPKD is shelf #297.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — prescribed increased water intake did not slow kidney growth over three years in the one randomised trial, despite achieving more dilute urine

title: The low-calcium diet for stones, overturned: normal calcium with less meat and salt recurred in 20% versus 38% over five years — because cutting calcium raised urinary oxalate
question: In idiopathic hypercalciuria with recurrent calcium stones, does a normal-calcium diet low in animal protein and salt prevent recurrence better than a traditional low-calcium diet?
balance: The traditional advice — restrict calcium — was tested head-to-head against the counter-intuitive alternative and lost. Borghi L et al. (PMID: 11784873) randomised 120 men with recurrent calcium oxalate stones and idiopathic hypercalciuria for five years: a normal-calcium diet (30 mmol/day) with reduced animal protein (52 g/day) and reduced salt (50 mmol of sodium chloride/day), versus the traditional low-calcium diet (10 mmol/day). Relapse struck 12 of 60 men on the normal-calcium, low-protein, low-salt diet versus 23 of 60 on low calcium — an unadjusted relative risk of recurrence of 0.49 (95% CI 0.24 to 0.98; P=0.04), i.e. a 51% relative reduction in recurrence, printed beside the absolute rates of 20% versus 38%. Urinary calcium fell by about 170 mg/day in both groups, which is what makes the result interesting: the low-calcium diet matched on calcium excretion but lost on stones, because urinary oxalate rose by an average of 5.4 mg/day on low calcium while falling by 7.2 mg/day on the normal-calcium diet — dietary calcium binds gut oxalate, and removing it frees oxalate for absorption. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): for men with hypercalciuric recurrent calcium oxalate stones, keep calcium normal and cut animal protein and salt — five-year randomised evidence from a single trial, in men only. Drug prevention with thiazides (shelf #483) and potassium citrate (shelf #2645) answers different questions.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a normal-calcium diet low in animal protein and salt halved stone recurrence in relative terms versus a low-calcium diet over five years, in men with hypercalciuria

title: Vancomycin versus metronidazole for C. difficile: a tie in mild disease, a clear vancomycin win in severe disease — severity, not habit, should pick the drug
question: In adults with Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhoea, is oral vancomycin superior to metronidazole — and does the answer depend on disease severity?
balance: SPLIT — severity decides. The only prospective, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled head-to-head trial (Zar FA et al., PMID: 17599306; 172 enrolled, 150 completing) found the two drugs effectively tied in mild disease (clinical cure 90% on metronidazole vs 98% on vancomycin, P=.36) and clearly separated in severe disease (76% vs 97%, P=.02), with recurrence much the same either way (15% vs 14%). The 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis of CDI antibiotic therapy (Stabholz Y et al., PMID: 37690610) points the same way at scale: initial treatment failure was higher with metronidazole than with glycopeptides (RR 1.58, 95% CI 1.10 to 2.27; 5 RCTs, 843 patients), while all-cause mortality did not differ significantly between vancomycin and metronidazole (RR 0.78, 95% CI 0.46 to 1.32; 4 RCTs, 808 patients; very low certainty). Neither drug is the modern recurrence story — fidaxomicin and recurrence prevention live on shelf #170 — but as a cure question, this trial is why severity, not habit, should pick between these two. PROPOSED SPLIT: metronidazole matches vancomycin in mild disease; vancomycin is superior in severe disease.
stamp: SPLIT — metronidazole matches vancomycin in mild C. difficile disease, but vancomycin is superior in severe disease (cure 97% vs 76%)
