title: MERINO: the carbapenem-sparing shortcut cost lives — piperacillin-tazobactam mortality 12.3% versus 3.7% on meropenem in resistant bloodstream infection
question: In patients with ceftriaxone-resistant Escherichia coli or Klebsiella pneumoniae bloodstream infection, is piperacillin-tazobactam non-inferior to meropenem for 30-day mortality?
balance: LIKELY (harm) — the carbapenem-sparing idea failed its fairest test. MERINO (Harris PNA et al., PMID: 30208454) randomised 379 patients with ceftriaxone-resistant Escherichia coli or Klebsiella pneumoniae bloodstream infection — organisms susceptible to both study drugs — and piperacillin-tazobactam did not come close to non-inferiority: 30-day mortality was 12.3% (23/187) versus 3.7% (7/191) on meropenem, a risk difference of 8.6 percentage points against a 5-point margin (P=.90 for non-inferiority). The later meta-analysis (Gatti M et al., PMID: 39173739), pooling MERINO with nine retrospective studies (1,962 patients), found a smaller, non-significant mortality difference overall (OR 1.41, 95% CI 0.96 to 2.07) but a significantly higher mortality with piperacillin-tazobactam where fewer than half the infections came from urinary or biliary sources (OR 2.02, 95% CI 1.00 to 4.07) — observational softening of a randomised signal, not a refutation of it. PROPOSED LIKELY (harm): for ceftriaxone-resistant E. coli or K. pneumoniae bloodstream infection, definitive piperacillin-tazobactam carries a mortality price the randomised trial measured and the pooled literature does not erase.
stamp: LIKELY (harm) — definitive piperacillin-tazobactam was not non-inferior to meropenem and carried higher 30-day mortality (12.3% vs 3.7%) in ceftriaxone-resistant bloodstream infection

title: TANGO II: meropenem-vaborbactam doubled clinical cure over best available therapy in carbapenem-resistant infection — 65.6% versus 33.3%, in just 47 confirmed cases
question: In patients with carbapenem-resistant Gram-negative infections, is meropenem-vaborbactam superior to best available therapy for clinical cure and mortality?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — TANGO II (Wunderink RG et al., PMID: 30270406) randomised just 77 patients with confirmed or suspected carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae infection, and only 47 with confirmed CRE formed the primary population — yet the direction was consistent across endpoints: clinical cure at end of treatment 65.6% (21/32) versus 33.3% (5/15) on best available therapy, day-28 mortality 15.6% versus 33.3%, and fewer renal adverse events (4.0% vs 24.0%). A 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of novel beta-lactam/beta-lactamase inhibitors versus best available therapy (Al Shammari et al., PMID: 42792078; 9 studies, 2,892 patients) found a 27% relative reduction in mortality (pooled RR 0.73, 95% CI 0.59 to 0.90), with meropenem-vaborbactam the most effective agent against KPC-producing strains (RR 0.65, 95% CI 0.49 to 0.94) and no combination effective against metallo-beta-lactamase producers. Small numbers, an open-label design, a heterogeneous comparator and a trial that stopped short of its ambitions keep this at possible, not likely. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): meropenem-vaborbactam probably improves cure and spares kidneys in CRE infection, with the mortality advantage plausible but not proven by the trial alone.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — meropenem-vaborbactam improved clinical cure and reduced renal harm versus best available therapy in CRE infection, in one small open-label trial

title: EPIC: once-daily plazomicin matched meropenem for complicated UTI — and was ahead at test of cure, 81.7% versus 70.1%, with more creatinine rises
question: In adults with complicated urinary tract infection, is once-daily plazomicin non-inferior to meropenem for clinical and microbiological cure?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — EPIC (Wagenlehner FME et al., PMID: 30786187) randomised 609 patients with complicated urinary tract infection or acute pyelonephritis and met its non-inferiority objective at both primary time points: composite cure (clinical cure plus microbiological eradication) at day 5 was 88.0% (168/191) on once-daily plazomicin versus 91.4% (180/197) on meropenem (difference −3.4 points, 95% CI −10.0 to 3.1), and at the test-of-cure visit plazomicin was ahead, 81.7% versus 70.1% (difference 11.6 points, 95% CI 2.7 to 20.3), with fewer microbiological recurrences (3.7% vs 8.1%) and clinical relapses (1.6% vs 7.1%) at late follow-up. The aminoglycoside price tag showed in the expected place: creatinine rises of 0.5 mg/dL or more occurred in 7.0% versus 4.0%. The 2023 meta-analysis of novel antibiotics for complicated UTI (Hung KC et al., PMID: 37100354) supports the class direction — higher clinical cure at test of cure (83.6% vs 80.3%; OR 1.37, 95% CI 1.08 to 1.74) with similar adverse events — while warning its own clinical-cure evidence remains inconclusive. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): plazomicin is a credible once-daily meropenem alternative for complicated UTI caused by Enterobacteriaceae, including multidrug-resistant strains, with kidney monitoring as the condition.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — once-daily plazomicin was non-inferior to meropenem for complicated UTI, with higher composite cure at test of cure and a creatinine-rise cost (7.0% vs 4.0%)

title: Two weeks versus four after the washout: 99% cured on the short course in native joint arthritis — but two-thirds of the joints were hands and wrists
question: In adults with native joint bacterial arthritis treated with surgical drainage, are 2 weeks of antibiotics as effective as 4 weeks for remission?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one prospective randomised non-inferiority trial (Gjika E et al., PMID: 30992295) asked the duration question after surgical drainage of native joint bacterial arthritis and found almost nothing separating the courses: among 154 cases (77 per arm), recurrence occurred in 3 patients in total — cure 99% on 2 weeks versus 97% on 4 weeks — with no difference in adverse events or sequelae, and a significantly shorter hospital stay on the shorter course. The catch is the case mix: 99 of the 154 cases were hand and wrist infections, where the per-protocol subgroup analysis likewise found cure of 97% versus 96% but sequelae in about half of patients either way (50% vs 55%). No systematic review of antibiotic duration in native joint arthritis was found to corroborate the trial, so the shelf stands on this single study: after adequate surgical lavage, two weeks of targeted therapy looks sufficient for hand and wrist septic arthritis, and is unproven — not disproven — for large joints. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the shorter course halves antibiotic exposure without a measured cure cost, within the population actually studied.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — 2 weeks of antibiotics after surgical drainage was non-inferior to 4 weeks for native joint arthritis (cure 99% vs 97%), mostly hand and wrist

title: Five days was not enough for the under-twos: clinical failure 34% on the short course versus 16% on ten days of amoxicillin-clavulanate
question: In young children with acute otitis media, does a shortened 5-day course of amoxicillin-clavulanate produce worse outcomes than the standard 10-day course?
balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — in the youngest children, the short course lost. Hoberman A et al. (PMID: 28002709) randomised 520 children aged 6 to 23 months with rigorously diagnosed acute otitis media to 5 days of amoxicillin-clavulanate (then 5 days of placebo) or the standard 10 days, and clinical failure was twice as common on the short course: 34% (77/229) versus 16% (39/238), a difference of 17 percentage points (95% CI 9 to 25). The shorter regimen bought nothing in exchange — no significant difference in recurrence, adverse events, or nasopharyngeal colonisation with penicillin-nonsusceptible pathogens. The older meta-analysis (Kozyrskyj AL et al., PMID: 9624028) had found 5-day courses broadly comparable by 20 to 30 days in children aged 4 weeks to 18 years (odds ratio 1.22, 95% CI 0.98 to 1.54) — but its children were older, its diagnoses less strict, and even it found more early failures on short courses (OR 1.52 at 8 to 19 days). The two records reconcile by age and diagnostic certainty: shortening is a gamble that the under-twos, diagnosed strictly, demonstrably lose. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm): in children 6 to 23 months old with certain acute otitis media, cutting amoxicillin-clavulanate to 5 days worsens outcomes without reducing resistance or side effects.
stamp: POSSIBLE (harm) — a shortened 5-day course of amoxicillin-clavulanate produced worse outcomes than 10 days in children 6–23 months (clinical failure 34% vs 16%)

title: Antibiotics at catheter removal: a meta-analysis finds about 6 fewer symptomatic urine infections per 100 removals (NNT 17) — a real gain with an uncounted resistance cost
question: In patients having a urinary catheter removed, does antibiotic prophylaxis at removal reduce subsequent urinary tract infection?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — across seven controlled studies (six randomised) of short-term catheterisation, antibiotic prophylaxis at catheter removal was associated with fewer subsequent symptomatic urinary tract infections: risk ratio 0.45 (95% CI 0.28 to 0.72), an absolute risk reduction of 5.8%, and a number needed to treat of 17 (95% CI 12 to 30). That is a 55% relative risk reduction, stated alongside the 5.8% absolute reduction. The limits are real: five of the seven studies were in surgical patients, the antibiotics and observation periods varied, and the review could not weigh the harms that decide policy in practice — side effects, cost, and antimicrobial resistance — against a modest absolute gain. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): prophylaxis at removal probably prevents some symptomatic infections after short-term catheterisation, most clearly in surgical patients, but which patients benefit enough to justify routine antibiotic use remains unresolved.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Doravirine for first HIV treatment: non-inferior suppression to darunavir and efavirenz regimens in two phase 3 trials, with far fewer brain and sleep side effects than efavirenz
question: In antiretroviral-naive adults with HIV-1, is doravirine-based therapy non-inferior to ritonavir-boosted darunavir or to efavirenz-based therapy for viral suppression, with better tolerability?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — two phase 3 non-inferiority trials point the same way. Against ritonavir-boosted darunavir (DRIVE-FORWARD), doravirine-based therapy suppressed HIV-1 RNA below 50 copies/mL in 84% versus 80% at week 48 (difference 3.9%, 95% CI −1.6 to 9.4). Against efavirenz-based therapy (DRIVE-AHEAD), the fixed-dose doravirine combination suppressed 84.3% versus 80.8% (difference 3.5%, 95% CI −2.0 to 9.0), with significantly less dizziness (8.8% vs 37.1%), fewer sleep disorders (12.1% vs 25.2%), and essentially flat lipids where efavirenz raised them. A systematic review and meta-analysis of the randomised record likewise ranked doravirine 100 mg highest for efficacy among the strategies compared, with no significant pairwise difference against boosted darunavir. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): doravirine-based initial therapy is non-inferior for viral suppression with a tolerability advantage over efavirenz — benefit here means an equally effective, better-tolerated option, not superior suppression.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: Switching suppressed HIV patients to the doravirine single tablet: suppression held in the one DRIVE-SHIFT trial, with better lipids for those leaving a boosted protease inhibitor
question: In virologically suppressed adults with HIV-1, does switching to doravirine/lamivudine/tenofovir disoproxil maintain suppression versus continuing the current regimen?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in the single DRIVE-SHIFT trial, switching suppressed adults to once-daily doravirine/lamivudine/tenofovir disoproxil fumarate maintained suppression: 93.7% versus 94.6% still below 50 copies/mL at week 24 against continuing the baseline regimen (difference −0.9, 95% CI −4.7 to 3.0), and 90.8% at week 48 met non-inferiority against the baseline regimen's week-24 result. In participants switching from a boosted protease inhibitor, fasting lipids fell significantly more. The costs: adverse events were more frequent after switching by week 24 (68.9% vs 52.5%) and discontinuation for adverse events was 2.5% versus 0.4%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): switching maintains suppression in this one trial, with a lipid gain for protease-inhibitor switchers and a small early tolerability price. Tier C is set because this is a single trial.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Fostemsavir for multidrug-resistant HIV: a clear 8-day randomised effect and suppression in about half of salvage patients at 48 weeks in the single BRIGHTE trial
question: In heavily treatment-experienced adults with multidrug-resistant HIV-1, does fostemsavir added to optimised background therapy achieve viral suppression?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in BRIGHTE, a phase 3 trial in multidrug-resistant HIV-1, adding fostemsavir to a failing regimen cut HIV-1 RNA by a mean 0.79 log10 copies/mL in 8 days versus 0.17 log10 on placebo (P<0.001), in the cohort that still had at least one fully active drug available. By week 48, 54% of that randomised cohort and 38% of the cohort with no remaining options had HIV-1 RNA below 40 copies/mL, with mean CD4 gains of 139 and 64 cells respectively. An indirect-comparison analysis found significantly higher odds of suppression than optimised background therapy alone from an older trial programme (OR 3.26, 95% CI 2.08 to 5.11), but non-significant differences against ibalizumab-based therapy. Seven percent stopped fostemsavir for adverse events, and gp120 substitutions appeared in 43% of randomised-cohort virologic failures. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a genuinely new mechanism with sustained responses in about half of a salvage population — meaningful where options are exhausted, on single-trial evidence. Tier C is set for that reason.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Ibalizumab for multidrug-resistant HIV: 83% responded within a week of the loading dose — in one single-arm study of 40 patients with no control group
question: In adults with multidrug-resistant HIV-1 failing current therapy, does ibalizumab added to an optimised regimen suppress viral load?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the entire case rests on one single-arm, open-label phase 3 study of 40 adults with multidrug-resistant HIV-1. After a 7-day control period on their failing therapy, a single loading dose of ibalizumab was followed by a decrease of at least 0.5 log10 copies/mL in 33 of 40 patients (83%) by day 14 (P<0.001 against the control period), with a mean fall of 1.1 log10. By week 25 on ibalizumab plus an optimised background regimen, the mean fall was 1.6 log10, 43% were below 50 copies/mL and 50% below 200 copies/mL. But there was no parallel control group, the background regimen (which had to include at least one fully active agent) shares credit for every later result, 9 of 10 patients with failure or rebound showed reduced ibalizumab susceptibility in vitro, and the commonest adverse event was diarrhoea (20%). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): real antiviral activity in a desperate population, demonstrated only against each patient's own control week. Tier C is set because the evidence is a single-arm study.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — antiviral activity is shown only in a single-arm study of 40 patients, with no randomised comparison

title: Point-of-care HIV testing for exposed infants: treatment started within 60 days for 90% versus 13% with laboratory referral in one Mozambican cluster trial
question: In HIV-exposed infants in low-resource settings, does point-of-care early infant diagnosis increase antiretroviral initiation and retention versus standard laboratory testing?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in one cluster-randomised trial across 16 primary health centres in Mozambique, point-of-care early infant diagnosis transformed the treatment cascade: 89.7% of HIV-positive infants started antiretroviral therapy within 60 days of sample collection versus 12.8% with standard laboratory referral (adjusted relative risk 7.34; P<0.001), median time to initiation was under 1 day versus 127 days, and retention at 90 days among those who started was 61.6% versus 42.9% (adjusted relative risk 1.40; P<0.027). The effect sizes are unusually large for a delivery intervention, which is itself a caution: a single programme, in one country's clinic system, where the standard-care arm performed exceptionally poorly (only 13 of 102 infants started within 60 days). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): same-day infant testing very probably speeds treatment and improves early retention where laboratory referral leaks patients, with the size of the gain depending on how weak the referral system is. Tier C is set because this is a single trial programme.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Assisted partner services for HIV: partners tested 67% versus 13% and five times the new diagnoses in the Kenyan cluster trial, with a smaller but consistent pooled effect
question: In people newly diagnosed with HIV, does assisted partner notification (provider-supported partner services) increase partner testing and new diagnoses versus passive referral?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in a Kenyan cluster-randomised trial of 18 clinics, immediate assisted partner services multiplied partner testing nearly fivefold at 6 weeks: 67% of partners tested versus 13% with delayed services (incidence rate ratio 4.8, 95% CI 3.7 to 6.4), new HIV diagnoses in 23% versus 4% of partners (5.0, 3.2 to 7.9), and new enrolment in care in 15% versus 3% (4.4, 2.6 to 7.4), with one intimate-partner-violence event related to notification in each group. A WHO systematic review of the wider literature found a more modest pooled effect (partner test uptake relative risk 1.46, 95% CI 1.22 to 1.75, across three individually randomised trials) with few reports of harm — the Kenyan cluster effect is larger than the pooled average, likely reflecting its delayed-service comparator. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): provider-supported partner services find substantially more partners, diagnoses, and care enrolments than passive referral, without a demonstrated increase in partner violence in these studies. Tier C is set because the anchor is a single cluster trial.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Hepatitis C treatment with almost no monitoring: 95% cured in the single-arm MINMON study — feasibility demonstrated, equivalence to monitored care untested
question: In adults with chronic hepatitis C, does a minimal-monitoring direct-acting antiviral approach (no scheduled on-treatment visits or labs) achieve cure rates comparable to standard monitored care?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — MINMON was a single-arm phase 4 study: 399 people with hepatitis C across five countries took 12 weeks of sofosbuvir-velpatasvir with no pre-treatment genotyping, the whole course dispensed at entry, no scheduled on-treatment visits or laboratory monitoring, and only remote contacts at weeks 4 and 22. Overall 379 of 399 (95.0%, 95% CI 92.4 to 96.7) achieved sustained virological response, 89% of those assessed reported taking 100% of the medication, serious adverse events occurred in 4% (none treatment-related), and only 4% had unplanned visits (none treatment-related). Those cure figures resemble standard monitored care in real-world data — but resemblance is not a comparison: with no control arm, the study cannot show minimal monitoring costs nothing, only that high cure is achievable under it in trial-supported conditions. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): minimal monitoring is feasible and achieved 95% cure in this cohort; equivalence to monitored care is unproven. Tier C is set because the evidence is a single-arm study.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — cure rates under minimal monitoring are shown in a single-arm study only, with no monitored comparison

title: Hepatitis B vaccine for prior nonresponders with HIV: the CpG vaccine protected 93–99% versus 81% for repeating the standard vaccine in BEe-HIVe
question: In people with HIV who previously did not respond to hepatitis B vaccination, does the 2-dose CpG-adjuvanted hepatitis B vaccine achieve seroprotection where the alum-adjuvanted vaccine failed?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in BEe-HIVe, a phase 3 randomised trial of 561 people with HIV who had previously not responded to hepatitis B vaccination, the CpG-adjuvanted vaccine outperformed the conventional alum-adjuvanted vaccine on seroprotection (antibody at least 10 mIU/mL): 93.1% after 2 doses of HepB-CpG, 99.4% after 3 doses, versus 80.6% after 3 doses of HepB-alum. The 2-dose regimen beat the alum regimen by a stratified difference of 12.5% (97.5% CI 4.1% to 20.9%) — non-inferior and superior — and the 3-dose CpG regimen by 18.4% (repeated 97.5% CI 10.4% to 26.2%); over 90% of CpG recipients were protected by week 12, and 78.1% of the 3-dose CpG group exceeded 1000 mIU/mL versus 35.2% on alum. No unexpected safety issues were observed. The outcome is an antibody threshold, not prevented hepatitis B infections, and durability beyond the primary timepoints is not shown in this record. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): in prior nonresponders with HIV, HepB-CpG — especially 3 doses — achieves seroprotection in substantially more people than repeating the alum vaccine. Tier C is set because this is a single trial with a surrogate outcome.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Oteseconazole for recurrent yeast infections: only about 4–7% recurred over 48 weeks versus about 40% on placebo, in two phase 3 trials
question: In women with recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis, does oteseconazole reduce recurrence versus placebo over 50 weeks?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — the VIOLET programme comprises two global phase 3, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials (656 women whose screening episode had first cleared with fluconazole induction). Through week 48, the averaged proportion with one or more recurrent episodes was 6.7% and 3.9% on oteseconazole in the two trials versus 42.8% and 39.4% on placebo (P<0.001 for both) — roughly a 36–39 percentage-point absolute reduction, with hazard ratios for time to recurrence of 0.11 (95% CI 0.06 to 0.21) and 0.08 (0.04 to 0.17), an 89–92% relative reduction in recurrence hazard alongside those absolute rates. Mean time to recurrence among those who did recur was about 46–47 weeks on oteseconazole versus 28–33 weeks on placebo. Treatment-emergent adverse events were similar between groups, with no drug-related serious events and no adverse effects on pregnancy outcomes, liver function, or QT interval reported. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): oteseconazole maintenance after fluconazole induction prevents most recurrences for a year in women with recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: Ibrexafungerp for an acute yeast infection: one day of tablets cured 50.5% versus 28.6% on placebo in VANISH 303 — effective, with no fluconazole comparison
question: In women with acute vulvovaginal candidiasis, is oral ibrexafungerp superior to placebo for clinical cure?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in VANISH 303, a phase 3 randomised superiority trial, one day of oral ibrexafungerp (300 mg twice for 1 day) beat placebo on every efficacy endpoint at test-of-cure (day 11): clinical cure 50.5% versus 28.6% (P=0.001) — a 21.9 percentage-point absolute gain — mycological eradication 49.5% versus 19.4% (P<0.001), and overall success 36.0% versus 12.6% (P<0.001), with symptom resolution at follow-up (day 25) of 59.6% versus 44.9% (P=0.009). Adverse events were primarily gastrointestinal and mild. The honest framing: half of treated patients were not clinically cured at day 11, and placebo itself produced a 28.6% cure rate, so the drug adds about one extra cure for every five women treated over doing nothing. There is no comparison here against fluconazole, the standard oral treatment. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): ibrexafungerp is an effective oral option for acute vulvovaginal candidiasis versus placebo, with its place relative to azole therapy untested in this trial.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Weekly fluconazole for recurrent yeast infections: 91% stayed disease-free on treatment versus 36% on placebo — but the advantage largely faded within six months of stopping
question: In women with recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis, does weekly maintenance fluconazole for 6 months keep the infection suppressed versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in the single classic trial, after remission was induced with three fluconazole doses, weekly fluconazole 150 mg for 6 months kept 90.8% of women disease-free at 6 months versus 35.9% on placebo (P<0.001) — a 54.9 percentage-point absolute difference during treatment. The protection then decayed off therapy: disease-free proportions were 73.2% versus 27.8% at 9 months and 42.9% versus 21.9% at 12 months, and median time to recurrence was 10.2 versus 4.0 months (P<0.001). There was no evidence of fluconazole resistance in Candida albicans isolates or superinfection with Candida glabrata, and one patient stopped fluconazole for headache. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): weekly fluconazole suppresses recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis while it is taken, but a long-term cure after stopping remains difficult to achieve — the trial's own conclusion. Tier C is set because this is a single trial.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: One big dose of liposomal amphotericin B for disseminated histoplasmosis: response looked comparable in a 118-person trial, but the authors themselves say a confirmatory trial is needed
question: In people with HIV and disseminated histoplasmosis, does a single high dose of liposomal amphotericin B achieve clinical response comparable to standard daily dosing, with less toxicity?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the modern randomised trial (118 people with AIDS-related disseminated histoplasmosis) found day-14 clinical response of 84% with a single 10 mg/kg dose of liposomal amphotericin B, 69% with a two-dose regimen, and 74% with standard daily dosing for 2 weeks, with no significant difference (P=0.69); day-14 survival was 89.0%, 78.0%, and 92.1% respectively (P=0.82), and infusion, kidney, and laboratory toxicities were similar across arms. The authors state response may be non-inferior but a confirmatory phase III trial is needed — this trial did not prove non-inferiority. Supporting biology comes from an older comparison across two separate trials (Wheat 2001): liposomal amphotericin B and itraconazole produced similar clinical response (86% vs 85%), but fungemia cleared faster with liposomal amphotericin B (over 85% vs 53% culture-negative at 2 weeks; P=0.0008), and the Cochrane review of disseminated histoplasmosis treatment in HIV found liposomal amphotericin B may raise clinical success versus the deoxycholate form (risk ratio 1.46, 95% CI 1.01 to 2.11; low certainty) with less nephrotoxicity. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): single-dose induction looks comparable and was no more toxic in a small trial, but equivalence is a hypothesis awaiting a confirmatory trial, not a result. Tier C is set for that reason.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — a single small trial found no significant difference, which does not establish that one dose is equivalent to standard dosing

title: Talaromycosis in HIV: amphotericin B and itraconazole tied at 2 weeks, but 6-month deaths were 11.3% versus 21.0% — induction choice decides survival
question: In HIV-associated talaromycosis, is amphotericin B deoxycholate induction superior to itraconazole for 6-month mortality?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in IVAP, an open-label trial of 440 adults with HIV-associated talaromycosis, amphotericin B deoxycholate and itraconazole looked equal at the 2-week primary endpoint (death 6.5% vs 7.4%; absolute difference 0.9 percentage points, 95% CI −3.9 to 5.6; non-inferiority met) but diverged by 6 months: death 11.3% versus 21.0% (absolute difference 9.7 percentage points, 95% CI 2.8 to 16.6; P=0.006), with faster clinical resolution and fungal clearance and lower relapse and immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome rates on amphotericin. A meta-analysis of 975 patients (only one randomised trial among eight studies) found the same direction: initial amphotericin B was associated with lower mortality than initial itraconazole (risk ratio 0.61, 95% CI 0.41 to 0.90). The price of amphotericin was significantly more infusion reactions, renal failure, hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, and anaemia. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): amphotericin B induction saves lives at 6 months compared with itraconazole induction, at a real toxicity cost — start with amphotericin where it can be given and monitored. Tier C is set because the randomised evidence is a single trial.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Steroids for moderate-to-severe Pneumocystis pneumonia in HIV: 31-day deaths 11% versus 23% in the 1990 trial that set the standard of care
question: In patients with moderate-to-severe Pneumocystis pneumonia and HIV, do adjunctive corticosteroids reduce mortality and respiratory failure versus antibiotics alone?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — in the California Collaborative Treatment Group trial (Bozzette 1990), 333 patients with AIDS and Pneumocystis pneumonia were randomised to early adjunctive corticosteroids or standard therapy alone. Among patients with confirmed or presumed pneumonia, cumulative risk at 31 days was lower with corticosteroids for respiratory failure (0.14 vs 0.30; P=0.004) and for death (0.11 vs 0.23; P=0.009) — absolute reductions of 16 and 12 percentage points — and death within 84 days was 0.16 versus 0.26 (P=0.026); intention-to-treat analysis of the entire cohort confirmed the findings. Benefit could not be demonstrated in mild disease (oxygenation ratio above 350, equivalent to arterial oxygen above 75 torr on room air), and corticosteroid patients had more localised herpetic lesions (26% vs 15%; P=0.04) without excess other infections or neoplasms. The NIH-University of California expert panel's consensus statement, published alongside, formalised corticosteroids as adjunctive therapy for this condition. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): early adjunctive corticosteroids reduce respiratory failure and death in moderate-to-severe Pneumocystis pneumonia in HIV — a foundational result that has structured practice since 1990, scoped to moderate-to-severe disease.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: Stopping Pneumocystis prophylaxis after CD4 recovery: zero cases in 262 patients who stopped — the upper confidence limit, not certainty, is what the cohort buys
question: In adults with HIV whose CD4 counts have recovered on antiretroviral therapy, can primary prophylaxis against Pneumocystis pneumonia be stopped safely?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the Swiss HIV Cohort Study (Furrer H et al., PMID: 10219064) prospectively stopped primary prophylaxis in 262 adults whose CD4 counts had risen to at least 200 cells per cubic millimeter and at least 14 percent of total lymphocytes, sustained for at least 12 weeks on combination antiretroviral therapy, and followed them for a median of 11.3 months: there were no cases of Pneumocystis pneumonia and no cases of toxoplasmic encephalitis. Zero events is reassuring but not proof of zero risk — the one-sided upper 99 percent confidence limit was 1.9 cases per 100 patient-years for Pneumocystis pneumonia (238 patient-years) and 4.2 per 100 patient-years for toxoplasmic encephalitis (110 patient-years, among the 121 participants seropositive for Toxoplasma gondii). This is a prospective cohort, not a randomised trial: patients whose counts recovered may differ from those whose did not, follow-up was under a year at the median, and prophylaxis was resumed in nine patients. No systematic review or meta-analysis of prophylaxis discontinuation itself was found in-session, so the shelf rests on this cohort and the consistent discontinuation studies of its era that the miner entry cites. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): for patients meeting the CD4 and lymphocyte-percentage thresholds on effective antiretroviral therapy, stopping primary prophylaxis is a reasonable, evidence-supported step that removes drug burden and toxicity risk — with restarting if counts fall again.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — stopping primary Pneumocystis prophylaxis appears safe once CD4 counts have risen to at least 200 cells/mm³ and 14% of lymphocytes for at least 12 weeks on combination antiretroviral therapy

title: Toxoplasmic encephalitis in AIDS: the one head-to-head trial stopped early and found no significant difference — the cheaper, available regimen remains unproven, not disproven
question: In patients with HIV-associated toxoplasmic encephalitis, is trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole as effective as pyrimethamine plus sulfadiazine for clinical and radiological response?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the randomised record for this comparison is a single Thai trial (Kongsaengdao S et al., PMID: 17517949) that randomised AIDS patients with toxoplasmic encephalitis to six weeks of pyrimethamine 50 mg/day plus sulfadiazine, pyrimethamine 100 mg/day plus sulfadiazine, or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, and was terminated prematurely; its abstract reports that failure rates were not significantly different among the three groups and that the 50 mg pyrimethamine combination gave the best primary outcome (death in the first six weeks), while its authors themselves call for further evaluation of intravenous trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. The systematic review of randomised toxoplasmosis trials (Rajapakse S et al., PMID: 23816507) likewise found the efficacy of pyrimethamine plus sulfadiazine and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole similar for toxoplasmic encephalopathy, while grading most encephalitis trials as high risk of bias and poor methodological quality, with adverse effects seemingly more common on pyrimethamine plus sulfadiazine. 'No significant difference' in a small, stopped-early trial is not demonstrated equivalence, and the abstract of the anchor record reports no arm sizes or event rates to extract. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is a plausible alternative where pyrimethamine is unavailable or unaffordable, but equivalence is a hope the trials have not yet earned. Tier C is set because the evidence base is one prematurely terminated trial and a low-quality trial literature.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — one prematurely terminated trial found no significant difference in failure rates between trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and pyrimethamine plus sulfadiazine, which is too little evidence to call the regimens equivalent

title: Delamanid for multidrug-resistant TB: culture conversion at 2 months rose from 29.6% to 45.4% at the 100 mg dose — a surrogate gain with a QT-prolongation price
question: In multidrug-resistant pulmonary tuberculosis, does adding delamanid to an optimised background regimen improve sputum culture conversion at 2 months?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in the multinational randomised trial (Gler MT et al., PMID: 22670901), 481 patients with pulmonary multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (nearly all HIV-negative) received delamanid 100 mg twice daily, delamanid 200 mg twice daily, or placebo for 2 months on top of a WHO-guideline background regimen. Sputum culture conversion in liquid broth at 2 months was 45.4 percent with 100 mg (P=0.008 versus placebo), 41.9 percent with 200 mg (P=0.04), and 29.6 percent with placebo — an absolute gain of about 16 and 12 percentage points respectively, with similar findings on solid medium. Most adverse events were mild to moderate and evenly distributed, but QT prolongation on electrocardiography was reported significantly more frequently with delamanid, though no clinical events due to QT prolongation were observed. A later systematic review and meta-analysis of bedaquiline and delamanid studies (Ahmed SH et al., PMID: 38296395) found a pooled 6-month culture conversion proportion of 0.849 in delamanid cohorts and a pooled QTc prolongation incidence of 0.344, but those pooled proportions come largely from non-randomised cohorts and cannot substitute for a mortality or cure end point. Two months of a surrogate marker, in one trial, is what this shelf has. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): delamanid plausibly improves early culture conversion as part of a multidrug regimen, with cardiac monitoring owed for the QT signal. Tier C is set because the evidence is a single trial on a surrogate outcome.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — delamanid added to a background regimen increased 2-month sputum culture conversion by about 16 percentage points at 100 mg twice daily, on a surrogate end point, with more QT prolongation

title: TB-CHAMP: tuberculosis in 1.1% of children on levofloxacin versus 2.6% on placebo — a halving that the trial could not confirm (hazard ratio 0.44, 95% CI 0.15 to 1.25)
question: In children with household exposure to multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, does 24 weeks of levofloxacin preventive treatment prevent tuberculosis disease versus placebo?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — TB-CHAMP (Hesseling AC et al., PMID: 39693542) randomised 497 South African households, enrolling 922 children with household exposure to an adult with bacteriologically confirmed multidrug-resistant pulmonary TB, to 24 weeks of daily levofloxacin or placebo. By week 48, tuberculosis had developed in 5 of 453 children (1.1 percent) on levofloxacin and 12 of 469 (2.6 percent) on placebo — hazard ratio 0.44 (95% CI 0.15 to 1.25), a difference that was not significant; sensitivity analyses agreed. Grade 3 or higher possibly-related adverse events occurred in 4 children on levofloxacin and 8 on placebo, and grade 2 tendonitis in one levofloxacin-treated child. The wider literature looks stronger than the trial: a systematic review and meta-analysis of preventive treatment for MDR-TB contacts (Zhou G et al., PMID: 37741621) pooled a relative risk of 0.34 (95% CI 0.16 to 0.72) for progression — but from 11 mostly observational studies of 1,105 contacts, not from randomised comparisons. The honest summary is that the point estimates all lean the same way while the one randomised test in children ran out of events: only 17 children developed TB in total. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): levofloxacin prophylaxis for child contacts is biologically and observationally supported and was safe in the trial, but its efficacy is not yet proven by randomised evidence. Tier C is set because this rests on a single underpowered trial.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — levofloxacin preventive treatment was associated with a lower incidence of tuberculosis in exposed children, but the difference was not significant and the confidence interval spans from a large benefit to a small harm

title: V-QUIN: confirmed TB in 0.6% on levofloxacin versus 1.1% on placebo over 30 months — again a halving, again not significant (incidence rate ratio 0.55, 95% CI 0.19 to 1.62)
question: In household contacts of people with multidrug-resistant tuberculosis in Vietnam, does 6 months of daily levofloxacin prevent tuberculosis versus placebo?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — V-QUIN (Fox GJ et al., PMID: 39693541) randomised 2,041 household contacts of people with bacteriologically confirmed rifampicin-resistant or multidrug-resistant TB in Vietnam to 6 months of daily levofloxacin or placebo, following them for 30 months. Confirmed tuberculosis occurred in 6 participants (0.6 percent) on levofloxacin and 11 (1.1 percent) on placebo — incidence rate ratio 0.55 (95% CI 0.19 to 1.62), not significant. Tolerability is the counterweight: adverse events of any grade were reported by 306 participants (31.9 percent) taking levofloxacin versus 125 (13.0 percent) on placebo (risk difference 18.9 percentage points, 95% CI 14.2 to 23.6), although grade 3 or 4 events differed little (risk difference 1.0 percentage point, −0.3 to 2.4) and no acquired fluoroquinolone resistance was observed. The systematic review of preventive treatment for MDR-TB contacts (Zhou G et al., PMID: 37741621) pools a relative risk of 0.34 (95% CI 0.16 to 0.72), but from mostly observational studies. With only 17 confirmed cases across 2,041 contacts, V-QUIN — like its paediatric sibling TB-CHAMP — was defeated by how rare the outcome was. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): the direction of effect is consistent across both randomised trials and the observational literature, but randomised proof of efficacy is still missing, and a third of treated contacts report some adverse event. Tier C is set because this rests on a single trial for its population.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — levofloxacin was associated with a lower incidence of tuberculosis in household contacts, but the difference was not significant, and any-grade adverse events were substantially more common on levofloxacin

title: Aspirin for tuberculous meningitis: infarct-or-death in 15.8% on high-dose aspirin versus 28.9% on placebo in a 120-patient phase 2 trial — a trend, with a significant signal only in confirmed cases
question: In tuberculous meningitis, does adjunctive aspirin reduce new cerebral infarction and mortality versus placebo?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the phase 2 trial (Mai NTH et al., PMID: 29482717) randomised 120 HIV-uninfected adults with tuberculous meningitis to aspirin 81 mg, aspirin 1000 mg, or placebo daily for the first 60 days, all with anti-tuberculosis drugs and dexamethasone. The primary efficacy outcome — new brain infarction on MRI or death by 60 days — occurred in 11 of 38 (28.9 percent) on placebo, 8 of 36 (22.2 percent) on aspirin 81 mg, and 6 of 38 (15.8 percent) on aspirin 1000 mg (p=0.40): a dose-ordered trend that is not significant. The safety outcome (gastrointestinal or cerebral bleeding by 60 days) occurred in 13.9 percent on placebo and 22.9 percent and 20.0 percent on the two aspirin doses (p=0.59). A pre-planned subgroup analysis found a significant interaction with diagnostic category, with a possible reduction in microbiologically confirmed disease (34.4 percent on placebo versus 14.8 percent and 10.7 percent on aspirin; p=0.06), and spinal-fluid analysis showed dose-dependent thromboxane suppression. The systematic review and meta-analysis (Rizvi I et al., PMID: 31512620; 4 trials, 546 patients) found aspirin did not significantly reduce mortality (risk ratio 0.66, 95% CI 0.42 to 1.02; low-quality evidence) but did reduce new infarctions (risk ratio 0.52, 0.29 to 0.92; moderate-quality evidence). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): aspirin may prevent infarctions in tuberculous meningitis — the phase 3 trial the phase 2 authors call for is the test that matters. Tier C is set for the small phase 2 base.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — a small phase 2 trial showed a non-significant trend toward fewer new infarctions or deaths with aspirin, and a meta-analysis found fewer new infarctions but no mortality benefit, all at low-to-moderate quality

title: TEMPRANO long-term follow-up: 6 months of isoniazid preventive therapy cut the hazard of death by about a third (hazard ratio 0.63) — a benefit still visible at 6 years in people with high CD4 counts
question: In adults with HIV and high CD4 counts in West Africa, does 6 months of isoniazid preventive therapy reduce death or severe HIV illness when added to early antiretroviral therapy?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — the long-term follow-up of the TEMPRANO ANRS 12136 factorial trial (Badje A et al., PMID: 29025631) followed 2,056 HIV-infected adults in Côte d'Ivoire (mean baseline CD4 count 477 cells per microliter) for 9,404 patient-years (median 4.9 years), comparing those randomised to 6 months of isoniazid preventive therapy (IPT) with those randomised to none, across both early and deferred antiretroviral therapy (ART) strategies. Eighty-six deaths occurred: the 6-year probability of death was 4.1 percent (95% CI 2.9 to 5.7) with IPT versus 6.9 percent (5.1 to 9.2) without — hazard ratio 0.63 (95% CI 0.41 to 0.97) adjusted for ART strategy, and 0.61 (0.39 to 0.94) after fuller adjustment, with no interaction with ART timing (p=0.77) or with time (p=0.94). The mechanism is credible: the Cochrane review of preventive therapy in HIV (Akolo C et al., PMID: 20091503; 12 trials, 8,578 participants) found preventive therapy reduced active tuberculosis (relative risk 0.68, 95% CI 0.54 to 0.85), most strongly in tuberculin-positive people (0.38, 0.25 to 0.57), with a mortality reduction for isoniazid monotherapy in that subgroup (0.74, 0.55 to 1.00). The absolute mortality gain here is modest — about 2.8 percentage points over 6 years — in a setting with TB incidence of 159 per 100,000, and one factorial trial carries the mortality claim. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): at high CD4 counts on early ART, 6 months of IPT adds a durable survival benefit beyond ART alone. Tier C is set because the mortality result rests on a single trial analysis.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — in a 2,056-person factorial trial, 6 months of isoniazid preventive therapy reduced all-cause mortality over a median 4.9 years (hazard ratio 0.63, 95% CI 0.41 to 0.97), independent of antiretroviral timing, with Cochrane evidence of fewer tuberculosis cases behind it

title: Typhoid in children: cure in 91% on oral azithromycin versus 97% on ceftriaxone in a 64-child culture-positive trial — close on cure, and all four relapses fell in the ceftriaxone arm
question: In children with uncomplicated typhoid fever, is azithromycin as effective as ceftriaxone for fever clearance and cure?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the head-to-head trial (Frenck RW et al., PMID: 11073741) randomised 108 children aged 4 to 17 years with uncomplicated typhoid fever to 7 days of oral azithromycin (10 mg/kg/day) or ceftriaxone (75 mg/kg/day); among the 64 with Salmonella typhi isolated from blood, cure was achieved in 31 of 34 (91 percent) on azithromycin and 29 of 30 (97 percent) on ceftriaxone (P>.05) — a 6-percentage-point gap the trial was far too small to resolve. All 64 isolates were susceptible to both drugs, no serious side effects occurred in either arm, and the one asymmetry was relapse: 4 ceftriaxone-treated patients subsequently relapsed, none reported on azithromycin. The Cochrane review of azithromycin for enteric fever (Effa EE et al., PMID: 18843701; 7 trials, 773 participants) points the same way on relapse: versus ceftriaxone, azithromycin significantly reduced relapse (odds ratio 0.09, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.70; 132 participants, 2 trials) with no significant difference in other outcomes, and versus fluoroquinolones it reduced clinical failure (odds ratio 0.48, 0.26 to 0.89). Those pooled estimates rest on few participants and open-label trials from 2008 and earlier — before today's extensively drug-resistant strains. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): once-daily oral azithromycin is a credible, more convenient alternative to ceftriaxone for uncomplicated childhood typhoid where isolates are susceptible. Tier C is set because the direct comparison is a single small older trial.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — oral azithromycin cured 91 percent versus 97 percent on ceftriaxone in the one small head-to-head trial, with no relapses on azithromycin versus four on ceftriaxone, and Cochrane evidence of fewer relapses with azithromycin across two trials

title: Severe leptospirosis: ceftriaxone and penicillin G performed identically (median fever 3 days, 5 deaths in each arm) — while the Cochrane review finds antibiotics themselves unproven against placebo
question: In adults with severe leptospirosis, is intravenous ceftriaxone as effective as intravenous penicillin G — and has antibiotic therapy itself been shown to improve outcomes?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — two different uncertainties sit inside this question. The head-to-head part is settled as far as one trial can settle it: Panaphut T et al. (PMID: 12802748) randomised 173 patients with severe leptospirosis in Thailand to intravenous ceftriaxone 1 g daily or sodium penicillin G 1.5 million units every 6 hours, each for 7 days; the median duration of fever was 3 days in both groups, 10 patients died (5 in each group), and there were no statistically significant differences in the duration of organ dysfunction — the authors conclude the two are equally effective, with once-daily dosing and broader spectrum as ceftriaxone's practical advantages. The deeper part is unsettled: the Cochrane review of antibiotics for leptospirosis (Brett-Major DM et al., PMID: 22336839; 7 trials) found, across the four placebo-controlled trials, deaths of 16/200 (8.0 percent) on antibiotics versus 11/203 (5.4 percent) on placebo — fixed-effect odds ratio 1.56 (95% CI 0.70 to 3.46), random-effects 1.16 (0.23 to 5.95) — with all trials at high risk of bias and no significant effect on hospital stay in the one trial reporting it (8.9 versus 8.8 days). Note the miner question's framing (antibiotics versus no therapy, anchored on Panaphut) does not match the anchor trial, which compares two antibiotics; this shelf answers both parts with the records that actually address them. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): choose between ceftriaxone and penicillin on logistics, not efficacy — and recognise that antibiotic benefit in severe leptospirosis, though standard practice, has never been cleanly demonstrated in randomised trials. Tier C is set for the single head-to-head trial and the high-bias placebo literature.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — ceftriaxone and penicillin G were equally effective for severe leptospirosis in the one head-to-head trial, but randomised evidence that any antibiotic improves mortality over no treatment remains inconclusive

title: Brucellosis: the all-oral doxycycline-rifampin regimen is NOT as effective — relapse 16% versus 5.3%, and combined failure 24% versus 7.45%, with a meta-analysis agreeing (odds ratio 3.17)
question: In human brucellosis, is doxycycline plus rifampin as effective as doxycycline plus streptomycin for cure without relapse?
balance: LIKELY (harm) — the answer to this shelf's question is no, and two independent sources say so consistently. In the GECMEI multicentre trial (Solera J et al., PMID: 8540716), 194 patients with acute brucellosis (without endocarditis or neurobrucellosis) received doxycycline for 45 days plus either rifampin 900 mg/day for 45 days or streptomycin 1 g/day intramuscularly for 14 days. Initial lack of efficacy occurred in 8 of 100 (8 percent) on doxycycline-rifampin versus 2 of 94 (2 percent) on doxycycline-streptomycin (P=0.10); relapses occurred in 16 of 100 (16 percent) versus 5 of 94 (5.3 percent) (P=0.02); and the combined failure outcome — the number that matters to patients — was 26 of 100 (24 percent) versus 7 of 94 (7.45 percent) (P=0.0016). Tolerability did not rescue the oral regimen: adverse effects forcing discontinuation occurred in 4 percent versus 2 percent (P>0.2). The systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised brucellosis trials (Solís García del Pozo J et al., PMID: 22393379 — the record's first author; the miner entry cites it as Skalsky et al.) pooled the same comparison and found it favoured doxycycline-streptomycin (odds ratio 3.17, 95% CI 2.05 to 4.91 for relapse/failure with the rifampin regimen), while finding no significant difference between doxycycline-streptomycin and doxycycline-gentamicin (odds ratio 1.89, 0.81 to 4.39). PROPOSED LIKELY (harm): the convenience of an all-oral regimen is bought with roughly triple the failure rate; where injections are feasible, an aminoglycoside partner is the better-evidenced choice. Tier C is not set — a consistent trial-plus-meta-analysis record is above the weak tier.
stamp: LIKELY (harm) — doxycycline plus rifampin produces significantly more relapse and combined treatment failure than doxycycline plus streptomycin (24 percent versus 7.45 percent in the pivotal trial; meta-analytic odds ratio 3.17, 95% CI 2.05 to 4.91)

title: Single-dose azithromycin for cholera: clinical success 73% versus 27% and bacteriological success 78% versus 10% against single-dose ciprofloxacin — a rout driven by ciprofloxacin's lost potency against local strains
question: In adults with severe cholera, does a single dose of azithromycin match a single dose of ciprofloxacin for clinical and bacteriological cure?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — note first a correction to the miner question, which asked about multi-day tetracycline: the anchor trial (Saha D et al., PMID: 16760445) actually compared single 1-gram doses of azithromycin and ciprofloxacin in 195 men hospitalised with severe cholera caused by Vibrio cholerae O1 or O139 in Bangladesh, alongside fluid therapy. The result was one-sided: clinical success (cessation of watery stools within 48 hours) in 71 of 97 patients (73 percent) on azithromycin versus 26 of 98 (27 percent) on ciprofloxacin (P<0.001), and bacteriological success in 76 of 97 (78 percent) versus 10 of 98 (10 percent) (P<0.001). Azithromycin patients also had shorter diarrhoea (median 30 versus 78 hours), less vomiting (43 percent versus 67 percent), fewer stools (median 36 versus 52), and lower stool volume (median 114 versus 322 ml per kilogram). The explanation sits in the microbiology: the median ciprofloxacin minimum inhibitory concentration for the 177 O1 isolates was 0.25 micrograms per milliliter, 11 to 83 times higher than in previous studies at the site — ciprofloxacin had not become a bad drug everywhere, it had stopped working against these strains. The Cochrane review of antimicrobials for cholera (Leibovici-Weissman Y et al., PMID: 24944120; 39 trials, 4,623 participants) supplies the class context: antimicrobial therapy shortened diarrhoea by about a day and a half versus placebo or no treatment (mean difference −36.77 hours, 95% CI −43.51 to −30.03; moderate quality evidence), halved stool volume, and cut rehydration fluid needs by 40 percent. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): where ciprofloxacin susceptibility has eroded, single-dose azithromycin is the better-evidenced single-dose choice — an inherently local verdict that susceptibility surveillance must keep re-earning. Tier C is set because the head-to-head evidence is a single trial in men at one site.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single-dose azithromycin was far superior to single-dose ciprofloxacin for clinical and bacteriological success in severe cholera in a setting where circulating Vibrio cholerae had diminished ciprofloxacin susceptibility

title: Treating sick young infants when hospital referral is impossible: all three simplified regimens matched the standard injections on treatment failure (5–8% across arms) in a 3,564-infant equivalence trial
question: In young infants with possible serious bacterial infection whose families cannot accept hospital referral, do simplified oral/injectable antibiotic regimens match the standard injectable procaine benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin regimen?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — AFRINEST (Tshefu A et al., PMID: 25842221) randomised 3,564 young infants aged 0 to 59 days with clinical signs of severe infection, whose families did not accept hospital referral, across sites in DR Congo, Kenya and Nigeria, to the standard regimen (injectable procaine benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin for 7 days) or one of three simplified regimens: gentamicin injections plus oral amoxicillin for 7 days; 2 days of the standard injections then oral amoxicillin for 5 days; or 2 days of gentamicin injections plus oral amoxicillin for 7 days. In the per-protocol analysis, treatment failure by day 8 was 8 percent on the standard regimen versus 6 percent (risk difference −1.9 percent, 95% CI −4.4 to 0.1), 8 percent (−0.6 percent, −3.1 to 2.0), and 5 percent (−2.7 percent, −5.1 to 0.3) on the three simplified regimens — all within the prespecified 5 percent similarity margin. Deaths within 15 days were 1 to 2 percent across arms. The pooled analysis of the three African and Asian trials (Longombe AL et al., PMID: 36403158; 7,617 infants) went further: the oral amoxicillin plus gentamicin regimen had a lower risk of poor clinical outcome than the standard regimen (per-protocol risk difference −2.1 percent, 95% CI −3.8 to −0.4; P=0.016), and the switch regimen did not increase poor outcomes (−1.1 percent, −2.8 to 0.6). These results apply only where referral is genuinely not possible — hospital care remains the standard when it can be had. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): simplified regimens, including one built on oral amoxicillin, are a proven fallback that should not be withheld when the alternative is no treatment. Tier C is not set — a large equivalence trial plus a consistent pooled analysis is above the weak tier.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — three simplified regimens were equivalent to the standard 7-day injectable regimen for treatment failure in young infants treated where referral was not possible, and a pooled analysis of 7,617 infants found the oral amoxicillin plus gentamicin regimen modestly superior on poor clinical outcome

title: Strong Treat 1 to 4: four doses of ivermectin cured no more than one dose (85% versus 86% at 12 months) and caused more adverse events — the trial was stopped early for futility
question: In Strongyloides stercoralis infection, are multiple doses of ivermectin superior to a single dose for parasitological cure?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the answer to this shelf's question is no: more doses did not cure more people. Strong Treat 1 to 4 (Buonfrate D et al., PMID: 31558376) randomised 309 patients older than 5 years with non-disseminated Strongyloides stercoralis infection at centres in Italy, Spain and the UK to a single dose of ivermectin 200 micrograms/kg or four doses (days 1, 2, 15 and 16). At 12 months, clearance in the modified full-analysis set was 86 percent (102 of 118) on a single dose versus 85 percent (96 of 113) on four doses (risk difference 1.48 percent, 95% CI −7.55 to 10.52; p=0.75), with similar per-protocol results; adverse events were generally mild but more frequent with multiple doses, and the trial was terminated early due to futility — continuing could not plausibly reveal the superiority it was designed to detect. The Cochrane review of ivermectin for strongyloidiasis (Henriquez-Camacho C et al., PMID: 26778150) is consistent on dosing: in its dosage comparison, a second dose of ivermectin was not associated with higher cure (risk ratio 1.02, 95% CI 0.94 to 1.11; 94 participants), while ivermectin beat albendazole on parasitological cure (risk ratio 1.79, 1.55 to 2.08; moderate quality evidence). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): for non-disseminated infection, one dose does the work of four — fewer adverse events, simpler delivery, same cure. Tier C is set because the dose comparison rests on this single trial, stopped early with about a quarter of randomised patients outside the modified analysis set.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single dose of ivermectin achieved the same 12-month clearance as four doses (86 percent versus 85 percent) with better tolerability, so the simpler regimen is preferred for non-disseminated strongyloidiasis

title: Giardiasis in children: single-dose tinidazole cured MORE than 3 days of nitazoxanide — 90.5% versus 78.4% parasitological cure in a 137-child trial (P<0.05)
question: In children with giardiasis, is single-dose tinidazole as effective as 3 days of nitazoxanide for clinical and parasitological cure?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the head-to-head trial (Escobedo AA et al., PMID: 18348774) randomised 166 Cuban children with microscopically proven Giardia lamblia infection to a single dose of tinidazole 50 mg/kg or nitazoxanide 7.5 mg/kg twice daily for 3 days; among the 137 children who completed the study, parasitological cure — no Giardia in either of two faecal samples collected 5 to 10 days after treatment — was significantly more frequent after tinidazole (90.5 percent) than after nitazoxanide (78.4 percent) (P<0.05). Both schedules were well accepted and well tolerated, with only mild, transient, self-limited side effects, and diarrhoea generally cleared 2 to 6 days after starting treatment. The Cochrane review of drugs for giardiasis (Granados CE et al., PMID: 23235648; 19 trials, 1,817 participants) puts this result in a sobering frame: its best-supported comparison is albendazole versus metronidazole (parasitological cure risk ratio 0.99, 95% CI 0.95 to 1.03; moderate quality evidence), while the shortened regimens — single-dose tinidazole, single-dose metronidazole, 3-day nitazoxanide — were evaluated in trials at high risk of bias and too small to reliably detect or exclude important differences (very low quality evidence). So the direct answer favours tinidazole, on one open trial with a per-protocol analysis. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a single supervised dose that cures at least as many children is operationally attractive, and nitazoxanide remains, in the trial authors' own words, a good candidate where tinidazole is unsuitable. Tier C is not set — the miner entry graded this trial-plus-Cochrane base above the weak tier — but the stamp stays at POSSIBLE for the single small open trial.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single-dose tinidazole achieved a higher parasitological cure rate than 3 days of nitazoxanide in the one head-to-head trial (90.5 percent versus 78.4 percent), though the wider Cochrane record grades shortened-regimen evidence as very low quality

title: Prophylactic platelet transfusion in dengue: bleeding in 21% transfused versus 26% on supportive care alone (not significant) — with 13 adverse events versus 2, including anaphylaxis and transfusion-related lung injury
question: In adults with dengue and thrombocytopenia without bleeding, does prophylactic platelet transfusion prevent bleeding versus supportive care alone?
balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — the randomised trial (Lye DC et al., PMID: 28283286) assigned 372 adults with laboratory-confirmed dengue and platelet counts of 20,000 per microliter or lower, without severe bleeding, at five hospitals in Singapore and Malaysia to prophylactic platelet transfusion (4 units of pooled platelets each day the count was 20,000 or lower) plus supportive care, or supportive care alone. Clinical bleeding by day 7 or discharge occurred in 40 of 187 patients (21 percent) in the transfusion group and 48 of 182 (26 percent) in the control group (risk difference −4.98 percent, 95% CI −15.08 to 5.34; relative risk 0.81, 95% CI 0.56 to 1.17; p=0.16) — no significant benefit, with an interval that still allows a moderate benefit or a small harm on bleeding itself. The harm side is clearer: 13 adverse events occurred in the transfusion group versus 2 in the control group (p=0.0064), including urticaria, rash, pruritus and chest pain, and one case each of anaphylaxis, transfusion-related acute lung injury and fluid overload as serious events; no deaths occurred in either group. The systematic review of interventions for dengue bleeding (Rajapakse S et al., PMID: 29385613; 11 studies, 1,904 patients) found no evidence that platelet transfusion or any other assessed intervention prevents or treats clinically significant bleeding in dengue. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm): routine prophylactic transfusion at a platelet threshold spends a scarce blood product and exposes patients to real transfusion risks without demonstrated protection — reserve platelets for clinically significant bleeding. Tier C is set because the randomised base is a single open-label trial.
stamp: POSSIBLE (harm) — prophylactic platelet transfusion did not significantly reduce clinical bleeding (21 percent versus 26 percent) and produced significantly more adverse events (13 versus 2) in the one randomised trial, and a systematic review found no evidence any prophylactic intervention prevents dengue bleeding

title: Natamycin beats voriconazole for fungal eye ulcers overall — but the win is Fusarium's: outside Fusarium the two drops performed the same
question: In fungal keratitis, is natamycin superior to voriconazole for visual acuity and perforation — especially in Fusarium infection?
balance: SPLIT — natamycin was the better drug overall in the Mycotic Ulcer Treatment Trial (Prajna NV et al., PMID: 23710492), with better 3-month visual acuity and fewer perforations or therapeutic keratoplasties, and a systematic summary of the randomised trials (Retamal J et al., PMID: 30562337) reached the same conclusion. But the advantage was concentrated almost entirely in Fusarium infection: in Fusarium cases the acuity and perforation differences were large, while in non-Fusarium cases acuity and perforation were essentially identical between the drugs. The practical reading is therefore organism-dependent, not a blanket verdict — natamycin first for filamentous keratitis, especially where Fusarium is likely, and no demonstrated natamycin advantage once a non-Fusarium organism is established. PROPOSED SPLIT: natamycin superior, driven by Fusarium; the two drugs look similar for non-Fusarium keratitis.
stamp: SPLIT — natamycin superior overall, driven by Fusarium infection; natamycin and voriconazole performed similarly in non-Fusarium keratitis

title: Six months of valganciclovir for symptomatic congenital CMV: no hearing gain at 6 months, but better hearing and language by age two
question: In neonates with symptomatic congenital cytomegalovirus disease, does 6 months of oral valganciclovir improve hearing and developmental outcomes versus 6 weeks?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the randomised trial (Kimberlin DW et al., PMID: 25738669) is a study in two halves: on its primary endpoint, best-ear hearing at 6 months, six months of valganciclovir did not beat six weeks (P=0.41). The benefit appeared later and on broader measures — total-ear hearing more often improved or stayed normal at 12 months (73% vs 57%) and 24 months (77% vs 64%), with better language-composite and receptive-communication scores at 24 months. A systematic review of (val)ganciclovir and hearing in congenital CMV (De Cuyper E et al., PMID: 35072277) supports treatment of symptomatic children with hearing loss, while stressing the lack of randomised evidence for asymptomatic or isolated-hearing-loss presentations. Grade 3 or 4 neutropenia affected about one in five infants in the first 6 weeks in both arms. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): longer treatment modestly improves longer-term hearing and developmental outcomes in symptomatic congenital CMV, at the price of months of drug exposure and monitoring.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Valacyclovir in early-pregnancy CMV infection cut fetal transmission from 30% to 11% in the one randomised trial
question: In pregnant women with primary cytomegalovirus infection in early pregnancy, does valacyclovir prevent vertical transmission to the fetus?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in the single randomised trial (Shahar-Nissan K et al., PMID: 32919517), high-dose valacyclovir (8 g/day) from enrolment to amniocentesis cut positive amniocenteses from 30% (14 of 47) to 11% (5 of 45), an odds ratio of 0.29 — with the effect concentrated in first-trimester infection (11% vs 48%). An individual patient data meta-analysis including this trial (Chatzakis C et al., PMID: 37473793; 3 studies, 527 women) found the same direction for vertical transmission (adjusted OR 0.34) and neonatal infection (adjusted OR 0.30), with severe side effects in 2.1%. The evidence base is still one small per-protocol trial plus largely non-randomised data in the pooled analysis, and the endpoint is amniocentesis positivity rather than long-term infant outcome. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): valacyclovir probably reduces vertical transmission after early primary maternal CMV infection; infant-outcome proof is still indirect.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Ceftriaxone for neurosyphilis: similar responses and shorter hospital stay in a French cohort — but no real trial has ever tested it against penicillin
question: In neurosyphilis, is ceftriaxone as effective as benzylpenicillin for clinical and serological outcomes?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — there is no adequate randomised comparison. The largest dataset is a French retrospective multicentre cohort (Bettuzzi T et al., PMID: 34051142) in which overall clinical response at one month was higher with ceftriaxone than benzylpenicillin in crude and propensity-weighted analyses, serological response at 6 months did not differ, and hospital stay was shorter with ceftriaxone — but only 42 of 208 patients received ceftriaxone, and confounding by who gets which drug is exactly what a retrospective design cannot remove. The Cochrane review (Buitrago-Garcia D et al., PMID: 31132142) found a single trial of 36 participants, graded very low quality, with inconclusive serological and clinical cure results. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): ceftriaxone is a plausible alternative where benzylpenicillin is impractical, but equivalence has not been shown by a design that can show it.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — ceftriaxone has not been shown equivalent to benzylpenicillin in any randomised trial; the supporting data are retrospective

title: A maternal group B strep vaccine raised protective-looking antibodies in most infants — phase 2 only, with no disease-prevention trial yet
question: In pregnant women, does a hexavalent group B streptococcus polysaccharide-protein conjugate vaccine produce antibody responses likely to protect infants, with acceptable safety?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — this is immunogenicity evidence, not protection evidence. In the phase 2 trial and parallel seroepidemiology study (Madhi SA et al., PMID: 37467497), the hexavalent conjugate vaccine GBS6 raised maternal antibodies to all six serotypes, transferred to infants at maternal-to-infant ratios of about 0.4 to 1.3, and 57 to 97% of infants exceeded the lowest putative protective threshold (0.184 µg/mL) with the most immunogenic formulation — thresholds themselves derived from natural-history association (IgG levels linked to 75–95% relative reductions in disease risk), not from a vaccine efficacy trial. No safety signals were seen in mothers or infants, with more local reactions in aluminium-phosphate formulations. No baby in this record was shown to be protected from group B streptococcal disease by vaccination. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): a promising maternal vaccine candidate whose clinical efficacy is untested.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — phase 2 immunogenicity only; no trial has yet shown the vaccine prevents infant group B streptococcal disease

title: Liver-cancer surveillance in hepatitis B cut HCC deaths by about a third in relative terms in the one large randomised trial
question: In adults with chronic hepatitis B at high risk, does regular ultrasound plus alpha-fetoprotein surveillance reduce hepatocellular carcinoma mortality versus no screening?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the one large randomised trial (Zhang BH et al., PMID: 15042359; 18,816 people with hepatitis B or chronic hepatitis in Shanghai) found biannual ultrasound plus alpha-fetoprotein surveillance reduced hepatocellular carcinoma mortality from 131.5 to 83.2 per 100,000 — a mortality rate ratio of 0.63, i.e. a 37% relative reduction — with far more subclinical, small and resectable cancers found in the screened group, though only 58.2% of offered screening was completed. A meta-analysis in cirrhosis (Singal AG et al., PMID: 24691105) is directionally consistent: surveillance was associated with earlier detection (OR 2.08), more curative treatment (OR 2.24) and prolonged survival (OR 1.90), but that literature is observational and lead-time bias is its known weakness. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): surveillance probably reduces HCC mortality in high-risk patients; the randomised proof is a single trial in a hepatitis B population.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Endoscopic screening for oesophageal cancer in rural China: incidence and deaths trended lower at 9 years, but neither reduction was significant
question: In a high-incidence rural Chinese population, does endoscopic screening for oesophageal cancer reduce oesophageal cancer incidence and mortality?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the ESECC randomised trial's 9-year report (Liu M et al., PMID: 38457759; 33,847 residents of a high-risk region of northern China) found endoscopic screening associated with 19% and 18% relative reductions in oesophageal cancer incidence and mortality in intention-to-treat analysis — but neither estimate was statistically significant (incidence aHR 0.81, 95% CI 0.60 to 1.09; mortality aHR 0.82, 95% CI 0.53 to 1.26), and per-protocol estimates (0.78 and 0.79) were likewise non-significant. Absolute rates were 60.9 versus 72.5 per 100,000 person-years for incidence and 29.7 versus 32.4 for mortality. The authors themselves describe the reductions as modest and call for a more efficient screening and management strategy. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): a single round of chromoendoscopy in a high-incidence population may reduce incidence and mortality, but this trial did not prove it.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — endoscopic screening showed modest, non-significant reductions in incidence and mortality in one trial

title: Spraying plus nets in Tanzania: each beat standard nets alone, but together they were redundant — the second intervention added little
question: In malaria-endemic Tanzania, does adding indoor residual spraying to long-lasting insecticidal nets (including piperonyl-butoxide nets) reduce malaria infection versus nets alone?
balance: SPLIT — the factorial cluster trial (Protopopoff N et al., PMID: 29655496) shows each intervention worked against standard nets where pyrethroid resistance was prevalent, but combining them was redundant rather than additive. At 9 months, malaria prevalence in children was lower with indoor residual spraying than without (28% vs 44%; OR 0.33) and lower with piperonyl-butoxide (PBO) nets than standard nets (29% vs 42%; OR 0.37), yet the significant interaction (OR 2.43) indicated the combination gave back part of that advantage; the PBO-net effect persisted at 21 months (45% vs 62%; OR 0.40). So adding spraying helps on top of standard nets, while a programme already deploying PBO nets should not assume spraying adds the same again. PROPOSED SPLIT: benefit depends on which net is underneath — additive with standard nets, redundant with PBO nets.
stamp: SPLIT — indoor residual spraying added benefit over standard nets, but was redundant when combined with piperonyl-butoxide nets

title: CHoBI7 in Bangladesh: hygiene help triggered by a hospital diarrhoea admission cut child diarrhoea and stunting over the next year
question: In households of patients hospitalised with diarrhoea in Bangladesh, does a hospital-delivered water, sanitation and hygiene programme (CHoBI7) reduce diarrhoea and improve child growth?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in the CHoBI7 cluster trial (George CM et al., PMID: 32761174; 769 households, 2,626 participants in Dhaka), a hospital-delivered water, sanitation and hygiene programme with mobile-health messaging reduced 12-month diarrhoea prevalence in children under five in both delivery arms — prevalence ratio 0.73 with two home visits and 0.82 with no home visits — and reduced stunting at 12 months in children under two (about 32–33% versus 45%; odds ratios 0.54–0.55). The broader WASH meta-analysis (Wolf J et al., PMID: 29537671) supports the direction for water, sanitation and handwashing interventions generally, while warning that correcting for non-blinding shrinks the associations. This is a single trial of a specific hospital-triggered programme, with reported (not observed) diarrhoea as the primary outcome. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): CHoBI7 lowered diarrhoea and stunting in the households it targeted.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: One-week rabies pre-exposure vaccination primed travellers well for a later simulated exposure — but it formally missed non-inferiority
question: In people exposed to rabies risk (travellers and occupational groups), is one-week pre-exposure prophylaxis (intramuscular or intradermal) non-inferior to the standard 3-week schedule for antibody response?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the phase 3 trial (Quiambao BP et al., PMID: 35933278; 570 participants) gives a genuinely mixed answer. One-week pre-exposure regimens (two visits, intramuscular or intradermal, with either vaccine) produced seroconversion of 96.7–97.2% fourteen days after the last injection, against 100% for the classic three-week regimen — and the trial's primary objective, formal non-inferiority of one-week intramuscular versus three-week, was NOT demonstrated. Yet the priming worked in the way that matters clinically: after simulated post-exposure vaccination a year later, every group mounted rapid, robust anamnestic responses, with all but one participant seroconverting, and no safety concerns arose. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): one-week PrEP primes reliably enough to answer a simulated exposure a year later, but it did not meet its own non-inferiority bar on the primary antibody endpoint, so 'non-inferior' must not be claimed.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — one-week PrEP primed effectively but did not demonstrate non-inferiority to the 3-week schedule on the primary antibody endpoint

title: Prednisolone for leprosy nerve damage: 20 weeks matched 32 in an 868-patient trial — and against placebo, benefit has never been shown
question: In leprosy patients, does prednisolone given early prevent or improve nerve function impairment and reactions versus placebo or shorter courses?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — two facts bound what can be claimed. First, on duration, the large TENLEP clinical trial (Wagenaar I et al., PMID: 28976976; 868 patients with recent nerve function impairment) found 32 weeks of prednisolone no better than 20 weeks — improvement or restoration at 78 weeks in 77.5% versus 78.1% — with more serious adverse events on the longer course, so 20 weeks is the preferred initial duration. Second, on whether prednisolone beats nothing at all, the Cochrane review (Van Veen NH et al., PMID: 27210895) found the two placebo-controlled trials (84 and 95 participants) showed no significant difference in nerve function improvement after 12 months, on moderate-to-low quality evidence. The TENLEP programme's companion subclinical trial — prednisolone for nerve damage detected only on conduction studies, to prevent clinical impairment — was set out in the TENLEP protocols (PMID: 23249098). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): steroids remain standard practice for recent leprosy nerve impairment, but placebo-controlled proof of benefit is lacking and longer courses add harm without benefit.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — prednisolone has not beaten placebo for nerve function in the Cochrane analysis, and 32 weeks was no better than 20 weeks in TENLEP
