title: Thalidomide for ENL leprosy reactions: it controls the reaction at either dose — a slower taper from 300 mg held it off longer, but relapse followed stopping
question: In erythema nodosum leprosum (type 2 leprosy reaction), is thalidomide effective for controlling the reaction, and at what dose?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — thalidomide works for erythema nodosum leprosum, and the dose question is about tapering, not just the starting dose. In the double-blind dose-comparison trial (Villahermosa LG et al., PMID: 15891124; 22 men), a 300 mg starting dose and a 100 mg starting dose produced comparable improvement by day 7 (7 of 10 versus 12 of 12 improved; P=0.08), but the slower taper from the higher dose showed significantly less re-emergence of ENL through week 7 (P=0.02) — while most patients in both groups developed new lesions soon after treatment stopped. The Cochrane review of ENL interventions (Van Veen NH et al., PMID: 19588412) found thalidomide significantly increased remission of skin lesions versus aspirin (RR 2.43) in one 92-participant trial, and that mild-to-moderate adverse events were significantly fewer at 100 mg than 300 mg daily (RR 0.46). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): thalidomide controls ENL; a higher start with a slow taper holds the reaction longer, at the cost of more adverse events, and relapse after stopping is the rule.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Vasopressin first after heart surgery: one double-blind trial cut death-or-major-complications from 49% to 32% — but the pooled mortality record is still silent
question: In adults with vasoplegic shock after cardiac surgery, does vasopressin reduce mortality and vasopressor duration compared with norepinephrine as the first-line vasopressor?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one well-conducted double-blind trial drives this shelf. In VANCS (Hajjar LA et al., PMID: 27841822), 300 patients with post-cardiotomy vasoplegic shock randomised to vasopressin or norepinephrine had a primary composite of death or severe complications in 32% versus 49% (hazard ratio 0.55, 95% CI 0.38 to 0.80), with much less atrial fibrillation on vasopressin (63.8% vs 82.1%) and no excess digital or mesenteric ischaemia, hyponatraemia, or myocardial infarction. The wider literature is less decisive: a 2023 systematic review and meta-analysis of ten studies (Szeles TF et al., PMID: 38055405) found no significant mortality difference between vasopressin and norepinephrine (odds ratio 1.60, 95% CI 0.47 to 5.50) and no significant difference in hospital stay, while judging vasopressin safe in postoperative vasoplegic shock. The question as asked — mortality and vasopressor duration head-to-head — is only partly answered: VANCS reports the composite and complications, not a mortality-only or duration-only win. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): vasopressin is a reasonable first-line choice in post-cardiotomy vasoplegia on one positive trial, but the pooled record does not confirm a mortality advantage, and a second large trial is still owed.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — vasopressin first-line reduced a death-or-severe-complications composite in one double-blind trial, but pooled mortality data show no confirmed advantage

title: More blood thinner in ICU COVID-19: INSPIRATION found identical outcomes at 30 days (45.7% vs 44.1%) — pooled data trade fewer lung clots for more bleeding
question: In critically ill adults with COVID-19, does intermediate-dose prophylactic anticoagulation reduce thrombotic events, need for organ support, or mortality compared with standard-dose prophylaxis?
balance: SPLIT — the dose question splits by outcome, and the split does not favour escalation. In the INSPIRATION trial (Sadeghipour P et al., PMID: 33734299), 562 ICU patients with COVID-19 randomised to intermediate-dose enoxaparin (1 mg/kg daily) versus standard prophylaxis (40 mg daily) had an identical primary composite of thrombosis, ECMO treatment, or 30-day death — 45.7% versus 44.1% (odds ratio 1.06, 95% CI 0.76 to 1.48) — while severe thrombocytopenia occurred only in the intermediate arm (6 vs 0 patients) and major bleeding was numerically higher (2.5% vs 1.4%, noninferiority not met). The 90-day report (Bikdeli B et al., PMID: 33865239) was the same story extended: primary outcome 47.8% versus 45.4% (hazard ratio 1.21, 95% CI 0.95 to 1.55). A systematic review and meta-analysis of six randomised trials (Bonfim LCMG et al., PMID: 37244209) found escalated dosing did not change mortality (relative risk 1.01, 95% CI 0.90 to 1.13) or deep vein thrombosis, but did reduce pulmonary embolism (relative risk 0.35, 95% CI 0.21 to 0.60) while increasing bleeding (relative risk 1.65, 95% CI 1.08 to 2.53). PROPOSED SPLIT: escalated prophylaxis buys fewer pulmonary emboli at the price of more bleeding, with no mortality or overall-composite benefit — routine intermediate dosing in unselected ICU patients is not supported by its own trial.
stamp: SPLIT — escalated prophylaxis reduced pulmonary embolism but increased bleeding, with no mortality or overall composite benefit

title: Alpha-2 sedation vs propofol: A2B's 1,404 patients got no faster extubation from dexmedetomidine or clonidine — and more agitation and slow heart rates
question: In mechanically ventilated critically ill adults, does sedation based on an alpha-2 agonist (dexmedetomidine or clonidine) improve outcomes compared with propofol-based sedation?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the largest direct test says no. In the A2B trial (Walsh TS et al., PMID: 40388916), 1,404 ventilated ICU patients randomised to dexmedetomidine-based, clonidine-based, or propofol-based sedation had time to successful extubation that was not significantly shorter on either alpha-2 agonist (subdistribution hazard ratio 1.09, 95% CI 0.96 to 1.25 for dexmedetomidine; 1.05, 95% CI 0.95 to 1.17 for clonidine), 180-day mortality was similar, and both alpha-2 arms had more agitation (risk ratio about 1.55) and more severe bradycardia (risk ratio about 1.6). The older Cochrane review (Chen K et al., PMID: 25879090) had leaned the other way for dexmedetomidine — duration of mechanical ventilation reduced by 22% (95% CI 10% to 33%) and ICU stay by 14% against traditional sedatives, on low to very low quality evidence, with bradycardia doubled (risk ratio 2.11) and no mortality effect (risk ratio 0.99); it found no eligible clonidine trials at all. A2B, pragmatic and ten times the typical older trial's size, is the record to weight. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): alpha-2-based sedation remains a legitimate choice for individual patients, but a general extubation or survival advantage over propofol is unproven — and A2B's agitation and bradycardia signals are part of the price.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — neither dexmedetomidine nor clonidine was superior to propofol for time to extubation in the large A2B trial

title: Breathing the sedative in: SAVE-ICU's 780 patients died at the same rate on isoflurane as on IV sedation (42.5% vs 43.8%) — with fewer delirium-free days
question: In mechanically ventilated adults with acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure, does inhaled isoflurane sedation improve outcomes compared with intravenous propofol sedation?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the first large trial of the strategy is neutral on survival and slightly adverse on brain outcomes. In SAVE-ICU (Jerath A et al., PMID: 42872958), 780 ventilated adults with acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure randomised to isoflurane-based inhaled sedation or usual intravenous sedation had hospital mortality of 42.5% versus 43.8% (risk ratio 0.98, 95% CI 0.84 to 1.14; P=0.85), no difference in ICU-, ventilator-, or hospital-free days, quality of life, or disability — and fewer delirium- and coma-free days in the inhaled group (between-group difference −0.95 days, 95% CI −1.69 to −0.22), alongside more use of adjunctive therapies for hypoxaemia (63.9% vs 55.0%). The earlier pooled literature (Kim HY et al., PMID: 29245269), thirteen small trials and 1,027 patients, had found volatile sedation shortened awakening time by 80 minutes and extubation time by 196 minutes versus intravenous sedation, with no difference in ICU or hospital stay — process gains that SAVE-ICU's free-day outcomes do not corroborate at scale. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): inhaled isoflurane sedation is feasible in this population, but no patient-important benefit over intravenous sedation has been shown, and the delirium/coma signal points the wrong way.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — inhaled isoflurane sedation did not reduce hospital mortality versus intravenous sedation in the SAVE-ICU trial

title: Methylene blue early in septic shock: pressors stopped a day sooner in the anchor trial, and six small trials pool to a mortality relative risk of 0.66 — on low certainty
question: In adults with septic shock on high-dose vasopressors, does early adjunctive methylene blue shorten vasopressor duration or reduce mortality compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a coherent but small evidence base. In the anchor trial (Ibarra-Estrada M et al., PMID: 36915146), 91 patients with septic shock randomised to early adjunctive methylene blue or placebo came off vasopressors sooner (median 69 vs 94 hours; p<0.001), gained one more vasopressor-free day at day 28 (p=0.008), and left the ICU 1.5 days and hospital 2.7 days sooner, with mortality similar and no serious adverse effects attributed to the drug. A systematic review and meta-analysis of six randomised trials and 302 patients (Fernando SM et al., PMID: 38904978) points the same way and further: short-term mortality relative risk 0.66 (95% CI 0.47 to 0.94), vasopressor duration 31.1 hours shorter, and hospital stay 2.1 days shorter — every one of those estimates rated low certainty, with the methemoglobin effect uncertain (very low certainty) and no difference in adverse events. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): early methylene blue probably shortens vasopressor time in septic shock; the mortality signal is real in the pooled data but rests on about 300 randomised patients in total, which is exactly why the stamp stops at possible.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — early methylene blue shortened vasopressor duration, and pooled low-certainty data suggest lower short-term mortality

title: Dexamethasone for established ARDS: 4.8 more ventilator-free days and 60-day mortality of 21% vs 36% in DEXA-ARDS, with the pooled literature pointing the same way
question: In adults with established acute respiratory distress syndrome, does dexamethasone increase ventilator-free days and reduce mortality compared with usual care?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — a large effect in a properly randomised multicentre trial, corroborated in direction by the pooled literature. In DEXA-ARDS (Villar J et al., PMID: 32043986), 277 patients with established moderate-to-severe ARDS randomised to dexamethasone (20 mg daily for 5 days, then 10 mg daily to day 10) or routine care gained 4.8 more ventilator-free days at day 28 (95% CI 2.57 to 7.03) and had 60-day mortality of 21% versus 36% (difference −15.3%, 95% CI −25.9 to −4.9; p=0.0047), with no significant difference in adverse events — hyperglycaemia was common in both arms (76% vs 70%). A systematic review and meta-analysis of four studies and 702 patients (Feng LH et al., PMID: 36181003) found dexamethasone significantly reduced all-cause mortality (odds ratio 0.62, 95% CI 0.44 to 0.88) and improved ventilator-free status at 28 days (mean difference 3.65 days, 95% CI 1.49 to 5.80), again without a significant difference in adverse events. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): in established moderate-to-severe ARDS, early dexamethasone on this schedule likely shortens ventilation and reduces mortality — held back from the strongest grade because the anchor trial stopped for low enrolment at 88% of its planned sample and the pooled base is still only four studies.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — dexamethasone increased ventilator-free days and reduced mortality in established moderate-to-severe ARDS

title: Thiamine alone in septic shock: two 88-patient trials missed their primary outcomes — the only positive signals sit in small thiamine-deficient subgroups
question: In adults with septic shock, does thiamine (alone, not in a combination cocktail) improve lactate clearance, kidney outcomes, or mortality compared with placebo?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — two small placebo-controlled trials of thiamine alone, and both miss their primary outcome. Donnino's pilot (Donnino MW et al., PMID: 26771781) randomised 88 septic-shock patients with lactate above 3 mmol/L to thiamine 200 mg twice daily or placebo and found no difference in 24-hour lactate (median 2.5 vs 2.6 mmol/L; p=0.40), shock reversal, severity of illness, or mortality overall — though in the predefined subgroup who were thiamine-deficient at baseline (35% of patients), lactate was lower on thiamine (2.1 vs 3.1 mmol/L; p=0.03) with a possible mortality decrease over time (p=0.047). TRPSS (Moskowitz A et al., PMID: 37364280), also 88 patients, found no significant difference in its primary outcome of creatinine change at 72 hours (mean difference −0.57 mg/dl, 95% CI −1.18 to 0.04; P=0.07), nor in kidney replacement therapy (14.3% vs 21.7%), stage-3 acute kidney injury (54.7% vs 73.9%), or mortality (35.7% vs 54.3%) — all numerically favouring thiamine, none significant — while ICU-free days were greater on thiamine (median 22.5 vs 0.0; P<0.01). No systematic review of thiamine alone (as distinct from the vitamin C–steroid combination) was found in-session, so this shelf rests on the two trials. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): thiamine alone is unproven for lactate, kidney, or survival outcomes in unselected septic shock; the deficiency-subgroup signal is a hypothesis for a targeted trial, not a result.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — thiamine alone did not significantly improve lactate, kidney outcomes, or mortality in two small placebo-controlled trials

title: The green-whistle question: methoxyflurane cut pain 17.4 mm more than placebo within 20 minutes and worked at a median 5 minutes — relief first, dizziness second
question: In adults with moderate-to-severe trauma pain in the emergency department, does low-dose inhaled methoxyflurane relieve pain compared with placebo or standard analgesics?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — for rapid short-term pain relief, the randomised record is consistent and the effect is fast. In the STOP! trial's adult subgroup (Coffey F et al., PMID: 27567918), 204 emergency-department patients with minor-trauma pain randomised to inhaled methoxyflurane (up to 6 mL via the Penthrox inhaler — Medical Developments International Limited, named in the publication) or placebo inhaler had a mean pain reduction across 5–20 minutes that was 17.4 mm greater on a visual analogue scale (95% CI −22.3 to −12.5 as a treatment effect favouring methoxyflurane; p<0.0001), a median time to first relief of 5 versus 20 minutes (hazard ratio 2.32), and rescue medication requested within 20 minutes by 2.0% versus 22.8% — at the price of more mostly mild, transient treatment-related adverse events, chiefly dizziness and headache (42.2% vs 14.9%). A systematic review and meta-analysis of pooled randomised data against standard-of-care analgesics (Fabbri A et al., PMID: 33505170) found the pain-intensity difference significantly superior for methoxyflurane (overall estimated treatment effect 11.88, 95% CI 9.75 to 14.00; P<0.0001), superior from 5 minutes onward, with more patients reaching pain at or below 30 mm and relative reductions of at least 30% and 50% — those responder outcomes are reported without absolute rates in the record, so they are not dressed up with invented percentages here. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): low-dose inhaled methoxyflurane is an effective, rapid, non-opioid analgesic for acute trauma pain in the emergency setting; the evidence is about the first minutes-to-hour of pain, not about downstream outcomes.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — low-dose inhaled methoxyflurane relieves acute trauma pain faster and more than placebo or standard analgesics

title: A block on arrival for the broken hip: pain beaten at every measurement and median morphine of 0 mg vs 6 mg — in the patients least able to tolerate opioids
question: In adults with hip fracture, does a preoperative fascia iliaca compartment block reduce pain and opioid use compared with systemic analgesia or placebo block?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — a small founding trial with an unusually clean design, backed by a consistent pooled literature. Foss (Foss NB et al., PMID: 17413915) randomised 48 hip-fracture patients on arrival — before X-ray confirmation — double-blind to a fascia iliaca compartment block with 1.0% mepivacaine plus a placebo intramuscular injection, or a placebo block plus intramuscular morphine 0.1 mg/kg: maximum pain relief was superior with the block at rest (P<0.01) and on movement (P=0.02), pain relief was superior at all times and all measurements, median total morphine consumption was 0 mg versus 6 mg (P<0.01), and more morphine-group patients were sedated at 180 minutes (P=0.05). A meta-analysis of eleven trials and 937 hip-fracture patients (Hong HK et al., PMID: 31305398) found the block significantly reduced pain intensity at 1–8, 12, 24, and 48 hours (standardised mean differences from −0.96 to −1.14) and reduced total morphine consumption and nausea, with no difference by 72 hours. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): a fascia iliaca block on arrival gives better early pain control than systemic morphine alone in hip fracture and spares opioids in exactly the fragile elderly population that tolerates them worst — the grade stops at likely because the founding trial is 48 patients and the pooled trials vary in technique and timing.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — fascia iliaca block gave superior early pain relief and spared morphine compared with systemic analgesia in hip fracture

title: Extra MRSA cover for plain cellulitis: cure 83.5% vs 85.5% in the big trial and 85% vs 82% in the small one — an unproven habit, kept honest by one wide interval
question: In adults with uncomplicated cellulitis, does adding trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole to cephalexin improve clinical cure compared with cephalexin alone?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — two randomised trials asked whether adding MRSA cover to cephalexin helps non-purulent cellulitis, and neither found it. Moran (Moran GJ et al., PMID: 28535235) randomised 496 analysed outpatients with uncomplicated cellulitis (ultrasound used to exclude abscess) to cephalexin plus trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole or cephalexin plus placebo: in the prespecified per-protocol primary analysis, cure was 83.5% versus 85.5% (difference −2.0%, 95% CI −9.7% to 5.7%; P=0.50), while the modified intention-to-treat analysis leaned the other way without significance (76.2% vs 69.0%; difference 7.3%, 95% CI −1.0% to 15.5%; P=0.07) — the authors note that imprecision leaves a clinically important difference possible. Pallin's earlier trial (Pallin DJ et al., PMID: 23457080), 146 analysed patients without abscess, diabetes, or immunosuppression, found cure in 85% versus 82% (risk difference 2.7%, 95% CI −9.3% to 15%; P=0.66), with no subgroup — including nasal MRSA colonisation or purulence — predicting response. A network meta-analysis of ten trials and 1,936 cellulitis or erysipelas patients (Shu Z et al., PMID: 39240378) likewise found no significant differences in cure rates among the antibiotics analysed, including the cephalexin-plus-trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole combination. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): for uncomplicated non-purulent cellulitis, routine added MRSA cover is unproven — the trials cannot exclude a moderate benefit (Moran's intention-to-treat interval reaches +15.5%), but two nulls and a null network are what a prescriber actually has.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — adding trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole to cephalexin has not been shown to improve cure in uncomplicated cellulitis

title: Glue vs stitches for a cut: the scar ties at 3 months and at 1 year, glue is faster and hurts less — and reopens about once in every 25 closures
question: In children and adults with traumatic lacerations, does octylcyanoacrylate tissue adhesive give equivalent closure, cosmesis, and infection outcomes compared with sutures?
balance: SPLIT — the outcomes split cleanly, and the split is the answer. On appearance, the methods tie: Singer's multicentre trial (Singer AJ et al., PMID: 11894031) of 814 patients with 924 lacerations and incisions found no difference at 3 months in optimal appearance (82% vs 83%; P=0.67) or dehiscence (1.6% vs 0.9%; P=0.35), and Quinn's trial (Quinn J et al., PMID: 9832658) found no difference at 1 year in optimal wound scores (73% vs 68%; P=0.60) or cosmetic visual-analogue scores (69 vs 69 mm; P=0.95). On process, adhesive wins: closure was faster (2.9 vs 5.2 minutes; P<0.001) and fewer adhesive wounds were erythematous at 1 week (18% vs 36%; P<0.001), though infection rates were similar (2.1% vs 0.7%; P=0.09). The Cochrane review (Farion K et al., PMID: 12137689), eight trials of adhesive versus standard closure for traumatic lacerations, found no cosmesis difference at any time point, pain scores favouring adhesives (parent visual-analogue weighted mean difference −15.7 mm, 95% CI −21.9 to −9.5) and procedure time favouring adhesives (−5.6 minutes, 95% CI −8.2 to −3.1) — against a small but significant increase in dehiscence favouring standard closure (number needed to harm 25, 95% CI 14 to 100) and less erythema with adhesives (number needed to harm 8 for standard closure, as printed). PROPOSED SPLIT: for suitable low-tension lacerations, tissue adhesive matches sutures on the scar, beats them on speed and pain, and loses slightly on wound reopening — the choice turns on the wound and the patient, not on a winner.
stamp: SPLIT — equivalent cosmesis and faster, less painful closure with tissue adhesive, at a small increased risk of dehiscence

title: Adductor canal block after knee replacement: less morphine and faster walking than placebo in the founding trial — and against femoral block, the same pain relief with a stronger quadriceps
question: In adults after total knee arthroplasty, does an adductor canal block reduce postoperative pain and opioid use while preserving quadriceps strength, compared with placebo or femoral nerve block?
balance: The placebo-controlled record is two small double-blind trials from one Danish group. In primary total knee arthroplasty (Jenstrup MT et al., PMID: 22221014), a continuous adductor canal block with ropivacaine cut 24-hour morphine consumption from 56 ± 26 mg to 40 ± 21 mg (P = 0.006), reduced pain during 45-degree knee flexion (P = 0.01, though not at rest, P = 0.06), and patients walked the Timed-Up-and-Go test faster at 24 hours (36 ± 17 vs 50 ± 29 seconds, P = 0.03). In the harder revision-arthroplasty population (Jæger P et al., PMID: 25386752) the block won only its primary endpoint — pain on flexion at 4 hours, 52 ± 22 vs 71 ± 25 mm (mean difference 19, 95% CI 1 to 37) — with area-under-curve pain and morphine use not significantly different, in a trial the authors call underpowered. Against the older femoral nerve block, a 33-study meta-analysis (Hasabo EA et al., PMID: 36042669) found no difference in pain (MD 0.06, 95% CI −0.06 to 0.17) or opioid consumption (SMD 0.08, −0.06 to 0.22), but better preserved quadriceps strength (MD 0.28, 0.11 to 0.46) and better mobilisation to day 2. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the block is a real analgesic against placebo and a strength-sparing equal against femoral block — but the placebo trials are small and single-group, so the stamp stops short of likely.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — adductor canal block reduces early opioid use and pain on movement versus placebo, and preserves quadriceps strength better than femoral nerve block with equal analgesia

title: Erector spinae plane block after breast cancer surgery: one small trial cut 24-hour morphine from 16.6 mg to 5.5 mg — in the network ranking of eleven techniques it sits mid-table, not at the top
question: In adults after breast cancer surgery, does an erector spinae plane block reduce postoperative pain and opioid consumption compared with placebo block or no block?
balance: The direct placebo-controlled evidence is a single small double-blind trial (Ben Amor M et al., PMID: 38372553): in 50 women having elective breast cancer surgery, an ultrasound-guided erector spinae plane block with ropivacaine lowered visual analogue pain scores at almost every time point over 24 hours and cut 24-hour morphine consumption to 5.5 ± 0.9 mg from 16.6 ± 2.8 mg on placebo (p < 0.001), with intraoperative fentanyl also far lower (9.1 ± 4.2 vs 50 ± 9.1 mcg). The wider comparative picture is less triumphant: in a network meta-analysis of 79 randomised trials and 5,686 patients across 11 regional techniques (Singh NP et al., PMID: 35102494), the erector spinae plane block's ranking for 24-hour resting pain (SUCRA 0.59) sat below continuous paravertebral block (0.83), serratus anterior plane block (0.76), and single-level paravertebral block (0.68), on evidence the reviewers graded moderate to very low certainty. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the block works against placebo and is simple and safe in the trial record, but nothing yet shows it is the best of the fascial-plane and paravertebral options, and its one placebo trial enrolled 50 patients at one centre.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — erector spinae plane block reduces postoperative pain scores and opioid use after breast cancer surgery, but the direct trial is small and the comparative ranking is middling

title: A single phenobarbital load for alcohol withdrawal: ICU admissions 8% versus 25% in the one placebo trial — but pooled against benzodiazepines alone, the admission advantage disappears
question: In adults with acute alcohol withdrawal in the emergency department, does a single loading dose of phenobarbital reduce ICU admission and withdrawal severity compared with placebo added to benzodiazepine-based care?
balance: The only placebo-controlled test of the exact question is Rosenson J et al. (PMID: 22999778): 102 analysed emergency-department patients with acute alcohol withdrawal all received a symptom-guided lorazepam protocol, and those randomised to a single intravenous phenobarbital load (10 mg/kg) were admitted to intensive care far less often than those given placebo saline — 8% versus 25% (95% CI for the difference 4 to 32) — with no difference in adverse events. The wider literature asks a neighbouring question, phenobarbital instead of or against benzodiazepines, and there the advantage vanishes: a systematic review and meta-analysis of eight studies and 1,507 patients (Lee CM et al., PMID: 37923363) found a pooled relative risk of ICU admission of 0.92 (95% CI 0.54 to 1.55), hospital admission 0.98 (0.89 to 1.07), and adverse events 1.1 (0.78 to 1.57), on low-to-moderate quality evidence with moderate-to-high risk of bias and only two randomised trials among the eight. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): the add-on loading-dose strategy is promising and was safe in its one trial, but a single 102-patient study whose headline outcome is a disposition decision — made by clinicians who may not have stayed blind to a sedated patient — cannot carry a stronger stamp against a null pooled record.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — a single phenobarbital load reduced ICU admission in one small placebo-controlled trial, but the pooled literature against benzodiazepines shows no admission or safety advantage

title: Prochlorperazine versus metoclopramide for ED migraine: dead even in the head-to-head trial (pain fell 5.5 versus 5.2 points) — a meta-analysis favouring prochlorperazine rests on other, older comparisons
question: In adults presenting to the emergency department with acute migraine, does intravenous prochlorperazine relieve headache more effectively than intravenous metoclopramide?
balance: Asked head-to-head, the question has one direct answer. In the randomised double-blind trial by Friedman BW et al. (PMID: 18006188), 77 emergency-department migraine patients received prochlorperazine 10 mg or metoclopramide 20 mg intravenously, both with diphenhydramine 25 mg, and pain relief at one hour was indistinguishable: numeric rating scale scores fell 5.5 versus 5.2 points (difference 0.3, 95% CI −1.0 to 1.6), with similar results at 2 and 24 hours, adverse events in 46% versus 32%, and about three quarters of each group wanting the same drug next time. A systematic review and meta-analysis (Golikhatir I et al., PMID: 30990883) pooling 11 studies and 771 patients reached a friendlier verdict for prochlorperazine — odds ratio 2.89 (95% CI 1.42 to 5.86) for headache relief against metoclopramide among its comparison arms — but that estimate leans on older and smaller trials at differing doses and co-treatments, and the same review found prochlorperazine raised akathisia/dystonia odds against active comparators (OR 2.55, 1.03 to 6.31). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): either drug is a reasonable first choice and the direct trial says they tie; the claim that prochlorperazine is the stronger of the two rests on indirect pooling the head-to-head does not confirm.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the only direct head-to-head trial found prochlorperazine and metoclopramide equally effective; a meta-analysis favouring prochlorperazine is indirect and inconsistent with it

title: MI FREEE: free post-heart-attack medicines raised adherence by 4–6 points and cut first major vascular events — but the trial's primary outcome, first event or revascularisation, did not significantly fall
question: In adults after myocardial infarction, does eliminating copayments for preventive medications improve medication adherence and reduce major vascular events compared with usual cost-sharing?
balance: MI FREEE (Choudhry NK et al., PMID: 22080794) randomised insurance-plan sponsors — 1,494 sponsors with 2,845 patients to full coverage and 1,486 with 3,010 patients to usual coverage — so that after myocardial infarction, statins, beta-blockers, and ACE inhibitors or ARBs cost patients nothing. Adherence, poor at baseline (35.9–49.0% under usual coverage), rose by 4 to 6 percentage points with full coverage (P < 0.001 for all comparisons). The event record splits: the primary outcome — first major vascular event or revascularisation — did not significantly differ (17.6 vs 18.8 per 100 person-years; HR 0.93, 95% CI 0.82 to 1.04; P = 0.21), yet total major vascular events or revascularisation were significantly reduced (21.5 vs 23.3 per 100 person-years; HR 0.89; P = 0.03), as was the rate of first major vascular events alone (11.0 vs 12.8; HR 0.86, 0.74 to 0.99; P = 0.03), and total spending did not rise ($66,008 vs $71,778; P = 0.68) while patient costs fell. A systematic review of cost-sharing interventions (Sensharma A et al., PMID: 30628493) generalises the adherence half of that story: across 28 studies, removing or reducing out-of-pocket costs usually improved adherence modestly, with higher plan drug spending generally offset by lower non-drug medical spending. PROPOSED SPLIT: free medicines after a heart attack are an adherence intervention with a real but modest clinical dividend — significant on several event measures, null on the one the trial named primary — and they pay for themselves in this record mainly by shifting, not shrinking, costs.
stamp: SPLIT — eliminating copayments improved adherence and reduced first and total major vascular events, but did not significantly reduce the primary outcome of first major vascular event or revascularisation

title: Video-observed tuberculosis therapy: 70% versus 31% of patients hit the observation target by phone video — superior on being watched, with treatment-outcome equivalence resting on the wider review, not this trial
question: In adults with drug-sensitive tuberculosis, does smartphone video-observed therapy achieve treatment observation and completion non-inferior or superior to clinic-based directly observed therapy?
balance: The head-to-head trial (Story A et al., PMID: 30799062) randomised 226 tuberculosis patients in 22 English clinics — a population in which 58% had a history of homelessness, imprisonment, drug use, alcohol problems, or mental-health problems — to daily smartphone video observation or to directly observed therapy three to five times a week. In intention-to-treat, 70% of the video group (78/112) achieved at least 80% of scheduled observations in the first two months versus 31% (35/114) on direct observation (adjusted OR 5.48, 95% CI 3.10 to 9.68; p < 0.0001); the restricted analysis was closer (77% vs 63%; adjusted OR 2.52, 1.17 to 5.54). A systematic review restricted to randomised trials (Areas Lisboa Netto T et al., PMID: 39405342) found video observation non-inferior for treatment adherence in every included trial, with lower observation costs, less professional supervision time, and higher patient satisfaction where those were measured. The gap in the record is the endpoint itself: what is proven is observation — doses seen taken — while cure, completion of the full course, and relapse were not the powered outcomes of the anchor trial. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): for the job of supervising daily doses, video observation is at least the equal of in-person observation and reaches far more of them; calling it better tuberculosis treatment, rather than better treatment observation, would go past the evidence.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — video-observed therapy achieved far more completed treatment observations than directly observed therapy in one multicentre trial, and randomised comparisons find adherence non-inferior with lower cost and higher satisfaction

title: Spacer versus nebuliser in acute asthma: across 39 trials and 2,626 patients, admissions and lung function were the same — and children using spacers left the emergency department 33 minutes sooner, with less tremor
question: In children and adults with acute asthma, does beta-agonist delivery by metered-dose inhaler with a holding chamber (spacer) work as well as delivery by nebuliser?
balance: The Cochrane review by Cates CJ et al. (PMID: 24037768) pools 39 trials — 1,897 children and 729 adults, 33 of them in emergency or equivalent community settings — in which beta-agonist treatment was repeated and titrated to response. The delivery method made no significant difference to hospital admission: risk ratio 0.94 (95% CI 0.61 to 1.43) in adults and 0.71 (0.47 to 1.08, moderate quality evidence) in children, and peak flow and forced expiratory volume were similar between methods in both age groups. Where the spacer did win was around the edges that matter to families and departments: children given spacer treatment spent 33 minutes less in the emergency department (95% CI −43 to −24; mean nebuliser stay 103 minutes), had a lower pulse rate (mean difference −5% of baseline, −8% to −2%), and developed tremor less often (RR 0.64, 0.44 to 0.95); adult length of stay was similar by either method. Nebulisers need power, maintenance, and cost more in the community; spacers need neither. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): not a stronger bronchodilator effect — the review's own conclusion is that nebuliser delivery produced outcomes not significantly better than a metered-dose inhaler with spacer — but equal efficacy with practical and small clinical advantages, on a moderate-quality paediatric evidence base, earns the benefit stamp for the device choice rather than for the drug.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — spacer delivery is as effective as nebuliser delivery for acute asthma, with shorter emergency-department stays and less tremor in children

title: Measuring the burn to set the feed: calorimetry-guided ICU nutrition hit its targets exactly and moved no outcome in its only direct trial
question: In critically ill adults, does nutrition guided by indirect calorimetry (early goal-directed energy and protein delivery) improve physical function and mortality compared with standard care?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the single direct trial is null and the pooled literature disagrees with itself at different time horizons. EAT-ICU (Allingstrup MJ et al., PMID: 28936712) randomised 203 ventilated patients to calorimetry- and urea-guided feeding aiming at 100% of measured requirements versus standard care: energy and protein balances were less negative, but the 6-month physical component score was identical (mean difference 0.0, 95% CI −5.9 to 5.8) and mortality, organ failure, infections, and length of stay did not differ. Two meta-analyses of the small-trial literature (e.g., Duan J et al., PMID: 33639997; 8 trials, 991 patients) found lower short-term mortality with calorimetry guidance (risk ratio 0.77, 0.60–0.98) without differences in ventilation duration or stay — a pooled signal built from trials individually too small to show it, which the largest and most rigorous single trial does not confirm at 6 months. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): measuring energy expenditure is physiologically attractive and may fine-tune delivery, but improved function or survival is unproven where it has been tested hardest.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — indirect-calorimetry-guided nutrition improves delivery accuracy, but improved function or survival is unproven

title: Getting the feed down: erythromycin beats metoclopramide for a day, the combination beats both for a week — and none of it has been shown to change survival
question: In critically ill adults with enteral feed intolerance, does erythromycin, metoclopramide, or their combination improve feeding success compared with placebo or each other?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for the narrow job of getting feed down in a critically ill patient who is not tolerating it, prokinetics work, combination therapy works best, and nothing here shows they change survival or stay. In the head-to-head trial (Nguyen NQ et al., PMID: 17205032), erythromycin beat metoclopramide at 24 hours (successful feeding 87% vs 62%), but both faded fast; in the companion trial (Nguyen NQ et al., PMID: 17828038), the erythromycin–metoclopramide combination beat erythromycin alone over 7 days, with more calories delivered and less postpyloric feeding, at the cost of more watery diarrhoea (20 of 37 vs 10 of 38). The meta-analysis (Lewis K et al., PMID: 27527069) confirms a moderate-certainty reduction in feeding intolerance (risk ratio 0.73, 95% CI 0.55–0.97; 17.3% absolute reduction) and high residual volumes, with no significant effect on vomiting, diarrhoea overall, ICU stay, or mortality. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): use a prokinetic — combination first where monotherapy fails — to rescue enteral feeding, expecting a feeding benefit that wanes over days, not an outcome benefit.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — prokinetics, especially combined erythromycin plus metoclopramide, improve feeding success in critically ill patients with feed intolerance, without shown outcome benefit

title: Selenium for sepsis: the 1,089-patient trial found mortality a touch higher on selenite (28.3% vs 25.5%) — the antioxidant hypothesis, properly tested, did not survive
question: In adults with severe sepsis or septic shock, does high-dose intravenous selenium (sodium selenite), with procalcitonin-guided antibiotic therapy, reduce mortality compared with placebo?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the largest and best trial is null, and the pooled literature cannot agree with itself. In SISPCT (Bloos F et al., PMID: 27428731), 1,089 patients with severe sepsis or septic shock received a 1,000 µg selenite loading dose then 1,000 µg daily: 28-day mortality was 28.3% versus 25.5% on placebo (p=0.30) — the point estimate favours placebo — and the trial's procalcitonin-guidance factor was likewise null (25.6% vs 28.2%, p=0.34) while reducing antimicrobial exposure by 4.5%. A later meta-analysis of just 5 trials (Kong L et al., PMID: 34394308) reports no 28-day mortality effect (risk ratio 0.93, 95% CI 0.73–1.19) yet a significant all-cause mortality effect (risk ratio 0.78, 0.63–0.98) — an internal inconsistency that signals small-study and timepoint selection rather than a real benefit hiding from the big trial. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): high-dose intravenous selenium should not be given for sepsis outside a trial; the honest summary is 'tested properly once, did not work, and the meta-analytic residue is noise-prone'.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — high-dose intravenous selenium has not been shown to reduce mortality in severe sepsis or septic shock

title: Too thin on paper, fine in person: vitamin K brought the INR down twice as fast and prevented no bleeding whatsoever (15.8% vs 16.3%)
question: In adults on warfarin with excessive anticoagulation (INR 4.5–10) and no bleeding, does low-dose oral vitamin K correct the INR faster without increasing thrombosis or later warfarin resistance, compared with placebo?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — vitamin K does exactly what the blood test asks and nothing the patient can feel. In the one large trial (Crowther MA et al., PMID: 19258557), 712 non-bleeding warfarin patients with INR 4.5–10.0 received 1.25 mg oral vitamin K or placebo: the INR fell faster (mean fall 2.8 vs 1.4 by the next day, p<0.001), but over 90 days bleeding occurred in 15.8% versus 16.3% (absolute difference −0.5 percentage points, 95% CI −6.1 to 5.1), major bleeding was numerically more frequent with vitamin K (2.5% vs 1.1%; difference 1.5 points, −0.8 to 3.7), and thromboembolism was similar (1.1% vs 0.8%). No systematic review answers this acute-correction question — the Cochrane vitamin K review addresses chronic low-dose supplementation for unstable control, a different intervention — so the shelf rests on the single trial. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): holding warfarin and watching is a defensible default for the non-bleeding patient in this INR range; low-dose oral vitamin K is a reasonable option where a faster fall is wanted, but no one should promise it prevents bleeding, because the trial that looked found none prevented.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — low-dose oral vitamin K corrects a high INR faster but has not been shown to reduce bleeding in non-bleeding warfarin patients

title: Iron instead of blood in the ICU: 39 fewer units transfused on iron — in a 140-patient trial too small to call that a finding rather than a hint
question: In critically ill adults with anaemia, does intravenous iron reduce red-cell transfusion and improve haemoglobin recovery compared with placebo?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — one small trial, a blood-count win and a transfusion trend that never reached significance. In IRONMAN (Litton E et al., PMID: 27686346), 140 anaemic ICU patients received intravenous iron or placebo: transfusion use was 97 versus 136 red-cell units (incidence rate ratio 0.71, 95% CI 0.43–1.18, p=0.19) — a point estimate suggesting fewer units, with a confidence interval spanning meaningful benefit and none — while haemoglobin at hospital discharge was significantly higher on iron (median 107 vs 100 g/L, p=0.02), and no safety outcome differed. No systematic review specific to intravenous iron in critically ill patients was found to strengthen the shelf (the available syntheses address surgical patients and exclude critical illness), so the claim must stay at the size of its evidence. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): intravenous iron in ICU anaemia plausibly reduces transfusion and speeds haemoglobin recovery, but with 140 patients the trial proves only the haemoglobin part; a transfusion-sparing claim awaits a trial powered for it.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — intravenous iron raises discharge haemoglobin in ICU anaemia, but a transfusion-sparing effect is unproven

title: Vitamin B6 for PMS: double the odds of feeling better across nine small trials — every one of them too weak to fully trust
question: In women with premenstrual syndrome, does vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) reduce premenstrual symptoms compared with placebo?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — a positive pooled result standing on low-quality legs. The BMJ systematic review (Wyatt KM et al., PMID: 10334745) pooled nine published randomised placebo-controlled trials in 940 women with premenstrual syndrome: the odds of overall symptom improvement were about double on vitamin B6 (odds ratio 2.32, 95% CI 1.95–2.54), and for premenstrual depressive symptoms the odds ratio was 1.69 (1.39–2.06) across four trials and 541 patients, at doses up to 100 mg/day. But the reviewers state plainly that conclusions are limited by the low quality of most included trials — small, old, and variably reported — and no large modern trial has since settled the question. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): vitamin B6 at up to 100 mg/day may ease premenstrual symptoms and is cheap and familiar, but the evidence would not survive the standards applied elsewhere in this library, and the dose ceiling matters — chronic high-dose B6 is itself a cause of neuropathy (shelf #60).
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — vitamin B6 up to 100 mg/day may improve premenstrual symptoms, but the supporting trials are small and low quality

title: Rhodiola SHR-5 for burnout fatigue: better than placebo on burnout and concentration scores in 60 people — in a literature reviewers call contradictory
question: In adults with stress-related fatigue, does the standardised Rhodiola rosea extract SHR-5 (Swedish Herbal Institute) reduce fatigue and improve concentration compared with placebo?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — one small trial of one named extract, positive on some measures, inside a literature a systematic review calls contradictory. The trial (Olsson EM et al., PMID: 19016404) randomised 60 adults with stress-related fatigue to the standardised Rhodiola rosea root extract SHR-5 (Swedish Herbal Institute; 576 mg/day) or placebo for 28 days: both groups improved, but SHR-5 was superior on the Pines burnout scale and on several attention indices (omissions, Hit RT SE, variability on the Conners test), with a blunted cortisol response to awakening and no serious attributable side-effects. The systematic review (Ishaque S et al., PMID: 22643043) found 11 trials, judged all at high or unclear risk of bias, and concluded efficacy cannot be accurately assessed. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): SHR-5 may reduce stress-related fatigue over four weeks; the claim belongs to that named extract and dose, and current Rhodiola products — which vary widely in extract and dose — cannot be assumed to share its safety or effectiveness.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the SHR-5 Rhodiola extract may reduce stress-related fatigue over 28 days, on a single small trial

title: Bacopa for the ageing memory: the tested extract was BacoMind, and it improved word-list learning and delayed recall — not the memory people complain about
question: In healthy older adults, does Bacopa monnieri extract (standardised extract CDRI 08, the KeenMind preparation) improve memory performance compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — small trials, consistent direction, narrow outcome. The direct trial (Morgan A & Stevens J, PMID: 20590480) randomised 98 healthy adults over 55 to the Bacopa monnieri extract BacoMind (Natural Remedies Pvt. Ltd.), 300 mg/day, or placebo for 12 weeks: the Bacopa group improved significantly on verbal learning, memory acquisition, and delayed recall on the Rey Auditory Verbal Learning Test (delayed recall p=0.001; total learning p=0.011), while visual memory, trail-making, and subjective memory scores did not differ significantly; gastrointestinal side-effects (increased stool frequency, abdominal cramps, nausea) were more frequent on Bacopa. A meta-analysis of nine trials (Kongkeaw C et al., PMID: 24252493) found improved attention speed (Trail B −17.9 ms; choice reaction time −10.6 ms). Note: the tested preparation in the record is BacoMind, not the CDRI 08/KeenMind preparation named in the mining note — the card follows the publication. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): standardised Bacopa extract probably improves some memory-test performance in healthy older adults over 12 weeks; whether that is a difference anyone notices in daily life, or any protection against dementia, is untested.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — standardised Bacopa monnieri extract (BacoMind) improves verbal memory test performance in healthy older adults over 12 weeks

title: Hawthorn WS 1442 in heart failure: more watts on the bike and less breathlessness across 14 trials — and not one usable number on staying alive
question: In adults with chronic heart failure (NYHA class II–III) on standard therapy, does hawthorn extract WS 1442 (Dr. Willmar Schwabe) improve exercise capacity and symptoms compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — symptom and exercise benefits, consistently shown, with the outcomes that matter most never measured. In the largest single trial (Tauchert M, PMID: 12040357), 209 patients with NYHA class III heart failure on diuretics received the hawthorn extract WS 1442 (Dr. Willmar Schwabe) at 1,800 mg or 900 mg daily or placebo for 16 weeks: maximal tolerated workload rose significantly more on 1,800 mg than on either comparator, typical heart-failure symptoms improved significantly at both doses, and adverse events — particularly dizziness and vertigo — were fewest in the high-dose group. The Cochrane review (Pittler MH et al., PMID: 18254076) pooled 10 trials (855 patients): maximal workload +5.35 watts (95% CI 0.71–10.00), exercise tolerance up, pressure–heart-rate product down, and breathlessness and fatigue significantly improved — but no mortality or cardiac-event data apart from one trial's unexplained death counts (three on hawthorn, one on control). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): as an add-on to standard therapy, WS 1442 probably improves exercise capacity and symptoms in chronic heart failure; it is not a substitute for prognostic heart-failure drugs, whose benefit it has never been shown to share.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — hawthorn extract WS 1442 improves exercise capacity and symptoms as add-on therapy in chronic heart failure, with no mortality data

title: Ivy leaf extract EA 575 (Prospan) for acute cough: two placebo-controlled trials and their pooled analysis show faster recovery — BSS down 8.6 versus 6.2 points at a week, and twice as many cough-free
question: In adults with acute bronchitis or acute cough, does ivy leaf dry extract EA 575 (Prospan, Engelhard Arzneimittel) reduce cough severity compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the tested product matters here: every positive trial used the same named preparation, ivy leaf dry extract EA 575 (Prospan, Engelhard Arzneimittel), not generic ivy products. In the Schaefer 2016 trial (PMID: 29441845), 181 adults with acute cough treated three times daily for one week showed statistically significant and clinically relevant reductions in cough severity on visual analogue scale, Bronchitis Severity Score and verbal category scores versus placebo, with a significant advantage detectable within 48 hours and persisting 7 days after treatment ended; all adverse events were non-serious, mild or moderate, and none was judged drug-related. The individual-patient-data meta-analysis of the two double-blind placebo-controlled trials of EA 575 (Völp A et al., PMID: 36414647; 228 on EA 575, 162 on placebo) found Bronchitis Severity Score reductions of 8.6 versus 6.2 points at 7 days (p < 0.001), with the placebo group's 7-day score reduction matching what EA 575 achieved by day 4, and cough-free proportions of 18.1% versus 9.3% at treatment end and 56.2% versus 25.6% after a further untreated week; adverse event rates were comparable. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): for this specific extract, two placebo-controlled trials and their pooled analysis point the same way — faster, greater cough relief than placebo with no safety signal — but the evidence base is two industry-era trials of one proprietary extract, the outcomes are symptom scores in a self-limiting illness, and the result cannot be extended to other ivy preparations, which may differ in safety and effectiveness.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — ivy leaf dry extract EA 575 (Prospan) speeds and deepens cough relief versus placebo in acute bronchitis/cough

title: Cineole (Soledum) for acute nonpurulent sinusitis: symptom score 3.0 versus 9.2 on placebo at 7 days in the one direct trial — a big gap resting on 152 patients
question: In adults with acute non-purulent rhinosinusitis, does cineole (1,8-cineole, the Soledum preparation) improve symptoms and sinus findings compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one well-conducted double-blind trial carries this shelf. In Kehrl 2004 (PMID: 15064633), 152 patients with acute nonpurulent rhinosinusitis took cineole (the Soledum preparation; two 100-mg capsules three times daily) or placebo for 7 days: the symptom-sum-score, 15.6 in both groups at baseline, fell to 6.9 versus 12.2 at day 4 and 3.0 versus 9.2 at day 7 — differences the authors describe as clinically relevant and statistically significant — with parallel improvements in headache on bending, frontal headache, trigeminal pressure-point sensitivity, general condition, nasal obstruction and secretion, and only two mild possibly-related side effects (heartburn and exanthema). A 2023 systematic review and network meta-analysis of herbal medicines for rhinosinusitis (Hoang MP et al., PMID: 36609950; 47 randomised trials, 18 herbal medicines) independently placed cineole among the most effective treatments for symptom control in acute post-viral rhinosinusitis, at moderate certainty of evidence. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the effect size in the single trial is large and the network synthesis concurs, but the direct evidence remains one 152-patient, 7-day trial of one named preparation in nonpurulent (largely viral/post-viral) disease — it says nothing about bacterial sinusitis, where the antibiotic question is separate, and other cineole products may differ in safety and effectiveness.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — cineole (Soledum) substantially reduced symptom scores versus placebo in one trial of acute nonpurulent rhinosinusitis, with network meta-analysis support

title: Bronchipret (thyme–ivy, Bionorica) for acute bronchitis: coughing fits down 68.7% versus 47.6% on placebo and 96% responders by day 10 — in a single 361-patient trial
question: In adults with acute bronchitis with productive cough, does the thyme–ivy fluid extract combination Bronchipret (Bionorica) shorten cough compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one large, well-reported double-blind trial of the named combination product. In Kemmerich 2006 (PMID: 17063641), 361 outpatients with acute bronchitis and productive cough took the thyme–ivy fluid extract combination Bronchipret (Bionorica), 5.4 mL three times daily, or matched placebo for 11 days: the mean reduction in daytime coughing fits on days 7–9 was 68.7% relative to baseline on Bronchipret versus 47.6% on placebo (p < 0.0001), a 50% relative reduction in coughing fits was reached 2 days earlier on the combination, and Bronchitis Severity Score responder rates were 83.0% versus 53.9% at day 4 and 96.2% versus 74.7% at day 10 (p < 0.0001), with no difference in the frequency or severity of adverse events and no severe or serious events. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the trial is big for this field and internally consistent across counted coughing fits, severity scores and responder rates — but it is a single trial of one proprietary combination (Bronchipret, Bionorica), in a self-limiting illness, with symptom-count outcomes; it cannot be read across to ivy alone (shelf #3039, a different product), to thyme alone, or to other thyme–ivy products, which may differ in safety and effectiveness. No qualifying systematic review or meta-analysis of this combination was found, so no synthesis card is added.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the thyme–ivy combination Bronchipret (Bionorica) reduced coughing fits and raised responder rates versus placebo in one large trial

title: Aquablation versus TURP: identical 15.1-point IPSS gains at 1 year, fewer ejaculatory problems, and a 5-year symptom edge in 50–80 mL prostates — all from the one WATER programme
question: In men with benign prostatic hyperplasia and prostates of 30–80 mL, does Aquablation (robot-assisted waterjet ablation) relieve urinary symptoms as well as transurethral resection of the prostate, with fewer sexual side effects?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one randomised programme, followed to 5 years, answers this directly. In the WATER trial's 1-year report (Gilling PJ et al., PMID: 30552937; 181 men, prostates 30–80 mL), symptom-score improvement was identical after Aquablation and transurethral resection of the prostate (IPSS reduction 15.1 points in both), maximum flow improved by 10.3 versus 10.6 mL/s (p = 0.8632), prostate-specific antigen fell by about 1 point in both groups, and surgical retreatment within a year was 2.6% versus 1.5% (not significant), with no procedure-related adverse events after month 6. The 5-year report in the 50–80 mL subgroup (Oumedjbeur K et al., PMID: 37838991; 96 men) found a larger IPSS reduction with Aquablation (−14.1 versus −10.8, p = 0.02), a lower rate of Clavien-Dindo grade 1 persistent or grade 2+ events at 3 months (risk difference −23.1%), notably less de novo ejaculatory dysfunction (risk difference −21.9%), similar bleeding risk after 6 months, and a lower retreatment rate at 6 months (risk difference −14.4%). A 2023 systematic review and meta-analysis (Chen DC et al., PMID: 37692142; 7 studies, 551 patients, mostly non-randomised) found IPSS improved by about 16.5 points at 3 months, sustained to 12 months, with sexual-function scores essentially unchanged (pooled effect −0.55, p = 0.321), while noting heterogeneity and publication-bias concerns. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): symptom relief matches TURP at 1 year and looks at least as durable at 5 years in medium prostates, with a genuine ejaculatory-function advantage — but the randomised base is a single trial programme, the 5-year figures come from a subgroup, and wider comparative durability data are still thin.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — Aquablation matches TURP for symptom relief with better ejaculatory preservation in the WATER trial programme

title: HoLEP versus TURP: identical symptom relief at a year, hospital stay 59 versus 86 hours and a much shorter catheter time — paid for with a longer operation and more early leakage
question: In men with benign prostatic hyperplasia, does holmium laser enucleation of the prostate (HoLEP) give symptom relief and flow rates at least as good as transurethral resection, with less bleeding and shorter catheter time?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — efficacy is a draw; the perioperative course is where HoLEP wins in the randomised record. In the two-centre trial of Montorsi 2008 (PMID: 18405765; 100 men with obstructive benign prostatic hyperplasia), HoLEP and TURP showed no statistically significant differences in urodynamic findings or subjective symptom scores at 1, 6 or 12 months; HoLEP took longer in the operating room (74 ± 19.5 versus 57 ± 15 minutes, p < 0.05) but catheterisation time was far shorter (31 ± 13 versus 57.78 ± 17.5 — units as printed in the record — p < 0.001) and hospital stay shorter (59 ± 19.9 versus 85.8 ± 18.9 hours, p < 0.001); transient stress and urge incontinence were more common after HoLEP, overall complication rates were comparable, and erectile function was maintained in both groups. The wider synthesis (Ahyai SA et al., PMID: 20825758; meta-analysis of 23 randomised trials, 2,245 patients, across transurethral techniques) concluded that functional results and overall morbidity of the minimally invasive techniques, HoLEP among them, were statistically comparable to contemporary TURP, with technique-specific safety profiles. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): for symptom relief HoLEP is TURP's equal on this record; its benefit is the shorter catheter time and hospital stay, bought with longer operating time, more transient incontinence, and a well-known operator learning curve that trial centres have already climbed — community results may lag trial results.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — HoLEP equals TURP for symptom relief with shorter catheterisation and hospital stay

title: Pregabalin for chronic prostatitis/pelvic pain: responders 47% versus 36% on placebo but p = 0.07 — the primary endpoint missed, and Cochrane calls it probably ineffective
question: In men with chronic prostatitis/chronic pelvic pain syndrome (category III), does pregabalin reduce pain and pelvic-pain symptom scores compared with placebo?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the one dedicated trial missed its primary endpoint, and the Cochrane synthesis sides with the miss. In the NIH-network trial (Pontari MA et al., PMID: 20876412), 324 men with chronic prostatitis/chronic pelvic pain syndrome received pregabalin (titrated 150 to 600 mg/day) or placebo for 6 weeks in a 2:1 ratio: the primary outcome — at least a 6-point decrease in the NIH Chronic Prostatitis Symptom Index total score — was reached by 47.2% (103/218) on pregabalin versus 35.8% (38/106) on placebo, which was not statistically significant (p = 0.07). Secondary measures leaned pregabalin's way (NIH-CPSI total and subscore reductions, p < 0.05; Global Response Assessment response 31.2% versus 18.9%, p = 0.02; McGill Pain Questionnaire improvement, p = 0.01), but the other outcomes did not differ, and the authors conclude pregabalin was not superior to placebo on the primary outcome. The Cochrane systematic review of pharmacological interventions for CP/CPPS (Franco JVA et al., PMID: 31899937; 99 studies, 9,119 men) states that moderate- to high-quality evidence indicates pregabalin may be ineffective for reducing prostatitis symptoms. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): a near-miss primary endpoint with supportive secondaries is exactly the pattern that most often evaporates on replication, and the field's own synthesis grades pregabalin among the probably-ineffective options — it remains a maybe for an individual neuropathic-pain phenotype, not an evidence-backed CPPS treatment.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — pregabalin missed its primary endpoint in the one CP/CPPS trial and Cochrane grades it probably ineffective

title: Tamsulosin to prevent post-operative retention: 10.3% versus 16.3% and 17.7% versus 19.8% in the two newest trials — both null, with only subgroup hints in the pooled hernia data
question: In adults having surgery under spinal anaesthesia or pelvic surgery, does perioperative tamsulosin prevent postoperative urinary retention compared with placebo?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the two recent placebo-controlled trials carded here are both null, and the pooled literature agrees overall while leaving subgroup doors open. In Seyedinnavadeh 2025 (PMID: 40602006), 179 men over 50 having inguinal hernia repair under spinal anaesthesia received tamsulosin 0.4 mg before and after surgery or placebo: retention requiring catheterisation occurred in 10.3% versus 16.3% — a 6-point absolute gap that was not statistically significant (p = 0.242), with logistic regression confirming no significant prophylactic effect (p = 0.171). In Leffelman 2025 (PMID: 40220053), 161 women having mid-urethral sling placement received a single preoperative tamsulosin 0.4 mg tablet or placebo: retention rates were 17.7% versus 19.8% (p = 0.7420), with no differences in unplanned admissions, urinary tract infections, or hypotension, and only a non-significant trend in the subgroup without concomitant prolapse surgery (7.5% versus 16.7%, p = 0.142). The hernia-repair meta-analysis (Drahman A et al., PMID: 36952050; 8 RCTs of prophylactic alpha-blockade) found no overall prevention of retention, but significant reductions in the laparoscopic subgroup and in patients over 60 — subgroup findings of the kind that need prospective confirmation. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): routine perioperative tamsulosin to prevent retention is unproven; a benefit confined to older patients or specific operations remains possible but rests on subgroups set against null primary results.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — perioperative tamsulosin has not been shown to prevent postoperative urinary retention overall

title: Shockwave therapy for erectile dysfunction: 54% of pill-nonresponders regained penetration-hard erections versus 0% on sham — in small, 1-month, single-group trials
question: In men with erectile dysfunction, does low-intensity extracorporeal shockwave therapy improve erectile function compared with sham treatment?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two small sham-controlled trials from one research group, pointing the same way, plus a supportive meta-analysis. In Vardi 2012 (PMID: 22425129), 67 men with organic erectile dysfunction who responded to phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors received 12 sessions of low-intensity shockwave therapy or sham after a washout month: the IIEF erectile-function domain rose by 6.7 ± 0.9 points versus 3.0 ± 1.4 (p = 0.0322), 19 treated men who initially could not achieve penetration-hard erections (hardness score ≤ 2) reached hardness ≥ 3 versus none on sham, and maximal post-ischaemic penile blood flow improved by 8.2 versus 0.1 mL/min/dL (p < 0.0001), with no discomfort or adverse effects reported. In Kitrey 2016 (PMID: 26694904), 58 men who had stopped phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors for lack of efficacy were randomised (37 shockwave, 18 sham analysed): 54.1% versus 0% achieved penetration-hard erections with the inhibitor after treatment (p < 0.0001), treatment was 'effective' by IIEF-EF change in 40.5% versus 0% (p = 0.001), and 56.3% of the sham group crossed over to shockwave then achieved penetration-hard erections. The meta-analysis of Dong L et al. (PMID: 31027441; 7 RCTs, 522 participants) found pooled IIEF-EF improvement favouring shockwave over sham (mean difference 1.99 points, 95% CI 1.35 to 2.63) and a large odds ratio for hardness-score improvement (OR 16.02, 95% CI 7.93 to 32.37). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): short-term erectile-function gains are consistent, but the trials are small, short (1 month post-treatment), largely from one group, use varying devices and protocols, and durability beyond the short term is unestablished in this record.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — low-intensity shockwave therapy improves erectile function over sham in small short-term trials

title: Efinaconazole for toenail fungus: complete cure 18% and 15% versus 3% and 5% on vehicle after 48 weeks — the strongest topical evidence there is, and still only one cure in six
question: In adults with toenail onychomycosis, does topical efinaconazole 10% solution achieve complete or mycological cure compared with vehicle?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — two identical phase 3 trials and a Cochrane review land in the same place, which is rare for topical nail treatments. In Elewski 2013 (PMID: 23177180), 1,655 patients with distal lateral subungual toenail onychomycosis (20–50% involvement) applied efinaconazole 10% solution or vehicle daily for 48 weeks: mycological cure was 55.2% and 53.4% in the two studies versus significantly lower vehicle rates (p < 0.001), and the primary endpoint, complete cure at week 52 (0% clinical involvement plus negative microscopy and culture), was 17.8% versus 3.3% and 15.2% versus 5.5% (both p < 0.001); adverse events were local site reactions in about 2%, clinically similar to vehicle. The Cochrane review of topical and device-based toenail treatments (Foley K et al., PMID: 31978269; 56 studies, 12,501 participants) found high-quality evidence that efinaconazole beats vehicle for complete cure (RR 3.54, 95% CI 2.24 to 5.60; 3 studies, 1,716 participants) and clinical cure (RR 3.07, 95% CI 2.08 to 4.53), moderate-quality evidence for mycological cure (RR 2.31, 95% CI 1.08 to 4.94), and a slightly higher adverse-event risk (RR 1.10, 95% CI 1.01 to 1.20), mainly dermatitis and vesicles. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): the relative effects are large and consistent, but keep the absolutes in view — complete cure is roughly one patient in six after a year of daily application, versus roughly one in twenty on vehicle; it is the best-evidenced topical option for patients avoiding oral antifungals, not a match for simply wanting the nail cured.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — efinaconazole 10% solution produces complete cure in about one in six patients versus one in twenty on vehicle, with high-quality Cochrane support

title: Ear drops for wax: 22% cleared versus 5% with no treatment in the one direct study — but no drop beat water, saline, or any rival drop in Cochrane's ten trials
question: In adults and children with impacted ear wax, do ear drops (cerumenolytics, oil-based, or water-based preparations) remove wax or ease syringing compared with no treatment or each other?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the honest Cochrane answer is that drops probably help a little versus doing nothing, and no drop has earned preference over another — or over plain water. In Aaron 2018 (PMID: 30043448), 10 randomised studies (623 participants, 900 ears) of oil-based, water-based and other cerumenolytic drops found, on low-quality evidence: active treatment versus no treatment in the single study addressing it cleared wax completely in 22% of ears versus 5% after five days (RR 4.09, 95% CI 1.00 to 16.80; 117 ears; NNTB = 8); active treatment versus water or saline showed no evidence of a difference (RR 1.47, 95% CI 0.79 to 2.75; 3 studies, 257 ears); water or saline versus no treatment likewise showed no evidence of a difference (RR 4.00, 95% CI 0.91 to 17.62; 76 ears); and head-to-head studies found no evidence that any one active treatment beat another, or that oil-based beat non-oil-based preparations. Adverse effects (discomfort, irritation, pain) were mild, infrequent (fewer than 30 participants across seven studies), and not significantly different between drop types; no emergencies or serious adverse effects occurred. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): using some drops for a few days before review or syringing is reasonable and harmless, but the evidence cannot name a best drop, cannot separate proprietary cerumenolytics from water or saline, and rests on small, mostly old studies (nine of ten over 15 years old at review).
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — ear drops may aid wax clearance versus no treatment, but no drop is shown better than another or than water/saline

title: Drops for swimmer's ear: steroid-containing drops cured more patients by days 14–21 and halved recurrence versus acetic acid — and adding antibiotic to steroid added nothing
question: In adults with acute otitis externa in primary care, do topical acetic acid, antibiotic drops, or antibiotic–steroid drops differ in cure and pain relief?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for steroid-containing drops over acetic acid alone. The one large primary-care trial (van Balen FA et al., PMID: 14630756) randomised 213 adults with acute otitis externa in Dutch general practice to acetic acid drops, corticosteroid-plus-acetic-acid drops, or steroid-plus-antibiotic drops: median symptom duration was 8.0 days on acetic acid, 7.0 days on steroid–acetic acid, and 6.0 days on steroid–antibiotic; overall cure rates were 38% at day 7, 68% at day 14 and 75% at day 21, and compared with acetic acid both steroid-containing regimens cured significantly more patients by day 14 (OR 2.4, 95% CI 1.1 to 5.3, and OR 3.5, 1.6 to 7.7) and day 21 (OR 5.3, 2.0 to 13.7, and OR 3.9, 1.7 to 9.1), with less recurrence between days 21 and 42 (29% overall recurred; OR 0.3, 0.1 to 0.7, and OR 0.4, 0.2 to 1.0, versus acetic acid) — while the two steroid-containing regimens were equally effective as each other. The Cochrane review (Kaushik V et al., PMID: 20091565; 19 RCTs, 3,382 participants, mostly low quality) found topical antimicrobial-plus-steroid drops significantly more effective than placebo (OR 11, 95% CI 2.00 to 60.57; one trial), no clinically meaningful differences among most topical interventions, and the same exception: acetic acid, comparable at week 1, was significantly less effective than antibiotic/steroid drops at weeks 2 and 3 (OR 0.29, 95% CI 0.13 to 0.62, and OR 0.25, 0.11 to 0.58), with symptoms lasting about two days longer. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): use a steroid-containing drop rather than acetic acid alone when treatment beyond a few days is likely; adding the antibiotic to the steroid bought nothing measurable in the primary-care trial.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — corticosteroid-containing ear drops cure acute otitis externa more reliably than acetic acid alone

title: Numbing ear drops for children's otitis media (CEDAR): antibiotics used by 3% versus 29% — a big signal from a trial that recruited a fraction of its target and never settled the pain question
question: In children with acute otitis media, do anaesthetic–analgesic ear drops reduce ear pain and antibiotic consumption compared with placebo drops or usual care?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — a well-designed pragmatic trial that fell far short of its recruitment target, leaving a large-looking effect on antibiotic use and no answer at all on pain. In CEDAR (Hay AD et al., PMID: 31304912), children aged 1–10 with acute otitis media and ear pain, not requiring immediate antibiotics, were randomised to anaesthetic–analgesic ear drops or usual care (with a smaller blinded three-group comparison against placebo drops): in the combined analysis, 1 of 39 children (3%) in the active-drops group consumed antibiotics within 8 days versus 11 of 38 (29%) in the usual-care group (unadjusted OR 0.09, 95% CI 0.02 to 0.55, p = 0.009; adjusted for delayed prescribing OR 0.15, 95% CI 0.03 to 0.87, p = 0.035); in the tiny placebo comparison, antibiotic consumption was 43% (3/7) on placebo drops versus 0% (0/10) on active drops (p = 0.051). Ear pain at day 2, however, was not shown to improve — the adjusted difference versus placebo (0.67, 95% CI −1.44 to 2.79; p = 0.51) is consistent with chance, on 17 children — and NHS costs were £12.66 (active drops) versus £11.36 (usual care), an estimated £5.19 per antibiotic prescription avoided with a high degree of uncertainty. No adverse events were reported in children receiving active drops. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): the antibiotic-sparing signal is intriguing and mechanistically plausible only if the drops relieve pain — the very outcome the trial was too small to test; the authors themselves say the effect requires replication in a larger study. No qualifying systematic review of anaesthetic–analgesic drops for otitis media pain was found, so no synthesis card is added.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — anaesthetic–analgesic ear drops may reduce antibiotic consumption in childhood otitis media, but the one trial was under-recruited and pain relief was not established

title: Antihistamine updosing for chronic hives: 41 of 80 difficult cases became symptom-free as the dose rose to fourfold — with a modest pooled advantage (RR 1.13) and a little more sleepiness
question: In adults with chronic spontaneous urticaria uncontrolled on standard-dose antihistamines, does updosing levocetirizine or desloratadine (up to four times the licensed dose) improve hive control compared with standard dosing?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the guideline's first escalation step has one neat dose-escalation trial and a supportive meta-analysis behind it. In Staevska 2010 (PMID: 20226302), 80 patients with difficult-to-treat chronic urticaria were randomised double-blind to levocetirizine or desloratadine starting at the conventional 5 mg daily, escalating weekly to 10 mg, then 20 mg, then 20 mg of the opposite drug if relief was incomplete: 13 patients became symptom-free at 5 mg (9 levocetirizine versus 4 desloratadine), and 28 more became symptom-free on the higher doses — at 10 mg (8 levocetirizine, 7 desloratadine) and at 20 mg (5 and 1); of 28 patients nonresponsive to 20 mg desloratadine, 7 became symptom-free on 20 mg levocetirizine, while none of 18 levocetirizine nonresponders benefited from 20 mg desloratadine. The authors summarise the responsiveness pattern as roughly 15% good responders, 10% nonresponders, and 75% responding to higher-than-conventional doses; increasing doses improved quality of life without increasing somnolence, and no serious or severe adverse effects occurred. The meta-analysis of Xiao X et al. (PMID: 37024900; 7 RCTs pooled) found high-dose second-generation antihistamines gave a significantly higher response rate than standard dose (RR 1.13, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.26; p = 0.02) — a modest relative gain — with significantly more somnolence (risk difference 0.05, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.09) but no difference in overall adverse events or withdrawals, and the authors caution the pooled doses studied were mostly up to twice standard, with few trials. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): updosing converts a substantial share of standard-dose nonresponders in the escalation trial and a small average advantage in the pool — worth doing before biologics, with the honest caveats that the pooled effect is modest, somnolence rises with dose, and the full fourfold strategy rests mainly on the single trial.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — updosing second-generation antihistamines up to fourfold improves hive control in patients uncontrolled on standard doses

title: STRONG-HF: pushing heart-failure drugs to full dose within two weeks of discharge, with four close visits, cut death or readmission by a third in relative terms
question: In adults hospitalised with acute heart failure, does a high-intensity strategy of rapid up-titration of guideline-directed medical therapy with close follow-up, compared with usual care, reduce death or heart-failure readmission?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — one large multinational randomised trial (1,078 patients) tested the whole strategy, not a single drug: rapid up-titration to full recommended doses within 2 weeks of discharge plus four close follow-up visits over 2 months, against usual local care. By day 90 the strategy plainly worked as a delivery system — full-dose renin-angiotensin blockers in 55% versus 2%, beta-blockers 49% versus 4%, mineralocorticoid antagonists 84% versus 46% — and the clinical endpoint followed: heart-failure readmission or all-cause death by day 180 in 15.2% versus 23.3% (adjusted risk difference 8.1%, risk ratio 0.66, a 34% relative reduction). The cautions are real: the trial was open-label, stopped early on the data monitoring board's advice (which can exaggerate effects), the primary endpoint was amended mid-trial with down-weighting, and adverse events were more frequent with high-intensity care (41% versus 29% by 90 days) although serious (16% versus 17%) and fatal (5% versus 6%) events were not. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): rapid up-titration with close follow-up after an acute heart-failure admission reduces death or readmission, provided the monitoring visits that make it safe are actually delivered.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — rapid up-titration of guideline-directed therapy with close follow-up after acute heart failure reduced 180-day death or heart-failure readmission (15.2% vs 23.3%)
