title: Digitoxin in modern HFrEF (DIGIT-HF): the death-or-admission composite fell (HR 0.82), but death alone did not — a single-trial, borderline result
question: In patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction on modern therapy, does digitoxin, compared with placebo, reduce cardiovascular death or worsening heart failure?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — digitoxin is not digoxin: it is a different cardiac glycoside, and this shelf asks what it does on top of modern guideline-directed therapy. DIGIT-HF (1,212 patients in the modified intention-to-treat population, median follow-up 36 months) found the composite of death from any cause or first hospital admission for worsening heart failure in 39.5% on digitoxin versus 44.1% on placebo (hazard ratio 0.82, 95% CI 0.69 to 0.98, p=0.03) — an 18% relative reduction. Neither component alone was significant: death 27.2% versus 29.5% (HR 0.86, 95% CI 0.69 to 1.07) and first worsening-heart-failure admission 28.1% versus 30.4% (HR 0.85, 95% CI 0.69 to 1.05). Serious adverse events were numerically more frequent on digitoxin (4.7% versus 2.8% of patients with at least one). It is a single trial with a borderline composite and no proven mortality benefit on its own. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): digitoxin modestly reduces the combined risk of death or worsening-heart-failure admission in HFrEF on modern therapy; a mortality benefit is not established.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — digitoxin reduced the composite of death or worsening-heart-failure admission (HR 0.82) in one modern trial; mortality alone was not significantly reduced

title: Fluid restriction in chronic heart failure (FRESH-UP): liberal drinking missed its quality-of-life endpoint, restriction bought nothing but thirst — four trials, no outcome benefit
question: In patients with chronic heart failure, does liberal fluid intake, compared with fluid restriction to 1.5 L/day, improve quality of life without increasing death or hospitalisation?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — fluid restriction to 1.5 L/day is widely advised in chronic heart failure, but the randomised record does not show it helps. In FRESH-UP (504 outpatients), advice for liberal fluid intake versus restriction gave a Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire overall score at 3 months of 74.0 versus 72.2 — an adjusted difference of 2.17 points (95% CI −0.06 to 4.39, p=0.06) favouring liberal intake that did not meet the primary outcome — while thirst distress was higher in the restriction group and safety events did not differ. A 2026 systematic review of all four randomised trials (682 patients) found no trial showed a difference in mortality or heart-failure hospitalisation, contradictory quality-of-life results, and more thirst distress with restriction; only one trial was at low risk of bias. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): liberal intake has not been shown to improve quality of life, but routine restriction has no demonstrated outcome benefit either and costs patients thirst — the honest reading is that the case for routine restriction is unproven, not that liberal intake is proven better.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — liberal fluid intake was not shown to improve quality of life, and fluid restriction has no demonstrated outcome benefit, only more thirst distress

title: Vitamin D in heart failure (VINDICATE): ejection fraction rose 6 points, walking distance did not move — a surrogate benefit with no outcomes trial behind it
question: In patients with chronic heart failure and vitamin D deficiency, does high-dose vitamin D supplementation improve cardiac function and exercise capacity?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — VINDICATE randomised 229 patients with chronic heart failure from left ventricular systolic dysfunction and vitamin D deficiency to 4,000 IU (100 µg) vitamin D3 daily or placebo for a year. The primary endpoint was negative: 6-minute walk distance did not improve. The secondary imaging endpoints moved — ejection fraction rose by 6.07% more than placebo (95% CI 3.20 to 8.95, p<0.0001), with reversal of remodelling (left ventricular end-diastolic diameter −2.49 mm; end-systolic diameter −2.09 mm). A 2021 meta-analysis of 13 randomised trials (1,215 patients) likewise found an ejection-fraction gain of 3.30% (95% CI 0.95 to 5.65). But ejection fraction is a surrogate: no trial here shows fewer deaths or hospitalisations, and the one patient-centred measure in the anchor trial — walking distance — was null. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): high-dose vitamin D improves the echocardiogram in deficient heart-failure patients; whether that translates into outcomes patients feel is untested.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — high-dose vitamin D improved ejection fraction but not walk distance in deficient HFrEF patients; no outcome benefit is shown

title: Allopurinol for hyperuricaemic heart failure (EXACT-HF): uric acid fell 4 points, every clinical measure stayed flat — the oxidative-stress hypothesis failed its direct test
question: In patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction and hyperuricaemia, does allopurinol, compared with placebo, improve clinical status, quality of life and left ventricular function?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the mechanistic story was attractive: xanthine oxidase generates oxidative stress, and hyperuricaemia tracks with worse heart failure. EXACT-HF tested it directly in 253 patients with symptomatic heart failure, ejection fraction ≤40% and uric acid ≥9.5 mg/dL, randomised to allopurinol (target 600 mg daily) or placebo for 24 weeks. Allopurinol lowered uric acid as intended (treatment difference −4.2 mg/dL at 12 weeks and −3.5 mg/dL at 24 weeks) and changed nothing else: the primary clinical-status composite was identical (worsened 45% versus 46%; improved 13% versus 19%, p=0.68), with no difference in quality-of-life scores, 6-minute walk distance or ejection fraction, and more rash (10% versus 2%). A 2020 meta-analysis of 11 studies went further, associating allopurinol with higher all-cause mortality (HR 1.24) and cardiovascular mortality (HR 1.42) — but with high heterogeneity (I²=73%) and a mix of study designs, that harm signal is hypothesis-raising, not proof. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): allopurinol does not improve clinical status, function or ejection fraction in hyperuricaemic HFrEF; treat gout if present, not the heart failure.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — allopurinol lowered uric acid but did not improve clinical status, quality of life, exercise capacity or ejection fraction in hyperuricaemic HFrEF

title: Sildenafil and nitrates in HFpEF (RELAX, NEAT-HFpEF): no gain in exercise capacity — and patients on the nitrate actually did less each day
question: In heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, do sildenafil or long-acting isosorbide mononitrate improve exercise capacity and daily activity compared with placebo?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — two well-run trials from the same network tested the two classic vasodilator ideas in HFpEF, and both failed. RELAX (216 outpatients, ejection fraction ≥50%) gave sildenafil for 24 weeks: peak oxygen consumption changed identically in both arms (median −0.20 ml/kg/min each, p=0.90), the clinical-status rank score was no different (94.2 versus 95.8, p=0.85), 6-minute walk distance was no different, and serious adverse events were numerically more frequent on sildenafil (22% versus 16%). NEAT-HFpEF (110 patients, crossover) gave isosorbide mononitrate up to 120 mg daily and patients were, if anything, less active on the drug: daily accelerometer units trended lower (−381, p=0.06) at the top dose and were significantly lower across all doses (−439, p=0.02), with fewer hours of activity per day (−0.30, p=0.02) and no gain in walk distance, quality of life or NT-proBNP. An earlier meta-analysis had found sildenafil improved peak VO2 in reduced-ejection-fraction heart failure but not in HFpEF — consistent with RELAX. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): neither sildenafil nor long-acting nitrate improves exercise capacity or daily activity in HFpEF, and nitrates may reduce activity; 'weak' reflects the modest trial sizes, not any positive signal.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — neither sildenafil nor long-acting isosorbide mononitrate improved exercise capacity or daily activity in HFpEF in direct randomised trials

title: Patisiran for cardiac amyloidosis (APOLLO-B): patients walked 15 metres further and felt slightly better at a year — the death and hospitalisation composites did not move
question: In patients with transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy, does patisiran, compared with placebo, slow decline in functional capacity and quality of life?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — APOLLO-B randomised 360 patients with hereditary (variant) or wild-type transthyretin cardiac amyloidosis to patisiran 0.3 mg/kg or placebo every 3 weeks for 12 months. The primary endpoint was met, modestly: the decline in 6-minute walk distance was smaller on patisiran (median difference 14.69 m, 95% CI 0.69 to 28.69, p=0.02), and quality of life moved in opposite directions in the two arms (KCCQ-OS least-squares mean difference 3.7 points, 95% CI 0.2 to 7.2, p=0.04). The harder composites did not follow: significant benefit was not observed for the composite of death, cardiovascular events and walk-distance change, and the record reports no significant result for the death/hospitalisation composite either. Infusion-related reactions, arthralgia and muscle spasms were more common on patisiran. A 2020 systematic review, written before APOLLO-B, could only call patisiran 'promising' from a polyneuropathy-trial subgroup — APOLLO-B is the first direct cardiomyopathy test, and it shows preserved function, not saved lives. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): patisiran slows functional and quality-of-life decline over 12 months in ATTR cardiac amyloidosis; an effect on death or hospitalisation is not established.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — patisiran slowed decline in walk distance and quality of life over 12 months in transthyretin cardiac amyloidosis; death and hospitalisation effects are not established

title: Bromocriptine for peripartum cardiomyopathy: hearts recovered impressively — in a trial where every woman received the drug, so its share of the credit is unknowable
question: In women with peripartum cardiomyopathy, does adding bromocriptine to standard heart-failure therapy improve recovery of left ventricular function?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the biology is coherent (a cleaved prolactin fragment is thought to drive peripartum cardiomyopathy, and bromocriptine blocks prolactin release), and recovery rates in the one randomised study look high — but that study had no placebo arm. Hilfiker-Kleiner 2017 randomised 63 women with peripartum cardiomyopathy and ejection fraction ≤35% to 1 week versus 8 weeks of bromocriptine, both on top of standard heart-failure therapy: ejection fraction rose from 28% to 49% (+21 points) and from 27% to 51% (+24 points) respectively (p=0.381 for the difference), full recovery (ejection fraction ≥50%) occurred in 52% versus 68%, heart-failure hospitalisations were 9.7% versus 6.5%, and no patient died, needed a transplant or an assist device. Without an untreated comparator, how much of that recovery is bromocriptine and how much is the well-known spontaneous recovery of peripartum cardiomyopathy cannot be separated from this trial. A 2023 meta-analysis (10 studies, only 3 randomised) found higher follow-up ejection fraction with bromocriptine (pooled mean differences 12.56 and 14.25 points in cohort and trial analyses) and higher odds of left ventricular recovery (OR 3.55), but no difference in all-cause mortality. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): bromocriptine may aid recovery of ventricular function in peripartum cardiomyopathy; the randomised record cannot prove it, because everyone in the trial received it.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — bromocriptine was associated with high ventricular recovery rates in peripartum cardiomyopathy, but the randomised trial had no untreated arm and mortality was unchanged in pooled data

title: Immune therapy for myocarditis splits by phenotype: TIMIC's virus-negative chronic patients improved on steroids — unselected myocarditis (Mason) and immune globulin (IMAC) did not
question: In biopsy-proven virus-negative inflammatory cardiomyopathy or lymphocytic myocarditis, does immunosuppressive therapy (prednisone with azathioprine or ciclosporin) or intravenous immune globulin improve left ventricular function and survival compared with conventional therapy alone?
balance: SPLIT — the answer splits cleanly by which myocarditis. In chronic, biopsy-proven, virus-negative inflammatory cardiomyopathy unresponsive to conventional therapy, TIMIC (85 patients, double-blind) found prednisone plus azathioprine improved ejection fraction and shrank ventricular dimensions and volumes over 6 months, while no placebo patient improved and placebo ejection fraction significantly worsened; 12% of treated patients did not respond, and no major adverse reactions were registered. In unselected biopsy-proven myocarditis, the Myocarditis Treatment Trial (111 patients) found no difference: ejection fraction rose 0.10 with immunosuppression versus 0.07 with conventional therapy alone, survival did not differ (p=0.96), and mortality was 20% at 1 year and 56% at 4.3 years in the whole cohort. And intravenous immune globulin in recent-onset dilated cardiomyopathy or myocarditis (IMAC, 62 patients) was a flat null — ejection fraction rose 0.14–0.16 in both arms alike. A 30-year meta-analysis (Cheng 2021) lands in the same place: a non-significant mortality trend in prospective studies (12.5% versus 18.2%; OR 0.7, 95% CI 0.3 to 1.64), a significant survival association only in retrospective studies (HR 0.82), and a conclusion that tailored immunosuppression may be considered depending on disease phase and type. PROPOSED SPLIT: immunosuppression helps the selected virus-negative chronic inflammatory phenotype (TIMIC); it does not help unselected myocarditis, and immune globulin does not help recent-onset disease.
stamp: SPLIT — immunosuppression improved ventricular function in virus-negative chronic inflammatory cardiomyopathy (TIMIC) but not in unselected myocarditis (Mason), and immune globulin did not help recent-onset disease (IMAC)

title: Drugs after Takotsubo syndrome: the biggest registry links ACE inhibitors and statins to lower mortality — and finds nothing for the beta-blockers everyone prescribes
question: In patients with Takotsubo syndrome, are beta-blockers, ACE inhibitors/ARBs or statins associated with lower long-term mortality?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — there is no randomised trial of any drug in Takotsubo syndrome; everything known comes from registries, and this shelf's anchor is the SWEDEHEART analysis of 1,724 Takotsubo patients (mean age 66, 77% women) identified among 228,263 angiography patients from 2009–2016. Mortality was 2.5% at 30 days and 16.6% at 6 years. In adjusted registry analyses, ACE inhibitors (HR 0.60, p=0.025) and statins (HR 0.62, p=0.040) were associated with lower long-term mortality, and heparins with lower 30-day mortality (HR 0.63, p=0.01), while beta-blockers — the drug most reflexively prescribed — showed no statistical correlation with mortality, nor did ARBs, oral anticoagulants, aspirin or P2Y12 inhibitors. Intravenous inotropes (HR 9.92) and diuretics (HR 3.22) were associated with higher 30-day mortality, which almost certainly marks sicker patients rather than drug harm. Every one of these associations is vulnerable to confounding by indication: clinicians give ACE inhibitors and statins to patients they expect to live. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): ACE inhibitors and statins are associated with lower long-term mortality after Takotsubo; beta-blockers, despite their intuitive appeal, have no mortality association in the largest registry — all of it observational and none of it a basis for certainty.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — in registry data ACE inhibitors and statins were associated with lower long-term mortality after Takotsubo syndrome and beta-blockers were not; no randomised evidence exists

title: Vigorous exercise in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (LIVE-HCM): 1,660 patients, event rates identical between vigorous exercisers and the rest — the blanket ban loses its evidence
question: In adolescents and adults with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, is vigorous exercise associated with a higher risk of death or ventricular arrhythmia than moderate or no exercise?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — for decades, vigorous exercise was simply forbidden in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy on the theory that exertion triggers lethal arrhythmia. LIVE-HCM is the first large prospective test of that assumption: 1,660 participants aged 8–60 with HCM (or genotype-positive/phenotype-negative) at 42 high-volume centres, classified by self-reported activity as sedentary (15%), moderate (43%) or vigorous (42%, of whom 37% competed). Over the study period, 77 participants (4.6%) reached the composite of death, resuscitated cardiac arrest, arrhythmic syncope or appropriate ICD shock — 4.7% of the vigorous group versus 4.6% of the non-vigorous group, event rates 15.9 versus 15.3 per 1,000 person-years, adjusted hazard ratio 1.01, with the upper one-sided 95% confidence bound (1.48) just inside the prespecified noninferiority boundary of 1.5. That is reassurance with edges: it is observational (people who choose vigorous exercise differ from those who do not), participants were cared for at expert centres, and the confidence bound cannot exclude a moderate increase in risk. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): in expert-centre HCM populations, vigorous exercise was not associated with higher rates of death or life-threatening arrhythmia than moderate exercise or sedentary life — enough to inform a shared decision, not enough to declare exertion proven safe for every patient.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — vigorous exercise was not associated with higher rates of death or ventricular arrhythmia than moderate or no exercise in a large prospective HCM cohort

title: Myectomy versus alcohol septal ablation: identical long-term survival in 8,453 patients — ablation trades a safer procedure day for a one-in-nine chance of needing it done again
question: In symptomatic obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, how do septal myectomy and alcohol septal ablation compare on long-term mortality and reintervention?
balance: SPLIT — there is no randomised comparison of septal myectomy and alcohol septal ablation for obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy; the evidence is a meta-analysis of 45 observational cohorts (Osman 2019: 22 ablation cohorts, 4,213 patients, mean follow-up 6.6 years; 23 myectomy cohorts, 4,240 patients, 6.8 years), and it splits by time horizon. Around the procedure, myectomy cost more: periprocedural mortality 2% versus 1.2% (p=0.009) and stroke 1.5% versus 0.8% (p=0.013), while ablation cost more pacemakers (10% versus 5%, p<0.001). Over the long term the survival lines converge — all-cause mortality 1.1% versus 1.5% per person-year (p=0.21), cardiovascular mortality 0.5% versus 0.4% (p=0.53), sudden death 0.3% in both (p=0.43) — but ablation patients needed repeat septal-reduction procedures far more often (11% versus 1.5%, p<0.001). PROPOSED SPLIT: long-term mortality is indistinguishable between the two procedures in observational data; the choice trades myectomy's higher upfront risk against ablation's higher pacemaker and reintervention rates — a trade shaped by age, anatomy and centre expertise, none of which a cohort meta-analysis can randomise away.
stamp: SPLIT — long-term mortality did not differ between alcohol septal ablation and myectomy, but ablation brought more pacemakers and reintervention while myectomy brought more periprocedural death and stroke

title: Lenient versus strict rate control in permanent AF (RACE II): a resting rate under 110 did everything under 80 did — with a tenth of the clinic visits
question: In patients with permanent atrial fibrillation, does lenient rate control (resting heart rate <110/min) match strict rate control on death, hospitalisation and symptoms?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — strict rate control in permanent atrial fibrillation was guideline doctrine without outcome evidence behind it; RACE II tested it head-to-head. In 614 patients with permanent AF, a lenient target (resting heart rate <110/min) was compared with a strict target (resting <80/min and <110/min during moderate exercise) over 2–3 years. The primary composite — cardiovascular death, heart-failure hospitalisation, stroke, systemic embolism, bleeding and life-threatening arrhythmic events — occurred in an estimated 12.9% with lenient control versus 14.9% with strict control (absolute difference −2.0 percentage points, 90% CI −7.6 to 3.5), meeting the prespecified noninferiority criterion (p<0.001 for noninferiority), with similar frequencies for every component. Lenient control was also far easier to live with: 97.7% of lenient patients met their target versus 67.0% of strict patients, with a median of 0 versus 2 extra visits (75 versus 684 total visits), and symptoms and adverse events were similar. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): lenient rate control matches strict control on outcomes in permanent AF while demanding fewer drugs, fewer visits and less titration — the benefit is equivalence with less burden, from a single moderately sized trial.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — lenient rate control (resting <110/min) was noninferior to strict control in permanent atrial fibrillation and far easier to achieve

title: Ablation in end-stage heart failure with AF: one small trial stopped early found death, LVAD or urgent transplant in 8% versus 30% — a huge signal that still needs a second trial
question: In patients with atrial fibrillation and end-stage heart failure eligible for transplantation or assist devices, does catheter ablation, compared with medical therapy, reduce death or urgent transplantation/LVAD?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in a single-centre, open-label German trial of 194 patients with symptomatic atrial fibrillation and end-stage heart failure referred for transplant evaluation, catheter ablation plus guideline-directed medical therapy produced a strikingly lower rate of the composite of death, left ventricular assist device implantation, or urgent transplantation than medical therapy alone (8% versus 30%; HR 0.24 relative, 95% CI 0.11 to 0.52), and death alone was lower too (6% versus 20%; HR 0.29 relative, 95% CI 0.12 to 0.72). The cautions are structural, not numerical: the trial was stopped early for efficacy after only 97 patients per arm, which tends to inflate effect sizes; it was unblinded; ablation was actually performed in only 84% of the ablation arm while 16% of the control arm crossed over to ablation; and procedure-related complications occurred in 3 ablation patients versus 1 control patient. An effect this large from one small stopped-early trial is a strong signal that needs a confirmatory multicentre trial before it can be called established. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): ablation probably helps this very specific end-stage population, but the size of the benefit is almost certainly overstated by the design that found it.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one small stopped-early trial found a large reduction in death, LVAD or urgent transplantation

title: Treating the causes underneath persistent AF: RACE 3's bundled upstream therapy kept 75% in sinus rhythm at a year versus 63% — one trial, a borderline P value, and no way to credit a single component
question: In patients with persistent atrial fibrillation, does targeted treatment of underlying risk factors and upstream therapy, added to rhythm control, improve sinus-rhythm maintenance compared with conventional management?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — RACE 3 randomised 245 patients with early persistent atrial fibrillation and mild-to-moderate heart failure to a bundled targeted-therapy programme (mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist, statin, ACE inhibitor/ARB optimisation, and cardiac rehabilitation with exercise, dietary counselling) on top of rhythm control, or to conventional management. At 1 year, sinus rhythm on 7-day Holter was present in 75% of the targeted group versus 63% of controls (odds ratio 1.765, lower limit of the 95% CI 1.021; P=0.042) — a real but borderline result, 12 percentage points absolute, from a single trial whose intervention was a bundle: the contrast was driven mainly by MRA use (85% versus 4%) and statin use (93% versus 48%), since ACE inhibitor/ARB use did not differ, so no single component can be credited. The endpoint is rhythm on a monitor at one year, not stroke, hospitalisation, or death. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): treating underlying conditions alongside rhythm control probably helps maintain sinus rhythm, but one 245-patient trial with a P value of 0.042 cannot say which part of the bundle does the work.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one trial found targeted risk-factor therapy improved 1-year sinus-rhythm maintenance (75% vs 63%)

title: Procainamide versus amiodarone for stable wide-complex tachycardia: the one randomised trial favours procainamide on safety (9% vs 41% major events) and speed (67% vs 38% terminated)
question: In patients with tolerated sustained monomorphic wide-QRS tachycardia, does intravenous procainamide terminate the arrhythmia more safely than intravenous amiodarone?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — PROCAMIO is the only randomised head-to-head trial of intravenous procainamide versus intravenous amiodarone for tolerated wide-QRS tachycardia, and it favoured procainamide on both of its main measures: major predefined cardiac adverse events within 40 minutes occurred in 9% of procainamide patients versus 41% of amiodarone patients (odds ratio 0.1; 95% CI 0.03 to 0.6; P=0.006), and the tachycardia terminated within 40 minutes in 67% versus 38% (OR 3.3; 95% CI 1.2 to 9.3; P=0.026). Over the following 24 hours adverse events were 18% versus 31% (OR 0.49; 95% CI 0.15 to 1.61; P=0.24), not significantly different. The restraint is size and design: 74 patients were enrolled, only 62 could be analysed, the trial was open-label, and the population was the selected minority whose tachycardia is haemodynamically tolerated. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): for the stable patient in front of you, procainamide looks both safer and faster than amiodarone — on the strength of one small open-label trial.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — procainamide terminated more episodes with fewer major cardiac adverse events than amiodarone in one small trial

title: Pill-in-the-pocket for paroxysmal AF: 94% of episodes ended at home in patients pre-tested in hospital — effective for the selected, never randomised
question: In patients with infrequent, well-tolerated paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, does self-administered "pill-in-the-pocket" flecainide or propafenone safely terminate episodes and reduce emergency visits?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the evidence for pill-in-the-pocket is a single prospective cohort, not a randomised trial. Alboni and colleagues first proved the approach in hospital in 268 patients with recent-onset, haemodynamically tolerated AF and mild or no heart disease, then sent the 210 patients (79% of those screened in) in whom it had worked and caused no problems home to self-treat: over a mean 15 months, 165 patients had 618 episodes, treatment succeeded in 94% of treated episodes, symptoms resolved in a mean 113 minutes, adverse effects occurred in 7% of patients (including one case of atrial flutter with rapid ventricular rate), and monthly emergency visits and hospitalisations fell significantly compared with the prior year (P<0.001 for both). The 2010 Health Technology Assessment systematic review found the strategy slightly less effective than continuous antiarrhythmic therapy or in-hospital treatment but also less costly, with the balance turning on age. The catch is in the funnel: 22% of patients were excluded before self-treatment even began because in-hospital treatment failed or caused side effects — the 94% success rate belongs to a pre-selected group in whom the drug was already known to work. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): in carefully selected, pre-tested patients this is a workable, visit-sparing strategy; it has never been randomised against the alternatives.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in pre-selected patients, self-administered flecainide or propafenone terminated 94% of episodes with fewer emergency visits

title: Ivabradine for hyperadrenergic POTS: heart rate down and quality of life up in a 22-patient crossover trial — promising, tiny, and one month long
question: In patients with hyperadrenergic postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome, does ivabradine, compared with placebo, reduce heart rate and improve quality of life?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one small randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial is the whole randomised record: 22 patients with hyperadrenergic postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (plasma norepinephrine >600 pg/ml with an abnormal tilt test; mean age 33.9 years, 95.5% women) each spent a month on ivabradine and a month on placebo. Heart rate was significantly lower on ivabradine (P<0.001), and patients reported significant improvements in quality of life on the RAND 36-Item Health Survey for physical functioning (P=0.008) and social functioning (P=0.021); standing norepinephrine showed a strong trend to reduction (P=0.056), and no significant side effects such as bradycardia or hypotension occurred. The 2023 systematic review of drug therapy in POTS found the same pattern across the whole field — midodrine, ivabradine, bisoprolol and others showed positive signals in studies of only 10–50 patients, most underpowered. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): ivabradine probably lowers heart rate and improves how these patients feel, but 22 patients treated for a month each cannot establish durability, and the result applies to the hyperadrenergic subtype that was enrolled, not to all POTS.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one 22-patient crossover trial found ivabradine reduced heart rate and improved quality of life in hyperadrenergic POTS

title: Which beta-blocker for long QT? The registries agree the class works and the drugs differ — nadolol covers LQT1 and LQT2, metoprolol reaches significance in neither
question: In patients with congenital long QT syndrome, do beta-blockers differ — in particular nadolol versus metoprolol, atenolol or propranolol — in preventing syncope, cardiac arrest and death?
balance: SPLIT — by genotype and by drug. All of this evidence is observational — there has never been a randomised trial of beta-blockers in long QT syndrome — but the registry data are large and consistent that beta-blockade as a class reduces first cardiac events. In the Rochester registry analysis of 1,530 patients, hazard ratios for a first cardiac event versus no beta-blocker were 0.71 for atenolol, 0.70 for metoprolol, 0.65 for propranolol and 0.51 for nadolol. The split appears by genotype: in LQT1 the four drugs looked similar, but in LQT2 nadolol was the only drug with a significant risk reduction (HR 0.40 relative, 95% CI 0.16 to 0.98). The 2017 meta-analysis of 10 studies and 9,727 patients agrees: nadolol significantly reduced risk in both LQT1 (HR 0.47 relative) and LQT2 (HR 0.27 relative), atenolol and propranolol reduced risk only in LQT1, and metoprolol showed no significant reduction in either genotype; in LQT3 the data were insufficient. A second split: among patients who had already had an event on a beta-blocker, propranolol was the least effective drug for preventing recurrence. PROPOSED SPLIT: beta-blockers work, but they are not interchangeable — nadolol has the broadest support across LQT1 and LQT2, and metoprolol the weakest.
stamp: SPLIT — beta-blockers reduce events as a class, but nadolol is the only drug with significant support in both LQT1 and LQT2; metoprolol in neither

title: Flecainide added to beta-blockade in CPVT: exercise arrhythmias nearly abolished in a 14-patient crossover trial — suppression proven, survival inferred
question: In patients with catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia, does adding flecainide to beta-blockade reduce exercise-induced ventricular arrhythmias?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the randomised evidence is a single small crossover trial: 14 patients with catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia and an implantable defibrillator (median age 16 years), all on maximally tolerated beta-blockade, received flecainide and placebo for 3 months each. The median exercise-test ventricular arrhythmia score (0 = no ectopy to 4 = nonsustained ventricular tachycardia) fell to 0 on flecainide versus 2.5 on placebo (P<0.01), with complete suppression of exercise-induced arrhythmia in 11 of 13 completers (85%), and no difference in overall or serious adverse events. The 2019 systematic review and meta-analysis (7 retrospective cohorts plus this 1 trial; 333 patients, 152 treated with flecainide) points the same way: combination flecainide plus beta-blocker beat beta-blocker alone for arrhythmic events (relative risk 0.29; 95% CI 0.13 to 0.69) and symptomatic events (RR 0.36 relative; 95% CI 0.20 to 0.62). What neither source can show is the outcome that matters most — no deaths were reported among flecainide-treated patients in the meta-analysis, but the samples are far too small and the follow-up too short to prove a survival effect; the proven endpoint is suppression of exercise-provoked arrhythmia, a close surrogate in this disease. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): adding flecainide to beta-blockade very likely suppresses CPVT arrhythmias; whether it saves lives is inferred, not shown.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — adding flecainide to beta-blockade suppressed exercise-induced arrhythmias in one small trial and pooled cohorts

title: Stent everything today or stage it? Immediate completion won both big trials' composites — and the pooled record flags more early cardiac deaths with doing it all at once
question: In patients with acute coronary syndrome and multivessel disease, does immediate complete revascularisation at the index procedure match staged complete revascularisation on death, myocardial infarction and unplanned revascularisation?
balance: SPLIT — the two large trials and the pooled record pull in different directions on different outcomes. In BIOVASC (1,525 patients with STEMI or non-ST acute coronary syndrome), immediate complete revascularisation was non-inferior to staged on the 1-year composite of death, myocardial infarction, unplanned ischaemia-driven revascularisation or cerebrovascular events (7.6% versus 9.4%; HR 0.78 relative, 95% CI 0.55 to 1.11), with fewer infarctions (1.9% versus 4.5%; HR 0.41 relative) but numerically more deaths (1.9% versus 1.2%; HR 1.56 relative, 95% CI 0.68 to 3.61). In MULTISTARS AMI (840 haemodynamically stable STEMI patients), immediate multivessel PCI clearly won its composite (8.5% versus 16.3%; risk ratio 0.52 relative, 95% CI 0.38 to 0.72), driven by fewer infarctions and revascularisations, with death, stroke and heart-failure hospitalisation similar. Against that, the updated meta-analysis of 9 trials and 4,213 STEMI patients found short-term all-cause mortality of 2.0% after immediate versus 1.2% after staged complete revascularisation (risk ratio 1.66 relative, 95% CI 0.99 to 2.78; P=0.053) and significantly increased short-term cardiac death (RR 2.19 relative, 95% CI 1.08 to 4.44), concluding that the pooled data currently favour staging for most patients. PROPOSED SPLIT: on composite endpoints immediate completion is at least as good and prevents early infarctions and repeat procedures; on the pooled early-mortality signal, staging looks safer — the honest answer depends on which outcome you weight.
stamp: SPLIT — composites and infarctions favour immediate completion, but pooled short-term cardiac death was higher with immediate than staged treatment

title: FFR-guided PCI versus bypass in three-vessel disease: FAME 3's answer was no — 10.6% versus 6.9% for death, MI, stroke or repeat revascularisation at one year
question: In patients with three-vessel coronary disease without left main involvement, does FFR-guided PCI match coronary artery bypass grafting on death, myocardial infarction or stroke at one year?
balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — FAME 3 asked the strongest version of the PCI question: in 1,500 patients with three-vessel disease (left main excluded), PCI guided by fractional flow reserve with current-generation stents was compared with CABG in a non-inferiority design, and it failed. The 1-year composite of death, myocardial infarction, stroke or repeat revascularisation occurred in 10.6% with PCI versus 6.9% with CABG (hazard ratio 1.5 relative; 95% CI 1.1 to 2.2; P=0.35 for non-inferiority, against a prespecified margin of 1.65 for the upper confidence bound) — that is 3.7 percentage points more events in absolute terms with PCI. The harder composite of death, infarction or stroke was 7.3% versus 5.2% (HR 1.4 relative; 95% CI 0.9 to 2.1). Surgery paid its usual upfront price: major bleeding, arrhythmia and acute kidney injury were all more frequent in the CABG group, and PCI patients received a mean of 3.7 stents. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm) — for PCI as the strategy: even with physiology guidance and modern stents, PCI did not match bypass surgery at one year in three-vessel disease; the harm framing applies to choosing PCI expecting equivalence, not to PCI where surgery is not an option.
stamp: POSSIBLE (harm) — FFR-guided PCI did not match CABG at 1 year in three-vessel disease (composite 10.6% vs 6.9%)

title: Cangrelor at PCI: fewer clots and stent thromboses in the first 48 hours (4.7% vs 5.9%), no more severe bleeding — and no mortality claim anywhere in the record
question: In patients undergoing PCI who are not pre-treated with oral P2Y12 inhibitors, does intravenous cangrelor, compared with clopidogrel, reduce periprocedural ischaemic events without excess severe bleeding?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in CHAMPION PHOENIX (11,145 patients undergoing urgent or elective PCI who had not been pre-treated), intravenous cangrelor reduced the 48-hour composite of death, myocardial infarction, ischaemia-driven revascularisation or stent thrombosis from 5.9% with clopidogrel loading to 4.7% (adjusted odds ratio 0.78 relative; 95% CI 0.66 to 0.93; P=0.005) — a 22% relative reduction, 1.2 percentage points absolute — and stent thrombosis from 1.4% to 0.8% (OR 0.62 relative; 95% CI 0.43 to 0.90). Severe bleeding at 48 hours was 0.16% versus 0.11% (OR 1.50 relative; 95% CI 0.53 to 4.22; P=0.44), not significantly different, though transient dyspnoea was more common with cangrelor (1.2% versus 0.3%). The prespecified patient-level pooled analysis of all three CHAMPION trials (24,910 patients, comparators clopidogrel or placebo) found the same shape: primary outcome 3.8% versus 4.7% (OR 0.81 relative; 95% CI 0.71 to 0.91), stent thrombosis 0.5% versus 0.8% (OR 0.59 relative), no difference in severe or life-threatening bleeding (0.2% in both groups), but more mild bleeding (16.8% versus 13.0%). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): cangrelor prevents early periprocedural ischaemic events, mostly periprocedural infarction and stent thrombosis, at the cost of more minor bleeding; neither record shows a mortality difference.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — cangrelor reduced 48-hour periprocedural ischaemic events and stent thrombosis without more severe bleeding

title: IV metoprolol before the artery opens: smaller infarcts in early anterior STEMI, nothing at all in the larger all-comer trial — a split verdict by phenotype
question: In patients with anterior STEMI undergoing primary PCI, does early intravenous metoprolol before reperfusion reduce infarct size and improve left ventricular function?
balance: SPLIT — by trial and by population. METOCARD-CNIC (270 patients with anterior STEMI, Killip class II or less, treated within 6 hours) found that intravenous metoprolol before reperfusion reduced infarct size on magnetic resonance imaging at 5–7 days (25.6±15.3 g versus 32.0±22.2 g; adjusted difference −6.52 g; 95% CI −11.39 to −1.78; P=0.012) and modestly raised ejection fraction (adjusted difference 2.67%; 95% CI 0.09 to 5.21; P=0.045), with no excess of the 24-hour composite of death, malignant arrhythmia, shock, heart block or reinfarction (7.1% versus 12.3%; P=0.21). EARLY-BAMI — larger (683 patients), double-blind and placebo-controlled, in an unselected STEMI population — found nothing: infarct size by magnetic resonance at 30 days was 15.3±11.0% of the left ventricle on metoprolol versus 14.9±11.5% on placebo (P=0.616), enzyme release and ejection fraction were the same, though malignant arrhythmias were fewer (3.6% versus 6.9%; P=0.050). The 2022 meta-analysis of 8 trials pools its way back to a positive average (infarcted myocardium lower by a mean 3.84 g at 6 months; ejection fraction higher by 3.57 points), but pooling cannot erase the fact that the one large blinded trial in a general STEMI population was neutral. PROPOSED SPLIT: a benefit is plausible in early-presenting anterior STEMI without heart failure — the METOCARD phenotype — and unproven for STEMI at large.
stamp: SPLIT — infarct size fell in early anterior STEMI (METOCARD-CNIC) but not in unselected STEMI in the larger blinded trial (EARLY-BAMI)

title: Remote ischaemic conditioning in STEMI: the cuff cycles were safe and the 5,401-patient answer was no — 9.4% versus 8.6% for cardiac death or heart-failure admission
question: In patients with acute myocardial infarction undergoing PCI, does remote ischaemic conditioning reduce cardiovascular death or heart-failure hospitalisation?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit not shown) — remote ischaemic conditioning is the cleanest negative on this shelf's run of shelves. In CONDI-2/ERIC-PPCI, 5,401 patients with suspected STEMI eligible for primary PCI were randomised to four cycles of arm-cuff inflation/deflation before PCI or standard treatment; in the intention-to-treat population (5,115 patients), cardiac death or hospitalisation for heart failure at 12 months occurred in 9.4% of the conditioning group versus 8.6% of controls (hazard ratio 1.10 relative; 95% CI 0.91 to 1.32; P=0.32) — the point estimate favours the control arm. No important unexpected adverse events were observed; the intervention is safe, it simply does not work on clinical outcomes. The updated meta-analysis (12 trials, 8,239 patients, 816 major adverse events) explains the history: earlier meta-analyses were positive, but once the three newest trials including CONDI-2 (5,712 patients) are added, the pooled effect on composite clinical endpoints is null (odds ratio 0.77 relative; 95% CI 0.59 to 1.01; P=0.105), and the pooled result only becomes significant if CONDI-2 itself is removed. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit not shown): a biologically elegant idea that reduced infarct size in small studies and then failed, definitively, at clinical-outcome scale.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit not shown) — remote ischaemic conditioning did not reduce cardiac death or heart-failure hospitalisation in a 5,401-patient trial

title: Anakinra after STEMI: the inflammatory surge was cut by two-thirds and new heart failure was rarer — in a 99-patient trial whose clinical endpoints were secondary
question: In patients with ST-elevation myocardial infarction, does interleukin-1 blockade with anakinra blunt the acute inflammatory response and prevent new heart failure?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — VCU-ART3 randomised just 99 patients with ST-elevation myocardial infarction to two weeks of anakinra once daily (33), anakinra twice daily (31) or placebo (35), and its primary endpoint was inflammatory, not clinical: the hsCRP area under the curve over 14 days was far lower on anakinra (median 67 versus 214 mg·day/L; P<0.001), with no difference between the two doses. The clinical signals are secondary and fragile at this size, but they point the right way: death or new-onset heart failure occurred in 9.4% on anakinra versus 25.7% on placebo (P=0.046), and death or heart-failure hospitalisation in 0% versus 11.4% (P=0.011), while left ventricular volumes and ejection fraction at 12 months did not differ (end-systolic volume change P=0.21; ejection fraction change P=0.61). The 2023 meta-analysis of NLRP3/IL-1/IL-6 pathway inhibition in STEMI (9 trials, 1,211 patients) supports the heart-failure signal for anakinra specifically (new-onset or worsening heart failure relative risk 0.32; 95% CI 0.13 to 0.77) alongside a clear CRP reduction, at the cost of more injection-site reactions — in VCU-ART3, 22% versus 3% (P=0.016), with serious infection no different (14% versus 14%). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the anti-inflammatory effect is certain and the heart-failure signal is consistent, but 99 patients cannot carry a clinical-outcome claim; a powered outcomes trial is still owed.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — anakinra blunted the post-STEMI inflammatory response and was associated with less new heart failure in small trials

title: Opening a chronic total occlusion: one trial found better angina scores, the other found no health-status gain at all — and neither found fewer deaths, infarctions or strokes
question: In patients with a chronic total coronary occlusion and angina or ischaemia, does PCI plus optimal medical therapy improve symptoms and quality of life compared with optimal medical therapy alone?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the two randomised trials point in different directions on the very outcome this question asks about. EuroCTO (Werner GS et al., PMID: 29722796; 396 patients) found PCI improved Seattle Angina Questionnaire angina-frequency scores by 5.23 points (95% CI 1.75 to 8.71) and quality of life by 6.62 points (1.78 to 11.46) at 12 months, with complete freedom from angina in 71.6% versus 57.8%. DECISION-CTO (Lee SW et al., PMID: 30813758; 834 randomised, median follow-up 4.0 years) found significant health-status improvement in both strategies with no between-group difference sustained through 36 months, and no difference in the composite of death, myocardial infarction, stroke or any revascularisation (22.3% versus 22.4%; HR 1.03, 95% CI 0.77 to 1.37). A meta-analysis of randomised and propensity-matched studies (Iannaccone M et al., PMID: 30549199; 3,971 patients) likewise found no difference in major adverse cardiac events, repeat PCI or infarction; its lower cardiovascular death signal (OR 0.52) was driven by the propensity-matched observational studies, not the trials. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): a symptom-driven, case-by-case decision after optimal medical therapy — not a prognostic intervention, and not a guaranteed symptomatic one.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — PCI of a chronic total occlusion may improve angina in selected patients, but the two randomised trials disagree on symptoms and neither showed a clinical-event benefit

title: DK crush for true left main bifurcation lesions: target-lesion failure halved at one year in one 482-patient trial (5.0% vs 10.7%) — a technique result from expert centres
question: In patients with complex left main distal bifurcation lesions, does a planned double-kissing crush two-stent strategy beat provisional stenting on target-lesion failure?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — DKCRUSH-V (Chen SL et al., PMID: 29096915) randomised 482 patients with true distal left main bifurcation lesions (Medina 1,1,1 or 0,1,1) at 26 centres and found one-year target-lesion failure in 5.0% with planned double-kissing (DK) crush versus 10.7% with provisional stenting (HR 0.42, 95% CI 0.21 to 0.85) — a relative reduction of about half, or 5.7 fewer events per 100 patients in absolute terms. The difference was carried by target-vessel myocardial infarction (0.4% versus 2.9%) and definite or probable stent thrombosis (0.4% versus 3.3%); cardiac death did not differ, and target-lesion revascularisation only tended to differ (3.8% versus 7.9%, P=0.06). A Bayesian meta-analysis of the three randomised trials of DK crush versus provisional stenting in bifurcation lesions (Kumar A et al., PMID: 38537883; 916 patients, not left-main-specific) is directionally consistent, with an absolute risk difference for target-lesion revascularisation centred at −0.05 (95% credible interval −0.08 to −0.03). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a real advantage for a planned two-stent strategy in this specific anatomy, resting substantially on one trial performed by operators expert in the technique.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a planned double-kissing crush strategy reduced one-year target-lesion failure compared with provisional stenting in true distal left main bifurcation lesions

title: Ultrasound for femoral access: first-pass success jumped (86.6% vs 70.0%) but bleeding and major vascular complications did not significantly fall in the 621-patient UNIVERSAL trial
question: In patients undergoing coronary procedures via femoral access, does routine ultrasound guidance reduce vascular access complications compared with fluoroscopic landmark guidance?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — UNIVERSAL (Jolly SS et al., PMID: 36116089) randomised 621 patients having coronary angiography or intervention with planned femoral access to ultrasound guidance or fluoroscopic landmarking alone. The primary composite of BARC 2, 3 or 5 bleeding or major vascular complications at 30 days occurred in 12.9% versus 16.1% (OR 0.77, 95% CI 0.49 to 1.20; P=0.25) — a point estimate favouring ultrasound that the trial could not distinguish from no effect; bleeding (10.0% versus 10.7%) and major vascular complications (6.4% versus 9.4%) were each likewise non-significant. What ultrasound clearly did was mechanical: first-pass success 86.6% versus 70.0%, fewer puncture attempts, and far fewer accidental venipunctures (3.1% versus 11.7%). An earlier meta-analysis of five smaller trials (Rashid MK et al., PMID: 31257213; 1,553 patients) found fewer vascular complications with ultrasound (1.9% versus 4.3%; OR 0.44), but the effect was driven by local haematomas and disappeared for other complications and for major bleeding. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) on the outcomes patients feel — major bleeding and vascular injury — with a genuine, separate gain in puncture efficiency.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — routine ultrasound guidance did not significantly reduce bleeding or major vascular complications, though it made puncture easier and avoided the vein

title: Ranolazine after incomplete revascularisation: the 2,651-patient RIVER-PCI trial found no reduction in ischaemia-driven revascularisation or hospitalisation (26% vs 28%)
question: In patients with angina and incomplete revascularisation after PCI, does ranolazine improve angina frequency and quality of life compared with placebo?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — RIVER-PCI (Weisz G et al., PMID: 26474810) is a large, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial: 2,651 patients with chronic angina and incomplete revascularisation after PCI were randomised to ranolazine 1000 mg twice daily or placebo, and over a median 643 days the composite of ischaemia-driven revascularisation or ischaemia-driven hospitalisation occurred in 26% versus 28% (HR 0.95, 95% CI 0.82 to 1.10; P=0.48), with neither component differing significantly. More patients stopped ranolazine for adverse events (14% versus 11%; P=0.04). That null needs one careful boundary: RIVER-PCI tested a prognostic endpoint in a post-PCI population. In the different population of symptomatic chronic stable coronary disease, a meta-analysis of six trials (Savarese G et al., PMID: 24063912; 9,223 patients) found ranolazine reduced weekly angina frequency and nitroglycerin consumption and prolonged exercise duration and time to ischaemia — symptom effects, with no substantial blood-pressure or heart-rate change. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): after incomplete revascularisation, ranolazine should not be prescribed expecting fewer procedures or admissions; any role is symptomatic, on evidence drawn from a different population.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — in the population and for the prognostic endpoint tested, ranolazine did not reduce ischaemia-driven revascularisation or hospitalisation after incomplete revascularisation

title: Enhanced external counterpulsation for refractory angina: one small sham-controlled trial, a longer time to exercise ischaemia, no clear gain in exercise duration — and more adverse events
question: In patients with refractory angina ineligible for revascularisation, does enhanced external counterpulsation improve exercise-induced ischaemia and angina compared with a sham procedure?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the entire sham-controlled randomised record in angina is MUST-EECP (Arora RR et al., PMID: 10362181): 139 outpatients with angina, documented coronary disease and a positive exercise test received 35 hours of active or inactive counterpulsation over four to seven weeks. Time to 1-mm ST-segment depression increased significantly with active treatment (P=0.01), and more active-treatment patients reported fewer angina episodes (P<0.05); but exercise duration — the outcome patients experience as stamina — increased in both groups with no significant between-group difference (P>0.3), and nitroglycerin use did not differ significantly between groups (P>0.7). The Health Technology Assessment systematic review (McKenna C et al., PMID: 19409154; five studies) put the ischaemia-time gain at a mean 41 seconds (95% CI 9.10 to 73.90), found no significant difference in exercise duration, self-reported angina episodes or daily nitroglycerin use, noted more withdrawals and adverse events with EECP (RR 2.13, 95% CI 1.35 to 3.38), and concluded the single trial does not provide firm evidence of clinical effectiveness. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): a non-invasive option with a plausible small physiological effect, unproven patient-important benefit, and a 35-hour time burden.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — enhanced external counterpulsation may extend time to exercise-induced ischaemia, but firm evidence of clinical benefit in refractory angina is lacking

title: Milrinone versus dobutamine in cardiogenic shock: the blinded DOREMI trial found no difference — composite 49% vs 54%, in-hospital death 37% vs 43%
question: In patients with cardiogenic shock, does milrinone differ from dobutamine on death or the composite of resuscitated arrest, transplantation/mechanical support, myocardial infarction, stroke or renal replacement?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — DOREMI (Mathew R et al., PMID: 34347952) is a double-blind randomised trial of 192 patients with cardiogenic shock, 96 per group. The primary composite — in-hospital death, resuscitated cardiac arrest, cardiac transplantation or mechanical circulatory support, nonfatal myocardial infarction, transient ischaemic attack or stroke, or initiation of renal replacement therapy — occurred in 49% on milrinone versus 54% on dobutamine (relative risk 0.90, 95% CI 0.69 to 1.19; P=0.47). In-hospital death, which this shelf reports separately as heart-failure and shock questions require, was 37% versus 43% (relative risk 0.85, 95% CI 0.60 to 1.21), and resuscitated arrest, mechanical support and renal replacement each likewise did not differ significantly. A meta-analysis dominated by observational data (Biswas S et al., PMID: 35545181) leans the other way — lower mortality with milrinone in acute heart failure overall (relative risk 0.87, 95% CI 0.79 to 0.97, event rates 9.4% versus 9.8%) — but in the cardiogenic-shock subgroup the difference was only a non-significant trend, and its bridge-to-transplant subgroup trended toward dobutamine. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): on randomised evidence the choice between these two inotropes in shock is not a survival decision; it is made on haemodynamics, rhythm, renal function and familiarity.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — in the one double-blind randomised trial, milrinone and dobutamine did not differ on death or the composite outcome in cardiogenic shock

title: Ticagrelor plus aspirin after bypass surgery: vein graft patency 88.7% vs 76.5% at one year in DACAB — a patency gain, with bleeding safety still thinly measured
question: In patients undergoing CABG, does ticagrelor plus aspirin improve saphenous vein graft patency at one year compared with aspirin alone, and at what bleeding cost?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — DACAB (Zhao Q et al., PMID: 29710164) randomised 500 patients having elective bypass surgery with saphenous vein grafting to ticagrelor plus aspirin, ticagrelor alone, or aspirin alone, started within 24 hours. One-year graft patency (FitzGibbon grade A) was 88.7% (432 of 487 grafts) with the combination versus 76.5% (371 of 485) with aspirin alone — an absolute difference of 12.2 percentage points (95% CI 5.2 to 19.2; P<0.001) — while ticagrelor alone (82.8%) did not differ significantly from aspirin alone (difference 6.3 points, 95% CI −1.1 to 13.7; P=0.10). The bleeding price in this trial was small in count and imprecise: five major bleeding episodes in a year (three on the combination, two on ticagrelor alone, none reported on aspirin alone). A network meta-analysis of ten post-CABG antiplatelet trials (Hasan SU et al., PMID: 39087882; 2,139 patients) is consistent, ranking aspirin plus ticagrelor lowest for saphenous vein graft occlusion (mean absolute risk 0.144) without a significantly higher major-bleeding signal. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the patency benefit is randomised and coherent, but patency is an imaging outcome, the trial was open-label, and neither source can yet show fewer infarctions or deaths — or exclude a real bleeding cost at scale.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — ticagrelor plus aspirin improved one-year saphenous vein graft patency compared with aspirin alone, with too few bleeding events to price the harm precisely

title: After TAVR, aspirin alone beat aspirin plus clopidogrel on bleeding (15.1% vs 26.6%) with no ischaemic penalty at one year — POPular TAVI cohort A
question: In patients without an indication for anticoagulation after successful TAVR, does aspirin alone, compared with aspirin plus clopidogrel, reduce bleeding without increasing ischaemic events?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — POPular TAVI cohort A (Brouwer J et al., PMID: 32865376) randomised 665 patients undergoing transcatheter aortic-valve implantation who had no indication for long-term anticoagulation to aspirin alone or aspirin plus clopidogrel for three months. At one year, all bleeding occurred in 15.1% on aspirin alone versus 26.6% on dual therapy (risk ratio 0.57, 95% CI 0.42 to 0.77; P=0.001) — about 12 fewer bleeding events per 100 patients — and non-procedure-related bleeding in 15.1% versus 24.9% (risk ratio 0.61). The composite of cardiovascular death, non-procedure-related bleeding, stroke or infarction favoured aspirin alone (23.0% versus 31.1%; risk ratio 0.74; P=0.04 for superiority), while the purely ischaemic composite was essentially identical (9.7% versus 9.9%; risk ratio 0.98), meeting non-inferiority. A meta-analysis of the randomised trials (Lin X et al., PMID: 33570686; four studies, 1,086 patients) agrees: by 6 to 12 months dual therapy increased bleeding (relative risk 1.67, 95% CI 1.24 to 2.24) with no difference in mortality, stroke or infarction. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): in patients without an anticoagulation indication, adding clopidogrel after TAVR buys bleeding and no measurable ischaemic protection.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — aspirin alone reduced bleeding compared with aspirin plus clopidogrel after TAVR, without increasing cardiovascular death, stroke or myocardial infarction

title: TAVR for moderate aortic stenosis in heart failure: TAVR UNLOAD missed its primary endpoint (win ratio 1.31, P=0.14) but improved quality of life at one year
question: In patients with systolic heart failure and moderate aortic stenosis, does TAVR, compared with medical therapy and surveillance, reduce death or heart-failure hospitalisation?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — TAVR UNLOAD (Van Mieghem NM et al., PMID: 39480381) randomised just 178 patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction on guideline-directed therapy and moderate aortic stenosis to transfemoral TAVR with a balloon-expandable valve or to clinical surveillance with valve replacement on progression to severe stenosis. Over a median 23 months the primary hierarchical endpoint — all-cause death, then disabling stroke, then disease-related hospitalisations and heart-failure equivalents, then change in Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire score — was not significantly better with TAVR (win ratio 1.31, 95% CI 0.91 to 1.88; P=0.14). The trial's structure blurs its own contrast: 38 of 89 surveillance patients (43%) underwent TAVR at a median of 12 months, 35 of them after progressing to severe stenosis, so the comparison became early versus deferred TAVR for nearly half the control group. The one clearly positive component was quality of life at one year (KCCQ improvement 12.8 versus 3.2 points; P=0.018), and the authors describe pre-emptive TAVR as safe. No systematic review of this intervention question exists in the record set searched, so the shelf rests on this single small trial. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): feeling better sooner is plausible; living longer or staying out of hospital is unproven, and surveillance with prompt treatment at severe stenosis remains a defensible strategy.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — pre-emptive TAVR for moderate aortic stenosis in HFrEF did not significantly improve the hierarchical composite of death, stroke, hospitalisation and quality of life, though quality of life alone improved

title: A dedicated transcatheter valve for pure aortic regurgitation: ALIGN-AR met its safety and one-year mortality performance goals — in a single-arm study of 180 high-risk patients
question: In patients at high surgical risk with severe symptomatic native aortic regurgitation, can dedicated transcatheter aortic valve implantation achieve acceptable one-year outcomes?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — ALIGN-AR (Vahl TP et al., PMID: 38552656) is a prospective single-arm study of the Trilogy transcatheter heart valve (JenaValve Technology, Irvine, CA, USA) — the specific tested product, named here because transcatheter valves for pure regurgitation are device-specific and not interchangeable — in 180 patients with symptomatic moderate-to-severe or severe native aortic regurgitation at high risk for surgical complications. Technical success was 95%. The 30-day composite safety endpoint occurred in 27% of patients, meeting non-inferiority against a prespecified performance goal of 40.5% (P<0.0001), and one-year all-cause mortality was 7.8%, meeting non-inferiority against a 25% goal (P<0.0001). The price on the face of the record: new pacemaker implantation in 24% of patients, with four deaths (2%) and four strokes (2% disabling, 2% non-disabling as counts of two each) by 30 days. A systematic review of transcatheter treatment for aortic regurgitation (Liu R et al., PMID: 38749505; 31 studies, 1,851 patients) found new-generation dedicated ('on-label') devices achieved 97.8% device success and 2.6% 30-day mortality, better than off-label devices on success, pacemaker, paravalvular leak and mortality. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): performance goals are a low bar set against historical surgical-era expectations, there is no concurrent control group, and durability beyond one year is unknown.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — a dedicated transcatheter valve achieved acceptable 30-day safety and one-year mortality against prespecified performance goals in high-risk aortic regurgitation, without a randomised comparison

title: Lower INR for the On-X mechanical aortic valve: major bleeding roughly halved (1.48% vs 3.26% per patient-year) with no significant rise in thromboembolism in PROACT's interim report
question: In patients with an On-X mechanical aortic valve, does reduced-intensity warfarin (lower INR target) plus aspirin match standard anticoagulation on thromboembolism and bleeding?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — PROACT (Puskas J et al., PMID: 24512654) randomised 375 patients three months after mechanical aortic valve replacement with the On-X bileaflet valve — the specific tested valve, named because the result is valve-specific — and higher-risk features for thromboembolism, to a test INR target of 1.5–2.0 or the standard 2.0–3.0, all on aspirin 81 mg daily with home INR monitoring. Over an average 3.82 years, major bleeding was significantly lower in the test group (1.48% versus 3.26% per patient-year; P=0.047), as was minor bleeding (1.32% versus 3.41%; P=0.021), while stroke, transient ischaemic attack, total neurological events and all-cause mortality were similar between groups. A systematic review of lower versus higher INR targets across left-sided mechanical valves (Pandey AK et al., PMID: 34622377; nine randomised trials) points the same way: thromboembolism 2.4% versus 2.3% (relative risk 1.14, 95% CI 0.82 to 1.60) and total bleeding 21.9% versus 40.9% (relative risk 0.46, 95% CI 0.28 to 0.78), though the reviewers downgraded the evidence for bias and imprecision. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the bleeding gain is consistent across both sources; the reassurance on thromboembolism is 'no significant increase in an interim, modest-sized trial', not proof of equality, and it belongs to this valve, this aspirin co-therapy and home-monitored patients.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — reduced-intensity warfarin for the On-X aortic valve lowered bleeding without a significant increase in thromboembolism, in one interim trial report supported by a broader meta-analysis

title: The Ross operation versus homograft root replacement: 10-year survival 97% vs 83% in the one randomised trial — a striking result from a single centre and 216 analysed patients
question: In adults needing aortic root replacement, does the Ross pulmonary autograft give better long-term survival and valve durability than a homograft root replacement?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the randomised evidence is one single-centre UK trial (El-Hamamsy I et al., PMID: 20684981): 228 adults under 69 needing aortic valve surgery were randomised to Ross pulmonary autograft or homograft aortic root replacement, with 108 per group analysed. At ten years, four autograft patients had died versus 15 homograft patients — actuarial survival 97% versus 83%, with a hazard ratio for death in the homograft group of 4.61 (95% CI 1.71 to 16.03; P=0.0060) — and autograft survival matched an age- and sex-matched British population (96%). Perioperative death was one versus three patients. A network meta-analysis of randomised and propensity-matched studies (Yokoyama Y et al., PMID: 36565200; 4,812 patients) extends the comparison beyond homografts: all-cause mortality was lower after Ross than after mechanical replacement (HR 0.58, 95% CI 0.35 to 0.97) or bioprosthetic replacement (HR 0.32, 95% CI 0.18 to 0.59), with less major bleeding and stroke than mechanical replacement — at the cost of more reintervention than mechanical valves, though less than bioprostheses. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the direction is consistent across both sources, but the head-to-head trial is small, single-centre and surgeon-specific, its comparator (homograft root) is now uncommon, and 19 deaths in total carry the survival claim.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the Ross autograft gave better 10-year survival than homograft root replacement in a single randomised trial, supported by a network meta-analysis against conventional valve replacement

title: Self-expanding transcatheter pulmonary valve (Harmony): 98% had acceptable valve function at a median 13 months in a 243-patient registry — but one in five needed treatment for ventricular arrhythmia
question: In children and young adults with right-ventricular outflow tract dysfunction after repaired congenital heart disease, does transcatheter pulmonary valve replacement with a self-expanding valve achieve durable valve function without surgery?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the evidence for the self-expanding Harmony transcatheter pulmonary valve (Medtronic) — the specific tested device, named because transcatheter pulmonary valves are device-specific — is a multicentre US registry (Goldstein BH et al., PMID: 38569760): 243 patients with native or surgically repaired right-ventricular outflow tract pulmonary regurgitation, median age 31 years, 71% with tetralogy of Fallot. Acute technical success was achieved in all but one case, hospital stay was one day in 86%, and at a median follow-up of 13 months 98% of patients had acceptable haemodynamic function, with estimated freedom from the composite of haemodynamic dysfunction or outflow-tract reintervention of 99% at one year and 96% at two years, and freedom from valve-related endocarditis of 98% at one year. The counterweights are on the same card: procedural serious adverse events in 4%, ventricular arrhythmia prompting treatment in 19%, and five deaths during follow-up (one COVID-19, two unknown causes, two bloodstream infection). A systematic review comparing transcatheter with surgical pulmonary valve replacement generally (Chongmelaxme B et al., PMID: 40392782; 28 studies, 16,150 patients, all observational) found lower mortality with the transcatheter route (OR 0.64, 95% CI 0.43 to 0.95 — a 36% relative reduction as reported, with absolute rates not given in the record) but three-fold higher odds of infective endocarditis (OR 3.10, 95% CI 2.22 to 4.33). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): short-term function is excellent in selected anatomy, but there is no randomised or controlled evidence for this device, and 'durable' beyond two years is exactly what a 13-month median follow-up cannot show.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — self-expanding transcatheter pulmonary valve replacement achieved excellent short-term valve function in a multicentre registry, with durability beyond two years and comparative benefit still unproven

title: A statin straight after a heart transplant: one small 1995 trial found less severe rejection, less graft vasculopathy and better one-year survival — and pooled data since point the same way
question: In heart transplant recipients, does pravastatin started soon after transplantation reduce rejection with haemodynamic compromise, cardiac allograft vasculopathy and death?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the randomised anchor is a single, small, unblinded 1995 trial of 97 patients, but its results were large and internally consistent: pravastatin started early after cardiac transplantation cut rejection with haemodynamic compromise (3 vs 14 patients), improved one-year survival (94% vs 78%), and reduced angiographic/autopsy vasculopathy (3 vs 10 patients), alongside the expected cholesterol fall (193 vs 248 mg/dL). A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis of 17 studies and 4,627 recipients (Mardani-Nafchi H et al., PMID: 38840403) points the same way for the outcomes that matter — lower odds of mortality (OR 0.49, 95% CI 0.32 to 0.75) and of cardiac allograft vasculopathy (OR 0.71, 0.53 to 0.96) among statin users — while its rejection result was null overall (OR 0.69, 0.41 to 1.15) and positive only in the randomised subgroup (OR 0.42, 0.21 to 0.82), and most of its weight is observational, with a possible publication-bias signal on Egger's test. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): early statin therapy after heart transplantation probably reduces vasculopathy and death, but the randomised base is one small pre-modern-immunosuppression trial, so the size of the effect in contemporary recipients is not pinned down.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Swapping the kidney-toxic immune drug out after a heart transplant: kidneys, graft vessels and CMV all did better on everolimus — rejection did worse
question: In de novo heart transplant recipients, does everolimus initiation with early calcineurin-inhibitor withdrawal preserve renal function without increasing treated rejection compared with standard calcineurin therapy?
balance: SPLIT — the trade is explicit in the one randomised trial. In SCHEDULE (Andreassen AK et al., PMID: 25041227), 115 de novo heart transplant recipients assigned to everolimus with ciclosporin withdrawal at 7–11 weeks had markedly better measured GFR at 12 months (79.8 vs 61.5 mL/min/1.73 m²), less progression of intimal thickening, a lower incidence of cardiac allograft vasculopathy (50.0% vs 64.6%), and far fewer cytomegalovirus infections (5.4% vs 30.5%) than standard ciclosporin — but biopsy-proven acute rejection after the withdrawal window was more frequent with everolimus. A network meta-analysis of 15 maintenance-immunosuppression studies (Ueyama H et al., PMID: 32424550) generalises the pattern without resolving it: no mortality difference between regimens, less vasculopathy with calcineurin inhibitor plus mTOR inhibitor, the lowest rejection rates in calcineurin-containing regimens, and better renal function and fewer CMV infections when the mTOR inhibitor replaced the calcineurin inhibitor. PROPOSED SPLIT: early calcineurin withdrawal on everolimus buys kidney function, vasculopathy and CMV advantages at the price of more treated rejection — a regimen choice to individualise, not a uniform upgrade.
stamp: SPLIT — renal and vasculopathy benefit, with more early rejection after calcineurin withdrawal

title: Hearts from donors after circulatory death: six-month survival matched brain-death donors in the randomised trial — pooled curves raise a question about years two to four
question: In patients awaiting heart transplantation, do hearts donated after circulatory death give non-inferior recipient survival compared with hearts donated after brain death?
balance: SPLIT — the answer depends on the time horizon. The one randomised trial (Schroder JN et al., PMID: 37285526) met its noninferiority endpoint clearly: risk-adjusted 6-month survival was 94% with hearts donated after circulatory death (DCD), reanimated and assessed on extracorporeal nonischemic perfusion, versus 90% with standard brain-death (DBD) hearts on cold storage — though the noninferiority margin was a generous 20 percentage points, follow-up was short, and graft-related serious adverse events at 30 days were similar. The pooled observational record is less settled: a 2025 meta-analysis reconstructing time-to-event data from six studies and 3,240 recipients (Al-Tawil M et al., PMID: 40121872) found no overall survival difference (HR 1.01, 95% CI 0.81 to 1.25), but the proportional-hazards assumption was violated, and landmark analyses suggested lower survival in DCD recipients from two years (HR 1.67) and four years (HR 2.78), on data that thin out beyond six years. PROPOSED SPLIT: early survival after DCD heart transplantation is non-inferior in randomised evidence; a possible late survival disadvantage in observational pooling is unresolved and is the number to watch.
stamp: SPLIT — early non-inferiority, possible late survival disadvantage

title: Balloon angioplasty versus riociguat for inoperable CTEPH: the balloon lowered lung-artery resistance far more — and caused serious adverse events in 42% versus 9%
question: In patients with inoperable chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension, does balloon pulmonary angioplasty improve haemodynamics and exercise capacity compared with riociguat?
balance: SPLIT — balloon pulmonary angioplasty (BPA) won the haemodynamic contest and lost the safety contest in the only head-to-head randomised trial. In RACE (Jaïs X et al., PMID: 35926542), 105 treatment-naive patients with inoperable chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH) randomised to BPA or riociguat had, at 26 weeks, a fall in pulmonary vascular resistance to 39.9% of baseline with BPA versus 66.7% with riociguat (ratio of geometric means 0.60, 95% CI 0.52 to 0.69) — but treatment-related serious adverse events in 42% versus 9%, driven by lung injury in 35% of the BPA group, with no treatment-related deaths. The trial's own follow-up softens the either/or framing: by week 52, after symptomatic patients crossed to add-on therapy, resistance reductions were similar (ratio 0.91, 0.79 to 1.04), and BPA after riociguat pretreatment caused fewer serious adverse events (14% vs 42%). A meta-analysis of BPA series (Guo Q et al., PMID: 37295014) confirms the direction of the haemodynamic and walking-distance gains without a randomised comparator. PROPOSED SPLIT: BPA lowers pulmonary vascular resistance more than riociguat at six months, at a substantially higher serious-adverse-event cost; the evidence points toward sequencing the two rather than choosing one.
stamp: SPLIT — greater haemodynamic improvement with BPA, more serious adverse events

title: A medium-dose statin plus ezetimibe matched a high-dose statin on three-year heart outcomes — with more patients at LDL goal and half the intolerance dropouts
question: In patients at high cardiovascular risk, does moderate-intensity statin plus ezetimibe match high-intensity statin monotherapy for cardiovascular outcomes, with fewer intolerance-related discontinuations?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the strategy question was tested head-on in one large open-label noninferiority trial. In RACING (Kim BK et al., PMID: 35863366), 3,780 patients with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease randomised to rosuvastatin 10 mg plus ezetimibe 10 mg or rosuvastatin 20 mg alone had near-identical three-year rates of the composite of cardiovascular death, major cardiovascular events, or non-fatal stroke (9.1% vs 9.9%; absolute difference −0.78%, 90% CI −2.39 to 0.83, inside the 2.0% noninferiority margin), while the combination put more patients below an LDL cholesterol of 70 mg/dL at every year checked (73% vs 55% at one year) and halved intolerance-related discontinuation or dose reduction (4.8% vs 8.2%). A 2025 meta-analysis of 20 randomised trials and 5,412 participants (Yasmin F et al., PMID: 40492183) supports the lipid half of the claim — greater LDL reduction with low/moderate-intensity statin plus ezetimibe (mean difference −6.59 mg/dL) — but found no significant difference in major adverse cardiovascular events, so the outcomes equivalence rests on RACING alone. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): combination therapy is a legitimate equal-outcomes, better-tolerated alternative to high-intensity statin monotherapy, proven in one Korean trial population rather than across many.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)
