title: Zodasiran silences ANGPTL3 and triglycerides fell by up to 63% in a 204-patient phase 2 trial — a lipid result only, with heart outcomes entirely untested
question: In adults with mixed hyperlipidaemia, does zodasiran (RNA interference against ANGPTL3) lower triglycerides and other atherogenic lipids compared with placebo?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — zodasiran, a small interfering RNA against ANGPTL3, does exactly what its mechanism promises to blood lipids, and nothing yet to clinical events. In the phase 2b ARCHES-2 trial (Rosenson RS et al., PMID: 38809174), 204 adults with mixed hyperlipidaemia had dose-dependent placebo-adjusted triglyceride falls of 51, 57, and 63 percentage points at 50, 100, and 200 mg at week 24, with parallel falls in non-HDL cholesterol (up to 36 percentage points), apolipoprotein B (up to 22), and LDL cholesterol (up to 20), and a transient rise in glycated haemoglobin at the highest dose in patients with pre-existing diabetes as the one flagged safety signal. A 2026 meta-analysis of target-specific RNA lipid therapies (Widjaja JS et al., PMID: 42863556; 16 trials, 5,604 participants) found adverse-event rates comparable with placebo across the class but states plainly that long-term clinical outcome data are lacking. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): a potent, durable lipid-lowering signal from a single 204-patient, 24-week surrogate-endpoint trial — whether silencing ANGPTL3 this way prevents cardiovascular events is untested.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — potent lipid lowering in one small phase 2 trial; no outcome data

title: A daily pill that inhibits PCSK9: enlicitide cut LDL by 58% versus placebo in familial hypercholesterolaemia — cholesterol proven, heart outcomes not yet
question: In adults with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia, does the oral PCSK9 inhibitor enlicitide lower LDL cholesterol compared with placebo on top of standard therapy?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — enlicitide is the first oral PCSK9 inhibitor to complete a phase 3 trial, and the LDL effect is large and durable over a year. In CORALreef HeFH (Ballantyne CM et al., PMID: 41206969), 303 adults with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia already on statins (81.5% high-intensity; 64.4% also on ezetimibe; mean baseline LDL 119.0 mg/dL) randomised to enlicitide 20 mg daily or placebo had a week-24 LDL change of −58.2% versus +2.6% (between-group difference −59.4 percentage points, 95% CI −65.6 to −53.2), sustained at week 52 (−55.3% vs +8.7%; difference −61.5 points), with parallel falls in non-HDL cholesterol, apolipoprotein B, and lipoprotein(a), and adverse-event, serious-adverse-event, and discontinuation rates similar to placebo. A 2026 dose-stratified meta-analysis of oral PCSK9 inhibitors (Marchetta M et al., PMID: 42765777; 4 trials, 949 participants, moderate GRADE certainty) confirms substantial atherogenic-lipoprotein reductions without a short-term safety signal — while stating that no cardiovascular outcome benefit or equivalence to injectable PCSK9 antibodies is established. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): proven, injectable-class-sized LDL lowering from a pill in HeFH; the outcomes trial that would make this LIKELY has not reported.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Blocking interleukin-6 in kidney patients: ziltivekimab lowered CRP by up to 92% in a 264-patient phase 2 trial — inflammation suppressed, events untested
question: In patients with chronic kidney disease, elevated interleukin-6 and high atherosclerotic risk, does ziltivekimab lower inflammatory biomarkers (hsCRP, fibrinogen, Lp(a)) compared with placebo?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — RESCUE (Ridker PM et al., PMID: 34015342) is a clean phase 2 biomarker trial and nothing more. In 264 patients with moderate-to-severe chronic kidney disease and high-sensitivity CRP of at least 2 mg/L, monthly subcutaneous ziltivekimab — a monoclonal antibody against the interleukin-6 ligand — reduced median hsCRP at 12 weeks by 77%, 88%, and 92% at 7.5, 15, and 30 mg versus 4% on placebo (pairwise differences −66.2, −77.7, and −87.8 percentage points, all p < 0.0001), with stable effects over 24 weeks and dose-dependent reductions in fibrinogen, serum amyloid A, haptoglobin, secretory phospholipase A2, and lipoprotein(a). It was well tolerated, with no serious injection-site reactions and no sustained grade 3 or 4 neutropenia or thrombocytopenia, and it did not affect the total-to-HDL cholesterol ratio. No cardiovascular event was an endpoint, no on-question systematic review pooling clinical outcomes exists yet, and the authors' own conclusion is that a large outcomes trial is the next step. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): profound, dose-ordered suppression of inflammatory biomarkers in exactly the high-risk CKD population of interest — with event prevention entirely unproven.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — profound biomarker suppression in one phase 2 trial; no outcome data

title: Asundexian versus apixaban in atrial fibrillation: the trial was stopped early — strokes nearly quadrupled (1.3% vs 0.4%) even though major bleeding fell (0.2% vs 0.7%)
question: In patients with atrial fibrillation at moderate-to-high stroke risk, does the factor XIa inhibitor asundexian, compared with apixaban, prevent stroke or systemic embolism without excess bleeding?
balance: LIKELY (harm) — this is a stopped-for-inferiority trial, and the numbers are not close. In OCEANIC-AF (Piccini JP et al., PMID: 39225267), 14,810 high-risk patients with atrial fibrillation randomised to asundexian 50 mg daily or standard-dose apixaban were followed until the independent data monitoring committee stopped the trial prematurely: stroke or systemic embolism occurred in 1.3% on asundexian versus 0.4% on apixaban (HR 3.79, 95% CI 2.46 to 5.83) — nearly four times the hazard, an absolute excess of about 0.9 percentage points over the truncated follow-up. The hoped-for safety advantage was real but smaller in absolute terms: major bleeding 0.2% versus 0.7% (HR 0.32, 0.18 to 0.55). A 2026 meta-analysis of factor XI/XIa inhibitors versus direct oral anticoagulants in atrial fibrillation (de Alcântara JPTL et al., PMID: 41734570) shows the same class pattern — major bleeding roughly a third (OR 0.30) but ischaemic stroke roughly tripled (OR 3.20, 1.85 to 5.55) — so this is not one trial's accident. PROPOSED LIKELY (harm): at the dose tested, asundexian traded away stroke prevention that apixaban demonstrably provides; less bleeding does not compensate for strokes not prevented.
stamp: LIKELY (harm)

title: Intensive statin, ACE inhibitor and aspirin for women with chest pain but open arteries: WARRIOR found no event reduction — 221 events versus 200 on usual care
question: In women with ischaemia and non-obstructive coronary arteries, does intensive medical therapy (high-intensity statin, ACE inhibitor/ARB and aspirin), compared with usual care, reduce angina burden and cardiovascular events?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — WARRIOR is the largest randomised trial of empiric intensive therapy in women with ischaemia and non-obstructive coronary arteries, and it found no benefit — but it also failed to recruit as planned and the population arrived already well treated. In WARRIOR (Pepine CJ et al., PMID: 41932694), 2,476 women (mean age 64) with suspected ischaemia referred for coronary angiography randomised to intensive medical therapy (high-intensity statin, ACE inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker, and aspirin) versus usual care had no difference in the primary composite of death, myocardial infarction, stroke or transient ischaemic attack, or hospitalisation for angina or heart failure at 2.5 years (221 vs 200 events; HR 1.13, 95% CI 0.94 to 1.37, p = 0.20), with hospitalisations for angina dominating the endpoint and no secondary outcome favouring intensive therapy. The authors note the trial was underpowered relative to plan, baseline blood pressure and LDL were already well controlled, and baseline use of statins and ACE inhibitors/ARBs was already high in usual care — a contamination problem a sensitivity analysis (estimated HR 0.74, 95% CI 0.352 to 1.558, p = 0.43) could not resolve. No on-question systematic review of intensive therapy for INOCA was found on a verified search. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): intensive empiric therapy did not reduce events in WARRIOR, and the trial's own limitations mean that is a negative trial, not proof of no effect.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — intensive therapy did not reduce events in the one trial, which was underpowered and contaminated

title: After a spontaneous coronary tear: beta-blockers were linked to far fewer recurrences, while two blood thinners fared worse than one — all from observational data
question: In patients with spontaneous coronary artery dissection managed conservatively, are beta-blockers and single versus dual antiplatelet therapy associated with lower recurrence and major adverse events?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — every number on this shelf is observational, and the two sources agree on one association and disagree in spirit on the other. In a prospective cohort of 327 patients with spontaneous coronary artery dissection (Saw J et al., PMID: 28838364), followed for a median 3.1 years, overall major adverse cardiac events occurred in 19.9% (death 1.2%, recurrent myocardial infarction 16.8%, recurrent SCAD 10.4%); in multivariable modelling only hypertension raised recurrence risk (HR 2.46) and beta-blocker use lowered it (HR 0.36, p = 0.004) — consistent with a 2022 meta-analysis of 14 studies and 4,206 patients (Chi G et al., PMID: 35866498), in which beta-blocker use was associated with a lower risk of recurrence (RR 0.51, 95% CI 0.33 to 0.77) while hypertension (RR 1.49) and fibromuscular dysplasia (RR 2.02) raised it. The antiplatelet question points the other way: in the DISCO registry's 199 conservatively managed patients (Cerrato E et al., PMID: 34338759), dual antiplatelet therapy had a higher 12-month MACE rate than single antiplatelet therapy (18.9% vs 6.0%; HR 2.62, 95% CI 1.22 to 5.61), driven by early non-fatal myocardial infarction or unplanned revascularisation, and DAPT was independently associated with MACE (OR 4.54) — but treatment was chosen by clinicians, so sicker or more complex dissections may have been given two drugs. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): beta-blockers look protective against recurrence in all observational sources; dual antiplatelets look worse, on data that cannot separate drug effect from confounding by indication.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — beta-blockers associated with less recurrence; DAPT signal against, all observational

title: Fish oil in chronic heart failure: one very large trial found a small survival edge — 27% vs 29% died over about four years — that a later pooled analysis did not confirm
question: In patients with chronic heart failure, does n-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid supplementation (1 g daily), compared with placebo, reduce death and hospital admission for cardiovascular reasons?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the GISSI-HF trial (Tavazzi L et al., PMID: 18757090) randomised 6,975 patients with chronic heart failure to n-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids 1 g daily or placebo and followed them for a median 3.9 years: death from any cause occurred in 27% on n-3 PUFA versus 29% on placebo (adjusted HR 0.91, 95.5% CI 0.833 to 0.998; p = 0.041) — a 9% relative reduction in the hazard of death, 2 percentage points in absolute terms, with 56 patients treated for 3.9 years to avoid one death — and death or admission for cardiovascular reasons occurred in 57% versus 59% (adjusted HR 0.92, 99% CI 0.849 to 0.999; p = 0.009). Gastrointestinal adverse effects were the commonest reaction and were equal (3% vs 3%). A 2024 meta-analysis of the randomised record (Dwiputra B et al., PMID: 38826182; 5 studies) found no significant association with cardiovascular mortality (OR 0.94, 95% CI 0.84 to 1.05) or heart-failure hospitalisation (OR 0.94, 0.88 to 1.02). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a real but small effect in one very large, well-run trial, with a confidence limit that only just excludes no effect and a pooled estimate that does not confirm it — and the trial predates modern heart-failure therapy, so the margin available on top of today's treatment is unknown.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one very large trial showed a small mortality advantage (27% vs 29%); a later pooled analysis did not confirm it

title: Distal radial access for coronary procedures: pooled trials show far fewer blocked radial arteries, but the largest trial — with meticulous conventional technique — found occlusion under 1% in both arms, with more crossovers from the distal site
question: In patients undergoing coronary angiography or intervention, does distal radial access, compared with conventional transradial access, reduce forearm radial artery occlusion without increasing crossover or access complications?
balance: SPLIT — the largest trial and the pooled record point in different directions on the primary question. In DISCO RADIAL (Aminian A et al., PMID: 35595673), 1,307 patients were randomised to distal or conventional radial access with systematic best practice to prevent occlusion: forearm radial artery occlusion at discharge was 0.31% with distal versus 0.91% with conventional access (P = 0.29) — no significant difference — while crossover was higher with distal access (7.4% vs 3.5%; P = 0.002), radial spasm was more frequent (5.4% vs 2.7%; P = 0.015), and haemostasis was shorter (median 153 vs 180 minutes; P < 0.001), with no difference in bleeding or vascular complications. An updated meta-analysis of 18 randomised trials and 8,205 patients (Mufarrih SH et al., PMID: 38432336) found occlusion risk much lower with distal access (RR 0.31, 95% CI 0.21 to 0.46) — a 69% relative reduction — and haemostasis about 51 minutes shorter, but crossover more than doubled (RR 2.39, 1.71 to 3.32), with longer access time, more pain and more multiple puncture attempts. PROPOSED SPLIT: distal access plausibly protects the forearm radial artery where conventional occlusion rates are not already driven below 1% by patent-haemostasis technique, and it shortens haemostasis — at the cost of a harder, more often abandoned puncture.
stamp: SPLIT — fewer radial artery occlusions in pooled trials and faster haemostasis, but more crossover and spasm; the largest trial found no occlusion difference

title: Epinephrine vs norepinephrine in shock after a heart attack: the same blood pressure and cardiac index, but refractory shock in 37% vs 7% stopped the only head-to-head trial early
question: In patients with cardiogenic shock after acute myocardial infarction, does epinephrine, compared with norepinephrine, improve haemodynamics without increasing refractory shock?
balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — for epinephrine. The only randomised head-to-head trial, OptimaCC (Levy B et al., PMID: 29976291), randomised 57 patients with cardiogenic shock after acute myocardial infarction to epinephrine or norepinephrine, double-blind: cardiac index evolution from baseline to 72 hours was similar between groups (p = 0.43), but refractory shock occurred in 37% of the epinephrine group (10 of 27) versus 7% of the norepinephrine group (2 of 30; p = 0.008), which led to early termination of the study; heart rate rose with epinephrine while remaining unchanged with norepinephrine (p < 0.0001), and cardiac double product and lactic acidosis were likewise unfavourable to epinephrine. The wider evidence base offers no counterweight: a systematic review and meta-analysis of 19 studies and 2,478 patients with infarction-related cardiogenic shock (Karami M et al., PMID: 32629772) found no routinely used vasopressor or inotrope associated with a mortality difference, on evidence graded low quality. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm): epinephrine buys no haemodynamic advantage over norepinephrine in this setting and carries a substantially higher risk of refractory shock, so norepinephrine is the safer default vasopressor after infarction — on the strength of one small trial stopped early, which is why the stamp is POSSIBLE, not LIKELY. Tier C is set because the direct evidence is that single small trial.
stamp: POSSIBLE (harm) — epinephrine matched norepinephrine haemodynamically but caused far more refractory shock (37% vs 7%) in the only direct trial

title: Testosterone in chronic heart failure: an early meta-analysis found better walking capacity, a later, larger one did not — and neither showed fewer deaths or hospital admissions
question: In patients with chronic heart failure, does testosterone supplementation, compared with placebo, improve exercise capacity, cardiac function, quality of life, or clinical outcomes?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — two meta-analyses of the same small trial record disagree. The earlier one (Toma M et al., PMID: 22511747; 4 trials, 198 patients) found testosterone therapy significantly improved exercise capacity versus placebo: 6-minute walk distance by 54.0 m (95% CI 43.0 to 65.0), incremental shuttle walk by 46.7 m (12.6 to 80.9) and peak oxygen consumption by 2.70 mL/kg per min, a pooled net effect of 0.52 SD (0.10 to 0.94), with no significant adverse cardiovascular events noted. The later, larger one (Tao J et al., PMID: 32231640; 8 randomised trials, 170 patients on testosterone and 162 controls) found no significant improvement in exercise capacity overall (standardised mean difference 0.36; p = 0.07), none in peak VO2, functional class or quality of life, no effect on ejection fraction or B-type natriuretic peptide, and no difference in the composite of death or heart-failure hospitalisation (RR 1.02; p = 0.96) — with benefit appearing only in the subgroup whose end-of-treatment testosterone reached at least 25 nmol/L (SMD 1.12; p = 0.02), and systolic blood pressure rising by 5.68 mmHg on treatment (p < 0.001). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): a few hundred patients in short, small trials, conflicting pooled answers on a surrogate outcome, and no evidence at all on the outcomes that matter.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — small trials conflict on exercise capacity and show no clinical-outcome benefit

title: Olanzapine with samidorphan: weight gain cut from 6.6% to 4.2% of body weight at 24 weeks — blunted, not abolished, with antipsychotic effect preserved
question: In adults with schizophrenia, does combining samidorphan with olanzapine reduce olanzapine-associated weight gain compared with olanzapine alone, without losing antipsychotic efficacy?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the weight effect is replicated across a phase 2 and a phase 3 trial and points the same way in both. In ENLIGHTEN-2 (Correll CU et al., PMID: 32791894), 561 adults with schizophrenia gained a least-squares mean of 4.21% of body weight on olanzapine/samidorphan versus 6.59% on olanzapine alone at 24 weeks (difference −2.38%); 17.8% versus 29.8% gained at least 10% of body weight (odds ratio 0.50). The phase 2 study (Martin WF et al., PMID: 30845818) found the same pattern at 12 weeks — 2.6% versus 4.1% mean gain — with PANSS improvement equivalent across groups, and ENLIGHTEN-2 likewise found similar symptom improvement between arms. But mitigation is not abolition: patients on the combination still gained weight, still reported weight gain as an adverse event in 24.8% of cases, and fasting metabolic measures changed little and similarly in both groups within 24 weeks. Whether sparing roughly 2.4 percentage points of weight gain prevents diabetes or cardiovascular events over years is untested. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a real, replicated reduction in olanzapine-associated weight gain with efficacy preserved — a partial answer to olanzapine's main liability, not a solution to it.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — olanzapine/samidorphan produces significantly less weight gain than olanzapine alone in two randomised trials, with antipsychotic efficacy preserved

title: Omaveloxolone in Friedreich ataxia: mFARS improved by 2.4 points against placebo at 48 weeks in the single registrational trial — a real signal on a rating scale, in a disease with no other drug
question: In people with Friedreich ataxia, does omaveloxolone slow neurological decline compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one registrational randomised trial, positive on its primary endpoint, in a progressive disease with no approved treatment at the time. In MOXIe part 2 (Lynch DR et al., PMID: 33068037), patients on omaveloxolone 150 mg daily improved by −1.55 points on the modified Friedreich's Ataxia Rating Scale over 48 weeks while placebo patients worsened by +0.85 — a between-group difference of −2.40 points (p=0.014). The delayed-start analysis of the open-label extension (Lynch DR et al., PMID: 36444905) found that difference preserved after the placebo group switched to drug (−2.91 points at 72 extension weeks), which is the pattern a disease-slowing drug should show and a purely symptomatic one should not — though extension analyses are not randomised comparisons. Harms were modest: reversible aminotransferase rises without bilirubin elevation, and more headache, nausea and fatigue. What 2.4 mFARS points mean in years of walking or independence is not established by these data. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the only randomised evidence in Friedreich ataxia favours omaveloxolone, on a rating-scale endpoint, from a single trial programme. Tier C is set because the evidence is one trial and its open-label extension.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single registrational trial showed a 2.4-point mFARS advantage over placebo at 48 weeks, with a delayed-start pattern suggesting persistence

title: Augmentation therapy in severe alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency: lung density fell more slowly at total lung capacity (p=0.03) but the combined primary endpoint missed (p=0.06) — one trial, a CT surrogate, and density never regained
question: In adults with severe alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency and emphysema, does weekly intravenous alpha-1 proteinase inhibitor (augmentation therapy) slow loss of lung density compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — biologically coherent, directionally consistent, and statistically fragile. In RAPID (Chapman KR et al., PMID: 26026936), the combined primary endpoint — annual lung-density loss at total lung capacity (TLC) and functional residual capacity (FRC) together — did not reach significance: −1.50 versus −2.12 g/L per year, difference 0.62 g/L per year (95% CI −0.02 to 1.26), p=0.06. The TLC measure alone did: difference 0.74 (0.06 to 1.42), p=0.03; FRC alone did not (p=0.18). The open-label extension (McElvaney NG et al., PMID: 27916480) showed the delayed-start group's loss rate falling from −2.26 to −1.26 g/L per year once they switched to active treatment, while the early-start group's benefit persisted to 48 months — and lost density was never recovered, which argues for early treatment if treatment is given at all. The endpoint throughout is CT lung density, a surrogate: no trial here shows fewer exacerbations, better breathlessness, or longer life. Treatment-emergent adverse events were similar between groups in RAPID. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): augmentation probably slows emphysema progression on imaging; what that buys a patient, and at what point in the disease, remains inference. Tier C is set because the randomised base is a single trial.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one randomised trial showed slower CT lung-density loss at TLC (p=0.03) while missing its combined primary endpoint (p=0.06); clinical outcomes untested

title: Sutimlimab in cold agglutinin disease: 73% met the composite response versus 15% on placebo in CADENZA — haemolysis halted within weeks, in 42 randomised patients
question: In adults with cold agglutinin disease, does sutimlimab reduce haemolysis and raise haemoglobin compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a large effect in a small randomised trial, backed by a single-arm study in a sicker population. In CADENZA (Röth A et al., PMID: 35687757), 42 patients without a transfusion in the prior six months met the composite endpoint — haemoglobin rise of at least 1.5 g/dL at assessment, no transfusion, no prohibited therapy — in 73% on sutimlimab versus 15% on placebo (odds ratio 15.9, 95% CI 2.9 to 88.0). In CARDINAL (Röth A et al., PMID: 33826820), 24 recently transfused patients on open-label sutimlimab gained a least-squares mean of 2.6 g/dL of haemoglobin, 54% met their composite endpoint, and 71% needed no transfusion from week 5 to 26. Bilirubin normalised within one to three weeks in both studies, tracking near-complete classical-pathway inhibition, and fatigue improved. The price in these short trials was mostly nuisance-grade — headache, hypertension, rhinitis, Raynaud phenomenon and acrocyanosis were commoner on drug — with three CADENZA discontinuations for adverse events and no meningococcal infections; the numbers are far too small to exclude rare complement-blockade harms, and neither trial ran beyond 26 weeks. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): sutimlimab clearly switches off haemolysis in cold agglutinin disease while it is given; durability, long-term safety and any effect beyond blood counts and fatigue are unproven. Tier C is set for the small, single-programme evidence base.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one small randomised trial (73% versus 15% composite response) plus a single-arm study show sutimlimab rapidly halts haemolysis in cold agglutinin disease

title: Crovalimab in untreated PNH: haemolysis control 79.3% versus 79.0% on eculizumab — non-inferior in the single phase 3 trial, with monthly self-administered injections as the practical gain
question: In adults with paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria not previously treated with a complement C5 inhibitor, is crovalimab non-inferior to eculizumab for haemolysis control and transfusion avoidance?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — non-inferiority to the standard C5 inhibitor, demonstrated once. In COMMODORE 2 (Röth A et al., PMID: 38884175), 204 C5-inhibitor-naive patients were randomised 2:1 to crovalimab or eculizumab for a 24-week primary period. Haemolysis control (LDH ≤1.5× the upper limit of normal) was achieved by 79.3% on crovalimab and 79.0% on eculizumab (odds ratio 1.0, 95% CI 0.6 to 1.8), and transfusion avoidance by 65.7% versus 68.1% (weighted difference −2.8 percentage points, 95% CI −15.7 to 11.1) — both meeting non-inferiority, neither suggesting superiority. Breakthrough haemolysis (10.4% versus 14.5%), haemoglobin stabilisation (63.4% versus 60.9%) and fatigue improvement were likewise similar, safety profiles were similar, and no meningococcal infections occurred. The genuine advantage is practical, and it is in the record: crovalimab is a low-volume subcutaneous self-administration every four weeks, and most patients who switched from eculizumab after the primary period preferred it. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): crovalimab matches eculizumab on the measured outcomes in a single open-label trial, with convenience — not efficacy — as the reason to choose it. Tier C is set for the single-trial base. Ravulizumab is compared with eculizumab at shelf #1804 and the proximal inhibitors at shelf #845.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — crovalimab was non-inferior to eculizumab on haemolysis control and transfusion avoidance in a single phase 3 trial, with monthly self-administration as its advantage

title: Routine nasogastric tubes after abdominal surgery: bowel function returned later and pulmonary complications were commoner with a routine tube across 33 trials — the Cochrane verdict was to abandon routine use
question: In adults having abdominal surgery, does routine nasogastric decompression until bowel function returns speed recovery compared with no tube or early tube removal?
balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — for the routine policy, not for the tube itself. Across 33 randomised trials and 5,240 patients (Nelson R et al., PMID: 17636780), patients managed without a routine nasogastric tube had an earlier return of bowel function (p<0.00001) and fewer pulmonary complications (p=0.01) than patients kept on routine decompression. Anastomotic leak did not differ (p=0.70); wound infection (p=0.22) and ventral hernia (p=0.09) trended against the no-tube group without reaching significance. The one outcome favouring routine tubes was vomiting — bought with increased patient discomfort — and length of stay was shorter without a tube, though heterogeneity makes that estimate soft. The reviewers' conclusion was unusually blunt: routine nasogastric decompression does not accomplish any of its intended goals and should be abandoned in favour of selective use. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm): keeping a tube in every abdominal-surgery patient until the bowel wakes up delays the recovery it is meant to speed and adds pulmonary risk; a tube placed for a specific indication is a different question, and this shelf does not answer it.
stamp: POSSIBLE (harm) — routine nasogastric decompression after abdominal surgery delays return of bowel function and increases pulmonary complications across 33 trials; selective use only

title: Decolonising nasal S. aureus carriers: hospital S. aureus infection 3.4% versus 7.7% with mupirocin–chlorhexidine after rapid screening — the benefit lives in carriers, not in everyone
question: In hospital patients who carry Staphylococcus aureus in the nose, does screening plus mupirocin–chlorhexidine decolonisation prevent hospital-acquired S. aureus infection, including surgical-site infection?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two randomised trials converge on the same point: the benefit is in confirmed carriers. In Bode (Bode LG et al., PMID: 20054045), carriers identified by rapid PCR screening and treated with mupirocin nasal ointment plus chlorhexidine soap had a hospital S. aureus infection rate of 3.4% (17/504) versus 7.7% (32/413) on placebo — a relative risk of 0.42 (95% CI 0.23 to 0.75), a 58% relative reduction with the absolute rates printed alongside — and the effect was strongest for deep surgical-site infections (relative risk 0.21, 0.07 to 0.62). In Perl (Perl TM et al., PMID: 12063371), intranasal mupirocin given to all-comers did not reduce S. aureus surgical-site infection overall (2.3% versus 2.4%), but among the 891 confirmed nasal carriers, nosocomial S. aureus infections fell from 7.7% to 4.0% (odds ratio 0.49, 0.25 to 0.92). Neither trial showed a mortality difference, and Bode's strains were all methicillin- and mupirocin-susceptible — a condition that cannot be assumed where resistance is common. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): screen-and-decolonise works for carriers; blanket mupirocin for unscreened surgical patients does not, on this record.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — decolonising confirmed nasal S. aureus carriers reduces hospital S. aureus infection (3.4% versus 7.7% in the screening-based trial); unscreened blanket treatment did not reduce surgical-site infection

title: Immunostimulants to prevent children's respiratory infections: about 1.1 fewer infections per child in pooled trials — a 39% relative reduction built on low-quality, heterogeneous evidence
question: In children prone to respiratory tract infections, do immunostimulants (including bacterial lysates such as OM-85) prevent acute respiratory infections compared with placebo?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the pooled effect looks substantial and the foundations look soft. The systematic review (Berber A et al., PMID: 36185547) gathered 72 placebo-controlled trials in 12,229 children; the 38 trials with usable data (4,643 children) showed a mean of 1.12 fewer acute respiratory infections per child (95% CI −1.39 to −0.85) and a ratio of means of 0.61 (0.54 to 0.69) — a 39% relative reduction, with the absolute difference of about one infection printed alongside. But the reviewers themselves graded the efficacy evidence low: heterogeneity was considerable to substantial, risk of bias was unclear in every domain in 32 of the 72 trials, only 14 trials reported adverse events at all, and publication bias is plausible. The best-known single product trial (Gutiérrez-Tarango MD et al., PMID: 11399700) randomised just 54 susceptible children and found large effects (about three fewer infections over 12 months) of a size that small trials produce more often than large ones confirm. The review's record carries no MeSH terms and no registered protocol number. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): immunostimulants may prevent roughly one respiratory infection per susceptible child per season — a claim the current trial base is too weak to carry with confidence, and safety reporting is thinner still.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — pooled trials suggest about 1.1 fewer respiratory infections per child, but the evidence is low quality, heterogeneous, and safety is barely reported

title: Endoscopic sleeve gastroplasty for class 1–2 obesity: 49% of excess weight lost versus 3% with lifestyle alone at one year in MERIT — one randomised trial, supported by observational series
question: In adults with class 1 or class 2 obesity, does endoscopic sleeve gastroplasty added to lifestyle modification produce more weight loss than lifestyle modification alone?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one well-run randomised trial with a large effect, surrounded by uncontrolled series. In MERIT (Abu Dayyeh BK et al., PMID: 35908555), 209 adults with class 1–2 obesity gained 49.2% excess weight loss at 52 weeks with endoscopic sleeve gastroplasty (ESG) plus lifestyle modification versus 3.2% with lifestyle alone (p<0.0001); total body weight loss was 13.6% versus 0.8%, and 77% of the ESG group versus 12% of controls reached at least 25% excess weight loss. Benefit persisted: 68% of followed ESG patients still held ≥25% excess weight loss at 104 weeks, and metabolic comorbidities improved in 80% of the ESG group versus 45% of controls. Serious ESG-related adverse events occurred in 2% (3 of 131 who underwent ESG, including crossovers), with no deaths and no need for intensive care or surgery. The supporting systematic review (Hedjoudje A et al., PMID: 31442601) pools only observational studies — 1,772 patients, total weight loss 15.1% at 6 months and 17.2% at 18–24 months, severe adverse events 2.2% — consistent with MERIT but incapable of confirming it. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): ESG produces substantial, two-year-durable weight loss against lifestyle care in the one randomised test; comparison with bariatric surgery and with modern obesity pharmacotherapy is not in this record. Tier C is set because the randomised base is a single trial.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single randomised trial showed 49.2% versus 3.2% excess weight loss at 52 weeks, maintained in most patients at 104 weeks, with 2% serious procedure-related adverse events

title: Lesinurad added to allopurinol: urate target reached by 54–66% versus 23–28% in two large trials — flares and tophi unmoved, kidneys paying at the higher dose, and the drug later discontinued
question: In adults with gout whose serum urate remains above target on allopurinol, does adding lesinurad increase the proportion reaching target urate — and does it reduce flares or tophi?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for the blood test, not yet for the disease. Two large phase 3 trials agree closely: adding lesinurad 200 mg to allopurinol put 54.2% (CLEAR 1, Saag KG et al., PMID: 27564409) and 55.4% (CLEAR 2, Bardin T et al., PMID: 27821644) of patients at the <6.0 mg/dL urate target at month 6, versus 27.9% and 23.3% on allopurinol alone (p<0.0001 in both). But in neither trial did the outcomes patients feel — gout flare rates in months 7–12, or complete resolution of tophi — differ significantly, so the proven benefit is a surrogate. The harm is renal and dose-related: creatinine elevations of at least 1.5× baseline occurred in 5.9% on 200 mg and 15.0% on the unmarketed 400 mg dose versus 3.4% on allopurinol alone in CLEAR 2, with serious treatment-emergent events at 9.5% on 400 mg versus 3.9% on allopurinol alone. Lesinurad was discontinued in the United States in February 2019 for business reasons, not for safety or efficacy findings — so this shelf now reads as the evidence record for a drug patients can no longer be started on there. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): lesinurad reliably delivers urate target on top of allopurinol at the 200 mg dose with a modest renal price; a flare or tophus benefit was never shown.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — adding lesinurad 200 mg to allopurinol roughly doubles urate-target achievement in two phase 3 trials, without demonstrated flare or tophus benefit and with dose-related renal adverse effects

title: Airway pressure release ventilation in ARDS: oxygenation rose by 56 mm Hg in the pooled trials, but survival, ventilator-free days and ventilation duration did not move
question: In adults with ARDS, does airway pressure release ventilation improve oxygenation and survival compared with conventional lung-protective ventilation?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — on survival, with better blood oxygen as the consolation. The 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Sajawal M et al., PMID: 42965657) pooled nine trials and 585 adults with or at risk for ARDS and found no mortality benefit for airway pressure release ventilation versus conventional ventilation (risk ratio 0.95, 95% CI 0.72 to 1.26), no clear difference in ventilator-free days (mean difference 3.83 days, 95% CI −1.69 to 9.34, I²=83%) or ventilation duration (mean difference −2.44 days, 95% CI −4.96 to 0.09), but a higher PaO2/FiO2 ratio (mean difference 56.21 mm Hg, 95% CI 24.63 to 87.79, I²=84%) and a shorter ICU stay (mean difference −2.53 days, 95% CI −4.43 to −0.64). The reviewers graded the certainty of evidence low to very low, with varied populations, protocols and outcome timing — so the oxygenation gain is a physiology signal, not a survival result, and the data establish neither superiority nor equivalence on mortality. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): APRV improves oxygenation numbers without demonstrated benefit on survival or ventilator-free days.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — APRV raised PaO2/FiO2 by a pooled 56 mm Hg but showed no mortality or ventilator-free-day benefit across nine randomised trials

title: Neurally adjusted ventilatory assist: pooled invasive-ventilation trials show lower ICU and hospital mortality — but the noninvasive trials show nothing, and an earlier synthesis found no mortality difference
question: In critically ill adults, does neurally adjusted ventilatory assist improve patient–ventilator synchrony, ventilation duration, and mortality compared with pressure-support ventilation?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in invasive ventilation only, and on one synthesis's reading. The 2026 meta-analysis (Wu RR et al., PMID: 43026034) pooled nine randomised trials and 842 patients and found that during invasive mechanical ventilation neurally adjusted ventilatory assist (NAVA) reduced ICU mortality (risk ratio 0.72, 95% CI 0.53 to 0.99) and hospital mortality (risk ratio 0.71, 95% CI 0.56 to 0.90) versus conventional modes — relative reductions of 28% and 29%, with the pooled absolute rates not printed in the abstract — and increased ventilation success (risk ratio 1.13, 95% CI 1.04 to 1.22) and 28-day ventilator-free days (mean difference 3.48 days, 95% CI 0.97 to 6.00). In noninvasive NAVA, no mortality or success benefit was shown. The earlier 2023 synthesis (Pinto CB et al., PMID: 36958129), five trials and 643 invasively ventilated patients, found more ventilator-free days (mean difference 3.42, 95% CI 1.21 to 5.62) and less weaning failure (odds ratio 0.51, 95% CI 0.29 to 0.88) but no significant ICU mortality difference (odds ratio 0.58, 95% CI 0.33 to 1.03) — so the mortality claim rests on the newer pooling and is not corroborated trial-by-trial. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): NAVA during invasive ventilation is associated with fewer deaths and more ventilator-free days in pooled small trials; the mortality signal needs a large confirmatory trial.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — invasive NAVA was associated with lower ICU and hospital mortality in a nine-trial meta-analysis, a signal an earlier synthesis did not confirm

title: Letting the ventilator run the weaning: automated systems shortened weaning time by 2.68 days in the 2014 Cochrane review, and the 62-trial update still finds less time on the ventilator — with no mortality difference
question: In mechanically ventilated adults, do automated weaning and spontaneous-breathing-trial systems shorten weaning time compared with clinician-led weaning?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for time, not for survival. The 2014 Cochrane review (Burns KEA et al., PMID: 25203308) pooled ten SmartCare trials and 654 participants and found automated weaning cut weaning time by a mean of 2.68 days (95% CI −3.99 to −1.37), shortened time to successful extubation by 0.99 days and ICU stay by 5.70 days, and reduced the proportions ventilated beyond seven days (risk ratio 0.44) and 21 days (risk ratio 0.39), with no effect on mortality or reintubation. The 2025 Cochrane update of the broader closed-loop literature (Rose L et al., PMID: 40678933) — 62 trials, 5,052 participants — found automated systems probably reduce ventilation duration (a 24% relative reduction, 95% CI 18% to 30%, with absolute durations varying by trial), ICU stay (14% relative reduction) and reintubation (risk ratio 0.73, 95% CI 0.59 to 0.89), again with little to no mortality difference (risk ratio 0.94, 95% CI 0.82 to 1.07). Two cautions ride on the face: the 2014 effect was largest against non-protocolised clinician weaning, so part of the gain may be protocolisation rather than automation; and the evidence certainty is low to moderate. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): automated weaning systems get patients off the ventilator sooner without a shown survival effect or a reintubation penalty.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — automated weaning and SBT systems shortened weaning time and ventilation duration in two Cochrane syntheses, with no mortality difference

title: Thirty minutes is enough: in 526 patients ready for weaning, a 30-minute breathing trial identified successful extubation as reliably as a 120-minute trial (75.9% vs 73.0% still extubated at 48 hours)
question: In patients ready for a spontaneous breathing trial, does a 30-minute trial identify successful extubation as reliably as a 120-minute trial?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the shorter trial reads the patient just as well. In the multicentre randomised comparison (Esteban A et al., PMID: 9927366), 526 ventilated patients considered ready for weaning were assigned target spontaneous-breathing-trial durations of 30 or 120 minutes: 87.8% versus 84.8% completed the trial without distress and were extubated (p=0.32), reintubation within 48 hours was 13.5% versus 13.4%, and the proportions still extubated at 48 hours were 75.9% versus 73.0% (p=0.43), with similar within-unit mortality (13% vs 9%) and in-hospital mortality (19% vs 18%). The 2025 SL-SBT trial (Hadda V et al., PMID: 39504619) asked the same question in the harder population — 119 patients who had already failed a first trial — and again found successful extubation in 58.3% on 30 minutes versus 59.3% on 120 minutes (p=0.91), with no differences in ICU or hospital stay or in in-hospital and 90-day mortality. Two randomised comparisons a quarter-century apart, in easy and difficult weaning alike, land in the same place. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): a 30-minute trial identifies successful extubation as reliably as a 120-minute trial, and the extra 90 minutes buy no information.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — 30-minute and 120-minute spontaneous breathing trials produced near-identical extubation success in two randomised trials

title: Wake up and breathe: pairing daily sedation interruption with breathing trials added 3.1 ventilator-free days and saved one life per seven treated in the ABC trial — the early cognitive gain had faded by 12 months
question: In mechanically ventilated adults, does pairing daily sedation interruption with spontaneous breathing trials increase ventilator-free days and improve long-term cognitive outcomes compared with usual care?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — on time off the ventilator and on survival in one trial; the cognitive half of the question is where the answer thins. In the Awakening and Breathing Controlled trial (Girard TD et al., PMID: 18191684), 336 ventilated patients randomised to a paired daily spontaneous awakening trial followed by a spontaneous breathing trial spent 14.7 versus 11.6 days breathing without assistance over 28 days (mean difference 3.1 days, 95% CI 0.7 to 5.6; p=0.02), left ICU earlier (median 9.1 vs 12.9 days) and hospital earlier (14.9 vs 19.2 days), and were less likely to die over the following year (hazard ratio 0.68, 95% CI 0.50 to 0.92; number needed to treat 7.4) — a mortality claim, which is why this shelf is Tier C. The harm on the face: more self-extubations in the intervention group (16 vs 6 patients; p=0.03), though reintubation after self-extubation and total reintubation rates (13.8% vs 12.5%) did not differ. The pre-planned long-term substudy (Jackson JC et al., PMID: 20299535) found cognitive impairment less common at 3 months (absolute risk reduction 20.2%, 95% CI 1.5% to 36.1%; p=0.03) but not at 12 months (absolute risk reduction −1.9%; p=0.89), with composite cognitive scores, depression, PTSD symptoms and functional outcomes similar throughout — so the survival benefit was not bought with worse brains, but a durable cognitive benefit was not shown either. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): paired awakening and breathing trials free patients from the ventilator sooner and improved one-year survival in a single trial; long-term cognition was no worse, and no better by 12 months.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — paired daily awakening and breathing trials added 3.1 ventilator-free days and improved 1-year survival in the ABC trial; long-term cognitive outcomes were similar by 12 months

title: Ultrasound at the bedside: diaphragm and lung ultrasound predict weaning success with an area under the curve near 0.87 — a prediction tool, with no trial yet showing ultrasound-guided extubation helps patients
question: In mechanically ventilated patients, can diaphragm and lung ultrasound predict weaning success accurately enough to guide extubation decisions?
balance: POSSIBLE — as a predictor, not as a treatment: this shelf grades a test, and no stamp of benefit attaches to scanning itself. The Chest meta-analysis (Llamas-Álvarez AM et al., PMID: 28864053) pooled 19 studies and 1,071 critically ill adults: for diaphragm thickening fraction the area under the summary receiver-operating characteristic curve was 0.87 with a diagnostic odds ratio of 21 (95% CI 11 to 40); for diaphragmatic excursion, pooled sensitivity and specificity were each 75% (diagnostic odds ratio 10, 95% CI 4 to 24); for lung ultrasound the area under the curve was 0.77 with a diagnostic odds ratio of 38 but a very wide interval (95% CI 7 to 198). The 2023 Critical Care meta-analysis of diaphragmatic ultrasound (Parada-Gereda HM et al., PMID: 37147688), 19 studies and 1,204 patients in the pooled analysis, found excursion sensitivity 0.80 and specificity 0.80 and thickening-fraction sensitivity 0.85 and specificity 0.75, both with an area under the curve of 0.87 — concordant numbers, alongside significant heterogeneity and cut-off values that varied between studies. Accuracy of this order can inform an extubation decision; it cannot make one, and no randomised trial has tested whether acting on these measurements improves outcomes. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: diaphragm ultrasound predicts weaning outcome with moderate, reproducible accuracy (sensitivity and specificity around 0.75–0.85); whether ultrasound-guided extubation decisions help patients is untested.
stamp: POSSIBLE — diaphragm and lung ultrasound predict weaning outcome with moderate accuracy (AUC ≈0.87 for diaphragm measures) across two meta-analyses; a diagnostic-accuracy shelf, not a treatment benefit

title: Training the breathing muscle: in prolonged ventilation, inspiratory muscle training tripled the odds of weaning success in the pooled small trials (OR 3.05) and strengthened the in-breath by 6.1 cm H2O — with protocols all over the map
question: In patients undergoing prolonged mechanical ventilation, does inspiratory muscle training improve weaning success and breathing-muscle strength compared with sham or usual care?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — from seven small recent trials whose protocols barely resemble each other. The 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis (Andrade-Rebolledo FA et al., PMID: 41608455) analysed seven randomised trials published since 2019, totalling 642 ICU patients across training strategies, in prolonged mechanical ventilation. In the pooled weaning-success analysis (three studies, IMT versus T-piece control), the odds ratio was 3.05 (95% CI 1.83 to 5.10; I²=0%) — an odds ratio from randomised comparisons, printed here without absolute success rates, which the review does not pool. High-intensity training improved maximal inspiratory pressure by a pooled mean difference of 6.13 cm H2O (95% CI 3.15 to 9.11; I²=59%) versus low-intensity training or usual care across six studies. The counterweight is inside the same review: several included trials (Bissett, Roceto Ratti, Sandoval, Réginault) found no significant difference in weaning success, the positive results concentrate in high-intensity protocols (loads above roughly 50–60% of maximal inspiratory pressure), and the authors themselves state that variability in protocols and populations limits generalisability and that standardisation is urgently needed. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): high-intensity inspiratory muscle training probably improves weaning success and inspiratory strength in prolonged ventilation, but the recipe — device, load, dose — is not yet standardised.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — inspiratory muscle training improved weaning success (pooled OR 3.05) and inspiratory pressure (+6.13 cm H2O) across seven small randomised trials in prolonged ventilation

title: A mask straight after the tube comes out: in hypercapnic patients, immediate NIV cut post-extubation respiratory failure from 48% to 15% and lowered 90-day mortality in the Ferrer trial
question: In hypercapnic patients recovering from acute respiratory failure, does starting noninvasive ventilation immediately after extubation prevent post-extubation respiratory failure compared with standard oxygen therapy?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in the hypercapnic, chronic-respiratory-disorder population the trials actually enrolled. In Ferrer 2009 (Ferrer M et al., PMID: 19682735), 106 patients with chronic respiratory disorders who were hypercapnic during a successful breathing trial were randomised to NIV for 24 hours after extubation or conventional oxygen: respiratory failure within 72 hours occurred in 15% versus 48% (odds ratio 5.32 for the control direction as printed, 95% CI 2.11 to 13.46; p<0.0001; adjusted odds ratio 0.17, 95% CI 0.06 to 0.44, for NIV), and 90-day mortality was lower with NIV (p=0.0146; the abstract prints no absolute mortality rates, so none are claimed here). In Nava 2005 (Nava S et al., PMID: 16276167), 97 patients at risk of post-extubation failure — hypercapnia was one of several qualifying risks — received NIV at least 8 hours a day for 48 hours or standard therapy: reintubation was 4 of 48 versus 12 of 49 (p=0.027), and ICU mortality risk fell by 10% (p<0.01), an effect the authors attribute to the avoided reintubations. The boundary matters: these are prevention trials in selected high-risk and hypercapnic patients, the opposite strategy from rescue NIV once failure is established, which harmed patients in the Esteban trial (shelf #3135). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): immediate post-extubation NIV prevents respiratory failure in hypercapnic patients, with a mortality signal in both trials.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — immediate NIV after extubation cut post-extubation respiratory failure from 48% to 15% in hypercapnic patients (Ferrer 2009) and reduced reintubation in at-risk patients (Nava 2005)

title: High-flow oxygen for the easy weans: in low-risk patients, post-extubation high-flow nasal cannula cut reintubation within 72 hours from 12.2% to 4.9%
question: In patients at low risk of extubation failure, does post-extubation high-flow nasal cannula reduce reintubation compared with conventional oxygen therapy?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one well-run multicentre trial in carefully defined low-risk patients. Hernández 2016 (Hernández G et al., PMID: 26975498) randomised 527 adults at low risk for reintubation — under 65, APACHE II below 12 on the extubation day, body mass index below 30, simple weaning, at most one comorbidity, and no heart failure, significant COPD, airway problems or prolonged ventilation — to high-flow nasal cannula or conventional oxygen for 24 hours after extubation. Reintubation within 72 hours occurred in 4.9% on high-flow versus 12.2% on conventional oxygen (absolute difference 7.2%, 95% CI 2.5% to 12.2%; p=0.004) — a relative reduction of about 60%, with the absolute rates printed alongside — and post-extubation respiratory failure was also less common (8.3% vs 14.4%; p=0.03). Time to reintubation did not differ (median 19 vs 15 hours), and no adverse effects were reported. The mirror-image caution: 'low risk' here is a strict checklist, and the same group's high-risk trial asked a different question (high-flow versus NIV) — this shelf's stamp belongs to the low-risk population only. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): in low-risk extubated patients, 24 hours of high-flow nasal cannula prevents roughly one reintubation for every 14 patients treated.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — post-extubation high-flow nasal cannula reduced 72-hour reintubation from 12.2% to 4.9% in low-risk patients in one multicentre randomised trial

title: The rescue that backfired: NIV for respiratory failure after extubation did not prevent reintubation (48% in both groups), delayed it by hours, and ICU mortality rose from 14% to 25%
question: In patients who develop respiratory failure after extubation, does rescue noninvasive ventilation improve survival — or delay reintubation and increase mortality — compared with prompt reintubation?
balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — the mask bought time, and the time cost lives. In the multicentre Esteban trial (Esteban A et al., PMID: 15190137), 221 patients in 37 centres in eight countries who developed respiratory failure within 48 hours of elective extubation were randomised to noninvasive positive-pressure ventilation by face mask or standard medical therapy. The need for reintubation was identical (48% in both groups; relative risk 0.99, 95% CI 0.76 to 1.30), but ICU mortality was higher with NIV (25% vs 14%; relative risk 1.78, 95% CI 1.03 to 3.20; p=0.048), and the median time from respiratory failure to reintubation was far longer in the NIV group (12 hours vs 2 hours 30 minutes; p=0.02) — the trial was stopped early at an interim analysis. The authors' interpretation, and the field's since, is that rescue NIV does not avert reintubation in unselected patients and that the delay it introduces is the plausible mechanism of the excess deaths. The contrast that keeps this shelf honest sits on shelf #3133: NIV started immediately after extubation, before failure, in selected hypercapnic and high-risk patients prevented failure — prevention and rescue are opposite strategies with opposite results. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm): rescue NIV for established post-extubation respiratory failure does not reduce reintubation and is associated with higher ICU mortality, most plausibly through delayed reintubation.
stamp: POSSIBLE (harm) — rescue NIV for respiratory failure after extubation did not reduce reintubation (48% vs 48%) and was associated with higher ICU mortality (25% vs 14%) in the Esteban trial

title: Less pressure, same result: in 980 ICU patients without ARDS, a lower-PEEP strategy was noninferior to higher PEEP for ventilator-free days (median 18 vs 17) — with a few more rescue treatments for low oxygen
question: In ICU patients ventilated without ARDS, does a lower-PEEP strategy reduce ventilator-free days or mortality compared with a higher-PEEP strategy?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — lower PEEP did not cost ventilator-free days or lives, which was the question the trial was built to answer. RELAx (Algera AG et al., PMID: 33295981) randomised 980 patients without ARDS, expected not to be extubated within 24 hours, in eight Dutch ICUs to the lowest PEEP level between 0 and 5 cm H2O or to a PEEP of 8 cm H2O. At day 28 the lower-PEEP group had a median of 18 ventilator-free days versus 17 with higher PEEP (mean ratio 1.04; p=0.007 for noninferiority, within the pre-set −10% margin). Mortality at 28 days was 38.4% versus 42.0% (hazard ratio 0.89, 95% CI 0.73 to 1.09) — a point estimate favouring lower PEEP that the trial was not powered to confirm. The harm on the face runs the other way: severe hypoxaemia occurred in 20.6% versus 17.6% (risk ratio 1.17, 95% CI 0.90 to 1.51) and a rescue strategy for hypoxaemia was needed in 19.7% versus 14.6% (risk ratio 1.35, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.79; adjusted p=0.54), with no significant differences in other secondary outcomes including ARDS development, pneumonia or pneumothorax. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): in patients without ARDS, lower PEEP is noninferior for ventilator-free days, so the burden of proof sits on higher PEEP, not on lower.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — a lower-PEEP strategy was noninferior to higher PEEP for ventilator-free days at day 28 in ICU patients without ARDS (RELAx)

title: Analgesia first: a 17-study meta-analysis found lower ICU mortality with analgosedation (OR 0.72) — but no difference in hospital mortality, and delirium was higher in the trial-only subgroup (OR 1.88)
question: In ventilated ICU patients, does an analgesia-first (analgosedation) strategy reduce ventilation duration, delirium, and mortality compared with conventional sedative-based regimens?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the three outcomes in the question point in three different directions, and the review says so itself. The 2019 systematic review and meta-analysis (Wang CT et al., PMID: 31395447) pooled 17 studies and 2,298 critically ill patients (1,170 analgosedation, 1,128 control) comparing analgesia-first strategies with conventional analgesia-plus-sedation. ICU mortality was lower with analgosedation (odds ratio 0.72, 95% CI 0.53 to 0.97; p=0.03), but 28-day/hospital mortality did not differ (odds ratio 0.91, 95% CI 0.70 to 1.18; p=0.48) and neither did the overall incidence of delirium (odds ratio 1.06, 95% CI 0.78 to 1.45; p=0.70) — while the subgroup analysis restricted to trials found delirium significantly increased (odds ratio 1.88, 95% CI 1.14 to 3.10; p=0.01), the harm printed on the face of this shelf. The review does not report a pooled ventilation-duration result in its abstract, so that part of the question goes unanswered by this record. The authors themselves warn of high clinical heterogeneity — varying analgesics and sedatives across studies, randomised trials mixed with cohort studies — and conclude the results must be interpreted cautiously. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): analgosedation may reduce ICU mortality, but the signal does not survive to hospital mortality, delirium may be worse in the trial data, and the evidence base is too heterogeneous to grade higher.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — analgosedation was associated with lower ICU mortality (OR 0.72) but not hospital mortality, and delirium was higher in the trial-only subgroup (OR 1.88), in a heterogeneous 17-study meta-analysis

title: The short-acting opioid: remifentanil-based sedation shortened mechanical ventilation (pooled mean difference −1.46) and time to extubation (−1.02) across 23 trials — with no difference in mortality, hospital stay or costs
question: In mechanically ventilated adults, does remifentanil-based sedation shorten ventilation and ICU stay compared with fentanyl- or morphine-based sedation?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — on the clock, not on survival, and with heterogeneity high enough to print on the face. The 2017 systematic review and meta-analysis (Zhu Y et al., PMID: 28774327) pooled 23 randomised trials and 1,905 mechanically ventilated patients comparing remifentanil with other opioids (chiefly fentanyl and morphine based regimens). Remifentanil was associated with a shorter duration of mechanical ventilation (mean difference −1.46, 95% CI −2.44 to −0.49), a shorter time to extubation after sedation was stopped (mean difference −1.02, 95% CI −1.59 to −0.46) and a shorter ICU stay (mean difference −0.10, 95% CI −0.16 to −0.03) — the ICU-stay figure is small and its scale, as pooled across trials reporting stay differently, should not be read as a tenth of a day saved. There were no significant differences in hospital stay (mean difference −0.05, 95% CI −0.25 to 0.15), costs (mean difference −709.71, 95% CI −1590.98 to 171.55; I²=88%), mortality (mean difference −0.64, 95% CI −1.33 to 0.06; I²=87%) or agitation (I²=93%). The pharmacology predicts the pattern — remifentanil is cleared by blood esterases independently of liver and kidney function, so it should wear off faster — but pooled effects with I² values of 87–93% on several outcomes are averages over very unlike trials. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): remifentanil-based sedation probably shortens ventilation and time to extubation modestly versus fentanyl- or morphine-based sedation, with no shown effect on mortality, hospital stay or cost.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — remifentanil-based sedation shortened ventilation duration and time to extubation in a 23-trial meta-analysis, with no difference in mortality or hospital stay

title: One small trial, one clear signal: nocturnal dexmedetomidine kept 80% of ICU patients delirium-free versus 54% on placebo — and did not improve sleep quality
question: In ICU patients at risk of delirium, does a low-dose nocturnal dexmedetomidine infusion prevent delirium compared with placebo?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — a real delirium signal from a single 100-patient trial, with sleep unchanged. In the two-centre double-blind Skrobik trial (Skrobik Y et al., PMID: 29498534), delirium-free survival through the ICU stay was 80% (40 of 50) on nocturnal dexmedetomidine versus 54% (27 of 50) on placebo — delirium in 20% versus 46%, a relative risk of 0.44 (95% CI 0.23 to 0.82; P=0.006), with the absolute rates printed alongside. Patient-reported sleep quality (Leeds Sleep Evaluation Questionnaire) was similar between groups, and hypotension and bradycardia did not differ significantly. That is the whole evidence base for the nocturnal strategy: one small trial, however clean its design, in patients already receiving sedatives whose other sedative doses were halved during the infusion — so the result is one trial away from changing. This is a different question from postoperative prophylaxis after surgery (live shelf #791) and from dexmedetomidine as the primary ICU sedative. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): nocturnal low-dose dexmedetomidine may prevent ICU delirium, but a single 100-patient trial cannot carry a stronger stamp, and it did not make patients sleep better by their own report.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — low-dose nocturnal dexmedetomidine reduced ICU delirium in one small double-blind trial (delirium 20% vs 46%), with no improvement in patient-reported sleep quality

title: Rivastigmine added to haloperidol did not shorten ICU delirium — the trial was stopped early with mortality 22% versus 8%
question: In ICU patients with delirium treated with haloperidol, does adding rivastigmine shorten delirium — or increase mortality — compared with haloperidol alone?
balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — the only randomised trial of the strategy was stopped early by its safety board, pointing the wrong way on both outcomes. In van Eijk's multicentre double-blind trial (van Eijk MM et al., PMID: 21056464), 104 ICU patients with delirium received rivastigmine or placebo as an adjunct to haloperidol-based usual care; the trial had planned 440 patients but was halted because mortality was 22% (12 of 54) on rivastigmine versus 8% (4 of 50) on placebo (p=0.07), and median delirium duration was longer, not shorter, on rivastigmine (5.0 days, IQR 2.7–14.2, versus 3.0 days, IQR 1.0–9.3; p=0.06). Neither difference reached conventional significance — an early-stopped trial cannot prove harm — but a treatment that trends toward longer delirium and higher death, with no favourable signal anywhere, has no case for use. This shelf is about the rivastigmine adjunct specifically, not about antipsychotics for delirium (live shelf #341). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm): adding rivastigmine to haloperidol should not be used to treat ICU delirium; the randomised evidence points toward harm and the trial's own authors recommend against it.
stamp: POSSIBLE (harm) — adding rivastigmine to haloperidol did not shorten ICU delirium and was associated with higher mortality in a trial stopped early on safety grounds

title: Non-drug sleep bundles in the ICU: the pooled delirium benefit belongs to the dexmedetomidine trials — light, earplugs and multicomponent care alone showed no significant delirium effect
question: In ICU patients, do non-drug sleep-promotion protocols (noise, light, and care-clustering bundles) improve sleep and reduce delirium compared with usual care?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — for delirium, the non-drug components are the null part of a positive-looking pool. Teng's meta-analysis of 15 randomised trials (Teng J et al., PMID: 37302381) found sleep interventions overall associated with less ICU delirium (risk ratio 0.73, 95% CI 0.58 to 0.93 — a relative effect), but the pooled dexmedetomidine trials drove it (risk ratio 0.43, 95% CI 0.32 to 0.59), while the nonpharmacological subgroups — light therapy, earplugs, melatonin, and multicomponent nonpharmacologic treatments — showed no significant effect on delirium incidence or duration, and the authors conclude non-pharmacological sleep interventions are not effective for preventing delirium. Sleep itself may still improve: Huang's network meta-analysis of 31 trials and 2,036 patients (Huang D et al., PMID: 38206715) found eye masks, and earplugs plus eye masks, improved sleep quality versus routine care (P<.05), though its abstract reports no pooled effect sizes and it measured no delirium outcome. So the honest split is: bundles may make the night feel better; they have not been shown to prevent delirium. This shelf is broader than the earplugs-and-eye-masks question on live shelf #1328. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): non-drug sleep-promotion protocols have not been shown to reduce ICU delirium; any benefit is on subjective sleep quality, chiefly from eye masks and earplugs.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — nonpharmacological sleep interventions did not significantly reduce ICU delirium in the non-drug subgroups of a 15-trial meta-analysis, though eye masks and earplugs may improve subjective sleep quality

title: CLONES pilot: one night of low-dose clonidine bought postoperative high-dependency patients about 100 extra minutes of sleep (497 vs 396 minutes) — 80 patients, one night, one centre
question: In postoperative ICU patients, does a low-dose clonidine infusion improve sleep quality compared with placebo or standard care?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — a genuine sleep gain in a pilot trial too small and too short to settle anything. In the double-blind CLONES pilot (Liu D et al., PMID: 39311905), 80 analysed postoperative high-dependency patients slept a mean of 497.2 minutes on low-dose clonidine versus 396.4 minutes on placebo on the night of surgery — a mean difference of 100.8 minutes (95% CI 38.2 to 163.4; p=0.002) — and reported better sleep overall. The price signal was small but real: four clonidine patients had the infusion stopped for bradycardia and hypotension (none needed additional treatment), and safety outcomes otherwise did not differ. Delirium was essentially absent in this elective population, so the trial says nothing about it. Note the setting honestly: these were elective-surgery high-dependency patients, not general ICU patients, sleep was measured with a consumer actigraphy/photoplethysmography device, and the exposure was a single night. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): low-dose clonidine probably lengthens one night's postoperative sleep, on pilot evidence that needs a larger confirmatory trial.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — low-dose clonidine lengthened total sleep time by about 100 minutes on the night of surgery in one 80-patient pilot trial in postoperative high-dependency patients

title: Esmolol in septic shock: one open-label 154-patient trial reported 28-day mortality of 49.4% versus 80.5% — a benefit too large to take at face value without a blinded confirmatory trial
question: In patients with septic shock and persistent tachycardia despite fluids and norepinephrine, does heart-rate control with esmolol improve survival compared with standard care?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the direction is consistent and the size is implausible; both things are true. Morelli's open-label phase 2 trial (Morelli A et al., PMID: 24108526) randomised 154 septic-shock patients with heart rates of at least 95/min on high-dose norepinephrine: 28-day mortality was 49.4% on esmolol versus 80.5% on standard care (adjusted hazard ratio 0.39, 95% CI 0.26 to 0.59; P<.001), with lower norepinephrine requirements and less fluid given. Hasegawa's meta-analysis of seven small trials (613 patients; esmolol or landiolol) (Hasegawa D et al., PMID: 33434497) pools to a 28-day mortality risk ratio of 0.68 (95% CI 0.54 to 0.85) — a relative effect, reported alongside an absolute risk reduction of 18.2% and a number needed to treat of 5.5. The counterweights are structural: Morelli's trial was open-label and single-centre, its primary outcome was heart-rate control rather than mortality, and a control-group mortality of 80.5% is far above what comparable septic-shock cohorts show, which inflates any relative benefit. No large blinded trial has tested the claim. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): heart-rate control with an ultrashort beta-blocker may improve survival in tachycardic septic shock, but the mortality claim rests on small open-label trials and must not be read as established.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — esmolol heart-rate control was associated with much lower 28-day mortality in one small open-label trial and in a pooled analysis of small trials, but no large blinded trial has confirmed a survival benefit

title: LeoPARDS: levosimendan in sepsis did not reduce organ dysfunction (SOFA 6.68 vs 6.06) or mortality (34.5% vs 30.9%) — and weaning was slower, with more tachyarrhythmia
question: In patients with septic shock, does levosimendan improve organ dysfunction and survival compared with placebo on top of standard care?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — a well-run double-blind trial whose point estimates lean, if anything, against the drug. In LeoPARDS (Gordon AC et al., PMID: 27705084), 516 adults with sepsis received levosimendan or placebo on top of standard care: mean daily SOFA score was 6.68 on levosimendan versus 6.06 on placebo (mean difference 0.61, 95% CI −0.07 to 1.29; P=0.053 — higher is worse), and 28-day mortality was 34.5% versus 30.9% (absolute difference 3.6 percentage points, 95% CI −4.5 to 11.7; P=0.43). Two secondary outcomes favoured placebo: ventilated patients on levosimendan were less likely to be weaned successfully (hazard ratio 0.77, 95% CI 0.60 to 0.97), and supraventricular tachyarrhythmia was more common (3.1% versus 0.4%; P=0.04). Chang's meta-analysis of ten trials and 1,036 patients with severe sepsis or septic shock (Chang W et al., PMID: 29602841) agrees on the outcome that matters: mortality odds ratio 0.89 (95% CI 0.69 to 1.16; P=0.39), despite better lactate and cardiac-function measures. Note the population honestly: LeoPARDS enrolled adults with sepsis, not exclusively septic shock. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): levosimendan added to standard care does not reduce organ dysfunction or mortality in sepsis, and carries a tachyarrhythmia and weaning cost.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — levosimendan did not reduce organ dysfunction or mortality in the 516-patient LeoPARDS trial, with slower ventilator weaning and more supraventricular tachyarrhythmia

title: SEPSIS-ACT: selepressin stopped for futility — ventilator- and vasopressor-free days 15.0 versus 14.5, 90-day mortality 40.6% versus 39.4%
question: In adults with septic shock, does selepressin increase ventilator- and vasopressor-free days compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — an 868-patient adaptive trial that stopped itself for futility. In SEPSIS-ACT (Laterre PF et al., PMID: 31577035), adults with septic shock requiring more than 5 µg/min of norepinephrine were randomised to one of three selepressin dosing regimens or placebo: the primary endpoint, ventilator- and vasopressor-free days within 30 days, was 15.0 on selepressin versus 14.5 on placebo (difference 0.6 days, 95% CI −1.3 to 2.4; P=.30), and 90-day mortality was 40.6% versus 39.4% (difference 1.1%, 95% CI −6.5% to 8.8%; P=.77), with kidney-replacement-therapy-free days and ICU-free days likewise similar. Ischaemic and arrhythmic adverse events ran numerically higher on selepressin (cardiac ischaemia 6.6% versus 5.6%; mesenteric ischaemia 3.2% versus 2.6%) without reaching a proven harm. A selective V1a agonist was an elegant idea — pressor effect without catecholamines — and the trial was large and honest enough to kill it. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): selepressin does not increase ventilator- and vasopressor-free days or improve any key secondary outcome in septic shock.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — selepressin did not improve ventilator- and vasopressor-free days in the 868-patient SEPSIS-ACT trial, which was stopped for futility

title: Drotrecogin alfa in septic shock: the 1,697-patient PROWESS-SHOCK trial found mortality 26.4% versus 24.2% — reversing the 2001 PROWESS result that launched the drug
question: In adults with septic shock, does drotrecogin alfa (activated protein C) reduce mortality compared with placebo?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — the definitive trial in the exact population reversed the founding trial. In PROWESS-SHOCK (Ranieri VM et al., PMID: 22616830), 1,697 patients with septic shock on fluids and vasopressors received drotrecogin alfa (activated) or placebo for 96 hours: 28-day mortality was 26.4% (223 of 846) on the drug versus 24.2% (202 of 834) on placebo (relative risk 1.09, 95% CI 0.92 to 1.28; P=0.31), 90-day mortality 34.1% versus 32.7% (relative risk 1.04, 95% CI 0.90 to 1.19), and even the predefined subgroup with severe protein C deficiency — the patients the drug most plausibly suits — showed no benefit (28.7% versus 30.8%; risk ratio 0.93, 95% CI 0.74 to 1.17). Serious bleeding during treatment was similar (10 versus 8 patients; P=0.81). The earlier PROWESS trial in severe sepsis (Bernard GR et al., PMID: 11236773) had found mortality of 24.7% versus 30.8% — a 19.4% relative risk reduction with a 6.1-percentage-point absolute reduction (P=0.005) — and more serious bleeding (3.5% versus 2.0%). Two large double-blind trials, opposite answers; the later one asked the question in septic shock itself, the population of this shelf, and its answer governs. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): drotrecogin alfa does not reduce mortality in septic shock.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — drotrecogin alfa did not reduce 28- or 90-day mortality in the 1,697-patient PROWESS-SHOCK trial in septic shock, reversing the earlier positive PROWESS result in severe sepsis

title: RACE: levocarnitine in septic shock missed its own phase 2 bar — SOFA improvement at the best dose had a posterior probability of 0.78 against a 0.90 threshold, mortality 43.3% versus 45.9%
question: In patients with septic shock, does adjunctive levocarnitine improve organ failure and one-year survival compared with placebo?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — a dose-finding phase 2 trial that did not clear the bar it set itself. In RACE (Jones AE et al., PMID: 30646314), 250 patients with septic shock and moderate organ dysfunction were adaptively randomised to levocarnitine 6 g, 12 g or 18 g, or placebo, as a 12-hour infusion: the fitted change in SOFA score at 48 hours was −1.97 at the most promising (18 g) dose versus −1.63 on placebo, and the posterior probability that the 18 g dose was superior was 0.78 — short of the trial's prespecified 0.90 threshold for proceeding. Twenty-eight-day mortality was 43.3% (45 of 104) at 18 g versus 45.9% (34 of 74) on placebo. On the one-year survival half of this shelf's question, this record is silent: RACE as published reports organ failure at 48 hours and mortality at 28 days, and no one-year outcome appears in its record — so no one-year claim is made here. A phase 2 trial designed to pick a dose cannot prove or disprove efficacy; what it establishes is that the organ-failure signal was too weak to meet the investigators' own go/no-go criterion. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): adjunctive levocarnitine has not been shown to improve organ failure in septic shock, and its one-year survival effect is untested in this record.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — levocarnitine did not meet its prespecified phase 2 organ-failure threshold in the 250-patient RACE trial, and one-year survival was not reported in the trial record
