title: Passive leg raising predicts fluid responsiveness well (AUC 0.95 when cardiac output is measured) — but prediction is not outcome: no PLR-guided resuscitation outcome trial sits in this record
question: In patients with septic shock, does resuscitation guided by passive-leg-raise fluid-responsiveness testing improve outcomes compared with usual assessment?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — for the outcome question as asked, there is no direct evidence here at all; what exists is diagnostic accuracy, and it is strong only when flow is measured directly. Monnet's meta-analysis of 21 studies and 991 adults (Monnet X et al., PMID: 26825952) found PLR-induced changes in cardiac output predicted fluid responsiveness with pooled sensitivity 0.85 and specificity 0.91 and an area under the ROC curve of 0.95, at a best threshold of a cardiac-output rise of at least 10%; read by pulse pressure instead, sensitivity fell to 0.56 (AUC 0.77). Cherpanath's meta-analysis of 23 trials and 1,013 patients (Cherpanath TGV et al., PMID: 26741579) agrees: sensitivity 86%, specificity 92%, AUC 0.95, with pulse-pressure readings clearly inferior to flow variables. Neither review reports a trial of PLR-guided resuscitation against usual assessment on mortality, organ failure, or any patient outcome — they validate a measurement, not a strategy. So this shelf separates the two claims the question conflates: as a test, PLR with a cardiac-output measurement is reliable; as a resuscitation strategy, its outcome benefit is untested in this record. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): PLR reliably predicts fluid responsiveness when cardiac output is measured, but whether guiding resuscitation by it improves outcomes in septic shock has not been shown.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — passive leg raising reliably predicts fluid responsiveness when cardiac output is measured (AUC 0.95 in two meta-analyses), but no outcome trial of PLR-guided resuscitation is present in this record

title: Lactate clearance versus ScvO2: the EMShockNet trial met non-inferiority (in-hospital mortality 17% versus 23%) — a blood test can stand in for the central-line oxygen target
question: In emergency-department patients with severe sepsis, is a lactate-clearance-guided resuscitation strategy non-inferior to central venous oxygen saturation-guided therapy for survival?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — non-inferior in the trial that asked, and favoured in the pool; the benefit claimed is substitutability, not superiority of a drug. In the EMShockNet randomised non-inferiority trial (Jones AE et al., PMID: 20179283), 300 emergency-department patients with severe sepsis and hypoperfusion or septic shock were resuscitated for up to 6 hours to normalise central venous pressure and mean arterial pressure plus either lactate clearance of at least 10% or ScvO2 of at least 70%: in-hospital mortality was 17% (25 of 150) with lactate clearance versus 23% (34 of 150) with ScvO2, and the observed difference did not cross the predefined −10% non-inferiority threshold (95% CI for the 6% difference, −3% to 15%), with no differences in treatments given over the first 72 hours or in adverse events. Pan's meta-analysis of seven randomised trials and 1,301 patients (Pan J et al., PMID: 30813144) goes further, finding lower in-hospital mortality with lactate-clearance-guided therapy (risk ratio 0.68, 95% CI 0.56 to 0.82 — a relative effect; the abstract does not report pooled absolute mortality rates), plus shorter ICU stay and ventilation time. The anchor trial's own absolute rates are the anchor for practice: lactate guidance performed at least as well without requiring the ScvO2 catheter target. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): lactate-clearance-guided resuscitation is a non-inferior, less invasive substitute for ScvO2-guided therapy in early severe sepsis.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — lactate-clearance-guided resuscitation was non-inferior to ScvO2-guided therapy for in-hospital mortality in the EMShockNet trial (17% vs 23%), with pooled estimates favouring lactate guidance

title: Drawing less blood in the ICU: conservation devices cut the volume taken by 19–80% in small studies — but the one large trial of small-volume tubes did not significantly cut transfusions in its primary analysis
question: In ICU patients, do small-volume blood-collection tubes and other blood-conservation devices reduce iatrogenic blood loss and transfusion compared with standard tubes?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the devices clearly take less blood; whether that saves transfusions is unproven. The systematic review behind this shelf (Siegal DM et al., PMID: 30482081) found 8 studies (1,204 patients) of arterial access devices and reduced-volume tubes, every one reporting less blood taken for laboratory testing than standard practice (range 19%–80%), but all at serious risk of bias and too heterogeneous to pool, with no pooled transfusion result. The one large randomised test, STRATUS (Siegal DM et al., PMID: 37824152), switched 25 Canadian ICUs to small-volume tubes in a stepped-wedge design: in its primary analysis of 21,201 patients, red-cell units per patient per ICU stay did not differ significantly (relative risk 0.91, 95% CI 0.79 to 1.05; P=.19; absolute reduction 7.24 units per 100 patients, 95% CI −3.28 to 19.44); only a prespecified secondary analysis including the COVID-hiatus period reached significance (relative risk 0.88, 95% CI 0.77 to 1.00; P=.04). Specimens with insufficient volume for testing stayed rare (≤0.03%) on both strategies, so the laboratory harm feared from smaller tubes did not materialise. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): blood-conservation devices reliably reduce the volume of blood drawn, but a transfusion benefit rests on a secondary analysis of a single trial and on small studies at serious risk of bias.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — blood-conservation devices reduce the volume of blood taken for testing, but the large STRATUS trial found no significant reduction in red-cell transfusion in its primary analysis

title: Transfusing children at 7 g/dL: TRIPICU's restrictive threshold matched 9.5 g/dL on organ dysfunction (12% in both groups) and 54% of children needed no transfusion at all
question: In critically ill children, does a restrictive red-cell transfusion threshold (7 g/dL) give equivalent outcomes to a liberal threshold (9.5 g/dL)?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — on outcomes, with substantially less blood used. In TRIPICU (Lacroix J et al., PMID: 17442904), 637 stable critically ill children with haemoglobin below 9.5 g/dL were randomised to transfusion thresholds of 7 or 9.5 g/dL: new or progressive multiple-organ dysfunction developed in 12% in both groups (38 vs 39 patients; absolute risk reduction with the restrictive strategy 0.4%, 95% CI −4.6 to 5.4), deaths within 28 days were 14 in each group, and the restrictive group received 44% fewer transfusions — 54% of its children were never transfused, versus 2% in the liberal group. The trial's own sepsis subgroup (Karam O et al., PMID: 21057356; 137 children) read the same way: new or progressive multiple-organ dysfunction in 18.8% vs 19.1% (P=.97), with no difference in PICU stay or mortality. This is the paediatric question, distinct from the adult threshold trials on the adult umbrella shelf: in stable critically ill children, waiting until 7 g/dL costs nothing measurable in organ outcomes and spares about half the children any transfusion. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): a 7 g/dL threshold in stable critically ill children gives equivalent organ-dysfunction outcomes to 9.5 g/dL while markedly reducing transfusion exposure.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — in stable critically ill children a 7 g/dL transfusion threshold matched 9.5 g/dL on multiple-organ dysfunction and mortality in TRIPICU, while cutting transfusions by 44%

title: Extended daily dialysis versus continuous therapy in ICU kidney injury: mortality the same in the randomised trials (relative risk 0.90) — the apparent EDD advantage lives only in observational studies
question: In ICU patients with acute kidney injury, does extended daily dialysis (sustained low-efficiency dialysis) give equivalent clearance, haemodynamic stability, and survival to continuous renal replacement therapy?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — in the randomised evidence, the hybrid and the continuous machine are interchangeable on outcomes. The meta-analysis behind this shelf (Zhang L et al., PMID: 25843704) pooled 7 randomised trials (533 patients) and 10 observational studies (675 patients) of extended daily dialysis (EDD, sessions of more than 6 and less than 24 hours on a conventional machine) versus continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT): in the randomised trials, mortality did not differ (relative risk 0.90, 95% CI 0.74 to 1.11; P=0.3), nor did kidney recovery, fluid removal, or ICU days, and biochemical efficacy (urea, creatinine, phosphate) was similar. The lower mortality with EDD (relative risk 0.86, 95% CI 0.74 to 1.00; P=0.05) appeared only in the observational studies, where allocation bias is the obvious explanation, as the reviewers themselves state. The largest single randomised comparison (Schwenger V et al., PMID: 22839577; 232 patients, 12-hour sustained low-efficiency dialysis versus 24-hour continuous haemofiltration) found 90-day mortality of 49.6% vs 55.6% (P=0.43) with similar haemodynamic stability — and fewer ventilator days (17.7 vs 20.9; P=0.047), fewer ICU days (19.6 vs 23.7; P=0.04), and lower nursing time and cost with the extended-daily approach. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): extended daily dialysis matches CRRT on survival, kidney recovery, and clearance in the randomised trials, with practical advantages in time and cost — and no proven survival advantage for either mode.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — extended daily dialysis and CRRT gave similar mortality, kidney recovery, and clearance in the randomised trials; an EDD survival advantage appears only in observational data

title: Where to put the central line: subclavian carried the lowest infection-and-thrombosis risk in 3SITES (1.5 vs 3.6 vs 4.6 events per 1,000 catheter-days) — and the highest pneumothorax risk
question: In critically ill adults needing a central venous catheter, how do subclavian, jugular, and femoral insertion sites compare for bloodstream infection and thrombosis?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for the subclavian site on infection and thrombosis, with its mechanical price on the same face. In 3SITES (Parienti JJ et al., PMID: 26398070), 3,471 catheters in 3,027 ICU patients were randomised by site: the composite of catheter-related bloodstream infection and symptomatic deep-vein thrombosis occurred at 1.5 per 1,000 catheter-days with the subclavian vein, 3.6 with the jugular, and 4.6 with the femoral (P=0.02); pairwise, risk was higher for femoral than subclavian (hazard ratio 3.5, 95% CI 1.5 to 7.8; P=0.003) and for jugular than subclavian (hazard ratio 2.1, 95% CI 1.0 to 4.3; P=0.04), with femoral and jugular similar (hazard ratio 1.3, 95% CI 0.8 to 2.1). The harm runs the other way: pneumothorax requiring a chest tube followed 13 (1.5%) of subclavian insertions versus 4 (0.5%) of jugular insertions. A network meta-analysis of 13 randomised trials (6,201 patients) (Sakuraya M et al., PMID: 36106316) points the same direction for infection — subclavian lower than jugular (relative risk 0.30, 95% CI 0.11 to 0.81, moderate certainty) and femoral higher than subclavian (relative risk 2.56, 95% CI 1.02 to 6.44) — with no significant site differences for thrombosis and fewer mechanical complications at the femoral site. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): when all three sites are available, subclavian insertion minimises bloodstream infection and symptomatic thrombosis, at the cost of the highest pneumothorax risk.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — subclavian insertion gave the lowest rate of bloodstream infection and symptomatic thrombosis in the 3SITES trial, with pneumothorax as its counterweight

title: Treating fever with acetaminophen in infected ICU patients: HEAT's 700 patients gained no ICU-free days (23 vs 22) and died at the same rate (15.9% vs 16.6% at 90 days)
question: In critically ill patients with suspected infection, does acetaminophen for fever increase or decrease mortality and ICU-free days compared with placebo?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — the best blinded test of fever treatment in infection is neutral on both of its outcomes. In HEAT (Young P et al., PMID: 26436473), 700 ICU patients with fever (temperature ≥38°C) and known or suspected infection were randomised to intravenous acetaminophen 1 g or placebo every 6 hours: ICU-free days to day 28 were 23 (interquartile range 13 to 25) on acetaminophen versus 22 (12 to 25) on placebo (absolute difference 0 days, 96.2% CI 0 to 1; P=0.07), and 90-day mortality was 15.9% (55 of 345) versus 16.6% (57 of 344) (relative risk 0.96, 95% CI 0.66 to 1.39; P=0.84) — neither benefit nor harm, in either direction the question asks about. The wider randomised literature reads identically: a meta-analysis of antipyretic therapy in critically ill septic adults (Drewry AM et al., PMID: 28221185) found no reduction in 28-day/hospital mortality across 8 randomised studies (1,507 patients; relative risk 0.93, 95% CI 0.77 to 1.13), no change in shock reversal or nosocomial infection, and a mean temperature reduction of only 0.38°C (95% CI −0.63 to −0.13). PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): acetaminophen lowers the thermometer slightly and changes neither survival nor ICU-free days in infected critically ill patients — fever treatment here is a comfort decision, not a survival decision.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — acetaminophen for fever in ICU patients with suspected infection changed neither ICU-free days nor 90-day mortality in the HEAT trial, matching the pooled antipyretic literature

title: Cooling the febrile septic-shock patient: Schortgen's 200 patients needed less vasopressor early and day-14 mortality was 19% vs 34% — in one open-label trial whose own primary endpoint was not met
question: In patients with septic shock and fever, does fever control with external cooling reduce vasopressor requirements and early mortality compared with no cooling?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — an early-mortality signal from a single small open-label trial whose primary endpoint was missed, uncorroborated by the pooled fever-control literature. In Schortgen's trial (Schortgen F et al., PMID: 22366046), 200 febrile patients with septic shock on vasopressors, ventilation, and sedation were randomised to external cooling to normothermia (36.5–37°C) for 48 hours or no cooling: the primary endpoint — a 50% decrease in baseline vasopressor dose at 48 hours — did not differ significantly (72% vs 61%; absolute difference 11%, 95% CI −23 to 2), although the same endpoint at 12 hours did (54% vs 20%; absolute difference 34%, 95% CI −46 to −21; P<0.001), shock reversal during the ICU stay was more common with cooling (86% vs 73%; P=0.021), and day-14 mortality was lower (19% vs 34%; absolute difference −16%, 95% CI −28 to −4; P=0.013). Against that stands the individual-patient-data meta-analysis of fever-control trials (Young PJ et al., PMID: 30741326; 1,413 participants): more active fever management did not significantly change survival time overall (hazard ratio 0.91, 95% CI 0.75 to 1.10; P=0.32) or in any prespecified subgroup with limited physiological reserve. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): external cooling speeds vasopressor weaning in the first hours and may reduce early mortality in septic shock, but the claim rests on one 200-patient trial and a secondary time point — it is a reason for a larger trial, not a practice verdict.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — external cooling in febrile septic shock sped early vasopressor weaning and was associated with lower day-14 mortality in one small trial, but its primary endpoint was not met and pooled fever-control data show no survival effect

title: Running beta-lactams continuously in sepsis: BLING III's 7,031 patients died at 24.9% vs 26.8% (P=.08) with clearly better clinical cure — and the 18-trial meta-analysis puts 90-day mortality at a relative risk of 0.86
question: In critically ill patients with sepsis, does continuous (prolonged) infusion of beta-lactam antibiotics improve clinical cure and survival compared with intermittent bolus dosing?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the largest trial leans toward benefit without proving it on mortality, and the pooled trials cross the line. In BLING III (Dulhunty JM et al., PMID: 38864155), 7,031 critically ill adults with sepsis receiving piperacillin-tazobactam or meropenem were randomised to the same 24-hour dose by continuous or intermittent infusion: 90-day mortality was 24.9% (864 of 3,474) on continuous infusion versus 26.8% (939 of 3,507) on intermittent (absolute difference −1.9%, 95% CI −4.9 to 1.1; odds ratio 0.91, 95% CI 0.81 to 1.01; P=.08), while clinical cure was clearly higher with continuous infusion (55.7% vs 50.0%; absolute difference 5.7%, 95% CI 2.4 to 9.1), with no significant difference in resistant-organism acquisition or Clostridioides difficile infection. The companion systematic review and meta-analysis of 18 randomised trials (9,108 patients) (Abdul-Aziz MH et al., PMID: 38864162) found prolonged infusion associated with lower 90-day mortality (pooled risk ratio 0.86, 95% credible interval 0.72 to 0.98 — a 14% relative reduction, graded high certainty, with a 99.1% posterior probability of benefit), lower ICU mortality (risk ratio 0.84, 95% credible interval 0.70 to 0.97), and higher clinical cure (risk ratio 1.16, 95% credible interval 1.07 to 1.31; moderate certainty). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): continuous or prolonged beta-lactam infusion in sepsis improves clinical cure and probably reduces mortality modestly in relative terms; BLING III's own absolute mortality gap was 1.9 points and not significant on its own.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — continuous/prolonged beta-lactam infusion improved clinical cure in BLING III and was associated with lower 90-day mortality across 18 randomised trials (relative risk 0.86)

title: Sitting the ventilated patient up: the network meta-analysis gives semirecumbent positioning a relative risk of 0.38 for pneumonia — but the trial that measured the actual angle never reached 45° and found no benefit
question: In ventilated ICU patients, does nursing in a semirecumbent (head-of-bed elevated) position prevent ventilator-associated pneumonia compared with a supine position?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — on the pooled trial evidence, with a feasibility warning built into the same shelf. The network meta-analysis behind this shelf (Pozuelo-Carrascosa DP et al., PMID: 35193688), pooling randomised trials of body position in ventilated ICU patients, found the semirecumbent position reduced ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) incidence compared with the supine position (risk ratio 0.38, 95% CI 0.25 to 0.52 — a 62% relative reduction; the abstract reports relative effects, with no pooled absolute VAP rates), and ranked semirecumbent positioning first for reducing VAP (71.4% ranking probability), hospital stay, and duration of ventilation; prone positioning, a different intervention, ranked first for mortality (risk ratio 0.70, 95% CI 0.50 to 0.91). The cautionary card is the randomised feasibility trial (van Nieuwenhoven CA et al., PMID: 16424720): assigned to a target backrest elevation of 45°, patients actually achieved 28.1° on day 1 and 22.6° on day 7, the target was not achieved for 85% of the study time, and VAP was diagnosed in 10.7% of the semirecumbent group versus 6.5% of the supine group (not significant), with no differences in mortality or duration of ventilation or ICU stay. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): semirecumbent positioning probably prevents VAP as tested in trials, but the delivered angle in real units is far below the 45° the policy names — the benefit belongs to achieving elevation, not to writing it on the chart.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — semirecumbent positioning was associated with substantially less ventilator-associated pneumonia than supine positioning in the pooled randomised trials (relative risk 0.38), though the one trial that measured achieved elevation could not sustain 45° and found no benefit

title: Immediate angiography after resuscitated cardiac arrest without ST elevation: no survival gain in COACT or TOMAHAWK — 64.5% vs 67.2% alive at 90 days in one, and a harm lean (54.0% vs 46.0% dead at 30 days) in the other
question: In comatose survivors of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest without ST elevation, does immediate coronary angiography improve survival compared with a delayed or selective strategy?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — rushing to the cath lab did not save lives in either large trial. In COACT (Lemkes JS et al., PMID: 30883057), 552 resuscitated patients without signs of STEMI had 90-day survival of 64.5% with immediate angiography versus 67.2% with angiography delayed until after neurologic recovery (odds ratio 0.89, 95% CI 0.62 to 1.27; P = 0.51). In TOMAHAWK (Desch S et al., PMID: 34459570), 554 patients had 30-day mortality of 54.0% with immediate angiography versus 46.0% with initial intensive care assessment and delayed or selective angiography (hazard ratio 1.28, 95% CI 1.00 to 1.63; P = 0.06), and the composite of death or severe neurologic deficit also leaned against the immediate strategy (64.3% vs 55.6%; relative risk 1.16, 95% CI 1.00 to 1.34), while bleeding, stroke and renal-replacement therapy were similar. The meta-analysis of all three randomised trials (Freund A et al., PMID: 35900214; 1,167 patients) found short-term mortality odds ratio 1.19 (95% CI 0.94 to 1.52; p = 0.15) for the early approach, with no difference in severe neurological deficit, renal replacement or significant bleeding. The harm is on the face of this shelf: every point estimate in TOMAHAWK favours waiting, though none quite reaches significance. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): after resuscitated out-of-hospital cardiac arrest without ST elevation, immediate coronary angiography does not improve survival over a delayed or selective strategy, and the larger trial's estimates lean toward harm.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — immediate coronary angiography did not improve survival over a delayed or selective strategy in two randomised trials and a 1,167-patient meta-analysis

title: Music the patient chooses, whenever they want it: anxiety 19.5 points lower and roughly a third less sedation by day 5 in Chlan's 373-patient trial — though headphones alone explain part of it
question: In mechanically ventilated patients, does patient-directed music listening reduce anxiety and sedative exposure compared with usual care or noise-cancelling headphones?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the patient's own music, started by the patient, measurably calmed patients and spared sedatives. In the anchor trial (Chlan LL et al., PMID: 23689789), 373 ventilated patients randomised to patient-directed music (PDM), noise-cancelling headphones (NCH) or usual care had anxiety scores 19.5 points lower on a 100-mm scale with PDM than usual care at any time point (95% CI −32.2 to −6.8; P = .003), with anxiety reduced by 36.5% by the fifth study day; sedation frequency fell by −0.21 points/day (P = .01) and sedation intensity by −0.18 points/day (P = .05) versus usual care — about 2 fewer sedative doses (a 38% reduction) and 36% lower sedation intensity by day 5. Against headphones alone, music reduced sedation frequency (−0.18 points/day; P = .04) but not anxiety or sedation intensity, so part of the effect is simply shutting the ICU out. A meta-analysis of 14 randomised trials (Xiao M et al., PMID: 38619185) points the same way (anxiety SMD −1.09, 95% CI −1.52 to −0.67) and reported no adverse events in any included study. The economic analysis of the same trial cohort (Chlan LL et al., PMID: 29727366) estimated costs $2,322 per patient lower with music. The honest limits: the median patient listened only 12 minutes a day, anxiety is self-rated by patients who knew their group, and the whole programme rests on one trial group. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): patient-directed music reduces anxiety and sedative exposure in ventilated ICU patients, at trivial cost and with no reported harm.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — patient-directed music reduced anxiety and sedative exposure versus usual care in a 373-patient randomised trial, with a concordant meta-analysis of 14 trials and no reported harm

title: In-bed cycling on top of usual mobilisation: the largest trial found no function gain (PFIT-s 7.7 vs 7.5) — and the two newest meta-analyses disagree with each other
question: In ventilated ICU patients, does adding early in-bed cycling to usual mobilisation improve physical function at hospital discharge compared with usual mobilisation alone?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the pooled signals point toward benefit, but the largest single trial found none on function, and the two newest meta-analyses disagree with each other. The 2026 meta-analysis (Lu D et al., PMID: 41731824; 41 randomised trials, 3,781 patients) found adding in-bed cycling to routine rehabilitation improved the Barthel Index (SMD 1.06, 95% CI 0.66 to 1.46), 6-minute walking distance (SMD 0.80) and muscle strength (SMD 0.53), and lowered ICU-acquired weakness (OR 0.49, 95% CI 0.37 to 0.67) and delirium (OR 0.50) — but graded its own certainty very low to moderate, with ICU mortality unchanged (OR 0.95, 95% CI 0.76 to 1.19). The 2025 meta-analysis (Pazo-Palacios R et al., PMID: 40107080; 32 studies, 3,052 participants) found shorter ICU stay (−0.93 days), hospital stay (−1.78 days) and ventilation duration (−0.51 days) and better functional status, yet no significant difference in mortality, muscle strength, ICU-acquired weakness or quality of life — directly contradicting the other review on strength and weakness. And in the CYCLE trial (Kho ME et al., PMID: 38865147), the largest randomised test at 360 ventilated patients, adding 30 minutes of early in-bed cycling to usual physiotherapy did not improve physical function 3 days after ICU discharge (PFIT-s 7.7 vs 7.5; difference 0.23 points, 95% CI −0.19 to 0.65; P = 0.29), with no serious adverse events in either group. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): in-bed cycling is safe and may shorten stays, but an improvement in physical function — the outcome this shelf asks about — is not established.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — in-bed cycling added to usual mobilisation has not been shown to improve physical function in the largest randomised trial, and two recent meta-analyses disagree on strength and ICU-acquired weakness

title: Percutaneous versus open surgical tracheostomy: wound infection risk ratio 0.24 in the Cochrane review — mortality, serious events and major bleeding not significantly different, technical difficulties slightly more
question: In critically ill adults needing a tracheostomy, does percutaneous dilatational tracheostomy cause fewer complications than open surgical tracheostomy?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for the wound, not for survival: the percutaneous route infects far fewer wounds, and on every grave outcome the two techniques are indistinguishable. The Cochrane review (Brass P et al., PMID: 27437615; 20 trials, 1,652 participants) found percutaneous techniques reduced wound infection/stomatitis with risk ratio 0.24 (95% CI 0.15 to 0.37; moderate-quality evidence — a 76% relative reduction; the review's abstract does not print pooled absolute rates) and unfavourable scarring with risk ratio 0.25 (95% CI 0.07 to 0.91; low quality), while procedure-related mortality (Peto odds ratio 0.52, 95% CI 0.10 to 2.60), serious intraoperative events (risk ratio 0.93, 95% CI 0.57 to 1.53), serious postoperative events (risk ratio 0.72, 95% CI 0.41 to 1.25) and major bleeding (risk ratio 0.70, 95% CI 0.45 to 1.09) did not differ significantly. A 24-trial meta-analysis (Klotz R et al., PMID: 29282535; 1,795 procedures) agrees: no difference in life-threatening events (risk difference 0.01, 95% CI −0.03 to 0.05) or mortality (risk difference 0.00), fewer stomal infections with the percutaneous route (risk difference −0.05, 95% CI −0.08 to −0.02) — but more technical difficulties with it (risk difference 0.04, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.08), the harm on the face of this shelf. The candidate-named 2016 meta-analysis (Johnson-Obaseki S et al., PMID: 27075530) reads the same way qualitatively: no significant difference in mortality or haemorrhage, infection rates and operative time favouring percutaneous. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): percutaneous dilatational tracheostomy causes fewer wound infections than open surgical tracheostomy, with no demonstrated difference in mortality, serious adverse events or major bleeding, and slightly more technical difficulty.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — percutaneous dilatational tracheostomy causes fewer wound infections than open surgical tracheostomy, with no demonstrated difference in mortality, serious adverse events or major bleeding

title: Low tidal volumes without ARDS: PReVENT's 961 patients got the same 21 ventilator-free days — and no fewer cases of ARDS (3.8% vs 5.0%) — as intermediate volumes
question: In ICU patients ventilated without ARDS, does a low tidal-volume strategy prevent lung injury and reduce ventilation duration compared with intermediate tidal volumes?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the lung-protective reflex does not transfer to patients whose lungs are not yet injured. In PReVENT (Simonis FD et al., PMID: 30357256), 961 ICU patients without ARDS randomised to low versus intermediate tidal volumes had exactly the same median ventilator-free days at day 28 — 21 days in both groups (mean difference −0.27, 95% CI −1.74 to 1.19; P = .71) — with no difference in ICU stay (median 6 vs 6 days) or hospital stay (median 14 vs 15 days), and mortality that leaned, non-significantly, against the low-volume arm: 28-day mortality 34.9% vs 32.1% (hazard ratio 1.12, 95% CI 0.90 to 1.40; P = .30) and 90-day mortality 39.1% vs 37.8% (hazard ratio 1.07, 95% CI 0.87 to 1.31; P = .54). New lung injury was not prevented either: ARDS developed in 3.8% vs 5.0% (P = .38), pneumonia in 4.2% vs 3.7% (P = .67), severe atelectasis in 11.4% vs 11.2% (P = .94) and pneumothorax in 1.8% vs 1.3% (P = .55). The earlier individual-patient meta-analysis (Serpa Neto A et al., PMID: 24811940; 7 investigations, 2,184 patients) had associated tidal volumes ≤6 ml/kg with more patients breathing unassisted by day 28 (93.1% vs 88.6% for ≥10 ml/kg; p = 0.027) — an association from largely non-randomised comparisons that the randomised trial then failed to confirm, and its sedation analysis (only 187 patients) found no difference in sedative, opioid or neuromuscular-blockade needs. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): in ICU patients without ARDS, a low tidal-volume strategy neither prevents lung injury nor shortens ventilation compared with intermediate tidal volumes.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — a low tidal-volume strategy did not increase ventilator-free days, prevent ARDS or reduce mortality versus intermediate tidal volumes in the PReVENT trial

title: Inhaled prostacyclin in ARDS: oxygenation rises in uncontrolled series (PaO2/FiO2 +40, very low certainty) — the one multicentre trial missed its primary endpoint and survival was unchanged
question: In adults with ARDS, does inhaled prostacyclin improve oxygenation, ventilation duration, or survival compared with standard care?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the oxygen numbers move in uncontrolled series; the one proper trial missed its target and survival did not move. The systematic review and meta-analysis (Torbic H et al., PMID: 37303944) pooled 23 studies (1,658 patients) and found inhaled prostacyclins raised the PaO2/FiO2 ratio from baseline (mean difference 40.35, 95% CI 26.14 to 54.56; p < 0.00001) and PaO2 (mean difference 12.68 mm Hg, 95% CI 2.89 to 22.48), and lowered mean pulmonary artery pressure in the 3 studies measuring it (mean difference −3.67 mm Hg) — all graded very low quality evidence with extreme heterogeneity (I² = 95–96%) and high risk of bias, and almost all of it before-versus-after physiology rather than controlled comparison. The single multicentre randomised trial (Haeberle HA et al., PMID: 36805707) randomised 150 patients with moderate to severe ARDS to inhaled prostacyclin or saline placebo three times daily for 5 days: the primary analysis was negative (oxygenation improved by 20 mmHg more than placebo; p = 0.17), mortality did not differ between groups (the abstract prints no rates), and secondary organ failure and adverse events were similar; a secondary analysis in COVID-19-positive patients showed a 34 mmHg oxygenation advantage (p = 0.04), a subgroup signal, not a primary result. No study in this record shows shorter ventilation or better survival. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): inhaled prostacyclin may raise oxygenation indices in ARDS, but no patient-important benefit has been demonstrated.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — inhaled prostacyclin raises oxygenation indices in uncontrolled series, but the only multicentre randomised trial was negative on its primary endpoint and no survival or ventilation-duration benefit has been shown

title: Remimazolam versus propofol for ICU sedation: non-inferior in two single-blind trials (success 97.5% vs 97.5% and 98.1% vs 96.2%) — the promised fewer hypotensive episodes are not in the record
question: In mechanically ventilated ICU patients, is remimazolam non-inferior to propofol for light-to-moderate sedation, with fewer hypotensive episodes?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — remimazolam sedates as well as propofol in head-to-head trials; the advertised blood-pressure advantage is not in this record. In SHOSREB (Yang X et al., PMID: 41915173), a multicentre single-blind non-inferiority trial in 164 ventilated patients needing light sedation (RASS −2 to +1), successful sedation was 97.5% in both groups (difference 0, 95% CI −6.5% to 6.4%), comfortably inside the −8% non-inferiority margin, with time in target range 88.6% versus 89.4%. In the phase 3 trial (Guan X et al., PMID: 41855428), 211 postoperative ventilated patients had sedation success of 98.1% on remimazolam tosylate versus 96.2% on propofol (difference 1.9%, 95% CI −3.3 to 7.8%), time in target range 95.1% versus 95.0%, and adverse events in 76.4% versus 73.3%, all mild to moderate except one severe event on propofol. The long-term pilot (Tang Y et al., PMID: 36114552; 60 patients ventilated over 24 hours) found time in target range 73.2% versus 82.8% (p = 0.269) with no differences in ventilator-free days, ICU stay, 28-day mortality or adverse events. The meta-analysis of 6 randomised trials (Nakahara S et al., PMID: 42981695; 705 patients) found no significant difference in time within target range (mean difference −0.45%, 95% CI −2.46 to 1.55) nor in sedation success, 28-day or ICU mortality, ICU stay, ventilation duration or safety outcomes — including hypotension — while noting several estimates were imprecise. So the second half of this shelf's question must be answered plainly: fewer hypotensive episodes with remimazolam have not been demonstrated in any abstract-level result here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): remimazolam is non-inferior to propofol for light-to-moderate ICU sedation in single-blind trials, with no demonstrated outcome or hypotension advantage.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — remimazolam was non-inferior to propofol for light-to-moderate ICU sedation in single-blind randomised trials, with no demonstrated reduction in hypotensive episodes

title: Tele-ICU: the randomised studies found no mortality or stay difference — the pooled 'benefit' (OR 0.80–0.82) comes from before–after studies
question: In adult ICUs, does telemedicine coverage (tele-ICU) reduce ICU mortality and length of stay compared with usual on-site care?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the randomised evidence says no difference; the mortality 'benefit' lives in before–after studies at effect sizes this library does not accept from observational data. The 2025 Cochrane-standard systematic review (Pscheidl T et al., PMID: 41397018) found 26 controlled studies covering about 2,164,508 patients, but only three were randomised (one cluster RCT of 15,230 patients and two stepped-wedge trials totalling 5,915): for ICU mortality two found no evidence of a difference and one favoured standard care (very low certainty); ICU length of stay showed no evidence of a difference in the randomised data; heterogeneity prevented any meta-analysis. The positive pooled numbers come from non-randomised designs: the meta-analysis by Kalvelage C et al. (PMID: 33710032; 20 studies, 477,637 patients) found ICU mortality risk ratio 0.82 (95% CI 0.71 to 0.94) only where the remote team held decision-making authority, while consultative tele-ICU showed no advantage and slightly longer ICU stay (mean difference +0.31 days, 95% CI 0.10 to 0.53); and the earliest meta-analysis (Young LB et al., PMID: 21444842) pooled 13 studies that were all before-and-after designs (41,374 patients), finding ICU mortality odds ratio 0.80 (95% CI 0.66 to 0.97) but in-hospital mortality odds ratio 0.82 (95% CI 0.65 to 1.03; P = .08) and no hospital length-of-stay benefit. Ratios of 0.80–0.82 sit inside the 0.5–2.0 band that is not solid evidence for observational associations — and before–after ICU studies are exactly where secular improvement masquerades as intervention effect. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): tele-ICU coverage has not been shown to reduce ICU mortality or length of stay; whether granting the remote team decision-making authority changes that is untested by randomisation.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — tele-ICU coverage has not been shown to reduce ICU mortality or length of stay in randomised studies; the pooled reductions come from before–after studies at effect sizes inside the range treated as not solid for observational evidence

title: Nurse-led ICU follow-up programmes: no gain in quality of life at 12 months in the PRaCTICaL trial (SF-36 physical 42.0 vs 40.8) — and a Cochrane review of five studies agrees
question: After ICU discharge, do nurse-led intensive-care follow-up clinics improve quality of life and reduce post-traumatic stress compared with standard follow-up?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the clinics are well liked and well organised, but the outcomes they were built to move did not move. In PRaCTICaL, 286 ICU survivors randomised to nurse-led follow-up programmes or standard care had indistinguishable SF-36 physical component scores at 12 months (42.0 vs 40.8; effect size 1.1, 95% CI -1.9 to 4.2; P=0.46), with no significant difference in the mental component score or any secondary outcome, and the programmes cost significantly more. The Cochrane review of follow-up services (5 studies, 1,707 participants) found the same pattern: little or no difference in health-related quality of life at 12 months, little or no difference in all-cause mortality (RR 0.96, 95% CI 0.76 to 1.22), and little or no difference in post-traumatic stress (SMD -0.05, 95% CI -0.19 to 0.10). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): nurse-led ICU follow-up, as tested, does not improve quality of life, survival, or PTSD at one year, and costs more than standard care.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — a 286-patient pragmatic RCT and a Cochrane review of five studies both found no improvement in quality of life, mortality, or PTSD from ICU follow-up services

title: Exchanging a dialysis catheter over a guidewire: no more colonisation (5.6% vs 5.6%) but more than double the dysfunction (37.6% vs 15.7%, HR 3.67)
question: In ICU patients needing a temporary dialysis catheter change, is guidewire exchange as safe as new-site placement for infection and dysfunction?
balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — the wire preserves the vein, and on infection it delivers what it promises; the price is a catheter that stops working. In the matched-cohort analysis nested in the ELVIS randomised trial (1,496 ICU adults needing a dialysis catheter), colonisation was identical after guidewire exchange and new-site venipuncture (5.6% in both groups), but dysfunction was far commoner after exchange: 37.6% vs 15.7% (HR 3.67, 95% CI 2.07 to 6.49; p<0.01). The older systematic review of central venous catheter replacement (12 randomised trials) points the same way on infection — trends toward more colonisation (RR 1.26, 95% CI 0.87 to 1.84) and catheter-related bacteraemia (RR 1.72, 95% CI 0.89 to 3.33) with guidewire exchange, offset by fewer mechanical complications (RR 0.48, 95% CI 0.12 to 1.91). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm): guidewire exchange does not increase colonisation, but it more than doubles catheter dysfunction — a harm that costs dialysis sessions even when it costs no infections.
stamp: POSSIBLE (harm) — guidewire exchange of temporary dialysis catheters did not raise colonisation but was associated with over twice the dysfunction (HR 3.67) in a matched analysis of randomised-trial data

title: Ketamine as an adjunct sedative: a meta-analysis finds less opioid use, but the largest blinded trial found none — while delirium fell from 37% to 21%
question: In mechanically ventilated patients, does ketamine as an adjunctive sedative reduce opioid and propofol requirements compared with standard sedation alone?
balance: SPLIT — the opioid-sparing claim splits by which evidence you stand on. The meta-analysis of randomised trials found ketamine regimens reduced opioid consumption (six RCTs, 494 participants; -13.19 µg/kg/h morphine equivalents, 95% CI -22.10 to -4.28; P=0.004), with no difference in sedative consumption, ventilation duration, length of stay, or mortality. But the largest double-blind trial inside that literature found no opioid sparing at all: remifentanil use was 7.9 vs 9.3 µg/kg/h with ketamine versus placebo (P=0.548) under a nurse-driven sedation protocol — while delirium incidence fell from 37% (30/82) on placebo to 21% (17/80) on ketamine (P=0.03). The pilot ATTAINMENT trial (83 patients) found feasibility and similar sedative use, with more patients at goal sedation scores on ketamine. PROPOSED SPLIT: ketamine's opioid-sparing is real in small heterogeneous trials and absent in the best blinded one; its most reproducible signal in that trial was less delirium, an outcome the meta-analysis was not built to judge.
stamp: SPLIT — opioid consumption fell in a meta-analysis of small RCTs but not in the largest double-blind trial, where delirium instead fell from 37% to 21%

title: Terlipressin versus norepinephrine in septic shock: 28-day mortality 40% vs 38% — no survival difference, and serious adverse events 30% vs 12%
question: In septic shock, does terlipressin infusion improve blood pressure, organ function, and survival compared with norepinephrine?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — terlipressin raises blood pressure and spares catecholamines, but in the only large head-to-head trial it did not save lives, and it caused more serious harm. In 617 randomised patients with septic shock across 21 Chinese ICUs (526 in the modified intention-to-treat analysis), 28-day mortality was 40% on terlipressin and 38% on norepinephrine (odds ratio 0.93, 95% CI 0.55 to 1.56; p=0.80), day-7 SOFA change and vasopressor-free days were similar, and serious adverse events were more than twice as common on terlipressin (30% vs 12%; p<0.001). The earlier TERLIVAP pilot (45 patients) showed the pharmacology clearly — open-label norepinephrine requirements at 48 hours of 0.2 µg/kg/min on terlipressin versus 1.2 µg/kg/min on norepinephrine — without any power for outcomes. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): as a first-line infusion, terlipressin matches norepinephrine for survival and organ function while adding serious adverse events.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — a 617-patient double-blind trial found identical mortality for terlipressin and norepinephrine in septic shock, with more serious adverse events on terlipressin

title: High-volume haemofiltration in septic shock with kidney injury: 28-day mortality 37.9% vs 40.8% in IVOIRE — doubling the dose changed nothing
question: In septic shock with acute kidney injury, does high-volume haemofiltration improve survival compared with standard-volume haemofiltration?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — an attractive idea, tested at full dose, with a flat result. IVOIRE randomised 140 patients with septic shock and acute kidney injury to high-volume haemofiltration at 70 mL/kg/h or standard-volume at 35 mL/kg/h for 96 hours; 28-day mortality was 37.9% versus 40.8% (p=0.94), with no significant difference in any secondary endpoint, and the trial stopped early for slow accrual. The meta-analysis of four trials (470 participants) found the same: 28-day mortality odds ratio 0.76 (95% CI 0.45 to 1.29), no significant difference in kidney recovery or lengths of stay, and more hypophosphataemia and hypokalaemia at high volume. The Cochrane review (four trials, 200 participants) pooled a 28-day mortality risk ratio of 0.89 (95% CI 0.60 to 1.32) on low-quality evidence. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): high-volume haemofiltration, as applied in these trials, does not reduce mortality in septic shock with AKI and cannot be recommended for that purpose.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — IVOIRE and two syntheses found no mortality benefit from high-volume over standard-volume haemofiltration in septic shock with AKI

title: ROSE-AHF: neither low-dose dopamine nor low-dose nesiritide added urine or protected the kidney — 72-hour urine 8,524 and 8,574 mL vs 8,296 mL on placebo
question: In acute heart failure with kidney dysfunction, does low-dose dopamine or nesiritide improve kidney function and urine output compared with placebo?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — two beloved 'renal-dose' strategies, tested properly in the same trial, both flat. ROSE randomised 360 hospitalised patients with acute heart failure and an eGFR of 15–60 mL/min/1.73 m² to low-dose dopamine (2 µg/kg/min), low-dose nesiritide (0.005 µg/kg/min), or pooled placebo, each added to diuretic therapy. At 72 hours, cumulative urine volume was 8,524 mL on dopamine and 8,574 mL on nesiritide versus 8,296 mL on placebo (P=0.59 and P=0.49), and the change in cystatin C — the kidney co-primary endpoint — was likewise indistinguishable (dopamine difference 0.01 mg/L, P=0.72; nesiritide difference -0.04 mg/L, P=0.36). No secondary decongestion, renal, or clinical endpoint favoured either drug. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): in acute heart failure with renal dysfunction, neither low-dose dopamine nor low-dose nesiritide enhances decongestion or preserves kidney function when added to diuretics.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — one rigorous 360-patient double-blind trial tested both strategies against placebo and neither improved urine output or cystatin C

title: A statin load before angiography prevents contrast kidney injury in two trials: 6.7% vs 15.1% in acute coronary syndrome, 2.3% vs 3.9% in diabetes with CKD
question: In patients undergoing coronary angiography or PCI, does a high-dose statin beforehand prevent contrast-associated acute kidney injury compared with placebo or low-dose statin?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two randomised trials, two different at-risk populations, the same direction. In PRATO-ACS, statin-naïve patients with non-ST-elevation acute coronary syndrome randomised to high-dose rosuvastatin on admission (40 mg, then 20 mg/day) developed contrast-induced acute kidney injury in 6.7% versus 15.1% without statin (adjusted odds ratio 0.38, 95% CI 0.20 to 0.71; p=0.003), and the 30-day composite of death, dialysis, myocardial infarction, stroke, or persistent renal damage was 3.6% versus 7.9% (p=0.036). In TRACK-D, 2,998 patients with type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease randomised to rosuvastatin 10 mg/day for five days around angiography developed contrast injury in 2.3% versus 3.9% on standard care (p=0.01), with less worsening heart failure at 30 days (2.6% vs 4.3%; p=0.02). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a short rosuvastatin course around contrast exposure reduces contrast-associated kidney injury; the absolute gains are modest where baseline risk is low (1.6 points in TRACK-D) and larger where it is high (8.4 points in PRATO-ACS).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two randomised trials found less contrast-induced AKI with rosuvastatin loading around angiography, with absolute reductions of 8.4 and 1.6 percentage points

title: POSEIDON: letting the left-ventricular filling pressure set the drip rate cut contrast kidney injury from 16.3% to 6.7% (RR 0.41)
question: In patients at risk of contrast-associated kidney injury, does hydration guided by left-ventricular end-diastolic pressure prevent kidney injury better than standard hydration?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one well-conducted trial, a large relative effect, and a mechanism that makes sense: give more fluid to the hearts that can take it, less to those that cannot. POSEIDON randomised 396 patients with eGFR ≤60 mL/min/1.73 m² plus at least one risk factor, undergoing cardiac catheterisation, to hydration titrated to left-ventricular end-diastolic pressure or a standard protocol; contrast-induced acute kidney injury occurred in 6.7% (12/178) of the guided group versus 16.3% (28/172) of controls (relative risk 0.41, 95% CI 0.22 to 0.79; p=0.005) — a 59% relative reduction and 9.6 absolute points. Hydration was stopped for shortness of breath in three patients in each group. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: the result rests on a single trial, and the strategy requires the filling pressure the catheterisation itself provides — it generalises to the cath lab, not to every contrast study.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single randomised trial found LVEDP-guided hydration reduced contrast-induced AKI from 16.3% to 6.7% (RR 0.41)

title: AASK: the drug class separated, the blood-pressure target did not — ramipril cut the kidney composite by 22–38%, the lower target added nothing
question: In Black adults with hypertensive chronic kidney disease, which drug class — ACE inhibitor, beta-blocker, or calcium-channel blocker — and which blood-pressure target best slow kidney progression?
balance: SPLIT — AASK answered its two questions in opposite directions. In 1,094 Black adults with hypertensive kidney disease (GFR 20–65 mL/min/1.73 m²) randomised in a 3×2 factorial design, the lower blood-pressure goal (mean arterial pressure ≤92 mmHg; achieved 128/78) did not slow GFR decline versus the usual goal (achieved 141/85): slopes -2.21 vs -1.95 mL/min/1.73 m² per year (P=0.24), and the clinical composite (GFR halving, kidney failure, or death) differed by 2% (95% CI -22% to 21%; P=0.85). The drug comparison did separate: ramipril reduced the clinical composite by 22% versus metoprolol (95% CI 1% to 38%; P=0.04) and by 38% versus amlodipine (95% CI 14% to 56%; P=0.004), though GFR slopes did not differ consistently by drug. The trial's cardiovascular analysis found 202 cardiovascular events (4.5% per patient-year) with no significant relation to either randomised drug class or blood-pressure goal. PROPOSED SPLIT: ACE inhibition first for the kidney in this population; pushing below the usual target bought no renal protection in AASK.
stamp: SPLIT — in AASK, ramipril beat metoprolol and amlodipine on the kidney composite (22% and 38% relative reductions) while the lower blood-pressure goal conferred no benefit

title: Sibeprenlimab in IgA nephropathy: proteinuria halved at 9 months, and the final analysis shows eGFR slope 0.3 vs -4.2 mL/min per year on placebo
question: In IgA nephropathy at risk of progression, does the anti-APRIL antibody sibeprenlimab reduce proteinuria compared with placebo?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — the APRIL hypothesis, confirmed at every step it has been tested. In the phase 2 ENVISION trial, 12 months of sibeprenlimab cut the 24-hour urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio by 47.2%, 58.8%, and 62.0% at 2, 4, and 8 mg/kg versus 20.0% on placebo, with eGFR changes of -2.7, 0.2, and -1.5 versus -7.4 mL/min/1.73 m². In the phase 3 VISIONARY interim analysis, proteinuria fell 50.2% on sibeprenlimab while rising 2.1% on placebo at 9 months (adjusted ratio 51.2% lower; P<0.001), and the trial's final analysis delivered the kidney-function endpoint: an annualised eGFR slope of 0.3 versus -4.2 mL/min/1.73 m² per year (difference 4.5; P<0.001), with a composite kidney event in 0.4% versus 11.2% (hazard ratio 0.029, 95% CI 0.004 to 0.214). Serious adverse events were no commoner on drug (8.1% vs 12.7% in the final analysis) and no deaths were reported. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): sibeprenlimab halves proteinuria and, over 24 months, essentially flattens eGFR decline in IgA nephropathy at risk of progression.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — phase 2 and phase 3 randomised trials agree: proteinuria roughly halved, and the phase 3 final analysis showed eGFR slope preserved (0.3 vs -4.2 mL/min/1.73 m²/yr)

title: Atacicept in IgA nephropathy: proteinuria down 35% vs placebo at 36 weeks, and the phase 3 final analysis shows eGFR slope -0.6 vs -5.6 per year
question: In IgA nephropathy, does the dual BAFF/APRIL inhibitor atacicept reduce proteinuria compared with placebo?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — the second B-cell-targeting strategy in IgA nephropathy to clear both the proteinuria bar and the eGFR bar. In the ORIGIN phase 2b trial (116 patients), atacicept reduced the urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio by 34% at week 36 while placebo rose 2% — a 35% reduction versus placebo — with galactose-deficient IgA1 down 60% and eGFR stabilised (between-group difference about 5.7 mL/min/1.73 m²). In the ORIGIN 3 phase 3 final analysis (431 randomised), the annualised eGFR slope through week 104 was -0.60 versus -5.60 mL/min/1.73 m² per year on placebo (difference 5.00; P<0.001), composite kidney-disease progression occurred in 5.1% versus 17.8% (hazard ratio 0.24, 95% CI 0.12 to 0.48), and no atacicept patient progressed to dialysis, transplantation, or death versus 7 on placebo. Serious adverse events were fewer on drug (7.0% vs 15.4%). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): atacicept reduces proteinuria and slows eGFR decline over two years in IgA nephropathy.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — phase 2b and phase 3 randomised trials agree: proteinuria reduced by about a third, and eGFR slope preserved by 5.0 mL/min/1.73 m²/yr over 104 weeks

title: Fish oil in IgA nephropathy: one positive 1994 trial (kidney failure or death 10% vs 40% at four years) that the pooled trials never confirmed for kidney function
question: In IgA nephropathy, does fish oil slow the loss of kidney function compared with placebo or control?
balance: SPLIT — the shelf splits between its founding trial and everything pooled since. Donadio's 1994 multicentre placebo-controlled trial (106 patients, fish oil 12 g/day for two years) found a ≥50% creatinine rise in 6% on fish oil versus 33% on olive-oil placebo (P=0.002), and death or kidney failure in 10% versus 40% by four years (P=0.006). But when the same group later randomised 73 patients with severe disease to high-dose versus low-dose omega-3, the doses were indistinguishable (creatinine slope 0.10 vs 0.08 mg/dL per year; P=0.51; kidney failure 8 vs 10 patients), and the meta-analysis of five randomised trials (233 patients) concluded omega-3 fatty acids ameliorate proteinuria but have no beneficial effect on preserving renal function, at any dose. PROPOSED SPLIT: fish oil lowers proteinuria modestly across trials, but the kidney-protection claim rests on a single small 1994 trial whose result the pooled evidence does not confirm — Tier C, because the positive claim is single-trial and includes mortality.
stamp: SPLIT — a single 1994 RCT showed large kidney protection, but the meta-analysis of five RCTs found proteinuria improved and renal function not preserved

title: Tonsillectomy plus steroid pulses in IgA nephropathy: the one randomised trial found no remission benefit — the glowing meta-analysis is built on retrospective studies
question: In IgA nephropathy, does tonsillectomy combined with steroid pulses improve remission and kidney survival compared with steroids alone or supportive care?
balance: SPLIT — the answer splits cleanly by study design. The only multicentre randomised trial (72 patients) compared tonsillectomy plus steroid pulses with steroid pulses alone over 12 months: the percentage fall in proteinuria was significantly larger with tonsillectomy, but the frequency of disappearance of proteinuria, haematuria, or both (clinical remission) was not statistically different between groups, and the authors concluded the added operation had no beneficial effect on haematuria or remission, with the antiproteinuric difference marginal. Against that, the meta-analysis of 14 studies (1,794 patients) — mostly retrospective cohorts — reports far higher odds of clinical remission with tonsillectomy (pooled OR 3.40, 95% CI 2.58 to 4.48) and lower odds of kidney failure (OR 0.25, 95% CI 0.12 to 0.52), including for tonsillectomy plus steroid pulses versus pulses alone (remission OR 3.15, 95% CI 1.99 to 5.01). PROPOSED SPLIT, Tier C: randomised evidence says the operation adds little to steroid pulses; the large observational effects are exactly the size that confounding by indication manufactures, and kidney survival has never been randomised.
stamp: SPLIT — the single RCT found no remission benefit from adding tonsillectomy to steroid pulses, while a meta-analysis dominated by retrospective studies reports remission OR 3.40 and kidney-failure OR 0.25

title: Mycophenolate in IgA nephropathy: the largest trial cut progression from 21.2% to 7.1% (aHR 0.23) — while the meta-analysis of nine earlier trials found nothing
question: In IgA nephropathy with persistent proteinuria, does mycophenolate mofetil reduce proteinuria and slow progression compared with control?
balance: SPLIT — this shelf is two literatures facing each other. The MAIN trial randomised 170 Chinese patients with progressive IgA nephropathy (proteinuria >1 g/day, eGFR 30–60 or persistent hypertension), all after three months of optimised supportive care with losartan, to mycophenolate plus supportive care or supportive care alone for three years: the composite of creatinine doubling, kidney failure, or kidney/cardiovascular death occurred in 7.1% versus 21.2% (adjusted hazard ratio 0.23, 95% CI 0.09 to 0.63), and chronic kidney disease progression in 8.2% versus 27.1% (aHR 0.23, 95% CI 0.10 to 0.57). Yet the meta-analysis of the nine earlier randomised trials (587 patients) found mycophenolate — alone or with low/medium-dose steroid — did not differ from full-dose steroid or placebo on remission, proteinuria, or creatinine, with more infection but less Cushing syndrome and diabetes. PROPOSED SPLIT, Tier C: a single large positive trial in one population against a null pooled literature — the honest stamp is that mycophenolate's benefit in IgA nephropathy is population- and protocol-dependent and unconfirmed outside China.
stamp: SPLIT — the 170-patient MAIN trial found progression cut by three quarters (aHR 0.23), while the meta-analysis of nine earlier RCTs (587 patients) found no significant benefit

title: LUNAR: adding rituximab to mycophenolate and steroids did not significantly raise renal response at one year — 56.9% vs 45.8% (P=0.18), primary endpoint missed
question: In proliferative lupus nephritis, does adding rituximab to mycophenolate and steroids increase complete renal remission compared with mycophenolate and steroids alone?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — a biologically beautiful idea that missed its endpoint. LUNAR randomised 144 patients with class III or IV lupus nephritis to rituximab (1,000 mg on days 1, 15, 168, and 182) or placebo, both on mycophenolate and corticosteroids. At week 52 the overall (complete plus partial) renal response rate was 56.9% on rituximab versus 45.8% on placebo (P=0.18) — a numerical gap carried mostly by partial responses that did not reach significance, so the primary endpoint was not achieved. Rituximab did what it does to blood tests: B cells were depleted in 71 of 72 patients, complement C3 and C4 rose and anti-dsDNA fell significantly, and no rituximab patient needed cyclophosphamide rescue versus eight on placebo. Serious adverse events, including infections, were similar; neutropenia, leukopenia, and hypotension were commoner on rituximab. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference), Tier C: a single trial, and its lesson is that depleting B cells on top of mycophenolate improves serology without proven clinical gain at one year.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the single phase 3 trial missed its primary endpoint (renal response 56.9% vs 45.8%, P=0.18) despite complete B-cell depletion and improved serology

title: Multitarget therapy for lupus nephritis: complete remission 45.9% vs 25.6% with IV cyclophosphamide at 24 weeks — and 65% vs 15% in the earlier class V+IV trial
question: In proliferative lupus nephritis, does multitarget therapy with tacrolimus plus mycophenolate induce remission faster than intravenous cyclophosphamide?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two randomised trials from the same research tradition, both clearly positive on remission, both short. In the 362-patient multicentre trial, multitarget therapy (tacrolimus 4 mg/day plus mycophenolate 1.0 g/day plus steroids) produced complete remission at 24 weeks in 45.9% versus 25.6% on intravenous cyclophosphamide (difference 20.3 percentage points, 95% CI 10.0 to 30.6; P<0.001), with overall response 83.5% versus 63.0% and a median time to response 4.1 weeks shorter; adverse events were similar (50.3% vs 52.5%). In the earlier 40-patient trial in class V+IV disease, complete remission on multitarget therapy reached 50% at 6 months and 65% at 9 months versus 5% and 15% on cyclophosphamide. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): multitarget induction induces remission faster and more often than IV cyclophosphamide in the populations studied — with the standing caveat that both trials are Chinese, the larger one is open-label, and neither follows patients long enough to judge kidney survival or relapse.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two randomised trials found higher complete-remission rates with tacrolimus plus mycophenolate than with IV cyclophosphamide (45.9% vs 25.6% at 24 weeks in the larger)

title: Pegcetacoplan in C3 glomerulopathy: proteinuria down 67.2% vs up 2.9% on placebo at 26 weeks — composite renal endpoint met by 49% vs 3%
question: In C3 glomerulopathy, does the C3 inhibitor pegcetacoplan reduce proteinuria and stabilise kidney function compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a rare-disease trial with an unusually unambiguous primary result. VALIANT randomised 124 adolescents and adults with C3 glomerulopathy or primary immune-complex MPGN (including post-transplant recurrence) to pegcetacoplan or placebo for 26 weeks: proteinuria fell 67.2% on drug while rising 2.9% on placebo, a 68.1% relative reduction (95% CI 57.3 to 76.2). The composite renal endpoint (eGFR stabilisation plus ≥50% proteinuria reduction) was met by 49% versus 3%, and ≥50% proteinuria reduction by 60% versus 5%. In the open-label extension, patients switched from placebo cut proteinuria 53.9% within 26 weeks of starting drug, and the treated group held its 67.2% reduction at week 52. Pegcetacoplan was not associated with more adverse events than placebo; no serious infections from encapsulated bacteria occurred, and one pegcetacoplan patient died of COVID-19 pneumonia. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: one randomised trial in a rare disease, with proteinuria — not kidney survival — as its proven endpoint.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single phase 3 trial in C3 glomerulopathy/IC-MPGN found a 68.1% relative proteinuria reduction and composite renal response in 49% vs 3%

title: Ravulizumab in atypical HUS: complete TMA response in 53.6% of adults and 77.8% of children — from single-arm trials with no comparator
question: In atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome, does the long-acting C5 inhibitor ravulizumab achieve haematological normalisation and improve kidney function?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — dramatic responses in a disease that does not remit on its own, from trials with no control arm. In Study 311, 58 complement-inhibitor-naïve adults with atypical HUS received ravulizumab every 8 weeks: complete thrombotic microangiopathy response (platelet and LDH normalisation plus ≥25% creatinine improvement) was achieved by 53.6%, with platelet normalisation in 83.9%, LDH normalisation in 76.8%, creatinine improvement in 58.9%, and eGFR improvement by at least one stage in 68.1% by day 183; four deaths occurred, none judged treatment-related. In Study 312, 18 naïve children achieved complete response in 77.8% by week 26 and 94.4% by week 50, with a median eGFR increase of 80 mL/min/1.73 m² by week 26 and no deaths or meningococcal infections. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: the evidence is two single-arm phase 3 studies — persuasive against the known natural history of untreated aHUS, but incapable of pricing the drug against eculizumab or of excluding selection effects.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two single-arm phase 3 trials found complete TMA response in 53.6% of adults and 77.8% of children with aHUS on ravulizumab

title: Somatostatin analogues in ADPKD: kidneys grow more slowly on octreotide and lanreotide — but the largest trial found eGFR falling at exactly the same rate
question: In autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease, do somatostatin analogues (octreotide or lanreotide) slow kidney growth and function decline compared with placebo?
balance: SPLIT — the class splits by drug, by trial, and by endpoint. On kidney growth the signal is consistent: in ALADIN, octreotide-LAR limited total kidney volume growth at one year (46.2 vs 143.7 mL on placebo; p=0.032), though the three-year difference was not significant (220.1 vs 454.3 mL; p=0.25); in ALADIN 2, in later-stage disease, octreotide reduced volume growth by 96.8 mL at one year (p=0.027) and 422.6 mL at three years (p=0.002) and cut progression to creatinine doubling or kidney failure (9 vs 21 patients; HR 0.307, 95% CI 0.127 to 0.742; p=0.009), while its GFR-decline difference (0.56 mL/min/1.73 m² per year) was not significant (p=0.295). Then DIPAK 1 — the largest trial, 309 patients — found lanreotide did not slow eGFR decline at all (-3.53 vs -3.46 mL/min/1.73 m² per year; difference -0.08, 95% CI -0.71 to 0.56; P=0.81), even though kidney growth was slower (4.15% vs 5.56% per year; P=0.02), at the cost of loose stools in 91% and hepatic cyst infections in 5.2%. PROPOSED SPLIT: somatostatin analogues reliably slow cyst growth; whether they preserve kidney function is unproven — positive only as a secondary composite in one small octreotide trial, null as the primary endpoint of the large lanreotide trial.
stamp: SPLIT — kidney-volume growth slowed in all three trials, but eGFR decline was unchanged in the largest trial (difference -0.08/yr) and significantly better only on a secondary composite in one small octreotide trial

title: TAME-PKD: metformin was safe and tolerable in ADPKD, but the efficacy signals were not significant — eGFR decline -1.71 vs -3.07 per year in a 97-patient phase 2 trial
question: In autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease, does metformin slow kidney-function decline compared with placebo?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference) — a safety trial that answered its safety question and could not answer the efficacy one. TAME-PKD randomised 97 adults with ADPKD and eGFR above 50 mL/min/1.73 m² to metformin or placebo twice daily for two years, with safety and tolerability as primary outcomes: serious adverse events were similar, gastrointestinal symptom scores stayed low, and dose reductions for intolerance occurred in 21 metformin versus 14 placebo participants (not significant). The secondary efficacy signals leaned toward metformin on function — annual eGFR change -1.71 versus -3.07 mL/min/1.73 m² (mean difference 1.37, 95% CI -0.70 to 3.44) — and against it on growth (height-adjusted kidney volume +3.87% versus +2.16% per year; difference 1.68%, 95% CI -2.11 to 5.62), neither significant. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference): metformin in ADPKD is safe and tolerable at the doses tested; whether it slows progression is unknown and awaits an adequately powered trial.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference) — a single 97-patient phase 2 trial designed for safety found no significant difference in eGFR decline or kidney growth

title: Pravastatin in children and young adults with ADPKD: the composite progression endpoint hit 69% vs 88% on placebo over three years — driven by slower kidney growth
question: In children with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease, does pravastatin slow kidney growth and left-ventricular mass increase compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the only randomised trial of early intervention in paediatric ADPKD, and it met its endpoint. In 110 children and young adults with ADPKD and normal kidney function — all receiving lisinopril — pravastatin versus placebo over three years produced the composite primary endpoint (a ≥20% change in height-corrected total kidney volume, left ventricular mass index, or urine microalbumin excretion) in 69% versus 88% (P=0.03). The driver was kidney growth: a ≥20% rise in height-corrected kidney volume occurred in 46% versus 68% (P=0.03), and adjusted three-year kidney-volume growth was 23% ± 3% versus 31% ± 3% (P=0.02). Left ventricular mass progression (25% vs 38%; P=0.18) and microalbuminuria progression (47% vs 39%; P=0.50) did not differ significantly. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: a single trial, on structural endpoints, in young patients with normal kidney function — it shows early pravastatin slows the anatomical march of ADPKD, not yet that it prevents kidney failure decades later.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single randomised trial in 110 children/young adults found pravastatin slowed kidney-volume growth over 3 years (composite endpoint 69% vs 88%)

title: Kidneys from hepatitis-C-viremic donors: every recipient cured in THINKER (20/20) and MYTHIC (30/30) with direct-acting antivirals — graft function matching HCV-negative kidneys
question: In kidney transplantation, can kidneys from hepatitis-C-viremic donors be used safely when recipients receive direct-acting antivirals?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a discarded organ supply, reclaimed in two prospective trials with a perfect cure record. In THINKER, 20 hepatitis-C-negative recipients of genotype-1 HCV-viremic kidneys received elbasvir-grazoprevir from post-transplant day 3: all 20 achieved HCV cure, complications were transient or manageable, and 12-month eGFR (median 72.8 mL/min/1.73 m²) matched recipients of HCV-negative kidneys (67.2). In the multicentre MYTHIC trial, 30 recipients of HCV-viremic deceased-donor kidneys received 8 weeks of glecaprevir-pibrentasvir starting about day 3: all 30 achieved sustained virologic response, median eGFR at 6 months was 57 mL/min/1.73 m², three developed acute cellular rejection, and one recipient died of sepsis four months after achieving cure — with no severe adverse event judged likely related to HCV or its treatment. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: single-arm trials without randomised comparators — the claim is feasibility and safety of the strategy, and on that claim 50 consecutive cures is strong evidence.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two prospective single-arm trials transplanted HCV-viremic kidneys into 50 uninfected recipients with 100% HCV cure on direct-acting antivirals and good graft function

title: Imlifidase for highly sensitised transplant candidates: 89.5% of positive crossmatches turned negative within 24 hours — and 38.9% then had early antibody-mediated rejection
question: In highly sensitised patients awaiting kidney transplantation, does imlifidase enable transplantation and improve graft outcomes compared with remaining on dialysis or conventional desensitisation?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — imlifidase unquestionably does the thing it is designed to do, for about a day; what happens next is the honest uncertainty. In the international phase 2 Highdes trial, imlifidase converted a positive crossmatch to negative within 24 hours in 89.5% of transplanted, highly sensitised patients (median calculated panel-reactive antibody 99.83%), enabling transplantation that conventional desensitisation could not offer; patient survival was 100% and graft survival 88.9% at 6 months — but donor-specific antibodies rebounded at 3–14 days and 38.9% developed early biopsy-proven antibody-mediated rejection. In the first French real-world series of 9 deceased-donor recipients (cPRA 99–100%, on dialysis a mean of 123 months), all crossmatches turned negative after one injection, five patients had antibody rebound within 14 days (four with clinical or subclinical rejection), and eGFR at about 7 months was 56 ± 22 mL/min/1.73 m² with no graft loss or death. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): imlifidase opens a transplant window for patients with essentially no other route to a deceased-donor kidney; comparative outcomes against remaining on dialysis are untested in any controlled design, and early rejection is the rule's price, not its exception.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — single-arm phase 2 and case-series evidence: crossmatch conversion in 89.5% within 24 hours, graft survival 88.9% at 6 months, early antibody-mediated rejection in 38.9%

title: Clazakizumab for chronic antibody-mediated rejection: the phase 3 IMAGINE trial was stopped for futility — eGFR fell 8.0 points on drug vs 5.2 on placebo
question: In kidney transplant recipients with chronic active antibody-mediated rejection, does the anti-interleukin-6 antibody clazakizumab slow the decline in kidney function compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — a phase 2 promise that phase 3 dismantled. The phase 2 study (10 patients, open-label) had shown eGFR stabilising after clazakizumab (38.1 mL/min/1.73 m² at initiation, 41.6 at 12 months, 38.1 at 24 months) with falling donor-specific antibodies and biopsy inflammation scores — enough to launch IMAGINE, the largest placebo-controlled trial in chronic active antibody-mediated rejection. IMAGINE randomised kidney transplant recipients to clazakizumab 12.5 mg monthly or placebo; its one-year interim analysis (115 patients) showed the trial was unlikely to meet its primary outcome, and it was terminated early. In the final analysis (191 patients), eGFR change at week 52 was -8.0 mL/min/1.73 m² on clazakizumab versus -5.2 on placebo (P=0.959 as reported), and allograft loss or irreversible loss of function occurred in 28.3% versus 22.2% — numerically worse on drug, with no safety concerns and the expected fall in C-reactive protein. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): interleukin-6 blockade with clazakizumab does not slow kidney-function decline in chronic active antibody-mediated rejection, and this shelf stands as the library's record of a phase 2 signal that did not survive randomisation.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the phase 3 IMAGINE trial was terminated for futility; eGFR decline and graft-loss outcomes were no better (numerically worse) than placebo

title: Rituximab added to IVIG for desensitisation: the one randomised trial stopped early at 15 patients — rejection episodes clustered in the IVIG-only arm, but nothing was significant
question: In sensitised kidney transplant candidates, does rituximab plus intravenous immunoglobulin reduce panel-reactive antibodies and improve transplantation rates compared with immunoglobulin alone?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — the randomised evidence for adding rituximab to IVIG is one small trial that was stopped early. Vo AA et al. (PMID: 24770617) randomised 15 highly HLA-sensitised deceased-donor candidates to IVIG plus rituximab or IVIG plus placebo; 13 received transplants, but entry was discontinued after five serious adverse events. No significant difference was seen in donor-specific antibody levels at transplant, and all antibody-mediated rejection episodes occurred in the IVIG-plus-placebo arm (P=0.06), with the two graft losses also in the placebo group; renal function at 6 and 12 months favoured IVIG plus rituximab (P=0.04). The systematic review by Macklin PS et al. (PMID: 25321163) found only two randomised trials among 21 studies of rituximab desensitisation and concluded the evidence in highly sensitised recipients was of limited quality. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): rituximab added to IVIG may prevent antibody rebound and rejection after desensitisation, but the claim rests on a single stopped-early trial of 15 patients.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — one stopped-early randomised trial of 15 patients hints at less antibody-mediated rejection when rituximab is added to IVIG; nothing reached significance
