title: Oxygenated machine perfusion of donor kidneys: fewer graft failures in DCD kidneys in one trial, no gain at all when added briefly before implantation in expanded-criteria kidneys in another
question: In deceased-donor kidney transplantation, does oxygenated hypothermic machine perfusion reduce delayed graft function and improve graft survival compared with static cold storage or standard (non-oxygenated) perfusion?
balance: SPLIT — the answer splits by how and in which kidneys the oxygen is given. In COMPARE (Jochmans I et al., PMID: 33220737), a paired double-blind phase 3 trial in kidneys donated after circulatory death, continuous oxygenated hypothermic machine perfusion did not significantly improve the primary outcome — 12-month eGFR was 50.5 versus 46.7 mL/min/1.73 m2 (mean difference 3.7, 95% CI -1.0 to 8.4; p=0.12) — but graft failure was lower (3 of 106 [3%] versus 11 of 106 [10%]; hazard ratio 0.27, 95% CI 0.07 to 0.95; p=0.028) and severe complications were fewer (11% versus 16%; p=0.032). In Husen P et al. (PMID: 33881456), short end-perfusion with oxygen after static cold storage in expanded-criteria brain-dead-donor kidneys changed nothing: 1-year graft survival was 92.1% versus 93.3% (P=.71), with no significant differences in delayed graft function, primary nonfunction, eGFR, or acute rejection. PROPOSED SPLIT: continuous oxygenation throughout preservation may protect DCD kidneys (secondary outcomes only, primary null); a brief oxygenated reconditioning at the end of cold storage does not help expanded-criteria kidneys.
stamp: SPLIT — continuous oxygenated perfusion in DCD kidneys: primary eGFR outcome null but graft failure 3% vs 10% on secondary analysis; brief end-perfusion after cold storage in expanded-criteria kidneys: no benefit on any outcome

title: Everolimus with reduced-dose calcineurin inhibitor: noninferior to mycophenolate with standard-dose CNI at 12 and 24 months — fewer viral infections, far more patients stopping the drug
question: In de novo kidney transplant recipients, does everolimus with reduced-dose calcineurin inhibitor preserve kidney function without more rejection than mycophenolate with standard-dose calcineurin inhibitor?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — in the TRANSFORM trial (Pascual J et al., PMID: 29752413), 2,037 de novo kidney transplant recipients were randomised to everolimus with reduced-exposure calcineurin inhibitor or mycophenolic acid with standard-exposure CNI. The primary endpoint (treated biopsy-proven acute rejection or eGFR below 50 mL/min/1.73 m2 at month 12) occurred in 48.2% versus 45.1% (difference 3.2%; 95% CI, -1.3% to 7.6%), meeting the 10% noninferiority margin. Cytomegalovirus (3.6% versus 13.3%) and BK virus infections (4.3% versus 8.0%) were less frequent with everolimus, but 23.0% versus 11.9% discontinued the study drug for adverse events. At 24 months (Berger SP et al., PMID: 31152476), noninferiority held (47.9% versus 43.7%; difference 4.2%; 95% CI -0.3 to 8.7), mean eGFR was 52.6 versus 54.9 mL/min/1.73 m2, and discontinuation for adverse events had risen to 27.2% versus 15.0%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): everolimus with reduced CNI exposure matches mycophenolate with standard CNI on efficacy and graft function for two years, trading fewer viral infections for roughly double the drug discontinuations.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — TRANSFORM met noninferiority at 12 and 24 months for rejection-or-low-eGFR; viral infections fewer, adverse-event discontinuations about twice as common

title: Esaxerenone on top of RAS blockade: albuminuria remission 22% versus 4% at one year in phase 3, dose-dependent albuminuria cuts in phase 2 — potassium the price
question: In type 2 diabetes with albuminuric kidney disease, does the mineralocorticoid antagonist esaxerenone reduce albuminuria compared with placebo on top of RAS blockade?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for albuminuria, a surrogate, in Japanese trial populations. In the phase 3 ESAX-DN trial (Ito S et al., PMID: 33239409), 455 patients with type 2 diabetes and microalbuminuria on RAS inhibitors were randomised to esaxerenone or placebo for 52 weeks: albuminuria remission was achieved by 22% versus 4% (absolute difference 18%; 95% CI, 12% to 25%; P<0.001), and the urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio changed by -58% versus +8% (ratio to placebo 0.38, 95% CI 0.33 to 0.44). The earlier phase 2 trial (Ito S et al., PMID: 31248950) found dose-dependent reductions at 12 weeks — 38%, 50%, and 56% at 1.25, 2.5, and 5 mg/day versus 7% on placebo (all P<0.001). The harm is potassium: in phase 3, a serum potassium of at least 5.5–6.0 mEq/L on two consecutive measurements occurred in 9% on esaxerenone versus 2% on placebo, asymptomatic and resolving with dose reduction or discontinuation. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): esaxerenone reliably and substantially reduces albuminuria on top of RAS blockade; no trial here measured kidney failure or cardiovascular outcomes.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two concordant randomised trials show large albuminuria reductions (remission 22% vs 4% at 52 weeks); hyperkalaemia in 9% vs 2%; hard kidney outcomes untested

title: Eplerenone added to an ACE inhibitor: albuminuria down 41–48% versus 7% on ACE inhibitor alone at 12 weeks — the class review confirms the proteinuria effect and doubles hyperkalaemia
question: In diabetic kidney disease, does eplerenone added to an ACE inhibitor reduce albuminuria compared with ACE inhibitor alone?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for albuminuria, over 12 weeks, in the one diabetes-specific randomised trial. Epstein M et al. (PMID: 17699311) randomised patients with type 2 diabetes and albuminuria, all on enalapril, to added eplerenone 50 mg, eplerenone 100 mg, or placebo: at week 12 the urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio had fallen by 41.0% and 48.4% on eplerenone versus 7.4% on placebo (both P<0.001 versus placebo), with significant reductions already at week 4, and incidences of sustained and severe hyperkalaemia not significantly different between arms. The Cochrane review by Chung EY et al. (PMID: 33107592), covering 44 studies and 5,745 participants with proteinuric CKD, found aldosterone antagonists added to ACE inhibitor or ARB may reduce protein excretion (standardised mean difference -0.51, 95% CI -0.82 to -0.20) but probably increase hyperkalaemia (risk ratio 2.17, 95% CI 1.47 to 3.22) and acute kidney injury (risk ratio 2.04, 95% CI 1.05 to 3.97), with effects on kidney failure, death, and cardiovascular events uncertain. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): eplerenone added to an ACE inhibitor reduces albuminuria substantially in the short term; the class price is potassium and kidney-function monitoring, and no hard-outcome benefit is established.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — albuminuria fell 41–48% vs 7% in the diabetes RCT at 12 weeks; class review: proteinuria down but hyperkalaemia risk ratio 2.17; hard outcomes uncertain

title: BI 690517, an aldosterone synthase inhibitor: albuminuria down 39% at the 10 mg dose versus 3% on placebo at 14 weeks, with or without empagliflozin — hyperkalaemia in up to 18%
question: In chronic kidney disease with albuminuria, does the aldosterone synthase inhibitor BI 690517, alone or with empagliflozin, reduce albuminuria compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one phase 2 trial, 14 weeks, a urine surrogate. Tuttle KR et al. (PMID: 38109916) randomised 586 people with CKD (eGFR 30 to <90 mL/min/1.73 m2, urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio 200 to <5,000 mg/g, potassium at most 4.8 mmol/L, all on an ACE inhibitor or ARB) to BI 690517 3, 10, or 20 mg or placebo, after an empagliflozin-or-placebo run-in. Percentage change in first-morning UACR at week 14 was -3% (95% CI -19 to 17) on placebo, -22% (-36 to -7) on 3 mg, -39% (-50 to -26) on 10 mg, and -37% (-49 to -22) on 20 mg monotherapy, with similar reductions when BI 690517 was added to empagliflozin. Investigator-reported hyperkalaemia occurred in 10% (3 mg), 15% (10 mg), and 18% (20 mg) versus 6% on placebo, though 86% of affected participants needed no intervention; adrenal insufficiency was reported in 2% on BI 690517 versus 1% on placebo, and there were no treatment-related deaths. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): BI 690517 dose-dependently reduces albuminuria over 14 weeks, alone or with empagliflozin; this is a single short phase 2 trial and no kidney-outcome data exist yet.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single phase 2 trial: UACR -39% at 10 mg vs -3% on placebo at 14 weeks, similar with empagliflozin; hyperkalaemia up to 18% vs 6%

title: Empagliflozin in stone formers (SWEETSTONE): calcium-phosphate supersaturation down 36% in calcium stone formers and uric-acid supersaturation down 30% in uric-acid stone formers — calcium-oxalate supersaturation unmoved
question: In patients with calcium kidney stones, does empagliflozin reduce urinary supersaturation for calcium stones compared with placebo?
balance: SPLIT — the effect splits by stone chemistry, and it is a two-week urine-chemistry effect, not a stone-prevention result. In the SWEETSTONE trial (Anderegg MA et al., PMID: 39747681), 53 non-diabetic adults with calcium (n=28) or uric acid (n=25) stones were randomised in a double-blind crossover to empagliflozin 25 mg daily and placebo, two weeks each. In calcium stone formers, empagliflozin reduced the relative supersaturation ratio for calcium phosphate (relative difference to placebo -36%; 95% CI -48% to -21%; P<0.001) but not for calcium oxalate or uric acid. In uric acid stone formers, it reduced the uric-acid supersaturation ratio (-30%; 95% CI -44% to -12%; P=0.002) but not the calcium-oxalate or calcium-phosphate ratios. No serious or prespecified adverse events occurred. PROPOSED SPLIT: empagliflozin lowers the supersaturation that drives calcium-phosphate stones (in calcium formers) and uric-acid stones (in uric-acid formers), but leaves calcium-oxalate supersaturation — the commonest stone chemistry — unchanged; whether any of this prevents actual stones is untested.
stamp: SPLIT — by stone type: calcium-phosphate supersaturation -36% relative in calcium formers and uric-acid supersaturation -30% relative in uric-acid formers, but calcium-oxalate supersaturation unchanged; 2-week surrogate, single small trial

title: Allopurinol for hyperuricosuric calcium stones (Ettinger 1986): stone events 0.12 versus 0.26 per patient-year — but the placebo group also improved by 63%, in the only randomised trial
question: In recurrent calcium oxalate stones with hyperuricosuria, does allopurinol reduce stone recurrence compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — from a single small double-blind trial conducted in the 1980s. Ettinger B et al. (PMID: 3534570) randomised 60 patients with hyperuricosuria and normocalciuria and a history of calcium oxalate calculi to allopurinol 100 mg three times daily or placebo. During the study the mean rate of calculous events was 0.12 per patient per year on allopurinol versus 0.26 on placebo, and actuarial analysis showed a significantly longer time before recurrence on allopurinol (P<0.02). The caution is built into the record: compared with their pre-study rates, the placebo group had 63.4 percent fewer calculi (P<0.001) and the allopurinol group 81.2 percent fewer (P<0.001) — most of the apparent improvement happened on placebo too, the 'positive treatment bias' the authors themselves flag in stone-prophylaxis trials that use historical controls. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): allopurinol roughly halved the on-trial stone-event rate in hyperuricosuric calcium stone formers, on the strength of one 60-patient trial; the effect has never been re-tested in a modern randomised trial.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single 1986 trial (n=60): stone events 0.12 vs 0.26 per patient-year, time to recurrence longer (P<0.02); placebo group also improved 63.4% from its pre-study rate

title: Fruits and vegetables versus sodium bicarbonate for CKD acidosis: matched on acidosis correction and eGFR preservation in two trials from one research group — both beat usual care
question: In chronic kidney disease with metabolic acidosis, does a base-producing diet of fruits and vegetables correct acidosis and preserve kidney function as well as sodium bicarbonate?
balance: SPLIT — between the two alkali strategies there is no difference that matters; against usual care, both work. In Goraya N et al. (PMID: 24694986), 108 patients with stage 3 CKD and plasma total CO2 of 22–24 mmol/l were randomised for three years to usual care, sodium bicarbonate, or fruits and vegetables dosed to halve dietary acid: plasma total CO2 fell in usual care but rose with either alkali treatment, urine angiotensinogen rose in usual care but fell with either, and eGFR loss at three years was less with bicarbonate or fruits and vegetables than with usual care, with no separation between the two alkali arms. In Goraya N et al. (PMID: 39990902), 153 patients with stage G1 CKD and normal eGFR were randomised for five years to fruits and vegetables (n=51), matched oral bicarbonate (n=51), or usual care (n=51): five-year acid accumulation was lower in the fruits-and-vegetables (-1.2 [11.0] mmol) and bicarbonate (-1.7 [10.8] mmol) groups than in usual care (5.2 [10.3] mmol, P<0.003), and urine albumin, N-acetyl-β-D-glucosamine, and angiotensinogen excretion were lower in both treated groups. PROPOSED SPLIT: fruits and vegetables match bicarbonate on acidosis and kidney-injury markers wherever the two have been compared head-to-head — the benefit is in giving alkali, not in which form it takes.
stamp: SPLIT — head-to-head: no difference between fruits-and-vegetables and bicarbonate on acidosis or eGFR preservation; versus usual care: both reduce acid accumulation and kidney-injury markers

title: Higher dialysis dose and high-flux membranes (HEMO; MPO): no survival benefit overall in 2,584 randomised patients — the only signal is high-flux in patients with albumin at most 4 g/dL
question: In maintenance haemodialysis, does a higher dialysis dose or a high-flux membrane reduce death and hospitalisation compared with a standard dose and low-flux membrane?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the two definitive randomised trials agree on the main question. In the HEMO Study (Eknoyan G et al., PMID: 12490682), 1,846 patients on thrice-weekly dialysis were randomised in a two-by-two factorial design to standard or high dialysis dose and low-flux or high-flux dialyser: the relative risk of death was 0.96 (95% CI, 0.84 to 1.10; P=0.53) for high versus standard dose and 0.92 (95% CI, 0.81 to 1.05; P=0.23) for high-flux versus low-flux, and none of the main secondary outcomes (cardiac hospitalisation or death, infection hospitalisation or death, albumin fall or death, all hospitalisations) differed significantly. In the MPO study (Locatelli F et al., PMID: 19092122), 738 incident patients randomised to high-flux or low-flux membranes and followed for 3 to 7.5 years showed no significant survival difference overall, but patients with serum albumin at most 4 g/dl had significantly higher survival with high-flux membranes (P=0.032), with a secondary signal in patients with diabetes. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): pushing dose above standard targets, or switching flux, does not reduce death or hospitalisation for the average maintenance haemodialysis patient; the low-albumin high-flux signal is a subgroup finding, not a general rule.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — HEMO: death RR 0.96 for dose and 0.92 for flux, both non-significant, secondaries null; MPO: no overall survival difference, high-flux benefit only in the albumin ≤4 g/dL subgroup

title: Extended-hours haemodialysis (ACTIVE): quality of life unchanged at 12 months — phosphate and potassium lower and fewer medicines, sleep no better, deaths 5 versus 2
question: In maintenance haemodialysis, do extended treatment hours improve phosphate control, blood pressure, and quality of life compared with conventional hours?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — for the outcomes patients feel, in the one large randomised trial. In ACTIVE (Jardine MJ et al., PMID: 28151412), 200 adults on maintenance haemodialysis were randomised to extended weekly hours (at least 24 hours; median achieved 24.0) or standard hours (target 12–15; median 12.0) for 12 months. The primary outcome, change in EQ-5D quality-of-life score, did not differ (mean difference 0.04; 95% CI, -0.03 to 0.11; P=0.29), blood pressure did not differ at study end, and left ventricular mass index in a 95-patient substudy did not differ (mean difference -6.0; 95% CI, -14.8 to 2.7 g/m2; P=0.18). Extended hours were associated with lower phosphate and potassium and higher haemoglobin, and with fewer blood-pressure-lowering and phosphate-binding medicines; five deaths occurred in the extended group and two in the standard group (P=0.44). The prespecified sleep analysis (Liao JL et al., PMID: 29424935) found no significant improvement in overall sleep quality (average intervention effect 0.44, 95% CI -0.01 to 0.89; P=0.053) or the sleep subscale (3.58, 95% CI -0.02 to 7.18; P=0.051). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): doubling weekly dialysis hours buys better phosphate and potassium numbers and a smaller pill burden, but not better quality of life, blood pressure, or sleep over 12 months.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — ACTIVE: EQ-5D difference 0.04 (P=0.29), blood pressure and sleep unchanged; phosphate/potassium lower and medication burden reduced; deaths 5 vs 2 (P=0.44)

title: Probing dry weight in haemodialysis hypertension (DRIP): about 1 kg of extra ultrafiltration lowered ambulatory systolic pressure by 6.6–6.9 mm Hg at 4–8 weeks
question: In haemodialysis patients with hypertension, does probing dry weight with additional ultrafiltration lower ambulatory blood pressure compared with usual care?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one well-conducted randomised trial, eight weeks long. In the DRIP trial (Agarwal R et al., PMID: 19153263), 150 hypertensive haemodialysis patients were randomised to additional ultrafiltration (dry weight probed without extra dialysis time; n=100) or control (physician visits only; n=50). Post-dialysis weight fell by 0.9 kg at 4 weeks, with systolic ambulatory blood pressure changing by -6.9 mm Hg (95% CI, -12.4 to -1.3; P=0.016) and diastolic by -3.1 mm Hg (95% CI, -6.2 to -0.02; P=0.048); at 8 weeks, with dry weight reduced by 1 kg, systolic changed by -6.6 mm Hg (95% CI, -12.2 to -1.0; P=0.021) and diastolic by -3.3 mm Hg (95% CI, -6.4 to -0.2; P=0.037). The combined odds ratio for a systolic reduction of at least 10 mm Hg was 2.24 (95% CI, 1.32 to 3.81; P=0.003). No domain of the kidney-disease quality-of-life survey deteriorated, despite more intradialytic signs and symptoms of hypotension. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): probing dry weight by roughly a kilogram lowers interdialytic ambulatory pressure by about 7/3 mm Hg within two months; whether the gain persists, and at what long-term cost in cramps and access or myocardial stunning, the trial does not say.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single RCT (n=150): ambulatory systolic BP -6.6 to -6.9 mm Hg at 4–8 weeks from ~1 kg dry-weight reduction; more intradialytic hypotension symptoms

title: Intravenous L-carnitine in haemodialysis: 49 randomised trials pooled — no improvement in haemoglobin, erythropoietin dose, or quality of life; LDL and CRP shifts too small or too soft to act on
question: In maintenance haemodialysis, does intravenous L-carnitine improve anaemia, muscle symptoms, cramps, or hypotension compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — two independent meta-analyses of the randomised literature land in the same place. Chen Y et al. (PMID: 24368434) pooled 49 randomised trials (1,734 participants) of L-carnitine in maintenance haemodialysis: no significant differences in haemoglobin (mean difference 0.68 g/dL; 95% CI, 0.14 to 1.50 — an interval the authors read as failing to confirm an anaemia benefit), haematocrit, albumin, or required erythropoietin dose (-0.76 KU/week; 95% CI, -1.75 to 0.23); LDL cholesterol fell slightly (-5.82 mg/dL; 95% CI, -11.61 to -0.04) and C-reactive protein by -3.65 mg/L (95% CI, -6.19 to -1.12), changes the authors call clinically irrelevant (LDL) or of unclear relevance to hard endpoints (CRP). Yang SK et al. (PMID: 24535997), in a separate meta-analysis, found L-carnitine did not improve quality-of-life total score (standardised mean difference 0.76; 95% CI, -0.13 to 1.65; P=0.09), CRP, oxidised LDL, albumin, haemoglobin, cholesterol, triglycerides, or parathyroid hormone, concluding there is no evidence of benefit for inflammation, nutrition, anaemia, dyslipidaemia, or quality of life. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): routine L-carnitine in haemodialysis has no demonstrated benefit on anaemia, erythropoietin requirements, or quality of life; cramps and intradialytic hypotension were never adequately measured in the pooled trials.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — two meta-analyses (49 RCTs in the larger): haemoglobin, erythropoietin dose and quality of life all non-significant; only small LDL/CRP laboratory shifts

title: Nalfurafine for uraemic pruritus: itch, sleep disturbance, and excoriations significantly better than placebo in two pooled trials — a 9.5 mm advantage on a 100 mm itch scale, over 2–4 weeks
question: In haemodialysis patients with uraemic pruritus, does the kappa-opioid agonist nalfurafine reduce itch severity compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a real but modest itch reduction, measured over weeks. Wikström B et al. (PMID: 16251241) report two multicentre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled studies enrolling 144 haemodialysis patients with uraemic pruritus, treated with post-dialysis intravenous nalfurafine or placebo for 2 to 4 weeks: a meta-analytic assessment found statistically significant reductions in worst itching (P=0.0212), itching intensity (P=0.0410), and sleep disturbances (P=0.0003), with improvements in itching (P=0.0025) and excoriations (P=0.0060), and drug-related adverse events of similar type and incidence to placebo. The systematic review by Jaiswal D et al. (PMID: 28270926) pooled the nalfurafine trials and found a 9.50 mm (95% CI, 6.27 to 12.74; P<0.001) greater reduction in itch severity on a 100-mm visual analogue scale than placebo. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): nalfurafine reduces uraemic itch by roughly a tenth of the scale over a few weeks — meaningful for a symptom with few options, but the trials are short, small, and largely from the Japanese development programme where the drug is approved.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two pooled RCTs (144 patients) significant on itch and sleep outcomes; meta-analysis: 9.50 mm greater itch reduction than placebo on a 100-mm scale; follow-up only 2–4 weeks

title: Endovascular fistula creation: 87% physiologically suitable and 84% cumulative patency at 12 months in the single-arm NEAT study — but no randomised comparison with surgical fistulas exists
question: In patients needing a new arteriovenous fistula, does endovascular fistula creation achieve maturation and patency comparable to surgical creation?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference) — the technology works in its own series; the comparison the question asks for has never been randomised. In the NEAT study (Lok CE et al., PMID: 28624422), a prospective single-arm multicentre study of 60 full-analysis-set patients, endovascular fistulas were created in 98%, 87% were physiologically suitable for dialysis within 3 months (mean brachial artery flow 918 mL/min, vein diameter 5.2 mm), functional usability was 64% among participants who received dialysis, and 12-month primary and cumulative patencies were 69% and 84%; 8% had a serious procedure-related adverse event (2% device-related). The meta-analysis by Sun JB et al. (PMID: 36148078), pooling 14 case series and 5 cohort studies with 1,929 patients, found endovascular technique success of 98.00% and maturation of 87.00%, with no statistically significant differences versus surgical fistulas in the three cohort studies reporting procedural success (odds ratio 0.69; 95% CI, 0.04 to 11.98; P=0.80) or maturation (odds ratio 0.73; 95% CI, 0.20 to 2.63; P=0.63) — intervals so wide they exclude neither substantial inferiority nor superiority. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): endovascular creation reliably produces usable fistulas in selected anatomy, but 'comparable to surgery' is an unproven claim resting on non-randomised cohorts.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference) — no randomised comparison exists; single-arm NEAT: 87% suitable, 84% 12-month cumulative patency; cohort comparisons vs surgery non-significant with very wide intervals

title: Exercise for fistula maturation: isometric hand exercise improved maturation (RR 1.56–1.80) and vein diameter (+0.84 mm) in small trials; ordinary isotonic exercise barely moved ultrasound maturation (RR 1.09)
question: After arteriovenous fistula creation, does a programme of hand and arm exercise improve fistula maturation and usable diameter compared with usual care?
balance: SPLIT — it splits by exercise type, and the certainty is low throughout. The Cochrane review by Nantakool S et al. (PMID: 36184076) included nine studies (579 participants) of upper-limb exercise around fistula creation. Compared with no intervention, isotonic exercise may make little or no difference to ultrasound maturation (two studies, 263 participants: risk ratio 1.09; 95% CI, 0.94 to 1.25) but may improve clinical maturation (risk ratio 1.14; 95% CI, 1.02 to 1.27), both low-certainty. Compared with isotonic exercise, isometric exercise may improve ultrasound maturation (three studies, 160 participants: risk ratio 1.56; 95% CI, 1.21 to 2.00) and clinical maturation (risk ratio 1.80; 95% CI, 1.18 to 2.76), with greater venous diameter (mean difference 0.84 mm; 95% CI, 0.45 to 1.23) and inflow-artery blood flow (mean difference 140.62 mL/min; 95% CI, 38.72 to 242.52). The systematic review by Ramanarayanan S et al. (PMID: 36805738) found hand exercise increased distal cephalic vein calibre by 0.24 mm (95% CI, 0.03 to 0.45) overall, and by 0.29 mm (95% CI, 0.11 to 0.47) when restricted to the two randomised trials with independent control groups, and was well tolerated, especially in the first four weeks. PROPOSED SPLIT: isometric hand exercise probably helps maturation modestly; generic isotonic exercise has little measurable effect on ultrasound maturation — all on low-certainty evidence from small trials.
stamp: SPLIT — by exercise type: isometric exercise improves maturation (RR 1.56 ultrasound, 1.80 clinical) and vein diameter (+0.84 mm); isotonic exercise vs none: ultrasound maturation RR 1.09 (non-significant), clinical RR 1.14; low certainty throughout

title: Taurolidine–citrate catheter locks: pooled citrate-lock data favour antimicrobial locks for bloodstream infection, but the one double-blind taurolidine trial missed its primary endpoint and doubled thrombolytic use
question: In haemodialysis patients with central venous catheters, does a taurolidine–citrate lock reduce catheter-related bloodstream infection compared with a heparin lock?
balance: SPLIT — the pooled and the best-blinded evidence point in different directions. The double-blind randomised trial by Solomon LR et al. (PMID: 20207458) assigned 110 haemodialysis patients with new tunneled catheters to taurolidine-citrate or heparin locks: there were 11 bacteraemic episodes on taurolidine-citrate versus 23 on heparin (1.4 versus 2.4 episodes per 1,000 patient-days; P=0.1), no significant benefit for time to first bacteraemia (hazard ratio 0.66; 95% CI, 0.2 to 1.6; P=0.4), fewer Gram-negative infections (0.2 versus 1.1 per 1,000 patient-days; P=0.02) but no difference for Gram-positive organisms — and a greater need for thrombolytic therapy (hazard ratio 2.5; 95% CI, 1.3 to 5.2; P=0.008). The smaller randomised trial by Betjes MG et al. (PMID: 14993498), covering 76 catheters in 58 patients, found catheter colonisation and exit-site infections similar between locks, with four cases of catheter-related sepsis on heparin versus none on citrate-taurolidine, a difference the record does not show to be statistically significant. The meta-analysis by Zhao Y et al. (PMID: 24125729) of 13 citrate-lock trials (1,770 patients) found citrate locks reduced catheter-related bloodstream infection overall (risk ratio 0.39; 95% CI, 0.27 to 0.56), with the advantage confined to antimicrobial-containing citrate locks (including citrate plus taurolidine) rather than citrate alone. PROPOSED SPLIT: antimicrobial citrate locks probably reduce catheter-related bloodstream infection on pooled evidence, but taurolidine-citrate's own double-blind trial was null on its primary endpoint and cost more thrombolytic use.
stamp: SPLIT — pooled citrate-lock meta-analysis favours antimicrobial locks (CRBSI RR 0.39), but the double-blind taurolidine-citrate RCT was null for all-cause bacteraemia (HR 0.66, NS) with more thrombolytic therapy (HR 2.5)

title: Acute peritoneal dialysis versus haemodialysis for AKI: mortality 58% versus 53% and kidney recovery 28% versus 26% in the one head-to-head trial — the Cochrane pool agrees there is little or no difference
question: In acute kidney injury needing dialysis in low-resource or critical-care settings, does acute peritoneal dialysis match haemodialysis for survival and kidney recovery?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — on survival and recovery, the two modalities match wherever they have been compared head-to-head. In Gabriel DP et al. (PMID: 18379555), 120 patients with acute tubular necrosis were randomised to high-volume peritoneal dialysis or daily haemodialysis: mortality was 58% versus 53% and renal function recovery 28% versus 26%, both similar, although delivered weekly Kt/V was lower with peritoneal dialysis (3.6 versus 4.7; P<0.01) and time to recovery of renal function was significantly shorter with peritoneal dialysis. The Cochrane review by Liu L et al. (PMID: 29199769), pooling six studies (484 participants), found peritoneal dialysis probably makes little or no difference to all-cause mortality versus extracorporeal therapy (four studies, 383 participants: risk ratio 1.12; 95% CI, 0.81 to 1.55; moderate certainty) or to kidney function recovery (three studies, 333 participants: risk ratio 0.95; 95% CI, 0.68 to 1.35; moderate certainty), with probably slightly less fluid removal (mean difference -0.59 L/day; 95% CI, -1.19 to 0.01; low certainty) and little or no difference in infectious complications (risk ratio 1.03; 95% CI, 0.60 to 1.78). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): acute peritoneal dialysis is a legitimate substitute for haemodialysis in AKI where machines, water, or vascular access are limiting — accepting somewhat weaker clearance and fluid removal.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — Gabriel RCT: mortality 58% vs 53%, recovery 28% vs 26%; Cochrane: mortality RR 1.12 and recovery RR 0.95, both compatible with no difference (moderate certainty)

title: Antifungal prophylaxis during antibiotic treatment in peritoneal dialysis: fungal peritonitis 0.92% versus 6.45% of treated bacterial-peritonitis episodes with fluconazole; pooled risk ratio 0.28
question: In peritoneal dialysis patients receiving antibiotics for peritonitis, does antifungal prophylaxis prevent fungal peritonitis compared with no prophylaxis?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for the specific, dangerous niche of fungal peritonitis following an antibiotic course. In the randomised trial by Restrepo C et al. (PMID: 20634438), patients in a peritoneal dialysis programme who developed bacterial peritonitis, exit-site infection, or tunnel infection were randomised to oral fluconazole 200 mg every 48 hours throughout antibiotic treatment or no prophylaxis: among bacterial-peritonitis episodes, fungal peritonitis followed in 0.92% of fluconazole-covered episodes versus 6.45% without prophylaxis (p=0.0051), with three occurrences of fungal peritonitis in the prophylaxis group versus 15 in the control group within 30–150 days across the studied infections. The Cochrane review by Campbell D et al. (PMID: 28390069) pooled the randomised evidence: antifungal prophylaxis with oral nystatin or fluconazole, compared with placebo or no treatment, may reduce the risk of fungal peritonitis occurring after an antibiotic course (two studies, 817 patients: risk ratio 0.28; 95% CI, 0.12 to 0.63; low quality evidence). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): covering antibiotic courses with an oral antifungal substantially reduces subsequent fungal peritonitis in peritoneal dialysis; the evidence is two trials and rated low quality, and it does not extend to preventing bacterial peritonitis or preserving the catheter.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — fluconazole RCT: fungal peritonitis after bacterial peritonitis 0.92% vs 6.45% (p=0.0051); Cochrane pool of 2 studies: RR 0.28 (95% CI 0.12 to 0.63), low-quality evidence

title: Vitamin K1 in haemodialysis (VitaVasK): aortic calcification progression 56% lower and coronary 68% lower at 18 months — in a trial stopped early with only 40 of 60 patients analysed
question: In patients on dialysis, does vitamin K supplementation slow the progression of vascular calcification compared with placebo?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — a promising signal from a trial that could not finish. In VitaVasK (Saritas T et al., PMID: 37216675), 60 haemodialysis patients with pre-existing coronary calcification were randomised to standard care alone or with vitamin K1 5 mg orally three times weekly, with calcification progression on CT at 18 months as the hierarchically ordered primary endpoints. Twenty patients dropped out for reasons unrelated to vitamin K1, leaving 23 control and 17 vitamin K1 patients; the trial was stopped early for slow recruitment. Average thoracic aortic calcification progression at 18 months was 56% lower in the vitamin K1 group than control (p=.039); coronary artery calcification progressed significantly within the control group but not within the vitamin K1 group, with average progression 68% lower than control (P=.072 — not significant). Vitamin K1 reduced plasma uncarboxylated matrix Gla protein by 69% at 18 months, and no treatment-related adverse events were noted. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): vitamin K1 may slow vascular calcification progression in haemodialysis, but the entire result rests on 40 analysed patients in an open-label trial stopped early — a hypothesis, not a basis for practice.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — single open-label RCT stopped early, 40 of 60 analysed: aortic calcification progression 56% lower (p=.039), coronary 68% lower (P=.072, NS); imaging surrogate only

title: Early ramipril in children with Alport syndrome (EARLY PRO-TECT): progression hazard ratio 0.51 — not significant in the 22 randomised children, with a clean safety record over 216 patient-years
question: In children with Alport syndrome, does early ramipril delay progression to kidney failure compared with placebo?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — the direction is consistent, the randomised numbers are tiny, and the firmest finding is safety. In EARLY PRO-TECT (Gross O et al., PMID: 32299679), 66 oligosymptomatic children with Alport syndrome were enrolled at 14 German sites; only 22 could be randomised to ramipril or placebo for three to six years, while 44 joined an open-arm comparison. In the randomised arm, ramipril decreased the risk of disease progression by almost half (hazard ratio 0.51; 95% CI 0.12 to 2.20 — not significant), diminished the slope of albuminuria progression, and slowed glomerular filtration decline. Adjusted analysis of the open-label treated children versus untreated children again suggested progression reduced by almost half (0.53; 95% CI 0.22 to 1.29), and Bayesian synthesis combining the data gave a hazard ratio of 0.52 (95% CI 0.19 to 1.39). Safety was the co-primary endpoint and was met: over 216.4 patient-years on ramipril there were no safety issues (adverse event rate-ratio 1.00; 95% CI 0.66 to 1.53). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): early ramipril appears safe in children with Alport syndrome and may halve progression, but the randomised evidence is 22 children and every efficacy interval crosses 1.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — single trial, only 22 randomised: progression HR 0.51 (95% CI 0.12 to 2.20, NS); Bayesian synthesis HR 0.52 (0.19 to 1.39); safety clean (AE rate-ratio 1.00)

title: Nasal mupirocin in peritoneal dialysis carriers: S. aureus exit-site infections cut from 44 to 14 episodes — total exit-site infections and peritonitis not significantly changed
question: In peritoneal dialysis patients, does nasal mupirocin eradication of Staphylococcus aureus carriage reduce exit-site infection and peritonitis compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for staphylococcal exit-site infection specifically, in proven nasal carriers; not for peritonitis. The Mupirocin Study Group trial (PMID: 8959632) screened 1,144 continuous ambulatory peritoneal dialysis patients in nine European centres and randomised 267 confirmed nasal carriers of Staphylococcus aureus to calcium mupirocin 2% nasal ointment or placebo, used twice daily for five days every four weeks for up to 18 months. Nasal carriage fell to 10% on mupirocin versus 48% on placebo. Total exit-site infections were 33 in 1,390 patient-months on mupirocin versus 55 in 1,236 patient-months on placebo (not significant), but S. aureus caused 14 episodes in the mupirocin group versus 44 in the control group (P=0.006); there were no differences in tunnel infection or peritonitis, and no progressive increase in mupirocin resistance over time. The meta-analysis by Tacconelli E et al. (PMID: 14689344), pooling ten studies and 2,445 dialysis patients, found mupirocin reduced S. aureus infections by 68% relative (95% CI, 57% to 76%) overall, with relative reductions among peritoneal dialysis patients of 66% for peritonitis and 62% for exit-site infections. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): in PD patients who carry S. aureus in the nose, periodic nasal mupirocin prevents staphylococcal exit-site infections; the one large trial did not significantly reduce all-cause exit-site infection or peritonitis.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — RCT in 267 nasal carriers: S. aureus exit-site infections 14 vs 44 episodes (P=0.006), total exit-site infections NS, peritonitis unchanged; meta-analysis: S. aureus infections reduced 68% relative across dialysis patients

title: Oral magnesium lowers blood pressure a little — about 2 mmHg systolic at 300 mg a day or more, in two concordant meta-analyses of placebo-controlled trials
question: In adults with hypertension, does oral magnesium supplementation lower blood pressure in a dose-dependent way versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a small, real, dose-related effect. Zhang X et al. (PMID: 27402922), pooling 34 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trials (2,028 participants), found oral magnesium at a median dose of 368 mg/day for a median of 3 months lowered systolic blood pressure by 2.00 mmHg (95% CI 0.43–3.58) and diastolic by 1.78 mmHg (95% CI 0.73–2.82), with a dose–response analysis suggesting 300 mg/day for 1 month is enough to raise serum magnesium and lower blood pressure. Kass L et al. (PMID: 22318649), pooling 22 trials (1,173 participants, mean dose 410 mg/day), found a similar 3–4 mmHg systolic and 2–3 mmHg diastolic fall, larger at intakes above 370 mg/day. Neither meta-analysis reports clinical events, and individual trials were mostly small and short — this is a blood-pressure effect of a few mmHg, not a substitute for antihypertensive drugs. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): oral magnesium lowers blood pressure modestly and dose-dependently, on the pooled evidence of two concordant meta-analyses of placebo-controlled trials.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two concordant meta-analyses of randomised placebo-controlled trials show a small dose-related fall in blood pressure (about 2–4 mmHg systolic) at intakes around or above 300–370 mg/day

title: Nutritional rickets heals best with calcium in the regimen: calcium beat vitamin D alone in Nigeria, and daily vitamin D matched weekly high-dose vitamin D in India
question: In children with nutritional rickets, what vitamin D and calcium treatment regimens heal rickets — daily dosing versus single large (stoss) doses?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for calcium-containing regimens, and for daily vitamin D over no treatment; the daily-versus-bolus question itself is a draw. In the Nigerian randomised trial (Thacher TD et al., PMID: 10451461), 123 children with rickets treated for 24 weeks reached the combined healing endpoint (alkaline phosphatase ≤350 U/L plus near-complete radiographic healing) in 61% on calcium alone and 58% on calcium plus vitamin D, versus only 19% on vitamin D alone (600,000 U intramuscularly, a stoss-style regimen) (P<0.001) — in a population whose dietary calcium intake was very low (median 203 mg/day). In India, Dabas A et al. (PMID: 35550679) randomised 132 children to daily vitamin D3 2,000 IU for 12 weeks or weekly 60,000 IU for 3 or 6 weeks: complete radiological healing at 12 weeks was 75% with daily dosing versus 60.5% and 61.9% with the weekly regimens, a non-significant difference (P=0.15). No trial here tested a single one-off oral stoss dose against daily dosing head-to-head. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): where dietary calcium is low, calcium (with or without vitamin D) heals rickets far better than vitamin D alone; daily and weekly high-dose vitamin D regimens heal at similar rates.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — calcium-containing regimens healed rickets in 58–61% versus 19% for vitamin D alone in one randomised trial, and daily vitamin D matched weekly high-dose vitamin D in a second; no direct single-dose stoss trial was found

title: High-dose multivitamins at the start of HIV treatment made no difference to progression or death — and raised liver enzymes; the pre-treatment-era mortality signal did not survive the ART era
question: In adults starting antiretroviral therapy for HIV, does high-dose multivitamin supplementation reduce disease progression or death versus standard-dose multivitamins?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — for the question as asked, in the treatment era. Isanaka S et al. (PMID: 23073950) randomised 3,418 adults initiating HAART in Tanzania to high-dose versus standard-dose multivitamins (B complex, C, and E) for 24 months: the absolute risk of HIV progression or death was 72% in both groups (risk ratio 1.00; 95% CI 0.96–1.04), with no effect on CD4 count, viral load, BMI, or haemoglobin — and the trial was stopped early because high-dose supplementation increased alanine transaminase elevations (risk ratio 1.44; 95% CI 1.11–1.87). The older, pre-HAART-era trial by Jiamton S et al. (PMID: 14600517) in Bangkok (481 patients, 48 weeks) found a lower death rate on multiple micronutrients that was not significant overall (hazard ratio 0.53; 95% CI 0.22–1.25; P=0.1), with significant subgroup signals only at CD4 counts below 200 and below 100. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): at ART initiation, high-dose multivitamins do not reduce progression or death compared with standard-dose, and they carry a liver-enzyme price.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — in 3,418 adults starting HAART, high-dose versus standard-dose multivitamins gave identical progression-or-death risk (72% vs 72%; RR 1.00) with more ALT elevations (RR 1.44)

title: Vitamin A for extremely-low-birth-weight infants: death or chronic lung disease in 55% versus 62% — one extra survivor without lung disease for every 14–15 treated
question: In extremely-low-birth-weight infants, does vitamin A supplementation reduce chronic lung disease (bronchopulmonary dysplasia) and death versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a slight but real reduction in the composite of death or chronic lung disease. In the NICHD Neonatal Research Network trial (Tyson JE et al., PMID: 10379020), 807 extremely-low-birth-weight infants needing respiratory support received intramuscular vitamin A 5,000 IU three times a week for four weeks or sham treatment: death or chronic lung disease at 36 weeks' postmenstrual age occurred in 55% versus 62% (relative risk 0.89; 95% CI 0.80–0.99) — one additional infant survived without chronic lung disease for every 14 to 15 treated — while death alone was 15% versus 14%, essentially unchanged. The Cochrane review by Darlow BA et al. (PMID: 21975731; 9 trials) found the same pattern: oxygen requirement at 36 weeks reduced (risk ratio 0.87; 95% CI 0.77–0.98; number needed to treat 13) and death or oxygen requirement at one month reduced (risk ratio 0.93; 95% CI 0.88–0.99), with no difference in neurodevelopment at 18–22 months in the largest trial. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): vitamin A slightly reduces chronic lung disease in extremely-low-birth-weight infants; it does not reduce death on its own.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — death or chronic lung disease 55% vs 62% (RR 0.89) in the 807-infant NICHD trial, confirmed in direction by a 9-trial Cochrane review; death alone unchanged

title: Ferric maltol in IBD iron-deficiency anaemia: haemoglobin up 2.25 g/dL more than placebo at 12 weeks, normalised in two-thirds — one trial programme, in patients who had already failed ordinary oral iron
question: In adults with inflammatory bowel disease and iron-deficiency anaemia who do not tolerate standard oral iron, does ferric maltol correct anaemia versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a clear haemoglobin effect in a single phase 3 programme. Gasche C et al. (PMID: 25545376) randomised 128 patients with quiescent or mild-to-moderate ulcerative colitis or Crohn's disease and mild-to-moderate iron-deficiency anaemia, all with documented failure on previous oral ferrous products, to ferric maltol 30 mg twice daily or placebo for 12 weeks: haemoglobin rose by a mean of 2.25 g/dL (SE 0.19) more than placebo at week 12 (P<0.0001), with significant separation already at week 4 (1.04 g/dL), and haemoglobin normalised in two-thirds of patients by week 12; the safety profile was comparable to placebo with no impact on IBD severity. In the open-label extension (Schmidt C et al., PMID: 27237709), haemoglobin gains were maintained to week 64 (rise of 3.07 g/dL from baseline in those continued on ferric maltol), with normal haemoglobin in 89% of continued and 83% of switched patients — but with no placebo comparator after week 12. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): ferric maltol corrects iron-deficiency anaemia in IBD patients who failed ferrous iron, on one randomised trial plus its extension.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — haemoglobin rose 2.25 g/dL more than placebo at 12 weeks in the single AEGIS phase 3 trial (n=128), with gains maintained in an uncontrolled 52-week extension

title: Low-dose iron after blood donation: haemoglobin recovery in about a month instead of five — and low-haemoglobin deferral cut to a third in the pooled trials
question: In regular blood donors, does low-dose iron supplementation prevent iron deficiency and donor deferral versus placebo?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — for recovery of haemoglobin and iron stores after donation, with more minor side effects as the price. In the STRIDE randomised trial (Kiss JE et al., PMID: 25668261), 215 donors took ferrous gluconate (37.5 mg elemental iron) daily or no iron for 24 weeks after donating a unit of whole blood: time to recover 80% of the haemoglobin lost was a mean of 32 days versus 158 days in low-ferritin donors (≤26 ng/mL) and 31 versus 78 days in higher-ferritin donors, and without iron 67% of participants had not recovered their iron stores by 168 days. The Cochrane review by Smith GA et al. (PMID: 24990381; 30 trials, 4,704 participants) found iron supplementation cut deferral for low haemoglobin to a risk ratio of 0.34 (95% CI 0.21–0.55) at the first donation after starting iron and 0.25 (95% CI 0.15–0.41) at subsequent donations, with higher haemoglobin (mean difference 2.36 g/L) and ferritin (mean difference 13.98 ng/mL) — and more adverse effects (risk ratio 1.60; 95% CI 1.23–2.07). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): low-dose iron after donation speeds haemoglobin and iron-store recovery and prevents deferral.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — a randomised trial and a 30-trial Cochrane review agree: faster haemoglobin recovery (32 vs 158 days in low-ferritin donors) and deferral risk ratio 0.34, at the cost of more minor adverse effects (RR 1.60)

title: Folinic acid for language impairment in autism: verbal communication improved by 5.7 standardised points in one small trial — strongest in children with folate-receptor autoantibodies
question: In children with autism spectrum disorder and language impairment, does folinic acid (leucovorin) improve verbal communication versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — from a single small trial, with a plausible responder subgroup. Frye RE et al. (PMID: 27752075) randomised 48 children with non-syndromic autism and language impairment to high-dose folinic acid (2 mg/kg/day, maximum 50 mg/day) or placebo for 12 weeks: verbal communication improved by 5.7 standardised points more on folinic acid (95% CI 1.0–10.4; Cohen's d=0.70), and by 7.3 points (95% CI 1.4–13.2; d=0.91) in children positive for folate receptor-α autoantibodies, with no significant difference in adverse effects. The systematic review by Rossignol DA et al. (PMID: 34834493) found 21 leucovorin studies in autism — only four of them placebo-controlled — reporting improvements in communication with medium-to-large effect sizes, alongside mostly mild adverse effects (agitation or excitement 11.7%, aggression 9.5%, insomnia 8.5%). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): promising, FRAA-guided, and still resting on one small randomised trial.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one small double-blind trial (n=48) found a 5.7-point verbal-communication advantage (d=0.70), larger in folate-receptor-autoantibody-positive children (7.3 points, d=0.91)

title: Doubling third-trimester choline sped up infants' information processing — in a controlled-feeding trial of 26 women; the attention benefit was still visible at age 7 in the 20 children followed
question: In healthy pregnant women, does higher-dose choline supplementation in the third trimester improve infant information-processing speed versus standard intake?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — a genuine randomised signal from a very small, tightly controlled trial. Caudill MA et al. (PMID: 29217669) randomised 26 women entering the third trimester to 480 mg choline/day or 930 mg/day until delivery, with all food provided: infants of the 930 mg group had significantly faster mean reaction times (information-processing speed) averaged across testing at 4, 7, 10, and 13 months (24 infants tested), and within the 480 mg group, longer exposure predicted faster reaction times. In the 7-year follow-up (Bahnfleth CL et al., PMID: 34962672), 20 children from the same trial were tested on a sustained-attention task: the 930 mg group performed superiorly on the primary endpoint (P=0.02) and maintained correct detections across the session (P=0.02), while the 480 mg group showed a 22.9% decline in hits for the briefest signals versus a 1.5% increase in the 930 mg group (P=0.04). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): one small trial and its own follow-up point the same way, but 26 mothers is a narrow base for advice to all pregnant women.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — one controlled-feeding RCT of 26 women found faster infant processing speed with 930 vs 480 mg choline/day, with a sustained-attention advantage persisting at age 7 in 20 children

title: Vitamin D repletion in type 2 diabetes: HbA1c lower by 0.30 percentage points across 24 controlled trials — a small average gain, with the deficiency-specific trial evidence still pilot-sized
question: In adults with type 2 diabetes and documented vitamin D deficiency, does vitamin D repletion improve glycaemic control (HbA1c) versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — small, and not yet proven to be a deficiency-only effect. Mirhosseini N et al. (PMID: 28957454) pooled 24 controlled trials (1,528 people with type 2 diabetes): vitamin D supplementation reduced HbA1c by a mean difference of 0.30 percentage points (95% CI −0.45 to −0.15; P<0.001), fasting glucose by 4.9 mg/dL (95% CI −8.1 to −1.6), and HOMA-IR by 0.66 (95% CI −1.06 to −0.26), while raising serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D by about 17 ng/mL; the authors note a minimum dose of 100 µg/day (4,000 IU/day) in the trials showing these effects. The deficiency-specific randomised pilot by Upreti V et al. (PMID: 29580871) — 60 patients with type 2 diabetes and hypovitaminosis D, 6 months — found within the supplemented group a fall in HbA1c from 7.29% to 7.02% (P=0.01) and in fasting glucose from 131.4 to 102.6 mg/dL (P=0.04), though the abstract reports within-group rather than between-group comparisons. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): repletion improves glycaemic measures modestly on average; whether deficient patients gain more is plausible but under-tested.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a 24-trial meta-analysis found HbA1c 0.30 points lower with vitamin D; the one deficiency-specific placebo-controlled pilot (n=60) was positive within-group but small

title: Weekly vitamin A in pregnancy: maternal deaths cut by about 40% in Nepal — and no effect at all in Ghana's 207,000-woman trial; the answer splits by setting
question: In pregnant women in a vitamin-A-deficient population, does weekly low-dose vitamin A or beta-carotene supplementation reduce maternal mortality versus placebo?
balance: SPLIT — the two large trials flatly disagree. In Nepal (West KP Jr et al., PMID: 10037634; NNIPS-2), 44,646 women received weekly vitamin A (7,000 µg retinol equivalents), beta-carotene (42 mg), or placebo for over 3.5 years: pregnancy-related mortality was 704 per 100,000 pregnancies on placebo versus 426 on vitamin A (relative risk 0.60; 95% CI 0.37–0.97) and 361 on beta-carotene (relative risk 0.51; 95% CI 0.30–0.86) — reductions of 40% and 49%, with the maternal mortality ratio falling from 645 to 385 per 100,000 live births on combined supplementation. In Ghana (Kirkwood BR et al., PMID: 20435345; ObaapaVitA), 207,781 women received weekly vitamin A (25,000 IU) or placebo: pregnancy-related deaths were 348 versus 377 per 100,000 pregnancies (adjusted odds ratio 0.92; 95% CI 0.73–1.17; P=0.51) and all-cause female mortality was identical (rate ratio 1.01; 95% CI 0.93–1.09). PROPOSED SPLIT: a large mortality benefit in the deficient Nepali population, none in Ghana — baseline deficiency, dose, and setting appear to decide the answer.
stamp: SPLIT — pregnancy-related mortality fell ~40% with weekly vitamin A/beta-carotene in Nepal (RR 0.60/0.51) but was unchanged in Ghana (OR 0.92); the effect splits by population and setting

title: Magnesium oxide for chronic constipation: overall improvement in 68.3% versus 11.7% on placebo at 28 days — matching senna (69.2%) in the only head-to-head placebo-controlled trial
question: In adults with chronic constipation, does magnesium oxide improve bowel movements and quality of life versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — from one well-run 28-day trial. Morishita D et al. (PMID: 32969946) randomised 90 adults with chronic idiopathic constipation to senna 1.0 g, magnesium oxide 1.5 g, or placebo daily for 28 days: the response rate for overall improvement was 68.3% on magnesium oxide and 69.2% on senna versus 11.7% on placebo (P<0.0001); changes in spontaneous bowel movements and complete spontaneous bowel movements were significantly greater on both active treatments than placebo (P<0.001 and P<0.01), constipation quality-of-life scores improved significantly on magnesium oxide (P<0.001), and severe treatment-related adverse events were 0%. The systematic review by Kang SJ et al. (PMID: 34642269) of 23 randomised trials of laxatives in elderly patients likewise found magnesium-based osmotic laxatives among the agents more effective than placebo in the short term, with adverse-effect frequency and severity similar between arms. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): magnesium oxide is an effective short-term osmotic laxative, on a single placebo-controlled trial supported by the elderly-laxative review literature.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one double-blind placebo-controlled trial (n=90) found overall improvement in 68.3% on magnesium oxide vs 11.7% on placebo over 28 days, equal to senna

title: Vitamin D for chronic musculoskeletal pain: pain scores fell a little more than placebo on change-score analysis (−0.57) but not on final scores (−0.06) — a small, analysis-dependent signal
question: In adults with chronic musculoskeletal pain, does vitamin D supplementation reduce pain versus placebo?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — the signal depends on how the trials are pooled. Wu Z et al. (PMID: 27676659), pooling 19 randomised trials (3,436 participants), found a significantly greater mean decrease in pain score with vitamin D than placebo (mean difference −0.57; 95% CI −1.00 to −0.15; P=0.007) in the 8 trials reporting change scores — but no difference in mean pain score at final follow-up (mean difference −0.06; 95% CI −0.44 to 0.33; P=0.78) across 14 studies, and a non-significant relative risk of 1.38 (95% CI 0.93–2.05) for reported pain improvement. Yong WC et al. (PMID: 28812209), pooling 4 trials (287 subjects) in chronic widespread pain and fibromyalgia, found lower visual analogue pain scores with vitamin D (mean difference 0.46; 95% CI 0.09–0.89, favouring treatment). In the small fibromyalgia trial by Wepner F et al. (PMID: 24438771), 30 women with low calcifediol randomised to cholecalciferol titrated to 32–48 ng/mL for 20 weeks showed a significant group effect on pain scores versus placebo. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): a small average pain reduction is possible, concentrated in patients with pre-existing pain, but the evidence is fragile to analysis choice.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — change-score pooling favours vitamin D (−0.57 points) while final-score pooling is null (−0.06); a 4-trial widespread-pain meta-analysis and one small fibromyalgia trial lean positive

title: Home blood-pressure telemonitoring with pharmacist case management: control in 57.2% versus 30.0% at 12 months — and the advantage persisted 6 months after the intervention stopped
question: In adults with uncontrolled hypertension, does home blood-pressure telemonitoring combined with pharmacist case management improve blood-pressure control versus usual care?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — two randomised trials of the same model, a decade apart, agree. In the HyperLink cluster trial (Margolis KL et al., PMID: 23821088), 450 adults with uncontrolled blood pressure in 16 Minnesota clinics received home telemonitoring with pharmacist case management or usual care: blood pressure was controlled at both 6 and 12 months in 57.2% versus 30.0% (P=0.001), systolic pressure fell 9.7 mmHg more than usual care at 12 months (P<0.001), and at 18 months — six months after the intervention stopped — control remained higher at 71.8% versus 57.1% (P=0.003). In the earlier e-BP trial (Green BB et al., PMID: 18577730), 778 patients randomised to home monitoring plus web-based pharmacist care achieved control in 56% versus 31% on usual care (P<0.001), while home monitoring with web training but no pharmacist did not significantly improve control (36% versus 31%; P=0.21). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): the pharmacist acting on transmitted home readings is the ingredient that doubles control rates.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — two concordant RCTs: BP control 57.2% vs 30.0% (HyperLink) and 56% vs 31% (e-BP) with pharmacist case management on home readings; monitoring without the pharmacist was not effective

title: The Diabetes Prevention Program in the real world: about 4% of body weight lost at 12 months survives translation — roughly half the trial's punch, and more with every session attended
question: When the Diabetes Prevention Program lifestyle intervention is translated into community and primary-care settings, how much weight loss and diabetes prevention survives the move?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — attenuated but real. Ali MK et al. (PMID: 22232096) pooled 28 US studies translating the Diabetes Prevention Program lifestyle intervention into real-world settings: average weight change at 12 months was a loss of about 4% of baseline weight, similar whether programmes were delivered by clinically trained professionals or lay educators, and each additional lifestyle session attended added 0.26 percentage points of weight loss. Dunkley AJ et al. (PMID: 24652723) pooled 25 translational studies (22 in the primary weight analysis) and found a mean weight loss of 2.12 kg at 12 months (95% CI −2.61 to −1.63; I²=91.4%), with greater weight loss where programmes adhered more closely to international guideline recommendations (0.3 kg more per point on a 12-point adherence scale). Neither meta-analysis could pool diabetes incidence the way the original trial reported it, so the 'prevention survives' half of the question rests on weight loss as the standing surrogate. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): translated programmes deliver roughly half the original trial's weight loss, reliably, and fidelity plus attendance are the levers that protect it.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two meta-analyses of translated DPP programmes found ~4% body-weight loss (Ali) and 2.12 kg (Dunkley) at 12 months, with high heterogeneity and diabetes incidence not poolable

title: Reciprocal peer support beat nurse care management on HbA1c by 0.58 points at 6 months in veterans — but the wider peer-support literature improves control in only a minority of trials
question: In veterans with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes, does reciprocal peer support — patients paired to support each other — improve glycaemic control versus nurse care management?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — proven in one well-run trial against an active comparator, unproven as a class. Heisler M et al. (PMID: 20956707) randomised 244 male veterans with HbA1c above 7.5% to reciprocal peer support (paired peers, weekly telephone contact, optional group sessions) or nurse care management: at 6 months HbA1c fell by 0.29 points in the peer group and rose by 0.29 points under nurse management — a between-group difference of 0.58 points (P=0.004) — and among those starting above 8.0% the peer group fell 0.88 points versus 0.07 (difference 0.81; P<0.001); blood pressure, self-reported adherence, and distress did not differ. The systematic review by Dale JR et al. (PMID: 22804713; 25 studies, 14 randomised or comparative trials) found peer support improved glycaemic control in only 3 of 14 trials, with no consistent pattern by model of support. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the reciprocal, paired model worked in its trial; generic 'peer support' should not inherit the claim.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one RCT (n=244) found HbA1c 0.58 points better with reciprocal peer support than nurse care management; a 25-study review found glycaemic improvement in only 3 of 14 trials overall

title: Reminder packaging works on the pill count: 11% more pills taken in the Cochrane pooling — with diastolic pressure and HbA1c gains in the few trials that measured them, and huge heterogeneity throughout
question: Does reminder packaging for medicines — calendar blister packs and pill organisers with date cues — improve adherence versus ordinary bottles?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for adherence itself; clinical spillovers are thinner. Mahtani KR et al. (PMID: 21901694), in the Cochrane review of reminder packaging (12 studies, 2,196 participants), found reminder packaging increased the percentage of pills taken by a mean difference of 11% (95% CI 6–17) across six intervention groups in four trials — with notable heterogeneity (I²=96.3%) — while self-reported adherent-patient proportions did not significantly change (odds ratio 0.89; 95% CI 0.56–1.40). In the two trials measuring each clinical outcome, diastolic blood pressure fell by 5.89 mmHg (95% CI −6.70 to −5.09) and HbA1c by 0.72 points (95% CI −0.83 to −0.60), with no effect on systolic pressure. The wider Cochrane adherence review by Nieuwlaat R et al. (PMID: 25412402; 182 randomised trials) is the cautionary frame: even the most effective adherence interventions did not lead to large improvements, and only 5 of the 17 lowest-bias trials improved both adherence and clinical outcomes. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): dated packaging makes people take measurably more of their medicine; expect modest, not transformative, clinical gains.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — Cochrane pooling found 11% more pills taken with reminder packaging (heterogeneity I²=96.3%), with diastolic BP and HbA1c gains in the few trials measuring them

title: The New Medicine Service: adherence 71% versus 61% at 10 weeks with a pharmacist follow-up — an advantage that faded to non-significance by 26 weeks
question: In people starting a new medicine for a long-term condition, does a community-pharmacist follow-up service (the New Medicine Service) improve adherence versus usual pharmacy care?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — early, with fading. Elliott RA et al. (PMID: 26647412) randomised 504 people starting a new medicine for asthma/COPD, hypertension, type 2 diabetes, or anticoagulation/antiplatelet therapy in 46 English community pharmacies to the New Medicine Service (pharmacist consultations 7–14 days and 14–21 days after starting) or normal practice: at 10 weeks, self-reported adherence was 71% with the service versus 61% without (adjusted odds ratio 1.67; 95% CI 1.06–2.62; P=0.027), with a non-significant NHS cost saving of £21 per patient. At the 26-week follow-up (Elliott RA et al., PMID: 31732700), adherence was 65.6% versus 57.1% unadjusted, but the adjusted odds ratio of 1.50 (95% CI 0.93–2.44; P=0.095) was no longer significant, with attrition a stated concern; modelling suggested an 89% probability of cost-effectiveness at £20,000 per quality-adjusted life-year, with high uncertainty. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a real early adherence gain from two brief pharmacist consultations, durability unproven.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one pragmatic RCT (n=504): adherence OR 1.67 at 10 weeks, attenuating to a non-significant OR 1.50 at 26 weeks

title: Medication reconciliation finds discrepancies — most of them harmless: the systematic review and the big pharmacist RCT agree it does not, by itself, cut errors that hurt patients or post-discharge utilisation
question: Does structured medication reconciliation at admission, transfer, and discharge reduce medication errors and adverse drug events versus usual care?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — for patient-level outcomes, on the evidence as it stands. Kwan JL et al. (PMID: 23460096) reviewed 18 studies of 20 hospital-based medication-reconciliation interventions (pharmacist-led in 17 of 20) and concluded that most unintentional discrepancies identified had no clinical significance, and that medication reconciliation alone probably does not reduce post-discharge hospital utilisation, though it may do so when bundled with broader care-transition interventions. In the PILL-CVD randomised trial (Kripalani S et al., PMID: 22751755), 851 patients discharged after acute coronary syndromes or heart failure received pharmacist-assisted reconciliation plus counselling and follow-up or usual care: 50.8% had at least one clinically important medication error within 30 days regardless, and the intervention did not significantly change errors per patient (incidence rate ratio 0.92; 95% CI 0.77–1.10) or adverse drug events (1.09; 95% CI 0.86–1.39), with only a trend toward fewer potential adverse drug events (0.80; 95% CI 0.61–1.04). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): reconciliation reliably finds discrepancies, but most are trivial, and no reduction in clinically important errors or utilisation has been shown for reconciliation alone.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — a systematic review and an 851-patient RCT agree: reconciliation finds mostly trivial discrepancies and does not significantly reduce clinically important errors (IRR 0.92) or adverse drug events (IRR 1.09) by itself

title: Teach-back discharge education: 30-day readmission odds nearly halved in a five-study review (OR 0.55) — but the studies were few, small, and at high risk of selection bias
question: In patients discharged with heart failure, does discharge education using the teach-back method reduce 30-day readmission versus standard discharge education?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — a large-looking effect on a thin base. Oh EG et al. (PMID: 30882616) reviewed experimental studies of discharge education with the teach-back method (5 studies: 3 in heart failure, 1 in total joint replacement, 1 in coronary artery bypass grafting): across the 3 studies pooled, the odds ratio for 30-day readmission with teach-back versus usual care was 0.55 (95% CI 0.34–0.91; P=0.02), described by the authors as a 45% relative reduction in readmission odds — but the included studies were few and showed a high risk of selection bias. The earlier systematic review by Ha Dinh TT et al. (PMID: 26878928) of teach-back in chronic-disease education (12 studies) found improved disease-specific knowledge in 4 studies and significant self-efficacy gains in 2 (P=0.0026 and P<0.001), while 5 studies found reductions in readmission or hospitalisation that were not always statistically significant, and the single heart-failure quality-of-life study was null (P=0.59). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): teach-back is cheap, safe, and plausibly reduces readmissions — the heart-failure-specific claim awaits a proper randomised trial.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — pooled OR 0.55 for 30-day readmission across 3 small studies at high risk of selection bias; broader teach-back evidence is positive but inconsistent

title: Automatic referral plus a liaison conversation: cardiac-rehab enrolment in 73.5% versus 29.0% with usual referral — the referral system, not the patient, was the barrier
question: After a cardiac event, do systematic referral strategies — automatic referral plus a liaison visit — increase cardiac-rehabilitation enrolment versus usual physician referral?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for enrolment, from a large prospective controlled comparison. Grace SL et al. (PMID: 21325114) followed 2,635 inpatients with coronary artery disease at 11 Ontario hospitals using four referral strategies: combined automatic referral (discharge order or electronic record) plus a liaison discussion achieved 85.8% referral and 73.5% enrolment (odds ratio 8.41 versus usual care), ahead of automatic only (70.2% referral, 60.0% enrolment; OR 3.27) and liaison only (59.0%, 50.6%; OR 3.35), versus usual referral at 32.2% and 29.0%; among referred patients, attendance did not differ by strategy (mean 82.87% of classes). The Cochrane review by Karmali KN et al. (PMID: 24963623) of interventions to promote cardiac-rehabilitation uptake (10 studies, 1,338 participants) found 8 of 10 studies increased uptake, with successful interventions including structured nurse- or therapist-led contacts, early appointments, and motivational letters. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): systematising referral roughly doubles-to-triples enrolment; the mortality benefit of rehabilitation itself is claimed on rehabilitation's own shelves, not this one.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — automatic-plus-liaison referral gave 73.5% enrolment vs 29.0% usual (OR 8.41) in a 2,635-patient prospective controlled study; 8 of 10 uptake interventions were positive in the Cochrane review

title: Home-based pulmonary rehabilitation matched centre-based rehabilitation at programme end in two randomised trials — and by 12 months neither model had held its gains
question: In adults with COPD, is a home-based pulmonary rehabilitation programme non-inferior to centre-based rehabilitation for dyspnoea and exercise capacity?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — equivalence at the end of the programme, honestly time-limited. Holland AE et al. (PMID: 27672116) randomised 166 people with stable COPD to 8 weeks of centre-based rehabilitation or a minimal-resource home model (one home visit plus seven weekly physiotherapist telephone calls): the between-group difference in 6-minute walk distance at programme end favoured home by 18.6 m (95% CI −3.3 to 40.7), meeting non-inferiority without excluding superiority, and dyspnoea-related quality of life was equivalent at 12 months (difference 0.05 points; 95% CI −2.0 to 2.1) — but at 12 months the walk-distance interval (−5.1 m; 95% CI −29.2 to 18.9) did not exclude inferiority, and neither group maintained its gains. Maltais F et al. (PMID: 19075206) randomised 252 patients with moderate-to-severe COPD to self-monitored home rehabilitation or hospital outpatient rehabilitation after a shared 4-week education programme: at 1 year, dyspnoea improved by 0.62 units (95% CI 0.43–0.80) at home and 0.46 (95% CI 0.28–0.64) in outpatients, a difference of 0.16 (95% CI −0.08 to 0.40) inside the 0.5-unit non-inferiority margin. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): home-based rehabilitation is a genuine equivalent for patients who cannot reach a centre — for as long as either model works.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two RCTs found home-based rehabilitation non-inferior to centre-based at programme end (walk difference +18.6 m; dyspnoea difference 0.16 units, inside the 0.5 margin); 12-month equivalence was not established

title: COPD telemonitoring: admissions unchanged in the large pragmatic TELESCOT trial (HR 0.98) — the earlier Cochrane pooling of telehealthcare packages had found fewer admissions (OR 0.46); the split is the service around the monitor
question: In adults with COPD already under specialist services, does adding home telemonitoring reduce hospital admissions for exacerbations versus usual care alone?
balance: SPLIT — the biggest, cleanest trial is null; the older pooled literature is positive. Pinnock H et al. (PMID: 24136634; TELESCOT) randomised 256 adults with a previous COPD admission in Lothian, Scotland, to telemonitoring (daily symptom questionnaire and oxygen saturation with algorithm-generated alerts) or conventional self-monitoring, with both groups receiving the same existing clinical services: time to hospital admission for exacerbation did not differ (adjusted hazard ratio 0.98; 95% CI 0.66–1.44), mean admissions were 1.2 versus 1.1 per person over a year (P=0.59), and quality of life did not improve (St George's Respiratory Questionnaire 68.2 versus 67.3). The earlier Cochrane review by McLean S et al. (PMID: 21735417; 10 trials) found telehealthcare associated with fewer patients having one or more hospital admissions over 12 months (odds ratio 0.46; 95% CI 0.33–0.65; 6 trials, 604 participants) and fewer emergency attendances (odds ratio 0.27; 95% CI 0.11–0.66), with no difference in deaths (odds ratio 1.05; 95% CI 0.63–1.75) — but telehealthcare there was embedded in complex packages including nurse case management. PROPOSED SPLIT: telemonitoring bolted onto an already-good service adds nothing; the positive trials bundled monitoring with an enhanced clinical service, which is the likelier active ingredient.
stamp: SPLIT — the large pragmatic TELESCOT RCT found no admission benefit (HR 0.98) when both arms shared the same clinical service, while an earlier Cochrane review of telehealthcare bundled with case management found fewer admissions (OR 0.46)

title: CPAP telemonitoring: automated feedback raised use by about an hour a night in a 556-patient trial — clinician-contact telemonitoring in a smaller trial did not
question: In adults starting CPAP for obstructive sleep apnoea, does telemonitoring with feedback improve CPAP adherence versus usual follow-up?
balance: SPLIT — the kind of telemonitoring decides it. In the large Tele-OSA factorial trial (Hwang D et al., PMID: 28858567), CPAP telemonitoring with automated patient feedback raised 90-day use to 4.4 hours a night and telemonitoring plus web education to 4.8 hours, versus 3.8 hours with usual care (P=0.0002 for both); Medicare adherence criteria were met by 65.6% and 73.2% versus 53.5%. Education alone did not significantly raise use (4.0 hours, P=0.10). In the smaller European trial (PMID: 28179438), telemonitoring that triggered clinician contact changed nothing: use was 5.1±2.1 versus 4.9±2.2 hours a night, although telemonitoring cost less (€123.65 versus €170.97, P=0.022) and satisfaction was lower (74% versus 96% rating it high or very high, P=0.034). PROPOSED SPLIT: automated feedback messaging improves early CPAP use by roughly an hour a night; telemonitoring as surveillance plus clinician contact does not, and may satisfy patients less.
stamp: SPLIT — automated-feedback telemonitoring improves CPAP use (Tele-OSA); clinician-contact telemonitoring did not (Turino 2017)

title: Supported asthma self-management: 270 trials say unscheduled care falls and control improves — the support, not the plan alone, is what works
question: In adults with asthma, does supported self-management — a personalised action plan plus regular professional review — reduce hospitalisations and emergency attendances versus usual care?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — two independent syntheses of the randomised literature agree. The PRISMS meta-review (Pinnock H et al., PMID: 28302126) combined 27 systematic reviews (244 randomised trials) with 13 update trials and found supported self-management reduces hospitalisations, accident and emergency attendances and unscheduled consultations, and improves markers of control and quality of life across cultural, demographic and healthcare settings, with total costs offset by reduced hospital and emergency care (standard mean difference 0.13, 95% CI -0.09 to 0.34). The 2020 network meta-analysis (PMID: 32816816; 105 trials, 27,767 participants) found regularly supported self-management beat usual care on healthcare use (standardised mean difference -0.30, 95% credible interval -0.46 to -0.15) and quality of life (0.54, 0.11 to 0.96). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): a written action plan plus regular professional review — totalling at least two hours of support — reduces unscheduled asthma care and improves quality of life.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — supported self-management reduces unscheduled care and improves control across a meta-review of 270 trials and a 105-trial network meta-analysis
