title: Pharmacist inhaler-technique training works — and reminder labels stop the skill fading: correct technique retained by 67% versus 12% at 3 months in one trial
question: In adults with asthma, does pharmacist-led inhaler-technique training and follow-up improve asthma control versus usual care?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — pharmacist training corrects technique, and a personalised reminder label protects the gain. In the Australian cluster study (Basheti IA et al., PMID: 18314294), patients of trained pharmacists improved their inhaler technique score (of 9) by 2.8±1.6 points versus 0.9±1.4 with control pharmacists over 6 months (P<0.001), with asthma severity also significantly improved (P=0.015). In the Jordanian single-blind randomised trial (PMID: 28184045), every patient reached a perfect 9/9 after training, but at 3 months technique had declined significantly less in patients whose inhalers carried labels flagging their own errors (mean difference -1.04 points for Accuhaler, -1.61 for Turbuhaler), and label patients used less reliever medication (2.19 versus 3.42 puffs/day, P=0.002). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): brief pharmacist show-and-tell training improves inhaler technique and short-term control; labels extend the benefit, but the trials are small and from one research group.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — pharmacist training improves inhaler technique in two small trials from one research group; reminder labels slow skill decay

title: Once a day beats four times a day for taking medicines — 79% versus 51% of doses taken — but once versus twice daily is a small step, not a leap
question: Does simplifying dosing frequency — once-daily instead of multiple daily doses — improve medication adherence across chronic conditions?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — adherence falls as daily doses multiply, with the cliff beyond twice daily. The electronic-monitoring systematic review (Claxton AJ et al., PMID: 11558866; 76 studies) found mean dose-taking compliance of 79%±14% for once-daily, 69%±15% for twice-daily, 65%±16% for three-times-daily and 51%±20% for four-times-daily regimens (P<0.001 across schedules); once-daily beat three-times (P=0.008) and four-times daily (P<0.001), but once-daily versus twice-daily was not significantly different. In cardiovascular medicines specifically (PMID: 27144286; 26 studies), regimen adherence was 83.1% once-daily versus 73.8% twice-daily, with adjusted adherence 14.2% worse (95% CI 6.8 to 21.7) on twice-daily dosing. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): cutting doses per day improves adherence — decisively when regimens drop from three or four doses to one or two, modestly from two to one. Tier C: the comparisons are pooled across studies, not randomised head-to-head.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — fewer daily doses, better adherence in pooled electronic-monitoring data; the once- versus twice-daily gap is modest and non-randomised

title: Showing patients their own dosing history lifts adherence by about 9–20 points — the largest single component effect in the electronic-monitoring literature
question: Does electronically compiled dosing-history feedback — showing patients and clinicians their actual dosing pattern — improve medication adherence versus monitoring without feedback?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — feedback is the best-supported single adherence component, on process outcomes. The meta-analysis of 79 randomised trials with electronically compiled dosing histories (Demonceau J et al., PMID: 23588595) found intervention groups averaged 74.3% adherence versus 60.2% in controls, and that adding feedback of the patient's own dosing history (EM-feedback) was associated with a 19.8% adherence improvement (95% CI 10.7 to 28.9) versus 10.3% (7.5 to 13.1) for interventions without it (P<0.01); meta-regression attributed an independent 8.8% increase to feedback (P<0.01). The later focused systematic review (PMID: 28991903) of 10 randomised trials found significant positive effects on full adherence in all five studies reporting it, but a significant clinical-outcome benefit in only one of seven studies. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): dosing-history feedback improves measured adherence; whether it improves health outcomes is unproven.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — feedback of electronically compiled dosing histories improves adherence in meta-analysis; clinical-outcome benefit unproven

title: Paying for viral suppression worked modestly in the big US trial — suppression up 3.8 points, continuity up 8.7 — but paying for linkage to care did nothing
question: In people with HIV attending clinics, do financial incentives for viral suppression increase the proportion virally suppressed versus usual care?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a real but small effect, confined to people already in care. In HPTN 065 (El-Sadr WM et al., PMID: 28628702), a site-randomised trial in the Bronx and Washington DC, $70 gift cards paid quarterly for viral suppression raised the proportion suppressed by 3.8 percentage points overall (95% CI 0.7 to 6.8, P=0.01) and by 4.9 points (1.4 to 8.5, P=0.007) among patients not previously consistently suppressed, and raised continuity of care by 8.7 points (4.2 to 13.2, P<0.001); $125 linkage coupons did not increase linkage to care (adjusted odds ratio 1.10, 95% CI 0.73 to 1.67, P=0.65). The meta-analysis of 22 randomised trials (PMID: 32968885; 38,119 participants) found incentives improved ART adherence (risk ratio 1.30, 95% CI 1.13 to 1.50) and continuity (1.24, 1.09 to 1.41), with viral-suppression benefit clearest in high-income-country studies. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: the suppression claim rests mainly on one large trial.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — incentives raised viral suppression by 3.8 points in HPTN 065 and adherence in meta-analysis; no effect on linkage to care

title: Adherence clubs at city scale: 95.2% retained at a year and 97.2% suppressed among those tested — reassuring numbers, but from selected stable patients with no comparison group
question: For stable patients on antiretroviral therapy, do adherence clubs and other differentiated service-delivery models maintain viral suppression with fewer clinic visits versus standard clinic care?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the outcomes inside clubs look excellent; the comparison the question asks for was never randomised. In the Cape Town scale-up sample (Tsondai PR et al., PMID: 28770595), 3,216 adults in adherence clubs had retention of 95.2% (95% CI 94.0 to 96.4) at 12 months and 89.3% (87.1 to 91.4) at 24 months, and 97.2% (96.5 to 97.8) of those with a viral load in the prior 13 months were suppressed (≤400 copies/mL). The implementation report (PMID: 27097834) shows the model reached 32,425 patients in 1,308 clubs at 55 facilities by March 2015 — 25.2% of the district's ART cohort — offsetting 51% of the cohort's doubling. But club members are chosen for being stable and adherent, and neither report compares them with matched clinic patients. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): clubs demonstrably sustain high retention and suppression in selected stable patients at scale; superiority or equivalence to clinic care is not established by these data.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — high retention and suppression within clubs at scale, but observational data in pre-selected stable patients without a comparator

title: A GP's signature on the screening invitation is worth about 6 points of uptake — 11.8 points combined with a better leaflet in the English factorial trial
question: Does adding a GP endorsement letter and a patient leaflet to a colorectal screening invitation raise screening participation versus the standard invitation?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one well-conducted factorial trial, consistent with the wider screening-intervention literature. In the English Bowel Cancer Screening Programme trial (Hewitson P et al., PMID: 21829202; 1,288 invitees of 20 GPs), a GP endorsement letter raised participation by 5.8 percentage points (95% CI 4.1 to 7.8) and an enhanced procedural leaflet by 6.0 points (4.3 to 8.1), with no important interaction — adjusted rate ratios 1.11 (P=0.038) and 1.12 (P=0.029) — so receiving both added 11.8 points (8.5 to 16). The US systematic review of 73 screening trials (PMID: 30326005) confirms invitation-side interventions work, with larger effects for mailed test outreach (risk ratio 2.26; risk difference 22%) and navigation (2.01; 18%) than for education (1.20; 4%) or reminders (1.20; 3%) alone. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: the endorsement estimate itself rests on a single trial.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — GP endorsement +5.8 points and enhanced leaflet +6.0 points in one factorial RCT; combined +11.8 points

title: Targeted lung-screening invitations did not raise uptake — 52.3% versus 52.9% — but the stepped Lung Health Check invitation itself drew over half of deprived smokers in
question: In deprived heavy smokers, do targeted, stepped invitation materials increase uptake of lung cancer screening versus standard invitations?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — for the targeted leaflet, in the only randomised test. In the Lung Screen Uptake Trial (Quaife SL et al., PMID: 31825647; 2,012 people aged 60–75 recorded as current smokers, from 16 primary care practices), uptake of a Lung Health Check appointment was 52.6% overall with no difference between the targeted low-burden leaflet and the control leaflet (52.3% versus 52.9%; odds ratio 0.98, 95% CI 0.82 to 1.16). Current smokers attended less than former smokers (adjusted odds ratio 0.70, 0.56 to 0.86). The screening-round report (PMID: 32759387) records what that uptake yielded: 768 of 996 analysed attendees scanned, 36 lung cancers (4.7%), 72.2% at stage I/II. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): psychologically targeted materials added nothing over a well-designed stepped invitation; the high uptake in both arms is the service finding, not a leaflet effect.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — targeted invitation leaflet did not change uptake in LSUT (OR 0.98); both arms exceeded 52%

title: Diabetes medication conversation aids: patients know more and join in more — adherence and HbA1c unmoved in both randomised trials, and once better in usual care
question: In primary-care consultations for type 2 diabetes, does an encounter decision aid for glucose-lowering medicines improve knowledge, decisional comfort, and adherence versus usual care?
balance: SPLIT — decision quality improves; the downstream outcomes do not. In the multicentre cluster trial of the Diabetes Medication Choice conversation aid (Kunneman M et al., PMID: 34499328; 350 patients, 99 clinicians, 20 practices), knowledge rose (52% versus 45% correct answers, P=0.02) and observed patient involvement rose (OPTION12 difference 7.3, 95% CI 3 to 12, P=0.003), with no between-arm differences in treatment choice, satisfaction, encounter length, medication adherence or glycaemic control. The earlier pilot trial (PMID: 19786674) found the same pattern — knowledge +1.10 of 10 questions (95% CI 0.11 to 2.09) and involvement +21.8 of 100 (13.0 to 30.5) — but adherence at 6 months was better in usual care (9% more days covered, 4 to 14) and HbA1c identical (difference 0.01, -0.49 to 0.50). PROPOSED SPLIT: conversation aids do what they are built to do — inform and involve — and should not be sold as adherence or glycaemic interventions.
stamp: SPLIT — knowledge and involvement improve in two cluster RCTs; adherence and HbA1c do not (adherence favoured usual care in the pilot)

title: Midwife-led continuity of care: preterm birth down by about a quarter (RR 0.76) and fetal loss/neonatal death down (RR 0.84) across 15 trials — with fewer interventions and no caesarean penalty
question: In pregnant women and new mothers, does midwife-led continuity of care — the same midwife or team throughout — reduce preterm birth and interventions versus other models of care?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — a high-quality Cochrane synthesis, with a mortality-adjacent outcome that puts this shelf in Tier C for personal review. Across 15 trials with 17,674 women (Sandall J et al., PMID: 27121907), midwife-led continuity models reduced preterm birth before 37 weeks (average risk ratio 0.76, 95% CI 0.64 to 0.91; 13,238 women, 8 trials), all fetal loss plus neonatal death (0.84, 0.71 to 0.99; 17,561 women, 13 trials), regional analgesia (0.85, 0.78 to 0.92) and instrumental vaginal birth (0.90, 0.83 to 0.97), and increased spontaneous vaginal birth (1.05, 1.03 to 1.07) — all graded high-quality evidence — with no difference in caesarean birth. The largest single caseload trial (PMID: 22830446; 2,314 low-risk women) did find fewer caesareans (19.4% versus 24.9%; risk ratio 0.78, 0.67 to 0.91), a setting-specific result the pooled analysis does not reproduce overall. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): continuity models reduce preterm birth and interventions with at least comparable safety.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — Cochrane review of 15 trials (17,674 women): preterm birth RR 0.76 and fetal loss/neonatal death RR 0.84, high-quality evidence

title: Telephone triage splits by setting: out-of-hours nurse consultation halved GP workload safely — in-hours triage raised total contacts by a third to a half at no cost saving
question: In general practice, does telephone triage by GPs or nurses change same-day consultation demand, safety, and costs versus usual appointment booking?
balance: SPLIT — the two big randomised tests answer different questions and point opposite ways on workload. For same-day requests in UK general practice (Campbell JL et al., PMID: 25098487; ESTEEM, 42 practices, 20,990 patients), GP telephone triage increased contacts over 28 days by 33% (2.65 versus 1.91 per person; rate ratio 1.33, 95% CI 1.30 to 1.36) and nurse triage by 48% (2.81; 1.48, 1.44 to 1.52), with similar costs (about £75 per patient) and eight deaths within 7 days across arms that were not associated with trial group. For out-of-hours care (PMID: 9774295; 14,492 calls), nurse telephone consultation let nurses manage 49.8% of calls without a GP, cut GP telephone advice by 69%, primary-care-centre attendance by 38% and home visits by 23% — about a 50% workload reduction — with statistical equivalence in deaths, emergency admissions and A&E attendances. PROPOSED SPLIT: triage reorganises demand rather than abolishing it; out-of-hours nurse consultation substitutes safely, in-hours triage adds contacts.
stamp: SPLIT — out-of-hours nurse triage halved GP workload with no safety signal (Lattimer); in-hours GP/nurse triage increased contacts 33–48% at similar cost (ESTEEM)

title: Community paramedics in social housing: blood pressure and quality of life improved in both trial reports — the ambulance-call reduction was clear in the first, not significant in the full trial
question: In older adults living in social housing, does a community paramedicine wellness programme (CP@clinic) improve blood pressure and diabetes risk versus usual access to care?
balance: SPLIT — health measures improve; the headline service outcome is unstable across reports of the same trial programme. In the first cluster-randomised report (Agarwal G et al., PMID: 29807936; 6 buildings, 1,092 residents), CP@clinic lowered mean monthly ambulance calls (3.11 versus 3.99 per 100 units/month; adjusted difference -0.88, 95% CI -0.45 to -1.30 as printed), systolic blood pressure (mean change 5.0, 1.0 to 9.0) and diastolic pressure (4.8, 1.9 to 7.6), and improved quality-adjusted life years (difference 0.09, 0.01 to 0.17). In the larger multi-site report (PMID: 30624150; 30 buildings), the primary intention-to-treat analysis found no significant difference in EMS calls (-0.37 per 100 units/month, -0.98 to 0.24), though a sensitivity analysis excluding two ineligible building pairs did (-0.90, -1.54 to -0.26), and blood pressure and quality-of-life gains persisted (systolic -3.65, quality-adjusted life years +0.06); the cost analysis put the programme at about $C2,933 per quality-adjusted life year (PMID: 33109643, cited in synthesis). PROPOSED SPLIT, Tier C: a single trial programme with successive reports.
stamp: SPLIT — BP and quality of life improve; ambulance-call reduction significant in the 6-building report but not in the 30-building primary analysis

title: Text reminders get people through the door: attendance 78.6% versus 67.8% in the Cochrane review — matching phone calls at roughly half the cost
question: Do mobile-phone text-message reminders improve attendance at healthcare appointments versus no reminders or other reminder types?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two concordant syntheses, on attendance rather than health outcomes. The meta-analysis by Guy R et al. (PMID: 22091980) pooled eight randomised trials and found a summary effect of 1.48 (95% CI 1.23 to 1.72) for SMS reminders on attendance, with heterogeneity (I²=90%) driven by the ten included observational studies rather than the trials. The Cochrane update (PMID: 24310741; 8 randomised trials, 6,615 participants) found moderate-quality evidence that text reminders improved attendance versus no reminder (risk ratio 1.14, 1.03 to 1.26; attendance 78.6% versus 67.8%), matched phone-call reminders (risk ratio 0.99, 0.95 to 1.02; 80.3% attended after calls), and cost 55% and 65% less per attendance than calls in the two costing studies. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a cheap, reliable nudge for attendance — distinct from the adherence-texting shelf, which asks a different question.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — Cochrane: attendance RR 1.14 versus no reminder (78.6% vs 67.8%), equivalent to phone calls and cheaper

title: OpenNotes: most patients who read their notes said they felt more in control and took medicines more reliably — self-reported, from volunteers, with almost no doctors quitting
question: Does giving patients open access to their clinicians' visit notes (OpenNotes) improve engagement, understanding, and medication adherence versus usual record access?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — large, consistent patient-reported gains; objectively weak designs, hence Tier C. In the original quasi-experimental study (Delbanco T et al., PMID: 23027317; 105 primary care physicians, 13,564 patients at three US systems), 11,155 patients opened at least one note; of 5,219 survey respondents who opened a note, 59–77% across sites said open notes helped them feel more in control of their care and 60–78% of those taking medications reported increased medication adherence, while 26–36% had privacy concerns and only 1–8% reported confusion, worry or offence; 99% of patients wanted open notes to continue and no doctor elected to stop. The later mixed-methods evaluation (PMID: 26826154; 576 free-text responses, 13 interviews) found the same themes — improved understanding, relationships, self-care and perceived adherence — with fewer concerns among experienced note-readers. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): patients value and report benefiting from open notes; measured adherence or outcome effects have not been demonstrated.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — patient-reported control and adherence gains in a 13,564-patient quasi-experimental study; evidence is self-reported, Tier C

title: Organised anticoagulation care keeps INRs in range about 12 points more of the time than community practice — event-rate benefits come from observational comparisons, not trials
question: In patients on warfarin, does management through a dedicated anticoagulation clinic or management service improve time in therapeutic range and reduce bleeding and thrombosis versus usual physician care?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the control advantage is consistent; the clinical-event advantage is observational. The systematic review and metaregression (van Walraven C et al., PMID: 16685005; 67 studies, 50,208 patients, 57,154.7 patient-years) found patients were in therapeutic range 63.6% of the time overall (95% CI 61.6 to 65.6), with community-practice care significantly worse than anticoagulation clinics or trials (-12.2%, -19.5 to -4.8, P<0.0001) and self-management better (+7.0%, 0.7 to 13.3, P=0.03). The pharmacist-led service review (PMID: 26100092; 24 studies, 11,607 patients) found, in non-randomised studies, time in range of 72.1% versus 56.7% (P=0.013) with less major bleeding (0.6% versus 1.7%), thromboembolism (0.6% versus 2.9%) and hospitalisation (3% versus 10%) — while its four randomised trials showed only comparability with usual care. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: dedicated services improve INR control; claims of fewer bleeds and clots rest on non-randomised data.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — anticoagulation clinics beat community practice on time in range by ~12 points; event benefits are observational only, Tier C

title: Virtual wards split by diagnosis: no effect in the large mixed high-risk trial — fewer deaths and readmissions only in heart-failure trials
question: After hospital discharge, does a virtual ward — daily interdisciplinary rounds on patients monitored at home — reduce readmission or death versus usual post-discharge care?
balance: SPLIT — by diagnosis, and the largest single trial is null. In the Toronto randomised trial (Dhalla IA et al., PMID: 25268437; 1,923 high-risk patients), a post-discharge virtual ward did not significantly change the composite of readmission or death at 30 days (21.2% (203/959) versus 24.6% (235/956); absolute difference 3.4%, 95% CI -0.3 to 7.2, P=0.09) or at 90 days, 6 months or 1 year. The meta-analysis of 24 randomised trials (PMID: 35763296; 10,876 patients) found virtual wards associated with fewer deaths (risk ratio 0.86, 0.76 to 0.97) and readmissions (0.84, 0.74 to 0.96) only in heart-failure trials, with no such associations in other diagnoses (mortality 0.93, 0.83 to 1.04; readmissions 0.96, 0.88 to 1.05), though emergency department visits fell overall (0.83, 0.70 to 0.98). PROPOSED SPLIT, Tier C for the heart-failure mortality component: build virtual wards for heart failure if at all; the generic high-risk model failed its test.
stamp: SPLIT — null in mixed high-risk patients (Dhalla, n=1,923); fewer deaths/readmissions only in heart-failure trials in meta-analysis

title: Barcode medication administration: non-timing errors fell 41% relative and potential harm events halved — provided every dose is scanned; scanning one dose of many made harm events rise
question: In hospital inpatients, does barcode medication administration reduce medication administration errors and potential adverse drug events versus manual checking?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — large, directly observed before-and-after evidence with a crucial configuration warning; Tier C because nothing here is randomised. In the academic-centre study (Poon EG et al., PMID: 20445181; 14,041 observed administrations, 3,082 transcriptions), barcode eMAR cut non-timing administration errors from 11.5% to 6.8% (41.4% relative reduction, P<0.001) and potential adverse drug events from 3.1% to 1.6% (50.8% relative reduction, P<0.001), and eliminated transcription errors (6.1% to 0%). In the same group's pharmacy study (PMID: 16983130; 369,148 observed doses), target potential adverse drug events fell 74% relative overall — but in the configuration that scanned only one dose of a multi-dose fill, target potential adverse events rose 2.4-fold (P=0.014), while scan-every-dose configurations cut target errors 93–96% relative. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): barcode verification works when the workflow forces a scan of every dose, every time.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — administration errors -41% relative and potential ADEs halved in before-and-after studies; benefit depends on scanning every dose, Tier C

title: The WHO Surgical Safety Checklist: deaths 1.5% to 0.8% and complications 11.0% to 7.0% in the eight-hospital study — consistent in meta-analysis, but never randomised
question: Across hospitals, does implementing the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist reduce surgical complications and death versus care without the checklist?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a large consistent signal from non-randomised evidence; Tier C for the mortality claim and design. In the Safe Surgery Saves Lives study (Haynes AB et al., PMID: 19144931; eight hospitals in eight cities, 3,733 patients before and 3,955 after checklist introduction), inpatient death fell from 1.5% to 0.8% (P=0.003) and complications from 11.0% to 7.0% (P<0.001) in patients aged 16+ undergoing noncardiac surgery. The systematic review and meta-analysis (PMID: 24469615; seven studies) found risk ratios of 0.59 (95% CI 0.47 to 0.74) for any complication, 0.77 (0.60 to 0.98) for mortality and 0.57 (0.41 to 0.79) for surgical-site infection, with effectiveness correlated with adherence to the checklist's embedded care processes (Q=0.82, P=0.042) — while cautioning the evidence 'cannot be regarded as definitive' without higher-quality studies. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the checklist probably reduces complications and deaths when actually used as designed; the size of the true effect is uncertain.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — death 1.5% to 0.8% and complications 11.0% to 7.0% after checklist implementation; meta-analysis RR 0.59 for complications, Tier C

title: X-PERT structured diabetes education: HbA1c -0.6% versus +0.1% at 14 months in its trial, with one medication increase prevented for every four participants
question: In people with newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes, does the X-PERT structured education programme improve glycaemic control versus usual care?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one good trial of the named programme, backed by a consistent meta-analysis of its class; Tier C because the X-PERT claim itself is single-trial. In the X-PERT randomised trial (Deakin TA et al., PMID: 16922700; 314 adults with type 2 diabetes in Lancashire), six 2-hour group sessions produced an HbA1c change of -0.6% versus +0.1% in individual-appointment controls at 14 months (P<0.001), with a number needed to treat of 4 (95% CI 3 to 7) to prevent a diabetes medication increase and 7 (5 to 11) for medication reduction, plus significant improvements in weight, waist circumference, total cholesterol, knowledge, empowerment and treatment satisfaction; 95% attended and 82% attended at least four sessions. The meta-analysis of group-based education generally (PMID: 22824531; 21 studies, 2,833 participants) found HbA1c reductions of 0.44 points at 6 months, 0.46 at 12 months and 0.87 at 2 years. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): X-PERT improves glycaemic control at about a year; durability beyond the trial and in newly diagnosed-only populations is less certain.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — X-PERT HbA1c -0.6% vs +0.1% at 14 months in a single RCT, supported by group-education meta-analysis, Tier C

title: Intensive case management (the ACT family): about 0.86 fewer hospital days a month versus standard care — and the benefit concentrates where hospital use is high and teams follow the ACT model
question: In adults with severe mental illness living in the community, does assertive community treatment reduce hospital use and improve engagement versus standard community care?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a large randomised literature with honestly low-grade certainty. The Cochrane review of intensive case management (Dieterich M et al., PMID: 28067944; 40 randomised trials, 7,524 participants — the successor to the withdrawn Marshall & Lockwood review) found, versus standard care, slightly fewer hospital days per month (mean difference -0.86, 95% CI -1.37 to -0.34; 24 trials, 3,595 participants, low-quality evidence) and fewer people leaving care early (risk ratio 0.68, 0.58 to 0.79), with little or no difference in suicide (0.68, 0.31 to 1.51); versus less-intensive case management, hospital days did not differ (-0.08, -0.37 to 0.21, moderate-quality evidence). The meta-regression (PMID: 17631513) explains the inconsistency across trials: effects grow with baseline hospital use (coefficient -0.23, -0.36 to -0.09) and with fidelity to the assertive community treatment team model (-0.31, -0.59 to -0.03). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): deploy intensive, ACT-faithful teams for high hospital users; expect little where bed use is already low.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — ICM reduces hospital days (MD -0.86/month) and dropout (RR 0.68) versus standard care in Cochrane review of 40 RCTs; low-quality evidence

title: Pharmacist-led care splits by outcome: blood pressure falls clearly (-7.6/-3.9 mmHg across 39 trials) — but broad medication therapy management evidence is 'insufficient' for most health outcomes
question: In adults with chronic conditions managed in primary care, does pharmacist-led medication therapy management improve disease control and reduce hospital use versus usual care?
balance: SPLIT — by outcome and by how tightly the intervention is defined. The AHRQ systematic review of medication therapy management in outpatients (Viswanathan M et al., PMID: 25401788; 44 studies) graded evidence insufficient for most outcomes — drug therapy problems, adverse drug events, morbidity, mortality and harms — while finding low-strength evidence of improved medication appropriateness (4.9 versus 0.9 points on the medication appropriateness index, P<0.001), adherence (about +4.6%) and lower odds of hospitalisation in diabetes (odds ratio 0.91 to 0.93) and heart failure (adjusted hazard ratio 0.55, 95% CI 0.39 to 0.77). The focused meta-analysis of pharmacist interventions for hypertension (PMID: 24721801; 39 randomised trials, 14,224 patients) found systolic pressure 7.6 mmHg lower (95% CI -9.0 to -6.3) and diastolic 3.9 lower (-5.1 to -2.8) than usual care, albeit with wide prediction intervals. PROPOSED SPLIT: pharmacist care is a proven blood-pressure intervention and a plausible medication-safety one; it is not yet a proven general outcome intervention.
stamp: SPLIT — pharmacist interventions lower BP in 39 RCTs; broad MTM evidence insufficient for most health outcomes (AHRQ review)

title: Six-monthly ART refills hold the line: retention 92.6% versus 93.6% and suppression actually higher (+4.6 points) at 24 months in the adherence-club trial — with far fewer visits
question: In people with HIV established on antiretroviral therapy, does multi-month (three- to six-monthly) dispensing maintain viral suppression and retention in care versus monthly dispensing?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — maintained outcomes on far fewer visits, shown in randomised programmes. In the Khayelitsha cluster trial (Cassidy T et al., PMID: 33340284; 2,150 adherence-club patients, 88 clubs), six-monthly refills gave 24-month retention of 92.6% (905/977) versus 93.6% (1,098/1,173) with standard club refills (risk difference -1.0%, 95% CI -3.2 to 1.3; non-inferior), with higher viral load completion (90.8% (887/977) versus 85.1% (999/1,173); +5.5%, 1.5 to 9.5) and suppression (87.3% (853/977) versus 82.6% (969/1,173); +4.6%, 0.2 to 9.0). The pooled analysis of two cluster trials in Zimbabwe and Lesotho (PMID: 34713614; 599 newly stable adults) found six-monthly community dispensing non-inferior for retention (95.8% versus 93.4%; adjusted risk difference +1.7%, -2.5 to 5.9) with suppression of 98.1–99.3% across arms. The meta-analysis of 16 randomised trials (PMID: 37655428; 13,886 participants) found differentiated models at least comparable (retention risk ratio 1.09, 1.08 to 1.11; suppression 1.01, 1.00 to 1.02). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): for stable patients, multi-month dispensing maintains suppression and retention while cutting visit burden.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — six-monthly dispensing non-inferior for retention and suppression in cluster RCTs and a 16-trial meta-analysis, with fewer visits

title: Cutting down drinking lowers blood pressure only in heavier drinkers: about 5.5/4.0 mm Hg in those drinking six or more drinks a day who halved their intake, and nothing measurable at two drinks a day or fewer
question: In adults with hypertension who drink alcohol regularly, does reducing alcohol intake lower blood pressure compared with continuing usual drinking?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — with a threshold. Two meta-analyses of randomised trials, 15 years apart, agree that cutting alcohol lowers blood pressure in a dose-dependent way. Roerecke 2017 (36 trials, 2,865 participants) found no significant blood-pressure reduction in people drinking two or fewer drinks per day, but a mean reduction of −5.50 mm Hg systolic (95% CI −6.70 to −4.30) and −3.97 mm Hg diastolic (−4.70 to −3.25) in participants drinking six or more drinks per day who reduced intake by about 50%. Xin 2001 (15 trials, 2,234 participants) found an overall reduction of −3.31 mm Hg systolic (−4.10 to −2.52) and −2.04 mm Hg diastolic (−2.58 to −1.49), with a dose–response between the percentage of alcohol reduction and the blood-pressure fall, and larger effects at higher baseline blood pressure. The benefit is real but belongs to heavier drinkers; at low intake there is nothing to gain on blood pressure. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): alcohol reduction lowers blood pressure dose-dependently in people drinking more than two drinks a day, with the largest falls in the heaviest drinkers.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two concordant meta-analyses of randomised trials show dose-dependent blood-pressure lowering from alcohol reduction, confined to people drinking more than two drinks per day

title: Device-guided slow breathing: the small pooled blood-pressure fall vanishes when manufacturer-linked trials are removed, and the 2022 meta-analysis finds no significant effect at all
question: In adults with hypertension, does device-guided slow breathing lower office and ambulatory blood pressure compared with usual care or a control device?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — once the manufacturer's own trials are set aside. Mahtani 2012 pooled eight trials of the RESPeRATE device (InterCure Ltd) in 494 adults and found systolic pressure lower by 3.67 mm Hg (95% CI −5.99 to −1.39) and diastolic by 2.51 mm Hg (−4.15 to −0.87) — but five of the eight trials were sponsored by or involved the manufacturer, and excluding them left no overall effect. The independent 2022 meta-analysis (de Freitas Gonçalves et al.) likewise found device-guided slow breathing did not significantly reduce systolic (mean difference −2.13 mm Hg, 95% CI −12.71 to 8.44) or diastolic pressure (−0.90, −3.97 to 2.11) versus usual care, with high heterogeneity. The honest reading is that any effect is small, short-term (maximum trial duration 9 weeks in Mahtani), and unproven independently. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): device-guided slow breathing has not been shown to lower blood pressure in trials independent of the device manufacturer.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the pooled benefit in early meta-analysis rests on manufacturer-linked trials and disappears without them; a 2022 meta-analysis found no significant effect

title: Spironolactone lowers blood pressure more than eplerenone in primary aldosteronism — diastolic 12.5 versus 5.6 mm Hg in the one blinded trial — but causes far more breast side effects; a small unrandomised series found the two similar
question: In primary aldosteronism, is spironolactone more effective than eplerenone at controlling blood pressure, and how do their side effects compare?
balance: SPLIT — spironolactone wins on blood pressure, eplerenone wins on sex-hormone side effects. In the one double-blind randomised head-to-head trial (Parthasarathy 2011), titrated spironolactone (75–225 mg daily) lowered seated diastolic pressure by 12.5 mm Hg versus 5.6 mm Hg on eplerenone (100–300 mg daily) over 16 weeks — a difference of −6.9 mm Hg (95% CI −10.6 to −3.3; P<0.001), so eplerenone failed its non-inferiority test. The price was hormonal: male gynaecomastia in 21.2% on spironolactone versus 4.5% on eplerenone (P=0.033) and female mastodynia in 21.1% versus 0.0% (P=0.026). A small unrandomised Japanese comparison (Karashima 2016, 54 patients treated for 12 months) found the two decreased blood pressure and raised potassium to similar degrees — a weaker design that does not overturn the blinded trial. PROPOSED SPLIT: choose spironolactone for maximum blood-pressure effect, eplerenone when anti-androgen side effects bite — accepting less pressure reduction.
stamp: SPLIT — spironolactone lowers blood pressure more (one blinded RCT), eplerenone causes fewer sex-hormone side effects; a small unrandomised series found them similar

title: TONE: in older hypertensive patients, cutting sodium or losing weight each cut the risk of needing medication again by about 30% in relative terms — combined, the hazard ratio was 0.47 — with no excess of cardiovascular events
question: In older adults with hypertension, does combining sodium reduction with weight loss lower blood pressure and reduce the need for antihypertensive medication compared with usual care?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — from a single large randomised trial. In TONE (Whelton 1998), 975 men and women aged 60–80 whose blood pressure was controlled on a single drug attempted medication withdrawal after 3 months of intervention. The combined endpoint (high blood pressure at follow-up, restarting medication, or a cardiovascular event) was less frequent with reduced sodium intake (relative hazard ratio 0.69, 95% CI 0.59–0.81; P<0.001) and, in the 585 obese participants, with weight loss (0.70, 0.57–0.87; P<0.001). Among obese participants versus usual care, hazard ratios were 0.60 for sodium reduction alone, 0.64 for weight loss alone, and 0.47 (0.35–0.64; P<0.001) for the two combined — relative effects; the trial reports hazards, not absolute event rates, in its record. Cardiovascular events were similar across all six groups. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): sodium reduction, and weight loss in obese patients, genuinely delay the return of hypertension after drug withdrawal in older adults; the combination is best.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single large randomised trial (TONE) showed sodium reduction and weight loss each delayed recurrent hypertension after medication withdrawal, combined hazard ratio 0.47 in relative terms

title: A short course of furosemide after delivery speeds blood-pressure recovery in severe pre-eclampsia: day-2 systolic 142 versus 153 mm Hg in the first trial, fewer severe episodes and less add-on treatment in two more — no shortening of hospital stay
question: In women with pre-eclampsia, does a short course of furosemide after delivery improve blood-pressure control and reduce the need for other antihypertensive treatment?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for blood-pressure recovery after severe pre-eclampsia, not for milder disease. In Ascarelli 2005 (264 patients), the benefit was confined to the severe subgroup (n=70): systolic pressure on postpartum day 2 was 142 ± 13 mm Hg on furosemide 20 mg daily for 5 days versus 153 ± 19 mm Hg on no therapy (P<0.004), and antihypertensive treatment at discharge was needed by 6% versus 26% (P=0.045); patients with mild (n=169) or superimposed (n=25) pre-eclampsia gained nothing, and neither hospital stay nor delayed complications improved. Veena 2017 (108 women with severe pre-eclampsia) found additional antihypertensive drugs were required by 8.0% on furosemide plus nifedipine versus 26.0% on nifedipine alone (P=0.017). Cursino 2025 (120 women, triple-masked, placebo-controlled) found lower mean daily systolic and diastolic pressures on furosemide 40 mg daily (P<0.001), fewer severe hypertensive episodes on days 2 and 5 (P=0.04), and faster blood-pressure control (P=0.01). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): five days of oral furosemide after delivery accelerates blood-pressure recovery in severe pre-eclampsia.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — three randomised trials show a short postpartum furosemide course lowers blood pressure faster and reduces add-on antihypertensive treatment in severe pre-eclampsia, without shortening hospital stay

title: POTS: low-dose propranolol (20 mg) acutely slows the standing heart rate and eases symptoms — a higher 80 mg dose slows the heart more but helps symptoms less; midodrine helped only the neuropathic subtype in one small adolescent crossover trial
question: In postural tachycardia syndrome, do low-dose propranolol or midodrine improve standing heart rate and orthostatic symptoms compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — acute, low-dose, and subtype-specific. Raj 2009 randomised 54 patients with POTS in a crossover design to single doses: propranolol 20 mg lowered supine and standing heart rates versus placebo (both P<0.001) and improved symptom burden at 2 hours more than placebo (median −4.5 versus 0 arbitrary units; P=0.044), while 80 mg lowered standing heart rate further yet improved symptoms less than 20 mg (−2 versus −6 units; P=0.041) — less is more. Arnold 2013 found a single 20 mg dose raised peak oxygen consumption in POTS (27.6 ± 1.0 versus 24.5 ± 0.7 mL/min/kg on placebo; P=0.024). For midodrine, Ross 2014 (20 patients aged 12–20, double-blind crossover) found haemodynamic improvement in neuropathic POTS but a placebo-like pattern in hyperadrenergic POTS. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): low-dose propranolol acutely improves tachycardia and symptoms in POTS; chronic-dosing and hard-outcome evidence does not exist in this record.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — small acute crossover trials show low-dose propranolol improves standing tachycardia, symptoms, and exercise capacity in POTS, and midodrine helps the neuropathic subtype; no long-term trials

title: Sacubitril/valsartan lowers blood pressure a few mm Hg more than an ARB alone: central systolic −3.7 mm Hg versus olmesartan at 12 weeks in older patients, and sitting systolic −2.3 to −3.5 mm Hg at 8 weeks in Asian patients
question: In adults with hypertension, does sacubitril/valsartan lower blood pressure more than an angiotensin receptor blocker alone?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a real but small extra fall in blood pressure. In PARAMETER (Williams 2017), 454 older patients (mean age 67.7 years, mean seated systolic 158.6 mm Hg) randomised to sacubitril/valsartan or olmesartan showed a greater fall in central aortic systolic pressure at 12 weeks with sacubitril/valsartan (−3.7 mm Hg versus olmesartan; P=0.010), with 24-hour ambulatory systolic lower by 4.1 mm Hg (P<0.001); by 52 weeks pressures were similar, though fewer sacubitril/valsartan patients needed add-on therapy (32% versus 47%; P<0.002). In Huo 2019 (1,438 Asian patients), sacubitril/valsartan 200 mg beat olmesartan 20 mg on sitting systolic pressure at 8 weeks by −2.33 mm Hg (95% CI −4.00 to −0.66) and the 400 mg dose by −3.52 mm Hg (−5.19 to −1.84). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): sacubitril/valsartan lowers blood pressure modestly more than olmesartan alone in hypertension — a few mm Hg, with no hypertension outcome trial behind it.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two randomised double-blind trials show sacubitril/valsartan lowers blood pressure about 2–4 mm Hg more than olmesartan in hypertension

title: Meditation lowers blood pressure modestly in randomised trials: Transcendental Meditation pooled at −4.7/−3.2 mm Hg, and −10.7/−6.4 mm Hg versus an education control in the one older trial in African American patients
question: In adults with hypertension, do meditation and mindfulness-based stress-reduction programmes lower office and ambulatory blood pressure compared with usual care?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — modest falls, from trials of uneven quality. Anderson 2008 meta-analysed nine randomised controlled trials of Transcendental Meditation versus control and found systolic pressure lower by 4.7 mm Hg (95% CI −7.4 to −1.9) and diastolic by 3.2 mm Hg (−5.4 to −1.3), with similar reductions in hypertensive subgroups and in the three high-quality studies. The largest single trial in the pool's tradition, Schneider 1995, randomised 127 older African American patients (aged 55–85) with mild hypertension: Transcendental Meditation reduced systolic pressure by 10.7 mm Hg (P<0.0003) and diastolic by 6.4 mm Hg (P<0.00005) versus a lifestyle-education control over 3 months, beating progressive muscle relaxation as well. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): meditation — best evidenced for the Transcendental Meditation technique — lowers clinic blood pressure by roughly 3–5 mm Hg in pooled randomised evidence; ambulatory-pressure and outcome data are thin.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a meta-analysis of nine randomised trials found Transcendental Meditation lowered blood pressure by 4.7/3.2 mm Hg versus control, with trial quality varying widely

title: POST: metoprolol did not prevent vasovagal syncope — 208 patients with a median of 9 lifetime spells, recurrences no different from placebo over a year, in any age group
question: In recurrent vasovagal syncope, does metoprolol prevent syncope recurrence compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the definitive placebo-controlled trial was flatly negative. In POST (Sheldon 2006), 208 patients (mean age 42 ± 18 years) with more than two syncopal spells and a positive tilt test — a median of 9 spells over a median of 11 years — were randomised to metoprolol or placebo at highest-tolerated doses of 25–200 mg daily for 1 year. Seventy-five patients had at least one recurrence, and the likelihood of recurrent syncope was not significantly different between groups; neither age (<42 versus ≥42 years) nor needing isoproterenol for a positive tilt test predicted benefit. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): metoprolol does not prevent recurrent vasovagal syncope in tilt-positive patients.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the single large randomised placebo-controlled trial (POST, 208 patients) found metoprolol did not reduce syncope recurrence over 1 year

title: Growth hormone in chronic heart failure: pooled small trials show ejection fraction up about 3–5 points and better exercise capacity — and a 2025 meta-analysis claims fewer death/worsening events (relative risk 0.59), a hard-endpoint claim built on small trials that no large trial has tested
question: In chronic heart failure, does growth hormone supplementation improve exercise capacity, cardiac function, or clinical outcomes compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for function and symptoms, on small-trial evidence. Le Corvoisier 2007 pooled 12 trials and found growth hormone improved left ventricular ejection fraction by 5.10% (weighted mean difference), maximal oxygen uptake by 2.48 mL/kg/min, exercise duration by 103.7 seconds, and NYHA class by −0.97, alongside thicker walls and smaller cavity dimensions. The updated Theodorakis 2025 meta-analysis of 17 randomised placebo-controlled studies found ejection fraction +3.34% (95% CI 1.09–5.59; P=0.0037), peak oxygen consumption +2.84 mL/kg/min (1.32–4.36; P=0.0002), NYHA class −0.44, and a composite of death, worsening heart failure, or ventricular tachycardia reduced with a relative risk of 0.59 (0.39–0.90; P=0.013) — a relative effect from small trials, with no large event-driven trial behind it. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: the hard-endpoint claim rests on pooled small trials and goes to the developer personally.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two meta-analyses of small randomised trials show improved ejection fraction, exercise capacity, and symptoms; the claimed reduction in death/worsening events (relative risk 0.59) is untested in any large trial

title: Thiamine for heart failure: the one positive trial was 30 patients selected for furosemide-induced deficiency; pooling all seven randomised trials (274 patients) shows no significant effect on ejection fraction, walk distance, or symptoms
question: In patients with heart failure, does thiamine supplementation improve ejection fraction and symptoms compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — except for correcting deficiency itself. Shimon 1995 randomised 30 patients with moderate-to-severe heart failure on furosemide ≥80 mg/day: after intravenous thiamine, ejection fraction rose from 0.28 ± 0.11 to 0.32 ± 0.09 (P<0.05) and diuresis increased, in patients selected for biochemical thiamine deficiency. But He 2024 pooled all seven randomised double-blind trials (274 patients) and found no significant effect of thiamine versus placebo on ejection fraction (weighted mean difference 1.653%, 95% CI −1.098 to 4.405; P=0.239), 6-minute walk (16.526 m, −36.582 to 69.634; P=0.542), NT-proBNP, or NYHA class — while confirming thiamine does correct thiamine deficiency. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): routine thiamine supplementation does not improve cardiac function or symptoms in heart failure; treating documented deficiency is a different, narrower claim.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — a meta-analysis of seven randomised trials (274 patients) found no significant effect of thiamine on ejection fraction, walk distance, or symptoms in heart failure

title: Repeated levosimendan infusions in advanced heart failure: LION-HEART (69 patients) cut NT-proBNP and heart-failure hospitalisations (hazard ratio 0.25), but LevoRep (120 patients) missed its functional primary endpoint — a split verdict from two small trials
question: In advanced heart failure with recurrent decompensation, do repeated intermittent levosimendan infusions reduce hospitalisation and death compared with placebo?
balance: SPLIT — the biomarker and hospitalisation signals point one way, the functional endpoint the other, and death is unanswered. LION-HEART (Comín-Colet 2018) randomised 69 outpatients with advanced heart failure to levosimendan 0.2 µg/kg/min for 6 hours every 2 weeks for 12 weeks or placebo: NT-proBNP exposure was significantly lower on levosimendan (area under the curve 344 × 10³ versus 535 × 10³ pg·day/mL; P=0.003) and heart-failure hospitalisation was reduced (hazard ratio 0.25, 95% CI 0.11–0.56; P=0.001) — a relative effect in 69 patients. LevoRep (Altenberger 2014, 120 patients) found its primary endpoint — combined ≥20% improvement in 6-minute walk and ≥15% improvement in quality-of-life score — in 19% on levosimendan versus 15.8% on placebo (odds ratio 1.25, 0.44–3.59; P=0.810). Neither trial was powered for death. PROPOSED SPLIT: promising hospitalisation signal, unproven function, unknown mortality — an adequately powered event-driven trial is still owed.
stamp: SPLIT — LION-HEART showed lower NT-proBNP and fewer heart-failure hospitalisations (hazard ratio 0.25, relative) while LevoRep missed its functional primary endpoint; neither small trial addresses mortality

title: Hypertonic saline with high-dose furosemide: SMAC-HF reported readmissions 18.5% versus 34.2% and mortality 12.9% versus 23.8% — huge effects from one research group's single-blind programme, pooled at relative risk 0.55 for death, that independent replication has not confirmed
question: In acute decompensated heart failure, does adding hypertonic saline to high-dose furosemide improve diuresis, kidney function, and outcomes compared with furosemide alone?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — with the strongest caveat on this shelf: the effects are implausibly large and trace mainly to one group. In SMAC-HF (Paterna 2011), 1,771 patients with NYHA class III heart failure were single-blind randomised to furosemide 250 mg plus hypertonic saline 150 mL twice daily with a moderate sodium diet, or furosemide alone with a low-sodium diet: hospital stay was 3.5 ± 1 versus 5.5 ± 1 days (P<0.0001), and over 57 ± 15 months readmissions were 18.5% versus 34.2% (P<0.0001) and mortality 12.9% versus 23.8% (P<0.0001). Liu 2021 pooled 11 randomised trials (2,987 patients) and found hypertonic saline plus furosemide associated with lower all-cause mortality (relative risk 0.55, 95% CI 0.46–0.67) and fewer heart-failure readmissions (relative risk 0.50, 0.33–0.76), with greater diuresis (mean difference 583.87 mL/day) — relative effects, with certainty graded only low to moderate. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: a mortality claim dominated by one investigator group's trials goes to the developer personally.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — hypertonic saline plus furosemide improved diuresis and, in one group's large single-blind trial and a meta-analysis dominated by it, readmissions and mortality (relative risk 0.55); independent replication is lacking

title: ATHENA-HF: high-dose spironolactone (100 mg) in acute heart failure changed nothing — NT-proBNP, congestion, dyspnoea, urine output, weight, and 30-day death or hospitalisation all no different from usual care at 96 hours
question: In acute heart failure, does high-dose spironolactone improve decongestion and dyspnoea compared with usual care?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — a clean null in a properly blinded trial. ATHENA-HF (Butler 2017) randomised 360 patients hospitalised with acute heart failure (median ejection fraction 34%, median NT-proBNP 4,601 pg/mL in the high-dose group and 3,753 pg/mL in usual care) to spironolactone 100 mg daily or usual care (placebo or 25 mg) for 96 hours. The primary endpoint, change in log NT-proBNP, did not differ (−0.55 [95% CI −0.92 to −0.18] versus −0.49 [−0.98 to −0.14]; P=0.57), and neither did the congestion score, dyspnoea, net urine output, weight change, or day-30 all-cause mortality or heart-failure hospitalisation; potassium and kidney function changed similarly. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): 96 hours of high-dose spironolactone is well tolerated in acute heart failure but does not decongest faster than usual care.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the single randomised trial (ATHENA-HF, 360 patients) found high-dose spironolactone did not improve NT-proBNP, congestion, dyspnoea, or 30-day outcomes in acute heart failure

title: DICTATE-AHF: early dapagliflozin in acute heart failure missed its primary diuretic-efficiency endpoint (odds ratio 0.65; P=0.06) — patients lost the same weight on less loop diuretic (560 versus 800 mg), with no safety penalty
question: In acute heart failure, does early dapagliflozin improve diuretic efficiency and decongestion compared with usual care alone?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — on the endpoint the trial chose, with a diuretic-sparing signal underneath. DICTATE-AHF (Cox 2024) randomised 240 patients within 24 hours of presentation with hypervolaemic acute heart failure, open-label, to dapagliflozin 10 mg daily or structured usual care with protocolised diuretic titration to day 5 or discharge. Diuretic efficiency (cumulative weight change per cumulative loop diuretic dose) did not differ significantly (odds ratio 0.65, 95% CI 0.41–1.02; P=0.06). Dapagliflozin patients achieved equivalent weight loss on lower loop diuretic doses (560 mg [Q1–Q3 260–1,150] versus 800 mg [380–1,715]; P=0.006) with fewer intravenous diuretic up-titrations, better 24-hour natriuresis (P=0.03) and urine output (P=0.005), and no increase in diabetic, renal, or cardiovascular safety events. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for diuretic efficiency as defined; the shelf records the diuretic-sparing findings without upgrading them past the missed primary endpoint.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the single open-label trial (DICTATE-AHF, 240 patients) missed its primary diuretic-efficiency endpoint (P=0.06), though equivalent weight loss was achieved with less loop diuretic

title: TRUE-AHF: ularitide lowered blood pressure and NT-proBNP but not cardiovascular death — 21.7% versus 21.0% (hazard ratio 1.03) over a median 15 months in 2,157 patients with acute heart failure
question: In acute heart failure, does the natriuretic peptide ularitide improve dyspnoea, cardiovascular death, or heart-failure hospitalisation compared with placebo?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — a large, definitive null. TRUE-AHF (Packer 2017) randomised 2,157 patients with acute heart failure, a median of 6 hours after initial evaluation, to a 48-hour infusion of ularitide 15 ng/kg/min or placebo on top of standard therapy. Cardiovascular death occurred in 236 patients on ularitide and 225 on placebo (21.7% versus 21.0%; hazard ratio 1.03, 96% CI 0.85–1.25; P=0.75) over a median follow-up of 15 months, and the hierarchical composite of the initial 48-hour clinical course also did not differ significantly. Ularitide did lower systolic blood pressure and NT-proBNP more than placebo, but cardiac troponin T changes did not differ — the physiological effects never became clinical benefit. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): early ularitide infusion does not improve the clinical course or reduce cardiovascular mortality in acute heart failure.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — one large definitive randomised trial (TRUE-AHF, 2,157 patients) found ularitide did not reduce cardiovascular death (21.7% versus 21.0%) or improve the early clinical course in acute heart failure

title: Baroreflex activation therapy in HFrEF: quality of life, walk distance, and NT-proBNP improved durably — but the long-term primary endpoint of cardiovascular death and heart-failure morbidity was neutral (rate ratio 0.94) in BeAT-HF
question: In heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, does baroreflex activation therapy improve symptoms, exercise capacity, and heart-failure hospitalisation compared with medical therapy alone?
balance: SPLIT — symptoms and function improve and stay improved; hard outcomes do not. In BeAT-HF's FDA-intended-use cohort (Zile 2020; 245 patients with HFrEF, ejection fraction ≤35%, no CRT indication), baroreflex activation therapy plus medical management beat medical management alone at 6 months on quality of life (Δ −14.1 points, 95% CI −19 to −9; P<0.001), 6-minute walk distance (Δ +60 m, 40–80; P<0.001), and NT-proBNP (Δ −25%, −38% to −9%; P=0.004), with a 97% freedom rate from major adverse neurological/cardiovascular events. But the long-term report (Zile 2024; median follow-up 3.6 years per patient, 332 primary events) found the primary endpoint of cardiovascular mortality and heart-failure morbidity not significantly different (rate ratio 0.94, 0.57–1.57; P=0.82), while the symptom gains remained durable. PROPOSED SPLIT: an implanted symptom treatment with neutral hard outcomes — hospitalisation benefit, part of the candidate question, was not shown.
stamp: SPLIT — baroreflex activation therapy durably improves quality of life, walk distance, and NT-proBNP in HFrEF, but its long-term primary endpoint (cardiovascular death and heart-failure morbidity, rate ratio 0.94) was neutral

title: Cardiac contractility modulation in narrow-QRS HFrEF: the confirmatory trial grew from a post-hoc subgroup of a negative parent trial — peak oxygen uptake +0.84 mL/kg/min and better quality of life at 24 weeks, unblinded, with a Bayesian analysis borrowing from that subgroup
question: In heart failure with reduced ejection fraction and a narrow QRS, does cardiac contractility modulation improve exercise capacity and quality of life compared with sham or usual care?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — real functional gains, fragile provenance. The parent FIX-HF-5 trial (428 patients, ejection fraction ≤35%) missed its primary endpoint overall; its subgroup analysis (Abraham 2011) found that patients with NYHA class III symptoms and ejection fraction ≥25% (206 patients) responded: peak oxygen uptake rose by 0.34 ± 3.11 versus −0.97 ± 2.31 mL/kg/min on medical therapy alone (P=0.001), with ≥1-class NYHA improvement in 44% versus 23% (P=0.002). The confirmatory FIX-HF-5C trial (Abraham 2018) randomised 160 such patients (ejection fraction 25–45%, QRS <130 ms), unblinded, and met its primary endpoint: peak oxygen uptake difference 0.84 mL/kg/min (95% Bayesian credible interval 0.123–1.552), with better quality of life (P<0.001), NYHA class (P<0.001), and 6-minute walk (P=0.02), and a composite of cardiovascular death and heart-failure hospitalisation of 2.9% versus 10.8% (P=0.048). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for exercise capacity and quality of life in this narrow subgroup — no sham control exists in either trial.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — cardiac contractility modulation improved peak oxygen uptake and quality of life in the ejection-fraction 25–45%, narrow-QRS subgroup across FIX-HF-5's subgroup analysis and the unblinded FIX-HF-5C confirmatory trial

title: ACE inhibitors and ARBs in HFpEF: three large trials, three missed primary endpoints — candesartan 22% versus 24% (P=0.118), irbesartan hazard ratio 0.95 (P=0.35), perindopril 100 versus 107 events (P=0.545); only hospitalisation hints survive
question: In heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, do ACE inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers improve death or hospitalisation compared with placebo?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — three concordant large placebo-controlled trials. CHARM-Preserved (Yusuf 2003; 3,023 patients, ejection fraction >40%) found the primary outcome of cardiovascular death or heart-failure admission in 333 (22%) on candesartan versus 366 (24%) on placebo (unadjusted hazard ratio 0.89, 95% CI 0.77–1.03; P=0.118), with cardiovascular death identical (170 versus 170) though first heart-failure admissions were fewer (230 versus 279; P=0.017). I-PRESERVE (Massie 2008; 4,128 patients, ejection fraction ≥45%) found the primary outcome at 100.4 versus 105.4 per 1,000 patient-years on irbesartan versus placebo (hazard ratio 0.95, 0.86–1.05; P=0.35) and death rates of 52.6 versus 52.3 per 1,000 patient-years (hazard ratio 1.00). PEP-CHF (Cleland 2006; 850 patients aged ≥70) found the primary endpoint in 100 patients on perindopril versus 107 on placebo (hazard ratio 0.919, 0.700–1.208; P=0.545). PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): renin–angiotensin blockade does not improve death or the primary composites in HFpEF.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — three large concordant placebo-controlled trials (CHARM-Preserved, I-PRESERVE, PEP-CHF) found ACE inhibitors/ARBs did not significantly improve death or primary hospitalisation composites in HFpEF

title: Obese older HFpEF: diet and exercise each raised peak oxygen consumption (by 1.3 and 1.2 mL/kg/min), and together the gains added up (2.5) — quality of life, oddly, did not significantly improve in the SECRET trial
question: In older obese patients with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, does combining caloric restriction with aerobic exercise improve exercise capacity more than either alone?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for exercise capacity, in one centre's programme of two trials. In SECRET (Kitzman 2016), 100 obese older patients with stable HFpEF (mean age 67 years, body mass index 39.3) were randomised in a 2×2 factorial design to 20 weeks of caloric restriction, aerobic exercise, both, or attention control. By main-effects analysis, peak oxygen consumption rose with exercise (+1.2 mL/kg/min, 95% CI 0.7–1.7; P<0.001) and with diet (+1.3, 0.8–1.8; P<0.001), and the combination was additive (joint effect 2.5 mL/kg/min); weight fell 7% on diet, 3% on exercise, and 10% on both. Neither intervention significantly changed the Minnesota Living with Heart Failure quality-of-life score. Brubaker 2023 then showed adding resistance training to diet plus aerobic exercise (88 patients) improved leg strength and muscle quality without further raising peak oxygen consumption. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): combined caloric restriction and aerobic exercise additively improve exercise capacity in obese older HFpEF.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a factorial randomised trial (SECRET, 100 patients) showed caloric restriction and aerobic exercise each improved peak oxygen consumption in obese HFpEF and combined additively (joint effect 2.5 mL/kg/min), without a significant quality-of-life gain

title: Non-invasive ventilation in cardiogenic pulmonary oedema: breathing and acidosis improve within an hour and intubation falls in pooled trials — but the largest trial (3CPO, 1,069 patients) found 7-day mortality identical at 9.5% versus 9.8%
question: In acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema, does non-invasive ventilation reduce intubation and mortality compared with standard oxygen therapy?
balance: SPLIT — intubation and early physiology favour ventilation; mortality depends on which evidence you trust. In 3CPO (Gray 2008), 1,069 patients (mean age 77.7 years) randomised to standard oxygen, CPAP, or non-invasive positive-pressure ventilation showed no difference in 7-day mortality (9.8% on oxygen versus 9.5% on non-invasive ventilation; P=0.87) and no difference between CPAP and NIPPV in death or intubation (11.7% versus 11.1%; P=0.81) — though dyspnoea, heart rate, acidosis, and hypercapnia all improved faster at 1 hour on ventilation. The Cochrane review (Berbenetz 2019; 24 studies, 2,664 participants) pooled a mortality benefit (risk ratio 0.65, 95% CI 0.51–0.82; low-quality evidence; number needed to treat 17) and a clearer intubation reduction (risk ratio 0.49, 0.38–0.62; moderate-quality evidence; NNT 13) — relative effects driven by smaller, older trials that 3CPO outweighs. PROPOSED SPLIT: use non-invasive ventilation to relieve distress and avoid intubation; a mortality benefit is claimed by the pooled small trials and contradicted by the one large trial.
stamp: SPLIT — non-invasive ventilation improves early physiology and reduces intubation (pooled relative risk 0.49), but the largest trial found no mortality difference (9.5% versus 9.8%) while a Cochrane pool of smaller trials claims relative risk 0.65 for death

title: Multidisciplinary heart-failure programmes cut hospitalisations — and, when a specialist team follows patients, death too (relative risk 0.75): telephone-only programmes cut heart-failure admissions but not mortality in two concordant McAlister reviews
question: In chronic heart failure, do multidisciplinary disease-management programmes reduce hospitalisation and death compared with usual care?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — for programmes built around a specialist multidisciplinary team. McAlister 2001 pooled 11 randomised trials (2,067 patients): disease-management programmes reduced hospitalisations (risk ratio 0.87, 95% CI 0.79–0.96) but not all-cause mortality (0.94, 0.75–1.19), were cost-saving in 7 of 8 trials reporting costs, and worked when follow-up was by a specialised multidisciplinary team (hospitalisation risk ratio 0.77, 0.68–0.86; n=1,366) but not when they were telephone-only with primary-care coordination (1.15, 0.96–1.37; n=646). McAlister 2004, across 29 trials (5,039 patients), found specialised multidisciplinary follow-up also reduced mortality (risk ratio 0.75, 0.59–0.96), heart-failure hospitalisations (0.74, 0.63–0.87), and all-cause hospitalisations (0.81, 0.71–0.92), with cost-saving in 15 of 18 trials reporting costs — all relative effects. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): multidisciplinary team follow-up reduces hospitalisation in heart failure, with a mortality reduction in the larger review; programme design decides the result.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — two concordant systematic reviews of randomised trials show multidisciplinary heart-failure programmes reduce hospitalisations, and specialist-team follow-up also reduced mortality (relative risk 0.75) in the larger review

title: Rolofylline in acute heart failure with kidney dysfunction: the 2,033-patient PROTECT trial was neutral on symptoms, kidneys and 60-day outcomes — the pilot's promise did not survive phase 3
question: In acute heart failure with renal dysfunction, does the adenosine A1 antagonist rolofylline improve dyspnoea and kidney outcomes compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the definitive trial is neutral on every outcome the drug was designed to move. In PROTECT (Massie BM et al., PMID: 20925544), 2,033 patients hospitalised with acute heart failure and impaired renal function were randomised 2:1 to intravenous rolofylline 30 mg daily for up to 3 days or placebo: the primary clinical composite (treatment success, failure, or no change) did not differ (odds ratio 0.92, 95% CI 0.78 to 1.09; P=0.35), persistent renal impairment developed in 15.0% on rolofylline versus 13.7% on placebo (P=0.44), and death or cardiovascular/renal readmission by 60 days occurred in 30.7% versus 31.9% (P=0.86). The earlier 301-patient pilot (Cotter G et al., PMID: 18926433) had shown the trends that justified phase 3 — better dyspnoea, stable creatinine, and a trend to fewer 60-day events at the 30 mg dose (hazard ratio 0.55, 95% CI 0.28 to 1.04) — none of which the large trial confirmed. The one clear harm signal was seizures, which occurred only in rolofylline patients. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): adenosine A1 blockade with rolofylline does not improve dyspnoea, kidney function, or 60-day outcomes in acute heart failure with renal dysfunction.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — phase 3 PROTECT (n=2,033) neutral on the clinical composite, renal function and 60-day death or readmission, against positive pilot trends

title: SERCA2a gene therapy for heart failure: a 39-patient phase 2 trial met its success criteria — the 250-patient CUPID 2 trial then found nothing (recurrent events HR 0.93)
question: In heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, does SERCA2a gene therapy delivered by intracoronary infusion improve outcomes compared with placebo?
balance: SPLIT — by trial size and rigour. The phase 2 CUPID trial (Jessup M et al., PMID: 21709064) randomised just 39 patients with advanced heart failure to intracoronary AAV1/SERCA2a or placebo and met its prespecified success criteria at group, individual and outcome level at 6 months, with a hazard ratio of 0.12 (P=0.003) for time to clinical events at 12 months and cardiovascular hospitalisation duration of 0.4 versus 4.5 days. The phase 2b CUPID 2 trial (Greenberg B et al., PMID: 26803443) then randomised 250 patients at 67 centres to a single intracoronary infusion of AAV1/SERCA2a or placebo and found no improvement in time to recurrent heart-failure events (104 vs 128 events; hazard ratio 0.93, 95% CI 0.53 to 1.65; p=0.81), with deaths in 21% on gene therapy versus 16% on placebo. No safety signals were noted in CUPID 2. PROPOSED SPLIT: the small phase 2 result was positive on its own terms; the adequately sized confirmatory trial was neutral, and the therapy as tested does not improve the clinical course of heart failure.
stamp: SPLIT — phase 2 (n=39) positive on prespecified composite criteria; phase 2b (n=250) neutral on recurrent heart-failure events

title: Cell therapy for advanced heart failure: both large sham-controlled trials missed their primary endpoints — DREAM-HF's heart-attack and stroke signal is exploratory only
question: In advanced heart failure, do mesenchymal or cardiopoietic cell therapies improve death and hospitalisation compared with control?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — on the endpoints these trials were built to answer. In DREAM-HF (Perin EC et al., PMID: 36858705), 565 patients with high-risk heart failure with reduced ejection fraction were randomised to a single transendocardial administration of mesenchymal precursor cells or sham control: the primary endpoint of recurrent decompensated heart-failure or resuscitated ventricular-arrhythmia events was similar between groups (hazard ratio 1.17, 95% CI 0.81 to 1.69; P = 0.41), as were terminal cardiac events and the hierarchical secondary endpoints. In CHART-1 (Bartunek J et al., PMID: 28025189), 315 patients with ischaemic heart failure were randomised to cardiopoietic cells or sham: the 39-week hierarchical composite primary endpoint was neutral (Mann-Whitney estimator 0.54, 95% CI 0.47 to 0.61; P = 0.27). The counterweight sits inside DREAM-HF: mesenchymal precursor cells reduced myocardial infarction or stroke by a relative 58% (hazard ratio 0.42, 95% CI 0.23 to 0.76) in the analysis population — but the trial's own conclusion is that the primary and secondary endpoints were negative and these are prespecified and post hoc exploratory signals, strongest in patients with inflammation. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): neither cell therapy improved its primary heart-failure endpoint; the anti-inflammatory event signal is a hypothesis for another trial, not a result.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — DREAM-HF and CHART-1 both neutral on their primary endpoints; the myocardial-infarction/stroke reduction in DREAM-HF is exploratory

title: Interatrial shunt for heart failure with preserved ejection fraction: it lowered exercise wedge pressure in a 44-patient phase 2 trial — then the 626-patient sham-controlled trial found no fewer heart-failure events and no better health status
question: In heart failure with preserved or mildly reduced ejection fraction and raised left atrial pressure, does an interatrial shunt device improve symptoms and outcomes compared with sham?
balance: SPLIT — the mechanism works and the clinical benefit does not follow. In the phase 2 REDUCE LAP-HF I trial (Feldman T et al., PMID: 29142012), 44 patients with ejection fraction ≥40% and exercise wedge pressure ≥25 mm Hg were randomised to the Corvia interatrial shunt device or sham: at 1 month the device produced a greater reduction in exercise pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (P=0.028 across exercise stages; peak wedge fell 3.5 ± 6.4 versus 0.5 ± 5.0 mm Hg, P=0.14). In the phase 3 REDUCE LAP-HF II trial (Shah SJ et al., PMID: 35120593), 626 patients were randomised to the device or sham: the hierarchical primary endpoint was exactly neutral (win ratio 1.0, 95% CI 0.8 to 1.2; p=0.85), no component differed, and the composite safety endpoint occurred in 38% on the device versus 31% on sham (p=0.11). Prespecified subgroups with high exercise pulmonary artery pressure, large right atria, and men fared worse on heart-failure events with the device. PROPOSED SPLIT: a real haemodynamic effect in phase 2; no reduction in heart-failure events or improvement in health status in the definitive sham-controlled trial.
stamp: SPLIT — exercise wedge pressure reduced in phase 2; no benefit on heart-failure events or health status in the phase 3 sham-controlled trial

title: Vagus nerve stimulation for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction: no reduction in death or heart-failure events (INOVATE-HF HR 1.14) and no reverse remodelling (NECTAR-HF) — quality of life improved in both trials, only one of them sham-controlled
question: In heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, does vagus nerve stimulation improve symptoms, remodelling, or outcomes compared with control?
balance: SPLIT — patients felt better; hearts and event rates did not change. In INOVATE-HF (Gold MR et al., PMID: 27058909), 707 patients with NYHA class III heart failure and ejection fraction ≤40% were randomised 3:2 to vagus nerve stimulation or continued medical therapy: the primary composite of death or first worsening-heart-failure event occurred in 30.3% versus 25.8% (hazard ratio 1.14, 95% CI 0.86 to 1.53; p = 0.37), while quality of life, NYHA class and 6-minute walk distance favoured stimulation (p < 0.05) and left ventricular end-systolic volume index did not differ (p = 0.49). In the sham-controlled NECTAR-HF trial (Zannad F et al., PMID: 25176942), 96 implanted patients were randomised 2:1 to stimulation on or off: the primary remodelling endpoint, change in left ventricular end-systolic diameter at 6 months, was -0.04 ± 0.25 cm on therapy versus -0.08 ± 0.32 cm on control (P = 0.60), every other echo, exercise and biomarker endpoint was neutral, and quality-of-life measures again improved significantly. PROPOSED SPLIT: no effect on death, heart-failure events or remodelling in either trial; a consistent improvement in symptoms and quality of life, proven against sham only in the small trial.
stamp: SPLIT — death, heart-failure events and remodelling neutral in both trials; symptoms and quality of life improved, against sham only in NECTAR-HF

title: Pulmonary-artery-catheter-guided care in severe heart failure: ESCAPE found the same days alive out of hospital (133 vs 135) and more in-hospital adverse events — and a 13-trial meta-analysis found no mortality benefit in any setting
question: In hospitalised acute heart failure, does management guided by a pulmonary artery catheter improve death or hospitalisation compared with clinical assessment alone?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — a large trial and the pooled randomised literature agree. In ESCAPE (Binanay C et al., PMID: 16204662), 433 patients hospitalised with severe symptomatic recurrent heart failure were randomised to therapy guided by clinical assessment plus a pulmonary artery catheter or by clinical assessment alone: days alive out of hospital in 6 months were 133 versus 135 (hazard ratio 1.00, 95% CI 0.82 to 1.21; P = .99), mortality was 10% versus 9% (odds ratio 1.26, 95% CI 0.78 to 2.03; P = .35), and in-hospital adverse events were more common with the catheter (21.9% vs 11.5%; P = .04). The accompanying meta-analysis of 13 randomised trials and 5,051 critically ill patients (Shah MR et al., PMID: 16204666) found a combined mortality odds ratio of 1.04 (95% CI 0.90 to 1.20; P = .59) and no difference in hospital days, with catheter-guided care associated with more inotrope (OR 1.58) and vasodilator (OR 2.35) use. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): catheter numbers change what doctors prescribe, not whether patients live or how long they stay in hospital.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — ESCAPE neutral on days alive out of hospital and mortality with more adverse events; 13-trial meta-analysis concordant

title: Disopyramide for obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy still obstructed on a beta-blocker: outflow gradients roughly halved and symptoms improved in two large cohorts — but no randomised trial has ever tested it
question: In obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, does disopyramide reduce the outflow gradient and symptoms in patients still obstructed on a beta-blocker?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — consistent before-and-after improvement in the only evidence there is: uncontrolled cohorts. In the four-centre study (Sherrid MV et al., PMID: 15837258), 118 patients with obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy treated with disopyramide (mean dose 432 ± 181 mg/day, 97% also on beta-blockers) for a mean of 3.1 years saw resting outflow gradient fall from 75 ± 33 to 40 ± 32 mm Hg (p < 0.0001) and NYHA class from 2.3 ± 0.7 to 1.7 ± 0.6 (p < 0.0001); 66% were managed without myectomy, alcohol ablation or pacing, and annual cardiac mortality was 1.4% versus 2.6% per year in 373 untreated obstructed patients (p = 0.07). In the later single-centre series (Sherrid MV et al., PMID: 23704138), disopyramide was added in 221 of 299 patients still symptomatic after beta-blockade or verapamil, and pharmacological control of symptoms was achieved in 141 (64%). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): disopyramide probably lowers gradient and symptoms in patients who remain obstructed on first-line therapy, on cohort evidence only — there is no randomised, placebo-controlled, or blinded evidence at all.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — gradient and symptom improvement consistent across two uncontrolled cohorts; no randomised evidence exists
