title: Benznidazole in established Chagas cardiomyopathy: parasite cleared from the blood (PCR conversion 66.2% vs 33.5%) but cardiac deterioration unchanged over five years (primary outcome 27.5% vs 29.1%)
question: In established Chagas cardiomyopathy, does benznidazole reduce parasite detection, disease progression, or cardiovascular death compared with placebo?
balance: SPLIT — the drug does exactly what it is meant to do to the parasite, and it does not change the disease. In the BENEFIT trial (Morillo CA et al., PMID: 26323937), 2,854 patients with established Chagas cardiomyopathy were randomised to benznidazole or placebo for up to 80 days and followed for a mean of 5.4 years: the primary composite (death, resuscitated cardiac arrest, sustained ventricular tachycardia, device insertion, transplantation, new heart failure, stroke or thromboembolism) occurred in 27.5% on benznidazole versus 29.1% on placebo (hazard ratio 0.93, 95% CI 0.81 to 1.07; P=0.31). Parasite detection told the opposite story: conversion to negative PCR was 66.2% versus 33.5% at the end of treatment, 55.4% versus 35.3% at 2 years and 46.7% versus 33.1% at 5 years or more (P<0.001 for all comparisons), though the size of the PCR effect varied sharply by region and did not correspond to clinical effects. PROPOSED SPLIT: trypanocidal therapy clears parasites from blood without significantly reducing cardiac clinical deterioration in established cardiomyopathy — by the time the heart is damaged, the damage, not the parasite load in blood, drives events.
stamp: SPLIT — parasite detection clearly reduced; clinical cardiac outcomes not significantly different over a mean 5.4 years in one large trial

title: Amiodarone, sotalol or propafenone to keep atrial fibrillation away: amiodarone holds sinus rhythm longest in two randomised trials (median 487 vs 74 days against sotalol in SAFE-T) — and is stopped for side effects most often
question: In atrial fibrillation needing rhythm control, how do amiodarone, sotalol, and propafenone compare at keeping patients in sinus rhythm?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — amiodarone is the most effective of the three at maintaining sinus rhythm, in two concordant randomised trials, and the least tolerable. In SAFE-T (Singh BN et al., PMID: 15872201), 665 anticoagulated patients with persistent atrial fibrillation were randomised double-blind to amiodarone, sotalol or placebo: median time to recurrence was 487 days on amiodarone versus 74 days on sotalol and 6 days on placebo (intention-to-treat), with spontaneous conversion in 27.1%, 24.2% and 0.8% respectively — though in patients with ischaemic heart disease amiodarone and sotalol did not differ significantly (569 vs 428 days; P=0.53). In the three-arm Kochiadakis trial (Kochiadakis GE et al., PMID: 11139949), 214 patients with recurrent symptomatic atrial fibrillation had recurrence in 25 of 75 on amiodarone, 51 of 75 on sotalol and 24 of 64 on propafenone, while adverse effects forcing discontinuation struck 14 on amiodarone, 5 on sotalol and 1 on propafenone. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): for keeping sinus rhythm, amiodarone first, propafenone a close and better-tolerated second, sotalol last — an efficacy ranking bought with amiodarone's side-effect burden.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — amiodarone superior for maintaining sinus rhythm in two randomised trials, with the most treatment-stopping side effects

title: Restarting anticoagulation after a brain haemorrhage in atrial fibrillation: two small trials and their pooled analysis — ischaemic events clearly fewer (HR 0.27), haemorrhagic events possibly more, the net still unresolved
question: In atrial fibrillation after a spontaneous intracerebral haemorrhage, does restarting oral anticoagulation reduce ischaemic stroke enough to outweigh recurrent bleeding?
balance: SPLIT — the trade-off is real in both directions and neither small trial could settle it. In SoSTART (SoSTART Collaboration, PMID: 34487722), 203 survivors of spontaneous intracranial haemorrhage with atrial fibrillation were randomised to start or avoid oral anticoagulation: recurrent intracranial haemorrhage occurred in 8% versus 4% (adjusted HR 2.42, 95% CI 0.72 to 8.09), non-inferiority of starting was not shown (p=0.152), and 22% versus 11% died. In APACHE-AF (Schreuder FHBM et al., PMID: 34687635), 101 patients were randomised to apixaban or no anticoagulation after anticoagulant-associated intracerebral haemorrhage: non-fatal stroke or vascular death occurred in 26% versus 24% (adjusted HR 1.05, 95% CI 0.48 to 2.31; p=0.90). Pooling all four eligible trials (412 participants) in the COCROACH individual-participant meta-analysis (Al-Shahi Salman R et al., PMID: 37839434), starting anticoagulation gave a pooled HR of 0.68 (95% CI 0.42 to 1.10) for any stroke or cardiovascular death, 0.27 (95% CI 0.13 to 0.56) for ischaemic major cardiovascular events, and 1.80 (95% CI 0.77 to 4.21) for haemorrhagic major events. PROPOSED SPLIT: restarting prevents ischaemic events convincingly and may cause haemorrhagic ones; whether the net favours restarting awaits the adequately powered trials still running.
stamp: SPLIT — restarting reduces ischaemic events (pooled HR 0.27) with an uncertain increase in haemorrhagic events; net effect on stroke or cardiovascular death not established

title: Standardised perioperative DOAC interruption without bridging (PAUSE): major bleeding 0.90–1.85% and arterial thromboembolism 0.16–0.60% at 30 days in 3,007 patients — a large prospective cohort, not a randomised trial
question: In patients on a direct oral anticoagulant who need an elective procedure, does a standardised interruption protocol without bridging keep bleeding and thromboembolism acceptably low?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a simple rule, applied prospectively to 3,007 patients, produced low event rates. In the PAUSE cohort (Douketis JD et al., PMID: 31380891), patients with atrial fibrillation on apixaban, dabigatran or rivaroxaban stopped their drug 1 day before a low-bleeding-risk procedure and 2 days before a high-bleeding-risk procedure, resuming 1 day or 2–3 days afterwards, with no heparin bridging and no coagulation testing: 30-day major bleeding was 1.35% in the apixaban cohort, 0.90% in the dabigatran cohort and 1.85% in the rivaroxaban cohort, and arterial thromboembolism was 0.16%, 0.60% and 0.37% respectively; in high-bleeding-risk procedures major bleeding reached 2.96% (apixaban) and 2.95% (rivaroxaban). The randomised PAUSE-2 pilot (Douketis JD et al., PMID: 40086754) found preoperative residual drug levels nearly identical under PAUSE-based and ASRA-based management (<30 ng/mL in 94.4% vs 95.6% of tested patients). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the standardised interruption protocol is associated with acceptably low bleeding and thromboembolism, on prospective-cohort evidence — no trial has randomised patients against bridging or against unstructured care.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — standardised interruption without bridging or testing was associated with low bleeding and thromboembolism rates in a 3,007-patient prospective cohort; randomised evidence is pilot-stage only

title: Direct oral anticoagulants versus warfarin around cardioversion: three randomised trials, stroke and bleeding rates at or under 1% on both sides — each DOAC strategy matched the vitamin-K-antagonist strategy
question: Before cardioversion for atrial fibrillation, do direct oral anticoagulants match warfarin for stroke, embolism, and bleeding?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — three dedicated randomised trials, one per drug, all telling the same story of very low event rates on both strategies. In X-VeRT (Cappato R et al., PMID: 25182247), 1,504 patients were randomised to rivaroxaban or dose-adjusted vitamin K antagonists around early or delayed cardioversion: the primary efficacy composite occurred in 0.51% versus 1.02% (risk ratio 0.50, 95% CI 0.15 to 1.73) and major bleeding in 0.6% versus 0.8%. In ENSURE-AF (Goette A et al., PMID: 27590218), 2,199 patients were randomised to edoxaban or enoxaparin-warfarin: the efficacy composite occurred in under 1% versus 1% (odds ratio 0.46, 95% CI 0.12 to 1.43) and major plus clinically relevant non-major bleeding in 1% versus 1% (OR 1.48, 95% CI 0.64 to 3.55). In EMANATE (Ezekowitz MD et al., PMID: 29659797), 1,500 patients had 0 strokes on apixaban versus 6 on heparin/VKA, with major bleeding in 3 versus 6 patients. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): DOACs are a safe, effective alternative to warfarin around cardioversion — the trials establish comparability at low event rates, not superiority, and none was powered for the rare events that matter most.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — three randomised trials show DOAC strategies match heparin/VKA around cardioversion with very low event rates in both arms; none was powered to prove superiority

title: Colchicine after atrial fibrillation ablation: three months of it halved early recurrence in one trial (16% vs 33.5%) — ten days of it did nothing for recurrence in a larger later trial, though pericarditis chest pain fell from 15% to 4%
question: After catheter ablation for atrial fibrillation, does colchicine reduce early arrhythmia recurrence and pericarditis compared with placebo?
balance: SPLIT — by regimen, era and population. In the 2012 trial (Deftereos S et al., PMID: 23040570), 161 patients with paroxysmal atrial fibrillation undergoing pulmonary vein isolation were randomised to colchicine 0.5 mg twice daily or placebo for 3 months, without antiarrhythmic drugs: recurrence within 3 months occurred in 16% (13/81) on colchicine versus 33.5% (27/80) on placebo (odds ratio 0.38, 95% CI 0.18 to 0.80), alongside larger falls in C-reactive protein and interleukin-6, at the cost of diarrhoea in 8.6% versus 1.3%. In the 2024 trial (Benz AP et al., PMID: 38126206), 199 patients were randomised to colchicine 0.6 mg twice daily or placebo for just 10 days starting before ablation: atrial arrhythmia recurrence was 31% versus 32% at 2 weeks (hazard ratio 0.98, 95% CI 0.59 to 1.61) and 14% versus 15% at 3 months (HR 0.95, 95% CI 0.45 to 2.02), but post-ablation chest pain consistent with pericarditis fell from 15% to 4% (HR 0.26, 95% CI 0.09 to 0.77; P=0.02) while diarrhoea rose from 7% to 26% (HR 4.74). PROPOSED SPLIT: a 3-month course after isolation of paroxysmal AF reduced early recurrence in one small trial; a 10-day course in a broader modern population did not — its demonstrable benefit is less pericarditis pain.
stamp: SPLIT — a 3-month course reduced early recurrence in paroxysmal AF (2012); a 10-day course did not reduce recurrence in a broader population (2024) but did reduce pericarditis pain

title: Ablation for persistent atrial fibrillation with unexplained cardiomyopathy: ejection fraction rose 18 points versus 4 with rate control in a 68-patient trial — a large effect on a surrogate endpoint, in a small, carefully selected group
question: In persistent atrial fibrillation with reduced ejection fraction and suspected tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy, does catheter ablation improve ejection fraction compared with medical rate control?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the effect is large, mechanistically coherent, and rests on very few patients. In CAMERA-MRI (Prabhu S et al., PMID: 28855115), 68 patients with persistent atrial fibrillation and idiopathic cardiomyopathy (ejection fraction ≤45%) were randomised to catheter ablation or continued medical rate control: at 6 months, ejection fraction had improved by 18 ± 13% with ablation versus 4.4 ± 13% with rate control (p < 0.0001), and normalised (≥50%) in 58% versus 9% (p = 0.0002), with post-ablation AF burden of 1.6 ± 5.0%; patients without ventricular fibrosis on MRI improved most. The earlier meta-analysis of ablation versus rate control in persistent AF with heart failure (Zhu M et al., PMID: 27472728) pooled just 3 randomised trials and 143 patients, finding an ejection-fraction advantage of 6.22% (95% CI 0.7 to 11.74; P = 0.03) and better peak oxygen consumption and NYHA class. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): in AF with unexplained cardiomyopathy, restoring sinus rhythm by ablation recovers ventricular function far more than rate control — on surrogate endpoints, in small selected trials, with no mortality or hospitalisation data.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one small randomised trial with a large ejection-fraction effect, supported by a small meta-analysis; no hard-outcome data

title: Hybrid surgical–catheter ablation for long-standing persistent atrial fibrillation: freedom from arrhythmia 68–72% versus 39–50% with catheter ablation alone in two randomised trials, without more major complications
question: In long-standing persistent atrial fibrillation, does hybrid surgical–catheter ablation improve freedom from arrhythmia compared with catheter ablation alone?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — two independent randomised trials agree, with large absolute differences. In CONVERGE (DeLurgio DB et al., PMID: 33185144), 153 patients with persistent or long-standing persistent atrial fibrillation were randomised 2:1 to the hybrid convergent procedure or catheter ablation: primary effectiveness (freedom from AF/flutter/tachycardia without new or increased previously failed antiarrhythmic drugs) at 12 months was 67.7% versus 50.0% (P=0.036), and 53.5% versus 32.0% off antiarrhythmic drugs (P=0.0128); major adverse events occurred in 2.9% within 7 days and 4.9% between days 8 and 30, with no deaths, perforations or atrioesophageal fistulas. In CEASE-AF (Doll N et al., PMID: 37425372), 154 patients were randomised 2:1 to hybrid or catheter ablation: freedom from arrhythmia off class I/III drugs at 12 months was 71.6% versus 39.2% — an absolute benefit increase of 32.4% (95% CI 14.3% to 48.0%; p < 0.001) — with major complications in 7.8% versus 5.8% (p = 0.75). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): for symptomatic drug-refractory persistent and long-standing persistent AF, hybrid ablation keeps substantially more patients arrhythmia-free at one year than catheter ablation alone, at similar major-complication rates in trial centres.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — two concordant randomised trials show higher 12-month freedom from atrial arrhythmia with hybrid ablation and no significant excess of major complications

title: Adding linear lesions or fractionated-signal ablation to pulmonary vein isolation in persistent atrial fibrillation: STAR AF II found no fewer recurrences (freedom 59% with isolation alone vs 49% and 46% with more ablation) — only longer procedures
question: In persistent atrial fibrillation, does adding linear lesions or ablation of complex fractionated signals to pulmonary vein isolation improve freedom from arrhythmia?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — the definitive trial and the pooled literature point the same way. In STAR AF II (Verma A et al., PMID: 25946280), 589 patients with persistent atrial fibrillation were randomised to pulmonary vein isolation alone (n = 67), isolation plus ablation of complex fractionated electrograms (n = 263), or isolation plus linear ablation (n = 259): after 18 months, freedom from recurrent atrial fibrillation was 59% with isolation alone versus 49% and 46% with the adjunctive strategies (P=0.15), with no differences in secondary endpoints, and procedure time was significantly shorter with isolation alone (P<0.001). The meta-analysis of adjunctive strategies (Scott PA et al., PMID: 26559915) pooled 10 studies and 1,821 patients: adding fractionated-electrogram ablation (risk ratio 0.86, 95% CI 0.64 to 1.16; P = 0.32) or linear ablation (RR 0.64, 95% CI 0.37 to 1.09; P = 0.10) did not significantly improve arrhythmia-free survival, while increasing procedure and fluoroscopy times. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): in persistent AF, more ablation is not better ablation — pulmonary vein isolation alone remains the benchmark these strategies failed to beat.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — the definitive randomised trial and a concordant meta-analysis both show no arrhythmia benefit from adjunctive substrate ablation

title: Fish oil around cardiac surgery: the 1,516-patient OPERA trial found postoperative atrial fibrillation in 30.0% on fish oil versus 30.7% on placebo — while a pooled analysis of 19 smaller trials still claims a modest reduction
question: After cardiac surgery, does fish oil (omega-3) supplementation prevent postoperative atrial fibrillation compared with placebo?
balance: SPLIT — the best trial says no; the average of all trials says a little. In OPERA (Mozaffarian D et al., PMID: 23128104), 1,516 patients scheduled for cardiac surgery in three countries were randomised double-blind to fish oil (preoperative loading of 10 g over 3–5 days, then 2 g/day) or placebo: postoperative atrial fibrillation occurred in 30.0% versus 30.7% (odds ratio 0.96, 95% CI 0.77 to 1.20; P = .74), with no difference in any secondary endpoint and no excess bleeding. The updated systematic review and meta-analysis (Langlois PL et al., PMID: 27293143) pooled 19 randomised trials and 4,335 cardiac-surgery patients: omega-3 reduced postoperative atrial fibrillation (odds ratio 0.78, 95% CI 0.68 to 0.90; P = 0.004) and hospital stay (weighted mean difference -1.37 days) but not ICU stay, ventilation duration or mortality — with, in the authors' own words, considerable clinical and statistical heterogeneity weakening the findings. PROPOSED SPLIT: the largest, broadest, best-blinded trial is flatly null; the pooled estimate leans positive on the strength of smaller trials, the pattern that most often means the true effect is small or absent.
stamp: SPLIT — the largest trial (OPERA, n=1,516) is null; a meta-analysis of 19 mostly smaller trials estimates a modest reduction (OR 0.78) with considerable heterogeneity

title: Amiodarone prophylaxis after cardiac surgery: atrial tachyarrhythmias in 16.1% versus 29.5% in the PAPABEAR trial, and roughly halved odds across 14 trials — with no difference in mortality or serious complications
question: After cardiac surgery, does prophylactic amiodarone prevent postoperative atrial fibrillation and shorten hospital stay compared with placebo?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — a large double-blind trial and the pooled literature agree on fewer arrhythmias, and neither shows a mortality price. In PAPABEAR (Mitchell LB et al., PMID: 16380589), 601 patients listed for bypass and/or valve surgery were randomised to oral amiodarone 10 mg/kg daily or placebo from 6 days before to 6 days after surgery: atrial tachyarrhythmias lasting ≥5 minutes and prompting therapy occurred in 16.1% (48/299) versus 29.5% (89/302) (hazard ratio 0.52, 95% CI 0.34 to 0.69; P<.001), consistently across age, surgery type and beta-blocker subgroups, with postoperative sustained ventricular tachyarrhythmias in 0.3% versus 2.6% (P = .04), more dose reductions on amiodarone (11.4% vs 5.3%; P = .008), and no differences in serious complications, in-hospital mortality, 6-month readmission or 1-year mortality. The dose-and-timing meta-analysis (Buckley MS et al., PMID: 17316148) pooled 14 trials and 2,864 patients: odds ratios for postoperative AF were 0.58 (low dose), 0.45 (medium) and 0.44 (high), with no significant difference between preoperative (OR 0.50) and postoperative (OR 0.48) initiation. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): a short perioperative amiodarone course roughly halves postoperative atrial tachyarrhythmias; it has not been shown to shorten stay or save lives, and the question's hospital-stay limb remains unanswered by these records.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — one large double-blind trial and a concordant 14-trial meta-analysis show fewer postoperative atrial arrhythmias; no mortality or serious-complication difference

title: Intravenous magnesium added to standard treatment for rapid atrial fibrillation: rate control achieved more often in two meta-analyses (63% vs 40% in the largest pool), conversion to sinus rhythm modestly more often — flushing the main side effect
question: In acute atrial fibrillation in the emergency department, does intravenous magnesium added to standard therapy improve rate control or conversion compared with standard therapy alone?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two independent meta-analyses of small randomised trials agree. The 2021 analysis (Ramesh T et al., PMID: 34162502) pooled 6 randomised trials and 745 patients receiving intravenous magnesium plus standard care versus standard care alone for rapid atrial fibrillation: rate control was achieved in 63% versus 40% (odds ratio 2.49, 95% CI 1.80 to 3.45) and conversion to sinus rhythm in 21% versus 14% (OR 1.75, 95% CI 1.08 to 2.84), with flushing in 9% versus 0.4% (OR 19.79, 95% CI 4.30 to 91.21); lower doses (≤5 g) performed better for rhythm control than higher doses in subgroup analysis. The 2023 analysis (Enayati A et al., PMID: 37186322) pooled 9 trials and 1,048 non-postoperative patients: rate control OR 1.87 (95% CI 1.13 to 3.11; p = .02) and rhythm control OR 1.45 (95% CI 1.04 to 2.03; p = .03), with no significant difference in side effects as reported. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): as an adjunct — not a substitute — intravenous magnesium improves the odds of rate control by roughly twofold and conversion modestly, on pooled small-trial evidence.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two concordant meta-analyses of randomised trials show better rate control and modestly better conversion when magnesium is added to standard care

title: Diltiazem versus metoprolol for acute atrial fibrillation with a rapid rate: randomised trials favour diltiazem for reaching rate control (OR 4.75) — observational studies show no difference, and hypotension looks similar
question: In acute atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response, does intravenous diltiazem control heart rate faster and more reliably than intravenous metoprolol?
balance: SPLIT — the answer changes with the study design. The largest meta-analysis (Bolton A et al., PMID: 37856044) pooled 16 studies — 7 randomised and 9 observational — of intravenous diltiazem versus metoprolol for atrial fibrillation or flutter with rapid ventricular response: in randomised trials, diltiazem was more effective for rate control (odds ratio 4.75, 95% CI 2.50 to 9.04; I² = 14%), but in observational studies there was no significant difference (OR 1.26, 95% CI 0.89 to 1.80; I² = 55%), and observational data showed no difference in hypotension (OR 1.12, 95% CI 0.51 to 2.45). The earlier emergency-medicine systematic review (Martindale JL et al., PMID: 25564459) found only two randomised double-blind trials (n = 92) and a combined relative risk of acute rate control of 1.8 (95% CI 1.2 to 2.6) favouring diltiazem. PROPOSED SPLIT: on randomised evidence diltiazem reaches rate control more reliably; the observational record, which reflects sicker and more hypotension-prone real-world selections, cannot confirm it — and neither body of evidence shows a hypotension penalty for either drug.
stamp: SPLIT — by study design: randomised trials favour diltiazem for acute rate control; observational studies show no difference; hypotension similar in observational data

title: Aspirin 81 mg versus 325 mg in established cardiovascular disease: 15,076 patients, no difference in death, myocardial infarction or stroke hospitalisation (7.28% vs 7.51%) and none in major bleeding — in a trial where 41.6% of the high-dose group switched down
question: In established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, is aspirin 81 mg daily as effective and as safe as 325 mg daily?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — one very large pragmatic trial, flat on both effectiveness and safety. In ADAPTABLE (Jones WS et al., PMID: 33999548), 15,076 patients with established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease were randomised open-label to aspirin 81 mg or 325 mg daily and followed for a median of 26.2 months: death, hospitalisation for myocardial infarction, or hospitalisation for stroke occurred in 590 patients (estimated 7.28%) on 81 mg versus 569 (7.51%) on 325 mg (hazard ratio 1.02, 95% CI 0.91 to 1.14), and hospitalisation for major bleeding in 53 (0.63%) versus 44 (0.60%) (HR 1.18, 95% CI 0.79 to 1.77). The trial's own caveat is adherence to the assigned strategy: 41.6% of the 325 mg group switched dose (versus 7.1% of the 81 mg group), and median exposure to the assigned dose was 434 versus 650 days — and 96.0% of patients with prior-use data were already taking aspirin before randomisation, 85.3% of them 81 mg. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): in established cardiovascular disease there is no demonstrated advantage — in events prevented or bleeding caused — to 325 mg over 81 mg, and patients vote for the lower dose with their feet.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — a very large pragmatic trial found no effectiveness or safety advantage for 325 mg over 81 mg; heavy dose-switching blurs the contrast actually tested

title: Omega-3 carboxylic acids in STRENGTH: 12.0% versus 12.2% major cardiovascular events — no difference in 13,078 high-risk patients, the trial stopped early for futility, and gut side effects nearly doubled
question: In statin-treated patients with raised triglycerides, do omega-3 carboxylic acids reduce cardiovascular events compared with placebo?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — one very large double-blind trial answers this formulation's question directly. In STRENGTH (Nicholls SJ et al., PMID: 33190147), 13,078 statin-treated patients at high cardiovascular risk with hypertriglyceridemia and low HDL cholesterol were randomised to omega-3 carboxylic acids (a carboxylic acid formulation of EPA and DHA) 4 g/d or corn oil. The primary composite — cardiovascular death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke, coronary revascularisation, or unstable angina requiring hospitalisation — occurred in 785 patients (12.0%) on omega-3 CA versus 795 (12.2%) on corn oil (hazard ratio 0.99, 95% CI 0.90–1.09; P = .84). The trial was halted prematurely, after 1,384 patients had experienced a primary end point event of a planned 1,600 events, on an interim analysis indicating a low probability of clinical benefit. The only clear difference was harm-side and modest: gastrointestinal adverse events in 24.7% on omega-3 CA versus 14.7% on corn oil. This is a statement about the EPA+DHA carboxylic-acid formulation, not about icosapent ethyl, a different agent tested in a different trial. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): in statin-treated high-risk patients with raised triglycerides, omega-3 carboxylic acids did not reduce major adverse cardiovascular events versus corn oil, and the record does not support using this formulation for that purpose.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — in one 13,078-patient double-blind trial stopped for futility, omega-3 carboxylic acids 4 g/d gave a primary-event rate of 12.0% versus 12.2% on corn oil (HR 0.99, 95% CI 0.90–1.09), with more gastrointestinal adverse events (24.7% versus 14.7%)

title: Dalcetrapib after acute coronary syndrome: HDL up 31–40%, events unchanged (8.0% vs 8.3%) — a 15,871-patient trial stopped for futility
question: In patients after acute coronary syndrome with raised HDL cholesterol, does the CETP inhibitor dalcetrapib reduce cardiovascular events compared with placebo?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — dalcetrapib did exactly what it was designed to do to the blood test and nothing to outcomes. In dal-OUTCOMES (Schwartz GG et al., PMID: 23126252), 15,871 patients after an acute coronary syndrome received dalcetrapib 600 mg daily or placebo on top of best evidence-based care; HDL cholesterol rose 31–40% with dalcetrapib versus 4–11% with placebo, with minimal effect on LDL cholesterol. Over a median 31 months the primary composite (coronary death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, ischaemic stroke, unstable angina, or resuscitated cardiac arrest) occurred in 8.0% on dalcetrapib and 8.3% on placebo (hazard ratio 1.04, 95% CI 0.93–1.16; p=0.52), and the trial was stopped for futility at a prespecified interim analysis. Total mortality did not differ, while median C-reactive protein was 0.2 mg/L higher and mean systolic blood pressure 0.6 mm Hg higher on dalcetrapib (p<0.001 for both). PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): a very large, well-powered trial shows raising HDL with dalcetrapib after acute coronary syndrome does not reduce cardiovascular events.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — dal-OUTCOMES (n=15,871) stopped for futility; primary events 8.0% vs 8.3% (HR 1.04) despite a 31–40% HDL rise

title: Evacetrapib in high-risk vascular disease: LDL down 31%, HDL up 133% — and events identical (12.9% vs 12.8%), trial stopped for lack of efficacy
question: In patients with atherosclerotic disease, does the CETP inhibitor evacetrapib reduce cardiovascular events compared with placebo?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — the strongest lipid changes in the CETP class bought no events at all. In ACCELERATE (Lincoff AM et al., PMID: 28514624), 12,092 patients with high-risk vascular disease received evacetrapib 130 mg daily or placebo on top of standard therapy. At 3 months LDL cholesterol had fallen 31.1% on evacetrapib versus a 6.0% rise on placebo, and HDL cholesterol had risen 133.2% versus 1.6%. Yet after a median 26 months a primary end-point event (cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, stroke, coronary revascularisation, or hospitalisation for unstable angina) occurred in 12.9% on evacetrapib and 12.8% on placebo (hazard ratio 1.01, 95% CI 0.91–1.11; p=0.91), and the trial was terminated early for lack of efficacy after 1,363 of 1,670 planned events. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): evacetrapib's favourable effects on lipid biomarkers did not reduce cardiovascular events.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — ACCELERATE (n=12,092) stopped early for lack of efficacy; primary events 12.9% vs 12.8% (HR 1.01) despite LDL −31.1% and HDL +133.2%

title: Statins in children with familial hypercholesterolaemia: LDL falls at every time point across nine placebo trials, carotid wall thickness regressed over two years on pravastatin — long-term safety still not firmly established
question: In children and adolescents with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia, do statins lower LDL cholesterol safely compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for cholesterol and the artery wall, with event prevention inferred, not shown. The Cochrane review (Vuorio A et al., PMID: 31696945) pooled nine randomised placebo-controlled studies in 1,177 participants up to 18 years old with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia: statins reduced mean LDL cholesterol at all time points (high-quality evidence), with little or no difference in liver enzymes, creatine kinase, myopathy measures, or clinical adverse events, though follow-up was short (median 24 weeks, range 6 weeks to 2 years). The largest single trial (Wiegman A et al., PMID: 15265847) randomised 214 children aged 8–18 to pravastatin 20–40 mg daily or placebo for 2 years: LDL cholesterol fell 24.1% on pravastatin versus a 0.3% rise on placebo (p<0.001), carotid intima-media thickness trended to regression on pravastatin (−0.010 mm) versus progression on placebo (+0.005 mm; between-group difference significant, p=0.02), and there were no differences in growth, maturation, hormone levels, or muscle and liver enzymes. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): statins lower LDL substantially and appear safe over up to two years in children with familial hypercholesterolaemia; whether starting in childhood prevents adult heart attacks is biologically plausible but has never been tested in a trial with clinical events.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — nine placebo-controlled trials (n=1,177) lower LDL at all time points; pravastatin over 2 years lowered LDL 24.1% and regressed carotid thickness, with no growth or maturation signal; long-term safety and event prevention untested

title: Intravenous magnesium in acute myocardial infarction: a 24% relative mortality reduction in LIMIT-2, nothing at all in MAGIC's 6,213 high-risk patients — the early promise did not survive bigger trials
question: In acute myocardial infarction, does intravenous magnesium reduce mortality compared with placebo?
balance: SPLIT — the answer splits by trial size and era. The early evidence was strongly positive: an overview of seven small randomised trials (Teo KK et al., PMID: 1838289; 1,301 patients) found short-term mortality of 3.8% on magnesium versus 8.2% on control, and LIMIT-2 (Woods KL et al., PMID: 1351547; 2,316 patients) found 28-day mortality of 7.8% on intravenous magnesium versus 10.3% on saline — a 24% relative reduction (95% CI 1–43%; p=0.04) — with left ventricular failure in the coronary care unit reduced by 25% relative. But the largest dedicated trial, MAGIC (PMID: 12401244; 6,213 high-risk patients with ST-elevation infarction), found 30-day mortality of 15.3% on magnesium versus 15.2% on placebo (odds ratio 1.0, 95% CI 0.9–1.2; p=0.96), with no benefit in any prespecified subgroup. The 58,050-patient ISIS-4 factorial trial — carded on shelf #3334 for its captopril question — also tested intravenous magnesium and is named here without figures. PROPOSED SPLIT: benefit in the small early trials and LIMIT-2, none in MAGIC's high-risk reperfusion-era population; routine intravenous magnesium in acute myocardial infarction is not supported by the largest evidence.
stamp: SPLIT — LIMIT-2 (n=2,316) cut 28-day mortality (7.8% vs 10.3%; 24% relative reduction) and the early overview was positive, but MAGIC (n=6,213 high-risk STEMI) found 15.3% vs 15.2% (OR 1.0)

title: Glucose–insulin–potassium in acute infarction: hospital mortality 16.1% vs 21% in the small old trials — 10.0% vs 9.7% in the 20,201-patient CREATE-ECLA trial that settled it
question: In acute myocardial infarction, does glucose–insulin–potassium infusion reduce death compared with usual care?
balance: SPLIT — the answer splits by era. The early trials pointed to real benefit: an overview of nine randomised placebo-controlled trials (Fath-Ordoubadi F et al., PMID: 9286943; 1,932 patients) found hospital mortality of 16.1% on glucose–insulin–potassium versus 21% on placebo (odds ratio 0.72, 95% CI 0.57–0.90; p=0.004) — a 28% proportional relative reduction, about 49 lives saved per 1,000 treated. The definitive modern trial reversed the picture: CREATE-ECLA (Mehta SR et al., PMID: 15671428) randomised 20,201 patients with ST-elevation infarction presenting within 12 hours to high-dose GIK for 24 hours plus usual care or usual care alone, and 30-day mortality was 10.0% on GIK versus 9.7% on control (hazard ratio 1.03, 95% CI 0.95–1.13; p=0.45), with no differences in cardiac arrest, cardiogenic shock, reinfarction, or heart failure, and consistency across subgroups including patients with and without diabetes and with and without reperfusion. PROPOSED SPLIT: a genuine signal in small pre-reperfusion trials, and no effect in the one trial large enough and modern enough to decide routine use.
stamp: SPLIT — nine small early trials pooled to a mortality benefit (16.1% vs 21%; OR 0.72), but CREATE-ECLA (n=20,201) found 30-day mortality 10.0% vs 9.7% (HR 1.03)

title: Routine nitrates after myocardial infarction: intravenous nitrates cut mortality in the small early trials (136 vs 193 deaths), transdermal GTN in 19,394 GISSI-3 patients did not (OR 0.94)
question: After acute myocardial infarction, do routine nitrates reduce mortality compared with placebo?
balance: SPLIT — the answer splits by formulation and era. The early evidence for intravenous nitrates was positive: an overview of ten randomised trials (Yusuf S et al., PMID: 2896919; about 2,000 patients) counted 136 deaths on intravenous nitroglycerin or nitroprusside versus 193 on control — a typical 35% relative reduction in the odds of death (p<0.001), concentrated in the first week. But when nitrates were given systematically to an unselected modern population, the effect vanished: in GISSI-3 (PMID: 7910229), 19,394 patients randomised within 24 hours of infarction to transdermal glyceryl trinitrate (intravenous for 24 hours, then transdermal 10 mg daily) or open control showed no independent effect of GTN on 6-week mortality (odds ratio 0.94, 95% CI 0.84–1.05) or on mortality plus severe ventricular dysfunction (0.94, 0.87–1.02). The 58,050-patient ISIS-4 trial — carded on shelf #3334 for its captopril question — also randomised an oral mononitrate and is named here without figures. PROPOSED SPLIT: intravenous nitrates reduced mortality in small pre-reperfusion trials; routine scheduled nitrates for every infarct patient did not reduce mortality in the mega-trial era.
stamp: SPLIT — Yusuf 1988 overview of IV nitrates: 136 vs 193 deaths (35% relative odds reduction); GISSI-3 (n=19,394) transdermal GTN: 6-week mortality OR 0.94 (95% CI 0.84–1.05)

title: Calcium-channel blockers after infarction: verapamil cut major events (18.0% vs 21.6%) in DAVIT II, diltiazem was neutral overall in MDPIT — and harmful when the chest film showed pulmonary congestion (HR 1.41)
question: After myocardial infarction, do calcium-channel blockers improve survival — and does the answer differ for diltiazem in patients with heart failure?
balance: SPLIT — the answer splits by drug and, decisively, by left-ventricular function. In MDPIT (PMID: 2899840), 2,466 patients after infarction received diltiazem 240 mg daily or placebo for a mean of 25 months: total mortality was nearly identical (167 vs 166 deaths), and first recurrent cardiac events were 11% fewer on diltiazem without reaching significance (202 vs 226; hazard ratio 0.90, 95% CI 0.74–1.08) — but a significant bidirectional interaction (p=0.0042) split the result: in 1,909 patients without pulmonary congestion diltiazem reduced cardiac events (HR 0.77, 0.61–0.98), while in 490 patients with pulmonary congestion it increased them (HR 1.41, 1.01–1.96). In DAVIT II (PMID: 2147813), 1,775 patients received verapamil 360 mg daily or placebo for up to 18 months: 18-month mortality was 11.1% on verapamil versus 13.8% on placebo (HR 0.80, 0.63–1.05; p=0.108), and major events (death or reinfarction) were significantly fewer on verapamil (18.0% vs 21.6%; HR 0.80, 0.64–0.99; p=0.027). PROPOSED SPLIT: verapamil modestly reduced major events without a proven mortality benefit; diltiazem was neutral on average and harmful in patients with pulmonary congestion — left-ventricular dysfunction is the dividing line for this class after infarction.
stamp: SPLIT — DAVIT II verapamil: major events 18.0% vs 21.6% (p=0.027), mortality not significant; MDPIT diltiazem: neutral overall (HR 0.90) but harmful with pulmonary congestion (HR 1.41) and beneficial without it (HR 0.77)

title: Low-dose rivaroxaban after acute coronary syndrome: events 8.9% vs 10.7%, cardiovascular death 2.7% vs 4.1% at the 2.5 mg dose — paid for with major bleeding 2.1% vs 0.6% and intracranial bleeding 0.6% vs 0.2%
question: After an acute coronary syndrome, does adding low-dose rivaroxaban to antiplatelet therapy reduce cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, and stroke enough to justify the bleeding?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a real event reduction, bought with real bleeding, and the dose decides the trade. In ATLAS ACS 2–TIMI 51 (Mega JL et al., PMID: 22077192), 15,526 patients with a recent acute coronary syndrome received rivaroxaban 2.5 mg or 5 mg twice daily or placebo, on top of antiplatelet therapy, for a mean of 13 months. The primary composite (cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, or stroke) occurred in 8.9% on rivaroxaban versus 10.7% on placebo (hazard ratio 0.84, 95% CI 0.74–0.96; p=0.008). The 2.5 mg twice-daily dose reduced cardiovascular death (2.7% vs 4.1%; p=0.002) and death from any cause (2.9% vs 4.5%; p=0.002) — a survival benefit not seen with the 5 mg dose. The cost: major bleeding not related to bypass surgery in 2.1% versus 0.6% (p<0.001) and intracranial haemorrhage in 0.6% versus 0.2% (p=0.009), without a significant increase in fatal bleeding (0.3% vs 0.2%); fatal bleeding was less frequent on the 2.5 mg dose than the 5 mg dose (0.1% vs 0.4%; p=0.04). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): at 2.5 mg twice daily, rivaroxaban after acute coronary syndrome reduces events and cardiovascular death, at the price of roughly triple the major bleeding and triple the intracranial haemorrhage — a trade that has to be made patient by patient.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — ATLAS ACS 2–TIMI 51 (n=15,526): primary events 8.9% vs 10.7% (HR 0.84); 2.5 mg dose cut cardiovascular death (2.7% vs 4.1%); major bleeding 2.1% vs 0.6%, intracranial haemorrhage 0.6% vs 0.2%

title: An ACE inhibitor on day one of infarction: captopril saved about 5 lives per 1,000 in ISIS-4 (7.19% vs 7.69%) — intravenous enalapril in CONSENSUS II saved none and caused early hypotension in 12% vs 3%
question: In unselected patients with acute myocardial infarction, does starting an oral ACE inhibitor in the first day reduce mortality compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — small, real, and route-dependent. ISIS-4 (PMID: 7661937) randomised 58,050 patients with suspected acute infarction to one month of oral captopril or placebo: 5-week mortality was 7.19% on captopril versus 7.69% on placebo — a 7% relative reduction (p=0.02), an absolute difference of about 4.9 fewer deaths per 1,000 patients treated for one month, maintained at 12 months (5.4 fewer per 1,000), at the cost of hypotension severe enough to stop treatment in 52 more patients per 1,000. The Chinese Cardiac Study (CCS-1, PMID: 7885123; 13,634 patients) pointed the same way without reaching significance: 4-week mortality 9.05% on captopril versus 9.59% on placebo (p=0.3). The strategy that failed was intravenous-first: CONSENSUS II (Swedberg K et al., PMID: 1495520) gave intravenous enalaprilat within 24 hours followed by oral enalapril to 6,090 patients and found 6-month mortality of 11.0% on enalapril versus 10.2% on placebo (relative risk 1.10, 95% CI 0.93–1.29), with early hypotension in 12% versus 3% (p<0.001). (GISSI-3's lisinopril result — mortality OR 0.88 — is carded on shelf #3331, where that trial's nitrate question lives.) PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): starting a modest oral ACE inhibitor within the first day of infarction saves roughly 5 lives per 1,000 treated for a month; the intravenous loading strategy does not share the benefit.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — ISIS-4 (n=58,050): 5-week mortality 7.19% vs 7.69% (7% relative reduction; ~5 fewer deaths per 1,000); CCS-1 concordant but not significant; CONSENSUS II intravenous enalapril null (11.0% vs 10.2%) with hypotension 12% vs 3%

title: Nicorandil in stable angina (IONA): the composite fell (13.1% vs 15.5%; HR 0.83) — driven by hospital admissions for chest pain, while coronary death or infarction did not reach significance (4.2% vs 5.2%; p=0.068)
question: In stable angina, does nicorandil reduce coronary events compared with placebo on top of standard therapy?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a positive composite whose hard core did not quite follow. In IONA (IONA Study Group, PMID: 11965271), 5,126 patients with stable angina and additional risk factors received nicorandil 20 mg twice daily or placebo on top of standard antianginal therapy for a mean of 1.6 years. The primary composite (coronary heart disease death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, or unplanned hospital admission for cardiac chest pain) occurred in 13.1% on nicorandil versus 15.5% on placebo (hazard ratio 0.83, 95% CI 0.72–0.97; p=0.014). But the secondary endpoint of coronary death or nonfatal infarction was not significantly different (4.2% vs 5.2%; HR 0.79, 0.61–1.02; p=0.068); acute coronary syndromes (6.1% vs 7.6%; p=0.028) and all cardiovascular events (14.7% vs 17.0%; p=0.027) did fall. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): nicorandil reduces coronary event composites in stable angina, with the reduction carried mainly by admissions and acute coronary syndrome presentations rather than by a proven fall in death or infarction.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — IONA (n=5,126): primary composite 13.1% vs 15.5% (HR 0.83; p=0.014), but coronary death or MI 4.2% vs 5.2% (p=0.068, not significant)

title: Trimetazidine after successful PCI (ATPCI): primary events 23.3% vs 23.7% over four years in 6,007 patients — no reduction in angina recurrence or cardiac events
question: After successful PCI, does trimetazidine reduce angina recurrence and cardiovascular events compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — a large, long, clean null. In ATPCI (Ferrari R et al., PMID: 32877651), 6,007 patients who had undergone successful PCI — elective for stable angina, or urgent for unstable angina or non-ST-elevation infarction — received trimetazidine 35 mg modified-release twice daily or placebo on top of standard evidence-based therapy. After a median follow-up of 47.5 months, the primary composite (cardiac death; hospital admission for a cardiac event; recurrence or persistence of angina requiring a change in antianginal therapy; or recurrence or persistence of angina requiring coronary angiography) occurred in 23.3% on trimetazidine versus 23.7% on placebo (hazard ratio 0.98, 95% CI 0.88–1.09; p=0.73), with no significant differences in any individual component, and similar results in the elective and urgent PCI subgroups. Serious adverse events were also similar (40.9% vs 41.1% of patients). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): routine trimetazidine after successful PCI does not reduce angina recurrence or cardiac events over four years.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — ATPCI (n=6,007): primary events 23.3% vs 23.7% (HR 0.98; p=0.73) over a median 47.5 months, no component different

title: Allopurinol in chronic stable angina: 43 seconds longer to ST depression and 58 seconds longer total exercise than placebo — one 65-patient crossover trial, no events measured
question: In stable angina, does allopurinol improve exercise capacity and time to chest pain compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a clean physiological result in a very small trial. Noman A et al. (PMID: 20542554) randomised 65 patients with angiographically documented coronary disease, a positive exercise test, and stable angina to allopurinol 600 mg daily or placebo for 6 weeks before crossover (60 analysed in the second period). Allopurinol lengthened the median time to ST depression to 298 seconds versus 249 seconds on placebo — an absolute difference of 43 seconds (95% CI 31–58; p=0.0002) — lengthened total exercise time by 58 seconds (95% CI 45–77; p=0.0003), and lengthened time to chest pain by 38 seconds (95% CI 17–55; p=0.001). No adverse effects of treatment were reported. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): high-dose allopurinol improves exercise capacity in chronic stable angina by a modest margin; whether that translates into fewer events is untested, and this shelf rests on a single small crossover trial.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — Noman 2010 (n=65, crossover): time to ST depression +43 s (95% CI 31–58), total exercise time +58 s, time to chest pain +38 s vs placebo; no clinical events measured

title: Vasospastic angina: in the only double-blind head-to-head, nifedipine and isosorbide mononitrate each cut spontaneous ischaemic attacks by about 90% with no difference between them — the whole randomised base is a few dozen patients
question: In vasospastic angina, how do calcium-channel blockers compare with nitrates and with placebo for preventing angina attacks?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — calcium-channel blockers clearly suppress attacks in the clinic, but the randomised record behind that confidence is remarkably thin. In the only double-blind trial comparing the two classes head-to-head (Lombardi M et al., PMID: 8325315), 21 patients with angina at rest underwent Holter monitoring and ergonovine testing on placebo and on treatment: isosorbide-5-mononitrate reduced spontaneous ischaemic attacks by 87% and nifedipine by 95%, and induced attacks by 66% and 75% respectively, with no significant difference between the two drugs. A second small double-blind crossover (Ardissino D et al., PMID: 1746458) in 30 patients with Prinzmetal's angina found felodipine once daily and nifedipine four times daily similarly effective, with ischaemic episodes or attacks in 19% of patients on nifedipine and 11–26% on felodipine depending on dose. The larger literature is observational: a meta-analysis of four Japanese cohort studies (Nishigaki K et al., PMID: 20668353; 1,997 patients with positive spasm provocation tests, 143 major adverse cardiovascular events) compared calcium blockers against each other — benidipine's hazard ratio for major events was significantly lower than diltiazem's (adjusted HR 0.41; p=0.016) — but included no placebo or nitrate arm. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): calcium-channel blockers and long-acting nitrates each suppress vasospastic attacks in tiny short trials, with no proven difference between the classes and no randomised evidence on hard outcomes.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — Lombardi 1993 (n=21): spontaneous attacks cut 87% (isosorbide mononitrate) and 95% (nifedipine) vs placebo, no difference between drugs; all other support is small crossovers or observational cohorts

title: Drug-eluting stents beat bare-metal stents even when antiplatelet therapy must be short: safety composite 9.4% vs 12.9% in high-bleeding-risk patients, major events 12% vs 16% in the over-75s — bleeding no higher in either trial
question: In patients at high bleeding risk, do drug-eluting stents beat bare-metal stents on death, myocardial infarction, and revascularisation without excess bleeding on short dual antiplatelet therapy?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — two trials, two high-risk populations, the same answer. In LEADERS FREE (Urban P et al., PMID: 26466021), 2,466 patients at high bleeding risk received a polymer-free umirolimus-coated stent or a very similar bare-metal stent, all with just one month of dual antiplatelet therapy: at 390 days the primary safety composite (cardiac death, myocardial infarction, or stent thrombosis) occurred in 9.4% on the drug-coated stent versus 12.9% on the bare-metal stent (hazard ratio 0.71, 95% CI 0.56–0.91; p=0.005 for superiority), and clinically driven target-lesion revascularisation in 5.1% versus 9.8% (HR 0.50, 0.37–0.69; p<0.001). In SENIOR (Varenne O et al., PMID: 29102362), 1,200 patients aged 75 or older received a drug-eluting or bare-metal stent with short dual therapy (one month if stable, six months if unstable): the primary composite (all-cause mortality, myocardial infarction, stroke, or ischaemia-driven target-lesion revascularisation) occurred in 12% versus 16% (relative risk 0.71, 95% CI 0.52–0.94; p=0.02), with bleeding complications no different (5% vs 5%; p=0.68) and stent thrombosis infrequent in both groups (1% vs 1%). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): with short dual antiplatelet therapy, a drug-eluting (or drug-coated) stent is both safer and more effective than a bare-metal stent in patients at high bleeding risk or of advanced age — the historical reason for choosing bare metal no longer holds.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — LEADERS FREE (n=2,466): safety composite 9.4% vs 12.9% (HR 0.71), revascularisation 5.1% vs 9.8%; SENIOR (n=1,200, age ≥75): major events 12% vs 16% (RR 0.71), bleeding 5% vs 5%

title: Bioresorbable scaffolds: within the noninferiority margin for target-lesion failure at one year in ABSORB III (7.8% vs 6.1%) — but device thrombosis ran at 3.5% vs 0.9% through two years in AIDA (HR 3.87)
question: In coronary disease, do bioresorbable scaffolds match metallic drug-eluting stents on target-lesion failure and stent thrombosis?
balance: SPLIT — the answer splits by endpoint: the scaffold matched on the composite it was designed to match, and lost on the complication that ended it. In ABSORB III (Ellis SG et al., PMID: 26457558), 2,008 patients with stable or unstable angina received an everolimus-eluting bioresorbable (Absorb) scaffold or an everolimus-eluting cobalt-chromium stent: target-lesion failure at one year occurred in 7.8% versus 6.1% (difference 1.7 percentage points, 95% CI −0.5 to 3.9; p=0.007 for noninferiority, p=0.16 for superiority), with device thrombosis in 1.5% versus 0.7% (p=0.13). In AIDA (Wykrzykowska JJ et al., PMID: 28402237), 1,845 patients undergoing routine PCI received the scaffold or a metallic stent: two-year target-vessel failure was 11.7% versus 10.7% (HR 1.12, 95% CI 0.85–1.48; p=0.43), but definite or probable device thrombosis occurred in 3.5% versus 0.9% (HR 3.87, 1.78–8.42; p<0.001), and the data and safety monitoring board recommended early reporting because of safety concerns. PROPOSED SPLIT: bioresorbable scaffolds were noninferior for one-year target-lesion failure in selected lesions, but carried a roughly fourfold device-thrombosis rate in routine practice — a harm that led to the Absorb scaffold's withdrawal from the market.
stamp: SPLIT — ABSORB III (n=2,008): 1-year target-lesion failure 7.8% vs 6.1% (noninferior); AIDA (n=1,845): target-vessel failure 11.7% vs 10.7% but device thrombosis 3.5% vs 0.9% (HR 3.87; p<0.001)

title: Drug-coated balloon for small coronary vessels (BASKET-SMALL 2): major events 7.5% vs 7.3% at one year — noninferior to a drug-eluting stent, with nothing left behind
question: In small native coronary vessels, does a drug-coated balloon match a drug-eluting stent for late lumen loss and clinical events?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — in the one randomised test, the balloon matched the stent on events. In BASKET-SMALL 2 (Jeger RV et al., PMID: 30170854), 758 patients with de-novo lesions in coronary vessels under 3 mm in diameter were randomised after successful predilatation to a paclitaxel drug-coated balloon or a second-generation drug-eluting stent. At 12 months, major adverse cardiac events (cardiac death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, target-vessel revascularisation) occurred in 7.5% on the balloon versus 7.3% on the stent (hazard ratio 0.97, 95% CI 0.58–1.64; p=0.9180), and noninferiority was formally shown in the per-protocol population (absolute difference 95% CI −3.83 to 3.93%, inside the 4% margin; p=0.0217). Cardiac deaths were 12 (3.1%) on the balloon versus 5 (1.3%) on the stent — a numerical imbalance the trial was not powered to resolve — while probable or definite stent thrombosis (0.8% vs 1.1%) and major bleeding (1.1% vs 2.4%) were similar. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): in small native vessels, a drug-coated balloon gives one-year clinical results statistically indistinguishable from a drug-eluting stent; the question the candidate asked about late lumen loss was not this trial's primary measure, and the shelf says so.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — BASKET-SMALL 2 (n=758): 12-month major events 7.5% (balloon) vs 7.3% (stent), HR 0.97; noninferiority met; cardiac deaths numerically higher on balloon (3.1% vs 1.3%), unresolved

title: Drug-coated balloon for in-stent restenosis: clearly better than a plain balloon (target-lesion failure 17.9% vs 28.6% in AGENT IDE) — clinically level with a repeat drug-eluting stent in RIBS V, though the stent left a wider lumen
question: For in-stent restenosis, does a drug-coated balloon match repeat drug-eluting stenting or balloon angioplasty for recurrence and events?
balance: SPLIT — the answer splits by comparator. Against a plain balloon, the drug-coated balloon wins outright: in AGENT IDE (Yeh RW et al., PMID: 38460161), 600 patients with in-stent restenosis received a paclitaxel-coated or an uncoated balloon; one-year target-lesion failure occurred in 17.9% versus 28.6% (hazard ratio 0.59, 95% CI 0.42–0.84; p=0.003), with target-lesion revascularisation in 13.0% versus 24.7% and target-vessel myocardial infarction in 5.8% versus 11.1%, though cardiac death was numerically higher on the coated balloon (2.9% vs 1.6%; HR 1.75, 0.49–6.28; p=0.38). Against a repeat drug-eluting stent, it is a draw clinically and a loss angiographically: in RIBS V (Alfonso F et al., PMID: 24412457), 189 patients with bare-metal-stent restenosis received a drug-eluting balloon or an everolimus-eluting stent; the combined clinical outcome was 6% versus 8% (HR 0.76, 0.26–2.18; p=0.6) and target-vessel revascularisation 2% versus 6%, but minimal lumen diameter at follow-up was significantly larger with the stent (2.36 mm vs 2.01 mm; p<0.001). PROPOSED SPLIT: for in-stent restenosis, a drug-coated balloon beats plain angioplasty and matches repeat stenting on clinical events, while leaving a narrower lumen than a new stent.
stamp: SPLIT — AGENT IDE (n=600): target-lesion failure 17.9% vs 28.6% vs uncoated balloon (HR 0.59); RIBS V (n=189): clinical outcome 6% vs 8% vs everolimus stent (NS), but lumen diameter 2.01 vs 2.36 mm favoured the stent

title: Rotational atherectomy in calcified lesions: it gets the stent in (strategy success 98% vs 81% in PREPARE-CALC) — but late lumen loss was worse, not better, in ROTAXUS (0.44 vs 0.31 mm), and clinical events never differed
question: In heavily calcified coronary lesions, does rotational atherectomy before stenting improve procedural success and outcomes compared with balloon preparation?
balance: SPLIT — the answer splits by what 'improve' means: delivery yes, vessel healing no, events unchanged. In PREPARE-CALC (Abdel-Wahab M et al., PMID: 30354632), 200 patients with severely calcified lesions were randomised to lesion preparation with rotational atherectomy or modified (scoring/cutting) balloons before a third-generation drug-eluting stent: strategy success was significantly more common with atherectomy (98% vs 81%; relative risk of failure with a balloon-first strategy 9.5, 95% CI 2.3–39.7; p=0.0001), at the cost of longer fluoroscopy (23.9 vs 19.6 minutes; p=0.03), while 9-month in-stent late lumen loss was similar (0.22 vs 0.16 mm; noninferiority met) and target-lesion revascularisation (2% vs 7%), stent thrombosis (0% vs 0%), and target-vessel failure (6% vs 8%) did not differ significantly. In ROTAXUS (Abdel-Wahab M et al., PMID: 23266232), 240 patients with complex calcified lesions received atherectomy or standard preparation before a paclitaxel-eluting stent: despite a higher acute lumen gain (1.56 vs 1.44 mm; p=0.01) and higher strategy success (92.5% vs 83.3%; p=0.03), in-stent late lumen loss at 9 months was higher with atherectomy (0.44 vs 0.31 mm; p=0.04), while binary restenosis (11.4% vs 10.6%), target-lesion revascularisation (11.7% vs 12.5%), definite stent thrombosis (0.8% vs 0%), and major adverse cardiac events (24.2% vs 28.3%) were similar. PROPOSED SPLIT: upfront rotational atherectomy reliably delivers and expands the stent in calcified lesions, but it does not improve late lumen loss or clinical outcomes over balloon preparation with bailout atherectomy.
stamp: SPLIT — PREPARE-CALC (n=200): strategy success 98% vs 81% (p=0.0001), late loss similar; ROTAXUS (n=240): late lumen loss worse with atherectomy (0.44 vs 0.31 mm; p=0.04), major events 24.2% vs 28.3% (NS)

title: Upstream glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibition in non-ST-elevation ACS: no benefit in EARLY ACS (primary events 9.3% vs 10.0%) or in a 19,929-patient meta-analysis — and more bleeding both times
question: In non-ST-elevation acute coronary syndrome, does routine upstream glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibition improve outcomes compared with provisional use during PCI?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — starting the drug early, before the angiogram, bought nothing and cost blood. In EARLY ACS (Giugliano RP et al., PMID: 19332455), 9,492 patients with non-ST-elevation acute coronary syndromes assigned to an invasive strategy received early routine eptifibatide (started at least 12 hours before angiography) or placebo with provisional eptifibatide after angiography: the primary composite at 96 hours occurred in 9.3% versus 10.0% (odds ratio 0.92, 95% CI 0.80–1.06; p=0.23), death or myocardial infarction at 30 days in 11.2% versus 12.3% (OR 0.89, 0.79–1.01; p=0.08), and the early group had significantly higher rates of bleeding and red-cell transfusion. The wider randomised record agrees: a meta-analysis of seven trials (De Luca G et al., PMID: 21211597; 19,929 high-risk ACS patients undergoing an invasive strategy) found upstream glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibition did not decrease 30-day mortality (2.0% vs 2.0%; p=0.84) or myocardial infarction (7.0% vs 7.6%; p=0.11), but increased major bleeding (1.8% vs 1.3%; p=0.0002). PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): routine upstream glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibition does not improve outcomes over provisional use at PCI, and it increases bleeding.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — EARLY ACS (n=9,492): primary events 9.3% vs 10.0% (p=0.23), bleeding and transfusion higher; meta-analysis of 7 trials (n=19,929): mortality 2.0% vs 2.0%, major bleeding 1.8% vs 1.3%

title: Enoxaparin versus heparin in primary PCI: ATOLL missed its primary endpoint (28% vs 34%; p=0.06) but won its ischaemic secondary endpoints — and a 30,966-patient meta-analysis, partly non-randomised, favoured enoxaparin on death and bleeding
question: In primary PCI for STEMI, does enoxaparin match unfractionated heparin for death, myocardial infarction, and bleeding?
balance: SPLIT — the randomised trial and the pooled literature tell adjacent but different stories. In ATOLL (Montalescot G et al., PMID: 21856483), 910 STEMI patients received an intravenous bolus of enoxaparin 0.5 mg/kg or unfractionated heparin before primary PCI: the primary endpoint (death, complication of myocardial infarction, procedure failure, or major bleeding at 30 days) occurred in 28% on enoxaparin versus 34% on heparin (relative risk 0.83, 95% CI 0.68–1.01; p=0.06) — a miss — while the main secondary endpoint (death, recurrent acute coronary syndrome, or urgent revascularisation) fell significantly (7% vs 11%; RR 0.59, 0.38–0.91; p=0.015), as did death, complication of MI, or major bleeding (10% vs 15%; p=0.03), with major bleeding itself no different (5% vs 5%; p=0.79). The broader pooled evidence is more favourable: a systematic review and meta-analysis of 23 studies (Silvain J et al., PMID: 22306479; 30,966 PCI patients, of whom 10,243 were primary PCI) found enoxaparin associated with lower death (relative risk 0.66, 95% CI 0.57–0.76), death or MI (0.68, 0.57–0.81), and major bleeding (0.80, 0.68–0.95), with the mortality reduction largest in primary PCI (relative risk 0.52, 0.42–0.64) — but that pool mixes randomised and non-randomised studies. PROPOSED SPLIT: in the head-to-head randomised trial enoxaparin matched heparin on its primary endpoint and bleeding while reducing ischaemic secondary endpoints; the stronger mortality claims come from a meta-analysis whose non-randomised components cannot carry them alone.
stamp: SPLIT — ATOLL (n=910): primary endpoint 28% vs 34% (p=0.06, missed), main secondary 7% vs 11% (p=0.015), major bleeding 5% vs 5%; Silvain 2012 meta-analysis (23 studies, 30,966 patients, partly non-randomised): death RR 0.66, major bleeding RR 0.80

title: Vascular closure devices after catheterisation: haemostasis is faster, major complications are no different — but groin infection is more frequent (0.6% vs 0.2%) in a meta-analysis of 31 randomised trials
question: After coronary stenting, do vascular closure devices reduce access-site complications and time to walking compared with manual compression?
balance: SPLIT — the answer splits by endpoint: speed yes, safety neutral-to-worse. A meta-analysis of 31 prospective randomised studies (Biancari F et al., PMID: 20362708) including 7,528 patients randomised to a vascular closure device or manual/mechanical compression after diagnostic angiography and/or endovascular procedures found similar results for groin haematoma, bleeding, pseudoaneurysm, and blood transfusion. Lower-limb ischaemia and other arterial ischaemic complications (0.3% vs 0%; p=0.07) and the need for surgery for vascular complications (0.7% vs 0.4%; p=0.10) were somewhat more frequent with closure devices, and groin infection was significantly more frequent (0.6% vs 0.2%; p=0.02). The one uniform advantage was a significantly shorter time to haemostasis with closure devices, more evident in patients undergoing PCI than in those undergoing diagnostic angiography, among whom adverse-event rates were similar. PROPOSED SPLIT: closure devices shorten time to haemostasis (and so may shorten recovery) without reducing access-site complications, and they add a small excess of groin infection and device-specific arterial complications.
stamp: SPLIT — Biancari 2010 meta-analysis (31 RCTs, 7,528 patients): time to haemostasis significantly shorter; haematoma, bleeding, pseudoaneurysm and transfusion similar; groin infection 0.6% vs 0.2% (p=0.02)

title: Pharmaco-invasive care for STEMI: STREAM matched primary PCI on death, shock, heart failure or reinfarction (12.4% vs 14.3%) with more intracranial bleeding — and TRANSFER-AMI showed routine early transfer beat delayed standard care (11.0% vs 17.2%)
question: In STEMI patients who cannot reach primary PCI quickly, does a pharmaco-invasive strategy — early fibrinolysis with routine transfer for angiography — match primary PCI for death and ischaemic events?
balance: SPLIT — the strategy matches primary PCI in the trial that asked that question, and beats doing less in the trial that asked the other one. In STREAM (Armstrong PW et al., PMID: 23473396), 1,892 patients with STEMI presenting within 3 hours who could not undergo primary PCI within 1 hour received either prehospital fibrinolysis (tenecteplase, with angiography 6–24 hours later or urgently if lysis failed) or primary PCI: the primary composite (death, shock, congestive heart failure, or reinfarction at 30 days) occurred in 12.4% versus 14.3% (relative risk 0.86, 95% CI 0.68–1.09; p=0.21), with emergency angiography required in 36.3% of the fibrinolysis group and more intracranial haemorrhages (1.0% vs 0.2%; p=0.04 — 0.5% vs 0.3% after the protocol amendment halving tenecteplase in patients 75 or older). In TRANSFER-AMI (Cantor WJ et al., PMID: 19553646), 1,059 high-risk STEMI patients lysed at non-PCI centres were randomised to routine transfer for PCI within 6 hours or standard treatment (rescue PCI if required, or delayed angiography): the primary composite at 30 days occurred in 11.0% versus 17.2% (relative risk 0.64, 95% CI 0.47–0.87; p=0.004), with no significant difference in major bleeding. PROPOSED SPLIT: when primary PCI cannot be delivered promptly, fibrinolysis with routine early transfer achieves outcomes statistically indistinguishable from primary PCI in STREAM — at the price of more intracranial bleeding — and is clearly better than lysis with delayed, selective transfer.
stamp: SPLIT — STREAM (n=1,892): composite 12.4% (pharmaco-invasive) vs 14.3% (primary PCI), RR 0.86 (NS), intracranial haemorrhage 1.0% vs 0.2%; TRANSFER-AMI (n=1,059): routine early transfer 11.0% vs 17.2% standard care (RR 0.64; p=0.004)

title: Opening a persistently occluded infarct artery days later (OAT): no reduction in death, reinfarction, or heart failure over four years (17.2% vs 15.6%) — and a trend toward more reinfarction with PCI (7.0% vs 5.3%)
question: In stable patients days to weeks after myocardial infarction with a persistently occluded infarct artery, does PCI improve death, reinfarction, or heart failure compared with medical therapy alone?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the open-artery hypothesis, tested properly, failed. In the Occluded Artery Trial (Hochman JS et al., PMID: 17105759), 2,166 stable high-risk patients with a totally occluded infarct-related artery 3–28 days after myocardial infarction (ejection fraction under 50% or proximal occlusion) were randomised to routine PCI with stenting plus optimal medical therapy or optimal medical therapy alone. The four-year cumulative primary event rate (death, reinfarction, or NYHA class IV heart failure) was 17.2% with PCI versus 15.6% with medical therapy (hazard ratio 1.16, 95% CI 0.92–1.45; p=0.20). Reinfarction occurred in 7.0% versus 5.3% (HR 1.36, 0.92–2.00; p=0.13) — nonfatal reinfarction 6.9% versus 5.0% (HR 1.44, 0.96–2.16; p=0.08), with only 0.6% of reinfarctions related to the assigned PCI procedures — while class IV heart failure (4.4% vs 4.5%) and death (9.1% vs 9.4%) were similar, and no subgroup interaction was found. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): routinely opening a persistently occluded infarct artery in stable patients days to weeks after infarction does not reduce death, reinfarction, or severe heart failure, and may increase reinfarction.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — OAT (n=2,166): 4-year primary events 17.2% (PCI) vs 15.6% (medical), HR 1.16 (p=0.20); reinfarction 7.0% vs 5.3% (trend against PCI); death 9.1% vs 9.4%

title: Cyclosporine at reperfusion in STEMI: no better clinical outcomes in CIRCUS (59.0% vs 58.1%) and no better ST resolution or troponin in CYCLE — the reperfusion-injury idea failed both its tests
question: In STEMI treated with primary PCI, does intracoronary cyclosporine at reperfusion reduce infarct size or clinical events compared with placebo?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — two trials, two designs, one answer; note the candidate asked about intracoronary cyclosporine, and both trials in fact gave it intravenously, which the shelf states plainly. In CIRCUS (Cung TT et al., PMID: 26321103), 970 patients with anterior STEMI and a completely occluded culprit artery received an intravenous bolus of cyclosporine 2.5 mg/kg or placebo before recanalisation in primary PCI: the one-year primary outcome (death, worsening heart failure during the initial hospitalisation, rehospitalisation for heart failure, or adverse left-ventricular remodelling) occurred in 59.0% on cyclosporine versus 58.1% on placebo (odds ratio 1.04, 95% CI 0.78–1.39; p=0.77), with no reduction in any clinical component and no safety difference. In CYCLE (Ottani F et al., PMID: 26821623), 410 patients with large STEMI and TIMI flow 0–1 received intravenous cyclosporine 2.5 mg/kg or control before primary PCI: ST-segment resolution of at least 70% occurred in 52.0% versus 49.0% (p=0.55), day-4 high-sensitivity troponin T was similar (median 2,160 vs 2,068 ng/L; p=0.85), and ejection fraction, remodelling, and six-month clinical events did not differ, with six-month mortality numerically higher on cyclosporine (5.7% vs 3.2%; p=0.17). PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): cyclosporine given at reperfusion does not reduce infarct size surrogates or improve clinical outcomes in STEMI.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — CIRCUS (n=970): primary outcome 59.0% vs 58.1% (OR 1.04; p=0.77); CYCLE (n=410): ST resolution ≥70% in 52.0% vs 49.0% (p=0.55), troponin similar

title: Erythropoietin at reperfusion in STEMI: infarct size unchanged in REVEAL (15.8% vs 15.0% of LV mass) and ejection fraction unchanged in HEBE III — with a safety signal in REVEAL's older patients and event composite
question: In STEMI, does erythropoietin at reperfusion reduce infarct size or improve outcomes compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — no infarct-size benefit in either trial, and the safety leans are all in one direction. In REVEAL (Najjar SS et al., PMID: 21558517), 222 STEMI patients who had undergone successful PCI received a single intravenous bolus of epoetin alfa (60,000 units in the efficacy phase) or placebo within 4 hours of reperfusion: infarct size on cardiac MRI was 15.8% of left-ventricular mass on epoetin versus 15.0% on placebo at the first scan (p=0.67) and 10.6% versus 10.4% at 12 weeks (p=0.89); in a prespecified analysis of patients aged 70 or older, infarct size was larger on epoetin (19.9% vs 11.7% of LV mass; p=0.03), and in the safety cohort the composite of death, MI, stroke, or stent thrombosis occurred in 4.0% of epoetin patients versus 0% on placebo (p=0.04). In HEBE III (Voors AA et al., PMID: 20802250), 529 patients received a single 60,000 IU bolus of epoetin alfa after successful primary PCI or standard care alone: ejection fraction at six weeks was 0.53 versus 0.52 (p=0.41), enzymatic infarct size did not differ significantly, though major adverse cardiac events were fewer on epoetin (8 vs 19 events; p=0.032) on very small numbers. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): erythropoietin at reperfusion does not reduce infarct size or improve ventricular function after STEMI, and REVEAL raises a specific concern in older patients.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — REVEAL (n=222): infarct size 15.8% vs 15.0% of LV mass (p=0.67), larger in patients ≥70 on epoetin (19.9% vs 11.7%; p=0.03), safety composite 4.0% vs 0% (p=0.04); HEBE III (n=529): ejection fraction 0.53 vs 0.52 (p=0.41)

title: Bone-marrow cells after a heart attack: ejection fraction rose 2.5 points more than placebo in REPAIR-AMI, but the larger BAMI trial found no fewer deaths — 3.3% versus 3.8% at two years
question: After myocardial infarction, does intracoronary bone-marrow cell therapy improve ejection fraction, death, or reinfarction compared with control?
balance: SPLIT — a surrogate moved, survival did not. In REPAIR-AMI (Schächinger V et al., PMID: 16990384), 204 patients received intracoronary bone-marrow-derived progenitor cells or placebo 3–7 days after reperfused myocardial infarction: ejection fraction rose 5.5 points on cells versus 3.0 on placebo at 4 months (p=0.01), and the prespecified 1-year composite of death, recurrent infarction, or any revascularisation was significantly reduced (p=0.01). BAMI (Mathur A et al., PMID: 32860406), the larger mortality trial, recruited only 375 of its planned patients and found all-cause mortality at 2 years of 3.26% on cells versus 3.82% on control — no difference it could meaningfully test — with heart-failure hospitalisation in 2.7% versus 8.1% and stroke hospitalisations in 4 cell patients versus none. PROPOSED SPLIT: a modest ejection-fraction gain in one placebo-controlled trial, no demonstrated effect on death or reinfarction in the trial built to measure them.
stamp: SPLIT — ejection fraction improved modestly in REPAIR-AMI, but BAMI showed no mortality difference and was too under-recruited to settle clinical benefit

title: Adenosine in STEMI: no clinical benefit in 2,118 patients and no smaller infarcts in REFLO-STEMI — with a per-protocol harm signal in the smaller trial
question: In STEMI treated with primary PCI, does intracoronary or intravenous adenosine reduce infarct size or microvascular obstruction compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — on the endpoints both trials prespecified. AMISTAD II (Ross AM et al., PMID: 15936605) randomised 2,118 anterior-STEMI patients to intravenous adenosine or placebo: the primary composite of new heart failure, heart-failure rehospitalisation, or death at 6 months occurred in 17.9% on placebo versus 16.3% on pooled adenosine (16.5% and 16.1% by dose; p=0.43). REFLO-STEMI (Nazir SA et al., PMID: 27147610) gave high-dose intracoronary adenosine during primary PCI and found infarct size of 10.1% of left-ventricular mass versus 8.3% on control (p=0.062) and microvascular obstruction no different — with a per-protocol analysis showing more major adverse cardiac events on adenosine (hazard ratio 5.39 at 30 days). The one positive signal anywhere is a subset: infarct size 11% versus 27% (p=0.023) at the higher AMISTAD II dose in 243 imaged patients. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): two randomised trials, two null primary endpoints, one hypothesis-generating dose subset.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — AMISTAD II's clinical composite and REFLO-STEMI's infarct-size endpoint were both null; only a high-dose imaging subset favoured adenosine

title: Ischaemic postconditioning at primary PCI: death or heart-failure admission in 10.5% versus 11.2% over 38 months in DANAMI-3 — and reperfusion no better in POST
question: In STEMI, does ischaemic postconditioning at reperfusion reduce infarct size or clinical events compared with conventional primary PCI?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — two multicentre randomised trials, concordantly null. In DANAMI-3 iPOST (Engstrøm T et al., PMID: 28249094), 1,234 STEMI patients were randomised to postconditioning or conventional primary PCI: the composite of all-cause death and heart-failure hospitalisation occurred in 10.5% with postconditioning versus 11.2% without over a median 38 months (hazard ratio 0.93; 95% CI 0.66–1.30; p=0.66), with hazard ratios of 0.75 for death and 0.99 for heart failure, both non-significant. In POST (Hahn JY et al., PMID: 24068776), 700 patients showed complete ST-segment resolution in 40.5% versus 41.5% (p=0.79) and 30-day major adverse cardiac events in 4.3% versus 3.7% (p=0.70). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): the balloon ritual added minutes and hope, and neither reperfusion quality nor clinical outcomes moved.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — DANAMI-3 iPOST (n=1,234) and POST (n=700) were both null on clinical and reperfusion endpoints

title: Metformin after STEMI in people without diabetes: ejection fraction 53.1% on metformin versus 54.8% on placebo at 4 months — numerically the wrong way (GIPS-III)
question: In non-diabetic patients with STEMI, does metformin after primary PCI improve ejection fraction compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — one well-run trial, null on every measure. GIPS-III (Lexis CPH et al., PMID: 24687169) randomised 380 patients without diabetes presenting with STEMI to metformin 500 mg twice daily or placebo for 4 months after primary PCI. Ejection fraction by MRI at 4 months was 53.1% (95% CI 51.6–54.6%) on metformin versus 54.8% (95% CI 53.5–56.1%) on placebo (p=0.10) — the point estimate favours placebo. NT-proBNP was identical at 167 ng/L in both groups (p=0.66), major adverse cardiac events occurred in 6 patients (3.1%) on metformin versus 2 (1.1%) on placebo (p=0.16), and no lactic acidosis occurred. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): the animal-data promise of metformin as post-infarction cardioprotection did not survive contact with 380 randomised humans.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — GIPS-III's ejection fraction, NT-proBNP, and event measures were all null, with point estimates favouring placebo
