title: Tocilizumab in STEMI: myocardial salvage index 5.6 points higher (p=0.04) in one 199-patient trial — but final infarct size itself was not significantly smaller (7.2% versus 9.1%, p=0.08)
question: In STEMI, does interleukin-6 blockade with tocilizumab improve myocardial salvage compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for a scan measure, in one small trial. ASSAIL-MI (Broch K et al., PMID: 33858620) randomised 199 STEMI patients at three Norwegian PCI centres to a single 280 mg infusion of tocilizumab or placebo before PCI. The primary endpoint, myocardial salvage index on MRI at 3–7 days, was larger on tocilizumab by an adjusted 5.6 percentage points (95% CI 0.2 to 11.3; p=0.04), and microvascular obstruction was less extensive — but final infarct size, the measure patients would care about, was 7.2% versus 9.1% of myocardial volume (p=0.08), not significant, and adverse events were evenly distributed. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a single small trial moved the salvage index while its own final-infarct-size endpoint missed significance — promising physiology, unproven therapy. Tier C: single-trial benefit claim.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — ASSAIL-MI improved the MRI salvage index (adjusted difference 5.6 points, p=0.04) but not final infarct size (p=0.08), in a single 199-patient trial

title: Complete revascularisation in MI patients aged 75+: death, MI, stroke, or revascularisation in 15.7% versus 21.0% at one year (FIRE) — one trial, composite-driven
question: In older patients with myocardial infarction and multivessel disease, does physiology-guided complete revascularisation beat culprit-only PCI for death and reinfarction?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one large trial in exactly the population the question asks about. FIRE (Biscaglia S et al., PMID: 37634150) randomised 1,445 patients aged 75 or older (median 80) with myocardial infarction and multivessel disease to physiology-guided complete revascularisation or culprit-only PCI. The primary composite — death, myocardial infarction, stroke, or any revascularisation at 1 year — occurred in 113 patients (15.7%) on complete revascularisation versus 152 (21.0%) on culprit-only (hazard ratio 0.73; 95% CI 0.57–0.93; p=0.01), and cardiovascular death or myocardial infarction in 8.9% versus 13.5% (hazard ratio 0.64; 95% CI 0.47–0.88). The safety composite of contrast-associated kidney injury, stroke, or bleeding was 22.5% versus 20.4% (p=0.37). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a real reduction in a composite that includes revascularisation, from a single trial — Tier C, because a cardiovascular-event benefit claim resting on one trial is the developer's to review.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — FIRE reduced the 1-year composite (15.7% versus 21.0%; HR 0.73) and cardiovascular death or MI (8.9% versus 13.5%) in patients ≥75, in a single trial

title: Routine invasive strategy in older NSTEMI patients: cardiovascular death or MI in 25.6% versus 26.3% over four years (SENIOR-RITA) — nonfatal MI lower, cardiovascular death numerically higher
question: In frail older patients with non-ST-elevation acute coronary syndrome, does a routine invasive strategy improve death or myocardial infarction compared with conservative management?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — on the composite the trial prespecified. SENIOR-RITA (Kunadian V et al., PMID: 39225274) randomised 1,518 patients aged 75 or older with NSTEMI (mean age 82; 32% frail) at 48 UK sites to an invasive strategy of angiography and revascularisation plus best medical therapy, or best medical therapy alone. Over a median 4.1 years, cardiovascular death or nonfatal myocardial infarction occurred in 193 patients (25.6%) on the invasive strategy versus 201 (26.3%) on conservative care (hazard ratio 0.94; 95% CI 0.77–1.14; p=0.53). The components pointed in opposite directions: cardiovascular death 15.8% versus 14.2% (hazard ratio 1.11) and nonfatal MI 11.7% versus 15.0% (hazard ratio 0.75; 95% CI 0.57–0.99), with procedural complications in fewer than 1%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): the largest trial in this population found no net gain from routinely taking older NSTEMI patients to the catheter lab.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — SENIOR-RITA's primary composite was null (25.6% versus 26.3%; HR 0.94) over a median 4.1 years, with components in opposite directions

title: Early invasive strategy at 80+: composite events in 40.6% versus 61.4% (After Eighty) — driven by fewer infarctions and urgent revascularisations, with death itself unmoved (HR 0.89)
question: In patients aged 80 or older with NSTEMI or unstable angina, does an early invasive strategy improve death or myocardial infarction compared with a selective invasive strategy?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for the composite, not for survival. The After Eighty study (Tegn N et al., PMID: 26794722) randomised 457 patients aged 80 or older with NSTEMI or unstable angina in Norway to an early invasive strategy or conservative optimum medical treatment. Over a median 1.53 years, the primary composite of myocardial infarction, need for urgent revascularisation, stroke, and death occurred in 93 patients (40.6%) invasively managed versus 140 (61.4%) conservatively managed (hazard ratio 0.53; 95% CI 0.41–0.69; p=0.0001). But the components split: myocardial infarction hazard ratio 0.52 (p=0.0010) and urgent revascularisation 0.19 (p=0.0010), while stroke was 0.60 (p=0.2650) and death from any cause 0.89 (95% CI 0.62–1.28; p=0.5340) — no significant difference. Major bleeding was 1.7% versus 1.8%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): fewer infarctions and far fewer urgent procedures, no shown survival gain, in a single 457-patient trial — Tier C.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — After Eighty halved its composite (40.6% versus 61.4%; HR 0.53) via MI and urgent revascularisation, with no significant effect on death (HR 0.89) or stroke

title: OCT versus IVUS guidance for PCI: target-vessel failure 2.5% versus 3.1% in OCTIVUS and 5.2% versus 4.9% in OPINION — the light-based camera matched ultrasound in both trials
question: For guiding PCI, does optical coherence tomography match intravascular ultrasound for death, myocardial infarction, and revascularisation?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — two randomised head-to-head trials, both meeting noninferiority. OCTIVUS (Kang DY et al., PMID: 37634092) randomised 2,008 patients to OCT-guided or IVUS-guided PCI: the composite of cardiac death, target-vessel myocardial infarction, or ischaemia-driven target-vessel revascularisation at 1 year occurred in 25 patients (2.5%) on OCT guidance versus 31 (3.1%) on IVUS guidance (absolute difference −0.6 percentage points; p<0.001 for noninferiority), with contrast-induced nephropathy in 1.4% versus 1.5% and major procedural complications in 2.2% versus 3.7% (p=0.047). OPINION (Kubo T et al., PMID: 29121226) found target-vessel failure in 5.2% on optical frequency-domain imaging versus 4.9% on IVUS at 12 months (noninferiority p=0.042), with identical in-stent restenosis rates of 1.6%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): OCT is not better than IVUS — it is, on two trials, its equal.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — OCT-guided PCI was noninferior to IVUS-guided PCI in both OCTIVUS (2.5% versus 3.1%) and OPINION (5.2% versus 4.9%)

title: TAVR versus surgery in low/intermediate-risk aortic stenosis: death or stroke at one year in 5.4% versus 10.0% (DEDICATE) — noninferior, and numerically ahead, at one year only
question: In low- or intermediate-risk severe aortic stenosis, does transcatheter replacement match surgery for death or stroke at one year?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — at one year, in one trial. DEDICATE (Blankenberg S et al., PMID: 38588025) randomised 1,414 patients with severe aortic stenosis at low or intermediate surgical risk (median STS risk score 1.8%; mean age 74) at 38 German sites to transcatheter aortic-valve implantation or surgical replacement, with valve choice at operator discretion. The primary composite of death from any cause or fatal or nonfatal stroke at 1 year occurred in an estimated 5.4% on TAVI versus 10.0% on surgery (hazard ratio 0.53; 95% CI 0.35–0.79; p<0.001 for noninferiority). Death from any cause was 2.6% versus 6.2% (hazard ratio 0.43; 95% CI 0.24–0.73) and stroke 2.9% versus 4.7% (hazard ratio 0.61; 95% CI 0.35–1.06); procedural complications were 1.5% versus 1.0%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): TAVI more than matched surgery at one year — but one year is where TAVI's advantages are largest and its durability questions unasked, and a mortality claim from a single trial is Tier C.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — DEDICATE found death or stroke at 1 year in 5.4% on TAVI versus 10.0% on surgery (HR 0.53), with death 2.6% versus 6.2%, in a single trial

title: Small-annulus TAVR: clinical events matched (9.4% versus 10.6%), but valve dysfunction was 9.4% on the self-expanding valve versus 41.6% on the balloon-expandable (SMART)
question: In severe aortic stenosis with a small annulus, does a balloon-expandable valve match a self-expanding valve for valve function and clinical outcomes?
balance: SPLIT — the patients fared the same; the valves did not. SMART (Herrmann HC et al., PMID: 38587261) randomised 716 patients with severe aortic stenosis and an annulus area of 430 mm² or less (mean age 80; 87% women) to a self-expanding supraannular valve or a balloon-expandable valve. The clinical coprimary endpoint — death, disabling stroke, or heart-failure rehospitalisation through 12 months — occurred in an estimated 9.4% with the self-expanding valve versus 10.6% with the balloon-expandable valve (difference −1.2 percentage points; p<0.001 for noninferiority). The valve-function coprimary endpoint split wide open: bioprosthetic-valve dysfunction in 9.4% versus 41.6% (difference −32.2 points; p<0.001 for superiority), mean gradient 7.7 versus 15.7 mmHg, effective orifice area 1.99 versus 1.50 cm², and moderate or severe prosthesis–patient mismatch at 30 days in 11.2% versus 35.3%. PROPOSED SPLIT: balloon-expandable matches on 12-month clinical outcomes and loses decisively on haemodynamics — whether that loss becomes clinical over time is the unanswered part. Tier C: single-trial, industry-funded.
stamp: SPLIT — clinical outcomes noninferior (9.4% versus 10.6%) but bioprosthetic-valve dysfunction far lower with the self-expanding valve (9.4% versus 41.6%) in SMART

title: Valve-in-valve TAVR versus redo surgery for a failed surgical valve: early death 2.8% versus 5.0% in pooled observational data — but midterm mortality equal and the new valve leaks and pinches more
question: In failed surgical bioprosthetic aortic valves, does valve-in-valve TAVR match redo surgical replacement for death and stroke?
balance: SPLIT — valve-in-valve wins the first month and loses the echo. There are no randomised trials; two meta-analyses of observational studies agree on the shape. Raschpichler M et al. (PMID: 36533610) pooled 15 studies and 8,881 patients: short-term mortality was 2.8% after valve-in-valve TAVR versus 5.0% after redo surgery (risk ratio 0.55; 95% CI 0.34–0.91; p=0.02) and acute kidney failure was less frequent (risk ratio 0.54), but midterm mortality did not differ (hazard ratio 1.27; 95% CI 0.72–2.25), while prosthetic regurgitation (risk ratio 4.18) and severe prosthesis–patient mismatch (risk ratio 3.12) were more frequent after valve-in-valve and gradients were higher. Nasir MM et al. (PMID: 38723857), pooling 24 studies and 25,216 patients, found 30-day mortality odds ratio 0.50, major bleeding odds ratio 0.28, and no difference in 1-year mortality — with more paravalvular leak and higher gradients after valve-in-valve. PROPOSED SPLIT: an early-survival advantage bought with worse valve haemodynamics, all of it confounded by who gets chosen for which procedure. Tier C: observational evidence throughout.
stamp: SPLIT — valve-in-valve TAVR shows lower short-term mortality (2.8% versus 5.0%) but equal midterm mortality and more regurgitation and mismatch, in observational data only

title: Prosthetic valve thrombosis: ultraslow low-dose thrombolysis freed 90% of valves in PROMETEE with 6.7% complications — but the older pooled comparison says surgery embolises and bleeds less
question: In prosthetic valve thrombosis, does slow-infusion low-dose thrombolysis match surgery for success, embolism, and bleeding?
balance: SPLIT — the modern regimen looks gentle; the comparative evidence is old and points the other way. PROMETEE (Özkan M et al., PMID: 26299240) treated 114 patients (120 episodes of prosthetic valve thrombosis, 64.2% obstructive) at a single centre with transoesophageal-echo-guided ultraslow infusion of low-dose alteplase (25 mg over 25 hours, no bolus): overall thrombolytic success was 90% (95% CI 0.85–0.95) with an overall complication rate of 6.7% (3.3% nonfatal major, 2.5% minor, 0.8% death). The comparative record is a meta-analysis of observational studies (Karthikeyan G et al., PMID: 23329151) pooling 690 episodes: complete restoration of valve function in 86.5% with urgent surgery versus 69.7% with fibrinolysis (odds ratio 2.53; p=0.066, not significant), death in 13.5% versus 9% (odds ratio 1.95; not significant), but thromboembolism in 1.6% versus 16% (odds ratio 0.10; p<0.001), major bleeding in 1.4% versus 5% (odds ratio 0.27), and recurrent thrombosis in 7.1% versus 25.4% (odds ratio 0.25) — all favouring surgery. PROPOSED SPLIT: ultraslow thrombolysis succeeds often with few complications in expert hands, but it has never been randomised against surgery, and the regimens in the comparative pool predate it. Tier C.
stamp: SPLIT — PROMETEE's ultraslow regimen achieved 90% success with 6.7% complications in a single-arm series, while the pooled observational comparison favoured surgery for embolism, bleeding, and recurrence

title: INR self-testing and self-management: pooled trials show thromboembolism halved and mortality cut by a third — but the benefit sits in self-management, and the largest trial of self-testing alone found nothing
question: In patients on warfarin, does self-testing or self-management of the INR reduce thromboembolism, bleeding, and death compared with clinic management?
balance: SPLIT — who adjusts the dose decides whether this works. The Cochrane review (Garcia-Alamino JM et al., PMID: 20393937) pooled 18 randomised trials with 4,723 participants: self-monitoring or self-management reduced thromboembolic events (risk ratio 0.50; 95% CI 0.36–0.69) and all-cause mortality (risk ratio 0.64; 95% CI 0.46–0.89) versus standard monitoring, with no increase in harm. Split by mode, self-management alone reduced thromboembolism (risk ratio 0.47) and mortality (risk ratio 0.55), while self-testing alone — phoning the result to a clinic — did not significantly reduce either, though it did reduce major haemorrhage (risk ratio 0.56). The individual-patient meta-analysis (Heneghan C et al., PMID: 22137798; 11 trials, 6,417 participants) likewise found thromboembolism halved (hazard ratio 0.51; 95% CI 0.31–0.85) but mortality (hazard ratio 0.82) and major haemorrhage (hazard ratio 0.88) not significantly reduced. And the largest single trial, THINRS (Matchar DB et al., PMID: 20961244; 2,922 patients), found weekly home self-testing no better than monthly high-quality clinic testing for stroke, major bleeding, or death (hazard ratio 0.88; p=0.14). PROPOSED SPLIT: teach suitable patients to manage their own dose and events fall; hand them a meter and a phone number and the advantage evaporates. Tier C: mortality benefit claim.
stamp: SPLIT — self-management reduced thromboembolism (RR 0.47–0.51) and mortality in pooled trials, while self-testing alone was null in THINRS and in the self-monitoring subgroups

title: Leadless versus transvenous pacemakers in Medicare: fewer chronic complications (adjusted HR 0.69) and reinterventions (HR 0.62) at two years — but pericardial effusion or perforation doubled at implant (0.8% versus 0.4%)
question: In patients who need permanent pacing but not defibrillation, does a leadless pacemaker reduce complications compared with a transvenous pacemaker?
balance: SPLIT — safer by the year, riskier on the day. The Micra Coverage with Evidence Development study compared leadless with transvenous single-chamber ventricular pacemakers in US Medicare patients. At implant, adjusted acute complication rates were 7.7% versus 7.4% (Piccini JP et al., PMID: 34319383; risk difference 0.3 points; p=0.49), but pericardial effusion and/or perforation was significantly higher with the leadless device (0.8% versus 0.4%; p=0.004), while 6-month complications already favoured leadless (adjusted hazard ratio 0.77). At 2 years (El-Chami MF et al., PMID: 34788416), leadless patients had fewer reinterventions (adjusted hazard ratio 0.62; 95% CI 0.45–0.85) and fewer chronic complications (adjusted hazard ratio 0.69; 95% CI 0.60–0.81), with adjusted all-cause mortality no different (hazard ratio 0.97; 95% CI 0.91–1.04). PROPOSED SPLIT: no leads means no lead problems — the trade is a doubled, still uncommon, risk of perforating the heart at implant. Tier C: all observational, in patients who were sicker at baseline (end-stage kidney disease in 12.0% versus 2.3%).
stamp: SPLIT — leadless pacing showed fewer chronic complications and reinterventions at 2 years but more pericardial effusion/perforation at implant, in observational Medicare data

title: Extravascular ICD: defibrillation succeeded in 98.7% at implant and 92.6% were free of major complications at 6 months — against performance goals, not against a transvenous control
question: In patients who need a defibrillator without pacing, does a fully extravascular ICD defibrillate reliably with fewer lead complications than transvenous systems?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for reliability; the 'fewer complications than transvenous' half of the question has no comparative data at all. The Extravascular ICD Pivotal Study (Friedman P et al., PMID: 36036522) was a prospective single-group premarket study: of 356 enrolled patients, 316 had an implantation attempt, and among 302 in whom ventricular arrhythmia was induced and testing completed, successful defibrillation at implantation was 98.7% (lower boundary of the one-sided 97.5% CI 96.6%, against a performance goal of 88%). Freedom from major system- or procedure-related complications at 6 months was 92.6% (lower boundary 89.0%, goal 79%); 25 major complications occurred in 23 of 316 patients (7.3%), with no major intraprocedural complications. Over a mean 10.6 months, 29 patients received 118 inappropriate shocks, antitachycardia pacing succeeded in an estimated 50.8% of episodes, and 8 systems were explanted without replacement. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the device demonstrably shocks — whether it beats the transvenous systems it is meant to displace is untested. Tier C: single-arm evidence, sponsor-funded.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the extravascular ICD met its defibrillation (98.7%) and safety (92.6% complication-free) performance goals in a single-arm pivotal study, with no transvenous comparator

title: Antibiotic envelope at device implant: major infection in 0.7% versus 1.2% at 12 months (WRAP-IT) — a 40% relative reduction on a 1-in-200 baseline, with no added complications
question: In patients receiving a cardiac implantable electronic device, does an absorbable antibiotic envelope reduce device infection compared with standard prophylaxis?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — real, relative, and small in absolute terms. WRAP-IT (Tarakji KG et al., PMID: 30883056) randomised 6,983 patients undergoing pocket revision, generator replacement, system upgrade, or initial CRT-defibrillator implantation to an absorbable antibiotic-eluting envelope (minocycline and rifampin) or standard prophylaxis alone. The primary infection endpoint — infection causing extraction or revision, long-term antibiotics with recurrence, or death — occurred in 25 envelope patients versus 42 controls (12-month Kaplan–Meier rates 0.7% versus 1.2%; hazard ratio 0.60; 95% CI 0.36–0.98; p=0.04), a 40% relative reduction worth 0.5 percentage points absolute: about 200 envelopes to prevent one major infection. Procedure- or system-related complications were 6.0% versus 6.9% (hazard ratio 0.87; noninferior), and major infections over the full follow-up (mean 20.7 months) remained lower (hazard ratio 0.63; 95% CI 0.40–0.98). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): worth it where baseline infection risk is high; arithmetic, not enthusiasm, should decide where it is routine. Tier C: single trial, sponsor-funded.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — WRAP-IT reduced major device infection (0.7% versus 1.2%; HR 0.60) with no excess complications, in a single trial

title: Defibrillation testing at ICD implant: skipping it was noninferior in 3,577 randomised patients — first-shock efficacy and arrhythmic death unchanged (SIMPLE; NORDIC ICD)
question: In ICD recipients, does omitting defibrillation threshold testing at implant worsen shock efficacy or survival compared with routine testing?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — where 'the treatment' is the test itself. SIMPLE (Healey JS et al., PMID: 25715991) randomised 2,500 first-ICD patients to implantation with or without defibrillation testing: the composite of arrhythmic death or failed appropriate shock occurred in 90 patients in the no-testing group versus 104 with testing (hazard ratio 0.86; 95% CI 0.65–1.14; p<0.0001 for noninferiority) over a mean 3.1 years, and 30-day safety composites were 5.6% versus 6.5% (p=0.33) and 3.2% versus 4.5% (p=0.08). NORDIC ICD (Bänsch D et al., PMID: 26112885) randomised 1,077 patients and found model-based first-shock efficacy noninferior without testing (difference 3.0% in favour of no testing; p for noninferiority <0.001), with procedure-related serious adverse events in 17.6% of tested patients versus 13.9% untested (p=0.095). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): routine testing at first implant can be omitted — it found nothing, fixed nothing, and its own risks were the only ones that showed up at all.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — omitting defibrillation testing was noninferior for shock efficacy and arrhythmic death in both SIMPLE and NORDIC ICD

title: His-bundle and physiologic pacing versus right-ventricular pacing: ejection fraction preserved (+5.3 points pooled) where RV pacing let it fall — mortality unchanged, heart-failure hospitalisation unmeasured in the pool
question: In patients who need ventricular pacing, does His-bundle pacing preserve ejection fraction and reduce heart-failure hospitalisation compared with right-ventricular pacing?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for the ventricle's measurements, not yet for its events. The systematic review prepared for the 2018 ACC/AHA/HRS bradycardia guideline (Slotwiner DJ et al., PMID: 30412708) pooled 8 studies and 679 patients with ejection fraction above 35% needing pacing for heart block: physiologic pacing — biventricular or His-bundle — left ventricular volumes lower (end-diastolic −2.77 mL; end-systolic −7.09 mL) and ejection fraction preserved or increased by 5.328 percentage points (95% CI 2.86–7.8; p<0.0001) compared with right-ventricular pacing over a mean ~1.6 years; there was no effect on mortality, data on hospitalisations were unavailable, and functional benefit was clearest in patients with chronic atrial fibrillation after AV-node ablation. The randomised His-SYNC pilot (Upadhyay GA et al., PMID: 31096064) compared His-bundle resynchronisation with biventricular pacing — not RV pacing — in 41 CRT patients: QRS narrowed far more on His pacing (125 versus 164 ms on-treatment; p<0.001) with a trend to more echocardiographic response (80% versus 57%; p=0.14) and no difference in cardiovascular hospitalisation or mortality, amid 48% crossover from the His arm. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): physiologic pacing protects the ejection fraction that RV pacing spends; whether that converts into fewer heart-failure admissions is, on this record, unmeasured rather than shown. Tier C.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — physiologic (His-bundle or biventricular) pacing preserved ejection fraction versus right-ventricular pacing in a guideline systematic review, with no mortality effect and no pooled hospitalisation data

title: Pacing for carotid sinus hypersensitivity in older fallers: falls cut from a mean 9.3 to 4.1 per year and injurious events by 70% in SAFE PACE — one 175-patient trial
question: In older patients with carotid sinus hypersensitivity and unexplained falls or syncope, does dual-chamber pacing reduce falls and syncope compared with no pacing?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a large effect in a single small trial. SAFE PACE (Kenny RA et al., PMID: 11691528) randomised 175 consecutive patients older than 50 (mean age 73; 60% women) attending an emergency facility after a non-accidental fall, all with cardioinhibitory carotid sinus hypersensitivity, to dual-chamber pacemaker implantation or standard treatment. Over one year, falls were reduced by two-thirds: control patients reported 669 falls (mean 9.3; range 0–89) versus 216 (mean 4.1; range 0–29) in paced patients, who were significantly less likely to fall (odds ratio 0.42; 95% CI 0.23–0.75). Syncopal episodes were also fewer (28 in paced patients versus 47 in controls), and injurious events were reduced by 70% (61 versus 202). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): pacing a hypersensitive carotid sinus kept older fallers upright in the only randomised trial — an effect size this large, from 175 unblinded patients counting their own falls, invites both belief and a second trial that never came. Tier C: single-trial benefit claim.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — SAFE PACE reduced falls (mean 4.1 versus 9.3 per year; OR 0.42) and injurious events by 70% with dual-chamber pacing in carotid sinus hypersensitivity, in a single trial

title: Low-risk pulmonary embolism treated at home: recurrence 0.6% and death 0.6% in the randomised trial, 0.6% recurrence in HoT-PE — with 3.4 fewer days in hospital
question: In low-risk pulmonary embolism, can patients be treated safely at home from the start rather than admitted?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the benefit is the bed not occupied, at no measured cost in events. Aujesky D et al. (PMID: 21703676) randomised 344 patients with acute pulmonary embolism and low risk of death (PESI classes I–II) to discharge within 24 hours or inpatient care, both on enoxaparin then oral anticoagulation: recurrent venous thromboembolism within 90 days occurred in 1 outpatient (0.6%) versus no inpatients (noninferiority p=0.011), death within 90 days in 1 patient (0.6%) in each group, and major bleeding by 90 days in 3 outpatients (1.8%) versus no inpatients — while mean length of stay was 0.5 days versus 3.9 days. HoT-PE (Barco S et al., PMID: 31120118), a single-arm management trial of early discharge on rivaroxaban in 525 carefully selected low-risk patients (no instability, no right-ventricular dysfunction, no serious comorbidity), found symptomatic recurrence in 3 patients (0.6%), major bleeding in 6 (1.2%), and 2 cancer-related deaths (0.4%). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): in rigorously selected low-risk PE, home treatment is as safe as admission and returns three-plus days of hospital to the patient. Tier C: one randomised trial plus a single-arm study carry the safety claim.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — home treatment of selected low-risk PE matched inpatient care on recurrence and death (0.6% each) while cutting stay from 3.9 to 0.5 days

title: Direct oral anticoagulants in children with VTE: rivaroxaban recurrence 1% versus 3% on standard care, dabigatran noninferior on the composite (46% versus 42%) — bleeding no higher in either trial
question: In children and adolescents with venous thromboembolism, do direct oral anticoagulants match standard anticoagulation for recurrence and bleeding?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — which, for a child facing injections and INR checks, is the win. EINSTEIN-Jr (Male C et al., PMID: 31699660) randomised 500 children aged 0–17 with acute venous thromboembolism to bodyweight-adjusted rivaroxaban or standard anticoagulants: symptomatic recurrence occurred in 4 children (1%) on rivaroxaban versus 5 (3%) on standard care (hazard ratio 0.40; 95% CI 0.11–1.41), thrombotic burden on repeat imaging improved more with rivaroxaban (p=0.012), and major or clinically relevant non-major bleeding occurred in 3% versus 2% (hazard ratio 1.58; 95% CI 0.51–6.27), with no major bleed on rivaroxaban and no treatment-related deaths. DIVERSITY (Halton J et al., PMID: 33290737) randomised 267 analysed children to dabigatran by an age- and weight-adjusted nomogram or standard care: the composite of complete thrombus resolution, freedom from recurrence, and freedom from VTE-related death was met by 46% on dabigatran versus 42% on standard care (weighted difference −0.04; 90% CI −0.14 to 0.07; p<0.0001 for noninferiority), with major bleeding in 2% of each group. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): two randomised trials, two DOACs, efficacy and bleeding statistically indistinguishable from the heparin-and-warfarin standard they replace.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — rivaroxaban and dabigatran each matched standard anticoagulation for recurrence and bleeding in randomised paediatric VTE trials

title: High-intensity warfarin in antiphospholipid syndrome: recurrence 10.7% on high intensity versus 3.4% on moderate in Crowther, 11.1% versus 5.5% in WAPS — more anticoagulation, numerically more clots, more minor bleeding
question: In antiphospholipid syndrome, does high-intensity warfarin prevent recurrent thrombosis better than standard-intensity warfarin?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — and the point estimates lean against the intensive strategy. Crowther MA et al. (PMID: 13679527) randomised 114 patients with antiphospholipid antibodies and previous thrombosis to warfarin targeted to INR 3.1–4.0 or 2.0–3.0: over a mean 2.7 years, recurrent thrombosis occurred in 6 of 56 patients (10.7%) on high intensity versus 2 of 58 (3.4%) on moderate intensity (hazard ratio 3.1; 95% CI 0.6–15.0), with major bleeding in 3 versus 4 patients (hazard ratio 1.0). WAPS (Finazzi G et al., PMID: 15869575) randomised 109 patients to high-intensity warfarin (INR 3.0–4.5) or conventional treatment (mostly warfarin INR 2.0–3.0): over a median 3.6 years, recurrent thrombosis occurred in 11.1% versus 5.5% (hazard ratio 1.97; 95% CI 0.49–7.89), while any bleeding occurred in 27.8% versus 14.6% (hazard ratio 2.18; 95% CI 0.92–5.15), major bleeding in 2 versus 3 patients. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): two randomised trials agree that pushing the INR above 3 buys no protection — standard intensity is the evidence-based target, and the extra intensity is paid for in minor bleeding.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — high-intensity warfarin was not superior in either Crowther (recurrence 10.7% versus 3.4%) or WAPS (11.1% versus 5.5%), with more minor bleeding in WAPS

title: Dalteparin in pregnancy for women with thrombophilia: the composite of pre-eclampsia, small babies, pregnancy loss and clots was 17.1% on dalteparin versus 18.9% without — no benefit, more minor bleeding
question: In pregnant women with thrombophilia and prior pregnancy complications, does antepartum dalteparin reduce placenta-mediated complications compared with no prophylaxis?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the large TIPPS trial and the individual-patient meta-analysis point the same way. In TIPPS, the composite of severe or early pre-eclampsia, small-for-gestational-age infant, pregnancy loss or venous thromboembolism occurred in 17.1% on antepartum dalteparin versus 18.9% on no dalteparin (risk difference −1.8%, 95% CI −10.6 to 7.1). The individual-patient meta-analysis of eight trials (963 women) likewise found no significant reduction in recurrent placenta-mediated complications (14% versus 22%; relative risk 0.64, 95% CI 0.36–1.11, p=0.11), with a signal only in the subgroup whose previous complication was placental abruption in multicentre trials. The cost in TIPPS was minor bleeding: 19.6% versus 9.2% (p=0.01), with no difference in major bleeding. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): prophylactic dalteparin does not prevent placenta-mediated complications in thrombophilic pregnancy and adds minor bleeding.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — TIPPS (n=289 analysed) and an 8-trial individual-patient meta-analysis agree: no reduction in placenta-mediated complications; minor bleeding increased

title: Highlow: intermediate-dose heparin in pregnancy after a previous clot — recurrence 2% versus 3% on low dose, not significantly lower, bleeding identical at 4%
question: In pregnant women with a previous venous thromboembolism, does an intermediate dose of low-molecular-weight heparin prevent recurrence better than a fixed low dose?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — in the 1,110-woman Highlow trial, recurrent venous thromboembolism occurred in 11/555 (2%) on weight-adjusted intermediate-dose low-molecular-weight heparin versus 16/555 (3%) on fixed low-dose (relative risk 0.69, 95% CI 0.32–1.47, p=0.33), with the antepartum split identical at 1% versus 1% and the small gap arising post partum (1% versus 2%). Major bleeding was the same in both groups (23/520, 4%, versus 20/525, 4%; relative risk 1.16, 95% CI 0.65–2.09). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): the higher dose buys no proven protection, so the fixed low dose is the appropriate thromboprophylaxis dose in pregnancy after a previous clot.

title: IDEAL DVT: stopping compression stockings early when symptoms settle was non-inferior to a fixed two years — post-thrombotic syndrome 29% versus 28%, and two-thirds could stop early
question: After a first deep-vein thrombosis, does individualising compression-stocking duration by symptoms match a fixed two years for preventing post-thrombotic syndrome?

title: SURPRISE: a rivaroxaban tablet matched daily fondaparinux injections for superficial-vein thrombosis — events 3% versus 2% at 45 days, non-inferior, no major bleeding in either group
question: In acute superficial-vein thrombosis, does rivaroxaban match fondaparinux for preventing deep-vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, and extension?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — as an equally effective, less burdensome substitute: in the SURPRISE trial the composite of symptomatic deep-vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism, progression or recurrence of superficial-vein thrombosis, and all-cause death at 45 days occurred in 7/211 (3%) on rivaroxaban 10 mg daily versus 4/224 (2%) on fondaparinux 2.5 mg daily (hazard ratio 1.9, 95% CI 0.6–6.4; p=0.0025 for non-inferiority against a 4.5% margin). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): rivaroxaban is a non-inferior oral alternative to 45 days of fondaparinux injections for superficial-vein thrombosis with additional risk factors — the benefit is convenience at equal protection, not greater protection.

title: API-CAT: after six months of treatment for cancer-associated clots, halving the apixaban dose kept recurrence at 2.1% versus 2.8% — non-inferior — and cut clinically relevant bleeding from 15.6% to 12.1%
question: In cancer-associated venous thromboembolism that has completed six months of anticoagulation, does continuing a reduced dose of apixaban match the full dose for recurrence and bleeding?

title: FIT every year versus every two or three years: at the repeat round the detection of advanced neoplasia was the same whatever the interval — 1.9% overall, with no interval effect (p=0.62); mortality was never tested
question: In average-risk adults screened with faecal immunochemical testing, does annual testing detect more colorectal cancers and advanced adenomas than biennial testing, and does the interval change colorectal cancer mortality?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — for detection at the repeat round, within a 1–3-year range: in the Dutch randomised comparison of 7,501 invitees, second-round participation was 63.2% with a 1-year interval, 62.5% with 2 years and 64.0% with 3 years; positivity in the second round (6.0%, down from 8.4% in round one) did not depend on interval length (p=0.23), and neither did the detection rate of advanced neoplasia (1.9% in round two versus 3.3% in round one; interval comparison p=0.62). No trial has randomised the FIT interval and followed participants to colorectal cancer mortality, so that half of the question is unanswered by direct evidence. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): annual testing finds no more advanced neoplasia at the repeat round than biennial or triennial testing; any mortality difference between intervals is untested, not disproven.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — single randomised interval comparison: advanced-neoplasia detection independent of 1–3-year interval (p=0.62); no mortality data

title: Endoscopic screening for gastric cancer: a large Chinese cluster trial cut upper-GI cancer deaths in high-risk areas (0.77% versus 0.99%), but the gastric-specific 12-year trial found 13.1 versus 13.5 deaths per 100,000 person-years — not significant
question: In high-incidence populations, does population endoscopic screening for gastric cancer reduce gastric cancer mortality versus no screening?
balance: SPLIT — by population and by how specific the endpoint is. In the multicentre Chinese cluster-randomised trial (234,635 participants), an invitation to endoscopic screening reduced upper gastrointestinal cancer mortality in high-risk areas — adjusted cumulative risk 0.77% versus 0.99% over 7.5 years (risk ratio 0.78, 95% CI 0.66–0.91) — but not significantly in non-high-risk areas (0.26% versus 0.30%; risk ratio 0.86, 95% CI 0.65–1.13). The trial aimed squarely at non-cardia gastric cancer (Hua County, 33,847 residents, 12 years) found mortality of 13.1 versus 13.5 per 100,000 person-years (adjusted rate ratio 0.85, 95% CI 0.49–1.50) — a non-significant 15% relative reduction, with per-protocol estimates (0.70) also non-significant. PROPOSED SPLIT: screening probably reduces upper-GI cancer deaths where incidence is high, but a gastric-cancer-specific mortality benefit is not yet statistically secured.
stamp: SPLIT — mortality benefit significant for combined upper-GI cancers in high-risk areas (RR 0.78), non-significant for non-cardia gastric cancer alone over 12 years (aRR 0.85)

title: WISDOM: risk-based breast screening was non-inferior to annual mammography for stage ≥IIB cancers (30.0 versus 48.0 per 100,000 person-years) with far fewer mammograms — but biopsies were not reduced
question: In women invited to breast screening, does risk-based screening (interval and modality set by individual risk) detect cancer as safely as standard annual mammography, with fewer false positives?
balance: SPLIT — safe on the cancer endpoint, unsuccessful on the biopsy endpoint. In WISDOM (28,372 women randomised), stage ≥IIB cancer rates were 30.0 per 100,000 person-years with risk-based screening versus 48.0 with annual screening (rate difference −18.0, 95% CI −40.2 to 4.1), meeting non-inferiority, and mammograms were far fewer (rate difference −3,835.9 per 100,000 person-years). But the co-primary hope of fewer biopsies failed: biopsy rates were not lower (rate difference +98.7 per 100,000 person-years, 95% CI −17.9 to 215.3; 1,029 versus 943 biopsies). In the parallel observational cohort, 89% of women (15,980/18,031) chose risk-based screening when offered the choice. PROPOSED SPLIT: risk-based screening safely reallocates intensity — less screening for low-risk women, more for high-risk — without the promised reduction in biopsies.
stamp: SPLIT — non-inferior for stage ≥IIB cancer and far fewer mammograms, but biopsy rates not reduced (rate difference +98.7 per 100,000 person-years)

title: HPV self-sampling: with PCR-based tests, a self-collected vaginal sample finds CIN2+ as accurately as a clinician's sample (pooled sensitivity ratio 0.99) — but signal-amplification tests lose accuracy (0.85), and specificity dips 2–4%
question: How accurately does HPV testing on a self-collected vaginal sample detect cervical precancer (CIN2+) compared with clinician-collected samples?
balance: SPLIT — by assay technology. The updated Arbyn meta-analyses (56 accuracy studies) found PCR-based high-risk HPV assays on self samples were as sensitive as on clinician samples for CIN2+ and CIN3+ (pooled sensitivity ratio 0.99, 95% CI 0.97–1.02), whereas signal-amplification assays were less sensitive on self samples (ratio 0.85, 95% CI 0.80–0.89); specificity to exclude CIN2+ was 2% (PCR) to 4% (signal amplification) lower on self samples. The earlier 2014 analysis (36 studies, 154,556 women) had found self-sample sensitivity lower overall (ratio 0.88 for CIN2+) because signal-based assays dominated. Mailing kits home also raised participation among underscreened women (relative participation 2.33, 95% CI 1.86–2.91 versus invitation letters). PROPOSED SPLIT: self-sampling is accurate enough with PCR-based assays and reaches women clinics miss; with older signal-based assays it is a second-best test.
stamp: SPLIT — PCR-based assays: equal sensitivity on self samples (ratio 0.99); signal-amplification assays: less sensitive (0.85); specificity 2–4% lower

title: Liver-cancer surveillance in cirrhosis: cohort evidence links it to earlier detection and better survival (hazard ratio 0.67), but scanning every 3 months instead of 6 found no more small cancers in the one randomised trial
question: In patients with cirrhosis, does regular ultrasound surveillance improve early-stage detection and survival from hepatocellular carcinoma, and is 6-monthly surveillance better than 3-monthly?
balance: SPLIT — surveillance itself versus surveillance intensity. For intensity, the randomised answer is clear: in Trinchet's trial of 1,278 patients with compensated cirrhosis, ultrasound every 3 months detected more tiny focal lesions (≤10 mm: 41% versus 28%, p=0.002) but no more hepatocellular carcinomas ≤30 mm (79% versus 70%, p=0.30) and no difference in HCC incidence (p=0.13) versus every 6 months. For surveillance versus none there is no cirrhosis randomised trial; the 2022 cohort meta-analysis (59 studies, 145,396 patients) associated surveillance with earlier-stage detection (risk ratio 1.86, 95% CI 1.73–1.98), more curative treatment (risk ratio 1.83, 1.69–1.97) and better survival after lead-time adjustment (hazard ratio 0.67, 95% CI 0.61–0.72), with physical harms from false positives in 8.8–27.5%. PROPOSED SPLIT: 6-monthly surveillance is the supported standard; 3-monthly adds false alarms, not curable cancers.
stamp: SPLIT — 6-monthly surveillance supported by cohort evidence (survival HR 0.67); 3-monthly adds nothing in the randomised interval trial

title: BEST3: offering a swallowable Cytosponge test in primary care found ten times more Barrett's oesophagus — 140 cases versus 13 — including 9 treatable dysplasias or stage I cancers versus none
question: In primary-care patients with chronic reflux symptoms, does a non-endoscopic Cytosponge-TFF3 test identify Barrett's oesophagus accurately enough to target endoscopy?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for detection, which is the outcome the trial measured: in BEST3 (13,514 patients randomised across 109 English general practices), offering Cytosponge-TFF3 to patients on long-term acid suppression produced 140 Barrett's diagnoses (2% of 6,834) versus 13 (<1% of 6,388) with usual care over 12 months (absolute difference 18.3 per 1,000 person-years; adjusted rate ratio 10.6, 95% CI 6.0–18.8, p<0.0001), including 9 cases of dysplastic Barrett's or stage I oesophago-gastric cancer versus none. title: Skin-cancer screening and melanoma deaths: the Schleswig-Holstein pilot was followed by a halving of mortality — but nationwide German screening from 2008 produced no mortality decline, and the pilot region's rate climbed back to the national level
question: Does organised population skin-cancer screening reduce melanoma mortality, or mainly increase detection of thin and in-situ lesions?
balance: SPLIT — the pilot region and the national programme tell different stories. After the 2003–04 SCREEN pilot (360,288 people examined in Schleswig-Holstein), age-standardised melanoma mortality there fell 47% in men (1.9 to 1.0 per 100,000) and 49% in women (1.4 to 0.7) by 2008/09, while adjacent regions and Germany overall were stable. But when Germany rolled screening out nationally in 2008, incidence rose ~28% to 18.2 per 100,000 by 2010 with no downward mortality trend (2.3 deaths per 100,000 in 2013), and Schleswig-Holstein's mortality rose back to 2.4 per 100,000 — the same as Germany overall. PROPOSED SPLIT: an intensive one-off regional campaign coincided with a temporary mortality fall; routine nationwide screening has shown detection gains without a measurable mortality benefit — overdiagnosis is the demonstrated effect, mortality reduction is not.
stamp: SPLIT — pilot-region ecological mortality fall (47–49%) not reproduced by nationwide screening (no mortality trend; pilot region rebounded to 2.4/100,000)

title: Thyroid cancer screening: detection has risen 4.5% a year while mortality stands still — the USPSTF recommends against screening asymptomatic adults (grade D), judging harms at least moderate and benefits no greater than small
question: Does ultrasound screening for thyroid cancer in asymptomatic adults reduce thyroid cancer deaths, or only multiply diagnoses of indolent cancers?
balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — net harm, in the USPSTF's bounded judgement: thyroid cancer detection in the US rose 4.5% per year over a decade to an incidence of 15.3 cases per 100,000 (2013) with no corresponding change in mortality, and overall 5-year survival is already 98.1%. The Task Force found inadequate direct evidence on screening benefits but bounded them as no greater than small — the cancer is rare, treated and monitored patients fare alike for the common types, and mass screening elsewhere changed incidence without changing mortality — while bounding harms as at least moderate, given proven treatment harms and substantial overdiagnosis and overtreatment. Its conclusion: the net benefit of screening asymptomatic adults is negative (grade D, recommend against). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm): population thyroid ultrasound screening multiplies diagnoses of cancers that would never have caused harm, exposing people to surgery and lifelong treatment without a shown mortality gain.
stamp: POSSIBLE (harm) — USPSTF grade D: benefits bounded as ≤small, harms ≥moderate; detection rising 4.5%/year with mortality unchanged

title: ANCHOR: treating anal precancer in people with HIV cut progression to anal cancer by 57% in relative terms — 173 versus 402 cases per 100,000 person-years
question: In people living with HIV aged 35 and over, does treating anal high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions prevent anal cancer versus active monitoring?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in ANCHOR, among 4,446 people living with HIV aged ≥35 with biopsy-proven anal high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions, progression to anal cancer occurred at 173 per 100,000 person-years with treatment versus 402 per 100,000 person-years with active monitoring over a median 25.8 months — a 57% relative reduction (95% CI 6–80; p=0.03), on absolute counts of 9 versus 21 cancers. title: Lynch syndrome colonoscopy intervals: 3-yearly surveillance in Finland produced no more colorectal cancer than 2-yearly-or-closer elsewhere — cumulative incidence by age 70 was 41%/36% (men/women) versus 58%/55%, and survival after cancer was 89–92% whatever the interval
question: In carriers of Lynch syndrome, how often should colonoscopic surveillance be performed — does a 1–2-year interval prevent more colorectal cancers than a 3-year interval?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — for interval length, on prospective observational data: in the Prospective Lynch Syndrome Database, path_MLH1 carriers under 3-yearly colonoscopy in Finland (n=505) had cumulative colorectal cancer incidence by age 70 of 41% (men) and 36% (women), versus 58% and 55% under 2-yearly-or-more-frequent protocols elsewhere (n=439) — differences not significant (p>0.05), with mean time from last colonoscopy to cancer virtually identical (32.7 versus 31.0 months). In the companion survival analysis, 10-year survival after colon cancer was 89%, 90%, 90% and 92% whether the last colonoscopy was <1.5, 1.5–2.5, 2.5–3.5 or >3.5 years before diagnosis (p=0.91), while stage strongly predicted survival (93%, 94% and 82% for stages I–III, p<0.001). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): shortening surveillance below a 3-year interval has not been shown to prevent more Lynch colorectal cancers or improve survival — surveillance itself is not in question here, only its frequency.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — prospective database: CRC incidence and post-cancer survival flat across 3-yearly vs ≤2-yearly intervals

title: IBIS-II: five years of anastrozole halved breast cancer in high-risk postmenopausal women — 85 versus 165 cases over a median 131 months (hazard ratio 0.51), and the protection persisted after treatment stopped
question: In postmenopausal women at increased risk of breast cancer, does anastrozole for 5 years prevent invasive breast cancer versus placebo, and do benefits persist after treatment stops?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — large and durable, from one trial reported twice: IBIS-II randomised 3,864 high-risk postmenopausal women to anastrozole 1 mg daily or placebo for 5 years. At the first report (median 5.0 years), breast cancer had developed in 40 women (2%) on anastrozole versus 85 (4%) on placebo (hazard ratio 0.47, 95% CI 0.32–0.68). At the long-term report (median follow-up 131 months), cases were 85 versus 165 (hazard ratio 0.51, 95% CI 0.39–0.66) — a 49% relative reduction — with benefit continuing in the post-treatment period (hazard ratio 0.64 after year 5) and invasive oestrogen-receptor-positive cancer reduced by 54% in relative terms (hazard ratio 0.46). Deaths did not differ (69 versus 70), and there was no excess of fractures or cardiovascular disease. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): anastrozole prevents breast cancer in high-risk postmenopausal women with protection outlasting the five treatment years; a mortality benefit has not been shown.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single RCT with long-term follow-up: 85 vs 165 cases (HR 0.51) at 131 months; no mortality difference

title: MAP.3: exemestane cut invasive breast cancer by 65% in relative terms in high-risk postmenopausal women — 11 cancers versus 32 over a median 35 months (0.19% versus 0.55% per year), with no serious toxicity signal
question: In postmenopausal women at increased risk, does exemestane prevent invasive breast cancer versus placebo, and at what cost in menopausal symptoms and bone health?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — from the single MAP.3 trial: 4,560 postmenopausal women at moderately increased risk were randomised to exemestane or placebo; at a median 35 months, invasive breast cancer was detected in 11 women on exemestane versus 32 on placebo — annual incidence 0.19% versus 0.55%, a 65% relative reduction (hazard ratio 0.35, 95% CI 0.18–0.70, p=0.002). Invasive plus non-invasive cancers: 0.35% versus 0.77% per year (hazard ratio 0.47, 95% CI 0.27–0.79). Adverse events were slightly commoner on exemestane (88% versus 85%, p=0.003) but there were no significant differences in skeletal fractures, cardiovascular events, other cancers or treatment-related deaths, and quality-of-life differences were minimal. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): exemestane substantially reduces invasive breast cancer over three years in at-risk postmenopausal women, with symptom costs that were small in-trial; longer-term bone safety rests on the aromatase-inhibitor class record rather than this trial's 35 months.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single RCT: invasive cancer 11 vs 32 (HR 0.35, 65% relative reduction); no fracture or cardiovascular excess at 35 months

title: TAM-01: tamoxifen at a quarter of the standard dose (5 mg for 3 years) halved new breast events after intraepithelial neoplasia — 14 versus 28 events at 5 years, still 25 versus 41 at 10 years, without extra serious harm
question: In women with breast intraepithelial neoplasia (atypical hyperplasia, LCIS or DCIS), does low-dose tamoxifen 5 mg/day prevent recurrence and new breast events versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in TAM-01, 500 women with hormone-sensitive or unknown breast intraepithelial neoplasia were randomised to tamoxifen 5 mg daily for 3 years or placebo. At median 5.1 years there were 14 neoplastic events on tamoxifen versus 28 on placebo (11.6 versus 23.9 per 1,000 person-years; hazard ratio 0.48, 95% CI 0.26–0.92, p=0.02), with contralateral events reduced by 75% in relative terms (3 versus 12; hazard ratio 0.25) and a 5-year number needed to treat of 22. At the 10-year report (median 9.7 years), events were 25 versus 41 (hazard ratio 0.58, 95% CI 0.35–0.95) and the NNT had improved to 14. Serious adverse events did not differ (12 versus 16 in the first report, including one deep-vein thrombosis and one stage I endometrial cancer on tamoxifen). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): low-dose tamoxifen prevents recurrence and new events after intraepithelial neoplasia with a durable effect and limited toxicity.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single RCT with 10-year follow-up: events 14 vs 28 (HR 0.48) at 5 years, 25 vs 41 (HR 0.58) at 10 years; NNT 14 at 10 years

title: Metformin after polypectomy: one year of low-dose metformin (250 mg) cut adenoma recurrence to 30.6% versus 51.6% on placebo in non-diabetic patients — a small single-country trial of 133 completers
question: In patients without diabetes after polypectomy, does low-dose metformin for one year prevent metachronous colorectal adenomas and polyps versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — promising but thin: in the Higurashi phase 3 trial, non-diabetic Japanese patients with resected adenomas were randomised to metformin 250 mg daily or placebo for one year, after which adenomas were found in 22/71 (30.6% as reported) on metformin versus 32/62 (51.6%) on placebo (risk ratio 0.60, 95% CI 0.39–0.92, p=0.016), and total polyps in 38.0% versus 56.5% (risk ratio 0.67, 95% CI 0.47–0.97, p=0.034); median polyp count was 0 versus 1 (p=0.041). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): one year of low-dose metformin reduced one-year adenoma recurrence in this trial — a single small study at an unusually low dose, awaiting replication before it can be called established.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single small RCT: adenomas 30.6% vs 51.6% (RR 0.60) at 1 year

title: Celecoxib prevents colorectal adenomas — recurrence 43.2% and 37.5% versus 60.7% over three years — at a cardiovascular price that rises with dose: event risk ratios 2.6 and 3.4 in the APC trial
question: In patients with a recently removed colorectal adenoma, does celecoxib prevent adenoma recurrence versus placebo, and at what cardiovascular cost?
balance: SPLIT — a real preventive effect bought with dose-related cardiovascular harm. In the APC trial (2,035 patients with removed adenomas), the cumulative incidence of one or more adenomas by year 3 was 60.7% on placebo versus 43.2% on celecoxib 200 mg twice daily (risk ratio 0.67, 95% CI 0.59–0.77) and 37.5% on 400 mg twice daily (risk ratio 0.55, 95% CI 0.48–0.64). But adjudicated cardiovascular events (death, myocardial infarction, stroke or heart failure) rose with dose: risk ratio 2.6 (95% CI 1.1–6.1) at 200 mg twice daily and 3.4 (95% CI 1.5–7.9) at 400 mg twice daily in APC, with the pooled APC+PreSAP hazard ratio 1.9 (95% CI 1.1–3.1) and dose-related systolic blood-pressure rises of up to 5.2 mm Hg at 3 years. Serious adverse events overall were 18.8% (placebo), 20.4% and 23.0%. PROPOSED SPLIT: celecoxib demonstrably prevents adenoma recurrence and demonstrably harms the cardiovascular system at these doses — which is why it is not routinely recommended for this indication.
stamp: SPLIT — adenoma recurrence reduced (RR 0.67/0.55 by dose) while cardiovascular events increased (RR 2.6/3.4 by dose)

title: Taiwan's universal infant hepatitis B vaccination: childhood liver-cancer incidence fell from 0.70 to 0.36 per 100,000 within a decade, and vaccinated birth cohorts carried a relative risk of 0.31 into early adulthood
question: Did universal infant hepatitis B immunisation reduce the incidence of hepatocellular carcinoma in children and young adults?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — the first demonstration that a vaccine prevents a human cancer, from Taiwan's nationwide programme (launched July 1984) tracked through the national cancer registry: average annual hepatocellular carcinoma incidence in children aged 6–14 fell from 0.70 per 100,000 (1981–86) to 0.57 (1986–90) and 0.36 (1990–94) (p<0.01), and in children aged 6–9 from 0.52 per 100,000 in those born 1974–84 to 0.13 in those born 1984–86 (p<0.001), with mortality falling in parallel. The 20-year follow-up found the protection extended to age 29: 64 cancers in 37.7 million person-years among vaccinated cohorts versus 444 in 78.5 million among unvaccinated — an age- and sex-adjusted relative risk of 0.31 (p<0.001). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): universal infant hepatitis B immunisation prevents hepatocellular carcinoma from childhood into early adulthood; residual cases concentrate in children of highly infectious carrier mothers and in incomplete vaccination.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — national programme registry data: childhood HCC incidence 0.70 → 0.36 per 100,000; vaccinated-cohort relative risk 0.31 at 20 years

title: Quadrivalent HPV vaccine in women aged 24–45: 90.5% efficacy against vaccine-type infection and disease in women not already infected — but only 30.9% in the whole randomised population, because many were already exposed
question: In women aged 24–45, does quadrivalent HPV vaccination prevent vaccine-type HPV infection and disease versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — sharply split by prior exposure: in the randomised trial of 3,819 women aged 24–45, per-protocol efficacy against the composite of persistent infection and disease from HPV types 6, 11, 16 and 18 was 90.5% (95% CI 73.7–97.5; 4/1,615 cases on vaccine versus 41/1,607 on placebo), and 83.1% against types 16/18 endpoints (4/1,601 versus 23/1,579). But in the intention-to-treat population — everyone randomised, including women already infected at baseline — efficacy against the first endpoint was only 30.9% (95% CI 11.1–46.5; 108/1,886 versus 154/1,883) and 22.6% (95% CI −2.9 to 41.9) for types 16/18. No vaccine-related serious adverse events were recorded. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the vaccine works in mid-adult women who have not yet met the vaccine types; its population yield at this age is limited by prior exposure, which is why programmes target adolescents.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single RCT: per-protocol efficacy 90.5% in type-naive women vs 30.9% intention-to-treat

title: Quitting smoking after an early-stage lung cancer diagnosis: continuing smokers carried nearly triple the mortality hazard in non-small-cell cancer (HR 2.94) — modelled five-year survival 70% for quitters versus 33% for continuing smokers
question: In people diagnosed with early-stage lung cancer, does quitting smoking after diagnosis improve survival versus continuing to smoke?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational but with effects beyond the usual confounding range: Parsons' systematic review of longitudinal studies found continued smoking after diagnosis associated with significantly increased all-cause mortality in early-stage non-small-cell lung cancer (hazard ratio 2.94, 95% CI 1.15–7.54) and recurrence (hazard ratio 1.86, 95% CI 1.01–3.41), and in limited-stage small-cell cancer with increased mortality (hazard ratio 1.86, 95% CI 1.33–2.59), second primary tumours (hazard ratio 4.31, 95% CI 1.09–16.98) and recurrence (hazard ratio 1.26, 95% CI 1.06–1.50). Life-table modelling from these data estimated five-year survival for a 65-year-old with early-stage non-small-cell cancer at 70% if they quit versus 33% if they continued, and 63% versus 29% in limited-stage small-cell cancer. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): quitting at diagnosis is associated with substantially better survival — the modelled gains exceed what fewer cardiorespiratory deaths would explain, implicating slower cancer progression.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational meta-analysis: continued smoking HR 2.94 for mortality in early NSCLC; modelled 5-year survival 70% (quit) vs 33% (continued)

title: Salpingectomy with delayed oophorectomy in BRCA1/2 carriers: menopause symptoms clearly milder than after immediate salpingo-oophorectomy — but cancer safety is still unproven
question: In women carrying a BRCA1/2 pathogenic variant, does salpingectomy with delayed oophorectomy preserve quality of life and menopause-related health versus immediate risk-reducing salpingo-oophorectomy, without compromising safety?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for menopause-related quality of life only, in a trial where women chose their own operation. In the Dutch TUBA study (Steenbeek MP et al., PMID: 34081085), 577 BRCA1/2 carriers chose risk-reducing salpingectomy with delayed oophorectomy or immediate salpingo-oophorectomy; over the first year the rise in climacteric symptoms on the Greene Climacteric Scale was 6.7 points (95% CI 5.0–8.4) greater after salpingo-oophorectomy without hormone therapy than after salpingectomy alone, and 3.6 points (2.3–4.8) greater even when hormone therapy followed salpingo-oophorectomy. Cancer worry, tracked in the same cohort (van Bommel MHD et al., PMID: 34997316), was high before surgery in 57% of women and fell after surgery in 54%, with only 6% persistently highly worried — and it fell after either operation. The decisive unknown is stated plainly by the trialists: whether delaying oophorectomy is oncologically safe is being tested in a separate international follow-up study and is not answered here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): salpingectomy with delayed oophorectomy preserves menopause-related quality of life better than immediate salpingo-oophorectomy, on nonrandomised evidence, with cancer safety unproven.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — menopause-related quality of life is better after salpingectomy with delayed oophorectomy than after immediate salpingo-oophorectomy in the nonrandomised TUBA study, but oncologic safety of the delay is unproven

title: Oral contraceptives in BRCA1/2 carriers: ovarian cancer risk roughly halved in two meta-analyses — the breast cancer signal splits by measure, hazard ratio 1.55 versus odds ratio 1.06
question: In carriers of BRCA1/2 mutations, do oral contraceptives reduce ovarian cancer risk, and is there an offsetting increase in breast cancer risk?
balance: SPLIT — the ovarian side of the ledger is consistent, the breast side is not. The 2023 systematic review and meta-analysis (van Bommel MHD et al., PMID: 36383189) found ovarian cancer risk lower in oral contraceptive users (hazard ratio 0.62, 95% CI 0.52–0.74; odds ratio 0.49, 0.38–0.63), with the protection vanishing after stopping; for breast cancer the same review found a hazard ratio of 1.55 (1.36–1.76) in seven studies yet an odds ratio of 1.06 (0.90–1.25) in four others. The earlier meta-analysis (Iodice S et al., PMID: 20537530) agrees on the ovary — summary relative risk 0.50 (0.33–0.75), with a further 36% relative reduction per additional 10 years of use — and found no significant breast cancer association overall (summary relative risk 1.13, 0.88–1.45), except for formulations used before 1975 (1.47, 1.06–2.04). All of this is observational evidence graded low or very low quality, in women whose baseline risks are very high. PROPOSED SPLIT: ovarian protection is the consistent finding; a breast cancer increase is possible but unproven for modern formulations.
stamp: SPLIT — ovarian cancer risk is lower with oral contraceptive use (odds ratio 0.49, hazard ratio 0.62) while the breast cancer signal splits by study measure (hazard ratio 1.55 versus odds ratio 1.06), all in observational meta-analyses

title: Simple hysterectomy in low-risk cervical cancer: pelvic recurrence 2.52% versus 2.17% at 3 years — noninferior, with far less urinary retention and better sexual health
question: In low-risk early-stage cervical cancer, is simple hysterectomy non-inferior to radical hysterectomy for pelvic recurrence, with fewer bladder and bowel complications?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — less surgery, the same pelvic control, and measurably less harm, in the one randomised trial that asked. In SHAPE (Plante M et al., PMID: 38416430), 700 women with low-risk cervical cancer (lesions ≤2 cm with limited stromal invasion) were randomised to simple or radical hysterectomy, both with lymph-node assessment: pelvic recurrence at 3 years was 2.52% after simple and 2.17% after radical hysterectomy (absolute difference 0.35 percentage points; 90% CI −1.62 to 2.32), inside the prespecified 4-point noninferiority margin. The harm gradient ran the other way: urinary retention beyond 4 weeks in 0.6% versus 9.9%, incontinence beyond 4 weeks in 4.7% versus 11.0%. The trial’s sexual-health and quality-of-life analysis (Ferguson SE et al., PMID: 39353164) favoured simple hysterectomy on desire, arousal, pain, lubrication, sexual-vaginal functioning, body image, and global health status at 36 months. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): de-escalation to simple hysterectomy in strictly low-risk disease, resting on a single trial.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — simple hysterectomy was noninferior for 3-year pelvic recurrence (2.52% versus 2.17%) with substantially less urinary and sexual harm in the single SHAPE randomised trial

title: Minimally invasive radical hysterectomy harms survival: disease-free survival 86.0% versus 96.5% at 4.5 years in LACC, and 4-year mortality 9.1% versus 5.3% in the companion cohort
question: In early-stage cervical cancer, does minimally invasive radical hysterectomy worsen recurrence and survival versus open abdominal radical hysterectomy?
balance: LIKELY (harm) — the randomised trial and the population data point the same way, and the effect is large. In LACC (Ramirez PT et al., PMID: 30380365), 631 women with early-stage cervical cancer were randomised to minimally invasive or open radical hysterectomy: disease-free survival at 4.5 years was 86.0% versus 96.5% (difference −10.6 percentage points; 95% CI −16.4 to −4.7), with a hazard ratio for recurrence or death from cervical cancer of 3.74 (1.63–8.58) and for death from any cause of 6.00 (1.77–20.30). The companion epidemiologic study (Melamed A et al., PMID: 30379613) found 4-year mortality of 9.1% after minimally invasive versus 5.3% after open surgery (hazard ratio 1.65; 1.22–2.22) in 2,461 US women, and a survival decline that began exactly when minimally invasive surgery was adopted. PROPOSED LIKELY (harm): open radical hysterectomy is the safer operation for early-stage cervical cancer.
stamp: LIKELY (harm) — minimally invasive radical hysterectomy lowered disease-free survival (86.0% versus 96.5% at 4.5 years; recurrence hazard ratio 3.74) and overall survival in the LACC randomised trial, corroborated by a national cohort

title: Sentinel-node mapping in endometrial cancer: sensitivity 97.2% and negative predictive value 99.6% in FIRES, with a 97% per-patient negative predictive value in SENTI-ENDO
question: In women with apparent early-stage endometrial cancer, does sentinel-lymph-node mapping stage the cancer as accurately as full lymphadenectomy?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for staging accuracy, from two prospective diagnostic cohorts checked against the full dissection they would replace. In FIRES (Rossi EC et al., PMID: 28159465), 340 women with clinical stage 1 endometrial cancer had indocyanine-green sentinel-node mapping followed by complete pelvic lymphadenectomy: of 36 node-positive patients with successful mapping, the sentinel node caught 35 — sensitivity 97.2% (95% CI 85.0–100) and negative predictive value 99.6% (97.9–100). In SENTI-ENDO (Ballester M et al., PMID: 21489874), dual-label mapping in 111 women gave a per-patient negative predictive value of 97% (91–99) and sensitivity of 84% (62–95), with all three false negatives in type 2 cancers; ultrastaging found metastases conventional histology missed in 47% of node-positive patients. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): mapping stages accurately enough to spare most women a full lymphadenectomy, on prospective cohort — not randomised — evidence.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — sentinel-node mapping detected node-positive disease with 97.2% sensitivity and 99.6% negative predictive value in FIRES, corroborated by SENTI-ENDO, in prospective diagnostic cohorts

title: Chemotherapy first in advanced ovarian cancer: survival noninferior in two trials (hazard ratios 0.98 and 0.87) — with far fewer postoperative deaths and severe complications
question: In advanced ovarian cancer, does neoadjuvant chemotherapy with interval debulking give survival as good as primary debulking surgery, with less perioperative morbidity?
balance: SPLIT — survival is a draw in both randomised trials; the perioperative harm is not. In EORTC 55971 (Vergote I et al., PMID: 20818904), the hazard ratio for death with neoadjuvant chemotherapy and interval debulking versus primary surgery was 0.98 (90% CI 0.84–1.13; P=0.01 for noninferiority), and residual tumour ≤1 cm was achieved in 80.6% after interval versus 41.6% after primary debulking. In CHORUS (Kehoe S et al., PMID: 26002111), median overall survival was 24.1 versus 22.6 months (hazard ratio 0.87; 95% CI 0.72–1.05), while grade 3–4 postoperative adverse events occurred in 14% versus 24% and deaths within 28 days of surgery in under 1% versus 6%. In both trials, complete resection of all macroscopic disease — whenever achieved — was the strongest predictor of survival. PROPOSED SPLIT: chemotherapy-first is a legitimate, gentler route to the same survival in bulky stage IIIC/IV disease, not a better one.
stamp: SPLIT — overall survival noninferior with neoadjuvant chemotherapy in two randomised trials (hazard ratios 0.98 and 0.87), while postoperative severe adverse events (14% versus 24%) and 28-day surgical deaths (under 1% versus 6% in CHORUS) favoured chemotherapy first

title: Lenvatinib versus sorafenib in unresectable liver cancer: survival noninferior (13.6 versus 12.3 months) — different toxicities, and slower deterioration of fatigue, pain and diarrhoea
question: In unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma, is lenvatinib non-inferior to sorafenib for overall survival as first-line therapy, and how do toxicity and quality of life compare?
balance: SPLIT — survival is statistically a tie, the side-effect profiles are genuinely different, and patient-reported deterioration comes later on some symptom scales with lenvatinib. In REFLECT (Kudo M et al., PMID: 29433850), median overall survival was 13.6 months on lenvatinib versus 12.3 months on sorafenib (hazard ratio 0.92; 95% CI 0.79–1.06), meeting the 1.08 noninferiority margin. The commonest adverse events diverged by drug: hypertension 42%, diarrhoea 39%, decreased appetite 34% and weight loss 31% on lenvatinib, versus hand–foot syndrome 52%, diarrhoea 46%, hypertension 30% and decreased appetite 27% on sorafenib. The trial’s patient-reported-outcomes analysis (Vogel A et al., PMID: 34087115) found nominally significant delays in definitive deterioration with lenvatinib for fatigue (hazard ratio 0.83), pain (0.80) and diarrhoea (0.52), but not for global health status (0.89). PROPOSED SPLIT: an equal-survival choice between two different toxicity and quality-of-life profiles, from a single trial.
stamp: SPLIT — overall survival noninferior for lenvatinib (13.6 versus 12.3 months; HR 0.92) in the single REFLECT trial, with a different toxicity profile and delayed deterioration in fatigue, pain and diarrhoea scores

title: NALIRIFOX in metastatic pancreatic cancer: survival 11.1 versus 9.2 months (hazard ratio 0.83) — a real but modest gain, with grade ≥3 adverse events in 87%
question: In metastatic pancreatic cancer, does NALIRIFOX improve overall survival versus gemcitabine plus nab-paclitaxel as first-line therapy?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a statistically real survival gain of about two months in the median, at full chemotherapy cost. In NAPOLI-3 (Wainberg ZA et al., PMID: 37708904), 770 patients with metastatic pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma were randomised to NALIRIFOX or nab-paclitaxel plus gemcitabine: median overall survival was 11.1 versus 9.2 months (hazard ratio 0.83; 95% CI 0.70–0.99; p=0.036). Grade 3 or higher treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 87% on NALIRIFOX and 86% on the comparator, with treatment-related deaths in 2% of each group. A pooled individual-patient-data meta-analysis (Nichetti F et al., PMID: 38190183) places the result in context: NALIRIFOX and FOLFIRINOX produced near-identical survival (11.1 versus 11.7 months; hazard ratio 1.06), both ahead of gemcitabine–nab-paclitaxel — so NAPOLI-3 establishes a new reference regimen, not a uniquely effective one. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): first-line NALIRIFOX extends survival versus gemcitabine–nab-paclitaxel, on a single phase 3 trial.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — NALIRIFOX improved median overall survival to 11.1 versus 9.2 months (HR 0.83) in the single NAPOLI-3 phase 3 trial, a mortality benefit claim resting on one trial

title: BTK-inhibitor regimens beat chemoimmunotherapy in untreated CLL: 3-year progression-free survival 89.4% versus 72.9% in E1912 and 42-month 74.6% versus 24.8% in GLOW
question: In previously untreated chronic lymphocytic leukaemia, do BTK-inhibitor-based regimens improve progression-free survival versus chemoimmunotherapy, and in whom?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — two phase 3 trials in two different age-and-fitness populations, both decisively positive. In E1912 (Shanafelt TD et al., PMID: 31365801), patients aged 70 or younger received ibrutinib–rituximab or fludarabine–cyclophosphamide–rituximab: progression-free survival at 3 years was 89.4% versus 72.9% (hazard ratio 0.35; 95% CI 0.22–0.56), and overall survival at 3 years was 98.8% versus 91.5% (hazard ratio 0.17; 0.05–0.54) at a planned interim analysis, with grade ≥3 infections in 10.5% versus 20.3%. In GLOW (Niemann CU et al., PMID: 37944541), older or comorbid patients received fixed-duration ibrutinib–venetoclax or chlorambucil–obinutuzumab: at 46 months the progression-free-survival hazard ratio was 0.214 (0.138–0.334), with 42-month rates of 74.6% versus 24.8%, and 15 versus 30 deaths. The benefit in E1912 was clearest without IGHV mutation (90.7% vs 62.5% at 3 years); with mutated IGHV the 3-year rates were nearly identical (87.7% vs 88.0%). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): BTK-based first-line therapy is superior to chemoimmunotherapy for progression-free survival across both populations.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — BTK-inhibitor regimens improved progression-free survival versus chemoimmunotherapy in two phase 3 trials (HR 0.35 in E1912; HR 0.214 in GLOW), with an interim overall-survival advantage in E1912

title: Bendamustine–rituximab over R-CHOP in indolent lymphoma: progression-free survival 69.5 versus 31.2 months in StiL, complete response noninferior in BRIGHT — with less alopecia, neuropathy and infection
question: In indolent non-Hodgkin lymphoma, does bendamustine plus rituximab improve progression-free survival versus R-CHOP as first-line therapy, with less toxicity?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — a large progression-free-survival advantage and a kinder toxicity profile in one trial, response noninferiority in the other. In StiL NHL1-2003 (Rummel MJ et al., PMID: 23433739), median progression-free survival was 69.5 months on bendamustine–rituximab versus 31.2 months on R-CHOP (hazard ratio 0.58; 95% CI 0.44–0.74; p<0.0001), with haematological toxicity in 30% versus 68%, infections in 37% versus 50%, peripheral neuropathy in 7% versus 29%, and alopecia in 0% versus 100% of patients receiving at least three cycles. In BRIGHT (Flinn IW et al., PMID: 24591201), complete response was 31% on bendamustine–rituximab versus 25% on R-CHOP/R-CVP (noninferiority met), with overall response 97% versus 91% (P=.0102). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): bendamustine–rituximab is at least as effective as R-CHOP-class therapy first-line in indolent lymphoma, with a longer progression-free survival in StiL and fewer of the toxicities patients notice most.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — bendamustine–rituximab prolonged progression-free survival versus R-CHOP (69.5 versus 31.2 months; HR 0.58) in StiL and was noninferior for complete response in BRIGHT, with less alopecia, neuropathy, and haematological toxicity

title: Adding daratumumab to VRd in transplant-eligible myeloma: 48-month progression-free survival 84.3% versus 67.7% in PERSEUS, MRD negativity 51.0% versus 20.4% in GRIFFIN
question: In transplant-eligible newly diagnosed multiple myeloma, does adding daratumumab to VRd induction and consolidation improve progression-free survival versus VRd alone?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — a large phase 3 trial and a randomised phase 2 trial agree that the four-drug regimen deepens responses and delays progression. In PERSEUS (Sonneveld P et al., PMID: 38084760), 709 transplant-eligible patients received daratumumab plus VRd or VRd alone, both with lenalidomide maintenance: estimated progression-free survival at 48 months was 84.3% versus 67.7% (hazard ratio for progression or death 0.42; 95% CI 0.30–0.59; P<0.001), complete response or better in 87.9% versus 70.1%, and MRD-negative status in 75.2% versus 47.5%; deaths numbered 34 versus 44. In GRIFFIN (Voorhees PM et al., PMID: 32325490), stringent complete response after consolidation was 42.4% versus 32.0%, deepening with follow-up (62.6% vs 45.4%), with MRD negativity 51.0% versus 20.4% and 24-month progression-free survival 95.8% versus 89.8%. The price is haematological: grade 3–4 neutropenia 62.1% versus 51.0% in PERSEUS, and serious adverse events 57.0% versus 49.3%. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): daratumumab-VRd is the stronger induction for transplant-eligible patients.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — adding daratumumab to VRd improved 48-month progression-free survival (84.3% versus 67.7%; HR 0.42) in PERSEUS, with deeper responses and MRD negativity corroborated by the randomised GRIFFIN trial
