title: Early transplant in myeloma buys progression-free survival, not life: 67.5 versus 46.2 months in DETERMINATION and 50 versus 36 months in IFM 2009 — overall survival identical in both
question: In newly diagnosed multiple myeloma, does early autologous stem-cell transplantation added to RVd improve progression-free and overall survival versus RVd alone with transplant reserved for relapse?
balance: SPLIT — the same split in two large trials on two continents: transplant first delays progression by roughly a year and a half to two years, and does not extend life. In DETERMINATION (Richardson PG et al., PMID: 35660812), median progression-free survival was 67.5 months with RVd plus transplant versus 46.2 months with RVd alone (hazard ratio for progression or death in the RVd-alone group 1.53; 95% CI 1.23–1.91), while 5-year survival was 80.7% versus 79.2% (hazard ratio for death 1.10; 0.73–1.65), with grade ≥3 treatment-related adverse events in 94.2% versus 78.2%. In IFM 2009 (Attal M et al., PMID: 28379796), median progression-free survival was 50 versus 36 months (adjusted hazard ratio 0.65; P<0.001), complete response 59% versus 48%, MRD undetectable 79% versus 65% — and 4-year overall survival 81% versus 82%. PROPOSED SPLIT: early transplant is a progression-delaying choice with a real toxicity price, not a life-extending one.
stamp: SPLIT — early autologous transplant prolonged progression-free survival in two randomised trials (67.5 versus 46.2 months; 50 versus 36 months) but overall survival did not differ in either (5-year 80.7% versus 79.2%; 4-year 81% versus 82%), with more grade ≥3 toxicity

title: Intensive follow-up after colorectal cancer surgery finds more curable recurrences but saves no lives: 5-year mortality 13.0% versus 14.1% in COLOFOL, deaths 18.2% versus 15.9% in FACS
question: In patients with stage II–III colorectal cancer, does high-frequency follow-up testing (CEA and CT) improve overall survival versus less frequent follow-up?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — to survival, which is what patients are usually told the scans are for. In COLOFOL (Wille-Jørgensen P et al., PMID: 29800179), 2,509 patients with stage II–III colorectal cancer were randomised to CT and CEA testing at 6, 12, 18, 24, and 36 months versus at 12 and 36 months only: 5-year overall mortality was 13.0% versus 14.1% (risk difference 1.1%; 95% CI −1.6 to 3.8; P=.43), colorectal-cancer-specific mortality 10.6% versus 11.4% (P=.52), and recurrence 21.6% versus 19.4% (P=.15). In FACS (Primrose JN et al., PMID: 24430319), intensive CEA, CT, or combined follow-up did triple the rate of curative-intent surgery for recurrence (6.6–8.0% versus 2.3% with minimum follow-up) — yet deaths were 18.2% in the combined intensive groups versus 15.9% with minimum follow-up, not significantly different. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): intensive surveillance detects more treatable recurrences without a demonstrated survival benefit.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — high-frequency CEA/CT follow-up did not reduce 5-year overall or cancer-specific mortality in COLOFOL (13.0% versus 14.1%), and FACS found more curative-intent recurrence surgery but no significant mortality difference

title: Stopping imatinib in deep molecular remission: about half stay treatment-free — 41% in persistent complete molecular remission at 12 months in STIM, 50% molecular relapse-free survival at 24 months in EURO-SKI
question: In chronic-phase chronic myeloid leukaemia with a sustained deep molecular response, can imatinib be stopped safely — how many patients stay in treatment-free remission?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — roughly half of carefully selected patients stay off treatment, relapses come early and are recaptured, and nobody in these studies progressed. In STIM (Mahon FX et al., PMID: 20965785), imatinib was stopped in 100 patients in complete molecular remission for at least 2 years: among 69 patients with at least 12 months of follow-up, 42 (61%) relapsed molecularly — 40 of them within 6 months — leaving a 41% probability (95% CI 29–52) of persistent complete molecular remission at 12 months; every relapsing patient responded to imatinib reintroduction, 26 regaining sustained complete molecular remission. In EURO-SKI (Saussele S et al., PMID: 29735299), 755 evaluable patients stopping any tyrosine kinase inhibitor after at least 3 years of therapy and at least 1 year of deep molecular response had molecular relapse-free survival of 61% (57–64) at 6 months and 50% (46–54) at 24 months, with estimated savings of €22 million and no serious adverse events from stopping. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): discontinuation is a realistic, monitored option for sustained deep responders — about a coin-flip of staying treatment-free.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — about half of patients with sustained deep molecular responses stay in treatment-free remission after stopping (50% at 24 months in EURO-SKI; 41% persistent complete molecular remission at 12 months in STIM), with relapses recaptured on restarting, in prospective non-randomised studies

title: Adjuvant capecitabine after biliary tract cancer resection: median survival 51.1 versus 36.4 months — but the primary intention-to-treat analysis missed significance (p=0.097)
question: After resection of biliary tract cancer, does adjuvant capecitabine improve overall survival versus observation?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a clinically large survival difference whose primary analysis fell just short of significance, with every prespecified sensitivity analysis pointing the same way. In BILCAP (Primrose JN et al., PMID: 30922733), 447 patients with resected cholangiocarcinoma or muscle-invasive gallbladder cancer were randomised to eight cycles of capecitabine or observation: median overall survival was 51.1 versus 36.4 months, but the intention-to-treat hazard ratio was 0.81 (95% CI 0.63–1.04; p=0.097); the protocol-specified adjusted sensitivity analysis gave 0.71 (0.55–0.92; p=0.010) and the per-protocol analysis 0.75 (0.58–0.97; p=0.028), with median recurrence-free survival 24.4 versus 17.5 months. The long-term analysis (Bridgewater J et al., PMID: 35316080), at a median follow-up of 106 months, found median survival 49.6 versus 36.1 months with the same pattern (intention-to-treat hazard ratio 0.84, 0.67–1.06; adjusted 0.74, 0.59–0.94). Grade 3 toxicity affected 44% of capecitabine patients, led by hand–foot syndrome in 20%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): adjuvant capecitabine probably extends survival after biliary tract resection — adopted as standard of care on evidence that is suggestive rather than decisive.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — adjuvant capecitabine was associated with longer median survival (51.1 versus 36.4 months) in the single BILCAP trial, but the primary intention-to-treat analysis was not significant (HR 0.81; p=0.097), with adjusted and per-protocol analyses significant

title: Bevacizumab plus capecitabine in older patients with metastatic colorectal cancer: progression-free survival 9.1 versus 5.1 months in AVEX, pooled survival hazard ratio 0.79 in meta-analysis
question: In older or frail patients with advanced colorectal cancer, does capecitabine plus bevacizumab improve progression-free survival versus capecitabine alone?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — progression delayed by four months in the one randomised trial in this population, with a pooled survival signal behind it. In AVEX (Cunningham D et al., PMID: 24028813), 280 patients aged 70 or older (median 76) who were not candidates for oxaliplatin- or irinotecan-based therapy received capecitabine with or without bevacizumab: median progression-free survival was 9.1 versus 5.1 months (hazard ratio 0.53; 95% CI 0.41–0.69; p<0.0001), with grade ≥3 treatment-related adverse events in 40% versus 22% and haemorrhage in 25% versus 7%. A systematic review and meta-analysis of bevacizumab plus fluoropyrimidine monotherapy in unfit or older patients (Pinto C et al., PMID: 27687553) pooled 782 patients and found hazard ratios of 0.52 (0.43–0.64) for progression-free survival and 0.79 (0.64–0.98) for overall survival, with more hypertension, bleeding, thromboembolism, and proteinuria on bevacizumab. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the combination is an effective gentler-intent regimen for older patients, on one randomised trial plus a mixed-design meta-analysis.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — bevacizumab plus capecitabine prolonged progression-free survival versus capecitabine alone in AVEX (9.1 versus 5.1 months; HR 0.53), with a pooled overall-survival HR of 0.79 in meta-analysis, at the cost of more grade ≥3 toxicity (40% versus 22%)

title: Maintenance capecitabine–bevacizumab after CAPOX-B induction: time to second progression 11.7 versus 8.5 months — benefit in every mutational subgroup, quality of life preserved
question: In metastatic colorectal cancer responding to induction chemotherapy, does maintenance capecitabine plus bevacizumab improve progression-free survival versus observation?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — maintenance delays the endpoint that matters in this design, second progression after re-induction, in the one phase 3 trial that tested it. In CAIRO3 (Simkens LH et al., PMID: 25862517), 558 patients with metastatic colorectal cancer who had stable disease or better after six cycles of CAPOX-B were randomised to maintenance capecitabine plus bevacizumab or observation, with CAPOX-B reintroduced at first progression in both groups: median time to second progression (PFS2) was 11.7 months on maintenance versus 8.5 months on observation (hazard ratio 0.67; 95% CI 0.56–0.81; p<0.0001), hand–foot syndrome occurred in 23% during maintenance, and global quality of life did not deteriorate or differ between groups. The updated analysis (Goey KKH et al., PMID: 28911067), at a median follow-up of 87 months, found the PFS2 benefit in every molecular subgroup — hazard ratios 0.57 in RAS/BRAF wild-type, 0.74 in RAS-mutant, and 0.28 in BRAF-mutant tumours. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): maintenance capecitabine–bevacizumab after CAPOX-B induction, resting on a single trial.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — maintenance capecitabine plus bevacizumab improved time to second progression versus observation (11.7 versus 8.5 months; HR 0.67) in the single CAIRO3 phase 3 trial, without compromising quality of life

title: Nanoliposomal irinotecan plus fluorouracil after gemcitabine: survival 6.1 versus 4.2 months in NAPOLI-1, maintained at final analysis (6.2 versus 4.2) — the liposomal drug alone did nothing
question: In metastatic pancreatic cancer progressing on gemcitabine-based therapy, does nanoliposomal irinotecan plus fluorouracil improve overall survival versus fluorouracil alone?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a two-month median survival gain in a disease with almost no second-line options, from a single trial whose internal control arm usefully isolates the active ingredient. In NAPOLI-1 (Wang-Gillam A et al., PMID: 26615328), 417 patients with metastatic pancreatic cancer previously treated with gemcitabine-based therapy were randomised to nanoliposomal irinotecan plus fluorouracil and folinic acid, nanoliposomal irinotecan alone, or fluorouracil and folinic acid: median overall survival was 6.1 months on the combination versus 4.2 months on fluorouracil alone (hazard ratio 0.67; 95% CI 0.49–0.92; p=0.012), while the monotherapy arm did no better than control (4.9 versus 4.2 months; hazard ratio 0.99). The final analysis (Wang-Gillam A et al., PMID: 30654298) confirmed the combination’s advantage (6.2 versus 4.2 months; hazard ratio 0.75; 0.57–0.99), with estimated 1-year survival of 26% versus 16%. Grade 3–4 neutropenia (27%), diarrhoea (13%), vomiting (11%), and fatigue (14%) were the commonest severe toxicities of the combination. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): nanoliposomal irinotecan plus fluorouracil extends survival after gemcitabine — as a combination, not as a single agent.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — nanoliposomal irinotecan plus fluorouracil improved median overall survival versus fluorouracil alone (6.1 versus 4.2 months; HR 0.67) in the single NAPOLI-1 trial, while the liposomal drug alone did not (HR 0.99)

title: Adding an NK1 antagonist to standard antiemetics in cisplatin chemotherapy: complete response 72.7% versus 52.3% and 62.7% versus 43.3% in two phase 3 trials
question: In patients receiving highly emetogenic chemotherapy, does adding an NK1 receptor antagonist (aprepitant/fosaprepitant) to a 5-HT3 antagonist and dexamethasone improve complete response versus standard dual prophylaxis?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — two large double-blind phase 3 trials, run on different continents, land within a point of each other on a twenty-point absolute gain. In the first (Hesketh PJ et al., PMID: 14559886), patients receiving cisplatin ≥70 mg/m² for the first time had a complete response (no emesis and no rescue therapy, days 1–5) in 72.7% on the aprepitant regimen versus 52.3% on standard ondansetron–dexamethasone (P<.001), with the advantage largest on days 2–5. In the second (Poli-Bigelli S et al., PMID: 12784346), complete response was 62.7% (163/260) versus 43.3% (114/263) (P<0.001), with day-1 rates of 82.8% versus 68.4% and days 2–5 rates of 67.7% versus 46.8%. Tolerability was indistinguishable: overall adverse events 72.8% versus 72.6% in Poli-Bigelli, with similar serious events, discontinuations, and deaths. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): adding aprepitant to a 5-HT3 antagonist plus dexamethasone prevents chemotherapy-induced vomiting in about one extra patient in five receiving high-dose cisplatin.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — adding aprepitant improved complete response (no emesis, no rescue) over days 1–5 in two phase 3 double-blind trials (72.7% versus 52.3%; 62.7% versus 43.3%) with no added tolerability burden

title: Cognitive behavioural therapy for severe post-cancer fatigue: clinically significant improvement in 54% versus 4% on a waiting list — pooled data name CBT the strongest psychosocial strategy
question: In patients with severe cancer-related fatigue during or after chemotherapy, does cognitive behavioural therapy reduce fatigue versus usual care?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a striking result in the one dedicated randomised trial, backed by pooled individual-patient data across the psychosocial literature. In Gielissen’s trial (Gielissen MF et al., PMID: 17050873), 112 disease-free cancer survivors with somatically unexplained severe fatigue received CBT designed for fatigue or waited: fatigue severity fell 13.3 points more (95% CI 8.6–18.1) and functional impairment 383.2 points more (197.1–569.2) with CBT, and clinically significant improvement occurred in 54% versus 4% for fatigue and 50% versus 18% for function. The POLARIS individual-patient-data meta-analyses (Abrahams HJG et al., PMID: 33448521), pooling 14 randomised trials in 1,091 women with breast cancer and 1,008 men with prostate cancer, found small overall effects of psychosocial interventions on fatigue (β −0.19 and −0.11), with the largest effects for CBT as the strategy (β −0.27), for fatigue-specific interventions (β −0.48), and for interventions targeting only clinically fatigued patients (β −0.85). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): fatigue-focused CBT reduces severe post-treatment fatigue — the trial evidence is strong in effect size but narrow in provenance.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — fatigue-specific CBT produced clinically significant improvement in 54% versus 4% of severely fatigued survivors in one randomised trial, with CBT the largest-effect strategy in pooled individual-patient-data meta-analyses

title: CBT for insomnia in breast-cancer survivors: benefits maintained to 12 months in Savard 2005 — and professional delivery beat video delivery, remission 71.3% versus 44.3%, in 2014
question: In breast-cancer survivors with insomnia, does cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia improve sleep versus control, and do gains persist?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two randomised trials from the same programme, a decade apart, showing the therapy works in person and still works, less well, by video. In the first (Savard J et al., PMID: 16135475), 57 women with insomnia caused or aggravated by breast cancer received eight weekly group CBT sessions or waited: subjective sleep indices (sleep diary and Insomnia Severity Index) improved significantly, medicated nights fell, depression and anxiety decreased, and global quality of life rose — with effects generally clinically significant and maintained at 3, 6, and 12 months, though polysomnographic results were more equivocal. In the second (Savard J et al., PMID: 25083010), 242 women were randomised to professionally administered CBT-I, video-based CBT-I, or no treatment: both active formats beat no treatment on subjective sleep, but professional delivery was superior on insomnia severity and remission (Insomnia Severity Index <8 in 71.3% versus 44.3%; P<0.005). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): CBT-I improves insomnia in breast-cancer survivors, durably to at least 12 months, with face-to-face delivery the stronger format.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — CBT-I improved subjective sleep in two randomised trials in breast-cancer survivors, with gains maintained to 12 months and higher remission with professional (71.3%) than video-based (44.3%) delivery

title: Acupuncture for chronic pain in cancer survivors: electroacupuncture cut pain by 1.9 points and auricular by 1.6 versus usual care in PEACE — but auricular treatment caused more dropouts
question: In cancer survivors with chronic musculoskeletal pain, do electroacupuncture or auricular acupuncture reduce pain versus usual care?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a well-run three-arm trial with a clinically meaningful margin over usual care, set against a wider literature that is positive but heterogeneous. In PEACE (Mao JJ et al., PMID: 33734288), 360 cancer survivors with chronic musculoskeletal pain received ten weekly sessions of electroacupuncture or auricular acupuncture, or usual care: pain severity on the Brief Pain Inventory fell 1.9 points more with electroacupuncture (97.5% CI 1.4–2.4; P<.001) and 1.6 points more with auricular acupuncture (1.0–2.1; P<.001) than with usual care by week 12; auricular treatment was not shown noninferior to electroacupuncture, and 10.5% of the auricular group versus 0.7% of the electroacupuncture group stopped because of adverse events (P<.001). A systematic review and meta-analysis of acupuncture and acupressure for cancer pain (He Y et al., PMID: 31855257) found real acupuncture beat sham by a mean difference of −1.38 points across seven high-quality sham-controlled trials, with substantial heterogeneity (I²=81%) and a moderate evidence grade. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): acupuncture reduces chronic musculoskeletal pain in cancer survivors versus usual care, on one large trial plus a supportive but heterogeneous meta-analysis.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — electroacupuncture and auricular acupuncture reduced pain versus usual care in the PEACE trial (−1.9 and −1.6 points on the Brief Pain Inventory), corroborated by a sham-controlled meta-analysis (mean difference −1.38) graded moderate quality

title: Gabapentin 900 mg for hot flushes in breast cancer: severity scores fell 49% versus 21% on placebo at 4 weeks — the 300 mg dose failed, and pooled trials show more dizziness and dropouts
question: In women with hot flushes during breast-cancer treatment, does gabapentin reduce hot-flush frequency and scores versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one large, clean, dose-split trial, supported in direction and shadowed on harms by the pooled literature. In the 420-woman trial (Pandya KJ et al., PMID: 16139656), hot-flush severity scores fell by 49% at 4 weeks and 46% at 8 weeks on gabapentin 900 mg/day, versus 21% and 15% on placebo (P=0.0001 and P=0.007 for overall treatment effect), while gabapentin 300 mg/day (33% and 31%) was not significantly different from placebo — only the higher dose worked, on both frequency and severity. The systematic review and meta-analysis of gabapentin for hot flashes (Toulis KA et al., PMID: 19302896) pooled four randomised trials and found greater percentage reductions in frequency (weighted mean difference 23.72%; 95% CI 16.46–30.97) and composite score (27.26%; 21.24–33.29) with gabapentin, but with extreme heterogeneity (I²=97.8% and 95.6%) and more dropouts for adverse events (relative risk 2.09; 1.13–3.85), dizziness or unsteadiness (relative risk 6.94; 3.19–15.13), and fatigue or somnolence (4.78; 2.23–10.25). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): gabapentin 900 mg/day reduces hot flushes in women with breast cancer, at a real cost in dizziness and sedation.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — gabapentin 900 mg/day reduced hot-flush severity scores by 49% versus 21% on placebo in one large randomised trial (the 300 mg dose did not), with pooled data confirming direction but showing more dizziness, somnolence, and dropouts

title: Exercise during androgen deprivation: three randomised trials agree fatigue falls and fitness rises — fat gain is blunted when training starts with treatment, but weight and bone are unmoved
question: In men receiving androgen deprivation therapy for prostate cancer, does structured exercise improve fatigue, body composition and physical function versus usual care?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for fatigue, fitness and body composition, not for weight or bone. Three randomised trials in men on androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) point the same way. Segal RJ et al. (PMID: 12721238) randomised 155 men to 12 weeks of resistance exercise: fatigue interfered less with daily activities (P=.002), quality of life was higher (P=.001) and upper- and lower-body muscular fitness improved, but body composition did not change. Cormie P et al. (PMID: 24467669) started supervised aerobic plus resistance exercise within 10 days of the first ADT injection in 63 men: over 3 months lean mass was preserved (P=.019) and whole-body fat gain was prevented (between-group difference -1.4 kg, P=.001; percentage fat -1.3%, P<.001), with better fatigue scores (difference 3.1, P=.042). Taaffe DR et al. (PMID: 28249801) followed 163 men for 12 months: fatigue fell by about 5 points with impact-loading plus resistance training at 6 and 12 months (p=0.005), with comparable gains from aerobic plus resistance training by 12 months, and the most fatigued men improved most. No trial showed a survival, fracture or falls outcome. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): structured exercise during ADT reduces fatigue and improves fitness and quality of life across three concordant randomised trials, and blunts fat gain when started at ADT initiation; effects on weight, bone and hard outcomes are unshown.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — three concordant randomised trials show less fatigue, better fitness and quality of life, and blunted fat gain when exercise starts with ADT; no hard-outcome data

title: Bioimpedance surveillance with early compression (PREVENT): progression to chronic lymphoedema 7.9% versus 19.2% after a triggered intervention — one trial, reported twice
question: In women at risk after breast-cancer surgery, does prospective bioimpedance surveillance with early compression prevent progression to chronic lymphoedema versus tape-measure surveillance?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — from a single large randomised trial, reported at interim and at final analysis. In PREVENT, women after breast-cancer surgery were randomised to surveillance by bioimpedance spectroscopy (BIS) or tape measurement (TM), with a 4-week compression sleeve and gauntlet triggered by subclinical change. In the final report (Ridner SH et al., PMID: 35099283), 879 women were analysed: BIS triggered intervention less often (20.1% vs 27.5%, p=0.011) and later (median 9.7 vs 3.9 months), and among women who triggered, progression to chronic lymphoedema needing complex decongestive physiotherapy was 7.9% with BIS versus 19.2% with TM (relative risk 0.41; absolute reduction 11.3 percentage points, 95% CI 2.3 to 20.3; p=0.016). The earlier interim analysis (Ridner SH et al., PMID: 31054038) pointed the same way but was not significant for progression (4.9% vs 14.7%, p=0.130). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): BIS-triggered early compression reduced progression to chronic lymphoedema in the one trial that has tested it; the comparison is against tape-measure surveillance with the same compression trigger, not against no surveillance.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one large randomised trial (PREVENT): bioimpedance-triggered early compression cut progression to chronic lymphoedema (7.9% vs 19.2% of triggered patients)

title: Urea cream prevents sorafenib hand–foot skin reactions (any grade 56.0% versus 73.6%) but did not prevent capecitabine hand–foot syndrome (56% versus 62.4%)
question: In patients receiving sorafenib or capecitabine, does prophylactic urea-based cream prevent hand–foot skin reactions versus control?
balance: SPLIT — the answer splits by drug. For sorafenib, one large open-label randomised trial (Ren Z et al., PMID: 25667293) in 871 patients with advanced hepatocellular carcinoma found 10% urea-based cream three times daily cut any-grade hand–foot skin reaction over 12 weeks from 73.6% to 56.0% (odds ratio 0.457, 95% CI 0.344 to 0.608) and grade ≥2 reactions from 29.2% to 20.7% (odds ratio 0.635), delaying first occurrence (median 84 vs 34 days). For capecitabine, a smaller double-blind-era trial (Wongkraisri C et al., PMID: 39962445) in 216 patients found no prevention: any-grade hand–foot syndrome 56% with urea cream versus 62.4% with usual care (p=0.36), grade 3 in 41.1% versus 47.7% (p=0.34), and no delay in onset. PROPOSED SPLIT: prophylactic urea cream reduces sorafenib-associated hand–foot skin reactions in a single open-label trial; it does not prevent capecitabine-associated hand–foot syndrome.
stamp: SPLIT — prevents sorafenib hand–foot skin reactions in one large open-label trial (OR 0.46 for any grade); no prevention of capecitabine hand–foot syndrome (p=0.36)

title: Neutropenic diet does not reduce infections: pooled relative risk 1.02 for major infections across 15 studies and 4,320 patients — with one bacteremia signal in transplant trials
question: In patients receiving chemotherapy or stem-cell transplantation, does a neutropenic diet reduce infection versus a regular/liberalised diet?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — for infection prevention in the populations studied. A 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis (Jamal F et al., PMID: 42721418) pooled 15 comparative studies with 4,320 patients with cancer: the neutropenic diet was not associated with fewer major infections (relative risk 1.02, 95% CI 0.88 to 1.18), bacteremia/fungemia (0.97, 0.78 to 1.22), pneumonia (0.98) or deaths (0.94, 0.77 to 1.15), and results restricted to randomised trials were consistent. An earlier systematic review (Matteucci S et al., PMID: 37513590) found the same null for infection and mortality across 12 studies, with worse quality of life on the restricted diet. One subgroup cuts the other way: in randomised trials limited to haematologic malignancy/HSCT patients (6 studies, 855 patients), the neutropenic diet was associated with lower bacteremia/fungemia (relative risk 0.67, 95% CI 0.47 to 0.95) — hypothesis-generating, not practice-settling. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): routine neutropenic diets do not reduce infections or mortality versus a liberalised diet; a possible bacteremia benefit in prolonged-neutropenia transplant patients is the open exception.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — meta-analysis of 15 studies (4,320 patients): no reduction in major infections (RR 1.02), bacteremia or mortality; HSCT randomised subgroup showed a bacteremia signal (RR 0.67)

title: Erythropoiesis-stimulating agents in cancer: transfusions fall by a third, but on-study mortality rises (HR 1.17) and thromboembolism rises by half (RR 1.52)
question: In chemotherapy-induced anaemia, do erythropoiesis-stimulating agents increase mortality and thromboembolism even as they reduce transfusions?
balance: LIKELY (harm) — on mortality and clots, with a real transfusion benefit on the other side of the scale. Bohlius J et al. (PMID: 19410717) pooled individual data from 53 randomised trials with 13,933 patients with cancer: erythropoiesis-stimulating agents (ESAs) increased mortality during the active study period (combined hazard ratio 1.17, 95% CI 1.06 to 1.30) and worsened overall survival (1.06, 1.00 to 1.12), with little heterogeneity. The updated Cochrane review (Tonia T et al., PMID: 23235597), covering 91 trials and 20,102 participants, found the same mortality signal (hazard ratio 1.17, 95% CI 1.06 to 1.29), more thromboembolic complications (risk ratio 1.52, 95% CI 1.34 to 1.74), and — the benefit — fewer red-cell transfusions (risk ratio 0.65, 95% CI 0.62 to 0.68; on average one unit of blood less per patient). PROPOSED LIKELY (harm): in patients with cancer, ESAs increase deaths during treatment and thromboembolism while reducing transfusion need by about a third; the harm claim is why this shelf is Tier C for the developer's personal review.
stamp: LIKELY (harm) — two concordant meta-analyses (13,933 and 20,102 patients): on-study mortality HR 1.17 and thromboembolism RR 1.52, against a transfusion reduction (RR 0.65)

title: Subcutaneous ketamine for refractory cancer pain: response 31% versus 27% on placebo in the one phase 3 trial — with twice the adverse events and a number-needed-to-harm of 6
question: In refractory cancer pain, does subcutaneous ketamine added to opioids improve pain control versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — in the only adequately sized trial, with harm on the face. Hardy J et al. (PMID: 22965960) randomised 185 patients with chronic uncontrolled cancer pain on opioids and standard co-analgesics to dose-escalated subcutaneous ketamine or placebo over 3 to 5 days: positive responses were 31% (29/93) on ketamine versus 27% (25/92) on placebo (difference 0.04, 95% CI -0.10 to 0.18; P=.55), a number needed to treat of 25, while adverse events worse than baseline occurred at almost twice the rate (incidence rate ratio 1.95, 95% CI 1.46 to 2.61) and the number needed to harm through toxicity-related withdrawal was 6. The Cochrane review (Bell RF et al., PMID: 28657160) found only two other eligible trials (20 and 10 participants, crossover, intrathecal and intravenous routes) and judged the overall evidence very low quality — insufficient to assess benefit or harm for ketamine as an opioid adjuvant in refractory cancer pain generally. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): for subcutaneous dose-escalated ketamine the phase 3 answer is no net benefit; for other routes and regimens the honest answer is that the evidence is too thin to tell. Tier C: a single trial carries the null, and the shelf carries a harm signal.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — one phase 3 trial: response 31% vs 27% (P=.55), adverse events doubled (IRR 1.95), NNH 6; Cochrane rates all other evidence very low quality

title: GnRH agonist during chemotherapy: ovarian failure 8% versus 22% (POEMS) and early menopause 8.9% versus 25.9% (PROMISE) — with 12-year safety data now reassuring
question: In premenopausal women receiving adjuvant chemotherapy for breast cancer, does a GnRH agonist protect ovarian function and future fertility versus chemotherapy alone?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two randomised trials agree on ovarian protection, and the long-term follow-up answers the safety worry. In POEMS (Moore HC et al., PMID: 25738668), 257 premenopausal women with hormone-receptor-negative breast cancer were randomised to chemotherapy with or without goserelin: ovarian failure at 2 years was 8% versus 22% (odds ratio 0.30, 95% CI 0.09 to 0.97; P=.04), and pregnancies occurred in 21% versus 11% (P=.03). In PROMISE-GIM6 (Del Mastro L et al., PMID: 21771987), 281 women randomised to chemotherapy with or without triptorelin had early-menopause rates of 8.9% versus 25.9% at 12 months (absolute difference -17 percentage points; odds ratio 0.28, 95% CI 0.14 to 0.59). At a median 12.4 years (Lambertini M et al., PMID: 34850043), PROMISE showed no difference in disease-free survival (65.7% vs 69.2%; HR 1.16) or overall survival (81.2% vs 81.3%; HR 1.17), including in hormone-receptor-positive disease, with 9 versus 4 post-treatment pregnancies. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a GnRH agonist during chemotherapy roughly halves-to-thirds chemotherapy-induced ovarian failure across two trials, with more pregnancies and no survival penalty at 12 years; POEMS' missing primary-endpoint data keep this at POSSIBLE, not LIKELY.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two concordant randomised trials: ovarian failure 8% vs 22% (OR 0.30) and early menopause 8.9% vs 25.9% (OR 0.28); 12-year survival identical in PROMISE

title: Pilocarpine for radiation dry mouth: salivary flow and global relief improve in two placebo-controlled trials totalling 369 patients — sweating is the price, and 5 mg three times daily was the sweet spot
question: In patients with xerostomia after radiotherapy for head and neck cancer, does pilocarpine improve salivary flow and dry-mouth symptoms versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — old but properly blinded evidence. LeVeque FG et al. (PMID: 8501499) randomised 162 patients with significant xerostomia after at least 40 Gy to dose-titrated oral pilocarpine or placebo for 12 weeks: pilocarpine produced significant improvement in overall global assessment (P=.035), significantly reduced use of oral comfort agents such as artificial saliva (P=.020), improved dryness nearly significantly (P=.057), and significantly increased whole and parotid salivary flow after dosing. The integrated analysis of both placebo-controlled trials (Rieke JW et al., PMID: 7852133; 369 patients) confirmed significant improvements in salivary flow and global condition in both studies, with the fixed-dose study also showing significant gains in dryness, mouth comfort and speaking; adverse effects were those of a cholinergic agonist — sweating commonest — rising with dose, and 5.0 mg three times daily gave the best balance. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): pilocarpine improves salivary flow and gives clinically significant symptomatic relief of postradiation xerostomia, with dose-related cholinergic side effects; the trials are from the pre-IMRT era, which caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two placebo-controlled trials (369 patients pooled): significant gains in salivary flow and global relief; sweating and other cholinergic effects rise with dose

title: Whole-brain radiotherapy for lung-cancer brain metastases (QUARTZ): no survival or quality-of-life gain over supportive care alone — HR 1.06 for death, and more drowsiness, hair loss and nausea
question: In non-small-cell lung cancer with brain metastases and poor prognosis, does whole-brain radiotherapy improve survival or quality of life versus best supportive care alone?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — from the one phase 3 trial that asked. QUARTZ (Mulvenna P et al., PMID: 27604504) randomised 538 patients with brain metastases from non-small-cell lung cancer, unsuitable for resection or stereotactic radiotherapy, to optimal supportive care including dexamethasone with or without whole-brain radiotherapy (20 Gy in five fractions). There was no difference in overall survival (hazard ratio 1.06, 95% CI 0.90 to 1.26), overall quality of life, or dexamethasone use. The primary outcome, quality-adjusted life-years, differed by 4.7 days (46.4 QALY days with WBRT versus 41.7 without; two-sided 90% CI -12.7 to 3.3) — a difference whose confidence interval includes the prespecified 7-day non-inferiority margin, so formal non-inferiority was not cleanly established even though no outcome favoured WBRT. Patients receiving WBRT reported significantly more drowsiness, hair loss, nausea and dry or itchy scalp, with no difference in serious adverse events. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): in this poor-prognosis population WBRT added toxicity without demonstrable survival or quality-of-life benefit. Tier C: a single trial carries the shelf.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — single phase 3 trial (QUARTZ, n=538): survival HR 1.06 (0.90–1.26), no quality-of-life difference, QALY difference 4.7 days with CI crossing the non-inferiority margin

title: Conquer Fear: a structured psychological intervention cuts fear of recurrence versus relaxation control — face-to-face in 2017, and again online in groups in 2023 (effect size 0.47)
question: In cancer survivors with clinically significant fear of recurrence, does a structured psychological intervention (Conquer Fear) reduce fear versus relaxation control?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two randomised trials of the same programme family, eight years and two delivery modes apart. Butow PN et al. (PMID: 29095681) randomised 222 survivors of curable breast or colorectal cancer or melanoma with above-cutoff fear of recurrence to five face-to-face ConquerFear sessions or a relaxation attention control: Fear of Cancer Recurrence Inventory (FCRI) total scores improved significantly more with ConquerFear immediately post-therapy (P<.001), and the advantage was maintained at 3 months (P=.017) and 6 months (P=.018), with parallel gains in cancer-specific distress. Tauber NM et al. (PMID: 37489745) randomised 85 breast-cancer survivors to online group ConquerFear-Group or online group relaxation: fear fell more with the intervention (Cohen's d=0.47, p=0.001; severity d=0.57, p<0.001), with effects stable over 6 months. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): Conquer Fear reduces fear of recurrence versus an active relaxation control in survivors screened for clinically significant fear; effects are moderate and measured on the programme's own target scale.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two randomised trials versus relaxation control: FCRI total improved (P<.001, maintained at 6 months) face-to-face; online group version d=0.47 (p=0.001)

title: GP-led follow-up after breast cancer: recurrence confirmed in 22 versus 21 days (1996) and serious clinical events 3.5% versus 3.7% (2006) — two randomised trials, no safety signal
question: After treatment for early breast cancer, is GP-led follow-up as safe as hospital specialist follow-up for recurrence detection, quality of life and satisfaction?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — on every outcome the trials measured, across a decade of replication. Grunfeld E et al. (PMID: 8811760) randomised 296 women with breast cancer in remission to routine follow-up in general practice or hospital: median time from presentation to hospital confirmation of recurrence was 22 days in the GP group versus 21 days in the hospital group, most recurrences (18/26, 69%) presented as interval events between scheduled visits, and quality-of-life differences were small. Grunfeld E et al. (PMID: 16418496) randomised 968 women with early-stage breast cancer to family-physician or cancer-centre follow-up: recurrence-related serious clinical events occurred in 3.5% versus 3.7% (difference 0.19 percentage points, 95% CI -2.26 to 2.65), recurrences in 11.2% versus 13.2% and deaths in 6.0% versus 6.2%, with no significant differences on any quality-of-life questionnaire. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): GP-led follow-up detected recurrence as promptly and as safely as specialist follow-up in two randomised trials; satisfaction was the question's third limb and the trials' quality-of-life instruments showed no penalty for GP care.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — two randomised trials (n=296 and n=968): time to recurrence confirmation 22 vs 21 days; serious clinical events 3.5% vs 3.7%; quality of life indistinguishable

title: Daily aspirin during vascular-prevention trials: cancers on aspirin metastasised less (HR 0.64) — a post hoc analysis of trials that were never designed to treat cancer
question: Does daily aspirin during randomised trials reduce distant metastasis of incident cancers?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a striking signal from analyses that were not the trials' purpose. Rothwell PM et al. (PMID: 22440947) reviewed every incident cancer arising in five large UK randomised trials of daily aspirin (≥75 mg) versus control for vascular prevention (17,285 participants; 987 new solid cancers over a mean 6.5 years): allocation to aspirin reduced the risk of cancer with distant metastasis (hazard ratio 0.64, 95% CI 0.48 to 0.84, p=0.001), driven by adenocarcinoma (HR 0.54, 0.38 to 0.77) rather than other solid cancers (HR 0.82, 0.53 to 1.28). Aspirin reduced metastasis present at diagnosis (HR 0.69), metastasis appearing later in initially localised cancers (HR 0.45), and fatal adenocarcinoma overall (HR 0.65, 0.53 to 0.82). The companion individual-patient analysis (Rothwell PM et al., PMID: 21144578) found aspirin reduced cancer death across eight trials (odds ratio 0.79, 0.68 to 0.92), with benefit emerging after 5 years and a 20-year risk of death from solid cancer still lower on aspirin (HR 0.80, 0.72 to 0.88). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): daily aspirin taken during these trials was associated with substantially less distant metastasis of incident adenocarcinomas; Tier C, because this is a mortality/metastasis benefit claim resting on post hoc analysis of trials randomised for another purpose — the developer reviews it personally.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — pooled post hoc analyses of vascular-prevention trials: distant metastasis HR 0.64 (adenocarcinoma 0.54); cancer death OR 0.79; no trial randomised patients to treat cancer

title: Barrett's surveillance (BOSS): 2-yearly endoscopy did not improve survival over 12.8 years — deaths 333 versus 356 (HR 0.95), and surveillance cost $115,563 per QALY
question: In people with Barrett's oesophagus without dysplasia, does regular endoscopic surveillance detect earlier cancer and improve survival versus no surveillance?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — on survival, in the first randomised trial of the practice. BOSS (Old O et al., PMID: 40180292) randomised 3,453 patients with Barrett's oesophagus at 109 UK centres to 2-yearly surveillance endoscopy or endoscopy only when symptoms required it, with a minimum of 10 years of follow-up (median 12.8 years). Overall survival did not differ: 333 deaths among 1,733 surveillance patients versus 356 among 1,719 at-need patients (hazard ratio 0.95, 95% CI 0.82 to 1.10). Cancer-specific survival did not differ (108 versus 106 cancer deaths; HR 1.01), nor did time to oesophageal adenocarcinoma diagnosis (40 versus 31 diagnoses; HR 1.32, CI crossing 1) or cancer stage at diagnosis; serious adverse events were similar (0.46% versus 0.41%). The alongside economic evaluation (Deidda M et al., PMID: 40383306) found surveillance cost more ($5,309 versus $3,182) for a negligible QALY gain (8.647 versus 8.629) — $115,563 per QALY gained over a modelled 22.8-year horizon. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): regular 2-yearly surveillance did not improve overall or cancer-specific survival in BOSS and is unlikely to be cost-effective at that interval. Tier C: a single trial carrying a mortality null — for the developer's personal review.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — one very large randomised trial (BOSS, n=3,453, median 12.8 years): overall survival HR 0.95 (0.82–1.10), cancer-specific survival HR 1.01; surveillance cost $115,563/QALY

title: Oxybutynin for hot flushes on androgen deprivation (Alliance A222001): flushes per day fell by 6.89 on 5 mg versus 2.15 on placebo — one small 6-week trial
question: In men receiving androgen-deprivation therapy for prostate cancer who have hot flushes, does oxybutynin reduce flush frequency versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one small, short, well-blinded trial with a clear dose response. Alliance A222001 (Stish BJ et al., PMID: 41587370) randomised 88 men on a stable androgen-deprivation regimen with at least 28 hot flushes per week to oxybutynin 2.5 mg twice daily, oxybutynin 5 mg twice daily, or placebo for 6 weeks; 81 were analysed. Hot flushes per day fell by 2.15 on placebo, 4.77 on 2.5 mg (P=.02) and 6.89 on 5 mg (P<.001) from a baseline average of 10.1 flushes per day; daily hot-flush scores fell by 4.85, 9.94 (P=.07) and 13.95 points (P=.002) respectively. Interference with daily life (HFRDIS) improved by 14.2 points on 2.5 mg (P=.042) and 20.7 points on 5 mg (P<.01) versus 3.1 on placebo. No treatment-related grade 3 or higher adverse events occurred. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): oxybutynin reduces hot-flush frequency and interference in men on ADT over 6 weeks, with a dose gradient favouring 5 mg twice daily; Tier C because a single small trial carries the benefit claim.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single small randomised trial (A222001, n=81 analysed, 6 weeks): hot flushes/day -6.89 on 5 mg twice daily vs -2.15 on placebo (P<.001), dose-responsive

title: Brentuximab vedotin plus AVD in advanced Hodgkin lymphoma (ECHELON-1): 6-year survival 93.9% versus 89.4% on ABVD (HR 0.59) — bought with more neutropenia and neuropathy, less lung toxicity
question: In adults with advanced-stage Hodgkin lymphoma, does brentuximab vedotin plus AVD chemotherapy improve progression-free and overall survival versus ABVD?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — one large phase 3 trial whose survival advantage grew with follow-up. ECHELON-1 randomised 1,334 patients with previously untreated stage III or IV classic Hodgkin lymphoma to brentuximab vedotin plus AVD (A+AVD) or ABVD. At the primary report (Connors JM et al., PMID: 29224502), 2-year modified progression-free survival was 82.1% versus 77.2% (difference 4.9 percentage points; HR 0.77, 95% CI 0.60 to 0.98; P=.04), with interim deaths 28 versus 39. At a median of 73 months (Ansell SM et al., PMID: 35830649), 39 patients on A+AVD and 64 on ABVD had died (HR 0.59, 95% CI 0.40 to 0.88; P=.009); 6-year overall survival was 93.9% versus 89.4%, and progression-free survival HR was 0.68. The costs: neutropenia in 58% versus 45% (febrile neutropenia reduced by primary G-CSF prophylaxis, 11% versus 21% without it in early experience) and peripheral neuropathy in 67% versus 43%, mostly resolving; against that, grade ≥3 pulmonary toxicity was under 1% with A+AVD versus 3% with ABVD, and fewer A+AVD patients needed subsequent therapy or developed second cancers (23 versus 32). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): A+AVD improves progression-free and overall survival over ABVD in advanced Hodgkin lymphoma. Tier C: a mortality benefit resting on a single trial goes to the developer personally.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — single large phase 3 trial (ECHELON-1, n=1,334): overall survival HR 0.59 at 6 years (93.9% vs 89.4%); modified PFS HR 0.77 at 2 years

title: Acalabrutinib versus ibrutinib in relapsed CLL (ELEVATE-RR): identical progression-free survival (38.4 months both arms, HR 1.00) with less atrial fibrillation (9.4% versus 16.0%)
question: In adults with previously treated chronic lymphocytic leukaemia, does acalabrutinib match ibrutinib for progression-free survival with less atrial fibrillation and hypertension?
balance: SPLIT — equal efficacy, unequal tolerability, in the first head-to-head randomised trial of BTK inhibitors. ELEVATE-RR (Byrd JC et al., PMID: 34310172) randomised 533 patients with previously treated CLL harbouring del(17p) or del(11q) to acalabrutinib 100 mg twice daily or ibrutinib 420 mg once daily. At a median follow-up of 40.9 months, acalabrutinib was noninferior for progression-free survival: median 38.4 months in both arms (hazard ratio 1.00, 95% CI 0.79 to 1.27). All-grade atrial fibrillation/flutter was significantly less frequent with acalabrutinib (9.4% versus 16.0%, P=.02), and fewer patients stopped acalabrutinib for adverse events (14.7% versus 21.3%). Grade ≥3 infections were comparable (30.8% versus 30.0%), Richter transformation similar (3.8% versus 4.9%), and median overall survival was not reached in either arm (HR 0.82, 0.59 to 1.15; deaths 23.5% versus 27.5%). PROPOSED SPLIT: acalabrutinib matches ibrutinib on progression-free survival in high-risk relapsed CLL and wins on atrial fibrillation and treatment discontinuation; the trial record does not report the hypertension comparison the question also asks about. Tier C: a single trial carries the shelf.
stamp: SPLIT — noninferior progression-free survival (HR 1.00; median 38.4 months both arms) with significantly less atrial fibrillation (9.4% vs 16.0%) and fewer adverse-event discontinuations (14.7% vs 21.3%)

title: Oral supplements after hip fracture: fewer patients with complications in the pooled trials (RR 0.71) — but no clear effect on mortality, on low- or very-low-quality evidence
question: After hip fracture, do oral nutritional supplements reduce complications and mortality versus routine care?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for complications, not for survival. The Cochrane review of nutritional interventions after hip fracture (Avenell et al., PMID: 27898998; 41 trials, 3,881 participants) found low-quality evidence that oral multinutrient feeds may reduce the number of participants with complications (123/370 versus 157/367; RR 0.71, 95% CI 0.59 to 0.86; 11 trials) but had little effect on mortality (24/486 versus 31/481; RR 0.81, 95% CI 0.49 to 1.32; 15 trials), and very-low-quality evidence of fewer 'unfavourable outcomes' (death or complications; RR 0.67, 95% CI 0.51 to 0.89). A single-blind randomised trial in a rehabilitation ward (Myint et al., PMID: 22685164; 126 patients) points the same way: less BMI loss, a rehabilitation stay shortened by 3.80 days, and significantly fewer infection episodes on supplements, with no difference in albumin change, functional independence, or mobility scores. Vomiting and diarrhoea were not increased in the pooled data (RR 0.99). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): oral supplements after hip fracture probably prevent some complications; a mortality benefit is unproven and the underlying trials are methodologically weak.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — oral multinutrient supplements after hip fracture reduce participants with complications (pooled RR 0.71) with no clear mortality effect, on low-quality evidence

title: Supplements in malnourished COPD: weight up about 1.7 kg and grip and breathing-muscle strength improved in pooled trials — lung function unmoved, quality-of-life results mixed
question: In malnourished patients with COPD, do oral nutritional supplements improve weight, grip strength, and quality of life versus dietary advice alone?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for weight and strength in the malnourished, not for lung function. The Cochrane review (Ferreira et al., PMID: 23235577; 17 trials, 632 participants) found that in undernourished patients supplementation produced significant weight gain (MD 1.65 kg, 95% CI 0.14 to 3.16, as final values; MD 1.73 kg, 95% CI 1.29 to 2.17, as change from baseline), better respiratory-muscle strength (maximal inspiratory pressure MD 5.02 cmH₂O and maximal expiratory pressure MD 12.73 cmH₂O in the malnourished), and a clinically significant pooled St George's Respiratory Questionnaire improvement (MD −6.55, 95% CI −11.7 to −1.41) — while FEV₁ did not change (SMD −0.01). A functional-outcomes meta-analysis (Collins et al., PMID: 23432923; 12 RCTs, 448 patients) agrees on strength: handgrip +1.35 kg (P = 0.05), inspiratory and expiratory muscle strength significantly up, with gains concentrated in patients who gained at least 2 kg; quality of life improved in some trials but could not be pooled. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): in malnourished COPD, supplements buy weight and measurable strength; they do not change the lungs themselves, and the quality-of-life evidence is inconsistent.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — nutritional supplementation in malnourished COPD improves weight (~1.7 kg), grip and respiratory-muscle strength in two concordant meta-analyses, without changing lung function

title: Supplements for undernourished older people at home: a 49-person pilot hinted at fewer hospital admissions — the larger follow-up trial found none (29% versus 32% admitted)
question: In undernourished older people in the community, do oral nutritional supplements reduce complications and hospital admissions versus dietary advice?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — on the only direct community evidence, and with a large caveat: in both trials the supplement was bundled with testosterone, never tested alone against dietary advice. The pilot (Chapman et al., PMID: 19144729) randomised 49 community-dwelling undernourished people over 65 to testosterone, a 475 kcal/day oral supplement, both, or nothing for a year: the combined group had no hospital admissions versus 9 admissions in 13 untreated subjects, and significantly fewer people admitted (0 versus 5, P = 0.03); the supplement-alone arm had 5 admissions in 13 subjects, between the two and not separable at this size. The larger multicentre follow-up (Visvanathan et al., PMID: 27499311) tested the combined package against placebo in 53 undernourished community-dwelling older people for a year and found no difference: 8 of 28 (29%) admitted on treatment versus 8 of 25 (32%) on placebo, with no difference in number or length of hospitalisations (P = 0.842 and P = 0.645) or quality of life. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): the community supplement question has never been cleanly tested alone, and the bundled intervention that was tested failed its confirmatory trial.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the confirmatory community trial of a supplement-containing package found no reduction in hospital admissions (29% vs 32%); the supplement was never tested alone against dietary advice

title: Dietary counselling during head and neck radiotherapy: weight and quality of life held up better than with supplements alone or ad lib eating — counselling was the ingredient that lasted
question: In head and neck cancer patients undergoing radiotherapy, does intensive dietary counselling with oral supplements preserve weight and quality of life versus ad lib advice?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — with counselling, not supplements alone, as the active ingredient. In the three-arm Ravasco trial (PMID: 15920748; 75 head and neck cancer patients referred for radiotherapy), dietary counselling with regular foods and supplements-plus-usual-diet both raised energy and protein intake during radiotherapy while the ad lib group's intake fell significantly; at 3 months only the counselled group maintained intake, and the reduction in grade 1+2 anorexia, nausea/vomiting, xerostomia and dysgeusia was seen in 90% of counselled patients versus 67% on supplements and 51% ad lib (p < .0001), with quality-of-life function scores tracking nutritional intake. Isenring's trial (PMID: 15226773; 60 outpatients receiving radiotherapy to the gastrointestinal or head and neck area) found the same shape: intensive individualised dietitian counselling with supplements as required produced statistically smaller deteriorations in weight (P < 0.001), nutritional status (P = 0.020) and global quality of life (P = 0.009) than usual practice. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): intensive dietary counselling during radiotherapy preserves weight, intake and quality of life; handing over supplements without counselling did not hold its gains at 3 months.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — intensive dietary counselling during head and neck radiotherapy preserves weight, intake and quality of life in two small randomised trials; supplements without counselling did not sustain benefit

title: Feeding to a measured calorie target in the ICU: a pilot's mortality trend (32.3% versus 47.7%) came with longer ventilation — the 417-patient international trial found no difference in infections or death
question: In critically ill patients, does tight calorie control guided by repeated indirect calorimetry reduce infections versus weight-based feeding targets?
balance: SPLIT — the pilot and the multicentre trial point different ways. The single-centre TICACOS pilot (Singer et al., PMID: 21340655; 130 ventilated patients) fed the calorimetry group more (2,086 versus 1,480 kcal/day) and saw a trend to lower hospital mortality (32.3% versus 47.7%, p = 0.058) — but ventilation lasted longer (16.1 versus 10.5 days, p = 0.03) and ICU stay likewise (17.2 versus 11.7 days, p = 0.04), and infections were not its demonstrated win. The multicentre TICACOS International trial (Singer et al., PMID: 32534949; 417 patients, stopped early after 6 years of slow recruitment) targeted 80–100% of measured expenditure and found infection rates, pneumonia, ventilation length, ICU and hospital stay all not different between groups, with mortality numerically lower but not significantly different (21 versus 30 deaths). PROPOSED SPLIT: a single-centre pilot suggested benefit at a morbidity price; the larger international test of the same idea found no significant benefit on infections or mortality.
stamp: SPLIT — pilot trial suggested a mortality trend with longer ventilation; the multicentre calorimetry trial found no significant difference in infections or mortality

title: Feeding while prone: pooled data link it to more vomiting (OR 2.38), more pneumonia (OR 2.11) and more feed interruptions (OR 4.75) — yet a protocolised unit fed more, not less safely, and mortality did not differ
question: In mechanically ventilated patients fed while prone, does enteral nutrition increase vomiting or aspiration versus feeding supine?
balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — to tolerance, not to survival, on mostly observational evidence. A meta-analysis of enteral nutrition during prone ventilation (Pan et al., PMID: 40176759; 5 studies, 319 patients) found prone feeding associated with more vomiting (OR 2.38, 95% CI 1.61 to 3.50), greater gastric residual volume (OR 2.72, 95% CI 1.47 to 5.03), more ventilator-associated pneumonia (OR 2.11, 95% CI 1.12 to 3.96) and far more feeding interruptions (OR 4.75, 95% CI 2.22 to 10.17), with no significant mortality difference (OR 1.11, 95% CI 0.65 to 1.88). The primary studies are less alarming: in a before–after study of a standardised protocol (Reignier et al., PMID: 19709786), patients fed prone with 25-degree head elevation and prophylactic erythromycin received larger volumes (median 1,170 versus 774 mL/day) without increases in residual volume, vomiting, or pneumonia; and in a 19-patient crossover study (van der Voort & Zandstra, PMID: 11511335), gastric residual volumes did not differ between prone and supine periods. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm): feeding prone measurably worsens tolerance markers in pooled data, but protocolised delivery appears to offset much of it, and no mortality penalty has been shown.
stamp: POSSIBLE (harm) — enteral feeding in the prone position is associated with more vomiting, gastric residuals, pneumonia and interruptions in pooled (mostly observational) data, without a mortality difference

title: Higher-calorie refeeding in anorexia nervosa: medical stability restored sooner (HR 1.67) and 4 days saved — with no excess electrolyte harm; in atypical anorexia the same fixed dose underfeeds
question: In adolescents with anorexia nervosa, does higher-calorie refeeding shorten hospital stay without increasing refeeding syndrome versus lower-calorie refeeding?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — from one multicentre trial programme. The StRONG trial (Garber et al., PMID: 33074282; 120 adolescents and young adults aged 12–24 hospitalised with anorexia or atypical anorexia nervosa, 111 in the modified intention-to-treat analysis) compared refeeding beginning at 2,000 kcal/day and advancing 200 kcal/day against 1,400 kcal/day advancing 200 kcal every other day: higher-calorie refeeding restored medical stability significantly earlier (hazard ratio 1.67, 95% CI 1.10 to 2.53, P = .01), electrolyte abnormalities and other adverse events did not differ by group, and hospital stay was 4.0 days shorter (95% CI −6.1 to −1.9), saving $19,056 in charges per participant. The trial's atypical-anorexia analysis (Garber et al., PMID: 38179719) adds the catch: patients with atypical anorexia (≥85% of median BMI) restored heart rate more slowly (8.7 versus 6.5 days), gained less weight, and had more hypomagnesaemia (29% versus 11%, OR 3.29) because the fixed starting dose delivered fewer kcal/kg (32.4 versus 43.4 kcal/kg) — dose per kilogram, not the diagnosis, predicted outcomes. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): starting higher and advancing faster is safe and quicker in hospitalised adolescents — dosed generously enough per kilogram for heavier patients.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — higher-calorie refeeding restored medical stability sooner (HR 1.67) and shortened stay by 4.0 days with no increase in electrolyte events, in a single multicentre trial

title: Devil's claw for chronic low back pain: two small placebo trials (315 people) favoured extracts standardised to 50–100 mg harpagoside — low-quality evidence, short-term only
question: In adults with chronic low back pain, does devil's claw (Harpagophytum procumbens, e.g. the Doloteffin preparation) reduce pain versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — short-term, on low-quality evidence. The Cochrane review of herbal medicine for low back pain (Oltean et al., PMID: 25536022) concluded that daily doses of Harpagophytum procumbens standardised to 50 mg or 100 mg harpagoside may be better than placebo for short-term improvements in pain and may reduce use of rescue medication (two trials, 315 participants, low-quality evidence), with a further trial showing relative equivalence to rofecoxib 12.5 mg/day on very-low-quality evidence. The largest placebo trial (Chrubasik et al., PMID: 10101629; 197 patients with exacerbations of chronic back pain) counted patients pain-free without rescue tramadol in the last treatment week: 3 on placebo, 6 on extract providing 50 mg harpagoside/day, and 10 on 100 mg/day (P = 0.027 for the dose trend) — real, but absolute responder numbers are small. Neither record names the Doloteffin preparation or its maker: the trial extract is identified as WS 1531, and the review by standardised harpagoside dose; current commercial products may differ in safety and effectiveness. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a modest short-term pain benefit is the most the evidence supports.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — devil's claw standardised to 50–100 mg harpagoside/day beat placebo short-term in two small trials (low-quality evidence); responder counts are small in absolute terms

title: Flaxseed and blood pressure: one PAD trial found a striking −10/−7 mmHg — the pooled effect across 15 trials is a tenth of that (−2.85/−2.39 mmHg)
question: In hypertensive patients with peripheral arterial disease, does milled flaxseed (30 g/day in food) lower blood pressure versus placebo?
balance: SPLIT — one remarkable trial, one modest pool. In FLAX-PAD (Rodriguez-Leyva et al., PMID: 24126178), 110 patients with peripheral artery disease ate foods containing 30 g/day of milled flaxseed or placebo for 6 months: systolic pressure was ≈10 mmHg lower and diastolic ≈7 mmHg lower on flaxseed, and patients entering with systolic ≥140 mmHg fell 15 mmHg systolic and 7 mmHg diastolic — described by its authors as one of the most potent antihypertensive effects achieved by a dietary intervention. But the meta-analysis of flaxseed trials (Ursoniu et al., PMID: 26071633; 15 trials, 1,302 participants) found much smaller average effects: systolic −2.85 mmHg (95% CI −5.37 to −0.33) and diastolic −2.39 mmHg (95% CI −3.78 to −0.99), with significant systolic reduction for flaxseed powder specifically (−1.81 mmHg) but not for oil or lignan extract. PROPOSED SPLIT: in the PAD population asked about, the single dedicated trial is strongly positive; across hypertensive populations generally, expect a small average effect — the FLAX-PAD number should not be quoted as the typical result.
stamp: SPLIT — the single PAD trial found ≈10/7 mmHg reductions, but the 15-trial pooled effect of flaxseed on blood pressure is only ≈2.9/2.4 mmHg

title: Olive leaf extract (EFLA 943) for blood pressure: it matched captopril in one trial (−11.5 versus −13.7 mmHg systolic) — but no placebo-controlled trial exists, and the only other human study was open-label in 40 twins
question: In adults with mild hypertension, does the olive leaf extract EFLA 943 (Benolea) lower blood pressure versus placebo — and how did it compare with captopril in a head-to-head trial?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — the placebo question has never been tested. The head-to-head trial (Susalit et al., PMID: 21036583) randomised patients with stage-1 hypertension to olive leaf extract EFLA 943, 500 mg twice daily, or captopril 12.5 mg twice daily titrated to 25 mg, for 8 weeks: systolic pressure fell −11.5 ± 8.5 mmHg on the extract and −13.7 ± 7.6 mmHg on captopril, diastolic −4.8 ± 5.5 versus −6.4 ± 5.2, with no significant difference between groups — but with no placebo arm, the trial cannot show the extract beats doing nothing, since stage-1 pressures commonly fall on trial entry alone. The earlier human study (Perrinjaquet-Moccetti et al., PMID: 18729245) was an open study in 40 borderline-hypertensive monozygotic twins: blood pressure was unchanged in the lifestyle-advice controls and the 500 mg/day group, and fell significantly only at 1,000 mg/day (137 ± 10/80 ± 10 to 126 ± 9/76 ± 6 mmHg). Neither record names a manufacturer; both test the extract identified as EFLA 943. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): a real pharmacological signal is plausible, but 'similar to captopril in an unblinded-by-design comparison without placebo' is not evidence of efficacy.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — EFLA 943 matched captopril's reductions in one active-comparator trial, but there is no placebo-controlled trial and the supporting twin study was open-label

title: Skipping the antibiotic in uncomplicated UTI: uva-ursi did nothing for symptoms or antibiotic use — ibuprofen advice cut antibiotic use in one trial, but as a replacement treatment it cured fewer women and caused 7 cases of pyelonephritis
question: In women with uncomplicated urinary tract infection, does uva-ursi extract combined with ibuprofen reduce antibiotic use without worsening symptoms versus usual antibiotic-first care?
balance: SPLIT — the herb failed; the painkiller strategy trades antibiotics for a small, real risk. In the ATAFUTI factorial trial (Moore et al., PMID: 30685500; 382 women with suspected uncomplicated UTI, all given a back-up antibiotic prescription), uva-ursi extract did not improve frequency symptoms versus placebo (−0.06, 95% CI −0.33 to 0.21, p = 0.661) and did not significantly reduce antibiotic consumption (39.9% versus 47.4%; OR 0.59, 95% CI 0.22 to 1.58, p = 0.293); ibuprofen advice likewise did not improve symptoms (−0.01, p = 0.951) but did reduce antibiotic use (34.9% versus 51.0%; OR 0.27, 95% CI 0.10 to 0.72, p = 0.009 — one less antibiotic user for every seven women advised), with no upper-tract infections recorded. The companion evidence is colder: when ibuprofen was tested as a replacement for an antibiotic (Vik et al., PMID: 29763434; 383 women), only 38.7% felt cured by day 4 versus 73.6% on pivmecillinam, and 7 cases of pyelonephritis occurred, all on ibuprofen (number needed to harm 26), though 53% of the ibuprofen group recovered without antibiotics. PROPOSED SPLIT: uva-ursi — no effect; ibuprofen with a safety-net prescription — fewer antibiotics, slower relief, and a pyelonephritis risk that the back-up prescription exists to catch.
stamp: SPLIT — uva-ursi showed no benefit on symptoms or antibiotic use; ibuprofen strategies reduce antibiotic consumption but cure fewer women and carry a pyelonephritis risk (7 cases in one trial)

title: Curcumin to keep ulcerative colitis quiet: relapse 4.65% versus 20.51% over 6 months in one 89-patient trial — never replicated, and the benefit faded after stopping
question: In adults with ulcerative colitis in remission, does curcumin maintenance therapy reduce relapse versus placebo on top of standard aminosalicylates?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — from a single small trial, unreplicated in this role. Hanai and colleagues (PMID: 17101300) randomised 89 patients with quiescent ulcerative colitis to curcumin 1 g twice daily or placebo, each on top of sulfasalazine or mesalamine, for 6 months: among completers, 2 of 43 patients (4.65%) relapsed on curcumin versus 8 of 39 (20.51%) on placebo (P = .040), with the intention-to-treat comparison also significant (P = .049), and curcumin improved both the clinical activity index (P = .038) and the endoscopic index (P = .0001). In the 6 months after treatment stopped — both groups on aminosalicylates alone — 8 more curcumin-group patients and 6 more placebo-group patients relapsed, eroding the separation. The record names no curcumin product or manufacturer, so no branded preparation can claim this result. (Curcumin for inducing remission in active colitis is a different question, answered on its own shelf from a different trial; it is not carded here.) PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a promising maintenance signal that one 89-patient trial cannot carry further than POSSIBLE.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — curcumin 2 g/day halved-to-quartered 6-month relapse in a single 89-patient maintenance trial (4.65% vs 20.51%); unreplicated and the effect faded after stopping

title: Liquorice raises blood pressure and lowers potassium, dose-dependently: pooled systolic +5.45 mmHg, diastolic +3.19 mmHg, potassium −0.33 mmol/L at ≥100 mg glycyrrhizic acid a day
question: Does regular liquorice (glycyrrhizin) consumption raise blood pressure and lower potassium in a dose-dependent way?
balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — a consistent, dose-related physiological effect in feeding studies, sitting on top of a case-report literature of severe events. The systematic review and meta-analysis (Penninkilampi et al., PMID: 28660884) pooled 18 studies (337 participants) of products providing at least 100 mg of glycyrrhizic acid daily: chronic ingestion raised mean systolic blood pressure by 5.45 mmHg (95% CI 3.51 to 7.39) and diastolic by 3.19 mmHg (95% CI 0.10 to 6.29), and lowered plasma potassium by 0.33 mmol/L, plasma renin activity by 0.82 ng/mL per hour, and plasma aldosterone by 173.24 pmol/L — the hormonal signature of apparent mineralocorticoid excess. Daily glycyrrhizic acid dose correlated with the systolic (r² = 0.55) and diastolic (r² = 0.65) rises, supporting the dose-dependence this question asks about. The authors note the effect appears even at modest doses and matters most for people with existing cardiovascular disease; the review's background records case reports of severe adverse events including deaths after chronic liquorice ingestion. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm): regular liquorice at these doses measurably raises pressure and lowers potassium — a food with a drug-like effect, not a benign sweet.
stamp: POSSIBLE (harm) — chronic liquorice ingestion (≥100 mg glycyrrhizic acid/day) raised systolic pressure 5.45 mmHg and lowered potassium 0.33 mmol/L in pooled studies, with a dose–response relationship

title: Black seed oil in asthma: control scores improved modestly in one 4-week trial (ACT 21.1 versus 19.6) and eosinophils fell — lung function did not significantly change
question: In adults with asthma, does Nigella sativa (black seed) supplementation improve asthma control and lung function versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for symptom control scores, from one small short trial. Koshak and colleagues (PMID: 28093815) randomised 80 asthmatic patients to Nigella sativa oil capsules 500 mg twice daily or placebo for 4 weeks as supplementary treatment (60 patients completed; ten withdrew from each group): the Asthma Control Test score was significantly higher on the oil (21.1 ± 2.6 versus 19.6 ± 3.7, p = 0.044), blood eosinophils fell significantly (median change −50 versus +15 cells/µL, p = 0.013), and FEV₁ as percent predicted improved by a median of 4 versus 1 points without reaching significance (p = 0.170). Total serum IgE is listed among the secondary outcomes but no comparative result for it appears in the record. The record names no brand or manufacturer for the oil capsules. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a borderline-significant 1.5-point control-score gain over 4 weeks in 60 completers is a signal worth a larger trial — it is not yet a treatment.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — Nigella sativa oil improved asthma control scores (21.1 vs 19.6, p = 0.044) and eosinophils over 4 weeks in a single 80-patient trial; lung function not significantly improved

title: Ginkgo (EGb 761) as dementia treatment: pooled cognition favoured ginkgo (SMD −0.58) across 9 trials — daily functioning did not reach significance overall, and the trials are heterogeneous
question: In adults with dementia, does the standardised ginkgo biloba extract EGb 761 improve cognition and daily functioning versus placebo as a treatment (as distinct from prevention)?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — modest, heterogeneous, and confined to the standardised extract. The systematic review and meta-analysis (Weinmann et al., PMID: 20236541) pooled nine trials of the standardised extract EGb 761 in Alzheimer's, vascular or mixed dementia (2,372 patients, 12–52 weeks): change scores for cognition favoured ginkgo (SMD −0.58, 95% CI −1.14 to −0.01, p = 0.04), while activities of daily living did not differ significantly overall (SMD −0.32, 95% CI −0.66 to 0.03, p = 0.08); in the Alzheimer subgroup both cognition and daily-living effects were larger and the ADL effect was significant (SMD −0.44, 95% CI −0.77 to −0.12, p = 0.008), with high heterogeneity throughout and no difference in drop-outs or side effects. The largest single trial carded here (Ihl et al., PMID: 22086747; 404 outpatients, 240 mg once daily for 24 weeks) found EGb 761 superior on the SKT cognitive battery (drug–placebo difference 1.7 points in Alzheimer's disease, p < 0.001; 1.4 in vascular dementia, p < 0.05) and on neuropsychiatric symptoms. Neither record names the extract's manufacturer. This shelf is treatment of established dementia only: ginkgo to prevent dementia is a separate question with two large null trials, answered on its own shelf. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): effect sizes are moderate on paper and, as the reviewers note, of difficult-to-determine clinical relevance.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — EGb 761 improved cognition versus placebo in a 9-trial meta-analysis (SMD −0.58) with daily-living benefit significant only in the Alzheimer subgroup; heterogeneity is high

title: American ginseng blunts warfarin: peak INR fell significantly after 2 weeks of ginseng in a placebo-controlled trial — in 20 healthy volunteers, not patients
question: In patients taking warfarin, does American ginseng reduce warfarin's anticoagulant effect (INR) versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — a pharmacokinetic interaction demonstrated under controlled conditions, in the wrong population to size the clinical risk. Yuan and colleagues (PMID: 15238367) randomised 20 healthy volunteers who received warfarin for 3 days in weeks 1 and 4, with American ginseng or placebo given from week 2: after 2 weeks of ginseng, peak INR fell significantly compared with placebo (between-group difference −0.19, 95% CI −0.36 to −0.07, P = 0.0012), and INR area under the curve, peak plasma warfarin level, and warfarin AUC were all significantly reduced, with peak INR correlating positively with peak warfarin level — a coherent exposure-and-effect reduction. The record names no ginseng product or manufacturer. The authors themselves flag the limitation that decides how far this travels: the volunteers were young and healthy and received brief low-intensity warfarin, not therapeutic anticoagulation for atrial fibrillation or a mechanical valve. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm): the interaction is real in the laboratory sense; its size in a patient whose INR must stay between 2 and 3 is unmeasured — which is precisely why the safe advice is to ask about ginseng, as the authors conclude, rather than to assume the effect is trivial.
stamp: POSSIBLE (harm) — American ginseng significantly reduced warfarin exposure and peak INR (−0.19) in a single small placebo-controlled trial in healthy volunteers

title: St John's wort switches on drug-clearing enzymes: it cut indinavir exposure by 57% in volunteers, and the interaction literature runs from transplant rejection to contraceptive failure
question: Can St John's wort preparations cause clinically serious interactions — transplant rejection, contraceptive failure, loss of drug effect — by inducing drug-metabolising enzymes?
balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — the enzyme induction is trial-proven; the catastrophic outcomes rest on case reports, and both halves belong on the shelf. The updated systematic review (Izzo & Ernst, PMID: 19719333) assembled 128 case reports or case series and 80 clinical trials across seven herbs: clinical trials show St John's wort, via cytochrome P450 and/or P-glycoprotein induction, reduces plasma concentrations (or increases clearance) of a long list including ciclosporin, tacrolimus, oral contraceptives, indinavir, irinotecan, imatinib, digoxin, warfarin, simvastatin, atorvastatin, omeprazole and methadone, while case reports link it to transplant-relevant ciclosporin and tacrolimus failures, contraceptive failure, and serotonin-toxicity combinations. The cleanest single demonstration (Piscitelli et al., PMID: 10683007): in healthy volunteers, St John's wort reduced the area under the curve of the HIV protease inhibitor indinavir by a mean of 57% (SD 19) and the extrapolated 8-hour trough by 81% (SD 16) — a loss of exposure the authors warn could produce drug resistance and treatment failure. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm): no other common herbal product has this breadth of documented, mechanism-backed interaction — treat it as an interacting drug, not a benign supplement.
stamp: POSSIBLE (harm) — St John's wort induces CYP/P-glycoprotein and reduces concentrations of many critical drugs in clinical trials (indinavir AUC −57%); rejection and contraceptive-failure reports complete the picture
