title: Passionflower for anxiety: it matched oxazepam over 4 weeks in one 36-patient trial with less job impairment — and cut pre-operative anxiety versus placebo in another; no placebo trial in generalised anxiety exists
question: In adults with generalised anxiety disorder, does passionflower (Passiflora incarnata) extract reduce anxiety versus placebo — and how did it compare with oxazepam in the head-to-head trial?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — two small trials, neither of which is the trial the question really needs. The head-to-head study (Akhondzadeh et al., PMID: 11679026) randomised 36 outpatients with generalised anxiety disorder to Passiflora incarnata extract 45 drops/day or oxazepam 30 mg/day for 4 weeks: both treatments were effective, no significant difference was observed between the protocols at trial end, oxazepam acted faster, and significantly more problems with impairment of job performance occurred on oxazepam. There was no placebo arm, so the trial cannot exclude that both arms simply rode the natural course and expectation effects. The only placebo-controlled anxiety trial carded (Movafegh et al., PMID: 18499602) is a different setting — a single 500 mg oral dose of Passiflora incarnata (the record names the product Passipy, from IranDarouk) before ambulatory surgery in 60 patients — where anxiety scores were significantly lower than placebo (P < 0.001) without sedation or psychomotor impairment. The Akhondzadeh record names no product or manufacturer. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): passionflower is plausibly anxiolytic; for generalised anxiety disorder the evidence is one small active-comparator pilot, exactly as its authors said in calling for a large-scale trial.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — passionflower matched oxazepam in a 36-patient GAD pilot (no placebo arm) and beat placebo for pre-operative anxiety in a 60-patient single-dose trial

title: Fenugreek for type 2 diabetes: a meta-analysis reports HbA1c −1.16% — but the named placebo-controlled trial found fasting and 2-hour glucose no different between groups
question: In adults with type 2 diabetes, does fenugreek seed powder lower fasting glucose and HbA1c versus placebo?
balance: SPLIT — the pooled answer and the checkable trial disagree. The meta-analysis (Gong et al., PMID: 27496582; 10 articles, 12 studies in diabetes and prediabetes) pooled significant reductions with fenugreek: fasting blood glucose −0.84 mmol/L (≈-15 mg/dL) (95% CI −1.38 to −0.31, p = 0.002), 2-hour glucose −1.30 mmol/L (≈-23 mg/dL) (95% CI −1.78 to −0.83, p < 0.0001), HbA1c −1.16 (95% CI −1.23 to −1.09, p < 0.00001) and total cholesterol −0.30 mmol/L (≈-12 mg/dL), while triglycerides, LDL and HDL effects were not significant — with the authors' own caveat that some included studies were of low quality, and the main side effects gastrointestinal discomfort. Yet the double-blind placebo-controlled trial carded here (Gupta et al., PMID: 11868855; 25 newly diagnosed patients, fenugreek seed extract 1 g/day for 2 months) found fasting glucose and 2-hour glucose not different between groups at the end, with benefit confined to glucose and insulin areas under the curve, HOMA insulin-resistance indices, triglycerides and HDL. Neither record names a fenugreek product or manufacturer. PROPOSED SPLIT: small, low-quality pooled trials say fenugreek lowers glucose and HbA1c by amounts that would matter; the individual placebo-controlled evidence is far weaker — do not dose diabetes treatment around it.
stamp: SPLIT — meta-analysis of small trials reports fasting glucose −0.84 mmol/L (≈-15 mg/dL) and HbA1c −1.16, but a placebo-controlled trial found fasting and 2-hour glucose no different between groups

title: Artichoke leaf extract for functional dyspepsia: symptom improvement beat placebo over 6 weeks (8.3 versus 6.7 points) and quality of life improved more — in a single 247-patient trial
question: In adults with functional dyspepsia, does artichoke leaf extract improve dyspeptic symptoms and quality of life versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one well-sized trial, never independently replicated in this record set. Holtmann and colleagues (PMID: 14653829) randomised 247 patients with functional dyspepsia to a commercial artichoke leaf extract preparation (two 320 mg capsules three times daily) or placebo for 6 weeks (244 in the intention-to-treat analysis): the primary outcome — overall change in dyspeptic symptoms on the patient's weekly four-point rating — improved significantly more on the extract (8.3 ± 4.6 versus 6.7 ± 4.8, P < 0.01), as did disease-specific quality of life on the Nepean Dyspepsia Index (−41.1 ± 47.6 versus −24.8 ± 35.6, P < 0.01). The record describes the preparation only as a commercial artichoke leaf extract and names no brand or manufacturer, so no product on sale today can claim this trial. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a statistically solid 1.6-point advantage on the trial's symptom scale over 6 weeks — real, modest, short-term, and resting on a single trial.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — artichoke leaf extract improved dyspepsia symptoms (8.3 vs 6.7, P < 0.01) and quality of life versus placebo over 6 weeks in a single 247-patient trial

title: Pycnogenol for knee osteoarthritis: WOMAC scores fell 56% versus 9.6% in one small trial and symptoms improved in a second — 3 months, small numbers, a branded extract
question: In adults with knee osteoarthritis, does Pycnogenol (French maritime pine bark extract, Horphag Research) reduce pain and improve function versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two small 3-month placebo trials of the same branded extract point the same way. In the SVOS study (Belcaro G et al., PMID: 18386255), 100 mg/day Pycnogenol in 156 patients with osteoarthritis cut the global WOMAC score by 56% versus 9.6% on placebo, and treadmill walking distance rose from 68 m to 198 m versus 65 m to 88 m. In the second trial (Cisár P et al., PMID: 18570266), 150 mg/day in 100 patients with stage I–II knee osteoarthritis significantly improved the WOMAC index (p<0.05) and visual-analogue pain (p<0.04) while placebo had no effect, and analgesic use fell on Pycnogenol but rose on placebo. Both trials tested Pycnogenol, the French maritime pine bark extract of Horphag Research — the specific tested product named in the question — so the shelf vouches for that extract, not for generic pine bark products, which may differ in safety and effectiveness. Neither trial runs beyond 3 months or reports structural joint outcomes. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): short-term symptom relief in two small concordant trials of one branded extract; durability and any effect on the joint itself are unproven.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two small 3-month placebo trials of Pycnogenol (Horphag Research) improved WOMAC symptoms and pain in knee osteoarthritis; no long-term or structural data

title: Micronised purified flavonoid fraction for chronic venous disease: a meta-analysis of 7 trials favours it on most leg symptoms — but the two largest individual trials were null or inconclusive on their main measures
question: In chronic venous insufficiency, does micronised purified flavonoid fraction (diosmin/hesperidin) reduce leg oedema and symptoms compared with placebo?
balance: SPLIT — the pooled evidence and the biggest single trials tell different stories. The meta-analysis of 7 randomised double-blind placebo trials (1,692 patients; Kakkos SK et al., PMID: 29385792) found MPFF (Daflon, Laboratoires Servier) significantly improved nine defined leg symptoms, with categorical risk ratios of 0.53 for leg pain (NNT 4.2), 0.35 for heaviness (NNT 2.0) and 0.39 for feeling of swelling (NNT 3.1), and reduced ankle circumference (standardised mean difference −0.59). But the largest prospective trial (Rabe E et al., PMID: 25972136; 1,137 patients) was inconclusive on its primary oedema measure (water-displacement volumetry, for methodological reasons) and found only a −0.5 cm pain/heaviness difference in a post-hoc symptomatic subgroup, and an earlier 101-patient trial (Danielsson G et al., PMID: 11748952) found no significant symptom benefit at all except night cramps. PROPOSED SPLIT: symptom relief is supported by pooling many small trials; objective oedema reduction rests on much thinner ice, and no trial here addresses ulcers, thrombosis, or long-term disease course.
stamp: SPLIT — meta-analysis of 7 small trials favours MPFF for leg symptoms and ankle circumference, but the largest individual trials were null (symptoms) or inconclusive (oedema) on their primary measures

title: Ashwagandha root extract in novice resistance trainees: bench press up 46.0 kg versus 26.4 kg and testosterone up 96 ng/dL in one 57-man, 8-week trial
question: In resistance-training men, does the ashwagandha root extract KSM-66 increase muscle strength, size, and testosterone versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — on a single small, short trial. In 57 young men (18–50 years) with little resistance-training experience, ashwagandha root extract 300 mg twice daily for 8 weeks (Wankhede S et al., PMID: 26609282) produced greater strength gains than placebo — bench press 46.0 kg versus 26.4 kg (p=0.001), leg extension 14.5 kg versus 9.8 kg (p=0.04) — greater arm and chest muscle-size gains, a larger testosterone rise (96.2 versus 18.0 ng/dL, p=0.004) and a larger fall in body-fat percentage (3.5% versus 1.5%, p=0.03). The question names the KSM-66 extract; the PubMed record itself identifies the intervention only as ashwagandha root extract 300 mg twice daily and names no brand or manufacturer, so this shelf cannot vouch for any specific commercial product — products on sale may differ in safety and effectiveness. Eight weeks in novices, whose strength rises fast on any programme, is the easiest possible test-bed. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a real signal in one small trial; replication in trained men over longer periods does not exist in this record.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one 8-week trial (57 novice trainees) found greater strength, size and testosterone gains on ashwagandha root extract 300 mg twice daily versus placebo

title: Curcumin extract in prediabetes: 0 of the curcumin group developed diabetes in 9 months versus 16.4% on placebo — one 240-person trial, so a delay signal awaiting replication
question: In adults with prediabetes, does a standardised curcumin extract delay progression to type 2 diabetes versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a striking result from exactly one trial. In 240 people with prediabetes randomised to curcumin extract capsules or placebo for 9 months (Chuengsamarn S et al., PMID: 22773702), 16.4% of the placebo group were diagnosed with type 2 diabetes and none of the curcumin group were; beta-cell function was better on curcumin (HOMA-β 61.58 versus 48.72, P<0.01), insulin resistance lower (HOMA-IR 3.22 versus 4.04, P<0.001) and adiponectin higher (22.46 versus 18.45, P<0.05), with very minor adverse effects. In this library's language that is, at most, a delay in the formal diagnosis over 9 months — whether the effect persists, or merely postpones crossing the diagnostic threshold while treatment continues, is untested, and a zero-event arm in a single-centre trial is exactly the kind of result that shrinks on replication. The record identifies the intervention only as curcumin extract capsules and names no brand or manufacturer, so no commercial curcumin product can claim this result; current products may differ in safety and effectiveness. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): one small trial with a zero-event treatment arm — promising, fragile, and unreplicated.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one 9-month trial (240 people with prediabetes) found 0% versus 16.4% progression to diabetes on curcumin extract; a delay signal from a single centre, unreplicated

title: White willow bark for low back pain: pain-free in the last week in 39% on the high salicin dose, 21% on the low dose, 6% on placebo — one 210-patient exacerbation trial
question: In adults with chronic low back pain, does white willow bark extract reduce pain versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a dose-ordered result in one good-sized trial, graded moderate at best by the Cochrane reviewers. In 210 patients with an exacerbation of chronic low back pain (Chrubasik S et al., PMID: 10936472), the proportion pain-free without rescue tramadol for at least 5 days of the final week was 39% on willow bark extract providing 240 mg salicin/day, 21% on 120 mg/day, and 6% on placebo (P<0.001), with significantly more placebo patients needing tramadol in every week; one patient had a severe allergic reaction, perhaps to the extract. The Cochrane review update (Gagnier JJ et al., PMID: 26630428) concluded that Salix alba (white willow bark), like several other herbs, seems to reduce pain more than placebo, but that the evidence was of moderate quality at best and trial reporting was poor. The tested preparation is a standardised extract dosed by salicin content; the records name no brand or manufacturer, so shop products — whose salicin content varies — cannot be assumed equivalent. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): short-term relief of back-pain exacerbations at the 240 mg salicin dose; steady chronic pain, function, and longer use are untested here.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one 210-patient trial found pain-free rates of 39% (240 mg salicin), 21% (120 mg) and 6% (placebo) in back-pain exacerbations; Cochrane grades the willow evidence moderate quality at best

title: SURPASS-4: tirzepatide beat insulin glargine on HbA1c by about 1 percentage point in high-cardiovascular-risk type 2 diabetes — with less hypoglycaemia and no excess of cardiovascular events, in an open-label trial
question: In type 2 diabetes on background metformin-based therapy, does once-weekly tirzepatide lower HbA1c and weight more than once-daily insulin glargine?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one large open-label phase 3 trial. In 1,995 treated patients with type 2 diabetes and established cardiovascular disease or high risk, inadequately controlled on oral agents (Del Prato S et al., PMID: 34672967), HbA1c at 52 weeks fell by 2.43% on tirzepatide 10 mg and 2.58% on 15 mg versus 1.44% on titrated insulin glargine (estimated differences −0.99% and −1.14%). Hypoglycaemia (glucose <54 mg/dL or severe) occurred in 6–9% on tirzepatide versus 19% on glargine. Adjudicated MACE-4 events were not increased on tirzepatide (hazard ratio 0.74, 95% CI 0.51 to 1.08), with 25 deaths (3%) on tirzepatide versus 35 (4%) on glargine — reassuring on safety, but the confidence interval is too wide to claim cardiovascular benefit, and this library does not stamp one from it. Gastrointestinal effects were the price: nausea 12–23%, diarrhoea 13–22% and vomiting 5–9% on tirzepatide versus 2%, 4% and 2% on glargine. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): clearly better glycaemic control than basal insulin with less hypoglycaemia in a single open-label trial; a cardiovascular-outcome benefit is not shown by this record.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — tirzepatide lowered HbA1c ~1 percentage point more than glargine with less hypoglycaemia in one open-label phase 3 trial; MACE hazard ratio 0.74 (0.51–1.08) does not establish cardiovascular benefit

title: SURPASS-1: tirzepatide alone lowered HbA1c by 1.87–2.07% versus +0.04% on placebo in drug-naive type 2 diabetes — and 31–52% reached an HbA1c below 5.7%
question: In drug-naive type 2 diabetes, does once-weekly tirzepatide monotherapy lower HbA1c and weight versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one double-blind placebo trial in early, mild diabetes. In 478 adults whose type 2 diabetes was managed by diet and exercise alone (mean baseline HbA1c 7.9%, mean duration 4.7 years; Rosenstock J et al., PMID: 34186022), 40 weeks of once-weekly tirzepatide lowered HbA1c by 1.87% (5 mg), 1.89% (10 mg) and 2.07% (15 mg) versus a 0.04% rise on placebo (treatment differences −1.91% to −2.11%, all p<0.0001); 87–92% reached HbA1c below 7.0% versus 20%, and 31–52% reached below 5.7% versus 1%. Weight fell dose-dependently by 7.0 to 9.5 kg. Gastrointestinal events were the main cost (nausea 12–18% versus 6%, diarrhoea 12–14% versus 8%), with no clinically significant or severe hypoglycaemia reported on tirzepatide. These are large effects in the easiest population to treat — short-duration diabetes on no medicines — and say nothing about durability beyond 40 weeks or about outcomes. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): potent monotherapy glycaemic and weight effects in a single placebo trial in early diabetes.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — tirzepatide monotherapy lowered HbA1c by ~1.9–2.1 percentage points more than placebo and weight by 7.0–9.5 kg in one 40-week trial in drug-naive patients

title: SURPASS-3: tirzepatide lowered HbA1c more than insulin degludec and weight fell 7.5–12.9 kg while degludec added 2.3 kg — hypoglycaemia 1–2% versus 7%
question: In type 2 diabetes, does once-weekly tirzepatide lower HbA1c more than insulin degludec, and with what weight and hypoglycaemia trade-off?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one large open-label trial against a modern basal insulin. In 1,437 insulin-naive patients on metformin with or without an SGLT2 inhibitor (Ludvik B et al., PMID: 34370970), HbA1c at 52 weeks fell by 1.93% (tirzepatide 5 mg), 2.20% (10 mg) and 2.37% (15 mg) versus 1.34% on titrated insulin degludec (treatment differences −0.59% to −1.04%, p<0.0001 for all doses), and HbA1c below 7.0% was reached by 82–93% versus 61%. The weight contrast was stark: −7.5 kg to −12.9 kg on tirzepatide versus +2.3 kg on degludec. Hypoglycaemia (<54 mg/dL or severe) occurred in 1–2% on tirzepatide versus 7% on degludec. The trade was gastrointestinal: nausea 12–24%, diarrhoea 15–17% and vomiting 6–10% on tirzepatide versus 2%, 4% and 1% on degludec, and treatment discontinuation for adverse events was more common on tirzepatide. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): better glycaemia, large weight advantage and less hypoglycaemia than degludec in a single open-label trial, paid for in gastrointestinal tolerability.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — tirzepatide beat degludec on HbA1c (−0.59% to −1.04%) and weight (−9.8 to −15.2 kg difference) with less hypoglycaemia in one open-label phase 3 trial

title: SURPASS-5: adding tirzepatide to insulin glargine lowered HbA1c by a further 1.24–1.53 percentage points versus placebo and weight fell instead of rising — at the cost of 10–18% discontinuation
question: In type 2 diabetes already on insulin glargine, does adding once-weekly tirzepatide improve HbA1c and weight versus glargine titration alone?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one placebo-controlled add-on trial. In 475 adults inadequately controlled on insulin glargine with or without metformin (mean HbA1c 8.31%; Dahl D et al., PMID: 35133415), adding once-weekly tirzepatide for 40 weeks lowered HbA1c by 2.11% (5 mg), 2.40% (10 mg) and 2.34% (15 mg) versus 0.86% on placebo added to titrated glargine (differences −1.24% to −1.53%, P<0.001), and 85–90% reached HbA1c below 7% versus 34%. Weight moved the 'wrong' way for insulin therapy — in the patient's favour: −5.4 to −8.8 kg on tirzepatide versus +1.6 kg on placebo (differences −7.1 to −10.5 kg). The costs were gastrointestinal (diarrhoea 12–21% versus 10%; nausea 13–18% versus 3%) and persistence: premature discontinuation was 10%, 12% and 18% across the tirzepatide doses versus 3% on placebo. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a large add-on glycaemic and weight effect in a single trial, with tolerability — not efficacy — as the limiting factor.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — adding tirzepatide to glargine improved HbA1c by 1.24–1.53 percentage points and weight by 7.1–10.5 kg versus placebo in one 40-week trial; discontinuation reached 18% at 15 mg

title: SUSTAIN 7: semaglutide beat dulaglutide head-to-head at both dose pairs — HbA1c by an extra 0.40–0.41 points and weight by an extra 2.3–3.6 kg, with gastrointestinal events in 43–44%
question: In type 2 diabetes, how do once-weekly semaglutide and dulaglutide compare head-to-head on HbA1c and weight?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one open-label head-to-head trial, consistent across both dose pairs. In 1,201 patients on metformin alone (Pratley RE et al., PMID: 29397376), at 40 weeks semaglutide 0.5 mg lowered HbA1c by 1.5 points versus 1.1 on dulaglutide 0.75 mg (difference −0.40 points, p<0.0001), and semaglutide 1.0 mg by 1.8 versus 1.4 on dulaglutide 1.5 mg (difference −0.41, p<0.0001). Weight showed the same pattern: −4.6 versus −2.3 kg at the low doses (difference −2.26 kg) and −6.5 versus −3.0 kg at the high doses (difference −3.55 kg), both p<0.0001. Gastrointestinal disorders were the most frequent adverse events, occurring in 43–44% of patients on semaglutide. The comparison is between the doses as marketed at the time — dulaglutide has since been tested at 3.0 and 4.5 mg (AWARD-11, on its own shelf) — so this shelf settles semaglutide versus dulaglutide 0.75/1.5 mg, not versus today's higher dulaglutide doses. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): semaglutide the stronger drug at the compared doses, in a single open-label trial.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — semaglutide lowered HbA1c 0.40–0.41 points more and weight 2.26–3.55 kg more than dulaglutide at matched dose pairs in one open-label head-to-head trial

title: PIONEER 2: oral semaglutide beat empagliflozin on HbA1c at 26 weeks (−1.3% versus −0.9%) — but weight superiority was not confirmed until the 52-week on-treatment analysis
question: In type 2 diabetes on metformin, does once-daily oral semaglutide lower HbA1c as much as empagliflozin 25 mg?
balance: SPLIT — the answer depends on the endpoint and the week. In 822 patients uncontrolled on metformin (Rodbard HW et al., PMID: 31530666), oral semaglutide 14 mg daily beat empagliflozin 25 mg on the primary HbA1c endpoint at 26 weeks: −1.3% versus −0.9% (treatment-policy difference −0.4%, P<0.0001), a gap that persisted at 52 weeks. But the confirmatory weight endpoint failed at 26 weeks — superior weight loss was not confirmed under the treatment-policy estimand — and only at 52 weeks, in the on-treatment (trial-product) estimand, was weight significantly better on oral semaglutide (−4.7 versus −3.8 kg, P=0.0114). Gastrointestinal adverse events were more common with oral semaglutide. So: yes for blood sugar, from 26 weeks onward; for weight, only later and only counting patients who stayed on treatment. Neither arm's cardiovascular-outcome evidence is tested here — empagliflozin's outcome data come from its own outcomes trial, and a glycaemic head-to-head does not transfer them. PROPOSED SPLIT: HbA1c superiority shown; weight superiority estimand- and time-dependent.
stamp: SPLIT — oral semaglutide was superior to empagliflozin for HbA1c at 26 and 52 weeks, but weight superiority was not confirmed at 26 weeks and appeared only in the 52-week on-treatment analysis

title: AWARD-11: escalating dulaglutide from 1.5 mg to 4.5 mg bought an extra 0.24–0.34 points of HbA1c and 1.6 kg of weight — the 3.0 mg step was significant only in the on-treatment analysis
question: In type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled on dulaglutide 1.5 mg, does escalating to 3.0 mg or 4.5 mg lower HbA1c and weight further?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — real but modest gains from a higher dose of the same drug. In 1,842 patients on metformin (mean HbA1c 8.6%; Frias JP et al., PMID: 33397768), dulaglutide 4.5 mg lowered HbA1c at 36 weeks by 1.77% versus 1.54% on 1.5 mg under the treatment-regimen estimand (difference −0.24%, P<0.001) and by 1.87% versus 1.53% on-treatment (difference −0.34%). The 3.0 mg step was superior only on-treatment (difference −0.17%, P=0.003) and not under the treatment-regimen estimand (difference −0.10%, P=0.096). Weight at 4.5 mg fell 4.6 kg versus 3.0 kg (difference −1.6 kg, P<0.001). Nausea rose with dose (13.4%, 15.6%, 16.4% across 1.5, 3.0 and 4.5 mg) and vomiting likewise (5.6%, 8.3%, 9.3%). Note the candidate question frames this as escalation in patients already on 1.5 mg; the trial randomised metformin-treated patients to the three doses in parallel rather than stepping up non-responders, so it answers 'higher dose versus standard dose', not 'rescue after failing 1.5 mg'. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): dose escalation to 4.5 mg gives a small, dose-ordered improvement; whether it beats switching drugs is a different question this trial does not ask.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — dulaglutide 4.5 mg beat 1.5 mg by 0.24–0.34 HbA1c points and 1.6 kg in one trial; the 3.0 mg advantage was significant only on-treatment

title: SUSTAIN 11: once-weekly semaglutide matched and slightly beat three-times-daily insulin aspart on HbA1c (−1.5 versus −1.2 points) — with weight down 4.1 kg instead of up 2.8 kg
question: In type 2 diabetes on basal insulin plus metformin, does adding once-weekly semaglutide control HbA1c as well as adding three-times-daily insulin aspart?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one open-label trial against the burdensome standard. In 1,748 adults on optimised insulin glargine plus metformin whose HbA1c remained 7.5–10.0% (Kellerer M et al., PMID: 35546450), adding once-weekly semaglutide lowered HbA1c over 52 weeks by 1.5 points versus 1.2 points on three-times-daily insulin aspart (difference −0.29 points [95% CI −0.38 to −0.20]; P<0.0001 for non-inferiority). Weight diverged sharply: −4.1 kg on semaglutide versus +2.8 kg on aspart (difference −6.99 kg [−7.41 to −6.57]). Severe hypoglycaemic episodes were few in both groups with no statistically significant difference. Adverse events were more frequent on semaglutide (58.5% versus 52.1%), mostly mild to moderate. The candidate question's framing — control 'as well as' prandial insulin — is answered yes and slightly better, with one weekly injection replacing three daily ones and weight falling instead of rising; what the trial cannot show is whether that holds beyond 52 weeks or in patients whose post-prandial excursions are the dominant problem. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): non-inferior-to-superior glycaemia with a large weight advantage over basal-bolus intensification, in a single open-label trial.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — adding weekly semaglutide beat adding thrice-daily aspart on HbA1c by 0.29 points and on weight by 6.99 kg in one open-label trial, with few severe hypoglycaemic episodes in either arm

title: Linagliptin versus glimepiride in CAROLINA: cardiovascular events tied at 11.8% versus 12.0% over 6.3 years — but hypoglycaemia in 10.6% versus 37.7%, the widest safety gap in the gliptin trials
question: In type 2 diabetes at high cardiovascular risk, does linagliptin cause fewer cardiovascular events or less hypoglycaemia than glimepiride over years of follow-up?
balance: SPLIT — LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for cardiovascular events / LIKELY (benefit) for hypoglycaemia. CAROLINA (Rosenstock J et al., PMID: 31536101) is the only active-comparator cardiovascular outcomes trial of a dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitor: 6,033 adults with relatively early type 2 diabetes and elevated cardiovascular risk were randomised double-blind to linagliptin 5 mg daily or glimepiride 1–4 mg daily on top of usual care, and followed for a median 6.3 years. On the primary composite — cardiovascular death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, or nonfatal stroke — the drugs tied: 356 of 3,023 (11.8%) on linagliptin versus 362 of 3,010 (12.0%) on glimepiride (hazard ratio 0.98, 95.47% CI 0.84–1.14; P<.001 for noninferiority, P=.76 for superiority). On hypoglycaemia they did not tie at all: at least one hypoglycaemic adverse event occurred in 320 (10.6%) on linagliptin versus 1,132 (37.7%) on glimepiride (hazard ratio 0.23, 95% CI 0.21–0.26). Overall adverse events were similar (93.4% versus 94.9%), as was adjudicated-confirmed acute pancreatitis (15 participants, 0.5%, versus 16, 0.5%). So the head-to-head answer splits cleanly: linagliptin buys no cardiovascular advantage over modern glimepiride, and glimepiride is acquitted of excess cardiovascular events in this trial — what linagliptin buys is freedom from most of the hypoglycaemia a sulfonylurea causes. PROPOSED SPLIT: cardiovascular events — the treatment made no difference over 6.3 years; hypoglycaemia — a large, definitive benefit for linagliptin, from a single large trial (Tier C).
stamp: SPLIT — LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for cardiovascular events (11.8% vs 12.0%, HR 0.98) / LIKELY (benefit) for hypoglycaemia (10.6% vs 37.7%, HR 0.23), in one large double-blind active-comparator trial

title: SCORED: sotagliflozin cut the composite of cardiovascular death, heart-failure hospitalisation and urgent heart-failure visits by 26% relative in diabetes with kidney disease — in a trial that changed its primary endpoint and stopped early for lost funding
question: In type 2 diabetes with chronic kidney disease, does sotagliflozin reduce cardiovascular death and heart-failure hospitalisations versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a positive composite with two structural cautions on its face. In 10,584 patients with type 2 diabetes, chronic kidney disease (eGFR 25–60) and cardiovascular risk (Bhatt DL et al., PMID: 33200891), the primary composite — total cardiovascular deaths, heart-failure hospitalisations and urgent heart-failure visits — occurred at 5.6 versus 7.5 events per 100 patient-years on sotagliflozin versus placebo (hazard ratio 0.74 [95% CI 0.63 to 0.88], P<0.001; a 26% relative reduction). But cardiovascular death alone did not fall (2.2 versus 2.4 per 100 patient-years; HR 0.90 [0.73 to 1.12], P=0.35) — the composite is carried by heart-failure events. And the primary endpoint was changed during the trial, which then ended early owing to loss of funding, at a median follow-up of 16 months. Diarrhoea, genital mycotic infections, volume depletion and diabetic ketoacidosis were all more common on sotagliflozin. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: a heart-failure-event benefit in one trial whose endpoint was redefined mid-course; no mortality claim is made.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — sotagliflozin reduced the cardiovascular-death/heart-failure composite (HR 0.74) in one trial, driven by heart-failure events; cardiovascular death alone was unchanged (HR 0.90) and the endpoint was changed mid-trial

title: DARE-19: dapagliflozin did not significantly prevent organ dysfunction or death in hospitalised COVID-19 patients — 11.2% versus 13.8% (HR 0.80, p=0.17) — but was well tolerated
question: In hospitalised patients with COVID-19 and cardiometabolic risk factors, does dapagliflozin prevent organ dysfunction or death?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — a well-run trial that missed both its primary endpoints. In 1,250 patients hospitalised with COVID-19 and at least one cardiometabolic risk factor (hypertension, type 2 diabetes, atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, heart failure or chronic kidney disease), excluding the critically ill at screening (Kosiborod MN et al., PMID: 34302745), organ dysfunction or death occurred in 70 patients (11.2%) on dapagliflozin 10 mg daily for 30 days versus 86 (13.8%) on placebo (HR 0.80 [95% CI 0.58 to 1.10]; p=0.17), and the hierarchical recovery outcome also missed significance (win ratio 1.09 [0.97 to 1.22]; p=0.14). Deaths were 41 (6.6%) versus 54 (8.6%) (HR 0.77 [0.52 to 1.16]) — a point estimate in dapagliflozin's favour whose confidence interval comfortably includes no effect and which this library does not convert into a benefit claim. Serious adverse events were fewer on dapagliflozin (10.6% versus 13.3%), so the honest summary is: safe in this setting, not shown to protect organs or save lives. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): both dual primary outcomes non-significant in a single adequately sized trial.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — dapagliflozin did not significantly reduce organ dysfunction or death (HR 0.80, p=0.17) or improve recovery (win ratio 1.09, p=0.14) in hospitalised COVID-19 patients

title: inTandem3: adding sotagliflozin in type 1 diabetes doubled clean target achievement (28.6% versus 15.2%) — and quintupled ketoacidosis (3.0% versus 0.6%)
question: In type 1 diabetes on insulin, does adding sotagliflozin improve HbA1c and weight — and how much does diabetic ketoacidosis increase?
balance: SPLIT — the benefit and the harm arrive in the same trial, in similar absolute sizes. In 1,402 patients with type 1 diabetes on any insulin regimen (Garg SK et al., PMID: 28899222), adding sotagliflozin 400 mg daily for 24 weeks achieved the composite primary endpoint — HbA1c below 7.0% with no severe hypoglycaemia and no ketoacidosis — in 200 of 699 patients (28.6%) versus 107 of 703 (15.2%) on placebo (P<0.001); HbA1c fell by an extra 0.46 points, weight by an extra 2.98 kg, systolic pressure by 3.5 mmHg and daily bolus insulin by 2.8 units. Severe hypoglycaemia was similar (3.0% versus 2.4%), but diabetic ketoacidosis occurred in 21 patients (3.0%) on sotagliflozin versus 4 (0.6%) on placebo — an absolute excess of about 2.4 points over 24 weeks, against an absolute gain of about 13.4 points in clean target achievement. Whether that trade is worth it is a judgement this shelf presents, not settles: ketoacidosis in type 1 diabetes can be life-threatening and can occur at near-normal glucose. PROPOSED SPLIT: glycaemic and weight benefit shown; a fivefold ketoacidosis rate is the standing price in this population.
stamp: SPLIT — sotagliflozin improved the net glycaemic endpoint (28.6% versus 15.2%) and weight (−2.98 kg) in type 1 diabetes, but ketoacidosis rose from 0.6% to 3.0% over 24 weeks

title: ORIGIN: six years of early insulin glargine in dysglycaemia changed cardiovascular outcomes not at all (HR 1.02) — new diabetes fell borderline-significantly while severe hypoglycaemia tripled
question: In people with dysglycaemia at cardiovascular risk, does early basal insulin glargine prevent cardiovascular events or delay progression to diabetes versus standard care?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — one of the largest and longest nulls in diabetes. In 12,537 people (mean age 63.5 years) with cardiovascular risk factors plus impaired fasting glucose, impaired glucose tolerance or type 2 diabetes, randomised to insulin glargine titrated to fasting glucose at or below 95 mg/dL or standard care and followed a median 6.2 years (Gerstein HC et al., PMID: 22686416), the first coprimary cardiovascular outcome occurred at 2.94 versus 2.85 per 100 person-years (HR 1.02 [95% CI 0.94 to 1.11]; P=0.63) and the expanded coprimary at 5.52 versus 5.28 (HR 1.04 [0.97 to 1.11]; P=0.27). Cancers were identical (HR 1.00). New diabetes among the 1,456 participants without diabetes at baseline was diagnosed in 30% versus 35% about 3 months after therapy stopped (odds ratio 0.80 [0.64 to 1.00]; P=0.05) — a borderline delay signal at the edge of significance, with an association ratio inside this library's 0.5–2.0 zone of clinical uncertainty, bought with severe hypoglycaemia at 1.00 versus 0.31 per 100 person-years and 1.6 kg of weight gain versus 0.5 kg lost. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): normalising fasting glucose with basal insulin for six years neither prevented cardiovascular events nor, convincingly, delayed the onset of diabetes.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — early glargine over 6.2 years was neutral for cardiovascular outcomes (HR 1.02 and 1.04) and cancers (HR 1.00), with more severe hypoglycaemia (1.00 versus 0.31 per 100 person-years)

title: AdDIT: neither quinapril nor atorvastatin changed albumin excretion in adolescents with type 1 diabetes at higher risk — the trial's primary outcome was flat for both drugs
question: In adolescents with type 1 diabetes, do atorvastatin or quinapril slow early kidney or retinal disease versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — a factorial trial that answers its own primary question in the negative for both drugs. From 4,407 screened adolescents with type 1 diabetes aged 10–16, the 1,287 with albumin-to-creatinine ratios in the upper third were identified and 443 randomised in a 2-by-2 factorial design to an ACE inhibitor (quinapril), a statin (atorvastatin), both, or neither, over 2 to 4 years (Marcovecchio ML et al., PMID: 29091568). The primary outcome — change in albumin excretion as the area under the albumin-to-creatinine curve — was not affected by ACE inhibitor therapy, statin therapy, or the combination. The ACE inhibitor arm showed a lower incidence of microalbuminuria (HR 0.57 [95% CI 0.35 to 0.94]), but the authors state that, in the context of the negative primary outcome and the statistical analysis plan, this was not considered significant. The statin did what statins do to lipids (significant reductions in total, LDL and non-HDL cholesterol, triglycerides and the apoB/apoA1 ratio), but neither drug significantly affected carotid intima-media thickness, glomerular filtration rate, other cardiovascular markers, or progression of retinopathy. Adherence was 75% and serious adverse events were similar across groups. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): in adolescents selected for higher albumin excretion, starting these drugs in the teenage years did not move the early kidney measure the trial was built on.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — in AdDIT neither quinapril nor atorvastatin changed the primary albumin-excretion outcome over 2–4 years in adolescents with type 1 diabetes, and neither affected retinopathy progression or GFR

title: COR-Diabetes: naltrexone-bupropion produced −5.0% versus −1.8% weight loss and −0.6% versus −0.1% HbA1c in type 2 diabetes — with nausea in 42.3%
question: In type 2 diabetes with overweight or obesity, does naltrexone-bupropion produce weight loss and HbA1c reduction versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one placebo trial with honest effect sizes and a heavy nausea burden. In 505 overweight or obese patients with type 2 diabetes (mean weight 106 kg, BMI 37, HbA1c 8.0%), all receiving standardised lifestyle intervention (Hollander P et al., PMID: 24144653), 56 weeks of naltrexone sustained-release 32 mg / bupropion sustained-release 360 mg produced weight loss of 5.0% versus 1.8% on placebo (P<0.001); 5% or greater weight loss was achieved by 44.5% versus 18.9%, HbA1c fell by 0.6% versus 0.1% (P<0.001), and HbA1c below 7% was reached by 44.1% versus 26.3%. Triglycerides and HDL cholesterol also improved. The tolerability ledger: nausea 42.3% versus 7.1%, constipation 17.7% versus 7.1%, vomiting 18.3% versus 3.6%; no difference was observed in depression, suicidal ideation or hypoglycaemia. A 3.2-point weight advantage over placebo is real but modest next to the incretin-era trials on neighbouring shelves, and nearly half the treated group felt nauseated. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a genuine but modest weight and glycaemic effect from a single trial, limited by gastrointestinal tolerability.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — naltrexone-bupropion beat placebo on weight (−5.0% versus −1.8%) and HbA1c (−0.6% versus −0.1%) in one 56-week trial, with nausea in 42.3% versus 7.1%

title: SCALE Diabetes: liraglutide 3.0 mg produced 6.0% weight loss versus 2.0% on placebo in type 2 diabetes — and 5%-or-more loss in 54.3% versus 21.4%
question: In type 2 diabetes with obesity, does liraglutide 3.0 mg daily produce weight loss and glycaemic improvement versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one large placebo trial of the obesity dose in diabetes. In 846 adults with overweight or obesity and type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 7.0–10.0% on 0–3 oral agents), all on a 500 kcal/day deficit diet and increased activity (Davies MJ et al., PMID: 26284720), 56 weeks of liraglutide 3.0 mg daily produced weight loss of 6.0% (6.4 kg) versus 2.0% (2.2 kg) on placebo (estimated difference −4.00% [95% CI −5.10% to −2.90%]; P<0.001); the standard 1.8 mg diabetes dose gave 4.7% (difference −2.71%). Weight loss of 5% or more occurred in 54.3% on 3.0 mg versus 21.4% on placebo, and more than 10% in 25.2% versus 6.7%. More gastrointestinal disorders were reported with liraglutide 3.0 mg than with 1.8 mg and placebo; no pancreatitis was reported. The candidate question also asks about glycaemic improvement; the record's abstract reports the weight coprimary endpoints in full but does not give the HbA1c numbers, so this shelf claims the weight result and leaves the glycaemic figures unclaimed rather than importing them from outside the record. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a clear, dose-ordered weight effect in a single trial in type 2 diabetes.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — liraglutide 3.0 mg beat placebo on weight (−6.0% versus −2.0%; ≥5% loss in 54.3% versus 21.4%) in one 56-week trial in type 2 diabetes

title: STEP 2: semaglutide 2.4 mg weekly produced −9.6% weight change versus −3.4% on placebo in type 2 diabetes with overweight or obesity — at least 5% loss in 68.8% versus 28.5%
question: In type 2 diabetes with overweight or obesity, does once-weekly semaglutide 2.4 mg improve HbA1c and weight versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one large placebo trial of the obesity dose in diabetes, with the diabetes penalty visible: weight loss is smaller than in the non-diabetes STEP trials. In 1,210 adults with BMI at least 27 and type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 7–10%), all receiving lifestyle intervention (Davies M et al., PMID: 33667417), 68 weeks of semaglutide 2.4 mg weekly changed bodyweight by −9.6% versus −3.4% on placebo (estimated difference −6.2 percentage points [95% CI −7.3 to −5.2]; p<0.0001), and at least 5% weight loss was achieved by 68.8% versus 28.5% (odds ratio 4.88 [3.58 to 6.64]). A semaglutide 1.0 mg arm (the diabetes dose) was included as a reference. Gastrointestinal adverse events — mostly mild to moderate — occurred in 63.5% on 2.4 mg versus 34.3% on placebo, and overall adverse events in 87.6% versus 76.9%. As with the neighbouring SCALE shelf, the record's abstract quantifies the weight coprimary endpoints but does not print the HbA1c change, so the glycaemic half of the question is left unclaimed here rather than filled in from outside the record. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a large, clinically meaningful weight effect of the 2.4 mg dose in type 2 diabetes, in a single trial.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — semaglutide 2.4 mg beat placebo on weight (−9.6% versus −3.4%; ≥5% loss in 68.8% versus 28.5%) in one 68-week trial in type 2 diabetes, with gastrointestinal events in 63.5% versus 34.3%

title: Tirzepatide in type 2 diabetes with obesity: weight down 12.8–14.7% versus 3.2% on placebo at 72 weeks (SURMOUNT-2) — one trial, gut effects throughout, and the HbA1c figures live on the monotherapy shelf
question: In type 2 diabetes with overweight or obesity, does once-weekly tirzepatide improve weight and HbA1c versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — substantial weight loss in the one large trial that asked the weight question in this population. In SURMOUNT-2 (Garvey WT et al., PMID: 37385275), 938 adults with type 2 diabetes and BMI ≥27 kg/m² lost 12.8% of body weight on tirzepatide 10 mg and 14.7% on 15 mg at 72 weeks, versus 3.2% on placebo (estimated differences −9.6 and −11.6 percentage points, p<0.0001); 79–83% reached at least 5% weight loss versus 32% on placebo. The most frequent adverse events were gastrointestinal — nausea, diarrhoea, and vomiting — mostly mild to moderate, with discontinuation under 5%; serious adverse events occurred in 68 participants (7%) overall. Two honest limits: the record's abstract reports the weight outcomes and does not print the HbA1c change figures, so this shelf does not state them — the glycaemic potency of the same drug is carded on the tirzepatide monotherapy shelf built from SURPASS-1 — and no cardiovascular-outcome result is in this record. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): tirzepatide produces large, dose-ordered weight loss in type 2 diabetes with obesity over 72 weeks; Tier C because a single trial carries the claim.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — tirzepatide 10–15 mg weekly lost 12.8–14.7% of body weight versus 3.2% on placebo at 72 weeks in type 2 diabetes with obesity (SURMOUNT-2, single trial); gastrointestinal effects common

title: Once-monthly maridebart cafraglutide (MariTide): weight down 12.3–16.2% versus 2.5% on placebo at one year in a phase 2 trial — monthly dosing, frequent gut effects, no phase 3 result yet
question: In adults with obesity, does once-monthly maridebart cafraglutide (a GLP-1 agonist / GIP antagonist antibody conjugate) produce weight loss versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one phase 2 dose-ranging trial, large weight effects, no confirmatory trial yet. In 592 participants (Jastreboff AM et al., PMID: 40549887), mean bodyweight change at week 52 in the obesity cohort (n=465) ranged from −12.3% to −16.2% across maridebart cafraglutide regimens versus −2.5% on placebo; in the smaller obesity-with-type-2-diabetes cohort (n=127), weight change ranged from −8.4% to −12.3% versus −1.7% on placebo, and HbA1c changed by −1.2 to −1.6 percentage points versus +0.1 on placebo. Gastrointestinal adverse events were common, though less frequent with dose escalation and a lower starting dose; no unexpected safety signals emerged. The drug is a peptide–antibody conjugate given every 4 weeks (one arm every 8 weeks) — the monthly schedule is its distinguishing claim, and it is unproven beyond this single trial. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): substantial one-year weight loss in a single phase 2 trial; Tier C because one trial, however large the effect, has carried phase 2 obesity drugs astray before.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — once-monthly maridebart cafraglutide lost 12.3–16.2% of body weight versus 2.5% on placebo at 52 weeks in one phase 2 trial; gastrointestinal effects common

title: Teplizumab in newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes: C-peptide preserved at 78 weeks (difference 0.13 pmol/mL) and 95% kept meaningful beta-cell function versus 79% — but insulin dose, HbA1c and time in range did not differ
question: In children and adolescents with newly diagnosed stage 3 type 1 diabetes, does teplizumab preserve stimulated C-peptide versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for the beta-cell marker, not yet for anything a patient can feel. In PROTECT (Ramos EL et al., PMID: 37861217), 328 children and adolescents with newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes received two 12-day courses of intravenous teplizumab or placebo; at week 78, stimulated C-peptide was higher with teplizumab (least-squares mean difference 0.13 pmol/mL, 95% CI 0.09 to 0.17; P<0.001), and 94.9% of teplizumab patients maintained a peak C-peptide of at least 0.2 pmol/mL versus 79.2% on placebo. But the key secondary endpoints — insulin dose needed, HbA1c, time in target range, and clinically important hypoglycaemia — did not differ significantly between groups. Adverse events clustered around administration: headache, gastrointestinal symptoms, rash, lymphopenia, and mild cytokine release syndrome. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a real, single-trial preservation of the C-peptide surrogate whose clinical payoff — less insulin, better control — was not shown in the same trial; Tier C.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two courses of teplizumab preserved stimulated C-peptide at 78 weeks in newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes (PROTECT), with no significant difference in insulin dose, HbA1c, or time in range

title: Golimumab in youth with new-onset type 1 diabetes: C-peptide 0.64 versus 0.43 pmol/mL at 52 weeks, partial remission in 43% versus 7% — one small phase 2 trial, HbA1c unchanged
question: In children and young adults with newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes, does golimumab preserve endogenous insulin production versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a clear C-peptide signal in one small phase 2 trial. In T1GER (Quattrin T et al., PMID: 33207093), 84 children and young adults (ages 6–21) with newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes received subcutaneous golimumab or placebo for 52 weeks. The 4-hour C-peptide AUC at week 52 was 0.64 pmol/mL on golimumab versus 0.43 pmol/mL on placebo (P<0.001); a partial-remission response occurred in 43% versus 7% (difference 36 percentage points, 95% CI 22 to 55), and insulin use was lower with golimumab — while HbA1c, managed treat-to-target in both groups, did not differ. Hypoglycaemic events recorded as adverse events were reported in 23% on golimumab versus 7% on placebo, and anti-drug antibodies developed in 30 participants who received golimumab. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): beta-cell preservation in a single small trial, with the clinical endpoints (HbA1c) equal by design; Tier C.

title: One course of rituximab in new type 1 diabetes: C-peptide decline slowed and HbA1c and insulin dose lower at one year — a partial, temporary preservation in a single phase 2 trial
question: In newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes, does a single course of rituximab preserve C-peptide at one year versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — partial preservation, honestly bounded. In the phase 2 trial (Pescovitz MD et al., PMID: 19940299), 87 patients aged 8–40 with newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes received four rituximab infusions (days 1, 8, 15, 22) or placebo. At one year the C-peptide AUC during a mixed-meal test was significantly higher with rituximab, the rate of C-peptide decline between months 3 and 12 was significantly slower, and the rituximab group had significantly lower HbA1c and insulin dose (the record's abstract reports these as significant without printing the group means). B lymphocytes were depleted but had recovered to 69% of baseline by 12 months — matching the temporary nature of the effect. Adverse events were mostly grade 1–2 infusion reactions after the first dose, with no increase in infections or neutropenia. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): one small trial, a surrogate endpoint, and an effect that wanes as B cells return; Tier C.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single four-dose rituximab course partially preserved C-peptide at 1 year in new-onset type 1 diabetes in one phase 2 trial, with lower HbA1c and insulin dose

title: Imatinib in recent-onset type 1 diabetes: primary endpoint met at 12 months by a whisker (difference 0.095, one-tailed p=0.048) — gone by 24 months, with grade ≥2 adverse events in 71%
question: In adults with recently diagnosed type 1 diabetes, does daily imatinib preserve beta-cell function versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the weakest 'positive' in the new-onset immunotherapy set, and the shelf says so. In the phase 2 trial (Gitelman SE et al., PMID: 34214479), 67 adults aged 18–45 with recent-onset type 1 diabetes received imatinib 400 mg daily or placebo for 26 weeks. The primary endpoint was met: the adjusted difference in 2-hour C-peptide AUC at 12 months was 0.095 (90% CI −0.003 to 0.191; p=0.048 on a one-tailed test) — a confidence interval that touches zero. The effect was not sustained to 24 months. The cost was real: grade 2 or worse adverse events in 71% on imatinib versus 59% on placebo, dose modifications in 38%, and permanent discontinuation for adverse events in 13% versus none on placebo. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a borderline, transient surrogate effect bought with a cancer drug's toxicity profile; Tier C, and a candidate for MAYBE (weak evidence) if the developer reads the one-tailed p-value strictly.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — 26 weeks of imatinib met its 12-month C-peptide endpoint by a one-tailed margin in adults with recent-onset type 1 diabetes, with the effect gone by 24 months and frequent adverse events

title: Screening toddlers for islet autoantibodies (Fr1da): 0.31% found presymptomatic type 1 diabetes and only 2 of 90,632 screened children presented in ketoacidosis — population yield from an observational programme, not a trial
question: Does general-population screening of young children for islet autoantibodies identify presymptomatic type 1 diabetes early enough to prevent ketoacidosis at diagnosis?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the programme finds the children and, in its own follow-up, almost none arrived in ketoacidosis; what it cannot show is the comparison against no screening. In Fr1da (Ziegler AG et al., PMID: 31990315), 90,632 Bavarian children aged 1.75–5.99 years were screened in primary care between 2015 and 2019; 280 (0.31%) had presymptomatic type 1 diabetes (196 stage 1, 17 stage 2, 26 stage 3, 41 unstaged). The 3-year cumulative risk of stage 3 diabetes among those 280 was 24.9%, and only two children had diabetic ketoacidosis. Parental psychological stress scores rose at staging (median PHQ-9 3 vs 2 in mothers of antibody-negative children) and fell back by 12 months. There is no unscreened control group in this record, so the ketoacidosis rate cannot be causally credited to screening from this shelf alone. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): screening demonstrably identifies presymptomatic disease at population scale with very low ketoacidosis in follow-up; Tier C because the evidence is a single observational programme.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — general-population islet-autoantibody screening found presymptomatic type 1 diabetes in 0.31% of 90,632 young children, with diabetic ketoacidosis in only 2 children during follow-up (Fr1da, observational)

title: In youth type 2 diabetes, empagliflozin lowered HbA1c by 0.84 points versus placebo — linagliptin, tested in the same trial, did not (DINAMO)
question: In adolescents with type 2 diabetes, does empagliflozin (with or without linagliptin) improve HbA1c versus placebo?
balance: SPLIT — the two drugs in one trial part company. In DINAMO (Laffel LM et al., PMID: 36738751), 158 young people aged 10–17 with type 2 diabetes were randomised to empagliflozin, linagliptin, or placebo. At 26 weeks the adjusted HbA1c change with pooled empagliflozin was −0.84 percentage points versus placebo (95% CI −1.50 to −0.19; p=0.012), while linagliptin managed −0.34 points (95% CI −0.99 to 0.30; p=0.29) — not significant. Adverse events occurred in 77% on empagliflozin, 71% on linagliptin, and 64% on placebo up to week 26; hypoglycaemia was the commonest event and commoner on active treatment, with no severe hypoglycaemia. PROPOSED SPLIT: empagliflozin POSSIBLE (benefit) on a single trial in a population with almost no licensed options; linagliptin POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) on the same trial's own numbers. Tier C: one trial carries both halves.
stamp: SPLIT — empagliflozin lowered HbA1c by 0.84 points versus placebo at 26 weeks in youth type 2 diabetes (DINAMO); linagliptin did not significantly differ from placebo in the same trial

title: Liraglutide in children and adolescents with type 2 diabetes: HbA1c −1.06 points versus placebo at 26 weeks, widening to −1.30 at 52 — paid for in gastrointestinal adverse events (Ellipse)
question: In children and adolescents with type 2 diabetes, does daily liraglutide improve HbA1c versus placebo on background metformin?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a clean, single-trial result in a population where metformin alone fails half the time. In Ellipse (Tamborlane WV et al., PMID: 31034184), 134 children and adolescents aged 10 to under 17 with type 2 diabetes, all on metformin (with or without basal insulin), received liraglutide up to 1.8 mg daily or placebo. At 26 weeks HbA1c had fallen 0.64 points on liraglutide and risen 0.42 on placebo — an estimated difference of −1.06 points (P<0.001) — and the gap widened to −1.30 points by 52 weeks; fasting glucose moved the same way. Adverse events were reported by similar proportions (84.8% vs 80.9%), but overall and gastrointestinal event rates were higher with liraglutide. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): one well-conducted trial, a surrogate endpoint, a daily injection for teenagers; Tier C.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — liraglutide added to metformin lowered HbA1c by 1.06 points versus placebo at 26 weeks in youth type 2 diabetes (Ellipse), with more gastrointestinal adverse events

title: Youth type 2 diabetes (TODAY): metformin alone failed in 51.7% within four years — adding rosiglitazone cut failure to 38.6%, adding lifestyle did not significantly help
question: In youth-onset type 2 diabetes, how do metformin alone, metformin plus rosiglitazone, and metformin plus lifestyle compare on durable glycaemic control?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for the combination over metformin alone, inside a trial whose headline is how badly youth type 2 diabetes behaves. In TODAY (Zeitler P et al., PMID: 22540912), 699 young people aged 10–17 with recent-onset type 2 diabetes were randomised to metformin alone, metformin plus rosiglitazone, or metformin plus an intensive lifestyle programme, and followed for a mean of 3.86 years. Loss of glycaemic control (HbA1c ≥8% for 6 months or decompensation needing insulin) struck 51.7% on metformin alone, 38.6% on metformin plus rosiglitazone (superior to metformin alone, P=0.006), and 46.6% on metformin plus lifestyle — intermediate and not significantly different from either. Serious adverse events were reported in 19.2% of participants. Rosiglitazone is now little used, so the practical residue is the prognosis: roughly half of youth lose control on metformin within a few years, and lifestyle added to metformin did not significantly change that. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): metformin plus rosiglitazone beat metformin alone on durability in the only large trial of its kind; Tier C.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in youth type 2 diabetes, metformin plus rosiglitazone maintained glycaemic control better than metformin alone (failure 38.6% vs 51.7% over ~3.9 years, TODAY); metformin plus lifestyle was not significantly better

title: Preserving beta cells in early dysglycaemia (RISE): glargine, liraglutide and metformin all improved beta-cell function on treatment — and none of it survived three months off treatment
question: In adults with impaired glucose tolerance or early type 2 diabetes, can glargine-metformin, liraglutide-metformin, or sitagliptin-metformin preserve beta-cell function after treatment withdrawal?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — after withdrawal, which is the only version of the question that matters for 'preservation'. In the RISE Adult Medication Study (RISE Consortium, PMID: 31178434), 267 adults with impaired glucose tolerance (74%) or type 2 diabetes diagnosed within 12 months received 12 months of metformin alone, insulin glargine for 3 months followed by metformin, liraglutide plus metformin, or placebo. On treatment, all three active arms improved HbA1c, weight, and clamp-measured beta-cell responses — most with liraglutide plus metformin. Three months after everything stopped, no treatment group showed any sustained improvement in beta-cell function versus baseline. (The candidate question also names a sitagliptin-metformin arm; that comparison belongs to the RISE paediatric study, not this adult record, and the shelf is built on the adult arms the record reports.) PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): drug-induced beta-cell improvement in early dysglycaemia is a rental, not a purchase — it lasts only while treatment continues; Tier C, single consortium trial.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — in RISE, 12 months of glargine-metformin, liraglutide-metformin, or metformin improved beta-cell function on treatment but none preserved it 3 months after withdrawal

title: Insulin detemir versus NPH in pregnant women with type 1 diabetes: A1C noninferior at 36 weeks (6.27% vs 6.33%), fasting glucose lower, perinatal outcomes alike — one trial, two reports
question: In pregnant women with type 1 diabetes, does insulin detemir achieve glycaemic control and perinatal outcomes comparable to NPH insulin?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — which, for a noninferiority question, is the finding the trial was built to deliver. In the randomised trial (Mathiesen ER et al., PMID: 22851598), 310 pregnant women with type 1 diabetes (or planning pregnancy) received insulin detemir or NPH, both with prandial aspart. A1C at 36 gestational weeks was 6.27% on detemir versus 6.33% on NPH (difference −0.06%, 95% CI −0.21 to 0.08), meeting the 0.4% noninferiority margin; fasting glucose was significantly lower with detemir at 24 weeks (96.8 vs 113.8 mg/dL, P=0.012) and 36 weeks (85.7 vs 97.4 mg/dL, P=0.017), with similar hypoglycaemia rates. The companion perinatal report (Hod M et al., PMID: 23617228) found 128 versus 136 live births, perinatal deaths of two versus one, and malformations in 5.6% versus 5.5% — no perinatal safety signal. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): detemir is a comparable basal insulin in pregnancy on this single trial, with a fasting-glucose edge; Tier C because one trial carries both reports.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — insulin detemir was noninferior to NPH for A1C in pregnancy in type 1 diabetes (6.27% vs 6.33% at 36 weeks), with lower fasting glucose and similar perinatal outcomes in one trial

title: Severely obese adolescents with type 2 diabetes: surgery cohorts' HbA1c fell 6.8%→5.5% over two years while medical cohorts' rose 6.4%→7.8% — a non-randomised comparison, with reoperation in 23%
question: In adolescents with severe obesity and type 2 diabetes, does metabolic surgery produce diabetes remission more often than medical therapy over five years?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — large glycaemic separation, observational design, and a question trimmed to what the record actually covers: two years, not five. Comparing the Teen-LABS surgical cohort with the TODAY medical-therapy cohort (Inge TH et al., PMID: 29532078), mean HbA1c over 2 years fell from 6.8% to 5.5% in 30 surgical adolescents while rising from 6.4% to 7.8% in 63 medically treated adolescents; BMI fell 29% with surgery and rose 3.7% with medical therapy. The surgical price inside the same window: 23% of Teen-LABS participants required a subsequent operation within the 2-year follow-up. This is a secondary analysis comparing two separately enrolled cohorts — not a randomised trial — and baseline ages differed (16.9 vs 15.3 years). The candidate question's five-year frame is not in this record; the five-year Teen-LABS report is already carded on the live adolescent-surgery shelf, so this shelf is anchored on the uncarded head-to-head comparison instead (declared as a swap in the part summary). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): surgery outperformed medical therapy on glycaemia over two years in the only direct comparison, at a real reoperation cost; Tier C — observational evidence throughout.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in severely obese adolescents with type 2 diabetes, metabolic surgery was associated with far better 2-year glycaemic control than medical therapy in a non-randomised cohort comparison (HbA1c 5.5% vs 7.8%), with reoperation in 23%

title: After gestational diabetes, lifestyle and metformin each cut progression to diabetes by about half over the DPP years — and metformin worked in these women as well as lifestyle, unlike in women without prior GDM
question: In women with prior gestational diabetes, do intensive lifestyle or metformin prevent diabetes over ten years compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a prespecified subgroup of a landmark trial, with the ten-year frame softened to what this record shows (the DPP treatment period; the decade-long follow-up is a separate report). Among 350 women with a history of gestational diabetes in the Diabetes Prevention Program (Ratner RE et al., PMID: 18826999), diabetes incidence on placebo ran 71% higher than in parous women without prior GDM at the same glucose levels — this is a genuinely high-risk group. Both intensive lifestyle and metformin reduced incidence by approximately 50% versus placebo in the prior-GDM women; in parous women without GDM the reductions were 49% for lifestyle but only 14% for metformin. So in women after gestational diabetes, metformin performed like lifestyle — the reverse of the pattern in other women. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): lifestyle and metformin each roughly halve progression after GDM on this analysis; Tier C because the shelf rests on a subgroup analysis of one trial, however prespecified and plausible.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in women with prior gestational diabetes in the DPP, intensive lifestyle and metformin each reduced progression to diabetes by ~50% versus placebo (Ratner 2008 subgroup analysis)

title: Intensive insulin therapy in type 1 diabetes (DCCT): retinopathy risk cut 76% in prevention and progression slowed 54%, microalbuminuria cut 39% and neuropathy 60% — at two-to-three times the severe hypoglycaemia, with a cardiovascular dividend 17 years later
question: In type 1 diabetes, does intensive insulin therapy prevent or slow retinopathy, nephropathy, and neuropathy versus conventional therapy over the long term?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — the foundational trial of diabetes care, with its harm printed in the same breath. In the DCCT (Diabetes Control and Complications Trial Research Group, PMID: 8366922), 1,441 patients with type 1 diabetes were randomised to intensive therapy (pump or ≥3 daily injections, frequent monitoring) or conventional therapy (1–2 injections) for a mean of 6.5 years. Intensive therapy reduced the adjusted mean risk of developing retinopathy by 76% (95% CI 62 to 85) in the primary-prevention cohort, slowed retinopathy progression by 54% (39 to 66) in the secondary cohort, and reduced microalbuminuria by 39%, albuminuria by 54%, and clinical neuropathy by 60% — all relative reductions, from a trial where the chief adverse event was a two-to-threefold increase in severe hypoglycaemia. The long echo came from EDIC follow-up (Nathan DM et al., PMID: 16371630): over 17 years, prior intensive treatment reduced any cardiovascular event by 42% and the composite of nonfatal myocardial infarction, stroke, or cardiovascular death by 57%. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): concordant microvascular benefits in the trial itself plus a cardiovascular legacy in follow-up; Tier C is set because the shelf claims a cardiovascular-event benefit, which the developer reviews personally.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — DCCT intensive therapy reduced retinopathy, nephropathy and neuropathy by 39–76% (relative) versus conventional therapy, with 2–3× severe hypoglycaemia, and a 42% relative reduction in cardiovascular events over 17 years of EDIC follow-up

title: Steno-2: intensive multifactorial treatment in type 2 diabetes with microalbuminuria halved cardiovascular events (HR 0.47) — and at 13 years, deaths were 24 versus 40 (HR 0.54) in a single 160-patient trial
question: In type 2 diabetes with microalbuminuria, does intensive multifactorial intervention (glucose, blood pressure, lipids, aspirin) reduce cardiovascular events and mortality versus conventional care?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — striking hazard ratios from one small, open, single-centre trial; the size of the effect is exactly why it needs the caution. In Steno-2 (Gaede P et al., PMID: 12556541), 160 patients with type 2 diabetes and microalbuminuria received target-driven intensive multifactorial therapy or conventional guideline care for a mean of 7.8 years. Intensive therapy lowered the cardiovascular composite (hazard ratio 0.47, 95% CI 0.24 to 0.73) and the risks of nephropathy (HR 0.39), retinopathy (HR 0.42), and autonomic neuropathy (HR 0.37) — relative effects the authors summarise as 'about 50%'. In the follow-up report (Gaede P et al., PMID: 18256393), at 13.3 years 24 intensive-group patients had died versus 40 on conventional therapy (HR 0.54, 95% CI 0.32 to 0.89), with cardiovascular death HR 0.43 and cardiovascular events HR 0.41; progression to end-stage renal disease occurred in 1 versus 6 patients. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a mortality claim from a single 160-patient trial is Tier C by rule, and the stamp stays at POSSIBLE until a larger trial speaks.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — Steno-2's intensive multifactorial intervention reduced cardiovascular events (HR 0.47) and, at 13.3 years, all-cause death (24 vs 40 deaths; HR 0.54) in type 2 diabetes with microalbuminuria — one 160-patient trial

title: Painful diabetic neuropathy (OPTION-DM): all three first-line pathways cut pain from 6.6 to 3.3 and none beat the others — adding the second drug beat staying on one (extra 1.0 versus 0.2 points)
question: In painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy, which first-line pathway — amitriptyline, duloxetine, or pregabalin, alone or combined — gives the best pain relief?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — between pathways; the trial's actionable finding is about combining, not choosing. In OPTION-DM (Tesfaye S et al., PMID: 36007534), 130 patients with diabetic peripheral neuropathic pain (mean daily pain ≥4/10) rotated through three 16-week pathways — amitriptyline supplemented with pregabalin, pregabalin supplemented with amitriptyline, and duloxetine supplemented with pregabalin — with the second drug added at week 6 only if pain remained above 3. Pain fell from a mean 6.6 at baseline to 3.3 at week 16 in all three pathways, with between-pathway differences of −0.1, −0.1, and 0.0 points — none significant. Patients who went on to combination therapy gained a further mean 1.0-point reduction versus 0.2 in those who stayed on monotherapy. Adverse events were the familiar ones, split by pathway: more dizziness with pregabalin-first, nausea with duloxetine-first, dry mouth with amitriptyline-first. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) between the three pathways: start with any first-line drug, and add a second when one is not enough; Tier C, single trial.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — OPTION-DM found the amitriptyline, pregabalin-first and duloxetine pathways equally effective for painful diabetic neuropathy (pain 6.6→3.3 in all), while adding a second drug beat continuing monotherapy

title: After standard-dose failure in diabetic neuropathic pain (COMBO-DN): combining duloxetine with pregabalin was not significantly better than pushing either drug to its maximum dose (pain −2.35 vs −2.16, p=0.370)
question: In painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy inadequately controlled on monotherapy, does combining duloxetine with pregabalin beat high-dose monotherapy?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — on the primary endpoint, with every secondary signal leaning the combination's way and none reaching significance. In COMBO-DN (Tesfaye S et al., PMID: 23732189), patients with diabetic peripheral neuropathic pain who had not responded to 8 weeks of standard-dose duloxetine (60 mg) or pregabalin (300 mg) were randomised to the combination (duloxetine 60 mg + pregabalin 300 mg) or to high-dose monotherapy (duloxetine 120 mg or pregabalin 600 mg). Among 339 patients in the combination/high-dose phase, mean 24-hour pain change was −2.35 on combination versus −2.16 on high-dose monotherapy (P=0.370); 50% response rates were 52.1% versus 39.3% (P=0.068). Both strategies were well tolerated. An exploratory analysis of the initial phase found standard-dose duloxetine superior to standard-dose pregabalin (P<0.001, uncorrected). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): combination and dose-escalation are both reasonable next steps after standard-dose failure; this trial does not crown either; Tier C, single trial.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — in COMBO-DN, duloxetine plus pregabalin was not significantly superior to high-dose monotherapy for diabetic neuropathic pain after standard-dose non-response (primary outcome p=0.370)

title: G-POEM for severe refractory gastroparesis: treatment success 71% versus 22% after sham at 6 months — a 41-patient sham-controlled trial stopped early, strongest in diabetic gastroparesis (89% vs 17%)
question: In diabetic gastroparesis refractory to medical therapy, does gastric peroral endoscopic myotomy (G-POEM) improve symptoms versus a sham procedure?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the first sham-controlled test of G-POEM, positive and small in equal measure. In the trial (Martinek J et al., PMID: 35470243), 41 patients with severe gastroparesis (17 diabetic, 13 postsurgical, 11 idiopathic) were randomised to G-POEM or a sham endoscopic procedure. Treatment success at 6 months (≥50% fall in the Gastroparesis Cardinal Symptom Index) was 71% (95% CI 50 to 86) after G-POEM versus 22% (8 to 47) after sham (p=0.005). In the diabetic subgroup — the population of the candidate question — success was 89% (56 to 98) versus 17% (3 to 57); postsurgical and idiopathic results were weaker and, in the authors' words, 'not entirely conclusive'. Median 4-hour gastric retention fell from 22% to 12% after G-POEM and was unchanged after sham. Twelve sham patients crossed over to G-POEM, 9 (75%) successfully. Enrolment was stopped early at interim analysis, short of the planned 86 patients. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a real sham-controlled effect, from a single small trial stopped early — the classic recipe for an overestimated effect size; Tier C.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — G-POEM beat sham for severe gastroparesis at 6 months (success 71% vs 22%) in one small sham-controlled trial stopped early, with the clearest effect in diabetic gastroparesis

title: Small-particle diet for diabetic gastroparesis: nausea, fullness and bloating all improved significantly in the only randomised diet trial — 56 patients, 20 weeks, symptoms only
question: In diabetic gastroparesis, does a diet of small-particle food improve cardinal symptoms versus a standard diabetic diet?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for symptoms, on one small randomised trial plus a mechanistic meal study. In the only randomised trial of diet in diabetic gastroparesis (Olausson EA et al., PMID: 24419482), 56 insulin-treated patients randomised to a small-particle diet or the standard recommended diabetic diet for 20 weeks had significantly greater reductions in nausea/vomiting (P=0.01), postprandial fullness (P=0.02), bloating (P=0.006) and regurgitation/heartburn (P=0.02), but not abdominal pain, with no difference in body weight or HbA1c. The mechanism is supported by a randomised crossover meal study in 7 patients with type 1 diabetes and gastroparesis (Olausson EA et al., PMID: 18237818): a small-particle solid meal emptied faster (significantly less radioactivity remaining in the stomach at 120 minutes) and produced a smaller, shorter postprandial glucose dip than an identical large-particle meal. Anxiety also fell on the intervention diet, but depression and quality of life did not change in either group. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): grinding food to small particle size is a low-risk dietary change with randomised evidence for the cardinal upper-gut symptoms — but the trial base is one 56-patient, 20-week study, so this is Tier C.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a small-particle diet significantly reduced nausea/vomiting, fullness and bloating versus standard diabetic diet in one 56-patient randomised trial, with faster gastric emptying shown mechanistically

title: Ultra-rapid lispro in type 1 diabetes: HbA1c non-inferior to lispro, 1-hour post-meal excursions 1.55 mmol/L (≈28 mg/dL) lower — at the price of ~14× the injection-site reactions
question: In type 1 diabetes, does ultra-rapid lispro (Lyumjev) improve postprandial glucose and HbA1c versus conventional lispro?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for postprandial glucose, not for HbA1c. In PRONTO-T1D (Klaff L et al., PMID: 32488923), 1,222 adults with type 1 diabetes were randomised to mealtime ultra-rapid lispro (URLi), conventional lispro, or open-label post-meal URLi for 26 weeks. HbA1c change was non-inferior for both URLi arms (treatment difference −0.08% for mealtime, +0.13% for post-meal, versus lispro), but mealtime URLi was superior on the meal-test excursions: −1.55 mmol/L (≈-28 mg/dL) at 1 hour and −1.73 mmol/L (≈-31 mg/dL) at 2 hours (both P<0.001). Hypoglycaemia rates were similar overall, with a 37% lower rate more than 4 hours after meals on mealtime URLi (P=0.013); injection-site reactions were reported by 2.9% on mealtime URLi versus 0.2% on lispro. The 52-week extension (Bue-Valleskey J et al., PMID: 33458803) showed the pattern held: HbA1c 7.47% versus 7.54%, 1-hour post-meal glucose 9.23 versus 10.14 mmol/L (≈166 versus 183 mg/dL) (P<0.001), injection-site reactions 3.3% versus 0.9%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a real but narrow win — flatter post-meal curves at equal HbA1c, from a single trial programme, so Tier C.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — ultra-rapid lispro is non-inferior for HbA1c and superior for 1–2 hour postprandial excursions versus lispro in the single PRONTO-T1D trial programme, with more injection-site reactions

title: Patient self-titration of basal insulin (AT.LANTUS): HbA1c fell 1.22% versus 1.08% with physician-led titration in 4,961 patients — severe hypoglycaemia 1.1% versus 0.9%
question: In type 2 diabetes starting basal insulin, does a simple patient self-titration algorithm achieve control as safely as physician-led titration?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — patients titrating their own glargine did at least as well as physicians, in one very large pragmatic trial. AT.LANTUS (Davies M et al., PMID: 15920040) randomised 4,961 people with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes (72% already on insulin, mean duration 12.3 years) to investigator-led titration or a simple subject-administered algorithm for 24 weeks. HbA1c fell from 8.9% to 7.8% overall, with a significantly greater decrease on self-titration (−1.22% versus −1.08%, P<0.001) and a greater fasting glucose fall (−62 versus −57 mg/dL, P<0.001); self-titrators also ended on a higher mean dose increase (21.6 versus 18.7 IU, P<0.003). Severe hypoglycaemia was uncommon and not significantly different: 1.1% self-titration versus 0.9% investigator-led. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a simple self-titration algorithm is safe and marginally more effective than physician-led titration — a single (though very large) open-label trial, so Tier C.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — patient self-titration of glargine achieved slightly greater HbA1c and fasting-glucose reductions than physician-led titration with no significant difference in severe hypoglycaemia, in one 4,961-patient trial
