title: Liraglutide for antipsychotic-associated prediabetes: normal glucose tolerance in 63.8% versus 16.0% at 16 weeks — but glucose back to baseline a year after stopping
question: In people with prediabetes and glucose intolerance treated with antipsychotics, does liraglutide reverse prediabetes and reduce weight versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — while the drug is taken. In the Larsen trial (Larsen JR et al., PMID: 28601891), 103 patients with schizophrenia-spectrum disorders on clozapine or olanzapine, overweight or obese with prediabetes, were randomised to liraglutide or placebo for 16 weeks. Glucose tolerance improved significantly more on liraglutide (P<0.001): 63.8% of liraglutide-treated participants developed normal glucose tolerance versus 16.0% on placebo (P<0.001; number needed to treat 2), and body weight fell by 5.3 kg more than placebo (−5.3 kg; 95% CI −7.0 to −3.7). The 1-year follow-up after treatment stopped (Svensson CK et al., PMID: 30374965) is the catch: fasting glucose, HbA1c, C-peptide and lipids had all returned to baseline, though a placebo-subtracted weight loss of −3.8 kg (95% CI −7.3 to −0.2, P=0.04) persisted. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): liraglutide reverses antipsychotic-associated prediabetes in about two-thirds of patients during treatment — a single small trial, and the glycaemic benefit does not survive stopping, so Tier C.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — liraglutide restored normal glucose tolerance in 63.8% versus 16.0% and cut weight by 5.3 kg over 16 weeks in one trial in antipsychotic-treated prediabetes; glycaemic gains reversed within a year of stopping

title: KCNJ11 neonatal diabetes: 90% came off insulin onto sulfonylurea tablets, HbA1c 8.1% to 6.4% — and 93% were still tablet-only a decade later
question: In permanent neonatal diabetes due to KCNJ11 mutations, can patients transfer from insulin to oral sulfonylureas with better control?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — one of the clearest pharmacogenetic wins in medicine, though never randomised. In the transfer series (Pearson ER et al., PMID: 16885550), 44 of 49 consecutive patients (90%) with diabetes due to KCNJ11 (Kir6.2) mutations successfully discontinued insulin after switching to sulfonylureas, and glycated haemoglobin improved in every patient who switched, from 8.1% before treatment to 6.4% after 12 weeks (P<0.001), sustained at one year. The 10-year international cohort (Bowman P et al., PMID: 29880308) shows the win lasts: of 81 patients followed a median 10.2 years, 75 (93%) remained on sulfonylurea therapy alone, median HbA1c was 6.4% at most recent follow-up versus 8.1% before transfer, and no severe hypoglycaemia was recorded in 809 patient-years. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): consistent, large, mechanism-anchored cohort evidence — but it is observational, so Tier C, and it applies only to genetically confirmed KCNJ11 neonatal diabetes.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — 90% of patients with KCNJ11 neonatal diabetes transferred from insulin to sulfonylureas with HbA1c 8.1%→6.4%, and 93% remained on tablets alone at 10 years with no severe hypoglycaemia; cohort evidence only

title: HNF1A-MODY and gliclazide: fasting glucose fell 4.7 mmol/L (≈85 mg/dL) on gliclazide versus 0.9 on metformin — a 5.2-fold sensitivity in a 36-patient crossover trial
question: In HNF1A maturity-onset diabetes of the young, are patients unusually sensitive to low-dose gliclazide compared with type 2 diabetes?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a marked, mechanism-backed drug sensitivity shown in one small randomised crossover trial. Pearson ER et al. (PMID: 14575972) randomised 36 patients — HNF1A-mutation diabetes or type 2 diabetes matched for BMI and fasting glucose — to crossover treatment with gliclazide and metformin. Patients with HNF1A diabetes had a 5.2-fold greater response to gliclazide than to metformin (fasting plasma glucose reduction 4.7 versus 0.9 mmol/L (≈85 versus 16 mg/dL), P=0.0007) and a 3.9-fold greater response to gliclazide than patients with type 2 diabetes (P=0.002). The mechanism fitted: a strong insulin secretory response to intravenous tolbutamide despite a small response to intravenous glucose, greater insulin sensitivity than type 2 diabetes, and similar sulfonylurea metabolism in both groups. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): HNF1A diabetes is unusually sensitive to low-dose gliclazide — one 36-patient crossover trial from 2003, never replicated at scale, so Tier C.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — patients with HNF1A diabetes showed a 5.2-fold greater fasting-glucose response to gliclazide than to metformin and 3.9-fold greater than type 2 diabetes, in one 36-patient randomised crossover trial

title: Metformin in obese pregnancy: weight gain trimmed in two trials (4.6 versus 6.3 kg in EMPOWR) — baby's birth weight unchanged in both, preeclampsia signal in one
question: In obese pregnant women without diabetes, does metformin reduce maternal weight gain or improve pregnancy outcomes versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for maternal weight gain, not for the baby's size. Two double-blind placebo-controlled trials agree on the shape of the answer. In EMPOWR (Syngelaki A et al., PMID: 26840133), 450 women with BMI over 35 without diabetes were randomised to metformin 3.0 g daily or placebo from 12–18 weeks until delivery: the primary outcome, median neonatal birth-weight z score, did not differ (0.05 versus 0.17, P=0.66), but median maternal gestational weight gain was lower on metformin (4.6 versus 6.3 kg, P<0.001) and preeclampsia was less frequent (3.0% versus 11.3%; odds ratio 0.24; 95% CI 0.10 to 0.61; P=0.001), with more side effects on metformin. In GRoW (Dodd JM et al., PMID: 30528218), 514 overweight or obese women receiving dietary and lifestyle advice were randomised to metformin (up to 2,000 mg) or placebo: birthweight over 4,000 g did not differ (16% versus 14%; adjusted risk ratio 0.97; 95% CI 0.65 to 1.47), weekly weight gain was slightly lower on metformin (adjusted mean difference −0.08 kg/week, P=0.007), and total weight gain and other pregnancy outcomes did not differ significantly. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): metformin trims gestational weight gain in obese pregnancy; a neonatal benefit was not shown in either trial, and the preeclampsia signal rests on one trial.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — metformin reduced gestational weight gain in two placebo-controlled trials in obese pregnancy, with no difference in neonatal birth weight in either and a preeclampsia reduction seen in only one

title: Inpatient CGM: time in range not significantly better in either randomised trial (54.5% versus 48.6%, P=0.14) — hypoglycaemia events and recurrence clearly down
question: In hospitalised patients with diabetes, does real-time continuous glucose monitoring improve time in range versus point-of-care fingerstick testing?
balance: SPLIT — no significant time-in-range gain in either inpatient trial, but hypoglycaemia burden fell. In Spanakis EK et al. (PMID: 35984478), 185 general medicine and surgery patients on basal-bolus insulin were randomised to insulin adjustment guided by real-time CGM or by point-of-care (POC) fingerstick testing: time in range 70–180 mg/dL did not differ significantly (54.51% versus 48.64%, P=0.14), nor did mean daily glucose (183.2 versus 186.8 mg/dL, P=0.36); among patients who had a hypoglycaemic event, CGM guidance cut recurrence (1.80 versus 2.94 events/patient, P=0.03) and time below 70 mg/dL (1.89% versus 5.47%, P=0.02). In Singh LG et al. (PMID: 32759361), 72 high-risk insulin-treated patients with type 2 diabetes on general wards randomised to real-time CGM with glucose telemetry or POC testing had fewer hypoglycaemic events per patient (0.67 versus 1.69, P=0.024) and fewer events below 54 mg/dL (0.08 versus 0.75, P=0.003), with time below 70 mg/dL 0.40% versus 1.88% (P=0.002) — but again no difference in time in range. PROPOSED SPLIT: CGM in hospital is a hypoglycaemia-safety intervention, not a proven time-in-range intervention, on current randomised evidence.
stamp: SPLIT — real-time CGM in hospital significantly reduced hypoglycaemic events and time below range in two randomised trials, but did not significantly improve time in range in either

title: Insulin glargine versus NPH in pregnancy: no significant difference on any maternal or neonatal outcome in 702 women — reassurance, not proof of equivalence
question: In pregnant women with type 1 or type 2 diabetes, does insulin glargine achieve control comparable to NPH insulin without worse perinatal outcomes?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — glargine and NPH looked alike on every maternal and neonatal outcome measured, in the only synthesis available. The meta-analysis (Lepercq J et al., PMID: 22685467) pooled 8 studies of women with gestational or pregestational diabetes using insulin glargine (331 women) or NPH insulin (371 women), comparing maternal weight gain, HbA1c, severe hypoglycaemia, hypertension, preeclampsia and caesarean section, and neonatal congenital malformations, birth weight, macrosomia, large-for-gestational-age, NICU admission, respiratory distress, neonatal hypoglycaemia and hyperbilirubinaemia. No significant differences in efficacy or safety outcomes were found between glargine and NPH. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): comparable control and no safety signal — but the underlying studies are small and mostly non-randomised, so this is Tier C and 'no difference found' is not 'equivalence proven'.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — a meta-analysis of 8 studies (702 women) found no significant differences between insulin glargine and NPH in pregnancy on any maternal or neonatal outcome; evidence largely observational

title: Metformin XR versus IR: pooled trials show no gut advantage except dyspepsia (RR 0.58) — and HbA1c a shade worse on XR (0.09%)
question: In type 2 diabetes, does extended-release metformin cause fewer gastrointestinal side effects than immediate-release at equal HbA1c?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the widely repeated claim that extended-release metformin is much gentler on the gut does not survive meta-analysis. Abrilla AA et al. (PMID: 33887354) pooled 9 randomised trials (2,609 adults) comparing equal daily doses of extended-release (MXR) and immediate-release (MIR) metformin: immediate-release was statistically associated with slightly better HbA1c lowering (mean difference 0.09%; 95% CI 0.01 to 0.17), extended-release reduced only dyspepsia among the gastrointestinal symptoms (risk ratio 0.58; 95% CI 0.34 to 0.98 — a relative reduction), and the cumulative incidence of abdominal discomfort or pain, diarrhoea, and nausea and vomiting was similar with both formulations. A small single-centre randomised trial (Hameed M et al., PMID: 28718236) pointed the other way on tolerability — diarrhoea, dyspepsia and flatulence in 40% on immediate-release 1,000 mg twice daily versus less than half that rate on the same dose of extended-release — with no statistical difference in HbA1c reduction at 3 months (1.0% versus 0.7%). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): at equal doses the formulations are glycaemically near-identical and, dyspepsia aside, gastrointestinal tolerability is similar in the pooled randomised evidence.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — across 9 randomised trials at equal doses, extended-release metformin reduced only dyspepsia versus immediate-release, with similar diarrhoea, nausea and abdominal pain and marginally worse HbA1c

title: Ustekinumab in new type 1 diabetes: C-peptide 49% higher at 12 months in a 72-adolescent phase 2 trial — a surrogate signal awaiting a larger trial
question: In newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes, does ustekinumab preserve stimulated C-peptide versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a phase 2 signal in adolescents, nothing more yet. In the UST1D trial (Tatovic D et al., PMID: 39079992), 72 adolescents aged 12–18 years with recent-onset type 1 diabetes were randomised double-blind to ustekinumab or control: treatment was well tolerated with no increase in adverse events, and at 12 months stimulated C-peptide was 49% higher in the intervention group (P=0.02) — a relative difference — meeting the prespecified primary outcome. C-peptide preservation correlated with reductions in IL-17A/interferon-γ co-secreting TH17.1 cells. The earlier phase 1b dose-finding study in 20 young adults (Marwaha AK et al., PMID: 35072168) had found ustekinumab safe at psoriasis doses, with the 90 mg maintenance cohort showing the smallest mean C-peptide decline at 1 year (0.1 pmol/ml). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): IL-12/23 blockade preserved measurably more C-peptide at 12 months in one small phase 2 trial — Tier C, and C-peptide is a surrogate for the outcomes that matter (insulin dose, hypoglycaemia, complications).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — ustekinumab preserved stimulated C-peptide (49% higher at 12 months, P=0.02) in one 72-patient phase 2 trial in adolescents with recent-onset type 1 diabetes, with no increase in adverse events

title: Flash CGM on tablets only (IMMEDIATE): time in range up 9.9 points (2.4 h/day) and HbA1c down 0.3% in 16 weeks — one open-label trial of 116 patients
question: In type 2 diabetes treated only with oral agents, does intermittently scanned or real-time CGM improve HbA1c versus fingerstick monitoring?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in the one trial aimed exactly at this population. IMMEDIATE (Aronson R et al., PMID: 36546594) randomised 116 adults with type 2 diabetes on non-insulin therapy only (at least one oral agent, HbA1c ≥7.5%, mean 8.6%) to intermittently scanned CGM plus diabetes self-management education, or education alone, for 16 weeks. Time in range in the final 2 weeks was greater by 9.9 percentage points (2.4 hours/day) with the sensor (P<0.01), time above range was less by 8.1 percentage points (1.9 hours/day, P=0.037), and HbA1c fell by 0.3% more than control (P=0.048). Time below range was low and not significantly different, hypoglycaemic events were few in both groups, and glucose-monitoring satisfaction was higher among sensor users. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a real but modest glycaemic gain from scanning in oral-agent-only type 2 diabetes — one open-label 16-week trial, so Tier C.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — intermittently scanned CGM improved time in range by 9.9 percentage points and HbA1c by 0.3% versus education alone in one 116-patient trial in type 2 diabetes treated only with oral agents

title: Stem cells for diabetic foot ulcers: complete healing up in pooled trials (RR 1.63) but only for ulcers under 5 cm² — amputation and recurrence unmoved
question: In non-healing diabetic foot ulcers, does cellular (stem-cell-based) therapy increase complete healing versus standard care?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for complete healing of smaller ulcers; not for amputation or recurrence. The meta-analysis of randomised trials (Mei XH et al., PMID: 40530428) pooled 6 RCTs of mesenchymal stem cell therapy for diabetic foot ulcers: complete healing rates were significantly higher with cell therapy (risk ratio 1.63; 95% CI 1.23 to 2.16; P=0.0007 — a relative effect), driven by small ulcers under 5 cm² (RR 1.71; 95% CI 1.11 to 2.63; P=0.02), with no efficacy for large ulcers (RR 1.18; 95% CI 0.75 to 1.86; P=0.46) and no significant differences in amputation risk (P=0.16), serious adverse events (P=0.38) or recurrence (P=0.33). The largest single trial, of placenta-derived cells PDA-002 (Pollak R et al., PMID: 41077558; the tested product is PDA-002, human placenta-derived cells — Celularity), randomised 159 patients with chronic ulcers with and without peripheral artery disease to one of three intramuscular doses or placebo: the best result was in the peripheral-artery-disease subgroup at the lowest dose (complete closure 38.5% versus 22.6% on placebo, sustained 4 weeks), and no treatment-related serious adverse events occurred. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): cell therapy probably helps some chronic ulcers close — heterogeneous small trials, a subgroup-driven largest trial, and no amputation benefit, so Tier C.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — mesenchymal stem cell therapy increased complete healing of diabetic foot ulcers in a 6-trial meta-analysis (RR 1.63), confined to ulcers under 5 cm², with no reduction in amputation or recurrence

title: Glargine versus NPH (Treat-to-Target): identical HbA1c, 6.96% versus 6.97% — the difference is nocturnal hypoglycaemia, 33.2% versus 26.7% reaching target without it
question: In type 2 diabetes, does insulin glargine titrated to fasting glucose achieve HbA1c comparable to NPH insulin with less nocturnal hypoglycaemia?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — equal control, less nocturnal hypoglycaemia. In the Treat-to-Target trial (Riddle MC et al., PMID: 14578243), 756 patients with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled on oral agents were randomised to bedtime glargine or NPH, both titrated to fasting glucose ≤100 mg/dL for 24 weeks: endpoint fasting glucose (117 versus 120 mg/dL) and HbA1c (6.96% versus 6.97%) were essentially identical, and about 60% on each insulin reached HbA1c ≤7% — but 25% more patients reached target without documented nocturnal hypoglycaemia on glargine (33.2% versus 26.7%, P<0.05), and rates of other symptomatic hypoglycaemia categories were 21–48% lower (relative reductions). The Cochrane review (Semlitsch T et al., PMID: 33166419) pooling 16 glargine-versus-NPH trials found HbA1c changes comparable, with glargine reducing confirmed and confirmed nocturnal hypoglycaemia; the severe-hypoglycaemia risk ratio was 0.68 (95% CI 0.46 to 1.01; P=0.06; absolute risk reduction −1.2%), on very low-certainty evidence. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): glargine's advantage over NPH is hypoglycaemia — chiefly nocturnal — not glycaemic potency.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — glargine and NPH achieve identical HbA1c when titrated to the same fasting target, but glargine causes significantly less nocturnal hypoglycaemia in the Treat-to-Target trial and across 16 pooled trials

title: Insulin plus metformin (HOME): weight gain prevented (−3.07 kg) and insulin dose cut by ~20 units/day over 4.3 years — primary vascular endpoint null, macrovascular signal secondary
question: In type 2 diabetes, does combining insulin with metformin improve control and reduce weight gain and hypoglycaemia versus insulin alone?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — continuing metformin after starting insulin prevents weight gain, improves control and cuts insulin dose; the hard-outcome win is a secondary endpoint. In the HOME trial (Kooy A et al., PMID: 19307526), 390 insulin-treated patients with type 2 diabetes were randomised to metformin 850 mg (1–3 times daily) or placebo added to insulin for 4.3 years. The primary endpoint — an aggregate of microvascular and macrovascular morbidity and mortality — was not improved. But metformin prevented weight gain (mean difference −3.07 kg; P<0.001), improved glycaemic control (HbA1c 0.4 percentage points lower; P<0.001) despite the aim of similar control in both groups, and reduced insulin requirements by 19.63 IU/day (P<0.001). The secondary macrovascular endpoint favoured metformin (hazard ratio 0.61; 95% CI 0.40 to 0.94; P=0.02; number needed to treat 16.1), partly explained by the weight difference. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the metabolic benefits are primary-analysis-grade; the macrovascular claim is a secondary endpoint in a single trial, and because it is a cardiovascular-event benefit claim this shelf is Tier C.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — adding metformin to insulin prevented weight gain (−3.07 kg), improved HbA1c (−0.4 points) and reduced insulin dose (−19.6 IU/day) in the HOME trial; its primary vascular composite was null and the macrovascular reduction (HR 0.61) was a secondary endpoint

title: Acarbose versus metformin first-line (MARCH): HbA1c −1.11% versus −1.12% at 48 weeks in 784 newly diagnosed Chinese patients — a dead heat
question: In newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes in Chinese patients, is acarbose as effective initial therapy as metformin for HbA1c?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — acarbose matched metformin almost exactly as initial therapy in Chinese patients. In the MARCH trial (Yang W et al., PMID: 24622668), 784 patients with newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes (mean HbA1c 7.5%) at 11 Chinese sites were randomised open-label to acarbose or metformin monotherapy for 24 weeks, followed by 24 weeks in which add-on therapy was allowed if targets were missed. HbA1c reduction at week 24 was −1.17% on acarbose and −1.19% on metformin; at week 48 it was −1.11% versus −1.12% (difference 0.01%; 95% CI −0.12 to 0.14; P=0.8999), inside the 0.3% non-inferiority margin. Serious adverse events occurred in 2% of each group and hypoglycaemic episodes in 1% of each. The BMI-stratified analysis (Wang G et al., PMID: 25148570) found the similarity held in normal-weight, overweight and obese strata: HbA1c reductions and the proportion reaching HbA1c ≤6.5% were similar, though metformin lowered fasting glucose more in the overweight stratum (−1.73 versus −1.37 mmol/L (≈-31 versus -25 mg/dL), P<0.05) and acarbose lowered 2-hour post-challenge glucose more (−3.34 versus −2.35 mmol/L (≈-60 versus -42 mg/dL), P<0.01). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): a genuine non-inferiority result — from a single open-label trial programme in one population, so Tier C.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — acarbose was non-inferior to metformin as initial therapy in newly diagnosed Chinese type 2 diabetes (HbA1c −1.11% versus −1.12% at 48 weeks) in the single MARCH trial

title: Exenatide weekly versus liraglutide daily (DURATION-6): HbA1c −1.28% versus −1.48% — liraglutide wins on glucose, exenatide on nausea (9% versus 21%)
question: In type 2 diabetes, how does once-weekly exenatide compare with daily liraglutide on HbA1c and weight?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for liraglutide on HbA1c, and for exenatide on tolerability; the head-to-head splits. In DURATION-6 (Buse JB et al., PMID: 23141817), 911 patients with type 2 diabetes on oral agents were randomised open-label to liraglutide 1.8 mg once daily or exenatide 2 mg once weekly for 26 weeks. HbA1c fell more on liraglutide (−1.48%) than on exenatide (−1.28%); the treatment difference of 0.21% (95% CI 0.08 to 0.33) failed the predefined non-inferiority criterion for exenatide (upper confidence limit <0.25%). Gastrointestinal adverse events were commoner on liraglutide: nausea 21% versus 9%, diarrhoea 13% versus 6%, vomiting 11% versus 4% — falling in frequency over time in both groups — and discontinuation for adverse events was 5% versus 3%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): daily liraglutide lowers HbA1c by about 0.2% more than weekly exenatide, at roughly double the gastrointestinal side-effect rates — a single open-label trial, so Tier C. The candidate question asks how the two compare; the stamp direction is liraglutide's glycaemic edge, with exenatide's tolerability and weekly dosing on the face of the shelf.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — liraglutide once daily lowered HbA1c 0.21% more than exenatide once weekly in DURATION-6, but with roughly double the rates of nausea, diarrhoea and vomiting; a single open-label trial

title: Exenatide plus dapagliflozin (DURATION-8): HbA1c −2.0% for the pair versus −1.6% and −1.4% for each drug alone — superior on every secondary endpoint
question: In type 2 diabetes on metformin, does combining once-weekly exenatide with dapagliflozin lower HbA1c more than either drug alone?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — the combination beat each drug alone on every efficacy measure in its one large double-blind trial. In DURATION-8 (Frías JP et al., PMID: 27651331), 685 patients with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled on metformin (mean HbA1c 9.3%) were randomised to exenatide once weekly plus dapagliflozin daily, exenatide plus placebo, or dapagliflozin plus placebo for 28 weeks. HbA1c fell −2.0% on the combination versus −1.6% on exenatide alone and −1.4% on dapagliflozin alone (combination versus exenatide −0.4%; 95% CI −0.6 to −0.1; P=0.004; versus dapagliflozin −0.6%; 95% CI −0.8 to −0.3; P<0.001). The combination was significantly superior to either drug alone for all secondary efficacy endpoints — fasting and postprandial glucose, the proportion reaching HbA1c <7.0%, weight loss, the proportion losing ≥5% of weight, and systolic blood pressure (all P≤0.025). Adverse events were recorded in 57% (combination), 54% (exenatide) and 52% (dapagliflozin), with no episodes of major or minor hypoglycaemia reported. A mechanistic substudy (Ferrannini E et al., PMID: 31469220) showed the combination abolished the dapagliflozin-induced rise in β-hydroxybutyrate while maintaining glycosuria. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): a large, double-blind, internally consistent trial — held at LIKELY rather than higher because it remains a single trial programme, and flagged Tier C on that basis.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — exenatide plus dapagliflozin lowered HbA1c more than either drug alone (−2.0% versus −1.6% and −1.4%) and won every secondary endpoint in the double-blind DURATION-8 trial, with no hypoglycaemia reported

title: Empagliflozin plus metformin from day one: HbA1c −1.9% to −2.1% versus −1.4% and −1.2% to −1.8% for the single drugs in 1,364 drug-naïve patients
question: In type 2 diabetes, does starting empagliflozin and metformin together beat starting either component alone?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — starting both drugs together beat starting either alone in one large double-blind trial. Hadjadj S et al. (PMID: 27493136) randomised 1,364 drug-naïve patients with type 2 diabetes (HbA1c >7.5% to ≤12%; mean baseline 8.6–8.9%) to twice-daily empagliflozin+metformin combinations at two dose levels of each drug, empagliflozin once daily (10 or 25 mg), or metformin twice daily (500 or 1,000 mg), for 24 weeks. HbA1c fell −1.9% to −2.1% on the twice-daily combination regimens, −1.4% on both empagliflozin once-daily regimens, and −1.2% to −1.8% on metformin twice daily; the combination reductions were significantly greater than with empagliflozin once daily (P<0.001) and with metformin twice daily (P<0.01). Weight fell significantly more on the combinations (−2.8 to −3.8 kg) than on metformin (−0.5 to −1.3 kg; P<0.001 for all). Adverse-event rates were similar across groups (56.7–66.3%), and no hypoglycaemic events required assistance. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): a big, clean, double-blind win on HbA1c and weight — a single 24-week trial with surrogate endpoints, so Tier C.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — initial empagliflozin plus metformin lowered HbA1c (−1.9% to −2.1%) and weight (−2.8 to −3.8 kg) significantly more than either drug started alone in one 1,364-patient double-blind trial in drug-naïve type 2 diabetes

title: Pioglitazone and the death/MI/stroke composite: 4.4% versus 5.7% across 19 trials (hazard ratio 0.82) — with serious heart failure raised from 1.8% to 2.3%
question: In type 2 diabetes with established macrovascular disease, does pioglitazone reduce the composite of death, myocardial infarction, and stroke versus placebo?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — for ischaemic events, with a heart-failure price printed on the same card. The PROactive trial record itself (Dormandy et al., PMID: 16214598) is already carded on the live thiazolidinedione-harms shelf, so this shelf is built on the patient-level meta-analysis of 19 randomised pioglitazone trials (16,390 patients): death, myocardial infarction or stroke occurred in 375 of 8,554 patients (4.4%) on pioglitazone versus 450 of 7,836 (5.7%) on control (hazard ratio 0.82, 95% CI 0.72–0.94, P=.005), an 18% relative reduction. Serious heart failure went the other way: 200 (2.3%) versus 139 (1.8%) (hazard ratio 1.41, 95% CI 1.14–1.76, P=.002), without an associated increase in mortality. In the PROactive prior-stroke subgroup (984 patients), pioglitazone reduced fatal or nonfatal stroke from 10.2% to 5.6% (hazard ratio 0.53, 95% CI 0.34–0.85, P=0.0085), while the main secondary composite in that subgroup (15.6% versus 19.7%; hazard ratio 0.78) did not reach significance. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): pioglitazone lowers the death/MI/stroke composite by about a fifth relative, at the cost of more serious heart failure. Tier C is set because this is a mortality/cardiovascular-event benefit claim.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — patient-level meta-analysis of 19 trials: death/MI/stroke hazard ratio 0.82 (4.4% vs 5.7%), offset by serious heart failure hazard ratio 1.41

title: Linagliptin and kidney progression in CARMELINA: no difference in renal death, end-stage kidney disease or sustained ≥40% eGFR fall (HR 1.04) at any level of kidney function — albuminuria progression fell, events did not
question: In type 2 diabetes, does linagliptin increase kidney disease progression versus placebo over long follow-up?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — linagliptin neither increased nor decreased hard kidney progression in CARMELINA. The trial's main JAMA record (Rosenstock et al., PMID: 30418475) is already carded on the live DPP-4 cardiovascular-safety shelf, so this shelf is built on the trial's kidney-focused secondary analyses. Across 6,979 participants followed for a median 2.2 years, the secondary kidney outcome (renal death, end-stage kidney disease, or sustained ≥40% decrease in eGFR) had a hazard ratio of 1.04 (95% CI 0.89–1.22) for linagliptin versus placebo, consistent across all baseline eGFR categories; progression of albuminuria was reduced and HbA1c fell without more hypoglycaemia. In the 646 participants with nephrotic-range proteinuria, the kidney composite likewise showed no clear benefit (hazard ratio 0.80, 95% CI 0.63–1.01 for the ≥40% eGFR-decline definition, with significant heterogeneity against the non-nephrotic subgroup), and renal death or end-stage kidney disease did not differ (hazard ratio 0.88, 95% CI 0.64–1.21). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): over 2.2 years linagliptin is kidney-neutral on hard outcomes — it does not increase progression, and it does not prevent it either.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — CARMELINA kidney composite hazard ratio 1.04 (0.89–1.22) over 2.2 years; albuminuria progression reduced, hard kidney events unchanged

title: Text-message support for type 2 diabetes: HbA1c fell about 0.4 points more than usual care — in one tailored-programme trial and across an 11-trial meta-analysis
question: In type 2 diabetes, does a text-messaging support programme improve HbA1c versus usual care?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — modest, consistent, and small. In the SMS4BG randomised trial (366 adults with poorly controlled type 1 or type 2 diabetes, HbA1c ≥8%), nine months of individually tailored text-message support reduced HbA1c by 8.85 mmol/mol versus 3.96 mmol/mol with usual care (adjusted mean difference −4.23 mmol/mol, 95% CI −7.30 to −1.15, P=0.007) — roughly 0.4 percentage points. A systematic review and meta-analysis of 11 randomised trials in type 2 diabetes (1,710 participants) found a closely similar pooled HbA1c reduction of 0.38% (95% CI −0.53 to −0.23, P<0.001), with five of the eleven trials individually significant. Only 4 of 21 secondary outcomes in SMS4BG improved significantly, and the trialists themselves note the clinical significance of a 0.4-point fall is unclear. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): text-message support lowers HbA1c by about 0.4 percentage points on average — a real but small effect from a cheap intervention.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — HbA1c about 0.4 percentage points lower with text-message support in both the SMS4BG trial and an 11-trial meta-analysis

title: Degludec versus detemir in children with type 1 diabetes: equal HbA1c at one year (7.9% versus 7.8%), a 30% lower basal dose — and significantly fewer hyperglycaemia-with-ketosis episodes (rate ratio 0.41)
question: In children and adolescents with type 1 diabetes, does insulin degludec achieve control comparable to insulin detemir with lower rates of ketosis?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for ketosis, on top of equal glucose control. In the BEGIN Young trial (350 children aged 1–17 years), degludec once daily was non-inferior to detemir (once or twice daily) for HbA1c at 26 weeks (estimated treatment difference 0.15%, 95% CI −0.03 to 0.32), and at 52 weeks HbA1c was 7.9% versus 7.8% with fasting glucose significantly lower on degludec (treatment difference −1.62 mmol/L (≈-29 mg/dL), P=0.0090) at a lower basal dose (0.38 versus 0.55 units/kg). Hypoglycaemia rates did not differ significantly, but hyperglycaemia with ketosis was significantly less frequent on degludec (0.7 versus 1.1 events per patient-year; treatment ratio 0.41, 95% CI 0.22–0.78, P=0.0066). A pooled analysis of the two paediatric degludec trials confirmed lower ketosis rates with degludec-based treatment despite similar hyperglycaemia rates. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): degludec matches detemir for control in children and cuts ketosis episodes by more than half relative.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — non-inferior HbA1c versus detemir in children, with hyperglycaemia-with-ketosis rate ratio 0.41 and a 30% lower basal dose

title: Teplizumab as treatment for new-onset type 1 diabetes: C-peptide decline slowed at 2 years in two randomised programmes — a 75% smaller decline in AbATE, preservation concentrated in early, younger, better-controlled patients
question: In recent-onset type 1 diabetes, does teplizumab treatment (as distinct from prevention) delay C-peptide decline over two years?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for beta-cell function as measured by C-peptide, a surrogate, over two years. In the AbATE trial (52 patients with new-onset type 1 diabetes given two 2-week courses of teplizumab, at diagnosis and after 1 year), the decline in C-peptide at 2 years was −0.28 nmol/L on teplizumab versus −0.46 nmol/L in controls (P=0.002), described by the authors as a 75% improvement in the decline. In the larger phase 3 Protégé trial (516 randomised patients), the 14-day full-dose regimen reduced the loss of C-peptide area under the curve at 2 years versus placebo — a prespecified secondary endpoint, the primary composite endpoint having been missed in the trial's first-year report — with preservation concentrated in patients treated within 6 weeks of diagnosis, aged 8–17, with HbA1c below 7.5% and lower insulin use. The common adverse events were rash, transient upper respiratory infections, headache and nausea; antidrug antibodies developed in some Protégé patients without apparent loss of effect. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): two courses of teplizumab slow the loss of endogenous insulin secretion for at least two years in a responder subgroup — this shelf is about treatment after diagnosis, not the separate prevention question (stage 2 disease) shelved elsewhere.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — C-peptide decline at 2 years reduced in AbATE (−0.28 vs −0.46 nmol/L, P=0.002) and in Protégé's full-dose arm, with response concentrated in early-treated younger patients

title: GAD65 vaccine for new-onset type 1 diabetes: a promising small trial missed its primary endpoint, and the 334-patient phase 3 trial showed no preservation of C-peptide at all (P=0.10)
question: In newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes, does GAD65 (glutamic acid decarboxylase) vaccine preserve beta-cell function versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — at the dose and schedule tested in the definitive trial. The first randomised trial (70 patients aged 10–18, GAD-alum on days 1 and 30) missed its primary endpoint: no significant effect on the change in fasting C-peptide at 15 months, though over 30 months fasting C-peptide declined less on GAD-alum (−0.21 versus −0.27 nmol/L, P=0.045) and stimulated secretion likewise (P=0.04), with no effect in patients treated 6 months or more after diagnosis. The phase 3 trial (334 patients aged 10–20, treated within 3 months of diagnosis) then found the stimulated C-peptide level declined to a similar degree in all groups, with no significant difference between the combined active groups and placebo at 15 months (P=0.10), and no effect on insulin dose, HbA1c, or hypoglycaemia rate; adverse events were infrequent and mild in both programmes. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): GAD-alum as tested does not preserve beta-cell function — the small trial's late secondary signals were not confirmed when the question was asked properly at scale.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — phase 3 trial of 334 patients: no significant C-peptide preservation at 15 months (P=0.10), no effect on insulin dose, HbA1c or hypoglycaemia

title: Low-dose interleukin-2 in type 1 diabetes: regulatory T cells rose dose-dependently (up to +4.8 percentage points versus +0.5 on placebo) with no deterioration in glucose control — in two small early-phase studies
question: In type 1 diabetes, does low-dose interleukin-2 expand regulatory T cells safely without worsening glycaemic control?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — the immunological aim was met in tiny early-phase studies; no clinical benefit has been tested. In the randomised phase 1/2 trial (24 adults with established type 1 diabetes), a 5-day course of interleukin-2 at 0.33, 1 or 3 million IU/day increased the proportion of regulatory T cells (Tregs) as a percentage of CD4+ cells by 2.8, 3.9 and 4.8 percentage points respectively, versus 0.5 on placebo (P=0.0039 at each dose), with no serious adverse events and no deleterious changes in glucose-metabolism variables; non-serious events (injection-site reactions, influenza-like syndrome) rose with dose. In the DILT1D adaptive dose-finding study (40 adults, single subcutaneous doses of aldesleukin), the doses estimated to raise Treg frequency by 10% and 20% were 0.101×10⁶ and 0.497×10⁶ IU/m², though even the lowest doses transiently pushed plasma IL-2 above the in-vitro Treg-specific window and caused an early dose-dependent dip in circulating Tregs before the rebound. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): low-dose IL-2 reliably expands Tregs over days and did not worsen glucose control in these small studies — whether that translates into preserved beta-cell function is unanswered by either record. Tier C is set: early-phase, small, surrogate-endpoint evidence.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — dose-dependent Treg expansion (+2.8 to +4.8 points vs +0.5 on placebo) and no glucose deterioration in two small early-phase studies; clinical efficacy untested

title: Zimislecel stem-cell islets in type 1 diabetes with severe hypoglycaemia: all 12 full-dose patients were free of severe hypoglycaemic events at a year and 10 of 12 were insulin-independent — in an uncontrolled 14-patient study, with neutropenia and two deaths
question: In type 1 diabetes with recurrent severe hypoglycaemia, do stem-cell-derived islet cells (zimislecel) restore endogenous insulin and eliminate severe hypoglycaemic events?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — striking results in a very small, uncontrolled, interim study, bought with full immunosuppression. In the phase 1–2 FORWARD study, 14 patients with type 1 diabetes and impaired hypoglycaemia awareness (C-peptide undetectable at baseline in all) received zimislecel — allogeneic stem-cell-derived fully differentiated islets, a product of Vertex Pharmaceuticals — by portal-vein infusion with glucocorticoid-free immunosuppression; 2 received a half dose and 12 a full dose. All 14 had engraftment with detectable C-peptide after infusion. Among the 12 full-dose patients, all were free of severe hypoglycaemic events from day 90 to 365 and had HbA1c below 7% (the part C primary endpoint), spent more than 70% of time in the 70–180 mg/dL range, and 10 of 12 (83%) were insulin-independent at day 365. Neutropenia was the most common serious adverse event (3 participants), and two deaths occurred — one from cryptococcal meningitis and one from progression of preexisting neurocognitive impairment. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): zimislecel restored endogenous insulin and abolished severe hypoglycaemia for a year in this first small cohort — Tier C, because a single uncontrolled 14-patient interim analysis, however dramatic, is not yet a proven therapy.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — 12/12 full-dose patients free of severe hypoglycaemic events with HbA1c <7% at 1 year and 10/12 insulin-independent, in a single uncontrolled 14-patient phase 1–2 study

title: Tighter glucose targets in gestational diabetes: large-for-gestational-age unchanged (14.7% versus 15.1%), serious infant outcomes fewer (1.3% versus 2.6%) but serious maternal outcomes more (5.9% versus 3.0%) — and no benefit visible 4.5 years later
question: In gestational diabetes, do tighter glycaemic targets improve perinatal outcomes versus less-tight targets?
balance: SPLIT — the primary outcome was null and the secondary outcomes point in opposite directions for baby and mother. In the TARGET stepped-wedge cluster trial (1,100 women with gestational diabetes in 10 New Zealand hospitals), tighter targets (fasting ≤5.0, 1-hour ≤7.4, 2-hour ≤6.7 mmol/L — ≈90, 133 and 121 mg/dL) versus less-tight targets did not reduce large-for-gestational-age infants (88/599, 14.7% versus 76/502, 15.1%; adjusted relative risk 0.96, 95% CI 0.66–1.40, P=0.839). The composite of serious infant outcomes (perinatal death, birth trauma, shoulder dystocia) was lower with tighter targets (8/599, 1.3% versus 13/505, 2.6%; adjusted relative risk 0.23, 95% CI 0.06–0.88, P=0.032), but the composite of serious maternal outcomes was higher (35/595, 5.9% versus 15/501, 3.0%; adjusted relative risk 2.29, 95% CI 1.14–4.59, P=0.020), and more women on tighter targets needed pharmacological treatment (67.9% versus 58.5%). At 4.5-year follow-up, maternal HbA1c and child BMI z-score did not differ, and several child motor and behavioural measures favoured the less-tight group. PROPOSED SPLIT: tighter targets did not deliver their primary aim and traded a possible infant gain against a maternal cost, with no long-term advantage — whether to tighten is a values-weighted decision, not an evidence mandate.
stamp: SPLIT — large-for-gestational-age null (aRR 0.96); serious infant composite lower (aRR 0.23) but serious maternal composite higher (aRR 2.29), and no difference at 4.5 years

title: Duodenal mucosal resurfacing in type 2 diabetes: the sham-controlled REVITA-2 trial missed its primary endpoint overall (P=0.147) — the HbA1c signal lived in the European subgroup and in patients with high fasting glucose
question: In type 2 diabetes, does duodenal mucosal resurfacing improve HbA1c versus a sham endoscopic procedure?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — a negative primary endpoint with subgroup signals, preceded by an encouraging open-label study. REVITA-2 (108 patients in Europe and Brazil) found median HbA1c change at 24 weeks of −10.4 mmol/mol with duodenal mucosal resurfacing (DMR, using the Revita system as named in the publication) versus −7.1 mmol/mol with sham (P=0.147, not significant), and liver-fat change at 12 weeks of −5.4% versus −2.9% (P=0.096). Marked heterogeneity between regions (interaction P=0.063) led to stratified reporting: in the European cohort HbA1c fell −6.6 versus −3.3 mmol/mol (P=0.033) and liver fat −5.4% versus −2.2% (P=0.035), while Brazil showed a large sham effect; in the per-protocol population, patients with baseline fasting glucose ≥10 mmol/L (≈180 mg/dL) had significantly greater HbA1c reductions with DMR (P=0.002). The earlier open-label first-in-human programme (36 patients analysed) saw HbA1c fall 0.9% at 24 weeks and remain improved at 12 months, with 52% of patients having a procedure-related adverse event, 81% of them mild. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): DMR may lower HbA1c modestly in selected patients, but its only sham-controlled trial did not prove it overall. Tier C is set: the benefit claim rests on subgroups of a single sham-controlled trial.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — REVITA-2 primary endpoint not significant overall (HbA1c P=0.147); benefit confined to the European subgroup (P=0.033) and high-fasting-glucose patients

title: Oral semaglutide alone in drug-naive type 2 diabetes: HbA1c fell 1.1–1.4 points more than placebo at the 14 mg dose over 26 weeks, with 2.3–2.6 kg more weight loss
question: In drug-naive type 2 diabetes, does oral semaglutide monotherapy lower HbA1c and weight versus placebo?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — as monotherapy against placebo, the cleanest comparison in the PIONEER programme. In PIONEER 1 (703 patients with type 2 diabetes managed by diet and exercise alone, mean baseline HbA1c 8.0%), 26 weeks of once-daily oral semaglutide reduced HbA1c versus placebo by 0.6% (3 mg), 0.9% (7 mg) and 1.1% (14 mg) on the treatment-policy estimand, and by 0.7%, 1.2% and 1.4% on the trial-product estimand (P<0.001 for all doses); body weight fell by an additional 2.3 kg (treatment policy) to 2.6 kg (trial product) at 14 mg (P<0.001). Gastrointestinal events were the most common adverse events, mild-to-moderate and transient, with discontinuations in 2.3–7.4% on semaglutide versus 2.2% on placebo. A systematic review and meta-analysis of 10 oral-semaglutide trials (8,536 patients) confirms the pattern against placebo and active comparators alike: lower HbA1c, weight and fasting glucose, more patients reaching HbA1c below 7.0%, and more nausea, diarrhoea and vomiting, without increased hypoglycaemia or pancreatitis. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): oral semaglutide monotherapy lowers HbA1c by about 1–1.4 points versus placebo at the top dose — this shelf covers monotherapy versus placebo only; comparisons with sitagliptin and liraglutide live on the PIONEER glycaemic-trials shelf.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — PIONEER 1: placebo-adjusted HbA1c −1.1% (treatment policy) to −1.4% (trial product) at 14 mg over 26 weeks, confirmed across a 10-trial meta-analysis

title: Glargine 300 versus glargine 100 in type 1 diabetes: identical HbA1c control (difference 0.04%), fewer severe hypoglycaemic events in pooled trials (6.2% versus 9.3% of patients), and less weight gain
question: In type 1 diabetes, does insulin glargine 300 U/mL achieve control comparable to glargine 100 U/mL with less nocturnal hypoglycaemia?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — equal control with a hypoglycaemia edge that is clearest early and for severe events. In EDITION 4 (549 adults with long-duration type 1 diabetes), glargine 300 U/mL was non-inferior to glargine 100 U/mL for HbA1c change at 6 months (difference 0.04%, 95% CI −0.10 to 0.19, from a baseline of 8.1%); overall hypoglycaemia did not differ, except in the first 8 weeks, when nocturnal confirmed or severe hypoglycaemia was lower with glargine 300 (rate ratio 0.69, 95% CI 0.53–0.91), and weight gain was lower. A pooled meta-analysis of the three 6-month phase 3 trials in type 1 diabetes (EDITION 4, EDITION JP 1, EDITION JUNIOR; 1,255 patients) found fewer patients with at least one severe hypoglycaemic event on glargine 300 (6.2% versus 9.3%) and a lower risk of a first severe event (hazard ratio 0.65, 95% CI 0.44–0.98, P=0.038), with similar HbA1c reductions. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): in type 1 diabetes glargine 300 matches glargine 100 for control and buys a modest reduction in severe and early nocturnal hypoglycaemia — the type 2 diabetes EDITION comparisons live on their own shelf.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — non-inferior HbA1c in EDITION 4 (difference 0.04%); pooled severe hypoglycaemia 6.2% versus 9.3% of patients (HR 0.65 for first event)

title: Enalapril or losartan in normotensive type 1 diabetes: five years of renin–angiotensin blockade did not slow kidney structural progression — but cut the odds of retinopathy progression by about two-thirds
question: In normotensive type 1 diabetes, do enalapril or losartan prevent progression of nephropathy or retinopathy versus placebo over five years?
balance: SPLIT — the kidney answer is no, the eye answer is yes, from the same five-year trial. In the Renin-Angiotensin System Study (285 normotensive, normoalbuminuric patients with type 1 diabetes randomised to losartan 100 mg, enalapril 20 mg, or placebo for 5 years, with kidney biopsies), the primary renal endpoint — change in mesangial fractional volume — did not differ between placebo (0.016 units) and enalapril (0.005, P=0.38) or losartan (0.026, P=0.26), and no other biopsy-assessed structural variable favoured treatment. Microalbuminuria developed in 6% on placebo, 4% on enalapril (P=0.96) — and 17% on losartan (P=0.01), a paradoxical harm signal for the ARB. Retinopathy told the opposite story: the odds of progression by two or more steps were reduced by 65% with enalapril (odds ratio 0.35, 95% CI 0.14–0.85) and by 70% with losartan (odds ratio 0.30, 95% CI 0.12–0.73), independently of blood-pressure changes. Chronic cough occurred in 12 patients on enalapril, 6 on losartan and 4 on placebo; three biopsy-related serious adverse events resolved completely. PROPOSED SPLIT: early renin–angiotensin blockade in normotensive type 1 diabetes does not prevent nephropathy — and losartan may hasten microalbuminuria — while both drugs slowed retinopathy progression in this single trial. Tier C is set: the benefit and the harm signals each rest on one trial.
stamp: SPLIT — nephropathy: no structural benefit over 5 years (primary endpoint null; microalbuminuria 17% on losartan vs 6% on placebo); retinopathy: progression odds reduced 65–70% by both drugs in one trial

title: Continuous glucose monitoring in young people with type 1 diabetes: in the JDRF trial the HbA1c benefit was confined to adults 25 and older (−0.53%) — ages 8–14 (−0.13%) and 15–24 (+0.08) showed no significant gain, and teenagers wore the sensor least
question: In children, adolescents, and young adults with type 1 diabetes, does continuous glucose monitoring improve HbA1c versus fingerstick monitoring?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — in the age groups this question asks about, in the trial that defined the field. The JDRF Continuous Glucose Monitoring trial (322 children and adults on intensive therapy, HbA1c 7.0–10.0%) found the HbA1c effect varied markedly by age (P=0.003 for interaction): among patients 25 years and older, CGM improved HbA1c change by −0.53% (95% CI −0.71 to −0.35, P<0.001), but among 15–24-year-olds the difference was +0.08 (95% CI −0.17 to 0.33, P=0.52) and among 8–14-year-olds −0.13 (95% CI −0.38 to 0.11, P=0.29) — neither significant. Use tracked the result: sensor wear of 6.0 or more days per week was achieved by 83% of adults 25 and older, 50% of 8–14-year-olds, and only 30% of 15–24-year-olds. Severe hypoglycaemia rates were low and did not differ. In the 6-month extension, the 83 adults who continued CGM sustained their benefit (A1C −0.4±0.6% at 12 months in those starting at or above 7.0%), confirming the adult effect without adding paediatric evidence. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): for children, adolescents and young adults as studied in 2008-era devices, CGM did not significantly improve HbA1c — the proven benefit belonged to the adults, and adherence, not sensor accuracy, was the binding constraint.

title: Sensor-augmented pump versus injections in type 1 diabetes: HbA1c 7.5% versus 8.1% at one year in STAR 3 — in adults and children alike, with no difference in severe hypoglycaemia
question: In type 1 diabetes with suboptimal control, does sensor-augmented pump therapy lower HbA1c more than multiple daily injections with fingerstick monitoring?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one large, well-run trial, unblinded by necessity. In STAR 3 (485 patients — 329 adults and 156 children — with inadequately controlled type 1 diabetes, baseline HbA1c 8.3% in both groups), sensor-augmented pump therapy brought HbA1c to 7.5% at 1 year versus 8.1% with multiple daily injections plus fingerstick monitoring (P<0.001), and a greater proportion of both adults and children reached the below-7% target on the pump. Severe hypoglycaemia did not differ (13.31 versus 13.48 events per 100 person-years, P=0.58), and neither group gained significant weight. A post hoc analysis of the North American cohort found the incremental pump benefit similar in the United States (−0.93% versus −0.31% A1C change, pump versus injections) and Canada (−1.14% versus −0.67%), alongside higher sensor use in Canada (79% versus 68% of the time). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): sensor-augmented pump therapy lowers HbA1c by about 0.6 points more than injections over a year. Tier C is set because the benefit rests on a single trial programme — its post hoc analyses are the same patients, not independent confirmation.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — STAR 3: HbA1c 7.5% versus 8.1% at 1 year (P<0.001), severe hypoglycaemia unchanged; single trial programme, Tier C

title: Mini-dose glucagon in sick children with type 1 diabetes: glucose rose from 3.44 to 8.11 mmol/L (≈62 to 146 mg/dL) within 30 minutes in 33 episodes — from one uncontrolled case series, with no comparator
question: In children with type 1 diabetes and impending hypoglycaemia during exercise or fasting, does mini-dose glucagon avert hypoglycaemia without rebound hyperglycaemia?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — a physiologically coherent rescue that has only ever been described, never tested against a comparator. The single study behind this shelf reports 33 episodes of impending or mild hypoglycaemia in 28 children with type 1 diabetes (mean age about 6.6 years) during gastroenteritis or poor oral intake, treated at home with small subcutaneous glucagon doses measured in insulin-syringe units (20 µg for children aged 2 years or under; 1 unit per year of age up to 150 µg above that age). Blood glucose rose from 3.44±0.15 mmol/L (≈62±3 mg/dL) before treatment to 8.11±0.72 mmol/L (≈146±13 mg/dL) at 30 minutes; in 14 children hypoglycaemia recurred and responded to a doubled repeat dose (3.48±0.18 to 6.94±0.72 mmol/L (≈63±3 to 125±13 mg/dL)), and four children needed a third dose. In 28 of the 33 episodes the children stayed home and recovered fully; five were taken to hospital for dehydration or fever concerns, none for hypoglycaemia. The authors do not report rebound hyperglycaemia as a problem, but with no control group there is no way to know how many episodes would have resolved with oral carbohydrate or time alone. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): mini-dose glucagon appears to avert hypoglycaemia in sick children who cannot keep carbohydrate down — a practice supported by one small case series and two decades of clinical use, not by a trial. Tier C is set: uncontrolled observational evidence.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — glucose 3.44 to 8.11 mmol/L (≈62 to 146 mg/dL) at 30 minutes across 33 episodes in one uncontrolled 28-child case series; no comparator, no randomised trial

title: Insulin aspart versus human insulin in pregnant type 1 diabetes: equal HbA1c in the second and third trimesters, smaller postprandial glucose rises, and a non-significant halving of major nocturnal hypoglycaemia
question: In pregnant women with type 1 diabetes, does insulin aspart control postprandial glucose and HbA1c as well as human regular insulin without worse perinatal outcomes?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for postprandial control, on a base of equal HbA1c and comparable safety in one open-label trial. In the randomised trial of 322 pregnant women with type 1 diabetes (aspart versus regular human insulin as the mealtime insulin, both with NPH basal), HbA1c was comparable in the second trimester (difference −0.04, 95% CI −0.18 to 0.11) and third trimester (−0.08, 95% CI −0.23 to 0.06), with 80% of participants reaching HbA1c at or below 6.5%. Average postprandial plasma glucose increments were significantly lower with aspart at the end of the first and third trimesters (P=0.003 and P=0.044), as was mean glucose 90 minutes after breakfast (P=0.044 and P=0.001). Major hypoglycaemia occurred at 1.4 versus 2.1 episodes per year of exposure (relative risk 0.720, 95% CI 0.36–1.46), and the risk of major or major nocturnal hypoglycaemia was 52% lower in relative terms with aspart (relative risk 0.48, 95% CI 0.20–1.143) without reaching significance. Maternal safety profiles and pregnancy outcomes were similar between treatments, per the record. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): aspart matches human insulin for HbA1c in pregnancy and improves the postprandial profile it was designed to improve. Tier C is set: a single trial carries the shelf. The candidate anchor (Hod et al. 2008) is a perinatal-outcomes report of this same trial programme; the shelf is built on the trial's primary randomised report — a swap declared for the coordinator.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single RCT (n=322): HbA1c equivalent to human insulin in trimesters 2–3, postprandial increments significantly lower (P=0.003–0.044), perinatal outcomes similar; Tier C

title: Lidocaine 5% plaster for painful diabetic neuropathy: response matched pregabalin in an open-label trial (66.7% versus 69.1% responders in the diabetic subgroup) — with far fewer drug-related adverse events (5.8% versus 41.2%)
question: In painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy, does the lidocaine 5% medicated plaster relieve pain versus placebo or pregabalin?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — comparable pain response to pregabalin in one open-label non-inferiority programme, with no placebo arm to prove the plaster beats nothing. In the two-stage adaptive trial (204 patients with painful diabetic polyneuropathy and 96 with postherpetic neuralgia), 4-week responder rates (a fall of at least 2 points, or a score of 4 or less, on the 11-point pain scale) were 66.4% on the lidocaine 5% medicated plaster versus 61.5% on pregabalin overall; within the diabetic polyneuropathy subgroup the per-protocol responder rates were 66.7% (plaster) versus 69.1% (pregabalin). Tolerability clearly favoured the plaster: any adverse event in 18.7% versus 46.4% of patients, drug-related adverse events in 5.8% versus 41.2%, with fewer treatment-related discontinuations. In the 8-week second phase, patients who had responded inadequately to either monotherapy gained additional clinically relevant pain reduction when the two were combined. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): the plaster relieves diabetic neuropathic pain about as well as pregabalin in head-to-head open-label data and is much better tolerated — but without a placebo comparison in this population, the size of its true drug effect is unknown. Tier C is set: open-label, mixed-indication, single-programme evidence.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — open-label non-inferiority versus pregabalin (diabetic subgroup responders 66.7% vs 69.1%), drug-related adverse events 5.8% vs 41.2%; no placebo arm

title: Voglibose in impaired glucose tolerance: diabetes onset delayed — 50 cases versus 106 on placebo (hazard ratio 0.595) in a trial stopped early at its interim analysis after a mean of only 48 weeks
question: In impaired glucose tolerance, does voglibose delay progression to type 2 diabetes versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one large trial, stopped early, in a single population; in line with this library's standing language for prediabetes, the effect is a delay in the formal diagnosis, not prevention of the disease. In the Japanese trial (1,780 people with impaired glucose tolerance, all on standard diet and exercise advice), voglibose 0.2 mg three times daily reduced progression to type 2 diabetes versus placebo (50 of 897 versus 106 of 881 patients; hazard ratio 0.595, 95% CI 0.433–0.818, P=0.0014) — a 40% relative reduction — and more patients achieved normoglycaemia on voglibose (599 of 897 versus 454 of 881; hazard ratio 1.539, 95% CI 1.357–1.746, P<0.0001). But the trial was stopped at a pre-planned interim analysis after a mean treatment duration of only 48.1 weeks, although the protocol envisaged a minimum of 3 years, and early stopping is known to inflate effect estimates. Adverse events were reported by 90% of the voglibose group versus 85% on placebo. The Cochrane review of alpha-glucosidase inhibitors for delaying type 2 diabetes rated the voglibose-versus-placebo evidence (this single trial) as low certainty (risk ratio 0.46, 95% CI 0.34–0.64), with the class's firmer data coming from acarbose. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): voglibose delays the diagnosis of type 2 diabetes in Japanese adults with impaired glucose tolerance over about a year of treatment — Tier C, a single early-stopped trial.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — diabetes onset 50/897 versus 106/881 (HR 0.595) in one trial stopped early at interim analysis (mean 48 weeks); Cochrane rates the voglibose evidence low certainty; Tier C

title: Canagliflozin and amputation: the pooled patient-level analysis could not explain why CANVAS showed an increase and CREDENCE did not (heterogeneity P=0.02) — and the class-wide trial meta-analysis finds no significant increase (risk ratio 1.24, 95% CI 0.96–1.60)
question: Does canagliflozin increase amputation risk compared with other SGLT2 inhibitors or placebo when CANVAS and CREDENCE are pooled?
balance: SPLIT — the answer splits by trial, and the pooled analysis says so itself. In the patient-level pooled analysis of CANVAS (10,142 participants, median follow-up 2.4 years; 187 amputations, 1.8% annual event rate) and CREDENCE (4,401 participants, median 2.5 years; 133 amputations, 3.0% annual rate), the effect of canagliflozin on amputation risk differed significantly between the two trials (P for heterogeneity 0.02, I²=82%): increased in CANVAS, null in CREDENCE, with no explanation found in participant or trial differences and no evidence that the foot-care protocols introduced during CREDENCE accounted for it; a previous amputation was the strongest predictor of a future one in both trials. The authors conclude the CANVAS finding may have been the result of chance. The trial-level meta-analysis of all SGLT2-inhibitor cardiovascular outcome trials (6 trials, 51,713 participants, 858 amputations) found amputation rates of 2.0% on SGLT2 inhibitors versus 1.3% on control and a pooled risk ratio of 1.24 (95% CI 0.96–1.60) that was not statistically significant, with substantial heterogeneity (I²=67.5%) and no significant increase in any subgroup, including patients with peripheral artery disease. PROPOSED SPLIT: a canagliflozin-specific amputation signal exists in CANVAS and nowhere else — neither the same drug's kidney trial nor the class-wide evidence confirms it. Tier C is set: a harm claim resting on discordant trial data.
stamp: SPLIT — CANVAS showed increased amputation risk, CREDENCE (same drug) did not (heterogeneity P=0.02); class-wide meta-analysis null (RR 1.24, 95% CI 0.96–1.60)

title: Switching mealtime insulin to inhaled insulin in type 1 diabetes: HbA1c non-inferior to usual care at 17 weeks (adjusted difference 0.11%) — with smaller post-meal excursions, more patients worsening by >0.5%, and cough the commonest side effect
question: In type 1 and type 2 diabetes, does switching mealtime insulin to inhaled insulin maintain HbA1c versus usual care over 17 weeks?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — non-inferior HbA1c maintenance over 17 weeks in type 1 diabetes, with a postprandial advantage and a wider spread of individual responses. In INHALE-3 (123 adults with type 1 diabetes, mostly previously on automated insulin delivery or multiple daily injections), a regimen of inhaled Technosphere insulin plus insulin degludec was non-inferior to usual care for HbA1c at 17 weeks (7.62%±1.06% versus 7.54%±0.77% from baselines of 7.57% and 7.59%; adjusted difference 0.11%, 95% CI −0.10 to 0.33, P for non-inferiority=0.01). More patients improved by over 0.5% on inhaled insulin (12 of 62, 21% versus 3, 5%) — but more also worsened by over 0.5% (15, 26% versus 2, 3%). The commonest side effect was a brief cough, and eight participants discontinued inhaled insulin because of side effects. In the trial's meal-challenge study (122 adults), the glucose area above 180 mg/dL over 2 hours after a meal was smaller with inhaled insulin than with rapid-acting analogue (adjusted difference −12 mg/dL, 95% CI −22 to −2, P=0.02), with a lower peak reached sooner; in the 30-week extension, patients continuing inhaled insulin plus degludec held HbA1c at 7.4%±1.0% with time in range 54%±20%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): inhaled insulin maintains HbA1c as well as usual care over 17 weeks in type 1 diabetes and flattens the post-meal rise — noting that the trial enrolled type 1 diabetes only, although the candidate question also names type 2. Tier C is set: a single trial programme.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — INHALE-3: HbA1c non-inferior at 17 weeks (adjusted difference 0.11%, P-NI=0.01) in type 1 diabetes, post-meal excursion smaller (−12 mg/dL AUC>180, P=0.02); single programme, Tier C

title: Risankizumab for ulcerative colitis: remission in 20.3% versus 6.2% at induction and about 40% versus 25% at one year in two phase 3 trials
question: In moderately to severely active ulcerative colitis, does risankizumab induce and maintain clinical remission versus placebo?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — two large phase 3 trials, reported together, point the same way. In INSPIRE, intravenous risankizumab 1200 mg put 20.3% (132/650) of patients in clinical remission at week 12 versus 6.2% (20/325) on placebo (adjusted difference 14.0%, P<.001). In COMMAND, responders re-randomised to subcutaneous risankizumab stayed in remission at week 52 in 40.2% (180 mg) and 37.6% (360 mg) versus 25.1% on withdrawal to placebo. No new safety risks were detected in either trial. The absolute remission rates remain a minority of patients, and follow-up ends at 52 weeks. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): risankizumab induces and maintains remission in moderately to severely active ulcerative colitis, with roughly one in five remitting on induction and two in five responders still in remission at a year.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — clinical remission 20.3% vs 6.2% at week 12 (INSPIRE) and 40.2%/37.6% vs 25.1% at week 52 (COMMAND) in two phase 3 trials

title: Upadacitinib for ulcerative colitis: remission in 26–34% versus 4–5% at 8 weeks and 42–52% versus 12% at a year across three phase 3 trials
question: In moderately to severely active ulcerative colitis, does upadacitinib induce remission at 8 weeks and maintain it at 52 weeks versus placebo?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — three phase 3 trials in one programme agree. Upadacitinib 45 mg induced clinical remission at week 8 in 26% (U-ACHIEVE induction) and 34% (U-ACCOMPLISH) versus 5% and 4% on placebo. Among induction responders, maintenance remission at week 52 was 42% on 15 mg and 52% on 30 mg versus 12% on placebo. Serious adverse events were less frequent on upadacitinib than placebo in the induction studies; the adverse events that did cluster on the drug were acne, nasopharyngitis and creatine phosphokinase elevation. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): upadacitinib is an effective oral induction and maintenance therapy for moderately to severely active ulcerative colitis, with a JAK-inhibitor monitoring burden the trials' size cannot fully price.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — remission 26% and 34% vs 5% and 4% at week 8 in two induction trials, and 42%/52% vs 12% at week 52 in maintenance

title: Filgotinib 200 mg for ulcerative colitis: remission in 26.1% versus 15.3% (biologic-naive) and 11.5% versus 4.2% (biologic-experienced) at week 10, held at week 58 — the 100 mg dose mostly missed
question: In moderately to severely active ulcerative colitis, does filgotinib 200 mg induce and maintain clinical remission versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one phase 2b/3 programme, positive at the 200 mg dose only. In SELECTION, filgotinib 200 mg induced clinical remission at week 10 in 26.1% versus 15.3% on placebo in biologic-naive patients (difference 10.8%, p=0.0157) and 11.5% versus 4.2% in biologic-experienced patients (difference 7.2%, p=0.0103); at week 58, remission was 37.2% versus 11.2% in the 200 mg maintenance comparison. The 100 mg dose did not separate from placebo at week 10 and reached significance only at week 58 (23.8% vs 13.5%). Serious adverse events were similar across groups (about 4–5% in induction). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): filgotinib 200 mg induces and maintains remission in ulcerative colitis; the effect is dose-specific and the absolute induction gain is modest, especially after biologics.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — filgotinib 200 mg beat placebo on remission at weeks 10 and 58 in the single SELECTION programme; the 100 mg dose did not separate at induction

title: Vedolizumab for Crohn's disease: maintenance remission 39.0% versus 21.6% at a year — but induction is slow, and the week-6 remission endpoint failed outright after TNF failure
question: In moderately to severely active Crohn's disease, does vedolizumab induce and maintain remission versus placebo?
balance: SPLIT — maintenance works, induction barely does. In GEMINI 2, week-6 clinical remission was 14.5% on vedolizumab versus 6.8% on placebo (P=0.02), but the CDAI-100 response endpoint was not significant (31.4% vs 25.7%, P=0.23); among induction responders, remission at week 52 was 39.0% (every 8 weeks) and 36.4% (every 4 weeks) versus 21.6% on placebo. In GEMINI 3, in patients whose TNF-antagonist treatment had failed, the week-6 remission endpoint was missed (15.2% vs 12.1%, P=0.433) and separation appeared only at week 10 (26.6% vs 12.1%). Serious adverse events were more common on vedolizumab in GEMINI 2 (24.4% vs 15.3%). PROPOSED SPLIT: vedolizumab maintains remission in Crohn's disease and can induce it, but slowly — it is the wrong drug to judge at six weeks, especially after TNF failure.
stamp: SPLIT — maintenance remission clearly positive (39.0% vs 21.6% at week 52); induction weak at week 6 and the primary endpoint missed in TNF-failure patients (GEMINI 3)

title: Acute severe ulcerative colitis after steroid failure: ciclosporin and infliximab are a dead heat in two randomised trials — treatment failure 60% versus 54%, colectomy 48% versus 41%
question: In acute severe ulcerative colitis that has failed intravenous steroids, is ciclosporin as effective as infliximab at avoiding colectomy?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — two randomised head-to-head trials, a decade of practice apart in style, agree there is nothing between the drugs. In CYSIF, treatment failure occurred in 60% on ciclosporin versus 54% on infliximab (absolute difference 6%, 95% CI −7 to 19, p=0.52). In the pragmatic CONSTRUCT trial, quality-adjusted survival did not differ (p=0.603), nor did colectomy: 48% on ciclosporin versus 41% on infliximab (p=0.223). Deaths were few and serious adverse reactions similar in both trials. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): for steroid-refractory acute severe ulcerative colitis, ciclosporin and infliximab are equally effective rescue therapies — the choice turns on centre experience, prior drug exposure and patient factors, not on efficacy.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — treatment failure 60% vs 54% (CYSIF) and no difference in quality-adjusted survival or colectomy (CONSTRUCT) between ciclosporin and infliximab

title: Stopping infliximab in Crohn's remission: about 4 in 10 relapse within a year — but retreatment recaptures remission in almost 9 in 10
question: In Crohn's disease in sustained remission on combination therapy, does stopping infliximab lead to relapse — and can it be recaptured on retreatment?
balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — stopping infliximab in deep remission is usually followed by relapse, though relapse is usually reversible. In the prospective STORI cohort, the 1-year relapse rate after stopping infliximab was 43.9%, and retreatment was effective and well tolerated in 88% of those who relapsed. In the randomised SPARE trial, 2-year relapse was 36% after infliximab withdrawal versus 14% on continued combination therapy (hazard ratio 3.45, 95% CI 1.56–7.69), while stopping the immunosuppressant instead gave 10%; of relapsed patients retreated per protocol, 25 of 28 regained remission, including 22 of 23 after infliximab withdrawal. A low-risk minority exists: STORI patients with at most 2 of its risk factors had a 15% 1-year relapse risk. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm): withdrawing infliximab roughly triples relapse over two years; the harm is bounded by high recapture on retreatment, which is why this is POSSIBLE, not LIKELY.
stamp: POSSIBLE (harm) — relapse 43.9% at 1 year after stopping (STORI cohort) and 36% vs 14% at 2 years in the randomised SPARE trial (HR 3.45); retreatment recaptured remission in 88% (STORI) and 22 of 23 (SPARE)

title: After Crohn's resection: colonoscopy at 6 months with step-up treatment cut endoscopic recurrence at 18 months to 49% versus 67% with standard care (POCER)
question: After ileocolonic resection for Crohn's disease, does colonoscopy-guided step-up treatment prevent endoscopic recurrence better than standard care alone?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one well-run randomised trial. In POCER, patients managed with colonoscopy at 6 months and treatment step-up for endoscopic recurrence had recurrence at 18 months in 49% (60/122) versus 67% (35/52) on standard care (p=0.03), and complete mucosal normality was maintained in 22% versus 8% (p=0.03). Of patients who stepped up for 6-month recurrence, 38% were in remission 12 months later. Adverse events did not differ between groups. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): risk-stratified drug therapy plus a 6-month colonoscopy with step-up prevents endoscopic recurrence after Crohn's resection better than drug therapy alone — a single-trial result, and an endoscopic rather than clinical endpoint.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — endoscopic recurrence at 18 months 49% vs 67% (p=0.03) with 6-month colonoscopy-guided step-up in the single POCER trial

title: Budesonide in Crohn's disease: it induces remission (47% versus 22% on placebo) but does not maintain it — and it is weaker than conventional steroids for induction
question: In ileal or ileocolonic Crohn's disease, does budesonide induce and maintain remission versus placebo or mesalazine?
balance: SPLIT — budesonide starts remission but cannot hold it. For induction, the Cochrane review found budesonide 9 mg superior to placebo at 8 weeks: remission in 47% (115/246) versus 22% (29/133) (relative risk 1.93, 95% CI 1.37–2.73) — but inferior to conventional corticosteroids (52% vs 61% remission; relative risk 0.85, 0.75–0.97), and markedly inferior in severe disease (relative risk 0.52). For maintenance, budesonide 6 mg was no better than placebo at 3, 6 or 12 months (12-month remission 55% vs 48%; relative risk 1.13, 0.94–1.35), with only small gains in CDAI scores and about 60 extra days to relapse. PROPOSED SPLIT: a reasonable gentler induction option for ileal Crohn's, clearly weaker than systemic steroids, and not a maintenance drug.
stamp: SPLIT — induction: superior to placebo (RR 1.93) but inferior to conventional steroids (RR 0.85); maintenance: no better than placebo at 12 months (RR 1.13, not significant)

title: Methotrexate for refractory Crohn's disease: weekly intramuscular high-dose treatment worked in the one large trial (failure to remit 61% versus 81%) — low-dose oral treatment never beat placebo
question: In refractory Crohn's disease, does weekly methotrexate induce remission versus placebo?
balance: SPLIT — the answer splits by dose and route. The Cochrane review of 7 trials (495 patients) found the small low-dose oral methotrexate studies uniformly negative: failure to enter remission was 81% versus 77% on placebo at 12.5 mg/week (relative risk 1.05) and numerically worse than placebo at 15 mg/week (33% vs 11% failing; relative risk 3.00, very wide interval). The one large placebo-controlled trial, using high-dose intramuscular methotrexate, did show benefit: 61% failed to enter remission versus 81% on placebo (relative risk 0.75, 95% CI 0.61–0.93; number needed to treat 5) — at a price: 17% withdrew for adverse events versus 2% on placebo (relative risk 8.00). PROPOSED SPLIT: intramuscular high-dose methotrexate can induce remission in refractory Crohn's; the oral low-dose regimens actually used for convenience have no supporting trial result.
stamp: SPLIT — high-dose intramuscular methotrexate beat placebo in one large trial (RR 0.75 for failure to remit; withdrawals 17% vs 2%); low-dose oral regimens showed no benefit in small trials

title: Infected necrotising pancreatitis: a minimally invasive step-up approach cut death or major complications to 40% versus 69% with open necrosectomy — and the advantage held at 7 years
question: In infected necrotising pancreatitis, does a minimally invasive step-up approach reduce death or major complications versus primary open necrosectomy?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one randomised trial and its own long-term follow-up, both strongly positive on the composite. In PANTER, death or major complications occurred in 40% (17/43) with the step-up approach (percutaneous drainage, then minimally invasive necrosectomy only if needed) versus 69% (31/45) with primary open necrosectomy (risk ratio 0.57, 95% CI 0.38–0.87, p=0.006); 35% of step-up patients needed drainage only. Death alone did not differ (19% vs 16%, p=0.70), but new-onset multiple-organ failure did (12% vs 40%, p=0.002). At a mean of 86 months, death or major complications remained lower with step-up (44% vs 73%, p=0.005), with fewer incisional hernias and less pancreatic insufficiency. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): step-up is the better strategy for infected necrotising pancreatitis; the win is in complications, not in mortality alone.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — death or major complications 40% vs 69% (RR 0.57) in PANTER and 44% vs 73% at 86-month follow-up; mortality alone not significantly different

title: After ERCP in high-risk patients: adding a pancreatic stent to rectal indomethacin does help — pancreatitis 11.3% versus 14.9%, and indomethacin alone failed the non-inferiority test
question: In high-risk patients undergoing ERCP, does a prophylactic pancreatic stent reduce post-ERCP pancreatitis beyond rectal indomethacin?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for the stent, from one large rigorous trial that answered the question the other way than its designers hoped. In 1,950 high-risk patients, post-ERCP pancreatitis occurred in 14.9% (145/975) on rectal indomethacin alone versus 11.3% (110/975) on indomethacin plus a prophylactic pancreatic stent (risk difference 3.6%, 95% CI 0.6–6.6); indomethacin alone failed non-inferiority (p=0.18 for non-inferiority) and a post-hoc analysis found it frankly inferior (p=0.011). Serious adverse events, ICU admission and hospital stay did not differ. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): in high-risk ERCP, the stent adds real protection on top of indomethacin — about 3–4 fewer pancreatitis cases per 100 procedures — so the technically harder combined strategy remains the standard this trial set out to retire.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — post-ERCP pancreatitis 11.3% with indomethacin plus stent vs 14.9% with indomethacin alone in one 1,950-patient non-inferiority trial; indomethacin alone was not non-inferior
