title: Acute pancreatitis fluids: lactated Ringer's beat normal saline on inflammation in a small blinded trial, and a 4-trial meta-analysis found less moderately severe or severe disease (OR 0.49) — on only 248 patients in total
question: In acute pancreatitis, does lactated Ringer's solution reduce systemic inflammation and organ failure compared with normal saline?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — consistent direction, very small evidence base. In the triple-blind de-Madaria trial (40 patients), C-reactive protein at 48 hours was 28 mg/L on lactated Ringer's versus 166 mg/L on normal saline (p=0.037), with a similar gap at 72 hours (25 vs 217 mg/L, p=0.043), though SIRS criteria counts did not differ significantly. Pooling all 4 randomised trials (248 patients), the meta-analysis found lactated Ringer's halved the odds of moderately severe or severe pancreatitis (odds ratio 0.49, 95% CI 0.25–0.97) and reduced ICU admission (odds ratio 0.33, 0.13–0.81) and local complications (odds ratio 0.42, 0.2–0.88) — but found no difference in SIRS at 24 or 48 hours or in organ failure, the outcomes in this shelf's question. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): lactated Ringer's probably causes less inflammation and less severe disease than saline in acute pancreatitis, on evidence far thinner than the confidence of current practice.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — CRP markedly lower in one 40-patient blinded trial and pooled odds of moderately severe/severe pancreatitis 0.49 across 4 small trials; no pooled difference in SIRS or organ failure

title: Faecal microbiota transplant for recurrent hepatic encephalopathy: in a 20-man trial, no FMT patient developed another episode in 5 months versus 5 on standard care — a pilot, not a proof
question: In cirrhosis with hepatic encephalopathy, does faecal microbiota transplant improve cognition and reduce encephalopathy episodes versus standard care?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a striking result in a trial too small to trust on its own. In Bajaj's open-label randomised trial in men with cirrhosis and recurrent hepatic encephalopathy, 5 standard-care patients developed further encephalopathy episodes over 5 months versus none after a single FMT enema (from one rationally selected donor, after antibiotic pretreatment) (P=0.03); serious adverse events occurred in 8 of 10 standard-care patients (11 events) versus 2 of 10 FMT patients, both unrelated to FMT (P=0.02), and cognition improved in the FMT group but not on standard care. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): FMT looks safe and promising for recurrent hepatic encephalopathy in this single small pilot; the effect size is exactly the kind that small open-label trials overstate, so it is held at POSSIBLE and Tier C.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — further encephalopathy episodes in 0 vs 5 patients and fewer serious adverse events over 5 months in one 20-patient open-label trial

title: Peptic ulcer bleeding: scheduled second-look endoscopy does not reduce rebleeding — pooled rebleeding relative risk 0.78 (0.53–1.14) across 1,513 patients, and the one high-risk-selected trial was null too
question: In high-risk peptic ulcer bleeding after successful endoscopic haemostasis, does scheduled second-look endoscopy reduce rebleeding versus on-demand endoscopy?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the routine second look is a ritual the trials do not support. The 2024 systematic review pooled 10 randomised trials (1,513 patients) and found no difference in rebleeding (relative risk 0.78, 95% CI 0.53–1.14), surgery (0.58, 0.29–1.15), mortality (0.89, 0.46–1.71) or transfusion (−0.01 units) between scheduled second-look and single endoscopy, at moderate quality of evidence. The 2022 trial that selected patients predicted to be at high risk of rebleeding — the subgroup most likely to benefit — likewise found no significant difference: clinical bleeding within 30 days in 11.8% with second-look versus 18.2% with observation (absolute difference 6.4%, −5.0 to 17.8), though 30.4% of scoped patients received further endoscopic treatment. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): scheduled second-look endoscopy does not demonstrably reduce rebleeding after successful haemostasis; on-demand re-endoscopy for suspected rebleeding remains the fallback.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — pooled rebleeding RR 0.78 (95% CI 0.53–1.14) across 10 RCTs and no significant benefit in the high-risk-selected RCT

title: Adding Lactobacillus to H. pylori therapy: eradication relative risk 1.063 across 26 trials — a few extra cures per hundred, with genuinely fewer antibiotic side effects
question: Does adding a probiotic to standard eradication therapy improve Helicobacter pylori eradication rates and reduce antibiotic side effects?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — a real but very small eradication gain, and a clearer side-effect gain. Pooling 26 randomised trials, the 2024 meta-analysis found Lactobacillus supplementation raised eradication rates with a per-protocol relative risk of 1.063 (p<0.001) — roughly a 6% relative improvement, a few extra eradications per 100 patients treated — with the clearest subgroup result for adding Lactobacillus to triple therapy (relative risk 1.124). Gastrointestinal side effects fell more substantially: diarrhoea relative risk 0.324, abdominal pain 0.438, nausea/vomiting 0.566, with no significant effect on bloating (0.820). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): the eradication effect is too small to change regimen choice, and this record's own reporting is internally inconsistent (its printed confidence intervals do not match its risk ratios), so the shelf claims only a modest adjunctive nudge, mostly on tolerability.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — eradication RR 1.063 across 26 RCTs (a few extra cures per 100) with larger reductions in diarrhoea (RR 0.324) and abdominal pain (RR 0.438); the record's printed confidence intervals are internally inconsistent

title: Pancreatic enzyme replacement in chronic pancreatitis: fat absorption rose from about 67% to 83% of intake versus placebo across the trials — nutrition and pain improved, on heterogeneous small studies
question: In chronic pancreatitis with exocrine insufficiency, does pancreatic enzyme replacement improve fat absorption, nutrition and pain versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the physiology works in the trials, with wide scatter. The 2017 systematic review pooled 17 studies (511 patients with chronic pancreatitis and exocrine insufficiency): the coefficient of fat absorption on enzyme replacement was 83.2% versus 67.4% on placebo (p=0.0001), and 83.7% versus a 63.1% baseline without treatment (p<0.00001). Enzyme replacement also improved nitrogen absorption, reduced faecal fat, faecal weight and abdominal pain, and follow-up studies showed better nutritional parameters, symptoms and quality of life, without significant adverse events. Heterogeneity was very high (I²=86–89%), and high-dose or enteric-coated preparations trended better. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): enzyme replacement demonstrably corrects fat malabsorption in chronic pancreatitis; the size of the gain in any one patient varies far more than the pooled average suggests.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — coefficient of fat absorption 83.2% vs 67.4% versus placebo across 14 pooled studies, with very high heterogeneity (I²=86%)

title: Vonoprazan for non-erosive reflux heartburn: 44.8% of days heartburn-free versus 27.7% on placebo over 4 weeks — no PPI comparison in the trial
question: In non-erosive reflux disease, does vonoprazan relieve heartburn versus placebo — and versus a proton pump inhibitor?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — versus placebo, clearly; versus a PPI, this record says nothing. In the US randomised trial of 772 patients with non-erosive reflux disease, the percentage of 24-hour heartburn-free days over 4 weeks was 44.8% on vonoprazan 10 mg and 44.4% on 20 mg versus 27.7% on placebo (least-squares mean differences 17.1% and 16.7%, both P<.0001), with separation already on day 1 (8.3% and 11.6% more patients heartburn-free) and benefit persisting through the 20-week extension (61–63% heartburn-free days). The two doses were indistinguishable. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): vonoprazan relieves heartburn in non-erosive reflux disease against placebo in a single trial; the head-to-head against a PPI that the question also asks about was not tested here and remains open.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — 24-hour heartburn-free days 44.8%/44.4% vs 27.7% on placebo at 4 weeks in one 772-patient trial; no PPI arm

title: Mirtazapine for functional dyspepsia with weight loss: early satiation, weight and quality of life improved in a 34-patient pilot — the headline symptom comparison missed significance at week 8
question: In functional dyspepsia with weight loss, does mirtazapine improve early satiation, dyspeptic symptoms and body weight versus placebo?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — a pilot trial whose parts point in different directions. In 34 patients with functional dyspepsia and over 10% weight loss, mirtazapine 15 mg reduced dyspepsia symptom severity from baseline at weeks 4 and 8 (P=.003 and P=.017) while placebo did not — but the between-group difference in change, the comparison that matters, was only a trend at week 4 (P=.059) and not significant at week 8 (P=.55). Improvements from baseline were significantly larger on mirtazapine than placebo for early satiation, quality of life, gastrointestinal-specific anxiety, weight and nutrient tolerance, mostly with large effect sizes. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): in this selected subgroup (weight loss without depression or anxiety), mirtazapine plausibly helps the early-satiation/weight cluster of symptoms; a 34-patient pilot with a missed primary-style comparison cannot carry more than MAYBE.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — secondary endpoints (early satiation, weight, quality of life) favoured mirtazapine in a 34-patient pilot, but the between-group symptom-severity difference was not significant at week 8 (P=.55)

title: Variceal bleeding prophylaxis: a network meta-analysis ranks carvedilol first among beta blockers for survival — but the mortality claim is indirect, and the direct win is on portal-pressure response
question: For primary prophylaxis of variceal bleeding, is carvedilol as effective as propranolol or other non-selective beta blockers?
balance: SPLIT — carvedilol looks at least as good as the older beta blockers everywhere, and better on the measures that are indirect. The 2023 network meta-analysis of 33 randomised trials (3,188 patients with gastroesophageal varices) found, against placebo, variceal-bleeding relative risks of 0.25 for nadolol, 0.33 for carvedilol and 0.52 for propranolol. Carvedilol beat propranolol directly on achieving a hepatic venous pressure gradient response (relative risk 0.43, 95% credible interval 0.26–0.69 for failure to respond), and ranked first for all-cause mortality (relative risk 0.32, 0.17–0.57 versus placebo) — a ranking built largely on indirect comparisons across trials of mixed primary and secondary prophylaxis, which is why the mortality part cannot be stamped as proven. PROPOSED SPLIT: for preventing variceal bleeding, carvedilol is at least propranolol's equal with a better portal-pressure response; the claimed survival advantage rests on network geometry, not on a head-to-head trial, and awaits one.
stamp: SPLIT — bleeding prevention at least equal (network RR vs placebo 0.33 carvedilol, 0.52 propranolol) and HVPG response directly better (RR 0.43), but the first-ranked mortality benefit (RR 0.32) is an indirect network estimate

title: Vaptans in cirrhosis: sodium rose by 1.8 mmol/L and ascites eased slightly — mortality and every cirrhosis complication were unchanged, and adverse events were four times as common
question: In cirrhosis with hyponatraemia or ascites, do vasopressin V2-receptor antagonists (vaptans) raise serum sodium and improve outcomes versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — to the outcomes that matter, with the harm on the face. The 2012 meta-analysis of 12 randomised trials (2,266 patients with cirrhosis and ascites or hyponatraemia) found vaptans raised serum sodium by a weighted mean of 1.8 mmol/L (95% CI 0.79–2.96) and modestly reduced weight and time to first paracentesis — but mortality was unchanged (relative risk 1.06, 0.90–1.26), as were variceal bleeding, hepatic encephalopathy, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, hepatorenal syndrome and renal failure. Adverse events were more frequent on vaptans (relative risk 3.97, 1.78–8.83), including excessive urine volume (relative risk 9.96). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): vaptans correct the number and mobilise some water in cirrhosis, but no trial evidence shows they keep anyone alive or out of the complications that define the disease — and they add adverse events.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — mortality RR 1.06 and no effect on cirrhosis complications across 12 RCTs (2,266 patients), despite a 1.8 mmol/L sodium rise; adverse events RR 3.97

title: Probiotic prophylaxis in predicted severe acute pancreatitis (PROPATRIA): infections unmoved at 30% versus 28% — and mortality doubled, 16% versus 6%, with bowel ischaemia in 9 patients versus none
question: In predicted severe acute pancreatitis, does probiotic prophylaxis prevent infectious complications — or increase mortality?
balance: LIKELY (harm) — the prophylaxis did not prevent infection, and more patients died. In PROPATRIA (Besselink MG et al., PMID: 18279948), 298 patients with predicted severe acute pancreatitis were randomised within 72 hours of symptom onset to a multispecies probiotic preparation (n=153) or placebo (n=145), given enterally twice daily for 28 days; after one incorrect diagnosis was excluded in each group, 152 and 144 patients were analysed. The primary endpoint — the composite of infectious complications (infected pancreatic necrosis, bacteraemia, pneumonia, urosepsis, or infected ascites) during admission and 90-day follow-up — occurred in 46 patients (30%) on probiotics versus 41 (28%) on placebo (relative risk 1.06, 95% CI 0.75–1.51): no benefit. Mortality went the other way: 24 patients (16%) in the probiotics group died, compared with 9 (6%) in the placebo group (relative risk 2.53, 95% CI 1.22–5.25). Nine patients in the probiotics group developed bowel ischaemia (eight with fatal outcome), compared with none in the placebo group (p=0.004). The authors' conclusion was plain: probiotic prophylaxis with this combination of probiotic strains did not reduce infectious complications, was associated with an increased risk of mortality, and should therefore not be administered in this category of patients. The record describes the intervention only as a multispecies probiotic preparation and names no branded product or company, so the harm is pinned to this preparation, given enterally in this dose schedule, in predicted severe disease — not to probiotics in milder illness. PROPOSED LIKELY (harm): in predicted severe acute pancreatitis, probiotic prophylaxis with the PROPATRIA multispecies preparation gave no reduction in infectious complications and doubled mortality, with a bowel-ischaemia signal that supplies a mechanism.
stamp: LIKELY (harm) — in one 298-patient randomised double-blind trial, probiotic prophylaxis did not reduce infectious complications (30% versus 28%; relative risk 1.06) but was associated with doubled mortality (16% versus 6%; relative risk 2.53, 95% CI 1.22–5.25) and bowel ischaemia in 9 patients versus none

title: Predicted severe gallstone pancreatitis without cholangitis: urgent ERCP with sphincterotomy did not reduce death or major complications (38% versus 44%, p=0.37) — cholangitis was the only component that fell
question: In predicted severe acute gallstone pancreatitis without cholangitis, does urgent ERCP with sphincterotomy improve outcomes versus conservative treatment?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — one multicentre randomised trial, adequately sized for its composite, says wait. In APEC, the composite of mortality or major complications within 6 months occurred in 45/117 (38%) with urgent ERCP and sphincterotomy (within 24 hours) versus 50/113 (44%) with conservative treatment (relative risk 0.87, 95% CI 0.64–1.18, p=0.37), with no relevant differences in any component except cholangitis itself (2% vs 10%; relative risk 0.18, 0.04–0.78). Adverse events were reported in 74% versus 80%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): without cholangitis or persistent cholestasis, urgent ERCP does not improve outcomes in predicted severe gallstone pancreatitis — conservative care with ERCP reserved for cholangitis is the strategy the trial supports.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — death or major complications 38% vs 44% (RR 0.87, p=0.37) in the single APEC trial; cholangitis alone fell (2% vs 10%)

title: Gallstone dissolution: adding chenodeoxycholic acid to ursodeoxycholic acid gained nothing — complete dissolution at 2 years 30% versus 28% on ursodeoxycholic acid alone, in a trial with no placebo arm
question: In adults with cholesterol gallstones, does ursodeoxycholic acid — alone or with chenodeoxycholic acid — dissolve stones and prevent symptoms versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — between the two regimens actually compared; the placebo question in this shelf's title was never put to a trial in this record. In the British-Italian Gallstone Study Group trial of 154 patients with radiolucent cholesterol stones up to 15 mm in functioning gallbladders, complete dissolution at 24 months was 28% on ursodeoxycholic acid alone (10 mg/kg/day) versus 30% on the combination with chenodeoxycholic acid (5 mg/kg/day each), with mean dissolution rates of 47% versus 44% at 6 months and 59% versus 59% at 12 months; biliary pain frequency fell on both regimens, with no significant difference in side effects or dropouts. Because there was no placebo or untreated arm, how much dissolution exceeds the natural history of small radiolucent stones cannot be read from this trial. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): combination bile-acid therapy adds nothing to ursodeoxycholic acid alone for stone dissolution; the versus-placebo half of the question is flagged as untested by the anchor record.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — complete dissolution at 24 months 30% (combination) vs 28% (ursodeoxycholic acid alone) in one 154-patient trial with no placebo arm; the placebo comparison in the question is untested by this record

title: Hepatitis C after direct-acting antiviral failure: sofosbuvir–velpatasvir–voxilaprevir cured 96% versus 0% on placebo after NS5A-inhibitor failure, and 98% versus 90% against sofosbuvir–velpatasvir in POLARIS-4
question: In hepatitis C with prior direct-acting antiviral failure, does sofosbuvir–velpatasvir–voxilaprevir achieve sustained virological response?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — two phase 3 trials in the hardest-to-cure population, with response rates near the ceiling. In POLARIS-1 (prior NS5A-inhibitor failure), sustained virological response was 96% on sofosbuvir–velpatasvir–voxilaprevir versus 0% on placebo. In POLARIS-4 (prior direct-acting antiviral failure without an NS5A inhibitor), response was 98% on the triple combination versus 90% on sofosbuvir–velpatasvir. Across both trials 46% of actively treated patients had compensated cirrhosis, results spanned genotypes, and 1% or fewer discontinued for adverse events; the commonest events were headache, fatigue, diarrhoea and nausea. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): 12 weeks of sofosbuvir–velpatasvir–voxilaprevir is a highly effective salvage regimen after direct-acting antiviral failure.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — sustained virological response 96% vs 0% (placebo, POLARIS-1) and 98% vs 90% (sofosbuvir–velpatasvir, POLARIS-4) in two phase 3 trials

title: Gastroparesis drugs ranked: only oral dopamine antagonists and tachykinin-1 antagonists beat placebo in a 29-trial network meta-analysis — clebopride first, domperidone second, confidence low to moderate
question: In gastroparesis, do prokinetic and antiemetic drugs — including domperidone — improve symptoms versus placebo, and how do they rank?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for two drug classes only, on low-to-moderate confidence evidence. In a network meta-analysis of 29 randomised trials (3,772 patients), clebopride ranked first for global gastroparesis symptoms (relative risk of not improving 0.30, 95% CI 0.16–0.57) and domperidone second (RR 0.68, 95% CI 0.48–0.98); no other drug was superior to placebo. At class level, oral dopamine antagonists (RR 0.58, 95% CI 0.44–0.77) and tachykinin-1 antagonists (RR 0.69, 95% CI 0.52–0.93) were the only efficacious classes. Oral metoclopramide ranked first for nausea, fullness and bloating, but on only one small trial. Only prucalopride was more likely than placebo to cause adverse events. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): dopamine antagonists (domperidone the best-evidenced familiar name) and tachykinin-1 antagonists improve global gastroparesis symptoms; most other tested drugs did not beat placebo.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — network meta-analysis of 29 RCTs: oral dopamine antagonists and tachykinin-1 antagonists beat placebo on global symptoms; no other drug class did

title: Tegaserod in women under 65 with IBS-C and no cardiovascular disease: response 44.1% versus 36.5% on placebo across four pooled trials — a real but modest edge, in a drug once withdrawn over cardiac fears
question: In women under 65 with irritable bowel syndrome with constipation and no cardiovascular disease, does tegaserod improve global IBS symptoms versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — modest, and confined to the population the FDA re-approved it for. Pooling four 12-week randomised placebo-controlled trials of tegaserod 6 mg twice daily in IBS-C, the indicated population (women younger than 65 with no history of cardiovascular ischaemic events; 2,752 participants) responded at 44.1% on tegaserod versus 36.5% on placebo (pooled odds ratio 1.38, 95% CI 1.18–1.61; p<0.001); the overall female population (2,939 participants) responded at 43.3% versus 35.9% (OR 1.37, 95% CI 1.18–1.59). Adverse events were similar between groups, and no significant cardiovascular events related to tegaserod were observed in patients with at most one cardiac risk factor. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): tegaserod lifts global IBS-C response by roughly 8 percentage points over placebo in women under 65 without cardiovascular disease.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — pooled analysis of 4 RCTs: tegaserod response 44.1% vs 36.5% on placebo in the FDA-indicated population of women <65 without cardiovascular disease

title: Norursodeoxycholic acid in primary sclerosing cholangitis: alkaline phosphatase fell 12–26% dose-dependently over 12 weeks versus a 1.2% rise on placebo — a blood test, in a disease with no proven therapy
question: In primary sclerosing cholangitis, does norursodeoxycholic acid improve cholestasis biochemistry versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for cholestasis biochemistry only, from a single 12-week phase 2 trial. In 161 patients with primary sclerosing cholangitis and elevated alkaline phosphatase (ALP), norursodeoxycholic acid (norUDCA) reduced ALP by −12.3%, −17.3% and −26.0% at 500, 1,000 and 1,500 mg/day (p=0.029, p=0.003 and p<0.0001 versus placebo), while placebo rose +1.2%; secondary enzymes (ALT, AST, γ-GT) moved the same dose-dependent way. Serious adverse events were scattered across arms (seven, five and two patients on ascending norUDCA doses, three on placebo) with no difference in pruritus. No clinical outcome — transplant, decompensation, death — was or could be tested in 12 weeks. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): norUDCA lowers ALP dose-dependently with a placebo-like safety profile; whether that buys liver outcomes is a phase 3 question.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single phase 2 RCT: norUDCA reduced alkaline phosphatase 12–26% dose-dependently vs +1.2% on placebo over 12 weeks; clinical outcomes untested

title: Maralixibat in childhood PFIC (MARCH-PFIC): itch scores fell 1.1 points more than placebo and serum bile acids by 187 µmol/L more — with diarrhoea in 57% versus 20%
question: In progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis, does maralixibat reduce pruritus and serum bile acids versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one phase 3 trial in a rare childhood disease, hitting both its symptom and its biomarker endpoint. In MARCH-PFIC (93 children aged 1–17 years with PFIC and persistent pruritus), maralixibat improved morning itch scores in the primary BSEP cohort by −1.7 points versus −0.6 on placebo (between-group difference −1.1, 95% CI −1.8 to −0.3; p=0.0063) and cut total serum bile acids by −176 µmol/L versus a rise of 11 µmol/L on placebo (difference −187 µmol/L, 95% CI −293 to −80; p=0.0013). The price was gastrointestinal: diarrhoea in 57% on maralixibat versus 20% on placebo, all mild or moderate and mostly transient; serious treatment-emergent events occurred in 11% versus 7%, with no treatment-related deaths. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): maralixibat relieves PFIC pruritus and lowers bile acids over 26 weeks; longer-term liver outcomes rest on the bile-acid surrogate.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single phase 3 RCT in children with PFIC: itch difference −1.1 points and bile-acid difference −187 µmol/L vs placebo at 26 weeks; diarrhoea 57% vs 20%

title: Naldemedine for opioid-induced constipation (COMPOSE-1 and COMPOSE-2): responders 47.6% and 52.5% versus 34.6% and 33.6% on placebo — pain relief untouched, gut side effects the cost
question: In opioid-induced constipation with chronic non-cancer pain, does naldemedine increase spontaneous bowel movements versus placebo without worsening pain?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two identical phase 3 trials, one answer. In COMPOSE-1 (547 patients with chronic non-cancer pain and opioid-induced constipation), responders — at least three spontaneous bowel movements a week with an increase of at least one over baseline, sustained — were 47.6% on naldemedine 0.2 mg daily versus 34.6% on placebo (difference 13.0%, 95% CI 4.8–21.3; p=0.002); in COMPOSE-2 (553 patients), 52.5% versus 33.6% (difference 18.9%, 95% CI 10.8–27.0; p<0.0001). Overall adverse-event rates matched placebo (49–50% versus 45–48%); the excess was gastrointestinal — treatment-related gut events in 15–16% on naldemedine versus 7% on placebo. As a peripherally acting antagonist, naldemedine is designed not to reach the central receptors that carry analgesia, and the trials enrolled patients on stable opioid regimens. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): naldemedine converts roughly one in six to eight treated patients into responders over placebo, at the price of gut upset in about one in twelve.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two concordant phase 3 RCTs: naldemedine responders 47.6% and 52.5% vs 34.6% and 33.6% on placebo over 12 weeks

title: Green kiwifruit, prunes or psyllium for chronic constipation: all three raised complete spontaneous bowel movements in one small 4-week trial — kiwifruit best tolerated, none proven better than another
question: In chronic constipation, how do green kiwifruit, psyllium and prunes compare for stool frequency and gastrointestinal comfort?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — three familiar foods all helped in one small, short, unblinded trial, and none beat the others. In 79 US adults with chronic constipation randomised to green kiwifruit (2/day), prunes (100 g/day) or psyllium (12 g/day) for 4 weeks, the proportions meeting the primary responder endpoint (an increase of at least one complete spontaneous bowel movement per week for at least 2 of 4 weeks) were similar across groups, while weekly complete spontaneous bowel movement rates rose significantly with all three treatments (p≤0.003). Stool consistency improved with kiwifruit (p=0.01) and prunes (p=0.049); straining improved with all three. Adverse events were most common with psyllium and least with kiwifruit, and fewer kiwifruit patients were dissatisfied at the end of treatment (p=0.02). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): each of the three is a reasonable first food-based step for chronic constipation; superiority of any one is unproven.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — one small 4-week unblinded trial (n=79): kiwifruit, prunes and psyllium each improved stool frequency, with no significant difference between them on the primary endpoint

title: Liraglutide in NASH without needing diabetes (LEAN): steatohepatitis resolved in 39% versus 9% on placebo — in 45 biopsied patients, with fibrosis progression in 9% versus 36%
question: In non-alcoholic steatohepatitis without diabetes, does liraglutide achieve resolution of steatohepatitis versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a striking relative effect on a very small base. In the LEAN trial, 52 overweight patients with clinical evidence of non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (with or without diabetes) were randomised to liraglutide 1.8 mg daily or placebo for 48 weeks; among those with end-of-treatment biopsy, resolution of definite steatohepatitis without worsening fibrosis occurred in 9 of 23 (39%) on liraglutide versus 2 of 22 (9%) on placebo (relative risk 4.3, 95% CI 1.0–17.7; p=0.019), and fibrosis progressed in 2 of 23 (9%) versus 8 of 22 (36%) (RR 0.2, 95% CI 0.1–1.0; p=0.04). Gastrointestinal disorders were commoner on liraglutide (81% versus 65% of patients), including diarrhoea in 38% versus 19%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): LEAN is a genuine proof of concept for GLP-1 therapy in steatohepatitis — and, at 45 biopsied patients, only a proof of concept.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single small phase 2 RCT (LEAN): NASH resolution 39% vs 9% on placebo (RR 4.3) and less fibrosis progression, in 45 patients with paired biopsies

title: Preoperative biliary drainage before pancreatic head cancer surgery: serious complications 74% with drainage versus 39% with early surgery — the drainage itself caused complications in 46%
question: In pancreatic head cancer with obstructive jaundice, does preoperative biliary drainage improve outcomes versus surgery alone?
balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — routine drainage hurt, in the one large randomised trial and in the network evidence behind it. In van der Gaag's multicentre trial, 202 patients with pancreatic head cancer and obstructive jaundice (bilirubin 40–250 µmol/L) were randomised to preoperative biliary drainage for 4–6 weeks or surgery alone within a week: serious complications within 120 days struck 74% of the drainage group versus 39% of the early-surgery group (relative risk in the early-surgery group 0.54, 95% CI 0.41–0.71; p<0.001), with drainage-related complications in 46% of drained patients; surgery-related complications (47% versus 37%), mortality and hospital stay did not differ significantly. A 2018 network meta-analysis of 32 studies likewise ranked no preoperative drainage as the best approach for postoperative complications. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm): routine preoperative biliary drainage in resectable pancreatic head cancer adds complications without improving surgical outcomes — drainage keeps its place for cholangitis, delay or neoadjuvant plans, which this trial did not test.
stamp: POSSIBLE (harm) — one large RCT: serious complications 74% with preoperative drainage vs 39% with early surgery; mortality unchanged; network meta-analysis concordant

title: Single-stage laparoscopic duct exploration versus two-stage ERCP then cholecystectomy: mortality and overall morbidity equal — ERCP clears more ducts and leaks less, LCBDE avoids pancreatitis and shortens stay
question: In choledocholithiasis, does single-stage laparoscopic common bile duct exploration achieve duct clearance and outcomes equal to two-stage ERCP plus laparoscopic cholecystectomy?
balance: SPLIT — the two routes trade complications, and neither wins the outcomes that matter most. In Lyu's meta-analysis of 12 randomised trials (1,545 patients), preoperative ERCP plus laparoscopic cholecystectomy achieved a significantly higher duct stone clearance rate and a significantly lower postoperative bile leakage rate than single-stage laparoscopic common bile duct exploration plus cholecystectomy — but a significantly higher rate of pancreatitis; LCBDE shortened overall hospital stay, and morbidity and mortality did not differ. The Cochrane review (Dasari 2013; five trials, 580 participants for the laparoscopic comparison) likewise found no significant difference in mortality (0.7% versus 1%) or morbidity between laparoscopic clearance and preoperative ERCP. PROPOSED SPLIT: choose by local expertise and by which complication the patient can least afford — pancreatitis and a second procedure on the ERCP side, bile leak and a longer stay on the surgical side.
stamp: SPLIT — clearance and bile leak favour two-stage ERCP, pancreatitis and hospital stay favour single-stage LCBDE; mortality and morbidity do not differ in either meta-analysis

title: Balloon dilation versus sphincterotomy for bile duct stones: overall clearance favours sphincterotomy — unless the balloon is large (≥10 mm), when clearance and pancreatitis match; bleeding is rarer with dilation throughout
question: For removal of common bile duct stones, does endoscopic papillary balloon dilation preserve sphincter function without losing clearance compared with endoscopic sphincterotomy?
balance: SPLIT — by balloon size. In Tringali's cumulative meta-analysis of 25 randomised trials, endoscopic papillary balloon dilation (EPBD) matched sphincterotomy for stone removal at first attempt (odds ratio 0.95, 95% CI 0.65–1.38) but was inferior for overall stone clearance in studies published since 2002 (OR 0.65, 95% CI 0.43–0.99) — except with large balloons (≥10 mm), where clearance matched (OR 1.37, 95% CI 0.72–2.62). Pancreatitis overall did not differ significantly (OR 1.35, 95% CI 0.90–2.03), but was commoner with EPBD when balloons were <10 mm (OR 1.78, 95% CI 1.07–2.97) and not with large balloons (OR 0.84, 95% CI 0.46–1.53); EPBD had lower rates of bleeding and cholecystitis. The earlier Baron meta-analysis (8 trials) found the same shape: similar overall removal (94.3% versus 96.5%) and complications (10.5% versus 10.3%), less bleeding with EPBD (0% versus 2.0%), more pancreatitis (7.4% versus 4.3%). PROPOSED SPLIT: small-balloon dilation loses on clearance and pancreatitis; large-balloon dilation matches sphincterotomy while sparing the sphincter and bleeding less.
stamp: SPLIT — sphincterotomy clears more overall, but large-balloon (≥10 mm) dilation matches its clearance and pancreatitis rates with less bleeding; small-balloon dilation is inferior

title: Metal versus plastic stents for malignant biliary obstruction: metal stays patent far longer (hazard ratio 0.36), needs fewer re-interventions, and pooled survival favoured metal (HR 0.74) across 10 randomised trials
question: In malignant biliary obstruction, do self-expandable metal stents stay patent longer than plastic stents — and at what cost in complications?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — patency decisively, survival modestly, in trial populations. Hong's updated meta-analysis of 10 randomised trials found metal stents associated with significantly longer stent patency than plastic stents (hazard ratio 0.36, 95% CI 0.28–0.47, I²=0%), fewer re-interventions (weighted mean difference 0.59, 95% CI 0.28–0.90) and longer patient survival (HR 0.74, 95% CI 0.64–0.85, I²=16.0%); results held in sensitivity analyses, and no publication bias was observed. The one soft spot: in the hilar-obstruction subgroup, the re-intervention advantage did not reach significance. The record reports no pooled complication penalty against metal to set against these gains — but it also predates much of the covered-versus-uncovered metal stent refinement. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): for palliation of malignant biliary obstruction, metal stents outlast plastic, spare re-interventions and were associated with longer survival; Tier C because the shelf carries a mortality benefit claim.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — meta-analysis of 10 RCTs: metal stents longer patency (HR 0.36), fewer re-interventions, longer survival (HR 0.74) vs plastic stents

title: Tacrolimus versus ciclosporin after liver transplantation: deaths and graft loss lower at one year (RR 0.85 and 0.73), rejection down — de novo diabetes up (RR 1.38), across 16 randomised trials
question: After liver transplantation, does tacrolimus-based immunosuppression reduce rejection and graft loss compared with ciclosporin-based immunosuppression?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — the calcineurin contest was settled by 16 randomised trials, with one named price. McAlister's meta-analysis found one-year mortality (relative risk 0.85, 95% CI 0.73–0.99) and graft loss (RR 0.73, 95% CI 0.61–0.86) significantly reduced with tacrolimus versus ciclosporin, alongside less acute rejection (RR 0.81, 95% CI 0.75–0.88) and far less steroid-resistant rejection (RR 0.54, 95% CI 0.47–0.74). In absolute terms, treating 100 recipients with tacrolimus instead of ciclosporin would avoid graft loss in five and death in two, and rejection in nine — but four additional patients would develop de novo diabetes (RR 1.38, 95% CI 1.01–1.86). More patients stopped ciclosporin than tacrolimus (RR 0.57, 95% CI 0.49–0.66); lymphoproliferative disorder and dialysis rates did not differ. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): tacrolimus is the better default foundation after liver transplantation; Tier C because the shelf carries a mortality benefit claim.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — meta-analysis of 16 RCTs: tacrolimus vs ciclosporin — mortality RR 0.85, graft loss RR 0.73, acute rejection RR 0.81 at 1 year; de novo diabetes RR 1.38

title: Benralizumab in eosinophilic oesophagitis (MESSINA): tissue eosinophils cleared in 87.4% versus 6.5% — but swallowing symptoms did not improve (DSQ difference 3.0 points, p=0.18)
question: In eosinophilic oesophagitis, does benralizumab deplete tissue eosinophils and improve dysphagia versus placebo?
balance: SPLIT — the drug did exactly what it was built to do to the tissue, and the patient felt no better. In the phase 3 MESSINA trial (211 patients aged 12–65 with symptomatic, histologically active eosinophilic oesophagitis), benralizumab produced a histologic response (≤6 eosinophils per high-power field) in 87.4% versus 6.5% on placebo at week 24 (difference 80.8 percentage points, 95% CI 72.9–88.8; p<0.001) — but the change in Dysphagia Symptom Questionnaire score did not differ significantly (difference in least-squares means 3.0 points, 95% CI −1.4 to 7.4; p=0.18), and neither did the endoscopic reference score. Adverse events were reported in 64.1% on benralizumab and 61.7% on placebo, with no discontinuations for adverse events. PROPOSED SPLIT: benralizumab is a proven eosinophil-depleting drug and an unproven dysphagia treatment — in EoE, clearing eosinophils and relieving symptoms have come apart.
stamp: SPLIT — histologic response 87.4% vs 6.5% (p<0.001) but dysphagia scores unchanged (p=0.18) in the single phase 3 MESSINA trial

title: Pure oats on a gluten-free diet in coeliac disease: no signal of mucosal relapse, symptoms or serology harm across 28 studies — but the evidence quality is low and every trial used uncontaminated oats
question: In coeliac disease, can pure oats be added safely to a gluten-free diet without causing mucosal relapse?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference) — adding pure oats changed nothing measurable, in low-quality evidence. Pinto-Sánchez's systematic review and meta-analysis (28 eligible studies; eight controlled trials totalling 661 patients, the rest observational) found oat consumption for 12 months did not affect symptoms (standardised mean difference −0.22, 95% CI −0.56 to 0.13; p=0.22), histologic findings (relative risk 0.24, 95% CI 0.01–4.8; p=0.35) or serologic tests, with no adult-versus-child subgroup differences — but the overall quality of evidence was rated low. The landmark Janatuinen trial behind much of the data randomised 92 adults to gluten-free diets with or without 50–70 g/day of oats and found no differences in symptoms, nutrition or duodenal architecture over 6–12 months. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference): pure, uncontaminated oats appear safe for most people with coeliac disease — the catch is 'pure', since commercial oats are commonly contaminated with wheat, and the trial evidence cannot vouch for those.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference) — meta-analysis of 28 studies found no effect of adding pure oats on symptoms, histology or serology; evidence quality low, all RCTs used uncontaminated oats

title: Transoral incisionless fundoplication (TEMPO) at 5 years: troublesome regurgitation eliminated in 86% and daily PPI use down from 100% to 34% — but after the 6-month randomised phase everyone had the procedure, so the long term is uncontrolled
question: In gastro-oesophageal reflux disease with incomplete response to a proton pump inhibitor, does transoral incisionless fundoplication eliminate reflux symptoms versus sham or continued PPI?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — durable symptom relief in the patients followed, on evidence that stops being randomised at 6 months. TEMPO randomised 63 patients with troublesome reflux refractory to PPI therapy, hiatal hernia ≤2 cm and abnormal acid exposure to transoral incisionless fundoplication (TIF 2.0) or continued PPI; after the 6-month evaluation every PPI-group patient elected crossover to TIF, so all 63 underwent the procedure. At 5 years (44 patients available), troublesome regurgitation was eliminated in 86% and troublesome atypical symptoms resolved in 80%; daily PPI use had fallen from 100% at screening to 34%; GERD health-related quality-of-life score improved from 22.2 to 6.8 (p<0.001); there were three reoperations and no serious adverse events. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): TIF gives sustained relief for most selected patients at 5 years — with the selection (small hernia, PPI-refractory but procedure-suitable) and the uncontrolled follow-up printed on the shelf, and no sham comparison anywhere in this record.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — TEMPO 5-year report: regurgitation eliminated in 86% and daily PPI use 34% vs 100% at screening; randomised comparison ended at 6 months by crossover, long-term data uncontrolled

title: Testosterone in men with cirrhosis and low testosterone: appendicular lean mass +1.69 kg and total lean mass +4.74 kg over 12 months versus placebo — mortality 16% versus 25.5%, not significant
question: In men with cirrhosis, low testosterone and sarcopenia, does testosterone therapy increase muscle mass versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for body composition, from the first and only randomised trial of its kind. Sinclair randomised 101 men with established cirrhosis and low testosterone to intramuscular testosterone undecanoate or placebo for 12 months: appendicular lean mass was higher on testosterone (mean adjusted difference +1.69 kg, 95% CI +0.40 to +2.97; p=0.021), as was total lean mass (+4.74 kg, 95% CI +1.75 to +7.74; p=0.008), while fat mass fell (−4.34 kg, 95% CI −6.65 to −2.04; p<0.001); bone mass, femoral-neck bone density, haemoglobin (+10.2 g/L) and HbA1c (−0.35%) also favoured testosterone. Mortality was 16% versus 25.5% — lower, but not significantly (p=0.352) — and adverse events were not increased. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): testosterone rebuilds muscle and bone in hypogonadal men with cirrhosis over a year; whether that converts into survival needs the larger trial the authors call for.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single RCT (n=101): testosterone increased appendicular lean mass by +1.69 kg and total lean mass by +4.74 kg vs placebo at 12 months; mortality difference not significant

title: Sertraline versus rifampicin for cholestatic pruritus: itch improved on both, no difference between them (p=0.740) — in 36 patients over 4 weeks, with liver enzymes favouring sertraline
question: In cholestatic pruritus, is sertraline as effective as rifampicin for itch relief?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference) — between the two drugs, in one very small single-blind trial. Ataei randomised 36 patients with primary sclerosing cholangitis or primary biliary cholangitis and cholestatic pruritus to sertraline 100 mg/day or rifampin (rifampicin) 300 mg/day for 4 weeks: pruritus relieved in both groups with no significant difference between sertraline and rifampin (p=0.740), and total bilirubin likewise did not differ significantly (p=0.106), while ALT, AST and ALP levels differed significantly between groups (p<0.01) in sertraline's favour on hepatic safety. With 18 patients per arm and no placebo group, 'no difference found' is a long way from 'equally effective' — the trial could not have detected anything but a very large gap. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference): sertraline is a plausible rifampicin alternative when rifampicin's interactions or hepatotoxicity loom, on evidence that is suggestive at best.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference) — one single-blind RCT (n=36, 4 weeks): no significant difference in itch relief between sertraline and rifampin (p=0.740); liver enzymes favoured sertraline

title: Soluble fibre (psyllium) for IBS in primary care: responders 57% versus 35% on placebo in month 1 and 59% versus 41% in month 2 — bran helped later and worsened symptoms early, dropping out more
question: In irritable bowel syndrome in primary care, does soluble fibre (psyllium) improve symptoms versus placebo or insoluble bran?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for psyllium, not for bran, in the one large primary-care trial, backed by the wider meta-analysis. Bijkerk randomised 275 patients aged 18–65 with IBS in general practice to 10 g/day psyllium (n=85), bran (n=97) or placebo (rice flour, n=93) for 12 weeks: responders were 57% versus 35% for psyllium versus placebo in month 1 (relative risk 1.60, 95% CI 1.13–2.26) and 59% versus 41% in month 2 (RR 1.44, 95% CI 1.02–2.06); bran beat placebo only in month 3 (57% versus 32%; RR 1.70, 95% CI 1.12–2.57), a result that lost significance in the worst-case analysis. Symptom severity fell 90 points on psyllium versus 49 on placebo (p=0.03); quality of life did not differ. Ford's meta-analysis of 12 fibre trials (591 patients) likewise found the fibre effect limited to ispaghula (psyllium): RR of persistent symptoms 0.78 (95% CI 0.63–0.96), versus 0.87 (0.76–1.00) for fibre overall. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): psyllium is the only fibre with a demonstrated IBS benefit in primary care — and the distinction between soluble and insoluble fibre is the point of the shelf.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — psyllium responders 57% vs 35% (month 1) and 59% vs 41% (month 2) vs placebo in a 275-patient primary-care RCT, supported by a meta-analysis limited to ispaghula

title: Total (Nissen) versus posterior partial (Toupet) fundoplication: reflux recurrence equal (OR 0.69, p=0.31) but long-term dysphagia far commoner after Nissen (OR 2.92) across 8 randomised trials
question: In gastro-oesophageal reflux disease, does posterior partial fundoplication cause less dysphagia than total (Nissen) fundoplication without losing reflux control?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — posterior partial fundoplication keeps reflux control and spares swallowing, in pooled randomised evidence. Peristeri's systematic review and meta-analysis of eight randomised trials (1,545 patients; 799 total [Nissen] and 746 posterior partial [Toupet]) found long-term recurrence of gastro-oesophageal reflux disease was not statistically different between the techniques (odds ratio 0.69, 95% CI 0.34–1.41; p=0.31), while long-term dysphagia was statistically lower with posterior partial fundoplication (OR 2.92, 95% CI 1.49–5.72; p=0.002) with low between-study heterogeneity (I²=0%). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): for patients without dysmotility disorders, posterior partial fundoplication is the better balance — equivalent reflux control with less dysphagia.

title: Outpatient diverticulitis without antibiotics (DINAMO): admissions 3.3% versus 5.8% with antibiotics — noninferior at 90 days, but read alongside the inpatient no-antibiotic trials on live shelf #178
question: In mild acute uncomplicated diverticulitis, is outpatient treatment without antibiotics as safe and effective as treatment with antibiotics?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — for the outpatient setting specifically, in one open-label noninferiority trial. DINAMO randomised 480 patients with CT-diagnosed mild acute diverticulitis presenting to the emergency department to outpatient treatment without antibiotics (n=242) or with amoxicillin/clavulanic acid (n=238), plus anti-inflammatory and symptomatic care: hospital admissions were 3.3% (8/242) without antibiotics versus 5.8% (14/238) with antibiotics (mean difference 2.58%, 95% CI −1.17 to 6.32), confirming noninferiority; emergency revisits were 7.0% versus 6.7% (mean difference −0.3, 95% CI −4.83 to 4.22), and poor pain control at 2 days was 2.3% versus 5.7%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): mild diverticulitis can be managed at home without antibiotics; the shelf is deliberately distinct from — and cross-points to — live shelf #178, which asks the no-antibiotics question for CT-proven uncomplicated diverticulitis without the outpatient setting (the coordinator's one-home adjudication is requested on the face of the summary).
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — single RCT (DINAMO, n=480): outpatient treatment without antibiotics noninferior — admissions 3.3% vs 5.8%, revisits 7.0% vs 6.7% at 90 days

title: Laparoscopic lavage versus sigmoidectomy for perforated diverticulitis (LOLA, 3 years): no difference in morbidity (84% vs 72%) or mortality (16% vs 18%) — but fewer reoperations and fewer stomas alive at 3 years, at the price of sigmoidectomy in 45% of lavage patients
question: In perforated diverticulitis with purulent peritonitis, does laparoscopic peritoneal lavage avoid stoma and match sigmoidectomy on outcomes?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — for morbidity and mortality, with a real stoma benefit bought at a cost. In the LOLA arm of the LADIES trial, 88 patients with purulent perforated diverticulitis were randomised to laparoscopic lavage or sigmoidectomy: at 12 months the composite of major morbidity and mortality occurred in 67% after lavage versus 60% after sigmoidectomy (odds ratio 1.28, 95% CI 0.54–3.03; p=0.58), with four deaths after lavage and six after sigmoidectomy. By 36 months, in the 77 patients with long-term follow-up, cumulative morbidity was 84% versus 72% (p=0.272) and mortality 16% versus 18% (p=1.000); reoperations were significantly fewer after lavage (45% versus 69%, p=0.039), patients alive with a stoma were fewer (11% versus 17%, log-rank p=0.0268) — but 45% of lavage patients had eventually undergone sigmoidectomy. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): lavage does not match sigmoidectomy's safety case at 12 months and leaves nearly half needing the operation it was meant to avoid — the stoma advantage is real but selective, and better patient selection is the open question.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — LADIES/LOLA: morbidity and mortality equal at 12 months (67% vs 60%) and 36 months; reoperations fewer (45% vs 69%) and stoma rates lower, but 45% of lavage patients later had sigmoidectomy

title: Dapagliflozin for liver fat in type 2 diabetes with fatty liver: MRI liver fat fell significantly versus control at 24 weeks — but the absolute fat loss is unpublished in the abstract, and monotherapy did not beat placebo in the second trial
question: In type 2 diabetes with fatty liver, does dapagliflozin reduce liver fat content versus control treatment?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — on MRI fat, in two small 12–24-week trials whose reporting leaves the effect size half-told. Shi randomised 84 patients with type 2 diabetes and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease to dapagliflozin or a control group: at week 24 liver fat content (p<0.001) and pancreatic fat content (p=0.033) were significantly reduced versus control, along with ALT (p<0.001), TNF-α (p=0.004) and IL-6 (p=0.001) — but the abstract prints no absolute liver-fat values, so the size of the reduction cannot be stated from this record. Eriksson's EFFECT-II (84 participants, 12 weeks, four arms) found dapagliflozin reduced liver PDFF by 13% relative to baseline, omega-3 carboxylic acids by 15% and the combination by 21% — yet only the combination reduced liver PDFF versus placebo (p=0.046; liver fat volume −24%, p=0.037), while dapagliflozin monotherapy reduced all measured hepatocyte injury biomarkers. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): dapagliflozin reduces liver fat, with the honest caveat that the placebo-controlled trial found monotherapy's fat reduction significant only against baseline, not against placebo.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two small RCTs: dapagliflozin significantly reduced MRI liver fat vs control at 24 weeks (Shi), but monotherapy did not beat placebo on liver fat in EFFECT-II; Tier C

title: Green-Mediterranean diet in fatty liver (DIRECT PLUS): intrahepatic fat fell 38.9% proportionally versus 19.6% on a standard Mediterranean diet and 12.2% on healthy guidelines — at the same weight loss as Mediterranean
question: In fatty liver disease, does a green-Mediterranean diet reduce intrahepatic fat more than other healthy diets?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one large, long dietary trial with imaging endpoints. In DIRECT PLUS, 294 participants with abdominal obesity or dyslipidaemia were randomised for 18 months to healthy dietary guidelines, a Mediterranean diet, or a green-Mediterranean diet (further restricted in red/processed meat, enriched with green tea, walnuts and the aquatic plant Mankai — Wolffia globosa, as named in the publication): intrahepatic fat fell by 38.9% proportionally on green-Mediterranean versus 19.6% on Mediterranean (p=0.035, weight-loss adjusted) and 12.2% on healthy guidelines (p<0.001), despite similar weight loss in the two Mediterranean groups. Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease prevalence after 18 months was 31.5% on green-Mediterranean versus 47.9% on Mediterranean and 54.8% on guidelines (p=0.012 between groups). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the green-Mediterranean pattern roughly doubles intrahepatic fat loss over a standard Mediterranean diet at equal weight loss — a single-trial, surrogate-imaging result, Tier C.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single RCT (DIRECT PLUS, n=294, 18 months): green-Mediterranean diet reduced intrahepatic fat by 38.9% proportionally vs 19.6% (Mediterranean) and 12.2% (guidelines)

title: Band ligation versus beta blockers to prevent first variceal bleeding: bleeding was lower with ligation only in trials with unclear bias control (RR 0.56) — in adequately controlled trials there was no difference (RR 0.86), and mortality never differed (116/573 vs 115/594)
question: For primary prevention of variceal bleeding, does endoscopic band ligation prevent first bleeding better than beta blockers — and does either reduce mortality?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for first bleeding only, and only on the weaker half of the evidence. Gluud's meta-analysis of 16 randomised trials of band ligation versus beta blockers for primary prophylaxis of oesophageal varices found no mortality difference in any analysis — 116 of 573 patients died on ligation versus 115 of 594 on beta blockers overall; relative risk 1.22 (95% CI 0.84–1.78) in trials with adequate bias control and 1.02 (0.75–1.39) in trials with unclear bias control. Bleeding told two stories: no significant difference in the adequately controlled trials (RR 0.86, 95% CI 0.55–1.35), but significantly less bleeding with ligation in the unclear-bias trials (RR 0.56, 95% CI 0.41–0.77); metaregression showed ligation's estimated benefit grew the shorter the follow-up and when trials were published as abstracts. The best-known single trial (Sarin 1999) did favour ligation: actuarial bleeding probability at 18 months 15% versus 43% on propranolol (p=0.04), with five deaths in each group. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): ligation probably prevents some first bleeds that beta blockers do not — the unbiased trials cannot confirm it — and neither strategy has ever been shown to save lives in this comparison; Tier C, because the benefit claim rests on bias-prone trials.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — meta-analysis of 16 RCTs: ligation reduced first bleeding only in unclear-bias trials (RR 0.56); adequate-bias trials RR 0.86 (NS); mortality identical (116/573 vs 115/594)

title: Spironolactone alone matched spironolactone plus furosemide for moderate ascites — 94% versus 98% responded, and the single drug needed half as many dose reductions
question: In moderate ascites in cirrhosis, is spironolactone alone as effective as spironolactone combined with furosemide?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — for clearing moderate ascites, starting with two diuretics bought nothing over starting with one. In the one head-to-head randomised trial (Santos J et al., PMID: 12873814), ascites responded in 98% on spironolactone plus furosemide versus 94% on spironolactone alone, with similar speed of mobilisation and similar complication rates — but the combination group needed its dose reduced far more often (68% versus 34%, P=0.002), the practical price of starting with both. The older head-to-head that frames the question (Pérez-Ayuso RM et al., PMID: 6339312) found spironolactone alone answered in 18 of 19 patients (95%) against 11 of 21 (52%) on furosemide alone (p<0.01), and 9 of the 10 furosemide failures later responded to spironolactone — spironolactone is the load-bearing drug of the pair. Neither trial was powered for survival, kidney failure, or hospitalisation, and both predate modern ascites care. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): spironolactone alone clears moderate ascites as reliably as the combination, with fewer dose adjustments; the combination remains the escalation step, not the starting step.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — spironolactone alone responded in 94% versus 98% on the combination in the single head-to-head trial, with half as many dose reductions

title: Larazotide in coeliac gluten challenge: the permeability endpoint failed in both trials — symptoms and antibody rises were blunted at the lowest dose instead
question: In coeliac disease undergoing gluten challenge, does larazotide acetate prevent gluten-induced mucosal injury and symptoms versus placebo?
balance: SPLIT — the endpoint the drug was built for failed; the symptoms moved. Larazotide acetate, a tight-junction regulator peptide, did not significantly change the urinary lactulose-to-mannitol (LAMA) permeability ratio versus placebo in either gluten-challenge trial (Kelly CP et al., PMID: 23163616, n=184; Leffler DA et al., PMID: 22825365, n=86) — and neither trial measured mucosal histology, so 'mucosal injury prevented' was never directly tested. What did move were symptoms and immune reactivity at the lowest dose: in Kelly 2013, larazotide 1 mg limited gluten-induced symptoms (P=0.002 versus placebo), and the anti-tissue-transglutaminase IgA rise was a mean ratio of 19.0 over baseline on placebo versus 5.78, 3.88, and 7.72 on larazotide 1, 4, and 8 mg (P=0.010, 0.005, and 0.025). The 2022 meta-analysis of four randomised trials (626 patients; Hoilat GJ et al., PMID: 34339872) confirms the split: no LAMA difference in any analysis, significantly better symptom scores only in the gluten-challenge subgroup. Adverse event rates were similar to placebo in both trials. PROPOSED SPLIT: larazotide blunts gluten-induced symptoms and antibody response at low doses, but its permeability primary endpoint — the closest proxy these trials offer for mucosal protection — was null throughout.
stamp: SPLIT — permeability endpoint null in both challenge trials and in meta-analysis; gastrointestinal symptoms and anti-transglutaminase rise improved at the 1 mg dose

title: Survodutide in MASH with fibrosis: steatohepatitis improved without worsening fibrosis in 47%, 62% and 43% across the three doses versus 14% on placebo — one phase 2 trial, a biopsy surrogate, and a dose response that peaked in the middle
question: In metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis with fibrosis, does survodutide improve steatohepatitis without worsening fibrosis versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — on liver histology at 48 weeks, in a single phase 2 trial. In Sanyal AJ et al. (PMID: 38847460), 293 adults with biopsy-confirmed metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) and fibrosis stage F1 through F3 were randomly assigned in a 1:1:1:1 ratio to once-weekly subcutaneous survodutide 2.4 mg, 4.8 mg or 6.0 mg, or placebo, over 48 weeks (a 24-week rapid-dose-escalation phase followed by a 24-week maintenance phase). The primary end point — histologic improvement in MASH with no worsening of fibrosis — occurred in 47% of the 2.4-mg group, 62% of the 4.8-mg group and 43% of the 6.0-mg group, versus 14% on placebo (P<0.001 for the quadratic dose-response curve as best-fitting model). Secondary end points moved the same way: a decrease in liver fat content by at least 30% occurred in 63%, 67% and 57% across the survodutide doses versus 14% on placebo, and improvement in fibrosis by at least one stage in 34%, 36% and 34% versus 22%. The price was gastrointestinal: nausea in 66% on survodutide versus 23% on placebo, diarrhoea in 49% versus 23%, and vomiting in 41% versus 4%; serious adverse events occurred in 8% with survodutide and 7% with placebo. The authors concluded that survodutide was superior to placebo for improvement in MASH without worsening of fibrosis, warranting further investigation in phase 3 trials. The catches are on the face of the record: the end point is a biopsy surrogate with no liver-outcome data, the dose response was non-monotonic (the highest dose did worse than the middle dose on the primary end point), and one phase 2 trial is the whole evidence base. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): in MASH with fibrosis stage F1–F3, once-weekly survodutide improved steatohepatitis without worsening fibrosis in roughly half to three-fifths of patients versus 14% on placebo at 48 weeks, with frequent gastrointestinal adverse events — a single-trial, surrogate-endpoint result awaiting phase 3 confirmation.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in one 293-patient phase 2 trial, survodutide improved MASH without worsening fibrosis in 47% (2.4 mg), 62% (4.8 mg) and 43% (6.0 mg) versus 14% on placebo at 48 weeks, with nausea in 66% versus 23%; histology is a surrogate and the dose response peaked at the middle dose

title: Which lifestyle change cuts liver fat most? The Cochrane network meta-analysis of 59 trials could not rank them — the data were too sparse for any clinical outcome
question: In non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, which lifestyle modification — aerobic exercise, resistance exercise, diet, or combinations — reduces liver fat most?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference) — not because lifestyle change was shown not to work, but because the comparative evidence cannot crown a winner. The Cochrane network meta-analysis built for exactly this question (Buzzetti E et al., PMID: 34114650) included 59 randomised trials with 3,631 participants and 33 different interventions, yet found the data too sparse for the clinical outcomes: only 28 trials (1,942 participants) reported any outcome of interest, follow-up ran from 1 month to 24 months, and clinical events — death, cirrhosis, decompensation, transplantation, liver cancer — were so sparse that the planned network rankings could not be estimated and only direct head-to-head comparisons were performed. All but two trials were at high risk of bias. The review's own conclusion is that there is considerable uncertainty about the effects of lifestyle interventions versus no additional intervention on any clinical outcome over this follow-up, and it proposes aerobic exercise plus dietary advice as the combination to test in long trials — a research agenda, not a ranking. No liver-fat effect sizes that would order aerobic against resistance against diet are reported in the record. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference): on current randomised evidence no lifestyle modality can be ranked above the others for fatty liver; the honest answer to 'which most' is that the trials have not been built to say.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference) — the 59-trial Cochrane network meta-analysis found data too sparse to rank lifestyle interventions or show clinical-outcome differences

title: Branched-chain amino acids in hepatic encephalopathy: oral trials improve symptoms (Marchesini 1990: 80% vs 35% improved) — acute intravenous trials null, survival unchanged (RR 0.88)
question: In hepatic encephalopathy, do branched-chain amino acids improve symptoms or survival versus control diets?
balance: SPLIT — but the split runs by route and by outcome, and the oral limb is stronger than a bare SPLIT implies. ORAL BCAA for encephalopathy manifestations: the classic trials line up. Marchesini 1990 (PMID: 2204661; double-blind, casein-controlled, n=64) improved the portal-systemic encephalopathy index (40→21% vs 37→36%) with 80% vs 35% of patients improving on two or more measures (p<0.001); the double-blind crossovers Egberts 1985 (PMID: 3882509) and Plauth 1993 (PMID: 8315258) each found significant psychomotor gains in latent encephalopathy; and Horst 1984 (PMID: 6706302) showed oral BCAA lets protein-intolerant patients take protein-equivalent nitrogen with far fewer encephalopathy episodes (stage 2 or greater: 1 of 17 vs 7 of 20). Against that: Eriksson 1982 (PMID: 6749604) was null — in 7 patients — and the largest oral trial, Les 2011 (PMID: 21326220, n=116), missed its recurrence endpoint (47% vs 34% remaining episode-free, P=0.274) while still improving neuropsychological tests and muscle mass. The Cochrane pool (Gluud 2017, PMID: 28518283; 16 trials, 827 participants) puts failure to improve at RR 0.73 (0.61–0.88), graded high-quality evidence — a LIKELY-grade symptom benefit for the oral route. ACUTE INTRAVENOUS BCAA is a different story: Wahren 1983 (PMID: 6345330; improvement 14 of 25 vs 12 of 25), Vilstrup 1990 (PMID: 2195106; 17 woke in each group) and Michel 1985 (PMID: 4079669; improved 12 of 36 vs 10 of 34) are all null, Rossi-Fanelli 1982 (PMID: 6749458) was not significant against lactulose (complete recovery 70% vs 47%), and the single positive acute trial, Cerra 1985 (PMID: 3892073), beat neomycin — an active control — without printing event counts. SURVIVAL: no trial shows a mortality benefit; pooled mortality is RR 0.88 (0.69–1.11), not significant. Two large trials in broader cirrhosis populations (Marchesini 2003, PMID: 12806613; Muto 2005, PMID: 16206505) found fewer composite cirrhosis events on long-term oral BCAA — context for biological activity, not encephalopathy or mortality evidence. Against lactulose or neomycin directly, no significant symptom edge was shown (RR 0.66, 0.34–1.30), and gastrointestinal upset is the cost (nausea/vomiting RR 5.56 in the review's fixed-effect analysis). PROPOSED SPLIT: LIKELY benefit for encephalopathy symptoms with oral BCAA; no demonstrated benefit for acute intravenous use or for survival. EXPANSION (Nov 18, 2026 — 10 references added, developer's verdict pending): the Cochrane review has been updated (Aamann 2026, PMID: 41542879; 18 trials, 934 participants): encephalopathy non-improvement RR 0.79 (0.64–0.96) and mortality RR 0.89 (0.71–1.12), with certainty graded low and very low respectively — the point estimates confirm the 2017 pool while the certainty language softens. The intravenous limb gains a modern trial and its own meta-analysis: Mehtani 2023 (PMID: 37975059) found a 24-hour improvement that was not sustained in ACLF, and Yokobori 2025 (PMID: 39780295) pooled the acute intravenous trials to a null (consciousness RR 1.26, 0.96–1.66; mortality RR 0.90, 0.70–1.16). The oral limb gains one modern pilot (Vidot 2019, PMID: 31390762) whose BCAA-alone arm did not separate from placebo. Six nutritional-context references now support the surrounding limbs without changing the stamp: albumin (Konstantis 2022, PMID: 35500317, SMD 0.52 across 20 cirrhosis trials; Nakaya 2007, PMID: 17234504; Takeshita 2009, PMID: 19285598), muscle (Ismaiel 2022, PMID: 35155535 — indices up, grip unchanged), late evening snacks (Chen 2019, PMID: 30883904 — less ascites and encephalopathy with snacks of mixed composition) and Japanese granules (Kobayashi 2008, PMID: 18297438 — null in compensated cirrhosis). The stamp is unchanged by the expansion.
stamp: SPLIT — LIKELY (benefit) for encephalopathy symptoms with oral BCAA; POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for acute intravenous BCAA; mortality not improved (RR 0.88, not significant)

title: Mobile stroke units: 90-day outcomes better in both large prospective studies and the pooled analysis — excellent outcome odds up by about two-thirds, thrombolysis about half an hour sooner
question: In acute ischaemic stroke, does dispatching a mobile stroke unit — a CT-equipped ambulance that starts thrombolysis before hospital arrival — improve functional outcome at 90 days versus conventional ambulance care?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — consistent, sizeable, and entirely non-randomised at the level of the individual patient. In Berlin's B_PROUD study (Ebinger M et al., PMID: 33528537; 1,543 patients), dispatch of a mobile stroke unit (MSU) was associated with lower disability at 3 months (median modified Rankin Scale 1 versus 2; common odds ratio for worse outcome 0.71, 95% CI 0.58 to 0.86), with death in 7.1% versus 8.8% on the coprimary disability scale. In the US BEST-MSU study (Grotta JC et al., PMID: 34496173; 1,515 enrolled, 1,047 thrombolysis-eligible), patients on MSU weeks reached thrombolysis at a median 72 versus 108 minutes, 97.1% of eligible patients were treated versus 79.5%, excellent outcome (mRS 0–1) was 55.0% versus 44.4%, and 90-day mortality was 8.9% versus 11.9%. The 2022 systematic review and meta-analysis (Turc G et al., PMID: 35129584) pools the field in the same direction: excellent outcome adjusted odds ratio 1.64 (1.27 to 2.13; 5 studies, 3,228 patients), onset-to-thrombolysis shortened by a median 31 minutes, and no increase in mortality or symptomatic haemorrhage. No study randomised individual patients — B_PROUD allocated by MSU availability and BEST-MSU by alternating weeks — so system and selection effects cannot be fully excluded. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): MSUs speed thrombolysis and are associated with better 90-day function, on prospective but non-randomised evidence.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — excellent 90-day outcome adjusted OR 1.64 in meta-analysis and better disability scores in both large prospective studies, all non-randomised designs

title: Straight to thrombectomy versus the drip first: the largest trial met its non-inferiority margin — the pooled analysis of all six trials did not
question: In large-vessel-occlusion stroke treated with thrombectomy, does going straight to thrombectomy match bridging intravenous thrombolysis first — or does skipping the drip lose recanalisation and outcome?
balance: SPLIT — the answer depends on which evidence you stand on, and the bigger evidence is the cautious one. The IRIS collaboration's individual-participant meta-analysis of all six randomised trials (Majoie CB et al., PMID: 37640037; 2,313 patients presenting directly to thrombectomy centres) found a 90-day outcome shift favouring bridging (median mRS 2 with thrombolysis plus thrombectomy versus 3 with thrombectomy alone; adjusted common odds ratio 0.89, 95% CI 0.76 to 1.04 for thrombectomy alone) and did NOT establish non-inferiority against its prespecified 0.82 lower boundary; symptomatic haemorrhage and mortality did not differ significantly, though any intracranial haemorrhage was less frequent without the drip (odds ratio 0.82, 0.68 to 0.99). The largest single trial, DIRECT-MT (Yang P et al., PMID: 32374959; 656 patients in China), did meet its own wider non-inferiority margin (adjusted common OR 1.07, 0.81 to 1.40) — yet even there, successful reperfusion before thrombectomy was 2.4% without alteplase versus 7.0% with it, and overall successful reperfusion was 79.4% versus 84.5%; mortality was 17.7% versus 18.8%. So skipping the drip loses early reperfusion, has not been proven equal on outcome in the pooled data, and saves some non-symptomatic bleeding. PROPOSED SPLIT: non-inferiority shown in one large trial under its own margin, not established when all six trials are pooled.
stamp: SPLIT — DIRECT-MT met its non-inferiority margin (acOR 1.07) but the six-trial IRIS pooled analysis did not (acOR 0.89, lower CI below its 0.82 boundary)

title: Late-window thrombectomy works: functional independence 49% versus 13% (DAWN) and 45% versus 17% (DEFUSE 3) in imaging-selected patients 6–24 hours after onset
question: In patients with large-vessel occlusion presenting 6–24 hours after onset selected by clinical–core or perfusion mismatch, does thrombectomy improve functional outcome versus medical care alone?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — two trials, stopped early for efficacy, with effects too large to be fragile. In DAWN (Nogueira RG et al., PMID: 29129157; 206 patients last known well 6–24 hours earlier with a clinical-deficit/infarct mismatch), functional independence at 90 days was 49% with thrombectomy versus 13% with standard care (adjusted difference 33 percentage points, 95% credible interval 24 to 44), and the utility-weighted disability score was 5.5 versus 3.4 (adjusted difference 2.0 points); symptomatic haemorrhage was 6% versus 3% (P=0.50) and mortality 19% versus 18%. In DEFUSE 3 (Albers GW et al., PMID: 29364767; 182 patients at 6–16 hours with perfusion mismatch), functional independence was 45% versus 17% (P<0.001), the outcome distribution shifted favourably (odds ratio 2.77, P<0.001), and mortality was 14% versus 26% (P=0.05), with symptomatic haemorrhage 7% versus 4% (P=0.75). Both trials selected patients by imaging or clinical mismatch — small infarct, large threatened territory — so the benefit belongs to that selected minority, not to all late presenters. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): in mismatch-selected large-vessel occlusion 6–24 hours from onset, thrombectomy roughly triples functional independence.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — functional independence 49% versus 13% and 45% versus 17% in two early-stopped randomised trials of mismatch-selected patients

title: Tenecteplase at 4.5–24 hours (TIMELESS): median Rankin 3 in both groups — no benefit in perfusion-selected patients, most of whom had thrombectomy anyway
question: In perfusion-selected ischaemic stroke 4.5–24 hours from onset, does tenecteplase improve functional outcome versus placebo without excess symptomatic haemorrhage?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — a clean null in exactly the population chosen to favour the drug. In TIMELESS (Albers GW et al., PMID: 38329148), 458 patients with middle-cerebral or internal-carotid occlusion and perfusion-proven salvageable tissue were randomised to tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg or placebo at 4.5–24 hours (median about 12–13 hours from last known well); 77.3% then underwent thrombectomy. The median 90-day modified Rankin score was 3 in each group, and the adjusted common odds ratio for the outcome distribution was 1.13 (95% CI 0.82 to 1.57; P=0.45). Safety was as the question hoped — mortality 19.7% versus 18.2% and symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage 3.2% versus 2.3%, no significant excess — but with no efficacy signal to weigh it against. The plausible reading is that once thrombectomy is coming, a late drip adds nothing measurable; the trial cannot speak to late thrombolysis where thrombectomy is unavailable. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): tenecteplase at 4.5–24 hours did not improve 90-day function in perfusion-selected patients, without a significant haemorrhage penalty.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — adjusted common OR 1.13 (0.82–1.57) for 90-day outcome in the single TIMELESS trial; symptomatic haemorrhage 3.2% versus 2.3%

title: Alteplase for minor nondisabling stroke: no gain over antiplatelet care in either trial — PRISMS stopped at a third of its sample with a 3.2% bleed signal, ARAMIS found dual antiplatelets non-inferior
question: In minor ischaemic stroke (low NIHSS) within 4.5 hours, does alteplase improve excellent outcome versus aspirin-based care — or does bleeding erase any gain?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — in minor nondisabling stroke, thrombolysis has never beaten tablets. PRISMS (Khatri P et al., PMID: 29998337) randomised 313 patients with NIHSS 0–5 and non-disabling deficits to alteplase or aspirin 325 mg within 3 hours, then stopped far short of its planned 948 patients: favourable outcome (mRS 0–1) at 90 days was 78.2% on alteplase versus 81.5% on aspirin (adjusted risk difference −1.1%, 95% CI −9.4% to 7.3%), while symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage occurred in 5 alteplase patients (3.2%) versus none on aspirin (risk difference 3.3%, 0.8% to 7.4%). ARAMIS (Chen HS et al., PMID: 37367978) then tested the stronger antiplatelet strategy in 760 patients within 4.5 hours: dual antiplatelet therapy was non-inferior to alteplase for excellent outcome (93.8% versus 91.4%; risk difference 2.3%, −1.5% to 6.2%; P for non-inferiority <.001), with symptomatic haemorrhage in 0.3% versus 0.9%. Most minor-stroke patients recover well anyway — the ceiling is high, the bleed is real, and no trial has found headroom for the drip. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): alteplase does not improve excellent outcome over aspirin-based care in minor nondisabling stroke, and carries a small haemorrhage excess.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — favourable outcome 78.2% versus 81.5% in the stopped-early PRISMS trial and dual antiplatelets non-inferior in ARAMIS, with symptomatic haemorrhage 3.2% versus 0% in PRISMS
