title: Cilostazol dual therapy in high-risk stroke (CSPS.com): recurrence 3% versus 7% (HR 0.49) with no excess of severe bleeding — in one open-label Japanese trial stopped at half its target
question: In high-risk non-cardioembolic ischaemic stroke, does dual antiplatelet therapy with cilostazol plus aspirin or clopidogrel prevent recurrence better than single antiplatelet therapy without more major bleeding?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a halving of recurrence, from a single open-label trial that stopped early. In CSPS.com (Toyoda K et al., PMID: 31122494), 1,884 Japanese patients with high-risk non-cardioembolic stroke (at least 50% stenosis of a major artery, or two or more vascular risk factors) were randomised to cilostazol 100 mg twice daily added to aspirin or clopidogrel, versus aspirin or clopidogrel alone, for up to 3.5 years. Recurrent ischaemic stroke occurred in 29 of 932 (3%; annualised 2.2%) on dual therapy versus 64 of 947 (7%; annualised 4.5%) on monotherapy (hazard ratio 0.49, 95% CI 0.31 to 0.76; P=0.0010) — a 51% relative reduction, printed beside the absolute rates. Severe or life-threatening bleeding was not increased (annualised 0.6% versus 0.9%; HR 0.66, 0.27 to 1.60; P=0.35), and any bleeding events were 4% in both groups. The cautions are structural: the trial was open-label, enrolled 1,884 of a planned 4,000 patients before stopping for slow recruitment, and studied only Japanese patients — a population in which cilostazol is licensed and commonly used. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): cilostazol-based dual therapy cut recurrence without a bleeding penalty in this single trial; confirmation outside Japan does not exist.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — recurrent stroke HR 0.49 (0.31–0.76) with severe bleeding HR 0.66 (not significant) in the single CSPS.com trial

title: ARCADIA: apixaban for cryptogenic stroke with atrial cardiopathy — recurrent stroke 4.4% per year on both drugs (HR 1.00); the trial stopped for futility
question: In cryptogenic stroke with atrial cardiopathy but no atrial fibrillation, does apixaban prevent recurrent stroke versus aspirin?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — as clean a futility result as stroke prevention produces. ARCADIA (Kamel H et al., PMID: 38324415) randomised 1,015 patients with cryptogenic stroke and atrial cardiopathy (an abnormal P-wave measure, NT-proBNP over 250 pg/mL, or a left atrial diameter index of at least 3 cm/m²) but no atrial fibrillation, to apixaban 5 or 2.5 mg twice daily or aspirin 81 mg daily. After a mean 1.8 years the trial was stopped for futility at a planned interim analysis: recurrent stroke occurred in 40 patients in each group, an annualised rate of 4.4% in both (hazard ratio 1.00, 95% CI 0.64 to 1.55). The safety ledger ran the other way from expectation — symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage occurred in 0 patients on apixaban versus 7 on aspirin (annualised 1.1%), and other major haemorrhage in 5 patients in each group (annualised 0.7% versus 0.8%; HR 1.02, 0.29 to 3.52). Atrial cardiopathy, as these three markers define it, marks risk but does not identify patients whose strokes are clot-driven in a way apixaban can prevent. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): apixaban did not reduce recurrent stroke versus aspirin in cryptogenic stroke with atrial cardiopathy and no fibrillation.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — recurrent stroke HR 1.00 (0.64–1.55) in the futility-stopped ARCADIA trial; symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage 0 versus 7 patients

title: Organised stroke-unit care: for every 100 patients, about 2 more survive, 6 more go home, and 6 more live independently at one year (29 trials, Cochrane)
question: Does organised inpatient stroke-unit care reduce death and dependency versus care on a general ward?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — the oldest, most replicated result in stroke care. The Cochrane network meta-analysis (Langhorne P et al., PMID: 32324916) pooled 29 randomised trials with 5,902 participants comparing organised inpatient stroke-unit care with an alternative service, and at a median one year found less poor outcome (odds ratio 0.77, 95% CI 0.69 to 0.87), less death (OR 0.76, 0.66 to 0.88), less death or institutional care (OR 0.76, 0.67 to 0.85), and less death or dependency (OR 0.75, 0.66 to 0.85) — all moderate-quality evidence, and robust when restricted to securely randomised trials with blinded outcome assessment. In absolute terms the review equates this to two extra survivors, six more patients living at home, and six more living independently for every 100 treated. The benefit was independent of age, sex, initial stroke severity, and stroke type, was clearest for units in a discrete stroke ward (network OR 0.74, 0.62 to 0.89 for poor outcome), and came with no systematic increase in length of stay. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): organised stroke-unit care reduces death and dependency versus general-ward care.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — death OR 0.76 (0.66–0.88) and death or dependency OR 0.75 (0.66–0.85) across 29 randomised trials in the Cochrane analysis

title: VERSE: intensive speech therapy started within two weeks of stroke did not improve communication recovery — 50.3% versus 52.1% recovered at 12 weeks
question: In acute stroke, does intensive early speech therapy within the first weeks improve communication recovery versus usual-care therapy — the VERSE question?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — more therapy, started earlier, did not buy more recovery in the window the trial allowed. VERSE (Godecke E et al., PMID: 33019888) randomised 246 patients with aphasia after acute stroke at 17 hospitals in Australia and New Zealand to usual-care therapy, or to one of two intensive regimens (20 sessions of usual-care-plus or prescribed VERSE therapy) beginning within 14 days. At 12 weeks, communication recovery on the Western Aphasia Battery–Revised Aphasia Quotient was 50.3% (95% CI 45.7 to 54.8) in the combined high-intensity groups versus 52.1% (46.1 to 58.1) on usual care — a difference of −1.8 points (95% CI −8.7 to 5.0), with no difference in non-fatal or fatal adverse events (P=0.72). The null is about intensity and timing in the first 12 weeks, not about therapy itself: usual care in this trial was itself active therapy, and the dose question over longer horizons is a separate shelf. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): intensive aphasia therapy within 14 days did not improve 12-week communication recovery versus usual-care therapy.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — communication recovery 50.3% versus 52.1% (difference −1.8, −8.7 to 5.0) in the single VERSE trial

title: How much speech therapy for aphasia? The RELEASE participant-level analysis: gains clustered above 20 hours total, at 2–4 or 9+ hours a week — under 20 hours, comprehension gains vanished
question: In post-stroke aphasia, how much does the dose, intensity and timing of speech–language therapy change language recovery — what does the individual-participant evidence say?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for enough therapy, delivered often enough; the dose itself was never randomised, so this is a map, not a proof. The RELEASE collaboration (PMID: 34847708) pooled individual data from 959 participants in 25 trials and modelled how speech–language therapy (SLT) regimen relates to language gains. The greatest overall-language and comprehension gains were associated with a total dosage of more than 20 to 50 hours (overall language +18.37 points on the Western Aphasia Battery–Aphasia Quotient, 95% CI 10.58 to 26.16; comprehension +5.23, 1.51 to 8.95 on the Aachen Token Test), with the greatest clinical gains at 2–4 and at 9+ hours per week and at a frequency of 3–5+ days per week for overall language and functional communication. Below the floor there was nothing: evidence of comprehension gains was absent for SLT of 20 hours or less, under 3 hours per week, and 3 days per week or less. Mixed receptive–expressive therapy, functionally tailored, with prescribed home practice, was associated with the greatest overall gains. Because dose was observed, not assigned, motivated and less-impaired patients may simply accumulate more therapy — the analysis adjusted for age, sex, time since stroke, and baseline severity, but cannot fully remove that confounding. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): language recovery is greatest with frequent, functionally tailored therapy totalling well over 20 hours; very low doses show no measurable gain.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — greatest gains at >20–50 hours total dose and 2–4 or 9+ hours/week in the RELEASE participant-level network analysis; no comprehension gain at ≤20 hours

title: Modafinil for debilitating post-stroke fatigue (MIDAS): fatigue scores fell by 7.4 points and quality of life rose in a 36-patient crossover trial
question: In debilitating post-stroke fatigue, does modafinil improve fatigue severity versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a real signal in a very small room. MIDAS (Bivard A et al., PMID: 28404841) was a single-centre phase 2 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial in stroke survivors at least 3 months out with severe fatigue (Multidimensional Fatigue Inventory score of at least 60): 232 survivors were screened and 36 randomised to modafinil 200 mg daily or placebo for 6 weeks, a 1-week washout, then the opposite treatment for 6 weeks. Patients on modafinil reported significantly less fatigue than on placebo (within-person difference −7.38 points on the 0–100 fatigue inventory, 95% CI −21.76 to −2.99 as printed in the record; P<0.001) and better stroke-specific quality of life (+11.81 points, 95% CI 2.31 to 21.31; P=0.0148), while cognition (Montreal Cognitive Assessment) and depression/anxiety/stress scores did not significantly improve (P>0.05). Post-stroke fatigue has few tested treatments, which makes the signal valuable — and a 36-patient single-centre crossover, with fatigue measured by self-report in a condition where expectation effects are plausible despite blinding, is exactly the design most prone to flattering a drug. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): modafinil reduced fatigue severity and improved quality of life in one small crossover trial; replication in a larger parallel-group trial is still owed.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — fatigue inventory −7.38 points (P<0.001) and quality of life +11.81 points in the single 36-patient MIDAS crossover trial

title: Fitness training after stroke: disability scores improved (SMD 0.52 for cardiorespiratory training) and walking and balance with them — deaths were too few to judge (19 in 3,017)
question: After stroke, does structured physical-fitness training — cardiorespiratory, resistance, or mixed — improve disability, walking and death versus usual care?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for function and fitness, with mortality honestly untested. The Cochrane review (Saunders DH et al., PMID: 32196635) pooled 75 randomised studies with 3,017 mostly ambulatory stroke survivors: cardiorespiratory training improved disability scores at the end of intervention (standardised mean difference 0.52, 95% CI 0.19 to 0.84; 8 studies, 462 participants; moderate-certainty evidence), mixed training improved them modestly (SMD 0.23, 0.03 to 0.42; low-certainty), and cardiorespiratory fitness itself rose (VO2 peak mean difference 3.40 mL/kg/min, 2.98 to 3.83), alongside benefits for walking speed and balance. Death was not influenced by any intervention — risk differences were all 0.00 — but with only 19 deaths among 3,017 participants at end of intervention and 19 among 1,469 at follow-up, the review is explicit that it cannot determine whether training reduces death or dependence. The constituent trials agree at the intensive end: in Globas C et al. (PMID: 21885867), 3 months of high-intensity aerobic treadmill training in chronic stroke improved VO2 peak by 6.4 mL/kg/min (P<.001) and 6-minute walk distance by 53 m (P<.001) versus conventional physiotherapy. No serious adverse events were attributed to training in the review. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): fitness training after stroke improves disability, fitness, and walking; an effect on death is unknown, not disproven.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — disability SMD 0.52 (0.19–0.84) for cardiorespiratory training across 75 Cochrane trials; mortality risk difference 0.00 with too few deaths to judge

title: Preventing post-stroke depression: escitalopram cut new depression to 8.5% versus 22.4% on placebo — problem-solving therapy helped in the main analysis but not the conservative one
question: In patients without depression after stroke, do escitalopram or problem-solving therapy prevent new post-stroke depression versus placebo or usual care?
balance: SPLIT — the drug passed every analysis; the therapy passed only some. In the single prevention trial (Robinson RG et al., PMID: 18505948), 176 non-depressed patients within 3 months of stroke were randomised to escitalopram (59), placebo (58), or problem-solving therapy (59) for 12 months. New depression developed in 8.5% on escitalopram (3 major, 2 minor cases) and 11.9% on problem-solving therapy (5 major, 2 minor) versus 22.4% on placebo (11 major, 2 minor) — adjusted hazard ratios for placebo versus each treatment of 4.5 (95% CI 2.4 to 8.2) and 2.2 (1.4 to 3.5), both P<.001, with adverse events not significantly different between groups. Under the conservative intention-to-treat analysis — counting all 27 patients who never started treatment as depressed — escitalopram remained superior (23.1% versus 34.5%; adjusted HR 2.2, 1.2 to 3.9; P=.007) while problem-solving therapy did not (30.5% versus 34.5%; adjusted HR 1.1, 0.8 to 1.5; P=.51). A later re-examination of the same cohort over 8–10 years (Robinson RG et al., PMID: 28029510) found problem-solving therapy independently associated with longer time to death in an adjusted survival model — a model-based finding without absolute mortality rates in the record, from a post-hoc analysis. PROPOSED SPLIT: escitalopram prevents post-stroke depression in this trial under both analyses; problem-solving therapy's prevention effect is analysis-dependent, with a hypothesis-generating survival association.
stamp: SPLIT — escitalopram prevented depression under both analyses (8.5% versus 22.4%); problem-solving therapy was significant in the main analysis (11.9%) but not the conservative intention-to-treat analysis

title: SPRINT MIND: intensive blood-pressure control cut mild cognitive impairment (HR 0.81) but not dementia itself (HR 0.83, not significant) — the trial stopped early with too few dementia cases
question: In hypertensive adults, does intensive systolic control (target <120 mm Hg) reduce mild cognitive impairment and dementia versus standard control (<140 mm Hg)?
balance: SPLIT — the earlier, softer endpoint moved; the disease endpoint did not reach significance. In SPRINT MIND (Williamson JD et al., PMID: 30688979), 9,361 hypertensive adults (mean age 67.9 years; 35.6% women; no diabetes or prior stroke) were randomised to a systolic target under 120 mm Hg (4,678) or under 140 mm Hg (4,683); over a median 5.11 years of follow-up, adjudicated probable dementia occurred in 149 versus 176 patients (7.2 versus 8.6 cases per 1,000 person-years; hazard ratio 0.83, 95% CI 0.67 to 1.04 — not significant). Mild cognitive impairment was significantly reduced (14.6 versus 18.3 per 1,000 person-years; HR 0.81, 0.69 to 0.95), as was the composite of impairment or dementia (20.2 versus 24.1 per 1,000 person-years; HR 0.85, 0.74 to 0.97). The parent trial's early stop for cardiovascular benefit (median intervention 3.34 years) left fewer dementia cases than planned, and the authors state the dementia analysis may be underpowered. The brain-imaging substudy (Nasrallah IM et al., PMID: 31408137) leans the same way: white-matter lesion volume grew less on intensive treatment (increase 0.92 versus 1.45 cm³; between-group difference −0.54 cm³, −0.87 to −0.20), while total brain volume fell slightly more (−3.7 cm³ difference, −6.3 to −1.1) — small, opposing-direction anatomical signals. PROPOSED SPLIT: intensive control reduces mild cognitive impairment and slows white-matter lesion accrual, with dementia prevention suggested but not proven.
stamp: SPLIT — mild cognitive impairment HR 0.81 (0.69–0.95) and the impairment-or-dementia composite HR 0.85 (0.74–0.97), but probable dementia HR 0.83 (0.67–1.04) not significant

title: ASPREE: daily aspirin did not prevent dementia, Alzheimer's disease, or cognitive decline in 19,114 healthy older adults (dementia HR 1.03)
question: In healthy older adults, does daily low-dose aspirin prevent dementia and cognitive decline versus placebo?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — the largest prevention experiment ever run on the question, and flat. In ASPREE's cognitive analysis (Ryan J et al., PMID: 32213642), 19,114 community-dwelling adults aged 70 or older (65 for US minorities), free of cardiovascular disease, disability, and diagnosed dementia, were randomised to aspirin 100 mg daily or placebo and followed a median 4.7 years, with 964 participants triggered into full dementia assessment and 575 adjudicated dementia cases (41% clinically probable Alzheimer's disease). There was no substantial difference in all-dementia risk (hazard ratio 1.03, 95% CI 0.91 to 1.17), probable Alzheimer's disease (HR 0.96, 0.74 to 1.24), or mild cognitive impairment (HR 1.12, 0.92 to 1.37), and cognitive change over time was similar in both groups. The record is graded Class II evidence that low-dose aspirin does not significantly reduce dementia, Alzheimer's disease, mild cognitive impairment, or cognitive decline in healthy older adults. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): aspirin started in healthy old age does not prevent dementia or cognitive decline.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — dementia HR 1.03 (0.91–1.17), Alzheimer's HR 0.96, MCI HR 1.12 in 19,114 randomised older adults

title: Statins do not prevent dementia: 31 dementia cases on statin versus 31 on placebo in 26,340 randomised patients (Cochrane) — and no cognitive test moved
question: Do statins prevent dementia or cognitive decline in people at risk — and does stopping a statin in established dementia change cognition or quality of life?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — the prevention half of this question has a large, consistent randomised answer. The Cochrane review (McGuinness B et al., PMID: 26727124) found two double-blind placebo-controlled trials totalling 26,340 participants aged 40 to 82 (11,610 aged 70 or older), all with vascular disease or vascular risk factors, treated with simvastatin or pravastatin for a mean 3.2 and 5 years, at low risk of bias. The one trial reporting dementia incidence (20,536 participants) found 31 cases in each group (odds ratio 1.00, 95% CI 0.61 to 1.65). Both trials assessed cognition on five different tests with no differences between statin and placebo (high-quality evidence), and withdrawal for adverse events did not differ (OR 0.94, 0.83 to 1.05; discontinuation under 5%). The review's verdict is that there is good evidence statins given in late life to people at vascular risk do not prevent cognitive decline or dementia — the observational promise that prompted the question did not survive randomisation. The question's second half — whether stopping a statin in established dementia changes cognition or quality of life — has no verified randomised trial behind it in this build, and this shelf claims nothing for it. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): statins do not prevent dementia or cognitive decline in at-risk adults.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — dementia incidence OR 1.00 (0.61–1.65) and no difference on five cognitive tests across two trials totalling 26,340 participants (Cochrane)

title: Galantamine in mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's: cognition better by 3.3–3.9 ADAS-cog points at 16–24 mg/day in two large trials — a symptomatic gain, with global and daily-function benefits alongside
question: In mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's disease, does galantamine improve cognition, daily function and behaviour versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two concordant registration trials with the class's familiar small, real, symptomatic effect. In the USA-10 trial (Tariot PN et al., PMID: 10881251; 978 patients with mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's disease), galantamine at 16 and 24 mg/day beat placebo on cognition at 5 months by 3.3 and 3.6 ADAS-cog points (both P<0.001), with significantly better clinician-rated global change (CIBIC-plus), activities of daily living, and behavioural symptoms; discontinuations for adverse events were 6–10% on galantamine versus 7% on placebo, and adverse events were predominantly mild gastrointestinal symptoms. In USA-1 (Raskind MA et al., PMID: 10881250; 636 patients), the pattern repeated at 6 months — treatment effects of 3.9 points (24 mg/day) and 3.8 points (32 mg/day) on ADAS-cog (both P<0.001), better CIBIC-plus outcomes (P<0.05), no modification by APOE genotype, and scores maintained near baseline at 12 months in patients continuing 24 mg/day. The Cochrane class review (Birks J, PMID: 16437532) puts the cholinesterase inhibitors' shared effect at about −2.7 ADAS-cog points (95% CI −3.0 to −2.3) across 13 trials, with about 29% leaving treatment for adverse events versus 18% on placebo. Nothing here slows the disease itself; the benefit is a few points of cognition and function for some months. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): galantamine 16–24 mg/day produces small, consistent symptomatic improvements in cognition, global state, daily function, and behaviour in mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's disease.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — ADAS-cog advantages of 3.3–3.6 points (USA-10) and 3.8–3.9 points (USA-1) at 16–32 mg/day in two concordant placebo-controlled trials

title: Donepezil in vascular dementia: cognition improved by about 2 ADAS-cog points in two pooled trials (1,219 patients) — global benefit clearest at 5 mg, withdrawals doubled at 10 mg
question: In vascular dementia, does donepezil improve cognition and global function versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a small symptomatic gain in a condition with no approved treatment, from two identical industry trials. The combined analysis (Román GC et al., PMID: 16192723) pooled two 24-week randomised, double-blind trials totalling 1,219 patients with vascular dementia: both donepezil doses (5 and 10 mg/day) improved cognition versus placebo on ADAS-cog and MMSE (P<0.01), global function improved on CIBIC-plus at 5 mg/day (P<0.001 versus placebo; the 10 mg comparison was P=0.006) and on the Clinical Dementia Rating sum-of-boxes at 10 mg/day (P<0.01), and instrumental daily-living function improved at both doses (P<0.05). In the larger constituent trial reported separately (Black S et al., PMID: 12970516; 603 patients, mean age 73.9 years), week-24 ADAS-cog effect sizes were −1.90 points at 5 mg/day (P=0.001) and −2.33 at 10 mg/day (P<0.001), daily-living scores improved by −1.31 points at both doses (P=0.02), and withdrawals for adverse events were 11.1% on placebo, 11.1% on 5 mg, and 21.8% on 10 mg (P=0.005 versus placebo). The dose lesson cuts against escalation: the lower dose carried the cleanest global result with placebo-level tolerability. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): donepezil produces small improvements in cognition and some global and functional measures in vascular dementia, best supported at 5 mg/day.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — ADAS-cog effect sizes −1.90 (5 mg) and −2.33 (10 mg) points at 24 weeks across two pooled trials totalling 1,219 patients

title: Donepezil in Lewy-body dementia: the phase 2 trial was strongly positive (MMSE +3.8 at 5 mg) — the confirmatory phase 3 missed both co-primary endpoints, with MMSE benefit only at 10 mg
question: In dementia with Lewy bodies, does donepezil improve cognition and neuropsychiatric symptoms versus placebo?
balance: SPLIT — the small trial promised more than the confirmatory trial delivered. In the exploratory phase 2 trial (Mori E et al., PMID: 22829268; 140 Japanese patients), donepezil 5 and 10 mg/day beat placebo on the MMSE at 12 weeks (mean differences 3.8 points, 95% CI 2.3 to 5.3, and 2.4 points, 0.9 to 3.9; P<0.001 and P=0.001), on clinician-rated global change (P<0.001 at every dose including 3 mg), and on behavioural measures (P<0.001 at 5 and 10 mg), with caregiver burden reduced at 10 mg (P=0.004) and safety consistent with the known donepezil profile. The larger confirmatory phase 3 trial (Ikeda M et al., PMID: 25713599; 142 patients) then missed its predefined bar: superiority required significance on both co-primary endpoints (MMSE and the NPI-2 hallucinations/fluctuations score), and neither dose achieved it — MMSE improved significantly only at 10 mg (2.2 ± 0.4 versus 0.6 ± 0.5 points on placebo; P=0.016; the 5 mg change was not significant, P=0.232), NPI-2 differences from placebo were not significant at either dose, and parkinsonism was slightly more frequent at 10 mg though UPDRS motor scores barely changed. The cognition signal survived confirmation at the higher dose; the neuropsychiatric claim — half the original question — did not. PROPOSED SPLIT: donepezil improves cognition modestly in Lewy-body dementia (clearest at 10 mg), while a neuropsychiatric benefit was shown in phase 2 but not confirmed in phase 3.
stamp: SPLIT — cognition improved (phase 2 MMSE +3.8 at 5 mg; phase 3 significant only at 10 mg) but the phase 3 co-primary neuropsychiatric endpoint was not met

title: Music-based therapy in dementia: depressive symptoms slightly better and overall behavioural problems possibly better at the end of treatment — agitation, cognition and every long-term outcome unmoved
question: In people with dementia, do music-based therapeutic interventions reduce agitation, depression and behavioural symptoms versus usual care?
balance: SPLIT — the benefit is narrow and short-lived. The 2025 Cochrane review (30 randomised trials, 1,720 participants) found moderate-certainty evidence that music-based interventions probably improved depressive symptoms slightly at the end of treatment (standardised mean difference −0.23, 95% CI −0.42 to −0.04; 9 studies, 441 participants) and low-certainty evidence they may have improved overall behavioural problems (SMD −0.31, 95% CI −0.60 to −0.02; 10 studies, 385 participants) versus usual care. But the symptoms families ask about most did not move: agitation or aggression likely did not improve (SMD −0.05, 95% CI −0.27 to 0.17; 11 studies, 503 participants, moderate certainty), and neither did anxiety, social behaviour or cognition; at four or more weeks after treatment ended there was no evidence of benefit for any outcome. A second meta-analysis of 22 trials (1,780 patients) reached more optimistic conclusions on cognition, quality of life and neuropsychiatric symptoms, but its abstract reports vote counts of positive trials rather than pooled effect sizes, so the Cochrane GRADE-rated estimates govern the stamp. No serious adverse events were reported in the Cochrane set. PROPOSED SPLIT: a small, real, end-of-treatment gain in depressive symptoms (and possibly overall behavioural problems), with agitation, cognition and durability null.
stamp: SPLIT — depressive symptoms slightly improved and overall behavioural problems possibly improved at end of treatment versus usual care; agitation/aggression, anxiety, cognition and all long-term (≥4-week) outcomes showed no benefit

title: Solanezumab in preclinical Alzheimer's disease (A4): no slowing of cognitive decline over 240 weeks — amyloid accumulated more slowly, cognition did not follow
question: In amyloid-positive preclinical Alzheimer's disease, does solanezumab slow cognitive decline versus placebo — the prevention-stage anti-amyloid test?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — in the prevention-stage test of anti-amyloid therapy, solanezumab did not slow cognitive decline. In the A4 trial, 1,169 cognitively normal older adults with elevated brain amyloid were randomised to solanezumab (up to 1,600 mg intravenously every 4 weeks) or placebo for 240 weeks: the mean change in Preclinical Alzheimer Cognitive Composite score was −1.43 on solanezumab versus −1.13 on placebo (difference −0.30, 95% CI −0.82 to 0.22; P=0.26) — numerically favouring placebo. Brain amyloid did accumulate more slowly on solanezumab (mean increase 11.6 versus 19.3 centiloids on PET), so the drug engaged amyloid biology without converting it into cognition. Amyloid-related imaging abnormalities with oedema occurred in less than 1% in each group; ARIA with microhaemorrhage or haemosiderosis occurred in 29.2% on solanezumab versus 32.8% on placebo. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): four and a half years of monomeric-amyloid targeting in preclinical Alzheimer's disease produced no cognitive benefit in its single large phase 3 trial.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — solanezumab did not slow cognitive decline over 240 weeks in preclinical Alzheimer's disease (PACC difference −0.30, P=0.26), despite slower amyloid accumulation on PET

title: Shunt valves in normal-pressure hydrocephalus: starting pressure and valve design changed overdrainage complications — 5 versus 29 cases in SVASONA — but not who improved
question: In idiopathic normal-pressure hydrocephalus, do shunt-valve pressure settings change gait and clinical outcome after ventriculoperitoneal shunting?
balance: SPLIT — valve choices move overdrainage complications, not clinical improvement. In the DEPSS trial (58 patients with suspected idiopathic normal-pressure hydrocephalus), an adjustable Strata valve preset at the highest performance level (2.5, lowered stepwise) produced no statistically significant difference in clinical improvement versus a valve preset low (performance level 1.0), but significantly more subdural effusions were observed in the improved patients in the low-preset group — the authors recommend starting high and lowering until improvement or radiological overdrainage appears, accepting slower improvement and more adjustments. The companion valve trial, SVASONA (145 patients), compared gravitational with programmable valves: overdrainage signs at 6 months occurred in 5 patients on gravitational valves versus 29 on standard valves (risk difference −36%, 95% CI −49% to −23%; p<0.001 — about one overdrainage complication avoided for every third patient), while disease-specific outcome scales did not differ between groups. PROPOSED SPLIT: start-high/valve-design strategies cut overdrainage harm; neither trial showed better gait or disease-specific clinical outcome from the valve choice itself.
stamp: SPLIT — initial pressure setting and valve design changed overdrainage complications (fewer effusions starting high; 5 versus 29 overdrainage cases with gravitational valves) but did not change clinical improvement or disease-specific outcome

title: Lithium augmentation in resistant depression: response odds 2.89 in the 2014 pooling and 2.06 in 2026 — an effect that bias adjustment and trial sequential analysis then erase
question: In depression unresponsive to antidepressants, does lithium augmentation improve response and remission versus placebo or continued antidepressant alone?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the conventional meta-analyses say yes; the robustness checks say 'not proven'. Pooling nine placebo-controlled trials (237 patients), Nelson 2014 found lithium augmentation more than doubled the odds of response versus placebo (odds ratio 2.89, 95% CI 1.65 to 5.05; p=0.0002), with effects for both tricyclic and second-generation antidepressant backbones and no excess discontinuation for adverse events. The 2026 bias-adjusted reappraisal (56 augmentation trials, 13,616 patients) still found a conventional lithium benefit across 17 trials (OR 2.06, 95% CI 1.30 to 3.27), but trial sequential analysis did not support it — the accrued evidence reached only 8% of the required information size — and the effect became statistically non-significant after publication-bias adjustment (PET-PEESE and selection models). Most lithium trials also predate the modern operational definition of treatment-resistant depression. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): lithium augmentation probably helps some antidepressant non-responders, on an evidence base that is positive but small, old, and fragile to bias adjustment.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — lithium augmentation roughly doubled-to-tripled response odds in conventional meta-analyses (OR 2.06–2.89), but the 2026 trial-sequential and bias-adjusted analyses do not confirm the effect

title: T3 augmentation in resistant depression: 10 of 17 responded versus 3 of 16 on placebo in the one head-to-head trial — but double-blind-only pooling has never been significant
question: In treatment-resistant depression, does triiodothyronine (T3) augmentation improve response versus lithium augmentation or placebo?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — the positive signal lives in the weaker designs. The one head-to-head randomised trial (Joffe 1993, 50 tricyclic non-responders) found response in 10 of 17 patients on triiodothyronine, 9 of 17 on lithium and 3 of 16 on placebo over two weeks — T3 and lithium indistinguishable from each other, both ahead of placebo. But the 1996 meta-analysis of eight studies (292 patients) that pooled a relative response of 2.09 (95% CI 1.31 to 3.32) also reported that among the four randomised double-blind studies alone, the pooled effect was not significant (relative response 1.53, 95% CI 0.70 to 3.35; P=.29). The SSRI-era review (Cooper-Kazaz 2008) found five randomised trials too disparate to pool and called the enhancement evidence inconclusive. The 2026 bias-adjusted reappraisal carded on the companion lithium shelf (#3656) likewise found T3 response no better than control (OR 1.19, 95% CI 0.53 to 2.70; 6 trials) — it is mentioned here, not re-carded. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): T3 augmentation may help a subgroup of tricyclic-era non-responders, but the double-blind-only evidence has never reached significance.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — one small trial favoured T3 over placebo (10/17 versus 3/16 responders) and all-design pooling gives relative response 2.09, but the double-blind-only pooling is non-significant (1.53, P=.29) and SSRI-era trials are inconclusive

title: Pramipexole for treatment-resistant bipolar depression (PAX-BD): primary endpoint missed in 39 patients — late response 46% versus 6%, with hypomania ratings up
question: In treatment-resistant bipolar depression already on mood stabilisers, does adjunctive pramipexole improve depressive symptoms versus placebo?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — a clinically large signal in a trial too small to confirm it. PAX-BD randomised just 39 patients with treatment-resistant bipolar depression (of a much larger planned sample; recruitment closed early) to pramipexole (maximum 2.5 mg/day) or placebo added to mood stabilisers. At the 12-week primary endpoint, the QIDS-SR reduction was 4.4 points (SD 4.8) on pramipexole versus 2.1 (5.1) on placebo — a medium effect (d=−0.72) that was not statistically significant (95% CI −0.4 to 6.3; p=0.087). Later timepoints tilted pramipexole's way: a significant 6.28-point QIDS-SR advantage at 36 weeks (95% CI 1.85 to 10.71), and at trial exit response in 46% versus 6% (p=0.026) and remission in 31% versus 0% (p=0.030). Against that, hypomania ratings were significantly higher on pramipexole at 12 weeks. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): pramipexole may help treatment-resistant bipolar depression over months, but the only randomised trial enrolled 39 patients, missed its primary endpoint, and raised hypomania ratings — a hypothesis, not an answer.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — the single 39-patient trial missed its 12-week primary endpoint (p=0.087) but showed significant late advantages in symptoms, response (46% versus 6%) and remission, alongside higher hypomania ratings

title: Minocycline in treatment-resistant depression: small trials pool positive (SMD −0.59) — the one large trial found nothing on any outcome
question: In treatment-resistant depression, does adjunctive minocycline improve depressive symptoms versus placebo?
balance: SPLIT — the meta-analysis of small trials is positive; the one large rigorous trial is null. Pooling five randomised trials (374 patients), Qiu 2023 found minocycline reduced depression severity scores versus control (standardised mean difference −0.59, 95% CI −0.98 to −0.20; P=0.003), including in the treatment-resistant subgroup (SMD −0.36, 95% CI −0.64 to −0.09; P=0.010). But the largest single trial — Hellmann-Regen 2022, 168 patients in the intention-to-treat population, minocycline 200 mg/day added to usual antidepressant treatment for six weeks — found no difference in MADRS change (difference 1.46, 95% CI −1.04 to 3.96; P=.25) and no significant effect on any secondary outcome. Minocycline was well tolerated in the large trial, and the meta-analysis found no excess of adverse events other than dizziness or of discontinuation. PROPOSED SPLIT: small-trial pooling says minocycline helps depression scores; the best-powered test in treatment-resistant depression says it does not — the large trial governs for the resistant population.
stamp: SPLIT — five small trials pool to a severity benefit (SMD −0.59), but the largest trial in treatment-resistant depression (n=168) found no effect on MADRS or any secondary outcome (P=.25)

title: Extended-release ketamine tablets in resistant depression: 180 mg held MADRS 6.1 points below placebo and halved relapse — in a phase 2 trial of patients pre-selected for responding
question: In treatment-resistant depression, do extended-release ketamine tablets improve depressive symptoms versus placebo?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — one phase 2 trial, in a population pre-selected for responding. In Glue 2024, 231 adults with treatment-resistant depression and MADRS scores of at least 20 entered an open-label enrichment phase on extended-release ketamine tablets (R-107, 120 mg/day for 5 days); the 168 who responded by day 8 were randomised to twice-weekly R-107 at 30, 60, 120 or 180 mg, or placebo, for 12 further weeks, mostly dosed at home. The primary objective was met at the top dose: the least-square mean MADRS difference for 180 mg versus placebo at 13 weeks was −6.1 (P=0.019), and relapse during double-blind treatment showed a dose response from 70.6% on placebo to 42.9% on 180 mg. Tolerability was excellent by ketamine standards — no blood-pressure changes, minimal sedation and minimal dissociation; headache, dizziness and anxiety were the commonest adverse events. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): in patients already shown to respond to the tablets, continuing the 180 mg dose held depression scores down better than switching to placebo — an enriched-withdrawal result that says nothing about starting the drug in unselected patients.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — a single enriched phase 2 trial: continuing 180 mg tablets beat placebo on MADRS (−6.1, P=0.019) and relapse (42.9% versus 70.6%) in patients pre-selected for responding

title: Gepirone extended-release for major depression: two positive 8-week trials, remission 28.7% versus 14.9% — and dizziness in 45% on the drug versus 10% on placebo
question: In major depressive disorder, does gepirone extended-release — a selective 5-HT1A agonist — improve depressive symptoms versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two placebo-controlled trials, both positive on their primary scale, neither printing the size of the score difference in its record. Feiger 2003 randomised 209 outpatients with moderate-to-severe major depression to gepirone extended-release (20–80 mg/day) or placebo for 8 weeks: HAM-D-17 change was significantly greater on gepirone at weeks 3 (p=.013) and 8 (p=.018), with response in 33.7% versus 18.8% at week 3 and remission in 28.7% versus 14.9% at week 8. Bielski 2008, a second 8-week trial in the same population, found significantly greater HAM-D-17 reductions on gepirone-ER from week 4 (p=.004) through week 8 (p=.032), with secondary scales also favouring gepirone. The price is early dizziness and nausea: in Bielski, dizziness occurred in 45% on gepirone versus 10% on placebo and nausea in 36% versus 13%, concentrated during up-titration; in Feiger, 9.8% versus 2.8% discontinued for adverse events. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): gepirone-ER beats placebo on depression scores over 8 weeks in two concordant trials, with a characteristic early dizziness/nausea burden.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — gepirone-ER beat placebo on HAM-D-17 in two concordant 8-week trials (remission 28.7% versus 14.9% in Feiger 2003), with dizziness in 45% versus 10% during titration

title: Esketamine in acute suicidal depression (ASPIRE I & II): MADRS down an extra ~4 points within 24 hours in both trials — suicidal ideation itself no different from placebo
question: In major depression with active suicidal ideation with intent, does esketamine nasal spray plus standard care reduce depressive symptoms within 24 hours versus placebo nasal spray — and does it change suicidal ideation itself?
balance: SPLIT — depressive symptoms fell faster on esketamine; suicidal ideation itself did not separate from placebo. In ASPIRE I (226 hospitalised adults with major depression and active suicidal ideation with intent), esketamine 84 mg nasal spray plus comprehensive standard care beat placebo spray plus standard care on MADRS change at 24 hours (least-squares mean difference −3.8; 95% CI −6.56 to −1.09; P=.006). ASPIRE II (230 randomised) replicated it almost exactly: MADRS −15.7 versus −12.4 points, difference −3.9 (95% CI −6.60 to −1.11; P=.006), with separation already at 4 hours (−4.2; 95% CI −6.38 to −1.94). But in both trials the key secondary endpoint — severity of suicidality on the CGI-SS-r — did not differ significantly between groups (ASPIRE I: median treatment difference 0.0, 95% CI −1.00 to 0.00; P=.107): suicidal ideation fell rapidly in both arms under hospitalisation and optimised antidepressants. Dizziness, dissociation, nausea, headache and somnolence were the commonest esketamine adverse events. PROPOSED SPLIT: a rapid, replicated ~4-point antidepressant advantage at 24 hours, with no demonstrated advantage on suicidal ideation itself — the outcome the admission was for.
stamp: SPLIT — depressive symptoms improved faster on esketamine in both ASPIRE trials (MADRS −3.8 and −3.9 at 24 hours, P=.006 each), but severity of suicidality did not differ significantly from placebo plus standard care in either trial

title: Adjunctive celecoxib for major depression: pooled Hamilton advantage 3.26 points — from four trials totalling just 150 patients, with odds ratios too large to take at face value
question: In major depressive disorder, does adjunctive celecoxib improve response versus antidepressant alone?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — large-looking effects from a very small evidence base. The 2014 meta-analysis (Na) pooled the four randomised trials of adjunctive celecoxib in major depression — 150 patients in total — and found a Hamilton score advantage of 3.26 points (weighted mean difference, 95% CI 1.81 to 4.71), with remission odds of 6.58 (95% CI 2.55 to 17.00) and response odds of 6.49 (95% CI 2.89 to 14.55) versus antidepressant plus placebo. The component trials are pilots: Müller 2006 added celecoxib 400 mg/day to reboxetine in 40 patients for 6 weeks and found significantly greater Hamilton improvement; Akhondzadeh 2009 added celecoxib 400 mg/day to fluoxetine in 40 outpatients for 6 weeks with the same directional result and no significant difference in observed side effects. Odds ratios above 6 from 150 randomised patients are the signature of small-study inflation, and neither component record prints its own effect size. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): adjunctive celecoxib may add a few Hamilton points to an antidepressant over six weeks, on pilot-trial evidence that a larger trial could shrink or erase.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — four small trials (150 patients) pool to a 3.26-point Hamilton advantage with implausibly large remission/response odds ratios (~6.5), the signature of pilot-trial inflation

title: Deprexis internet CBT for depression (EVIDENT): PHQ-9 effect d=0.39 over usual care in 1,013 patients, holding at 6 months — a small effect with a large reach
question: In major depression, does a guided internet-delivered CBT programme (Deprexis) reduce symptoms versus waitlist or care as usual?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a large pragmatic trial of the named programme, backed by an individual-participant meta-analysis of the wider class. In EVIDENT, 1,013 adults with mild-to-moderate depressive symptoms (PHQ-9 score 5–14) were randomised to usual care alone or usual care plus the 12-week internet intervention Deprexis: the between-group effect on PHQ-9 at 3 months was d=0.39 (95% CI 0.13 to 0.64), holding at 6 months (d=0.32, 95% CI 0.06 to 0.69), and 35.6% versus 20.2% achieved at least a minimally important PHQ-9 change — a number needed to treat of 7 (95% CI 5 to 10). The individual-participant-data meta-analysis of self-guided internet CBT (13 studies, 3,876 participants) found a smaller average effect (Hedges g=0.27) with a response odds ratio of 1.95 (95% CI 1.52 to 2.50; NNT 8), and adherence predicted better outcomes. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): Deprexis added to usual care produces a small-to-moderate, durable symptom reduction in mild-to-moderate depression — an access intervention with a modest per-person effect, not a substitute for therapy in severe illness.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — Deprexis added to usual care improved PHQ-9 by d=0.39 at 3 months in a 1,013-patient trial (NNT 7), consistent with the IPD meta-analysis of internet CBT (g=0.27, response OR 1.95)

title: Vortioxetine and cognition in depression (FOCUS): DSST up 5.6 and 5.0 points over placebo in working patients, 9.2 and 9.0 in professionals — an effect that survived adjustment for mood
question: In working adults with major depression, does vortioxetine improve objective cognitive performance — processing speed and executive function — versus placebo, beyond its antidepressant effect?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for objective processing-speed performance, in the one dedicated cognition trial and its working-patient analysis. FOCUS randomised adults with major depression who self-reported cognitive dysfunction to vortioxetine 10–20 mg, duloxetine 60 mg (active reference), or placebo for 8 weeks, with the Digit Symbol Substitution Test (DSST) as the prespecified primary endpoint: vortioxetine was statistically superior to placebo on the DSST (P<0.05), on the subjective Perceived Deficits Questionnaire (P<0.01), and on the performance-based UPSA functional-capacity measure (P<0.001), while duloxetine did not separate from placebo on the DSST or UPSA. In the post hoc working-patient analysis (McIntyre 2017), the DSST effect versus placebo was 5.6 points at 10 mg and 5.0 at 20 mg (P<0.001 for both) — larger than the 4.0-point effect in the total population, and reaching 9.2 and 9.0 points in patients in professional positions — and it remained significant after adjusting for change in depression (MADRS) scores, with path analysis in FOCUS likewise attributing the cognitive benefit primarily to a direct effect rather than to mood improvement. A 2022 meta-analysis of six randomised trials (1,782 patients) confirmed significant DSST, PDQ and MADRS advantages at both 10 and 20 mg, without printing pooled effect sizes in its record. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): vortioxetine improves DSST performance more than placebo over 8 weeks, with the largest gains in working patients, and the effect is not fully explained by feeling less depressed.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — vortioxetine beat placebo on the DSST in the dedicated FOCUS cognition trial (effect 5.6 and 5.0 points in working patients, 9.2 and 9.0 in professional positions), independent of mood change, with a concordant six-trial meta-analysis

title: Catatonia treatment: lorazepam remits 55% and ECT responds at 59–100% across the case-series literature — the lorazepam-first sequence has never been tested head-to-head
question: In catatonia, how do benzodiazepines (lorazepam) and ECT compare — who responds to lorazepam first, and what does the systematic evidence support when it fails?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — a consistent, large clinical signal with no controlled trials behind it. The 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis (Bot) screened 1,336 articles and included 53 studies, most of them case series of lorazepam at doses from 2 to 60 mg/day (median 8 mg/day), usually for no more than a week: the overall remission rate was 55% and the overall response rate 77%, with a pooled Bush–Francis Catatonia Rating Scale improvement of −11.88 points (Cohen's d=−3.15) and no significant dose–response relationship in meta-regression. The earlier systematic review (Pelzer 2018; 31 articles) found lorazepam and ECT the most investigated treatments, with response percentages of 66% to 100% for lorazepam in Western studies and 59% to 100% for ECT, and no evidence supporting antipsychotics in catatonia without an underlying psychotic disorder. No randomised head-to-head trial of lorazepam versus ECT exists: the sequence the literature supports is lorazepam first, ECT when lorazepam fails — a practice consensus built on case series, not a tested comparison. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): benzodiazepines, usually lorazepam, remit about half of reported catatonia cases and produce some response in about three quarters, with ECT the established fallback — all on uncontrolled evidence.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — benzodiazepines remit 55% and produce response in 77% of reported catatonia cases across 53 mostly case-series studies, and ECT series respond at 59–100%, but no controlled or head-to-head trial exists

title: ECT in acute mania: randomised pooling favours adding ECT to medication — but the pooled SMD of −3.50 is too large to believe, and memory impairment rose
question: In acute mania, does electroconvulsive therapy improve response versus pharmacotherapy in patients who have not responded to drugs?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — a meta-analysis of randomised trials whose headline effect is too large to take at face value. Zhang 2021 pooled 12 randomised trials (863 patients) of ECT combined with medication versus medication alone in acute mania: the combination outperformed medication alone on manic-symptom reduction (standardised mean difference −3.50, 95% CI −4.57 to −2.44; p<0.00001), with the difference appearing after 3–5 treatments or one week. An SMD of −3.50 would be among the largest effects in psychiatry and arrives with high heterogeneity across mostly small, unblindable trials — the direction is consistent, the magnitude is not credible. The combination also increased memory impairment (the record prints the statistic as SMD 8.33, 95% CI 2.73 to 25.45; p=0.0002 — an odds-ratio-shaped figure), with no other significant differences in side effects or dropout. The 80-year clinical review (Elias 2021) places ECT where guidelines now do: no longer first-line for mania, reserved largely for pharmacological resistance, with randomised trials 'in limited numbers'. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): adding ECT to medication probably speeds and deepens manic-symptom reduction in acute mania, at a real cost in memory effects, on trial evidence too heterogeneous to quantify honestly.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — 12 small heterogeneous RCTs pool to a manic-symptom advantage for ECT plus medication whose size (SMD −3.50) is not credible, with significantly increased memory impairment; direction positive, magnitude unknown

title: Antipsychotic augmentation in SRI-resistant OCD: aripiprazole −5.4 Y-BOCS points and risperidone −3.3 in network pooling — the two agents that carry the effect
question: In treatment-resistant obsessive–compulsive disorder, does antipsychotic augmentation of a serotonin reuptake inhibitor improve response versus continuing the SRI alone — and which agents carry the effect?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for antipsychotic augmentation, aripiprazole carries the clearest effect and risperidone a smaller one. In the Maiti 2023 Bayesian network meta-analysis (59 trials of SRI augmentation in OCD), the antipsychotics significantly reduced Yale–Brown Obsessive–Compulsive Scale scores versus control: aripiprazole by a mean difference of −5.4 points (95% credible interval −9.1 to −1.6) and risperidone by −3.3 points (−6.4 to −0.20); several non-antipsychotic agents also separated (memantine −6.2, lamotrigine −6.0, ondansetron −5.7, pregabalin −8.1, topiramate −5.3, granisetron −5.6), with augmentation working better in SRI-refractory than non-refractory patients. The Suhas 2023 network meta-analysis, restricted to SRI-resistant OCD (55 RCTs, 2,011 participants), likewise found aripiprazole effective (standardised mean difference −1.36, 95% CI −2.56 to −0.17) and ranked it among the first-line options alongside ondansetron, deep TMS and therapist-administered CBT. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): adding aripiprazole (best supported) or risperidone to an SRI reduces Y-BOCS scores in resistant OCD — network estimates built from many small trials, with wide intervals.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — antipsychotic augmentation of an SRI reduces Y-BOCS in resistant OCD in two network meta-analyses: aripiprazole −5.4 points / SMD −1.36 in both, risperidone −3.3 points in one

title: Memantine augmentation in OCD: remission 89% versus 32% in a 42-patient trial and SMD −1.17 in pooling — numbers that outrun their evidence base
question: In obsessive–compulsive disorder with inadequate SRI response, does adjunctive memantine improve obsessive–compulsive symptoms versus placebo?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — striking percentages from very small trials. The one double-blind trial carded in full (Ghaleiha 2013) randomised 42 patients with moderate-to-severe OCD to memantine (20 mg/day) or placebo added to fluvoxamine for 8 weeks: by week 8, all patients in the memantine group versus 32% on placebo met partial-or-complete response criteria, and 89% versus 32% achieved remission. The 2025 meta-analysis of seven randomised trials (315 participants) found memantine augmentation superior to placebo on Y-BOCS (standardised mean difference −1.17, 95% CI −2.14 to −0.20; p=0.02), with significant heterogeneity, benefit concentrated at 20 mg/day and at eight weeks (SMD −1.06, 95% CI −1.77 to −0.36), and a significantly increased risk of mild rash (relative risk 7.00, 95% CI 1.31 to 37.47). The 2023 network meta-analysis carded on shelf #3668 also ranked memantine its most effective SRI augmenter (mean difference −6.2 Y-BOCS points) — mentioned here, not re-carded. Effect sizes above one standard deviation from trials of a few dozen patients are the classic small-study pattern. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): memantine 20 mg/day added to an SRI may substantially reduce OCD symptoms over eight weeks, on evidence whose size is exactly what makes it suspect.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — memantine augmentation beat placebo across seven small trials (Y-BOCS SMD −1.17) and produced 89% remission versus 32% in the index trial, effects too large for their sample sizes to be taken at face value

title: Guanfacine for PTSD in veterans: no effect on symptoms, sleep or mood in either of the two placebo-controlled trials
question: In veterans with PTSD, does guanfacine reduce PTSD symptoms versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — two placebo-controlled trials in veterans, both null on every outcome. Neylan 2006 randomised 63 veterans with chronic PTSD to guanfacine (29) or placebo (34) for 8 weeks: guanfacine had no effect on PTSD symptoms, subjective sleep quality, or general mood disturbances, and was associated with a number of side effects; the authors concluded the results do not support alpha-2 agonists in veterans with chronic PTSD. Davis 2008 randomised veterans with chronic PTSD to 8 weeks of double-blind guanfacine or placebo (with stable antidepressants allowed) and found no significant differences on clinician-administered or self-report measures — CAPS, MADRS, CGI-S, CGI-I and the Davidson Trauma Scale — though the drug was well tolerated in that small, predominantly male combat-veteran sample. The noradrenergic rationale was reasonable; the trials simply did not confirm it. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): guanfacine does not reduce PTSD symptoms in veterans in the two randomised trials that tested it.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — guanfacine showed no effect on PTSD symptoms, sleep or mood in two concordant placebo-controlled trials in veterans with chronic PTSD

title: Topiramate for PTSD: overall effect not significant (p=.082) in five small trials — only hyperarousal symptoms improved significantly
question: In PTSD, does topiramate — as monotherapy or adjunctive treatment — reduce symptom severity versus placebo?
balance: SPLIT — the overall effect is a non-significant trend, and only the hyperarousal cluster reached significance. Varma 2018 meta-analysed the randomised placebo-controlled trials of topiramate as monotherapy or adjunctive treatment in adults with PTSD (six trials identified; one excluded from the statistical analysis for a high dropout rate of 16 of 40 participants, leaving five). For overall symptomatology, topiramate showed a medium but not significant effect (standardised mean difference 0.55; p=.082). By symptom cluster, hyperarousal fell by a small, significant amount (SMD 0.35, 95% CI 0.029 to 0.689; p=.033), while re-experiencing (SMD 0.29, 95% CI −0.019 to 0.597; p=.067) and avoidance (SMD 0.20, 95% CI −0.105 to 0.509; p=.198) did not reach significance. Results did not differ significantly between veteran and non-veteran subjects, or between monotherapy and adjunctive use. The authors note prescribers' reluctance given topiramate's commonly reported cognitive impairment, sedation, fatigue and headache. PROPOSED SPLIT: a possible small benefit confined to hyperarousal symptoms, with overall PTSD severity not significantly improved — on five small trials.
stamp: SPLIT — overall PTSD severity not significantly improved (SMD 0.55, p=.082) across five small trials; hyperarousal symptoms alone fell significantly (SMD 0.35, p=.033), with re-experiencing and avoidance null

title: Omega-3 in ultra-high-risk psychosis (NEURAPRO): transition 11.5% versus 11.2% at 12 months — the multicentre trial that failed to replicate the single-centre promise
question: In young people at ultra-high risk of psychosis, do omega-3 fatty acids prevent transition to psychosis versus placebo when both groups receive cognitive–behavioural case management?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the large multicentre replication of a famous single-centre result found nothing. NEURAPRO randomised 304 young people at ultrahigh risk for psychotic disorders (mean age 19.1 years) to omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids 1.4 g/day (153) or paraffin-oil placebo (151), both with up to 20 sessions of cognitive-behavioural case management over 6 months. Transition to psychosis at 6 months was 6.7% on omega-3 versus 5.1% on placebo, and at 12 months 11.5% versus 11.2% (hazard ratio 1.1, 95% CI 0.55 to 2.23; P=.76) — the point estimate favours placebo. Both groups improved substantially in symptoms and functioning on the psychosocial intervention, which the authors suggest may have created a ceiling effect; they also note the lower-than-expected transition rate may have limited the test. Their stated conclusion is nonetheless plain: omega-3 fatty acids are not effective under conditions where good-quality evidence-based psychosocial treatment is available, and the trial clearly failed to replicate the original single-centre finding. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): added to good psychosocial care, omega-3 does not prevent transition to psychosis in ultrahigh-risk young people.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — omega-3 did not reduce transition to psychosis versus placebo when both groups received cognitive-behavioural case management (12-month transition 11.5% versus 11.2%; HR 1.1, P=.76)

title: Cannabidiol in schizophrenia: positive symptoms down 1.4 PANSS points at 1,000 mg/day in one small trial — cognition null in both trials, 600 mg null throughout
question: In schizophrenia, does adjunctive cannabidiol improve positive symptoms and cognition versus placebo added to antipsychotic treatment?
balance: SPLIT — a small positive-symptom gain at the higher dose in one exploratory trial; cognition null in both trials, and the lower-dose trial null on symptoms too. McGuire 2018 randomised 88 patients with schizophrenia to cannabidiol 1,000 mg/day (43) or placebo (45) added to existing antipsychotics for 6 weeks: positive symptoms were lower on CBD (PANSS treatment difference −1.4, 95% CI −2.5 to −0.2), clinicians rated more CBD patients improved (CGI-I difference −0.5, 95% CI −0.8 to −0.1), but cognitive performance (BACS difference 1.31, 95% CI −0.10 to 2.72) and functioning (GAF difference 3.0, 95% CI −0.4 to 6.4) fell short of significance. Boggs 2018 randomised 36 stable outpatients to CBD 600 mg/day or placebo for 6 weeks with cognition as the target: there was no drug effect on the MATRICS battery — only the placebo group improved over time — and no significant drug-by-time effect on PANSS total scores (p=0.18); sedation was more prevalent on CBD, with other side effects similar. PROPOSED SPLIT: adjunctive CBD may trim positive symptoms slightly at 1,000 mg/day; at 600 mg/day it did nothing measurable, and no trial shows a cognitive benefit.
stamp: SPLIT — adjunctive CBD 1,000 mg/day trimmed positive symptoms by 1.4 PANSS points in one exploratory trial, but cognition was not significantly improved in either trial and the 600 mg/day trial was null on symptoms and cognition alike

title: AVATAR therapy for distressing voices: severity down 3.82 points at 12 weeks and distress improved at 16 weeks in two trials — gone by 28 weeks in the larger one
question: In people with psychosis who hear distressing voices, does AVATAR therapy — dialogue with a digital avatar of the persecutory voice — reduce voice severity versus supportive counselling?
balance: SPLIT — voice severity and distress improve by the end of therapy in both trials; the distress benefit was gone by 28 weeks in the larger one. In the first AVATAR trial (Craig 2018), 150 people with persistent auditory verbal hallucinations despite treatment were randomised to AVATAR therapy — facilitated dialogue with a digital avatar of the persecutory voice, voiced by the therapist and conceding power over the sessions — or supportive counselling: at 12 weeks the reduction in hallucination severity (PSYRATS-AH) was significantly greater with AVATAR (mean difference −3.82, 95% CI −6.70 to −0.94; p=0.0093), with no adverse events attributable to either therapy. AVATAR2 (Garety 2024) randomised 345 participants to AVATAR-Brief, AVATAR-Extended, or treatment as usual: voice-related distress improved versus usual care at 16 weeks for both forms (Brief: −1.05 points, Cohen's d=0.38, P=0.035; Extended: −1.60 points, d=0.58, P=0.029) but not at 28 weeks (P=0.316 and P=0.175); voice severity likewise improved at 16 weeks only, while voice frequency was reduced in the Extended form at both timepoints. No related serious adverse events occurred. PROPOSED SPLIT: a real, moderate short-term reduction in voice severity and distress — strongest for the Extended protocol — whose distress benefit did not persist to 28 weeks.
stamp: SPLIT — AVATAR therapy reduced voice severity (−3.82 PSYRATS-AH points at 12 weeks) and voice distress at 16 weeks (Extended form d=0.58) versus controls, but the distress and severity benefits were not significant at 28 weeks in AVATAR2

title: Roluperidone for negative symptoms: phase 2 positive at both doses (d=0.45 and 0.57) — phase 3 primary missed in the full analysis (P=.064), functioning endpoint hit
question: In schizophrenia with predominant negative symptoms, does roluperidone improve negative symptoms versus placebo?
balance: SPLIT — the phase 2 trial was cleanly positive; the larger phase 3 missed its primary endpoint in the full analysis set and hit it only in the modified set, while its functioning endpoint succeeded in both. In phase 2 (Davidson 2017), 244 stabilised patients with prominent negative symptoms were randomised to roluperidone (then MIN-101) 32 mg/day, 64 mg/day, or placebo for 12 weeks after antipsychotic washout: the PANSS negative factor score improved significantly more on both doses, with effect sizes of d=0.45 and d=0.57, supported by the Brief Negative Symptom Scale and CGI severity, with no significant difference in positive symptoms and no clinically significant changes in weight, metabolic indices, or movement scores. In phase 3 (Davidson 2022), 513 patients with moderate-to-severe negative symptoms received the same doses or placebo for 12 weeks: at 64 mg the Negative Symptom Factor Score marginally missed significance in the intention-to-treat analysis (P≤.064) and reached nominal significance in the modified intention-to-treat set (P≤.044), while the Personal and Social Performance functioning score was significantly better than placebo in both analyses (P≤.021 and P≤.017). PROPOSED SPLIT: roluperidone probably improves everyday functioning at 64 mg/day, with its negative-symptom score effect confirmed in phase 2 but only borderline in the phase 3 primary analysis.
stamp: SPLIT — roluperidone improved negative-symptom scores significantly in phase 2 (d=0.45–0.57) and functioning in phase 3 (PSP, P≤.021), but the phase 3 primary symptom endpoint missed significance in the intention-to-treat analysis (P≤.064)

title: Glycine-site agents added to antipsychotics: small-to-medium gains in negative symptoms across two meta-analyses — and nothing added to clozapine, where glycine made positive symptoms worse
question: In schizophrenia, do glycine-site agents (D-serine, sarcosine, glycine) improve negative symptoms added to antipsychotics versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — real but modest, and fenced off from clozapine. Two meta-analyses of double-blind placebo-controlled add-on trials agree: Singh SP et al. (PMID: 21936588), pooling 29 trials and 1,253 patients, found adjunctive NMDA-receptor modulators improved negative symptoms with a standardised mean difference of -0.27 and total symptoms with -0.40, with D-serine (negative-symptom SMD -0.53) and sarcosine (SMD -0.39) among the better agents when added to non-clozapine antipsychotics. Goh KK et al. (PMID: 33406959), pooling 40 trials and 4,937 patients, likewise found glycine, D-serine and sarcosine had the better treatment profiles of the seven glutamatergic agents analysed. The fence is consistent in both: augmentation worked only alongside antipsychotics other than clozapine, and in Singh's analysis glycine added to clozapine worsened positive symptoms (SMD +0.56). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): glycine-site agents give small-to-medium symptom gains as add-ons to non-clozapine antipsychotics; they are not a clozapine add-on.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two meta-analyses of placebo-controlled add-on trials show small-to-medium negative- and total-symptom gains for glycine, D-serine and sarcosine alongside non-clozapine antipsychotics only

title: Bipolar maintenance: lithium plus valproate beat valproate alone (relapse hazard ratio 0.59) but not lithium alone (0.82, not significant) — and lithium alone beat valproate alone (0.71) in BALANCE
question: In bipolar disorder, how do lithium, valproate and their combination compare for preventing relapse in maintenance treatment?
balance: SPLIT — the combination wins only against the weaker partner. In BALANCE (Geddes JR et al., PMID: 20092882), 330 patients with bipolar I disorder were randomised to lithium, valproate, or both for up to 24 months; a new intervention for an emergent mood episode occurred in 54% on the combination, 59% on lithium, and 69% on valproate. The hazard ratios were 0.59 (95% CI 0.42–0.83) for combination versus valproate, 0.82 (0.58–1.17, not significant) for combination versus lithium, and 0.71 (0.51–1.00) for lithium versus valproate. The Cochrane review of valproate maintenance (Cipriani A et al., PMID: 24132760) points the same way: no difference between valproate and lithium (RR 1.02, 95% CI 0.87–1.20), and combination therapy more likely to prevent relapse than valproate alone (RR 0.78, 0.63–0.96). PROPOSED SPLIT: if the choice is between the two single drugs, lithium has the edge; adding valproate to lithium was not shown to help, but adding lithium to valproate was.

title: Acute mania: 13 drugs beat placebo on response in a 72-trial network meta-analysis — cariprazine among them — but only four beat placebo on staying in the trial
question: In acute mania in bipolar I disorder, how do antipsychotics including cariprazine compare with placebo for response at three weeks?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — for the class, with acceptability splitting the field. Kishi T et al. (PMID: 34642461) pooled 72 double-blind randomised trials of 23 drugs and placebo (n=16,442, mean study duration 3.96 weeks): aripiprazole, asenapine, carbamazepine, cariprazine, haloperidol, lithium, olanzapine, paliperidone, quetiapine, risperidone, tamoxifen, valproate and ziprasidone all outperformed placebo on treatment response (56 trials, n=14,503), but only aripiprazole, olanzapine, quetiapine and risperidone had lower all-cause discontinuation than placebo. The earlier network meta-analysis by Yildiz A et al. (PMID: 25036226) — 14,256 patients, 18 treatments — found the same shape: standardised mean differences against placebo of 0.32 to 0.66 for the 12 effective drugs, with no single drug superior to the rest except risperidone over aripiprazole and valproate. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): antimanic efficacy at about three weeks is established for the class including cariprazine; the choice between agents turns on tolerability and discontinuation, not on a proven efficacy champion.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — two concordant network meta-analyses (72 and ~95-trial pools) show 12–13 agents including cariprazine beat placebo on mania response, with acceptability separating only a few

title: Allopurinol added to lithium for acute mania: one 180-patient trial with a small effect (d=0.32) and a five-trial meta-analysis at d=0.294 — promising, thin, and unreplicated at scale
question: In acute mania, does adjunctive allopurinol improve response versus placebo added to mood stabilisers?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a small effect on a thin base. The anchor trial (Machado-Vieira R et al., PMID: 18681754) randomised 180 inpatients with bipolar I mania to allopurinol 600 mg/day, dipyridamole 200 mg/day, or placebo, each added to lithium for 4 weeks: allopurinol produced greater reductions in Young Mania Rating Scale scores at day 21 (p<0.001) and day 28 (p=0.003), with an effect size of d=0.32 (95% CI 0.07 to 0.57), and remission rates significantly higher than with dipyridamole or placebo (p=0.008). The meta-analysis by Chen AT et al. (PMID: 29017068) found five placebo-controlled trials: four showed efficacy on the primary outcome and one did not, with an overall effect size of d=0.294 across the four positive studies, and no significant difference in side effects. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): adjunctive allopurinol probably trims mania scores modestly on top of a mood stabiliser; Tier C because the whole base is five small trials and one 180-patient anchor.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one 180-patient double-blind trial (d=0.32) plus a five-trial meta-analysis (d=0.294) for adjunctive allopurinol in acute mania; Tier C for the thin base

title: Nurse-delivered sleep restriction therapy in primary care: insomnia severity 10.9 versus 13.9 at six months in 642 patients — four sessions, and cost-effective at £2,076 per QALY (HABIT)
question: In primary-care insomnia, does nurse-delivered sleep restriction therapy improve insomnia severity versus sleep hygiene alone?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one large, well-run pragmatic trial. In HABIT (Kyle SD et al., PMID: 37573859), 642 adults with insomnia disorder from 35 general practices in England were randomised to four sessions of nurse-delivered sleep restriction therapy plus a sleep hygiene booklet, or the booklet alone: at 6 months the mean Insomnia Severity Index score was 10.9 (SD 5.5) with sleep restriction versus 13.9 (5.2) with sleep hygiene (adjusted mean difference -3.05, 95% CI -3.83 to -2.28; p<0.0001; Cohen's d -0.74). The incremental cost per QALY gained was £2,076, with a 95.3% probability of being cost-effective at a £20,000 threshold. Serious adverse events numbered eight in each group, none judged related to the intervention. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a brief, nurse-delivered single-component therapy delivers a moderate insomnia gain in primary care; Tier C because it is a single (open-label) trial awaiting replication.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one large pragmatic randomised trial (n=642) of nurse-delivered sleep restriction therapy, ISI difference -3.05 points (d -0.74) at 6 months; Tier C as a single open-label trial

title: Prolonged-release melatonin 2 mg after 55: responders 26% versus 15% in one trial, better sleep quality and morning alertness in both — a three-week, questionnaire-scale benefit
question: In insomnia in adults aged 55 and over, does prolonged-release melatonin improve sleep quality and next-day alertness versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — modest, short-horizon, and specific to the prolonged-release formulation in older patients. Wade AG et al. (PMID: 17875243) randomised 354 primary-care patients aged 55–80 to prolonged-release melatonin 2 mg (the publication names the formulation Circadin) or placebo for 3 weeks: the responder rate (combined improvement in sleep quality and morning alertness) was 26% versus 15% (p=0.014), and sleep latency shortened by -24.3 versus -12.9 minutes (p=0.028). Lemoine P et al. (PMID: 18036082), in 170 outpatients aged 55 and over on the same 2 mg prolonged-release formulation for 3 weeks, found better quality of sleep (-22.5 versus -16.5 mm, p=0.047) and morning alertness (-15.7 versus -6.8 mm, p=0.002), with no rebound or withdrawal on stopping. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): prolonged-release melatonin improves perceived sleep quality and next-morning alertness in insomnia over 55 — over three weeks, on questionnaires, with no objective sleep-architecture claim.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two concordant 3-week double-blind trials of prolonged-release melatonin 2 mg in insomnia aged ≥55 (responders 26% vs 15%; alertness and sleep-quality scores better), questionnaire outcomes only

title: Trazodone for insomnia: sleep quality and continuity improve in a 44-trial meta-analysis, subjective total sleep time does not (difference 0.73 minutes) — and patients drop out for adverse effects at twice the placebo rate
question: In chronic insomnia, does trazodone improve subjective sleep onset and maintenance versus placebo — and how thin is the randomised evidence behind its widespread off-label use?
balance: SPLIT — it improves how sleep feels and some measured sleep, but not the outcome patients name first. Kokkali M et al. (PMID: 39123094) pooled 44 randomised trials with 3,935 participants: trazodone did not significantly change subjective total sleep time (weighted mean difference 0.73 minutes, 95% CI -24.62 to 26.07; p=0.96), but improved sleep quality (SMD -0.58, 95% CI -0.87 to -0.28), reduced nocturnal awakenings (SMD -0.57) and time awake after sleep onset (-13.47 minutes), and lengthened polysomnography-measured total sleep time by 27.98 minutes. The price: dropouts due to adverse effects were more than doubled (RR 2.30, 95% CI 1.45 to 3.64). The Cochrane review of antidepressants for insomnia (Everitt H et al., PMID: 29761479) is the colder read: for trazodone specifically there were too few studies to draw clear conclusions, with a possible small improvement in sleep quality on short-term low-dose use. PROPOSED SPLIT: a real but modest continuity/quality effect on a thin primary-insomnia base, no gain in perceived sleep duration, and a tolerability cost — Tier C so the developer sees how thin the insomnia-specific evidence is.
stamp: SPLIT — sleep quality, awakenings and objective sleep time improve modestly, subjective total sleep time does not, and adverse-effect dropouts double; the primary-insomnia trial base is thin (Tier C)

title: Eptinezumab: about one extra migraine day a month beyond placebo in episodic migraine (-4.3 versus -3.2 days) and about two in chronic migraine (-8.2 versus -5.6) in the PROMISE trials
question: In episodic and chronic migraine, does intravenous eptinezumab prevent attacks versus placebo — the PROMISE programme?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — two concordant phase 3 trials, with the size of the prize stated plainly. In PROMISE-1 (Ashina M et al., PMID: 32075406; episodic migraine, 888 patients, baseline about 8.6 monthly migraine days), eptinezumab 100 mg and 300 mg reduced monthly migraine days over weeks 1–12 by -3.9 and -4.3 versus -3.2 on placebo (p=0.0182 and p=0.0001); the 30 mg dose (-4.0) did not meet the primary endpoint comparison as reported. In PROMISE-2 (Lipton RB et al., PMID: 32209650; chronic migraine, 1,072 patients, baseline about 16.1 monthly migraine days), the reductions were -7.7 (100 mg) and -8.2 (300 mg) versus -5.6 on placebo (both p<0.0001). Treatment-emergent adverse events ran at placebo-like rates (57.6–63.2% across eptinezumab arms in PROMISE-1 versus 59.5% on placebo), with upper respiratory infection and fatigue the common excess events. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): quarterly intravenous eptinezumab prevents roughly one to two more migraine days a month than placebo over 12 weeks, in line with the rest of the CGRP class.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — two phase 3 placebo-controlled trials (PROMISE-1 and PROMISE-2, 1,960 patients) with concordant monthly-migraine-day reductions at 100 mg and 300 mg
