title: Zavegepant nasal spray for acute migraine: pain freedom at 2 hours in 24% versus 15% on placebo in phase 3 — a real, modest gain, paid for in bad taste (dysgeusia up to 16.1%)
question: In acute migraine, does zavegepant nasal spray achieve pain freedom at two hours versus placebo nasal spray?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — modest absolute gains, twice replicated. In the phase 3 trial (Lipton RB et al., PMID: 36804093), 1,269 patients in the efficacy set treated a single moderate-to-severe attack: pain freedom at 2 hours occurred in 24% on zavegepant 10 mg versus 15% on placebo (risk difference 8.8 percentage points, 95% CI 4.5 to 13.1; p<0.0001), and freedom from the most bothersome symptom in 40% versus 31% (risk difference 8.7 points, 3.4 to 13.9; p=0.0012). The earlier dose-ranging trial (Croop R et al., PMID: 36239038) found the same shape: pain freedom 22.5% (10 mg) and 23.1% (20 mg) versus 15.5% on placebo, with the 5 mg dose not significant. The commonest adverse events were dysgeusia (13.5% to 16.1% versus 3.5%), nausea (2.7% to 4.1% versus 0.5%) and nasal discomfort (1.3% to 5.2% versus 0.2%). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): zavegepant nasal spray gives roughly one extra pain-free response per 11 treated attacks over placebo, as the non-oral gepant option.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — two double-blind placebo-controlled trials (phase 2/3 and phase 3) concordant on pain freedom at 2 hours (about 23–24% vs 15–16%)

title: Candesartan for migraine prevention: headache days 13.6 versus 18.5 over 12 weeks in the first crossover trial, and responders 43% versus 23% on placebo in the second — matching propranolol head-to-head
question: In episodic migraine, does candesartan prevent migraine days versus placebo — and how does it compare with propranolol?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two small crossover trials, both positive, one with an active comparator. Tronvik E et al. (PMID: 12503978) randomised 60 patients with 2–6 attacks a month to candesartan 16 mg and placebo in crossover: over 12 weeks, days with headache averaged 13.6 on candesartan versus 18.5 on placebo (p=0.001), days with migraine 9.0 versus 12.6 (p<0.001), and 40.4% were responders for migraine days. Stovner LJ et al. (PMID: 24335848), in a triple-blind double-crossover study of 72 patients, found migraine days per month of 2.95 on candesartan and 2.91 on propranolol slow-release 160 mg versus 3.53 on placebo (p=0.02 for both comparisons), with responders at 43% on candesartan and 40% on propranolol versus 23% on placebo, and candesartan non-inferior to propranolol. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): candesartan 16 mg prevents migraine about as well as propranolol 160 mg in these small trials — a useful option when beta-blockers are unsuitable, pending a large parallel-group trial.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two small double-blind crossover trials (n=60 and n=72) concordant against placebo, with candesartan non-inferior to propranolol in the second

title: Melatonin for migraine prevention splits by age: adults gained 2.7 fewer migraine days a month versus 1.1 on placebo — the children's trial found a difference of 0 days and closed early, underpowered
question: In migraine prevention, does melatonin reduce attack frequency versus placebo — in adults, and in children and adolescents?
balance: SPLIT — positive in adults, unproven in children. In adults, Gonçalves AL et al. (PMID: 27165014) randomised 196 patients with 2–8 attacks a month to melatonin 3 mg, amitriptyline 25 mg, or placebo for 3 months: headache frequency fell by 2.7 migraine days on melatonin, 2.2 on amitriptyline, and 1.1 on placebo, with melatonin significantly better than placebo (p=0.009) but not different from amitriptyline (p=0.19), and better tolerated. In children and adolescents, Gelfand AA et al. (PMID: 37466211) randomised just 42 patients aged 10–17 (the trial closed early for slow enrolment, aiming at 210): median migraine days in the final treatment weeks were 2 on melatonin and 2 on placebo, a difference in medians of 0 days (95% CI -9 to 3), with heavy missing diary data — a result the authors say should not be read as proof of inefficacy. PROPOSED SPLIT: melatonin 3 mg probably prevents migraine in adults about as well as low-dose amitriptyline with fewer side effects; in children the question remains open, not answered no.
stamp: SPLIT — adult trial positive versus placebo and comparable to amitriptyline 25 mg; the paediatric trial was null on its face but closed early and underpowered, so the child question is unresolved

title: Laser ablation versus open resection for mesial temporal lobe epilepsy: pooled data give open surgery the seizure-freedom edge (72.5% versus 57.1% beyond two years), laser the gentler recovery — all of it observational
question: In mesial temporal lobe epilepsy resistant to drugs, does MRI-guided laser interstitial thermal therapy match open resection on seizure freedom — and at what cost to memory and reoperation?
balance: SPLIT — the trade-off is the finding, and no randomised trial exists. The meta-analysis by Ekman FR et al. (PMID: 39332763), pooling comparative studies with follow-up beyond 24 months, found seizure freedom in 72.5% after open temporal lobe resection versus 57.1% after MRI-guided laser interstitial thermal therapy (p<0.01), while minor (transient) complications were commoner with open surgery (9.9% versus 4.1%, p=0.04) and major complications did not differ (2.0% versus 2.7%). The propensity-matched cohort by Mo J et al. (PMID: 37800596) found no significant differences in memory preservation (p=0.95) or surgical outcomes (p=0.96) in 26 matched pairs — a much smaller, shorter comparison than the pooled analysis. Visual field deficits were frequent after both (79.4% open versus 49.8% laser in the meta-analysis, p=0.08, not significant). PROPOSED SPLIT: open resection probably buys more seizure freedom; laser ablation probably buys a gentler recovery; Tier C because every number here is observational and confounding by case selection runs in both directions.
stamp: SPLIT — open resection ahead on seizure freedom in pooled observational data (72.5% vs 57.1%), laser ablation ahead on minor complications (4.1% vs 9.9%); no randomised evidence (Tier C)

title: Modified Atkins diet for drug-resistant epilepsy: at least half of seizures gone in 26.2% versus 2.5% on drugs alone at six months in the randomised trial — and a paediatric network meta-analysis at odds ratio 11.3
question: In adults with drug-resistant epilepsy, does a modified Atkins diet reduce seizure frequency versus control diet?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a striking responder gap in one open trial, backed by the paediatric diet-therapy literature. Manral M et al. (PMID: 36599697) randomised 160 adolescents and adults with drug-resistant epilepsy to a modified Atkins diet plus standard drug therapy or standard therapy alone: at 6 months, a greater than 50% seizure reduction occurred in 26.2% on the diet versus 2.5% on drugs alone (95% CI for the difference 13.5 to 33.9; p<0.001), and quality of life improved more (mean difference 9.6 points, 95% CI 4.3 to 14.9). The network meta-analysis by Devi N et al. (PMID: 36716045) — 12 randomised trials, 907 children — found the modified Atkins diet more efficacious than care as usual for at least 50% seizure reduction in the short term (odds ratio 11.3, 95% CI 5.1 to 25.1), with adverse-event discontinuation also raised (odds ratio 6.5, 1.4 to 31.2). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): for drug-resistant epilepsy, adding a modified Atkins diet gives roughly one in four patients a halving of seizures within six months, against roughly one in forty without it — in trials that cannot be blinded.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one randomised trial in adolescents/adults (>50% seizure reduction 26.2% vs 2.5%) plus a 12-trial paediatric network meta-analysis (OR 11.3) for dietary therapy including modified Atkins

title: High-intensity treadmill exercise in new Parkinson's: motor scores stood still (change 0.3) while usual care worsened (3.2) over six months in the SPARX phase 2 trial — enough to justify a phase 3, not enough to claim disease modification
question: In de novo Parkinson's disease with motor symptoms, does high-intensity treadmill exercise slow motor progression versus usual care?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a phase 2 nonfutility signal, honestly labelled. In SPARX (Schenkman M et al., PMID: 29228079), 128 patients with de novo Parkinson disease (Hoehn and Yahr stages 1–2, not yet on dopaminergic medication) were randomised to high-intensity treadmill exercise (80–85% of maximum heart rate, 4 days a week), moderate-intensity exercise (60–65%), or wait-list usual care for 6 months. The mean change in Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale motor score was 0.3 (95% CI -1.7 to 2.3) in the high-intensity group versus 3.2 (1.4 to 5.1) in the usual-care group (p=0.03); the high-intensity group, but not the moderate-intensity group, met the predefined nonfutility threshold. Patients actually exercised 2.8 days per week at 80.2% of maximum heart rate in the high-intensity arm, and anticipated musculoskeletal adverse events were not severe. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): high-intensity treadmill exercise may slow early motor progression; Tier C because this is a single phase 2 trial designed to justify — not replace — a phase 3 efficacy trial.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single phase 2 randomised trial (n=128): UPDRS motor change 0.3 on high-intensity treadmill versus 3.2 on usual care at 6 months, nonfutility met; Tier C

title: Lixisenatide in early Parkinson's: motor disability scores improved by -0.04 points while placebo worsened by 3.04 over 12 months (difference 3.08) in LIXIPARK — with nausea in 46% and vomiting in 13%
question: In early Parkinson's disease, does the GLP-1 agonist lixisenatide slow motor disability progression versus placebo over 12 months?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one positive phase 2 trial, read alongside the class's phase 3 failure elsewhere in this library. In LIXIPARK (Meissner WG et al., PMID: 38598572), 156 patients with Parkinson disease diagnosed less than 3 years earlier, on stable symptomatic medication and without motor complications, received daily subcutaneous lixisenatide or placebo for 12 months: Movement Disorder Society UPDRS part III scores changed by -0.04 points on lixisenatide versus 3.04 points of worsening on placebo (difference 3.08; 95% CI 0.86 to 5.30; p=0.007), assessed in the on-medication state. After a 2-month washout, off-medication motor scores were 17.7 on lixisenatide versus 20.6 on placebo. The cost was gastrointestinal: nausea in 46% and vomiting in 13% of the lixisenatide group. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): lixisenatide slowed measured motor progression over one year in early Parkinson disease; Tier C — a single phase 2 trial, and the related exenatide programme's phase 3 was null, so replication is the whole question.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single phase 2 double-blind trial (n=156): MDS-UPDRS part III difference 3.08 points at 12 months favouring lixisenatide, with substantial gastrointestinal adverse effects; Tier C

title: Tai chi in Parkinson's: balance measures beat both resistance training and stretching in one 195-patient trial, and falls fell versus stretching — but not versus resistance training
question: In Parkinson's disease, does tai chi improve postural stability and reduce falls versus resistance training or stretching?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one well-conducted trial, with the falls claim fenced to the weaker comparator. Li F et al. (PMID: 22316445) randomised 195 patients with Hoehn and Yahr stage 1–4 Parkinson disease to tai chi, resistance training, or stretching, in 60-minute sessions twice weekly for 24 weeks. On the primary limits-of-stability outcomes, tai chi beat both comparators: maximum excursion improved by 5.55 percentage points more than resistance training (95% CI 1.12 to 9.97) and 11.98 points more than stretching (7.21 to 16.74), with directional control ahead by 10.45 and 11.38 points respectively. Tai chi also beat stretching on all secondary outcomes and beat resistance training on stride length and functional reach. Falls were fewer with tai chi than with stretching, but not significantly fewer than with resistance training; effects persisted 3 months after the intervention ended, and no serious adverse events occurred. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): tai chi improves postural stability in mild-to-moderate Parkinson disease; Tier C because a single trial carries the shelf and the falls result is comparator-dependent.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single randomised trial (n=195): tai chi superior to resistance training and stretching on limits-of-stability outcomes; falls reduced versus stretching only; Tier C

title: LSVT LOUD for Parkinson's dysarthria: voice handicap scores 8.0 points better than no therapy and 9.6 better than standard NHS speech therapy in PD COMM — while standard therapy itself showed no benefit over none
question: In Parkinson's disease with dysarthria, does Lee Silverman Voice Treatment (LSVT LOUD) improve voice and communication versus NHS speech therapy or no treatment?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one large pragmatic trial with an uncomfortable second finding. In PD COMM (Sackley CM et al., PMID: 38986549), 388 people with Parkinson disease and dysarthria were randomised to LSVT LOUD (four 50-minute sessions a week for four weeks, plus home practice), standard NHS speech and language therapy, or no therapy. At 3 months, self-reported Voice Handicap Index scores were lower (better) with LSVT LOUD than with no therapy by -8.0 points (99% CI -13.3 to -2.6; p<0.001) and lower than with NHS therapy by -9.6 points (-14.9 to -4.4; p<0.001) — while NHS therapy showed no evidence of difference from no therapy (1.7 points, -3.8 to 7.1; p=0.43). Adverse events, predominantly vocal strain, numbered 93 in the LSVT LOUD group, 46 in the NHS group and none in the no-therapy group, with no serious adverse events. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the intensive, protocolised LSVT LOUD programme — a named non-drug programme — improves patient-reported voice handicap where usual-dose therapy did not; Tier C as a single unblinded trial with a self-reported endpoint.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single pragmatic randomised trial (n=388): LSVT LOUD beat no therapy (-8.0 Voice Handicap Index points) and NHS speech therapy (-9.6), which itself did not beat no therapy; Tier C

title: Ublituximab versus teriflunomide in relapsing multiple sclerosis: relapse rates roughly halved in both ULTIMATE trials (0.08–0.09 versus 0.18–0.19 a year) and MRI lesions nearly abolished — disability worsening not significantly different
question: In relapsing multiple sclerosis, does ublituximab reduce relapses and MRI lesions versus teriflunomide?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — two identical twin trials, concordant on relapses and lesions, null on disability. In ULTIMATE I (Steinman L et al., PMID: 36001711), the annualised relapse rate was 0.08 on ublituximab versus 0.19 on teriflunomide (rate ratio 0.41, 95% CI 0.27 to 0.62; p<0.001); in ULTIMATE II, 0.09 versus 0.18 (rate ratio 0.51, 0.33 to 0.78; p=0.002). Mean gadolinium-enhancing lesions numbered 0.02 versus 0.49 in ULTIMATE I and 0.01 versus 0.25 in ULTIMATE II. But pooled 12-week confirmed disability worsening was 5.2% on ublituximab versus 5.9% on teriflunomide (hazard ratio 0.84, 0.50 to 1.41; p=0.51) — not significant. Infusion-related reactions occurred in 47.7% of the ublituximab group, and serious infections in 5.0% versus 2.9%. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): ublituximab suppresses relapses and MRI activity more than teriflunomide over 96 weeks; a disability advantage was not shown.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — two identical phase 3 trials (ULTIMATE I and II, 1,094 participants) concordant on relapse rate and MRI lesions versus teriflunomide; disability worsening not significantly different

title: Clemastine in multiple sclerosis: visual evoked potential latency shortened by 1.7 ms per eye in the 50-patient ReBUILD crossover — the first randomised remyelination signal, on a surrogate, with fatigue as the price
question: In multiple sclerosis with chronic optic neuropathy, does clemastine fumarate improve visual evoked potential latency — the first remyelination signal in a randomised trial?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a genuine first, at surrogate scale. In ReBUILD (Green AJ et al., PMID: 29029896), 50 patients with relapsing multiple sclerosis and chronic demyelinating optic neuropathy, on stable immunomodulatory therapy, were randomised in a double-blind crossover to clemastine fumarate 5.36 mg twice daily and placebo in sequence over 150 days. The primary endpoint was met: clemastine reduced the P100 visual evoked potential latency delay by 1.7 ms per eye (95% CI 0.5 to 2.9; p=0.0048) in the crossover analysis. Clemastine treatment was associated with fatigue; no serious adverse events were reported. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): clemastine produced the first randomised evidence that a drug can improve a remyelination marker in chronic multiple sclerosis lesions — 1.7 milliseconds on an evoked potential, not a demonstrated gain in vision or function; Tier C for a single small single-centre trial on a surrogate endpoint.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single small double-blind crossover trial (n=50): P100 latency delay reduced by 1.7 ms/eye on clemastine; surrogate endpoint, fatigue signal; Tier C

title: Ozanimod versus weekly interferon beta-1a in relapsing multiple sclerosis: relapse rates 0.18 versus 0.35 a year in SUNBEAM and 0.17 versus 0.28 over two years in RADIANCE at the 1 mg dose
question: In relapsing multiple sclerosis, does ozanimod reduce relapses versus weekly interferon beta-1a?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — two phase 3 trials, one result. In SUNBEAM (Comi G et al., PMID: 31492651; 1,346 participants, at least 12 months), the adjusted annualised relapse rate was 0.18 on ozanimod 1.0 mg versus 0.35 on weekly intramuscular interferon beta-1a (rate ratio 0.52, 95% CI 0.41 to 0.66; p<0.0001), and 0.24 on the 0.5 mg dose (rate ratio 0.69, 0.55 to 0.86). In RADIANCE (Cohen JA et al., PMID: 31492652; 1,320 participants, 24 months), the adjusted rates were 0.17 on ozanimod 1.0 mg versus 0.28 on interferon (rate ratio 0.62, 0.51 to 0.77; p<0.0001), and 0.22 on 0.5 mg (rate ratio 0.79, 0.65 to 0.96). No first-dose clinically significant bradycardia or second- or third-degree atrioventricular block was reported in SUNBEAM. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): ozanimod roughly halves the relapse rate of weekly interferon beta-1a — against a comparator the field already regards as modest-efficacy.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — two concordant phase 3 active-comparator trials (SUNBEAM and RADIANCE, 2,666 participants): annualised relapse rate about halved versus interferon beta-1a at the 1 mg dose

title: Ponesimod versus teriflunomide in relapsing multiple sclerosis: relapses 0.202 versus 0.290 a year (a 30.5% relative rate reduction) and 56% fewer active MRI lesions in OPTIMUM — confirmed disability accumulation not significantly different
question: In relapsing multiple sclerosis, does ponesimod reduce relapses versus teriflunomide?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one large active-comparator trial. In OPTIMUM (Kappos L et al., PMID: 33779698), 1,133 patients with relapsing multiple sclerosis were randomised to ponesimod 20 mg or teriflunomide 14 mg daily for 108 weeks: the annualised relapse rate was 0.202 on ponesimod versus 0.290 on teriflunomide (a 30.5% relative rate reduction; p<0.001), and combined unique active MRI lesions per year numbered 1.405 versus 3.164 (a 56% relative risk reduction; p<0.001). Fatigue symptom scores also favoured ponesimod (mean difference -3.57; p<0.001). But time to 12-week and 24-week confirmed disability accumulation did not differ significantly (10.1% versus 12.4%, p=0.29; and 8.1% versus 9.9%, p=0.37). Treatment-emergent adverse events were near-identical (88.8% versus 88.2%), as were serious events (8.7% versus 8.1%). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): ponesimod controls relapses and MRI activity better than teriflunomide; Tier C because a single trial carries the claim and its disability endpoints were null.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single phase 3 active-comparator trial (n=1,133): annualised relapse rate 0.202 vs 0.290 and 56% fewer active lesions versus teriflunomide, disability accumulation not significantly different; Tier C

title: Tenecteplase 4.5–24 hours after stroke: disability-free survival 33.0% versus 24.2% where thrombectomy was not available (TRACE-III) — but a null result where most patients went on to thrombectomy (TIMELESS), with symptomatic bleeding 3.0% versus 0.8%
question: In Chinese patients with perfusion-selected stroke 4.5–24 hours from onset and no thrombectomy access, does tenecteplase improve outcome versus standard care?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in the population the question names. In TRACE-III (Xiong Y et al., PMID: 38884324), 516 Chinese patients with large-vessel occlusion, perfusion-imaging salvageable tissue, and no access to endovascular thrombectomy were randomised 4.5–24 hours after last-known-well to tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg or standard medical treatment: absence of disability (modified Rankin scale 0–1) at 90 days occurred in 33.0% on tenecteplase versus 24.2% on standard care (relative rate 1.37, 95% CI 1.04 to 1.81; p=0.03). Mortality was 13.3% versus 13.1%, and symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage within 36 hours was 3.0% versus 0.8%. The boundary, stated without its numbers because that trial is carded on its own shelf in this library: the same drug and window in patients most of whom went on to thrombectomy was null — the late-window drug has its proven case where no thrombectomy follows. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): late-window tenecteplase helps perfusion-selected patients who cannot get thrombectomy; Tier C — a single trial with a stroke-outcome benefit claim and a quadrupled symptomatic-bleed rate.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single randomised trial (TRACE-III, n=516): mRS 0–1 at 90 days 33.0% vs 24.2% without thrombectomy access, symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage 3.0% vs 0.8%; Tier C

title: Mobile stroke units in intracerebral haemorrhage: imaging 17.75 minutes sooner and arrival blood pressure 16.31 mmHg lower in the Berlin B_PROUD cohort — 7-day mortality and functional outcome no different
question: In intracerebral haemorrhage, does mobile stroke unit dispatch improve early blood-pressure management and outcome versus conventional care?
balance: SPLIT — the process wins are real, the outcome wins are absent, in haemorrhage specifically. In the B_PROUD intracerebral haemorrhage cohort (Schwabauer E et al., PMID: 38014623), 95 patients received additional mobile stroke unit dispatch and 78 conventional ambulance care in Berlin: after inverse-probability weighting, dispatch-to-imaging time was 17.75 minutes shorter (95% CI -27.16 to -8.21) and systolic blood pressure at hospital arrival was 16.31 mmHg lower (-30.64 to -6.19) with the mobile unit. But the primary outcome, 7-day mortality, did not differ significantly (adjusted odds ratio 1.43, 0.68 to 3.31), nor did favourable functional outcome (adjusted odds ratio 0.67, 0.27 to 1.67). The same Berlin programme's ischaemic-stroke analysis — carded on its own shelf in this library, and not re-carded here — did find better functional outcomes with dispatch, which makes the haemorrhage null a finding about haemorrhage, not about the vehicle. PROPOSED SPLIT: mobile stroke units deliver faster imaging and earlier blood-pressure control in intracerebral haemorrhage, with no demonstrated outcome benefit in that population; Tier C — non-randomised evidence throughout.
stamp: SPLIT — mobile stroke unit dispatch improved imaging time (-17.75 min) and arrival systolic pressure (-16.31 mmHg) in intracerebral haemorrhage but not 7-day mortality or functional outcome in the only ICH-specific controlled cohort; Tier C (non-randomised)

title: Anti-inflammatory add-ons fail in bipolar depression: minocycline and celecoxib, alone or together, no better than placebo in a 266-patient factorial trial
question: In bipolar depression, do adjunctive minocycline, celecoxib, or their combination improve depressive symptoms versus placebo in a factorial design?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — in a 266-patient 2×2 factorial trial in Pakistan, HAMD-17 scores fell in all four groups (from 24.5–25.2 to 11.3–12.8 over 12 weeks), but neither minocycline (adjusted difference 1.48, 95% CI −0.41 to 3.36; p=0.123) nor celecoxib (−0.74, −2.61 to 1.14; p=0.443) beat placebo. title: Treating insomnia with digital CBT-I (Sleepio) also eases anxiety: effect g 0.39–0.44, with 84% of the anxiety gain mediated by better sleep
question: In people with insomnia and comorbid anxiety, does digital CBT-I (Sleepio) improve anxiety outcomes as well as sleep versus control?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — pooling individual data from 2,172 people with insomnia and clinically significant anxiety in two large Sleepio trials, digital CBT-I beat control on insomnia (Hedges' g 0.77–0.81) and on anxiety (g 0.39–0.44, both p<0.001) at post-treatment and follow-up, and 84% of the follow-up anxiety improvement was mediated by the earlier sleep improvement. The catch: participants had anxiety symptoms, not a formal anxiety disorder diagnosis, and the analysis was run by authors employed by or consulting for the company that sells Sleepio. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): digital CBT-I for insomnia produces a moderate knock-on reduction in anxiety symptoms, apparently by fixing sleep first.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — individual-participant analysis of two large Sleepio RCTs (n=2,172) shows moderate anxiety improvement (g 0.39–0.44) mediated by sleep gains

title: Internet CBT (Amiria) cuts depression in multiple sclerosis: BDI-II about 6 points better than usual care, effect size near 1.0, in a 279-patient phase 3 trial
question: In people with multiple sclerosis and depressive symptoms, does internet-delivered CBT reduce depression versus waitlist?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in a five-centre phase 3 trial, 279 people with multiple sclerosis and depressive symptoms randomised to stand-alone or therapist-guided internet CBT (the MS-specific programme Amiria) or usual care: at 12 weeks the BDI-II score was 6.32 points better with stand-alone iCBT (95% CI 3.37–9.27; effect size d=0.97) and 5.80 points better with guided iCBT (2.71–8.88; d=0.96) than control, both p<0.0001. Clinically relevant worsening occurred in three control participants, one stand-alone participant and no guided participants; there were no deaths and no suicidality. The limits: one trial, an unblinded waitlist-style control, and 18% dropout by week 12. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a scalable online programme produced a large short-term reduction in MS depressive symptoms in its single confirmatory trial.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single phase 3 RCT (n=279) found internet CBT lowered BDI-II by ~6 points versus usual care in MS depression

title: Cariprazine maintenance does not prevent bipolar relapse: relapse 16.8–17.9% on drug versus 19.7% on placebo, hazard ratios 0.83–0.89 with confidence intervals crossing 1
question: In bipolar I disorder, does cariprazine maintenance prevent relapse into mood episodes versus placebo after stabilisation?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — 896 patients with bipolar I disorder entered open-label cariprazine 3.0 mg/day; the 440 who stabilised were randomised to cariprazine 1.5 mg, 3.0 mg, or placebo for up to 39 weeks. Relapse rates were 16.8% (1.5 mg), 17.9% (3.0 mg) and 19.7% (placebo), and neither dose beat placebo on time to relapse (HR 0.83, 95% CI 0.5–1.4; HR 0.89, 0.5–1.5). The authors note relapse on placebo was unusually low — an enriched, stabilised population in which a maintenance effect is hardest to show. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): in this trial, continuing cariprazine after stabilisation did not prevent relapse better than switching to placebo.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — a single randomised withdrawal trial found cariprazine maintenance no better than placebo for bipolar I relapse

title: PTSD: trauma-focused psychotherapy first — at long-term follow-up it beats medication (SMD −0.83 in network, −0.63 pairwise), though nothing separates the approaches at end of treatment
question: In PTSD, does trauma-focused psychotherapy outperform pharmacotherapy as first-line treatment — and how do their effects compare head to head in the meta-analytic evidence?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for psychotherapy as the first-line choice. Lee 2016 found trauma-focused psychotherapies produced larger effects against active controls than medications did against placebo, with more sustained benefit over time, while several drugs (paroxetine, fluoxetine) improved symptoms only slightly and others (bupropion, citalopram, topiramate and more) failed to separate from placebo at all. Merz 2019's network meta-analysis of the 12 head-to-head RCTs (922 participants) found no approach superior at end of treatment, but at last follow-up psychotherapy beat pharmacotherapy (network SMD −0.83, 95% CI −1.59 to −0.07; pairwise SMD −0.63, −1.18 to −0.09), with no difference in dropout acceptability. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the durable advantage sits with trauma-focused psychotherapy; medication is a second-line or adjunct option, not an equal first-line one.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two meta-analyses favour trauma-focused psychotherapy over pharmacotherapy for durable PTSD benefit; no difference at end of treatment

title: GLP-1 agonists reverse antipsychotic weight gain: 3.71 kg more lost than control in participant-level data, 6.74 kg in a 2026 pooled analysis — nausea the price
question: In people with schizophrenia and antipsychotic-induced weight gain, do GLP-1 receptor agonists reduce weight versus control?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — Siskind 2019's individual-participant meta-analysis of three randomised trials (n=164, mean weight 105.8 kg) found GLP-1 agonists (exenatide weekly ×2 trials, liraglutide daily ×1) produced 3.71 kg more weight loss than control over ~16 weeks (95% CI 2.44–4.99; p<0.001), with a number-needed-to-treat of 3.8 for ≥5% weight loss, and larger effects on clozapine/olanzapine (4.70 kg) than other antipsychotics (1.5 kg, CI crossing zero). A 2026 GRADE-assessed meta-analysis of 8 RCTs (664 patients) found a larger pooled difference (−6.74 kg, −10.05 to −3.43), with semaglutide the strongest agent (−11.06 kg). The price is gastrointestinal: nausea in 53.6% versus 27.5% in the participant-level data (number-needed-to-harm 3.8). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): GLP-1 agonists are the best-evidenced pharmacological answer to antipsychotic weight gain, on short trials with small total numbers.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two meta-analyses of RCTs show 3.7–6.7 kg greater weight loss with GLP-1 agonists in antipsychotic-treated patients, with more nausea

title: Acupuncture for insomnia: better scores on subjective sleep scales in low-quality trials, objective sleep unproven — an umbrella review and an electroacupuncture meta-analysis agree on the caveats
question: In chronic insomnia, does acupuncture improve sleep quality versus sham acupuncture or no treatment?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — an umbrella review of 15 systematic reviews found acupuncture significantly improved subjective sleep quality and insomnia severity, but effects on objectively measured sleep were inconclusive and the quality of the underlying studies was rated low. A 2024 meta-analysis of electroacupuncture (31 trials, 2,226 subjects) found a higher clinical response rate than mixed controls (RR 1.21, 95% CI 1.16–1.27) and a PSQI advantage of −3.23 points (−4.29 to −2.17), with no significant difference in adverse events (RR 1.48, 0.91–2.40) — but its trials were single-centre, small, and some of poor quality, and its controls mixed sham, no treatment, usual care and ordinary acupuncture. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): people report sleeping better after acupuncture; whether the needles beat a credible sham on objective sleep is not established.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — acupuncture improves subjective sleep scores in low-quality trials; objective benefit versus sham unproven

title: Argentine tango in Parkinson's: motor scores improved 28.7% over 12 months while controls stood still — small, unblinded trials from one research group
question: In Parkinson's disease, does Argentine tango dance training improve balance, gait and quality of life versus an exercise control?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in Duncan and Earhart's 12-month randomised trial, 62 people with Parkinson's disease assigned to twice-weekly community Argentine tango or a no-intervention control: the tango group's MDS-UPDRS-3 motor score fell 28.7% (12.8 points) while controls showed no significant change, with significant group-by-time interactions favouring tango on the MiniBESTest balance test, Freezing of Gait Questionnaire, 6-Minute Walk Test, forward and dual-task walking velocity, and the Nine-Hole Peg Test. A 2-year pilot extension in just 10 participants found the same pattern. The honest limits: the control was no intervention (not the exercise control the question poses), participants cannot be blinded to dancing, and both trials come from one group. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a year of tango improved motor severity and balance measures versus doing nothing; superiority over other exercise is untested in this record.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — randomised trials show tango improves motor and balance measures versus no intervention in Parkinson's; no exercise-control comparison

title: Coenzyme Q10 for migraine prevention: half of patients responded in the one good small trial (47.6% versus 14.4%), and a meta-analysis finds 1.52 fewer attacks — severity unmoved
question: In migraine prevention, does coenzyme Q10 reduce attack frequency versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — Sándor 2005 randomised 42 migraine patients to coenzyme Q10 300 mg/day or placebo: by the third month CoQ10 was superior on attack frequency, headache days and days with nausea, with a 50%-responder rate of 47.6% versus 14.4% (number-needed-to-treat 3). Sazali 2021's meta-analysis of six studies (371 participants) found CoQ10 reduced attack frequency (mean difference −1.52, 95% CI −2.40 to −0.65; p<0.001) and attack duration (−0.19, −0.27 to −0.11) versus control, but found no statistically significant reduction in headache severity. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): CoQ10 probably reduces how often migraines come, modestly, on small-trial evidence; it does not demonstrably make attacks milder. The publication names no branded product or company, and current products may differ in content and quality.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a small RCT and a 6-study meta-analysis show fewer migraine attacks on CoQ10 versus placebo; severity not reduced

title: SMILE self-management course for poorly controlled epilepsy: no gain in quality of life, seizure control or distress at 12 months in a 404-patient pragmatic trial
question: In epilepsy, does a seizure self-management programme reduce seizure frequency and improve quality of life versus usual care?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — SMILE (UK) randomised 404 adults with poorly controlled epilepsy (≥2 seizures in the prior year) to a 2-day group self-management course plus usual care or usual care alone. At 12 months, quality of life (QOLIE-31-P) was 67.4 in the course group and 69.5 in controls — no significant difference — and no secondary outcome (seizure frequency or recency, psychological distress, impact or stigma of epilepsy, self-mastery, medication adherence, adverse effects) differed either. The companion HTA report adds that the course was cost-saving and possibly cost-effective despite the lower quality of life, and that interviewed participants said the group increased their confidence. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): a well-run pragmatic trial of the flagship self-management course found no measurable clinical benefit at a year.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — a single large pragmatic RCT (n=404) found a 2-day epilepsy self-management course improved no clinical outcome at 12 months

title: Baclofen for alcohol use disorder splits its two big trials: Bacloville hit its consumption target (57% versus 36%) on a contested analysis, ALPADIR missed abstinence entirely (11.9% versus 10.5%) — with more serious adverse events on baclofen
question: In adults with alcohol use disorder, does baclofen reduce return to heavy drinking versus placebo?
balance: SPLIT — by trial and by endpoint. Bacloville (Rigal 2020; 320 primary-care patients drinking 129 g/day, baclofen titrated to up to 300 mg/day) met its primary endpoint: success (no or low-risk drinking in the final month) in 57% on baclofen versus 36% on placebo, a 21-percentage-point difference (95% CI 8–34; p=0.003) — but when patients who switched to open-label baclofen were not automatically counted as failures, the difference shrank to 62% versus 55% (6 points, CI −7 to 20), and serious adverse events occurred in 85 patients on baclofen (7 deaths) versus 36 on placebo (3 deaths). ALPADIR (Reynaud 2017; 320 alcohol-dependent patients, target 180 mg/day) missed its primary endpoint: 20 weeks of continuous abstinence in 11.9% versus 10.5% (OR 1.20, 0.58–2.50; p=0.618), with consumption differences non-significant (10.9 g/day at month 6, p=0.095) though craving fell (p=0.017). PROPOSED SPLIT: baclofen may reduce consumption in high-risk primary-care drinkers on one contested analysis; it does not maintain abstinence after detoxification, and its high-dose adverse-event burden is real.
stamp: SPLIT — Bacloville positive on consumption (57% vs 36%, sensitive to analysis) with more serious adverse events; ALPADIR null on abstinence (11.9% vs 10.5%)

title: Noisy knees do predict arthritis symptoms: crepitus 'always' carried 3.0-fold odds of incident symptomatic knee osteoarthritis in 3,495 people — but most cases arose in knees already abnormal on X-ray
question: Do noisy, clicking knees (crepitus) mean arthritis is coming — and does anything prevent it or help?
balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — as a prognostic signal, not a treatment effect. In the Osteoarthritis Initiative cohort (3,495 people without symptomatic knee osteoarthritis at baseline, followed to 48 months), the odds of developing symptomatic knee osteoarthritis rose stepwise with crepitus frequency: adjusted odds ratios 1.5 (rarely), 1.8 (sometimes), 2.2 (often) and 3.0 (always) versus never (p<0.0001 for trend). The catch matters for the visitor's question: knees that already had radiographic osteoarthritis without symptoms were 26% of observations but contributed over 75% of the incident cases — crepitus mostly flags knees whose joint is already changed, and this record tests no treatment or prevention. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm): frequent knee crepitus is a genuine risk marker for symptomatic osteoarthritis within four years, strongest where X-ray change already exists; nothing in this evidence says the noise itself damages the joint or that any intervention prevents the outcome.
stamp: POSSIBLE (harm) — a large cohort found a dose-graded association between crepitus frequency and incident symptomatic knee OA (adjusted OR up to 3.0); prognostic, not causal

title: Baricitinib beats adalimumab head-to-head in RA-BEAM: ACR20 at week 12 in 70% versus 61% (and 40% on placebo), with less radiographic progression than placebo
question: In rheumatoid arthritis with inadequate response to conventional DMARDs, does baricitinib beat adalimumab on disease activity when both are combined with methotrexate?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in RA-BEAM, 1,307 patients with active rheumatoid arthritis and inadequate response to methotrexate (all continuing methotrexate) were randomised to baricitinib 4 mg daily, adalimumab 40 mg every other week, or placebo. ACR20 at week 12: 70% on baricitinib versus 61% on adalimumab (p=0.014) and 40% on placebo (p<0.001). Radiographic progression at week 24 was lower on baricitinib than placebo (mean mTSS change 0.41 versus 0.90; p<0.001). The trial's patient-reported-outcome analysis found baricitinib also beat adalimumab on function, pain, fatigue and quality of life at week 12, maintained to week 52. Adverse events including infections were more frequent on baricitinib and adalimumab than placebo through week 24; cancers were reported in five patients (two on baricitinib, three on placebo); baricitinib lowered neutrophil counts and raised creatinine and LDL cholesterol. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): one large phase 3 trial puts the oral JAK inhibitor ahead of adalimumab on response, structure and symptoms — a single-trial superiority claim, so Tier C.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single phase 3 trial (RA-BEAM, n=1,307) found baricitinib superior to adalimumab and placebo on ACR20 with methotrexate

title: ADACTA: tocilizumab alone beats adalimumab alone when methotrexate cannot be used — DAS28 fell 3.3 versus 1.8 points at 24 weeks
question: In rheumatoid arthritis when methotrexate cannot be used, is tocilizumab monotherapy superior to adalimumab monotherapy?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — ADACTA randomised 325 patients with severe rheumatoid arthritis who were intolerant to methotrexate or inappropriate for it to tocilizumab 8 mg/kg intravenously every 4 weeks or adalimumab 40 mg subcutaneously every 2 weeks (each with the other's placebo) for 24 weeks. Mean DAS28 change was −3.3 on tocilizumab versus −1.8 on adalimumab (difference −1.5, 95% CI −1.8 to −1.1; p<0.0001). Serious adverse events were similar (12% tocilizumab versus 10% adalimumab); tocilizumab produced more raised LDL cholesterol, raised alanine aminotransferase, and reduced platelet and neutrophil counts. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the one head-to-head monotherapy trial favours tocilizumab clearly on disease activity — a single-trial claim, so Tier C.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single head-to-head trial (ADACTA, n=325) found tocilizumab monotherapy superior to adalimumab monotherapy on DAS28

title: Guselkumab works in psoriatic arthritis in both DISCOVER trials: ACR20 at week 24 in 52–64% versus 22–33% on placebo, in biologic-naive and TNF-experienced patients alike
question: In active psoriatic arthritis, does guselkumab improve joint and skin responses versus placebo — in biologic-naive patients and after TNF inhibitors?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — two phase 3 trials agree. DISCOVER-1 (381 patients, about 30% previously treated with TNF inhibitors): ACR20 at week 24 in 59% on guselkumab every 4 weeks and 52% every 8 weeks versus 22% on placebo (differences 37 and 30 percentage points; both p<0.0001). DISCOVER-2 (741 biologic-naive patients): 64% and 64% versus 33% (differences 31 points each; both p<0.0001). Serious adverse events to week 24 were no more frequent on guselkumab than placebo in either trial (DISCOVER-1: 0% and 3% versus 4%; DISCOVER-2: 3% and 1% versus 3%), and no guselkumab-treated patient died in DISCOVER-1 or had more serious infections than placebo overall. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): two large concordant trials, both dosing schedules, across biologic-naive and TNF-experienced disease.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — two concordant phase 3 trials (DISCOVER-1 and -2, n=1,122) show ACR20 roughly doubled versus placebo at week 24

title: HOPE: six weeks of prednisolone 10 mg relieves inflammatory hand osteoarthritis pain — finger pain fell 21.5 points versus 5.2 on placebo
question: In inflammatory hand osteoarthritis, does a short course of prednisolone 10 mg reduce finger pain versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the HOPE trial randomised 92 patients with painful hand osteoarthritis and ultrasound/clinical signs of synovial inflammation to prednisolone 10 mg daily or placebo for 6 weeks (then a 2-week taper and 6 weeks off treatment). Finger pain (100-mm VAS) fell by 21.5 points on prednisolone versus 5.2 on placebo — a between-group difference of −16.5 (95% CI −26.1 to −6.9; p=0.0007). Non-serious adverse events were similar; five serious adverse events occurred (one myocardial infarction on prednisolone; four events on placebo). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a short prednisolone course works for an inflammatory hand-OA flare — in one small, carefully phenotyped trial of patients selected for synovitis and an NSAID-washout flare, so Tier C.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single small RCT (HOPE, n=92) found 6 weeks of prednisolone 10 mg reduced finger pain by 16.5 VAS points versus placebo in inflammatory hand OA

title: Metformin for knee osteoarthritis pain: 11.4 mm better than placebo on a 100-mm scale at 6 months — statistically real, below the 15-mm difference patients were said to need
question: In overweight or obese adults with knee osteoarthritis, does metformin reduce knee pain versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a community-based telemedicine trial randomised 107 people with symptomatic knee osteoarthritis and BMI ≥25 to metformin 2,000 mg/day or placebo for 6 months. Knee pain (100-mm VAS) fell 31.3 mm on metformin and 18.9 mm on placebo — a between-group difference of −11.4 mm (95% CI −20.1 to −2.6; p=0.01; standardised effect 0.43). That is smaller than the trial's own stated minimum clinically important difference of 15 mm. Diarrhoea occurred in 15% on metformin versus 8% on placebo, and abdominal discomfort in 13% versus 9%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a real but modest average pain effect in one small trial, awaiting the larger confirmatory trial the authors call for — Tier C.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single small RCT (n=107) found metformin reduced knee OA pain by 11.4 mm versus placebo at 6 months, below the 15-mm clinical-importance threshold

title: Genicular artery embolisation no better than a sham procedure for knee osteoarthritis pain: 21.4 versus 18.4 points of pain reduction at 4 months
question: For symptomatic knee osteoarthritis, does genicular artery embolisation reduce pain versus sham embolisation?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — in a double-blind sham-controlled trial, 58 adults with symptomatic mild-to-moderate knee osteoarthritis not improving with conservative treatment were randomised to real or sham genicular artery embolisation. At 4 months, KOOS pain improved 21.4 points (95% CI 13.9–28.8) with embolisation and 18.4 points (11.6–25.1) with sham — a between-group difference of 3.0 points (−7.1 to 13.0), effect size d=0.15, with group allocation not a significant contributor (p=0.31). No serious adverse events occurred; 23 mild adverse events occurred in the embolisation group and 5 in the sham group. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): the large improvements after an invasive knee procedure were produced equally by its sham — the honest headline for embolisation in mild-to-moderate disease.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — a single sham-controlled RCT (n=58) found genicular artery embolisation no better than sham for knee OA pain

title: Topical capsaicin eases osteoarthritis pain for up to 3 months (SMD −0.84) — and burns: application-site burning RR 5.56, number-needed-to-harm 3
question: Does topical capsaicin cream relieve osteoarthritis pain versus placebo cream?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a 2024 systematic review pooled eight double-blind RCTs (498 patients) of topical capsaicin (0.0125%–5%) versus placebo in osteoarthritis: pain severity on visual analogue scale was lower with capsaicin (standardised mean difference −0.84, 95% CI −1.48 to −0.19; p=0.01). The trade-off is on the face of the result: burning sensation at the application site was far more common (risk ratio 5.56, 1.75–17.69; p=0.004; number-needed-to-harm 3). The reviewers rate the certainty low to very low, with short study durations, small samples and high heterogeneity; follow-up extended only to 3 months. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a genuine short-term pain effect for patients who cannot take NSAIDs, bought with predictable local burning — the publication names no branded product or company, and preparations vary widely in strength.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a meta-analysis of 8 RCTs (n=498) shows topical capsaicin reduces OA pain (SMD −0.84) with frequent application-site burning (NNH 3)

title: Glyceryl trinitrate patches split by tendon: Achilles tendinopathy improved (78% versus 49% asymptomatic at 6 months), patellar tendinopathy did not (no treatment effect, p=0.80)
question: In chronic Achilles and patellar tendinopathy, do topical glyceryl trinitrate patches improve pain and function versus placebo patches?
balance: SPLIT — by tendon. For chronic noninsertional Achilles tendinopathy, Paoloni 2004 randomised 65 patients (84 tendons) to glyceryl trinitrate patches (1.25 mg/24 h) plus rehabilitation or rehabilitation alone: the GTN group had less pain with activity at 12 and 24 weeks, less night pain and tenderness at 12 weeks, and 78% of tendons (28/36) were asymptomatic in daily activities at 6 months versus 49% (20/41) on placebo (p=0.001) — though the mean effect size across all outcome measures was only 0.14. For chronic patellar tendinopathy, Steunebrink 2013 randomised patients to GTN or placebo patches, both with eccentric training: VISA-P scores improved over time in both groups (to 75.0 and 80.7 at 24 weeks) with no treatment-by-time effect (p=0.80), no difference in pain during sports (p=0.38) or satisfaction (p=0.25); three GTN patients reported rash. PROPOSED SPLIT: a positive Achilles result driven by one small trial with p-value-led reporting, and a clean patellar null — tendon by tendon, not a class effect.
stamp: SPLIT — GTN patches positive in one small Achilles trial (78% vs 49% asymptomatic) but null in a patellar tendinopathy trial (p=0.80)

title: Glyceryl trinitrate for rotator cuff tendinopathy: one small trial positive at 6 months (46% versus 24% asymptomatic), a Cochrane review calling the whole field too weak to be sure
question: In rotator cuff tendinopathy, does topical glyceryl trinitrate improve pain versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — Paoloni 2005 randomised 53 patients (57 shoulders) with chronic supraspinatus tendinopathy to glyceryl trinitrate patches (1.25 mg/24 h) plus rehabilitation or placebo plus rehabilitation: at 24 weeks the GTN group had significantly less pain with activity, at night and at rest, less impingement, better range of motion and greater muscle force, and 46% of GTN patients were asymptomatic in daily activities at 6 months versus 24% on rehabilitation alone (p=0.007) — with a mean effect size across outcomes of 0.26. The Cochrane review of topical GTN for rotator cuff disease (three small studies, one at moderate and two at high risk of bias) could not meta-analyse them, found extractable pain data in only one study, and concluded longer-term benefit is uncertain, with headache a common side effect. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a single small positive trial, honestly framed by a sceptical Cochrane review — Tier C.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single small RCT (n=53) favours GTN patches in supraspinatus tendinopathy; the Cochrane review rates the overall evidence insufficient

title: Shock wave therapy for midportion Achilles tendinopathy: no better than placebo shock waves in the sham-controlled trial — everyone improved with physiotherapy
question: In midportion Achilles tendinopathy, does extracorporeal shock wave therapy improve pain and function versus sham or placebo treatment?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — against a true placebo, shock wave therapy has not separated. In the single-blinded placebo-controlled trial (Gatz 2021, PMID: 33586526), VISA-A scores improved in all three arms over 24 weeks (+23 points with point-focused ESWT, +18 with line-focused ESWT, +15 with placebo ESWT), with no significant time-by-group interaction (P = 0.24) — every group also did daily physiotherapy. Against no treatment the picture differs: in Rompe 2007 (PMID: 17244902), 52% on repetitive low-energy shock-wave therapy reported complete recovery or much improvement at 4 months versus 24% on a wait-and-see policy, a result statistically indistinguishable from eccentric loading (60%). So shock waves beat doing nothing, but not their own placebo — the honest reading is a large contextual/physiotherapy effect and no proven specific effect. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): versus sham treatment, ESWT has not been shown to improve Achilles pain or function beyond placebo plus physiotherapy.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the only placebo-controlled trial found no significant benefit of point- or line-focused ESWT over placebo ESWT, although ESWT beat wait-and-see in an earlier unblinded comparison

title: Cemented hemiarthroplasty for intracapsular hip fracture: modestly better quality of life and far fewer periprosthetic fractures (0.5% vs 2.1%) — no proven survival gain
question: For an intracapsular hip fracture, does cemented hemiarthroplasty improve quality of life and reduce reoperation versus uncemented hemiarthroplasty?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — cement wins on the outcomes that separate the two operations, modestly. In WHiTE 5 (Fernandez 2022, PMID: 35139272; 1,225 patients), health-related quality of life at 4 months was better with cement (EQ-5D utility 0.371 vs 0.315; adjusted difference 0.055, 95% CI 0.009 to 0.101; P = 0.02 — at the bottom of the 0.050–0.075 range considered clinically important), and periprosthetic fractures were much less frequent (0.5% vs 2.1%; odds ratio for uncemented vs cemented 4.37). Mortality at 12 months was 23.9% versus 27.8% (odds ratio 0.80, 95% CI 0.62 to 1.05) — a difference that was not significant. The earlier meta-analysis of 8 randomised trials (Li 2020, PMID: 32080078; 1,577 hips) agrees on the fracture harm of uncemented stems (periprosthetic fracture odds ratio 8.32; loosening/subsidence odds ratio 5.33) and on no significant 12-month mortality difference (odds ratio 1.22, 95% CI 0.94 to 1.59), while noting uncemented surgery is quicker and had fewer pulmonary emboli. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): cemented hemiarthroplasty gives a small quality-of-life edge and a clear reduction in periprosthetic fracture, at the price of a longer operation; a survival benefit is unproven.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — cemented hemiarthroplasty modestly improved quality of life and reduced periprosthetic fracture versus modern uncemented stems in a 1,225-patient trial, with concordant meta-analysis; no significant mortality difference

title: Trochanteric hip fracture: intramedullary nail and sliding hip screw tie at one year in the 850-patient INSITE trial — the cheaper screw is an acceptable alternative
question: For trochanteric (intertrochanteric) hip fractures, does an intramedullary nail give better outcomes than a sliding hip screw?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — with modern implants, the nail's dominance is not matched by better outcomes. In INSITE (Schemitsch 2023, PMID: 37278998; 850 patients), 1-year quality of life was identical in practical terms (EQ-5D mean difference 0.02 points, 95% CI −0.03 to 0.07; P = 0.42), with no between-group differences in revision surgery, fracture healing, adverse events, mobility or hip function, and no interaction with fracture stability. The older Cochrane comparison (Parker & Handoll 2010, PMID: 20824825; 22 trials, 3,749 participants for Gamma nail vs sliding hip screw) if anything leaned against the early nails: the Gamma nail was associated with more operative and later femoral fractures and a higher reoperation rate, with no differences in wound infection, mortality or medical complications. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): for AO/OTA 31-A1/A2 trochanteric fractures, nail and screw deliver the same 1-year outcomes, so cost and surgeon familiarity can decide.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — INSITE found no difference in 1-year quality of life or any secondary outcome between intramedullary nail and sliding hip screw, and the older Cochrane review found no advantage for nails

title: Romosozumab in men with osteoporosis: spine density up 12.1% vs 1.2% on placebo in a year — a density trial, with a numerical cardiovascular imbalance and no fracture endpoint
question: In men with osteoporosis, does romosozumab increase bone mineral density versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for bone density, in the only placebo-controlled trial in men. In BRIDGE (Lewiecki 2018, PMID: 29931216; 245 men), 12 months of monthly romosozumab 210 mg raised lumbar spine BMD by 12.1% versus 1.2% on placebo and total hip BMD by 2.5% versus −0.5% (P < 0.001 for both). That is a large, unambiguous effect on the surrogate the trial was powered for — but the trial reports no fracture outcomes, and its safety table carries the signal that has followed this drug: positively adjudicated cardiovascular serious adverse events in 8 men (4.9%) on romosozumab versus 2 (2.5%) on placebo, a numerical imbalance in a trial far too small to judge it, with overall adverse and serious adverse events otherwise balanced. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): romosozumab clearly increases spine and hip density in men over 12 months; whether that converts into fewer fractures in men, and at what cardiovascular price, this record does not say.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — romosozumab increased lumbar spine BMD by 12.1% vs 1.2% and total hip BMD by 2.5% vs −0.5% over 12 months in the single placebo-controlled trial in men; fracture outcomes untested and a numerical cardiovascular imbalance noted

title: Teriparatide after osteoporotic fracture: treatment failure 11.0% vs 17.6% — not significant; one meta-analysis finds better function, neither finds faster healing
question: Does teriparatide speed healing and improve outcomes in osteoporotic fractures versus control treatment?
balance: SPLIT — the healing claim fails, a functional claim survives weakly. Pooling the 5 randomised trials in osteoporotic hip and pelvic fractures (Moon 2020, PMID: 33335866), treatment failure — non-union, varus collapse, screw perforation or revision for mechanical failure — occurred in 11.0% on teriparatide versus 17.6% on control, an odds ratio of 0.81 (95% CI 0.42 to 1.53; P = 0.16) that is not significant. The broader meta-analysis of PTH analogues across fracture types (Eastman 2021, PMID: 33559713) reaches the matching verdict in words: PTH treatment improved functional outcomes but did not affect the fracture healing rate or reduce pain, across trials that were mostly in elderly patients with osteoporosis and of heterogeneous, limited quality. PROPOSED SPLIT: no demonstrated acceleration of healing or reduction in mechanical failure; a possible functional benefit that the underlying trials are too weak to quantify.
stamp: SPLIT — healing and mechanical failure not significantly improved (odds ratio 0.81, CI 0.42–1.53), while a second meta-analysis reports improved functional outcomes without faster healing or less pain

title: rhBMP-2 for open tibial fractures: 44% relative reduction in reintervention with unreamed nails (Govender) — no healing advantage at all with reamed nails (Aro)
question: In open tibial fractures, does recombinant human bone morphogenetic protein-2 reduce reintervention for delayed union versus standard care alone?
balance: SPLIT — the answer turns on the nail. In the 450-patient BESTT trial (Govender 2002, PMID: 12473698), where fractures were fixed predominantly with unreamed nails, the 1.50 mg/mL rhBMP-2 implant produced a 44% relative reduction in the risk of secondary intervention for delayed union (relative risk 0.56, 95% CI 0.40 to 0.78; p = 0.0005), with faster fracture and wound healing (wound healing at 6 weeks 83% vs 65%) and fewer hardware failures and infections in severe injuries. In the later trial restricted to reamed nail fixation (Aro 2011, PMID: 21454742; 277 patients), the same 1.5 mg/mL dose did nothing measurable: fracture healing at week 20 was 68% with rhBMP-2 versus 67% with standard care, secondary procedures were 12% in each group, and infections were numerically more frequent with rhBMP-2 (19% vs 11%; p = 0.0645). PROPOSED SPLIT: a real reintervention benefit in the unreamed-nail setting of the original trial; no demonstrated benefit when the fracture is fixed with a reamed nail.
stamp: SPLIT — rhBMP-2 reduced secondary interventions by a relative 44% in the unreamed-nail BESTT trial, but showed no healing benefit in the reamed-nail trial

title: Scaphoid waist fracture: surgery did not beat a cast at one year in SWIFFT (439 patients) — and carried a 14% serious-complication rate against 1%
question: In adults with a bicortical scaphoid waist fracture, does surgical fixation improve function versus cast immobilisation?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — on function, with the harms pointing against routine early surgery. In SWIFFT (Dias 2020, PMID: 32771106; 439 adults with bicortical scaphoid waist fractures displaced by 2 mm or less), patient-rated wrist evaluation at 52 weeks was 11.9 after early surgical fixation versus 14.0 with cast immobilisation (adjusted mean difference −2.1, 95% CI −5.8 to 1.6; p = 0.27) — no significant difference. The complication trade was lopsided: potentially serious surgical complications in 31 of 219 patients (14%) in the surgery group versus 3 of 220 (1%) in the cast group, while cast-related complications ran the other way (5 patients [2%] after surgery vs 40 [18%] in the cast group), and medical complications were similar (2% in both groups). The cast strategy in SWIFFT was not 'cast and hope': fractures that failed to unite were fixed promptly. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): initial cast immobilisation with surgery reserved for confirmed non-union gives the same one-year function without exposing everyone to surgical risk.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — SWIFFT found no significant difference in 1-year wrist function between early surgical fixation and cast immobilisation, with more serious complications from surgery

title: End-stage ankle arthritis: replacement and fusion improved walking/standing scores by statistically indistinguishable amounts at one year in TARVA — different complications, same totals
question: In end-stage ankle osteoarthritis, does total ankle replacement give better pain and function than ankle arthrodesis (fusion)?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — at one year, in the only randomised trial. In TARVA (Goldberg 2022, PMID: 36375147; 303 patients aged 50–85), both operations improved Manchester-Oxford Foot Questionnaire walking/standing scores substantially; the adjusted difference in change at 52 weeks was −5.6 points in favour of replacement (95% CI −12.5 to 1.4), which the authors judged neither clinically nor statistically significant. Adverse events were similar in total (109 vs 104) but different in kind: more wound-healing problems and nerve injuries with replacement; more thromboembolic events and nonunion with fusion, whose symptomatic nonunion rate was 7%. A post hoc analysis suggested fixed-bearing replacement implants did beat fusion (−11.1, 95% CI −19.3 to −2.9) — a hypothesis, not the trial's verdict. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): on one-year scores the two operations tie; the choice turns on complication profiles, implant longevity questions this trial cannot answer, and patient preference.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — TARVA found no clinically or statistically significant difference in 1-year walking/standing scores between total ankle replacement and arthrodesis, with similar total adverse events of different types

title: Humeral shaft fracture: surgery did not significantly improve 12-month function in FISH — but one in four braced fractures never united, and pooled data trade nonunion against infection and nerve injury
question: In fractures of the humeral shaft (diaphysis), does operative plate fixation improve function versus non-operative functional bracing?
balance: SPLIT — function ties in the trial; the failure modes do not. In the FISH trial (Rämö 2020, PMID: 32396179; 82 patients), DASH scores at 12 months were 8.9 after plate fixation versus 12.0 with functional bracing (difference −3.1 points, 95% CI −9.6 to 3.3; P = 0.34) — no significant difference, against a 10-point minimal clinically important difference. But 13 of 44 braced patients (30%) crossed over to surgery to promote healing, 11 (25%) developed nonunion, and 3 surgical patients (8%) had a temporary radial nerve palsy. The wider meta-analysis of comparison studies (Beyer 2023, PMID: 37459427; 18 studies, 706 patients) shows the same trade at scale: revision, nonunion and malunion risks were significantly higher with bracing (p < 0.0001, p < 0.0001, p = 0.004), infection and radial nerve injury higher with surgery (p = 0.04 and p = 0.01), and Constant shoulder scores higher after surgery (p = 0.004). PROPOSED SPLIT: average function at a year is similar either way; bracing buys avoidance of surgical complications at the price of roughly a one-in-four nonunion risk and frequent late surgery, while plating buys union at the price of infection and nerve risk.
stamp: SPLIT — 12-month function did not differ significantly in the FISH trial, but bracing carried ~25% nonunion and 30% crossover to surgery while surgery carried infection and radial-nerve risks in pooled data

title: Non-displaced Lisfranc injury: surgery and non-operative care scored 91.8 vs 96.1 at two years — in a trial that recruited 27 of its planned 60 patients and says so itself
question: In Lisfranc injuries, does operative treatment improve outcomes versus non-operative treatment in non-displaced injuries?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference) — the only randomised trial is frankly underpowered. Ponkilainen 2025 (PMID: 39584430) randomised 27 patients with CT-confirmed non-displaced Lisfranc injuries against a target sample of 60: at 2 years the mean VAS Foot and Ankle overall score was 96.1 with non-operative care and 91.8 with open reduction and internal fixation (mean difference 4.3, 95% CI −2.4 to 11) — no statistically significant difference, in the authors' own words an underpowered trial from which robust conclusions cannot be drawn. Both groups ended near the top of the scale, which is itself informative: non-displaced injuries do well. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference): no demonstrated advantage for operating on non-displaced Lisfranc injuries, on evidence too thin to close the question.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference) — the single randomised trial (27 of a planned 60 patients) found no significant difference between operative and non-operative care at 2 years and is explicitly underpowered

title: Lisfranc surgery: primary fusion beat fixation on function scores in the small 2006 ligamentous-injury trial (88 vs 68.6) — the larger 2024 displaced-injury trial found no difference
question: In Lisfranc injuries requiring surgery, does primary arthrodesis give better outcomes than open reduction and internal fixation?
balance: SPLIT — by injury type and by era. In the prospective randomised trial of primarily ligamentous Lisfranc injuries (Ly & Coetzee 2006, PMID: 16510816; 41 patients), primary arthrodesis of the medial rays produced a mean AOFAS Midfoot score of 88 at two years versus 68.6 after open reduction and screw fixation (p < 0.005); 5 fixation patients developed persistent pain with deformity or osteoarthrosis and went on to arthrodesis, and arthrodesis patients rated their activity at 92% of preinjury level versus 65% (p < 0.005). In the multicentre randomised trial of displaced Lisfranc injuries (Ponkilainen 2024, PMID: 38482816; 43 patients), the primary outcome told the opposite story: VAS-FA overall at 24 months was 86.5 with fixation versus 80.1 with arthrodesis (difference 6.5, 95% CI −5.3 to 18.2) — no evidence of a difference, in a trial that also fell short of its planned 60 patients. PROPOSED SPLIT: fusion ahead for purely ligamentous injuries in one small older trial; no demonstrated difference for displaced injuries in the newer trial — both underpowered, so neither verdict is secure.
stamp: SPLIT — primary arthrodesis scored better in the small ligamentous-injury trial (AOFAS 88 vs 68.6), while the displaced-injury trial found no significant difference (VAS-FA 86.5 vs 80.1); both trials underpowered

title: Tranexamic acid in hip and knee replacement: intravenous and topical routes tie — combining both cuts blood loss further and more than halves transfusion versus a single route
question: In primary total knee and hip arthroplasty, how do intravenous, topical and combined tranexamic acid routes compare for blood loss and transfusion?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for the combined route; the two single routes are interchangeable. Pooling 26 randomised trials (Sun 2019, PMID: 30696680), intravenous versus topical tranexamic acid did not differ substantially on total blood loss (weighted mean difference 30.92 mL, p = 0.31), haemoglobin decline, hospital stay, transfusion rate (relative risk 1.08, p = 0.75) or venous thromboembolism (relative risk 1.89, p = 0.15). But single-route patients fared worse than combined-route patients on every bleeding measure: total blood loss was 198.07 mL greater, haemoglobin decline 0.56 g/dL greater, and transfusion rate higher (relative risk 2.51, p < 0.05) — i.e., the combined route roughly halved transfusion relative to a single route. The earlier meta-analysis (Zhang 2017, PMID: 28602763; 6 trials, 704 patients) concurs: combined administration reduced total blood loss by a mean 134.65 mL and the transfusion rate by a risk difference of −0.07 (7 fewer transfusions per 100 patients, 95% CI −0.11 to −0.03). Neither analysis found a venous-thromboembolism penalty for combining routes. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): if tranexamic acid is given, give it both ways; if only one way, route does not matter.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — combined intravenous plus topical tranexamic acid reduced blood loss and transfusion versus single-route use in two concordant meta-analyses of randomised trials, while intravenous and topical routes alone did not differ

title: Tourniquet in knee replacement: it buys a drier field and a shorter operation — and costs more pain, less early motion, and the highest thrombosis rate in the network analyses
question: In total knee arthroplasty, does using a tourniquet improve the surgical field without worsening pain, function or thromboembolism?
balance: SPLIT — the tourniquet wins the operation and loses the recovery. In the 2022 Bayesian network meta-analysis of pain, function and thromboembolism (Migliorini 2022, PMID: 33967006; 54 articles, 5,497 procedures), the no-tourniquet group had the lowest rate of deep vein thrombosis, the lowest pain scores at 24–48 hours and at 1, 3 and 12 months, the greatest gain of motion at every time point from 3 days to 12 months, and the highest Knee Society scores at 1, 3 and 12 months. In the companion peri-operative network analysis (Migliorini 2021, PMID: 33417033; 68 studies, 7,413 procedures), full-time tourniquet use gave the shortest surgical duration and the lowest intra-operative blood loss, while hospitalisation was shortest with no tourniquet — and the total-blood-loss data were so inconsistent that no conclusion could be drawn on them. PROPOSED SPLIT: the field/duration benefit the question asks about is real but intra-operative only; on every patient-facing outcome the network evidence favours operating without a tourniquet, or limiting its inflation time.
stamp: SPLIT — tourniquet use shortened surgery and reduced intra-operative blood loss, but no-tourniquet surgery ranked best for pain, motion, function scores, hospital stay and deep vein thrombosis in two Bayesian network meta-analyses

title: Cervical disc replacement vs fusion: higher overall success (odds ratio 2.10), half the secondary surgery (0.50) and less adjacent-segment disease (0.46) in pooled long-term trial data
question: In cervical radiculopathy or myelopathy from disc disease, does cervical disc arthroplasty preserve motion and match fusion on long-term outcomes and reoperation?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — pooled randomised evidence favours the artificial disc on success, satisfaction and reoperation, which is why this shelf sits above POSSIBLE. In the long-term meta-analysis of 11 randomised trials (Wang 2020, PMID: 31863642; 3,505 patients), arthroplasty beat fusion on overall success (odds ratio 2.10, 95% CI 1.70 to 2.59), neurological success (1.65) and patient satisfaction (2.14), with less neck and arm pain, and significantly less symptomatic adjacent-segment disease (odds ratio 0.46, 95% CI 0.34 to 0.63), less total secondary surgery (0.50, 95% CI 0.29 to 0.87) and less surgery at both the index level (0.46) and the adjacent level (0.37) — with no significant difference in total adverse events (1.14, 95% CI 0.92 to 1.42). The earlier synthesis of 14 trials (Findlay 2018, PMID: 30062947; 3,160 patients, follow-up to 10 years) concurs: disc replacement was superior on patient-reported outcomes between 4 and 7 years and produced significantly less adjacent-segment disease at both 2 years and 4–7 years. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): arthroplasty matches or beats fusion on function and halves reoperation and adjacent-segment disease in the pooled trial record; the residual uncertainty is prosthesis durability beyond the trial horizon, not the direction of the evidence.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — two concordant meta-analyses of randomised trials (3,505 and 3,160 patients) found higher success and satisfaction, less adjacent-segment disease (odds ratio 0.46) and less secondary surgery (odds ratio 0.50) with cervical disc arthroplasty than with fusion

title: Degenerative spondylolisthesis: SLIP's small trial favoured adding fusion (reoperation 14% vs 34%) — the four-times-larger NORDSTEN-DS trial found decompression alone non-inferior at five years (responders 63% vs 63%)
question: In degenerative lumbar spondylolisthesis with stenosis, does laminectomy plus fusion improve outcomes versus laminectomy alone?
balance: SPLIT — the two randomised trials point in opposite directions, and the larger one is the null. In SLIP (Ghogawala 2016, PMID: 27074067; only 66 patients), adding instrumented fusion produced a greater improvement in SF-36 physical-component scores at 2 years (15.2 vs 9.5; difference 5.7, 95% CI 0.1 to 11.3; P = 0.046) sustained at 3 and 4 years, and a lower cumulative reoperation rate (14% vs 34%; P = 0.05) — but the Oswestry disability change did not differ significantly (−26.3 vs −17.9; P = 0.06), and fusion cost more blood loss and longer hospital stays (P < 0.001 for both). In NORDSTEN-DS (Kgomotso 2024, PMID: 39111800; 267 patients, 5-year follow-up), decompression alone was non-inferior: 63% of each group achieved at least a 30% Oswestry improvement (difference 0.4 percentage points, 95% CI −11.2 to 11.9, against a −15-point non-inferiority margin), with identical mean Oswestry changes (−17.8 in both groups). PROPOSED SPLIT: fusion may protect against reoperation in selected stable grade-I slips (SLIP), but for the average patient the bigger, longer trial says decompression alone does just as well at five years while avoiding the bigger operation.
stamp: SPLIT — SLIP (n = 66) favoured fusion on physical-component scores and reoperation, while NORDSTEN-DS (n = 267) found decompression alone non-inferior at 5 years with identical responder rates (63% vs 63%)

title: Starting allopurinol during a gout flare: pain, resolution time and repeat flares all unchanged in two randomised trials — the old 'wait until it settles' rule has no trial support
question: In acute gout, does starting allopurinol during the flare prolong or worsen the attack versus starting after it settles?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — starting during the flare neither prolongs nor worsens it, in two concordant randomised trials. In Taylor 2012 (PMID: 23098865; 57 men with crystal-proven gout), allopurinol 300 mg started at first medical contact versus placebo for 10 days (both groups on indomethacin and colchicine prophylaxis, all on open allopurinol from day 11) produced identical pain trajectories — visual analogue scores fell from 6.72 versus 6.28 at baseline to 0.18 versus 0.27 at day 10, with no significant difference on any day — and similar subsequent flares (2 vs 3 patients; P = 0.60), while urate fell rapidly on allopurinol (7.8 to 5.9 mg/dL by day 3). ELAG (Satpanich 2022, PMID: 34406530; 117 patients) found the same for timing: median time to complete resolution was 6 days in both the day-1 and day-14 start groups (p = 0.14), and median time to clinical resolution was 4 days in both (p = 0.12), with no serious adverse events in either group. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): the flare runs its course regardless — starting urate lowering during the attack is safe and saves a second visit's worth of delay.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — two randomised trials found no difference in pain, time to resolution or recurrent flares between starting allopurinol during an acute gout flare and starting it after the flare
