title: Erosive gout: pushing urate below 0.20 mmol/L (≈3.4 mg/dL) instead of 0.30 did not improve CT bone erosion scores over two years — and the intensive target was harder to hit (62% vs 83%) despite much higher drug doses
question: In erosive gout, does intensive serum urate lowering to a very low target improve outcomes versus standard target treatment?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — more drug, lower urate, same bones. In the 2-year double-blind randomised trial (Dalbeth 2022, PMID: 34927391; 104 patients with erosive gout), an intensive serum urate target of <0.20 mmol/L (≈3.4 mg/dL) versus the standard <0.30 mmol/L (≈5.0 mg/dL) produced significantly lower urate levels over the study (P = 0.002), yet CT bone erosion scores rose slightly in both groups with no between-group difference (P = 0.20), and every OMERACT core outcome — flares, tophi, pain, patient global assessment, quality of life, activity limitation — improved in both groups without between-group differences. The intensive strategy was also harder to execute: only 62% of the intensive group reached their target by year 2 versus 83% of the standard group (P < 0.05), despite a mean allopurinol dose of 746 mg/day versus 497 mg/day (P < 0.001) and significantly more combination therapy (P = 0.0004), with similar adverse-event rates. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): below the standard <0.30 mmol/L (≈5.0 mg/dL) target, further urate lowering bought no measurable structural or clinical gain over two years in erosive gout — at a substantially higher medication burden.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — intensive urate lowering to <0.20 mmol/L (≈3.4 mg/dL) did not improve CT erosion scores or any clinical outcome versus a <0.30 mmol/L (≈5.0 mg/dL) target over 2 years in the single randomised trial, despite significantly lower urate and higher drug doses

title: Tranexamic acid in hip fracture surgery: transfusion relative risk 0.72 in the pooled trials — a real reduction, with thromboembolic safety still under-powered rather than proven
question: In hip fracture surgery, does tranexamic acid reduce blood transfusion versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — transfusion falls; the safety file stays open. The pooled randomised evidence (Haj-Younes 2020, PMID: 31835969; 10 trials, 842 patients) shows tranexamic acid reduced the proportion of patients transfused with a relative risk of 0.72 (95% CI 0.59 to 0.88) — a 28% relative reduction — with no significant differences in mortality (relative risk 1.17, 95% CI 0.65 to 2.10), deep vein thrombosis (1.14), pulmonary embolism (0.53), acute coronary syndrome (1.52) or cerebrovascular events (0.78), all on low event counts. The best-known single trial (Zufferey 2010, PMID: 19926634; 110 patients) points the same way on efficacy — transfusion 42% on tranexamic acid versus 60% on placebo (P = 0.06) — while carrying the caution in its own data: vascular events at 6 weeks occurred in 16% versus 6% (P = 0.10), prompting the authors to warn of a possible hypercoagulable state and to call for further safety evaluation. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): expect roughly a quarter to a third fewer patients transfused, relatively speaking; do not read the pooled safety rows as proof of thromboembolic innocence.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — tranexamic acid reduced transfusion in hip fracture surgery (pooled relative risk 0.72, 95% CI 0.59–0.88) across 10 randomised trials, with thromboembolic safety estimates too imprecise to close the question

title: Hip fracture anaemia: iron plus tranexamic acid halved transfusion (15% vs 30%, RR 0.51) in HiFIT — but neither drug alone beat placebo (26% and 27% vs 30%)
question: In hip fracture patients with anaemia, does intravenous iron — alone or with tranexamic acid — reduce transfusion versus usual care?
balance: SPLIT — the combination works; the components, alone, were not shown to. In the HiFIT factorial trial (Lasocki 2023, PMID: 37524101; 413 hip-fracture patients with preoperative haemoglobin 9.5–13.0 g/dL), transfusion during hospitalisation occurred in 31 of 103 patients (30%) on double placebo, versus 16 of 104 (15%) on ferric derisomaltose plus tranexamic acid (relative risk 0.51, 98.3% CI 0.27 to 0.97; p = 0.012) — but in 27 patients (26%) on iron alone (relative risk 0.81, 95% CI 0.50 to 1.29; p = 0.28) and 28 (27%) on tranexamic acid alone (relative risk 0.85, 95% CI 0.54 to 1.33; p = 0.39), neither significantly different from placebo. Adverse events were similar across groups (487 events in total); severe postoperative anaemia (haemoglobin <8 g/dL) was more frequent on double placebo. The trial was stopped early for efficacy at its planned interim analysis. PROPOSED SPLIT: give both or expect little — in this trial the transfusion benefit belonged to the combination, and a single preoperative iron infusion by itself did not significantly reduce transfusion.
stamp: SPLIT — in the HiFIT factorial trial, iron plus tranexamic acid significantly reduced transfusion (15% vs 30%; RR 0.51), while iron alone (26%) and tranexamic acid alone (27%) did not differ significantly from double placebo (30%)

title: Prehabilitation before hip or knee replacement: better early function and pain after knee replacement in pooled trials — but 24 of 28 trials at high risk of bias, and the hip evidence is two contradictory trials
question: Before total hip or knee arthroplasty, does prehabilitation improve postoperative pain, function and length of stay versus usual care?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a real-looking early advantage after knee replacement, resting on a weak trial base. Pooling the randomised trials in osteoarthritis arthroplasty (Adebero 2024, PMID: 38349251; 28 trials), prehabilitation improved post-knee-replacement function (standardised mean difference 0.50, 95% CI 0.23 to 0.77), pain (0.44, 0.17 to 0.71), quality of life (0.28), strength (0.72) and functional mobility (0.39) — but 24 of the 28 trials were at high risk of bias, heterogeneity was significant for every outcome, hip-replacement evidence rested on 2 limited and contradictory trials, and the authors state these problems prevent conclusions about effectiveness up to one year. The wider orthopaedic synthesis (Punnoose 2023, PMID: 37052919; 48 trials, 3,570 participants) graded the postoperative evidence for knee replacement function at 6 weeks as moderate certainty (standardised mean difference −0.51, 95% CI −0.85 to −0.17, on scales where lower is better), with most other postoperative differences low to very low certainty. Neither record reports a pooled length-of-stay benefit, so that part of the question is unanswered here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): prehabilitation probably improves early recovery after knee replacement; for hip replacement, and for hospital stay, the evidence is not there yet.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — prehabilitation improved early postoperative function, pain and strength after knee arthroplasty in two meta-analyses, but the trial base is largely high risk of bias and hip arthroplasty evidence is limited and contradictory

title: NSAIDs and fracture healing: the large adjusted synthesis finds no significant nonunion increase (OR 1.11, 0.99–1.23) — the small randomised-trial pool finds harm (OR 3.47), concentrated in use beyond 4 weeks and in indomethacin
question: Do NSAIDs delay fracture healing or increase non-union?
balance: SPLIT — the two evidence layers disagree, and the disagreement is informative. The updated systematic review (Chuang 2024, PMID: 39319252; 20 studies, 523,240 patients, mostly observational) found no significant difference in non-union or delayed union between NSAID users and non-users (pooled adjusted odds ratio 1.11, 95% CI 0.99 to 1.23); an initial reoperation association (crude odds ratio 1.42, 95% CI 0.88 to 2.28) also became insignificant on sensitivity analysis. The meta-analysis restricted to randomised trials (Al Farii 2021, PMID: 34746650; 6 trials, 609 patients) found the opposite: nonunion odds ratio 3.47 with NSAIDs — but when trials were split by treatment duration, courses under 2 weeks showed no significant nonunion risk while courses over 4 weeks did, and indomethacin specifically carried odds ratios from 1.66 to 9.03 while other NSAIDs showed no significant risk. PROPOSED SPLIT: short courses look safe in both layers; prolonged use — and indomethacin in particular — carries a randomised-trial harm signal that the big observational pool, with its cruder exposure data, may simply miss. Because this is a harm claim, the shelf is Tier C.
stamp: SPLIT — a large mostly-observational synthesis found no significant nonunion association (adjusted OR 1.11), while the randomised-trial meta-analysis found increased nonunion (OR 3.47) confined to longer courses (>4 weeks) and indomethacin; short courses (<2 weeks) showed no significant risk

title: Knee cartilage defects ≥3 cm²: the MACI implant's pain-and-function advantage over microfracture was maintained at five years in SUMMIT (P = 0.022) — with no difference in MRI defect filling
question: In knee cartilage defects, does matrix-applied autologous chondrocyte implantation give better outcomes than microfracture?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one well-conducted randomised trial, followed to five years. In SUMMIT (Brittberg 2018, PMID: 29565642; 144 patients randomised, 128 in the 5-year extension), symptomatic knee cartilage defects of 3 cm² or larger treated with the MACI implant — autologous cultured chondrocytes on a porcine collagen membrane, as named in the record, which does not name a manufacturer — maintained a clinically and statistically significant advantage over microfracture on the co-primary endpoint of KOOS pain and function at 5 years (P = 0.022), with activities-of-daily-living improvements also significantly better (P = 0.007); quality-of-life and other-symptom scores remained numerically higher but lost statistical significance versus the 2-year analysis. MRI at year 5 (120 patients) showed improved defect filling in both groups with no statistically significant difference between treatments — the structural pictures tie while the patients' scores do not. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): for larger cartilage defects, MACI gives durably better pain and function than microfracture at five years, on the strength of a single trial programme.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the SUMMIT randomised trial's 5-year follow-up found MACI maintained a significant advantage over microfracture in KOOS pain and function (P = 0.022) for defects ≥3 cm², with no MRI structural difference

title: First-time kneecap dislocation: operating on the MPFL roughly halves redislocation (22% vs 43% in children; pooled OR 0.17) — but the operated children scored their knees slightly worse
question: After a first-time traumatic patellar dislocation, does medial patellofemoral ligament reconstruction prevent re-dislocation better than rehabilitation or bracing?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for preventing the next dislocation, with a function caveat and a population flag. In the randomised trial in skeletally immature patients aged 9–14 (Askenberger 2018, PMID: 29847145; 74 patients), arthroscopic-assisted MPFL repair cut 2-year redislocation to 8 of about 37 patients (22%) versus 16 (43%) with a knee brace (P = 0.047) — yet the repair group's mean Kujala score was lower (90.9, 'good') than the brace group's (95.9, 'excellent'), and the KOOS-child sport/play and quality-of-life subscales favoured the brace group among those with redislocations. The 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis (Elnewishy 2024, PMID: 39703292; 6 studies, 325 patients) pools a larger surgical advantage: redislocation odds ratio 0.17 (95% CI 0.09 to 0.32; P < 0.00001) and Kujala scores higher with surgery (mean difference 8.10) — but with severe heterogeneity (I² = 95%) and mostly non-randomised studies. A second randomised trial (Straume-Næsheim 2022, PMID: 35347375) is in recurrent — not first-time — dislocation: persistent instability at 12 months in 2 of 30 (6.7%) after MPFL reconstruction versus 13 of 31 (41.9%) with active rehabilitation (relative risk 6.3 for rehabilitation). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): MPFL surgery prevents redislocation better than bracing or rehabilitation; whether the average first-time dislocator's knee feels better for it is much less clear, and the randomised base is paediatric repair plus a recurrent-dislocation trial, not adult first-time reconstruction — hence Tier C.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — MPFL surgery reduced redislocation versus bracing in the paediatric randomised trial (22% vs 43%) and in a pooled analysis (OR 0.17), with a concordant trial in recurrent dislocation; functional scores did not favour surgery in the randomised trial

title: Ankle syndesmosis injury: suture-button fixation beats screws on function scores (AOFAS ~95 vs ~87) and implant problems (breakage 0% vs 25.4%, removal 6.0% vs 22.4%) in pooled randomised trials
question: For acute ankle syndesmosis (diastasis) injuries, does suture-button fixation give better outcomes than syndesmotic screws?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — consistent across two independent meta-analyses of the same small randomised literature. Shimozono 2019 (PMID: 30475639; 5 trials, 285 patients) found suture-button patients scored higher on the American Orthopaedic Foot & Ankle Society scale at a mean of 20.8 months (95.3 vs 86.7; P < 0.001), with no broken implants (0.0% vs 25.4%; P < 0.001), fewer implant removals (6.0% vs 22.4%; P = 0.01) and less joint malreduction (0.8% vs 11.5%; P = 0.05). Onggo 2020 (PMID: 30503612; 5 trials, 280 patients) confirms the pattern with a cooler head: the 1-year AOFAS advantage was a mean difference of 5.46 points (95% CI 0.40 to 10.51; p = 0.03) — statistically significant but, the authors note, of unlikely clinical significance — while implant failure was dramatically lower with the button (odds ratio 0.03, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.15; p < 0.001) and infection/wound problems were marginally, non-significantly higher (odds ratio 1.4, 95% CI 0.4 to 4.85; p = 0.60). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the button's clearest wins are mechanical — nothing to break, rarely anything to remove, better reduction — with a small functional edge on top.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two meta-analyses of randomised trials found better AOFAS scores and markedly fewer implant failures, removals and malreductions with suture-button fixation than with syndesmotic screws

title: One botulinum toxin A injection into the thumb base cut pain more than saline at 3 months in a 60-patient phase 3 trial — with transient thenar weakness in nearly half
question: In painful base-of-thumb osteoarthritis, does intra-articular botulinum toxin A reduce pain versus placebo injection?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — one small, well-blinded trial, a real pain difference, and a conspicuous side effect. In RHIBOT (Nguyen C et al., PMID: 38294016), 60 adults with painful trapeziometacarpal osteoarthritis received an ultrasound-guided injection of botulinum toxin A 50 units or saline, both with rigid splinting: at 3 months thumb pain had fallen by -25.7 points (0-100 scale) on botulinum toxin versus -9.7 on saline, an absolute difference of -16.0 points (95% CI -28.1 to -3.9; p=0.043). But 14 of 30 (47%) botulinum patients reported a mild transient motor deficit of the thenar muscle, versus 2 of 30 (7%) on saline, and no serious adverse events occurred in either group. A 2023 narrative review of intra-articular therapies for hand osteoarthritis (Oo WM et al., PMID: 36633823) places this among investigational injectates whose supporting studies are mostly small and short. There is no second randomised trial of botulinum toxin for this joint, no data on repeat injections, and no structural outcome. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): a single injection probably eases thumb-base pain for at least 3 months, at the price of temporary thumb weakness in many — one small trial is all there is.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — one 60-patient double-blind phase 3 trial showed a 16-point greater pain reduction than saline at 3 months, with transient thenar weakness in 47%

title: Tai chi matched physical therapy for knee osteoarthritis over a full year — WOMAC improvement 167 versus 143 points, a non-significant 24-point gap, with better depression scores on tai chi
question: For knee osteoarthritis, is tai chi as effective as physical therapy for pain and function?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — between the two active treatments, in the only head-to-head trial. Wang C et al. (PMID: 27183035) randomised 204 adults with symptomatic knee osteoarthritis to tai chi twice weekly for 12 weeks or standard physical therapy (twice weekly for 6 weeks, then 6 weeks of monitored home exercise). At 12 weeks the WOMAC score had fallen by 167 points on tai chi and 143 points on physical therapy — a between-group difference of 24 points (95% CI -10 to 58) that was not significant — and most secondary outcomes improved similarly in both groups, with benefits maintained to 52 weeks. Tai chi did significantly better on depression and on the physical component of quality of life, and no serious adverse events occurred. This is a comparison of two active therapies, not of tai chi against nothing: the trial cannot say how much of either group's improvement was the treatment itself. One trial, unblindable, at one centre. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): tai chi performed comparably to a standard physical-therapy course over 12 months, with a mood advantage — equivalence shown once, not replicated head-to-head.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — in one 204-patient trial tai chi and physical therapy improved WOMAC scores similarly at 12 weeks and benefits held to 52 weeks; tai chi scored better on depression

title: Opioids for acute low back and neck pain (OPAL): pain at 6 weeks no better than placebo — 2.78 versus 2.25 on a 10-point scale, the point estimate favouring placebo — with more opioid-related adverse events
question: In acute low back pain and neck pain, do opioids relieve pain better than placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — a judicious short opioid course did not beat placebo for the commonest acute spinal pain. In OPAL (Jones CMP et al., PMID: 37392748), 347 adults presenting to 157 primary care or emergency department sites in Sydney, Australia, with 12 weeks or less of low back or neck pain (or both) of at least moderate severity were randomly assigned to guideline-recommended care plus an opioid (oxycodone-naloxone, up to 20 mg of oxycodone per day orally; n=174) or guideline-recommended care plus an identical placebo (n=173), for up to 6 weeks, in a triple-blinded design. The primary outcome — pain severity at 6 weeks on the 10-point pain severity subscale of the Brief Pain Inventory, analysed in 151 opioid and 159 placebo participants who provided at least one post-randomisation pain score — was a mean of 2.78 (SE 0.20) in the opioid group versus 2.25 (0.19) in the placebo group (adjusted mean difference 0.53, 95% CI -0.00 to 1.07, p=0.051): no significant difference, and the point estimate favoured placebo. More participants in the opioid group had discontinued by week 6 (33 of 174, 19%, versus 25 of 172, 15%). At least one adverse event was reported by 61 participants (35%) on the opioid versus 51 (30%) on placebo (p=0.30), and opioid-related adverse events were more frequent on the opioid — constipation, for example, in 13 participants (7.5%) versus 6 (3.5%). The authors concluded that opioids should not be recommended for acute non-specific low back pain or neck pain. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): in one triple-blinded placebo-controlled trial of 347 patients, a short course of oxycodone-naloxone added to guideline care gave no pain advantage over placebo at 6 weeks for acute low back or neck pain, with more opioid-related adverse events.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — in one 347-patient triple-blinded placebo-controlled trial, oxycodone-naloxone up to 20 mg/day added to guideline care did not significantly reduce pain at 6 weeks versus placebo (mean 2.78 versus 2.25 on a 10-point scale; adjusted mean difference 0.53, 95% CI -0.00 to 1.07, p=0.051), with more opioid-related adverse events

title: Calcitonin eases acute vertebral fracture pain within a week — pooled effect large at week 1 (SMD -1.54, NNT about 2) in two systematic reviews, fading into uncertainty by week 4
question: In acute painful osteoporotic vertebral compression fractures, does calcitonin relieve pain versus placebo or usual care?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for the first days of pain, on pooled small trials. The updated systematic review (Boucher E et al., PMID: 32188529) included 11 studies in adults 60 and over with recent atraumatic compression fractures and found pain lower on salmon calcitonin (100-200 IU daily, injected or nasal) than control at week 1 with high certainty: standardised mean difference -1.54 (95% CI -2.02 to -1.06), a number needed to treat of about 2; by week 4 heterogeneity made the effect unclear, and adverse events overall were not significantly increased (nausea/vomiting risk ratio 2.10, 95% CI 0.87 to 5.08). The earlier review of five double-blind placebo-controlled trials, 246 patients (Knopp JA et al., PMID: 15614441), found the same pattern: pain at rest already lower at week 1 (weighted mean difference 3.08 on a 10-point scale, 95% CI 2.64 to 3.52) and still lower at week 4 (4.03, 3.70 to 4.35), with minor gastrointestinal side effects. Neither review shows any effect on fracture healing, function beyond mobilisation, or later outcomes. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): calcitonin is a reasonable short-term analgesic adjunct for the acute fracture week, not a treatment for the osteoporosis itself.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two systematic reviews of small placebo-controlled trials agree calcitonin reduces acute vertebral fracture pain within 1 week (SMD -1.54); the effect beyond 4 weeks is uncertain

title: Denosumab raised spine density 5.7% in a year in men with low bone density (ADAMO) — and 8.0% by two years — but the trial measured density, not fractures
question: In men with low bone mineral density, does denosumab increase bone density and is it safe over two years?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for bone density, from a single trial programme. ADAMO randomised 242 men with low bone mineral density to denosumab 60 mg every 6 months or placebo: at 12 months (Orwoll E et al., PMID: 22723310) lumbar spine density had risen 5.7% on denosumab, with gains of 2.4% at total hip, 2.1% at femoral neck, 3.1% at trochanter and 0.6% at the one-third radius, all significant versus placebo, and adverse-event incidence similar between groups. In the 12-month open-label extension (Langdahl BL et al., PMID: 25607608), continued treatment brought cumulative 24-month gains to 8.0% at the spine, 3.4% at total hip and 3.4% at femoral neck, men crossing over from placebo gained similarly in their first denosumab year, and no new safety signals appeared. What ADAMO never measured is the outcome that matters: it was not powered for fractures, so fracture protection in men is extrapolated from the women's trials, not shown here. One trial, one surrogate. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): denosumab reliably increases bone density in men over two years with a clean short-term safety record in this population; fracture benefit in men is inferred, not demonstrated.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the single ADAMO trial showed spine BMD +5.7% at 12 months and +8.0% by 24 months in men with low BMD, with no fracture endpoint and no new safety signals

title: Robotic knee replacement lines the implant up better — alignment outliers roughly halved — but patients feel no difference: WOMAC difference -0.35 points in pooled randomised trials
question: Does robotic-assisted total knee arthroplasty improve alignment, pain or function versus conventional surgery?
balance: SPLIT — the x-ray improves, the patient does not (yet). A systematic review of 12 randomised trials, 2,200 patients (Ruangsomboon P et al., PMID: 36805771) found robotic-assisted total knee arthroplasty probably makes little to no difference to patient-reported outcomes (WOMAC mean difference -0.35, 95% CI -0.78 to 0.07) or range of motion (mean difference -0.73 degrees, CI -7.5 to 6.0), while likely reducing mechanical-alignment outliers (risk ratio 0.43, CI 0.27 to 0.67 — a 57% relative reduction) and deviation from neutral alignment (mean difference -0.94 degrees, CI -1.1 to -0.73). A second meta-analysis of 7 randomised trials, 1,942 knees (Alrajeb R et al., PMID: 38133653), found the same split: significantly better anatomical and mechanical restoration on imaging, with clinical and functional scores and complication rates statistically similar. Neither review could settle revision rates — the outcome better alignment is supposed to improve — because follow-up is too short. PROPOSED SPLIT: robotic assistance is a radiological improvement in search of a clinical one; on current randomised evidence patients should not expect to feel better, move better, or have fewer complications.
stamp: SPLIT — robotic assistance improves alignment (outliers RR 0.43) across pooled RCTs, but patient-reported outcomes, motion and complications are the same as conventional surgery

title: Filgotinib beat placebo in all three FINCH trials — ACR20 up to 77% versus 50% on methotrexate background — and the 200 mg dose matched adalimumab on low disease activity
question: In rheumatoid arthritis, does filgotinib induce remission versus placebo — and how does it compare with adalimumab?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — three large double-blind phase 3 trials, one direction. In FINCH 1 (Combe B et al., PMID: 33504485; 1,755 patients with inadequate response to methotrexate), ACR20 at week 12 was 76.6% on filgotinib 200 mg and 69.8% on 100 mg versus 49.9% on placebo (both p<0.001), and filgotinib 200 mg was non-inferior to adalimumab for low disease activity (DAS28-CRP ≤3.2) at week 12, while the 100 mg dose was not. In FINCH 2 (Genovese MC et al., PMID: 31334793; 448 patients refractory to biologics), ACR20 was 66.0% (200 mg) and 57.5% (100 mg) versus 31.1% on placebo (both p<0.001). In FINCH 3 (Westhovens R et al., PMID: 33452004; 1,252 methotrexate-naive or limited-exposure patients), ACR20 at week 24 was 81% on filgotinib 200 mg plus methotrexate and 80% on 100 mg plus methotrexate versus 71% on methotrexate alone (p<0.001 and p=0.017), with remission (DAS28-CRP <2.6) in 54% and 43% versus 29%; filgotinib monotherapy (78%) did not significantly beat methotrexate (p=0.058). Adverse events were comparable across arms in each trial; herpes zoster cases appeared on filgotinib in FINCH 2, and none of the trials ran long enough to settle the JAK-class cardiovascular and malignancy questions. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): filgotinib induces response and remission well beyond placebo in every population tested, and at 200 mg stands comparison with adalimumab — with long-term class safety still the open file.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — three phase 3 trials show ACR20 responses 58-81% on filgotinib versus 31-50% on placebo, remission up to 54% versus 29% on methotrexate, and 200 mg non-inferior to adalimumab

title: Tapering works for many, stopping fails for most: remission held in 81% continuing, 59% tapering and 43% stopping DMARDs (RETRO) — while guided TNF dose reduction matched usual care on major flares (DRESS)
question: In rheumatoid arthritis in sustained remission on a biologic, can the biologic be tapered or stopped without flare?
balance: SPLIT — tapering is a reasonable, monitored gamble; stopping is a losing bet for most. In RETRO (Tascilar K et al., PMID: 38297524), 282 patients in sustained remission were randomised to continue full-dose DMARDs, taper to 50%, or taper then stop: remission at 12 months was maintained by 81.2% continuing, 58.6% tapering and 43.3% stopping (p=0.0005 for trend), with relapse hazard ratios of 3.02 for tapering and 4.34 for stopping versus continuing — though most who relapsed regained remission when full dose was reintroduced. The DRESS study (van Herwaarden N et al., PMID: 25858265) asked the narrower biologic question: in 180 patients with low disease activity on adalimumab or etanercept, a disease-activity-guided dose-reduction strategy was non-inferior to usual care for major flare at 18 months (12% versus 10%; difference 2%, 95% CI -12 to 12), with the drug stopped successfully in 20% and the interval extended in 43% — but short-lived flares were far commoner (73% versus 27%). So: about two in three patients can reduce a TNF inhibitor under close monitoring without a major flare; complete withdrawal, in RETRO, kept barely two in five in remission. PROPOSED SPLIT: taper — yes, with monitoring and a restart plan; stop outright — expect relapse in the majority.
stamp: SPLIT — guided dose reduction of TNF inhibitors is non-inferior for major flare and succeeds in about two-thirds, but full DMARD withdrawal keeps remission in only 43% versus 81% on continued treatment

title: Glucocorticoid bridging gets early rheumatoid arthritis down faster, but methotrexate alone catches up on remission by two years — 72% versus 67% in CareRA's low-risk group
question: In early rheumatoid arthritis, does initial combination therapy with a glucocorticoid bridging scheme beat methotrexate alone for remission and damage?
balance: SPLIT — bridging wins the early months, not the two-year remission count. CareRA (Stouten V et al., PMID: 31236568) randomised 379 DMARD-naive early rheumatoid arthritis patients by prognostic risk. In high-risk patients, methotrexate plus a prednisone step-down bridge (COBRA-Slim, starting 30 mg) put 72% into remission (DAS28-CRP <2.6) at two years — statistically indistinguishable from the heavier COBRA-Classic (65%, prednisone from 60 mg plus sulfasalazine) and COBRA-Avant-Garde (74%, plus leflunomide) regimens, with fewer therapy-related adverse events. In low-risk patients, COBRA-Slim reached 67% remission versus 72% on methotrexate alone without prednisone (Tight Step Up) — no significant difference — although the bridged group ran lower longitudinal disease-activity scores over the two years and needed fewer glucocorticoid injections. The COBRA-light trial (den Uyl D et al., PMID: 23606682) confirms the early pharmacology: prednisolone-based combination therapy drove DAS44 down by about -2.2 to -2.5 points within 6 months, with minimal disease activity in 41-49%. So the honest answer to 'does bridging beat methotrexate alone' is: faster and smoother control early, yes; more remission or less damage at two years, not shown. PROPOSED SPLIT: early benefit, long-term equivalence — and the lightest bridge (methotrexate plus prednisone step-down) did everything the heavier combinations did.
stamp: SPLIT — glucocorticoid bridging speeds early disease control, but two-year remission on methotrexate plus bridging (67%) did not beat methotrexate alone (72%) in CareRA's low-risk group; heavier combinations added adverse events, not remission

title: Denosumab slowed structural damage in erosive hand osteoarthritis in one 100-patient trial — joint scores diverged by 14.3 points at 48 weeks and new erosive joints were fewer (OR 0.24)
question: In erosive hand osteoarthritis, does denosumab slow structural damage versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for joint structure, from a single small phase 2a trial, with symptoms not the story. Wittoek R et al. (PMID: 38361122) randomised 100 patients with erosive hand osteoarthritis to denosumab 60 mg every 3 months or placebo for 48 weeks. The primary radiographic endpoint — change in the Ghent University Scoring System (GUSS), where positive change means remodelling and negative change erosive progression — favoured denosumab by an estimated 8.9 points at week 24 (95% CI 1.0 to 16.9; p=0.024) and by 14.3 points at week 48 (95% CI 4.6 to 24.0; p=0.003). Fewer new erosive joints developed on denosumab (odds ratio 0.24, 95% CI 0.08 to 0.72; p=0.009). Adverse events were actually more frequent on placebo (125 events in 90% of patients) than on denosumab (97 events in 80%). What the record does not show is that patients felt better: the demonstrated effect is radiographic, in one centre, in 100 patients, over 48 weeks. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): denosumab has genuine structure-modifying signal in erosive hand osteoarthritis — the first for any drug in this disease — but one phase 2a trial is a beginning, not a basis for routine use, and pain benefit is unproven here.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one double-blind phase 2a trial (n=100) showed less erosive progression on denosumab (GUSS difference 14.3 points at 48 weeks; new erosive joints OR 0.24); symptom benefit not shown

title: Hydrodilatation helped frozen shoulder more than placebo in the one low-bias trial in the Cochrane review — but adding it to a steroid injection changed nothing at 8 weeks in a 2025 double-blind trial
question: In frozen shoulder, does hydrodilatation (arthrographic distension) improve pain and movement versus corticosteroid injection or physiotherapy?
balance: SPLIT — better than placebo or physiotherapy alone in the older small trials; no better than a plain steroid injection in the newest blinded test. The Cochrane review (Buchbinder R et al., PMID: 18254123) found five trials, 196 people: the single low-risk-of-bias trial showed distension with saline and steroid beat placebo for pain (number needed to treat to benefit 2), function (NNTB 3) and range of movement at 3 weeks, with function benefit partly maintained to 12 weeks; a second trial found distension plus physiotherapy beat physiotherapy alone on movement and percentage pain improvement at 8 weeks; three further trials comparing distension against steroid injection alone gave conflicting results, all at high risk of bias. The 2025 double-blind trial (Konarski A et al., PMID: 40495621; 79 patients) directly tested the add-on: steroid injection with hydrodilatation versus steroid injection alone improved similarly (SPADI 57.7 to 32.7 versus 57.4 to 35.8), with no significant difference in any outcome at 8 weeks — and hydrodilatation was the more painful procedure. PROPOSED SPLIT: distension is an active treatment against inert comparators in the short term, but the fluid-stretch itself has not been shown to add anything to the steroid it is usually delivered with.
stamp: SPLIT — hydrodilatation beat placebo/physiotherapy short-term in small older trials (Cochrane 'silver' evidence), but a 2025 double-blind trial found no added benefit over corticosteroid injection alone

title: Surgery did not beat a cast for displaced distal radius fractures — wrist scores identical at 12 months in DRAFFT2 and at 24 months in older patients in CROSSFIRE, though 13% of casts later needed fixation
question: In adults with a dorsally displaced distal radius fracture, does surgical fixation improve function versus cast treatment?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — to wrist function, in two multicentre randomised trials, with one honest catch. DRAFFT2 (Costa ML et al., PMID: 35045969) randomised 500 adults with dorsally displaced distal radius fractures to moulded cast or K-wire fixation after manipulation: the Patient Rated Wrist Evaluation (PRWE) score at 12 months was 21.2 on cast versus 20.7 on K-wires (adjusted difference -0.34, 95% CI -4.33 to 3.66; p=0.87), with no difference at 3 or 6 months either. The catch: 33 cast patients (13%) needed surgical fixation for loss of fracture position in the first six weeks, versus one revision in the K-wire group. CROSSFIRE's 24-month analysis (Lawson A et al., PMID: 35476128), in patients 60 and over randomised to volar locking plate or closed reduction and cast, found the same functional equivalence (PRWE 13.6 versus 15.8; difference 2.1, 95% CI -4.2 to 8.5; p=0.50) and similar complications — though more plate patients called their treatment 'very successful' (75.0% versus 44.6%; p=0.002). PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): routine fixation does not buy better wrist function than a cast at 1-2 years; what it buys is insurance against the roughly one-in-eight chance the casted fracture slips and needs the operation anyway.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — two multicentre RCTs found no functional advantage to surgical fixation over casting at 12-24 months (PRWE differences -0.34 and 2.1, both non-significant); 13% of cast patients crossed to fixation

title: Bisphosphonates take about a year to pay off: 12.4 months of treatment to prevent one nonvertebral fracture per 100 women — 20.3 months for one hip fracture per 200
question: After starting a bisphosphonate, how long until fracture risk actually falls — what is the time to benefit?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — arriving on a measurable schedule, pooled from ten randomised trials. Deardorff WJ et al. (PMID: 34807231) fitted survival curves to 10 randomised trials of alendronate, risedronate and zoledronic acid in 23,384 postmenopausal women with osteoporosis (mean ages 63-74, follow-up 12-48 months). The pooled time to benefit was 12.4 months (95% CI 6.3 to 18.4) to prevent one nonvertebral fracture per 100 women treated (absolute risk reduction 0.010); 12.1 months (95% CI 6.4 to 17.8) to prevent one clinical vertebral fracture per 200 women (absolute risk reduction 0.005); and 20.3 months (95% CI 11.0 to 29.7) to prevent one hip fracture per 200 women (absolute risk reduction 0.005). In other words, the drugs work — but a woman whose life expectancy is under about a year is unlikely to live long enough to collect the nonvertebral benefit, and hip protection takes the longest to arrive. These are population averages from trial populations with established osteoporosis, not a promise for any individual. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): bisphosphonate fracture prevention is real but deferred — roughly a year for nonvertebral and vertebral fractures, nearer two years for hip — which is precisely the number deprescribing and goals-of-care conversations need.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a meta-analysis of 10 RCTs (23,384 women) puts bisphosphonate time to benefit at 12.4 months for one nonvertebral fracture prevented per 100 treated, and 20.3 months for one hip fracture per 200

title: Low-dose colchicine while allopurinol starts cut gout flares from 2.91 to 0.52 per patient in the one double-blind trial — 43 patients, flares also milder and shorter on colchicine
question: In gout, does low-dose colchicine prophylaxis during initiation of urate-lowering therapy prevent acute flares versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a large effect in a very small trial, never replicated under blind. Borstad GC et al. (PMID: 15570646) randomised 43 patients with crystal-proven chronic gouty arthritis starting allopurinol to colchicine 0.6 mg twice daily or placebo, continuing study drug until 3 months after serum urate fell below 6.5 mg/dL. Patients on colchicine had fewer total flares (0.52 versus 2.91 per patient; p=0.008), fewer flares in months 0-3 (0.57 versus 1.91; p=0.022) and months 3-6 (0 versus 1.05; p=0.033), less severe flares (visual analogue scale 3.64 versus 5.08; p=0.018) and fewer recurrent flares (p=0.001). Colchicine was well tolerated in this small sample. The relative reduction in flare count is about 82% relative — but it rests on 43 patients studied two decades ago, with no second placebo-controlled trial of prophylaxis at allopurinol initiation in this record, and modern practice (lower starting doses, treat-to-target titration) may flare less at baseline than this trial's placebo arm did. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): prophylactic colchicine during allopurinol initiation prevents and softens flares on the best available evidence — which is one small trial, so the shelf is Tier C.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single double-blind trial (n=43) found 0.52 versus 2.91 flares per patient on colchicine 0.6 mg twice daily versus placebo during allopurinol initiation, with milder flares

title: Rilonacept cut gout flares during allopurinol initiation in two blinded trials — 0.21-0.29 flares per patient versus 1.06 on placebo in phase 3, with injection-site reactions the price
question: In patients starting urate-lowering therapy, does rilonacept (interleukin-1 blockade) prevent gout flares versus placebo?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — two double-blind placebo-controlled trials, same direction, dose response in the larger one. In the phase II trial (Schumacher HR et al., PMID: 22223180), 83 patients starting allopurinol received weekly rilonacept 160 mg (after a 320 mg loading dose) or placebo: mean flares per patient over 12 weeks were 0.15 (6 flares) versus 0.79 (33 flares) (p=0.0011), and the proportion experiencing any flare was 14.6% versus 45.2% (p=0.0037). In the phase III confirmatory trial (Schumacher HR et al., PMID: 22549879), 241 patients starting allopurinol received 16 weekly injections of placebo, rilonacept 80 mg or rilonacept 160 mg: flares per patient over 16 weeks were 1.06 on placebo versus 0.29 on 80 mg and 0.21 on 160 mg (both p<0.001) — about a 73-80% relative reduction, with the absolute counts alongside — and patients with at least one flare numbered 46.8% on placebo versus 18.8% and 16.3%. The cost was injection-site reactions (19.8% on 160 mg versus 1.3% on placebo in phase III); other adverse events were broadly balanced. Rilonacept is a weekly injection for a problem oral colchicine also addresses, and it is not marketed for this indication — the shelf records efficacy, not a recommendation to seek it. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): IL-1 blockade with rilonacept prevents initiation flares as reliably as anything tested, at injection burden and cost the trials do not weigh.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — two double-blind trials show rilonacept cuts flares per patient from 0.79-1.06 on placebo to 0.15-0.29 during urate-lowering initiation, with more injection-site reactions

title: Cabergoline roughly halves moderate-to-severe ovarian hyperstimulation in high-risk IVF patients — pooled risk ratio 0.38 in one meta-analysis, class odds ratio 0.27 in the Cochrane review — without lowering pregnancy rates
question: In women at high risk of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome, does cabergoline prevent moderate or severe OHSS versus placebo or no treatment?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — two independent syntheses of randomised trials agree. The meta-analysis restricted to cabergoline (Leitao VM et al., PMID: 24360566; 7 studies, 858 women) found moderate-to-severe OHSS risk ratio 0.38 (95% CI 0.29 to 0.51) — a 62% relative reduction — with no signal of harm to clinical pregnancy (risk ratio 1.02, 95% CI 0.78 to 1.34) or oocyte yield (mean difference 1.15, 95% CI -0.76 to 3.07), though estimates for live birth (one study, 200 women) and miscarriage were imprecise. The Cochrane review of dopamine agonists (Tang H et al., PMID: 27901279; 16 trials, 2,091 high-risk women) found the class reduced moderate or severe OHSS versus placebo or no intervention with odds ratio 0.27 (95% CI 0.19 to 0.39) — in absolute terms, from an expected 29% of women to between 7% and 14% — again with no difference in live birth, clinical pregnancy, multiple pregnancy or miscarriage, and cabergoline specifically beat human albumin (odds ratio 0.21, 95% CI 0.12 to 0.38). Gastrointestinal adverse effects were increased for the class, driven by quinagolide data. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): for high-risk women in assisted reproduction, cabergoline prevents a large share of moderate-to-severe OHSS without costing pregnancies — live-birth safety rests on thinner data than the OHSS benefit.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — cabergoline reduces moderate-to-severe OHSS (RR 0.38, 95% CI 0.29 to 0.51) across randomised trials, with no demonstrated effect on clinical pregnancy rates

title: Aspirin, heparin, or both did not raise live births in unexplained recurrent miscarriage — ALIFE: 54.5% on combination, 50.8% on aspirin, 57.0% on placebo; Cochrane agrees in low-bias studies
question: In women with unexplained recurrent miscarriage, do aspirin, heparin, or both increase live births versus placebo?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — the biggest trial and the bias-restricted synthesis land in the same place. ALIFE (Kaandorp SP et al., PMID: 20335572) randomised 364 women with unexplained recurrent miscarriage to aspirin 80 mg plus nadroparin, aspirin alone, or placebo: live-birth rates were 54.5%, 50.8% and 57.0% respectively — the combination was 2.6 percentage points below placebo (95% CI -15.0 to 9.9) and aspirin 6.2 points below (95% CI -18.8 to 6.4); among women who became pregnant the rates were 69.1%, 61.6% and 67.0%. The Cochrane review (de Jong PG et al., PMID: 24995856; 9 studies, 1,228 women) found that two of three high-bias-risk studies claimed benefits, but in sensitivity analyses excluding them, no anticoagulant regimen improved live birth: aspirin versus placebo risk ratio 0.94 (95% CI 0.80 to 1.11), low-molecular-weight heparin versus aspirin 1.08 (0.93 to 1.26), heparin plus aspirin versus no treatment 1.01 (0.87 to 1.16). The harms are real if modest: more bruising, and injection-site skin reactions in almost 40% on heparin in one study. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): in unexplained recurrent miscarriage without antiphospholipid syndrome, anticoagulants are an intervention with costs and no demonstrated live-birth benefit — this shelf does not address antiphospholipid syndrome, where the evidence and practice differ.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — ALIFE and the low-bias Cochrane analyses show no live-birth benefit from aspirin, heparin, or both in unexplained recurrent miscarriage (live birth 50.8-57.0% across ALIFE arms, placebo highest)

title: Drospirenone contraceptive pills ease premenstrual symptoms modestly — symptom scores SMD -0.41 versus placebo in Cochrane's pooling, response 48% versus 36% in the largest trial — with more adverse effects and dropouts
question: Does a drospirenone-containing oral contraceptive improve premenstrual syndrome and premenstrual dysphoric disorder versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a small-to-moderate symptom benefit on low-quality evidence, bought with more side effects. The Cochrane review (Ma S et al., PMID: 37365881) pooled five randomised trials, 858 women, mostly with premenstrual dysphoric disorder: drospirenone plus ethinylestradiol improved overall premenstrual symptoms versus placebo (standardised mean difference -0.41, 95% CI -0.59 to -0.24; 2 trials, 514 women; low-quality evidence), with small improvements in productivity, social activities and relationships, but withdrawal due to adverse effects was more than three times as likely (odds ratio 3.41, 95% CI 2.01 to 5.78) and total adverse effects more than doubled (odds ratio 2.31, 95% CI 1.71 to 3.11; an assumed 28% risk on placebo becomes 40-54%). In the largest single trial (Yonkers KA et al., PMID: 16135578; 450 women, 24/4 regimen), symptom scores fell by -37.49 on drospirenone versus -29.99 on placebo (adjusted difference -7.5, 95% CI -11.2 to -3.8; p<0.001), and response (halving of symptom scores) occurred in 48% versus 36% — a number needed to treat of about 8. Placebo itself did a great deal in both records. Nothing shows benefit beyond three cycles, in milder PMS, or against other contraceptive pills. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): for women with PMDD who also want contraception, drospirenone pills offer a real but modest edge over placebo, with a clear adverse-effect price.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — drospirenone contraceptives improve premenstrual symptoms modestly versus placebo (SMD -0.41; response 48% versus 36% in the largest trial) on low-quality evidence, with more adverse effects and withdrawals

title: Anti-androgens for PCOS: better than metformin for hirsutism in pooled trials, but not better than placebo — the 2023 guideline review says pills first, anti-androgens when pills can't be used
question: In polycystic ovary syndrome, do anti-androgens such as spironolactone improve hirsutism and other hyperandrogenic symptoms?
balance: SPLIT — the answer depends on the comparator, and against placebo the case is not made. The systematic review prepared for the 2023 International PCOS Guideline (Alesi S et al., PMID: 37583655; 20 unique studies, 13 meta-analysed with 961 women, testing spironolactone, finasteride, flutamide and bicalutamide) found anti-androgens plus lifestyle beat metformin plus lifestyle for hirsutism (weighted mean difference -1.59, 95% CI -3.06 to -0.12; p=0.03) but were NOT superior to placebo plus lifestyle for hirsutism (-0.93, -3.37 to 1.51; p=0.45) or SHBG; daily dosing beat every-third-day dosing for hirsutism (-3.48, -4.58 to -2.39), and adding an anti-androgen to a combined oral contraceptive worsened lipid profiles without improving other outcomes. The reviewers' conclusion: evidence does not support anti-androgens in preference to contraceptive pills; they are an option for hirsutism when pills are contraindicated, poorly tolerated, or insufficient after six months. In the one head-to-head trial carded here (Alpañés M et al., PMID: 28912358; 46 women), a contraceptive pill plus spironolactone 100 mg beat metformin over one year on hirsutism (mean difference 4.6 points, 95% CI 2.6 to 6.7) and androgen levels, with similar cardiometabolic safety. PROPOSED SPLIT: anti-androgens outperform metformin-based care for hirsutism; superiority over placebo is unproven in this record, and they sit behind contraceptive pills in the guideline the review was written for.
stamp: SPLIT — anti-androgens beat metformin for hirsutism (WMD -1.59) but did not beat placebo plus lifestyle (-0.93, non-significant) in the 2023 guideline meta-analysis; contraceptive pills remain first-line

title: Levonorgestrel coil versus dienogest for adenomyosis: pain fell equally in the randomised trial — the coil controlled bleeding better (90% versus 77% lighter), dienogest scored better on quality of life; a meta-analysis leans the other way on pain
question: In adenomyosis, how do the levonorgestrel intrauterine system and dienogest compare for pain and bleeding?
balance: SPLIT — each treatment wins a different outcome, and the two records do not fully agree. In the randomised trial (Choudhury S et al., PMID: 38283750; 68 women analysed, 12 weeks), pain scores fell significantly in both groups — visual analogue scale 6.41 to 3.41 on the levonorgestrel intrauterine system (LNG-IUS) and 6.41 to 3.12 on dienogest — with no significant between-group difference; lighter menstrual bleeding was commoner on LNG-IUS (27/30, 90%, versus 17/22, 77.2%; p=0.006), while quality-of-life improvement was larger on dienogest (48.26 versus 28.76 points on the WHOQOL-BREF change; p=0.04), and neither drug caused major adverse reactions. The systematic review and meta-analysis (Akhigbe RE et al., PMID: 39032312; 6 studies, 707 women, all from Asia) leaned toward dienogest for pelvic pain (lower visual analogue scores) and uterine-volume reduction, while LNG-IUS patients had higher haemoglobin — consistent with better bleeding control — and side-effect rates (weight gain, breast tenderness, headache, insomnia, mood and skin effects) were comparable. PROPOSED SPLIT: for bleeding-dominant adenomyosis the coil has the edge; for pain-dominant disease dienogest may have it; overall the two are close substitutes, and the evidence is one small short trial plus a six-study synthesis.
stamp: SPLIT — LNG-IUS and dienogest reduced pain similarly in the randomised trial; LNG-IUS controlled bleeding better (90% versus 77%) while dienogest improved quality of life more, and a 6-study meta-analysis favoured dienogest for pain and uterine volume

title: Timing is the treatment: oestradiol started within 6 years of menopause slowed carotid thickening (0.0044 versus 0.0078 mm/year) in ELITE — started 10+ years out, it did nothing (0.0100 versus 0.0088)
question: Does starting oestradiol soon after menopause slow atherosclerosis progression compared with starting it late?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for early starters only, on a surrogate endpoint, in the single trial designed to test the timing hypothesis. ELITE (Hodis HN et al., PMID: 27028912) randomised 643 healthy postmenopausal women, stratified by time since menopause, to oral 17beta-estradiol 1 mg daily (plus sequential vaginal progesterone gel for women with a uterus) or placebo, with carotid intima-media thickness (CIMT) measured every 6 months over a median of 5 years. The treatment effect differed significantly by stratum (p=0.007 for interaction): in women under 6 years from menopause, CIMT progressed at 0.0044 mm/year on estradiol versus 0.0078 mm/year on placebo (p=0.008) — about a 44% relative slowing, with the absolute rates alongside; in women 10 or more years out, progression was 0.0100 on estradiol versus 0.0088 on placebo (p=0.29) — nothing. Cardiac CT measures (coronary calcium, stenosis, plaque) did not differ significantly in either stratum, and clinical cardiovascular events were not the endpoint. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): ELITE supports the timing hypothesis on arterial imaging — oestradiol slows subclinical atherosclerosis when begun early and not when begun late — but it is one trial, the endpoint is a surrogate, and the coronary CT half of its own record is null.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in the single ELITE trial, estradiol slowed CIMT progression only when started <6 years after menopause (0.0044 versus 0.0078 mm/year; p=0.008), not when started ≥10 years after (p=0.29); coronary CT measures were null in both strata

title: Sertraline after delivery cut postpartum depression recurrence from 50% to 7% — in a pilot trial of just 22 women, the only sertraline prevention trial Cochrane could find
question: In women with a previous postpartum depression, does sertraline started immediately after delivery prevent recurrence versus placebo?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — a dramatic percentage gap on a handful of patients. The pilot trial (Wisner KL et al., PMID: 15229064) randomised non-depressed women with at least one previous episode of postpartum major depression to sertraline or placebo immediately after birth for 17 weeks: recurrence occurred in 1 of 14 women on sertraline (7%) versus 4 of 8 on placebo (50%), a significant difference, with time to recurrence also significantly longer on sertraline. The Cochrane review (Molyneaux E et al., PMID: 29669175) found only two eligible prevention trials in total (81 women, both from the same research group): the sertraline trial, expressed as risk ratio 0.14 (95% CI 0.02 to 1.07) — very low quality evidence, its confidence interval just crossing 1 — and a nortriptyline trial that found nothing (postnatal depression in 23% on nortriptyline versus 24% on placebo; risk ratio 0.96, 95% CI 0.36 to 2.59). One woman on sertraline had a hypomanic episode; dizziness and drowsiness were commoner on sertraline. No new eligible trial has appeared in over a decade. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): sertraline prophylaxis may prevent recurrence in women with previous postpartum depression — the signal is large, the denominator is 22 women, and the honest grade is weak evidence.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — recurrence 7% on sertraline versus 50% on placebo in a 22-woman pilot trial (RR 0.14, 95% CI 0.02 to 1.07 in Cochrane's analysis); the only other prevention trial, of nortriptyline, was null

title: HPV vaccination after excision treatment was followed by far fewer CIN2+ recurrences — pooled risk ratio 0.43 in the BMJ meta-analysis — but almost all the evidence is observational, and the least-biased studies show less
question: Does HPV vaccination after surgical treatment (conisation) for cervical intraepithelial neoplasia reduce recurrence of HPV-related disease?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a large association (risk ratio 0.43, below the 0.5 threshold this library asks of observational evidence) that shrinks as study quality rises, which is exactly why it is Tier C. The BMJ meta-analysis (Kechagias KS et al., PMID: 35922074; 18 studies in the meta-analyses, mostly observational) found recurrent CIN2+ risk ratio 0.43 (95% CI 0.30 to 0.60) in vaccinated versus unvaccinated women after local surgical treatment — a 57% relative reduction — and 0.26 (95% CI 0.16 to 0.43) for recurrence related to HPV16/18, over a median 36 months; evidence for CIN3, other HPV-related lesions and persistent infection was lacking or very uncertain, and GRADE confidence ranged from very low to moderate. The second meta-analysis (Eriksen DO et al., PMID: 35470865; 9 studies, 19,971 women) found the same direction with a warning label: pooling only the two randomised trials gave odds ratio 0.29 (95% CI 0.16 to 0.53) and unadjusted observational data 0.35 (0.18 to 0.67), but adjusted observational estimates were 0.54 (0.21 to 1.35) — not significant — and most studies carried serious risk of bias. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): post-treatment HPV vaccination is associated with substantially fewer CIN2+ recurrences, plausibly causally given the randomised-trial pooling, but the definitive large placebo-controlled trial does not yet exist and vaccinated women differ from unvaccinated women in ways adjustment only partly removes.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — HPV vaccination after excisional treatment is associated with reduced CIN2+ recurrence (RR 0.43, 95% CI 0.30 to 0.60), but the evidence is mostly observational and adjusted estimates are weaker (OR 0.54, non-significant)

title: Tamoxifen relieves mastalgia in pooled randomised trials — response risk ratio 2.04 versus placebo in the 2022 meta-analysis, 1.92 in the earlier one — with 10 mg doing what 20 mg does
question: In women with cyclical mastalgia, does tamoxifen reduce breast pain versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a doubled chance of pain relief versus placebo in the pooled randomised trials, in a condition with a large placebo response. The 2022 meta-analysis (Sinha MK et al., PMID: 35752405; 9 randomised trials) found oral tamoxifen beat placebo for mastalgia relief with risk ratio 2.04 (95% CI 1.49 to 2.78; p<0.001), and no significant efficacy difference between the 10 mg and 20 mg doses over 3 months (risk ratio 1.08, 95% CI 0.97 to 1.21; p=0.18) — supporting 10 mg as the dose, typically for 3-6 months in long-standing mastalgia. An earlier meta-analysis of mastalgia treatments reached the same conclusion for tamoxifen; that record is carded at home on the danazol shelf (#3776) and is not re-carded here. Neither record is specific to strictly cyclical mastalgia — the trials enrolled mastalgia broadly — and tamoxifen's serious-harm profile (thromboembolism, endometrial effects) comes from its oncology literature, not these small pain trials, so the benefit shown here is for severe, persistent pain where that trade-off has been weighed. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): tamoxifen, usually 10 mg for a few months, roughly doubles the chance of pain relief over placebo in persistent mastalgia.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — tamoxifen roughly doubles pain-relief response versus placebo in pooled RCTs (RR 2.04, 95% CI 1.49 to 2.78), with 10 mg as effective as 20 mg

title: Danazol eases breast pain more than placebo — a mean pain-score gain of about 20 points in pooled trials — but its androgenic side effects are why it is not first choice
question: In women with mastalgia, does danazol reduce breast pain versus placebo — and at what cost in side effects?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — danazol relieves mastalgia pain versus placebo, at a real side-effect price. The meta-analysis of randomised trials (Srivastava A et al., PMID: 17509880) found a weighted mean pain-score difference of -20.23 (95% CI -28.12 to -12.34) in danazol's favour, and the small double-blind crossover trial behind it (Mansel RE et al., PMID: 6122770) found a significant, progressive fall in pain and nodularity on danazol, faster at 400 mg/day than 200 mg/day but with greater side effects at the higher dose. The same meta-analysis judged tamoxifen — not danazol — the drug of first choice because it carried the fewest side effects, so danazol's place is for severe, hormone-related breast pain when gentler options fail. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): pain relief is consistent across the pooled trials, but the evidence is old and small, and tolerability limits use.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — danazol reduces mastalgia pain versus placebo in pooled randomised trials (mean pain-score difference -20.23), with dose-related side effects that keep it from first-line use

title: Word catheter matches marsupialisation for Bartholin cyst or abscess: recurrence 12% versus 10% at one year — with less analgesia (33% versus 74%) and faster treatment (1 versus 4 hours)
question: For a Bartholin cyst or abscess, does Word catheter placement match marsupialisation on recurrence and healing?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — on recurrence, the Word catheter and marsupialisation are a draw, and the catheter wins on the day itself. In the WoMan randomised trial (Kroese JA et al., PMID: 27640367), recurrence within one year was 12% after Word catheter versus 10% after marsupialisation (relative risk 1.1, 95% CI 0.64-1.91; P=0.70), pain scores after treatment were comparable, but analgesics were used in the first 24 hours by 33% versus 74% (P<0.001) and time from diagnosis to treatment was 1 hour versus 4 hours (P=0.001). The systematic review of all eight randomised trials (Illingworth B et al., PMID: 31876985) likewise found the evidence consistent with effects in either direction (risk ratio 0.76, 95% CI 0.41-1.40 for marsupialisation versus Word catheter approaches). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): recurrence is equivalent within the trial's precision; choose on setting, speed and patient preference, not on expected recurrence.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — Word catheter and marsupialisation give comparable one-year recurrence (12% versus 10%) in the WoMan trial, with less early analgesia use and faster treatment for the catheter

title: After endometriosis surgery, hormonal suppression cuts recurrence versus no treatment (RR 0.41 pooled) — and PRE-EMPT shows long-acting progestogen and the pill tie on pain at 3 years, both about 40% better than before surgery
question: After surgery for ovarian endometrioma, does postoperative hormonal suppression reduce recurrence versus no suppression?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — postoperative hormonal suppression reduces endometriosis recurrence compared with no suppression, and the choice between the two main strategies is a tie on pain. The systematic review and meta-analysis (Zakhari A et al., PMID: 33020832) pooled 17 studies (2,137 patients; 13 randomised trials and 4 cohorts) and found recurrence significantly lower with suppression than with expectant management or placebo (relative risk 0.41, 95% CI 0.26 to 0.65), with lower pain scores too (standardised mean difference -0.49, 95% CI -0.91 to -0.07). The PRE-EMPT trial (Cooper KG et al., PMID: 38749550) randomised 405 women after conservative surgery to a long-acting progestogen or the combined pill — notably, it had no untreated arm — and found pain at three years identical between strategies (adjusted mean difference -0.8, 95% CI -5.7 to 4.2; P=0.76), improved by around 40% in both groups, with fewer repeat surgical procedures on the long-acting progestogen (73 versus 97 events; hazard ratio 0.67, 95% CI 0.44 to 1.00). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): suppress after surgery if pregnancy is not sought immediately; pick the agent on preference and tolerability. Tier C is set because the versus-no-treatment pooling mixes randomised and cohort studies.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — postoperative hormonal suppression lowers endometriosis recurrence versus no suppression (pooled RR 0.41), and long-acting progestogen versus the combined pill tie on 3-year pain in PRE-EMPT

title: Cystectomy beats drainage and ablation for endometrioma on pain and recurrence — recurrence 5–17% versus 37% at one year — but it costs more ovarian reserve: AMH falls by 1.08 versus 0.40 ng/mL-equivalent units after ablation
question: In surgery for endometrioma, does cystectomy reduce recurrence and pain compared with drainage and coagulation — and what does it cost ovarian reserve?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — for pain and recurrence, excision wins; for ovarian reserve, excision is the costlier operation, and both halves belong on the shelf. The Cochrane review (Kalra R et al., PMID: 39588841) pooled nine randomised trials (578 women): at up to two years, excision versus ablation may reduce dysmenorrhoea recurrence (odds ratio 0.25, 95% CI 0.12 to 0.52; recurrence 49% after ablation versus 10-34% after excision) and dyspareunia recurrence (OR 0.09, 95% CI 0.03 to 0.22); at one year it may reduce endometrioma recurrence (OR 0.17, 95% CI 0.09 to 0.34; 37% after ablation versus 5-17% after excision) and further surgery (OR 0.16, 95% CI 0.07 to 0.41), with little or no difference in spontaneous pregnancy (OR 1.27, 95% CI 0.33 to 4.87). The reserve cost comes from the second meta-analysis (Paik H et al., PMID: 38509401): anti-Müllerian hormone fell by a weighted mean 1.08 after cystectomy versus 0.40 after ablation, while recurrence was higher after ablation (risk ratio 1.51, 95% CI 1.08 to 2.12). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): cystectomy for symptom and recurrence control, chosen with open eyes about reserve — especially for bilateral cysts or women banking on future fertility.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — cystectomy reduces pain recurrence, endometrioma recurrence and reoperation versus drainage/ablation in randomised trials, at a larger measured fall in ovarian reserve (AMH)

title: Pravastatin to prevent pre-eclampsia: three tiny trials, 213 women — pooled risk ratio 0.62 with a confidence interval (0.33–1.14) that settles nothing; safety in a 20-woman pilot looked clean
question: In women at high risk of pre-eclampsia, does pravastatin prevent pre-eclampsia versus placebo?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference) — shown so far, in far too few women to close the question. The meta-analysis with trial sequential analysis (Provinciatto H et al., PMID: 38109997) pooled the entire randomised prevention literature — three trials, 213 women — and found no significant effect on pre-eclampsia incidence (risk ratio 0.62, 95% CI 0.33-1.14; P=.12), concluding that adequately powered trials are still needed. The largest contributing pilot (Costantine MM et al., PMID: 34033812) randomised just 20 women with previous early pre-eclampsia to pravastatin 20 mg or placebo from 12-16 weeks and was designed for safety and pharmacokinetics: no significant differences in adverse or serious adverse events, congenital anomalies or cord-blood chemistries, with pregnancy outcomes described as more favourable on pravastatin but not quantified in the abstract. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference): a biologically plausible idea with a clean early safety signal and no demonstrated prevention benefit — Tier C, because a prevention claim resting on 213 randomised women belongs in front of the developer.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference) — pravastatin has not significantly reduced pre-eclampsia in the three small randomised trials pooled to date (RR 0.62, 95% CI 0.33-1.14; 213 women)

title: Adding azithromycin to standard prophylaxis at non-elective caesarean halved postoperative infection: 6.1% versus 12.0% in the 2,013-woman C/SOAP trial
question: In non-elective caesarean delivery, does adjunctive azithromycin added to standard prophylaxis reduce postoperative infection versus placebo?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — one large trial, confirmed by the pooled randomised literature. In C/SOAP (Tita AT et al., PMID: 27682034), 2,013 women having a non-elective caesarean during labour or after membrane rupture received azithromycin 500 mg or placebo on top of standard prophylaxis: the composite of endometritis, wound infection or other infection within six weeks occurred in 6.1% versus 12.0% (relative risk 0.51, 95% CI 0.38 to 0.68; P<0.001) — about a 49% relative reduction, 5.9 percentage points absolute — with endometritis 3.8% versus 6.1% and wound infection 2.4% versus 6.6%, and fewer serious maternal adverse events (1.5% versus 2.9%); the neonatal composite did not differ (14.3% versus 13.6%). The 2022 meta-analysis of randomised trials (Yang M et al., PMID: 35091057) found the same direction: endometritis relative risk 0.62 (95% CI 0.49-0.79) and wound infection 0.40 (95% CI 0.27-0.58). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): adjunctive azithromycin for non-elective caesarean, where membranes or labour have raised the infection risk — the trial does not speak to elective, pre-labour caesarean.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — adjunctive azithromycin halves postoperative infection after non-elective caesarean (6.1% versus 12.0%; RR 0.51) in C/SOAP, with concordant meta-analysis

title: Remifentanil PCA beats pethidine for labour pain when an epidural is declined or unsuitable: epidural conversion 19% versus 41% in RESPITE — but an epidural itself still relieves pain better
question: For labour analgesia when an epidural is unsuitable or declined, does patient-controlled remifentanil relieve pain and satisfy mothers versus other options?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — against pethidine, the usual fallback, remifentanil patient-controlled analgesia is clearly better; against an epidural, it is not. In RESPITE (Wilson MJA et al., PMID: 30115484), 400 women at term who requested opioid pain relief were randomised to intravenous remifentanil PCA or intramuscular pethidine: progression to epidural analgesia was 19% versus 41% (risk ratio 0.48, 95% CI 0.34-0.66; p<0.0001), with no serious adverse events attributable to either drug. The earlier meta-analysis of 12 randomised trials (Schnabel A et al., PMID: 22273829) found the same pattern — lower pain scores at one hour, higher satisfaction and less conversion to epidural than pethidine — while epidural analgesia decreased pain scores compared with remifentanil (P=0.003). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): when an epidural is unsuitable, declined or delayed, remifentanil PCA is the better opioid option; it is not an epidural substitute of equal strength.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — remifentanil PCA halves epidural conversion versus pethidine (19% versus 41%; RR 0.48) with higher satisfaction in pooled trials, though epidural analgesia itself relieves pain more

title: Tocolysis for external cephalic version splits by drug: beta-mimetics raise success, nifedipine does not (42% versus 37% on placebo), and atosiban does worse than beta-agonists (36.7% versus 45.3%)
question: For breech presentation at term, does external cephalic version with tocolysis increase cephalic presentation and vaginal birth versus version without tocolysis?
balance: SPLIT — the answer depends entirely on which tocolytic. The drug class with evidence of benefit is the beta-mimetics: the systematic review (Wilcox CB et al., PMID: 21199292) records that ECV success rates are improved with betamimetic tocolytics, and found nifedipine worse than terbutaline head-to-head (pooled risk ratio 0.67, 95% CI 0.48-0.93). Nifedipine against placebo failed in its adequately sized trial (Kok M et al., PMID: 18669722): success 42% versus 37% (relative risk 1.1, 95% CI 0.85-1.5), caesarean delivery 51% versus 46%. Atosiban fared worse than beta-agonist controls in its meta-analysis (Riemma G et al., PMID: 33421816): success 36.7% versus 45.3% (RR 0.78, 95% CI 0.6 to 0.98), though with fewer drug side effects (16.0% versus 42.9%; RR 0.38, 95% CI 0.31 to 0.47) and no difference in caesarean rates. PROPOSED SPLIT: tocolysis helps ECV when it is a beta-mimetic; substituting nifedipine or atosiban for convenience loses the benefit.
stamp: SPLIT — beta-mimetic tocolysis improves ECV success, but nifedipine does not beat placebo (42% versus 37%) and atosiban underperforms beta-agonists (36.7% versus 45.3%)

title: Needle aspiration matches incision and drainage for breast abscess cure (RR 0.96) — and wins on healing time (about 11 days shorter), fistula (RR 0.21) and keeping breastfeeding going (interrupted breastfeeding RR 0.28)
question: In lactating women with a breast abscess, does ultrasound-guided needle aspiration match incision and drainage for cure — with better cosmetic and breastfeeding outcomes?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — cure is a tie; everything around the cure favours the needle. The meta-analysis of nine randomised trials (Zhou F et al., PMID: 37350731; 703 patients) found no significant difference in cure rate (relative risk 0.96, 95% CI 0.86-1.07) or recurrence (RR 0.68, 95% CI 0.35-1.30), but aspiration healed faster (weighted mean difference -11.02 days, 95% CI -15.14 to -6.90), caused fewer breast fistulas (RR 0.21, 95% CI 0.06-0.72), far less interrupted breastfeeding (RR 0.28, 95% CI 0.20-0.39) and higher appearance satisfaction (RR 1.51, 95% CI 1.03-2.21). The Cochrane review restricted to breastfeeding women (Irusen H et al., PMID: 26279276; four contributing studies, 325 women) could not pool its resolution-time data for heterogeneity (I²=97%) and found one small study favouring aspiration by 6.07 days — directionally the same, statistically fragile. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): aspiration first for most lactational abscesses, reserving incision and drainage for large, multiloculated or aspiration-refractory collections, exactly as the meta-analysis concludes.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — needle aspiration cures as often as incision and drainage (RR 0.96) with shorter healing, fewer fistulas and much less interrupted breastfeeding in pooled randomised trials

title: Pessary self-management matches clinic care for prolapse quality of life at 18 months and at 4 years (TOPSY) — with fewer complications (16.7% versus 22.0%) and lower cost
question: In women using a vaginal pessary for prolapse, is self-management as effective as clinic-based care for symptoms and complications?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — on quality of life, self-management neither improves nor worsens outcomes, and it is cheaper with fewer complications. In TOPSY (Hagen S et al., PMID: 38078194), 340 women using a pessary for prolapse were randomised to a 30-minute self-management teaching session with telephone support or to routine clinic-based care: pelvic-floor quality of life (PFIQ-7) at 18 months was 32.3 versus 32.5 (adjusted mean difference -0.03, 95% CI -9.32 to 9.25), complications were fewer with self-management (16.7% versus 22.0%; adjusted mean difference -3.83%, 95% CI -6.86% to -0.81%), and self-management cost less (incremental net benefit £564). The four-year follow-up (Bugge C et al., PMID: 40832737) found the same picture in 186 responders: PFIQ-7 32.9 versus 31.4 (adjusted mean difference 4.86, 95% CI -6.41 to 16.12), complications 17.7% versus 22.0%, and self-management still cost-effective (incremental net benefit £2,240). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): offer self-management to women who can and want to do it — the gain is convenience, cost and slightly fewer complications, not better prolapse control. Tier C is set: one trial and its own follow-up carry the shelf.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — pessary self-management gives the same prolapse quality of life as clinic care at 18 months and 4 years in TOPSY, with fewer complications and lower cost

title: Soy isoflavone extracts cut hot flush frequency by about a fifth versus placebo (20.6% relative reduction) in one meta-analysis — but Cochrane pooling of the wider phytoestrogen literature found no conclusive effect
question: Do soy isoflavones reduce the frequency and severity of menopausal hot flushes versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a real but modest effect for extracted or synthesised soy isoflavones specifically, with a dissenting Cochrane read of the broader literature. The dedicated meta-analysis (Taku K et al., PMID: 22433977) pooled double-blind randomised trials of extracted or synthesised soybean isoflavones (median 54 mg aglycone equivalents, six weeks to 12 months) and found hot flush frequency reduced by 20.6% relative to placebo (95% CI -28.38 to -12.86; P<0.00001) and severity by 26.2% relative (95% CI -42.23 to -10.15; P=0.001), with supplements providing more than 18.8 mg of genistein more than twice as potent as lower-genistein ones — though heterogeneity was high (I²=67% for frequency, 86% for severity). The Cochrane review of all phytoestrogens (Lethaby A et al., PMID: 24323914; 43 trials, 4,364 participants) concluded there was no conclusive evidence that phytoestrogen supplements reduce flush frequency or severity, while noting high-genistein extracts consistently reduced frequency in four trials and a strong placebo effect (frequency reductions of 1% to 59% on placebo). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): expect, at best, about a one-fifth relative trim in flushes from a genistein-rich extract — not the abolition hormone therapy can give. No specific commercial product is named in either record, so none is named here; products on sale may differ in genistein content, safety and effectiveness.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — extracted soy isoflavones reduce hot flush frequency by 20.6% relative to placebo in a dedicated meta-analysis, an effect Cochrane's wider phytoestrogen review did not confirm as conclusive

title: Hypnosis cuts hot flashes well beyond control conditions: scores fell 80% with clinician-led hypnosis versus 15% on attention control, and self-administered hypnosis beat sham (53.4% versus 40.9% score fall) in 2025
question: Does hypnosis reduce hot flush frequency and severity in postmenopausal women and breast cancer survivors versus sham or control?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — two randomised trials from the same programme, against two different controls, point the same way. The clinician-delivered trial (Elkins GR et al., PMID: 23435026) randomised 187 postmenopausal women with at least seven flushes a day to five weekly hypnosis sessions or structured-attention control: by week 12, subjective flush frequency had fallen 74.16% versus 17.13% and flush score 80.32% versus 15.38% (both P<0.001), with physiologically monitored flushes down 56.86% versus 9.94%. The self-administered trial (Elkins G et al., PMID: 41217756) randomised 250 women (24.8% with a history of breast cancer) to six weeks of self-hypnosis audio or sham white-noise hypnosis: flush scores fell 53.4% versus 40.9% (P=.04) — a much smaller margin, because the sham was an active control carrying the full placebo and expectancy load. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): hypnosis works for hot flashes; how much of the gain survives a rigorous sham depends on delivery, and self-administration is the accessible, smaller-effect version.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — hypnosis reduces hot flash frequency and scores versus attention control (74% versus 17% frequency fall) and versus sham self-hypnosis (53.4% versus 40.9% score fall) in two randomised trials
