title: Clonidine trims hot flashes by about one flush a day versus placebo (pooled mean difference -0.95) — a modest drug effect bought with dry mouth, constipation and, in the breast-cancer trial, worse sleep (41% versus 21%)
question: Does clonidine reduce menopausal hot flushes versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — clonidine works, a little. The JAMA systematic review and meta-analysis (Nelson HD et al., PMID: 16670414) pooled four placebo-controlled clonidine trials and found daily hot flash frequency reduced by a mean 0.95 flushes versus placebo (95% CI -1.44 to -0.47) — less than the pooled effects of the antidepressants (-1.13) and gabapentin (-2.05) in the same review, and less than oestrogen. The largest single trial (Pandya KJ et al., PMID: 10819701) randomised 194 postmenopausal women with breast cancer on tamoxifen to clonidine 0.1 mg daily or placebo: flush frequency fell 37% versus 20% at four weeks and 38% versus 24% at eight weeks, but difficulty sleeping was reported by 41% on clonidine versus 21% on placebo (P=0.02). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a genuine but small effect — roughly one flush a day — reasonable when hormones are off the table and better-evidenced non-hormonal options do not suit, with sleep and anticholinergic-type side effects counted in.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — clonidine reduces daily hot flash frequency by about 0.95 flushes versus placebo in pooled trials, a modest effect with measurable side effects including worse sleep

title: Endometrial ablation beats the levonorgestrel intrauterine system on blood loss at 2 years (PBAC 14.2 versus 64.8) and surgical reintervention (10% versus 27%) — satisfaction and quality of life tie, and by 7 years hysterectomy rates converge
question: For heavy menstrual bleeding, how does endometrial ablation compare with the levonorgestrel intrauterine system on bleeding control, satisfaction and further surgery?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for ablation, on the mechanical outcomes; for the intrauterine system, on reversibility and avoiding a procedure, with satisfaction equal either way. In the MIRA randomised trial (Beelen P et al., PMID: 32795428), 270 women with heavy menstrual bleeding were allocated to a levonorgestrel intrauterine system or bipolar radiofrequency endometrial ablation: at 24 months the intrauterine system was not shown non-inferior on blood loss (Pictorial Blood Loss Assessment Chart scores 64.8 versus 14.2; difference 50.5 points, 95% CI 4.3-96.7; non-inferiority P=.87), and surgical reintervention was 27% versus 10% (relative risk 2.64, 95% CI 1.49-4.68), while satisfaction and quality of life did not differ significantly. At a mean 7.4 years (Huijs DPC et al., PMID: 38280433; 196 women), total reintervention was 40.0% versus 28.7% (RR 1.39, 95% CI 0.92-2.10), surgical reintervention remained higher after starting with the system (35.3% versus 19.1%; RR 1.84, 95% CI 1.11-3.10), but hysterectomy rates were similar (11.8% versus 18.1%; RR 0.65, 95% CI 0.32-1.34) and median bleeding scores were 0.0 in the follow-up sample. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for ablation on bleeding control and durability — Tier C, because one trial and its own follow-up carry the comparison.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — endometrial ablation controls blood loss better and needs less surgical reintervention than starting with a levonorgestrel intrauterine system in the MIRA trial, with equal satisfaction and quality of life

title: Misoprostol alone aborts about 9 in 10 early pregnancies after extra doses — sublingual beats buccal at preventing continuing pregnancy (1.1% versus 5.5%), buccal causes less chills and fever
question: How effective is a misoprostol-alone regimen for early abortion, and does route (buccal versus sublingual) change success?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — misoprostol alone works, and the route changes the failure mode more than the final success rate. In the multicentre randomised trial (Sheldon WR et al., PMID: 30831103), 401 women received three doses of misoprostol 800 µg every three hours, buccal or sublingual: continuing pregnancy at first follow-up was 1.1% (2/189) sublingual versus 5.5% (11/201) buccal (p=.02), but after additional misoprostol was offered, complete abortion reached 93.7% sublingual and 92.5% buccal — statistically indistinguishable — with chills and fever reported more often sublingually. The Cochrane review of medical methods for first-trimester abortion (Zhang J et al., PMID: 35608608) places this in context: combined regimens (misoprostol with mifepristone or letrozole) may be more effective than misoprostol alone, failure may be slightly lower sublingual than vaginal (risk ratio 0.69, 95% CI 0.37 to 1.28; low-certainty), and oral misoprostol alone may fail more than vaginal (RR 3.68, 95% CI 1.56 to 8.71). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): where mifepristone is unavailable, a three-dose misoprostol-alone regimen with a follow-up dose available succeeds in roughly 92-94% — choose sublingual to minimise continuing pregnancy, buccal to minimise fever and chills.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — misoprostol alone (800 µg × 3) achieves complete abortion in about 92-94% after follow-up doses; sublingual lowers continuing pregnancy versus buccal (1.1% versus 5.5%) at the cost of more chills and fever

title: Adding letrozole to misoprostol splits by trimester: pooled first-trimester trials show more complete abortions (RR 1.45) and faster expulsion — the one blinded second-trimester trial found no gain at all
question: Does adding letrozole to misoprostol improve complete abortion rates versus misoprostol alone?
balance: SPLIT — by stage of pregnancy and by evidence quality. The 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis (Miller KAR et al., PMID: 41774466) pooled 12 randomised trials (1,524 women) of letrozole pretreatment plus misoprostol versus misoprostol alone for pharmacological abortion and miscarriage management: complete abortion was higher with letrozole (risk ratio 1.45, 95% CI 1.25-1.68; p<0.00001), time to abortion shorter (mean difference -5.47 hours, 95% CI -8.68 to -2.26) and haemoglobin decline smaller (mean difference +0.26 g/dL, 95% CI 0.13-0.39), with comparable side effects (RR 1.04, 95% CI 0.88-1.23) — but heterogeneity was very high (I²=73% for complete abortion, 99% for time to abortion). Against that stands the cleanest single trial, in the second trimester (Lee VC et al., PMID: 22078193): 130 women randomised double-blind to letrozole 7.5 mg for three days or placebo before misoprostol had near-identical abortion rates at 24 hours (93.8% versus 90.8%) and 48 hours (98.5% versus 95.4%). PROPOSED SPLIT: a probable first-trimester gain on pooled, heterogeneous trials; no demonstrated gain in the second trimester.
stamp: SPLIT — letrozole pretreatment raises complete abortion in pooled (heterogeneous) trials (RR 1.45), but the blinded second-trimester trial found abortion rates of 93.8% versus 90.8% at 24 hours, no better than misoprostol alone

title: Miscarriage management: infection is 2–3% however you manage it (MIST) — surgery completes fastest, expectant and medical care trade that for far more unplanned admissions and curettage
question: For first-trimester miscarriage, how do expectant, medical and surgical management compare on complete evacuation, infection and later pregnancy?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — for surgery, on completion; with infection a tie across all three strategies, which is what makes the choice a preference decision. In the MIST trial (Trinder J et al., PMID: 16707509), 1,200 women under 13 weeks with early fetal demise or incomplete miscarriage were randomised to expectant, medical (vaginal misoprostol, preceded by mifepristone for early fetal demise) or surgical management: confirmed infection within 14 days was 3% expectant, 2% medical and 3% surgical — no significant differences — but unplanned admissions and unplanned surgical curettage were far commoner after expectant and medical management (risk differences for unplanned curettage versus surgery: -39% and -30% respectively, in surgery's favour). The Cochrane network meta-analysis (Ghosh J et al., PMID: 34061352; 78 trials, 17,795 women) ranked every method against expectant care for complete miscarriage: suction aspiration after cervical preparation RR 2.12 (95% CI 1.41 to 3.20), dilatation and curettage 1.49, suction aspiration 1.44, mifepristone plus misoprostol 1.42 (moderate-certainty) and misoprostol alone 1.30 — all surgical methods above all medical methods, and medical above expectant. Neither record reports later-pregnancy outcomes, a declared gap for that part of the question. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): surgery for speed and certainty of completion; medical or expectant care are safe alternatives for women who accept a one-in-three-ish chance of ending up with surgery anyway.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — surgical management completes miscarriage most reliably (network RR up to 2.12 versus expectant) with infection equally low (2-3%) across surgical, medical and expectant care in MIST

title: Antibiotics before miscarriage surgery: AIMS found pelvic infection 4.1% versus 5.3% — not significant on its pragmatic definition (P=0.09), significant on the strict one (RR 0.60); Cochrane's low-bias sensitivity analysis agrees (RR 0.57)
question: Do prophylactic antibiotics before miscarriage surgery reduce pelvic infection versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the effect is probably real and modest, and the headline trial technically missed. In AIMS (Lissauer D et al., PMID: 30865795), 3,412 women and adolescents in Malawi, Pakistan, Tanzania and Uganda were randomised to a single preoperative dose of doxycycline 400 mg plus metronidazole 400 mg or placebo before miscarriage surgery: pelvic infection within 14 days was 4.1% (68/1,676) versus 5.3% (90/1,684) — risk ratio 0.77 (95% CI 0.56 to 1.04; P=0.09) on the pragmatic definition adopted before unblinding, but 1.5% versus 2.6% (RR 0.60, 95% CI 0.37 to 0.96) on the original strict definition, with no significant difference in adverse events. The 2025 Cochrane review (Ahmed SI et al., PMID: 40231786; six trials, 4,371 women) found the overall estimate equally equivocal (RR 0.78, 95% CI 0.47 to 1.28; low-certainty) but, in the sensitivity analysis limited to low-risk-of-bias studies (3,737 women), a 43% relative reduction in uterine infection (RR 0.57, 95% CI 0.37 to 0.86; high-certainty). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a single cheap preoperative dose likely prevents roughly one pelvic infection per 80-90 operations in high-baseline-risk settings; in low-risk settings the absolute gain shrinks with the baseline rate.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — preoperative doxycycline plus metronidazole probably reduces pelvic infection after miscarriage surgery (AIMS strict-definition RR 0.60; Cochrane low-bias sensitivity RR 0.57), though AIMS's primary pragmatic analysis was not significant (RR 0.77; P=0.09)

title: Intravenous ferric carboxymaltose clears postpartum anaemia faster and more completely than oral iron: still anaemic at 6 weeks in 18% versus 32% in the 1,400-woman Nigerian trial (RR 0.54)
question: In postpartum anaemia, does intravenous ferric carboxymaltose restore haemoglobin faster than oral iron?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — intravenous ferric carboxymaltose beats oral ferrous sulphate on speed, completeness and tolerability, in trials a decade and a half apart. The IVON-PP trial (Afolabi BB et al., PMID: 41865415) randomised 1,400 Nigerian women with moderate-to-severe postpartum anaemia (haemoglobin under 100 g/L) to a single intravenous ferric carboxymaltose dose (20 mg/kg, maximum 1,000 mg) or oral ferrous sulphate twice daily for six weeks: at six weeks, 18% (115/655) versus 32% (214/662) remained anaemic (risk ratio 0.54, 95% CI 0.44-0.66; p<0.001), and adverse events were less common intravenously (8% versus 20%). The earlier US trial (Van Wyck DB et al., PMID: 17666600; 352 women, haemoglobin 10 g/dL or less) found the same pattern: a haemoglobin rise of at least 2.0 g/dL came earlier (7.0 versus 14.0 days; P<.001), a rise of at least 3.0 g/dL was commoner (86.3% versus 60.4%), and haemoglobin above 12.0 g/dL was reached by 90.5% versus 68.6%, with no serious adverse drug reactions. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): where intravenous access and the drug are available, one infusion replaces six weeks of tablets that many women do not finish — the gain is largest exactly where postpartum anaemia is commonest and follow-up hardest.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — single-dose intravenous ferric carboxymaltose leaves fewer women anaemic at six weeks than oral ferrous sulphate (18% versus 32%; RR 0.54) and raises haemoglobin about twice as fast in the earlier trial

title: CORONIS (15,935 women): none of the five caesarean technique choices — entry, exteriorisation, uterine closure layers, peritoneal closure, suture material — changed death, infection, reoperation or transfusion, at 6 weeks or at 3 years
question: Which caesarean surgical techniques — closure, suture materials, bladder flap, peritoneal closure — change infection, pain and later outcomes?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — across every technique pair CORONIS randomised, in the short term and at three years. The main trial (CORONIS Collaborative Group; first author Abalos E et al., PMID: 23721753) randomised 15,935 women at 19 sites in seven countries in a fractional factorial design across five pairs — blunt versus sharp abdominal entry, exteriorisation versus intra-abdominal uterine repair, single- versus double-layer uterine closure, peritoneal closure versus non-closure, and chromic catgut versus polyglactin-910 — and found no significant difference in the composite of death, maternal infectious morbidity, further operations or transfusion for any pair (risk ratios 0.90 to 1.06, every confidence interval crossing 1). The three-year follow-up (Abalos E et al., PMID: 27155903; 13,153 women, 84%) likewise found no differences in hernia, infertility, ectopic pregnancy, adhesion-type symptoms or subsequent pregnancy complications, including uterine rupture (RR 3.05, 95% CI 0.32-29.29 for catgut versus polyglactin-910 — a wide interval on a rare event). One element in the question — bladder flap formation — was not among CORONIS's five randomised pairs, a declared gap. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): surgeons may choose these techniques on time, cost and habit; the trial gives no outcome reason to prefer one over another.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — no CORONIS technique pair (entry, exteriorisation, closure layers, peritoneal closure, suture material) significantly changed short-term maternal morbidity or three-year outcomes in 15,935 randomised women

title: Probiotics prevent lactational mastitis in trials (incidence RR 0.49 pooled; one strain trial 6% versus 14%) — but the asked comparison, probiotics versus antibiotics for treating established mastitis, has no randomised trial here
question: In lactational mastitis, do probiotics reduce pain and recurrence compared with antibiotics?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for prevention, which is what the randomised evidence actually tests; the treatment-versus-antibiotics comparison in the question is a declared gap with no carded trial. The systematic review and meta-analysis (Yu Q et al., PMID: 36084006; six randomised trials) found oral probiotics during pregnancy reduced mastitis incidence (risk ratio 0.49, 95% CI 0.35 to 0.69; p<0.0001) and reduced milk bacterial counts in both healthy women (mean difference -0.19, 95% CI -0.23 to -0.16) and women with mastitis (-0.89, 95% CI -1.34 to -0.43). The strain-specific trial (Jiménez E et al., PMID: 34576828) randomised 328 women to Ligilactobacillus salivarius PS2 — the strain named in the publication; no manufacturer is named in the record — from week 35 of pregnancy to week 12 postpartum, or placebo: mastitis occurred in 9 women (6%) versus 20 (14%), hazard ratio 0.41 (95% CI 0.190-0.915; p=0.029). Neither record compares a probiotic with an antibiotic for treating established mastitis, and neither reports pain or recurrence as a treatment outcome. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for prevention in pregnancy and lactation, Tier C: small trials, one strain carrying much of the effect, and the clinical question as asked — treatment instead of antibiotics — remains untested in the carded evidence.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — oral probiotics in pregnancy and lactation reduce mastitis incidence (pooled RR 0.49; strain trial HR 0.41) versus placebo; no carded trial compares probiotics with antibiotics for treating established mastitis

title: Menopausal symptoms beyond placebo splits in two: plant-based phytoestrogens trim daily hot flashes by about 1.3, while acupuncture ties sham exactly (hot flash scores 15.36 versus 15.04)
question: Does acupuncture — or other plant-based and complementary therapies — reduce menopausal symptoms beyond placebo?
balance: SPLIT — the plant-based half shows a modest effect over placebo; the acupuncture half, tested against a proper sham, shows none. The JAMA systematic review and meta-analysis (Franco OH et al., PMID: 27327802) pooled 62 trials (6,653 women): phytoestrogens were associated with 1.31 fewer daily hot flashes than control (pooled mean difference of changes -1.31, 95% CI -2.02 to -0.61) and a small improvement in vaginal dryness score (-0.31, 95% CI -0.52 to -0.10), but no significant reduction in night sweats (-2.14, 95% CI -5.57 to 1.29); several herbal remedies, though not Chinese medicinal herbs, were associated with fewer vasomotor symptoms — with the warning that 74% of the trials were at high risk of bias in at least three quality areas. The acupuncture trial (Ee C et al., PMID: 26784863) randomised 327 women with at least seven moderate flushes daily to standardised Chinese-medicine acupuncture or non-insertive sham over eight weeks: end-of-treatment hot flash scores were 15.36 versus 15.04 (mean difference 0.33, 95% CI -1.87 to 2.52; P=0.77), with no serious adverse events. PROPOSED SPLIT: phytoestrogen supplements — a small, low-quality-evidence gain; acupuncture — no gain beyond a credible sham.
stamp: SPLIT — plant-based phytoestrogens reduce daily hot flashes by about 1.31 versus control in pooled trials (low-quality evidence), while acupuncture does not beat sham acupuncture (score difference 0.33; P=0.77)

title: Pelvic-floor physical therapy beat overnight lidocaine for provoked vestibulodynia pain — 1.8 points better on a 0–10 scale, held at 6 months
question: In provoked vestibulodynia and vulvodynia, do medical, physical-therapy or surgical treatments reduce pain versus placebo or usual care?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for multimodal pelvic-floor physical therapy, on the one large head-to-head trial. In 212 women randomised to 10 weeks of weekly physical therapy (education, pelvic-floor exercises with biofeedback, manual therapy, dilation) or overnight 5% lidocaine ointment, pain during intercourse fell 1.8 points more on a 0–10 scale with physical therapy (95% CI 1.2 to 2.3, P<.001), the gap held at 6 months (1.8; 95% CI 1.2 to 2.5), and 79% of the physical-therapy group rated themselves very much or much improved versus 39% on lidocaine. An older three-way trial (78 women) found vestibulectomy, group cognitive–behavioural therapy and biofeedback all reduced pain by 6 months, with surgery ahead on completer analysis — but 7 women assigned to surgery never had it, and there is no placebo arm anywhere in this evidence. No drug has beaten placebo in a trial carded here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): physical therapy is the best-supported first treatment; surgery helps selected patients in one small old trial; the drug evidence is thin.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — multimodal physical therapy beat topical lidocaine by 1.8 points (0–10) in one large randomised trial; older small trial supports behavioural therapy and vestibulectomy, with no placebo-controlled drug win

title: Laser for vulvar lichen sclerosus: one small trial's dual laser beat clobetasol on the clinician's score but not on symptoms — and pooled ablative-laser trials show no significant benefit
question: In vulvar lichen sclerosus, does laser treatment control disease as well as ultrapotent topical corticosteroid (clobetasol)?
balance: SPLIT — the answer depends on which laser and which outcome. In the one head-to-head randomised trial (66 women), non-ablative Nd:YAG/Er:YAG dual laser (4 treatments over 4 months) lowered the objective clinical lichen sclerosus score by −2.34 points versus −0.95 on clobetasol propionate over 6 months (P<0.001), and satisfaction was higher with laser (P=0.035) — but symptom scores improved similarly in both arms with no significant difference. The 2026 meta-analysis of the different, ablative approach (fractional CO2 laser; 3 randomised trials, 151 patients) found no statistically significant benefit on symptom burden (mean difference 1.04; 95% CI −4.71 to 6.79) or disease severity (standardised mean difference −0.27; 95% CI −1.47 to 0.94). PROPOSED SPLIT: a possible objective-score edge for one dual-laser protocol in one small unblinded trial; no demonstrated benefit for ablative CO2 laser; clobetasol remains the proven standard, and this premalignant disease needs follow-up whichever treatment is used.
stamp: SPLIT — non-ablative dual laser beat clobetasol on objective score but not symptoms in one small trial; ablative fractional CO2 laser shows no significant benefit in pooled randomised trials

title: Topical progesterone is not a clobetasol substitute in vulvar lichen sclerosus: clinician score improved 4.6→2.9 on clobetasol but only 4.6→4.5 on progesterone in the one double-blind trial
question: In vulvar lichen sclerosus, is topical progesterone as effective as clobetasol propionate?
balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — harm here means a worse disease outcome than standard care, not toxicity. The single double-blind randomised trial (37 premenopausal women with previously untreated, biopsy-confirmed early vulvar lichen sclerosus) compared progesterone 8% ointment with clobetasol propionate 0.05% for 12 weeks. The clinician-rated severity score improved from 4.6 to 2.9 on clobetasol but barely moved on progesterone (4.6 to 4.5); the between-group difference favoured clobetasol by 1.61 points (95% CI 0.44 to 2.77, P=0.009). Symptoms also improved more on clobetasol (score 4.7→1.9 versus 4.5→3.1; difference 1.32, 95% CI −0.25 to 2.89, P=0.095), and complete remission on biopsy was seen in 13 of 16 (81.3%) on clobetasol versus 6 of 10 (60%) on progesterone. No drug-related serious adverse event occurred in either arm. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm): progesterone 8% is inferior to clobetasol at 12 weeks — patients swapped to it would be under-treated, on one small pilot trial.
stamp: POSSIBLE (harm) — topical progesterone 8% was inferior to clobetasol propionate on the clinician severity score in the one double-blind randomised trial (difference 1.61 points favouring clobetasol, P=0.009)

title: Intravenous calcium prevents ovarian hyperstimulation about as well as cabergoline — moderate/severe OHSS 10.6% on calcium vs 8.2% on cabergoline head-to-head, and 7% vs 23% against placebo
question: In ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome prevention, is intravenous calcium as effective as cabergoline?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — yes, on the randomised record, calcium looks as effective as cabergoline, and it has its own placebo-controlled win. In the head-to-head trial (170 high-risk IVF patients), moderate or severe OHSS occurred in 8.24% on cabergoline (7 of 85) versus 10.59% on intravenous calcium gluconate (9 of 85) (P=.599; OR 0.76, 95% CI 0.27 to 2.14), with one severe case in each group and similar implantation, clinical and ongoing pregnancy rates. In the earlier double-blind placebo-controlled trial (200 high-risk women), calcium infusion cut overall OHSS from 23% on saline placebo to 7% (moderate 1% vs 8%; severe 0% vs 4%). Neither trial was powered to prove equivalence formally, and both come from single research groups in one region. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): calcium infusion is a credible, cheap alternative to cabergoline for OHSS prevention in high-risk cycles.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — intravenous calcium matched cabergoline for moderate/severe OHSS in a head-to-head trial (10.59% vs 8.24%) and beat placebo in a double-blind trial (7% vs 23%)

title: Programmed intermittent epidural bolus beats continuous infusion for labour analgesia in pooled trials — less drug, less breakthrough pain, higher spontaneous delivery rate
question: For maintenance of labour epidural analgesia, does programmed intermittent epidural bolus give better analgesia and less motor block than continuous infusion?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — pooled randomised trials favour programmed intermittent epidural bolus (PIEB) over continuous epidural infusion (CEI) for maintaining labour analgesia. The 2022 meta-analysis found PIEB used less ropivacaine (weighted mean difference −15.83; 95% CI −19.06 to −12.60) and less sufentanil (WMD −4.93), with fewer patients needing patient-controlled boluses (OR 0.27; 95% CI 0.14 to 0.51), less breakthrough pain (OR 0.47; 95% CI 0.28 to 0.80), lower pain scores at 2–5 hours, a higher spontaneous vaginal delivery rate (OR 1.37; 95% CI 1.08 to 1.75), shorter first and second stages, and higher satisfaction (weighted mean difference 0.91; 95% CI 0.42 to 1.39). Within PIEB itself, the Wong 2011 randomised trial (190 women) showed a 10 mL bolus every 60 minutes used less bupivacaine per hour (median 8.8 mg) than 5 mL every 30 minutes (10.0 mg) or 2.5 mL every 15 minutes (10.4 mg) (P=0.005), with no difference in pain or satisfaction. Heterogeneity in the pooled analysis is high for several outcomes, and motor block — asked about in the question — was not consistently separated in the pooled record. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): PIEB is the better-supported maintenance mode, with the widest bolus interval the most drug-sparing regimen tested.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — meta-analysis of randomised trials favours programmed intermittent bolus over continuous infusion for drug use, breakthrough pain, delivery mode and satisfaction, with high heterogeneity

title: Amnioinfusion for meconium-stained liquor: large perinatal gains only where monitoring is limited (aspiration syndrome RR 0.17, perinatal death RR 0.24) — no substantive benefit where surveillance is standard
question: In labour with meconium-stained liquor, does amnioinfusion reduce caesarean delivery and neonatal morbidity?
balance: SPLIT — by setting, and the split is the finding. The Cochrane review (14 studies, 4,435 women with moderate or thick meconium staining) found, in settings with limited peripartum surveillance (3 studies), meconium aspiration syndrome at a relative risk of 0.17 (95% CI 0.05 to 0.52; 1,144 women) and perinatal mortality at a relative risk of 0.24 (95% CI 0.11 to 0.53; 1,151 women) with amnioinfusion, alongside fewer caesareans for fetal distress and overall. In settings with standard peripartum surveillance there was no significant reduction in meconium aspiration syndrome, perinatal death or severe morbidity, or maternal death or severe morbidity; caesareans for fetal distress (but not overall) fell, and when the reviewers excluded higher-risk-of-bias trials in a sensitivity analysis, the benefits for every outcome disappeared. The trials are too small to exclude rare serious maternal harms. PROPOSED SPLIT: amnioinfusion is a substantive intervention where fetal monitoring is limited, and an unproven one where it is standard.
stamp: SPLIT — substantive perinatal benefit only in limited-surveillance settings (meconium aspiration syndrome RR 0.17; perinatal mortality RR 0.24); no significant benefit with standard surveillance, and sensitivity analysis removes even the smaller gains

title: Pharmacist-led education aimed at both patient and physician (D-PRESCRIBE): inappropriate prescriptions stopped by 43% versus 12% at 6 months — one cluster trial, four Beers drug classes, one province
question: In older adults on potentially inappropriate medicines, does a pharmacist-led educational intervention for patients and physicians increase deprescribing versus usual care?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a pharmacist writing to both the patient and the physician got far more inappropriate prescriptions stopped than usual care did. In D-PRESCRIBE (Martin P et al., PMID: 30422193), a cluster randomised trial in 69 community pharmacies in Quebec, Canada, 489 community-dwelling adults aged 65 years and older (mean age 75 years; 66% women) were prescribed 1 of 4 Beers Criteria medications — sedative-hypnotics, first-generation antihistamines, glyburide, or nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. Pharmacists in the intervention group were encouraged to send patients an educational deprescribing brochure in parallel to sending their physicians an evidence-based pharmaceutical opinion to recommend deprescribing; pharmacists in the control group provided usual care. At 6 months, 106 of 248 patients (43%) in the intervention group no longer filled prescriptions for inappropriate medication, compared with 29 of 241 patients (12%) in the control group (risk difference 31% [95% CI, 23% to 38%]). By drug class, discontinuation in the intervention versus control group was 43.2% versus 9.0% for sedative-hypnotics, 30.6% versus 13.8% for glyburide, and 57.6% versus 21.7% for nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs; the first-generation antihistamine class was too small to analyse (n=12). No adverse events requiring hospitalization were reported, although 29 of 77 patients (38%) who attempted to taper sedative-hypnotics reported withdrawal symptoms. The proven gain is discontinuation itself — a prescribing outcome at 6 months — not a fall, fracture, hospitalisation, or mortality outcome, and it rests on this one trial in one province. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a pharmacist-led educational intervention aimed at both patients and physicians increased deprescribing of potentially inappropriate medicines at 6 months in a single cluster randomised trial, with no hospitalisation-level harm reported but with withdrawal symptoms common during sedative-hypnotic tapering.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in one 489-patient cluster randomised trial, a pharmacist-led educational intervention for patients and physicians raised discontinuation of inappropriate medication at 6 months to 43% versus 12% on usual care (risk difference 31% [95% CI, 23% to 38%])

title: Masked taper plus placebo-targeted behavioural therapy got 73.4% off benzodiazepine-receptor agonists at 6 months versus 58.6% with a standard open taper — insomnia no worse
question: In long-term benzodiazepine-receptor-agonist users, does a masked taper combined with behavioural intervention achieve discontinuation versus an unmasked taper with standard behavioural therapy?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in the one randomised trial, hiding the dose during the taper helped more people finish it. Among 188 adults aged 55 or older who had used a benzodiazepine-receptor agonist (lorazepam, alprazolam, clonazepam, temazepam and/or zolpidem) at least 2 nights a week for at least 3 months, discontinuation 6 months after treatment ended was achieved by 73.4% with the masked taper plus augmented cognitive–behavioural therapy for insomnia (MTcap) versus 58.6% with standard CBT-I plus a supervised unmasked gradual taper (odds ratio 1.95; 95% CI 1.03 to 3.70; P=.04). The gap was larger 1 week post-treatment (88.4% vs 67.4%; OR 3.68; 95% CI 1.67 to 8.12). Insomnia Severity Index scores improved in both groups with no significant between-group difference, so the extra discontinuation was not bought with worse sleep. The comparator is an active best-practice taper, not usual care — usual-care discontinuation rates would be far lower. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): masked tapering is a promising upgrade to standard taper-plus-CBT-I, from a single two-centre trial.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — masked taper plus augmented CBT-I beat unmasked taper plus standard CBT-I on 6-month discontinuation (73.4% vs 58.6%; OR 1.95) in one randomised trial

title: Admission-avoidance hospital at home: no mortality or readmission difference at 6 months (RR 0.88 and 1.14), but far fewer older patients living in residential care (RR 0.53)
question: In older adults, does admission-avoidance hospital-at-home care match or beat inpatient hospital care on mortality, readmission and living at home?
balance: SPLIT — hospital-level care at home neither saves lives nor costs them in the pooled trials, but it does keep more older people out of residential care. The 2024 Cochrane review (20 randomised trials, 3,100 participants; in older populations) found admission-avoidance hospital at home probably makes little or no difference to mortality at 6 months (RR 0.88; 95% CI 0.68 to 1.13; 5 trials, 1,502 participants; moderate-certainty evidence) and little or no difference to readmission within 3–12 months (RR 1.14; 95% CI 0.97 to 1.34; 8 trials, 1,757 participants), while probably reducing the likelihood of living in residential care at 6 months (RR 0.53; 95% CI 0.41 to 0.69; 4 trials, 1,271 participants). Self-reported health status probably differed little; satisfaction may be improved; initial hospital length of stay was shorter by design. This shelf covers the admission-avoidance model in predominantly older populations; the broader hospital-at-home question for acutely ill adults of all ages sits on its own shelf. PROPOSED SPLIT: equivalent on death and readmission, better on staying out of residential care.
stamp: SPLIT — no difference in 6-month mortality (RR 0.88) or readmission (RR 1.14), but lower likelihood of living in residential care at 6 months (RR 0.53), in a 20-trial Cochrane review

title: After an ED fall visit, multifactorial prevention programmes did not reduce falls in pooled trials (rate ratio 0.78; 95% CI 0.58–1.05) — one older positive trial is the exception, not the rule
question: In older adults presenting to the emergency department after a fall, do multifactorial falls-prevention programmes reduce further falls versus usual care?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — as a class, these programmes have not earned their pooled result. The 2019 systematic review and meta-analysis (12 randomised trials, 3,986 community-dwelling older adults presenting to an emergency department with a fall) found no reduction in falls (rate ratio 0.78; 95% CI 0.58 to 1.05), number of fallers (RR 1.02; 95% CI 0.88 to 1.18), fractured neck of femur (RR 0.82; 95% CI 0.53 to 1.25), fall-related ED re-presentations (rate ratio 0.99; 95% CI 0.84 to 1.16) or hospitalisations (rate ratio 1.14; 95% CI 0.69 to 1.89). One well-known earlier trial points the other way: Davison 2005, in 313 cognitively intact recurrent fallers, found 36% fewer falls with multifactorial assessment and intervention (RR 0.64; 95% CI 0.46 to 0.90) — though the proportion still falling was unchanged (65% vs 68%) and admissions did not fall. The reviewers' conclusion stands: insufficient evidence to support these programmes for this population. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): pooled across programmes and settings, no outcome improved significantly.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — meta-analysis of 12 ED-based multifactorial falls trials found no significant reduction in falls, fallers, fractures, re-presentations or admissions

title: Comprehensive geriatric assessment outside hospital: most reviews find no effect on admissions, function or quality of life — frailty may improve, mortality signals appear in only 2 of 10 reviews
question: In community-dwelling frail older adults at risk of decline, does home-based comprehensive geriatric assessment improve function and reduce hospital use versus usual care?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference) — for the headline outcomes, the accumulated review literature is mostly a null. The 2025 overview of systematic reviews (22 reviews, 478 primary studies, more than 136,336 participants, mostly community and home settings) found most reviews reported no effect of comprehensive geriatric assessment (CGA) on hospital or long-term-care admissions, quality of life or function; of 10 reviews reporting mortality, only 2 found reductions (13% and 14% relative reductions at longest follow-up), and of 3 reviews reporting frailty, 2 found benefit (one meta-analysis: frailty RR 0.77; 95% CI 0.64 to 0.93). A 2026 meta-analysis of home-based interventions in frail or pre-frail older adults (24 studies, 3,826 participants) — broader than CGA alone — found small improvements in frailty scores (standardised mean difference −0.27) and grip strength, but no significant change in overall or physical quality of life, and physical-function gains only in professionally supervised programmes. CGA models vary so much in content, dose and duration (6–36 months) that 'CGA' barely names one intervention. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference): no consistent benefit on admissions or function; a possible frailty effect is the live lead.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference) — overview of 22 systematic reviews finds mostly no effect on admissions, function or quality of life; frailty benefit in a minority of reviews

title: Collaborative care for Alzheimer's disease in primary care: behavioural symptoms improved by 5.6 NPI points at 12 months and caregiver distress fell — cognition, function and hospital use did not change
question: In older adults with Alzheimer's disease in primary care, does collaborative care management with a nurse care manager improve behavioural symptoms and caregiver burden versus usual care?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for behaviour and caregivers, from one well-run trial. Callahan 2006 randomised 153 older adults with Alzheimer disease and their caregivers (by physician) to 1 year of collaborative care management led by an advanced-practice nurse working with the family caregiver inside primary care, or augmented usual care. Behavioural and psychological symptoms (Neuropsychiatric Inventory total) were significantly lower in the intervention group at 12 months (mean difference −5.6; P=.01) and 18 months (−5.4; P=.01); caregivers reported significantly less distress at 12 months and less depression (PHQ-9) at 18 months. Intervention patients were more likely to receive cholinesterase inhibitors (79.8% vs 55.1%; P=.002) and antidepressants (45.2% vs 27.5%; P=.03), without significantly more antipsychotics or sedative-hypnotics. There were no group differences in depression-in-dementia scores, cognition, activities of daily living, hospitalisation, nursing-home placement or death. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a nurse-led collaborative model improves the symptoms families struggle with most; it does not slow the disease.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — collaborative care improved behavioural symptoms (−5.6 NPI points at 12 months) and caregiver distress in one randomised trial, with no effect on cognition, function or institutional outcomes

title: Advance-care-planning videos in nursing homes changed nothing measured: hospital transfers 3.7 vs 3.9 per 1,000 days in long-stay residents — and only 21.9% of residents ever saw a video
question: In long-stay nursing-home residents with dementia, does an advance-care-planning video intervention increase goal-concordant care and reduce burdensome hospital transfers versus usual care?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the PROVEN pragmatic trial is a large, honest null. Across 360 nursing homes (119 intervention, 241 control), offering five 6–10-minute advance-care-planning videos to long-stay residents with advanced illness (4,171 intervention; 8,308 control) did not significantly reduce the primary outcome, hospital transfers per 1,000 person-days alive (3.7 vs 3.9; rate difference −0.2; 95% CI −0.5 to 0.2), and secondary outcomes — burdensome treatments and hospice enrolment — did not differ in residents with or without advanced illness. The companion short-stay analysis was likewise null (12.3 vs 13.2 transfers per 1,000 days; rate difference −0.8; 95% CI −1.8 to 0.2). The caveat is delivery: champions reported only 21.9% of long-stay residents with advanced illness actually viewed a video (14–15% of short-stay patients), and 11.8% of intervention facilities showed videos to no one. Goal-concordant care itself was not directly measured. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): as implemented at scale, the video programme did not move transfers, burdensome treatment or hospice use.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — a 360-home pragmatic cluster trial found no reduction in hospital transfers, burdensome treatments or hospice enrolment from an ACP video programme, with low viewing fidelity

title: Group pelvic-floor training matched individual training in older women: leakage episodes fell 74% in groups versus 70% individually at 1 year — noninferiority confirmed
question: In older women with urinary incontinence, does group-based pelvic floor muscle training match individual training on leakage episodes?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — group delivery is not a diluted version of the real thing. In the GROUP randomised noninferiority trial (362 community-dwelling women aged 60 or older with stress or mixed urinary incontinence, in two Canadian centres), women learned pelvic-floor contraction in one individual session, then trained for 12 weeks either in groups of 8 (178 women) or individually (184). At 1 year, the median percentage reduction in incontinence episodes was 74% (95% CI 46% to 86%) in the group arm versus 70% (95% CI 44% to 89%) individually; the difference was 4% (95% CI −10% to 7%), with the upper confidence bound below the pre-specified 10% noninferiority margin — noninferiority confirmed. All secondary outcomes (lower urinary tract symptoms, quality of life) were similar at 1 year, and adverse events were minor and uncommon. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): group-based training delivers individual-level results at group-level cost, on one trial's evidence.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — group-based pelvic floor training was noninferior to individual training for leakage reduction at 1 year (74% vs 70% median reduction) in one randomised trial

title: Fludrocortisone for orthostatic hypotension rests on 28 randomised patients: 3 tiny crossover trials, very low-certainty evidence on blood pressure, symptoms and harms alike
question: In orthostatic hypotension, does fludrocortisone raise standing blood pressure and improve symptoms versus placebo — and on how much randomised evidence?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference) — 'no difference shown' is the honest reading, because almost nothing has been shown at all. The 2021 Cochrane review found 13 studies (513 participants) but only 3 crossover randomised trials totalling 28 participants, each 2–3 weeks long, in just two conditions (diabetes and Parkinson disease). Against placebo, the entire randomised dataset is one 6-person crossover study in diabetes: standing blood-pressure drop was −26 mmHg systolic on fludrocortisone versus −39 mmHg on placebo (−7 vs −11 mmHg diastolic), and 4 of 5 analysed participants reported improved orthostatic symptoms — all graded very low-certainty evidence. In Parkinson disease, fludrocortisone was compared with pyridostigmine and domperidone, not placebo, with mixed findings. Observational studies fill gaps without resolving them, and adverse-event evidence is likewise very low certainty (reported side effects minimal in these tiny samples). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference): a first-line drug by custom, resting on 28 randomised patients — the shelf's real content is the size of the evidence hole.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference) — Cochrane found only 3 crossover RCTs (28 participants) with very low-certainty evidence for blood pressure, symptoms and harms

title: HMB in sarcopenia: grip strength rose 4.6 kg more than placebo over 12 weeks in one 34-person trial — muscle mass itself did not change; a bed-rest trial shows HMB can preserve lean mass under catabolic stress
question: In older adults with sarcopenia, does beta-hydroxy-beta-methylbutyrate (HMB) improve muscle mass and function versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for strength and performance, not for mass, and the sarcopenia trial is very small. Yang 2023 randomised 34 older adults with sarcopenia to HMB or placebo twice daily for 12 weeks, both groups doing resistance exercise twice weekly: handgrip strength improved 4.61 kg more with HMB (95% CI 2.93 to 6.28; P<0.001), gait speed 0.11 m/s more (95% CI 0.02 to 0.20), five-times chair-stand time 3.65 seconds faster (95% CI −5.72 to −1.58), and muscle quality rose — but skeletal muscle mass and muscle index did not differ significantly between groups. The mechanistic support comes from Deutz 2013: in healthy older adults confined to 10 days of bed rest, HMB (3 g/day) prevented the lean-body-mass loss seen on placebo (−0.17 kg vs −2.05 kg change; P=0.02), though functional differences could not be detected at that sample size. The publication record for the sarcopenia trial does not name a branded HMB product or its manufacturer, so no product can be endorsed from it — current products may differ in formulation and effect. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): HMB added to resistance training improved strength and performance in one small trial; the mass claim it is usually sold on was not shown in sarcopenic patients.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — HMB plus resistance training improved grip strength, gait speed and chair-stand performance versus placebo in one small sarcopenia trial, without a significant muscle-mass difference

title: Oral nutritional supplements in hospitalised older people at nutritional risk: mortality RR 0.46 and serious adverse events RR 0.56 in a Cochrane IPD network meta-analysis — low-certainty, and individualised nutritional care showed no mortality effect (RR 0.98)
question: In hospitalised older people at nutritional risk, do oral nutritional supplements reduce mortality and complications versus usual hospital care?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — with the certainty label doing heavy work. The 2026 Cochrane network meta-analysis of individual participant data (21 randomised trials, 3,309 hospitalised older participants at risk of or with malnutrition; 12 trials contributing IPD for 1,863 participants) found oral nutritional supplements (ONS) may reduce all-cause mortality versus control (RR 0.46; 95% CI 0.25 to 0.84; absolute difference 57 fewer deaths per 1,000 people, 95% CI 79 fewer to 17 fewer; low-certainty evidence) and may reduce serious adverse events (RR 0.56; 95% CI 0.32 to 0.95; 84 fewer per 1,000). By contrast, comprehensive individualised nutritional care may show little to no mortality effect (RR 0.98; 95% CI 0.55 to 1.73) and little to no difference in activities of daily living (standardised mean difference 0.06; 95% CI −0.08 to 0.20); for most other comparisons the evidence was very uncertain. Only 16.1% of outcome assessments were at low risk of bias. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the pooled point estimate is large, but it is low-certainty and sits beside a null for the more intensive individualised-care strategy — a combination that should temper, not erase, the claim.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — oral nutritional supplements may reduce mortality (RR 0.46) and serious adverse events (RR 0.56) in hospitalised older people at nutritional risk, low-certainty IPD network meta-analysis evidence

title: DO-HEALTH: three years of vitamin D, omega-3s and home exercise changed none of six primary outcomes in healthy adults over 70 — one borderline falls signal for omega-3s aside
question: In adults aged 70 and over, does the DO-HEALTH combination — vitamin D, omega-3s and a home exercise programme — improve blood pressure, cognition, fractures and infections versus control?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — in the factorial DO-HEALTH trial of 2,157 adults aged 70 or older followed for 3 years, none of vitamin D3 2000 IU/day, omega-3s 1 g/day, or a strength-training exercise programme, alone or combined, significantly improved any of the six primary outcomes: systolic blood pressure (difference in change −0.8 mm Hg for both vitamin D and omega-3s, 99% CI −2.1 to 0.5), physical performance (SPPB), cognition (MoCA), nonvertebral fractures, or infections (omega-3 infection-rate difference −0.13, rate ratio 0.89, 99% CI 0.78–1.01, p=0.02 against a p<0.01 threshold). The trial's falls analysis found one borderline signal — omega-3s reduced total falls by 10% in relative terms (incidence rate ratio 0.90, 95% CI 0.81–1.00, p=0.04) — while vitamin D and the exercise programme had no falls benefit. The participants were unusually healthy and active, which limits how far the null travels to frailer populations. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): in healthy, active adults over 70, this popular trio does not improve blood pressure, cognition, fractures, infections or physical performance over 3 years.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — one large factorial trial found no significant benefit of vitamin D, omega-3s or home exercise on any of six primary outcomes over 3 years in healthy adults ≥70

title: Deprescribing in nursing homes reliably cuts inappropriate medicines — but the two meta-analyses split on whether falls, admissions or deaths follow
question: In nursing-home residents, do deprescribing interventions reduce falls, hospitalisations and mortality versus usual care?
balance: SPLIT — the prescribing outcome moves, the clinical outcomes are contested. A 2019 meta-analysis of 41 randomised trials (18,408 residents) found deprescribing cut the number of residents with potentially inappropriate medications by a relative 59% (odds ratio 0.41, 95% CI 0.19–0.89), and in its medication-review subgroup, mortality fell by a relative 26% (OR 0.74, 95% CI 0.65–0.84) and fallers by a relative 24% (OR 0.76, 95% CI 0.62–0.93). A larger 2026 meta-analysis (38 studies, 22 of them RCTs) confirmed fewer drugs per patient (−0.89 within 12 months; −1.60 at ≥12 months) and fewer potentially inappropriate medications, but found no significant effect on falls, hospitalisations or mortality, with moderate-to-high risk of bias across most studies. PROPOSED SPLIT: deprescribing in nursing homes — benefit for prescribing appropriateness is consistent; benefit for falls, hospitalisation and mortality appears in one meta-analysis's subgroup and vanishes in the other's full pool.
stamp: SPLIT — prescribing appropriateness improves consistently; falls/mortality benefit found in one meta-analysis's medication-review subgroup but not in the 2026 pooled analysis

title: Adding CBT-I to a supervised hypnotic taper roughly doubles benzodiazepine-free rates in older adults — 85% versus 48%, and 70% versus 24% at one year in the second trial
question: In older adults with insomnia who take hypnotics, does CBT-I delivered alongside a supervised taper get patients off sleeping tablets and sleeping better versus taper alone?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two small randomised trials from the same research tradition agree that adding cognitive behaviour therapy for insomnia to a supervised benzodiazepine taper gets far more older adults off the drug than tapering alone. In Morin 2004, 85% of the combined-treatment group were benzodiazepine-free after the 10-week intervention versus 48% with taper alone (54% with CBT-I alone), with gains maintained at 12 months. In Baillargeon 2003, complete withdrawal immediately after treatment was 77% (26/34) on combined treatment versus 38% (11/29) on taper alone (odds ratio 5.3, 95% CI 1.8–16.2), and at 12 months 70% (23/33) versus 24% (7/29) (OR 7.2, 95% CI 2.4–23.7). Sleep improvements in the CBT groups were largely subjective at first and became more noticeable over the following months; no significant withdrawal symptoms or adverse events were associated with tapering in Morin. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): CBT-I alongside a supervised taper approximately doubles durable benzodiazepine discontinuation in older adults with chronic insomnia.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two concordant randomised trials show CBT-I added to a supervised taper roughly doubles benzodiazepine-free rates, sustained to 12 months

title: Urinary incontinence in women over 60: across 43 trials, pelvic-floor-based physical therapies top the network for cure — on low- to very-low-certainty evidence
question: In older women with urinary incontinence, how do conservative, drug and combined interventions compare across the network of randomised trials?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — the 2025 Cochrane network meta-analysis of 43 randomised trials (8,506 women aged 60 and over) found every treatment category might beat its control, with physical therapies — mainly pelvic floor muscle training, with or without complementary therapies or education — performing best for 'cure': physical therapies combined with complementary therapies OR 17.79 (95% CI 2.97–106.46; 1 study, 71 participants), physical therapies alone OR 7.20 (95% CI 2.59–20.03; 4 studies, 310 participants), and physical therapies with education OR 3.25 (95% CI 1.19–8.84; 4 studies, 364 participants). For 'cure or improvement', physical therapies (OR 3.98, 95% CI 2.02–7.82) and physical therapies with education (OR 3.20, 95% CI 1.45–7.02) again led, ahead of β3-adrenergic agonists (OR 2.44, 95% CI 1.28–4.62) and antimuscarinics (OR 1.90, 95% CI 1.19–3.03). But the reviewers rated the evidence low to very low certainty, with sparse data and wide intervals — the ranking is a signal, not a verdict. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): pelvic-floor-based therapy ranks first for cure in older women, on evidence too imprecise to rank the rest with confidence.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — a 43-trial Cochrane network meta-analysis ranks pelvic-floor physical therapies best for cure in women ≥60, at low to very low certainty

title: Preventing falls in hospital: tailored education and service-model change probably cut fall rates; exercise and medication optimisation alone remain unproven
question: In hospitalised older people, do falls-prevention interventions — exercise, medication review, environmental and multifactorial programmes — reduce falls and fall injuries versus usual care?
balance: SPLIT — what works in hospital depends on the intervention class. The 2026 Cochrane review (55 trials, 104,474 participants, mean age 79) found tailored education (patient, staff or multicomponent) probably reduces the rate of falls (rate ratio 0.73, 95% CI 0.56–0.94; 3 trials, 4,868 participants; moderate-certainty) and the risk of falling (RR 0.61, 95% CI 0.40–0.92). Service model change in acute settings probably reduces the fall rate (RaR 0.45, 95% CI 0.27–0.74; 6 trials, 10,825 participants; moderate-certainty). Multifactorial interventions probably reduce the fall rate (RaR 0.87, 95% CI 0.69–1.08; 5 trials, 42,256 participants) and risk of falling (RR 0.82, 95% CI 0.63–1.07), but both intervals include no effect. Exercise was uncertain (rate RaR 0.62, 95% CI 0.28–1.36; risk RR 0.73, 95% CI 0.36–1.46), and medication optimisation as a single intervention was likewise uncertain (rate RaR 1.71, 95% CI 0.95–3.07). Pooled across everything, any intervention gave RaR 0.85 (95% CI 0.71–1.02) at very low certainty. Fracture outcomes were poorly reported. PROPOSED SPLIT: education and organisational change carry the hospital falls evidence; exercise and medication review alone do not, yet.
stamp: SPLIT — tailored education and service-model change probably reduce hospital fall rates (moderate certainty); exercise and medication optimisation alone are unproven

title: HMB during 10 days of bed rest in older adults: lean body mass preserved (−0.17 kg versus −2.05 kg on placebo) in one 19-evaluable-person trial — function unmoved and a larger trial still needed
question: In older adults confined to bed rest, does HMB preserve lean body mass versus control over 10 days of bed rest?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for lean body mass over 10 days of bed rest only, on one very small trial. Deutz 2013 randomised 24 healthy older adults (SPPB ≥9; 20 women, 4 men) to calcium HMB 1.5 g twice daily (3 g/day) or inactive placebo powder, starting 5 days before 10 days of complete bed rest and continuing through 8 weeks of resistance-training rehabilitation; 19 were evaluable at the end of bed rest (11 HMB, 8 control). Bed rest caused a significant decrease in total lean body mass in the control group (−2.05 ± 0.66 kg; P=0.02), while HMB treatment prevented the decline (−0.17 ± 0.19 kg change; P=0.23 within group), with a statistically significant between-group difference in lean-mass change over bed rest (P=0.02); the female sub-analysis also favoured HMB (P=0.04). Differences in functional parameters could not be observed, which the authors attribute to sample size, and the authors conclude that HMB supplementation preserves muscle mass during 10 days of bed rest in healthy older adults and that these results need to be confirmed in a larger trial. The fetched record describes the intervention only as calcium HMB (the calcium salt) and names no branded HMB product or company, so no commercial product is named on this shelf and current products may differ in safety and effectiveness. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): in one small double-blind trial, HMB preserved lean body mass over 10 days of bed rest in healthy older adults, without a demonstrated functional benefit.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in one small randomised double-blind trial of healthy older adults (24 randomised, 19 evaluable), calcium HMB 3 g/day prevented the lean-body-mass loss seen on placebo over 10 days of bed rest (−0.17 kg versus −2.05 kg change; P=0.02), with no functional difference detected

title: Adding electromyographic biofeedback to pelvic floor training changed nothing at two years: incontinence severity 8.2 versus 8.5 on the ICIQ in a 600-woman trial
question: In women with urinary incontinence, does pelvic floor muscle training with electromyographic biofeedback beat pelvic floor training alone?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — in the 600-woman OPAL trial, women newly presenting with stress or mixed urinary incontinence received six continence-therapist appointments over 16 weeks, with or without electromyographic biofeedback built into clinic and home training. At 24 months, self-reported incontinence severity (ICIQ-UI SF) was 8.2 (SD 5.1) with biofeedback versus 8.5 (SD 4.9) without — a mean difference of −0.09 (95% CI −0.92 to 0.75; p=0.84). Costs were similar (mean difference £121, 95% CI −£409 to £651) and quality-adjusted life years did not differ (−0.04, 95% CI −0.12 to 0.04). Forty-eight participants reported an adverse event, 23 possibly related to the interventions. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): routine electromyographic biofeedback adds cost and kit to pelvic floor training without improving continence at two years.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — one large multicentre RCT found no benefit of adding electromyographic biofeedback to PFMT at 24 months

title: Adding mirabegron to tibial nerve stimulation cut urgency incontinence episodes further — a 9.4 versus 5.3 episode improvement in one 54-woman trial
question: In adults with overactive bladder, does posterior tibial nerve stimulation combined with mirabegron beat stimulation alone?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — a single small double-blind randomised trial (54 women with refractory urgency urinary incontinence) compared 12 weeks of posterior tibial nerve stimulation plus mirabegron against stimulation plus placebo. The improvement in urgency incontinence episodes on a 3-day bladder diary was significantly greater with the combination: a mean pre- to post-treatment change difference of 9.4 ± 3.9 episodes with mirabegron versus 5.3 ± 5.5 with placebo (p=0.007), with significant between-arm differences also in urinary frequency and Overactive Bladder Questionnaire symptom-bother and quality-of-life scores. Twelve weeks is short, the sample is small, and no second trial of percutaneous stimulation plus mirabegron was found. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): the combination beat stimulation alone on diary and symptom outcomes in one small trial; replication is needed before this is more than a promising signal.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — one small double-blind RCT (n=54) found PTNS plus mirabegron improved urgency incontinence episodes more than PTNS plus placebo at 12 weeks

title: Hip bone structure after menopause: resistance-and-impact exercise and risedronate each nudged some strength estimates versus control — neither beat the other, and density itself did not move
question: In postmenopausal women, does a programme of resistance and impact exercise — or risedronate — better preserve hip bone structure?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — one 12-month randomised trial in 276 women within 6 years of menopause (mean age 54.5) compared weighted jogging plus progressive resistance exercise, monthly risedronate 150 mg, and control, all with calcium and vitamin D. Volumetric bone density and other pQCT outcomes did not differ between groups. On hip structural analysis, exercise beat control on intertrochanteric cross-sectional area (+2.25%, 95% CI 0.28 to 4.12), moment of inertia (+5.67%, 95% CI 1.47 to 9.87) and section modulus (+4.38%, 95% CI 1.02 to 7.74); risedronate beat control on intertrochanteric moment of inertia (+4.28%) and section modulus (+3.35%) and on several shaft measures. Exercise and risedronate did not differ significantly from each other on the remaining measures, and no fractures were assessed. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): both strategies produced small favourable shifts in estimated hip strength versus control in a single trial, with no winner between them and no fracture evidence.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — one 276-woman RCT found small hip-structure benefits for both exercise and risedronate versus control, none between them, and no density or fracture effect

title: MID-FRAIL: a multicomponent programme improved physical performance by 0.85 SPPB points in frail older people with diabetes — and the gains outlasted the training blocks
question: In frail older adults with type 2 diabetes, does a multicomponent intervention — exercise, nutrition, and education — improve physical function versus usual care?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the MID-FRAIL cluster-randomised trial (964 frail and pre-frail adults over 70 with type 2 diabetes, 74 sites in seven European countries) combined a 16-week individualised progressive resistance-exercise programme, a seven-session diabetes and nutrition education programme, and optimised care against usual care. At 12 months the intervention group's Short Physical Performance Battery scores were a mean 0.85 points higher than usual care (95% CI 0.44 to 1.26; p<0.0001) — a clinically relevant margin on a 12-point scale — with an estimated saving of €428.02 per patient per year; no other secondary outcome differed significantly. The trial's two-year follow-up found each 16-week intervention block raised SPPB performance by a mean 36.1% at week 18 and 10.2% at week 68, with values still above baseline at 2 years. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a structured exercise-plus-education programme improves physical function in frail older people with diabetes, at no net cost in the trial's economic analysis.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one large cluster-RCT found a 0.85-point SPPB advantage at 12 months, sustained above baseline at 2 years, with cost savings

title: CHIPPS: a weekly pharmacist-prescriber service in care homes did not reduce falls (rate ratio 0.91, CI 0.66–1.26) — it did reduce drug burden, safely
question: In care-home residents, does a pharmacist-led structured medication review reduce falls and hospital admissions versus usual care?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — CHIPPS randomised 49 triads (pharmacist independent prescriber, GP practice, care homes) covering 882 residents aged 65 and over across England, Scotland and Northern Ireland to a weekly pharmacist-prescriber service for six months or usual care. The primary outcome did not move: 697 falls (1.55 per resident) in the intervention group versus 538 falls (1.26 per resident) in controls, an adjusted fall rate ratio of 0.91 (95% CI 0.66–1.26). Secondary outcomes — quality of life, Barthel score, hospital admissions and mortality — were not significantly different, except the Drug Burden Index, which significantly favoured the intervention. A third of the pharmacists' 566 interventions (185; 32.7%) involved medicines associated with falls, and no adverse events or safety concerns were identified. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): intensive pharmacist prescribing in care homes is safe and lightens drug burden, but six months of it did not reduce falls or admissions.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — one large cluster-RCT found no fall reduction from pharmacist independent prescribing in care homes (rate ratio 0.91), though drug burden fell

title: Geriatric emergency-department interventions: reviews call the evidence weak and inconsistent, while one large nurse-led programme raised discharges (hazard ratio 1.19) without more deaths or returns
question: In older adults presenting to the emergency department, does a geriatric emergency department intervention — geriatric assessment with dedicated staff and transitional care — reduce hospital admission and return visits versus standard emergency care?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — the evidence is suggestive and structurally weak. A 2021 review of reviews found 15 review articles covering 83 primary studies of ED interventions for older people, with 26 different outcomes reported inconsistently; no individual intervention stood out, though interventions begun in the ED and continued into other settings tended to produce more favourable patient and service outcomes. The largest single evaluation, the nurse-led, physician-championed Geriatric Emergency Department Intervention (GEDI) in Queensland (44,983 presentations by people over 70), found patients seen when the GEDI team was working were more likely to be discharged (hazard ratio 1.19, 95% CI 1.13–1.24) with shorter ED stays (HR 1.42, 95% CI 1.33–1.52), no increase in mortality (HR 1.01, 95% CI 0.23–4.43) and no significant increase in same-cause re-presentation within 28 days (HR 1.21, 95% CI 0.99–1.49), saving an average $35 per presentation and $1,469 per admission. But GEDI was a pre-post pragmatic evaluation, not a randomised trial. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): geriatric ED teams probably help some older patients go home sooner; randomised proof that they cut admissions or return visits is still missing.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — a review of reviews finds the ED-intervention evidence weak and inconsistent; one large non-randomised programme evaluation showed more discharges without more deaths or returns

title: For acute extremity pain in the ED, one dose of ibuprofen plus acetaminophen matched three opioid combinations — pain down 4.3 points versus 3.5 to 4.4 at two hours
question: In adults with acute extremity pain in the emergency department, does a single oral dose of a non-opioid combination (ibuprofen plus acetaminophen) relieve pain as well as opioid combinations?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — in a double-blind trial of 416 adults (aged 21–64) with moderate to severe acute extremity pain at two Bronx emergency departments, a single oral dose of ibuprofen 400 mg plus acetaminophen 1,000 mg reduced pain at 2 hours by 4.3 points on an 11-point scale (95% CI 3.6–4.9), statistically and clinically indistinguishable from oxycodone/acetaminophen (4.4 points), hydrocodone/acetaminophen (3.5 points) and codeine/acetaminophen (3.9 points). The largest between-group difference, 0.9 points, was below the prespecified minimum clinically important difference of 1.3. Adverse events were not assessed in the trial. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): for a single dose in acute extremity pain, the non-opioid combination relieves pain as well as standard opioid combinations — the opioid adds nothing measurable at two hours.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — one double-blind RCT found single-dose ibuprofen plus acetaminophen equal to three opioid combinations for acute extremity pain at 2 hours

title: Low-dose ketamine added to morphine deepens early pain relief — an extra 0.76 points at 60 minutes in the pooled trials, below the clinically important line, with less rescue analgesia
question: In adults with acute pain in the emergency department, does low-dose ketamine added to morphine improve pain relief compared with morphine alone, and at what cost in adverse effects?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — modest and time-limited. In the Beaudoin double-blind trial (60 ED patients with moderate to severe acute pain), summed pain-intensity difference over 2 hours was 4.0 with morphine alone versus 7.0 with morphine plus ketamine 0.15 mg/kg and 7.8 with 0.3 mg/kg (p<0.02), with rescue analgesia needed by 35% of controls versus 20% in each ketamine group and more dysphoria and dizziness on ketamine. The 2023 meta-analysis of 8 RCTs (903 patients) found pain scores significantly lower only at 60 minutes (mean difference −0.76, 95% CI −1.19 to −0.33) — a reduction the reviewers themselves note was not clinically significant — with no difference at other time points, less rescue analgesia, no excess of serious side effects, and higher patient satisfaction. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): adjunctive low-dose ketamine buys a small, brief analgesic edge and some opioid sparing, paid for in minor dissociative effects.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — an RCT and an 8-trial meta-analysis agree on a small early analgesic gain and reduced rescue analgesia, below the clinically important threshold, with more minor adverse effects

title: Shoulder dislocation: injecting lidocaine into the joint reduces as successfully as intravenous sedation — with a sixth of the adverse events and a shorter ED stay
question: In adults undergoing closed reduction of a dislocated shoulder, does intra-articular lidocaine give equivalent reduction success with fewer complications than intravenous analgesia and sedation?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a 2022 systematic review and meta-analysis of 12 randomised trials (630 patients; 327 intra-articular lidocaine, 303 intravenous sedation) for closed reduction of acute anterior shoulder dislocation in the ED found no difference in reduction success (risk ratio 0.93, 95% CI 0.86–1.01), no difference in pain scores after analgesia or in ease of reduction — but significantly fewer adverse events with intra-articular lidocaine (RR 0.16, 95% CI 0.07–0.33) and a shorter ED length of stay (mean difference −1.48, units as reported in the review; 95% CI −2.48 to −0.47). Heterogeneity was substantial for success (I²=69%) and length of stay (I²=93%), nil for adverse events (I²=0%). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): intra-articular lidocaine is an equally effective, safer, faster-throughput alternative to IV sedation for anterior shoulder reduction, particularly when sedation is contraindicated or unavailable.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a 12-trial meta-analysis found equal reduction success with intra-articular lidocaine, far fewer adverse events (RR 0.16) and shorter ED stay than IV sedation

title: Distal radius fracture reduction: haematoma block achieves the same radiographic result as sedation — dexmedetomidine relieved pain faster at 10 minutes in the one head-to-head trial
question: In patients with a distal radius fracture, does a haematoma block provide adequate analgesia for reduction compared with procedural sedation or other regional techniques?
balance: SPLIT — adequacy splits by outcome. The direct randomised comparison (60 ED patients with distal radius fractures) found no difference between haematoma block and dexmedetomidine conscious sedation in post-reduction radiographic quality (Sarmiento criteria, p=0.89) or physician satisfaction (p=0.512), and no adverse effects in either group — but pain scores 10 minutes after the intervention were significantly lower with dexmedetomidine (p=0.009). A 2026 best-evidence review of haematoma block versus procedural sedation (7 studies, including 4 RCTs) likewise found no consistent difference in procedural success, with the highest-quality RCTs showing no difference in radiographic outcome. PROPOSED SPLIT: for getting the fracture reduced as well, the block is adequate; for how the first minutes feel, sedation acted faster in the single direct trial.
stamp: SPLIT — reduction quality and physician satisfaction equal in the direct trial and the evidence review; early pain relief (10 minutes) favoured dexmedetomidine sedation

title: Antibiotics after mammal bites: the old Cochrane evidence supports prophylaxis for human bites and hand bites (OR 0.10) — and finds no benefit for ordinary dog or cat bites
question: In patients presenting after mammalian bites, does prophylactic antibiotic treatment prevent wound infection compared with no prophylaxis, and does the answer differ for dog, cat, and human bites?
balance: SPLIT — by bite type and site, on old and thin evidence. The 2001 Cochrane review pooled 8 randomised trials of prophylactic antibiotics after mammalian bites. Antibiotics were associated with a statistically significant reduction in infection after human bites (the reviewers note this rests on one trial and needs confirmation). For bites by cats or dogs, prophylaxis did not appear to reduce infection rates. Site mattered independently: prophylaxis after hand bites significantly reduced infection (odds ratio 0.10, 95% CI 0.01–0.86; number needed to treat 4, 95% CI 2–50). Wound type (laceration versus puncture) did not appear to modify the effect. PROPOSED SPLIT: prophylaxis — supported for human bites and for hand bites of any species; not supported by trial evidence for uncomplicated dog or cat bites elsewhere on the body.
stamp: SPLIT — prophylaxis reduced infection after human bites and hand bites (OR 0.10) in an 8-trial Cochrane review, with no demonstrated benefit for dog or cat bites; key subgroups rest on single trials

title: Packing a drained perianal abscess cavity bought nothing but pain: 38.2 versus 28.2 on a 100-point pain scale, with fistula and recurrence no lower
question: After surgical drainage of a perianal abscess, does prolonged packing of the cavity improve healing or reduce recurrence compared with no packing — or mainly add pain?
balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — for the packing, not the patient outcomes it was meant to protect. In PPAC2, 433 adults admitted for incision and drainage of a primary perianal abscess across 50 NHS sites were randomised to continued postoperative cavity packing or no packing. Packing hurt more: mean maximum pain scores were 38.2 with packing versus 28.2 without (mean difference 9.9 points on a 100-point scale; p<0.0001). In return, packing bought no significant protection — fistula-in-ano occurred in 15% (32/213) with packing versus 11% (24/220) without (OR 0.69, 95% CI 0.39–1.22; p=0.20), and abscess recurrence in 3% (7/213) with packing versus 6% (13/223) without (OR 1.85, 95% CI 0.72–4.73; p=0.20), both intervals wide and compatible with small effects either way. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm): routine packing of perianal abscess cavities adds significant pain without demonstrated benefit on healing complications.
stamp: POSSIBLE (harm) — one multicentre RCT found packing increased pain (difference 9.9 of 100 points) with no significant reduction in fistula or recurrence

title: Absorbable sutures close traumatic lacerations as cosmetically as non-absorbable ones — 79 versus 66 in children, 54.1 versus 54.5 mm in the adult-inclusive trial — with no removal visit
question: In traumatic lacerations closed in the emergency department, do absorbable sutures give equivalent long-term cosmetic outcomes to non-absorbable sutures that require removal?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — two randomised trials agree. In children (95 enrolled), plain-gut absorbable versus nylon sutures gave similar short-term optimal wound scores (63% versus 49%; RR 0.73, 95% CI 0.45–1.17) and, at four months in the 63 children followed, blinded plastic-surgeon cosmesis scores of 79 (95% CI 73–85) versus 66 (95% CI 55–76), with no differences in infection or dehiscence. In the second trial (115 enrolled, children and adults, trunk and extremity lacerations), absorbable Vicryl Rapide versus non-absorbable Prolene gave mean cosmesis scores of 54.1 mm versus 54.5 mm on a 100-mm scale (mean difference 0.5 mm, 95% CI −12.1 to 17.2), meeting the trial's 13-mm noninferiority margin, with no significant complication differences. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): absorbable sutures match non-absorbable ones for long-term cosmesis in simple traumatic lacerations, and spare the removal visit.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — two RCTs found long-term cosmetic outcomes equivalent between absorbable and non-absorbable sutures for traumatic lacerations

title: Staples versus sutures for skin closure: infection and dehiscence are a wash (OR 0.98) — staples are faster, sutures look better and satisfy patients more; after hip replacement, staples carried more superficial infection
question: For skin closure, do staples close wounds faster than sutures, and do they differ in infection and cosmetic outcomes?
balance: SPLIT — by outcome and by operation. In abdominal surgery (7 RCTs, 3,705 patients), staples and subcuticular sutures did not differ in surgical-site infection (OR 0.98, 95% CI 0.79–1.22) or dehiscence; staple closure was faster, while sutures gave better cosmesis and patient satisfaction. In hip arthroplasty (5 RCTs and 1 cohort), the balance tilted: superficial infection and prolonged wound discharge were more frequent with staples than with sutures, with no significant differences in dehiscence, abscess, wound-score or satisfaction outcomes — and suturing again took longer. PROPOSED SPLIT: staples win on speed everywhere; on infection they tie in abdominal surgery and lose after hip replacement; on appearance and satisfaction, sutures lead where they were measured.
stamp: SPLIT — staples are faster; infection ties in abdominal surgery (OR 0.98) but favours sutures after hip arthroplasty; cosmesis and satisfaction favour sutures
