title: Canadian Syncope Risk Score: superb in its Canadian validation (area under the curve 0.91; very-low-risk patients had a 0.3% event rate) — but in its first validation abroad it matched clinical judgement overall and its low-risk group still had a 6.7% event rate
question: In adults presenting to the emergency department with syncope, does the Canadian Syncope Risk Score accurately identify patients at low risk of serious adverse events within 30 days who can be safely discharged?
balance: SPLIT — by where it was validated. In the Canadian multicentre validation (3,819 ED patients with syncope, 3.6% with 30-day serious outcomes), the score discriminated excellently (area under the receiver operating curve 0.91, 95% CI 0.88–0.93), calibration was near-perfect (slope 1.0), event rates rose from 0.3% (3 of 1,631) in the very-low-risk group to 51.3% (40 of 78) in the very-high-risk group, no very-low- or low-risk patient died or had a ventricular arrhythmia, and at a threshold of −1 the sensitivity was 97.8% (95% CI 93.8–99.6) with specificity 44.3%. In the first validation outside Canada (345 Italian ED patients, 12% with serious adverse events), discrimination fell to 0.75 (95% CI 0.68–0.81) — similar to clinical judgement at 0.68 — and patients labelled low risk by the score still had a 6.7% event rate, versus 2% for clinician-judged low risk; score sensitivity was 70% (95% CI 54–83) versus 95% (95% CI 84–99) for judgement. PROPOSED SPLIT: the score stratifies beautifully in its home system; abroad, it did not beat — and at the discharge threshold did not match — clinician judgement.
stamp: SPLIT — excellent discrimination and safe low-risk strata in the Canadian validation (AUC 0.91), but weaker abroad (AUC 0.75) where score-defined low-risk patients still had 6.7% serious events versus 2% for clinical judgement

title: Implementing the Canadian C-Spine Rule cut cervical imaging by about an eighth in a 12-hospital cluster trial — no fractures missed, and the rule itself beat NEXUS head-to-head
question: In emergency-department patients with possible cervical spine injury, does implementing the Canadian C-Spine Rule reduce imaging rates without missing clinically important injuries?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for imaging use, with the safety record the trial could show. In a 12-centre matched-pair cluster randomised trial of 11,824 alert, stable adults with blunt head or neck trauma, an active implementation strategy (education, policy, real-time requisition reminders) produced a 12.8% relative reduction in cervical spine imaging (61.7% before to 53.3% after), while control hospitals rose 12.5% relative (52.8% to 58.9%); no fractures were missed and no adverse outcomes occurred (Stiell IG et al., PMID: 19875425). The rule being implemented had itself beaten the NEXUS low-risk criteria head-to-head in 8,283 patients: sensitivity 99.4% versus 90.7% and specificity 45.1% versus 36.8%, missing 1 important injury versus 16 (PMID: 14695411). The catch is reach: even after active implementation, 53.3% of these alert, stable patients were still imaged, so the rule trims imaging rather than transforming it. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): implementation measurably reduces cervical imaging with no missed fractures in the trial, on a rule independently shown more accurate than NEXUS.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — active implementation of the Canadian C-Spine Rule reduced cervical imaging (12.8% relative reduction) with no missed fractures in one cluster randomised trial, and the rule outperformed NEXUS on accuracy

title: Ottawa ankle rules in practice: ankle X-rays down 28% relative, no fractures missed, shorter waits and lower costs — and a systematic review puts the post-test fracture risk below 1.4%
question: In emergency-department patients with acute ankle injury, does implementing the Ottawa ankle rules reduce radiography without increasing missed fractures?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — less radiation and waiting, with sensitivity at or near 100% in the studies that measured it. In the original controlled implementation study of 2,342 adults, introducing the Ottawa ankle rules produced a 28% relative reduction in ankle radiography at the intervention hospital against a 2% increase at the control hospital (P<0.001), foot radiography fell 14% relative, patients discharged without radiography spent 80 versus 116 minutes in the department, and no fractures were missed — sensitivity was 1.0 for both malleolar (74 fractures) and midfoot (19 fractures) injuries (Stiell IG et al., PMID: 8114236). A systematic review of 27 studies and 15,581 patients found pooled negative likelihood ratios of 0.08 for ankle and mid-foot, which at a 15% fracture prevalence leaves under a 1.4% probability of fracture after a negative rule (PMID: 12595378). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the rules safely cut ankle and foot radiography by roughly a quarter to a third wherever they have been implemented and measured.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — implementing the Ottawa ankle rules reduced radiography (28% relative reduction in the controlled implementation study) with no missed fractures, backed by a 27-study accuracy review

title: PECARN head-injury rules: in 42,412 children the low-risk groups carried a 100% and 99.95% negative predictive value for clinically important brain injury — and an external validation in 20,137 more children agreed
question: In children with head injury, does the PECARN decision rule safely identify those at very low risk of clinically important traumatic brain injury in whom CT can be avoided?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — as a rule-out instrument, this is about as well validated as decision rules get. In the derivation-and-validation cohort of 42,412 children with Glasgow Coma Scale scores of 14–15 presenting within 24 hours of head trauma, clinically important traumatic brain injury (ciTBI) occurred in 0.9% and neurosurgery in 0.1%; in validation, the under-2 rule had a negative predictive value of 100.0% (1176/1176) and sensitivity of 100% (25/25), and the age-2-and-older rule a negative predictive value of 99.95% (3798/3800) and sensitivity of 96.8% (61/63), with neither rule missing a child who needed neurosurgery (Kuppermann N et al., PMID: 19758692). External validation in 20,137 Australian and New Zealand children again found PECARN sensitivities of 100.0% (under 2 years, 38/38) and 99.0% (2 years and older, 97/98) (PMID: 28410792). About a fifth to a quarter of CT-imaged children fell in the low-risk groups — that is the imaging the rule can obviate. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): two very large prospective cohorts agree the low-risk strata can safely forgo CT.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — PECARN low-risk strata showed 100% and 99.95% negative predictive value for clinically important brain injury in 42,412 children, confirmed in a 20,137-child external validation

title: Ultrasound-first for suspected kidney stones: in 2,759 randomised patients, high-risk missed diagnoses were 0.4% on every strategy — the only clear winner was the radiation bill, lower with ultrasound
question: In emergency-department patients with suspected kidney stones, does an ultrasound-first imaging strategy give equivalent outcomes to CT-first, with less cumulative radiation?
balance: SPLIT — clinical outcomes drawn, radiation not. In a multicentre pragmatic randomised trial of 2,759 emergency-department patients aged 18–76 with suspected nephrolithiasis, initial point-of-care ultrasonography, radiology ultrasonography, or CT produced the same low rate of high-risk diagnoses with complications at 30 days (0.4% overall, no difference by strategy), the same serious adverse event rates (12.4%, 10.8% and 11.2%; P=0.50), the same pain scores at 7 days (2.0 in each group), and no significant differences in return visits, hospitalisations, or diagnostic accuracy — but mean 6-month cumulative radiation exposure was significantly lower in both ultrasonography groups (P<0.001) (Smith-Bindman R et al., PMID: 25229916). A systematic review tempers the enthusiasm: pooled point-of-care ultrasound sensitivity for nephrolithiasis was only 70.2% and specificity 75.4%, though moderate-or-greater hydronephrosis was 94.4% specific (PMID: 29427476). PROPOSED SPLIT: ultrasound-first is as safe on patient outcomes and kinder on radiation, but it is the weaker test stone-by-stone, and many ultrasound-first patients still end up scanned.
stamp: SPLIT — patient outcomes identical across ultrasound-first and CT-first strategies in one large randomised trial (high-risk diagnoses 0.4%), with significantly lower cumulative radiation for ultrasound-first but only modest test accuracy (sensitivity 70.2%)

title: FAST in stable children with blunt torso trauma: a 975-child randomised trial found no gain — CT use 52.4% versus 54.6%, stays and charges the same, and pooled sensitivity in children is only 0.63
question: In children with blunt abdominal trauma, does the FAST examination improve outcomes — time to surgery, CT use, length of stay, and mortality — compared with usual care without FAST?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — in the population where it was actually tested. Among 925 randomised haemodynamically stable children with blunt torso trauma, adding a FAST examination to standard evaluation changed nothing measured: abdominal CT in 52.4% versus 54.6% (difference −2.2%, 95% CI −8.7% to 4.2%), emergency-department stay 6.03 versus 6.07 hours, median hospital charges $46,415 versus $47,759, and one missed intra-abdominal injury in the FAST group versus none without (difference 0.2%, −0.6% to 1.2%) (Holmes JF et al., PMID: 28609532). The accuracy literature explains why expectations should stay modest: in the Cochrane review, pooled sensitivity of point-of-care sonography in children was 0.63 (95% CI 0.46 to 0.77) against 0.78 in adults, at specificities of 0.91 and 0.97 (PMID: 30548249). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): routine FAST in stable injured children did not improve care, resource use, or outcomes in the only randomised trial.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — adding FAST to standard evaluation of stable children with blunt torso trauma changed neither CT use (52.4% vs 54.6%), stay, charges, nor missed injuries in a 925-child randomised trial

title: Fomepizole for toxic-alcohol poisoning: acidosis resolved and no survivor lost vision in the two prospective series — 19 ethylene-glycol and 11 methanol patients, and never a comparison group
question: In patients with toxic alcohol (methanol or ethylene glycol) poisoning, does fomepizole prevent visual loss, acidosis complications, and death, and can it avert dialysis in early presenters?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — the pharmacology is proven in patients; the outcomes are not, because nobody has ever run the comparison. In the prospective ethylene-glycol series, 19 patients received intravenous fomepizole: acid–base status normalised within hours, glycolate and oxalate fell uniformly, one patient with extreme acidosis died, and none of the 10 patients with normal creatinine at enrolment developed renal injury — every case of renal deterioration occurred in patients who arrived with high creatinine and markedly elevated glycolate (Brent J et al., PMID: 10080845). In the methanol series of 11 patients, formic acid fell and metabolic abnormalities resolved in all, nine survived (the two deaths had anoxic brain injury present at enrolment), and none of the seven patients with initial visual abnormalities had detectable visual deficits at the end (PMID: 11172179). Whether fomepizole averts dialysis in early presenters is asserted from mechanism and these series, not tested — dialysis decisions in both studies followed preset criteria alongside the antidote. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): consistent, mechanism-concordant case-series results in 30 patients total, with no comparator arm anywhere in the literature.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — two small prospective series (19 ethylene-glycol and 11 methanol patients) showed resolution of acidosis and no visual loss in survivors, but fomepizole has never been compared with ethanol, dialysis, or no antidote in a controlled study

title: Lipid emulsion for local anaesthetic toxicity: 81 of 83 reported human cases survived — but the only controlled human study was in volunteers with subclinical toxicity, and it showed no difference
question: In local anaesthetic systemic toxicity, does intravenous lipid emulsion improve resuscitation success compared with standard advanced life support alone?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — a treatment carried by case reports, graded 'very low quality' by the reviewers who collected them. The collaborative systematic review found 76 human studies: one randomised crossover trial in 16 healthy volunteers with subclinical toxicity, which showed no difference between lipid emulsion and saline, and 73 case reports plus a case series covering 83 patients with real toxicity — 45 (54%) with CNS features, 49 (59%) with seizures, 39 (47%) with cardiovascular features, and 18 (22%) in cardiac arrest — of whom 81 (98%) survived and 63 (76%) had no reported sequelae (Hoegberg LC et al., PMID: 26853119). The companion evidence-based recommendations endorse lipid emulsion for bupivacaine cardiac arrest and, if other therapies fail, for life-threatening toxicity from other local anaesthetics — every recommendation explicitly based on very low quality evidence (PMID: 27608281). Publication bias hangs over the 98% survival figure: failed rescues are far less likely to be written up. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): plausible, widely endorsed, and unproven against standard resuscitation in any controlled human study.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — human evidence for lipid emulsion in local anaesthetic toxicity is 83 case-report patients (98% survival) plus one negative volunteer crossover trial; the systematic reviewers graded it very low quality

title: Digoxin antibody fragments: in life-threatening intoxication, 80% of 150 patients had complete resolution in an uncontrolled series — in chronic poisoning, the only comparative study found Fab no better than observation
question: In patients with life-threatening digoxin poisoning, does early treatment with digoxin-specific antibody fragments improve survival and arrhythmia resolution compared with supportive care?
balance: SPLIT — by poisoning type, because the two halves of the evidence answer different questions. In life-threatening digitalis intoxication, the classic multicentre series treated 150 patients with digoxin-specific Fab: of 148 evaluable patients, 119 (80%) had resolution of all signs and symptoms, 14 (10%) improved, and 15 (10%) showed no response, with a median time to initial response of 19 minutes; 54% of patients who had suffered cardiac arrest survived to hospital discharge — but there was no comparison group (Antman EM et al., PMID: 2188752). In chronic digoxin poisoning, the prospective ATOM-4 comparison of 78 patients given initial Fab versus 50 managed supportively found mortality of 12% versus 14% (risk difference −2.5%, 95% CI −14% to 9%), identical median stays of six days, and no difference in heart-rate or potassium change at 4 hours (PMID: 30585517). ATOM-4 excluded patients presenting with ventricular arrhythmias, so the life-threatening question itself has still never had a comparative study. PROPOSED SPLIT: dramatic uncontrolled responses in acute life-threatening poisoning; no measurable benefit over observation in chronic poisoning.
stamp: SPLIT — uncontrolled series in life-threatening intoxication shows 80% complete resolution with Fab, while the only comparative study, in chronic poisoning (ventricular arrhythmias excluded), found no benefit over supportive care (mortality 12% vs 14%)

title: Hydroxocobalamin for smoke-inhalation cyanide poisoning: 72% of a prospective treated series survived — and the one comparative study found mortality identical (29% versus 28%)
question: In suspected cyanide poisoning from smoke inhalation, does hydroxocobalamin improve survival and neurological outcome compared with other antidotes or supportive care?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — an antidote whose reputation rests on a case series, with the only comparative data showing no survival difference. In the prospective Paris series, 69 adult smoke-inhalation victims with suspected cyanide poisoning received hydroxocobalamin 5 g (up to 15 g) at the fire scene or in intensive care; 50 (72%) survived, and among the 42 patients with cyanide poisoning confirmed afterwards, 28 (67%) survived; adverse events were mostly chromaturia and skin discolouration, with no serious event attributed to the drug (Borron SW et al., PMID: 17481777). In a burn-centre comparison with historical controls, mortality was 29% with hydroxocobalamin versus 28% without (P=0.90), though the treated group had less pneumonia (23% vs 49%), fewer ventilator days (4 vs 7), and shorter ICU stays (6 vs 10 days) — differences wide open to era effects, since controls were treated in 2002–2008 and the treated group in 2008–2014 (PMID: 27554631). Neurological outcome, the outcome families care about most, was not comparatively measured in either study. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): safe and mechanistically direct, but a survival or neurological benefit over supportive care has never been shown.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — a prospective series reports 72% survival after hydroxocobalamin in suspected smoke-inhalation cyanide poisoning, but the single comparative study found identical mortality (29% vs 28%) and no study measures neurological outcome comparatively

title: High-dose insulin for calcium-channel-blocker and beta-blocker shock: success rates of 80–100% in published case series — and not one comparative human study behind them
question: In calcium-channel-blocker or beta-blocker poisoning with shock, does high-dose insulin euglycaemia therapy improve haemodynamics and survival compared with conventional vasopressor therapy?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — a mainstay therapy whose entire human evidence base is case reports, case series, and one observational study. The systematic review of treatments for calcium-channel-blocker poisoning screened 15,577 citations and analysed 216 studies, of which 117 were case reports; for high-dose insulin (bolus 1 unit/kg, infusion 0.5–2.0 units/kg/h) it found an association with improved haemodynamic parameters and lower mortality at low quality of evidence, with hypoglycaemia and hypokalaemia as the costs — and noted that the only observational human study in the whole review examined high-dose insulin and extracorporeal life support (St-Onge M et al., PMID: 25283255). A focused review of high-dose insulin euglycaemia therapy in calcium-channel-blocker and beta-blocker overdose reports success rates of 80.4–100% across published case series, with regular insulin typically bolused at 1 unit/kg then infused at 0.5–1 unit/kg/h alongside dextrose (PMID: 30141827). No study has compared the therapy with vasopressors head-to-head, so 'improves survival compared with conventional therapy' remains an unasked experimental question. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): physiologically coherent and consistently reported, formally untested.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — high-dose insulin in calcium-channel-blocker/beta-blocker poisoning rests on case reports and series (reported success 80.4–100%); the systematic review graded the evidence low quality and no comparative human study exists

title: Ketofol versus propofol alone for emergency-department sedation: five trials, 1,250 patients — fewer respiratory adverse effects with the mixture, sedation quality a draw
question: For adult emergency-department procedural sedation, does a ketamine–propofol combination (ketofol) cause fewer adverse events than propofol alone, with equally effective sedation?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a modest safety edge, not a better sedation. A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials in adult emergency-department procedural sedation pooled five eligible trials totalling 1,250 patients (615 ketofol, 635 propofol): two of the five studies found better sedation quality with ketofol and three found no significant difference, while the review found a lower incidence of respiratory adverse effects in the ketofol group than with propofol alone (Ghojazadeh M et al., PMID: 31011553). The theoretical logic — lower doses of each agent trimming both drugs' adverse effects — is thus half confirmed: the respiratory side improved, the sedation itself did not clearly. The record reports the respiratory advantage without a pooled effect size, so its size cannot be stated from this record. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): fewer respiratory adverse events across five small trials, with equivalent sedation quality in most.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a meta-analysis of five randomised trials (1,250 adults) found fewer respiratory adverse effects with ketofol than propofol alone, with no consistent difference in sedation quality

title: Nitrous oxide for children's painful procedures: 30 trials say it works for needles and lacerations, matches ketamine-based regimens for fractures — nausea 4.4%, vomiting 3.6%, and worse when combined with other sedatives
question: In children undergoing painful procedures, does nitrous oxide provide effective and safe procedural analgesia and sedation compared with other agents?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — real analgesia for short, mildly-to-moderately painful procedures, with the indication mattering more than the gas. A systematic review and meta-analysis of 30 trials in children and youth found 70% nitrous oxide beat topical anaesthetic cream (EMLA) for intravenous-insertion pain by 16.5 points on a 0–100 scale (95% CI −28.6 to −4.4; P=0.008), nitrous oxide was 'favourable' against subcutaneous lidocaine, oxygen, and oral midazolam for laceration repair, and 'neutral' — no winner — against intravenous ketamine regimens for fracture reduction (Poonai N et al., PMID: 37171705). Common adverse effects were nausea (4.4%), agitation (3.7%), and vomiting (3.6%), and adverse effects were far commoner when nitrous oxide was combined with midazolam (92.3%) or fentanyl (61.2%) than used alone (24.2%). An earlier systematic review put serious adverse events at under 0.5% and minor events at 4–8% for brief procedures (PMID: 23743110). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): effective and acceptably safe as a single agent for brief procedures; not a substitute for deeper sedation in fracture reduction.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — across 30 trials, nitrous oxide beat topical anaesthetic for IV-insertion pain and matched ketamine-based regimens for fracture reduction, with nausea 4.4% and vomiting 3.6% and serious events under 0.5%

title: Intranasal dexmedetomidine versus nitrous oxide for children's procedural sedation: worst pain scores identical (median FLACC 4 in both) in a 148-child non-inferiority trial
question: In children needing procedural sedation in the emergency department, does intranasal dexmedetomidine achieve adequate sedation as reliably as nitrous oxide or other standard agents?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — in the one head-to-head trial, the spray matched the gas on pain. In an open-label randomised non-inferiority trial in a paediatric emergency department, 148 previously healthy children aged 3–15 years with an extremity fracture or luxation or a burn were randomised to intranasal dexmedetomidine or inhaled 50% nitrous oxide; the highest pain score during the procedure (FLACC) was a median of 4 in both groups (IQR 3–6 versus 2–6), and the median between-group difference was 0 (95% CI 0 to 1), meeting non-inferiority (Nikula A et al., PMID: 39568028). Acceptance was a touch lower for the spray: 82.5% of children and 91.5% of parents would accept the same method again, versus 88.1% and 94.6% with nitrous oxide. No serious adverse events were reported in either group. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): equivalent procedural pain control in a single trial — a genuine alternative where nitrous oxide is impractical, not an improvement on it.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — intranasal dexmedetomidine was non-inferior to 50% nitrous oxide for procedural pain (median worst FLACC 4 in both groups) in one 148-child randomised trial, with no serious adverse events

title: Intravenous magnesium for acute migraine in the emergency department: seven trials, 545 patients — pain better at 60–120 minutes, not earlier, and the 50%-relief results point in three directions at once
question: In adults with acute migraine in the emergency department, does intravenous magnesium sulfate relieve headache compared with placebo or standard therapy?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — the reviewers themselves declined to draw a firm conclusion, and the shelf follows them. A systematic review of randomised trials of intravenous magnesium sulfate for non-traumatic headache in the emergency department found seven eligible trials with 545 participants (six in migraine): pain intensity was improved with magnesium versus comparators at 60–120 minutes but not at earlier time points; for the endpoint of pain reduction by 50%, three studies variously reported headache improved, unchanged, and worse with magnesium; complete pain relief was improved in one study and in the migraine-with-aura subgroup of another; rescue-analgesia need and 24-hour recurrence each improved in one study and were unchanged in another (Miller AC et al., PMID: 31566727). Heterogeneity prevented any meta-analysis. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): a late, inconsistent pain signal across small trials — a reasonable adjunct candidate, not a proven abortive.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — seven small randomised trials (545 patients) show intravenous magnesium improving migraine pain only at 60–120 minutes, with conflicting results for 50% pain relief and no meta-analysis possible

title: Intravenous valproate for acute migraine: a seven-trial meta-analysis found it worse than the standard drugs it was compared with — less relief (odds ratio 0.51) and nearly four times the odds of needing rescue therapy
question: In adults with acute migraine in the emergency department, does intravenous valproate relieve headache as effectively as standard therapies such as metoclopramide or ketorolac?
balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — 'harm' here in the comparative sense this library uses: patients given intravenous valproate did worse than patients given the standard alternatives. A meta-analysis of seven double-blind randomised trials involving 682 emergency-department patients with acute migraine found those receiving intravenous valproate had less improvement in headache intensity than those receiving other active treatments (standardised mean difference −0.39, 95% CI −0.73 to −0.06; P=0.02), a lower rate of headache relief (odds ratio 0.51, 95% CI 0.33 to 0.77; P=0.002), and higher odds of needing rescue therapy (odds ratio 3.76, 95% CI 1.96 to 7.20; P<0.0001) (Wang F et al., PMID: 32740903). The exceptions are narrow: valproate was comparable to dexamethasone, and in migraine without aura there was no significant difference in headache-intensity improvement (standardised mean difference −0.00, −0.54 to 0.54). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm): as a first-choice abortive it underperforms the comparators studied; the authors leave it a salvage role, particularly floated for migraine with aura and status migrainosus, on thinner data.
stamp: POSSIBLE (harm) — intravenous valproate was inferior to other active migraine treatments in a seven-trial meta-analysis (headache relief odds ratio 0.51; rescue-therapy odds ratio 3.76), though comparable to dexamethasone

title: Corticosteroids for vestibular neuritis: vestibular function recovered better in the one factorial trial (62.4 versus 39.6 percentage points of improvement) — whether patients feel better is, in the guideline synthesis's words, very uncertain
question: In patients with acute vestibular neuritis, do corticosteroids improve recovery of vestibular function and symptoms compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for the caloric test, with the symptom question honestly open. In a randomised double-blind two-by-two factorial trial of 141 patients with acute vestibular neuritis, mean improvement in peripheral vestibular function at 12 months was 62.4 percentage points with methylprednisolone versus 39.6 with placebo (valacyclovir made no difference, P=0.43; the methylprednisolone effect was significant at P<0.001) (Strupp M et al., PMID: 15269315). The emergency-medicine guideline evidence synthesis, an umbrella review of the systematic reviews (12 studies, 660 patients), found corticosteroids associated with higher complete caloric recovery in a meta-analysis of two trials totalling only 50 patients (risk ratio 2.81, 95% CI 1.32 to 6.00; low certainty), while patient-reported vertigo and dizziness-disability estimates were so imprecise that translation into clinical improvement is 'very uncertain' (PMID: 35975654). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): steroids speed the laboratory recovery of the vestibular organ; a patient-felt benefit has never been shown with comparable rigour.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — methylprednisolone improved caloric recovery of vestibular function (62.4 vs 39.6 percentage points at 12 months) in one factorial trial, but patient-reported vertigo benefit remains very uncertain in the guideline evidence synthesis

title: Steroids and antihistamines in anaphylaxis: the Cochrane review found zero eligible randomised trials — these routine adjuncts rest on no controlled evidence at all
question: In anaphylaxis, do corticosteroids or antihistamines added to adrenaline improve outcomes or prevent biphasic reactions — or is the evidence for these routine adjuncts absent?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference) — read precisely: no difference has ever been demonstrated, because the trials have never been done; that is an absence of evidence, not a proven absence of effect. The Cochrane review of glucocorticoids for anaphylaxis, searching to September 2011, found no randomised or quasi-randomised study that satisfied its inclusion criteria, and concluded it was unable to make any recommendations for or against glucocorticoids in anaphylaxis (Choo KJ et al., PMID: 22513951). A later systematic review found 30 original papers (22 human studies) in which corticosteroids were used in an average of 68% of anaphylaxis treatments (range 48–100%); steroids appeared to reduce length of hospital stay but not emergency-department revisits, there was no consensus on whether they reduce biphasic reactions, and none of the human studies had data capable of comparing outcomes between treatment groups (PMID: 28884986). Adrenaline remains the only treatment in anaphylaxis with a claim on the outcome evidence — such as it is. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference): the adjuncts are unproven, widely given, and not shown harmful in these reviews; the stamp records the missing evidence, not a demonstrated null effect.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference) — no randomised trial of corticosteroids in anaphylaxis exists (Cochrane found zero eligible studies) and no human study compares outcomes with versus without adjuncts; benefit is undemonstrated rather than disproven

title: Intramuscular beats subcutaneous adrenaline: peak levels at 8 minutes versus 34 in children, and the thigh beats the arm — two small randomised pharmacokinetic studies settled the route
question: For anaphylaxis, is intramuscular adrenaline absorbed faster and more reliably than subcutaneous adrenaline?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — faster and higher peaks by the intramuscular route, in both age groups studied, on pharmacokinetic rather than outcome evidence. In children with a history of anaphylaxis randomised to a single dose, intramuscular adrenaline from an autoinjector reached a mean maximum plasma concentration of 2,136±351 pg/mL at a mean of 8±2 minutes, while subcutaneous injection reached 1,802±214 pg/mL at 34±14 minutes (range 5–120) — and only two of nine subcutaneous children had peaked by 5 minutes, versus six of eight intramuscular (Simons FE et al., PMID: 9449498). In adults, a randomised blinded six-way crossover study found peak plasma concentrations significantly higher after intramuscular injection into the thigh than after intramuscular or subcutaneous injection into the upper arm (P<0.01) (PMID: 11692118). No serious adverse effects occurred in the children's study. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): intramuscular-into-thigh is the reliably faster route — the finding behind every modern autoinjector instruction — proven on blood levels in small studies, not on anaphylaxis outcomes.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — intramuscular adrenaline peaked faster than subcutaneous in randomised pharmacokinetic studies in children (8 vs 34 minutes to peak) and adults (thigh intramuscular highest, P<0.01)

title: Take-home ondansetron after a gastroenteritis visit: moderate-to-severe illness over the next week in 5.1% versus 12.5% on placebo — but return visits and IV fluids did not fall
question: In children discharged after an emergency visit for gastroenteritis, does a multidose ondansetron course at home reduce return visits and intravenous rehydration compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the illness ran milder at home, even though the utilisation outcomes the question names did not move. In a double-blind randomised trial in six paediatric emergency departments, 1,030 children aged 6 months to under 18 years with gastroenteritis-associated vomiting were given six doses of oral ondansetron or placebo to use against ongoing vomiting over 48 hours: moderate-to-severe gastroenteritis over the following 7 days (modified Vesikari score ≥9) occurred in 5.1% (23/452) on ondansetron versus 12.5% (55/441) on placebo — an absolute difference of −7.4 percentage points (95% CI −11.2 to −3.7) and an adjusted odds ratio of 0.50 (0.40 to 0.60) (Freedman SB et al., PMID: 40673584). Vomiting episodes within 48 hours were fewer (adjusted rate ratio 0.76, 0.67 to 0.87), but the presence and duration of vomiting, unscheduled physician visits, and receipt of intravenous fluids did not differ substantially, and adverse events were similar (odds ratio 0.99, 0.61 to 1.61). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a take-home course softens the week's illness — roughly one moderate-to-severe course avoided for every 14 children treated — without demonstrably keeping children out of the clinic or off the drip.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — multidose home ondansetron halved moderate-to-severe gastroenteritis over 7 days (5.1% vs 12.5%; adjusted odds ratio 0.50) in one 1,030-child randomised trial, without reducing return visits or intravenous fluids

title: Oral prednisone for acute sciatica: function improved modestly at 3 weeks and a year, pain did not improve at all — and adverse events doubled (49.2% versus 23.9%)
question: In adults with acute radiculopathy (sciatica) from a herniated lumbar disc, does a short course of oral prednisone improve function and pain compared with placebo?
balance: SPLIT — function yes (a little), pain no. In a randomised double-blind trial of 269 adults with radicular pain for 3 months or less, an Oswestry Disability Index score of at least 30, and an MRI-confirmed herniated disc, a tapering 15-day course of prednisone (60/40/20 mg, 600 mg total) produced a 6.4-point greater improvement in disability at 3 weeks than placebo (95% CI 1.9 to 10.9; P=0.006) and 7.4 points at 52 weeks (2.2 to 12.5; P=0.005) — but leg-pain reduction differed by only 0.3 points at 3 weeks (P=0.34) and 0.6 at a year (P=0.15), surgery rates were the same, and one or more adverse events occurred in 49.2% on prednisone versus 23.9% on placebo (P<0.001) (Goldberg H et al., PMID: 25988461). The broader drug review for sciatica found pooled corticosteroid trials showing a short-term mean pain advantage of −12.2 points on a 0–100 scale (−20.9 to −3.4) across two trials, on evidence it graded low quality overall (PMID: 22331277). PROPOSED SPLIT: a real but modest functional gain that patients may or may not notice, bought with a doubled adverse-event rate, and no analgesia in the best-powered trial.
stamp: SPLIT — prednisone modestly improved disability (6.4 points at 3 weeks) but not pain (0.3 points, P=0.34) in a 269-patient randomised trial, with adverse events in 49.2% vs 23.9%

title: Endoscopy within 6 hours for high-risk upper GI bleeding: mortality 8.9% versus 6.6% with endoscopy at 6–24 hours — rushing found more bleeding lesions and treated more of them, and helped no one measurably
question: In acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding, does endoscopy within 6 hours improve mortality or further bleeding compared with endoscopy within 24 hours?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — in the highest-risk patients, where the case for rushing was strongest. In a randomised trial of 516 patients with overt acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding and a Glasgow-Blatchford score of 12 or higher, endoscopy within 6 hours of gastroenterology consultation gave 30-day mortality of 8.9% (23/258) versus 6.6% (17/258) with endoscopy between 6 and 24 hours (difference 2.3 percentage points, 95% CI −2.3 to 6.9), and further bleeding in 10.9% versus 7.8% (difference 3.1 points, −1.9 to 8.1) (Lau JYW et al., PMID: 32242355). The urgent group did get more endoscopic treatment (60.1% vs 48.4%), because ulcers found earlier were more often actively bleeding or showed visible vessels (66.4% vs 47.8%) — earlier scopes find more to treat without changing what happens to patients. A meta-analysis of five randomised trials (926 patients) likewise found no significant benefit of very early over early endoscopy for rebleeding, mortality, ICU admission, transfusion, surgery, or stay, with a higher need for haemostatic treatment when scoping very early (risk ratio 1.23, 1.06 to 1.42) (PMID: 33570742). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): within-24-hours endoscopy is the evidence-based deadline; within-6-hours adds procedures, not survival.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — endoscopy within 6 hours did not lower 30-day mortality versus 6–24 hours in high-risk bleeders (8.9% vs 6.6%) in a 516-patient randomised trial, confirmed by a five-trial meta-analysis

title: Offering families the chance to witness CPR: relatives in the control group had 1.7 times the odds of PTSD symptoms at 90 days — and resuscitation, survival, team stress, and legal claims were all unaffected
question: Should family members be offered the chance to witness cardiopulmonary resuscitation, and does witnessing reduce their post-traumatic stress compared with not being offered?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for the relatives, with no cost detected for the patient or the team. In a cluster-randomised trial across 15 French prehospital emergency units, 570 relatives of patients in cardiac arrest were in units assigned either to systematically offer the opportunity to observe CPR or to follow standard practice: 79% of offered relatives witnessed CPR versus 43% under standard practice, and PTSD-related symptoms at day 90 were significantly commoner in the control group (adjusted odds ratio 1.7, 95% CI 1.2 to 2.5; P=0.004) and among relatives who did not witness CPR versus those who did (adjusted odds ratio 1.6, 1.1 to 2.5; P=0.02) (Jabre P et al., PMID: 23484827). Witnessing did not affect resuscitation characteristics, patient survival, or the medical team's emotional stress, and produced no medicolegal claims; non-witnessing relatives also had more anxiety and depression symptoms. A 2022 systematic review of 31 studies (including two randomised trials) found the wider evidence low or very low certainty, with family outcomes mixed across studies (PMID: 36087636). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the offer itself appears protective for relatives' mental health; the trial supports offering, not compelling, presence.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — systematically offering family presence during CPR reduced relatives' PTSD-related symptoms at 90 days (adjusted odds ratio 1.7 against the control group) in a 570-relative cluster randomised trial, with no effect on resuscitation or survival

title: Hypotensive resuscitation in bleeding trauma: pooled odds ratio for death 0.70 across five randomised trials (1,158 patients) — a real signal built from small, mostly underpowered trials
question: In bleeding trauma patients, does a hypotensive (restricted) resuscitation strategy targeting a lower systolic pressure before bleeding control improve survival compared with conventional resuscitation?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a mortality signal the reviewers themselves call underpowered. A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials comparing permissive hypotension with conventional resuscitation after traumatic injury pooled five trials and 1,158 patients: the pooled odds ratio for 30-day or in-hospital mortality was 0.70 (95% CI 0.53 to 0.92) favouring hypotensive resuscitation, and the hypotensive groups received fewer blood products and had less estimated blood loss (Tran A et al., PMID: 29370058). Intervention targets ranged from systolic 50–70 mmHg or mean arterial pressure ≥50, against control targets of systolic 65–100 or MAP ≥65. Four of the five trials suggested a survival benefit but three were insufficiently powered to show it individually, and study quality was poor to moderate. The largest component experience, a randomised trial targeting MAP 50 versus 65 mmHg during operative resuscitation in 90 patients in haemorrhagic shock, found significantly less blood product and intravenous fluid use, significantly lower early postoperative mortality, less postoperative coagulopathy, and a non-significant trend to lower 30-day mortality in the low-MAP group (PMID: 21610356). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the direction is consistent and the mechanism (less clot disruption, dilution, and hypothermia) coherent — the definitive large trial still does not exist.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — permissive hypotension reduced mortality in a meta-analysis of five randomised trauma trials (pooled odds ratio 0.70, 0.53 to 0.92), with less blood-product use, though most component trials were underpowered

title: Lung ultrasound for pneumonia: pooled sensitivity 0.95 against chest X-ray's 0.77 in head-to-head meta-analysis, with similar specificity — the better bedside test where the expertise exists
question: In emergency-department patients with suspected pneumonia, is lung ultrasound more accurate than chest X-ray for diagnosis when compared with CT or clinical follow-up?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — as a diagnostic test, judged against the reference standards the studies used. A systematic review and meta-analysis of 16 studies (2,359 participants) found lung ultrasonography highly accurate for pneumonia in adults, with an area under the summary receiver-operating curve of 0.93 and a diagnostic odds ratio at the optimal cutpoint of 50 (95% CI 21 to 120) (Llamas-Álvarez AM et al., PMID: 27818332). The head-to-head meta-analysis is the sharper result: across five studies comparing both tests, lung ultrasound had pooled sensitivity 0.95 (0.93–0.97) and specificity 0.90 (0.86–0.94), while chest radiography had sensitivity 0.77 (0.73–0.80) and specificity 0.91 (0.87–0.94); against CT as the reference (138 patients), the area under the curve was 0.901 for ultrasound versus 0.590 for radiography (P=0.002) (PMID: 26107512). The catch is operator dependence: these accuracies come from studies where ultrasound was performed and interpreted by enthusiasts, and both reviews found significant heterogeneity. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): more pneumonias found at the bedside at no cost in false positives — in trained hands.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — lung ultrasound outperformed chest X-ray for pneumonia diagnosis in two concordant meta-analyses (sensitivity 0.95 vs 0.77 at similar specificity ~0.90; area under the curve 0.93 overall)

title: PERC rule in low-risk ED patients: the PROPER randomised trial found no excess missed clots (0.1% vs 0%) and 10 percentage points fewer CT pulmonary angiograms — pooled sensitivity 0.97, specificity only 0.23
question: In emergency-department patients with suspected pulmonary embolism, can a negative PERC rule safely exclude the diagnosis without D-dimer testing or imaging?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a PERC-negative result in a patient already judged low-risk can end the workup safely, and the one randomised test of that strategy found no safety cost. In the PROPER crossover cluster-randomised trial (Freund Y et al., PMID: 29450523), a thromboembolic event missed at presentation occurred in 0.1% of the PERC group versus 0% of controls over 3 months, while CT pulmonary angiography fell from 23% to 13% (difference −10%, 95% CI −13% to −6%), median ED stay fell by a mean of 36 minutes, and hospital admission fell by 3.3 percentage points. The pooled diagnostic accuracy behind the rule (Singh B et al., PMID: 22177109) is sensitivity 0.97 (95% CI 0.96 to 0.98) with specificity only 0.23 — PERC rules out; it never rules in. Both records apply only after a clinician has already judged the pretest probability low: PERC was never tested as a stand-alone screen in unselected chest-pain patients. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): in gestalt low-risk patients, PERC-negative safely avoids D-dimer and imaging, on one randomised strategy trial plus a concordant accuracy meta-analysis.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — PERC-based rule-out in low-risk ED patients caused no excess 3-month thromboembolism in the PROPER randomised trial and cut CT pulmonary angiography by 10 percentage points; pooled sensitivity 0.97

title: Droperidol and the heart: mean QTc barely moved (424 to 428 ms) in the largest ED series and torsades occurred once in 16,546 patients (0.006%) — a real but very small risk at usual doses
question: In patients sedated with droperidol in the emergency department, how large is the risk of QT prolongation and torsades at usual doses?
balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — the harm is real but, at usual emergency-department doses, very small, and both large series agree on that scale. In the largest record (Cole JB et al., PMID: 32726229), 15,374 non-critical patients received 18,020 droperidol doses; among patients with ECGs before and after, mean QTc was 424.3 ms before and 427.6 ms after droperidol, and a single case of torsades occurred in a patient with multiple risk factors who tolerated rechallenge — an incidence of 1 in 16,546 (0.006%, 95% CI 0.00015 to 0.03367%). In critically ill patients the mean QTc was 435.7 ms before and 435.8 ms after. A later series (Alshehri AM et al., PMID: 39695417) found a composite of QTc prolongation, torsades, ventricular arrhythmia or hypotension in 9.1% of 327 administrations, with no episode of torsades or serious ventricular arrhythmia and no event rated probable or definite on the Naranjo scale; higher cumulative dose was associated with QTc prolongation (OR 1.27). All of this evidence is observational — there is no randomised cardiac-safety trial — so the shelf is Tier C. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm): droperidol prolongs QTc slightly on average and torsades is documented but rarer than 1 in 16,000 at usual ED doses; dose and patient risk factors, not the drug name alone, drive the risk.
stamp: POSSIBLE (harm) — droperidol causes small average QTc prolongation with torsades in about 1 of 16,546 ED patients in the largest series; observational evidence only

title: Buccal midazolam stopped children's seizures in 56% versus 27% on rectal diazepam in the one head-to-head hospital trial — with no extra respiratory depression
question: In children with seizures in the emergency department, is buccal midazolam more effective than rectal diazepam at stopping seizures?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — when there is no intravenous access, the cheek beats the rectum. In the multicentre randomised trial (McIntyre J et al., PMID: 16023510), therapeutic success — seizure cessation within 10 minutes lasting at least 1 hour without respiratory depression requiring intervention — was 56% (61 of 109) on buccal midazolam versus 27% (30 of 110) on rectal diazepam (difference 29%, 95% CI 16 to 41), and the rate of respiratory depression did not differ between groups. The Cochrane review (McTague A et al., PMID: 29320603) pooled the comparison at a risk ratio for seizure cessation of 1.25 (95% CI 1.13 to 1.38) across 4 trials and 690 children, but rated that evidence low to very low quality — smaller than the single big trial's own estimate, and the reason this shelf is POSSIBLE rather than LIKELY. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): buccal midazolam stops acute seizures in children more often than rectal diazepam, with no demonstrated increase in respiratory depression.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — buccal midazolam achieved therapeutic success in 56% vs 27% on rectal diazepam in the largest trial; Cochrane pooling (RR 1.25) is low- to very-low-quality evidence

title: Early tracheostomy after severe stroke (SETPOINT2): survival without severe disability at 6 months was 43.5% early versus 47.1% standard — no significant difference, with confidence intervals too wide to exclude real benefit or harm
question: In patients with severe stroke requiring prolonged ventilation, does early tracheostomy improve long-term functional outcome compared with a standard (later) tracheostomy strategy?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — on the outcome that matters, timing did not deliver. In SETPOINT2 (Bösel J et al., PMID: 35506515), 382 ventilated patients with severe ischaemic or haemorrhagic stroke were randomised to tracheostomy within 5 days or to continued weaning with tracheostomy if needed from day 10; a tracheostomy was performed in 95.2% of the early group (median day 4) and 67% of the standard group (median day 11). Survival without severe disability at 6 months (modified Rankin Scale 0–4) was 43.5% early versus 47.1% standard (difference −3.6%, 95% CI −14.3% to 7.2%; adjusted OR 0.93, 95% CI 0.60 to 1.42; P=.73). Tracheostomy-related serious adverse events were 5.0% of reported serious events in the early group versus 3.4% in the standard group. The confidence interval is wide enough to include a clinically important difference in either direction, so this is a single-trial null, not proof of equivalence — Tier C. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): early tracheostomy did not significantly improve 6-month functional outcome in the one large stroke-specific trial.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — SETPOINT2 found no significant difference in survival without severe disability at 6 months (43.5% vs 47.1%) for early versus standard tracheostomy after severe stroke

title: GFAP/UCH-L1 blood test after head injury: sensitivity 0.976 and negative predictive value 0.996 for CT injury in ALERT-TBI — but no trial has yet shown it actually reduces CT scanning
question: In adults with mild traumatic brain injury, does a blood biomarker test (GFAP and UCH-L1) safely reduce head CT scanning compared with usual clinical decision-making?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the test is an accurate rule-out; the scanning reduction the question asks about has never been randomised. In ALERT-TBI (Bazarian JJ et al., PMID: 30054151), 1,959 adults with Glasgow Coma Scale 9–15 who had a head CT as standard care had serum GFAP and UCH-L1 measured at prespecified cutoffs: 125 (6%) had CT-detected intracranial injury, the combined test was negative in 671 (34%), and for detection of injury it had sensitivity 0.976 (95% CI 0.931 to 0.995) and negative predictive value 0.996 (0.987 to 0.999), with 3 patients CT-positive despite a negative test. The rapid point-of-care version, tested on banked plasma from the same cohort (Bazarian JJ et al., PMID: 34358399), performed similarly in the 1,901 patients with GCS 13–15: sensitivity 0.958 (95% CI 0.906 to 0.982), specificity 0.404, negative predictive value 0.993, positive predictive value 0.098. Because every patient in both records was scanned anyway, the records show who could have avoided a CT, not that using the test safely reduces scanning in practice — that gap, and the single-cohort base, make this Tier C. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a negative GFAP/UCH-L1 test identifies a group at very low risk of CT injury; a management trial proving safe CT reduction is still missing.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — GFAP/UCH-L1 testing showed sensitivity 0.976 and NPV 0.996 for CT-detected injury in ALERT-TBI, but no study has randomised its effect on actual CT use

title: Late parenteral nutrition in critically ill children (PEPaNIC): new infections 10.7% versus 18.5% and ICU stay 6.5 versus 9.2 days when parenteral nutrition was withheld for the first week — mortality similar
question: In critically ill children, does withholding parenteral nutrition for the first week in intensive care (late parenteral nutrition) improve recovery compared with starting it within 24 hours?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — withholding parenteral nutrition for the first week sped recovery in one large paediatric intensive care trial, without a mortality difference. In PEPaNIC (Fivez T et al., PMID: 26975590), 1,440 critically ill children were randomised to early parenteral nutrition, started within 24 hours of ICU admission (n=723), or late parenteral nutrition, not provided until the morning of the 8th day in the ICU (n=717); in both groups enteral nutrition was attempted early, intravenous micronutrients were provided, and fluid loading was similar. New infection acquired during the ICU stay — a primary endpoint — occurred in 10.7% of the late group versus 18.5% of the early group (adjusted odds ratio 0.48, 95% CI 0.35 to 0.66). The other primary endpoint, ICU dependency, also favoured late nutrition: mean ICU stay was 6.5±0.4 days versus 9.2±0.8 days, with a higher likelihood of earlier live discharge from the ICU at any time (adjusted hazard ratio 1.23, 95% CI 1.11 to 1.37). Late parenteral nutrition was also associated with a shorter duration of mechanical ventilatory support (P=0.001), a smaller proportion of patients receiving renal-replacement therapy (P=0.04), and a shorter hospital stay (P=0.001). Mortality was similar in the two groups — the record gives no mortality rates — so the benefit shown is faster recovery and fewer new infections, not survival. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): in critically ill children, withholding parenteral nutrition for the first week (late parenteral nutrition) reduced new infections and shortened ICU stay in one large multicentre randomised trial, with mortality similar between groups.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in one 1,440-child multicentre randomised trial, withholding parenteral nutrition for 1 week reduced new infections (10.7% versus 18.5%; adjusted odds ratio 0.48, 95% CI 0.35 to 0.66) and shortened ICU stay (6.5 versus 9.2 days), with mortality similar

title: MIS-C / PIMS-TS: methylprednisolone matched IVIG on hospital stay in both randomised trials (median 6.0 vs 6.0 days head-to-head; RECOVERY stay 6.9 days on steroid vs 7.6 on usual care, IVIG 7.4) — no winner, steroid far cheaper
question: In children with multisystem inflammatory syndrome (MIS-C / PIMS-TS), does methylprednisolone alone match intravenous immunoglobulin — alone or combined — for fever resolution and cardiac recovery?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — head-to-head, the steroid matched the immunoglobulin on the outcome both trials measured, hospital stay. In the Swissped randomised trial (Welzel T et al., PMID: 36746174), median stay was 6.0 days on methylprednisolone and 6.0 days on intravenous immunoglobulin (effect size −0.037 of log10-transformed stay, 95% CI −0.13 to 0.065; p=0.42), although fewer methylprednisolone patients needed respiratory support (27% versus 55%, p=0.025). In RECOVERY's first randomisation (RECOVERY Collaborative Group, PMID: 38272046), mean stay was 6.9 days with methylprednisolone (difference from usual care −0.7 days, 95% credible interval −1.9 to 0.6) and 7.4 days with IVIG (difference −0.1 days, 95% CrI −1.3 to 1.0) against 7.6 days on usual care. Neither trial randomised a combined IVIG-plus-steroid arm, and neither record reports the fever-resolution or cardiac-recovery endpoints in the question — stay is the measured proxy, and that gap is stated plainly. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): methylprednisolone alone performed indistinguishably from IVIG on hospital stay in two open-label randomised trials.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — methylprednisolone matched IVIG on length of hospital stay in the Swissped head-to-head trial and in RECOVERY; fever and cardiac endpoints were not reported

title: Prednisolone for children's Bell's palsy (BellPIC): complete recovery at 1 month was 49% on prednisolone versus 57% on placebo — an underpowered trial, and most children recover anyway (93–99% by 6 months)
question: In children with Bell's palsy, does early prednisolone improve complete facial recovery compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the one placebo-controlled trial in children found no benefit, and its point estimate at the primary timepoint favoured placebo. In BellPIC (Babl FE et al., PMID: 36008143), complete recovery at 1 month was 49% (43 of 87) on prednisolone versus 57% (50 of 87) on placebo (risk difference −8.1%, 95% CI −22.8 to 6.7; adjusted OR 0.7, 95% CI 0.4 to 1.3); by 3 months recovery was 90% versus 85% and by 6 months 99% versus 93%, neither significant. The 12-month follow-up of the same cohort (Babl FE et al., PMID: 38320457) found clinician-rated recovery in 96% versus 92% at 12 months (OR 3.12, 95% CI 0.61 to 15.98). The trial recruited 187 children against a target of 540, so it lacked the precision to exclude an important benefit or harm — a single underpowered trial, hence Tier C. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): early prednisolone has not been shown to improve complete recovery in children, most of whom recover without it.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — BellPIC found no significant recovery benefit from prednisolone in children (49% vs 57% complete recovery at 1 month), in a trial that reached only 187 of its 540 target

title: Amoxicillin for children's chest infections in primary care (ARTIC PC): moderately bad symptoms lasted a median 5 days on antibiotic versus 6 on placebo (HR 1.13, 0.90–1.42) — no benefit overall or in any prespecified subgroup
question: In children presenting in primary care with acute lower respiratory tract infection, does amoxicillin reduce symptom duration or severity compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the one large placebo-controlled trial found nothing worth prescribing for. In ARTIC PC (Little P et al., PMID: 34562391), 432 children aged 6 months to 12 years with uncomplicated, non-pneumonic lower respiratory tract infection in English primary care received amoxicillin 50 mg/kg per day or placebo for 7 days; the median duration of moderately bad or worse symptoms was 5 days (IQR 4 to 11) on amoxicillin versus 6 days (4 to 15) on placebo (hazard ratio 1.13, 95% CI 0.90 to 1.42). No difference appeared in any of the five prespecified subgroups in whom antibiotics are commonly prescribed — children with chest signs, fever, a physician rating of unwell, sputum or chest rattle, or shortness of breath — and complete-case and per-protocol analyses agreed with the primary analysis. A single trial, however large and well blinded, is Tier C. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): amoxicillin does not meaningfully shorten uncomplicated chest infections in children when pneumonia is not suspected.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — ARTIC PC found no reduction in symptom duration from amoxicillin for uncomplicated childhood LRTI (median 5 vs 6 days; HR 1.13, 95% CI 0.90 to 1.42), overall or in any subgroup

title: Nebulised epinephrine for croup: croup scores improve at 30 minutes (SMD −0.94) but the effect is gone by 2 hours — a bridge treatment, pooled from just 225 children
question: In children with moderate-to-severe croup, does nebulised epinephrine shorten symptoms and reduce intubation or return visits compared with placebo or supportive care?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a real, fast, and deliberately temporary effect. The Cochrane review (Bjornson C et al., PMID: 24114291) pooled 8 studies with 225 children, mostly under two years old with moderate-to-severe croup: nebulised epinephrine improved croup scores at 30 minutes (standardised mean difference −0.94, 95% CI −1.37 to −0.51, across 3 trials), but the effect was not significant at two or six hours, and one trial found a shorter hospital stay (mean difference −32.0 hours, 95% CI −59.1 to −4.9). No study in the review sought or reported data on adverse effects, and none reported the intubation or return-visit outcomes named in the question — those limbs are unanswered on this record, and the small total (225 children) is why the stamp is POSSIBLE, not LIKELY. Racemic and L-epinephrine did not differ at 30 minutes, and delivery by intermittent positive pressure breathing added nothing over simple nebulisation. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): nebulised epinephrine relieves croup symptoms within 30 minutes for a couple of hours; evidence that it prevents intubation or return visits is absent from the pooled record.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — nebulised epinephrine improves croup scores at 30 minutes (SMD −0.94) with no significant effect by 2 hours; intubation and return-visit outcomes were not reported in the pooled trials

title: Nebulised magnesium sulfate in children's acute severe asthma (MAGNETIC): severity score 4.72 versus 4.95 at 60 minutes — a statistically significant 0.25-point difference the trial itself judged not clinically significant, and no admission result in the record
question: In children with acute severe asthma, does nebulised magnesium sulfate added to standard bronchodilator therapy improve asthma severity and reduce hospital admission?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a real but small average effect on a severity score, below the difference the trial itself set as clinically significant, and with no admission result in the record. In MAGNETIC (Powell C et al., PMID: 24429155), 508 children aged 2–16 years with severe acute asthma who did not respond to standard inhaled treatment, enrolled at 30 hospitals in the UK, were randomly assigned to nebulised salbutamol and ipratropium bromide with either isotonic magnesium sulfate (2.5 mL, 250 mmol/L; 151 mg per dose; n=252) or isotonic saline placebo (n=256), on three occasions at 20-min intervals. The primary outcome, the mean Yung Asthma Severity Score (ASS) at 60 min post-randomisation, was 4.72 (SD 1.37) in the magnesium sulfate group versus 4.95 (SD 1.40) in the placebo group — an adjusted difference of −0.25 (95% CI −0.48 to −0.02; p=0.03). The trial had set a between-group ASS difference of 0.5 as the minimal clinically significant treatment effect, and the authors concluded that this difference was not clinically significant. The clinical effect was larger in children with more severe asthma exacerbation (p=0.03) and in those with symptoms present for less than 6 h (p=0.049), and no difference in the occurrence of adverse events was detected between groups. On the question's second half — hospital admission — the fetched record reports no admission outcome and no admission figures at all: every child was already recruited in hospital with a severe attack, so no admission benefit can be claimed from this trial. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): one large masked randomised trial found a statistically significant but clinically sub-threshold average improvement in asthma severity score at 60 minutes from adding nebulised magnesium sulfate to standard bronchodilators, with the largest response in the most severe, earliest-presenting attacks; no admission effect is reported in the record.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in one 508-child randomised placebo-controlled trial, adding nebulised magnesium sulfate to standard bronchodilators lowered the 60-minute asthma severity score by an adjusted 0.25 points (95% CI −0.48 to −0.02; p=0.03), below the 0.5-point difference the trial set as clinically significant, with no admission result reported in the record

title: Preemptive high-dose fluticasone at the first sniffle: rescue oral steroid courses fell from 18% to 8% of colds (OR 0.49) — at the cost of measurably less height and weight gain in one trial
question: In preschool children with virus-induced wheezing, does preemptive high-dose inhaled fluticasone at the first sign of an upper respiratory infection reduce rescue oral corticosteroid courses?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — with the growth price printed on the same line. In the one randomised trial (Ducharme FM et al., PMID: 19164187), 129 children aged 1 to 6 years with recurrent virus-induced wheezing took fluticasone propionate 750 µg twice daily or placebo from the onset of each upper respiratory infection, for up to 10 days, over 6 to 12 months: 8% of infections in the fluticasone group led to rescue systemic corticosteroids, versus 18% on placebo (odds ratio 0.49, 95% CI 0.30 to 0.83). Children on fluticasone gained less height (z-score difference from baseline to endpoint −0.24, 95% CI −0.40 to −0.08) and less weight (z-score difference −0.26, 95% CI −0.41 to −0.09), with no significant differences in basal cortisol, bone mineral density, or adverse events. The trial's own authors concluded the approach should not be adopted in practice until long-term adverse effects are clarified — a single-trial benefit with a measured harm, hence Tier C. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): preemptive high-dose fluticasone roughly halves rescue steroid courses per cold, and slows growth velocity while it is used.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — preemptive high-dose fluticasone cut rescue oral corticosteroid use to 8% vs 18% of infections (OR 0.49) in one trial, with significantly smaller height and weight gains

title: Azithromycin for asthma-like episodes in 1–3-year-olds (COPSAC): episodes lasted 3.4 days on azithromycin versus 7.7 on placebo — a 63% shortening in one single-centre trial, with resistance never measured
question: In young children aged 1–3 years with episodes of asthma-like symptoms, does a short course of azithromycin shorten the episode and reduce treatment escalation?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a large effect on episode duration from a single, small, single-centre trial. In COPSAC (Stokholm J et al., PMID: 26704020), 158 episodes of asthma-like symptoms in 72 children aged 1 to 3 years were randomised to a 3-day course of azithromycin 10 mg/kg per day or placebo: mean episode duration after treatment was 3.4 days on azithromycin versus 7.7 days on placebo, a shortening of 63.3% (95% CI 56.0 to 69.3; p<0.0001), larger when treatment began before day 6 of the episode (83% reduction) than on or after day 6 (36%). Clinical adverse events did not differ (23% of azithromycin episodes versus 30% of placebo episodes, p=0.30), but bacterial resistance after treatment was not investigated. The record does not report the treatment-escalation outcomes named in the question, and episodes rather than children were the unit of randomisation — Tier C. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): azithromycin substantially shortened asthma-like episodes in toddlers in one trial; whether it reduces escalation, and what it costs in resistance, is unmeasured.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — azithromycin shortened asthma-like episodes in 1–3-year-olds from 7.7 to 3.4 days (63.3% reduction) in the single COPSAC trial; escalation and resistance outcomes unreported

title: Antibiotics for sore throat: sore throat at day 3 falls (RR 0.70) and rheumatic fever was cut in the old trials (OR 0.36) — but 82% are better by a week anyway, and the complication data come from the 1950s
question: In children and adults with sore throat, do antibiotics shorten illness and prevent suppurative complications and acute rheumatic fever compared with placebo?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — a small, real symptom benefit and a real complication benefit, both resting largely on trials from an era when complications were common. The Cochrane review (Spinks A et al., PMID: 34881426) pooled 29 trials with 15,337 cases of sore throat: antibiotics reduced sore throat at day three (risk ratio 0.70, 95% CI 0.60 to 0.80; 16 studies, 3,730 participants; number needed to treat for one fewer sore throat under six) and at one week (RR 0.50, 95% CI 0.34 to 0.75; NNTB 18), although 82% of the placebo group were symptom-free by one week. Headache at day three fell (RR 0.49, 95% CI 0.34 to 0.70); fever at day three did not significantly (RR 0.75, 95% CI 0.53 to 1.07). Antibiotics reduced acute otitis media within 14 days (Peto OR 0.21, 95% CI 0.11 to 0.40), quinsy within two months (Peto OR 0.16, 95% CI 0.07 to 0.35), and acute rheumatic fever within two months (Peto OR 0.36, 95% CI 0.26 to 0.50; 18 studies, 12,249 participants) — but the majority of included studies were conducted in the 1950s, when rheumatic fever rates were far higher than today, and harms were too poorly reported to quantify. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): antibiotics modestly shorten sore throat and prevent suppurative complications; the rheumatic-fever protection is proven in high-incidence settings and unquantifiable where the disease is now rare.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — antibiotics reduce sore throat at day 3 (RR 0.70) and at 1 week (RR 0.50), otitis media (OR 0.21), quinsy (OR 0.16) and rheumatic fever (OR 0.36) in a 29-trial Cochrane review, with absolute gains small where complications are now rare

title: Antibiotics for children's acute sinusitis: cure 50% versus 14% in the strict 2009 trial, but only a small average symptom gain in 2023 — and almost none in children without bacterial pathogens in the nose
question: In children with acute sinusitis, do antibiotics improve clinical cure compared with placebo — and which presenting features identify the children who benefit?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the benefit is real but concentrated, and the two trials show its two faces. In the strictly diagnosed 2009 trial (Wald ER et al., PMID: 19564277), high-dose amoxicillin-clavulanate cured 50% of children versus 14% on placebo, with treatment failure in 14% versus 68%. In the larger 2023 trial (Shaikh N et al., PMID: 37490085), mean symptom scores were modestly lower on amoxicillin-clavulanate (9.04 versus 10.60 on a 0–40 scale; between-group difference −1.69, 95% CI −2.07 to −1.31) and symptoms resolved at 7.0 versus 9.0 days — but children without nasopharyngeal bacterial pathogens benefited much less (difference −0.88, 95% CI −1.63 to −0.12) than those with pathogens detected (−1.95, 95% CI −2.40 to −1.51), and the colour of nasal discharge made no difference to efficacy (interaction P=.52). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): antibiotics help children with acute sinusitis, most clearly when bacterial pathogens are present; coloured discharge does not identify the beneficiaries.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — antibiotics improved cure in two randomised trials of childhood acute sinusitis, with the 2023 trial showing minimal benefit in children without nasopharyngeal pathogens and no effect modification by discharge colour

title: Adjuvant adenoidectomy for persistent glue ear (TARGET): no extra hearing gain over grommets in the first 6 months, but +4.2 dB through the second year and repeat-surgery eligibility halved (31% to 14%)
question: In children with persistent bilateral otitis media with effusion, does adjuvant adenoidectomy improve hearing and reduce later surgery compared with watchful waiting or grommets alone?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the adenoidectomy dividend arrives late, after the grommets have stopped working. In the TARGET trial (MRC Multicentre Otitis Media Study Group, PMID: 22443163), 376 children with persistent bilateral effusion and hearing level at least 20 dB were randomised to observation, ventilation tubes alone, or tubes plus adenoidectomy: adenoidectomy added nothing to the tubes' hearing benefit of 8.8 dB (95% CI 7.1 to 10.5) averaged over 3–6 months, but averaged over 12, 18 and 24 months adenoidectomy provided 4.2 dB of benefit (95% CI 2.6 to 5.7) while tubes alone gave none, and it halved the proportion meeting the 25 dB cut-off for repeat tube surgery — 31% to 14% at 12 months and 33% to 15% at 18 months — with an absolute reduction in actual re-insertion surgery of 21%. One of 165 children having adenoidectomy (0.6%) had haemorrhage requiring return to theatre. The earlier randomised trial (Maw R et al., PMID: 8490338) agrees on durability: a single grommet resolved effusion for a mean of 9.5 months, while the effect of adenoidectomy was sustained throughout follow-up, and combined treatment resolved fluid fastest. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): adding adenoidectomy to grommets extends better hearing into the second year and roughly halves later repeat surgery, at a small operative risk.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — adjuvant adenoidectomy added 4.2 dB of hearing benefit in year 2 and halved repeat-surgery eligibility in TARGET, concordant with the earlier Maw randomised trial

title: Oral antibiotics first for febrile infant UTI (Hoberman 1999): urine sterile within 24 hours in every child either way, fever gone in 25 vs 24 hours, kidney scarring at 6 months 9.8% oral versus 7.2% IV — at half the cost
question: In young febrile children with urinary tract infection, is initial oral antibiotic therapy as effective as initial intravenous therapy for cure and kidney scarring?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — route did not matter; the drug did the work in both arms. In the multicentre randomised trial (Hoberman A et al., PMID: 10390264), 306 children aged 1 to 24 months with fever and urinary tract infection received either oral cefixime for 14 days or intravenous cefotaxime for 3 days followed by oral cefixime: repeat urine cultures were sterile within 24 hours in all children, mean time to defervescence was 25 hours oral versus 24 hours intravenous, symptomatic reinfections occurred in 4.6% versus 7.2%, and renal scarring at 6 months was 9.8% oral versus 7.2% intravenous, with mean extent of scarring approximately 8% in both groups. Mean costs were at least twofold higher for initial intravenous therapy ($3,577 versus $1,473). One trial from 1999, with scarring confidence limits the abstract does not print — Tier C. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): initial oral therapy matched initial intravenous therapy on sterilisation, fever, reinfection and scarring in febrile infants with UTI.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — oral cefixime matched initial IV cefotaxime on urine sterilisation, defervescence, reinfection and 6-month renal scarring in one randomised trial of 306 febrile infants

title: Circumcision to prevent urinary infections in boys: febrile UTI risk 3% with circumcision plus prophylaxis versus 20% on prophylaxis alone in the CIRCUP randomised trial — in posterior urethral valves, with observational data (OR 0.23) for reflux
question: In boys with vesicoureteral reflux or recurrent urinary tract infection, does circumcision reduce further urinary tract infections compared with no circumcision?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the one randomised trial is dramatic and narrow in equal measure. In CIRCUP (Harper L et al., PMID: 34563412), 91 newborn boys with posterior urethral valves were randomised to neonatal circumcision plus antibiotic prophylaxis or prophylaxis alone: the probability of a febrile urinary tract infection over 2 years was 3% with circumcision versus 20% without (hazard ratio for the uncircumcised group 10.3, 95% CI 1.3 to 82.5). No randomised trial in boys with vesicoureteral reflux — the population named in the question — was found on the record; for reflux the evidence is observational, pooled in a meta-analysis of boys with antenatal hydronephrosis (Chan JY et al., PMID: 37563014): circumcision was associated with reduced odds of UTI overall (OR 0.26, 95% CI 0.21 to 0.32) and in the vesicoureteral reflux subgroup specifically (OR 0.23, 95% CI 0.13 to 0.42), across 23 studies and 9,093 boys. The candidate anchor for this shelf, a Pennesi randomised trial of circumcision in reflux, could not be verified on PubMed — no such record exists — so the shelf is built on CIRCUP plus the meta-analysis and is Tier C. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): circumcision substantially reduces febrile UTI in high-risk boys, randomised in posterior urethral valves and observational in reflux.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — circumcision cut febrile UTI risk (3% vs 20% over 2 years) in the CIRCUP randomised trial in posterior urethral valves, with concordant observational evidence in vesicoureteral reflux (OR 0.23)

title: Phentermine/topiramate in adolescents with obesity: BMI fell 10.4 percentage points more than placebo at the top dose and 8.1 points at the mid dose over 56 weeks — one trial, with two serious adverse events at the top dose
question: In adolescents with obesity, does once-daily phentermine/topiramate reduce BMI compared with placebo on top of lifestyle therapy?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a large weight effect in a single trial. In the 56-week randomised double-blind trial (Kelly AS et al., PMID: 36968652), 223 adolescents aged 12 to under 17 years with obesity received lifestyle therapy plus placebo (n=56), mid-dose phentermine/topiramate 7.5 mg/46 mg (n=54), or top-dose 15 mg/92 mg (n=113): the difference from placebo in mean percent change in BMI at week 56 was −10.44 percentage points (95% CI −13.89 to −6.99; P<0.001) at the top dose and −8.11 percentage points (95% CI −11.92 to −4.31; P<0.001) at the mid dose. Triglyceride and HDL-cholesterol changes nominally favoured the drug at both doses. At least one adverse event was reported by 51.8% on placebo, 37.0% on mid dose and 52.2% on top dose, and serious adverse events were reported for two participants in the top-dose group. One trial only — Tier C — and the record carries no MeSH terms. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): phentermine/topiramate produces substantial BMI reduction in adolescents over a year, on single-trial evidence.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — phentermine/topiramate reduced BMI by 10.44 and 8.11 percentage points more than placebo (top and mid doses) at 56 weeks in one adolescent trial
