title: Orlistat in adolescents with obesity: BMI fell 0.55 while placebo gained 0.31 over a year — 26.5% versus 15.7% lost at least 5% of BMI, paid for in gastrointestinal adverse events in 9–50%
question: In adolescents with obesity, does orlistat reduce weight and BMI compared with placebo, and at what gastrointestinal cost?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a statistically solid, clinically modest effect, with the cost itemised. In the multicentre randomised trial (Chanoine JP et al., PMID: 15956632), 539 adolescents aged 12 to 16 years took orlistat 120 mg three times daily or placebo for a year, all with a mildly hypocaloric diet, exercise and behavioural therapy: BMI changed by −0.55 on orlistat versus +0.31 on placebo (P=.001), weight by +0.53 kg versus +3.14 kg (P<.001), and 26.5% on orlistat versus 15.7% on placebo achieved at least a 5% BMI decrease (P=.005), with at least a 10% decrease in 13.3% versus 4.5% (P=.002). Waist circumference fell 1.33 cm on orlistat and rose 0.12 cm on placebo (P<.05), and dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry attributed the weight difference to fat mass. Generally mild-to-moderate gastrointestinal adverse events occurred in 9% to 50% of the orlistat group versus 1% to 13% on placebo. One trial — Tier C. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): orlistat adds a small BMI advantage over lifestyle therapy alone in adolescents, and most users will feel why it works.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — orlistat improved BMI change by about 0.9 units versus placebo over 1 year in one adolescent trial (26.5% vs 15.7% achieving ≥5% BMI loss), with gastrointestinal adverse events in 9–50%

title: Metformin for childhood obesity: pooled BMI fell by about 1.07 kg/m² across 38 trials — but the best-stratified trial found the BMI z-score benefit only before puberty
question: In children and adolescents with obesity, does metformin reduce BMI and insulin resistance compared with placebo or lifestyle alone?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a consistent small pooled effect that dissolves by pubertal stage when one trial looks carefully. The meta-analysis (Sadeghi A et al., PMID: 32068434) pooled 38 trials with 2,199 children and adolescents: metformin reduced BMI by a weighted mean difference of −1.07 kg/m² (95% CI −1.43 to −0.72), body weight by −2.51 kg (95% CI −3.14 to −1.89) and waist circumference by −1.93 cm (95% CI −2.69 to −1.16). The stratified randomised trial (Pastor-Villaescusa B et al., PMID: 28759403) gave metformin 1 g daily or placebo for 6 months to 160 prepubertal and pubertal children: BMI z score fell more on metformin only in the prepubertal group (−0.8 versus −0.6; difference 0.2; P=.04), alongside better insulin-sensitivity and adiponectin-leptin measures in that group, while no differential effect between prepubertal and pubertal children was formally demonstrated and the authors caution that dose per kilogram may explain the pattern. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): metformin produces a small average BMI reduction in children with obesity, clearest before puberty; an insulin-resistance benefit is shown only in subgroup measures, not as a pooled clinical endpoint.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — metformin reduced BMI (weighted mean difference −1.07 kg/m²) across 38 paediatric trials, with the clearest randomised benefit in prepubertal children

title: Family-based behavioural treatment in primary care: children's percentage above median BMI changed 0.00% on treatment versus +6.48% on usual care over 24 months — and untreated siblings improved too
question: In children with obesity treated in primary care, does family-based behavioural treatment reduce BMI compared with usual care?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the treated children held their trajectory while usual-care children gained, in one large pragmatic trial. In the primary-care trial (Epstein LH et al., PMID: 37314275), 452 children aged 6 to 12 years with overweight or obesity, their parents and 106 siblings were randomised to family-based behavioural treatment (a goal of 26 coached sessions over 24 months) or usual care: at 24 months the difference in change in percentage above median BMI favoured treatment by −6.21 percentage points (95% CI −10.14 to −2.29), with 0-to-24-month changes of 0.00% on treatment versus +6.48% on usual care in children, −1.05% versus +2.92% in parents, and 0.03% versus +5.35% in siblings who were not directly treated. Benefits were evident by 6 months and maintained through 24 months. A single trial, however pragmatic — Tier C. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): family-based treatment delivered in paediatric primary care prevents the BMI rise seen under usual care, with spillover to parents and siblings.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — family-based behavioural treatment in primary care improved 24-month weight trajectories versus usual care (difference −6.21 percentage points of percentage above median BMI) in one randomised trial

title: Clonidine extended-release for ADHD: symptoms improved significantly more than placebo both alone (8-week fixed-dose trial) and added to a stimulant (week-5 difference CI −7.83 to −1.13) — somnolence the commonest cost
question: In children and adolescents with ADHD, does clonidine extended-release — alone or added to a stimulant — reduce ADHD symptoms compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two placebo-controlled trials, one for each way the drug is used, both positive. As monotherapy (Jain R et al., PMID: 21241954), clonidine extended-release 0.2 mg/day and 0.4 mg/day each improved ADHD Rating Scale-IV total scores significantly more than placebo at week 5 in 236 children and adolescents, with significant gains on both inattention and hyperactivity/impulsivity subscales and on global-impression measures; the most common treatment-emergent adverse event was mild-to-moderate somnolence, and electrocardiogram changes were minor. Added to a stimulant in children with an inadequate stimulant response (Kollins SH et al., PMID: 21555501), clonidine extended-release improved the ADHD Rating Scale-IV total score more than placebo at week 5 (95% CI for the difference −7.83 to −1.13; P=.009), with concordant parent-rating and global-impression results and generally mild adverse events. Neither abstract prints the point estimate of symptom change — magnitudes rest on the add-on trial's confidence interval — a declared gap that, with symptom scores rather than functional outcomes, keeps the stamp at POSSIBLE. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): clonidine extended-release reduces ADHD symptom scores versus placebo, alone and as stimulant add-on, with somnolence the principal cost.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — clonidine extended-release beat placebo on ADHD symptom scores in two phase 3 trials, as monotherapy and as stimulant add-on; abstracts report significance and one confidence interval rather than point estimates

title: AKL-T01 digital therapeutic for ADHD (STARS-ADHD): objective attention index improved by a median 0.88 versus 0.03 mean change on control (p=0.006) — a computerised attention gain, with symptom change not the primary outcome
question: In children with ADHD, does the prescription digital therapeutic AKL-T01 improve objective attention compared with a control digital activity?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for the attention test it was built to move, in the one trial that exists. In STARS-ADHD (Kollins SH et al., PMID: 33334505), 348 children aged 8 to 12 years with confirmed ADHD and impaired Test of Variables of Attention (TOVA) Attention Performance Index scores (−1.8 or below), taking no ADHD medication, played AKL-T01 or a control digital activity for 25 minutes a day, 5 days a week, for 4 weeks: the median change in TOVA Attention Performance Index was 0.88 (95% CI 0.24 to 1.49; p=0.0060) on AKL-T01, with mean change 0.93 (SD 3.15) versus 0.03 (SD 3.16) on control. There were no serious adverse events or discontinuations; treatment-related adverse events were mild — frustration in 5 of 180 children (3%) and headache in 3 (2%) — and children completed a mean of 83 of 100 expected sessions. The primary outcome is a computerised attention measure, not ADHD symptoms or school function, and the trial was sponsored by the product's maker, Akili Interactive Labs — a named programme/product tested as specified, single-trial, hence Tier C. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): AKL-T01 improves objectively measured attention over 4 weeks versus a control game, with minimal adverse events; whether that becomes symptom or classroom benefit is not shown here.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — AKL-T01 improved the TOVA Attention Performance Index versus a control digital activity (median change 0.88; p=0.006) in one 4-week trial in unmedicated children with ADHD

title: Aripiprazole cuts irritability scores in autistic disorder in two 8-week trials — with weight gain of 1.3–2.0 kg and sedation the price
question: In children and adolescents with autism, does aripiprazole reduce irritability and aggression compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two concordant 8-week placebo-controlled trials. In Owen et al. (PMID: 19948625), flexibly dosed aripiprazole beat placebo on the Aberrant Behavior Checklist irritability subscale from week 1 through week 8, with mean weight gain 2.0 kg versus 0.8 kg on placebo and extrapyramidal symptom-related events in 14.9% versus 8.0%. In Marcus et al. (PMID: 19797985), all three fixed doses improved irritability scores more than placebo at week 8 (-12.4, -13.2 and -14.4 points for 5, 10 and 15 mg/day versus -8.4 on placebo; all p<.05), with mean weight change +1.3 to +1.5 kg versus +0.3 kg on placebo. The benefit is real but short-term and symptom-scored, and clinically significant residual symptoms may persist. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): aripiprazole reduces irritability in autistic disorder over 8 weeks, at the cost of weight gain and sedation.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two randomised placebo-controlled trials show greater irritability reduction than placebo over 8 weeks, with weight gain and sedation as the main costs

title: Lubiprostone did not beat placebo for childhood functional constipation: response 18.5% versus 14.4% (p=.2245) in the one large trial
question: In children and adolescents with functional constipation, does lubiprostone increase spontaneous bowel movements compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the one large randomised trial missed its primary endpoint. In Benninga et al. (PMID: 33838349), overall spontaneous bowel movement response was 18.5% on lubiprostone versus 14.4% on placebo (P=.2245) in 606 children aged 6–17 years. The 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis of pharmacological therapies for functional constipation in children (PMID: 41101321), covering 59 randomised trials and 7,045 participants, found polyethylene glycol probably more effective than placebo (RR 1.74, 95% CI 1.25–2.41, moderate certainty) — a contrast that underlines lubiprostone's null rather than rescuing it. Tolerability was acceptable in both records. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): lubiprostone has not been shown to increase spontaneous bowel movements over placebo in children.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the single large placebo-controlled trial found response 18.5% versus 14.4% (p=.2245), and the 2025 meta-analysis gives lubiprostone no winning result

title: Tricyclics dry the bed while the child takes them — 78% versus 95% fail to reach 14 dry nights on imipramine versus placebo — then 96% are wet again after stopping, and alarms beat them
question: In children with nocturnal enuresis that alarms and desmopressin have not settled, do tricyclic drugs such as imipramine produce dryness — and does it last after stopping?
balance: SPLIT — tricyclics work during treatment and stop working when treatment stops. The Cochrane review (Caldwell et al., PMID: 26789925; 64 trials, 4,071 children) found imipramine gave one fewer wet night per week than placebo (mean difference -0.95, 95% CI -1.40 to -0.50; 4 trials, 347 children), with 78% failing to achieve 14 consecutive dry nights versus 95% on placebo (RR 0.74, 95% CI 0.61 to 0.90; 12 trials, 831 children). After treatment ceased, 96% on imipramine were wetting again versus 97% on placebo. Alarms beat imipramine head-to-head: 67% failed to achieve 14 consecutive dry nights on imipramine versus 17% on alarms (RR 4.00, 95% CI 1.06 to 15.08; 1 trial, 24 children), with a more sustained alarm effect after stopping (100% versus 58% wetting at follow-up). Minor adverse effects were common across 30 reporting trials. PROPOSED SPLIT: a real on-treatment effect, no cure, and a better non-drug alternative.
stamp: SPLIT — tricyclics reduce wet nights while taken (imipramine: one fewer wet night/week; 78% vs 95% failing to reach 14 dry nights) but relapse is near-universal after stopping (96% vs 97%), and alarms outperform them

title: Succimer lowered blood lead by 4.5 µg/dL but bought no cognition: IQ 1 point lower (not significant) at 36 months, and still no benefit at age 7
question: In toddlers with raised blood lead levels, does chelation with succimer improve neuropsychological development compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — one large, well-run trial programme, reported twice, with the same answer. In the Treatment of Lead-exposed Children trial (Rogan et al., PMID: 11346806), succimer lowered mean blood lead by 4.5 µg/dL (95% CI 3.7 to 5.3) over the first six months, yet at 36 months the succimer group's mean IQ was 1 point lower than placebo and parent-rated behaviour slightly worse, with slightly better scores on one neuropsychological battery — all differences small and none statistically significant. The age-7 follow-up of the same cohort (Dietrich et al., PMID: 15231903; 647 children remaining) again found no benefit in cognitive, behavioural or neuromotor endpoints. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): chelation cleans the blood test, not the brain outcome, at blood lead levels of 20–44 µg/dL.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — succimer lowered blood lead by 4.5 µg/dL but produced no significant cognitive, behavioural or neuropsychological benefit at 36 months or at age 7 in the TLC trial

title: Iron-fortified formula in infancy tracked with lower scores a decade later: every 10-year outcome lower, and 16-year-olds scored lower on visual memory, arithmetic and reading
question: In infancy, does iron-fortified formula, compared with low-iron formula, change cognitive and developmental outcomes into adolescence in non-anaemic infants?
balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — a single randomised cohort followed twice, pointing the same way. At 10 years (Lozoff et al., PMID: 22064877), children randomised as infants to iron-fortified formula (12.7 mg/L) scored lower than the low-iron group (2.3 mg/L) on every outcome measured — 1.4–4.6 points lower, significantly so for spatial memory and visual-motor integration — with the deficit concentrated in infants whose 6-month haemoglobin was high (>12.8 g/dL: 10.7–19.3 points lower), while infants with low haemoglobin (<10.5 g/dL) scored better on iron-fortified formula. At 16 years (Gahagan et al., PMID: 31253407), the iron-fortified group again scored lower on visual memory, arithmetic achievement and reading comprehension. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm): in iron-replete infants, the higher-iron formula was followed by poorer long-term cognitive scores; infants who were iron-deficient may still need the iron.
stamp: POSSIBLE (harm) — one randomised cohort followed to age 10 and 16 scored lower on cognitive outcomes after iron-fortified versus low-iron formula, with harm concentrated in infants with high baseline haemoglobin

title: Daily penicillin in toddlers with sickle cell anaemia cut pneumococcal septicaemia by 84% — 2 infections versus 13, and 0 deaths versus 3, in a trial stopped early
question: In infants and young children with sickle cell anaemia, does daily penicillin prophylaxis prevent pneumococcal septicaemia and death?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — an early-stopped trial with a very large effect, backed by a Cochrane synthesis. In the PROPS trial (Gaston et al., PMID: 3086721), pneumococcal septicaemia occurred in 2 of 105 children on penicillin versus 13 of 110 on placebo — an 84% relative reduction (P=0.0025) — with no deaths from pneumococcal septicaemia on penicillin versus three deaths on placebo; the trial was terminated 8 months early. The Cochrane review of prophylactic antibiotics in sickle cell disease (Rankine-Mullings & Owusu-Ofori, PMID: 33724440) found an odds ratio of 0.37 (95% CI 0.16 to 0.86; 2 trials, 457 children) for pneumococcal infection when starting penicillin, graded low-certainty evidence. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): prophylactic penicillin prevents pneumococcal septicaemia in young children with sickle cell anaemia. Tier C is set because the shelf carries a mortality claim resting substantially on one trial.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — penicillin prophylaxis cut pneumococcal septicaemia by 84% relative (2/105 vs 13/110) with 0 versus 3 deaths in PROPS, concordant with the Cochrane odds ratio of 0.37

title: Early azithromycin did not prevent chronic lung disease of prematurity: survival without moderate or severe disease 42% versus 45% (adjusted OR 0.84, p=0.43) in 796 preterm infants
question: In preterm infants, does early azithromycin prevent chronic lung disease of prematurity (bronchopulmonary dysplasia) compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — one large, adequately powered trial settles what smaller conflicting reviews could not. In AZTEC (Lowe et al., PMID: 38679042), survival without moderate or severe chronic lung disease at 36 weeks' postmenstrual age occurred in 166 of 394 infants (42%) on azithromycin versus 179 of 402 (45%) on placebo (adjusted OR 0.84, 95% CI 0.55–1.29, p=0.43), and pulmonary Ureaplasma colonisation did not influence the treatment effect. Serious adverse events were reported in seven infants in the azithromycin group and six in the placebo group. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): prophylactic azithromycin cannot be recommended to prevent chronic lung disease of prematurity.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — survival without moderate or severe chronic lung disease was 42% on azithromycin versus 45% on placebo (adjusted OR 0.84, 95% CI 0.55–1.29) in the 796-infant AZTEC trial

title: Inhaled nitric oxide does not save preterm babies or prevent lung disease: death or bronchopulmonary dysplasia risk ratio 0.94 in every timing group in the Cochrane review
question: In preterm infants with respiratory failure, does inhaled nitric oxide reduce death or bronchopulmonary dysplasia compared with placebo or usual care?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — 17 trials grouped three ways, all null on the outcome that matters. The Cochrane review (Barrington et al., PMID: 28045472) found no significant effect of inhaled nitric oxide on death or bronchopulmonary dysplasia in any group: early rescue treatment (typical RR 0.94, 95% CI 0.87–1.01; 958 infants), routine use with respiratory support (RR 0.94, 95% CI 0.87–1.02; 1,924 infants), or later treatment for bronchopulmonary dysplasia risk (RR 0.92, 95% CI 0.85–1.01; 1,075 infants), and no effect on neurodevelopmental impairment. The largest single trial (Kinsella et al., PMID: 16870914; 793 infants) likewise found death or bronchopulmonary dysplasia in 71.6% on nitric oxide versus 75.3% on placebo (P=0.24). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): inhaled nitric oxide is not an effective rescue or preventive therapy in preterm respiratory failure.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — across 17 trials, death or bronchopulmonary dysplasia risk ratios were 0.92–0.94 with confidence intervals crossing 1 in every timing group

title: Cooling started 6–24 hours after birth for hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy: death or disability 24.4% versus 27.9% — a 76% Bayesian probability of benefit, not proof
question: In newborns with hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy who present late, does therapeutic hypothermia started between 6 and 24 hours of age reduce death or disability compared with normothermia?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — one trial, analysed Bayesianly precisely because it could not settle the question. In Laptook et al. (PMID: 29067428), death or moderate/severe disability at 18–22 months occurred in 19 of 78 cooled infants (24.4%) versus 22 of 79 noncooled infants (27.9%) — an absolute difference of 3.5% (95% CI -1% to 17%). Bayesian analysis with a neutral prior gave a 76% posterior probability of reduced death or disability with hypothermia (adjusted posterior risk ratio 0.86, 95% credible interval 0.58–1.29), and a 64% probability of at least a 2% absolute reduction. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): late cooling may help, with genuine uncertainty — the trial's own conclusion.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — a single Bayesian trial found death or disability 24.4% versus 27.9% with a 76% posterior probability of benefit and a credible interval (0.58–1.29) that includes harm

title: Procalcitonin guidance cut neonatal antibiotic courses by about 10 hours (55.1 versus 65.0 hours) — but non-inferiority for reinfection or death could not be shown
question: In neonates with suspected early-onset sepsis, does procalcitonin-guided decision-making safely shorten antibiotic therapy compared with standard care?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for antibiotic exposure; the safety half of the question stays open. In the NeoPInS trial (Stocker et al., PMID: 28711318), procalcitonin-guided decision-making shortened antibiotic therapy versus standard care (intention-to-treat 55.1 versus 65.0 hours, p<0.0001; per protocol 51.8 versus 64.0 hours, p<0.0001) in 1,710 neonates. But reinfection or death was so rare — 5 of 866 (0.6%) versus 4 of 844 (0.5%), risk difference 0.1% (95% CI -4.6 to 4.8) against a 2.0% non-inferiority margin, with no sepsis-related deaths and 9 possible reinfections overall — that non-inferiority could not be shown. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): procalcitonin guidance safely-appearing but unproven-safe shortening of neonatal antibiotic courses, Tier C as a single trial.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one large trial shortened antibiotics by about 10 hours (55.1 vs 65.0 h, p<0.0001), but reinfection was too rare (0.6% vs 0.5%) for non-inferiority to be shown

title: Preschool vision screening finds amblyopia risk accurately — but no trial has ever compared screening with no screening, so better later vision is inferred, not shown
question: In preschool children, does vision screening detect amblyopia and improve later visual outcomes compared with no screening or later detection?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — detection is proven; the outcome chain is indirect. The US Preventive Services Task Force evidence report (Jonas et al., PMID: 28873167; 40 studies, 34,709 children) found no randomised trial comparing screening with no screening and no studies of school performance, function or quality of life, while test accuracy was genuinely good: positive likelihood ratios of 5–10 for amblyopia risk factors in most studies and above 10 for combinations of clinical tests. Treatment links the chain only part-way: patching improved the amblyopic eye by less than 1 line after 5–12 weeks in pretreated children, and 45% versus 21% achieved at least a 2-line improvement with patching versus no patching (P=.003; 1 trial, 180 participants). The Vision in Preschoolers studies (Kulp et al., PMID: 35044337) confirm which tests perform best and that children unable to perform the tests (<2%) are more likely to have vision disorders and should be referred. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): screening detects the right children; that population screening improves later vision has never been randomised.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — screening tests detect amblyopia risk with positive likelihood ratios of 5–10 or more, but no trial compares screening with no screening and the outcome evidence is indirect

title: Babies whose hearing loss was confirmed by 9 months had language 0.70–0.82 standard deviations higher at age 8 — the case for universal newborn hearing screening rests on this cohort
question: Does universal newborn hearing screening improve language development in children with permanent hearing loss compared with later, distraction-test detection?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — consistent observational evidence from one large birth cohort, never randomised. In Kennedy et al. (PMID: 16707750), among 120 children with bilateral permanent hearing impairment assessed at a mean age of 7.9 years, confirmation of hearing impairment by 9 months of age was associated with higher adjusted language scores relative to nonverbal ability (receptive language adjusted mean difference 0.82, 95% CI 0.31 to 1.33; expressive language 0.70, 95% CI 0.13 to 1.26), and birth during periods with universal newborn screening was associated with higher receptive language scores (adjusted mean difference 0.60, 95% CI 0.07 to 1.13), though not significantly higher expressive language; speech scores did not differ significantly. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): earlier detection through universal screening is associated with better language — but not better speech — in mid-childhood. Tier C: observational evidence throughout.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in the Wessex cohort, confirmation of hearing impairment by 9 months was associated with receptive and expressive language 0.82 and 0.70 SD higher at about age 8, with no significant speech difference

title: Early prednisolone does not prevent kidney involvement in IgA vasculitis: proteinuria at 12 months in 15% on prednisolone versus 10% on placebo (OR 1.46, not significant)
question: In children with IgA vasculitis (Henoch–Schönlein purpura), does early prednisolone prevent kidney involvement compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the largest trial of the question found nothing, with the point estimate leaning the wrong way. In Dudley et al. (PMID: 23845696), proteinuria at 12 months was present in 18 of 123 children (15%) on prednisolone versus 13 of 124 (10%) on placebo (OR 1.46, 95% CI 0.68 to 3.14; adjusted OR 1.29, 95% CI 0.58 to 2.82), and there was no significant difference in time to needing additional renal treatment (HR 0.53, 95% CI 0.18 to 1.59). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): a 14-day course of prednisolone at presentation does not prevent nephropathy in IgA vasculitis.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — in the largest trial (352 children), proteinuria at 12 months was 15% on prednisolone versus 10% on placebo (OR 1.46, 95% CI 0.68–3.14)

title: Intranasal fentanyl matched intravenous morphine for children's fracture pain: pain scores indistinguishable at every time point, with a 10-minute difference of -5 mm (95% CI -16 to 7)
question: In children with acute limb-fracture pain, is intranasal fentanyl as effective as intravenous morphine for pain relief?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one small double-blind equivalence trial, with a concordant systematic review behind it. In Borland et al. (PMID: 17067720), 67 children aged 7–15 years with deformed closed long-bone fractures received intranasal fentanyl (mean total dose 1.7 µg/kg) or intravenous morphine (mean total dose 0.11 mg/kg) under double-dummy blinding; visual analogue pain scores did not differ significantly before analgesia or at 5, 10, 20 or 30 minutes (P=.333), the 10-minute between-group difference was -5 mm (95% CI -16 to 7 mm), and there were no serious adverse events. The systematic review of intranasal fentanyl in children (Mudd, PMID: 21867860) found all reviewed studies showed similar or improved pain scores compared with other opioids and routes, with no severe adverse outcomes reported. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): intranasal fentanyl relieves fracture pain as effectively as intravenous morphine, without needing a cannula first. Tier C: the head-to-head trial is single and small.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — intranasal fentanyl gave pain relief indistinguishable from intravenous morphine in the one double-blind fracture trial (10-minute difference -5 mm, 95% CI -16 to 7), with concordant systematic-review evidence

title: Rituximab did not reduce proteinuria in resistant childhood nephrotic syndrome: -12% at 3 months (95% CI -73% to 110%, P=0.77) in the one randomised trial
question: In children with steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome, does rituximab induce remission compared with standard therapy?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the one randomised trial was frankly null, and the 2025 Cochrane review rates the rituximab evidence as very low certainty. In Magnasco et al. (PMID: 22581994), adding two doses of rituximab to prednisone plus calcineurin inhibitors in 31 children with resistant idiopathic nephrotic syndrome changed proteinuria by -12% at 3 months (95% CI -73% to 110%; P=0.77). The Cochrane review of interventions for idiopathic steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome in children (Liu et al., PMID: 40337980; 29 studies, 1,248 children) concludes it is uncertain whether rituximab combined with cyclosporin and prednisolone increases remission compared with cyclosporin and prednisolone, because the certainty of the evidence is very low. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): rituximab has no demonstrated remission benefit in steroid-resistant disease — a different picture from steroid-dependent disease.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the single randomised trial found a -12% proteinuria change (95% CI -73% to 110%, P=0.77), and the Cochrane review calls the rituximab remission evidence very low certainty and uncertain

title: Amitriptyline did not beat placebo for children's functional abdominal pain: 63% versus 57.5% felt better (P=.63), and the Cochrane pooled risk ratio is 1.17 (95% CI 0.87–1.56)
question: In children with functional abdominal pain or irritable bowel syndrome, does amitriptyline improve pain and quality of life compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — a multicentre trial and a Cochrane meta-analysis agree. In Saps et al. (PMID: 19596010), 63% of children on amitriptyline reported feeling better versus 57.5% on placebo (P=.63), with excellent or good pain relief in 50% versus 45% (P=.85) and no difference on logistic regression (P=.83) — while both groups improved substantially. The Cochrane review of antidepressants for functional abdominal pain disorders in children (de Bruijn et al., PMID: 33560523) pooled treatment success at RR 1.17 (95% CI 0.87 to 1.56; 2 studies, 205 participants), low-certainty evidence of no difference. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): the large placebo response in this condition is the story; amitriptyline adds nothing measurable to it.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the multicentre trial found 63% versus 57.5% feeling better (P=.63) and the Cochrane pooled RR for treatment success is 1.17 (95% CI 0.87–1.56)

title: Internet-delivered family CBT reduced pain and activity limitations in two randomised trials — significantly greater activity-limitation reduction than education control at 6 months in 273 adolescents
question: In children and adolescents with chronic pain, does internet-delivered cognitive behavioural therapy improve pain and disability compared with waiting list or education control?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two randomised trials from one programme, both positive on function. In Palermo et al. 2009 (PMID: 19695776), 48 children aged 11–17 with chronic pain showed significantly greater reductions in activity limitations and pain intensity on internet-delivered family CBT than wait-list control, maintained at 3-month follow-up, with a greater rate of clinically significant improvement in pain. In the larger multicentre trial (Palermo et al. 2016, PMID: 26335910; 273 adolescents), internet CBT produced significantly greater reduction in activity limitations from baseline to 6 months than internet education (b=-1.13, P=0.03), with benefits also on sleep quality (b=0.14, P=0.04) and parent behaviours. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): internet-delivered CBT improves function and pain modestly, and reaches families far from pain centres.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two randomised trials found greater reductions in activity limitations (and pain in the first) with internet-delivered family CBT than wait-list or education controls

title: Trauma-focused CBT is the best-supported treatment for childhood PTSD: largest symptom reductions in a 70-trial network meta-analysis (g=1.06 versus passive control), and a head-to-head win over child-centred therapy
question: In children and adolescents with PTSD, does trauma-focused CBT reduce symptoms versus usual care or waitlist?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — a large network meta-analysis plus a rigorous head-to-head trial. The 2025 network meta-analysis (Hoppen et al., PMID: 39630422; 70 randomised trials, 5,528 patients) found trauma-focused CBTs produced the largest short-term reductions in paediatric PTSD versus passive controls (Hedges g 1.06, 95% CI 0.86–1.26, P<.001), were superior to both passive and active controls across sensitivity analyses, and held their effects at mid-term and long-term follow-up; 52 of the 70 trials (74%) examined trauma-focused CBTs. In the multisite randomised trial (Cohen et al., PMID: 15187799; 229 children aged 8–14 with sexual-abuse-related PTSD), trauma-focused CBT produced significantly more improvement than child-centred therapy in PTSD, depression, behaviour problems, shame and abuse-related attributions, with parents also improving more. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): trauma-focused CBT reduces PTSD symptoms in children and adolescents more than waiting, usual or non-trauma-focused care.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — a 70-trial network meta-analysis gives trauma-focused CBT the largest PTSD reduction (g=1.06 vs passive control), concordant with a 229-child head-to-head randomised win over child-centred therapy

title: First-line stimulants in childhood ADHD: amphetamines lead on clinician ratings (SMD -1.02 versus -0.78 for methylphenidate) — but methylphenidate is the authors' first choice in children, on teacher ratings and tolerability
question: In children with ADHD, do methylphenidate and amphetamine formulations differ in efficacy and tolerability as first-line stimulant treatment?
balance: SPLIT — the two stimulant classes split by outcome: amphetamines win on clinician-rated efficacy, methylphenidate wins on tolerability and teacher ratings, and the authors name methylphenidate the preferred first choice in children and adolescents. In the Cortese 2018 network meta-analysis (Cortese S et al., PMID: 30097390) of 133 double-blind randomised controlled trials (81 in children and adolescents), the efficacy analysis closest to 12 weeks covered 10,068 children and adolescents and the tolerability analysis 11,018. On clinicians' ratings of ADHD core symptoms versus placebo, amphetamines had the largest effect (standardised mean difference -1.02, 95% CI -1.19 to -0.85), ahead of methylphenidate (-0.78, 95% CI -0.93 to -0.62), and head-to-head efficacy differences favoured amphetamines over methylphenidate (standardised mean differences -0.46 to -0.24). The picture reverses on the other measures: on teachers' ratings, only methylphenidate (-0.82, 95% CI -1.16 to -0.48) among the stimulants was more efficacious than placebo, and on tolerability amphetamines were inferior to placebo in children and adolescents (odds ratio for dropout because of side-effects 2.30, 95% CI 1.36 to 3.89), whereas methylphenidate was listed as less well tolerated than placebo in adults only. Taking efficacy and safety together, the authors concluded that the evidence supports methylphenidate in children and adolescents as the preferred first-choice medication for the short-term treatment of ADHD — with no sufficient data at 26 or 52 weeks. PROPOSED SPLIT: short-term clinician-rated efficacy favours amphetamines, but tolerability and teacher ratings favour methylphenidate, which the synthesis names first choice in children and adolescents.
stamp: SPLIT — clinician-rated efficacy favours amphetamines (SMD -1.02 versus placebo; head-to-head -0.46 to -0.24 over methylphenidate), but tolerability (amphetamine dropout odds ratio 2.30 versus placebo; methylphenidate not worse than placebo in this age group) and teacher ratings favour methylphenidate, the authors' preferred first choice in children and adolescents for short-term treatment

title: Outpatient care for low-risk febrile neutropenia in children looks as safe as inpatient care: treatment failure RR 1.04 (95% CI 0.55–1.99) and mortality RR 0.63 (0.15–2.70) in the Cochrane child trials
question: In children at low risk with febrile neutropenia, is outpatient oral antibiotic therapy as safe as inpatient intravenous therapy?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — two systematic reviews find no clear safety penalty for stepping down care in carefully selected low-risk children. The Cochrane review (Rivas-Ruiz et al., PMID: 30887505) found, in children, no clear difference between outpatient and inpatient treatment in treatment failure (RR 1.04, 95% CI 0.55 to 1.99; 4 studies) or mortality (RR 0.63, 95% CI 0.15 to 2.70; 3 studies, 329 participants), both moderate-certainty evidence, with hospital stay shorter by 3.9 days in the one child study measuring it (mean difference -3.90, 95% CI -5.37 to -2.43). The systematic review of reduced-therapy regimens (Morgan et al., PMID: 26757936; 37 studies, 3,205 episodes) found odds ratios for treatment failure of 0.98 (95% CI 0.44–2.19) for outpatient treatment and 1.05 (95% CI 0.74–1.48) for oral treatment in the randomised trials, with only four safety events (two deaths, two intensive care admissions) across all included studies. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): in low-risk children, outpatient/oral strategies have not been shown to cost treatment failures or lives.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — child trials show treatment failure RR 1.04 (95% CI 0.55–1.99) and mortality RR 0.63 (0.15–2.70) for outpatient versus inpatient care, with wide intervals that demand careful low-risk selection

title: Walnut oral immunotherapy desensitised 89% (49/55) versus 0% (0/18) on avoidance in a non-randomised cohort — with cross-desensitisation to pecan in all co-allergic patients and cashew in part
question: In children with cashew or walnut allergy, does oral immunotherapy raise the tolerated dose compared with avoidance or placebo?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — one prospective cohort, allocated by order of presentation rather than randomisation, with a very large effect. In the Nut CRACKER study (Elizur et al., PMID: 30926371), 49 of 55 patients (89%) on walnut oral immunotherapy were desensitised to walnut (passing a 4,000 mg walnut protein challenge) versus none of 18 in the avoidance control group. Cross-desensitisation followed for co-allergies: all 46 patients co-allergic to pecan were desensitised to pecan, and 18 of 30 patients (60%) co-allergic to hazelnut or cashew were fully desensitised or responded. The cost was reactions: 47 of 55 patients (85%) had an adverse reaction during clinic up-dosing (mostly grade 1–2) and eight required intramuscular epinephrine for a dose taken at home. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): walnut oral immunotherapy probably desensitises most treated children — randomised, placebo-controlled confirmation for tree nuts does not yet exist in this record.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — a single non-randomised cohort found walnut desensitisation in 89% versus 0% on avoidance, with reactions in 85% during up-dosing and no placebo-controlled tree-nut trial behind it

title: Intramuscular vitamin K at birth nearly abolishes late bleeding (pooled RR 0.02 versus none); a single oral dose leaves risk 24.5-fold higher than intramuscular, while weekly oral dosing in Denmark recorded zero cases
question: In newborn infants, does vitamin K prophylaxis prevent vitamin K deficiency bleeding — and does a single intramuscular dose beat oral dosing?
balance: SPLIT — prophylaxis works, and the route decides how completely. The systematic review (Sankar et al., PMID: 27109090) puts the median burden of late vitamin K deficiency bleeding at 35 per 100,000 live births (interquartile range 10.5–80) in infants who received no prophylaxis, and surveillance data show intramuscular or subcutaneous prophylaxis reduces late bleeding versus none (pooled RR 0.02, 95% CI 0.00 to 0.10). Against intramuscular dosing, a single oral dose increased the risk of vitamin K deficiency bleeding (RR 24.5, 95% CI 7.4 to 81.0), while multiple oral doses did not clearly differ (RR 3.64, 95% CI 0.82 to 16.3). Denmark's weekly oral regimen performed at the intramuscular level in practice (Hansen et al., PMID: 12892158): among about 396,000 infants given oral prophylaxis within 507,850 live births, no cases of vitamin K deficiency bleeding were found (incidence 0–0.9 per 100,000), with 94% of surveyed infants completing the course. PROPOSED SPLIT: one intramuscular dose is the reliable single-act protection; oral dosing protects only as a completed multi-dose course.
stamp: SPLIT — prophylaxis prevents late vitamin K deficiency bleeding (IM vs none pooled RR 0.02), a single oral dose is far weaker than IM (RR 24.5), but a completed weekly oral course recorded zero cases in Denmark

title: Five days of prednisone matched 14 days in COPD exacerbations: re-exacerbation 37.2% versus 38.4% at six months — with less than half the steroid dose
question: In patients hospitalised with a COPD exacerbation, is a 5-day course of systemic glucocorticoids non-inferior to a conventional 14-day course for re-exacerbation within six months?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — the shorter course is as effective and halves exposure. In the REDUCE trial (314 patients presenting to emergency departments with acute COPD exacerbation), 5 days of prednisone 40 mg was noninferior to 14 days for re-exacerbation within 180 days: hazard ratio 0.95 (90% CI 0.70 to 1.29), with estimated re-exacerbation rates of 37.2% on 5 days versus 38.4% on 14 days (difference −1.2%, 95% CI −12.2% to 9.8%), while mean cumulative prednisone dose was 379 mg versus 793 mg (p<0.001). A Cochrane review of eight trials (582 participants) likewise found no difference between courses of seven or fewer days and longer courses in treatment failure (odds ratio 0.72, 95% CI 0.36 to 1.46), relapse (OR 1.04, 95% CI 0.70 to 1.56), adverse events, or hospital stay. The honest catch: adverse reactions such as hyperglycaemia and hypertension did not actually fall in REDUCE despite the halved dose, and the pooled evidence was graded moderate quality for imprecision — the gain proven is equal efficacy with less drug, not fewer side effects in the short term. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): five days of systemic glucocorticoid treats a hospitalised COPD exacerbation as well as 14 days, at roughly half the cumulative exposure.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — 5-day glucocorticoid course noninferior to 14 days for re-exacerbation in a large double-blind trial and a Cochrane review, with cumulative dose roughly halved

title: Eosinophil-guided steroids in COPD exacerbations: exposure cut from a median 5 days to 2 days, days alive and out of hospital unchanged — a small mortality imbalance keeps this at POSSIBLE
question: In patients hospitalised with a COPD exacerbation, can blood-eosinophil-guided prednisolone treatment safely reduce steroid exposure without increasing treatment failure compared with standard care?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the biomarker strategy spares steroids without a shown cost in the outcomes measured, in two randomised trials in different settings. In hospitalised patients (CORTICO-COP, 318 patients), giving prednisolone only on days when the blood eosinophil count was at least 0.3 × 10⁹ cells/L cut median systemic corticosteroid duration from 5 days to 2 days (p<0.0001), with days alive and out of hospital within 14 days of 8.9 versus 9.3 (difference −0.4, 95% CI −1.3 to 0.5) and treatment failure at 30 days of 26% in both groups — but deaths at 30 days were 6% guided versus 4% standard (difference 1.9%, 95% CI −2.8 to 6.5), a small imbalance the trial could not resolve. In UK primary care (STARR2), eosinophil-directed prednisolone was likewise non-inferior, with treatment failure at 30 days in 19% of guided versus 32% of standard-care exacerbations (relative risk 0.60, 95% CI 0.33 to 1.04). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): eosinophil guidance safely reduces steroid exposure in COPD exacerbations; a mortality cost has not been excluded, which is why this is not LIKELY.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — eosinophil-guided prednisolone halved steroid exposure with non-inferior short-term outcomes in hospital and primary-care trials, with an unresolved small mortality imbalance in the hospital trial

title: Tiotropium beat salmeterol head-to-head in COPD: first exacerbation at 187 versus 145 days, severe exacerbations 0.09 versus 0.13 a year — a modest, real edge
question: In patients with COPD at risk of exacerbations, does once-daily tiotropium prevent exacerbations better than twice-daily salmeterol?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — in the one large direct comparison, tiotropium prevented exacerbations better than salmeterol, and a Cochrane pool of seven trials points the same way. In POET-COPD (7,376 patients with moderate-to-very-severe COPD and a prior exacerbation), tiotropium 18 µg once daily delayed the first exacerbation versus salmeterol 50 µg twice daily (187 versus 145 days; hazard ratio 0.83, 95% CI 0.77 to 0.90 — a 17% relative reduction in risk), cut the annual rate of moderate or severe exacerbations (0.64 versus 0.72; rate ratio 0.89, 95% CI 0.83 to 0.96) and of severe exacerbations (0.09 versus 0.13; rate ratio 0.73, 95% CI 0.66 to 0.82), with deaths of 1.7% versus 2.1% and similar serious adverse events. The Cochrane review of tiotropium versus long-acting beta-agonists (seven studies, 12,223 participants) found fewer patients experiencing one or more exacerbations on tiotropium (odds ratio 0.86, 95% CI 0.79 to 0.93) and fewer exacerbations leading to hospitalisation (OR 0.87, 95% CI 0.77 to 0.99), with no mortality difference. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): if a single long-acting bronchodilator is chosen for exacerbation prevention, tiotropium has the better of this direct evidence — by weeks of delay and fractions of an exacerbation a year, not by a transformation.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — tiotropium prevented COPD exacerbations better than salmeterol in a 7,376-patient head-to-head trial, concordant with a Cochrane comparison against long-acting beta-agonists as a class

title: Metoprolol did not prevent COPD exacerbations: first exacerbation at 202 versus 222 days, and hospitalised exacerbations nearly doubled (HR 1.91) — the observational promise failed its randomised test
question: In patients with moderate-to-very-severe COPD and no significant cardiac disease, does metoprolol prevent acute exacerbations compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — started purely to prevent exacerbations, metoprolol did not help and the severe end of the outcome worsened. In BLOCK COPD (532 patients with moderate-to-very-severe COPD, no established indication for a beta-blocker, and no significant cardiac disease), extended-release metoprolol did not change time to first exacerbation (median 202 versus 222 days on placebo; hazard ratio 1.05, 95% CI 0.84 to 1.32), while exacerbations leading to hospitalisation were more frequent on metoprolol (HR 1.91, 95% CI 1.29 to 2.83); deaths were 11 versus 5, and the trial was stopped early for futility and safety concerns. The contrast matters: pooled observational data had associated beta-blocker therapy with fewer exacerbations (HR 0.77, 95% CI 0.70 to 0.85) — an association inside the range that confounding by indication can manufacture, and one the randomised test did not confirm. This shelf is about starting a beta-blocker for COPD alone; it says nothing against beta-blockers given for a cardiac indication. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm): no exacerbation benefit, with a hospitalisation signal, from the single randomised trial.
stamp: POSSIBLE (harm) — a single randomised trial stopped early found no exacerbation prevention from metoprolol in COPD without cardiac indication, with more hospitalised exacerbations (HR 1.91)

title: Simvastatin did not prevent COPD exacerbations: 1.36 versus 1.39 per person-year, first exacerbation at 223 versus 231 days, deaths 28 versus 30 — another retrospective statin promise that failed prospectively
question: In patients with COPD at risk of exacerbations, does daily simvastatin prevent exacerbations compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — in the large prospective trial built to test the retrospective claims, simvastatin changed nothing it was asked to change. In STATCOPE (885 patients with moderate-to-severe COPD at high exacerbation risk, deliberately excluding anyone with a cardiovascular or diabetes indication for a statin), simvastatin 40 mg daily gave 1.36 exacerbations per person-year versus 1.39 on placebo (p=0.54), a median time to first exacerbation of 223 versus 231 days (p=0.34), and 28 versus 30 deaths (p=0.89), despite LDL cholesterol falling as expected. A 2026 meta-analysis of the three randomised trials (1,190 patients) likewise found no significant difference in annualised exacerbation rates (weighted mean difference −0.21 per person-year, 95% CI −0.61 to 0.20), though it reported lower exacerbation hospitalisation (relative risk 0.87, 95% CI 0.77 to 0.97) at low GRADE certainty — a signal the largest trial's own event rates do not corroborate. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): simvastatin should not be started to prevent COPD exacerbations; its proven uses remain cardiovascular.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the large STATCOPE trial found identical exacerbation rates on simvastatin and placebo, and a three-trial meta-analysis found no difference in annualised exacerbation rates

title: Lung volume reduction surgery in severe emphysema: no overall survival advantage (0.11 deaths per person-year in both groups) — survival better with upper-lobe disease and low exercise capacity (RR 0.47), worse without them (RR 2.06)
question: In patients with severe emphysema, does lung volume reduction surgery improve survival, exercise capacity, and quality of life compared with medical therapy alone — and in which subgroups does it harm?
balance: SPLIT — by anatomy and exercise capacity, and the split is the whole answer. In NETT (1,218 patients with severe emphysema, all after pulmonary rehabilitation), overall mortality was identical at 0.11 deaths per person-year in the surgery and medical groups (risk ratio 1.01), while exercise capacity improved by more than 10 W at 24 months in 15% of surgical versus 3% of medical patients (p<0.001). Within that null average, patients with predominantly upper-lobe emphysema and low baseline exercise capacity had lower mortality with surgery (risk ratio for death 0.47, p=0.005), while patients with non-upper-lobe emphysema and high exercise capacity had higher mortality with surgery (risk ratio 2.06, p=0.02). A prespecified high-risk subgroup of 140 patients (very low FEV1 with homogeneous disease or very low diffusion capacity) had such high early surgical mortality that enrolment of that subgroup was halted; over 15 years of follow-up their survival curves eventually crossed (log-rank p=0.95), but the high 30-day operative death risk remains the practical deterrent. PROPOSED SPLIT: benefit — exercise capacity for many, survival for the upper-lobe/low-exercise subgroup; harm — early death in high-risk and non-upper-lobe/high-exercise patients.
stamp: SPLIT — survival benefit only in upper-lobe emphysema with low exercise capacity (RR for death 0.47), harm in non-upper-lobe disease with high exercise capacity (RR 2.06) and in the halted high-risk subgroup; exercise capacity improved overall (15% versus 3% gaining >10 W)

title: Endobronchial coils for severe emphysema: walk distance improved by 14.6 m — below the 25 m threshold patients can feel — quality of life by 8.9 points, at a price of major complications in 34.8% versus 19.1%
question: In patients with severe heterogeneous emphysema, do endobronchial coils improve lung function, exercise capacity, and quality of life compared with usual care?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — statistically real, clinically modest, and bought with complications. In RENEW (315 patients with severe emphysema and severe air trapping), bilateral endobronchial coils plus usual care beat usual care alone on the primary outcome by a median 14.6 m of six-minute walk distance at 12 months (10.3 m gained versus 7.6 m lost) — less than the 25 m difference prespecified as clinically important — although 40.0% versus 26.9% achieved at least a 25 m gain, the St George's Respiratory Questionnaire improved by 8.9 points more with coils, and the between-group FEV1 difference was 7.0%. Against that, major complications occurred in 34.8% of coil patients versus 19.1% on usual care (p=0.002), including pneumonia in 20% versus 4.5% and pneumothorax in 9.7% versus 0.6%. The earlier, smaller RESET trial (47 patients) found the same quality-of-life direction at 90 days (−8.36 points, 95% CI −16.24 to −0.47) with no difference in serious adverse events detected at that size. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): coils improve quality-of-life scores and lung function modestly in severe hyperinflation, with a complication burden that must be weighed patient by patient.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two randomised trials show modest quality-of-life and lung-function gains from endobronchial coils, with the walk-distance gain below the clinically important threshold and major complications in about a third of treated patients

title: Hospital at home for COPD exacerbations: readmissions lower (RR 0.76) and mortality a non-significant trend (RR 0.65) — but only in the selected minority judged safe to send home
question: For acute COPD exacerbations, does hospital-at-home or early supported discharge give equivalent mortality and readmission outcomes to inpatient care in selected patients?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for carefully selected patients, being treated at home did at least as well as a hospital bed, and readmissions fell. A Cochrane review of eight randomised trials (870 patients presenting to emergency departments with COPD exacerbations, excluding anyone with impaired consciousness, acute confusion, arterial pH below 7.35, or other features making home treatment irresponsible) found hospital at home reduced readmission compared with inpatient care (risk ratio 0.76, 95% CI 0.59 to 0.99; p=0.04), with a trend toward lower mortality that did not reach significance (RR 0.65, 95% CI 0.40 to 1.04; p=0.07), on evidence graded moderate quality; quality of life, lung function, and cost evidence was too weak for firm conclusions. In the largest early trial within that pool, only 192 of 583 patients referred for admission (33%) even met home-care criteria — the selection is the intervention's boundary. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): hospital at home is a safe, readmission-sparing alternative for the selected minority, not a substitute for admission in unselected exacerbations.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in selected patients, hospital at home for COPD exacerbations reduced readmissions (RR 0.76) with a non-significant mortality trend, in a Cochrane pool of eight randomised trials

title: Intravenous magnesium in acute COPD exacerbations: peak flow better at 45 minutes and admission odds halved in pooled small trials (OR 0.45) — but no trial large enough to trust, and length of stay unmoved
question: In acute COPD exacerbations, does intravenous magnesium sulfate as an adjunct to standard therapy improve lung function and reduce admission or ventilation compared with placebo?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — the pooled signal points one way, but it is built from small trials and a 45-minute flow measurement. A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis of nine studies (seven randomised trials and two observational studies) found adjunctive intravenous magnesium sulfate improved peak expiratory flow at 45 minutes (mean difference 18.50, 95% CI 6.36 to 30.65) and reduced hospital admission from the emergency department (odds ratio 0.45, 95% CI 0.23 to 0.88), with no significant difference in length of stay (mean difference −0.83 days, 95% CI −2.99 to 1.33) or adverse events (OR 0.79, 95% CI 0.20 to 3.13). An earlier meta-analysis of seven studies found the same pattern — admission odds ratio 0.453 (95% CI 0.233 to 0.882) and small FEV1 gains during exacerbations but not in stable COPD. Neither pool reports a ventilation or mortality outcome, the two pools substantially overlap, and neither record carries MeSH indexing. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): a plausible, cheap adjunct with a consistent small-trial signal on admission — unproven where it matters most.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — two overlapping meta-analyses of small trials associate adjunctive intravenous magnesium with better early peak flow and lower admission odds (OR 0.45), with no data on ventilation or mortality

title: Supported self-management in COPD: hospitalisations fell 26.9% over two years in the Canadian programme trial, but the large European COMET trial missed its primary endpoint — and its startling mortality gap (1.9% versus 14.2%) is not credible at face value
question: In patients with COPD, does a supported self-management programme with an exacerbation action plan reduce hospital admissions and improve quality of life compared with usual care?
balance: SPLIT — the two big programme trials disagree on admissions, and the mortality number in one of them should not be believed as printed. In COMET (319 patients with severe COPD across Europe; self-management programme plus home telemonitoring, care coordination, and medical management versus usual care), the primary endpoint — unplanned all-cause hospitalisation days per year — was 17.4 versus 22.6 days, a difference that was not significant (mean difference −5.3, 95% CI −13.7 to −3.1 as printed; p=0.16), with no difference in exacerbation frequency; yet mortality was reported at 1.9% versus 14.2% (p<0.001), a gap far too large for the intervention and arising in a trial whose patient profiles and hospitalisation practices varied substantially across countries. In the Canadian multicentre trial of the named 'Living Well with COPD' self-management programme (191 patients with a prior hospitalisation), all-cause hospitalisations fell by a relative 26.9% and emergency visits by a relative 21.1% at two years compared with standard care. PROPOSED SPLIT: hospitalisation benefit shown for a supervised, action-plan programme in previously hospitalised patients; the broader multicomponent European programme missed its primary endpoint, and its mortality claim is flagged Tier C for personal review.
stamp: SPLIT — a supervised self-management programme reduced hospitalisations over two years in one randomised trial, while the larger multicomponent COMET programme missed its primary hospitalisation endpoint; COMET's mortality difference is implausibly large and country-confounded

title: Adding tiotropium to inhaled steroid plus LABA in uncontrolled asthma: severe exacerbations delayed (282 versus 226 days; HR 0.79) and FEV1 up by 86–154 mL in two replicate trials
question: In asthma uncontrolled on inhaled corticosteroid plus long-acting beta-agonist, does adding tiotropium improve lung function and reduce exacerbations compared with doubling the steroid or adding a leukotriene antagonist?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — two replicate trials agree, and a crossover trial answers the 'instead of what' question for the steroid-doubling option. In the PrimoTinA-asthma programme (two replicate randomised trials, 912 patients symptomatic on inhaled corticosteroid plus LABA with at least one severe exacerbation in the prior year), adding tiotropium 5 µg once daily improved peak FEV1 at 24 weeks by 86 mL (trial 1) and 154 mL (trial 2) over placebo, delayed the first severe exacerbation (282 versus 226 days), and reduced severe-exacerbation risk by a relative 21% (hazard ratio 0.79; p=0.03), with adverse events similar and no deaths. In the TALC crossover trial (210 patients uncontrolled on inhaled corticosteroid alone), tiotropium beat doubling the steroid dose on morning peak flow (difference 25.8 L/min; p<0.001), FEV1 (0.10 L; p=0.004), and symptom scores, and was non-inferior to adding salmeterol. The leukotriene-antagonist comparison in the candidate question was not tested in either record and is declared a gap, not answered here. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): tiotropium is a proven add-on when steroid-plus-LABA asthma remains uncontrolled — with modest lung-function gains and a real, moderate exacerbation delay.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — two replicate randomised trials show tiotropium add-on improves lung function and delays severe exacerbations (HR 0.79) in asthma uncontrolled on ICS plus LABA, and a crossover trial found it superior to doubling the steroid dose

title: Heliox for acute severe asthma: no significant improvement in pulmonary function (SMD −0.28, −0.56 to 0.01) and no reduction in hospital admission (RR 0.83, 0.66 to 1.08) across ten small trials
question: In non-intubated patients with acute severe asthma, does heliox-driven nebulisation improve airflow and reduce admission compared with oxygen-driven nebulisation?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — for routine use in non-intubated acute asthma, the pooled trials show no benefit that reaches significance on either airflow or admission. The Cochrane review (ten randomised trials, 544 patients in emergency departments, seven adult and three paediatric) found no significant difference in pulmonary function between heliox and oxygen or air (standardised mean difference −0.28, 95% CI −0.56 to 0.01, with significant heterogeneity) and no significant difference in hospital admission (risk ratio 0.83, 95% CI 0.66 to 1.08; p=0.17). An earlier systematic review of seven trials (392 patients) found the same: no significant pulmonary-function difference (SMD −0.20, 95% CI −0.91 to 0.51) and no admission difference in the nebuliser-driven subgroup (odds ratio 1.07, 95% CI 0.46 to 2.48). Both reviews note a possible signal confined to the subgroup with the most severe baseline obstruction — a hypothesis from a small number of studies, not a finding. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): heliox has no established role in the initial treatment of acute asthma outside that unproven severe-obstruction niche.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — Cochrane and earlier systematic reviews of small randomised trials found no significant airflow or admission benefit from heliox in non-intubated acute asthma

title: Noninvasive ventilation in acute severe asthma: used widely, proven barely — the intubation data are two events in 86 patients (RR 4.48, CI 0.23 to 89.13), and the one positive pilot randomised 30 people
question: In acute severe asthma with respiratory failure, does noninvasive positive-pressure ventilation reduce intubation and mortality compared with standard therapy?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — the honest summary is that the question is unanswered, with one small pilot leaning positive. The Cochrane review found six trials of noninvasive positive-pressure ventilation (NPPV) in severe acute asthma, with five studies and 206 participants contributing data; for endotracheal intubation, the only outcome that matters most here, two studies contributed just two intubations among 45 NPPV patients and none among 41 controls (risk ratio 4.48, 95% CI 0.23 to 89.13) — a confidence interval that excludes nothing — and there were no deaths in either study. The single small hospitalisation result favoured NPPV (3 of 17 versus 10 of 16 admitted; RR 0.28, 95% CI 0.09 to 0.84). The pilot trial behind that signal randomised 30 emergency-department patients: 80% on bilevel ventilation reached a 50% FEV1 rise versus 20% on sham (p<0.004), with mean FEV1 rises of 53.5% versus 28.5%. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): lung function and admission lean NPPV's way in tiny trials; any claim about intubation or mortality is currently unfounded in either direction.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — one 30-patient pilot showed faster lung-function recovery and fewer admissions with bilevel ventilation, but pooled intubation data are two events with a confidence interval spanning 0.23 to 89.13 and mortality is unmeasured

title: Escalating treatment in children's acute asthma: intravenous magnesium is the only option with high-certainty evidence of shorter stay and fewer admissions — aminophylline mainly adds vomiting, and almost every comparison rests on one to three tiny trials
question: In children with acute asthma exacerbations not responding to first-line therapy, which escalation treatment — intravenous salbutamol, aminophylline, or magnesium — works best?
balance: SPLIT — the three named options do not stand equal, and 'best' can only be answered by elimination. A Cochrane overview of 13 reviews (67 trials) of second-line treatment for children with acute asthma found intravenous magnesium sulfate was the only intervention shown to reduce hospital length of stay (high-certainty evidence) and one of the interventions reducing hospital admission (also high-certainty); no intervention was shown to reduce intensive care admission. Aminophylline increased vomiting compared with placebo (moderate-certainty evidence) and nausea compared with intravenous beta2-agonists (low-certainty), with no compensating benefit finding highlighted. A 2025 meta-analysis of intravenous magnesium specifically (nine randomised trials, 473 children) found lower hospitalisation and less need for non-invasive ventilation (risk ratio 0.17, 95% CI 0.15 to 0.54 as printed) at low certainty, with asthma scores, intensive care admission, invasive ventilation, and length of stay similar. Crucially, there are no adequate head-to-head trials between the options — most comparisons involve one to three trials and fewer than 100 children — so intravenous salbutamol's place is 'unproven', not 'disproven'. PROPOSED SPLIT: magnesium — supported; aminophylline — harm without shown benefit; intravenous salbutamol — no demonstrated advantage in this evidence.
stamp: SPLIT — intravenous magnesium is the only escalation drug with high-certainty evidence of benefit in children (shorter stay, fewer admissions); aminophylline adds vomiting without a shown benefit; intravenous salbutamol has no demonstrated advantage and no head-to-head trials exist

title: Adding clarithromycin to a beta-lactam in hospitalised pneumonia: the early combined response endpoint was met by 68% versus 38% at 72 hours — a single trial, on a composite of symptoms, organ score, and procalcitonin
question: In hospitalised patients with community-acquired pneumonia and a strong inflammatory response, does adding clarithromycin to standard beta-lactam therapy improve early clinical outcomes compared with beta-lactam alone?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one well-blinded trial, on an early composite endpoint, in an inflammation-selected population. In ACCESS (278 adults hospitalised with community-acquired pneumonia who had systemic inflammatory response syndrome, a SOFA score of at least 2, and procalcitonin of at least 0.25 ng/mL), adding oral clarithromycin 500 mg twice daily for seven days to standard beta-lactam care met the primary composite endpoint — at least 50% improvement in respiratory symptom score plus at least 30% SOFA improvement or favourable procalcitonin kinetics at 72 hours — in 68% of patients versus 38% on placebo (difference 29.6%, 95% CI 17.7 to 40.3; odds ratio 3.40, 95% CI 2.06 to 5.63), with serious treatment-emergent adverse events in 43% versus 53% (p=0.14), none judged treatment-related. The supporting trial is a caution rather than a confirmation: in Garin's randomised comparison in moderately severe pneumonia, beta-lactam monotherapy failed to prove non-inferior to beta-lactam plus macrolide for clinical stability at day 7 (41.2% versus 33.6% not yet stable), with the combination's advantage concentrated in atypical-pathogen infection and the most severe stratum, and no mortality difference. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: a single trial carrying a benefit claim on a composite early-response endpoint — mortality and hospital stay benefits are not shown in either record.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single double-blind trial found adding clarithromycin raised the 72-hour combined clinical-and-inflammatory response from 38% to 68% in inflammation-selected hospitalised pneumonia, with no mortality data

title: Adjunctive prednisone in hospitalised community-acquired pneumonia (STEP): clinical stability in 3.0 versus 4.4 days — faster stability with no survival claim, at a hyperglycaemia price of 19% versus 11%
question: In adults hospitalised with non-severe community-acquired pneumonia, does adjunctive prednisone shorten time to clinical stability and hospital stay compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for speed to clinical stability, not for survival. In STEP (Blum CA et al., PMID: 25608756), 785 patients admitted to hospital with community-acquired pneumonia at seven tertiary care hospitals in Switzerland were randomly assigned within 24 hours of presentation to prednisone 50 mg daily for 7 days (n=392) or placebo (n=393). Median time to clinical stability — the primary endpoint, defined as time until stable vital signs for at least 24 hours — was shorter on prednisone: 3.0 days (IQR 2.5-3.4) versus 4.4 days (4.0-5.0) on placebo (hazard ratio 1.33, 95% CI 1.15-1.50, p<0.0001). Pneumonia-associated complications until day 30 did not differ significantly: 11 patients (3%) on prednisone versus 22 (6%) on placebo (odds ratio 0.49, 95% CI 0.23-1.02; p=0.056). The price was glucose: in-hospital hyperglycaemia needing insulin treatment occurred in 76 patients (19%) on prednisone versus 43 (11%) on placebo (odds ratio 1.96, 95% CI 1.31-2.93, p=0.0010), while other adverse events compatible with corticosteroid use were rare and similar in both groups. The authors concluded that prednisone for 7 days in patients admitted to hospital with community-acquired pneumonia shortens time to clinical stability without an increase in complications. The fetched record reports no hospital length-of-stay figure and makes no survival claim, so this shelf claims neither: the proven gain is reaching stable vital signs about a day and a half sooner. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): adjunctive prednisone 50 mg daily for 7 days shortened time to clinical stability in one large double-blind trial of hospitalised community-acquired pneumonia, with more insulin-treated hyperglycaemia and no demonstrated effect on complications or survival.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in one 785-patient randomised double-blind trial, adjunctive prednisone 50 mg daily for 7 days shortened median time to clinical stability from 4.4 to 3.0 days (hazard ratio 1.33, 95% CI 1.15-1.50), with no survival claim and more in-hospital hyperglycaemia needing insulin (19% versus 11%)

title: Early switch from intravenous to oral antibiotics in severe pneumonia: cure 83% versus 85%, mortality 4% versus 6% — and two fewer days in hospital
question: In patients with severe community-acquired pneumonia who have stabilised, is an early switch from intravenous to oral antibiotics as effective as a full intravenous course?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — switching stabilised patients to oral antibiotics after three intravenous days matched a full intravenous course on cure and mortality, and shortened both intravenous treatment and hospital stay, in a randomised trial and a concordant meta-analysis. In the Dutch multicentre trial (302 patients with severe community-acquired pneumonia on non-intensive-care wards; 265 in the intention-to-treat analysis), clinical cure was 83% with early switch versus 85% with seven intravenous days (difference 2%, 95% CI −7% to 10%) and day-28 mortality was 4% versus 6% (difference 2%, 95% CI −3% to 8%), while intravenous treatment was 3.4 days shorter (3.6 versus 7.0 days) and hospital stay 1.9 days shorter (9.6 versus 11.5 days). A meta-analysis of six randomised trials (1,219 patients with moderate-to-severe pneumonia) found treatment success, mortality (odds ratio 0.81, 95% CI 0.49 to 1.33), and recurrence no different, hospitalisation 3.34 days shorter, and fewer drug-related adverse events with early switch (OR 0.65, 95% CI 0.48 to 0.89). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): for the patient who has stabilised, the oral switch is the adequately proven default — the benefit is time and freedom from the drip, at no shown clinical cost.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — early intravenous-to-oral switch in stabilised severe pneumonia matched full intravenous therapy on cure and mortality in a randomised trial and a six-trial meta-analysis, shortening hospital stay by about two to three days

title: A negative MRSA nasal PCR in pneumonia: vancomycin courses about a day shorter (−0.98 days) with no shown harm — and a negative predictive value of 96.5% at 10% prevalence, but only 94.8% in ventilator-associated pneumonia
question: In hospitalised patients with pneumonia, can a negative MRSA nasal PCR safely guide stopping or withholding anti-MRSA therapy, shortening vancomycin exposure without worse outcomes?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the diagnostic logic is strong and the stewardship outcomes point the right way, but every outcome study behind the practice is retrospective. A 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of six observational retrospective studies (1,649 hospitalised pneumonia patients) found MRSA nasal PCR screening was associated with vancomycin duration shorter by 0.98 days (95% CI −1.61 to −0.59), with no significant difference in acute kidney injury (odds ratio 0.53, 95% CI 0.26 to 1.08), hospital stay (−0.20 days, 95% CI −0.85 to 0.45), or mortality (OR 0.68, 95% CI 0.45 to 1.02) — the safety intervals are wide and all lean favourable without proving safety. The diagnostic foundation is a 2018 meta-analysis of 22 studies (5,163 patients): nasal screening had sensitivity 70.9% and specificity 90.3% for MRSA pneumonia, giving a negative predictive value of 96.5% at a 10% prevalence (98.1% in community- and healthcare-associated pneumonia) — but in ventilator-associated pneumonia sensitivity fell to 40.3% and the negative predictive value to 94.8%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: a negative swab is a reasonable de-escalation prompt in non-ventilator pneumonia; the evidence is observational, and the ventilator-associated subgroup is exactly where the test is weakest.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — MRSA nasal PCR-guided de-escalation shortened vancomycin by about a day in retrospective studies with no significant harm signal, resting on a diagnostic meta-analysis showing 96.5% negative predictive value (94.8% in ventilator-associated pneumonia)

title: Inhaled amikacin–fosfomycin added to intravenous therapy for Gram-negative ventilator pneumonia: bacterial counts fell, clinical outcomes did not — infection score change identical (p=0.70), deaths 24% versus 17%
question: In ventilator-associated pneumonia caused by Gram-negative bacilli, does adjunctive inhaled amikacin–fosfomycin improve clinical cure compared with standard intravenous therapy alone?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the one randomised trial of this specific inhalation system sterilised airways without helping patients. In the IASIS trial (143 patients with Gram-negative ventilator-associated pneumonia), the amikacin fosfomycin inhalation system (300 mg amikacin/120 mg fosfomycin aerosol twice daily for up to 10 days, added to standard intravenous care) did not differ from placebo aerosol on the primary endpoint of change in Clinical Pulmonary Infection Score (p=0.70), on the hierarchical endpoint of no mortality with clinical cure by day 14 (p=0.68), or on ventilator-free days (p=0.06); deaths were 17 of 71 (24%) on the system versus 12 of 72 (17%) on placebo (p=0.32), despite significantly fewer positive tracheal cultures on days 3 and 7. A broader meta-analysis of adjunctive inhaled antibiotics in ventilator-associated pneumonia (11 randomised trials, 1,210 patients, mostly other agents) found clinical cure modestly higher (relative risk 1.13, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.26) and microbiological eradication higher (RR 1.45, 95% CI 1.19 to 1.76) but mortality unchanged (RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.82 to 1.21) and bronchospasm increased (RR 2.74, 95% CI 1.31 to 5.73) — its own authors do not support routine use. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): for the amikacin–fosfomycin system the answer is a direct randomised no; for inhaled adjuncts as a class, cure-score gains have never converted into survival.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the randomised IASIS trial found no clinical benefit from adjunctive inhaled amikacin–fosfomycin in Gram-negative ventilator-associated pneumonia despite reduced bacterial burden, and a class meta-analysis found no mortality benefit
