title: Vitamin D added to tuberculosis treatment does not speed sputum conversion: pooled trials show no significant difference in smear or culture conversion — symptoms scores improve slightly, bacteria clear at the same rate
question: In patients being treated for pulmonary tuberculosis, does adjunctive vitamin D accelerate sputum culture conversion or improve clinical outcomes compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — on the outcome the question asks about, the pooled randomised answer is no. A 2025 meta-analysis of 26 randomised trials (19,586 participants, spanning prevention and treatment) found no significant differences between vitamin D and control in sputum smear conversion, sputum culture conversion, or time to sputum culture conversion during anti-tuberculosis treatment, although tuberculosis symptom scores were lower at eight weeks (mean difference −0.39, 95% CI −0.57 to −0.22) and 12 weeks (−0.53, 95% CI −0.84 to −0.22), safety profiles were similar, and a daily-dosing subgroup showed higher smear conversion at six and eight weeks. The best-known individual trial points the same way: in 146 London patients with smear-positive pulmonary tuberculosis, four 2.5 mg doses of vitamin D3 gave a median time to culture conversion of 36.0 versus 43.5 days (adjusted hazard ratio 1.39, 95% CI 0.90 to 2.16; p=0.14) — not significant — with a significant hastening only in the small subgroup carrying one vitamin-D-receptor genotype (HR 8.09, 95% CI 1.36 to 48.01), a subgroup finding with a confidence interval too wide to act on. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): vitamin D may ease symptom scores, but it does not clear sputum faster, and it is not a substitute for, or an accelerator of, standard therapy.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — a 26-trial meta-analysis and the largest named trial found no significant acceleration of sputum smear or culture conversion from adjunctive vitamin D in pulmonary tuberculosis

title: Exercise rehabilitation after pulmonary embolism: early programmes after the clot show no clear between-group benefit in four small trials (250 patients) — but targeted rehabilitation for persistent breathlessness improved the shuttle walk by 53 m
question: After an acute pulmonary embolism, does a structured exercise and rehabilitation programme improve exercise capacity and quality of life compared with usual care?
balance: SPLIT — by timing and by who is enrolled. A 2026 systematic review of randomised trials of structured exercise training started within three months of acute venous thromboembolism found only four trials (250 patients in total; two after pulmonary embolism, one after deep vein thrombosis, one mixed): exercise capacity, cardiopulmonary function, or quality of life improved within the exercise groups in three studies, but differences between exercise and control groups were nonsignificant, limited by small samples and risk of bias — while no trial reported safety concerns from starting exercise within three months. The clearer positive result comes later and in a selected group: in a randomised trial of 211 survivors with persistent dyspnoea six to 72 months after pulmonary embolism, an eight-week programme of twice-weekly exercise plus one education session beat usual care on the incremental shuttle walk test by 53.0 m (95% CI 17.7 to 88.3; p=0.0035) and on the disease-specific quality-of-life questionnaire (mean difference −4%, 95% CI −0.09 to 0.00; p=0.041), with no differences in generic quality of life, dyspnoea scores, or endurance shuttle performance, and no adverse events. PROPOSED SPLIT: early routine rehabilitation after a clot — safe, benefit unproven; rehabilitation aimed at survivors still breathless months later — exercise capacity genuinely improved in one randomised trial.
stamp: SPLIT — structured exercise begun within three months of acute VTE was safe but showed no significant between-group benefit across four small trials, while rehabilitation targeted at PE survivors with persistent dyspnoea improved shuttle-walk capacity by 53 m in one randomised trial

title: Rituximab versus cyclophosphamide in connective-tissue-disease lung fibrosis: lung function improved equally in both groups (FVC +97 versus +99 mL at 24 weeks) — rituximab's edge was tolerability, with 445 versus 646 adverse events
question: In connective-tissue-disease-associated interstitial lung disease that is progressing despite immunosuppression, is rituximab as effective as intravenous cyclophosphamide for lung function, with fewer adverse events?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — not because rituximab beat cyclophosphamide on the lung, but because it matched it while costing less harm. In RECITAL (101 patients with severe or progressive interstitial lung disease related to scleroderma, idiopathic inflammatory myositis, or mixed connective tissue disease), forced vital capacity improved from baseline at 24 weeks in both groups (+99 mL on cyclophosphamide, +97 mL on rituximab), and the adjusted difference of −40 mL (95% CI −153 to 74; p=0.49) showed rituximab was not superior; quality-of-life scores improved clinically importantly in both groups, survival, progression-free survival, and time to treatment failure did not differ, and deaths were three (6%) on rituximab versus two (4%) on cyclophosphamide, all from complications of the underlying diseases. The tolerability gap was real: 445 adverse events were reported on rituximab versus 646 on cyclophosphamide, serious adverse events numbered 29 versus 33, and corticosteroid exposure over 48 weeks was lower with rituximab. A 2025 meta-analysis of the head-to-head literature (six studies) likewise found no significant difference in FVC change (weighted mean difference 0.86, 95% CI −1.51 to 3.24), a possible DLCO advantage for rituximab (6.43, 95% CI 1.62 to 11.23) resting on only three studies, and fewer adverse events with rituximab. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: a single phase 2b trial carries the comparison — rituximab is a legitimate alternative where cyclophosphamide's toxicity is the deciding concern, not a more effective drug.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single double-blind phase 2b trial found rituximab matched cyclophosphamide on lung-function improvement in CTD-ILD with fewer adverse events and lower steroid exposure; superiority was not shown

title: Pirfenidone in progressive fibrotic lung disease beyond IPF (RELIEF): FVC decline slowed on a rank analysis in a trial stopped early for futility — median difference 1.69 points with an interval crossing zero
question: In patients with progressive fibrotic interstitial lung diseases other than idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis who are not responding to standard therapy, does pirfenidone slow forced vital capacity decline compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a real but fragile signal from one stopped-early trial. In RELIEF (Behr J et al., PMID: 33798455), 127 patients with progressive fibrotic ILD other than IPF were randomised to pirfenidone or placebo for 48 weeks before the trial was terminated early for futility at an interim analysis triggered by slow recruitment. The prespecified rank ANCOVA showed significantly less decline in FVC % predicted on pirfenidone (p=0.043), and the slope analysis estimated a difference of 3.53 FVC % predicted (95% CI 0.21 to 6.86) — yet the median difference for the primary endpoint was 1.69 FVC % predicted (95% CI -0.65 to 4.03), an interval that crosses zero. Deaths were 1 of 64 (2%) on pirfenidone versus 5 of 63 (8%) on placebo, far too few to read. A 2024 meta-analysis of antifibrotics in non-IPF progressive fibrosing ILD (Chong WH et al., PMID: 39089077) found less FVC decline with antifibrotics overall but substantially more gastrointestinal harm (nausea/vomiting 54.2% versus 20.3%; diarrhoea 65.2% versus 27.6%; discontinuation 18.4% versus 9.9%). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): pirfenidone probably attenuates FVC decline in progressive non-IPF fibrotic ILD, but the one pirfenidone trial was small, stopped early, and its headline interval includes no effect — Tier C.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one early-terminated phase 2b trial (RELIEF) showed slower FVC decline on pirfenidone in non-IPF progressive fibrotic ILD, with a primary-endpoint interval crossing zero

title: Nalbuphine for IPF cough (CORAL): objective cough frequency fell 48–60% relative across doses versus 17% on placebo in six weeks — one phase 2b trial, adverse-event rates not in the abstract
question: In patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and chronic cough, does extended-release nalbuphine reduce cough frequency compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a large, dose-ordered effect on objectively counted cough in a single phase 2b trial. In CORAL (Molyneaux PL et al., PMID: 41569557), 165 patients with IPF and chronic cough were randomised to nalbuphine extended-release 27 mg, 54 mg, or 108 mg twice daily or placebo for 6 weeks. Mean relative decreases in 24-hour cough frequency were 47.9% (27 mg, P=.008), 53.4% (54 mg, P<.001), and 60.2% (108 mg, P<.001), compared with 16.9% on placebo; in absolute terms cough fell from 24.6 to 11.9, 28.0 to 14.9, and 31.5 to 11.9 coughs per hour across the dose groups, versus 29.4 to 28.1 on placebo. Patient-reported cough frequency improved significantly at the two higher doses (-40.6% and -40.2% versus -21.9% on placebo) but not at 27 mg (-31.4%, P=.14). The published abstract reports no adverse-event rates, so the tolerability price of an opioid antitussive cannot be weighed from this record. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): nalbuphine ER substantially reduces objectively measured cough in IPF over six weeks; durability, safety rates, and any effect beyond cough counting are unshown — Tier C.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one phase 2b trial (CORAL) showed dose-ordered 48–60% relative reductions in objective cough frequency versus 17% on placebo at six weeks

title: Sildenafil in advanced IPF (STEP-IPF): the walk-distance primary endpoint was missed — 10% versus 7% improved by 20% or more (P=0.39) — with small secondary gains in oxygenation, breathlessness and quality of life
question: In patients with advanced idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, does sildenafil improve six-minute walk distance and breathlessness compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — on the outcome the trial was built around. In STEP-IPF (Zisman DA et al., PMID: 20484178), 180 patients with advanced IPF (diffusing capacity under 35% predicted) were randomised to sildenafil or placebo for 12 weeks. The primary outcome — an increase of 20% or more in 6-minute walk distance — occurred in 9 of 89 patients (10%) on sildenafil versus 6 of 91 (7%) on placebo (P=0.39). Small but significant differences favoured sildenafil for arterial oxygenation, diffusing capacity, degree of dyspnoea, and quality of life, and serious adverse events were similar between groups. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): sildenafil did not deliver the prespecified walk-distance benefit in advanced IPF; the secondary signals are hypothesis-generating only — Tier C, a single trial.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — STEP-IPF missed its primary walk-distance endpoint (10% versus 7% responders, P=0.39), with only small secondary-outcome differences favouring sildenafil

title: High-dose N-acetylcysteine added to prednisone plus azathioprine in IPF (IFIGENIA): vital capacity decline slowed by 0.18 litres at one year — on a background regimen later abandoned, in a single trial
question: In idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, does high-dose N-acetylcysteine added to prednisone and azathioprine slow the decline in vital capacity compared with the same immunosuppression without N-acetylcysteine?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for the lung-function measures, in a trial whose background therapy is no longer used. In IFIGENIA (Demedts M et al., PMID: 16306520), 182 patients with IPF were randomised to high-dose acetylcysteine 600 mg three times daily or placebo, each added to prednisone plus azathioprine, for one year. At 12 months the absolute differences in change from baseline favouring acetylcysteine were 0.18 litres (95% CI 0.03 to 0.32) for vital capacity — a 9% relative difference, P=0.02 — and 0.75 mmol/min/kPa (95% CI 0.27 to 1.23) for diffusing capacity — a 24% relative difference, P=0.003. Mortality was 9% on acetylcysteine versus 11% on placebo (P=0.69), and adverse events did not differ significantly except for fewer myelotoxic effects on acetylcysteine (P=0.03). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): acetylcysteine preserved vital capacity and diffusing capacity on top of immunosuppression in this single trial — Tier C, and the prednisone–azathioprine backbone it was added to has since been abandoned in IPF, which limits what the result can mean today.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — IFIGENIA showed acetylcysteine added to prednisone and azathioprine slowed vital-capacity and DLCO decline at one year, with no mortality difference

title: Methotrexate in acute sarcoidosis: prednisone dose in months 7–12 was a median 8 versus 16 mg/day — in the 15 of 24 patients who stayed on therapy six months, with the all-patient analysis negative
question: In acute pulmonary sarcoidosis requiring treatment, is methotrexate steroid-sparing compared with prednisone alone?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — a steroid-sparing signal that survives only in a completers analysis of a very small trial. Baughman RP et al. (PMID: 10746262) randomised 24 patients with new-onset symptomatic sarcoidosis starting prednisone to methotrexate or placebo for one year, with a predetermined prednisone taper. Only 15 patients received at least six months of therapy and were evaluated. Among them, median prednisone dose in the second six months was 8 mg/day (range 1–22) on methotrexate versus 16 mg/day (range 11–22) on placebo (p<0.01 between groups), with less weight gain on methotrexate and no difference in toxicity. Crucially, the difference was not seen when all patients including dropouts were analysed. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): methotrexate may halve the maintenance prednisone dose in acute sarcoidosis after six months, but the evidence is 15 analysed patients with a negative all-patient analysis — Tier C.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — one tiny trial found lower second-half prednisone doses with methotrexate in completers only (median 8 versus 16 mg/day), with the all-patient analysis negative

title: Mucoactive agents including hypertonic saline in non-CF bronchiectasis: pooled exacerbations did not fall (mean difference -0.40/year, interval crossing zero) and FEV1 rose a small 3.23% predicted — at very low certainty
question: In non-cystic-fibrosis bronchiectasis, does inhaled hypertonic saline improve lung function, exacerbations, and quality of life compared with isotonic saline or usual care?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — the pooled record does not show the outcome patients care about most. The 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of mucoactive agents in bronchiectasis (McCullough B et al., PMID: 42342264) pooled seven randomised studies (n=1,259) reporting exacerbations and found no statistically significant difference in annualised exacerbation incidence (mean difference -0.40 per patient per year, 95% CI -1.04 to 0.24; p=0.22; I²=91%; very low certainty), while nine studies (n=767) showed a small increase in FEV1 % predicted of 3.23% (95% CI 0.31 to 6.15; p=0.03; very low certainty), with no significant differences in quality of life or adverse events. The earlier review of mucoactives in chronic non-CF lung disease (Tarrant BJ et al., PMID: 28397992) reported that normal and hypertonic saline improved spirometry, health-related quality of life, and sputum burden in non-CF bronchiectasis, while dornase alfa was detrimental there. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): hypertonic saline may give small lung-function and symptom gains in bronchiectasis, but an exacerbation benefit is unproven and the certainty is very low — Tier C.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — mucoactive therapy including hypertonic saline showed a small pooled FEV1 gain but no significant exacerbation reduction in bronchiectasis, at very low certainty

title: Talc through an indwelling pleural catheter (IPC-PLUS): pleurodesis at day 35 in 43% versus 23% with the catheter alone (HR 2.20) — no difference in hospital days, mortality, or adverse events
question: In patients with malignant pleural effusion, does administering talc slurry through an indwelling pleural catheter increase pleurodesis success compared with the catheter alone?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a doubling of pleurodesis success in one well-run trial, on a procedural endpoint. In IPC-PLUS (Bhatnagar R et al., PMID: 29617585), patients with malignant pleural effusion and no substantial lung entrapment at 10 days after catheter insertion were randomised to 4 g talc slurry or placebo through the indwelling pleural catheter as outpatients. Successful pleurodesis at day 35 occurred in 30 of 69 patients (43%) on talc versus 16 of 70 (23%) on placebo (hazard ratio 2.20, 95% CI 1.23 to 3.92; P=0.008). There were no significant differences in effusion size or complexity, inpatient days, mortality, or adverse events, and no significant excess of catheter blockages with talc. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): talc via the catheter roughly doubles the chance of pleurodesis by day 35 without added harm in this trial — Tier C, a single trial, and pleurodesis is a mechanical endpoint rather than breathlessness or survival.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — IPC-PLUS showed talc through an indwelling pleural catheter raised day-35 pleurodesis from 23% to 43% (HR 2.20), with no difference in hospital days, mortality, or adverse events

title: Surgery for pleural empyema (Cochrane): no mortality difference versus tube drainage in 8 small trials (391 patients) — hospital stay was shorter with VATS in adults, by a mean 5.90 days with thoracotomy in the one child trial
question: In pleural infection (empyema), does early video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery improve drainage, hospital stay, and mortality compared with chest-tube drainage with or without fibrinolytics?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for hospital stay only; survival was not shown to differ. The Cochrane review of surgical versus non-surgical management for pleural empyema (Redden MD et al., PMID: 28304084) included eight randomised trials with 391 participants — six in children and two in adults — comparing tube thoracostomy drainage, with or without intrapleural fibrinolytics, against video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS) or thoracotomy. For VATS versus tube drainage (seven pooled studies) there was no statistically significant difference in mortality or procedural complications in adults or children; mortality data were sparse — one study reported one death in each arm and seven reported none. Hospital stay was significantly shorter with VATS, with the subgroup result clear in adults and insufficient evidence in children; the single thoracotomy-versus-drainage trial in children found a mean 5.90 days shorter stay and fewer procedural complications with thoracotomy. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): early surgery shortens hospital stay in empyema without a demonstrated mortality advantage, on low-to-moderate quality evidence dominated by paediatric trials — Tier C.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — Cochrane review of 8 trials found shorter hospital stay with surgery (VATS/thoracotomy) versus tube drainage in empyema, but no mortality difference, on sparse mostly paediatric data

title: CPAP in older adults with sleep apnoea (PREDICT): sleepiness fell by 2.1 Epworth points at 3 months and 2.0 at 12 months — quality-adjusted life-years did not differ (0.01, interval crossing zero)
question: In older adults with obstructive sleep apnoea, does CPAP improve sleepiness, quality of life, and cognitive function compared with best supportive care?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for sleepiness, the symptom CPAP is prescribed for, in the age group trials usually exclude. In PREDICT (McMillan A et al., PMID: 25172769), 278 patients aged 65 years or older with newly diagnosed obstructive sleep apnoea syndrome were randomised to CPAP plus best supportive care or best supportive care alone for 12 months. CPAP reduced the Epworth sleepiness score by 2.1 points (95% CI -3.0 to -1.3; p<0.0001) at 3 months and by 2.0 points (95% CI -2.8 to -1.2; p<0.0001) at 12 months, with larger effects in patients with higher CPAP use or higher baseline sleepiness. Quality-adjusted life-years were similar (treatment effect 0.01, 95% CI -0.03 to 0.04; p=0.787), mood, functionality, nocturia, accidents, cognitive function, and cardiovascular events were unchanged, and 37 serious adverse events occurred on CPAP versus 22 on supportive care — all classified as unrelated to the trial. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): CPAP durably reduces sleepiness in older patients with OSA; broader quality-of-life, cognitive, and cardiovascular gains were not shown — Tier C, a single trial.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — PREDICT showed CPAP reduced sleepiness by about 2 Epworth points sustained to 12 months in patients 65 and older, without quality-of-life, cognitive, or cardiovascular-event gains

title: Bariatric surgery for obstructive sleep apnoea: cohorts show apnoea remission in 65% — but the one randomised trial found no significant AHI advantage over conventional weight loss despite 27.8 kg versus 5.1 kg lost, so apnoea usually persists
question: In obese adults with obstructive sleep apnoea, does weight-loss (bariatric) surgery reduce apnoea severity compared with conservative weight management, and how often does apnoea persist after surgery?
balance: SPLIT — the observational and randomised records point in different directions. In the only randomised trial (Dixon JB et al., PMID: 22990273), 60 obese patients with recently diagnosed OSA lost a mean of 27.8 kg (95% CI 20.9 to 34.7) with laparoscopic adjustable gastric banding versus 5.1 kg (95% CI 0.8 to 9.3) with a conventional weight-loss programme over two years — yet the apnoea–hypopnoea index fell by 25.5 events/hour with surgery versus 14.0 events/hour conventionally, a between-group difference of -11.5 events/hour (95% CI -28.3 to 5.3; P=.18), not significant. In the pooled cohort literature (Al Oweidat K et al., PMID: 37145243; 32 studies, 2,310 patients), bariatric surgery was associated with an AHI reduction of 19.3 events/hour (weighted mean difference -19.3, 95% CI -23.9 to -14.6) and an OSA remission rate of 65% (95% CI 54% to 76%) — meaning roughly a third of patients still had apnoea after surgery even in the favourable uncontrolled data. PROPOSED SPLIT: surgery produces large weight loss and lower AHI on average, apnoea persists in a substantial minority, and superiority over good conservative care for AHI itself is unproven by randomisation — Tier C.
stamp: SPLIT — cohort data show large AHI falls and 65% remission after bariatric surgery, but the single RCT found no significant AHI advantage over conventional weight loss (-11.5 events/h, 95% CI -28.3 to 5.3), and apnoea persists in about a third

title: Acetazolamide in sleep apnoea: apnoea–hypopnoea index fell clearly in central sleep apnoea (mean difference -22.60) but not significantly in obstructive sleep apnoea (mean difference -10.29, interval from -33.34 to +12.77)
question: In adults with obstructive sleep apnoea, does acetazolamide reduce the apnoea–hypopnoea index compared with placebo?
balance: SPLIT — by apnoea type, and the obstructive half of the split is the null. The systematic review and meta-analysis of acetazolamide in sleep apnoea at sea level (Ni YN et al., PMID: 33538687) pooled 15 controlled trials with only 256 patients in total. Acetazolamide reduced the apnoea–hypopnoea index overall (mean difference -15.82, 95% CI -21.91 to -9.74; P<.00001) and in central sleep apnoea (mean difference -22.60, 95% CI -29.11 to -16.09; P<.00001), but in obstructive sleep apnoea the reduction was not significant (mean difference -10.29, 95% CI -33.34 to 12.77; P=.38). It also improved arterial oxygen (mean difference 11.62, 95% CI 9.13 to 14.11), mean oxygen saturation (mean difference 1.78, 95% CI 0.53 to 3.04), and total sleep time (mean difference 25.74 minutes, 95% CI 4.10 to 47.38) across the pooled population, with high heterogeneity flagged by the authors. PROPOSED SPLIT: acetazolamide lowers AHI in central sleep apnoea; for obstructive sleep apnoea — the question on this shelf — a benefit is unproven on 256 pooled patients — Tier C.
stamp: SPLIT — acetazolamide reduced AHI in central sleep apnoea (mean difference -22.60) but the obstructive sleep apnoea estimate was non-significant (mean difference -10.29, 95% CI -33.34 to 12.77) in a 15-trial, 256-patient meta-analysis

title: Sulthiame in obstructive sleep apnoea: AHI fell 41% relative on 400 mg and 32% relative on 200 mg versus 5% on placebo in four weeks — with paraesthesia in 79% and 67% versus 18%, in one small dose-guiding trial
question: In adults with obstructive sleep apnoea, does the carbonic anhydrase inhibitor sulthiame reduce apnoea severity and improve oxygenation compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one of the largest drug effects on AHI reported, from one small four-week trial with a heavy side-effect signature. Hedner J et al. (PMID: 35202553) randomised patients with moderate-to-severe OSA who did not tolerate positive airway pressure to sulthiame 400 mg (n=34), sulthiame 200 mg (n=12), or placebo (n=22) for four weeks. The apnoea–hypopnoea index fell from 55.2 to 33.0 events/hour on 400 mg (a 41.0% relative reduction) and from 61.1 to 40.6 events/hour on 200 mg (a 32.1% relative reduction), versus 53.9 to 50.9 events/hour on placebo (a 5.4% relative reduction; P<0.001 for both dose comparisons); relative reductions are labelled relative as reported. Mean overnight oxygen saturation improved by 1.1% at both doses. But intermittent paraesthesia was reported by 79% on 400 mg, 67% on 200 mg, and 18% on placebo; dyspnoea occurred in 18% on 400 mg; and six patients in the higher-dose group withdrew because of adverse events. A prespecified endotypic analysis of the same trial programme (Hoff E et al., PMID: 37776971) showed sulthiame reduced loop gain and improved ventilation measures that correlated with the AHI fall. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): sulthiame substantially reduces AHI and improves oxygenation over four weeks, at a paraesthesia cost most patients will feel — Tier C, a single trial programme.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one small 4-week RCT showed sulthiame cut AHI by 41% relative (400 mg) and 32% relative (200 mg) versus 5% on placebo, with paraesthesia in up to 79%

title: Dornase alfa in cystic fibrosis (Fuchs): exacerbations needing intravenous antibiotics occurred in 27% on placebo versus 22% once daily and 19% twice daily over 24 weeks, with FEV1 up about 5.8%
question: In cystic fibrosis, does daily inhaled recombinant human DNase (dornase alfa) reduce pulmonary exacerbations and slow lung-function decline compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the founding trial of a now-standard therapy, still a single trial on this shelf. Fuchs HJ et al. (PMID: 7503821) randomised 968 adults and children with cystic fibrosis to recombinant human DNase once daily, twice daily, or placebo for 24 weeks as outpatients. One or more exacerbations of respiratory symptoms requiring parenteral antibiotics occurred in 27% of patients on placebo, 22% on once-daily DNase, and 19% on twice-daily DNase — age-adjusted relative risk reductions of 28% (P=0.04) and 37% (P<0.01) respectively, relative reductions labelled relative with the absolute rates alongside. FEV1 improved during the study by a mean of 5.8% with once-daily and 5.6% with twice-daily dosing. No patient had anaphylaxis; voice alteration and laryngitis were more frequent on DNase but rarely severe and resolved within 21 days. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): daily dornase alfa modestly reduces exacerbations and improves lung function over 24 weeks — Tier C by the single-trial rule, despite the therapy's later standard-of-care status.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one large RCT (968 patients) showed dornase alfa cut exacerbations from 27% (placebo) to 22% once daily and 19% twice daily over 24 weeks, with FEV1 up about 5.8%

title: Intermittent inhaled tobramycin in cystic fibrosis (Ramsey): FEV1 rose 10% versus a 2% fall on placebo across two concordant trials, and hospitalisation risk fell 26% relative over 24 weeks
question: In cystic fibrosis patients chronically infected with Pseudomonas aeruginosa, does intermittent inhaled tobramycin improve lung function and reduce exacerbations and hospitalisation compared with placebo?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — two concordant double-blind trials reported in a single record. Ramsey BW et al. (PMID: 9878641) conducted two multicentre, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials totalling 520 patients with cystic fibrosis and Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection, using 300 mg inhaled tobramycin or placebo twice daily in three four-weeks-on, four-weeks-off cycles over 24 weeks. FEV1 rose by an average of 10% at week 20 from week 0 on tobramycin versus a 2% decline on placebo (P<0.001). Sputum Pseudomonas density fell by 0.8 log10 colony-forming units per gram on tobramycin versus a rise of 0.3 on placebo (P<0.001), and patients on tobramycin were 26% less likely to be hospitalised (95% CI 2 to 43) — a relative reduction, reported without absolute hospitalisation rates in the abstract. No detectable ototoxic or nephrotoxic effects and no serum accumulation were seen, though the proportion of isolates with a tobramycin minimum inhibitory concentration of 8 µg/mL or higher rose from 25% to 32% on tobramycin versus falling from 20% to 17% on placebo. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): intermittent inhaled tobramycin improves lung function, lowers bacterial density, and reduces hospitalisation in chronically infected cystic fibrosis, with a measurable resistance drift as the price to watch.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — two concordant double-blind trials (520 patients) showed intermittent inhaled tobramycin raised FEV1 by 10% versus a 2% placebo decline and reduced hospitalisation risk by 26% relative

title: Lumacaftor–ivacaftor in Phe508del-homozygous cystic fibrosis (TRAFFIC/TRANSPORT): FEV1 improved by 2.6–4.0 percentage points and pulmonary exacerbations ran 30–39% lower relative across two phase 3 trials
question: In cystic fibrosis patients homozygous for Phe508del, does lumacaftor–ivacaftor improve lung function and reduce exacerbations compared with placebo?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — two concordant phase 3 trials with a modest lung-function gain and a clearer exacerbation gain. Wainwright CE et al. (PMID: 25981758) report TRAFFIC and TRANSPORT, two randomised double-blind trials totalling 1,108 patients aged 12 years or older with cystic fibrosis homozygous for Phe508del, comparing lumacaftor (600 mg once daily or 400 mg every 12 hours) plus ivacaftor 250 mg every 12 hours against placebo for 24 weeks, from a mean baseline FEV1 of 61% predicted. The mean absolute improvement in FEV1 % predicted differed from placebo by 2.6 to 4.0 percentage points across the dose groups in both studies (P<0.001) — a 4.3 to 6.7% mean relative treatment difference, labelled relative. Pooled pulmonary exacerbation rates were 30 to 39% lower in the lumacaftor–ivacaftor groups than on placebo (relative reductions), and rates of events leading to hospitalisation or intravenous antibiotics were also lower. Adverse events were generally similar between groups, but discontinuation due to an adverse event was 4.2% on lumacaftor–ivacaftor versus 1.6% on placebo. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): the first CFTR corrector–potentiator combination delivered a small FEV1 gain and a substantial relative reduction in exacerbations for Phe508del-homozygous patients.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — TRAFFIC and TRANSPORT (1,108 patients) showed FEV1 gains of 2.6–4.0 percentage points and 30–39% lower relative pulmonary exacerbation rates with lumacaftor–ivacaftor

title: Azithromycin in cystic fibrosis with chronic Pseudomonas (Saiman): FEV1 rose 0.097 L versus 0.003 L on placebo and exacerbation hazard fell (HR 0.65) over 24 weeks — with nausea, diarrhoea and wheeze each 13–17% more common
question: In cystic fibrosis patients chronically infected with Pseudomonas aeruginosa, does thrice-weekly azithromycin improve lung function and reduce exacerbations compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single well-conducted trial with a small lung-function gain, a clearer exacerbation signal, and a noticeable gastrointestinal price. Saiman L et al. (PMID: 14519709) randomised 185 patients aged 6 years or older with cystic fibrosis and at least one year of Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection to azithromycin 250 mg or 500 mg by weight, three days a week, or placebo, for 168 days. FEV1 rose by a mean of 0.097 L on azithromycin versus 0.003 L on placebo (mean difference 0.094 L, 95% CI 0.023 to 0.165; P=.009). The hazard of a pulmonary exacerbation was lower on azithromycin (hazard ratio 0.65, 95% CI 0.44 to 0.95; P=.03), and patients gained an average of 0.7 kg more weight (95% CI 0.1 to 1.4; P=.02). Against that, nausea occurred in 17% more participants on azithromycin (P=.01), diarrhoea in 15% more (P=.009), and wheezing in 13% more (P=.007). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): thrice-weekly azithromycin modestly improves lung function and reduces exacerbation hazard in chronically infected cystic fibrosis — Tier C, a single trial.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one RCT (185 patients) showed thrice-weekly azithromycin improved FEV1 by 0.094 L and reduced exacerbation hazard (HR 0.65) in CF with chronic Pseudomonas, with more nausea, diarrhoea and wheeze

title: Physiotherapy and speech-therapy cough suppression (PSALTI): cough quality of life improved by 1.53 Leicester points and objective cough frequency fell 41% relative versus lifestyle advice in refractory chronic cough
question: In adults with refractory chronic cough, does physiotherapy and speech-and-language-therapy cough-suppression treatment reduce cough frequency and improve quality of life compared with healthy-lifestyle advice?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a non-drug treatment that beat an active control on both quality of life and objectively counted cough, in one small trial. Chamberlain Mitchell SA et al. (PMID: 27682331) randomised 75 patients with refractory chronic cough to four weekly one-to-one sessions of a physiotherapy and speech-and-language-therapy intervention (education, laryngeal hygiene and hydration, cough-suppression techniques, breathing exercises, and psychoeducational counselling) or to healthy-lifestyle advice. Health-related quality of life on the Leicester Cough Questionnaire improved by 1.53 points more with the intervention (95% CI 0.21 to 2.85; p=0.024) at week 4, and 24-hour cough frequency decreased by 41% relative to control (p=0.030) — a relative reduction as reported, with the confidence interval printed in the record as 36% to 95%. Improvements within the intervention group were sustained to three months, and capsaicin cough-reflex sensitivity did not differ between groups. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): PSALTI improves cough quality of life and reduces objective cough frequency in refractory chronic cough — Tier C, a single small trial with an assessor-blinded (single-blind) design.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one RCT (75 patients) showed PSALTI improved Leicester Cough Questionnaire scores by 1.53 points and cut objective cough frequency by 41% relative versus lifestyle advice

title: Home treatment triage for low-risk pulmonary embolism (HOME-PE): Hestia was non-inferior to sPESI — 30-day adverse outcomes 3.82% versus 3.57% per protocol, with about 37–38% of patients treated at home under either rule
question: In low-risk acute pulmonary embolism, does a Hestia-based home-treatment strategy perform as well as a simplified (sPESI-based) strategy for safe outpatient care?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — a large strategy trial that found the two triage rules interchangeable in practice. In HOME-PE (Roy PM et al., PMID: 34363386), 1,975 normotensive patients with acute pulmonary embolism at 26 hospitals in four European countries were randomised to triage by the Hestia rule or by the simplified Pulmonary Embolism Severity Index (sPESI), with discharge home if the tool was negative and the responsible physician agreed. In the per-protocol population, the 30-day composite of recurrent venous thromboembolism, major bleeding, or all-cause death occurred in 3.82% (34 of 891) in the Hestia arm versus 3.57% (32 of 896) in the sPESI arm (P=0.004 for non-inferiority against a 2.5% absolute margin). In intention-to-treat, 38.4% of Hestia patients (378 of 984) versus 36.6% of sPESI patients (361 of 986) were treated at home (P=0.41), with 30-day composite rates among home-treated patients of 1.33% (5 of 375) and 1.11% (4 of 359); no recurrent or fatal pulmonary embolism occurred in either home-treatment arm. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): Hestia and sPESI triage are equally safe routes to home treatment for roughly a third of normotensive PE patients — Tier C, a single (large) strategy trial.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — HOME-PE (1,975 patients) found Hestia triage non-inferior to sPESI for 30-day outcomes (3.82% versus 3.57%), with similar home-treatment rates (38.4% versus 36.6%)

title: Nintedanib plus add-on pirfenidone in IPF (INJOURNEY): tolerable over 12 weeks — gastrointestinal events 69.8% versus 52.9% on nintedanib alone — with only an exploratory FVC signal (-13.3 versus -40.9 mL)
question: In idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, is combining nintedanib with pirfenidone safe and does it slow lung-function decline more than either drug alone?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — safety was the question this trial could answer, and efficacy it could not. In INJOURNEY (Vancheri C et al., PMID: 28889759), 104 patients with IPF who had tolerated a 4–5-week nintedanib run-in were randomised open-label to nintedanib 150 mg twice daily with add-on pirfenidone (titrated to 801 mg three times daily) or nintedanib alone for 12 weeks. The primary endpoint — on-treatment gastrointestinal adverse events — occurred in 37 of 53 patients (69.8%) on the combination versus 27 of 51 (52.9%) on nintedanib alone, a profile the authors describe as manageable and in line with each drug's known effects; nintedanib plasma concentrations were similar with and without pirfenidone. The exploratory efficacy readout was a mean FVC change at week 12 of -13.3 mL (SE 17.4) on the combination versus -40.9 mL (SE 31.4) on nintedanib alone — descriptive only, from 48 and 44 patients, in an open-label 12-week window far too short and small to establish added benefit. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): the combination is tolerable in run-in-selected patients; whether it slows decline more than a single antifibrotic is unproven — Tier C.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — INJOURNEY showed the nintedanib–pirfenidone combination was tolerable over 12 weeks (GI events 69.8% versus 52.9%), with efficacy limited to an exploratory, descriptive FVC difference

title: Continuous alternating inhaled antibiotics in cystic fibrosis: the one head-to-head trial (90 patients) found no difference from intermittent tobramycin on any outcome — while inhaled antibiotics versus placebo do cut exacerbations (RR 0.66)
question: In cystic fibrosis with chronic Pseudomonas infection, do continuous alternating inhaled antibiotic regimens suppress infection better than intermittent single-agent therapy?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — for the alternating-versus-intermittent comparison specifically. The Cochrane review of inhaled anti-pseudomonal antibiotics for long-term therapy in cystic fibrosis (Smith S et al., PMID: 36373968) included 18 trials with 3,042 participants; exactly one trial (90 participants) compared intermittent tobramycin with continuous tobramycin alternating with aztreonam, and it found no differences between groups in any outcome. The wider review found inhaled antibiotics may improve lung function versus placebo (4 trials, 814 participants) and may reduce exacerbation frequency (risk ratio 0.66, 95% CI 0.47 to 0.93; 3 trials, 946 participants; low-certainty evidence) — so suppressive inhaled therapy itself has support, but intensifying it into a continuous alternating regimen showed no added benefit in the only direct test. Other single-trial comparisons in the review: aztreonam lysine probably improved FEV1 % predicted versus tobramycin by a mean difference of -3.40% as printed (95% CI -6.63 to -0.17; 1 trial, 273 participants; moderate-certainty evidence, with endpoint-definition caveats), and levofloxacin produced fewer hospitalisations for respiratory exacerbations than tobramycin (risk ratio 0.62, 95% CI 0.40 to 0.98; 1 trial, 282 participants). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): continuous alternating regimens have not beaten intermittent single-agent therapy where directly compared — Tier C, resting on one 90-patient comparison inside a low-certainty review.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the single trial comparing continuous alternating with intermittent inhaled antibiotics in CF (90 patients, within a Cochrane review) found no difference on any outcome

title: Mucolytics for children with chronic suppurative lung disease (Cochrane): one small crossover trial of 3% hypertonic saline reported 2.50 versus 7.80 exacerbations per child-year — at very low certainty and high risk of bias
question: In children with chronic suppurative lung disease and bronchiectasis, do mucolytic therapies improve lung function or reduce exacerbations?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — a strikingly large effect from exactly the kind of trial that most often misleads. The Cochrane review of mucolytics for children with chronic suppurative lung disease (O'Farrell HE et al., PMID: 40152354) found only one eligible randomised trial: a crossover study of nebulised 3% hypertonic saline before chest physiotherapy versus physiotherapy alone, each phase eight weeks, with analysable first-phase data for 52 children (26 per arm) with non-cystic-fibrosis bronchiectasis. The mean number of exacerbations per child-year was 2.50 (SD 0.64) on hypertonic saline versus 7.80 (SD 1.05) on control (mean difference -5.30, 95% CI -5.77 to -4.83), and improvement in FEV1 % predicted was greater on saline (mean difference 9.11%, 95% CI 6.11 to 12.11), as was FVC improvement (mean difference 6.23%, 95% CI 3.33 to 9.13) — all graded very low-certainty evidence from a study the reviewers judged at high risk of bias (unblinding, missing data, deviations, and reporting bias). No quality-of-life data existed, no studies covered exacerbation-state treatment, oral mucolytics, or protracted bacterial bronchitis, and no dropouts due to adverse events were reported. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): hypertonic saline may help children with bronchiectasis, but the entire evidence base is one small high-bias crossover trial — Tier C.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — a Cochrane review found a single small high-risk-of-bias crossover trial (52 children) reporting far fewer exacerbations with 3% hypertonic saline, at very low certainty

title: Targeted lung denervation in severe COPD (AIRFLOW-2): respiratory adverse events 32% versus 71% with sham in the 3–6.5-month window (OR 0.19) — but 83% versus 90% over the full 12.5 months, with symptoms and lung function unchanged
question: In patients with severe COPD, does targeted lung denervation reduce exacerbations and improve quality of life compared with sham bronchoscopy?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a real reduction in a prespecified safety-window event rate, which fades when the whole follow-up is counted. In AIRFLOW-2 (Slebos DJ et al., PMID: 31404499), 82 patients with symptomatic moderate-to-severe COPD (FEV1 30–60% predicted) were randomised double-blind to targeted lung denervation (bronchoscopic radiofrequency ablation of parasympathetic nerves) plus optimal pharmacotherapy or sham bronchoscopy. During the predefined 3- to 6.5-month window, respiratory adverse events (a composite including exacerbation, wheeze, bronchitis, dyspnoea, pneumonia, and respiratory failure) occurred in 32% on denervation versus 71% on sham (P=0.008; odds ratio 0.19, 95% CI 0.0750 to 0.4923; P=0.0006). Over 0 to 12.5 months, however, the rates were 83% versus 90% (P=0.52). The risk of COPD exacerbation requiring hospitalisation over 0–12.5 months was lower with denervation (hazard ratio 0.35, 95% CI 0.13 to 0.99; P=0.039), but there was no statistical difference in time to first moderate or severe exacerbation, patient-reported symptoms, or other physiological measures. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): denervation reduced hospitalised exacerbations in this small sham-controlled trial, without improving symptoms or lung function — Tier C, a single trial, and the quality-of-life half of the question is answered negatively by this record.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one small sham-controlled RCT (82 patients) showed fewer respiratory adverse events in a prespecified window (32% versus 71%) and fewer hospitalised exacerbations (HR 0.35), with no symptom or lung-function improvement

title: Isolated subsegmental pulmonary embolism: anticoagulation has never been shown to cut recurrence (RR 0.61, interval crossing 1) but triples bleeding (RR 3.10) in pooled observational data — while surveillance itself carried a 3.1% 90-day recurrence in a prospective cohort
question: In patients with isolated subsegmental pulmonary embolism and no deep-vein thrombosis, does anticoagulation improve outcomes compared with clinical surveillance alone?
balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — for routine anticoagulation: the pooled record shows a bleeding price without a proven recurrence benefit, though surveillance is not free either. The 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis (Nicoletto M et al., PMID: 41962426) pooled observational comparisons of anticoagulation versus clinical surveillance in isolated subsegmental pulmonary embolism: venous thromboembolism recurrence did not differ significantly (risk ratio 0.61, 95% CI 0.28 to 1.35; 8 studies, 674 patients), all-cause mortality did not differ (risk ratio 0.70, 95% CI 0.44 to 1.12), but any bleeding was significantly more frequent with anticoagulation (risk ratio 3.10, 95% CI 1.39 to 6.88; 9 studies, 862 patients), with a similar association for major bleeding. The surveillance side's own risk is quantified by the prospective cohort of Le Gal G et al. (PMID: 34807722): among 266 low-risk patients with isolated subsegmental PE and no deep-vein thrombosis managed without anticoagulation, recurrent venous thromboembolism occurred in 3.1% (95% CI 1.6% to 6.1%) over 90 days — 2.1% (95% CI 0.8% to 5.5%) for a single subsegmental embolism and 5.7% (95% CI 2.2% to 14.4%) for multiple — with no fatal recurrent pulmonary embolism; recruitment was stopped early because the predefined stopping rule was met. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm): on current observational evidence, routine anticoagulation for isolated subsegmental PE buys bleeding without demonstrated protection — Tier C, observational evidence throughout, and a randomised trial is still owed.
stamp: POSSIBLE (harm) — pooled observational data show anticoagulation for isolated subsegmental PE increases bleeding (RR 3.10) without a significant recurrence reduction (RR 0.61, 95% CI 0.28 to 1.35)

title: Hib conjugate vaccine in Gambian infants: invasive disease cut by 95% and radiological pneumonia by 21% in a 42,848-infant randomised trial
question: In infants in high-burden settings, does Haemophilus influenzae type b conjugate vaccine prevent pneumonia and meningitis versus control?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — in the Gambian double-blind randomised trial of 42,848 infants, three doses of Hib polysaccharide–tetanus protein (PRP-T) conjugate vaccine prevented 95% of all invasive Hib disease (1 case in vaccinees versus 19 in controls), 100% of Hib pneumonia after two or three doses (0 versus 10), and reduced radiologically defined pneumonia of any cause by 21.1% (198 versus 251 cases). Observational evidence since is concordant: a systematic review and meta-analysis of 30 studies in 17 countries estimated vaccine effectiveness against invasive Hib disease of 97% after three doses and against Hib meningitis of 96% after two or three doses. The catch is schedule, not direction: one dose protects far less well (59% against invasive disease), so the benefit belongs to a completed primary series. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): a completed Hib conjugate series prevents nearly all invasive Hib disease and about a fifth of radiological pneumonia in high-burden infancy.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — one large double-blind randomised trial (95% efficacy against invasive disease) concordant with a 30-study observational meta-analysis (97% after three doses)

title: Pneumococcal conjugate vaccines in young children: invasive disease cut by 65–100% across three randomised trials — pneumonia by a fifth, ear infections by only 6%
question: In young children, do pneumococcal conjugate vaccines prevent invasive pneumococcal disease, pneumonia and acute otitis media versus control?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — three randomised trials agree on invasive disease and split honestly on the softer endpoints. In Soweto, a 9-valent conjugate vaccine cut first episodes of vaccine-serotype invasive pneumococcal disease by 83% in children without HIV (3 versus 17 cases) and by 65% in children with HIV (9 versus 26), and radiologically confirmed pneumonia by 20%. In Finland's cluster-randomised FinIP trial, the ten-valent vaccine's effectiveness against vaccine-type invasive disease was 100% on the 3+1 schedule (0 cases) and 92% on 2+1 (1 case, versus 12 in controls). For ear infections the same vaccine class is far weaker: the Finnish otitis trial found 57% fewer episodes caused by vaccine serotypes but only 6% fewer episodes of acute otitis media from any cause (95% CI −4 to 16). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): conjugate vaccines prevent most vaccine-serotype invasive disease and about a fifth of confirmed pneumonia in young children; the ear-infection benefit is real for pneumococcal episodes but small for ear infections overall.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — three randomised trials concordant on invasive disease (65–100% efficacy) and pneumonia (~20%), with a much smaller effect on all-cause otitis media (6%)

title: MenAfriVac mass vaccination: meningitis incidence 2.48 versus 43.8 per 100,000 in Chad, no serogroup A cases in vaccinated regions, and serogroup A carriage eliminated in Burkina Faso
question: In the African meningitis belt, does mass vaccination with the meningococcal A conjugate vaccine (MenAfriVac) reduce meningococcal A carriage and epidemics?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — the evidence is ecological rather than randomised, but it is large, abrupt and biologically coherent. In Chad, roughly 1.8 million people aged 1–29 years were vaccinated with the serogroup A polysaccharide–tetanus toxoid conjugate vaccine (PsA-TT, MenAfriVac) in December 2011; in the 2012 meningitis season, incidence in the three vaccinated regions was 2.48 per 100,000 (57 cases in 2.3 million people) versus 43.8 per 100,000 (3,809 cases in 8.7 million) in unvaccinated regions — an incidence rate ratio of 0.096 (95% CI 0.046–0.198) — and no serogroup A case was reported in the vaccinated regions despite enhanced surveillance. In Burkina Faso, serogroup A carriage, 0.39% at baseline, was not identified at all after mass vaccination in 25,521 oropharyngeal samples, disappearing in unvaccinated people too — the signature of herd immunity. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): mass MenAfriVac campaigns collapse serogroup A meningitis and carriage, including in the unvaccinated.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — community studies in two countries: meningitis incidence rate ratio 0.096 in Chad and serogroup A carriage eliminated (0.39% to none detected) in Burkina Faso

title: A third MMR dose in a university mumps outbreak: attack rate 6.7 versus 14.5 per 1,000 and a 78.1% lower adjusted risk — one observational study, no trial
question: During a mumps outbreak in a vaccinated population, does a third dose of MMR vaccine reduce the risk of mumps versus two doses?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single large observational outbreak study. Among 20,496 students at the University of Iowa during the 2015–2016 outbreak, mumps was diagnosed in 259 students; the attack rate was 6.7 per 1,000 among the 4,783 students who received a third MMR dose during the campaign versus 14.5 per 1,000 among those with two doses (P<0.001). At 28 days after vaccination, a third dose was associated with a 78.1% lower risk of mumps than two doses (adjusted hazard ratio 0.22, 95% CI 0.12–0.39), after adjustment for years since the second dose. The same study shows why outbreaks happen in vaccinated populations: students whose second dose was 13 or more years earlier had more than nine times the risk of mumps. There is no randomised trial of a third dose, and students who came forward for the campaign dose may differ from those who did not. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a third MMR dose probably helps control a mumps outbreak in a young-adult population whose second dose is distant — on one study's evidence, flagged Tier C.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single observational outbreak study: attack rate 6.7 vs 14.5 per 1,000, adjusted hazard ratio 0.22 for a third dose

title: Early BCG for low-birthweight infants: neonatal mortality rate ratio 0.70 in the third trial (not significant alone), 0.62 pooled across three randomised trials
question: In low-birthweight infants in high-mortality settings, does early BCG vaccination at birth reduce neonatal and infant mortality versus delayed BCG?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — three randomised trials in Guinea-Bissau of early BCG-Denmark (Statens Serum Institut) for infants weighing under 2,500 g point the same way, though the largest single trial does not reach significance on its own. In that trial (4,172 infants), early BCG was associated with a neonatal mortality rate ratio of 0.70 (95% CI 0.47–1.04), and 0.66 (0.44–1.00) when follow-up was censored at oral polio vaccine campaigns; infectious-disease mortality fell by 43% (rate ratio 0.57, 0.35–0.93) with no reduction in non-infectious mortality. Pooling all three trials, early BCG reduced neonatal mortality by 38% (rate ratio 0.62, 0.46–0.83) and mortality by 12 months by 16% (0.84, 0.71–1.00). The trials were unblinded, and the pooled estimate leans on two smaller earlier trials. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): early BCG probably reduces neonatal deaths in low-birthweight infants in high-mortality settings, mainly by preventing infectious deaths — a mortality claim, so Tier C.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — three randomised trials pooled: neonatal mortality rate ratio 0.62 (0.46–0.83); largest trial alone 0.70 (0.47–1.04)

title: BCG vaccination in older adults (ACTIVATE): new infections 25.0% versus 42.3% over 12 months — a 198-patient trial stopped at an interim analysis
question: In older adults, does BCG vaccination reduce new infections and respiratory infections versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one small double-blind randomised trial. In ACTIVATE, 198 elderly patients received BCG or placebo at hospital discharge and were followed for 12 months for new infections. The incidence of new infections was 25.0% (95% CI 16.4–36.1) after BCG versus 42.3% (31.9–53.4) after placebo, and the median time to first infection was 16 weeks versus 11 weeks. Most of the protection was against respiratory tract infections of probable viral origin (hazard ratio 0.21, p=0.013). No difference in the frequency of adverse effects was found. The cautions are size and stopping: 198 patients, and the result was reported at an interim analysis, which tends to exaggerate effects. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): BCG revaccination probably reduces infections in older adults over the following year, on a single small trial — Tier C, and the authors themselves call for larger studies.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single small double-blind trial: new infections 25.0% vs 42.3%, respiratory infection hazard ratio 0.21

title: ASSIST peer-led school programme: smoking odds ratio 0.77 at one year (significant) fading to 0.85 at two years — a real but modest and decaying effect
question: In adolescents in schools, does a peer-led anti-smoking programme (ASSIST) reduce uptake of regular smoking versus usual education?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one large cluster-randomised trial, supported weakly by the wider school-programme literature. ASSIST trained influential 12–13-year-olds in 30 schools to act as peer supporters discouraging smoking in informal interactions; 29 schools continued usual education (10,730 students in total). The odds ratio for being a smoker in intervention versus control schools was 0.75 (95% CI 0.55–1.01) immediately after the intervention, 0.77 (0.59–0.99) at one year, and 0.85 (0.72–1.01) at two years — a benefit that is statistically secure only at the one-year point and fades thereafter. The Cochrane review of school-based prevention programmes found a similar overall pattern at longest follow-up (odds ratio 0.88, 0.82–0.96 across programmes), with social-competence curricula doing best. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): peer-led prevention probably delays or reduces smoking uptake modestly for about a year; it is not a durable one-off inoculation.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one large cluster trial: smoking odds ratio 0.77 (0.59–0.99) at 1 year, fading to 0.85 (0.72–1.01) at 2 years; Cochrane school-programme pool 0.88

title: Tobacco taxes: over 100 studies show higher prices cut use, especially in the young and the poor — but the evidence is population studies, not trials, and no single pooled number exists
question: Do tobacco tax and price increases reduce smoking prevalence and cigarette consumption at population level?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — the direction is among the most consistent findings in tobacco control, but the evidence form is weak by this library's standards: no randomised trials exist or could exist, and the reviews report consistency rather than a pooled effect size. Chaloupka and colleagues, assessing well over 100 studies including a growing number from low- and middle-income countries, conclude that significant tax increases that raise prices encourage current users to stop, prevent potential users from starting, and reduce consumption among those who continue, with the greatest impact on the young and the poor. The Community Guide economic review found that a conservative 20% price increase generates substantial healthcare cost savings, with seven of eight modelling studies estimating healthcare savings and three estimating productivity gains. Neither record gives a single pooled percentage for prevalence or consumption that this shelf can print as a verified figure. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): higher tobacco prices almost certainly reduce smoking at population level; the size of the reduction per tax rise varies by country and cannot be stated as one number from these records — Tier C, as a policy claim resting on observational evidence.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — 100+ population studies consistently link higher prices to lower use, but no trials and no pooled effect size in the records

title: Daily aspirin and colorectal cancer 20 years on: colon cancer incidence hazard ratio 0.76 and mortality 0.65 — benefit concentrated in the proximal colon and in those treated 5+ years
question: In average-risk adults, does long-term daily aspirin reduce colorectal cancer incidence and mortality 10–20 years later?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a delayed benefit shown in pooled individual-patient follow-up of randomised trials, with the anatomy and duration caveats on the face. Across four trials of aspirin versus control (14,033 patients, median follow-up 18.3 years), 391 patients (2.8%) developed colorectal cancer; allocation to aspirin reduced the 20-year risk of colon cancer (incidence hazard ratio 0.76, 95% CI 0.60–0.96; mortality 0.65, 0.48–0.88) but not rectal cancer (0.90, 0.63–1.30; mortality 0.80, 0.50–1.28). The benefit was concentrated in the proximal colon (incidence 0.45, 0.28–0.74) and grew with at least five years of scheduled treatment (proximal colon incidence 0.35, 0.20–0.63). A second pooled analysis of 51 trials found cancer deaths reduced overall (odds ratio 0.85, 0.76–0.96), particularly from five years onwards (0.63, 0.49–0.82). These are post-trial observational follow-ups of trials designed for vascular endpoints, in mostly male, vascular-risk populations — not average-risk screening populations randomised for cancer. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): years of daily aspirin probably reduce colon cancer incidence and death a decade or two later; the bleeding price of those years is a separate shelf's question and is not netted off here.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — pooled 20-year follow-up of randomised trials: colon cancer incidence HR 0.76, mortality HR 0.65; no rectal-cancer effect

title: Statins at 75 and over without cardiovascular disease: trial meta-analysis shows vascular events still fall per mmol/L of LDL lowering, but the over-75 primary-prevention evidence is thin and a 46,864-person cohort found nothing without diabetes
question: In adults aged 75 and over without cardiovascular disease, does statin therapy reduce major cardiovascular events versus placebo or usual care?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the trial evidence leans positive but thins exactly where the question asks. The Cholesterol Treatment Trialists' individual-patient meta-analysis of 28 trials (186,854 participants, 14,483 of them older than 75) found statin therapy or a more intensive regimen produced a 21% relative reduction in major vascular events per 1.0 mmol/L (≈39 mg/dL) reduction in LDL cholesterol overall (rate ratio 0.79, 95% CI 0.77–0.81), with significant reductions in all age groups — but the proportional reduction appeared smaller among older people without pre-existing vascular disease (trend p=0.05), and the authors state plainly that there is less direct evidence of benefit among patients older than 75 without occlusive vascular disease. A meta-analysis restricted to primary prevention over 75 (35 trials) found no significant mortality difference on frequentist analysis (p=0.16), though a Bayesian analysis favoured statins (p=0.03). And in a retrospective cohort of 46,864 people aged 75 or over without atherosclerotic disease, statin use in those without diabetes was associated with hazard ratios of 0.94 (0.86–1.04) for cardiovascular events and 0.98 (0.91–1.05) for mortality at ages 75–84 — no measurable benefit. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): statins probably still reduce vascular events after 75 in proportion to LDL lowering, but a mortality benefit in primary prevention at this age is unproven and the direct trial base is small — Tier C.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — CTT meta-analysis: 21% relative reduction in major vascular events per 1 mmol/L (≈39 mg/dL) LDL reduction overall, with less direct evidence over 75 without vascular disease; primary-prevention mortality unproven

title: Folic acid added to enalapril cut first stroke in hypertensive adults in China: 2.7% versus 3.4% over 4.5 years (a 21% relative reduction) — in a low-folate population with no folic-acid food fortification
question: In hypertensive adults in China, does folic acid added to enalapril reduce first stroke versus enalapril alone?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in the one large trial that asked exactly this question, in exactly this population. In CSPPT (Huo Y et al., PMID: 25771069), 20,702 Chinese adults with hypertension and no history of stroke or myocardial infarction were randomised to a single-pill combination of enalapril 10 mg plus folic acid 0.8 mg daily (n=10,348) or enalapril 10 mg alone (n=10,354). Over a median treatment duration of 4.5 years, first stroke occurred in 2.7% on enalapril–folic acid versus 3.4% on enalapril alone (hazard ratio 0.79, 95% CI 0.68–0.93) — a 21% relative reduction, an absolute difference of 0.7 percentage points. First ischemic stroke (2.2% versus 2.8%; hazard ratio 0.76, 95% CI 0.64–0.91) and the composite of cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction and stroke (3.1% versus 3.9%; hazard ratio 0.80, 95% CI 0.69–0.92) also favoured the combination, while hemorrhagic stroke, myocardial infarction and all-cause death did not differ significantly, and adverse-event frequencies did not differ significantly between groups. The supporting meta-analysis (Huo Y et al., PMID: 22607506; 55,764 participants) points the same way only where food is not fortified: across the 10 trials with no or partial folic acid fortification (n=43,426) folic acid supplementation was associated with an 11% relative reduction in stroke risk (relative risk 0.89, 95% CI 0.82–0.97), while in the five trials in fortified populations (n=12,338) it had no effect (relative risk 1.03, 95% CI 0.88–1.21). The population boundary is part of the finding: CSPPT was run in China, which does not fortify food with folic acid, in adults the authors describe as having low baseline folate levels — the result must not be generalised to folate-replete, fortified populations. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): adding folic acid 0.8 mg to enalapril reduced first stroke in hypertensive Chinese adults in one large double-blind trial, with a concordant meta-analysis signal confined to non-fortified populations; a single pivotal trial carries the claim, so the shelf is Tier C for the developer's personal verdict.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one large randomised double-blind trial (CSPPT, n=20,702) found first stroke in 2.7% on enalapril plus folic acid 0.8 mg versus 3.4% on enalapril alone over a median 4.5 years (hazard ratio 0.79, 95% CI 0.68–0.93; a 21% relative reduction), with a supporting meta-analysis signal only in populations without folic-acid food fortification

title: Depression screening in primary care, with treatment systems attached: pooled odds ratio 0.60 for still being depressed at 6–12 months — screening alone, and suicide-risk screening, have no such evidence
question: In adults in primary care, does screening for depression — with systems for follow-up care — improve depression outcomes versus usual care?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for depression screening programmes, not for screening as a bare test. The USPSTF evidence report (105 studies) found that depression screening interventions — many of which included additional components beyond screening, such as treatment protocols and follow-up systems — were associated with a lower prevalence of depression or clinically important depressive symptoms after 6 to 12 months (pooled odds ratio 0.60, 95% CI 0.50–0.73; 8 randomised trials, 10,244 participants). The instruments themselves are accurate enough to build on: the PHQ-9 at a cutoff of 10 or more had pooled sensitivity 0.85 and specificity 0.85 (47 studies, 11,234 participants), and a large body of evidence supports psychological and pharmacological treatment once depression is found. The boundary is suicide risk: the same report found the suicide-prevention studies generally did not demonstrate improvement over usual care, and one trial of suicide-risk screening found no difference in suicidal ideation after two weeks. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): screening for depression improves outcomes when it is a programme wired to treatment and follow-up; this record does not show that a questionnaire alone, or screening for suicide risk, does — Tier C, because the active ingredient cannot be separated from the bundle.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — USPSTF evidence report: screening programmes (with follow-up systems) pooled OR 0.60 for depression at 6–12 months; no demonstrated benefit for suicide-risk screening

title: Lipid screening in childhood: no trial has ever tested screening itself; FH is found in 0.2–0.4% and statins lower LDL by 81–82 mg/dL in FH trials — benefit is an inference chain, not a demonstration
question: In children and adolescents, does universal lipid screening identify familial hypercholesterolaemia and other lipid disorders better than targeted screening, and does early treatment help?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — the USPSTF evidence report is unusually candid: no randomised trial directly addressed the effectiveness or harms of lipid screening in children and adolescents, and no direct evidence on the benefits or harms of screening was identified at all. What exists is a chain. Screening finds familial hypercholesterolaemia (FH) at a prevalence of 0.2% to 0.4% (1 in 250 to 1 in 500) in three US studies totalling 395,465 children, and elevated total cholesterol (≥200 mg/dL) in 7.1% to 9.4%. In children with FH, ten randomised trials (1,230 participants) showed statins produced an 81- to 82-mg/dL greater reduction in total and LDL cholesterol than placebo, and observational studies suggest starting statins in childhood or adolescence reduces long-term cardiovascular risk. For the much commoner multifactorial dyslipidaemia, no evidence was found that treatment is effective, and two behavioural-counselling trials (934 participants) produced only 3- to 6-mg/dL greater cholesterol reductions that did not persist. Whether universal screening beats targeted screening was not answered by any study in the report. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): screening certainly identifies FH and treatment certainly lowers its cholesterol; that screening children improves adult outcomes is inferred, never tested — Tier C.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — no screening trial exists; FH prevalence 0.2–0.4%, statins lower LDL-C by 81–82 mg/dL in FH trials, long-term benefit observational only

title: Screening asymptomatic adults for sleep apnoea: no study has ever compared screening with no screening; treatment improves sleepiness scores but no trial shows fewer deaths, cardiovascular events or crashes
question: In asymptomatic adults, does screening for obstructive sleep apnoea improve health outcomes versus no screening?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — the direct evidence does not exist. The USPSTF evidence report (86 studies, 11,051 participants) states plainly that no study directly compared screening with no screening. The chain that does exist: a two-step strategy (Multivariable Apnea Prediction score followed by home sleep testing) detected severe OSA syndrome with an area under the curve of 0.80 (95% CI 0.78–0.82) and 0.83 (0.77–0.90) in two studies (702 participants), while five studies of other screening tools were heterogeneous and inconsistent. Treatment of found OSA improves symptoms: positive airway pressure versus inactive control improved Epworth Sleepiness Scale scores by a pooled 2.33 points (95% CI −2.75 to −1.90; 47 trials, 7,024 participants) and sleep-related quality of life (standardised mean difference 0.30, 0.19–0.42), and lowered blood pressure by a small 2–3 mm Hg in three systematic reviews. But no included trial found a significant benefit of treatment on mortality, cardiovascular events or motor vehicle crashes. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): screening can find severe OSA and treatment relieves sleepiness; that screening asymptomatic adults improves health outcomes is unproven — Tier C.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — no screening-vs-no-screening study exists; PAP improves sleepiness by 2.33 ESS points in treatment trials, with no demonstrated mortality, cardiovascular or crash benefit

title: Intermittent preventive malaria treatment in infancy (sulfadoxine–pyrimethamine): clinical malaria down 30.3% and anaemia down 21.3% across six pooled trials — deaths unchanged (56 versus 53)
question: In infants in malaria-endemic Africa, does perennial malaria chemoprevention (intermittent preventive treatment in infancy) with sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine reduce clinical malaria and anaemia versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a pooled analysis of six double-blind, placebo-controlled trials (7,930 infants) of intermittent preventive treatment in infancy (IPTi) with sulfadoxine–pyrimethamine, given at routine Expanded Program on Immunization vaccination visits. IPTi had a protective efficacy of 30.3% (95% CI 19.8–39.4) against clinical malaria, 21.3% (8.2–32.5) against anaemia, 38.1% (12.5–56.2) against hospital admissions associated with malaria parasitaemia, and 22.9% (10.0–34.0) against all-cause hospital admissions, up to 12 months of age. Mortality did not fall: 56 deaths in the IPTi group versus 53 in the placebo group (rate ratio 1.05, 0.72–1.54). Safety was reassuring in this record — four of 676 non-fatal admissions in the IPTi group were judged possibly treatment-related, versus five of 860 on placebo. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): IPTi with sulfadoxine–pyrimethamine prevents about a third of clinical malaria episodes and a fifth of anaemia in the first year of life in endemic Africa; it has not been shown to save lives, and sulfadoxine–pyrimethamine resistance has grown since these trials.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — pooled six placebo-controlled trials (7,930 infants): clinical malaria protective efficacy 30.3%, anaemia 21.3%, mortality unchanged (rate ratio 1.05)

title: Post-discharge malaria chemoprevention after severe anaemia: readmission or death hazard ratio 0.65 in the Kenyan–Ugandan trial, mortality rate ratio 0.23 during the intervention period in the three-trial pooled analysis — protection ends when the drug stops
question: In children discharged after treatment for severe malarial anaemia, does post-discharge malaria chemoprevention reduce readmission and death versus placebo?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — during the months the drug is given. In a multicentre placebo-controlled trial in Kenya and Uganda, 1,049 children under five discharged after severe anaemia received three monthly 3-day courses of dihydroartemisinin–piperaquine or placebo: from week 3 to week 26 there were 184 readmission-or-death events in the chemoprevention group versus 316 on placebo (hazard ratio 0.65, 95% CI 0.54–0.78), concentrated in the intervention period (weeks 3–14: hazard ratio 0.30, 0.22–0.42) and absent after it (weeks 15–26: 1.13, 0.87–1.47). The individual-patient meta-analysis of all three post-discharge trials (3,663 children) found the same shape: during the intervention period, mortality was reduced by 77% in relative terms (rate ratio 0.23, 0.08–0.70) and all-cause readmissions by 55% in relative terms (hazard ratio 0.45, 0.36–0.56), with protection not sustained after the drugs' pharmacological effect waned. No serious adverse events were attributed to dihydroartemisinin–piperaquine in the trial. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): post-discharge chemoprevention strongly protects recently discharged children with severe anaemia while it is being taken — and only while it is being taken, which is a delivery problem, not a reason to withhold it. Tier C is set because the pooled claim includes a mortality reduction.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — randomised trial HR 0.65 for readmission or death; three-trial IPD meta-analysis mortality RR 0.23 during intervention; benefit confined to the treatment period

title: HIV post-exposure prophylaxis after needlestick injury: zidovudine use associated with odds ratio 0.19 for seroconversion in the only case-control study — and full 28-day prescriptions complete better than starter packs (70% versus 53.2%)
question: After occupational exposure to HIV, does post-exposure prophylaxis reduce the risk of HIV transmission, and which regimens are completed?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the efficacy evidence is a single case-control study, because a placebo trial of PEP after occupational exposure has never been run and could not now be run. Among health-care workers with percutaneous exposure to HIV-infected blood, the 33 who seroconverted were significantly less likely to have taken zidovudine after exposure than 665 exposed controls who did not seroconvert (odds ratio 0.19, 95% CI 0.06–0.52) — against a background average transmission risk of 0.3% per percutaneous exposure. The same study defines who is at risk: deep injury (odds ratio 15, 6.0–41), a device visibly contaminated with blood (6.2, 2.2–21), a needle placed in the source patient's artery or vein (4.3, 1.7–12), and a source patient who died of AIDS within two months (5.6, 2.0–16). On completion, a systematic review of 54 studies (11,714 PEP initiations) found outcomes were better with a full 28-day prescription at first presentation than with starter packs: fewer refusals (11.4% versus 22%) and higher completion (70% versus 53.2%), with 28% of starter-pack recipients never returning for the rest of the course. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): PEP probably prevents most transmissions it could plausibly reach — an 81% relative reduction in the odds of seroconversion in the only direct study — and giving the whole course up front gets it finished; Tier C, as a single observational efficacy study.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single case-control study: zidovudine PEP odds ratio 0.19 (0.06–0.52) for seroconversion; completion 70% with full-course prescribing vs 53.2% with starter packs
