title: Home safety education and equipment: safety practices clearly improve (smoke alarms odds ratio 1.81, fire escape plans 2.01) but injuries fall only in home-delivered programmes (rate ratio 0.75) — and the one large equipment trial found no injury reduction at all
question: In families with young children, do home safety education and provision of safety equipment reduce childhood injuries versus usual care?
balance: SPLIT — practices versus injuries. The Cochrane review (98 studies, 2,605,044 people; 54 studies in at least one meta-analysis) found home safety interventions reliably changed what families do: safe hot tap water temperatures (odds ratio 1.41, 95% CI 1.07–1.86), functional smoke alarms (1.81, 1.30–2.52), a fire escape plan (2.01, 1.45–2.77), and storing medicines (1.53, 1.27–1.84) and cleaning products (1.55, 1.22–1.96) out of reach. Injury rates were a different story: after adjusting controlled before-and-after studies for baseline rates, the pooled incidence rate ratio was 0.89 (0.78–1.01) — not significant overall — with greater reductions for interventions delivered in the home (0.75, 0.62–0.91) and, counterintuitively, for interventions not providing safety equipment (0.78, 0.66–0.92); there was a lack of evidence that interventions reduced thermal injuries or poisoning. The largest single randomised trial (3,428 families) of advice plus free fitted equipment found no reduction in medically attended injuries (odds ratio 1.14, 0.98–1.50) despite improved safety practices. PROPOSED SPLIT: home safety education improves safety behaviour and probably reduces injuries when delivered in the home; handing over equipment, by itself, has not been shown to reduce injuries — Tier C.
stamp: SPLIT — safety practices improve (OR 1.41–2.01) and home-delivered programmes reduce injury rates (IRR 0.75), but overall injury reduction is non-significant (IRR 0.89) and the largest equipment trial was null (OR 1.14)

title: Helmet-promotion programmes roughly double children's helmet wearing — and helmets themselves cut head-injury odds by about 60% in crash studies, though no promotion trial measured injuries
question: Do interventions promoting bicycle helmet use increase helmet wearing and reduce head injuries in children?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — promotion works on wearing; the injury benefit is inferred, not trialled. The Cochrane review of non-legislative interventions (Owen R et al., PMID: 22071810) pooled 11 studies and found observed helmet wearing roughly doubled (OR 2.08, 95% CI 1.29 to 3.34), with the largest effects for community-based programmes (OR 4.30) and free-helmet provision (OR 4.35), and a smaller effect for education alone (OR 1.43). Whether wearing prevents injury rests on crash data, not trials: the Attewell meta-analysis of case-control studies (PMID: 11235796) found helmet use associated with lower odds of head injury (OR 0.40, 95% CI 0.29 to 0.55), brain injury (OR 0.42) and fatal injury (OR 0.27), against a possible neck-injury signal (OR 1.36, 95% CI 1.00 to 1.86). No promotion trial measured head injuries directly, and the injury evidence is observational — which is why this shelf is Tier C. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): programmes — especially community-based ones giving helmets away — increase wearing, and the observational crash evidence says wearing matters.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — non-legislative promotion doubles observed helmet wearing in pooled controlled studies, and case-control meta-analysis associates helmet use with ~60% lower odds of head injury; injury outcome itself is observational, hence Tier C

title: Giving parents a child seat plus education works — education alone does not: distribution programmes carry the strongest evidence for getting children restrained
question: Do child safety-seat distribution and education programmes increase correct seat use and reduce injuries versus usual care?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for the programmes that hand over a seat, not for leaflets. The Community Preventive Services Task Force reviews (Zaza S et al., PMID: 11691560) screened 72 studies and found strong evidence of effectiveness for child safety-seat laws and for distribution-plus-education programmes, sufficient evidence for community-wide information with enhanced enforcement and for incentive-plus-education programmes, and insufficient evidence for education-only programmes. The Cochrane review of booster-seat interventions for 4–8-year-olds (Ehiri JE et al., PMID: 16437484) pooled 5 studies (3,070 children) and found interventions increased booster use (RR 1.43, 95% CI 1.05 to 1.96), with free distribution plus education strongest (RR 2.34, 95% CI 1.50 to 3.63). The injury link is background effectiveness: correctly used seats reduce hospitalisation by 69% and death by about 70% in infants and 47–54% in toddlers, as summarised in the Task Force review. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): distribution plus education reliably raises correct restraint use; education alone is unproven.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — distribution-plus-education programmes have strong review-level evidence for increasing child seat use (booster use RR 1.43, free distribution RR 2.34); education-only programmes have insufficient evidence

title: BARCODE1: screening only the top genetic-risk decile found cancer in 40% of men biopsied — over half needing treatment, most of whom the standard UK pathway would have missed; no outcomes data yet
question: In prostate screening, does a polygenic risk score identify a high-risk group in whom targeted PSA screening finds more clinically significant cancers?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for finding clinically significant cancer in a pre-selected high-risk group; whether that saves lives is untested. In BARCODE1 (McHugh JK et al., PMID: 40214032), 6,393 UK men aged 55–69 had a 130-variant polygenic risk score calculated; the 745 (11.7%) in the top decile were offered MRI and biopsy regardless of PSA. Of 468 men biopsied, 187 (40.0%) had prostate cancer, and 103 (55.1%) of those cancers were intermediate-risk or higher, so treatment was indicated — 74 (71.8%) of those 103 would not have been detected by the current UK diagnostic pathway. The pilot (Benafif S et al., PMID: 34214236) showed the approach is feasible but uptake is the constraint: only 26% of invited men took part. There is no randomised comparison and no mortality, metastasis or overdiagnosis outcome — detection yield is a surrogate, and some detected cancers would never have caused harm. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): risk-targeted screening concentrates significant cancers where it looks, at the price of biopsying a group in whom 60% have no cancer found.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — top-decile polygenic-risk targeting found cancer in 40.0% of men biopsied, 55.1% of cancers treatment-indicated; single-arm study with no mortality or overdiagnosis outcomes, hence Tier C

title: HPV vaccine and oral infection in men: no trial in men exists — vaccinated young men had no vaccine-type oral infections at all in US survey data (0.0% vs 2.13%), and the one randomised proof comes from women (93% efficacy)
question: In boys and men, does HPV vaccination prevent vaccine-type oral HPV infection, a precursor pathway to oropharyngeal cancer?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — strongly suggestive, never randomised in men. In US NHANES 2011–2014 data (Chaturvedi AK et al., PMID: 29182497), vaccine-type oral HPV prevalence was 0.11% in vaccinated versus 1.61% in unvaccinated young adults (an adjusted 88.2% relative reduction), and among men specifically 0.0% versus 2.13%. The biological bridge is a vaccine trial in 150 mid-adult men (Pinto LA et al., PMID: 27511896): all developed serum anti-HPV-16/18 antibodies and over 90% had detectable oral-cavity antibodies after vaccination with the quadrivalent vaccine (Gardasil, as named in the publication). The only randomised efficacy evidence against oral infection is in women: the Costa Rica trial found 93.3% efficacy against prevalent oral HPV16/18 infection four years after bivalent vaccination (Herrero R et al., PMID: 23873171). Because the male evidence is cross-sectional and immunogenicity-based, this shelf is Tier C. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): every available strand points the same way, but a male efficacy trial remains undone.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — vaccinated men had 0.0% vs 2.13% vaccine-type oral HPV prevalence in US survey data and vaccination induces oral antibodies in men; no randomised efficacy trial in men, hence Tier C

title: Tirzepatide in obesity with prediabetes: diabetes diagnosed in 1.3% versus 13.3% over three years — a 93% relative reduction in onset, still evident after 17 weeks off the drug
question: In adults with obesity and prediabetes, does tirzepatide reduce progression to type 2 diabetes versus placebo over three years?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — one large trial, an effect too big to be fragile, on delaying the formal diagnosis. In the three-year SURMOUNT-1 analysis (Jastreboff AM et al., PMID: 39536238), among 1,032 participants with obesity and prediabetes, type 2 diabetes was diagnosed in 1.3% on tirzepatide versus 13.3% on placebo over 176 weeks (hazard ratio 0.07, 95% CI 0.0 to 0.1) — a 93% relative reduction, 12.0 percentage points absolute. After 17 weeks off treatment the gap persisted (2.4% versus 13.7%; HR 0.12). Weight fell 12.3% to 19.7% by dose versus 1.3% on placebo, consistent with the parent trial's 72-week results (PMID: 35658024). Consistent with the developer's framing, this is best described as delaying progression to a diabetes diagnosis — driven by weight loss — rather than proof of permanent prevention: what happens over a decade, or after years off the drug, is unknown. Tier C: a single trial carrying a diabetes-onset benefit claim. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): tirzepatide delays progression from prediabetes to diabetes for at least three years.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — diabetes onset 1.3% vs 13.3% over 176 weeks (HR 0.07) in the single large SURMOUNT-1 prediabetes cohort, persisting 17 weeks off treatment; single trial, hence Tier C

title: High-dose flu vaccine in nursing homes: respiratory hospital admissions 3.4% versus 3.9% over one season in an 823-home cluster trial — a real but modest edge (adjusted RR 0.87)
question: In nursing-home residents, does high-dose influenza vaccine reduce respiratory-related hospital admissions versus standard-dose vaccine?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a modest relative effect on a common outcome, from one very large pragmatic trial. The cluster-randomised trial across 823 US nursing homes (Gravenstein S et al., PMID: 28736045) found respiratory-related hospital admissions in 3.4% of residents in high-dose facilities versus 3.9% in standard-dose facilities over six months (0.185 versus 0.211 per 1,000 resident-days; adjusted relative risk 0.873, 95% CI 0.776 to 0.982, p=0.023) — a 13% relative reduction, 0.5 percentage points absolute. Supporting evidence in community-dwelling older adults points the same way: a meta-analysis of 15 publications over 10 seasons (Lee JKH et al., PMID: 33422382) found high-dose vaccine relatively more effective against pneumonia admissions (relative VE 27.3%) and influenza admissions (relative VE 11.7%). Tier C: the nursing-home claim rests on a single trial, and its unadjusted analysis was not significant (RR 0.888, p=0.061). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): high-dose vaccine gives nursing-home residents a small reduction in respiratory admissions.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — respiratory admissions 3.4% vs 3.9% over one season (adjusted RR 0.873) in one 823-facility cluster trial; single trial for the nursing-home claim, hence Tier C

title: School hand-hygiene programmes: illness absence may fall a little (pooled IRR 0.82, very low certainty) — but the largest trial, 60 schools in Addis Ababa, found no effect on absence at all
question: In primary-school children, do school-based hand-hygiene programmes reduce illness-related absence versus usual practice?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — the signal is small, the certainty very low, and the biggest trial is null on absence. The Cochrane review of rinse-free hand washing (Munn Z et al., PMID: 32270476; 19 studies, 30,747 children) found illness-related absenteeism may be reduced (IRR 0.82, 95% CI 0.69 to 0.97; 6 studies) but rated the evidence very low certainty, and found little to no difference for absenteeism for any reason (IRR 0.91, 95% CI 0.82 to 1.01). The WISE cluster trial in 60 Addis Ababa primary schools (Bick S et al., PMID: 39218883; 6,229 pupils) found no effect on roll-call absence (adjusted OR 1.07) or diarrhoea, with only a borderline reduction in reported respiratory illness (adjusted OR 0.84, 95% CI 0.71 to 1.00). A small US trial (Sandora TJ et al., PMID: 18519460) did reduce gastrointestinal-illness absence with sanitizer plus surface disinfection. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): programmes are cheap and safe, but a dependable absence reduction is not established.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — pooled illness-absence IRR 0.82 at very low certainty, contradicted on absence by the largest cluster trial; Tier C for the weak, mixed base

title: Screen-and-treat for malaria in pregnancy matches preventive treatment on birth outcomes in low-resistance areas — but in high-resistance Malawi it left more malaria at delivery and more fetal loss
question: In pregnant women in malaria-endemic Africa, does intermittent screening and treatment for malaria match intermittent preventive treatment for preventing placental malaria and low birthweight?
balance: SPLIT — the answer depends on where the parasites stand on sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine (SP) resistance. In four West African countries with low SP resistance, the Tagbor trial (PMID: 26258474; 5,354 women) found screen-and-treat with artemether-lumefantrine non-inferior to IPTp-SP on low birthweight (15.6% versus 15.1%), anaemia and placental malaria (24.2% versus 24.5%). In Malawi, where SP resistance is high, the Madanitsa trial (PMID: 27622558; 1,873 women) found similar adverse birth outcomes (29.9% versus 28.8%) but more malaria at delivery with screen-and-treat (48.7% versus 40.8%) and more fetal loss (2.6% versus 1.3%; RR 2.06). The individual-participant meta-analysis of five trials (Gutman JR et al., PMID: 34746720; 10,821 pregnancies) found no difference in adverse pregnancy outcomes (RR 1.00) and no superiority for screening, with more subpatent infections missed by rapid tests. PROPOSED SPLIT: birth outcomes match, infection control does not — screening is not a superior replacement for preventive treatment anywhere it has been tested.
stamp: SPLIT — birth outcomes match IPTp in both low- and high-resistance settings (IPD meta-analysis RR 1.00), but screening leaves more malaria infection at delivery where SP resistance is high, with a fetal-loss signal in the Malawi trial

title: Preventive zinc in young children: diarrhoea falls modestly (RR 0.91 in 96 modern trials) — the pneumonia claim from the 1999 pooled analysis (OR 0.59) was not reproduced for respiratory morbidity (RR 1.01)
question: In young children in low-income settings, does zinc supplementation prevent diarrhoea and pneumonia versus placebo?
balance: SPLIT — diarrhoea yes, modestly; pneumonia not on current evidence. The 1999 pooled analysis of randomised trials (Bhutta ZA et al., PMID: 10586170) found continuous zinc supplementation reduced diarrhoea incidence (OR 0.82, 95% CI 0.72 to 0.93) and pneumonia incidence (OR 0.59, 95% CI 0.41 to 0.83). The much larger 2023 Cochrane review (Imdad A et al., PMID: 36994923; 96 trials, 219,584 children) confirmed a small diarrhoea reduction (RR 0.91, 95% CI 0.90 to 0.93, moderate certainty) but found little to no difference in lower-respiratory-tract morbidity (RR 1.01, 95% CI 0.95 to 1.08, high certainty) and little to no difference in all-cause mortality (RR 0.93, 95% CI 0.84 to 1.03). Vomiting increased (RR 1.29). PROPOSED SPLIT: a real but small diarrhoea benefit; the pneumonia prevention claim rests on the older, smaller analysis and did not survive the larger one.
stamp: SPLIT — diarrhoea incidence modestly reduced in both eras (OR 0.82 in 1999; RR 0.91 across 96 trials in 2023), but pneumonia/LRTI prevention appears only in the older pooled analysis (OR 0.59) and not in the 2023 Cochrane review (RR 1.01)

title: STROKESTOP II: NT-proBNP triage concentrated AF detection where it aimed (4.4% new AF in the high-peptide group, almost none below the cut-off) — but screening did not reduce stroke at five years (HR 0.96)
question: In asymptomatic older adults at high stroke risk, does NT-proBNP-guided systematic ECG screening detect more atrial fibrillation than standard screening invitation?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for detection, with the outcome caveat on the face. In STROKESTOP II (Kemp Gudmundsdottir K et al., PMID: 39217615), all 75–76-year-olds in the Stockholm region were randomised to screening invitation or control (28,712 people); among participants without known AF, NT-proBNP ≥125 ng/L triggered two weeks of four-times-daily ECG recordings, while those below the cut-off had a single ECG. The stepwise report (PMID: 31790147) found new AF in 4.4% of the high-NT-proBNP group versus a single case in the low group, raising known AF prevalence from 8.1% to 10.5% among participants, with anticoagulation started in 94.5% of those newly diagnosed. Yet at a median 5.1 years there was no difference in stroke or systemic embolism between invited and control groups (HR 0.96, 95% CI 0.86 to 1.06). Tier C: a single trial, and a screening claim. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the peptide triage demonstrably finds AF where it looks — the stroke payoff was not shown.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — NT-proBNP-guided screening detected new AF in 4.4% of the high-peptide group versus ~0% below the cut-off, but the trial found no stroke reduction at 5 years (HR 0.96); single trial, hence Tier C

title: Varenicline in adolescent smokers: two placebo-controlled trials, two null primary results — end-of-treatment abstinence 8.9% versus 8.9%, and 20–27% versus 18% at higher enrolment, neither significant
question: In adolescents who smoke, does varenicline increase abstinence versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — on the primary outcomes of both trials. In the US trial (Gray KM et al., PMID: 31609433; 157 smokers aged 14–21), cotinine-confirmed 7-day abstinence at end of treatment was identical: 8.9% on varenicline and 8.9% on placebo (RR 0.97, 95% CI 0.29 to 2.99). Secondary measures favoured varenicline — earlier first abstinence (HR 1.91) and higher self-reported weekly abstinence during treatment (RR 1.81) — but the pre-selected primary endpoint was flat. The larger multinational trial (Gray KM et al., PMID: 32979939; 312 smokers aged 12–19) found continuous abstinence at weeks 9–12 of 20% on high-dose and 27% on low-dose varenicline versus 18% on placebo, neither significant (OR 1.18 and 1.73). Treatment was generally well tolerated in both. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): adult efficacy does not transfer to adolescents on the evidence of these two trials.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — both placebo-controlled trials missed their primary abstinence endpoints (8.9% vs 8.9%; 20%/27% vs 18%, NS), with only secondary self-report measures favouring varenicline

title: Church-based colorectal screening programmes: screening rose in intervention and comparison churches alike — the faith-based programmes themselves added nothing measurable (+6.4 vs +4.7 points, p=.25)
question: In communities, do faith-based programmes increase colorectal cancer screening among church-going adults versus control education?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — for the faith-based programme as the active ingredient. In the ACTS of Wellness cluster trial (Leone LA et al., PMID: 26515276; 19 urban African American churches), up-to-date colorectal screening rose by 6.4 percentage points in intervention churches and 4.7 points in comparison churches (p=.25) — no significant programme effect, in a population already 74–76% screened at baseline. In the Holt trial (PMID: 23033548; 16 churches), a spiritually themed education series and an identical non-spiritual series both improved awareness and self-reported screening, with no significant group differences except fecal occult blood test uptake, which rose more in the non-spiritual arm. Screening improved more, within the ACTS intervention arm, among members who actually spoke with a peer counsellor or recalled the newsletters — engagement, not faith content, is the plausible lever. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): churches are workable venues, but the programmes tested did not beat their comparisons.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — in both church-based randomised trials, screening rose similarly in intervention and comparison arms (ACTS +6.4 vs +4.7 points, p=.25); spiritual content added nothing over identical secular education

title: Fractional-dose IPV: one-fifth doses boost immunity as well as full doses in primed people (non-inferior in the Cuban trial) and match seroconversion by three doses — but a single fractional dose is clearly weaker (RR 0.61)
question: In outbreak response, does fractional-dose (one-fifth) intradermal inactivated poliovirus vaccine boost immunity comparably to a full intramuscular dose?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for boosting and multi-dose schedules, not for a single priming dose. The systematic review and meta-analysis (Mashunye TR et al., PMID: 33939958) found seroconversion after fractional versus full-dose IPV in children diverged by dose count for poliovirus type 2: risk ratio 0.61 (95% CI 0.51 to 0.72) after one dose, 0.90 (0.82 to 1.00) after two, and 0.95 (0.91 to 1.00) after three, with antibody titres lower after fractional doses at every count. The outbreak-relevant evidence is the Cuban boosting trial (Resik S et al., PMID: 28073858): in OPV-primed adults, one-fifth intradermal doses produced immune responses in 94.8–98.0% across serotypes versus 98.0–99.2% for full intramuscular doses, meeting non-inferiority at days 7, 28 and 56. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): in an outbreak, fractional doses stretch supply fivefold and boost primed populations comparably — they are not a like-for-like substitute for a first full dose in a naive child.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — fractional doses were non-inferior for boosting primed adults and matched seroconversion by three doses (RR 0.95), but a single fractional dose seroconverts far fewer children (RR 0.61) and titres run lower throughout

title: Early aflibercept in severe diabetic retinopathy without macular oedema: complications fall by two-thirds (16–19% versus 50% in PANORAMA; HR 0.32 in Protocol W) — but vision itself is no better at two years
question: In severe non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy without macular oedema, does early aflibercept prevent vision-threatening complications compared with sham and deferred treatment?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for preventing complications and retinopathy progression, with no demonstrated vision advantage yet. In PANORAMA (Brown DM et al., PMID: 34351414; 402 eyes with severe NPDR), a ≥2-step retinopathy improvement at one year occurred in 65.2% (every-16-week dosing) and 79.9% (every-8-week/PRN) versus 15.0% on sham, and through week 100 vision-threatening complications or centre-involved macular oedema developed in 16.3% and 18.7% versus 50.4% on sham. In Protocol W (Maturi RK et al., PMID: 33784735; 399 eyes), the two-year cumulative probability of proliferative disease or vision-losing macular oedema was 16.3% with aflibercept versus 43.5% with sham (HR 0.32, 95% CI 0.21 to 0.50) — yet mean visual acuity change was −0.9 versus −2.0 letters, a non-significant 0.5-letter difference, because the sham group was treated promptly when complications appeared. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): early injections prevent anatomical complications; whether patients see better for it is unproven against a watch-and-treat strategy.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two randomised trials show early aflibercept cuts vision-threatening complications roughly threefold (16.3% vs 43.5%; HR 0.32), but Protocol W found no visual-acuity advantage over deferred treatment at 2 years

title: Aflibercept 8 mg every 12–16 weeks matches 2 mg every 8 weeks on vision in both wet AMD and diabetic macular oedema — the gain is fewer injections, not better sight
question: In neovascular age-related macular degeneration and diabetic macular oedema, does aflibercept 8 mg dosed every 12–16 weeks match standard aflibercept 2 mg every 8 weeks on vision?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — benefit in the form of durability: equal vision with a third fewer visits is the whole claim, and both trials support it. In PULSAR (Lanzetta P et al., PMID: 38461841; 1,009 treated patients with neovascular AMD), vision gains at 48 weeks were +6.7 letters (8 mg every 12 weeks) and +6.2 letters (every 16 weeks) versus +7.6 letters on 2 mg every 8 weeks — differences of −0.97 and −1.14 letters, within the 4-letter non-inferiority margin. In PHOTON (Brown DM et al., PMID: 38461843; 658 treated patients with diabetic macular oedema), gains were +8.8 and +7.9 letters versus +9.2 letters, likewise non-inferior. Ocular adverse-event rates in PULSAR were near-identical across arms (~38–39%). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): 8 mg buys interval, not acuity — patients trade nothing measurable in vision for fewer injections over the first year.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — aflibercept 8 mg at 12–16-week intervals was non-inferior to 2 mg every 8 weeks on 48-week vision in both PULSAR (+6.7/+6.2 vs +7.6 letters) and PHOTON (+8.8/+7.9 vs +9.2), with similar ocular adverse events

title: Ranibizumab port implant refilled twice a year matches monthly injections on vision through two years — paid for with more ocular adverse events (23.8% versus 10.2%), including endophthalmitis in 1.6%
question: In neovascular age-related macular degeneration, does the ranibizumab port delivery system refilled every 24 weeks match monthly ranibizumab injections on vision?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — vision equivalence is real; so is the surgical harm ledger. In Archway (Holekamp NM et al., PMID: 34597713; 418 patients previously responsive to anti-VEGF), vision change averaged over weeks 36–40 was +0.2 letters with the port delivery system refilled every 24 weeks versus +0.5 letters with monthly injections (difference −0.3 letters, 95% CI −1.7 to 1.1) — both non-inferior and equivalent — and 98.4% of port patients needed no supplemental injection before their first refill. At two years (Regillo C et al., PMID: 36870451) non-inferiority held at every timepoint, but prespecified ocular adverse events of special interest had accumulated in 23.8% of port patients versus 10.2% on injections, including endophthalmitis in 1.6%, implant dislocation in 1.6% and conjunctival erosion in 4.0%. Tier C: a single trial programme carrying a device benefit claim with a material harm profile. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the port trades injection burden for surgical risk, at equal vision.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — port delivery with 24-week refills was non-inferior and equivalent to monthly ranibizumab on vision through 2 years, with ocular adverse events of special interest in 23.8% vs 10.2%; single trial programme, hence Tier C

title: Dexamethasone implant in diabetic macular oedema: ≥15-letter gains in 22.2% versus 12.0% on sham over three years — with cataract adverse events in 67.9% of phakic eyes and pressure rises in 27.7%
question: In diabetic macular oedema, does the sustained-release dexamethasone intravitreal implant improve vision compared with sham, and at what cost in cataract and raised intraocular pressure?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a real vision benefit with the steroid bill itemised. In the pooled MEAD trials (Boyer DS et al., PMID: 24907062; two identical phase 3 trials, 1,048 patients), ≥15-letter vision gains at study end occurred in 22.2% on the 0.7 mg dexamethasone implant and 18.4% on the 0.35 mg implant versus 12.0% on sham, with mean retinal-thickness reductions of −111.6 and −107.9 µm versus −41.9 µm. The costs: cataract-related adverse events in 67.9% and 64.1% of phakic eyes versus 20.4% on sham. The MEAD pressure analysis (Maturi RK et al., PMID: 26871523) found ≥10 mmHg pressure rises in 27.7% and 24.8% versus 3.7%, pressure-lowering medication use in 41.5% and 37.6% versus 9.1%, but filtering surgery in only 0.3% per implant group, and vision gains were preserved in eyes whose pressure rose. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): effective, with cataract near-expected in phakic eyes and pressure usually manageable medically.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — ≥15-letter gains 22.2% vs 12.0% (sham) across two pooled phase 3 trials, against cataract adverse events in 67.9% of phakic eyes and ≥10 mmHg pressure rises in 27.7%, usually controlled with drops

title: PreserFlo MicroShunt is NOT trabeculectomy's equal on pressure: success 53.9% versus 72.7% and pressure 14.3 versus 11.1 mmHg at one year — its case is fewer interventions (40.8% versus 67.4%) and less hypotony
question: In open-angle glaucoma, is the PreserFlo MicroShunt non-inferior to trabeculectomy for lowering intraocular pressure, with fewer complications?
balance: SPLIT — the non-inferiority claim fails on efficacy and succeeds only on parts of safety. In the randomised trial (Baker ND et al., PMID: 34051211; 527 patients with primary open-angle glaucoma), one-year surgical success (≥20% pressure reduction without more medication) was 53.9% with the MicroShunt versus 72.7% with trabeculectomy (P<0.01), and mean pressure fell to 14.3 mmHg (−29.1%) versus 11.1 mmHg (−45.4%). Against that, postoperative interventions were fewer with the MicroShunt (40.8% versus 67.4%) and transient hypotony less common (28.9% versus 49.6%), with vision-threatening complications uncommon in both arms (~1.0% MicroShunt). The 2025 meta-analysis (Governatori L et al., PMID: 39394492; 10 studies, 1,833 eyes) agrees: trabeculectomy achieved lower pressure (mean difference ~1.6–2.5 mmHg in trabeculectomy's favour), while the MicroShunt carried lower hypotony-maculopathy risk (OR 0.30) but higher reintervention rates in several subgroups. PROPOSED SPLIT: choose trabeculectomy for maximum pressure lowering; the MicroShunt trades pressure for a quieter postoperative course.
stamp: SPLIT — MicroShunt is inferior on pressure and success (53.9% vs 72.7%; 14.3 vs 11.1 mmHg) but needs fewer postoperative interventions (40.8% vs 67.4%) and causes less transient hypotony (28.9% vs 49.6%); single RCT plus meta-analysis, hence Tier C

title: Newer glaucoma drops versus timolol: latanoprostene bunod beat timolol at every timepoint (pressure ≤18 mmHg in 22.9% versus 11.3%) — netarsudil only matched it in eyes starting below 25 mmHg, with red eye in half of users
question: In open-angle glaucoma and ocular hypertension, do the newer drops — netarsudil (a Rho-kinase inhibitor) and latanoprostene bunod (a nitric-oxide-donating prostaglandin) — lower pressure as well as timolol or latanoprost?
balance: SPLIT — the two 'newer drops' have opposite stories against timolol. Latanoprostene bunod 0.024% once nightly beat timolol 0.5% twice daily in APOLLO (Weinreb RN et al., PMID: 26875002): mean pressure was significantly lower at all 9 assessment timepoints (P≤0.002), with 22.9% versus 11.3% of subjects at ≤18 mmHg at every timepoint and 34.9% versus 19.5% achieving ≥25% reductions. Netarsudil 0.02% once daily, in the pooled ROCKET-1 and ROCKET-2 report (Serle JB et al., PMID: 29199013; 1,167 patients), was non-inferior to timolol only in the per-protocol population whose baseline pressure was below 25 mmHg — and conjunctival hyperaemia occurred in 50–59% on netarsudil versus 8–11% on timolol. Neither trial compared against latanoprost, the usual first-line prostaglandin, so the shelf cannot place either drug against it. PROPOSED SPLIT: latanoprostene bunod is timolol's superior on pressure; netarsudil is its conditional equal with a cosmetic cost.
stamp: SPLIT — latanoprostene bunod lowered pressure more than timolol at all 9 timepoints (APOLLO), while netarsudil was non-inferior only in eyes with baseline pressure <25 mmHg and caused conjunctival hyperaemia in 50–59% vs 8–11% (ROCKET-1/2)

title: Multifocal and EDOF lenses after cataract surgery: spectacle dependence falls (RR 0.63) and near vision improves, distance vision is unchanged — and haloes are 3.6 times as likely
question: After cataract surgery, do multifocal or extended-depth-of-focus intraocular lenses improve spectacle independence compared with monofocal lenses, and at what cost in glare and contrast?
balance: SPLIT — spectacle independence is bought with optical phenomena, and the exchange rate is now quantified. The Cochrane review (de Silva SR et al., PMID: 27943250; 20 trials, 2,230 people) found distance acuity no different between multifocal and monofocal lenses (RR 0.96 for unaided acuity worse than 6/6), better near vision with multifocals (RR 0.20 for near acuity worse than J3/J4), less spectacle dependence (RR 0.63, 95% CI 0.55 to 0.73), but more glare (RR 1.41) and haloes (RR 3.58, 95% CI 1.99 to 6.46). The 2022 network meta-analysis (Cho JY et al., PMID: 36136323; 27 trials, 2,605 patients) adds the modern lens types: trifocals gave the best near acuity (mean difference −0.32 logMAR versus monofocal), EDOF lenses the best intermediate acuity, distance acuity was comparable for all, and it found no statistical differences in contrast sensitivity, glare or haloes — a softer harm picture than Cochrane's, from indirect comparisons. PROPOSED SPLIT: patients who prize glasses-free near vision gain it; patients who prize clean night vision pay for it.
stamp: SPLIT — multifocal/EDOF lenses reduce spectacle dependence (RR 0.63) and improve near vision with distance acuity unchanged, at the cost of more glare (RR 1.41) and haloes (RR 3.58) in the Cochrane analysis

title: Preventing macular oedema after cataract surgery: in non-diabetics the bromfenac-plus-dexamethasone combination beat either drop alone (clinically significant oedema 1.5% versus 3.6% and 5.1%) — in diabetics, an added triamcinolone injection thinned the macula further
question: Does perioperative topical bromfenac, dexamethasone, or their combination prevent cystoid macular oedema after cataract surgery in patients with and without diabetes?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for the combination in non-diabetics, from one large multicentre trial. In PREMED report 1 (Wielders LHP et al., PMID: 29778106; 914 non-diabetic patients), six-week central macular thickness was 284.5 µm on combined bromfenac plus dexamethasone versus 288.3 µm on bromfenac alone and 296.0 µm on dexamethasone alone (overall P=.006), and clinically significant macular oedema within 12 weeks occurred in 1.5% versus 3.6% and 5.1% (overall P=.043). In diabetics (report 2, PMID: 30055692; 213 patients), everyone received the bromfenac-plus-dexamethasone base; adding a subconjunctival triamcinolone injection lowered macular thickness by a further 12.3 µm at 6 weeks and 9.7 µm at 12 weeks, with no macular oedema cases in the triamcinolone group, while intravitreal bevacizumab added nothing. Tier C: each population's claim rests on a single trial. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): combination drops are the best-tested prophylaxis in non-diabetics; diabetics may gain from an added depot steroid injection.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — combination bromfenac + dexamethasone gave the least macular thickening and oedema (1.5% vs 3.6%/5.1%) in 914 non-diabetics; in diabetics an added triamcinolone injection helped further; one trial per population, hence Tier C

title: Same-day surgery on both eyes: no sign of extra harm in the Cochrane review — endophthalmitis in 1 of 14,076 same-day patients versus 55 of 556,246 delayed, vision and refraction the same, costs lower, but certainty only moderate to very low
question: Is immediate sequential bilateral cataract surgery as safe and effective as delayed sequential surgery for people needing both eyes done?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — operating on both eyes on the same day looked as safe and as effective as operating on separate days, and cheaper. The Cochrane review (Dickman MM et al., PMID: 35467755) of 14 studies and 276,260 participants found endophthalmitis in 1 of 14,076 same-day participants versus 55 of 556,246 delayed-surgery participants, no difference in the share of eyes missing the refractive target (risk ratio 0.84, 95% CI 0.57 to 1.26 in the randomised trials) and no difference in postoperative complications (risk ratio 1.33, 95% CI 0.52 to 3.40), with lower total costs per participant for same-day surgery. An earlier meta-analysis (Malvankar-Mehta MS et al., PMID: 26121673) likewise found no significant difference in best-corrected visual acuity between the two approaches (standardised mean difference -0.18, 95% CI -0.37 to 0.01). The honest catch is certainty: Cochrane graded the evidence moderate to very low, the randomised base is only two trials, and bilateral simultaneous endophthalmitis — the catastrophic event same-day surgery is feared for — is too rare for any of these data to exclude. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): same-day bilateral cataract surgery shows no measurable disadvantage on any outcome the evidence can actually measure, at lower cost; the unmeasurable rare bilateral disaster remains a judgement call, not a data point.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — Cochrane review of 14 studies (276,260 participants) found no evidence of higher endophthalmitis, complications or worse refraction with same-day bilateral surgery, and lower costs, but certainty was moderate to very low

title: Clascoterone 1% cream: clear or almost clear in 18.4% and 20.3% versus 9.0% and 6.5% on vehicle at 12 weeks in two phase 3 trials — a real but modest win, with mostly mild local redness
question: In moderate-to-severe facial acne, does clascoterone 1% cream — a topical androgen-receptor inhibitor — clear lesions better than vehicle?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the first topical androgen-receptor inhibitor beat vehicle in two identical phase 3 trials, by a modest margin. Treatment success (clear or almost clear with at least a 2-grade improvement) at week 12 was 18.4% and 20.3% on clascoterone cream 1% twice daily versus 9.0% and 6.5% on vehicle (Hebert A et al., PMID: 32320027), with inflammatory lesion counts falling by 19.3 and 20.0 versus 15.5 and 12.6 on vehicle. In the open-label extension (Eichenfield LF et al., PMID: 37556524), 18.1% of patients reported treatment-emergent adverse events over up to 9 further months, the commonest local reactions being erythema and scaling/dryness, and 48.9% of per-protocol completers had clear or almost-clear faces at study end. The catch is scale: roughly four of five treated patients did not reach clear/almost-clear at 12 weeks, and there is no comparison against any established acne treatment. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): clascoterone 1% cream is a genuinely effective, well-tolerated addition for moderate-to-severe facial acne — an incremental option, not a replacement for standard therapy.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two phase 3 vehicle-controlled trials show treatment success in 18–20% versus 7–9% at 12 weeks, with low, mostly mild local adverse events

title: Trifarotene cream for face and trunk acne: both PERFECT phase 3 trials positive on every endpoint (all P<.001) — the abstracts report significance without success percentages; a 52-week open-label study reached 65.1% clear or almost clear on the face
question: In moderate-to-severe acne of the face and trunk, does trifarotene 50 µg/g cream improve lesion counts and success rates compared with vehicle?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — trifarotene, a retinoid selective for the skin-predominant RAR-γ receptor, beat vehicle on every primary and secondary endpoint in two phase 3 trials covering both face and trunk (Tan J et al., PMID: 30802558): facial success, truncal success, and inflammatory and noninflammatory lesion counts on both sites were all highly significant (P<.001) at week 12. The published abstract does not state the absolute success percentages, so the size of the win cannot be quoted from the record — a declared gap on this shelf. What can be sized is durability: in the 52-week open-label study (Blume-Peytavi U et al., PMID: 31306527), facial success rose from 26.6% at week 12 to 65.1% at week 52 and truncal success from 38.6% to 66.9%, with trifarotene-related treatment-emergent adverse events in 12.6% and local irritation concentrated in the first weeks. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): trifarotene works on face and trunk acne with the usual early retinoid irritation; the pivotal abstracts' missing percentages keep this at POSSIBLE rather than LIKELY.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two phase 3 vehicle-controlled trials positive on all face and trunk endpoints (P<.001), with 52-week open-label success of 65.1% (face) and 66.9% (trunk); pivotal abstracts do not report absolute success rates

title: Combined oral contraceptives for acne in women: all nine placebo-controlled trials in the Cochrane review favoured the pill — a drospirenone pill gave clear or almost-clear skin at about four times the placebo odds; which progestin is best stays unclear
question: In women with acne, do combined oral contraceptives improve lesion counts compared with placebo or other acne treatments?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — combined oral contraceptives reduce facial acne lesions versus placebo, consistently. The Cochrane review (Arowojolu AO et al., PMID: 22786490) covered 31 trials with 12,579 participants; all nine placebo-controlled trials with analysable data showed combined pills reducing lesion counts, severity grades and self-assessed acne. A levonorgestrel pill cut total lesion counts by a mean 9.98 more than placebo; a drospirenone pill roughly tripled the odds of investigator-assessed clear or almost-clear skin (odds ratio 3.02, 95% CI 1.99 to 4.59). The largest single drospirenone trial (Koltun W et al., PMID: 18342647) put the odds of clear or almost-clear skin at 4.31 (95% CI 2.11 to 9.60) versus placebo over six cycles. What the evidence does not settle is ranking: differences between progestin types were inconsistent, and only one trial compared a pill with an antibiotic. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): for women who also want contraception, a combined pill is a well-evidenced acne treatment; choosing between pills on acne grounds alone is not evidence-based.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — Cochrane review of 31 trials (12,579 women): every placebo-controlled trial favoured combined oral contraceptives for lesion counts and global improvement; comparative ranking of progestins unclear

title: Dapsone 5% gel: two identical 12-week trials (3,010 patients) beat vehicle on global assessment and every lesion count (all P<.001) — the report gives p-values, not percentages; a year of open-label use cut inflammatory lesions by 58.2%
question: In moderate acne, does dapsone 5% gel reduce inflammatory lesions compared with vehicle?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — dapsone 5% gel beat vehicle in two identically designed 12-week trials totalling 3,010 patients (Draelos ZD et al., PMID: 17208334): superior on the investigator's global assessment and on mean percentage reductions in inflammatory, noninflammatory and total lesion counts (all P<.001), with inflammatory-lesion separation apparent by 4 weeks. The pivotal report gives p-values without the actual percentages — a declared gap that caps this shelf at POSSIBLE. The size signal comes from the 12-month open-label study (Lucky AW et al., PMID: 17966175): mean inflammatory lesion counts fell 30.6% by one month and 58.2% by 12 months, with application-site reactions in 8.2% and no significant haematology or blood-chemistry changes — including in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase-deficient patients in the controlled trials. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): dapsone 5% gel is an effective, well-tolerated twice-daily option for acne, on trials whose published record proves direction more clearly than size.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two identical vehicle-controlled trials (3,010 patients) positive on all endpoints (P<.001) but reported without percentages; 12-month open-label inflammatory lesion reduction 58.2%

title: Oral minoxidil 5 mg versus topical 5%: no superiority on hair-density measures at 24 weeks in the only head-to-head trial — a photographic win on the vertex only, and unwanted hair growth in 49% of the oral group
question: In androgenetic alopecia, is low-dose oral minoxidil as effective as topical minoxidil for hair density, and how do their side effects compare?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — in the only randomised head-to-head trial, oral minoxidil 5 mg daily did not demonstrate superiority over topical minoxidil 5% twice daily on the prespecified hair-density outcomes (Penha MA et al., PMID: 38598226). At 24 weeks, between-group differences in terminal hair density were 3.1 hairs/cm² on the frontal scalp (95% CI -18.2 to 21.5; P=.27) and 23.4 hairs/cm² on the vertex (95% CI -0.3 to 43.0; P=.09); total hair density differences were likewise non-significant. Blinded photographic evaluation favoured oral minoxidil on the vertex (24%; 95% CI 0 to 48; P=.04) but not the frontal scalp. The price of the tablet was hypertrichosis in 22 of 45 men (49%) and headache in 6 of 45 (14%). A network meta-analysis of monotherapies (Gupta AK et al., PMID: 38725143) ranked dutasteride 0.5 mg most effective for hair density and found oral 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors more effective than oral minoxidil — context that oral minoxidil is not the strongest oral option either. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): on density measures the oral and topical routes performed alike in one small trial; the choice turns on convenience, scalp irritation and tolerance of body-wide hair growth, not proven efficacy.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — single double-blind trial (90 men): oral minoxidil 5 mg not superior to topical 5% on frontal or vertex hair density at 24 weeks; hypertrichosis in 49% on oral

title: Ciclosporin versus methotrexate for severe childhood eczema (TREAT): ciclosporin clearly ahead at 12 weeks (o-SCORAD difference -5.69), methotrexate ahead by week 60 — speed versus staying power, with similar harms
question: In children and young people with severe atopic dermatitis, how does ciclosporin compare with methotrexate for disease control, speed of response and tolerability?
balance: SPLIT — ciclosporin works faster, methotrexate lasts longer. In the TREAT trial (Flohr C et al., PMID: 37722926), 103 children and young people aged 2–16 years with severe atopic dermatitis were randomised to ciclosporin 4 mg/kg daily or methotrexate 0.4 mg/kg weekly for 36 weeks. Ciclosporin improved disease severity more by week 12 (mean o-SCORAD difference -5.69, 97.5% CI -10.81 to -0.57; P=0.01), with more children reaching o-SCORAD 50 (odds ratio 2.60, 95% CI 1.23 to 5.49). After treatment stopped, the picture reversed: by week 60 methotrexate was superior (odds ratio 0.33, 95% CI 0.13 to 0.85 for the ciclosporin comparison), and participant-reported flares after stopping were higher in the ciclosporin arm (odds ratio 3.22, 95% CI 0.42 to 6.01). Adverse events were comparably frequent; serious adverse events occurred in 10% on ciclosporin and 14% on methotrexate. A network meta-analysis of systemic eczema treatments (Chu AWL et al., PMID: 37678577) likewise rates the evidence for both drugs as less certain than for newer biologics. PROPOSED SPLIT: choose ciclosporin when speed matters, methotrexate when durable control after stopping matters — one trial, 103 children, decides it.
stamp: SPLIT — ciclosporin faster (better o-SCORAD at week 12), methotrexate more durable (superior at week 60, fewer post-treatment flares); harms similar in the single TREAT trial

title: Nemolizumab plus topical therapy (ARCADIA 1 & 2): clear or almost-clear skin in 36% and 38% versus 25% and 26%, EASI-75 in 44% and 42% versus 29% and 30% at week 16 — itch relief from week 1, responses largely maintained to week 48
question: In adolescents and adults with moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis, does nemolizumab with background topical therapy reduce itch and skin severity compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — nemolizumab, an interleukin-31 receptor blocker aimed at itch, improved both skin clearance and itch on top of topical therapy in two replicate phase 3 trials (Silverberg JI et al., PMID: 39067461). At week 16, Investigator's Global Assessment success was 36% versus 25% in ARCADIA 1 (adjusted difference 11.5%) and 38% versus 26% in ARCADIA 2 (adjusted difference 12.2%), and EASI-75 responses were 44% versus 29% and 42% versus 30%. Itch improved significantly from week 1 and sleep by week 16. In the maintenance phase (Wollenberg A et al., PMID: 42272192), week-16 responders rerandomised to nemolizumab every 4 or 8 weeks maintained IGA success at week 48 in 61.5% and 60.4% versus 49.7% after withdrawal to placebo. Adverse-event rates were similar to placebo in the initial period (50% and 41% versus 45% and 44%). The gains are real but incremental — about one extra clear/almost-clear patient for every eight or nine treated. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): nemolizumab adds a modest, itch-led benefit over topical therapy alone, maintained with continued dosing.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two replicate phase 3 trials: IGA success 36–38% versus 25–26% and EASI-75 42–44% versus 29–30% at week 16 on background topicals, with maintenance to week 48

title: Abrocitinib 200 mg versus dupilumab (JADE DARE): faster itch relief (48% versus 26% responding by week 2) and more EASI-90 at week 4 (29% versus 15%) — one trial, and more adverse events (74% versus 65%)
question: In moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis, is abrocitinib 200 mg more effective than dupilumab for early itch relief and skin clearance, and how do their harms compare?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — on the early endpoints it was designed around, abrocitinib 200 mg beat dupilumab in the single head-to-head JADE DARE trial (Reich K et al., PMID: 35871814). A 4-point itch improvement by week 2 was reached by 172 (48%) of 357 on abrocitinib versus 93 (26%) of 364 on dupilumab (difference 22.6%), and EASI-90 at week 4 by 101 (29%) of 354 versus 53 (15%) of 364 (difference 14.1%; both p<0.0001). Treatment-emergent adverse events were more frequent on abrocitinib (268 of 362, 74%, versus 239 of 365, 65%), and two non-treatment-related deaths occurred in the abrocitinib group. Supporting evidence that abrocitinib works even after dupilumab comes from JADE EXTEND (Shi VY et al., PMID: 35439608), where 12 weeks of abrocitinib produced EASI-75 in 80.0% of prior dupilumab nonresponders on 200 mg. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): abrocitinib 200 mg is the faster drug for itch and early clearance in this one trial — a speed advantage bought with more adverse events, in a comparison that says nothing about long-term control or rare JAK-inhibitor harms.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single head-to-head phase 3 trial: abrocitinib 200 mg beat dupilumab on week-2 itch response (48% vs 26%) and week-4 EASI-90 (29% vs 15%), with more treatment-emergent adverse events (74% vs 65%)

title: Roflumilast 0.15% cream for mild-to-moderate atopic dermatitis: clear or almost clear in 32.0% and 28.9% versus 15.2% and 12.0% on vehicle at 4 weeks in two phase 3 trials — gentle on skin, and twice-weekly proactive use held clear skin a median 281 days
question: In mild-to-moderate atopic dermatitis, does roflumilast cream 0.15% achieve clear or almost-clear skin compared with vehicle?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — roflumilast cream 0.15%, a once-daily non-steroidal PDE4 inhibitor, beat vehicle in two phase 3 trials in mild-to-moderate atopic dermatitis (Simpson EL et al., PMID: 39292443). Validated IGA success at week 4 was 32.0% versus 15.2% in INTEGUMENT-1 and 28.9% versus 12.0% in INTEGUMENT-2 (both P<.001), with EASI-75 in 43.2% versus 22.0% and 42.0% versus 19.7%. Tolerability was the standout: investigators saw no irritation at the application site in at least 95% of roflumilast-treated patients at each time point. In the open-label extension (PMID: 39792455), 657 patients treated for up to 52 weeks reported adverse events in 36.7% (4.7% treatment-related), and patients who cleared and switched to twice-weekly proactive application maintained clear or almost-clear skin for a median of 281 days. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a modest-clearance, high-tolerability topical for mild-to-moderate disease, including in children from age 6 — with efficacy sized at 4 weeks and durability evidence uncontrolled.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two phase 3 vehicle-controlled trials: IGA success 32.0%/28.9% versus 15.2%/12.0% at week 4, EASI-75 ~42–43% versus ~20–22%, with minimal application-site irritation

title: Proactive twice-weekly treatment of eczema-prone skin: flares cut to a relative risk of 0.46 with fluticasone and 0.78 with tacrolimus versus vehicle in the meta-analysis — long-term safety unproven
question: In atopic eczema that keeps flaring, does twice-weekly proactive tacrolimus (or topical corticosteroid) applied to previously affected skin prevent flares compared with reactive treatment alone?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — treating previously affected skin on a twice-weekly schedule, before any flare, prevents flares better than vehicle in the randomised evidence. The systematic review and meta-analysis (Schmitt J et al., PMID: 20819086) pooled eight vehicle-controlled trials: the relative risk of experiencing at least one flare was 0.46 (95% CI 0.38 to 0.55) with proactive fluticasone propionate — a 54% relative reduction — and 0.78 (95% CI 0.60 to 1.00) with proactive tacrolimus, with methylprednisolone aceponate also efficacious in its single trial. In the largest tacrolimus paradigm trial (Paller AS et al., PMID: 19015204), children whose eczema had stabilised and who applied tacrolimus three times weekly to previously affected skin had significantly more disease-free days and a significantly longer time to first relapse than those on vehicle. The open questions are long-term: the trials were too short and too small to establish the safety of years of proactive anti-inflammatory use. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): proactive maintenance is a proven flare-prevention strategy, strongest for topical corticosteroid, with its long-term safety still asserted rather than shown.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — meta-analysis of 8 vehicle-controlled trials: flare relative risk 0.46 (0.38–0.55) for proactive fluticasone and 0.78 (0.60–1.00) for proactive tacrolimus; long-term safety not established

title: Emollients for eczema: fewer flares (relative risk 0.40) and a sixfold longer time to flare (median 180 versus 30 days), but the average severity gain (-2.42 SCORAD points) is far below the 8.7 points patients would notice — low-quality evidence throughout
question: In people with atopic eczema, do standard emollients and moisturisers improve severity and reduce flares compared with no moisturiser or vehicle?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — moisturisers probably help eczema a little, and the Cochrane review is honest about how little certainty there is. Across 77 studies with 6,603 participants (van Zuuren EJ et al., PMID: 28166390), the six studies comparing moisturiser with no moisturiser found lower SCORAD scores (mean difference -2.42, 95% CI -4.55 to -0.28, in three studies) — well short of the 8.7-point minimal important difference — alongside fewer flares (relative risk 0.40, 95% CI 0.23 to 0.70, in two studies), a prolonged time to flare (median 180 versus 30 days), and less topical corticosteroid needed (mean difference -9.30 g). Evidence for these no-treatment comparisons was low quality; most individual moisturisers beat their vehicles on some measures, and the reviewers found no reliable evidence that one moisturiser is better than another. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): emollients are a reasonable, low-harm foundation of eczema care with a small average effect — flare prevention and steroid-sparing are their best-supported benefits, not severity transformation.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — Cochrane review of 77 studies: versus no moisturiser, SCORAD -2.42 points (below the 8.7-point minimal important difference) but flare relative risk 0.40 and median time to flare 180 vs 30 days; evidence low quality

title: Wet-wrap therapy for atopic dermatitis: the meta-analysis of six small trials (19–51 patients each) could not show it beats topical steroids alone — low-quality evidence, with an imprecise infection signal (relative risk 6.35, 95% CI 0.83 to 48.55)
question: In moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis in children, does wet-wrap therapy added to topical treatment improve severity compared with topical treatment alone?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — wet wraps are widely used as a crisis intervention for severe eczema, but the randomised evidence that they add anything to topical steroids is thin. The systematic review and meta-analysis (González-López G et al., PMID: 27861727) found six trials of 19 to 51 patients each; severity and quality-of-life results were reported incompletely and were too heterogeneous to pool, the overall quality of evidence was low, and there was a non-significant tendency to more mild skin infections with wet wraps (pooled relative risk 6.35, 95% CI 0.83 to 48.55). The best single trial (Janmohamed SR et al., PMID: 24698702) compared wet wraps with diluted corticosteroid against wet wraps with emollient in children with severe eczema and found the steroid version acted faster and was more efficacious on objective SCORAD at every measuring point — which shows the steroid under the wrap matters, not that the wrap itself adds benefit. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): wet-wrap therapy remains a plausible short-term rescue on weak evidence; its added value over the topical treatment it delivers is unproven.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — systematic review of 6 small trials: efficacy over topical steroids alone unproven and low-quality; one trial shows diluted-steroid wraps beat emollient wraps in severe childhood eczema

title: Alitretinoin for severe chronic hand eczema: clear or almost-clear hands in up to 48% versus 17% on placebo in the 1,032-patient BACH trial — dose-dependent headache, lipid and thyroid effects, and relapse a median 5.5–6.2 months after stopping
question: In severe chronic hand eczema that topical steroids cannot control, does oral alitretinoin clear the hands compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — oral alitretinoin cleared severe, steroid-refractory chronic hand eczema in the large BACH trial (Ruzicka T et al., PMID: 18294310): responses (clear or almost-clear hands on the Physician Global Assessment) reached up to 48% on alitretinoin versus 17% on placebo (P<0.001), with up to a 75% median reduction in disease signs and symptoms. Benefit came with the retinoid price list — dose-dependent headache, mucocutaneous events, hyperlipidaemia, and decreased free thyroxine and thyroid-stimulating hormone — and it did not last: median time to relapse after stopping was 5.5–6.2 months. For patients who did not fully respond, an extended further course (Lynde C et al., PMID: 22731739) produced response rates of 39% to 51% depending on prior treatment, with no late-arising toxicities over up to 48 weeks of total exposure. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): alitretinoin is an effective oral option for severe hand eczema that topicals cannot control — Tier C because one pivotal trial carries it, and a maintenance commitment rather than a cure.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single large placebo-controlled trial (1,032 patients): clear/almost-clear hands in up to 48% versus 17%; dose-dependent retinoid adverse effects and relapse a median ~6 months after stopping

title: Adalimumab versus methotrexate in children with severe plaque psoriasis: PASI-75 in 58% versus 32% at week 16 — but clear or minimal disease (61% versus 41%) was not significant, in the only head-to-head trial (114 children)
question: In children with moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis, is adalimumab more effective than methotrexate for skin clearance, and how do their safety profiles compare?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — adalimumab 0.8 mg/kg beat methotrexate on the first of two ranked primary endpoints in the only head-to-head trial in children with severe plaque psoriasis (Papp K et al., PMID: 28478975): PASI-75 at week 16 was achieved by 22 (58%) of 38 on adalimumab versus 12 (32%) of 37 on methotrexate (p=0.027), while the second endpoint, clear or minimal Physician Global Assessment, favoured adalimumab without reaching significance (61% versus 41%; p=0.083). Infections were the commonest adverse events in all groups (45% on adalimumab 0.8 mg/kg, 57% on methotrexate during initial treatment), and no new safety risks emerged. The 52-week extension (Thaçi D et al., PMID: 31017657) found efficacy maintained or improved with continued adalimumab — including in children switched from methotrexate, whose PASI-75 rates rose from 31% to 86% across the reported range — with no serious infections. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): adalimumab clears more children's skin than methotrexate at 16 weeks, on one small trial whose second primary endpoint did not confirm the first. Tier C for that single-trial base.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single phase 3 trial (114 children): adalimumab 0.8 mg/kg PASI-75 58% versus methotrexate 32% (p=0.027) at week 16; clear/minimal PGA 61% versus 41% not significant; efficacy maintained in 52-week extension

title: Home versus hospital UVB phototherapy for psoriasis (PLUTO): equally effective (SAPASI-50 in 82% versus 79%) and equally safe, with lower treatment burden and no higher costs (€800 versus €752 at end of therapy)
question: In plaque psoriasis needing ultraviolet B phototherapy, is home phototherapy as effective as outpatient phototherapy — and is it as safe?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — where the treatment is delivered made no difference to what it achieved in the pragmatic PLUTO trial (Koek MB et al., PMID: 19423623): SAPASI-50 was reached by 82% of home-treated versus 79% of outpatient-treated patients (difference 2.8%, 95% CI -8.6 to 14.2), PASI-50 by 70% versus 73%, cumulative ultraviolet doses and short-term side effects were similar, and quality of life improved equally — while treatment burden was significantly lower at home and 42% of home patients rated the experience 'excellent' versus 23% of outpatients. The economic evaluation of the same trial (Koek MB et al., PMID: 20406865) found total costs of €800 for home versus €752 for outpatient treatment at end of therapy (difference €48, 95% CI -77 to 174) and near-identical QALY gains (0.296 versus 0.291). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): home UVB is as effective and safe as outpatient UVB for eligible patients, with less burden and no cost penalty — on one Dutch trial, so Tier C.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — single pragmatic non-inferiority trial (196 patients): home UVB matched outpatient UVB on SAPASI-50 (82% vs 79%), safety and QALYs, with lower burden and similar costs

title: Imiquimod versus surgery for low-risk basal cell carcinoma (SINS): success 84% versus 98% at 3 years and 82.5% versus 97.7% at 5 years — the cream works for most, but it is not a substitute for excision
question: For nodular and superficial basal cell carcinoma, is imiquimod 5% cream an acceptable substitute for surgical excision on tumour clearance at three and five years?
balance: SPLIT — imiquimod clears most low-risk basal cell carcinomas but is clearly inferior to surgery, so 'substitute' depends on what the patient is trading. In the SINS trial (Bath-Hextall F et al., PMID: 24332516), clinical success at 3 years was 178 (84%) of 213 on imiquimod versus 185 (98%) of 188 on surgical excision (relative risk 0.84, 98% CI 0.78 to 0.91), failing the prespecified non-inferiority margin. At 5 years (Williams HC et al., PMID: 27932240) success was 82.5% (170/206) versus 97.7% (173/177), with most imiquimod failures occurring in year 1 — lesions that respond early tend to stay clear. The Cochrane review of BCC interventions (Thomson J et al., PMID: 33202063) expresses the same gap as recurrence: 16.4% after imiquimod versus 1.6% after excision at 3 years (relative risk 10.30), while noting cosmetic outcomes can favour non-surgical treatment. Itching (211 versus 129 patients) and weeping (160 versus 81) were commoner with the cream. PROPOSED SPLIT: surgery remains the standard; imiquimod is a legitimate, knowingly less effective option for small low-risk lesions when surgery is declined, impractical, or cosmetically costly.
stamp: SPLIT — imiquimod succeeds in ~83–84% of low-risk BCCs at 3–5 years but is clearly inferior to surgery (98%); an option for selected lesions and patients, not an equivalent substitute

title: Mohs surgery versus standard excision for facial basal cell carcinoma: no proven gain for primary tumours (10-year recurrence 4.4% versus 12.2%, p=0.10), a clear gain for recurrent ones (3.9% versus 13.5%, p=0.023) — at higher cost
question: For primary basal cell carcinoma of the face, does Mohs micrographic surgery reduce recurrence compared with standard surgical excision — for primary and for recurrent tumours?
balance: SPLIT — Mohs micrographic surgery earns its extra cost and complexity for recurrent facial basal cell carcinoma, not demonstrably for primary tumours. In the Dutch randomised trial's 5-year report (Mosterd K et al., PMID: 19010733), recurrences among primary tumours were 4 (2.5%) after Mohs versus 7 (4.1%) after excision (p=0.397), while among recurrent tumours they were 2 (2.4%) after Mohs versus 10 (12.1%) after excision (p=0.015). At 10 years (van Loo E et al., PMID: 25262378) cumulative recurrence probabilities were 4.4% after Mohs versus 12.2% after excision for primary tumours (p=0.100) and 3.9% versus 13.5% for recurrent tumours (p=0.023) — the primary-tumour gap widened numerically without reaching significance. Treatment costs were higher for Mohs (€1,248 versus €990 for primary; €1,284 versus €1,043 for recurrent tumours), giving an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio of €23,454 for primary but €3,171 for recurrent disease. PROPOSED SPLIT: reserve Mohs for recurrent facial BCC (and judge primary cases on site and histology), because the trial proves a recurrence benefit only there. Tier C: a single trial, with substantial loss to follow-up.
stamp: SPLIT — Mohs reduces recurrence for recurrent facial BCC (10-year 3.9% vs 13.5%, p=0.023) but not significantly for primary BCC (4.4% vs 12.2%, p=0.10); costs higher in both

title: One course of fluorouracil 5% cream to prevent skin cancer in high-risk veterans: squamous cell carcinoma surgery cut from 4% to 1% in year 1 only — no effect on basal cell carcinoma and no overall benefit across the full trial
question: In veterans at high risk of keratinocyte carcinoma, does a single course of topical fluorouracil 5% cream prevent new squamous and basal cell carcinomas?
balance: SPLIT — one short course of fluorouracil 5% cream bought exactly one year of protection against squamous cell carcinoma, and nothing else. In the Veterans Affairs trial (Weinstock MA et al., PMID: 29299592), 932 veterans with at least two prior keratinocyte carcinomas applied fluorouracil or vehicle to the face and ears twice daily for 2–4 weeks. In year 1, squamous cell carcinoma developed in 5 (1%) on fluorouracil versus 20 (4%) on control — a 75% relative reduction (95% CI 35% to 91%; P=.002) — while basal cell carcinoma was unaffected (45 [10%] versus 50 [11%], not significant). Over the whole study there was no difference in time to first keratinocyte, basal cell or squamous cell carcinoma. The economic analysis (Yoon J et al., PMID: 29505863) found the intervention arm's treatment and dermatology costs lower at 1 year ($2,106 versus $2,444) and $771 less per patient by 3 years. PROPOSED SPLIT: a real but brief chemopreventive effect against squamous cell carcinoma in very-high-risk skin, with no basal-cell effect and no durable overall prevention. Tier C: a single trial carries the claim.
stamp: SPLIT — single trial (932 veterans): year-1 squamous cell carcinoma 1% versus 4% (75% relative reduction) but no basal-cell effect and no difference over full follow-up; costs lower by $771 per patient at 3 years

title: Low-dose minocycline (DFD-29, 40 mg) for papulopustular rosacea: IGA success beat placebo by 32.9 and 34.1 percentage points and doxycycline 40 mg by 18.0 and 28.3 points in two phase 3 trials
question: In papulopustular rosacea, does once-daily low-dose minocycline (DFD-29) reduce inflammatory lesions better than doxycycline 40 mg and placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — DFD-29, a 40 mg low-dose modified-release minocycline formulation (the specific tested product in the MVOR trials), beat both placebo and the standard low-dose doxycycline 40 mg in two phase 3 trials (Bhatia N et al., PMID: 40042869). Investigator's Global Assessment success exceeded placebo by 32.9 percentage points in MVOR-1 and 34.1 points in MVOR-2, and exceeded doxycycline by 18.0 and 28.3 points (all significant). Inflammatory lesion reductions likewise favoured DFD-29 over placebo (least-squares mean differences -9.2 and -6.8 lesions) and over doxycycline (-4.7 and -3.5). Adverse events on DFD-29 were reported by 26.4% and 41.8% of participants, against 21.6% and 33.1% on doxycycline and 35.5% and 36.6% on placebo, with nasopharyngitis and COVID-19 the commonest events. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the most effective oral agent yet tested head-to-head for papulopustular rosacea on these records — two industry trials of 16 weeks, with no data beyond that horizon and no comparison with topical standards.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two phase 3 trials: DFD-29 (minocycline 40 mg) IGA success +32.9/+34.1 points versus placebo and +18.0/+28.3 points versus doxycycline 40 mg, with adverse-event rates comparable to both

title: Brimonidine 0.5% gel for rosacea redness: significantly more two-grade improvement than vehicle from 30 minutes to 12 hours on days 1, 15 and 29 in two pivotal trials (all P<.001) — a same-day effect, not a cure; the abstracts report no percentages
question: In moderate-to-severe facial erythema of rosacea, does brimonidine tartrate gel 0.5% reduce redness on the day of application compared with vehicle?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — brimonidine tartrate gel 0.5%, a vasoconstrictive alpha-2 agonist, reduces rosacea redness for the day it is applied. In the two pivotal randomised trials (Fowler J et al., PMID: 23839181), once-daily brimonidine was significantly more efficacious than vehicle throughout the 12 hours after application on days 1, 15 and 29, with a significant difference as early as 30 minutes after the first dose (all P<.001), and no tachyphylaxis, rebound or aggravation of other rosacea signs over 4 weeks. The earlier dose-finding programme (Fowler J et al., PMID: 22050040) showed a dose-dependent effect, with a single application of the 0.5% gel significantly reducing measured redness from 30 minutes to 12 hours, and the same two-grade success advantage on days 1, 15 and 29. Neither abstract reports the success percentages — a declared gap that caps the stamp at POSSIBLE. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a reliable same-day cosmetic pharmacology for persistent facial erythema — it treats the day, not the disease.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two pivotal vehicle-controlled trials: significantly greater two-grade erythema improvement than vehicle from 30 minutes to 12 hours on days 1, 15 and 29 (all P<.001), no rebound; absolute rates not reported in the records

title: Spesolimab for a generalised pustular psoriasis flare: pustules cleared in 54% versus 6% at one week in a 53-patient trial — infections in 47% by week 12 and systemic drug reactions keep this a specialist rescue treatment
question: In an acute flare of generalised pustular psoriasis, does a single intravenous dose of spesolimab clear pustules within a week compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single intravenous dose of spesolimab, an interleukin-36 receptor blocker, cleared pustules within a week in the Effisayil 1 trial (Bachelez H et al., PMID: 34936739): a pustulation subscore of 0 (no visible pustules) at week 1 was reached by 19 of 35 patients (54%) on spesolimab versus 1 of 18 (6%) on placebo (difference 49 percentage points, 95% CI 21 to 67; P<0.001), and a total score of 0 or 1 by 15 (43%) versus 2 (11%) (difference 32 points, 95% CI 2 to 53; P=0.02). The harms are not incidental: infections occurred in 6 of 35 (17%) through week 1 and in 24 of 51 patients (47%) who received spesolimab at any time by week 12; drug reactions occurred in 2 patients, one with concurrent drug-induced liver injury; and antidrug antibodies were detected in 23 of 50 (46%). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a dramatic one-week effect in a rare, life-threatening flare — Tier C because a single 53-patient phase 2 trial, with an infection burden that demands specialist supervision, carries the whole claim.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single phase 2 trial (53 patients): pustule clearance at week 1 in 54% versus 6% (difference 49 points); infections in 47% of ever-treated patients by week 12

title: Silicone gel sheeting for hypertrophic and keloid scars: the Cochrane review found fewer hypertrophic scars (relative risk 0.46) and thinner, better-coloured scars — but every trial was highly susceptible to bias, and a later randomised trial found no Vancouver Scar Scale difference between gel, sheet and pressure alone
question: For preventing and treating hypertrophic and keloid scars, do silicone gel sheeting and silicone gel improve scar outcomes compared with no treatment or other dressings?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — silicone gel sheeting is a standard scar treatment resting on unusually weak trials. The Cochrane review (O'Brien L et al., PMID: 24030657) included 20 trials with 873 people: in prevention studies, silicone sheeting reduced hypertrophic scarring in people prone to scarring versus no treatment (relative risk 0.46, 95% CI 0.21 to 0.98), and in treatment studies it reduced scar thickness (mean difference -2.00) and improved colour (relative risk 3.49, 95% CI 1.97 to 6.15) — but the reviewers stress these studies were highly susceptible to bias, so a great deal of uncertainty prevails. A later intraindividual randomised trial in hand-burn patients (Pruksapong C et al., PMID: 33173695) found no significant differences on any Vancouver Scar Scale parameter between silicone gel plus pressure garment, silicone sheet plus pressure garment, and pressure garment alone, though some patient-and-observer scale parameters favoured the silicone combinations and scar thickness improved earlier with gel. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): cheap, safe and plausibly helpful — and after four decades of use, still not properly proven.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — Cochrane review of 20 trials (873 people): prevention relative risk 0.46 (0.21–0.98) and better thickness/colour in treatment, but all evidence highly bias-prone; a later RCT found no scale difference versus pressure alone

title: Adding silver nitrate cautery to antiseptic nasal cream changed nothing: improvement in 89% versus 91% — and the children's review calls the whole field inconclusive
question: In children with recurrent anterior nosebleeds, does antiseptic nasal cream alone match silver nitrate cautery plus cream for stopping recurrences?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference) — cautery added nothing measurable to antiseptic cream in the one randomised comparison. In Murthy 1999 (PMID: 10384851), 91% of patients on chlorhexidine–neomycin antiseptic cream alone improved versus 89% on cream plus silver nitrate cautery (P = 0.7569), with no difference between the under-16 and over-16 age groups (P = 1.000). The Cochrane review of interventions for recurrent idiopathic epistaxis in children (Qureishi 2012, PMID: 22972071) found five small trials of 468 participants in total and concluded the results were inconclusive, with no statistically significant difference between any compared treatments; its one clear finding was procedural — 75% silver nitrate beat 95% silver nitrate at two weeks (88% versus 65% complete resolution, P = 0.01) and hurt less (mean pain score 1 versus 5, P = 0.001). So cream alone matching cautery-plus-cream is the best-supported reading, but it rests on one small mixed-age trial inside an inconclusive field. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference): no added benefit from cautery over antiseptic cream was shown, and the evidence base in children is thin.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference) — the single randomised comparison found no added benefit from silver nitrate cautery over antiseptic cream alone, and the Cochrane review in children judged the whole field inconclusive

title: Intranasal steroids for acute sinusitis: 73% improved or resolved versus 66.4% on placebo — a real but modest edge, larger at higher doses
question: In acute rhinosinusitis, do intranasal corticosteroids added to antibiotics (or alone) speed symptom resolution compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a modest, dose-related gain in symptom resolution. The Cochrane review (Zalmanovici Trestioreanu 2013, PMID: 24293353) pooled four double-blind trials of 1,943 participants with acute sinusitis: resolution or improvement of symptoms occurred in 73% on intranasal corticosteroids versus 66.4% on placebo (risk ratio 1.11, 95% CI 1.04 to 1.18). Higher doses worked better — for mometasone furoate, 400 µg gave a risk ratio of 1.10 (95% CI 1.02 to 1.18) versus 1.04 (95% CI 0.98 to 1.11) for 200 µg. No significant adverse events were reported and drop-out and recurrence rates did not differ. The trials tested the spray as monotherapy or as an adjunct to antibiotics over 15 or 21 days, so the shelf cannot separate the alone-versus-added question; what it supports is a small average benefit either way. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): intranasal steroids raise the chance of improvement or resolution by about 7 percentage points over placebo in acute sinusitis.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a Cochrane meta-analysis of four double-blind trials found resolution or improvement in 73% versus 66.4% on placebo (RR 1.11), with a dose gradient and no significant adverse events
