title: Ciclosporin for antihistamine-resistant chronic urticaria: responders in both randomised trials — 8 of 19 versus 0 of 10 in the small one — with relapse the rule after stopping
question: In chronic spontaneous urticaria refractory to antihistamines, does ciclosporin induce remission compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two placebo-controlled trials agree, both on background antihistamine. In Grattan 2000 (PMID: 10951147), patients with severe disease and a positive autologous serum skin test responded in 8 of 19 cases on ciclosporin 4 mg/kg daily versus 0 of 10 on placebo at 4 weeks (P < 0.05), with mean weekly urticaria activity score falling by 12.7 points versus 2.3 on placebo (P = 0.005). In Vena 2006 (PMID: 17010756), therapeutic failures were fewer on 16 weeks of ciclosporin (3) than on placebo (11), with symptom scores significantly improved at 8 and 16 weeks. The catch is durability: six of Grattan's eight randomised responders relapsed within 6 weeks of stopping, and only five of 19 responders overall (26%) had not relapsed by study end — this is suppression while taking it, not remission after it. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): ciclosporin controls antihistamine-resistant urticaria while taken, at immunosuppressant cost, with relapse common on withdrawal.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two concordant placebo-controlled trials show ciclosporin controls antihistamine-resistant chronic urticaria while taken, with relapse common after stopping

title: Peanut sublingual immunotherapy: 70% responders versus 15% on placebo at 44 weeks in the randomised trial — and a quarter of young children passed a 5,000 mg challenge after up to 5 years
question: In young children with peanut allergy, does sublingual immunotherapy raise the tolerated peanut dose and produce sustained unresponsiveness after stopping, compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — desensitisation is real; sustained unresponsiveness is shown in a minority, without a placebo arm. The randomised trial (Fleischer 2013, PMID: 23265698) found responders in 14 of 20 (70%) on peanut SLIT versus 3 of 20 (15%) on placebo after 44 weeks (P < .001), with median successfully consumed dose in responders rising from 3.5 mg to 496 mg. The long-term study in younger children (Kim 2019, PMID: 31493887) treated children aged 1 to 11 years with 2 mg/day for up to 5 years: 67% (32/48) consumed at least 750 mg at the final challenge and 25% (12/48) passed a 5,000 mg challenge, of whom 10 of 12 showed sustained unresponsiveness after 2 to 4 weeks off therapy. Side effects were mostly transient mouth itching (4.8% of doses in Kim; no epinephrine used). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): SLIT raises the tolerated dose in most treated children, but full sustained unresponsiveness after stopping was demonstrated in only about a fifth of the long-term cohort and never against placebo. Tier C is set: the young-child and sustained-unresponsiveness claims rest on a single uncontrolled long-term study.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one randomised trial shows clear desensitisation versus placebo, but sustained unresponsiveness in young children rests on a single uncontrolled long-term study (Tier C)

title: Tinea capitis: the fungus decides — terbinafine beats griseofulvin for Trichophyton (complete cure RR 1.47), griseofulvin beats terbinafine for Microsporum (RR 0.68)
question: In children with tinea capitis, does terbinafine clear infection faster and more completely than griseofulvin — and does the answer depend on whether the fungus is Trichophyton or Microsporum?
balance: SPLIT — the answer splits by species. The Cochrane review (Chen 2017, PMID: 27816294; 25 randomised trials, 4,449 children) found terbinafine and griseofulvin similar for mixed infections (risk ratio 1.08, 95% CI 0.94 to 1.24), but terbinafine clearly better for Trichophyton tonsurans complete cure (RR 1.47, 95% CI 1.22 to 1.77) and griseofulvin clearly better for Microsporum-only infections (RR 0.68, 95% CI 0.53 to 0.86). The largest trial programme (Elewski 2008, PMID: 18378354; 1,286 children in the efficacy population) matches: complete cure 45.1% on terbinafine versus 39.2% on griseofulvin overall, with terbinafine significantly better on every cure measure for T. tonsurans and griseofulvin significantly better for M. canis. Neither drug is 'the winner' — identifying the organism is what chooses the drug. PROPOSED SPLIT: terbinafine for Trichophyton, griseofulvin for Microsporum, either for mixed or unknown infections.
stamp: SPLIT — terbinafine wins for Trichophyton (complete cure RR 1.47) and griseofulvin wins for Microsporum (RR 0.68); the two are equivalent for mixed infections

title: Varenicline nasal spray for dry eye: Schirmer responders 47–49% versus 27.8% on vehicle in phase 3 — tear production clearly up, symptom relief less consistent
question: In dry eye disease, does varenicline solution nasal spray increase tear production and improve symptoms compared with vehicle?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the sign is solid, the symptom is softer. In ONSET-2 (Wirta 2022, PMID: 34767866), a Schirmer improvement of at least 10 mm at week 4 was achieved by 47.3% on varenicline 0.03 mg and 49.2% on 0.06 mg versus 27.8% on vehicle (P < 0.0001 for both). In ONSET-1 (Wirta 2022, PMID: 36107843), the mean Schirmer advantage over vehicle was 7.7 mm (95% CI 3.8 to 11.7) at 0.03 mg and 7.5 mm (95% CI 3.4 to 11.6) at 0.06 mg (both P < 0.001). Symptoms split: eye dryness improved significantly at 0.03 mg in ONSET-1 (P = 0.021) but the ONSET-2 dryness difference was not significant in the controlled-environment chamber and only nominally significant in clinic. The price is nasal, not ocular: sneezing in 62–84% in ONSET-1 and at least one treatment-emergent event in 97–99% on active spray versus 57% on vehicle in ONSET-2, mostly mild sneezing, cough and throat irritation. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): varenicline nasal spray reliably increases tear production over 4 weeks; how much patients feel it is less certain.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two randomised trials show a clear tear-production gain versus vehicle, with inconsistent symptom benefit and mostly mild nasal side effects

title: Perfluorohexyloctane for evaporative dry eye: corneal staining and dryness both significantly better than saline in two phase 3 trials — differences of about 1 staining point and 8–10 dryness points
question: In evaporative dry eye from meibomian gland dysfunction, does perfluorohexyloctane ophthalmic solution improve corneal staining and dryness compared with hypotonic saline control?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — two large phase 3 trials, both primary endpoints met in both. In GOBI (Tauber 2023, PMID: 36574848), the week-8 advantage over hypotonic saline was −0.97 points for total corneal fluorescein staining (95% CI −1.40 to −0.55) and −7.6 points for eye dryness on a 0–100 scale (95% CI −11.8 to −3.4), both P < 0.001. In MOJAVE (Sheppard 2023, PMID: 36948372), staining change was −2.3 versus −1.1 (difference −1.2, 95% CI −1.7 to −0.8) and dryness change −29.4 versus −19.2 (difference −10.2, 95% CI −14.4 to −6.1), both P < .001, with differences present from week 2. Ocular adverse events were similar to saline (12.9% versus 12.3% in MOJAVE) and no serious ocular events occurred in either trial. The effects are statistically robust but modest in size — about one staining point on a 15-point scale — and the trials run only 8 weeks. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): perfluorohexyloctane improves both the staining sign and the dryness symptom of meibomian-gland dry eye over 8 weeks, by a modest margin.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — two concordant phase 3 trials met both sign and symptom primary endpoints versus saline, with an adverse-event profile similar to saline

title: After pterygium excision, conjunctival autograft halves 6-month recurrence versus amniotic membrane (RR 0.53) — and bare-sclera excision recurs in up to 80%
question: After pterygium excision, does conjunctival autograft reduce recurrence compared with amniotic membrane graft or bare sclera?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — for autograft over amniotic membrane; the bare-sclera comparison is historical, not randomised. The Cochrane review (Clearfield 2016, PMID: 26867004; 20 randomised trials, 1,947 eyes) found recurrence at 6 months ranging from 3.3% to 16.7% after conjunctival autograft versus 6.4% to 42.3% after amniotic membrane graft, a pooled risk ratio of 0.53 (95% CI 0.33 to 0.85) — a 47% relative reduction. For recurrent pterygia the advantage was larger (RR 0.45, 95% CI 0.21 to 0.99). At 3 months there was no difference (RR 0.87, 95% CI 0.43 to 1.77). Against bare sclera the review offers only background: recurrence with simple excision leaving bare sclera 'has been reported to be upwards of 80%', which is why grafting is standard — no randomised bare-sclera arm is pooled here. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): conjunctival autograft is the better graft for preventing 6-month recurrence, especially for recurrent pterygium.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — a 20-trial Cochrane meta-analysis found 6-month recurrence roughly halved with conjunctival autograft versus amniotic membrane graft (RR 0.53)

title: Blocked tear duct in infants: balloon dilation succeeded in 82% and intubation in 84% in prospective series — but no randomised trial has ever shown either beats simple probing
question: In infants and children with congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction that has not resolved, does balloon catheter dilation or nasolacrimal intubation beat simple probing for resolution?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference) — not because the procedures fail, but because the head-to-head randomised evidence does not exist. In the PEDIG prospective series, primary balloon catheter dilation succeeded in 82% of eyes (95% CI 74% to 88%; Repka 2008, PMID: 18929305) — with no comparison group, so it cannot show superiority over probing. After a failed probing, balloon dilation and intubation performed alike: success in 77% of balloon eyes versus 84% (adjusted) of intubation eyes, risk ratio 1.08 (0.95 to 1.22) (Repka 2009, PMID: 19433712). And the one randomised trial in this area (Lee 2013, PMID: 23954210) compared timing, not technique: immediate office probing versus 6 months of observation then facility probing gave bilateral success in 66% versus 76% (difference −10%, 95% CI −35% to 14%), with 56% of observed infants resolving in both eyes without any surgery. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference): balloon and intubation are reasonable escalations after failed probing, but 'beats probing' is unproven. Tier C is set: the technique comparison rests on non-randomised prospective cohorts.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference) — no randomised trial compares balloon dilation or intubation against probing; prospective series show similar success rates for all three (Tier C)

title: Screening for HLA-B*1502 before carbamazepine in Taiwan: zero cases of Stevens–Johnson syndrome in 4,877 screened patients, against about 10 expected historically
question: In populations with high HLA-B*15:02 prevalence, does screening for HLA-B*15:02 before starting carbamazepine prevent Stevens–Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a large prospective screening programme with a historical comparator, not a randomised trial. In Chen 2011 (PMID: 21428768), 4,877 carbamazepine candidates in Taiwan were genotyped: 372 (7.7%) carried HLA-B*1502 and were advised to avoid carbamazepine, while the 92.3% who tested negative took it. Stevens–Johnson syndrome or toxic epidermal necrolysis developed in none of the screened-negative patients taking carbamazepine, against an estimated historical incidence of 0.23% — about 10 expected cases in this cohort (P < 0.001). Mild transient rash still occurred in 4.3% and a more widespread rash requiring hospitalisation in 0.1%, so screening removes the catastrophic reaction, not all rash. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): in a high-prevalence population, pre-treatment HLA-B*1502 screening with avoidance in carriers was associated with eliminating carbamazepine-induced SJS-TEN in nearly 5,000 patients. Tier C is set: the evidence is a single prospective cohort against historical incidence, an observational design.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one large prospective screening cohort (4,877 patients) saw zero SJS-TEN cases versus about 10 expected historically; observational evidence (Tier C)

title: TPMT testing before thiopurines (TOPIC): no overall reduction in blood toxicity (7.4% versus 7.9%) — but variant carriers given a reduced dose had a tenth the events (2.6% versus 22.9%)
question: In patients with inflammatory bowel disease starting thiopurines, does pre-treatment TPMT genotyping with genotype-guided dosing reduce haematological adverse events versus standard dosing?
balance: SPLIT — the trial's two answers point opposite ways depending on who you look at. Overall, TOPIC (Coenen 2015, PMID: 26072396) found haematological adverse events in 7.4% of the genotype-guided group versus 7.9% on standard care (relative risk 0.93, 95% CI 0.57 to 1.52) — no benefit, because variant carriers are uncommon. But among carriers themselves, dose reduction worked dramatically: 2.6% of screened carriers developed a haematological event versus 22.9% of unscreened carriers (relative risk 0.11, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.85). Disease activity did not differ between groups (P = .18 for Crohn's disease, P = .14 for ulcerative colitis), so the dose reduction did not cost efficacy. PROPOSED SPLIT: population-level screening did not lower the overall event rate in this trial, while identified carriers who received a reduced starting dose were strongly protected.
stamp: SPLIT — no overall reduction in haematological events (RR 0.93), but a tenfold reduction among TPMT variant carriers given genotype-guided doses (RR 0.11)

title: UGT1A1-guided irinotecan dosing: febrile neutropenia in 6.5% of dose-reduced poor metabolisers versus 24% in historical full-dose poor metabolisers — and €183 saved per patient
question: In patients with UGT1A1 poor-metaboliser genotypes starting irinotecan, does pre-emptive genotype-guided dose reduction reduce severe neutropenia and diarrhoea versus standard dosing?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a prospective implementation study against historical controls, backed by the genetics of the toxicity. In Hulshof 2022 (PMID: 34998046), 31 of 350 patients (8.9%) were UGT1A1 poor metabolisers and received a median 30% initial dose reduction; febrile neutropenia in the first two cycles occurred in 6.5% of them versus 24% in a historical poor-metaboliser cohort treated at full dose (P = 0.04), a rate comparable to non-poor-metabolisers on full dose. The meta-analysis card (Zhang 2017, PMID: 28585035) confirms the underlying risk the strategy targets: UGT1A1*6 variant carriers had roughly double the odds of severe neutropenia (OR 2.03, 95% CI 1.54 to 2.68; homozygous OR 2.95, 1.83 to 4.75). Dose reduction was cost-saving (€183 per patient). The record reports neutropenia outcomes; a diarrhoea benefit is not quantified in it. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): pre-emptive genotyping with a 30% starting-dose reduction in poor metabolisers cut febrile neutropenia to the background rate. Tier C is set: the dosing study is non-randomised with a historical comparator.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one prospective non-randomised study found febrile neutropenia of 6.5% with genotype-guided dose reduction versus 24% historically (Tier C)

title: CYP3A5-guided tacrolimus starting dose: 43.2% in target range at day 3 versus 29.1% with standard dosing — faster to target, fewer dose changes, clinical outcomes unchanged
question: In kidney transplant recipients, does adapting the starting tacrolimus dose to CYP3A5 genotype get patients into the target range faster versus standard weight-based dosing?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for the blood level, not (yet) for the patient. In Thervet 2010 (PMID: 20393454), 280 kidney transplant recipients were randomised to a CYP3A5-adapted or standard starting dose: at day 3, 43.2% of the adapted group were within the target trough range versus 29.1% of controls (P = 0.03), the adapted group needed fewer dose modifications, and 75% of them reached target sooner. Clinical endpoints, however, were similar in the two groups — no rejection or survival advantage was shown. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): genotype-adapted starting doses get tacrolimus into range faster with less titration, a process benefit whose clinical payoff remains unproven. Tier C is set: a single trial carrying a benefit claim.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single randomised trial found more patients in target range at day 3 with CYP3A5-adapted dosing, with no difference in clinical endpoints (Tier C)

title: Rapid MT-RNR1 testing before gentamicin in newborn intensive care: 80.6% of antibiotic-treated babies tested in 26 minutes, 3 carriers identified and spared aminoglycosides, no delay to antibiotics
question: In neonatal intensive care, does a rapid point-of-care test for the MT-RNR1 m.1555A>G variant, used before gentamicin, prevent aminoglycoside-induced hearing loss versus standard prescribing?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the pathway works end-to-end; prevented deafness itself is inferred, not counted. In the PALOH implementation study (McDermott 2022, PMID: 35311942), 751 neonates at two UK intensive care units were tested with a point-of-care assay giving a result in 26 minutes, with 100% sensitivity (95% CI 93.9% to 100%) and specificity (98.5% to 100%) on preclinical validation. Three babies carried the m.1555A>G variant and all three avoided aminoglycosides; 424 infants (80.6%) receiving antibiotics were successfully tested, and mean time to antibiotics was equivalent to previous practice. No baby in the study was followed to a hearing outcome — the prevented harm rests on the established variant–ototoxicity link and on those three avoided exposures. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): rapid testing can be integrated without delaying antibiotics and does divert carriers away from aminoglycosides. Tier C is set: a single non-randomised implementation study with a process outcome.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single prospective implementation study showed rapid testing integrated without delaying antibiotics and diverted all 3 identified carriers from aminoglycosides (Tier C)

title: SLCO1B1 and simvastatin myopathy: odds ratio 4.5 per copy of the rs4149056 C allele — 16.9 in CC homozygotes — replicated at the lower dose and in a second genome-wide study
question: In patients taking high-dose simvastatin, does the SLCO1B1 variant identify who is at high risk of myopathy — and should it change statin choice or dose?
balance: LIKELY (harm) — for carrying the variant on high-dose simvastatin; the testing-policy half of the question has no trial. The SEARCH genome-wide study (Link 2008, PMID: 18650507) found myopathy odds rising 4.5-fold per copy of the SLCO1B1 rs4149056 C allele (95% CI 2.6 to 7.7), and 16.9-fold (4.7 to 61.1) in CC versus TT homozygotes, with more than 60% of myopathy cases in the 80 mg trial attributable to the variant; the association replicated in a 40 mg simvastatin trial. An independent genome-wide study (Carr 2019, PMID: 31220337) again found only this variant genome-wide significant for severe myopathy (OR 5.15, 95% CI 3.13 to 8.45). No record carded here randomised patients to genotype-guided statin choice, so 'should it change prescribing' is answered by risk magnitude, not by an outcomes trial. PROPOSED LIKELY (harm): the C allele identifies a genuinely high-risk group for simvastatin myopathy, strongest at 80 mg. Tier C is set: observational genetic association evidence behind a harm claim.
stamp: LIKELY (harm) — the SLCO1B1 rs4149056 C allele confers an odds ratio of 4.5 per copy (16.9 in homozygotes) for simvastatin myopathy, replicated across studies; observational evidence (Tier C)

title: CYP2D6-guided opioid prescribing after surgery (ADOPT-PGx): prescribing concordance rose from 27% to 64% — pain scores and opioid use did not move (SIA difference 2.8, P = .80)
question: In patients with acute postoperative pain, does CYP2D6-guided opioid selection improve pain control and reduce adverse effects versus usual opioid prescribing?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — a well-run pragmatic trial whose intervention changed prescriptions but not outcomes. In ADOPT-PGx (Cavallari 2026, PMID: 41719044), among 351 poor or intermediate CYP2D6 metabolisers, phenotype-concordant opioid treatment was 64% in the guided arm versus 27% in controls (difference 37 percentage points, 95% CI 27 to 46; P < .001). Yet the 10-day primary outcome was identical: mean Silverman integrated analgesic assessment score 1.4 versus −1.4 (difference 2.8, 95% CI −18.3 to 23.8; P = .80), with pain intensity 5.2 versus 5.1 and opioid use 13.7 versus 13.2 morphine milligram equivalents per day. Adverse-effect differences are not reported in the record. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): in contemporary multimodal postoperative care, CYP2D6 guidance changed what was prescribed without improving pain or reducing opioid use. Tier C is not set — this is a null from a single large randomised trial, not a benefit or harm claim; it is flagged in the summary for the coordinator's attention on single-trial null calibration.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — one large pragmatic randomised trial found CYP2D6 guidance changed prescribing (64% versus 27% concordance) without changing pain or opioid use

title: CYP2C19-tailored H. pylori therapy: first-line eradication 96.0% versus 70.0% with standard triple therapy — at no extra cost per cure
question: In patients with Helicobacter pylori infection, does CYP2C19 genotype-guided acid-suppression therapy improve eradication rates versus standard empirical therapy?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one randomised trial, a very large effect. In Furuta 2007 (PMID: 17215846), 300 H. pylori-positive patients were randomised to standard triple therapy or a regimen tailored by CYP2C19 genotype and bacterial clarithromycin susceptibility: intention-to-treat eradication was 96.0% (144/150; 95% CI 91.5 to 98.2) in the tailored group versus 70.0% (105/150; 62.2 to 77.2) on standard therapy (P < 0.001) — a 26-percentage-point absolute gain. Final cost per successful eradication was essentially identical ($669 tailored versus $657 standard), because fewer tailored patients needed second-line treatment. The catch: the tailored arm bundled two personalisations (genotype-guided acid suppression and susceptibility-guided antibiotics), so the trial cannot credit CYP2C19 alone. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): pharmacogenomically tailored first-line therapy eradicated H. pylori in 96% versus 70%. Tier C is set: a single trial carrying a benefit claim.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single randomised trial found eradication of 96.0% with genotype-tailored therapy versus 70.0% with standard therapy (Tier C)

title: SHIVA: choosing targeted drugs from tumour profiling did not improve progression-free survival (2.3 versus 2.0 months; HR 0.88, P = 0.41) in advanced cancer
question: In adults with advanced cancer, does choosing targeted therapy from tumour molecular profiling improve progression-free survival versus conventional physician-choice therapy?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the first randomised test of profile-matched prescribing was negative. In SHIVA (Le Tourneau 2015, PMID: 26342236), 195 patients with refractory metastatic solid tumours and a matchable molecular alteration were randomised to a matched targeted agent or physician's-choice treatment: median progression-free survival was 2.3 months (95% CI 1.7 to 3.8) versus 2.0 months (1.8 to 2.1), hazard ratio 0.88 (95% CI 0.65 to 1.19; P = 0.41). Grade 3–4 adverse events occurred in 43% on targeted agents versus 35% on chemotherapy (P = 0.30). Only 40% of the 741 screened patients had an alteration matching one of the trial's ten regimens at all. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): molecular profiling with the panel and drug set of this trial did not improve progression-free survival over physician's choice, and off-label matched use outside trials was discouraged by its authors.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — one randomised phase 2 trial found no progression-free survival benefit from profile-matched targeted therapy (HR 0.88, P = 0.41)

title: Child–parent screening at immunisation visits: 40 children and 40 parents identified per 10,095 toddlers screened — 8 people per 1,000 — a screening-yield study, not an outcomes trial
question: At routine childhood immunisation visits, does child–parent screening — testing the child for familial hypercholesterolaemia and then the parents — identify new FH cases effectively versus usual practice?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for case identification only; no outcome benefit was tested. In Wald DS et al. (PMID: 27783906), capillary blood samples were obtained to measure cholesterol levels and to test for familial hypercholesterolemia mutations in 10,095 children 1 to 2 years of age during routine immunization visits in primary care. Using a prespecified cholesterol cutoff value of 1.53 multiples of the median (MoM), 28 children had positive screening results for familial hypercholesterolemia (0.3% of the 10,095 children; 95% CI, 0.2 to 0.4). A lower initial cutoff strategy — 1.35 MoM plus a mutation, or two cholesterol values of at least 1.50 MoM — identified 40 children (0.4%) and 40 parents who had positive screening results. The overall mutation prevalence was 1 in 273 children (37 in 10,095; 95% CI, 1 in 198 to 1 in 388). For every 1000 children screened, 8 persons (4 children and 4 parents) were identified as having positive screening results for familial hypercholesterolemia. The study had no usual-practice comparison group and measured no cardiovascular outcomes, so it establishes the identification yield and feasibility of the strategy — not that screening this way prevents heart attacks or deaths, and not a head-to-head advantage over usual practice. This shelf is a re-card: Wald 2016 also serves as a supporting card on live shelf #476, which asks about cascade screening of relatives of people already known to have FH; child–parent screening at immunisation visits (screen the child first, then the parents) is a different screening strategy and a genuinely different question. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): child–parent screening at routine immunisation visits feasibly identifies new FH cases in both generations — 8 persons per 1,000 children screened — on the evidence of one large prospective study, with any outcome benefit unproven.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in one large prospective primary-care study (10,095 children aged 1–2 years), child–parent screening at routine immunisation visits identified 40 children (0.4%) and 40 parents with positive results — 8 persons per 1,000 children screened; the claim is identification yield only, with no usual-practice comparator and no cardiovascular outcomes measured

title: After direct-to-consumer genomic testing (PGen): vegetable intake rose 0.11 servings a day and strength exercise 0.14 days a week — changes unrelated to the genetic results themselves
question: After direct-to-consumer personal genomic testing, do people change diet, exercise, screening, or other health behaviours — and do they share results with clinicians?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — tiny average behaviour changes, driven by the experience of testing rather than by what the results said. In the PGen cohort (Nielsen 2017, PMID: 28464943; 1,002 participants with 6-month follow-up), vegetable intake rose by 0.11 servings/day (95% CI 0.05 to 0.17; P = 0.0003) and strength exercise by 0.14 days/week (0.03 to 0.25; P = 0.0153), with larger gains confined to participants who rated their health poorly at baseline; genetic results were not consistently associated with any change. On sharing and clinical contact (Carere 2017, PMID: 27657683), 5.6% (54/961) reported changing or starting a prescription medication because of their results, and 83.3% of those consulted a health-care provider first — fewer than 1% reported unsupervised changes. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): testing is followed by small, mostly healthy shifts and usually clinician-mediated medication changes, but nothing here shows the genomic information itself caused them. Tier C is set: observational survey evidence.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — observational cohort data show only tiny average diet and exercise changes after testing, unrelated to the results received (Tier C)

title: Whole-genome sequencing in healthy primary-care patients (MedSeq): new clinical actions for 34% versus 16% — behaviour change no different (41% versus 30%), and 2 of 11 flagged results judged inappropriately managed
question: In healthy adults in primary care, does whole-genome sequencing added to standard care find clinically useful results and change management versus standard care alone?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — sequencing changed what doctors did; whether patients were better off is unknown. In the MedSeq pilot trial (Vassy 2017, PMID: 28654958), 100 generally healthy patients aged 40–65 were randomised to family-history assessment alone or family history plus an interpreted whole-genome report. Eleven of 50 sequenced patients (22%) had new monogenic disease-risk results, but only 2 (4%) had any evidence of the predicted phenotype. Physicians recommended new clinical actions for 34% of sequenced patients versus 16% of controls, while reported health-behaviour change at 6 months was 41% versus 30% — not a significant difference at this size. A clinician-geneticist panel rated management of 8 of 11 results (73%) appropriate and 2 (18%) inappropriate. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): whole-genome sequencing in healthy adults generates findings and extra clinical actions of uncertain value. Tier C is set: a single small pilot trial.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — a single 100-patient pilot trial found sequencing prompted more clinical actions without demonstrated patient benefit (Tier C)

title: Thrombophilia testing after a first clot: recurrence hazard ratios of 0.6–1.8 for every laboratory defect — while being male (2.7×) and having an unprovoked event (HR 1.9) actually predicted recurrence
question: In patients with a first unprovoked venous thromboembolism, does testing for inherited thrombophilia (factor V Leiden and the prothrombin G20210A mutation) change management or prevent recurrence?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the laboratory results do not predict the outcome they are ordered to predict. In the Leiden follow-up cohort (Christiansen 2005, PMID: 15900005), 474 patients after a first thrombotic event were followed a mean 7.3 years; recurrence risks by laboratory abnormality ran from a hazard ratio of 0.6 (95% CI 0.3 to 1.1) for elevated factor XI to 1.8 (0.9 to 3.7) for anticoagulant deficiencies — none significant — while male sex (2.7 times the risk) and an unprovoked first event (HR 1.9, 1.2 to 2.9) did predict recurrence. In patients on warfarin (Kearon 2008, PMID: 18791166), factor V Leiden carried a recurrence hazard ratio of 0.7 (0.2 to 2.6), the prothrombin mutation 0, and one or more defects together 0.7 (0.2 to 2.3) — testing could not identify who needed stronger or longer treatment. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): inherited-thrombophilia results after a first unprovoked clot do not usefully stratify recurrence risk, so basing anticoagulation duration on them is unsupported. Tier C is set: observational and secondary-analysis evidence.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — cohort and trial-cohort data show thrombophilia results do not predict recurrence (HRs 0.6–1.8, none significant), unlike clinical factors (Tier C)

title: Dutasteride on active surveillance: progression in 38% versus 48% at 3 years in the one trial — but the endpoint is biopsy change or starting treatment, and sexual and breast effects were more common
question: In men on active surveillance for low-risk localised prostate cancer, does dutasteride delay pathological or therapeutic progression compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in the single randomised trial, dutasteride slowed the clock on a composite endpoint. In REDEEM, 54 of 144 men (38%) on dutasteride 0.5 mg daily and 70 of 145 (48%) on placebo had pathological or therapeutic progression by 3 years (hazard ratio 0.62, 95% CI 0.43–0.89; p=0.009). The catch is what progression means here: a worse biopsy or a decision to start treatment — there were no prostate-cancer deaths and no metastases in either group, so nothing in this record shows dutasteride changes the outcomes surveillance is ultimately trying to protect. The price was modest and mostly sexual: sexual adverse events or breast enlargement or tenderness in 35 men (24%) on dutasteride versus 23 (15%) on placebo, with cardiovascular events equal at 5% in both groups. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): one well-run trial shows dutasteride delays biopsy-or-treatment progression on surveillance, at a small sexual and breast side-effect cost; a mortality or metastasis benefit was not shown.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in the single REDEEM trial dutasteride delayed pathological or therapeutic progression (38% vs 48% at 3 years, HR 0.62), with more sexual and breast adverse events and no deaths or metastases in either arm

title: One year of enzalutamide on active surveillance: progression risk cut by 46% relative while on treatment — the advantage was gone a year after stopping, and fatigue and breast swelling were common
question: In men on active surveillance for low- or intermediate-risk prostate cancer, does adding enzalutamide for one year reduce progression compared with surveillance alone?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — while the drug is being taken. In the open-label ENACT trial, one year of enzalutamide 160 mg daily reduced the risk of pathological or therapeutic progression versus surveillance alone (hazard ratio 0.54, 95% CI 0.33–0.89; p=.02 — a 46% relative reduction), the odds of a negative biopsy at 1 year were 3.5 times higher, and PSA progression was delayed by 6 months (hazard ratio 0.71, 95% CI 0.53–0.97). But the biopsy and PSA advantages seen at 1 year were no longer significant at 2 years, a year after treatment stopped — this looks like suppression while on therapy, not a changed trajectory. The burden was real: fatigue in 55.4% and gynecomastia in 36.6% of treated men, and three deaths occurred in the enzalutamide arm, none judged treatment-related and none while receiving the drug. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): one open-label trial shows enzalutamide delays progression during a year of treatment, with effects that fade after stopping and a substantial fatigue and breast-symptom cost.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in the single open-label ENACT trial, one year of enzalutamide reduced progression versus surveillance alone (HR 0.54), but the advantage was not significant a year after stopping and fatigue (55.4%) and gynecomastia (36.6%) were common

title: Metformin on active surveillance: no delay in progression in a 408-man phase 3 trial (HR 1.09) — and a prespecified signal of more pathological progression in obese men
question: In men on active surveillance for low-risk prostate cancer, does metformin delay progression compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the preclinical and observational promise did not survive a proper trial. In the MAST phase 3 trial, progression occurred in 70 of 205 men on metformin 850 mg twice daily and 74 of 203 on placebo over a median 36 months, with no significant difference in progression-free survival (hazard ratio 1.09, 95% CI 0.79–1.52; P=.59). Negative biopsy rates at 36 months were 41.0% on metformin versus 31.1% on placebo, also not significant (P=.181). The one signal ran the wrong way: in the prespecified subgroup of obese men (BMI ≥30), metformin was associated with more pathological progression (hazard ratio 2.36, 95% CI 1.21–4.59; P=.0092) — a subgroup finding that needs confirmation but removes any case for casual use. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): metformin does not delay progression on active surveillance in the one large blinded trial, and it may hasten pathological progression in obese men.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — in the MAST phase 3 trial metformin did not delay progression on active surveillance (HR 1.09, 95% CI 0.79–1.52), with a prespecified subgroup signal of more pathological progression in obese men (HR 2.36)

title: Alfuzosin for chronic prostatitis / pelvic pain in alpha-blocker-naive men: 49.3% responded — exactly the same 49.3% as on placebo
question: In men with chronic prostatitis / chronic pelvic pain syndrome who have not had an alpha-blocker before, does alfuzosin improve pain and urinary symptoms compared with placebo?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — as clean a null as this literature produces. In the NIH network's multicentre trial, restricted to men diagnosed within the previous 2 years who had never taken an alpha-blocker — the group earlier small trials suggested would benefit most — 49.3% of men on alfuzosin 10 mg daily and 49.3% on placebo achieved the prespecified response of at least a 4-point fall in the NIH Chronic Prostatitis Symptom Index at 12 weeks (rate difference 0.1%, 95% CI −11.2 to 11.0; P=0.99). Global response assessment was likewise identical (34.8% versus 33.6%, P=0.90), and adverse-event rates were similar. The confidence interval excludes the minimum clinically important difference the trial was built around, so this is evidence of no useful effect in this population, not an underpowered shrug. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): alfuzosin does not improve symptoms of chronic prostatitis / chronic pelvic pain syndrome in alpha-blocker-naive men.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — in the NIH network trial, response rates on alfuzosin and placebo were identical (49.3% vs 49.3%; difference 0.1%, 95% CI −11.2 to 11.0) in alpha-blocker-naive men with chronic prostatitis / chronic pelvic pain syndrome

title: Varicocele repair in subfertile men: pregnancy rates may rise (pooled RR 1.55, low-certainty evidence) — but on live birth, the outcome that matters, the two trials point opposite ways
question: In subfertile men with varicocele, does surgical repair or embolisation improve pregnancy rates compared with no treatment or delayed treatment?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — treatment may improve pregnancy rates, but the evidence is weak where it counts. The Cochrane review (48 studies, 5,384 participants) found that surgical or radiological treatment may improve pregnancy rates compared with delayed or no treatment (risk ratio 1.55, 95% CI 1.06–2.26; 13 RCTs, 1,193 participants; low-certainty evidence), corresponding to a pregnancy chance of 21% with no or delayed treatment and between 22% and 48% after treatment. For live birth, however, the only two trials disagreed in direction, leaving the effect frankly uncertain (risk ratio 2.27, 95% CI 0.19–26.93; 204 participants; very low-certainty evidence). One comparison does reach moderate certainty: microscopic subinguinal surgery probably improves pregnancy slightly versus other surgical techniques (risk ratio 1.18, 95% CI 1.02–1.36) and probably halves varicocele recurrence (risk ratio 0.48, 95% CI 0.29–0.79). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): varicocele treatment may raise pregnancy rates, but a live-birth benefit is unproven and the choice between surgery and radiological treatment is unresolved.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — a Cochrane review finds treatment may improve pregnancy rates versus no or delayed treatment (RR 1.55, low-certainty), but the live-birth effect is uncertain (RR 2.27, 95% CI 0.19–26.93, very low-certainty)

title: Tadalafil 5 mg daily for prostate symptoms: symptom scores improve about 2–3 points beyond placebo — peak urine flow does not move at any dose
question: In men with lower urinary tract symptoms from benign prostatic hyperplasia, does tadalafil 5 mg once daily improve symptom scores and flow compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for symptoms, not for flow. In the dose-finding trial, the International Prostate Symptom Score fell by 4.9 points on tadalafil 5 mg versus 2.3 points on placebo over 12 weeks (p<0.001), and the 2018 meta-analysis of 13 randomised trials (3,973 patients) found the same direction across symptom and erectile-function scores, with more discontinuations for adverse events on tadalafil (odds ratio 1.79, 95% CI 1.12–2.85). The consistent negative is the plumbing: in the dose-finding trial no tadalafil dose — 2.5, 5, 10 or 20 mg — produced a statistically significant effect on peak urine flow versus placebo. So tadalafil makes men feel better and can treat erectile dysfunction at the same time, but it is not doing what an alpha-blocker does to the outlet. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): tadalafil 5 mg daily improves prostate symptom scores modestly beyond placebo across many trials, with no demonstrated improvement in urine flow rate.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — tadalafil 5 mg daily improves IPSS by roughly 2–3 points beyond placebo across the pivotal trial and a 13-trial meta-analysis, with no significant effect on peak urine flow at any dose

title: Vibegron for overactive bladder: about half a void and half a leakage episode a day better than placebo at 12 weeks in the one phase 3 trial — blood-pressure signal no worse than placebo
question: In adults with overactive bladder, does vibegron 75 mg reduce urgency incontinence and daily voids compared with placebo, and how does it compare with tolterodine?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — real but modest, from a single trial. In EMPOWUR, 1,518 patients with overactive bladder were randomised to vibegron 75 mg, placebo, or tolterodine extended-release 4 mg for 12 weeks. Daily voids fell by an adjusted mean of 1.8 on vibegron versus 1.3 on placebo (p<0.001) and 1.6 on tolterodine; among incontinent patients, urge incontinence episodes fell by 2.0 versus 1.4 per day (p<0.0001) and 1.8 on tolterodine. The trial was not designed to declare vibegron superior to tolterodine, so the honest comparison is 'in the same range'. Tolerability was good: discontinuation for adverse events in 1.7% on vibegron versus 1.1% on placebo and 3.3% on tolterodine, and hypertension incidence was 1.7% on both vibegron and placebo. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): vibegron improves overactive bladder symptoms modestly beyond placebo at 12 weeks in one large phase 3 trial, with a clean short-term safety profile.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in the single EMPOWUR phase 3 trial, vibegron 75 mg reduced daily voids (−1.8 vs −1.3) and urge incontinence episodes (−2.0 vs −1.4) versus placebo at 12 weeks, with adverse-event discontinuation of 1.7%

title: Formal one-to-one pelvic-floor training after prostate surgery: incontinence at 12 months was 76% versus 77% after prostatectomy and 65% versus 62% after TURP — no benefit, at extra cost
question: In men with urinary incontinence after prostate surgery, does formal one-to-one pelvic-floor muscle training speed recovery of continence compared with lifestyle advice alone?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — tested properly, in two parallel trials, and found wanting. In MAPS, men incontinent 6 weeks after radical prostatectomy or transurethral resection were randomised to four one-to-one therapist sessions over 3 months or to standard care with lifestyle advice. At 12 months, incontinence rates were 76% (148 of 196) with training versus 77% (151 of 195) with standard care after prostatectomy (absolute difference −1.9%, 95% CI −10 to 6), and 65% (126 of 194) versus 62% (125 of 203) after TURP (difference 3.4%, 95% CI −6 to 13). The training cost more (£180 and £209 extra per patient) with no economically important difference in quality-adjusted life years. The sobering background finding: about two-thirds to three-quarters of men were still incontinent at a year in every arm — a large unmet need that supervised training, at least in settings where exercise information is already widely available, does not meet. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): formal one-to-one pelvic-floor training does not improve continence recovery after prostate surgery beyond standard care and lifestyle advice.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — in the two MAPS trials, one-to-one pelvic-floor training did not reduce incontinence at 12 months after prostatectomy (−1.9%, 95% CI −10 to 6) or TURP (3.4%, 95% CI −6 to 13), and cost more

title: Whole-gland or subtotal HIFU versus prostatectomy (HIFI): salvage-therapy-free survival not inferior at 30 months and continence and erections better preserved — in a non-randomised comparison where HIFU patients were nearly a decade older
question: In men with low- or intermediate-risk localised prostate cancer, does whole-gland or subtotal high-intensity focused ultrasound preserve continence and erections without compromising cancer control compared with radical prostatectomy?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — on functional outcomes, in a comparison that cannot fully be trusted on cancer outcomes. The French HIFI study prospectively followed 3,328 men (1,967 HIFU, 1,361 prostatectomy) with low- to intermediate-risk prostate cancer. At 30 months, salvage therapy-free survival was not inferior with HIFU (hazard ratio 0.71, 95% CI 0.52–0.97; p=0.008 for noninferiority). Function favoured HIFU: deterioration in urinary continence at 12 months in 29% versus 44%, and a smaller fall in erectile-function scores (median IIEF-5 change −7 versus −13); about 10% of HIFU patients had urinary retention, and grade >IIIa complications were similar (54 of 1,967 versus 29 of 1,361, p=0.3). The structural problem is allocation: this was not randomised, and the HIFU group was much older (median 74.7 versus 65.1 years), so the men, their cancers' management thresholds, and their salvage decisions all differed before treatment began. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): HIFU preserves continence and erections better than prostatectomy with noninferior short-term salvage-free survival in this large prospective non-randomised study; randomised confirmation is lacking.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in the non-randomised HIFI study, HIFU was noninferior to prostatectomy for 30-month salvage therapy-free survival (HR 0.71) with less continence deterioration (29% vs 44%), but the HIFU group was a decade older and allocation was not randomised

title: Oral fosfomycin for chronic bacterial prostatitis: cure in roughly three quarters of men in small uncontrolled series — including resistant organisms — with no comparative trial to say what would have happened otherwise
question: In men with chronic bacterial prostatitis, does oral fosfomycin achieve clinical and microbiological cure, including against resistant organisms?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — promising numbers, no controls. In the largest prospective series, 44 men with chronic bacterial prostatitis — 59% with multidrug-resistant organisms and all strains fosfomycin-susceptible — were treated with fosfomycin 3 g daily for a week then every 48 hours for 6–12 weeks: the cure rate was 82% at the end of treatment and 73% at 6 months, with microbiological eradication in 86% and 77% respectively, and diarrhoea in 18%. A smaller pilot combining fosfomycin with N-acetyl-L-cysteine in 28 difficult-to-treat men (68% ESBL strains) found microbiological eradication in 75% and clinical cure in 71.4%. What is missing is any comparison: chronic bacterial prostatitis relapses and remits, and without a control group these cure rates cannot be separated from natural history, prior-treatment washout, or selection of men whose organisms happened to be susceptible. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): oral fosfomycin cures about three quarters of selected men with chronic bacterial prostatitis in uncontrolled series, and is a reasonable salvage option where fluoroquinolones have failed — comparative evidence does not exist.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — oral fosfomycin achieved cure in 73–82% of men with chronic bacterial prostatitis in small uncontrolled series (including multidrug-resistant strains), but no comparative trial exists

title: Duloxetine for incontinence after prostatectomy: leakage episodes fall by about half while taking it — and continence flips back within weeks of stopping
question: In men with stress incontinence after radical prostatectomy, does duloxetine speed return of continence compared with placebo or pelvic-floor training alone?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — only while the drug is on board. In the small placebo-controlled trial, incontinence episode frequency fell by 52.2% on duloxetine 80 mg daily over 3 months while rising 19.0% on placebo (mean difference 71.2%, 95% CI 41.0–101.4; p<0.0001), with parallel improvements in incontinence quality-of-life scores. The larger trial, of duloxetine added to rehabilitation versus rehabilitation alone, found more men dry at 16 weeks on the combination (39 versus 27, p=0.007) — but four weeks after duloxetine was stopped the picture reversed (23 dry versus 38, p=0.008), converging by 24 weeks (31 versus 41, p=0.08). So duloxetine rents continence rather than restoring it: it suppresses leakage pharmacologically while taken, at an adverse-event rate of 15.2% in the larger trial, and the underlying sphincter recovery proceeds at its own pace underneath. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): duloxetine reduces leakage after prostatectomy in two randomised trials, but the benefit does not survive stopping the drug.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — duloxetine cut incontinence episodes by 52.2% versus a 19.0% rise on placebo in one trial and increased dry rates on treatment in another, but continence reversed within 4 weeks of stopping (23 vs 38 dry)

title: Silodosin versus tamsulosin for prostate symptoms: no better on symptoms or flow in the head-to-head trial — but absent or reduced ejaculation in 14% versus 2%
question: In men with benign prostatic hyperplasia, does silodosin relieve symptoms better than tamsulosin — and how much more ejaculatory dysfunction does it cause?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — on efficacy; the difference between these drugs is in the bedroom, not the bathroom. In the European head-to-head trial (955 men randomised), the placebo-subtracted improvement in total symptom score was −2.3 points (95% CI −3.2 to −1.4) for silodosin 8 mg and −2.0 points (95% CI −2.9 to −1.1) for tamsulosin 0.4 mg, with responder rates of 66.8% versus 65.4% versus 50.8% on placebo; the 5-trial meta-analysis likewise found no significant difference between the drugs in total symptom score, storage symptoms, peak flow, or quality of life. The one clear separation was ejaculation: reduced or absent ejaculation during orgasm in 14% of silodosin-treated men versus 2% on tamsulosin (1.3% stopped silodosin because of it), an effect the trial attributes to silodosin's potent alpha-1A selectivity and describes as reversible. Discontinuation for adverse events was otherwise low and similar (2.1% versus 1.0% versus 1.6% on placebo). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): silodosin is not superior to tamsulosin for symptoms or flow, and it costs substantially more ejaculatory dysfunction.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — silodosin was not superior to tamsulosin on symptom scores or flow in the head-to-head trial or the 5-trial meta-analysis, but caused reduced or absent ejaculation in 14% versus 2%

title: Steroid cover for radioiodine in Graves' disease: progression of eye disease cut to near zero when ophthalmopathy is already present (pooled OR 0.14) — no benefit shown in patients without eye disease
question: In Graves' disease treated with radioiodine, do prophylactic glucocorticoids prevent new or worsening orbitopathy versus no prophylaxis?
balance: SPLIT — the answer depends entirely on whether the eyes are already involved. The systematic review and meta-analysis (8 trials, 850 patients) found that in patients with preexisting Graves' ophthalmopathy, standard-dose prednisone (0.4–0.5 mg/kg tapered over 3 months) was very effective at preventing progression after radioiodine (odds ratio 0.14, 95% CI 0.06–0.35), and low-dose prednisone also looked effective on indirect comparisons (odds ratio 0.20, 95% CI 0.07–0.60). In patients without preexisting ophthalmopathy, steroid prophylaxis had no beneficial effect (odds ratio 1.87, 95% CI 0.81–4.3). The anchor randomised trial shows the same split in absolute terms: after radioiodine alone, ophthalmopathy developed or worsened in 23 of 150 patients (15%), whereas among 145 patients given radioiodine plus a 3-month prednisone course, no patient had progression and 50 of 75 (67%) with baseline ophthalmopathy improved. Steroid prophylaxis did not change whether the hyperthyroidism resolved (odds ratio 1.05, 95% CI 0.69–1.58), and glucocorticoid side effects were common but mild. PROPOSED SPLIT: give steroid cover to patients with existing ophthalmopathy or high progression risk; it is not supported for patients with no eye involvement.
stamp: SPLIT — benefit in patients with preexisting Graves' ophthalmopathy (progression OR 0.14 with standard-dose prednisone); no benefit shown in patients without preexisting ophthalmopathy (OR 1.87, not significant)

title: Antithyroid drugs in early pregnancy: birth defects in 9.1% after methimazole and 8.0% after propylthiouracil versus 5.7% unexposed — different defect patterns, and switching drugs in early pregnancy did not remove the risk (10.1%)
question: In pregnancy, how do propylthiouracil and methimazole compare on congenital malformations, and does switching drugs in early pregnancy remove the risk?
balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — both drugs carry risk; they differ in pattern, not in safety. In the Danish nationwide cohort of 817,093 children, birth defects diagnosed before age 2 occurred in 9.1% of children exposed to methimazole/carbimazole in early pregnancy, 8.0% exposed to propylthiouracil, and 10.1% exposed to both (switched in early pregnancy), versus 5.7% in never-exposed children and 5.4% in children whose mothers used antithyroid drugs but not in pregnancy. Adjusted odds ratios were 1.66 (95% CI 1.35–2.04) for methimazole/carbimazole, 1.41 (1.03–1.92) for propylthiouracil, and 1.82 (1.08–3.07) for switching — so switching in early pregnancy did not remove the excess. The defect spectra differed: methimazole/carbimazole was linked to a characteristic group (choanal atresia, oesophageal atresia, omphalocele, omphalomesenteric duct anomalies, aplasia cutis; combined adjusted odds ratio 21.8, 95% CI 13.4–35.4), while propylthiouracil was associated with face/neck and urinary malformations. The extended 2019 cohort (1,243,353 children) corroborated the rates — 9.6% after methimazole/carbimazole and 8.3% after propylthiouracil versus 6.7% unexposed — and found maternal thyroid dysfunction itself was not a major risk factor. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm): early-pregnancy exposure to either antithyroid drug is associated with more birth defects than no exposure, with methimazole's pattern more severe, and switching does not abolish the risk.
stamp: POSSIBLE (harm) — in nationwide Danish cohorts, early-pregnancy antithyroid drug exposure was associated with more birth defects (methimazole/carbimazole 9.1–9.6%, propylthiouracil 8.0–8.3%, versus 5.7–6.7% unexposed), and switching drugs in early pregnancy did not remove the excess (10.1%)

title: Liquid levothyroxine when tablets are not absorbed: in 24 patients whose proton-pump inhibitors blocked tablet absorption, switching to the oral solution at the same dose brought TSH from 5.4 to 1.7 mU/L
question: In hypothyroid patients with impaired levothyroxine absorption, does liquid levothyroxine normalise TSH more reliably than tablets?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — a neat pharmacological story tested only in a small uncontrolled switch study. Twenty-four adults whose tablet levothyroxine absorption was impaired by proton-pump inhibitors were switched to the oral solution at the same daily dose. Mean TSH fell from 5.4 ± 4.3 mU/L on tablets to 1.7 ± 1.0 on the solution in the replacement group, and from 2.1 ± 2.7 to 0.1 ± 0.3 in the group needing TSH suppression (both P<.0001). In the suppression group, no pre-switch measurement (0 of 22) reached the target TSH of at most 0.10 mU/L, versus 26 of 35 measurements (74.3%) after switching. There was no parallel control group, no randomisation, and no blinding — patients switched because tablets were failing, so regression to the mean and intensified follow-up are built into the design. The mechanism is plausible (the solution does not need gastric dissolution), and the within-patient consistency is striking, but 24 patients in one centre is the whole of this card's evidence. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): liquid levothyroxine appears to restore TSH control when proton-pump inhibitors impair tablet absorption, on small uncontrolled evidence.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — in one uncontrolled switch cohort of 24 patients, liquid levothyroxine at the same dose lowered mean TSH from 5.4 to 1.7 mU/L where proton-pump inhibitors had impaired tablet absorption

title: Block-and-replace versus dose titration in Graves' disease: relapse in 51% versus 54% across 12 trials — no stability or remission advantage, and more rashes and treatment withdrawals
question: In Graves' hyperthyroidism, does block-and-replace therapy produce more stable control or higher remission than dose titration with antithyroid drugs?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — on remission; block-and-replace simply costs more side effects. The Cochrane review (26 randomised trials, 3,388 participants) pooled 12 trials of block-replace versus titration regimens: relapse rates were 51% in the block-replace group and 54% in the titration group (odds ratio 0.86, 95% CI 0.68–1.08), a difference compatible with no effect. Adverse effects ran the other way: rashes in 10% versus 6%, and withdrawal due to side effects in 16% versus 9%, both significantly more frequent with block-replace — unsurprising, since the regimen uses higher antithyroid doses plus levothyroxine. On duration, the review found 12 months of titration superior to 6 months for relapse, with no benefit in extending treatment beyond 18 months. No trial in the review measured hypothyroidism incidence, weight change, quality of life, ophthalmopathy progression, or costs. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): block-and-replace does not improve remission over dose titration in Graves' disease and causes more adverse effects.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — across 12 trials in the Cochrane review, block-and-replace gave relapse rates of 51% versus 54% for titration (OR 0.86, 95% CI 0.68–1.08), with more rashes (10% vs 6%) and withdrawals (16% vs 9%)

title: Gene-expression classifier for indeterminate thyroid nodules: a 'benign' result was right 94–95% of the time in the validation study — but the test still called half of all benign nodules suspicious
question: In indeterminate thyroid nodules, does gene-expression classifier testing reduce unnecessary diagnostic surgery versus standard management?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — as a rule-out test, with a specific arithmetic patients should hear. In the prospective multicentre validation study, 265 cytologically indeterminate nodules with surgical histology were tested: 85 were malignant, and the classifier identified 78 of the 85 as suspicious (sensitivity 92%, 95% CI 84–97), with specificity of 52% (95% CI 44–59). The negative predictive value of a benign classifier result — the number that matters for a decision to observe rather than operate — was 95% for atypia of undetermined significance, 94% for follicular neoplasm, and 85% for suspicious cytology. The flip side: with specificity of 52%, roughly half of benign nodules are still labelled suspicious and head to surgery anyway, so the test spares an operation mainly for the minority whose result comes back benign. Of the 7 false-negative aspirates, 6 had a paucity of thyroid follicular cells, flagging sampling as the failure mode. The study was funded by the test's manufacturer, Veracyte, and it validates accuracy against surgical histology — it does not itself randomise patients to testing versus standard management or measure how many operations are actually avoided in practice. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a benign gene-expression classifier result identifies indeterminate nodules that can reasonably be observed, on a single manufacturer-funded validation study.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in the prospective validation study, the gene-expression classifier had 92% sensitivity and negative predictive values of 94–95% for the commonest indeterminate categories, but only 52% specificity, so about half of benign nodules still test suspicious

title: Ethanol instillation for recurrent benign thyroid cysts: cure in 82% versus 48% with saline flushing in a double-blind trial — with moderate-to-severe pain in a fifth of patients
question: In benign recurrent thyroid cysts, does percutaneous ethanol injection achieve lasting volume reduction versus aspiration or saline injection?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a small, well-blinded trial with a clear result. Sixty-six patients with benign thyroid cysts that had already recurred after aspiration were randomised to aspiration plus ethanol flushing or aspiration plus saline flushing, repeated up to three times if the cyst returned. Cure — cyst volume at most 1 ml at 6 months — was achieved in 27 of 33 patients (82%, 95% CI 65–93) with ethanol versus 16 of 33 (48%, 95% CI 31–66) with saline (P=0.006), and cure after a single session in 64% versus 18% (P=0.002). Success fell with more previous aspirations and with larger baseline cyst volume. The cost was pain: 7 patients (21%) in the ethanol group had moderate-to-severe pain (median duration 5 minutes) and one had transient dysphonia; laryngoscopy was normal in all patients. Follow-up was 6 months, so 'lasting' beyond that horizon is unproven here, and the trial predates modern cyst-ablation comparisons. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): ethanol instillation roughly doubles the cure rate of recurrent benign thyroid cysts over aspiration with saline, in one small double-blind trial.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in the single double-blind trial, ethanol instillation cured 82% of recurrent benign thyroid cysts versus 48% with saline flushing (p=0.006), with moderate-to-severe pain in 21%

title: Alendronate in mild primary hyperparathyroidism: lumbar spine density up 6.85% over two years in a 44-patient trial — the distal radius, the site this disease hits hardest, did not improve
question: In mild primary hyperparathyroidism, does alendronate improve bone mineral density versus placebo over two years?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for spine and hip density, in a very small trial with a crossover design. Forty-four patients with asymptomatic primary hyperparathyroidism who did not meet surgical guidelines or refused surgery were randomised to alendronate 10 mg daily or placebo, with the placebo group crossing to alendronate at 12 months. Lumbar spine bone mineral density rose 6.85% over 2 years on alendronate (P<0.001 versus baseline); total hip density rose 4.01% at 12 months (P<0.001) and held; femoral neck density gained 3.67% at 24 months (P=0.038). The placebo group showed no significant change at any site at 12 months, and after crossing over gained 4.1% at the spine and 1.7% at the hip in its year on treatment — an internal replication. The exception matters: the distal one-third radius, the cortical site primary hyperparathyroidism characteristically erodes, showed no significant change at 12 or 24 months. Bone turnover markers fell sharply (urinary NTX down 66% by 3 months), while serum calcium, PTH and urinary calcium did not change — alendronate treats the bone consequence, not the parathyroid disease, and no fracture outcomes were measured. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): alendronate improves spine and hip bone density in primary hyperparathyroidism over two years, without improving the distal radius and without touching calcium or PTH.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in one 44-patient crossover trial, alendronate raised lumbar spine BMD by 6.85% and total hip by 4.01% over 1–2 years in primary hyperparathyroidism, with no significant gain at the distal radius and no change in calcium or PTH

title: Vitamin D repletion in primary hyperparathyroidism: PTH fell 17% and spine density rose 2.5% on 2,800 IU daily — with no rise in blood or urine calcium in a 46-patient trial
question: In primary hyperparathyroidism with vitamin D insufficiency, does cholecalciferol repletion lower parathyroid hormone without raising serum calcium?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the feared harm did not appear, and the hormone moved the right way. In this double-blind trial, 46 patients with primary hyperparathyroidism received cholecalciferol 70 µg (2,800 IU) daily or placebo for 52 weeks, spanning their parathyroidectomy at week 26. Vitamin D levels rose from 50 to 94 nmol/L on treatment while falling from 57 to 52 nmol/L on placebo (P<.001). Before surgery, PTH was 17% lower on vitamin D than on placebo (P=.01), lumbar spine bone density was 2.5% higher (P=.01), and the bone-resorption marker C-terminal β-CrossLaps was 22% lower (P<.005); postoperatively, PTH remained lower in the cholecalciferol group (P=.04). The safety point of the question: plasma creatinine and plasma and urinary calcium did not differ between groups at any stage. The trial was small and single-centre, PTH and density are surrogates, and all patients proceeded to parathyroidectomy — so this supports repletion as safe preparation, not as an alternative to surgery. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): high-dose cholecalciferol safely repletes vitamin D in primary hyperparathyroidism, lowering PTH modestly without raising calcium, in one small trial.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in one 46-patient double-blind trial, cholecalciferol 2,800 IU daily lowered PTH by 17% and raised spine BMD by 2.5% in primary hyperparathyroidism, with no difference in plasma or urinary calcium versus placebo

title: Starting lenvatinib lower (18 mg versus 24 mg) in radioiodine-refractory thyroid cancer: response rate fell from 57.3% to 40.3% — and severe toxicity did not fall with it (57.1% versus 61.3%)
question: In radioiodine-refractory differentiated thyroid cancer, does a lower starting dose of lenvatinib (18 mg) preserve efficacy with less toxicity than 24 mg?
balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — starting lower trades away responses and buys no safety. Study 211 randomised patients with radioiodine-refractory differentiated thyroid cancer double-blind to a starting dose of lenvatinib 18 mg or the approved 24 mg daily. The objective response rate at week 24 was 40.3% (95% CI 29.3–51.2) on 18 mg versus 57.3% (95% CI 46.1–68.5) on 24 mg (odds ratio 0.50, 95% CI 0.26–0.96), so the lower dose failed its noninferiority criterion by a clinically meaningful margin. The hoped-for compensation never arrived: grade 3 or worse treatment-emergent adverse events at week 24 occurred in 57.1% on 18 mg versus 61.3% on 24 mg (difference −4.2%, 95% CI −19.8 to 11.4), and the companion quality-of-life analysis found no significant differences between arms on EQ-5D or FACT-G scores. The trial's logic is now the standard one for this drug: start at 24 mg and reduce for toxicity in the individual patient, rather than pre-emptively underdosing everyone. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm): a lower lenvatinib starting dose (18 mg) reduces tumour responses without reducing severe toxicity or improving quality of life, compared with starting at 24 mg.
stamp: POSSIBLE (harm) — in Study 211, starting lenvatinib at 18 mg instead of 24 mg lowered the week-24 response rate (40.3% vs 57.3%; OR 0.50) without reducing grade ≥3 toxicity (57.1% vs 61.3%) or improving quality of life

title: Selenium in TPO-antibody-positive pregnancy: postpartum thyroid dysfunction in 28.6% versus 48.6% on placebo in the one randomised trial — permanent hypothyroidism also halved, but the trial stands alone
question: In women with thyroid-peroxidase antibodies, does selenium supplementation during pregnancy prevent postpartum thyroiditis?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — on one trial's evidence. In the single randomised placebo-controlled trial, pregnant women positive for thyroid peroxidase antibodies who took selenomethionine 200 micrograms daily during pregnancy and after delivery developed postpartum thyroid dysfunction in 28.6% of cases versus 48.6% on placebo (P<0.01), and permanent hypothyroidism in 11.7% versus 20.3% (P<0.01) (Negro R et al., PMID: 17284630). The absolute differences — about 20 percentage points for postpartum dysfunction and about 9 points for permanent hypothyroidism — are large, but they come from one centre's trial of 151 antibody-positive women, the abstract reports no adverse-event rates, and no second randomised trial in this session's records confirms the result. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): selenium during and after pregnancy reduced postpartum thyroid dysfunction and later permanent hypothyroidism in the one randomised trial; confirmation is still missing, so this is Tier C.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — selenomethionine 200 µg/day cut postpartum thyroid dysfunction from 48.6% to 28.6% and permanent hypothyroidism from 20.3% to 11.7% in one randomised trial of 151 TPO-antibody-positive pregnant women

title: Levothyroxine suppression for benign nodules: ≥50% shrinkage in 16% versus 10% in the Cochrane pooling — a small edge bought with hyperthyroid symptoms in 25% versus 7%
question: In benign nodular goitre, does levothyroxine suppression shrink nodules or prevent growth versus placebo?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — the shrinkage edge is small and the price is real. The Cochrane review found levothyroxine, versus no treatment or placebo, gave a nodule volume reduction of 50% or more in 16% of participants versus 10% after 6 to 24 months (risk ratio 1.57, 95% CI 1.04 to 2.38; 958 participants, 10 studies, moderate-quality evidence) (Bandeira-Echtler E et al., PMID: 24941398). The largest double-blind trial inside that evidence base found the same pattern for solitary nodules: a clinically relevant volume reduction in 26.6% on levothyroxine versus 16.9% on placebo (P=0.04) (Wémeau JL et al., PMID: 12414852). Against that, signs and symptoms of hyperthyroidism appeared in 25% of levothyroxine-treated versus 7% of placebo-treated participants in the trials that reported them. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): suppression shrinks a minority of nodules a little more often than placebo, with hyperthyroid symptoms in a quarter of treated patients in the reporting trials.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — levothyroxine suppression produced ≥50% nodule shrinkage in 16% versus 10% (RR 1.57) in the Cochrane pooling of randomised trials, with hyperthyroid symptoms in 25% versus 7% where reported

title: Denosumab in primary hyperparathyroidism (DENOCINA): spine bone density up 6.9% versus placebo in one year in a 45-patient proof-of-concept trial — bone, not calcium, is what it treats
question: In primary hyperparathyroidism in patients unfit for or declining surgery, does denosumab improve bone mineral density versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for bone density, in one small trial. In DENOCINA, patients with primary hyperparathyroidism randomised to denosumab (with placebo tablets) gained bone mineral density over one year compared with placebo at the lumbar spine (6.9%, 95% CI 4.2 to 9.6), total hip (4.1%, 95% CI 2.5 to 5.8) and femoral neck (3.8%, 95% CI 1.4 to 6.3); the combination arm with cinacalcet gained similarly (5.4%, 5.0% and 4.5% respectively) (Leere JS et al., PMID: 32333877). Six non-fatal serious adverse events occurred across the arms (2 combination, 1 denosumab, 3 placebo), overall adverse-event prevalence did not differ between groups, and there were no fatal events. The trial enrolled patients selected for low bone density (T-score −1.0 to −3.5), not specifically patients unfit for surgery, and it measured density and turnover — not fractures or calcium control. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): denosumab improves bone mineral density over one year in primary hyperparathyroidism; fracture and calcium outcomes are untested, and the single small trial makes this Tier C.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — denosumab raised lumbar spine bone density by 6.9% versus placebo at one year in the single DENOCINA randomised trial, with fractures and calcium control untested

title: Pralsetinib in RET-mutant medullary thyroid cancer (ARROW): tumours responded in 60% of previously treated and 71% of treatment-naive patients — single-arm evidence, with hypertension in 17% at grade 3 or worse
question: In advanced RET-mutant medullary thyroid cancer, does pralsetinib produce durable tumour responses in previously treated and treatment-naive patients?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — deep responses, but from a single-arm study with no comparator. In ARROW, pralsetinib 400 mg daily produced overall responses in 33 of 55 patients (60%, 95% CI 46 to 73) with previously treated RET-mutant medullary thyroid cancer and 15 of 21 (71%, 95% CI 48 to 89) with treatment-naive disease (Subbiah V et al., PMID: 34118198). The updated analysis of the same study, with more patients and longer follow-up, found responses in 55.7% of previously treated and 77.4% of treatment-naive patients, with median duration of response and progression-free survival both 25.8 months in the previously treated group (Subbiah V et al., PMID: 38009200). The price in the updated safety population was substantial: 97.1% reported a treatment-related adverse event, 52.6% needed a dose reduction, and grade 3 or worse treatment-related hypertension occurred in 17% in the primary report. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): response rates of this size in a cancer with few options are unlikely to be spontaneous, but without a randomised comparator the survival benefit is unproven — Tier C.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — pralsetinib produced tumour responses in 60% of previously treated and 71% of treatment-naive RET-mutant medullary thyroid cancers in the single-arm ARROW study, with no randomised comparator

title: Total thyroidectomy versus lobectomy in low-risk papillary cancer: 5-year recurrence-free survival 95% versus 96% in the pooled cohorts — no survival advantage for taking the whole gland
question: In low-risk papillary thyroid cancer, does total thyroidectomy improve outcomes versus lobectomy?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — more surgery did not buy better cancer outcomes in the observational record. A 2025 meta-analysis of 10 studies (17,082 patients) found 5-year recurrence-free survival in intermediate-risk papillary cancer of 96% after lobectomy and 95% after total thyroidectomy (hazard ratio 1.19, 95% CI 0.69 to 2.04), raw recurrence of 3% versus 4% across low-to-intermediate-risk cohorts, and no mortality benefit for total thyroidectomy in any risk group (Wong RSH et al., PMID: 40891682). An earlier systematic review of 13 studies of 1.0–4.0 cm tumours reached the same conclusion on disease-specific survival, while noting that four of six studies reporting disease-free survival found a small statistically significant edge for total thyroidectomy of uncertain clinical significance (Gartland RM et al., PMID: 29855833). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): for low-risk papillary cancer, total thyroidectomy has not been shown to improve recurrence or survival over lobectomy — Tier C, because every study behind this is observational and confounding by indication runs against the bigger operation.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — pooled observational data show 5-year recurrence-free survival of 96% after lobectomy versus 95% after total thyroidectomy and no mortality benefit for total thyroidectomy in low-risk papillary cancer

title: Rituximab for Graves' orbitopathy: two randomised trials, two answers — 100% improved versus intravenous steroid in Italy, 31% versus 25% on placebo at Mayo
question: In moderate-to-severe Graves' orbitopathy, does rituximab improve disease activity versus intravenous methylprednisolone or placebo?
balance: SPLIT — the two randomised trials disagree, and the split follows the comparator. Against intravenous methylprednisolone, rituximab won clearly: at 24 weeks 100% of rituximab patients had improved versus 69% after intravenous methylprednisolone, disease reactivation occurred in five steroid patients and in no rituximab patient, and fewer rehabilitative operations followed (5 in 15 versus 12 in 16 patients) (Salvi M et al., PMID: 25494967). Against placebo, rituximab won nothing: clinical activity score improvement at 24 weeks in 31% on rituximab versus 25% on placebo (P=0.75), no difference in any secondary endpoint, and more moderate or severe adverse events on rituximab (Stan MN et al., PMID: 25343233). PROPOSED SPLIT: rituximab beat an active steroid comparator in one small trial and matched placebo in another — whether it works at all is unresolved, which is why this shelf is Tier C.
stamp: SPLIT — rituximab beat intravenous methylprednisolone (improvement 100% versus 69% at 24 weeks) in one randomised trial but matched placebo (31% versus 25%) in another; efficacy is unresolved
