title: Routine calcitonin screening in nodular thyroid disease: medullary cancer in about 1 in 250 patients screened, found earlier, with complete remission in 59% versus 2.7% in a pre-screening era cohort — no randomised test
question: In nodular thyroid disease, does routine calcitonin screening detect medullary carcinoma earlier and change outcomes versus no screening?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — screening finds the cancer early; whether it saves lives is inferred, not trialled. In 5,817 consecutive patients with nodular thyroid disease, systematic calcitonin measurement identified 15 medullary cancers (and 7 cases of C-cell hyperplasia); every patient with a basal calcitonin above 100 pg/ml had medullary cancer, though the positive predictive value at the 20 pg/ml threshold was only 23.1%, so stimulation testing was needed to sort most positives (Costante G et al., PMID: 17119000). In a 10,864-patient screening experience, medullary cancer prevalence was 0.40% (44 patients, about 1 in 250), cancers were diagnosed at an earlier stage than in a pre-screening historical group (P=0.004), and complete remission at the end of follow-up was 59% versus 2.7% (P=0.0001) (Elisei R et al., PMID: 14715844). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): routine calcitonin measurement detects medullary cancer earlier and at a more curable stage — Tier C, because the outcome comparison is against a historical era, not a randomised or concurrent control.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — routine calcitonin screening found medullary cancer in 0.40% of nodular-disease patients, at earlier stage, with complete remission in 59% versus 2.7% in a historical pre-screening cohort

title: When to take levothyroxine: with breakfast, TSH rose to 2.93 versus 1.06 fasting in one crossover trial — but a second trial found bedtime and pre-meal dosing non-inferior, and coffee alone cuts absorption by about a third
question: In hypothyroidism, does levothyroxine absorption timing with food and interacting drugs (iron, calcium, coffee) change TSH control?
balance: SPLIT — the food effect is consistent, the clock effect is not. In a three-period crossover trial, mean TSH was 1.06 mIU/litre when levothyroxine was taken fasting, 2.93 when taken with breakfast, and 2.19 at bedtime — both non-fasting regimens significantly higher and more variable (Bach-Huynh TG et al., PMID: 19584184). A second crossover trial, testing half an hour before breakfast against an hour before the main meal and against bedtime (at least 2 hours after dinner), found all three timings non-inferior with no significant TSH difference between any regimen (Skelin M et al., PMID: 30043093). The interacting-drinks evidence is mechanistic but direct: swallowing levothyroxine with coffee lowered the incremental rise in serum thyroxine by 36% in patients and 29% in volunteers and delayed its peak by about 40 minutes (Benvenga S et al., PMID: 18341376). PROPOSED SPLIT: taking levothyroxine with breakfast worsens TSH control in the trial that isolated breakfast; bedtime dosing split the two trials; coffee demonstrably impairs absorption — Tier C for small crossover evidence throughout.
stamp: SPLIT — levothyroxine taken with breakfast raised TSH (2.93 versus 1.06 mIU/litre fasting) in one crossover trial, while a second found pre-meal and bedtime timings non-inferior; coffee reduced thyroxine absorption by about a third

title: Mailed FIT outreach in underserved care: screening in 40.7% versus 12.1% on usual care at one year — and colonoscopy outreach wins the three-year process while FIT wins the single test
question: In underserved primary-care populations, does mailed FIT outreach with reminders increase colorectal cancer screening completion versus usual care?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — two large pragmatic trials in safety-net systems agree that mailing the test beats waiting for a clinic visit. In the first, screening participation within a year was 40.7% with mailed FIT outreach versus 12.1% with usual care (colonoscopy outreach reached 24.6%) (Gupta S et al., PMID: 23921906). In the second, completion of the full three-year screening process was 28.0% with FIT outreach and 38.4% with colonoscopy outreach versus 10.7% with usual care — FIT outreach's absolute advantage over usual care was 17.3 percentage points (95% CI 14.8 to 19.8) (Singal AG et al., PMID: 28873161). The honest nuance is inside the second trial: a mailed colonoscopy invitation completed the multi-year process more often than repeated FIT, even though FIT wins any single round. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): mailed FIT outreach roughly triples screening completion versus usual care in underserved populations, on two concordant randomised trials — not Tier C.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — mailed FIT outreach raised screening participation to 40.7% versus 12.1% on usual care at one year and three-year process completion to 28.0% versus 10.7% in two large safety-net randomised trials

title: Patient navigation after an abnormal screening test: resolution came faster in the randomised trial, and the multisite programme's benefit appeared after day 90 (adjusted HR 1.51 for resolution by one year)
question: After an abnormal cancer screening test, does patient navigation shorten time to diagnostic resolution versus usual care?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — navigation speeds resolution, but the benefit is delayed and uneven across abnormality types. In the individually randomised Denver trial, time to diagnostic resolution was significantly shorter with lay patient navigation across breast, colorectal and prostate abnormalities combined (stratified log-rank P<0.001), with clear gains for mammographic BI-RADS 3 (P=0.0003) and colorectal abnormalities (P=0.0017) but not for BI-RADS 4/5 or abnormal clinical breast examinations (Raich PC et al., PMID: 23045537). The multisite Patient Navigation Research Program's pooled analysis of 10,521 participants found no benefit in the first 90 days, then a benefit from day 91 to 365 for both diagnostic resolution (adjusted hazard ratio 1.51, 95% CI 1.23 to 1.84) and treatment initiation (adjusted HR 1.43, 95% CI 1.10 to 1.86), largest in centres whose usual-care delays were greatest (Freund KM et al., PMID: 24938303). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): navigation shortens time to resolution mainly for the patients usual care is slowest to resolve — Tier C, because the pooled effect is a modest hazard ratio assembled across heterogeneous centres.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — patient navigation shortened time to diagnostic resolution in a randomised trial (P<0.001 overall) and in the multisite programme analysis (adjusted HR 1.51 after day 90), with no benefit in the first 90 days

title: A lung screening decision aid for people who smoke: 67.4% felt well prepared to decide versus 48.2% with standard information — knowledge and values clarity up, screening uptake unchanged
question: In people who smoke and are eligible for lung screening, does a patient decision aid improve knowledge and decision quality about low-dose CT screening versus standard information?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for decision quality, which is what a decision aid is for; it did not change behaviour. In the randomised trial among tobacco-quitline clients eligible for lung screening, the video decision aid left 67.4% of viewers well prepared to make a screening decision versus 48.2% with standard educational material (odds ratio 2.31, 95% CI 1.56 to 3.44); 50.0% versus 28.3% felt informed (OR 2.56, 95% CI 1.72 to 3.79) and 68.0% versus 47.4% were clear about their values on the harms and benefits (OR 2.37, 95% CI 1.60 to 3.51), and the aid group was more knowledgeable at every follow-up (Volk RJ et al., PMID: 32003822). Intentions to be screened and actual screening within six months did not differ between groups. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a decision aid measurably improves knowledge, preparedness and values clarity without steering uptake either way — a single trial, so Tier C.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a video decision aid improved preparation for decision-making (67.4% versus 48.2%; OR 2.31), feeling informed (50.0% versus 28.3%) and values clarity (68.0% versus 47.4%) in one randomised trial, with no change in screening uptake

title: Genetic-risk disclosure in MI-GENES: statins started by 39% versus 22% and LDL cholesterol 96.5 versus 105.9 mg/dL at 6 months — a prescribing effect in one small trial, with no heart outcomes tested
question: Does disclosing a genetic (polygenic) risk score for coronary heart disease change statin use and LDL cholesterol versus conventional risk disclosure?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for prescribing and a cholesterol number, not for heart outcomes. In MI-GENES (Kullo IJ et al., PMID: 26915630), 203 people aged 45–65 years at intermediate risk for coronary heart disease and not on statins were randomly assigned to receive their 10-year probability of coronary heart disease based either on a conventional risk score alone (n=100) or on the conventional score plus a genetic risk score (n=103); risk was disclosed by a genetic counselor followed by shared decision making regarding statin therapy with a physician. At 6 months the genetic-score group had a lower LDL cholesterol than the conventional group (96.5±32.7 versus 105.9±33.3 mg/dL; P=0.04), a difference of 9.4 mg/dL, and statins had been initiated more often in the genetic-score group (39% versus 22%, P<0.01). The LDL difference was concentrated in participants with a high genetic risk score (92.3±32.9 mg/dL; P=0.02 versus the conventional group), while participants with an average/low genetic risk score did not differ significantly (100.9±32.2 mg/dL; P=0.18). No significant differences in dietary fat intake or physical activity levels were noted, so the LDL effect ran through statin prescribing, not through lifestyle change. The trial measured no heart attacks, strokes, or deaths, and this shelf claims behaviour and LDL effects only — no outcome benefit. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): in one small randomised trial, disclosing coronary risk that incorporated a genetic risk score led to more statin initiation and a modestly lower LDL cholesterol at 6 months than conventional risk disclosure alone.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in one 203-patient randomised trial (MI-GENES), disclosing a genetic risk score with conventional risk led to more statin initiation (39% versus 22%, P<0.01) and lower LDL cholesterol at 6 months (96.5 versus 105.9 mg/dL, P=0.04), with no heart-outcome data

title: Paying people $24 to vaccinate against COVID-19: uptake rose 4.2 percentage points from a 71.6% baseline in an 8,286-person Swedish randomised trial — nudges moved intentions only
question: Do small monetary incentives increase COVID-19 vaccination uptake versus no incentive?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a modest payment produced a modest, real increase, verified in records rather than self-report. In the preregistered Swedish randomised trial of 8,286 participants, a guaranteed payment of 200 Swedish kronor (about US $24) increased vaccination by 4.2 percentage points from a baseline rate of 71.6% (P=0.005), with uptake measured in population-wide administrative vaccination records (Campos-Mercade P et al., PMID: 34618594). Behavioural nudges in the same trial raised stated intentions but had only small, non-significant effects on actual vaccination. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): small guaranteed payments increase vaccination uptake by a few percentage points — a single trial in a high-baseline setting, so Tier C, and the absolute gain will differ where baseline uptake differs.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a guaranteed payment of about US $24 increased COVID-19 vaccination by 4.2 percentage points from a 71.6% baseline in one large preregistered randomised trial with registry-verified uptake

title: Adding the GP's name to a bowel scope reminder letter: attendance 4% versus 3% — no significant effect (adjusted OR 1.30, 95% CI 0.69–2.43) in previous non-participants
question: Does a GP-endorsed reminder letter increase uptake of bowel cancer screening among previous non-participants versus a standard reminder?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the endorsement, at least in this unpersonalised form, did not move attendance. In the North West London randomised trial, previous non-participants who received a GP-endorsed reminder letter a year after their original bowel scope (flexible sigmoidoscopy) invitation attended in 4% of cases versus 3% with the standard reminder letter — an adjusted odds ratio of 1.30 (95% CI 0.69 to 2.43), not statistically significant (Kaushal A et al., PMID: 33022321). The authors' own reading is that the endorsement may not have been personalised enough. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): a GP endorsement added to a reminder letter did not significantly increase bowel scope attendance among previous non-participants — a single trial, so Tier C, and the null applies to this endorsement format, not to every form of GP involvement.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — GP endorsement of a reminder letter gave bowel scope attendance of 4% versus 3% (adjusted OR 1.30, 95% CI 0.69–2.43, not significant) in one randomised trial of previous non-participants

title: Contacting at-risk relatives directly instead of relying on the patient: cascade testing uptake 62% versus 40% in first-degree relatives in the meta-analysis — from non-randomised comparisons
question: For hereditary cancer and familial hypercholesterolaemia families, does direct contact of at-risk relatives by health services increase cascade testing uptake versus family-mediated contact?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — direct contact reaches more relatives, on evidence that is comparative but not randomised. In the hereditary-cancer meta-analysis, direct relative contact by the medical team or laboratory produced genetic counselling uptake of 63% (95% CI 49 to 75) versus 35% (95% CI 24 to 48) with patient-mediated contact, and genetic testing in first-degree relatives of 62% (95% CI 49 to 73) versus 40% (95% CI 32 to 48); overall, only 48% of relatives underwent counselling and 41% testing by any route (Frey MK et al., PMID: 35960887). In familial hypercholesterolaemia, a systematic review of 24 non-comparative studies likewise found the direct strategy gave the largest yield of index cases participating in cascade testing (94%, 8 studies), while a combined strategy — letting the index case choose the contact method — produced the largest yields of relatives tested among those contacted (Leonardi-Bee J et al., PMID: 34753031). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): direct contact increases cascade uptake over family-mediated contact — Tier C, because the underlying studies are non-randomised and the reviewers themselves call for randomised confirmation.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — direct contact of relatives gave cascade genetic testing uptake of 62% versus 40% (first-degree relatives) and counselling uptake of 63% versus 35% versus patient-mediated contact in meta-analysis of non-randomised studies

title: Pay-for-performance and payment incentives in primary care: screening and process measures improve in some schemes, patient outcomes mostly do not — and cancer-screening incentives showed partial or no effects in most studies
question: Do pay-for-performance schemes in primary care improve preventive care quality and screening rates versus fee-for-service alone?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — the reviews agree the effects are inconsistent and mostly confined to process measures. A systematic review focused on cancer screening found that most studies showed partial or no effects of financial incentives on breast and cervical screening delivery rates, with only a few positive or partial effects for colorectal screening (Mauro M et al., PMID: 31587819). A broader 2026 systematic review of randomised and cluster-randomised trials of payment and financial-incentive models in primary care (10 studies, including pay-for-performance) found that selected interventions may improve provider adherence, preventive screening, chronic-disease management and vaccination uptake, but that improvements in patient-centred clinical outcomes were less consistent, every included study carried some concerns or a high risk of bias, and certainty of evidence ranged from very low to moderate (Alrashed A et al., PMID: 42764853). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): pay-for-performance may lift some preventive process measures; a reliable improvement in screening rates or patient outcomes is not established — Tier C.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — payment and pay-for-performance incentives in primary care improved some preventive process measures in a 10-trial review, while a screening-specific review found partial or no effects in most studies and patient-outcome gains were inconsistent

title: Text messages and bowel screening: adding an SMS reminder raised kit return to 82.6% versus 77.7% — but swapping the reminder letter for an SMS cut participation to 17.2% versus 21.9%
question: Does adding a text-message (SMS) component to screening invitations increase bowel cancer screening participation versus invitation alone?
balance: SPLIT — adding a text helps; replacing the letter with a text hurts. In the Catalan screening programme, people who had collected a FIT kit but not returned it within 14 days completed screening more often when an SMS reminder was added: 64.2% versus 53.7% at 30 days and 82.6% versus 77.7% at 126 days (Vives N et al., PMID: 39083331). But when an SMS was sent instead of the routine postal reminder to non-completers at six weeks, participation fell to 17.2% versus 21.9% on the letter (odds ratio 0.71, 95% CI 0.62 to 0.82), and the trial was stopped early; only after a recovery postal reminder did the SMS group's final participation (29.3%) overtake the control group's (26.5%) (Vives N et al., PMID: 39742454). PROPOSED SPLIT: an SMS added to the standard pathway increases participation; an SMS substituted for the letter decreases it — Tier C, as both trials come from one programme.
stamp: SPLIT — adding an SMS reminder increased FIT completion (82.6% versus 77.7% at 126 days), while replacing the postal reminder with an SMS decreased participation (17.2% versus 21.9%; OR 0.71) in trials from the same programme

title: Opt-out hepatitis C testing in emergency departments: programmes found 182 new cases in one Dublin series and linked 86.2% of new diagnoses to care — but a Canadian universal programme found new cases in only 0.23% and linked just two patients
question: In emergency departments, does opt-out universal hepatitis C screening identify more new infections and link more people to care than risk-based testing?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — opt-out testing demonstrably finds new infections; no study here compares it head-to-head with risk-based testing, and linkage varied from excellent to poor. In Dublin's three-year opt-out programme, 61.7% of patients who had blood taken accepted screening, 267 of 41,535 individual patients screened (12.1% of all positives) were newly diagnosed — including 182 new hepatitis C diagnoses — and 86.2% of new diagnoses were linked to care (Grant C et al., PMID: 31806726). In a Canadian university emergency department's universal opt-out programme, 62.1% of eligible patients were tested, the prevalence of new hepatitis C cases was 0.23% (95% CI 0.12 to 0.45), and only two newly diagnosed hepatitis C patients were linked to care at three months (Martel-Laferriere V et al., PMID: 35042704). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): universal opt-out screening identifies new hepatitis C infections that risk-based testing is designed to miss, but the yield and linkage dividend depend entirely on local prevalence and follow-up infrastructure — Tier C, observational evidence with no direct comparator.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — opt-out emergency-department screening programmes identified new hepatitis C diagnoses (182 in one three-year programme; new-case prevalence 0.23% in another) with linkage to care ranging from 86.2% of new diagnoses to only two patients, and no head-to-head comparison with risk-based testing

title: Home self-collection kits for chlamydia and gonorrhoea: testing uptake 2.61 times higher than clinic collection in a 15-trial meta-analysis — and mailing men a kit directly made testing 11.1 times as likely as usual care
question: Does offering home self-collection kits for chlamydia and gonorrhoea increase STI screening uptake versus clinic-based testing invitations?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — offering people a home kit gets substantially more of them tested, and those who test positive reach care at the same rate. A systematic review and meta-analysis of 19 studies, including 15 randomised trials with 62,369 participants, found uptake of chlamydia or gonorrhoea testing was 2.61 times higher with home self-collection than with clinic-based collection, with high concordance between home and clinic specimens and no significant difference in linkage to care (prevalence ratio 0.96, 95% CI 0.91 to 1.01) (Smith AC et al., PMID: 39191483). In the largest single outreach trial pattern inside that evidence, mailing young men a sampling kit directly produced a relative risk of being tested of 11.1 (95% CI 7.3 to 16.9) versus usual care — though absolute return rates stayed low, at 7.8% (Scholes D et al., PMID: 17538514). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): home self-collection multiplies screening uptake severalfold over clinic invitations — a solid randomised-trial meta-analysis, so not Tier C; the caveat is that multiplied uptake can still be a small absolute number.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — home self-collection increased chlamydia/gonorrhoea testing uptake 2.61-fold versus clinic collection in a meta-analysis of 15 randomised trials (62,369 participants), with linkage to care unchanged (prevalence ratio 0.96)

title: Community health workers and cancer screening in underserved communities: uptake odds 2.25 for colorectal screening in minority populations and 1.90 across breast, cervical and bowel screening in two randomised-trial meta-analyses
question: In underserved communities, do community health worker programmes increase cancer screening uptake versus usual outreach?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two independent meta-analyses of randomised trials point the same way. For colorectal screening in racial and ethnic minority populations, community-health-worker-led interventions increased uptake versus no intervention with an odds ratio of 2.25 (95% CI 1.48 to 3.44; P<0.001) across 10 US randomised trials, and multicomponent interventions worked best across all groups (Rana T et al., PMID: 36927698). Across breast, cervical and bowel screening, a second meta-analysis of 30 randomised trials found participation associated with an odds ratio of 1.901 (95% CI 1.60 to 2.26; P<0.001), with larger effects in people previously non-adherent to screening schedules and 25 of 30 studies conducted in ethnic minority groups (Bellhouse S et al., PMID: 29080378). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): community health worker programmes increase cancer screening uptake in underserved communities — not Tier C, because two concordant randomised-trial meta-analyses carry it; the stamp stays at POSSIBLE because study quality in the larger review was generally poor.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — community health worker interventions increased colorectal screening uptake (OR 2.25, 95% CI 1.48–3.44) and overall breast/cervical/bowel screening receipt (OR 1.90, 95% CI 1.60–2.26) in two meta-analyses of randomised trials

title: Bimodal neuromodulation for tinnitus (sound plus tongue stimulation, the Lenire device): symptoms fell in two large studies — but neither had a sham control, so how much is the device is unproven
question: In adults with chronic tinnitus — the phantom ringing a visitor simply asked about as 'what is tinnitus' — does bimodal neuromodulation (sound delivered to the ears paired with electrical stimulation of the tongue) reduce tinnitus symptom severity?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — the symptom scores move, the control group is missing. In the randomised TENT-A1 study of 326 adults with chronic subjective tinnitus (Conlon B et al., PMID: 33028707), all three bimodal stimulation arms improved on the Tinnitus Handicap Inventory (effect sizes -0.87 to -0.92) and Tinnitus Functional Index (-0.77 to -0.87) over 12 weeks, with gains persisting to 12 months in some settings — but every arm received active stimulation, so there was no sham or untreated comparator. In the TENT-A3 pivotal study of 112 participants (Boedts M et al., PMID: 39160146), adding tongue stimulation after 6 weeks of sound-only stimulation raised the responder rate in moderate-to-severe tinnitus from 43.2% to 58.6% on the THI (p=0.022) — a within-person comparison, not a parallel control — and the difference was not seen in the full cohort. No treatment-related serious adverse events were reported in either study, and the device has FDA De Novo authorisation. This shelf exists because the visitor question 'what is tinnitus' is already answered live (Shelf #2298, and CBT at #634); bimodal neuromodulation is the cardable tinnitus intervention not already asked. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): symptom improvement is consistent and durable, but with no sham-controlled trial the specific effect of the device over sound therapy, attention and time is unmeasured.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — tinnitus scores improved in a 326-person randomised study and a 112-person pivotal study of the Lenire device, but neither included a sham control

title: Unable to belch (retrograde cricopharyngeus dysfunction): botulinum toxin into the cricopharyngeus restored belching in 92–100% across three series — with no randomised trial and no placebo arm anywhere
question: In people who have never been able to belch — 'I have trouble burping' — with retrograde cricopharyngeus dysfunction, does botulinum toxin injection into the cricopharyngeus muscle restore the ability to belch and relieve the associated symptoms?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — a dramatic, consistent effect in uncontrolled data, and nothing stronger exists. In the only controlled study, a prospective comparison of manometry-diagnosed patients (Sanagapalli S et al., PMID: 39589004), 92% of 52 patients given endoscopic cricopharyngeal botulinum toxin injection could belch at 3 months versus 0 of 7 untreated controls (p<0.001), with global symptom scores improving from 7.3 to 1.8 while controls were static. In the syndrome-defining series (Bastian RW et al., PMID: 31236539), all 51 patients achieved belching and symptom relief after injection. In a retrospective series of 72 patients given 100 units under general anaesthesia (Karagama Y, PMID: 33893849), all could burp within 4 weeks and the ability persisted beyond 3 months in 96%. The pattern — an all-or-nothing mechanical outcome, restored immediately and often durably after the toxin wears off — is biologically coherent for a muscle that fails to relax. But there is no randomised or placebo-controlled trial, samples are small and self-selected, and diagnosis in two series was partly confirmed by response to the treatment itself. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): the signal is about as strong as uncontrolled evidence gets, and it is still uncontrolled — Tier C for the developer's personal review.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — botulinum toxin restored belching in 92% of treated patients versus 0% of controls in one small prospective study, with two concordant case series and no randomised trial

title: After high-risk adenomas: starting surveillance colonoscopy at 5 years was noninferior to 3 years for colorectal cancer at 5 years in EPoS II — an interim read of a 10-year trial
question: In patients who have had high-risk adenomas removed, can the first surveillance colonoscopy wait until 5 years instead of the currently recommended 3 years without increasing colorectal cancer incidence?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — on the interim evidence, waiting longer found no more cancer. EPoS II randomised 10,799 patients with high-risk adenomas in eight European countries to a first surveillance colonoscopy at 5 years or at 3 years (Jover R et al., PMID: 42748427). At the 5.5-year interim analysis, the 5-year cumulative colorectal cancer incidence was 0.77% with 5-year surveillance and 0.82% with 3-year surveillance (difference -0.05 percentage points; upper boundary of the 99.12% CI 0.68, inside the prespecified 0.7-point noninferiority margin), with 5 colorectal cancer deaths in total (3 vs 2). The supporting UK cohort of 21,318 post-polypectomy patients (Cross AJ et al., PMID: 33674342) shows why the question matters: without surveillance, high-risk patients' cancer incidence ran above the general population's (SIR 1.30), so surveillance itself is not being questioned — only its timing. This is a single trial, reported at interim, with the definitive 10-year analysis still to come, and noninferiority margins are a judgement, not a fact. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): at 5 years, a 5-year first interval performed no worse than 3 years in high-risk adenomas — Tier C because it rests on one interim trial report bearing on a cancer endpoint.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — in EPoS II's interim analysis, colorectal cancer incidence at 5 years was 0.77% with first surveillance at 5 years versus 0.82% at 3 years, meeting the noninferiority margin

title: Chlorfenapyr-pyrethroid bed nets beat standard nets where mosquitoes resist pyrethroids: malaria prevalence 25.6% vs 45.8% and incidence halved in two cluster trials — pyriproxyfen nets did not
question: In areas with pyrethroid-resistant mosquitoes, do dual-active-ingredient insecticidal nets (chlorfenapyr-pyrethroid or pyriproxyfen-pyrethroid) protect against malaria better than standard pyrethroid-only nets?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — for one of the two new net types, in two independent cluster-randomised trials. In Tanzania (Mosha JF et al., PMID: 35339225), malaria infection prevalence in children at 24 months was 25.6% under chlorfenapyr-pyrethroid nets versus 45.8% under pyrethroid-only nets (adjusted odds ratio 0.45, 95% CI 0.30 to 0.67). In Benin (Accrombessi M et al., PMID: 36706778), mean malaria incidence over 2 years was 0.56 cases per child-year under chlorfenapyr nets versus 1.03 under standard nets (hazard ratio 0.54, 95% CI 0.42 to 0.70). Pyriproxyfen-pyrethroid nets did not significantly beat standard nets in either trial (aOR 0.79 and HR 0.86, both non-significant), and piperonyl-butoxide nets also failed in Tanzania (aOR 0.99). Chlorfenapyr nets were cost-effective in the Tanzanian economic analysis at US$19–28 per DALY averted. Both trials were run where pyrethroid resistance is high; where mosquitoes remain susceptible, standard nets may do as well. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): two concordant cluster trials, one clear winner among the dual-ingredient nets.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — chlorfenapyr-pyrethroid nets reduced malaria versus pyrethroid-only nets in two cluster-randomised trials (prevalence aOR 0.45; incidence HR 0.54); pyriproxyfen nets did not

title: Probiotics for preterm infants: necrotising enterocolitis roughly halved in the pooled trials and in ProPrems — late-onset sepsis and mortality not moved by the one large named-product trial
question: In preterm infants, do probiotics prevent necrotising enterocolitis, late-onset sepsis and death compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — strongest for necrotising enterocolitis (NEC), the outcome that kills. A network meta-analysis of 106 trials in 25,840 preterm infants (Wang Y et al., PMID: 37782505) found multiple-strain probiotics associated with less severe NEC than placebo (risk ratio 0.38, 95% CI 0.30 to 0.50; absolute risk difference -3.7%) and with lower all-cause mortality (RR 0.69, 0.56 to 0.86; risk difference -1.7%), at moderate-to-high certainty. The largest single named-product trial, ProPrems (Jacobs SE et al., PMID: 24249817), randomised 1,099 very preterm infants to a three-strain combination or placebo: NEC of Bell stage 2 or more occurred in 2.0% versus 4.4% (relative risk 0.46, 0.23 to 0.93), but definite late-onset sepsis (the primary outcome) and mortality did not differ. Products, strains and doses vary across the pooled trials, and probiotics for preterm infants are not regulated as medicines in many countries — strain identity is the intervention, so this shelf names the ProPrems combination (Bifidobacterium infantis, Streptococcus thermophilus and Bifidobacterium lactis) exactly as published, and the pooled result should not be read onto any other product. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a real NEC reduction across two evidence layers, with sepsis unproven and the mortality signal resting on the pooling — Tier C because a mortality benefit is among the claims.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — probiotics reduced severe necrotising enterocolitis in a 106-trial network meta-analysis (RR 0.38) and in the ProPrems trial (2.0% vs 4.4%); sepsis was not reduced in ProPrems

title: One round of cervical screening in rural India: HPV testing cut cervical cancer deaths by about half (HR 0.52); visual inspection worked in one trial (HR 0.65) and not in the other
question: In low-resource settings without organised cytology programmes, does a single round of screening — HPV testing, cytology, or visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA) — reduce cervical cancer incidence and death?
balance: SPLIT — the answer depends on the test. In the Osmanabad cluster-randomised trial of 131,746 women aged 30–59 (Sankaranarayanan R et al., PMID: 19339719), a single round of HPV testing produced 34 cervical cancer deaths versus 64 in the control group (hazard ratio 0.52, 95% CI 0.33 to 0.83) and fewer advanced cancers (HR 0.47); neither cytology nor VIA significantly reduced advanced cancers or deaths in that trial. In the Dindigul cluster trial of about 80,000 women (Sankaranarayanan R et al., PMID: 17679017), one round of nurse-delivered VIA did reduce mortality (83 vs 92 deaths; HR 0.65, 95% CI 0.47 to 0.89) and incidence (HR 0.75). The difference between the VIA results plausibly reflects training and quality assurance, which the Dindigul team emphasise. Both trials are single-round, single-region, and two decades old; organised repeat HPV screening is a different, stronger intervention. PROPOSED SPLIT: HPV testing — benefit shown on deaths in one very large trial; VIA — benefit in one of two trials, contingent on programme quality. Tier C because mortality benefit claims rest substantially on single trials.
stamp: SPLIT — HPV testing reduced cervical cancer deaths (HR 0.52) in one large cluster trial; VIA reduced deaths in one of two trials (HR 0.65) and not in the other

title: Handwashing promotion cuts diarrhoea episodes by about a third in day-care and by about a quarter in communities — and a behaviour-change campaign lifted actual handwashing with soap from 2% to 37%
question: Does promoting handwashing with soap prevent diarrhoea in children and adults, in day-care, school, community and hospital settings?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — one of the oldest ideas in prevention, and the randomised evidence supports it. The Cochrane review of 29 trials (Ejemot-Nwadiaro RI et al., PMID: 33539552) found handwashing promotion prevented about a third of diarrhoea episodes in child day-care and schools in high-income countries (incidence rate ratio 0.70, 95% CI 0.58 to 0.85; high-certainty) and probably about a quarter in communities in low- and middle-income countries (IRR 0.71, 0.62 to 0.81; moderate-certainty), with larger effects where soap was provided free (RR 0.66) than with education alone (RR 0.84). The SuperAmma cluster trial in India (Biran A et al., PMID: 25102847) shows the behaviour itself can be moved at scale: observed handwashing with soap at key events rose from about 1–2% at baseline to 37% in intervention villages versus 6% in controls at 6 months. No trial in the review measured diarrhoea deaths or cost-effectiveness, follow-up was short, and behaviour measurement is easily biased. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): many trials, consistent direction, honest surrogate — episodes, not deaths.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — handwashing promotion reduced diarrhoea episodes across 29 randomised trials (IRR 0.70 in day-care/schools; 0.71 in LMIC communities)

title: Zoledronate every 18 months in women with osteopenia: fragility fractures in 122 vs 190 women over 6 years (HR 0.63, NNT 15) — one large trial, in women not yet osteoporotic
question: In older women with osteopenia (bone density below normal but above the osteoporosis threshold), does zoledronate prevent fragility fractures compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single, large, well-run trial in exactly the population where most fractures occur. Reid IR et al. (PMID: 30575489) randomised 2,000 women aged 65 or older with osteopenia (T score -1.0 to -2.5) to four infusions of zoledronate 5 mg or saline at 18-month intervals over 6 years. A nonvertebral or vertebral fragility fracture occurred in 122 women on zoledronate versus 190 on placebo (hazard ratio 0.63, 95% CI 0.50 to 0.79; number needed to treat 15), with concordant reductions in nonvertebral (HR 0.66), symptomatic (HR 0.73) and vertebral (odds ratio 0.45) fractures. Most fractures in postmenopausal women occur in women with osteopenia, so the population is the right one; but this is one trial, from one country, in women selected for a median 10-year hip fracture risk of only 2.3%, and bisphosphonate treatment of osteopenia commits many women who would never fracture to a drug with rare but serious harms not quantifiable at this sample size. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: a single-trial benefit claim on a fracture endpoint, for the developer's personal review.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one 2,000-woman 6-year trial found zoledronate reduced fragility fractures in osteopenia (122 vs 190 women; HR 0.63; NNT 15)

title: Vaccinating children against influenza protected their unvaccinated neighbours: 3.1% vs 7.6% confirmed influenza in non-recipients in the Hutterite colony trial (61% protective effectiveness)
question: Does vaccinating children and adolescents against influenza reduce influenza illness in unvaccinated members of their communities (herd protection)?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one well-designed cluster trial, with a wide confidence interval. Loeb M et al. (PMID: 20215608) randomised 49 Hutterite colonies to vaccinate children aged 36 months to 15 years with inactivated influenza vaccine or hepatitis A vaccine (an active control), achieving about 83% coverage. Among community members who did not receive study vaccine, PCR-confirmed influenza occurred in 39 of 1,271 (3.1%) in influenza-vaccine colonies versus 80 of 1,055 (7.6%) in control colonies — a protective effectiveness of 61% (95% CI 8% to 83%; p=0.03); across all residents the rates were 4.5% versus 10.6% (effectiveness 59%). No serious vaccine adverse events were observed. The setting — closed, rural, communal colonies — maximises measurable herd effects and may flatter what school-based programmes achieve in open populations; the confidence interval reaches down to 8%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: a single cluster trial carrying a population-level claim.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one cluster-randomised trial found vaccinating children reduced confirmed influenza in unvaccinated community members by 61% in relative terms (3.1% vs 7.6%)

title: Hepatitis B immunoglobulin plus vaccine at birth: only 6% of infants of highly infectious mothers became carriers, versus 88% of controls in the founding trial
question: In newborn infants of hepatitis B surface antigen-positive (especially e-antigen-positive) mothers, does hepatitis B immunoglobulin plus hepatitis B vaccine at birth prevent perinatal hepatitis B infection and the carrier state?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — among the most decisive prevention results in the library, from the pre-vaccine-era trial record. In the founding randomised blinded trial in Taipei (Beasley RP et al., PMID: 6138642), infants of e-antigen-positive carrier mothers received HBIG at birth plus vaccine on one of three schedules: persistent HBs antigenaemia developed in only 9 of 159 infants (6%), versus 88% of controls; the combined efficacy was 94%, compared with 71% for HBIG alone and 75% for vaccine alone in the programme's comparisons. The Cochrane review of 29 randomised trials (Lee C et al., PMID: 16625613) found vaccine plus HBIG reduced hepatitis B occurrence versus vaccine alone (relative risk 0.54, 95% CI 0.41 to 0.73, 10 trials) and versus placebo or no intervention (RR 0.08, 0.03 to 0.17, 3 trials), with vaccine alone also effective (RR 0.28). The trials are old — plasma-derived vaccine era — because the question became untestable once the answer was known; modern recombinant vaccines inherit the result. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): a near-total effect on the carrier state, consistent across the trial record.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — HBIG plus vaccine at birth prevented the hepatitis B carrier state in 94% of infants of e-antigen-positive mothers in the founding trial, confirmed across 29 trials in Cochrane review

title: Telephone counselling and quitlines help smokers quit: risk ratio 1.37 for call-back counselling to helpline callers and 1.27 in other settings, across 77 trials
question: Does telephone counselling — proactive call-back support from quitlines, or telephone counselling offered in other settings — help smokers stop smoking?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — a modest relative effect, replicated at scale. The Cochrane review of 77 trials (Stead LF et al., PMID: 23934971) found that among smokers who contacted helplines, those randomised to multiple sessions of proactive call-back counselling quit at higher rates than controls (risk ratio 1.37, 95% CI 1.26 to 1.50; 9 studies, over 24,000 participants). Telephone counselling offered outside quitline settings also increased quitting (RR 1.27, 1.20 to 1.36; 51 studies, over 30,000 participants), with some evidence of a dose response — one or two brief calls are less likely to help, three or more calls increase the chances — and a smaller relative increment when counselling was added to pharmacotherapy than when the comparison was self-help material alone. Effects are relative gains on low absolute quit rates, which the review reports as risk ratios rather than percentages; at typical control quit rates of around 5–10%, an RR of 1.3 is roughly 2–3 extra quitters per 100 smokers counselled. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): many trials, consistent direction, honestly modest size.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — telephone counselling increased quitting across 77 randomised trials (RR 1.37 for quitline call-back counselling; RR 1.27 in other settings)

title: CMV hyperimmune globulin in pregnancy did not prevent congenital cytomegalovirus: 22.7% vs 19.4% in the large blinded trial stopped for futility — the earlier smaller trial was also null (30% vs 44%, p=0.13)
question: In pregnant women with primary cytomegalovirus infection, does CMV hyperimmune globulin prevent congenital CMV infection in the baby?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — a hopeful uncontrolled signal that two randomised trials could not confirm. An uncontrolled 2005 study had suggested transmission falling from 40% to 16%, but the phase 2 randomised trial (Revello MG et al., PMID: 24693891) found congenital infection in 30% on hyperimmune globulin versus 44% on placebo (difference 14 percentage points, 95% CI -3 to 31; p=0.13), with more obstetric adverse events on treatment (13% vs 2%). The definitive multicentre double-blind trial (Hughes BL et al., PMID: 34320288) screened 206,082 pregnant women, randomised 399 with primary CMV infection before 24 weeks to monthly hyperimmune globulin or placebo, and was stopped early for futility: the primary outcome occurred in 22.7% versus 19.4% (relative risk 1.17, 95% CI 0.80 to 1.72), with point estimates for fetal/neonatal death (4.9% vs 2.6%), preterm birth and low birth weight all leaning the wrong way, none significantly. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): two randomised trials, the larger one blinded and futility-stopped, agree there is no demonstrated benefit to prevent.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — two randomised trials found no significant reduction in congenital CMV infection with hyperimmune globulin; the large blinded trial was stopped for futility

title: Lactoferrin for very preterm infants split: sepsis cut from 17.3% to 5.9% in a 472-infant Italian trial — and no effect at all (29% vs 31%) in the 2,203-infant UK ELFIN trial
question: In very preterm infants, does enteral bovine lactoferrin supplementation prevent late-onset infection and sepsis compared with placebo?
balance: SPLIT — the small trial said yes, the large trial said no, and size wins arguments in this library. Manzoni P et al. (PMID: 19809023) randomised 472 very-low-birth-weight infants in Italy to bovine lactoferrin, lactoferrin plus Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG, or placebo: first late-onset sepsis occurred in 5.9% and 4.6% in the lactoferrin groups versus 17.3% on placebo (risk ratios 0.34 and 0.27). The ELFIN trial (PMID: 30635141) randomised 2,203 very preterm infants in 37 UK hospitals to lactoferrin 150 mg/kg/day or sucrose: late-onset infection occurred in 29% versus 31% (adjusted risk ratio 0.95, 95% CI 0.86 to 1.04) — no effect, with serious adverse events numerically more frequent on lactoferrin (16 vs 10, two assessed as possibly related). Differences in baseline infection rates (17.3% placebo sepsis in Italy vs a broader 31% infection outcome in the UK), product, dose and case mix could explain part of the split, but a clinician choosing today faces the larger, null trial. PROPOSED SPLIT: benefit claimed by one moderate trial, refuted for routine use by one large trial — the honest shelf keeps both on its face.
stamp: SPLIT — one 472-infant trial found lactoferrin cut late-onset sepsis (5.9% vs 17.3%); the 2,203-infant ELFIN trial found no effect on late-onset infection (29% vs 31%)

title: Umbilical cord milking versus delayed clamping in preterm infants: the trial was stopped early — severe brain bleeding was higher with milking (8% vs 3%), and 22% vs 6% in babies born before 28 weeks
question: In preterm infants, is umbilical cord milking as safe as delayed cord clamping for death or severe intraventricular haemorrhage?
balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — a safety signal from a trial that had to stop. Katheria A et al. (PMID: 31742630) randomised preterm infants born at 23–31 weeks to cord milking or delayed clamping in a noninferiority design, but enrolment was halted at the first interim analysis (474 of a planned 1,500 infants) because severe intraventricular haemorrhage was imbalanced: 8% (20/236) with milking versus 3% (8/238) with delayed clamping (risk difference 5%, 95% CI 1% to 9%; p=0.02), concentrated in the youngest stratum — 22% (20/93) versus 6% (5/89) at 23–27 weeks (risk difference 16%). The composite of death or severe haemorrhage did not differ significantly (12% vs 8%; p=0.16) and death alone did not differ. The earlier meta-analysis of seven small trials (Al-Wassia H et al., PMID: 25365246) had found no mortality difference and less intraventricular haemorrhage of all grades with milking (RR 0.62) — the large trial's severe-haemorrhage signal in the most immature infants reverses the reassurance for exactly the babies at highest risk. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm), Tier C: one stopped-early trial, post hoc analysis, but a harm signal the developer should see personally.
stamp: POSSIBLE (harm) — in the largest trial, stopped early, severe intraventricular haemorrhage was higher with cord milking than delayed clamping (8% vs 3%; 22% vs 6% before 28 weeks)

title: Advance provision of emergency contraception: women used it twice as often and faster — and pregnancy rates did not fall (8% in every group of the largest trial; pooled OR 1.0)
question: Does giving women emergency contraception in advance (or direct pharmacy access) reduce unintended pregnancy rates compared with standard clinic access?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — to pregnancies, while clearly changing behaviour. In the largest trial (Raine TR et al., PMID: 15632336), 2,117 women aged 15–24 were randomised to pharmacy access, advance provision of three packs of levonorgestrel emergency contraception, or clinic access: advance provision nearly doubled use (37.4% vs 21.0%) yet pregnancy rates were 8% in all groups (adjusted OR for advance provision 1.10, 95% CI 0.66 to 1.84), sexually transmitted infections did not increase, and contraceptive and condom use did not deteriorate. The Cochrane review of 8 trials in 6,389 women (Polis CB et al., PMID: 17443596) found the same pattern pooled: no reduction in pregnancies at 12 months (OR 1.0, 0.78 to 1.29) despite more use (single use OR 2.52) and faster use (about 14.6 hours sooner), and no increase in unprotected intercourse or STIs. Easier access is justified on autonomy and per-episode efficacy grounds; it is not, on this record, a population pregnancy-prevention strategy, because too many episodes of unprotected intercourse still go uncovered. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — for the pregnancy-rate claim specifically.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — advance provision increased and hastened emergency contraception use across 8 trials but did not reduce pregnancy rates (pooled OR 1.0)

title: Sanitation campaigns built latrines and grew taller children — but did not reduce diarrhoea in either large trial (Mali prevalence ratio 0.93; Odisha 0.97)
question: Do community sanitation programmes (community-led total sanitation and latrine-promotion campaigns) reduce child diarrhoea, helminth infection and malnutrition?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — for diarrhoea, the outcome the programmes are sold on. In Mali's cluster trial of community-led total sanitation (Pickering AJ et al., PMID: 26475017), 121 villages were randomised: latrine access nearly doubled (65% vs 35% of households) and reported open defecation fell sharply, yet diarrhoea prevalence in under-5s was 22% versus 24% (prevalence ratio 0.93, 95% CI 0.76 to 1.14) — while children in CLTS villages were taller (height-for-age Z +0.18) and less often stunted (35% vs 41%). In Odisha, India (Clasen T et al., PMID: 25442689), a government sanitation campaign raised village latrine coverage from 9% to 63% of households (vs 8% to 12% in controls), but 7-day diarrhoea prevalence in under-5s was 8.8% versus 9.1% (period prevalence ratio 0.97, 0.83 to 1.12), with no clear gains in helminth infection or malnutrition. Coverage is not exposure reduction: partial uptake leaves transmission pathways open. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — for diarrhoea in these two trials; the Mali growth finding is recorded on the face of the shelf as the unexplained exception.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — two large cluster trials raised latrine coverage substantially without reducing child diarrhoea (PR 0.93 and 0.97)

title: Screening houses against mosquitoes: indoor mosquito counts fell by about half (ratio 0.41–0.53) and childhood anaemia was less common (OR ~0.5) in the Gambian randomised trial
question: Does screening houses (full screening of doors, windows and eaves, or screened ceilings) reduce malaria mosquito entry and childhood anaemia in malaria-endemic areas?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one randomised trial with an entomological primary endpoint and a supportive clinical secondary, plus observational housing evidence behind it. Kirby MJ et al. (PMID: 19732949) randomised 500 houses in The Gambia to full screening, screened ceilings, or no screening: mean Anopheles gambiae caught per trap per night were 15.2 with full screening and 19.1 with screened ceilings versus 37.5 unscreened (ratios of means 0.41, 95% CI 0.31 to 0.54, and 0.53, 0.40 to 0.70). Among 731 children, anaemia (haemoglobin <80 g/L) affected 12% in both screened groups versus 19% in control houses (adjusted OR 0.53 and 0.51), while parasitaemia did not differ. The systematic review of housing and malaria (Tusting LS et al., PMID: 26055986) found residents of modern houses had lower odds of malaria infection (adjusted OR 0.53) and clinical malaria across observational studies, at low to very low quality. No trial has yet measured clinical malaria incidence as a primary endpoint for screening alone. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: the clinical claim rests on a secondary endpoint of one trial plus observational data.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — house screening halved indoor malaria mosquito counts in a randomised trial and was associated with less childhood anaemia (OR ~0.5); clinical malaria was not a primary endpoint

title: Preventive zinc in children: diarrhoea and pneumonia episodes fell by about 13–19% in the pooled trials — all-cause mortality did not reach significance in either major review
question: In children in low- and middle-income countries, does preventive zinc supplementation reduce diarrhoea, pneumonia, malaria and death compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for illness episodes; the mortality claim is where two big reviews part company with the headline version of this story. Yakoob MY et al. (PMID: 21501441), pooling the preventive trials in under-5s, found diarrhoea incidence reduced by 13% in relative terms (RR 0.87, 95% CI 0.81 to 0.94) and pneumonia incidence by 19% (RR 0.81, 0.73 to 0.90), with a non-significant 9% lower all-cause mortality (RR 0.91, 0.82 to 1.01) and no effect on malaria. The Cochrane review of 80 trials in 205,401 children aged 6 months to 12 years (Mayo-Wilson E et al., PMID: 24826920) similarly found all-cause mortality compatible with benefit or slight harm (RR 0.95, 0.86 to 1.05), diarrhoea incidence reduced (RR 0.87, 0.85 to 0.89), no clear effect on lower respiratory infection incidence (RR 1.00) or malaria (RR 1.05), a very small height gain, and more vomiting (RR 1.29). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): episodes of diarrhoea clearly fewer; pneumonia and mortality unsettled between reviews — the shelf prints both.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — preventive zinc reduced diarrhoea incidence (RR 0.87) across the pooled trials; mortality effects were non-significant in both major reviews (RR 0.91 and 0.95)

title: Routine iron and folic acid for preschool children where malaria is intense: the 24,000-child Pemba trial was stopped early — death or hospital admission was 12% higher on iron
question: In preschool children in a high malaria-transmission setting, does routine preventive iron and folic acid supplementation (with or without zinc) increase or decrease death and hospital admission?
balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — one of the most consequential safety trials in child health, with an important modern qualification. In Pemba, Zanzibar, Sazawal S et al. (PMID: 16413877) randomised 24,076 children aged 1–35 months to iron plus folic acid, iron plus folic acid plus zinc, or placebo; the iron-containing arms were stopped early on the data safety board's recommendation because children receiving iron and folic acid (with or without zinc) were 12% more likely in relative terms to die or need hospital treatment for an adverse event (95% CI 2% to 23%; p=0.02) and 11% more likely to be admitted (p=0.03), with 15% more deaths (CI -7% to 41%, non-significant). The Cochrane review of oral iron in malaria-endemic areas (Neuberger A et al., PMID: 26921618; 35 trials, 31,955 children) reframed the finding: overall, iron did not increase clinical malaria (RR 0.93, 0.87 to 1.00), and where malaria prevention and treatment services were provided, iron may reduce clinical malaria (RR 0.91) — while where such services were unavailable, iron may increase it (RR 1.16, 1.02 to 1.31). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm), Tier C: the harm claim rests on one very large stopped-early trial in one service context, and the Cochrane subgroup reading is the condition attached to it.
stamp: POSSIBLE (harm) — routine iron/folic acid increased death or hospital admission by 12% in relative terms in the Pemba trial (stopped early); Cochrane found the risk concentrated where malaria services are absent

title: Preventing depression and anxiety in older people who already have symptoms: stepped care halved new disorders at 12 months (12% vs 24%) in 75-year-olds; problem-solving therapy halved incidence at 2 months in macular degeneration, fading by 6
question: In older adults with subthreshold depression or anxiety (symptoms but no disorder), do preventive psychological programmes — stepped care or problem-solving therapy — prevent onset of major depression and anxiety disorders?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — prevention aimed at people already symptomatic ('indicated' prevention), tested in two randomised trials with the same direction and the same caveat about durability. In 33 Dutch primary care practices, van't Veer-Tazelaar PJ et al. (PMID: 19255379) randomised 170 people aged 75 and older with subthreshold depression or anxiety to a stepped-care programme (watchful waiting, then bibliotherapy, then problem-solving treatment, then medication referral if needed) or usual care: the 12-month cumulative incidence of major depression or anxiety disorder was 0.12 (10/86) versus 0.24 (20/84) — relative risk 0.49 (95% CI 0.24 to 0.98). In age-related macular degeneration, Rovner BW et al. (PMID: 18515689) found problem-solving therapy halved 2-month incidence of depressive disorders (11.6% vs 23.2%; OR 0.43, 0.20 to 0.95), but most benefits had diminished by 6 months. Absolute gains are about 12 prevented disorders per 100 treated in both trials at their best timepoint. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): two concordant trials, one durable to a year, one not — maintenance is the open problem.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — indicated preventive therapy halved 12-month incidence of depression/anxiety disorders in older adults with subthreshold symptoms (RR 0.49), with a second trial positive at 2 months but faded by 6

title: Universal newborn hearing screening finds deaf babies months earlier: 71 more babies per 100,000 referred before 6 months in the Wessex controlled trial — detection proven, better life outcomes inferred
question: Does universal neonatal hearing screening, added to the later distraction test, increase early identification, confirmation and management of permanent childhood hearing impairment?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for the outcome the trial measured: finding the babies early. The Wessex controlled trial (PMID: 9872244) alternated periods with and without universal neonatal screening across hospitals between 1993 and 1996, covering 53,781 babies (25,609 born in screening periods). Screening achieved 87% coverage with a 1.5% false-alarm rate and a yield of 90 cases of bilateral permanent hearing impairment of 40 dB or more per 100,000 babies — about 80% of expected prevalence. Seventy-one more babies per 100,000 with moderate or severe impairment were referred before 6 months of age during screening periods, early confirmation and management increased significantly, and the screening test's false-negative rate was lower than the distraction test's (4% vs 27%). What the trial does not show is the downstream claim — better language, education and employment — which rests on the plausible, separately studied link between early management and development. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: a single controlled (non-randomised) trial whose endpoint is detection, carrying a programme adopted worldwide.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — universal newborn hearing screening increased referral before 6 months by 71 babies per 100,000 and improved early confirmation and management in one large controlled trial

title: Screening newborns' hips with ultrasound: no trial shows fewer late dislocations or less surgery — universal ultrasound mainly increases the number of babies treated
question: Do screening programmes for developmental dysplasia of the hip (universal or targeted ultrasound, versus clinical examination alone) reduce late-diagnosed hip dislocation and surgery in infants?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference) — an entrenched programme whose randomised record is, on inspection, nearly empty. The Cochrane review (Shorter D et al., PMID: 21901691) found no study at all comparing screening with early treatment against no screening with later treatment. Universal ultrasound versus clinical examination alone did not significantly reduce late-diagnosed dysplasia or surgery but did significantly increase treatment; targeted ultrasound likewise showed no significant reduction in late diagnosis or surgery. Meta-analysis of two studies found universal versus targeted ultrasound also did not significantly change late diagnosis or surgery rates. For infants with unstable or mildly dysplastic hips, delayed ultrasound with targeted splinting reduced treatment without significantly increasing late diagnosis, compared with immediate splinting. The trials are substantially underpowered for the rare outcome that matters (late dislocation), so this is absence of evidence in both directions — but the treatment increase is the one effect that is demonstrated. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference): screening strategy choice currently rests on tradition and observational data, not on randomised proof of better hips.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference) — no randomised evidence that ultrasound hip screening reduces late dislocation or surgery; universal ultrasound significantly increases treatment rates

title: House dust mite avoidance for asthma: 49 trials and 2,733 patients — no effect on peak flow, symptoms, medication use or the number improved (Cochrane)
question: In people with mite-sensitive asthma, do chemical, physical or combined house dust mite control measures improve asthma outcomes compared with placebo or no treatment?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — one of the most thoroughly negative records in the library, and it concerns advice still routinely given. The Cochrane review (Gøtzsche PC et al., PMID: 15495009) assembled 49 randomised trials with 2,733 patients with mite-sensitive asthma: 31 trials of physical methods (such as allergen-impermeable covers), 10 of chemical methods (acaricides) and 8 of combined methods. Despite many trials being of poor quality — which would be expected to exaggerate effects — there was no effect on the most reported outcome, morning peak flow (standardised mean difference -0.02, 95% CI -0.13 to 0.08; 1,339 patients), and no significant differences in patients improved (relative risk 1.01, 0.80 to 1.27), symptom scores (SMD -0.01) or medication use (SMD -0.05). The reviewers concluded such methods cannot be recommended. Later versions of this review have not reversed the finding. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): mite allergen can be reduced in the mattress while asthma, measurably, does not care.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — 49 randomised trials of dust mite control measures in mite-sensitive asthma found no effect on peak flow, symptoms, medication or improvement rates

title: Pictorial cigarette pack warnings beat text-only warnings: quit attempts 40% vs 34% and 7-day quitting 5.7% vs 3.8% in a 2,149-smoker randomised trial
question: Do pictorial warnings on cigarette packs change smoking behaviour — quit attempts and quitting — compared with text-only warnings?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a policy intervention with a genuine randomised trial of behaviour, which is rarer than it should be. Brewer NT et al. (PMID: 27273839) randomised 2,149 adult smokers in California and North Carolina to smoke for 4 weeks from packs bearing pictorial warnings or the existing text-only Surgeon General's warnings: smokers with pictorial warnings were more likely to attempt to quit during the trial (40% vs 34%; odds ratio 1.29, 95% CI 1.09 to 1.54) and more likely to have quit for at least 7 days at trial end (5.7% vs 3.8%; OR 1.53, 1.02 to 2.29), with more forgoing of cigarettes, quit intentions and conversations about quitting, and no demographic subgroup differences. The meta-analysis of the experimental literature (Noar SM et al., PMID: 25948713; 37 studies, 33,613 participants) found pictorial warnings outperformed text on 12 of 17 effectiveness outcomes — attention, cognitive and emotional reactions, attitudes and quit intentions — while noting that most experiments measured reactions and intentions rather than behaviour. Four weeks is short, the sample was a convenience sample, and population-level effects after real implementation are a further step. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): behaviour moved in the one large trial designed to measure it.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — pictorial pack warnings increased quit attempts (40% vs 34%) and short-term quitting (5.7% vs 3.8%) in a 2,149-smoker randomised trial, supported by a 37-study experimental meta-analysis

title: Repeated ivermectin mass administration cut malaria episodes in young children (2.00 vs 2.49 episodes per child in one season) — in a single trial of eight villages where most young children were too short to be treated
question: In malaria-endemic villages, does frequently repeated mass administration of ivermectin to the whole community reduce malaria episodes in young children?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — an ingenious idea (make human blood lethal to the mosquitoes that bite) with exactly one cluster trial behind it. In RIMDAMAL (Foy BD et al., PMID: 30878222), eight villages in Burkina Faso were randomised: in intervention villages, eligible residents received six single doses of ivermectin at 3-week intervals across one rainy season (both groups received one combined ivermectin–albendazole dose). In the active case-detection cohort of children aged 5 and under, cumulative malaria incidence was 2.00 episodes per child (648 episodes among 327 children) versus 2.49 per child in controls (647 among 263) — a risk difference of -0.49 episodes (95% CI -0.79 to -0.21; p=0.0009). Adverse events did not differ significantly (3% vs 2% of participants) and no adverse reactions were reported. The catches are structural: eight clusters is very few, most young children were themselves ineligible for treatment (height under 90 cm), so the effect is entirely indirect, and one season in one district cannot speak to resistance, repeat seasons or other transmission settings. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit), Tier C: a single small-cluster trial of a community-level intervention.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — one 8-village cluster trial found repeated ivermectin mass administration reduced child malaria episodes by about 0.5 per child over one season

title: PCI on top of modern medical therapy in severe ischaemic left ventricular dysfunction: no fewer deaths or heart-failure hospitalisations in REVIVED-BCIS2
question: In patients with severe ischaemic left ventricular systolic dysfunction, extensive coronary artery disease and demonstrable myocardial viability, does adding percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) to optimal medical therapy reduce death from any cause or hospitalisation for heart failure?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — in the one dedicated randomised trial, event rates were essentially identical: a primary-outcome event (death or heart-failure hospitalisation) occurred in 37.2% with PCI plus medical therapy and 38.0% with medical therapy alone over a median of 41 months (hazard ratio 0.99), and ejection fraction did not improve at 6 or 12 months. Pooled individual-patient data with the older surgical STICHES trial show that patients treated with medical therapy alone in the modern era fared better than medical-therapy patients in STICHES (adjusted hazard ratio 0.60), which is the most plausible explanation for why PCI added nothing: contemporary drug and device therapy has moved the baseline. Quality of life favoured PCI early but the difference had diminished by 24 months. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): in severe ischaemic left ventricular dysfunction, PCI added to optimal medical therapy does not reduce death or heart-failure hospitalisation.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — a 700-patient randomised trial found identical rates of death or heart-failure hospitalisation with PCI added to optimal medical therapy (hazard ratio 0.99), and pooled individual-patient data confirm modern medical therapy alone performs far better than in the surgical-trial era

title: EDTA chelation after myocardial infarction: TACT reported fewer events, but TACT2 — the replication trial in patients with diabetes — found none
question: In patients with a previous myocardial infarction, does an edetate disodium (EDTA)-based chelation regimen reduce cardiovascular events — and does the effect hold in patients with diabetes, the population chosen for the replication trial?
balance: SPLIT — the two trials disagree. TACT (1,708 patients after myocardial infarction) reported its composite endpoint in 26% on chelation versus 30% on placebo (hazard ratio 0.82; 95% CI 0.69 to 0.99), with no effect on total mortality (10% versus 11%; hazard ratio 0.93). TACT2 was built to replicate TACT in 959 patients who all had diabetes and a previous infarction — exactly where benefit was expected to be largest — and found the primary endpoint in 35.6% on chelation versus 35.7% on placebo (adjusted hazard ratio 0.93; 95% CI 0.76 to 1.16), despite chelation demonstrably lowering blood lead (median 9.03 to 3.46 µg/L by infusion 40). A treatment whose pivotal replication fails in the target population cannot be recommended on the first trial alone. PROPOSED SPLIT: one positive trial with borderline significance and high consent withdrawal, one adequately designed null replication in diabetes — the chelation question stays open in name but the diabetes claim is refuted.
stamp: SPLIT — TACT reported an 18% relative reduction in its composite endpoint (hazard ratio 0.82), but TACT2, the dedicated replication trial in patients with diabetes and previous myocardial infarction, found no effect (35.6% versus 35.7%; adjusted hazard ratio 0.93)

title: Apabetalone after acute coronary syndrome in type 2 diabetes: the phase 3 BETonMACE trial missed its endpoint (10.3% versus 12.4%) despite a promising pooled phase 2 signal
question: In patients with a recent acute coronary syndrome, type 2 diabetes and low HDL cholesterol, does the BET protein inhibitor apabetalone, added to standard therapy, reduce cardiovascular death, nonfatal myocardial infarction or stroke?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the definitive trial did not confirm the early signal. A pooled analysis of three short phase 2 trials (798 patients) had found fewer major adverse cardiovascular events on apabetalone (5.9% versus 10.4%; P = 0.02), but those trials were lipid and imaging studies with events counted secondarily. In BETonMACE — 2,425 patients after an acute coronary syndrome, all with type 2 diabetes and low HDL cholesterol — the primary outcome occurred in 10.3% on apabetalone versus 12.4% on placebo over a median of 26.5 months (hazard ratio 0.82; 95% CI 0.65 to 1.04; P = .11), and more patients stopped apabetalone for liver-enzyme elevations (2.9% versus 0.9%). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): apabetalone does not significantly reduce major adverse cardiovascular events after acute coronary syndrome in type 2 diabetes; the phase 2 event signal was not reproduced at phase 3 scale.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the phase 3 BETonMACE trial found no significant reduction in cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction or stroke (10.3% versus 12.4%; hazard ratio 0.82, 95% CI 0.65 to 1.04), superseding a positive pooled phase 2 event analysis

title: Carotid revascularisation on top of modern medical therapy: neither ECST-2 nor SPACE-2 showed added benefit for asymptomatic or low-risk stenosis
question: In patients with asymptomatic carotid stenosis, or symptomatic stenosis at low-to-intermediate predicted stroke risk, does adding carotid revascularisation (endarterectomy or stenting) to optimised modern medical therapy reduce stroke or death compared with medical therapy alone?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — both modern trials point the same way, though neither is definitive alone. In SPACE-2 (513 patients with asymptomatic stenosis of at least 70%), the 5-year primary endpoint (any stroke or death within 30 days, or ipsilateral stroke within 5 years) occurred in 2.5% with endarterectomy plus medical therapy, 4.4% with stenting plus medical therapy and 3.1% with medical therapy alone; endarterectomy versus medical therapy alone gave a hazard ratio of 0.93 (95% CI 0.22 to 3.91), and five strokes occurred in the 30 days after each procedure type. In ECST-2 (429 patients, asymptomatic or low-to-intermediate-risk symptomatic stenosis), the 2-year hierarchical primary outcome produced a win ratio of 1.01 (95% CI 0.60 to 1.70) — no benefit either way — with non-fatal stroke in 11 patients on medical therapy alone versus 16 with added revascularisation. Event rates on modern medical therapy are now so low that the procedural risk consumes any plausible gain in these risk groups. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): for asymptomatic or low-to-intermediate-risk carotid stenosis, revascularisation added to optimised medical therapy has not been shown to reduce stroke or death.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — two randomised trials of revascularisation added to modern medical therapy (SPACE-2, 5-year hazard ratio 0.93 for endarterectomy versus medical therapy alone; ECST-2, 2-year win ratio 1.01) found no benefit, with low event rates on medical therapy alone

title: Iron reduction by phlebotomy in peripheral arterial disease (FeAST): mortality 20% versus 23% — no significant benefit from lowering iron stores
question: In patients with symptomatic peripheral arterial disease, does reducing body iron stores by regular phlebotomy reduce all-cause mortality, or death combined with nonfatal myocardial infarction and stroke?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the iron hypothesis failed its randomised test. In FeAST (1,277 patients with symptomatic but stable peripheral arterial disease), all-cause deaths occurred in 125 patients (20%) in the iron-reduction group and 148 (23%) in the control group (hazard ratio 0.85; 95% CI 0.67 to 1.08; P = .17), and the secondary endpoint of death plus nonfatal myocardial infarction and stroke in 180 (28%) versus 205 (32%) (hazard ratio 0.88; 95% CI 0.72 to 1.07; P = .20). A biomarker substudy of the same trial found that patients who died had had higher average ferritin (132.5 versus 83.6 ng/mL) and higher interleukin-6 — ferritin tracks inflammation and prognosis, but lowering iron stores did not convert that association into fewer events. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): scheduled phlebotomy to reduce iron stores does not significantly reduce mortality or major cardiovascular events in peripheral arterial disease.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — in the 1,277-patient FeAST randomised trial, iron reduction by phlebotomy did not significantly reduce all-cause mortality (hazard ratio 0.85, 95% CI 0.67 to 1.08) or death plus nonfatal myocardial infarction and stroke (hazard ratio 0.88)

title: Carvedilol after myocardial infarction with left ventricular dysfunction (CAPRICORN): all-cause mortality 12% versus 15%, though the primary composite endpoint was neutral
question: In patients with left ventricular dysfunction after an acute myocardial infarction, treated with contemporary therapy including ACE inhibitors, does carvedilol reduce mortality and cardiovascular hospitalisation?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one large trial, with its headline composite neutral and its mortality result favourable. In CAPRICORN (1,959 patients with ejection fraction of 40% or less after infarction), the primary endpoint of all-cause mortality or cardiovascular hospital admission occurred in 35% on carvedilol versus 37% on placebo (hazard ratio 0.92; 95% CI 0.80 to 1.07), but all-cause mortality alone was lower on carvedilol — 116 deaths (12%) versus 151 (15%), hazard ratio 0.77 (0.60 to 0.98; P = 0.03) — as were cardiovascular mortality and recurrent non-fatal infarction. A prespecified arrhythmia analysis of the same trial found substantially less atrial fibrillation or flutter (2.3% versus 5.4%; hazard ratio 0.41) and ventricular tachyarrhythmia (0.9% versus 3.9%; hazard ratio 0.24) on carvedilol. Because the mortality claim rests on a single trial whose primary composite was neutral, this shelf is flagged Tier C for the developer's eye. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): carvedilol after infarction with left ventricular dysfunction probably reduces mortality, on one trial whose primary composite endpoint did not reach significance.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in the single CAPRICORN trial, all-cause mortality was 12% on carvedilol versus 15% on placebo (hazard ratio 0.77), although the primary composite of mortality or cardiovascular admission was neutral (hazard ratio 0.92)

title: Amlodipine in severe chronic heart failure: PRAISE was neutral overall, its striking non-ischaemic subgroup signal (46% relative mortality reduction) was tested in PRAISE-2 — and disappeared
question: In patients with severe chronic heart failure and ejection fraction below 30%, does amlodipine reduce death or major cardiovascular events — overall, and specifically in non-ischaemic cardiomyopathy, where the first trial suggested a large benefit?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — a textbook subgroup rise and fall. In PRAISE (1,153 patients with severe heart failure), the primary endpoint occurred in 39% on amlodipine versus 42% on placebo (a 9% relative reduction; P = 0.31) and death in 33% versus 38% (a 16% relative reduction; P = 0.07) — neutral overall — but in the non-ischaemic subgroup amlodipine appeared to cut death by 46% in relative terms (P < 0.001). PRAISE-2 then randomised 1,654 patients with non-ischaemic cardiomyopathy specifically: 278 deaths on amlodipine versus 262 on placebo (hazard ratio 1.09; 95% CI 0.92 to 1.29), and pooling both trials' non-ischaemic patients gave a mortality hazard ratio of 0.97 (0.83 to 1.13). Amlodipine caused more peripheral and pulmonary oedema. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): amlodipine neither prolongs nor shortens survival in severe heart failure of either cause; it appears safe when needed for angina or hypertension, but it is not a heart-failure treatment.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PRAISE was neutral overall and its non-ischaemic subgroup mortality signal was refuted by the dedicated PRAISE-2 trial (hazard ratio 1.09; pooled non-ischaemic hazard ratio 0.97)
