title: Tumour necrosis factor blockade in chronic heart failure: etanercept did not help (RENEWAL), and high-dose infliximab increased death or heart-failure hospitalisation (ATTACH)
question: In patients with chronic heart failure and reduced ejection fraction, does blocking tumour necrosis factor-alpha — with etanercept or infliximab — improve clinical status, or reduce death and hospitalisation for heart failure?
balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — the anti-cytokine idea in heart failure failed, with a dose-related harm signal. The pooled RENEWAL analysis of the RECOVER and RENAISSANCE trials found etanercept had no effect on the combined outcome of death or heart-failure hospitalisation (relative risk 1.1; 95% CI 0.91 to 1.33) and no effect on clinical status; both trials were stopped early for lack of benefit. In ATTACH (150 patients), infliximab did not improve clinical status at either dose, and the 10 mg/kg dose increased the combined risk of death or heart-failure hospitalisation through 28 weeks (hazard ratio 2.84; 95% CI 1.01 to 7.97). Because this is a harm claim, the shelf is flagged Tier C. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm): TNF-alpha blockade does not help chronic heart failure and, at higher infliximab doses, probably harms — a caution whenever anti-TNF drugs are used in patients who also have heart failure.
stamp: POSSIBLE (harm) — etanercept showed no benefit on death or heart-failure hospitalisation (relative risk 1.1), and high-dose infliximab increased death or heart-failure hospitalisation (hazard ratio 2.84) in randomised trials in chronic heart failure

title: The SUPRIM cognitive behavioural stress-management programme after a coronary event: 41% relative fewer recurrent cardiovascular events over 8 years in one randomised trial
question: In patients recovering from a coronary heart disease event, does adding the SUPRIM programme — a structured, group cognitive behavioural therapy programme focused on stress management — to traditional care reduce recurrent cardiovascular events and myocardial infarction?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one well-followed trial of a named programme, against a mixed wider literature. In SUPRIM (362 patients after a coronary event), the group offered 20 two-hour CBT sessions over 1 year had, over a mean of 94 months, a 41% relative lower rate of fatal and nonfatal first recurrent cardiovascular events (hazard ratio 0.59; 95% CI 0.42 to 0.83), 45% relative fewer recurrent myocardial infarctions (hazard ratio 0.55; 0.36 to 0.85), and a non-significant 28% relative lower all-cause mortality (hazard ratio 0.72; 0.40 to 1.30), with a dose-response by attendance. The broader Cochrane review of psychological interventions in coronary disease (35 trials, 10,703 people) is cooler: no reduction in total mortality (risk ratio 0.90; 0.77 to 1.05) or non-fatal infarction (0.82; 0.64 to 1.05), with a possible reduction in cardiac mortality (0.79; 0.63 to 0.98) on low-quality evidence. Because the hard-outcome benefit rests substantially on one trial, this shelf is Tier C. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the SUPRIM stress-management CBT programme probably reduces recurrent events after a coronary event; psychological therapy in general has, at most, smaller and less certain effects.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the single SUPRIM randomised trial found 41% relative fewer recurrent cardiovascular events (hazard ratio 0.59) with its CBT stress-management programme, while the wider Cochrane literature on psychological interventions shows no total-mortality benefit

title: Wait-and-see cardioversion in recent-onset atrial fibrillation (RACE 7 ACWAS): sinus rhythm at 4 weeks in 91% with delayed versus 94% with early cardioversion — noninferior, and 69% converted on their own
question: In haemodynamically stable patients presenting to the emergency department with recent-onset symptomatic atrial fibrillation, is a wait-and-see strategy (rate control first, cardioversion only if the arrhythmia persists beyond 48 hours) noninferior to early cardioversion for being in sinus rhythm at 4 weeks?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — waiting did not cost rhythm outcomes, because most episodes stop by themselves. In RACE 7 ACWAS (437 patients with recent-onset, symptomatic atrial fibrillation in the emergency department), sinus rhythm at 4 weeks was present in 91% of the delayed-cardioversion group and 94% of the early-cardioversion group (difference -2.9 percentage points; 95% CI -8.2 to 2.2; P = 0.005 for noninferiority against a -10 margin). In the wait-and-see group, 69% converted spontaneously within 48 hours and only 28% needed the delayed cardioversion; atrial fibrillation recurred in 30% versus 29%, and cardiovascular complications occurred in 10 versus 8 patients within 4 weeks. A prespecified substudy found that when fibrillation recurred, heart rates were better controlled after the delayed strategy (median 100 versus 112 beats per minute). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): for stable recent-onset atrial fibrillation, initial rate control with cardioversion in reserve achieves the same 4-week rhythm outcome as immediate cardioversion, while sparing most patients the procedure.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — in the single RACE 7 ACWAS randomised trial, a wait-and-see approach was noninferior to early cardioversion for sinus rhythm at 4 weeks (91% versus 94%), with 69% of the delayed group converting spontaneously

title: Angiotensin-receptor blockers to prevent atrial fibrillation recurrence: valsartan (GISSI-AF) and olmesartan (ANTIPAF) both failed against placebo
question: In patients with a history of atrial fibrillation who are in sinus rhythm, does an angiotensin II-receptor blocker — valsartan or olmesartan — reduce recurrence of atrial fibrillation or lower AF burden, compared with placebo?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — two placebo-controlled trials, in two different AF populations, both flat. In GISSI-AF (1,442 patients with prior atrial fibrillation plus cardiovascular disease, diabetes or atrial enlargement), recurrence occurred in 51.4% on valsartan versus 52.1% on placebo over 1 year (adjusted hazard ratio 0.97; 96% CI 0.83 to 1.14), and more-than-one recurrence in 26.9% versus 27.9%. In ANTIPAF (430 patients with paroxysmal atrial fibrillation and no structural heart disease, monitored with daily transtelephonic ECG — 87,818 recordings), the primary endpoint of AF burden did not differ between olmesartan and placebo (P = 0.770). Whatever ARBs do for blood pressure and ventricular remodelling, they do not keep atrial fibrillation away. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): ARBs should not be prescribed to prevent AF recurrence; their use in these patients stands or falls on their other indications.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — two randomised placebo-controlled trials found no reduction in AF recurrence with valsartan (51.4% versus 52.1%; hazard ratio 0.97) or in AF burden with olmesartan (P = 0.770)

title: Clopidogrel versus ticagrelor or prasugrel after NSTE-ACS at age 70 and older (POPular AGE): less bleeding on clopidogrel (18% versus 24%) with noninferior net clinical benefit
question: In patients aged 70 years or older with non-ST-elevation acute coronary syndrome, is clopidogrel — rather than the more potent ticagrelor or prasugrel — the better P2Y12 inhibitor when bleeding and net clinical benefit are weighed over 12 months?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in the one trial dedicated to older patients, the gentler drug won on bleeding without losing on net benefit. In POPular AGE (1,002 patients aged 70 or older with non-ST-elevation acute coronary syndrome), the primary bleeding outcome (PLATO major or minor bleeding) occurred in 88 patients (18%) on clopidogrel versus 118 (24%) on ticagrelor or prasugrel (hazard ratio 0.71; 95% CI 0.54 to 0.94; P = 0.02 for superiority), and the co-primary net clinical benefit outcome (death, myocardial infarction, stroke, and major or minor bleeding) was noninferior on clopidogrel — 139 patients (28%) versus 161 (32%), an absolute difference of -4% (95% CI -10.0 to 1.4). Nearly half the ticagrelor group (47%) stopped their drug early, versus 22% on clopidogrel. Because the bleeding-benefit claim rests on a single trial, this shelf is Tier C. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): in NSTE-ACS patients aged 70 and older, clopidogrel probably causes less bleeding than ticagrelor-based therapy without a net clinical penalty.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in the single POPular AGE randomised trial in patients aged 70 or older with NSTE-ACS, clopidogrel caused less PLATO major or minor bleeding than ticagrelor or prasugrel (18% versus 24%; hazard ratio 0.71) and was noninferior for net clinical benefit

title: Unguided DAPT de-escalation from ticagrelor to clopidogrel one month after myocardial infarction (TALOS-AMI): net events 4.6% versus 8.2%, with bleeding halved and no ischaemic penalty
question: In stabilised patients with acute myocardial infarction who have completed one month of aspirin plus ticagrelor after PCI without events, does switching the P2Y12 inhibitor to clopidogrel (unguided de-escalation) improve net clinical outcomes over months 1 to 12 compared with continuing ticagrelor?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — a large trial and a patient-level meta-analysis of four trials agree. In TALOS-AMI (2,697 stabilised post-infarction patients switched at 1 month), the primary net endpoint (cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, stroke, or BARC type 2, 3 or 5 bleeding) occurred in 4.6% with de-escalation versus 8.2% continuing ticagrelor (hazard ratio 0.55; 95% CI 0.40 to 0.76), driven by bleeding (3.0% versus 5.6%; hazard ratio 0.52), while the ischaemic composite was not significantly different (2.1% versus 3.1%; hazard ratio 0.69; 0.42 to 1.14). The individual-patient meta-analysis of four de-escalation trials (10,133 patients) found both fewer ischaemic events with de-escalation (2.3% versus 3.0%; hazard ratio 0.761) and less bleeding (6.5% versus 9.1%; hazard ratio 0.701), with no difference in all-cause death or major bleeding. Because the claim includes a cardiovascular-event composite benefit, this shelf is flagged Tier C. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): switching from ticagrelor to clopidogrel after the first event-free month following myocardial infarction reduces bleeding and net events without an ischaemic penalty.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — TALOS-AMI found fewer net clinical events with unguided de-escalation to clopidogrel at 1 month (4.6% versus 8.2%; hazard ratio 0.55), and a four-trial individual-patient meta-analysis confirmed less bleeding (hazard ratio 0.701) and fewer ischaemic events (hazard ratio 0.761)

title: Gastric bypass for hypertension in obesity (GATEWAY): 84% cut their antihypertensive load by at least 30% at 1 year versus 13% on medical therapy — and the advantage held at 5 years
question: In patients with obesity and hypertension requiring at least two antihypertensive medications, does Roux-en-Y gastric bypass plus medical therapy reduce medication burden and produce hypertension remission more than medical therapy alone, at 1 year and at 5 years?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a large, durable effect in one small, single-centre, unblinded trial. In GATEWAY (100 patients with obesity and hypertension on at least two drugs), the primary endpoint — cutting total antihypertensive medications by at least 30% while keeping blood pressure below 140/90 mm Hg — was met at 12 months by 83.7% of the gastric bypass group versus 12.8% on medical therapy alone (rate ratio 6.6; 95% CI 3.1 to 14.0), and hypertension remission occurred in 51% (office measurement) versus 0%. At 5 years the pattern persisted: medication reduction in 80.7% versus 13.7% (relative risk 5.91), remission in 46.9% versus 2.4% (relative risk 19.66), and a mean medication count of 0.80 versus 2.97. Because this is a single small trial, the shelf is Tier C. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): gastric bypass probably produces large, durable reductions in antihypertensive burden and frequent hypertension remission in obesity — an effect on medication load and blood pressure, with no randomised data on cardiovascular events from this trial.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in the single GATEWAY randomised trial, gastric bypass far outperformed medical therapy for reducing antihypertensive medication load at 1 year (83.7% versus 12.8%) and 5 years (80.7% versus 13.7%), with hypertension remission in about half of surgical patients

title: Oral inotropic drugs in chronic heart failure killed: milrinone raised mortality by 28% relative (PROMISE), vesnarinone dose-dependently (VEST), ibopamine by a relative risk of 1.26 (PRIME II)
question: In patients with severe chronic heart failure, does long-term oral inotropic therapy — milrinone, vesnarinone or ibopamine — improve survival, or does it increase mortality despite better haemodynamics and symptoms?
balance: LIKELY (harm) — three large randomised trials of three different oral inotropes, one direction. PROMISE (1,088 patients with severe heart failure): oral milrinone was associated with a 28% relative increase in all-cause mortality (95% CI 1 to 61; P = 0.038) and a 34% relative increase in cardiovascular mortality, with the worst effect in NYHA class IV (a 53% relative increase), plus more hospitalisations (44% versus 39%). VEST (3,833 patients): deaths were significantly fewer on placebo (242 deaths, 18.9%) than on vesnarinone 60 mg daily (292 deaths, 22.9%; P = 0.02), attributed to sudden arrhythmic death, even though quality of life improved more on vesnarinone. PRIME II (1,906 patients) was stopped early: 232 deaths (25%) on ibopamine versus 193 (20%) on placebo (relative risk 1.26; 95% CI 1.04 to 1.53). As a harm claim this shelf is Tier C. PROPOSED LIKELY (harm): chronic oral inotropic therapy increases mortality in severe heart failure — feeling better and pumping harder did not mean living longer.
stamp: LIKELY (harm) — three large randomised trials each found higher mortality with long-term oral inotropes in severe heart failure: milrinone (+28% relative), vesnarinone 60 mg (22.9% versus 18.9% deaths), and ibopamine (relative risk 1.26)

title: Treating depression in heart failure with an SSRI: sertraline (SADHART-CHF) and escitalopram (MOOD-HF) improved neither mood more than placebo nor cardiovascular outcomes
question: In patients with chronic heart failure and major depression, does SSRI treatment — sertraline or escitalopram — reduce depression severity and improve cardiovascular outcomes, including death and hospitalisation, compared with placebo?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — two placebo-controlled trials, concordant on both mood and events. In SADHART-CHF (469 patients with heart failure and major depression), 12 weeks of sertraline changed the Hamilton depression score by -7.1 points versus -6.8 on placebo (between-group difference -0.4; 95% CI -1.7 to 0.92; P = 0.89 between groups) — both groups improved, the drug added nothing — and the composite cardiovascular status did not differ (P = 0.78). In MOOD-HF (372 patients, 24 months of escitalopram), the primary outcome of death or hospitalisation occurred in 63% on escitalopram versus 64% on placebo (hazard ratio 0.99; 95% CI 0.76 to 1.27), and depression scores again improved equally (between-group difference -0.9 points on the Montgomery-Åsberg scale; P = .26). Both drugs were safe in heart failure — that is the only positive finding. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): SSRIs do not treat depression better than placebo-plus-support in heart failure, and do not reduce death or hospitalisation; depression in heart failure still needs care, but not on the expectation these drugs change cardiac outcomes.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — two randomised trials found SSRIs no better than placebo for depression in heart failure (SADHART-CHF between-group difference -0.4 points) and no effect on death or hospitalisation (MOOD-HF hazard ratio 0.99)

title: Screening asymptomatic diabetes for silent coronary disease: neither stress imaging (DIAD) nor CT angiography (FACTOR-64) reduced cardiac events
question: In people with diabetes who have no symptoms of coronary artery disease, does routine screening for silent coronary disease — by stress myocardial perfusion imaging or by CT coronary angiography — reduce cardiac death, myocardial infarction and related events?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — two randomised screening trials, two imaging technologies, one answer. In DIAD (1,123 asymptomatic patients with type 2 diabetes), cardiac death or nonfatal myocardial infarction over 4.8 years occurred in 2.7% of the screened group and 3.0% of the unscreened group (hazard ratio 0.88; 95% CI 0.44 to 1.88); overall event rates were low (2.9% cumulative), and even moderate-to-large perfusion defects had a positive predictive value of only 12%. In FACTOR-64 (900 patients with type 1 or type 2 diabetes), CT-angiography screening gave a primary outcome (death, nonfatal infarction, or unstable-angina hospitalisation) in 6.2% versus 7.6% on standard care (hazard ratio 0.80; 95% CI 0.49 to 1.32), and the ischaemic composite was numerically worse with screening (4.4% versus 3.8%; hazard ratio 1.15). Finding silent disease did not translate into preventing events, largely because background preventive therapy rose equally in both arms. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): routine imaging screening for coronary disease in asymptomatic diabetes does not reduce cardiac events.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — two randomised trials found no event reduction from screening asymptomatic diabetes for coronary disease, by stress perfusion imaging (hazard ratio 0.88) or by CT angiography (hazard ratio 0.80, with the ischaemic composite numerically worse)

title: Adding mitral-valve repair to CABG in moderate ischaemic mitral regurgitation: less residual regurgitation, but no better remodelling or survival at 2 years — and more early harm (CTSN)
question: In patients with moderate ischaemic mitral regurgitation undergoing coronary-artery bypass grafting, does adding mitral-valve repair to CABG improve left ventricular remodelling, survival and clinical outcomes compared with CABG alone?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the valve leaks less, the patient does no better. In the CTSN trial (301 patients with moderate ischaemic mitral regurgitation), adding mitral repair to CABG did not improve the primary endpoint of ventricular remodelling at 1 year (left ventricular end-systolic volume index change -9.3 versus -9.4 mL/m²) and death was 6.7% with the combined procedure versus 7.3% with CABG alone (hazard ratio 0.90); at 2 years death was 10.0% versus 10.6% (hazard ratio 0.90; 95% CI 0.45 to 1.83), again with no remodelling difference. Repair did durably reduce moderate-or-severe residual regurgitation (11.2% versus 32.3% at 2 years), but at the cost of longer bypass time, longer hospital stay, and more neurologic events and supraventricular arrhythmias. The small RIME trial (73 patients) found better peak oxygen consumption and remodelling measures with repair (+3.3 versus +0.8 mL/kg/min) with similar deaths (9% versus 5% at 1 year) — surrogate gains the larger trial's clinical outcomes do not confirm. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): routine addition of mitral repair to CABG for moderate ischaemic regurgitation fixes the echocardiogram, not the prognosis.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — in the 301-patient CTSN trial, adding mitral repair to CABG did not improve remodelling or survival at 1 or 2 years (2-year mortality hazard ratio 0.90) despite less residual regurgitation, and increased early adverse events

title: Transcatheter edge-to-edge repair versus mitral surgery for secondary mitral regurgitation (MATTERHORN): noninferior on efficacy at 1 year, with far fewer major adverse events (14.9% versus 54.8%)
question: In patients with heart failure and secondary (functional) mitral regurgitation who remain symptomatic on guideline-directed medical therapy, is transcatheter edge-to-edge repair noninferior to mitral-valve surgery for death, heart-failure hospitalisation, reintervention, assist-device implantation or stroke at 1 year — and how do early major adverse events compare?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single, small noninferiority trial in which the catheter strategy matched surgery on outcomes and clearly beat it on early harm. In MATTERHORN (210 patients with heart failure and secondary mitral regurgitation, symptomatic despite guideline-directed therapy), the primary efficacy composite (death, heart-failure hospitalisation, mitral reintervention, assist-device implantation, or stroke within 1 year) occurred in 16.7% after transcatheter edge-to-edge repair versus 22.5% after surgery (estimated difference -6 percentage points; 95% CI -17 to 6; P < 0.001 for noninferiority). The primary safety endpoint — major adverse events within 30 days — occurred in 14.9% after repair versus 54.8% after surgery (difference -40 percentage points; 95% CI -51 to -27; P < 0.001). Because the claim rests on one trial of 210 patients with a composite that includes mortality, this shelf is Tier C. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): for suitable patients with secondary mitral regurgitation, edge-to-edge repair probably achieves surgical-level 1-year outcomes with a much smaller early adverse-event burden.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in the single MATTERHORN randomised trial, transcatheter edge-to-edge repair was noninferior to mitral surgery for the 1-year efficacy composite (16.7% versus 22.5%) and caused far fewer 30-day major adverse events (14.9% versus 54.8%)

title: Salsalate in type 2 diabetes: HbA1c about 0.4 percentage points lower over 48 weeks in TINSAL-T2D — a real glycaemic effect, with rising urine albumin and no outcome data
question: In patients with type 2 diabetes, does salsalate — a salicylate prodrug with anti-inflammatory action — improve glycaemic control compared with placebo, and what safety signals accompany it?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for the blood test only: two stages of one research programme show a consistent, modest HbA1c reduction and a renal signal to watch. In the 14-week dose-ranging trial (108 patients), HbA1c fell by 0.36, 0.34 and 0.49 percentage points more than placebo at salsalate doses of 3.0, 3.5 and 4.0 g/day. In the 48-week TINSAL-T2D trial (286 patients), mean HbA1c was 0.37 percentage points lower on salsalate 3.5 g/day than on placebo (95% CI -0.53 to -0.21; P < 0.001), achieved despite more reductions in other diabetes medications in the salsalate group; triglycerides and adiponectin improved, but weight and LDL cholesterol rose, and urinary albumin increased (reversing on discontinuation, with estimated GFR unchanged). No trial measured cardiovascular or renal outcomes. As a single-programme surrogate benefit, this shelf is Tier C. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): salsalate probably lowers HbA1c by roughly 0.4 percentage points in type 2 diabetes; whether that helps or harms patients over years is unknown.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two randomised trials from one programme found salsalate lowered HbA1c by about 0.4 percentage points versus placebo (48-week difference -0.37, 95% CI -0.53 to -0.21), with increased urine albumin and no hard-outcome data

title: Oral insulin to delay type 1 diabetes in autoantibody-positive relatives (TrialNet): diabetes in 28.5% versus 33% — no significant delay overall, with a signal in one small secondary stratum
question: In autoantibody-positive relatives of patients with type 1 diabetes who still have normal glucose tolerance, does daily oral insulin delay the onset of clinical type 1 diabetes compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the prespecified main analysis was null; one small subgroup keeps the hypothesis alive but cannot carry it. In the TrialNet oral insulin trial, the main study group comprised 389 autoantibody-positive relatives with preserved first-phase insulin release: over a median of 2.7 years, diabetes was diagnosed in 28.5% on oral insulin versus 33% on placebo, and time to diabetes did not differ significantly (hazard ratio 0.87; 1-sided 95% CI reported as 0 to 1.2; P = .21). In secondary stratum 1 — just 55 participants with lower first-phase insulin release — diabetes developed in 48.1% versus 70.3%, with a significantly longer time to diabetes on oral insulin (hazard ratio 0.45; P = .006); the other secondary strata combined showed nothing (hazard ratio 1.03). A 55-person subgroup inside a null 560-person trial is a reason to run another trial, not to treat. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): oral insulin has not been shown to delay type 1 diabetes in at-risk relatives overall; the low-insulin-release subgroup signal is hypothesis-generating only.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — in the TrialNet randomised trial, oral insulin did not significantly delay diabetes onset in the main at-risk group (28.5% versus 33%; hazard ratio 0.87; P = .21); a positive result in one 55-person secondary stratum is hypothesis-generating only

title: Short intensive insulin therapy at diagnosis of type 2 diabetes: 1-year drug-free remission in 51% (pump) and 45% (multiple injections) versus 27% on oral agents in the Weng trial
question: In patients with newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes, does a short course of intensive insulin therapy (continuous subcutaneous infusion or multiple daily injections), stopped once normoglycaemia is achieved, produce higher drug-free remission rates at 1 year than initial treatment with oral hypoglycaemic agents?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one randomised trial with a striking remission difference, supported by a meta-analysis whose underlying studies are mostly non-randomised. In the Weng trial (382 patients with newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes in China), target glycaemic control was reached by 97.1% on pump therapy and 95.2% on multiple daily injections versus 83.5% on oral agents, and faster (4.0 and 5.6 days versus 9.3 days); after treatment stopped and patients were followed on diet and exercise alone, 1-year remission rates were 51.1% (pump), 44.9% (injections) and 26.7% (oral agents; P = 0.0012). A systematic review of short-term intensive insulin studies (7 studies, 839 participants) found drug-free remission in about 46.3% at 12 months and 42.1% at 24 months, with beta-cell function improved (HOMA-B pooled increase 1.13) — but five of its seven studies were non-randomised. Because the benefit claim (remission, a surrogate for disease modification) rests substantially on one randomised trial, this shelf is Tier C. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a short intensive insulin course at diagnosis probably induces drug-free remission in roughly half of newly diagnosed patients at 1 year — about double the rate with oral agents — though durability beyond 2 years and hard outcomes are unproven.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the single randomised Weng trial found 1-year drug-free remission in 51.1% and 44.9% after short intensive insulin versus 26.7% on oral agents, and a systematic review (mostly non-randomised studies) found about 46% in remission at 12 months

title: Physician-optimised blood-pressure self-management after hypertensive pregnancy (POP-HT): 24-hour diastolic pressure 5.8 mm Hg lower at 9 months, with favourable cardiac remodelling
question: In women who have had a hypertensive pregnancy (gestational hypertension or pre-eclampsia), does postpartum self-monitoring of blood pressure with physician-guided remote titration of antihypertensive medication achieve lower blood pressure at about 9 months than usual postnatal care?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one single-centre trial with a large, coherent effect on pressure and cardiac structure. In POP-HT (220 women after hypertensive pregnancy), 24-hour diastolic blood pressure at about 8 months postpartum was 5.8 mm Hg lower with self-monitoring plus physician-optimised titration than with usual care (71.2 versus 76.6 mm Hg; difference -5.80; 95% CI -7.40 to -4.20; P < .001), and systolic pressure was 6.5 mm Hg lower (114.0 versus 120.3 mm Hg; difference -6.51; -8.80 to -4.22). The imaging substudy (187 women) found the intervention group had lower relative wall thickness (-0.06), lower left ventricular mass (-6.37 g/m²), smaller ventricular volumes and higher ejection fractions (left +2.6%, right +2.8%) at follow-up — a remodelling pattern associated with better long-term outcomes. Because the claim rests on a single trial, this shelf is Tier C. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): structured postpartum blood-pressure self-management probably achieves meaningfully lower pressure after hypertensive pregnancy; whether it prevents later hypertension or cardiovascular events is untested.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in the single POP-HT randomised trial, physician-optimised self-management lowered 24-hour diastolic blood pressure by 5.8 mm Hg and systolic by 6.5 mm Hg at about 9 months after hypertensive pregnancy, with favourable cardiac remodelling on imaging

title: Suppressing ventricular ectopy after myocardial infarction (CAST): encainide and flecainide tripled arrhythmic death (relative risk 3.6) and raised total mortality 2.5-fold; moricizine harmed too
question: In survivors of myocardial infarction with asymptomatic or mildly symptomatic ventricular ectopy that can be suppressed by an antiarrhythmic drug, does long-term suppression with encainide, flecainide or moricizine reduce arrhythmic death and total mortality?
balance: LIKELY (harm) — the trial that taught medicine not to treat the surrogate. In CAST, patients whose ventricular ectopy was suppressed on encainide or flecainide were randomised to drug or placebo: death from arrhythmia or nonfatal cardiac arrest occurred in 33 of 730 patients (4.5%) on active drug versus 9 of 725 (1.2%) on placebo (relative risk 3.6; 95% CI 1.7 to 8.5), and total mortality was 7.7% versus 3.0% (relative risk 2.5; 1.6 to 4.5) over about 10 months, at which point the encainide/flecainide arms were stopped. The full report counted 43 arrhythmic deaths on drug versus 16 on placebo (P = 0.0004). CAST-II then tested moricizine: its 14-day initiation phase was stopped for excess deaths or cardiac arrests (17 of 665 versus 3 of 660), and the long-term phase showed no benefit (49 versus 42 arrhythmic deaths or arrests; adjusted P = 0.40). As a harm claim this shelf is Tier C. PROPOSED LIKELY (harm): suppressing asymptomatic ventricular ectopy after infarction with class I antiarrhythmic drugs increases mortality — the drugs did exactly what they were prescribed to do to the ECG, and patients died more.
stamp: LIKELY (harm) — in CAST, encainide and flecainide increased arrhythmic death or cardiac arrest (4.5% versus 1.2%; relative risk 3.6) and total mortality (7.7% versus 3.0%; relative risk 2.5) after myocardial infarction, and moricizine in CAST-II was also harmful at initiation with no long-term benefit

title: Dofetilide in severe left ventricular dysfunction (DIAMOND): no effect on mortality after infarction or in heart failure (41% versus 42%; 31% versus 32%), but fewer heart-failure hospitalisations and effective rhythm control — at a 3.3% torsades price
question: In patients with severe left ventricular dysfunction — with chronic heart failure or after a recent myocardial infarction — does the class III antiarrhythmic dofetilide reduce all-cause mortality, and what does it do to heart-failure hospitalisation, atrial fibrillation and torsades de pointes?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — for survival, the outcome these trials were built to test; the morbidity and rhythm effects are real but secondary. In DIAMOND-CHF (1,518 patients with symptomatic heart failure and severe ventricular dysfunction), 311 patients (41%) died on dofetilide versus 317 (42%) on placebo over a median of 18 months (hazard ratio 0.95; 95% CI 0.81 to 1.11), while hospitalisation for worsening heart failure fell (risk ratio 0.75; 0.63 to 0.89). In DIAMOND-MI (1,510 patients with severe dysfunction after infarction), all-cause mortality was 31% versus 32%, with cardiac and arrhythmic deaths also no different. Dofetilide converted atrial fibrillation (12% versus 1% at one month in DIAMOND-CHF) and maintained sinus rhythm (recurrence hazard ratio 0.35), but caused torsade de pointes in 25 patients (3.3%) versus none on placebo in DIAMOND-CHF, and in 7 patients (all on dofetilide) in DIAMOND-MI. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): dofetilide does not prolong life in severe ventricular dysfunction; it is a rhythm drug with a hospitalisation benefit and a proarrhythmic price that mandates in-hospital initiation.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — two DIAMOND trials found no mortality effect of dofetilide in severe left ventricular dysfunction (hazard ratio 0.95 in heart failure; 31% versus 32% after infarction), though heart-failure hospitalisation fell (risk ratio 0.75) and torsades occurred in 3.3%

title: Novel oral polio vaccine type 2 (nOPV2): two doses seroprotected 92.9% of Gambian infants and 99% of Bangladeshi newborns — but giving it together with bivalent OPV blunted the type 2 response (86% alone versus 65% combined)
question: In infants and young children, does the genetically stabilised novel oral poliovirus vaccine type 2 (nOPV2) produce protective type 2 antibody responses comparable to the Sabin vaccines it replaces — and what happens when it is given together with bivalent OPV?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — for antibody protection, the outcome these trials can measure. In the phase 3 Gambian trial (Ochoge M et al., PMID: 38402887), two doses of nOPV2 left 92.9% of infants and 95.5% of young children seroprotected against type 2 poliovirus, with seroconversion in 85.6% of baseline-seronegative infants; in Bangladeshi newborns (Zaman K et al., PMID: 36495882), two doses at birth and 4 weeks seroconverted 90% and left 99% seroprotected. In Panama (Sáez-Llorens X et al., PMID: 33308427), the novel candidates' day-28 seroprotection in infants (91–95%) was non-inferior to Sabin monovalent OPV2 (94%). The catch is co-administration: in Dhaka (Wilkinson AL et al., PMID: 37178706), giving nOPV2 together with bivalent OPV cut the type 2 response to 65% versus 86% for nOPV2 alone — non-inferiority for type 2 was not met, though types 1 and 3 were unaffected. No trial measures paralysis prevented; the vaccine's reason to exist — greater genetic stability, hence fewer vaccine-derived outbreaks — is a design property the immunogenicity trials support only indirectly, through similar shedding and response profiles. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): nOPV2 reliably immunises infants against type 2 poliovirus at Sabin-like rates, but it should not be co-administered with bivalent OPV when the type 2 response is the point.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — nOPV2 produces Sabin-comparable type 2 seroprotection across phase 2–3 trials in newborns, infants and children, with co-administration alongside bivalent OPV blunting the type 2 response

title: Pentavalent meningococcal vaccine NmCV-5 (A, C, W, Y and X): non-inferior to the licensed quadrivalent vaccine for the four shared serogroups in 2-to-29-year-olds, with a 97.2% response to serogroup X — the serogroup no licensed vaccine covered
question: In children, adolescents and young adults in the African meningitis belt, does a single dose of the pentavalent meningococcal conjugate vaccine NmCV-5 produce antibody responses non-inferior to a licensed quadrivalent vaccine for serogroups A, C, W and Y — and does it immunise against serogroup X?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — on immunogenicity, the endpoint meningococcal conjugate vaccines are licensed on. In the phase 3 trial in Mali and Gambia (Haidara FC et al., PMID: 37224196), a single dose of NmCV-5 produced seroresponses of 70.5% (serogroup A) to 98.5% (W) across the shared serogroups, non-inferior to MenACWY-D on both seroresponse differences (1.2 to 20.5 percentage points in NmCV-5's favour) and geometric mean titre ratios (1.7 to 2.8), and a 97.2% seroresponse to serogroup X, which no licensed vaccine covers. In Malian toddlers (Tapia MD et al., PMID: 34077644), bactericidal titres ≥128 were reached by 99–100% for all five serogroups after two doses. In infants given the vaccine alongside routine 9- or 15-month vaccinations (Diallo F et al., PMID: 40086461), NmCV-5 was non-inferior to MenACWY-TT for all five serogroups at both ages. Systemic adverse events were similar to the licensed comparators (11.1% versus 9.2% in phase 3), with no vaccine-related serious events in the infant trial. No trial measures meningitis cases prevented; that inference rides on the bactericidal-antibody correlate every predecessor vaccine was licensed on. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): NmCV-5 matches the licensed quadrivalent vaccines serogroup for serogroup and adds X, the gap in the meningitis belt's cover.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — NmCV-5 is non-inferior to licensed quadrivalent meningococcal conjugate vaccines across three randomised trials and adds a 97.2% seroresponse against serogroup X

title: One 200 mg dose of doxycycline after a deer-tick bite: erythema migrans in 0.4% versus 3.2% in the one randomised trial — an 87% relative reduction built on nine events, with nausea in 15%
question: After a bite from an Ixodes scapularis tick in a Lyme-endemic area, does a single 200 mg dose of doxycycline prevent Lyme disease compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a large relative effect on a small absolute risk, from one trial. In the randomised, double-blind New York trial (Nadelman RB et al., PMID: 11450675), erythema migrans developed in 1 of 235 subjects (0.4%) given a single 200 mg dose of doxycycline within 72 hours of removing an attached Ixodes scapularis tick, versus 8 of 247 (3.2%) on placebo (p<0.04) — an 87% relative reduction in efficacy terms (95% CI 25 to 98), an absolute reduction of about 2.8 percentage points, and no extracutaneous Lyme disease or asymptomatic seroconversion in anyone. The updated meta-analysis of all randomised prophylaxis trials (Zhou G et al., PMID: 34749665) pools 3,766 people: unfavourable events in 0.4% treated versus 2.2% control (pooled RR 0.38, 95% CI 0.22–0.66), with the single-dose doxycycline subgroup at RR 0.29 (0.14–0.60). The price is gastrointestinal: adverse effects in 30.1% on doxycycline versus 11.1% on placebo, nausea 15.4% versus 2.6% and vomiting 5.8% versus 1.3%. Risk concentrates in engorged nymphal ticks (erythema migrans after 9.9% of untreated bites from partially engorged nymphs, 0% after adult female bites in this trial), so the absolute case for the dose is strong after an engorged nymph and thin after a briefly attached adult tick. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): one dose very likely prevents most early Lyme disease after a high-risk bite; the trial base is a single study with nine outcome events, so the shelf is Tier C.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single-dose doxycycline after an Ixodes scapularis bite cut erythema migrans from 3.2% to 0.4% in one randomised trial, supported by a meta-analysis of six trials (pooled RR 0.38)

title: Babesiosis: atovaquone plus azithromycin cleared parasites as completely as clindamycin plus quinine — with adverse effects in 15% versus 72% (tinnitus in 39% on the old regimen)
question: In non-life-threatening babesiosis, is atovaquone plus azithromycin as effective as clindamycin plus quinine — and how do the two regimens compare on adverse effects?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the benefit is tolerability at equal efficacy, in the only randomised trial. In that trial (Krause PJ et al., PMID: 11078770), 58 subjects with non-life-threatening babesiosis in southern New England received seven days of atovaquone plus azithromycin (40 subjects) or clindamycin plus quinine (18 subjects). Parasite clearance was complete in both groups: three months after treatment, no parasites were visible on microscopy and no Babesia microti DNA was detectable in any subject, and by six months no patient in either group had symptoms (symptom resolution at three months: 65% versus 73%, p=0.66). The difference was harm: adverse effects in 15% on atovaquone–azithromycin versus 72% on clindamycin–quinine (p<0.001) — on the older regimen, tinnitus in 39%, diarrhoea in 33% and decreased hearing in 28%, against diarrhoea and rash at 8% each on the newer one. The trial was small and nonblinded, and it excluded life-threatening disease, so it says nothing about severe babesiosis, exchange transfusion, or immunocompromised patients, where this evidence does not reach. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): for non-severe babesiosis, atovaquone plus azithromycin is the regimen patients can actually finish — Tier C, a single small trial.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — atovaquone plus azithromycin matched clindamycin plus quinine on parasite clearance in the only randomised trial, with adverse effects in 15% versus 72%

title: A synbiotic for newborns in rural India: sepsis or death reduced by 40% relative (RR 0.60) in one 4,556-baby trial — driven by fewer sepsis cases, not fewer deaths (6 versus 4)
question: In healthy newborn infants in a low-resource community setting, does a daily oral synbiotic (Lactobacillus plantarum plus fructooligosaccharide) for the first week of life prevent sepsis and death over the first 60 days?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one large, well-blinded community trial, with the mortality caveat on its face. In rural India (Panigrahi P et al., PMID: 28813414), 4,556 newborns (birth weight at least 2,000 g, at least 35 weeks' gestation, no signs of sepsis) received an oral synbiotic — Lactobacillus plantarum (the strain named in the record is ATCC-202195) plus fructooligosaccharide — or placebo, and were monitored for 60 days. The primary outcome, the combination of sepsis and death, fell with a risk ratio of 0.60 (95% CI 0.48–0.74), a 40% relative reduction; culture-positive sepsis, culture-negative sepsis and lower respiratory tract infections were also significantly reduced. Deaths themselves were few and not fewer on the synbiotic: 6 in the synbiotic arm versus 4 on placebo — the composite is carried by sepsis episodes prevented, not lives shown to be saved. The wider neonatal probiotic literature in low- and middle-income countries points the same way (Imdad A et al., PMID: 32192165: neonatal sepsis RR 0.78, 95% CI 0.70–0.86, across 33 mostly hospital-based trials), but those trials used other organisms in mostly preterm, hospitalised babies. The record names the strain but no manufacturer or commercial product, so none is stated — and strain identity is the whole intervention here, so other probiotic products cannot borrow this result. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a one-week synbiotic course prevented sepsis episodes in community newborns in a single large trial; a mortality benefit was not shown. Tier C: single trial, and the composite touches mortality.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a 7-day synbiotic course reduced the sepsis-or-death composite by 40% relative (RR 0.60) in one large community trial of newborns, with deaths themselves not reduced (6 versus 4)

title: Chlorhexidine wipes in labour: the big randomised trial found nothing (neonatal sepsis 3% versus 4%) — the striking Malawi benefit came from a before-and-after study, and the pooled randomised evidence is null
question: In women in labour in low-resource settings, does chlorhexidine cleansing of the birth canal (with wiping of the newborn) reduce neonatal sepsis and maternal postpartum infection?
balance: SPLIT — the answer splits cleanly by study design. The only large randomised trial (Cutland CL et al., PMID: 19846212) assigned 8,011 women in Soweto to chlorhexidine vaginal wipes in labour plus full-body chlorhexidine washes for their babies, or water wipes and foot washes: neonatal sepsis occurred in 141 (3%) of 4,072 versus 148 (4%) of 4,057 (p=0.65), and newborn group B streptococcal colonisation was identical (54% versus 55%). The famous positive result is non-randomised: in Malawi (Taha TE et al., PMID: 9253269), a phased before-and-after introduction of 0.25% chlorhexidine birth-canal cleansing was followed by neonatal sepsis admissions of 7.8 versus 17.9 per 1,000 live births, neonatal mortality of 28.6 versus 36.9 per 1,000, and postpartum infection admissions of 1.7 versus 5.1 per 1,000 deliveries — but phase comparisons absorb every other change in the hospital over those six months. The meta-analysis of the randomised trials (Bell C et al., PMID: 29739349; 11 trials, 20,101 women) found no significant difference for any maternal or neonatal colonisation or infection outcome. PROPOSED SPLIT: as tested in randomised trials, intrapartum chlorhexidine wipes do not prevent neonatal sepsis; the observational Malawi signal remains unexplained by — and unconfirmed in — randomised evidence. Tier C: the shelf's positive arm rests on a non-randomised study.
stamp: SPLIT — randomised evidence null (8,011-woman trial and an 11-trial meta-analysis) versus a large non-randomised Malawi before-and-after study showing fewer sepsis admissions and deaths

title: Recurrent staph skin infections in children: decolonising the whole household cut recurrence in cases from 72% to 52% over a year — though carriage eradication was no better, and targeting only previously infected members later proved non-inferior
question: In households of children with community-associated Staphylococcus aureus skin infections, does decolonising every household member prevent recurrent skin and soft tissue infections better than decolonising the affected child alone — and can the effort be narrowed to members with a prior infection?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — infections fell even though carriage did not, in one open-label trial programme. In St Louis (Fritz SA et al., PMID: 22198793), 183 children with community-onset S. aureus skin abscesses and colonisation were randomised to a 5-day decolonisation regimen (hygiene education, twice-daily intranasal mupirocin, daily chlorhexidine body washes) performed by the index child alone or by all household members. Eradication of carriage did not differ — 50% versus 51% at one month (p=1.00) and 54% versus 66% at 12 months (p=0.28) — but recurrent skin and soft tissue infection over 12 months was reported in 52% of cases in household households versus 72% in index-only households (p=0.02), and infection incidence in household contacts was significantly lower in the first six months. The follow-on HOME2 trial (Hogan PG et al., PMID: 32521007) then showed the burden can be trimmed: decolonising only household members who had an infection in the prior year was non-inferior to decolonising everyone for 3-month cumulative infection (9.7% versus 10.8%; difference −1.1 percentage points, 95% CI −6.7 to 4.5). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): household-wide decolonisation prevents recurrent infections in this setting, and the targeted version keeps the benefit with less work — Tier C, because the anchor comparison is a single open-label trial with self-reported infections.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — household-wide decolonisation reduced recurrent SSTI in index cases from 72% to 52% over 12 months in one randomised trial, and targeting only previously infected members was non-inferior in its successor trial

title: Neurocysticercosis: albendazole cut seizures with generalisation by 67% relative but not total seizures — and adding praziquantel raised complete cyst resolution from 37% to 64%
question: In people with viable parenchymal brain cysticercosis and seizures, does antiparasitic treatment (albendazole, with corticosteroids) reduce seizures versus placebo — and does adding praziquantel to albendazole destroy more cysts than albendazole alone?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — real but narrower than the headline version. In the double-blind placebo-controlled trial (Garcia HH et al., PMID: 14724304), 120 patients with living brain cysticerci and seizures received albendazole 800 mg/day plus dexamethasone 6 mg/day for 10 days, or double placebo, alongside antiepileptic drugs. Over months 2–30, the total number of seizures fell 46% relative on albendazole — but that reduction was not statistically significant (95% CI −74 to 83), and the proportions having partial seizures were similar (19 of 57 versus 16 of 59); what did fall significantly was seizures with generalisation, down 67% relative (95% CI 20 to 86), with a greater tendency to generalise on placebo (22 of 59 versus 13 of 57; RR 1.63, 0.91–2.92). More cysts resolved on albendazole, and side effects other than abdominal pain did not differ. A decade later, the same group's phase 3 trial (Garcia HH et al., PMID: 24999157) showed how to kill more cysts: complete resolution at 6-month MRI in 25 (64%) of 39 patients on combined albendazole plus praziquantel versus 15 (37%) of 41 on standard albendazole (RR 1.75, 1.10–2.79), with no significant difference in adverse events; higher-dose albendazole alone (53%) did not significantly beat standard dosing. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): antiparasitic therapy clears cysts and reduces generalised seizures, with the combination the most cysticidal regimen tested — Tier C, because the seizure claim rests on the single 2004 trial and its primary count was not significant.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — albendazole (with dexamethasone) reduced seizures with generalisation by 67% relative in one placebo-controlled trial, and albendazole plus praziquantel achieved complete cyst resolution in 64% versus 37% on albendazole alone

title: Trachoma mass treatment: community azithromycin beat tetracycline ointment (infection down 93% versus 77% in Egypt at one year) — but twice-yearly rounds added nothing over annual, and narrowing treatment to young children let infection creep back up
question: For trachoma control in endemic communities, does mass azithromycin distribution reduce ocular chlamydial infection better than community tetracycline treatment — and does giving it twice a year, or targeting it to young children, do better than annual whole-community rounds?
balance: SPLIT — mass azithromycin works against the old standard; intensifying or narrowing it does not. In the three-country village trial (Schachter J et al., PMID: 10466664), community-wide oral azithromycin cleared infection in 866 (95%) of 924 initially positive people versus 482 (82%) of 587 on prolonged topical tetracycline, and at one year village infection rates had fallen further with azithromycin than tetracycline (relative reductions 93% versus 77% in Egypt, 78 versus 66% in The Gambia, 64 versus 55% in Tanzania). In hyperendemic Ethiopia (Gebre T et al., PMID: 22192488), however, twice-yearly distribution bought nothing over annual: after 42 months, infection prevalence in children was 3.2% in twice-yearly subdistricts versus 1.9% in annual ones, from baselines of 38.3% and 41.9% (pooled comparison p>0.99), though elimination may have been about 7.5 months faster with twice-yearly rounds (p=0.10). And after years of mass treatment, narrowing the target failed: in TANA II (Mahmud H et al., PMID: 37021692), communities randomised to treat only preschool children, or only households with an active case, saw childhood infection prevalence rise over 36 months (4.3% to 8.7% age-targeted; 2.8% to 6.3% household-targeted), with no difference between the two targeted strategies (adjusted difference 2.4 percentage points, 95% CI −4.8 to 9.6). PROPOSED SPLIT: annual whole-community azithromycin is the effective core; extra rounds add cost without prevalence benefit, and targeted rounds let transmission re-establish.
stamp: SPLIT — community azithromycin beats tetracycline for trachoma infection, but twice-yearly distribution adds nothing over annual (42-month prevalence 3.2% versus 1.9%), and child- or household-targeted treatment lets infection rise again

title: Deworming in pregnancy: no gain in anaemia, birthweight or perinatal survival in two randomised trials — treatment looked safe for the pregnancy, but infants of albendazole-treated mothers had more eczema (HR 1.82)
question: In pregnant women in helminth-endemic settings, does anthelminthic treatment (albendazole for soil-transmitted worms, praziquantel for schistosomiasis) improve maternal anaemia, birthweight and perinatal outcomes — and is it safe for mother and baby?
balance: SPLIT — safe for the pregnancy, unhelpful for the outcomes it was given for, with an infant-allergy price signal. In Entebbe, Uganda (Ndibazza J et al., PMID: 20067426), 2,507 pregnant women (68% with helminths, 45% hookworm, 18% Schistosoma mansoni, 40% anaemic) were randomised in a 2×2 factorial design to single-dose albendazole and/or praziquantel or placebos, all receiving haematinics and malaria presumptive treatment. Neither drug moved the targets: maternal anaemia at delivery (35% overall) had odds ratios of 0.95 (95% CI 0.79–1.15) for albendazole and 1.00 (0.83–1.21) for praziquantel; mean birthweight differences were −0.00 kg and −0.01 kg; and there was no effect on low birthweight, perinatal mortality or congenital anomalies — the one hint was albendazole against anaemia in moderate-to-heavy hookworm infection (OR 0.45, 0.21–0.98; interaction p=0.15). The dedicated safety trial in the Philippines (Olveda RM et al., PMID: 26511959) treated 370 women infected with S. japonicum at 12–16 weeks: birthweight was 2.85 kg in both arms (β −0.002, 95% CI −0.088 to 0.083), with no significant differences in abortion, fetal death or congenital anomalies. The price signal came from the Entebbe offspring follow-up (Mpairwe H et al., PMID: 21255083): maternal albendazole was associated with more doctor-diagnosed infantile eczema (HR 1.82, 1.26–2.64) and recurrent wheeze (HR 1.58, 1.13–2.22), and praziquantel with more eczema among infants of S. mansoni-infected mothers (HR 2.65, 1.16–6.08). PROPOSED SPLIT: in low-intensity infection settings, routine deworming in pregnancy is a null for mother and newborn outcomes — reassuring on birth safety, disappointing on benefit, and not free for the infant's allergy risk. Tier C: the harm signal rests on one trial programme.
stamp: SPLIT — no benefit on maternal anaemia, birthweight or perinatal mortality across two randomised trials (birthweight identical at 2.85 kg in the praziquantel trial), no excess of abortion or anomalies, but a higher infant eczema rate after maternal albendazole (HR 1.82)

title: Rabies monoclonal antibodies instead of human rabies immunoglobulin: two randomised trials met non-inferiority on day-14 antibody responders (90.2% versus 94.4% for the Twinrab cocktail; antibody levels fourfold higher with SII RMAb)
question: For people with WHO category III suspected rabies exposures, can a manufactured monoclonal antibody (or cocktail) replace scarce human rabies immunoglobulin as the passive component of post-exposure prophylaxis, alongside vaccine?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — on the antibody endpoint rabies prophylaxis is judged by, since a placebo-controlled efficacy trial after a rabid bite would be unethical. In the phase 3 trial (Kansagra K et al., PMID: 32556113), 308 patients with WHO category III suspected rabies exposures received the monoclonal cocktail Twinrab (docaravimab and miromavimab, as named in the publication) or human rabies immunoglobulin (Imogam Rabies-HT, as named in the publication), each with vaccine: day-14 responders (neutralising antibody ≥0.5 IU/mL) were 90.21% on Twinrab versus 94.37% on HRIG in the per-protocol population, geometric mean titres 4.38 versus 4.85 IU/mL, non-inferiority confirmed with protection maintained to day 84, and no deaths or serious adverse events. In the earlier phase 2/3 trial (Gogtay NJ et al., PMID: 29020321), 199 participants received the single monoclonal SII RMAb (as named in the publication) or HRIG with five vaccine doses: the day-14 geometric mean concentration ratio was 4.23 (95% CI 2.59–6.94) in the monoclonal's favour (24.90 versus 5.88 IU/mL), meeting non-inferiority, with adverse reactions mostly mild to moderate in both groups. Neither publication names a manufacturer for its monoclonal product in the record, so none is stated. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): manufactured monoclonals match the blood product on the protective-antibody window — the supply, cost and safety rationale for replacing HRIG is strong, though no trial can or does count rabies cases prevented.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — rabies monoclonal antibodies were non-inferior to human rabies immunoglobulin for day-14 neutralising antibody responses in two randomised trials of category III exposures

title: Dengue shock syndrome fluids: Ringer's lactate matched both colloids for moderate shock (rescue-colloid risk ratio 1.08) — colloids recovered children marginally faster, dextran caused more reactions, and mortality was under 0.2% on any fluid
question: In children with dengue shock syndrome, does initial resuscitation with a colloid (dextran or hydroxyethyl starch) improve outcomes compared with the crystalloid Ringer's lactate — and does the answer change with shock severity?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — for the choice between crystalloid and colloid in moderate shock, which is where most children sit. In the double-blind Vietnamese trial (Wills BA et al., PMID: 16135832), 383 children with moderately severe dengue shock were randomised to Ringer's lactate, 6% dextran 70 or 6% hydroxyethyl starch, and 129 with severe shock to one of the colloids. Only one patient died (mortality under 0.2%). The primary outcome — needing rescue colloid — was similar across fluids: relative risk 1.08 (95% CI 0.78–1.47) for Ringer's lactate versus either colloid in moderate shock, and 1.13 (0.74–1.74) for dextran versus starch in severe shock. Ringer's lactate improved the haematocrit less rapidly and took marginally longer to initial recovery, but no other response measure differed; bleeding, coagulation derangement and fluid overload were similar, while dextran caused significantly more adverse reactions than starch. The earlier four-fluid trial (Ngo NT et al., PMID: 11170909) in 230 children likewise found no survivor difference (all children survived) and no clear advantage to any fluid, with the longest recovery times on Ringer's lactate and a suggestion that colloids helped most in children presenting with the narrowest pulse pressures. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): with prompt resuscitation, the fluid brand matters far less than giving fluid — crystalloid first for moderate shock is the trial-supported default.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — in dengue shock syndrome, colloids did not beat Ringer's lactate on rescue-fluid need or any major outcome in two double-blind trials; recovery was marginally faster on colloids and dextran caused more reactions

title: Severe melioidosis intensive phase: ceftazidime halved mortality against the old four-drug regimen (37% versus 74%) — and imipenem later matched ceftazidime on survival, with fewer early treatment failures
question: In acute severe melioidosis, which intravenous intensive-phase regimen saves most lives — ceftazidime against the older conventional combination, and how does imipenem compare with ceftazidime?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — for ceftazidime over the regimen it replaced, on mortality, from the trial that changed practice. In the open randomised Thai trial (White NJ et al., PMID: 2570956), ceftazidime 120 mg/kg/day was compared with conventional therapy (chloramphenicol, doxycycline, trimethoprim and sulfamethoxazole) in severe melioidosis; the sequential trial was stopped after 22 months because ceftazidime was associated with a 50% relative lower overall mortality (95% CI 19–81) — 37% versus 74% (p=0.009) — among the 65 culture-confirmed patients (54 septicaemic) of 161 entered. A decade later (Simpson AJH et al., PMID: 10476746), 296 patients with suspected severe melioidosis (214 culture-confirmed) were randomised to high-dose imipenem or ceftazidime for at least 10 days: overall mortality in confirmed disease was 36.9%, with no difference in survival overall (p=0.96) or after 48 hours (p=0.3), but treatment failure after 48 hours was more common on ceftazidime (p=0.011), and both drugs were well tolerated. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): ceftazidime (or a carbapenem) is the intensive-phase standard because it halved mortality against what came before; between ceftazidime and imipenem, survival is a tie. Tier C is set because the mortality claim that anchors the shelf comes from the single 1989 trial, stopped early.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — ceftazidime halved mortality versus conventional four-drug therapy in severe melioidosis (37% versus 74%), and imipenem matched ceftazidime's survival in the head-to-head trial

title: Posaconazole for invasive aspergillosis: non-inferior to voriconazole on day-42 mortality (15% versus 21% overall; 19% versus 19% in proven/probable disease), with fewer treatment-related adverse events (30% versus 40%)
question: In patients with invasive aspergillosis needing primary treatment, is posaconazole non-inferior to voriconazole for all-cause mortality — and how do the two compare on treatment-related harm?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — an alternative first-line azole, proven non-inferior in one large double-blind trial. In that trial (Maertens JA et al., PMID: 33549194), 575 patients aged 13 years or older with proven, probable or possible invasive aspergillosis at 91 sites in 26 countries received posaconazole or voriconazole for up to 12 weeks. All-cause mortality to day 42 in the intention-to-treat population was 15% (44 of 288) on posaconazole versus 21% (59 of 287) on voriconazole — a treatment difference of −5.3 percentage points (95% CI −11.6 to 1.0), meeting non-inferiority (p<0.0001 for the non-inferiority test); in the subpopulation with proven or probable disease the rates were identical, 19% (31 of 163) versus 19% (32 of 171), difference 0.3 points (−8.2 to 8.8). Treatment-related adverse events were fewer on posaconazole: 30% versus 40% overall (difference −10.2 points, 95% CI −17.9 to −2.4), with liver-enzyme rises, nausea, hypokalaemia and vomiting the commonest on posaconazole, and hallucinations and blurred vision featuring on voriconazole. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): posaconazole is a first-line option with a gentler treatment-related profile — Tier C, a single trial, whose ITT mortality gap is driven partly by 'possible' cases the proven/probable analysis does not reproduce.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — posaconazole was non-inferior to voriconazole for day-42 mortality in invasive aspergillosis in one phase 3 trial, with treatment-related adverse events in 30% versus 40%

title: Male circumcision beyond HIV: HSV-2 seroconversion 7.8% versus 10.3% at two years (adjusted HR 0.72) and high-risk HPV prevalence 18.0% versus 27.9% (adjusted RR 0.65) — but no effect on syphilis (HR 1.10)
question: In adolescent boys and men, does medical male circumcision reduce acquisition of herpes simplex virus type 2, human papillomavirus and syphilis — the sexually transmitted infections beyond HIV that the circumcision trials also measured?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for HSV-2 and HPV, with a clean null for syphilis in the same men. The analysis pools the two Rakai, Uganda randomised trials (Tobian AAR et al., PMID: 19321868): 5,534 HIV-negative uncircumcised males aged 15–49 were randomised to immediate circumcision or circumcision deferred 24 months. Among the 3,393 who were HSV-2-seronegative at enrolment, cumulative HSV-2 seroconversion at 24 months was 7.8% in the intervention group versus 10.3% in controls (adjusted hazard ratio 0.72, 95% CI 0.56–0.92; p=0.008) — a 28% relative reduction. In the subgroup evaluated for HPV, high-risk genotype prevalence at 24 months was 18.0% versus 27.9% (adjusted risk ratio 0.65, 0.46–0.90; p=0.009), a 35% relative reduction. Syphilis incidence did not differ (adjusted HR 1.10, 0.75–1.65; p=0.44). The HPV figure is prevalence at a single 24-month sweep, not measured incidence, and both positive endpoints are secondary analyses of HIV trials — the reason this is POSSIBLE rather than LIKELY. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): circumcision modestly reduces HSV-2 acquisition and high-risk HPV carriage in men; it does not prevent syphilis.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — male circumcision reduced HSV-2 acquisition (adjusted HR 0.72) and high-risk HPV prevalence (adjusted RR 0.65) at 24 months in the Rakai randomised trials, with no effect on syphilis

title: Asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy: untreated positive women had pyelonephritis in 2.4% versus 0.6% of negative women — but treating it changed nothing (composite 2.5% treated versus 2.9% untreated), and it was not linked to preterm birth
question: In women with uncomplicated singleton pregnancies, does screening for and treating asymptomatic bacteriuria prevent pyelonephritis and preterm birth — the policy built on trials from over 30 years ago?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — in the modern reassessment. The Dutch multicentre study (Kazemier BM et al., PMID: 26255208) screened 5,132 eligible women at 16–22 weeks; in the final cohort of 4,283, 248 were asymptomatic-bacteriuria positive — 85 entered the embedded double-blind trial of nitrofurantoin 100 mg twice daily for 5 days versus placebo, and 163 were followed untreated. The composite of pyelonephritis, preterm birth or both did not differ between untreated/placebo-positive women and bacteriuria-negative women (6 [2.9%] of 208 versus 77 [1.9%] of 4,035; adjusted OR 1.5, 95% CI 0.6–3.5), nor between nitrofurantoin-treated positive women and untreated/placebo-positive women (1 [2.5%] of 40 versus 6 [2.9%] of 208; risk difference −0.4 points, 95% CI −3.6 to 9.4). Bacteriuria was associated with pyelonephritis specifically — 5 (2.4%) of 208 untreated/placebo-positive women versus 24 (0.6%) of 4,035 negative women (adjusted OR 3.9, 1.4–11.4) — but the absolute risk was low, and bacteriuria was not associated with preterm birth. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): in this low-risk population, a routine screen-and-treat policy found no measurable benefit to buy — Tier C, because the embedded randomised comparison is only 85 women and the rest is cohort evidence.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — treating asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy did not reduce pyelonephritis or preterm birth in the Dutch cohort-plus-trial reassessment; untreated bacteriuria carried a low absolute pyelonephritis risk (2.4%)

title: Early two-dose measles vaccination and child survival: the first Guinea-Bissau trial pointed to lower mortality (rate ratio 0.78, not significant; 0.59 without neonatal vitamin A) — the larger replication found none (HR 1.38), with a possible harmful interaction with polio campaigns
question: In high-mortality settings, does giving measles vaccine early — at about 4.5 months, with a second dose at 9 months — reduce all-cause childhood mortality compared with the standard single dose at 9 months, beyond preventing measles itself?
balance: SPLIT — two large randomised trials from the same research setting point in opposite directions, and the shelf keeps both. The first (Aaby P et al., PMID: 21118875) randomised 6,648 Guinea-Bissau children to Edmonston-Zagreb measles vaccine at 4.5 and 9 months or a single dose at 9 months: the intention-to-treat mortality rate ratio from 4.5 to 36 months was 0.78 (95% CI 0.59–1.05) — not significant overall, though significant in girls (0.64, 0.42–0.98) and in the 3,402 children who had not received neonatal vitamin A (0.59, 0.39–0.89), and 0.65 (0.43–0.99) when measles cases were censored, which is why the result was read as a non-specific (non-measles) effect. The replication (Nielsen S et al., PMID: 35747181), 6,598 children randomised 2:1 to two doses (4 and 9 months) versus one dose, found a mortality hazard ratio of 1.38 (0.92–2.06) between 4 and 60 months (90 versus 33 deaths) — no benefit, with a significant interaction: HR 0.81 (0.29–2.22) in children with no oral polio vaccine campaigns, but 4.73 (1.44–15.6) in children exposed to campaigns before and after enrolment (interaction p=0.027), while early vaccination in the presence of maternal measles antibody was associated with 50% lower mortality (20–68%). A third trial, in Burkina Faso (PMID: 29523450), found no effect of an additional early dose on hospitalisation or mortality (HR 1.00, 0.83–1.20). PROPOSED SPLIT: the early two-dose strategy's survival benefit appeared in one trial's subgroups, vanished in its replication, and may depend on the surrounding campaign environment — it is not a settled reason to move the measles schedule.
stamp: SPLIT — early two-dose measles vaccination showed a non-significant mortality reduction in the first trial (rate ratio 0.78) with significant subgroup effects, no benefit in the larger replication (HR 1.38) or a third trial (HR 1.00), and a possible adverse interaction with oral polio campaigns

title: Routine antibiotics with therapeutic food in severe acute malnutrition: recovery 88.7% (amoxicillin) and 90.9% (cefdinir) versus 85.1% (placebo) — and mortality 4.8% and 4.1% versus 7.4%
question: For children with uncomplicated severe acute malnutrition treated as outpatients with ready-to-use therapeutic food, does adding a routine 7-day antibiotic (amoxicillin or cefdinir) improve recovery and survival compared with therapeutic food alone?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — one large, rigorous trial is the evidence, and it is a mortality trial, which is why it is Tier C for the developer. In Malawi (Trehan I et al., PMID: 23363496), 2,767 children aged 6–59 months with severe acute malnutrition were randomised double-blind to amoxicillin, cefdinir or placebo for 7 days, all with ready-to-use therapeutic food as outpatients. Nutritional recovery was 88.7% with amoxicillin, 90.9% with cefdinir and 85.1% with placebo — relative risks of treatment failure with placebo of 1.32 (95% CI 1.04–1.68) versus amoxicillin and 1.64 (1.27–2.11) versus cefdinir. Mortality was 4.8%, 4.1% and 7.4% respectively — relative risk of death with placebo 1.55 (1.07–2.24) versus amoxicillin and higher still versus cefdinir (the record's text is truncated at that point, so only the amoxicillin comparison is quoted). In absolute terms, placebo cost about 2.6–3.3 extra deaths per 100 children treated. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): routine antibiotics alongside therapeutic food improved both recovery and survival in the only large trial — a single-trial mortality claim, held as Tier C.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — adding 7 days of amoxicillin or cefdinir to therapeutic food raised recovery (88.7%/90.9% vs 85.1%) and cut mortality (4.8%/4.1% vs 7.4%) in one large double-blind trial in Malawian children

title: Tetanus: giving antitetanus immunoglobulin intrathecally as well as intramuscularly — pooled mortality relative risk 0.71 across 12 small trials; the largest trial showed better progression and shorter spasms, stay and ventilation
question: In patients being treated for tetanus, does adding intrathecal antitetanus immunoglobulin (or antiserum) to the standard intramuscular dose improve survival and clinical course compared with intramuscular treatment alone?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — an old, small-trial literature with a consistent direction, held as Tier C. The meta-analysis (Kabura L et al., PMID: 16827708) pooled 12 randomised trials, 942 patients (484 intrathecal, 458 intramuscular): the combined relative risk of mortality for intrathecal versus intramuscular administration was 0.71 (95% CI 0.62–0.81) — a 29% relative reduction — with superiority also in the adult and neonatal subcategories and at high and low intrathecal doses. The largest single trial (Miranda-Filho DB et al., PMID: 15003976), 120 ICU patients in Brazil randomised to intrathecal plus intramuscular human immunoglobulin or intramuscular alone, found better clinical progression (difference in proportion improved 20%, 95% CI 4% to 35%; p=0.005), more patients with spasms lasting 10 days or fewer (difference 36%, 18% to 55%), shorter hospital stay and respiratory assistance (69.2% versus 30.8% needing assistance for 10 days or fewer; difference 38%, 12% to 65%); its abstract does not report the mortality split, so the survival claim rests on the pooled analysis. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): intrathecal antitoxin probably improves the course of tetanus and may reduce mortality — but the trials are small, old, and mix human immunoglobulin with equine serum, which is why this stays Tier C.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — intrathecal plus intramuscular antitetanus immunoglobulin improved clinical progression in the largest trial and was associated with lower pooled mortality (RR 0.71) across 12 small randomised trials

title: Plague treatment: gentamicin and doxycycline both worked — favourable responses 94% versus 97% in the only randomised trial (65 patients, Tanzania); 3 early deaths were from advanced disease
question: For patients with naturally occurring plague (bubonic, septicaemic or pneumonic), is gentamicin — available where streptomycin no longer is — as effective as doxycycline in a randomised comparison?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — between the two drugs, in the only randomised trial there is. In Tanzania (Mwengee W et al., PMID: 16447105), 65 adults and children with bubonic, septicaemic or pneumonic plague of 3 days' duration or less were randomised open-label to gentamicin (2.5 mg/kg intramuscularly every 12 hours for 7 days; n=35) or doxycycline (100 mg in adults, 2.2 mg/kg in children, orally every 12 hours for 7 days; n=30). Three patients died on the first or second day — 2 on gentamicin, 1 on doxycycline — with deaths attributed to advanced disease (pneumonia, septicaemia, haemorrhage, renal failure at presentation). All other patients were cured or improved: favourable response 94% (95% CI 81.1–99.0) with gentamicin and 97% (83.4–99.8) with doxycycline. Yersinia pestis isolates (biotype antigua) were susceptible to both drugs, serum concentrations were in range, adverse events were infrequent, and gentamicin produced a modest rise in mean serum creatinine. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): with 65 patients the trial cannot prove equivalence — it shows both drugs performed well in real plague, which is the evidence base guidelines actually rest on. Tier C: a single small open-label trial for a lethal disease.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — gentamicin and doxycycline both produced favourable responses above 94% in the only randomised plague trial; the trial was far too small to prove equivalence

title: A third mRNA COVID-19 vaccine dose in organ transplant recipients: neutralising responses against Delta in 55% versus 18% on placebo (difference 37 points) — an antibody trial, with no proven clinical endpoint
question: In organ transplant recipients who have had two doses of COVID-19 vaccine, does a third dose of mRNA-1273 vaccine raise neutralising antibody responses against SARS-CoV-2 variants compared with placebo?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — for the antibody outcome the trial actually measured; the shelf claims nothing about infections prevented. The randomised, double-blind trial (Hall VG et al., PMID: 34379917; neutralisation analysis PMID: 34807716) assigned organ transplant recipients to a third dose of mRNA-1273 vaccine or placebo; 117 recipients were analysed (60 vaccine, 57 placebo), with sera before and 4–6 weeks after the third dose. After two doses, the proportion with positive neutralisation against all three variants was small compared with wild-type virus. After the third dose, positive neutralisation by the pseudovirus assay against the Delta variant was present in 33 of 60 (55%) vaccine recipients versus 10 of 57 (18%) on placebo — a difference of 37 percentage points (95% CI 19–53); differences were 36 points (17–51) for Alpha and 31 points (15–46) for Beta, with neutralisation values lower for variants than wild-type, especially Beta. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): a third dose clearly raised variant neutralisation in transplant recipients — with the analysis's own stated limitation printed on the shelf: there is no clear correlate of protection for neutralising antibody, and this was a secondary analysis of an immunogenicity trial.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — a third mRNA-1273 dose raised neutralising antibody responses against variants in transplant recipients (Delta 55% vs 18% positive); an immunogenicity result, not a proven reduction in infections

title: Non-severe scrub typhus (and undifferentiated fever with leptospirosis): azithromycin matched doxycycline — cure 100% versus 93.5% for a single 500 mg dose against a 7-day course in mild disease, with fewer adverse events in the Thai fever trial (10.6% versus 27.6%)
question: For non-severe scrub typhus — and for the undifferentiated acute fever in Southeast Asia where scrub typhus and leptospirosis are the leading treatable causes — is azithromycin as effective as doxycycline, the standard drug?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — on efficacy, with a tolerability edge to azithromycin; severe scrub typhus lives on its own shelf (INTREST) and is not this question. In South Korea (Kim YS et al., PMID: 15494910), 93 patients with mild scrub typhus were randomised open-label to a single 500 mg dose of azithromycin or doxycycline 200 mg daily for a week: cure was achieved in 47 (100%) of 47 on azithromycin and 43 (93.5%) of 46 on doxycycline (p=0.117), median time to defervescence 21 versus 29 hours (p=0.097), no serious adverse events and no relapses in either group over one month. In Thailand (Phimda K et al., PMID: 17638700), 296 adults with acute undifferentiated fever were randomised to 7 days of doxycycline or 3 days of azithromycin; among the 151 with a determined cause — 69 leptospirosis, 57 scrub typhus, 14 murine typhus, 11 mixed — azithromycin was not inferior to doxycycline for both leptospirosis and scrub typhus with comparable fever clearance times (the record reports no arm-specific cure rates, so none are quoted), and adverse events were less frequent with azithromycin (10.6% versus 27.6%; p=0.02), against which the authors set azithromycin's higher cost and lower availability. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): in mild disease the drugs performed alike in both randomised comparisons — two small open-label trials, so the stamp stays POSSIBLE.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — azithromycin matched doxycycline for mild scrub typhus and for empirical treatment of undifferentiated fever (leptospirosis/scrub typhus) in two randomised trials, with fewer adverse events
