title: Rice-based oral rehydration solution in cholera: first-24-hour stool output cut by 36% in adults and 32% in children versus glucose ORS (13-trial meta-analysis) — but only 18% in non-cholera diarrhoea
question: For severe dehydrating diarrhoea, does oral rehydration solution made with rice instead of glucose reduce stool losses compared with the standard glucose-based WHO solution — and does the answer differ between cholera and other diarrhoeas?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — for cholera, where the effect is large and consistent; much weaker elsewhere, and the shelf says so. The meta-analysis of the 13 randomised trials (Gore SM et al., PMID: 1531430; 1,367 patients — 668 standard WHO glucose solution, 699 rice-based) found the rice solution significantly reduced the rate of stool output during the first 24 hours by 36% (95% CI 28–44%) in adults with cholera and by 32% (19–45%) in children with cholera, but by only 18% (6–30%) in infants and children with acute non-cholera diarrhoea; the authors concluded the benefit in cholera is sufficiently great to warrant its use, while the smaller non-cholera benefit needed sharper definition. A four-arm randomised trial in 182 adults with cholera (Alam NH et al., PMID: 1582603) agreed qualitatively: a substantial and significant reduction in stool output in the rice-ORS groups irrespective of feeding, and food itself did not potentiate either solution (the record reports no arm-level volumes, so none are quoted). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): rice-based ORS reduces purging in cholera by about a third in the first day — a stool-output benefit, in trials run against the older standard-osmolarity glucose solution; the library's separate shelf on reduced-osmolarity ORS asks the neighbouring formulation question.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — rice-based ORS cut first-24-hour stool output by about a third in cholera (36% adults, 32% children) across 13 randomised trials; the benefit in non-cholera diarrhoea was smaller (18%)

title: Whipple's disease: ceftriaxone or meropenem induction, then trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole — every patient in the randomised trial achieved remission (endpoint OR 0.95 between inductions), and a follow-on study found 3 months of oral therapy did the work of 12
question: In previously untreated Whipple's disease, which induction antibiotic — ceftriaxone or meropenem — followed by oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole cures the infection, and is 3 months of the oral phase enough instead of 12?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — between the two induction drugs, in a disease so rare that 40 patients is a landmark trial; the duration answer comes from a non-randomised extension and is labelled as such. The randomised trial (Feurle GE et al., PMID: 19879276) assigned 40 previously untreated central-European patients to daily ceftriaxone (2 g once daily, n=20) or meropenem (1 g three times daily, n=20) infusions for 14 days, both followed by oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for 12 months: all patients were followed for the entire period (median 89 months), all achieved clinical and laboratory remission, and remission was maintained in all except 2 who died of unrelated causes; the odds ratio for the endpoint (remission for at least 3 years) was 0.95 (95% CI 0.05–16.29; p=1.0). One patient with asymptomatic cerebrospinal-fluid infection resistant to both treatments responded to chloroquine and minocycline. The extension study (Feurle GE et al., PMID: 23291038) treated a further 40 patients identically except for 3 months of oral therapy: 12 months was not more effective than 3 months on clinical, laboratory (p=0.405, p=0.631) or histological (p=0.456) measures, and 36 of 37 surviving patients — including 14 with cerebrospinal infection — were in remission without recurrence after a median 80 months, with one arthritis recurrence at 63 months. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): either induction cures; the shorter oral course rests on a sequential, non-randomised comparison — Tier C for the single small trial at the shelf's core.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — ceftriaxone and meropenem induction cured all 40 randomised Whipple's patients; a non-randomised extension found 3 months of trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole as effective as 12

title: Micafungin versus caspofungin for candidaemia and invasive candidiasis: success 76.4% (micafungin 100 mg), 71.4% (150 mg) and 72.3% (caspofungin) — non-inferior, with no mortality or safety separation
question: In adults with candidaemia or other invasive candidiasis, is micafungin — at 100 mg or 150 mg daily — as effective and safe as standard-dose caspofungin in a head-to-head randomised trial?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — a properly blinded head-to-head that found the class behaving like a class. The international double-blind trial (Pappas PG et al., PMID: 17806055) randomised 595 adults with candidaemia and other invasive candidiasis to micafungin 100 mg daily, micafungin 150 mg daily, or caspofungin (70 mg loading, then 50 mg daily); in the modified intention-to-treat population (191, 199 and 188 patients), about 85% had candidaemia. At the end of blinded intravenous therapy, treatment success (clinical plus mycological) was 76.4% with micafungin 100 mg, 71.4% with micafungin 150 mg and 72.3% with caspofungin; median time to culture negativity was 2 days in the micafungin 100 mg and caspofungin groups and 3 days in the micafungin 150 mg group. There were no significant differences in mortality, relapsing or emergent infections, or adverse events between the arms, and both micafungin doses were non-inferior to caspofungin. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): the higher micafungin dose bought nothing measurable — the shelf's practical content is dose discipline (100 mg suffices) and free choice between the two drugs on other grounds.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — micafungin 100 mg and 150 mg were non-inferior to caspofungin for candidaemia/invasive candidiasis (success 76.4%/71.4% vs 72.3%), with no mortality or safety differences

title: Alexander technique lessons: 24 lessons cut disability by 3.4 points and pain days from 21 to 3 a month in back pain — and lessons matched acupuncture for chronic neck pain a year on
question: In adults with chronic or recurrent back pain, or chronic neck pain, do one-to-one Alexander technique lessons reduce pain and disability compared with usual care, massage or exercise advice?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two large UK primary-care trials, one for back pain and one for neck pain, both show durable benefit a year after lessons end. In ATEAM (Little P et al., PMID: 18713809), 579 patients with chronic or recurrent back pain randomised to 24 Alexander lessons had a Roland Morris disability score 3.4 points better than normal care at one year (95% CI -4.76 to -2.03), six lessons gave -1.40 points, and six lessons plus exercise prescription achieved 72% of the effect of 24 lessons alone; median days in pain in the previous four weeks fell from 21 on control to 3 after 24 lessons (reported as -18 days). Massage, by contrast, was not significantly better than control at one year (-0.58, 95% CI -1.94 to 0.77). In ATLAS (MacPherson H et al., PMID: 26524571), 517 people with chronic neck pain had Northwick Park Questionnaire scores 3.79 percentage points lower with Alexander lessons than usual care at 12 months (95% CI 0.91 to 6.66; p=0.010), a 31% relative reduction from baseline, essentially matching acupuncture (3.92 points). No significant harms were reported in ATEAM, and no serious adverse events were judged related in ATLAS. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): Alexander lessons from registered teachers produce modest, durable improvements in chronic back and neck pain — the catch is access, cost and the number of lessons needed.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — 24 lessons improved back disability by 3.4 Roland Morris points at 1 year in ATEAM, and lessons matched acupuncture for neck pain in ATLAS, with no significant harms in either trial

title: Pilates for low back pain: about 14 points better than doing almost nothing on a 100-point pain scale — but no better than other exercise
question: In adults with non-specific low back pain, does Pilates reduce pain and disability compared with minimal intervention — and is it better than other forms of exercise?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — against minimal intervention only. The Cochrane review (Yamato TP et al., PMID: 26133923) pooled 10 trials with 510 participants: Pilates reduced pain versus minimal intervention by a mean 14.05 points on a 0-100 scale at short-term follow-up (95% CI -18.91 to -9.19; low-quality evidence) and by 10.54 points at intermediate term (moderate-quality evidence), with disability improved by 7.95 points short term and 11.17 points at intermediate term. Against other exercise, however, there was no significant difference in disability either short term (mean difference -3.29, 95% CI -6.82 to 0.24) or intermediate term (-0.91, 95% CI -5.02 to 3.20). A single-assessor-blinded trial of 60 patients (Natour J et al., PMID: 24965957) found Pilates plus NSAIDs beat NSAIDs alone on pain, function and quality of life (all p<0.001 for pain and function) with fewer NSAIDs taken at 45, 90 and 180 days (p<0.010). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): Pilates is a reasonable exercise choice for back pain — the evidence supports exercise, not Pilates specifically.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — Pilates beats minimal intervention by ~14 pain points (0-100) short term in the Cochrane pool, but shows no advantage over other exercise

title: The McKenzie method for recent back pain: a slight short-term pain dip the Cochrane reviewers judged not clinically important — and no better than motor-control exercise in chronic pain
question: In adults with non-specific low back pain, does the McKenzie method (directional-preference exercises) reduce pain and disability compared with minimal intervention, manual therapy or other exercise?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the best synthesis is unusually blunt. The 2023 Cochrane review of the McKenzie method for (sub)acute non-specific low back pain (Almeida MO et al., PMID: 37017272; 5 trials, 563 participants) found a slight short-term pain reduction versus minimal intervention (mean difference -7.3 on a 0-100 scale, 95% CI -12.0 to -2.56) that was gone by intermediate term (-5.0, 95% CI -14.3 to 4.3), no disability reduction at either point, and no advantage over manual therapy — with a slight pain increase versus manual therapy at intermediate term (+7.0, 95% CI 0.7 to 13.3). The reviewers concluded the effects were not clinically important and that the method is not an effective treatment for (sub)acute back pain. In chronic back pain with a directional preference, a 70-patient trial (Halliday MH et al., PMID: 27170524) found no significant between-group differences in pain (p=.99) or function (p=.26) between McKenzie and motor-control exercise over 8 weeks. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): McKenzie assessment may help clinicians sort patients, but as a treatment it has not beaten booklets, manual therapy or rival exercise by any margin that matters.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — Cochrane: short-term pain -7.3/100, judged not clinically important, no disability gain; chronic-pain trial ties motor-control exercise

title: Massage for low back pain: better than doing nothing for a few weeks (pooled pain SMD -0.75) — the Cochrane reviewers still say they have 'very little confidence' it works
question: In adults with non-specific low back pain, does massage therapy reduce pain and improve function compared with inactive or active controls, and for how long?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — short-term only, on low-confidence evidence. The Cochrane review (Furlan AD et al., PMID: 26329399) pooled 25 trials with 3,096 participants: for sub-acute and chronic back pain, massage beat inactive controls for pain in the short term (SMD -0.75, 95% CI -0.90 to -0.60; 761 participants) and function (SMD -0.72, 95% CI -1.05 to -0.39), but not in the long term; against active controls the pain advantage was smaller (SMD -0.37 short term; -0.40 long term) with no functional difference. The reviewers rated the evidence low to very low quality and concluded they have very little confidence massage is effective. The best-known single trial (Cherkin DC et al., PMID: 11322842; 262 patients) found massage superior to self-care education at 10 weeks on symptoms (3.41 versus 4.71 on a 0-10 scale; p=.01) and disability (5.88 versus 8.92; p<.001), but by 1 year massage was no longer better than self-care. Increased pain was the commonest adverse event, reported in 1.5% to 25% of participants across trials; no serious adverse events were reported. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): expect weeks of relief, not a cure — and the ATEAM trial on shelf #4201 likewise found massage's back-pain benefit gone by one year.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — short-term pain and function gains versus inactive controls in the Cochrane pool (SMD -0.75 and -0.72), not sustained long term and rated low to very low quality

title: Dry needling for trigger-point pain: neck pain down 2.31 points more than sham in the short term — and no measurable effect left by mid-term in either review
question: In adults with musculoskeletal pain from myofascial trigger points, does dry needling reduce pain and disability compared with sham needling, no treatment or other physical therapy?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a short-term effect that fades. The broad review (Gattie E et al., PMID: 28158962; 13 randomised trials) found very low- to moderate-quality evidence that dry needling by physical therapists reduced pain more than control, sham or other treatments in the immediate-to-12-week window and raised pressure pain threshold, but at 6-12 months the pain advantage was no longer statistically significant, and functional outcomes beat only no-treatment/sham, not other therapies. The neck-specific update (Navarro-Santana MJ et al., PMID: 33066556; 28 trials) found pain lower than sham/placebo/waiting-list by 1.53 points immediately (95% CI -2.29 to -0.76) and 2.31 points at short term (95% CI -3.64 to -0.99), disability better (SMD -0.87, 95% CI -1.60 to -0.14), but no difference versus other physical therapy interventions and no between-treatment effect on any outcome at mid-term; cervical range of motion did not improve. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): dry needling buys short-term trigger-point pain relief comparable to other hands-on therapy — it has not shown a durable or unique effect.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — short-term pain relief versus sham in two meta-analyses (neck pain MD -2.31 at short term), with no mid-term effect and no advantage over other physical therapy

title: TENS machines: pain is lower while the current is on (SMD -0.96 versus placebo across 91 trials) — the older back-pain-only review found just two trials and they disagreed
question: In adults with acute or chronic pain, does transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS) reduce pain compared with placebo or standard care — and does the effect persist after the device is switched off?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — strictly during or immediately after use. The meta-TENS collaboration (Johnson MI et al., PMID: 35144946) pooled 381 randomised trials with 24,532 participants: pain intensity was lower during or immediately after TENS than placebo (91 trials, 4,841 participants; SMD -0.96, 95% CI -1.14 to -0.78; moderate-certainty evidence) and lower than standard-care pharmacological and non-pharmacological treatments (61 trials, 3,155 participants; SMD -0.72, 95% CI -0.95 to -0.50; low-certainty evidence), with adverse events generally mild and no different from comparators. The narrower older Cochrane review for chronic low back pain (Khadilkar A et al., PMID: 16034883) found only two eligible trials (175 patients) which disagreed — one positive, one null across multiple outcomes — and judged the evidence inconsistent for TENS as a single treatment for back pain. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a TENS unit is a reasonable, low-harm way to take the edge off pain while it runs; neither review establishes relief that outlasts the session, and back-pain-specific evidence is the weakest part of the record.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — pain lower during/immediately after TENS versus placebo (SMD -0.96, moderate certainty, 381-trial pool); durability unproven and back-pain-only evidence inconsistent

title: Back belts and lumbar supports: moderate evidence they do not prevent back pain — yet one trial in workers with previous pain found 52.7 fewer pain days a year, with no fewer sick days
question: Do lumbar supports (back belts/braces) prevent low back pain, prevent its recurrence, or treat existing non-specific low back pain?
balance: SPLIT — prevention in general: no; recurrence in workers who already have back pain: maybe; treatment: unknown. The Cochrane review (van Duijvenbode IC et al., PMID: 18425875) included seven prevention studies (14,437 people) and eight treatment studies (1,361 people): there was moderate evidence that lumbar supports are not more effective than no intervention or training in preventing low back pain, conflicting evidence on supports as supplements to other prevention, and it remained unclear whether supports beat no treatment or other interventions for treating back pain; only five of fifteen studies met half or more of the internal validity items. Against that background, one well-sized trial (Roelofs PD et al., PMID: 18025444) randomised 360 home care workers with a history of back pain: those given patient-directed lumbar supports reported on average 52.7 fewer days with low back pain over 12 months (95% CI -59.6 to -45.1) than a healthy-working-methods course alone, with small significant advantages in pain intensity and function — but total sick days did not fall (-5 days, 95% CI -21.1 to 6.8). PROPOSED SPLIT: do not buy a belt to prevent a first back problem or to treat one; a support may reduce the number of painful days for people whose work provokes recurrences, without reducing time off work.
stamp: SPLIT — moderate evidence of no preventive effect in general (Cochrane, 14,437 people), but 52.7 fewer pain days over a year in one 360-worker secondary-prevention trial, with sick leave unchanged; treatment effect remains unclear

title: Low-level laser therapy for neck pain: pain down about 20 mm on a 100 mm scale in the pooled trials, with relief persisting up to 22 weeks in chronic pain
question: In adults with acute or chronic neck pain, does low-level laser therapy (photobiomodulation) reduce pain compared with placebo or active treatment?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — an older but large pooled signal, with mild side effects. The Lancet systematic review (Chow RT et al., PMID: 19913903) pooled 16 randomised trials with 820 patients: in acute neck pain, two trials gave a relative risk of 1.69 for pain improvement with laser versus placebo (95% CI 1.22 to 2.33); in chronic neck pain, five trials reporting categorical data gave a relative risk of 4.05 (95% CI 2.74 to 5.98), and 11 trials reporting visual analogue scores showed pain intensity reduced by 19.86 mm on a 100 mm scale (95% CI 10.04 to 29.68), with relief persisting 1-22 weeks after treatment ended (reduction 22.07 mm, 95% CI 17.42 to 26.72). Side effects were mild and not different from placebo. A double-blind placebo-controlled trial in a narrower group — 60 patients with acute neck pain with radiculopathy (Konstantinovic LM et al., PMID: 20704667) — found significantly better arm pain (p=0.003, effect size d=0.92) and neck extension (p=0.003, d=0.94) after 15 treatments over 3 weeks. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): laser therapy probably eases neck pain by a clinically noticeable margin — but the trials span many wavelengths and doses, and the evidence base is from 2009 and earlier.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — pooled pain reduction of 19.86 mm/100 in chronic neck pain and RR 4.05 for categorical improvement (16 trials, 820 patients); mild side effects, ageing evidence base

title: Shock wave therapy for tennis elbow: 'Platinum' level evidence of little or no benefit across nine placebo trials — one positive trial in tennis players is the exception, and steroid injection beat it head-to-head
question: In adults with lateral elbow pain (tennis elbow), does extracorporeal shock wave therapy reduce pain and improve function compared with placebo or steroid injection?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the pooled verdict is one of the firmest nulls in this territory. The Cochrane review (Buchbinder R et al., PMID: 16235324) included nine placebo-controlled trials with 1,006 participants: 11 of 13 pooled analyses found no significant benefit of shock wave therapy over placebo — for example, improvement in pain at 4-6 weeks differed by -9.42 points on a 100-point scale (95% CI -20.70 to 1.86) and pain on resisted wrist extension at 12 weeks by -9.04 (95% CI -19.37 to 1.28). The reviewers graded this 'Platinum' level evidence of little or no benefit. Two pooled results favoured treatment (success relative risk 2.2, 95% CI 1.55 to 3.12), but four other trials that could not be pooled did not support them. The best-known positive trial (Rompe JD et al., PMID: 15090392) enrolled only tennis players with MRI-confirmed elbow pain of at least 12 months: 65% achieved at least 50% pain reduction versus 28% on sham (p=.001). In the one head-to-head trial, steroid injection beat shock wave therapy at 3 months (84% versus 60% achieving 50% pain reduction; p<0.05) — though shelf #684 records that steroid's own advantage reverses by one year. Adverse effects were minimal: transient pain, skin reddening and nausea. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): outside a narrow recalcitrant tennis-player subgroup, shock wave therapy for tennis elbow is an expensive placebo-grade intervention on current evidence.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — 11 of 13 pooled analyses null across 1,006 participants ('Platinum' evidence, Cochrane); one positive sham-controlled trial confined to tennis players with year-long symptoms

title: Morton's neuroma injections: adding steroid to the anaesthetic made no difference in the placebo-controlled trial — ultrasound guidance is where the Cochrane pool finds a gain (pain -15.01 mm at 6 months)
question: In adults with Morton's neuroma, does a corticosteroid-plus-anaesthetic injection relieve pain better than anaesthetic alone — and does ultrasound guidance improve the result?
balance: SPLIT — the steroid itself: no proven gain; the guidance: probably a gain. The 2024 Cochrane review (Matthews BG et al., PMID: 38334217; six trials, 373 participants) found low-certainty evidence that corticosteroid plus local anaesthetic results in little to no difference in pain at 3-6 months versus anaesthetic alone (mean difference -6.31 mm on a 100 mm scale, 95% CI -14.23 to 1.61; two trials, 157 participants) and little to no difference in function (SMD -0.30, 95% CI -0.61 to 0.02), while ultrasound-guided injection probably reduces pain versus unguided injection at 6 months (mean difference -15.01 mm, 95% CI -27.88 to -2.14; moderate-certainty) and probably increases function (SMD -0.47, 95% CI -0.84 to -0.10). The double-blind placebo-controlled trial (Lizano-Díez X et al., PMID: 28617064; 41 patients, three injections) found no significant between-group differences in pain or function at 3 and 6 months, and 48.5% of all patients went on to request surgical excision — 44% of the steroid group and 53% of controls (p=1.0). The guidance trial (Mahadevan D et al., PMID: 27037432; 45 feet) itself found pain improved in both groups (from 64 to 29 mm guided; 69 to 37 mm unguided) with no statistical difference between them, and 12-month failure rates of 48% and 55% (p=0.458). Steroid adverse events in the review included skin atrophy (3.9%), hypopigmentation (3.9%) and plantar fat pad atrophy (2.6%). PROPOSED SPLIT: inject if you like — the anaesthetic may be doing the work; if you inject, guidance probably helps; about half of patients still end up wanting surgery within a year.
stamp: SPLIT — steroid adds little to anaesthetic alone (pain MD -6.31 mm, CI crosses zero; ~half proceed to surgery), while ultrasound guidance probably improves pain (MD -15.01 mm at 6 months, Cochrane pool) despite a null guidance trial

title: Foot orthoses for plantar heel pain: a small medium-term edge over sham insoles (SMD -0.27) — custom-made no better than prefabricated, and the head-to-head with steroid injection never reached a difference patients would notice
question: In adults with plantar heel pain (plantar fasciitis), do foot orthoses reduce pain and improve function compared with sham orthoses, and how do they compare with corticosteroid injection?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — small, delayed and possibly below what patients can feel. The systematic review (Whittaker GA et al., PMID: 28935689) pooled 19 trials with 1,660 participants: in the medium term (7-12 weeks) there was moderate-quality evidence that foot orthoses reduced pain more than sham orthoses (standardised mean difference -0.27, 95% CI -0.48 to -0.06), but no improvement in function; in the short term (0-6 weeks) and longer term (13-52 weeks) the evidence was very low quality and showed no pain or function benefit; customised and prefabricated orthoses did not differ at any time point. The head-to-head SOOTHE trial (Whittaker GA et al., PMID: 31130060; 103 participants) found corticosteroid injection ahead on foot pain at week 4 (adjusted mean difference 8.2 points, 95% CI 0.6 to 15.8) and orthoses ahead at week 12 (8.5 points, 95% CI 0.2 to 16.8) — but neither difference met the pre-calculated minimal important difference of 12.5 points. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a prefabricated arch-supporting insole is a reasonable, low-harm buy for heel pain at around two to three months — paying for custom moulding buys nothing the trials can detect.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — medium-term pain SMD -0.27 versus sham (moderate-quality, 19 trials); no function gain, no custom-versus-prefabricated difference, and sub-threshold differences versus steroid injection

title: A night splint for thumb-base arthritis: nothing at 1 month — then pain 14.3 mm better and disability improved at 12 months, in the one randomised trial
question: In adults with osteoarthritis at the base of the thumb, does wearing a custom-made splint reduce pain and disability compared with usual care?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a slow-burn result from a single trial, so this shelf is Tier C. Rannou F et al. (PMID: 19451573) randomised 112 patients (101 women) with base-of-thumb osteoarthritis in two French tertiary hospitals to a custom-made neoprene splint worn at night or usual care. At 1 month there was no difference in pain change (adjusted mean change -10.1 versus -10.7; between-group difference 0.6, 95% CI -7.9 to 9.1; p=0.89). At 12 months the splint group had improved more on pain (adjusted mean change -22.2 versus -7.9; between-group difference -14.3, 95% CI -23.4 to -5.2; p=0.002), on the Cochin Hand Function Scale (between-group difference -6.3, 95% CI -10.9 to -1.7; p=0.008) and on patient-perceived disability (-13.1, 95% CI -21.8 to -4.4; p=0.003). Adherence was high — 86% of the splint group wore it more than five nights a week at 12 months — and no adverse effects were observed. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a night splint is cheap and harmless, but patients should be told the trial found nothing at one month — the benefit, if real, took a year of nightly wear.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single trial: pain difference -14.3 mm at 12 months (p=0.002) after a null result at 1 month; no adverse effects; Tier C single-trial shelf

title: Avocado-soybean unsaponifiables for knee and hip arthritis: pain down 20.8 mm versus 10.4 mm on placebo at 6 months in one trial — but the 3-year structure trial found no difference in joint-space loss
question: In adults with symptomatic osteoarthritis of the knee or hip, do avocado/soybean unsaponifiables (ASU) reduce pain, disability and NSAID use compared with placebo — and do they slow joint-space narrowing?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for symptoms over months, from two 1990s French trials of one preparation family; the structure claim failed its main test. In Maheu E et al. (PMID: 9433873; 164 patients, 6 months), pain fell from 56.1 mm to 35.3 mm on ASU versus 56.1 to 45.7 mm on placebo (p=0.003), the Lequesne functional index improved significantly more (to 6.8 versus 8.9; p<0.001), success rate was 39% versus 18%, and fewer ASU patients required NSAIDs (48% versus 63%; p=0.054). In Blotman F et al. (PMID: 9476272; 163 evaluable patients, 3 months), 43.4% of the ASU group resumed NSAID therapy after a protocol stop versus 69.7% on placebo (p<0.001), with a better functional index (-2.3 versus -1.0; p<0.01) but similar pain scores. The 3-year ERADIAS trial (Maheu E et al., PMID: 23345601; 399 patients with hip osteoarthritis, testing the named product Piascledine — avocado-soybean unsaponifiable-Expanscience, ASU-E) found no significant difference in mean joint-space-width loss (-0.638 mm versus -0.672 mm; p=0.72) and no difference in clinical outcomes, though progressors (loss of at least 0.5 mm) were fewer on ASU-E (40% versus 50%; p=0.040); safety was excellent. The two symptom trials' records do not name the tested product or its maker; ERADIAS names Piascledine (Expanscience) — current ASU products may differ in composition, safety and effectiveness. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a modest symptomatic effect over 2-6 months is supported; a joint-saving effect is not.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two double-blind trials show less pain and less NSAID resumption than placebo over 3-6 months; the 3-year Piascledine structure trial was null on joint-space loss and on symptoms

title: Muscle rubs (salicylate rubefacients): the older small trials said they work (acute NNT 3.2) — the larger, more recent trials showed no effect, and Cochrane will not support their use
question: In adults with acute or chronic musculoskeletal pain, do salicylate-containing rubefacient creams and gels (muscle rubs) relieve pain compared with placebo?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — a fading signal that lives in the oldest trials. The Cochrane review (Derry S et al., PMID: 25425092) found, for clinical success at seven days in acute conditions (mostly sprains, strains and acute low back pain), a relative risk of 1.9 (95% CI 1.5 to 2.5) and a number needed to treat of 3.2 (95% CI 2.4 to 4.9) for salicylate rubefacients versus placebo — but rated this very low quality evidence and not robust; in chronic conditions (mostly osteoarthritis, bursitis and chronic back pain) the relative risk was 1.6 (95% CI 1.2 to 2.0) with an NNT of 6.2 (95% CI 4.0 to 13), also very low quality. The reviewers state plainly that in both categories any evidence of efficacy came from the older, smaller studies, while the larger, more recent studies showed no effect, and conclude the evidence does not support the use of topical salicylate rubefacients for acute injuries or chronic conditions. The overview of all topical analgesics (Derry S et al., PMID: 28497473; 13 Cochrane reviews, 206 studies, around 30,700 participants) likewise graded salicylate rubefacient evidence low or very low quality — in sharp contrast to topical diclofenac gel in acute pain (78% achieving at least 50% relief versus 20% on placebo; NNT 1.8, 95% CI 1.5 to 2.1), which sits on shelf #577's territory. Adverse events were more common with salicylate than placebo but concentrated in a few studies, and local events were nearly all in one study combining salicylate with another irritant. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): the rub probably does something for a few days in acute aches — the warmth and the rubbing are unmeasured co-treatments — but anyone choosing a rub over a proven topical NSAID gel is choosing the weaker record.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — acute clinical-success RR 1.9 (NNT 3.2) and chronic RR 1.6 on very low quality evidence, with larger recent trials showing no effect and Cochrane concluding use is not supported

title: Chlorhexidine mouthwash: plaque down by about a quarter and gingivitis measurably lower within weeks — a real effect on gum scores, paid for in tooth staining and altered taste
question: In people with gingivitis, does chlorhexidine mouthrinse used alongside brushing reduce plaque and gum inflammation compared with brushing alone or a placebo rinse — and at what cost in side effects?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for plaque and mild gingivitis scores, with staining as the certain price. The Cochrane review (James P et al., PMID: 28362061) included 51 studies analysing 5,345 participants: after 4-6 weeks, chlorhexidine mouthrinse reduced gingivitis by 0.21 on the 0-3 Gingival Index (95% CI 0.11 to 0.31; 10 trials, 805 participants with mild gingival inflammation; high-quality evidence) — an effect the reviewers note was not considered clinically relevant at that mild level — and reduced plaque by a large standardised amount (SMD 1.45 lower, 95% CI 1.00 to 1.90; 12 trials, 950 participants), with similar effects at 6 months. Extrinsic tooth staining increased by a large standardised amount at 4-6 weeks (SMD 1.07 higher, 95% CI 0.80 to 1.34; moderate-quality evidence), and taste disturbance, mucosal soreness/irritation and burning were commonly reported. A general-practice trial (Eaton KA et al., PMID: 9083904; 121 subjects, 98 completing) found 0.12% chlorhexidine reduced plaque accumulation by 28% and gingival inflammation by 25% over 12 weeks versus placebo rinse (plaque score 1.33 to 0.96 versus 1.31 to 1.13; p<0.001; gingival bleeding 0.56 to 0.42 versus unchanged 0.54-0.55). There were insufficient data for moderate or severe gingivitis. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): chlorhexidine rinse does what the bottle claims on plaque and mild gum inflammation for as long as it is used — it is an adjunct to brushing, not a substitute, and it stains teeth.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — gingivitis down 0.21 (0-3 scale) and plaque SMD 1.45 lower at 4-6 weeks (Cochrane, 51 studies), with a large increase in tooth staining (SMD 1.07)

title: Pepto-Bismol before the trip: bismuth subsalicylate cut travellers' diarrhoea from 40% to 14% at the high dose — 65% protection in students in Mexico, confirmed in a volunteer challenge study
question: In travellers to high-risk regions, does taking bismuth subsalicylate prophylactically prevent travellers' diarrhoea compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — old but genuinely randomised evidence for prevention (treatment of established diarrhoea is a different question, housed with the acute-diarrhoea shelves). In DuPont HL et al. (PMID: 3820443), 182 US students in Mexico were randomised within 48 hours of arrival to two tablets (high dose, 2.1 g/day), one tablet (low dose) or placebo, each four times daily for three weeks: among completers, diarrhoea occurred in 14% (7/51) on high dose, 24% (15/63) on low dose and 40% (23/58) on placebo — protection rates of 65% relative and 40% relative respectively; diarrhoea caused by enterotoxigenic E. coli occurred in one high-dose student, no low-dose students and seven on placebo. In a volunteer challenge study (Graham DY et al., PMID: 6352386), 32 healthy volunteers were dosed with bismuth subsalicylate or placebo around an oral challenge with enterotoxigenic E. coli strain H10407: diarrhoea occurred in 13% (2/15) on bismuth versus 56% (9/16) on placebo (p<0.03), and the organism was recovered less often from the bismuth group. Bismuth was well tolerated in DuPont; the commonest effects were blackening of tongue and stools, with tinnitus reported at a low frequency of 1.2 days per 100 days of treatment. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): four-times-daily tablets buy roughly two-thirds protection for trips of up to three weeks — a real effect that has to be weighed against the dosing burden and the salicylate load.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — travellers' diarrhoea 14% versus 40% on placebo at 2.1 g/day (65% relative protection) in a 182-student trial, confirmed in a 32-volunteer E. coli challenge study (13% versus 56%)

title: Flurbiprofen throat lozenges: sore-throat relief significantly better than a plain demulcent lozenge from about 30 minutes, lasting 2-4 hours — in two industry-era double-blind trials totalling over 600 patients
question: In adults with sore throat from an upper respiratory infection, does a flurbiprofen 8.75 mg lozenge relieve throat pain better than a placebo (demulcent) lozenge, and how quickly and how long does it work?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — real but modest symptomatic relief, measured in hours. In Watson N et al. (PMID: 11198725), 301 patients with subjective and objective signs of sore throat were randomised to flurbiprofen 8.75 mg lozenges (129), flurbiprofen 12.5 mg (43) or a demulcent placebo lozenge (129): the 8.75 mg lozenge was superior to placebo on a number of efficacy parameters, notably throat soreness, which was significantly reduced after 15 minutes (p<0.05) with effects sustained for at least 2 hours (p<0.05), and multiple dosing continued to provide effective relief over the 4-day treatment period; both treatments were well tolerated. In Benrimoj SI et al. (PMID: 27517548), 320 patients with sore throat from an upper respiratory tract infection were randomised to flurbiprofen 8.75 mg (128), 12.5 mg (64) or placebo lozenges (128): the 8.75 mg lozenge was significantly superior to placebo for total pain relief summed over 15-120 minutes and for throat soreness over 2 hours and swollen throat over 2 and 6 hours (all p<0.05); relief began within 15 minutes (attributed by the authors partly to the lozenge's demulcent effect), statistically significant differences from placebo were detected within 30 minutes and sustained over 4 hours, and there were no significant differences in adverse events once taste perversion reports were removed (p=0.776). The higher 12.5 mg dose was not significantly better than 8.75 mg in either trial. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a flurbiprofen lozenge is a reasonable purchase for a bad sore throat — expect a measurable edge over a plain lozenge for a few hours per lozenge, not a shorter illness.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two double-blind trials (301 and 320 patients) show significantly better pain relief than demulcent placebo from ~30 minutes, sustained 2-4 hours per dose; no benefit from the higher dose

title: Artificial tears for dry eye: symptoms improve in trials, but after 43 randomised comparisons Cochrane could not say any ordinary tear beats another — one polyacrylic-acid gel beat polyvinyl alcohol in two small trials
question: In adults with dry eye syndrome, do over-the-counter artificial tear drops relieve symptoms — and is any formulation demonstrably better than the others or than placebo?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — improvement is consistently reported, superiority is not. The Cochrane review (Pucker AD et al., PMID: 26905373) included 43 randomised trials with 3,497 participants with dry eye, almost all comparing one over-the-counter tear against another rather than against placebo: it found general uncertainty whether different tears provide similar relief of signs and symptoms compared with each other or placebo, with the single consistent result that 0.2% polyacrylic acid-based tears were more effective for dry eye symptoms than 1.4% polyvinyl alcohol-based tears in two trials (175 participants); all other comparisons produced contradictory results or no between-group differences. Evidence quality was low, and 18 further registered trials enrolling 2,079 participants had no published results — a high risk of publication bias. A modern head-to-head trial (Downie LE et al., PMID: 31734510; 242 subjects over 90 days) compared a nano-emulsion tear containing carboxymethylcellulose, glycerin, flaxseed and castor oils and osmoprotectants (named in the record as OM3) with a similar tear without trehalose and flaxseed oil (named in the record as Refresh Optive Advanced): both groups improved significantly on the Ocular Surface Disease Index, staining and tear breakup time, with small between-group differences favouring the nano-emulsion on combined staining at all timepoints and corneal staining at day 90 (p<0.05); treatment-related adverse events were 6.7% versus 9.8%. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): tears are safe and symptoms do improve while using them — but the trial record gives no reason to pay a premium for one ordinary formulation over another. Prescription drops and omega-3 for dry eye are housed at live shelf #611.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — 43 trials (3,497 participants) show symptom improvement but low-quality, mostly head-to-head evidence with no formulation clearly superior, except polyacrylic acid over polyvinyl alcohol in two small trials

title: Ipratropium nasal spray for a cold: nasal discharge down 26% versus a salt-water spray and runny-nose severity down 31% — congestion untouched, nosebleeds and dryness up
question: In children and adults with the common cold, does intranasal ipratropium bromide spray reduce runny nose (rhinorrhoea) and nasal congestion compared with placebo spray or no treatment?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for the dripping nose only; it does nothing for the blocked nose. The Cochrane review (AlBalawi ZH et al., PMID: 23784858) included seven trials with 2,144 participants: the four studies reporting subjective rhinorrhoea severity (1,959 participants) were consistent in finding statistically significant changes favouring ipratropium, two studies found better global improvement, but nasal congestion showed no significant change in any of the four studies reporting it; side effects were more frequent with ipratropium (odds ratio 2.09, 95% CI 1.40 to 3.11), mainly nasal dryness, blood-tinged mucus and nosebleeds, and overall risk of bias was moderate. The largest single trial (Hayden FG et al., PMID: 8678385; 411 healthy people aged 14-56 with colds of under 36 hours and at least moderate rhinorrhoea) measured the discharge itself: ipratropium 0.06% spray recipients had 26% less nasal discharge than the buffered-salt control spray (p=0.0024) and 34% less than untreated patients (p=0.0001), subjective rhinorrhoea severity was reduced by 31% relative versus control and 78% relative versus no treatment (p=0.0001 for both), and sneezing was reduced on days 2 and 4 (20% and 30% differences) — again with no reduction in nasal congestion. Blood-tinged mucus occurred in 16.8% on ipratropium versus 3.6% on control (p=0.01) and nasal dryness in 11.7% versus 3.6% (p=0.021). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the one cold spray with a specific, measured anti-drip effect — useless for congestion, and it dries the nose it dries out.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — rhinorrhoea significantly improved in all four reporting trials (2,144 participants, Cochrane) and discharge objectively 26% lower than control spray; no effect on congestion; side effects OR 2.09

title: Salt-water nasal rinsing for colds: Cochrane says 'possibly' — the trials are small and biased, and the one big children's trial's symptom gains (about 0.3 points on a 4-point scale) may be too small to notice
question: In adults and children with acute upper respiratory infections (colds, rhinosinusitis), does saline nasal irrigation relieve symptoms compared with routine care or other sprays?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — cheap, safe, and supported by evidence its own reviewers call weak. The Cochrane review (King D et al., PMID: 25892369) found five randomised trials (544 children and 205 adults) comparing saline irrigation with routine care or other nose sprays — none against a placebo rinse: most results showed no difference between saline and control, and the trials were generally small and of low quality with unclear risk of bias. The one larger children's trial showed a significant reduction in nasal secretion score (mean difference -0.31, 95% CI -0.48 to -0.14) and nasal obstruction score (-0.33, 95% CI -0.47 to -0.19) — but the reviewers note a 0.33 difference on a four-point scale may have minimal clinical significance; that trial also found significantly less decongestant use in the saline group, and minor nasal discomfort or irritation was the only side effect reported, by a minority. That larger trial is Slapak I et al. (PMID: 18209140): 401 children aged 6-10 with uncomplicated cold or flu, randomised openly to standard medication alone or plus an isotonic seawater nasal wash (the tested product is named in the record as Physiomer), followed 12 weeks: at the second visit the saline group had better nasal secretion (mean 1.79 versus 2.10) and obstruction (1.25 versus 1.58) scores (p<0.05 for both), and by eight weeks fewer saline children were using antipyretics (9% versus 33%), decongestants (5% versus 47%), mucolytics (10% versus 37%) and systemic antiinfectives (6% versus 21%), with fewer reported illness days (31% versus 75%), school absences (17% versus 35%) and complications (8% versus 32%) (all p<0.05). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): rinsing may take a small edge off a cold and clearly substitutes for other medicines in one open trial — but that trial's very large prevention effects come from an unblinded design, and the blinded evidence base does not confirm them. Chronic rhinosinusitis irrigation is a different question, housed at live shelf #637.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — Cochrane (5 trials, 749 participants): most outcomes null, one larger trial showing ~0.3-point symptom gains of doubtful clinical significance; the big prevention effects rest on a single open-label trial

title: Isotretinoin for acne: lesion counts fall by a clinically relevant amount in every trial — against antibiotics plus topicals the Cochrane pool found no lesion-count advantage (RR 1.01), with 67% more minor adverse effects
question: In people with acne vulgaris, does oral isotretinoin improve acne compared with placebo or oral antibiotics plus topical treatment — and what adverse effects accompany it?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — effective, on evidence weaker than its reputation, with frequent minor harms and unresolved serious-harm questions in the trial record. The Cochrane review (Costa CS et al., PMID: 30484286) included 31 randomised trials with 3,836 participants aged 12-55 with mild to severe acne: against oral antibiotics plus topical agents in moderate-to-severe acne, isotretinoin made no difference to investigator-assessed inflammatory lesion count (RR 1.01, 95% CI 0.96 to 1.06; three studies, 400 participants; very low-quality evidence), may slightly improve physician global assessment (RR 1.15, 95% CI 1.00 to 1.32; 351 participants), and caused more less-serious adverse effects (RR 1.67, 95% CI 1.42 to 1.98) such as dry lips and skin, cheilitis, vomiting and nausea; one serious adverse event (Stevens-Johnson syndrome) occurred in an isotretinoin group. Within isotretinoin dose comparisons, one trial reported 58%, 80% and 90% of participants achieving a 95% decrease in total inflammatory lesion count at 0.1, 0.5 and 1 mg/kg/day respectively. A second review (Vallerand IA et al., PMID: 28542914; 11 trials, 760 patients) found isotretinoin reduced lesion counts by a clinically relevant amount in all trials, always by more than control (placebo in two studies, oral antibiotics in seven), with statistically significant differences in two of three low-bias trials; adverse events were twice as frequent as control (751 versus 388 events), more than half dermatological dryness-related, and 12 participants withdrew for adverse events including Stevens-Johnson syndrome, cheilitis, acne flare, photophobia, raised liver enzymes and depressed mood. No included trial reported birth defects — trials exclude pregnancy, so the teratogenicity that dominates real-world isotretinoin governance is outside this trial record and is not quantified here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): isotretinoin works, including where the comparison is honest; what the trials cannot tell you is how much better than good antibiotic-plus-topical care it is, and its serious-harm management rests on regulation, not on these trials.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — lesion counts fall more than control in all 11 trials of one review, but Cochrane found no lesion-count advantage over antibiotics plus topicals (RR 1.01, very low quality) and 67% more minor adverse effects

title: Triple-combination cream for melasma: complete clearing in 26.1% versus 4.6% for any two-ingredient version at 8 weeks — and 'none or mild' severity in 64.2% versus 39.4% against hydroquinone alone, at triple the irritation rate
question: In adults with moderate-to-severe facial melasma, does the fixed triple-combination cream (fluocinolone acetonide 0.01%, hydroquinone 4%, tretinoin 0.05%) clear pigmentation better than hydroquinone alone or dual-combination creams?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — clearly the strongest topical in its trials, over eight weeks, with irritation in about half of users. In two combined 8-week multicentre investigator-blind studies (Taylor SC et al., PMID: 12889718; 641 adults, predominantly female, with moderate-to-severe melasma and Fitzpatrick skin types I-IV), complete clearing at week 8 occurred in 26.1% on the triple combination versus 4.6% across the dual-combination groups (tretinoin+hydroquinone, tretinoin+fluocinolone, hydroquinone+fluocinolone, all at the same concentrations; p<.0001), and a 75% reduction in pigmentation was seen in more than 70% on triple therapy versus 30% on the dual agents; the commonest reactions in all groups were erythema, peeling, burning and stinging, mostly mild. In Asian patients with moderate-to-severe melasma (Chan R et al., PMID: 18616780; 242 randomised, 8 weeks), the triple cream (once nightly) beat hydroquinone 4% alone (twice daily) on the primary outcome: global severity 'none' or 'mild' at week 8 in 64.2% (77/120) versus 39.4% (48/122) (p<0.001), with patient satisfaction also favouring triple therapy (70.8% versus 49.6%; p=0.005) — but related adverse events occurred in 48.8% (63/129) versus 13.7% (18/131), none severe. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): for an eight-week course, the triple cream outperforms its own ingredients in pairs and hydroquinone alone by wide margins — the trials say nothing about staying clear after stopping, and melasma is a relapsing condition.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — complete clearing 26.1% versus 4.6% versus dual combinations (641 patients) and severity none/mild 64.2% versus 39.4% versus hydroquinone alone; related adverse events 48.8% versus 13.7%

title: Ketoconazole shampoo for tinea versicolor: healed with a negative tape test in 73% after three days of use — versus 5% on placebo shampoo; a single application did nearly as well (69%)
question: In people with tinea (pityriasis) versicolor, does ketoconazole 2% shampoo applied briefly to the skin clear the infection compared with placebo shampoo — and how does selenium sulfide shampoo compare?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a strikingly large effect in one large double-blind trial, for clearing an episode (this condition characteristically recurs, which the trial's 31 days cannot judge). In Lange DS et al. (PMID: 9843006), 312 patients with mycologically confirmed tinea versicolor were randomised to ketoconazole 2% shampoo as a single application, daily applications for three days, or placebo shampoo: clinical response at day 31 — defined as a global evaluation score of healed plus a negative cellophane tape test — was 73% in the 3-day group, 69% in the 1-day group and 5% on placebo (both ketoconazole regimens significantly more effective than placebo at p<.001 on clinical response, global scores and mycologic outcomes); the two ketoconazole regimens did not differ significantly from each other, and adverse events did not differ between groups, with no serious events and no withdrawals for adverse events. A smaller double-blind trial (Lusiana et al., PMID: 38021181) compared selenium sulfide 1.8% shampoo (described in its abstract as SeS2) with ketoconazole 2% shampoo: mycological efficacy was 94% versus 86% in the order reported (ketoconazole versus selenium; p=0.182, not significant), with side effects in 22% versus 8% as reported. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a few applications of an antifungal shampoo clear most versicolor episodes within a month — expect the pale patches to fade more slowly than the fungus, and expect recurrence eventually, which no card here measures.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — clinical response 73% (3-day) and 69% (1-day) versus 5% on placebo at day 31 in a 312-patient double-blind trial; selenium sulfide shampoo statistically indistinguishable in a smaller trial

title: Amlexanox for mouth ulcers: pain and ulcer size significantly reduced by days 4-6 in two blinded trials — but neither record reports how much, and both come from one research group
question: In people with recurrent minor aphthous ulcers (canker sores), does topical amlexanox (adhesive tablets, pellicles or paste) reduce ulcer size and pain compared with a vehicle/placebo preparation?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — significant p-values without published effect sizes, from a single research programme. In Liu J et al. (PMID: 16997114), 212 subjects with recurrent minor aphthous ulceration completed a double-blind vehicle-controlled multicentre trial of amlexanox oral adhesive tablets applied four times daily for five days (104 amlexanox, 108 vehicle): group differences favoured amlexanox for pain, ulcer size change and efficacy index at both day 4 and day 6 (all p<0.05), and for erythema and exudation at day 6; no systemic side effects were reported. In Meng W et al. (PMID: 19419555; Registry ID: NTR1727), 216 patients with minor recurrent aphthous ulcers were randomised to amlexanox adhesive pellicles or placebo pellicles four times daily for five days: ulcer size was significantly reduced (p=0.017 at day 4; p=0.038 at day 6) and ulcer pain significantly alleviated (p=0.021 at day 4; p=0.036 at day 6), with no significant difference in effectiveness between the pellicle and the tablet form studied previously by the same group. Neither record reports the actual size or pain differences, so how many hours or millimetres amlexanox buys cannot be stated from the sources. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): amlexanox probably speeds ulcer healing and pain relief a little over five days — the trials establish direction, not magnitude, and independent replication outside this one Chinese research programme is absent from the record.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — ulcer size and pain significantly better than vehicle/placebo at days 4-6 in two blinded trials (212 completers; 216 patients), with no effect sizes reported and a single research group behind both

title: Ciclopirox nail lacquer for toenail fungus: mycological cure 29% and 36% versus 11% and 9% on vehicle after 48 weeks — a year of daily painting for a one-in-three fungus cure in mild-to-moderate disease
question: In adults with mild-to-moderate toenail onychomycosis, does ciclopirox 8% nail lacquer cure the fungus compared with vehicle lacquer or amorolfine lacquer?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a real but slow and partial cure, in carefully selected nails. The report of the two identically designed US pivotal trials (Gupta AK et al., PMID: 11051136) randomised 223 and 237 patients with mild-to-moderate dermatophyte toenail onychomycosis (20-65% of the target nail involved, no lunula involvement) to daily ciclopirox 8% lacquer or vehicle for 48 weeks: mycological cure (negative culture and negative microscopy) at the end of treatment was 29% versus 11% in study I and 36% versus 9% in study II; non-US studies reported mycological cure rates from 46.7% to 85.7% under more varied regimens. Causally related adverse effects were described as extremely uncommon in the review's summary, mostly transient local reactions such as erythema and application-site reaction, generally mild and clearing while patients continued use. A later formulation trial (Iorizzo M et al., PMID: 27171791; 120 evaluable patients with mild-to-moderate toenail onychomycosis, 48 weeks) compared a ciclopirox 8% HPCH lacquer (named P-3051 in the record) daily against amorolfine 5% lacquer twice weekly: treatment success was 58.3% versus 26.7% (p<0.001), complete cure 35.0% versus 11.7% (p<0.001), and mycological cure 100% versus 81.7% (p<0.001). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): for a patient who cannot or will not take oral terbinafine (live shelf #1156) and whose infection is mild-to-moderate without matrix involvement, a year of daily lacquer cures the fungus in roughly one in three — the newer efinaconazole record (pack #3048) shows complete cure in 15-18% on a stricter endpoint, and cross-trial comparisons between these lacquers are not randomised comparisons.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — mycological cure 29% and 36% versus 11% and 9% on vehicle at 48 weeks in two pivotal trials; a newer ciclopirox formulation beat amorolfine on complete cure (35.0% versus 11.7%)

title: Pessary first for prolapse: surgery reported improvement a little more often (81.5% vs 76.3%) and noninferiority was not shown — but 54% crossed over to surgery and the pessary strategy cost about €1,800 less
question: In women with symptomatic pelvic organ prolapse, is starting with a pessary noninferior to surgery for patient-reported improvement at 24 months?
balance: SPLIT — improvement is close and the pessary is cheaper, but noninferiority was not proven and most pessary users eventually had surgery. In the PEOPLE randomised trial (van der Vaart LR et al., PMID: 36538310), subjective improvement at 24 months was reported by 76.3% starting with a pessary versus 81.5% with surgery (risk difference −6.1%, 1-sided 95% CI −12.7 to ∞; P for noninferiority .16), and the per-protocol gap was wider (70.3% vs 83.3%). Crossover from pessary to surgery occurred in 54.1% of the pessary group. The alongside economic evaluation (Ben ÂJ et al., PMID: 38692718) found no significant QALY difference (−0.03, 95% CI −0.07 to 0.002) but significantly lower healthcare costs with the pessary strategy (mean difference −€1807, 95% CI −€2172 to −€1446). PROPOSED SPLIT: as a first strategy the pessary buys similar reported improvement at lower cost for the roughly half who stay with it, while surgery remains the more reliable single treatment — the trial does not support calling the two equivalent.
stamp: SPLIT — pessary-first gives close patient-reported improvement at significantly lower cost, but noninferiority to surgery was not shown and 54.1% crossed over to surgery within 24 months

title: Levonorgestrel coil for endometrial hyperplasia: every woman responded in the randomised trial (53 of 53) versus 96% on continuous oral progestogen and only 69% on cyclical oral progestogen
question: In women with endometrial hyperplasia without atypia (low or medium risk), does the levonorgestrel intrauterine system normalise the endometrium more reliably than oral progestogen — and does how the oral drug is scheduled matter?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the coil and continuous oral therapy both work; cyclical oral therapy is the weak option. In the Norwegian multicentre randomised trial (Ørbo A et al., PMID: 24286192), histological response at 6 months was obtained in all women on the levonorgestrel intrauterine system (53 of 53), 96% on continuous oral medroxyprogesterone (46 of 48), and only 69% on cyclical oral medroxyprogesterone (36 of 52). The earlier systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies (Gallos ID et al., PMID: 20934679) pointed the same way: pooled regression with the intrauterine system versus oral progestogens was 92% versus 66% in complex hyperplasia and 90% versus 69% in atypical hyperplasia, with no significant difference in simple hyperplasia (96% vs 89%). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): for hyperplasia without atypia, the levonorgestrel intrauterine system is at least as reliable as continuous oral progestogen and clearly better than cyclical oral regimens, which should not be used for this purpose.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — levonorgestrel intrauterine system normalised hyperplasia in 53 of 53 women in the one randomised trial, matching continuous oral progestogen (96%) and beating cyclical oral therapy (69%), with concordant observational pooling

title: ECHO: HIV acquisition did not differ substantially between the injectable, the copper IUD and the implant — hazard ratios 1.04, 1.23 and 1.18, all non-significant, in 7,829 randomised women
question: In women at high risk of HIV who want contraception, does intramuscular depot medroxyprogesterone acetate raise HIV acquisition compared with a copper intrauterine device or a levonorgestrel implant?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the randomised comparison found no substantial HIV-risk difference between the three methods. In the ECHO trial (Evidence for Contraceptive Options and HIV Outcomes (ECHO) Trial Consortium, PMID: 31204114), 7,829 women in eSwatini, Kenya, South Africa and Zambia were randomised to depot medroxyprogesterone acetate, a copper intrauterine device, or a levonorgestrel implant; 397 HIV infections occurred (incidence 3.81 per 100 woman-years). Hazard ratios for HIV acquisition were 1.04 (96% CI 0.82–1.33, p=0.72) for the injectable versus the copper device, 1.23 (0.95–1.59, p=0.097) versus the implant, and 1.18 (0.91–1.53, p=0.19) for the copper device versus the implant. All three methods were highly effective contraceptives: 255 pregnancies occurred, 71% of them after the assigned method had been discontinued. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): within this trial's precision, the long-feared injectable–HIV signal from observational data was not confirmed — the confidence intervals still allow up to roughly a 1.3- to 1.6-fold relative difference, so 'no substantial difference', not proof of exact equality, is the honest claim.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — in one large randomised trial, HIV acquisition did not differ substantially between depot medroxyprogesterone, copper IUD and levonorgestrel implant (HRs 1.04–1.23, all non-significant)

title: Gabapentin for vulvodynia: tampon-test pain 4.0 on gabapentin versus 4.3 on placebo (difference −0.3, P=.07) in the one double-blind crossover trial — and no tested treatment beat placebo on pain in the pooled record
question: In women with vulvodynia (provoked vestibulodynia), does extended-release gabapentin reduce pain compared with placebo — and does any tested treatment improve pain in the randomised record?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the one rigorous trial of gabapentin missed its endpoint, and pooling the few randomised treatments shows the same pattern. In the multicentre double-blind crossover trial (Brown CS et al., PMID: 29742655), tampon-test pain was 4.0 on extended-release gabapentin (1,200–3,000 mg/day) versus 4.3 on placebo (adjusted difference −0.3, 95% CI −0.7 to 0.0; P=.07), with no benefit for intercourse pain or daily pain. The systematic review and meta-analysis of vestibulodynia treatments (Pérez-López FR et al., PMID: 31364893) found four randomised trials (n=275) across oestrogen cream, desipramine with or without lidocaine, lidocaine, laser and transcranial stimulation, and no intervention reduced dyspareunia (mean difference 0.08, 95% CI −0.49 to 0.64) or daily vestibular symptoms. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): gabapentin should not be recommended on this record, and no pooled randomised treatment has yet beaten placebo on vulvodynia pain itself.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — gabapentin did not reduce vulvodynia pain versus placebo in its one double-blind trial (difference −0.3 points, P=.07), and a meta-analysis of four randomised vestibulodynia trials found no pain benefit for any modality

title: Linzagolix for endometriosis pain: dysmenorrhoea responders 72.9% on 200 mg with add-back versus 23.5% on placebo in EDELWEISS 3 — the 75 mg dose helped periods (44.0%) but not non-menstrual pain
question: In women with moderate-to-severe endometriosis-associated pain, does the oral GnRH antagonist linzagolix reduce dysmenorrhoea and non-menstrual pelvic pain versus placebo — at 75 mg alone, or at 200 mg with hormonal add-back?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — linzagolix reduces endometriosis pain, with the full effect at the high dose plus add-back. In the phase 3 EDELWEISS 3 trial (Donnez J et al., PMID: 38648863), responders for dysmenorrhoea at 3 months were 72.9% on linzagolix 200 mg with add-back therapy versus 23.5% on placebo (P<0.001), and for non-menstrual pelvic pain 47.3% versus 30.9% (P=0.007); the 75 mg dose without add-back improved dysmenorrhoea only (44.0% vs 23.5%, P<0.001; non-menstrual pain not significant, P=0.279). The earlier dose-ranging trial (Donnez J et al., PMID: 32505383) found the same dose pattern at 12 weeks — overall pelvic-pain responders 61.5%, 56.4% and 56.3% at 75, 100 and 200 mg versus 34.5% on placebo — with dose-dependent bone loss reaching a mean 2.6% at the spine on 200 mg without add-back. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): pain relief is real and dose-graded; the 200 mg dose needs add-back to protect bone, and no trial here compares linzagolix with standard hormonal treatments.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — linzagolix beat placebo for endometriosis pain in a phase 2 dose-ranging trial and the phase 3 EDELWEISS 3 trial, most completely at 200 mg with add-back (dysmenorrhoea responders 72.9% vs 23.5%)

title: Immediate postpartum contraception and breastfeeding: milk intake and continuation were noninferior with immediate implant or coil — the price is coil expulsion in 19% versus 2%
question: In women who plan to breastfeed, does inserting a levonorgestrel intrauterine device or an etonogestrel implant immediately after delivery harm breastfeeding compared with delayed insertion or no method?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — immediate insertion did not measurably harm breastfeeding in two randomised trials, but immediate coils are expelled far more often. In the noninferiority trial of immediate versus delayed levonorgestrel intrauterine device insertion (Turok DK et al., PMID: 28842126), any breastfeeding at 8 weeks was 79% with immediate insertion versus 84% with delayed insertion — noninferior within the prespecified 15% margin — and time to lactogenesis was 65.3 versus 63.6 hours; expulsions, however, were 19% versus 2% (P<.001). In the implant trial (Braga GC et al., PMID: 26209863), infants' breast-milk intake measured by deuterium dilution was essentially identical with an implant inserted within 48 hours versus no method (median 340 vs 330 mL/day after the first dose; 845 vs 785 mL/day after the second). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): for breastfeeding itself, immediate long-acting contraception looks safe on this record; the trade-off to counsel is expulsion and possible unnoticed loss of contraception, not milk supply.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — immediate postpartum IUD insertion was noninferior for breastfeeding continuation (79% vs 84% at 8 weeks) and immediate implant did not change measured milk intake, but immediate IUD expulsion was 19% vs 2%

title: Ondansetron versus metoclopramide for hyperemesis gravidarum: vomiting and well-being tied at 24 hours (median 1 vs 2 episodes; well-being 9 vs 9) — ondansetron won on side effects, not on sickness
question: In women hospitalised with hyperemesis gravidarum, is ondansetron more effective than metoclopramide at controlling vomiting and nausea in the first 24 hours — and how do their side effects compare?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — for efficacy, the head-to-head trial is a tie; the separation is tolerability and price. In the double-blind randomised trial (Abas MN et al., PMID: 24807340), women with hyperemesis gravidarum received intravenous ondansetron 4 mg or metoclopramide 10 mg every 8 hours for 24 hours: median well-being scores were 9 versus 9 (P=.33), vomiting episodes 1 versus 2 (P=.38), and nausea trajectories did not differ (P=.22). Drowsiness (12.5% vs 30%; number needed to treat to benefit, 6), dry mouth (10.0% vs 23.8%; NNTB 8) and persistent ketonuria at 24 hours (12.5% vs 30%; NNTB 6) were all less frequent on ondansetron, while hospital stay was similar and metoclopramide was significantly cheaper. The JAMA systematic review of treatments for nausea and vomiting in pregnancy and hyperemesis (McParlin C et al., PMID: 27701665) likewise found ondansetron associated with improvement across severity ranges on low-quality overall evidence, with one small trial favouring ondansetron over metoclopramide on day-4 nausea scores. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): choose between these two on side effects, availability and cost — not on expected antiemetic power.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — ondansetron and metoclopramide controlled hyperemesis equally at 24 hours in the one double-blind head-to-head trial; ondansetron caused less drowsiness, dry mouth and persistent ketonuria but cost more

title: Endocuff Vision at colonoscopy: adenoma detection rose from 36.2% to 40.9% in ADENOMA, driven by screening patients (61.7% vs 50.9%) — but the same device changed nothing at flexible sigmoidoscopy (13.3% vs 12.2%)
question: Does attaching the Endocuff Vision mucosal-exposure device to the endoscope increase adenoma detection — at colonoscopy, and at flexible sigmoidoscopy screening?
balance: SPLIT — the device helped where baseline detection and lesion yield were high, and did nothing where they were low. In the ADENOMA colonoscopy trial (Ngu WS et al., PMID: 29363535), adenoma detection was 40.9% with Endocuff Vision versus 36.2% with standard colonoscopy (P=0.02), driven by a 10.8-point gain in faecal-occult-blood-positive screening patients (61.7% vs 50.9%, P<0.001), with more cancers found (4.1% vs 2.3%, P=0.02). In the B-ADENOMA flexible sigmoidoscopy trial (Rees CJ et al., PMID: 32245908), detection was 13.3% with the device versus 12.2% without (p=0.353), with no differences in polyp yield, procedure time or experience. PROPOSED SPLIT: Endocuff Vision is a detection aid with a real but context-dependent effect — worthwhile in screening colonoscopy on this record, unproven at one-off sigmoidoscopy — and detection remains a surrogate for cancer prevention in both trials.
stamp: SPLIT — Endocuff Vision raised adenoma detection at colonoscopy (40.9% vs 36.2%, concentrated in screening patients) but not at flexible sigmoidoscopy screening (13.3% vs 12.2%)

title: Buspirone for functional dyspepsia: overall symptom severity 7.5 versus 11.5 on placebo and gastric accommodation nearly doubled in one 17-patient crossover trial — promising physiology, tiny evidence base
question: In adults with functional dyspepsia, does buspirone — a fundus-relaxing 5-HT1A agonist — improve meal-related symptoms and gastric accommodation compared with placebo?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — one very small crossover trial with a coherent mechanism and a clear symptom result, and nothing behind it. In that trial (Tack J et al., PMID: 22813445), 17 patients with functional dyspepsia took buspirone 10 mg three times daily or placebo for 4 weeks each: overall dyspepsia severity was 7.5 ± 1.3 on buspirone versus 11.5 ± 1.2 on placebo (P<.005), with significant gains in postprandial fullness, early satiation and bloating, and gastric accommodation rose from 141 ± 32 mL on placebo to 229 ± 28 mL on buspirone (P<.05), while sensitivity to gastric distension and solid emptying were unchanged and adverse events were similar between treatments. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): buspirone is a physiologically plausible, apparently well-tolerated option for postprandial-distress dyspepsia whose entire clinical case rests on 17 patients — it needs a real trial before it needs a stronger stamp.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — buspirone improved dyspepsia severity (7.5 vs 11.5) and gastric accommodation (229 vs 141 mL) versus placebo in a single 17-patient crossover trial

title: STW 5 (Iberogast) for functional dyspepsia: complete relief in 43.3% versus 3.3% at 8 weeks in the STW 5-II trial, and a pooled odds ratio of 0.22 for the most bothersome symptom across the placebo trials
question: In adults with functional dyspepsia, does the herbal preparation STW 5 (Iberogast) — or its STW 5-II variant — improve dyspeptic symptoms compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — an old, small but concordant placebo-controlled record for one named herbal mixture. In the multicentre double-blind trial of STW 5-II (Madisch A et al., PMID: 14755152), the gastrointestinal symptom score fell significantly more on active treatment than placebo in the first 4 weeks (p<0.001), and after 8 weeks 43.3% on active treatment versus 3.3% on placebo reported complete relief of symptoms (p<0.001). The meta-analysis of STW 5 itself (Melzer J et al., PMID: 15606389) re-pooled three placebo-controlled trials (138 on verum, 135 on placebo) and found STW 5 more effective for the severity of the most bothersome gastrointestinal symptom (P=0.001; odds ratio 0.22, 95% CI 0.11–0.47), with adverse events similar to placebo and no serious adverse events. The tested products are the named preparations STW 5 (Iberogast) and STW 5-II as described in the publications; neither record names the manufacturer in its abstract, and other herbal mixtures cannot borrow this result. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): for patients who want a herbal option, this specific preparation has genuine placebo-controlled support — from trials run two decades ago, at modest size.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the named herbal preparation STW 5 / STW 5-II beat placebo for functional dyspepsia symptoms in a double-blind trial (complete relief 43.3% vs 3.3% at 8 weeks) and a pooled re-analysis of three placebo trials (OR 0.22 for the most bothersome symptom)

title: Eosinophilic oesophagitis diets: milk-only elimination matched six-food elimination (remission 34% vs 40%, difference 6%, p=0.58) — and a step-up strategy spared endoscopies while reaching 79% remission at its widest step
question: In eosinophilic oesophagitis, is eliminating animal milk alone (one-food elimination) as effective as six-food elimination for histological remission — and what does a step-up dietary strategy achieve?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — between the two diets, that is: starting with milk alone performed statistically indistinguishably from starting with six foods. In the randomised trial (Kliewer KL et al., PMID: 36863390), histological remission at 6 weeks was 34% on one-food (milk) elimination versus 40% on six-food elimination (difference 6%, 95% CI −11 to 23; p=0.58), although complete remission (≤1 eosinophil per high-power field) favoured six foods (difference 13%, 95% CI 2 to 25; p=0.031); 43% of one-food non-responders then remitted on six foods, and 82% of six-food non-responders remitted on swallowed fluticasone. In the prospective step-up study (Molina-Infante J et al., PMID: 29074457), a two-food elimination (milk and gluten cereals) remitted 43%, rising to 60% at four foods and 79% at six foods, while cutting endoscopies and diagnostic time by 20% versus starting at six foods. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): milk-first is an acceptable, far less restrictive opening move — with escalation paths that recover most non-responders.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — one-food (milk) elimination was statistically indistinguishable from six-food elimination for histological remission in the randomised trial (34% vs 40%), with step-up escalation recovering many non-responders

title: RBX2660 microbiota enema for recurrent C. difficile: model-estimated success 70.6% versus 57.5% on placebo in phase 3 — after the phase 2b trial missed its own primary endpoint
question: In adults with recurrent Clostridioides difficile infection who have completed standard antibiotics, does a single RBX2660 microbiota-based enema reduce recurrence within 8 weeks compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a real but modest absolute gain, carried by a Bayesian phase 3 analysis after a conventionally negative phase 2b. In PUNCH CD3 (Khanna S et al., PMID: 36287379), model-estimated treatment success (no recurrence within 8 weeks) was 70.6% on RBX2660 versus 57.5% on placebo — an estimated 13.1-point difference with a posterior probability of superiority of 0.991 — and over 90% of successes in both groups stayed recurrence-free through 6 months. In the earlier PUNCH CD2 trial (Dubberke ER et al., PMID: 36544075), intention-to-treat success was 56.8% (one RBX2660 dose plus one placebo dose) and 55.6% (two RBX2660 doses) versus 43.2% on placebo — differences that were not significant (both p=0.2), so the phase 2b trial missed its predefined primary endpoint. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): RBX2660 — the standardised stool-derived microbiota product tested under that name in these records (the records do not name its manufacturer) — probably prevents roughly one recurrence in eight treated patients beyond placebo, with mostly mild gastrointestinal adverse effects.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — RBX2660 raised 8-week recurrence-free success by an estimated 13.1 points over placebo in the Bayesian phase 3 PUNCH CD3 trial (70.6% vs 57.5%), though its phase 2b trial missed its primary endpoint
