title: Split-dose bowel preparation: satisfactory cleansing in roughly two-and-a-half times the odds of day-before regimens across 47 trials (OR 2.51) — and patients prefer repeating it
question: For colonoscopy, does splitting the bowel-preparation dose between the evening before and the morning of the procedure clean the colon better than taking the whole preparation the day before?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — two meta-analyses of randomised trials, seven years of literature apart, agree that splitting the dose cleans better. The larger analysis (Martel M et al., PMID: 25863216) pooled 47 trials with 13,487 patients: split-dose preparations beat day-before preparations for colon cleansing (odds ratio 2.51, 95% CI 1.86–3.39), including against day-before polyethylene glycol specifically (OR 2.60, 1.46–4.63), and more patients were willing to repeat a split regimen (OR 1.90, 1.05–3.46). The earlier polyethylene-glycol-only analysis (Kilgore TW et al., PMID: 21628016) found the same direction with a larger estimate — satisfactory preparations OR 3.70 (2.79–4.91) across five trials (N=1,232) — plus fewer discontinuations (OR 0.53) and less nausea (OR 0.55). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): split dosing is the better default schedule for colonoscopy preparation; the remaining questions are about product and volume, not about whether to split.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — split-dose bowel preparation cleans the colon better than day-before dosing in two concordant meta-analyses of randomised trials (OR 2.51 across 47 trials; OR 3.70 for polyethylene glycol in the earlier analysis)

title: Propofol versus midazolam-based sedation for colonoscopy: satisfaction higher by half a standard deviation and recovery about 3 minutes shorter — with no difference in cardiorespiratory events across 9 trials
question: For colonoscopy sedation, does propofol give better patient satisfaction, recovery and safety than midazolam with or without a short-acting opioid?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — propofol's advantages are real but marginal, and its safety record in these trials is a tie. The meta-analysis of nine randomised trials (Dossa F et al., PMID: 31926966; 1,427 patients) found no significant differences in hypotension, hypoxia or bradycardia between propofol and midazolam (with or without opioids); patient satisfaction favoured propofol (standardised mean difference 0.54, 95% CI 0.30–0.79, with considerable heterogeneity), and recovery was shorter (SMD 0.41, 0.08–0.74) — a median difference of just 3 minutes 6 seconds. In the inflammatory bowel disease trial of nurse-administered propofol sedation (Steenholdt C et al., PMID: 33371995), satisfaction scores were 60.1 on propofol versus 51.2 on midazolam–fentanyl (P<.001), with less pain and more willingness to repeat colonoscopy, and no safety signals. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): patients prefer propofol and wake marginally faster; nothing here shows it to be safer or more dangerous than midazolam-based sedation in trial populations.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — propofol beat midazolam-based sedation on satisfaction (SMD 0.54) and recovery time (median 3 minutes shorter) across 9 randomised trials, with no difference in cardiorespiratory adverse events

title: Flavonoid tablets (MPFF) for acute haemorrhoid bleeding: bleeding stopped by day 3 in 80% versus 38% on placebo in one trial — and the Cochrane class review found less bleeding (OR 0.12) across the phlebotonics
question: In adults with an acute episode of internal haemorrhoids, does micronised purified flavonoid fraction (MPFF) stop bleeding and settle symptoms faster than placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — consistent short-term symptom control from two small double-blind trials and a supportive class review, all with wide error bars. In the largest single trial (Misra MC et al., PMID: 10931020), bleeding from acute internal haemorrhoids had stopped by day 3 in 40 of 50 patients (80%) on micronised purified flavonoid fraction versus 19 of 50 (38%) on placebo (P<0.01), bleeding duration was 2.1 days shorter (95% CI 1.2–2.9), and continued treatment prevented relapse in 30 of 47 versus 12 of 30 patients (P<0.05). The second trial (Jiang ZM et al., PMID: 16846547) found significantly better evolution of pain, oedema and bleeding over 7 days on MPFF (bleeding p=0.021 at day 4 and p=0.047 at day 7), with tolerability similar to placebo. The Cochrane review of the wider phlebotonic class (Perera N et al., PMID: 22895941) found significantly less bleeding versus control (OR 0.12, 95% CI 0.04–0.37) and better overall symptom improvement across 20 controlled studies (2,344 participants), while noting methodological limitations. The publications name the product only as micronised purified flavonoid fraction; neither trial record names a manufacturer. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): MPFF probably shortens an acute bleeding episode by a couple of days — useful for deferring a procedure, not a substitute for one.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — MPFF stopped acute haemorrhoid bleeding faster than placebo in two small double-blind trials (cessation by day 3 in 80% vs 38% in the larger), with a concordant Cochrane class review

title: Diltiazem cream versus GTN ointment for chronic anal fissure: healing tied (24 of 31 vs 25 of 29) but headaches halved — side effects in 13 of 31 versus 21 of 29 patients
question: In adults with chronic anal fissure, is topical diltiazem as effective as glyceryl trinitrate (GTN) ointment for healing — and does it cause fewer headaches and other side effects?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for tolerability, not healing: the one head-to-head trial found equal healing and clearly fewer headaches on diltiazem. In that double-blind trial (Kocher HM et al., PMID: 11952579), healing or improvement was achieved by 24 of 31 patients on 2% diltiazem cream versus 25 of 29 on 0.2% GTN ointment (no significant difference), while side effects occurred in 13 of 31 versus 21 of 29 (relative risk 1.84 for GTN, 95% CI 1.11–3.04; P=0.01) and headaches in 8 of 31 versus 17 of 29 (RR 2.06, 1.18–3.59; P=0.01). The Cochrane review of non-surgical fissure therapy (Nelson RL et al., PMID: 22336789) places both creams in context: GTN healed only marginally better than placebo (48.9% vs 35.5%), botulinum toxin and calcium-channel blockers (diltiazem, nifedipine) were equivalent to GTN with fewer adverse events, late recurrence approached 50% of initial cures, and no medical therapy came close to surgery. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): diltiazem is the reasonable first cream — same modest healing as GTN, about half the headaches — with surgery still the definitive option behind both.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — diltiazem cream matched GTN ointment for fissure healing in the head-to-head trial (24/31 vs 25/29) with significantly fewer side effects and headaches (RR 1.84 and 2.06 for GTN), and the Cochrane review rates calcium-channel blockers equivalent to GTN with fewer adverse events

title: Dextrose prolotherapy for knee osteoarthritis: WOMAC improvement beat blinded saline in both randomised trials (change 15.3 vs 7.6 points at a year; pain difference −10.34 points)
question: In adults with painful knee osteoarthritis, do dextrose prolotherapy injections improve pain, function and stiffness compared with blinded saline injections?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two small blinded trials from different continents point the same way. In the US three-arm trial (Rabago D et al., PMID: 23690322), composite WOMAC scores at 52 weeks improved by 15.3 ± 3.5 points on dextrose prolotherapy versus 7.6 ± 3.4 on blinded saline and 8.2 ± 3.3 on at-home exercise (P<.05), exceeding the WOMAC minimal clinically important difference, with high satisfaction and no adverse events. In the Hong Kong trial (Sit RWS et al., PMID: 32393559), the WOMAC pain difference-in-difference at 52 weeks favoured intra-articular hypertonic dextrose by −10.34 points (95% CI −19.20 to −1.49; P=0.022), with parallel gains in function (−9.55), composite score (−9.65) and visual-analogue pain (−10.98), and no adverse events reported. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): prolotherapy probably improves knee osteoarthritis symptoms beyond a saline injection ritual — by amounts patients can feel — but the trials are small, single-centre and unblinded at the level of the treating clinician in one case, so the stamp stays at POSSIBLE.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — dextrose prolotherapy improved WOMAC scores more than blinded saline injections in two randomised trials (15.3 vs 7.6 points change; pain difference −10.34 points at 52 weeks)

title: Calf stretching for nocturnal leg cramps: one trial found 1.2 fewer cramps a night, the other — in quinine users — found nothing; the record splits by who was studied
question: In older adults with nocturnal leg cramps, do nightly calf and hamstring stretching exercises before sleep reduce cramp frequency and severity?
balance: SPLIT — the two randomised trials disagree, and their populations explain the split better than their methods do. In untreated older adults with nocturnal cramps (Hallegraeff JM et al., PMID: 22341378), six weeks of nightly calf and hamstring stretching cut cramp frequency by 1.2 more cramps per night than control (95% CI 0.6 to 1.8) and severity by 1.3 cm more on a 10-cm scale (0.9 to 1.7). In patients already prescribed quinine for night cramps (Coppin RJ et al., PMID: 15808033), a factorial trial found no significant effect of stretching advice on cramp numbers in the previous 4 weeks at 12 weeks (difference 1.95, 95% CI −3.01 to 6.90) or on symptom burden — while advice to stop quinine did let 26.5% more patients (13.3% to 39.7%) stay off quinine (odds ratio 3.32, 1.37–8.06) without major problems. PROPOSED SPLIT: stretching is a reasonable, harmless first try for untreated cramps on one positive trial; in established quinine users the trial evidence says it adds nothing measurable — the useful intervention there was a supervised trial off quinine.
stamp: SPLIT — nightly stretching reduced cramps in untreated older adults (1.2 fewer per night) but showed no effect in a factorial trial of patients already on quinine, where stopping quinine was the intervention that worked

title: Lumbar traction for low back pain: the sham-controlled trial found nothing at 12 weeks or 6 months, and the Cochrane review of 32 trials (2,762 people) found little or no difference on pain, function or return to work
question: In adults with low back pain, with or without sciatica, does lumbar traction — alone or added to physiotherapy — reduce pain and disability compared with sham traction, no treatment or other treatments?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — this is one of the more thoroughly negative records in physical therapy. The Cochrane review (Wegner I et al., PMID: 23959683) pooled 32 randomised trials with 2,762 participants and found low- to moderate-quality evidence that traction makes little or no difference to pain intensity, functional status, global improvement or return to work versus placebo, sham traction or no treatment — in mixed back-pain populations, in back pain with sciatica, and for chronic pain without sciatica versus sham — with adverse effects (increased pain, aggravated neurological signs, subsequent surgery) reported in seven studies. The methodologically strongest single trial (Beurskens AJ et al., PMID: 9431610) compared high-dose motorised traction with sham low-dose traction in 151 patients, with patients and assessors blinded, and found no significant differences on any outcome at 12 weeks or 6 months — every 95% confidence interval included zero. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): traction, alone or added to physiotherapy, should not be sold as pain relief for low back pain on this record.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — traction showed little or no effect on pain, function, global improvement or return to work across 32 randomised trials (2,762 participants) in the Cochrane review, and the blinded sham-controlled trial was null on every outcome

title: Inhaled levodopa for Parkinson's OFF periods: motor scores improve about 4 points more than placebo 30 minutes after a dose — proven in clinic, not yet in daily life
question: In people with Parkinson's disease who have daily OFF periods on oral levodopa, does self-administered inhaled levodopa powder improve motor function during an OFF period compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for getting out of an OFF period faster, measured in the clinic. In the phase 3 SPAN-PD trial, inhaled levodopa 84 mg improved the UPDRS motor score from predose to 30 minutes postdose by -9.83 points versus -5.91 on placebo inhaler (between-group difference -3.92 [95% CI -6.84 to -1.00]; p=0.0088). An earlier phase 2 study of a single 50 mg dose in 24 patients found 77% reached a plasma levodopa rise of more than 400 ng/ml within 10 minutes versus 27% after oral carbidopa/levodopa, with significant motor improvement at the earliest assessments. Severe adverse events were uncommon and similar across arms (4% on 84 mg, 6% on 60 mg, 2% on placebo in SPAN-PD); cough at inhalation was the characteristic side effect in the phase 2 work. What is not shown: benefit on OFF time across an ordinary day at home, or any long-term efficacy — the pivotal endpoint was a single in-clinic OFF episode at week 12. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): inhaled levodopa speeds motor recovery from an OFF period by a modest margin over placebo, with the real-world and long-term value still untested in the carded record.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — inhaled levodopa 84 mg beat placebo by 3.92 UPDRS motor points at 30 minutes in one phase 3 in-clinic trial, supported by a small single-dose phase 2 study

title: IncobotulinumtoxinA for chronic drooling: salivary flow and global impression both beat placebo at 4 weeks in adults (SIAXI) and in children (SIPEXI)
question: In adults and children with chronic sialorrhea (drooling) from neurological disorders, do incobotulinumtoxinA injections into the salivary glands reduce salivary flow and improve global impression compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two placebo-controlled phase 3 trials, one in adults and one in children, agree. In adults (SIAXI), incobotulinumtoxinA 100 U significantly reduced unstimulated salivary flow rate at week 4 versus placebo (p=0.004) and improved patients' Global Impression of Change scores (p=0.002), with an effect lasting to week 16; dry mouth (2.7% at 100 U) and dysphagia (0.0% at 100 U) were the commonest treatment-related adverse events. In children aged 6-17 (SIPEXI), the same drug beat placebo on both coprimary endpoints — mean salivary flow decrease difference -0.06 g/min (p=0.0012) and carers' global impression difference 0.28 points (p=0.032) — with adverse-event rates comparable to placebo. The absolute flow reductions are small; the claim rests on the pairing of an objective flow measure with a global-impression benefit in two independent trials. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): gland injections of incobotulinumtoxinA modestly reduce drooling in adults and children with neurological sialorrhea, with dry mouth and dysphagia as the trade-off to watch.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — incobotulinumtoxinA beat placebo on salivary flow and global impression at week 4 in two phase 3 trials, adults (SIAXI) and children (SIPEXI)

title: Mexiletine for ALS muscle cramps: cramp frequency fell to 16-31% of placebo rates at 300-900 mg in one trial, and from 5.3 to 3.5 cramps a day in a crossover trial
question: In people with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis troubled by muscle cramps, does mexiletine reduce cramp frequency and severity compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for cramps specifically, not for the disease. In a 60-patient phase 2 trial, mexiletine cut muscle cramp frequency to 31% of the placebo rate at 300 mg/day (p=0.047) and 16% at 900 mg/day (p=0.002), with cramp intensity at 25% of placebo on the higher dose (p=0.005); rates of decline in ALSFRS-R and slow vital capacity did not differ from placebo. A second, crossover trial in 20 patients found cramps fell from 5.3 per day on placebo to 3.5 on mexiletine 150 mg twice daily, with cramp severity down 15 units on a 100-unit scale (p=0.01). Tolerability splits by dose: 300 mg/day was well tolerated, while 32% of patients on 900 mg/day discontinued study drug versus 5% on placebo (p=0.026). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): mexiletine at about 300 mg/day substantially reduces ALS cramp frequency and severity in two small randomised trials, with no shown effect on disease progression.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — mexiletine reduced ALS cramp frequency in two small randomised trials (to 16-31% of placebo rates; 5.3 to 3.5 cramps/day in crossover), with dose-related discontinuation at 900 mg/day

title: Rotigotine patch for restless legs syndrome: severity scores fell about 5 points more than placebo at the 2-3 mg doses in two 6-month trials — skin reactions in up to 43%
question: In adults with moderate-to-severe idiopathic restless legs syndrome, does the once-daily rotigotine transdermal patch reduce symptom severity compared with placebo over 6 months?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two 6-month placebo-controlled trials of the dopamine-agonist patch agree. In the European-led trial (458 patients), IRLS severity scores fell by -16.2 (2 mg/24 h) and -16.8 (3 mg/24 h) versus -8.6 on placebo (p<0.0001 for each dose versus placebo), with parallel gains in clinical global impression. In the US trial (505 patients), adjusted IRLS differences versus placebo were -4.5 (95% CI -6.9 to -2.2) at 2 mg/24 h and -5.2 (-7.5 to -2.9) at 3 mg/24 h (both p<0.001 on the coprimary measures). The price is the patch itself: skin reactions in 145 (43%) of 341 rotigotine patients versus 2 (2%) of 117 on placebo in the first trial, and in 27% in the second, alongside nausea (18.1%) and headache (11.6%). No augmentation was noted within the 6-month trial period — but augmentation is a longer-horizon harm these trials cannot exclude. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): rotigotine 2-3 mg/24 h relieves restless legs symptoms over 6 months, with application-site reactions as its signature cost.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — rotigotine 2-3 mg/24 h patches beat placebo by about 4.5-5.2 IRLS points in two 6-month trials, with skin reactions in 27-43% of users

title: Ravulizumab for generalised myasthenia gravis: MG-ADL improved -3.1 versus -1.4 on placebo at 26 weeks in a single phase 3 trial (CHAMPION MG)
question: In adults with anti-acetylcholine-receptor antibody-positive generalised myasthenia gravis, does the long-acting C5 complement inhibitor ravulizumab improve daily-function and clinician-rated weakness scores compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one well-conducted phase 3 trial. In CHAMPION MG, 175 adults with anti-AChR antibody-positive generalised myasthenia gravis were randomised to intravenous ravulizumab (loading dose, then maintenance every 8 weeks) or placebo for 26 weeks. The patient-reported MG-ADL score improved by -3.1 on ravulizumab versus -1.4 on placebo (P<0.001), and the clinician-reported QMG score by -2.8 versus -0.8 (P<0.001); improvements appeared within 1 week and were sustained to week 26, and a QMG improvement of at least 5 points occurred in 30.0% versus 11.3% (P=0.005). No notable differences in adverse events were observed between groups in the trial window. What is missing: a second trial, any comparison with the other complement and FcRn therapies now used in this disease, and outcomes beyond 26 weeks of blinded treatment. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): ravulizumab improves MG-ADL and QMG scores over 26 weeks in AChR-positive generalised myasthenia gravis, on the strength of a single trial.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — ravulizumab improved MG-ADL by -3.1 versus -1.4 and QMG by -2.8 versus -0.8 at 26 weeks in the single CHAMPION MG phase 3 trial

title: Optic neuritis steroids (ONTT): intravenous methylprednisolone speeds visual recovery but does not improve final acuity — and oral prednisone alone raises recurrence (relative risk 1.79)
question: In adults with acute optic neuritis, does corticosteroid treatment — intravenous methylprednisolone followed by oral prednisone, or oral prednisone alone — improve visual recovery compared with placebo, and does either change the risk of new episodes?
balance: SPLIT — the route decides. In the Optic Neuritis Treatment Trial (457 patients), intravenous methylprednisolone followed by oral prednisone sped recovery of visual function versus placebo — most clearly for visual-field defects (P=0.0001) — and left slightly better visual fields (P=0.054), contrast sensitivity (P=0.026) and colour vision (P=0.033) at 6 months, but not better visual acuity (P=0.66). Oral prednisone alone did not differ from placebo on visual outcomes at all, and it carried a higher rate of new episodes of optic neuritis in either eye (relative risk 1.79; 95% CI 1.08 to 2.95 versus placebo) — a relative effect printed with its confidence interval in the record. So the intravenous regimen buys speed, not a better final result, and the oral-only regimen buys nothing and adds recurrence risk. PROPOSED SPLIT: intravenous methylprednisolone for faster recovery when speed matters; oral prednisone alone should not be used for acute optic neuritis.
stamp: SPLIT — intravenous methylprednisolone speeds recovery without improving 6-month acuity; oral prednisone alone is ineffective and increases recurrence (relative risk 1.79)

title: Uveitis first-line steroid-sparing therapy (FAST): mycophenolate did not beat methotrexate — success 57.1% versus 66.7% at 6 months, with a posterior-disease subgroup favouring methotrexate
question: In adults with noninfectious intermediate, posterior or pan-uveitis needing corticosteroid-sparing immunosuppression, is mycophenolate mofetil superior to methotrexate for achieving controlled inflammation on low-dose steroids?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — for the superiority question asked. In the FAST trial, 216 adults with noninfectious uveitis needing steroid-sparing therapy were randomised to oral methotrexate 25 mg weekly or mycophenolate mofetil 3 g daily. Treatment success at 6 months — controlled inflammation in both eyes on no more than 7.5 mg prednisone daily and no more than 2 drops of prednisolone acetate, without failure for safety or intolerability — occurred in 66.7% on methotrexate versus 57.1% on mycophenolate (difference 9.5% [95% CI -5.3% to 21.8%]; odds ratio 1.50 [0.81 to 2.81]; P=0.20): mycophenolate was not superior. A prespecified anatomical split leaned the other way by site — posterior uveitis or panuveitis success 74.4% (methotrexate) versus 55.3% (mycophenolate), P=0.02, against 33.3% versus 63.6% in intermediate uveitis (P for interaction=0.004) — hypothesis-generating, not a verdict. Elevated liver enzymes were the commonest laboratory adverse event (13.0% methotrexate, 7.4% mycophenolate). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): as first-line steroid-sparing therapy, mycophenolate is not superior to methotrexate; either drug controls about three in five patients by 6 months.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — in the single FAST trial, mycophenolate was not superior to methotrexate for steroid-sparing uveitis control at 6 months (57.1% versus 66.7% success)

title: Cenegermin (nerve growth factor drops) for neurotrophic keratitis: corneal healing 55-75% versus 20-43% on vehicle across two randomised trials
question: In patients with moderate-to-severe neurotrophic keratitis (neurotrophic keratopathy), does topical cenegermin (recombinant human nerve growth factor) heal the corneal lesion compared with vehicle eye drops?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two randomised vehicle-controlled trials of the same 8-week, six-drops-daily regimen point the same way. In the European REPARO phase 2 trial (156 patients), corneal healing at week 4 was 54.9% on cenegermin 10 µg/ml and 58.0% on 20 µg/ml versus 19.6% on vehicle (P<0.001 for both), rising at week 8 to 74.5% and 74.0% versus 43.1%. In the US NGF0214 trial (48 patients), healing by the conventional measure at week 8 was 69.6% on cenegermin 20 µg/ml versus 29.2% on vehicle (+40.4%; P=0.006), and by the conservative 0-mm-staining measure 65.2% versus 16.7% (P<0.001). More than 96% of healed REPARO patients stayed recurrence-free during follow-up. Adverse effects in both trials were mostly local, mild and transient. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): cenegermin roughly doubles corneal healing in neurotrophic keratitis over 8 weeks — a rare-disease evidence base of two small trials, one of them phase 2.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — cenegermin healed corneal lesions in 54.9-74.5% versus 19.6-43.1% on vehicle across the REPARO and NGF0214 randomised trials

title: Idebenone for Leber's hereditary optic neuropathy: the single randomised trial missed its primary endpoint — benefit appeared only in a post hoc subgroup with discordant vision between the eyes
question: In patients with Leber's hereditary optic neuropathy, does idebenone 900 mg/day improve visual acuity compared with placebo over 24 weeks?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — a possible benefit in a subgroup, from a trial that missed its primary endpoint. RHODOS randomised 85 patients with Leber's hereditary optic neuropathy (m.3460G>A, m.11778G>A or m.14484T>C mutations) to idebenone 900 mg/day or placebo for 24 weeks. The primary endpoint — best recovery in visual acuity — did not reach statistical significance in the intention-to-treat population, and the record reports no significant overall effect size. A post hoc interaction analysis found a different response in patients with discordant visual acuities between the eyes at baseline; in that subgroup, all secondary endpoints differed significantly between idebenone and placebo. Idebenone was safe and well tolerated. A post hoc subgroup inside a small, primary-negative trial is the weakest form of randomised evidence — it identifies who might benefit, it does not prove that anyone does. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): idebenone may help the subgroup of LHON patients whose two eyes differ in acuity, on post hoc evidence only.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — the single RHODOS trial missed its primary endpoint; benefit was confined to a post hoc subgroup with discordant baseline visual acuities

title: Inhaled aztreonam for bronchiectasis: two phase 3 trials missed their quality-of-life endpoint — one nominal 'win' was judged not clinically significant, and airway side effects rose
question: In adults with non-cystic-fibrosis bronchiectasis colonised with Gram-negative bacteria, does aztreonam for inhalation solution improve respiratory-symptom quality of life compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — two large phase 3 trials of the same regimen failed to show clinical benefit. AIR-BX1 (266 randomised) and AIR-BX2 (274 randomised) tested aztreonam for inhalation solution 75 mg three times daily, in two 4-week courses, against placebo in bronchiectasis with Gram-negative colonisation; the primary endpoint was change in Quality of Life-Bronchiectasis Respiratory Symptoms score at 4 weeks. The adjusted difference was 0.8 points (95% CI -3.1 to 4.7; p=0.68) in AIR-BX1 and 4.6 points (1.1 to 8.2; p=0.011) in AIR-BX2 — the second result statistically significant but explicitly judged not clinically significant by the trialists (the scale's minimal important difference is 8.0 points). Treatment-related adverse events and discontinuations were more common on aztreonam in both trials, with dyspnoea, cough and increased sputum each more frequent than on placebo. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): inhaled aztreonam does not provide clinically significant symptom benefit in non-CF bronchiectasis and adds airway side effects.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — AIR-BX1 and AIR-BX2 both failed to deliver a clinically significant quality-of-life benefit from inhaled aztreonam, with more airway adverse events than placebo

title: Itraconazole for allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis: responses in 46% versus 19% on placebo in the one steroid-dependent trial — exacerbations cut from 1.3 to 0.4 per patient in the pooled record
question: In patients with allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, does adding itraconazole to corticosteroid-based care improve response, reduce exacerbations and lower IgE compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a small, old, but genuinely randomised evidence base. In the double-blind trial in corticosteroid-dependent ABPA, a composite response (at least 50% steroid-dose reduction, at least 25% IgE fall, plus improvement in exercise tolerance, lung function or infiltrates) occurred in 13 of 28 patients (46%) on itraconazole 200 mg twice daily for 16 weeks versus 5 of 27 (19%) on placebo (P=0.04), with similar adverse-event rates. The Cochrane review of azoles in ABPA (three randomised trials, 94 participants) found itraconazole-treated patients more likely to achieve a decline in serum IgE of 25% or more (Peto odds ratio 3.30; 95% CI 1.30 to 8.15), and in one trial exacerbations requiring oral corticosteroids numbered 0.4 per patient on itraconazole versus 1.3 on placebo (p<0.03), with sputum eosinophils down 35% versus 19% (p<0.01). The caveat is scale and era: fewer than 100 randomised patients, 16-week horizons, and a flagged interaction concern — adrenal suppression when itraconazole is combined with inhaled corticosteroids. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): itraconazole improves immunologic and clinical response in ABPA over 16 weeks, on small-trial evidence.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — itraconazole produced composite responses in 46% versus 19% on placebo in steroid-dependent ABPA, with pooled IgE-response odds ratio 3.30 in the Cochrane review

title: Tezepelumab for COPD (COURSE): the primary endpoint missed — exacerbations 1.75 versus 2.11 a year (rate ratio 0.83, not significant), with the signal confined to higher-eosinophil subgroups
question: In adults with moderate-to-very-severe COPD on triple inhaled therapy who keep exacerbating, does tezepelumab reduce the annualised rate of moderate or severe exacerbations compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — in the overall trial population. COURSE randomised 333 patients with moderate-to-very-severe COPD on triple therapy and at least two exacerbations in the prior year to tezepelumab 420 mg every 4 weeks or placebo for 52 weeks. The annualised rate of moderate or severe exacerbations was 1.75 on tezepelumab versus 2.11 on placebo (rate ratio 0.83 [90% CI 0.64-1.06]; p=0.10 one-sided) — the primary endpoint was not met. Prespecified eosinophil subgroups leaned favourable at higher counts (rate ratio 0.66 [95% CI 0.42-1.04] at 150 to <300 cells/µL and 0.54 [0.25-1.15] at ≥300 cells/µL) but harmful-leaning below 150 cells/µL (1.19 [0.75-1.90]), and every subgroup interval crosses 1. Adverse events occurred in 81% versus 75% and serious adverse events in 30% in both groups; five patients died on treatment (two tezepelumab, three placebo), none judged treatment-related. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): tezepelumab did not significantly reduce COPD exacerbations overall in its phase 2a trial; the eosinophil-high hypothesis is unproven and is being tested further.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — tezepelumab missed its primary exacerbation endpoint in the single COURSE phase 2a COPD trial (rate ratio 0.83 [90% CI 0.64-1.06])

title: Montelukast for chronic asthma: morning FEV1 improved about 7-10% more than placebo in its 1998 dose-ranging trials — symptom and reliever-use gains were fractions of a point and a puff
question: In adolescents and adults with chronic persistent asthma, does oral montelukast improve lung function, symptoms and reliever use compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — real but modest, from the drug's original dose-ranging trials. In a 343-patient 6-week trial, pooled montelukast doses beat placebo on morning FEV1 percentage change by 10.30% (95% CI 5.56 to 15.04), with as-needed beta-agonist use down 0.98 puffs (95% CI -1.53 to -0.44) and morning peak flow up 18.80 L/min (8.62 to 28.98). In a second, 3-week trial, pooled 10 and 50 mg doses beat placebo on FEV1 change by 7.1%, morning peak flow by 19.23 L/min, daytime symptom score by -0.29 points and beta-agonist use by -0.82 puffs/day. Adverse experiences were similar to placebo and not dose-related in both trials, and doses above 10 mg once daily added nothing — the 10 mg evening dose is where the effect plateaus. These are short trials in mild-to-moderate asthma using lung function and symptom scores, not exacerbations or hospitalisations. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): montelukast improves asthma control measures modestly over 3-6 weeks in chronic asthma, at the 10 mg dose.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — montelukast beat placebo on FEV1 (+7.1% to +10.30%), peak flow and reliever use in two short 1998 randomised trials, with effects plateauing at 10 mg daily

title: Buteyko breathing for asthma: reliever use fell (by 904 µg/day in one trial, two puffs/day in another) and symptoms improved — lung function and airway responsiveness never moved
question: In people with asthma, does the Buteyko breathing technique reduce symptoms and medication use compared with control classes or placebo devices, and does it change lung function or bronchial responsiveness?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for symptoms and reliever use only; the objective measures are null in both trials. In Bowler's blinded trial (39 subjects), the Buteyko group cut daily beta-agonist dose by a median 904 µg at 3 months versus 57 µg in controls (P=0.002), with inhaled steroid dose falling 49% versus 0 (P=0.06) and a trend to better quality of life (P=0.09) — but no change in daily peak flow or FEV1 in either group. In Cooper's 6-month three-arm trial (90 patients on inhaled corticosteroids), symptom scores improved most with Buteyko (median change -3 versus 0 on placebo device; p=0.003 between groups) and bronchodilator use fell by two puffs/day (p=0.005), while methacholine responsiveness (PD20), FEV1, exacerbations and ability to reduce inhaled steroids did not differ between groups. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): Buteyko training reduces reliever use and symptoms in asthma without changing the underlying airway physiology — patients should not read it as a substitute for controller therapy, which neither trial showed could be safely withdrawn.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — Buteyko breathing reduced reliever use and symptoms in two randomised trials, with no improvement in lung function or bronchial responsiveness in either

title: Antimicrobial urinary catheters: silver-alloy catheters did not reduce symptomatic catheter infection at all (12.5% versus 12.6%) in a 7,102-patient trial; nitrofural catheters fell short of the worthwhile threshold
question: In adults needing short-term urinary catheterisation in hospital, do antimicrobial catheters (silver alloy-coated or nitrofural-impregnated) reduce symptomatic catheter-associated urinary tract infection compared with a standard catheter?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — one very large pragmatic trial settles the silver question and nearly settles the nitrofural one. Among 7,102 randomised adults needing short-term catheterisation, symptomatic urinary tract infection for which an antibiotic was prescribed occurred by 6 weeks in 263 (12.5%) of 2,097 patients with a silver alloy-coated catheter versus 271 (12.6%) of 2,144 with a standard PTFE catheter (difference -0.1% [95% CI -2.4 to 2.2]), and in 228 (10.6%) of 2,153 with a nitrofural-impregnated catheter (difference -2.1% [-4.2 to 0.1]) — short of the 3.3% absolute reduction the trialists had set as the threshold for recommending routine use, and bought with higher rates of catheter-related discomfort. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): routine antimicrobial catheters are not supported for short-term hospital catheterisation — silver alloy does not work, and nitrofural's smaller, uncertain effect comes with more discomfort.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — in a 7,102-patient trial, silver-alloy catheters matched standard catheters on symptomatic infection (12.5% versus 12.6%) and nitrofural's -2.1% difference fell below the worthwhile threshold

title: Prostatic urethral lift (UroLift) for BPH: symptom scores beat sham at 3 months and held to 5 years (IPSS improvement 36%, retreatment 13.6%) — and beat TURP on recovery and ejaculation preservation in BPH6
question: In men with lower urinary tract symptoms from benign prostatic hyperplasia, does the prostatic urethral lift procedure improve symptoms and flow compared with sham — and how does it compare with transurethral resection on recovery and sexual function?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a sham-controlled win plus a favourable head-to-head on the outcomes TURP puts at risk. In the L.I.F.T. study (206 men randomised 2:1 to lift or sham), IPSS improvement after the lift was 88% greater than that of sham at 3 months; improvements in IPSS, quality of life, BPH impact index and peak flow were durable through 5 years at 36%, 50%, 52% and 44% respectively, with surgical retreatment in 13.6% over 5 years and no de novo, sustained erectile or ejaculatory dysfunction. In BPH6 (80 men, lift versus TURP), the lift was noninferior and superior on the composite BPH6 responder endpoint, with superior preservation of ejaculation and quality of recovery (p<0.01) and significant symptom relief in both arms. The trade: roughly one in seven lift patients needed surgical retreatment within 5 years, and the studied prostates were 30-80 cc — the evidence does not cover large glands. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): prostatic urethral lift gives durable, sham-beating symptom relief for men with 30-80 cc prostates, preserving ejaculation at the price of a 13.6% 5-year retreatment rate.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — prostatic urethral lift beat sham on symptoms (effect 88% greater at 3 months) with durability to 5 years and ejaculation preservation superior to TURP in BPH6

title: Aquablation versus TURP (WATER): symptom relief noninferior at 6 months, fewer persistent complications (26% versus 42%) and far less anejaculation (10% versus 36%)
question: In men with moderate-to-severe lower urinary tract symptoms from benign prostatic hyperplasia, is robot-assisted Aquablation (waterjet ablation) noninferior to transurethral resection for symptom relief, and does it differ on complications and ejaculatory dysfunction?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — as a comparative claim: equal symptom relief with a better safety and ejaculation profile, in one trial. WATER randomised 181 men with moderate-to-severe BPH symptoms to Aquablation or TURP in a double-blind design. At 6 months both groups had large IPSS improvements and the prespecified noninferiority hypothesis for symptom relief was met (p<0.0001). The primary safety endpoint (persistent Clavien-Dindo grade 1, or grade 2 or higher complications) occurred in 26% after Aquablation versus 42% after TURP — meeting noninferiority and then superiority (p=0.0149) — and among sexually active men anejaculation occurred in 10% versus 36% (p=0.0003). Operative time was similar (33 versus 36 minutes) though resection itself was far quicker with the waterjet (4 versus 27 minutes; p<0.0001). The record suggests larger prostates (50-80 ml) gained the most, but 6 months is early for a prostate operation whose comparator is judged over years. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): Aquablation matches TURP's early symptom relief with fewer persistent complications and much less anejaculation, on a single trial with 6-month primary outcomes.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — Aquablation was noninferior to TURP for symptom relief at 6 months in the single WATER trial, with fewer persistent complications (26% versus 42%) and less anejaculation (10% versus 36%)

title: Rezūm water-vapour therapy for BPH: IPSS fell 11.2 points versus 4.3 on sham at 3 months, flow up 6.2 ml/s, sustained to 12 months with sexual function preserved
question: In men with lower urinary tract symptoms from benign prostatic hyperplasia, does transurethral convective water-vapour (steam) ablation with the Rezūm system improve symptoms and flow compared with a sham control procedure?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one sham-controlled trial with a large symptom margin. McVary's multicentre trial randomised 197 men (prostate 30-80 cc, IPSS at least 13, flow 15 ml/s or less) 2:1 to Rezūm water-vapour ablation or a rigid-cystoscopy sham with simulated treatment sounds. At 3 months IPSS had fallen by 11.2 ± 7.6 points on active treatment versus 4.3 ± 6.9 on sham (p<0.0001); in treated men the baseline IPSS of 22 fell by 50% or more at 3, 6 and 12 months, and peak flow rose by 6.2 ml/s at 3 months and stayed up through 12 months (p<0.0001). No de novo erectile dysfunction was reported, and adverse events were mild to moderate and resolved quickly. What one trial cannot show: how steam ablation compares with resection or with the lift procedure, and durability beyond a year. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): Rezūm gives rapid, sham-beating symptom and flow improvement sustained to 12 months in men with 30-80 cc prostates, preserving erectile and ejaculatory function in the trial record.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — Rezūm steam ablation beat sham on IPSS by about 7 points at 3 months in a single randomised trial, with gains sustained to 12 months

title: Low-intensity shockwave therapy for erectile dysfunction: 57% could have intercourse without medication after treatment versus 9% on placebo at 5 weeks — but the validated IIEF erectile score did not significantly improve
question: In men with organic erectile dysfunction, does low-intensity extracorporeal shockwave therapy improve erectile function compared with placebo (sham) treatment?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — one small placebo-controlled trial whose two outcome measures disagree. Olsen randomised 112 men with organic erectile dysfunction who could not have intercourse with or without medication to five weekly shockwave treatments or placebo; 105 were assessed (51 active, 54 placebo). Five weeks after treatment, 29 men (57%) in the active group could obtain an erection and have intercourse without medication versus 5 (9%) on placebo (p=0.0001), and Erection Hardness Scale scores improved significantly — but the IIEF Erectile Function domain, the field's standard validated score, showed no significant result. By 24 weeks, after the placebo group had crossed to active treatment, only 7 (19%) of the active group and 9 (23%) of the crossed-over group remained able to have intercourse without medication. The trialists themselves call for a larger multicentre trial. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): shockwave therapy may restore medication-free intercourse in some men with organic ED, but the single small trial's null validated-score result and fading effect keep this at MAYBE.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — one small placebo-controlled trial found more men able to have medication-free intercourse after shockwave therapy (57% versus 9%), but the IIEF erectile-function domain was not significant and the effect faded by 24 weeks

title: Five-grass pollen SLIT tablet: symptom scores cut by about a quarter to a third versus placebo in adults and in children — and the benefit was still there a season after three years of treatment stopped
question: In children and adults with grass-pollen allergic rhinitis, does five-grass pollen sublingual immunotherapy reduce symptom-and-medication scores compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two concordant randomised double-blind trials of the same five-grass pollen tablet, one in each age group, plus a post-treatment season. In 628 adults (Didier A et al., PMID: 17935764), mean Rhinoconjunctivitis Total Symptom Score in the first pollen season was 3.58 on the 300-IR dose and 3.74 on the 500-IR dose versus 4.93 on placebo (P=.0001 and P=.0006), while the 100-IR dose (4.70) did not separate from placebo. In 278 children and adolescents aged 5–17 (Wahn U et al., PMID: 19046761), the 300-IR tablet improved the total symptom score versus placebo (P=.001), a mean relative improvement of 28.0% and a median relative improvement of 39.3%, with rescue-medication scores and days on rescue medication also lower (P=.0064 and P=.0146). After three consecutive pre- and co-seasonal years, benefit persisted into the untreated fourth season (Didier A et al., PMID: 23600548): adjusted symptom-score differences versus placebo of −1.14 and −1.43 points, relative differences of −22.9% and −28.5%, in 435 patients. Adverse events in the paediatric trial were generally mild or moderate and no serious side effects were reported in either first-season trial. The tested product is the five-grass pollen sublingual tablet (300 IR) of Stallergènes, Antony, France, named in the paediatric record — a different product from the single-grass tablet homed on Shelf #379. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the five-grass tablet reduces symptom and rescue-medication scores by roughly a quarter to a third relative to placebo across adults and children, with a post-treatment season of carry-over after three years of use.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — five-grass pollen SLIT tablet (300 IR) improves symptom scores versus placebo in concordant adult and paediatric randomised trials, with lower rescue-medication use and one post-treatment season of carry-over

title: Ataluren in nonsense-mutation Duchenne dystrophy: the phase 3 trial missed its walking endpoint (13.0 m difference, p=0.213) — the only significant signal sits in one prespecified middle subgroup
question: In ambulant boys with Duchenne muscular dystrophy, does ataluren improve walking distance compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — on the trials' own primary endpoints. In the phase 3 ACT DMD trial (McDonald CM et al., PMID: 28728956), change in 6-minute walk distance at week 48 was −47.7 m on ataluren versus −60.7 m on placebo, a difference of 13.0 m (95% CI −7.4 to 33.4; p=0.213) — not significant. The earlier phase 2b trial (Bushby K et al., PMID: 25042182) likewise only favoured its low dose in a post hoc analysis (difference 31.3 m, post hoc p=0.056). The one nominally significant result in either trial is a prespecified ACT DMD subgroup — boys with a baseline walk distance of 300 m to less than 400 m, difference 42.9 m (95% CI 11.8–74.0; p=0.007) — while the subgroups below 300 m (−7.7 m; p=0.749) and at 400 m or more (−9.5 m; p=0.580) showed nothing. Ataluren was generally well tolerated in both trials; in ACT DMD, serious adverse events occurred in 8 patients (3%), 4 per group. Two randomised blinded trials that both miss their primary endpoint cannot carry a benefit stamp; the middle-subgroup signal is hypothesis-generating only. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): ataluren has not been shown to improve walking distance overall in nonsense-mutation Duchenne dystrophy; a possible effect confined to boys in the transitional 300–400 m walk range rests on a single subgroup analysis.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — two randomised blinded trials missed their primary walking endpoints; the only significant signal is one prespecified subgroup of the phase 3 trial

title: Satralizumab in NMOSD: relapses cut in two phase 3 trials — 20% versus 43% added to immunosuppressants (HR 0.38) and 30% versus 50% alone (HR 0.45) — with the effect concentrated in aquaporin-4-positive patients
question: In patients with neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder, does satralizumab reduce relapse risk compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two phase 3 trials, one answer. Added to stable immunosuppressant treatment (SAkuraSky, Yamamura T et al., PMID: 31774956), satralizumab 120 mg subcutaneously every 4 weeks produced a first protocol-defined relapse in 8 of 41 patients (20%) versus 18 of 42 (43%) on placebo (hazard ratio 0.38; 95% CI 0.16–0.88) — a 62% relative reduction in relapse hazard. As monotherapy (SAkuraStar, Traboulsee A et al., PMID: 32333898), relapses occurred in 19 of 63 patients (30%) versus 16 of 32 (50%) (hazard ratio 0.45; 95% CI 0.23–0.89; p=0.018) — a 55% relative reduction. The benefit concentrates in aquaporin-4-IgG-seropositive patients: in SAkuraSky their hazard ratio was 0.21 (95% CI 0.06–0.75), against 0.66 (95% CI 0.20–2.24) in seronegative patients. Neither trial showed an effect on pain or fatigue scores, and rates of serious adverse events and infections did not differ between groups in SAkuraSky. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): satralizumab roughly halves relapse risk in NMOSD, as add-on therapy and alone, with the clearest effect in aquaporin-4-positive disease; the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE in this band.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two concordant phase 3 trials show relapse hazard ratios of 0.38 (add-on) and 0.45 (monotherapy), strongest in aquaporin-4-positive patients

title: THALES: ticagrelor plus aspirin cut 30-day stroke or death to 5.5% versus 6.6% on aspirin alone after minor stroke or TIA — a 1.1-point absolute gain bought with five times the severe bleeding (0.5% versus 0.1%)
question: In adults after TIA or minor ischaemic stroke, does ticagrelor plus aspirin reduce subsequent stroke compared with aspirin alone?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — from a single large trial, flagged single-trial. In THALES (Johnston SC et al., PMID: 32668111), 11,016 patients with mild-to-moderate acute noncardioembolic ischaemic stroke (NIHSS score 5 or less) or TIA, randomised within 24 hours and not receiving thrombolysis or thrombectomy, took 30 days of ticagrelor plus aspirin or aspirin alone. The composite of stroke or death within 30 days occurred in 303 patients (5.5%) on ticagrelor–aspirin versus 362 (6.6%) on aspirin alone (hazard ratio 0.83; 95% CI 0.71–0.96; p=0.02) — a 17% relative reduction, and 1.1 percentage points absolute. Ischaemic stroke occurred in 276 patients (5.0%) versus 345 (6.3%) (hazard ratio 0.79; 95% CI 0.68–0.93; p=0.004). Disability at 30 days did not differ significantly. The price was bleeding: severe bleeding in 28 patients (0.5%) versus 7 (0.1%) (p=0.001). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): 30 days of ticagrelor plus aspirin modestly reduces early stroke or death after minor stroke or TIA, at a real severe-bleeding cost — one trial only, so the developer decides whether a single-trial shelf stands.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single large trial (THALES): stroke or death 5.5% versus 6.6% at 30 days, severe bleeding 0.5% versus 0.1%

title: Bimekizumab versus adalimumab in plaque psoriasis: clear or almost-clear skin in 85% versus 57% at week 16 in BE SURE — with oral candidiasis and diarrhoea as the price, and a 91% versus 1% placebo-controlled clearance rate behind it
question: In adults with plaque psoriasis, does bimekizumab achieve complete skin clearance more often than adalimumab?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one head-to-head trial against adalimumab, backed by one placebo-controlled trial of the same drug. In BE SURE (Warren RB et al., PMID: 33891379), 478 patients with moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis were randomised to bimekizumab 320 mg every 4 weeks (with or without a switch to every 8 weeks after week 16) or adalimumab 40 mg every 2 weeks: at week 16 a PASI 90 response (at least 90% improvement) occurred in 275 of 319 (86.2%) on bimekizumab versus 75 of 159 (47.2%) on adalimumab (adjusted risk difference 39.3 percentage points; P<0.001 for noninferiority and superiority), and an Investigator's Global Assessment score of 0 or 1 (clear or almost clear) in 272 of 319 (85.3%) versus 91 of 159 (57.2%). In BE READY (Gordon KB et al., PMID: 33549192), bimekizumab achieved PASI 90 in 317 of 349 (91%) versus 1 of 86 (1%) on placebo at week 16, with IGA 0 or 1 in 323 of 349 (93%) versus 1 of 86 (1%). The harm ledger is the IL-17 class signature: oral candidiasis and diarrhoea occurred more frequently with bimekizumab in BE SURE, and treatment-emergent adverse events in BE READY's first 16 weeks ran 61% on bimekizumab versus 41% on placebo. Neither record's abstract reports PASI 100 (literally complete clearance), so this shelf's claim is clear-or-almost-clear skin and PASI 90, not total clearance. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): bimekizumab clears or nearly clears skin substantially more often than adalimumab at week 16 in a single head-to-head phase 3 trial, at the cost of more oral candidiasis and diarrhoea; Tier C because the adalimumab comparison rests on that one trial.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — bimekizumab beat adalimumab on PASI 90 (86.2% vs 47.2%) and IGA clear/almost-clear (85.3% vs 57.2%) at week 16 in the single head-to-head BE SURE trial, with a concordant placebo-controlled trial (BE READY) and more oral candidiasis and diarrhoea

title: Autologous cell therapy for 'no-option' critical limb ischaemia: amputations fell by about 60% across 16 small trials — deaths did not move at all
question: In adults with chronic limb-threatening ischaemia and no revascularisation options, does autologous cell therapy improve amputation-free survival compared with standard care?
balance: SPLIT — amputations down, mortality unchanged, and no trial pooled amputation-free survival directly. A meta-analysis of 16 randomised trials in 775 patients with no-option critical limb ischaemia (Wahid FSA et al., PMID: 29532760) found all-cause mortality rates similar between autologous cell-based therapy and non-cell-based care on high-quality evidence, while amputation rates fell by approximately 60% on moderate-quality evidence — a relative effect that clears the developer's floor for benefit — alongside improvements in ulcer healing, ankle–brachial index, transcutaneous oxygen, pain-free walking capacity and collateral vessel formation. Intramuscular bone marrow mononuclear cells and mobilised peripheral blood stem cells were the products that appeared to reduce amputation; bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells improved perfusion measures but not amputation. A Cochrane review of head-to-head trials (Abdul Wahid SF et al., PMID: 30155883) found only seven randomised trials (359 participants) comparing one cell source, dose or route against another, and identified no other comparisons — so no cell product or regimen is proven best. Because deaths did not fall, any gain in amputation-free survival would be carried entirely by the amputation reduction, and that composite was not the pooled endpoint. PROPOSED SPLIT: fewer amputations (POSSIBLE benefit on moderate-quality pooled evidence), no mortality benefit, regimen unsettled.
stamp: SPLIT — POSSIBLE (benefit) for amputation; POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for all-cause mortality

title: Soy isoflavones do not preserve bone density after menopause: three placebo-controlled trials (202, 131 and 431 women) and a 1,433-woman meta-analysis all null
question: In postmenopausal women with low bone density, do soy isoflavones reduce bone loss compared with placebo?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — three concordant null trials plus a null pooling. Kreijkamp-Kaspers 2004 (PMID: 15238592) gave 202 postmenopausal women soy protein containing 99 mg isoflavones daily or milk protein for 12 months: bone mineral density of hip and lumbar spine did not differ significantly. Kenny 2009 (PMID: 19474141), in 131 older women randomised across soy protein and/or isoflavone tablets (105 mg aglycone equivalents) for 1 year, found no significant differences in BMD between groups. Tai 2012 (PMID: 21901480), the largest and longest, gave 431 women 300 mg/day isoflavones or placebo for 2 years: BMD differences were not significant at lumbar spine (p = 0.42) or total femur (p = 0.39), with bone loss proceeding in both groups. Ricci 2010 (PMID: 20673147) pooled 12 studies and 1,433 women: the lumbar-spine BMD difference was 9.86 mg/cm² (95% CI −2.64 to 22.36), not statistically significant. None of the records names a branded product or company. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): soy isoflavone mixtures, at doses up to 300 mg/day for up to 2 years, did not slow postmenopausal bone loss versus placebo.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — three placebo-controlled trials and a 12-study meta-analysis found no significant bone-density preservation from soy isoflavones

title: Ginkgo biloba does not help tinnitus: 34 of 360 versus 35 of 360 called it less troublesome in the largest trial, and the Cochrane pool of 1,543 patients found no evidence of effect
question: In adults with subjective tinnitus, does Ginkgo biloba extract improve tinnitus severity compared with placebo?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — a large trial, a small trial with its own meta-analysis, and a Cochrane review agree. Drew & Davies 2001 (PMID: 11154618) randomised matched participants with stable tinnitus to Ginkgo biloba extract LI 1370, 50 mg three times daily, or placebo for 12 weeks: 34 of 360 on ginkgo and 35 of 360 on placebo reported their tinnitus less troublesome, with no significant differences on primary or secondary outcomes; the record names the extract (LI 1370) but names no company. Rejali 2004 (PMID: 15142066) found no significant difference on the Tinnitus Handicap Inventory in its own 66-patient trial, and its meta-analysis of six trials found benefit in 21.6% on ginkgo versus 18.4% on placebo (odds ratio 1.24, 95% CI 0.89–1.71). Hilton 2013 (PMID: 23543524, Cochrane) pooled four trials with 1,543 participants and found no evidence that Ginkgo biloba was effective in patients whose primary complaint was tinnitus. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): ginkgo extract did not improve tinnitus severity over placebo in any adequate comparison.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — largest trial numerically identical to placebo (34/360 vs 35/360 improved) and Cochrane pooling of 1,543 participants found no evidence of effect

title: Melatonin advances sleep onset by about 27 minutes and adds about 20 minutes of sleep in children with ADHD and chronic sleep-onset insomnia — with no effect on behaviour, cognition, or ADHD symptoms
question: In children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder and insomnia, does melatonin improve sleep onset and total sleep time compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for sleep timing only, in two concordant double-blind trials. Van der Heijden 2007 (PMID: 17242627) randomised 105 medication-free children aged 6–12 years with ADHD and chronic sleep-onset insomnia to melatonin 3 or 6 mg (by body weight) or placebo for 4 weeks: sleep onset advanced by 26.9 minutes on melatonin and was delayed by 10.5 minutes on placebo (p < .0001), dim-light melatonin onset advanced by 44.4 minutes versus a 12.8-minute delay (p < .0001), and total time asleep increased by 19.8 minutes versus a 13.6-minute decrease (p = .01) — with no significant effect on behaviour, cognition, or quality of life. Weiss 2006 (PMID: 16670647), in 27 stimulant-treated children with ADHD and initial insomnia, found melatonin 5 mg reduced initial insomnia by 16 minutes relative to placebo in the crossover phase (effect size 0.6), after sleep hygiene alone had resolved insomnia in 5 children; improved sleep had no demonstrable effect on ADHD symptoms. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): melatonin modestly advances and lengthens sleep in children with ADHD and sleep-onset insomnia; it is not a treatment for ADHD itself.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two double-blind trials: sleep onset advanced ~27 minutes and total sleep increased ~20 minutes versus placebo, with no effect on behaviour, cognition, or ADHD symptoms

title: Elacestrant in pretreated ER-positive, HER2-negative advanced breast cancer: progression-free survival hazard ratio 0.70 overall and 0.55 in ESR1-mutated tumours — one open-label phase 3 trial, nausea in 35%
question: In patients with metastatic hormone-receptor-positive breast cancer and ESR1 mutations after endocrine therapy, does elacestrant improve progression-free survival compared with standard endocrine therapy?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — on a single randomised trial. In EMERALD (Bidard FC et al., PMID: 35584336), 477 patients with ER-positive, HER2-negative advanced breast cancer after one to two lines of endocrine therapy (all pretreated with a CDK4/6 inhibitor) were randomised to elacestrant or standard endocrine monotherapy: progression-free survival hazard ratio was 0.70 (95% CI 0.55 to 0.88; P=.002) in all patients and 0.55 (95% CI 0.39 to 0.77; P=.0005) in the 47.8% with detectable ESR1 mutations — the subgroup this question asks about, where the benefit was largest. Treatment-related grade 3/4 adverse events occurred in 7.2% on elacestrant versus 3.1% on standard care, and nausea of any grade in 35.0% versus 18.8%. Single-trial flag under the relaxed beyond-4,000 intake tier. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): elacestrant prolonged progression-free survival in one phase 3 trial, most clearly in ESR1-mutated disease; no survival result is reported in this record.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single phase 3 trial: PFS HR 0.70 overall and 0.55 in ESR1-mutated tumours versus standard endocrine therapy; no overall-survival result in the record

title: Tisotumab vedotin in recurrent cervical cancer after chemotherapy: median survival 11.5 versus 9.5 months (HR 0.70) and response 17.8% versus 5.2% — one open-label phase 3 trial
question: In patients with recurrent or metastatic cervical cancer previously treated with chemotherapy, does tisotumab vedotin improve survival compared with investigator-choice chemotherapy?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — on a single randomised trial. In innovaTV 301 (Vergote I et al., PMID: 38959480), 502 patients with recurrent or metastatic cervical cancer were randomised to tisotumab vedotin or investigator's-choice chemotherapy as second- or third-line therapy: median overall survival was 11.5 months (95% CI 9.8 to 14.9) versus 9.5 months (95% CI 7.9 to 10.7) — a hazard ratio of 0.70 (95% CI 0.54 to 0.89; P=0.004), a 30% relative reduction in the risk of death — median progression-free survival 4.2 versus 2.9 months (HR 0.67), and confirmed response 17.8% versus 5.2%. Grade 3 or greater adverse events occurred in 52.0% on tisotumab vedotin versus 62.3% on chemotherapy, and 14.8% stopped tisotumab vedotin because of toxic effects. Single-trial flag under the relaxed beyond-4,000 intake tier. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): tisotumab vedotin extended survival by a median 2.0 months in one phase 3 trial in a setting with few options.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single phase 3 trial: median overall survival 11.5 vs 9.5 months (HR 0.70) and response 17.8% vs 5.2% versus investigator-choice chemotherapy

title: Idecabtagene vicleucel in triple-class-exposed relapsed myeloma: median progression-free survival 13.3 versus 4.4 months (HR 0.49) and complete response 39% versus 5% — one open-label phase 3 trial, cytokine release syndrome in 88%
question: In patients with relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma, does idecabtagene vicleucel improve progression-free survival compared with standard regimens?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — on a single randomised trial. In KarMMa-3 (Rodriguez-Otero P et al., PMID: 36762851), 386 patients with relapsed and refractory myeloma after two to four prior regimens (66% triple-class-refractory, 95% daratumumab-refractory) were randomised 2:1 to idecabtagene vicleucel or one of five standard regimens: at median follow-up 18.6 months, median progression-free survival was 13.3 versus 4.4 months (hazard ratio 0.49; 95% CI 0.38 to 0.65; P<0.001), response 71% versus 42%, and complete response 39% versus 5%; overall-survival data were immature. Grade 3–4 adverse events occurred in 93% versus 75%; among 225 patients who received ide-cel, cytokine release syndrome occurred in 88% (grade ≥3 in 5%) and neurotoxic effects in 15% (grade ≥3 in 3%). Single-trial flag under the relaxed beyond-4,000 intake tier. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): ide-cel roughly tripled median progression-free survival in one phase 3 trial, with survival benefit not yet shown and substantial CAR T toxicity.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single phase 3 trial: median PFS 13.3 vs 4.4 months (HR 0.49) and complete response 39% vs 5%; overall survival immature, cytokine release syndrome in 88%

title: Axicabtagene ciloleucel as second-line therapy for early relapsed large B-cell lymphoma: median event-free survival 8.3 versus 2.0 months (HR 0.40) and 24-month event-free survival 41% versus 16% — one phase 3 trial, grade ≥3 neurologic events in 21%
question: In patients with early relapsed or refractory large B-cell lymphoma, does axicabtagene ciloleucel improve event-free survival compared with standard second-line care?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — on a single randomised trial. In ZUMA-7 (Locke FL et al., PMID: 34891224), 359 patients whose large B-cell lymphoma was refractory to or had relapsed within 12 months of first-line chemoimmunotherapy were randomised to axicabtagene ciloleucel or standard care (salvage chemoimmunotherapy, then high-dose therapy with autologous transplant in responders): at median follow-up 24.9 months, median event-free survival was 8.3 versus 2.0 months and 24-month event-free survival 41% versus 16% (hazard ratio for event or death 0.40; 95% CI 0.31 to 0.51; P<0.001), response 83% versus 50% with complete response 65% versus 32%, and estimated 2-year overall survival 61% versus 52% at interim analysis. Grade 3 or higher adverse events occurred in 91% versus 83%; among axi-cel recipients, grade ≥3 cytokine release syndrome occurred in 6% and grade ≥3 neurologic events in 21%, with no deaths from either. Single-trial flag under the relaxed beyond-4,000 intake tier. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): axi-cel markedly improved event-free survival in one phase 3 trial, with high-grade toxicity on both arms.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single phase 3 trial: median event-free survival 8.3 vs 2.0 months (HR 0.40), 24-month event-free survival 41% vs 16%; grade ≥3 neurologic events in 21% of axi-cel recipients

title: Fixed-duration ibrutinib plus venetoclax in untreated CLL in older or comorbid patients: progression-free survival hazard ratio 0.216 versus chlorambucil–obinutuzumab, undetectable MRD in marrow 55.7% versus 21.0% — one phase 3 trial (GLOW)
question: In patients with treatment-naive chronic lymphocytic leukaemia, does fixed-duration ibrutinib plus venetoclax improve progression-free survival compared with chemoimmunotherapy?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — on a single randomised trial. In GLOW (Kater AP et al., PMID: 38319255), 211 previously untreated patients with CLL who were 65 or older or had comorbidities were randomised to fixed-duration ibrutinib–venetoclax (3 cycles of ibrutinib lead-in, then 12 cycles of the combination) or 6 cycles of chlorambucil–obinutuzumab: at median follow-up 27.7 months there were 22 progression-free-survival events versus 67 (hazard ratio 0.216; 95% CI 0.131 to 0.357; P<0.001), best undetectable minimal residual disease in bone marrow was 55.7% versus 21.0% (P<0.001), and only 4 versus 27 patients had required subsequent therapy. Single-trial flag under the relaxed beyond-4,000 intake tier. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): fixed-duration ibrutinib–venetoclax gave a large progression-free-survival advantage in one trial in older or comorbid patients; a survival advantage was not shown at this follow-up.

title: Sunitinib in advanced GIST after imatinib failure: median time to tumour progression 27.3 versus 6.4 weeks (HR 0.33) — one double-blind placebo-controlled trial, unblinded early at interim analysis
question: In patients with advanced gastrointestinal stromal tumour progressing on imatinib, does sunitinib improve time to tumour progression compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — on a single randomised trial. In the pivotal trial (Demetri GD et al., PMID: 17046465), 312 patients with advanced GIST resistant to or intolerant of imatinib were randomised 2:1 to sunitinib 50 mg daily (4 weeks on, 2 weeks off) or placebo: median time to tumour progression was 27.3 weeks (95% CI 16.0 to 32.1) versus 6.4 weeks (95% CI 4.4 to 10.0), hazard ratio 0.33 (P<0.0001) — a 67% relative reduction in the hazard of progression, with the absolute medians printed alongside. The trial was unblinded early after a planned interim analysis showed the difference. The most common treatment-related adverse events were fatigue, diarrhoea, skin discolouration and nausea. Single-trial flag under the relaxed beyond-4,000 intake tier; sunitinib is mentioned as prior therapy on other GIST shelves but this trial had no card-home. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): sunitinib quadrupled median time to progression after imatinib failure in one double-blind trial stopped early at interim analysis.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single double-blind placebo-controlled trial: median time to tumour progression 27.3 vs 6.4 weeks (HR 0.33); trial unblinded early at interim analysis

title: Denosumab on androgen deprivation: new vertebral fractures 1.5% versus 3.9% at 36 months in one large trial — bone density up at every site, adverse events no higher
question: In men receiving androgen deprivation therapy for non-metastatic prostate cancer, does denosumab reduce fractures compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one large double-blind trial, a fracture endpoint actually won. In HALT (Smith MR et al., PMID: 19671656), 1,468 men on androgen-deprivation therapy for nonmetastatic prostate cancer received denosumab 60 mg every 6 months or placebo. New vertebral fractures at 36 months occurred in 1.5% on denosumab versus 3.9% on placebo (relative risk 0.38; 95% CI 0.19 to 0.78; P=0.006) — a 62% relative reduction, 2.4 percentage points absolute. Lumbar-spine bone mineral density at 24 months rose 5.6% on denosumab versus a 1.0% loss on placebo (P<0.001), with gains at hip, femoral neck and radius. Rates of adverse events were similar between groups. The catch is scope: the fracture win is vertebral fractures in a single trial; non-vertebral and hip fracture rates are not reported as won in this record. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): denosumab reduces new vertebral fractures and raises bone density in men on androgen deprivation, on the strength of one trial.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — denosumab halved-plus new vertebral fractures (1.5% vs 3.9%, RR 0.38) and raised BMD in one large double-blind trial in men on ADT; single-trial

title: Trabectedin versus dacarbazine in pretreated liposarcoma/leiomyosarcoma: progression-free survival 4.2 versus 1.5 months — overall survival a draw (12.4 versus 12.9 months)
question: In patients with advanced liposarcoma or leiomyosarcoma after anthracycline therapy, does trabectedin improve progression-free survival compared with dacarbazine?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for disease control, not for survival. In the single phase 3 trial (Demetri GD et al., PMID: 26371143), 518 patients with metastatic liposarcoma or leiomyosarcoma after an anthracycline and at least one further regimen were randomised 2:1 to trabectedin or dacarbazine. Median progression-free survival was 4.2 versus 1.5 months (hazard ratio 0.55; P<.001) — a 45% relative reduction in the risk of progression or death. Overall survival, the trial's primary endpoint, did not differ: median 12.4 versus 12.9 months (hazard ratio 0.87; P=.37) at an interim analysis with 64% of patients censored. The commonest grade 3–4 adverse effects on trabectedin were myelosuppression and transient transaminase elevations. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): trabectedin delays progression versus dacarbazine in heavily pretreated L-sarcomas; a survival benefit was not shown.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — trabectedin improved PFS versus dacarbazine (4.2 vs 1.5 months, HR 0.55) in one phase 3 trial, with no overall-survival difference; single-trial

title: Regorafenib after sorafenib in liver cancer (RESORCE): median survival 10.6 versus 7.8 months — the first second-line survival win, paid for in hypertension and hand-foot reactions
question: In patients with hepatocellular carcinoma progressing on sorafenib, does regorafenib improve survival compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a real survival gain in one double-blind trial. In RESORCE (Bruix J et al., PMID: 27932229), 573 patients with hepatocellular carcinoma who had tolerated and progressed on sorafenib, with Child-Pugh A liver function, were randomised 2:1 to regorafenib 160 mg (weeks 1–3 of each 4-week cycle) plus best supportive care or placebo. Median overall survival was 10.6 months versus 7.8 months (hazard ratio 0.63; 95% CI 0.50–0.79; one-sided p<0.0001) — a 37% relative reduction in the risk of death, 2.8 months at the median. The price: grade 3–4 hypertension in 15% versus 5%, hand-foot skin reaction in 13% versus 1%, fatigue in 9% versus 5%; adverse events occurred in 100% of regorafenib recipients versus 93% on placebo, though deaths attributed to study drug were 2% versus 1%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): regorafenib extends survival after sorafenib in patients fit enough to have tolerated sorafenib, with substantial symptomatic toxicity.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — regorafenib improved median OS after sorafenib (10.6 vs 7.8 months, HR 0.63) in one double-blind phase 3 trial; single-trial

title: Cabozantinib in previously treated liver cancer (CELESTIAL): median survival 10.2 versus 8.0 months — high-grade adverse events roughly double (68% versus 36%)
question: In patients with previously treated advanced hepatocellular carcinoma, does cabozantinib improve survival compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a survival gain in one double-blind trial, with a heavy toxicity bill. In CELESTIAL (Abou-Alfa GK et al., PMID: 29972759), 707 patients with advanced hepatocellular carcinoma previously treated with sorafenib (up to two prior systemic regimens) were randomised 2:1 to cabozantinib 60 mg daily or placebo. Median overall survival was 10.2 versus 8.0 months (hazard ratio for death 0.76; 95% CI 0.63 to 0.92; P=0.005) — a 24% relative reduction in the risk of death. Median progression-free survival was 5.2 versus 1.9 months (HR 0.44; 95% CI 0.36 to 0.52), and objective response rates were 4% versus less than 1% (P=0.009). Grade 3–4 adverse events occurred in 68% versus 36% — palmar-plantar erythrodysesthesia 17% versus 0%, hypertension 16% versus 2%, raised aspartate aminotransferase 12% versus 7%, fatigue 10% versus 4%, diarrhoea 10% versus 2%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): cabozantinib extends survival after sorafenib, at roughly double the high-grade adverse-event rate.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — cabozantinib improved median OS in previously treated HCC (10.2 vs 8.0 months, HR 0.76) in one double-blind phase 3 trial; single-trial

title: Ramucirumab in liver cancer with alpha-fetoprotein ≥400 ng/mL (REACH-2): median survival 8.5 versus 7.3 months — the first biomarker-selected win in this disease
question: In patients with advanced hepatocellular carcinoma and elevated alpha-fetoprotein after sorafenib, does ramucirumab improve survival compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a modest survival gain in one double-blind trial, in a biomarker-defined subgroup. In REACH-2 (Zhu AX et al., PMID: 30665869), 292 patients with advanced hepatocellular carcinoma, Child-Pugh A, and alpha-fetoprotein of at least 400 ng/mL after first-line sorafenib were randomised 2:1 to ramucirumab 8 mg/kg every 2 weeks or placebo, both with best supportive care. Median overall survival was 8.5 versus 7.3 months (hazard ratio 0.710; 95% CI 0.531–0.949; p=0.0199) — a 29% relative reduction in the risk of death, 1.2 months at the median. Median progression-free survival was 2.8 versus 1.6 months (HR 0.452; p<0.0001); objective response did not differ significantly (5% versus 1%; p=0.1697), and neither time to symptom deterioration nor time to performance-status deterioration differed. Grade 3 or worse hypertension occurred in 13% versus 5% and hyponatraemia in 6% versus 0%; serious adverse events in 35% versus 29%, with three treatment-related deaths on ramucirumab. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): ramucirumab extends survival modestly in AFP-high hepatocellular carcinoma after sorafenib.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — ramucirumab improved median OS in AFP ≥400 ng/mL HCC after sorafenib (8.5 vs 7.3 months, HR 0.71) in one double-blind phase 3 trial; single-trial

title: Fruquintinib in refractory metastatic colorectal cancer: two trials, one answer — median survival 9.3 versus 6.6 months (FRESCO) and 7.4 versus 4.8 months (FRESCO-2)
question: In patients with metastatic colorectal cancer after standard therapies, does fruquintinib improve overall survival compared with placebo?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — two concordant double-blind trials, one in China and one global. In FRESCO (Li J et al., PMID: 29946728), 416 Chinese patients whose metastatic colorectal cancer had progressed after at least two chemotherapy lines (no prior VEGFR inhibitor) were randomised 2:1 to fruquintinib 5 mg (21 days on, 7 off) or placebo: median overall survival 9.3 versus 6.6 months (hazard ratio 0.65; 95% CI 0.51–0.83; P<.001) and median progression-free survival 3.7 versus 1.8 months (HR 0.26). In FRESCO-2 (Dasari A et al., PMID: 37331369), 691 heavily pretreated patients across 14 countries (median four prior lines; all had received standard therapies and progressed on or were intolerant to trifluridine-tipiracil or regorafenib or both): median overall survival 7.4 versus 4.8 months (HR 0.66; 95% CI 0.55–0.80; p<0.0001). Grade 3–4 treatment-emergent events occurred in 61.2% versus 19.7% in FRESCO; grade 3 or worse events in 63% versus 50% in FRESCO-2, hypertension the commonest (14% on fruquintinib in FRESCO-2). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): fruquintinib extends survival by roughly 2.6–2.7 months at the median in refractory metastatic colorectal cancer, with substantial toxicity.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — fruquintinib improved median OS in two double-blind phase 3 trials (9.3 vs 6.6 months, HR 0.65; 7.4 vs 4.8 months, HR 0.66)
