title: Perioperative durvalumab with neoadjuvant chemotherapy in bladder cancer (NIAGARA): 24-month event-free survival 67.8% versus 59.8%, overall survival 82.2% versus 75.2% — no added grade 3–4 toxicity
question: In patients with muscle-invasive bladder cancer, does perioperative durvalumab added to neoadjuvant chemotherapy improve event-free and overall survival compared with chemotherapy alone?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — event-free and overall survival both improved in one large open-label trial. In NIAGARA (Powles T et al., PMID: 39282910), 1,063 cisplatin-eligible patients with muscle-invasive bladder cancer were randomised to neoadjuvant durvalumab plus gemcitabine–cisplatin for four cycles, then radical cystectomy and eight cycles of adjuvant durvalumab, or to neoadjuvant gemcitabine–cisplatin then cystectomy alone. Estimated event-free survival at 24 months was 67.8% versus 59.8% (hazard ratio 0.68; 95% CI 0.56 to 0.82; P<0.001) — a 32% relative reduction in the risk of progression, recurrence, not undergoing cystectomy, or death. Estimated overall survival at 24 months was 82.2% versus 75.2% (HR 0.75; 95% CI 0.59 to 0.93; P=0.01) — a 25% relative reduction in the risk of death, 7.0 percentage points absolute. Grade 3–4 treatment-related adverse events were 40.6% versus 40.9%, treatment-related deaths 0.6% in each group, and cystectomy was performed in 88.0% versus 83.2%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): perioperative durvalumab improves event-free and overall survival around cystectomy without measurably adding high-grade toxicity.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — perioperative durvalumab improved 24-month EFS (67.8% vs 59.8%, HR 0.68) and OS (82.2% vs 75.2%, HR 0.75) in one phase 3 trial; single-trial

title: Tivozanib versus sorafenib as third- or fourth-line therapy in kidney cancer (TIVO-3): progression-free survival 5.6 versus 3.9 months in an open-label trial — survival not the endpoint won
question: In patients with relapsed or refractory advanced renal cell carcinoma, does tivozanib improve progression-free survival compared with sorafenib?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a progression-free survival gain in one open-label trial. In TIVO-3 (Rini BI et al., PMID: 31810797), 350 patients with metastatic renal cell carcinoma who had received at least two previous systemic treatments (including at least one VEGFR inhibitor) were randomised to tivozanib 1.5 mg daily in 4-week cycles or sorafenib 400 mg twice daily. Median progression-free survival by independent review was 5.6 versus 3.9 months (hazard ratio 0.73; 95% CI 0.56–0.94; p=0.016) — a 27% relative reduction in the risk of progression or death, 1.7 months at the median, at a median follow-up of 19.0 months. The commonest grade 3–4 treatment-related adverse event was hypertension: 20% on tivozanib versus 14% on sorafenib. Serious treatment-related adverse events occurred in 11% versus 10%, with no treatment-related deaths. The authors report tivozanib was better tolerated overall than sorafenib. Overall survival was not the endpoint this record reports as won. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): tivozanib delays progression versus sorafenib as third- or fourth-line therapy; a survival benefit is not shown in this record.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — tivozanib improved median PFS versus sorafenib as third/fourth-line therapy (5.6 vs 3.9 months, HR 0.73) in one open-label phase 3 trial; single-trial

title: Aspirin in hospitalised COVID-19: 17% died within 28 days in both groups in RECOVERY — fewer thrombotic events, more major bleeding, and discharge about a day sooner
question: In hospitalised adults with COVID-19, does aspirin reduce 28-day mortality compared with usual care?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — for survival, in one very large open-label trial. In RECOVERY, 17% of patients allocated aspirin 150 mg daily and 17% allocated usual care alone died within 28 days (rate ratio 0.96, 95% CI 0.89–1.04; p=0.35). Aspirin did shift secondary outcomes in opposite directions: thrombotic events fell (4.6% vs 5.3%) while major bleeding rose (1.6% vs 1.0%), hospital stay was slightly shorter (median 8 vs 9 days), and slightly more patients were discharged alive within 28 days (75% vs 74%; rate ratio 1.06, 95% CI 1.02–1.10). The composite of invasive mechanical ventilation or death among those not ventilated at baseline was 21% vs 22% (risk ratio 0.96, 95% CI 0.90–1.03). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): aspirin does not reduce 28-day mortality in hospitalised COVID-19; its small antithrombotic gain is offset by a small bleeding cost. Single-trial shelf — flagged in the summary.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — 28-day mortality identical at 17% in both groups in the single large RECOVERY comparison; thrombotic events down, major bleeding up

title: Remdesivir in hospitalised COVID-19: recovery five days faster in the blinded ACTT-1 trial, but no significant mortality benefit in any trial — and none at all once patients were ventilated
question: In hospitalised adults with COVID-19, does remdesivir shorten time to recovery and reduce mortality compared with placebo or standard care?
balance: SPLIT — recovery is faster, survival is not proven. In the double-blind ACTT-1 trial, remdesivir shortened median recovery from 15 to 10 days (rate ratio for recovery 1.29, 95% CI 1.12–1.49; p<0.001), while day-29 mortality was 11.4% vs 15.2% (hazard ratio 0.73, 95% CI 0.52–1.03) — not significant. The smaller blinded Wang trial in severe disease found no significant difference in time to clinical improvement (hazard ratio 1.23, 95% CI 0.87–1.75). The open-label WHO Solidarity final analysis, the largest comparison, found in-hospital mortality of 14.5% vs 15.6% (rate ratio 0.91, 95% CI 0.82–1.02), with a small effect in patients not yet ventilated (rate ratio 0.86, 95% CI 0.76–0.98 for those not ventilated initially) and none in those already ventilated (rate ratio 1.13, 95% CI 0.89–1.42). PROPOSED SPLIT: a real recovery-time benefit in non-ventilated hospitalised patients; no demonstrated mortality benefit overall and no benefit once ventilated.
stamp: SPLIT — POSSIBLE (benefit) for time to recovery; POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for mortality

title: Convalescent plasma in hospitalised COVID-19: 28-day mortality 24% versus 24% in RECOVERY's 11,558 patients — and no benefit in the critically ill or in CONCOR-1 either
question: In hospitalised adults with COVID-19, does high-titre convalescent plasma reduce mortality compared with usual care?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — three randomised trials agree. In RECOVERY, 28-day mortality was 24% in both groups (rate ratio 1.00, 95% CI 0.93–1.07; p=0.95), including in patients seronegative at randomisation, and discharge within 28 days was 66% vs 66%. In critically ill patients in REMAP-CAP, plasma met the prespecified futility criterion: median organ support-free days 0 vs 3, median-adjusted odds ratio 0.97 (95% credible interval 0.83–1.15), in-hospital mortality 37.3% vs 38.4%, and serious adverse events 3.0% vs 1.3%. In CONCOR-1, intubation or death by day 30 was 32.4% on plasma vs 28.0% on standard care (relative risk 1.16, 95% CI 0.94–1.43), with more serious adverse events on plasma (33.4% vs 26.4%; relative risk 1.27, 95% CI 1.02–1.57). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): high-titre convalescent plasma given after hospital admission does not improve survival or other clinical outcomes. The early outpatient plasma question is a different shelf (#2212) and is not duplicated here.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — mortality identical in RECOVERY (24% vs 24%), futility in REMAP-CAP, and a numerically worse primary outcome in CONCOR-1

title: Casirivimab–imdevimab in hospitalised COVID-19: 28-day mortality 24% versus 30% in patients with no antibodies of their own — and no benefit in those who already had them
question: In hospitalised adults with COVID-19, does casirivimab–imdevimab reduce mortality in patients without their own antibodies compared with usual care?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — confined to seronegative patients, in a single large open-label trial. In RECOVERY's primary efficacy population of patients without detectable anti-SARS-CoV-2 antibodies at randomisation, 24% (396 of 1,633) allocated casirivimab 4 g plus imdevimab 4 g died within 28 days versus 30% (452 of 1,520) on usual care (rate ratio 0.79, 95% CI 0.69–0.91; p=0.0009) — a 21% relative reduction in mortality with the absolute rates printed alongside. In all randomised patients regardless of antibody status, mortality was 19% vs 21% (rate ratio 0.94, 95% CI 0.86–1.02; p=0.14), and the effect differed significantly by serostatus (p for heterogeneity = 0.002). No deaths were attributed to the treatment and prespecified safety outcomes did not differ meaningfully. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the antibody combination reduces mortality only in hospitalised patients who have not mounted their own antibody response. Single-trial shelf — flagged in the summary.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — 28-day mortality 24% vs 30% (rate ratio 0.79) in seronegative patients in the single RECOVERY comparison; no benefit in seropositive patients

title: Doxycycline for community COVID-19: recovery half a day sooner at most and hospitalisation 5.3% versus 4.5% in PRINCIPLE — the trial was stopped for futility
question: In adults with COVID-19 in the community, does doxycycline improve recovery and reduce hospitalisation compared with usual care alone?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — from a single large open-label community trial, stopped for futility. In PRINCIPLE, median time to first self-reported recovery was 9.6 days on doxycycline versus 10.1 days on usual care (hazard ratio 1.04, 95% Bayesian credible interval 0.93–1.17), an estimated benefit of 0.5 days with a probability of only 0.10 that the benefit reached the 1.5-day threshold for clinical meaningfulness. Hospitalisation or death related to COVID-19 occurred in 5.3% of the doxycycline group and 4.5% of the usual care group (estimated absolute difference −0.5%, 95% Bayesian credible interval −2.6 to 1.4), and there were five deaths (0.6%) on doxycycline versus two (0.2%) on usual care. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): doxycycline should not be used as a routine community treatment for COVID-19. Single-trial shelf — flagged in the summary.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — recovery 9.6 vs 10.1 days and hospitalisation or death 5.3% vs 4.5% in the single PRINCIPLE comparison, stopped for futility

title: Higher-dose dexamethasone in COVID-19: mortality rose from 12% to 19% in RECOVERY's patients on simple oxygen — while 12 mg versus 6 mg in sicker patients in COVID STEROID 2 was a non-significant trend the other way
question: In adults with hospitalised COVID-19 on oxygen, does higher-dose dexamethasone improve survival compared with usual-dose corticosteroid care?
balance: SPLIT — by how sick the patient is. In RECOVERY's comparison in patients with hypoxia receiving no oxygen or simple oxygen only, higher-dose corticosteroids (dexamethasone 20 mg daily for 5 days, then 10 mg for 5 days) increased 28-day mortality: 19% (123 of 659) versus 12% (75 of 613) on usual care, in which 87% received low-dose corticosteroids (rate ratio 1.59, 95% CI 1.20–2.10; p=0.0012) — recruitment to this group was stopped early on safety grounds. Non-COVID pneumonia (10% vs 6%) and hyperglycaemia requiring more insulin (22% vs 14%) were also more frequent. In COVID STEROID 2, in patients with severe hypoxemia, dexamethasone 12 mg versus 6 mg daily did not significantly change days alive without life support at 28 days (median 22.0 vs 20.5 days; adjusted mean difference 1.3 days, 95% CI 0–2.6; p=0.07), with 28-day mortality of 27.1% vs 32.3% (adjusted relative risk 0.86, 99% CI 0.68–1.08). PROPOSED SPLIT: higher-dose corticosteroids harm patients on simple oxygen; in severe hypoxemia the question remains open, with a non-significant trend favouring 12 mg that the trial may have been underpowered to settle.
stamp: SPLIT — POSSIBLE (harm) for higher-dose corticosteroids in patients on no/simple oxygen; MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) for 12 mg vs 6 mg in severe hypoxemia (unresolved)

title: Azithromycin for community COVID-19: recovery no faster and hospitalisation 3% in both groups in PRINCIPLE — and 28-day mortality 22% versus 22% when RECOVERY tested it in hospital
question: In patients with suspected COVID-19 in the community, does azithromycin improve recovery and reduce hospitalisation compared with usual care?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — in the community and in hospital alike. In PRINCIPLE, among people at increased risk of an adverse course with suspected COVID-19 in the community, 80% on azithromycin 500 mg daily for 3 days and 77% on usual care reported feeling recovered within 28 days, with little evidence of a meaningful benefit in time to first reported recovery (hazard ratio 1.08, 95% Bayesian credible interval 0.95–1.23; estimated benefit in median time to recovery 0.94 days, 95% BCI −0.56 to 2.43; probability of a clinically meaningful benefit of at least 1.5 days was 0.23). Hospitalisation was 3% in both groups (16 of 500 vs 28 of 823; absolute benefit 0.3%, 95% BCI −1.7 to 2.2), and there were no deaths in either group. In hospital, RECOVERY found 28-day mortality of 22% in both groups (rate ratio 0.97, 95% CI 0.87–1.07; p=0.50). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): azithromycin does not speed recovery or reduce hospitalisation in community COVID-19, and its routine use carries an antibiotic-stewardship cost the PRINCIPLE authors state plainly.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — no recovery or hospitalisation benefit in the community PRINCIPLE trial, and no mortality benefit in hospital in RECOVERY

title: Corticosteroids in dengue do not prevent shock or save lives: a 225-patient placebo trial found no clinical benefit, and a Cochrane review of 8 trials (948 patients) found no effect on death
question: In patients with dengue, do corticosteroids improve outcomes in early dengue or dengue shock compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — corticosteroids are biologically plausible in dengue, where complications are thought to be immunologically mediated, and the trials say they do not work. In Vietnam (Tam DT et al., PMID: 22865871), 225 patients aged 5–20 years admitted within 72 hours of fever were randomised to low-dose (0.5 mg/kg) or high-dose (2 mg/kg) oral prednisolone for 3 days or placebo: all patients recovered fully, and apart from a trend toward hyperglycaemia in steroid recipients there was no association between treatment and any predefined clinical, haematological or virological endpoint, and no reduction in shock or other complications. The Cochrane review (Zhang F et al., PMID: 24984082) pooled eight trials enrolling 948 participants: in dengue shock, four trials in 284 children detected no effect on death, transfusion, pulmonary haemorrhage, convulsions or hospital stay; in early dengue, four trials in 664 patients found no evidence of an effect on mortality or on severe complications such as shock. The review's honest caveat is that the shock trials are old and small, so a modest effect in shock is not excluded — but nothing in the record supports giving steroids. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): corticosteroids show no benefit in early dengue or dengue shock in the randomised evidence.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — a placebo-controlled trial and a Cochrane review of 8 trials found no effect of corticosteroids on dengue death, shock or complications

title: Hyperbaric oxygen for carbon monoxide poisoning: one positive trial (cognitive sequelae 25.0% versus 46.1%) against two that found nothing — and harm signals when treatment was pushed harder
question: In patients with acute carbon monoxide poisoning, does hyperbaric oxygen reduce delayed cognitive sequelae compared with normobaric oxygen?
balance: SPLIT — the three randomised trials point in three directions. Weaver 2002 (PMID: 12362006), the only double-blind trial stopped early for benefit, found cognitive sequelae at six weeks in 25.0% on three hyperbaric sessions versus 46.1% on normobaric oxygen (P=0.007). Scheinkestel 1999 (PMID: 10092916) found no outcome measure worse on normobaric oxygen, more additional treatments on hyperbaric oxygen (28% versus 15%, P=0.01), and delayed neurological sequelae restricted to the hyperbaric group (P=0.03). Annane 2011 (PMID: 21125215) found one-month complete recovery of 58% with one hyperbaric session versus 61% on normobaric oxygen alone in patients with transient loss of consciousness, and significantly worse recovery with two hyperbaric sessions than one in comatose patients (47% versus 68%). PROPOSED SPLIT: benefit shown in one early-stopped trial, no benefit in two others, and worse outcomes when hyperbaric treatment was intensified — the question remains genuinely unsettled.
stamp: SPLIT — Weaver 2002 positive for cognitive sequelae, Scheinkestel 1999 and Annane 2011 null, with harm signals at higher hyperbaric dose in Annane trial B and Scheinkestel

title: Lofexidine eases opioid withdrawal and keeps more people in treatment: completion 41.5% and 39.6% versus 27.8% on placebo in the larger trial, with symptom scores lower in both trials
question: In patients with opioid withdrawal, does lofexidine reduce withdrawal severity and improve treatment completion compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two concordant double-blind placebo-controlled trials. Gorodetzky 2017 (PMID: 28527421, n=264) found lower Day 3 withdrawal scores on lofexidine than placebo (SOWS-Gossop 6.32 versus 8.67, p=0.0212) and fewer early terminators (59 versus 80). Fishman 2019 (PMID: 30531234, n=603) found significantly lower overall SOWS-Gossop scores at both doses (differences −0.21 and −0.26 on log-transformed scores; P=0.02 and P=0.003) and higher 7-day completion: 41.5% on 2.16 mg/day and 39.6% on 2.88 mg/day versus 27.8% on placebo — absolute gains of about 14 and 12 percentage points (relative increases of 85% and 71% as printed in the record). The price is cardiovascular: orthostatic hypotension, hypotension and bradycardia were the common adverse events, though they rarely stopped treatment. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): lofexidine modestly reduces withdrawal symptoms and meaningfully improves completion of a withdrawal episode.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two double-blind placebo-controlled trials with lower withdrawal scores and higher completion on lofexidine; hypotension and bradycardia are the common adverse events

title: Rifaximin shortens travellers' diarrhoea by about a day: time to last unformed stool 32–33 hours versus 60–66 hours on placebo in two double-blind trials — for non-invasive pathogens
question: In travellers with travellers' diarrhoea, does rifaximin shorten illness compared with placebo?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — two double-blind placebo-controlled trials agree. Taylor 2006 (PMID: 16760520, n=399) found a median time to last unformed stool of 32.0 hours on rifaximin 200 mg three times daily versus 65.5 hours on placebo (P=0.001), essentially matching ciprofloxacin (28.8 hours). Steffen 2003 (PMID: 12809830, n=380) found 32.5 and 32.9 hours on rifaximin 600 and 1200 mg/day versus 60.0 hours on placebo (p=0.0001). The catch is the pathogen: rifaximin was less effective than ciprofloxacin against invasive intestinal bacterial pathogens, so the benefit is for the non-invasive, non-bloody illness that makes up most travellers' diarrhoea. No relevant side effects were reported in Steffen; Taylor found rifaximin safe. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): about a day less illness for non-invasive travellers' diarrhoea.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — two double-blind placebo-controlled trials halving time to last unformed stool (about 32 versus 60–66 hours); weaker against invasive pathogens

title: Ibuprofen cut acute mountain sickness on rapid ascent in two trials (43% versus 69%; 24.4% versus 40.4% in intention-to-treat) — but the larger trial's per-protocol analysis went null, and ibuprofen can mask the headache that defines the diagnosis
question: In people ascending rapidly to high altitude, does ibuprofen prevent acute mountain sickness compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two double-blind placebo-controlled trials, positive on their primary analyses, with an honest crack in the larger one. Lipman 2012 (PMID: 22440488) found acute mountain sickness in 43% on ibuprofen 600 mg three times daily versus 69% on placebo on ascent to 3,810 m (odds ratio 0.3, 95% CI 0.1 to 0.8; number needed to treat 3.9), with lower severity scores (3.2 versus 4.4). Gertsch 2012 (ASCENT, PMID: 23098412) found acute mountain sickness in 24.4% versus 40.4% in the intention-to-treat analysis (P=.01) and less high-altitude headache (42.3% versus 60.5%, P<.01) — but among the 183 of 294 recruits who completed the trial per protocol, the difference was not significant (22.7% versus 32.9%, P=.129). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): ibuprofen probably reduces acute mountain sickness on rapid ascent, with the per-protocol null and the headache-masking problem printed on the face of the shelf.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two double-blind placebo-controlled trials positive on primary analyses; the larger trial's per-protocol analysis was not significant, and headache masking may artefact the diagnosis

title: Ocriplasmin injection: vitreomacular adhesion released in 26.5% versus 10.1% and macular holes closed without surgery in 40.6% versus 10.6% — but most eyes still need watching or surgery, and transient ocular side effects are common
question: In patients with symptomatic vitreomacular traction, does a single intravitreal ocriplasmin injection release the traction and close macular holes compared with placebo injection?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two concordant phase 3 trials, a real but minority anatomical win. In the pooled MIVI-TRUST trials (Stalmans P et al., PMID: 22894573), vitreomacular adhesion resolved by day 28 in 26.5% of ocriplasmin eyes versus 10.1% on placebo (P<0.001), and macular holes closed without surgery in 40.6% versus 10.6% (P<0.001). The price is transient ocular adverse events in 68.4% versus 53.5% (floaters, photopsia, injection pain, conjunctival haemorrhage), with serious ocular events similar between groups. Three of four treated eyes did not achieve release, so this is an option that spares a minority an operation, not a replacement for vitrectomy. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a single ocriplasmin injection releases traction and closes holes in a substantial minority, best in younger, phakic eyes with focal adhesion and small holes.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two phase 3 trials show adhesion release in 26.5% versus 10.1% and non-surgical hole closure in 40.6% versus 10.6%, with frequent transient ocular adverse events

title: Dexamethasone implant for macular oedema after retinal vein occlusion: vision improves faster and more often than sham in two identical trials — the gain peaks by day 90, and repeated implants bring cataract progression in 29.8% of phakic eyes
question: In macular oedema after retinal vein occlusion, does the dexamethasone intravitreal implant improve vision compared with sham — and at what cataract and pressure cost?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — faster, more frequent visual improvement, paid for in pressure rises and, with repeat dosing, cataract. In the two identical GENEVA trials (Haller JA et al., PMID: 20417567), eyes on the dexamethasone implant reached a ≥15-letter gain significantly sooner than sham (P<0.001), with the advantage concentrated at days 30–90; intraocular pressure ≥25 mmHg peaked at 16% at day 60 and was back to sham levels by day 180. Over 12 months with a second implant (PMID: 21764136), ≥15-letter gains were seen in 30% and 32% of patients 60 days after the first and second implants, but cataract progression occurred in 29.8% of phakic eyes receiving two 0.7 mg implants versus 5.7% on sham. This shelf is a different drug and question from the ranibizumab shelf for the same condition (live #894). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a real short-horizon visual gain with a steroid's predictable ocular price.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two sham-controlled trials show faster ≥15-letter improvement versus sham, with transient pressure rises and cataract progression in 29.8% of phakic eyes after two implants

title: Fluocinolone implant in diabetic macular oedema (FAME): ≥15-letter gains in 28.7% versus 18.9% on sham at three years — but the benefit lives in chronic oedema (34.0% versus 13.4%), is absent in newer oedema, and nearly every phakic eye develops cataract
question: In diabetic macular oedema, does the fluocinolone acetonide implant sustain vision compared with sham or laser in the FAME trials?
balance: SPLIT — benefit in chronic oedema, none shown in non-chronic oedema, with a heavy steroid price either way. In the two FAME trials (Campochiaro PA et al., PMID: 22727177), ≥15-letter gains at month 36 were 28.7% (low-dose insert) and 27.8% (high-dose) versus 18.9% on sham (P=0.018). The preplanned duration analysis (Cunha-Vaz J et al., PMID: 24935282) splits the result: in oedema present ≥3 years, low-dose gains were 34.0% versus 13.4% on sham (P<0.001); in oedema under 3 years, 22.3% versus 27.8% (P=0.275) — no benefit. Almost all phakic patients on the insert developed cataract, and incisional glaucoma surgery by month 36 was needed in 4.8% (low dose) and 8.1% (high dose). This is a different implant from the dexamethasone implant shelf in diabetic macular oedema (pack #4021). PROPOSED SPLIT: reserve judgement for chronic, previously laser-treated oedema; the trials do not support it earlier in the disease.
stamp: SPLIT — POSSIBLE (benefit) in chronic (≥3 years) diabetic macular oedema / no benefit shown in non-chronic oedema, with near-universal cataract in phakic eyes and glaucoma surgery in 4.8–8.1%

title: Steroid irrigations after sinus surgery: one small double-blind trial found better symptom and endoscopy scores with budesonide rinses, a Samter's-triad trial found no added benefit over saline — and neither measured relapse or revision surgery
question: After endoscopic sinus surgery for chronic rhinosinusitis, do high-volume corticosteroid irrigations reduce relapse and revision surgery compared with saline irrigation?
balance: SPLIT — the two double-blind trials disagree, and the outcome the question asks about was never measured. In a general chronic rhinosinusitis population after surgery (Ahamed S et al., PMID: 38440477), budesonide irrigation (0.5 mg in 200 mL, twice daily) beat saline on 3-month symptom scores (SNOT-22 26.69 versus 30.54; p<0.0001) and endoscopy scores. In Samter's triad patients (Rotenberg BW et al., PMID: 21997904), adding budesonide — as spray or mixed into irrigation — gave no benefit over saline irrigation alone at 6 or 12 months. Neither trial reported relapse rates or revision surgery, so any claim about preventing re-operation is unsupported by this record. This shelf is distinct from live #905 (surgery versus clarithromycin in chronic rhinosinusitis). PROPOSED SPLIT: possible short-term symptom benefit in ordinary post-surgical rhinosinusitis; no shown benefit in Samter's triad; revision surgery unstudied.
stamp: SPLIT — POSSIBLE (benefit) for short-term symptom/endoscopy scores in general post-surgical chronic rhinosinusitis / no added benefit in Samter's triad, and relapse or revision surgery measured in neither trial

title: Articaine versus lidocaine for dental anaesthesia: success odds roughly doubled overall (OR 2.44) and nearly quadrupled for infiltration (OR 3.81) — the edge shrinks for nerve blocks and vanishes in symptomatic teeth; paraesthesia was not a randomised-trial finding
question: For dental extractions and oral surgery, is articaine more effective than lidocaine for successful local anaesthesia, and does it carry more paraesthesia?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for anaesthetic success, with the advantage depending on technique. Pooling the randomised trials (Brandt RG et al., PMID: 21531931), articaine's odds of successful pulpal anaesthesia were 2.44 times lidocaine's (95% CI 1.59–3.76), rising to an odds ratio of 3.81 (2.71–5.36) for infiltration but only 1.57 (1.12–2.21) for mandibular block, with no difference in symptomatic teeth. A second meta-analysis (Katyal V et al., PMID: 20006669) found a relative success risk of 1.31 (1.12–1.54) in the posterior first molar and no difference in post-injection adverse events (relative risk 1.05, 0.66–1.65). On paraesthesia: neither meta-analysis of the randomised trials reports a paraesthesia excess — that concern rests on observational reports outside this randomised record, and this shelf does not card it as a trial finding. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): choose articaine where infiltration success matters; do not expect a block advantage in hot, symptomatic teeth.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two meta-analyses of randomised trials show higher anaesthetic success with articaine (OR 2.44 overall; 3.81 infiltration; 1.57 block; none in symptomatic teeth) and no difference in post-injection adverse events

title: Dexamethasone around third-molar surgery: pooled trials show less early pain (NNT 4) and less swelling (NNT 5) with submucosal injection — the trismus gain is under 5 mm and not clinically significant
question: In patients having surgical removal of impacted third molars, does pre- or peri-operative dexamethasone reduce swelling, trismus and pain compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — consistent across two meta-analyses for pain and swelling, weakest exactly where patients hope most (jaw opening). The larger pooled analysis (O'Hare PE et al., PMID: 31078366; 17 trials of submucosal dexamethasone) found the greatest clinical effects were early postoperative pain (number needed to treat 4) and early oedema (NNT 5), with moderate-quality evidence for late pain and early oedema reduction — but the trismus reduction was under 5 mm and not clinically significant. The earlier meta-analysis (Moraschini V et al., PMID: 26458538; 8 articles) agrees: oedema and pain reduced, no statistically significant difference for trismus. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a peri-operative dexamethasone injection buys a modest, real reduction in pain and swelling over the first days; it does not meaningfully loosen a stiff jaw.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two meta-analyses of randomised trials: submucosal dexamethasone reduces early pain (NNT 4) and oedema (NNT 5) after third-molar surgery; trismus effect <5 mm and not clinically significant

title: Tranexamic acid mouthwash after dental extraction on anticoagulants: in the warfarin era it cut bleeding patients from 8 of 20 to 1 of 19 — in the modern NOAC trial the primary outcome was null (26.4% versus 28.6%), with fewer delayed bleeds only
question: In patients on oral anticoagulants having dental extractions, does tranexamic acid mouthwash reduce postoperative bleeding compared with placebo or standard care?
balance: SPLIT — by anticoagulant era and by bleeding timing. In 1989, in patients continuing warfarin-type anticoagulation (Sindet-Pedersen S et al., PMID: 2648144), tranexamic acid mouthwash (4.8% solution, four times daily for 7 days) left 1 of 19 patients with a postoperative bleed versus 8 of 20 patients (10 episodes) on placebo (P=0.01), with no systemic side effects. In the modern EXTRACT-NOAC trial (Ockerman A et al., PMID: 33939696), 10% tranexamic acid mouthwash did not reduce any post-extraction bleeding by day 7 (26.4% versus 28.6%; relative risk 0.92, 95% CI 0.60–1.42; P=0.72), though delayed bleeding (rate ratio 0.32, 0.12–0.89) and bleeding after multiple extractions (rate ratio 0.40, 0.20–0.78) were lower. PROPOSED SPLIT: a large benefit in the small older warfarin trial; in today's NOAC patients, no overall benefit, with a possible delayed-bleed advantage.
stamp: SPLIT — large benefit in the 1989 warfarin-era trial (1/19 versus 8/20 patients bleeding) / primary outcome null in the modern NOAC trial (RR 0.92), with fewer delayed and multiple-extraction bleeds

title: Socket preservation grafting: about 2 mm less horizontal and 1.7 mm less vertical ridge shrinkage across 22 randomised trials — whether that buys better implants later was not shown
question: In patients having a tooth extracted, does socket (ridge) preservation grafting reduce ridge resorption and improve later implant outcomes compared with unassisted healing?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for ridge dimensions, a surrogate; the implant-outcome half of the question is unverified. Across 22 randomised trials (Avila-Ortiz G et al., PMID: 30623987), socket grafting (ridge preservation) versus extraction alone prevented horizontal resorption by a pooled 1.99 mm (95% CI 1.54–2.44; p<0.00001), vertical mid-buccal resorption by 1.72 mm (0.96–2.48) and vertical mid-lingual resorption by 1.16 mm (0.81–1.52) at 3–6 months, with the largest preservation where the buccal wall was thicker than 1.0 mm (3.2 mm versus 1.29 mm for thinner walls, allograft subgroup). No superior graft modality could be determined, and patient-reported outcomes were comparable in the two studies reporting them. Neither this record nor any card below demonstrates fewer failed implants, fewer later augmentations, or better prosthetic outcomes. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): grafting preserves roughly 1–2 mm of ridge that would otherwise be lost; whether that millimetre changes the implant story is asserted by practice, not shown by these trials.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — meta-analysis of 22 RCTs: socket grafting reduces horizontal resorption by 1.99 mm and vertical buccal resorption by 1.72 mm at 3–6 months; later implant outcomes not demonstrated

title: Antibiotic prophylaxis at dental implant placement: older pooled trials suggested fewer failures (RR 0.40, NNT 33) — the largest modern placebo trial found failures of 2.5% versus 3.0% and no significant benefit
question: In patients receiving dental implants, does antibiotic prophylaxis reduce early implant failure and postoperative infection compared with placebo?
balance: SPLIT — by era and baseline risk. The Cochrane-based review (Esposito M et al., PMID: 20623035) pooled 4 randomised trials and found significantly more implant failures without antibiotics (risk ratio 0.40, 95% CI 0.19–0.84, favouring prophylaxis), translating to a number needed to treat of 33 at a 5% control failure rate, with no significant difference in infections or adverse events. The largest single trial since (Momand P et al., PMID: 35075765; 474 patients, 2 g amoxicillin versus placebo, double-blind) found implant failures in 2.5% on antibiotics versus 3.0% on placebo and infections in 0.8% versus 2.1% — both non-significant — and its authors conclude prophylaxis is likely of small benefit and should be avoided in most cases. PROPOSED SPLIT: where baseline failure risk is low, routine prophylaxis buys little; the older pooled benefit was estimated at higher baseline risk.
stamp: SPLIT — older pooled RCTs favour prophylaxis (failure RR 0.40; NNT 33 at 5% baseline risk) / largest modern double-blind trial null (failures 2.5% versus 3.0%, infections 0.8% versus 2.1%, both non-significant)

title: Full-mouth disinfection within 24 hours versus quadrant-by-quadrant cleaning: across 20 randomised trials there was no benefit in pocket depth (MD 0.11 mm) or attachment at 6–8 months — one visit or four, the gums end up the same
question: In patients with chronic periodontitis, does full-mouth disinfection within 24 hours improve probing depth compared with quadrant-wise scaling and root planing over weeks?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — a well-pooled null. The Cochrane review (Jervøe-Storm PM et al., PMID: 35763286) included 20 randomised trials with 944 participants: at 6–8 months, full-mouth disinfection versus conventional quadrant scaling and root planing showed no evidence of benefit for probing pocket depth (mean difference 0.11 mm, 95% CI −0.04 to 0.27; 6 trials, 224 participants; low-certainty) or clinical attachment gain (0.07 mm, −0.11 to 0.24), and full-mouth scaling without antiseptic was likewise null (pocket depth mean difference 0.03 mm, −0.14 to 0.20). The head-to-head trial of the three protocols (Swierkot K et al., PMID: 19236536) agrees: all improved, with no group differences by 8 months. This shelf answers the periodontal-outcome question only; live #462 homes the different question of periodontal treatment and HbA1c in diabetes. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): compressing treatment into 24 hours, with or without antiseptic disinfection, does not deepen the result — choose the schedule on logistics and patient preference.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — Cochrane review of 20 RCTs: full-mouth disinfection versus quadrant scaling showed no benefit in probing depth (MD 0.11 mm, −0.04 to 0.27) or attachment at 6–8 months

title: Closing a significant ductus in preterm infants: high-dose oral ibuprofen ranked best across 68 trials; paracetamol matched ibuprofen head-to-head (81.2% versus 78.8% closure) with less hyperbilirubinaemia and gut bleeding
question: In preterm infants with a haemodynamically significant patent ductus arteriosus, how do ibuprofen, indomethacin and paracetamol compare for duct closure and adverse events?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the drugs close the ductus; they differ in dose, route and side-effects, not in the hard outcomes. A Bayesian network meta-analysis of 68 randomised trials in 4,802 preterm infants (Mitra S et al., PMID: 29584842) found the overall closure rate was 67.4% (2,867 of 4,256), and that a high dose of oral ibuprofen beat a standard dose of intravenous ibuprofen (odds ratio 3.59, 95% credible interval 1.64–8.17; 199 more closures per 1,000 infants) and standard-dose intravenous indomethacin (odds ratio 2.35, 95% credible interval 1.08–5.31; 124 more per 1,000), ranking first for closure and for avoiding surgical ligation — while no treatment, including placebo, differed significantly on mortality, necrotising enterocolitis or intraventricular haemorrhage. Head-to-head, oral paracetamol closed the ductus in 81.2% versus 78.8% on oral ibuprofen, within the non-inferiority margin, with significantly less hyperbilirubinaemia and gastrointestinal bleeding (Dang D et al., PMID: 24223740). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): for closure itself, high-dose oral ibuprofen has the strongest randomised support and paracetamol is a credible gentler alternative; no regimen has shown a mortality or brain-injury advantage.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — high-dose oral ibuprofen ranks first for ductal closure across 68 trials and paracetamol is non-inferior to ibuprofen head-to-head, with no regimen differing on mortality, necrotising enterocolitis or intraventricular haemorrhage

title: Cooling encephalopathic newborns in low-resource settings (HELIX): death or disability 50% versus 47% — no benefit — and death alone significantly higher with hypothermia (42% versus 31%)
question: In term infants with hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy in low-resource settings, does therapeutic hypothermia improve survival without disability compared with usual care (HELIX)?
balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — the intervention that helps in high-income nurseries did not transfer. In HELIX (Thayyil S et al., PMID: 34358491), 408 term infants with moderate or severe neonatal encephalopathy in India, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh were randomised to whole-body hypothermia at 33.5°C for 72 hours or usual care, in tertiary units with ventilation, cardiovascular support and MRI. Death or moderate or severe disability at 18–22 months occurred in 50% (98 of 195) on hypothermia versus 47% (94 of 199) on usual care (risk ratio 1.06, 95% CI 0.87–1.30, p=0.55) — and death alone was significantly higher with cooling: 42% versus 31% (p=0.022), including neonatal hospital deaths of 36% versus 24% (p=0.0087). The trial's own conclusion: therapeutic hypothermia should not be offered for neonatal encephalopathy in low-income and middle-income countries, even where tertiary intensive care is available. This is a different question from the high-resource cooling trials homed at live shelves #145 and #260. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm): in low-resource settings, cooling encephalopathic newborns increased death without reducing disability.
stamp: POSSIBLE (harm) — in HELIX, hypothermia did not reduce death or disability (50% vs 47%) and significantly increased death alone (42% vs 31%) in low-resource settings

title: Upright in the second stage splits by epidural: without one, fewer assisted births (RR 0.75) and episiotomies (RR 0.75) but more blood loss over 500 mL (RR 1.48); with one, upright gave fewer spontaneous births (35.2% versus 41.1%, BUMPES)
question: In women in the second stage of labour, do upright positions reduce instrumental birth and episiotomy compared with supine or lithotomy positions?
balance: SPLIT — the answer reverses with epidural analgesia. Without an epidural, the Cochrane review of 30 trials in 9,015 women (Gupta JK et al., PMID: 28539008) found upright positions reduced assisted deliveries (relative risk 0.75, 95% CI 0.66–0.86) and episiotomies (average relative risk 0.75, 95% CI 0.61–0.92) and shortened the second stage by about 6 minutes (mean difference −6.16 minutes, 95% CI −9.74 to −2.59), at the cost of more estimated blood loss over 500 mL (relative risk 1.48, 95% CI 1.10–1.98) and a possible increase in second-degree tears (relative risk 1.20, 95% CI 1.00–1.44), with no clear difference in caesarean section (relative risk 1.22, 95% CI 0.81–1.81). With a low-dose epidural, the large BUMPES trial (PMID: 29046273) found the opposite for its primary outcome: spontaneous vaginal birth in 35.2% upright versus 41.1% lying down (adjusted risk ratio 0.86, 95% CI 0.78–0.94). PROPOSED SPLIT: upright helps women without an epidural on instrumental birth and episiotomy while raising measured blood loss; with an epidural, lying down gave more spontaneous births.
stamp: SPLIT — without epidural, upright positions reduce assisted delivery and episiotomy but increase blood loss >500 mL; with epidural (BUMPES), upright reduced spontaneous vaginal birth (35.2% vs 41.1%)

title: PRP versus hyaluronic acid for knee osteoarthritis: a 34-trial meta-analysis favours PRP at 6–12 months on low-quality evidence — the two double-blind head-to-head trials found no difference at all
question: In adults with knee osteoarthritis, do platelet-rich plasma injections reduce pain compared with hyaluronic acid injections?
balance: SPLIT — the pooled literature and the best individual trials point in different directions. A meta-analysis of 34 randomised trials (1,403 PRP knees, 1,426 control knees) found WOMAC scores favoured PRP over hyaluronic acid at 6 and 12 months (P<0.001 for both), while rating the quality of evidence low and noting superiority did not reach the minimal clinically important difference for all outcomes (Filardo 2021, PMID: 32551947). But the double-blind head-to-head trials do not reproduce it: Wang 2022 (PMID: 36013495, n=110, single-injection PRP versus crosslinked HA) found no significant between-group difference in WOMAC change at 1, 3 or 6 months, and Fossati 2024 (PMID: 39367905, n=174, three injections of PRP, HA, or both) found no significant differences among the groups on any outcome at 6 or 12 months (WOMAC p=0.45 and p=0.64). Note the separate question — PRP versus saline placebo — is homed at live shelf #457, where blinded trials were null; this shelf asks only whether PRP beats the active comparator HA. PROPOSED SPLIT: pooled small trials say yes at a year, the rigorous double-blind trials say no difference — paying a PRP premium over HA is not supported by the best evidence.
stamp: SPLIT — a 34-trial meta-analysis favours PRP over hyaluronic acid at 6–12 months on low-quality evidence, but both double-blind head-to-head trials found no significant difference

title: PRP for rotator-cuff tendinopathy: no better than saline at one year in the double-blind trial — better than dry needling in a smaller one, and a meta-analysis pools the two kinds of control into a positive answer
question: In adults with rotator-cuff tendinopathy, do platelet-rich plasma injections improve pain and function compared with corticosteroid or saline?
balance: SPLIT — the answer flips with the comparator. Against saline placebo, the rigorous trial is null: Kesikburun 2013 (PMID: 23893418), a double-blind trial of 40 patients with chronic rotator-cuff tendinopathy, found no significant difference between PRP and saline on WORC, SPADI or pain scores at one year (P=0.174, 0.314 and 0.904), though both groups improved with their exercise programme. Against dry needling, PRP won: Rha 2013 (PMID: 23035005, n=39) found Shoulder Pain and Disability Index scores of 17.7 versus 29.5 at six months favouring PRP (P<0.05). A meta-analysis of eight RCTs (A Hamid 2021, PMID: 33970936) — four against saline, four against rehabilitation or dry needling — concluded PRP was effective for long-term pain control and function, pooling those unlike controls together. The candidate's corticosteroid comparison could not be verified as a discrete carded trial this session; the verified split is saline versus active-needling controls. PROPOSED SPLIT: PRP beats needling a tendon without injecting anything active; it has not beaten salt water.
stamp: SPLIT — no benefit over saline placebo in the double-blind trial at one year, but superior to dry needling at six months in a smaller trial; pooled positivity depends on mixing those controls

title: Spinal manipulation for acute low back pain: it did not speed recovery by a single day against placebo manipulation (hazard ratio 1.01) — yet a JAMA meta-analysis pooling other comparators finds a modest 10 mm pain improvement at six weeks
question: In adults with acute non-specific low back pain, does spinal manipulative therapy reduce pain and speed recovery compared with sham manipulation or inert treatment?
balance: SPLIT — against sham manipulation the answer is no; against the mixed bag of other comparators it is a modest yes. Hancock 2007 (PMID: 17993364), a 240-patient factorial trial in acute low back pain on top of advice and paracetamol, found spinal manipulative therapy did not appreciably reduce days to recovery versus placebo manipulation (hazard ratio 1.01, 95% CI 0.77 to 1.31; p=0.955); 99% had recovered or were censored by 12 weeks regardless. Paige 2017 (PMID: 28399251), a JAMA systematic review of 26 RCTs, found moderate-quality evidence that manipulation was associated with a pooled pain improvement of −9.95 mm on a 100-mm scale (95% CI −15.6 to −4.3; 15 trials, 1,711 patients) and a function effect size of −0.39 (12 trials, 1,381 patients) at up to six weeks — with large heterogeneity the reviewers could not explain, and minor transient harms (increased pain, stiffness, headache) reported 50–67% of the time in large case series. The pragmatic question — manipulation added to usual care for established low back pain — is homed at live shelf #785; this shelf covers the acute, sham-controlled question only. PROPOSED SPLIT: no faster recovery than placebo manipulation, but a small short-term pain and function advantage over the range of alternatives trials have used.
stamp: SPLIT — no effect on time to recovery versus placebo manipulation in the factorial trial (HR 1.01), but a modest pooled pain (−9.95 mm) and function benefit versus mixed comparators in meta-analysis, with large heterogeneity

title: Aquatic exercise for hip and knee osteoarthritis: pain and disability about 5 points better than control on a 0–100 scale in the Cochrane pool of 13 trials — small, short-term, and never tested against a blinded comparator
question: In adults with hip or knee osteoarthritis, does aquatic exercise improve pain and function compared with land-based exercise or control?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a consistent small short-term gain against non-exercise controls, with the land-based comparison essentially untested in the carded evidence. The Cochrane review (Bartels 2016, PMID: 27007113; 13 trials, 1,190 participants, mean programme 12 weeks) found aquatic exercise improved pain (SMD −0.31, 95% CI −0.47 to −0.15; 12 trials, 1,076 participants) and disability (SMD −0.32, −0.47 to −0.17) versus control, corresponding to about five points lower pain and disability scores on a 0–100 scale, with a small quality-of-life effect (SMD −0.25) and no serious adverse events — moderate-quality evidence. The largest single trial, Hinman 2007 (PMID: 17142642; n=71), found 72% of aquatic-therapy participants reported improved pain and 75% improved function versus 17% each in controls after six weeks, with benefits maintained six weeks later. This shelf covers structured exercise in water; passive spa/balneotherapy for knee OA and fibromyalgia is homed at pack #2699 and is not rebuilt here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): pool-based exercise is a reasonable, low-harm way to buy a small short-term improvement — superiority over equivalent land exercise is asserted by enthusiasts, not shown here.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — Cochrane pool of 13 trials shows small short-term pain and disability improvements (about 5 points on 0–100) versus control, moderate-quality evidence; no carded trial establishes superiority over land-based exercise

title: Epidural steroids for sciatica from a herniated disc: a flicker of leg-pain relief at 3–6 weeks in two double-blind trials — no gain in function, and surgery rates identical at a year (about 25% in both arms)
question: In adults with sciatica from lumbar disc herniation, do epidural corticosteroid injections reduce leg pain and disability compared with placebo injections?
balance: SPLIT — brief symptom relief, no durable benefit. In Carette S et al. (PMID: 9171065; 158 patients with sciatica from a herniated nucleus pulposus), epidural methylprednisolone improved leg pain more than saline at 6 weeks (P=0.03) but disability did not differ at 3 weeks (Oswestry change −8.0 versus −5.5; 95% CI for the difference −7.1 to 2.2) or at 3 months (−17.3 versus −15.4; 95% CI −9.3 to 5.4), and the cumulative probability of back surgery at 12 months was 25.8% versus 24.8% (P=0.90). The WEST trial (Arden NK et al., PMID: 16030082; 228 patients) found 75% disability improvement at 3 weeks in 12.5% on epidural triamcinolone versus 3.7% on placebo injections (number needed to treat 11.4) and no benefit at any point from 6 to 52 weeks, no gain in physical function or return to work, and no reduction in surgery. Two concordant double-blind trials say the injection buys a few weeks of partial relief and changes nothing else. PROPOSED SPLIT: transient leg-pain/disability benefit at 3–6 weeks; no benefit on function, work or surgery from 6 weeks to 1 year.
stamp: SPLIT — POSSIBLE (benefit) at 3–6 weeks only; (the treatment made no difference) on function, return to work and surgery at 6–52 weeks

title: Greater occipital nerve blocks for chronic migraine: headache days fell from 18.1 to 8.8 on bupivacaine versus 16.9 to 13.2 on saline at one month in the larger of two small placebo trials
question: In adults with migraine or cluster headache, do greater occipital nerve blocks reduce attack frequency or pain compared with sham or placebo injection?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for chronic migraine only; no placebo trial for cluster headache was verified for this shelf. Inan LE et al. (PMID: 25765043) randomised 84 patients with chronic migraine to four weekly greater occipital nerve blocks with bupivacaine or saline: after 1 month headache days had fallen from 18.1 to 8.8 on bupivacaine versus 16.9 to 13.2 on saline (between-group P=0.004), and pain scores fell from 8.4 to 5.3 versus 8.1 to 6.7 (P=0.004), while headache duration did not differ between groups (P=0.767). Gul HL et al. (PMID: 27910088), in 44 patients with chronic migraine given the same four-weekly regimen, found significant decreases in headache frequency and pain scores on bupivacaine at the first, second and third months of follow-up, whereas the placebo group's improvement was significant only at the first month; no severe adverse effects occurred in either trial. Two small short trials from similar settings agree, but neither exceeds 84 patients or a few months of blinded follow-up. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): weekly bupivacaine occipital blocks reduce headache days in chronic migraine for at least a month beyond placebo, on small-trial evidence.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — headache days 18.1→8.8 vs 16.9→13.2 at 1 month (P=0.004) in the larger of two small placebo-controlled chronic-migraine trials; no verified placebo trial in cluster headache

title: Stimulus control alone for insomnia: small-to-large gains against passive controls (g 0.38–0.85) that shrink to negligible (g 0.06–0.30) against active treatments — in 11 mostly decades-old trials a modern meta-analysis calls uncertain
question: In adults with insomnia, does stimulus-control therapy alone improve sleep compared with control?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — the component works against doing nothing and adds little against anything active. Jansson-Fröjmark M et al. (PMID: 37496454) meta-analysed 11 randomised and experimental studies of stimulus control for insomnia, the majority published between 1978 and 1998: against passive comparators, stimulus control produced small-to-large improvements in sleep onset latency and total sleep time (Hedges g = 0.38–0.85), but against active comparators the improvements were negligible (g = 0.06–0.30), with methodological uncertainties throughout. Verreault MD et al. (PMID: 37586843) included 23 randomised studies in a network meta-analysis and likewise found stimulus control effective against control conditions, while rating the included studies generally poor quality with inconsistencies in the network. The one modern primary trial verified, Goodhines PA et al. (PMID: 35943968), was a pilot in 82 college students in which a single-session peer-led stimulus-control arm (n=14) improved within-group insomnia severity (d = 1.66) — a feasibility signal, not a confirmatory test. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): stimulus control alone probably improves sleep versus passive control, on old, small, low-quality trials.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — pooled g 0.38–0.85 vs passive comparators but 0.06–0.30 vs active comparators, across 11 mostly 1978–1998 trials rated methodologically uncertain

title: Specific neck exercise for chronic neck pain: pain and disability fell versus control at 12 months in a 180-woman trial (P<0.001), and deep cervical flexor training added gains on top of conventional exercise in a 65-teacher trial
question: In adults with chronic neck pain, does specific neck exercise (deep cervical flexor training) reduce pain and disability compared with general exercise or control?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — specific neck training beats advice and general activity; the deep-flexor-specific claim rests on smaller work. Ylinen J et al. (PMID: 12759322) randomised 180 women with chronic nonspecific neck pain to intensive isometric neck strength training, lighter neck endurance training, or a control group advised on aerobic and stretching exercise: at 12 months both training groups had decreased neck pain and disability compared with control (P<0.001), and maximal isometric neck strength improved in flexion by 110% in the strength group versus 28% in the endurance group and 10% in controls. Iqbal ZA et al. (PMID: 33521131) randomised 65 school teachers with neck pain to deep cervical flexor training with pressure biofeedback plus conventional exercises or conventional exercises alone, finding statistically significant additional improvement in muscle endurance, pain and disability at days 14 and 42. A systematic review of nine randomised trials of deep cervical flexor programmes (Amiri Arimi S et al., PMID: 28225440) found eight of nine supported low-load craniocervical flexion training for deep-flexor impairments, with one trial finding no difference against other cervical exercise. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): specific neck exercise reduces pain and disability versus control, with deep cervical flexor training a reasonable specific form.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — pain and disability reduced vs control at 12 months in a 180-woman RCT (P<0.001), with deep-flexor training adding benefit over conventional exercise in a 65-patient trial and 8 of 9 reviewed RCTs

title: Prednisolone versus dexamethasone for croup: three head-to-head trials, including a 1,252-child noninferiority trial, found no clinically important difference
question: In children with croup, is oral prednisolone equivalent to dexamethasone for symptom relief, return visits and length of stay?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — between the two steroids. Three randomised head-to-head trials compared single-dose oral prednisolone with dexamethasone in childhood croup. The largest (Parker CM et al., PMID: 31416827) enrolled 1,252 children and demonstrated noninferiority of prednisolone 1 mg/kg and of low-dose dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg against standard dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg: adjusted Westley score differences at 1 hour were 0.05 (95% CI −0.07 to 0.17) for prednisolone, and unscheduled re-attendance within 7 days was 21.7% on prednisolone versus 17.8% on standard-dose dexamethasone (not significant). Two smaller trials agree: Fifoot AA et al. (PMID: 17305661, n=99) found no significant differences between prednisolone 1 mg/kg and either dexamethasone dose, and Garbutt JM et al. (PMID: 24092872, n=87) found no differences in additional care (7% versus 2%), symptom duration or parent outcomes. An earlier trial suggesting prednisolone inferiority (Sparrow & Geelhoed 2006) is already carded at live shelf #239 and is not re-carded here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): prednisolone performs equivalently to dexamethasone for croup in the direct comparisons.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — prednisolone noninferior to dexamethasone in a 1,252-child trial, with two smaller concordant head-to-head trials

title: Heliox in bronchiolitis: distress scores ease within an hour in small trials, but the 319-infant phase III trial found no shorter treatment overall — benefit only by tight facemask or CPAP
question: In children with moderate-to-severe croup or bronchiolitis, does helium–oxygen (heliox) reduce respiratory distress and intubation compared with oxygen alone?
balance: SPLIT — scores versus hard outcomes, and delivery route decides. The phase III trial (Chowdhury MM et al., PMID: 23509160) randomised 319 infants with bronchiolitis to heliox or a nitrogen–oxygen control gas (airox): median length of treatment was 1.90 versus 1.87 days (P=.41), and the proportion needing CPAP was 17% versus 19% (OR 0.87). Benefit appeared only where the gas was actually delivered undiluted — by tight-fitting facemask (1.46 versus 2.01 days, P=.03) or CPAP (1.55 versus 2.26 days, P=.02) — and not by nasal cannula. Small intensive-care trials split: Cambonie G et al. (PMID: 16537867, n=20) found the respiratory distress score lower after 1 hour on heliox (3.05 versus 5.5, P<.01), while Liet JM et al. (PMID: 16356437, n=39) found positive-pressure ventilation was needed in 22.2% on heliox versus 19.0% on control gas (RR 1.17). No randomised trial of heliox in croup against oxygen alone with usable outcome data was found; the croup heliox record is a small pilot and a comparison against racemic epinephrine. PROPOSED SPLIT: heliox may ease distress scores and shorten treatment when delivered by facemask or CPAP in bronchiolitis, but it has not reduced ventilation or overall treatment length.
stamp: SPLIT — POSSIBLE (benefit) for distress scores and facemask/CPAP-subgroup treatment length in bronchiolitis; (the treatment made no difference) on the phase III primary outcome and ventilation rates

title: Antibiotics for glue ear: the founding trial said effusion cleared twice as often, its own reanalysis said the result was measurement bias — and hearing, the outcome that matters, remains unproven
question: In children with otitis media with effusion, do antibiotics improve hearing and effusion resolution compared with placebo or watchful waiting?
balance: SPLIT — effusion on paper versus hearing in the child. The founding double-blind trial (Mandel EM et al., PMID: 2880294) randomised 518 children with otitis media with effusion to 2 weeks of amoxicillin, with or without a decongestant–antihistamine, or placebo: effusion resolution at 4 weeks was twice as high on amoxicillin (P<.001), yet 69.8% of amoxicillin-treated children still had effusion, and about half of those who cleared relapsed within 3 months in both groups. A published reanalysis of the same trial (Cantekin EI et al., PMID: 1683673) concluded the apparent benefit rested on biased otoscopic judgement: by tympanometry the estimated efficacy was 4.8% (P=.171), recurrence after treatment was two to six times higher in the amoxicillin group (P=.001), and resolution at about 10 weeks was 13.6% versus 11.3% (P=.477). The 2023 Cochrane review (Mulvaney CA et al., PMID: 37870130; 19 studies, 2,581 children) rated the evidence low to very low certainty: return to normal hearing at 2 months rested on a single study (20/49 versus 0/37), persistent effusion at 6–12 months was 48% versus 54% against placebo (RR 0.89, 95% CI 0.68–1.17), and against no treatment effusion resolved more by 3 months (RR 0.64, 95% CI 0.50–0.80) with little to no difference in hearing threshold. PROPOSED SPLIT: antibiotics may clear effusion a little sooner; a hearing benefit is unproven and the flagship result is contested by its own reanalysis.
stamp: SPLIT — POSSIBLE (benefit) for short-term effusion resolution; hearing benefit unproven (very low certainty)

title: Cranberry in children with recurrent urinary infection: the largest trial missed its primary endpoint (16% versus 22%), while two small trials found far fewer infections
question: In children with recurrent urinary tract infection, does cranberry prophylaxis reduce recurrence compared with placebo or antibiotic prophylaxis?
balance: SPLIT — by trial size and by endpoint. The largest trial (Salo J et al., PMID: 22100577) randomised 263 children treated for urinary tract infection to cranberry juice or placebo for 6 months: at least one recurrence occurred in 16% on cranberry versus 22% on placebo (difference −6%, 95% CI −16 to 4%; P=.21) — not significant — although total episodes were fewer (27 versus 47; incidence density 0.16 lower per person-year, P=.035) and antimicrobial days were 6 fewer per patient-year (P<.001). Two small trials were positive: Afshar K et al. (PMID: 22910239, n=40) found urinary infection incidence of 0.4 versus 1.15 per patient-year on high-proanthocyanidin cranberry juice versus proanthocyanidin-free juice (P=.045), a 65% relative reduction; Ferrara P et al. (PMID: 19921981, n=84 girls) found at least one infection in 18.5% on daily cranberry juice versus 48.1% in controls over 6 months (P<.05). No child trial against antibiotic prophylaxis was found; the adult-women question lives at live shelves #50 and #489. PROPOSED SPLIT: episode counts fall in all three trials, but the only adequately sized trial did not significantly reduce the proportion of children with a recurrence.
stamp: SPLIT — POSSIBLE (benefit) for total episode counts and antimicrobial days; (the treatment made no difference) on ≥1 recurrence in the largest trial

title: Pain relief for endometrial sampling: lidocaine spray cut pain scores from 5.11 to 3.51 against placebo, and intrauterine lidocaine beat paracervical block after the procedure
question: In women having outpatient endometrial sampling, does a paracervical block or intrauterine lidocaine reduce procedural pain compared with placebo or no analgesia?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — local lidocaine, by spray, intrauterine infusion or added to a block, reduces sampling pain in randomised trials. Aksoy H et al. (PMID: 26471087) randomised 120 women having office endometrial biopsy to 10% lidocaine spray or placebo spray, double-blind: mean pain during the procedure was 3.51 ± 1.51 on lidocaine versus 5.11 ± 1.66 on placebo (P<.001). Cengiz H et al. (PMID: 24071820) randomised 120 women to intrauterine lidocaine or paracervical block: pain immediately after the procedure was similar (P=.079), but pain 30 minutes after was significantly lower with intrauterine lidocaine (P=.0001). Rattanachaiyanont M et al. (PMID: 16135583), in 66 women having fractional curettage under paracervical block, found adding intrauterine lidocaine lowered the median maximum pain score from 4.7 to 2.3 (P=.022) and cut the proportion with pain above 4 from 60.6% to 33.3% (number needed to treat 3.7). Paracervical block alone, tested against placebo in outpatient hysteroscopy with biopsy (live evidence at shelf #4728's Lau 1999 card), helped only at instrument insertion. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): lidocaine-based local anaesthesia — spray or intrauterine — reduces endometrial sampling pain; the block alone is the weakest of the tested options.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — lidocaine spray beat placebo (pain 3.51 versus 5.11) and intrauterine lidocaine beat or augmented paracervical block in randomised trials

title: Analgesia for outpatient hysteroscopy: vaginal misoprostol helped in one trial and not in another, an NSAID alone did not beat placebo, and paracervical block helped only at insertion — with more bradycardia
question: In women having outpatient hysteroscopy, which analgesia (local anaesthetic, NSAIDs, misoprostol priming) reduces pain compared with placebo?
balance: SPLIT — by technique, and the trials pull in different directions. Lau WC et al. (PMID: 10426243) randomised 100 women having outpatient hysteroscopy and endometrial biopsy to paracervical block with 2% lignocaine or saline, double-blind: the block significantly reduced pain only at insertion of the hysteroscope, not at subsequent stages, and caused a higher incidence of bradycardia and hypotension. Issat T et al. (PMID: 24768981) randomised 150 women to vaginal misoprostol 400 µg, intravenous ketoprofen, or placebo: median pain scores during and immediately after hysteroscopy were significantly lower with misoprostol than with ketoprofen (P=.02) or placebo (P=.006), with no difference by 15 minutes (P=.16). Hassa H et al. (PMID: 23850898), in 158 nulliparous infertile women having vaginoscopic diagnostic hysteroscopy, found neither vaginal misoprostol nor rectal diclofenac beat placebo (median pain 4.75 and 5.01 versus 4.15 on placebo; P=.57). PROPOSED SPLIT: misoprostol priming may reduce pain in conventional outpatient hysteroscopy but showed nothing in vaginoscopic technique; NSAID alone and paracervical block have, at best, narrow and stage-specific effects.
stamp: SPLIT — POSSIBLE (benefit) for misoprostol in conventional hysteroscopy (1 of 2 trials) and for paracervical block at insertion only (with harm: more bradycardia/hypotension); (the treatment made no difference) for NSAIDs and for misoprostol in vaginoscopic technique

title: Misoprostol before operative hysteroscopy: the cervix opens wider and dilates in about 50 seconds instead of 178 — a process win, bought with more side effects
question: In women having operative hysteroscopy, does preoperative misoprostol ease cervical dilation and reduce complications compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for cervical priming, the process outcome; a reduction in complications is not established. Nada AM et al. (PMID: 27523921) randomised 390 women having operative hysteroscopy to oral misoprostol 400 µg, vaginal misoprostol 400 µg, or placebo 12 hours before: mean width of the endocervical canal was 4.79 ± 1.07 mm (oral) and 4.25 ± 0.71 mm (vaginal) versus 3.92 ± 0.92 mm on placebo (P<.001 for both), and mean time to dilatation was 48.98 and 46.55 seconds versus 178.05 seconds on placebo (P<.001), with no significant difference in adverse effects between groups in this trial. Zhuo Z et al. (PMID: 30907209) randomised 253 women to 600 µg misoprostol orally or vaginally or vitamin B6 control: cervical width after administration was 7.2 ± 0.9 mm (vaginal) and 7.5 ± 1.4 mm (oral), significantly greater than control; dilatation took 75 ± 24 and 82 ± 22 seconds versus 148 ± 31 seconds on control; uterine false tract was substantially increased in the placebo group, but side effects increased in the misoprostol groups, and the priming effect was significantly stronger in premenopausal women. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): misoprostol reliably primes the cervix before operative hysteroscopy by either route; whether that converts into fewer serious complications is suggested (false tract) but not proven, and side effects rise.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two double-blind trials show wider cervical canal and dilatation roughly three times faster with misoprostol; complication reduction unproven and side effects increased in one trial

title: Seasonal malaria chemoprevention in the Sahel: three large blinded trials cut clinical malaria by 70–86% and severe malaria sharply, on top of bednets — vomiting is the commonest side effect
question: In children in the Sahel, does seasonal malaria chemoprevention (sulfadoxine–pyrimethamine plus amodiaquine) reduce clinical malaria and severe malaria compared with no chemoprevention?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — the largest preventive effect in this band. Three large randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials in Sahelian children aged 2–59 months agree: monthly chemoprevention during the transmission season cut clinical malaria by 86% (95% CI 80–90) in Senegal (Cissé B et al., PMID: 16503464), by 82% (78–85) in Mali (Dicko A et al., PMID: 21304923) and by 70% (66–74) in Burkina Faso (Konaté AT et al., PMID: 21304925). Severe malaria fell too — 2 versus 15 episodes in Mali (87% protective efficacy) and a 69% relative reduction in Burkina Faso — and in Mali and Burkina Faso the protection was on top of insecticide-treated bednets, which more than 93% of children slept under. The commonest harm is vomiting: children on chemoprevention were 2.8 times more likely to vomit in Burkina Faso, and vomiting was also increased in Senegal; no drug-related serious adverse event was recorded in any trial. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): seasonal chemoprevention is a large, consistent preventive win for Sahelian children, capped at POSSIBLE by this band's stamp cap — the trials themselves would support more.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — three large blinded trials cut clinical malaria by 70–86% and severe malaria sharply, on top of bednets; vomiting is the main side effect

title: Methotrexate in giant cell arteritis: three small trials disagreed, but pooled patient-level data show fewer relapses (hazard ratio 0.65 for a first relapse) and about 842 mg less prednisone over 48 weeks
question: In patients with giant-cell arteritis, does methotrexate reduce relapses and steroid dose compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — three small randomised trials, individually discordant, positive when pooled patient by patient. Jover JA et al. (PMID: 11177313) found at least one relapse in 45% on methotrexate plus prednisone versus 84.2% on prednisone alone (P=0.02), with a mean cumulative prednisone dose lower by 1,302 mg (95% CI 350 to 2,253; P=0.009). Hoffman GS et al. (PMID: 12115238), the largest trial at 98 patients, found treatment failure in 57.5% on methotrexate versus 77.3% on placebo (P=0.26) and no significant difference in cumulative corticosteroid dose. Spiera RF et al. (PMID: 11579707), with 21 patients, found no corticosteroid-sparing benefit. The individual patient data meta-analysis of all three (Mahr AD et al., PMID: 17665429; 161 patients) found hazard ratios of 0.65 for a first relapse (P=0.04) and 0.49 for a second relapse (P=0.02) — relative effects — a reduction in cumulative corticosteroid dose of 842 mg within 48 weeks (P<0.001), and a higher probability of sustained corticosteroid discontinuation for at least 24 weeks (hazard ratio 2.84, P=0.001), with no difference in dropout rates or adverse events. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): adjunctive methotrexate modestly reduces relapse and steroid exposure in giant cell arteritis, on pooled small-trial evidence.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — three small discordant randomised trials whose pooled individual patient data show fewer relapses (hazard ratio 0.65, relative) and about 842 mg less corticosteroid over 48 weeks with adjunctive methotrexate

title: Adding baloxavir to a neuraminidase inhibitor in hospitalised severe influenza: no faster recovery — 97.5 versus 100.2 hours to clinical improvement in the one double-blind trial (FLAGSTONE)
question: In hospitalised patients with influenza, does oseltamivir plus baloxavir combination therapy beat monotherapy?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — one large double-blind trial, a clean null on its primary endpoint. In FLAGSTONE (Kumar D et al., PMID: 35085510), 366 hospitalised patients aged 12 years or older with severe influenza were randomised to baloxavir plus a standard-of-care neuraminidase inhibitor or placebo plus a neuraminidase inhibitor. Median time to clinical improvement was 97.5 hours on the combination versus 100.2 hours on neuraminidase inhibitor alone (median difference −2.7 hours, 95% CI −53.4 to 25.9; p=0.467). The combination was well tolerated: serious adverse events occurred in 12% versus 15%, and deaths in 2% (4 patients) versus 6% (7 patients), none considered treatment-related — but the trial was not powered to settle mortality, so the death gap is a numerically favourable wobble, not a finding. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): adding baloxavir to a neuraminidase inhibitor does not speed clinical improvement in hospitalised severe influenza; single-trial shelf, held for the developer's verdict.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — in the single FLAGSTONE double-blind trial, baloxavir plus a neuraminidase inhibitor did not shorten time to clinical improvement versus the neuraminidase inhibitor alone (97.5 vs 100.2 hours; p=0.467)

title: Switching suppressed HIV patients to two-drug dolutegravir–lamivudine: suppression held in two phase 3 trials — virological failure 0.3–0.4% on two drugs versus 0.5–1.2% on three or four
question: In people with HIV on antiretroviral therapy who are virologically suppressed, does switching to two-drug therapy (dolutegravir–lamivudine) maintain suppression compared with continuing three-drug therapy (TANGO, SALSA)?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the benefit is simplification without losing suppression, shown the same way in two phase 3 switch trials. In TANGO (van Wyk J et al., PMID: 31905383), suppressed adults randomised to switch to dolutegravir–lamivudine or stay on a tenofovir-alafenamide-based regimen had HIV-1 RNA ≥50 copies/mL at week 48 in 0.3% versus 0.5% (adjusted difference −0.3 percentage points, 95% CI −1.2 to 0.7; non-inferior). In SALSA (Llibre JM et al., PMID: 35235656), switching to dolutegravir–lamivudine versus continuing a varied 3- or 4-drug regimen gave 0.4% versus 1.2% with RNA ≥50 copies/mL (adjusted difference −0.8 percentage points, 95% CI −2.4 to 0.8; non-inferior). No participant on two-drug therapy in either trial met confirmed virological withdrawal criteria, and no resistance emerged. The price was tolerability noise early after the switch: drug-related adverse events were more frequent on dolutegravir–lamivudine in SALSA (20% versus 6% through week 48, converging to 5% versus 2% after week 24), and drug-related grade ≥2 events in TANGO were 4.6% versus 0.8%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): in already-suppressed patients without prior virological failure, switching to dolutegravir–lamivudine maintains suppression as reliably as staying on three or four drugs, at the cost of more early drug-related symptoms.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — switching suppressed patients to dolutegravir–lamivudine was non-inferior to continuing 3- or 4-drug therapy in two phase 3 trials (TANGO, SALSA), with no virological failure or resistance on two drugs

title: Probiotics in cirrhosis: fewer encephalopathy hospitalisations than placebo in the blinded VSL#3 trial, no better than lactulose in the pooled record, and no mortality benefit
question: In patients with cirrhosis and hepatic encephalopathy, do probiotics improve recovery, recurrence or hospitalisation compared with placebo or lactulose?
balance: SPLIT — probiotics beat placebo or no treatment on the softer outcomes and match lactulose, but no trial shows a mortality benefit. In the one double-blind trial, the named preparation VSL#3 (CD Pharma India Private Limited) did not significantly cut breakthrough encephalopathy (34.8% versus 51.6%; HR 0.65, 95% CI 0.38–1.11; P=.12) yet did cut hospitalisation for encephalopathy (19.7% versus 42.2%; HR 0.45, 95% CI 0.23–0.87) and for any cirrhosis complication (24.2% versus 45.3%; HR 0.52) over 6 months (Dhiman RK et al., PMID: 25450083). An open-label primary-prophylaxis trial found overt encephalopathy in 7 of 86 on probiotics versus 14 of 74 controls (Lunia MK et al., PMID: 24246768). Pooling 14 randomised trials (1,152 patients), probiotics versus no treatment/placebo improved minimal encephalopathy (OR 3.91), progression to overt encephalopathy (OR 0.40) and hospitalisation (OR 0.53), but versus lactulose every one of those comparisons was null, and mortality was unchanged against either comparator (Saab S et al., PMID: 26561214). PROPOSED SPLIT: POSSIBLE (benefit) against placebo for progression and hospitalisation; no demonstrated advantage over lactulose and no mortality benefit.
stamp: SPLIT — POSSIBLE (benefit) versus placebo/no treatment for progression to overt encephalopathy and hospitalisation; no advantage over lactulose and no mortality benefit in the pooled randomised record
