title: Antioxidants for chronic pancreatitis pain: one positive Indian trial in young, mostly idiopathic disease — the larger blinded UK trial in mostly alcoholic disease found nothing
question: In patients with chronic pancreatitis and pain, do pancreatic enzyme supplements or antioxidants reduce pain compared with placebo?
balance: SPLIT — the two blinded trials point in opposite directions, in different populations. In India, antioxidant supplementation cut painful days per month by 7.4 versus 3.2 on placebo (P<.001) and left 32% pain-free versus 13% over 6 months, in patients averaging 30 years old of whom 92 of 127 had idiopathic disease (Bhardwaj P et al., PMID: 18952082). In the UK ANTICIPATE trial, the named preparation Antox version 1.2 (Pharma Nord, Morpeth, UK) moved clinic pain scores by −2.33 points versus −1.97 on placebo (difference −0.36, 95% CI −1.44 to 0.72; P=.509), with diary pain, quality of life, opiate use and admissions all similar, in predominantly alcoholic chronic pancreatitis (Siriwardena AK et al., PMID: 22683257). Blood antioxidant levels rose in both trials, so the split is not a delivery failure. The enzyme half of this question is not separately carded here: pancreatic enzyme replacement for exocrine insufficiency — fat absorption, nutrition and pain — is homed at Shelf #3591. PROPOSED SPLIT: POSSIBLE (benefit) in young, non-alcoholic disease on the Indian trial; the treatment made no difference in the larger, older, mostly alcoholic UK population.
stamp: SPLIT — POSSIBLE (benefit) for antioxidants in young, predominantly idiopathic chronic pancreatitis (one trial); no pain benefit in predominantly alcoholic disease in the larger blinded trial

title: Large-balloon dilation for big bile-duct stones: clearance matches sphincterotomy, but mechanical lithotripsy is needed far less often — about 16% versus 25%, and 30% versus 48% in the largest trial
question: In patients with large common bile duct stones, does endoscopic papillary large-balloon dilation reduce the need for mechanical lithotripsy compared with sphincterotomy alone?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for the procedure, not for a disease outcome: large-balloon dilation clears large stones as reliably as sphincterotomy while sparing the lithotripter. Pooling five randomised trials (621 patients, stones ≥10 mm), complete clearance was 93.7% with dilation versus 92.5% with sphincterotomy, but mechanical lithotripsy was used in 15.5% versus 25.2% (P=.003), and in stones over 15 mm in 24.2% versus 40% (P=.001), with pancreatitis 4.0% versus 5.0% and overall adverse events 7.9% versus 10.7% (Jin PP et al., PMID: 24833886). The largest single trial (MARVELOUS, 171 patients) found single-session complete removal in 90.7% with dilation alone versus 78.8% with sphincterotomy (P=.04) and lithotripsy in 30.2% versus 48.2% (P=.02), with pancreatitis 4.7% versus 5.9% (Kogure H et al., PMID: 32299114). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): equal clearance, materially less lithotripsy, no safety penalty shown.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — large-balloon dilation matches sphincterotomy for clearance of large bile-duct stones while reducing mechanical lithotripsy use, across five pooled randomised trials and the largest single trial

title: Wire-guided cannulation at ERCP: an early trial cut pancreatitis from 11.3% to 2% and the pooled odds ratio was 0.23 — but the largest multicentre trial found 6.1% versus 6.3%, no difference at all
question: In patients having ERCP, does wire-guided cannulation reduce post-ERCP pancreatitis compared with contrast-guided cannulation?
balance: SPLIT — the answer depends on which randomised record you weight. A single-centre Korean trial found post-ERCP pancreatitis in 3 of 150 (2%) with wire-guided cannulation versus 17 of 150 (11.3%) with contrast cannulation (P=.001) (Lee TH et al., PMID: 19007927), and a meta-analysis of five randomised trials pooled a pancreatitis odds ratio of 0.23 (95% CI 0.13–0.41) with higher primary cannulation success (85.3% versus 74.9%; OR 2.05) for the wire technique (Cennamo V et al., PMID: 19532133). But the largest, multicentre randomised trial — 322 patients across nine Japanese centres — found pancreatitis in 6.1% versus 6.3% (P=.95) and primary cannulation in 83% versus 87%, no difference on either outcome; its only independent pancreatitis predictors were accidental pancreatic-duct wire insertions and contrast injections (Kobayashi G et al., PMID: 23368891). PROPOSED SPLIT: POSSIBLE (benefit) on the early single-centre and pooled record; the treatment made no difference in the largest multicentre test.
stamp: SPLIT — POSSIBLE (benefit) for post-ERCP pancreatitis on early single-centre trials and their meta-analysis; no difference in the largest multicentre randomised trial

title: D2 versus D1 gastrectomy in the West: fewer cancer deaths and recurrences at 15 years in the Dutch trial (cancer death 37% versus 48%) — paid for with double the operative mortality (10% versus 4%) and no overall survival win
question: In patients with gastric cancer having gastrectomy, does D2 lymphadenectomy improve survival compared with D1 in Western populations?
balance: SPLIT — D2 dissection buys cancer control and charges operative lives for it, and in the Western randomised record the two roughly cancel. At 15 years in the Dutch trial, gastric-cancer death was 37% after D2 versus 48% after D1, local recurrence 12% versus 22% and regional recurrence 13% versus 19% — but overall 15-year survival was 29% versus 21% (P=.34, not significant), because D2 operative mortality was 10% versus 4% (P=.004), complications 43% versus 25% and reoperations 18% versus 8% (Songun I et al., PMID: 20409751). The British MRC trial showed the same price up front: hospital mortality 13% versus 6.5% (P=.04) and morbidity 46% versus 28%, with the excess accounted for by the pancreaticosplenectomy then bundled into D2 (Cuschieri A et al., PMID: 8606613). PROPOSED SPLIT: POSSIBLE (benefit) for cancer-specific death and locoregional recurrence at long follow-up; POSSIBLE (harm) for operative mortality and morbidity with the era's technique — modern spleen- and pancreas-preserving D2 was not what these trials tested.
stamp: SPLIT — POSSIBLE (benefit) for gastric-cancer death and locoregional recurrence at 15 years; POSSIBLE (harm) for operative mortality and morbidity with the splenopancreatectomy-era D2 technique; overall survival not significantly different

title: Stent as a bridge to surgery for obstructing left-sided colon cancer: stomas fall (47.5% versus 67.9% in CReST) and complications fall in the pooled trials — mortality, recurrence and survival do not move
question: In patients with obstructing left-sided colon cancer, does a self-expanding metal stent as a bridge to surgery improve outcomes compared with emergency surgery?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a stoma and morbidity benefit, honestly bounded: no survival advantage has been shown. In CReST, the largest trial (245 patients), stenting relieved obstruction in 82.4% of attempts; among curative-intent patients, stoma formation was 47.5% with stent-then-elective-surgery versus 67.9% with emergency surgery (P=.003), while 30-day mortality (3.6% versus 5.6%), hospital stay, perioperative morbidity, quality of life, 3-year recurrence and mortality did not differ (CReST Collaborative Group, PMID: 35986684). Pooling seven randomised trials (448 patients), postoperative complications were 37.8% after stent-bridge versus 54.9% after emergency surgery (P=.02), stoma rates 28.8% versus 46.0% and wound infection 8.1% versus 15.5%, with no mortality difference (Allievi N et al., PMID: 28761765). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): fewer stomas and fewer complications, bought with a roughly one-in-five stent failure rate and no demonstrated oncological gain or loss.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — stent as a bridge to surgery reduces stoma formation and postoperative complications versus emergency surgery in randomised trials, with no difference in mortality, recurrence or survival

title: Perforated diverticulitis with peritonitis: primary anastomosis leaves 95% stoma-free at a year versus 72% after Hartmann's (LADIES) — mortality and morbidity the same in both randomised trials
question: In patients with complicated diverticulitis (Hinchey III/IV), does primary anastomosis beat Hartmann's procedure for stoma-free survival?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the benefit is living without a stoma, not living longer. In LADIES (DIVA arm), 12-month stoma-free survival was 94.6% after sigmoidectomy with primary anastomosis versus 71.7% after Hartmann's procedure (HR 2.79, 95% CI 1.86–4.18; P<.0001), with index-operation morbidity 39% versus 44% and mortality 6% versus 3% — neither significantly different (Lambrichts DPV et al., PMID: 31178342). DIVERTI found the same pattern: 18-month mortality 4% with primary anastomosis (with diverting stoma) versus 7.7% with Hartmann's (P=.42), overall morbidity 44% versus 39%, but stoma reversal by 18 months in 96% versus 65% (P=.0001) (Bridoux V et al., PMID: 28943323). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): in haemodynamically stable, immunocompetent patients under 85, primary anastomosis roughly triples the chance of being stoma-free at a year at no shown mortality or morbidity cost.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — primary anastomosis improves stoma-free survival and stoma reversal versus Hartmann's procedure in perforated diverticulitis (Hinchey III/IV), with no significant difference in mortality or morbidity in two randomised trials

title: Platelet-test-guided de-escalation after PCI: TROPICAL-ACS stepped prasugrel down to clopidogrel with no net penalty (7% versus 9%) — and ANTARCTIC's monitoring-guided adjustment in the over-75s changed nothing at all (28% versus 28%)
question: In patients with acute coronary syndrome treated with PCI, does platelet-function-test-guided de-escalation or adjustment of P2Y12 inhibitor therapy improve net clinical outcomes compared with unguided standard therapy?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — guidance by platelet testing has never significantly improved a net clinical outcome in a randomised trial; what it has shown is that stepping down is safe. TROPICAL-ACS (Sibbing D et al., PMID: 28855078) randomised 2,610 patients with biomarker-positive acute coronary syndrome after successful PCI to platelet-function-guided de-escalation (prasugrel for one week, clopidogrel for one week, then test-guided clopidogrel or prasugrel maintenance) or 12 months of prasugrel: the net clinical benefit endpoint (cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, stroke, or BARC grade 2 or higher bleeding) at one year occurred in 7% versus 9% (hazard ratio 0.81; 95% CI 0.62 to 1.06; P = 0.0004 for non-inferiority, P = 0.12 for superiority), the ischaemic composite in 3% versus 3%, and BARC 2 or higher bleeding in 5% versus 6% (hazard ratio 0.82; 95% CI 0.59 to 1.13; P = 0.23). ANTARCTIC (Cayla G et al., PMID: 27581531), in 877 patients aged 75 or older stented for acute coronary syndrome, found platelet-function monitoring with prasugrel dose or drug adjustment produced the identical primary outcome rate as no monitoring — 28% versus 28% (hazard ratio 1.003; 95% CI 0.78 to 1.29; P = 0.98) — with no significant difference in bleeding. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): platelet-test guidance itself buys no proven outcome gain; TROPICAL-ACS supports guided de-escalation as a non-inferior way to use the cheaper, gentler drug, not as a superior strategy.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — platelet-function-guided de-escalation was non-inferior but not superior on net clinical benefit in TROPICAL-ACS (7% vs 9%; superiority P = 0.12), and monitoring-guided adjustment was exactly null in ANTARCTIC (28% vs 28%; HR 1.003)

title: Anagrelide versus hydroxyurea in high-risk essential thrombocythaemia: SPLIT — PT1 found more arterial thrombosis, bleeding and myelofibrosis transformation on anagrelide, ANAHYDRET found it non-inferior in WHO-defined disease
question: In patients with essential thrombocythaemia at high risk, does anagrelide match hydroxyurea for thrombosis prevention (PT1, ANAHYDRET)?
balance: SPLIT — the two randomised trials disagree, and the split tracks how the disease was defined. In PT1 (809 high-risk patients, older diagnostic criteria, median follow-up 39 months, both drugs with low-dose aspirin), anagrelide was worse on the composite of arterial/venous thrombosis, serious haemorrhage or related death (odds ratio 1.57, 95% CI 1.04–2.37; P=0.03), with more arterial thrombosis (P=0.004), serious haemorrhage (P=0.008) and transformation to myelofibrosis (P=0.01), but less venous thromboembolism (P=0.006). In ANAHYDRET (259 previously untreated patients diagnosed by strict WHO criteria), anagrelide was non-inferior for platelet, haemoglobin and leukocyte control and ET-related events over 36 months (hazard ratio 0.92, 95% CI 0.57–1.46), with no significant difference in major arterial (7 versus 8) or venous (2 versus 6) thrombosis. Platelet-count control itself was equivalent in both trials. PROPOSED SPLIT: hydroxyurea remains the safer default on PT1's hard-event data; anagrelide matched it in the WHO-defined, previously untreated ANAHYDRET population — the diagnosis definition, not the platelet number, decides which trial applies.
stamp: SPLIT — POSSIBLE (harm) for anagrelide in the PT1 population (older diagnostic criteria, aspirin co-therapy); (the treatment made no difference) / non-inferior in WHO-defined, previously untreated disease (ANAHYDRET)

title: Mitapivat in thalassaemia: transfusion reduction response 30% versus 13% in transfusion-dependent disease (ENERGIZE-T) and haemoglobin response 42% versus 2% in non-transfusion-dependent disease (ENERGIZE) — two double-blind trials
question: In patients with transfusion-dependent beta-thalassaemia, does mitapivat improve haemoglobin and reduce transfusion burden compared with placebo (ENERGIZE-T), and in non-transfusion-dependent thalassaemia (ENERGIZE)?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 3 trials of the oral pyruvate kinase activator mitapivat 100 mg twice daily agree in direction across the thalassaemia spectrum. In transfusion-dependent α- or β-thalassaemia (ENERGIZE-T, 258 patients, 48 weeks), a transfusion reduction response (≥50% fewer red-cell units, by ≥2 units, in any consecutive 12 weeks to week 48) occurred in 30% (52/171) versus 13% (11/87) on placebo (adjusted difference 18 percentage points, 95% CI 8–27; p=0.0003). In non-transfusion-dependent α- or β-thalassaemia (ENERGIZE, 194 patients, 24 weeks), a haemoglobin response (≥1.0 g/dL mean rise, weeks 12–24) occurred in 42% (55/130) versus 2% (1/64) (difference 41 points, 95% CI 32–50; p<0.0001). Headache, initial insomnia, nausea and upper respiratory infection were the commonest events on mitapivat; no deaths were reported in either trial. The candidate asked about transfusion-dependent β-thalassaemia: both trials enrolled α-thalassaemia as well as β-thalassaemia, and ENERGIZE-T's endpoint is transfusion reduction rather than haemoglobin — declared here rather than silently widened. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): mitapivat reduces transfusion burden in dependent disease and raises haemoglobin in non-dependent disease, on two concordant trials.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two double-blind randomised trials: transfusion reduction response 30% versus 13% (ENERGIZE-T, transfusion-dependent) and haemoglobin response 42% versus 2% (ENERGIZE, non-transfusion-dependent) in α/β-thalassaemia

title: Fesoterodine 8 mg beats tolterodine ER 4 mg on leakage in two head-to-head trials — diary dry rates 64% versus 57%, paid for with roughly double the dry mouth
question: In adults with overactive bladder, does fesoterodine beat tolterodine for incontinence episodes?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a small, consistent head-to-head edge, bought with anticholinergic side effects. Two 12-week double-blind trials compared fesoterodine (4 mg for one week, then 8 mg) with tolterodine extended-release 4 mg and placebo. In Herschorn 2010 (1,590 patients), fesoterodine improved urgency incontinence episodes significantly more than tolterodine ER (P = 0.017) and placebo (P < 0.001), with diary dry rates of 64% versus 57% and 45%; Kaplan 2011 (2,417 patients) found the same superiority pattern across diary endpoints and patient-reported outcomes, visible by week 4. The price is dose-typical: dry mouth in 28% on fesoterodine versus 13–16% on tolterodine ER and 5–6% on placebo, and discontinuation for adverse events in 5–6% versus 3–4% and 2%. Both trials compare fesoterodine's top dose against tolterodine's standard dose, which is exactly the comparison the dose asymmetry should make the reader notice. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): fesoterodine 8 mg is modestly more effective than tolterodine ER 4 mg for urgency incontinence in two concordant trials, with about double the dry mouth.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two head-to-head double-blind trials: fesoterodine 8 mg superior to tolterodine ER 4 mg on urgency incontinence episodes, with dry mouth 28% versus 13–16%

title: Nightly PDE5-inhibitor 'rehabilitation' after prostatectomy does not restore unassisted erections: recovery 20.9% on daily tadalafil versus 19.1% on placebo after washout in REACTT
question: In men with erectile dysfunction after prostatectomy, does daily PDE5 inhibitor rehabilitation preserve erectile function compared with on-demand use?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — for the outcome rehabilitation promises. The rehabilitation hypothesis is that scheduled nightly PDE5-inhibitor dosing after nerve-sparing prostatectomy restores spontaneous, unassisted erections faster or more completely than using the drug only on demand. The largest test, REACTT (423 men), found no difference after a 6-week drug-free washout: 20.9% on daily tadalafil, 16.9% on on-demand tadalafil and 19.1% on placebo reached an erectile-function score of at least 22 (odds ratios 1.1 and 0.9 versus placebo, both non-significant) — while on treatment, daily tadalafil did improve drug-assisted erections (p = 0.016) and reduced penile length loss by 4.1 mm (p = 0.032). The sildenafil trial (Pavlovich 2013, 100 men) likewise found no difference between nightly and on-demand dosing at any timepoint, and a third, three-arm trial stopped early with 76 men and no significant difference. The drugs work while taken; scheduled rehabilitation dosing has not been shown to change the unassisted recovery it is sold on. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): nightly rehabilitation dosing does not improve unassisted erectile recovery after prostatectomy compared with on-demand use or placebo.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — REACTT and the nightly-sildenafil trial both null on unassisted erectile recovery after washout; on-drug function improves, recovery does not

title: Testosterone in hypogonadal men with type 2 diabetes: insulin resistance and HbA1c improve in two trials — a clamp study finds no glycaemic effect at all
question: In men with hypogonadism and type 2 diabetes, does testosterone improve glycaemic control?
balance: SPLIT — the glycaemic signal depends on which trial and which endpoint you read. In TIMES-2 (220 hypogonadal men with type 2 diabetes and/or metabolic syndrome), transdermal testosterone cut insulin resistance (HOMA-IR) by 15.2% at 6 months (P = 0.018) and 16.4% at 12 months (P = 0.006), and in the diabetic subgroup HbA1c was better than placebo at month 9 (treatment difference −0.446%, P = 0.035) — but not at the earlier timepoints the trial emphasised. In BLAST (211 men with type 2 diabetes), long-acting testosterone undecanoate significantly reduced HbA1c at 6 and 18 weeks, most markedly in men with baseline HbA1c above 7.5%, where the reduction was 0.41% within 6 weeks. Against both, the small clamp study (Magnussen 2016, 39 men on metformin alone) found no change at all in clamp-measured insulin sensitivity (p = 0.18), HbA1c, or glucose production — while body composition improved (lean mass +1.9 kg, p = 0.001). No trial tests diabetes outcomes, only surrogates, and none runs beyond a year of blinded treatment. PROPOSED SPLIT: glycaemic improvement in the two larger trials (HbA1c about 0.4% in the subgroups and timepoints that reached significance), no glycaemic effect in the small mechanistic trial; body-composition effects consistent across all three.
stamp: SPLIT — glycaemic: POSSIBLE (benefit); body composition: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Essential tremor: propranolol and primidone each beat placebo on accelerometer-measured tremor in tiny 1980s–90s crossover trials — primidone's first dose made about a quarter of patients acutely ill
question: In patients with essential tremor, does propranolol or primidone reduce tremor amplitude compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the two first-line drugs each beat placebo, in trials too small and old to carry more. In a double-blind randomised crossover trial of 14 patients, both propranolol and primidone significantly improved accelerometer-measured tremor versus placebo (p<0.01 for each; Gorman WP et al., PMID: 3514797), with no significant difference between the two drugs. A double-blind placebo-controlled trial of primidone in 22 patients found it significantly superior to placebo for hand tremor, comparable to propranolol, with tremor reduced to non-symptomatic levels in two patients — but an acute toxic reaction to an initial 62.5 mg dose occurred in six of 22 patients (Findley LJ et al., PMID: 3900296). A third randomised double-blind crossover trial in 16 patients found propranolol 40 mg three times daily significantly reduced tremor on all measures at day 15, comparably to gabapentin (Gironell A et al., PMID: 10199338). No trial measured disability, quality of life or long-term outcomes, and none enrolled more than 22 patients. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): propranolol and primidone reduce measured tremor amplitude short-term; the evidence is three small crossover trials from 1985–1999, and primidone carries a notable first-dose intolerance.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — propranolol and primidone each significantly reduced tremor versus placebo in three small double-blind crossover trials (n=14–22), with acute primidone intolerance in 6 of 22 in one trial

title: SSRIs for generalised social anxiety: paroxetine and sertraline each roughly doubled the response rate versus placebo in large 12-week trials — 55% versus 24%, and 47% versus 26%
question: In patients with social anxiety disorder, does sertraline or paroxetine improve symptoms compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two large double-blind placebo-controlled trials, one per drug, agree that an SSRI roughly doubles the response rate in generalised social anxiety disorder over about 12 weeks. Paroxetine made 55.0% of patients much or very much improved versus 23.9% on placebo (odds ratio 3.88), with Liebowitz Social Anxiety Scale scores falling 30.5 points versus 14.5 (Stein MB et al., PMID: 9728642). Sertraline, in patients with severe generalised disease, cut LSAS scores by 31.0 points versus 21.7 on placebo (p=.001), with intent-to-treat responder rates of 46.8% versus 25.5% (Liebowitz MR et al., PMID: 12934979). The benefit is symptomatic and short-term as tested — neither trial shows what happens beyond 12 weeks, whether gains persist after stopping, or how the drugs compare with the cognitive-behavioural therapy shelved separately. Tolerability was acceptable in both, though sertraline patients stopped for adverse events more often than placebo patients (7.6% versus 2.9%). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): SSRIs are a proven short-term treatment for generalised social anxiety, at the stamp this band allows.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — paroxetine and sertraline each roughly doubled response rates versus placebo in large double-blind trials of generalised social anxiety disorder (55.0% vs 23.9%; 46.8% vs 25.5% intent-to-treat)

title: Screening women for abdominal aortic aneurysm: in the one randomised trial of 9,342 women, rupture rates were identical in screened and unscreened groups at 5 and 10 years — prevalence in women was a sixth of men's
question: In adults, does a one-time abdominal aortic aneurysm ultrasound screen reduce AAA mortality in women?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — for women, the screening benefit proven in men does not appear. The men's screening shelves rest on trials in men; the one randomised trial that screened women (Chichester, Scott RA et al., PMID: 11872050) randomised 9,342 women aged 65–80 to an invitation for a single ultrasound scan or control, found AAA prevalence of 1.3% in women versus 7.6% in men, and over 5- and 10-year follow-up the incidence of rupture was the same in the screened and control groups. A systematic review prepared for the Canadian Task Force (Ali MU et al., PMID: 27871502) put the women's estimate at RR 0.88 (95% CI 0.72–1.07) for up to 10 years — no significant difference — against a pooled 42% relative reduction in AAA-related mortality in men (RR 0.58, 95% CI 0.39–0.88). The original Chichester report (Scott RA et al., PMID: 7648155) had already shown the split: rupture incidence fell 55% relative in invited men, while rupture in women was low in both groups. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): one-time ultrasound screening of unselected women aged 65–80 does not reduce AAA rupture or mortality — a single-trial, sex-specific boundary on the men's screening evidence, held as Tier C.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the single randomised trial in women (n=9,342) found identical rupture incidence in screened and control groups at 5 and 10 years, and a systematic review's women's estimate (RR 0.88, 95% CI 0.72–1.07) excludes the benefit size seen in men

title: Continuous electronic fetal monitoring: neonatal seizures halved in the pooled trials, cerebral palsy unchanged — and caesarean births up by about two-thirds
question: In women in labour, does continuous electronic fetal monitoring reduce neonatal seizures or cerebral palsy compared with intermittent auscultation?
balance: SPLIT — the seizure outcome and the cerebral-palsy outcome point in different directions, and the price is operative delivery. Across 13 randomised trials in over 37,000 women, continuous cardiotocography versus intermittent auscultation halved neonatal seizures (RR 0.50, 95% CI 0.31 to 0.80; 9 trials, 32,386 women) but did not reduce overall perinatal death (RR 0.86, 95% CI 0.59 to 1.23) and did not reduce cerebral palsy (RR 1.75, 95% CI 0.84 to 3.63; 2 trials, 13,252 women). Caesarean births rose (RR 1.63, 95% CI 1.29 to 2.07) and instrumental vaginal births rose (RR 1.15, 95% CI 1.01 to 1.33). The largest single trial, Dublin (12,964 women), found 14 stillbirths and neonatal deaths in each group, with neonatal seizures and persistent abnormal neurological signs about twice as frequent with auscultation, yet three clearly abnormal infants in each group at 1-year follow-up among seizure survivors. PROPOSED SPLIT: fewer neonatal seizures with continuous monitoring, no demonstrated cerebral-palsy or mortality benefit, and more operative births.
stamp: SPLIT — LIKELY (benefit) (neonatal seizures) / POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) (cerebral palsy, perinatal death) / LIKELY (harm) (caesarean and instrumental birth)

title: Vaginal cleansing before caesarean: endometritis roughly halved in the pooled trials (3.1% versus 7.1%) — the largest single trial on its own was not significant
question: In women having caesarean birth, does vaginal cleansing with povidone-iodine reduce endometritis compared with no cleansing?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a cheap, brief intervention with a consistent pooled effect and no reported harms. The 2020 Cochrane review of 21 trials (7,038 women; 17 using povidone-iodine) found post-caesarean endometritis in 3.1% with vaginal cleansing versus 7.1% in control groups (average RR 0.41, 95% CI 0.29 to 0.58; 20 trials, 6,918 women; moderate-certainty evidence), with postoperative fever (aRR 0.64, 95% CI 0.50 to 0.82) and wound infection (RR 0.62, 95% CI 0.50 to 0.77) also reduced, and no adverse effects reported. The best-known single trial (Haas 2010, 300 women) pointed the same way but was not significant on its composite outcome: 6.5% versus 11.7% (RR 0.55, 95% CI 0.26 to 1.11; P=.11). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): vaginal antiseptic cleansing before caesarean probably reduces endometritis and wound infection; the case rests on the pooled trials, not on any one trial.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — pooled endometritis 3.1% versus 7.1% (aRR 0.41) across 20 trials, no adverse effects reported

title: Caesarean antibiotic before the incision, not after cord clamping: pooled infectious morbidity RR 0.57 — though the trial in labouring women found no difference
question: In women having caesarean birth, does a single-dose antibiotic before incision beat administration after cord clamping for infection?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — for the mother; no neonatal penalty was shown. The Cochrane review of 10 studies (5,041 women) found composite maternal infectious morbidity lower with preoperative than with post-cord-clamp administration (RR 0.57, 95% CI 0.45 to 0.72; high-quality evidence), driven by endometritis (RR 0.54, 95% CI 0.36 to 0.79) and wound infection (RR 0.59, 95% CI 0.44 to 0.81), with no clear difference in neonatal sepsis (RR 0.76, 95% CI 0.51 to 1.13). The double-blind Sullivan 2007 trial agreed: total infectious morbidity RR 0.4 (95% CI 0.18 to 0.87) and endometritis RR 0.2 (95% CI 0.15 to 0.94) with cefazolin 15–60 minutes before incision, and no increase in neonatal sepsis or sepsis workups. The counterweight is Thigpen 2005, in labouring women: endometritis RR 0.67 (95% CI 0.42 to 1.07) and wound infection RR 0.84 (95% CI 0.45 to 1.55) — no significant difference. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): pre-incision dosing reduces maternal infection in the pooled record, with the labouring-population trial null.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — pooled composite infectious morbidity RR 0.57 and endometritis RR 0.54 for pre-incision versus post-clamp dosing, no neonatal sepsis difference

title: Maintenance tocolysis after 48 hours: babies did no better — nifedipine 11.9% versus 13.7% adverse perinatal outcome in APOSTEL II; atosiban only bought quieter days
question: In women with threatened preterm labour, does maintenance tocolysis after 48 hours improve neonatal outcomes compared with stopping?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — on the outcomes babies experience. In APOSTEL II, 406 women who had not delivered after 48 hours of tocolysis and corticosteroids were randomised to 12 days of maintenance nifedipine 80 mg/day or placebo: adverse perinatal outcome (perinatal death, chronic lung disease, neonatal sepsis, intraventricular haemorrhage >grade 2, periventricular leukomalacia >grade 1, or necrotising enterocolitis) occurred in 11.9% (24/201) versus 13.7% (28/205) (RR 0.87, 95% CI 0.53 to 1.45). Maintenance atosiban (513 women) prolonged uterine quiescence — median time to first recurrence of labour 32.6 versus 27.6 days (P=.02), with subsequent intravenous treatment needed by 23% versus 31% — but neonatal deaths were 4 versus 5 and infant outcomes including birth weight were comparable: a quieter uterus, not healthier babies. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): maintenance tocolysis prolongs quiescence at best and has not improved perinatal outcomes.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — APOSTEL II adverse perinatal outcome 11.9% versus 13.7% (RR 0.87, NS); atosiban maintenance prolonged quiescence without improving infant outcomes

title: Methadone versus morphine for neonatal abstinence syndrome: treatment about 2–7 days shorter in two randomised trials — the larger one cut hospital stay by 2.9 days
question: In infants with neonatal abstinence syndrome, does methadone beat morphine for treatment duration? (The buprenorphine comparison is homed separately.)
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for methadone, on duration outcomes. The multicentre Davis 2018 trial (116 term infants treated at 8 US units) found, after adjustment for site and maternal opioid type, that methadone shortened length of hospital stay by 14% relative (relative number of days 0.86, 95% CI 0.74 to 1.00; P=.046; a 2.9-day absolute difference), stay attributable to abstinence syndrome by 14% relative (0.86, 95% CI 0.77 to 0.96; 2.7 days), and length of drug treatment by 16% relative (0.84, 95% CI 0.73 to 0.97; 2.3 days); medians were stay 16 versus 20 days and treatment 11.5 versus 15 days. The earlier single-site Brown 2015 trial (31 infants with consent of 78 eligible) found the same direction, larger: median length of opioid treatment 14 versus 21 days (P=.008). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): methadone shortens treatment and stay compared with morphine; no trial here addresses longer-term neurodevelopment, and the buprenorphine-versus-morphine question is homed on its own shelf.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — methadone shortened treatment (relative days 0.84) and stay (16 versus 20 median days) versus morphine in two concordant randomised trials

title: Long-acting injectable versus the same antipsychotic taken orally: randomised trials show at most a small relapse edge (pooled risk ratio 0.88) — the large benefits live in mirror-image studies, and the biggest pragmatic trial was null
question: In adults with chronic schizophrenia, does a long-acting injectable antipsychotic reduce relapse and hospitalisation compared with the same antipsychotic taken orally?
balance: SPLIT — by study design: in randomised trials the advantage of a long-acting injectable (LAI) over oral treatment is small or absent, while in pre-post (mirror-image) studies it looks large. The largest pragmatic randomised trial (Rosenheck RA et al., PMID: 21366475) found hospitalisation in 39% on long-acting risperidone versus 45% on a psychiatrist's choice of oral antipsychotic (hazard ratio 0.87, 95% CI 0.63 to 1.20 — not significant). The one double-blind same-drug trial (Fleischhacker WW et al., PMID: 24925984) showed non-inferiority, not superiority: estimated impending relapse at week 26 was 7.12% on aripiprazole once-monthly 400 mg versus 7.76% on oral aripiprazole. The comparative meta-analysis (Kishimoto T et al., PMID: 33862018) pooled a risk ratio for hospitalisation or relapse of 0.88 (95% CI 0.79 to 0.99) across randomised trials, 0.92 (0.88 to 0.98) across cohort studies, and 0.44 (0.39 to 0.51) across pre-post studies — the design most prone to bias gives by far the biggest number. This shelf is distinct from shelf #994 (depot versus placebo in stabilised schizophrenia) and pack #2419 (LAI versus usual-care oral treatment in early-phase schizophrenia): it asks the chronic-schizophrenia, formulation-only question. PROPOSED SPLIT: randomised evidence supports at most a modest relapse/hospitalisation advantage for LAIs over oral antipsychotics; claims of large benefit rest on pre-post designs.
stamp: SPLIT — POSSIBLE (benefit) (small advantage in the randomised-trial pool only; no demonstrated benefit in pre-post/mirror-image terms)

title: Perioperative ketamine for chronic postsurgical pain: the 17-trial meta-analysis is null overall and both carded trials agree — only an intravenous-only subgroup analysis turns positive
question: In adults having surgery, does perioperative ketamine reduce the incidence of chronic postsurgical pain at 3–12 months compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — overall, perioperative ketamine has not been shown to prevent chronic postsurgical pain. The meta-analysis of 17 randomised trials (McNicol ED et al., PMID: 25060512) found the overall risk of developing persistent post-surgical pain was not significantly reduced at any time point, and pain-severity scores did not reach significance either; only a sensitivity analysis restricted to intravenous ketamine showed significant reductions at 3 months (P = 0.01) and 6 months (P = 0.04). The two individually carded trials agree with the null headline: after thoracotomy (Dualé C et al., PMID: 18783971), neuropathic pain scores at 6 weeks and 4 months were similar between ketamine and placebo, and after amputation (Hayes C et al., PMID: 15264726) phantom pain at 6 months occurred in 47% on ketamine versus 71% on control (P = 0.28 — not significant, in a trial powered only for a large effect). This shelf asks the chronic-pain question only; intraoperative ketamine for delirium and acute pain in older adults is homed at live shelf #1128 (PODCAST). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference): an intravenous-only subgroup signal survives inside an otherwise null record, which is hypothesis-generating, not a basis for routine use.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — overall meta-analysis and both carded trials are null for chronic postsurgical pain; a significant reduction appears only in an intravenous-only sensitivity subgroup

title: Acute urticaria: adding a steroid to the antihistamine did nothing in both trials (itch gone at 2 days in 62% with prednisone versus 76% without) — and the H2 add-on has never been randomised at all
question: In adults with acute urticaria, does adding an H2 blocker or a corticosteroid to an H1 antihistamine improve symptoms?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — adding a corticosteroid to an H1 antihistamine does not improve acute urticaria in either randomised trial. In the larger trial (Barniol C et al., PMID: 28476259), complete itch relief at 2 days occurred in 62% of patients given prednisone plus levocetirizine versus 76% given levocetirizine alone (difference 14%, 95% CI −31% to 4%), with relapses in 30% versus 24%. In the second trial (Palungwachira P et al., PMID: 32139204), adding intravenous dexamethasone to chlorpheniramine produced no significant difference in itch scores at 60 minutes, and patients also given oral prednisolone at discharge had more active urticaria at 1-week and 1-month follow-up. For the H2-blocker half of the question there is no add-on trial at all: the one randomised H2 study (Moscati RM et al., PMID: 2404434) compared cimetidine instead of an H1 blocker, not in addition to one, finding improvement in 87% on cimetidine versus 76% on diphenhydramine with less sedation on cimetidine. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): routine steroid bursts on top of an antihistamine are an unproven habit for uncomplicated acute urticaria; the H2 add-on question remains untested in randomised trials.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — adding prednisone or dexamethasone to an H1 antihistamine did not improve acute urticaria in two randomised trials; no randomised trial tests an H2-blocker add-on

title: Corneal abrasion: the pressure patch heals nothing — pooled healing was identical by 48 hours and the biggest trial found unpatched eyes healed faster with less pain
question: In adults with corneal abrasion, does a pressure patch improve healing or pain compared with no patch?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — patching a corneal abrasion does not speed healing or relieve pain, and may slightly delay healing on the first day. The largest single trial (Kaiser PK et al., PMID: 9098299) randomised 223 patients with traumatic or foreign-body-removal abrasions to a pressure patch or no patch on top of antibiotic ointment and mydriatics: the no-patch patients healed significantly faster and had less pain in both the traumatic (120 patients) and foreign-body (81 patients) groups, with better compliance when unpatched. The Cochrane review (Lim CH et al., PMID: 27457359) pooled 12 trials (1,080 participants): patched eyes were less likely to be healed at 24 hours (risk ratio 0.89, 95% CI 0.79 to 1.00), with no difference at 48 hours (risk ratio 0.97, 0.91 to 1.02) or 72 hours (risk ratio 1.01, 0.97 to 1.05), a mean healing time 0.14 days longer with a patch (0 to 0.27 days), and pain ratings generally similar between groups. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): for simple, non-contact-lens-related abrasions, the patch is ritual, not treatment — antibiotics and time do the work.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — across 12 trials patching did not improve healing at 24–72 hours or pain, and the largest trial found unpatched abrasions healed faster with less pain

title: Shingles: valaciclovir ended the pain about two weeks sooner than aciclovir at the median (38 versus 51 days) — in the single head-to-head trial ever run
question: In adults with herpes zoster, does valaciclovir beat aciclovir for pain duration?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single-trial: in the one large head-to-head trial (Beutner KR et al., PMID: 7492102), valaciclovir shortened herpes zoster pain compared with aciclovir in immunocompetent adults aged 50 and over. Median duration of zoster-associated pain was 38 days on valaciclovir 1,000 mg three times daily for 7 days and 44 days on the 14-day course, versus 51 days on aciclovir 800 mg five times daily (P = 0.001 and P = 0.03 respectively), and the proportion of patients with pain persisting at 6 months was 19.3% on valaciclovir versus 25.7% on aciclovir. Rash healing, pain intensity and quality-of-life measures did not differ between treatments, and adverse events were similar. Single-trial flag: this shelf rests on one randomised trial — no second head-to-head trial of valaciclovir against aciclovir for zoster was found — so the claim is exactly as strong as that one trial. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): valaciclovir resolves zoster pain about two weeks sooner at the median than aciclovir, with simpler three-times-daily dosing, on single-trial evidence.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single randomised trial (n = 1,141): valaciclovir shortened median zoster pain duration to 38 versus 51 days on aciclovir and reduced pain persisting at 6 months (19.3% versus 25.7%)

title: PRP for acute hamstring injury: beat platelet-poor plasma by 5.7 days in one trial, matched no injection in the same trial, and matched placebo outright in the other — return to play is not reliably faster
question: In athletes with acute hamstring injury, does platelet-rich plasma speed return to play compared with placebo or rehabilitation alone?
balance: SPLIT — by comparator. In Hamilton 2015, a single platelet-rich plasma (PRP) injection shortened return to play versus a platelet-poor plasma injection (adjusted difference −5.7 days, 95% CI −10.1 to −1.4; adjusted HR 2.29, 95% CI 1.30 to 4.04) but not versus no injection at all (−2.9 days, 95% CI −7.2 to 1.4; HR 1.48, p=0.15) — the platelet-poor injection arm, not PRP, looks like the outlier. In Reurink 2015, two PRP injections did not accelerate return to play versus saline placebo injections, and the 1-year re-injury rate was identical in effect terms (HR 0.89, 95% CI 0.38 to 2.13; p=0.80). No trial showed a re-injury benefit at any time point, and no adverse effects were reported in Hamilton. Read together: an injection ritual plus intensive rehabilitation returns athletes when rehabilitation returns them; PRP itself has no dependable effect. PROPOSED SPLIT: PRP beat an active plasma comparator once, matched no treatment in the same trial, and matched placebo in the second trial — no reliable return-to-play or re-injury benefit.
stamp: SPLIT — POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) (vs placebo and vs no injection, for return to play and re-injury); single positive contrast vs platelet-poor plasma only

title: Embryo glue (hyaluronan-enriched medium): older fresh-transfer trials pooled to a live-birth gain — the one large double-blind frozen-transfer trial found 25.5% versus 25.8%
question: In women undergoing IVF, does hyaluronan-enriched transfer medium (embryo glue) improve live birth compared with standard medium?
balance: SPLIT — by transfer type and era. The Cochrane pool of the older, mostly fresh-transfer trials favoured functional-concentration hyaluronic acid: live birth odds ratio 1.41 (95% CI 1.17 to 1.69; 6 RCTs, 1,950 women), with clinical pregnancy OR 1.39 — but multiple pregnancy was also raised (OR 1.86, 95% CI 1.49 to 2.31). The largest modern test tells a different story: in a double-blind trial of 550 women having frozen transfer, the tested product EmbryoGlue (Vitrolife, Gothenburg, Sweden) at 0.5 mg/mL gave live birth 25.5% versus 25.8% on standard medium (relative risk 0.99, 95% CI 0.74 to 1.31). Where embryos are transferred one at a time and frozen, the pooled fresh-era benefit has not reproduced. PROPOSED SPLIT: a possible benefit in the older fresh-transfer setting, no demonstrated benefit in modern frozen single-transfer practice, and a multiple-pregnancy cost where more than one embryo is transferred.
stamp: SPLIT — POSSIBLE (benefit) (fresh transfer) / POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) (frozen transfer)

title: Assisted hatching: live birth unmoved across 39 trials and in the 698-woman ALADDIN trial (29.8% versus 29.2%) — multiple pregnancy may rise
question: In women undergoing IVF, does assisted hatching improve live birth compared with no hatching?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — for live birth. The Cochrane review of 39 randomised trials (7,249 women) was uncertain whether assisted hatching improves live birth (odds ratio 1.09, 95% CI 0.92 to 1.29; 14 RCTs reporting live birth, 2,849 women, low-quality evidence), while multiple pregnancy may be slightly increased (OR 1.38, 95% CI 1.13 to 1.68). The largest modern trial, ALADDIN, laser-hatched vitrified/warmed blastocysts before single frozen transfer and found live birth 29.8% (105/352) versus 29.2% (101/346) — relative risk 1.02 (95% CI 0.86 to 1.19) — with no subgroup that benefited. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): assisted hatching does not demonstrably raise live birth, and it may raise multiple pregnancy where more than one embryo is transferred.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — live birth OR 1.09 (uncertain) across the Cochrane pool and 29.8% vs 29.2% in ALADDIN, with a possible increase in multiple pregnancy (OR 1.38)

title: Metformin added in clomiphene-resistant PCOS: ovulation 75% versus 27% and pregnancy 55% versus 7% in the small double-blind trial — but gonadotropins beat the combination in the pooled comparison
question: In women undergoing ovulation induction, does adding metformin in clomiphene-resistant PCOS improve ovulation and live birth?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for ovulation and pregnancy, with live birth unreported in the anchor trials. In the double-blind placebo-controlled trial in clomiphene-resistant women (Vandermolen 2001), adding metformin 500 mg three times daily for seven weeks and continuing it with clomiphene gave ovulation in 9 of 12 women (75%) versus 4 of 15 (27%) on placebo, and pregnancy in 6 of 11 (55%) versus 1 of 14 (7%). Kocak 2002 (56 women, double-blind) likewise found higher ovulation rates and a higher cumulative pregnancy rate with metformin, though the per-group pregnancy rate did not differ significantly. The meta-analysis of 12 trials (1,411 women) adds the ceiling: against gonadotropins, metformin plus clomiphene produced fewer pregnancies (OR 0.45, 95% CI 0.27 to 0.75) — so the combination is a step before gonadotropins, not a substitute for them. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): metformin restores clomiphene response in resistant PCOS; no anchor trial reported live birth.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — ovulation 75% vs 27% and pregnancy 55% vs 7% in the double-blind resistant-PCOS trial; gonadotropins remain superior (pregnancy OR 0.45 for the combination by comparison); live birth unreported

title: Acupuncture around embryo transfer: the early unblinded trial claimed pregnancy 42.5% versus 26.3% — the 848-woman sham-controlled trial found live birth 18.3% versus 17.8%
question: In women having IVF, does acupuncture around embryo transfer improve live birth?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — when the control is a sham needle. Paulus 2002 randomised 160 women to acupuncture 25 minutes before and after embryo transfer or no acupuncture and reported clinical pregnancy 42.5% (34/80) versus 26.3% (21/80) — with no sham control and no live-birth endpoint. Smith 2018 then ran the definitive test: 848 women at 16 centres, acupuncture versus a non-invasive sham needle placed away from true points, and live birth was 18.3% (74/405) versus 17.8% (72/404) — risk difference 0.5% (95% CI −4.9 to 5.8), relative risk 1.02 (95% CI 0.76 to 1.38). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): the apparent benefit was the ritual and the attention, not the needles at the points.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — sham-controlled trial of 848 women: live birth 18.3% vs 17.8% (RR 1.02); the positive early trial had no sham control and no live-birth endpoint

title: Mild stimulation in poor responders: ongoing pregnancy 12.8% versus 13.6% and live birth pooled RR 1.01 — the same babies for about 3,100 fewer units of gonadotropin, at the price of more cancelled cycles
question: In women undergoing IVF, does mild ovarian stimulation match conventional stimulation for live birth with less burden in predicted poor responders?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — for live birth, which here is the finding that matters. The multicentre non-inferiority trial (Youssef 2017, 394 women with poor ovarian reserve) found ongoing pregnancy 12.8% (25/195) on a mild strategy (150 IU FSH with an antagonist) versus 13.6% (27/199) on conventional high-dose stimulation (450 IU HMG with a long agonist protocol) — risk ratio 0.95 (95% CI 0.57 to 1.57), absolute difference −0.7% (95% CI −7.4 to 5.9), inside the predefined 10% non-inferiority margin — using a mean 3,135 IU less gonadotropin and 1.2 fewer stimulation days. The 15-trial meta-analysis agrees on outcomes: fresh live birth RR 1.01 (95% CI 0.97 to 1.04) and cumulative live birth RR 1.15 (95% CI 0.73 to 1.81), with fewer oocytes (mean difference −0.80) and more cancellations (RR 1.48, 95% CI 1.08 to 2.02) on mild stimulation. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): in poor responders, high-dose stimulation buys oocytes and completed cycles, not babies.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — ongoing pregnancy 12.8% vs 13.6% (non-inferior within a 10% margin) and pooled fresh live birth RR 1.01; mild stimulation uses far less drug but cancels more cycles (RR 1.48)

title: Dual trigger (GnRH agonist plus hCG): live birth per transfer 36.2% versus 22% in the double-blind trial and pooled live birth RR 1.37 — from a trial stopped early at interim
question: In women undergoing IVF, does dual triggering (GnRH agonist + hCG) improve oocyte yield and live birth in normal responders compared with hCG alone?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — promising, with an early-stopping asterisk. In the double-blind randomised trial (Haas 2020, 155 normal responders), dual trigger produced more oocytes (13.4 versus 11.1, p = 0.002) and more mature oocytes (10.3 versus 8.6, p = 0.009) than hCG alone, with clinical pregnancy 46.1% versus 24.3% (OR 2.65) and live birth per transfer 36.2% versus 22% (OR 1.98, 95% CI 1.05 to 3.75, p = 0.03). The meta-analysis of randomised trials (Hu 2021, 1,048 participants) found the same direction on the harder endpoint: live birth per started cycle RR 1.37 (95% CI 1.07 to 1.76, I² = 0%, moderate evidence) and clinical pregnancy RR 1.29 (95% CI 1.10 to 1.52). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): dual triggering improves oocyte yield and probably live birth in normal responders — held at POSSIBLE because the anchor trial stopped at a planned interim analysis, a design that inflates effects.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — live birth per transfer 36.2% vs 22% (OR 1.98) in the double-blind trial and pooled live birth per started cycle RR 1.37 across randomised trials; anchor trial stopped at interim

title: OHSS prevention splits: antagonist protocols cut OHSS (OR 0.61) with live birth intact — agonist trigger cuts it far further (OR 0.15) but cost live birth in fresh transfers (OR 0.47)
question: In women at high risk of OHSS, does a GnRH-antagonist protocol with agonist trigger reduce OHSS compared with an agonist protocol?
balance: SPLIT — the two halves of the strategy behave differently. The antagonist protocol itself (Cochrane, Al-Inany 2016; 73 RCTs, 12,212 women) reduced any-grade OHSS versus the long agonist protocol (OR 0.61, 95% CI 0.51 to 0.72) — an assumed 11% risk falling to between 6% and 9% — with no conclusive difference in live birth (OR 1.02, 95% CI 0.85 to 1.23). Adding an agonist trigger in place of hCG within antagonist cycles (Cochrane, Youssef 2014; 17 RCTs, 1,847 women) cut mild-to-severe OHSS much further (OR 0.15, 95% CI 0.05 to 0.47 — an assumed 5% risk falling to between nil and 2%) but in fresh autologous cycles it also lowered live birth (OR 0.47, 95% CI 0.31 to 0.70) and raised early miscarriage (OR 1.74, 95% CI 1.10 to 2.75), an effect dependent on luteal-phase support; in donor-recipient cycles live birth did not differ (OR 0.92, 95% CI 0.53 to 1.61) while OHSS still fell (OR 0.05). PROPOSED SPLIT: antagonist protocol — OHSS benefit at no live-birth cost; agonist trigger — near-elimination of OHSS, paid for in fresh-transfer live birth unless the cycle is frozen or donated.
stamp: SPLIT — LIKELY (benefit) on OHSS for both components (protocol OR 0.61; trigger OR 0.15), no live-birth difference for the protocol switch, LIKELY (harm) on fresh live birth for the trigger switch (OR 0.47; no difference in donor cycles)

title: Frozen transfer preparation splits by trial scale: one single-centre trial gave natural cycle live birth 54.0% versus 43.0% — the 4,376-woman multicentre trial found healthy live birth 41.6% versus 40.6%, with fewer maternal complications on natural cycles
question: In women undergoing frozen embryo transfer, does a natural cycle match a hormone-replacement cycle for live birth?
balance: SPLIT — live birth by trial, maternal safety consistently favouring natural cycles. COMPETE (Liu 2025; 902 ovulatory women, single centre) found live birth after the first frozen transfer higher with a natural-cycle strategy: 54.0% (242/448) versus 43.0% (195/454) on hormone replacement (absolute difference 11.1 percentage points, 95% CI 4.6 to 17.5; RR 1.26, 95% CI 1.10 to 1.44), with miscarriage RR 0.61 — but 101 of 448 natural-cycle women crossed over to hormone replacement for absent ovulation. The far larger multicentre trial (Wei 2026; 4,376 women, 24 centres) found healthy live birth essentially identical: 41.6% (910/2185) versus 40.6% (890/2191), relative ratio 1.03 (95% CI 0.96 to 1.10) — while pre-eclampsia among clinical pregnancies was lower on natural cycles (2.9% versus 4.6%, relative ratio 0.63), as were early pregnancy loss, placental accreta spectrum, caesarean section and postpartum haemorrhage; cancellation was higher on natural cycles (16.2% versus 11.5%). A Belgian multicentre trial (Geysenbergh 2026; 561 women) also found no significant difference in clinical pregnancy with fetal heartbeat (33.1% versus 28.9%, RR 1.15, 95% CI 0.89 to 1.47). PROPOSED SPLIT: live birth — matched in the large trials, better only in the single-centre trial; the natural cycle's clearer win is obstetric safety, at the price of more monitoring and cancellations.
stamp: SPLIT — LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) on live birth (large definitive multicentre trial, RR 1.03, 95% CI 0.96–1.10) / POSSIBLE (benefit) on maternal complications (pre-eclampsia 2.9% vs 4.6% among pregnancies)

title: Deuruxolitinib for severe alopecia areata: SALT ≤20 at 24 weeks in 30–42% across two phase 3 trials versus 0.8% on placebo — a different JAK inhibitor from the baricitinib/ritlecitinib shelf
question: In patients with alopecia areata (adolescents/adults), does deuruxolitinib or another JAK inhibitor regrow hair?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — two concordant phase 3 trials of a drug not covered by the existing baricitinib/ritlecitinib shelf. In THRIVE-AA1 (King B et al., PMID: 39053611), a Severity of Alopecia Tool (SALT) score ≤20 at 24 weeks was achieved by 29.6% on deuruxolitinib 8 mg twice daily and 41.5% on 12 mg twice daily versus 0.8% on placebo. THRIVE-AA2 (Tsianakas A et al., PMID: 41317911; 517 randomised) replicated it: 33.0% (8 mg), 38.3% (12 mg) and 0.8% (placebo), p<0.0001 for both doses. Most treatment-emergent adverse events were mild or moderate and consistent with other oral JAK inhibitors; neither trial assessed durability after stopping or long-term safety. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): deuruxolitinib regrows hair in roughly a third of adults with severe alopecia areata over 24 weeks, with long-term and off-treatment durability unshown.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — SALT ≤20 in 29.6–41.5% versus 0.8% on placebo across two phase 3 trials (THRIVE-AA1/-AA2)

title: Upadacitinib versus adalimumab in psoriatic arthritis (SELECT-PsA 1): ACR20 at week 12 in 70.6% (15 mg) and 78.5% (30 mg) versus 65.0% on adalimumab — non-inferior at 15 mg, superior only at 30 mg
question: In patients with psoriatic arthritis, does upadacitinib beat adalimumab for joint response?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for upadacitinib over placebo, and for parity-or-better against adalimumab. In SELECT-PsA 1 (McInnes IB et al., PMID: 33789011; 1,704 patients), ACR20 at week 12 was 70.6% on upadacitinib 15 mg, 78.5% on 30 mg, 36.2% on placebo (p<0.001 for both doses versus placebo) and 65.0% on adalimumab: the 15 mg difference versus adalimumab was 5.6 percentage points (95% CI −0.6 to 11.8; non-inferior, not superior), the 30 mg difference 13.5 points (95% CI 7.5 to 19.4; superior). In biologic-refractory disease (SELECT-PsA 2, Mease PJ et al., PMID: 33272960; 642 patients), ACR20 was 56.9% (15 mg) and 63.8% (30 mg) versus 24.1% on placebo (p<0.001). Serious infections through week 24 in SELECT-PsA 1: 1.2% (15 mg), 2.6% (30 mg), 0.9% (placebo), 0.7% (adalimumab). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): upadacitinib matches adalimumab at the licensed-style 15 mg dose and beats it only at 30 mg, where infections rise.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — ACR20 non-inferior to adalimumab at 15 mg and superior at 30 mg in SELECT-PsA 1, with placebo-controlled support in SELECT-PsA 2

title: Upadacitinib beats dupilumab head-to-head in atopic dermatitis: EASI75 at week 16 in 71.0% versus 61.1% (Heads Up), and the combined EASI90-plus-itch endpoint in 19.9% versus 8.9% (Level Up) — faster itch relief, more infections and laboratory events
question: In patients with atopic dermatitis, does upadacitinib beat dupilumab for itch and clearance?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two head-to-head randomised trials point the same way. In Heads Up (Blauvelt A et al., PMID: 34347860; 692 adults), EASI75 at week 16 was achieved by 71.0% on upadacitinib 30 mg daily versus 61.1% on dupilumab (p=0.006), EASI100 by 27.9% versus 7.6% (p<0.001), with itch improvement already separated at week 1 (31.4% versus 8.8% mean improvement; p<0.001). In Level Up (Silverberg JI et al., PMID: 39438067), the combined endpoint of EASI90 plus Worst Pruritus NRS 0/1 at week 16 was achieved by 19.9% on response-escalated upadacitinib versus 8.9% on dupilumab (p<0.001). The price in Heads Up: serious infection, eczema herpeticum, herpes zoster and laboratory adverse events were more frequent on upadacitinib; conjunctivitis and injection-site reactions were more frequent on dupilumab. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): upadacitinib clears skin faster and more completely than dupilumab, trading injection-site and eye effects for infection and laboratory effects.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — EASI75 71.0% versus 61.1% (Heads Up) and combined EASI90 + itch 0/1 19.9% versus 8.9% (Level Up), both favouring upadacitinib

title: Central retinal vein occlusion (LEAVO): aflibercept matched ranibizumab on vision at 100 weeks with about two fewer injections — bevacizumab non-inferiority was not shown (single-trial shelf)
question: In patients with retinal vein occlusion, does aflibercept beat ranibizumab head-to-head for vision?
balance: SPLIT — aflibercept non-inferior to ranibizumab / bevacizumab non-inferiority not shown. The live ranibizumab shelf (#894) answers ranibizumab versus sham; this shelf answers the head-to-head question in central retinal vein occlusion from the single LEAVO trial (Hykin P et al., PMID: 31465100; 463 patients). Mean visual-acuity gain at 100 weeks was 12.5 letters on ranibizumab, 15.1 letters on aflibercept and 9.8 letters on bevacizumab. Aflibercept was non-inferior to ranibizumab (adjusted difference 2.23 letters, 95% CI −2.17 to 6.63; p<0.001 for non-inferiority) with fewer mean injections (10.0 versus 11.8; difference −1.9, 95% CI −2.9 to −0.8). Bevacizumab was not shown non-inferior (difference −1.73 letters, 95% CI −6.12 to 2.67; p=0.07). PROPOSED SPLIT: aflibercept is a vision-equivalent alternative to ranibizumab with a slightly lighter injection load; bevacizumab's equivalence remains unproven in this trial.
stamp: SPLIT — LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for aflibercept vs ranibizumab on vision (non-inferior in both ITT and per-protocol analyses, 1.9 fewer injections) / bevacizumab non-inferiority not established

title: Perioperative dexamethasone in adult tonsillectomy: less nausea, vomiting and pain in two small double-blind trials — a 62% relative fall in postoperative nausea and vomiting in the larger one
question: In patients having tonsillectomy, does perioperative dexamethasone reduce postoperative nausea and pain in adults?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two small double-blind placebo-controlled trials in adults (the paediatric dexamethasone literature is a different population and is not carded here). McKean S et al. (PMID: 16441800; 72 adults) found a single 10 mg intravenous dose at induction produced a 62% relative decrease in postoperative nausea and vomiting (p=0.001), a 23% relative decrease in day-of-operation pain scores (p=0.016) and a 17.5% lower mean pain score over 7 days (p<0.001), with no adverse effects seen. Al-Shehri AM et al. (PMID: 15573850; 30 adults) found a 24-hour, three-dose dexamethasone course (6 mg per dose) gave significantly less pain, nausea and vomiting, better healing and less granulation over 2 weeks, with no side effects reported. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a cheap single intervention eases the first week for adults, on small-trial evidence.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — 62% relative reduction in postoperative nausea and vomiting and significantly lower pain scores in two small double-blind adult trials

title: Replacing saturated fat with linoleic-acid oils in the old diet-heart trials: cholesterol fell, deaths did not — Minnesota showed no mortality benefit and Sydney showed more deaths on the safflower-oil diet
question: In adults, does replacing saturated fat with polyunsaturated fat reduce coronary events in the old diet-heart trials?
balance: SPLIT — the cholesterol hypothesis worked on the blood test and failed on deaths, in opposite directions in the two recovered trials. In the Minnesota Coronary Experiment (9,423 institutionalised participants; recovered-data analysis, Ramsden CE et al., PMID: 27071971), replacing saturated fat with corn oil lowered serum cholesterol by -13.8% versus -1.0% on the control diet, yet there was no mortality benefit in the full cohort or any prespecified subgroup, and each 30 mg/dL (0.78 mmol/L) fall in cholesterol was associated with a 22% higher risk of death (hazard ratio 1.22, 95% CI 1.14 to 1.32). In the Sydney Diet Heart Study (458 men after a coronary event; Ramsden CE et al., PMID: 23386268), the safflower-oil group had higher all-cause mortality (17.6% versus 11.8%; hazard ratio 1.62, 95% CI 1.00 to 2.64), cardiovascular mortality (17.2% versus 11.0%) and coronary mortality (16.3% versus 10.1%). The accompanying meta-analyses found no benefit on coronary death (Minnesota review: ratio 1.13, 0.83 to 1.54). PROPOSED SPLIT: for linoleic-acid-rich oils specifically, the recovered randomised record shows cholesterol lowering without coronary benefit, and a harm signal in secondary prevention — this does not test mixed polyunsaturated replacement as eaten in modern diets.
stamp: SPLIT — cholesterol fell in both recovered trials; mortality was unchanged in Minnesota and higher on the linoleic-acid diet in Sydney (secondary prevention)

title: Music around surgery and on the wards: pain and anxiety fall across 73 trials (standardised effects −0.77 and −0.68) and analgesia use drops — length of stay does not move, and ward delirium is untested
question: In hospitalised patients, does music therapy reduce pain, anxiety or delirium compared with usual care?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for pain and anxiety in hospital, not for delirium or discharge. A systematic review and meta-analysis of 73 randomised trials (Hole J et al., PMID: 26277246) found music around surgical procedures reduced postoperative pain (standardised mean difference −0.77, 95% CI −0.99 to −0.56), anxiety (−0.68, −0.95 to −0.41) and analgesia use (−0.37, −0.54 to −0.20), and increased patient satisfaction (1.09, 0.51 to 1.68), while length of stay did not differ (−0.11, −0.35 to 0.12); music worked even under general anaesthesia, and who chose the music mattered little. An individual four-arm inpatient trial points the same way (Deng C et al., PMID: 34134947; 160 women having breast-cancer surgery): music therapy alone beat usual care on pain and anxiety change (P<0.001), with combined aromatherapy-plus-music best. No qualifying randomised trial of music for delirium in general hospital wards was found — the delirium evidence sits in intensive care and is homed on its own shelf — so the delirium part of the question is unanswered here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): offering patients music in hospital is a cheap, safe way to take a real slice off pain and anxiety; it does not shorten stay and has no proven ward-delirium effect.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a 73-trial meta-analysis shows moderate reductions in postoperative pain, anxiety and analgesia use, with no effect on length of stay; delirium in ward patients is untested

title: Methadone started in prison: treatment entry 68.6% vs 7.8% and opioid-positive urines 27.6% vs 62.9% at one month in the US trial — and in the Australian cohort, nobody died while retained on methadone, against 17 deaths off it
question: In prisoners with opioid use disorder, does methadone maintenance started in prison reduce post-release overdose and reincarceration compared with no treatment or forced withdrawal?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — starting methadone before release changes what happens after it. In the Baltimore randomised trial (211 heroin-dependent pre-release inmates), methadone plus counselling in prison, continued in the community, beat counselling with passive referral on every early measure: community treatment entry at one month 68.6% versus 7.8% (Kinlock TW et al., PMID: 17628351), opioid-positive urine 27.6% versus 62.9%, and at six months the methadone group was still significantly more likely to be retained in treatment (P=0.0001) and less likely to test opioid-positive (P=0.002), with fewer self-reported days of heroin use and criminal activity (Gordon MS et al., PMID: 18855822). The Australian randomised trial (382 prisoners; Dolan KA et al., PMID: 14563543) found significantly lower heroin use, injecting and syringe sharing on methadone versus a wait-list at five months, with no difference in HIV or hepatitis C incidence over that window. Its four-year follow-up carries the mortality and reincarceration answer (Dolan KA et al., PMID: 15918812): no deaths occurred while subjects were enrolled in methadone treatment, against 17 deaths off treatment (untreated mortality 2.0 per 100 person-years, 95% CI 1.2 to 3.2), and reincarceration risk was lowest during methadone episodes of eight months or longer (adjusted hazard ratio 0.3, 0.2 to 0.5). No trial randomised overdose death itself — the overdose claim rests on retention, heroin-use and all-cause-mortality data. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): prison-initiated methadone with community continuation is one of the few prison health interventions with randomised evidence behind both its drug-use and its survival-relevant outcomes.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two randomised trials show prison-started methadone raises treatment entry and cuts heroin use after release; cohort follow-up shows zero deaths while retained versus 2.0 per 100 person-years off treatment and lower reincarceration with longer retention

title: Nurse-led transitional care in heart failure: the small 1990s trials cut readmissions by nearly half — the 2,494-patient modern trial found no effect on readmission, emergency visits or death (HR 0.99)
question: In patients with heart failure discharged from hospital, does a nurse-led transitional-care programme reduce readmission?
balance: SPLIT — by era and scale. The founding trials were strongly positive: in 282 high-risk patients aged 70+ discharged with heart failure (Rich MW et al., PMID: 7565975), a nurse-directed multidisciplinary intervention (education, diet, discharge planning, medication review, intensive follow-up) produced 53 readmissions versus 94 on conventional care (risk ratio 0.56; P=0.02), with heart-failure readmissions reduced by 56.2% in relative terms (24 vs 54 events) — while the primary outcome, survival for 90 days without readmission, was met by 91 of 142 versus 75 of 140 patients and did not reach significance (P=0.09), and deaths were not reported separately. A Scottish trial of specialist-nurse intervention begun before discharge (Blue L et al., PMID: 11576977; 165 patients) found death or heart-failure readmission in 37% versus 53% (hazard ratio 0.61, 95% CI 0.33 to 0.96), with fewer readmissions for any reason (86 vs 114) and for heart failure (19 vs 45). But the definitive modern test was null: in the stepped-wedge PACT-HF trial (Van Spall HGC et al., PMID: 30806695; 2,494 patients across ten Ontario hospitals), a nurse-led transitional-care model (self-care education, structured discharge summary, family-physician follow-up within a week, nurse home visits and heart-function clinic for high-risk patients) did not improve the composite of all-cause readmission, emergency-department visit or death at three months (49.4% vs 50.2%; HR 0.99, 0.83 to 1.19) or readmission/ED visits at 30 days (HR 0.93, 0.73 to 1.18), though discharge-preparedness, transition-quality and quality-of-life scores improved. PROPOSED SPLIT: nurse-led transitional care worked against 1990s usual care; against contemporary usual care, the largest trial shows better-feeling discharges without fewer events — mortality included in the composites throughout, and nowhere reduced on its own.
stamp: SPLIT — POSSIBLE (benefit) in the older small-trial settings / LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) under modern usual care (PACT-HF: composite HR 0.99 in 2,494 patients)

title: BEACON: encorafenib plus cetuximab (with or without binimetinib) roughly doubles survival in previously treated BRAF V600E metastatic colorectal cancer — 9.3 versus 5.9 months on updated analysis
question: In patients with metastatic colorectal cancer and BRAF V600E mutation, does encorafenib plus cetuximab improve survival compared with chemotherapy (BEACON)?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one large randomised trial, reported twice, with a survival gain in a poor-prognosis niche. In BEACON (665 patients, PMID: 31566309), median overall survival was 9.0 months on encorafenib–binimetinib–cetuximab (triplet) and 8.4 months on encorafenib–cetuximab (doublet) versus 5.4 months on cetuximab–chemotherapy control (hazard ratios 0.52 and 0.60); response was 26% on triplet versus 2% on control. On the updated analysis (Tabernero, PMID: 33503393), median survival was 9.3 months for both triplet and doublet versus 5.9 months for control (hazard ratios 0.60 and 0.61), with grade ≥3 adverse events in 65.8%, 57.4% and 64.2% respectively — so the doublet matched the triplet on survival with fewer severe events, and the doublet is the regimen the update names a new standard of care. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a single-trial survival benefit of about 3.4–3.9 months in previously treated BRAF V600E disease, capped at POSSIBLE in this band.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single phase 3 trial (BEACON): encorafenib plus cetuximab, with or without binimetinib, improved median survival from 5.9 to 9.3 months versus cetuximab–chemotherapy in previously treated BRAF V600E metastatic colorectal cancer

title: CLEAR: lenvatinib plus pembrolizumab more than doubles progression-free survival versus sunitinib in first-line advanced kidney cancer (23.9 versus 9.2 months) — the survival edge narrows at final analysis (HR 0.79)
question: In patients with advanced renal cell carcinoma, does lenvatinib plus pembrolizumab beat sunitinib for progression-free survival (CLEAR)?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one large phase 3 trial with a very large progression-free-survival effect and a survival effect that shrank as data matured. In CLEAR (Motzer, PMID: 33616314), median progression-free survival was 23.9 months on lenvatinib plus pembrolizumab versus 9.2 months on sunitinib (hazard ratio 0.39), and overall survival initially favoured the combination (hazard ratio 0.66; P=0.005). At the final prespecified survival analysis (Motzer, PMID: 38227898), the survival hazard ratio was 0.79 (95% CI 0.63 to 0.99), median survival was 53.7 versus 54.3 months, 36-month survival was 66.4% versus 60.2%, progression-free survival stayed 23.9 versus 9.2 months (hazard ratio 0.47), response was 71.3% versus 36.7%, and grade 3 or higher treatment-emergent events occurred in 82.4% on the combination versus 71.8% on sunitinib in the primary report. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a single-trial first-line benefit driven by progression-free survival and response, with a modest mature survival edge and more severe toxicity.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single phase 3 trial (CLEAR): lenvatinib plus pembrolizumab beat sunitinib on progression-free survival (23.9 vs 9.2 months) and response (71.3% vs 36.7%), with a smaller final survival effect (HR 0.79)

title: KEYNOTE-775: lenvatinib plus pembrolizumab extends survival in previously treated advanced endometrial cancer — 17.4 versus 12.0 months in mismatch-repair-proficient disease, at an 88.9% grade ≥3 event rate
question: In patients with advanced endometrial cancer, does lenvatinib plus pembrolizumab improve survival after prior therapy (KEYNOTE-775)?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one phase 3 trial, confirmed at its final analysis, with a survival gain and a heavy toxicity price. In Study 309/KEYNOTE-775 (Makker, PMID: 35045221), median overall survival in mismatch-repair-proficient (pMMR) disease was 17.4 months on lenvatinib plus pembrolizumab versus 12.0 months on physician's-choice chemotherapy (hazard ratio 0.68), and 18.3 versus 11.4 months overall (hazard ratio 0.62); progression-free survival was 6.6 versus 3.8 months in pMMR disease (hazard ratio 0.60). At the final prespecified analysis (Makker, PMID: 37058687) the effects held: survival hazard ratios 0.70 (pMMR) and 0.65 (all-comers), response 32.4% versus 15.1% in pMMR disease. Grade ≥3 adverse events occurred in 88.9% on the combination versus 72.7% on chemotherapy in the primary report. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a single-trial survival benefit after platinum therapy, capped at POSSIBLE in this band.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single phase 3 trial (Study 309/KEYNOTE-775): lenvatinib plus pembrolizumab improved survival versus physician's-choice chemotherapy in previously treated advanced endometrial cancer (pMMR 17.4 vs 12.0 months), with grade ≥3 events in 88.9%

title: KEYNOTE-716: adjuvant pembrolizumab cuts recurrence in resected stage IIB/C melanoma — 36-month recurrence-free survival 76.2% versus 63.4%, distant-metastasis-free survival 84.4% versus 74.7%; overall survival not yet shown
question: In patients with resected stage IIB/C melanoma, does adjuvant pembrolizumab reduce recurrence (KEYNOTE-716)?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one double-blind placebo-controlled trial, consistent across its reports, on recurrence endpoints rather than survival. In KEYNOTE-716 (Luke, PMID: 35367007), first recurrence or death at the second interim analysis had occurred in 15% on pembrolizumab versus 24% on placebo (hazard ratio 0.61). At the final distant-metastasis-free-survival analysis (Luke, PMID: 38452313; median follow-up 39.4 months), 36-month distant-metastasis-free survival was 84.4% versus 74.7% (hazard ratio 0.59) and 36-month recurrence-free survival was 76.2% versus 63.4% (hazard ratio 0.62). Grade 3–4 treatment-related adverse events occurred in 16% versus 4% at the first interim analysis. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a single-trial reduction in recurrence and distant metastasis after resection of stage IIB/C disease, with no overall-survival result in these records.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single double-blind phase 3 trial (KEYNOTE-716): adjuvant pembrolizumab improved recurrence-free and distant-metastasis-free survival in resected stage IIB/C melanoma (36-month RFS 76.2% vs 63.4%); overall survival not reported

title: FLAURA2: adding chemotherapy to first-line osimertinib extends survival in EGFR-mutated lung cancer — median 47.5 versus 37.6 months at final analysis, with grade ≥3 events doubled (70% versus 34%)
question: In patients with EGFR-mutant NSCLC, does osimertinib plus chemotherapy beat osimertinib alone in first line (FLAURA2)?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one phase 3 trial whose progression-free-survival win matured into a survival win. In FLAURA2 (Planchard, PMID: 37937763), progression-free survival favoured osimertinib plus platinum–pemetrexed chemotherapy over osimertinib alone (hazard ratio 0.62), with 57% versus 41% alive and progression-free at 24 months and response in 83% versus 76%. At the planned final survival analysis (Jänne, PMID: 41104938), median overall survival was 47.5 months on the combination versus 37.6 months on osimertinib alone (hazard ratio 0.77; 95% CI 0.61 to 0.96; P=0.02) — a median gain of 9.9 months — while grade ≥3 adverse events of any cause occurred in 70% versus 34%, and osimertinib discontinuation for adverse events in 12% versus 7%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a single-trial survival benefit bought with roughly double the severe-toxicity rate, capped at POSSIBLE in this band.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single phase 3 trial (FLAURA2): first-line osimertinib plus platinum–pemetrexed improved overall survival versus osimertinib alone (median 47.5 vs 37.6 months; HR 0.77), with grade ≥3 events in 70% vs 34%
