title: The mRNA RSV vaccine cut lower-respiratory disease by 83.7% relative in its first season in over-60s — one trial, a median of only 112 days watched, and a rougher two days after the jab
question: In older adults, does an mRNA RSV vaccine prevent RSV lower-respiratory disease compared with placebo (a platform boundary vs live #980's pregnancy question)?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — strong first-season protection from the mRNA platform, in a single trial that had watched participants for a median of only 112 days when the primary analysis was run. ConquerRSV randomised 35,541 adults aged 60 and over to one dose of mRNA-1345 (n=17,793) or placebo (n=17,748). Vaccine efficacy was 83.7% relative (95.88% CI 66.0 to 92.2) against RSV-associated lower respiratory tract disease with at least two signs or symptoms, 82.4% relative (96.36% CI 34.8 to 95.3) against disease with at least three signs or symptoms, and 68.4% relative (95% CI 50.9 to 79.7) against RSV-associated acute respiratory disease, with protection against both RSV subtypes A and B. The price was reactogenicity: solicited local reactions in 58.7% versus 16.2% and systemic reactions in 47.7% versus 32.9%, mostly mild to moderate and transient; serious adverse events occurred in 2.8% of each group. The protein-based RSV vaccines for this age group live on their own shelf (live #320); this shelf is the mRNA platform's separate record — and durability beyond one season is not in it. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a single dose of mRNA-1345 prevents RSV lower-respiratory disease in adults 60 and over, on one large trial with short median follow-up.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single randomised double-blind trial (ConquerRSV, n=35,541): mRNA-1345 efficacy 83.7% relative against RSV lower-respiratory disease with ≥2 symptoms at a median 112 days, with higher transient reactogenicity than placebo

title: Rapid troponin pathways discharge more chest-pain patients within hours — 0/1-hour protocol freed 45.1% from the ED versus 32.3%, and a single undetectable troponin freed 46% within 4 hours, with no excess 30-day death or infarction in either randomised trial
question: In patients with chest pain, does a high-sensitivity troponin 0/1-hour pathway discharge safely compared with standard serial testing?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for flow, with safety shown only to a non-inferiority standard over 30 days. In RAPID-TnT (Chew DP et al., PMID: 31478763), 3,288 patients with suspected acute coronary syndrome randomised to a 0/1-hour high-sensitivity troponin T protocol versus a masked 0/3-hour protocol were discharged from the ED in 45.1% versus 32.3% of cases (p<0.001), with median ED stay 4.6 versus 5.6 hours and less functional testing (7.5% versus 11.0%); 30-day death or myocardial infarction was 1.0% in both arms (incidence rate ratio 1.06, 95% CI 0.53–2.11; non-inferiority p=0.006), and negative predictive value among those discharged was 99.6%. In LoDED (Carlton EW et al., PMID: 32371401), a single undetectable troponin plus a non-ischaemic ECG discharged 46% within 4 hours without a 30-day major adverse cardiac event versus 37% on usual care (adjusted OR 1.58, 95% CI 0.84–2.98), and no patient with an undetectable first troponin had an event within 30 days. Neither trial was powered for rare missed events beyond its non-inferiority margin, and RAPID-TnT saw more myocardial injury recognised in the rapid arm. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): rapid troponin pathways safely speed discharge in two randomised trials; the benefit is hours and avoided tests, not lives.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two randomised trials show rapid troponin pathways discharge substantially more patients hours earlier with 30-day death/MI non-inferior to standard serial testing

title: Moxifloxacin alone matched ofloxacin plus metronidazole for uncomplicated pelvic inflammatory disease in three randomised trials — resolution 90.2% versus 90.7% in the double-blind trial — with fewer drug-related adverse events on the single drug
question: In patients with pelvic inflammatory disease, does moxifloxacin match ofloxacin plus metronidazole for cure?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — moxifloxacin monotherapy cured uncomplicated pelvic inflammatory disease at the same rate as the two-drug regimen in every randomised comparison. In the double-blind trial (Ross JD et al., PMID: 16723364), clinical resolution at test of cure was 90.2% on moxifloxacin versus 90.7% on ofloxacin plus metronidazole (95% CI for the difference −5.7% to 4.0%). A second, larger trial (Aşicioğlu O et al., PMID: 23993130) found clinical cure in 79.5% versus 82.7% (p=0.172). A third trial, against the closely related levofloxacin plus metronidazole (Judlin P et al., PMID: 20716255), found cure in 78.4% versus 81.6% and met its non-inferiority margin. The single drug's edge was tolerability and simplicity: drug-related adverse events were 22.5% versus 30.9% (p=0.01) in the double-blind trial and 37.5% versus 46.4% (p=0.003) in the larger trial. All three trials enrolled uncomplicated disease only — no tubo-ovarian abscess, no sepsis — so nothing here extends to complicated pelvic infection. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): once-daily moxifloxacin alone matches fluoroquinolone-plus-metronidazole combinations for clinical and bacteriological cure in uncomplicated pelvic inflammatory disease, with fewer drug-related adverse events.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — moxifloxacin monotherapy matches ofloxacin (or levofloxacin) plus metronidazole for cure of uncomplicated pelvic inflammatory disease across three randomised trials, with fewer drug-related adverse events

title: Pentoxifylline for claudication: the largest trial found it indistinguishable from placebo (+64 m versus +65 m walked at 24 weeks) — and the Cochrane review could not pool the smaller, inconsistent trials that leaned its way
question: In adults with intermittent claudication from peripheral artery disease, does pentoxifylline improve pain-free and maximal walking distance compared with placebo?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference) — the honest summary is that pentoxifylline has never been shown, at any usable certainty, to make claudicants walk further. The Cochrane review (Broderick C et al., PMID: 33063850) gathered 24 studies with 3,377 participants, 17 of them against placebo, and could not pool them: the percentage improvement in pain-free walking distance over placebo ranged from −33.8% to 73.9% across trials, and in total walking distance from 1.2% to 155.9%, with the review rating any benefit low-certainty and finding no difference in ankle-brachial index or quality of life at moderate certainty. The largest single double-blind trial (Dawson DL et al., PMID: 11063952; 698 patients, 24 weeks) is blunter: maximal walking distance rose 64 m on pentoxifylline and 65 m on placebo (P=0.82 between them) — the drug and the dummy were indistinguishable, while cilostazol in the same trial gained 107 m. The drug is well tolerated (mainly gastrointestinal upset), so the question is not safety but whether there is any effect to buy. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference): on the record as it stands, pentoxifylline's walking benefit is unproven — the biggest trial is a flat null and the pooled record is too inconsistent to overturn it.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference) — the largest double-blind trial found pentoxifylline identical to placebo on maximal walking distance, and the Cochrane review of 24 trials (3,377 patients) could not pool the smaller inconsistent trials and rated any benefit low-certainty

title: Statins and walking distance in PAD: pain-free walking improved in trials of two different statins — atorvastatin 80 mg and simvastatin 40 mg — but maximal walking time did not move in the largest trial
question: In adults with peripheral artery disease and intermittent claudication, do statins improve walking distance — and do trials of two different statins agree?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for the distance walked before pain stops you, shown for two different statins. In the largest trial (Mohler ER 3rd et al., PMID: 12952839; 354 patients, 12 months), atorvastatin did not significantly change maximal walking time, but pain-free walking time improved on the 80 mg dose versus placebo (P=0.025), and a physical-activity questionnaire improved on both the 10 mg and 80 mg doses (P=0.011). Simvastatin carries the cleaner walking numbers: in 86 hypercholesterolaemic claudicants (Mondillo S et al., PMID: 12714124), six months of simvastatin 40 mg increased pain-free walking distance by 90 m more than placebo (95% CI 64 to 116) and total walking distance by 126 m more (95% CI 101 to 151), with ankle-brachial index gains alongside; and in older patients (Aronow WS et al., PMID: 12972114) simvastatin lengthened treadmill time to claudication onset by 24% at six months and 42% at one year while placebo did not significantly change. So the answer to 'two different statins?' is yes on the face of the trials — atorvastatin and simvastatin each improved pain-free walking — with the catch that the trials are small and old, and the biggest one's headline endpoint (maximal walking time) was null. None of this displaces the reason these patients take statins anyway: event prevention, for which the walking gain is a symptom bonus. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): statins modestly improve pain-free walking distance in claudication, on concordant small trials of two different agents.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two small double-blind trials of two different statins (atorvastatin 80 mg; simvastatin 40 mg) improved pain-free walking distance in claudication, with a third small placebo-controlled simvastatin trial concordant; the largest trial's maximal-walking-time endpoint was null

title: Vitamin C and iron absorption: a real dose-response at the meal — relative absorption up 1.65-fold at 25 mg and 9.57-fold at 1,000 mg — that shrinks to +30% relative for a supplement dose and to nothing for anaemia recovery
question: In people taking oral iron or eating iron-containing meals, does adding vitamin C (ascorbic acid) in different amounts increase iron absorption, and by how much?
balance: SPLIT — the answer depends on which claim is being made. For a single meal, the absorption effect is real and dose-graded: in the classic semisynthetic-meal experiments (Cook & Monsen 1977, PMID: 835510; 63 men), the relative ratio of iron absorption with versus without ascorbic acid rose from 1.65 at 25 mg to 9.57 at 1,000 mg, directly proportional to dose — and substantially less when the meal contained meat. Across real meals in 299 subjects (Hallberg 1986, PMID: 3700141), the enhancement was most pronounced in meals rich in inhibitors such as phytates and tannins, food vitamin C matched synthetic, and about 50 mg per main meal was judged enough for optimum effect; phytate itself inhibited absorption dose-dependently (by 18% relative at 2 mg and 82% relative at 250 mg) and ascorbic acid significantly counteracted it (Hallberg 1989, PMID: 2911999). With a modern supplement dose the gain is smaller and saturates early: 80 mg of ascorbic acid raised fractional absorption of a 100 mg ferrous fumarate dose by 30% relative, and 500 mg added nothing further (von Siebenthal 2023, PMID: 37357807). But the effect does not scale up to whole diets or to anaemia treatment: across complete diets at vitamin C intakes of 51–247 mg/day, absorption did not differ significantly (Cook & Reddy 2001, PMID: 11124756); and in 440 patients with iron-deficiency anaemia, iron plus 200 mg vitamin C three times daily was equivalent to iron alone for haemoglobin and ferritin recovery (Li 2020, PMID: 33136134), with a pooled advantage across trials of just 0.14 g/dL of haemoglobin (Deng 2024, PMID: 40765927). So the routine advice to pair vitamin C with iron rests on genuine meal-level physiology — and on the clinical question patients actually ask, the added vitamin C makes no measurable difference. PROPOSED SPLIT: vitamin C dose-dependently increases nonheme iron absorption from single meals and modestly from a supplement dose, but adding it to oral iron does not improve anaemia recovery (the treatment made no difference).
stamp: SPLIT — absorption: vitamin C increases nonheme iron absorption dose-dependently at a single meal (relative ratio 1.65 at 25 mg rising to 9.57 at 1,000 mg; +30% relative from a supplement dose at 80 mg, no further gain at 500 mg) · treatment: adding vitamin C to oral iron in iron-deficiency anaemia made no difference to haemoglobin or ferritin recovery (equivalence in the 440-patient randomised trial; pooled haemoglobin advantage 0.14 g/dL, judged clinically insignificant)

title: Psyllium (Metamucil) for diarrhoea: it halves faecal incontinence episodes with loose stools (2.5 vs 5.5 per week on placebo) and matches loperamide in chronic diarrhoea — but it did not prevent tube-feeding diarrhoea, and it has never been trialled in acute infectious diarrhoea
question: In adults with diarrhoea, does psyllium (Metamucil) help — and for which kinds of diarrhoea (chronic diarrhoea, faecal incontinence, diarrhoea-predominant IBS as an adjunct) — and where does it not help (acute infectious diarrhoea)?
balance: SPLIT — the answer depends on the kind of diarrhoea. Faecal incontinence with loose or liquid stools is where psyllium has its clearest trial support: in the largest fibre trial (Bliss 2014, PMID: 25155992; 189 community-living adults, 16 g/day for 32 days), estimated incontinence episodes were 2.5 per week on psyllium versus 5.5 per week on placebo, and psyllium was the only fibre of the three tested that significantly reduced frequency (carboxymethylcellulose increased it); an earlier 39-person trial from the same group (Bliss 2001, PMID: 11480529) found the proportion of incontinent stools on psyllium or gum arabic was less than half that on placebo. Against an active drug, psyllium matched loperamide: in an 80-person double-blind crossover trial (Markland 2015, PMID: 26347971) there were no differences between psyllium and loperamide for incontinence episodes, severity or quality of life, both improved within-group, and constipation was less frequent on psyllium (10% versus 29%). In chronic diarrhoea proper, the one direct trial is small and old: ispaghula husk plus calcium halved stool frequency just as loperamide did in 19 completers, and was significantly better for urgency and stool consistency (Qvitzau 1988, PMID: 3074458). The mechanism is demonstrated experimentally — psyllium, unlike calcium polycarbophil or wheat bran, made stools firmer and increased faecal viscosity dose-dependently in phenolphthalein-induced secretory diarrhoea (Eherer 1993, PMID: 8385040) — but that study had only 9 subjects. Where psyllium does NOT help: in enteral tube feeding, the psyllium-specific randomised trials found no reduction in diarrhoea incidence (Lertpipopmetha 2019, PMID: 30561029: 42.9% versus 31.7% with at least one diarrhoea day, P=0.41; Belknap 1997, PMID: 9176691: no significant difference in incidence), even though fibre in enteral feeds overall reduced diarrhoea in a 16-trial meta-analysis (relative risk 0.64, 95% CI 0.49–0.82) — an effect driven by mixed fibre and partially hydrolysed guar gum, with the psyllium subgroup itself unclear (Kaewdech 2022, PMID: 36505240). For acute infectious diarrhoea there is no trial evidence at all: explicit PubMed searches this session found no randomised trial of psyllium in acute infectious diarrhoea or gastroenteritis — the only 'acute' data are the experimental laxative-induced model above and in-vitro work — so psyllium cannot be recommended there on evidence; oral rehydration therapy is the treatment used for dehydration caused by diarrhoea (Fontaine 2000, PMID: 10796624). Boundaries: diarrhoea-predominant IBS as an adjunct is NOT re-carded here — psyllium in IBS overall, including the primary-care trial and the fibre meta-analysis, is homed on Shelf #3619, and no diarrhoea-subgroup-specific psyllium trial was found to card separately; psyllium for constipation is compared on Shelf #3606; and bile-acid diarrhoea has a different drug — colesevelam — on Shelf #2773, cross-pointed here and not re-carded. PROPOSED SPLIT: psyllium helps faecal incontinence with loose stools and probably chronic diarrhoea (small, old evidence); it made no difference to tube-feeding diarrhoea incidence; and it is untested in acute infectious diarrhoea.
stamp: SPLIT — faecal incontinence with loose stools: POSSIBLE (benefit) (2.5 vs 5.5 episodes/week vs placebo, Bliss 2014, n=189; matched loperamide, Markland 2015) · chronic diarrhoea: POSSIBLE (benefit) on one small 1988 crossover trial (ispaghula + calcium halved frequency, better urgency/consistency than loperamide) · enteral tube-feeding diarrhoea: (the treatment made no difference) to incidence in both psyllium-specific RCTs · acute infectious diarrhoea: no trial evidence found — untested, not a substitute for oral rehydration · IBS-D adjunct: see Shelf #3619 (not re-carded)

title: Loperamide beyond a week in chronic diarrhoea: effective at about 4–6 mg a day over 4–13 weeks in small double-blind trials, with few side-effects at therapeutic doses — the life-threatening cardiac record belongs to supratherapeutic abuse doses (median 200 mg a day), not to labelled use
question: In adults with chronic diarrhoea, is loperamide effective and safe when taken for more than a week — including long-term daily use?
balance: BOUNDARY: this shelf is chronic diarrhoea only. Acute diarrhoea is homed separately at Shelf #2478 (loperamide versus placebo, racecadotril and rifaximin in acute and travellers' diarrhoea) and its acute trials are not re-carded here; the azithromycin-plus-loperamide travellers' question at #4603 is an adjunct question, not this one. EFFICACY BEYOND A WEEK: in chronic diarrhoea of mixed causes, loperamide beat placebo in small double-blind trials at ordinary doses — Mainguet 1977 (PMID: 326642; 18 completers with ileocolic disease or resection, median 6 mg/day) found stool frequency and weight significantly decreased, stools more solid and transit prolonged, with gastrointestinal side-effects few and comparable to placebo; Tytgat 1976 (PMID: 779663) found 11 of 15 patients improved in an open phase (optimal dose 4–14 mg/day) and relapse on blinded placebo substitution was obvious enough that the investigator guessed the code in 10 of 11 cases, while ileostomy output fell by 22% relative on loperamide (P less than 0.001). Benefit was sustained over multi-week treatment: Palmer 1980 (PMID: 7002706; 30 patients, three randomised 4-week periods) found loperamide 4.6 mg/day matched codeine and beat diphenoxylate on stool solidity and urgency, with the fewest central side-effects of the three; Cann 1984 (PMID: 6365490; 28 patients with irritable bowel syndrome, 5 weeks per period) found further significant improvement over placebo in diarrhoea, urgency and stool frequency, and 15 of the 18 patients who preferred loperamide remained satisfied at follow-up; Lavö 1987 (PMID: 3306903; 13 weeks, the longest placebo-controlled test) found significant advantages for stool consistency (p less than 0.001), pain (p less than 0.02), urgency (p less than 0.05) and overall response (p less than 0.03). SAFETY — THE TWO RECORDS MUST NOT BE MERGED. At therapeutic doses the trial record is quiet: side-effects few and comparable to placebo (Mainguet), least with loperamide among the antidiarrhoeals compared (Palmer; its discontinuations were for abdominal pain and constipation), and a single nightly self-titrated dose was described as safe over 13 weeks (Lavö). The FDA states loperamide 'is a safe drug when used as directed' and 'safe at approved doses', with labelled maxima of 8 mg/day over-the-counter and 16 mg/day prescription. The serious cardiac record — QT interval prolongation, Torsades de Pointes, other ventricular arrhythmias, syncope, cardiac arrest and death — is a supratherapeutic record: the FDA's 2016 Drug Safety Communication (updated 30 January 2018) concerns 'much higher than the recommended doses', primarily intentional misuse or abuse, and the systematic review of supratherapeutic exposure (Bekka 2026, PMID: 41817965; 129 published cases) found a median daily dose of 200 mg, 57% with known or suspected substance use disorder, severe toxicity in 64% of reported cases and fatalities in 13% — with severity dose-dependent (adjusted OR 1.04 per 10 mg) and severe toxicity reported at doses as low as 20–40 mg/day, just above the labelled maximum. So: effective and apparently well tolerated for weeks at 4–6 mg/day in the trials; no controlled trial runs beyond 13 weeks, so truly long-term daily safety rests on the absence of a therapeutic-dose signal rather than on long controlled follow-up; and the dose must not creep — the toxicology literature begins just above the labelled ceiling. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) at therapeutic doses, Tier C.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — in chronic diarrhoea at therapeutic doses (trials used about 4–6 mg/day; labelled maxima 8 mg/day over-the-counter, 16 mg/day prescription), sustained over 4–13 weeks of double-blind treatment with side-effects few and comparable to placebo; no controlled evidence beyond 13 weeks. The serious cardiac harm (QT prolongation, Torsades de Pointes, ventricular tachycardia, cardiac arrest, death) is a supratherapeutic-abuse record — median 200 mg/day in 129 published cases, fatalities in 13% of reported cases — not a therapeutic-dose record, but severe toxicity has been reported from 20–40 mg/day, just above the labelled maximum

title: Standby antibiotics for travellers' diarrhoea: carry one and reserve it for moderate-to-severe illness — azithromycin first (the only defensible default for South-East Asia and for dysentery), ciprofloxacin undermined by resistance (75% of Campylobacter isolates fluoroquinolone-nonsusceptible), rifaximin only for non-invasive illness — and every course taken raises resistant gut colonisation
question: Should travellers to high-risk regions carry a standby antibiotic to self-treat travellers' diarrhoea — and if so, which one: azithromycin, ciprofloxacin (or another fluoroquinolone), or rifaximin — given current fluoroquinolone-resistance patterns?
balance: LIKELY — yes, carry one, but the carrying is not the treatment decision: the graded expert-panel guideline (Riddle 2017, PMID: 28521004) advises that most if not all travellers be provided with loperamide and an antibiotic for self-treatment, then gates its use by severity — no antibiotic for mild diarrhoea, antibiotics may be used for moderate diarrhoea, and antibiotics should be used for severe diarrhoea, with azithromycin preferred in severe illness and single-dose regimens acceptable. The benefit being bought is time: in the fluoroquinolone-susceptible era a single carried 500 mg dose of ciprofloxacin cut mean diarrhoea duration from 50.4 hours on placebo to 20.9 hours (Salam 1994, PMID: 7983954). The drug choice has since been decided by resistance, not by preference. In Thailand, 51 of 57 Campylobacter isolates (89%) were ciprofloxacin-resistant while azithromycin resistance was 2% (Mason 2017, PMID: 28883983); fluoroquinolone resistance in Campylobacter rose in Thailand from zero in 1990 to 84% in 1995 and has since spread to enterotoxigenic and enteroaggregative Escherichia coli, Shigella and non-typhoidal Salmonella (Tribble 2017, PMID: 28520997); and in the current GeoSentinel series (859 cases, 2015–2022), fluoroquinolone nonsusceptibility was 75% in Campylobacter, 32% in non-typhoidal Salmonella, 22% in Shigella and 18% in diarrhoeagenic E. coli, against macrolide nonsusceptibility of 12% in Campylobacter — though 35% in Shigella (Amatya 2025, PMID: 41591385). Hence the guideline's regional rule: azithromycin for South-East Asia; a fluoroquinolone, azithromycin or rifaximin elsewhere. Rifaximin is the narrowest choice, not a substitute: it is less effective against invasive pathogens, with failure to achieve wellness in up to 50% of treated subjects in the guideline's summary, invasive pathogens account for approximately 10–20% of cases, and it is not appropriate for dysentery at any severity — if rifaximin is the carried first-line agent, azithromycin should also be carried for dysentery or febrile diarrhoea (Riddle 2017). The counterweight is colonisation, and it is quantified: among 430 travellers, ESBL-producing Enterobacteriaceae acquisition was 11% with neither diarrhoea nor antibiotic, 21% with diarrhoea alone and 37% with diarrhoea plus an antibiotic — reaching 80% in South Asia and 69% in South-East Asia when diarrhoea and an antibiotic combined (Kantele 2015, PMID: 25613287); and among 288 travellers with diarrhoea, colonisation was 21% with no medication, 20% with loperamide alone, 40% with an antimicrobial alone and 71% with the guideline-style combination of loperamide plus an antimicrobial (Kantele 2016, PMID: 26691898). So: carry azithromycin as the default standby (the only one of the three that covers dysentery and fluoroquinolone-resistant Campylobacter), hold it for moderate-to-severe illness, and treat ciprofloxacin as a legacy choice whose susceptibility can no longer be assumed. The head-to-head treatment trials behind these choices are homed elsewhere and are not re-carded here: rifaximin treatment at Shelf #4602, azithromycin plus loperamide at Shelf #4603, the single-dose azithromycin Thailand trial and TrEAT TD at Shelf #1213; prophylaxis questions sit at Shelf #4216 (bismuth) and Shelf #1214 (rifaximin prophylaxis) — this shelf is the carry-and-self-treat decision and the drug choice only.
stamp: LIKELY — travellers to high-risk regions should carry a standby antibiotic for self-treatment of moderate-to-severe travellers' diarrhoea, with azithromycin as the default choice (preferred for severe illness and dysentery, and the guideline choice for South-East Asia); ciprofloxacin and other fluoroquinolones can no longer be assumed active (Campylobacter fluoroquinolone nonsusceptibility 75% overall and 89% ciprofloxacin resistance in Thailand isolates, azithromycin resistance 2% in the same series); rifaximin is an option only for non-invasive, non-dysenteric illness and needs azithromycin carried alongside it for dysentery or fever; the price of taking the antibiotic is resistant gut colonisation (ESBL-producing Enterobacteriaceae in 37% of travellers who had diarrhoea and took an antibiotic versus 11% with neither, and 71% when loperamide and an antimicrobial were combined), which is why mild illness should be managed without it

title: Single-dose live oral cholera vaccine CVD 103-HgR (Vaxchora) for travellers: 90.3% efficacy at 10 days and 79.5% at 3 months in the human challenge trial — but 14% and not significant in the one large field trial
question: In adults travelling to cholera-risk areas, does the single-dose live oral cholera vaccine CVD 103-HgR (Vaxchora) prevent cholera, and by how much — and how does its challenge-trial record sit with its field record?
balance: SPLIT — the answer depends on which test of the vaccine is being read. In the human challenge model the protection is large and replicated: in the randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled pivotal trial behind US licensure (Chen 2016, PMID: 27001804; 197 volunteers aged 18–45), moderate (≥3.0 L) to severe (≥5.0 L) diarrhoeal purge after ingesting wild-type Vibrio cholerae O1 El Tor occurred in 39 of 66 (59.1%) placebo recipients versus 2 of 35 (5.7%) vaccinees challenged at 10 days (vaccine efficacy 90.3%, a relative measure) and 4 of 33 (12.1%) vaccinees challenged at 3 months (efficacy 79.5%). An earlier randomised double-blind challenge trial found the same pattern at 3 months (Tacket 1999, PMID: 10569747: moderate or severe diarrhoea in 9 of 23 [39%] placebo recipients versus 1 of 28 [4%] vaccinees; protective efficacy 91%), and the earliest onset/duration studies reported 100% protection against diarrhoea on homologous challenge at 8 days and at 6 months (Tacket 1992, PMID: 1527420). In the field, the same vaccine did not reproduce this: in the randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of 67,508 people aged 2–41 in North Jakarta (Richie 2000, PMID: 10738097), 93 evaluable cholera cases occurred over four years — 43 in vaccinees and 50 in placebo recipients — for an efficacy of 14%, not significant, and the authors concluded that single-dose CVD 103-HgR did not confer long-term protection in Jakarta; only seven cases occurred within six months, so short-term field efficacy could not be assessed. A Jakarta immunogenicity study hints at one reason the field is harder than the challenge ward: the dose that seroconverts over 90% of people in industrialised countries seroconverted only 16% of Indonesian children, and a ten-fold higher dose was needed for 75–87% seroconversion (Suharyono 1992, PMID: 1355798). The vaccine was licensed by the US FDA in 2016 for travellers (Saluja 2020, PMID: 31339792), and ACIP recommends it only for travellers aged 2–64 years going to an area with active cholera transmission (Collins 2022, PMID: 36173766) — cholera is rare in travellers, so this vaccine is rarely recommended for ordinary travellers. BOUNDARY: this shelf covers ONLY the live vaccine CVD 103-HgR (Vaxchora). The killed whole-cell oral cholera vaccines and their field efficacy in endemic settings (Kolkata two-dose 65% over 5 years; Bangladesh single-dose 40% / 63% against severe cholera) are homed on Shelf #1180 and are not re-carded here. PROPOSED SPLIT: strong, replicated protection in the volunteer challenge model at 10 days to 3 months; no significant protection shown in the one large field trial over four years.
stamp: SPLIT — challenge model: single-dose CVD 103-HgR (Vaxchora) prevented moderate/severe cholera after experimental challenge, vaccine efficacy 90.3% at 10 days (5.7% vaccine vs 59.1% placebo attack rates) and 79.5% at 3 months (12.1% vs 59.1%), corroborated by an earlier challenge trial (91% at 3 months) · field record: in the 67,508-person Indonesia field trial, efficacy was 14% (43 vaccine vs 50 placebo cases over four years) and not significant — long-term field protection (the treatment made no difference) on that test; short-term field efficacy was never assessable. Recommended only for travel to areas with active cholera transmission; rarely recommended for ordinary travellers

title: Wildfire smoke and health: in a meta-analysis of over 124 million people, each extra 10 μg/m³ of wildfire PM2.5 came with a 2% relative rise in all-cause mortality and a 4% relative rise in respiratory hospital admissions and emergency visits — all of it observational
question: What does wildfire smoke do to your health? When wildfire smoke raises fine particulate matter (PM2.5) in the air, what happens to deaths, hospital admissions and emergency department visits — especially for lung and heart disease?
balance: POSSIBLE (harm — observational only). Nobody can ethically randomise people to breathe wildfire smoke, so this entire shelf is observational epidemiology, and it should be read that way. In the largest synthesis (Wang 2025: 45 studies, a meta-analysis of over 124 million patients), each 10 μg/m³ rise in wildfire PM2.5 was associated with a relative risk of 1.02 (95% CI 1.01–1.03) for all-cause mortality, 1.04 (1.02–1.05) for respiratory hospital admission and 1.04 (1.02–1.06) for respiratory emergency department visits. A global time-series study of 749 cities (Chen 2021) found nearly identical relative risks for death (1.019 per 10 μg/m³) and estimated that 0.62% of all deaths each year are attributable to wildfire PM2.5. The cardiovascular signal is weaker and inconsistent between studies. The per-person relative risks are small, but smoke exposes whole populations at once, so the absolute number of extra deaths and admissions is large. These studies measure outdoor particle levels, not what any one person breathed, and smoke days differ from ordinary days in heat and behaviour, so residual confounding cannot be excluded.
stamp: POSSIBLE (harm — observational evidence only) — wildfire PM2.5 is consistently associated with more deaths and more respiratory hospital and emergency care (relative risks 1.02–1.04 per 10 μg/m³), but every study is observational: smoke exposure cannot be randomised, so this shelf shows association, not proof of causation

title: Stopping simple snoring (no sleep apnoea): a jaw-advancement device beat a combined nasal/positional bundle in the one head-to-head pilot trial (partner-rated response 91% versus 58%) — and palatal radiofrequency beat sham in one small trial, modestly
question: How do I stop snoring? In adults who snore without obstructive sleep apnoea (primary/simple snoring), do mandibular advancement devices, combined nasal and positional measures, or soft-palate radiofrequency surgery reduce snoring?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the trial record for simple snoring is thin: one small pilot randomised trial and one small sham-controlled surgical trial, with no large or long-term study. In the pilot randomised trial in primary snoring (Ioerger 2024, PMID: 38780959; 50 couples randomised, 42 dyads completed, 4 weeks), a mandibular advancement device (MAD) was rated a responder by the sleeping partner in 21 of 23 snorers (91%) versus 11 of 19 (58%) on combined airway and positional therapy (CAPT — external nasal dilator, nasal saline lavage with mometasone, mouth taping, and lateral positional therapy): a difference of 33 percentage points (95% CI 8–58), number needed to treat 3; both options reduced snoring, and adverse-effect withdrawals were 2 in each group. For surgery, the only placebo-controlled trial of soft-palate radiofrequency in primary snoring (Stuck 2005, PMID: 16124664; 26 patients, 23 completed) found partner-rated snoring scores improving from 8.1 to 5.2 on a 10 cm scale with radiofrequency versus 8.4 to 8.0 with sham needle insertion (P < 0.05) — a real but moderate effect, in the authors' own words. The systematic review of palatal radiofrequency (Bäck 2009, PMID: 19365852; 30 studies, only 2 randomised) confirms that this single sham-controlled trial is the controlled core of the surgical literature, that radiofrequency causes less postoperative pain than other procedures, and that most studies were uncontrolled with short follow-up, precluding solid conclusions. BOUNDARY: this shelf is simple snoring only. External nasal dilator strips used alone are homed on Shelf #2530 and are not re-carded here (the dilator appears here only as one component of the CAPT bundle); mandibular advancement devices versus CPAP for obstructive sleep apnoea are homed on Shelf #923, and oropharyngeal exercises for OSA on Shelf #1507 — different questions, not re-carded. Anyone whose snoring comes with witnessed apnoeas or daytime sleepiness needs an apnoea evaluation, not this shelf. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a MAD is the best-tested option on a small evidence base; the combined nasal/positional bundle also helped most users in the same small trial; palatal radiofrequency has one small positive sham-controlled trial and a mostly uncontrolled literature behind it.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in the only head-to-head pilot trial in primary snoring (42 couples completing), a mandibular advancement device was partner-rated a responder in 91% versus 58% for a combined nasal/positional bundle (NNT 3); palatal radiofrequency beat sham in one small trial (snoring score 8.1→5.2 versus 8.4→8.0). Small, short trials only

title: Paracetamol (acetaminophen) in pregnancy and child neurodevelopment: ordinary cohort analyses show a small association (pooled ADHD risk ratio 1.34) — but the 2.48-million-child Swedish sibling-control analysis found none (hazard ratio 0.98 for autism and for ADHD)
question: Is paracetamol (acetaminophen) safe in pregnancy? In pregnant people who use paracetamol/acetaminophen for pain or fever, is use associated with autism, ADHD, or intellectual disability in their children — and does the association survive sibling-control analysis?
balance: SPLIT / CONTESTED — all of this evidence is observational; no randomised trial of paracetamol in pregnancy with child neurodevelopment follow-up exists, and the answer changes with the study design. The association side: in the Danish National Birth Cohort (Liew 2014, PMID: 24566677; 64,322 children), children of mothers who used acetaminophen in pregnancy had higher risk of a hospital diagnosis of hyperkinetic disorder (hazard ratio 1.37, 95% CI 1.19–1.59), ADHD medication use (HR 1.29, 1.15–1.44), and ADHD-like behaviours at age 7 (risk ratio 1.13, 1.01–1.27), with stronger associations for use in more than one trimester. Pooling seven cohorts (Masarwa 2018, PMID: 29688261; 132,738 mother–child pairs) gave a risk ratio of 1.34 (1.21–1.47) for ADHD and 1.19 (1.14–1.25) for autistic spectrum disorder. The confounding side: the largest study (Ahlqvist 2024, PMID: 38592388; 2,480,797 Swedish children, 185,909 [7.49%] exposed) found only marginal associations before sibling control (autism HR 1.05; ADHD HR 1.07; intellectual disability HR 1.05; crude absolute risks at age 10 in unexposed versus exposed children 1.33% versus 1.53% for autism, 2.46% versus 2.87% for ADHD, 0.70% versus 0.82% for intellectual disability) — and in matched full-sibling analyses, which compare children of the same mother and so strip out shared family factors, there was no association at all: autism HR 0.98 (0.93–1.04), ADHD HR 0.98 (0.94–1.02), intellectual disability HR 1.01 (0.92–1.10), with no dose–response pattern. The authors' reading is that the ordinary-model associations may be attributable to familial confounding — the reasons and family background behind paracetamol use, not the drug. The counterweight, stated plainly: paracetamol is the analgesic and antipyretic most commonly used in pregnancy (Masarwa 2018), it is taken for pain and for fever, and the cohort studies compare users with non-users — they do not test the alternative of leaving significant pain or fever untreated, which is itself a clinical problem in pregnancy; this shelf therefore cannot be read as 'never take it' or as 'proven harmless'. PROPOSED SPLIT: a small association in conventional cohort analyses that disappears under sibling control in the largest and best-controlled study — causality unproven either way, evidence contested and observational throughout.
stamp: SPLIT (contested, observational only) — pooled conventional cohorts: ADHD risk ratio 1.34 and ASD 1.19 with prenatal acetaminophen; the largest study's sibling-control analysis (2,480,797 children): hazard ratio 0.98 for autism, 0.98 for ADHD, 1.01 for intellectual disability — no association, no dose–response. Familial confounding is the leading explanation; causality is not established in either direction

title: Stopping nail biting: habit reversal training beat wait-list and a rival behavioural method in a 91-child trial — N-acetylcysteine beat placebo at one month in a 42-child pilot, then lost its edge by month two
question: How do I stop biting my nails? In children, adolescents and adults with chronic nail biting (onychophagia), do habit reversal training, object manipulation, or the supplement N-acetylcysteine (NAC) help nails grow and biting stop?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) for habit reversal training (HRT); MAYBE (weak evidence) for N-acetylcysteine. HRT — awareness training plus a competing response — is the best-tested treatment for nail biting: in a 91-child randomised trial, HRT and object manipulation training both increased nail length versus wait-list at 1 month (P<0.001 each), and by 3 months HRT was ahead of object manipulation (P<0.021), with complete stopping in 8 of 30 children on HRT and 7 of 30 on object manipulation, versus 0 on wait-list during its month of waiting. NAC 800 mg/day beat placebo on nail growth at 1 month in a 42-child double-blind pilot (5.21 mm versus 1.18 mm) but not at 2 months, and dropout was high. An uncontrolled retrospective series of 93 children given NAC for mixed habit disorders (nail biting among them) rated 49 of 93 (53%) significantly better or completely clear — without a control group that cannot separate a drug effect from time, expectation and staying on treatment. No trial in this area is large, and none follows patients beyond 3 months.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — habit reversal training increased nail length versus wait-list (P<0.001 at 1 month) and beat object manipulation long-term in one 91-child randomised trial; NAC's one positive pilot (42 children) showed a difference at 1 month (nail growth 5.21 mm versus 1.18 mm) that was gone by 2 months. Small trials, short follow-up

title: Side effects of GLP-1 drugs: nausea affects about 1 in 5 users in trials (relative risk 2.90 versus placebo), vomiting about 1 in 11 — and the rare serious signals (gastroparesis, thyroid cancer) come with conflicting answers
question: What are the side effects of GLP-1 drugs? In people taking GLP-1 receptor agonists such as semaglutide, liraglutide, exenatide, dulaglutide or tirzepatide for diabetes or weight loss, how common are gut side effects, and what is the evidence on gastroparesis, bowel obstruction, pancreatitis, thyroid cancer, and retained stomach contents at endoscopy or surgery?
balance: SPLIT. The common side effects are not in doubt: across 101 randomised trials (Joy 2026), nausea (22.8% of users; relative risk 2.90 versus placebo), vomiting (9.12%; RR 3.60), diarrhoea (13%; RR 1.97), constipation (7.39%; RR 2.41) and decreased appetite (2.61%; RR 3.51) are class effects, and the same analysis found pancreatitis at 1.07% incidence with a relative risk of 2.24. The rarer, more serious signals rest on observational data and conflict. A US claims study (Sodhi 2023) found higher rates of gastroparesis, bowel obstruction and pancreatitis than with bupropion-naltrexone, but on only 613 semaglutide users and with very wide confidence intervals. For thyroid cancer, a French case-control study found an association after 1–3 years of use (adjusted HR 1.58), while a Scandinavian active-comparator cohort of 437,077 starters found none (HR 0.93; upper confidence limit consistent with no more than a 31% relative increase). Around procedures, GLP-1 users much more often have retained stomach contents at endoscopy (OR 6.30) and more aborted procedures (OR 5.50), but aspiration itself was not significantly increased (OR 1.26, 95% CI 0.86–1.87).
stamp: SPLIT — the everyday gut effects are LIKELY and common (in 101 randomised trials: nausea in 22.8% of users, relative risk 2.90 versus placebo; vomiting 9.12%, relative risk 3.60; diarrhoea 13%, relative risk 1.97). The rare serious harms are contested: one claims study links the drugs to gastroparesis, bowel obstruction and pancreatitis, and the two large thyroid-cancer studies disagree (France: adjusted HR 1.58 for 1–3 years of use; Scandinavia: HR 0.93)

title: Antibiotics for acute bronchitis: no difference in overall clinical improvement (relative risk 1.07), cough shorter by about half a day on average — and adverse effects more common (relative risk 1.20; one extra person harmed per 24 treated)
question: Do antibiotics help bronchitis? In people with acute bronchitis (an acute chesty cough, without pneumonia and without underlying lung disease), do antibiotics shorten the cough or speed recovery — and what harms do they cause?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for the outcome patients care about — getting better. The Cochrane review of 17 trials (Smith 2017) found no difference in the proportion clinically improved (RR 1.07, 95% CI 0.99–1.15), with small average gains on some cough measures (mean cough duration 0.46 days shorter; cough still present at follow-up RR 0.64, NNTB 6) set against more adverse effects (RR 1.20; NNTH 24). The largest placebo-controlled trial, GRACE (Little 2013; 2,061 adults with acute lower-respiratory-tract infection, pneumonia not suspected), found amoxicillin did not shorten moderately-bad symptoms (HR 1.06, P=0.229), caused nausea, rash or diarrhoea in one extra patient per 21 treated, and produced one case of anaphylaxis; its one positive finding — fewer new or worsening symptoms (15.9% versus 19.3%; NNT 30) — is a secondary outcome. If a prescription feels hard to withhold, delayed prescribing is the evidence-based compromise: in the Cochrane prescribing review (Spurling 2023), cough outcomes did not differ between delayed, immediate and no antibiotics in any study, while delaying cut antibiotic use from 93% to 30% with similar satisfaction (86% versus 91%).
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for overall recovery — the Cochrane review found no significant difference in clinical improvement (RR 1.07, 95% CI 0.99–1.15) and a mean cough just 0.46 days shorter, while adverse effects increased (RR 1.20; number needed to harm 24). The largest single trial (2,061 patients) found amoxicillin did not shorten 'moderately bad or worse' symptoms at all (HR 1.06, P=0.229)

title: Best medicine for acute low back pain: NSAIDs beat placebo by 7.3 points on a 100-point pain scale — an effect the Cochrane authors call small and probably not clinically relevant; paracetamol was no better than placebo at all
question: What is the best medicine for back pain? For acute low back pain, scoped here to the drug class with the best trial record — non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) versus placebo — how much do they reduce pain and disability, and how do the other drug classes compare?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), small. Scoped to NSAIDs for acute low back pain, this is the honest answer to 'best medicine': NSAIDs are the best-supported drug class, and their average advantage over placebo is small — pain −7.29 points on a 0–100 scale (van der Gaag 2020, Cochrane, 32 trials, 5,356 participants) and disability −2.02 points on a 0–24 scale, with the review's authors concluding the effects are 'small and probably not clinically relevant'. A second meta-analysis of spinal pain (Machado 2017) puts it in patient terms: 6 people need treatment for 1 extra person to achieve a clinically important pain reduction, and gastrointestinal reactions were 2.5 times more common on NSAIDs. The Cochrane overview of all drug classes (Cashin 2023; 7 reviews, 103 studies, 22,238 participants) found no high- or moderate-certainty evidence that any drug gives a large or medium effect on pain in acute or chronic low back pain, and high-certainty evidence that paracetamol is no better than placebo for acute low back pain (pain MD 0.49, 95% CI −1.99 to 2.97). BOUNDARY: this shelf covers NSAIDs alone. Whether adding a muscle relaxant to an NSAID helps is a separate question, homed on Shelf #786 ('Muscle relaxants for acute low back pain: the null shelf'); its studies are not re-carded here.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — NSAIDs give a small average benefit over placebo in acute low back pain (pain −7.29 points on a 0–100 scale, moderate certainty; disability −2.02 on a 0–24 scale, high certainty) that the Cochrane authors judge probably not clinically relevant; no drug class provides a large or medium effect, and paracetamol is no better than placebo. Boundary: adding a muscle relaxant to an NSAID is a different question, homed on Shelf #786 — not covered here

title: Do antidepressants work — and which is best? All 21 drugs beat placebo across 522 trials (response odds ratios 1.37–2.13, relative measures), but the average drug–placebo difference is 1.75 Hamilton points, and only about 15% of patients get a substantial drug-specific benefit
question: Do antidepressants work — and which is best? In adults with major depressive disorder, how much do antidepressants beat placebo, how big is the benefit in absolute terms, how does it change with severity, and which drugs rank best for efficacy and for staying on treatment?
balance: LIKELY (benefit), modest average size, growing with severity. The anchor is Cipriani 2018: 522 double-blind trials, 116,477 participants, and all 21 antidepressants beat placebo on response (odds ratios — relative measures — from 2.13 for amitriptyline down to 1.37 for reboxetine); between drugs the differences were smaller (ORs 1.15–1.55 across all trials), and only agomelatine and fluoxetine had fewer dropouts than placebo. Absolute framing comes from Stone 2022's individual-participant analysis of 232 FDA-submitted trials (73,388 participants): the mean drug–placebo difference was 1.75 Hamilton points, responses were trimodal, and a large response occurred in 24.5% on drug versus 9.6% on placebo — the authors' estimate that about 15% of participants obtain a substantial antidepressant effect beyond placebo. Fournier 2010's patient-level analysis adds the severity gradient: below a Hamilton score of 23 the drug–placebo effect size was under 0.20, crossing the NICE clinical-significance threshold only at a score of 25. So: the drugs work on average, 'which is best' has only small separations (escitalopram, mirtazapine, paroxetine, venlafaxine, vortioxetine and agomelatine ranked higher for efficacy; agomelatine, citalopram, escitalopram, fluoxetine, sertraline and vortioxetine for acceptability), and the expected benefit is least in mild depression. Certainty in the network analysis was moderate to very low.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) for the class in major depressive disorder — all 21 antidepressants were more effective than placebo across 522 trials (116,477 participants) — with the size stated plainly: an average advantage of 1.75 Hamilton points, a large response in 24.5% of patients on drug versus 9.6% on placebo, and a drug–placebo difference that may be minimal or nonexistent in mild-to-moderate symptoms (effect size d<0.20 below a Hamilton score of 23 in patient-level data)

title: MCT oil: swapping it for other fats lost an extra 0.51 kg across 13 small trials — and the Alzheimer's cognition claim failed its 413-patient confirmatory trial (ADAS-Cog difference 0.76 points, P=0.2458, not significant)
question: Should I take MCT oil? In adults, does medium-chain triglyceride (MCT) oil — swapped for other dietary fats, or taken as a ketogenic medical food — reduce weight and body fat, or improve memory and thinking in Alzheimer's disease?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence). For weight: the meta-analysis of 13 randomised trials (Mumme & Stonehouse 2015; 749 adults) found that replacing long-chain triglycerides with MCTs reduced body weight by 0.51 kg (95% CI −0.80 to −0.23), waist circumference by 1.46 cm and total body fat (SMD −0.39), with no difference in blood lipids — but many trials lacked information for full quality assessment, commercial bias was detected, and the design was substitution: adding MCT oil (extra calories) on top of an unchanged diet was not what was tested. For cognition, the tested products were specific caprylic-triglyceride medical foods, named here per library rule: AC-1202 and AC-1204, developed by the sponsoring company (Accera, Inc. — the first author's affiliation on the 2009 record; Cerecin, Inc. on the 2020 record). AC-1202 (Henderson 2009; 152 patients with mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's) differed from placebo on ADAS-Cog at day 45 (1.9 points, P=0.0235) and at day 90 only within the APOE4-non-carrier subgroup (3.36 points, P=0.0148); the larger confirmatory trial of AC-1204 (Henderson 2020; 413 patients, 26 weeks) found no benefit in that same pre-specified subgroup (difference 0.76 points, P=0.2458) and no drug effect on secondary outcomes. Generic MCT oil and coconut oil sold as supplements were not the tested products in the cognition trials.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — replacing long-chain fats with MCTs lost an extra 0.51 kg (95% CI −0.80 to −0.23) across 13 small trials in which commercial bias was detected, and the trials swapped fats rather than adding MCT oil on top; the cognition claim rests on one maker-run 152-person trial positive at day 45 and in a genetic subgroup, while its 413-person confirmatory trial found no benefit (P=0.2458)

title: Bringing down a fever in adults: fever medicines lower temperature (0.38 °C on average in sepsis) but do not improve survival — mortality relative risk 0.93 (95% CI 0.77–1.13) across the randomised trials; the big ICU paracetamol trial (HEAT) lives on Shelf #3160
question: How do I bring down a fever (in adults)? In febrile adults — the trial evidence is almost entirely in critically ill patients with infection — do paracetamol (acetaminophen), ibuprofen or physical cooling improve survival and other patient-important outcomes, or only the thermometer reading?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for outcomes beyond the thermometer. Fever can certainly be lowered: across the randomised trials in Drewry 2017's meta-analysis, antipyretic therapy reduced body temperature by 0.38 °C (95% CI −0.63 to −0.13) — but 28-day/hospital mortality was not improved (relative risk 0.93, 95% CI 0.77–1.13; 8 randomised studies, 1,507 patients), nor were shock reversal (RR 1.13, 0.68–1.90) or nosocomial infection (RR 1.13, 0.61–2.09). The largest single drug trial, Bernard 1997 (455 septic patients), found intravenous ibuprofen lowered temperature, heart rate and oxygen consumption with no extra renal or bleeding harm, yet 30-day mortality was 37% versus 40% on placebo — not significant. Physical cooling has the one positive signal: Schortgen 2012 (200 patients with septic shock) found lower day-14 mortality with external cooling (19% versus 34%), but the trial's primary endpoint — vasopressor reduction at 48 hours — was not met (72% versus 61%), so the mortality finding is hypothesis-generating, not settled. The landmark ICU paracetamol trial, HEAT, is homed on Shelf #3160 ('Treating fever with acetaminophen in infected ICU patients: HEAT's 700 patients gained no ICU-free days (23 vs 22), mortality 15.9% vs 16.6% at 90 days') and is not re-carded here. Almost all of this evidence is in critically ill patients with sepsis; there are no comparable outcome trials for ordinary fever at home, where the rational target is comfort rather than a number.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for patient-important outcomes — antipyretics reliably lower temperature, but the randomised evidence in sepsis shows no mortality benefit (RR 0.93, 95% CI 0.77–1.13); intravenous ibuprofen in 455 septic patients gave 30-day mortality of 37% versus 40% on placebo, not significant; the one external-cooling trial with lower day-14 mortality missed its own primary endpoint. The ICU paracetamol trial (HEAT) is homed on Shelf #3160 and is cross-pointed here, not re-carded

title: Motion sickness: scopolamine and first-generation antihistamines prevent it better than placebo when taken before travel — ginger's evidence is one small sea trial — and no drug has ever been trial-tested for treating symptoms once they start
question: What helps motion sickness? In people prone to motion sickness in cars, boats and planes, do scopolamine, antihistamines (meclizine, dimenhydrinate) or ginger prevent symptoms — and can anything treat symptoms once they have started?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for PREVENTION only, taken before the journey. Two Cochrane reviews carry the shelf. For scopolamine (Spinks 2011, PMID: 21678338; 14 randomised trials, 1,025 subjects), scopolamine was more effective than placebo at preventing symptoms, was superior to methscopolamine and equivalent to antihistamines in the few head-to-head comparisons, and caused more dry mouth but no more drowsiness, blurred vision or dizziness than comparators; the trials were small and of varying quality, and the review prints no pooled effect size. For first-generation antihistamines (Karrim 2022, PMID: 36250781; 9 RCTs, 658 participants), the natural-motion studies (cinnarizine and dimenhydrinate only) found symptoms prevented in 40% on antihistamines versus 25% on placebo (risk ratio 1.81, 95% CI 1.23 to 2.66 — a relative measure, printed beside the absolute rates of 40% and 25%; moderate-certainty, 3 studies, 240 participants), at the cost of more sedation (66% versus 44% on placebo; RR 1.51, relative). Ginger rests on much thinner ice: one double-blind sea trial of 80 naval cadets (Grøntved 1988, PMID: 3277342) found less vomiting and cold sweating on 1 g ginger root than placebo (P<0.05) with nausea and vertigo differences not statistically significant, and the systematic review that contains it (Ernst 2000, PMID: 10793599) found exactly one seasickness trial among its six studies and called ginger 'promising' but the data insufficient for firm conclusions. The shelf's sharpest finding is a shared negative: BOTH Cochrane reviews found no randomised trial of any of these drugs for TREATING motion sickness that has already started — every positive result is prevention taken in advance. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): prevention with scopolamine or a first-generation antihistamine is supported at low-to-moderate certainty; ginger is a MAYBE within that; treatment of established symptoms is untested, not disproven.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — prevention only: scopolamine beat placebo across 14 small trials (Cochrane) and first-generation antihistamines prevented symptoms in 40% versus 25% on placebo (RR 1.81, relative; moderate-certainty) with more sedation; ginger rests on one 80-cadet sea trial; no randomised trial has tested any of these drugs for treating symptoms once started

title: Metformin and heart attacks: UKPDS 34's overweight substudy showed 32–42% relative reductions in diabetes endpoints and death — but the abstract prints no absolute rates, the pooled trial record is non-significant, and the 10-year legacy result lives on Shelf #284
question: Does metformin prevent heart attacks? In people with type 2 diabetes — particularly the overweight patients studied in UKPDS 34 — does taking metformin reduce myocardial infarction and cardiovascular death compared with diet alone, other glucose-lowering drugs, or no metformin?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a famous claim resting on a narrow base. The claim comes from one substudy: UKPDS 34 (PMID: 9742977), in which 342 overweight patients with newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes allocated intensive control with metformin, versus 411 allocated a conventional diet-first policy, had relative risk reductions of 32% (95% CI 13–47; P=0.002) for any diabetes-related endpoint, 42% for diabetes-related death (9–63; P=0.017) and 36% for all-cause mortality (9–55; P=0.011) over a median 10.7 years, at HbA1c 7.4% versus 8.0%. Every one of those numbers is a RELATIVE reduction: the abstract prints no absolute event rates, so no honest absolute benefit can be quoted from this record — a gap this shelf states rather than fills. The same paper contains the counter-signal: in its supplementary randomised trial, early addition of metformin to sulphonylurea-treated patients was associated with a 96% relative INCREASE in diabetes-related death (95% CI 2–275; P=0.039) versus continuing sulphonylurea alone — although the paper's own combined analysis (19% relative reduction in diabetes-related endpoints, P=0.033) and its epidemiological assessment in 4,416 patients (5% relative reduction, P=0.78) did not confirm the harm. The one other randomised test, SPREAD-DIMCAD (Hong 2013, PMID: 23230096; 304 patients with type 2 diabetes and coronary artery disease), found fewer composite cardiovascular events on metformin than glipizide (adjusted HR 0.54, 95% CI 0.30–0.90 — relative; P=0.026) over a median 5.0 years, but it is a single small trial against an active comparator, not placebo. When Griffin (2017, PMID: 28770324) pooled the 13 randomised trials that isolate metformin against diet, lifestyle or placebo (2,079 people allocated metformin), NO outcome reached significance — all-cause mortality RR 0.96 (0.84–1.09), cardiovascular death 0.97 (0.80–1.16), myocardial infarction 0.89 (0.75–1.06), stroke 1.04 (0.73–1.48) — and UKPDS itself supplied 52.3% to 70.5% of the weight, so the pool is not independent corroboration. The 10-year post-trial legacy follow-up, in which the metformin group showed myocardial infarction 33% relatively lower (P=0.005) and death 27% relatively lower (P=0.002), is homed on Shelf #284 (how tight should glucose control be) and is cross-pointed, not re-carded, under the one-home rule. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): metformin probably reduces cardiovascular events when started early in overweight type 2 diabetes, but the direct evidence is one positive substudy plus one small active-comparator trial, the pooled isolated-effect estimate is non-significant, and the absolute size of any heart-attack benefit has never been printed in the landmark abstract.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — UKPDS 34's overweight substudy showed 32–42% relative reductions in diabetes endpoints and death versus diet-first policy (no absolute rates printed), SPREAD-DIMCAD favoured metformin over glipizide (HR 0.54, relative), but the pooled isolated-effect meta-analysis is non-significant on every outcome and UKPDS 34's own supplementary trial raised an unconfirmed mortality signal for early combination use; the 10-year legacy follow-up is homed on Shelf #284

title: Rivaroxaban (Xarelto) in stage 3 kidney disease: trial-supported for atrial fibrillation at a creatinine-clearance dose — 15 mg at CrCl 30–49 matched warfarin in ROCKET-AF — with exposure up only ~1.5-fold and no trial data below CrCl 30
question: Can I take Xarelto (rivaroxaban) with stage 3 kidney disease? In a person with stage 3 chronic kidney disease (eGFR 30–59) who needs anticoagulation — chiefly for atrial fibrillation — is rivaroxaban safe and effective, and at what dose?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — yes-with-conditions for atrial fibrillation, and the condition is creatinine clearance (CrCl), not the CKD stage label alone. The pharmacokinetic foundation (Kubitza 2010, PMID: 21039764; 32 subjects given a single 10 mg dose) is that renal impairment raises rivaroxaban exposure only moderately: plasma AUC was 1.44-fold higher in mild impairment (CrCl 50–79 mL/min), 1.52-fold in moderate (30–49) and 1.64-fold in severe (<30) than in healthy controls, with factor Xa inhibition AUC up to 2.0-fold in severe impairment — the drug is only partly renally cleared, so exposure climbs but does not multiply. The outcome evidence is the ROCKET-AF renal subgroup (Fox 2011, PMID: 21873708): of 14,264 randomised patients, the 2,950 (20.7%) with CrCl 30–49 mL/min received the reduced 15 mg/day dose and had stroke or systemic embolism at 2.32 per 100 patient-years versus 2.77 on warfarin (HR 0.84, 95% CI 0.57–1.23 — relative, printed beside the absolute rates), with the principal safety outcome (major plus clinically relevant non-major bleeding) at 17.82 versus 18.28 per 100 patient-years (P=0.76), intracranial bleeding 0.71 versus 0.88 (P=0.54), and fatal bleeding lower on rivaroxaban (0.28 versus 0.74 per 100 patient-years; P=0.047). Note what that means for 'stage 3': stage 3 spans CrCl/eGFR 30–59, and ROCKET-AF dosed by CrCl — 20 mg/day at CrCl ≥50, 15 mg/day at 30–49, and CrCl <30 was outside the trial. Real-world stage III data agree in direction: in a Quebec cohort of 8,899 patients with AF and stage III CKD (Perreault 2023, PMID: 38230301), rivaroxaban 15 mg and 20 mg each presented a similar effectiveness and safety composite risk to warfarin. In the XARENO registry (Kreutz 2024, PMID: 38939389; 1,455 patients, eGFR 15–49, mean eGFR ≈37), rivaroxaban was associated with fewer adverse kidney outcomes than vitamin K antagonists (HR 0.62, 95% CI 0.43–0.88 — relative, observational) and lower all-cause death (HR 0.76, 0.59–0.98), with no significant difference in net clinical benefit. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the randomised support is a subgroup with confidence intervals that include harm, and everything beyond it is observational — so the honest answer is 'studied and usable in AF down to CrCl 30 at the reduced dose, with bleeding rates at least as high as the kidney disease itself makes them, and not trial-tested below CrCl 30'.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — GAP-E: for atrial fibrillation, rivaroxaban is trial-supported in stage 3 kidney disease at a creatinine-clearance dose (20 mg/day at CrCl ≥50 mL/min; 15 mg/day at CrCl 30–49, where it matched warfarin on stroke prevention and composite bleeding in ROCKET-AF's renal subgroup); exposure rises only ~1.5-fold at CrCl 30–49, observational stage III data show no detected penalty — but there is no trial evidence below CrCl 30 and none for VTE dosing on this shelf

title: Toothache and dental pain: ibuprofen plus acetaminophen beats opioids — first in the systematic reviews, first in the 82-trial network analysis, first-line in the ADA guideline
question: What helps a toothache? For acute dental pain — toothache before a dentist can treat the cause, or pain after a tooth extraction — which painkillers actually work best: ibuprofen, acetaminophen, the two together, or prescription opioids?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) for ibuprofen plus acetaminophen as the first-line answer — this is one of the rare everyday questions where the evidence hierarchy speaks with one voice. The Moore 2018 overview of five systematic reviews (PMID: 29599019) found that ibuprofen-and-acetaminophen combinations had the highest association with treatment benefit and the highest proportion of adults achieving maximum pain relief of any oral analgesic strategy reviewed, while opioid-containing medicines were the ones most frequently associated with acute adverse events in both children and adults. The ADA's own evidence base — the Miroshnychenko 2023 network meta-analysis of 82 post-extraction trials (PMID: 36631957) — put numbers on it: for 6-hour pain relief (0–4 scale, versus placebo), ibuprofen 200–400 mg plus acetaminophen 500–1,000 mg scored a mean difference of 1.68 (95% CI 1.06–2.31), ibuprofen 400 mg alone 1.31 (1.17–1.45), naproxen 400–440 mg 1.44 (1.07–1.80), while acetaminophen 650 mg plus oxycodone 10 mg scored 1.19 (0.85–1.54) and oxycodone 5 mg, codeine 60 mg and tramadol 37.5 mg/acetaminophen 325 mg were no better than placebo. The 2024 ADA guideline, summarised for emergency settings by Green 2025 (PMID: 39764906), converts this into practice: NSAIDs with or without acetaminophen are first-line for toothache when definitive dental treatment is not immediately available, and opioids are reserved for when first-line therapy fails or NSAIDs are contraindicated. Two honest limits. First, most trial data come from pain after tooth extraction (the standard dental pain model) rather than the throbbing pulpitis toothache of the question; the guideline explicitly extends the recommendation to temporary toothache management, but the trials themselves are post-surgical. Second, analgesics only buy time: no card here shows a painkiller curing the pulp or periapical disease causing the pain, and definitive dental treatment remains the treatment. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) for NSAID ± acetaminophen as first-line analgesia; opioids show no advantage and more harm.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — ibuprofen plus acetaminophen is the best-supported first-line treatment for acute dental pain: it ranked first for benefit and maximum relief in the Moore 2018 overview of systematic reviews, gave the largest 6-hour relief in the 82-trial ADA network meta-analysis (MD 1.68 vs placebo, ahead of every opioid combination), and is first-line in the 2024 ADA guideline; opioids add harm without added relief

title: Can a UTI go away on its own? Often, yes — 28% symptom-free at one week on placebo, up to 42% improved by 9 days — but most women are still symptomatic without antibiotics, and one placebo patient developed pyelonephritis
question: "Can a UTI go away on its own?" In a non-pregnant woman with uncomplicated cystitis (burning, frequency, urgency, no fever or flank pain), how often do symptoms and infection clear without antibiotics, how long does that take, and what is risked by waiting?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) for the honest answer 'often, yes — but slower, and not always'. The largest placebo dataset (Ferry 2004, PMID: 15198188; 1,143 women randomised, 288 in the placebo arm) found spontaneous symptom cure in 28% after the first week and 37% with neither symptoms nor bacteriuria at 5–7 weeks; the adjusted spontaneous cure of both symptoms and bacteriuria at study end was 24%. The natural-history systematic review (Hoffmann 2020, PMID: 32958533; 3 trials, 346 placebo participants) found the proportion symptom-free or improved rising to 42% over the first 9 days and standing at 36% by 6 weeks — but up to 39% had failed to improve by 6 weeks, and pyelonephritis occurred in one placebo participant. The one small placebo-controlled trial with a direct comparison (Christiaens 2002, PMID: 12236276; 78 women) shows what antibiotics add: symptomatic improvement or cure by day 7 was 30/34 on nitrofurantoin versus 17/33 on placebo (about 88% versus 52%; NNT 2.7), and bacteriological cure by day 3 was 21/26 versus 5/25 (NNT 1.6) — so roughly half of placebo patients were better by a week anyway, and antibiotics roughly doubled the chance and sped it up. The delayed-antibiotic trial (Little 2010, PMID: 20139214; 309 women) found no significant difference in symptom duration or severity between immediate antibiotics and waiting at least 48 hours, while delayed prescribing cut antibiotic use (77% versus 97% still took them) at the cost of 37% longer symptoms among those who waited and then consulted. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for the strategy of watchful waiting with a safety net in uncomplicated cystitis: the natural history is genuinely favourable for a substantial minority, but the majority are still symptomatic at a week without treatment, a small pyelonephritis risk exists, and all of this evidence is in non-pregnant women with uncomplicated lower-tract symptoms — not men, not pregnancy, not fever or flank pain. The ibuprofen-first strategy trial is homed on Shelf #2489 and is not re-carded here.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for watchful waiting in uncomplicated cystitis: spontaneous symptom cure was 28% at one week on placebo in the largest trial (Ferry 2004), up to 42% were symptom-free or improved by 9 days across placebo arms (Hoffmann 2020), but most women do not recover quickly without antibiotics (day-7 cure 17/33 on placebo vs 30/34 on nitrofurantoin), delayed prescribing traded 37% longer symptoms for less antibiotic use, and pyelonephritis, though rare, occurred on placebo

title: Taking ibuprofen every day: cardiovascular events matched other NSAIDs in PRECISION, but ibuprofen was the worst of the three for blood pressure, kidneys and stomach lining
question: "Is it safe to take ibuprofen every day?" For a person taking ibuprofen daily for months or years — usually for arthritis or chronic pain — what does the long-term evidence show about heart, stomach, kidney and blood-pressure harm, and how does ibuprofen compare with celecoxib and naproxen?
balance: SPLIT — the honest answer splits by organ system, and PRECISION (Nissen 2016, PMID: 27959716; 24,081 arthritis patients at increased cardiovascular risk, NCT00346216) is the anchor: at the doses actually used (mean ibuprofen 2,045 mg/day — a high, prescription-level dose), cardiovascular event rates were close across all three drugs (primary outcome: celecoxib 2.3%, naproxen 2.5%, ibuprofen 2.7%), so daily ibuprofen was not shown to be a cardiovascular outlier among NSAIDs. But ibuprofen was the worst of the three on two other systems: gastrointestinal events were significantly fewer on celecoxib than on ibuprofen (P=0.002) or naproxen (P=0.01), and renal events were significantly fewer on celecoxib than on ibuprofen (P=0.004) but not naproxen (P=0.19). The blood-pressure substudy (Ruschitzka 2017, PMID: 29020251; 444 patients) sharpens the renal/vascular picture: over 4 months, mean 24-hour systolic pressure changed by −0.3 mmHg on celecoxib, +1.6 on naproxen and +3.7 on ibuprofen, and new hypertension developed in 23.2% of previously normotensive ibuprofen patients versus 19.0% on naproxen and 10.3% on celecoxib. The older placebo-controlled record (CNT Collaboration, PMID: 23726390; 280 trials, 124,513 participants) supplies the absolute frame: ibuprofen carried the highest relative rate of upper gastrointestinal complications of the traditional NSAIDs (RR 3.97, 95% CI 2.22–7.10 — relative), a non-significant relative rate for major vascular events (RR 1.44, 0.89–2.33) and for major coronary events (RR 2.22, 1.10–4.48) in the NSAID-versus-placebo comparisons, all NSAIDs roughly doubled heart-failure risk, and the collaboration's absolute anchor — about 3 extra major vascular events per 1,000 patients treated for a year with a coxib or diclofenac, one of them fatal — shows that relative risks of this size translate into small absolute numbers for most people, but real ones. PROPOSED SPLIT: daily ibuprofen at arthritis doses is not uniquely dangerous to the heart among NSAIDs, but it is measurably the hardest of the three compared drugs on blood pressure, kidneys and gut — so 'safe every day' depends on dose, duration, and the taker's stomach, kidneys, blood pressure and other medicines. Shelf #330 covers strategies to prevent NSAID harm; this shelf prices the harm itself.
stamp: SPLIT — in PRECISION, daily ibuprofen (≈2,000 mg/day) matched celecoxib and naproxen on cardiovascular events (2.7% vs 2.3% and 2.5%) but was significantly worse for gastrointestinal events (vs celecoxib, P=0.002) and renal events (P=0.004), raised 24-hour systolic pressure by 3.7 mmHg with new hypertension in 23.2% of normotensive users, and in the CNT meta-analysis carried the highest relative rate of upper GI complications (RR 3.97) of the traditional NSAIDs

title: Alcohol on antibiotics: the blanket ban outruns the evidence for most drugs — the metronidazole reaction is unproven under blinded challenge, but MTT-side-chain cephalosporins are a real risk
question: "Can I drink alcohol while taking antibiotics?" For a person prescribed a common antibiotic, which drug–alcohol combinations are genuinely dangerous, which are merely traditional warnings, and what does the evidence actually show for metronidazole — the most famous warning of all?
balance: SPLIT — the blanket warning ('never drink on any antibiotic') outruns the evidence, but the warning is not baseless for a specific few drugs. The systematic review (Mergenhagen 2020, PMID: 31871085) found the published data support safe use with alcohol for many common agents — oral penicillins, cefdinir, cefpodoxime, fluoroquinolones, azithromycin, tetracycline, nitrofurantoin, secnidazole, tinidazole and fluconazole — with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole equivocal. For the famous one, metronidazole, the evidence is strikingly weak: the double-blind challenge study (Visapää 2002, PMID: 12022894; 12 volunteers) found metronidazole did not raise blood acetaldehyde and produced no objective or subjective disulfiram-like effects after 0.4 g/kg ethanol; and the case-literature review (Williams & Woodcock 2000, PMID: 10676835) found that reports from 1969–1982 provided no convincing evidence the reaction exists, and that of 6 case reports covering 8 patients, 4 cases were serious (including one death) but every report simply presumed the reaction was an established fact without providing justifying evidence. Mergenhagen nonetheless records the metronidazole reaction as occurring 'with uncertain frequency and with varied severity' and the label still advises avoiding alcohol during therapy and for at least 72 hours after the last dose — so the shelf's position is: unproven, not disproven, and the official advice stands until better evidence exists. Where the interaction is on firmer ground: cephalosporins carrying a methylthiotetrazole (MTT) side chain or methylthiodioxotriazine (MTDT) ring, plus ketoconazole and griseofulvin, are associated with increased disulfiram-like reaction risk. Two non-interaction reasons to abstain survive any debunking: alcohol worsens many infections' symptoms and recovery, and several antibiotics plus alcohol share side effects (nausea, dizziness, sedation). PROPOSED SPLIT.
stamp: SPLIT — the blanket 'no alcohol on antibiotics' warning outruns the evidence for most agents (the 2020 systematic review found data supporting safe use with penicillins, several cephalosporins, fluoroquinolones, azithromycin, tetracycline and nitrofurantoin), the famous metronidazole reaction is unproven under double-blind challenge and in the case literature — though the label's 72-hour abstinence advice stands — and a real disulfiram-like risk attaches to MTT/MTDT-side-chain cephalosporins, ketoconazole and griseofulvin
