title: Hangover: no treatment has been shown to work — two systematic reviews found only single, small, unreplicated trials, and the reviewers' verdict is that abstinence or moderation is the only effective prevention
question: "How do I get rid of a hangover?" After alcohol, do any medicines, supplements or remedies — painkillers, anti-sickness drugs, prickly pear, ginseng, pear juice, fructose, anything — actually prevent or treat hangover symptoms better than placebo?
balance: (no treatment shown to work) — stated plainly, because two systematic reviews seventeen years apart reached the same conclusion. Pittler 2005 (BMJ, PMID: 16373736) reviewed the randomised trials of hangover interventions — eight double-blind trials covering propranolol, tropisetron, tolfenamic acid, fructose/glucose, borage, artichoke, prickly pear and a yeast preparation — and found significant differences favouring treatment in only a few single trials (tolfenamic acid, the γ-linolenic acid in borage, and the yeast preparation), concluding: 'No compelling evidence exists to suggest that any conventional or complementary intervention is effective for preventing or treating alcohol hangover. The most effective way to avoid the symptoms of alcohol induced hangover is to practise abstinence or moderation.' Roberts 2022 (Addiction, PMID: 34972259) updated the search to August 2021 and found 21 placebo-controlled trials with only 386 participants in total; no two studies tested the same intervention, so no meta-analysis was possible, and every efficacy outcome in every study was rated very low quality by GRADE — a scatter of single small trials with statistically significant results (clove extract, tolfenamic acid, pyritinol, Hovenia dulcis, L-cysteine, red ginseng, Korean pear juice) that have never been replicated. The best-executed single trial on the shelf, Wiese 2004 (PMID: 15226168; 64 young adults, crossover), found a prickly-pear (Opuntia ficus-indica) extract taken before drinking reduced three of nine symptoms (nausea, dry mouth, anorexia) and the odds of a severe hangover (OR 0.38, 95% CI 0.16–0.88 — relative), but the overall symptom index difference was not significant (2.7 points; 95% CI −0.2 to 5.5; P=0.07). PROPOSED (no treatment shown to work): after decades of trials, nothing — drug, supplement or folk remedy — has replicated, adequately powered evidence of relieving a hangover; time, fluids, food and sleep are unproven comforts, and prevention by drinking less is the only intervention with a coherent evidence story.
stamp: (no treatment shown to work) — two systematic reviews (BMJ 2005; Addiction 2022) found no intervention with replicated, adequately reliable evidence for preventing or treating hangover: 21 placebo-controlled trials totalling 386 participants, no two testing the same remedy, every outcome rated very low quality; the best single prevention trial (prickly pear extract) missed significance on its overall symptom index

title: Acetaminophen (paracetamol) safety in a day: 4 g/day — the labelled ceiling — pushed ALT past 3 times the upper limit of normal in 31–44% of healthy volunteers, while the liver-failure cohorts took a median of 24 g and staggered overdoses were stratified by the presenting AST
question: 'How much acetaminophen (paracetamol) is safe in a day?' — What does the evidence say about the 4 g/day ceiling: liver-enzyme effects at the ceiling in healthy adults and in newly abstinent alcoholics, and where liver injury actually concentrates in the repeated supratherapeutic-ingestion and acute-liver-failure cohorts?
balance: SPLIT — the answer depends on which side of the 4 g/day line the evidence sits. AT the ceiling: in the randomised trial of healthy adults taking exactly 4 g/day, the maximum recommended dose, 31–44% of acetaminophen recipients (including the acetaminophen-alone group) had a maximum ALT more than 3 times the upper limit of normal, versus none of 39 on placebo (Watkins 2006, PMID: 16820551) — a common laboratory signal, though no clinical liver injury was reported in that trial; and in newly abstinent alcoholic patients, 4 g/day for 3 days produced peak mean ALT values indistinguishable from placebo (57 ± 45 versus 55 ± 48 IU/L), with no transaminase increase attributed to the drug (Kuffner 2007, PMID: 17537264). ABOVE the ceiling is where the injury cohorts live: in the prospective poison-centre series of repeated supratherapeutic ingestion (>4 g/24 h), no patient whose presenting AST was below 50 IU/L went on to hepatotoxicity, while 15% of those presenting with AST 50–1,000 IU/L did and 16% of those above 1,000 IU/L died or were transplanted (Daly 2004, PMID: 15459622); and in the US acute liver failure registry, acetaminophen caused 42% of all cases, the median dose ingested was 24 g — six times the daily ceiling — and nearly half the cases (48%) were unintentional, often assembled from two or more acetaminophen products taken at once (Larson 2005, PMID: 16317692). PROPOSED SPLIT: at 4 g/day the demonstrated harm is a frequent, usually transient enzyme rise rather than liver failure; the catastrophic outcomes in the fetched record come from doses well above the ceiling or from staggered supratherapeutic use — which is why the practical safety question is less the single-product dose than the total from all products combined.
stamp: SPLIT — at the 4 g/day ceiling, healthy volunteers commonly show ALT rises (31–44% above 3x ULN) but trials show no clinical liver injury at or below the ceiling; the liver-failure record is dominated by median doses of 24 g and staggered supratherapeutic use, where a normal presenting AST (<50 IU/L) predicted no hepatotoxicity

title: Treatment for optic nerve atrophy: none has been shown to work for optic atrophy in general — idebenone's only randomised trial is in Leber hereditary optic neuropathy (Shelf #4253), and its dominant-optic-atrophy data are uncontrolled (an 87-patient cohort and a 16-patient open-label phase 2 trial)
question: 'Is there a treatment for optic nerve atrophy?' — For optic atrophy in general, and for its commonest inherited forms (dominant optic atrophy and Leber hereditary optic neuropathy), has any treatment been shown to preserve or restore vision?
balance: No treatment has been shown to work for optic atrophy in general, and the fetched record supports that scoping exactly. For dominant optic atrophy (DOA), the commonest inherited form, the 2025 systematic review of its natural history states plainly that there is currently no disease-modifying treatment for DOA, and it quantifies why weak studies mislead here: untreated visual acuity declines at only 0.022 LogMAR per year, a rate not significantly different from zero (95% CI −0.008 to 0.052; p=0.155) (Ovens 2025, PMID: 40329928). The only treatment signal in DOA comes from idebenone used off-label: a non-randomised historical cohort of 87 OPA1 patients found stabilisation or recovery of acuity in 92% of treated versus 75.7% of untreated patients (adjusted OR 4.37; 95% CI 1.01–18.9 — a relative measure whose confidence interval nearly touches 1) (Romagnoli 2020, PMID: 32243103), and a 16-patient open-label phase 2 trial reported improved best recovery of visual acuity over 12 months but, being uncontrolled, cannot separate drug effect from placebo effect or natural history (Valentin 2023, PMID: 38130806). The one randomised placebo-controlled idebenone trial in any optic atrophy is in a different disease — Leber hereditary optic neuropathy (RHODOS) — and it is homed on Shelf #4253 (Klopstock 2011, PMID: 21788663); it is cross-pointed here, not re-carded, under the one-home rule. PROPOSED (the treatment made no difference): for optic atrophy as a whole, no therapy has beaten control or natural history in a fetched record; idebenone in DOA remains an uncontrolled, off-label hypothesis, and idebenone's trial and licensing history belongs to LHON.
stamp: (the treatment made no difference) — no treatment has been shown to work for optic atrophy in general; idebenone's only randomised trial is in Leber hereditary optic neuropathy (homed on Shelf #4253), and its dominant-optic-atrophy evidence is a non-randomised cohort and a 16-patient uncontrolled trial

title: Ingrown toenail: adding phenol after nail avulsion cuts recurrence — relative risk 0.13 in the 2023 meta-analysis of 36 studies and 14% versus 41% in the one like-for-like trial — but the trial quality is rated very low and phenol raised post-operative infection in the earlier Cochrane review
question: 'How do I treat an ingrown toenail?' — In people with an ingrowing toenail, how do surgical treatments (especially partial nail avulsion with phenolisation of the matrix) compare with conservative care and with avulsion alone for recurrence, and what harms come with phenol?
balance: The consistent finding across three successive syntheses is that destroying part of the nail matrix with phenol after avulsion lowers recurrence — but the underlying trials are poor. The 2005 Cochrane review found avulsion plus phenol beat surgical excision for symptomatic recurrence at 6 months or more (OR 0.44; 95% CI 0.24–0.80, relative) and beat avulsion alone by a wide relative margin (OR 0.07; 0.04–0.12), at the cost of more post-operative infection (OR 5.69; 1.93–16.77) (Rounding 2005, PMID: 15846620). The 2012 Cochrane update (24 RCTs, 2,826 participants) found surgery better than gutter treatment at preventing recurrence and probably better than orthonyxia (brace), and in the single like-for-like study — partial nail avulsion with matrix excision with or without phenol, 117 participants — recurrence was 14% with phenol versus 41% without (RR 0.34; 0.17–0.69, relative; an absolute difference of 27 percentage points) (Eekhof 2012, PMID: 22513901). The 2023 meta-analysis (36 studies, 3,756 participants) again found phenol plus avulsion far below avulsion alone for recurrence (RR 0.13; 0.06–0.27, relative) but rated that evidence very low quality and concluded the research in this area is poor (Exley 2023, PMID: 37301845). PROPOSED POSSIBLE: phenolisation probably reduces recurrence after avulsion — the direction is consistent across every synthesis — but certainty is capped by very-low-quality trials, and the older review's infection signal has not been cleanly resolved.
stamp: POSSIBLE — phenolisation after partial nail avulsion consistently reduces recurrence across three syntheses (14% vs 41% in the one like-for-like trial; RR 0.13 in the 2023 meta-analysis), but the underlying trial evidence is rated very low quality and an early infection signal (OR 5.69) is unresolved

title: Long-term damage from tick-borne infections: after hospitalised Rocky Mountain spotted fever, 38% of interviewed survivors reported ongoing symptoms and 23% had neurologic sequelae on examination; after treated Lyme disease, persistent symptoms ran only about 4–6 percentage points above background rates
question: 'What long-term damage can tick-borne infections do?' — After Rocky Mountain spotted fever and after treated Lyme disease, how often do symptoms, disability or organ damage persist long-term, and how do those rates compare with people who never had the infection?
balance: SPLIT — the two infections leave very different long-term records. After Rocky Mountain spotted fever severe enough to hospitalise for weeks, lasting damage is common and concrete: in the classic series, 9 of 20 followed patients had at least one sequela persisting a year or more — paraparesis, hearing loss, peripheral neuropathy, bladder and bowel incontinence, cerebellar and motor dysfunction, language disorders (Archibald 1995, PMID: 7619986) — and in a modern Arizona series of 80 hospitalised cases, 38% of interviewed survivors reported ongoing symptoms or reduced function and 23% had neurologic sequelae on examination, with longer hospitalisation and delayed doxycycline marking the worse outcomes (Drexler 2022, PMID: 36324320). After treated Lyme disease the picture is a small excess over a high background: a Connecticut cohort found symptom frequencies similar to matched controls without Lyme disease (Seltzer 2000, PMID: 10665700); the large Dutch prospective cohort found persistent symptoms in 27.2% of Lyme patients versus 21.2% of the general population and 23.3% of tick-bitten controls — absolute excesses of 6.0 and 3.9 percentage points (Ursinus 2021, PMID: 34557833); and a rigorous prospective US study of erythema migrans found no significant difference from matched controls in any symptom at 6 or 12 months (Wormser 2020, PMID: 31996890). PROPOSED SPLIT: RMSF's long-term damage is real, organ-based, and concentrated in severe, late-treated disease; post-treatment Lyme symptoms are common in absolute terms but only modestly more common than in comparable people who never had Lyme.
stamp: SPLIT — after severe hospitalised RMSF, lasting neurological sequelae are documented in a substantial minority of survivors (9 of 20 followed in 1995; 23% with neurologic sequelae on examination in 2022); after treated Lyme disease, persistent symptoms exceed background rates by only ~4–6 percentage points (27.2% vs 21.2–23.3%), and two controlled studies found no significant excess at all

title: Knock knees (genu valgum) at 23: no trials — realignment osteotomy is the adult treatment in the published series, correcting the mechanical axis accurately (96.1% in a 31-procedure series) with osteotomy survival of roughly 74–90% at 10 years in valgus knees with lateral arthritis
question: 'I am 23 with knock knees — what treatment is there?' — In a skeletally mature young adult with genu valgum, what do the published series show for realignment osteotomy (femoral or tibial): correction achieved, durability, and complications? (Guided growth is a children's treatment and does not apply at 23.)
balance: There are no trials for a 23-year-old with knock knees — the entire fetched record is retrospective series and systematic reviews of series, and most of it concerns older patients whose valgus deformity comes with lateral compartment arthritis. What the record does show: realignment osteotomy corrects the deformity accurately — in a consecutive series of 31 procedures (23 patients, mean age 41.2 years), the mechanical axis deviation moved from 32.5 mm lateral to 2.44 mm medial with 96.1% correction accuracy, one stable hinge fracture and one chronic regional pain syndrome, and no non-union or revision (Sheridan 2024, PMID: 39359363). For durability, the distal femoral osteotomy reviews report mean survival of 80% at 10 years in one synthesis (Chahla 2016, PMID: 27331074) and survival of 74–90% at 10 years in a 2025 synthesis of 18 studies, with conversion to knee replacement reaching 48.4% in the longest series (Yazdi 2025, PMID: 41082590) — survival figures that mean 'not yet converted to arthroplasty' in arthritic knees, a different endpoint from what a 23-year-old without arthritis needs. Guided growth (hemiepiphysiodesis), the low-morbidity option in children, requires open growth plates and is not available at 23. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: osteotomy is a real, mechanically effective treatment for adult genu valgum on consistent case-series evidence — but for a young adult without arthritis there is no comparative evidence at all, and the durability numbers are borrowed from an older, arthritic population.
stamp: POSSIBLE — retrospective case series only: osteotomy corrects adult genu valgum accurately (96.1% correction accuracy in a 31-procedure series) with 10-year survival of ~74–90% in valgus knees with lateral arthritis, but there are no trials and almost no data in young adults without arthritis

title: Taken off bupropion (Wellbutrin) suddenly, without a taper: across antidepressants about 1 in 6–7 people get symptoms attributable to stopping (about 15%), severe symptoms in about 2.8% — and bupropion sits in the lower-risk group, with no bupropion-specific incidence study
question: 'I was taken off bupropion (Wellbutrin) completely without tapering — what happens?' — After abrupt antidepressant discontinuation, how common and how severe are discontinuation symptoms, and where does bupropion sit in the risk ranking? (Depression relapse after stopping is a different question — Shelf #705.)
balance: Across antidepressants as a class, stopping brings symptoms in roughly a third of people — but about half of that is the nocebo/placebo rate: the 2024 Lancet Psychiatry meta-analysis of 21,002 patients found at least one discontinuation symptom in 31% after stopping an antidepressant versus 17% after stopping placebo, severe symptoms in 2.8% versus 0.6%, and estimated the incidence truly attributable to the drug at about 15% — roughly 1 in every 6–7 people who stop (Henssler 2024, PMID: 38851198). The 2025 JAMA Psychiatry meta-analysis of randomised trials found the average excess was about one extra symptom (from the Discontinuation-Emergent Signs and Symptoms scale) in the first week — below the threshold for a clinically significant discontinuation syndrome — with dizziness the most prevalent symptom, and, importantly, discontinuation was not associated with depressive symptoms, so later depression signals relapse rather than withdrawal (Kalfas 2025, PMID: 40632531). For bupropion specifically: Henssler's high-frequency list names desvenlafaxine, venlafaxine, imipramine and escitalopram — bupropion is not on it — and the pharmacist practice review's risk table places bupropion XL in the lower-risk category for discontinuation syndrome (Geen 2023, PMID: 38222887). No bupropion-specific incidence study was found in the fetched record. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: a person taken off bupropion abruptly will most likely have few or no discontinuation symptoms; if symptoms come, the class pattern is onset within 2–4 days, flu-like symptoms, insomnia, nausea, imbalance, sensory disturbances and hyperarousal, usually settling over weeks.
stamp: POSSIBLE — class data put drug-attributable discontinuation symptoms at ~15% (1 in 6–7) with severe symptoms ~2.8%, and bupropion ranks in the lower-risk group on both fetched stratifications, so abrupt cessation is usually tolerated — but no bupropion-specific incidence study exists

title: Ear-lobe creases (Frank's sign) and heart disease: a real observational association — pooled diagnostic odds ratio 3.27 with sensitivity 62% and specificity 67% across 37 studies — but association only, not causation, and too weak to diagnose or exclude coronary disease
question: 'Are ear-lobe creases a sign of heart disease?' — Is a diagonal earlobe crease (Frank's sign) associated with coronary artery disease, how strong and how diagnostically useful is the association, and is any of it causal?
balance: The association is real, replicated, and weak — and it is association only. The 2014 meta-analysis of 37 studies and 31,188 participants pooled a sensitivity of 0.62 (95% CI 0.56–0.67) and specificity of 0.67 (0.61–0.73) for diagonal earlobe crease as a marker of coronary artery disease, with a diagnostic odds ratio of 3.27 (2.47–4.32, relative) (Lucenteforte 2014, PMID: 24866080) — performance far too poor to diagnose or exclude disease in an individual. The strongest design, the Copenhagen City Heart Study's 10,885 initially disease-free adults followed for 35 years, found earlobe crease among the visible ageing signs associated with ischaemic heart disease and myocardial infarction after adjustment for age and known risk factors, with risk rising stepwise by number of signs (hazard ratio up to 1.40 for ischaemic heart disease and 1.57 for infarction with 3–4 signs versus none — relative measures for the bundle of signs) (Christoffersen 2014, PMID: 24334176). The 2025 systematic review likewise found about a four-fold likelihood of coronary disease in people with the crease across 12 studies, independent of age and risk factors in all 10 studies that examined confounding (Curtis 2025, PMID: 34924071). No fetched study shows the crease causes coronary disease, that it adds usefully to standard risk factors for an individual patient, or that acting on it changes outcomes — it travels with age and with the same risk factors that cause the disease. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: an ear-lobe crease is a genuine statistical sign of higher coronary risk at group level, best read as a prompt to check the conventional risk factors — not as evidence that any individual has, or will get, heart disease.
stamp: POSSIBLE — diagonal earlobe crease is consistently associated with coronary artery disease (pooled diagnostic OR 3.27; sensitivity 0.62, specificity 0.67; prospective adjusted association in a 10,885-person cohort), but the evidence is observational only: association, not causation, and too weak to diagnose or exclude disease

title: Hairy cell leukaemia: the purine analogues work — cladribine gave 91% complete responses in 349 evaluable patients in the pivotal single-arm series, and pentostatin beat interferon in the one randomised trial (complete remission 76% versus 11%)
question: 'My father has hairy cell leukaemia — is there treatment, how well does it work?' — In classic hairy cell leukaemia, what response rates and durability do the purine analogues cladribine and pentostatin achieve, and how do they compare with each other and with the older interferon treatment?
balance: Yes — hairy cell leukaemia is one of the most treatment-responsive leukaemias, and the purine analogues cladribine and pentostatin are the reason. The one randomised trial in the record compared pentostatin with the older interferon alfa-2a in 313 eligible previously untreated patients: confirmed complete remission 76% on pentostatin versus 11% on interferon, complete plus partial remission 79% versus 38%, both response and relapse-free survival favouring pentostatin at P<.0001 (Grever 1995, PMID: 7707126). Cladribine's pivotal evidence is single-arm and is labelled as such on its card: in the Scripps series of 349 evaluable patients, a single 7-day course gave 91% complete and 7% partial responses, with overall survival of 96% at 48 months — though 26% relapsed at a median of 29 months (Saven 1998, PMID: 9731048). The long retrospective comparisons find the two purine analogues equivalent: complete remission about 81–82% for either as first-line treatment, median disease-free survival 15 years (pentostatin) and 11+ years (first-line cladribine) at 12.5 years of follow-up (Else 2005, PMID: 16245328), and at 16 years a median relapse-free survival of 16 years with only 8 of 233 patients dying of hairy-cell-leukaemia-related causes (Else 2009, PMID: 19344416). The honest limit in the same records: remissions are long but the disease-free curve shows no plateau — relapse continues for decades, second courses work again (69% complete remission second-line), and cure remains elusive. PROPOSED LIKELY: first-line purine analogue therapy very likely produces a complete remission lasting many years; it is control measured in decades, not guaranteed cure.
stamp: LIKELY — purine analogues produce complete remission in ~76–91% of patients (pentostatin 76% vs interferon 11% in the one RCT; cladribine 91% in the pivotal single-arm series), with median relapse-free survival up to 16 years, though relapse continues for decades and cure is not established

title: Blood sugar 94 mg/dL (≈5.2 mmol/L) at bedtime but 165 mg/dL (≈9.2 mmol/L) in the morning: the dawn phenomenon typically adds only about 16–22 mg/dL (≈0.9–1.2 mmol/L) overnight and about 0.4% to HbA1c, no oral drug eliminated it, and acarbose blunted it in one small trial analysis (n=50)
question: 'My blood sugar is 94 at bedtime but 165 in the morning — how can I lower it?' — 94 mg/dL (≈5.2 mmol/L) at bedtime, 165 mg/dL (≈9.2 mmol/L) before breakfast: how big is the dawn phenomenon in type 2 diabetes, how much does it contribute to HbA1c, and what has been shown to blunt the overnight rise?
balance: The dawn phenomenon is real, common, and modest in size — which is the first thing to set against this person's numbers. In 248 non-insulin-treated patients with type 2 diabetes wearing continuous glucose monitors, the median overnight rise from the nocturnal low to the pre-breakfast value was 16.0 mg/dL (≈0.9 mmol/L), and its average impact was 4.3 ± 1.3 mmol/mol (0.39 ± 0.12%) on HbA1c and 12.4 ± 2.4 mg/dL (≈0.7 mmol/L) on 24-hour mean glucose; crucially, the impact was not eliminated by any available oral agent class (Monnier 2013, PMID: 24170753). An age-stratified study found dawn increments of 18.0–22.0 mg/dL (≈1.0–1.2 mmol/L) across age groups, present (a rise over 10 mg/dL, ≈0.6 mmol/L) in 52–70% of patients (Monnier 2012, PMID: 22991448). The gap in the question — 94 mg/dL (≈5.2 mmol/L) at bedtime to 165 mg/dL (≈9.2 mmol/L) in the morning, a 71 mg/dL (≈3.9 mmol/L) difference — is three to four times the typical dawn increment, and the studies measure from the overnight low, not from a bedtime reading, so either this rise is unusually large or something beyond the classic dawn effect contributes. On blunting it, the fetched record is thin: in a post-hoc analysis of a randomised trial in 50 patients on metformin, adding acarbose reduced the dawn magnitude from 35.9 ± 15.7 to 28.3 ± 16.5 mg/dL (≈2.0 to ≈1.6 mmol/L; p=0.037) while glibenclamide did not (Wang 2021, PMID: 34394904) — one small secondary analysis, not a treatment trial. No fetched record carded a bedtime snack or insulin-timing intervention, so this shelf makes no claim for them. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): the dawn rise itself is well documented; proven ways to blunt it are not.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the dawn phenomenon is well measured (typical rise ~16–22 mg/dL ≈ 0.9–1.2 mmol/L; ~0.4% of HbA1c; not eliminated by any oral agent class), but the only blunting evidence is one small post-hoc trial analysis (acarbose, n=50), and nothing cardable was found for bedtime snacks or insulin timing

title: Goodpasture syndrome (anti-GBM disease): plasma exchange added to steroids and cyclophosphamide — the one randomised trial had just 17 patients (dialysis in 2 of 8 versus 6 of 9), and the big cohorts say how far the kidneys have fallen decides the outcome
question: What are the treatments for Goodpasture syndrome (anti-GBM disease) — in people with anti-glomerular basement membrane antibody disease, does plasma exchange added to corticosteroids and cyclophosphamide improve survival and kidney recovery compared with immunosuppression alone, and what do the cohort renal-survival numbers show?
balance: POSSIBLE — the standard treatment (plasma exchange plus prednisolone and cyclophosphamide) rests on one very small randomised trial and consistent cohort data, not on any large trial. In the only randomised trial (Johnson 1985, PMID: 3892220; n = 17 printed on the face), adding plasma exchange to prednisone and cyclophosphamide cleared anti-GBM antibodies about twice as fast, left end-of-treatment serum creatinine at 4.1 mg/dL versus 9.2 mg/dL, and left 2 of 8 exchange patients dialysis-dependent versus 6 of 9 on drugs alone. The 25-year Hammersmith cohort (Levy 2001, PMID: 11388816; 71 treated patients, all given plasma exchange, prednisolone and cyclophosphamide) shows the dominant fact of this disease: outcome is set by kidney function at presentation — creatinine below 500 micromol/L (5.7 mg/dL): 100% patient survival and 95% renal survival at 1 year; dialysis-dependent at presentation: 65% patient survival but only 8% renal survival at 1 year. The largest regimen comparison (Cui 2011, PMID: 21862934; 221 patients) found combination therapy associated with lower mortality (hazard ratio 0.31, a relative measure) and lower renal-failure risk (HR 0.60) than the other regimens, while steroids plus cyclophosphamide without exchange did not improve renal outcome (P = 0.73). PROPOSED POSSIBLE: benefit is plausible and consistent, the randomised base is 17 patients, and no regimen rescues kidneys that present dialysis-dependent with 100% crescents.
stamp: POSSIBLE — plasma exchange plus steroids and cyclophosphamide is the standard on one 17-patient randomised trial (dialysis 2 of 8 versus 6 of 9) and concordant cohorts; presenting kidney function, not regimen choice, dominates renal survival (95% at 1 year if creatinine <5.7 mg/dL versus 8% if dialysis-dependent)

title: Ménétrier disease: cetuximab is the only treatment with numbers — 7 of 7 completers improved in a single-arm trial of just 9 patients, with a 2-patient report behind it and no comparative trial of anything
question: What are the treatments for Ménétrier disease — in people with severe Ménétrier disease (giant gastric folds with protein loss), does the EGFR antibody cetuximab improve symptoms, gastric acidity and histology, and what is the prognosis that makes gastrectomy the historical alternative?
balance: POSSIBLE — the entire treatment evidence for Ménétrier disease is one single-arm trial of n = 9 and a two-patient chronic-treatment report, both of the EGFR antibody cetuximab (Erbitux), with n printed on the face of each card as this library's small-n rule requires. In the single-arm trial (Fiske 2009, PMID: 20368185; 9 enrolled, 7 completing one month), all 7 completers improved significantly on quality-of-life indices and biochemically — parietal cell mass rose from 20.9 to 61.2 (P = 0.01) and mean gastric pH fell from 6.0 to 4.1 (P = 0.05) — all 7 elected to continue treatment, and 4 later showed near-complete histological remission. The earlier chronic-treatment report (Settle 2005, PMID: 16206497; n = 2) describes one patient whose albumin stabilised enough to stop parenteral nutrition and albumin infusions over a 1-year course, and one whose twice-monthly transfusions were eliminated over 4 months. The backdrop is a disease with real mortality: in the Mayo case-control series (Almazar 2021, PMID: 32184187; 76 patients), 5- and 10-year survival were 72.7% and 65.0% versus 100% in controls, and gastric cancer developed in 8.9% by 10 years versus 3.7% of controls (P = .09) — the reason gastrectomy was the historical default and surveillance endoscopy is advised. There is no randomised or comparative trial of any treatment. PROPOSED POSSIBLE, capped by the tiny uncontrolled base.
stamp: POSSIBLE — cetuximab improved all 7 completers of a 9-patient single-arm trial and both patients in a 2-patient chronic-treatment report; no comparative trial of any Ménétrier treatment exists, and every n is printed on the face

title: Posterior urethral valves in newborns: vesicostomy versus primary valve ablation — no kidney-outcome difference in any comparison, more surgery with diversion, and bladder studies that disagree
question: What are the treatments for urine blockage in newborns (posterior urethral valves) — in newborn boys with posterior urethral valves, how do initial vesicostomy and primary valve ablation compare on kidney outcomes, bladder function and burden of surgery?
balance: POSSIBLE (the two operations made no difference to kidney outcomes) — every comparison fetched is observational, and on kidney outcomes they agree: no significant difference between initial vesicostomy and primary valve ablation. In the matched newborn cohort (Weitzner 2025, PMID: 40750022; 12 versus 12 matched neonates), creatinine did not differ at 6 weeks (P = .74) or 1 year (P = .89) and time to renal replacement therapy did not differ (hazard ratio 1.32, 95% CI 0.32–5.45; P = .70). In the London comparison (Godbole 2007, PMID: 18947754; 54 boys), adjusted GFR and 1-year creatinine did not differ (P = 0.16 and P = 0.87). In the 100-patient long-term series (Smith 1996, PMID: 8627873), 13% had end-stage renal disease by age 15 with no statistical difference in age at end-stage disease between initial treatments — but diversion meant significantly more surgery. Bladder function is where the studies pull apart: one comparative urodynamic study (Puri 2002, PMID: 12415375; 67 patients) found vesicostomy bladders smaller and less compliant (mean maximal cystometric capacity 62% of normal versus 96% after fulguration; P = 0.002). Observational-only evidence caps this shelf at POSSIBLE.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatments made no difference to kidney outcomes) — in matched and unmatched observational comparisons alike, vesicostomy and primary valve ablation did not differ on creatinine or renal replacement therapy; diversion cost more operations, and bladder-function signals conflict

title: Acanthosis nigricans: metformin and pioglitazone both improved the skin in small head-to-head trials — but there is no placebo arm anywhere, and no treatment has ever beaten another
question: How is acanthosis nigricans treated — in people with insulin-resistance-associated acanthosis nigricans (the dark, velvety skin thickening of the neck and folds), do metformin, pioglitazone or other systemic treatments improve the skin, and how do they compare?
balance: POSSIBLE — the evidence is three small randomised head-to-head trials with no placebo arm and no blinded skin assessment in the largest, so every positive finding is a within-group improvement. Metformin 500 mg twice daily and pioglitazone 7.5 mg twice daily both significantly improved lesion grading over 12 weeks with no significant difference between them (Jain 2026, PMID: 41449989; 65 patients), metformin producing the greater BMI and weight fall. Metformin and the branded fixed combination Canthex (alpha-lipoic acid, biotin, calcium pantothenate and zinc sulfate) likewise both significantly reduced neck lesion severity and texture with no intergroup difference at any follow-up (Sett 2019, PMID: 30983607; 33 patients analysed, double-blind). A second metformin-versus-pioglitazone report (Jain 2026, PMID: 40826852; 50 patients) found the same pattern — both improved, no significant between-group difference — with larger metabolic falls on pioglitazone (HOMA-IR −35.8% versus −28.56%). Because no trial compares any drug with placebo or with no treatment, spontaneous improvement, weight change and regression to the mean cannot be excluded. PROPOSED POSSIBLE, capped by design: treating the underlying insulin resistance is the consistent thread, and no agent has beaten another.
stamp: POSSIBLE — metformin, pioglitazone and a branded antioxidant combination each improved lesions within their own trial arms, but no trial has a placebo arm and no agent has beaten another; the honest reading is that treating insulin resistance may help, unproven against doing nothing

title: Acoustic neuroma (vestibular schwannoma): radiosurgery shrank tumours observation let grow in the one randomised trial, microsurgery controls best in pooled series but costs facial nerve function — and hearing ends up the same
question: How is an acoustic neuroma (vestibular schwannoma) treated — in people with a small or medium vestibular schwannoma, how do stereotactic radiosurgery, microsurgical removal and watch-and-scan observation compare on tumour control, hearing preservation and facial nerve function?
balance: SPLIT — the answer depends on which comparison you mean, and the records correct one common assumption: a randomised trial does exist for one of them. In V-REX (Dhayalan 2023, PMID: 37526718; NCT02249572; 100 patients with tumours under 2 cm), upfront Gamma Knife radiosurgery beat watch-and-scan on the primary outcome — tumour volume ratio at 4 years 0.87 versus 1.51 (between-group ratio 1.73, 95% CI 1.23–2.44; P = .002) — while 25 of 26 secondary outcomes, including quality of life and hearing measures, showed no significant difference, and 42% of the observation group crossed over to radiosurgery for growth within 4 years. Matched observational data agree that radiosurgery controls tumours observation cannot (VISAS, PMID: 38588868: control 99% at 5 years and 91.9% at 10 years versus 45.8% and 22% under observation), with serviceable hearing preservation statistically indistinguishable (P = .53). For microsurgery versus radiosurgery there is no randomised trial — only a 32-study systematic review (Savardekar 2022, PMID: 34838768): tumour control favoured microsurgery (98% versus 92%, P < 0.0001), hearing preservation did not differ (56% versus 59% at about 65 months, P = 0.1527), and facial nerve dysfunction was five times as common after microsurgery (10% versus 2%, P < 0.0001). PROPOSED SPLIT: radiosurgery over observation for tumour control with no proven patient-outcome advantage; microsurgery over radiosurgery for control at a facial-nerve price; observation remains defensible for small tumours, since about a third grow within 3 years and most observed patients in V-REX still needed no treatment at 4 years (56% untreated).
stamp: SPLIT — radiosurgery controls tumours better than observation (one randomised trial: volume ratio 0.87 versus 1.51) without improving patient-reported outcomes; microsurgery controls better than radiosurgery in non-randomised pools (98% versus 92%) at five times the facial-nerve dysfunction (10% versus 2%); hearing preservation is the same across all three

title: Anal fistula surgery: cut the sphincter on a simple fistula and it heals either way you cut it; spare the sphincter on a complex one and a quarter to a third fail — with the plug and fibrin glue beaten by the flap in randomised comparisons
question: How is an anal fistula treated — in people with fistula-in-ano, how do fistulotomy, fistulectomy, advancement flap, LIFT, the fistula plug and other operations compare on healing, recurrence and continence?
balance: SPLIT — the fistula literature splits cleanly by anatomy. For simple fistulas, the sphincter-cutting operations heal almost everyone and the two variants are equivalent: a meta-analysis of 13 randomised trials (Quinn 2025, PMID: 40125894; 1373 patients) found no significant difference between fistulotomy and fistulectomy in healing time, recurrence or incontinence, with less pain at 24 hours after fistulectomy (mean difference −0.49) and less bleeding after fistulotomy (odds ratio 3.81, a relative measure). For complex fistulas, where the sphincter must be spared, a network meta-analysis of 16 randomised trials (Sierra Fernández 2025, PMID: 40442569) found LIFT, VAAFT, cutting seton and fistulotomy with sphincter reconstruction statistically indistinguishable from the advancement-flap control on failure — while the fistula plug (OR 3.6, 95% CI 1.1–11.5), fibrin glue (OR 7.5, 2.2–25) and platelet-rich plasma (OR 11.5, 1.3–99) all failed significantly more often (relative measures), and only the cutting seton raised incontinence (OR 8.6). A second network analysis (Fuschillo 2025, PMID: 40392371; 49 articles, 3520 patients) puts absolute failure at 22–29% for LIFT, VAAFT and flap, 43.9% for laser closure (FiLaC), with continence disturbance of 1.5% after LIFT versus 7.3% after flap. PROPOSED SPLIT: cut the sphincter for simple fistulas and it heals; spare it for complex ones and roughly a quarter to a third fail whatever you choose — with plug and glue measurably worse.
stamp: SPLIT — for simple fistulas fistulotomy and fistulectomy are equivalent and near-definitive; for complex fistulas every sphincter-sparing option fails 22–44% of the time, LIFT/VAAFT/flap are statistically alike, and the plug, fibrin glue and platelet-rich plasma failed significantly more than the flap in randomised comparisons

title: Unruptured brain aneurysm: treat or watch? Five-year rupture risk runs from 0% (small, front of the brain) to 50% (giant, back of the brain) — so the evidence answers by risk stratum, not with one rule
question: Should an unruptured brain aneurysm be treated — in people with an unruptured intracranial aneurysm found before any bleed, what is the rupture risk if it is left alone, by size, location and risk score, and how does that frame the decision to clip, coil or watch?
balance: SPLIT — whether to treat an unruptured aneurysm is a comparison between a rupture risk that varies a hundred-fold by size, site and patient, and a treatment risk that is front-loaded — and no randomised trial of treatment versus observation exists in the records fetched. The natural-history anchor is ISUIA (Wiebers 2003, PMID: 12867109; 4060 patients): 5-year cumulative rupture rates in patients without prior subarachnoid haemorrhage were 0%, 2.6%, 14.5% and 40% for anterior-circulation aneurysms under 7 mm, 7–12 mm, 13–24 mm and 25 mm or more, versus 2.5%, 14.5%, 18.4% and 50% for posterior-circulation and posterior-communicating aneurysms of the same sizes. The PHASES pooled analysis (Greving 2014, PMID: 24290159; 8382 participants, 230 ruptures) puts the mean 5-year rupture risk at 3.4% (95% CI 2.9–4.0) but the individual range at 0.25% to over 15% depending on age, hypertension, prior haemorrhage, size, site and population. A 36-year conservatively-managed cohort (Dodier 2025, PMID: 40446344; 661 patients, 767 aneurysms) observed rupture in 3.5% (annual haemorrhage rate 0.6%), with 87% of haemorrhages in the first 5 years, none after 10 years, and no rupture or aneurysm-related death at all among patients with PHASES under 8 or ELAPSS under 15. PROPOSED SPLIT: small anterior aneurysms without risk factors rupture so rarely that observation is the evidence-based default; large, posterior or high-PHASES aneurysms carry double-digit 5-year risks that justify treatment despite its up-front risk. Boundary: this shelf is unruptured aneurysms only — ruptured aneurysm treatment (ISAT and subarachnoid haemorrhage care) is homed elsewhere in this library (Shelf #2389 and neighbours) and is deliberately not re-carded.
stamp: SPLIT — observation for the small anterior low-risk aneurysm (5-year rupture 0–2.6%, and no ruptures at all under PHASES 8 in a 36-year conservative cohort), treatment for the large, posterior or high-score aneurysm (5-year rupture up to 40–50%); no randomised trial of treatment exists

title: Anxiety in pregnancy: individual CBT-based sessions halved-and-more postnatal illness in a large trial and internet CBT helped anxiety — brief group CBT did not beat a booklet, and the SSRI malformation signal fades against the right comparison
question: How is anxiety treated in pregnancy — in pregnant women with anxiety, do psychological therapies (CBT-based programmes, internet CBT, group CBT) reduce anxiety, and what does the safety evidence say about SSRI use in pregnancy?
balance: SPLIT — the two halves of this question have very different evidence. For psychological treatment of anxiety in pregnancy, the largest trial is strongly positive: the HMHB trial (Surkan 2024, PMID: 38365951; NCT03880032), a CBT-based intervention delivered by non-specialists to pregnant women with at least mild anxiety and no clinical depression, cut major depressive episodes at 6 weeks postpartum to 12% versus 41% with enhanced usual care, with adjusted odds (relative measures) of 0.19 for depression-or-anxiety combined, 0.19 for depressive episode and 0.26 for moderate-to-severe anxiety. Unguided internet CBT also beat treatment as usual on anxiety in a small trial (Loughnan 2019, PMID: 30266030; 87 women; GAD-7 effect size g = 0.76). But brief group CBT in an earlier trial did not beat an information booklet (Austin 2008, PMID: 17490753; anxiety diagnoses fell similarly in both groups) — so format and intensity matter. For SSRI safety, the records allow only pregnancy-wide data, not anxiety-specific cohorts: a meta-analysis of 29 cohort studies and 9,085,954 births (Gao 2018, PMID: 30415641) found small relative increases in major congenital anomalies (RR 1.11, 95% CI 1.03–1.19) and heart defects (RR 1.24, 1.11–1.37) with first-trimester exposure — which disappeared when the analysis was restricted to women with a psychiatric diagnosis (RR 1.04 and 1.06, both non-significant), the signature of confounding by indication. PROPOSED SPLIT: structured CBT-based help for antenatal anxiety is supported (one large trial, one small positive, one null); SSRI malformation risk, if real, is small in relative terms and not separable from the underlying illness in these data. Boundary declared: postpartum depression treatment (brexanolone, zuranolone, sertraline recurrence prevention) and postpartum prevention programmes are homed on other shelves (#229, #836, #2743, #3773) and are not re-carded here.
stamp: SPLIT — structured CBT-based treatment for anxiety in pregnancy is supported (postnatal depression 12% versus 41% in the one large trial; internet CBT anxiety effect g = 0.76), brief group CBT was no better than a booklet, and SSRI malformation signals are small relative risks (1.11–1.24) that disappear when women with a psychiatric diagnosis are compared fairly (1.04–1.06, non-significant)

title: Auditory processing disorder in children: three small randomised trials, all positive on questionnaires or trained tasks and null or untested on blinded behaviour — 120 children is the whole evidence base
question: How is auditory processing disorder treated — in children diagnosed with auditory processing disorder, do auditory training programmes, language training, FM systems or remote-microphone hearing aids improve listening, and how strong is the trial evidence?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — three small randomised trials exist, and each is positive on some outcomes and null on others, with the gains concentrated in trained tasks and parent/teacher questionnaires rather than in blinded real-world measures. Computer-based speech auditory training added to standard school strategies improved all its outcome measures in the trained group only, with effect sizes of 0.76 to 1.7, and speech-in-noise gains that persisted at 3 months (Loo 2016, PMID: 26418044; 39 children). A five-arm trial of bottom-up training, top-down language training and FM systems reported positive outcomes on several measures with an unchanged control group, but published no extractable effect sizes in its record (Sharma 2012, PMID: 22512470; 55 children). Remote-microphone hearing aids improved children's self-reported classroom listening at 3 and 6 months (mean difference 7.31 points at 3 months, P = 0.014) while behavioural listening-in-noise and attention measures did not change significantly (Stavrinos 2020, PMID: 32973443; NCT02353091; 26 children). Total randomised evidence: 120 children across three trials, no blinded outcome assessment in any, and the diagnosis itself remains contested. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): something in these interventions moves questionnaire and trained-task scores; whether auditory processing disorder treatment changes real-world listening is unproven.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — three small randomised trials (120 children in total) show gains on trained tasks and self-report questionnaires, with behavioural measures null where they were tested separately; nothing here is blinded and the diagnosis itself is contested

title: Bird flu (avian influenza H5N1/H7N9): oseltamivir is associated with better survival in observational registry data — 60% survived with oseltamivir versus 24% with no antiviral in H5N1 — and earlier treatment looks better; no randomised trial exists
question: How is bird flu (avian influenza) treated? In people with confirmed H5N1 or H7N9 avian influenza, does oseltamivir improve survival, and does starting it earlier matter?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only, and the shelf says so on its face: there is NO randomised trial of oseltamivir (or any antiviral) in human avian influenza, and none is likely, because cases are sporadic and often fulminant. What exists is registry and case-series evidence that points consistently one way. In the Global Patient Registry analysis of 308 confirmed H5N1 cases from 12 countries (Adisasmito 2010, PMID: 20831384), crude survival was 60% in patients who received at least one dose of oseltamivir alone versus 24% in patients with no evidence of anti-influenza antiviral treatment (P<.001), and propensity-adjusted multivariate modelling showed a 49% relative reduction in mortality with oseltamivir treatment; the survival advantage persisted when treatment began up to 6–8 days after symptom onset. Timing analyses point the same way: in 215 oseltamivir-treated registry patients, early initiation was particularly protective in patients without respiratory failure (odds ratio 0.17; Chan 2012, PMID: 22927451); in the Indonesian case series of 127 confirmed cases (103 deaths, 81%), survival by treatment timing was 36.4% (4 of 11) when oseltamivir started at 2–4 days, 37.5% (6 of 16) at 5–6 days and 18.5% (10 of 44) at 7 days or later (Kandun 2008, PMID: 18706688); and in 193 registry children, each day of delay in starting oseltamivir raised the adjusted odds of death by 75% (Oner 2012, PMID: 22423125). For H7N9, the one comparative study found adding peramivir to oseltamivir was NOT superior to oseltamivir alone (mortality 43.59% combination versus 25.58% monotherapy, p>0.05; Zhang 2016, PMID: 26864456) — a reminder that sicker patients get more drugs in observational data. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): consistent observational survival association, strongest with early treatment, unproven by any randomised test and vulnerable to confounding (patients who live long enough and reach care get treated).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only (no RCT exists): in 308 registry H5N1 cases survival was 60% with oseltamivir versus 24% with no antiviral, with a 49% relative mortality reduction on adjusted modelling, and earlier initiation was consistently associated with better survival

title: Baker's cyst: draining the cyst and injecting steroid eases knee pain for a few weeks — one small randomised trial (n=60) and small series only, and about 1 in 8 cysts needed draining again
question: How is a Baker's cyst treated? I have a swelling behind my knee — will draining it or injecting steroid help, and will it come back? Clinical question underneath: in adults with a symptomatic popliteal (Baker's) cyst, usually alongside knee osteoarthritis, does ultrasound-guided aspiration with corticosteroid injection (into the cyst or into the joint) improve pain, function and cyst size, and how often does the cyst recur?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the honest summary is that needle treatment of a Baker's cyst probably eases knee pain in the short term, but the evidence is one small randomised trial with only 4 weeks of follow-up plus small uncontrolled or partly controlled series, and nothing here tests surgery. In the randomised trial (Di Sante 2012, PMID: 22525511; 60 patients with knee osteoarthritis and a Baker's cyst), ultrasound-guided aspiration plus corticosteroid injection kept pain lower at 4 weeks while electrical 'horizontal therapy' alone did not, and the combination arm had the lowest pain scores — yet the cyst's maximum axial area did not shrink in any group (P=0.259). A 40-patient comparison (Bandinelli 2012, PMID: 22200813) found cyst diameters fell further when the steroid was injected directly into the aspirated cyst than into the joint (p<0.01 at 4 and 8 weeks). The largest series (Smith 2015, PMID: 26502415; 47 patients) reported WOMAC scores improving from 48.55 to 17.15 after aspiration, fenestration and steroid injection, with 6 of 47 (12.7%) needing re-aspiration for recurrence and no infections. Because most of this is short-term and partly uncontrolled, the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): aspiration with corticosteroid injection likely gives short-term pain relief; durability beyond a few weeks and the value of arthroscopic surgery on the underlying knee are not established by the studies carded here.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one small randomised trial (n=60, 4-week follow-up) and small series support short-term pain relief from aspiration plus corticosteroid injection; recurrence needing re-aspiration was 12.7% in the largest series; no surgical trial is carded

title: Bile duct cancer (advanced biliary tract cancer): gemcitabine + cisplatin beats gemcitabine alone — median survival 11.7 vs 8.1 months in the ABC-02 trial — and adding a third chemotherapy drug did not help
question: How is bile duct cancer (cholangiocarcinoma) treated? If the cancer cannot be removed by surgery, which chemotherapy actually helps people live longer? Clinical question underneath: in adults with locally advanced or metastatic biliary tract cancer (cholangiocarcinoma, gallbladder or ampullary cancer), does first-line gemcitabine plus cisplatin improve overall survival compared with gemcitabine alone, and does intensifying the regimen further add benefit?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) for the chemotherapy backbone — two randomised trials point the same way. The phase 3 ABC-02 trial (Valle 2010, PMID: 20375404; 410 patients) found median overall survival of 11.7 months on cisplatin plus gemcitabine versus 8.1 months on gemcitabine alone (hazard ratio 0.64, 95% CI 0.52-0.80, P<0.001 — a relative reduction in the risk of death of about a third, alongside the absolute 3.6-month median gain), with progression-free survival 8.0 vs 5.0 months and tumour control 81.4% vs 71.8% (P=0.049); neutropenia was more common on the combination but neutropenia-associated infections were similar. The smaller Japanese randomised study (Okusaka 2010, PMID: 20628385; 84 patients) was consistent: 1-year survival 39.0% vs 31.0%, median survival 11.2 vs 7.7 months. Intensifying further did not help: in SWOG S1815 (Shroff 2025, PMID: 39671534; 452 randomised), adding nab-paclitaxel to gemcitabine-cisplatin gave median survival 14.0 vs 13.6 months (HR 0.91, 95% CI 0.72-1.14, P=.41) with more toxicity. BOUNDARY: the modern immunotherapy additions are homed elsewhere and are NOT re-carded here — durvalumab (TOPAZ-1) and pembrolizumab added to this same backbone are on Shelf #858; second-line FOLFOX (ABC-06) is on Shelf #1885; adjuvant capecitabine after surgery is on Shelf #3415. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): gemcitabine plus cisplatin is the proven first-line chemotherapy backbone for advanced biliary tract cancer.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — gemcitabine + cisplatin improved survival over gemcitabine alone in a 410-patient phase 3 trial (11.7 vs 8.1 months; HR 0.64) with a consistent smaller randomised study; adding nab-paclitaxel did not improve survival. Immunotherapy additions are homed on Shelf #858, not here

title: Bladder stones: all three operations clear the stone — in the 805-patient global registry, complete clearance was 95.5% through the urethra, 84.6% percutaneous and 100% open, with the fewest early complications by the transurethral route; no randomised trial exists
question: How are bladder stones treated? If a stone in the bladder has to be removed, which operation — through the urethra, through a small hole above the pubic bone, or open surgery — clears it best and with fewest problems? Clinical question underneath: in patients with bladder calculi, how do transurethral cystolithotripsy, percutaneous cystolithotomy and open cystolithotomy compare on stone-free rates, hospital stay and complications?
balance: POSSIBLE — every comparative dataset here is observational, so the stamp is capped: there is no randomised trial of bladder-stone surgery in the record carded. The largest dataset is the prospective BLAST registry (Gauhar 2026, PMID: 42867550; 805 patients, 31 centres, 16 countries): complete (Grade A) stone clearance was 95.5% for transurethral surgery (n=741), 84.6% for percutaneous (n=39) and 100% for open surgery (n=25); median stay was 2 days transurethral versus 3 days for the other routes; early complications were most frequent after open surgery (48.0% vs 18.6% transurethral and 17.9% percutaneous); and reintervention for residual fragments was most frequent after percutaneous surgery (10.3% vs 1.3% and 0%). But the groups were not comparable — transurethral patients had smaller stones (median 2.1 cm vs 3.0 cm) — and the registry authors state their findings describe treatment patterns and observed outcomes rather than comparative effectiveness. A geriatric series (Tunçekin 2025, PMID: 40495496; n=76, age 65+) found stone-free rates of 85.7% transurethral versus 100% open and 100% percutaneous, with no significant differences in stay or complications. In children, a meta-analysis of 7 studies (Zhao 2025, PMID: 40354160; 397 patients) found percutaneous surgery quicker but with longer hospitalisation than transurethral surgery, other differences not significant. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: all three routes clear bladder stones effectively; the transurethral route is the usual default for ordinary stones, with percutaneous and open routes reserved for larger or complex cases — a pattern of practice supported by, but not proven by, these observational data.
stamp: POSSIBLE — no randomised trials; an 805-patient prospective registry, a 76-patient geriatric series and a 397-patient paediatric meta-analysis all show high stone clearance by every route, with route choice in practice driven by stone size and anatomy rather than proven superiority

title: Simple (unicameral) bone cyst in children: steroid injection healed 42% versus 23% for bone-marrow injection in the one randomised trial — but most cysts fail a first treatment whichever method is used, and percutaneous curettage healed 70% in a comparative series
question: How is a simple bone cyst treated? In children and adolescents with a unicameral (simple) bone cyst, how do intralesional steroid (methylprednisolone) injection, bone-marrow injection and curettage compare on healing?
balance: SPLIT — the methods rank differently in different study designs, and no method heals most cysts first time. The one randomised trial (Wright 2008, PMID: 18381307; 90 children randomised, 77 followed for 2 years, blinded radiographic assessment) found healing in 16 of 38 (42%) cysts injected with methylprednisolone acetate versus 9 of 39 (23%) injected with bone marrow (p=0.01), with no significant difference in function, pain, number of injections, additional fractures or complications — steroid beat marrow, but both healed a minority. The large retrospective three-treatment comparison (Sung 2008, PMID: 18679761; 167 patients under 20, mean follow-up 7.3 years) found failure after one treatment in 84% of steroid-injected cysts versus 64% with curettage plus bone grafting and 50% with a combined steroid/demineralised-bone-matrix/bone-marrow injection (SDB), with steroids alone an independent predictor of failure — almost the reverse ranking for steroids, in a design where treatment was chosen, not randomised. A smaller retrospective comparison (Canavese 2011, PMID: 21150732; 46 children, at least 24 months' follow-up) found satisfactory healing at 2 years in 70% after percutaneous curettage versus 41% after methylprednisolone injection and 21% after bone-marrow injection (P=0.03). PROPOSED SPLIT: steroid injection is superior to bone-marrow injection on the only randomised test, yet retrospective series rank curettage-based approaches above steroid injection alone, and repeat treatment is the norm under every method.
stamp: SPLIT — randomised trial: methylprednisolone injection healed 42% versus 23% for bone-marrow injection (p=0.01), both a minority · retrospective series: failure after one treatment was 84% for steroids versus 64% for curettage and 50% for combined injection, and percutaneous curettage healed 70% versus 41% (steroid) and 21% (marrow) in another series

title: Bowel (faecal) incontinence: anal bulking injections beat sham (52% vs 31% halved their episodes), tibial nerve stimulation did not beat sham, injections matched biofeedback training, and sphincter repair helps but fades over years — a SPLIT record
question: How is bowel (faecal) incontinence treated? Beyond pads and diet, which treatments have actually been tested — injections, nerve stimulation, exercises, surgery — and which ones worked? Clinical question underneath: in adults with faecal incontinence that has not settled with conservative measures, how effective are anal bulking-agent injections, percutaneous tibial nerve stimulation, sphincter training with biofeedback, and overlapping sphincter repair? (Fibre/psyllium for loose-stool incontinence and sacral nerve stimulation are homed on their own shelves — see the boundary note.)
balance: SPLIT — the tested treatments genuinely divide. Anal bulking injections worked against sham: in the double-blind NASHA Dx trial (Graf 2011, PMID: 21420555; 206 randomised), 52% of injected patients versus 31% of sham patients at least halved their incontinence episodes (odds ratio 2.36, 95% CI 1.24-4.47, p=0.0089), with 128 treatment-related adverse events including 2 serious abscesses. But the same injections were no better than sphincter training with biofeedback in a second randomised trial (Dehli 2013, PMID: 23298304; 126 patients), in which both groups improved similarly over 2 years. Percutaneous tibial nerve stimulation failed its sham test: in CONFIDeNT (Knowles 2015, PMID: 26293315; 227 randomised), 38% versus 31% responded (adjusted OR 1.28, 95% CI 0.72-2.28, p=0.396). Sphincter repair is uncontrolled evidence: in a 23-woman series with mean follow-up of 87 months (Lamblin 2014, PMID: 25185844), 85% were satisfied and 60% had good continence, but the proportion keeping their continence correction fell from 85% at 1 year to 48% at 84 months. BOUNDARIES: psyllium/fibre for loose-stool incontinence is homed on Shelf #5267, and sacral nerve stimulation is homed on Shelf #2659 — neither is re-carded here. PROPOSED SPLIT: one positive sham-controlled result (bulking injections), one large negative sham-controlled trial (tibial nerve stimulation), equivalence with exercises in a head-to-head trial, and surgical repair that helps many patients but wanes.
stamp: SPLIT — bulking injections beat sham (52% vs 31% responders) but only matched biofeedback training head-to-head; tibial nerve stimulation did not beat sham (p=0.396); sphincter repair satisfaction 85% but continence correction fell to 48% by 84 months. Fibre (#5267) and sacral nerve stimulation (#2659) are homed elsewhere

title: Brain abscess: aspiration versus excision/resection is an observational question — reoperation was 39.4% after aspiration versus 20.7% after resection in a 2025 multicentre series, while older series found no significant mortality difference between the operations
question: How is a brain abscess treated? In patients with a pyogenic brain abscess, how do aspiration and excision/resection compare on reoperation, recovery and death — and what does the observational record actually show?
balance: POSSIBLE — for resection over aspiration on reoperation, observational only; there is no randomised trial comparing aspiration with excision for brain abscess, and treatment choice is driven by abscess size, depth and the patient's state. The largest modern comparison (Eibl 2025, PMID: 41175405; 148 patients with primary superficial pyogenic abscesses at five German/Austrian university centres, 2008–2023) found reoperation in 39.4% of the aspiration group versus 20.7% of the microsurgical resection group (p=0.018), five in-hospital deaths all in the aspiration group (overall mortality 3.4%; p=0.005), no significant difference in surgical complication rates, and comparable favourable outcomes at discharge, 3 and 6 months, with faster early recovery after resection. The older record is less decisive: in a 400-case review from China (Yang 1981, PMID: 7310502), mortality was 22% with aspiration as initial treatment, 17.2% with excision alone and 25% with aspiration followed by excision, with no significant difference between treatment groups — the dominant predictor was the patient's condition on arrival (mortality 64% with signs of herniation versus 8.4% without). In a 96-patient retrospective series (Hakan 2006, PMID: 16183134), 7 of 72 aspiration patients and 1 of 14 excision patients died, 10 patients were treated medically alone, and there was no significant correlation between treatment group and outcome. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: resection may halve reoperation in superficial abscesses on the newest series, but confounding by indication (deep, multiple or sicker-patient abscesses are aspirated, not resected) pervades every comparison, and antibiotics — given to all — are the untested constant underneath both operations.
stamp: POSSIBLE — observational only (no RCT): reoperation 39.4% after aspiration versus 20.7% after resection in the 2025 multicentre series, with comparable functional outcomes; older series found no significant mortality difference between aspiration and excision, and admission condition dominated prognosis

title: Breast cancer in men: no randomised trials exist in men — registry data say tamoxifen, not an aromatase inhibitor, is the endocrine treatment with the survival record (deaths 17.9% vs 32.0% in 257 men)
question: How is breast cancer in men treated? Do the hormone treatments proven in women work the same in men? Clinical question underneath: in men with hormone-receptor-positive breast cancer, what male-specific evidence exists for surgery and adjuvant endocrine therapy — in particular tamoxifen versus aromatase inhibitors — given that the randomised trials were done in women and men were excluded?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — capped, because every scrap of male-specific evidence is observational: there are no randomised trials of breast cancer treatment in men, and standard care is extrapolated from trials in women. That extrapolation fails at one tested point. In 257 men with hormone-receptor-positive disease from German registries (Eggemann 2013, PMID: 23224235), 37 of 207 men on tamoxifen died (17.9%) versus 16 of 50 on an aromatase inhibitor (32.0%) over a median 42.2 months (log-rank p=0.007); after adjustment, aromatase inhibitor treatment carried a higher mortality risk (HR 1.55, 95% CI 1.13-2.13) — the reverse of the female-trial ordering. In a prospectively enrolled cohort of 448 men (Eggemann 2020, PMID: 32367072), men who did not receive tamoxifen had significantly worse disease-free survival (P=0.002); the reported recurrence-and-mortality figure was 18.2% without tamoxifen versus 11.2% with it, and adjusted analysis gave a hazard ratio of 0.32 (95% CI 0.14-0.74) for recurrence with tamoxifen — a 68% relative reduction. The descriptive picture comes from Portugal's national registry (Montenegro 2025, PMID: 40079376; 620 men, 2001-2021): median age 68; 60.3% localised, 24.5% locally advanced, 15.2% metastatic; oestrogen-receptor-positive in 96.6%; mastectomy the primary surgery and tamoxifen the most-used adjuvant endocrine therapy; median survival 86 months (localised), 70 (locally advanced) and 41 (metastatic). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): in men, tamoxifen is the endocrine therapy with male-specific outcome data behind it; aromatase inhibitors alone performed worse in the male registry data, contrary to what female trials would predict.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational male-specific data only (no male RCTs exist): tamoxifen was associated with better survival than aromatase inhibitors (deaths 17.9% vs 32.0%; adjusted HR 1.55 for AI) and with better disease-free survival than no tamoxifen (adjusted recurrence HR 0.32); the rest of care is extrapolated from women's trials

title: Broken collarbone (displaced midshaft clavicle fracture): plate fixation cuts nonunion — 0.8% versus 11% at 9 months in the UK trial, relative risk 0.14 in the meta-analysis — and speeds early function, but final function differs little and second operations are common either way
question: How is a broken collarbone (clavicle fracture) treated? In adults with a displaced midshaft clavicle fracture, does operative plate fixation beat nonoperative sling treatment on union, function and reoperation?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for plate fixation on union and early recovery, with the limits printed beside it. Two multicentre randomised trials and a meta-analysis of six randomised trials agree that fixation markedly reduces nonunion: in the Canadian Orthopaedic Trauma Society trial (COTS 2007, PMID: 17200303; 132 randomised, 111 completing 1 year), nonunion occurred in 2 operative versus 7 nonoperative patients (p=0.042), symptomatic malunion in 0 versus 9 (p=0.001), and mean time to union was 16.4 versus 28.4 weeks (p=0.001), with Constant and DASH scores significantly better in the operative group at all time-points. In the larger UK Clavicle Trial (Ahrens 2017, PMID: 28816894; 301 randomised), nonunion at 9 months was 0.8% operative versus 11% nonoperative (p<0.001), function and satisfaction were better at 6 weeks and 3 months, and 12 (11%) of 147 nonoperative patients needed secondary surgery. The meta-analysis of six randomised trials (614 patients; Woltz 2017, PMID: 28632595) put the relative risk of nonunion at 0.14 (95% CI 0.06–0.32) with fixation — a relative measure; the absolute rates in the UK trial were 0.8% versus 11% — but found 1-year Constant and DASH advantages of only 4.4 and 5.1 points, judged not clinically relevant, and when plate removals were counted, secondary operations were as common after fixation (17.6%) as after nonoperative care (16.6%; relative risk 1.01). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): fixation is the surer route to union and a faster early recovery for a completely displaced fracture, not a guarantee of better final function — and it trades nonunion surgery later for hardware surgery sooner in a similar share of patients.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — plate fixation reduces nonunion (0.8% vs 11% at 9 months in the 301-patient UK trial; relative risk 0.14, 95% CI 0.06–0.32, across 6 RCTs) and speeds early function, but 1-year function gains were small (4.4–5.1 points, not clinically relevant) and total secondary operations were similar once plate removal is counted (17.6% vs 16.6%)

title: Broken finger or thumb: buddy taping matched splinting for children's reduced finger fractures, splint choice changed mallet-finger failure rates, and one small trial favoured a wire over a splint patients kept removing
question: I've broken my finger or thumb — should it be buddy-taped, splinted, or fixed with an operation, and does the choice change how well it heals?
balance: SPLIT — the answer depends on which finger injury is being treated, because the comparative evidence is injury-specific. For displaced extra-articular finger fractures in children that have been put back into place (closed reduction), one randomised trial (Weber 2025, PMID: 39487748; 81 children) found buddy taping non-inferior to splinting for keeping the fracture aligned, and more comfortable; a systematic review of children's Salter-Harris II finger fractures (Sohail 2026, PMID: 40304136) found every fracture healed without complications whichever method was used. For mallet finger (the fingertip droops because the extensor tendon is injured, with or without a small fracture), a multicentre randomised trial (O'Brien 2011, PMID: 21272714; 64 patients) found no difference in the final droop between three splint types, but treatment failure was 23.8% with a Stack splint and 23.8% with a dorsal aluminium splint versus 0% with a custom thermoplastic splint. And in one small randomised comparison (Mendoza 2022, PMID: 35572082; 41 patients), a Kirschner wire outperformed a Stack splint for mallet finger — but mainly because most splint patients did not keep the splint on. BOUNDARY: this shelf cards only the comparative immobilisation and wire-versus-splint evidence actually found. Fractures needing surgery for other reasons (open fractures, joint involvement, rotation that cannot be corrected) and thumb fractures specifically have no comparative trial carded here — no randomised comparison for thumb fractures was found. PROPOSED SPLIT: taping and splinting look equivalent for children's reduced finger fractures; for mallet finger the splint must fit and be worn, and a wire beat a poorly worn splint in one small study.
stamp: SPLIT — children's reduced phalangeal fractures: buddy taping non-inferior to splinting in one RCT (81 children) and more comfortable · mallet finger: no difference in final extensor lag between splint types in one RCT (64 patients), but failure 23.8% with Stack and dorsal splints versus 0% with a custom thermoplastic splint · mallet finger wire versus splint: Kirschner wire beat Stack splint in one small randomised comparison (41 patients), driven by splint non-compliance

title: Broken leg (tibial shaft fracture): reamed versus unreamed nailing — no overall difference in the 1,319-patient SPRINT trial, with closed fractures favouring reamed nailing and open fractures trending the other way
question: I've broken my leg — for a tibial shaft fracture fixed with a nail down the centre of the bone, should the surgeon ream the canal before inserting the nail, or use an unreamed nail?
balance: SPLIT — the answer differs for closed and open fractures. SCOPE DECLARED: this shelf covers one question within 'broken leg' — for an adult tibial shaft fracture treated with an intramedullary nail, should the medullary canal be reamed before the nail is inserted? In the SPRINT trial (PMID: 19047701; 1,319 adults, the dominant study in this field), the overall composite of major events (re-operation and related endpoints) did not differ significantly: 105 events with reamed versus 114 with unreamed nailing (relative risk 0.90, 95% CI 0.71–1.15). The split is in the subgroups: in CLOSED fractures, events occurred in 45 of 416 (11%) reamed versus 68 of 410 (17%) unreamed patients (relative risk 0.67, 95% CI 0.47–0.96; p=0.03) — a relative reduction of about a third, an absolute difference of about 6 percentage points, driven largely by dynamization procedures. In OPEN fractures the trend ran the other way: 60 of 206 (29%) reamed versus 46 of 194 (24%) unreamed (relative risk 1.27, 95% CI 0.91–1.78; p=0.16), not significant. The Cochrane review (Duan 2012, PMID: 22258982) found insufficient evidence overall, with moderate-quality evidence of no clear difference in major re-operations, though reamed nailing clearly reduced implant failure (relative risk 0.42). The SPRINT economic analysis (Briel 2011, PMID: 21669369) found near-identical costs and quality-adjusted life years for closed fractures. BOUNDARY: rhBMP-2 for open tibial fractures is homed on Shelf #3731 and is not re-carded here; femoral fractures and non-nailing treatments (plates, external fixation, casting) are outside this shelf's declared scope. PROPOSED SPLIT: no overall winner; reamed nailing favoured for closed tibial shaft fractures, no advantage — and a possible disadvantage — shown for open fractures.
stamp: SPLIT — overall no significant difference (SPRINT: relative risk 0.90, 95% CI 0.71–1.15) · closed tibial shaft fractures favour reamed nailing (events 11% versus 17%; relative risk 0.67) · open fractures trend against reamed nailing (29% versus 24%; relative risk 1.27, not significant)

title: Broken nose: closed reduction under local anaesthetic matched general anaesthetic in the comparative studies, and one cohort reported earlier reduction gave better results
question: I've broken my nose — does closed reduction work as well under local anaesthetic as under general anaesthetic, and does having it done sooner give a better result?
balance: POSSIBLE — the comparative evidence for broken-nose treatment is small and old, and it points to local anaesthesia being an acceptable substitute for general anaesthesia for closed reduction, with a suggestion that earlier reduction gives a better cosmetic result. A small randomised trial (Watson 1988, PMID: 3228992; 29 patients) found no significant differences between local and general anaesthesia in appearance or measured nasal airway after manipulation of a displaced fractured nose, and local anaesthesia was acceptable to all but one patient. A 2023 prospective comparison (Jana 2024, PMID: 38440457; 40 patients) likewise found no significant difference in pain scores between local and general anaesthesia, and 90% of local-anaesthesia patients said they would choose it again. On timing, one prospective cohort (Raghvi 2023, PMID: 37974860; 54 patients) reported better outcomes with reduction within 6 hours than after 2 weeks — but its abstract reports pooled results for all patients rather than per-group numbers, so the size of any timing advantage cannot be extracted. No comparative evidence on splinting after reduction was found that could be carded. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: local-anaesthetic reduction is a reasonable alternative to general anaesthesia for suitable fractures; the timing advantage is plausible but unquantified in the records fetched.
stamp: POSSIBLE — local anaesthesia for closed reduction matched general anaesthesia in one small RCT (29 patients) and one prospective comparison (40 patients); early reduction reported better than late in one cohort (54 patients) without per-group numbers

title: Broken ribs: a serratus anterior plane block added to standard care doubled early pain control and halved 24-hour opioid use in the 210-patient SABRE trial
question: I've broken my ribs and it hurts to breathe — does a serratus anterior plane block (a regional nerve block into the chest wall) control the pain better than standard painkillers alone?
balance: LIKELY (for early pain relief and opioid sparing) — SCOPE DECLARED: this shelf covers one analgesic technique for rib fractures, the ultrasound-guided serratus anterior plane block (SAPB), a regional block injected into the chest-wall fascial plane. In the SABRE trial (Partyka 2024, PMID: 38691350; 210 emergency-department patients, median age 71), adding a single SAPB to standard care roughly doubled the proportion achieving the composite pain goal at 4 hours (38 of 92 patients, 41%, versus 18 of 92, 19.6%) and halved median 24-hour opioid use (45 versus 91 milligram morphine equivalents). A smaller randomised trial (Teksen 2021, PMID: 33383266; 60 patients) found significantly lower 24-hour tramadol consumption and lower pain scores at every time point to 24 hours with SAPB, and less chronic pain afterwards (1 versus 9 patients). A third randomised trial (Zengin 2025, PMID: 40082780) compared SAPB head-to-head with intercostal nerve block: both worked, intercostal block was better in the first 4 hours, SAPB was better from 8 to 24 hours and no SAPB patient needed extra analgesia versus 43.3% of intercostal-block patients. No trial showed a difference in pneumonia or death. BOUNDARY: epidural analgesia for traumatic rib fractures is homed on Shelf #1313 and surgical stabilisation of rib fractures on Shelf #1268 — neither is re-carded here. Bruised ribs without fracture were not separately studied in these trials. PROPOSED LIKELY for the narrow claim: SAPB added to standard care improves early pain control and reduces opioid requirement after rib fractures.
stamp: LIKELY — serratus anterior plane block added to standard care improves early pain control (41% versus 19.6% met the 4-hour pain goal in SABRE, 210 patients) and halves 24-hour opioid use (median 45 versus 91 mg morphine equivalents); no pneumonia or mortality benefit shown
