title: Cavernoma (cerebral cavernous malformation): no definitive trial of surgery or radiosurgery versus watching — the CARE pilot showed a real trial is feasible, and the cohort comparisons are confounded by selection
question: I have a cavernoma (cerebral cavernous malformation) — should it be removed surgically or treated with radiosurgery, or is it safer to watch it with scans?
balance: POSSIBLE — stated plainly: there is NO definitive randomised trial of surgery or radiosurgery versus conservative management for cerebral cavernous malformation (cavernoma), and none of the numbers on this shelf comes from one. What exists: (1) the CARE pilot trial (Al-Shahi Salman 2025, PMID: 40820590), which randomised only 72 patients to test whether a definitive trial is feasible — it was (93% retention, 91% adherence) — and found the same number of primary clinical events in both arms (2 of 33 with intervention versus 2 of 34 without), far too few to judge benefit; the authors calculate a definitive trial would need 590–1,900 participants. (2) A systematic comparison of 100 published cohorts (Bubenikova 2022, PMID: 35273070; 8,994 patients) reporting haemorrhage prevention of 97% after surgery, 86% after radiosurgery and 77% with conservative care — figures built from non-randomised series in which patients chosen for surgery differ systematically from patients watched, so the gaps cannot be read as treatment effects. (3) A conservatively managed cohort (PMID: 38624046; 265 patients) quantifying the risk of watching: symptomatic haemorrhage in 19% during follow-up, at about 6.0% per year after a haemorrhagic presentation versus 1.5% per year without one. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — intervention plausibly prevents future haemorrhage in selected patients, but the only randomised evidence is a feasibility pilot with 4 events in total; the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE because the comparative evidence is observational.
stamp: POSSIBLE — no definitive RCT exists; the CARE pilot (72 patients) showed a definitive trial is feasible but had 2 events in each arm; observational cohort comparisons favour intervention but are confounded by selection

title: Cervical spondylosis with radiculopathy: surgery relieved pain faster, but physiotherapy caught up by 1–2 years on most measures in both randomised trials
question: I have cervical spondylosis with a trapped nerve in my neck (radiculopathy — pain, weakness or numbness down the arm) — is surgery better than physiotherapy or a collar, and does any advantage last?
balance: SPLIT (over time) — SCOPE DECLARED: this shelf covers cervical RADICULOPATHY (arm pain, weakness or sensory loss from a spondylotic trapped nerve root in the neck). Cervical myelopathy (spinal cord compression) is a different question — the Cochrane review found only one small myelopathy trial with no differences over 3 years and substantial loss to follow-up — and is not this shelf's subject. The pattern across the radiculopathy trials is consistent: surgery relieves pain faster, and conservative care catches up. The Cochrane review (Nikolaidis 2010, PMID: 20091520) found surgical decompression superior in the short term for pain, weakness and sensory loss versus physiotherapy or a collar, with no significant differences at 1 year — on low/very-low quality evidence from a single trial of 81 patients. That trial (Persson 1997, PMID: 9106315) found surgery gave less early pain than physiotherapy or a collar, but by final follow-up there were no differences in pain, function or mood between the three groups. The later randomised trial (Engquist 2013, PMID: 23778373; 63 patients) found the same shape over 24 months: surgery plus physiotherapy beat physiotherapy alone on neck pain (P=0.039) and on patients rating themselves better at 12 months (87% versus 62%), but disability (NDI) never differed significantly (P=0.23) and the global ratings had converged by 24 months (81% versus 69%, P=0.28). PROPOSED SPLIT: surgery buys speed of relief in the first months; by 1–2 years structured physiotherapy reaches a similar place on most measures.
stamp: SPLIT — surgery relieves cervical radiculopathy pain faster (better short-term pain outcomes in both randomised trials), but physiotherapy/collar care catches up: no significant differences at 1 year (Cochrane/Persson) and disability never differed over 24 months (Engquist, P=0.23)

title: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 1A: ascorbic acid (vitamin C) made no difference in six randomised trials — and one combination drug (PXT3003) showed a small benefit in a single manufacturer-run trial
question: I have Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 1A — does ascorbic acid (vitamin C) slow the neuropathy down, and has any other drug treatment been shown to help?
balance: (the treatment made no difference) — for ascorbic acid, this is one of the cleanest negative records in this library: six randomised trials of oral ascorbic acid (vitamin C, 1–4 g/day) versus placebo in Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 1A (CMT1A), gathered in a Cochrane review (Gess 2015, PMID: 26662471; 5 adult trials, 622 participants), with high-quality evidence of no improvement in the CMT Neuropathy Score at 12 months (mean difference −0.37, 95% CI −0.83 to 0.09; 5 studies, 533 participants) or 24 months (mean difference −0.21, 95% CI −0.81 to 0.39; 3 studies, 388 participants), and no clinical benefit in the one children's trial (80 children). The two largest trials agree individually: CMT-TRIAAL/CMT-TRAUK (Pareyson 2011, PMID: 21393063; 277 randomised, 1.5 g/day for 24 months) found CMTNS worsening of 0.2 points in both arms (mean difference 0.0, 95% CI −0.6 to 0.7; p=0.93), and the 4 g/day futility trial (Lewis 2013, PMID: 23797954; 110 randomised) found the placebo group numerically did better than the ascorbic-acid group (−0.92 versus −0.21 CMTNS change), with both arms faring better than natural history — a placebo/context effect, not a drug effect. Adverse effects did not differ from placebo: ascorbic acid is safe here, it simply does not work. The one positive signal on this shelf is a different treatment: PXT3003 (a fixed combination of baclofen, naltrexone and D-sorbitol) improved the Overall Neuropathy Limitations Scale by a mean of −0.37 points versus placebo (97.5% CI −0.68 to −0.06; p=0.008) in a single phase 3 trial (Attarian 2021, PMID: 34656144; 323 patients) whose high-dose arm was disrupted by a formulation defect and whose authors were all paid consultants of, or funded by, the manufacturer. PROPOSED: (the treatment made no difference) for ascorbic acid at any tested dose; POSSIBLE for PXT3003, pending independent replication.
stamp: (the treatment made no difference) — ascorbic acid for CMT1A: six RCTs, high-quality evidence of no benefit (Cochrane; largest trial mean difference 0.0, p=0.93) · PXT3003 separately POSSIBLE: one phase 3 trial, ONLS −0.37 points (p=0.008), manufacturer-run with a disrupted high-dose arm

title: Chiari malformation type I with syringomyelia: adding tonsil resection or reduction to decompression improved syrinx shrinkage across observational series — clinical improvement did not differ, and no randomised trial exists
question: I have Chiari malformation type I with a syrinx (syringomyelia) and am having decompression surgery — does also reducing or removing the cerebellar tonsils give a better result than decompression alone?
balance: POSSIBLE — every number on this shelf is observational: there is NO randomised trial of posterior fossa decompression techniques for Chiari malformation type I (CM-I) with syringomyelia, and the comparisons below come from retrospective series in which the choice of technique was the surgeon's, not chance. The consistent direction: adding cerebellar tonsil work (resection or reduction) to decompression shrinks the syrinx more. In a retrospective comparison of 162 patients (Zhang 2025, PMID: 40098683), decompression with tonsil resection beat decompression alone on 6-month favourable-outcome rates (78.8% versus 56.9% on the Chicago Chiari Outcome Scale) and syrinx recovery (76% versus 55.2%), with no significant difference in complications. A radiological meta-analysis of 20 studies and 3,063 patients (Prasad 2025, PMID: 41111088) found tonsillar reduction modestly superior to decompression with duraplasty on the syrinx-to-cord ratio (mean difference 0.04) — statistically detectable, clinically small. The largest series, a propensity-matched single-centre cohort of 1,231 patients (Yuan 2026, PMID: 42080534), found syrinx regression over 50% in 78% with a tonsil-resecting modified decompression versus 60% with standard decompression with duraplasty, and far fewer revision operations (4.1% versus 15.5%) — while clinical improvement did not differ significantly between techniques. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: tonsil resection/reduction probably improves syrinx resolution and reduces re-operation, on consistent but non-randomised evidence; whether patients feel better is not shown to differ.
stamp: POSSIBLE — observational evidence only (no RCT): adding tonsil resection/reduction to posterior fossa decompression improves syrinx regression (78% versus 60% for >50% regression in the largest cohort) and may reduce revision surgery (4.1% versus 15.5%), but clinical improvement did not differ significantly

title: Childhood cataracts (IATS): after surgery for a one-sided congenital cataract in infancy, a contact lens gave the same vision as an implanted lens at 1 year and at 4½ years — with far fewer adverse events and reoperations
question: My baby has a cataract in one eye — after the cataract is removed in infancy, is it better to implant an artificial lens straight away or to correct the eye with a contact lens, in terms of vision, complications and further operations?
balance: POSSIBLE — vision (the treatment made no difference), with fewer harms on contact lens: the single randomised trial behind this question, the Infant Aphakia Treatment Study (IATS, 114 infants with a unilateral congenital cataract, surgery at 1–6 months, 12 US sites, NCT00212134), found identical median visual acuity in the two groups at age 4½ years (both 0.90 logMAR, 20/159; P=.54; Lambert 2014, PMID: 24604348) and no significant difference in grating acuity at 1 year (contact lens 0.80 vs IOL 0.97 logMAR; P=.19). The difference was in harm and reoperation: by age 5, at least one adverse event had occurred in 81% of the IOL group versus 56% of the contact-lens group (P=.02), and at least one additional intraocular operation in 72% versus 21% (P<.001) (Lambert 2014; Plager 2014, PMID: 25077835). Glaucoma or glaucoma suspect did not differ (35% contact lens vs 28% IOL; P=.55). The trial's own recommendation: leave infants under 7 months aphakic and correct with a contact lens, reserving primary IOL implantation for infants in whom contact-lens handling would likely leave the eye uncorrected for long periods. BOUNDARY: this shelf covers unilateral congenital cataract operated on before 7 months of age — the IATS population. It does not cover bilateral cataracts, cataract surgery in older children, or traumatic cataract, where the balance may differ and no comparable randomised trial was carded here.
stamp: POSSIBLE — in the one randomised trial (IATS, 114 infants), contact-lens correction and primary IOL implantation gave identical median vision at 4½ years (both 0.90 logMAR), but the IOL group had more adverse events (81% vs 56%) and far more additional intraocular operations (72% vs 21%) by age 5

title: Chipped, broken or cracked tooth: cracked teeth restored without covering the cusps failed more (pulpal complications relative risk 3.2, extraction relative risk 8.1 versus full crowns in pooled observational data) — and repairing a defective filling performed no worse than replacing it over seven years
question: I have chipped, broken or cracked a tooth — should it be repaired, crowned or replaced, and if the pulp is exposed can it be capped rather than having root canal treatment?
balance: POSSIBLE — the comparative record is mostly observational, with one modern randomised pulp-therapy trial. For cracked teeth keeping a vital pulp, the systematic review and meta-analysis of 27 studies (Zhang 2024, PMID: 38272437) found tooth survival of 92.8–97.8% at 1–6 years, but direct restorations without cuspal coverage carried a relative risk of pulpal complications of 3.2 (95% CI 1.51–6.82) and of tooth extraction of 8.1 (95% CI 1.05–62.5) compared with full-crown restorations — relative measures from observational studies, with wide intervals. For a defective existing restoration, a prospective comparative study of 113 restorations followed for seven years (Gordan 2011, PMID: 21719808) found degradation in every group including full replacement, with no significant difference in failure rate — supporting repair over replacement for localised defects. For pulp exposure (studied in carious, not traumatic, exposures), a double-blind randomised trial of 140 teeth (Taha 2025, PMID: 40617285) found 1-year success of 91.5% for partial pulpotomy versus 81.3% for direct pulp capping, a difference that was not significant (P=.08). BOUNDARY: toothache pain relief itself is homed on Shelf #5287 and is not re-carded here; this shelf is about restoring and keeping the tooth.
stamp: POSSIBLE — cuspal-coverage (crown/onlay) restoration of a cracked vital tooth is associated with fewer pulpal complications and extractions than an uncovered direct filling in pooled observational data; repairing a defective restoration was no worse than replacing it in the one long comparative study; and pulp capping and partial pulpotomy both succeeded in over 80% at one year in the one randomised trial (carious exposures)

title: Cleft lip and palate: in the Scandcleft randomised trials of 431 children, no primary-surgery protocol beat the others — speech proficiency was 86–92% across all four protocols at 10 years and dental arches did not differ at 5, 8 or 10 years
question: My child has a cleft lip and palate — treatment is staged surgery, but does the timing or technique of the primary repairs (including vomer flap closure or delaying hard-palate closure), or the timing of alveolar bone grafting, change speech, dental and growth outcomes?
balance: LIKELY (no difference) between the tested primary-surgery protocols — cleft lip and palate care is staged surgery, and the one large randomised programme, Scandcleft (three parallel randomised trials, 431 children with non-syndromic unilateral cleft lip and palate, nine teams in five countries, ISRCTN29932826), tested four sequences of lip and palate closure — including hard-palate closure delayed to 36 months, simultaneous hard and soft palate closure at 12 months, and a vomer-flap single-layer hard-palate closure at 3–4 months — against a common protocol. It found no winner: dental arch relationships did not differ within any trial at 5, 8 or 10 years (Heliövaara 2022, PMID: 34476476), and at 10 years consonant proficiency ranged only 86–92% across arms with contradictory velopharyngeal patterns, the authors concluding there is 'no obvious evidence to recommend any of the protocols as superior' (Willadsen 2023, PMID: 36541222). Maxillary growth likewise did not differ within trials. For the later staged step, alveolar bone grafting, there are no randomised timing trials in the fetched record: a systematic review of 15 studies (Mundra 2022, PMID: 34967522) reports grafting with pre- and post-operative orthodontics as standard care and recommends the early mixed dentition phase, typically 6–8 years, without consensus on how graft success should even be measured.
stamp: LIKELY (no difference) — in the Scandcleft randomised trials (431 children with unilateral cleft lip and palate), none of the four primary-surgery protocols — including delayed hard-palate closure and vomer-flap closure — was superior on speech at 10 years or dental arch relationships at 5–10 years; alveolar bone graft timing (recommended 6–8 years) rests on observational review evidence only

title: Acute compartment syndrome: the diastolic-minus-compartment (delta-P) threshold under 30 mmHg missed no case in 116 monitored fractures — while cohorts disagree on how much fasciotomy timing itself changes death and amputation
question: I have acute compartment syndrome — how quickly must the fasciotomy be done, does pressure monitoring change outcomes, and which pressure threshold (absolute or diastolic-minus-compartment) should trigger decompression?
balance: SPLIT / POSSIBLE — there are no randomised trials of fasciotomy (withholding decompression cannot be randomised), so everything here is cohort evidence, capped at POSSIBLE. Two findings are consistent. First, the diagnostic threshold: in 116 tibial fractures monitored continuously, using a differential pressure (diastolic minus compartment pressure) under 30 mmHg as the fasciotomy trigger produced no missed compartment syndromes, while an absolute 30 mmHg threshold would have flagged 43% for fasciotomy (McQueen 1996, PMID: 8898137). Second, monitored patients reached fasciotomy sooner (16 vs 32 hours) and 0 of 12 survivors had sequelae versus 10 of 11 unmonitored survivors with weakness and contractures (McQueen 1996, PMID: 8898136) — a tiny, non-randomised comparison. On timing itself the cohorts disagree: in earthquake crush injuries, amputation was 0% with fasciotomy within 24 hours, 11.5% at 24–48 hours and 31.4% after 48 hours (Demir 2025, PMID: 39853473), yet in the largest series — 546 patients at two Level I trauma centres — neither death (6.6%) nor amputation (9.5%) was associated with time from injury to fasciotomy at all; patient and injury-severity factors were (Zhang 2020, PMID: 31560102). Fasciotomy remains the emergency standard of care; this shelf cards what the comparative cohorts can and cannot show about timing and pressure thresholds, and does not question decompressing a clinically evident compartment syndrome.
stamp: POSSIBLE — observational cohorts only: a differential pressure (diastolic minus compartment) under 30 mmHg was the threshold that missed no case in 116 monitored tibial fractures, and monitored patients were decompressed sooner with fewer sequelae; but on timing itself cohorts conflict — amputation rose with delay after earthquake crush injury (0% <24 h to 31.4% >48 h) while a 546-patient series found no association between time to fasciotomy and death or amputation

title: Corns and calluses: salicylic acid plasters resolved more corns than scalpel debridement (34% versus 21% at 3 months) — but for callus pain the scalpel beat a sham procedure by only 2–7 mm, not significantly
question: I have corns and calluses — do salicylic acid corn plasters work better than having them cut out (scalpel debridement), and does debridement itself relieve callus pain?
balance: SPLIT — the answer splits by lesion and by treatment. For corns, one randomised trial of 202 adults (Farndon 2013, PMID: 24063387) found 40% salicylic acid plasters beat usual scalpel debridement: complete resolution at 3 months in 34% (32/95) versus 21% (20/94), reduced size in 83% versus 56%, less pain at 3 months, and longer time to recurrence over 12 months. For painful plantar callus in older people, the scalpel itself barely beat doing nothing real: against sham debridement, real debridement's pain advantage was only 2–7 mm on a 100-mm scale, never significant and never clinically worthwhile (Landorf 2013, PMID: 23915078; 80 participants), and a 300-person trial found full and partial debridement indistinguishable, both only marginally better than simulated debridement (Garcia 2020, PMID: 32997761). A small three-arm trial found podiatry (scalpel) treatment changed callus skin measures and pain immediately, with lesser, slower changes from two home keratolytics (Hashmi 2016, PMID: 27189190). Safety boundary: salicylic acid plasters in the corn trial were applied under podiatrist supervision in selected patients — corns that were infected or neurovascular were excluded — and keratolytics are generally avoided on broken skin and in people with diabetes or poor circulation, who were not the studied population.
stamp: SPLIT — corns: 40% salicylic acid plasters beat scalpel debridement in the one randomised trial (resolution 34% vs 21% at 3 months, longer time to recurrence) · calluses: scalpel debridement's pain advantage over sham was only 2–7 mm and non-significant, and full versus partial debridement did not differ — its specific effect on callus pain is small

title: Cradle cap: no treatment has been shown to beat the rash's own course — Cochrane found six tiny trials (310 infants, all very low-certainty) and no randomised test of antifungals, oils or salicylic acid at all
question: My baby has cradle cap (infantile seborrhoeic dermatitis) — do antifungal creams, steroid creams or any other treatment clear it faster than leaving it alone?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — cradle cap (infantile seborrhoeic dermatitis) is benign and self-limiting, and its trial record is exceptionally thin. The Cochrane review (Victoire 2019, PMID: 30828791) found just six randomised trials with 310 children (297 analysed), rated every comparison very low-certainty, and found NO trials of the treatments actually used — mineral oils, salicylic acid or antifungals. Within the trials that exist: a non-steroidal proprietary cream scored 96% success versus 92% on placebo at day 14; a moisturising gel plus shampoo reduced lesional score by 81.4% versus 70.2% for shampoo only (P=0.0092); hydrocortisone 1% lotion cured 95.8% versus 97.1% for licochalcone lotion — no difference; and oral biotin versus placebo (35 children in two trials) produced no reportable severity benefit. The one direct antifungal comparison is a non-randomised split-side study of 48 infants (Wannanukul 2004, PMID: 16083165): lesions cleared in 31% on the ketoconazole 2% side versus 35% on the hydrocortisone 1% side at one week, with all lesions in both groups cleared by the end of week two — the natural history of the condition doing most of the work. No trial measured quality of life. The honest summary: nothing has been shown to beat time, and the commonly recommended antifungal and oil treatments have never been randomised in infants.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the Cochrane review found only six small randomised trials (310 infants), all very low-certainty, and no trials of the antifungals, mineral oils or salicylic acid actually used for cradle cap; the one antifungal-versus-steroid comparison (48 infants, non-randomised) found no difference, with all lesions cleared by two weeks on both sides

title: Detached retina: the best operation depends on the eye — buckling won on vision in phakic eyes and vitrectomy on first-time reattachment in pseudophakic eyes (SPR), while a gas bubble beat vitrectomy on vision but not first-time success in selected detachments (PIVOT)
question: I have a detached retina — which operation is best: vitrectomy, scleral buckling, or pneumatic retinopexy (a gas-bubble procedure), for vision and for getting the retina back in place?
balance: SPLIT — the randomised answer depends on the eye's lens status and on which detachments are eligible for the least invasive operation. In the SPR study (681 patients; Heimann 2007, PMID: 18054633), the largest randomised comparison of scleral buckling (SB) versus primary vitrectomy (PPV): in phakic eyes, vision improved more with buckling (mean BCVA change −0.71 vs −0.56 logMAR; P=0.0005) and cataract progressed more after vitrectomy; in pseudophakic eyes, vision did not differ, but primary anatomical success was significantly better with vitrectomy (72.0% [95/132] vs 53.4% [71/133]; P=0.0020) with fewer secondary operations — the authors recommend PPV in pseudophakic eyes. In PIVOT (176 patients; Hillier 2019, PMID: 30468761), restricted to detachments with breaks in the upper retina within one clock hour, pneumatic retinopexy (PnR) gave better 12-month vision than vitrectomy (79.9 vs 75.0 ETDRS letters, a 4.9-letter difference; P=0.024) and less vertical metamorphopsia, but lower primary anatomical success (80.8% vs 93.2%; P=0.045), with final (secondary) success equal at about 99% in both groups — and cataract surgery by 12 months in 65% of phakic PPV eyes versus 16% of PnR eyes. One-home note: retinal-detachment surgery was checked against the existing library before building; no prior shelf homes this SPR/PIVOT comparison.
stamp: SPLIT — phakic eyes: scleral buckling improved vision more than vitrectomy in the SPR study (−0.71 vs −0.56 logMAR) · pseudophakic eyes: vitrectomy reattached first time more often (72.0% vs 53.4%) with equal vision · PIVOT-eligible detachments: pneumatic retinopexy gave better 12-month vision (+4.9 letters) but lower primary success (80.8% vs 93.2%), final success ~99% both ways

title: Developmental co-ordination disorder (dyspraxia): CO-OP and task-oriented therapy improve the goals children practise — but the Cochrane review found no motor-performance effect in the randomised trials alone, and rated the evidence very low to low quality
question: My child has developmental co-ordination disorder (dyspraxia) — do task-oriented therapy or the CO-OP approach actually improve their motor skills?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — children with developmental co-ordination disorder (DCD, dyspraxia) are usually offered task-oriented therapy, and the best synthesis is unusually candid about how little certainty it provides. The Cochrane review of task-oriented interventions (Miyahara 2017, PMID: 28758189; 15 studies, 649 children aged 5–12) found its main pooled analysis — two RCTs plus four quasi-RCTs, 169 children — favoured task-oriented intervention over no intervention for motor performance (mean difference −3.63, 95% CI −5.88 to −1.39; P=0.002), but rated that very low-quality evidence; restricted to the two true RCTs (51 children), there was no effect (mean difference −2.34, 95% CI −7.50 to 2.83; P=0.38). The largest single trial of the flagship approach, CO-OP (Cognitive Orientation to daily Occupational Performance), randomised 78 children aged 8–12 to immediate treatment or a waitlist (Izadi-Najafabadi 2022, PMID: 35466705; NCT02597751): goal performance and movement quality improved markedly after treatment in children with DCD with and without ADHD (both P<0.001) and gains were maintained at three months, but transfer to overall motor skills appeared only in the DCD-only group. The original CO-OP pilot (Miller 2001, PMID: 11471396) compared CO-OP with contemporary therapy in just 20 children, with greater improvement on self-rated and observer-rated goal measures but not on the standardised motor test. Stamp is held at MAYBE (weak evidence): goal-specific gains are repeatedly seen, a general motor-performance effect is not established.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — task-oriented therapy and CO-OP improve performance on the goals children practise (waitlist RCT: goal scores 2.7 to 7.0, P<0.001, maintained at 3 months), but the Cochrane review's RCT-only analysis found no effect on motor performance (51 children), and it rated all its evidence very low to low quality

title: Psychotherapy for dissociative disorders: an adjunctive online programme beat a waitlist in one interim RCT (n=291), while a stabilising group programme added nothing immediate in the other RCT (n=59)
question: In people with dissociative disorders (including dissociative identity disorder), does psychotherapy — phase-oriented treatment or structured add-on programmes — improve symptoms and functioning compared with waiting list or with individual therapy alone?
balance: SPLIT — the two randomised trials test different add-ons and point in different directions. In the interim report of an ongoing RCT (Brand BL et al., PMID: 40014495; 291 outpatients with dissociative identity disorder, dissociative PTSD, other specified dissociative disorders, complex PTSD or unspecified dissociative disorder, all continuing their own outpatient psychotherapy), immediate access to the online Finding Solid Ground (FSG) psychoeducational programme produced significantly greater improvement than a 6-month waitlist in emotion regulation, PTSD symptoms, self-compassion and adaptive capacities at 6 months; by 12 months the immediate group showed large within-group effect sizes versus entry (|g| = 0.95–1.32), and the waitlist group improved comparably after it too received FSG. The abstract prints no between-group effect sizes, and this is an interim report of an ongoing trial. In the only other RCT (Bækkelund H et al., PMID: 35578194; 59 patients with complex dissociative disorders), adding 20 sessions of manualised stabilising group treatment to individual therapy produced no immediate advantage over individual therapy alone on functioning or any secondary outcome, although both groups improved significantly over 6 months of follow-up. A 2025 systematic review of phase-oriented treatment (Griffiths TA et al., PMID: 40891466) screened 6,088 articles and found only 19 pre–post studies, nearly all uncontrolled: every treatment type was associated with improvement, and the reviewers state plainly that high-powered controlled trials are needed. PROPOSED SPLIT: one specific adjunctive programme (FSG) has a positive waitlist-controlled interim result; structured group stabilisation as an add-on does not; and the core phase-oriented therapy itself has never been randomised.
stamp: SPLIT — adjunctive online Finding Solid Ground programme: significant gains versus waitlist at 6 months in an interim RCT of 291 patients (no between-group effect sizes printed) · stabilising group treatment added to individual therapy: no immediate advantage in the RCT of 59 patients · phase-oriented therapy itself: 19 studies, essentially all uncontrolled

title: Donepezil for cognition in Down syndrome: both large randomised trials were null on their primary measures (n=129 children; n=123 young adults) — only post-hoc and small-study signals remain
question: In people with Down syndrome, does donepezil improve cognition, adaptive behaviour or daily functioning compared with placebo — in children and young adults without dementia, and in adults with Alzheimer's dementia?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference) — scoped exactly to donepezil for cognition in Down syndrome, the tested question. Two large multicentre randomised double-blind trials anchor the shelf, and both missed: in children aged 10–17 (Kishnani PS et al., PMID: 21108390; 129 participants, 10 weeks, donepezil 2.5–10 mg/day), Vineland-II v-scores improved significantly in BOTH groups (P < 0.0001) with no significant between-group difference — the trial 'failed to demonstrate any benefit'. In young adults aged 18–35 without Alzheimer's disease (Kishnani PS et al., PMID: 19606472; 123 participants, 12 weeks, 5–10 mg/day), Severe Impairment Battery scores likewise improved in both groups with no significant between-group difference on the primary measure; the encouraging findings were post hoc (Vineland scores in observed cases, P = 0.03 but P = 0.07 by last-observation-carried-forward; responder analyses significant on three of five definitions). The Cochrane review of all pharmacological interventions for cognitive decline in adults with Down syndrome (Livingstone N et al., PMID: 26513128; 9 RCTs, 427 participants; 4 donepezil studies, 192 participants) found donepezil's cognitive scores similar to placebo (standardised mean difference 0.52, 95% CI −0.27 to 1.13 — an interval spanning no effect) and behaviour likewise (SMD 0.42, 95% CI −0.06 to 0.89), with significantly more adverse events on donepezil and the body of evidence rated low quality. The one small trial in Down syndrome with Alzheimer's dementia (n=30, inside the Cochrane review) showed at best a non-significant trend. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference): where it has been properly tested, donepezil has not beaten placebo on any pre-specified primary outcome in Down syndrome. BOUNDARY: memantine in Down syndrome is homed separately on Shelf #1399 (MEADOWS, also null) and is not re-carded here; this shelf is donepezil only.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference) — the two large randomised trials (129 children, 123 young adults) found no significant between-group difference on their primary measures, and the Cochrane pooling of the adult donepezil studies (192 participants) spans no effect, with more adverse events on donepezil

title: GnRH analogues for central precocious puberty: treated girls end about 4.8 cm taller than untreated girls in the comparative pooling — from observational studies, with no randomised trial
question: In children whose puberty has started too early (central precocious puberty), do GnRH analogue injections suppress puberty and leave them taller as adults than they would have been without treatment?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — there has never been a randomised placebo-controlled trial of GnRH analogues in central precocious puberty (CPP); the entire case rests on comparative observational studies, which caps this stamp at POSSIBLE. The systematic review and meta-analysis (Luo X et al., PMID: 33387371; 98 studies, 5,475 individuals) found, in its comparative studies, that GnRH analogue treatment increased final adult height in girls with idiopathic CPP versus no treatment by a mean difference of 4.83 cm (95% CI 2.32 to 7.34; 4 studies, n=242; I² = 49%) and decreased BMI by 1.01 kg/m² (95% CI −1.64 to −0.37; 3 studies, n=334), with no significant difference in polycystic ovary syndrome incidence (risk ratio 1.21, 95% CI 0.46 to 3.15; 3 studies, n=179); the reviewers graded the evidence very low to moderate and called the evidence for other long-term outcomes very weak. A direct treated-versus-untreated comparison (Poomthavorn P et al., PMID: 21501002) found adult height 158.6 (SD 5.2) cm in 47 treated girls versus 154.8 (5.6) cm in 11 untreated girls (P < 0.05), a 4.7 cm gain over pre-treatment predicted adult height in the treated group, and menstruation resuming 0.9 (0.5) years after stopping treatment — pubertal suppression is reversible. A large treated-only series (Yang EH et al., PMID: 37015776; 246 girls) shows predicted adult height rising on treatment in both CPP and early-puberty (onset 8–9 years) girls, but with no untreated comparator it cannot separate drug effect from prediction drift. BOUNDARY: delayed puberty is a different question — constitutional delay in boys is homed on Shelf #2907 (letrozole/testosterone) — and adding growth hormone to a GnRH analogue is not covered here. The height benefit is best supported for girls treated young with rapidly progressive CPP; for slowly progressive or borderline early puberty the comparative data are thinnest.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — comparative observational pooling puts final adult height 4.83 cm higher (95% CI 2.32 to 7.34) in treated versus untreated girls with idiopathic CPP, and suppression reverses after stopping (menarche ~0.9 years later); no randomised trial exists, so the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE

title: Celiprolol for vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome: arterial rupture or dissection in 20% on celiprolol versus 50% untreated in the one randomised trial (n=53, stopped early) — with cohort survival data behind it
question: In people with vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, does celiprolol prevent arterial rupture and dissection and improve survival compared with no preventive treatment?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — scoped exactly to the one Ehlers-Danlos question with comparative treatment data: celiprolol in the vascular type (vEDS, COL3A1). The single randomised trial (BBEST; Ong KT et al., PMID: 20825986) randomised 53 patients with clinical vEDS (33 COL3A1-positive) to celiprolol titrated to 400 mg/day or no treatment, open-label with blinded endpoint assessment: over a mean 47 months, arterial rupture or dissection occurred in 5 of 25 (20%) on celiprolol versus 14 of 28 (50%) controls — hazard ratio 0.36 (95% CI 0.15 to 0.88; P = 0.040), a 64% relative reduction and a 30-percentage-point absolute difference — and the trial was stopped early for benefit, which inflates effect estimates. The large French referral-centre cohort (Frank M et al., PMID: 30999998; 144 molecularly confirmed patients, median follow-up 5.3 years, 90.3% on celiprolol by study end) found celiprolol-treated patients survived better than others (P = 0.0004), with dose-dependent protection (400 mg/day better than <400 mg/day, P = 0.003) — observational, so confounded by everything that goes with being treated at a national centre. A 2025 systematic review (Saputra PBT et al., PMID: 40559232) gathered 323 participants across the 2010–2023 studies and reached the same direction of conclusion. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): one small open randomised trial stopped early plus concordant cohort data is a real signal for a disease with no other preventive drug, but it is not LIKELY-grade evidence, and celiprolol does not abolish events — events continue on treatment. BOUNDARY: there are no disease-modifying treatment trials for the other EDS types (classical, hypermobile and the rest); physiotherapy and bracing evidence in hypermobile EDS has no cardable comparative data and is not on this shelf.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in the one randomised trial (53 patients, open, blinded endpoints, stopped early), arterial rupture/dissection occurred in 20% on celiprolol versus 50% on no treatment (HR 0.36, a 64% relative reduction; 30-percentage-point absolute difference), and the 144-patient national cohort found better, dose-dependent survival on celiprolol

title: Birch-bark gel (Oleogel-S10, Filsuvez) for epidermolysis bullosa wounds: complete target-wound closure by day 45 in 41.3% versus 28.9% on control gel in the phase III EASE trial
question: In people with epidermolysis bullosa, does the birch-bark extract gel Oleogel-S10 (Filsuvez) heal wounds faster and reduce wound burden compared with a control gel?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one phase III randomised trial programme (EASE) carries this shelf, and a single trial caps the stamp at POSSIBLE. In the double-blind phase (Kern JS et al., PMID: 36689495; 223 patients with dystrophic or junctional EB, 109 Oleogel-S10 versus 114 control gel), first complete closure of the target wound within 45 days occurred in 41.3% on Oleogel-S10 versus 28.9% on control gel (relative risk 1.44, 95% CI 1.01 to 2.05; P = 0.013) — a 44% relative increase, and a 12.4-percentage-point absolute difference; adverse events were near-identical (81.7% versus 80.7%, predominantly mild-to-moderate). In the 24-month open-label phase (Murrell DF et al., PMID: 39821055; 205 patients, all on Oleogel-S10), wound burden fell and stayed down in those treated throughout (body-surface-area percentage change −5.9% at 12 months and −3.7% at 24 months from double-blind baseline), with adverse events in 77.1% (severe 18.0%, serious 24.4% — in a population with severe disease), 7.8% withdrawing for adverse events, and nine deaths, none attributed to treatment. A post-hoc analysis in patients who began with daily dressing changes (Bruckner AL et al., PMID: 40908727) found fewer daily changes needed by day 90 in 35.6% versus 10.6% (P = 0.005). The tested product is named exactly as trialled: Oleogel-S10 (birch triterpenes / birch bark extract), marketed as Filsuvez, developed by Amryt (now Chiesi). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): faster closure of a chosen target wound, by a modest absolute margin, in the only randomised trial — meaningful in a disease with no other approved wound therapy, but one trial, industry-run, with a confidence interval whose lower bound (1.01) sits just above no effect.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the single phase III EASE trial found first complete target-wound closure within 45 days in 41.3% on Oleogel-S10 versus 28.9% on control gel (RR 1.44, a 44% relative increase; 12.4-percentage-point absolute difference; P = 0.013), with sustained wound-burden reduction over 24 months open-label

title: Suppressive acyclovir for recurrent erythema multiforme: median attacks 0 versus 3 over 6 months in the one double-blind trial — of 20 patients
question: In people whose erythema multiforme keeps coming back, usually after herpes simplex, does taking acyclovir every day prevent further attacks compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — scoped exactly to the tested question: continuous suppressive acyclovir for recurrent (mostly herpes-simplex-associated) erythema multiforme. The entire randomised evidence is one small double-blind trial (Tatnall FM et al., PMID: 7888365): 20 patients with more than four attacks a year (15 herpes-precipitated) took acyclovir 400 mg twice daily or placebo for 6 months; median attacks on treatment were 0 on acyclovir versus 3 on placebo (P < 0.0005), 7 of 11 acyclovir patients had no attacks at all, and two went into complete remission after treatment while every placebo patient continued to have attacks. The large referral series behind it (Schofield JK et al., PMID: 8504046; 65 patients, 71% herpes-precipitated) found 55% of patients derived benefit from acyclovir regimens (continuous, or a patient-initiated 5-day course at herpes onset), with the most resistant 11 patients achieving complete suppression on azathioprine. A systematic review of all EM interventions (de Risi-Pugliese T et al., PMID: 30680804) found, from 1,558 references, exactly one RCT and six case series in the whole field, and graded the acyclovir evidence low-level. A single 20-patient trial caps the stamp at POSSIBLE however clean its result. BOUNDARY: this shelf is prevention of recurrent EM only. Acute EM and EM major are managed supportively; no trial evidence for treating an acute attack was found, and steroids for acute EM are untested in RCTs.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in the only double-blind trial (20 patients with >4 attacks/year), continuous acyclovir 400 mg twice daily gave a median of 0 attacks versus 3 on placebo over 6 months (P < 0.0005), with 7 of 11 attack-free; a single small trial caps the stamp

title: Oral oxybutynin for excessive sweating: responders 60% versus 27% on placebo in the largest RCT — three small, short trials, with dry mouth in 43–100%
question: In people with hyperhidrosis (excessive sweating) of the palms, armpits, feet or generalised, does oral oxybutynin reduce sweating compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — three small, short randomised placebo-controlled trials of oral oxybutynin, all positive, none longer than 6 weeks. The largest (Schollhammer M et al., PMID: 26114588; 62 patients with localised or generalised hyperhidrosis, oxybutynin titrated 2.5 to 7.5 mg/day) found 60% of oxybutynin patients improved at least one point on the Hyperhidrosis Disease Severity Scale (HDSS) at 6 weeks versus 27% on placebo (P = 0.009) — a 33-percentage-point absolute difference — with mean Dermatology Life Quality Index improvement of 6.9 versus 2.3 points, and dry mouth in 43% versus 11%. The first trial (Wolosker N et al., PMID: 22341836; 50 patients with palmar/axillary hyperhidrosis, titrated to 5 mg twice daily) reported improvement in over 70% of oxybutynin patients for palmar and axillary sweating and over 90% for plantar sweating at 6 weeks, with quality of life improved in 65.2% and dry mouth in 47.8%. In women with persistent plantar hyperhidrosis after sympathectomy (Costa Jr AS et al., PMID: 24519200; 32 patients, oxybutynin 10 mg/day, 30 days), quality-of-life scores improved on oxybutynin (40.4 to 17.5; P = 0.001) with objectively measured transepidermal water loss falling significantly (P = 0.001) versus no change on placebo (P = 0.95) — but dry mouth in 100% versus 43.8%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): consistent direction across three trials, but small samples, 30-day to 6-week horizons, mostly subjective outcomes, and an anticholinergic side-effect burden that is part of the treatment, not an accident of it. BOUNDARY: botulinum toxin injections and the glycopyrronium cloth for armpit sweating are homed on Shelf #2476 and are not re-carded here; iontophoresis has no cardable comparative trial data in this build (see summary flag).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — HDSS responders 60% versus 27% on placebo at 6 weeks in the largest of three small short RCTs (n=62, 50 and 32), with dry mouth in 43% versus 11% (and 100% at 10 mg/day in the post-sympathectomy trial)

title: Eye cancer (uveal melanoma): plaque brachytherapy versus removing the eye — the COMS randomised trial of 1,317 patients found no survival difference at 5 years (81% vs 82%) or 12 years, but vision in the radiated eye usually deteriorated
question: I have been told I have an eye cancer (uveal melanoma, a medium choroidal melanoma) — should I have the eye removed, or can a radiation plaque save the eye without shortening my life? How do survival and vision compare after iodine-125 plaque brachytherapy versus enucleation?
balance: LIKELY (no difference in survival) — this shelf is scoped to MEDIUM choroidal melanoma, the tumour size the Collaborative Ocular Melanoma Study (COMS) randomised. In the trial's initial mortality report (Diener-West 2001, PMID: 11448319; 1,317 patients: 660 enucleation, 657 iodine-125 brachytherapy), deaths were 188 of 660 (28%) after enucleation versus 176 of 657 (27%) after brachytherapy; 5-year survival was 81% versus 82% (P=.48), the adjusted relative risk of death was 0.99 (95% CI 0.80–1.22), and 5-year death with confirmed melanoma metastasis was 11% versus 9% (adjusted relative risk 0.91, 95% CI 0.66–1.24); the trial was powered to exclude a ±25% relative difference. At 12 years (COMS Group 2006, PMID: 17159027; NCT00000124), 471 of 1,317 patients had died, cumulative all-cause mortality was 43% after brachytherapy versus 41% after enucleation, and death with confirmed metastasis at 5, 10 and 12 years was 10%, 18% and 21% after brachytherapy versus 11%, 17% and 17% after enucleation. What brachytherapy buys is the eye, not sight: among 623 brachytherapy patients analysed for vision (Melia 2001, PMID: 11158813), median visual acuity fell from 20/32 at baseline to 20/125 at 3 years, the proportion at 20/40 or better fell from 70% to 34%, and 45% were at 20/200 or worse by 3 years. BOUNDARY: small and large choroidal melanomas were studied in separate COMS arms and are not carded here; metastatic uveal melanoma treatment (tebentafusp) is homed on Shelf #1903 and is not re-carded here. PROPOSED LIKELY (no difference in survival): removing the eye did not make patients live longer in the only randomised test, so the choice turns on keeping the eye against its expected visual decline.
stamp: LIKELY (no difference in survival) — in the COMS randomised trial (1,317 patients with medium choroidal melanoma), 5-year survival was 81% after enucleation versus 82% after iodine-125 plaque brachytherapy (P=.48; adjusted relative risk of death 0.99, 95% CI 0.80–1.22), and 12-year all-cause mortality was 41% versus 43%; brachytherapy keeps the eye, but median vision in the treated eye fell to 20/125 by 3 years

title: Eye injuries — patching for corneal abrasion: 12 randomised trials found no faster healing with a patch (healed at 48 hours, relative risk 0.97); a bandage contact lens, not a patch, sped return to normal activities
question: I scratched my eye (a corneal abrasion) — should it be patched? Does an eye patch speed healing or reduce pain compared with no patch, and how does a bandage contact lens compare?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference) — scoped to traumatic/mechanical corneal abrasion, the injury for which comparative trials exist; no cardable comparative evidence was fetched for chemical, penetrating or other eye injuries, and none is claimed. The Cochrane review (Lim 2016, PMID: 27457359) pooled 12 trials with 1,080 participants: the proportion healed did not differ between patch and no patch at 24 hours (relative risk 0.89, 95% CI 0.79–1.00; 7 trials, 531 participants, low certainty), 48 hours (RR 0.97, 0.91–1.02; 6 trials, 497, moderate certainty) or 72 hours (RR 1.01, 0.97–1.05; 4 trials, 430, moderate certainty), and time to heal differed by a mean of +0.14 days (95% CI 0 to 0.27; 6 trials, 642). Pain at 24 hours leaned against the patch (RR 1.51, 0.86–2.65; 2 trials, 193, low certainty), analgesic use did not differ (RR 0.95, 0.69–1.32; 256), and complications leaned against patching without reaching significance (RR 3.24, 0.87–12.05; 8 trials, 660); 22% of patched patients in three trials did not keep the patch on, and in one children's study walking was harder with a patch (activity score 1.7 vs 0.3 cm on a visual analogue scale). Head-to-head randomised comparisons found patching, a bandage contact lens and antibiotic ointment alone all reduced abrasion area equally (Menghini 2013, PMID: 23652196; 66 patients, all healed by day 7), while a bandage contact lens let patients return to normal activities sooner than a patch and adding a topical NSAID reduced pain (Donnenfeld 1995, PMID: 7777307; 47 patients). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference): patching a simple corneal abrasion does not speed healing and may add pain and inconvenience; comfort measures and, where used, a bandage lens address symptoms instead.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference) — across 12 randomised trials (1,080 participants) patching did not speed healing at 24, 48 or 72 hours (relative risks 0.89, 0.97, 1.01) and time to heal differed by +0.14 days; pain and complications leaned against the patch without reaching significance

title: Food intolerance — lactase for lactose intolerance: tablets blunted a lactose challenge (breath hydrogen down 55%, relative), but at a normal glass of milk blinded symptoms were negligible with or without aids
question: Milk gives me bloating and diarrhoea (lactose intolerance) — do lactase tablets or lactose-free milk actually reduce symptoms, or would I feel the same anyway?
balance: SPLIT — the answer depends on the dose of lactose being faced. This shelf is scoped strictly to lactase enzyme and lactose-hydrolysed (lactose-reduced) milk for lactose intolerance, the interventions with fetched trial numbers; IgG-test-based elimination diets and other 'food intolerance' treatments had no credible trials to card and are excluded, not endorsed. In breath-test-confirmed intolerance, a randomised double-blind crossover trial of 47 adults found lactase chewable tablets (the tested product was Yamoo lactase 4500 FCC, named in the full text) reduced cumulative breath hydrogen over 180 minutes by 55% relative to placebo and improved symptom scores (P<0.05) after a lactose load (Baijal & Tandon 2021, PMID: 33490624). At ordinary intakes the picture reverses: in a randomised double-blind crossover trial in 30 self-described severely intolerant people drinking 240 ml of milk daily for a week on each milk, symptom severity scores on lactose-hydrolysed versus regular milk were 0.1–1.2 on a scale where 1 is trivial and 2 is mild, with no significant differences, and the authors concluded digestive aids are unnecessary at intakes of 240 ml/day or less (Suarez 1995, PMID: 7776987). The AHRQ systematic review (Shaukat 2010, PMID: 20404262; 36 RCTs) found moderate-quality evidence that most adults tolerate 12–15 g of lactose (about one cup of milk), and rated the evidence insufficient that lactose-reduced products reduce symptoms compared with larger lactose doses. PROPOSED SPLIT: lactase measurably blunts the response to a lactose challenge in the laboratory; at a normal glass of milk, symptoms are minimal either way and the review-level symptom evidence for aids is insufficient.
stamp: SPLIT — against a lactose load in breath-test-confirmed intolerance, lactase cut breath hydrogen 55% (relative) and improved symptoms in a 47-person crossover trial · at ordinary intakes (240 ml milk daily) blinded symptoms were trivial-to-mild and identical on regular and hydrolysed milk, and the AHRQ review (36 trials) rated the symptom evidence for lactose-reduced products insufficient

title: Food poisoning: antibiotics depend on the organism — Campylobacter illness shortened by 1.32 days, Shigella dysentery reduced, but Salmonella gastroenteritis gained nothing and carriage nearly doubled
question: I have food poisoning — should I take an antibiotic? When the stool grows Campylobacter, Salmonella or Shigella, do antibiotics shorten the illness?
balance: SPLIT — by organism, because the three classic bacterial causes of food poisoning answer the antibiotic question differently. For Campylobacter, a meta-analysis of 11 randomised placebo-controlled trials found antibiotics shortened intestinal symptoms by 1.32 days (95% CI 0.64–1.99; P<.0001), with the benefit concentrated in treatment started early, while the authors advised a restrictive attitude in uncomplicated cases because of resistance (Ternhag 2007, PMID: 17278062). For Shigella dysentery, the Cochrane review of 16 trials (1,748 participants) concluded antibiotics reduce the duration of dysentery; in the one three-armed trial in moderately severe illness, diarrhoea at follow-up occurred with relative risk 0.21 (95% CI 0.09–0.48; furazolidone vs no drug, 73 participants) and 0.30 (0.15–0.59; cotrimoxazole vs no drug, 76 participants) (Christopher 2010, PMID: 20687081). For non-typhoidal Salmonella, the Cochrane review of 12 trials (767 participants) found no benefit: mean difference in diarrhoea duration 0 days (95% CI −0.54 to 0.54), clinical failure relative risk 0.88 (0.62–1.25), and antibiotics made passage of the same serovar one month later almost twice as likely (RR 1.96, 1.29–2.98), with more non-severe adverse reactions (Onwuezobe 2012, PMID: 23152205). BOUNDARY: empiric antibiotics and loperamide for traveller's diarrhoea are homed on Shelves #1213, #1214 and #5269 and are not re-carded here; typhoid fever is a different, systemic disease (its vaccine is Shelf #726). Fluids and supportive care remain the base treatment for all of these infections. PROPOSED SPLIT: antibiotics shorten Campylobacter symptoms by about a day and treat Shigella dysentery, but for Salmonella gastroenteritis in otherwise healthy people they do nothing measurable and prolong carriage.
stamp: SPLIT — by organism: Campylobacter symptoms shortened 1.32 days (95% CI 0.64–1.99) across 11 randomised trials · Shigella dysentery shortened by antibiotics (diarrhoea at follow-up, relative risk 0.21–0.30 vs no drug) · non-typhoidal Salmonella: no benefit (duration differences ~0 days) and one-month carriage almost doubled (relative risk 1.96)

title: Gallbladder cancer after surgery: adjuvant chemotherapy — BILCAP's main analysis just missed significance (HR 0.81, p=0.097) while Japan's ASCOT trial showed 5-year survival of 64% versus 52% with S-1
question: My gallbladder cancer has been removed by surgery — should I have chemotherapy afterwards to stop it coming back? What do the adjuvant trials (capecitabine, S-1) show?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — scoped to ADJUVANT treatment after surgical resection of biliary tract cancers, which include gallbladder cancer; chemotherapy for ADVANCED biliary tract cancer is homed on Shelf #5314 (and immunotherapy combinations on #858, second-line FOLFOX on #1885) and is not re-carded here. No randomised trial has enrolled gallbladder cancer alone, so every estimate below is from mixed biliary-tract populations. In BILCAP (Primrose 2019, PMID: 30922733; 447 patients — 223 capecitabine, 224 observation — with resected cholangiocarcinoma or muscle-invasive gallbladder cancer), the primary intention-to-treat analysis did not reach significance: median overall survival 51.1 months (95% CI 34.6–59.1) versus 36.4 months (29.7–44.5), adjusted hazard ratio 0.81 (0.63–1.04), p=0.097; the pre-specified sensitivity analysis gave HR 0.71 (0.55–0.92), p=0.010, and the per-protocol analysis (210 vs 220 patients) median survival 53 versus 36 months, HR 0.75 (0.58–0.97), p=0.028; median recurrence-free survival was 24.4 versus 17.5 months, and grade 3 or worse toxicity occurred in 44% of treated patients. In Japan's ASCOT trial (Ikeda 2026 five-year report, PMID: 42777180; 440 patients — 218 S-1, 222 observation), adjuvant S-1 improved survival clearly: 5-year overall survival 64% versus 52% (an absolute difference of 12 percentage points), hazard ratio 0.72 (0.55–0.95), one-sided P=.01; median survival 8.2 versus 5.9 years; median recurrence-free survival 6.1 versus 3.5 years; the original 3-year figures were 77.1% versus 67.6%. A single-arm phase II study of chemoradiation after resection (SWOG S0809; Ben-Josef 2015, PMID: 25964250; 79 patients, 32% gallbladder) reported 2-year survival of 65% with no control group. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): adjuvant fluoropyrimidine after resection probably extends survival, on one formally negative-but-supportive trial and one positive trial, with gallbladder-specific benefit unmeasured.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — adjuvant fluoropyrimidine after resection of biliary tract cancer (including gallbladder): BILCAP's primary analysis missed significance (HR 0.81, p=0.097; medians 51.1 vs 36.4 months) though its sensitivity/per-protocol analyses were positive, and ASCOT was clearly positive for S-1 (5-year survival 64% vs 52%, HR 0.72); no gallbladder-only randomised estimate exists

title: Ganglion cyst of the wrist: surgery cured 94% versus 61% for aspiration in the small randomised trial — but long-term, recurrence was 39–58% after either procedure and symptoms settled just as often with no treatment
question: I have a ganglion cyst on my wrist — should I have it drained (aspirated), cut out, or just leave it alone? How often does each choice work, and how often does the cyst come back?
balance: SPLIT — the short-term and long-term records point different ways. In the only randomised trial (Khan & Hayat 2011, PMID: 23204769; 36 patients with dorsal wrist ganglion), surgical excision succeeded in 17 of 18 patients (94.4%) versus 11 of 18 (61.1%) for aspiration with intralesional triamcinolone and immobilisation (p=0.041). A non-randomised comparison of 86 patients found the two nearly equal at up to 12 months — success 86.8% (59/68) after aspiration with steroid versus 83.3% (15/18) after excision (Shah 2019, PMID: 31309054). The long view is humbling for both: in a prospective cohort of 236 patients followed a mean of 70 months, recurrence was 58% (45/78) after aspiration and 39% (40/103) after excision, symptom resolution did not differ between excision, aspiration and no treatment (p>0.3), 23 of 55 untreated ganglia resolved on their own, and the authors concluded neither intervention gave significant long-term benefit over no treatment — though satisfaction was higher after excision (p<0.0001) and 8 of 103 surgical patients had complications (Dias 2007, PMID: 17950209). PROPOSED SPLIT: excision wins the short-term cure comparison in a small trial; over years, recurrence is common after either procedure and symptoms settle at similar rates with observation alone.
stamp: SPLIT — short term: excision beat aspiration plus steroid in the only randomised trial (success 94.4% vs 61.1%, 36 patients) · long term (prospective cohort, mean 70 months): recurrence 39% after excision and 58% after aspiration, symptom resolution no different from no treatment, and 23 of 55 untreated ganglia resolved on their own

title: Gender dysphoria and incongruence: hormone therapy outcomes are observational only — youth cohorts report better mental-health scores on treatment, register data show no time-on-hormones association, long-term risks stay above the general population, and estrogen carries a clotting signal
question: I have gender dysphoria (gender incongruence) — if I start gender-affirming hormone treatment, what does the evidence say happens to mental health and to physical health such as blood clots?
balance: POSSIBLE — every study on this shelf is observational; there are no randomised trials of gender-affirming hormone therapy, so all findings are associations and the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE. The fetched record, stated plainly in both directions: (1) In a prospective US clinic cohort of 104 youths aged 13–20, those who had started puberty blockers and/or hormones had lower adjusted odds of depression (aOR 0.40, 95% CI 0.17–0.95 — 60% lower odds, a relative measure) and of suicidality (aOR 0.27, 0.11–0.65 — 73% lower odds, relative) over 12 months than those who had not, with no association for anxiety (aOR 1.01) (Tordoff 2022, PMID: 35212746). (2) In a prospective cohort of 315 transgender and nonbinary youth aged 12–20 followed through 2 years of hormones, appearance congruence, positive affect and life satisfaction increased and depression and anxiety symptoms decreased; suicidal ideation occurred in 11 participants (3.5%) and 2 died by suicide; there was no comparison group (Chen 2023, PMID: 36652355). (3) In Swedish national register data (2,679 people with a gender incongruence diagnosis), years since starting hormones were not associated with mental-health treatment (aOR 1.01, 0.98–1.03 per year); the paper's original analysis linked time since last gender-affirming surgery to reduced treatment (aOR 0.92, 0.87–0.98), but a published correction stated the design supported no such conclusion and a reanalysis showed no advantage of surgery on those outcomes (Bränström & Pachankis 2020, PMID: 31581798). (4) In long-term Swedish follow-up of 324 people after sex-reassignment surgery (1973–2003) versus matched general-population controls, overall mortality (adjusted HR 2.8, 1.8–4.3) and death by suicide (aHR 19.1, 5.8–62.9) remained higher than in the general population (Dhejne 2011, PMID: 21364939). (5) In a US health-system cohort (2,842 transfeminine and 2,118 transmasculine people), transfeminine participants had more venous thromboembolism than cisgender comparators — risk differences of 4.1 per 1,000 at 2 years and 16.7 per 1,000 at 8 years versus cisgender men — with differences more pronounced among those who initiated hormones during follow-up; overall stroke and myocardial infarction incidence was similar across groups (Getahun 2018, PMID: 29987313). PROPOSED POSSIBLE: short-term youth cohorts associate treatment with better mental-health scores; register and long-term data show persistently elevated risks relative to the general population and no demonstrated association between time on hormones and mental-health treatment; a venous thromboembolism signal accompanies transfeminine estrogen therapy.
stamp: POSSIBLE — observational evidence only (no randomised trials): youth cohorts associate starting hormones/blockers with better 12-month depression and suicidality odds (aOR 0.40 and 0.27, relative); Swedish registers found no association between years on hormones and mental-health treatment (aOR 1.01/year) and, after correction, no surgery advantage; long-term post-surgical mortality stayed above general-population levels (aHR 2.8); transfeminine estrogen carried a venous thromboembolism excess (16.7 per 1,000 by 8 years)

title: Genital warts beyond the two standard creams: cryotherapy matched topical treatments in 11 trials, sinecatechins ointment beat placebo (54.9% vs 35.4% complete clearance), and adding HPV vaccine to treatment did not demonstrably help
question: I have genital warts — apart from the imiquimod and podophyllotoxin creams (covered on another shelf), what else actually clears them: freezing, other ointments, or the HPV vaccine used as treatment?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — scoped to treatments BEYOND the two standard patient-applied creams: the head-to-head question of imiquimod cream versus podophyllotoxin is homed on Shelf #2198 and is not re-carded here. What remains is cardable and consistent. (1) Cryotherapy: a systematic review and meta-analysis of 11 randomised trials in immunocompetent adults found cryotherapy's complete clearance did not differ from trichloroacetic acid, podophyllin or imiquimod; electrosurgery was weakly better than cryotherapy (relative risk 0.80, 95% CI 0.65–0.99 for clearance with cryotherapy relative to electrosurgery); cryotherapy caused more immediate low-level adverse events (RR 3.02, 1.38–6.61) and more pain needing oral analgesics (RR 2.11, 1.07–4.17) but fewer erosions (RR 0.57, 0.36–0.90); all but one trial were at high risk of bias (Bertolotti 2017, PMID: 28651824). (2) Sinecatechins (Polyphenon E, a defined green tea catechin ointment — the specific tested product, named because botanical preparations differ by maker): pooling two phase III vehicle-controlled trials (1,005 patients), complete clearance of all warts was 53.6% on the 10% ointment and 54.9% on the 15% ointment versus 35.4% on vehicle (P<0.001; odds ratios 2.10 and 2.22, relative measures), with recurrence of about 6% in all groups over follow-up (Tatti 2010, PMID: 19709100). (3) HPV vaccine as treatment: in the HIPvac factorial trial (503 participants), adding quadrivalent HPV vaccine to cream treatment did not demonstrably improve the combined outcome of clearance at week 16 and remaining wart-free at week 48 (adjusted odds ratio 1.46, 0.97–2.20) (Gilson 2020, PMID: 32975189). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): freezing and sinecatechins are effective wart-clearing options beyond the standard creams; vaccination during treatment is unproven as a treatment, whatever its preventive role.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — beyond the standard creams (homed on #2198): cryotherapy clearance matched the topical treatments across 11 RCTs, sinecatechins beat vehicle (complete clearance 53.6–54.9% vs 35.4%, two phase III trials), and adding quadrivalent HPV vaccine to treatment was not shown to help (aOR 1.46, 95% CI 0.97–2.20)

title: Glandular fever (infectious mononucleosis): steroids eased sore throat for about 12 hours only, and antivirals showed no dependable benefit — both Cochrane reviews found the evidence insufficient or uncertain
question: I have glandular fever (infectious mononucleosis) — will steroids or antiviral medicines shorten it or ease the sore throat?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference) — for routine symptom control in uncomplicated infectious mononucleosis, neither steroids nor antivirals have a demonstrated lasting benefit. The Cochrane review of corticosteroids (Candy & Hotopf 2006, PMID: 16856045; 7 trials of 24–94 participants each) found a sore-throat benefit at 12 hours in two studies that was not maintained, one trial suggesting longer benefit only for a steroid-plus-antiviral combination, and one trial suggesting faster fatigue resolution at about 4 weeks with the combination question unresolved; two trials reported severe complications in steroid groups, and the reviewers concluded the evidence is insufficient to recommend steroids for symptom control. The Cochrane review of antivirals (De Paor 2016, PMID: 27933614; 7 RCTs, 333 participants, testing acyclovir, valomaciclovir and valacyclovir) rated the evidence very low quality throughout: of 12 outcomes, only time to clinical recovery (−5 days, 95% CI −8.04 to −1.08; 2 studies, 87 participants) and duration of lymphadenopathy (−9 days, −11.75 to −6.14; 2 studies, 61) reached significance, viral shedding was suppressed only while treatment continued, and the reviewers concluded effectiveness is uncertain. The single-dose steroid trial behind the 12-hour signal (Roy 2004, PMID: 14993084; 40 children) found adequate pain relief at 12 hours in 12 of 20 (60%) on dexamethasone versus 5 of 19 (26%) on placebo (P=.03), and no difference at 24, 48 or 72 hours or at day 7. BOUNDARY: these trials address symptom control in uncomplicated glandular fever; steroid use for severe complications such as airway obstruction is a different clinical question that these reviews do not test. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference): a single steroid dose may buy a few hours of throat comfort; nothing fetched shows steroids or antivirals shorten the illness.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference) — for routine symptom control: Cochrane found steroid benefit only at 12 hours and not maintained (7 trials), antiviral evidence very low quality with effectiveness uncertain (7 trials, 333 participants), and the single-dose dexamethasone trial's pain advantage (60% vs 26% at 12 hours) had vanished by 24 hours

title: Granuloma annulare: no randomised trials exist — in the largest systematic review (689 patients, all uncontrolled reports), complete clearance ranged from 17.7% with topical steroids to about 83% in small JAK-inhibitor case collections
question: I have granuloma annulare (ring-shaped skin plaques) — what treatments have been reported to clear it, and how much can I trust the numbers?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — there are no randomised trials of treatment for granuloma annulare; the entire quantitative record is uncontrolled case reports and series, pooled in one systematic review of generalised granuloma annulare (Bettolini 2025, PMID: 40586485; PROSPERO CRD42025632216): 689 patients (mean age 52.8 years, 72.6% female) and 754 recorded treatments. Complete-response rates in that pooled, uncontrolled record: topical corticosteroid monotherapy 17.7% (17 of 96) with 38.5% (37 of 96) showing no response; oral corticosteroids 85.7% (12 of 14 — a very small group, two of them also on topical steroids); intralesional corticosteroids 33.3% (3 of 9); PUVA phototherapy 49.4% (41 of 83); UVA1 34.2% (14 of 41); narrowband UVB 30.4% (17 of 56); hydroxychloroquine 44.2% (34 of 77) with 42.9% (33 of 77) not improving; dapsone 33.3% (17 of 51); methotrexate 28% (7 of 25); JAK inhibitors 82.8% (24 of 29); anti-TNF agents 84% (21 of 25). The review's authors themselves caution that outcomes from isolated case reports must be interpreted with care because spontaneous remission and placebo effects cannot be excluded, and that publication bias likely under-reports failures — the highest rates sit in the smallest, newest case collections (JAK inhibitors, anti-TNF), which is the classic signature of that bias. The review proposes a stepwise approach beginning with hydroxychloroquine and phototherapy, reserving anti-TNF and JAK inhibitors for refractory cases. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): treatments are reported to clear generalised granuloma annulare at the rates above, but with no control group anywhere in the record, no rate can be credited to the treatment rather than to the disease's own course.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — no controlled trials exist; in the one systematic review of generalised disease (689 patients, all case reports/series), complete response ranged from 17.7% on topical steroids to 82.8–84% in small JAK-inhibitor and anti-TNF case collections, with the review itself warning that spontaneous remission and publication bias cannot be excluded

title: IVIG for haemolytic disease of the newborn: exchange transfusions fall in the pooled trials (relative risk 0.35) — but the only two blinded, placebo-controlled trials show no benefit at all
question: In a newborn with haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn (Rh or ABO incompatibility) on phototherapy, does intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) reduce the need for exchange transfusion?
balance: SPLIT — the answer depends entirely on which trials are believed. In the unblinded randomised trial of Alpay 1999 (PMID: 10102158; 116 newborns with ABO and/or Rh incompatibility), exchange transfusion was needed in 8 of 58 babies given high-dose IVIG 1 g/kg versus 22 of 58 on phototherapy alone (P < 0.001). In the two double-blind, placebo-controlled trials, the effect vanishes: Santos 2013 (PMID: 22882285; NCT00288600; 92 newborns) found exchange transfusion in 6 of 46 (13%) on IVIG versus 7 of 46 (15.2%) on saline placebo (P = 0.765), and Smits-Wintjens 2011 (PMID: 21422084; 80 neonates with rhesus disease, 66% already transfused in utero) found 7 of 41 (17%) versus 6 of 39 (15%) (P = .99), with no differences in phototherapy duration, peak bilirubin or top-up transfusions. The Cochrane synthesis (Zwiers 2018, PMID: 29551014; 9 studies, 658 infants) pools to a typical relative risk of 0.35 (95% CI 0.25 to 0.49) with a risk difference of −0.22 and NNTB of 5 — but its own sensitivity analysis restricted to the two placebo-masked, blinded-outcome studies gives RR 0.98 (95% CI 0.48 to 1.98), and the authors state they have insufficient confidence to make even a weak recommendation for IVIG. PROPOSED SPLIT: a large apparent benefit where the treating team knew the allocation and controlled the exchange decision; no benefit where they did not. SCOPE NOTE: intrauterine transfusion outcomes were part of the commissioning question, but no comparative IUT-outcome record was carded this session; IUT exposure appears on this shelf only as background to the Smits-Wintjens population.
stamp: SPLIT — pooled across all trials, IVIG is associated with fewer exchange transfusions (typical RR 0.35, 95% CI 0.25 to 0.49; risk difference −0.22; NNTB 5) · in the only two trials that masked treatment with a placebo and blinded outcome assessment, there was no difference (RR 0.98, 95% CI 0.48 to 1.98) — the apparent benefit lives in the high-risk-of-bias trials

title: Severe hand, foot and mouth disease: IVIG shortens fever and rash times in pooled small Chinese RCTs — but the big hospital datasets show no advantage, and steroids and milrinone show none anywhere
question: In a child with severe hand, foot and mouth disease (mostly enterovirus 71), does anything beyond supportive care — IVIG, corticosteroids, milrinone — improve outcomes?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the randomised evidence for severe HFMD is thin and surrogate-only. Jiao 2019 (PMID: 30646003) pooled 8 RCTs and 1,450 children and found IVIG plus conventional therapy shortened fever clearance time, rash regression time and clinical cure time versus conventional therapy alone, with the 1 g/kg/day dose subgroup performing best on most measures — but the abstract prints no pooled effect sizes and no mortality or sequelae outcome. The observational record is much larger and colder. Zhang 2018 (PMID: 29925360; 3,778 hospitalised children in Shantou) found no advantage for steroids or IVIG: recovery was lower with IVIG in mild cases and hospital stays were longer with steroid/IVIG in severe cases — patterns the authors themselves attribute in part to sicker children receiving the drugs. Liu & Qi 2020 (PMID: 32754560; 637 severe cases among 50,651 reported in Xiangyang) found an association between IVIG given in early stage IV disease and improved progression (odds ratio 0.24, 95% CI 0.10 to 0.57), but no mortality benefit for methylprednisolone or milrinone at any stage. Nothing carded tests any antiviral; the magnesium-sulfate RCT for EV71 autonomic dysregulation found this session is a protocol without results (NCT01940250), and acyclovir rests on a single uncontrolled 13-person series from 1996 — neither is carded as evidence. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) for IVIG in severe HFMD; no difference shown for corticosteroids and milrinone on the records fetched.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — IVIG added to conventional therapy shortened fever clearance, rash regression and clinical cure times in a meta-analysis of 8 small RCTs (1,450 children), with no mortality outcome and no pooled effect sizes in the abstract; large retrospective hospital series find no advantage for IVIG or steroids, and one stage-stratified series found an IVIG association only in early stage IV disease; methylprednisolone and milrinone showed no mortality benefit at any stage

title: Tension-type headache: paracetamol and ibuprofen beat placebo modestly for acute attacks (NNT 22 and 14 for pain-free at 2 hours); tricyclics prevent about 5 headaches a month; acupuncture beats usual care clearly but sham only slightly
question: For my tension-type headaches, what actually works — a painkiller for an attack, a daily preventive such as amitriptyline, or acupuncture?
balance: SPLIT — acute and preventive treatment are different questions with different answers, and this shelf keeps them apart (migraine trials are a different question again and are not carded here). Acute: two Cochrane reviews find modest, real benefits over placebo for a single attack of frequent episodic tension-type headache — paracetamol 1000 mg made 24 of 100 people pain-free at 2 hours versus 19 of 100 on placebo (Stephens 2016, PMID: 27306653; 23 studies, 8,079 participants; NNT 22), and ibuprofen 400 mg made 23 of 100 versus 16 of 100 (Derry 2015, PMID: 26230487; 12 studies, 3,094 participants; NNT 14); neither drug separated from placebo at 1 hour, and adverse events matched placebo for both. Prevention: tricyclic antidepressants reduced headache frequency by a weighted mean of 4.8 headaches a month versus placebo (from roughly 21 to roughly 16 a month) across 22 RCTs, 8 of them placebo-controlled, and beat SSRIs, while tetracyclics did not beat placebo (Jackson 2017; DOI 10.1007/s11606-017-4121-z; PMID not captured this session). Acupuncture roughly doubled-to-tripled the ≥50%-responder rate versus routine care (48% vs 19%, RR 2.5) but exceeded sham acupuncture only slightly (51% vs 43%, RR 1.3) across 12 trials and 2,349 participants (Linde 2016, PMID: 27092807) — the signature of a mostly contextual effect. PROPOSED SPLIT: small genuine drug benefits for attacks; a moderate preventive benefit for tricyclics; acupuncture's advantage over sham is small.
stamp: SPLIT — acute treatment: paracetamol 1000 mg and ibuprofen 400 mg are each modestly better than placebo for a single attack (pain-free at 2 hours in 24 vs 19 and 23 vs 16 per 100 people) · prevention: tricyclic antidepressants reduce headache frequency by about 4.8 headaches/month versus placebo, and acupuncture roughly doubles-to-triples the responder rate versus routine care but exceeds sham acupuncture only slightly (relative risk 1.3)
