title: IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein purpura): prednisone eases abdominal and joint pain and steroids speed abdominal-pain resolution — but no treatment is proven for established kidney disease, and kidney prevention is homed on Shelf #3914
question: In a child with IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein purpura), do corticosteroids help the abdominal and joint symptoms — and can they treat kidney involvement once it appears? (Whether steroids prevent kidney involvement is a separate question, answered on Shelf #3914.)
balance: SPLIT, with an explicit boundary. BOUNDARY: whether early steroids PREVENT kidney involvement in IgA vasculitis is homed on Shelf #3914 (Dudley 2013: proteinuria at 12 months 15% on prednisolone versus 10% on placebo, OR 1.46 — no protection), and that question is not re-carded here; Dudley is not a card on this shelf. This shelf covers the two remaining questions: treating symptoms, and treating kidney disease once present. Symptoms: in the largest placebo-controlled trial, Ronkainen 2006 (PMID: 16887443; 171 children), prednisone 1 mg/kg/day for 2 weeks with a 2-week wean cut abdominal pain intensity scores (2.5 vs 4.8, P = .029) and joint pain scores (4.6 vs 7.3, P = .030), and renal symptoms, once present, resolved in 61% versus 34% (difference 27 percentage points, 95% CI 3 to 47; P = .024); the 8-year follow-up of the same cohort found no long-term differences (Jauhola 2012, PMID: 22311342). Weiss 2007 (PMID: 17974746; 15 studies) found steroids did not shorten the median time to abdominal-pain resolution but did shorten the mean and raised the odds of resolution within 24 hours. The small Huber 2004 trial (PMID: 15059282; ISRCTN85109383; 40 children) found no significant differences in renal involvement at one year (3/21 vs 2/19) or acute GI complications (2/21 vs 3/19). Established kidney disease: the Cochrane review (Hahn 2015, PMID: 26258874; 13 studies, 1,403 patients) found no significant benefit of prednisone for persistent kidney disease (RR 0.74, 95% CI 0.42 to 1.32) and no benefit for cyclophosphamide; a single heparin trial (228 children, RR 0.27 at 3 months) stands unreplicated. PROPOSED SPLIT: POSSIBLE benefit for symptom relief; no proven treatment effect for established kidney disease on the fetched record.
stamp: SPLIT — treating symptoms: prednisone eased abdominal and joint pain scores in the largest placebo-controlled trial and steroids speeded abdominal-pain resolution in the pooled record (POSSIBLE benefit) · treating established kidney disease: Cochrane found no significant effect of prednisone on persistent kidney disease (RR 0.74, 95% CI 0.42 to 1.32) and no benefit for cyclophosphamide · kidney-disease PREVENTION is not this shelf's question — it is homed on Shelf #3914

title: Oral branched-chain amino acids and ascites: fewer ascites events in pooled liver-cancer treatment trials (relative risk 0.55) and a positive composite endpoint after liver resection — but no trial in decompensated cirrhosis tests BCAA against ascites itself
question: 'Does oral branched-chain amino acid treatment reduce ascites in advanced liver disease?' — In adults with cirrhosis, does oral branched-chain amino acid (BCAA) supplementation reduce the occurrence or severity of ascites compared with control diets, placebo or no supplementation?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), with the population caveat printed on the face: every direct ascites signal comes from an adjacent setting, not from decompensated cirrhosis with ascites as the primary endpoint. In liver-cancer care, a meta-analysis of 11 studies (974 patients undergoing hepatocellular carcinoma interventions; Chen 2015, PMID: 26155840) found ascites occurred less often on oral BCAA (relative risk 0.545, 0.316–0.938) and oedema likewise (relative risk 0.494). Before major liver resection, the one randomised trial (Kikuchi 2016, PMID: 27338747; n=77) missed its primary endpoint — refractory ascites alone 5.1% vs 13.2%, p=0.263 — but the composite of refractory ascites and/or pleural effusion was significantly less frequent on BCAA (5.1% vs 21.1%, p=0.047). A systematic review of 40 reports (Ooi 2018, PMID: 30390892) concluded BCAA may improve ascites and oedema in adults, without a pooled estimate. Indirect support: the two large cirrhosis-events trials homed on shelf #3630 (Marchesini 2003; Muto 2005) counted aggravation of hepatic failure — including ascites — inside composite endpoints that BCAA reduced (Moriwaki 2008, PMID: 19125940), but neither published ascites counts separately, and the one randomised trial of a BCAA-containing nutrition bundle in refractory ascites is homed on the refractory-ascites nutrition shelf (Sorrentino 2012, PMID: 22142548). The intravenous route is a separate, null story and stays on shelf #3630: nothing here supports intravenous BCAA for ascites.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — oral BCAA may reduce ascites occurrence; the direct evidence is from liver-cancer treatment and pre-surgical settings, not from decompensated cirrhosis with ascites as the primary endpoint

title: Protein in hepatic encephalopathy: restriction does not improve encephalopathy and increases protein breakdown (Córdoba 2004); vegetable and dairy protein outperform meat in small crossover trials, and a vegetable-protein feeding trial reversed minimal encephalopathy in 71% vs 23%
question: 'Should people with hepatic encephalopathy eat less protein — and is vegetable or milk protein better than meat?' — In cirrhosis with hepatic encephalopathy, does the amount of dietary protein (restricted vs normal/high) or its source (vegetable and dairy vs meat) change encephalopathy outcomes?
balance: SPLIT, by question. AMOUNT: the only randomised test of restriction (Córdoba 2004, PMID: 15246205; n=30, episodic encephalopathy) found the outcome of the episode was not significantly different on a normal-protein diet versus a low-protein diet — while protein breakdown was higher on the restricted diet. Restriction is a treatment that does not treat, at a metabolic cost; current guidance (ESPEN 2019, PMID: 30712783) advises against it. SOURCE: the classic crossover trials consistently favour vegetable (and dairy) protein over meat — better nitrogen balance (Bianchi 1993, PMID: 8068051, n=8), better number-connection and EEG results (Uribe 1982, PMID: 6756833, n=10; de Bruijn 1983, PMID: 6336714, n=8) — and the largest trial, Maharshi 2016 (PMID: 26453952; n=120, minimal encephalopathy), used 1.0–1.5 g/kg/day of vegetable protein within full nutritional therapy and reversed minimal encephalopathy in 71.1% vs 22.8% on usual diet, with overt encephalopathy in 10% vs 21.7%. An uncontrolled series of 153 patients (Gheorghe 2005, PMID: 16200232) improved on a casein-vegetable high-protein diet, showing dairy protein at 1.2 g/kg/day is compatible with recovery. PROPOSED SPLIT: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for protein restriction vs normal protein in episodic encephalopathy — with restriction metabolically harmful; POSSIBLE (benefit) for vegetable/dairy protein over meat protein, and for protein-adequate nutritional therapy in minimal encephalopathy.
stamp: SPLIT — POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for normal vs restricted protein in episodic encephalopathy, with restriction increasing protein breakdown; POSSIBLE (benefit) for vegetable/dairy protein over meat protein and for protein-adequate nutritional therapy in minimal encephalopathy

title: Refractory ascites and feeding: in the only randomised trial (Sorrentino 2012, 120 patients), a protein-centred nutrition protocol reduced paracentesis requirements, and adding intravenous nutrition after each tap gave the lowest mortality
question: 'When ascites keeps coming back despite water pills, does intensive feeding — a protein-rich diet, an evening protein snack and intravenous nutrition after each tap — help?' — In cirrhotic patients with refractory ascites undergoing repeated large-volume paracentesis, does aggressive nutritional support improve nutritional status, paracentesis requirement, morbidity and mortality compared with a low-sodium diet alone?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) on a single randomised trial. Sorrentino 2012 (PMID: 22142548) randomised 120 patients with refractory ascites on serial large-volume paracentesis to (A) post-paracentesis intravenous nutritional support plus a balanced oral diet and a late-evening protein snack, (B) the same oral protocol without parenteral support, or (C) a low-sodium diet alone, and followed them for 12 months. The nutrition groups preserved nutritional parameters with less deterioration of liver function than controls, had lower morbidity and mortality, needed fewer paracentesis taps — and mortality was significantly better in the parenteral-support group than in either other group. The stakes are set by the observational record: protein-calorie malnutrition marks the sickest ascites patients (Sam 2009, PMID: 19602136; ascites in 64.6% vs 47.8% of admissions, adjusted mortality odds ratio 1.76, a relative measure). What this shelf does NOT show: the trial's intervention is a bundle, so the benefit cannot be credited to protein, the evening snack or the intravenous component separately; and no published study tests parenteral nutrition reversing ascites in hepatorenal syndrome specifically — this trial, in refractory ascites, is the nearest controlled evidence to that question, not an answer to it.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single randomised trial of a bundled nutrition protocol in refractory ascites; effects cannot be assigned to protein, the evening snack or the parenteral component separately

title: Protein, supplements and survival in cirrhosis: pooled supplement trials are null overall (relative risk 0.75) but positive in the oral subgroup (0.40); patients eating under 0.8 g/kg/day of protein had higher mortality in cohorts (adjusted hazard ratio 1.8, a relative measure)
question: 'Does eating enough protein — or taking oral nutritional supplements — help people with cirrhosis live longer?' — In adults with cirrhosis, does oral or enteral nutritional supplementation, or higher dietary protein intake, reduce mortality compared with a standard diet or lower intake?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), honestly hedged. The randomised pool is null at the top line: Ney 2013 (PMID: 23421379) meta-analysed 6 trials of oral or enteral nutritional supplementation (470 patients; BCAA and parenteral trials excluded) and found no overall mortality reduction (relative risk 0.75, 0.42–1.32) — but the oral-supplement subgroup showed a significant mortality reduction (relative risk 0.40, 0.18–0.90), in trials of low quality (median Jadad 2). The cohort evidence points the same way with a threshold shape: in 630 transplant-waitlist patients (Ney 2015, PMID: 25667232), protein intake below 0.8 g/kg/day independently predicted waitlist mortality (adjusted hazard ratio 1.8, 1.2–2.7, a relative measure) while only 24% of patients reached the recommended 1.2 g/kg/day; and in a 121-patient prospective cohort (Daftari 2023, PMID: 37400778), higher total and dairy protein intakes tracked with lower cirrhosis-related mortality (hazard ratio 0.38 for each, confidence intervals crossing 1.0) while higher animal protein tracked with higher mortality (hazard ratio 3.8). BCAA-specific survival is a different shelf (#3630: mortality not improved, relative risk 0.88–0.89 across Cochrane versions), and the refractory-ascites nutrition trial's mortality finding is homed on the refractory-ascites shelf. PROPOSED: POSSIBLE (benefit) — enough for 'do not let protein intake fall short' as practice, not enough to promise a survival effect from supplements.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — pooled randomised evidence is null overall with a positive oral-supplement subgroup; cohort evidence links very low protein intake to higher mortality (observational, relative measures)

title: Hoarding disorder: CBT beats waitlist and self-help books in small trials (about a quarter to a third off symptom scores); no drug has ever passed a placebo-controlled test — venlafaxine's 32–36% improvements are open-label only
question: For hoarding disorder, does cognitive behavioural therapy work — and is there any medication with real evidence behind it?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) for CBT; pharmacotherapy unproven. The CBT record is three small controlled trials pointing the same way. Steketee 2010 (PMID: 20336804) randomised 46 patients to manualised multicomponent CBT or waitlist: CBT was superior at 12 weeks on hoarding severity and mood, and by session 26, 71% were rated improved by therapists, 81% rated themselves improved, and 41% of completers were clinically significantly improved. Tolin 2019 (PMID: 31008633; NCT01956344) randomised 87 adults to 16-session group CBT or waitlist and found CBT efficacious, with 83% of CBT patients classified as responders. Muroff 2012 (DOI 10.1002/da.21923; PMID not captured this session) randomised 38 patients and found group CBT cut Saving Inventory–Revised scores by 23.3–29.9% while bibliotherapy alone managed 9% and did not significantly improve — the shelf's most practically useful negative, since unguided self-help is what most people with hoarding actually get. Against this, every control is a waitlist or a book: no trial compares CBT with an active psychological placebo, so expectancy effects are unmeasured and the stamp stays at POSSIBLE. For drugs there is nothing controlled at all: venlafaxine extended-release improved scores by 32–36% over 12 weeks in an open-label study of 24 patients (Saxena & Sumner 2014, PMID: 24722633), and the only other drug data (open-label paroxetine, mean decrease 31%, Saxena 2007, PMID: 16790250) are of the same uncontrolled kind; a 2019 review confirms no placebo-controlled drug trial for hoarding disorder exists. PROPOSED: POSSIBLE (benefit) for CBT; no stamp available for any medication.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) for CBT — waitlist- and bibliotherapy-controlled trials show consistent, moderate symptom reductions (SI-R down 23–30% with group CBT versus 9% for a self-help book; 83% responders in the largest trial) · pharmacotherapy: no placebo-controlled trial exists for any drug in hoarding disorder; open-label venlafaxine and paroxetine data cannot support a stamp

title: HHT nosebleeds: nasal sprays of bevacizumab, estriol and tranexamic acid all failed against saline; oral tranexamic acid shortens bleeds without reducing their number; pomalidomide improved severity scores in the one positive modern RCT
question: For hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia (HHT), which drug treatments for nosebleeds have actually beaten placebo in trials?
balance: SPLIT — the HHT epistaxis record divides cleanly by route and by rigour. Nasal sprays failed twice: in the NOSE trial (Whitehead 2016, PMID: 27599329; NCT01408030; 121 adults), bevacizumab, estriol and tranexamic acid sprays were indistinguishable from saline placebo on bleed frequency (P = .97; medians 7.0–8.0 episodes/week in every arm), and Dupuis-Girod 2016 (PMID: 27599328; NCT02106520; 80 patients) found nasal bevacizumab at three doses numerically worse than placebo on monthly bleed duration (215–259 vs 200 minutes; P = .57), stopped for futility. Oral tranexamic acid does something narrower: in ATERO (Gaillard 2014, PMID: 25040799; NCT00355108; 118 patients, crossover) it shortened monthly bleeding duration by 17.3% relative (15.7 minutes absolute, 95% CI 5.5 to 27.6; P = 0.005) without changing frequency, and in Geisthoff 2014 (PMID: 25005464; NCT01031992; 22 patients) it missed its haemoglobin endpoint (P = 0.33) while cutting the epistaxis score by 54% relative (P = 0.0031). The one positive modern systemic RCT is pomalidomide: PATH-HHT (Al-Samkari 2024, PMID: 39292928; NCT03910244; 144 patients) improved epistaxis severity by −0.94 points versus placebo (95% CI −1.57 to −0.31; P = 0.004), past the 0.71-point clinical-significance threshold, and closed early at interim analysis. Systemic bevacizumab's dramatic numbers (severity score −3.33; haemoglobin +2.38 g/dL) come from 10 uncontrolled cohorts totalling 225 patients (Li 2025, PMID: 40095741). Across all 8 placebo-controlled RCTs pooled by Hsu 2019 (PMID: 30200816), tamoxifen was the only drug superior to placebo for frequency and severity, and no treatment changed haemoglobin or quality of life. PROPOSED SPLIT as stamped. stamp: SPLIT — no difference: nasal bevacizumab, estriol and tranexamic-acid sprays (NOSE trial, n=121) and nasal bevacizumab dose-ranging (n=80, stopped for futility) · duration only: oral tranexamic acid shortened monthly bleeding time by 17.3% relative (15.7 minutes absolute) without changing bleed frequency · positive but early: pomalidomide beat placebo on epistaxis severity (−0.94 points, P = 0.004) in one 144-patient trial closed early at interim analysis; systemic bevacizumab's large effects come only from uncontrolled series; tamoxifen's pooled RCT signal rests on small old trials

title: Neonatal herpes: high-dose acyclovir (60 mg/kg/day for 21 days) improved survival in disseminated disease against historical controls, and 6 months of oral suppression after CNS disease improved 12-month mental development scores in a placebo-controlled trial
question: For a newborn with herpes simplex infection, what dose and duration of acyclovir should be used — and does months of oral suppressive acyclovir afterwards protect the developing brain?
balance: SPLIT — two different treatment questions, two different grades of evidence. Acute treatment: Kimberlin 2001 (PMID: 11483782) compared high-dose intravenous acyclovir (60 mg/kg/day for 21 days) with historical standard-dose (30 mg/kg/day) controls and found survival in disseminated disease significantly higher on high dose (odds ratio 3.3, 95% CI 1.4 to 7.9), with overall survival also higher (OR 3.3, 95% CI 1.5 to 7.3) but CNS-disease survival similar between doses; neutropenia occurred in 21% of high-dose recipients with localised disease. That is an observational-grade comparison — no randomised dose trial exists or ethically can — and the Seattle era cohort (Melvin 2022, PMID: 34894240) shows what accompanied the high-dose era: overall mortality fell from 20.9% to 5.6% as high-dose use rose from 0% to about 95%, yet disseminated disease still killed 40.9% and only 55% of CNS survivors were without obvious neurologic abnormality at 24 months. Suppression: the one double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (Kimberlin 2011, PMID: 21991950; NCT00031460 and NCT00031447; 74 neonates) found that 6 months of oral acyclovir 300 mg/m² three times daily after the intravenous course improved Bayley Mental Development Index scores at 12 months in CNS disease (adjusted mean 88.24 vs 68.12; P = 0.046), assessed in 28 of 45 CNS infants, with a trend to more neutropenia (P = 0.09). PROPOSED SPLIT: high-dose acute therapy is standard care resting on historical-control evidence (POSSIBLE on the fetched record); suppression after CNS disease has genuine randomised support, from a single small trial (POSSIBLE). title: Infected ear piercing (auricular perichondritis): Pseudomonas is the organism to cover - 94% resolved with culture-guided antibiotics in a 50-patient series
question: How should an infected ear piercing (auricular perichondritis) be treated, and which antibiotic cover is needed?
balance: Piercing infections of the ear cartilage (auricular perichondritis) have never been tested in a randomised trial; everything known comes from case series. In the prospective 50-patient series of Mostafa 2025 (PMID 40583650), ear piercing was the commonest cause (56.0%), Pseudomonas aeruginosa (41.9% of isolates) and Staphylococcus aureus (27.9%) dominated, and 94% resolved completely on culture-guided antibiotics over a mean 14.2 days. In 127 inpatients with refractory disease, Zhang 2024 (PMID 38312521) found Pseudomonas in 49.2% of isolates, high susceptibility to ceftazidime (90.9%) and cefepime (94.6%) but fluoroquinolone susceptibility of only 65.2-67.4%. Klug 2019 (PMID 31079204), 112 Danish patients, found Pseudomonas in 58% of abscess cases but Staphylococcus predominant (49%) without abscess, and no significant outcome difference between Staphylococcus-covering and Pseudomonas-covering regimens in non-abscess cases. The practical reading: treat early, cover Pseudomonas where there is an abscess, a cartilage (high) piercing, or a slow response, and let cultures refine therapy. Because all the evidence is observational, the stamp is capped: PROPOSED POSSIBLE.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Laser hair removal clears shaving bumps (pseudofolliculitis barbae): Nd:YAG laser plus eflornithine cream cut hair by a median 99.5% in a blinded trial
question: What treatments work for ingrown hairs and shaving bumps (pseudofolliculitis barbae)?
balance: Three small randomised trials, all in men, all point the same way: removing the hair removes the bumps. In the double-blind paired trial of Xia 2012 (PMID 22226431), 27 men with pseudofolliculitis barbae had long-pulsed Nd:YAG laser to the whole bearded neck every 4 weeks for 16 weeks, with eflornithine cream on one side and placebo cream on the other: median hair reduction 99.5% (range 48.5-100.0%) on the eflornithine side vs 85.0% (range 50.5-94.5%) on the placebo side (P<.001), with significantly fewer inflammatory papules on the eflornithine side. Amer 2021 (PMID 33559240) randomised 20 men to Nd:YAG laser or chemical peeling (up to 5 sessions, 3 months' follow-up): the reduction in papules/pustules was statistically significantly greater with laser in the mandibular and neck regions, though the abstract reports no numeric effect sizes. Leheta 2009 (PMID 20101340) randomised 20 men in a split-face design to long-pulse alexandrite laser (GentleLase, Candela Corp.) on one half and intense pulsed light (Chromolite, Chromogenex Technologies Ltd.) on the other: the alexandrite side reached about 80% improvement in 7 sessions, the IPL side needed 10-12 sessions for about 50% improvement, with less recurrence over 1 year on the alexandrite side. Harms were mild: pain with laser, transient hyperpigmentation, mild erythema and burning with peeling. The evidence is small, short-term and all-male, so the stamp stays at: PROPOSED POSSIBLE.

title: Keratosis pilaris: 10% lactic acid cut lesions by 66% and 5% salicylic acid by 52% in a randomised trial; laser looks most supported in a review of 47 articles
question: What treatments help keratosis pilaris (the rough bumps on the upper arms and thighs)?
balance: The evidence is thin and uneven. Kootiratrakarn 2015 (PMID 25802513) randomised patients with keratosis pilaris to 10% lactic acid or 5% salicylic acid cream twice daily for 3 months: mean lesion reduction from baseline was 66% with lactic acid and 52% with salicylic acid, both statistically significant, with only mild local irritation - but the abstract gives no total number of patients, so the card prints 'N not documented'. McCormick 2024 (PMID 38206153) was a 4-week open-label, noncomparative study of a 20% urea moisturising cream in 30 participants aged 18-65: the percent change in skin smoothness/texture was significant at 1 week and 4 weeks (P<=0.001), most were satisfied at 4 weeks, and there were no significant adverse events - but without a control group the improvement cannot be separated from natural variation or expectation. Maghfour 2022 (PMID 32886029) systematically reviewed 47 articles from 1,150 screened and found laser therapy, particularly Q-switched Nd:YAG, the most supported treatment, with topicals (mineral oil-hydrophil petrolat, tacrolimus, azelaic acid, salicylic acid) also effective at least for appearance - but outcome measures varied between studies, so no pooled effect size exists. Nothing here is strong or controlled enough to go beyond: PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence)

title: Labial fusion in young girls: topical betamethasone and estrogen both work in most cases - success 80-89% in one series, but only 15% in another
question: How should labial fusion (labial adhesions) in prepubertal girls be treated - estrogen cream, betamethasone cream, or both?
balance: All three studies are retrospective chart reviews, so the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE, and they disagree. Mayoglou 2009 (PMID 19646671) reviewed 151 prepubertal girls (mean age 3 years): time to resolution was 1.3 months with betamethasone versus 2.2 months with topical estrogen (Premarin), recurrence was lower with betamethasone, and estrogen caused breast budding and vaginal bleeding while betamethasone caused only local irritation. Ertürk 2014 (PMID not captured this session; DOI 10.3906/sag-1312-3) studied 39 girls with adhesions covering at least 50% of the vaginal opening: success was 16/20 (80%) with estrogen and 17/19 (89.4%) with betamethasone plus petroleum ointment (Vaseline); 2/20 estrogen patients and 1/19 betamethasone patients needed manual separation; labial enlargement occurred in 2 (10%) on estrogen and local irritation in 1 (5.2%) on betamethasone. But Eroğlu 2011 (PMID 21945628), 131 children, found far lower success - estrogen only 11/71 (15.4%), betamethasone only 5/32 (15.6%), combination 5/28 (28.5%) - with no significant differences (estrogen vs betamethasone P=1.00; combination vs pooled single therapies relative risk 1.85, 95% CI 0.89-3.89, P=.11). The honest reading is that both creams are used first-line, betamethasone looks at least as good with fewer systemic effects, and success rates vary widely between clinics: PROPOSED POSSIBLE.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Amifampridine (Firdapse) helps Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome: two phase 3 withdrawal trials met their endpoints on muscle strength and global impression
question: Does amifampridine (3,4-diaminopyridine) help people with Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome?
balance: Three randomised trials, all positive, in a rare disease. Oh 2009 (PMID 19722254) was a randomised, double-blind, cross-over trial of 3,4-diaminopyridine (up to 75-80 mg/day) versus placebo in only 7 patients with LEMS (QMG score >9) - the n is printed on the card face because it is under 10; one patient withdrew with major side effects. 3,4-DAP was significantly better than placebo on the subjective symptoms score (P=0.01), LEMS classification (P<0.001), muscle strength score (P<0.006), QMG score (P=0.02) and CMAP (P=0.03). Oh 2016 (PMID 26852139; registry NCT01377922, stated in the paper's full text and not printed in the PubMed record) was the phase 3 randomised, double-blind withdrawal trial of amifampridine phosphate (Firdapse): after an open-label run-in of 7-91 days, patients were randomised to continue amifampridine phosphate for 14 days or placebo (7-day taper, 7-day placebo). The co-primary endpoints - change at day 14 in QMG and Subject Global Impression - were met, and all 5 primary, secondary and tertiary endpoints were significant at day 8; the most common adverse events were oral and digital paresthesias, nausea and headache. The PubMed abstract gives no total N, so the card prints 'N not documented'. Shieh 2019 (PMID 30801481) was the confirmatory phase 3 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled withdrawal trial in 26 adults with LEMS (13 amifampridine phosphate vs 13 placebo over 4 days), all previously titrated to 30-80 mg/day: amifampridine phosphate showed significant benefit in QMG and Subject Global Impression at 4 days, with Clinical Global Impression-Improvement, timed up-and-go and QMG limb domain also improved; placebo-group events were mainly withdrawal effects (muscle weakness n=5, fatigue n=4). The tested product is amifampridine phosphate, sold as Firdapse. Two phase 3 trials plus a positive cross-over trial, consistently in the same direction, support: PROPOSED LIKELY.
stamp: LIKELY

title: Learning disabilities: targeted maths training helps dyscalculia, but generic working-memory training does not transfer to school skills
question: What interventions help children and adolescents with learning disabilities - does working-memory training work, or do targeted programmes work better?
balance: BOUNDARY: intensive remedial reading instruction for severe reading disability / dyslexia is homed on shelf #1396 and is not re-carded here; this shelf covers non-reading interventions. The evidence splits. On the positive side, Zotti 2026 (PMID 41602671; registry ISRCTN15190285) was a single-centre, two-arm randomised trial (pseudo-randomised allocation, no blinding, waitlist control) in 70 adolescents aged 13-17 with a recent first diagnosis of developmental dyscalculia: prismatic adaptation followed by targeted cognitive training using serious games (the paper names the MindLenses software, from Restorative Neurotechnologies Srl) produced large between-group gains - working memory index 16.51 (95% CI 13.59-19.44, p<0.001, eta-squared 0.66), processing speed index 12.40 (95% CI 9.73-15.70, p<0.001, eta-squared 0.58), mental calculation speed 0.74 (95% CI 0.55-0.93, p<0.001, eta-squared 0.46), mental calculation accuracy 0.43 (95% CI 0.14-0.71, p<0.001, eta-squared 0.17) and numerical fact retrieval 14.07 (95% CI 8.58-19.56, p<0.001, eta-squared 0.31). Peijnenborgh 2016 (PMID not captured this session) reviewed 13 studies of working-memory training programmes (Cogmed, Jungle Memory, Braingame Brian) in children and adolescents with learning disabilities and found a medium effect on verbal working memory (g=0.64), a small effect on visuospatial working memory (g=0.63) and a small-to-medium effect on decoding (g=0.36), with children over 10 benefiting more on verbal working memory - but 76% of the studies included children with ADHD, and the authors note heterogeneity, small samples and reduced methodological rigour. Against that, Melby-Lervåg & Hulme 2013 (PMID 22612437) pooled 23 studies with 30 group comparisons and found reliable short-term improvements in working-memory skills themselves, but no convincing evidence of generalisation to nonverbal or verbal ability, attention inhibition, word decoding or arithmetic - verbal working-memory gains were not sustained at follow-up. The split is therefore: targeted, maths-focused training shows real gains in the skill it trains, while generic working-memory training improves only the trained tasks and does not transfer. PROPOSED SPLIT.
stamp: SPLIT

title: Exercise training in cirrhosis: supervised exercise raised peak oxygen uptake by 5.3 mL/kg/min and added about 49 m to the 6-minute walk
question: Does exercise training help people with liver cirrhosis - fitness, walking distance, muscle and quality of life?
balance: BOUNDARY: specific liver diseases - hepatitis, cirrhosis complications, MASH, albumin and TIPS - are homed on their own shelves, and cirrhosis nutrition is homed on shelves #5367-#5370; this shelf covers only exercise training in cirrhosis. The evidence is small but consistent. Román 2014 (PMID 24599772; the PubMed record as fetched this session prints no registry ID, so the card says 'none in the record') was a randomised pilot in 17 outpatients with cirrhosis (exercise n=8, control n=9): supervised moderate exercise for 12 weeks, with all patients receiving oral leucine 10 g/day, improved the 6-minute walk test from 365 m (160-420) to 445 m (250-500) (p=0.01) and the 2-minute step test (p=0.02); lower thigh circumference rose from 41 cm (34-53) to 46 cm (36-56) (p=0.02), and SF-36 general health (p=0.03), vitality (p=0.01) and social function (p=0.04) improved; there were no cirrhosis complications in either group. Zenith 2014 (PMID 24768811; NCT01799785) randomised 19 stable patients with Child-Pugh A or B cirrhosis (n=9 exercise, n=10 usual care) to supervised cycle-ergometer exercise 3 days a week for 8 weeks at 60-80% of baseline peak VO2: at week 8, peak VO2 was 5.3 mL/kg/min higher in the exercise group than in controls (95% CI 2.9-7.8; P=.001), thigh circumference (P=.001), thigh muscle thickness (P=.01) and self-perceived health (P=.01) were higher, and fatigue subscores were lower (P=.01); no adverse events occurred. Rocha 2025 (PMID 40976129) pooled 6 randomised trials with 244 participants aged 53-63 years with Child-Pugh A, B or C cirrhosis, mostly men: quality of life with resistance training had a standardised mean difference of 0.36 (0.01-0.76, p=0.04), and the 6-minute walk test improved by a mean difference of 49.39 m (16.53-82.24, p=0.03) after resistance and aerobic training, with no difference for VO2peak, thigh circumference or BMI; GRADE certainty was very low to moderate. Two tiny pilots plus a small meta-analysis of small trials, with a leucine co-intervention in one: PROPOSED POSSIBLE.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Nirmatrelvir-ritonavir (Paxlovid) for established long COVID: three randomised trials found no significant benefit on symptoms
question: Does nirmatrelvir-ritonavir (Paxlovid) help people who already have long COVID?
balance: BOUNDARY: metformin to prevent long COVID after early COVID-19 (COVID-OUT) is homed on shelf #1935 and is not re-carded here; this shelf is about treating established long COVID with an antiviral. Three randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials tested nirmatrelvir-ritonavir in established long COVID, and all three found no significant benefit. Geng 2024 (STOP-PASC; PMID 38848477; NCT05576662) randomised 155 adults (102 nirmatrelvir-ritonavir vs 53 placebo-ritonavir) to 15 days of treatment, 300/100 mg twice daily, a mean 17.5 months after infection: there was no statistically significant difference in the pooled severity of 6 core symptoms at 10 weeks, nor in patient global impression, summative symptom scores or PROMIS fatigue, dyspnea, cognitive or physical function; adverse events were similar and mostly low grade. Sawano 2025 (PAX LC; PMID 40188838; NCT05668091) enrolled 100 adults (49 vs 51) for 15 days: the adjusted change in PROMIS-29 Physical Health Summary Score to day 28 was 0.45 (-0.93 to 1.83) on nirmatrelvir-ritonavir vs 1.01 (-0.30 to 2.31) on placebo, an adjusted mean difference of -0.55 (95% CI -2.32 to 1.21; p=0.54); drug-related adverse events were 35/46 (76%) vs 27/49 (55%), mostly dysgeusia; there were no deaths or serious adverse events to week 6. Baden 2026 (RECOVER-VITAL; PMID 42673984; NCT05595369), the largest trial, randomised 964 people (959 in the modified intention-to-treat population) across 69 US sites into cognitive, autonomic and exercise phenotypes, testing 15 days and 25 days of active drug against placebo: there was no statistically significant benefit for any phenotype on its primary endpoint - adjusted differences vs placebo for the 25-day course were 3.2% (95% CI -10.4 to 16.8, p=0.65) for cognitive, -6.4% (-18.5 to 5.7, p=0.30) for autonomic and -7.8% (-19.5 to 3.8, p=0.19) for exercise phenotypes; there were no deaths, and 52 serious adverse events in 42 (4%) of 963 participants. Three null trials, including one of nearly a thousand people: the treatment made no difference. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference).
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference)

title: Long QT syndrome beyond beta-blockers: left cardiac sympathetic denervation cut the yearly cardiac event rate by 86%, and mexiletine cut arrhythmic events in LQT3 from 22% to 3%
question: Beyond beta-blockers, what treatments help people with long QT syndrome - sympathetic denervation or mexiletine?
balance: BOUNDARY: which beta-blocker to use for long QT syndrome is homed on shelf #3074 and is not re-carded here; this shelf covers treatments beyond beta-blockers. All the evidence is observational, so the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE - but the effects are large. Dusi 2022 (PMID 35331422) reported a single centre's 50-year experience of left cardiac sympathetic denervation (LCSD) in 125 patients with long QT syndrome (58% women, mean QTc 527 +/- 60 ms, 90% on beta blockers), followed for 12.9 +/- 10.3 years: after LCSD, 17% of the very-high-risk group remained asymptomatic, compared with 52%, 47% and 97% in the aborted-cardiac-arrest, syncope/ICD-shock and primary-prevention groups (P<0.0001), with an overall 86% decrease in the mean yearly cardiac event rate (P<0.0001); among the 45 patients with only syncope or ICD shocks before LCSD, none had aborted cardiac arrest or sudden death as a first symptom afterwards, and a 6-month post-LCSD QTc under 500 ms predicted an excellent outcome. Mazzanti 2016 (PMID 26940925) studied 34 patients with long QT syndrome type 3 (LQT3) (56% male, median age at treatment start 22 years, median baseline QTc 509 ms) on oral mexiletine for a median 36 months at a mean dose of 8 +/- 0.5 mg/kg/day: QTc shortened by 63 +/- 6 ms (p<0.0001), the proportion with arrhythmic events fell from 22% to 3% (p=0.031), mean events per patient from 0.43 +/- 0.17 to 0.03 +/- 0.03 (p=0.027), and the annual event rate from 10.3% to 0.7% (p=0.0097) - a before-after comparison over equal-duration periods. Funasako 2016 (PMID 26632536) gave an intravenous mexiletine infusion test (2 mg/kg) to 31 genotype-positive patients (LQT3 n=15; LQT1 n=4, LQT2 n=12): QTc shortened in both groups (P<0.0001 vs baseline), but the shortening was larger in LQT3 (99 +/- 39 ms) than in LQT1/LQT2 (48 +/- 32 ms), P=0.0004, and the test identified LQT3 with 86.7% sensitivity, 81.3% specificity and 81.3% accuracy at an optimal delta-QTc cut-off of 69 ms, with no pro-arrhythmic event. LCSD and mexiletine are additions to, not replacements for, beta-blockers in these series - 90% of the LCSD patients were on beta blockers. PROPOSED POSSIBLE.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Long-sightedness (hyperopia): no randomised trials compare PRK with LASIK, and the best available data show LASIK is no better than PRK
question: For long-sightedness (hyperopia), is laser surgery with LASIK or with PRK better?
balance: There is no randomised evidence at all. Settas 2012 (PMID 22696365), a Cochrane review that planned to include only randomised controlled trials comparing PRK with LASIK for hyperopia, identified no studies meeting its inclusion criteria and concluded that no robust, reliable conclusions could be reached - although the non-randomised trials it discussed narratively appeared to show comparable efficacy, and high-quality open RCTs are needed. The best comparative data come from two meta-analyses of non-randomised studies. Almutairi 2025 (PMID 40102791; PROSPERO CRD42023469543) pooled 6 articles (419 participants, 585 eyes; 5 retrospective, 1 case-series): the final mean refractive spherical equivalent differed by a weighted mean difference of -0.05 (P=0.06; the 95% CI is printed in the record as 0.42 to 0.31, apparently missing a minus sign), the odds ratio for uncorrected distance visual acuity of 20/20 or better was 0.58 (95% CI 0.39-0.78, P=0.33) and for 20/40 or better 1.40 (95% CI 0.65-3.02, P=0.81) - LASIK had no significant benefits over PRK on clinical outcomes, with less corneal haze in LASIK-treated eyes at 1-3 months. Hassanzadeh 2025 (PMID 40287029) pooled PRK alone - 750 eyes from 481 patients (49.5% female): postoperative improvement in uncorrected visual acuity, spherical equivalent and cylindrical power was statistically significant (P=0.001), but overall corneal haze incidence was 32.5% (95% CI 26.5-38.4%), significantly higher than in myopic PRK. So the honest answer is that neither operation has been shown better than the other in a randomised trial, and PRK carries a roughly one-in-three chance of corneal haze: PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence)

title: MERS: ribavirin plus interferon has never been shown to cut deaths — in the largest cohort 90-day mortality was 73.6% with it versus 61.5% without, and identical after adjustment (adjusted odds ratio 1.03)
question: In people with Middle East respiratory syndrome (MERS), does ribavirin plus interferon improve survival compared with supportive care alone?
balance: No randomised trial of any MERS treatment has ever reported. Omrani 2014 (PMID: 25278221; Registry ID: none in the record), a single-centre retrospective cohort of ventilated patients, found 14-day survival of 70% (14/20) with ribavirin plus pegylated interferon alfa-2a versus 29% (7/24) with supportive care alone, but by 28 days the gap had closed (30% versus 17% survived). The largest study, Arabi 2020 (PMID: 31925415; Registry ID: none in the record), covering 349 critically ill patients in 14 Saudi hospitals with adjustment for time-varying confounders, found ribavirin/interferon was not associated with 90-day mortality (adjusted odds ratio 1.03, 95% CI 0.73 to 1.44) or faster viral clearance. The Morra 2018 systematic review and meta-analysis (PMID: 29664167; Registry ID: none in the record) likewise found case fatality of 71% in both the interferon-treated and supportive-only groups. All evidence is observational, so any stamp is capped at POSSIBLE; the adjusted data show no mortality effect. Proposed stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference to mortality in the adjusted analyses).
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference to mortality in the adjusted analyses)

title: Molar pregnancy: prophylactic chemotherapy after evacuation roughly halves later cancerous growth in high-risk complete moles in the pooled trials (relative risk 0.37; 19% versus 39.7% with a single actinomycin D dose in a 426-woman cohort) — but one single methotrexate dose did not significantly help, and routine prophylaxis is not recommended
question: In women whose molar pregnancy (hydatidiform mole) has been evacuated, does prophylactic chemotherapy reduce the later development of gestational trophoblastic neoplasia (GTN), and does the regimen matter?
balance: Evacuation cures most molar pregnancies; the contested question is prophylactic chemotherapy (P-Chem) against later GTN. Wang 2017 (PMID: 28892119; Registry ID: none in the record), the Cochrane review of 3 randomised trials (613 women), found P-Chem reduced GTN after complete mole with a relative risk of 0.37 (95% CI 0.24 to 0.57), but two of the three trials were poor quality; the one good small trial in high-risk women gave a relative risk of 0.28 (95% CI 0.10 to 0.73), and P-Chem delayed GTN diagnosis and increased the courses needed to cure it. Uberti 2025 (PMID: 39799786; Registry ID: none in the record), a 27-year retrospective cohort of 426 high-risk complete moles, found GTN in 19% (55/290) after a single actinomycin D bolus at evacuation versus 39.7% (54/136) without (relative risk 0.48, 95% CI 0.35 to 0.66; NNT 5). Akhavan 2024 (PMID: 39538177; Registry ID: none in the record) found a single methotrexate dose did not significantly reduce progression (18.2% versus 36.3%; p=0.12; n=80). Proposed stamp: SPLIT (multi-course or single-dose actinomycin D prophylaxis in high-risk complete mole: POSSIBLE benefit · single-dose methotrexate: no significant effect · routine use not recommended by the Cochrane authors).

title: Nappy rash: in small trials, breast milk added to zinc oxide shortened healing by about three-quarters of a day (2.52 versus 3.28 days), calendula left fewer rash sites than aloe vera, and bentonite started recovery within 6 hours in 93.3% versus 40% — no trial compared any cream with no treatment
question: In infants with nappy rash (diaper dermatitis), which topical treatments speed healing — barrier creams such as zinc oxide, breast milk, or plant/mineral preparations such as calendula, aloe vera and bentonite?
balance: No placebo- or no-treatment-controlled trial was found; every carded trial compares one topical preparation with another. Veysizadeh 2026 (PMID: 41204732; Registry ID: none in the record) randomised 42 infants to 25% zinc oxide with or without topical breast milk: complete recovery was similar (61.9% versus 66.6%) but lesions resolved faster with breast milk added (2.52 versus 3.28 days; p=0.012) and no infant in the combination group failed to respond (versus 14.3%). Panahi 2012 (PMID: 22606064; Registry ID: none in the record), a double-blind trial in 66 infants, found both calendula ointment and aloe vera cream improved severity, with fewer rash sites on calendula (p=0.001). Adib-Hajbaghery 2014 (PMID: 25097603; Registry ID: none in the record), a double-blind trial in 60 infants, found bentonite started recovery within 6 hours in 93.3% versus 40% on calendula, with complete improvement by 3 days in 90% versus 36.7%. All trials are small, single-centre and from one country. Proposed stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence).
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence)

title: Nasal and sinus cancer: endoscopic surgery matched or beat open surgery on margins and local control in cohort data (clear margins 85% versus 64%; 5-year local control 90% versus 82%), and 5-year survival after endoscopic resection plus tailored radiotherapy was 71.4% in intestinal-type adenocarcinoma
question: In people with cancer of the nasal cavity and paranasal sinuses (sinonasal cancer), how do surgery-based treatments perform — in particular endoscopic resection versus open approaches — for margin clearance, local control and survival?
balance: There are no randomised trials in sinonasal cancer; all evidence is retrospective and endoscopic cases are selected to be more favourable. Kobayashi 2026 (PMID: 42367673; Registry ID: none in the record), 110 patients at 10 Japanese centres, found negative margins in 85% with endoscopic surgery versus 64% with the open craniofacial approach, and 5-year local control of 90% versus 82% — but endoscopy was used in earlier-stage cases. Chen 2022 (PMID: 36132140; Registry ID: none in the record), 303 patients over 18 years, found 5-year overall survival of 61.0%, better survival with surgery than with radiotherapy/chemotherapy alone, better survival with the endoscopic than the open approach (p<0.05), and a clear benefit from margin-negative (R0) resection (p<0.001). Parys 2025 (PMID: 40224179; Registry ID: none in the record), 200 intestinal-type adenocarcinoma patients treated with endoscopic resection and tailored radiotherapy over 30 years, found 5-year overall survival 71.4% and disease-specific survival 85.1%, with local recurrence in 34.0%. Observational evidence caps the stamp at POSSIBLE. Proposed stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) for endoscopic surgery-based treatment in selected patients (observational evidence only).

title: Necrotising fasciitis: urgent surgery and antibiotics are the treatment — adjunctive IVIG made no difference in the blinded INSTINCT trial (physical function 36 versus 31, p=0.81) or across 4,127 US hospital cases (mortality 27.3% versus 23.6%; adjusted odds ratio 1.00)
question: In people with necrotising fasciitis (necrotising soft-tissue infection), does adjunctive intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) — on top of urgent surgical debridement and antibiotics — improve survival or recovery?
balance: The proven treatment is immediate surgical debridement plus broad-spectrum antibiotics; the contested adjunct is IVIG. Madsen 2017 (INSTINCT; PMID: 28421246; Registry ID: NCT02111161), the only blinded placebo-controlled trial in necrotising soft-tissue infection (n=100), found no effect of IVIG 25 g daily for 3 days on 6-month physical function (median scores 36 versus 31; adjusted difference 1, 95% CI -7 to 10; p=0.81). Kadri 2017 (PMID: 28034881; Registry ID: none in the record), a propensity-matched analysis of 4,127 debrided necrotising fasciitis cases with shock, found in-hospital mortality of 27.3% with IVIG versus 23.6% without (adjusted odds ratio 1.00, 95% CI 0.55 to 1.83), including in the toxic-shock/streptococcal subgroup. Darenberg 2003 (PMID: 12884156; Registry ID: none in the record), a blinded trial in streptococcal toxic shock syndrome stopped after 21 patients, found 28-day mortality 3.6-fold higher on placebo without reaching significance, with faster organ-failure improvement on IVIG. Proposed stamp: SPLIT (IVIG in unselected necrotising soft-tissue infection: (the treatment made no difference) in the blinded RCT and the large matched analysis · IVIG in streptococcal toxic shock syndrome: unproven signal from one 21-patient trial stopped early).
stamp: SPLIT (IVIG in unselected necrotising soft-tissue infection: (the treatment made no difference) in the blinded RCT and the large matched analysis · IVIG in streptococcal toxic shock syndrome: unproven signal from one 21-patient trial stopped early)

title: Oesophageal atresia and tracheo-oesophageal fistula: repair by day 2 of life is supported by 863 US cases (11 of 18 stomach perforations happened after day 2), while long-gap atresia drives strictures (adjusted odds ratio 4.44) and far longer recovery (hospital stay 186 versus 53 days)
question: In newborns with oesophageal atresia and tracheo-oesophageal fistula, how do the timing and type of surgical repair affect survival, complications and feeding — and what most determines the outcome?
balance: Repair is surgical and uncontested; the evidence concerns timing and prognostic factors, and is entirely observational. Patwardhan 2025 (PMID: 39261185; Registry ID: none in the record), 863 infants in the US Pediatric Health Information System, found most repairs already happen on day 2 (36%), weekend repair had equivalent outcomes, and 11 of 18 gastric perforations (61%) occurred after day 2 — supporting repair by day 2. Ali 2025 (PMID: 41496816; Registry ID: none in the record), 67 infants in Riyadh, found survival to discharge of 86% (excluding palliatively managed trisomy 18), primary repair in only 10% of long-gap cases, and long-gap atresia as the only independent predictor of stricture (adjusted odds ratio 4.44, 95% CI 1.27 to 15.55), with median stay 186 versus 53 days. Tawil 2026 (PMID: 41386345; Registry ID: none in the record), 139 open-repair cases in five West Bank and East Jerusalem hospitals, found mortality of 20.5%, long-term complications in 67.0%, and each day of delayed repair raising mortality odds (odds ratio 1.35 per day, 95% CI 1.08 to 1.71). Observational evidence caps the stamp at POSSIBLE. Proposed stamp: POSSIBLE (observational evidence only).
stamp: POSSIBLE (observational evidence only)

title: Oral thrush: fluconazole cured 91% versus 51% for nystatin in immunocompromised children, and miconazole gel cured 99% versus 54% in healthy infants — nystatin is the weaker standard
question: In oral candidiasis (oral thrush), how do fluconazole and miconazole gel compare with nystatin, and how effective is nystatin itself?
balance: SPLIT. The head-to-head randomised evidence consistently puts nystatin suspension last among the tested agents. Flynn 1995 (PMID: 7636666) randomised 182 immunocompromised children: fluconazole suspension cured 91% versus 51% on nystatin, with organism eradication 76% versus 11%, though relapse by one month was similar (28% versus 27%). Hoppe 1997 (DOI 10.1097/00006454-199703000-00007; PMID not captured this session) randomised 183 healthy infants: miconazole gel cured 99% versus 54% on nystatin by day 12. Rai 2022 (PMID: 36362833) shows nystatin is nonetheless an active topical drug — it matched photodynamic therapy for clinical remission of denture stomatitis and lowered Candida counts more at 60 days — and records nystatin pastilles beating placebo for denture stomatitis. No carded trial gives nystatin suspension a placebo-controlled win in ordinary thrush. Proposed stamp: SPLIT (azoles superior head-to-head; nystatin active but weaker).
stamp: SPLIT (fluconazole and miconazole gel clearly superior to nystatin in head-to-head RCTs — cure 91% vs 51% and 99% vs 54% · nystatin itself active topically but with no strong placebo-controlled win for the suspension)

title: Ovarian cysts: birth-control pills did not speed resolution in any of 8 trials (686 women) and aspiration matched plain observation (46% vs 45% resolved) — watching a benign-appearing cyst carried a 0.4% two-year cancer risk
question: For a woman with a functional or simple ovarian cyst, do oral contraceptives or needle aspiration speed resolution compared with watchful waiting, and how safe is watchful waiting?
balance: SPLIT. For an existing functional or simple cyst, the two active treatments tested both failed against simply waiting. Grimes 2014 (PMID: 24782304), the Cochrane review of eight RCTs in 686 women, found combined oral contraceptives did not hasten resolution in any trial. Zanetta 1996 (DOI 10.1136/bmj.313.7065.1110; PMID not captured this session) randomised 278 women: aspiration resolved 46% versus 44.6% with observation at six months. What supports management is the safety of waiting itself: in IOTA5 (Froyman 2019, PMID: 30737137; NCT01698632), 1,919 women with benign-appearing masses managed conservatively had 20.2% spontaneous resolution by two years, with invasive malignancy 0.4%, torsion 0.4% and rupture 0.2%. Proposed stamp: SPLIT (oral contraceptives: the treatment made no difference · aspiration: the treatment made no difference · watchful waiting: supported as safe for ultrasound-benign cysts).
stamp: SPLIT (oral contraceptives for an existing cyst: the treatment made no difference in 8 RCTs · needle aspiration: the treatment made no difference versus observation, 46% vs 45% resolved · watchful waiting of benign-appearing cysts: 0.4% invasive malignancy over 2 years)

title: Paget's disease of the nipple: conservation alone recurred in 21.2% versus 5.9% after mastectomy across 24,062 patients — adding radiotherapy closed most of the gap, and 82% have an underlying breast cancer
question: In Paget's disease of the nipple (mammary Paget disease), how do mastectomy, breast-conserving surgery with radiotherapy, and breast-conserving surgery alone compare for local recurrence?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), observational evidence only — there are no randomised trials. The governing fact is that the nipple change usually sits on a breast cancer: Kollmorgen 1998 (PMID: 9704964) found underlying cancer in 82% (93% with a palpable mass, 74% without). Across 38 studies and 24,062 patients, Lin 2022 (PMID: 36309195) found local recurrence of 21.2% after breast-conserving surgery alone versus 5.9% after mastectomy and about 8% after conservation plus radiotherapy (the radiotherapy figure is printed truncated in the record), concluding conservation alone is not recommended with underlying invasive cancer or DCIS. Pelorca 2023 (PMID: 37265790) found oncoplastic conservation feasible with no detectable recurrence or survival difference in 85 patients. Proposed stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) for conservation plus radiotherapy over conservation alone. Not Paget's disease of bone (Shelf #1822).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) for breast conservation with radiotherapy over conservation alone (local recurrence about 8% vs 21.2%; mastectomy 5.9%) — observational evidence only, no randomised trials

title: Perforated eardrum: acute traumatic perforations healed 94% overall with no advantage from paper patching in the randomised trial — patches only shortened healing time in large perforations, while office patching closed 59.8% of chronic small dry perforations
question: For a perforated eardrum (tympanic membrane perforation), does patching improve healing compared with watchful waiting — in acute traumatic perforations, and in chronic perforations?
balance: SPLIT. For acute traumatic perforations, two randomised trials agree that patching does not significantly raise the final closure rate: Lindeman 1987 (PMID: 3675893) found 94% healed by two months with no difference between paper patch and control, and Park 2011 (PMID: 21593464), in perforations over half the drum, found closure of 93.3% (Steri-Strips), 84.2% (paper patch) and 78.9% (observation), not statistically significant — though patching shortened healing time and reduced repeat procedures. For chronic, dry, small perforations the question is different: Yazdani 2026 (PMID: 41729596) reports 59.8% complete closure 8 weeks after office paper patching in an uncontrolled series of 204 perforations. Proposed stamp: SPLIT (acute traumatic: patching made no difference to final closure · chronic small dry: office patching POSSIBLE on uncontrolled evidence).
stamp: SPLIT (acute traumatic perforation: patching made no difference to final closure — 94% healed overall in the randomised trial · chronic small dry perforation: office paper patching closed 59.8% in an uncontrolled series)

title: Personality disorders beyond borderline: outpatient therapy beat usual care or waitlist across 54 trials (g = 0.78), Cluster A trials total only 468 people (g 0.60–0.91, exploratory), and for antisocial personality disorder no treatment has compelling evidence
question: For personality disorders other than borderline personality disorder (which has its own shelf), what does treatment — psychotherapy or medication — achieve: for personality disorder in general, for Cluster A disorders, and for antisocial personality disorder?
balance: SPLIT. Borderline personality disorder has its own shelf (#708) and is not re-carded here; this shelf covers the generic and other-disorder question, where the evidence splits sharply by diagnosis. Katakis 2023 (PMID: 36681805) pooled 54 outpatient RCTs (n=3,716) in personality disorder/complex emotional needs: psychosocial treatment beat usual care or waitlist with g = 0.78 for personality-disorder symptoms — but that outcome is borderline-weighted. For Cluster A disorders, Cheli 2025 (PMID: 40111791) found only 468 participants in 19 studies, with exploratory pooled effects of g 0.60 to 0.91 and large heterogeneity. For antisocial personality disorder, Gibbon 2020 (PMID: 32880104) found 19 trials and no intervention with compelling evidence of changing antisocial behaviour. Proposed stamp: SPLIT (general outpatient therapy: benefit shown on a borderline-weighted base · Cluster A: POSSIBLE on tiny samples · antisocial: no proven treatment).
stamp: SPLIT (outpatient psychosocial therapy beats usual care/waitlist, g = 0.78, on a borderline-weighted trial base · Cluster A disorders: POSSIBLE, pooled g 0.60–0.91 from only 468 participants · antisocial personality disorder: no intervention with compelling evidence)

title: Piles: excision beats banding for durability — recurrence 6.1% versus 47.5% in grade III disease — but banding hurts less (pain 1 versus 4) and returns people to work in 1 day versus 9
question: In symptomatic haemorrhoids (piles), how do rubber band ligation and excisional haemorrhoidectomy compare for symptom control, recurrence, pain and recovery — by grade of disease?
balance: SPLIT, scoped to banding versus excision — haemorrhoidal artery ligation versus banding is homed on Shelf #1938 and flavonoid (MPFF) tablets on Shelf #4240, and neither is re-carded here. The trade-off is consistent across two decades of trials. For grade III piles, excision is far more durable: in the HollAND trial (van Oostendorp 2025, PMID: 39952268; NCT04621695) recurrence was 6.1% after haemorrhoidectomy versus 47.5% after banding, but banding hurt less (first-week pain 1 versus 4) and returned patients to work in 1 versus 9 days. The Cochrane review (Shanmugam 2005, PMID: 16034963) found the same pattern by grade — remission relative risk 1.23 favouring excision in grade III, 1.07 (no difference) in grade II — with more pain and delayed complications after excision; Dekker 2021 (PMID: 33683503) found the same split across eight RCTs but judged trial quality too poor for a firm verdict. Proposed stamp: SPLIT (grade II: banding a reasonable first procedure · grade III: excision more durable at the cost of pain and recovery time).
stamp: SPLIT (grade II: banding and excision similar for remission, relative risk 1.07 · grade III: excision far more durable — recurrence 6.1% vs 47.5% — but more painful, pain 4 vs 1, and slower to work, 9 vs 1 days)

title: Pilonidal sinus: flap operations cut recurrence versus midline closure (relative odds ratio 0.31 across 50 trials, 5,762 people) and the Karydakis flap healed in a median 14 days versus 49 — though the one 11-year trial found recurrences equal
question: For chronic pilonidal sinus disease, how do flap operations (Karydakis, Limberg) compare with midline closure and with excision left to heal by secondary intention, for recurrence, infection and healing time?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) for off-midline flap closure over midline closure. Two systematic reviews point the same way: Wiinblad 2025 (PMID: 39982788), across 50 RCTs and 5,762 participants, found flap operations had lower recurrence than primary midline closure (relative odds ratio 0.31) and lower infection (relative odds ratio 0.33), with secondary-intention healing always slowest; Alsalaumy 2026 (PMID: 41854814) found the Karydakis flap beat midline closure on recurrence (relative odds ratio 0.30) and returned patients to work 6.5 days sooner. The caution comes from the only long-follow-up head-to-head RCT, Hemmingsson 2022 (NCT00412659; PMID not captured this session): healing was far faster with the Karydakis flap (median 14 versus 49 days) but recurrences were five in each group at a median 11 years. Certainty in the reviews is very low to low. Proposed stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) for off-midline flap surgery over midline closure (recurrence relative odds ratio 0.31 in pooled trials; healing 14 vs 49 days in the long-term RCT, though its 11-year recurrences were equal at 5 vs 5)

title: Pityriasis rosea: acyclovir probably improves the rash (relative risk 2.45 across 3 trials, 141 people; 86.66% vs 33.33% complete resolution in the double-blind trial) — but its effect on itch is unresolved
question: In pityriasis rosea, do acyclovir, macrolide antibiotics, steroids or other treatments improve the rash or the itch compared with placebo or no treatment?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) for oral acyclovir on rash improvement; the itch evidence is unsettled. Contreras-Ruiz 2019 (PMID: 31684696), the Cochrane review of 14 trials (761 participants), found acyclovir probably improves practitioner-rated rash (relative risk 2.45, 3 trials, 141 participants) while its itch results conflicted — one 21-patient trial found placebo better for itch resolution. Ciccarese 2024 (PMID: 39597810), a network meta-analysis of 12 RCTs, ranked acyclovir best for rash improvement (relative risk 2.55 versus placebo) and oral steroids best for itch. The primary trials bracket the plausible effect: Drago 2006 (PMID: 16384760), unblinded, found 79% versus 4% full regression by day 14; Ganguly 2014 (PMID: 24995231), double-blind, found complete resolution of 86.66% versus 33.33%. Macrolides other than erythromycin showed probably no difference from placebo. Proposed stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) for oral acyclovir on rash improvement (relative risk 2.45 in Cochrane pooling; 86.66% vs 33.33% complete resolution in the one double-blind trial) — its effect on itch is unresolved

title: Polyhydramnios: draining fluid was followed by delivery at a median 36.5 weeks with rare immediate complications in 86 pregnancies — but no study shows draining prolongs pregnancy, and indomethacin rests on one 22-woman series from the 1990s
question: In a pregnancy complicated by polyhydramnios (excess amniotic fluid), does amnioreduction (draining fluid) or indomethacin improve outcomes, and what are the risks?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), observational evidence only — no randomised or controlled trial of any treatment for polyhydramnios was found. Amnioreduction is done to relieve maternal symptoms: in Laoreti 2024 (PMID: 38671719), 86 pregnancies drained at a median 32.5 weeks delivered at a median 36.5 weeks, 30 days after the first drain, with one abruption and two preterm deliveries as immediate complications — but 79% had a fetal anomaly, and there is no untreated comparison. Zargarzadeh 2025 (PMID: 40254983) pooled seven studies (390 singleton pregnancies) and found low pooled odds of abruption (0.04) and delivery within 48 hours (0.10), while stating that evidence for fetal benefit or pregnancy prolongation is lacking. Indomethacin rests on Cabrol 1996 (PMID: 8735752): 22 women, fluid reduction reported, mean delivery at 37.5 weeks, uncontrolled. Proposed stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) for amnioreduction as a symptom-relieving procedure.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) for amnioreduction to relieve symptoms, with delivery at a median 36.5 weeks and low pooled complication odds — observational evidence only; no study shows it prolongs pregnancy, and indomethacin rests on one 22-woman retrospective series

title: Polymorphic light eruption: hydroxychloroquine beat placebo on rash in one small 1987 trial (13 vs 15 patients, P < 0.01) and edged chloroquine in 117 patients; calcipotriol cream cut provoked symptoms by 32% in 13 patients
question: In people with polymorphic light eruption, which treatments reduce or prevent the eruption, and how strong is the trial evidence?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) for antimalarials, on small old trials. The only placebo-controlled trial of hydroxychloroquine (Murphy 1987, PMID: 3552020; 13 patients on active treatment and 15 on placebo over June-August 1982) found moderate clinical improvement with a statistically significant improvement in skin rash (P less than 0.01). The larger head-to-head trial (Pareek 2008, PMID: 18187817; 117 patients) found hydroxychloroquine beat chloroquine on burning, itching and erythema severity scores (P < 0.05) but not scaling (P = 0.229), with good-to-excellent responses in 68.9% on hydroxychloroquine versus 63% on chloroquine and no placebo arm, so neither drug is proven against no treatment by this trial. A tiny intra-individual trial of calcipotriol cream (PMID: 21428979; NCT00871052; 13 patients, lesions provoked in 12) found pretreatment reduced the PLE test score by an average of 32% relative to placebo cream (95% CI 21-44%; P = 0.0022) after photoprovocation. No trial of topical or systemic corticosteroids or of desensitisation phototherapy was carded this session. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): hydroxychloroquine probably eases PLE, but the placebo-controlled evidence is one 28-patient trial from 1987.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Progressive supranuclear palsy: no drug has slowed it — davunetide (313 patients), gosuranemab (486) and tideglusib (146) all matched placebo on the PSP Rating Scale over 52 weeks
question: In people with progressive supranuclear palsy, does any drug treatment slow progression or improve function compared with placebo?
balance: No tested drug has slowed progressive supranuclear palsy. Davunetide (Boxer 2014, PMID: 24873720; NCT01110720; 313 patients) changed the PSP Rating Scale by a median 11.8 points on both arms (p=0.41) and the Schwab and England scale by -0.20 on both (p=0.92) over 52 weeks. Gosuranemab (Dam 2021, PMID: 34385707; NCT03068468; 486 dosed) changed the PSP Rating Scale by 10.4 versus 10.6 points (P = 0.85) despite cutting unbound N-terminal tau in spinal fluid by 98%. Tideglusib (Tolosa 2014, PMID: 24532007; 146 patients) showed no significant difference on the primary or any secondary endpoint at either dose; its MRI substudy's slower atrophy signal never translated into clinical benefit. Riluzole and tilavonemab are named in the synthesis watch-out as further negative trials not carded this session. PROPOSED MAYBE (the treatment made no difference): three adequately sized, blinded, placebo-controlled trials of three different tau-directed mechanisms all came back flat, so care remains symptomatic and supportive.
stamp: MAYBE (the treatment made no difference)

title: Prosopagnosia: face training gives modest laboratory gains — the one placebo-controlled trial (20 adults) improved face memory but not perception; everyday benefit unproven
question: In people with prosopagnosia (face blindness), do training or rehabilitation interventions improve face recognition?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence). Face training produces modest laboratory gains in developmental prosopagnosia, from small uncontrolled or waitlist-controlled studies. DeGutis 2014 (PMID: 24691394; 24 adults) found moderate but significant training-related improvement in front-view face discrimination versus a waiting period after a 3-week online holistic-processing programme, with the best trainees normalising holistic processing. Bate 2022 (PMID: 35386218) ran the only placebo-controlled trial (20 adults): face-specific gains in face memory, not perception, greatest in those worst at entry and persisting 2 weeks after training; in a 4-child case series (n=4 printed on the face), 3 children improved in face memory. The critical review (Bate & Bennetts 2014, PMID: 25100965) concludes gains across the rehabilitation literature are limited, with laborious compensatory techniques, limited generalisation to untrained faces and limited maintenance. No drug treatment exists. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): training helps test performance a little; everyday-life benefit is unproven.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence)

title: Pyoderma gangrenosum: ciclosporin and prednisolone heal identically (47% by 6 months on each in STOP GAP); infliximab beat placebo 46% vs 6% at week 2 in the one small placebo-controlled trial
question: In people with pyoderma gangrenosum, how do ciclosporin, prednisolone, infliximab and topical therapy compare for healing ulcers?
balance: SPLIT. The two standard systemic drugs are equal: in STOP GAP (Ormerod 2015, PMID: 26071094; ISRCTN35898459; 112 analysed), healing speed at 6 weeks differed by 0.003 cm2/day (95% CI -0.20 to 0.21; P=0.97) between ciclosporin and prednisolone, and 47% of each group had healed by 6 months, with serious adverse reactions, especially infections, commoner on prednisolone. Infliximab beat placebo in the only placebo-controlled trial (Brooklyn 2006, PMID: 16188920; 30 patients): improvement at week 2 in 46% (6/13) versus 6% (1/17) (p=0.025). For smaller ulcers managed topically, the STOP GAP prospective cohort (Thomas 2016, PMID: 27502313; 66 patients, no comparator) saw 28 of 66 (43.8%) healed by 6 months on mainly clobetasol or tacrolimus. PROPOSED SPLIT: choose between ciclosporin and prednisolone on side-effect profile; infliximab has real but small-trial placebo-controlled support; topical therapy heals a similar share of milder disease without systemic toxicity.
stamp: SPLIT

title: Q fever: doxycycline settles acute pneumonia fever about a day faster than erythromycin (3 vs 4.3 days, 48 patients); chronic endocarditis needs 18-24 months of doxycycline plus hydroxychloroquine on observational data
question: In people with Q fever, which antibiotic treatments work for acute disease, and what regimen and duration treat chronic Q fever endocarditis?
balance: SPLIT by form of disease. For acute Q fever pneumonia, the one randomised trial (Sobradillo 1992, PMID: 1585291; 48 proven cases) found fever settled faster on doxycycline than erythromycin (3 (1.6) versus 4.3 (2) days) with far fewer side effects (2 versus 11 patients, p less than 0.01), and 47 of 48 chest radiographs were normal by day 40 — the illness is largely self-limiting. For chronic Q fever endocarditis there is no randomised trial: the Marseille comparison (Raoult 1999, PMID: 9927100; 35 patients) found doxycycline plus hydroxychloroquine cured 17 of 21 with a mean treatment duration of 31 months and no relapses beyond 18 months of therapy, versus 7 relapses among 14 on doxycycline plus a quinolone needing a mean 55 months. The 104-patient long-term survey (Million 2010, PMID: 20637694) fixed the optimum at 18 months for native valves and 24 months for prosthetic valves, with treatment under 18 months a relative hazard for relapse of 9.69. PROPOSED SPLIT: doxycycline first for acute disease on one small RCT; the chronic regimen rests entirely on observational referral-centre data and caps at POSSIBLE.
stamp: SPLIT

title: Reactive arthritis: antibiotics fail overall (pooled relative risk of non-remission 0.74, 95% CI 0.49-1.10) — except one 42-patient trial in PCR-positive chronic Chlamydia disease (responders 63% vs 20%)
question: In people with reactive arthritis, do antibiotics improve remission — and does prolonged combination antibiotic therapy help chronic Chlamydia-induced disease?
balance: SPLIT by trigger and chronicity. Pooled across all reactive arthritis, antibiotics do not work: the Barber 2013 meta-analysis (DOI 10.3899/jrheum.121192; 12 trials) gives a relative risk of failure to achieve remission of 0.74 (95% CI 0.49-1.10) with heavy heterogeneity (I2 = 76.3%), attenuating to 0.87 (0.70-1.10) when unblinded trials are excluded, and a relative 97% increase in gastrointestinal adverse events. Single-agent ciprofloxacin for 3 months was flat against placebo (Sieper 1999, PMID: 10403266; 126 randomised). The exception is chronic Chlamydia-induced disease with PCR-proven persistent infection: Carter 2010 (PMID: 20155838; NCT00351273; 42 patients) found 6 months of combination antibiotics (doxycycline or azithromycin, each with rifampin) produced responders in 17 of 27 (63%) versus 3 of 15 (20%) on placebo, with complete remission in 6 of 27 versus 0 of 15. PROPOSED SPLIT: no antibiotics for ordinary or enteric reactive arthritis; POSSIBLE benefit for prolonged combination therapy in the narrow PCR-positive chronic Chlamydia subgroup, on one 42-patient trial.
stamp: SPLIT

title: Repetitive strain injury: no conservative treatment has consistent trial support — exercises did not improve pain in 6,580 pooled participants and the 2026 Cochrane update finds ergonomics make little to no difference
question: In adults with repetitive strain injury (work-related complaints of the arm, neck or shoulder), do exercises, ergonomic changes or other conservative treatments reduce pain, disability or sick leave?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — no conservative treatment for repetitive strain injury (work-related complaints of the arm, neck or shoulder, CANS) has a consistent effect. The Cochrane review (Verhagen 2013, PMID: 24338903; 44 studies, 6,580 participants, 25 interventions) found very low-quality evidence that exercises did not improve pain versus no treatment (SMD -0.52, 95% CI -1.08 to 0.03) and that ergonomic interventions did not reduce pain short-term (SMD -0.07, 95% CI -0.36 to 0.22) though they did at long-term follow-up (SMD -0.76, 95% CI -1.35 to -0.16), with sick leave lower in two studies (relative risk 0.48, 95% CI 0.32 to 0.76). The 2026 Cochrane ergonomics update (Mehta 2026, PMID: 42946017) tightened the verdict: ergonomic interventions may result in little to no difference in pain versus no treatment, usual care or placebo (SMD -0.23, 95% CI -0.54 to 0.08; 4 RCTs, 692 participants; low-certainty). The earlier RSI-specific review (Konijnenberg 2001, PMID: 11712610; 15 trials, 702 participants) likewise found no strong evidence for any conservative option. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): ergonomic changes and exercise are reasonable and low-harm, but trial evidence that they relieve RSI is inconsistent and low-certainty.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence)

title: Selective mutism: behavioural treatment beats no treatment with large effects (g = 0.87-1.06 across 5 small RCTs) — but remission and advantage over active treatment are unproven
question: In children with selective mutism, do psychological or behavioural treatments increase speaking and produce remission compared with no treatment or other care?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) for behavioural/psychological treatment. The RCT-only meta-analysis (Steains 2021, PMID: 34265102; 5 RCTs, 233 children) found psychological interventions more effective than no treatment with a large overall weighted effect (Hedges g = 0.87). The broader systematic review (Hipolito 2023, PMID: 37720585; 25 studies, 5 RCTs in the meta-analysis) found combined systems/behavioural approaches beat waitlist for speaking behaviour (Hedges g = 1.06, p < .0001, 95% CI 0.57-1.56), while the remission advantage (relative risk 4.25, 95% CI 0.52-34.84) was not significant and the two active-control RCTs pooled non-significantly (g = 0.55, 95% CI -0.47 to 1.57). The 2025 questionnaire meta-analysis (Iimura 2025, PMID: 40181492; 12 studies, 472 participants) found the mean Selective Mutism Questionnaire total improved by 0.51 (95% CI 0.32-0.70; g = 1.00), with face-to-face treatment improving scores by 0.59 versus 0.12 for web-based. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): effects are large against waitlist but the whole RCT base is five small trials, and drug treatment (SSRIs) has no placebo-controlled support and is not carded.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Shin splints (medial tibial stress syndrome): no treatment is proven — shockwave beat graded running alone by about 32 days in an unblinded study but matched a sham dose in the blinded trial, and arch-support insoles eased pain earlier (weeks 6–12) but not by week 18
question: In people with medial tibial stress syndrome (shin splints), do shockwave therapy, foot orthoses or any other treatment speed recovery or reduce pain compared with sham treatment, graded running or no treatment?
balance: No treatment for medial tibial stress syndrome is proven. The systematic review (Winters 2013, PMID: 23979968; 11 trials, 519 participants) found every randomised trial at high risk of bias and could recommend nothing: pooled lower-leg braces (SMD −0.06; 95% CI −0.44 to 0.32) and iontophoresis (SMD 0.09; 95% CI −0.50 to 0.68) showed no difference, and laser, stretching/strengthening, compression stockings and pulsed electromagnetic fields were unproven. Shockwave is the SPLIT at the centre of this shelf: in the non-randomised two-hospital comparison (Moen 2012, PMID: 21393260) adding ESWT to graded running cut recovery from 91.6 to 59.7 days, but in the double-blind sham-controlled pilot trial (Newman 2017, PMID: 27640922; n = 28) a standard dose beat a sham low dose by only 1.1 points of palpation pain out of 10 (95% CI −2.3 to 0.0) with no difference in running distance. Arch-support foot orthoses added to ice massage, exercise and shockwave (Naderi 2022, PMID: 33797477; n = 50) lowered pain and severity at weeks 6 and 12 but not at week 18 — earlier relief, not a better end result. PROPOSED: SPLIT (shockwave unproven against sham; orthoses give earlier relief only).
stamp: SPLIT (shockwave: positive only in unblinded studies, no difference against sham in the blinded trial · arch-support orthoses: earlier pain relief at 6–12 weeks, gone by week 18 · no treatment proven)
