title: Sick building syndrome: fixing the building helps — raising outdoor air eased symptoms within hours in a blinded experiment, and ultraviolet lights in the ventilation cut work-related symptoms (odds ratio 0.8) in 771 office workers; no treatment given to the person has been trialled
question: In people with sick building syndrome, which interventions — increased ventilation, ventilation-system decontamination, or treatments given to the person — reduce symptoms?
balance: Sick building syndrome is treated at the building, not the patient, and the carded evidence supports two building-level interventions. In a blinded crossover experiment (Wargocki 2000, PMID: 11089327; 30 subjects), raising outdoor air from 3 to 30 L/s per person reduced dry mouth/throat (P < 0.0006) and difficulty thinking clearly (P < 0.001) and improved office-task performance by 1.7% per doubling of ventilation. In a double-blind multiple crossover trial in three real office buildings (Menzies 2003, PMID: 14654316; 771 workers), ultraviolet germicidal irradiation of cooling coils and drip pans cut microbial/endotoxin surface contamination by 99% (relative) and was associated with fewer work-related symptoms overall (adjusted OR 0.8 [95% CI 0.7–0.99], relative), respiratory symptoms (OR 0.6) and mucosal symptoms (OR 0.7). The EUROVEN consensus (2002; 105 papers, 30 judged conclusive) agreed ventilation is strongly associated with SBS symptoms and that supply rates below 25 L/s per person increase SBS risk and sick leave. No carded trial tests any treatment given to the symptomatic person. PROPOSED: POSSIBLE (benefit) for building-level ventilation increase and ventilation-system decontamination.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — building-level interventions only: more outdoor air and ultraviolet decontamination of ventilation systems; no person-level treatment has trial evidence

title: Skin cysts: removing the whole cyst wall is what stops them coming back — punch incision matched elliptical excision on recurrence with a wound a third as long (0.73 vs 2.34 cm), and draining alone recurred more than excision across 1,303 patients
question: In people with a skin (epidermoid/epidermal inclusion) cyst, which removal technique — complete elliptical excision, punch or minimal incision, incision and drainage, or one-stage excision when inflamed — gives the lowest recurrence with the best cosmetic result?
balance: Complete removal of the cyst wall is what prevents recurrence, and the carded evidence is consistent on that: a 2026 systematic review (Guru Naidu, PMID: 41769601; 5 studies, 1,303 patients) found complete surgical excision consistently associated with lower recurrence than incision and drainage. How the wall is reached matters for the scar, not the recurrence: in the randomised trial (Lee 2006, PMID: 16681659; 60 patients) punch incision left a 0.73 cm wound in 12.7 minutes versus 2.34 cm and 21.6 minutes for elliptical excision, with no significant recurrence difference. For inflamed cysts, one-stage excision (Jun 2010; 351 patients, retrospective) halved antibiotic exposure (5.1 vs 10.9 days) and cost about a third of the conventional drain-first approach, but wound infection was higher (6.0% vs 1.6%). PROPOSED: SPLIT (complete excision beats drainage alone for recurrence; small-incision techniques match elliptical excision on recurrence with smaller scars; one-stage excision of inflamed cysts trades fewer antibiotics for more wound infections).
stamp: SPLIT (complete excision of the cyst wall: lower recurrence than incision and drainage · punch/minimal incision: same recurrence, wound 0.73 vs 2.34 cm · inflamed cysts excised in one stage: antibiotics 5.1 vs 10.9 days, wound infection 6.0% vs 1.6%)

title: Skin tags: scissors beat laser head-to-head (85% vs 71% fully healed at 12 weeks across 1,257 tags), electrosurgery beat freezing on satisfaction, and home freezing pens cleared anywhere from 7% to 64% of tags depending on the device
question: In people who want skin tags (acrochordons) removed, how do scissor snip excision, laser, cryotherapy, electrosurgery and home cryogenic devices compare on clearance, healing, pain and satisfaction?
balance: Three randomised comparisons, three different winners by setting. In the largest, a split-body trial (Haase 2025, PMID: 40347285; 68 patients, 1,257 tags), scissor snip excision beat non-ablative 532 nm laser on complete healing at 12 weeks (85% vs 71%), pain (2.6 vs 3.42) and patient preference (63% vs 19%). In an assessor-blind trial (PMID: 39512253), electrosurgery gave significantly higher patient and physician satisfaction than cryotherapy for skin tags, with cryotherapy leaving hypopigmentation in 3.1% and depigmentation in 6.3% of lesions (pooled across lesion types). For home treatment, device choice dominated: the Pixie cryogenic pen cleared 64.3% of tags completely versus 7.1% for a comparator pen (Antunes 2021, PMID: 34019230). No trial compares removal with leaving tags alone, and none reports recurrence. PROPOSED: SPLIT (clinic: scissors/electrosurgery ahead of laser/cryotherapy in head-to-head trials; home freezing: 7–64% clearance depending on device).
stamp: SPLIT (scissor snip: 85% healed at 12 weeks vs 71% for laser · electrosurgery: higher satisfaction than cryotherapy · home cryo pens: complete clearance 64.3% vs 7.1% by device)

title: Stretch marks: tretinoin cream improved early red marks (80% vs 8% much improved on placebo cream), while for white marks CO2 laser and microneedling helped equally — and neither has ever been tested against simply leaving them alone
question: In people with stretch marks (striae distensae), do topical tretinoin, fractional CO2 laser, microneedling or platelet-rich plasma improve the marks compared with vehicle, each other, or no treatment?
balance: The evidence splits by the age of the marks. For early, red, active stretch marks, the one double-blind vehicle-controlled trial (Kang 1996, PMID: 8624148; 22 patients) found 0.1% tretinoin clearly better than vehicle: 80% versus 8% with definite or marked improvement at 6 months, and treated marks shrank 14% in length while vehicle marks grew 10%. For mature white marks (striae alba), a randomised split-body trial (Saki 2022, PMID: 34796595; 40 patients) found fractional CO2 laser and microneedling both shrank striae significantly with no difference between them — but with no untreated control, improvement over natural fading is unproven. Adding platelet-rich plasma to CO2 laser (Madegowda 2023, PMID: 38189063; 24 patients) raised 'excellent' responses from 16.6% to 33.3%, with hyperpigmentation in 19 of 24 patients resolving by 6 months. PROPOSED: SPLIT (tretinoin POSSIBLE for early red marks only; devices improve white marks versus baseline, unproven versus doing nothing).
stamp: SPLIT (tretinoin 0.1%: 80% vs 8% much improved for early red marks in one small blinded trial · white marks: CO2 laser and microneedling indistinguishable, neither tested against no treatment)

title: Swollen legs from venous disease: compression works, and adjustable beats tight — self-adjustable Velcro wraps cut leg volume 26% versus 19% for high-pressure bandages in a week, moderate stockings matched bandages, and adding physiotherapy changed nothing
question: In adults with swollen ankles, feet and legs from chronic venous insufficiency (peripheral oedema), which treatments — compression stockings, bandages, adjustable compression devices, or added physiotherapy — reduce leg volume, and how do they compare?
balance: Scoped to chronic venous leg oedema — the form of swollen legs with randomised treatment trials; drug-induced, cardiac, renal and lymphatic oedema are different questions, and the library already homes venous-symptom drug treatments (horse chestnut, Shelf #2504; micronised flavonoid fraction, Shelf #3477). Compression is the base treatment in every carded trial. Moderate-pressure stockings (23–32 mmHg) matched high-pressure inelastic bandages at 7 days (leg volume −13.2% vs −15.6%, not significant; Mosti 2012, PMID: 22090466; 30 patients). Patient-adjustable Velcro devices beat bandages over the first week (median volume reduction 26% vs 19%, p < .001) because their pressure does not decay (Mosti 2015, PMID: 26160211; 36 patients). Adding a physiotherapy programme of exercise and self-drainage to compression made no difference to oedema or function (Moreno-Segura 2026, PMID: 41549735). PROPOSED: SPLIT (adjustable/moderate compression at least as good as high-pressure bandages in week 1; added physiotherapy: the treatment made no difference).
stamp: SPLIT (venous leg oedema: adjustable Velcro devices −26% vs bandages −19% leg volume at 7 days · moderate stockings ≈ high-pressure bandages · added physiotherapy: the treatment made no difference)

title: Swollen arm after breast cancer treatment: compression shrinks the swelling by about a quarter — but hands-on lymphatic drainage added nothing in the two best trials (0.0 and −0.2 percentage points versus placebo drainage in 194 women)
question: In women with a swollen arm and hand from breast cancer-related lymphoedema, does decongestive therapy — and specifically its manual lymphatic drainage component — reduce arm volume compared with compression garments alone or placebo drainage?
balance: Scoped to breast cancer-related arm lymphoedema — the cause of swollen arms and hands with randomised treatment evidence; prevention (Shelf #3427) and resistance exercise (Shelf #1786) are homed separately. Compression-based therapy reduces swelling in every trial arm: garments alone cut excess arm volume by 22.6% (Dayes 2013), and decongestive therapy arms fell by about a fifth to a quarter in relative terms over 3 weeks (EFforT-BCRL). The contested add-on is manual lymphatic drainage (MLD). Cochrane (Ezzo 2015, PMID: 25994425) pooled two small trials (83 participants) showing bandaging alone reducing swelling 30–38.6% with a further 7.11% from MLD — but the two best trials found no added effect: Dayes 2013 (103 women) gave 29.0% versus 22.6% for full decongestive therapy versus garments alone (difference 6.4%, 95% CI −6.8 to 20.5; P = .34), and the blinded EFforT-BCRL trial (De Vrieze 2022, PMID: 35428594; NCT02609724; 194 women) found differences of 0.0 and −0.2 percentage points versus traditional and placebo drainage. PROPOSED: SPLIT (compression-based therapy effective; added MLD: the treatment made no difference in the two best trials).
stamp: SPLIT (compression-based decongestive therapy reduces arm swelling ~23–39% · adding manual lymphatic drainage: +7.11% in small old trials, but the treatment made no difference in the two large/blinded trials)

title: Testicular cancer: less treatment, same cure — 3 cycles of BEP matched 4 in good-prognosis disease (2-year progression-free survival 90.4% vs 89.4%), and one adjuvant BEP course prevented more recurrences than major lymph-node surgery in stage I disease (2 vs 15)
question: In men with testicular germ cell cancer, how much treatment is enough — three versus four cycles of BEP for good-prognosis metastatic disease, and adjuvant chemotherapy versus retroperitoneal lymph node dissection (or surveillance) for stage I nonseminoma?
balance: Scoped to the randomised treatment choices in germ cell tumours; adjuvant treatment of stage I seminoma (carboplatin versus radiotherapy) is already homed on Shelf #1876 and is not re-carded. In good-prognosis metastatic disease, three cycles of BEP were equivalent to four (2-year progression-free survival 90.4% vs 89.4%; difference −1.0%, 80% confidence limits −3.8 to +1.8), and a 3-day schedule matched 5 days for efficacy (de Wit 2001, EORTC 30941/MRC TE20; 812 patients; PMID not captured this session, DOI 10.1200/JCO.2001.19.6.1629) — though the nested quality-of-life study (Fosså 2003, PMID: 12637478; 666 patients) found the 3-day schedule cost more gastrointestinal toxicity and tinnitus, so 5 days is preferred if four cycles are planned. In clinical stage I nonseminoma after orchidectomy, one course of adjuvant BEP prevented more recurrences than retroperitoneal lymph node dissection (2 vs 15 recurrences; 2-year recurrence-free survival 99.46% vs 91.87%; Albers 2008, PMID: 18458040; 382 patients). PROPOSED: SPLIT (de-escalation wins on both questions — fewer cycles for metastatic good-prognosis disease, one chemo course over big surgery for stage I nonseminoma).
stamp: SPLIT (good-prognosis metastatic: 3 BEP cycles equivalent to 4 — 2-year PFS 90.4% vs 89.4% · stage I nonseminoma: 1 adjuvant BEP course, 2 vs 15 recurrences against lymph-node surgery)

title: Thoracic outlet syndrome: almost no controlled evidence — one small trial favoured removing the first rib for pain, botulinum toxin matched placebo, and surgery's 76–85% 'success' comes entirely from uncontrolled case series with 13–26% complication rates
question: In people with thoracic outlet syndrome, do surgery (first rib resection, scalenectomy), botulinum toxin injections or conservative treatment improve pain, disability and paresthesias compared with each other, placebo or no treatment?
balance: Thoracic outlet syndrome has the thinnest controlled evidence on this shelf. Cochrane (Povlsen 2014, PMID: 25427003) found only two randomised trials with adequate follow-up: first rib resection decreased pain more than brachial plexus neuroplasty in 55 patients with 'disputed' TOS (high risk of bias), and botulinum toxin injection into the scalene muscles did not significantly improve pain or disability versus saline placebo in 37 patients (low risk of bias), though paresthesias improved. All surgical enthusiasm comes from uncontrolled series: pooled success rates of 76–85% and complete relief of 53–61%, with complication rates of 12.6–25.9% (2019 review, PMID: 30122304), and a 2023 meta-analysis (PMID: 37055338; 22 series, 2,010 patients) ranking rib-sparing scalenectomy best on DASH improvement (43.0 points) and complications (3.6%). No trial compares surgery with physiotherapy or no treatment, and the diagnosis lacks generally accepted criteria. PROPOSED: MAYBE (weak evidence) for surgery in selected patients failing conservative care.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — one small high-bias trial favours first rib resection for pain; botulinum toxin matched placebo; all other surgical data are uncontrolled series (success 76–85%, complications 12.6–25.9%)

title: Toe pain from a bunion (hallux valgus): surgery cut pain more than waiting or an insole at 1 year (about 19 points on a 0-100 scale in the one head-to-head trial) — but waiting a year first did not worsen the final result
question: In adults with toe pain from hallux valgus (a bunion), does surgery relieve pain better than an orthosis or watchful waiting, and does delaying surgery harm the final result?
balance: For painful hallux valgus (bunion) — the commonest specific, trial-tested cause of great-toe pain — surgery beats waiting and beats an orthosis on pain at one year, but the margin rests on one unblinded Finnish trial. Torkki 2001 (PMID: 11368700; 209 patients randomised to chevron osteotomy, foot orthosis or a 1-year waiting list) found pain fell more with surgery than with no treatment at 6 months (adjusted mean difference -20 points, 95% CI -28 to -12) and at 1 year (-19, 95% CI -28 to -10); the orthosis helped at 6 months (-14, 95% CI -22 to -6) but not by 1 year, and 83% of the surgery group versus 46% orthosis and 24% control felt improved at 1 year. The 2-year follow-up (PMID: 12807332) found waiting a year, with or without orthoses, did not jeopardise the final result. The Cochrane review (Dias 2024, PMID: 39051477; 25 RCTs, 1,597 participants) found surgery may give a clinically important pain reduction versus no treatment (mean pain 21 vs 39 points at 12 months, MD -18.00, 95% CI -26.14 to -9.86; low-certainty, from that same single trial), a slight function gain (AOFAS 75 vs 66), and little to no difference in quality of life (93 vs 93 points); complex osteotomies probably match simple ones for pain and may increase reoperation. Other toe-pain causes (acute gout flare, Morton's neuroma, plantar heel pain) are homed on their own shelves. PROPOSED STAMP: POSSIBLE (benefit) for surgery over conservative care for painful bunion, on low-certainty evidence dominated by one unblinded trial.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — surgery for painful hallux valgus (bunion) reduces pain more than waiting or an orthosis at 1 year (about 18-20 points on a 0-100 scale), on low-certainty evidence from essentially one unblinded trial; an orthosis helps for about 6 months, and waiting a year does not worsen the final result

title: Vaginal cancer: no randomised trial exists — in 2,517 registry patients, adding brachytherapy to radiotherapy was associated with median survival of 6.1 versus 3.6 years, and a brachytherapy boost with chemoradiation gave 5-year survival of 62.9% versus 49.3%
question: In women with primary vaginal cancer, how should the cancer be treated, and does including brachytherapy in definitive (chemo)radiation improve survival?
balance: There are no randomised trials in primary vaginal cancer; the record itself states that prospective randomised data do not exist. Treatment is definitive radiotherapy, and every large dataset says the brachytherapy component matters. In the SEER analysis of Orton 2016 (PMID: 27036631; 2,517 patients), median overall survival was 6.1 years with brachytherapy (alone or with external beam) versus 3.6 years with external beam alone, and brachytherapy was associated with a lower risk of death in the propensity-matched cohort (HR 0.77, 95% CI 0.68-0.86), across all FIGO stages and in tumours over 5 cm (HR 0.68, 95% CI 0.50-0.91). In the National Cancer Database analysis of Reshko 2021 (1,094 patients treated with definitive chemoradiation), adding a brachytherapy boost was associated with better 5-year overall survival (62.9% vs 49.3%, P=0.0126), and completing radiotherapy within 63 days was also associated with better survival (67.8% vs 54.5%, P=0.0031). A single-centre series (Merten 2024; 27 patients, FIGO I-III) reported 5-year overall survival of 90% and disease-free survival of 68% with brachytherapy with or without external beam and chemotherapy, with grade 3 late toxicity in 3 of 22 patients (13.6%) and one grade 4 event (4.5%). All of this is observational, so fitter patients may simply be the ones who receive brachytherapy. PROPOSED STAMP: POSSIBLE (benefit) for including brachytherapy in definitive radiotherapy — the observational cap applies.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — including brachytherapy in definitive radiotherapy for primary vaginal cancer is associated with longer survival in two large database cohorts (observational evidence only, so the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE)

title: Vaginismus: brief intensive therapist-aided exposure worked in 89% of women versus 11% waiting (one RCT) — standard CBT managed only 14%, and botulinum toxin's 75% in refractory cases comes from a series with no control group
question: In women with vaginismus, which treatments — psychological therapy, therapist-aided exposure, or botulinum toxin injection — actually enable penetration and intercourse?
balance: The strongest evidence in vaginismus is for brief, intensive therapist-aided exposure. In ter Kuile 2013 (PMID: 24060195; 70 women with lifelong vaginismus randomised to exposure or a 3-month waiting list), 31 of 35 treated women (89%, 95% CI 72-96%) achieved intercourse versus 4 of 35 controls (11%, 95% CI 4-28%), most within the first 2 weeks, after at most three 2-hour sessions in one week. The earlier, gentler CBT programme was far weaker: van Lankveld 2006 (PMID: 16551154; 117 women randomised to group CBT, bibliotherapy or waiting list) found successful intercourse in 14% of treated women versus 0% of controls after treatment, rising only to 21% (group therapy) and 15% (bibliotherapy) at 12 months. For refractory cases, botulinum toxin rests on a single uncontrolled series: Ghazizadeh & Nikzad 2004 (24 women with grade 3-4 vaginismus who had failed previous treatment) reported 23 of 24 (95.8%) with little or no vaginismus at examination one week after injection and 18 (75%) achieving satisfactory intercourse after the first injection, with no recurrence over a mean 12.3 months — but with no control group, none of that can be separated from expectation and natural course. PROPOSED STAMP: SPLIT — intensive therapist-aided exposure has a large randomised effect (LIKELY benefit within this shelf's scale is not used; the shelf proposes POSSIBLE-to-strong for exposure), standard CBT a small one, and botulinum toxin is unproven beyond an uncontrolled series (MAYBE). The formal proposed stamp below is SPLIT.
stamp: SPLIT (therapist-aided exposure: large randomised benefit, 89% vs 11% achieved intercourse · standard CBT/bibliotherapy: small benefit, 14% vs 0% · botulinum toxin for refractory cases: MAYBE (weak evidence), one uncontrolled series of 24 women)

title: Von Willebrand disease: for heavy periods, tranexamic acid beat recombinant VWF (blood-loss score 146 vs 213) and desmopressin in randomised trials; for severe frequent bleeding, VWF concentrate prophylaxis cut bleeds by 84% in a single-arm study
question: In people with von Willebrand disease, what works for heavy menstrual bleeding, and does regular von Willebrand factor concentrate prophylaxis prevent bleeds in severe disease?
balance: Treatment splits by problem. For heavy menstrual bleeding, the randomised VWDMin trial (Ragni 2023, PMID: 37385272; NCT02606045; 39 women enrolled, 36 completing, with mild or moderate VWD) found recombinant VWF was NOT superior to tranexamic acid: median pictorial blood-loss (PBAC) score after two cycles was 146 (95% CI 117-199) on tranexamic acid versus 213 (152-298) on recombinant VWF (adjusted mean difference 46, 95% CI 2-90; P=0.039), and neither treatment brought scores into the normal range (the primary endpoint was not met; the trial stopped early for slow recruitment). An earlier crossover RCT in women with menorrhagia and abnormal laboratory haemostasis (Kouides 2009, PMID: 19236375; 116 women) likewise found tranexamic acid reduced PBAC scores more than intranasal desmopressin (estimated fall -105.7 vs -64.1; difference 41.6, P=0.0002), with both improving quality of life. For frequent severe bleeding, the prospective WIL-31 study (Sidonio 2024, PMID: 38237075; NCT04052698; 33 patients aged 6+, two-thirds type 3) found plasma-derived VWF/FVIII concentrate prophylaxis (the tested product was wilate, Octapharma) cut the mean total annualised bleeding rate by 84.4% versus the patients' own prior on-demand period (to 5.2 bleeds/year) and spontaneous bleeding by 86.9%, with no treatment-related serious adverse events or thromboses — but there was no parallel control group. PROPOSED STAMP: SPLIT — tranexamic acid ahead of both recombinant VWF and desmopressin for heavy menstrual bleeding on randomised evidence (POSSIBLE); concentrate prophylaxis strongly positive but single-arm (POSSIBLE, capped).
stamp: SPLIT (heavy menstrual bleeding: POSSIBLE (benefit) for tranexamic acid, which beat recombinant VWF and intranasal desmopressin in randomised crossovers · frequent severe bleeding: POSSIBLE (benefit) for VWF concentrate prophylaxis, 84.4% fewer bleeds in a single-arm trial)

title: Vulval cancer: a negative sentinel node makes full groin clearance unnecessary (groin recurrence 2.3%, 3-year survival 97%); radiotherapy replaces clearance safely only for deposits up to 2 mm — larger deposits recurred in 22% versus 6.9%
question: In early-stage vulval (vulvar) cancer, can full groin lymph-node clearance be safely omitted after sentinel-node biopsy, and how should a positive sentinel node be treated?
balance: Early-stage vulval (vulvar) cancer treatment was transformed by the GROINSS-V programme, all prospective but none of it randomised. GROINSS-V I (van der Zee 2008, PMID: 18281661; 403 patients with tumours <4 cm) showed that when the sentinel node was negative, omitting full inguinofemoral lymphadenectomy left a groin recurrence rate of just 2.3% (6 recurrences among 259 patients with unifocal disease and a negative sentinel node; 3-year survival 97%). Long-term follow-up (te Grootenhuis 2016; 377 patients, median follow-up 105 months) confirmed an isolated groin recurrence rate of 2.5% in sentinel-node-negative patients versus 8.0% in node-positive patients, with 5- and 10-year disease-specific survival of 93.5% and 90.8% versus 75.5% and 64.5%. For a positive sentinel node, size decides: in GROINSS-V II (Oonk 2021, PMID: 34432481; 1,535 registered patients), radiotherapy (50 Gy) instead of lymphadenectomy gave a 2-year isolated groin recurrence rate of 1.6% in 126 treated patients with micrometastases (2 mm or less) — but 22% versus 6.9% with lymphadenectomy (P=0.011) in macrometastases, which forced a protocol amendment mid-trial; radiotherapy caused less treatment-related morbidity than lymphadenectomy. Chemoradiation for macrometastases is being tested in GROINSS-V III (NCT05076942) and has no results yet. PROPOSED STAMP: SPLIT — omitting lymphadenectomy after a negative sentinel node, and radiotherapy for micrometastases, are supported by large prospective cohorts (POSSIBLE, the observational cap); radiotherapy alone for macrometastases made things worse (more recurrences).
stamp: SPLIT (negative sentinel node or micrometastasis ≤2 mm: POSSIBLE (benefit) for de-escalated treatment — groin recurrence 1.6-2.5% without full node clearance · macrometastasis >2 mm: radiotherapy alone was worse than lymphadenectomy, 22% vs 6.9% recurrence)

title: Wolff-Parkinson-White: in asymptomatic patients with high-risk pathways, prophylactic ablation cut arrhythmic events from 60% to 5% over 5 years (relative risk 0.08) in the randomised trial, and no ablated patient in a 2,169-patient registry developed ventricular fibrillation
question: In Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome, does catheter ablation help — in particular, should asymptomatic patients at high risk of arrhythmia have prophylactic ablation?
balance: For symptomatic WPW, catheter ablation is the established definitive treatment; the trial evidence addresses the harder question of prophylactic ablation in asymptomatic people found to be at high risk on electrophysiological testing. In Pappone 2003 (PMID: 14602878; 72 high-risk asymptomatic patients randomised from 224 eligible), arrhythmic events over 5 years occurred in 2 of 37 ablated patients (5%) versus 21 of 35 controls (60%); the 5-year Kaplan-Meier incidence was 7% versus 77% (relative risk 0.08, 95% CI 0.02-0.33; P<0.001), and one control patient presented with ventricular fibrillation. The paediatric trial (Pappone 2004, PMID: 15371577) found the same pattern in high-risk children aged 5-12: events in 1 of 20 ablated (5%) versus 12 of 27 controls (44%), with two control children suffering ventricular fibrillation and one sudden death; three ablation complications occurred, one needing hospitalisation. The group's 8-year registry (Pappone 2014, PMID: 25052405; 2,169 patients) found ablation successful in 98.5%, no malignant arrhythmia or ventricular fibrillation after ablation, and ventricular fibrillation in 1.5% of untreated patients — almost all children — predicted by a short accessory-pathway refractory period rather than by symptoms. All of this comes from one Milan group, the trials are small, and the endpoint is arrhythmic events, not mortality. PROPOSED STAMP: POSSIBLE (benefit) for prophylactic ablation in asymptomatic patients with high-risk electrophysiological features; no randomised evidence supports ablating low-risk asymptomatic patients.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — prophylactic catheter ablation in asymptomatic WPW patients with high-risk electrophysiological features greatly reduces arrhythmic events (relative risk 0.08 in the adult RCT), on small single-centre randomised evidence

title: Ceftazidime-avibactam: non-inferior to carbapenems in all three approved uses — cUTI cure/eradication 71.2% vs 64.5%, cIAI cure 81.6% vs 85.1%, pneumonia cure 68.8% vs 73.0% in the phase 3 trials
question: In adults with complicated urinary tract infection, complicated intra-abdominal infection, or hospital-acquired/ventilator-associated pneumonia, is ceftazidime-avibactam as effective as a carbapenem?
balance: Across its three approved uses, ceftazidime-avibactam (Avycaz in the US; the tested combination of ceftazidime with the beta-lactamase inhibitor avibactam) was non-inferior to a carbapenem in large double-blind phase 3 trials. In cUTI (RECAPTURE; Wagenlehner 2016, PMID: 27313268; NCT01595438/NCT01599806; 1,033 randomised), symptomatic resolution at day 5 was 70.2% versus 66.2% on doripenem (difference 4.0%, 95% CI -2.39 to 10.42) and combined symptomatic resolution with microbiological eradication at test of cure was 71.2% versus 64.5% (difference 6.7%, 95% CI 0.30 to 13.12), with microbiological eradication itself higher on ceftazidime-avibactam (77.4% vs 71.0%). In cIAI (RECLAIM; Mazuski 2016, PMID: 26962078; NCT01499290/NCT01500239; 1,066 patients, ceftazidime-avibactam plus metronidazole versus meropenem), clinical cure in the microbiologically modified intention-to-treat population was 81.6% versus 85.1% (difference -3.5%, 95% CI -8.64 to 1.58), non-inferior in all analysis populations, with cure of 83.0% versus 85.9% in ceftazidime-resistant infections. In nosocomial pneumonia including VAP (REPROVE; Torres 2018, PMID: 29254862; NCT01808092; 879 randomised), clinical cure was 68.8% versus 73.0% on meropenem in the clinically modified intention-to-treat population (difference -4.2%, 95% CI -10.8 to 2.5), meeting non-inferiority, though serious adverse events were numerically more frequent on ceftazidime-avibactam (19% vs 13%). A pooled analysis of the phase 3 programme in beta-lactamase-producing pathogens (PMID: 37700689; 813 patients) found identical clinical cure rates of 88.1% in both arms among non-metallo-beta-lactamase producers. The drug has no activity against metallo-beta-lactamase producers, and none of these trials enrolled the carbapenem-resistant infections for which it is now mainly reserved. PROPOSED STAMP: LIKELY (non-inferior to carbapenems for cUTI, cIAI and HAP/VAP in the trial populations).
stamp: LIKELY (non-inferior to carbapenems) — ceftazidime-avibactam matched doripenem in cUTI and meropenem in cIAI (with metronidazole) and HAP/VAP in large double-blind phase 3 trials; inactive against metallo-beta-lactamase producers

title: Ceftolozane-tazobactam: non-inferior to meropenem in abdominal infection (cure 83.0% vs 87.3%) and ventilated pneumonia (28-day mortality 24.0% vs 25.3%), and ahead of levofloxacin in urinary infection (composite cure 76.9% vs 68.4%) — parity with standard agents, not superiority
question: In adults with complicated intra-abdominal infection (cIAI), complicated urinary tract infection (cUTI) or ventilated Gram-negative nosocomial pneumonia, is ceftolozane-tazobactam non-inferior to standard comparator antibiotics?
balance: Three double-blind phase 3 non-inferiority trials cover the approved uses. ASPECT-cIAI (Solomkin 2015, PMID: 25670823; NCT01445665 and NCT01445678): ceftolozane-tazobactam plus metronidazole vs meropenem in cIAI — clinical cure 83.0% (323/389) vs 87.3% (364/417), weighted difference -4.2% (95% CI -8.91 to 0.54), meeting the 10% margin; cure in ESBL-producing Enterobacteriaceae 95.8% (23/24) vs 88.5% (23/26). ASPECT-cUTI (Wagenlehner 2015, PMID: 25931244; NCT01345929 and NCT01345955): composite cure 76.9% (306/398) vs 68.4% (275/402) on high-dose levofloxacin, difference 95% CI 2.3 to 14.6 — the one superiority signal, against a comparator many enrolled pathogens already resisted. ASPECT-NP (Kollef 2019, PMID: 31563344; NCT02070757): 28-day mortality 24.0% (87/362) vs 25.3% (92/364) on meropenem and clinical cure 54% vs 53% in ventilated nosocomial pneumonia. Non-inferiority to an active comparator is parity, not proof of added benefit. Proposed stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — non-inferior to active comparators in all three approved uses; no superiority shown except against a resistance-handicapped levofloxacin comparator in cUTI

title: Imipenem-cilastatin-relebactam: in the small resistant-pathogen trial, overall response tied colistin plus imipenem (71% vs 70%) with far less kidney injury (nephrotoxicity 10% vs 56%); in pneumonia it was non-inferior to piperacillin-tazobactam (28-day mortality 15.9% vs 21.3%)
question: In adults with infections caused by imipenem-nonsusceptible Gram-negative pathogens, or with hospital-acquired/ventilator-associated bacterial pneumonia, is imipenem-cilastatin-relebactam an effective and safer alternative to colistin-based or piperacillin-tazobactam therapy?
balance: RESTORE-IMI 1 (Motsch 2020, PMID: 31400759; NCT02452047) randomised just 47 patients with imipenem-nonsusceptible infections: favourable overall response 71% on imipenem/relebactam vs 70% on colistin plus imipenem, day-28 clinical response 71% vs 40%, 28-day mortality 10% vs 30%, and treatment-emergent nephrotoxicity 10% vs 56% (P = .002). RESTORE-IMI 2 (Titov 2021, PMID: 32785589; NCT02493764) showed non-inferiority to piperacillin-tazobactam in HABP/VABP: 28-day mortality 15.9% vs 21.3% (difference -5.3%; 95% CI -11.9 to 1.2) and favourable clinical response 61.0% vs 55.8%. A paediatric phase 2/3 trial (Bradley 2026, PMID: 42400209; NCT03969901) found comparable outcomes against standard care in 115 children. Proposed stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — non-inferior in pneumonia and comparable in resistant infection with a clear kidney-safety edge, but the resistant-pathogen trial randomised only 47 patients

title: Eravacycline for complicated intra-abdominal infection: non-inferior to ertapenem (cure 86.8% vs 87.6% in IGNITE1) and to meropenem (90.8% vs 91.2% in IGNITE4) — an approved use resting entirely on parity trials; its urinary-tract programme failed and was never approved
question: In adults with complicated intra-abdominal infection, is intravenous eravacycline non-inferior to carbapenem therapy (ertapenem or meropenem)?
balance: IGNITE1 (Solomkin 2017, PMID: 27851857; NCT01844856 as printed in the record): clinical cure 86.8% on eravacycline vs 87.6% on ertapenem (difference -0.80%; 95% CI -7.1 to 5.5) in 541 patients. IGNITE4 (Solomkin 2019, PMID: 30561562; NCT01844856 as printed in that record also): cure 90.8% (177/195) vs 91.2% (187/205) on meropenem (difference -0.5%; 95% CI -6.3 to 5.3). An earlier phase 2 trial (Solomkin 2014, PMID: 24342651; NCT01265784) found clinical success above 90% in each arm in 139 patients. Both phase 3 trials were non-inferiority designs against carbapenems. The complicated urinary tract infection programme (IGNITE2, IGNITE3) failed its endpoints and produced no journal-published trial, so cIAI is the only approved use. Proposed stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — non-inferior to carbapenems in two phase 3 cIAI trials; no superiority shown and no other approved indication

title: Omadacycline: non-inferior to linezolid in skin infections (early response 84.8% vs 85.5% IV-to-oral in OASIS-1; 88% vs 83% oral-only in OASIS-2) and to moxifloxacin in pneumonia (early response 81.1% vs 82.7% in OPTIC) — parity in three phase 3 trials, with oral formulations as its practical edge
question: In adults with acute bacterial skin and skin-structure infections or community-acquired bacterial pneumonia, is omadacycline non-inferior to linezolid or moxifloxacin?
balance: OASIS-1 (O'Riordan 2019, PMID: 30726689; NCT02378480): early clinical response 84.8% on intravenous-to-oral omadacycline vs 85.5% on linezolid (difference -0.7 points; 95% CI -6.3 to 4.9) in skin infection. OASIS-2 (O'Riordan 2019, PMID: 31474458; NCT02877927): oral-only omadacycline, early response 88% (315/360) vs 83% (297/360) on oral linezolid (difference 5.0; 95% CI -0.2 to 10.3). OPTIC (Stets 2019, PMID: 30726692; NCT02531438): early clinical response 81.1% vs 82.7% on moxifloxacin in community-acquired bacterial pneumonia (difference -1.6; 95% CI -7.1 to 3.8), with post-treatment response 87.6% vs 85.1%. All three were non-inferiority trials. Proposed stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — non-inferior to standard agents in both approved uses; no superiority shown

title: Delafloxacin: non-inferior to vancomycin plus aztreonam in skin infections (objective response 83.7% vs 80.6% in the IV-to-oral trial; 81.3% vs 80.7% pooled) and to moxifloxacin in pneumonia (early response 88.9% vs 89.0%) — fluoroquinolone parity in both approved uses
question: In adults with acute bacterial skin and skin-structure infections or community-acquired bacterial pneumonia, is delafloxacin non-inferior to vancomycin plus aztreonam or to moxifloxacin?
balance: Two phase 3 skin-infection trials were pooled by Giordano 2019 (PMID: 30957167): objective response 81.3% on delafloxacin vs 80.7% on vancomycin plus aztreonam (difference 0.8%; 95% CI -3.2 to 4.7) in 1,510 adults. In pneumonia, DEFINE-CABP (Horcajada 2020, PMID: 31988972; NCT03534622 as printed in that record) gave early clinical response 88.9% vs 89.0% on moxifloxacin (difference -0.2; 95% CI -4.4 to 4.1) in 859 adults. All non-inferiority designs. Proposed stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — non-inferior to standard comparators in both approved uses; a fluoroquinolone, with that class's safety baggage and no superiority shown

title: Ceftaroline: non-inferior to ceftriaxone in pneumonia with numerically higher cure (84.3% vs 77.7% pooled FOCUS) and non-inferior to vancomycin plus aztreonam in skin infection including MRSA (cure 91.6% vs 92.7% pooled CANVAS; MRSA 93.4% vs 94.3%)
question: In adults with community-acquired pneumonia or complicated skin and skin-structure infections (including MRSA), is ceftaroline fosamil non-inferior to ceftriaxone or to vancomycin plus aztreonam?
balance: FOCUS 1 and 2 integrated (File 2010, PMID: 21067350): clinical cure 84.3% on ceftaroline vs 77.7% on ceftriaxone in the clinically evaluable population (difference 6.7%; 95% CI 1.6 to 11.8), with each trial individually non-inferior. CANVAS 1 and 2 integrated (Corey 2010, PMID: 20695801; NCT00424190 and NCT00423657): cure 91.6% vs 92.7% against vancomycin plus aztreonam in skin infection, and 93.4% vs 94.3% in MRSA infection. The trial-programme summary (File 2012, PMID: 22903949) reports the same pattern at early (day 3-4) assessment and pneumococcal cure of 85.5% (59/69) vs 68.6% (48/70). Proposed stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — non-inferior in both approved uses across four phase 3 trials; the pneumonia cure edge is numerical within non-inferiority trials, and MRSA pneumonia was never studied

title: Tedizolid: 6 days matched 10 days of linezolid in skin infections — early response 79.5% vs 79.4% in ESTABLISH-1 (oral) and 85% vs 83% in ESTABLISH-2 (IV-to-oral); pooled 81.6% vs 79.4% with less nausea (8.2% vs 12.2%)
question: In adults with acute bacterial skin and skin-structure infections, is tedizolid phosphate 200 mg once daily for 6 days non-inferior to linezolid 600 mg twice daily for 10 days?
balance: ESTABLISH-1 (Prokocimer 2013, PMID: 23403680; NCT01170221): early clinical response 79.5% on oral tedizolid for 6 days vs 79.4% on oral linezolid for 10 days (difference 0.1%; 95% CI -6.1 to 6.2) in 667 adults. ESTABLISH-2 (Moran 2014, PMID: 24909499; NCT01421511): intravenous-to-oral tedizolid, early response 85% vs 83% on linezolid (difference 2.6%; 95% CI -3.0 to 8.2). The pooled analysis (Shorr 2015, PMID: 25421472) gives early response 81.6% vs 79.4% across 1,333 patients, with nausea in 8.2% vs 12.2% (P = 0.02). Proposed stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — non-inferior to linezolid in two phase 3 trials with a shorter course; no superiority in efficacy shown

title: Adjunctive glycerol in bacterial meningitis: fewer severe neurological sequelae in children (relative odds 0.31) but higher mortality in adults in a high-HIV setting (63% vs 49%) - split by population
question: In bacterial meningitis, does adjunctive oral glycerol added to antibiotics improve survival or reduce neurological sequelae and deafness?
balance: Adjunctive dexamethasone in bacterial meningitis is homed on Shelf #236 and is not re-carded here; this shelf covers the other adjuvant tested in randomised trials, oral glycerol. In 654 Latin-American children on ceftriaxone (Peltola 2007, PMID: 17968821), glycerol did not change death or deafness but cut severe neurological sequelae (relative odds ratio 0.31, 95% CI 0.13-0.76) and the composite of sequelae or death (relative OR 0.44, 0.25-0.76). In 265 adults in Malawi, a high-HIV-prevalence setting (Ajdukiewicz 2011, PMID: 21334262, ISRCTN70121840), glycerol increased day-40 mortality - 86/136 (63%) versus 61/125 (49%) on placebo, adjusted relative OR 2.4 (1.3-4.2) - and the trial was stopped early. The Cochrane review of osmotic therapy (Wall 2018, PMID: 29405037; 5 trials, 1,451 participants) found glycerol made no difference to death (relative RR 1.08, 0.90-1.30) but may reduce neurological disability (relative RR 0.73, 0.53-1.00; low certainty) and deafness (relative RR 0.64, 0.44-0.93). Proposed stamp: SPLIT (child benefit vs adult harm).
stamp: SPLIT (child benefit vs adult harm)

title: Enterococcal endocarditis: ampicillin plus ceftriaxone matched ampicillin plus gentamicin on death and relapse, with far less kidney injury (new renal failure 0% vs 23%)
question: In Enterococcus faecalis infective endocarditis, is ampicillin plus ceftriaxone as effective as ampicillin plus gentamicin, and is it safer?
balance: Early valve surgery in infective endocarditis is homed on Shelf #1627 (EASE) and oral step-down therapy on Shelf #1628 (POET); neither is re-carded here. This shelf covers the unhomed antibiotic question for Enterococcus faecalis endocarditis. In the largest direct comparison, a nonrandomised multicentre cohort of 246 patients (Fernandez-Hidalgo 2013, PMID: 23392394), ampicillin plus ceftriaxone (AC) and ampicillin plus gentamicin (AG) had the same mortality on treatment (22% vs 21%) and at 3 months (8% vs 7%), but treatment had to be stopped for adverse events in 25% of the AG group versus 1% on AC, and new renal failure occurred in 23% versus 0%. A 2024 meta-analysis restricted to 10 observational studies at high risk of bias (Prosty 2024, PMID: 39041860; 911 patients) found no mortality difference (risk difference -0.8%, 95% CI -5.0 to 3.5) and a 26.3-percentage-point higher discontinuation-for-toxicity risk with gentamicin. A 2026 meta-analysis of 6 studies (Sugimoto 2026, PMID: 42581256; 619 patients) likewise found no difference in mortality (relative OR 1.10, 0.73-1.65) or relapse (relative OR 1.08, 0.39-3.01), with fewer total adverse events (relative OR 0.20, 0.08-0.53) and renal events (relative OR 0.34, 0.19-0.58) on AC. All evidence is observational - there is no randomised trial - so the stamp is capped. Proposed stamp: POSSIBLE (equal efficacy, less toxicity; observational evidence only).
stamp: POSSIBLE (equal efficacy, less toxicity; observational evidence only)

title: IL-6 inhibition in rheumatoid arthritis: tocilizumab and sarilumab beat placebo on ACR20 by about 22-33 percentage points across three phase 3 trials
question: In rheumatoid arthritis with an inadequate response to methotrexate or to TNF inhibitors, does IL-6 receptor inhibition with tocilizumab or sarilumab improve disease activity versus placebo?
balance: Tocilizumab versus adalimumab monotherapy (ADACTA) is homed on Shelf #3718 and is not re-carded here. This shelf covers placebo-controlled IL-6 receptor inhibition. OPTION (Smolen 2008, PMID: 18358926, NCT00106548): tocilizumab 8 mg/kg plus methotrexate gave ACR20 at week 24 in 59% versus 26% on placebo (relative OR 4.0). MOBILITY (Genovese 2015, PMID: 25733246, NCT01061736): sarilumab 200 mg plus methotrexate gave ACR20 66.4% versus 33.4%, and slowed radiographic progression (Sharp score change 0.25 vs 2.78 at week 52). TARGET (Fleischmann 2017, PMID: 27860410, NCT01709578), in patients who had failed TNF inhibitors: sarilumab ACR20 60.9% (200 mg) versus 33.7% on placebo. Serious infections ran slightly above placebo in OPTION and MOBILITY (up to 4.0% vs 2.3%) but not in TARGET (1.1% vs 1.1%); liver-enzyme and neutrophil effects are class effects. Proposed stamp: LIKELY (benefit).
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: Rituximab in rheumatoid arthritis: one course (2 infusions) roughly tripled ACR20 responses versus placebo - 51-55% versus 18-28% across three trials
question: In rheumatoid arthritis with an inadequate response to methotrexate or to TNF inhibitors, does rituximab plus methotrexate improve disease activity versus placebo plus methotrexate?
balance: Three placebo-controlled trials of rituximab plus methotrexate. REFLEX (Cohen 2006, PMID: 16947627), in patients who had failed TNF inhibitors: ACR20 at week 24 was 51% versus 18% on placebo, ACR50 27% versus 5%, with serious infections 5.2 versus 3.7 per 100 patient-years. DANCER (Emery 2006, PMID: 16649186), a dose-ranging trial: ACR20 55% (2 x 500 mg) and 54% (2 x 1,000 mg) versus 28%, and glucocorticoid premedication did not add efficacy. SERENE (Emery 2010, PMID: 20488885), in biologic-naive methotrexate inadequate responders: ACR20 54% and 51% versus 23%, with no difference between the 500 mg and 1,000 mg courses. No registry ID appears in any of the three records (all predate routine registration reporting). Proposed stamp: LIKELY (benefit).
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: JAK inhibitor efficacy in rheumatoid arthritis: tofacitinib and upadacitinib beat placebo on ACR20 by about 23-39 percentage points in three phase 3 trials
question: In rheumatoid arthritis, do JAK inhibitors (tofacitinib, upadacitinib) improve disease activity versus placebo - efficacy only, with safety covered separately?
balance: This shelf covers efficacy only: the JAK-inhibitor safety question (ORAL Surveillance) is homed on Shelf #384 and is not re-carded here; baricitinib is homed on Shelf #3717 and filgotinib on Shelf #3757. ORAL Solo (Fleischmann 2012, PMID: 22873530, NCT00814307): tofacitinib monotherapy ACR20 at month 3 was 59.8% (5 mg twice daily) and 65.7% (10 mg) versus 26.7% on placebo. ORAL Standard (van Vollenhoven 2012, PMID: 22873531, NCT00853385), on background methotrexate: ACR20 at month 6 was 51.5% and 52.6% on tofacitinib, 47.2% on adalimumab and 28.3% on placebo. SELECT-NEXT (Burmester 2018, PMID: 29908669, NCT02675426): upadacitinib ACR20 at week 12 was 64% (15 mg) and 66% (30 mg) versus 36% on placebo, with DAS28(CRP) of 3.2 or less in 48% versus 17%. Proposed stamp: LIKELY (benefit) for efficacy; the class safety balance sits on Shelf #384.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: Risankizumab in psoriatic arthritis: ACR20 at week 24 was 57.3% versus 33.5% (KEEPsAKE 1) and 51.3% versus 26.5% (KEEPsAKE 2) on placebo, sustained to week 100
question: In psoriatic arthritis, does the IL-23 inhibitor risankizumab improve joint disease versus placebo?
balance: Guselkumab in psoriatic arthritis (DISCOVER-1 and DISCOVER-2) is homed on Shelf #3719 and is not re-carded here; this shelf covers the other IL-23 inhibitor, risankizumab. KEEPsAKE 1 (Kristensen 2022, PMID: 34911706, NCT03675308), in conventional-DMARD inadequate responders: ACR20 at week 24 was 57.3% versus 33.5% on placebo. KEEPsAKE 2, reported at 52 weeks (Ostör 2023, PMID: 36282537, NCT03671148), which also enrolled biologic inadequate responders: ACR20 at week 24 was 51.3% versus 26.5%, rising to 58.5% at week 52 on continuous risankizumab. The 100-week KEEPsAKE 1 report (Kristensen 2024, PMID: 38498141, NCT03675308) shows durability: ACR20 64.3% at week 100 on continuous risankizumab, with 81.2% of week-52 responders maintaining their response. Serious infections in KEEPsAKE 1 were 1.0% on risankizumab versus 1.2% on placebo. Proposed stamp: LIKELY (benefit).
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: Ustekinumab in psoriatic arthritis: ACR20 at week 24 was 42.4-49.5% versus 22.8% on placebo (PSUMMIT-1), and joint damage progressed less (vdH-S change 0.4 vs 1.0)
question: In psoriatic arthritis, does ustekinumab (IL-12/23 p40 blockade) improve joint disease and slow radiographic progression versus placebo?
balance: PSUMMIT-1 (McInnes 2013, PMID: 23769296, NCT01009086): ACR20 at week 24 was 42.4% on ustekinumab 45 mg and 49.5% on 90 mg versus 22.8% on placebo, maintained to week 52. PSUMMIT-2 (Ritchlin 2014, PMID: 24482301, NCT01077362), in which 180 of 312 patients had already failed TNF inhibitors: ACR20 43.8% on combined ustekinumab versus 20.2% on placebo, and 35.6% versus 14.5% within the TNF-experienced subgroup. The preplanned integrated radiographic analysis of both trials (Kavanaugh 2014, PMID: 24553909; 927 patients) found less joint damage progression on ustekinumab at week 24 (mean van der Heijde-Sharp change 0.4 versus 1.0 on placebo, all P<0.02). Proposed stamp: LIKELY (benefit).
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: Apremilast in psoriatic arthritis: ACR20 at week 16 was 28-41% versus 18-19% on placebo across the three PALACE trials - real but modest gains
question: In psoriatic arthritis, does oral apremilast improve joint disease versus placebo?
balance: Three phase 3 placebo-controlled trials of the oral PDE4 inhibitor apremilast, all with an early-escape design. PALACE-1 (Kavanaugh 2014, PMID: 24595547, NCT01172938): ACR20 at week 16 was 31% (20 mg twice daily) and 40% (30 mg) versus 19% on placebo. PALACE-2 (Cutolo 2016, PMID: 27422893, NCT01212757): 37.4% and 32.1% versus 18.9% - note the 20 mg dose scored numerically above the 30 mg dose. PALACE-3 (Edwards 2016, PMID: 26792812, NCT01212770), in patients all with skin involvement: 28% and 41% versus 18%, with PASI50 in 41% versus 24% at the 30 mg dose. Absolute gains are modest (about 9-22 percentage points) and smaller than those on the biologic shelves; gastrointestinal effects (diarrhoea, nausea) were the commonest adverse events and usually settled. Proposed stamp: LIKELY (benefit), with modest effect size.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: Tofacitinib in psoriatic arthritis: ACR20 at month 3 was 50-61% versus 33% on placebo (OPAL Broaden) and 47-50% versus 24% after TNF-inhibitor failure (OPAL Beyond)
question: In psoriatic arthritis, does the JAK inhibitor tofacitinib improve joint disease versus placebo, including after TNF-inhibitor failure?
balance: Upadacitinib in psoriatic arthritis (SELECT-PsA 1 and 2) is homed on pack Shelf #5092 and is not re-carded here; this shelf covers tofacitinib. OPAL Broaden (Mease 2017, PMID: 29045212, NCT01877668), in conventional-DMARD inadequate responders: ACR20 at month 3 was 50% on tofacitinib 5 mg twice daily and 61% on 10 mg versus 33% on placebo, with adalimumab at 52% in the same trial. OPAL Beyond (Gladman 2017, PMID: 29045207, NCT01882439), in TNF-inhibitor inadequate responders: ACR20 50% and 47% versus 24% on placebo, with serious adverse events in 4% and 6% on the continuous tofacitinib doses. A post hoc analysis of the OPAL Balance extension (Gladman 2024, PMID: 39702318) found efficacy was maintained when patients switched directly from adalimumab to tofacitinib (n=91) or continued tofacitinib (n=89). Class safety for JAK inhibitors is covered on Shelf #384. Proposed stamp: LIKELY (benefit).
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: Non-radiographic axial spondyloarthritis: certolizumab, secukinumab, ixekizumab and upadacitinib all beat placebo — ASAS40 gains of about 12–23 percentage points across the phase 3 trials
question: In adults with active non-radiographic axial spondyloarthritis who have not responded to NSAIDs, do TNF inhibitors, IL-17 inhibitors or a JAK inhibitor improve disease activity versus placebo?
balance: Non-radiographic axial spondyloarthritis (nr-axSpA) treatment beyond the adalimumab trial homed on Shelf #4780 (ABILITY-1, PMID: 22772328) and the radiographic-disease shelf #680. Four placebo-controlled programmes are carded here. Certolizumab (RAPID-axSpA, PMID: 24013647, NCT01087762): ASAS20 at week 12 of 57.7% and 63.6% versus 38.3% on placebo in the whole axSpA population, with similar effects in the nr-axSpA subpopulation. Secukinumab (PREVENT, PMID: 32770640, NCT02696031): ASAS40 in TNFi-naive patients 41.5% versus 29.2% at week 16 and 39.8% versus 19.9% at week 52. Ixekizumab (COAST-X, PMID: 31813637, NCT02757352): ASAS40 35–40% versus 19% at week 16, sustained at week 52 (30–31% vs 13%). Upadacitinib (SELECT-AXIS 2, PMID: 38747163, NCT04169373): ASAS40 63% versus 43% at week 52. Every class clears its placebo bar; no head-to-head or structural-progression data are carded. Proposed stamp: LIKELY (benefit).
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: Axial spondyloarthritis after TNF failure: switching to an IL-17 inhibitor was NOT better than a second TNF inhibitor in the one randomised trial (ASAS40 15.2% vs 14.5%) — except possibly after primary non-response
question: In axial spondyloarthritis with an inadequate response to a first TNF inhibitor, does switching to an IL-17 inhibitor outperform cycling to a second TNF inhibitor — and which class should come first?
balance: The sequencing question has one randomised trial. ROC-SpA (NCT03445845; results reported as a 2025 congress abstract): 300 TNF-inadequate responders randomised to an IL-17 inhibitor or a second TNF inhibitor; ASAS40 at week 24 was 15.2% versus 14.5% (adjusted OR for non-response 0.96, 95% CI 0.68–1.34) — no superiority. Observational data point the same way overall: a Korean nationwide cohort of 1,660 switchers (PMID: 41743540) found similar persistence, except after primary TNF failure, where a second TNF inhibitor was discontinued more (adjusted HR 1.54–2.11); the CorEvitas registry axSpA cohort found similar or numerically better outcomes for switchers. For first-biologic choice, a network meta-analysis in nr-axSpA (Li 2025, DOI: 10.1159/000542744) ranked TNF inhibitors above IL-17 and JAK inhibitors on ASAS40. Proposed stamp: SPLIT (the two sequencing strategies made no difference overall, with a possible switch advantage after primary failure).
stamp: SPLIT (switching to an IL-17 inhibitor and cycling to a second TNF inhibitor made no difference overall)

title: Hip osteoarthritis: one triamcinolone injection eased pain versus advice alone (−1.43 points over 6 months) but not versus a plain lidocaine injection, pooled placebo data are null, and PRP matched saline
question: In adults with hip osteoarthritis, do intra-articular corticosteroid or platelet-rich plasma injections reduce pain compared with advice, local anaesthetic or placebo?
balance: Hip-specific treatment evidence (exercise for knee and hip OA is homed on Shelf #683). The HIT trial (Paskins 2022, ISRCTN50550256) found one ultrasound-guided triamcinolone injection added to advice and education improved pain over 6 months by −1.43 points versus advice alone, but by only −0.52 (not significant) versus a lidocaine-only injection, and the 2025 meta-analysis (PMID: 40375257) found no statistically significant corticosteroid benefit over placebo. Kullenberg 2004 (PMID: 15517641) found fluoroscopic triamcinolone beat local anaesthetic at 3 weeks. Platelet-rich plasma was no better than saline in a 60-patient double-blind trial (PMID: 38948640). Proposed stamp: SPLIT.
stamp: SPLIT (steroid injection: POSSIBLE short-term benefit, unproven against placebo injection · PRP: the treatment made no difference)

title: Hand osteoarthritis: exercises improved function and grip, a splint added nothing to good self-management at 8 weeks (OTTER II, 349 patients) — but a custom night splint worn for a year cut pain by 14.3 mm
question: In adults with hand osteoarthritis, do thumb splints/orthoses and hand exercise programmes reduce pain and improve function?
balance: Non-drug treatment of hand osteoarthritis; the drug shelves are already homed (methotrexate/hydroxychloroquine #2014, topical diclofenac #2567, prednisolone #3720, denosumab #3760) and are cross-pointed, not re-carded. OTTER II (Adams 2021, ISRCTN54744256; 349 patients) found adding a verum or placebo thumb splint to a supported self-management programme made no difference at 8 weeks (−0.5, 95% CI −1.4 to 0.4). Rannou 2009 (112 patients) found a custom night splint useless at 1 month but better by 14.3 mm at 12 months. Exercise trials were positive: Hennig 2015 (PMID: 24667900) improved activity performance (responders 16 vs 2) and Stamm 2018 (PMID: 30413191) improved grip strength. Proposed stamp: SPLIT.

title: CPPD (pseudogout): colchicine and prednisone were equivalent in the first head-to-head trial (pain −36 vs −38 mm at 24 h, 111 patients); anakinra helped 76% in uncontrolled series
question: In older adults with an acute calcium pyrophosphate crystal arthritis flare, how do colchicine, prednisone and anakinra compare for pain relief and safety?
balance: Treatment of calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease, scoped to the acute flare and IL-1 blockade; colchicine prophylaxis is homed on Shelf #2713 and methotrexate on Shelf #2723 and is not re-carded. COLCHICORT (Pascart 2023, NCT03128905; 111 patients, median age 88) showed low-dose colchicine and prednisone 30 mg are equivalent at 24 hours (pain −36 vs −38 mm; difference −1 mm, 95% CI −12 to 10; ~65% responders each). Anakinra rests on a 15-patient double-blind pilot versus prednisone (Dumusc 2021), a meta-analysis of mostly uncontrolled series (PMID: 41206733; 84 patients, 76% response) and a 292-patient mixed-crystal cohort (PMID: 41926750; 92.8% judged effective, 4.5% infection). Proposed stamp: SPLIT.

title: Spaceflight bone loss: alendronate plus ARED exercise protected spine, hip and pelvis bone density in 7 ISS astronauts — exercise alone left hip trabecular bone unprotected
question: In astronauts on long-duration spaceflight, does adding a bisphosphonate (alendronate) to resistive exercise prevent the bone mineral density loss, raised bone resorption and urinary calcium of microgravity?
balance: Spaceflight bone loss: the flight evidence is two small NASA/JAXA ISS cohorts. LeBlanc 2013 (PMID: 23334732): 7 astronauts on alendronate 70 mg weekly plus ARED exercise for ~5.5 months showed attenuation of essentially all bone-loss indices. Sibonga 2019 (PMID: 31400472): 10 ARED-only astronauts were only partially protected — hip trabecular bone and resorption markers were not protected — isolating the drug's contribution. A 17-week bed-rest analogue (NASA report; alendronate n=6) concurs mechanistically and is labelled an analogue on its card. Proposed stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit), capped by n=7 treated flight subjects and no randomisation.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: ARED resistance exercise in space: crews with the heavier device kept hip and pelvis bone density — but still lost 1.7% femoral neck BMD, 5.8% leg strength and 6.1% VO2peak per mission
question: In astronauts on long-duration spaceflight, how well do ARED resistance-exercise countermeasures protect bone mineral density, muscle strength and aerobic fitness?
balance: Resistance-exercise countermeasures in flight. Smith 2012 (DOI: 10.1002/jbmr.1647): among 13 ISS crewmembers, pelvis and hip BMD were unchanged from pre-flight only in the 5 with ARED access (up to 600 lbf) versus 8 iRED crew (297 lbf). English 2020 Sprint (PMID: 32864428; 26 crew): high-intensity lower-volume training matched the standard programme, but both groups lost femoral neck BMD (−1.7%), knee extensor torque (−5.8%) and VO2peak (−6.1%). Loehr 2011 (PMID: 20473227) is an Earth training analogue showing ARED loads muscle like free weights. The drug-plus-exercise contrast is homed on Shelf #5459. title: Potassium citrate in spaceflight: 20 mEq/day held calcium oxalate supersaturation at pre-flight levels and lowered urinary calcium in a double-blind ISS study of 30 crew
question: In astronauts on long-duration spaceflight, does potassium citrate supplementation reduce the urinary stone-forming risk created by microgravity?
balance: Spaceflight stone prevention. Whitson 2009 (J Urol, DOI: 10.1016/j.juro.2009.07.010): in 30 long-duration crew, potassium citrate 20 mEq/day (double-blind, placebo-controlled on the ISS) decreased urinary calcium and maintained calcium oxalate supersaturation at pre-flight levels, with higher urinary pH lowering uric acid stone risk. Zerwekh 2007 (PMID: 17509313) is the controlled bed-rest analogue (n=20) showing the same chemistry effect, labelled an analogue on its card. Whitson 1997 documents the underlying risk shift (323 post-flight crew). Earth stone prevention with potassium citrate is homed on Shelf #2645. Proposed stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) on surrogate endpoints.

title: Post-flight orthostatic intolerance: compression garments held standing heart rate and pressure at pre-flight levels — fluid loading helps for 1–3 hours, and midodrine failed in 2 of 5 astronauts tested
question: In astronauts returning from spaceflight, do fluid loading, midodrine or gradient compression garments prevent post-flight orthostatic intolerance?
balance: Post-flight orthostatic intolerance countermeasures. Gradient compression garments have the strongest flight data: Stenger 2013 (PMID: 23713210; 14 Shuttle astronauts) — heart-rate rise 11 vs 21 beats/min and systolic change +2 vs −9 mmHg on landing day; Lee 2020 (PMID: 32765292; 11 long-duration astronauts) — standing responses held at pre-flight levels while wearing the garment. Fluid loading rests on a head-down-tilt analogue (Cowings 2015; n=16) showing a 10 mmHg pressure advantage confined to hours 1–3. Midodrine's only flight test (Platts, NASA report; n=5) failed to prevent hypotension in 2 of 5 and routine use was judged unlikely. Terrestrial midodrine shelves #2498/#1557 are cross-pointed, not re-carded. Proposed stamp: SPLIT.
stamp: SPLIT (compression garments: POSSIBLE benefit · fluid loading: POSSIBLE partial benefit · midodrine in flight: unproven)

title: Sleep in spaceflight: crews get only ~6 hours despite 3 in 4 using sleeping pills — and melatonin 0.3 mg, the one drug trialled in flight, did not improve sleep at all
question: In spaceflight crewmembers, do melatonin, sleep-promoting medications or light-based circadian countermeasures improve sleep duration and circadian alignment?
balance: Sleep and circadian countermeasures in flight. Dijk 2001 (PMID: 11641138): 5 Shuttle astronauts slept ~6.5 hours/day and melatonin 0.3 mg on alternate nights did not improve sleep. Barger 2014 (PMID: 25127232): 85 astronauts obtained 5.96 hours (Shuttle) and 6.09 hours (ISS) per night, while 78% of Shuttle crew used sleep-promoting drugs on 52% of nights and 75% of ISS crew used them — use is pervasive but untested against placebo in flight. The 2023 review (PMID: 37533816) puts medication use at 71–78% of crewmembers. No cardable in-flight randomised trial of timed light was captured this session — flagged as a gap. Proposed stamp: SPLIT.

title: SANS eye swelling in space: only standing upright (in the Earth bed-rest model) kept retinal thickening under NASA's danger line (18.6 vs >20 µm) — suction trousers and thigh cuffs did nothing extra, and the B-vitamin idea rests on risk genes, not a treatment trial
question: In astronauts and in head-down bed-rest analogues of spaceflight-associated neuro-ocular syndrome (SANS), do countermeasures — fluid-shift reversal (upright posture, lower body negative pressure, thigh cuffs) or B-vitamin supplementation aimed at one-carbon metabolism — prevent optic disc edema, and who is at highest risk?
balance: SPLIT — fluid-shift reversal works in the analogue, no deployable countermeasure is proven, and the B-vitamin lead is risk genetics, not a treatment trial. In the randomised 30-day head-down bed-rest trial of He 2025 (PMID: 40545016; 47 volunteers), only intermittent upright posture kept retinal thickening below NASA's 20 µm disc-edema threshold (18.6 ± 5.5 µm); lower body negative pressure and exercise with thigh cuffs did not differ from no countermeasure. Susceptibility is real and measurable before flight: Zwart 2012 (PMID: 22298570) found one-carbon metabolites 25–45% higher (P < 0.001) in the 5 astronauts with eye changes than in 15 without, before, during and after flight, and Zwart 2019 (JAMA Ophthalmology, DOI: 10.1001/jamaophthalmol.2019.3124) found edema in 5 of 11 bed-rest subjects tracking MTRR/SHMT1 risk alleles and B-vitamin status. That makes B-vitamin supplementation a plausible, currently untested countermeasure — not a proven one. PROPOSED SPLIT (analogue posture effect: positive · mechanical countermeasures as tested: the treatment made no difference · B vitamins: association only, no trial).
stamp: SPLIT (upright posture in the bed-rest analogue kept thickening at 18.6 µm, below the 20 µm threshold · lower body negative pressure and thigh cuffs: the treatment made no difference · B-vitamin supplementation: untested, supported only by risk-factor associations)

title: Medicines in space: the one drug measured in flight reached blood levels 4–5 times higher than on Earth (4 crew), and after 28 months on the space station only 9 of 35 medicines still met potency standards versus 17 of 35 stored on Earth
question: During spaceflight, are drug pharmacokinetics altered in microgravity, and do medications lose stability or potency faster in the space environment than on Earth?
balance: SPLIT — exposure changes in flight, and long storage degrades medicines faster, but the evidence is one drug in 4 people plus formulation chemistry. Mampre 2026 (PMID: 42530224) made the first blood-sampled in-flight pharmacokinetic measurements: in 4 Polaris Dawn crew, acetaminophen Cmax rose from 9,110 to 43,300 ng/mL and AUC roughly quadrupled versus pre-flight, with changes still present 3 days after landing. For stability, Du 2011 (PMID: 21479701) found only 9 of 35 ISS formulations still met USP potency criteria after 28 months versus 17 of 35 ground controls, with faster degradation in space; Wotring 2015 (DOI: 10.1208/s12248-015-9834-5) found most of 9 medicines still potent after 550 days on the ISS, 4 of them up to 8 months past expiry. PROPOSED SPLIT (in-flight pharmacokinetics: changed, direction drug-specific · long-duration storage: faster degradation · ~18-month storage: potency mostly held).
stamp: SPLIT (in-flight acetaminophen exposure ~4–5× higher in 4 crew · 28-month ISS storage: 9/35 formulations still in specification vs 17/35 on Earth · 550-day storage: potency mostly held)

title: Dormant viruses wake up in space: 22 of 23 long-mission astronauts shed a herpesvirus — but the fittest crew had a 29–39% lower relative risk, and shedding fell after 2012 as exercise, food and scheduling countermeasures improved
question: In long-duration spaceflight, how common is immune dysregulation with latent herpesvirus reactivation, and do countermeasures — preflight fitness, exercise, nutritional supplementation, scheduling and other operational measures — reduce it?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational evidence only. Reactivation is near-universal on long missions: Mehta 2017 (PMID: 28649633) found 22 of 23 ISS astronauts shed a latent herpesvirus (15 VZV, 22 EBV, 14 CMV at some phase), with shedding heavier than on short shuttle flights. Two countermeasure signals, neither randomised: Agha 2020 (PMID: 31908052) found higher preflight cardiorespiratory fitness carried a 29% lower relative risk of reactivation and higher upper-body endurance a 39% lower relative risk in 22 crew; Crucian 2020 (PMID: 32464118) found stress, immune dysregulation and reactivation all improved across 12 years of ISS operations as the exercise, nutrition, supplementation and scheduling bundle improved from about 2012. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for fitness and the combined operational countermeasure bundle; no drug or vaccine countermeasure has been tested in flight.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — fitter crew reactivated less (29–39% lower relative risk) and reactivation fell in the post-2012 countermeasure era; all evidence observational, none randomised

title: Spinning as medicine: 30 minutes a day in a small centrifuge blunted fainting-proneness after 60 days of bed rest (standing tolerance fell ~300 vs 801 seconds) — but it did not protect blood volume or fitness, and spinning while exercising added nothing
question: Does artificial gravity from short-radius (short-arm) centrifugation, daily or combined with exercise, protect against cardiovascular and other deconditioning during spaceflight or its head-down bed-rest analogue?
balance: SPLIT — a real orthostatic benefit at rest in analogues; no protection for plasma volume or fitness, and no added benefit when combined with exercise. Linnarsson 2015 (PMID: 25342708; 11 men, crossover) found tilt tolerance after 5 days of bed rest was 78% of baseline with 6 × 5 min daily centrifugation versus 36% with no countermeasure, while plasma volume (85% of baseline) and aerobic power (95%) were unprotected. Hoenemann 2023 (PMID: 37347452; DRKS00015677; AGBRESA, 24 people, 60 days) found time to presyncope fell ~300 s in both centrifugation groups versus 801 s in controls (P = 0.0249). Hedge 2025 (PMID: 40953072; BRACE, 24 men, 60 days) found exercise during centrifugation protected aerobic fitness exactly as exercise alone did (Δ +4% vs 0%, controls −24%) and standing tolerance fell in all groups. PROPOSED SPLIT (orthostatic tolerance at rest: POSSIBLE benefit in analogues · plasma volume, fitness, and exercise-combined use: the treatment made no difference beyond exercise).
stamp: SPLIT (daily centrifugation at rest blunted orthostatic losses in bed-rest analogues — presyncope time fell ~300 s vs 801 s in controls · no protection of plasma volume or aerobic power, and no added benefit over exercise alone)

title: Vitamin D in space: levels fell after long missions despite the old supplement dose — in the Antarctic no-sunlight test, 1,000–2,000 IU a day raised levels about 60%, and bones were protected only when good nutrition came with heavy resistance exercise
question: In spaceflight, does vitamin D supplementation (and adequate energy/nutrition generally) maintain vitamin D status and protect bone, and what dose is needed when there is no ultraviolet light?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for vitamin D status and for bone as part of an inseparable exercise-plus-nutrition package; no isolated nutritional countermeasure has a flight trial. Smith 2005 (PMID: 15735075; 11 astronauts) found serum 25-hydroxycholecalciferol fell after 128–195-day missions despite supplement use (P < 0.01), with bone resorption increased. The blinded Antarctic winter-over dose study (Smith 2009, FASEB conference abstract; 66 volunteers) found 1,000 and 2,000 IU/day raised levels ~61–63% while no supplement meant a 13% fall. Smith 2012 (PMID: 22549960; 13 crew) found bone density maintained in most regions when ARED resistance exercise came with adequate energy intake and vitamin D status. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).

title: Drugs for space muscle loss: testosterone is the only one with trial evidence — added to exercise it increased lean mass in 70 days of bed rest, but it never improved strength beyond exercise alone, and no other muscle drug has human space-analogue data
question: Beyond exercise, do pharmacologic countermeasures (testosterone or other anabolic agents) prevent muscle atrophy and strength loss during spaceflight or its bed-rest analogue?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for lean mass as an adjunct to exercise, from two small bed-rest trials of one drug; no drug preserved strength beyond exercise, and no other drug has cardable human evidence. Dillon 2018 (PMID: 29924745; NCT00891449; 70-day head-down bed rest) found lean body mass decreased in controls, held with exercise plus placebo, and increased with exercise plus cycled testosterone 100 mg/week, while leg strength was protected equally by exercise with or without the drug. The same cohort's metabolic report (Dillon 2020, NCT00891449) found testosterone protected against insulin resistance (HOMA-IR 1.45→1.07 vs 1.74→2.24 in controls) though 2-hour glucose rose. Zachwieja 1999 (10 men, 28 days) found testosterone preserved nitrogen balance and lean mass but knee extensor strength fell as much as on placebo. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), lean-mass adjunct only.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — cycled testosterone plus exercise increased lean mass in 70-day bed rest where exercise alone only held it; strength was not improved beyond exercise in either trial

title: Space motion sickness: promethazine is the proven treatment — relief within 2 hours in 14 of 15 sick crew, and in a blinded test flight sickness on only 12.6% of parabolas versus 51.8% on placebo
question: In spaceflight and its analogues, how effective are promethazine and other drugs for preventing and treating space motion sickness, and what cognitive price do they carry?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) for promethazine as treatment. Davis 1993 (PMID: 11541638), comparing Shuttle debriefings, found intramuscular promethazine gave relief within 1–2 hours in 14 of 15 treated crew with no delayed symptom onset, while oral scopolamine-dextroamphetamine prophylaxis was dropped over delayed symptoms and variable early-flight absorption. Abbott 2025 (PMID: 41253367), a blinded parabolic-flight trial in 12 subjects, found motion sickness on 12.6% of parabolas with 25 mg oral promethazine versus 51.8% on placebo. Bos 2004 (PMID: 15451046; 67 volunteers) ranked the cognitive cost of the options: meclizine best, then scopolamine, promethazine, lorazepam worst. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — promethazine relieved in-flight sickness in 14 of 15 treated crew and cut sick parabolas to 12.6% vs 51.8% on placebo; its cognitive cost ranks mid-pack among alternatives

title: Heart and fitness in space: exercise programmes fully protected aerobic fitness in Earth bed-rest trials, yet on real station missions fitness still fell about 17% in the first two weeks despite daily exercise
question: In spaceflight and its bed-rest analogue, do exercise and other countermeasures (including post-exercise venoconstrictive thigh cuffs) prevent cardiovascular deconditioning — loss of aerobic capacity, plasma volume and cardiac function?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) for exercise-based countermeasures, with documented breakthrough in flight. Moore 2014 (PMID: 24970852; 14 astronauts) found VO2peak fell ~17% by flight day 15 despite routine in-flight exercise, then partly recovered but stayed below preflight until after landing. In randomised bed-rest analogues the programmes work better: Ploutz-Snyder 2018 (PMID: 29924746; NCT00891449; 34 subjects) found integrated SPRINT exercise held peak aerobic capacity while sedentary controls lost ~10%, and the 2025 thigh-cuff randomised trial (PMID: 40605173; 24 subjects) found exercise plus post-exercise thigh cuffs limited the VO2peak fall to −106 versus −607 mL/min in controls (P < 0.001) and blunted plasma volume, stroke volume and cardiac output losses — without protecting muscle. Artificial gravity is homed on its own shelf (#5467) and not re-carded here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — exercise programmes held aerobic capacity in bed-rest trials (controls lost ~10%, or 607 vs 106 mL/min), but in real flight VO2peak still fell ~17% early despite exercise

title: Stronger social relationships predict survival: across 148 studies (308,849 people) stronger relationships carried 50% higher odds of survival (OR 1.50), and the most isolated Alameda County residents died at 2.3 times (men) and 2.8 times (women) the rate of the most connected over 9 years — observational evidence only
question: In adults, do stronger social relationships, and the absence of loneliness/social isolation, predict lower all-cause mortality?
balance: Observational evidence only — no randomised trial can assign social relationships, so this shelf caps at POSSIBLE and the face says so. Two Holt-Lunstad meta-analyses agree: across 148 studies (308,849 participants) stronger social relationships carried OR 1.50 (95% CI 1.42 to 1.59) for survival (PMID: 20668659), and loneliness (OR 1.26), social isolation (OR 1.29) and living alone (OR 1.32) each predicted higher mortality (PMID: 25910392). The founding cohort points the same way: in 6,928 Alameda County adults followed 9 years, the most isolated died at age-adjusted relative risks of 2.3 (men) and 2.8 (women) versus the most connected, independent of baseline health, socioeconomic status and health practices (PMID: 425958). Residual confounding and reverse causation (illness shrinking networks) cannot be excluded. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm) for social isolation/loneliness as a mortality risk marker — observational only.
stamp: POSSIBLE (harm) — loneliness, social isolation and living alone are associated with 26–32% relative higher mortality and stronger relationships with 50% higher odds of survival in observational meta-analyses; observational evidence only, no trial proof

title: Loneliness and social isolation track with heart disease and stroke in the global longitudinal data — 29% relative higher risk of incident coronary heart disease (RR 1.29) and 32% relative higher risk of stroke (RR 1.32) — but an Australia/New Zealand meta-analysis found no association, and all evidence is observational
question: In adults, are loneliness and social isolation associated with incident coronary heart disease and stroke?
balance: Observational evidence only, so this shelf caps at POSSIBLE. The disease-specific meta-analysis (Valtorta 2016; 16 longitudinal datasets, 4,628 coronary heart disease and 3,002 stroke events, follow-up 3–21 years) found poor social relationships associated with a pooled relative risk of 1.29 (95% CI 1.04 to 1.59) for incident coronary heart disease and 1.32 (95% CI 1.04 to 1.68) for stroke (PMID: 27091846). The foundational 1988 Science review reached the same qualitative conclusion from prospective and experimental work (PMID: 3399889). Against that, a 2022 Australia/New Zealand meta-analysis of 3 longitudinal datasets (2,137 coronary and 590 stroke events) found no association in fully adjusted models and judged its own evidence inconclusive (PMID: 35263481). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm) — observational only, with a printed regional discordance.
stamp: POSSIBLE (harm) — poor social relationships are associated with 29% relative higher incident coronary heart disease and 32% relative higher stroke risk in pooled longitudinal studies, with one discordant regional null; observational evidence only
