title: Poor social engagement tracks with dementia: a poor social network carried a relative risk of 1.59 and poor support 1.28 across 2,370,452 participants, and loneliness carried a relative risk of 1.23 for dementia and 1.72 for Alzheimer's disease in a second meta-analysis — observational evidence only
question: In older adults, are low social engagement and loneliness associated with incident dementia?
balance: Observational evidence only, so this shelf caps at POSSIBLE. Penninkilampi 2018 (33 studies, 2,370,452 participants) found poor social network relative risk 1.59 (95% CI 1.31 to 1.96) and poor social support 1.28 (95% CI 1.01 to 1.62) for dementia, while its loneliness estimate was non-significant (RR 1.38, 95% CI 0.98 to 1.94) (PMID: 30452410). A 2022 loneliness-specific meta-analysis (16 cohorts, 62,345 people, 4,625 dementia cases) did find loneliness associated with dementia (RR 1.23, 95% CI 1.16 to 1.31) and Alzheimer's disease (RR 1.72, 95% CI 1.32 to 2.23), but not mild cognitive impairment or vascular dementia (PMID: 36530204). A third synthesis put prolonged loneliness/isolation at HR 1.49 (95% CI 1.37 to 1.61) (PMID: 34369248). The structural question (which relationship features predict onset) is homed separately on #5477. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm) — observational only.
stamp: POSSIBLE (harm) — low social engagement and loneliness are associated with roughly 20–60% relative higher dementia risk across observational meta-analyses totalling millions of participants; observational evidence only, reverse causation (preclinical dementia shrinking social life) not excluded

title: The relationship features that predict dementia are participation, contact and loneliness — low participation relative risk 1.41, infrequent contact 1.57, loneliness 1.58 across 19 cohorts — while network size was inconsistent and network satisfaction showed no significant association (RR 1.25, CI crossing 1)
question: Across longitudinal cohorts, which aspects of social relationships (network size, contact, support) predict dementia onset?
balance: Observational evidence only, so this shelf caps at POSSIBLE. Kuiper 2015 pooled 19 longitudinal cohorts and separated the relationship features: low social participation RR 1.41 (95% CI 1.13 to 1.75), less frequent social contact RR 1.57 (95% CI 1.32 to 1.85) and more loneliness RR 1.58 (95% CI 1.19 to 2.09) predicted incident dementia, while network-size results were inconsistent and low network satisfaction was not significant (RR 1.25, 95% CI 0.96 to 1.62) (PMID: 25956016). Marital status — the crudest structural measure — shows the same pattern in 15 studies (812,047 participants): widowed RR 1.20 and lifelong single RR 1.42 versus married, divorced not significant (PMID: 29183957). The 20-year Paquid cohort (2,854 people) found engagement in social, physical or intellectual pursuits related to lower dementia risk at population level, though social measures did not explain its cognitive-trajectory subgroups (PMID: 26499254). title: Loneliness and isolation are not interchangeable: in Amsterdam, feelings of loneliness predicted dementia (OR 1.64, 95% CI 1.05–2.56) while objective isolation did not; in Chicago both predicted decline and Alzheimer's, and isolated-but-not-lonely elders declined fastest
question: Do loneliness (subjective) and social isolation (objective) carry different risks for cognitive decline and Alzheimer's disease?
balance: Observational evidence only, so this shelf caps at POSSIBLE — and the honest answer to its question is 'partly different'. In the Amsterdam AMSTEL cohort (2,173 people, 3 years), feelings of loneliness predicted dementia onset (OR 1.64, 95% CI 1.05 to 2.56) while objective social isolation (living alone, unmarried, no support) did not survive adjustment (PMID: 23232034). In the Chicago CHAP cohort (7,760 people, mean follow-up 7.9 years) both predicted decline and Alzheimer's — isolation OR 1.183 per index point and loneliness OR 2.117 for incident Alzheimer's — and the isolated-but-not-lonely group showed accelerated decline without significantly raised Alzheimer's odds (PMID: 40015756). In the Rush cohort (823 people, up to 4 years) loneliness more than doubled Alzheimer's risk at the 90th versus 10th percentile, independent of isolation indicators, yet was unrelated to Alzheimer's pathology at autopsy in 90 brains (PMID: 17283291). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm) — observational only.
stamp: POSSIBLE (harm) — loneliness and social isolation each predict cognitive decline and Alzheimer's disease but not identically: loneliness predicted dementia where objective isolation did not in one cohort (OR 1.64), and both predicted Alzheimer's in another (OR 1.18 per isolation point; OR 2.12 for loneliness); observational evidence only

title: Women who attended religious services more than once a week had 33% relative lower all-cause mortality (HR 0.67, 95% CI 0.62–0.71) than never-attenders among 74,534 Nurses' Health Study women — observational, with healthy-attender confounding a standing concern
question: In women, is frequent religious-service attendance (a measurable form of community participation) associated with lower mortality?
balance: Observational evidence only, so this shelf caps at POSSIBLE, and the healthy-attender effect (people well enough to attend differ from those who cannot) must be printed — the slate requires it and this balance prints it. In the Nurses' Health Study (74,534 women, 13,537 deaths), attending services more than once a week was associated with HR 0.67 (95% CI 0.62 to 0.71) for all-cause mortality versus never attending, with cardiovascular HR 0.73 and cancer HR 0.79; social support explained 23% of the association (PMID: 27183175). In the same cohort programme (89,708 women), weekly-or-more attendance was associated with an approximately five-fold lower suicide rate (HR 0.16, 95% CI 0.06 to 0.46) (PMID: 27367927). A modelling paper translating the attendance–mortality literature estimated 2–3 added life-years for weekly attendance (PMID: 16513898). None of this is randomised; attendance cannot be prescribed from this evidence. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — frequent religious-service attendance is associated with 33% relative lower all-cause mortality in one large women's cohort (HR 0.67) and markedly lower suicide rates (HR 0.16 for weekly attendance); observational evidence only, healthy-attender effect must be printed

title: The widowhood effect survives its sharpest bias test: in over 1 million older Americans a current wife's death raised her husband's mortality while an ex-wife's death did not — arguing against homogamy bias — and a spouse's hospitalisation alone carried 16–22% as much mortality risk as a spouse's death
question: After a spouse's death, does the surviving spouse's mortality rise — and does the 'widowhood effect' survive homogamy controls?
balance: Observational evidence only, so this shelf caps at POSSIBLE. Elwert & Christakis 2008 (over 1 million elderly Americans) ran the homogamy test: a current wife's death showed a strong effect on her husband's mortality across three empirical tests, while an ex-wife's death — which shares the similarity/shared-exposure history but cannot plausibly cause grief-driven mortality — showed no statistically significant effect, strengthening the causal interpretation (PMID: 19110901; the record reports the tests qualitatively, with no pooled hazard ratio printed). The companion Medicare study of 518,240 couples quantified the neighbouring exposure: a spouse's hospitalisation raised partner mortality by diagnosis (e.g., HR 1.22 for dementia, 1.19 for psychiatric disease in men), at 22% (men) and 16% (women) of the mortality risk associated with a spouse's death itself (PMID: 16481639). A pooled-panel review found a consistent survival advantage for the married but little mortality difference between widowed, divorced/separated and never-married statuses (PMID: 21526396) — a caution printed on the face. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm) — observational only.
stamp: POSSIBLE (harm) — bereavement is associated with raised mortality in the surviving spouse, and the ex-wife comparison argues the effect is not mainly homogamy bias; observational evidence only, with the two key qualitative cards reporting no pooled effect size in their records

title: Social stress measurably slows healing and skews immune gene expression: high-hostile couples healed wounds at 60% of the rate of low-hostile couples, and perceived isolation showed the pro-inflammatory CTRA transcriptome pattern across 141 older adults — small mechanistic studies, not outcome trials
question: Do hostile marital interactions and perceived social isolation change inflammatory biology and wound healing?
balance: Mechanistic and small-study evidence, so this shelf caps at POSSIBLE and claims biology, not clinical outcomes. In a crossover experiment in 42 healthy married couples, blister wounds healed more slowly after a marital-conflict session than after a social-support session, with lower local cytokine production at wound sites; consistently high-hostile couples healed at 60% of the rate of low-hostile couples and showed larger next-morning rises in plasma interleukin-6 and tumour necrosis factor alpha after conflict (PMID: 16330726). In five longitudinal transcriptome surveys of 141 older adults, perceived social isolation showed the conserved transcriptional response to adversity — sympathetic up-regulation, classical-monocyte expansion, glucocorticoid desensitisation and down-regulated interferons — with the mechanism confirmed in a macaque isolation model (PMID: 26598672). The population-level check is weaker: a meta-analysis of 14 loneliness and 16 isolation papers found no loneliness association with C-reactive protein or fibrinogen and only analysis-dependent signals for interleukin-6 and fibrinogen (PMID: 32092313). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm) — mechanistic evidence only.
stamp: POSSIBLE (harm) — hostile marital interaction slowed wound healing (60% of the low-hostile rate) in a 42-couple crossover experiment and perceived isolation tracked a pro-inflammatory, antiviral-suppressed leukocyte programme in 141 older adults, while the inflammation meta-analysis was mixed/null for most markers; mechanistic evidence only

title: Loneliness interventions work modestly, and changing thinking beats adding contact: psychological interventions reduced loneliness with a small-to-medium effect (g = 0.43) across 28 randomised trials (3,039 people), and the strategies that addressed maladaptive social cognition were the most successful in randomised comparisons
question: Across randomised studies, do interventions reduce loneliness, and do interventions targeting maladaptive social cognition outperform those that only increase social contact?
balance: Two concordant syntheses plus a youth synthesis support a real but modest effect, capped at POSSIBLE because effects are small-to-medium and heterogeneous. Masi 2011 compared the four strategy families (social skills, social support, social contact, maladaptive social cognition) and found that among randomised comparison studies the cognition-targeting interventions were the most successful, while single-group and non-randomised designs inflated effects (PMID: 20716644). Hickin 2021 pooled 28 randomised trials (3,039 people; 31 studies, 3,959 people in the review) and found psychological interventions significantly reduced loneliness versus control with effect size g = 0.43, cognitive behavioural therapy being the most common type (PMID: 34339939). In young people (≤25 years), a 39-study meta-analysis (25 randomised trials) likewise found interventions reduced loneliness, though trials rarely targeted young people who actually reported loneliness (PMID: 32406165). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — psychological interventions reduce loneliness by a small-to-medium standardised effect (g = 0.43) in randomised-trial meta-analysis, with cognition-targeting approaches favoured over contact-only approaches; effects modest and heterogeneous

title: In older adults most intervention types show some success but the evidence is weak: a randomised-trial meta-analysis of 70 studies (8,259 people) found mostly small effects — animal therapy and videoconferencing in long-term care looked largest but with very low-quality, highly heterogeneous evidence
question: In older adults, which intervention types (group, one-to-one, technology, activity) reduce social isolation and loneliness?
balance: Three syntheses agree on breadth and agree on weakness, so the stamp is POSSIBLE with the weakness printed. The randomised-trial synthesis (Hoang 2022; 70 studies, 8,259 participants; 44 studies in the loneliness meta-analysis) found most interventions had small effects; animal therapy in long-term care (−1.86, 95% CI −3.14 to −0.59, I² = 86%) and videoconferencing technology in long-term care (−1.40, 95% CI −2.37 to −0.44, I² = 70%) looked largest but with high heterogeneity, and overall quality of evidence was very low (PMID: 36251294). Gardiner 2018 (38 studies) found most interventions reported some success with generally weak evidence, the most effective sharing adaptability, a community-development approach and productive engagement (PMID: 27413007). Poscia 2018 (20 studies, 18 interventions) found significant findings in 6 of 11 group interventions, 1 of 4 mixed and all 3 individual interventions, flagging new technologies and community arts as promising (PMID: 29199121). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — group, one-to-one, technology and activity interventions each show some reductions in loneliness/isolation in older adults, but pooled randomised effects are mostly small and the overall quality of evidence was rated very low in the largest synthesis

title: Treating isolation in mental illness: across 30 randomised trials only a minority significantly reduced isolation — supported socialisation and cognitive approaches are leads, not proven treatments
question: In people with mental-health conditions, do interventions reduce subjective and objective social isolation?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence). Three syntheses agree the trial base is thin and mixed. Ma/Mann 2020 (PMID: 31741017) found 30 randomised trials in people with mental-health problems, with significant isolation reductions in only a minority; cognitive modification (for subjective isolation) and supported socialisation within mixed strategies (for objective isolation) were the preliminary signals. Webber 2017 (PMID: 28286914) found only 6 of 19 social-participation interventions had been randomised, with the strongest network gains for supported community engagement. title: Befriending: pooled randomised trials show a modest cut in depressive symptoms (SMD −0.27 short term) — but whether visiting actually reduces loneliness is still very uncertain
question: Does befriending (a trained volunteer forming a social relationship with an isolated person) reduce depressive symptoms and distress?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) for depressive symptoms and distress; unproven for loneliness itself. Mead 2010 (PMID: 20118451) pooled randomised trials and found a modest significant reduction in depressive symptoms (SMD −0.27 short term; −0.18 long term). Fakoya 2021 (PMID: 34499682) identifies plausible mechanisms (reciprocity, empathy, autonomy, privacy). title: Volunteering and health: volunteers had 22% lower relative mortality in cohort meta-analysis (risk ratio 0.78) — observational evidence only, and the few experiments did not confirm it
question: Is volunteering associated with lower mortality and better health, and what do the cohort data actually support?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational evidence only, and the face says so. Two meta-analyses of cohort data agree: Jenkinson 2013 (PMID: 23968220) found volunteers at lower mortality risk (risk ratio 0.78, a 22% relative risk reduction) with favourable depression, life-satisfaction and wellbeing findings in cohorts; Okun 2013 (PMID: 23421326) found a 24% lower relative mortality risk after adjustment (47% unadjusted — the shrinkage itself measures confounding). Anderson 2014 (PMID: 25150681) found the same directions across 73 papers with only one randomised trial among them. Crucially, Jenkinson's experimental studies did not confirm the cohort findings, and reverse causation (healthy people volunteer) is uncontrolled. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), capped by the observational base.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: volunteers show 22–24% lower relative mortality in cohort meta-analyses, but adjustment halves the association and experimental studies have not confirmed it

title: Experience Corps: in the pilot randomised trial 53% of older volunteers became more active versus 23% of controls — and over 2 years in the full trial, men's brain volumes rose 0.7–1.6% while controls' shrank
question: In older adults, does intensive intergenerational school volunteering (Experience Corps) improve the volunteers' health and activity?

title: Community choirs for older adults: the Community of Voices trial (390 people, 12 centres) cut loneliness (effect size 0.34) and raised interest in life (0.39) at 6 months

balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). Two randomised trials of two different choir programmes point the same way. title: Yoga for depression: 12 randomised trials (619 people) showed a short-term effect versus usual care (SMD -0.69), but the largest adjunctive trial found no difference at 10 weeks
question: In major depression, does yoga improve symptoms versus control in randomised trials?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), short-term and as an adjunct — not established as monotherapy. Cramer 2013 (PMID: 23922209) meta-analysed 12 randomised trials with 619 participants and found moderate evidence for short-term effects on depression severity versus usual care (SMD -0.69, 95% CI -0.99 to -0.39). The two primary trials carded point both ways on timing: Prathikanti 2017 (PMID: 28301561; NCT01210651; 38 adults) found a significantly greater 8-week fall in Beck Depression Inventory scores with hatha yoga as monotherapy for mild-to-moderate major depression (P = 0.034), while Uebelacker 2017 (PMID: 28382883; 122 adults on antidepressants) found no significant difference at the 10-week primary endpoint (P = 0.36) but lower depression over the full follow-up and more responders at 6 months (51% vs 31%). This shelf is distinct from live #455, which homes exercise for depression generally. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — 12 randomised trials (619 people) showed a short-term severity effect versus usual care (SMD -0.69), but the largest adjunctive trial found no difference at its 10-week primary endpoint

title: Reminiscence and life review for late-life depression: meta-analyses found a large effect on depressive symptoms (d = 0.84), rising to 1.23 in older people with elevated symptoms
question: In older adults, do reminiscence/life-review interventions reduce depressive symptoms?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — consistent meta-analytic effects from controlled studies, but the base is older and not all randomised. Bohlmeijer 2003 (PMID: 14677140) found an overall effect size of 0.84 (95% CI 0.31 to 1.37) on depressive symptoms across 20 controlled studies, larger (d = 1.23) in people with elevated symptoms. Pinquart & Forstmeier 2012 (PMID: 22304736), across 128 controlled studies, found a moderate depression effect (g = 0.57), rising to g = 1.09 in depressed individuals and g = 1.28 for life-review therapy specifically. Pinquart 2007 (PMID: 18074252), in clinically depressed older adults, likewise rated reminiscence among the interventions with large effects. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — meta-analyses of controlled studies found effects of d = 0.84 overall and up to g = 1.28 for life-review therapy in depressed older adults, but the trial base is older and not all randomised

title: Assertive community treatment in homeless people with severe mental illness: randomised trials showed a 37% greater reduction in homelessness than standard case management (relative comparison)
question: In homeless populations with severe mental illness, does assertive community treatment improve housing and clinical outcomes?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) for housing and symptom outcomes in homeless populations specifically. Coldwell & Bender 2007 (PMID: 17329462) meta-analysed 10 studies with 5,775 homeless subjects: in randomised trials, assertive community treatment produced a 37% greater reduction in homelessness (relative comparison, 95% CI 18% to 55%) and a 26% greater improvement in psychiatric symptom severity (relative comparison, 95% CI 7% to 44%) than standard case management, with no significant difference in hospitalisation. Aubry 2015 (PMID: 26720504) reports the At Home/Chez Soi randomised project (1,158 Housing First vs 990 standard care), in which assertive community treatment or intensive case management supported rapid, stable housing with superior housing outcomes. Burns & Santos 1995 (PMID: 7552556) reviewed the randomised assertive community treatment trials of 1990-1994, including homeless populations. Assertive community treatment for severe mental illness generally (hospital use) is homed at live #3273 and is not re-carded here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in randomised trials in homeless populations, assertive community treatment gave a 37% greater reduction in homelessness (relative) than standard case management, with no significant difference in hospitalisation

title: Social skills training in schizophrenia: meta-analysis found moderate gains in community functioning (d = 0.52) and negative symptoms (d = 0.40), on evidence Cochrane rated very low quality
question: In schizophrenia, does social skills training improve social functioning and negative symptoms?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two syntheses agree on improved skills and functioning, but the Cochrane evidence is rated very low quality and the effect disappears against an active discussion-group control. Kurtz & Mueser 2008 (PMID: 18540742) meta-analysed 22 controlled studies with 1,521 clients: large effects on content mastery (d = 1.20), moderate effects on performance-based skills and community functioning (both d = 0.52) and negative symptoms (d = 0.40). Almerie 2015 (PMID: 26059249), the Cochrane review of 13 randomised trials with 975 participants, found social functioning, relapse (relative risk 0.52, 95% CI 0.34 to 0.79; 2 trials, 263 participants) and rehospitalisation favoured social skills programmes versus standard care, all on very low quality evidence, with no significant differences versus a discussion group. Kurtz 2015 (PMID: 25640526) shows the training used as a platform alongside other rehabilitation. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — meta-analysis found moderate effects on community functioning and negative symptoms (d = 0.52 and 0.40), but Cochrane rated the randomised evidence very low quality and found no advantage over a discussion group

title: Family-to-Family, the peer-taught family education programme: a randomised study of 318 family members improved coping and empowerment, though subjective burden did not differ
question: For families of people with mental illness, does the peer-taught Family-to-Family education programme improve family outcomes in a randomised study?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single randomised programme, consistently positive on coping and empowerment, not on subjective burden. Dixon 2011 (PMID: 21632725) randomised 318 family members: Family-to-Family participants improved significantly more in problem-focused coping (empowerment and illness knowledge), with exploratory gains in acceptance, distress and problem solving, but subjective illness burden did not differ. The earlier waitlist-controlled study (Dixon 2004, PMID: 14984393; 95 family members) found reduced subjective burden and increased empowerment, sustained at 6 months; the randomised programme's benefits were still present at 9 months (Lucksted 2013, PMID: 22804103), and a pre-post study in Mexico City (Domínguez-Martinez 2017, PMID: 27842466; 230 relatives) found reduced negative emotional attitudes and improved understanding. This is the peer-taught Family-to-Family programme, distinct from clinician family intervention in schizophrenia, homed at live #2685. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one randomised study (318 family members) improved coping, empowerment and illness knowledge, with benefits sustained at 9 months, but subjective burden did not differ

title: Peer-supported self-management after a mental-health crisis: readmission within a year was 29% versus 38% in the CORE randomised trial (441 people)
question: In people discharged from mental-health crisis care, does peer-supported self-management improve outcomes and cost-effectiveness?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) for the specific crisis-discharge programme; the wider peer-support trial literature is weak. Lloyd-Evans 2014 (PMID: 24528545) meta-analysed 18 randomised trials with 5,597 participants and found little or no evidence that peer support improved hospitalisation, overall symptoms or satisfaction, with some inconsistent evidence for hope, recovery and empowerment. The CORE randomised trial (Johnson 2018, PMID: 30102174; ISRCTN01027104; 441 people discharged from crisis teams) then found readmission to acute care within 1 year in 29% of the peer-supported self-management group versus 38% of controls (odds ratio 0.66 relative, 95% CI 0.43 to 0.99; P = 0.0438). Its cost-effectiveness analysis (Le Novere 2023, PMID: 37333912) put the probability of cost-effectiveness at a £20,000-per-QALY threshold between 57% and 96% depending on method. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one randomised trial (441 people) found readmission after crisis care of 29% versus 38% with peer-supported self-management, while a meta-analysis of 18 peer-support trials found little or no class-level benefit

title: Telephone peer support to prevent postnatal depression: in 701 high-risk women, probable depression at 12 weeks was 14% with peer support versus 25% with usual care
question: In high-risk women, does telephone-based peer support from experienced mothers prevent postnatal depression?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one large randomised trial plus supportive meta-analysis. Dennis 2009 (PMID: 19147637; ISRCTN68337727) randomised 701 high-risk women: at 12 weeks, 14% of the telephone peer-support group versus 25% of controls scored above 12 on the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (number needed to treat 8.8, 95% CI 5.9 to 19.6); groups did not differ at 24 weeks, after women identified with clinical depression at 12 weeks had been referred for treatment. Huang 2020 (PMID: 32738663) meta-analysed 10 randomised trials of peer support for perinatal depression: reduced depressive scores (standardised mean difference -0.37, 95% CI -0.66 to -0.08) and reduced risk of depression (relative risk 0.69, 95% CI 0.49 to 0.96). The Cochrane prevention review (Dennis 2013, PMID: 23450532) singled out lay (peer)-based telephone support among promising interventions (relative risk 0.54, 95% CI 0.38 to 0.77) — an estimate resting on the Dennis trial itself. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one large randomised trial (701 high-risk women) found probable postnatal depression at 12 weeks in 14% versus 25% with telephone peer support, and a 10-trial meta-analysis found a relative risk of 0.69 for depression

title: Group therapy in metastatic breast cancer: mood and pain improved in the 235-woman BEST trial, but survival was not prolonged (median 17.9 vs 17.6 months) — the 1989 survival claim failed both randomised replications
question: Does supportive-expressive group therapy prolong survival in metastatic breast cancer — the claim and its randomised refutation?
balance: The survival claim does not survive its randomised tests in metastatic disease. Spiegel 1989 (PMID: 2571815; 86 women) reported mean survival of 36.6 versus 18.9 months with weekly supportive group therapy plus self-hypnosis. The larger multicentre BEST trial, Goodwin 2001 (PMID: 11742045; 235 women), found median survival of 17.9 versus 17.6 months (hazard ratio for death 1.06, 95% CI 0.78 to 1.45) — the treatment made no difference to survival — while mood and pain perception improved, particularly in women who were initially more distressed. Spiegel's own replication attempt in 2007 (PMID: 17647221; NCT00226928; 125 women) again found no survival effect (median 30.7 versus 33.3 months). One positive outlier exists outside metastatic disease: Andersen 2008 (PMID: 19016270; 227 women with regional breast cancer) reported lower recurrence and breast-cancer death with a psychologist-led group intervention over a median 11 years, a different population and intervention that has not overturned the two metastatic trials. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for mood and pain only, with no survival benefit.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) for mood and pain only — survival was not prolonged in either metastatic-disease trial (median 17.9 vs 17.6 months in the largest; the treatment made no difference to survival)

title: Lay-led self-management programmes: small short-term gains in pain, fatigue, disability and self-efficacy across 17 trials and 7,442 participants — but no significant change in healthcare use or quality of life
question: Do lay-led self-management education programmes improve outcomes in chronic conditions?
balance: Small, short-term, self-reported gains — consistent across a Cochrane synthesis and the programme's own trials, with no demonstrated change in healthcare use or clinical outcomes. Foster 2007 (PMID: 17943839; 17 trials, 7,442 participants) found small statistically significant improvements in pain, disability, fatigue, depression, self-rated health, aerobic exercise and self-efficacy, and no significant differences in physician attendance, days in hospital or health-related quality of life. The founding randomised trial, Lorig 1999 (PMID: 10413387; 952 patients), found the same pattern at 6 months plus fewer hospitalisations, and a real-world before-after cohort, Lorig 2001 (PMID: 11769298; 489 with complete data), reproduced similar gains at 1 year with fewer emergency department visits. Only one trial in the Cochrane set reported outcomes beyond six months and only two reported clinical outcomes, so durability and disease control are unproven. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — small short-term gains in symptoms and self-efficacy across 17 trials (7,442 participants), with no significant change in healthcare use or quality of life

title: Safety planning after a suicidal crisis: suicidal behaviour was 3.03% with safety planning plus follow-up calls versus 5.29% with usual care over 6 months — from a non-randomised cohort comparison, with no randomised trial of the standalone intervention
question: In suicidal patients seen in emergency departments, does safety planning with follow-up reduce suicidal behaviour versus usual care?
balance: Promising but non-randomised throughout — this shelf's face says so. The standalone Safety Planning Intervention evidence rests on one large cohort comparison, Stanley 2018 (PMID: 29998307; 1,640 veterans in 9 Veterans Health Administration emergency departments): suicidal behaviour over 6 months was 3.03% with safety planning plus follow-up telephone contact versus 5.29% with usual care (odds ratio 0.56, 95% CI 0.33 to 0.95), and outpatient mental-health attendance more than doubled in relative terms (odds ratio 2.06). A meta-analysis of safety planning-type interventions, Nuij 2021 (PMID: 35048835; 6 studies, 3,536 participants), pooled a relative risk of suicidal behaviour of 0.570 (95% CI 0.408 to 0.795) with no significant effect on suicidal ideation, and a systematic review, Ferguson 2022 (PMID: 33913799; 26 studies), found supportive but heterogeneous evidence, half of it for safety planning combined with other interventions. No randomised trial of the standalone intervention is carded here. The ED-SAFE 2 system package, which includes safety planning as one component of a multicomponent programme, is homed at live shelf #1169 and is cross-pointed, not re-carded. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational and pooled non-randomised evidence only.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — non-randomised evidence only: suicidal behaviour 3.03% vs 5.29% over 6 months in the one large cohort comparison (odds ratio 0.56), with a pooled relative risk of 0.570 in meta-analysis

title: Caring letters after a suicidal crisis: suicide rates were lower in all five contact years in the 843-patient Motto trial (significant for the first two years, P = .04) — an effect that faded after the letters stopped
question: In patients hospitalised after depression/suicidal crisis who declined follow-up, do regular caring letters reduce suicide deaths?
balance: One landmark randomised trial, one supportive but imprecise synthesis, and one small pilot. Motto & Bostrom 2001 (PMID: 11376235) randomised 843 patients who had been hospitalised for a depressive or suicidal state and refused ongoing care: those sent caring letters at least four times a year for five years had a lower suicide rate in all five years, significantly so for the first two years (P = .04), with the difference gradually diminishing and gone by year 14. The updated systematic review and meta-analysis, Skopp 2023 (PMID: 35420858; 6 randomised trials, 6,218 participants), found summary risk ratios ranging from 0.57 to 1.29 across outcomes and time points, a protective effect for suicide attempts at 1 year, and 1-year interval estimates for suicide deaths consistent with either an increase or a decrease in risk. The military Caring Letters pilot, Luxton 2012 (PMID: 21940244; 110 inpatients), established feasibility only. A single trial carries the deaths outcome, so the stamp is capped. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one randomised trial found lower suicide rates for at least two years with sustained caring letters; pooled trial evidence favours fewer attempts but is imprecise for deaths

title: Postcards after self-poisoning: repeat episodes fell in Australia (risk ratio 0.55) and attempts fell in Iran (42% relative risk reduction), but the share of patients repeating was not significantly reduced and a New Zealand trial found no difference
question: After hospital-treated self-poisoning, do repeated postcards reduce repeat episodes?
balance: Three randomised trials, genuinely discordant. Carter 2005 (PMID: 16183654; 772 patients after deliberate self-poisoning in Australia) found no significant difference in the proportion of patients who repeated (15.1% versus 17.3%) but fewer repeat episodes per person (incidence risk ratio 0.55, 95% CI 0.35 to 0.87). Hassanian-Moghaddam 2011 (PMID: 21343332; 2,300 patients in Iran) found significant relative reductions in suicidal ideation and suicide attempts at 12 months. Beautrais 2010 (PMID: 20592434; New Zealand, after self-harm of any method) found no significant differences at all — the treatment made no difference in that trial. Effects may depend on population (self-poisoning versus all self-harm) and setting; no trial was powered for suicide deaths. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — repeat episodes fell in two self-poisoning trials (incidence risk ratio 0.55; 42% relative risk reduction in attempts), but the proportion of repeaters was not significantly reduced and one trial found no difference at all

title: Brief intervention and contact after a suicide attempt: suicide deaths were 0.2% versus 2.2% at 18 months in a 1,867-patient five-country trial — while a 200-patient trial of the same model found no difference in repeat presentations
question: After a suicide attempt, does brief intervention plus scheduled follow-up contact reduce repeat attempts and deaths?
balance: One strongly positive multisite trial on deaths, one null trial on repeat presentations, and a strategy review. Fleischmann 2008 (PMID: 18797646; 1,867 suicide attempters in five low- and middle-income countries) found suicide deaths at 18 months of 0.2% with brief intervention and contact versus 2.2% with treatment as usual (P < 0.001). Amadéo 2015 (PMID: 26605034; 200 randomised patients in French Polynesia, the WHO START study) found no significant differences in repeat hospital presentations for suicidal behaviour — the treatment made no difference on that outcome in that setting. Zalsman 2016 (PMID: 27289303), a 10-year systematic review of suicide-prevention strategies, found the strongest evidence for restricting access to lethal means and for school-based awareness programmes, placing brief contact interventions in a wider, mixed evidence base. Discordant trials cap the stamp. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — suicide deaths were 0.2% vs 2.2% at 18 months in one five-country trial, but a smaller trial of the same model found no difference in repeat presentations

title: Means restriction: locking away barbecue charcoal in one Taiwanese city was followed by a 30% fall in charcoal-burning suicide with no rise in other methods — and two systematic reviews conclude restricting lethal means reduces suicide rates
question: Does restricting access to lethal means (firearms, pesticides, charcoal, bridges, pack sizes) reduce method-specific and overall suicide rates?
balance: Policy and natural-experiment evidence only — no randomised trials of means restriction exist, and this shelf's face says so, which caps the stamp at POSSIBLE. Two expert systematic reviews converge: Mann 2005 (PMID: 16249421; 10 systematic reviews/meta-analyses, 18 randomised trials, 24 cohort and 41 ecological studies) concluded that restricting access to lethal methods reduces suicide rates, and Yip 2012 (PMID: 22726520) reviewed the empirical studies and concluded that means restriction is effective, with substitution, where it occurs, usually to less lethal methods. The one carded natural experiment with hard numbers, Chen 2015 (PMID: 26305374), found that moving barbecue charcoal to locked storage in New Taipei City was followed by a 30% reduction in charcoal-burning suicide after accounting for secular trends (95% CI 14% to 44%), no compensatory rise in other methods, and an estimated 91 lives saved over 20 months. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational/policy evidence only.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational/policy evidence only, no randomised trials exist: two systematic reviews conclude means restriction reduces suicide rates, and a controlled natural experiment found a 30% fall in method-specific suicide with no compensatory rise

title: Targeted grief therapy beats standard therapy in randomised trials: response 51% versus 28% for complicated-grief treatment over interpersonal therapy, CBT beat supportive counselling, and adding exposure cut still-meeting-criteria rates to 14.8% versus 37.9%
question: In complicated/prolonged grief disorder, does targeted grief therapy (complicated-grief treatment or CBT) beat supportive/interpersonal therapy?
balance: LIKELY (benefit). Three independent randomised trials point the same way. Shear 2005 (PMID: 15928281; 95 people with complicated grief) found response in 51% on complicated-grief treatment versus 28% on interpersonal psychotherapy (P = .02; number needed to treat 4.3). Boelen 2007 (PMID: 17469885; 54 mourners) found cognitive-behavioural therapy (cognitive restructuring plus exposure, in either order) produced more improvement in complicated grief and general psychopathology than supportive counselling, with exposure the stronger component. Bryant 2014 (PMID: 25338187; ACTRN12609000229279; 80 patients with prolonged grief disorder) found group CBT plus individual exposure sessions beat the same group CBT plus supportive counselling at 6 months, with fewer completers still meeting prolonged-grief criteria (14.8% vs 37.9%). The trials are small and use active comparators rather than no treatment, so the stamp is for targeted therapy over supportive/interpersonal therapy, not over nothing. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit).
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — three randomised trials: targeted treatment beat interpersonal therapy (response 51% vs 28%), CBT beat supportive counselling, and CBT plus exposure beat CBT alone at 6 months

title: START coping programme for dementia family carers: anxiety/depression scores 1.8 points lower at 8 months and 2.58 points lower at 2 years than usual care in its one randomised trial, with case-level depression odds cut (odds ratio 0.24)
question: In family carers of people with dementia, does the manual-based START coping programme improve carer mental health cost-effectively?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), single-trial programme cap. All three cards are reports of the same pragmatic randomised trial of START (STrAtegies for RelaTives), an 8-session manual-based coping programme delivered by supervised psychology graduates — the main clinical-effectiveness report pinned at this build gate is Livingston 2013 (PMID: 24162942). In 260 carers, affective symptoms (Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale total) were lower with START than treatment as usual over 8 months (adjusted difference −1.80 points; 95% CI −3.29 to −0.31; P = 0.02), case-level depression was less likely (odds ratio 0.24; 95% CI 0.07 to 0.76), and carer quality of life was higher. The nested economic report (PMID: 24162943) found a greater than 99% chance of cost-effectiveness at a £30,000-per-QALY threshold, and the 2-year report (PMID: 26361313) found the mood benefit persisted (difference −2.58 points; P = 0.003). REACH II and the Mittelman NYU intervention are NOT re-carded here — they are homed at live shelf #795; this shelf homes START only. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one randomised trial programme (260 carers): affective symptoms lower at 8 months and still lower at 2 years, and the economic report found a >99% chance of cost-effectiveness at £30,000 per QALY; single-trial cap applies

title: Telephone ACT for dementia caregivers: depressive symptoms were significantly lower after 8 weekly telephone sessions in the one telephone randomised trial (81 caregivers), with most effects gone by 6 months
question: In caregivers of people with dementia, does telephone-delivered ACT improve caregiver outcomes in a randomised trial?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), single-trial cap for the telephone question. The only randomised trial of telephone-delivered acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT) for family caregivers of people with dementia is Risch 2024 (PMID: 39169671; DRKS00006355; 81 caregivers): after 8 weekly telephone sessions, depressive symptoms were significantly lower than in an untreated control group, with several secondary benefits, but most effects were not maintained at 6 months and the authors call the results preliminary because of the small sample. Two neighbouring ACT records support the approach without answering the telephone question directly: a 19-person pilot randomised trial of videoconferencing ACT (PMID: 36591636; NCT04847986) and a 135-caregiver face-to-face trial in which ACT matched CBT against control on depression and beat it on anxiety at post-treatment (PMID: 26075381). This shelf is distinct from live shelf #795 (REACH II / Mittelman NYU) and from shelf #5515 (START), neither of which is re-carded here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the telephone evidence is one small randomised trial (81 caregivers) with benefits at post-treatment that mostly faded by 6 months, supported by a 19-person videoconferencing pilot and one face-to-face ACT trial; single-trial cap applies

title: AI therapy chatbots: two small, short randomised trials in students found less depression with Woebot (P = .01) and with Tess than with an information-only control — and no randomised evidence for AI 'companions' as a loneliness treatment was found
question: Do AI chatbots improve depression/anxiety symptoms — and what is actually randomised?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), with the honest-evidence limits printed on the face. What is actually randomised: Woebot, a fully automated CBT conversational agent, in 70 students over 2 weeks (PMID: 28588005) — depression symptoms fell significantly in the Woebot group and not in the information-only control (P = .01); and Tess, an integrative psychological AI, in 74 students over 2 to 4 weeks (PMID: 30545815; ISRCTN61214172) — depression and anxiety reductions versus the same kind of information-only control. What is only observational: Wysa (PMID: 30470676), where self-selected high users improved more than low users (mean 5.84 vs 3.52 points; P = .03) — a comparison that cannot separate the app from the motivation to use it. No randomised evidence for AI 'companions' as a loneliness treatment was found this session: the randomised agents are symptom-therapy chatbots tested in students for 2 to 4 weeks, and that absence is part of this shelf, not a gap to paper over. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two small randomised trials of therapy chatbots in students (70 and 74 participants, 2 to 4 weeks) found symptom reductions versus information-only controls; the Wysa evidence is observational only, and no randomised evidence for AI companions as a loneliness treatment was found

title: Socially assistive robots in older people's care: reviews report many positive small studies, but the meta-analysis of randomised trials found no statistically significant effect on agitation, anxiety or quality of life
question: What does the evidence support for socially assistive robots in elderly care?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence). Three syntheses, no strong pooled effect. The scoping review (PMID: 29440212) mapped 33 studies and 1,574 participants across 11 robots and found 28 of 33 papers reporting positive findings — alongside methodological issues limiting the utility of the results. The systematic review and meta-analysis restricted to randomised trials (PMID: 29897445; 11 randomised trials, 9 in the meta-analysis) found social robots appeared to have positive impacts on agitation, anxiety and quality of life, but no statistical significance was found in the meta-analysis, and risk of bias was relatively high. The depression-focused systematic review (PMID: 30198077; 7 studies, 6 of them randomised) found three studies with promising outcomes and three with decreased but non-significant depression scores, and concluded the evidence is not strong enough for recommendations on clinical effectiveness. Specific robot trials, including PARO, are homed on shelf #5519 and are not re-carded here. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — a scoping review and two systematic reviews describe mostly positive small studies, but the pooled meta-analysis of randomised trials found no statistically significant effects; the face says so

title: PARO companion robot: loneliness fell versus usual activities in a 40-resident randomised trial, quality of life held up in severe dementia in a cluster trial, and medication use fell in a third — three small trials, all under 65 participants
question: In older people in residential care, does the PARO companion robot improve psychosocial outcomes in a randomised trial?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). Three small randomised trials of the PARO companion robot, each positive on a different outcome. Robinson 2013 (PMID: 23545466; 40 residential-care residents, 12 weeks of twice-weekly hour-long sessions) found significant decreases in loneliness versus a control group attending normal activities. Petersen 2017 (PMID: 27716673; 61 patients in five secure dementia units) reported decreased stress and anxiety and reductions in psychoactive and pain medication use with PARO versus standard activity programmes. Jøranson 2016 (PMID: 27434512; NCT01998490; cluster-randomised, 53 participants) found quality of life stayed stable with group PARO activity while it decreased in controls among residents with severe dementia, with significantly less psychotropic medication use after the intervention. No single outcome is replicated across two trials, samples are 40 to 61, and the pooled meta-analysis of social robots on shelf #5518 was non-significant — so the stamp stays POSSIBLE, not higher. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — three small randomised trials (40, 61 and 53 participants) each found a benefit on a different outcome (loneliness, medication use, quality of life in severe dementia), but no outcome is confirmed by two trials and pooled robot evidence (shelf #5518) is non-significant

title: Animal-assisted therapy: a Cochrane review of 9 randomised trials (305 people with dementia) found people may be slightly less depressed (mean difference −2.87) but no quality-of-life improvement, on low-to-moderate certainty evidence
question: Does animal-assisted therapy improve outcomes in randomised trials, including agitation/depression in dementia?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), for depressive symptoms only and with the certainty limits on the face. The Cochrane review for dementia (PMID: 31763689; 9 randomised trials, 305 participants) found animal-assisted therapy may leave people slightly less depressed (mean difference −2.87; 95% CI −5.24 to −0.50; 2 studies, 83 participants; low-certainty evidence), with no quality-of-life improvement and no clear differences in social functioning, problematic behaviour, agitation or daily activities. The matched dementia trial (PMID: 23831177) found symptoms stayed constant with therapy while they worsened in controls — a delay-of-progression pattern, not an improvement. The broader systematic review of randomised trials across conditions (PMID: 24731910; 11 trials) judged the trials relatively low quality and could not meta-analyse them. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for depressive symptoms only: the Cochrane review found a small depression advantage on low-certainty evidence and no clear difference on agitation, behaviour or quality of life; the wider randomised literature is small and low quality

title: Pet ownership and mortality (observational only): dog ownership was associated with a relative risk of death of 0.76 in a meta-analysis of 3.8 million people, but one meta-analysis found no significant dog-specific association — an association, not proof that getting a pet extends life
question: Is pet (especially dog) ownership associated with lower cardiovascular and all-cause mortality?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only; this face says so because no randomised evidence exists or could readily exist for pet ownership. A meta-analysis of dog ownership (PMID: 31592726; 10 studies, 3,837,005 participants) found dog ownership associated with a relative risk of 0.76 for all-cause mortality and 0.69 for cardiovascular death (relative measures; absolute rates were not reported in the fetched record). A nationwide Swedish cohort of 3,432,153 people (PMID: 29150678) found lower death and cardiovascular-death hazard ratios in dog owners, strongest in single-person households — but its twin subcohort could not replicate the reduced risk. A broader pet-ownership meta-analysis (PMID: 31815850; 26 studies) found lower cardiovascular mortality in pet owners overall (adjusted hazard ratio 0.81) yet no significant association for dog owners specifically on overall or cardiovascular mortality — a discordance printed here, not smoothed over. Healthy-owner and socioeconomic confounding remain plausible explanations for all of it. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), association only.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational evidence only, capped at POSSIBLE and labelled as such on the face: pooled relative risks favour owners, but the studies cannot exclude confounding, one meta-analysis found no significant dog-specific association, and absolute rates were not reported in the fetched records

title: Hearing interventions in older adults — the economic evidence only: a 2026 systematic review of 27 studies generally found hearing aids and cochlear implants cost-effective, and two hearing-aid economic studies put the cost at about S$11,964 per QALY over 5 years (Singapore) with cost-effectiveness in China depending on the aid lasting over about 2.5 years
question: What do economic evaluations support for hearing interventions in older adults?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) for economic value only — this is an economics shelf, not a clinical-effectiveness shelf. The 2026 systematic review (PMID: 42862436; 27 studies in 28 articles) found cost-effectiveness analyses generally judged cochlear implants and hearing aids cost-effective compared with no intervention, and cost-benefit analyses showed positive net monetary benefits, while flagging omitted downstream costs, limited carer and societal impacts and inconsistent outcome measurement. Two individual hearing-aid evaluations agree in direction: a Singapore delayed-start cost-utility study (PMID: 33261603; 427 older adults) estimated S$42,790 per QALY at 3 months, improving to S$11,964 per QALY over 5 years if use continued; and a Chinese randomised-trial-based analysis (PMID: 37306959; 385 adults) found hearing aids cost-effective with high probability provided the devices lasted, with a quality-adjusted life year gain of 0.017. The clinical question of hearing treatment and cognition is homed at live shelf #350 (the ACHIEVE trial) and is NOT re-carded here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), economics only.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — economic value only: syntheses and two hearing-aid economic studies generally find cost-effectiveness versus no intervention, on heterogeneous methods; this shelf makes no clinical-effect claim, and the hearing-and-cognition question stays homed at live shelf #350 (ACHIEVE), not re-carded here

title: Dependent oedema and evening ankle swelling (visitor ask): calcium-channel blockers cause it in about 1 in 10 users (amlodipine 16.6% vs 6.2% on placebo), and reviewing the blocker — lower dose, adding a renin–angiotensin blocker, or switching agent — reduces it; compression evidence is homed at pack #5420
question: In adults whose ankles swell by the evening, what causes dependent oedema, and does anything help — leg elevation, compression stockings, or reviewing a calcium-channel blocker such as amlodipine?
balance: SPLIT — the cause and the remedy point in different directions on this shelf. As a cause, calcium-channel blockers are established culprits: across 106 randomised trials (99,469 participants), peripheral oedema occurred in 10.7% on a calcium-channel blocker versus 3.2% on control/placebo, rising with dose and duration (Makani 2011, PMID: 21558959), and for amlodipine specifically the rate was 16.6% versus 6.2% on placebo (relative risk 2.9), although about 37% of oedema cases on amlodipine were estimated unrelated to the drug (Vukadinović 2019, PMID: 31107359). As a remedy, three randomised-trial meta-analyses agree that reviewing the blocker helps: adding a renin–angiotensin system blocker cut oedema incidence by 38% relative (RR 0.62; Makani 2011, PMID: 21295192), lower doses carried lower risk, and switching to a lipophilic dihydropyridine such as lercanidipine carried a relative risk of 0.44 versus first-generation agents (Makarounas-Kirchmann 2009, PMID: 19808126). Compression stockings for venous leg oedema are homed at pack #5420 and are NOT re-carded here; no trial evidence for leg elevation alone was carded on this shelf, and other causes of evening ankle swelling (venous insufficiency, heart failure, kidney or liver disease, other drugs) are separate questions. PROPOSED SPLIT (calcium-channel blockers a common, dose-dependent cause — harm; dose reduction, adding a renin–angiotensin blocker, or switching agent reduces it — benefit).
stamp: SPLIT — calcium-channel blockers (amlodipine RR 2.9 vs placebo) are a common dose-dependent cause of dependent oedema (harm), while dose reduction, adding a renin–angiotensin blocker (38% relative reduction) or switching to a lipophilic dihydropyridine (RR 0.44) reduces it (benefit); compression is cross-pointed to pack #5420, not re-carded

title: Cardiac sarcoidosis steroid-sparing treatment: no randomised trial results exist yet (CHASM CS-RCT pending) — observational evidence only shows similar inflammation suppression on methotrexate-based regimens and prednisone, with clinical-event differences not significant
question: In cardiac sarcoidosis, does methotrexate-based steroid-sparing treatment match prednisone for arrhythmia and cardiac outcomes with less steroid harm?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only, printed on the face: there is no published randomised trial in cardiac sarcoidosis. The one randomised trial designed to answer this question, CHASM CS-RCT (NCT03593759; low-dose prednisone plus methotrexate versus standard-dose prednisone, 97 patients per group planned), has a published design paper (PMID: 31911261) but no published results in the records fetched this session, so it is described here and NOT carded as evidence. What exists is observational: a 61-patient retrospective cohort found FDG uptake fell similarly on prednisone, methotrexate, or both, with major adverse cardiovascular events in 33.3%, 20.0% and 10.0% respectively — a non-significant difference (P = 0.292; Vis 2023, PMID: 36640249); a 28-patient series found methotrexate-based maintenance reduced or eliminated FDG uptake in most patients after a short prednisone lead-in (Rosenthal 2019, PMID: 31538835); and a 2025 systematic review of 11 studies found all treatments reduced myocardial inflammation, with no statistically significant difference between subgroups (PMID: 40225494). Whether steroid harm is actually less has not been measured in a randomised comparison. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only; the randomised answer is still pending.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: retrospective cohorts and a systematic review show similar FDG suppression on methotrexate-based regimens and prednisone with no significant clinical-event difference; no randomised trial results are published (CHASM CS-RCT, NCT03593759, pending)

title: Sevelamer versus calcium-based binders in non-dialysis CKD: the single INDEPENDENT pilot programme (212 patients) found lower mortality and slower calcification signals with sevelamer — with no effect sizes in its records and no replication trial
question: In non-dialysis chronic kidney disease with hyperphosphataemia, does sevelamer improve phosphate control, vascular calcification, or survival compared with calcium-based binders?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single small trial programme (INDEPENDENT), and its records report direction more often than effect sizes. In the INDEPENDENT pilot randomised trial (212 patients with stage 3–4 CKD), all-cause mortality and the composite of death or dialysis inception were lower on sevelamer than calcium carbonate, with only a non-significant trend for dialysis inception alone; the record reports no effect size or event counts (Di Iorio 2012, PMID: 22241819). A post hoc analysis of the 113 participants with coronary calcification found sevelamer independently predicted lower risk only when calcification progression was absent or moderate (Russo 2015, PMID: 24599830). The programme's patient-level economic analysis found sevelamer gained 0.06 life-years and saved €5,615 per patient over 3 years, driven by the mortality difference (Ruggeri 2014, PMID: 25171148). On phosphate control itself, the trial record states only the target range both arms were held to (2.7–4.6 mg/dL in stage 3–4 CKD) and reports no comparative phosphate levels. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — single pilot trial programme; larger trials needed, as the trial's own authors state.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single pilot trial programme (INDEPENDENT, 212 patients): mortality and the death-or-dialysis composite favoured sevelamer, but the records report no effect sizes and no independent replication exists

title: Insulin-only bionic pancreas (iLet) in type 1 diabetes: one pivotal programme (NCT04200313) — HbA1c fell 0.5 percentage points and time in range rose 12–14% versus standard care with CGM over 13 weeks, with no increase in measured hypoglycaemia
question: In type 1 diabetes, does the insulin-only bionic pancreas (iLet) improve HbA1c and time in range versus standard care with CGM?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single trial programme (the Insulin-Only Bionic Pancreas Pivotal Trial, NCT04200313), so the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE despite consistent results. In the 13-week randomised trial (326 participants aged 6–79), HbA1c fell from 7.9% to 7.3% on the bionic pancreas and was unchanged at 7.7% on standard care with CGM (adjusted difference −0.5 percentage points), with time below 54 mg/dL non-inferior and no diabetic ketoacidosis in either group (Russell 2022, PMID: 36170500). The adult fast-acting-insulin-aspart report of the same programme found the same −0.5% HbA1c difference and 14% more time in range (3.4 h/day) versus standard care (Beck 2022, PMID: 36173235), and the single-arm extension, in which the former standard-care group crossed to the device, reproduced the improvement (HbA1c 7.7% to 7.1%; time in range 53% to 65%; Lynch 2022, PMID: 36173238). Severe hypoglycaemia rates did not differ significantly. The youth-specific pivotal report of this programme is homed at live shelf #561 (closed-loop umbrella) and is not re-carded here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — single trial programme.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single trial programme (NCT04200313): HbA1c −0.5 percentage points and time in range +12–14% versus standard care with CGM at 13 weeks, hypoglycaemia non-inferior; capped at POSSIBLE because all carded reports share the one programme

title: Aspirin in pregestational diabetes to prevent preeclampsia: unproven — the dedicated IRELAnD trial (134 women, 150 mg from the first trimester) found no difference in placental-dysfunction outcomes, and the pooled diabetes-specific estimate is non-significant
question: In pregestational diabetes, does low-dose aspirin started in pregnancy prevent preterm preeclampsia versus placebo or usual care?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) unproven — the diabetes-specific evidence does not demonstrate prevention, and the record for the one dedicated trial does not report preterm preeclampsia separately. The IRELAnD randomised trial (134 women with pregestational diabetes; aspirin 150 mg from 11–14 weeks to 36 weeks versus placebo) found no difference in its composite of placental dysfunction — 25% on aspirin versus 21% on placebo (P = .796; the treatment made no difference) — in a trial stopped far short of its planned 566 participants (Finnegan 2024, PMID: 38461094). The diabetes-specific systematic review found an individual-patient meta-analysis of 930 women with diabetes gave a non-significant odds ratio of 0.58 (95% CI 0.20–1.71) for preeclampsia (Zen 2022, PMID: 34806161), and a secondary analysis of the older Maternal-Fetal Medicine Units high-risk trial — which included insulin-treated pregestational diabetes among its risk groups, at 60 mg — found no preeclampsia reduction in any subgroup, with diabetes-specific results not reported separately (Tolcher 2020, PMID: 33345910). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) unproven — underpowered and null so far; a larger diabetes-specific trial is still needed.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) unproven — the single dedicated RCT in pregestational diabetes was null on its composite (the treatment made no difference: 25% vs 21%) and underpowered (134 of 566 planned), and the diabetes-specific pooled estimate was non-significant (OR 0.58, 95% CI 0.20–1.71); preterm preeclampsia is not separately reported in the trial record

title: Diabetic foot ulcers — non-removable beats removable: a walker made irremovable healed 80% versus 74% for a total contact cast (41 patients), and syntheses favour non-removable offloading (pooled RR 1.43; OR 2.64 in randomised trials), though one synthesis found the removable-walker contrast alone non-significant
question: In diabetic foot ulcers, does a non-removable total contact cast heal ulcers faster than a removable cast walker?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — making the device non-removable, not the cast brand, is what the evidence supports. The head-to-head trial of the two non-removable forms found them equivalent: in 41 patients, ulcers healed within 12 weeks in 80% on a removable walker rendered irremovable (iTCC) versus 74% on a standard total contact cast (Katz 2005, PMID: 15735187). The removable-versus-non-removable contrast is where the difference sits: a 2013 meta-analysis found non-removable devices healed more ulcers than removable devices overall (pooled RR 1.43, 95% CI 1.11 to 1.84), although its removable-cast-walker subgroup contrast alone was not statistically significant (Morona 2013, PMID: 23303652); a 2016 meta-analysis of 1,605 patients found improved healing with total contact casting over a removable cast walker (Elraiyah 2016, PMID: 26804369); and a 2024 meta-analysis of randomised trials found total contact cast or a non-removable knee-high walker healed more ulcers than other offloading devices (odds ratio 2.64, 95% CI 1.43 to 4.89) (Gauna 2024, PMID: 38489054). The slate anchor trial, Armstrong 2005 (PMID: 15735186), is already carded on live shelf #291 and is cross-pointed, not re-carded here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for a non-removable total contact cast over a removable cast walker.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — non-removable total contact casting over a removable cast walker: three syntheses favour non-removable offloading (one removable-walker subgroup contrast non-significant) and the one head-to-head trial shows a walker made irremovable matches a total contact cast; the Armstrong 2005 anchor is homed on live shelf #291 and cross-pointed, not re-carded

title: TSH suppression in differentiated thyroid cancer — a split picture: fewer major events in old mixed-risk data (RR 0.73), no benefit in low-risk disease, and observational harm signals for atrial fibrillation (HR 1.58) and postmenopausal bone loss
question: In differentiated thyroid cancer, does more intensive TSH suppression improve recurrence-free survival, and at what cost in atrial fibrillation and bone loss?
balance: SPLIT — the benefit and the harm sit in different patients and different outcomes, and the evidence is observational-heavy throughout (labelled as such). Benefit component, POSSIBLE (benefit): an older meta-analysis of thyroid hormone suppression therapy found fewer major adverse clinical events (disease progression, recurrence and death) with suppression (RR 0.73; 95% CI 0.60 to 0.88) across a cumulative cohort of 4,174 patients (McGriff 2002, PMID: 12553495) — but in low-risk small cancers after lobectomy, a propensity-matched cohort of 446 patients found no disease-free-survival benefit from suppression at all (Park 2017, PMID: 28699428). Harm component, POSSIBLE (harm, observational only): a 2023 meta-analysis of 195,879 differentiated thyroid cancer patients on long-term suppression found higher risks of atrial fibrillation (HR 1.58) and stroke (HR 1.14) (Yu 2023, PMID: 37295414), and a 2021 meta-analysis found lower lumbar-spine bone mineral density in postmenopausal women on suppression (Ku 2021, PMID: 34302730). No randomised trial of suppression intensity is carded on this shelf. PROPOSED SPLIT — POSSIBLE (benefit) for major-event reduction in the older mixed-risk data, no demonstrated benefit in low-risk disease, and POSSIBLE (harm, observational only) for atrial fibrillation and postmenopausal bone loss.
stamp: SPLIT — POSSIBLE (benefit) for major adverse events in older mixed-risk observational data (RR 0.73) with no benefit shown in low-risk disease; POSSIBLE (harm, observational only) for atrial fibrillation (HR 1.58) and postmenopausal bone-density loss; no randomised trial of suppression intensity exists in the carded evidence

title: Encaleret in autosomal dominant hypocalcaemia type 1 — promising but tiny evidence: calcium corrected and urinary calcium reduced over 24 weeks in N = 13 (open-label, no controls), with an N = 5 proof-of-concept study behind it and conventional therapy's renal harms as the rationale
question: In autosomal dominant hypocalcaemia type 1, does the calcilytic encaleret normalise serum calcium and reduce urinary calcium versus conventional therapy?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the human evidence for calcilytics in autosomal dominant hypocalcaemia type 1 (ADH1) totals 18 treated patients across two uncontrolled studies, with the study numbers printed on the face of this shelf. In the encaleret phase 2b study (N = 13 adults with ADH1), encaleret corrected hypocalcaemia and reduced hypercalciuria during inpatient dose-ranging and a 24-week outpatient period, with calcitriol and calcium supplements withheld, no serious adverse events and no discontinuations (Gafni 2023, PMID: 37754292; the report is a journal letter whose PubMed record carries no abstract, and its laboratory values are reported in its figure rather than as numbers in the text). An earlier calcilytic, NPSP795, raised plasma parathyroid hormone up to 129% above baseline in a 3-day proof-of-concept study (N = 5 adults; Roberts 2019, PMID: 31063613). The need is real: in the ADH1 systematic review, 75% of 57 patients assessed on conventional calcium and active vitamin D therapy had at least one renal or related complication, and starting conventional therapy increased the incidence of hypercalciuria by 91% in the 27 patients with before-and-after urine measures (Roszko 2022, PMID: 35879818). There is no randomised or controlled comparison of encaleret against conventional therapy. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — based on a very small total N = 18 across two uncontrolled calcilytic studies.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — based on a very small total N = 18: encaleret corrected calcium and reduced urinary calcium over 24 weeks in an open-label study of N = 13, supported only by an N = 5 proof-of-concept study of an earlier calcilytic and a systematic review documenting conventional therapy's renal harms; no controlled comparison exists

title: Sleepio for insomnia — daytime outcomes: one large trial (1,711 adults) found better sleep-related quality of life (−18.72 points), functional health and well-being than sleep-hygiene education at 24 weeks, with depressive-symptom and older-adult benefits in secondary analyses
question: In insomnia disorder, does digital CBT-I (Sleepio) improve sleep, daytime functioning and quality of life versus sleep-hygiene education or waitlist?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one large randomised trial of the named programme, Sleepio, plus secondary analyses of the Sleepio trial programme. In 1,711 adults with insomnia symptoms, digital CBT-I (Sleepio) beat sleep-hygiene education on all three primary outcomes at 24 weeks: functional health by an adjusted 1.76 points, psychological well-being by 2.95 points, and sleep-related quality of life by −18.72 points on a 1–100 impairment scale, with a large improvement in insomnia mediating the gains (Espie 2019, PMID: 30264137). Secondary analyses point the same way for the outcomes patients feel: in 3,352 participants with probable insomnia and significant depressive symptoms, Sleepio improved depressive symptoms (g = 0.48) and nearly tripled the odds of clinically significant improvement (OR 2.9) (Henry 2021, PMID: 32810921); and in 315 participants aged 65 and over pooled from three Sleepio trials, post-treatment insomnia remission was 60% versus 16% on control (Tarnai 2025, PMID: 40176550). The broader question of app- and web-delivered CBT-I for sleep itself is homed at live shelf #437 (which cards the OASIS trial and the 2012 Sleepio trial) and is cross-pointed, not re-carded here; this shelf stands on Sleepio's functioning and quality-of-life outcomes. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for digital CBT-I (Sleepio) on sleep-related quality of life, daytime functioning and well-being versus sleep-hygiene education.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single large randomised trial of Sleepio (N = 1,711) showed better sleep-related quality of life, functional health and well-being than sleep-hygiene education at 24 weeks, supported by secondary analyses for depressive symptoms and older adults; the sleep-outcome question for digital CBT-I stays homed at live shelf #437 (OASIS), cross-pointed, not re-carded

title: Mediterranean diet and frailty: cohorts consistently link highest adherence to about a third less incident frailty (relative risk 0.66), and the NU-AGE randomised diet year shifted frailty-linked gut microbes and inflammation — but no trial has yet proven the diet prevents frailty
question: In older adults at risk of frailty, does a Mediterranean-style diet intervention slow frailty progression versus usual diet?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational-heavy evidence, printed on the face. The incidence evidence is entirely observational: a 2018 meta-analysis of 4 prospective cohorts (5,789 older people) found the highest Mediterranean-diet adherence carried about half the incident-frailty odds of the lowest (pooled OR 0.44), and a 2023 dose-response meta-analysis of 12 cohorts (89,608 participants) found a relative risk of 0.66 for highest versus lowest adherence. The one randomised intervention, NU-AGE (612 non-frail or pre-frail older people, 1 year of a tailored Mediterranean diet across five European countries), shifted the gut microbiome in directions associated with lower frailty markers and lower inflammatory markers (C-reactive protein, interleukin-17) — but it did not report incident frailty as an outcome in this record, so there is no trial proof that prescribing the diet prevents frailty. Healthy-adherer confounding is the standing alternative explanation for the cohort findings. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only for incident frailty (two meta-analyses of cohorts, relative risk 0.66 / OR 0.44 for highest adherence), supported by one randomised diet intervention (NU-AGE) that improved frailty-linked microbiome and inflammatory markers without reporting a frailty endpoint; healthy-adherer confounding stated on the face

title: Stretching surveillance after low-risk adenomas: Norwegian low-risk patients offered no surveillance died of colorectal cancer less often than the general population (SMR 0.75, still ≤0.90 at 13 years), and UK low-risk patients without surveillance matched population incidence — observational evidence only
question: After removal of colorectal adenomas, can colonoscopic surveillance be safely stretched to 5–10 years in low-risk patients instead of 3-yearly surveillance, without missing interval cancers?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) for stretching surveillance in low-risk patients — observational evidence only, printed on the face. Three large registry/cohort datasets point the same way. In Norway, where guidelines recommended NO routine surveillance after low-risk adenomas, colorectal-cancer mortality in 40,826 post-adenoma patients was lower in the low-risk group than in the general population (SMR 0.75), and with follow-up extended to a median 13 years the low-risk SMR stayed at or below 1.0 in both sexes (women 0.90, men 0.70). In a 33,011-patient UK cohort, low-risk patients who had NO surveillance had a colorectal-cancer incidence statistically indistinguishable from the general population (SIR 0.86), although a single surveillance visit was associated with lower incidence (HR 0.56) in every risk group — the tension that keeps this at POSSIBLE rather than higher. No randomised trial of surveillance intervals in low-risk patients is carded. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: low-risk adenoma patients under no-routine-surveillance policies had colorectal-cancer mortality at or below general-population rates out to 13 years (SMR 0.75–0.90), tempered by UK data associating a single surveillance visit with lower incidence (HR 0.56); no randomised interval trial in low-risk patients

title: School-located flu vaccination: programmes add about 7–12 percentage points of coverage (randomised programme trial and Oakland's city-wide rollout), with fewer illness absences and fewer community flu hospitalisations in seasons when the vaccine worked
question: Does school-located influenza vaccination increase children's vaccination coverage and reduce illness-related school absence?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). The programme evidence is consistent across three designs. A 2010 systematic review of 59 studies found school-located influenza vaccination (SLIV) programmes feasible and effective, with consent-form design, incentives, education, reminders and offering both injected and intranasal vaccine raising consent and coverage. A randomised programme trial in western New York elementary schools raised the proportion of children vaccinated by 11.2 and 12.0 percentage points over control schools in its two years, at about $59.88 per additionally vaccinated child excluding vaccine purchase — falling to about $24 per child once averted parental costs were counted. A city-wide Oakland matched-cohort evaluation (at least 95 schools, 2014–2018) found coverage 7 and 11 percentage points higher in the later seasons, illness-related absences lower by 0.63–0.80 days per 100 school days, and fewer laboratory-confirmed influenza hospitalisations in the wider community in seasons when the vaccine was moderately effective. No individual-patient efficacy claim is made here — this is a delivery question. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one randomised programme trial (coverage +12.0 percentage points) plus a 59-study implementation review and a city-wide matched cohort showing higher coverage, fewer illness absences and indirect community effects in effective-vaccine seasons; a delivery-route claim, not a vaccine-efficacy claim
