title: PPI versus H2-blocker for stress-ulcer prophylaxis: trials say PPIs bleed less (relative risk 0.68), cohorts say PPIs bleed more (odds ratio 1.98) — a design-dependent split, with pneumonia and C. difficile unsettled
question: In ventilated ICU patients needing stress-ulcer prophylaxis, do proton-pump inhibitors prevent gastrointestinal bleeding better than histamine-2 receptor blockers, and at what cost in pneumonia and C. difficile infection?
balance: SPLIT — the answer depends on which design you trust. Randomised evidence: Deliwala 2022 (PMID: 34049377; 14 trials, 28,526 patients) found proton-pump inhibitors reduced clinically significant gastrointestinal bleeding versus histamine-2-receptor blockers (relative risk 0.68, a 32% relative reduction) and overt bleeding (relative risk 0.61), with no difference in mortality (relative risk 1.05) or pneumonia (relative risk 1.11, imprecise). Observational evidence points the other way: He 2022 (PMID: 34971320; 13 cohort studies, 145,149 patients) found PPIs associated with more bleeding (odds ratio 1.98) and higher mortality (odds ratio 1.27), graded low certainty — the classic signature of confounding by indication. Daou 2022 (PMID: 35714455), in neurocritical care, found no significant head-to-head difference. No carded record reports a Clostridioides difficile effect size for this comparison, so that part of the question is unanswered by the carded evidence. The large PEPTIC trial is homed elsewhere in the library and is not re-carded here. PROPOSED SPLIT — randomised evidence: POSSIBLE (benefit) for PPIs on bleeding prevention; observational evidence: POSSIBLE (harm) signal against PPIs at low certainty; pneumonia and C. difficile: no settled difference on the carded records.
stamp: SPLIT — randomised meta-analysis: POSSIBLE (benefit) for PPIs (less clinically significant bleeding, relative risk 0.68); cohort meta-analysis: POSSIBLE (harm) signal against PPIs at low certainty; no carded C. difficile effect size

title: Earlier antibiotics in suspected sepsis: every carded study is observational — delay is associated with higher mortality (about 4–12% relative per hour), steepest in septic shock, and no trial calibrates a fixed door-to-antibiotic target
question: In emergency-department patients with suspected sepsis, does earlier empirical antibiotic administration reduce mortality, and how strong is the evidence behind fixed door-to-antibiotic targets?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only, printed on the face: every carded record is a cohort study or a review of cohort studies; there is no randomised trial of antibiotic timing. The direction is consistent. Rodríguez 2025 (PMID: 39898946; 7 emergency-department cohort studies, 118,349 patients, no meta-analysis performed) found per-hour delay carried an adjusted odds ratio of 1.09 for hospital mortality in its high-quality studies. Kumar 2006 (PMID: 16625125; 2,731 patients with septic shock) found survival of 79.9% when effective antibiotics began within the first hour of hypotension, falling an average of 7.6% per hour over the next 6 hours. Seymour 2017 (PMID: 28528569; 49,331 patients under New York's mandated protocol) found a much shallower gradient — odds ratio 1.04 per hour to antibiotics. The evidence supports prompt treatment, fastest for the sickest; it does not calibrate a precise fixed door-to-antibiotic hour, because timing is confounded by how obviously ill the patient looks. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: cohort evidence consistently associates each hour of antibiotic delay with higher mortality (odds ratios 1.04–1.12 per hour), steepest in septic shock; no randomised timing trial exists

title: Home treatment of pulmonary embolism by the Hestia criteria: recurrence 2.0%, death 1.0% and major bleeding 0.7% at 3 months in the original 297-patient study — prospective management evidence, not a randomised comparison
question: In patients with acute pulmonary embolism who meet Hestia criteria, is outpatient (home) treatment as safe as hospital treatment for recurrent clots, bleeding, and death?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — management-study and cohort evidence only; no randomised home-versus-hospital comparison in Hestia-selected patients is carded. In the original Hestia Study (Zondag 2011, PMID: 21645235), 297 patients with acute pulmonary embolism who met the Hestia criteria were treated entirely as outpatients: recurrent venous thromboembolism 2.0%, death 1.0% (none from fatal pulmonary embolism), and major bleeding 0.7% over 3 months. Two later Hestia-based programmes agree at smaller scale — a United States protocol cohort (Kline 2016, PMID: 27143861; 253 patients, 67 with pulmonary embolism) recorded no recurrence or major haemorrhage among its pulmonary embolism patients at 30 days, and a French programme adding sPESI, biomarker and imaging requirements (Assayag 2022, PMID: 35940966; 43 outpatients) recorded no death or recurrence at 3 months. The randomised low-risk pulmonary embolism home-treatment question is homed at pack #3373 and is not re-carded here; this shelf is specifically about Hestia-criteria selection. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): Hestia-selected patients treated at home have low absolute event rates, on prospective management and cohort evidence.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — Hestia-selected outpatients had recurrence 2.0%, death 1.0% and major bleeding 0.7% in the original prospective study, with concordant small programme cohorts; no randomised comparison carded

title: Eradicating a new Pseudomonas isolate in bronchiectasis: about 40% clear at 12 months on observational evidence — 48% with combined systemic plus inhaled antibiotics — with no randomised test of eradication versus no eradication
question: In bronchiectasis with a first or new Pseudomonas aeruginosa isolate, does eradication therapy clear the organism and reduce exacerbations compared with no eradication treatment?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only for the eradication question, printed on the face: no randomised trial compares eradication with no eradication in the carded records. Conceição 2024 (PMID: 38296344), a systematic review of 6 observational studies in 289 patients, found a pooled 12-month eradication rate of 40%, higher with combined systemic plus inhaled antibiotics (48%) than with systemic antibiotics alone (27%). White 2012 (PMID: 22204744), a retrospective cohort of 30 patients treated after a first isolate, found initial clearance in 80.0% and exacerbations falling from 3.93 to 2.09 per year, though 11 of 24 clearers were later reinfected. Tejada 2021 (PMID: 33947626), a trial meta-analysis of inhaled antibiotics in chronic infection (not first isolation), supports sputum clearance (odds ratio 3.19–7.22) with a 10% relative reduction in exacerbations and doubled antimicrobial resistance. Whether eradication itself improves long-term outcomes versus no eradication is untested in the carded evidence. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: pooled 12-month eradication 40% (48% combined systemic plus inhaled versus 27% systemic alone) across 289 patients; no randomised eradication-versus-none trial carded

title: Transdermal versus oral oestrogen and venous thromboembolism (observational only): oral oestrogen carried higher VTE risk in every carded record (OR 2.5, OR 4.2, RR 1.49, HR 1.7) while transdermal oestrogen showed no detectable increase (1.2, 0.9, 1.01, 1.1)
question: Does transdermal oestrogen carry a lower risk of venous thromboembolism than oral oestrogen in postmenopausal women?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only. Across four carded records the direction is uniform: oral oestrogen is associated with increased venous thromboembolism (odds ratio 2.5 in the Canonico 2008 systematic review's observational meta-analysis, PMID: 18495631; odds ratio 4.2 in the ESTHER case-control study, PMID: 17309934; rate ratio 1.49 in 955,582 UK women, PMID: 20230416; hazard ratio 1.7 in the E3N cohort, PMID: 19834106), while transdermal oestrogen shows no detectable increase in any of them (odds ratios/rate ratios/hazard ratios 1.2, 0.9, 1.01 and 1.1, all with confidence intervals crossing 1). The progestogen partner modifies risk independently of route — norpregnanes carried increased risk in both ESTHER and E3N, micronised progesterone did not. No trial has randomised women by route, so this is an association, printed as observational on the face. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: transdermal oestrogen is associated with lower venous thromboembolism risk than oral oestrogen.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: oral oestrogen is consistently associated with increased venous thromboembolism and transdermal oestrogen with no detectable increase across a systematic review, a case-control study, a 955,582-woman database study and a prospective cohort; no randomised route comparison exists

title: Opportunistic salpingectomy and ovarian cancer (observational only): associated with fewer later ovarian cancers — HR 0.65 in a Swedish nationwide cohort, no serous cancers versus 5.27 expected in British Columbia, and an approximately 80% risk reduction summarised by a 2023 systematic review
question: Does opportunistic salpingectomy at the time of other pelvic surgery reduce later ovarian cancer?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only. A 2023 systematic review of 158 publications summarises salpingectomy as associated with an approximately 80% reduction in ovarian cancer risk, without earlier menopause (PMID: 37672283). The two population cohorts agree in direction with smaller, more precise estimates: hazard ratio 0.65 (95% CI 0.52 to 0.81) after salpingectomy in Sweden, with bilateral removal at 0.35 versus 0.71 for unilateral (PMID: 25628372); and no serous ovarian cancers among 25,889 British Columbia opportunistic-salpingectomy patients against 5.27 expected (PMID: 35138400). Follow-up in the most specific cohort is short (median 3.2 years) and no randomised evidence exists, so the association is printed as observational on the face. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: opportunistic salpingectomy is associated with fewer later ovarian cancers.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: a systematic review and two population cohorts associate salpingectomy with fewer later ovarian cancers (HR 0.65 in Sweden; no serous cancers vs 5.27 expected in British Columbia); no randomised evidence, and follow-up is short in the most specific cohort

title: Intravaginal boric acid for azole-refractory recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis (series evidence only, Ns on the face): remission in 64% and 71% of symptomatic Candida glabrata cases in one series (N = 141) and 81% of treated episodes in another (N = 60)
question: In recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis that azoles cannot control, does intravaginal boric acid achieve remission?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — retrospective series evidence only, with every N printed on the face. The 2011 clinical evidence review (PMID: 21774671; 14 studies, mostly case series) found mycological cure rates of 40% to 100% with intravaginal boric acid and no demonstrated difference in recurrence. The two carded series are in azole-refractory Candida glabrata vaginitis: boric acid 600 mg daily for 2 to 3 weeks succeeded in 64% and 71% of symptomatic women at two sites (N = 141 women cultured; PMID: 14634557), and 14 days of boric acid improved or cured 21 of 26 treated episodes (81%) where azoles had responded in under 50% (N = 60 symptomatic patients; PMID: 9145739). No randomised trial in the refractory recurrent population is carded. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — series evidence only: boric acid achieves short-term remission in a majority of azole-refractory cases in these series.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — retrospective series evidence only, Ns on the face (N = 141 and N = 60 in the carded series; review total N not documented): boric acid achieved short-term remission in 64–81% of azole-refractory Candida glabrata cases in specialist-clinic series; no randomised trial in this population is carded

title: School-based HPV vaccination delivery and coverage (programme evidence only): school-based programmes achieved high coverage across 17 countries and 45 low- and middle-income countries in two reviews, and 75% at least-one-dose coverage in South Africa — with no head-to-head trial against clinic-based delivery
question: Does offering school-based HPV vaccination delivery increase adolescent vaccine coverage versus clinic-based delivery alone?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — programme and review evidence only; no head-to-head trial of delivery settings is carded. A literature review of HPV delivery strategies (9 articles, 17 countries) found school-based programmes achieved high coverage in 9- to 13-year-old girls (PMID: 24295804). A systematic lessons synthesis from 45 low- and middle-income countries found school-based delivery supplemented by facility delivery for out-of-school girls attained high coverage, with limited data on facility-only strategies (PMID: 28575074). South Africa's national school-based programme reached 75% of 15-year-old girls with at least one dose and 61% with two doses by 2020, though coverage was declining (PMID: 35174123). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — school-based delivery is associated with higher adolescent HPV coverage in programme evidence; the comparison with clinic-based delivery alone is descriptive, not randomised.

title: Nurse staffing, skill mix and inpatient mortality (observational only): each additional patient per nurse was associated with about 7% higher odds of 30-day mortality in Pennsylvania and in nine European countries, and shifts staffed below target with higher mortality in a US centre
question: In hospital inpatients, do higher nurse staffing levels and richer skill mix reduce patient mortality versus leaner staffing?
balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — observational only, printed on the face: leaner registered-nurse staffing is associated with higher inpatient mortality. Each additional patient per nurse carried 7% higher odds of 30-day mortality in 168 Pennsylvania hospitals (odds ratio 1.07; PMID: 12387650) and in 300 European hospitals in RN4CAST (odds ratio 1.068; PMID: 24581683), where every 10% increase in bachelor's-degree nurses was associated with 7% lower mortality odds (0.929). title: Zinc and pneumonia in nursing-home residents (observational only for the outcome): normal serum zinc was associated with lower pneumonia incidence, almost 50% fewer antibiotic prescriptions and shorter pneumonia — but no completed trial has tested supplementation against pneumonia
question: In older adults living in nursing homes, does zinc supplementation reduce the incidence and duration of pneumonia versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only for the pneumonia outcome, printed on the face. The slated anchor is not a supplementation trial: Meydani 2007 (PMID: 17921398) is an observational analysis nested in a vitamin E trial, in which residents with normal serum zinc (70 µg/dL or above) had lower pneumonia incidence, almost 50% fewer new antibiotic prescriptions and shorter pneumonia than residents with low zinc. The only carded randomised supplementation trial (Barnett 2016, PMID: 26817502) tested 30 mg/day for 3 months in zinc-deficient residents and measured serum zinc and T-cell function, not pneumonia. A registered pilot for a pneumonia-outcome trial (NCT05527899) had reported no results as of its 2024 protocol (PMID: 38450236), whose authors state causality could not be inferred from the earlier work. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: adequate serum zinc is associated with less pneumonia; whether supplementation causes that benefit is untested in a completed trial.

title: Beta-blockers in HFpEF — a genuine split: observational data link them to lower mortality, randomised and large matched-registry data show no difference in death or hospitalisation
question: Should beta-blockers be continued in HFpEF?
balance: SPLIT — the evidence genuinely divides by study design, and the split is printed on the face. Two meta-analyses pooling mostly observational cohorts (Kaddoura 2024, PMID: 38184132, 27,188 patients; Bavishi 2015, PMID: 25034701, 27,099 patients) associate beta-blocker use with about a 19% relative reduction in all-cause mortality (OR/RR 0.81 in both), but neither shows a reduction in heart failure hospitalisation. Against that, the randomised trials inside Bavishi's pooling show no difference in mortality or hospitalisation, and the largest single dataset — the SwedeHF registry's propensity-matched analysis (Meyer 2021, PMID: 33971289; 4,412 matched users vs 2,206 non-users) — found beta-blocker use was not associated with HF admission (HR 0.95) or cardiovascular death (HR 0.94) (the treatment made no difference). No trial has randomised HFpEF patients already taking a beta-blocker to continuation versus withdrawal, so the 'continued' question is answered only indirectly. PROPOSED SPLIT — observational data link beta-blockers to lower mortality in HFpEF, but randomised and large matched-registry data show no difference in death or HF hospitalisation; there is no direct continuation-versus-withdrawal trial.
stamp: SPLIT — observational meta-analyses associate beta-blockers with ~19% relative lower all-cause mortality in HFpEF (OR/RR 0.81) but no fewer HF hospitalisations, while the randomised trials (RR 0.94 for mortality) and the 14,434-patient SwedeHF matched registry (HR 0.95 for HF admission, HR 0.94 for cardiovascular death) show the treatment made no difference; continuation versus withdrawal has never been tested in a randomised trial

title: LVAD versus medical therapy in advanced HFrEF: survival was 52% versus 25% at one year in the randomised REMATCH trial — a real survival benefit bought with far more serious adverse events
question: Does left ventricular assist device therapy improve survival in advanced HFrEF versus medical therapy?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — one definitive randomised trial plus concordant prospective comparative data. In REMATCH (PMID: 11794191), the only randomised trial of a durable LVAD against medical therapy, transplant-ineligible patients with class IV symptoms had 1-year survival of 52% on the device versus 25% on optimal medical management, a 48% relative reduction in the risk of death (relative risk 0.52). The prospective ROADMAP comparison (PMID: 26483097) in less ill, non-inotrope-dependent ambulatory patients found 12-month survival of 80% with an LVAD versus 63% on medical management on as-treated analysis, with better function and quality of life — at the cost of far more adverse events, chiefly bleeding. MOMENTUM 3's intent analysis (PMID: 31939996) shows modern magnetically levitated devices sustain that benefit in destination-therapy patients, though it compares pumps, not device versus drugs. The harm side is real and printed on the cards: serious adverse events ran 2.35 times as often with the first-generation device. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) — LVAD therapy improves survival over medical therapy in advanced HFrEF, with a heavy adverse-event burden.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — LVAD therapy improved survival versus medical therapy in the one randomised trial (1-year survival 52% vs 25%; 48% relative reduction in the risk of death, RR 0.52) and in a prospective ambulatory comparison (12-month survival 80% vs 63%), at the cost of substantially more serious adverse events (2.35 times as frequent in REMATCH, chiefly infection, bleeding and malfunction)

title: Ablate and pace for refractory AF: symptoms and heart-failure events improved in one small randomised trial (HF composite 20% vs 38%) — survival did not differ
question: Does AV node ablation with pacing improve symptoms in refractory AF?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single small randomised trial programme for the strategy itself, capped at POSSIBLE. In APAF-CRT (Brignole 2018, PMID: 30165479), AV junction ablation plus biventricular pacing beat pharmacological rate control on the composite of HF death, HF hospitalisation or worsening HF (20% vs 38%; HR 0.38) and produced a 36% decrease in AF symptoms and physical limitations at one year, in 102 elderly patients with severely symptomatic permanent AF and a prior HF hospitalisation. The AIRCRAFT long-term follow-up (Lim 2007, PMID: 17491103) agrees on symptoms — fewer symptoms of irregular heartbeat, chest pain and breathlessness with ablate-and-pace — but found no survival difference and a similar decline in ejection fraction in both groups. PAVE (Doshi 2005, PMID: 16302897) answers the companion question of which pacing to use after ablation: biventricular pacing improved 6-minute walk and ejection fraction over right ventricular pacing alone. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — symptoms and HF outcomes improved in one small randomised trial, with concordant symptom findings at long-term follow-up; no survival benefit has been shown.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single small trial programme: AV junction ablation plus biventricular pacing reduced AF symptoms and physical limitations by 36% and the HF composite (20% vs 38%, HR 0.38) versus drug rate control in 102 patients, with concordant symptom findings at 4–7 years in AIRCRAFT, but no survival difference has been shown

title: Three months of DAPT after a drug-eluting stent: noninferior to 12 months for net events in two randomised trials of stable coronary disease (6.0% vs 5.8%; 4.7% vs 4.7%)
question: Is 3 months of DAPT as safe as 12 months after drug-eluting stent in stable coronary disease?
balance: LIKELY — two randomised noninferiority trials in the target population agree, and a third trial of the same 3-month strategy in acute coronary syndrome points the same way. OPTIMIZE (Feres 2013, PMID: 24177257; 3,119 patients with stable coronary disease or low-risk ACS receiving zotarolimus-eluting stents) found net adverse clinical and cerebral events in 6.0% on 3 months of DAPT versus 5.8% on 12 months (P = .002 for noninferiority), with stent thrombosis between days 91–360 of 0.3% versus 0.1% (HR 3.97, interval very wide). RESET (Kim 2012, PMID: 22999717; 2,117 patients) likewise found its primary composite in 4.7% versus 4.7% (P < 0.001 for noninferiority), though its 3-month arm also received a specific stent, confounding duration with device. TICO (Kim 2020, PMID: 32543684) tested dropping aspirin at 3 months in ACS and found fewer net events (3.9% vs 5.9%; HR 0.66) driven by less major bleeding (1.7% vs 3.0%). The carded trials used zotarolimus- or sirolimus-eluting stents of their era. PROPOSED LIKELY — 3 months of DAPT was noninferior to 12 months for net events after drug-eluting stenting in stable coronary disease, with no demonstrated excess of stent thrombosis, and less bleeding when the second agent is dropped at 3 months.
stamp: LIKELY — 3 months of DAPT was noninferior to 12 months after drug-eluting stenting in two randomised trials in stable or low-risk coronary disease (net events 6.0% vs 5.8% in OPTIMIZE; primary composite 4.7% vs 4.7% in RESET), with no demonstrated excess stent thrombosis, and aspirin discontinuation at 3 months in ACS (TICO) reduced net events (3.9% vs 5.9%, HR 0.66) through less major bleeding (1.7% vs 3.0%)

title: Evolocumab in peripheral arterial disease: in FOURIER's PAD subgroup it cut the primary composite by 21% relative (HR 0.79) with a 3.5% absolute reduction, and limb events fell 42% relative — from one trial programme
question: Does evolocumab reduce events in patients with peripheral arterial disease?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single trial programme (FOURIER), capped at POSSIBLE. Within FOURIER's 27,564 statin-treated patients, the 3,642 with peripheral arterial disease had a 21% relative reduction in the primary composite with evolocumab (HR 0.79) and a 27% relative reduction in the key secondary composite (HR 0.73), with larger absolute risk reductions than in patients without PAD (3.5% for both composites) because their baseline risk was higher (Bonaca 2018, PMID: 29133605). The same trial showed evolocumab reduced major adverse limb events across all patients (HR 0.58) and, in a territory-wide analysis (Oyama 2021, PMID: 34537830), reduced first acute arterial events by 19% relative (HR 0.81), including peripheral vascular events (HR 0.58). A small dedicated randomised study in chronic limb-threatening ischaemia (Dhillon 2025, PMID: 39638643; N = 27, printed on the face) confirms large LDL-C lowering (82 to 34 mg/dL at 6 months) but reports no clinical events. The parent FOURIER trial's main record is homed on its own shelf and is not re-carded here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — evolocumab reduced cardiovascular and limb events in the PAD subgroup of one large trial; no second outcomes trial in PAD exists.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single trial programme (FOURIER): in 3,642 patients with PAD, evolocumab reduced the primary composite by 21% relative (HR 0.79) and cardiovascular death, MI or stroke by 27% relative (HR 0.73), each a 3.5% absolute reduction, and reduced major adverse limb events by 42% relative across the trial (HR 0.58); no PAD-specific outcomes trial exists

title: Inclisiran and cardiovascular events (unproven): LDL cholesterol falls by about half, and an exploratory pooled analysis found fewer composite events (OR 0.74) — but no dedicated outcomes trial has reported
question: Does inclisiran reduce cardiovascular events in high-risk patients?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — event reduction is unproven; the completed evidence is LDL-lowering plus one exploratory events analysis, printed on the face. No dedicated cardiovascular outcomes trial of inclisiran has reported in any record fetched this session. What exists: a prespecified exploratory, patient-level pooled analysis of the phase III LDL trials ORION-9, -10 and -11 (Ray 2023, PMID: 36331326; 3,655 patients, 18 months, events collected as non-adjudicated safety endpoints) found fewer composite major cardiovascular events with inclisiran (odds ratio 0.74, 95% CI 0.58-0.94) but no significant difference in fatal and non-fatal myocardial infarction (OR 0.80, 95% CI 0.50-1.27) or stroke (OR 0.86, 95% CI 0.41-1.81) separately. The underlying trials were designed and powered for LDL cholesterol: the pooled phase III analysis (Wright 2021, PMID: 33663735) shows a placebo-corrected LDL reduction of 50.7% at day 510, and the phase II ORION-1 follow-up (Ray 2019, PMID: 31553410) shows the reduction is durable over a year with twice-yearly dosing. The LDL trials themselves (ORION-9/-10/-11 primary reports) are homed on live shelf #1103 and are cross-pointed, not re-carded. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): inclisiran halves LDL cholesterol and an exploratory pooled analysis is compatible with fewer cardiovascular events, but whether it reduces events awaits the larger, longer cardiovascular outcomes trials the analysis itself names.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — inclisiran lowers LDL cholesterol by about half and an exploratory pooled analysis found fewer composite major cardiovascular events (OR 0.74), but no dedicated cardiovascular outcomes trial has reported, so event reduction is unproven

title: Extended DAPT after myocardial infarction: fewer ischaemic events (7.8% vs 9.0% at 3 years in PEGASUS) and less cardiovascular death — bought with roughly double the major bleeding, but no more fatal bleeding
question: Should DAPT be extended beyond 12 months after MI in high ischemic risk patients?
balance: LIKELY (benefit for ischaemic events, at the cost of more major bleeding) — one definitive large randomised trial in exactly this population plus a concordant collaborative meta-analysis. In PEGASUS-TIMI 54 (Bonaca 2015, PMID: 25773268), 21,162 patients 1 to 3 years after myocardial infarction were randomised to ticagrelor 90 mg or 60 mg twice daily or placebo, all on low-dose aspirin: at 3 years the composite of cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction or stroke occurred in 7.85% (90 mg) and 7.77% (60 mg) versus 9.04% on placebo (hazard ratios 0.85 and 0.84 — relative reductions), while TIMI major bleeding rose from 1.06% to 2.60% and 2.30%, with intracranial or fatal bleeding essentially unchanged (0.63%, 0.71%, 0.60%). The collaborative meta-analysis restricted to patients with prior MI (Udell 2016, PMID: 26324537; 33,435 patients, six trials) found the same pattern: major adverse cardiovascular events 6.4% versus 7.5% (relative risk 0.78), cardiovascular death reduced (relative risk 0.85), major bleeding increased (1.85% versus 1.09%; relative risk 1.73) but not fatal bleeding. The broader post-stent meta-analysis (Cassese 2015, PMID: 25903112) adds a caution from a different population: prolonged DAPT after drug-eluting stenting reduced stent thrombosis and myocardial infarction but was associated with higher all-cause death (odds ratio 1.25) — a signal not seen in the post-MI-restricted analysis, and one reason the answer is framed for high-ischaemic-risk post-MI patients rather than all-comers. Post-stent DAPT duration itself is homed on live shelf #264 and is cross-pointed, not re-carded. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): extending DAPT beyond 12 months after MI in high-ischaemic-risk patients reduces ischaemic events including cardiovascular death, and increases major (not fatal) bleeding — the trade-off, not the direction, is the clinical decision.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit, with increased major bleeding) — extending DAPT beyond 12 months after MI in high-ischaemic-risk patients reduced the composite of cardiovascular death, MI or stroke (7.8% vs 9.0% at 3 years in PEGASUS-TIMI 54) and cardiovascular death in meta-analysis, while major bleeding rose (2.3-2.6% vs 1.1%) without more fatal bleeding

title: Amlodipine oedema is dose-related and ARB combination reduces it: 5.4% on amlodipine/valsartan versus 8.7% on amlodipine alone — and 0.9% at 5 mg versus 9.1% at 10 mg inside the same combination
question: Does amlodipine cause less edema at lower dose combined with ARB?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — two randomised combination trials and a network meta-analysis point the same way: amlodipine oedema is dose-related, and pairing the amlodipine with a renin-angiotensin blocker lowers it. In the pivotal factorial trials (Philipp 2007, PMID: 17617280; 3,161 patients randomised across two studies), peripheral oedema occurred in 5.4% on amlodipine/valsartan combination versus 8.7% on amlodipine monotherapy (P = 0.014), while blood-pressure lowering was greater on the combination — so the lower oedema rate was not bought with weaker treatment. The dose gradient inside an ARB combination is direct in Sinkiewicz 2009 (PMID: 19192976; 947 patients uncontrolled on valsartan): peripheral oedema was reported in 9.1% on amlodipine 10 mg/valsartan 160 mg but only 0.9% on amlodipine 5 mg/valsartan 160 mg (valsartan alone 1.3%), with the 5-mg combination still lowering blood pressure significantly more than valsartan alone. The network meta-analysis of 71 trials (Liang 2022, PMID: 35234349; 56,283 patients) ranks dihydropyridine-plus-blocker combinations below dihydropyridine monotherapy for oedema as a class, while noting the mitigation is clearest for ACE-inhibitor combinations and was not shown for every ARB pairing (nifedipine plus ARB did not mitigate in its ranking). The earlier oedema meta-analyses carded in pack #5524 are cross-pointed, not re-carded. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): yes — amlodipine causes less oedema at a lower dose combined with an ARB, and the combination lowers blood pressure more, not less.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — amlodipine combined with an ARB caused less peripheral oedema than amlodipine alone (5.4% vs 8.7%), and within the combination the lower amlodipine dose caused far less (0.9% at 5 mg vs 9.1% at 10 mg), while lowering blood pressure more

title: Exercise versus medication for blood pressure (indirect evidence only): no detectable difference from single drugs in hypertensive subgroups of a 391-trial network analysis — but no head-to-head trial has ever been run
question: Does exercise lower blood pressure as much as medication in hypertension?
balance: POSSIBLE — the comparison rests entirely on indirect (network) evidence, printed on the face: no randomised trial has ever compared exercise head-to-head with an antihypertensive drug. In the network meta-analysis of 391 randomised trials (Naci 2019, PMID: 30563873; 197 exercise trials with 10,461 participants and 194 medication trials with 29,281 participants), medications achieved greater systolic reductions than exercise across all populations combined (mean difference -3.96 mm Hg, 95% credible interval -5.02 to -2.91) — but among hypertensive participants specifically (only 56 exercise trials, 3,508 individuals), there were no detectable differences between endurance or dynamic resistance exercise and ACE inhibitors, ARBs, beta-blockers or diuretics. The exercise effect itself is real and dose-related: aerobic exercise at 150 minutes/week lowered systolic BP by 7.23 mm Hg in hypertensive adults (Jabbarzadeh Ganjeh 2024, PMID: 37872373; 34 trials, 1,787 participants), and isometric training lowered systolic BP by 6.77 mm Hg across nine small trials (Carlson 2014, PMID: 24582191; 223 participants) — magnitudes in the range of a single drug. The larger network meta-analyses of exercise modalities (Edwards 2023; Cornelissen 2013) are already carded elsewhere in the library and were not re-carded. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: in hypertensive patients, structured exercise lowers systolic blood pressure by amounts statistically indistinguishable from single-drug therapy in indirect comparisons — 'as much as medication' is plausible, not demonstrated, and exercise trials in hypertension remain few and small next to the drug trials.
stamp: POSSIBLE — in hypertensive subgroups, exercise lowered systolic blood pressure by amounts statistically indistinguishable from single-drug therapy, but the comparison is indirect (network meta-analysis only; no head-to-head randomised trial exists) and medications achieved greater reductions across all populations combined

title: Stopping NSAIDs to improve blood-pressure control (indirect evidence): starting an NSAID raises mean BP by about 5 mm Hg in hypertensive patients — the expected gain from stopping is that rise reversed, and it depends heavily on which NSAID it is
question: Should NSAIDs be stopped to improve blood pressure control?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — indirect evidence, printed on the face: no randomised trial that randomises patients to stop versus continue an NSAID and measures blood pressure was found in the records fetched this session, so this shelf answers from the other direction — the size and drug-dependence of the pressor effect that stopping would remove. Two meta-analyses of randomised trials agree that starting an NSAID raises blood pressure in hypertensive patients: Johnson 1994 (PMID: 8037411; 38 placebo-controlled plus 12 comparative randomised trials) found a pooled rise in supine mean blood pressure of 5.0 mm Hg, with the largest antagonism against beta-blockers (6.2 mm Hg) and the largest pressor effect from piroxicam (6.2 mm Hg) and the least from sulindac and aspirin; Pope 1993 (PMID: 8435027; 54 studies, 1,324 participants, 92% hypertensive) found the effect confined to hypertensive subjects, with indomethacin raising mean arterial pressure by 3.59 mm Hg while sulindac, aspirin and ibuprofen had negligible average effects. A randomised ambulatory-BP trial in high-risk patients (Sowers 2005, PMID: 15668361; 404 patients with hypertension, osteoarthritis and type 2 diabetes) shows the effect is drug-specific in practice: rofecoxib raised 24-hour systolic BP by about 4 mm Hg and destabilised control in 30% of previously controlled patients, while celecoxib and naproxen did not significantly change 24-hour systolic BP. The PRECISION ambulatory-BP substudy is homed in pack #5289 and is cross-pointed, not re-carded. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): stopping an NSAID — particularly indomethacin, piroxicam or a strongly pressor agent in a patient whose control worsened on it — should be expected to improve blood pressure control by roughly the amount the drug raised it (a few mm Hg on average, more in susceptible patients), but that expectation is inferred from starting trials, not proven by a stopping trial.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — indirect evidence only: NSAIDs raise blood pressure in hypertensive patients by about 5.0 mm Hg on average in randomised-trial meta-analyses (drug-dependent: indomethacin and piroxicam most, sulindac and aspirin least), so stopping should improve control, but no randomised stopping trial was found

title: Muvalaplin lowers Lp(a) substantially: up to 85.8% versus placebo at 240 mg/day over 12 weeks (phase II, 233 participants) — a large surrogate effect with no cardiovascular outcomes evidence yet
question: Does muvalaplin lower Lp(a) levels?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single trial programme, capped at POSSIBLE, measuring a surrogate over 12 weeks. In the phase II KRAKEN trial (Nicholls 2025, PMID: 39556768), 233 participants with Lp(a) of 175 nmol/L or above and atherosclerotic disease, diabetes or familial hypercholesterolaemia were randomised to muvalaplin 10, 60 or 240 mg/day or placebo for 12 weeks: placebo-adjusted Lp(a) reductions were 47.6%, 81.7% and 85.8% respectively on the intact-Lp(a) assay (40.4%, 70.0% and 68.9% on the traditional apo(a)-based assay), with dose-dependent apolipoprotein B reductions and no safety or tolerability concerns. The phase I trial (Nicholls 2023, PMID: 37638695; 114 participants) had shown maximal placebo-adjusted reductions of 63-65% over 14 days with no clinically significant change in plasminogen. A 2024 landscape review (Anchouche 2024, PMID: 39576403) confirms the context: there are no approved Lp(a)-specific drugs and no completed outcomes trial for any of them, muvalaplin included. Muvalaplin is mentioned as fenced class context (explicitly 'not carded') on live shelf #1104, which homes the RNA-therapy Lp(a) trials; this shelf is its first evidence-card home. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): yes, muvalaplin lowers Lp(a) substantially and dose-dependently — by up to about 86% at 240 mg/day over 12 weeks — but whether that lowers cardiovascular events is entirely untested.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single trial programme: muvalaplin lowered Lp(a) by up to 85.8% versus placebo at 240 mg/day over 12 weeks in a 233-person phase II trial, but the endpoint is a surrogate and no cardiovascular outcomes data exist

title: Measure Lp(a) once in every adult? Consensus says yes (EAS 2022, NLA 2019) on cohort and genetic evidence — levels are stable for life and risk is continuous and causal — with no randomised screening trial behind the recommendation
question: Should Lp(a) be measured once in a lifetime in all adults?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational/prognosis evidence and expert consensus only, printed on the face: no randomised trial of Lp(a) screening (measure everyone once versus do not) with clinical outcomes exists in the records fetched this session, and this shelf does not pretend otherwise. The case for once-in-a-lifetime measurement rests on three legs, all carded. First, prognosis: in the Emerging Risk Factors Collaboration's individual-participant analysis of 36 prospective studies (Erqou 2009, PMID: 19622820; 126,634 participants, 1.3 million person-years), Lp(a) was continuously and independently associated with coronary heart disease — adjusted relative risk 1.13 per 3.5-fold higher usual Lp(a) — and with ischaemic stroke (relative risk 1.10), but not with nonvascular mortality, and Lp(a) was highly consistent within individuals over several years, which is the property that makes a single lifetime measurement informative. Second, causality: Copenhagen genetic data (Kamstrup 2009, PMID: 19509380; about 40,000 participants across three studies) show genetically elevated Lp(a) tracks with myocardial infarction risk in a dose-dependent way consistent with a causal association. Third, consensus: the 2022 European Atherosclerosis Society statement (Kronenberg 2022, PMID: 36036785) recommends testing Lp(a) at least once in adults, and the National Lipid Association statement (Wilson 2019, PMID: 31147269) likewise supports testing to inform prevention — while both are explicit that, without a specific Lp(a)-lowering therapy of proven outcome benefit, what a high result changes today is the intensity of management of everything else. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: measuring Lp(a) once in every adult is recommended by both major consensus statements and is prognostically sound because levels are stable and causal — but it is a consensus recommendation resting on cohort and genetic evidence, not on a randomised screening trial.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: Lp(a) is stable within individuals, continuously and probably causally associated with coronary disease and stroke, and both the EAS and NLA recommend measuring it at least once in adults — but no randomised trial of screening exists

title: Lipoprotein apheresis in familial hypercholesterolemia (observational only): LDL falls by about two-thirds per course and on-treatment event rates are far below pre-treatment rates in every registry — with no randomised trial and progression still seen in homozygous children
question: Does lipoprotein apheresis improve outcomes in familial hypercholesterolemia?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only, printed on the face: there is no randomised trial of lipoprotein apheresis, and every carded outcome study uses the same before-and-after design, comparing event rates in the years before apheresis started with the years on it — a design that flatters treatment, because patients start apheresis after events cluster. Within that limit the findings are consistent. In the prospective multicentre Pro(a)LiFe study (Leebmann 2013, PMID: 24056686; 170 patients with Lp(a)-hyperlipoproteinaemia and progressive disease on maximally tolerated therapy), mean annual major adverse coronary event rates fell from 0.41 in the two years before apheresis to 0.09 in the two years on it. The German registry (Schettler 2017, PMID: 28233268; 1,435 patients, 15,527 treatments) found the same pattern — a 78% lower MACE rate over two years on apheresis — with median per-session LDL reduction of 67.5% and side effects in 5.9% of treatments, mainly puncture problems. A small Polish FH series (Mickiewicz 2021, PMID: 33386762; 23 patients, N printed on the face) found event rates falling in parallel with 70% LDL reductions. In children with homozygous FH (Hudgins 2008, PMID: 18940291; 29 patients), biweekly apheresis lowered LDL by 75% acutely and 48% chronically and was well tolerated for years — yet atherosclerosis still progressed in 30%, and target LDL levels were not achieved. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: apheresis unquestionably removes LDL and Lp(a) at each session and event rates are much lower on treatment than before it in every registry, but the before-after design cannot separate the treatment effect from regression to the mean and the intensified care that surrounds it.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: lipoprotein apheresis lowers LDL cholesterol by about two-thirds per course and event rates are far lower on treatment than before it in registries (0.41 to 0.09 events/year in Pro(a)LiFe), but all outcome evidence is uncontrolled before-and-after comparison and no randomised trial exists

title: Intensive blood-pressure control and thoracic aneurysm growth (untested as a strategy): beta-blockade slowed Marfan aortic dilatation versus no treatment in one small 1994 trial — no study has randomised a blood-pressure target, in Marfan or in degenerative aneurysm
question: Does intensive blood pressure control slow thoracic aortic aneurysm growth?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — no trial has tested intensive versus standard blood-pressure targets for thoracic aortic aneurysm growth in any record fetched this session; the shelf is built from the nearest evidence, drug trials in Marfan aortopathy, and says so on its face. The one trial of a blood-pressure-lowering drug against no treatment (Shores 1994, PMID: 8152445; 70 patients with Marfan syndrome, open-label randomised propranolol, mean follow-up about 10 years) found the aortic-root dilatation rate was significantly slower on beta-blockade (slope 0.023 versus 0.084 per year, P < 0.001), with clinical endpoints reached in 5 treated versus 9 control patients. Adding an ARB on top of standard therapy splits: the COMPARE programme (van Andel 2020, PMID: 32548624; 233 randomised adults) found a small significant slowing of aortic-root dilatation over 3 years on losartan and, in self-selected long-term follow-up, fewer deaths (0 versus 5) and dissections (3 versus 11) among continuers — while a small double-blind add-on trial (Muiño-Mosquera 2017, PMID: 28657492; 22 patients, N on the face) found no additional effect of losartan on aortic growth (the treatment made no difference). The large losartan-versus-atenolol trial in young Marfan patients is homed on live shelf #1417 and is cross-pointed, not re-carded. Nothing carded here addresses degenerative (non-Marfan) thoracic aneurysm, and nothing compares BP targets or achieved BP levels. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): blood-pressure-lowering treatment probably slows aortic growth in heritable aortopathy — one small old open-label trial says yes for beta-blockade — but 'intensive control' as a strategy, and any benefit in ordinary degenerative thoracic aneurysm, are untested.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — no trial has tested intensive blood-pressure targets for thoracic aortic aneurysm growth; beta-blockade slowed Marfan aortic-root dilatation in one small open-label trial (slope 0.023 vs 0.084/year), and ARB add-on evidence is split, with a null result in the only double-blind trial

title: Balloon valvuloplasty as a bridge to TAVI (observational only, split): symptoms and gradients improve and patients do reach TAVI — but the largest registry associates the bridge strategy with higher in-hospital mortality than direct TAVR
question: Does balloon aortic valvuloplasty help as a bridge to TAVI?
balance: SPLIT — observational only, printed on the face. Balloon aortic valvuloplasty (BAV) reliably opens the valve for a time: in a 112-patient prospective cohort where 51.8% of procedures were bridges to TAVI, valve area rose from 0.59 to 0.82 cm2 and mean gradient fell from 58.0 to 40.5 mm Hg (Daniec 2017, PMID: 27514931), and in a 224-patient contemporary cohort 61% of BAV was bridging, half of patients improved by at least one NYHA class at 30 days, and 40% of the bridge group reached TAVI/AVR within 12 months — though 12-month mortality was still 26% in the bridge group (Dawson 2020, PMID: 32341170). A systematic review of 27 studies and 4,123 patients found BAV safer in the TAVI era (in-hospital mortality 4.6% vs 8.5% in the earlier era), with 23.4% of contemporary BAV done as a bridge to TAVR (Kumar 2016, PMID: 27466275). Against this, the largest record — a 27,600-patient Japanese national registry — found patients bridged with BAV before TAVR died in hospital more often than patients taken straight to TAVR (5.6% vs 1.3%), with bridging an independent correlate of death (Fujimoto 2024, PMID: 38977224); bridged patients are plausibly sicker and more often emergent, so confounding by indication likely explains part or all of that gap, but no randomised trial exists to settle it. PROPOSED SPLIT (symptom and haemodynamic benefit as a bridge in cohort data; a national-registry mortality signal against the bridge strategy versus direct TAVR) — observational only: BAV can carry selected unstable patients to TAVI, but the bridge strategy has never been shown to beat going straight to TAVI.
stamp: SPLIT (benefit in bridge cohorts; mortality signal against the bridge strategy in registry data) — observational only: balloon valvuloplasty relieves symptoms and bridges selected patients to TAVI, but a 27,600-patient national registry associates bridging with higher in-hospital mortality than direct TAVR (5.6% vs 1.3%), and no randomised trial compares the strategies

title: Exercise restriction in asymptomatic severe aortic stenosis (unproven, observational only): never tested directly — but supervised exercise testing caused no serious events in 769 patients across three cohorts
question: Does exercise restriction prevent events in asymptomatic severe aortic stenosis?
balance: MAYBE (restriction benefit unproven) — observational only, printed on the face. No study carded here, and none found this session, has ever randomised or compared asymptomatic patients with severe aortic stenosis who were told to restrict exercise against patients who were not — so the preventive value of restriction itself is untested. What the evidence does test is the danger restriction is meant to avert: supervised exertion. Across three cohorts totalling 769 patients, symptom-limited exercise testing caused no serious adverse events: 797 treadmill tests in 316 patients with moderate or severe stenosis with no serious adverse events (Saeed 2018, PMID: 29654094); maximal exercise tests in 106 asymptomatic patients with no complications (Peidro 2007, PMID: 17114879); and cardiopulmonary exercise testing in 347 patients — 137 with severe stenosis — with no major events and minor events in 28% (Dhoble 2012, PMID: 22560172). These same records show exercise testing is prognostically useful (revealed symptoms in 29% at baseline in Saeed 2018, marking patients headed for valve replacement), which is an argument about testing, not about everyday exertion or its restriction. PROPOSED MAYBE (benefit of exercise restriction unproven) — observational only: brief supervised exertion has repeatedly proved safe in asymptomatic severe aortic stenosis, but whether restricting ordinary exercise prevents events has never been tested.
stamp: MAYBE (benefit of exercise restriction unproven) — observational only: no study has tested exercise restriction itself in asymptomatic severe aortic stenosis; supervised exercise testing in three cohorts totalling 769 patients caused no serious adverse events

title: Supervised exercise in peripheral arterial disease: improves walking distance and symptoms (about 210 m more than walking advice at three months) — no effect on the ankle brachial index or hard outcomes
question: Does supervised exercise improve symptoms in peripheral arterial disease?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) for walking distance and symptoms. Two Cochrane reviews of randomised trials point the same way. Exercise programmes versus usual care or placebo improved pain-free walking distance by a mean of 82.11 m and maximum walking distance by 120.36 m, on high-quality evidence (Lane 2017, PMID: 29278423; 32 trials, 1,835 participants). Supervised exercise therapy specifically beat walking advice by a standardised mean difference of 0.80 — about 210 m more maximal walking distance at three months, high-quality evidence — and beat home-based exercise by about 120 m (Hageman 2018, PMID: 29627967; 21 studies, 1,400 participants). A third meta-analysis of 18 trials and 1,200 patients found intensive walking exercise improved maximal, pain-free and 6-minute walking distances over usual care with no excess of adverse events (relative risk 0.84; Lyu 2016, PMID: 25940390). The benefit is in walking capacity and some quality-of-life domains; exercise did not improve the ankle brachial index and no effect on mortality or amputation was shown. The head-to-head question against stenting is not re-asked here: CLEVER and ERASE are homed on live shelf #280 (supervised exercise vs stenting for claudication) and are cross-pointed, not re-carded. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): supervised exercise improves walking distance and symptoms in peripheral arterial disease compared with usual care and walking advice.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit): supervised exercise improves walking distance and symptoms in peripheral arterial disease — about 210 m more maximal walking distance than walking advice at three months in Cochrane randomised-trial evidence; no effect shown on ankle brachial index, mortality or amputation

title: Home-based walking in PAD (split by programme design): group-supported home walking prevented mobility loss — fully remote programmes did not improve walking distance
question: Does home-based walking exercise improve mobility in PAD?
balance: SPLIT (by programme design). Home-based walking helped when the programme brought patients together: in the GOALS trial, a group-mediated cognitive behavioural intervention promoting home walking — weekly on-site group meetings for six months, with 90% of exercise done at or near home — cut mobility loss at six months from 26.5% to 6.3% (odds ratio 0.19) and at 12 months from 18.5% to 5.2% (odds ratio 0.24) versus an attention control (McDermott 2015, PMID: 25994445; 194 randomised), and the same programme's 6-minute walk advantage persisted at 12 months (+34.1 m; McDermott 2014, PMID: 24850615). Home-based programmes without that on-site group structure did not improve walking: a wearable-monitor plus telephone-coaching intervention changed 6-minute walk by 5.5 m versus 14.4 m with usual care (difference −8.9 m, P = .31 — the treatment made no difference) in the HONOR trial (McDermott 2018, PMID: 29710165; 200 randomised), and a behavioural home-walking intervention in diabetes with PAD did not improve treadmill walking distance (24.5 m vs 39.2 m change, P = 0.60), though walking speed and mental-health quality of life improved (Collins 2011, PMID: 21873560; 145 randomised). PROPOSED SPLIT (benefit for group-supported home programmes; no walking benefit for fully remote programmes): whether home-based walking improves mobility in PAD depends on how the programme is built — periodic in-person group support appears to be the ingredient that makes home exercise work.
stamp: SPLIT (benefit for group-supported home programmes; no walking benefit for fully remote programmes): a home walking programme with weekly group support prevented mobility loss in PAD (6.3% vs 26.5% at six months), while wearable/telephone-only and behavioural programmes did not improve walking distance in two other randomised trials

title: Early ambulation after DVT: does not worsen outcomes — no excess pulmonary embolism, progression or death versus bed rest across meta-analysis, registry and cohort evidence
question: Does early ambulation worsen outcomes after DVT?
balance: POSSIBLE (no worsening). The fear behind prescribing bed rest after deep vein thrombosis — that walking will shake a clot loose — is not borne out by any carded record. A meta-analysis of five randomised studies and prospective registries totalling 3,048 patients found early ambulation was not associated with a higher incidence of new pulmonary embolism than bed rest (relative risk 1.03, 95% CI 0.65 to 1.63), with trends favouring ambulation for the composites of new embolism or thrombus progression and of embolism or death (Aissaoui 2009, PMID: 18691773). In the RIETE registry's 2,650 patients with acute DVT or pulmonary embolism, new symptomatic embolism over 15 days was uncommon (0.5% after DVT, 0.7% after PE) with no significant differences between bed-rest and ambulant patients in new embolism, fatal embolism or bleeding (Trujillo-Santos 2005, PMID: 15888839). And in 1,289 consecutive patients all treated with compression and walking exercises instead of bed rest, fatal pulmonary embolism occurred in 0.23% (Partsch 2001, PMID: 11582950). The randomised base inside the meta-analysis is small, which caps the stamp: the answer rests on concordant meta-analytic, registry and cohort evidence rather than one large trial. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (no worsening): early ambulation after DVT does not increase pulmonary embolism, thrombus progression or death in the available evidence.
stamp: POSSIBLE (no worsening): early ambulation after DVT was not associated with more pulmonary embolism, thrombus progression or death than bed rest in a meta-analysis of 3,048 patients (relative risk for new embolism 1.03), a 2,650-patient registry and a 1,289-patient cohort — the randomised base is small

title: DOACs in antiphospholipid syndrome (harm signal): more recurrent thrombosis — arterial events especially — than warfarin, with no bleeding advantage; worst in triple-positive disease
question: Is DOAC therapy safe in antiphospholipid syndrome?
balance: POSSIBLE (harm). The safety problem with direct oral anticoagulants in antiphospholipid syndrome is not bleeding — it is recurrent thrombosis, especially arterial. In the carded randomised trial, rivaroxaban failed to show noninferiority to dose-adjusted vitamin K antagonists over three years: recurrent thrombosis occurred in 11.6% on rivaroxaban versus 6.3% on a vitamin K antagonist (relative risk 1.83, 95% CI 0.71 to 4.76), stroke occurred in 9 patients on rivaroxaban versus 0 on the antagonist, and major bleeding was similar (6.3% vs 7.4%) (Ordi-Ros 2019, PMID: 31610549; 190 patients). A patient-level meta-analysis of 447 patients treated with a DOAC found 16% suffered a recurrent thrombosis while on treatment, with triple positivity carrying a four-fold risk (odds ratio 4.3) (Dufrost 2018, PMID: 30103045). Even in lower-risk single- or double-positive patients, a retrospective cohort found recurrent thromboembolism in 15.4% on a DOAC versus 5.3% on warfarin, not statistically significant in 96 patients, with no difference in major bleeding (Williams 2022, PMID: 34817786). The second randomised trial in this field — TRAPS, in triple-positive patients — is homed on live shelf #1548 and is cross-pointed, not re-carded; it points the same way. Because only one randomised trial is carded here, the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm): DOAC therapy in antiphospholipid syndrome is associated with more recurrent thrombosis — arterial events in particular — than vitamin K antagonist therapy, without a bleeding advantage.
stamp: POSSIBLE (harm): DOAC therapy in antiphospholipid syndrome is associated with more recurrent thrombosis than vitamin K antagonists — 11.6% vs 6.3% in the carded randomised trial, stroke 9 vs 0, 16% recurrence across 447 patients in a patient-level meta-analysis — with no bleeding advantage; triple positivity carries the highest risk

title: Acute pericarditis first-line therapy: NSAID plus colchicine — recurrence at 18 months cut from 32.3% to 10.7% (COPE) with a pooled hazard ratio of 0.40
question: Should NSAIDs plus colchicine be first line for acute pericarditis?
balance: LIKELY (benefit). The randomised evidence for adding colchicine to conventional anti-inflammatory therapy (aspirin or another NSAID) in a first episode of acute pericarditis is concordant. In the COPE trial, colchicine plus aspirin cut recurrence at 18 months from 32.3% to 10.7% (P = 0.004; number needed to treat 5) and symptom persistence at 72 hours from 36.7% to 11.7% (Imazio 2005, PMID: 16186437; 120 patients, open-label). The Cochrane review of the randomised trials found, for acute pericarditis, a hazard ratio of 0.40 (95% CI 0.27 to 0.61) for recurrence with colchicine added to an NSAID, and better symptom relief at 72 hours (risk ratio 1.4) (Alabed 2014, PMID: 25164988). A further meta-analysis of nine trials and 1,832 patients found recurrence odds ratio 0.42 and symptom persistence odds ratio 0.29, at the cost of more adverse events (relative risk 1.48), mainly gastrointestinal (Li 2016, PMID: 26979508). The second acute-pericarditis trial inside those reviews — ICAP, double-blind — is homed on live shelf #190 and is cross-pointed, not re-carded. No carded trial tests an NSAID alone against placebo, so 'first line' rests on the combination's randomised evidence plus the universal use of NSAIDs as the trials' backbone. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): NSAID plus colchicine should be first-line therapy for a first episode of acute pericarditis.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit): NSAID plus colchicine should be first line for a first episode of acute pericarditis — recurrence at 18 months 10.7% vs 32.3% in the COPE trial and pooled hazard ratio 0.40 in Cochrane randomised-trial evidence, with mainly gastrointestinal adverse effects

title: Corticosteroids and pericarditis recurrence (observational only): associated with two- to three-fold higher recurrence in adjusted analyses — confounding by indication unexcluded
question: Does corticosteroid use increase pericarditis recurrence?
balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — observational only, printed on the face, as the brief for this number anticipated: no trial has randomised patients to corticosteroids to test recurrence, so every card is an adjusted observational analysis. The signal is consistent. Within the CORE randomised trial's cohort, previous corticosteroid use was an independent risk factor for further recurrences (odds ratio 2.89, 95% CI 1.10 to 8.26) (Imazio 2005, PMID: 16186468; 84 patients). In a 175-patient myopericarditis cohort, corticosteroid use independently predicted recurrence (hazard ratio 2.27, 95% CI 1.15 to 4.47) (Collini 2024, PMID: 38238076). In a prospective 148-patient acute pericarditis cohort, recurrence risk was higher in patients switched to corticosteroids after NSAID failure (hazard ratio 3.22) and in those given corticosteroids first-line (hazard ratio 2.06) than in patients treated with NSAIDs only (Lazaros 2019, PMID: 29684577). A 2026 systematic review of 10 studies and 2,632 patients found the association inconsistent in acute pericarditis but present in most recurrent-pericarditis studies, with moderate risk of bias and limited adjustment for confounding (Razeghi 2026, PMID: 42552090). Confounding by indication — steroids go to the sickest, most refractory patients — runs through all of it and cannot be removed by these adjustments. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm) — observational only: corticosteroid use in pericarditis is associated with roughly two- to three-fold higher recurrence in adjusted analyses.
stamp: POSSIBLE (harm) — observational only: corticosteroid use in pericarditis is associated with roughly two- to three-fold higher recurrence in adjusted analyses (odds ratio 2.89; hazard ratios 2.06–3.22), with confounding by indication the standing alternative explanation and no randomised evidence

title: Exercise restriction in myocarditis (untested, observational only): never compared with continued exercise — athlete cohorts managed with restriction showed resolved inflammation and very few events
question: Does exercise restriction improve recovery in myocarditis?
balance: MAYBE — observational only, printed on the face. Exercise restriction after myocarditis has never been compared with continued exercise in any carded study, randomised or otherwise: in every athlete cohort here, restriction was simply what was done with athletes found to have myocarditis, so the shelf can report outcomes under restriction, not the effect of restriction. Those outcomes were benign. In the Big Ten registry, 37 of 1,597 screened athletes (2.3%) were diagnosed with clinical or subclinical myocarditis after COVID-19, and on follow-up imaging the T2 signal of inflammation had resolved in all 27 re-imaged athletes, though late gadolinium enhancement persisted in 40.7% (Daniels 2021, PMID: 34042947). Among 789 professional athletes screened before return to play, five (0.6%) had inflammatory heart disease that resulted in restriction from play, and no adverse cardiac events occurred in athletes who resumed professional sport (Martinez 2021, PMID: 33662103). In the ORCCA cohort of 3,018 COVID-positive athletes, cardiac involvement was found in 0.7% and exactly one adverse cardiac event (0.03%) occurred over a median 113 days — judged likely unrelated to the infection (Moulson 2021, PMID: 33866822). None of this shows restriction improves recovery; it shows that a screen-restrict-return pathway was followed by very few events. PROPOSED MAYBE — observational only: whether exercise restriction improves recovery in myocarditis is untested; outcomes under restriction-based management in screened athletes were good.
stamp: MAYBE — observational only: exercise restriction after myocarditis has never been tested against continued exercise in any comparative study; in screened athlete cohorts managed with restriction, imaging inflammation usually resolved and adverse cardiac events were very rare (1 event in 3,018 athletes, judged unrelated)

title: Yes — longer recording catches what one day misses: a 14-day patch found 96 arrhythmia events versus the Holter's 61 in the same patients, and randomised and Medicare evidence agree
question: Does a 14-day patch monitor diagnose palpitations better than 24-hour Holter?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — concordant evidence across four designs. Worn simultaneously in the same 146 patients, a 14-day adhesive patch detected 96 arrhythmia events against the 24-hour Holter's 61 (Barrett 2014, PMID: 24384108). Randomised evidence agrees in adjacent settings: after stroke/TIA a 14-day patch found paroxysmal atrial fibrillation in 16.3% versus 2.1% with short Holter (EPACS, PMID: 31349792), and in emergency-department palpitation patients prolonged symptom capture found a symptomatic rhythm in 55.6% versus 9.5% with standard care (IPED, PMID: 31193636). In 287,789 Medicare patients the long-term continuous/patch strategy had the highest adjusted odds of a new diagnosis and the lowest repeat testing (Reynolds 2024, PMID: 38072334). The mechanism is duration — intermittent rhythms are missed by a single day of recording — not superior sensing. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): a 14-day patch monitor diagnoses palpitations better than 24-hour Holter.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit): a 14-day patch monitor detected more arrhythmias than 24-hour Holter in a simultaneous head-to-head study (96 vs 61 events), with randomised and 287,789-patient claims evidence concordant — the advantage is longer recording time catching intermittent rhythms

title: Unproven in preserved LVEF (observational only): risk persists and MRI scar marks it, and ICDs fire appropriately in 39% of cardiac sarcoidosis recipients — but no ICD-versus-none comparison exists in this subgroup
question: Does an ICD prevent sudden death in cardiac sarcoidosis with preserved LVEF?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only, printed on the face. No trial has tested an ICD in cardiac sarcoidosis with preserved LVEF. What the observational record shows is: (1) risk is not confined to reduced ejection fraction — in 398 Finnish patients, 5-year sudden-death incidence was 4.8% even without a guideline ICD indication, and the indications themselves did not predict sudden death (Nordenswan 2022, PMID: 36000392); (2) in 51 patients with LVEF over 35%, MRI scar stratified that risk sharply (positive predictive value 22% for any scar, 100% for right-ventricular scar; Crawford 2014, PMID: 25266311); (3) ICDs in cardiac sarcoidosis deliver appropriate therapy in 39% of recipients but inappropriate therapy in 15%, in a meta-analysis whose pooled mean LVEF was only 38.4% (Halawa 2020, PMID: 32062788). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: an ICD plausibly prevents some sudden deaths in preserved-LVEF cardiac sarcoidosis, especially with MRI scar, but that prevention is unproven in this subgroup.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: sudden-death risk persists in cardiac sarcoidosis with preserved LVEF (5-year incidence 4.8% even without a guideline indication) and is scar-stratified on MRI, and ICDs fire appropriately in 39% of recipients — but no study has compared ICD versus no ICD in preserved LVEF

title: For cardiac or unexplained syncope, the observational case is real (observational only): ~1.9% events/year and devices that fire — for clearly vasovagal syncope, the pooled evidence does not show added risk
question: Should patients with Brugada syndrome and syncope receive an ICD?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only, printed on the face; there is no randomised trial. The registries consistently place syncope patients at intermediate, real risk: cardiac events at 1.9% per year with syncope versus 0.5% per year asymptomatic and 7.7% per year after aborted sudden death (FINGER, PMID: 20100972), with syncope plus a spontaneous type 1 ECG predicting events (hazard ratio 4.20, relative; PRELUDE, PMID: 22192666). Pooled data split syncope by type — cardiac (odds ratio 4.48) and unexplained (4.71) syncope were associated with major arrhythmic events, vasovagal syncope was not (PMID: 37021016) — and in ICD recipients syncope with type 1 ECG predicted appropriate shocks (hazard ratio 4.96, relative), while 20.2% had other device complications (PMID: 29025556). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: an ICD is most defensible for Brugada patients whose syncope is cardiac or unexplained, and least supported for clearly vasovagal syncope.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: Brugada patients with syncope had cardiac events at 1.9%/year (vs 0.5% asymptomatic), cardiac/unexplained syncope carried ~4.5-fold relative odds of major arrhythmic events while vasovagal syncope did not, and ICDs fired appropriately in 20.2% of recipients — at a 20.2% complication rate

title: Probably, in the series that report it (observational only): inducibility abolished in three-quarters or more and very low on-treatment event rates — uncontrolled evidence, with tolerability the main limit
question: Does quinidine reduce arrhythmias in Brugada syndrome?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only, printed on the face; there is no randomised trial of quinidine in Brugada syndrome. In electrophysiology-guided cohorts, hydroquinidine prevented VT/VF inducibility in 76% of asymptomatic inducible patients and abolished recurrences in all 4 patients with multiple ICD shocks (Hermida 2004, PMID: 15145111); over 33 years, 90% of retested patients responded to a class 1A drug (mostly quinidine) and no responder had an arrhythmic event on therapy, though 38% had side effects (Belhassen 2015, PMID: 26354972); and a long-term French cohort on hydroquinidine 600 mg/day recorded an arrhythmic event rate of 1.04% per year (Bouzeman 2014, PMID: 24068450). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: quinidine reduces arrhythmias in Brugada syndrome in every published series, with the strongest face-value case in patients with recurrent ICD shocks, but the evidence is uncontrolled and rests largely on a stimulation surrogate.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: quinidine/hydroquinidine abolished arrhythmia inducibility in 76–90% of tested Brugada patients and on-treatment event rates were ~1%/year, but there is no randomised or untreated-controlled evidence and side effects affected 38% in the largest series

title: Yes, as corroboration (diagnostic evidence only): pooled discrimination is good (AUC 0.84), but sensitivity is ~41–61% and healthy controls faint too — a negative tilt does not exclude vasovagal syncope
question: Does tilt-table testing help diagnose vasovagal syncope?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — diagnostic-accuracy evidence only; no study carded here tests patient outcomes. Pooled across 55 case-control studies (4,361 patients, 1,791 controls), head-up tilt testing discriminated vasovagal patients from controls with an area under the curve of 0.84 and an adjusted diagnostic odds ratio of 12.15 (relative; Forleo 2013, PMID: 23041006). In primary protocols the yield is modest: 61% positive in recurrent unexplained syncope with 93% specificity (Morillo 1995, PMID: 7732979), and 41–49% positive against 10–13% false positives in healthy controls (Raviele 2000, PMID: 10802000). A structured history alone reached 89% sensitivity and 91% specificity (Sheldon 2006, PMID: 16223744), so tilt corroborates rather than replaces the story. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): tilt-table testing helps diagnose vasovagal syncope as corroborating evidence — a positive test supports the diagnosis, a negative test does not exclude it.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — diagnostic evidence only: tilt testing discriminates vasovagal syncope from controls (pooled AUC 0.84, 55 studies) but primary protocols were positive in only 41–61% of unexplained-syncope patients with 7–13% false positives in controls, and a structured history performed at least as well

title: Yes — three randomised trials agree: the loop recorder finds the cause in roughly half of unexplained syncope, several-fold more than conventional testing
question: Does implantable loop recorder find the cause of unexplained syncope better than conventional testing?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — three randomised trials are concordant, which earns LIKELY for this diagnostic-yield question. Prolonged implantable monitoring diagnosed 52% versus 20% with conventional testing in the RAST trial (PMID: 11435336); early recorder use established a certain cause in 46.2% versus 5% in the FRESH randomised study (PMID: 25241220); and first-line recorder use reached an ECG diagnosis far faster (hazard ratio 35.5, relative), found a pacing indication in 22% versus 3%, and delayed the second syncope (EaSyAS II, PMID: 26462702). In the 570-patient PICTURE registry the recorder guided the diagnosis in 78% of recurrent events after a median of 13 prior inconclusive tests (PMID: 21097478). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): an implantable loop recorder finds the cause of unexplained syncope better than conventional testing.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit): an implantable loop recorder diagnosed unexplained syncope in 52% vs 20% (RAST) and 46.2% vs 5% (FRESH) of patients versus conventional testing in randomised trials, with a third randomised trial and a 570-patient registry concordant

title: Split answer: prescribing gets inactive adults moving (benefit), but blood-pressure lowering at exactly 150 minutes/week is divided — 6 mmHg in one walking trial, non-significant in the exact-dose hypertensive trial
question: In adults who are inactive, does prescribing 150 minutes of moderate exercise per week improve blood pressure?
balance: SPLIT — the split is named in the stamp. As behaviour change, prescribing works: in the 878-patient Green Prescription cluster trial, counselling raised leisure exercise by 34 minutes/week and increased the share reaching 2.5 hours/week by 9.72 percentage points (Elley 2003, PMID: 12689976) — but that trial reports no blood-pressure effect size, only a trend. On blood pressure itself the two dose trials divide: walking 30 minutes five days a week for 12 weeks was followed by a 6 mmHg systolic fall with no change in controls (Tully 2007, PMID: 17699531), while the exact-dose trial in sedentary hypertensive adults — 30 minutes five days a week for 6 weeks — found a net −3.4/−2.8 mmHg that was not statistically significant (Cooper 2000, PMID: 11224966; the treatment made no demonstrated difference). PROPOSED SPLIT (prescription increases activity: benefit; blood-pressure lowering at exactly 150 minutes/week: divided): expect inactive adults to move more; expect, on this evidence, only a small and uncertain average blood-pressure fall from the prescription itself.
stamp: SPLIT (prescription increases activity: benefit; blood-pressure lowering at exactly 150 minutes/week: divided) — a walking trial found a 6 mmHg systolic fall, the exact-dose trial in hypertensive adults found a non-significant −3.4 mmHg, and the 878-patient prescription trial raised activity by 34 min/week but reported no blood-pressure effect size

title: Associated with slower growth in all observational evidence (observational only): dose-dependent in a 998-man cohort and pooled at 0.82 mm/year slower — never tested in a randomised trial
question: Does statin therapy slow abdominal aortic aneurysm growth?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only, printed on the face; no randomised trial of statins for aneurysm growth was found in the records fetched. The observational evidence is concordant and dose-dependent: in 998 men with screening-detected small aneurysms, each extra defined daily dose of statin was associated with 0.22 mm/year slower growth, with relative hazards of 0.82 for repair and 0.83 for repair/rupture/death per doubling of dose (Skovbo 2025, PMID: 40631665). Meta-analyses of observational studies agree — 0.82 mm/year slower growth across 80,428 patients, though with I² = 86% heterogeneity (Salata 2018, PMID: 30371297), and a standardised mean difference of −0.42 across 4,647 patients (Takagi 2012, PMID: 22824348). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: statin therapy is associated with slower abdominal aortic aneurysm growth, but confounding by indication has never been excluded by randomisation.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: statin use was associated with slower aneurysm growth in every observational design (0.22 mm/year per defined daily dose, dose-dependent; pooled 0.82 mm/year slower across 80,428 patients), but no randomised trial exists and the pooled estimate carries I² = 86% heterogeneity

title: Preoperative statin loading before cardiac surgery: no reduction in clinical events in pooled randomised evidence (the treatment made no difference), with a possible increase in acute kidney injury — small trials show only biomarker and strain benefits
question: Does preoperative statin loading reduce events before cardiac surgery?
balance: The randomised evidence says no for clinical events. The anchor is a meta-analysis of randomised trials in cardiac surgery (Putzu 2016, PMID: 27919293; 23 RCTs, 5,102 patients): in trials at low risk of bias, statin therapy in the days before surgery made no difference to postoperative atrial fibrillation, myocardial infarction, stroke, infections or mortality (the treatment made no difference), and was associated with more acute kidney injury (23.82% vs 19.86%; OR 1.26, 95% CI 1.05 to 1.52). Individual loading trials agree on events while differing on biomarkers: a randomised trial of 60 mg rosuvastatin loading before off-pump bypass (Youn 2011, PMID: 22263153; N = 142) found 30-day major adverse cardiac events in 1.4% vs 5.6% (P = 0.37, not significant) with lower postoperative enzyme release, and a 2024 valve-replacement trial (Prajapathi, PMID: 38681712) found better strain recovery and lower biomarker release with 40 mg rosuvastatin started 7 days before surgery, without clinical-event power. The definitive large single trial of perioperative rosuvastatin (STICS) is homed on shelf #1316 and is not re-carded here; its presence inside the Putzu meta-analysis is part of why the pooled answer is null. PROPOSED MAYBE (benefit) unproven — preoperative statin loading made no difference to clinical events in randomised evidence and may increase acute kidney injury.
stamp: MAYBE (benefit) unproven — preoperative statin loading made no difference to postoperative atrial fibrillation, myocardial infarction, stroke, infection or mortality in pooled randomised evidence (the treatment made no difference), and was associated with more acute kidney injury (23.82% vs 19.86%, OR 1.26)
