title: Polypill in primary prevention: LDL cholesterol about 19 mg/dL lower and systolic blood pressure about 5.8 mm Hg lower than placebo, with fewer cardiovascular events in large randomised trials
question: Does a polypill improve blood pressure and cholesterol control in primary prevention?
balance: Yes on both control measures, and events fall too. In TIPS-3 (Yusuf 2021, PMID: 33186492; 5,713 people without cardiovascular disease at intermediate risk), the polypill lowered LDL cholesterol by approximately 19 mg/dL and systolic blood pressure by approximately 5.8 mm Hg versus placebo, with the primary event outcome at 4.4% vs 5.5% (HR 0.79, 95% CI 0.63 to 1.00). In PolyIran (Roshandel 2019, PMID: 31448738; 6,838 participants in a pragmatic cluster-randomised trial), major cardiovascular events occurred in 5.9% on the polypill vs 8.8% on minimal care (adjusted HR 0.66, 95% CI 0.55 to 0.80); the subgroup without pre-existing cardiovascular disease — the primary-prevention subgroup — had HR 0.80 (95% CI 0.51 to 1.12), not significant on its own. An individual-participant meta-analysis of the three large primary-prevention polypill trials (Joseph 2021, PMID: 34469765; 18,162 participants) found the primary outcome in 3.0% vs 4.9% (HR 0.62, 95% CI 0.53 to 0.73). Two or more large concordant randomised trials support the stamp. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) — a polypill improves blood pressure and cholesterol control in primary prevention and reduces cardiovascular events.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — a polypill improves blood pressure and cholesterol control in primary prevention (LDL cholesterol about 19 mg/dL lower, systolic blood pressure about 5.8 mm Hg lower in TIPS-3) and reduces cardiovascular events across large randomised trials (pooled 3.0% vs 4.9%, HR 0.62)

title: Intermittent statin dosing in statin intolerance: LDL cholesterol falls by about a quarter to a third and most patients tolerate it in observational series — lipid effectiveness shown, cardiovascular outcomes untested
question: Is intermittent statin dosing effective for statin-intolerant patients?
balance: For lowering LDL cholesterol and being tolerated, the observational and review evidence is consistently favourable; for cardiovascular outcomes there is no trial at all. In the largest series (Meek 2012, PMID: 22256801; 325 statin-intolerant patients), rosuvastatin 5 mg two to three times weekly lowered LDL cholesterol by 32% and once-weekly dosing by 23%, and 89% of patients tolerated rosuvastatin over a median 14.9 months. A review of the intermittent-dosing literature (Keating 2013, PMID: 23482733; 10 publications) found at least 70% of previously intolerant patients tolerated an intermittent regimen without recurrence of treatment-limiting effects, with LDL cholesterol lowering of 12–38%. The one randomised comparison (Backes 2012, PMID: 22836073; N = 20, printed on the face) found rosuvastatin 80 mg once weekly lowered LDL cholesterol by 29%, comparable to daily atorvastatin 10 mg — but in patients with dyslipidaemia, not documented statin intolerance. No study reports cardiovascular events, so effectiveness here means lipid lowering with tolerability. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — intermittent dosing lowers LDL cholesterol substantially and is tolerated by most statin-intolerant patients in observational evidence; outcome benefit is untested.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — intermittent statin dosing lowers LDL cholesterol substantially (32% at two to three doses weekly, 23% once weekly) and was tolerated by 89% of statin-intolerant patients in the largest series; evidence is observational and review-level, with no cardiovascular-outcome trial

title: Metformin for walking in PAD without diabetes: the PERMET randomised trial found no improvement in 6-minute walk distance (the treatment made no difference)
question: Does metformin improve walking in PAD patients without diabetes?
balance: No — the one completed randomised trial is a clean null. In PERMET (McDermott 2026, PMID: 41205146; 202 people with peripheral artery disease and without diabetes), 6-minute walk distance changed by −5.4 m on metformin and −5.3 m on placebo over 6 months (adjusted between-group difference 1.1 m, 95% CI −16.3 to 18.6; P = .90), and no secondary outcome improved (the treatment made no difference). The mechanistic rationale came from animal work in which metformin improved limb blood supply without improving physical performance (Krishna 2025, PMID: 40304545 — a mouse study, carded as preclinical rationale only, not human evidence). A second human trial, MOBILE IC (Reitz 2023, PMID: 36681798; NCT05132439), plans 200 non-diabetic veterans with claudication but had reported no results in its protocol record. PROPOSED MAYBE (benefit) unproven — metformin did not improve walking in PAD patients without diabetes in the completed randomised trial.
stamp: MAYBE (benefit) unproven — metformin did not improve 6-minute walk distance in PAD patients without diabetes in the completed PERMET trial (difference 1.1 m, P = .90; the treatment made no difference); a second trial (MOBILE IC, NCT05132439) has not reported

title: Generic vs brand-name levothyroxine: TSH in range at near-identical rates in large cohorts (75.4% vs 76.9% in new users) — generic is as effective for maintaining TSH, on observational evidence
question: In adults with hypothyroidism, is generic levothyroxine as effective as brand-name levothyroxine for maintaining TSH in range?
balance: Essentially yes, on the evidence carded. In the largest head-to-head cohort of new users (Brito 2020, PMID: 32997127; 4,570 propensity-matched patients), normal thyrotropin within 3 months was achieved by 75.4% on generic vs 76.9% on brand-name levothyroxine (P = .23, no significant difference), with similar maintenance of normal levels thereafter. A much larger matched cohort of persistent users (Wang 2022, PMID: 34905150; 18,382 per group) found a statistically significant but very small difference the other way: 78.5% in range on brand vs 77.2% on generic (P = .002) — 1.3 percentage points. The classic randomised crossover bioequivalence trial (Dong 1997, PMID: 9103344; 22 women) found the tested generic and brand products bioequivalent, with relative bioequivalence of 0.95 to 1.07. The clinical-outcome evidence is observational, which caps the stamp. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (generic is as effective) — observational only for the TSH outcome: generic and brand-name levothyroxine maintain TSH in range at near-identical rates.
stamp: POSSIBLE (generic is as effective) — observational only for the TSH outcome: generic and brand-name levothyroxine achieved normal TSH at near-identical rates (75.4% vs 76.9%, P = .23 in new users; 77.2% vs 78.5% in persistent users), and tested products were bioequivalent (0.95 to 1.07) in a randomised crossover

title: Levothyroxine starting dose after total thyroidectomy: weight-based dosing does not achieve euthyroidism faster — only about a third of patients are euthyroid at first follow-up on any scheme
question: After total thyroidectomy for benign disease, does weight-based levothyroxine dosing achieve euthyroidism faster than fixed low-dose starting?
balance: No faster or more reliable achievement is shown — on any scheme, only about a third of patients are euthyroid at the first follow-up. A systematic review and meta-analysis of dosing strategies after total thyroidectomy (Chiardi 2025, PMID: 40682434; 11 studies, 2,577 patients) found a pooled first-follow-up euthyroidism rate of 33.9%, with weight-based (dose/kg) methods at 29% and fixed or algorithm-based approaches at 40%, without statistical significance — no strategy consistently outperformed the others (the treatment made no difference between strategies). In the benign-disease cohort behind the leading dosing-scheme comparison (Zaborek 2019, PMID: 30413325; 598 patients), standard weight-based dosing at 1.6 µg/kg/day predicted the eventual euthyroid dose correctly in only 51.3% of patients, and an external validation in benign thyroidectomy (Valenzuela 2021, PMID: 33845415) found weight-based accuracy of 53.8% with overdosing errors in 32.1%. The carded studies compare prediction accuracy and first-follow-up rates rather than time-to-euthyroidism directly, and none shows weight-based dosing beating a fixed start. PROPOSED MAYBE (benefit) unproven — weight-based dosing has not been shown to achieve euthyroidism faster than fixed low-dose starting.
stamp: MAYBE (benefit) unproven — weight-based levothyroxine dosing has not been shown to achieve euthyroidism faster than fixed starting doses after total thyroidectomy: pooled first-follow-up euthyroidism was 33.9% overall (weight-based 29% vs fixed/algorithm 40%, not significant; the strategies made no difference)

title: Ultrasound surveillance after benign thyroid cytology: it detects growth in 15.4% and cancer in 0.3% over 5 years, but no evidence shows it improves outcomes versus clinical follow-up alone (observational only)
question: In adults with a solitary thyroid nodule and benign cytology, does routine repeat ultrasound surveillance improve outcomes versus clinical follow-up alone?
balance: No trial has ever compared the two strategies, so improved outcomes from routine repeat ultrasound are unproven; the observational record shows what surveillance finds and what it misses. In a prospective multicentre cohort under yearly ultrasound surveillance (Durante 2015, PMID: 25734734; 992 patients with benign nodules), growth occurred in 15.4% over 5 years and thyroid cancer was diagnosed in 5 original nodules (0.3%), only 2 of which had grown. In a large biopsy cohort with median 13.9 years of follow-up (Ng 2021, PMID: 33371796; 2,207 patients), the false-negative rate for benign cytology was 3.2% (1.5% excluding papillary microcarcinomas), and no patient with a false-negative diagnosis died of thyroid cancer. A major review (Durante 2018, PMID: 29509871) frames most benign nodules as safely managed with a surveillance programme aimed at the small subgroup harbouring significant cancer (about 10% as printed in the record), with the initial risk estimate determining follow-up intensity. All evidence is observational, which caps the stamp. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) unproven — observational only: routine ultrasound surveillance detects the rare missed cancer, but no evidence shows it improves outcomes versus clinical follow-up alone.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) unproven — observational only: no trial compares routine repeat ultrasound surveillance with clinical follow-up alone; under surveillance, benign nodules grew in 15.4% over 5 years and cancer was found in 0.3%, and no false-negative patient died of thyroid cancer over a median 13.9 years

title: Calcium citrate vs carbonate in PPI users: citrate absorbs far better in the fasting acid-free gut (0.452 vs 0.042), but PPI exposure itself did not reduce absorption and no bone-outcome trial exists
question: In adults with osteoporosis, does calcium citrate improve absorption and bone outcomes compared with calcium carbonate in people taking proton pump inhibitors?
balance: For absorption under acid-free conditions the physiology evidence favours citrate strongly; for people actually taking proton pump inhibitors (PPIs), and for bone outcomes, there is no direct trial evidence at all. The classic experiment (Recker 1985, PMID: 4000241) compared the two salts in fasting patients with achlorhydria (n = 11): fractional absorption was 0.452 for citrate versus 0.042 for carbonate (P < 0.0001), while in normal subjects the salts did not differ (0.243 vs 0.225) — and carbonate taken with breakfast was absorbed normally even without acid. A direct PPI test (Hansen 2010, PMID: 20578215; 21 postmenopausal women) found 30 days of omeprazole 40 mg did not decrease fractional calcium absorption at all (20–23% across visits, P = .07), undercutting the premise that PPI use creates the achlorhydric fasting problem. A practice review (van der Velde 2014, PMID: 25147494) reports intestinal absorption of citrate about 24% better than carbonate overall, and states plainly that data comparing the salts during simultaneous PPI use are lacking. No study in any carded record measures bone density or fractures by calcium salt in PPI users. PROPOSED MAYBE (benefit) — citrate is absorbed far better than carbonate when fasting without gastric acid, but benefit in PPI users, and any bone-outcome benefit, is untested.
stamp: MAYBE (benefit) — absorption physiology only: citrate was absorbed far better than carbonate in fasting achlorhydria (0.452 vs 0.042), but omeprazole did not reduce calcium absorption in the direct PPI test, head-to-head data in PPI users are lacking, and no bone-outcome evidence exists

title: Stopping biotin before thyroid testing (small volunteer studies): biotin falsely moved TSH, free T4 and thyroglobulin on Roche/Beckman/Siemens platforms, and accuracy recovered 8 hours to 2 days after stopping — no study enrolled hypothyroid patients
question: In adults with hypothyroidism taking biotin supplements, does stopping biotin before testing improve accuracy of thyroid function tests versus continuing it?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — stopping biotin before testing removes a real, platform-dependent interference, but the direct washout evidence is two small volunteer studies (N = 13 and N = 10) in healthy adults, not a trial in people with hypothyroidism. Ylli 2021 (PMID: 34042535) gave 13 adults biotin 10 mg/day for 8 days and found significant changes in thyrotropin (TSH), free thyroxine and total triiodothyronine on the Roche Cobas 6000 platform and falsely lower thyroglobulin on Siemens IMMULITE 2000, with maximal interference 2 hours after ingestion; Zhang 2020 (PMID: 32118725) gave 10 healthy adults 5 and 10 mg/day for 7 days and found interference on Roche and Beckman platforms but none on Abbott, lasting 8 hours after 5 mg/day and 1 to 2 days after 10 mg/day — so accuracy returns once biotin is stopped, on a timescale of hours to about 2 days at supplement doses. The clinical stakes are documented in Favresse 2018 (PMID: 29982406): across more than 150 reported patients with thyroid immunoassay interferences of all types, at least 50% led to misdiagnosis and/or inappropriate management. No carded study enrolled hypothyroid patients specifically, so the levothyroxine-titration risk is inferred from the assay data and the review, and is printed as such. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): stop biotin before thyroid testing on susceptible platforms; how long ahead depends on dose and platform (hours after 5 mg/day, up to 2 days after 10 mg/day in the washout study).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — stopping biotin before thyroid testing removes platform-dependent assay interference (maximal 2 hours post-dose; clears 8 hours after 5 mg/day and 1–2 days after 10 mg/day); direct washout evidence is two small volunteer studies (N = 13 and N = 10, healthy adults — no trial in hypothyroid patients)

title: Cholestyramine added to methimazole in Graves disease: hormone levels fell faster in all three small randomised trials (T4 −61% vs −43% at 4 weeks) — but symptom relief itself was never measured
question: In adults with Graves disease, does adding cholestyramine to methimazole speed symptom control versus methimazole alone?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — three small short randomised trials agree that adding cholestyramine makes thyroid hormone levels fall faster, but none measured symptom control directly, so the shelf answers the hormone-speed question and labels the symptom inference. Mercado 1996 (PMID: 8784067, N = 30) found 4 weeks of cholestyramine with methimazole and propranolol lowered total T4 by 61% versus 43%, free T4 by 78% versus 65% and T3 by 68% versus 50% compared with methimazole and propranolol alone. Solomon 1993 (PMID: 8435884, N = 15, double-blind crossover) found a more rapid decline in all thyroid hormone levels during cholestyramine phases in the first weeks of treatment. Kaykhaei 2008 (PMID: 18946743, N = 45, double-blind placebo-controlled) found even 1–2 g twice daily sped the decline, with every patient on 2 g twice daily euthyroid at 4 weeks. Total carded N = 90, follow-up 2–4 weeks, endpoints biochemical throughout. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): cholestyramine speeds biochemical control in the first month; whether patients feel better faster is untested in the carded trials.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — three small randomised trials (total N = 90) consistently show faster thyroid hormone decline in the first 2–4 weeks when cholestyramine is added to methimazole; symptom control itself was not measured in any carded trial

title: Erythromycin for diabetic gastroparesis flares (weak evidence for symptoms): gastric emptying normalises acutely, but only 43% of patients reported symptom improvement in the small trials reviewed
question: Is erythromycin effective for acute gastroparesis flares in adults with diabetes?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — erythromycin reliably speeds gastric emptying in the short term, but symptom relief, which is what a flare means to the patient, is unproven in the carded evidence. Janssens 1990 (PMID: 2320062, N = 10, double-blind crossover) found intravenous erythromycin 200 mg normalised emptying: solid retention at 120 minutes was 4% ± 1% on erythromycin versus 63% ± 9% on placebo. Desautels 1995 (PMID: 7821102, N = 10, double-blind) found a single oral 250 mg dose cut solid half-emptying time from 151 ± 40 minutes on placebo to 58 ± 10 minutes. But the systematic review of oral erythromycin for symptoms (Maganti 2003, PMID: 12591038) found improvement in only 26 of 60 patients (43%) across five weak trials, none of which used symptoms as a primary endpoint, all with 13 or fewer subjects and 4 or fewer weeks of treatment. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): a potent short-term prokinetic for emptying; effectiveness for flare symptoms rests on small, short, mostly open-label studies.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — erythromycin markedly speeds gastric emptying acutely (solid retention 4% vs 63% at 120 min; half-emptying 58 vs 151 min after one 250 mg dose), but symptom relief was shown in only 43% of patients across five small, short, mostly open-label trials; primary emptying studies are N = 10 each

title: Weight loss to reverse steatohepatitis: about 10% of body weight — 90% resolution at 10% or more, 58% at 5% or more, with 7% the randomised trial's separating goal
question: How much weight loss is needed to reverse steatohepatitis in adults with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease?
balance: LIKELY (benefit, dose-dependent) — the answer the carded evidence supports is a gradient with a threshold at the top: about 10% of body weight is the amount that reliably reverses steatohepatitis. In the largest paired-biopsy cohort (Vilar-Gomez 2015, PMID: 25865049, N = 293), every patient who lost 10% or more of body weight had a reduced activity score, 90% had resolution of steatohepatitis and 45% had fibrosis regression; at 5% or more, 58% had resolution. The one randomised trial (Promrat 2010, PMID: 19827166, N = 31) set a 7–10% goal: the lifestyle group lost 9.3% versus 0.2% and participants reaching 7% or more improved significantly more on every histologic component. A meta-analysis of 22 randomised trials (Koutoukidis 2019, PMID: 31260026, 2,588 participants) confirms weight-loss interventions reduce the presence of steatohepatitis (odds ratio 0.14, a relative measure) without a significant fibrosis effect. Below 5%, resolution was uncommon in the cohort. PROPOSED LIKELY: aim for 10% or more to reverse steatohepatitis; 7–10% helps most patients; 5% resolves it in a minority-to-half depending on the group studied.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit, dose-dependent) — about 10% body-weight loss is needed to reliably reverse steatohepatitis (90% resolution at ≥10% loss in the paired-biopsy cohort; 58% at ≥5%; randomised and meta-analytic evidence concordant)

title: Screening for prediabetes and offering lifestyle intervention: the intervention delays progression (4% vs 10% at one year in pooled trials), but the screening tests miss and misclassify many people
question: Does screening for prediabetes and offering lifestyle intervention delay progression to diabetes?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) for delaying progression in people found to have prediabetes, with a screening-accuracy caveat printed on the face. The definitive trials themselves (the Diabetes Prevention Program, PMID: 11832527, and the Finnish Diabetes Prevention Study, PMID: 11333990) are already homed on live shelf #111 and are NOT re-carded here; this shelf answers the screening-framed question from the screen-and-treat evidence. Barry 2017 (PMID: 28052845), a systematic review of 49 screening-test studies and 50 intervention trials in people identified through screening, found lifestyle intervention associated with a 36% relative reduction in progression to type 2 diabetes over six months to six years, attenuating to 20% relative after the trials ended — but also found the screening tests themselves inaccurate (HbA1c sensitivity 0.49; fasting glucose sensitivity 0.25), so many people are misclassified in both directions. Glechner 2018 (PMID: 30076075), pooling 16 randomised trials, found progression of 4% versus 10% at one year (RR 0.46) and 14% versus 23% at three years (RR 0.64) with lifestyle intervention versus usual care. Roberts 2017 (PMID: 29146638) found screening-plus-intervention programmes cost-effective in modelling, though intervention-only programmes were generally more cost-effective than programmes that also included screening, and population impact on incident cases was small (0.1%–1.6% reduction). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): offering lifestyle intervention to people identified with prediabetes delays diabetes for the individual; the weakness is the screening step, not the intervention.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit): offering lifestyle intervention to people identified with prediabetes delays progression to diabetes (pooled trials: 4% vs 10% at 1 year, 14% vs 23% at 3 years; 36% relative reduction in screen-identified populations) — but screening tests are inaccurate (HbA1c sensitivity 0.49), so population screen-and-treat impact is small

title: Finerenone and blood pressure in resistant hypertension with CKD: a modest reduction (about 6 mmHg vs placebo), smaller than spironolactone's but with far less hyperkalaemia — indirect comparison only
question: Does finerenone lower blood pressure in resistant hypertension with CKD?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single trial programme (FIDELIO-DKD / FIGARO-DKD / ARTS-DN), capped at POSSIBLE. In the subgroup that answers this shelf's question directly — 624 FIDELITY patients with treatment-resistant hypertension and CKD meeting AMBER-trial eligibility — finerenone lowered systolic blood pressure by a least-squares mean of 7.1 mmHg versus 1.3 mmHg on placebo (between-group difference −5.74 mmHg, 95% CI −7.99 to −3.49) at about 17 weeks, a smaller reduction than spironolactone achieved in AMBER (−11.7 and −10.8 mmHg in its two arms) but with far less hyperkalaemia: serum potassium 5.5 mmol/L (5.5 mEq/L) or above in 12% on finerenone versus 3% on placebo, against 35% and 64% in the spironolactone arms, and hyperkalaemia discontinuation of 0.3% versus 7% and 23% (Agarwal 2023, PMID: 36864892). The parent FIDELIO-DKD analysis (N = 5,669) confirms finerenone reduced office systolic pressure across all baseline quartiles, though blood-pressure change explained only 13.8% of its kidney-outcome effect (Ruilope 2022, PMID: 36252131), and 24-hour ambulatory monitoring in ARTS-DN showed placebo-adjusted systolic reductions of about 8–11 mmHg at the 10–20 mg doses in a 240-patient subset (Agarwal 2023, PMID: 36583355). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): finerenone lowers blood pressure modestly in resistant hypertension with CKD — less than spironolactone in indirect comparison, with a lower hyperkalaemia burden; there is no head-to-head randomised trial against spironolactone.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single trial programme: finerenone lowered systolic blood pressure in resistant hypertension with CKD (−5.74 mmHg vs placebo in the 624-patient resistant-hypertension subgroup; 8–11 mmHg on ambulatory monitoring at 10–20 mg), less than spironolactone in indirect comparison but with much less hyperkalaemia; no head-to-head trial exists

title: Bisphosphonates in osteoporosis with CKD stage 3 (SPLIT): bone density improves, but fracture benefit is unproven in stage 3 CKD and safety signals are unresolved
question: In adults with osteoporosis and chronic kidney disease stage 3, are bisphosphonates safe and effective versus no antiresorptive treatment?
balance: SPLIT — the evidence divides by outcome and by CKD substage, and the split is named in the stamp. For bone mineral density the direction is favourable: the AHRQ systematic review (Wilson 2017, PMID: 28395318; 13 trials, n = 9,850) found bisphosphonates may slow loss of BMD, and a large propensity-matched cohort in stage 3B+ CKD found femoral-neck BMD gaining 2.65% per year more in bisphosphonate users than in matched non-users (Robinson 2021, PMID: 33739919). For fractures — the outcome that matters — no carded source demonstrates a reduction in stage 3 CKD: Wilson rates fracture effects unclear; the individual-patient meta-analysis of ibandronate trials (Whitlock 2024, PMID: 39381071; 7,428 participants, 27.5% stage G3A and 3.0% G3B) found an overall fracture hazard ratio of 0.871 (95% CI 0.746 to 1.018) but an increased fracture risk in the small G3B subgroup (HR 3.862, 95% CI 1.156 to 12.903), and a 2023 meta-analysis of stage 3–5 CKD and transplant trials concluded there is no evidence these medications reduce fracture risk (Leng 2023, PMID: 37387531). On safety, the IPD analysis found no effect on eGFR over 12 months but more hypocalcaemia (HR 1.324); the cohort found a 12% relative excess of CKD progression (subdistribution HR 1.12) and no increase in acute kidney injury, hypocalcaemia or gastrointestinal events. PROPOSED SPLIT: BMD improves, fracture benefit is unproven in stage 3 CKD, and safety signals (hypocalcaemia, possible CKD progression, a G3B fracture signal) are unresolved — randomised fracture-outcome data in stage 3 CKD do not exist in the carded records.
stamp: SPLIT (BMD: benefit; fractures and safety in stage 3 CKD: unproven): bisphosphonates improve bone mineral density in CKD stage 3, but no carded source demonstrates fewer fractures in this population, and safety signals (hypocalcaemia HR 1.324; CKD progression HR 1.12 in a cohort; a fracture signal in the small G3B subgroup) are unresolved

title: Peritoneal dialysis versus hemodialysis survival in the first 2 years (SPLIT, observational only): similar or slightly better overall, worse in diabetic cohorts
question: In adults with end-stage kidney disease, is peritoneal dialysis associated with similar survival to hemodialysis in the first 2 years?
balance: SPLIT — observational only, printed on the face; the evidence divides by diabetes status. In the largest matched comparison, 6,337 propensity-matched pairs of incident US dialysis patients, survival modestly favoured peritoneal dialysis (PD) in exactly this shelf's window — 85.8% versus 80.7% at 12 months and 71.1% versus 68.0% at 24 months, overall hazard ratio 0.92 (95% CI 0.86 to 1.00) — with the PD advantage concentrated in patients under 65, without cardiovascular disease and without diabetes, and no difference from day 90 in the overall sensitivity analysis (HR 1.05) (Weinhandl 2010, PMID: 20133483). A Canary Islands incident cohort (1,469 patients) likewise found higher early survival on PD, including at 24 months (90% versus 65% unadjusted), though its adjusted first-year relative risk of 0.509 and its unadjusted gaps are large enough to suggest residual selection differences (Rufino 2011, PMID: 21461011). In patients with diabetes the direction reverses: a meta-analysis of 17 cohort studies in diabetic end-stage kidney disease found PD associated with a 20% relative higher mortality than hemodialysis (HR 1.20, 95% CI 1.10 to 1.30) (Xue 2019, PMID: 31216914). PROPOSED SPLIT — observational only: in the first 2 years survival on PD is similar to, or slightly better than, hemodialysis overall, but worse in diabetic cohorts; no randomised comparison exists and modality choice is heavily confounded by who is offered and who chooses each therapy.
stamp: SPLIT — observational only (by diabetes status): in the first 2 years, peritoneal dialysis survival was similar to or slightly better than hemodialysis in general incident populations (matched HR 0.92; 24-month survival 71.1% vs 68.0%), but diabetic cohorts associate peritoneal dialysis with higher mortality (HR 1.20); no randomised evidence exists

title: More frequent hemodialysis and left ventricular mass: imaging improves in small trials (15.3 g difference; −11% end-diastolic volume), on surrogate outcomes over 6–12 months
question: In adults on hemodialysis, does more frequent dialysis improve left ventricular mass versus conventional thrice-weekly dialysis?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — small randomised trials, concordant on the imaging outcome. The FHN Daily Trial's primary report (PMID: 21091062) is already homed on live shelf #293 and is NOT re-carded here; this shelf cards the trials' cardiac-imaging reports and the independent nocturnal trial. Culleton 2007 (PMID: 17878421), a randomised trial of 52 patients, found frequent nocturnal hemodialysis six times weekly improved left ventricular mass versus conventional thrice-weekly dialysis, with a between-group difference in mass change of 15.3 g (95% CI 1.0 to 29.6, P = .04) over 6 months, alongside fewer blood-pressure medications (16/26 versus 3/25 patients reducing or stopping). The FHN cardiac magnetic resonance analysis (Chan 2013, PMID: 23970131) found frequent in-center dialysis reduced left ventricular end-diastolic volume by 11.0% and end-systolic volume by 14.8% relative to conventional therapy in the Daily Trial (245 patients), and reduced left ventricular mass, while the FHN Nocturnal Trial (87 patients) showed no significant volume changes and neither trial changed the mass-to-volume remodeling ratio. A small non-randomised in-center nocturnal study (MIDNIGHT, 25 patients) found left ventricular mass falling by 14.75 g versus rising 6.54 g on conventional dialysis over 6 months (Graham-Brown 2017, PMID: 29084397). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): more frequent dialysis improves left ventricular mass and volumes on imaging over 6–12 months; the trials are small, short, and powered for surrogates, not for death or hospitalisation.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit): more frequent dialysis improved left ventricular mass and volumes on cardiac imaging in small randomised trials (between-group mass difference 15.3 g in the 52-patient nocturnal trial; −11.0% end-diastolic volume with frequent in-center dialysis in FHN) — surrogate outcomes over 6–12 months, no mortality-powered trial

title: Tacrolimus versus cyclosporine after kidney transplantation: rejection is clearly lower on tacrolimus (pooled relative risk 0.69), with more new diabetes as the trade-off
question: In kidney transplant recipients, is tacrolimus better than cyclosporine for preventing acute rejection?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) for preventing acute rejection, with a diabetes harm printed on the face. Two large randomised trials agree: in the US cadaveric-transplant trial (412 patients), biopsy-confirmed acute rejection at 1 year was 30.7% on tacrolimus versus 46.4% on cyclosporine (P = 0.001), with less antilymphocyte rescue therapy (10.7% versus 25.1%) but more posttransplant diabetes (19.9% versus 4.0%) (Pirsch 1997, PMID: 9112351); in the European trial against cyclosporine microemulsion (560 patients), biopsy-proven rejection at 6 months was 19.6% versus 37.3% — an absolute difference of 17.7 percentage points (95% CI 10.3 to 25.1) — and steroid-resistant rejection 9.4% versus 21.0%, with no significant difference in patient or graft survival (Margreiter 2002, PMID: 11888584). The BMJ meta-analysis of 30 trials (4,102 patients) confirms less acute rejection at 1 year (relative risk 0.69, 95% CI 0.60 to 0.79) and less graft loss (RR 0.56 at 6 months), at the cost of more insulin-requiring diabetes (RR 1.86) — treating 100 recipients with tacrolimus instead of cyclosporine avoids 12 acute rejections and 2 graft losses but causes 5 extra cases of insulin-dependent diabetes (Webster 2005, PMID: 16157605). The later ELITE-Symphony trial (PMID: 18094377) is homed on live shelf #737 and is not re-carded here. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): tacrolimus prevents acute rejection better than cyclosporine, with more new diabetes as the principal trade-off.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit): tacrolimus prevents acute rejection better than cyclosporine (30.7% vs 46.4% and 19.6% vs 37.3% in two large randomised trials; pooled relative risk 0.69 at 1 year, graft loss RR 0.56), with more posttransplant diabetes (19.9% vs 4.0%; pooled RR 1.86 for insulin-requiring diabetes) as the trade-off

title: Stopping GLP-1 drugs before endoscopy (observational only): users have more retained gastric contents and holding is associated with less retention — but no study shows holding prevents aspiration, and gastroparesis patients were excluded from the evidence
question: Should adults with gastroparesis stop GLP-1 receptor agonists before endoscopy or surgery?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only, printed on the face. No randomised trial has tested holding versus continuing a GLP-1 receptor agonist before endoscopy or surgery, and no carded study enrolled patients because they had diagnosed gastroparesis — the largest cohort (Wu 2024, PMID: 38485835) explicitly excluded known gastroparesis, so this shelf answers the holding question for GLP-1 users coming to endoscopy, with gastroparesis patients the plausibly highest-risk group the evidence does not directly measure. What the observational evidence does show is consistent on the intermediate outcome and null on the feared one: across 23 observational studies and 262,018 patients, GLP-1 use was associated with about 4.5-fold higher odds of residual gastric contents and of prematurely terminated endoscopy, but no difference in aspiration pneumonia (OR 0.96) (Baig 2025, PMID: 39694296). Holding the drug the way anaesthesia guidance advises was associated with less retention in the one multicentre study that classified holding (4.4% vs 12.7%), with no aspiration events in either group and no significant difference in intubation or aborted procedures (Phan 2025, PMID: 39016372); glycaemic control predicted retention at least as strongly as the drug itself. For surgery under general anaesthesia there is no direct comparative evidence in the carded records at all. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: holding a GLP-1 receptor agonist before elective endoscopy probably reduces retained gastric contents and abandoned procedures, but a reduction in aspiration itself has never been shown, and patients with gastroparesis were excluded from the very studies used to judge their risk.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: holding a GLP-1 receptor agonist before elective endoscopy was associated with less retained gastric content (4.4% vs 12.7% in the one study that classified holding), but no study shows fewer aspirations, no trial has randomised holding, and patients with diagnosed gastroparesis were excluded from the key cohort

title: Infliximab vs adalimumab in Crohn's disease (no head-to-head trial): indirect and real-world evidence leans modestly to infliximab for induction — clearest in perianal disease — with hard outcomes broadly equal
question: Is infliximab better than adalimumab for inducing remission in moderate to severe Crohn's disease?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit, infliximab) — no head-to-head trial exists; the lean rests on indirect and observational evidence only, printed on the face. No randomised trial has ever compared infliximab with adalimumab directly in Crohn's disease. The indirect evidence leans modestly toward infliximab for induction: in a network meta-analysis of 25 induction trials (8,720 patients), infliximab 5 mg/kg ranked first of all agents for induction of clinical remission in the overall population (relative risk of failure to achieve remission 0.67 versus placebo), although risankizumab ranked first in both the biologic-naive and biologic-exposed subgroups (Barberio 2023, PMID: 35907636). The direct observational comparisons are split by outcome type: a US Medicare cohort found persistence, surgery and hospitalisation statistically indistinguishable (Osterman 2014, PMID: 23811254); a single-centre electronic-record cohort found more symptomatic non-response with adalimumab (OR 1.62) but no difference in surgery, hospitalisation or steroid use (Ananthakrishnan 2016, PMID: 26933751); and in 13,222 UK BioResource patients the two anti-TNF agents were broadly similar first-line, with infliximab superior specifically in perianal Crohn's disease (Kapizioni 2024, PMID: 38041850). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit, infliximab) — indirect and observational only: infliximab is probably at least as good and modestly better for inducing remission, most clearly in perianal disease, but the difference has never been tested head-to-head and hard outcomes look equal.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit, infliximab) — indirect and observational only: no head-to-head randomised trial exists; infliximab ranked first for induction in a network meta-analysis and showed less symptomatic non-response in one cohort, while persistence, surgery and hospitalisation were equal — its clearest advantage is in perianal Crohn's disease

title: Anti-TNF drug levels in Crohn's disease — SPLIT by phase: maintenance monitoring and correcting a low trough helped (NOR-DRUM B, TAXIT), while monitoring from induction and level-guided escalation did not (NOR-DRUM A, TAILORIX)
question: Should adults with Crohn's disease have drug levels checked to guide anti-TNF dosing?
balance: SPLIT — the randomised trials genuinely divide, and the split is by phase of treatment and by what the level is used for. Proactive monitoring during maintenance helped in the largest trial: in NOR-DRUM part B, 458 patients on maintenance infliximab (mixed immune-mediated diseases, including Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis) had sustained disease control without worsening in 73.6% with therapeutic drug monitoring versus 55.9% without (adjusted difference 17.6%) (Syversen 2021, PMID: 34932077). TAXIT points the same way for one use — correcting a low level: dose escalation in patients with troughs under 3 µg/mL raised Crohn's remission from 65% to 88%, and after optimisation, concentration-based dosing produced fewer flares than clinically based dosing (7% vs 17%), although 1-year remission itself did not differ (69% vs 66%) (Vande Casteele 2015, PMID: 25724455). Against that, monitoring from the start did not improve remission in NOR-DRUM part A (50.5% vs 53.0% at week 30; the treatment made no difference) (Syversen 2021, PMID: 33944876), and in TAILORIX, escalating infliximab by symptoms plus biomarkers plus drug levels produced the primary remission endpoint in 27–33% versus 40% with symptom-based escalation alone (P = .50) (D'Haens 2018, PMID: 29317275). Two cautions travel with the positive trials: NOR-DRUM pooled six diseases and its record does not report the Crohn's subgroup separately, and TAXIT's maintenance phase was null on its primary endpoint. PROPOSED SPLIT (maintenance monitoring and low-level correction: benefit in NOR-DRUM B and TAXIT; induction-phase and escalation-algorithm monitoring: no benefit in NOR-DRUM A and TAILORIX).
stamp: SPLIT (maintenance monitoring: benefit — NOR-DRUM B sustained control 73.6% vs 55.9% and TAXIT flare reduction after level correction; induction/escalation monitoring: no benefit — NOR-DRUM A and TAILORIX both null on remission)

title: Calprotectin monitoring vs symptoms alone in IBD — SPLIT: composite and subgroup outcomes favour monitoring in ulcerative colitis, but no carded trial won on its primary endpoint and Crohn's treat-to-target was null
question: Is fecal calprotectin monitoring better than symptom monitoring alone to prevent relapse in inflammatory bowel disease?
balance: SPLIT — biomarker-guided management wins on some targets in some settings and makes no difference on others, and the strongest positive trial cannot be re-carded here. In ulcerative colitis in remission, monthly calprotectin with 5-aminosalicylate escalation above 300 µg/g did not significantly reduce relapse overall (35.3% vs 50.0%, P = 0.23), although among patients whose calprotectin actually rose, relapse was halved (28.6% vs 57.1%) (Lasson 2015, PMID: 25653861). In active mild-to-moderate ulcerative colitis, calprotectin home monitoring missed its primary endoscopic endpoint (Mayo endoscopic subscore 0: 37.0% vs 33.4%, not significant) but achieved significantly more composite clinical-plus-endoscopic control (OPTIMISE; Danese 2024, PMID: 39274360). In Crohn's disease on ustekinumab, a treat-to-target strategy built on endoscopy, biomarkers and symptoms did not significantly improve endoscopic response at week 48 (38% vs 30%, P = 0.087) and produced less clinical response than symptom-driven care (STARDUST; Danese 2022, PMID: 35120656). The field's landmark positive trial, CALM (Colombel 2017, PMID: 29096949 — tight control 46% vs 30% endoscopic remission), is already carded as an evidence card on live shelf #324 and is cross-pointed here, not re-carded, under the one-home rule; it enrolled active Crohn's disease, not patients in remission being watched for relapse. PROPOSED SPLIT (calprotectin-guided escalation: benefit on composite control in active ulcerative colitis and in the calprotectin-risen subgroup in remission; no significant benefit on the primary endpoints of any carded trial, and no benefit for ustekinumab treat-to-target in Crohn's disease).
stamp: SPLIT (calprotectin-guided management: benefit on composite and subgroup outcomes in ulcerative colitis — OPTIMISE composites and Lasson's calprotectin-risen subgroup; no significant benefit on any carded trial's primary endpoint, and none for treat-to-target in Crohn's disease in STARDUST; the positive CALM trial is homed on live shelf #324)

title: Low-residue diet in an ulcerative colitis flare — untested, not disproven: no trial has ever randomised flaring patients to residue restriction, and the only fibre-feeding trial (in remission) found high fibre tolerated
question: Is a low-residue diet needed during an ulcerative colitis flare?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the honest answer is that the practice has never been tested, not that it has been disproven. No carded record contains a randomised trial of a low-residue (low-fibre) diet during an ulcerative colitis flare. The Cochrane review of dietary interventions in inflammatory bowel disease (18 RCTs, 1,878 participants) found exactly one trial in active ulcerative colitis — a symptoms-guided diet in 21 participants, remission 36% vs 0%, relative risk 8.25 with a confidence interval running from 0.50 to 136.33, rated very low certainty — and concluded that the effects of dietary interventions are uncertain and no firm conclusions can be drawn (Limketkai 2019, PMID: 30736095). A systematic review of diet trials found low-residue/low-fibre diets were among the commonest interventions studied, but the few higher-quality trials showing significant symptom improvement tested exclusion or other specific diets, not residue restriction (Charlebois 2016, PMID: 25569442). The only carded trial that fed ulcerative colitis patients more fibre points the other way, in a different population: 17 patients in remission or with mild disease tolerated a catered low-fat, high-fibre diet for 4 weeks, all remained in remission, and quality of life and inflammatory markers improved (Fritsch 2021, PMID: 32445952) — reassuring about fibre, but not a flare trial. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): a low-residue diet during a flare is an untested tradition; there is no trial evidence that it is needed, and no flare trial evidence that fibre is safe either — the gap itself is the finding.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence): no randomised trial has ever tested a low-residue diet during an ulcerative colitis flare — the Cochrane review found the whole diet literature in IBD uncertain, so the practice is unproven rather than disproven

title: Ciprofloxacin plus metronidazole for acute pouchitis — never tested against metronidazole alone: the one small head-to-head trial favours ciprofloxacin by itself, and the combination's evidence is uncontrolled, in refractory disease
question: Does ciprofloxacin plus metronidazole treat acute pouchitis better than metronidazole alone?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the exact comparison in this shelf's question has never been randomised. A 2023 systematic review of all 20 randomised pouchitis trials (830 patients) found just one acute-pouchitis antibiotic comparison — ciprofloxacin alone versus metronidazole alone — and no trial of the combination against metronidazole alone (Alphonsus 2023, PMID: 37246609). That single trial was tiny (16 patients): ciprofloxacin produced a greater fall in the Pouchitis Disease Activity Index than metronidazole (6.9 vs 3.8 points, P = 0.002) with remission in 7 of 7 versus 6 of 9 (relative risk 1.44, 95% CI 0.88–2.35, very low certainty in the meta-analysis), and no adverse effects versus 33% with metronidazole (Shen 2001, PMID: 11720319). The combination itself has only single-arm evidence, in a different population: 44 patients with recurrent or refractory pouchitis given ciprofloxacin plus metronidazole for 4 weeks, of whom 82% entered remission (Mimura 2002, PMID: 11966499) — with no comparator, that number cannot show the combination beats either drug alone, and refractory patients are not first-episode acute pouchitis. The indirect logic (ciprofloxacin alone at least as good as metronidazole alone; the pair rescues refractory cases) is why combinations are used, but it is logic, not a trial result. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): whether adding ciprofloxacin to metronidazole improves acute pouchitis outcomes is untested; the one head-to-head trial suggests ciprofloxacin alone, not the combination, is the better-supported first choice.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence): the combination has never been randomised against metronidazole alone in acute pouchitis — the only head-to-head trial (N = 16) favours ciprofloxacin alone, and combination evidence is a single-arm study in refractory disease

title: Smoking cessation and ulcerative colitis — SPLIT, observational only: a small matched cohort found the disease worsened after quitting; a nationwide cohort found no difference at all
question: Does smoking cessation worsen ulcerative colitis symptoms?
balance: SPLIT — observational only, printed on the face; the two best cohorts point in opposite directions. The older matched cohort found clear worsening after quitting: in 32 patients who stopped smoking after an ulcerative colitis diagnosis, the years after cessation (mean 7 years) brought significantly more years with active disease, hospitalisation and major medical therapy than their own smoking years, and their need for immunosuppression rose to the level of matched never-smokers and above continuing smokers — while colectomy risk did not change (Beaugerie 2001, PMID: 11467641). The much larger modern study found nothing of the kind: among 6,754 incident ulcerative colitis patients (878 smokers at diagnosis), those who quit within 2 years of diagnosis had rates of flares, thiopurine use, corticosteroid dependency, hospitalisation and colectomy that were not significantly different from persistent smokers (Blackwell 2019, PMID: 31389044). A narrative review of the wider literature describes the same inconsistency — some studies show a more benign course in smokers, others do not verify it, and colectomy does not seem determined by smoking status (Bastida 2011, PMID: 21734782). Both carded cohorts' authors, and the review, agree on the clinical bottom line that smoking's overall harms outweigh any colitis benefit and patients should be counselled to quit. PROPOSED SPLIT — observational only (worsening after cessation: the small matched cohort; no worsening: the nationwide cohort 200 times larger).
stamp: SPLIT — observational only (quitting worsened colitis activity and treatment needs in a small matched cohort, Beaugerie 2001; a nationwide cohort of 6,754 patients found no worse outcomes in quitters than in persistent smokers, Blackwell 2019)

title: Continuing biologics in pregnancy in IBD (observational only): no harm signal in large prospective registry data — active disease, not the biologic, is the demonstrated pregnancy risk
question: Should women with inflammatory bowel disease continue biologics during pregnancy?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only, printed on the face; there is and can be no randomised trial of continuing versus stopping biologics in pregnancy. The largest prospective registry analysis (PIANO; 1,490 completed pregnancies) found that exposure to biologics (642 pregnancies), thiopurines (242), both (227) or neither (379) made no difference to congenital malformations, spontaneous abortion, preterm birth, low birth weight or first-year infant infections — while higher disease activity itself was associated with spontaneous abortion (HR 3.41) and with preterm birth plus infant infection (OR 1.73), which is the risk continuation exists to prevent (Mahadevan 2021, PMID: 33227283). The registry's newer-biologic analysis points the same way for vedolizumab (66 exposed pregnancies) and ustekinumab (47), with no increased risk on any measured outcome and a recommendation to continue both throughout pregnancy (Chugh 2024, PMID: 37796648). The one discordant signal in the carded set is older and concerns thiopurines, not biologics: a 2015 meta-analysis found congenital abnormalities increased in thiopurine-exposed pregnancies versus unmedicated controls (OR 2.95, 95% CI 1.03–8.43), while its anti-TNF cohort review found no increase in adverse outcomes (Mozaffari 2015, PMID: 25378092). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: continuing biologics through pregnancy is not associated with worse maternal or infant outcomes in large prospective registry data, and uncontrolled disease is the demonstrated risk.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: continuing biologics through pregnancy was not associated with malformations, abortion, preterm birth, low birth weight or infant infection in 1,490 PIANO-registry pregnancies, while higher disease activity was (spontaneous abortion HR 3.41)

title: Vitamin D and Crohn's relapse — SPLIT by setting: small remission trials lean positive (pooled relative risk 0.47), but the largest trial, after surgery, found no benefit at all
question: Does vitamin D supplementation reduce relapse in adults with Crohn's disease?
balance: SPLIT — the evidence divides by setting, and the divide is named in the stamp. In medical remission, the signal favours vitamin D but rests on small trials: the first randomised trial (94 analysed patients) found relapse in 13% on 1,200 IU/day versus 29% on placebo, a difference that did not reach significance (P = 0.06) (Jorgensen 2010, PMID: 20491740), while a 2024 meta-analysis of the small randomised trials pooled a relative risk of clinical relapse of 0.64 overall and 0.47 in Crohn's patients in clinical remission (Valvano 2024, PMID: 36579768). In the postoperative setting, the largest and best-powered trial is plainly null: 25,000 IU weekly after ileocolonic resection did not reduce endoscopic recurrence (58% vs 66%, P = .37) or clinical recurrence (18.1% vs 18.3%) despite raising blood levels as intended (de Bruyn 2021, PMID: 32461138). A relative risk reduction quoted from the meta-analysis is a relative measure built from trials of a few dozen patients each; the absolute relapse rates in the one trial that reports them are 13% versus 29%. Correcting deficiency for bone health is a separate, uncontroversial reason to supplement; this shelf answers only the relapse question. PROPOSED SPLIT (medical remission: possible benefit in a meta-analysis of small trials, anchored on one non-significant trial; postoperative recurrence: no benefit in the largest trial).
stamp: SPLIT (medical remission: possible benefit — pooled relative risk of relapse 0.47 across small trials, anchor trial 13% vs 29%, P = 0.06; postoperative recurrence: no benefit — the largest trial found endoscopic recurrence 58% vs 66% on high-dose vitamin D)

title: Testing for bile acid diarrhoea before rifaximin in IBS-D (diagnostic-yield evidence only): roughly one in four to one in three patients has bile acid malabsorption and a binder-responsive diagnosis rifaximin would miss
question: Should adults with irritable bowel syndrome be tested for bile acid diarrhea before starting rifaximin?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational/diagnostic-yield evidence only, printed on the face; no trial has randomised a test-first strategy against rifaximin-first. What the evidence establishes is yield and consequence. Yield: roughly one in four to one in three patients meeting criteria for diarrhoea-predominant irritable bowel syndrome has bile acid malabsorption on SeHCAT testing — a pooled rate of 28.1% (95% CI 22.6%–34%) across six studies and 908 individuals (Slattery 2015, PMID: 25913530), and 32% at the moderate threshold (7-day retention under 10%) across 18 studies and 1,223 patients, with 10% severe (Wedlake 2009, PMID: 19570102). Consequence: these patients have a specific, cheap, effective treatment that is not rifaximin — response to the bile acid binder colestyramine ran 96%, 80% and 70% by severity of malabsorption in the same review's pooled treatment data — so a positive test redirects therapy entirely, and a rifaximin course given first delays that redirect. The practical caveat is test availability: SeHCAT is unavailable in many countries including the United States, and the blood alternatives are imperfect — serum FGF19 at 145 pg/mL detected raised bile acid synthesis (C4 above 28 ng/mL) with only 58% sensitivity and 79% specificity in 258 patients with chronic diarrhoea (Pattni 2012, PMID: 23238290). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — diagnostic-yield evidence only: testing before rifaximin identifies a large, specifically treatable subgroup, but the test-first sequence itself is untested in a trial and the available tests miss cases.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — diagnostic-yield evidence only: about 28–32% of IBS-D patients have bile acid malabsorption on SeHCAT testing and most respond to a bile acid binder, so testing before rifaximin identifies a large treatable subgroup — but no trial has tested the test-first sequence, and blood tests miss cases (FGF19 sensitivity 58%)

title: Sodium restriction for ascites in cirrhosis (SPLIT): standard guideline practice, but the randomised comparison of 40 versus 120 mmol/day found the stricter diet made no difference to diuretic response and reviews call the trial evidence contradictory
question: Should adults with cirrhosis and ascites restrict dietary sodium to control fluid retention?
balance: SPLIT — the randomised evidence divides against the guideline habit, and the split is named on the face. Sodium restriction is standard, guideline-endorsed care for ascites, and the physiology (avid renal sodium retention) supports it. But the only carded randomised comparison of sodium intakes, Bernardi 1993 (PMID: 8336527), randomised 115 hospitalised patients to diets of 40 versus 120 mmol of sodium daily inside a stepped diuretic protocol and found the type of diet did not influence the response to treatment. A 2020 systematic review of randomised nutritional trials in cirrhosis and ascites (PMID: 33473347) likewise reports that studies reached contradictory conclusions regarding sodium restriction in patients taking combination diuretics. The 2016 protocol for the first dedicated systematic review (PMID: 27160239) states the concern plainly: some randomised trials have suggested a lack of benefit of a sodium-restricted over an unrestricted diet, and even an increase in ascites and renal complications has been reported. No carded record shows that stricter restriction improves fluid control, survival, or any hard outcome. PROPOSED SPLIT (guideline practice: benefit; randomised comparisons: no added benefit of stricter restriction, possible harm): moderate sodium restriction remains the usual adjunct to diuretics, but the randomised record does not show that restricting harder controls ascites better.
stamp: SPLIT (guideline practice: benefit; randomised comparisons: no added benefit, possible harm) — sodium restriction is standard adjunct care for ascites, but the carded randomised comparison of 40 versus 120 mmol/day found the diet made no difference to diuretic response, and reviews describe the trial conclusions on restriction as contradictory

title: Early liver transplantation for steroid-nonresponsive severe alcohol-related hepatitis (observational only): large survival advantage in strictly selected patients, post-transplant survival matching standard transplantation — with more high-intake alcohol relapse
question: Is early liver transplant evaluation appropriate for severe alcohol-related hepatitis that does not respond to steroids?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only, printed on the face: there is no randomised trial of early transplantation, and every carded study is a selected-cohort comparison. Within that limit the survival signal is large and consistent. In Mathurin 2011 (PMID: 22070476), 26 rigorously selected patients (first episode, Lille score 0.45 or higher, supportive family, commitment to abstinence — fewer than 2% of admissions) had 6-month survival of 77 ± 8% versus 23 ± 8% in matched non-transplanted patients. The prospective controlled Louvet 2022 study (PMID: 35202597) confirms an important survival benefit (2-year overall survival hazard ratio 0.27 relative against eligible-score failures who were not transplanted) with post-transplant survival similar to standard transplantation after 6 months of abstinence (hazard ratio 0.87) — but alcohol relapse was not shown non-inferior (34% versus 25%), and high alcohol intake was more frequent after early transplantation (absolute difference 16.7%). A 2018 meta-analysis (PMID: 30349998) found the same pattern. Evaluation is therefore appropriate for carefully selected nonresponders; the relapse cost is real and belongs in the selection process, not discovered afterwards. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: in strictly selected patients with severe alcohol-related hepatitis not responding to medical therapy, early transplantation was associated with much higher survival (6-month 77% vs 23% in the founding cohort) and post-transplant survival similar to standard transplantation, but alcohol relapse was not shown non-inferior and high-intake relapse was more frequent

title: Pancreatic enzyme timing in chronic pancreatitis (weak evidence): take the dose during the meal, spread through it, or just after — the single small timing trial found digestion tended to be better than with a dose just before eating
question: How should pancreatic enzyme doses be timed with meals in chronic pancreatitis?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the timing question rests on one small randomised crossover study, and the stamp says so. In Domínguez-Muñoz 2005 (PMID: 15813835), 24 patients with chronic pancreatitis and exocrine insufficiency took 40,000 units of lipase just before, just after, or distributed along with meals in randomised 1-week periods: fat digestion, measured by an optimised mixed 13C-triglyceride breath test, tended to be higher when capsules were taken along with meals (13CO2 recovery 61.4 ± 21.4%) or just after meals (60.6 ± 21.8%) than just before meals (53.9 ± 20.3%), and fat digestion normalised in 63%, 54% and 50% of patients respectively — differences the record reports as a tendency, with no significance test printed. The carded placebo-controlled pancrelipase trial (Whitcomb 2010, PMID: 20502447) dosed enzymes per meal and per snack and proved the drug class works (coefficient of fat absorption change 31.9 versus 8.7 points over placebo), but it did not randomise timing. The Cochrane timing review in cystic fibrosis (Ng 2021, PMID: 34339047) found no eligible randomised trial of dosing schedules at all. Practical answer on this evidence: take the dose during the meal, spread through it (or immediately after), not as a single dose beforehand — a reasonable instruction whose comparative evidence is one 24-patient study. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — one small randomised crossover trial (n = 24) found fat digestion tended to be better when enzymes were taken distributed along with meals or just after meals than just before; no other randomised timing evidence exists in the carded records

title: ESWL for large pancreatic duct stones: complete clearance in about 7 in 10 patients and pain-free follow-up in about 6 in 10 in pooled series, with ESWL alone matching ESWL plus endoscopy in the randomised trial
question: Does extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy work for large pancreatic duct stones in chronic pancreatitis?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the clearance and pain numbers come mainly from pooled observational series, with one randomised strategy trial, and the stamp is capped accordingly. The meta-analysis of van Huijgevoort 2020 (PMID: 32743061) pooled 22 studies and 3,868 patients treated with extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy (ESWL) for symptomatic pancreatic duct stones: complete ductal clearance 69.8%, complete absence of pain during follow-up 64.2%, complete stone fragmentation 86.3%, with post-procedural pancreatitis in 4.0% and cholangitis in 0.5%. The large single-centre cohort of Tandan 2013 (PMID: 23891416) found 60–69% of 636 followed patients pain-free at intermediate and long-term follow-up after ESWL with endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography, with stone recurrence in 14–23%. The one randomised trial (Dumonceau 2007, PMID: 17047101) did not compare ESWL against no ESWL: it showed ESWL alone performed as well as ESWL plus systematic endoscopic drainage for pain relapse (38% versus 45%; odds ratio 0.77 relative), at one-third of the cost — so the randomised evidence supports ESWL as the platform treatment, while the size of its effect against natural history rests on the observational record. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — pooled series show complete ductal clearance in 69.8% and complete pain relief in 64.2% after ESWL for large pancreatic duct stones, and the one randomised trial found ESWL alone matched ESWL plus endoscopy for pain relapse at one-third of the cost; no carded trial compares ESWL with no ESWL

title: Simethicone in bowel preparation: fewer bubbles, better cleansing and less bloating across the randomised record — the adenoma-detection gain is real in one meta-analysis, absent overall in the larger one, and confined to single-dose regimens
question: Does adding simethicone to bowel preparation improve colonoscopy visualization?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) for visualization — two meta-analyses of randomised trials and a double-blind trial agree that simethicone clears bubbles and foam and improves cleansing scores, while they divide on whether adenoma detection rises overall, and that division is printed rather than smoothed over. Rishi 2019 (PMID: 31236194) randomised 168 outpatients: high bubble grades requiring intervention occurred in 4 of 84 patients with simethicone versus 20 of 84 with placebo (P = 0.007), while total Boston Bowel Preparation Scale scores did not differ (7.42 versus 7.28; P = 0.542 — the treatment made no difference on that scale). Pan 2019 (PMID: 30069899) pooled 6 trials and 1,855 patients and found adenoma detection increased (27.9% versus 23.3%; relative risk 1.20 relative). Moolla 2019 (PMID: 31451919) pooled 16 trials and 5,630 patients: colon cleansing improved (odds ratio 1.48 relative), bloating was less frequent with simethicone, but adenoma detection overall did not significantly change (odds ratio 1.22 relative; 95% CI 0.81 to 1.83), with the detection benefit confined to single-dose (non-split) preparations. The visualization claim itself — fewer bubbles, better cleansing — is concordant across all three records. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) for visualization, with the adenoma-detection split stated in the stamp.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) for visualization — simethicone consistently reduced bubbles/foam and improved cleansing across randomised trials and two meta-analyses, and lessened bloating; adenoma detection divided the meta-analyses (increased in one, no significant overall increase in the larger one, with benefit confined to single-dose preparation)

title: GLP-1 drugs before colonoscopy (observational only): retained gastric contents are more common in relative terms and preparation was poorer in one cohort, but absolute aborted-procedure rates were low and no aspiration excess was shown — routine stopping is not established by the record
question: Should adults stop GLP-1 receptor agonists before colonoscopy because of retained gastric contents?
balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — observational only, printed on the face: every carded record is a retrospective cohort or a meta-analysis of such cohorts, and none tests stopping versus continuing the drug. What the record does show: retained gastric contents are clearly more frequent in GLP-1 receptor agonist users at endoscopy (pooled odds ratio 15.39 relative in Singh 2025, PMID: 39401599, across 23 studies and 77,152 patients), and aborted procedures were also more frequent in relative terms (odds ratio 13.86 relative) — but the absolute rates were low: in the largest single cohort (Dev 2025, PMID: 40021603), 0.6% of procedures in GLP-1 users were aborted for retained food versus 0.096% in non-users, with no aspiration episodes in patients with retained food, and the meta-analysis found no significant difference in aspiration events. For colonoscopy specifically, Yao 2024 (PMID: 37856247) found modestly worse bowel preparation in users (Boston Bowel Preparation Scale 7.0 versus 7.5; repeat colonoscopy for poor preparation 18.9% versus 11.1%), while the meta-analysis found no significant difference in subjective bowel preparation quality (odds ratio 0.94 relative). The carded record therefore documents a real but small absolute procedural problem and does not establish that routinely stopping GLP-1 therapy before colonoscopy is needed; it supports individualised management, as the largest cohort's authors conclude. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm) — observational only.
stamp: POSSIBLE (harm) — observational only: GLP-1 use is associated with more retained gastric contents and, in one cohort, poorer bowel preparation and more repeat colonoscopies, but absolute aborted-procedure rates were low (0.6%) and no aspiration excess was shown — the records do not establish that routine stopping before colonoscopy is needed

title: Prophylactic clipping after large-polyp resection: bleeding roughly halved for polyps ≥20 mm — above all in the proximal colon — with little to no benefit for smaller or distal lesions
question: Does prophylactic clipping after removal of large colon polyps prevent delayed bleeding?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — for large (20 mm or larger), especially proximal, polyps; the benefit does not extend to smaller or distal lesions, and both halves are on the face. The multicentre randomised trial of Pohl 2019 (PMID: 30885778) randomised 919 patients after resection of nonpedunculated polyps of 20 mm or more: postprocedure bleeding occurred in 3.5% with clip closure versus 7.1% without (absolute risk difference 3.6%), and serious adverse events were also fewer (4.8% versus 9.5%). The protection was concentrated in proximal polyps (3.3% versus 9.6%; absolute difference 6.3%) and absent — numerically reversed — in distal polyps (4.0% versus 1.4%). The randomised-trial meta-analysis of Chen 2021 (PMID: 33049265; 8 trials, 3,415 patients) agrees: relative risk 0.61 relative overall, 0.54 relative for polyps 20 mm or larger (number needed to treat 30) and 0.49 relative for proximal polyps (number needed to treat 25). Bishay 2022 (PMID: 33751224) found the randomised benefit confined to polyps of 20 mm or more (relative risk 0.47 relative), with the remaining randomised data and the observational data showing no benefit (observational relative risk 0.96 relative — the treatment made no difference). Two or more concordant randomised sources for the large-polyp claim support LIKELY. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) for polyps ≥20 mm, especially proximal.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — for polyps ≥20 mm, especially proximal: clip closure reduced postprocedure bleeding from 7.1% to 3.5% in the randomised trial (proximal: 9.6% to 3.3%), and randomised meta-analyses agree (relative risk 0.47–0.54 relative for ≥20 mm); little to no benefit for smaller or distal lesions

title: Elective resection for recurrent diverticulitis: quality of life better at 6 months and 5 years after sigmoidectomy in the DIRECT trial — weighed against an 11–15% anastomotic leak risk, and not a test of the old two-episode rule
question: Should adults have elective colon resection after two episodes of diverticulitis?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single trial programme, capped at POSSIBLE, whose enrolled population must be printed plainly: the DIRECT trial did not study a simple 'two episodes' rule. It randomised 109 patients with recurrent diverticulitis (three or more presentations within 2 years) or persistent complaints for 3 months or more after an episode (van de Wall 2017, PMID: 28404008; NTR1478). At 6 months, quality of life (Gastrointestinal Quality of Life Index) was significantly higher after elective sigmoidectomy than with conservative management (114.4 versus 100.4; mean difference 14.2), and the advantage persisted at 5 years (Bolkenstein 2019, PMID: 30247329: 118.2 versus 108.5; mean difference 9.7), with less pain. The price is real surgery: anastomotic leakage in 15% of operated patients at 6 months (11% in the 5-year report), reinterventions in 15%, and severe adverse events in about a third of the surgical group — while 23% of the conservative group crossed over to resection within 6 months and 46% by 5 years, which narrows the contrast. The trial was terminated early for recruitment difficulties. A 2026 systematic review (Sadiq, PMID: 42722921) found only 4 studies and 446 patients in the contemporary literature, with quality of life favouring surgery but reintervention commoner after it (21%). The old automatic rule — resect after the second episode — is not what this evidence tests; it supports offering elective resection to patients with recurrent or persisting complaints after weighing the quality-of-life gain against operative risk. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — single trial programme.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single trial programme (DIRECT): elective sigmoidectomy improved quality of life at 6 months and 5 years in patients with recurrent (≥3 presentations in 2 years) or persistent complaints, at the cost of anastomotic leakage in about 11–15% of operated patients; the trial did not test an automatic resection rule after exactly two episodes

title: Biofeedback for levator ani syndrome: adequate relief in 87% of tenderness-confirmed patients in the single randomised trial, ahead of electrogalvanic stimulation and massage — and no benefit shown without the examination sign
question: Should adults with chronic anal pain and levator ani syndrome try biofeedback?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single randomised trial programme, capped at POSSIBLE, with a selection condition that governs the answer. In Chiarioni 2010 (PMID: 20044997), 157 patients with levator ani syndrome and weekly pain were randomised to 9 sessions of biofeedback, electrogalvanic stimulation or massage (all with psychological counselling). Among patients 'highly likely' to have the syndrome — those with tenderness on traction on the levator muscles — adequate relief was reported by 87% with biofeedback, 45% with electrogalvanic stimulation and 22% with massage; pain days per month fell from 14.7 at baseline to 3.3 after biofeedback (8.9 and 13.3 for the other treatments), pain intensity fell from 6.8 to 1.8 on a 0–10 scale, and improvements were maintained for 12 months. Patients with only a 'possible' diagnosis (no tenderness) did not benefit from any treatment — so the shelf's answer is yes for examination-confirmed levator ani syndrome, and the trial gives no reason to expect benefit without that sign. The group's systematic review (PMID: 22110274) and a 2020 update (PMID: 32519087) both record biofeedback as the only treatment for this syndrome proven effective in a randomised setting. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — single trial programme, in patients with levator tenderness on examination.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single trial programme: in the one randomised trial, biofeedback gave adequate relief to 87% of patients with examination-confirmed levator ani syndrome versus 45% for electrogalvanic stimulation and 22% for massage, maintained at 12 months; patients without levator tenderness did not benefit from any treatment

title: Pancreatic enzymes in cystic fibrosis: dosing by fat intake is the convention and the regimen behind a positive trial — but it has never been tested against fixed dosing, and the Cochrane review says meal-size dose variation is an unanswered question
question: Should adults with cystic fibrosis have pancreatic enzyme doses adjusted based on fat intake?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — for the comparative question itself. Dosing pancreatic enzymes in proportion to fat eaten is how the therapy is described and how the positive placebo-controlled trials dosed it: Trapnell 2009 targeted 4,000 lipase units per gram of fat and achieved a coefficient of fat absorption of 88.6% versus 49.6% on placebo. But a fixed-dose regimen also beat placebo withdrawal in Borowitz 2011 (overall adjusted difference in fat absorption 10.6 percentage points), and the Cochrane review of 14 trials and 641 participants states plainly that there is no evidence on the relative dosages of enzymes needed or on variations based on differences in meals and meal sizes, and calls for a properly designed trial. No trial has ever randomised adults to fat-adjusted versus fixed dosing, so the adjustment strategy itself is untested even though enzyme therapy dosed that way works. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): fat-intake-based dosing is the conventional framework and the regimen used in the successful trials, but its superiority over fixed dosing has never been tested head-to-head.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — fat-intake-based enzyme dosing is the conventional framework and the regimen used in a positive placebo-controlled trial (fat absorption 88.6% vs 49.6%), but a fixed-dose regimen also beat placebo and no trial has ever compared fat-adjusted versus fixed dosing; the Cochrane review states there is no evidence on dose variations based on meals or meal sizes

title: Chewing gum after abdominal surgery (SPLIT): pooled small trials say bowel function returns about half a day sooner, but the largest trial inside enhanced-recovery care found no difference at all
question: Does chewing gum after abdominal surgery speed return of bowel function?
balance: SPLIT (small trials and their meta-analysis: benefit; the largest trial, run inside enhanced-recovery care: the treatment made no difference). The Cochrane review of 81 studies and 9,072 participants found chewing gum shortened time to first flatus by 10.4 hours, time to bowel movement by 12.7 hours and hospital stay by 0.7 days — but categorised many studies at high or unclear risk of bias. The largest single trial (Atkinson 2016, 402 patients analysed, all sites using enhanced recovery programmes) found identical median stays of 7 days in both groups and no difference in bowel function. Smaller colorectal trials split both ways (Byrne 2018: first bowel motion 40 vs 90 hours, but flatus and stay not significantly different; Hsu 2022, n = 60: flatus about 14 hours earlier). The likely reconciliation is that gum helps where baseline care leaves a long ileus, and adds little inside modern enhanced-recovery pathways. PROPOSED SPLIT (meta-analysis of mostly small trials: benefit; largest enhanced-recovery trial: no difference).
stamp: SPLIT (small trials/meta-analysis: benefit — flatus 10.4 hours and bowel movement 12.7 hours earlier across 81 trials; largest enhanced-recovery trial, n = 402: the treatment made no difference to bowel function or hospital stay)

title: Pulmonary valve replacement in repaired tetralogy of Fallot (observational only): associated with fewer deaths and ventricular tachycardia once the right ventricle is markedly dilated, with volumes normalising only if surgery precedes 160 mL/m2 — and no randomised evidence at all
question: Should adults with repaired tetralogy of Fallot undergo pulmonary valve replacement for severe pulmonary regurgitation?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only, printed on the face: no randomised trial exists, and the guideline meta-analysis found no eligible study that compared valve replacement with conservative therapy for mortality in adults. What exists is registry evidence that has strengthened with follow-up: the earlier INDICATOR analysis (977 patients, 5.3 years) found no significant association with death or sustained ventricular tachycardia (adjusted HR 0.65, 95% CI 0.31 to 1.36), while the later, larger analysis (1,143 patients, 8.3 years) found a lower risk of death or sustained ventricular tachycardia in propensity-matched patients (adjusted HR 0.41, 95% CI 0.21–0.81), concentrated in those with advanced right ventricular dilatation (end-systolic volume index over 80 mL/m2: HR 0.32) and absent at or below that threshold (HR 0.86). Volumes reliably fall after replacement and normalise only if preoperative end-diastolic volume is under 160 mL/m2 (Oosterhof 2007) — the anatomical argument for not waiting too long. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: replacement is associated with fewer deaths and sustained ventricular tachycardia, mainly once right ventricular dilatation is advanced, but every number here is non-randomised and confounding by indication runs in both directions.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: pulmonary valve replacement was associated with a lower risk of death or sustained ventricular tachycardia (adjusted HR 0.41) in a propensity-matched registry analysis, concentrated in advanced right ventricular dilatation, but no randomised or comparative mortality trial exists and an earlier analysis of the same registry was null
