title: An inhaled corticosteroid with every reliever use in asthma (LIKELY benefit): severe exacerbations fall versus reliever alone across three large trial designs, matching daily maintenance in mild asthma at a fraction of the steroid dose
question: Should adults with asthma use an inhaled corticosteroid whenever they use a short-acting bronchodilator?
balance: LIKELY (benefit). The strategy named in the question has been tested three ways, and each large trial points the same direction. In PREPARE (PARTICS), Black and Latinx adults with moderate-to-severe asthma who took beclomethasone 80 µg every time they used their reliever had a lower annualised rate of severe exacerbations than usual care (0.69 vs 0.82 per year; HR 0.85, 95% CI 0.72 to 0.999). In mild asthma, an inhaled corticosteroid carried in the reliever itself (budesonide–formoterol) halved the exacerbation rate versus albuterol alone in Novel START (0.195 vs 0.400 per year; relative rate 0.49) and was noninferior to daily maintenance budesonide in SYGMA 2 (0.11 vs 0.12 per year) at about a quarter of the steroid dose — with slightly worse day-to-day symptom scores than daily maintenance. The fixed albuterol–budesonide rescue inhaler's own exacerbation trials (MANDALA and BATURA) are homed on live shelf #1030 and are cross-pointed, not re-carded here; DENALI is carded here only for its component-contribution lung-function results. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): taking an inhaled corticosteroid with every reliever use reduces severe exacerbations versus reliever alone and matches daily maintenance for exacerbations in mild asthma.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — using an inhaled corticosteroid with every reliever use reduced severe exacerbations versus reliever alone or usual care (0.69 vs 0.82 per year, HR 0.85, in the reliever-triggered trial; 0.195 vs 0.400 per year, relative rate 0.49, for reliever-carried budesonide–formoterol) and matched daily maintenance for exacerbations in mild asthma

title: Nebuliser versus inhaler in severe COPD: not shown to be better — trials totalling 250 patients found no difference on the primary outcome, and the poor-technique patients this question is about have never been randomised
question: Is nebulized therapy better than inhaler therapy for adults with severe COPD and poor inhaler technique?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — nebulised therapy has not been shown to be better. The direct trial evidence is eight small randomised studies totalling 250 participants in COPD exacerbations (Cochrane 2016): on the primary outcome, FEV1 one hour after dosing, nebuliser and metered-dose inhaler plus spacer made no difference (the treatment made no difference), with similar serious adverse events; a secondary timing of the same measurement favoured the nebuliser by 83 mL. In stable COPD the device literature is smaller still (three studies, 61 patients). Crucially, no trial has randomised the population this question is actually about — patients whose inhaler technique is poor: the one severe-COPD hospital trial (Berry 1989, n = 20, mean FEV1 0.69 L) concluded the inhaler-plus-spacer worked 'provided patients are able to master the technique', which is precisely the condition these patients fail. The practical case for a nebuliser in a patient who cannot use an inhaler is a delivery argument, not a demonstrated outcome advantage. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): no demonstrated superiority of nebulised over inhaler therapy; the poor-technique subgroup is untested.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — nebulised therapy is not shown to be better than inhaler-plus-spacer therapy in COPD (primary outcome FEV1 at one hour: the treatment made no difference, across 8 trials and 250 participants), and no trial has enrolled the poor-inhaler-technique population this question is about

title: Lung cancer screening eligibility: 20 pack-years (not 30) at ages 50–80 is the modelling-supported line, the 15-year quit window is contested by the ACS, and risk-based selection beats pack-year rules in simulation
question: In adults at high risk for lung cancer, what pack-year and quit-time criteria best define eligibility for low-dose CT screening?
balance: The criteria question has a modelling answer, not a trial answer: the screening trials themselves used fixed entry rules (the National Lung Screening Trial's 30 pack-years and quit within 15 years — its mortality result is homed on live shelf #164 and is cross-pointed, not re-carded here). The comparative work is simulation and cohort analysis. The CISNET modelling for the USPSTF (Meza 2021) found annual strategies starting at age 50–55 with a minimum of 20 pack-years were efficient and beat the 2013 criteria (30 pack-years, ages 55–80): eligibility 20.6%–23.6% vs 14.1% of the population, lung cancer deaths averted 469–558 vs 381 per 100,000, at the cost of more false positives and overdiagnosis. The USPSTF's 2021 recommendation adopted exactly that: ages 50–80, at least 20 pack-years, quit within 15 years. The American Cancer Society's 2023 update kept 20 pack-years and ages 50–80 but dropped the quit-time limit altogether, judging years since quitting should not start or stop screening. Risk-model selection does better still on paper (Katki 2016: screening the same 9.0 million highest-risk ever-smokers was estimated to avert 20% more deaths, 55,717 vs 46,488, with a number needed to screen of 162 vs 194), and the 20 pack-year threshold specifically repairs a racial eligibility gap (Aldrich 2019). PROPOSED LIKELY (criteria as modelled): at least 20 pack-years with a quit window of 15 years (USPSTF) — with the quit-time limit itself contested by the ACS and risk-based selection estimated to outperform any pack-year rule.
stamp: LIKELY (criteria as modelled) — at least 20 pack-years and quit within 15 years, ages 50–80, is the modelling-supported eligibility rule (estimated 469–558 vs 381 deaths averted per 100,000 versus the old 30 pack-year rule); the quit-time limit is contested, with the American Cancer Society dropping it entirely, and risk-model selection estimated to outperform any pack-year rule

title: Sedating antihistamines for sleep in insomnia with depression: avoid — benefit is thin and tolerance rapid, harms are documented in older adults, and the depression population itself has never been trialled
question: Should adults with insomnia and depression avoid sedating antihistamines for sleep?
balance: POSSIBLE (harm/avoid) — with the central gap printed on the face: no carded trial has tested sedating antihistamines in adults who have insomnia AND depression. The harm/benefit case is assembled from adjacent populations. For benefit, the direct diphenhydramine trials are weak: in elderly insomniacs, 50 mg improved only the number of awakenings versus placebo (1.7 vs 2.0) while a benzodiazepine improved four sleep measures (Glass 2008); in mild insomnia, 50 mg modestly improved subjective measures and sleep efficiency over 14 days with no polysomnographic difference (Morin 2005); and the class review concludes trial results are mixed, large controlled trials are lacking, and tolerance to over-the-counter antihistamines develops rapidly (Vande Griend 2012). For harm, the sedative-hypnotic meta-analysis in older people — which explicitly excluded people with psychiatric disorders — found small sleep gains (25.2 extra minutes) against adverse cognitive events 4.78 times and daytime fatigue 3.82 times more common than placebo (Glass 2005). In a depressed population, none of this has been measured directly; the shelf's advice to avoid rests on thin benefit plus class harm signals, not on depression-specific evidence. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm): avoid as a sleep strategy — benefit is small and tolerance rapid, harms are documented in older adults, and the insomnia-with-depression population is untested.
stamp: POSSIBLE (harm) — avoid sedating antihistamines for sleep: diphenhydramine's trial benefit is small (one improved diary measure in elderly insomniacs; modest 14-day gains in mild insomnia), tolerance develops rapidly, and sedative harms are documented in older adults — and no trial has tested these drugs in adults with insomnia and depression at all

title: Mirtazapine after stroke: reasonable for post-stroke depression on single-trial and network evidence — but its sleep advantage is a 10-patient uncontrolled observation with a sleep-apnoea caution attached
question: Should mirtazapine be used for post-stroke depression in patients with poor sleep?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single small open trial programme for the depression outcome, and almost nothing for sleep itself. Niedermaier 2004 randomised 70 acute-stroke patients openly to mirtazapine 30 mg from day 1 or no antidepressant: post-stroke depression developed in 5.7% (2/35) versus 40% (14/35), and 15 of the 16 patients who did develop depression remitted once mirtazapine was started (an uncontrolled treatment phase). A network meta-analysis of 51 randomised trials ranked mirtazapine highest for response at endpoint and among the best at 8 weeks for post-stroke depression (Li 2020). But the poor-sleep half of the question rests on one 10-patient open study in non-depressed stroke patients with sleep apnoea (Brunner 2008): sleep efficiency rose from 63.1% to 75.7%, yet the respiratory disturbance index initially worsened and mirtazapine was stopped in four patients — a standing caution in a population where sleep apnoea is common. No trial has enrolled post-stroke depression patients selected for poor sleep or measured their sleep as an outcome. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for the depression, with the sleep benefit itself unproven and an apnoea caution on the face.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for post-stroke depression (one open 70-patient prevention trial: depression in 5.7% vs 40%; top response ranking in a 51-trial network meta-analysis), but the sleep benefit rests on a single uncontrolled 10-patient study that also showed worsened sleep apnoea in some patients

title: Tapering Z-drugs in older adults: stopping is achievable and often durable, but improved long-term sleep quality has never been measured — the one Z-drug trial counted discontinuation, not sleep
question: Does tapering Z-drugs improve sleep quality long term in older adults with insomnia?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — because the question's exact outcome, long-term sleep quality after tapering Z-drugs, has never been measured in a trial. What exists: one randomised trial in older adults shows Z-drugs can be stopped — patient education, with or without a pharmacist call, roughly doubled 6-month discontinuation versus usual care (56% and 55% vs 26%; adjusted odds ratios about 4.0 and 4.1, relative measures) — but it reported no sleep-quality outcome (Kuntz 2019). The long-term data come from benzodiazepine (not Z-drug) cohorts: among 47 older adults who had successfully stopped after taper-based programmes, 42.6% had resumed benzodiazepines by 24 months, with the taper-containing groups relapsing least (Morin 2005, the long-term follow-up of the supervised-taper programme homed on pack #3829, cross-pointed and not re-carded); and a secondary analysis found patients who stayed medication-free had less severe insomnia over the following six months (Belleville 2008) — an association that may run from better sleep to successful stopping rather than the reverse. A non-randomised primary-care protocol (which excluded zolpidem users) kept 85% of dose-reducers off benzodiazepines at 12 months (Fernandes 2022). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): tapering gets many older adults off Z-drugs, but whether their sleep is better long term is untested — the honest expectation from adjacent evidence is substantial relapse and no measured sleep-quality gain.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — tapering gets many older adults off Z-drugs (discontinuation 56%/55% vs 26% at 6 months in the one Z-drug trial), but no trial has measured long-term sleep quality after Z-drug tapering, and adjacent benzodiazepine follow-up shows 42.6% relapse by 24 months

title: Caffeine after midday and sleep: the timing evidence is real (45 minutes of sleep lost; coffee's modelled cutoff 8.8 hours before bed) — but a midday rule has never been trialled, and never in people with insomnia
question: For adults with insomnia, does limiting caffeine after midday improve sleep quality in a trial setting?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the direction is well supported and the specific intervention is untested. No carded trial has randomised adults with insomnia to a midday caffeine cutoff. What the trial literature shows is timing- and dose-dependent harm from caffeine near bedtime: 400 mg of caffeine disrupted sleep versus placebo even when taken 6 hours before bed (Drake 2013); and a meta-analysis of 24 studies found caffeine cut total sleep time by 45 minutes and sleep efficiency by 7%, and calculated that a standard coffee (107 mg caffeine) should be finished at least 8.8 hours before bedtime and a high-dose pre-workout drink (217.5 mg) at least 13.2 hours before (Gardiner 2023). A midday cutoff for a typical late-evening bedtime lands between those two lines — about 10–11 hours before bed — so it covers ordinary coffee on the meta-analysis's arithmetic but not high-dose products. The systematic review evidence (Clark 2017) adds that dose- and timing-response relationships are established, that older adults' sleep may be more sensitive, and that most studies were in young healthy men — not in people with insomnia. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): limiting caffeine after midday is consistent with the trial evidence on caffeine timing, but the cutoff itself, in insomnia patients, has never been trialled.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — caffeine taken even 6 hours before bed significantly disrupted sleep in a randomised timing study, and a 24-study meta-analysis put the latest safe time for a standard coffee at 8.8 hours before bed (13.2 hours for high-dose products), but a midday cutoff itself has never been trialled and no carded study enrolled adults with insomnia

title: Apixaban versus rivaroxaban in atrial fibrillation (observational only): apixaban was associated with less gastrointestinal and major bleeding — gastrointestinal bleeding hazard ratio 0.72 in a 527,226-patient multinational cohort — with no substantial difference in stroke prevention
question: Is apixaban safer than rivaroxaban for stroke prevention in AF?
balance: No randomised trial has ever compared apixaban with rivaroxaban head to head, so every card on this shelf is observational and the stamp is capped accordingly. The largest comparison (Lau 2022, PMID: 36315950; 527,226 new users across five databases in France, Germany, the United Kingdom and the United States) found apixaban associated with a lower risk of gastrointestinal bleeding than rivaroxaban (HR 0.72, 95% CI 0.66 to 0.79), consistently at standard dose, at reduced dose and in chronic kidney disease, and no substantial differences for ischaemic stroke or systemic embolism, intracranial haemorrhage or mortality. A meta-analysis of the ten real-world head-to-head studies (Mamas 2022, PMID: 34949473) points the same way and slightly further: stroke or systemic embolism HR 0.88 (0.81 to 0.95), major bleeding HR 0.62 (0.56 to 0.69) and gastrointestinal bleeding HR 0.57 (0.50 to 0.64), all relative measures favouring apixaban. In the highest-risk subgroup carded, US patients with atrial fibrillation and stage 4/5 chronic kidney disease (Fu 2024, PMID: 37839687), rivaroxaban was again associated with more major bleeding than apixaban (HR 1.69, 1.33 to 2.15) while the ischaemic-stroke comparison was imprecise (HR 0.71, 0.40 to 1.24). The direction is consistent everywhere it has been looked for — less bleeding on apixaban — but residual confounding in claims and registry data can manufacture exactly this pattern, which is why the stamp stays at POSSIBLE and carries its observational-only label on the face. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: apixaban appears safer than rivaroxaban on bleeding, with no consistent difference in stroke prevention.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: across large routine-practice cohorts apixaban was consistently associated with less major and gastrointestinal bleeding than rivaroxaban, with no consistent difference in stroke or systemic embolism prevention; no head-to-head randomised trial exists

title: Dual antiplatelet therapy after minor stroke with carotid stenosis: embolic signals fell by about 40% in relative terms in two small trials, but a reduction in clinical stroke itself has never been demonstrated in this group
question: Does dual antiplatelet therapy reduce stroke after minor stroke with carotid stenosis?
balance: The direct evidence is two small randomised trials that measured a surrogate — microembolic signals on transcranial Doppler — rather than stroke. In CARESS (PMID: 15851601), patients with recently symptomatic carotid stenosis of 50% or more who had embolic signals were randomised (107 patients) to clopidogrel plus aspirin or aspirin alone: by day 7, 43.8% of dual-therapy patients remained signal-positive versus 72.7% on monotherapy (relative risk reduction 39.8%), and the treatment-emergent clinical events ran the same way (no strokes and 4 TIAs on dual therapy versus 4 strokes and 7 TIAs on aspirin alone) in numbers far too small to settle the clinical question. CLAIR (PMID: 20335070) found the same surrogate effect (day-2 signal-positive 14 of 45 versus 27 of 50; relative risk reduction 42.4%) but its population was predominantly intracranial stenosis — 93 of 100 patients — so its carotid read-across is indirect and is printed as such on its card. The only analysis inside a large clinical-outcome trial, the CHANCE-2 post hoc (PMID: 39773886), included just 197 patients with symptomatic carotid stenosis and compared two dual regimens (aspirin–ticagrelor 12.15% stroke recurrence versus aspirin–clopidogrel 12.22%; adjusted HR 1.04), so it says nothing about dual versus single therapy. The large minor-stroke dual-therapy trials were not carotid-specific, and guideline practice for symptomatic carotid stenosis remains revascularisation plus single antiplatelet therapy. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): the embolisation biology responds to dual therapy; whether that converts into fewer strokes after minor stroke with carotid stenosis is unproven.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — dual antiplatelet therapy clearly reduced microembolic signals in two small randomised trials in symptomatic large-artery stenosis, but no trial has been powered to show it reduces clinical stroke after minor stroke with carotid stenosis, and the one carotid subgroup analysis compares two dual regimens rather than dual versus single therapy

title: Starting anticoagulation at day 4 versus day 14 after a moderate AF stroke: the earliest start was favoured in the one trial that randomised the exact days, and pooled data show fewer early recurrences with starts within 4 days — with no extra intracranial bleeding
question: Should a patient with atrial fibrillation start anticoagulation 4 days versus 14 days after a moderate ischemic stroke?
balance: This shelf is the narrow, day-specific cut of the general early-versus-late timing question, whose home is shelf #1612 (the ELAN, TIMING and OPTIMAS trials are carded there and are not re-carded here). What is carded here is the evidence that speaks to the exact days in the question. The START trial (Warach 2025, PMID: 40163159) randomised 200 patients with mild-to-moderate atrial-fibrillation stroke (median NIHSS 6.5) to start a direct oral anticoagulant on day 3–4, day 6, day 10 or day 14: ischaemic events numbered 0, 3, 2 and 2 across those groups and haemorrhagic events 1, 1, 1 and 0, and the response-adaptive design gave the day 3–4 start the highest posterior probability (0.41) of being optimal and the day-14 start the lowest (0.15) — suggestive, not decisive, at this size. The CATALYST individual-participant meta-analysis (Dehbi 2025, PMID: 40570866) pooled the four randomised timing trials (5,441 participants, including START) on exactly this shelf's cut — start within 4 days versus day 5 or later — and found the 30-day composite of recurrent ischaemic stroke, symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage or unclassified stroke in 2.1% of early starters versus 3.0% of later starters (OR 0.70, 95% CI 0.50 to 0.98), driven by fewer recurrent ischaemic strokes (1.7% versus 2.6%; OR 0.66) with symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage identical at 0.4% in both groups. Real-world practice is less tidy: in the Berlin Atrial Fibrillation Registry (Olma 2024, PMID: 39299734), severity-rule-based timing was followed in only 39.2% of patients and adherence to the rule was not associated with the 3-month composite outcome (the treatment made no difference in that observational comparison). FLAG for the developer: this pack is built under the wave 7–8 precedent for a genuinely narrower question on free reports, with #1612 cross-pointed rather than re-carded; CATALYST pools the #1612 trials, so if the developer prefers, this shelf can be folded into #1612 as an update instead of standing alone. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): for a moderate AF stroke, starting by day 4 rather than waiting to day 14 is the better-supported choice on the carded evidence.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — starting by day 4 rather than waiting to day 14: a small dedicated randomised trial in mild-to-moderate stroke favoured the earliest start, and a pooled analysis of 5,441 randomised patients found fewer 30-day recurrences with starts within 4 days and no increase in symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage; no trial isolates exactly day 4 versus day 14 within moderate stroke alone

title: Carotid endarterectomy within 14 days of symptoms: yes for stable patients — the pooled trials give a number needed to treat of 5 when surgery follows within 2 weeks, versus 125 when it waits beyond 12 weeks
question: Should carotid endarterectomy be done within 14 days of a symptomatic carotid stenosis stroke?
balance: The benefit of endarterectomy for symptomatic stenosis decays with delay, and the decay is steep. The pooled analysis of the two founding randomised trials (Rothwell 2004, PMID: 15043958; 5,893 patients from the European Carotid Surgery Trial and the North American Symptomatic Carotid Endarterectomy Trial, 33,000 patient-years) found that time from the last symptomatic event to randomisation modified the effectiveness of surgery (p = 0.009): for stenosis of 50% or more, the number needed to treat to prevent one ipsilateral stroke in 5 years was 5 for patients randomised within 2 weeks, versus 125 for those randomised after more than 12 weeks — most of the operation's value is spent by waiting. The safety half of the question is answered by the timing-and-risk systematic review (Rerkasem 2009, PMID: 19661467): across 47 operative series, neurologically stable patients with recent transient ischaemic attack or nondisabling stroke faced no significant difference in operative stroke and death between surgery within 1 week versus later (OR 1.2, 0.9 to 1.7) or within 2 weeks versus later (OR 1.2, 0.9 to 1.6) — while genuinely unstable presentations were dangerous whenever operated (stroke-in-evolution 20.2%, crescendo transient ischaemic attack 11.4%). The pooled individual-patient analysis of the four endarterectomy-versus-stenting trials (Rantner 2017, PMID: 28455318; 4,138 patients) adds that within the first week the endarterectomy arm's 30-day stroke-or-death risk was 1.3% — low in absolute terms, and far below early stenting (8.3%). Two independent pooled analyses of randomised data plus a concordant risk review support LIKELY. The carve-outs are on the cards: unstable neurology, and the pooled trials' era (medical therapy has improved since, which shrinks absolute benefit at every delay without changing the direction of the timing effect). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): do the endarterectomy within 14 days in a neurologically stable patient with symptomatic stenosis.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — carotid endarterectomy within 14 days of the symptomatic event: in the pooled randomised trials the benefit of surgery was greatest in patients randomised within 2 weeks (number needed to treat 5, versus 125 after more than 12 weeks), and in neurologically stable patients early surgery carried no higher operative risk than later surgery

title: Intensive blood pressure lowering after stroke (target below 120 versus below 140): the dedicated trial pointed the right way without proving it (HR 0.73, CI crossing 1) — the pooled trials show a 22% relative reduction in recurrent stroke
question: Does intensive blood pressure lowering to below 120 mm Hg systolic reduce recurrent stroke compared with a target below 140?
balance: Only one randomised trial has tested the exact targets in the question in patients with prior stroke. RESPECT (Kitagawa 2019, PMID: 31355878) randomised 1,280 Japanese patients with stroke in the previous 3 years to below 120/80 or below 140/90 mm Hg; the trial was stopped early, achieved mean systolic pressures were 126.7 versus 133.2 mm Hg (a separation of only about 6.5 mm Hg — the intensive arm never averaged below 120), and recurrent stroke gave HR 0.73 (95% CI 0.49 to 1.11; P = .15) — directionally favourable, not significant. The same paper's updated meta-analysis, pooling RESPECT with three previous relevant trials, found intensive control did reduce recurrent stroke: relative risk 0.78 (0.64 to 0.96), absolute risk difference −1.5 percentage points, number needed to treat 67. RESPECT's post hoc analysis in patients whose index event was ischaemic stroke (Kitagawa 2022, PMID: 35241817) localises the benefit: annual recurrence was 1.74% versus 2.17% overall (P = 0.351), ischaemic recurrence was identical (1.74% versus 1.75%), and haemorrhagic recurrence fell to 0.00% versus 0.39% per year (P = 0.005) — the gain, where it appeared, was in preventing brain haemorrhage, not ischaemic recurrence. The achievability caveat is carded directly: PAST-BP (Mant 2016, PMID: 26919870) showed that even a milder intensive target (below 130 versus below 140) produced only a 2.9 mm Hg extra systolic reduction in primary care. The related lacunar-stroke blood-pressure trial (SPS3, targets below 130 versus 130–149) asks a different target question and is homed on shelf #2842; it is cross-pointed here, not re-carded. One underpowered stopped-early trial plus its own supportive meta-analysis caps this shelf at POSSIBLE. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): aiming below 120 probably reduces recurrent stroke modestly, chiefly haemorrhagic recurrence, but the exact-target trial has not proven it on its own.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — intensive lowering toward below 120 mm Hg systolic: the one dedicated trial was stopped early and its own result was not significant (HR 0.73, 95% CI 0.49 to 1.11), but pooled with three earlier trials intensive control reduced recurrent stroke (relative risk 0.78, absolute difference 1.5 percentage points, number needed to treat 67); achieved pressures in the trials fell well short of the below-120 target

title: Baclofen versus tizanidine after stroke: no evidence baclofen is better — the only direct comparisons (270 patients, mixed multiple sclerosis and cerebrovascular lesions) found the two drugs equally effective on muscle tone
question: Does oral baclofen help post-stroke spasticity better than tizanidine?
balance: There is no randomised trial of oral baclofen against tizanidine in post-stroke spasticity alone — that absence is the finding of this shelf, and the stamp is MAYBE (weak evidence) because of it. The only head-to-head synthesis (Groves 1998, PMID: 10186943) pooled individual patient data from ten double-blind comparative trials (270 patients) of tizanidine against baclofen (seven trials) or diazepam (three trials) in patients with multiple sclerosis or cerebrovascular lesions: on total and lower-body Ashworth scores the drugs reduced spasticity similarly, muscle strength was affected less by tizanidine, and investigators judged tizanidine better tolerated. Nothing in that record separates the cerebrovascular patients' results, so it cannot be quoted as a post-stroke result — it is printed that way on the card. The systematic review of oral antispastics in nonprogressive neurologic disease (Montané 2004, PMID: 15505149) is blunter about the whole field: twelve trials, 469 patients, only two direct drug-versus-drug comparisons, small and short trials of inadequate methodologic quality, evidence 'weak', efficacy 'marginal if any', and adverse effects (drowsiness, sedation, muscle weakness) common. The post-stroke-specific review (Olvey 2010, PMID: 21353101) confirms the gap from the other side: of 54 studies of upper-limb spasticity after stroke, 51 concerned botulinum toxin; the oral-drug record is a single tizanidine study and two intrathecal baclofen studies, with no oral head-to-head trial identified. A randomised trial of early baclofen after stroke (the Baclotox study, botulinum toxin versus oral baclofen) is in progress as a protocol, but it does not compare baclofen with tizanidine either. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): on current evidence baclofen is not shown to help post-stroke spasticity better than tizanidine; the two look equivalent where they have been compared at all, in mixed populations.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — oral baclofen versus tizanidine for post-stroke spasticity: the only head-to-head data pool multiple sclerosis with cerebrovascular lesions and show similar tone reduction with either drug; no trial has compared the two drugs in post-stroke spasticity alone, and systematic reviewers rate the whole oral-antispastic evidence base as weak

title: rTMS for post-stroke aphasia: small randomised trials consistently favour stimulation — naming most reliably — but protocols vary and no large multicentre trial exists
question: Does repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation improve post-stroke aphasia recovery?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). The direction of the randomised evidence is consistently favourable: a 47-trial meta-analysis (2,190 patients) reports improvement in repetition, naming and spontaneous language (no pooled effect sizes in its record, printed plainly), a 4-trial meta-analysis finds a naming benefit (standardised mean difference 0.51) with no significant difference for repetition or comprehension, and one small sham-controlled trial of personalised theta-burst stimulation shows aphasia-quotient gains of about 13–15 points over sham. The stamp is capped at POSSIBLE because the individual trials are small, protocols and targets vary widely, and no large multicentre sham-controlled trial anchors the field. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): rTMS improves some language outcomes after stroke, most consistently naming, as an adjunct to speech-language therapy.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — rTMS improved naming and other language measures across small randomised trials (47-trial meta-analysis, 2,190 patients, no pooled effect size in its record; one sham-controlled trial, N = 44, aphasia-quotient gain ~13–15 points over sham); protocols vary and no large multicentre trial exists

title: Rivastigmine patch vs capsules: about two-thirds less nausea (7.2% vs 23.1%) and vomiting (6.2% vs 17.0%) at equal efficacy in the 1,195-patient IDEAL trial
question: Does rivastigmine patch cause fewer gastrointestinal side effects than oral rivastigmine in Alzheimer's disease?
balance: LIKELY (benefit — fewer gastrointestinal side effects). One definitive large randomised trial answers this question directly: in IDEAL (N = 1,195), the 9.5 mg/24 h patch matched the efficacy of 6 mg twice-daily capsules while nausea fell from 23.1% to 7.2% and vomiting from 17.0% to 6.2%, rates statistically indistinguishable from placebo. A post hoc analysis of the same programme confirms no loss of functional benefit, and the pharmacologic rationale (lower peak plasma levels with transdermal delivery) is coherent. The stamp is LIKELY rather than higher because the evidence is a single trial programme and the advantage belongs to the 9.5 mg/24 h dose — the 17.4 mg/24 h patch tolerates like capsules. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): the rivastigmine patch causes substantially fewer gastrointestinal side effects than oral rivastigmine at the standard dose.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit — fewer gastrointestinal side effects) — in the IDEAL randomised trial (N = 1,195) the 9.5 mg/24 h patch caused nausea in 7.2% vs 23.1% on capsules and vomiting in 6.2% vs 17.0%, at similar efficacy; single trial programme, standard dose only

title: Lecanemab and ApoE4: brain swelling (ARIA-E) in 34.5% of ε4 homozygotes vs 16.8% of carriers overall in trial safety data — risk rises steeply with ε4 copies
question: What is the risk of brain swelling or bleeding with lecanemab in patients who carry ApoE4?
balance: LIKELY (risk, graded by ApoE ε4 copy number) — evidence types labelled on the face: randomised-trial safety data plus real-world observational cohorts. In the Clarity AD safety update, ARIA-E (brain swelling) occurred in 34.5% of ApoE ε4 homozygotes and 16.8% of ε4 carriers overall, with ARIA-E in 13.6% and ARIA-H microhaemorrhages in 16.0% of all lecanemab-treated participants; a US real-world cohort found any ARIA in 44% of homozygotes (4 of 9, small denominator) versus 17% of heterozygotes. Most ARIA is asymptomatic and MRI-detected, but fatal intracerebral haemorrhage has occurred, including alongside thrombolysis and anticoagulation. The Clarity AD primary efficacy record is homed on live shelf #333 (anti-amyloid benefit and risk); this shelf answers the narrower ApoE4-stratified risk question from the programme's safety report and two independent cohorts, and does not re-card the homed record. PROPOSED LIKELY (risk): carrying two ApoE ε4 copies roughly triples the ARIA-E risk seen in carriers overall, and about one in three homozygotes develops brain swelling on lecanemab.
stamp: LIKELY (risk — trial safety data + observational cohorts, labelled on the face) — ARIA-E in 34.5% of ApoE ε4 homozygotes vs 16.8% of ε4 carriers overall on lecanemab (Clarity AD safety data); ARIA-H microhaemorrhages in 16.0% of all treated; real-world ARIA in 44% of homozygotes (4/9) vs 17% of heterozygotes

title: Agonist vs levodopa in early Parkinson's: fewer dyskinesias (odds ratio 0.51) but NOT equal motor efficacy — levodopa relieves symptoms better and agonists cause more dropouts
question: Is a dopamine agonist as effective as levodopa for motor symptoms in early Parkinson's disease with fewer dyskinesias?
balance: SPLIT (fewer dyskinesias: benefit; symptom control and tolerability: harm). The dyskinesia half of the question is answered yes: pooled across 29 trials, agonists halve the odds of dyskinesia versus levodopa (odds ratio 0.51), and a 5-year trial shows absolute dyskinesia rates of 9.5% versus 21.2%. The efficacy half is answered no: in both long head-to-head trials, levodopa gave significantly greater motor improvement, and the meta-analysis concludes symptom control is poorer with agonists, alongside more oedema, somnolence, hallucinations and a more-than-doubled odds of stopping for adverse events (odds ratio 2.49). PROPOSED SPLIT: an agonist-first strategy trades better long-term motor-complication rates for weaker symptom control and worse non-motor tolerability.
stamp: SPLIT (fewer dyskinesias: benefit — pooled odds ratio 0.51 vs levodopa, 29 trials, 5,247 participants; symptom control and tolerability: harm — levodopa gave significantly better motor relief in both long trials, and agonists doubled discontinuations for adverse events, odds ratio 2.49)

title: Extended-release levodopa cuts off time by ~1.2 extra hours/day vs immediate-release (23.8% vs 29.8% of waking hours) in phase 3 trials
question: Does extended-release levodopa reduce off time compared with immediate-release levodopa in advanced Parkinson's disease?
balance: LIKELY (benefit). Two concordant phase 3 randomised trials of the extended-release carbidopa-levodopa formulation show less off time than immediate-release treatment: in the direct head-to-head trial, off time was 23.82% versus 29.79% of waking hours, an extra 1.17 hours/day removed (Hauser 2013, N = 393), and against immediate-release plus entacapone the figures were 3.8 versus 5.2 hours/day (Stocchi 2014, N = 91), without increased troublesome dyskinesia. The honest caveat, printed on the cards, is that conversion raised the total levodopa dose, so the benefit belongs to the formulation as dosed in its trials. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): extended-release levodopa reduces off time compared with immediate-release levodopa in advanced Parkinson's disease.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — extended-release carbidopa-levodopa reduced off time vs immediate-release (23.8% vs 29.8% of waking hours; extra -1.17 h/day) in a phase 3 RCT (N = 393), with a concordant phase 3 win vs immediate-release plus entacapone (3.8 vs 5.2 h/day, N = 91); conversion raised total levodopa dose

title: Brand-to-generic antiseizure switch: associated with more breakthrough seizures in observational data (odds ratio 1.85) — no randomised evidence, pharmacokinetics unchanged on average
question: Does switching from brand to generic antiseizure medication increase breakthrough seizures?
balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — observational only, printed on the face. No randomised trial answers this question. The largest dataset (3,530 German patients) associates a manufacturer switch with breakthrough seizures (brand-to-generic odds ratio 1.85, a relative measure, with switch rates of 5.5% versus 2.4%), a solicited case series documents 50 breakthrough events after switching with lower drug levels in 21 of 26 paired cases, and a 67-study systematic review finds average pharmacokinetics unchanged but clinical reports inconsistent in both directions. The stamp is capped at POSSIBLE by the evidence type, and the prudent clinical reading — avoid manufacturer switches in seizure-free patients — is the cohort authors' own conclusion. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm) — observational only.
stamp: POSSIBLE (harm) — observational only: manufacturer switching was associated with breakthrough seizures in a nationwide cohort (brand-to-generic odds ratio 1.85, relative; switch rates 5.5% vs 2.4%), with case evidence of lower drug levels after switching; pharmacokinetic studies show no average difference and clinical reports conflict

title: Early high-efficacy vs escalation in MS: observational cohorts consistently favour starting high (0.6–0.9 fewer EDSS points at 5–10 years) — randomised proof still pending
question: Does early high-efficacy disease-modifying therapy improve long-term disability in relapsing multiple sclerosis compared with escalation therapy?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only, printed on the face. Three large observational comparisons agree: a population-based cohort found a 5-year EDSS rise of 0.3 with early intensive treatment versus 1.2 with escalation (adjusted difference -0.85), and two propensity-matched Italian registry analyses found the disability gap widening over a decade (0.30 EDSS points at 5 years, 0.63–0.67 at 10 years, with escalation carrying a hazard ratio of 1.36 for confirmed disability accrual, a relative measure). The stamp is capped at POSSIBLE because no randomised strategy trial has reported; confounding by indication is the standing caveat, and it conventionally biases against the early-intensive group. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: early high-efficacy therapy is associated with less long-term disability than escalation.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: early high-efficacy therapy was associated with less disability accrual than escalation in three large cohorts (5-year EDSS change 0.3 vs 1.2; 10-year gap 0.63–0.67 EDSS points; escalation hazard ratio 1.36 for confirmed accrual, relative); no randomised strategy trial has reported

title: Vitamin D for MS relapses: pooled trials show no reduction in relapse rate (rate difference -0.05, CI spans zero) — supplementation does not prevent relapses
question: Should vitamin D supplementation reduce relapse rate in multiple sclerosis?
balance: POSSIBLE (no benefit shown) — the treatment made no difference in the randomised evidence. The Cochrane review of 12 trials (933 participants) finds no effect on the annualised relapse rate at 52 weeks (rate difference -0.05, 95% CI -0.17 to 0.07, very low-quality evidence); a dose-ranging trial after clinically isolated syndrome found no delay in conversion at 1,000, 5,000 or 10,000 IU daily; and in a SOLAR substudy a verified rise in blood vitamin D to 281 nmol/L (about 112 ng/mL) left the nerve-injury marker neurofilament light chain unchanged. The SOLAR primary report is homed on pack #2364, which covers vitamin D in clinically isolated syndrome and early relapsing disease; this shelf answers the relapse-rate question in established multiple sclerosis from the pooled review and the free reports, cross-pointing #2364 rather than re-carding it. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (no benefit shown): vitamin D supplementation should not be expected to reduce the relapse rate in multiple sclerosis.
stamp: POSSIBLE (no benefit shown) — pooled randomised trials found no reduction in annualised relapse rate (rate difference -0.05, 95% CI -0.17 to 0.07; 12 trials, 933 participants; the treatment made no difference), a dose-ranging early-disease trial was null at all doses, and blood levels rose without moving a nerve-injury biomarker

title: Exercise for MS fatigue: yes — pooled randomised evidence shows a clear reduction (standardised mean difference -0.53), with combined and resistance programmes best
question: Does a structured exercise program reduce fatigue in multiple sclerosis?
balance: LIKELY (benefit). Two independent syntheses of randomised trials agree: the Cochrane review (45 trials, 2,250 participants) finds fatigue reduced versus no exercise (standardised mean difference -0.53, 95% CI -0.73 to -0.33), and a 58-study network meta-analysis ranks combined exercise and resistance training highest. A randomised trial enrolling only fatigued patients confirms a clinically relevant effect size (about 10 fatigue-scale points over 12 weeks of resistance training). The standing caveat is that fatigue is self-reported and exercise cannot be blinded. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): a structured exercise programme reduces fatigue in multiple sclerosis.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — exercise reduced fatigue vs no exercise across 45 randomised trials (2,250 participants; standardised mean difference -0.53, 95% CI -0.73 to -0.33), a 58-study network analysis ranked combined and resistance training best, and a trial in fatigued patients showed ~10-point fatigue-score gains

title: Plasma exchange for steroid-refractory MS relapses: yes, it helps — 42.1% vs 5.9% on sham in the randomised trial, best when given early
question: Does plasma exchange help severe relapses in multiple sclerosis that do not respond to steroids?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). The one randomised test is positive and large in relative terms: in severe demyelinating attacks that had failed intravenous steroids, moderate-or-better improvement occurred in 42.1% of plasma-exchange courses versus 5.9% on sham (Weinshenker 1999). Two observational cohorts in steroid-refractory disease point the same way (59% of 153 patients improving moderately to markedly; 78.8% of 118 multiple sclerosis patients improving markedly or mildly, with earlier treatment responding better). The stamp is capped at POSSIBLE because the randomised trial is single, small, counts courses rather than patients, and mixes multiple sclerosis with related demyelinating diseases. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): plasma exchange helps severe multiple sclerosis relapses that do not respond to steroids.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — plasma exchange beat sham (42.1% vs 5.9% of courses with moderate-or-better improvement) in the single small randomised trial of steroid-refractory attacks, with 59–79% improving in two observational cohorts (N = 153 and 118); earlier treatment responded better

title: IV immunoglobulin for multifocal motor neuropathy: improves strength — 78% versus 4% improved in the pooled crossover trials, with consistent results in both small placebo-controlled trials
question: Does IV immunoglobulin improve strength in multifocal motor neuropathy?
balance: LIKELY (benefit). Two small double-blind, placebo-controlled trials agree that intravenous immunoglobulin improves strength and function in multifocal motor neuropathy: in a 16-patient crossover trial the neurologic disability score improved by 6.7 points on IVIg while falling 2.1 points on placebo, and grip strength rose 6.4 kg on the weaker side versus a 1.0 kg fall on placebo; in a 19-patient trial, seven of nine patients given IVIg first were responders at month 4 versus two of nine given placebo first (P = 0.03). The 2022 Cochrane review of six crossover randomised trials (90 participants in total) found strength improved in 21 of 27 (78%) IVIg-naive participants on IVIg versus 1 of 27 (4%) on placebo (relative risk 11.00, 95% CI 2.86 to 42.25; low-certainty evidence), while the disability result was weaker (39% versus 11%; relative risk 3.00, 95% CI 0.89 to 10.12). The trials are individually tiny and mostly crossover, so the size of the effect is imprecise even though its direction is consistent. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): IV immunoglobulin improves strength in multifocal motor neuropathy.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit): IV immunoglobulin improves strength and function in multifocal motor neuropathy — two small placebo-controlled trials agree (disability score +6.7 vs −2.1 points; responders 7/9 vs 2/9), and the Cochrane synthesis of six crossover trials (90 participants) found strength improved in 78% on IVIg versus 4% on placebo (relative risk 11.00, low-certainty evidence)

title: Erenumab in chronic migraine after preventive failure: about 2.5–4.3 fewer migraine days than placebo in the failed-treatment subgroups of the one chronic-migraine trial
question: Does erenumab reduce monthly migraine days in chronic migraine after failure of other preventives?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single trial programme, capped at POSSIBLE. All three cards report one randomised trial (NCT02066415; 667 patients with chronic migraine): erenumab 70 mg and 140 mg each reduced monthly migraine days by 6.6 days versus 4.2 days on placebo (difference −2.5 days, 95% CI −3.5 to −1.4). The card that answers this shelf's question directly is the prespecified-style subgroup analysis of patients who had previously failed preventives: among those with at least one prior failed medication category, the advantage over placebo at month 3 was −2.5 days (70 mg) and −3.3 days (140 mg), and among those with at least two failed categories it was −2.7 and −4.3 days — if anything larger than in patients who had never failed (−2.2 and −0.5 days). Patient-reported outcomes (headache impact, disability, quality of life) improved in parallel. There is no second, independent trial in prior-failure chronic migraine in the records fetched, so the programme cap applies. The episodic-migraine erenumab trial (Goadsby 2017) is homed on its own live shelf and is not re-carded here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): erenumab reduces monthly migraine days in chronic migraine, including after failure of other preventives.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single trial programme: erenumab reduced monthly migraine days by 2.5 days more than placebo in chronic migraine (667 patients), and in the subgroup with at least one prior preventive failure the advantage was −2.5 days (70 mg) and −3.3 days (140 mg), rising to −4.3 days at 140 mg after at least two failures

title: Continuing a CGRP antibody after a <30% response at 3 months: one in five early non-responders respond by month 6, and no validated stopping rule exists (observational only)
question: Should a CGRP monoclonal antibody be continued after 3 months if migraine days fall by less than 30 percent?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit of continuing) — observational only, printed on the face. No randomised trial in the records fetched tests a 30%-at-3-months stopping rule. The one directly relevant dataset is a real-life erenumab study of 100 highly refractory patients with daily diaries over 6 months: 20% of patients who had NOT reached a 30% average reduction in monthly migraine days over the first 3 months went on to reach at least 30% in the last 3 months, and almost 90% of early responders sustained their response; its authors propose continuing treatment for at least 6 months before judging response. The two guideline records carded — the American Headache Society consensus statement (2021) and the European Headache Federation guideline update (2022) — recommend these antibodies and address long-term management, but neither abstract prints a numeric 30% stopping threshold, and the EHF states that for several clinical questions the evidence was insufficient and guidance rested on expert opinion. A hard stop at 3 months for a <30% response would therefore abandon roughly one in five patients who would have responded by month 6, on the basis of a threshold no carded trial has validated. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: continue to about 6 months before deciding, rather than stopping at 3 months solely for a <30% reduction.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit of continuing) — observational only: in the one real-life cohort, 20% of patients below a 30% response at 3 months reached at least 30% by months 4–6, and no carded guideline validates a 30%-at-3-months stopping rule — continue to about 6 months before deciding

title: Gabapentin plus nortriptyline for neuropathic pain: better than either drug alone by 0.6–0.9 points in the one direct crossover trial
question: Does combining gabapentin with nortriptyline work better than either drug alone for neuropathic pain?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). One double-blind crossover trial answers the question directly: in 47 analysed patients with diabetic polyneuropathy or postherpetic neuralgia, mean daily pain at maximum tolerated dose was 2.3 on the gabapentin–nortriptyline combination versus 3.2 on gabapentin alone and 2.9 on nortriptyline alone (combination lower by 0.9 points versus gabapentin, P = 0.001, and by 0.6 points versus nortriptyline, P = 0.02, on a 0–10 scale). The Cochrane review of combination pharmacotherapy found this was the only trial of this specific pairing (56 participants) among 21 combination studies, and — while several combinations beat their single agents — declined to recommend any one specific combination because trials were few, small and short. A second Gilron crossover trial of a different pairing (gabapentin plus morphine) found the same pattern — combination pain 3.06 versus 4.15 (gabapentin) and 3.70 (morphine) — supporting the combination principle without adding a second trial of this pairing. Dry mouth was the commonest adverse event on nortriptyline-containing treatment. A single direct trial caps the stamp. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the combination works better than either drug alone, by about 0.6–0.9 points on a 0–10 pain scale.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single direct trial: gabapentin plus nortriptyline reduced pain to 2.3/10 versus 3.2 on gabapentin alone and 2.9 on nortriptyline alone at maximum tolerated dose (differences −0.9 and −0.6 points), with the Cochrane combination review confirming this pairing rests on that one 56-patient trial

title: Tapentadol versus oxycodone for low back pain with a neuropathic component: SPLIT — the trial (against oxycodone/naloxone) favours tapentadol, routine-practice data favour the oxycodone combination
question: Does tapentadol work better than oxycodone for chronic low back pain with a neuropathic component?
balance: SPLIT. First, a correction the shelf must carry: every head-to-head record fetched compares tapentadol prolonged release with oxycodone/naloxone prolonged release — a fixed oxycodone combination product — not with oxycodone alone, and no carded record tests tapentadol against plain oxycodone in this condition. In the one randomised trial (open-label, phase 3b/4, in opioid-naive patients with severe chronic low back pain and a neuropathic component), tapentadol was noninferior on pain change and, in confirmatory analysis, superior (97.5% repeated confidence interval for the difference −1.820 to −0.184; P = 0.003 for superiority), with significantly better neuropathic-symptom scores and gastrointestinal tolerability, and lower constipation and vomiting in its companion tolerability report. Against that, a blinded end-point analysis of German Pain Registry routine data (128 patients started on oxycodone/naloxone, 133 on tapentadol) found the composite benefit–risk end point significantly favoured oxycodone/naloxone (39.8% versus 25.6%; odds ratio 1.93, a relative measure; P = 0.014), driven by superior analgesic response rates at stricter thresholds. A sponsored open-label trial says tapentadol is better; routine-practice data say the oxycodone combination is at least as good. PROPOSED SPLIT (randomised trial: tapentadol benefit; routine-data analysis: oxycodone/naloxone benefit) — and the comparison actually tested is against oxycodone/naloxone, not oxycodone alone.
stamp: SPLIT (randomised open-label trial: tapentadol benefit; routine-practice registry analysis: oxycodone/naloxone benefit) — and the tested comparator throughout is oxycodone/naloxone, not oxycodone alone, for which no head-to-head record was found

title: Amitriptyline 10 mg at night in older adults: a sensible lowest-dose convention no trial has tested — and the drug's efficacy evidence is weaker than its reputation (MAYBE)
question: Should amitriptyline be started at 10 mg at night in older adults with neuropathic pain?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) for the specific practice asked about. No carded record tests a 10 mg starting dose, at night, in older adults: that exact regimen is a prudence-based convention, not a trialled strategy, and this shelf says so plainly. What the evidence does show cuts in two directions. For efficacy, the Cochrane review of amitriptyline in neuropathic pain (17 studies, 1,342 participants) found no first- or second-tier evidence at all — only third-tier, very-low-quality evidence, with amitriptyline significantly better than placebo in only two of seven studies reporting usable data — while adverse events were commoner on amitriptyline (55% versus 36%; relative risk 1.5, 95% CI 1.3 to 1.8; number needed to harm 5.2). For the drug class, the NeuPSIG meta-analysis (Finnerup 2015) gives tricyclics the most favourable number needed to treat among first-line options and a strong first-line recommendation, without printing a starting dose in its record. For older adults specifically, the geriatric spine-pain review advises the lowest therapeutic doses for all analgesics in this age group and notes serotonin–noradrenaline reuptake inhibitors have a more favourable safety profile than tricyclics. A low, cautious start in an older adult is consistent with everything carded — but the 10 mg figure itself is untested, and even the underlying efficacy of amitriptyline is weaker than its reputation. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): starting at 10 mg at night in older adults is a reasonable, harm-avoiding convention that no trial has directly tested.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence): starting amitriptyline at 10 mg at night in older adults is an untested, prudence-based convention — no carded trial tests that dose or population, geriatric reviews advise lowest therapeutic doses, and amitriptyline's own efficacy evidence is third-tier only (adverse events 55% vs 36% on placebo, relative risk 1.5)

title: Physical therapy after lumbar discectomy: SPLIT by timing — starting immediately made no difference, starting at 4–6 weeks modestly improved pain and function
question: Does early physical therapy after lumbar discectomy improve recovery compared with usual care?
balance: SPLIT — the answer divides by timing. Programmes started immediately after surgery were not more effective than their control interventions in the Cochrane review (22 trials, 2,503 participants), and the largest directly relevant randomised trial found referral for early rehabilitation (6–8 weeks of exercise therapy starting immediately after discharge) was neither more effective nor more cost-effective than no referral: no significant difference on any outcome at 26 weeks, including global perceived recovery (odds ratio 1.0, 95% CI 0.6 to 1.7, a relative measure) and functional status (mean difference 1.5, 95% CI −3.6 to 6.7). The same Cochrane review found the benefit sits later: exercise programmes starting four to six weeks after surgery beat no treatment for short-term pain (standardised mean difference −0.90, 95% CI −1.55 to −0.24; very low quality) and function (SMD −0.67, 95% CI −1.22 to −0.12; low quality), and physiotherapy from four to six weeks led to better function than no treatment or education only. A trial comparing two early exercise programmes (specific versus general trunk exercises, starting at two weeks) found no difference between them, with both groups improving. So 'early' rehabilitation in the first days adds nothing carded; rehabilitation begun at four to six weeks probably helps modestly. PROPOSED SPLIT (immediate start: the treatment made no difference; start at 4–6 weeks: benefit, low-quality evidence).
stamp: SPLIT (immediate rehabilitation: the treatment made no difference — recovery odds ratio 1.0 and no outcome differed at 26 weeks; rehabilitation starting at 4–6 weeks: benefit over no treatment for pain and function, standardised mean differences −0.90 and −0.67, low-quality evidence)

title: Opioid tapering in long-term high-dose therapy: SPLIT — pain may ease slightly but function does not improve, and tapering is associated with more overdose and mental-health crises
question: Does tapering opioids improve pain and function in patients on long-term high-dose therapy for chronic noncancer pain?
balance: SPLIT. On pain, the tapering literature leans favourable but is weak: a 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis (57 studies reviewed, 34 meta-analysed) found a beneficial overall effect of tapering (effect size 0.917, 95% CI 0.61 to 1.22) with significant improvement in pain intensity — but no statistically significant effect on physical functioning, mental-health or physical-health quality of life, or pain self-efficacy, and most included studies were poor quality (30 poor, 24 fair, 3 good). The one carded randomised trial of tapering off long-term therapy largely failed as an experiment: of 75 patients included, 40 dropped out before the tapering phase, and among the 15 tapered versus 20 controls, pain intensity stayed stable rather than improving. On harm, the largest carded dataset points the other way: in 113,618 patients on stable long-term higher-dose opioids (at least 50 morphine milligram equivalents daily), tapering was associated with 9.3 overdose events per 100 person-years versus 5.5 without tapering (adjusted incidence rate ratio 1.68, a relative measure) and 7.6 versus 3.3 mental-health-crisis events per 100 person-years (adjusted rate ratio 2.28), with risk rising with faster dose reduction — an observational association its authors flag as design-limited. So: pain may improve slightly or hold steady when doses come down, function does not demonstrably improve, and tapering as actually practised is associated with serious harms. PROPOSED SPLIT (pain: possible small benefit, low-quality evidence, function unchanged; tapering events: associated with increased overdose and mental-health crisis in observational data).
stamp: SPLIT (pain: possible small improvement after tapering in a mostly poor-quality meta-analysis, with no significant improvement in physical functioning and only stable pain in the one randomised trial; harms: tapering associated with overdose 9.3 vs 5.5 and mental-health crisis 7.6 vs 3.3 per 100 person-years in a 113,618-patient cohort)

title: Folic acid dose in pregnancy on anti-seizure medications: SPLIT — guidelines say high-dose 5 mg, but register data show no dose benefit against malformations
question: Does folic acid dose need to be higher in pregnant women taking anti-seizure medications?
balance: SPLIT — guideline practice and outcome data point in different directions. International guidelines, as documented in a 10-year maternity-hospital review, recommend high-dose folic acid (5 mg daily, at least three months before conception) for women at increased neural-tube-defect risk, and women taking anti-seizure medications are treated as that group; in that review 65.6% of 250 women with epilepsy on anti-seizure medications took high-dose 5 mg before conception. But the largest dose-specific outcome dataset carded — the Australian pregnancy register, 2,104 folic-acid-treated pregnancies — found no statistically significant effect of folic acid dosage on overall fetal malformation rates (P = 0.640 for use before and during pregnancy) or on spina bifida (P = 0.409), and its authors conclude it would be misguided to hope 5 mg/day protects against valproate- and other drug-associated malformations. Safety is not settled either: a Scandinavian register cohort found prenatal high-dose folic acid exposure (mean 4.3 mg) in children of mothers with epilepsy was associated with childhood cancer at an adjusted hazard ratio of 2.7 (a relative measure; absolute risk 1.4% versus 0.6%), and a 2015 review urged against advocating high doses until safe, optimal dosing is known, citing drug interactions and animal data. So the higher dose is what guidelines direct, but no carded study demonstrates that the higher dose prevents more malformations than standard doses. PROPOSED SPLIT (guidelines: use high-dose 5 mg periconceptionally; register outcome data: no demonstrated dose benefit, with an unresolved safety signal).
stamp: SPLIT (guidelines recommend high-dose 5 mg folic acid periconceptionally for women on anti-seizure medications; the 2,104-pregnancy register analysis found no significant effect of folic acid dose on malformation rates or spina bifida, and a register cohort links high-dose exposure to childhood cancer at adjusted hazard ratio 2.7 relative, absolute 1.4% vs 0.6%)

title: Cannabis-based medicines for chronic neuropathic pain: a small real benefit for the tested standardised preparations (30% relief NNTB 11) with frequent nervous-system harms (NNTH 3)
question: Does cannabis-based medicine reduce chronic neuropathic pain compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a small benefit, product by product, with frequent harms. Cannabis-based products are not well regulated and differ by maker, so this shelf names the specific tested preparations exactly as the publications give them, and says plainly where they do not: the Cochrane review's trials tested a plant-derived tetrahydrocannabinol/cannabidiol oromucosal spray (10 studies — the spray is the nabiximols preparation, though the Cochrane record does not print a brand name or company), the synthetic tetrahydrocannabinol mimic nabilone (2 studies), inhaled herbal cannabis (2 studies) and plant-derived tetrahydrocannabinol as dronabinol (2 studies); no carded record names a manufacturer for these products. On benefit, 50% or greater pain relief was achieved by 21% on cannabis-based medicines versus 17% on placebo (risk difference 0.05; number needed to treat for benefit 20) and 30% or greater relief by 39% versus 33% (NNTB 11), on low-to-moderate quality evidence. The nabiximols-specific meta-analysis (9 trials, 1,289 participants) found a mean pain advantage of −0.40 points on an 11-point scale — statistically firm, clinically small. Harms are not small: nervous system adverse events in 61% versus 29% (number needed to harm 3), psychiatric disorders in 17% versus 5% (NNTH 10) and withdrawal for adverse events in 10% versus 5% (NNTH 25). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): cannabis-based medicines reduce chronic neuropathic pain slightly more than placebo for a minority of patients, at the cost of frequent nervous-system and psychiatric adverse effects, and results from one preparation must not be read across to unregulated products that differ by maker.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — small effect for the named tested preparations (THC/CBD oromucosal spray including nabiximols, dronabinol, nabilone, trial-prepared herbal cannabis; no manufacturer named in the records): 30% pain relief 39% vs 33% on placebo (NNTB 11) and 50% relief 21% vs 17% (NNTB 20), against nervous system adverse events 61% vs 29% (NNTH 3)

title: Switching after SSRI nonresponse works for a minority: a second SSRI remitted 23.5% of nonresponders in pooled trials — nearly as many as switching class (28%) — and switching early beat switching later by no significant margin
question: Does switching to a different SSRI work after nonresponse to a first SSRI in major depression?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). Switching after a first SSRI fails does help a minority: in the pooled randomised evidence (Papakostas 2008, PMID: 17919460; four trials, n = 1,496), 23.5% of patients switched to a second SSRI remitted, so a within-class switch is a real treatment and not a placebo manoeuvre. Switching out of class did modestly better (28% remission; relative risk 1.29, an absolute gain of about 4.5 percentage points, NNT about 22), and response rates did not differ. The EMC trial (Tadic 2016, PMID: 26899588) adds a caution about timing: an early-switch strategy at 2 weeks (24% remission) did not significantly beat guideline-based continuation with later switch (16%; p = 0.2056 — the treatment made no difference on the primary outcome). The only uncontrolled card (Kaplan 2002, PMID: 12182262) reports implausibly high open-label rates and is carded only to be discounted. The STAR*D switch trial itself (Rush 2006, PMID: 16554525) is homed on live shelf #230 and is not re-carded here; this shelf is built on the free comparative reports above, per the one-home rule — flagged for the developer. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a second SSRI remits roughly 1 in 4 SSRI nonresponders; switching class remits slightly more, and no fetched evidence shows that switching early beats switching after an adequate trial.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — switching after SSRI nonresponse remits about 1 in 4 patients: a second SSRI remitted 23.5% versus 28% for switching class in pooled randomised trials (relative risk 1.29, NNT about 22), and an early-switch strategy did not beat guideline care (24% versus 16%, not significant)

title: Valproate in women of childbearing potential (observational only): spina bifida odds ratio 12.7, malformation risk rising with dose, and age-6 IQ 97 versus 105–108 after alternatives — avoid in bipolar disorder whenever an effective alternative exists
question: Should valproate be avoided in women of childbearing potential with bipolar disorder?
balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — observational only, printed on the face: there are no randomised trials of valproate in pregnancy, and there never will be, so the stamp is capped by design type even though the observational evidence is large, concordant and dose-dependent. Four independent data systems point the same way: a case-control analysis of 3.8 million births found six specific malformations significantly more common after first-trimester valproate monotherapy, with an adjusted odds ratio of 12.7 for spina bifida (Jentink 2010, PMID: 20558369); the EURAP registry found malformation risk rose with dose for every drug studied and was significantly higher for valproate than for low-dose lamotrigine at all doses (Tomson 2011, PMID: 21652013); the prospective NEAD study found age-6 IQ of 97 after valproate exposure versus 105–108 after the comparator drugs, again dose-dependent (Meador 2013, PMID: 23352199); and a 3.18-million-child UK–Swedish cohort found more autism, intellectual disability and ADHD diagnoses after valproate exposure, with little evidence of such associations for lamotrigine (Madley-Dowd 2024, PMID: 39548057). All carded cohorts enrolled women treated mainly for epilepsy, because that is where pregnancy exposure data exist; the exposure — valproate at comparable doses in women of the same age — is the same in bipolar disorder, and no fetched record suggests the fetal risk differs by indication. The comparative malformation analysis homed on live shelf #2676 (EURAP 2018 and the North American registry) is cross-pointed, not re-carded. None of the carded records measures the maternal relapse risk of stopping valproate in bipolar disorder, which is the other side of the decision and must be weighed separately. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm) — observational only: yes, valproate should be avoided in women of childbearing potential with bipolar disorder whenever an effective alternative exists, and where it is used, the lowest effective dose with folate and specialist review is the risk-minimising course the evidence supports.
stamp: POSSIBLE (harm) — observational only: valproate in pregnancy is consistently associated with specific malformations (spina bifida adjusted odds ratio 12.7), a dose-dependent malformation risk, and lower child IQ (97 versus 105–108) — avoid in women of childbearing potential with bipolar disorder whenever an effective alternative exists

title: Buspirone add-on for generalised anxiety disorder after SSRI nonresponse is untested: it works as GAD monotherapy (NNT 4.4) and matched bupropion as an add-on in depression — but no trial has studied the asked use
question: Is buspirone effective as add-on therapy for generalized anxiety disorder after SSRI nonresponse?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence). No fetched record reports a trial of buspirone added to an SSRI in generalised anxiety disorder (GAD) after SSRI nonresponse — the exact use in the question is untested in the carded evidence, and the shelf says so on its face. What exists is indirect: as monotherapy, azapirones including buspirone beat placebo in GAD across 36 trials and 5,908 participants, with a number needed to treat of 4.4 on global impression (Chessick 2006, PMID: 16856115), and the 89-trial network meta-analysis also found buspirone efficacious versus placebo while warning its estimate rests on small samples (Slee 2019, PMID: 30712879). The only randomised add-on evidence for buspirone after SSRI failure is in a different illness — depression — where buspirone augmentation of citalopram remitted 30.1% of nonremitters in STAR*D, the same as bupropion augmentation (Trivedi 2006, PMID: 16554526). Extrapolating a depression augmentation result to anxiety after SSRI failure is a guess the evidence does not make. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): buspirone is a proven GAD monotherapy and a plausible add-on, but its effectiveness as add-on therapy for GAD after SSRI nonresponse has not been tested in any trial carded here.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — no trial has tested buspirone added to an SSRI for generalised anxiety disorder after SSRI nonresponse; buspirone beats placebo as GAD monotherapy (NNT 4.4) and matched bupropion as an add-on in depression (remission 30.1%), but neither result is the asked use

title: Depression in pregnancy (SPLIT): psychotherapy works and is the evidence-backed first step for moderate illness — antidepressant safety divides between a large adjusted null on cardiac defects and drug-specific signals in a depressed-women cohort
question: Should antidepressants be used in pregnancy for moderate depression, or does psychotherapy work as well?
balance: SPLIT — the evidence divides by question, and the stamp names the split. On whether psychotherapy works: two meta-analyses of randomised trials agree it does — a pooled effect of g = 0.67 with an NNT of 4.39 across 43 studies and 6,270 participants (Cuijpers 2023, PMID: 37310303), and CBT and interpersonal therapy each beating treatment as usual by about 1.7 Edinburgh scale points across 44 trials (Couch 2025, PMID: 41183344). On whether antidepressants are safe enough to use when therapy is insufficient or declined: the largest cohort (949,504 pregnancies) found the apparent cardiac-defect excess disappeared with full adjustment for depression and confounders (fully adjusted relative risk 1.06, 95% CI 0.93–1.22; Huybrechts 2014, PMID: 24941178), while a cohort restricted to depressed women found drug-specific signals — citalopram for major malformations overall and paroxetine for cardiac defects (Bérard 2017, PMID: 28082367). No head-to-head randomised trial of an antidepressant versus psychotherapy in pregnancy is carded, so 'works as well' cannot be answered directly; what the evidence supports is psychotherapy first for moderate depression in pregnancy, with antidepressants a reasonable option — not a proven-safe one — when therapy fails, is unavailable, or the illness is more severe. PROPOSED SPLIT (psychotherapy benefit consistent; antidepressant safety signals divide between cohorts).
stamp: SPLIT (psychotherapy benefit consistent; antidepressant safety signals divide) — psychotherapy beats control in 80+ randomised trials (NNT 4.39), the largest adjusted cohort found no cardiac-malformation increase (relative risk 1.06), but a depressed-women cohort found citalopram and paroxetine signals; no head-to-head drug-versus-therapy trial in pregnancy is carded

title: Sertraline in breastfeeding (exposure evidence): infant levels usually undetectable in pooled data and a calculated infant dose of 0.54% of the mother's — among the preferred antidepressants while nursing
question: Is sertraline the preferred antidepressant during breastfeeding?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — on exposure data, with evidence types labelled on every card as this shelf's brief requires. There are no randomised outcome trials of antidepressants in breastfeeding; the preference for sertraline rests on pharmacokinetic evidence of three labelled types, all pointing the same way. A pooled analysis of infant-level studies found sertraline (with nortriptyline and paroxetine) usually produces undetectable infant plasma levels, while fluoxetine left 22% of infants with levels above 10% of the maternal level (Weissman 2004, PMID: 15169695 — pooled analysis). A review and meta-analysis of sertraline levels found 87.4% of 167 infant sertraline levels below the limit of detection and no significant correlation between maternal and infant sertraline concentrations (Pinheiro 2015, PMID: 25589155 — meta-analysis of serum-level studies). A pharmacokinetic study of 26 nursing women put the infant's calculated sertraline dose at 0.54% of the maternal daily dose, with no adverse events in any infant (Stowe 2003, PMID: 12590627 — pharmacokinetic study). 'Preferred' therefore means lowest demonstrated infant exposure with no signal of harm in the level literature — paroxetine shares the undetectable-level property, so sertraline is a preferred choice rather than the only one, and infant clinical-outcome data beyond case reports do not exist in the carded records. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): yes — on concordant exposure evidence, sertraline is among the preferred antidepressants during breastfeeding.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — on exposure data (evidence types labelled on the cards): sertraline usually produces undetectable infant plasma levels in pooled level data, 87.4% of 167 infant levels were below detection in meta-analysis, and the calculated infant dose was 0.54% of the maternal dose — among the preferred antidepressants in breastfeeding

title: Giant cell myocarditis (observational only): combination immunosuppression was associated with 12.3 versus 3.0 months average survival and suppresses the infiltrate — but relapse continues for years and fulminant disease still ends in transplantation
question: Does immunosuppression help giant cell myocarditis?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only, printed on the face: giant cell myocarditis is too rare and too lethal for randomised trials, and none is carded. The signal comes from the Multicenter Giant Cell Myocarditis Study: among 63 patients (death or transplantation in 89%, median survival 5.5 months), the 22 patients treated with corticosteroids plus cyclosporine and/or azathioprine survived an average of 12.3 months versus 3.0 months for the 30 untreated patients (p = 0.001; Cooper 1997, PMID: 9197214). A small prospective protocol study of combination immunosuppression (20 patients) found biopsy inflammation, necrosis and giant cells significantly reduced at 4 weeks, with 1 death and 2 transplantations in a year — and one fatal recurrence after immunosuppression was withdrawn (Cooper 2008, PMID: 19026310). Long-term registry follow-up shows the disease is suppressed, not cured: among 26 patients who survived the first year without transplantation, the combined rate of death, transplantation, assist-device placement or recurrence reached 47% at 5 years, with recurrences up to 8 years out (Maleszewski 2015, PMID: 25882774). In fulminant disease on mechanical circulatory support, immunosuppression rarely averted transplantation — 9 of 13 patients were transplanted and none survived long-term transplant-free (Montero 2018, PMID: 29306448). Immunosuppression for virus-negative lymphocytic myocarditis is a different question, homed on shelf #3062 and not re-carded here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: combination immunosuppression appears to prolong survival in giant cell myocarditis and should not be stopped casually, but most patients still die or need transplantation.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: combination immunosuppression was associated with longer survival in the multicentre series (average 12.3 versus 3.0 months) and suppresses biopsy inflammation, but there is no randomised trial, relapse continues for years, and fulminant cases usually still require transplantation
