title: Pregabalin dose in postherpetic neuralgia: 300 mg/day works slightly better than 150 mg/day (placebo-adjusted pain relief 1.07 versus 0.88 points) — a small average gain, with 600 mg/day stronger and less well tolerated
question: Does pregabalin 300 mg work better than 150 mg for postherpetic neuralgia?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a real but small dose advantage. Only one carded trial randomised postherpetic neuralgia (PHN) patients to both doses head-to-head: van Seventer 2006 (PMID: 16466610; 370 patients) found placebo-adjusted endpoint pain reductions of 0.88 points at 150 mg/day and 1.07 points at 300 mg/day — so 300 mg beat 150 mg by about 0.19 points on a 0–10 scale on average, while 600 mg/day reached 1.79 points. The other carded trials frame the doses rather than compare them: Dworkin 2003 (PMID: 12707429) dosed by renal function (300 or 600 mg/day) and beat placebo clearly (endpoint pain 3.60 versus 5.29; 50% pain reduction in 50% versus 20%), and Freynhagen 2005 (PMID: 15911152) showed flexible titration through 150–600 mg/day works, consistent with individual dose-finding rather than a fixed best dose. The cost of higher doses is tolerability: 13.5% of pregabalin patients in the dose-ranging trial withdrew for adverse events, led by dizziness. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): yes, 300 mg/day works slightly better than 150 mg/day on average — a small increment that matters for some patients, bought with more dizziness and somnolence, which is why titration rather than a blanket 300 mg start is what the trials embody.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — 300 mg/day gave slightly more pain relief than 150 mg/day in the one direct dose-ranging trial (placebo-adjusted reductions 1.07 versus 0.88 points), a small average gain; 600 mg/day gave more relief (1.79 points) with more adverse effects

title: Corticosteroid injection for knee osteoarthritis: real but brief relief — clinically relevant for about 2–6 weeks, small to 13 weeks, and gone by 26 weeks
question: Does an intra-articular corticosteroid injection provide short-term relief in knee osteoarthritis, and how long does it last?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — short-term only, with the duration printed in the stamp. Three independent syntheses of the placebo-controlled trials agree on the shape of the effect: it is real early and gone by about 6 months. The Cochrane review (27 trials, 1,767 participants) found pain benefits that were moderate at 1–2 weeks (SMD −0.48), small to moderate at 4–6 weeks (SMD −0.41), small at 13 weeks (SMD −0.22) and absent at 26 weeks (SMD −0.07; Jüni 2015, PMID: 26490760). A duration-focused meta-analysis put the pooled effect at SMD −0.58 with an NNT of 5.1, approaching statistical insignificance at 4 months (Saltychev 2020, PMID: 31972612). The most clinically framed synthesis found the benefit reached the minimal clinically important difference only at short-term follow-up (6 weeks or less: pain mean difference −1.6, function −9.9), fell below it by mid-term, and showed no difference at 6 months or beyond (Bensa 2024, PMID: 38294103). Repeated scheduled injections and cartilage outcomes are a different question, homed on shelf #1481, and are not re-carded here. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) — short-term only: expect clinically relevant relief for roughly 2–6 weeks, a small residual benefit out to about 13 weeks, and no benefit by 26 weeks (the treatment made no difference at 6 months).
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — short-term only: clinically relevant pain relief for about 2–6 weeks after one injection, a small residual benefit to about 13 weeks, and no benefit by 26 weeks (the treatment made no difference at 6 months)

title: Tapering gabapentin after long-term use (weak evidence): no taper-schedule trial exists — reduce gradually rather than stopping abruptly, slower after long use, high doses, or a substance-use history
question: How should gabapentin be tapered in patients taking it long term for chronic pain?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence). No randomised trial of gabapentin taper schedules in chronic pain was found in the records fetched this session — the 'how' of tapering rests on gabapentinoid discontinuation data and the dependence literature, and the shelf grades itself accordingly. The closest controlled evidence is for the sister drug pregabalin: in a randomised trial programme, a 1-week taper after 12 or 24 weeks of treatment produced low discontinuation symptom scores (Physician Withdrawal Checklist increases of 1.7–2.8 points across pregabalin dose groups) and rebound anxiety rates of 0–6% (Kasper 2014, PMID: 24351233). The dependence reviews explain who needs a slower taper: across 106 studies there was no convincing evidence of strong addictive power in ordinary patients — only 4 reported cases of behavioural dependence without a prior abuse history — with risk concentrated in people with current or past substance-use disorders, especially opioid use (Bonnet 2017, PMID: 28988943); a second review put gabapentinoid abuse prevalence at 1.6% in the general population versus 3–68% among opioid abusers (Evoy 2017, PMID: 28144823). At the severe end, a 38-patient inpatient gabapentinoid detoxification cohort records that abrupt cessation is associated with adverse events such as seizures, and most patients completed a supervised detoxification (Priyam 2026, PMID: 42366702). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): taper gradually rather than stopping abruptly — a short taper sufficed after months of pregabalin in trial conditions, but long-term, high-dose gabapentin use, and any substance-use history, argue for a slower, monitored reduction; the specific week-by-week schedule is practice consensus, not trial evidence, and is not dressed up as such here.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — no randomised trial of gabapentin taper schedules in chronic pain was found in the records fetched; taper gradually rather than stopping abruptly (abrupt cessation is associated with seizures), with a short taper sufficient after months of use in trial conditions and slower, monitored tapers after long-term or high-dose use or a substance-use history

title: Tramadol for chronic low back pain beyond 12 weeks (split by duration): benefit is shown only in trials of about 13 weeks or less — beyond 12 weeks there is no placebo-controlled support, and the single 56-week trial's tramadol arm was null versus placebo
question: Is tramadol effective for chronic low back pain beyond 12 weeks?
balance: SPLIT by trial duration, printed on the face. In trials lasting about 13 weeks or less, tramadol (alone in the Cochrane pooling, and as tramadol/acetaminophen in the two 91-day trials) beat placebo on pain by a small-to-moderate amount. Beyond 12 weeks the placebo-controlled evidence essentially disappears: the Cochrane reviewers state there are no placebo-controlled randomised trials supporting long-term opioid therapy for chronic low back pain, and in the one trial that ran 56 weeks, tramadol prolonged-release did not improve patients' global assessment or pain-interference scores versus placebo at week 16 (the placebo comparison ended at week 16). So the honest answer is: benefit is shown only up to about 3 months; effectiveness beyond 12 weeks is unproven, and the single long trial's tramadol arm was null against placebo. PROPOSED SPLIT (short trials: benefit; beyond 12 weeks: no benefit shown) — tramadol reduced pain more than placebo in trials of about 13 weeks or less, but no placebo-controlled evidence supports effectiveness beyond 12 weeks, and the one 56-week trial found tramadol made no difference versus placebo at week 16 on global and pain-interference measures.
stamp: SPLIT (short trials: benefit; beyond 12 weeks: no benefit shown) — tramadol beat placebo in trials lasting about 13 weeks or less, but there are no placebo-controlled trials supporting effectiveness beyond 12 weeks, and the one 56-week trial found tramadol made no difference versus placebo at week 16

title: Stopping culprit medicines in orthostatic hypotension (observational only): withdrawal was followed by fewer falls (adjusted HR 0.48) and resolution of orthostatic hypotension on retesting — but no randomised trial has ever reported falls for this strategy
question: Does treating orthostatic hypotension by stopping culprit medications reduce falls and syncope?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only, printed on the face. No randomised trial of stopping culprit medicines in orthostatic hypotension has ever reported falls: the Cochrane review of antihypertensive withdrawal in older people (6 trials, 1,073 participants, updated 2025) states plainly that no studies reported falls. What exists is one prospective geriatric-outpatient cohort programme: withdrawing fall-risk-increasing drugs was followed by about half the fall hazard (adjusted HR 0.48; cardiovascular-drug withdrawal HR 0.35) and by significant normalisation of orthostatic hypotension on repeat tilt-table testing (adjusted OR 0.35 for an abnormal orthostatic result persisting). Withdrawal also raised blood pressure in the randomised literature (systolic +9.75 mmHg in the Cochrane pooling), so it is not cost-free. The randomised deprescribing trial most often cited for feasibility in the very old is carded on its own shelf elsewhere in this library and is cross-pointed, not re-carded, in the synthesis. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: stopping culprit medications was followed by fewer falls and by resolution of orthostatic hypotension in cohort data, but no randomised trial has tested the strategy on falls or syncope.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: withdrawing culprit (especially cardiovascular) medications was followed by about half the fall hazard and by resolution of orthostatic hypotension on retesting in prospective cohort data, but no randomised trial of stopping these drugs has ever reported falls or syncope

title: Procalcitonin guidance in pneumonia: LIKELY to safely shorten antibiotic courses — median 12 to 5 days in the pneumonia-only trial and 10.7 to 7.2 days in the large trial's pneumonia subgroup, with no worse outcomes
question: Does procalcitonin guidance safely reduce antibiotic duration in adults with pneumonia?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) for safely shortening antibiotic courses in pneumonia, on concordant randomised evidence — with the library cross-point printed here: the broader question of procalcitonin guidance across all acute respiratory infections is homed on live shelf #314, which cards the intensive-care and US emergency-department trials (including a large US trial that found no reduction in antibiotic use); those records are NOT re-carded here. This shelf asks the narrower pneumonia question, and its anchor trial was never carded. In pneumonia specifically: the pneumonia-only randomised trial cut median duration from 12 to 5 days with similar outcomes; the large Swiss trial's pneumonia subgroup (925 patients) cut mean duration from 10.7 to 7.2 days with a similar adverse-outcome rate; and the patient-level meta-analysis of 26 trials found 2.4 fewer antibiotic days, fewer antibiotic side-effects, and lower 30-day mortality with guidance (adjusted OR 0.83). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): procalcitonin guidance safely reduces antibiotic duration in adults with pneumonia.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — procalcitonin guidance safely reduces antibiotic duration in adults with pneumonia (median 12 to 5 days in the pneumonia-only trial; 10.7 to 7.2 days in the large trial's pneumonia subgroup), with no worse outcomes and fewer antibiotic side-effects

title: Prolonged tuberculosis treatment in diabetes: MAYBE (weak evidence) — diabetes brings more relapse on standard 6-month treatment, but no study has ever tested whether treating beyond 6 months helps
question: Should adults with tuberculosis and diabetes have prolonged treatment beyond 6 months?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — prolongation itself has never been randomised, printed on the face. The rationale for longer treatment is real but indirect: two systematic reviews find that people with diabetes fare worse on standard tuberculosis treatment — a relative risk of 1.69 for the combined outcome of failure and death and 3.89 for relapse in the 2011 review, and odds ratios of 1.88 for death and 1.64 for relapse in the 2019 update (56,122 patients with tuberculosis and diabetes). One older Japanese cohort found relapse after a 6-month regimen concentrated in patients with diabetes (6 of 54 vs 3 of 237). But no carded record — and no trial found this session — compares more than 6 months against 6 months in patients with diabetes, so worse outcomes on standard treatment do not by themselves prove that prolonging treatment fixes them; the reviews instead point to glucose control, monitoring and drug exposure as the open questions. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): routine prolongation beyond 6 months for tuberculosis with diabetes is untested — diabetes is associated with more failure, death and relapse on standard treatment, but no study shows that longer treatment removes that excess.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — prolongation beyond 6 months has never been tested in tuberculosis with diabetes: diabetes is associated with more failure, death and relapse on standard treatment (relapse relative risk 3.89), but no study shows longer treatment removes that excess

title: Early gabapentin after herpes zoster: POSSIBLE (no benefit shown) for preventing postherpetic neuralgia — the one randomised trial was null (pain at 12 weeks 18.2% vs 9.5% on placebo)
question: Does early gabapentin after herpes zoster prevent postherpetic neuralgia?
balance: POSSIBLE (no benefit shown), stated plainly. The one randomised trial of the exact strategy — gabapentin started within 72 hours of rash onset, titrated to up to 1,800 mg/day for 5 weeks, on top of valaciclovir — found pain at 12 weeks in 18.2% of the gabapentin group versus 9.5% with placebo (P = 0.144): the treatment made no difference, and the point estimate ran the wrong way, with worse quality of life and sleep in the gabapentin group. The sibling gabapentinoid pregabalin, started during acute zoster in a small trial (N = 29, printed on its card), likewise made no difference to acute pain or to postherpetic neuralgia onset. Context: even antiviral treatment started within 72 hours does not significantly reduce postherpetic neuralgia incidence in the Cochrane pooling (relative risk 0.75 at 4 months, 95% CI 0.51 to 1.11), so prevention by early drug treatment is a high bar that gabapentin does not clear. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (no benefit shown): early gabapentin does not prevent postherpetic neuralgia in the randomised evidence.
stamp: POSSIBLE (no benefit shown) — the one randomised trial of gabapentin started within 72 hours of rash onset found the treatment made no difference to pain at 12 weeks (18.2% vs 9.5% with placebo), and no early drug treatment, gabapentin included, has been shown to prevent postherpetic neuralgia

title: Antibiotic duration in acute prostatitis: MAYBE (weak evidence), observational only — duration has never been randomised in prostatitis; the supported standard is about 14 days of an adequate prostate-penetrating drug, and relapse tracks drug adequacy, not a tested number of days
question: In adults with acute prostatitis, how long should antibiotic treatment continue?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — observational only for prostatitis itself, printed on the face. No trial has randomised men with acute prostatitis to different durations: the one randomised duration trial in the neighbouring population (febrile urinary tract infection in men, where 7 days proved inferior to 14 days at short-term follow-up in men) is homed on live shelf #488 and is cross-pointed here, not re-carded — and it excluded patients judged to need at least 14 days, the group closest to prostatitis. What the prostatitis cohorts show is that relapse tracks whether the drug was adequate for the organism, not a tested duration: in 410 patients, inadequate antibiotic therapy carried an odds ratio of 12.3 for relapse (overall relapse 6.3%), and in 326 Escherichia coli episodes, recurrence occurred only with the poorly penetrating oral beta-lactam comparator. The 2026 French guideline-rationale review states the conventional standard plainly: 14 days remains the standard for acute prostatitis to prevent relapse, with 7 days sufficient only for selected bacteraemic presentations of male urinary infection. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — observational only: continue antibiotics for about 14 days in acute prostatitis; shorter courses are untested in prostatitis itself, and adequacy of the chosen drug against the cultured organism is the factor the cohort evidence actually supports.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — observational only: no trial has randomised treatment duration in acute prostatitis; cohorts show relapse tracks drug adequacy (OR 12.3 for inadequate therapy), and the standing guideline standard is about 14 days, with shorter courses validated only for male cystitis and selected bacteraemic urinary infections

title: COVID booster at ages 50–64 without major risk factors (observational only): relative hospitalisation risk falls by roughly half for the first weeks then wanes — but the absolute benefit is small, and no study isolates this exact subgroup
question: Does a COVID booster reduce hospitalization in adults aged 50 to 64 without major risk factors?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only, printed on the face: every carded estimate comes from test-negative or cohort designs, as no placebo-controlled booster trial exists in this age group. The relative benefit is consistent: the English test-negative study found the bivalent booster's incremental effectiveness against hospitalisation in people aged 50 and over peaked at 53.0% (relative) 2–4 weeks after the dose and waned to 35.9% after 10 or more weeks; the US networks found the updated 2023–2024 vaccine 52% and 43% effective (relative) against hospitalisation in immunocompetent adults. But the absolute benefit in a healthy 50–64-year-old is small, because baseline hospitalisation risk is low: in the US number-needed-to-vaccinate cohort of 1,285,032 adults, the median NNV to prevent one hospitalisation was 205 overall and was consistently lower (more favourable) in people aged 65 and over and in those with underlying conditions than in younger, healthier groups — the record does not print a separate NNV for 50–64-year-olds without risk factors, and none is invented here. No carded record isolates adults aged 50–64 without major risk factors as its own stratum; the age-specific claim is therefore an inference from the 50-and-over and all-adult estimates, printed as such. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: a booster reduces the relative risk of COVID hospitalisation by roughly half in the first weeks, waning thereafter; for a 50–64-year-old without major risk factors the absolute number of hospitalisations prevented is small.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: a COVID booster reduces the relative risk of hospitalisation by roughly half in the first weeks (53.0% at 2–4 weeks, waning to 35.9% after 10+ weeks), but the absolute benefit for adults aged 50–64 without major risk factors is small (overall median number needed to vaccinate 205 to prevent one hospitalisation, least favourable in younger, healthier adults) and no study isolates that exact subgroup

title: Antibiotic prophylaxis timing: earlier within the 60 minutes before incision made no difference to surgical site infection — the randomised trial and meta-analysis agree; only after-incision or >120-minute-early dosing raises risk
question: Does giving antibiotic prophylaxis within 60 minutes before incision reduce surgical site infection compared with earlier timing?
balance: LIKELY — earlier timing inside the window made no difference. The question behind the familiar 'within 60 minutes' rule is whether minutes matter inside that window, and the best evidence says they do not. In the only large randomised trial (Weber 2017, PMID: 28385346; 5,175 patients analysed), single-shot cefuroxime given a median of 42 minutes before incision in the anaesthesia room did not reduce 30-day surgical site infection compared with a median of 16 minutes before incision in the operating room (odds ratio 0.93, 95% CI 0.72–1.21). The WHO-commissioned meta-analysis (de Jonge 2017, PMID: 28723736; 54,552 patients) likewise found no difference between administration 120–60 and 60–0 minutes before incision; risk rose only when prophylaxis was given after incision (OR 1.89) or more than 120 minutes before it (OR 5.26). A 222,439-patient Swiss cohort (Sommerstein 2023, PMID: 37289455) found administration closer to incision associated with slightly lower adjusted odds of infection, but that is observational timing data, subject to confounding by workflow, and it supports staying within 60 minutes rather than any benefit from the early part of the window; the Dutch TAPAS cohort (PMID: 31663971) found no conclusive difference between 60–30 and 30–0 minutes (OR 0.82, 95% CI 0.57–1.19). PROPOSED LIKELY — giving prophylaxis earlier within the 60 minutes before incision made no difference to surgical site infection (the treatment made no difference within the window); what matters is giving it before incision and not more than about 120 minutes ahead.
stamp: LIKELY — earlier timing within the 60 minutes before incision made no difference: the randomised trial (OR 0.93) and the 54,552-patient meta-analysis agree there is no timing gradient inside the window; infection risk rises only when prophylaxis is given after incision (OR 1.89) or more than 120 minutes before it (OR 5.26)

title: Shingles antivirals after 72 hours: untested — every trial started treatment within 72 hours, where famciclovir shortened neuralgia but prevention of neuralgia is disputed; no evidence measures a late start
question: For adults with shingles, does starting antivirals after 72 hours still reduce pain?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the late start itself is untested. Every randomised trial behind antiviral treatment of shingles enrolled patients within 72 hours of rash onset, so there is no direct trial evidence that starting after 72 hours reduces pain; any benefit from a late start is extrapolation. What early treatment does is itself mixed: famciclovir started within 72 hours resolved postherpetic neuralgia about twice as fast as placebo (Tyring 1995, PMID: 7778840; hazard ratios 1.7–1.9, median duration shortened by about 2 months), and a meta-analysis of aciclovir trials found less residual pain at 6 months (Jackson 1997, PMID: 9129551; summary odds ratio 0.54), yet the Cochrane review (Chen 2014, PMID: 24500927) — which by design included only trials of treatment given within 72 hours — found oral aciclovir did not significantly reduce the incidence of postherpetic neuralgia at 4 months (RR 0.75, 95% CI 0.51–1.11) or 6 months (RR 1.05). The head-to-head valaciclovir-versus-aciclovir trial is homed on shelf #5031 and is cross-pointed here, not re-carded. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): starting antivirals after 72 hours may still help pain, but no trial has tested it — the proven window is within 72 hours, and even there the effect is on pain duration more than on whether neuralgia occurs.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — starting antivirals after 72 hours is untested: every trial enrolled patients within 72 hours of rash onset, where famciclovir shortened neuralgia by about 2 months but aciclovir did not significantly prevent neuralgia in the Cochrane review; no effect size exists for a late start

title: Blepharitis: warm compresses and lid hygiene relieve symptoms about as well as antibiotic ointment in the available evidence — but no adequate head-to-head trial exists, and no treatment is proven to cure chronic blepharitis
question: For blepharitis, is warm compress and lid hygiene as effective as antibiotic ointment?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — no head-to-head trial establishes either treatment as superior, and the Cochrane review (Lindsley 2012, PMID: 22592706; 34 studies, 2,169 participants) found topical antibiotics gave some symptomatic relief and eradicated bacteria from the lid margin in anterior blepharitis, while lid hygiene may provide symptomatic relief for both anterior and posterior blepharitis — and concluded there is no strong evidence for any treatment in terms of curing chronic blepharitis. Direct warm-compress studies are small and device-focused: in 42 patients, heated eye masks improved meibomian gland function while a warm face cloth did not (Murphy 2020, PMID: 31657234), and in a 75-patient randomised trial a steam device beat a warm towel on symptoms while the towel itself still helped about half of users (Sim 2014, PMID: 25156975). A meta-analysis of thermal pulsation versus warm compresses (Pang 2019, PMID: 30844843) shows device treatment can beat compresses on gland measures, which underlines that 'warm compress' is not one uniform treatment. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): warm compresses and lid hygiene appear to give symptomatic relief of the same order as antibiotic ointment and remain the reasonable first step, but equivalence has never been tested in an adequate head-to-head trial, and antibiotics additionally clear lid-margin bacteria in anterior disease.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — no head-to-head trial shows antibiotic ointment superior to warm compresses and lid hygiene, and the Cochrane review (34 studies, 2,169 participants) found symptomatic relief from both but no strong evidence any treatment cures chronic blepharitis; antibiotics additionally eradicate lid-margin bacteria in anterior disease

title: HIF prolyl hydroxylase inhibitors on dialysis: haemoglobin control matches ESAs in three large noninferiority programmes (vadadustat, roxadustat, daprodustat) — an oral alternative for the haemoglobin target, with shorter long-term safety experience
question: In adults on dialysis with anemia, do HIF prolyl hydroxylase inhibitors achieve hemoglobin control as effectively as erythropoiesis-stimulating agents?
balance: LIKELY (as effective for haemoglobin control). Three large phase 3 programmes, each randomised against an erythropoiesis-stimulating agent in dialysis patients, meet their haemoglobin noninferiority margins: vadadustat versus darbepoetin alfa in 3,923 patients (Eckardt 2021, PMID: 33913638 — haemoglobin differences of −0.07 to −0.31 g/dL against a −0.75 g/dL margin, with cardiovascular safety also noninferior, MACE hazard ratio 0.96); roxadustat versus epoetin alfa in 2,133 patients (Fishbane 2022, PMID: 35361724 — haemoglobin change 0.77 versus 0.68 g/dL, difference 0.09 g/dL); and daprodustat versus darbepoetin alfa in 312 incident-dialysis patients (Singh 2022, PMID: 35377393 — adjusted difference −0.10 g/dL). A network meta-analysis of 17 phase 3 trials (Sackeyfio 2024, PMID: 38250252; 11,124 dialysis patients for the haemoglobin outcome) finds the three agents broadly comparable. The class's two biggest dialysis trials are homed elsewhere in this library — ASCEND-D on shelf #1108 and the Chen 2019 roxadustat dialysis trial within shelf #731 — and are cross-pointed here in prose, not re-carded; this shelf is built on the remaining free programme reports, a genuinely narrower class-level haemoglobin question, flagged for the developer. PROPOSED LIKELY: for haemoglobin control on dialysis, HIF prolyl hydroxylase inhibitors match ESAs; the stamp is about haemoglobin only, not about long-term safety, where follow-up remains shorter than the decades of ESA experience.
stamp: LIKELY (as effective for haemoglobin control) — vadadustat (3,923 patients), roxadustat (2,133) and daprodustat (312) each met haemoglobin noninferiority against an ESA on dialysis, and a 17-trial network meta-analysis finds the class broadly comparable; the stamp covers haemoglobin, not long-term safety

title: Methadone for refractory neuropathic cancer pain (observational only): specialist-supervised rotation or low-dose add-on relieved pain in about half to two-thirds of patients in small series — no randomised trial exists for this indication
question: Is methadone effective for refractory cancer-related neuropathic pain under specialist supervision?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only, printed on the face. No randomised trial tests methadone specifically for refractory neuropathic cancer pain. The Cochrane review (Nicholson 2017, PMID: 28177515) found only 6 trials with 388 participants in cancer pain generally — too heterogeneous to pool, low-quality evidence — with methadone similar to morphine for pain relief and an explicit warning that methadone should be initiated only by experienced practitioners because of titration difficulty and potentially fatal arrhythmias. The refractory-neuropathic evidence is observational: in a prospective cohort of 48 palliative inpatients rotated to methadone for refractory neuropathic cancer pain, 47% gained at least 20 mm on a visual analogue scale by day 28 (Fawoubo 2023, PMID: 34620692); in 19 rotation patients, pain scores fell 4 points by day 7 and the neuropathic DN4 screen turned negative in 65% (Rhondali 2013, PMID: 24116946); and adding low-dose methadone to ongoing opioids produced a response (at least 33% pain reduction) in 68.4% of 19 patients with uncontrolled pain (Hasegawa 2025, PMID: 40674591). All three series are small, uncontrolled, and run in specialist palliative units — exactly the supervised setting the question specifies. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: under specialist supervision, rotation to or addition of methadone relieves refractory neuropathic cancer pain in a substantial share of patients, on small uncontrolled series; the randomised evidence base does not address this indication.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: rotation to or addition of methadone under specialist supervision relieved refractory neuropathic cancer pain in about half to two-thirds of patients in three small uncontrolled series (N = 48, 19, 19); no randomised trial tests methadone for this indication, and the Cochrane review restricts initiation to experienced practitioners

title: Adding a corticosteroid for opioid-resistant cancer pain: SPLIT — meta-analyses find a small one-week pain reduction, the dedicated randomised trial found none; benefit, if any, is small, brief and likeliest in inflammatory pain
question: For cancer pain that does not respond to opioids alone, does adding a corticosteroid help?
balance: SPLIT — the pooled trials and the dedicated trial point different ways, and the split is named in the stamp. Pooling six studies with one-week data, the Cochrane review (Haywood 2015, PMID: 25908299; 15 studies, 1,926 participants overall) found corticosteroids reduced pain by a mean of 0.84 points on a 0–10 scale at one week (95% CI 1.38 to 0.30 lower) — a small effect on low-quality evidence, with the reviewers calling the overall evidence for efficacy weak. A 2025 adjuvant meta-analysis (Zhang 2025, PMID: 41074978) likewise found a dexamethasone pain-score reduction (MD −1.43). But the one randomised trial designed exactly around this question — dexamethasone 8 mg daily added to opioids in 76 advanced-cancer patients (Mercadante 2007, PMID: 17347500) — found no differences in pain intensity, opioid consumption or opioid escalation (the treatment made no difference to pain), though gastrointestinal symptoms eased and well-being improved for some weeks. PROPOSED SPLIT: adding a corticosteroid may buy a small, short-lived pain reduction on pooled low-quality data, but the dedicated adjuvant trial found none; any benefit is most plausible for inflammation-driven pain (bone, nerve compression, capsular stretch) over days to a few weeks, weighed against steroid harms in advanced disease.
stamp: SPLIT — pooled trials show a small short-term pain reduction from adding a corticosteroid (0.84 points at one week, low-quality evidence), but the dedicated randomised adjuvant trial of dexamethasone 8 mg found no added analgesia (the treatment made no difference to pain intensity or opioid use)

title: Acupuncture for chemotherapy-induced nausea: a modest adjunct benefit — complete protection rose from 34.5% to 52.9% when electroacupuncture was added to triple antiemetics, though vomiting itself barely changed and certainty is low
question: Does acupuncture help chemotherapy-induced nausea in adults with cancer?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — as an adjunct to standard antiemetics, never instead of them. The Cochrane review (Ezzo 2006, PMID: 16625560; 11 trials, 1,247 patients, all receiving pharmacological antiemetics) found acupuncture-point stimulation reduced acute vomiting (relative risk 0.82, 95% CI 0.69–0.99) but did not reduce acute or delayed nausea severity. A 2023 meta-analysis (Yan 2023, PMID: 37226372; 38 RCTs, 2,503 patients) found acupuncture added to usual care increased complete control of acute vomiting (RR 1.13) and delayed vomiting (RR 1.47), with certainty rated low or very low. The strongest single trial — a 239-patient sham-controlled study adding electroacupuncture to standard triple antiemetic therapy in breast-cancer patients receiving highly emetogenic chemotherapy (Shen 2024, PMID: 39241208) — raised complete protection from 34.5% to 52.9% (an absolute gain of about 18 percentage points), driven by nausea outcomes: no-vomiting rates themselves were similar (76.7% versus 73.9%). A second sham-controlled trial (Li 2020, PMID: 32514290; 134 patients) found no significant difference in complete response, only modestly reduced severity. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): acupuncture, mainly electroacupuncture at the P6 point, modestly improves nausea control on top of modern antiemetics; the vomiting effect is small and the evidence certainty is low.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — as an adjunct to standard antiemetics: acupuncture-point stimulation modestly improves nausea control (complete protection 52.9% versus 34.5% in the best sham-controlled trial) and slightly reduces acute vomiting relatively (RR 0.82), on evidence of low certainty; it does not replace antiemetic drugs

title: Statins after MI past 80 (observational only for this exact question): continuation is associated with fewer events and lower mortality in the oldest cohorts, and trials prove benefit into the early 80s — continue in patients who tolerate them and are likely to live ~2 years
question: Should statins be continued in patients over 80 after MI?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only for the over-80 post-MI continuation question, printed on the face; no randomised trial has tested continuing versus stopping a statin after 80. The randomised foundation is one step removed: a meta-analysis of 9 secondary-prevention trials in 19,569 patients aged 65–82 (Afilalo 2008, PMID: 18174034) found statins cut all-cause mortality (15.6% versus 18.7%; relative risk 0.78) — but its oldest participants were 82 and it tested starting, not continuing. The two large ageing trial syntheses are homed elsewhere in this library (the Cholesterol Treatment Trialists' age meta-analysis on shelf #3986; PROSPER in pack #1564) and are cross-pointed, not re-carded. Directly on the question, the evidence is observational: in 3,900 patients aged 80 or older after a first MI, at least 2 years of statin prescriptions were associated with lower composite cardiovascular risk (adjusted HR 0.81) and mortality (adjusted HR 0.84), with numbers needed to treat of 59 and 36 over a median 4.5 years before correction for early deaths (Lefeber 2020, PMID: 31647578); and in Denmark, discontinuation among long-term users aged 75+ was associated with 13 excess major cardiovascular events per 1,000 person-years in the secondary-prevention cohort (Thompson 2021, PMID: 34854906). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: continue the statin after MI past 80 in patients tolerating it and likely to live long enough (about 2 years) to benefit; deprescribing trials in this exact population are still lacking.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only for the over-80 post-MI question: cohorts associate continuation with fewer events (HR 0.81) and discontinuation with 13 excess events per 1,000 person-years, and trial meta-analysis shows mortality benefit in elderly secondary prevention up to age 82 — but continuing versus stopping past 80 has never been randomised

title: Blood pressure over 85: no trial isolates this age — the best-supported target is systolic below 140, toward 120–130 mm Hg if tolerated, extrapolated from SPRINT at 75+ and HYVET at 80+, with frailty setting the limit
question: What blood pressure target is best for patients over 85 with hypertension?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) for treating hypertension and aiming lower in fit older adults — with the explicit caveat that no trial isolates patients over 85 or their ideal target, so the answer for 85+ is extrapolated. The nearest randomised evidence: in the SPRINT subgroup aged 75 or older (Williamson 2016, PMID: 27195814; 2,636 participants, mean age 79.9), a systolic target under 120 mm Hg beat under 140 mm Hg on the cardiovascular composite (HR 0.66) and all-cause mortality (HR 0.67), without more injurious falls. A meta-analysis of 16 target trials (Roush 2019, PMID: 30870246) found lower targets benefited older patients (mean age 77; RR 0.77) more than younger ones, with the number needed to treat falling steeply with age. For the over-80s specifically, HYVET proved treating to a target of 150/80 mm Hg saves lives — its main results are homed on live shelf #94 and the intensive-trials shelf #93 and are cross-pointed here, not re-carded — and HYVET's frailty analysis (Warwick 2015, PMID: 25880068) found no evidence that frailty removes the benefit. STEP's 6-year follow-up (Song 2025, PMID: 41105077) supports sustained intensive control in older patients, though STEP enrolled ages 60–80. PROPOSED LIKELY: treat hypertension past 85 and aim systolic roughly 120–139 mm Hg in ambulatory, reasonably fit patients — below 140, toward 130 or lower if tolerated without hypotension, kidney injury or falls — individualising downward ambition for frailty, since the trials excluded the most frail.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) for treating hypertension and aiming lower — systolic below 140 and toward 120–130 mm Hg if tolerated — in ambulatory older adults; no trial isolates patients over 85, so the target past 85 is extrapolated from trials at 75–80+ (SPRINT ≥75: HR 0.66 for events, 0.67 for mortality) and must be individualised for frailty

title: Intensive blood-pressure lowering and falls in frail older adults: no increase in injurious falls detected (4.9% vs 5.5% at age 75+) in the trial frailty and oldest-age analyses or a 21-trial review — in ambulatory volunteers, not care-home residents
question: Does intensive blood pressure lowering increase falls in frail elderly patients?
balance: POSSIBLE (no increase in falls detected) — the falls question about intensive lowering has been asked inside the one big trial programme that enrolled older, higher-risk patients, and the answer there is reassuring but bounded. In SPRINT participants aged 75 and older, injurious falls were 4.9% on intensive treatment versus 5.5% on standard treatment (hazard ratio 0.91, a relative measure; Williamson 2016); at age 80 and older there was no between-group difference in injurious falls (Pajewski 2020); frailty did not significantly modify serious-adverse-event risk (Wang 2023); and a 21-trial Veterans Affairs review concluded that lower targets do not increase falls or cognitive impairment, on low- to moderate-strength evidence (Weiss 2017). The harms that genuinely rose were hypotension, syncope numerically, electrolyte abnormalities and kidney injury. The bounds matter: these were ambulatory volunteers, the parent trial's cardiovascular question is homed on live shelf #93 and this shelf cards only its age and frailty safety reports, the age-75+ falls interval still permits a modest relative increase, and the review itself says frail-elderly data are limited. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (no increase in falls detected): intensive blood-pressure lowering did not increase injurious falls in the trial populations studied, including their frail subgroups — evidence that does not extend to institutionalised or already-falling patients.
stamp: POSSIBLE (no increase in falls detected) — intensive lowering did not increase injurious falls in SPRINT's age-75+ report (4.9% vs 5.5%), its age-80+ report, or its frailty analysis, and a 21-trial review agrees; one trial programme plus a review, in ambulatory volunteers rather than institutionalised frail patients

title: Deprescribing antihypertensives in frail elderly patients: no increase in cardiovascular events has been demonstrated — but the evidence is weak, imprecise, and thinnest in the frail long-term-care setting itself
question: Does deprescribing antihypertensives in frail elderly increase cardiovascular events?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — no increase in cardiovascular events has been demonstrated after supervised antihypertensive deprescribing, but the evidence is too small and imprecise to exclude one, and it is thinnest exactly where this question points: frail elderly patients. The Cochrane pool (6 trials, 1,073 participants) found little to no difference in mortality, stroke or hospitalisation with very wide intervals and low-to-very-low certainty (Gnjidic 2025). In TONE, cardiovascular event rates were flat before, during/after and after resumption of withdrawn therapy (5.5, 5.5 and 6.8 per 100 person-years; Kostis 1998), while withdrawal raised systolic pressure by about 5 mmHg and symptoms clustered during withdrawal (Juraschek 2022). In long-term care, the frailest setting, three randomised studies (1,548 residents) could not be pooled; mortality hazard ratios were 1.02 and 1.65 in the two reporting trials and cardiovascular events were sparsely measured (Jiang 2026). The large modern deprescribing trial programme in patients aged 80 and older is homed on live shelf #132; this shelf cards the wider withdrawal literature and the long-term-care synthesis that speak to frailty and to cardiovascular events specifically. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): deprescribing under supervision, with monitoring and restart rules, has not been shown to increase cardiovascular events — an absence of demonstrated harm on weak evidence, not proof of safety.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — no increase in cardiovascular events demonstrated after supervised deprescribing (TONE event rates flat; Cochrane differences null), but trials are small, intervals wide (mortality odds ratio 2.08, 95% CI 0.79–5.46, relative) and frail long-term-care data are sparse and unpooled

title: Hip protectors in nursing homes (SPLIT): pooled and cluster-trial evidence suggests fewer hip fractures, but the two individually randomised trials — including HIP PRO's within-person test — found the treatment made no difference
question: In older adults, does hip protector use reduce hip fractures in nursing home residents versus no hip protectors?
balance: SPLIT (cluster/pooled evidence: benefit; individually randomised evidence: the treatment made no difference) — hip protectors in nursing homes are a genuinely divided evidence base, and the divide follows study design. The pooled Bayesian estimate over 4 nursing-home trials is an odds ratio of 0.40 (relative; Sawka 2007) and the Hamburg cluster trial that raised wearing from 15% to 68% of fallers recorded 4.6% versus 8.1% hip fractures (relative risk 0.57, relative; P = 0.072; Meyer 2003). Against that, the two trials that randomised the pad itself found nothing: HIP PRO, comparing each resident's protected hip with their own unprotected hip in 1,042 residents with 73.8% adherence, recorded 3.1% versus 2.5% (the treatment made no difference; Kiel 2007), and Cameron 2001 recorded 8 versus 7 fractures (hazard ratio 1.46, relative). The library's umbrella hip-protector shelf, including the large Finnish cluster trial and the Cochrane review, is homed on live shelf #606; this shelf cards the nursing-home trials and their pooled analysis that frame the split. Adherence is the hinge throughout: no fracture in Cameron's trial happened while a protector was worn as directed, yet high supported adherence in HIP PRO still produced no benefit. PROPOSED SPLIT: whether hip protectors reduce hip fractures in nursing-home residents depends on which design you believe — programme-level provision may help; the pad's own measured effect in individually randomised trials is null.
stamp: SPLIT (cluster and pooled evidence: benefit, pooled odds ratio 0.40 relative; individually randomised trials: the treatment made no difference — HIP PRO 3.1% protected vs 2.5% unprotected hips)

title: Relaxing the A1C target in frail older adults (SPLIT): tighter targets cause severe hypoglycaemia in trials, but the A1C number itself does not predict hypoglycaemia in older adults — the drug regimen does, and the head-to-head target trial has not been done
question: In older adults with type 2 diabetes and frailty, does relaxing the A1C target to below 8.5% reduce hypoglycemia versus a target below 7.5%?
balance: SPLIT (trial evidence: tighter targets cause more severe hypoglycaemia; older-adult evidence: the A1C number itself does not predict hypoglycaemia — drug burden does) — and the direct trial this question names does not exist in the records fetched: no study randomised frail older adults to an A1C target under 8.5% versus under 7.5% and counted hypoglycaemia. What the evidence does show pulls in two directions. Randomised target trials prove the direction of harm: intensive targets more than doubled severe hypoglycaemia (relative risk 2.18, relative; Hemmingsen 2013). But in older adults themselves, hypoglycaemia duration on glucose monitoring did not differ across A1C groups from under 7% to over 9%, before or after de-intensification (Munshi 2017), and in 201,705 adults the A1C association was U-shaped and small beside regimen associations of 7- to 28-fold for sulfonylureas and insulin (McCoy 2020); modelled US data attribute roughly 9,578 hypoglycaemia hospital events over 2 years to intensive treatment, concentrated in clinically complex adults (Mahoney 2019). So relaxing the printed target without changing the prescription is unproven to reduce hypoglycaemia; the benefit, where it exists, runs through de-intensifying hypoglycaemia-causing drugs, which a relaxed target permits but does not itself accomplish. PROPOSED SPLIT, as stated above.
stamp: SPLIT (tighter targets cause severe hypoglycaemia in trials, relative risk 2.18 relative; but in older adults A1C level itself did not predict hypoglycaemia — insulin/sulfonylurea burden did; no trial has randomised frail patients to <8.5% vs <7.5% targets)

title: Stopping benzodiazepines in older adults (weak evidence): cognition and balance measures improve after withdrawal in small uncontrolled studies, but no carded study has counted falls after benzodiazepine-only discontinuation
question: Does stopping benzodiazepines improve cognition and reduce falls in older adults?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the cognition half of this question has small, uncontrolled, favourable evidence; the falls half has none in the carded set. After tapering off benzodiazepine hypnotics, nursing-home completers improved in postural sway and in immediate memory, language and attention scores, without subjective sleep worsening (Tsunoda 2010; 30 enrolled, 26 completers). In 89 older outpatients, grip strength improved within 3 weeks of starting withdrawal and balance from the first week (Nurminen 2014). Stopping is achievable — tapering achieved 62% discontinuation versus 21% on usual care, with no change in psychological functioning either way (Voshaar 2003) — and a 2025 review of 16 deprescribing studies confirms cessation is common while reporting no pooled falls or cognition effects, because the studies largely did not measure them (McEvoy 2025). The library's randomised trial of gradual psychotropic-medication withdrawal and falls is homed on live shelf #1490, and the big education-to-stop trials are homed on live shelf #500; this shelf cards the outcome studies for cognition and balance specifically. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): stopping benzodiazepines probably improves daytime cognition and balance measures in older adults; a reduction in falls themselves is plausible but unproven in this evidence.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — cognition and balance measures improved after stopping in small uncontrolled studies (n = 30 and n = 89, printed on their faces) and tapering is achievable (62% vs 21%), but no carded study counted falls after benzodiazepine-only discontinuation

title: Multicomponent delirium prevention after surgery: postoperative delirium fell in both surgical trials of Elder Life Programs (2.6% vs 19.4% and 6.6% vs 15.1%), with shorter hospital stays
question: In older adults after surgery, does a multicomponent delirium prevention program reduce postoperative delirium?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — two concordant cluster-randomised trials in surgical patients, backed by the program's wider meta-analysis, support a real reduction in postoperative delirium. The tailored, family-involved Elder Life Program cut delirium from 19.4% to 2.6% (relative risk 0.14, relative; number needed to treat 5.9; Wang 2020), and the modified three-protocol program cut it from 15.1% to 6.6% after abdominal surgery (relative risk 0.44, relative; Chen 2017), with shorter hospital stays in both. Across hospital care the program's meta-analytic odds ratio for delirium is 0.47 (relative; Hshieh 2018). The caution card matters: in the broad elective-surgery literature the multicomponent effect reaches significance only in sensitivity analyses excluding high-bias studies, and no pooled effect size is printed for it (Janssen 2019). The founding trial of the original program in hospitalised medical patients is homed on live shelf #340; this shelf cards the postoperative trials and reviews. Both surgical trials are single-centre and cluster-randomised with high control rates, so absolute benefit elsewhere scales with the local baseline. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): a multicomponent delirium prevention program reduces postoperative delirium in older adults after surgery.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — postoperative delirium fell in both carded surgical trials of multicomponent Elder Life Programs (2.6% vs 19.4%, relative risk 0.14 relative; 6.6% vs 15.1%, relative risk 0.44 relative), with a concordant program meta-analysis (odds ratio 0.47, relative)

title: Combined hormonal contraception and menstrual migraine (SPLIT): attacks concentrate in the hormone-free interval on standard pills, a step-down pill improved them in a small pilot — and with aura, observational stroke evidence says avoid estrogen
question: Does combined hormonal contraception worsen menstrual migraine, and should it be avoided with aura?
balance: SPLIT — observational only for the vascular risk. On worsening: combined hormonal contraception predictably manufactures a monthly estrogen-withdrawal window, and in users with menstrual migraine the attacks land there — a mean of 2.2 migraine days in the hormone-free interval, almost half lasting over 24 hours despite rescue medication (Merki-Feld 2017). Yet 'worsens menstrual migraine' is not universal: a small uncontrolled pilot of a step-down estradiol valerate/dienogest pill found fewer, shorter, less severe attacks (Nappi 2013; 32 women), so formulation and regimen decide the direction. On aura: the evidence is observational throughout and consistent — migraine with aura carried a relative ischaemic-stroke risk of 2.27 (relative), rising to 8.72 (relative) in oral-contraceptive users in the older meta-analysis (Etminan 2005), and all four low-dose case-control studies reported increased odds with combined exposure, apparently driven by aura (Ornello 2020). No carded record prints absolute stroke rates. PROPOSED SPLIT: standard combined contraception worsens the withdrawal-week pattern of menstrual migraine for many users while a step-down formulation improved it in one small pilot; and estrogen-containing contraception should be avoided in migraine with aura on consistent observational stroke evidence — a risk-based rule, not a trial finding.
stamp: SPLIT — observational only for vascular risk (headache course divides by regimen: withdrawal-interval worsening on standard pills, improvement in one small step-down-pill pilot; ischaemic-stroke risk with aura consistently increased in observational studies, relative risk up to 8.72 relative in the older meta-analysis)

title: Vaginal candidiasis in pregnancy: topical clotrimazole is effective in pregnancy trials and safer than oral fluconazole on consistent cohort evidence — but the two have never been randomised head-to-head in pregnancy
question: For vaginal candidiasis in pregnancy, is topical clotrimazole safer and as effective as oral fluconazole?
balance: POSSIBLE (topical safer; comparative effectiveness untested head-to-head in pregnancy) — observational only for the safety comparison. On effectiveness, the pregnancy trial literature supports topical treatment on its own terms: imidazoles beat nystatin (odds ratio 0.21, relative), clotrimazole beat placebo (odds ratio 0.14, relative), and 7-day courses beat 4-day courses in pregnancy (Young 2001) — but no included trial randomised topical clotrimazole against oral fluconazole in pregnancy, so 'as effective' cannot be printed as a measured result. On safety, three large cohorts point the same way with small absolute numbers: against topical azoles as comparator, oral fluconazole carried an adjusted relative risk of 1.30 (relative) for musculoskeletal malformations, about 12 extra cases per 10,000 pregnancies (Zhu 2020); against no exposure, dose-graded miscarriage odds of 2.23 at 150 mg and 3.20 above it, plus a cardiac-septal signal at high dose (Bérard 2019); and a tetralogy-of-Fallot signal (odds ratio 3.16, relative) despite an overall birth-defect null (Mølgaard-Nielsen 2013). PROPOSED POSSIBLE, as stated above: topical clotrimazole is the safer choice in pregnancy on consistent observational evidence, and it is effective in pregnancy trials — while the direct comparative-effectiveness trial does not exist in the records fetched.
stamp: POSSIBLE (topical safer; as effective untested head-to-head) — observational only for safety: topical imidazoles are effective in pregnancy trials (clotrimazole vs placebo odds ratio 0.14 relative), while oral fluconazole shows small absolute risk increases across three large cohorts (musculoskeletal adjusted relative risk 1.30 relative vs topical azoles; miscarriage odds ratio 2.23 relative at 150 mg)

title: Estrogen contraception in migraine with aura (observational only): the combined exposure carries the highest stroke odds (6.1, relative) — progestin-only methods are preferred, with headache evidence in their favour and their vascular safety unstudied rather than proven
question: In women with migraine with aura, is estrogen-containing contraception safe compared with progestin-only methods?
balance: POSSIBLE (harm for estrogen-containing methods) — observational only. The comparison this question asks for has never been run as an outcome trial, so the shelf assembles it honestly from its two sides. On the estrogen side, the signal is consistent: migraine with aura plus combined hormonal contraception carried the highest ischaemic-stroke odds in the largest study (odds ratio 6.1, relative, versus neither exposure; aura alone 2.7; Champaloux 2017), and the guidance systematic review found two- to fourfold stroke risks with combined pills in women with migraine across four studies (Tepper 2016). On the progestin-only side, that same review found no evidence at all on stroke — no studies — so 'safer' means 'no signal in an empty evidence base', not 'proven safe'. What progestin-only evidence exists is about headache: desogestrel reduced migraine frequency, intensity and triptan use in a prospective controlled study (Merki-Feld 2019) and over 180 days in a chart review (Merki-Feld 2015). Absolute context from the largest record: 11 strokes per 100,000 women aged 15–49 over the study window — relative risks multiply a rare outcome. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm) — observational only: estrogen-containing contraception is not safe to treat as risk-neutral in migraine with aura; progestin-only methods are the preferred alternative on a harm-signal asymmetry, with their own vascular safety unstudied rather than established.
stamp: POSSIBLE (harm) — observational only: estrogen-containing contraception carries the highest stroke odds in migraine with aura (odds ratio 6.1 relative for combined exposure); progestin-only methods show no stroke signal because the systematic review found no stroke studies of them — their supporting evidence is headache relief, not vascular outcomes

title: Transdermal versus oral estrogen for hot flashes: equally effective — transdermal estradiol matched oral estrogen in KEEPS and the head-to-head trials (the route made no difference to relief)
question: For menopausal hot flashes, is transdermal estradiol as effective as oral estrogen?
balance: LIKELY (equal benefit) — yes: in every carded head-to-head comparison, transdermal estradiol relieved hot flashes as effectively as oral estrogen, and the route made no difference to relief. In KEEPS (727 recently postmenopausal women), moderate-to-severe hot flashes at 6 months were 7.4% on transdermal estradiol 50 µg/day and 4.2% on oral conjugated estrogens 0.45 mg/day versus 28.3% on placebo — both routes clearly effective, not significantly different from each other, and sustained over 4 years (Santoro 2017). A double-blind, double-dummy trial in 321 highly symptomatic women found no significant differences between patch and pill at matched doses by week 12 (Good 1999). The 32-trial review's versus-placebo reductions (transdermal −22.4 versus oral estradiol −16.8 weekly flushes) did not differ significantly between agents (Nelson 2004), and the earliest patch-versus-pill studies agree (Gordon 1995). The reading is concordant non-significance across several trials rather than one formal non-inferiority trial, and it covers symptom relief only. PROPOSED LIKELY (equal benefit): transdermal estradiol is as effective as oral estrogen for menopausal hot flashes.
stamp: LIKELY (equal benefit) — transdermal estradiol matched oral estrogen for hot-flash relief in KEEPS (7.4% vs 4.2% still flushing at 6 months, vs 28.3% placebo; no significant difference between routes) and in the head-to-head trial and 32-trial review (the route made no difference)

title: Micronized progesterone and the endometrium — split by outcome: it matched synthetic progestins against hyperplasia over 3 years in PEPI (at 200 mg for 12 days a month), but a 65,630-woman cohort associates it with more endometrial cancer than synthetic derivatives, especially beyond 5 years
question: In postmenopausal women with a uterus, does micronized progesterone protect the endometrium as well as synthetic progestins?
balance: SPLIT — the answer divides by outcome and by time horizon, and the split is printed in the stamp. On the short-term histological outcome, the randomised PEPI trial found that cyclic micronized progesterone (200 mg/day for 12 days per cycle) protected the endometrium as well as either medroxyprogesterone regimen over 3 years: hyperplasia rates on all three estrogen-plus-progestogen regimens were similar to placebo, while estrogen alone produced simple hyperplasia in 27.7%, complex hyperplasia in 22.7% and atypical hyperplasia in 11.8% of women. An expert systematic review likewise concludes that oral micronized progesterone given sequentially for 12–14 days a month at 200 mg/day provides endometrial protection for up to 5 years (and that transdermal micronized progesterone does not). On the long-term cancer outcome, however, the large E3N cohort points the other way: estrogen plus micronized progesterone was associated with a higher endometrial cancer risk than never use (HR 1.80 relative), rising with duration (over 5 years HR 2.66 relative), whereas preparations containing other progesterone derivatives were not associated with increased risk (HR 0.79 relative). The cohort is observational and the doses and durations used in France may not match the PEPI regimen, but no randomised trial has followed women long enough to test the cancer outcome. PROPOSED SPLIT (short-term endometrial histology: protection comparable to synthetic progestins in a randomised trial; long-term endometrial cancer: a large cohort associates micronized progesterone — unlike synthetic derivatives — with increased risk, especially beyond 5 years).
stamp: SPLIT (short-term endometrial histology: protection comparable to synthetic progestins in a randomised trial; long-term endometrial cancer: a large cohort associates micronized progesterone — unlike synthetic derivatives — with increased risk, especially beyond 5 years)

title: Sertraline for postnatal depression during breastfeeding — split: efficacy is divided (no difference from placebo on the primary outcome; CBT beat it in a small trial), but infant exposure through milk is consistently very low (about 0.54% of the maternal dose) with no infant adverse events reported
question: In women with postnatal depression, is sertraline effective and safe during breastfeeding?
balance: SPLIT — efficacy and breastfeeding safety point in different directions and are graded separately on the face. Efficacy is divided: the one placebo-controlled trial (O'Hara 2019, 162 women, breastfeeding and non-breastfeeding) found no significant effect of sertraline on its primary outcome, the HamD-17 (the treatment made no difference on that measure), although sertraline scored better on a secondary self-report depression scale; and in a small three-arm trial (Milgrom 2015, 45 women) all groups improved but cognitive behavioural therapy alone was superior to sertraline alone at 12 weeks. Breastfeeding safety, by contrast, is consistent across the pharmacokinetic evidence: in Stowe 2003 the calculated infant dose was 0.54% of the maternal dose, sertraline itself was detectable in only 4 of 22 infants, and no adverse events were reported in any infant; a pooled analysis of 57 studies (Weissman 2004) likewise found sertraline usually produces undetectable infant levels and named it among the preferred antidepressants in breastfeeding women. That safety evidence is observational — drug-level studies, not randomised infant-outcome trials. PROPOSED SPLIT (efficacy: divided — null on the primary outcome of the one placebo-controlled trial and inferior to CBT in a small trial; breastfeeding safety: consistently very low infant exposure in observational pharmacokinetic data, with no infant adverse events reported).
stamp: SPLIT (efficacy: divided — null on the primary outcome of the one placebo-controlled trial and inferior to CBT in a small trial; breastfeeding safety: consistently very low infant exposure in observational pharmacokinetic data, with no infant adverse events reported)

title: Stopping cervical cancer screening at 65 — safe only with documented adequate prior screening and no high-risk history: a negative HPV exit test leaves a modelled lifetime risk of 1 in 6,525, versus 1 in 588 when the history is unknown
question: In women aged 65 and older, when can cervical cancer screening be safely stopped?
balance: POSSIBLE — observational and modelling evidence only (there is no randomised trial of stopping screening, and the stamp is capped accordingly). The convergent answer: screening can be stopped after age 65 in a woman who has had adequate prior screening and is not otherwise at high risk. The USPSTF (2018) recommends against screening women older than 65 who have had adequate prior screening and are not at high risk (D recommendation), and against screening after hysterectomy with removal of the cervix for non-cancer indications. The modelling evidence quantifies why an exit test matters: in Malagón 2018, a 70-year-old whose history was unknown had a remaining lifetime risk of 1 in 588 if she stopped, falling to 1 in 1,206 after a negative cytology exit test, 1 in 6,525 after a negative HPV test and 1 in 9,550 after a negative co-test — while a never-screened woman's lifetime risk was 1 in 45. The cautionary cohort (Sheu 2021) shows the flip side of the condition: among 296 women who met exit criteria but kept screening, no cervical cancer was found. The condition that does the work is documented adequate prior screening; where the history is inadequate or unknown, the evidence supports continuing (or an HPV exit test) rather than stopping on age alone. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — observational and modelling evidence only: stop at 65 when adequate prior screening is documented and the woman is not at high risk; do not stop on age alone when the screening history is inadequate or unknown.
stamp: POSSIBLE — observational and modelling evidence only: screening can be stopped at 65 when adequate prior screening is documented and the woman is not at high risk (USPSTF D recommendation against further screening in that group); a negative HPV exit test marks the lowest remaining risk (modelled 1 in 6,525 lifetime) — do not stop on age alone when the history is inadequate or unknown

title: Twice-daily PPI in childhood eosinophilic esophagitis (observational only): histological remission in about half to two-thirds of children in prospective cohorts — 68.6% responded to 8 weeks of twice-daily esomeprazole, 50.5% in the pooled literature, and a third do not respond
question: Does twice-daily proton pump inhibitor therapy heal eosinophilic esophagitis in children?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only, printed on the face: there is no placebo-controlled trial of proton pump inhibitors in children with eosinophilic esophagitis in the carded evidence. What exists is consistent prospective cohort evidence that twice-daily high-dose esomeprazole (1 mg/kg per dose) produces a histological response in about two-thirds of children with esophageal eosinophilia: 68.6% responded in Gutiérrez-Junquera 2016 (47% complete, 21.6% partial), and among children who remitted on that 8-week twice-daily trial, 70.1% remained in histological remission on once-daily maintenance at 1 year (Gutiérrez-Junquera 2018). The pooled literature (Lucendo 2016; 619 patients, 188 of them children) puts histologic remission on PPIs at 50.5% overall, with twice-daily dosing non-significantly ahead of once-daily (55.9% vs 49.7%) and no significant difference between children and adults — so 'heals' is true for roughly one-half to two-thirds of children, not all, and the twice-daily advantage over once-daily dosing is itself unproven. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: twice-daily PPI induces histological remission in about half to two-thirds of children in prospective cohorts; a substantial minority do not respond, and no randomised trial in children establishes the effect against placebo.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: twice-daily PPI (esomeprazole 1 mg/kg per dose) induced histological remission in about half to two-thirds of children in prospective cohorts (68.6% response at 8 weeks; 50.5% pooled remission), with no randomised trial in children and no significant twice-daily advantage over once-daily dosing in the pooled data

title: Group B streptococcus screening and treatment in pregnancy: yes for early-onset newborn infection — intrapartum antibiotics cut it in small trials (RR 0.17 relative) and universal screening beat risk-based care observationally (RR 0.43), but the trials are small and biased and no mortality effect is shown
question: Does screening and treatment for group B streptococcus in pregnancy reduce newborn infection?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the randomised evidence is small and at high risk of bias, and the screening-strategy evidence is observational, so the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE despite consistent direction. The treatment half of the question rests on the Cochrane review (Ohlsson 2014): in three small trials (488 infants), intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis for colonised women reduced early GBS infection with a risk ratio of 0.17 relative (risk difference −0.04; NNTB 25), but did not significantly reduce all-cause mortality or deaths from GBS or other bacteria, and the reviewers warn the result may well be due to bias. The screening half rests on a meta-analysis of 17 observational studies (Hasperhoven 2020): universal screening was associated with less early-onset GBS disease than risk-based protocols (RR 0.43 relative) and than no policy (RR 0.31 relative), while risk-based protocols did not differ significantly from no policy (RR 0.86 relative, the treatment made no significant difference), and screening was not associated with higher antibiotic use (31% vs 29%). Surveillance of 309 residual US cases (Verani 2014) found most involved implementation errors, consistent with a programme that works when delivered. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): screening-based prophylaxis is associated with substantially less early-onset newborn GBS infection, on small high-bias trials for treatment and observational comparisons for the screening strategy.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit): universal screening with intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis is associated with substantially less early-onset newborn GBS infection (treatment RR 0.17 relative in small trials; screening vs risk-based RR 0.43 relative observationally) — trial evidence small and at high risk of bias, strategy evidence observational, and no mortality effect shown

title: Rh(D) immune globulin in pregnancy: likely prevents hemolytic disease of the newborn by preventing alloimmunisation — postpartum anti-D cut alloimmunisation to RR 0.04 relative, and antenatal doses cut first-pregnancy alloimmunisation from about 1% to about 0.2%
question: Does Rh(D) immune globulin in pregnancy prevent hemolytic disease of the newborn in Rh-negative women?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — two Cochrane reviews of randomised trials point the same way, and the mechanism is direct: hemolytic disease of the newborn in a later pregnancy is caused by the maternal alloimmunisation that anti-D prevents. Postpartum anti-D (Crowther 2000; six trials, over 10,000 women) cut alloimmunisation at 6 months to a relative risk of 0.04 and in a subsequent pregnancy to 0.12 relative. Antenatal anti-D (Crowther 2013; two trials, over 4,500 women) did not reach significance on immunisation itself (RR 0.42 relative, confidence interval crossing 1) but significantly reduced positive Kleihauer tests, and the review puts the underlying risk at about 1% in a first pregnancy falling to about 0.2% with 100 µg antenatal anti-D; the antenatal programme data assembled by Urbaniak 1998 show the same gradient in first pregnancies (for example 1.6% in controls to 0.18% with a single 300 µg dose at 28 weeks). The honest limit, printed on the face: the trials measured alloimmunisation — the necessary precursor — not hemolytic disease itself, which had already become too rare to be a trial outcome. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): Rh(D) immune globulin in pregnancy (antenatal plus postpartum) prevents the alloimmunisation that causes hemolytic disease of the newborn in subsequent pregnancies.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit): Rh(D) immune globulin prevents alloimmunisation — postpartum anti-D cut it to RR 0.04 relative at 6 months (six trials, over 10,000 women) and antenatal prophylaxis reduced first-pregnancy alloimmunisation from about 1% to about 0.2% — thereby preventing hemolytic disease of the newborn in subsequent pregnancies; trials measured alloimmunisation, not hemolytic disease itself

title: MMR vaccine and autism (observational only): no association in over 1.9 million cohort children — adjusted HR 0.93 and RR 0.92, no clustering after vaccination, no risk in children with autistic siblings
question: In parents asking about timing, is the MMR vaccine associated with autism in children?
balance: POSSIBLE (no association) — observational only, printed on the face: this is an association question and every carded study is observational, so the house cap for observational evidence applies even though the cohorts are very large and closely concordant. Across more than 1.9 million children in the two Danish nationwide cohorts, MMR-vaccinated children were not more likely to be diagnosed with autism: adjusted hazard ratio 0.93 relative (Hviid 2019, 657,461 children) and relative risk 0.92 for autistic disorder and 0.83 for other autistic-spectrum disorders (Madsen 2002, 537,303 children), with no association by age at vaccination, time since vaccination, or calendar period, and no increased risk in subgroups with an autistic sibling or other risk factors. The meta-analysis (Taylor 2014; five cohort studies, 1,256,407 children) found the same: MMR and autism OR 0.84 relative (95% CI 0.70 to 1.01), vaccination and autism OR 0.99 relative. Every estimate sits at or below 1.0 with confidence intervals including 1.0 — there is no positive association to explain, and the timing pattern parents ask about (onset after vaccination) was specifically tested and not found. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (no association) — observational only: in nationwide cohorts totalling over 1.9 million children, MMR vaccination was not associated with autism (adjusted HR 0.93 relative; RR 0.92 relative), with no clustering after vaccination and no subgroup signal.
stamp: POSSIBLE (no association) — observational only: MMR vaccination was not associated with autism in nationwide cohorts of 657,461 and 537,303 children (adjusted HR 0.93 relative; RR 0.92 relative) or in a 1,256,407-child meta-analysis (OR 0.84 relative), with no clustering of diagnoses after vaccination and no increased risk in susceptible subgroups

title: Varicella at 12 months, combined or separate — split: MMRV protects as well as separate MMR + varicella injections, but doubles the relative risk of febrile seizure in the second week (1 extra seizure per 2,300 first doses)
question: Should children receive the varicella vaccine at 12 months or as part of MMRV?
balance: SPLIT — both options give varicella at 12 months; the real choice is one combined injection (MMRV) versus two separate injections (MMR + varicella at the same visit), and the evidence splits cleanly between equal protection and unequal side effects. Protection is equal: in the immunogenicity trial (Lieberman 2006, 3,928 children), MMRV induced responses comparable to MMR + varicella for all four antigens, with 1-year antibody persistence above 95% for each. Fever and febrile seizure are not equal: fever of 38.9 °C or more was more frequent after MMRV in that trial (39.1% vs 33.1%), and in the large Vaccine Safety Datalink cohorts the risk of febrile seizure 7–10 days after the first dose was about double after MMRV (Klein 2010: RR 1.98 relative; excess 4.3 per 10,000 doses — one additional febrile seizure for every 2,300 doses instead of separate vaccines), a finding Klein 2015 confirmed while finding no significant difference in seven other serious outcomes. So the trade-off is convenience (one fewer injection) against a small absolute increase in febrile seizures, most of which are brief and benign but frightening; the carded evidence supports either choice and quantifies the difference rather than dictating it. PROPOSED SPLIT (protection: equal — comparable immunogenicity and persistence; safety: MMRV carries about twice the relative risk of febrile seizure 7–10 days after the first dose, an excess of 4.3 per 10,000 doses, versus separate MMR + varicella).
stamp: SPLIT (protection: equal — MMRV immunogenicity and 1-year persistence comparable to separate MMR + varicella; safety: MMRV carries about twice the relative risk of febrile seizure 7–10 days after the first dose, RR 1.98 relative, an excess of 4.3 per 10,000 doses or 1 extra seizure per 2,300 doses)

title: Vitamin D on enzyme-inducing antiseizure drugs: deficiency in 54% (vs 37% on non-inducing drugs), supplementation prevents the fall — monitor and supplement when low; fracture benefit untested
question: Should vitamin D be monitored and supplemented in people taking enzyme-inducing antiseizure drugs?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). Deficiency is common and measurably worse on enzyme-inducing drugs: in 596 adults with epilepsy, vitamin D deficiency (under 20 ng/mL) was present in 54% of the enzyme-inducing group versus 37% of the non-enzyme-inducing group (Teagarden 2014). The one randomised supplementation trial carded (Viraraghavan 2019, 83 children newly started on antiepileptic drugs) shows the fall is preventable: without supplementation mean 25(OH)D fell significantly over 6 months (18 to 13 ng/mL), while monthly vitamin D3 maintained levels (25 to 26 ng/mL; between-group P = 0.005). A 2024 Epilepsia narrative review (Sourbron 2024) concludes regular vitamin D measurement is a cost-effective, practical monitoring method in people with epilepsy, with densitometry added in high-risk patients, but states there is not enough evidence to advocate continuous supplementation in everyone. No carded trial tests fractures or other clinical endpoints, so the case rests on deficiency prevalence plus a biochemical prevention trial. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): monitor vitamin D in people on enzyme-inducing antiseizure drugs and supplement when low — deficiency is frequent and drug-related, and supplementation prevents the measured fall, but clinical-outcome benefit is untested.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit): vitamin D deficiency is common on enzyme-inducing antiseizure drugs (54% vs 37% on non-inducing drugs in 596 adults) and a small randomised trial shows supplementation prevents the fall in levels — monitor and supplement when low; clinical-outcome (fracture) benefit is untested
