title: Bypass vs angioplasty below the knee — SPLIT: endovascular-first won on amputation-free survival in BASIL-2, vein bypass wins on patency in pooled series
question: Is bypass surgery better than angioplasty for infrapopliteal disease?
balance: SPLIT — the randomised trial and the patency literature point in opposite directions, and the split is named in the stamp. BASIL-2 (345 patients randomised to vein bypass-first or best endovascular-first for infrapopliteal chronic limb-threatening ischaemia) found amputation-free survival was WORSE with bypass-first: the primary outcome occurred in 63% versus 53% (adjusted HR 1.35, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.80), driven by more deaths (53% versus 45%). Against that, the pooled prospective literature finds vein grafts stay open longest: infrapopliteal great saphenous vein primary patency 87% at 1 year and 78% at 2 years, above all other interventions, while survival, major amputation and amputation-free survival at 2 years were broadly similar between endovascular treatment and vein bypass (Almasri 2019, 44 studies, 8,602 patients); and Romiti 2008 found crural angioplasty limb salvage (82.4% at 36 months) equivalent to bypass despite lower patency. So: bypass is not better on the trial's patient-centred outcome, and endovascular-first is not better on durability. PROPOSED SPLIT (trial outcome: endovascular-first; graft patency: vein bypass): for infrapopliteal disease, bypass-first did not improve amputation-free survival in BASIL-2, while vein grafts show the highest patency in pooled series.
stamp: SPLIT (amputation-free survival in the RCT: endovascular-first better; graft patency in pooled series: vein bypass better): bypass-first did not improve amputation-free survival in BASIL-2 (63% vs 53% primary outcome, adjusted HR 1.35), while vein grafts show the highest infrapopliteal patency (87% at 1 year)

title: Preoperative BNP improves risk prediction (observational only): pooled OR 19.3 for 30-day events and 58% net reclassification over the RCRI — prediction proven, BNP-guided care untested
question: Does a preoperative BNP test improve risk prediction before major surgery?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only, printed on the face: every carded study is a prognostic cohort or a meta-analysis of cohorts; no trial has tested BNP-guided management. The association is strong and independent: pooled across 9 studies (3,281 patients), an elevated preoperative BNP or NT-proBNP carried an odds ratio of 19.3 (95% CI 8.5 to 43.7) for 30-day cardiovascular events (Karthikeyan 2009). The added value over clinical scoring is directly measured in the individual-patient meta-analysis (850 vascular patients): BNP above its optimal cut point (116 pg/mL) independently predicted cardiac death or nonfatal MI (OR 7.9, 95% CI 4.7 to 13.3), and adding it to the Revised Cardiac Risk Index improved reclassification in all risk groups (net reclassification improvement 58%; 84% in the intermediate-risk group) (Rodseth 2011). Biccard 2012 adds that, once BNP strata are known, RCRI factors add nothing further (BNP intermediate OR 5.1; high-risk OR 25). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: yes, a preoperative BNP improves risk prediction beyond clinical scores, on consistent cohort evidence; whether acting on it improves outcomes is untested.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: preoperative BNP independently predicts perioperative cardiac events (pooled OR 19.3) and improves on the Revised Cardiac Risk Index (net reclassification improvement 58%, 84% in intermediate risk); no trial has tested BNP-guided management

title: Radioiodine vs surgery in toxic multinodular goiter (indirect evidence only): radioiodine preserves long-term euthyroidism in roughly 27–59% depending on dose — no head-to-head trial exists
question: In adults with toxic multinodular goiter, is radioactive iodine better than surgery for long-term hypothyroidism-free survival?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — indirect evidence only, printed on the face: no head-to-head trial of radioiodine versus surgery for this outcome was found in the records fetched this session, so the comparison is assembled from each treatment's own literature. After radioiodine, a substantial minority stay off thyroid hormone long term: in the Azizi 2019 randomised trial's radioiodine arm, 37% were euthyroid and 41% hypothyroid at 60–100 months; with a calculated-dose regimen, Kahraman 2012 found hypothyroidism in 73% by the end of up to 8 years of follow-up, so the radioiodine figure depends heavily on dose strategy. Total thyroidectomy, the definitive surgical option, removes the whole gland — the surgical meta-analysis carded (Bharath 2023) compares total with less-than-total thyroidectomy on recurrence and complications and reports no hypothyroidism rates, printed plainly on its card; a total thyroidectomy leaves no thyroid tissue to sustain hormone-free survival, while less-than-total surgery trades a chance of remaining euthyroid against recurrence and re-operation. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — indirect evidence only: radioiodine preserves a real chance of long-term hypothyroidism-free survival (roughly 27–59% across the carded series) that total thyroidectomy does not, but no direct comparison exists.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — indirect evidence only: radioiodine leaves roughly 27–59% of patients euthyroid long term (dose-dependent: 41% hypothyroid at 60–100 months in one trial arm; 73% with a 150 Gy regimen), a chance total thyroidectomy does not offer; no head-to-head trial versus surgery exists

title: Preoperative oral supplements before major surgery: complications roughly halved in pooled GI-cancer trials (relative risk 0.53) — major-complication benefit unproven
question: In adults undergoing major surgery, does preoperative oral nutritional supplementation reduce complications in malnourished patients versus no supplementation?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). The strongest carded synthesis is in gastrointestinal cancer surgery in low- and middle-income countries (Knight 2022: 7 randomised trials, 891 patients), where preoperative oral nutritional supplementation roughly halved complications — relative risk 0.53 (95% CI 0.46 to 0.60) for all postoperative surgical complications, 0.52 for infection, and 0.35 for all-cause mortality, with an absolute risk reduction of 0.14 (number needed to treat 7) for all complications. The individual trials are consistent in direction but smaller and softer: Smedley 2004 (179 randomised, lower gastrointestinal surgery) found significantly fewer minor complications with supplements before and after surgery but no difference in major complications; Kabata 2015 (102 patients) found significantly more serious complications in the unsupplemented control group — in patients who were NOT malnourished at entry, printed on its card. No carded trial isolates preoperative-only supplementation in strictly malnourished patients across major surgery generally, so the malnourished-specific claim rests mainly on the Knight meta-analysis population. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): preoperative oral supplementation reduces postoperative complications, with the clearest numbers in gastrointestinal cancer surgery; the effect on major complications is unproven.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit): preoperative oral supplementation reduced postoperative complications in pooled gastrointestinal-cancer trials (relative risk 0.53; absolute risk reduction 0.14, NNT 7), with individual trials agreeing on minor/serious complications but showing no difference in major complications

title: Surgery vs radioiodine for compressive goiter symptoms — MAYBE (weak evidence): both relieve symptoms in separate uncontrolled series; never compared head-to-head
question: In adults with multinodular goiter and compressive symptoms, is surgery better than radioactive iodine for symptom relief?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — no head-to-head comparison exists in the records fetched this session; each treatment's symptom relief is documented only in its own series, printed as such. Radioiodine: in Duick 2004, all 30 patients with symptomatic toxic or nontoxic multinodular goiter experienced symptomatic relief by 1–2 months after rhTSH-aided radioiodine; the Cochrane review of rhTSH-aided radioiodine (6 RCTs, 321 participants) found greater thyroid volume reduction than radioiodine alone (mean difference 11.9%) at the cost of more hypothyroidism (relative risk 2.53). Surgery: in Shires 2021, 60 patients undergoing thyroidectomy for benign goiter improved significantly on breathlessness, dysphagia and all 11 ThyPRO quality-of-life domains after surgery — the improvement concentrated in obese patients, who started worst. Neither literature measures the other treatment, and compressive-symptom patients are exactly those often steered to surgery, so the series are not comparable. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): both surgery and radioiodine relieve compressive symptoms in their own series; whether surgery is better is untested head-to-head.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence): surgery and radioiodine each relieve compressive symptoms in their own uncontrolled series (relief in all 30 radioiodine patients; significant post-thyroidectomy gains in breathlessness, dysphagia and quality of life) — no head-to-head comparison exists

title: Earlier cataract surgery vs waiting: vision improves sooner (OR 7.22 for acuity gain) — quality-of-life benefit inferred, falls benefit unproven
question: In adults with cataracts, does surgery at an earlier stage improve quality of life compared with waiting?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). The timing trials are small but point the same way: a meta-analysis of expedited versus routine cataract surgery (Desapriya 2010) found expedited surgery increased the odds of improved visual acuity more than seven-fold (OR 7.22, 95% CI 3.16 to 16.55), while the pooled falls result — the outcome patients fear most from waiting — was a non-significant reduction (OR 0.81, 95% CI 0.55 to 1.17, 2 RCTs, 535 participants), i.e. the treatment made no proven difference to falls. The Cochrane review of immediate versus 6-month-delayed surgery in patients with cataract and age-related macular degeneration (Casparis 2017, 2 RCTs, 114 participants) found better best-corrected visual acuity at 6 months with immediate surgery (mean difference −0.15 logMAR, 95% CI −0.28 to −0.02, moderate-certainty evidence). Quality of life itself is barely moved by timing in the carded evidence: in the 3,787-patient Quintana 2011 cohort, waiting over 5 months meant smaller visual-acuity gains than waiting under 3 months (P = .0348), but waiting time did not significantly influence VF-14 quality-of-life gains or complications — the benefit shown is better vision sooner, during the months waiting would otherwise spend impaired. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): earlier surgery improves vision sooner; a quality-of-life advantage is plausible and consistent with the acuity data but thinly measured, and no falls benefit is proven.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit): earlier (expedited/immediate) cataract surgery improves visual acuity sooner than waiting (OR 7.22 for acuity improvement; −0.15 logMAR at 6 months) — quality-of-life benefit is inferred from acuity, and no falls benefit is proven (OR 0.81, not significant)

title: Screening relatives for bicuspid aortic valve (observational only): echocardiography finds it in 6.6–14% of first-degree relatives — detection proven, outcome benefit modelled only
question: Does screening echocardiography detect bicuspid aortic valve disease in first-degree relatives?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only, printed on the face: detection yield is a cohort measurement, not a randomised comparison, and no trial shows screening changes outcomes. The yield is consistent and far above population background: bicuspid aortic valve was diagnosed in 14% of screened first-degree relatives in the Tessler 2022 family cohort, and in 6.6% of 482 screened first-degree relatives in the paediatric-cardiology programme of Massardier 2020 (which also found aortic valve dysfunction in 5.4% and ascending aorta dilatation in 2.9%). A cost-effectiveness model built on these yields (Tessler 2021) found screening dominant — more effective and less costly than no screening, saving €644 with a 0.3 quality-adjusted life-year gain — but that is a model, not an observed outcome. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: yes, screening echocardiography detects bicuspid aortic valve in roughly 1 in 7 to 1 in 15 first-degree relatives; whether detection improves their outcomes is untested in a trial.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: screening echocardiography detects bicuspid aortic valve in 6.6–14% of first-degree relatives (plus aortic dilatation in 2.9%); a model finds screening cost-saving, but no trial shows detection improves outcomes

title: Ambulatory monitoring in suspected white coat hypertension — MAYBE (weak evidence) for changing outcomes: it reclassifies patients and refines prognosis, but no trial tests monitoring-guided care
question: Does ambulatory blood pressure monitoring change outcomes in suspected white coat hypertension?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — for the question as asked. No carded trial randomises patients with suspected white coat hypertension to ambulatory monitoring versus office-only care and measures events; what monitoring demonstrably changes is classification and predicted risk, not proven outcomes. Office measurement agrees poorly with 24-hour ambulatory monitoring (accuracy 54.8%, specificity 31.9% in 569 primary-care patients; Grezzana 2017), so monitoring reclassifies a large share of suspected cases. The reclassified groups genuinely differ in prognosis: untreated white coat hypertension carried higher cardiovascular risk than normotension in two meta-analyses (hazard ratio 1.36 for cardiovascular events and 2.09 for cardiovascular mortality, Cohen 2019; 38% relative increase in cardiovascular disease in untreated cohorts, Huang 2017), while treated white coat effect showed no significant excess risk — meaning ambulatory confirmation separates people who need follow-up from people who may not need treatment escalation. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): ambulatory monitoring changes who is labelled hypertensive and refines prognosis on consistent observational evidence, but whether it changes hard outcomes has never been tested in a trial.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence): ambulatory monitoring reclassifies suspected white coat hypertension (office accuracy only 54.8%) and the confirmed group carries higher risk if untreated (HR 1.36 for events), but no trial shows monitoring-guided care changes hard outcomes

title: Survivorship mammography after breast cancer: annual mammography is the schedule the evidence was built on — observational data link each additional surveillance mammogram to lower breast cancer mortality, and no trial supports stretching the interval
question: In women who have completed breast cancer treatment, how often should mammography be done for survivorship screening?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only for the mortality association, printed on the face. No randomised trial has compared annual with less frequent surveillance mammography after breast cancer treatment. What the trials do show is that follow-up built on regular examination and yearly mammography is as effective as more intensive follow-up (Cochrane, Moschetti 2016: overall survival HR 0.98, 95% CI 0.84 to 1.15, in 2,563 women — the more intensive approach made no difference). The mortality case for surveillance itself is observational: each additional surveillance mammogram was associated with a 0.69-fold decrease in the odds of breast cancer mortality in older survivors (Lash 2007), and the association persisted, weaker and non-significant, beyond five years (IRR 0.82, 95% CI 0.56–1.19; Buist 2013). A modelling study estimates mammography's preclinical detectable phase at 35 months (Aarts 2019), which is why longer intervals are discussed — but the authors themselves say studies are needed before a longer interval can be recommended. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: annual mammography is the survivorship schedule the evidence was built on; a longer interval is a hypothesis, not a tested alternative.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only for the mortality association: annual surveillance mammography after treatment is the schedule tested in follow-up trials and linked in cohort data to lower breast cancer mortality; no randomised trial has compared annual with less frequent mammography

title: Combined pill versus progestin-only pill and venous thromboembolism (observational only): combined pills raised VTE risk about 3- to 7-fold versus non-use in two large studies, while oral progestin-only pills showed no increase (relative risk 1.06, not significant)
question: Does the combined oral contraceptive pill increase venous thromboembolism risk compared with the progestin-only pill?
balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — observational only, printed on the face; there is no randomised evidence for this question and the comparison is indirect. Two large observational anchors agree that combined oral contraceptives raise venous thromboembolism risk several-fold versus non-use: relative risks of 2.9 to 6.6 by progestogen in the Danish national cohort (Lidegaard 2011; absolute risk about 10 per 10,000 women-years in the higher-risk group) and an odds ratio of 5.0 in the MEGA case-control study (van Hylckama Vlieg 2009). Against the same non-user reference, the oral progestin-only pill shows no increase: the Danish cohort found no increased risk with progestogen-only pills, and a 19-study meta-analysis gives a pooled relative risk of 1.06 (95% CI 0.70–1.62) for oral progestin-only contraception (Glisic 2018) — while noting injectable progestin-only contraception did show an increase (relative risk 2.62) and is a different method. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm) — observational only: the combined pill increases venous thromboembolism risk compared with the (oral) progestin-only pill.
stamp: POSSIBLE (harm) — observational only: combined oral contraceptives are associated with a several-fold higher venous thromboembolism risk than non-use, whereas oral progestin-only pills are not associated with increased risk, so the combined pill carries the higher risk in an indirect comparison through non-users

title: How long can menopausal hormone therapy continue? (evidence types on the face: two randomised trials and one observational meta-analysis) — no duration is proven risk-free: breast cancer risk rises steadily with years of use, while 18-year mortality in the WHI trials was neutral
question: How long can menopausal hormone therapy be safely continued in women who started before age 60?
balance: SPLIT — by regimen, named here and in the stamp; evidence types are labelled on each card's face (randomised trials versus observational meta-analysis), as this question requires. The randomised WHI evidence is reassuring on the hardest endpoint: after median treatment durations of 5.6 years (oestrogen plus progestagen) and 7.2 years (oestrogen alone), all-cause, cardiovascular and cancer mortality over 18 years were neutral (pooled HR 0.99; Manson 2017). But the same trials split on breast cancer over 20+ years (Chlebowski 2020): oestrogen alone was associated with lower incidence (HR 0.78) and mortality (HR 0.60) in women with hysterectomy, while oestrogen plus progestagen raised incidence (HR 1.28). The observational duration evidence (Collaborative Group 2019) is the direct answer to 'how long': breast cancer relative risk rises steadily with years of use — 1.60 in years 1–4 and 2.08 in years 5–14 for oestrogen-progestagen — and some excess persists for more than 10 years after stopping, scaled by how long therapy was used. No carded study randomised duration or proves any number of years 'safe'; the honest statement is that risk accumulates with duration for combined therapy while trial mortality stayed neutral at the durations tested. PROPOSED SPLIT (oestrogen-only: lower breast cancer incidence and mortality in the WHI trial; oestrogen plus progestagen: higher breast cancer incidence, rising with duration) — all-cause mortality neutral over 18 years in both trials; no duration of combined therapy is shown to be free of breast cancer risk.
stamp: SPLIT (oestrogen-only: lower breast cancer incidence and mortality in the WHI trial; oestrogen plus progestagen: higher breast cancer incidence, rising with duration) — all-cause mortality neutral over 18 years in both trials; no duration of combined therapy is shown to be free of breast cancer risk

title: Antidepressants while breastfeeding (observational exposure evidence only): sertraline and paroxetine were undetectable in infant serum in the comparative study, citalopram was low, and fluoxetine carries the one growth signal — exposure data, not infant-outcome trials
question: Which antidepressants are safest to use while breastfeeding?
balance: POSSIBLE (safest-exposure ranking) — observational only, printed on the face. This shelf answers the comparative class question; the sertraline-specific evidence is homed on shelf #5734 (sertraline as the preferred antidepressant during breastfeeding) and shelf #5770 (sertraline for postnatal depression during breastfeeding), whose carded reports (PMIDs 15169695, 12590627, 25589155) are cross-pointed here and deliberately not re-carded. On the free comparative evidence carded here, the ranking is consistent: in the head-to-head exposure study, sertraline and paroxetine were undetectable in infant serum while venlafaxine was measurable in all exposed infants and citalopram was undetectable or low (Berle 2004); SSRI milk transfer overall was low (median relative infant dose 1.5%) with differences among drugs (Pogliani 2019); paroxetine-exposed infants grew normally to 12 months (Merlob 2004). The caution end is fluoxetine, the one agent with an adverse signal — a 392 g average growth deficit in exposed infants (Chambers 1999) — compounded by its long half-life, which the exposure literature consistently flags. All of this is small observational and pharmacokinetic evidence, not infant-outcome trials. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (safest-exposure ranking) — observational only: sertraline and paroxetine are the safest-supported choices while breastfeeding; fluoxetine is the one to avoid where an alternative exists.
stamp: POSSIBLE (safest-exposure ranking) — observational only: sertraline and paroxetine show the lowest measured infant exposure and fluoxetine the most concerning signal, but all carded evidence is small pharmacokinetic or cohort data with no randomised infant-outcome comparison

title: Foam dressings for pressure ulcers: no proven advantage over simple dressings — healing comparisons against basic contact dressings and hydrocolloids are all non-significant on very low-certainty evidence
question: In adults with pressure ulcers, are advanced foam dressings better than simple dressings for healing?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the honest answer is that superiority is unproven, stated plainly. The direct randomised comparisons of foam against simple dressings do not show better healing: versus basic wound contact dressings the pooled healing risk ratios were 1.33 (95% CI 0.62 to 2.88) short term and 1.17 (0.79 to 1.72) medium term, and versus hydrocolloid dressings 0.85 (0.54 to 1.34) — every interval crosses no-effect and the Cochrane reviewers graded the certainty very low (Walker 2017). Network meta-analyses lean favourable — foam versus saline gauze RR 1.52 (1.03 to 2.26) in Westby 2017 and foam versus hydroactive dressings RR 1.18 (0.95 to 1.48) in Furuya-Kanamori 2019 — but both sets of authors warn that the networks are sparse, the trials small and biased, and rankings unreliable. Where a comparison is null it is stated as such: on the direct evidence, foam made no proven difference to healing. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — foam dressings have not been shown to heal pressure ulcers better than simple dressings.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — foam dressings have not been shown to heal pressure ulcers better than simple dressings: pooled healing risk ratios versus basic wound contact dressings were 1.33 and 1.17 (both not significant) on very low-certainty evidence

title: When to stop mammography screening: routine biennial screening is recommended to age 74 — beyond 75 there are no trial data, mixed observational results, and consistent evidence of rising overdiagnosis
question: At what age should average-risk women stop routine mammography screening?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — because the question's honest answer is a boundary, not a tested age. The trial evidence for screening mammography runs to about age 69–74: the 2009 USPSTF review found mortality reduction for ages 39 to 69 with data lacking at 70 and older (Nelson 2009), and the 2024 USPSTF statement recommends biennial screening for women aged 40 to 74 while issuing an I statement — evidence insufficient — for women 75 and older (USPSTF 2024). Beyond 75, the dedicated systematic review found mixed mortality results, mixed false-positive findings, and consistently increased overdiagnosis across 36 studies (Mathieu 2024); modelling studies price continuation to 75 or 80 at $34,000–$88,000 per life-year gained but captured none of the harms fully (Mandelblatt 2003). So routine screening stopping at 74/75 is where the evidence stops; continuing beyond it is an individual judgement for women in good health, not an evidence-based default. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — for stopping at 74/75: no trial evidence establishes benefit beyond 74, and the balance at older ages is undetermined.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — for stopping at 74/75: the recommendation to screen to 74 rests on trials that included women only up to their early 70s; for women 75 and older the evidence is insufficient to determine the balance of benefits and harms, so there is no evidence-proven stopping age, only a boundary of the evidence at 74

title: Brief clinician advice helps smokers quit: physician brief advice raised quitting by a relative 66% (about 1–3 extra quitters per 100 advised) across 17 trials, with concordant Cochrane evidence for nurses and motivational interviewing
question: Does a brief intervention from a primary care clinician help adults who smoke quit?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — three concordant Cochrane meta-analyses of randomised trials support it, which is the standard this library requires for LIKELY. The direct evidence is the physician-advice review (Stead 2013): brief advice versus no advice gave a relative risk of quitting of 1.66 (95% CI 1.42 to 1.94) across 17 trials — a relative measure that the reviewers translate honestly into about 1 to 3 extra quitters per 100 people advised, on an unassisted quit rate of 2 to 3%. The effect is a class effect of clinician intervention rather than one profession's trick: nurse-delivered interventions gave RR 1.29 (1.20 to 1.39; Rice 2013) and motivational interviewing beat even brief advice or usual care, RR 1.26 (1.16 to 1.36; Lindson-Hawley 2015). Intensity adds little — direct comparison of intensive versus minimal advice gave RR 1.37 — which is precisely why the brief form is worth doing. No mortality benefit is claimed: the one study that looked found no significant difference at 20 years. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) — brief advice from a clinician increases quitting (relative risk 1.66; about 1–3 extra quitters per 100 advised).
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — brief advice from a clinician increases quitting (physician advice relative risk 1.66, an absolute gain of about 1–3 percentage points), supported by three concordant Cochrane meta-analyses of randomised trials

title: Treating asymptomatic candiduria: fluconazole clears the urine at 14 days (50% versus 29%) but cultures are equal again two weeks later, and no study shows a clinical outcome benefit — treatment made no difference to recurrence, candidemia or mortality
question: Does treating asymptomatic candiduria improve outcomes in hospitalized adults?
balance: POSSIBLE (no benefit) — anchored on the one randomised trial, with concordant observational follow-up. Sobel 2000 randomised 316 hospitalised patients with asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic candiduria to fluconazole or placebo: urine clearance at day 14 favoured fluconazole (50% versus 29%, P < .001), but cultures two weeks after therapy showed similar candiduria rates in treated and untreated patients, and the authors state eradication was not associated with clinical benefit — the treatment made no difference to anything durable. The observational record points the same way: treated asymptomatic patients were more likely to have later positive cultures over up to 48 months of follow-up, with candidemia rare and never attributed to the candiduria (Revankar 2011), and recurrence, mortality and length of stay were similar whether care followed IDSA guidance or not (He 2021). Treating is therefore exposure to an antifungal for a transient laboratory effect. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (no benefit) — treating asymptomatic candiduria clears the urine short-term but improves no clinical outcome in any carded study.
stamp: POSSIBLE (no benefit) — the one randomised trial shows short-term urine clearance without durable or clinical benefit (the treatment made no difference to candiduria rates two weeks after therapy), and cohort follow-up finds no outcome advantage for treated patients

title: Empagliflozin in chronic HFmrEF: the mildly-reduced subgroup benefits like the preserved group — pooled HFmrEF hazard ratio 0.77 for cardiovascular death or heart failure hospitalisation, driven by fewer hospitalisations
question: Does empagliflozin improve outcomes in heart failure with mildly reduced ejection fraction (HFmrEF)?
balance: PARTIAL completion: live shelf #1574 covers empagliflozin started in hospital for acute heart failure (the EMPULSE question); this shelf covers the uncovered slice — chronic heart failure with mildly reduced ejection fraction (HFmrEF, ejection fraction 41–49%). The empagliflozin trial that enrolled this population, EMPEROR-Preserved, is homed on its own shelf and is not re-carded here; this shelf is built on free reports that separate the HFmrEF slice. A meta-analysis separating the ejection-fraction bands found the HFmrEF subgroup (n = 4,555) benefited at least as much as the preserved group (hazard ratio 0.77 for cardiovascular death or heart failure hospitalisation; Banerjee 2023). The prespecified five-trial Lancet meta-analysis found the composite benefit in the mildly-reduced/preserved trials (hazard ratio 0.80 among 12,251 participants) was consistent across ejection-fraction subgroups, with the effect carried mainly by fewer heart failure hospitalisations (hazard ratio 0.74) rather than cardiovascular death (0.88, confidence interval touching 1.00) (Vaduganathan 2022). Within EMPEROR-Preserved itself, empagliflozin's outcome benefit was consistent across baseline health-status tertiles and health status improved modestly (Butler 2022). The honest limits: no trial has randomised HFmrEF patients alone, the mortality component is not separately significant, and the empagliflozin-specific evidence is one trial programme. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — empagliflozin improves the composite outcome in chronic HFmrEF, driven by fewer heart failure hospitalisations; capped at POSSIBLE because the empagliflozin evidence is a single trial programme read through its mildly-reduced subgroup.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — empagliflozin's HFmrEF evidence is the mildly-reduced subgroup of a single trial programme (EMPEROR-Preserved, homed elsewhere) plus concordant class-level pooling that separates HFmrEF (hazard ratio 0.77); a single trial programme caps this shelf at POSSIBLE

title: CRT in HFrEF with LBBB: survival and hospitalisation benefit is concentrated in left bundle branch block — composite events cut by about a third (relative risk 0.64), and by 44% at QRS ≥150 ms — with no benefit in non-LBBB morphologies
question: Does cardiac resynchronization therapy improve survival in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction and left bundle branch block?
balance: PARTIAL completion: live shelf #274 covers cardiac resynchronization therapy in wide QRS generally; this shelf covers the uncovered slice — the left bundle branch block (LBBB) population specifically, where the wide-QRS average conceals a morphology split. Trial-level meta-analysis found CRT reduced composite adverse clinical events in LBBB (relative risk 0.64) but made no difference in non-LBBB conduction abnormalities (relative risk 0.97, the treatment made no difference), with a highly significant difference between morphologies (Sipahi 2012). Patient-level pooling of eight pivotal trials (6,264 patients; 4,549 with LBBB) found the same pattern for heart failure hospitalisation or death — hazard ratio 0.56 in LBBB with QRS ≥150 ms, no significant association at QRS <150 ms or in right bundle branch block — with similar relationships for all-cause death alone (Friedman 2023). Long-term MADIT-CRT follow-up in LBBB patients showed an approximately 60% relative reduction in heart failure events in both US and European cohorts and a significant 38% relative mortality reduction in the US cohort (Biton 2015), and a dedicated non-LBBB meta-analysis confirms the null on the other side of the split (Cunnington 2015). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) — CRT improves survival-relevant outcomes in HFrEF with LBBB, most clearly at QRS ≥150 ms; the LBBB slice, not wide QRS alone, is where the benefit lives.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — in HFrEF with LBBB, cardiac resynchronization therapy reduces death or heart failure hospitalisation across concordant trial-level and patient-level meta-analyses; the benefit is morphology-specific and is not seen in non-LBBB wide QRS

title: ICD in nonischemic cardiomyopathy — SPLIT over time: older trials and their meta-analysis show lower all-cause mortality (hazard ratio 0.75), but DANISH's 13-year follow-up shows no all-cause mortality reduction (0.96) while sudden-death protection persists (0.54)
question: Does an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator reduce mortality in nonischemic cardiomyopathy?
balance: PARTIAL completion: live shelf #90 is the broader prophylactic ICD shelf; this shelf covers the uncovered slice — the nonischemic population specifically. The slice's largest trial, DANISH, is homed on the broader shelf and is not re-carded here; this shelf is built on free reports, including DANISH's own extended follow-up. The older randomised evidence favours the ICD: DEFINITE, in nonischemic dilated cardiomyopathy, cut sudden arrhythmic death sharply (hazard ratio 0.20) with a non-significant all-cause mortality trend (0.65) (Kadish 2004), and pooling the four pre-DANISH trials (1,874 patients) gave a significant all-cause mortality reduction (hazard ratio 0.75) (Al-Khatib 2017). Against that, DANISH's extended follow-up to a median 13.2 years found all-cause mortality essentially identical (52.9% versus 53.4%; hazard ratio 0.96 — the treatment made no difference to overall survival) while sudden cardiovascular death remained halved (hazard ratio 0.54), with the sudden-death benefit confined to patients aged 70 or younger (Butt 2025). The split is real and is named in the stamp: as background therapy improved and follow-up lengthened, preventing arrhythmic death stopped translating into longer overall survival in this population. PROPOSED SPLIT (older randomised evidence: benefit; DANISH long-term: no all-cause benefit, sudden-death benefit persists).
stamp: SPLIT (older randomised evidence: benefit on all-cause mortality; DANISH long-term follow-up: no all-cause mortality benefit, sudden-death benefit persists) — an ICD reliably prevents sudden arrhythmic death in nonischemic cardiomyopathy, but whether it prolongs overall survival divides by era and follow-up length

title: Early SGLT2 inhibitor initiation in acute heart failure: starting before or just after discharge is associated with fewer deaths (odds ratio 0.71) and fewer heart failure rehospitalisations (0.73) across 7 randomised trials — safety event rates were too low to judge
question: Does early initiation of an SGLT2 inhibitor during acute heart failure improve outcomes?
balance: PARTIAL completion: live shelf #70 covers SGLT2 inhibitors in established (chronic) heart failure, and live shelf #1574 covers empagliflozin started in hospitalised acute heart failure; this shelf covers the uncovered slice — the timing question itself: starting an SGLT2 inhibitor early, during the acute admission or immediately after it, across agents. The two big acute-setting trials' primary reports are homed on those shelves and are not re-carded here; this shelf is built on free reports. A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis of early initiation (before or within 3 days after discharge) across 7 randomised trials and 2,320 patients found lower all-cause death (odds ratio 0.71) and fewer heart failure rehospitalisations (odds ratio 0.73), with consistent results when initiation was before discharge — but safety outcomes could not be usefully determined because events were few (Cherbi 2025). The earliest pilot, EMPA-RESPONSE-AHF, found no difference on its primary symptom and diuretic outcomes (the treatment made no difference on dyspnoea score, diuretic response, NT-proBNP or length of stay) yet fewer combined worsening-heart-failure events at 60 days (Damman 2020). Programme secondary reports point the same way: empagliflozin improved symptoms and quality of life from day 15 in EMPULSE (Kosiborod 2022), and sotagliflozin increased days alive and out of hospital in SOLOIST-WHF, driven by fewer days dead (Szarek 2021). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — early initiation improves outcomes; the stamp is capped because the pooled timing evidence leans on small trials and its safety side is unresolved.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — early initiation in acute heart failure reduces death and rehospitalisation in a 7-trial meta-analysis, concordant with the acute-HF trial programmes homed elsewhere; capped at POSSIBLE because the timing-specific pooling rests substantially on small trials and safety outcomes could not be determined

title: Edoxaban versus warfarin in elderly AF: in patients aged 75 or older, major bleeding was lower with edoxaban (hazard ratio 0.83) with a larger absolute gain than in younger patients (−82 events per 10,000 patient-years; intracranial haemorrhage −73)
question: Does edoxaban reduce bleeding compared with warfarin in elderly patients with atrial fibrillation?
balance: PARTIAL completion: live shelf #2447 covers edoxaban versus a vitamin K antagonist only after transcatheter aortic valve implantation; this shelf covers the uncovered slice — general elderly patients with atrial fibrillation. The ENGAGE AF-TIMI 48 primary report is homed elsewhere in the library and is not re-carded here; this shelf is built on its prespecified elderly analysis and on the very-elderly ELDERCARE-AF programme. In ENGAGE, bleeding rates on warfarin climbed steeply with age (major bleeding 1.8%, 3.3% and 4.8% across the <65, 65–74 and ≥75 groups), and in the ≥75 group (n = 8,474) edoxaban significantly reduced major bleeding versus warfarin (hazard ratio 0.83) while stroke prevention was similar (hazard ratio 0.83, not significant), with absolute gains favouring edoxaban of 82 fewer major bleeds and 73 fewer intracranial haemorrhages per 10,000 patient-years (Kato 2016). The very-elderly evidence answers a neighbouring question — in patients aged 80 or older judged unsuitable for standard anticoagulation, 15 mg edoxaban prevented stroke versus placebo without a significant major-bleeding increase (Okumura 2020), consistently across the 80–84, 85–89 and ≥90 strata (Kuroda 2022) — which bounds the bleeding concern at the oldest ages but does not itself compare against warfarin. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — edoxaban bleeds less than warfarin in elderly AF; capped at POSSIBLE because the warfarin comparison rests on one trial programme.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in elderly patients with atrial fibrillation, edoxaban reduces major bleeding compared with warfarin (hazard ratio 0.83 at age ≥75, with greater absolute benefit at older ages); a single trial programme (ENGAGE AF-TIMI 48) caps this shelf at POSSIBLE

title: Anticoagulation after successful AF ablation: in moderate-risk patients, stopping was not associated with more thromboembolism in pooled randomised data (3 trials, 2,324 patients) and continuing cost more major bleeding (risk difference +1.0%) — the randomised base is still small
question: Should anticoagulation be continued after successful atrial fibrillation ablation?
balance: PARTIAL completion: live shelf #2248 covers one slice of this question — rivaroxaban versus aspirin in patients free of recurrence at least a year after ablation at moderate stroke risk (the OCEAN question); this shelf covers the uncovered slice — continued anticoagulation generally, versus stopping, after successful ablation. That home trial's primary report is not re-carded here; this shelf is built on free reports, including a meta-analysis that pools the randomised trials. Across three randomised trials and 2,324 patients at moderate baseline stroke risk (mean CHA2DS2-VASc about 2), discontinuation was not associated with a significant increase in stroke, systemic embolism, transient ischaemic attack or death, while continuation was associated with significantly more major bleeding (risk difference 1.0%), intracranial bleeding (0.6%), minor bleeding (2.2%) and clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding (2.5%) (Kaisaier 2026). The one randomised trial of continuation itself, ODIn-AF, randomised 200 AF-free patients six months after pulmonary vein isolation to dabigatran or no anticoagulation and found no difference in new cerebral embolic lesions on MRI and no clinical strokes in either arm, with more serious adverse events on anticoagulation (Schrickel 2024). Registry practice shows the question is live: in a large US registry, 23% of higher-risk ablated patients had anticoagulation discontinued anyway, at a median 6.2 months (Freeman 2019). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit of discontinuation in moderate-risk patients) — the direction is consistent, but the randomised base is small, follow-up is short, and none of it licenses stopping in higher-risk patients.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit of discontinuation in moderate-risk patients) — pooled randomised trials show no significant thromboembolic increase after stopping anticoagulation following successful ablation and significantly more bleeding with continuation; the total randomised base is 2,324 patients at moderate stroke risk, so this does not extend to higher-risk patients

title: Digoxin safety in AF with heart failure — SPLIT by study design: randomised data are neutral on mortality (risk ratio 0.99), while observational data link digoxin to higher mortality (hazard ratios 1.14–1.23), including in the AF-with-HF subgroup of one large cohort
question: Is digoxin safe for rate control in atrial fibrillation with heart failure?
balance: PARTIAL completion: live shelf #1173 covers digoxin versus bisoprolol for quality of life in AF with heart failure symptoms (the RATE-AF question); this shelf covers the uncovered slice — safety, specifically mortality, when digoxin is used for rate control in AF with heart failure. The evidence genuinely divides by design. Pooling by design, the BMJ systematic review found digoxin's mortality association shrank as methods improved — risk ratio 1.76 unadjusted, 1.61 adjusted, 1.18 in propensity-matched studies, and 0.99 (the treatment made no difference) in randomised trials — while hospital admissions fell slightly across all study types (Ziff 2015). An updated adjusted-data meta-analysis found the opposite headline: mortality hazard ratio 1.17 overall, 1.23 in AF and 1.11 in heart failure subgroups (Vamos 2019). Within AF specifically, one meta-analysis found digoxin associated with higher mortality overall (hazard ratio 1.23) but not in the AF-with-heart-failure subgroup (1.08, not significant) (Chamaria 2015), whereas a large propensity-matched Quebec cohort of patients ≥65 found higher mortality with digoxin in both the heart-failure (1.14) and no-heart-failure (1.17) groups (Shah 2014). No randomised trial of digoxin for rate control in AF with HF has been powered for mortality. PROPOSED SPLIT (randomised: neutral; observational: harm signal) — safety is not established in either direction.
stamp: SPLIT (randomised evidence: no mortality increase; observational evidence: higher mortality with digoxin) — digoxin's safety for rate control in AF with heart failure is unresolved: the harm signal lives in observational data prone to prescription bias, and the AF-with-HF subgroup itself divides between meta-analyses

title: Andexanet alfa in factor Xa inhibitor major bleeding: anti-Xa activity falls by over 90% and 80–82% achieve good or excellent haemostasis in the single-arm ANNEXA-4 programme, with lower in-hospital mortality than 4-factor PCC in observational comparison (odds ratio 0.50) — but no randomised trial covers major bleeding generally
question: Does andexanet alfa improve outcomes in major bleeding associated with a direct oral anticoagulant (factor Xa inhibitor)?
balance: PARTIAL completion: live shelf #849 covers factor Xa inhibitor intracerebral haemorrhage (the randomised ANNEXA-I slice); this shelf covers the uncovered slice — DOAC-related major bleeding generally, across bleeding sites. In the single-arm ANNEXA-4 programme, andexanet reduced anti-factor Xa activity by 92% and 82% of evaluable patients achieved excellent or good haemostasis at 12 hours, while 14% died and 10% had a thrombotic event within 30 days (Connolly 2019); the final programme report (479 patients, 69% intracranial and 23% gastrointestinal bleeding) found the same pattern — 80% good or excellent haemostasis, 10% thrombotic events (Milling 2023) — and the small edoxaban subgroup behaved similarly (Benz 2022; n = 36, printed on its card). The only comparative outcome evidence is observational: in 4,395 hospitalised patients, in-hospital mortality odds were 50% lower with andexanet than with 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate, consistently for intracranial and gastrointestinal bleeds (Dobesh 2023). There is no randomised comparison for major bleeding overall — the randomised evidence is confined to the intracranial slice homed on #849. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — haemostatic efficacy is consistent within a single-arm programme and the comparative signal is observational only, both printed on the face.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — andexanet alfa reverses anti-Xa activity and achieves good or excellent haemostasis in about 4 of 5 patients in a single-arm programme, and observational comparison favours it over 4-factor PCC for in-hospital mortality; with no randomised trial in major bleeding generally, this caps at POSSIBLE

title: Idarucizumab in dabigatran-related bleeding: reversal is near-universal (100% median within 4 hours) and bleeding stopped within 24 hours in 68.7% of gastrointestinal bleeds (median 2.4 hours), with >91% normal haemostasis when it enabled urgent surgery — all from a single-arm cohort, so clinical benefit is inferred, not randomised
question: Does idarucizumab reversal improve clinical outcomes in dabigatran-related bleeding?
balance: PARTIAL completion: live shelf #849 covers idarucizumab reversal (the reversal-effect question, including the RE-VERSE AD full-cohort report, which is homed there and not re-carded here); this shelf covers the uncovered slice — clinical bleeding outcomes after reversal: whether bleeding stops, how fast, and what happens to patients. The free reports are the programme's outcome-focused analyses. In gastrointestinal bleeding (137 patients), reversal was complete in 97.5% by diluted thrombin time, bleeding cessation within 24 hours was reported in 68.7% after a median 2.4 hours, and by 90 days 4.4% had a thromboembolic event and 14.6% had died (Van der Wall 2019). In patients needing urgent surgery (202 patients), normal haemostasis was achieved in over 91%, surgery began within 2 hours in most groups, 30-day thromboembolic events were 5% and mortality 12.6% (Levy 2021). Across the full cohort split by renal function, median reversal was 100% within 4 hours regardless of kidney function, bleeding cessation and procedural haemostasis were similar across renal strata, dabigatran levels re-rose by 12–24 hours in over half of severely impaired patients, and mortality was higher with severe renal impairment (Eikelboom 2019). No report includes a control group, so none of these outcome rates can be credited to idarucizumab against a counterfactual. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — reversal is certain and the ensuing clinical course is consistently favourable in a single-arm programme; outcome improvement itself remains unrandomised.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — idarucizumab rapidly and completely reverses dabigatran and is followed by timely bleeding cessation and normal procedural haemostasis in the single-arm RE-VERSE AD programme; with no comparator arm, improved clinical outcomes are plausible but unproven, capping this shelf at POSSIBLE

title: Ticagrelor monotherapy after 3 months of DAPT: major bleeding roughly halved or better in two individual-patient meta-analyses (0.8% versus 2.1%, hazard ratio 0.37; 2.4% versus 4.5%, hazard ratio 0.54) with no significant increase in death, myocardial infarction or stroke
question: Is ticagrelor monotherapy after 3 months of dual antiplatelet therapy safer than continued dual antiplatelet therapy after percutaneous coronary intervention?
balance: PARTIAL completion: live shelf #4163 covers a neighbouring de-escalation slice — switching from ticagrelor to clopidogrel at 1 month in stabilised myocardial infarction; this shelf covers the uncovered slice — dropping aspirin and continuing ticagrelor alone after 3 months of dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT). The primary reports of the two anchor trials (TWILIGHT and TICO) are homed elsewhere in the library and are not re-carded here; this shelf is built on free reports. Pooling individual data from both trials in acute coronary syndrome (7,529 patients), ticagrelor monotherapy after 3 months reduced BARC type 3 or 5 bleeding between months 3 and 12 (0.8% versus 2.1%; hazard ratio 0.37) with no significant difference in death, myocardial infarction or stroke (2.4% versus 2.7%; hazard ratio 0.91) (Baber 2024). An independent individual-patient pooling of TICO with T-PASS (5,906 patients) found the same pattern: major bleeding 2.4% versus 4.5% (adjusted hazard ratio 0.54) and the ischaemic composite 1.9% versus 2.5% (adjusted hazard ratio 0.79, not significant) (Lee 2024). The benefit is largest where it matters most: in TWILIGHT's high-bleeding-risk patients, monotherapy cut BARC 2, 3 or 5 bleeding (6.3% versus 11.4%) with a larger absolute reduction in severe bleeding than in non-high-risk patients (Escaned 2021), and a risk-modelling analysis found the bleeding benefit consistent across bleeding- and ischaemic-risk strata with no offsetting ischaemic increase (Mendieta 2023). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) — two independent individual-patient meta-analyses of randomised trials agree on a large relative bleeding reduction with no significant ischaemic cost.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — ticagrelor monotherapy after 3 months of DAPT reduces major bleeding without a significant ischaemic penalty, concordantly in two individual-patient meta-analyses of the randomised trials and in the high-bleeding-risk subgroup, where the absolute gain is largest

title: FFR-guided PCI in multivessel disease generally (partial completion of the STEMI-only shelf #2280): fewer stents and fewer early events than angiography guidance, with the stable-disease advantage gone by 5 years
question: Does FFR-guided PCI improve outcomes compared with angiography-guided PCI in multivessel disease?
balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #2280, which covers FFR versus angiography guidance only in STEMI with multivessel disease (the FLOWER-MI comparison); this shelf covers multivessel disease generally. The FAME primary 1-year report (PMID: 19144937) is already carded elsewhere in the library (pack #1537) and is not re-carded here; the free FAME 5-year report is carded instead. Across the general multivessel evidence the benefit is real but time-limited and setting-dependent: in FAME, FFR guidance cut major adverse cardiac events for up to 2 years and used far fewer stents (1.9 vs 2.7 per patient), but by 5 years events had converged (28% vs 31%; relative risk 0.91, 95% CI 0.75-1.10; p=0.31). In acute MI with multivessel disease (FRAME-AMI), FFR-guided selective PCI of non-infarct lesions beat angiography-guided PCI clearly (7.4% vs 19.7%; hazard ratio 0.43). A 2016 meta-analysis of 2,138 randomised patients found lower reinfarction with FFR guidance (odds ratio 0.67) but no significant mortality or overall MACE difference. Against that, routine pressure-wire assessment of all vessels at diagnostic angiography (RIPCORD 2) made no difference to cost, quality of life or events — FFR helps when it decides which identified multivessel lesions to stent, not as a blanket screening strategy. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) — FFR-guided PCI improves outcomes over angiography-guided PCI in multivessel disease, principally by avoiding unnecessary stents and reducing early events and reinfarction; the advantage attenuates by 5 years in stable multivessel disease.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — FFR-guided PCI improves outcomes over angiography-guided PCI in multivessel disease (fewer stents; FRAME-AMI primary endpoint 7.4% vs 19.7%, HR 0.43; FAME benefit up to 2 years, converging by 5 years at 28% vs 31%), while routine pressure-wire screening of all vessels adds nothing (RIPCORD 2, the treatment made no difference)

title: Left main disease with low complexity (partial completion of the general left-main shelf #551): CABG is not better on death — it wins on spontaneous MI and repeat revascularisation, PCI wins on early stroke
question: Is CABG better than PCI for left main coronary disease with low complexity?
balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #551, the general left-main shelf (PCI as an alternative to CABG, built on the EXCEL and NOBLE primary reports, which are not re-carded here); this shelf isolates the low-complexity (low SYNTAX score) slice. In that slice the strategies divide by outcome rather than one winning outright. The individual-patient-data meta-analysis of the four left-main trials (4,394 patients, median SYNTAX score 25.0 — largely low or intermediate complexity) found no statistically significant difference in 5-year all-cause death (11.2% with PCI vs 10.2% with CABG; hazard ratio 1.10, 95% CI 0.91-1.32), although a Bayesian analysis put an 85.7% probability on some excess mortality with PCI, most likely under 0.2% per year. A SYNTAX-stratified meta-analysis found clinical equipoise on major adverse cardiac or cerebrovascular events at low-to-intermediate SYNTAX scores (HR 1.20, 95% CI 0.85-1.70) with a CABG advantage only at high scores. What CABG does win, consistently and in this complexity band, is spontaneous myocardial infarction (6.2% vs 2.6%; HR 2.35 with PCI) and repeat revascularisation (18.3% vs 10.7%; HR 1.78); what PCI wins is early stroke (first-year HR 0.37). So for low-complexity left main disease CABG is not better on death or the main composite — it is better on infarction and durability, and worse on early stroke. PROPOSED SPLIT (death and the main composite at low complexity: the strategies made no significant difference; spontaneous MI and repeat revascularisation: CABG better; early stroke: PCI better).
stamp: SPLIT (at low complexity, death and the main composite: the strategies made no significant difference — 5-year death 11.2% PCI vs 10.2% CABG, HR 1.10; spontaneous MI and repeat revascularisation: CABG better — HR 2.35 and 1.78 with PCI; early stroke: PCI better — first-year HR 0.37)

title: Aspirin plus low-dose rivaroxaban in stable coronary disease (partial completion of the post-ACS shelf #3333): the COMPASS combination cut events and mortality, with more major gastrointestinal bleeding
question: Does aspirin plus low-dose rivaroxaban reduce events in stable coronary disease?
balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #3333, which covers low-dose rivaroxaban added to antiplatelet therapy after an acute coronary syndrome (the ATLAS ACS programme); this shelf covers the different population of stable coronary disease — the COMPASS population. The COMPASS primary report (PMID: 28844192) is already carded elsewhere in the library and is not re-carded here; this shelf is built on the trial's free stable-coronary-disease reports. In the dedicated coronary artery disease report (24,824 patients with stable CAD), rivaroxaban 2.5 mg twice daily plus aspirin 100 mg daily reduced the primary outcome of myocardial infarction, stroke or cardiovascular death versus aspirin alone (4% vs 6%; hazard ratio 0.74, 95% CI 0.65-0.86) and reduced mortality (3% vs 4%; HR 0.77) — a 26% relative reduction in the primary outcome alongside a 2-percentage-point absolute difference — at the cost of more major bleeding (3% vs 2%; HR 1.66), mostly gastrointestinal, with no significant increase in intracranial or critical-organ bleeding. The benefit was consistent in women and men (MACE HR 0.72 and 0.76) and in patients with and without diabetes (primary-endpoint HR 0.74 and 0.77, with larger absolute reductions in diabetes), and stroke was roughly halved (HR 0.58). Rivaroxaban alone (5 mg twice daily) did not significantly improve the primary outcome in the CAD report (HR 0.89, p=0.094) — the benefit belongs to the combination. Because this is a single trial programme, the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — single trial programme: aspirin plus low-dose rivaroxaban reduces cardiovascular events and mortality in stable coronary disease, with more major (mainly gastrointestinal) bleeding.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single trial programme (COMPASS): aspirin plus rivaroxaban 2.5 mg twice daily reduced the primary outcome in stable coronary disease (4% vs 6%; HR 0.74) and mortality (HR 0.77), with more major bleeding (3% vs 2%; HR 1.66), mainly gastrointestinal

title: Short DAPT then P2Y12-inhibitor monotherapy after complex PCI (partial completion of the stabilised-AMI shelf #4163): bleeding roughly halved in the TWILIGHT complex analysis, with no detected ischaemic penalty
question: Does short DAPT followed by P2Y12 inhibitor monotherapy reduce bleeding after complex PCI?
balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #4163, which covers DAPT de-escalation strategy in stabilised acute myocardial infarction; this shelf covers the different setting of complex PCI specifically, across presentations. The direct complex-PCI evidence points the same way on bleeding. In the TWILIGHT complex-PCI analysis (2,342 patients who had completed 3 months of ticagrelor plus aspirin), dropping aspirin and continuing ticagrelor alone halved clinically relevant bleeding (BARC type 2, 3 or 5: 4.2% vs 7.7%; hazard ratio 0.54) and major bleeding (BARC 3 or 5: 1.1% vs 2.6%; HR 0.41), with no significant difference in death, myocardial infarction or stroke (3.8% vs 4.9%; HR 0.77, 95% CI 0.52-1.15). A meta-analysis of 5 trials (8,328 complex-PCI patients) found major bleeding significantly reduced by P2Y12-inhibitor monotherapy after 1-3 months of DAPT, consistently in complex and non-complex strata, with similar death, stent thrombosis and stroke — and, unexpectedly, less myocardial infarction in the complex stratum (HR 0.77). The SMART-CHOICE complex post-hoc analysis (498 patients, mostly clopidogrel monotherapy) likewise found no ischaemic penalty. The honest counterweight is STOPDAPT-3's complex subgroup, where clopidogrel monotherapy after 1 month did not beat aspirin monotherapy on bleeding (2.1% vs 2.7%, no significant interaction) — a comparison of two monotherapies, not of monotherapy versus continued DAPT. The evidence is subgroup and post-hoc analyses of trials not randomised on complexity, so the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — short DAPT followed by P2Y12-inhibitor monotherapy reduces bleeding after complex PCI without a detected ischaemic penalty, on subgroup-level evidence.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — short DAPT (1-3 months) followed by P2Y12-inhibitor monotherapy reduces bleeding after complex PCI (TWILIGHT complex: BARC 3 or 5 bleeding 1.1% vs 2.6%, HR 0.41) without a detected ischaemic penalty, on subgroup and post-hoc evidence rather than complexity-randomised trials

title: Ranolazine in chronic coronary syndrome generally (partial completion of the post-PCI shelf #3087): consistent, modest symptom and exercise benefit across CARISA, TERISA and MERLIN — and no hard-event benefit
question: Does ranolazine improve angina symptoms in chronic coronary syndrome?
balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #3087, which covers ranolazine only in angina with incomplete revascularisation after PCI (the RIVER-PCI population); this shelf covers chronic coronary syndrome generally — stable angina on background antianginal therapy, most of it never randomised around a PCI. The general stable-angina trials are concordant on symptoms. CARISA (823 patients with severe chronic angina on atenolol, amlodipine or diltiazem) increased trough exercise duration more with ranolazine than placebo (115.6 vs 91.7 seconds gained; P=0.01) and cut angina attacks and nitroglycerin use by about 1 per week. TERISA (949 patients with type 2 diabetes and chronic stable angina) reduced weekly angina episodes (3.8 vs 4.3; p=0.008) and nitroglycerin doses (1.7 vs 2.1; p=0.003). In the MERLIN-TIMI 36 chronic-angina subgroup (3,565 patients with prior angina), ranolazine reduced recurrent ischaemia (HR 0.78) and worsening angina (HR 0.77) but made no difference to cardiovascular death or myocardial infarction (HR 0.97). An updated meta-analysis of 18 trials (12,995 patients) found exercise duration up by 30 seconds and time to angina onset up by 40 seconds versus placebo. The benefit is symptomatic and functional — modest in absolute terms (about half an angina episode and 30 seconds of exercise) — with no mortality or infarction benefit shown. The RIVER-PCI report and the earlier stable-disease meta-analysis carded on #3087 are not re-carded here. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) — ranolazine improves angina symptoms and exercise tolerance in chronic coronary syndrome, with no demonstrated reduction in death or myocardial infarction.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — ranolazine improves angina symptoms and exercise tolerance in chronic coronary syndrome (weekly angina 3.8 vs 4.3 episodes in TERISA; pooled exercise duration +30 seconds), with no demonstrated reduction in death or myocardial infarction (HR 0.97 in the MERLIN chronic-angina subgroup)

title: Pelacarsen and cardiovascular events (partial completion of the phase-2-lowering shelf #1104): Lp(a)HORIZON has now reported — large Lp(a) lowering, no event reduction (the treatment made no difference)
question: Does lowering Lp(a) with pelacarsen reduce cardiovascular events?
balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #1104, which covers pelacarsen's phase 2 Lp(a) lowering only, with no outcome data; this shelf covers the cardiovascular-events slice, and the evidence status has changed since that shelf was built: the outcomes trial has now reported. Lp(a)HORIZON randomised 8,350 patients with preexisting cardiovascular disease and Lp(a) of at least 70 mg/dL to monthly pelacarsen 80 mg or placebo. Pelacarsen lowered Lp(a) as expected (at 12 months, 64.4 nmol/L versus 233.4 nmol/L from a median baseline of 236 nmol/L), but over a median follow-up of 4.7 years the primary endpoint — cardiovascular death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke or urgent coronary revascularisation — occurred in 12.3% on pelacarsen and 12.1% on placebo (hazard ratio 1.02, 95% CI 0.90-1.15; P=0.76): the treatment made no difference. The extended analyses found no benefit in any reframing — on-treatment (HR 0.98), uninterrupted treatment (HR 1.09), total events (rate ratio 1.00), or by achieved Lp(a) reduction — and the result held in the subgroup with baseline Lp(a) of at least 90 mg/dL (HR 1.00). A separate phase 3b study confirms the surrogate effect is real and large (86% placebo-adjusted Lp(a) reduction in Black and Hispanic participants), so the null outcome result cannot be blamed on failure to lower Lp(a). One definitive large outcomes trial supports a LIKELY stamp for the null. PROPOSED LIKELY (no benefit — the treatment made no difference): pelacarsen lowers Lp(a) by roughly 70-86% but did not reduce cardiovascular events in Lp(a)HORIZON.
stamp: LIKELY (no benefit — the treatment made no difference) — pelacarsen lowered Lp(a) from a median 236 nmol/L to 64.4 vs 233.4 nmol/L at 12 months, but major adverse cardiovascular events in Lp(a)HORIZON were 12.3% vs 12.1% (HR 1.02, 95% CI 0.90-1.15; P=0.76) over a median 4.7 years

title: Evolocumab and clinical events in familial hypercholesterolemia (partial completion of the LDL-lowering shelf #1569): LDL lowering is proven in FH — event lowering in FH has never been trialled and rests on extrapolation
question: Does evolocumab lower events in familial hypercholesterolemia?
balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #1569, which covers LDL lowering in familial hypercholesterolemia and ASCVD; this shelf covers the different slice of clinical events in FH specifically — and the honest headline is that the slice is nearly empty. No randomised trial has tested evolocumab against clinical events in an FH population: the events evidence behind evolocumab comes from FOURIER in established ASCVD generally (its primary report, PMID: 28304224, is already carded elsewhere in the library and is not re-carded here), and no FH-subgroup events report was found in this session's searches. What exists in FH is: TAUSSIG, an open-label, non-randomised study in homozygous FH (106 patients, mean follow-up 1.7 years) in which only four positively adjudicated cardiovascular events occurred, with no comparator group; a Japanese postmarketing single-arm study (3,724 patients, including 2,117 with homozygous or heterozygous FH) reporting myocardial infarction in 0.7% and stroke in 0.3% over 104 weeks, again with no comparator; and a 23-trial meta-analysis of PCSK9-targeting therapies in FH (4,282 patients) whose endpoints are lipid biomarkers and adverse events — LDL cholesterol down 46.64% — not clinical events. LDL lowering in FH is therefore well proven (the #1569 slice) while event lowering in FH is an extrapolation from the general ASCVD trial, not a demonstrated FH result. The evidence is observational and uncontrolled for events, so the stamp is MAYBE. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — evolocumab lowers LDL cholesterol in FH, but whether it lowers clinical events in FH itself is unproven: no FH events trial exists, and the FH event data are four adjudicated events in an uncontrolled homozygous-FH study and uncontrolled registry incidence rates.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — evolocumab lowers LDL cholesterol in familial hypercholesterolemia, but no trial has tested clinical events in FH: the FH events record is four adjudicated events in the uncontrolled TAUSSIG study (N=106) and uncontrolled registry incidence (MI 0.7%, stroke 0.3% over 104 weeks), so event lowering in FH is unproven

title: Warfarin intensity after mechanical mitral valve replacement (partial completion of the On-X aortic shelf #3094): PROACT Mitral found no difference between INR targets — and did not prove the lower target noninferior
question: Does warfarin improve outcomes after mechanical mitral valve replacement compared with lower INR targets?
balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #3094, which covers lower-INR warfarin only for the On-X aortic valve (the PROACT aortic programme); this shelf covers the different and higher-risk mechanical mitral position. The mitral counterpart trial has now reported: PROACT Mitral randomised 401 patients with an On-X mechanical mitral valve, after at least 3 months of standard anticoagulation, to low-dose warfarin (target INR 2.0-2.5) or standard-dose warfarin (target INR 2.5-3.5), all on aspirin 81 mg. Over a mean 4.1 years the composite of thromboembolism, valve thrombosis and bleeding was virtually identical (11.9% vs 12.0% per patient-year; difference -0.07%, 95% CI -3.40% to 3.26%), as were its components (thromboembolism 2.3% vs 2.5%; valve thrombosis 0.5% vs 0.5%; bleeding 9.13% vs 9.04% per patient-year) — but the confidence interval crossed the 1.5% noninferiority margin, so low-dose was not proven noninferior: the trial shows no demonstrated advantage for standard intensity on the composite, and no proven safety of the lower target either. Older evidence leans the other way: a meta-analysis of 23,145 mechanical-valve patients found that in the mitral position higher intensity (mean target INR above 3.0) reduced thromboembolism (relative risk 0.74) and total events (RR 0.84) without a significant bleeding increase (RR 1.08, p=0.0524) — though its targets are higher than either PROACT Mitral arm. Supporting randomised data are mixed-population: a D-dimer-guided strategy (starting low, escalating on D-dimer) beat both fixed low and fixed standard intensity in 748 aortic-and-mitral patients, and the small LIWACAP pilot (198 aortic or mitral patients) found low intensity plus aspirin similar to standard-high intensity over the first 6 months (events 5.8% vs 4.3%; p=0.6). PROPOSED SPLIT (the one mitral-specific randomised trial: standard and lower INR targets made no difference to the composite, and noninferiority of the lower target was not achieved; the older meta-analysis: higher intensity reduced total events in mitral valves).
stamp: SPLIT (PROACT Mitral, the mitral-specific trial: low-dose INR 2.0-2.5 vs standard 2.5-3.5 made no difference to the composite — 11.9% vs 12.0% per patient-year — but noninferiority of the lower target was not achieved; the older intensity meta-analysis found higher intensity reduced thromboembolism and total events in mitral valves, RR 0.74 and 0.84)

title: Vorapaxar and limb events in peripheral arterial disease (partial completion of the broad prior-MI/PAD shelf #1544): acute limb ischaemia and revascularisation reduced, cardiovascular composite in PAD unchanged, bleeding increased
question: Does vorapaxar reduce limb events in peripheral arterial disease?
balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #1544, which covers vorapaxar in prior myocardial infarction or peripheral arterial disease broadly (cardiovascular events as the focus, built on the TRA 2°P-TIMI 50 and TRACER primary reports, which are not re-carded here); this shelf covers the limb-events outcome slice in PAD. Within the TRA 2°P PAD cohort (3,787 patients with symptomatic PAD), vorapaxar did not significantly reduce the cardiovascular composite (11.3% vs 11.9%; hazard ratio 0.94) — but it did reduce limb events: hospitalisation for acute limb ischaemia (2.3% vs 3.9%; HR 0.58) and peripheral revascularisation (18.4% vs 22.2%; HR 0.84). The dedicated acute-limb-ischaemia analysis found first ALI reduced by 41% relative (HR 0.58, 95% CI 0.39-0.86; p=0.006) and total ALI events likewise (risk ratio 0.59), consistently across ALI types, in a population where placebo ALI ran at 3.9% over 3 years and 17.6% of ALI presentations ended in amputation. In the broader PAD analysis (6,136 patients), vorapaxar reduced major adverse limb events (HR 0.70, 95% CI 0.53-0.92), with the largest absolute limb benefit in patients with prior peripheral revascularisation (absolute reduction 2.5%; NNT 40), and reduced peripheral revascularisation overall (15.4% vs 19.3%; HR 0.82) across all indications. The price is bleeding: in the symptomatic-PAD cohort, bleeding occurred in 7.4% versus 4.5% (HR 1.62). All of this is one trial programme's subgroup analyses, so the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — single trial programme: vorapaxar reduces limb events (acute limb ischaemia and peripheral revascularisation) in PAD, with increased bleeding.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single trial programme (TRA 2°P-TIMI 50 PAD analyses): vorapaxar reduces limb events in peripheral arterial disease (acute limb ischaemia HR 0.58; major adverse limb events HR 0.70; peripheral revascularisation HR 0.84), with increased bleeding (7.4% vs 4.5%; HR 1.62) and no significant reduction in the cardiovascular composite in PAD (HR 0.94)

title: Aortoiliac claudication (PARTIAL — the aortoiliac slice of live shelf #280): supervised exercise matched stenting for 18-month walking improvement in the CLEVER trial and cost less, though quality-of-life scales often favoured stenting
question: Does supervised exercise work as well as stenting for aortoiliac PAD?
balance: PARTIAL completion — home live shelf #280 asks what works better for intermittent claudication generally (supervised exercise, stenting, or medical care) and cards the CLEVER trial's 6-month primary report there; this shelf targets the slice #280 does not isolate: claudication due specifically to aortoiliac disease, using CLEVER's own later and secondary reports, which are not carded on #280. CLEVER randomised only patients with aortoiliac disease (111 patients), so its 18-month report (Murphy 2015), its cost-effectiveness analysis (Reynolds 2014) and its patient-reported-outcomes analysis (Murphy 2013) answer the aortoiliac question directly. At 18 months, peak walking time had improved by 5.0 minutes with supervised exercise and 3.2 minutes with stenting versus 0.2 minutes with medical care alone, and the exercise-versus-stent difference was not significant (P = 0.16) — exercise worked as well as stenting on the treadmill outcome, while many disease-specific quality-of-life scales favoured stenting. Exercise was also much cheaper ($9,804 vs $14,590 per patient over 18 months). One caution from within the trial: after exercise, treadmill gains correlated poorly with patients' own symptom relief, whereas after stenting they correlated well. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — single trial programme: in aortoiliac claudication, supervised exercise matches stenting for durable walking improvement at 18 months and costs less, though patient-reported quality-of-life gains were larger with stenting on many scales.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single trial programme (CLEVER, aortoiliac disease only): supervised exercise worked as well as stenting for durable walking improvement at 18 months (peak walking time +5.0 vs +3.2 minutes; difference not significant) and cost less ($9,804 vs $14,590 per patient), though many quality-of-life scales favoured stenting

title: Duration after a first unprovoked VTE (PARTIAL — the overall-duration slice of live shelf #1592): extending anticoagulation prevents recurrence for as long as it is taken, across warfarin, rivaroxaban and dabigatran extension trials
question: How long should anticoagulation last after a first unprovoked VTE?
balance: PARTIAL completion — home live shelf #1592 covers one management strategy for this decision, a D-dimer-guided strategy for stopping or resuming anticoagulation after a first unprovoked VTE; this shelf targets the slice #1592 does not cover: the overall trial evidence on treatment duration itself, from the placebo- and active-controlled extension trials. That evidence is consistent on one point and silent on another. While anticoagulation is continued, recurrence is rare: in Kearon 1999, extending warfarin beyond 3 months cut recurrence from 27.4% to 1.3% per patient-year (a 95% relative reduction); in the EINSTEIN continued-treatment study, rivaroxaban cut recurrence from 7.1% to 1.3% (HR 0.18); in RE-SONATE, dabigatran cut recurrence from 5.6% to 0.4% (HR 0.08), and in RE-MEDY dabigatran matched warfarin for recurrence with less major or clinically relevant bleeding. The cost is bleeding: major bleeding on extended therapy ran at 0.3–0.9% in the dabigatran trials and 0.7% with rivaroxaban, against 0% on placebo in the placebo-controlled studies. What no carded trial shows is a finite extension that keeps protecting after it stops — the trials compare continuing versus stopping, and protection belongs to the continuing. So the honest duration answer is: at least 3–6 months for all, and extended (indefinite) treatment prevents recurrence for as long as it is taken, at a bleeding price; the choice is therefore about bleeding risk and patient preference, not about a magic number of months. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) — extended anticoagulation beyond 3–6 months prevents recurrence after a first unprovoked VTE for as long as it is continued, with more bleeding than placebo.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — after a first unprovoked VTE, extending anticoagulation beyond 3–6 months prevents recurrence for as long as it is continued (recurrence ~0.4–1.3% on treatment vs 5.6–27.4% on placebo across three trial programmes), with major bleeding of 0.3–0.9% on treatment vs 0% on placebo; no finite extension has been shown to keep protecting after it stops
