title: Unprovoked PE — indefinite versus stopping at 6 months (PARTIAL — the PE-duration slice of live shelf #1592): benefit exists only while treatment continues (PADIS-PE), and a finite extension made no difference (WODIT-PE)
question: Is indefinite anticoagulation better than stopping after 6 months for unprovoked PE?
balance: PARTIAL completion — home live shelf #1592 covers a D-dimer-guided stopping/resuming strategy after a first unprovoked VTE; this shelf targets the slice #1592 does not cover: for pulmonary embolism specifically, is indefinite (extended) anticoagulation better than stopping at 6 months? The two PE-specific randomised trials divide, and the division is the answer. PADIS-PE (Couturaud 2015) randomised 371 patients after 6 months of treatment to 18 further months of warfarin or placebo: on treatment, the composite of recurrence or major bleeding fell (3.3% vs 13.5%; HR 0.22) and recurrence fell sharply (HR 0.15) — but by 42 months, after everyone had stopped, the composite no longer differed (20.8% vs 24.0%; HR 0.75, CI crossing 1): the benefit was rented, not bought. WODIT-PE (Agnelli 2003) found extending from 3 months to 6–12 months made no difference to recurrence at all (9.1% vs 11.2%; rate ratio 0.81, CI 0.42–1.56), including in idiopathic PE (relative risk 0.99). A PADIS-PE analysis (Tromeur 2018) shows who recurs after stopping: older patients and those with residual pulmonary vascular obstruction or antiphospholipid antibodies. So indefinite treatment is better than stopping only in the narrow sense that it suppresses recurrence while it continues; neither trial shows a lasting advantage once treatment ends, which is why the decision turns on bleeding risk and recurrence-risk features rather than on duration alone. PROPOSED SPLIT — PADIS-PE favours extending (on-treatment benefit, lost after discontinuation); WODIT-PE found no benefit from extending (the treatment made no difference).
stamp: SPLIT — PADIS-PE: 18 extra months of warfarin after 6 months cut the on-treatment composite (HR 0.22) but the benefit was lost by 42 months after stopping (HR 0.75); WODIT-PE: extending to 6–12 months made no difference to recurrence (rate ratio 0.81; idiopathic PE relative risk 0.99)

title: Reduced-dose apixaban after 6 months in non-cancer VTE (PARTIAL — the non-cancer slice of live shelf #3380): recurrence prevention proven in AMPLIFY-EXT (primary homed on #1580), with less bleeding than full dose in RENOVE
question: Does reduced-dose apixaban prevent recurrence after 6 months of VTE treatment?
balance: PARTIAL completion — home live shelf #3380 covers reduced-dose apixaban only in cancer-associated VTE; this shelf targets the uncovered slice: non-cancer VTE, the AMPLIFY-EXT population. FLAG for the developer (one-home precedent): the AMPLIFY-EXT primary report itself is already carded on live shelf #1580, so under the one-home rule it is NOT re-carded here; this shelf is built on the trial's free secondary report and on later free evidence, with the primary cross-pointed in this prose. What the free reports show: within AMPLIFY-EXT, both apixaban doses (2.5 mg and 5 mg twice daily) significantly reduced all-cause hospitalisations versus placebo over 12 months (HR 0.64 and 0.54) and delayed first hospitalisation by 43 and 49 days (Liu 2016) — a downstream signal of the recurrence prevention the primary report established. RENOVE (Couturaud 2025) then randomised 2,768 patients who had already had 6–24 months of full-dose treatment to reduced-dose versus full-dose direct oral anticoagulants (apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily or rivaroxaban 10 mg daily, versus full doses): recurrence stayed low in both groups (5-year cumulative incidence 2.2% reduced vs 1.8% full; adjusted HR 1.32), formal non-inferiority was not met (P = 0.23 for non-inferiority), but major or clinically relevant bleeding was substantially lower on the reduced dose (5-year cumulative incidence 9.9% vs 15.2%; adjusted HR 0.61). A network meta-analysis (Wang 2019) puts low-dose factor Xa inhibitors as a class well ahead of placebo for recurrence (OR 0.16). So: yes, reduced-dose apixaban prevents recurrence after 6 months in non-cancer VTE — the placebo-controlled proof is the homed AMPLIFY-EXT primary; the free evidence adds that the reduced dose keeps recurrence low with less bleeding than full dose, without formally proving non-inferiority. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — single trial programme for the apixaban-specific placebo comparison (primary homed on #1580), supported by RENOVE and class-level network meta-analysis.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — reduced-dose apixaban (2.5 mg twice daily) prevents recurrence after 6 months of treatment in non-cancer VTE: placebo-controlled proof in AMPLIFY-EXT (primary report carded on live shelf #1580; hospitalisations HR 0.64 in its secondary analysis), with RENOVE showing low 5-year recurrence on reduced dose (2.2%) and less major or clinically relevant bleeding than full dose (9.9% vs 15.2%; HR 0.61), though formal non-inferiority was not met

title: IVC filters when anticoagulation is impossible (PARTIAL — the cannot-anticoagulate slice of live shelf #1178): PE prevention plausible in established VTE, randomised trauma primary outcome neutral, thrombosis increased
question: Do IVC filters prevent PE in patients who cannot be anticoagulated?
balance: PARTIAL completion — home live shelf #1178 covers a filter ADDED to anticoagulation (the PREPIC question); this shelf targets the uncovered slice: patients who cannot be anticoagulated at all, where the filter is the only mechanical option. The evidence divides by setting, and the stamp names the split. In severely injured patients with a contraindication to anticoagulation, the one randomised trial (Ho 2019, N = 240) found early filter placement made no difference to the composite of symptomatic PE or death at 90 days (13.9% vs 14.4%; HR 0.99) — the treatment made no difference on its primary outcome — although in the subgroup who received no prophylactic anticoagulation within 7 days, PE occurred in 0 of 46 filtered patients versus 5 of 34 unfiltered (14.7%). In established cancer-associated VTE with contraindications, a propensity-matched RIETE cohort (Quezada 2020) found filters associated with lower PE-related mortality (0.8% vs 4.0%) but higher recurrence (7.3% vs 3.2%) and no difference in all-cause death or major bleeding. The controlled-evidence synthesis (Bikdeli 2017) found filters reduce subsequent PE (OR 0.50) and increase deep-vein thrombosis (OR 1.70) with no change in all-cause mortality (OR 0.91) — but most of its included studies anticoagulated their patients, so it only partly speaks to this slice. Net: a filter probably prevents some PEs in patients who cannot be anticoagulated — most plausibly fatal PE in established VTE — at the price of more thrombosis, and the only randomised test in a contraindicated population was neutral on its primary outcome. PROPOSED SPLIT — randomised trauma evidence neutral on PE-or-death; observational VTE evidence shows less PE-related death but more recurrence; meta-analysis shows fewer PEs, more DVT, no mortality change.
stamp: SPLIT — in patients who cannot be anticoagulated: the randomised trauma trial found early filters made no difference to PE or death at 90 days (13.9% vs 14.4%; HR 0.99), while a matched cancer-VTE cohort found lower PE-related mortality with filters (0.8% vs 4.0%) but higher recurrence (7.3% vs 3.2%); meta-analysis: fewer PEs (OR 0.50), more DVT (OR 1.70), no mortality change

title: Aspirin after stopping anticoagulation (PARTIAL — the aspirin-versus-placebo slice of live shelf #1581): WARFASA, ASPIRE and their pooled analysis show about a one-third relative reduction in VTE recurrence
question: Does aspirin prevent VTE recurrence after stopping anticoagulation?
balance: PARTIAL completion — home live shelf #1581 covers extended rivaroxaban therapy after VTE, where aspirin appears only as the comparator arm; this shelf targets the uncovered slice: aspirin versus placebo or no treatment after anticoagulation is stopped (the WARFASA and ASPIRE question). Two randomised trials and their pre-planned individual-patient pooled analysis answer it. WARFASA (Becattini 2012, N = 402) found aspirin 100 mg daily cut recurrence from 11.2% to 6.6% per year (HR 0.58) with one major bleed in each group. ASPIRE (Brighton 2012, N = 822) pointed the same way but its primary outcome narrowly missed significance (4.8% vs 6.5% per year; HR 0.74; P = 0.09), while its composite vascular outcomes fell significantly. The INSPIRE pooled analysis (Simes 2014, 1,224 patients) resolves the pair: aspirin reduced recurrent VTE from 7.5% to 5.1% per year (HR 0.68; P = 0.008) — a 32% relative reduction — and major vascular events from 8.7% to 5.7% per year (HR 0.66), with major bleeding of 0.5% versus 0.4% per year. Aspirin is much weaker than continued anticoagulation (see the duration evidence on pack #5829), but against nothing it works, cheaply and with little bleeding. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) — aspirin after stopping anticoagulation reduces VTE recurrence by about a third relative to placebo, without a significant increase in major bleeding.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — after stopping anticoagulation for a first unprovoked VTE, aspirin 100 mg daily reduces recurrence versus placebo (pooled 5.1% vs 7.5% per year; HR 0.68, a 32% relative reduction) and major vascular events (HR 0.66), with major bleeding 0.5% vs 0.4% per year; ASPIRE's own primary outcome narrowly missed significance (P = 0.09)

title: Beta-blockers versus no treatment in long QT syndrome (PARTIAL — the treated-versus-untreated slice of live shelf #3074): registry evidence associates therapy with far fewer cardiac events, observational only
question: Does beta-blocker therapy prevent events in long QT syndrome?
balance: PARTIAL completion — home live shelf #3074 compares beta-blockers with each other in congenital long QT syndrome (which agent is best); this shelf targets the uncovered slice: beta-blocker therapy versus no treatment at all. No randomised trial exists — withholding standard therapy was never randomised — so the evidence is entirely observational, from the International LQTS Registry, and the stamp is capped accordingly and printed on the face. Moss 2000 compared matched periods before and after starting beta-blockers in 869 treated patients: cardiac event rates fell from 0.97 to 0.31 events per year in probands and from 0.26 to 0.15 in affected family members (P < 0.001) — but events continued on therapy, especially in patients symptomatic before treatment (32% had another event within 5 years) and after aborted cardiac arrest (14% had another arrest within 5 years). Goldenberg 2010 quantified the treated-versus-untreated contrast in high-risk LQT1/LQT2 patients: beta-blocker therapy was associated with a 67% relative risk reduction in LQT1 males and 71% in LQT2 females. Barsheshet 2012 adds the genotype nuance: in LQT1, the life-threatening-event benefit concentrated in cytoplasmic-loop KCNQ1 mutations (HR 0.12) and was not significant in other mutation groups (HR 0.82). The direction is consistent across three registry analyses spanning three decades of patients; the size of the benefit in any individual depends on genotype, mutation location, sex, age and prior symptoms. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: beta-blocker therapy is associated with substantially fewer cardiac events in congenital long QT syndrome, with residual risk concentrated in previously symptomatic patients.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: beta-blocker therapy is associated with substantially fewer cardiac events in congenital long QT syndrome (event rates 0.97 to 0.31/year after starting in probands; 67–71% relative reductions in high-risk LQT1/LQT2 subsets), with residual events concentrated in previously symptomatic patients; no randomised trial exists

title: Phentermine-topiramate beats phentermine alone head-to-head (EQUATE): the combination lost 8.5–9.2% of body weight at 28 weeks versus 46.2% reaching 5% loss on phentermine 15 mg — one direct components trial, cross-pointed to the placebo-controlled shelf #746
question: In adults with obesity, does phentermine-topiramate produce more weight loss than phentermine alone?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single direct head-to-head trial, printed on the face. This is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #746 already covers phentermine-topiramate versus placebo (the EQUIP/CONQUER programme); the uncovered slice carded here is the head-to-head against phentermine alone. Only one trial has ever randomised that comparison directly: EQUATE (Aronne 2013), a 28-week, seven-arm components trial in which both combination doses beat their respective monotherapies on percentage weight loss (P < 0.05) and on the share reaching at least 5% loss (62.1% and 66.0% for the combinations versus 43.3% and 46.2% for phentermine 7.5 mg and 15 mg). The two network meta-analyses carded here frame but do not replace that comparison: the American College of Physicians living review (Damen 2026) includes phentermine and phentermine-topiramate as separate network interventions across 69 studies and 112,511 participants yet states plainly that direct head-to-head comparisons were limited and prints no pairwise estimate for this pairing in its record; the BMJ network meta-analysis (Nong 2026; 262 trials, 99,791 participants) puts phentermine-topiramate's one-year effect versus lifestyle modification at a mean difference of −8.1% (95% CI −9.7 to −6.5), again without a printed phentermine-alone contrast. One earlier network meta-analysis considered for this shelf (Shi 2022) was NOT carded because its PubMed record is flagged as a retracted publication. The direct evidence is therefore a single 28-week trial programme, which caps the stamp. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): phentermine-topiramate produces more weight loss than phentermine alone, on one direct randomised components trial; longer and replicated head-to-head evidence does not exist in the records fetched this session.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single direct head-to-head trial: in the one randomised components trial (EQUATE), phentermine-topiramate extended-release produced greater percentage weight loss than its respective phentermine monotherapy arms (P < 0.05) and more patients reaching at least 5% weight loss; no second direct comparison exists in the records fetched

title: Naltrexone-bupropion beats placebo on top of lifestyle intervention in general obesity (COR programme): −6.4% versus −1.2% at 56 weeks in COR-II and −9.3% versus −5.1% added to intensive behaviour modification in COR-BMOD
question: In adults with obesity, does naltrexone-bupropion produce more weight loss than placebo when combined with lifestyle intervention?
balance: LIKELY (benefit). This is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #3498 already covers naltrexone-bupropion in type 2 diabetes with obesity (the COR-Diabetes trial); the uncovered slice carded here is obesity generally — the rest of the COR programme, in which every participant received lifestyle intervention alongside drug or placebo. COR-II (Apovian 2013; 1,496 participants) found −6.5% versus −1.9% at week 28 and −6.4% versus −1.2% at week 56, with at least 5% weight loss in 55.6% versus 17.5% at week 28 and 50.5% versus 17.1% at week 56. COR-BMOD (Wadden 2011; 793 participants) layered the drug on intensive behaviour modification — 28 group sessions and an energy-reduced diet in both arms — and still found an added drug effect: −9.3% versus −5.1% at week 56. The pooled programme analysis (Fujioka 2016; 2,043 on drug, 1,319 on placebo across the four phase 3 trials) adds the responder rule: patients reaching at least 5% loss by week 16 went on to average 11.7% loss at week 56. The programme's first trial, COR-I (Greenway 2010), is already carded in the live library and is therefore cross-pointed here in prose rather than re-carded; its direction and size (−6.1% versus −1.3% at 56 weeks for the 32 mg dose) match the trials carded on this shelf. Nausea was the most common adverse event in every trial. Two large concordant phase 3 trials plus a pooled programme analysis support the stamp. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): naltrexone-bupropion produces more weight loss than placebo when combined with lifestyle intervention in adults with obesity.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit): across the carded COR phase 3 trials in adults with obesity generally, naltrexone-bupropion 32/360 mg produced consistently greater weight loss than placebo when both were combined with lifestyle intervention (−6.4% vs −1.2% at 56 weeks in COR-II; −9.3% vs −5.1% with intensive behaviour modification in COR-BMOD), with nausea the most common adverse event

title: Rituximab in frequently relapsing adult nephrotic syndrome (observational only): pooled complete remission 84.2% and relapse 27.4% in adult minimal change/FSGS series — but no randomised trial has compared it with calcineurin inhibitors in adults
question: In adults with nephrotic syndrome, does rituximab reduce relapses in frequently relapsing disease versus calcineurin inhibitors?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only, printed on the face. This is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #739 covers rituximab evidence in children with nephrotic syndrome; the uncovered slice carded here is adults, asked against calcineurin inhibitors. The honest headline is that the direct adult comparison does not exist in the records fetched: the Cochrane review of interventions for minimal change disease in adults (Azukaitis 2022; 15 randomised trials, 769 participants) evaluates calcineurin inhibitors against prednisolone (complete remission RR 0.99, 95% CI 0.93 to 1.05; relapse RR 0.73, 95% CI 0.51 to 1.03) and states that randomised data on rituximab in adults are awaited. What exists for rituximab in adults is observational: a systematic review and meta-analysis of 21 cohort studies and case series in frequently relapsing or steroid-dependent minimal change disease/FSGS (Xue 2021; 382 adults) found a pooled complete remission rate of 84.2% (91.6% in minimal change disease, 43% in FSGS) with 27.4% relapsing during 12–43 months of follow-up, and the largest single series carded (Guitard 2014; 41 adults with minimal-change nephrotic syndrome, many previously on steroids or calcineurin inhibitors) found an overall response of 78%, with relapse in 56% of responders at a median of 18 months and renewed responses to a second course. Rituximab therefore looks effective at inducing remission and sparing steroids/CNIs in relapsing adult disease, but relapse after B-cell recovery is common, and superiority — or even equivalence — to calcineurin inhibitors is unproven in adults. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: in pooled adult cohort studies and case series of frequently relapsing or steroid-dependent minimal change disease/FSGS, rituximab induced complete remission in 84.2% with 27.4% relapsing over 12–43 months; no randomised trial in adults has compared rituximab with calcineurin inhibitors, so the versus-CNI half of the question is untested in the records fetched

title: Pasireotide in acromegaly inadequately controlled on first-generation analogs: the PAOLA trial (homed on #745) showed control in 15–20% versus 0% on continued octreotide/lanreotide; switch and real-world reports carded here put IGF-1 control at 14.6% in a single-arm switch study and 57.9% pooled in practice
question: In adults with acromegaly, is pasireotide more effective than octreotide for biochemical control in people inadequately controlled on first-generation somatostatin analogs?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). This is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #745 frames pasireotide versus octreotide in medically untreated acromegaly, and the head-to-head trial for this shelf's population — PAOLA (Gadelha 2014), whose primary record is already carded in the live library — is cross-pointed here in prose rather than re-carded. In PAOLA, 198 patients inadequately controlled after at least 6 months of high-dose octreotide or lanreotide were randomised to pasireotide 40 mg, pasireotide 60 mg, or continued first-generation treatment: biochemical control at 24 weeks was 15% and 20% versus 0% on continued treatment (absolute differences 15.4 and 20.0 percentage points), with hyperglycaemia in 33%/31% versus 14%. The free reports carded here fill out that population without re-carding PAOLA's primary record: its planned biomarker analysis (Schmid 2016) shows responders started with lower growth hormone and IGF-1 and that 47% of pasireotide-treated patients never needed antidiabetic medication; a single-arm phase IIIb switch study (Gadelha 2019; 123 patients) found full biochemical control in 14.6% at week 36 after switching; and a real-world meta-analysis (Biagetti 2025; 12 studies, 409 patients resistant to first-generation ligands) pooled IGF-1 control at 57.9% with tumour shrinkage in 33.3%, alongside worsened glucose measures. The direction is consistent — pasireotide controls some patients whom octreotide/lanreotide cannot — but the carded slice evidence is a biomarker substudy, an uncontrolled switch study, and observational practice data, which caps the stamp at POSSIBLE even though the underlying randomised result is positive. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit): pasireotide achieves biochemical control in a minority of patients inadequately controlled on first-generation somatostatin analogs where continued octreotide/lanreotide achieved none in the head-to-head trial cross-pointed from #745; the reports carded on this shelf (a PAOLA biomarker analysis, a single-arm switch study, and a real-world meta-analysis) are supportive but indirect, and hyperglycaemia is the price

title: Cabergoline beats bromocriptine in prolactinoma: meta-analysis of the randomised trials favours cabergoline for prolactin normalization, and a 498-patient comparison found normalization in 87.4% versus 41.4% with tumour shrinkage of 79.8% versus 54.1%
question: In adults with prolactinoma, is cabergoline more effective than bromocriptine for normalizing prolactin and shrinking tumor?
balance: LIKELY (benefit). This is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #2070 covers this comparison in women with hyperprolactinaemic amenorrhoea (the Webster 1994 trial population); the uncovered slice carded here is prolactinoma in adults generally, including men and macroprolactinoma, with tumour shrinkage as an outcome. The meta-analysis of the randomised trials (dos Santos Nunes 2011; four randomised trials in prolactinoma and idiopathic hyperprolactinaemia) found a significant difference in favour of cabergoline for normalization of serum prolactin (RR 0.67, 95% CI 0.57 to 0.80, as printed in the record) and for restoration of ovulatory cycles (RR 0.74, 95% CI 0.67 to 0.83), with more adverse effects on bromocriptine (RR 1.43, 95% CI 1.03 to 1.98). A small randomised trial enrolling mostly prolactinoma patients (Sabuncu 2001; 34 patients, 22 with micro- or macroprolactinoma) found greater prolactin reduction on cabergoline (−93% vs −87.5%; P < 0.05) and normalization in 82% versus 59%. The largest comparison, a retrospective single-centre series (Arduc 2015; 498 patients), found prolactin normalization in 87.4% on cabergoline versus 41.4% on bromocriptine and mean tumour-volume shrinkage of 79.8% versus 54.1%, with side effects in 5.3% versus 29.1%. The randomised-trial meta-analysis pools the home shelf's Webster trial among its four trials; it is carded here as a distinct publication answering the broader prolactinoma question, and Webster's own record is not re-carded. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): cabergoline is more effective than bromocriptine for normalizing prolactin and shrinking prolactinoma, and is better tolerated.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit): across a meta-analysis of the randomised cabergoline-versus-bromocriptine trials in prolactinoma and idiopathic hyperprolactinaemia, a small randomised trial in prolactinoma patients, and a 498-patient retrospective comparison, cabergoline normalizes prolactin more often, shrinks tumour more, and causes fewer adverse effects than bromocriptine

title: Oral desmopressin maintains control in central diabetes insipidus after switching from intranasal (small old studies only): stable antidiuresis over 1 year on oral therapy in 10 adults, at roughly a 16–17-fold higher microgram dose
question: In adults with central diabetes insipidus, is oral desmopressin as effective as intranasal desmopressin for controlling symptoms?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit — equivalence in practice, on small old studies, printed on the face). This is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #2906 covers how long desmopressin's antidiuretic action lasts by formulation and dose; the uncovered slice carded here is the direct oral-versus-intranasal efficacy comparison in adults with central diabetes insipidus. The evidence is three small switch studies from the intranasal era. Lam 1996 compared the routes head-to-head in 10 adults previously controlled on intranasal desmopressin: oral dosing produced dose-dependent antidiuresis peaking at 4 hours, the bioequivalent intranasal-to-oral ratio was 1:16, and over a 1-year prospective phase oral desmopressin 300–600 µg/day maintained stable, satisfactory antidiuresis comparable with previous intranasal therapy, with no side effect warranting withdrawal. Carraro 1991 switched 13 patients to tablets (150–600 µg/day) for 4 weeks with daily urine volume and osmolarity compared against their intranasal period and very good compliance. Murakami 2014 retrospectively studied 15 Japanese patients switched from intranasal desmopressin to the orally disintegrating tablet and found it safe and effective at a mean oral-to-nasal dose ratio of 17.0. No study randomised patients to oral versus intranasal treatment or tested formal equivalence, and all three predate modern formulations — so 'as effective' rests on maintained control after switching in 38 patients total. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: oral desmopressin is as effective as intranasal for controlling central diabetes insipidus in adults who switch, provided the dose is re-titrated at roughly 16–17 times the intranasal microgram dose.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit — equivalence in practice): in three small switch studies totalling 38 adults, oral desmopressin maintained antidiuresis and symptom control comparable with previous intranasal therapy, at an oral-to-nasal dose ratio of about 16–17 to 1; no randomised equivalence trial exists in the records fetched

title: Leucine and muscle strength in older adults — SPLIT: leucine alone made no difference to strength in the randomised trials (meta-analysis of 17 trials and two long-term RCTs), while leucine combined with vitamin D improved handgrip strength
question: In older adults, does leucine-enriched protein supplementation improve muscle strength versus standard protein?
balance: SPLIT — the split is named in the stamp. This is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #1493 covers a leucine- and vitamin-D-enriched whey supplement in sarcopenic older adults for muscle mass and chair-stand outcomes; the uncovered slice carded here is muscle strength in older adults generally, across the leucine literature. For leucine on its own, the answer is a concordant null: the meta-analysis of 17 randomised trials (Guo 2022; 1,418 participants) found leucine-isolated supplementation had no effect on handgrip strength (weighted mean difference 1.23 kg, 95% CI −0.58 to 3.03; P = 0.183), leg press (−1.35 kg, 95% CI −7.46 to 4.77), or total lean mass (0.03 kg, 95% CI −0.51 to 0.57) — the treatment made no difference. The two long-term trials agree: 3 months of leucine 7.5 g/day in healthy elderly men (Verhoeven 2009; n = 30) and 6 months in elderly men with type 2 diabetes (Leenders 2011; n = 60) each found no change in muscle strength or mass versus placebo. The other half of the split: in the same meta-analysis, leucine-combined supplementation including vitamin D significantly improved handgrip strength (weighted mean difference 2.17 kg, 95% CI 0.24 to 4.10; P = 0.027) and gait speed (0.03 m/s, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.05) — a subgroup signal from combined formulations, not from leucine alone, and the enriched-whey version of that combination in sarcopenic patients homes on #1493. PROPOSED SPLIT: leucine alone does not improve muscle strength in older adults; leucine combined with vitamin D may.
stamp: SPLIT (leucine alone: no benefit — the treatment made no difference to muscle strength in pooled randomised trials; leucine combined with vitamin D: possible benefit, with handgrip strength improved by a weighted mean difference of 2.17 kg in the meta-analysis subgroup)

title: Slower initial feeding to prevent refeeding syndrome in at-risk adults — unproven: no randomised trial compares initial calorie rates in adults; consensus guidance advises starting low, while adult-ward observational series starting at 1,500–2,000 kcal/day reported no attributable refeeding syndrome
question: In adults at risk of refeeding syndrome, does slower initial calorie introduction reduce complications versus standard feeding advancement?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the honest answer is that the benefit of starting slow is assumed, not demonstrated, in adults. This is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #1065 covers caloric restriction AFTER refeeding syndrome has developed in critical illness (the Doig trial); the uncovered slice carded here is prevention — the initial feeding rate in adults at risk who do not yet have the syndrome. No randomised trial comparing initial calorie rates in at-risk adults was found in the records fetched. What exists: the ASPEN consensus recommendations (da Silva 2020), which propose a standard definition (a fall of 10–20%, 20–30%, or over 30% in phosphorus, potassium and/or magnesium, or organ dysfunction, within 5 days of reintroducing calories) and risk-stratified avoidance strategies — consensus built explicitly because the underlying literature varies too much to meta-analyse. The comparative data are observational and mostly from eating-disorder care: a scoping review of higher-calorie refeeding (at least 1,500 kcal/day) on adult hospital wards (Taylor 2026; 11 studies, 4,874 patients exposed) found no deaths or clinically defined refeeding syndrome attributable to higher-calorie starts, with hypophosphataemia in up to about a third, usually mild and managed with supplementation; and the one direct lower-versus-higher calorie comparison carded (Schlapfer 2022) is in patients aged 12–21, not adults — severe refeeding syndrome occurred in 4.4% on lower calories versus 2.6% on higher calories (P = .52), with shorter stays on higher calories. Neither direction of the adult question is established; monitoring and electrolyte replacement, not the starting rate alone, are what the observational series share. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence): whether slower initial calorie introduction reduces complications in at-risk adults has never been tested in a randomised trial in the records fetched; the recommendation to start low rests on consensus guidance, and the comparative observational data that exist (largely eating-disorder wards) do not show more refeeding syndrome with higher-calorie starts under monitoring

title: Treat-to-target beats symptom-driven gout care in the first head-to-head strategy trial (GO TEST Overture): remission in 39.4% versus 24.0%, with reaching urate under 6 mg/dL (0.36 mmol/L) associated with far fewer flares (27% versus 64% having at least one flare)
question: In adults with gout, does treat-to-target urate lowering reduce flare frequency versus treat-to-symptoms management?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single strategy trial, printed on the face. This is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #681 covers nurse-led treat-to-target care versus general-practitioner usual care (the Nottingham trial); the uncovered slice carded here is the formal strategy comparison — treat-to-target against treat-to-symptoms management itself. The GO TEST Overture trial (Moses 2026; 308 adults with gout and hyperuricaemia not on urate-lowering therapy, in Dutch secondary care) randomised exactly that: structured urate-guided titration to a serum urate under 0.36 mmol/L (≈6.1 mg/dL) versus symptom-driven management in which starting urate-lowering therapy was discretionary. Remission during months 18–24 — a composite requiring no flares in that window, no tophi, low pain, and high patient global assessment — occurred in 39.4% versus 24.0% (absolute difference 15.4 percentage points, 95% CI 6.4 to 24.4; P = 0.024), with adverse events in 42% versus 53%. On flares specifically, the supporting individual-patient analysis of two earlier trials (Stamp 2022; 588 participants) found that patients whose average serum urate fell under 6 mg/dL (0.36 mmol/L) had at least one flare in months 12–24 in 27% of cases versus 64% of non-responders (adjusted odds ratio 0.29, 95% CI 0.17 to 0.51) and fewer flares per month (adjusted mean difference −1.41) — an association independent of the original randomised allocation, so supportive rather than randomised strategy evidence. The large US primary-care strategy trial designed to answer this question definitively (Solomon 2025, TRUST) has published its design only, with no results in the record. One completed strategy trial therefore caps the stamp. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): treat-to-target urate lowering reduces flares and improves disease control versus treat-to-symptoms management.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single strategy trial: in the one randomised head-to-head comparison (GO TEST Overture, 308 participants), a treat-to-target strategy (serum urate under 0.36 mmol/L, ≈6.1 mg/dL) produced remission in 39.4% versus 24.0% under symptom-driven management, and pooled trial data show patients reaching target urate had fewer flares; the large US strategy trial (TRUST) has reported design only

title: Pioglitazone in MASH (formerly NASH) — steatohepatitis activity and resolution on biopsy: consistent benefit in every placebo-controlled trial and synthesis (fibrosis and stiffness are asked separately on shelf #5865)
question: In adults with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH — formerly nonalcoholic steatohepatitis, NASH), does pioglitazone improve steatohepatitis activity on biopsy — histologic improvement and resolution of steatohepatitis without worsening fibrosis — versus placebo?
balance: This shelf asks the ACTIVITY question only: does pioglitazone improve steatohepatitis activity on biopsy — histologic improvement and resolution of steatohepatitis without worsening fibrosis? The FIBROSIS and liver-stiffness questions are asked separately on the companion shelf #5865, which is where the record divides; nothing on this shelf claims a fibrosis benefit. Scope: live shelf #2114 holds pioglitazone in steatohepatitis with prediabetes or type 2 diabetes (Belfort 2006; Cusi 2016, primary outcome met in 58%, absolute difference 41 percentage points); this shelf holds the general steatohepatitis evidence anchored on the non-diabetic trial populations. THE ACTIVITY EVIDENCE — consistent benefit in every placebo-controlled trial: Aithal 2008 (74 non-diabetic patients, pioglitazone 30 mg/day, 12 months) improved hepatocellular injury (P = .005) and Mallory-Denk bodies (P = .004) versus placebo. Huang 2021 (90 Asian patients, 24 weeks) achieved steatohepatitis improvement without worsening fibrosis in 46.7% versus 11.1% (absolute difference 35.6 percentage points; P = 0.002), with the activity score falling 4.27 to 2.53 on pioglitazone and not changing on placebo. PIVENS (247 non-diabetic adults; primary record carded on shelf #26 and cross-pointed here) missed its primary composite at its prespecified threshold — 34% versus 19% (P = 0.04 against a required P < 0.025) — but its activity endpoints were strongly positive: steatosis (P < 0.001), lobular inflammation (P = 0.004) and resolution of steatohepatitis in 47% versus 21%. The pilots agree (Promrat 2004: histological improvement in two-thirds; Sanyal 2004: combination-therapy histology gains over vitamin E alone). THE SYNTHESES AGREE: Musso 2017 resolution OR 3.22 (a relative odds measure); Boettcher 2012 activity endpoints all positive (ballooning OR 2.11, lobular inflammation OR 2.58, steatosis OR 3.39, combined necroinflammation OR 6.52 — all relative odds measures); Wang 2023: histologic response does not differ by diabetes status; Shi 2025: pioglitazone ranks first among common medications for resolving steatohepatitis without worsening fibrosis (SUCRA 91.4%). THE ONE DISCORDANT NOTE is PIVENS' primary composite missing its strict prespecified alpha — a threshold miss on a composite, in the same trial whose individual activity endpoints were all strongly positive. THE COST is uniform: weight gain wherever it is measured (+2.77 kg versus −0.55 kg in Aithal 2008; +4.7 kg in PIVENS; +2.70% of body weight in Musso 2017), with oedema alongside. No carded study measures clinical liver outcomes. For fibrosis stage and liver stiffness (kPa), see the companion shelf #5865.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — steatohepatitis activity and resolution improve consistently across every placebo-controlled trial (Aithal 2008 injury P = .005; Huang 2021 improvement without worsening fibrosis 46.7% vs 11.1%) and every synthesis (Musso resolution OR 3.22; Shi 2025 ranked first, SUCRA 91.4%); the one discordant note is PIVENS' primary composite missing its prespecified threshold while its activity endpoints were strongly positive; this stamp claims activity/resolution only — fibrosis and stiffness are asked on the companion shelf #5865, and weight gain is the consistent cost

title: Denosumab versus zoledronic acid in hypercalcemia of malignancy (observational only for treatment): similar calcium lowering in the direct treatment cohort and better prevention in randomised trials — superiority for controlling established calcium is unproven — a partial completion of shelf #2904
question: In adults with hypercalcemia of malignancy, is denosumab more effective than zoledronic acid for controlling calcium?
balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #2904, which covers denosumab in bisphosphonate-refractory hypercalcemia of malignancy (HCM); this shelf homes the head-to-head comparison against zoledronic acid, and #2904's single-arm refractory-disease trial is cross-pointed, not re-carded. No randomised trial has compared the two drugs as treatment for established HCM in the records fetched. The direct treatment evidence is one retrospective cohort of 317 patients with established HCM (Kong 2025), in which denosumab lowered calcium by 2.0 mg/dL and intravenous bisphosphonate by 1.8 mg/dL — similar effectiveness — while bisphosphonate plus calcitonin lowered it most (2.7 mg/dL), and hypocalcemia was significantly less frequent with denosumab; that study's comparator was intravenous bisphosphonates as a class, not zoledronic acid alone, and that limit is printed on its card. The randomised head-to-head evidence is about prevention, not treatment: pooled phase III data (Diel 2015) showed denosumab delayed first on-study HCM versus zoledronic acid (1.7% vs. 2.7% of patients; hazard ratio 0.63, a 37% relative reduction in hazard). A bone-metastases dosing cohort (Nasser 2019) cuts the other way on calcium control, with more hypercalcemia episodes recorded on denosumab than zoledronic acid (8.5% vs. 3.1% of encounters). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only for treatment of established hypercalcemia: denosumab looks at least as effective as bisphosphonate treatment and better at preventing HCM than zoledronic acid, but superiority for controlling established calcium is unproven by any randomised head-to-head trial.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only for treatment of established hypercalcemia: denosumab lowered calcium similarly to intravenous bisphosphonate in the one direct treatment cohort (−2.0 vs. −1.8 mg/dL, with less hypocalcemia) and prevented hypercalcemia better than zoledronic acid in pooled randomised trials (first HCM 1.7% vs. 2.7%), but no randomised head-to-head treatment trial exists

title: Metformin versus lifestyle over 60 in prediabetes (SPLIT): lifestyle intervention was most effective in the oldest DPP group while metformin's effect faded with age — a partial completion of shelf #3519
question: In adults with prediabetes, does metformin delay progression to diabetes in people over 60 versus lifestyle intervention?
balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #3519, which covers metformin and lifestyle after gestational diabetes; this shelf homes the over-60 prediabetes comparison, and the DPP primary report and the DPP Outcomes Study follow-up carded elsewhere in the library are cross-pointed, not re-carded. The DPP's own predefined age analysis (Crandall 2006) answers the question directly: intensive lifestyle intervention (ILS) grew more effective with age — incidence 3.3 cases per 100 person-years at age 60–85, its best result in any age group — while metformin grew less effective with age, with incidence rising to 9.3 cases per 100 person-years at 60–85 and an adjusted hazard ratio of 1.63 for age 60–85 versus 25–44 within the metformin arm. Long-term DPPOS data show metformin itself was safe and durably weight-reducing over 10 years (Diabetes Prevention Program Research Group 2012), so the issue in older adults is comparative efficacy, not tolerability. A 2023 head-to-head meta-analysis of five trials found no significant overall difference between metformin and lifestyle (relative risk 1.14, not significant) — an average that conceals the age gradient the DPP analysis documents. PROPOSED SPLIT (lifestyle: strong benefit over 60; metformin: effect faded with age) — in people over 60, lifestyle intervention is the effective treatment for delaying diabetes and metformin should not be presented as its equal: its delaying effect was weakest, and trended to absent, in the oldest group.
stamp: SPLIT (lifestyle: strong benefit over 60; metformin: effect faded with age) — in the DPP age analysis, incidence at age 60–85 was 3.3 cases per 100 person-years on lifestyle intervention versus 9.3 on metformin, and metformin risk rose with age (hazard ratio 1.63, oldest vs. youngest); metformin was safe long-term, so the preference for lifestyle over 60 is about efficacy, not tolerability

title: Setmelanotide in POMC deficiency obesity (single-arm evidence only, total N = 10): large weight loss on treatment, but no placebo-controlled trial exists to answer 'versus placebo' — a partial completion of shelf #1093
question: In adults with obesity without diabetes, does setmelanotide produce weight loss in people with POMC deficiency obesity versus placebo?
balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #1093, which homes the primary phase 3 report of setmelanotide in POMC/LEPR deficiency; that report is cross-pointed here, not re-carded, and this shelf homes the placebo-comparison question it cannot answer. The honest answer is that the 'versus placebo' comparison does not exist: every POMC report in the records fetched is single-arm and open-label, with no placebo group at any point. What the free reports add is corroboration around that gap. A 2023 review of the phase 3 programme (Trapp 2023) records that 10 participants with POMC/PCSK1 deficiency were enrolled and 80% of POMC participants achieved at least 10% weight loss at 1 year. The natural-history analysis (Wabitsch 2022) shows the untreated trajectory these patients were on — above the 95th weight percentile throughout childhood with continuous gain and no long-term loss from diet, surgery or exercise — and that setmelanotide attenuated the trajectory over 1 year (POMC n = 8 of 17 analysed). Quality-of-life data from the two phase 3 trials (Kühnen 2022) show impaired baseline quality of life improving on treatment in most adults assessed. The trials also enrolled children and adolescents, so the evidence is not adults-only, and the total POMC evidence base is the pivotal cohort of 10 — both limits are printed on the stamp. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — single-arm evidence only, total N = 10 with POMC deficiency: substantial weight loss occurred on treatment against a documented history of continuous gain, but with no placebo-controlled trial the size of any placebo-adjusted effect is unknown.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single-arm evidence only, total N = 10 with POMC deficiency: 80% of the pivotal POMC cohort achieved at least 10% weight loss at 1 year on setmelanotide against a natural history of continuous gain, but no placebo-controlled trial exists, so no placebo-adjusted effect can be stated

title: Ursodiol prevents gallstone formation after bariatric surgery (LIKELY): formation fell from 22–32% on placebo to 2–8% on treatment in two placebo-controlled trials — a partial completion of shelf #1668
question: In adults after bariatric surgery, does ursodiol prevent gallstone formation versus placebo?
balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #1668, which covers ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) against symptomatic gallstone disease after bariatric surgery (the UPGRADE trial); this shelf homes the upstream outcome UPGRADE was not powered around — gallstone formation itself on imaging — and UPGRADE is cross-pointed, not re-carded. Two placebo-controlled trials measured formation directly and agree. Sugerman 1995 (gastric bypass; 233 patients with postoperative sonograms) found 6-month formation of 32% on placebo versus 2% on ursodiol 600 mg/day and 6% on 1,200 mg/day. Miller 2003 (gastric restrictive procedures; 152 randomised) found formation of 3% versus 22% at 12 months and 8% versus 30% at 24 months, favouring UDCA 500 mg/day, with fewer cholecystectomies (4.7% vs. 12%). The 2022 meta-analysis of 11 randomised trials (Mulliri) pools the same direction: gallstone formation odds ratio 0.25 relative, with symptomatic disease and cholecystectomy also reduced. Absolute differences in the two trials are large (roughly 20–30 percentage points), so the relative measures are not carrying the claim alone. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): six months of ursodiol after bariatric surgery prevents gallstone formation versus placebo, on two concordant placebo-controlled trials and a concordant 11-trial meta-analysis.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — six months of ursodiol after bariatric surgery prevents gallstone formation versus placebo: 32% vs. 2% at 6 months (600 mg/day, gastric bypass) and 22% vs. 3% at 12 months (500 mg/day, restrictive procedures), with a pooled formation odds ratio of 0.25 across 11 randomised trials

title: High-protein diet and muscle preservation in sarcopenic obesity (SPLIT): enriched protein supplements preserved muscle during weight loss, but a high-protein diet alone showed no significant effect in its factorial trial — a partial completion of pack #5126
question: In adults with sarcopenic obesity, does high-protein hypocaloric diet preserve muscle during weight loss versus standard calorie restriction?
balance: PARTIAL completion of pack #5126, which tested a protein-enriched diet combined with resistance exercise in sarcopenic obesity; this shelf homes the diet question during weight loss itself, and #5126's whey-plus-training trial is cross-pointed, not re-carded. The evidence divides on a distinction the question hides: enriched protein supplements versus simply eating a higher-protein diet. In Verreijen 2015, where both arms followed a hypocaloric diet plus resistance training, a whey protein-, leucine- and vitamin D-enriched supplement preserved appendicular muscle mass (+0.4 kg vs. −0.5 kg; between-group difference 0.95 kg, P = 0.03). Memelink 2020 found the same direction for an enriched protein drink during a combined lifestyle intervention (appendicular muscle mass +0.36 kg vs. control). But the one trial that isolated diet alone — Verreijen 2017's 2×2 factorial of high-protein diet (target 1.3 g/kg) and/or resistance exercise — found the high-protein diet did not significantly affect fat-free mass change (the treatment made no significant difference); only the combined diet-plus-exercise group significantly gained fat-free mass. A further limit is printed on every card: these trials enrolled obese older adults at risk of muscle loss, not patients with formally diagnosed sarcopenic obesity. PROPOSED SPLIT (enriched protein supplements during a weight-loss programme: benefit; higher-protein diet alone: no significant difference) — protein enrichment as a supplement preserved muscle during weight loss in two trials where exercise was present in both arms, but a high-protein diet by itself has not been shown to do so.
stamp: SPLIT (enriched protein supplements during a weight-loss programme: benefit; higher-protein diet alone: no significant difference) — whey/leucine/vitamin D supplements preserved appendicular muscle mass (+0.95 kg and +0.36 kg between-group) in two trials with exercise in both arms, but the factorial trial of a high-protein diet alone found no significant fat-free-mass effect; no trial required a formal sarcopenic-obesity diagnosis

question: In adults with diabetic gastroparesis, does gastric peroral endoscopic myotomy improve symptoms versus botulinum toxin injection?
balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #3525, which covers gastric peroral endoscopic myotomy (G-POEM) versus sham in diabetic gastroparesis; this shelf homes the head-to-head against botulinum toxin injection (BTI), and the sham trial is cross-pointed, not re-carded. The direct evidence is one small double-blind randomised trial (Gonzalez 2024; 40 patients with refractory gastroparesis) in which clinical success favoured G-POEM numerically at 3 months (65% vs. 40%) and 1 year (60% vs. 40%) but neither difference was statistically significant (P = 0.10 at 3 months). Two limits define this shelf and are printed on the cards: the trial was mixed-etiology — only 11 of its 40 patients had diabetic gastroparesis, with no diabetic-subgroup results in the record — and the supporting comparison (Tran 2023) sets one centre's G-POEM series (28 analysed patients, of whom 4 were diabetic) against BTI results from the published literature rather than a randomised comparator. A 2026 cost-effectiveness model built on the randomised data found BTI more cost-effective at 3 months and G-POEM at 12 months once repeat injections were counted — a durability argument, not new efficacy data. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): G-POEM probably improves symptoms at least as much as botulinum toxin injection and likely more durably, but the single head-to-head trial was too small to demonstrate superiority, and diabetic-specific comparative results have not been reported.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — G-POEM clinical success was numerically higher than botulinum toxin injection in the only double-blind randomised head-to-head (65% vs. 40% at 3 months, P = 0.10, not significant; 60% vs. 40% at 1 year), but the trial had 40 patients of mixed etiology (11 diabetic, with no diabetic-subgroup results reported), so superiority in diabetic gastroparesis is plausible, not demonstrated

title: Pioglitazone in MASH (formerly NASH) — liver fibrosis on biopsy and liver stiffness (kPa): benefit in the smaller trials and pioglitazone-only pooling, none in the largest trial; the stiffness evidence is thin (activity and resolution are asked separately on shelf #5857)
question: In adults with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH — formerly nonalcoholic steatohepatitis, NASH), does pioglitazone improve liver fibrosis on biopsy (fibrosis stage or score), and what does the liver-stiffness (elastography, kPa) evidence show?
balance: This shelf asks the FIBROSIS question, and its non-invasive counterpart: does pioglitazone improve liver fibrosis on biopsy (fibrosis stage or score), and what does the liver-stiffness (elastography, kPa) evidence show? The ACTIVITY and resolution question is asked separately on the companion shelf #5857, where the record is consistent and the answer is yes; nothing on this shelf borrows that consistency. Scope: live shelf #2114 holds pioglitazone in steatohepatitis with prediabetes or type 2 diabetes (Belfort 2006; Cusi 2016) and is cross-pointed here; PIVENS' primary record is carded on shelf #26 and cross-pointed here. FIBROSIS ON BIOPSY — the record divides by analysis, not by endpoint definition: Aithal 2008 (74 non-diabetic patients, pioglitazone 30 mg/day, 12 months) reduced fibrosis versus placebo at exactly P = .05. Boettcher 2012 found fibrosis improvement NOT significant for the thiazolidinedione class as a whole, but significant for pioglitazone alone (OR 1.68, 95% CI 1.02 to 2.77 — a relative odds measure whose interval only just excludes no effect). Musso 2017, the synthesis whose primary outcome was fibrosis, found advanced fibrosis OR 3.15 (95% CI 1.25 to 7.93) and any-stage fibrosis OR 1.66 (1.12 to 2.47), with similar results in patients without diabetes (advanced fibrosis OR 2.95) and all effects accounted for by pioglitazone. Luo 2022's network analysis ranks pioglitazone first among the compared drugs for reducing biopsy fibrosis score. AGAINST: PIVENS — the largest and longest trial (247 non-diabetic adults, 96 weeks; cross-pointed from shelf #26) — found fibrosis improvement in 44% on pioglitazone versus 31% on placebo (P = 0.12), not significant, and Boettcher's class pool was likewise null. Cusi 2016 (cross-pointed, shelf #2114) points with the smaller trials (fibrosis score treatment difference −0.5; P = 0.039). That is a genuine split — smaller trials and pioglitazone-only pooling positive, the largest trial negative — not mere absence of data. LIVER STIFFNESS (kPa) — the evidence is thin, and it comes late: Kamolvisit 2021, the only placebo-controlled elastography trial found (98 people with HIV and prediabetes and fatty liver; baseline stiffness 5.4 kPa — early disease), showed no stiffness difference at 24 weeks (+0.014 vs +0.403 kPa; P = 0.199) and a significant one at 48 weeks (−0.184 vs +0.554 kPa; P = 0.016), a between-arm difference of about 0.7 kPa; the fat measure (controlled attenuation parameter) improved earlier and larger. Pereira 2025 (65 Brazilian patients on pioglitazone 30–45 mg/day for up to 10 years, retrospective, no control group) found FibroScan-AST (FAST) scores improved in both duration groups and the attenuation parameter fell significantly only in the 4–10-year group, but liver stiffness reduction itself was not significant (the only stiffness signal in its regression was a non-significant dyslipidemia association, adjusted OR 1.92, 95% CI 0.58 to 6.45); the group's earlier conference report recorded median stiffness 8.1 → 7.2 kPa with attenuation in 63% of a smaller 12–24-month cohort. On the ELF blood fibrosis score, Luo 2022 ranks liraglutide, not pioglitazone, first. NO MR-elastography trial and NO FIB-4-endpoint trial of pioglitazone exists in the record — stated plainly, because stiffness is the endpoint clinicians most often reach for. THE COST is uniform: weight gain wherever it is measured (+2.77 kg versus −0.55 kg in Aithal 2008; +2.70% of body weight in Musso 2017; +4.7 kg in PIVENS), with oedema alongside. No carded study measures clinical liver outcomes. For steatohepatitis activity and resolution, see the companion shelf #5857.
stamp: SPLIT (fibrosis on biopsy: benefit in the smaller trials and in pioglitazone-only pooled analyses — Boettcher 2012 pioglitazone-only OR 1.68 (95% CI 1.02–2.77); Musso 2017 advanced fibrosis OR 3.15, any-stage OR 1.66; Luo 2022 ranks pioglitazone first for reducing biopsy fibrosis score — but no significant fibrosis benefit in the largest trial, PIVENS (improvement 44% vs 31%; P = 0.12, cross-pointed in the balance), and the thiazolidinedione-class pool was likewise not significant; liver stiffness: thin evidence — one small elastography trial in early disease positive at 48 weeks (−0.184 vs +0.554 kPa; P = 0.016), one retrospective series without a significant stiffness reduction, and no MR-elastography trial exists; steatohepatitis activity and resolution are asked on the companion shelf #5857, and weight gain is the consistent cost)

title: Metformin versus lifestyle in younger adults with obesity (SPLIT): near-equal in younger cohorts and strongest in the more obese, but pooled head-to-head data still favour lifestyle — a partial completion of shelf #3519
question: In adults with prediabetes, is metformin as effective as intensive lifestyle intervention for delaying diabetes in younger adults with obesity?
balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #3519, which covers metformin and lifestyle in women with prior gestational diabetes; this shelf homes the younger, obese general-prediabetes comparison, and the DPP primary report carded elsewhere is cross-pointed, not re-carded. The fairest summary is 'close, but not equal — and closest exactly in the young and heavy'. The DPP/DPPOS metformin review (Aroda 2017) records that metformin reduced diabetes incidence by 31% relative versus placebo overall, with a greater effect in those who were more obese, had higher fasting glucose, or had a history of gestational diabetes — the younger-heavier profile. The Indian Diabetes Prevention Programme (Ramachandran 2006), in a younger cohort (mean age 45.9 years), found lifestyle and metformin almost identical: 3-year cumulative incidence 39.3% on lifestyle and 40.5% on metformin versus 55.0% on control (relative risk reductions 28.5% and 26.4%). But the pooled head-to-head meta-analysis (Mousavi 2023; mean age 50, mean BMI 35.5) still favours lifestyle: diabetes incidence was 25.3% relatively lower with lifestyle modification than with metformin (relative risk 0.747, p = 0.007). PROPOSED SPLIT (lifestyle modestly ahead overall; metformin essentially as effective in younger, more obese cohorts) — metformin is a reasonable near-equal where lifestyle programmes are not feasible in younger adults with obesity, but the pooled direct comparison does not support calling the two equal.
stamp: SPLIT (lifestyle modestly ahead overall; metformin essentially as effective in younger, more obese cohorts) — pooled head-to-head data favour lifestyle (relative risk 0.747 for diabetes incidence), but in the younger IDPP cohort lifestyle and metformin were near-identical (3-year incidence 39.3% vs. 40.5%) and the DPP found metformin's effect greatest in the more obese

title: Renal denervation off medications (SPLIT): it lowered pressure without drugs in non-resistant hypertension, but the resistant-hypertension effect is smaller and resistant patients off medication are untested — a partial completion of shelf #160
question: Does renal denervation lower blood pressure in resistant hypertension off medications?
balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #160, which covers renal denervation versus sham overall; this shelf homes the off-medication cut, and the large off-medication pivotal trial carded on #160 is cross-pointed, not re-carded. The precise population in the question — resistant hypertension studied while off all antihypertensive medication — has never been randomised in the records fetched: every resistant-hypertension denervation trial kept patients on medication, for the obvious safety reason. What exists is the two halves of the question in different trials. Off medication, in non-resistant uncontrolled hypertension, denervation beat sham in both carded trials: the SPYRAL HTN-OFF MED proof-of-concept (Townsend 2017; between-group difference −5.0 mm Hg in 24-hour systolic pressure at 3 months) and RADIANCE-HTN SOLO (Azizi 2018; baseline-adjusted difference −6.3 mm Hg in daytime ambulatory systolic pressure at 2 months). In resistant hypertension, the subgroup meta-analysis of all ten sham-controlled trials (Ahmed 2023) found the ambulatory effect smaller and not significant (24-hour systolic raw mean difference −1.86 mm Hg, confidence interval crossing zero), versus a significant −4.19 mm Hg in non-resistant trials, with a significant subgroup interaction for diastolic pressure (p = 0.02). PROPOSED SPLIT (off-medication efficacy shown in non-resistant hypertension; resistant-hypertension effect smaller and unproven off medication) — denervation does lower blood pressure without medication on board, but in resistant hypertension specifically the sham-controlled effect is weaker, and resistant patients off medication are an untested population, so the answer for them is inference, not evidence.
stamp: SPLIT (off-medication efficacy shown in non-resistant hypertension; resistant-hypertension effect smaller and unproven off medication) — denervation beat sham off medication by −5.0 and −6.3 mm Hg in two trials of non-resistant hypertension, but pooled resistant-hypertension trials (all on medication) show a non-significant −1.86 mm Hg ambulatory effect, and no trial has studied resistant patients off medication

title: Renal denervation at 3 years: the blood-pressure fall is maintained — both sham-controlled programmes still favour denervation at 36 months and registry reductions persist, with no late safety signal reported
question: Does renal denervation maintain blood pressure lowering at 3 years?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — PARTIAL completion of live shelf #160, which homes renal denervation versus sham at its primary (6-month) horizon; this shelf answers only the uncovered slice, 3-year durability, and none of #160's carded records is re-carded here. Two sham-controlled programmes report 36-month outcomes and both still favour denervation: SPYRAL HTN-ON MED (Mahfoud 2022) found an adjusted ambulatory systolic difference of −10.0 mm Hg at 36 months on a similar medication burden, and the SYMPLICITY HTN-3 final report (Bhatt 2022) found adjusted differences of −22.1 mm Hg (office) and −16.5 mm Hg (ambulatory) — although HTN-3's 36-month contrast was built after unmasking, crossover and imputation, so it overstates the certainty of the gap. The uncontrolled evidence points the same way: Symplicity HTN-1 (Krum 2014) held −32.0/−14.4 mm Hg at 36 months, and the Global SYMPLICITY Registry (Mahfoud 2019) held −16.5 mm Hg office and −8.0 mm Hg ambulatory systolic reductions at 3 years in 1,742 patients, with eGFR declines of 7.1 (no CKD) and 3.7 (CKD) mL/min/1.73 m² and no long-term safety concerns reported. No carded record reports a late safety penalty. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): renal denervation's blood-pressure lowering is maintained at 3 years, with the caveat that the precise advantage over sham at 3 years is less certain than the trial reports' point estimates.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit): blood-pressure lowering after renal denervation is maintained at 3 years — adjusted 36-month differences versus sham of −10.0 mm Hg ambulatory systolic (SPYRAL HTN-ON MED) and −16.5 mm Hg ambulatory / −22.1 mm Hg office (SYMPLICITY HTN-3), with sustained reductions in open-label and registry cohorts and no late safety signal reported

title: Linagliptin in stage 4 CKD: safe and effective against placebo at full dose — but never randomised against dose-adjusted sitagliptin or vildagliptin, which show near-identical placebo-adjusted HbA1c effects in parallel trials
question: In adults with type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease stage 4, is linagliptin safe and effective versus other DPP-4 inhibitors requiring dose adjustment?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — PARTIAL completion of live shelf #3552, which covers linagliptin's cardiovascular and kidney outcomes versus placebo (CARMELINA); this shelf answers only the uncovered slice, the stage-4 head-to-head comparison against dose-adjusted DPP-4 rivals, and none of #3552's carded records is re-carded here. The honest headline is that the direct trial does not exist in the records fetched: the Cochrane CKD review (Lo 2018) found only one DPP-4-versus-DPP-4 study in the entire CKD literature (vildagliptin versus sitagliptin) and no linagliptin head-to-head. What exists is parallel placebo-controlled evidence at stage-4-range kidney function: full-dose linagliptin lowered HbA1c by 0.72 points more than placebo at 1 year in severe impairment with three severe hypoglycaemia cases per group (McGill 2013, N = 133); dose-adjusted vildagliptin (50 mg daily) lowered it by 0.7 points more than placebo in severe impairment with a placebo-like safety profile (Kothny 2012); and dose-adjusted sitagliptin (25 mg daily in severe insufficiency) matched glipizide with symptomatic hypoglycaemia in 6.2% versus 17.0% (Arjona Ferreira 2013). Each agent is individually safe and effective at low eGFR; which is best has never been randomised. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): linagliptin's no-adjustment convenience is real and its stage-4 efficacy and safety are trial-proven against placebo, but superiority or equivalence versus dose-adjusted rivals is unproven — the comparison is indirect only.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence): no head-to-head trial of linagliptin versus a dose-adjusted DPP-4 inhibitor in stage 4 CKD was found — linagliptin (HbA1c −0.72 points vs placebo at 1 year in severe impairment), dose-adjusted vildagliptin (−0.7 points vs placebo) and dose-adjusted sitagliptin (noninferior to glipizide, less hypoglycaemia) are each proven only in parallel, so the comparison is indirect only

title: Phosphate binders versus placebo in non-dialysis CKD: mortality benefit unproven — pooled relative risks favour binders but are low-certainty and cross no effect, while calcification progressed more on binders in the largest placebo trial
question: In adults with chronic kidney disease, do phosphate binders reduce mortality versus placebo in people not on dialysis?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — PARTIAL completion of pack #5527, which compares sevelamer with calcium-based binders in non-dialysis CKD; this shelf answers only the uncovered slice, binders versus placebo for mortality, and none of #5527's carded records is re-carded here. The direct answer is that no mortality benefit has been shown: the Cochrane review (Natale 2025) puts the relative risk of death versus placebo/usual care at 0.45 (95% CI 0.13 to 1.53) for sevelamer and 0.33 (0.10 to 1.05) for lanthanum — relative measures, graded low-certainty, both compatible with no effect — and cardiovascular death was not estimable because no events were reported in the placebo-controlled studies. The non-dialysis placebo trials explain why a benefit is hard to credit: binders lowered phosphate only modestly and coronary calcification progressed more on pooled binders than placebo (Block 2012); sevelamer made no difference to FGF23 or serum phosphate over 12 weeks (Liabeuf 2017, FRENCH); and lanthanum made no difference to vascular function or arterial stiffness (Jovanovich 2024). Gastrointestinal harms versus placebo are real (constipation relative risk about 3 for both binders; nausea relative risk 2.99 for lanthanum). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): phosphate binders have not been shown to reduce mortality versus placebo in people with CKD who are not on dialysis.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence): no mortality benefit shown versus placebo in non-dialysis CKD — relative risk of death 0.45 (95% CI 0.13 to 1.53) for sevelamer and 0.33 (0.10 to 1.05) for lanthanum, low-certainty with intervals crossing no effect, no cardiovascular deaths reported, and mechanistic trials showing no FGF23 or vascular benefit

title: Allopurinol for uric acid stones: unproven — no placebo trial exists; the only data bundle it with citrate and show the same recurrence rate, because acid urine, not urate load, is the main driver
question: In adults with uric acid kidney stones, does allopurinol reduce stone recurrence versus placebo?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — observational only. PARTIAL completion of live shelf #3209, which homes allopurinol versus placebo for calcium oxalate stones with hyperuricosuria (Ettinger 1986); this shelf answers only the uncovered slice, uric acid stones, and Ettinger 1986 is cross-pointed here in prose only and is NOT re-carded. For uric acid stones the fetched records contain no placebo-controlled trial of allopurinol at all: the comparative evidence bundles allopurinol with potassium citrate, in which form adherence was associated with smaller recurrences and fewer operations but an identical recurrence rate of 32% (Canales 2019), and a dissolution series using citrate alone or with allopurinol cleared 67% of treated patients with no comparator and no allopurinol-only arm (Gridley 2019). The standard account of this stone type (Wiederkehr 2011) attributes formation primarily to unduly acid urine — hyperuricosuria a less deciding factor — and names urinary alkalinisation to pH 6–6.5 as the essential drug treatment. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — observational only: whether allopurinol reduces uric acid stone recurrence versus placebo is untested; its benefit for this stone type is unproven.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — observational only: allopurinol has never been tested against placebo in uric acid stones in the records fetched; bundled with potassium citrate it was associated with smaller recurrences and fewer operations but the same recurrence rate (32%), so its benefit for uric acid stones is unproven

title: Tramadol in older adults with neuropathic pain: generally avoid — modest 4–6-week benefit, adverse events in 58%, a reproducible early hyponatraemia signal, and more fractures than codeine (though recorded falls did not differ)
question: Should tramadol be avoided in older adults with neuropathic pain because of hyponatremia and falls?
balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — observational only for the hyponatraemia and fracture outcomes. PARTIAL completion of live shelf #2696, which covers tramadol's benefit–harm balance in musculoskeletal and osteoarthritis pain; this shelf answers only the uncovered slice, older adults with neuropathic pain and the hyponatraemia/falls harms, and none of #2696's carded records is re-carded here. The benefit in neuropathic pain is modest and short-term: at least 50% relief in 53% versus 30% on placebo over 4–6 weeks (NNT 4.4, low-quality evidence), with adverse events in 58% versus 34% and adverse-event withdrawal in 16% versus 3% (Duehmke 2017, Cochrane). The hyponatraemia signal is consistent across designs and is concentrated at initiation: hospitalisation for severe hyponatraemia at an adjusted odds ratio of 2.34 in the first 90 days, with no increased risk in ongoing users (Falhammar 2019), and early laboratory hyponatraemia at a matched rate ratio of 1.57 versus acetaminophen alone (Lee 2023). On falls the record is more nuanced than the question assumes: the large tramadol-versus-codeine cohort found more fractures (hazard ratio 1.50; 12.26 vs 8.13 per 1,000 person-years) and higher mortality, but no significant difference in recorded falls (Xie 2021) — both facts are printed on the card. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm) — observational only for harms: in older adults with neuropathic pain, tramadol's modest, short-lived benefit does not justify its adverse-event burden and early hyponatraemia risk, and it should generally be avoided.
stamp: POSSIBLE (harm) — observational only for hyponatraemia and fractures: tramadol should generally be avoided in older adults with neuropathic pain — modest short-term relief (53% vs 30% achieving 50% relief) against adverse events in 58%, early hyponatraemia (adjusted OR 2.34 for hospitalisation in the first 90 days; rate ratio 1.57 for early laboratory hyponatraemia) and more fractures versus codeine (HR 1.50), though recorded falls did not differ significantly

title: Citrate intake and low urinary citrate: urinary citrate rises (lemonade +383 mg/day), but stone prevention by diet alone is unproven — no randomised trial, and the one long-term stone-rate fall missed significance
question: Does increasing citrate intake prevent kidney stones in adults with low urinary citrate?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — PARTIAL completion of live shelf #2645, which homes potassium citrate drug therapy for recurrent calcium stones; this shelf answers only the uncovered slice, dietary citrate intake (juices and lemonade) in people with low urinary citrate, and none of #2645's carded records is re-carded here. Intake does move the urine: long-term lemonade raised urinary citrate by a mean of 383 mg/day in hypocitraturic stone formers (Kang 2007), fruit juices raised citraturia by a pooled 167.2 mg/day across controlled studies (Pachaly 2016), and orange juice — unlike lemonade — delivered an alkali load that raised urinary pH and citrate and lowered calculated calcium oxalate supersaturation in a metabolic crossover (Odvina 2006). But prevention of stones themselves is unproven for intake: the only long-term stone-outcome report is Kang's retrospective 11-patient lemonade series, whose formation-rate fall from 1.00 to 0.13 stones per patient-year was reported as not statistically significant (p > 0.05), and the review authors themselves call for larger trials. A small randomised crossover of a lemonade beverage in 8 hypocitraturic stone formers exists but falls below this library's 10-human reference floor and is not carded. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): increasing citrate intake raises urinary citrate in low-citrate adults; whether it prevents kidney stones has not been shown in a randomised trial.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence): increasing citrate intake raises urinary citrate (lemonade +383 mg/day in hypocitraturic stone formers; fruit juices pooled +167.2 mg/day), but stone prevention is unproven — the only long-term stone-rate fall (1.00 to 0.13 per patient-year) was not statistically significant and no randomised trial has tested intake against stone recurrence

title: Late-evening snack in cirrhosis: nutrition improves — body protein accretes with nighttime feeding (+0.53 kg over 12 months) and albumin rises in pooled trials — but hard outcomes are unproven
question: In adults with cirrhosis and malnutrition, does a late-evening snack improve nitrogen balance and outcomes versus no snack?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — PARTIAL completion of live shelf #5369, where an evening protein snack appears only as one component of an intensive feeding bundle in refractory ascites; this shelf answers only the uncovered slice, the isolated late-evening snack in cirrhosis with malnutrition, and none of #5369's carded records is re-carded here. The best trial isolates timing: the same 710 kcal/day supplement given at night increased total body protein by 0.53 kg over 12 months while daytime feeding produced no significant change, at equal total intakes (Plank 2008, N = 103). Pooled snack trials show the metabolic side of the same picture — improved respiratory quotient and carbohydrate oxidation within weeks and higher serum albumin by 3–12 weeks (Guo 2018, 14 trials, 478 patients) — and a network meta-analysis found the snack better than no snack in direct randomised comparisons on nutritional indicators (Yu 2022). Nitrogen balance and nutritional status therefore improve; what does not exist in the carded records is a hard-outcome result — no mortality, ascites or encephalopathy effect size for the isolated snack is reported. (A further snack trial, Nakaya 2007, is homed on shelf #3630 and is cross-pointed here in prose only, not re-carded.) PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a late-evening snack improves nitrogen balance and nutritional status in adults with cirrhosis and malnutrition; benefit on survival and complications is unproven.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit): a late-evening snack improves nitrogen balance and nutritional status in cirrhosis — nighttime supplementation raised total body protein by 0.53 kg over 12 months where daytime feeding did not, and pooled trials show higher albumin and improved energy metabolism — but no survival or complication benefit is reported in the carded records

title: Bedtime alginate add-on on a PPI: plausible but untested as a specific strategy — general add-on evidence is positive in one trial, while the homed bedtime trial's confirmatory study found no advantage over placebo add-on
question: Does adding an alginate at bedtime help adults with reflux who still have nighttime symptoms on a proton pump inhibitor?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — PARTIAL completion of live shelf #2655, which covers alginate efficacy generally; this shelf answers only the uncovered slice, the bedtime add-on in patients still symptomatic on a proton pump inhibitor, and none of #2655's carded records is re-carded here. Flag for the developer: the one trial that dosed alginate-antacid after meals and at bedtime in PPI breakthrough patients (Coyle 2017) is already carded on #2655 — its exploratory study favoured the add-on but its confirmatory study found no significant difference versus placebo add-on (51% vs 48% response) — so it is cross-pointed here in prose only, its PMID kept out of the card source lines. title: Barrett's surveillance interval (no trial fixes it): longer-than-guideline intervals showed no curability or mortality penalty in a 726-patient prospective cohort — the frequency question is answered only by observational data
question: How often should adults with non-dysplastic Barrett's esophagus have surveillance endoscopy?
balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #3441, which covers surveillance versus endoscopy at need (the BOSS comparison); this shelf covers the uncovered slice — how often surveillance should be done. No randomised trial has compared one surveillance interval against another in non-dysplastic Barrett's esophagus. The best interval evidence is observational: in a multicentre prospective cohort of 726 patients (3,802 endoscopies), only 16% of non-dysplastic surveillance was adherent to the recommended interval, yet longer intervals than recommended showed no evidence of affecting endoscopic curability of adenocarcinoma or cause-specific mortality (Roumans 2023). A structured programme cohort detected high-grade dysplasia or T1 cancer at a combined rate of 1 per 77.6 endoscopy-years of follow-up (Bright 2009), and a Veterans Affairs cohort found most surveillance was non-adherent to the 3-year guideline interval with no difference in biopsy-positive endoscopies between adherent and non-adherent patients (Dalal 2018). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — observational only: no trial fixes the right interval; the observational record does not show that stretching beyond guideline intervals worsens curability or mortality, and does not show that shorter intervals help.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — observational only: no trial compares surveillance intervals in non-dysplastic Barrett's esophagus; a prospective cohort found no evidence that longer-than-recommended intervals worsen cancer curability or cause-specific mortality, and programme data put detection at about 1 high-grade dysplasia/T1 cancer per 77.6 endoscopy-years
