title: Aspirin plus PPI and Barrett's cancer risk alone (SPLIT): observational studies associate the drugs with less adenocarcinoma, but the bias-graded review and the trial's cancer-specific outcome show no significant association
question: Does aspirin plus a proton pump inhibitor reduce cancer risk in adults with Barrett's esophagus?
balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #773, which covers the AspECT trial on its composite of death, adenocarcinoma and high-grade dysplasia; this shelf covers the uncovered slice — cancer risk alone. FLAG FOR THE DEVELOPER (one-home precedent b): the AspECT record itself (PMID: 30057104) is already carded on the home shelf, so it is NOT re-carded here; this pack is built entirely on three free reports that address the cancer-specific outcome. They split. In a Veterans Affairs nested case-control study where PPI use was almost universal (94–95%), filled aspirin/NSAID prescriptions were associated with a lower risk of adenocarcinoma (adjusted incidence density ratio 0.64) — effectively aspirin on a PPI background (Nguyen 2010). A second cohort found PPI use associated with reduced high-grade dysplasia/cancer while aspirin/NSAID showed only a nonsignificant trend (Nguyen 2009). But the 2025 systematic review with bias assessment found aspirin not significantly associated with progression in pooled observational data (adjusted OR 0.84), graded all observational evidence serious-to-critical risk of bias, and reported that the single randomised trial found no significant association for high-grade dysplasia/cancer — very low certainty overall (Ko 2025). PROPOSED SPLIT (observational studies: aspirin/PPI use is associated with less cancer; the randomised trial's cancer-specific outcome and the bias-adjusted review: no significant association) — the combination's effect on cancer alone is unproven.
stamp: SPLIT (observational studies associate aspirin/PPI use with less Barrett's cancer — adjusted incidence density ratio 0.64 for aspirin/NSAIDs on a near-universal PPI background; the bias-adjusted 2025 review finds aspirin nonsignificant, adjusted OR 0.84, and the single randomised trial no significant cancer-specific association) — unproven for cancer alone

title: Steroid versus diet in eosinophilic esophagitis (no head-to-head trial): indirect evidence puts histologic response in the same range for both — 68–77% for swallowed steroids, 69% for six-food elimination
question: Is a swallowed topical steroid better than dietary elimination for eosinophilic esophagitis in adults?
balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #774, which covers swallowed budesonide versus placebo; this shelf covers the uncovered slice — the head-to-head against dietary elimination. No randomised trial has compared a swallowed topical steroid directly with dietary elimination in adults. The comparison exists only indirectly: a meta-regression of 51 articles found summary histologic response rates of the same order for fluticasone (68.3%), budesonide (76.8%) and six-food elimination diet (69.0%), with the authors stating plainly that heterogeneity prevents direct comparison of the modalities (Cotton 2017). A modelled cost-utility analysis built on the same literature found topical fluticasone about as effective as the elimination diet but more expensive over 5 years, with the diet more effective and less expensive in the base case (Cotton 2017). In adults, the comparative literature is otherwise about combining the two rather than choosing between them (Reed 2019). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): no head-to-head trial exists; indirect evidence puts steroid and diet response rates in the same range, so neither can be called better.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — no head-to-head trial in adults: indirect meta-regression puts histologic response in the same range for swallowed steroids (68.3–76.8%) and six-food elimination diet (69.0%), and a cost-utility model found them about as effective, so neither can be called better

title: Dupilumab after steroid failure in eosinophilic esophagitis (subgroup evidence): benefit held regardless of prior steroid inadequate response or intolerance, with 60.9% vs 0.0% histologic remission in the paediatric refractory subgroup
question: Is dupilumab effective for eosinophilic esophagitis that does not respond to topical steroids?
balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #396, the dupilumab eosinophilic esophagitis shelf without the steroid-refractory specification; this shelf covers the uncovered slice — patients whose disease has already failed, not tolerated, or cannot take swallowed topical corticosteroids (STC). The evidence is subgroup analysis of a single trial programme, so it caps at POSSIBLE. In the phase 3 LIBERTY EoE TREET programme, prespecified subgroup analysis found dupilumab 300 mg weekly improved histologic, symptomatic and endoscopic outcomes versus placebo at week 24, maintained at week 52, regardless of prior STC use or of inadequate response, intolerance or contraindication to STC — though the record prints no effect sizes for these subgroups (Bredenoord 2024). A second programme report reaches the same conclusion by prior budesonide/fluticasone use (Bredenoord 2025). The one subgroup report with numbers is paediatric: in EoE KIDS, children with prior inadequate response/intolerance/contraindication to STC achieved histologic remission in 60.9% on higher-exposure dupilumab versus 0.0% on placebo at week 16 (Chehade 2026). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — single trial programme, subgroup evidence: dupilumab works in the steroid-refractory population about as it does in steroid-naive disease, but no trial has enrolled a steroid-refractory population as its primary population.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single trial programme, subgroup evidence: dupilumab improved histologic, symptomatic and endoscopic outcomes irrespective of prior swallowed-steroid failure or intolerance in LIBERTY EoE TREET subgroup analyses, with histologic remission 60.9% vs 0.0% in the paediatric steroid-refractory subgroup

title: P-CAB versus PPI for severe erosive esophagitis with nighttime breakthrough (inferred, not trialled): better severe healing than lansoprazole and stronger night-time acid suppression in pH studies — in two separate evidence bases
question: Is potassium-competitive acid blocker therapy better than proton pump inhibitors for severe erosive esophagitis with nighttime breakthrough?
balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #1661, which covers vonoprazan versus lansoprazole for healing of erosive esophagitis overall; this shelf covers the uncovered slice — severe (LA grade C/D) disease together with nighttime breakthrough. The two halves of the slice rest on different evidence. For severe healing, a meta-analysis of 4 randomised trials (2,208 participants) found vonoprazan 20 mg superior to lansoprazole 30 mg for healing severe esophagitis at weeks 2, 4 and 8 (week 8 relative risk 1.175), but not for mild disease (Simadibrata 2024) — the home shelf's trials re-pooled by severity, not re-carded here. For the nighttime half, no trial enrols severe esophagitis patients with nighttime breakthrough: the evidence is pharmacodynamic — in healthy volunteers, night-time intragastric pH ≥4 was held 60.5% of the night on vonoprazan and 66.0% on tegoprazan versus 36.1% on esomeprazole (Yang 2022, N = 16), tegoprazan raised pH ≥4 within 2 hours versus 7 hours for dexlansoprazole (Han 2023, N = 24), and a 55-trial network meta-analysis ranked vonoprazan and tegoprazan best for nocturnal acid inhibition (Zou 2024). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the class heals severe esophagitis better than lansoprazole and suppresses night-time acid more than PPIs in healthy volunteers — but the exact population in the question has never been trialled.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — vonoprazan heals severe (LA C/D) erosive esophagitis better than lansoprazole (week 8 relative risk 1.175, 4 trials) and potassium-competitive acid blockers suppress night-time acid more than PPIs in healthy-volunteer pH studies, but no trial has tested the class in severe esophagitis patients with nighttime breakthrough

title: Bismuth in H. pylori salvage after first failure (LIKELY benefit): 98.0% vs 69.2% eradication for bismuth quadruple versus standard triple salvage, concordant across two network meta-analyses
question: Does adding bismuth to salvage therapy improve Helicobacter pylori eradication after a first treatment fails?
balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #777, which covers bismuth quadruple therapy as a regimen in the clarithromycin-resistance era; this shelf covers the uncovered slice — salvage after a first eradication attempt has failed, and specifically whether the bismuth component improves the salvage result. The direct trial randomised post-failure patients to a bismuth-containing quadruple salvage (esomeprazole, bismuth, tetracycline, levofloxacin) versus the standard non-bismuth levofloxacin triple: eradication was 98.0% versus 69.2% by intention-to-treat, an absolute difference of 28.8 percentage points (Hsu 2017). Two network meta-analyses of the second-line literature point the same way: bismuth quadruple regimens of 10–14 days sit among the most effective salvage options (Chang 2020, 54 studies, 8,752 participants), and non-quinolone bismuth quadruple therapy for 10 days or more beat 7-day triple therapy (odds ratio 2.25), with quinolone-based bismuth quadruple ranked the optimum second-line approach (Yeo 2019, 26 trials, 3,628 participants). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): concordant randomised and pooled evidence says adding bismuth to salvage therapy raises eradication after first-line failure, with duration of at least 10 days part of the effect.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — adding bismuth in salvage after first-line failure raised eradication to 98.0% vs 69.2% in the direct randomised trial (absolute difference 28.8 points) and bismuth quadruple regimens of 10–14 days ranked among the most effective across two network meta-analyses

title: Risankizumab induction in Crohn's disease (LIKELY benefit): remission 45% vs 25% and 42% vs 20% over placebo in ADVANCE and MOTIVATE, with endoscopic response to match
question: Does risankizumab induce remission in adults with moderate to severe Crohn's disease?
balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #771, which covers the head-to-head SEQUENCE comparison of risankizumab versus ustekinumab; this shelf covers the uncovered slice — the placebo-controlled induction evidence (ADVANCE and MOTIVATE). Both phase 3 induction trials met all coprimary endpoints at week 12 at both doses: in ADVANCE, CDAI clinical remission was 45% on risankizumab 600 mg versus 25% on placebo (adjusted difference 21 percentage points) and endoscopic response 40% versus 12%; in MOTIVATE, in biologic-experienced patients, remission was 42% versus 20% and endoscopic response 29% versus 11% (D'Haens 2022). An earlier phase 2 placebo-controlled trial pointed the same way (pooled remission 31% versus 15%; Feagan 2017), and a meta-analysis of the IL-23 class found a relative risk of 1.87 for inducing clinical remission versus placebo at high certainty (Vuyyuru 2023). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): two concordant phase 3 placebo-controlled trials, supported by phase 2 and class-level pooling, establish that risankizumab induces clinical remission and endoscopic response in moderate to severe Crohn's disease.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — two concordant phase 3 placebo-controlled trials: risankizumab 600 mg induced CDAI remission in 45% vs 25% (ADVANCE) and 42% vs 20% (MOTIVATE) at week 12, with endoscopic response roughly triple the placebo rate

title: Methotrexate for Crohn's relapse prevention (POSSIBLE, intramuscular only): continuing weekly injections after methotrexate-induced remission kept 65% vs 39% in remission at 40 weeks
question: Does methotrexate prevent relapse in adults with Crohn's disease in remission?
balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #3584, which covers methotrexate for inducing remission in refractory Crohn's disease; this shelf covers the uncovered slice — relapse prevention in patients already in remission. The pivotal trial took patients who had entered remission on intramuscular methotrexate and randomised them to continue low-dose intramuscular methotrexate or switch to placebo: at 40 weeks, 65% remained in remission on methotrexate versus 39% on placebo, an absolute reduction in relapse risk of 26.1 percentage points, and fewer methotrexate patients needed prednisone for relapse (28% vs 58%) (Feagan 2000). The Cochrane review of 5 studies (333 patients) confirms intramuscular methotrexate's superiority at 40 weeks (relative risk 1.67 for maintained remission) but finds the oral-route evidence thin and not statistically significant, and oral methotrexate no better than 6-mercaptopurine (Patel 2014). A small earlier oral trial showed only a nonsignificant trend to fewer flares (Arora 1999). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the maintenance benefit is proven for weekly intramuscular methotrexate after methotrexate-induced remission, in one 76-patient trial — the route, the induction history and the single-trial base all limit it.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single pivotal trial: continuing weekly intramuscular methotrexate after methotrexate-induced remission kept 65% vs 39% in remission at 40 weeks (absolute relapse-risk reduction 26.1 points); oral methotrexate maintenance is unproven

title: Probiotics for maintaining remission in ulcerative colitis: E coli Nissle 1917 and Lactobacillus GG matched mesalazine in trials, but placebo-controlled proof is lacking (PARTIAL completion of the pouchitis shelf #2776)
question: Do probiotics help maintain remission in adults with ulcerative colitis?
balance: This is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #2776 covers probiotic maintenance of remission in chronic pouchitis after ileal pouch surgery for ulcerative colitis; the slice carded here is ulcerative colitis itself, in adults whose disease is in remission. The strongest evidence is active-comparator, not placebo: Escherichia coli Nissle 1917 matched mesalazine in two double-blind trials (Kruis 1997, 12 weeks, relapse 16.0% on E coli Nissle vs 11.3% on mesalazine, not significant; Kruis 2004, 12 months, per-protocol relapse 36.4% vs 33.9%, significant equivalence P = 0.003). Lactobacillus GG likewise showed no difference in relapse rate versus mesalazine at 12 months (Zocco 2006, P = 0.77), though relapse-free time was longer (P < 0.05). The one placebo-controlled trial carded was small and negative: Lactobacillus acidophilus La-5 plus Bifidobacterium animalis subsp. lactis BB-12 maintained remission in 25% vs 8% on placebo, not significant (Wildt 2011, N = 32 printed on the face). No carded trial shows a probiotic beating placebo or standard therapy for maintaining remission in ulcerative colitis; the tested preparations are specific named strains/preparations, and results cannot be assumed for other probiotic products. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — specific tested preparations (E coli Nissle 1917, Lactobacillus GG) performed as well as mesalazine in maintenance trials, but placebo-controlled evidence is thin and the one small placebo trial made no significant difference.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the named tested preparations (Escherichia coli Nissle 1917; Lactobacillus GG) maintained ulcerative colitis remission as well as mesalazine in randomised trials (12-month per-protocol relapse 36.4% vs 33.9%, equivalence P = 0.003), but no carded trial shows a probiotic beating placebo: the one small placebo-controlled trial (N = 32) made no significant difference

title: How long on strict low FODMAP before reintroducing? No duration trial exists — services restrict for weeks to 2 months, then reintroduce, and completing reintroduction tracks with long-term benefit (PARTIAL completion of the low-FODMAP efficacy shelf #202)
question: How long should adults stay on the strict low FODMAP diet before reintroducing foods for irritable bowel syndrome?
balance: This is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #202 covers whether the low FODMAP diet works for irritable bowel syndrome; the slice carded here is the timing question — how long the strict restriction phase should last before reintroduction. The honest headline is that no carded study randomised patients to different strict-phase durations, so there is no trial-derived number of weeks. What the fetched records do show is how the phased diet is actually run and what happens after reintroduction: in the Bellini 2020 service cohort, patients started the reintroduction phase after 2 months of restriction, and symptoms, quality of life and nutritional adequacy were maintained long term on an adapted diet. Completion of reintroduction as per protocol was itself associated with long-term symptom improvement in the Foulkes 2025 service evaluation (P = 0.049), satisfactory relief was 69% after restriction and 57% long term in O'Keeffe 2018, and a personalised post-reintroduction diet sustained adequate relief in 67% at 12 months in the small Staudacher 2022 follow-up (N = 18, printed on the face). The evidence therefore supports treating restriction as a short diagnostic phase — weeks to about two months in the services reported — followed by structured reintroduction, rather than staying strict indefinitely; it does not support any precise week count. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — observational/service evidence only: no duration trial exists, and the timing answer is descriptive, not tested.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — observational only: no trial has randomised the length of the strict low FODMAP phase; in the reported services restriction ran weeks to 2 months before reintroduction, and completing reintroduction (not prolonged restriction) was associated with long-term improvement, so the strict phase should be treated as a short diagnostic phase followed by structured reintroduction

title: Rifaximin after relapse in IBS-D: repeat treatment beat placebo modestly in TARGET 3 (38.1% vs 31.5% responders) — evidence covers relapse after response, not non-response (PARTIAL completion of the general IBS-D rifaximin shelf #772)
question: Is rifaximin effective for irritable bowel syndrome with diarrhea after other treatments fail?
balance: This is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #772 covers rifaximin for irritable bowel syndrome with diarrhoea (IBS-D) in general; the slice carded here is the patient whose symptoms come back or persist after initial treatment — the retreatment question, answered almost entirely by one programme, TARGET 3. In TARGET 3 (Lembo 2016), patients who had responded to an open-label 2-week course of rifaximin 550 mg three times daily and then relapsed were randomised to repeat rifaximin or placebo: responders after the first repeat course were 38.1% vs 31.5% (P = .03) — a real but modest absolute gain of 6.6 percentage points, driven by abdominal pain (50.6% vs 42.2%, P = .018) rather than stool consistency (51.8% vs 50.0%, P = .42, the treatment made no difference on that component). A secondary analysis of the same programme (Cash 2017) found the minimally clinically important difference in quality of life in 38.6% on retreatment vs 29.6% on placebo (P = 0.009). Outside the programme, a retrospective tertiary-centre series (Pimentel 2011) found over 75% of initial responders responded again to retreatment, up to five courses, without shortening benefit. Because the randomised evidence is a single trial programme, the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — single trial programme: repeat rifaximin helps a modest extra fraction of relapsing IBS-D responders, with low and similar adverse-event rates.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single trial programme (TARGET 3): in IBS-D patients who responded to a first rifaximin course and then relapsed, repeat rifaximin produced responders in 38.1% vs 31.5% on placebo (P = .03), with no difference on stool consistency; no randomised evidence covers patients who never responded to a first course

title: Hypnotherapy for diet-refractory IBS: never trialled in diet non-responders — benefit is shown only indirectly, in refractory and referred IBS (PARTIAL completion of the refractory-IBS hypnotherapy shelf #2456)
question: Is gut-directed hypnotherapy effective for irritable bowel syndrome that does not respond to diet changes?
balance: This is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #2456 covers gut-directed hypnotherapy for irritable bowel syndrome refractory to standard management, carding the Lindfors trials and Whorwell 1984; the slice asked for here is narrower — irritable bowel syndrome that does not respond to diet changes specifically. That exact population has never been enrolled in a carded trial: no fetched record defines its patients by diet non-response. The evidence carded here is therefore indirect, from the neighbouring refractory/referred populations, and the stamp is discounted for that indirectness. In IMAGINE (Flik 2019), patients referred from primary and secondary care had adequate relief at 3 months in 40.8% (individual) and 33.2% (group) vs 16.7% on educational supportive therapy (odds ratio 2.9, 95% CI 1.2–7.4 for hypnotherapy vs control). In explicitly refractory patients, Moser 2013 found improvement in 60.8% vs 40.9% after treatment and 54.3% vs 25.0% over 15 months, while Dobbin 2013 found hypnotherapy improved symptom severity less than biofeedback at 12 weeks in refractory women, with the two equal by 24 weeks. A 2024 network meta-analysis found face-to-face gut-directed hypnotherapy efficacious for abdominal pain (relative risk of pain not improving 0.77, 95% CI 0.61–0.96), but detected no significant effect among trials recruiting only refractory patients for the therapies analysed. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — indirect evidence only for the diet-nonresponder slice: benefit is shown in refractory and referred IBS, not in diet-defined non-responders.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — indirect evidence only: no trial has enrolled IBS patients defined by non-response to diet changes; in the neighbouring refractory/referred populations hypnotherapy beat supportive control (adequate relief OR 2.9 in IMAGINE; 54.3% vs 25.0% improved over 15 months in refractory patients), but a network meta-analysis found no significant hypnotherapy effect in refractory-only trials

title: Standard Mediterranean diet and liver fat: beats a low-fat/high-carbohydrate control in a 12-person crossover, but no better than a low-fat diet in larger trials — a comparator split (PARTIAL completion of the green-Mediterranean shelf #3624)
question: Does a Mediterranean diet reduce liver fat in adults with metabolic associated fatty liver disease?
balance: This is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #3624 covers the green-Mediterranean variant in DIRECT PLUS; the slice carded here is the standard Mediterranean diet against control diets in fatty liver disease. The evidence splits by comparator, and the stamp names the split. Against a low-fat/high-carbohydrate control in the smallest trial, the Mediterranean diet won clearly: relative reduction in hepatic steatosis 39 ± 4% vs 7 ± 3% (P = 0.012) in a 12-person crossover (Ryan 2013, N printed on the face). In the two larger head-to-head trials against low-fat diets, it did not: Properzi 2018 found relative steatosis reductions of 32.4% on Mediterranean vs 25.0% on low-fat (between-group P = 0.32 — the treatment made no difference between diets, both improved), and MEDINA (George 2022) found no between-group differences, with intrahepatic lipid improving significantly within the low-fat group (−17%, P = .02) but not within the Mediterranean group (−8%, P = .069). Against no-treatment control, Katsagoni 2018 found a Mediterranean diet improved liver stiffness versus control (P < 0.001 after adjustment), with ALT normalisation seen only in the Mediterranean-lifestyle arm. A 2023 meta-analysis of 10 trials (737 adults) found no significant effect on liver enzymes and a non-significant stiffness change. PROPOSED SPLIT (comparator split: Mediterranean diet reduces liver fat versus the low-fat/high-carbohydrate control in one small crossover and improves stiffness versus usual care, but shows no advantage over a low-fat diet in the two larger head-to-head trials).
stamp: SPLIT (comparator split: benefit versus a low-fat/high-carbohydrate control in one small crossover — relative steatosis reduction 39% vs 7% — and versus usual care on liver stiffness; but no advantage over a low-fat diet in the two larger head-to-head trials, where the Mediterranean diet made no difference between groups)

title: Lactulose for covert hepatic encephalopathy: reverses the minimal form in about half to two-thirds of patients across four trials — LIKELY benefit, with grade 1 disease untested separately (PARTIAL completion of the minimal-HE shelf #2126)
question: Is lactulose effective for covert hepatic encephalopathy in adults with cirrhosis?
balance: This is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #2126 covers lactulose for minimal hepatic encephalopathy (MHE) on a single trial (Prasad 2007, cross-pointed here and not re-carded); the slice carded here is covert hepatic encephalopathy broadly — the term that groups minimal with grade 1 disease. The carded trial set is wider than the home shelf's and concordant: a multicentre randomised trial found MHE reversal at 60 days in 64.18% on lactulose vs 22.58% on no therapy (Wang 2019; number needed to treat 2.4 as printed); Mittal 2011 found recovery in 47.5% on lactulose vs 10% on no treatment (P = 0.006 for the treatment groups vs none); Sharma 2008 found psychometry normalisation in 54.8% on lactulose; and in Sidhu 2016 the lactulose arm reversed MHE in 69.1% (rifaximin 73.7%; rifaximin's non-inferiority was not established). A meta-analysis of 9 trials (434 patients) found lactulose reduced the relative risk of no improvement to 0.52 (95% CI 0.44–0.62) and of progression to overt encephalopathy to 0.17 (0.06–0.52), at the cost of more diarrhoea (relative risk 4.38). Two honest limits: every carded trial enrolled the minimal end of covert disease — no fetched trial isolated grade 1 covert encephalopathy — and most trials were open-label. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) — concordant randomised trials and a meta-analysis show lactulose reverses covert (minimal) hepatic encephalopathy and reduces progression to overt disease; the grade 1 end of covert disease is untested separately.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — four concordant randomised trials and a 9-trial meta-analysis: lactulose reversed covert (minimal) hepatic encephalopathy in 47.5–69.1% versus 10–22.6% untreated, halved the relative risk of no improvement (relative risk 0.52) and reduced progression to overt encephalopathy (relative risk 0.17), with more diarrhoea and no mortality difference; grade 1 covert disease was not trialled separately

title: Beta-blockers vs no treatment for first variceal bleeding: pooled placebo-controlled trials favour the drug, but they enrolled large varices — medium varices were never isolated (PARTIAL completion of the band-ligation comparison shelf #3625)
question: Should nonselective beta-blockers be used to prevent first variceal bleeding in adults with cirrhosis and medium varices?
balance: This is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #3625 covers primary-prevention beta-blockers versus band ligation, and live shelf #776 covers beta-blockers versus placebo for preventing decompensation in clinically significant portal hypertension (the PREDESCI programme, PMID 30910320 — already carded there and cross-pointed here, not re-carded). The slice carded here is the older, direct comparison the other shelves do not home: beta-blocker versus no treatment/placebo for first bleeding in patients with established varices. The pooled individual-patient analysis of the four placebo-controlled trials (Poynard 1991, 589 patients) found 78 ± 3% free of bleeding at 2 years on a beta-blocker vs 65 ± 3% on placebo (P = 0.002), with fatal bleeding also reduced (90 ± 2% vs 82 ± 3% free, P = 0.01) and overall survival not significantly different (71% vs 68%, P = 0.34). The individual trials split: Idéo 1988 found nadolol almost abolished first bleeding (1/30 vs 11/49 controls over a mean 24 months), while the Italian multicentre trial in large varices found no significant overall difference (74% vs 59% free of bleeding over 42 months), with benefit confined to patients without ascites. Two boundaries are printed plainly: the trials enrolled large varices, not medium varices as a defined stratum — no fetched trial isolated medium varices — and the modern placebo-controlled frontier has moved to small varices (the BOPPP protocol, 740 patients planned, no results in the record). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — pooled placebo-controlled evidence favours beta-blockers for preventing first bleeding, but the medium-varices population itself was never trialled as such and the individual large-varices trials divide.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — pooled individual-patient data from the four placebo-controlled trials (589 patients) show beta-blockers prevent first bleeding (78% vs 65% free of bleeding at 2 years, P = 0.002) and fatal bleeding, with no significant overall-survival difference; but the trials enrolled large varices and split individually, and no trial has isolated medium varices

title: TMP-SMX for SBP prophylaxis: beat no prophylaxis in one small trial and matched norfloxacin head-to-head — a plausible alternative, not a proven equal (PARTIAL completion of the norfloxacin-only shelf #1675)
question: Should adults with cirrhosis take norfloxacin or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole to prevent spontaneous bacterial peritonitis?
balance: This is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #1675 covers norfloxacin prophylaxis alone in advanced cirrhosis; the slice carded here is trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) and the head-to-head comparison. TMP-SMX has one small placebo-controlled trial: Singh 1995 found spontaneous bacterial peritonitis or spontaneous bacteraemia in 3% (1/30) on TMP-SMX vs 27% (8/30) on no prophylaxis (P = 0.025), with deaths 7% vs 20% (P = 0.15, not significant). Against norfloxacin, two small randomised trials found no difference: Alvarez 2005, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis 16.0% on TMP-SMX vs 9.4% on norfloxacin, deaths 20.0% vs 21.9%; and Lontos 2014, infections 9 vs 10 episodes and spontaneous bacterial peritonitis 2 patients in each group over 12 months, with more definite/probable adverse events on TMP-SMX (22.5% vs 0%, P = 0.01). The Cochrane network meta-analysis (Komolafe 2020, 29 trials, 3896 participants) found no evidence of differences between any antibiotic and no intervention for mortality or serious adverse events, at low or very low certainty — clinically important differences could not be ruled out. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — TMP-SMX prevented spontaneous bacterial peritonitis in one small trial and matched norfloxacin in two head-to-head trials, so it is a plausible alternative where norfloxacin is unsuitable; the pooled certainty is low.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole prevented spontaneous bacterial peritonitis in one small randomised trial (3% vs 27% on no prophylaxis, P = 0.025) and showed no detected difference from norfloxacin in two head-to-head trials, though with more definite/probable adverse events (22.5% vs 0%); the Cochrane network meta-analysis rates the whole prophylaxis evidence base low to very low certainty

title: Baclofen or acamprosate in alcohol-related liver disease: baclofen's evidence splits between a positive cirrhosis trial and null larger data; acamprosate is unproven in advanced liver disease — SPLIT (PARTIAL completion of the baclofen-in-cirrhosis shelf #1677)
question: Do baclofen or acamprosate help maintain abstinence in adults with alcohol-related liver disease?
balance: This is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #1677 covers baclofen in cirrhosis on its single positive trial (Addolorato 2007, cross-pointed here and not re-carded); the slice carded here is the broader alcohol-related liver disease population and, above all, acamprosate, which the home shelf does not cover. The evidence genuinely divides, drug by drug and study by study, and the stamp names the split. For baclofen beyond the homed trial: the largest free randomised trial, in 180 veterans with chronic hepatitis C and alcohol use disorder, found baclofen made no difference to percentage of days abstinent versus placebo (absolute difference 1.3%, P = 0.95; Hauser 2017), and a meta-analysis of baclofen in alcohol use disorder with liver disease found the pooled randomised comparison non-significant (relative risk of abstinence 1.42, 95% CI 0.41–4.92; Duan 2023). Against that, a 2024 systematic review of medications for alcohol use disorder in alcohol-associated cirrhosis (8 studies, 794 patients) found treatment associated with a relative risk of alcohol consumption of 0.68 (95% CI 0.48–0.97) — but baclofen supplied 6 of its 8 studies, including the homed trial, and heterogeneity was high (I2 = 67%). For acamprosate, the cirrhosis evidence is one study inside that review plus a real-world matched analysis in cirrhosis/alcohol-associated hepatitis that found no difference in abstinence or mortality at 1 year and higher readmission in the acamprosate group (85% vs 57%, P < 0.001; Oldroyd 2024) — confounding by severity is the likely explanation, but benefit is unproven in advanced liver disease. Safety across the review was reassuring (5 of 165 serious adverse events possibly/probably drug-related). PROPOSED SPLIT (baclofen: positive homed cirrhosis trial and positive pooled cirrhosis review, but null in the largest free randomised trial and in the baclofen-specific pooled randomised comparison; acamprosate: no abstinence benefit shown in advanced liver disease).
stamp: SPLIT (baclofen: the homed cirrhosis trial and a pooled cirrhosis review favour it — relative risk of alcohol consumption 0.68 — but the largest free randomised trial was null, P = 0.95, and the baclofen-specific pooled randomised comparison was non-significant, relative risk 1.42, 95% CI 0.41–4.92; acamprosate: no abstinence or mortality benefit demonstrated in advanced liver disease, with higher readmission in confounded real-world data)

title: Adding AFP to ultrasound surveillance in cirrhosis (partial completion of #3387): the combination detects far more early liver cancers — early-stage sensitivity 63-74% versus 45-52% for ultrasound alone — at the price of more false positives
question: Should adults with cirrhosis be screened for hepatocellular carcinoma every 6 months with ultrasound and alpha-fetoprotein?
balance: PARTIAL completion: live shelf #3387 covers ultrasound surveillance for hepatocellular carcinoma in cirrhosis, including the 6-monthly interval and its survival evidence; this shelf answers only the part #3387 does not — what adding alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) to ultrasound buys. The diagnostic evidence is consistent in direction: ultrasound alone detects early-stage HCC poorly (47% sensitivity in Tzartzeva 2018; 63% with AFP added versus 45% without in the head-to-head studies, P=.002), and the Cochrane diagnostic review found the combination reached 96% sensitivity versus 76% for ultrasound alone in direct comparisons, at the cost of more false positives (specificity 85% versus 93%). A 2022 network meta-analysis puts the same trade at 74.1% versus 51.6% early-stage sensitivity, with specificity falling from 87.9% to 83.9%. No carded study here is a randomised trial of the combined strategy against mortality — the case for adding AFP is a detection case, resting on the survival logic already weighed on #3387. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): adding AFP to 6-monthly ultrasound materially improves early HCC detection in cirrhosis, with a real false-positive cost; the mortality benefit of the combination itself is inferred, not trialled.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — adding alpha-fetoprotein to 6-monthly ultrasound raises early-stage HCC sensitivity in cirrhosis from about 45-52% to 63-74% (combination sensitivity 96% vs 76% for ultrasound alone in direct comparisons), at the cost of lower specificity and more false positives; diagnostic-accuracy evidence only, with no randomised mortality trial of the combined strategy (partial completion of live shelf #3387)

title: BCAA for muscle mass in cirrhosis with sarcopenia (partial completion of #5367): SPLIT — small trials report gains, but the two larger controlled trials found BCAA added nothing to protein and exercise
question: Does branched-chain amino acid supplementation improve muscle mass in adults with cirrhosis and sarcopenia?
balance: PARTIAL completion: live shelf #5367 covers oral branched-chain amino acids (BCAA) for ascites and encephalopathy outcomes in advanced liver disease; this shelf answers only the outcome #5367 does not — muscle mass in cirrhosis with sarcopenia. Four randomised trials divide. Two small trials are positive: a 32-patient pilot found a significant within-group muscle-mass gain only in the BCAA arm (Hernández-Conde 2021), and a 54-patient frailty trial found skeletal muscle index rose within the BCAA group alongside frailty reversal (Siramolpiwat 2023). The two larger, placebo- or active-controlled trials are null: 60 patients given BCAA with exercise gained no more muscle than placebo (the treatment made no difference; Mohta 2022), and the largest trial, 150 patients over 12 months, found BCAA no better than whey protein for grip strength or lean mass (the treatment made no difference; Hey 2024). The positive trials are the smallest and lean on within-group change; the null trials include the only one big enough to be definitive and used an active protein control, which may itself build muscle. PROPOSED SPLIT — small early trials report muscle-mass gains with BCAA, but the two larger controlled trials (N=60 and N=150) found no advantage over placebo or whey protein: whether BCAA adds anything beyond adequate protein and exercise is unresolved.
stamp: SPLIT (small trials: benefit; larger controlled trials: the treatment made no difference) — a 32-patient pilot and a 54-patient frailty trial report muscle gains with BCAA, but a 60-patient placebo-controlled trial and the largest trial (150 patients vs whey protein) found no muscle-mass advantage; partial completion of live shelf #5367

title: Colonoscopy after 3-4 small adenomas (partial completion of #5549): risk is low when every adenoma is under 10 mm — the evidence supports a longer interval than the traditional 3 years
question: How soon should colonoscopy be repeated after removal of 3 to 4 small adenomas?
balance: PARTIAL completion: pack #5549 covers safely stretching surveillance to 5-10 years in low-risk patients (1-2 small adenomas and the registry cohorts behind that question); this shelf answers only the group #5549 does not isolate — patients with 3 to 4 small (under 10 mm) adenomas, historically labelled intermediate-risk and scoped at 3 years. The carded cohorts say that label overstates their risk when every adenoma is small: in a Spanish screening cohort, patients with 3-4 small adenomas had a 5.07% advanced-lesion rate at first follow-up versus 16.67% when one adenoma was 10-20 mm, and small adenomas alone were not significantly associated with advanced lesions (Pérez-Cuadrado-Robles 2016); in a Korean multicentre cohort the 3-4-adenoma group's 3-year advanced-neoplasia risk was 2.1% (Park 2017). Size still matters within 'small': adenomas of 6-9 mm carried higher metachronous risk than 1-5 mm adenomas in every count group, including 3-4 (odds ratio 4.91 in screening examinations; Hartstein 2020). The British guideline carded here reserves its 3-year surveillance for higher-risk findings (five or more polyps, or two or more including an advanced polyp) — criteria that 3-4 small adenomas alone do not meet. All of this is observational; no trial has randomised this group to different intervals. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: the evidence supports repeating colonoscopy later than the traditional 3 years after 3-4 small adenomas, on the low-risk timetable weighed on #5549, rather than at 3 years — with the caveat that a 6-9 mm adenoma in the set argues for the shorter end of that range.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: after removal of 3-4 small (under 10 mm) adenomas, advanced neoplasia is uncommon (2.1% at 3 years; 5.07% at first follow-up when all adenomas are small), supporting a longer-than-3-year interval on the low-risk timetable rather than routine 3-year recall, with a 6-9 mm adenoma in the set arguing for the shorter end (partial completion of pack #5549)

title: Outpatient versus inpatient diverticulitis care (partial completion of #3621): in selected patients, home treatment is as safe as admission — pooled readmission 7%, emergency surgery 0.2% — at a third of the cost
question: Is outpatient management safe for adults with uncomplicated diverticulitis?
balance: PARTIAL completion: live shelf #3621 homes an outpatient cohort whose randomised comparison is antibiotics versus no antibiotics (DINAMO); this shelf answers the different comparison #3621 does not — outpatient versus inpatient management itself. The only randomised trial of the setting question, DIVER (132 patients), found treatment failure in 4 inpatients and 3 outpatients with no difference between groups (P=0.619), no quality-of-life difference, and an episode cost three times lower as an outpatient (Biondo 2014). Two meta-analyses of the wider, mostly observational literature agree: pooled outpatient failure was 4.3% across 1,781 patients (Cirocchi 2019), and pooled readmission was 7% across 2,303 outpatients, with only 0.2% needing emergency surgery (van Dijk 2018). The catch is selection: the underlying studies predominantly excluded patients with comorbidity or immunosuppression, inability to tolerate oral intake, or no adequate social support — outpatient management is proven safe for selected patients, not for everyone who walks in. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): in selected adults with CT-confirmed uncomplicated diverticulitis who can take oral treatment and have support at home, outpatient management is as safe as admission and much cheaper; the randomised base is a single 132-patient trial, which caps the stamp.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in selected adults with uncomplicated diverticulitis, outpatient management is as safe as hospitalisation (single randomised trial, 132 patients: failures 3 vs 4; pooled readmission 7%, emergency surgery 0.2%) and substantially cheaper; the randomised base is one small trial, and the evidence applies only to selected patients (partial completion of live shelf #3621)

title: Botulinum toxin after topical failure in chronic anal fissure (partial completion of #2472): effective and sphincter-sparing, but less healing and more recurrence than sphincterotomy in treatment failures
question: Is botulinum toxin injection effective for chronic anal fissure that does not heal with topical therapy?
balance: PARTIAL completion: live shelf #2472 covers chronic anal fissure treatment generally, including botulinum toxin against placebo and topical glyceryl trinitrate as first-line options; this shelf answers only the next step #2472 does not isolate — the patient whose fissure has already failed topical/conservative therapy, where the real choice is botulinum toxin injection versus lateral internal sphincterotomy (LIS). The one trial that explicitly enrolled conservative-treatment failures found surgery healed significantly more fissures than botulinum toxin, with significantly fewer recurrences, while botulinum toxin carried significantly less incontinence (Nasr 2010, 80 patients). A second randomised comparison found the same pattern over longer follow-up: healing equal by 3 months after an early surgical lead (88% vs 44% at 2 months), but higher recurrence after botulinum toxin and more early incontinence after surgery (Valizadeh 2012, 50 patients). A dose-ranging randomised study shows the injection itself, with retreatment of non-healers, heals most fissures by 2 months (89%-96%; Brisinda 2002, 150 patients) — so 'effective' is true in absolute terms, but in the topical-refractory patient it is the less durable of the two definitive options, bought with a lower continence risk. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): botulinum toxin heals a majority of topical-refractory fissures and avoids permanent sphincter damage, but heals fewer and recurs more than sphincterotomy — a reasonable step before, or instead of, surgery for patients who prioritise continence.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — botulinum toxin heals most topical-refractory chronic fissures (89-96% by 2 months with retreatment) and avoids permanent sphincter injury, but in patients who had failed conservative treatment it healed significantly fewer fissures than sphincterotomy and recurred significantly more; a continence-sparing step, not the most durable cure (partial completion of live shelf #2472)

title: Dupilumab in severe eosinophilic asthma (partial completion of #1031): exacerbation benefit is real and concentrates at eosinophil counts of 300/µL or above — though anti-IL-5 drugs may beat it in that stratum
question: Does dupilumab reduce exacerbations in adults with severe eosinophilic asthma?
balance: PARTIAL completion, built under the one-home precedent for homed anchors: the primary QUEST and VENTURE trial reports are already carded on live shelf #1031 (dupilumab in moderate-to-severe asthma), so they are cross-pointed here by shelf number only and are NOT re-carded; this shelf is built entirely on free reports that cut the evidence the way #1031 does not — by severity and by eosinophil count. A systematic review of placebo-controlled biologic trials found exacerbation reduction with all biologics, dupilumab included, in patients with baseline blood eosinophil count 300 cells/µL or above, and consistent dupilumab reduction (300 mg dose) in the 150 to under 300 band (Korn 2023). In oral-corticosteroid-dependent severe asthma, dupilumab reduced the severe exacerbation rate by 71% (relative) in patients on under 10 mg/day baseline steroid and by 48% (relative) in those on 10 mg/day or more, while freeing 72% and 37% respectively from steroids entirely (Domingo 2022, a VENTURE post hoc analysis). In allergic and nonallergic asthma alike, exacerbation rates fell by 60%-72% (relative) across the phase 2b and VENTURE populations (Brusselle 2023). One cautionary comparative cohort found that, in patients with eosinophils 300/µL or above, dupilumab users had more exacerbations than anti-IL-5 users (weighted rate ratio 2.85) — a between-biologic comparison without a placebo arm, not a failure of dupilumab against no treatment (Kimura 2025). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — single trial programme (post hoc and review evidence): dupilumab reduces exacerbations in severe eosinophilic asthma, with the effect concentrated at higher eosinophil counts; the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE because the primary trials are homed on #1031 and the slice-specific evidence here is post hoc, review-level and observational.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single trial programme (post hoc/review evidence): dupilumab reduces exacerbations in severe eosinophilic asthma, with demonstrated benefit at blood eosinophil counts of 300/µL or above (and at 150-300/µL for the 300 mg dose), relative reductions of 48-72% in severe-asthma strata; one comparative cohort favours anti-IL-5 biologics over dupilumab at counts of 300/µL or above (partial completion of live shelf #1031)

title: FeNO-guided asthma treatment in adults (partial completion of #1728): pooled trials show fewer exacerbations (odds ratio about 0.6) and no other benefit — useful for frequent exacerbators, not a universal guide
question: Should fractional exhaled nitric oxide guide asthma treatment adjustments in adults?
balance: PARTIAL completion: live shelf #1728 covers FeNO-guided treatment in adolescents and young adults; this shelf answers the same question for adults generally. Two meta-analytic generations agree on a narrow benefit: the Cochrane adult review found fewer patients with one or more exacerbations on FeNO-guided care (odds ratio 0.60, 95% CI 0.43-0.84; number needed to treat 12 over 52 weeks) but no difference in hospitalisation, rescue steroid courses, symptoms, lung function or final inhaled steroid dose — and its authors state the universal use of FeNO to guide therapy in adults cannot be advocated (Petsky 2016). The 2023 update, pooling 12 adult trials and 2,116 patients, found the same pattern (odds ratio 0.61 for having an exacerbation; rate ratio 0.67) with no demonstrable effect on severe exacerbations, quality of life, FEV1 or treatment dose (Korevaar 2023). The two landmark single trials are individually null on exacerbations: Smith 2005 achieved a much lower final steroid dose on FeNO guidance (370 vs 641 µg/day) with a non-significant 45.6% relative exacerbation reduction, and Shaw 2007 found no significant difference in severe exacerbations (-21%, 95% CI -57% to 43%). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): FeNO-guided adjustment probably prevents some exacerbations in adults — most plausibly in those with frequent exacerbations — without improving day-to-day control, and the evidence does not support it as a universal routine.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — FeNO-guided adjustment in adults reduces exacerbations (pooled odds ratio 0.60-0.61; rate ratio 0.59-0.67) but has no demonstrated effect on severe exacerbations, symptoms, lung function or steroid dose, and the Cochrane authors state universal use cannot be advocated; most plausible value is in adults with frequent exacerbations (partial completion of live shelf #1728)

title: Bronchial thermoplasty after biologics (partial completion of #1036): never directly tested in biologic non-responders — observational refractory-asthma cohorts, many biologic-experienced, show improvement
question: Is bronchial thermoplasty effective for severe asthma that does not respond to biologics?
balance: PARTIAL completion, built honestly on the evidence status: live shelf #1036 covers bronchial thermoplasty (BT) in severe asthma on inhaled therapy; this shelf asks about the population #1036 does not — patients whose severe asthma has not responded to biologics. The desk-check finding, stated plainly: no randomised trial, and no study of any design carded here, has enrolled patients specifically because they failed a biologic and then tested BT in them. What exists is observational evidence in refractory populations where biologic exposure was common. In the Australian BT Registry, 43% of 77 severe patients had already been treated with a monoclonal antibody before BT, and the cohort as a whole improved markedly (Asthma Control Questionnaire 3.2 to 1.6 at 6 months; exacerbations in the prior 6 months 3.7 to 0.7; 48.8% of steroid-dependent patients weaned off oral steroids entirely) — but outcomes were not reported separately for the post-biologic subgroup (Langton 2020). In an Italian real-world series, the 30 BT patients — who started worse than the biologic groups — achieved reductions in hospitalisations (93.7%) and exacerbations (73.5%) comparable to the biologic arms over 12 months (Menzella 2021). A 15-patient Japanese cohort (N on the face) found BT improved symptoms even in refractory asthma with severe airflow limitation (Inoue 2024). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: BT can help selected patients with refractory severe asthma, many of them biologic-experienced, but its effectiveness specifically after biologic failure has never been directly tested, and this shelf must not be read as if it has.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: bronchial thermoplasty improved control and exacerbations in refractory severe-asthma cohorts in which biologic exposure was common (43% in the largest registry), but no study has enrolled or separately reported patients after biologic failure — effectiveness in that exact population is untested (partial completion of live shelf #1036)

title: Prednisone duration for a home-treated COPD exacerbation (partial completion of #3926): 5 vs 14 days has never been tested at home — and the one home trial of 5 days found no benefit over placebo
question: How many days of prednisone are needed for a COPD exacerbation treated at home, 5 days or 14 days?
balance: PARTIAL completion, built honestly on the evidence status: live shelf #3926 homes REDUCE, the hospital trial that found 5 days of glucocorticoid non-inferior to 14 days in hospitalised exacerbations; this shelf asks whether that answer transfers to exacerbations treated at home — and the desk-check finding is that the 5-versus-14-day comparison has never been run in home-treated patients in any record fetched this session. The home evidence that exists cuts at a more basic question. A 10-day course of prednisone after emergency-department discharge modestly reduced 30-day relapse versus placebo (27% vs 43%, P=0.05; Aaron 2003, 147 patients). But the only primary-care trial of a 5-day course found prednisone no better than placebo — treatment failure was 42.0% versus 34.5% (relative risk 1.22, P=0.25), with respiratory-related failure significantly higher on prednisone (27.6% vs 13.6%; relative risk 2.00) — in a trial that reached only 43% of its planned sample (Thebault 2023, 175 patients). The one trial designed to optimise duration at home compares 3 days against 5, not 5 against 14, and its record is a protocol with no results (Urwyler 2019, RECUT, NCT02386735). So the honest answer to '5 or 14?' at home is: 14 days has no supporting evidence in this setting at all, 5 days is the longest course with any home-trial pedigree — and whether even 5 days helps a mild primary-care exacerbation is genuinely in doubt. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): no home-treated trial compares 5 with 14 days; practice extrapolates the hospital answer, while the one home trial of 5 days found no benefit over placebo.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the 5-vs-14-day question has never been trialled in home-treated COPD exacerbations: the only home trial of a 5-day course found no benefit over placebo (failure 42.0% vs 34.5%), a 10-day course after emergency discharge did reduce relapse (27% vs 43%), and the one home duration trial in progress compares 3 vs 5 days; the 5-day answer is extrapolated from hospitalised patients (partial completion of live shelf #3926)

title: Home ventilation in stable hypercapnic COPD (partial completion of #1645): SPLIT — targeted high-intensity ventilation cut 1-year mortality from 33% to 12%, while unselected stable-patient trials showed no survival benefit
question: Does home noninvasive ventilation improve survival in adults with stable hypercapnic COPD?
balance: PARTIAL completion: live shelf #1645 covers home ventilation started after an exacerbation in patients with persistent post-exacerbation hypercapnia; this shelf answers the different population #1645 does not — patients with stable hypercapnic COPD and no recent exacerbation. The evidence genuinely divides, and the dividing line is how the ventilation is delivered. The one large targeted trial, which set ventilators to reduce PaCO2 by at least 20%, found a striking survival benefit in stable stage IV disease: 1-year mortality 12% versus 33% (hazard ratio 0.24, 95% CI 0.11-0.49; Köhnlein 2014, 195 patients). But the earlier meta-analysis that separated stable from post-hospital patients found no survival benefit in the stable subgroup (relative risk 0.88, 95% CI 0.55-1.43 across 7 trials; Dretzke 2016) — its included trials largely predated high-intensity, CO2-targeted ventilation. The most recent meta-analysis (19 trials, 1,482 patients) finds an overall mortality reduction (relative risk 0.76, 95% CI 0.61-0.95) that concentrates exactly where Köhnlein aimed: baseline PaCO2 of 55 mmHg or above (relative risk 0.69) and larger achieved PaCO2 reductions (relative risk 0.42), with no significant benefit below those marks (Wu 2022). PROPOSED SPLIT — survival benefit is demonstrated when home ventilation is high-intensity and targeted at marked hypercapnia (one definitive trial plus the PaCO2-defined subgroups of the latest meta-analysis), while unselected stable-hypercapnia trials pooled in 2016 showed no benefit (the treatment made no difference): patient selection and ventilator targeting, not the machine alone, decide the answer.
stamp: SPLIT (targeted high-intensity ventilation in marked hypercapnia: benefit — 1-year mortality 12% vs 33%, hazard ratio 0.24; unselected stable-patient trials: the treatment made no difference — pooled relative risk 0.88) — survival benefit in stable hypercapnic COPD depends on baseline PaCO2 (55 mmHg or above) and achieving a large PaCO2 reduction (partial completion of live shelf #1645)

title: Antifibrotics and survival in progressive fibrosis other than IPF (weak evidence): modelled survival favours nintedanib and small observed counts point the same way — but no trial has shown a mortality benefit
question: Does antifibrotic therapy improve survival in adults with progressive pulmonary fibrosis other than idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis?
balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #2783, which answers the lung-function half of this question: on #2783 nintedanib slowed the annual FVC decline in progressive fibrosing ILD (INBUILD, difference 107.0 mL/year) — but the INBUILD record reports no mortality comparison, so survival was left uncovered there and is the whole subject here. The survival evidence is indirect and thin. A Bayesian modelling analysis (Langford 2022, PMID: 34957531) matched 654 INBUILD patients to IPF trial patients and estimated median overall survival of 6.34–6.50 years on nintedanib versus 3.42–3.76 years on control — modelled, not observed, survival. In the Japanese INBUILD population (108 patients), mortality hazard ratios favoured nintedanib at both reported horizons — 0.54 (95% CI 0.14–2.11) at 52 weeks (Inoue 2021, PMID: 34564020) and 0.41 (95% CI 0.11–1.51) over the whole trial (Ogura 2022, PMID: 35927208) — with every interval crossing no effect. The only other randomised antifibrotic trial in this population, RELIEF (pirfenidone), is homed on pack #3951 and is not re-carded here; its death counts (1 of 64 versus 5 of 63) are printed on that shelf and are far too few to read. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): every estimate points toward longer survival, but none is a powered, observed mortality result, so a survival benefit is unproven.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — antifibrotic survival benefit in non-IPF progressive fibrosis rests on a Bayesian modelled estimate (median 6.34–6.50 vs 3.42–3.76 years), a subgroup mortality HR of 0.54 (95% CI 0.14–2.11), and 1 vs 5 deaths in a stopped-early trial; no powered observed mortality result exists

title: Low-risk PE at home on a DOAC (POSSIBLE): no PE-related deaths in the DOAC-specific studies and no clear difference from inpatient care — on a small, mixed literature whose own review calls itself inconclusive
question: Should adults with pulmonary embolism and low risk be treated at home with a direct oral anticoagulant?
balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #3373, which establishes home treatment of low-risk PE in general — the Aujesky randomised trial (enoxaparin-based) and the single-arm HoT-PE rivaroxaban study are carded there and are not re-carded here. This shelf covers the slice #3373 leaves open: the specifically DOAC-based home strategy. The dedicated evidence is a 2025 systematic review of outpatient DOAC management (Khachatryan 2025, PMID: 41464832: 8 studies, 2 randomised and 6 non-randomised; no PE-related deaths in any included study, but heterogeneity prevented any meta-analysis and the authors state no robust conclusions could be drawn). The randomised home-triage evidence behind it includes the HOME-PE trial — whose primary record is already carded elsewhere in the library and is therefore cross-pointed here in prose only, not re-carded — and its cancer post-hoc analysis (Chaibi 2024, PMID: 38308882), in which home-treated patients with active cancer had a 30-day composite rate of 4.3% (2/47) versus 1.0% (7/691) without cancer, while among patients with cancer home treatment itself was not associated with the outcome (OR 1.19, 95% CI 0.15–9.47). The Cochrane comparison of outpatient versus inpatient care (Yoo 2019, PMID: 30839095; 2 trials, 451 participants, one of them a rivaroxaban-regimen trial) found no clear difference in mortality, bleeding or recurrence, on low-quality evidence with very wide intervals. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a DOAC-based home pathway for rigorously selected low-risk PE looks as safe as admission in the available studies, but the DOAC-specific literature is small, mixed-design and explicitly inconclusive in its own systematic review. FLAG for the developer: this pack is built under one-home precedent (b) — the HOME-PE anchor is homed elsewhere, the slice is genuinely the DOAC strategy, and the three carded reports address that slice directly.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — home treatment of selected low-risk PE with a DOAC: no PE-related deaths across 8 studies in the DOAC-specific review, but that review could not pool its heterogeneous studies and states no robust conclusions can be drawn

title: Ramelteon for sleep-onset insomnia in older adults (SPLIT): measured sleep latency shortens by about 8–10 minutes in both elderly trials — a meta-analysis subgroup found no subjective benefit over 65
question: Is ramelteon effective for sleep-onset insomnia in older adults?
balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #1500, which covers ramelteon in general adults with chronic primary insomnia (its carded trial enrolled ages 18–64) — the older-adult slice was uncovered there and is the whole subject here. The slice genuinely divides. Two randomised trials in patients aged 65 and over are positive: a 2-night crossover study (Roth 2007, PMID: 17519067, N = 100, mean age 70.7) found latency to persistent sleep of 28.7 minutes on ramelteon 4 mg and 30.8 minutes on 8 mg versus 38.4 minutes on placebo, with total sleep time and sleep efficiency also improved and no next-day residual effects; and a 35-night outpatient trial (Roth 2006, PMID: 16709464, N = 829) found patient-reported sleep latency of 70.2 minutes on either dose versus 78.5 minutes on placebo at week 1 (P = .008), sustained at weeks 3 and 5, with no rebound or withdrawal on discontinuation. Against that, the subgroup analysis of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 8 trials (Liu 2012, PMID: 22897464) found subjective sleep latency was reduced only in patients aged 18–64 — not in patients over 65. PROPOSED SPLIT — objective sleep latency improves in older adults in both elderly trials, while the meta-analytic subgroup found no subjective latency benefit over 65: ramelteon shortens measured sleep onset in older adults by roughly 8–10 minutes, but whether older patients themselves feel they fall asleep faster is unproven.
stamp: SPLIT — objective sleep latency improves in older adults (28.7–30.8 vs 38.4 min polysomnographic; 70.2 vs 78.5 min patient-reported at week 1), but a meta-analysis subgroup found subjective latency reduced only at ages 18–64, not over 65

title: Pitolisant and dependence in narcolepsy (POSSIBLE): Drug Liking matched placebo even at six times the therapeutic dose — efficacy itself is homed on shelf #920; this shelf covers only the dependence slice
question: Does pitolisant reduce daytime sleepiness in adults with narcolepsy without causing dependence?
balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #920, which covers pitolisant's efficacy against placebo and modafinil (and its cataplexy trial) — those efficacy records are homed there and are not re-carded here. This shelf covers the slice #920 leaves open: dependence. The direct test is a formal human abuse-potential study (Setnik 2020, PMID: 31626696, NCT03152123): in 38 completers — nondependent recreational stimulant users, not narcolepsy patients — Drug Liking scores for pitolisant at the therapeutic dose (35.6 mg) and at six times that dose (213.6 mg) were similar to placebo and significantly lower than for phentermine 60 mg (mean differences 21.4 and 19.7 points, P < 0.0001). Longer exposure data point the same way without measuring dependence directly: in the 1-year open-label Harmony III study (Dauvilliers 2019, PMID: 31529094, n = 102), sleepiness fell (ESS −4.6 points) and the record reports no dependence or withdrawal outcome; and in the European post-authorisation safety study (Plazzi 2025, PMID: 39978240, 364 patients dosed, interim at 42.6 months), discontinuation was mainly for safety reasons (14.3%), lack of response (8.7%) and patient decision (7.6%) — the record reports no abuse or dependence signal, and also reports no dedicated dependence endpoint, which is printed plainly on its card. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — low dependence potential: a single dedicated abuse-potential trial in non-patients, supported by up to 42.6 months of uneventful real-world exposure, supports 'no dependence signal'; it cannot prove zero dependence risk in patients taking the drug for years.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — low dependence potential: Drug Liking matched placebo at therapeutic and 6× doses in the dedicated abuse-potential study (N = 38 completers), with no dependence signal in 1-year and 42.6-month follow-up — but dependence was a measured endpoint only in that one small volunteer study

title: MAD versus CPAP in mild-to-moderate OSA (SPLIT): CPAP normalises breathing more, sleepiness improves the same — and patients adhere better to the device
question: Is a mandibular advancement device as effective as CPAP for mild to moderate obstructive sleep apnea?
balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #923, which compares a mandibular advancement device (MAD) with CPAP in OSA generally — its carded trials (a general-population crossover trial and the CRESCENT blood-pressure trial) are homed there and are not re-carded here. This shelf covers only the mild-to-moderate slice, and the answer is consistent across all three slice-specific sources: CPAP lowers the apnoea–hypopnoea index (AHI) more, while sleepiness improves about the same. In TOMADO and its updated systematic review (Sharples 2014, PMID: 25359435), pooled AHI fell by 25.4 events/hour on CPAP versus 9.3/hour on MADs (between-treatment difference 7.0/hour favouring CPAP, P < 0.001), while the Epworth Sleepiness Scale fell by 1.6 points on both; the review notes no trial compared CPAP with a MAD in mild OSAH specifically. In the 1-year randomised trial in mild/moderate OSA (Aarab 2011, PMID: 21454959, n = 43, mean AHI 20.8/hour), CPAP improved AHI by 4.1 events/hour more than the MAD (P = 0.000 as printed), sleepiness improved similarly in both groups (P = 0.367), and more CPAP patients withdrew for side effects. In the mild-OSA-only randomised trial (E Silva 2021, PMID: 33394328, n = 79, AHI 9.5/hour), both devices reduced AHI versus control at 6 and 12 months and MAD adherence was higher, but CPAP was superior on total and LDL cholesterol at 12 months. PROPOSED SPLIT — on the breathing index CPAP wins (AHI), on sleepiness the devices tie (sleepiness): a MAD is a reasonable, often better-tolerated alternative in mild-to-moderate OSA, but it is not as effective as CPAP at normalising breathing.
stamp: SPLIT — AHI: CPAP better (pooled −25.4 vs −9.3 events/hour; +4.1 events/hour advantage at 1 year in mild/moderate OSA); sleepiness: equal (ESS −1.6 on both) — with adherence and tolerability favouring the MAD

title: Timed light and circadian adaptation in night work (POSSIBLE): melatonin onset moves hours in the intended direction in every simulation study — full adaptation remains the exception
question: Does timed light therapy help night shift workers adapt their circadian rhythm?
balance: PARTIAL completion of pack #5050, which covers scheduled bright light and melatonin for alertness and sleep in night-shift workers — its carded studies are homed there and are not re-carded here (one of them also measured adaptation, which is why this shelf is scoped strictly to the circadian-phase outcome and cards three different studies). On the phase outcome itself, timed light works as chronobiology predicts. In a simulated-night-work study (Horowitz 2001, PMID: 11440916, n = 54), both 2,500-lux bright light during the night shift and a fixed 08:00–16:00 sleep/darkness schedule significantly delayed dim-light melatonin onset (DLMO), their effects combined additively, and light produced the larger shifts — though neither consistently shifted the rhythm fully into the sleep episode. A compromise-phase protocol (Smith 2008, PMID: 19090319, n = 24) — five 15-minute bright-light pulses during shifts, dark sunglasses outdoors, scheduled dark sleep and afternoon light as a 'brake' — moved final DLMO to about 04:30 versus about 00:30 in controls, with better night performance and near-complete allotted sleep. And daytime light control alone (Dumont 2009, PMID: 19755587, n = 38) shifted DLMO by +2.3 hours (advance profile) or −4.1 hours (delay profile) by design, with shifts differing between groups by the third night. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): timed light — during the shift, and controlled across the day — reliably moves circadian phase in the intended direction in simulation studies; complete adaptation is uncommon, the studies are small laboratory simulations rather than trials in working shift workers, and real-world adherence is untested in these records.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — timed light shifts circadian phase in the intended direction (DLMO delays of about 4 hours with a compromise-phase protocol; +2.3 h advance / −4.1 h delay with daytime light control), but complete adaptation was not consistently achieved and all evidence is from small laboratory simulations (total N = 116)

title: Melatonin in delayed sleep-wake phase disorder (POSSIBLE): timing beats dose — 0.5 mg and 3.0 mg shift the clock equally at their optimal times, and phase can be estimated from a sleep diary
question: Is melatonin timing more important than dose for adults with delayed sleep-wake phase disorder?
balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #2429, which answers whether timed low-dose melatonin (0.5 mg, 1 hour before the desired bedtime) plus behavioural scheduling beats placebo in delayed sleep-wake phase disorder (DSWPD) — that trial is homed there and is not re-carded here. This shelf covers the comparison #2429 does not make: timing versus dose. No trial in DSWPD patients has randomised timing against dose directly; the answer is assembled from three directions. First, melatonin timed to circadian phase works in this disorder: a meta-analysis of 5 adult trials (van Geijlswijk 2010, PMID: 21120122) found melatonin advanced endogenous melatonin onset by 1.18 hours (95% CI 0.89–1.48) and sleep onset by 0.67 hours (95% CI 0.45–0.89), and cut sleep-onset latency by 23.27 minutes (95% CI 4.83–41.72). Second, the only head-to-head dose comparison using one protocol (Burgess 2010, PMID: 20410229, phase response curves in 34 healthy adults) found the optimal administration time differs by dose — maximum advances with 0.5 mg taken 2–4 hours before DLMO — but that when each dose is given at its own optimal time, 0.5 mg and 3.0 mg yield similarly sized advances and delays: timing, not milligrams, sets the shift. Third, timing can only be got right if phase is known, and in 24 DSWPD patients self-reported sleep timing estimated DLMO within ±1.5 hours in up to 88% of the sample (Lovato 2016, PMID: 27611743) — the practical route to timing treatment without a laboratory. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — timing over dose: within the studied range, when melatonin is taken relative to the circadian clock matters more than whether the dose is 0.5 or 3 mg; the dose-comparison evidence is from healthy volunteers, not DSWPD patients, and that indirectness is printed on the face. The record for the meta-analysis names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — timing over dose: 0.5 mg and 3.0 mg melatonin yield similarly sized phase shifts when each is given at its optimal time relative to DLMO, while mistimed dosing shifts less or the wrong way; the dose comparison is from healthy volunteers, not DSWPD patients (printed on the face)

title: Clonazepam or melatonin for REM sleep behavior disorder — a split choice: clonazepam improved the polysomnography in the only head-to-head trial, melatonin was gentler (less sleepiness, no rise in depressive symptoms), and neither has been tested for falls or injuries
question: Should adults with REM sleep behavior disorder take clonazepam or melatonin for safety?
balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #1509, which covers melatonin versus placebo in REM sleep behavior disorder (RBD) — this pack covers the slice #1509 does not: the clonazepam comparison and the safety choice between the two first-line drugs. In the only head-to-head randomised trial (Byun 2023, PMID: 35141811; 34 patients with isolated RBD), 4 weeks of clonazepam 0.5 mg — but not prolonged-release melatonin 2 mg — improved REM sleep without atonia on polysomnography, and clinical global improvement tended to favour clonazepam (P = 0.068); but depressive symptoms increased on clonazepam, while daytime sleepiness and insomnia symptoms improved on melatonin and not on clonazepam, and mild-to-moderate adverse events were reported by 4 patients (13.3%), similar between groups. A meta-analysis of polysomnography studies (Que 2022, PMID: 36387478) found drug-specific objective effects for both agents without a direct safety verdict, and a 2026 systematic review of 18 video-polysomnography-confirmed studies in synucleinopathies (Byun 2026, PMID: 42623795) concluded clonazepam shows possible benefit but raises important safety concerns in vulnerable populations, while melatonin appears better tolerated with inconsistent efficacy. No trial is powered for falls, fractures or injuries — the outcomes the safety question most cares about. PROPOSED SPLIT (clonazepam: better objective efficacy on polysomnography; melatonin: better tolerated) — on the narrow safety-and-tolerability evidence available, melatonin is the gentler drug and clonazepam the more effective one, and the choice turns on which of those the individual patient needs.
stamp: SPLIT (clonazepam: better objective efficacy — it alone improved REM sleep without atonia in the 34-patient head-to-head trial; melatonin: better tolerated — sleepiness and insomnia improved on melatonin, depressive symptoms rose on clonazepam, and reviews judge melatonin the gentler drug in vulnerable patients). No trial measures falls or injuries head-to-head

title: Trazodone for sleep in Alzheimer's dementia: one small trial found 42.5 more minutes of night-time sleep on 50 mg versus placebo — promising, low-certainty, and never replicated
question: Does trazodone help sleep in Alzheimer's dementia better than placebo?
balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #3683, which covers trazodone in general chronic insomnia — this pack covers the slice #3683 does not: Alzheimer's dementia specifically. The entire randomised evidence is one small trial (Camargos 2014, PMID: 24495406): in 30 community-dwelling patients with probable Alzheimer's disease and sleep disturbance, trazodone 50 mg at night for 2 weeks increased actigraphic night-time sleep by 42.5 minutes and night-time percent sleep by 8.5 percentage points versus placebo, with no effect on cognition or function and no difference in adverse events. The Cochrane review of pharmacotherapies for sleep disturbances in dementia (McCleery 2020, PMID: 33189083) graded that same trial as low-certainty evidence (total nocturnal sleep time mean difference 42.46 minutes, 95% CI 0.9 to 84.0), and a 2024 meta-analysis of 14 randomised trials of sleep drugs in Alzheimer's disease (Bedward 2024, PMID: 38597219) likewise called trazodone promising while requiring more trials. One small, short, single-centre trial programme therefore caps this shelf at POSSIBLE. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): trazodone 50 mg probably buys roughly three-quarters of an hour more night-time sleep over 2 weeks in Alzheimer's dementia — a real but thinly evidenced gain, from a single trial of 30 patients.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single trial programme, total N = 30: trazodone 50 mg added 42.5 minutes of actigraphic night-time sleep versus placebo over 2 weeks in Alzheimer's dementia (Cochrane: low-certainty, mean difference 42.46 minutes, 95% CI 0.9 to 84.0), with no cognitive effect and no adverse-event difference detected

title: Amitriptyline vs topiramate for migraine prevention in poor sleepers — untested as asked: the adult head-to-head trial (in episodic migraine) found no difference in migraine frequency, only in sedation and weight, and chronic migraine has no amitriptyline trial at all
question: Is amitriptyline better than topiramate for chronic migraine prevention in patients with poor sleep?
balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #873, which covers amitriptyline and topiramate versus placebo in children and adolescents (the CHAMP trial) — this pack covers the slice #873 does not: adults, head-to-head, with poor sleep in view. The honest headline is a gap: no randomised trial has enrolled adults with chronic migraine selected for poor sleep, and none has compared these two drugs on sleep outcomes. The nearest evidence is a 26-week adult head-to-head noninferiority trial in episodic migraine (Dodick 2009, PMID: 19393844; 331 patients), in which monthly migraine episodes fell by 2.6 on topiramate and 2.7 on amitriptyline — the treatment made no difference on the primary outcome (95% CI -0.6 to 0.7) — while the side-effect profiles diverged in ways that matter for sleep: somnolence in 17.8% on amitriptyline versus 11.9% on topiramate, dry mouth 35.5% on amitriptyline, paresthesia 29.9% on topiramate, and mean weight change +2.4 kg on amitriptyline versus -2.4 kg on topiramate. A network meta-analysis of episodic migraine prophylaxis (Jackson 2015, PMID: 26172390) ranked amitriptyline above topiramate but called the evidence for that superiority weak. For chronic migraine specifically, a 2024 NIHR health technology assessment (Mistry 2024, PMID: 39365169) found topiramate trials to include but no amitriptyline trial meeting its criteria at all. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): in unselected adults the two drugs look equivalent for migraine prevention, amitriptyline is the more sedating of the two, and the asked question — chronic migraine in poor sleepers — is untested.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — no trial has tested amitriptyline versus topiramate in chronic migraine patients with poor sleep: the one adult head-to-head trial (episodic migraine, N = 331) found the treatment made no difference in migraine episodes (-2.6 vs -2.7 per month), amitriptyline was more sedating (somnolence 17.8% vs 11.9%) and added weight, and for chronic migraine no includable amitriptyline trial exists
