title: Extending sleep in short sleepers: feasible and metabolically promising in small short trials (less eating, lower blood pressure in some) — but the mortality question behind the 7-hour U-curve has never been trial-tested
question: How much sleep duration is associated with lowest mortality in adults, and does extending sleep in short sleepers help?
balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #493, which covers the observational duration–mortality association (the U-curve, lowest risk at about 7 hours) — this pack covers the slice #493 cannot answer from cohorts: whether deliberately extending sleep in habitual short sleepers improves health. No trial has tested sleep extension against mortality or cardiovascular events; the carded trials are small, short and surrogate-outcome. In the largest (Tasali 2022, PMID: 35129580; 80 adults with overweight sleeping under 6.5 hours), a single sleep-hygiene counselling session extended sleep by about 1.2 hours per night and cut objectively measured energy intake by 270 kcal/day (95% CI -393 to -147) versus control, with weight reduction. A 6-week cognitive-behavioural extension programme in 18 men (Hartescu 2022, PMID: 34459060) added 79 minutes of sleep and improved blood pressure and insulin-resistance markers. A meta-analysis of 13 experimental studies (Zhu 2022, PMID: 34279625) found extension feasible (+51 minutes of total sleep time), no overall blood-pressure effect, a blood-pressure reduction only in the pre-hypertension/hypertension subgroup, and no significant pooled effect on fasting glucose or insulin resistance (the treatment made no difference on those pooled outcomes). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): extending sleep in short sleepers is achievable and improves some short-term metabolic measures, but whether it moves the mortality curve that home shelf #493 describes is untested.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — short-term surrogate outcomes only: sleep extension in habitual short sleepers is feasible (about +51 minutes to +1.2 hours per night) and reduced energy intake by 270 kcal/day in the largest trial (N = 80), with blood-pressure benefit pooled only in pre-hypertension/hypertension; no trial has tested mortality or clinical events

title: Carotid stenting in symptomatic patients over 70: not as safe as endarterectomy — early stroke or death 12.0% vs 5.9% (relative risk 2.04) in the pooled symptomatic trials, and later durability is equal, so the early harm is never repaid
question: Is carotid stenting as safe as endarterectomy in symptomatic carotid stenosis over 70?
balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #335, which compares carotid stenting and endarterectomy overall — by age, symptoms and era, including the four-trial age analysis (Howard 2016) in its full population. This pack isolates the slice #335 does not present on its own: symptomatic patients aged 70 and over. FLAG FOR THE DEVELOPER (precedent-b build): the four-trial age anchor is already carded on home #335 and is NOT re-carded here; this pack is built on three free reports that address the symptomatic older-patient cut directly. In the pooled individual-patient analysis of the three European symptomatic trials (Bonati 2011, PMID: 21269847; 3,433 patients), age was the only variable that significantly modified the treatment effect (interaction P = 0.0053): under 70, 120-day stroke or death was 5.8% with stenting versus 5.7% with endarterectomy (relative risk 1.00); at 70 or over it was 12.0% versus 5.9% — a relative risk of 2.04 (95% CI 1.48 to 2.82), an absolute excess of about 6 extra strokes or deaths per 100 patients treated with stenting. The four-trial pooled long-term analysis (Brott 2019, PMID: 30738706) shows the excess is periprocedural: beyond 120 days, annual ipsilateral stroke rates were nearly identical (0.64% stenting vs 0.60% endarterectomy per person-year), yet combined risks still favoured endarterectomy by 2.8–4.1 percentage points out to 9 years. ICSS long-term follow-up (Bonati 2015, PMID: 25453443) agrees: fatal or disabling stroke did not differ (the treatment made no difference: 5-year risk 6.4% vs 6.5%), but any stroke was more frequent after stenting (5-year risk 15.2% vs 9.4%; HR 1.71). PROPOSED LIKELY (harm): in symptomatic patients over 70, stenting is not as safe as endarterectomy — its early stroke/death risk is about double, and later durability does not repay it.
stamp: LIKELY (harm) — in symptomatic carotid stenosis at age 70 or over, stenting is not as safe as endarterectomy: pooled 120-day stroke or death 12.0% vs 5.9% (relative risk 2.04, 95% CI 1.48 to 2.82), with no long-term catch-up (postprocedural ipsilateral stroke 0.64% vs 0.60% per year)

title: Mechanical thrombectomy in high-risk PE: treated cohorts show strikingly low mortality (1.9% in FLAME vs ~29% with other therapies) — but all the evidence is observational, and who gets the catheter may be the real treatment
question: Does mechanical thrombectomy improve outcomes in high-risk PE?
balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #1585, which covers large-bore mechanical thrombectomy versus catheter-directed thrombolysis in intermediate-risk pulmonary embolism (the randomised PEERLESS trial) — this pack covers the slice #1585 does not: high-risk (haemodynamically unstable, 'massive') PE, where no randomised trial exists and all evidence is observational, printed on the face. The dedicated study is FLAME (Silver 2023, PMID: 37847768): a prospective, nonrandomised comparison in which 53 high-risk patients treated with mechanical thrombectomy had an in-hospital primary composite rate of 17.0% (against a prespecified 32.0% performance goal) and in-hospital mortality of 1.9%, while 61 contemporaneous patients treated mostly with systemic thrombolysis or anticoagulation alone had a 63.9% composite rate and 29.5% mortality. Those context-arm figures match the background risk: a systematic review of 1,517 high-risk patients (Silver 2023, PMID: 39132523) puts in-hospital mortality at 28.3% and major bleeding at 13.8%. The FLASH registry (Toma 2023, PMID: 36349702) adds procedural safety in 800 mostly intermediate-risk patients — major adverse events 1.8%, 30-day mortality 0.8% — but only 7.9% of its patients were high-risk, printed plainly on its card. Selection decides who gets a thrombectomy catheter in every one of these datasets, so the mortality gap cannot be read as the device's effect. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: thrombectomy in high-risk PE is associated with strikingly low in-hospital mortality in selected patients, and a randomised answer does not exist.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: in high-risk PE, thrombectomy-treated patients in FLAME had in-hospital mortality of 1.9% versus 29.5% with contemporary therapy and a 28.3% pooled background rate, but treatment was chosen, not randomised, so selection may explain the gap; no randomised trial exists

title: Aerobic exercise for post-stroke fatigue (partial completion of #1522, which covers fitness and gait): interval training cut fatigue scores in a small trial and graded activity boosted fatigue-therapy response — POSSIBLE benefit, two small trials only
question: Does a structured aerobic exercise program reduce post-stroke fatigue?
balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #1522, which covers aerobic exercise in chronic stroke for fitness and gait (Macko 2005 treadmill trial, carded there and not re-carded here) but never measured fatigue. On the uncovered fatigue slice, the direct evidence is thin but concordant. A small 2026 randomised trial of home-based supervised cardiorespiratory interval training (Bråndal 2026, PMID: 42089147; 45 randomised) cut fatigue by 5.35 Swedish Fatigue Assessment Scale points versus usual care and raised peak oxygen uptake. A second randomised trial (Zedlitz 2012, PMID: 22308241) found that adding graded activity training to cognitive therapy produced clinical fatigue improvement in 58% versus 24% of patients with persistent post-stroke fatigue, though the activity component cannot be isolated from the cognitive therapy it was bundled with. The wider literature urges caution: the Cochrane review of post-stroke fatigue interventions (Wu 2015, PMID: 26133313) pooled no aerobic-exercise treatment trial and judged the evidence for every intervention insufficient, and an observational meta-analysis (Larsson 2023, PMID: 36622013) found only a weak association between fatigue and fitness (r = −0.24). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — a structured aerobic programme probably reduces post-stroke fatigue, on one small direct trial plus one combined-intervention trial; larger and longer trials are still needed.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — structured aerobic exercise probably reduces post-stroke fatigue: a small randomised trial of home-based cardiorespiratory interval training cut fatigue by 5.35 points versus usual care, and graded activity training added to cognitive therapy raised clinical fatigue improvement to 58% versus 24%; the wider fatigue-intervention literature remains insufficient

title: Ginkgo biloba (EGb 761) for cognition in Alzheimer's disease (partial completion of #3470, dementia broadly): small but consistent cognitive gains in the Alzheimer's trials — POSSIBLE benefit, confined to the tested standardised extract
question: Does ginkgo biloba extract improve cognition in Alzheimer's disease?
balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #3470, which covers the standardised ginkgo biloba extract EGb 761 in dementia broadly (its Weinmann 2010 meta-analysis and Ihl 2012 trial are carded there and are not re-carded here). This shelf narrows to the Alzheimer's disease slice and to cognition. The tested product in every carded trial is the standardised extract EGb 761, named as such in each record; the fetched trial records do not name the manufacturing company, so no company is printed here, and ginkgo products other than EGb 761 — which are not standardised to the same specification — may differ in safety and effectiveness. In the Alzheimer's-type populations of the older trials, EGb 761 beat placebo on cognitive scores by small margins: a 1.4-point ADAS-Cog advantage over 52 weeks (Le Bars 1997, PMID: 9343463), a significant responder advantage at 240 mg/day (Kanowski 1996, PMID: 8741021), and a roughly 1.9-point SKT advantage in dementia with neuropsychiatric symptoms (Herrschaft 2012, PMID: 22459264). An Alzheimer's-only meta-analysis of seven studies (Liao 2020, PMID: 32658034) found a relative response advantage for cognition (risk ratio 1.98). The effects are consistent but modest, the older trials mixed Alzheimer's with multi-infarct/vascular dementia, and no carded trial enrolled a purely Alzheimer's population with modern biomarker confirmation. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — EGb 761 probably improves cognition slightly in Alzheimer's disease; the size of the gain is small and product-specific.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the standardised extract EGb 761 improves cognition modestly in Alzheimer's disease (1.4 ADAS-Cog points over placebo at 52 weeks; SKT advantage about 1.9 points; Alzheimer's-only pooled relative response ratio 1.98); the tested product is EGb 761 specifically — the fetched records do not name its manufacturer, and other ginkgo products may differ in safety and effectiveness

title: Computerised cognitive training in mild cognitive impairment (partial completion of #2872, cognitively intact adults): test cognition improves, everyday function does not demonstrably follow — MAYBE (weak evidence) for function
question: Does computerized cognitive training improve everyday function in mild cognitive impairment?
balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #2872, which covers cognitive training in cognitively intact older adults (the ACTIVE trial, Ball 2002, carded there and not re-carded here). The uncovered slice is mild cognitive impairment, and within it the outcome that matters most: everyday function. The cognition half of the story is positive — a meta-analysis of 17 MCI trials (Hill 2017, PMID: 27838936) found a moderate effect on overall cognition (Hedges' g = 0.35) — but the function half is not demonstrated. The Cochrane review of at least 12 weeks of computerised training in MCI (Gates 2019, PMID: 30864747; 8 trials, 660 participants) could not determine any effect on functional performance because the evidence was very low quality. The one randomised trial that measured everyday function directly over two years (Wadley 2025, PMID: 40567104) found processing speed training made no difference to instrumental activities of daily living, driving or community mobility versus a control training protocol. A small virtual-reality training meta-analysis (Son 2022, PMID: 36497946) reports significant ADL/IADL effects but prints no effect sizes in its record and mixes MCI with Alzheimer's disease. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — computerised training improves test cognition in MCI, but an everyday-function benefit is unproven, and the only direct trial found the treatment made no difference.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — computerised cognitive training improves cognitive test scores in mild cognitive impairment (g = 0.35), but an everyday-function benefit is unproven: the Cochrane review could not determine any functional effect and the one two-year trial measuring IADL, driving and mobility directly found the treatment made no difference

title: Tai chi versus usual activity in Parkinson's disease (partial completion of #3693, which uses active comparators): falls roughly halved in the one no-intervention trial — POSSIBLE benefit
question: Does tai chi reduce falls in Parkinson's disease compared with usual activity?
balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #3693, which compares tai chi with resistance training and stretching in Parkinson's disease (Li 2012, carded there and not re-carded here; on that shelf falls were lower only against stretching). The uncovered slice is tai chi against usual activity — no intervention. On that comparison there is one direct randomised trial: Gao 2014 (PMID: 24519923) randomised 76 patients who had already fallen to 12 weeks of tai chi or no intervention, and over 6 months 21.6% of the tai chi group fell versus 48.7% of controls, with fewer falls per person. Two meta-analyses point the same way: Winser 2018 (PMID: 29737198) pooled a relative falls odds ratio of 0.47 in Parkinson's disease across tai chi trials with active or no-treatment controls, and Ni 2014 (PMID: 24927169) found falls reduction greater after tai chi (mostly added to medication) than in control groups, while printing no pooled falls effect size. The direct usual-activity evidence is therefore a single small trial in prior fallers, supported by concordant pooling that mixes comparators. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — tai chi probably reduces falls in Parkinson's disease versus usual activity, on one small direct trial plus supportive meta-analyses.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — tai chi probably reduces falls in Parkinson's disease compared with usual activity: in the one direct trial 21.6% fell versus 48.7% on no intervention over 6 months, and meta-analyses pool a relative falls odds ratio of 0.47; the direct evidence is a single small trial in prior fallers

title: Levetiracetam versus carbamazepine in newly diagnosed focal epilepsy (partial completion of #337, first-line comparisons broadly): equal seizure control, better tolerated and better retained — in trials of patients over 60
question: Is levetiracetam as effective as carbamazepine for newly diagnosed focal epilepsy with fewer side effects?
balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #337, which covers first-line antiseizure comparisons broadly — its SANAD II focal arm pits levetiracetam against lamotrigine (carded there and not re-carded here) but never against carbamazepine head-to-head. On that uncovered pairing, the direct randomised evidence sits in patients aged 60 and over, and it answers the question in two parts. For effectiveness, levetiracetam and controlled-release carbamazepine did not differ: seizure freedom rates were not different in the double-blind elderly trial (Werhahn 2015, PMID: 25684224), and time to first seizure was similar in the KOMET elderly subgroup (Pohlmann-Eden 2016, PMID: 27552848; hazard ratio 1.02). For tolerability, levetiracetam clearly won on staying on treatment: 58-week retention 61.5% versus 45.8%, with discontinuation for adverse events or death roughly half (17.2% versus 32.2%); in KOMET, 12-month withdrawal was 25.0% versus 46.6% and adverse-event discontinuation 11.3% versus 35.0%. The Cochrane individual-participant network meta-analysis (Nevitt 2022, PMID: 35363878) is concordant at network level: lamotrigine and levetiracetam did not differ on treatment failure (HR 1.01) and both performed better than carbamazepine (lamotrigine versus carbamazepine HR 1.26). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit — tolerability and retention, not seizure superiority): levetiracetam appears as effective as carbamazepine for newly diagnosed focal epilepsy with fewer treatment-limiting side effects, on direct evidence confined to older adults.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit — tolerability and retention, not seizure superiority): levetiracetam was as effective as controlled-release carbamazepine for newly diagnosed focal epilepsy (seizure freedom and time to first seizure not different) with roughly half the adverse-event discontinuations (17.2% versus 32.2%; 11.3% versus 35.0%) — on direct evidence confined to patients aged 60 and over

title: Buccal midazolam versus rectal diazepam in the community (partial completion of #3878, children in the ED): the one out-of-hospital trial and the pooled data favour the buccal route — POSSIBLE benefit, and easier to give
question: Should buccal midazolam be preferred over rectal diazepam for prolonged seizures in the community?
balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #3878, which covers buccal midazolam versus rectal diazepam in children in the emergency department (the McIntyre 2005 trial and the McTague 2018 Cochrane review are carded there and are not re-carded here). The uncovered slice is the community — seizures treated where they happen, by carers or nurses, before hospital. The only randomised trial conducted entirely outside hospital is Scott 1999 (PMID: 10030327), run at a residential school: buccal midazolam stopped 75% of seizures versus 59% for rectal diazepam, a difference that was not significant (p = 0.16) in 42 young people, with no clinically important cardiorespiratory events and universal staff acceptance of the buccal route. The pooled evidence, which mixes community and hospital trials, favours buccal midazolam on the specific pairing: a relative risk of 1.54 for seizure cessation in one meta-analysis (McMullan 2010, PMID: 20624136), while a second, larger meta-analysis found the advantage only on the odds scale (odds ratio 1.78; relative risk 1.15, not significant) (Brigo 2015, PMID: 25817929). Administration is also faster with non-intravenous midazolam. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — buccal midazolam should be preferred in the community: at least as effective as rectal diazepam, probably somewhat more effective, quicker and more socially acceptable to give, on one small out-of-hospital trial plus pooled analyses.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — buccal midazolam should be preferred over rectal diazepam for prolonged seizures in the community: at least as effective (75% versus 59% stopped in the one out-of-hospital trial, not significant), pooled buccal-versus-rectal relative risk 1.54 in one meta-analysis, faster and more socially acceptable to administer

title: Triptan overuse headache (partial completion of #2381, withdrawal strategies generally): triptan overusers improve most after stopping, and the supported strategy is stop-plus-preventive — POSSIBLE, triptan-specific evidence observational only
question: Should triptans be stopped and preventive therapy started in medication-overuse headache?
balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #2381, which compares withdrawal and preventive strategies in medication-overuse headache generally (the Carlsen 2020 three-strategy trial is carded there and is not re-carded here). The uncovered slice is triptan overuse specifically, and no randomised trial restricted to triptan overusers was found in the records fetched — the triptan-specific evidence is a subgroup of a prospective withdrawal cohort. In that cohort (Zeeberg 2006, PMID: 16707727), triptan/ergot overusers improved the most after a 2-month drug-free period (p < 0.0001), within an overall picture in which 45% of patients who stayed drug-free improved. The strategy evidence is drug-class-general: the one randomised strategy trial (Hagen 2009, PMID: 18823363; 56 patients) found no significant difference in headache days between prophylaxis-from-the-start, withdrawal alone and no specific treatment, though the prophylaxis group reduced total headache suffering more; and a systematic review (Chiang 2016, PMID: 26122645) concluded that adding preventive medication to early discontinuation led to a better outcome than discontinuation alone, while the evidence for discontinuation alone is low because controlled studies are absent. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — for triptan overuse, stop the triptan and start a preventive together: triptan overusers are the subgroup that responds best to withdrawal, and the combined strategy is the review-supported default, but the triptan-specific leg is observational only.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only for the triptan-specific claim: stop the overused triptan and start preventive therapy together — triptan overusers improved most after a drug-free period (p < 0.0001), and reviews find preventive-plus-discontinuation beats discontinuation alone; no randomised trial restricted to triptan overusers exists

title: Topiramate in medication-overuse headache (partial completion of #2381, withdrawal strategies generally): SPLIT — one small strongly positive trial against a 2023 verdict of insufficient population-specific evidence
question: Does topiramate reduce headache days in medication-overuse headache after withdrawal?
balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #2381, which covers withdrawal and preventive strategies in medication-overuse headache generally (Carlsen 2020 is carded there and is not re-carded here). The uncovered slice is topiramate's own effect on headache days in patients with medication overuse — and the evidence genuinely divides. A small double-blind trial in chronic migraine with analgesic overuse (Silvestrini 2003, PMID: 14510929) found a large effect at only 50 mg/day (8.1 versus 20.6 headache days per 28 days in the last maintenance month). A review of the two large chronic-migraine trials (Diener 2009, PMID: 19735529) reports topiramate was effective in patients both with and without medication overuse, but prints no effect sizes, and one of those underlying trials is already carded elsewhere in the library, so it is not re-carded here. Against that, a 2023 systematic review and meta-analysis restricted to randomised trials in chronic migraine with medication overuse (Giri 2023, PMID: 36856015) concluded there is currently insufficient evidence to determine the impact of topiramate in this population. The only post-withdrawal data carded (Valguarnera 2010, PMID: 20464616) combine topiramate with amitriptyline and inpatient withdrawal, so topiramate's isolated contribution cannot be separated. PROPOSED SPLIT (small positive trial and positive subgroup reviews versus a 2023 meta-analysis finding the randomised evidence in medication overuse insufficient) — topiramate may reduce headache days in medication-overuse headache, but its isolated effect, especially after withdrawal, is not established.
stamp: SPLIT (a small positive trial and positive subgroup reviews versus a 2023 meta-analysis finding insufficient randomised evidence in medication overuse) — topiramate cut headache days to 8.1 versus 20.6 per 28 days in one small trial in analgesic overuse, but its isolated effect in medication-overuse headache, especially after withdrawal, is not established

title: Rimegepant — one gepant, both jobs (partial completion of #689, acute treatment only): three concordant trials support every-other-day prevention, 0.8–1.6 fewer migraine days a month — LIKELY
question: Is rimegepant effective for both acute treatment and prevention of migraine?
balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #689, which covers the gepants for acute treatment only (the ACHIEVE II ubrogepant trial and the Croop 2019 acute rimegepant trial are carded there and are not re-carded here). The uncovered slice is prevention — and with it the dual-indication question, since rimegepant is the one gepant tested in both roles. Three placebo-controlled prevention trials of rimegepant 75 mg every other day are now carded here, and they agree: the phase 2/3 trial (Croop 2021, PMID: 33338437; 747 randomised) reduced monthly migraine days by 4.3 versus 3.5 on placebo (difference −0.8 days); the Japanese phase 3 trial (Kitamura 2025, PMID: 40542538; 484 in the efficacy analysis) found a difference of −1.1 days; and a phase 4 trial in patients who had already failed 2 to 4 categories of oral preventives (Pozo-Rosich 2025, PMID: 41255098; 652 treated) found −2.1 versus −0.5 days (difference −1.6) with a 20.1-percentage-point advantage in 50% responders. Tolerability resembled placebo in all three. Combined with the acute efficacy homed on #689, the dual claim holds. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) — rimegepant is effective for prevention of migraine (about 0.8 to 1.6 fewer migraine days per month than placebo across three concordant trials), and, with its acute benefit on #689, it is effective for both acute treatment and prevention.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — rimegepant is effective for both acute treatment and prevention of migraine: three concordant placebo-controlled prevention trials of 75 mg every other day found 0.8 to 1.6 fewer monthly migraine days than placebo, and its acute efficacy is homed on live shelf #689

title: Ubrogepant in triptan non-responders (partial completion of #689, gepants versus placebo generally): efficacy consistent across triptan-response subgroups — POSSIBLE benefit, post-hoc evidence only
question: Does ubrogepant work for acute migraine in patients who do not respond to triptans?
balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #689, which covers the gepants versus placebo for acute migraine generally (the ACHIEVE II primary report and the acute rimegepant trial are carded there and are not re-carded here). The uncovered slice is patients who do not respond to triptans — and for ubrogepant that evidence is entirely post hoc. A pooled post-hoc analysis of ACHIEVE I and II (Blumenfeld 2021, PMID: 33749826) classified 451 of 1,799 participants as triptan-insufficient responders and found ubrogepant's efficacy did not differ by historical triptan experience (interaction p = 0.290 for pain freedom), though the record does not print the subgroup's own pain-freedom rates. A companion post-hoc analysis (Lipton 2022, PMID: 35468729) found functional benefits in that subgroup: normal function at 2 hours in 38% on ubrogepant versus 29% on placebo, and satisfaction at 24 hours in 58% versus 28%. A network meta-analysis restricted to triptan-insufficient responders (Laohapiboolrattana 2024, PMID: 39516789; 5 trials, 3,004 patients) found lasmiditan, rimegepant and ubrogepant all significantly superior to placebo for 2-hour pain freedom, without printing ubrogepant-specific estimates separately. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — ubrogepant probably works in triptan non-responders about as well as in responders, but no trial has prospectively enrolled non-responders to test it, so the claim rests on subgroup analyses of trials homed on #689 — flagged here for the developer: these are secondary reports of those same trials, carded because the subgroup is the question, with distinct PMIDs not used on the home shelf.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — ubrogepant probably works for acute migraine in patients who do not respond to triptans: its efficacy did not differ by historical triptan response in the ACHIEVE trials and functional outcomes favoured it within the insufficient-responder subgroup (normal function 38% versus 29% at 2 hours), but all the evidence is post-hoc subgroup analysis, with no prospective non-responder trial

title: Atogepant after oral preventives have failed (PARTIAL completion of #1448): in ELEVATE, atogepant cut monthly migraine days by 2.4 days more than placebo in episodic migraine failed by 2–4 preventive classes — one trial programme
question: Does atogepant prevent episodic migraine in patients who failed two oral preventives?
balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #1448, which covers atogepant in episodic migraine generally (the ADVANCE trial) and in chronic migraine (PROGRESS); this shelf covers only the slice #1448 does not: patients whose episodic migraine had already been failed by two to four classes of conventional oral preventive treatments. In that dedicated population, the single phase 3b ELEVATE trial (Tassorelli 2024, PMID: 38364831) found monthly migraine days fell by 4.2 days on atogepant 60 mg daily versus 1.9 days on placebo over 12 weeks (difference −2.4 days, 95% CI −3.2 to −1.5). A post hoc pooled subgroup of high-frequency episodic migraine patients who had failed at least two preventive classes (Ashina 2026, PMID: 43036972) found a consistent −2.65-day difference, and a pooled patient-reported-outcomes analysis of three phase 3 trials (Gottschalk 2024, PMID: 39648617) found the largest quality-of-life and headache-impact gains of any of its trial populations in the ELEVATE population. Constipation was the commonest adverse event (10% versus 3%); serious adverse events occurred in 3% on atogepant versus none on placebo. All three cards come from one trial programme anchored on a single randomised trial, so the stamp is capped. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): atogepant 60 mg daily reduced monthly migraine days by about 2.4 days more than placebo over 12 weeks in episodic migraine patients who had failed two to four classes of oral preventives — a single-trial-programme result.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single trial programme (ELEVATE): atogepant 60 mg daily reduced monthly migraine days by 2.4 days more than placebo over 12 weeks (95% CI −3.2 to −1.5) in episodic migraine patients who had failed two to four classes of conventional oral preventives

title: Trigeminal neuralgia first-line ranking (PARTIAL completion of #5032): carbamazepine remains first — the guideline's only Level A drug, unbeaten head-to-head, on an old and poor-quality comparative base
question: Is carbamazepine still the most effective first treatment for trigeminal neuralgia?
balance: PARTIAL completion of pack #5032, which covers only carbamazepine versus placebo in the old crossover trials; this shelf covers the slice #5032 does not: how carbamazepine ranks against the alternatives as first treatment. The AAN–EFNS evidence-based practice parameter (Gronseth 2008, PMID: 18716236) graded carbamazepine Level A (established effective) — the only drug at that level — with oxcarbazepine Level B and baclofen and lamotrigine Level C. The one comparative meta-analysis found (Wang 2011, PMID: 21936587) pooled six small, poor-quality Chinese trials of topiramate versus carbamazepine (354 patients): no difference at 1 month, and a relative advantage for topiramate at 2 months (relative risk 1.20) that the authors themselves say is limited by trial quality. An evidence-based pharmacology review (Di Stefano 2018, PMID: 30178160) likewise keeps carbamazepine and oxcarbazepine as first choice, with lamotrigine or baclofen as add-ons. So no alternative has beaten carbamazepine in adequate head-to-head trials — but the comparative base is old, small and poor quality, which caps the stamp. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: carbamazepine remains the most effective first treatment for trigeminal neuralgia on current evidence — the guideline's only Level A drug, with no alternative shown superior in adequate trials.
stamp: POSSIBLE — carbamazepine remains the most effective first treatment for trigeminal neuralgia on current evidence: it is the AAN–EFNS guideline's only Level A drug and no alternative has beaten it in adequate head-to-head trials, but the comparative trial base is old, small and poor quality

title: Long-term opioids for neuropathic pain without functional gain (PARTIAL completion of #346): trials show pain relief but no functional improvement, and tapering usually leaves pain unchanged — continuation is not supported
question: Should opioids be continued long term for chronic neuropathic pain if function does not improve?
balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #346, which covers long-term opioid versus non-opioid strategy in chronic back and joint pain; this shelf covers the slices #346 does not: neuropathic pain specifically, and the continuation question when function does not improve. The neuropathic-pain trial base (McNicol 2013, PMID: 23986501, Cochrane) reaches only 12 weeks: intermediate-term trials showed modest pain relief (at least 33% relief in 57% on opioid versus 34% on placebo) but opioids did not demonstrate improvement in many aspects of emotional or physical functioning — the trials show pain scores moving without function moving. No randomised trial tests continuation beyond 12 weeks. The tapering literature (Mackey 2020, PMID: 33145689) finds pain scores mostly unchanged or improved after dose reduction, with low confidence, and observational signals of overdose and suicidal ideation after reduction or discontinuation that mandate monitoring. A voluntary patient-centred tapering cohort (Darnall 2018, PMID: 29459978; 2–3-year follow-up, PMID: 33490845) reduced doses durably with pain intensity unchanged on average. None of the tapering studies was restricted to neuropathic pain — printed plainly, that is the remaining gap. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm): continuing long-term opioids for chronic neuropathic pain when function does not improve — pain relief in trials is modest and function does not improve, while supervised tapering usually leaves pain unchanged.
stamp: POSSIBLE (harm) — continuing long-term opioids for chronic neuropathic pain when function does not improve: trials of ≤12 weeks show modest pain relief with no improvement in functioning, and tapering studies show pain is usually unchanged after dose reduction, so continuation without functional gain carries harm without demonstrated benefit (tapering should be voluntary and monitored)

title: Antidepressants after a second depressive episode (PARTIAL completion of #705): continue at least 12 months — PREVENT and the imipramine programme agree at 1, 2, 3 and 5 years
question: Should antidepressants be continued for at least 12 months after a second depressive episode to prevent relapse?
balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #705, which covers continuation versus tapering in primary-care patients already well on antidepressants (ANTLER) and the older maintenance base in general; this shelf covers the slice #705 does not isolate: patients with recurrent depression — the second-episode-and-beyond population — and durations of at least 12 months. Every dedicated trial in that population favours continuation, at every duration tested. In the Pittsburgh recurrent-depression programme (Frank 1990, PMID: 2244793), full-dose imipramine maintained over 3 years had a highly significant prophylactic effect against recurrence; its extension (Kupfer 1992, PMID: 1417428) found the protection persisted beyond 3 years and concluded patients whose episodes come less than 2½ years apart merit at least 5 years. In PREVENT, 12 months of maintenance venlafaxine ER halved recurrence versus placebo (23.1% versus 42.0%; Kocsis 2007, PMID: 17685736), a second maintenance year again favoured continuation (8.0% versus 44.8%; Keller 2007, PMID: 17854250), and the combined 24-month recurrence probability was 28.5% versus 47.3%. Two independent programmes, concordant, with large absolute differences — the stamp can be strong. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): continuing antidepressants for at least 12 months after a second (recurrent) depressive episode prevents relapse, and the trial evidence supports continuing well beyond 12 months in frequently recurring illness.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — continuing antidepressants for at least 12 months after a second (recurrent) depressive episode prevents relapse: PREVENT recurrence 23.1% versus 42.0% at 12 months and 28.5% versus 47.3% at 24 months, with the imipramine programme showing protection at 3–5 years

title: Repositioning plus mattress versus standard care (PARTIAL completion of #796): 4-hourly turning on viscoelastic foam cut grade II+ ulcers to 3.0% in nursing-home patients — one trial, reviews unsettled
question: Do regular repositioning and pressure-redistributing mattresses prevent pressure injuries in immobile older adults?
balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #796, which covers the slices of frequency (2- versus 4-hourly turning, TURN) and of mattress-versus-mattress comparison (PRESSURE 2); this shelf covers the slice #796 does not: whether repositioning plus a pressure-redistributing mattress prevents pressure injuries at all, against standard care, in immobile older adults. Only one trial answers that directly (Defloor 2005, PMID: 15582638): in 838 nursing-home patients, turning every 4 hours on a viscoelastic foam mattress produced grade II-or-worse ulcers in 3.0%, versus 14.3–24.1% across the other regimens including standard preventive care — while early skin redness (non-blanchable erythema) did not differ (34.8–38.1%). The Cochrane repositioning review (Gillespie 2020, PMID: 32484259) found the frequency evidence very low certainty (2- versus 4-hourly relative risk 1.06), and the Cochrane foam review (Shi 2021, PMID: 34097765) found foam may be worse than air surfaces — neither review contains a trial of the combined package versus no prevention. So the package is supported by one large trial against standard care; the optimal frequency and surface remain unsettled. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): regular repositioning combined with a pressure-redistributing mattress prevents grade II-or-worse pressure injuries in immobile older adults, on single-trial evidence against standard care.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — regular repositioning on a pressure-redistributing mattress prevents grade II-or-worse pressure injuries in immobile older adults: 3.0% versus 14.3–24.1% against other regimens including standard care in one 838-patient nursing-home trial; Cochrane reviews leave the best frequency and surface uncertain

title: Nutrition to prevent pressure injuries (PARTIAL completion of #1223): SPLIT — a 2005 meta-analysis found prevention, the larger 2024 Cochrane review finds little to no difference
question: Does nutritional supplementation with protein and energy prevent pressure injuries in malnourished older adults?
balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #1223, which covers a nutrition formula for HEALING established pressure ulcers; this shelf covers the different slice #1223 does not: PREVENTION in malnourished older adults. Here the evidence genuinely divides. The older meta-analysis (Stratton 2005, PMID: 16081325) found oral nutritional supplements associated with a significantly lower incidence of pressure ulcer development (odds ratio 0.75, 95% CI 0.62 to 0.89; 4 trials, 1,224 at-risk patients). The current Cochrane review (Langer 2024, PMID: 38345088), pooling more and later trials, found energy, protein and micronutrient supplements may result in little to no difference versus standard diet (relative risk 0.92, 95% CI 0.71 to 1.19; 248 versus 269 per 1,000) and protein supplements likewise (relative risk 0.75, 95% CI 0.49 to 1.14) — both low-certainty. The one double-blind trial in a defined malnourished-risk group (Houwing 2003, PMID: 12880608, hip-fracture patients) found overall incidence did not differ (55% versus 59%) though stage II ulcers were less frequent (18% versus 28%). PROPOSED SPLIT: an older meta-analysis found a significant preventive effect of supplementation, while the 2024 Cochrane review of the larger trial base finds little to no difference — prevention by protein-and-energy supplementation is unproven on current evidence.
stamp: SPLIT (older meta-analysis: benefit; 2024 Cochrane review: little to no difference) — protein-and-energy supplementation to prevent pressure injuries: odds ratio 0.75 (95% CI 0.62 to 0.89) in Stratton 2005 versus relative risk 0.92 (95% CI 0.71 to 1.19) in the larger Cochrane 2024 pooling; prevention is unproven on current evidence

title: Esketamine versus quetiapine augmentation (PARTIAL completion of #407): ESCAPE-TRD remission 27.1% versus 17.6% at week 8 — one open-label head-to-head trial
question: Is esketamine nasal spray effective for treatment-resistant depression compared with augmentation with quetiapine?
balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #407, which covers esketamine as an add-on to a newly started oral antidepressant versus that antidepressant alone; this shelf covers the slice #407 does not: the head-to-head comparison against an active augmentation strategy, quetiapine extended-release, in ESCAPE-TRD. In that single open-label, rater-blinded trial (Reif 2023, PMID: 37792613), remission at week 8 was 27.1% on esketamine versus 17.6% on quetiapine XR (P = 0.003), and 21.7% versus 14.1% were relapse-free through week 32 after remitting at week 8. The trial's safety reports (McIntyre 2024, PMID: 38954874; Mattingly 2024, PMID: 43010384) show adverse events were more frequent on esketamine (91.9% versus 78.0%) but usually resolved the same day (92.0% versus 12.1% of events), and fewer esketamine patients discontinued for adverse events (4.2% versus 11.0%). Absolute remission remained low on both arms, the trial was open-label, and patients who discontinued were counted as failures — a convention that interacts with the differing discontinuation rates. One trial programme only, so the stamp is capped. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): esketamine nasal spray beat quetiapine XR augmentation on remission at week 8 and on sustained remission to week 32 in the single head-to-head trial.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single trial programme (ESCAPE-TRD): esketamine nasal spray beat quetiapine XR augmentation on remission at week 8 (27.1% versus 17.6%) and on relapse-free remission through week 32 (21.7% versus 14.1%) in treatment-resistant depression, in one open-label, rater-blinded trial

title: rTMS versus ECT in nonpsychotic depression (PARTIAL completion of #574): SPLIT — matched ECT in nonpsychotic illness on small trials, clearly beaten in severe ECT-referred illness
question: Is repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation as effective as electroconvulsive therapy for nonpsychotic major depression?
balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #574, which covers rTMS versus sham; this shelf covers the slice #574 does not: rTMS against the active standard, ECT, in nonpsychotic major depression. The evidence splits by population. In the one trial restricted to nonpsychotic depression (Grunhaus 2003, PMID: 12586451; 40 patients referred for ECT), response was 12 of 20 on ECT versus 11 of 20 on rTMS — no significant difference. In a larger multicentre trial of severe depression in ECT-referred patients (Eranti 2007, PMID: 17202547), ECT was clearly superior at the end of treatment (remission 59.1% versus 16.7%), though Hamilton scores no longer differed at 6 months. The meta-analysis (Ren 2014, PMID: 24556538; 9 trials, 425 patients) found ECT superior overall for response (64.4% versus 48.7%; relative risk 1.41) and remission (52.9% versus 33.6%; relative risk 1.38), but its subgroup analysis found the superiority concentrated in psychotic depression, with high-frequency rTMS as effective as ECT in nonpsychotic depression; specific cognitive domains (visual memory, verbal fluency) were more impaired after ECT in the few studies reporting them. PROPOSED SPLIT: rTMS matched ECT in the nonpsychotic-restricted trial and in the meta-analysis's nonpsychotic subgroup, but ECT was superior in severe, ECT-referred populations and overall — 'as effective' holds only for the nonpsychotic, less severe end of the spectrum, on small trials.
stamp: SPLIT (nonpsychotic, less severe depression: rTMS as effective as ECT on small-trial evidence; severe or psychotic-spectrum depression: ECT superior) — response 12/20 versus 11/20 in the nonpsychotic-restricted trial, versus remission 59.1% versus 16.7% for ECT in severe ECT-referred patients; meta-analysis relative risk 1.41 for response favouring ECT overall, with equivalence in its nonpsychotic subgroup

title: Lamotrigine's polarity (PARTIAL completion of #1436, flagged): its maintenance benefit is preventing bipolar depression (hazard ratio 0.59), not mania (hazard ratio 0.91; worse than lithium for mania)
question: Is lamotrigine effective for prevention of bipolar depression rather than mania?
balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #1436, which covers lamotrigine maintenance against any mood episode (the Calabrese and Bowden 18-month trials) — and which already reports, on its cards, that lamotrigine's advantage in those trials was against depressive episodes. This shelf was nonetheless built under the one-home precedent for a genuinely different outcome cut, on three free reports that address the polarity question directly and are NOT carded on #1436; it is flagged prominently in the part summary for the developer's ruling. The pooled analysis of the two home trials (Goodwin 2004, PMID: 15096085) found lamotrigine superior to placebo for time to intervention for depression, with 'more robust activity against depression' than mania. A meta-analysis restricted to women of childbearing age across four maintenance trials (Vieta 2024, PMID: 37775363) found lamotrigine delayed intervention for depressive episodes (hazard ratio 0.59, 95% CI 0.39 to 0.90) with no difference for manic episodes (hazard ratio 0.91, 95% CI 0.52 to 1.58 — the treatment made no difference for mania). The Cochrane review (Hashimoto 2021, PMID: 34523118) found the mirror image against lithium: manic recurrence at one year was higher on lamotrigine than lithium (relative risk 2.13, 95% CI 1.32 to 3.44), while its abstract reports no depression-specific pooled estimate. All underlying trials used enriched designs (randomising only patients stabilised on open-label lamotrigine), as disclosed on #1436. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit, for depression prevention specifically): lamotrigine maintenance prevents bipolar depressive episodes rather than manic ones — the polarity is consistent across the pooled analysis, the four-trial subgroup meta-analysis and the Cochrane comparison with lithium.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit, for bipolar depression prevention rather than mania) — lamotrigine maintenance delayed intervention for depressive episodes (hazard ratio 0.59, 95% CI 0.39 to 0.90) with no effect on manic episodes (hazard ratio 0.91) and higher manic recurrence than lithium (relative risk 2.13); enriched trial designs, as on home shelf #1436

title: Trauma-focused CBT vs EMDR for PTSD (PARTIAL, split): no consistent winner head-to-head — EMDR modestly ahead immediately in one meta-analysis, no difference in two others, exposure ahead in the one direct trial, and nothing between them at follow-up
question: Does trauma-focused cognitive behavioral therapy work better than EMDR for posttraumatic stress disorder?
balance: SPLIT — PARTIAL completion of live shelf #2408. That shelf compares EMDR with an antidepressant (fluoxetine) and asks whether EMDR's gains persist; it does not card the psychotherapy head-to-head. This shelf covers the uncovered slice: trauma-focused CBT against EMDR in adults. The direct evidence genuinely divides. The adult Cochrane review found no statistically significant difference between individual trauma-focused CBT and EMDR immediately after treatment (both clearly better than waitlist/usual care), and graded that comparison very low quality (Bisson 2013). One direct meta-analysis of randomised trials found EMDR modestly better for post-traumatic symptoms immediately after treatment (standardised mean difference −0.43, 11 trials, n = 547) but not at 3-month follow-up (Khan 2018); a second found no difference for PTSD symptoms at treatment end or at 3- and 6-month follow-up (Hudays 2022). The one carded three-way randomised trial (N = 60) found exposure therapy — a trauma-focused CBT — produced larger reductions in avoidance and re-experiencing than EMDR, with EMDR no better than relaxation (Taylor 2003). No carded analysis shows either treatment ahead at follow-up. PROPOSED SPLIT (EMDR modestly ahead immediately in one meta-analysis; no difference in the Cochrane and second meta-analysis; exposure ahead on some symptoms in the single direct trial — and no difference at follow-up in any).
stamp: SPLIT — one direct meta-analysis gives EMDR a modest immediate edge for PTSD symptoms (standardised mean difference −0.43), the Cochrane adult review and a second meta-analysis find no difference, and the one three-way trial favours exposure therapy on avoidance and re-experiencing; at follow-up no analysis separates trauma-focused CBT and EMDR

title: Buprenorphine vs methadone for illicit opioid use (PARTIAL, split): no advantage in the randomised trials — positive-urine rates did not differ; only completer and non-randomised analyses favour buprenorphine
question: Does buprenorphine maintenance reduce illicit opioid use better than methadone?
balance: SPLIT — PARTIAL completion of live shelf #402. That shelf homes the two drugs' mortality comparison and cards the Cochrane review (Mattick 2014), whose retained-patient analysis already notes that suppression of illicit opioid use did not differ between the drugs; the review itself is NOT re-carded here. This shelf covers the uncovered slice — illicit opioid use as the primary question — from the free individual reports. In the largest randomised double-blind trial (405 patients, 13 weeks) there were no significant differences in morphine-positive urines or self-reported heroin use (Mattick 2003), and among completers of a second double-blind trial the drugs produced very similar outcomes on opioid-positive urines (Strain 1996). The reports tilting toward buprenorphine are weaker cuts: completers of a small open trial (N = 60) had lower illicit opiate consumption on buprenorphine (P = 0.04; Fischer 1999), and a non-randomised comparison (N = 154) found fewer illicit-opioid users on buprenorphine at week 12 (25.6% vs 32.1%; Gerra 2004). Retention favoured methadone where reported. FLAG for the developer: the anchor review is homed on #402, so this pack is built on the free individual trials under the standing precedent for genuinely different slices, with the home cross-pointed here and the review's PMID kept out of the card source lines. PROPOSED SPLIT (randomised trials: the treatment made no difference to illicit opioid use; completer and observational analyses tilt to buprenorphine).
stamp: SPLIT — in the randomised double-blind trials buprenorphine did not reduce illicit opioid use better than methadone (the treatment made no difference); completer analyses of a small open trial and one non-randomised comparison tilt toward buprenorphine

title: Cinacalcet and bone in non-surgical primary hyperparathyroidism (PARTIAL): calcium normalises, bone does not — density unchanged against placebo and over 5.5 years, and no fracture data
question: In adults with primary hyperparathyroidism who do not meet surgical criteria, does cinacalcet improve bone outcomes versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference to bone density) — PARTIAL completion of live shelf #1753. That shelf covers cinacalcet for calcium and PTH normalisation and cards the pooled Peacock 2011 analysis, which mentions bone density only in passing (no significant change except a total-femur decrease at 1 year); its record is NOT re-carded here. This shelf covers the uncovered slice: bone outcomes, in the population that does not go to surgery. Against placebo in the 1-year randomised trial (n = 78), cinacalcet normalised calcium in 73% vs 5% but bone mineral density was unchanged, while bone resorption and formation markers increased (Peacock 2005). In the open-label extension, density z-scores at spine, hip and wrist did not change over up to 5.5 years (Peacock 2009). A randomised-trial meta-analysis in exactly this population — asymptomatic patients or those who decline surgery — found bone-density increases with alendronate, denosumab, vitamin D and estrogen, and reports no density increase for cinacalcet (Ye 2022); a medical-management review states bisphosphonates improved density while cinacalcet had no effect (Leere 2017). No carded record reports a fracture outcome for cinacalcet. Note the DENOCINA trial, which also reports bone outcomes with cinacalcet, is already carded elsewhere in the library and was therefore not carded here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference to bone density): cinacalcet is a calcium-and-PTH drug; on the carded evidence it does not improve bone outcomes.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference to bone density) — cinacalcet normalised calcium but bone mineral density was unchanged versus placebo at 1 year and unchanged over 5.5 years; no carded record reports a fracture benefit

title: Calcium plus vitamin D and hip fractures in community-dwelling older adults (PARTIAL): no prevention — 33 trials and two mega-trials are null, unlike the deficient nursing-home population on the home shelf
question: In older adults, does calcium plus vitamin D supplementation prevent hip fractures in community-dwelling people versus placebo?
balance: LIKELY (no benefit) — PARTIAL completion of live shelf #1498. That shelf covers calcium plus vitamin D in nursing-home elderly women, where the deficient institutionalised population benefited; it does not cover the community-dwelling population. This shelf covers the uncovered slice: community-dwelling older adults. The evidence is concordantly null. A JAMA meta-analysis of 33 randomised trials with 51,145 community-dwelling participants older than 50 found combined calcium and vitamin D was not associated with hip fracture (relative risk 1.09; 95% CI 0.85 to 1.39; absolute risk difference 0.00; Zhao 2017). The RECORD trial (5,292 people aged 70 or older after a low-trauma fracture) found no difference between combination treatment and placebo for new fractures (12.6% vs 13.4%; Grant 2005), and the Women's Health Initiative trial (36,282 postmenopausal women, 7 years) found a non-significant hip-fracture hazard ratio of 0.88 (95% CI 0.72 to 1.08) with significantly more kidney stones (HR 1.17; Jackson 2006). The deficiency-correcting nursing-home result on #1498 does not generalise to the replete community population. PROPOSED LIKELY (no benefit) — calcium plus vitamin D supplementation does not prevent hip fractures in community-dwelling older adults (the treatment made no difference in intention-to-treat analyses).
stamp: LIKELY (no benefit) — calcium plus vitamin D did not prevent hip fractures in community-dwelling older adults: pooled relative risk 1.09 (95% CI 0.85 to 1.39), with concordant null results in the RECORD and Women's Health Initiative trials (the treatment made no difference)

title: Vitamin D alone and falls in nursing homes (PARTIAL, split by regimen): daily 800–1,000 IU cut fall rates in two trials; a quarterly bolus in the largest trial did nothing
question: In older adults in nursing homes, does vitamin D supplementation reduce falls versus placebo?
balance: SPLIT — PARTIAL completion of live shelf #1498. That shelf covers calcium plus vitamin D for fractures in nursing-home women; it does not cover vitamin D alone for falls. This shelf covers the uncovered slice: vitamin D supplementation and falls in nursing-home and residential-care residents. The evidence splits by dose and regimen. In a small multiple-dose trial, only 800 IU daily reduced falls (20% of residents fell vs 44% on placebo; adjusted fall rate ratio 0.28), while 200, 400 and 600 IU did not differ from placebo (Broe 2007). In a 2-year placebo-controlled trial of 625 residents (all on background calcium), about 1,000 IU daily reduced the fall rate (incidence rate ratio 0.73; 95% CI 0.57 to 0.95), though ever-falling was not significantly reduced (Flicker 2005). In the largest trial — 3,717 residents given ergocalciferol as a quarterly bolus equivalent to about 1,100 IU/day — falls were 44% on treatment vs 43% on control and fractures did not differ (Law 2006). PROPOSED SPLIT (daily vitamin D at 800 IU or more: fewer falls in two trials; quarterly bolus in the largest trial: the treatment made no difference).
stamp: SPLIT — daily vitamin D (800–1,000 IU) reduced fall rates in two nursing-home trials (rate ratios 0.28 and 0.73), but a quarterly-bolus regimen in the largest trial (3,717 residents) made no difference to falls (44% vs 43%)

title: Proton pump inhibitors and fractures with long use (PARTIAL, observational only): risk about 30% higher in relative terms and rising with duration — an association the randomised evidence on the home shelf did not confirm
question: Does taking a proton pump inhibitor increase the risk of bone fractures in adults who use it for more than a year?
balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — observational only. PARTIAL completion of live shelf #325. That shelf weighs fractures as one of several long-term PPI harms and cards the randomised pantoprazole evidence (no fracture difference over 3 years); this shelf covers the uncovered slice: fracture risk alone, with duration of use at its centre, from the observational literature the home does not card. Across 11 observational studies, PPI use was associated with hip fracture relative risk 1.30, spine 1.56 and any-site 1.16 (Yu 2011). An updated meta-analysis of 33 studies (2,714,502 individuals) found fracture incidence of 22.04% in users vs 15.57% in controls (pooled relative effect 1.28) with a duration gradient — odds ratio 1.29 for short use, 1.33 for medium and 1.62 for long use — but no bone-density difference (Nassar 2018). In the Nurses' Health Study, regular use for at least 2 years carried hip-fracture hazard ratio 1.35 (absolute risk 2.02 vs 1.51 per 1,000 person-years), rising with longer use and confined to ever-smokers (Khalili 2012). Every carded report here is observational, the relative effects sit in the confounding-prone range, and the randomised evidence on #325 found no fracture difference. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm) — observational only: long-term PPI use is associated with a modestly higher fracture risk, increasing with duration; causation is unproven.
stamp: POSSIBLE (harm) — observational only: long-term proton pump inhibitor use is associated with a modestly higher fracture risk (relative risks about 1.3, rising to odds ratio 1.62 with long use), with absolute hip-fracture risk 2.02 vs 1.51 per 1,000 person-years in the largest cohort; no carded randomised evidence confirms the association

title: Capsaicin 8% patch vs pregabalin for postherpetic neuralgia (PARTIAL): longer relief unproven — no PHN head-to-head trial; the mixed-neuropathic-pain trial shows equal 8-week relief and faster onset, not longer duration
question: Does high-concentration capsaicin patch provide longer relief for postherpetic neuralgia than pregabalin?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — PARTIAL completion of live shelf #2565. That shelf covers the 8% capsaicin patch versus control in postherpetic neuralgia; it does not card any comparison with pregabalin. This shelf covers the uncovered slice: the head-to-head with pregabalin, on duration of relief. The direct evidence is thin and off-target. The only head-to-head randomised trial (559 patients) enrolled peripheral neuropathic pain of mixed causes — not postherpetic neuralgia specifically, with no PHN subgroup in the record — and ran only 8 weeks: the patch was non-inferior to optimised pregabalin (≥30% pain decrease 55.7% vs 54.5%) with faster onset (median 7.5 vs 36.0 days) and fewer systemic adverse effects (Haanpää 2016; allodynia analysis, Cruccu 2018). Faster onset is not longer relief, and duration beyond 8 weeks was not compared. The PHN-specific comparative literature is a cost-effectiveness model that states no head-to-head studies were identified and whose results hinge on the assumed retreatment frequency (Armstrong 2011), and a network meta-analysis printing no direct capsaicin-versus-pregabalin estimate (Guo 2025). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — whether the patch's relief lasts longer than pregabalin's in postherpetic neuralgia is unproven on the carded evidence.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — longer relief than pregabalin in postherpetic neuralgia is unproven: no PHN head-to-head trial exists in the carded records; the one head-to-head trial (mixed peripheral neuropathic pain, 8 weeks) found non-inferior relief with faster onset for the patch (55.7% vs 54.5% achieving ≥30% relief), and duration beyond 8 weeks was never compared

title: Opioids for osteoarthritis in older adults (PARTIAL, observational only): falls and fractures consistently higher than with NSAIDs across three designs — a harm ledger with no offsetting pain advantage on the home shelf
question: Should opioids be avoided for chronic osteoarthritis pain in older adults because of falls and fractures?
balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — observational only. PARTIAL completion of live shelf #346. That shelf compares opioid with non-opioid strategies for pain in chronic back and joint pain generally (finding no opioid advantage); it does not isolate older adults or the falls-and-fractures outcome. This shelf covers the uncovered slice: opioids for chronic osteoarthritis pain in older adults, judged on falls and fractures. Three observational designs agree. In propensity-matched Medicare beneficiaries with arthritis (mean age 80), opioid initiators had a fracture hazard ratio of 4.47 versus non-selective NSAID initiators (Solomon 2010). In 13,354 osteoarthritis patients aged 65–89, a narcotic prescription carried odds ratios of 3.3 (vs COX-2 inhibitors) and 4.1 (vs NSAIDs) for falls/fractures, rising with the number of prescriptions (Rolita 2013). In 100,358 osteoarthritis patients, tramadol initiation carried hip-fracture hazard ratios of 1.4–1.6 versus NSAIDs — an absolute excess of about 2 hip fractures per 1,000 person-years (Li 2022). All of this is observational and confounding by frailty and pain severity cannot be excluded; but combined with the absence of a pain advantage on #346, it supports avoiding opioids as routine first-line treatment for osteoarthritis in older adults. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm) — observational only.
stamp: POSSIBLE (harm) — observational only: opioid use for osteoarthritis in older adults is associated with substantially more falls and fractures than NSAID use (fracture hazard ratio 4.47 in one matched cohort; fall/fracture odds ratios 3.3–4.1 in another; hip-fracture hazard ratio 1.4–1.6 for tramadol, about 2 extra hip fractures per 1,000 person-years)

title: Low-dose naltrexone for fibromyalgia pain (PARTIAL, split): pooled small trials say yes, the largest trial says no — and the 'general population' evidence is still women-only
question: Does low-dose naltrexone help fibromyalgia pain?
balance: SPLIT — PARTIAL completion of live shelf #1455. That shelf covers low-dose naltrexone in women with fibromyalgia only, from a single small positive crossover trial at 4.5 mg; this shelf covers the uncovered slice: the general fibromyalgia population and the wider trial literature. FLAG for the developer, printed on the cards: the wider literature does not in fact widen the population — every randomised trial in the carded records enrolled women only or almost only, and no trial in men was found in the records fetched this session, so the general-population answer is the women's evidence pooled, stated plainly. That pooled evidence splits. Two overlapping meta-analyses of the small trials find a pain benefit (mean difference −0.86 across 4 trials and 222 patients, Vatvani 2024; standardised mean difference −0.61 across 5 trials, Nazir 2025 — both pools include the home shelf's trial, which is NOT re-carded here). The largest double-blind trial, of 6 mg in 99 women, found no significant pain difference versus placebo (−0.34 points; P = 0.27; Due Bruun 2024), and a single-blind dose-response study in 25 women (Bruun-Plesner 2020) supplies the dose rationale without efficacy evidence. Tolerability was good throughout, with vivid dreams the consistent excess adverse effect. PROPOSED SPLIT (pooled small trials: benefit; largest trial: the treatment made no difference; population: women only in the carded trials).
stamp: SPLIT — meta-analyses of the small trials find low-dose naltrexone reduces fibromyalgia pain (mean difference −0.86), but the largest double-blind trial (6 mg, 99 women) found no difference from placebo (−0.34 points, P = 0.27); all carded trials enrolled women only

title: Cryotherapy vs salicylic acid for plantar warts (PARTIAL): no — clearance was 13.6% vs 14.3% in the dedicated trial and cryotherapy costs more; the general-wart advantage on the home shelf does not extend to plantar warts
question: In adults with plantar warts, is cryotherapy more effective than salicylic acid?
balance: POSSIBLE — cryotherapy is not more effective (the treatment made no difference). PARTIAL completion of live shelf #622. That shelf covers cutaneous warts generally — its trial's plantar subgroup (n = 124) found no significant difference between cryotherapy, salicylic acid and waiting, and its Cochrane review reports a feet subgroup — and those records are NOT re-carded here. This shelf covers the uncovered slice: plantar warts specifically, from the plantar-only trials. In EVerT, the dedicated multicentre trial (240 patients aged 12 and over), complete clearance at 12 weeks was 13.6% on cryotherapy vs 14.3% on daily 50% salicylic acid (P = 0.89), with no difference in time to clearance or 6-month clearance (Cockayne 2011). In VRAIE, in plantar warts that had already failed a salicylic-acid course, second-line complete remission at day 90 was 11% on liquid nitrogen vs 20% on salicylic acid, in an under-enrolled trial (Chanal 2025). A 26-patient study found a salicylic-acid-containing combination cream (cantharidin–podophylotoxin–salicylic acid — not salicylic acid alone, labelled on its card) cleared more patients than cryotherapy (Kaçar 2012). Absolute clearance is low on both treatments. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — cryotherapy is not more effective than salicylic acid for plantar warts (the treatment made no difference in the two direct randomised trials).
stamp: POSSIBLE — cryotherapy is not more effective than salicylic acid for plantar warts: complete clearance 13.6% vs 14.3% at 12 weeks in the dedicated trial (the treatment made no difference), and 11% vs 20% as second-line treatment; absolute clearance is low on both

title: Early corticosteroid injection in frozen shoulder (PARTIAL completion of #3761): injection beat placebo on early pain, disability and range of motion, but by 12 months there was no difference
question: In adults with frozen shoulder, does early corticosteroid injection improve range of motion?
balance: PARTIAL completion — home live #3761 asks whether hydrodilatation beats corticosteroid injection or physiotherapy in frozen shoulder and cards the injection only as a comparator; this shelf asks the slice #3761 does not: whether an early corticosteroid injection itself, against placebo injection or no injection, improves range of motion. The direct evidence is old and small but consistent in direction and time course. In the only placebo-controlled trial (Carette 2003, 93 patients with adhesive capsulitis of under 1 year's duration), a single fluoroscopy-guided intra-articular corticosteroid injection improved pain-and-disability scores significantly more than saline injection by 6 weeks, with the steroid-plus-physiotherapy arm gaining the most range of motion, and the advantage was gone by 12 months. A 2017 meta-analysis of 5 studies (225 patients) found greater range-of-motion improvement with corticosteroid than placebo at both 0–8 and 9–24 weeks, while the pain advantage did not persist past 8 weeks. A primary-care randomised trial against physiotherapy (van der Windt 1998) shows the same early-speed pattern (77% vs 46% treatment success at 7 weeks, differences small by 26–52 weeks) but answers an injection-versus-physiotherapy question, not injection-versus-nothing. No carded record isolates an 'early versus late injection' comparison, so 'early' here means injection given in the first year of symptoms, as the trials enrolled. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): an early corticosteroid injection speeds recovery of range of motion and pain in the first weeks to months, but by about a year outcomes converge with no injection (the treatment made no difference at 12 months in the placebo-controlled trial).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — an early corticosteroid injection speeds range-of-motion and pain recovery in frozen shoulder over the first weeks to months (placebo-controlled and pooled evidence), but by 12 months outcomes converge with no injection

title: Early vasopressors and dialysis in septic shock (PARTIAL completion of #1070): dialysis prevention is unproven — the favourable renal signal is cohort-heavy and sizeless, and dialysis-free days did not differ in trial-inclusive pooling
question: In adults with septic shock at risk of AKI, does early vasopressor use prevent dialysis versus fluid-first resuscitation?
balance: PARTIAL completion — home live #1070 covers the restrictive-fluid/early-vasopressor strategy for mortality (CLASSIC, CLOVERS and ARISE FLUIDS, all null on mortality) and is cross-pointed here, not re-carded; this shelf asks only the slice #1070 does not answer: dialysis. On dialysis specifically, the evidence is thin and divided. One meta-analysis dominated by cohort studies (Ye 2023, 23 studies of which 21 were cohorts) reports that early vasopressor initiation (within 1–6 hours) was associated with a lower incidence of kidney injury (P = 0.001) and less renal replacement therapy use (P = 0.022) — but its record prints P values without a pooled effect size for either renal outcome, so the size of any protection cannot be stated. The most trial-inclusive meta-analysis (Ahn 2024, 12 studies, 7,281 patients) prespecified days free from renal replacement therapy and found no difference in that or the other secondary outcomes (the treatment made no difference to dialysis-free days). The updated 2025 meta-analysis (Shi 2025, 10 studies, 4,767 patients) also listed renal-replacement-therapy-free days as a secondary outcome but does not report its result in the record, while finding mortality associations driven substantially by non-randomised designs. No individual randomised trial carded here reports dialysis as an outcome, and the large strategy trials sit on #1070. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): early vasopressor use has not been shown to prevent dialysis; the only favourable renal signal comes from cohort-heavy pooling without a printed effect size, and the trial-inclusive pooling found no difference in dialysis-free days.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — early vasopressor use has not been shown to prevent dialysis: a cohort-heavy meta-analysis reports less renal replacement therapy use without printing an effect size, while the trial-inclusive meta-analysis found no difference in dialysis-free days

title: Antivirals in chronic hepatitis B with normal liver enzymes (PARTIAL completion of #326): the evidence splits by how strictly the immune-tolerant subgroup is defined, and treatment is proven only to suppress virus in this group
question: Should adults with chronic hepatitis B and normal liver enzymes receive antiviral treatment?
balance: PARTIAL completion — home live #326 covers long-term antiviral therapy in chronic hepatitis B broadly (progression, cirrhosis and liver cancer) and is cross-pointed here, not re-carded; this shelf asks only the slice #326 does not isolate: patients whose liver enzymes are normal, including the immune-tolerant phase. The observational evidence genuinely divides, and the split turns on how strictly the subgroup is defined. In a Korean cohort using normal ALT alone (Kim 2018), untreated immune-tolerant patients fared worse than treated immune-active patients (10-year liver cancer 12.7% vs 6.1%; hazard ratio 2.54 relative). But when the immune-tolerant phase is defined stringently — under 40 years old, very high viral load, ALT under 40 U/L (Lee 2021) — no liver cancer at all occurred in 194 untreated patients over a median 62 months, and a natural-history cohort (Lee 2020) found the risk concentrated in patients with intermediate viral loads, with zero cancers in the truly immune-tolerant subgroup. The one randomised trial in exactly this population (Chan 2014) shows treatment suppresses the virus (76% vs 55% suppressed at 192 weeks on combination versus single-agent therapy) but produced HBeAg seroconversion in only 5% and no surface-antigen loss, and no trial tests whether treating normal-enzyme patients prevents cancer or death. All hard-outcome evidence here is observational. PROPOSED SPLIT (observational only — risk definition decides: broadly defined normal-ALT cohorts show excess liver cancer when untreated, stringently defined immune-tolerant cohorts show negligible risk; whether treatment itself improves hard outcomes in this subgroup is untested in a trial).
stamp: SPLIT (observational only — by subgroup definition: broadly defined normal-ALT cohorts show excess liver cancer when untreated, hazard ratio 2.54 relative, while stringently defined immune-tolerant cohorts show negligible risk with zero events; no trial shows treating normal-enzyme patients prevents liver cancer or death)

title: Corticosteroids in all community-acquired pneumonia (PARTIAL completion of #159, which covers severe pneumonia only): no demonstrated mortality reduction across all severities — about a day faster recovery instead
question: Should adults with community-acquired pneumonia receive corticosteroids to reduce mortality?
balance: PARTIAL completion — home live #159 covers corticosteroids in severe community-acquired pneumonia only (its mortality signal rests on the ICU-severe CAPE COD trial) and is cross-pointed here, not re-carded; this shelf asks the slice #159 does not: all adults with community-acquired pneumonia, most of them not severely ill. Across all severities, a mortality reduction is not demonstrated. The individual-patient-data meta-analysis of 6 placebo-controlled trials (Briel 2018, 1,506 patients) found 30-day mortality of 5.0% on corticosteroids vs 5.9% on placebo (adjusted odds ratio 0.75, 95% CI 0.46 to 1.21 — the treatment made no significant difference), with no effect modification by severity or inflammation. An earlier aggregate meta-analysis (Siemieniuk 2015) was more favourable on its face (risk ratio 0.67 relative, 95% CI 0.45 to 1.01; risk difference 2.8%) but its interval also crosses no effect and its certainty was rated moderate. The two all-comer/non-ICU randomised trials carded here agree on the pattern: steroids shorten time to stability and hospital stay by about a day (Wittermans 2021: stay 4.5 vs 5.0 days; 30-day mortality did not differ) and in one trial bought nothing at all while increasing late failure (Snijders 2010). The consistent price is hyperglycaemia (22.1% vs 12.0% in the individual-patient analysis) and more pneumonia-related rehospitalisation (5.0% vs 2.7%). One carded trial (STEP) already sits on home #159 and is not re-carded here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — unproven for mortality in all-comer pneumonia: the demonstrated gain is about a day faster recovery, not fewer deaths, outside the severe subgroup homed at #159.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — unproven for mortality in all-comer community-acquired pneumonia: pooled mortality differences were not significant (5.0% vs 5.9%; adjusted odds ratio 0.75, 0.46–1.21); the consistent gain is about one day faster stability and discharge, with more hyperglycaemia and readmission

title: RSV vaccination, chronic lung disease and hospitalisation (PARTIAL completion of #320 and #5203): strong protection in the broader cardiorespiratory group and against hospitalisation generally — a lung-specific hospitalisation estimate is not reported
question: Is RSV vaccination effective at preventing hospitalization in older adults with chronic lung disease?
balance: PARTIAL completion — home live #320 covers RSV vaccines in adults 60 and older generally (lower respiratory tract disease efficacy and its waning) and home live #5203 covers the mRNA vaccine trial; both are cross-pointed here, not re-carded. This shelf asks the slice neither isolates: older adults with chronic lung disease, and the hospitalisation outcome. Two honest gaps frame the answer. First, no carded record reports a vaccine effectiveness figure for chronic lung disease alone: the pivotal trial's prespecified subgroup analysis (Feldman 2024, an AReSVi-006 report) groups lung with cardiac conditions as 'cardiorespiratory' and found efficacy against lower respiratory tract disease of 92.1% relative in that combined group (94.6% relative with any condition of interest), and hospitalisation was not an outcome in that record. Second, the hospitalisation evidence is real-world and all-older-adult: the US IVY test-negative study (Surie 2025) estimated effectiveness against RSV-associated hospitalisation at 58% relative over two seasons (69% relative same-season, 48% relative prior-season), and a 2026 meta-analysis of 8 real-world studies pooled an odds ratio of 0.23 for hospitalisation; neither reports a chronic-lung-disease subgroup in its record, and both found effectiveness lower in immunocompromised patients. So the lung-specific hospitalisation number a reader wants does not exist in the carded records; what exists is high trial efficacy in the broader cardiorespiratory group plus substantial real-world protection against hospitalisation in older adults generally. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — the hospitalisation evidence is observational and the chronic-lung-disease-specific hospitalisation estimate is not separately reported in any carded record.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — trial efficacy was 92.1% relative against lower respiratory tract disease in the combined cardiorespiratory subgroup and real-world effectiveness against RSV hospitalisation was 58% relative over two seasons, but no carded record reports a chronic-lung-disease-specific hospitalisation estimate (hospitalisation evidence observational)
