title: RSV vaccination over age 75 (PARTIAL completion of #5203 and #320): effectiveness does not drop off at 75+ in real-world data, but no trial reports an over-75-only efficacy estimate
question: Does RSV vaccination prevent lower respiratory illness in adults over 75?
balance: PARTIAL completion — home live #5203 is the older-adult mRNA RSV vaccine shelf (one trial, all older adults) and home live #320 covers RSV vaccines in adults 60 and older generally; both are cross-pointed here, not re-carded. This shelf asks the slice neither isolates: adults over 75, across RSV vaccine types. The central fact is a reporting gap: no carded trial record publishes an efficacy estimate for the over-75 group alone — the trials enrolled 60+ populations and their records report pooled estimates (the pooled randomised efficacy against lower respiratory tract disease was 81.38% relative in the first season across five vaccines, Riccò 2024; one vaccine's two-season efficacy was 67.2% relative, Ison 2024 — neither record separates the over-75s). What does speak directly to age is real-world: in a US test-negative study of 787,822 tested adults (Fry 2025), vaccine effectiveness against RSV acute respiratory illness was 75.1% relative overall and was similar in the 60–74 and 75-and-older groups, including in immunocompromised patients (73.1% relative at 75+); the same record quantifies the Guillain-Barré ledger (excess 5.2 cases per million doses for the adjuvanted vaccine and 18.2 per million for the bivalent vaccine). So protection in the over-75s is supported by age-stratified real-world data showing no drop-off, resting on trial efficacy proven only for the pooled 60+ population. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — no over-75-only trial estimate exists in the carded records; the age-specific support is observational.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — real-world effectiveness was similar at 75+ and 60–74 (75.1% relative overall against RSV illness), but no randomised trial record reports an over-75-only efficacy estimate; trial efficacy (81.38% relative pooled, first season) is proven for the pooled 60+ population

title: Pneumococcal vaccination in diabetes (PARTIAL completion of #444, older adults generally): fewer pneumonia hospitalisations in observational diabetes data, and the highest trial efficacy in the diabetes subgroup
question: In adults with diabetes, does pneumococcal vaccination reduce pneumonia hospitalizations?
balance: PARTIAL completion — home live #444 covers pneumococcal vaccines in older adults generally (vaccine-type disease prevented; all-cause pneumonia and mortality not shown) and is cross-pointed here, not re-carded; this shelf asks only the diabetes-specific slice. The diabetes evidence is thinner and mostly observational, but it points the same way and one randomised-trial cut is striking. A post-hoc analysis of the CAPiTA trial (Huijts 2017) found the conjugate vaccine's efficacy against vaccine-type pneumonia was modified by diabetes: 89.5% relative in participants with diabetes vs 24.7% relative in those without — but that rests on only 139 vaccine-type pneumonia cases, with wide intervals, and the outcome is vaccine-type pneumonia, not hospitalisation. For hospitalisation itself, the evidence is observational: a 2024 meta-analysis of diabetes-specific studies (Silverii 2024) found hospitalisation for overall pneumonia in the year after polysaccharide vaccination lower in vaccinated diabetic patients (odds ratio 0.63, unadjusted, relative measure) with no significant differences for other outcomes, and a Taiwanese population cohort in diabetic elderly (Kuo 2016) found less invasive pneumococcal disease (adjusted odds ratio 0.86 relative) and less respiratory failure with the polysaccharide vaccine, with shorter hospital stays. People with diabetes are also at higher pneumococcal risk to begin with (invasive disease odds ratio 2.42 in the same meta-analysis), so even a modest relative effect acts on a higher baseline. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only for the hospitalisation outcome: pneumococcal vaccination is associated with fewer pneumonia hospitalisations in adults with diabetes, and the one randomised dataset shows high vaccine-type efficacy in the diabetes subgroup, but no trial has tested hospitalisation in diabetic patients directly.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only for hospitalisation: pneumonia hospitalisation after polysaccharide vaccination was lower in diabetic patients (unadjusted odds ratio 0.63 relative), and the conjugate vaccine's vaccine-type efficacy was 89.5% relative in the trial's diabetes subgroup, but no trial has tested hospitalisation in diabetes directly

title: Direct-acting antivirals in compensated cirrhosis (PARTIAL completion of #593): cure is nearly as high with compensated cirrhosis as without — about 98% vs 99% — with defined exceptions
question: In adults with hepatitis C, do direct-acting antivirals cure infection in people with compensated cirrhosis as well as in those without cirrhosis?
balance: PARTIAL completion — home live #593 covers direct-acting antiviral cure across genotypes and is cross-pointed here, not re-carded; this shelf asks only the slice #593 does not isolate: compensated cirrhosis versus no cirrhosis, head to head. The answer across three independent large datasets is that cure is nearly as high with compensated cirrhosis, with a small, consistent penalty. In the largest real-world analysis (Mangia 2020, 5,552 patients on sofosbuvir/velpatasvir), sustained virological response was 98.9% overall and 97.9% (1,055/1,078) in compensated cirrhosis — and cirrhosis was the only factor significantly associated with virological failure (P = .002), on only 55 virological failures in total. In the prospective HCV-TARGET cohort (Terrault 2016, 2,099 patients, 41% cirrhotic), overall cure was 95–97% by regimen duration and absence of cirrhosis was one of the factors predicting cure, though the record does not print a cirrhosis-specific percentage. The trial-side integrated analysis restricted to compensated cirrhosis (Jacobson 2017, 402 patients with Child-Pugh A cirrhosis across 6 trials of elbasvir/grazoprevir) found cure of 97.8% in treatment-naive patients on 12 weeks, with lower rates in treatment-experienced patients (88.9% on 12 weeks) and in genotype 1a with baseline resistance substitutions (73%) — the exceptions that define where 'as well' stops holding. Decompensated cirrhosis is a different question and is not covered here. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): direct-acting antivirals cure hepatitis C in compensated cirrhosis nearly as well as without cirrhosis (about 98% vs about 99%), with cure modestly lower in treatment-experienced patients and in genotype 1a with resistance substitutions.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — direct-acting antivirals cure hepatitis C in compensated cirrhosis nearly as well as without cirrhosis (97.9% vs 98.9% overall in 5,552 real-world patients), with cure lower in treatment-experienced patients (88.9% on 12 weeks) and genotype 1a with resistance substitutions (73%)

title: Procalcitonin in febrile infants under 3 months: untested in this age group — the nearest randomised trials (enrolling from 7 days and 1 month) found revealing the result made no difference to antibiotic prescribing
question: In febrile infants under 3 months, can procalcitonin testing safely reduce antibiotic use?
balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #3911, which covers procalcitonin-guided antibiotic duration in neonates with suspected early-onset sepsis (NeoPInS); this shelf covers the different population of febrile infants under 3 months presenting with fever without source, and does not re-card #3911's trial. The honest headline is that no randomised trial has tested procalcitonin guidance specifically in infants under 3 months. The two randomised trials that enrolled from the first weeks of life — a Lab-score (procalcitonin, C-reactive protein and urine dipstick) trial enrolling from 7 days (Lacroix 2014) and a procalcitonin-reveal trial enrolling from 1 month (Manzano 2010) — both found that revealing the biomarker result made no difference to actual antibiotic prescribing (41.2% versus 42.1%, and 9% versus 10% among undiagnosed children respectively; the treatment made no difference), although strict adherence to the Lab-score would hypothetically have cut prescriptions by about a quarter. A 2022 meta-analysis of procalcitonin-guided therapy in children with infectious disease more broadly (Li 2022) found antibiotic courses 2.22 days shorter and fewer antibiotic adverse events, but no difference in prescription rates — and its patients were children generally, not young infants. On safety, procalcitonin alone discriminates serious bacterial infection in febrile infants under 91 days less well than clinical prediction rules (England 2014), and the Lab-score missed about 15% of serious bacterial infections (sensitivity 85.1%), so a biomarker-only rule cannot yet be trusted to withhold antibiotics in this age group. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): procalcitonin testing has not been shown to safely reduce antibiotic use in febrile infants under 3 months — the infant-specific trial does not exist, and the nearest randomised evidence, in populations dominated by older infants and children, is null for prescribing.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — no randomised trial has tested procalcitonin guidance in febrile infants under 3 months; the two trials enrolling from the first weeks of life found revealing the result made no difference to antibiotic prescribing, and procalcitonin alone discriminates serious bacterial infection in infants under 91 days less well than clinical prediction rules

title: Moderate acne: benzoyl peroxide plus a retinoid ranks above a topical antibiotic alone in network meta-analyses — an indirect, low-confidence advantage, clearest for noninflammatory lesions
question: For moderate acne, is topical benzoyl peroxide plus a retinoid better than a topical antibiotic alone?
balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #619, which covers the fixed adapalene–benzoyl peroxide gel against its own components (and oral spironolactone in adult women); this shelf covers the comparison #619 does not make — the benzoyl peroxide–retinoid combination against a topical antibiotic used alone — and does not re-card #619's trials. No large head-to-head trial of the combination against antibiotic monotherapy was found in the records fetched; the answer rests on network meta-analyses that rank all topical options on a common scale. In the mild-to-moderate acne network (Stuart 2021; 40 trials, 18,089 participants), benzoyl peroxide with adapalene was ranked the most effective topical treatment for self-reported improvement, ahead of benzoyl peroxide alone and of monotherapies, with slightly more withdrawals (2.5%) than adapalene alone (1.0%). In the all-severity pharmacological network (Huang 2023; 221 trials, 65,601 patients), combination regimens containing a retinoid and benzoyl peroxide ranked just below oral isotretinoin and the triple combination, while topical antibiotic monotherapy was comparable to other monotherapies for inflammatory lesions and weaker for noninflammatory lesions — the lesion type retinoids treat. The Cochrane benzoyl peroxide review (Yang 2020) adds the caution that benzoyl peroxide alone was essentially indistinguishable from clindamycin alone on participant-reported improvement (relative risk 0.95), so the combination's edge over an antibiotic alone comes from adding the retinoid, not from benzoyl peroxide itself, and overall confidence in the network evidence was rated low. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): for moderate acne, benzoyl peroxide plus a retinoid is probably more effective than a topical antibiotic alone, particularly for noninflammatory lesions, at the cost of slightly more local irritation and withdrawal.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — network meta-analyses rank benzoyl peroxide plus a retinoid above topical antibiotic monotherapy for moderate acne (clearest for noninflammatory lesions), but the comparison is indirect, confidence was rated low, and no direct head-to-head trial was found in the records fetched

title: Stroke with high-target ESA therapy in CKD anaemia: risk was doubled in TREAT (5.0% vs 2.6%) and raised across every target-trial meta-analysis — the clearest harm of chasing a normal haemoglobin
question: In adults with anemia of CKD, does a higher hemoglobin target with ESAs increase stroke risk versus a lower target?
balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #179, which covers high- versus low-target erythropoiesis-stimulating agent (ESA) therapy for cardiovascular outcomes as a composite, with stroke inside it; this shelf isolates the stroke outcome specifically, cross-pointing #179 for the primary CHOIR, CREATE and TREAT reports, which are homed there and are not re-carded here. The stroke-specific record is consistent and one-directional. In TREAT's dedicated stroke analysis (Skali 2011; a secondary analysis of the trial homed on #179, carded here as a distinct report because stroke is this shelf's question), darbepoetin alfa doubled stroke: 101 of 2,012 patients (5.0%) versus 53 of 2,026 (2.6%) on placebo (hazard ratio 1.9; 95% CI 1.4 to 2.7; relative measure), and no baseline feature, blood-pressure, haemoglobin, platelet or dose pattern explained or could mitigate it. Across the target trials, Palmer 2010 (27 trials, 10,452 patients) found a higher haemoglobin target increased stroke (relative risk 1.51; 95% CI 1.03 to 2.21; relative measure), and Vinhas 2012, restricting to large trials of at least a year (5 trials, 7,902 participants), found the same (relative risk 1.735; 95% CI 1.323 to 2.275; relative measure). The absolute excess in TREAT was 2.4 percentage points (5.0% versus 2.6%). PROPOSED LIKELY (harm): a higher haemoglobin target with ESAs increases stroke risk versus a lower target — shown in the dedicated analysis of the largest trial and in two independent meta-analyses of the target trials.
stamp: LIKELY (harm) — a higher haemoglobin target with ESAs increases stroke: 5.0% versus 2.6% with darbepoetin in TREAT (hazard ratio 1.9) and relative risk 1.51–1.74 for higher versus lower targets across the target-trial meta-analyses

title: Intravenous iron for fatigue without anaemia: pooled evidence favours iron and the benefit concentrates at ferritin 15 ng/mL or below — but the one dedicated trial was null overall and the evidence is rated low quality
question: In adults with iron deficiency without anemia, does intravenous iron improve fatigue versus placebo?
balance: PARTIAL completion of pack shelf #2458, which covers ORAL iron for fatigue in non-anaemic women with low ferritin; this shelf covers the intravenous route and the broader non-anaemic iron-deficient adult population, and does not re-card #2458's oral-iron trials. The one dedicated randomised trial (Krayenbuehl 2011; 90 non-anaemic premenopausal women, ferritin 50 ng/mL or below) missed its overall comparison — fatigue fell by 1.1 points on intravenous iron versus 0.7 on placebo at 6 weeks (P = 0.07; the treatment made no difference overall) — but in women with ferritin of 15 ng/mL or below the benefit was clear (fall of 1.8 versus 0.4 points, P = 0.005; 82% versus 47% reported improved fatigue). The abridged Cochrane synthesis of intravenous iron in non-anaemic iron deficiency (Dugan 2022; 21 trials, 3,514 participants) found fatigue improved overall (standardised mean difference 0.30 in favour of iron, as printed in the record) and peak oxygen consumption higher by 1.77 mL/kg/min, while rating the evidence low or very low quality for every outcome except fatigue. Houston 2018, pooling iron by all routes (18 trials, 1,170 patients), likewise found self-reported fatigue reduced (standardised mean difference −0.38) with no improvement in objective physical capacity. Adverse events on intravenous iron were more frequent but mild (21% versus 7% in Krayenbuehl; relative risk 1.77 for mild events in Dugan), with no difference in serious events. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): intravenous iron probably improves fatigue in iron deficiency without anaemia — most convincingly when ferritin is genuinely low (15 ng/mL or below) — on evidence the field itself rates low quality.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — intravenous iron improved fatigue in pooled non-anaemic iron-deficiency evidence and in the ferritin ≤15 ng/mL subgroup of the one dedicated trial (82% versus 47% improved), but the trial's overall comparison was null (P = 0.07) and the syntheses rate the evidence low quality

title: Iron when oral iron is not tolerated: intravenous iron works in prior oral failures (81.1% vs 5.5% response) and beats or matches oral iron head-to-head with far fewer intolerance dropouts
question: In adults with iron deficiency anemia, is intravenous iron more effective than oral iron when oral iron is not tolerated?
balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #369 (and its parent #294), which cover intravenous versus oral iron in chronic kidney disease anaemia; this shelf covers the general oral-intolerant iron-deficiency anaemia population outside CKD, and does not re-card the CKD trials homed there. In the population this question names — patients whose oral iron had already failed or could not be used — the definitive trial could not ethically re-randomise patients to the oral iron they had failed, so it tested intravenous ferumoxytol against placebo (Vadhan-Raj 2014; 812 patients): a haemoglobin rise of 2.0 g/dL or more by week 5 in 81.1% on ferumoxytol versus 5.5% on placebo, with mean haemoglobin up 2.7 versus 0.1 g/dL and fatigue scores also favouring iron. Where head-to-head testing against oral iron is possible, in inflammatory bowel disease anaemia, intravenous iron was more effective (odds ratio 1.57 for a haemoglobin rise of 2.0 g/dL or more) and better tolerated, with discontinuation for adverse events or intolerance much lower on intravenous iron (odds ratio 0.27) (Bonovas 2016; 5 trials, 694 patients). In cancer chemotherapy anaemia, intravenous iron isomaltoside was noninferior to oral iron for haemoglobin rise, acted faster, and oral iron caused far more intolerance dropouts (8.0% versus 0.9%) (Birgegård 2016, PROFOUND; 350 patients). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): when oral iron is not tolerated or has failed, intravenous iron is more effective — it reliably raises haemoglobin in exactly that population, and head-to-head evidence where it exists shows equal or better efficacy with far fewer intolerance discontinuations.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — in patients whose oral iron had failed or could not be used, intravenous ferumoxytol produced a ≥2.0 g/dL haemoglobin rise in 81.1% versus 5.5% on placebo, and head-to-head evidence shows intravenous iron at least as effective as oral iron with far fewer intolerance discontinuations (0.9% versus 8.0% in PROFOUND; odds ratio 0.27 in the IBD meta-analysis)

title: ESAs and transfusion in CKD anaemia: transfusion is reliably prevented (odds ratios ~0.2–0.3 vs placebo) — the class's most consistent benefit, with no survival gain attached
question: In adults with anemia of chronic kidney disease, do erythropoiesis-stimulating agents reduce transfusion needs?
balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #179, which covers erythropoiesis-stimulating agents (ESAs) in CKD for haemoglobin targets and cardiovascular outcomes; this shelf covers the outcome #179 does not isolate — transfusion needs — and does not re-card #179's target trials. The transfusion evidence is the oldest and most consistent benefit of these drugs. The 2023 Cochrane network meta-analysis (Chung 2023; 117 studies, 25,237 participants) found epoetin alfa (odds ratio 0.28), epoetin beta (odds ratio 0.19) and darbepoetin alfa (odds ratio 0.27) each superior to placebo for preventing blood transfusion, at low-to-moderate certainty, while effects on death were uncertain and hypertension odds rose. The 2014 edition of the same network (Palmer 2014; 56 studies, 15,596 adults) found the same pattern for every proprietary ESA (odds ratios 0.09 to 0.18 versus placebo). In pre-dialysis patients specifically, the Cochrane recombinant erythropoietin review (Cody 2016; 19 studies, 993 participants) found the number of patients requiring transfusion fell (relative risk 0.32; 95% CI 0.12 to 0.83; relative measure), alongside improved quality of life and exercise capacity. The same reviews are equally clear that preventing transfusion did not translate into a survival advantage, and that hypertension is more frequent on ESAs — and live shelf #179 and pack #5970 carry the high-target stroke harm that bounds how hard transfusion avoidance should be chased. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): ESAs reduce transfusion needs in anaemia of CKD — a large, consistent effect against placebo across two Cochrane network editions and the pre-dialysis review.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — ESAs reduce transfusion needs in CKD anaemia: odds ratios 0.19–0.28 versus placebo for epoetin alfa, epoetin beta and darbepoetin alfa in the 2023 Cochrane network meta-analysis (117 studies, 25,237 participants), with relative risk 0.32 for requiring transfusion in pre-dialysis patients; no survival benefit accompanies the effect

title: Preoperative iron beyond abdominal surgery: transfusion fell modestly in cardiac surgery (61.1% vs 68.2% in ITACS) and across pooled major-surgery trials — but not at hip-fracture operation, and not in the abdomen
question: Does preoperative anemia treatment with iron reduce transfusion after major surgery?
balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #1126, which covers preoperative intravenous iron before major open ABDOMINAL surgery (PREVENTT, null); this shelf covers the other major-surgery settings — cardiac surgery and hip-fracture surgery — and does not re-card PREVENTT. The picture outside the abdomen is more favourable but smaller in effect than guidelines once assumed. ITACS (Myles 2026; 955 anaemic adults before elective cardiac surgery, 1,000 mg intravenous iron versus placebo) reduced red-cell transfusion (61.1% versus 68.2%; relative risk 0.90; 95% CI 0.82 to 0.99; relative measure — an absolute reduction of 7.1 percentage points) and added a median 1.0 day alive and at home at 90 days, with no difference in major complications. The small INITIATE trial (Kong 2022; 156 cardiac-surgery patients) found lower transfusion odds with intravenous iron PLUS an erythropoiesis-stimulating agent versus oral iron (adjusted odds ratio 0.33) — a combination intervention, so the iron-only contribution cannot be separated. In hip-fracture surgery, IRON NOF (O'Loughlin 2023; 143 anaemic patients, terminated early) found no significant difference in transfusion (26% versus 37%; P = 0.15; the treatment made no difference on its primary outcome), though haemoglobin at 6 weeks was higher on iron. The cross-surgery meta-analysis (Elhenawy 2021; 10 trials, 1,039 participants) found preoperative intravenous iron reduced transfusion (relative risk 0.84; 95% CI 0.71 to 0.99; relative measure — a 16% relative reduction) at moderate certainty. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): preoperative iron treatment probably reduces transfusion modestly after major surgery outside the abdomen — shown best in cardiac surgery — a smaller and less certain effect than the abdominal-surgery null on #1126 might suggest is impossible, and than enthusiasts claim.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — preoperative intravenous iron reduced transfusion in the large cardiac-surgery trial ITACS (61.1% versus 68.2%; relative risk 0.90) and across major-surgery trials pooled (relative risk 0.84), but the hip-fracture trial was null and the abdominal-surgery trial on home shelf #1126 was null, so the benefit is modest and setting-dependent

title: ESAs in lower-risk MDS anaemia (PARTIAL completion of pack #4869's comparator question): epoetin alfa and darbepoetin alfa both beat placebo — transfusion incidence 36.1% versus 59.2% with darbepoetin, erythroid response 31.8% versus 4.4% with epoetin
question: In adults with myelodysplastic syndrome and anemia, do erythropoiesis-stimulating agents reduce transfusion needs?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) for transfusion reduction in lower-risk MDS. Two phase 3 placebo-controlled trials point the same way: epoetin alfa raised erythroid response to 31.8% versus 4.4% on placebo (45.9% after blinded review-committee re-assessment) and reduced red-cell transfusions (Fenaux 2018), and darbepoetin alfa lowered transfusion incidence from weeks 5-24 to 36.1% versus 59.2% on placebo (Platzbecker 2017) — an absolute difference of 23.1 percentage points. A meta-analysis of 30 studies (1,314 patients) found pooled erythroid response rates of 57.6% for epoetin alfa and 59.4% for darbepoetin alfa in studies using standardised criteria (Moyo 2008). PARTIAL completion: pack #4869 covers epoetin alfa only as the comparator arm against luspatercept in ESA-naive lower-risk MDS (COMMANDS); this shelf answers the prior question that pack presupposes — ESA versus placebo/control for transfusion needs — without re-carding the COMMANDS record. The evidence is in low- or intermediate-1-risk MDS with haemoglobin at or below 10 g/dL and low transfusion burden, and does not extend to higher-risk MDS. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit).
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — in lower-risk MDS, ESAs reduce transfusion needs: darbepoetin alfa transfusion incidence 36.1% versus 59.2% on placebo and epoetin alfa erythroid response 31.8% versus 4.4%, in two phase 3 placebo-controlled trials

title: Scalp cooling beyond breast cancer (PARTIAL completion of live #1780): cooling reduced substantial alopecia by 43% relative in randomised trials and kept about half of 7,424 registry patients out of a head cover — with success set by regimen, from 95% on paclitaxel to 8% on TAC
question: For chemotherapy-induced hair loss, does scalp cooling reduce alopecia?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) beyond breast cancer. The randomised evidence pooled by Rugo 2018 (10 trials, 654 patients with solid tumours) found scalp cooling reduced the relative risk of more-than-50% alopecia by 43% (RR 0.57) — but 66% of those patients had breast cancer, so the randomised base is still breast-dominated. The broader-population evidence is the Dutch Scalp Cooling Registry: in 1,411 cooled patients across regimens, 50% needed no head cover at their last session, with success ranging from 8% satisfaction after TAC to 95% after paclitaxel (van den Hurk 2012); in the expanded registry of 7,424 patients, 56% needed no head cover and 53% reported minimal hair loss, with results determined by drug and dose rather than by patient characteristics, and no gender effect in non-gender-specific cancers (Brook 2024). PARTIAL completion: live shelf #1780 covers women with breast cancer on taxane/anthracycline regimens (the SCALP trial and its companion cohort, not re-carded here); this shelf covers the broader chemotherapy population, where the honest summary is that cooling works for most regimens but fails for some, and the non-breast evidence is registry-based rather than randomised. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — scalp cooling reduces alopecia across chemotherapy regimens (randomised meta-analysis RR 0.57 for substantial alopecia; 50-56% of 7,424 registry patients needed no head cover), but randomised evidence remains breast-cancer-dominated and some regimens (TAC) largely defeat cooling

title: Exercise during chemotherapy in breast cancer (PARTIAL completion of live #1793's colon-cancer question): supervised exercise reduced physical fatigue in PACES, and pooled randomised trials give a fatigue SMD of -0.38 during chemotherapy
question: Does exercise during chemotherapy reduce treatment-related fatigue in breast cancer?
balance: LIKELY (benefit). In the PACES randomised trial of 230 women on adjuvant chemotherapy for breast cancer, the supervised moderate-to-high-intensity programme (OnTrack) significantly reduced physical fatigue versus usual care (P < .001), and both exercise programmes preserved cardiorespiratory fitness and physical functioning (van Waart 2015). In the OptiTrain randomised trial (240 women), a mechanistic analysis of 86 participants found the resistance-plus-interval programme blunted the chemotherapy-driven rise in interleukin-6, and that change mediated about 32% of the exercise effect on general fatigue and about 28% on physical fatigue (Hiensch 2021). A meta-analysis of 20 randomised trials (1,793 participants) found exercise reduced fatigue overall (SMD -0.46), with the chemotherapy-period subgroup at SMD -0.38 and supervised combined resistance-plus-aerobic training the most effective format (SMD -1.13) (Medeiros Torres 2022). PARTIAL completion: live shelf #1793 covers exercise during adjuvant chemotherapy for fatigue in colon cancer (the PACES pilot report in colon patients); this shelf covers breast cancer, the population in which the full PACES and OptiTrain trials were run. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit).
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — exercise during adjuvant chemotherapy reduces fatigue in breast cancer: significant physical-fatigue benefit in the PACES randomised trial and a pooled SMD of -0.38 during chemotherapy across randomised trials, strongest for supervised combined resistance-plus-aerobic training

title: Levothyroxine and cardiovascular events at 80-plus (PARTIAL completion of live #354's symptom question): SPLIT — the pooled randomised trials (including IEMO 80-plus) show no cardiovascular reduction, while a large observational analysis claims one
question: In adults over 80 with subclinical hypothyroidism, does levothyroxine reduce cardiovascular events versus observation?
balance: SPLIT — the randomised evidence says no cardiovascular benefit; a large observational analysis says the opposite, and the designs are not equal. The pooled individual-participant analysis of the two randomised trials (TRUST, age 65 and over, n = 737; IEMO 80-plus, age 80 and over, n = 105; 842 participants in total) found levothyroxine did not significantly change cardiovascular events (HR 0.74, 95% CI 0.41-1.25), atrial fibrillation (HR 0.69), heart failure (HR 0.41) or all-cause mortality (HR 1.28), irrespective of cardiovascular history and age (Zijlstra 2021). A meta-analysis of 7 studies (21,055 adults) likewise found no association with all-cause (pooled RR 0.95) or cardiovascular (pooled RR 0.99) mortality, and specifically no association in the older subgroup (Peng 2021). Against that, a UK emulated target trial of 22,621 adults over 50 (median age 66 — not an over-80 population) reported lower cardiovascular risk on levothyroxine (adjusted HR 0.82), with benefit limited to patients above age-specific TSH ranges and after at least 5 years of treatment (Holley 2026) — an observational design open to the confounding the randomised trials were built to remove. PARTIAL completion: live shelf #354 covers subclinical hypothyroidism treatment for symptoms, tiredness and quality of life (TRUST and the 80-plus symptom analysis are carded there and are NOT re-carded here); this shelf covers the cardiovascular-events outcome, including the 80-plus trial's contribution to the pooled randomised analysis. For the over-80 cardiovascular question specifically, the only randomised data are the pooled analysis above, and they show no reduction (the treatment made no difference). PROPOSED SPLIT (randomised: no benefit; observational: apparent benefit).
stamp: SPLIT (randomised: no benefit; observational: apparent benefit) — pooled randomised data including the 80-plus trial show levothyroxine made no difference to cardiovascular events (HR 0.74, interval crossing 1), while a large observational emulated trial reports lower cardiovascular risk on treatment (adjusted HR 0.82) in a younger (median 66) population

title: Conservative care versus dialysis in frail older adults (PARTIAL completion of live #2644's general older-adult question): no survival advantage for dialysis was found in the frailty-defined strata — observational evidence only
question: In older adults with end-stage kidney disease and frailty, does conservative kidney management provide similar survival to dialysis?
balance: POSSIBLE — observational only, printed on the face: in the frailest older patients, no survival advantage for dialysis has been shown. In the GOLD cohort, where frailty was measured by formal geriatric assessment (192 dialysis and 89 conservative patients), no survival benefit for dialysis could be found in patients over 80, hospitalisation was twice as common on dialysis (50% versus 24%), and quality of life held steady on dialysis while declining slightly on conservative care (van Loon 2019). In the Leeds cohort (269 renal replacement versus 172 conservative patients over 70), the survival advantage of renal replacement was lost in patients over 80 and in those with a WHO performance score of 3 or more — the frailty-defined stratum — at every level of kidney-function severity (Hussain 2013). Frailty itself, however measured, predicts shorter survival and earlier dialysis initiation in advanced kidney disease (Hussien 2024, 240 patients), which is why these comparisons are so confounded: frailer patients are both likelier to choose conservative care and likelier to die. PARTIAL completion: live shelf #2644 covers older kidney failure generally (Murtagh, Chandna, Carson and Da Silva-Gane cohorts, none frailty-defined, not re-carded here); this shelf covers the frailty-defined subgroup, where the evidence is thinner and entirely observational. No randomised trial has compared the two strategies in frail patients. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (no survival advantage shown for dialysis in frail older adults) — observational only.
stamp: POSSIBLE (no survival advantage shown for dialysis in frail older adults) — observational only: in geriatric-assessment and performance-status strata, dialysis showed no survival benefit over conservative management over age 80 or at poor performance status, with about twice the hospitalisation

title: Deprescribing in older adults with diabetes (PARTIAL completion of live #930's general medication-review question): benefit on adverse drug events is unproven — very-low-certainty review evidence and a results-pending randomised trial (OMED2)
question: In older adults with diabetes and polypharmacy, does a structured deprescribing review reduce adverse drug events versus usual care?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — for diabetes specifically, no completed trial has yet shown that a structured deprescribing review reduces adverse drug events. The updated systematic review of deprescribing antihyperglycaemic medicines in older adults with type 2 diabetes found only 4 controlled studies (2 randomised, 2 cohort): 3 reported no clinically significant change in glucose control after deprescribing and 2 reported reductions in adverse events such as hypoglycaemia, but the certainty of the evidence was rated very low for risk of bias, imprecision and indirectness (Deng 2022). A broader review of deprescribing preventive medicines in older people with cardiometabolic conditions in long-term care or at end of life (13 studies) found deprescribing success rates of 27-94.7%, no significant changes in laboratory values or adverse outcomes, mixed hospitalisation results, and a slight increase in mortality in intervention versus control groups — with a lack of good-quality randomised trials (Hickman 2023). The trial designed to answer this shelf's question directly, the Dutch OMED2 cluster-randomised trial of a general-practice deprescribing programme for insulin and sulfonylureas in overtreated older patients (86 practices, target 406 patients, ISRCTN50008265), has published its protocol only; no results were in the record fetched this session (Andriessen 2024). PARTIAL completion: live shelf #930 covers structured medication review in multimorbid older adults generally (the OPERAM and SPPiRE programmes and drug-related admissions, not re-carded here); this shelf covers the diabetes-specific deprescribing question and its adverse-drug-event outcome, where the honest current answer is 'plausibly safe, benefit unproven'. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — diabetes-specific deprescribing has not been shown in a completed trial to reduce adverse drug events: the review evidence is very low certainty (adverse events fell in 2 of 4 controlled studies), and the dedicated OMED2 randomised trial has published a protocol only

title: How long is safe on benzodiazepine receptor agonists for insomnia? (PARTIAL completion of live #3816's tapering question): no trial defines a threshold — the 4-week ceiling is where the efficacy evidence ends, not a tested safety boundary
question: How long can adults safely use benzodiazepine receptor agonists for insomnia before tapering?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — stated honestly: no trial defines a safe-use duration threshold for benzodiazepine receptor agonists in insomnia. What exists is a guideline ceiling, not a tested threshold. The European insomnia guideline found benzodiazepines and benzodiazepine receptor agonists effective only for short-term treatment (at most 4 weeks; weak recommendation, moderate-quality evidence), with cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia the recommended first-line treatment (Riemann 2017). A European review of long-term use repeats the same boundary: use is recommended for at most 4 weeks because long-term efficacy is unproven and because of tolerance, dependence and misuse risk — while in practice these drugs are the most widely used insomnia treatments in the five countries surveyed and are commonly used far longer than recommended (Soyka 2023). The harm side of longer use is observational: in a meta-analysis of 14 studies, Z-drugs were associated with more fractures (OR 1.63; 830,877 participants) and more injuries on zolpidem (OR 2.05), with a non-significant trend to more falls (OR 2.40, interval crossing 1) (Treves 2018). So the defensible answer to 'how long is safe?' is: efficacy is established only out to about 4 weeks, no study has randomised patients to different durations to find where harm begins, and beyond the guideline ceiling the user is outside the tested evidence. PARTIAL completion: live shelf #3816 covers tapering and discontinuation strategies in people already using these drugs long-term; this shelf covers the prior question — the duration boundary itself — and its evidence status. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — no trial defines a safe-use duration: efficacy is established only for short-term use (at most 4 weeks in the European guideline), long-term efficacy is unproven with tolerance/dependence risk, and harm data are observational only

title: Regular acetaminophen alone for agitation in dementia (PARTIAL completion of live #2758's stepwise-protocol question): no agitation benefit in either direct trial — Q-PID and Chibnall both null — despite a real paracetamol pain-score effect in the Husebo programme
question: Does pain treatment with regular acetaminophen reduce agitation in nursing home residents with dementia?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — unproven for agitation, with the direct trials null. The Q-PID crossover trial randomised 95 residents with advanced dementia to 6 weeks of regular paracetamol (acetaminophen) and 6 weeks of placebo in random order: there was no difference in neuropsychiatric symptoms (NPI-NH change +1.5 on paracetamol versus -2.1 on placebo, intervals overlapping), nor in quality of life, discomfort or pain (van Dam 2020). The earlier Chibnall crossover trial (25 residents, N printed on the face) gave 4 weeks of acetaminophen 3,000 mg/day versus placebo and found no effects on agitation (Cohen-Mansfield Agitation Inventory), emotional well-being or as-needed psychotropic use — though residents were more socially engaged and active on acetaminophen (Chibnall 2005). The Husebo programme's placebo-controlled DEP.PAIN.DEM trial (162 patients) tested analgesia for depression, not agitation; its paracetamol subgroup did show a significant pain reduction versus placebo from week 6 to 13 (-1.11 points), without a depression change — evidence that regular paracetamol can reduce measured pain in dementia even though the agitation trials are null (Erdal 2018). PARTIAL completion: live shelf #2758 covers the stepwise multi-drug pain protocol (paracetamol as first step, escalating to morphine, buprenorphine or pregabalin), which did reduce agitation in the Husebo cluster trial; this shelf isolates step 1 alone — regular acetaminophen by itself — where the treatment made no difference to agitation in either direct trial. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — regular acetaminophen alone is unproven for agitation: both direct placebo-controlled trials found no difference on agitation/neuropsychiatric outcomes (the treatment made no difference), though a paracetamol subgroup did show reduced pain scores

title: Stopping statins in primary prevention at the oldest ages (PARTIAL completion of live #3986's statin-benefit question): SPLIT — the completed SITE trial found stopping non-inferior on 3-year mortality, while French cohort data link stopping to more cardiovascular admissions
question: Should statins be stopped in adults over 80 without cardiovascular disease?
balance: SPLIT — the randomised stopping trial and the large observational cohort point in opposite directions, and the trial is the stronger design for the mortality question it asked. The SITE trial (published as SAGA/SITE) randomised 1,180 adults aged 75 and over (median age 80) who had taken a statin for at least a year for primary prevention and had no history of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, to stop or continue, with 3 years of follow-up: mortality was 7.2% (35/484) in the stopping group versus 7.9% (48/604) on continuation, an absolute difference of -0.68 percentage points (95% CI -3.95 to 2.60), meeting the prespecified 5-point non-inferiority margin (Bonnet 2026). The trial's protocol records the design honestly: open-label, pragmatic, powered on mortality and cost-effectiveness, not on cardiovascular events (Bonnet 2020). Against it, the French nationwide cohort of 120,173 adherent 75-year-olds found statin discontinuation associated with a 33% relative increase in hospital admission for a cardiovascular event (adjusted HR 1.33), with coronary HR 1.46 and cerebrovascular HR 1.26 (Giral 2019) — observational data in which people stop statins for reasons (illness, frailty, end of life) that themselves predict events. PARTIAL completion: live shelf #3986 covers whether starting/continuing statins benefits over-75s without cardiovascular disease; this shelf covers the distinct stopping question in the over-80-centred population SITE actually enrolled (75 and over, median 80 — printed plainly, since no trial has enrolled over-80s only). SITE status, per the fetched records: the trial is completed and its results are now published (Lancet Healthy Longevity, 2026; NCT02547883 marked completed in the record) — it is no longer a protocol-only question. PROPOSED SPLIT (randomised: stopping non-inferior on 3-year mortality; observational: stopping associated with more cardiovascular admissions).
stamp: SPLIT (randomised: stopping non-inferior on mortality; observational: stopping associated with more cardiovascular admissions) — in SAGA/SITE (75 and over, median 80, no cardiovascular disease) 3-year mortality was 7.2% stopping versus 7.9% continuing, while the French nationwide cohort found discontinuation associated with cardiovascular admission (adjusted HR 1.33)

title: High-dose vitamin D and falls (PARTIAL completion of live #30's annual-bolus question): no fall prevention at 1,000-4,000 IU/day, with significantly more serious and fracture falls at higher doses in STURDY
question: Does high-dose vitamin D increase falls in older adults compared with standard dose?
balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — regular high-dose vitamin D does not reduce falls, and the one dose-ranging trial raises harm signals rather than benefit. In STURDY, 688 adults aged 70 and over at elevated fall risk with serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D of 25-72.5 nmol/L (10-29 ng/mL) were randomised to 200 IU/day (control) or 1,000, 2,000 or 4,000 IU/day: in the confirmatory stage, the best dose (1,000 IU/day) did not differ from 200 IU/day on time to first fall or death (HR 0.94, 95% CI 0.76-1.15), while falls with adverse outcomes were more frequent with the best dose (serious fall HR 1.87; fall with hospitalisation HR 2.48), and dose-finding event rates were higher at 2,000 and 4,000 IU/day than at 1,000 (Appel 2021). STURDY's fall-type analysis found the pooled higher doses (≥1,000 IU/day) carried a greater risk of a first fall with fracture than 200 IU/day (HR 2.66) (Wanigatunga 2021). The large VITAL trial (25,871 adults, 2,000 IU/day versus placebo for a median 5.3 years) found no fall reduction at all (2 or more falls in 9.8% versus 9.4%; OR 0.97) — a standard-versus-nothing comparison that rules out a hidden benefit the dose-ranging trial might have missed (LeBoff 2020). PARTIAL completion: live shelf #30 covers the single annual 500,000-IU bolus (Sanders), a different exposure entirely; this shelf covers regular daily high-dose versus standard-dose supplementation. The accurate summary is not 'high-dose vitamin D increases all falls' — overall fall rates were not significantly higher — but 'high-dose vitamin D does not prevent falls, and serious and fracture falls were significantly more frequent at higher doses in the one trial that ranged doses'. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm).
stamp: POSSIBLE (harm) — regular high-dose vitamin D did not reduce falls versus 200 IU/day in STURDY (HR 0.94) or versus placebo in VITAL (OR 0.97), and STURDY found significantly more serious falls (HR 1.87) and fracture falls (HR 2.66) at doses of 1,000 IU/day or more; harm rests on a single trial programme

title: Multicomponent exercise in frail community-dwellers (partial completion of #459): strength, balance and mobility improve, but the frail-specific trials that counted falls — LIFE and Fairhall — found no fall reduction
question: Does a multicomponent exercise program prevent falls in frail older adults living in the community?
balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #459, which covers exercise — including the Otago home strength-and-balance programme — for fall prevention in community-dwelling older adults generally; this shelf asks the narrower frail-specific question #459 does not separate out. The answer divides. The two randomised trials that enrolled frail or functionally limited community-dwellers and counted falls found no fall reduction: in the LIFE programme's prespecified fall-injury analysis (Gill 2016), serious fall injuries ran 9.2% on structured physical activity versus 10.3% on health education (hazard ratio 0.90, 95% CI 0.66 to 1.23; the treatment made no difference), and Fairhall 2014's frailty-targeted multifactorial programme improved strength, sway, physical performance and walking speed yet left the fall rate unchanged (incidence rate ratio 1.12, 95% CI 0.78 to 1.63; the treatment made no difference to falls). Against that, a systematic review of exercise in physically frail older adults (Cadore 2013) found seven of ten fall-incidence trials reported fewer falls after training and judged multicomponent training the best strategy. The LIFE programme's mobility-disability benefit is homed on live shelves #130 and #343 and is not re-carded here; what this slice adds is that preventing disability and preventing falls are not the same outcome in frail people. PROPOSED SPLIT (function improves, falls unproven in frail-specific trials): multicomponent programmes reliably improve the physical risk factors for falling in frail community-dwellers, smaller and review-level evidence leans toward fewer falls, but the two frail-population randomised trials that counted falls found no reduction in fall rates or serious fall injuries.
stamp: SPLIT (function improves, falls unproven in frail-specific trials) — multicomponent programmes improved strength, balance and mobility in frail community-dwellers, and a review of smaller trials leans toward fewer falls, but LIFE (serious fall injuries, hazard ratio 0.90, not significant) and Fairhall 2014 (fall rate ratio 1.12, not significant) found no fall reduction (the treatment made no difference to falls in either trial). Partial completion of live #459

title: Prompted voiding on its own in care homes (partial completion of #2869): fewer wet episodes while the programme is actively delivered — short-term, small-trial evidence, nothing beyond six months
question: Does scheduled toileting and prompted voiding reduce incontinence episodes in care home residents?
balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #2869, which covers prompted voiding only as one half of functional incidental training (prompted voiding combined with exercise, Ouslander 2005); this shelf asks what prompted voiding and scheduled toileting do on their own. The evidence is old, small and short-term, but it points one way. The Cochrane review (Eustice 2000) gathered five trials in 355 elderly people and found prompted voiding increased self-initiated voiding and decreased incontinent episodes in the short term, with no evidence about long-term effects and insufficient evidence for firm conclusions. A staff-delivered randomised trial (Lai 2017, N = 52) found the benefit could be sustained by ordinary nursing-home staff over six months, with a 9.1% decrease in the incontinence rate in the intervention group. An implementation study (Schnelle 1993) showed wet checks falling from 43% to 21% over six months when supervisory nurses ran a quality-control system for the toileting programme — evidence about keeping the programme delivered, not a randomised comparison. Nothing here separates the effect of the schedule itself from the staff attention and positive reinforcement that prompted voiding, by definition, bundles with it. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): prompted voiding/scheduled toileting probably reduces wet episodes in care-home residents while it is actively delivered, on short-term and small-trial evidence; durability beyond six months and any effect independent of staff attention are unproven.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — prompted voiding/scheduled toileting reduced incontinent episodes in the short term across five small trials (Cochrane, 355 people) and in one six-month staff-delivered randomised trial (N = 52); long-term effects unstudied. Partial completion of live #2869 (which covers prompted voiding only combined with exercise)

title: Magnesium for menstrual migraine (partial completion of #2442): one small 1991 trial of magnesium pyrrolidone carboxylic acid favours benefit — weak, unreplicated evidence, named preparations on the face
question: Does magnesium supplementation reduce migraine frequency in women with menstrual migraine?
balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #2442, which covers magnesium (the Peikert trial) for migraine prevention in people with migraine generally; this shelf asks the menstrual-migraine slice in women, which #2442 does not separate out. The direct evidence is a single small trial. Facchinetti 1991 randomised 20 women with menstrual migraine to magnesium pyrrolidone carboxylic acid — the exact tested preparation named in the record — 360 mg/day from day 15 of the cycle until the next menses, or placebo: headache days fell only on active treatment and the pain index was lowest on magnesium. The supporting cards are adjacent, and are labelled as such: ionised magnesium deficiency was found in 45% of women during menstrual attacks (Mauskop 2002, observational — a mechanism signal, not a treatment result), and the same preparation improved premenstrual symptoms in a 32-woman randomised trial (Facchinetti 1991, Obstetrics and Gynecology), as did a named modified-release product, Sincromag 250 mg, in a 41-woman open pilot (Quaranta 2007) — neither of those two trials measured migraine frequency. Supplement rule applied: the tested preparations are named exactly as the publications give them (magnesium pyrrolidone carboxylic acid; Sincromag modified-release magnesium 250 mg tablet); no other carded record names a brand or formulation beyond its salt, and current shop products may differ from these preparations. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): one 20-woman double-blind trial favours cycle-timed magnesium for menstrual migraine, and everything else carded is mechanism or premenstrual-symptom evidence — the slice is real but thin, and no larger or modern trial was found in PubMed this session.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — a single double-blind trial of 20 women found cycle-timed magnesium pyrrolidone carboxylic acid 360 mg/day reduced headache days in menstrual migraine; supporting evidence is observational (ionised magnesium deficiency in 45% of menstrual attacks) or from premenstrual-symptom trials of named preparations. Partial completion of live #2442 (general migraine prevention)

title: Low-dose vaginal estrogen for vaginal dryness (partial completion of #2736): dryness relieved, systemic estradiol stays near postmenopausal levels, endometrial events extremely rare
question: Does low-dose vaginal estrogen relieve vaginal dryness without increasing systemic estrogen risks?
balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #2736, which covers low-dose vaginal oestrogen safety in breast-cancer survivors specifically; this shelf asks the general-population question #2736 does not — dryness efficacy plus systemic risk in postmenopausal women generally. On efficacy the evidence is concordant: the systematic review behind the specialty guideline (Rahn 2014; 44 eligible studies) found vaginal estrogens improved dryness and dyspareunia versus placebo across preparations, and the pivotal randomised trial (Bachmann 2008, N = 230) found both 25 mcg and 10 mcg estradiol vaginal tablets significantly improved vaginal health and symptoms versus placebo over 12 weeks. On systemic exposure, Santen 2020's assay-critical review found systemic estradiol on low-dose products stays dose-dependent and low — roughly 4.6 to 14.8 pg/mL on the 10-mcg tablet by sensitive assays, against a proposed untreated postmenopausal range up to about 10.7 pg/mL — and Rahn 2014 found endometrial hyperplasia and adenocarcinoma extremely rare, with serum estradiol remaining within postmenopausal norms for all preparations except high-dose conjugated equine estrogen cream. The caution card is small and old: Handa 1994 (N = 20) relieved symptoms in 19 of 20 women on 0.3 mg conjugated estrogens three nights a week with no significant change in serum estrogens or endometrial thickness — but endometrial proliferation in one case. The breast-cancer-survivor population stays on #2736 and is not re-carded here. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): low-dose vaginal estrogen relieves vaginal dryness, and at the low doses carded systemic estradiol stays within or near the postmenopausal range with extremely rare endometrial events — the residual uncertainty is the absence of long-term randomised safety outcomes, printed here rather than smoothed over.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — low-dose vaginal estrogen relieves vaginal dryness (44-study review; randomised trial N = 230, P < .001 versus placebo), systemic estradiol stays within or near the postmenopausal range at 4–10 mcg doses, and endometrial hyperplasia/cancer were extremely rare; long-term randomised safety outcomes are absent. Partial completion of live #2736 (breast-cancer survivors)

title: Embolization versus hysterectomy, long term (partial completion of #830): quality of life equal at five and ten years — one in three embolization patients eventually has the hysterectomy
question: In women with uterine fibroids, does uterine artery embolization preserve quality of life as well as hysterectomy in the long term?
balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #830, whose randomised comparison is uterine artery embolization (UAE) versus myomectomy (FEMME) with the EMMY two-year report riding along; this shelf asks the comparison #830 does not isolate — UAE versus hysterectomy over the long term. The EMMY trial followed its randomised women for a decade: at five years (van der Kooij 2010) health-related quality of life had improved significantly in both groups and remained stable with no differences between them, while 28.4% of UAE patients had undergone hysterectomy for insufficient improvement; at ten years (de Bruijn 2016) quality of life remained comparably stable with no between-group differences and comparable satisfaction (78% versus 87% at least satisfied), with 35% of the UAE group having had a secondary hysterectomy in total — meaning about two-thirds avoided hysterectomy altogether. The REST trial (Edwards 2007) found no significant difference in any SF-36 component at one year against a surgical group that was mostly hysterectomy (43 of 51), with faster recovery after embolization and 9% needing reintervention within the year; the four-trial meta-analysis (van der Kooij 2011, 515 patients) agrees: comparable mid- and long-term quality of life and equal satisfaction, at the price of a higher reintervention rate after UAE. The FEMME myomectomy comparison stays on #830 and is not re-carded here. PROPOSED LIKELY (as good as hysterectomy for long-term quality of life): quality of life after UAE matches hysterectomy at five and ten years in the only long-term randomised record, with the trade-off — roughly one in three women eventually needs a hysterectomy — printed on the face of the stamp and every card.
stamp: LIKELY (as good as hysterectomy for long-term quality of life) — quality of life was indistinguishable at 5 and 10 years in the EMMY randomised trial and comparable across four trials, with the trade-off printed here: 28.4% of embolization patients had a hysterectomy by 5 years and 35% by 10 years. Partial completion of live #830 (UAE versus myomectomy)

title: Vaginal progesterone for preterm birth beyond the short cervix (PARTIAL completion of live #418): pooled benefit in high-risk singletons, a null largest trial, and no benefit in twins
question: In women at risk of preterm birth, does vaginal progesterone reduce preterm delivery?
balance: SPLIT (population: pooled benefit in high-risk singletons; no benefit in the largest single trial's primary outcomes or in twins) — printed on the face. This pack is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #418 already answers vaginal progesterone for singleton pregnancies with a short cervix (≤25 mm) at the patient level; this shelf asks the wider question — women at risk for any reason. The widest test, OPPTIMUM (1,228 women at risk through previous preterm birth, short cervix, or positive fetal fibronectin with risk factors), found no significant effect on its obstetric, neonatal or childhood primary outcomes (the treatment made no difference). The patient-level pooling of 31 trials (EPPPIC, 11,644 women) found vaginal progesterone did reduce preterm birth before 34 weeks in high-risk singleton pregnancies (relative risk 0.78), with the largest absolute gains where baseline risk is highest — the short-cervix group homed on #418. In twins, both EPPPIC (relative risk 1.01) and the dedicated PREDICT trial (15.3% vs 18.5%) found no benefit (the treatment made no difference). PROPOSED SPLIT (population): vaginal progesterone reduces early preterm birth in pooled high-risk singleton pregnancies, but the largest broad-population trial was null on its primary outcomes and there is no benefit in twin pregnancies.
stamp: SPLIT (population) — vaginal progesterone reduced preterm birth before 34 weeks in pooled high-risk singleton pregnancies (EPPPIC relative risk 0.78), but the largest broad-population trial (OPPTIMUM) made no difference on its primary outcomes and neither EPPPIC nor PREDICT found any benefit in twin pregnancies

title: HPV every 5 years versus Pap every 3 years (PARTIAL completion of live #1348): the longer HPV interval protects at least as well — a negative HPV test carries less 5-year cancer risk than a negative Pap carries in 3
question: For cervical cancer screening, is primary HPV testing every 5 years as effective as Pap testing every 3 years?
balance: LIKELY — on the interval question as asked. This pack is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #1348 already answers whether primary HPV testing beats cytology at detecting CIN3+ by 48 months (the HPV FOCAL trial); this shelf asks the different question FOCAL cannot answer — whether stretching the HPV interval to 5 years gives up the protection that 3-yearly cytology provides. Three randomised-programme records answer it directly. Pooled across four European trials (176,464 women), HPV-based screening cut invasive cervical cancer versus cytology (rate ratio 0.60, a relative measure), and among women negative at entry the cumulative cancer incidence at 5.5 years was 8.7 per 100,000 after a negative HPV test versus 36.0 per 100,000 after negative cytology — the 5-year HPV-negative risk sitting below the 3.5-year cytology-negative risk (15.4 per 100,000). In Swedescreen's 13-year follow-up, the sensitivity of HPV testing at five years (86.40% for CIN2+) matched cytology at three years (85.94%), with cumulative CIN2+ incidence eventually identical — earlier detection, not overdiagnosis. And in POBASCAM's 14-year follow-up, HPV-negative women screened in 5-yearly rounds carried the same cancer incidence (0.09%) as cytology-negative women after fewer rounds. PROPOSED LIKELY: primary HPV testing every 5 years is at least as effective as Pap testing every 3 years at preventing invasive cervical cancer.
stamp: LIKELY — primary HPV testing every 5 years is at least as effective as Pap testing every 3 years: pooled randomised evidence shows fewer invasive cancers with HPV-based screening (rate ratio 0.60, relative), 5-year HPV sensitivity matching 3-year cytology sensitivity, and a lower 5.5-year cancer risk after a negative HPV test (8.7 per 100,000) than after a negative Pap (36.0 per 100,000)

title: Levonorgestrel IUD versus tranexamic acid for heavy menstrual bleeding (PARTIAL completion of live #2490): the IUD cut blood loss further at 6 months (85.8% vs 60.8%) in the one small head-to-head trial
question: In women using an IUD, does the levonorgestrel IUD reduce heavy menstrual bleeding more than oral tranexamic acid?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the direct head-to-head rests on one small randomised trial, printed on the face. This pack is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #2490 already answers tranexamic acid versus placebo and versus norethisterone; this shelf asks the comparison #2490 does not make — tranexamic acid head-to-head against the levonorgestrel intrauterine system. In the one direct three-arm trial (84 women enrolled, 62 evaluated), six months of the levonorgestrel system cut measured blood loss by 85.8% against 60.8% on tranexamic acid and 53.1% on norethisterone, and it corrected anaemia more efficiently than tranexamic acid. The large pragmatic ECLIPSE trial (571 women) points the same way against usual medical treatment as a bundle — a 13.4-point advantage on the Menorrhagia Multi-Attribute Scale at two years — but its usual-treatment arm mixed tranexamic acid with mefenamic acid, combined hormonal contraception and progesterone alone, so it cannot isolate tranexamic acid, and its advantage was no longer significant by five years (3.9 points) or at ten. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the levonorgestrel IUD probably reduces heavy menstrual bleeding more than oral tranexamic acid, on one small direct trial supported by a large pragmatic trial against mixed usual treatment.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the levonorgestrel IUD reduced measured blood loss more than oral tranexamic acid at 6 months in the one small direct head-to-head trial (85.8% vs 60.8% reduction; 62 women evaluated), with a large pragmatic trial concordant against usual medical treatment as a bundle but not against tranexamic acid alone

title: Amoxicillin versus broader-spectrum antibiotics in childhood pneumonia (PARTIAL completion of live #1140): narrow-spectrum treatment was never worse across 265,000 children — on observational evidence only
question: In children with community-acquired pneumonia, is amoxicillin as effective as broader-spectrum antibiotics?
balance: POSSIBLE — observational only, printed on the face: no randomised trial has compared antibiotic spectrum in childhood pneumonia. This pack is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #1140 already answers how much amoxicillin and for how long (the CAP-IT dose-and-duration trial and SAFER); this shelf asks the different question #1140 does not — whether the narrow aminopenicillin itself (amoxicillin in outpatients, ampicillin/penicillin in hospital) matches broader-spectrum agents. Three large cohort records agree. In 15,564 hospitalised children, narrow-spectrum therapy matched broad-spectrum cephalosporins on stay (median 3 days in both), intensive-care admission (0.8% vs 1.1%) and readmission (2.4% vs 2.3%). A propensity-matched cohort found narrow therapy associated with a 10-hour shorter stay and no difference in fever, oxygen or readmission. And in 252,177 ambulatory visits, later hospitalisation was rare (0.59%) and was not lower with broad-spectrum treatment (adjusted odds ratio 1.34 versus narrow-spectrum, an association the design cannot show is causal). PROPOSED POSSIBLE — observational only: amoxicillin-class narrow-spectrum treatment performs at least as well as broader-spectrum antibiotics for children with community-acquired pneumonia.
stamp: POSSIBLE — observational only: narrow-spectrum aminopenicillin treatment (amoxicillin in outpatients, ampicillin/penicillin in hospital) was as effective as broader-spectrum antibiotics across three large cohorts (same stay, intensive-care and readmission rates in hospital; no fewer hospitalisations with broad-spectrum treatment in outpatients); no randomised trial compares spectrum

title: Short-course oral steroids at home in childhood asthma/wheeze (PARTIAL completion of live #2664): parent-initiated courses made no difference — the benefit appears only when the course is started in the emergency department
question: In children with asthma, is a short course of oral steroids effective for an acute exacerbation at home?
balance: SPLIT (setting: a course started in the emergency department shortened hospital stay; courses started by parents at home made no difference) — printed on the face. This pack is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #2664 answers oral versus intravenous steroids in (largely adult) exacerbations, and the hospital-admission preschool-wheeze trial is homed on live shelf #1362; this shelf asks the remaining question — whether a short course started at home, by parents, works. The dedicated home evidence says it does not: in the parent-initiated randomised trial, symptom scores and admissions were identical on prednisolone and placebo (the treatment made no difference), even in children with high eosinophil priming, and the Cochrane review of parent-initiated courses (2 trials, 303 children) found no benefit on admissions, reviews or symptoms. The contrasting positive result comes from a different setting: a 3-day course started in the emergency department shortened time to discharge readiness (median 370 vs 540 minutes). PROPOSED SPLIT (setting): parent-initiated oral steroids at home have no demonstrated benefit for children's acute wheeze/asthma exacerbations, while a clinician-started short course in the emergency department shortened hospital stay.
stamp: SPLIT (setting) — parent-initiated oral prednisolone at home made no difference to symptoms or admissions in the dedicated randomised trial and the Cochrane review of home courses found no benefit, while a clinician-started 3-day course in the emergency department shortened hospital stay (median 370 vs 540 minutes)

title: Probiotics for infant colic beyond L. reuteri (PARTIAL completion of live #640): BB-12 and LGG each beat placebo on crying — strain by strain, in small trials
question: For infant colic, are probiotics effective compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — strain-specific, printed on the face: the benefit belongs to named strains, not to 'probiotics' as a class. This pack is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #640 already answers Lactobacillus reuteri DSM 17938 in breastfed infants; this shelf covers the other tested strains. Two clear the bar. Bifidobacterium animalis subsp. lactis BB-12 (1 × 10^9 CFU/day) beat placebo in two randomised trials (80 and 192 infants), with more infants reaching a ≥50% cut in crying and crying episodes roughly halving. Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG (ATCC 53103; now classified Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus) reduced median daily crying to 104 versus 242 minutes in one small trial of 45 breastfed infants run alongside maternal cow's-milk elimination, and a 2024 meta-analysis of four LGG trials (168 infants) found crying time lower by a mean 32.59 minutes/day. The publications name the strains exactly; none of the carded records names a manufacturer or branded product, and the shelf says so — current products carrying the same strain names may differ. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): BB-12 and LGG each have randomised evidence of reduced crying in colic, on small trials; no class-wide probiotic claim is made.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — strain-specific: Bifidobacterium animalis subsp. lactis BB-12 (two randomised trials, 272 infants) and Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus GG ATCC 53103 (one small trial plus a four-trial meta-analysis) each reduced crying versus placebo; the records name strains and doses but no manufacturer or branded product, and no class-wide probiotic claim is supported

title: Biologics versus methotrexate for plaque psoriasis (PARTIAL completion of live #377): far greater clearance on biologics — PASI 75 79.6% vs 35.5% in the direct trial
question: For chronic plaque psoriasis, how do biologic therapies compare with methotrexate for skin clearance?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — biologics clear skin substantially more completely than methotrexate. This pack is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #377 already answers how completely each modern biologic class clears skin against placebo and older biologics; this shelf asks the comparison #377 does not make — biologics against methotrexate, the conventional first systemic. The one large direct randomised comparison, CHAMPION, found PASI 75 at 16 weeks in 79.6% on adalimumab versus 35.5% on methotrexate and 18.9% on placebo, with complete clearance in 16.7% versus 7.3%; its benefit–risk analysis counted about four times as many adverse-event-free response days on adalimumab (36.9 vs 8.3 days), while methotrexate had the most discontinuations, chiefly hepatic. The Cochrane network meta-analysis of all systemic treatments ranks the biologic classes far above the conventional agents for PASI 90 and places methotrexate down with the non-biologics — finding no significant difference between methotrexate and the small molecules apremilast or tofacitinib — while cautioning that methotrexate itself rests on few trials in the network. The paediatric head-to-head (adalimumab versus methotrexate in children) is homed on live pack #4040 and is not re-carded here. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): for skin clearance, biologic therapies beat methotrexate — shown directly for adalimumab and consistently across classes in network evidence.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — biologic therapies clear skin substantially more than methotrexate: in the direct CHAMPION trial PASI 75 was 79.6% on adalimumab versus 35.5% on methotrexate at 16 weeks, and the Cochrane network meta-analysis ranks the biologic classes far above methotrexate and the other conventional systemics for PASI 90

title: Apremilast as the primary question (PARTIAL completion of live #1155): effective versus placebo in three trials — the oral option when biologics cannot be taken, with partial rather than complete clearance
question: In adults with psoriasis, is apremilast effective for those who cannot take biologics?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) versus placebo — with the population caveat printed on the face. This pack is a PARTIAL completion: on live shelf #1155 apremilast appears only as the comparator arm inside the deucravacitinib POETYK trials; this shelf makes apremilast the question. No trial has enrolled only patients who cannot take biologics — that population is defined by exclusion in practice, not by a trial — but three placebo-controlled phase III trials in moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis, the setting in which an oral non-biologic option is chosen, agree: PASI 75 at week 16 in 33.1% (ESTEEM 1, 844 patients) and 28.8% (ESTEEM 2, 411 patients) on apremilast 30 mg twice daily versus 5.3% and 5.8% on placebo, and 39.8% versus 11.9% in the biologic-naive LIBERATE population, with responses maintained to week 52 and a mild-to-moderate adverse-event profile (nausea, diarrhoea, nasopharyngitis, headache) and no biologic-style immunosuppression monitoring in the trial reports. Clearance is partial, not complete — roughly a third reach PASI 75, far below biologic rates on live shelf #377 — which is exactly the trade a biologic-ineligible patient is making. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): apremilast is effective versus placebo for adults with moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis, the evidence base for its use when biologics cannot be taken, though that specific population has not been trialled as such.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — apremilast beat placebo in three randomised trials (PASI 75 at week 16: 33.1% vs 5.3%, 28.8% vs 5.8%, and 39.8% vs 11.9% in biologic-naive patients), with responses maintained to 52 weeks; no trial enrolled only biologic-ineligible patients, so that use rests on this moderate-to-severe psoriasis evidence

title: Topical minoxidil versus placebo in women with hair loss (PARTIAL completion of live #4031): more hair per cm² in two double-blind trials and the Cochrane pooling
question: In women with hair loss, does topical minoxidil improve hair density?
balance: LIKELY — topical minoxidil improves hair density in women with female pattern hair loss: two large double-blind placebo-controlled trials (Lucky 2004, 381 women; Tsuboi 2007, 280 women) and the Cochrane pooling (relative risk 1.93 for participant-rated moderate-to-marked regrowth; +13.18 hairs/cm² versus placebo) all point the same way, across 1%, 2% and 5% formulations. This pack is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #4031 covers oral versus topical minoxidil in men; the topical-versus-placebo question in women is answered here, and no card from #4031 is re-used. The gains are real but modest in absolute terms — roughly 6–13 extra hairs per cm² over placebo — and the 5% strength buys a small patient-rated edge over 2% at the cost of more itching, irritation and unwanted facial hair growth.
stamp: LIKELY — topical minoxidil improved hair density versus placebo in two large double-blind trials in women (381 and 280 participants) and in the Cochrane pooling (regrowth relative risk 1.93; +13.18 hairs/cm²), with modest absolute gains

title: Sunscreen and melanoma specifically (PARTIAL completion of live #221): the observational literature splits by study design
question: Does daily sunscreen use prevent melanoma in adults at average risk?
balance: SPLIT — the carded observational literature disagrees with itself by study design: hospital-based case-control studies and one large cohort comparison of high- versus low-SPF use suggest protection, while population-based case-control studies show no association and cohort studies pooled in Rueegg 2019 show a positive association (hazard ratio 1.27) — the signature of confounding by indication, because sunscreen users are the people who burn, holiday in the sun and use tanning devices. This pack is a PARTIAL completion: the only randomised daily-use evidence (the Nambour trial and its melanoma follow-up) is homed on live shelf #221 and is NOT re-carded here; this shelf cards the wider sunscreen–melanoma literature for average-risk adults, all of it observational and therefore capped at POSSIBLE-grade reasoning. On this evidence, a protective effect of sunscreen on melanoma is unproven in average-risk adults — and so is any harmful effect.
stamp: SPLIT — observational evidence disagrees by study design (protective in hospital case-control studies and a high-SPF cohort comparison; null in population case-control pooling; positive association in other cohorts), so a melanoma-preventive effect in average-risk adults is unproven outside the single randomised trial homed on #221

title: Ketoconazole versus selenium sulfide shampoo, head-to-head (PARTIAL completion of live #2494): no efficacy winner in three randomised trials
question: For seborrheic dermatitis of the scalp, is ketoconazole shampoo more effective than selenium sulfide?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference between the two shampoos) — across three head-to-head randomised trials spanning 1993–2026, ketoconazole shampoo was not more effective than selenium sulfide/disulfide shampoo on symptom and scale scores: the one early advantage (Danby 1993, superiority at day 8 only) did not persist, and the two modern double-blind trials found no significant between-group difference at any time point. Note the modern trials tested specific formulated selenium disulfide shampoos (1% and 0.6% micronized); where the fetched record does not name the brand or company, the card says so plainly.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — three head-to-head randomised trials: ketoconazole shampoo was not more effective than selenium sulfide/disulfide shampoo (one day-8 advantage in 1993 that did not persist; no significant between-group difference in the 2024 and 2026 double-blind trials)

title: Total body skin examination screening and melanoma deaths in average-risk adults (PARTIAL completion of live #3389): no mortality benefit shown
question: In adults at average risk, does screening for skin cancer with total body examination reduce melanoma deaths?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — no study has shown that screening average-risk adults with a total body (whole-body/visual) skin examination reduces melanoma deaths. There are no randomised trials; the direct programme evidence is nonrandomised and, in the 2023 USPSTF evidence report, suggested no melanoma mortality benefit at population level over 4–10 years. The best supporting signal is a surrogate: in the Queensland case-control study, a whole-body examination in the prior 3 years was associated with fewer thick melanomas (odds ratio 0.86) — alongside 38% more thin melanomas, the overdiagnosis signature. All carded evidence is observational, which caps the stamp. This pack is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #3389 homes the German population-screening mortality story (the Schleswig-Holstein pilot and the nationwide programme); this shelf asks the narrower question — the clinician total body examination itself, in average-risk asymptomatic adults — and does not re-card the German programme studies.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — no randomised trials; nonrandomised programme analyses suggested no melanoma mortality benefit from total body/visual skin examination screening in average-risk adults, and the only positive signal is a surrogate (fewer thick melanomas, OR 0.86) alongside more thin melanomas (OR 1.38)
