title: Antihistamine eye drops versus oral antihistamines for allergic eye symptoms (PARTIAL completion of live #2518): drops win on itching in three direct comparisons
question: For allergic eye symptoms, are antihistamine eye drops more effective than oral antihistamines?
balance: POSSIBLE — in direct comparisons, antihistamine eye drops relieved ocular itching better than an oral antihistamine alone: ketotifen drops beat oral desloratadine at every measured time point in an allergen-challenge trial (Crampton 2003), adding olopatadine drops to loratadine beat loratadine alone within 20 minutes of the first dose (Lanier 2001), and topical levocabastine beat oral terfenadine on ocular itching in a small 8-week seasonal trial (Bahmer 1994). The stamp stays at POSSIBLE because the trials are small, two rest on laboratory allergen challenge or adjunctive designs, and the oldest comparator (terfenadine) has since been withdrawn for cardiac toxicity. This pack is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #2518 covers antihistamine eye drops versus placebo; the head-to-head against oral antihistamines is answered here, and no #2518 card is re-used. Eye drops treat the eye only — the oral drug remains the one that also treats the nose.
stamp: POSSIBLE — antihistamine eye drops relieved ocular itching better than an oral antihistamine alone in three small direct comparisons (challenge trial, adjunctive trial, and an 8-week seasonal trial), with no advantage for nasal symptoms

title: Nasal steroid spray versus oral antihistamine, head-to-head in allergic rhinitis (PARTIAL completion of live #2666): the spray wins on nasal symptoms
question: In adults with allergic rhinitis, is a nasal steroid spray more effective than an oral antihistamine?
balance: LIKELY — for nasal symptoms, a nasal steroid spray is more effective than an oral antihistamine: the meta-analysis of 16 head-to-head randomised trials (Weiner 1998, 2,267 subjects) found significantly greater relief of blockage, discharge, sneezing, itch and total nasal symptoms with intranasal corticosteroids, and the largest single trial (Ratner 1998, 600 patients) found fluticasone spray significantly better than loratadine, which itself did not separate from placebo on symptom scores. The one place the spray does not win is eye symptoms, where Weiner found no significant difference. This pack is a PARTIAL completion: on live shelf #2666 the steroid spray and the oral antihistamine appear only as comparators to montelukast; the direct head-to-head is answered here, and no #2666 card is re-used. Adding the antihistamine tablet to the spray added little or nothing in the carded trials.
stamp: LIKELY — intranasal corticosteroids beat oral antihistamines on nasal blockage, discharge, sneezing, itch and total nasal symptoms in a 16-trial meta-analysis and the largest head-to-head trial, with no difference for eye symptoms

title: Hearing aids, quality of life and cognition in older adults (PARTIAL completion of live #350): quality of life improves; a cognitive benefit is unproven in trials
question: Do hearing aids improve quality of life and cognition in older adults with hearing loss?
balance: SPLIT — the two halves of the question have different answers. Quality of life: hearing aids consistently improve hearing-specific quality of life (Cochrane pooling: Hearing Handicap Inventory difference −26.47 points) and general quality of life by a smaller amount, in trials and reviews spanning 1990–2017. Cognition: the only randomised cognitive-function signal is a small subscale improvement inside the 1990 Mulrow trial; the large pooled association (19% lower hazard of cognitive decline in hearing-aid users) comes from observational studies, labelled observational here, and the one large randomised cognition trial — ACHIEVE — is homed on live shelf #350, where its primary result was null, and is not re-carded on this shelf. This pack is a PARTIAL completion of #350: it answers the quality-of-life question that shelf does not ask, and gathers the non-ACHIEVE cognition evidence without duplicating the homed trial.
stamp: SPLIT — quality of life: hearing aids consistently improved hearing-specific quality of life in trials and reviews (HHIE −26.47 points pooled); cognition: benefit shown only in observational data (HR 0.81) and one small trial subscale, with the large randomised cognition trial homed on #350 null on its primary outcome

title: Catheter ablation and survival in AF with HFrEF (PARTIAL completion of live #271, precedent (b)): pooled benefit driven by the homed CASTLE-AF trial; free-standing trials split
question: Does catheter ablation improve survival in atrial fibrillation with HFrEF?
balance: SPLIT — with a prominent precedent-(b) flag. The trial that drives the survival claim, CASTLE-AF, is already homed on live shelf #271 and is therefore NOT carded here (its PMID is kept out of every card source line); this PARTIAL-completion shelf is built only on the free-standing HFrEF evidence around it. That surrounding evidence genuinely splits: meta-analyses pooling CASTLE-AF with smaller trials show lower mortality with ablation (9.0% vs 17.6%; relative risk 0.52) but state their results are driven primarily by that one homed trial; AATAC found lower mortality with ablation versus amiodarone as a secondary endpoint (8% vs 18%); while the two free-standing trials least dependent on CASTLE-AF found no significant hard-outcome benefit — RAFT-AF's primary composite missed significance (hazard ratio 0.71, P = 0.066; stopped early for futility) and AMICA found no difference at all (the treatment made no difference). A second positive trial, CASTLE-HTx in end-stage heart failure, is already carded elsewhere in the library and is likewise not re-carded here. Net: a survival benefit in AF with HFrEF is POSSIBLE on the pooled record, but it has not been independently confirmed by a free-standing trial in this slice.
stamp: SPLIT — pooled/meta-analytic mortality benefit for ablation in AF with HFrEF (relative risk 0.52) driven primarily by the CASTLE-AF trial homed on #271, with AATAC positive on a secondary endpoint but RAFT-AF (HR 0.71, P = 0.066) and AMICA null

title: Catheter ablation and mortality in ischaemic ventricular tachycardia (PARTIAL completion of live #713): ablation cuts shocks and ICD therapy, but no randomised report shows fewer deaths
question: Does catheter ablation reduce mortality in ventricular tachycardia with ischemic cardiomyopathy?
balance: POSSIBLE — printed on the face. This pack is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #713 already answers ablation versus escalating antiarrhythmic drugs in ICD patients with recurrent VT (VANISH, PMID 27149033, and PARTITA, PMID 35369700 — both homed there and not re-carded here), where death sat inside composite endpoints. This shelf asks the narrower question those composites leave open: does ablation itself reduce mortality? Five free randomised reports answer it, and none shows a mortality reduction. SMASH-VT (128 patients) found deaths of 9% with ablation versus 17% without (P=0.29 — the treatment made no difference) while ICD therapy fell sharply (hazard ratio 0.35). VTACH (110 patients) recorded five deaths against four. BERLIN VT, testing preventive against deferred ablation, found more deaths in the preventive arm (7.9% vs 2.4%, P=0.18) and was stopped early for futility. Pooling the three prophylactic-ablation trials (346 patients), the all-cause mortality odds ratio was 0.77 (95% CI 0.41–1.46) — no significant difference. The largest and newest trial, VANISH 2 (416 patients), lowered a composite that includes death (50.7% vs 60.6%; hazard ratio 0.75), but its record does not report mortality separately, so it cannot carry a survival claim. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: ablation's proven benefit is fewer shocks and less ICD therapy (homed on #713); a mortality benefit remains unproven, and every trial here was powered for arrhythmia endpoints, not death, so a modest survival effect is not excluded.
stamp: POSSIBLE — catheter ablation has not been shown to reduce mortality in ischaemic ventricular tachycardia: every randomised comparison is null for death (the treatment made no difference), though all were powered for arrhythmia outcomes rather than survival

title: Pelvic floor exercises in community-dwelling older women (PARTIAL completion of live #3831): real but modest improvement in four randomised trials — and a self-help booklet came close in one
question: Do pelvic floor exercises improve urinary incontinence in older women living in the community?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — printed on the face. This pack is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #3831 homes the 43-trial Cochrane network meta-analysis of all conservative, drug and combined treatments in women over 60 (Vesentini 2025, PMID 41307301 — homed there, not re-carded here), which ranks treatments against each other but does not isolate pelvic floor muscle training against no treatment in community-dwelling women. Four free randomised trials fill that slice. The largest, GLADIOLUS (463 women aged 55 and over), found a one-time group behavioural class built around pelvic floor exercises beat no treatment on incontinence scores at every time point, though the 3-month difference (−0.96 points) fell short of the trial's own 3-point target for clinical importance. A Hong Kong programme trial (55 women over 65) found 6.4 fewer leakage episodes per week than pamphlet advice alone. An Australian trial (83 women over 65) found intensive pelvic floor training beat bladder training on measured leakage. Against that, Burgio 2002 (222 women) found coached behavioural training reduced episodes by 63–69%, but a self-help booklet alone achieved 58.6%, with no significant difference between groups. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): pelvic floor exercises help older women living in the community, modestly; how much the coaching adds beyond a good booklet is unsettled.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — pelvic-floor-based exercise programmes improve incontinence in community-dwelling older women in randomised trials, but effects are modest and one trial found a self-help booklet nearly as effective

title: When should the PSA discussion start? (PARTIAL completion of live #212): the mortality trials screened men from 50, proved benefit at 55–69, and a PSA at 60 sorts who benefits
question: In men, at what age should PSA screening be discussed for prostate cancer detection?
balance: POSSIBLE — printed on the face. This pack is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #212 already answers whether PSA screening reduces prostate-cancer deaths (ERSPC 2009 and PLCO, homed there and not re-carded here; the developer's verdict there is MAYBE (weak evidence)). This shelf asks the question #212 does not: at what age should the discussion happen? The trials' own designs bracket the answer. ERSPC pre-specified its core age group as 55–69 and showed its mortality benefit there (rate ratio 0.79 at 13 years). The Göteborg trial began inviting men at 50–64 and, screening to about age 69, halved prostate-cancer mortality (rate ratio 0.56) — evidence that a programme starting at 50 sits inside the tested range. Two observational analyses then refine the discussion by PSA level rather than birthday alone: a single PSA at 60 separated men who benefit from continued screening (≥2 ng/mL; 23 men screened per death averted) from those who do not (<1 ng/mL, where the authors recommend no further screening), and PSA measured at 45–55 identified the small high-risk group (top decile) in whom 44% of later prostate-cancer deaths occurred, supporting a baseline test in the late 40s with long intervals for the low-risk majority. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: discuss from about age 50, expect benefit mainly at 55–69, and let the age-60 PSA steer continuation — the age-specific evidence beyond the two big trials is observational and is labelled as such on its cards.
stamp: POSSIBLE — the evidence supports opening the PSA discussion at about age 50 (with a baseline PSA in the late 40s usable for risk stratification); the demonstrated mortality benefit is concentrated at ages 55–69, and the age-60 PSA level should steer whether screening continues

title: Glutamine in general critical illness (PARTIAL completion of live #1049): no mortality benefit across two trials, a harm signal in one bundled formula, and a Cochrane long-term mortality ratio of exactly 1.00
question: In adults with critical illness, does glutamine supplementation reduce mortality versus standard nutrition without glutamine?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — on mortality, printed on the face. This pack is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #1049 homes glutamine in severe burns only (RE-ENERGIZE), and the high-dose glutamine-and-antioxidants trial REDOXS (PMID 23594003) is homed on live shelf #79 and is not re-carded here. FLAG (precedent b): the field's largest trial is homed elsewhere, so this shelf answers the wider question — standard-dose glutamine in general critical illness — from the remaining free reports, which are concordant. SIGNET (502 ICU patients needing parenteral nutrition) found a 6-month mortality odds ratio of 1.18 (95% CI 0.82–1.70) for parenteral glutamine — no difference. The Scandinavian trial (413 patients) found lower ICU mortality only in its per-protocol subgroup and no difference at 6 months. The Cochrane review (53 trials, 4,671 participants) put short-term mortality at relative risk 0.89 (95% CI 0.78–1.02) and long-term mortality at exactly 1.00 (95% CI 0.89–1.12). The one discordant note is MetaPlus, an enteral formula bundling glutamine with omega-3 fatty acids, selenium and antioxidants: infections were unchanged (53% vs 52%) and 6-month mortality in the medical subgroup ran higher on the formula (adjusted hazard ratio 1.57) — a bundle effect that cannot be laid on glutamine alone, but which points the same way as the REDOXS harm signal on #79. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): glutamine supplementation does not reduce mortality in general critical illness; an infection benefit (Cochrane relative risk 0.79) has not translated into survival.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — on mortality in general critical illness: two randomised trials and the Cochrane pooling (long-term mortality relative risk 1.00) agree that glutamine supplementation does not reduce deaths

title: Six-food elimination diet in adults with eosinophilic oesophagitis (PARTIAL completion of live #2768): about half to two-thirds reach histologic remission in three adult cohorts — all observational
question: Does the six-food elimination diet induce remission in adults with eosinophilic esophagitis?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational evidence only, printed on the face. This pack is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #2768 homes elimination diets across children and adults together (Arias 2014 meta-analysis, PMID 24534634 — homed there, not re-carded here), reporting six-food remission of 72.1% in the mixed-age pool. This shelf asks about adults alone, from the three free adult-specific reports. In the original prospective adult series (Gonsalves 2012, 50 adults), 6 weeks of six-food elimination (milk, wheat, egg, soy, peanut/tree nuts, fish/shellfish) brought peak counts to ≤5 eosinophils per high-power field in 64% and to ≤10 in 70%, and systematic reintroduction brought the inflammation back — the closest thing to an internal control this literature has. The largest adult cohort (Zalewski 2022, 213 adults) found 54% below 15 eosinophils per high-power field after the diet, rising to 58% after an extended round. A UK–Italian series (Visaggi 2023, 58 adults) found a 56.9% response overall, but only 21.4% in pollen-sensitised patients assessed during pollen season versus 77.3% outside it. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), observational: the diet induces remission in about half to two-thirds of adults who complete it; there is no randomised adult trial of the diet against no treatment, and the one randomised diet trial in this field (one-food versus six-food elimination) is already carded elsewhere in the library and is not re-carded here.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational evidence only: in three adult cohorts the six-food elimination diet induced histologic remission in roughly 54–70% of adults with eosinophilic oesophagitis, with no randomised or untreated comparison carded

title: Folic acid in pregnancies exposed to antiseizure medication (PARTIAL completion of live #48): the direct studies find no demonstrated reduction in birth defects — guidelines recommend it anyway, by extrapolation
question: Does folic acid supplementation reduce birth defects in women taking antiseizure medication?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — printed on the face, and the evidence is observational throughout. This pack is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #48 homes periconceptional folic acid preventing neural tube defects in the general population (the MRC recurrence trial and the Hungarian trial). This shelf asks the separate question for women taking antiseizure medication, whose drugs raise malformation risk and several of which are folate antagonists. The direct evidence does not show the protection seen in the general population. In the UK Epilepsy and Pregnancy Register (Morrow 2009), major congenital malformations were actually more frequent in women who took folic acid before conception than in those who took it late or not at all (3.9% vs 2.2%), and neural tube defects were near-identical (0.4% vs 0.34%) — confounding by indication (higher-risk women are likelier to be prescribed folate) may explain the direction, but no protective effect is visible. In the Slone case-control data (Hernández-Díaz 2000), folic-acid multivitamins blunted the harm of dihydrofolate-reductase inhibitors but did not diminish the adverse effects of antiepileptic drugs. A third direct register analysis (Australian Register, Vajda 2021, PMID 33272896) is already carded elsewhere in the library and is not re-carded here; it likewise found no folic-acid dose effect. Against this, the 2024 AAN/AES/SMFM guideline still recommends at least 0.4 mg of folic acid daily before and during pregnancy for anyone on an antiseizure medication — a recommendation resting on extrapolation from the general population and on possible neurodevelopmental benefit, not on demonstrated malformation prevention in this population. Supplement note (clarification exception): none of the carded publications names a specific tested brand or manufacturer — the exposures are generic folic acid preparations (0.4 mg daily in the 2024 recommendation; higher doses are commonly prescribed in this population but were not shown to work better), so no product can be endorsed from this evidence. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): folic acid has not been shown to reduce birth defects in antiseizure-medication-exposed pregnancies; it is recommended anyway, and this shelf reports both halves of that sentence.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — in women taking antiseizure medication, a reduction in birth defects from folic acid has not been demonstrated in the direct observational evidence; supplementation is still recommended by guideline, extrapolated from the general population

title: Vitamin D alone in adults not selected for deficiency (PARTIAL completion of live #56): two large trials and an 81-trial pool all found no fracture prevention
question: In adults without vitamin D deficiency, does vitamin D supplementation prevent fractures?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — for vitamin D ALONE in adults not selected for deficiency, the slice live shelf #56 leaves open (its home question is calcium plus vitamin D in healthy adults). Two large placebo-controlled trials of vitamin D alone agree: VITAL (25,871 US adults not recruited for deficiency, low bone mass or osteoporosis; vitamin D3 2000 IU daily for a median 5.3 years) found total fractures in 769 of 12,927 on vitamin D versus 782 of 12,944 on placebo (HR 0.98), with no effect on nonvertebral (HR 0.97) or hip fractures (HR 1.01) and no modification by baseline 25-hydroxyvitamin D level; D-Health (20,326 Australians aged 60–84; 60,000 IU monthly for up to 5 years) found fractures in 5.6% versus 5.9% (HR 0.94). The 81-trial pool (Bolland 2018; 44,790 participants in the total-fracture analysis) gives a relative risk of exactly 1.00 for total fracture, and trial sequential analysis crossed the futility boundary for even a 5% relative reduction. Correcting deficiency is a different question, and institutionalised deficient older women are homed elsewhere (live #1498); the annual mega-dose harm signal is homed on live #30 and is not re-carded here.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — vitamin D alone did not prevent total, nonvertebral or hip fractures in adults not selected for deficiency: HR 0.98 in VITAL (25,871 participants), HR 0.94 in D-Health (20,326), and a pooled relative risk of 1.00 across 81 trials

title: Spironolactone-centred medical treatment in primary aldosteronism not treated surgically (PARTIAL completion of live #3279): blood pressure falls substantially, but complete control is uncommon and renin suppression on treatment marks residual risk
question: Does spironolactone reduce blood pressure in primary aldosteronism unsuitable for surgery?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only, for the slice live shelf #3279 leaves open: that shelf compares spironolactone WITH eplerenone head-to-head; this shelf asks what spironolactone-based medical treatment itself achieves in patients who are not treated surgically. The blood-pressure effect is large where it is measured directly: in 24 patients with aldosterone-producing adenomas managed medically for at least 5 years, blood pressure fell from 175/106 to 129/79 mm Hg (Ghose 1999). But complete control is uncommon at cohort scale: in the 1,258-patient international PAMO cohort on targeted medical treatment (spironolactone the dominant drug; median dose 40 mg daily in complete biochemical responders versus 25 mg), only 18.3% achieved a complete clinical response at 6–12 months and 18.2% had an absent response (Yang 2025). A 394-patient spironolactone series found doses above 50 mg bought no better blood-pressure control than 50 mg or less, at the cost of more adverse effects — 128 of 394 patients, mostly men (Sconfienza 2026). And blood-pressure control is not the whole story: medically treated patients whose renin stayed suppressed on treatment carried a higher cardiovascular event rate than essential-hypertension controls (adjusted HR 1.91 relative), while those titrated to unsuppressed renin did not (Hundemer 2018). No randomised trial has tested spironolactone against no treatment in non-surgical primary aldosteronism, so the stamp caps at POSSIBLE and is labelled observational.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: spironolactone-based medical treatment lowered blood pressure substantially in non-surgical primary aldosteronism (175/106 to 129/79 mm Hg over at least 5 years in one adenoma cohort), but complete clinical response was only 18.3% in the 1,258-patient PAMO cohort, and no randomised trial tests spironolactone against no treatment in this population

title: TAVI versus surgery at 10 years in intermediate-risk aortic stenosis (PARTIAL completion of live #3360): the answer splits by valve generation and access route
question: Is TAVI as durable as surgery at 10 years in intermediate-risk patients?
balance: SPLIT (device generation and access route) — the 10-year answer live shelf #3360 could not give from its 1-year DEDICATE result. In the only fully randomised 10-year intermediate-risk comparison, PARTNER 2A (Thourani 2026; 1,910 patients who received a valve, mean STS score 5.8%), TAVI with the second-generation SAPIEN XT valve was associated with higher 10-year mortality than surgery (86.1% versus 82.8%; HR 1.13 relative; P=0.02) and four times the reintervention rate (6.3% versus 1.6%) — but the mortality gap was concentrated in the transthoracic (transapical/transaortic) access cohort (93.2% versus 85.1%), while transfemoral patients fared similarly (83.9% versus 82.1%). With the third-generation SAPIEN 3 valve, a propensity-matched comparison against the same surgical cohort found mortality (83.4% versus 82.3%; HR 1.01 relative) and reintervention (2.0% versus 1.9%) essentially identical at 10 years (Nazif 2026). On structural durability itself, the lower-risk NOTION trial found severe structural valve deterioration LESS often after TAVI than after surgical bioprostheses at 10 years (1.5% versus 10.0%; HR 0.2 relative), with bioprosthetic valve failure similar (9.7% versus 13.8%). PROPOSED SPLIT: durability at 10 years depends on which valve and which route — the early-generation transthoracic experience was worse than surgery; transfemoral and newer-generation results match it.
stamp: SPLIT (device generation and access route) — at 10 years in intermediate-risk patients, second-generation SAPIEN XT TAVI had higher mortality than surgery (86.1% vs 82.8%; HR 1.13 relative) and more reintervention (6.3% vs 1.6%), driven by transthoracic access, while third-generation SAPIEN 3 TAVI matched surgery on mortality (HR 1.01 relative) and reintervention (2.0% vs 1.9%); in lower-risk NOTION, severe structural valve deterioration was less frequent after TAVI (1.5% vs 10.0%)

title: How long to anticoagulate after surgery-provoked VTE (PARTIAL completion of live #1581): recurrence after stopping is the lowest of any VTE type — about 0.7% per patient-year — so 3 months is the supported course unless enduring risk factors coexist
question: How long should anticoagulation last after provoked VTE from surgery?
balance: SPLIT (enduring risk factors) — for the slice live shelf #1581 leaves open: that shelf covers extended rivaroxaban in equipoise VTE after 6–12 months of treatment; this shelf asks how long anticoagulation should run from the start after VTE provoked by surgery. Surgery-provoked VTE has the lowest recurrence risk of any VTE category once treatment stops: 0.7% per patient-year at 24 months, versus 4.2% for nonsurgical transient factors and 7.4% for unprovoked VTE (Iorio 2010). The 22-trial duration meta-analysis (Li 2025) found that for primary treatment — including VTE provoked by transient factors — longer courses (over 6 months) versus shorter (3–6 months) probably reduced recurrent PE only modestly (relative risk 0.66, CI crossing 1) while doubling major bleeding (relative risk 2.02); its authors conclude shorter courses are more beneficial for primary treatment of all VTE types, reserving indefinite treatment for unprovoked or chronic-risk VTE. The exception is the patient whose provoking surgery coexists with enduring risk factors: in HI-PRO (Piazza 2025), such patients randomised after at least 3 months of treatment to 12 further months of low-dose apixaban had recurrence in 1.3% versus 10.0% on placebo. PROPOSED SPLIT: 3 months for surgery-provoked VTE without enduring risk factors; extended low-dose treatment is trial-supported when enduring risk factors coexist.
stamp: SPLIT (enduring risk factors) — 3 months of anticoagulation fits VTE provoked by surgery alone (recurrence after stopping about 0.7% per patient-year, the lowest of any VTE category, and longer primary treatment doubled major bleeding, relative risk 2.02, in the 22-trial duration pool); where enduring risk factors coexist with the provocation, 12 further months of low-dose apixaban cut recurrence from 10.0% to 1.3% in one trial (HI-PRO)

title: Early versus delayed cholecystectomy for acute cholecystitis in older adults (PARTIAL completion of live #650): no elderly randomised trial exists; observational data favour operating early in selected patients, and delay invites recurrence
question: Is early laparoscopic cholecystectomy better than delayed surgery for acute cholecystitis in older adults?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only, for the older-adult slice live shelf #650 leaves open (its ACDC and Roulin trials enrolled general adult populations). No randomised trial has tested timing in older adults specifically — the dedicated international study in patients 70 and over (GOLDENEYE) is still a protocol — so this shelf rests on elderly-specific observational evidence. Early cholecystectomy in patients aged 70 and over is feasible but not benign: across 8 series totalling 592 patients (mean age 81), conversion was 23%, perioperative morbidity 24% and mortality 3.5% (Loozen 2017). In 21,392 NSQIP patients, surgery delayed to day 3 or beyond carried significantly higher bleeding and mortality, and the authors report the delay penalty was most marked in the elderly subgroup (Daniel 2021). The one elderly head-to-head cohort found emergency surgery and medical treatment followed by elective surgery produced similar overall outcomes — with the emergency arm's 53% morbidity reflecting how much sicker its patients were (Sánchez Beorlegui 2009). And when older patients are drained first, waiting is expensive: in octogenarians, cholecystectomy delayed 6 weeks or more after drainage brought recurrent cholecystitis in 52.9% versus 4.9% with earlier surgery (Pan 2023). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), observational only: in selected older adults, operating early beats delaying — with selection, not age alone, doing the work.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only, with no randomised trial in older adults specifically: early cholecystectomy at age 70 and over carried 24% morbidity and 3.5% mortality in the pooled series, delay beyond 72 hours was associated with higher bleeding and mortality in NSQIP (a penalty the authors found most significant in the elderly), and in octogenarians drained first, waiting 6 weeks or more brought recurrent cholecystitis in 52.9% versus 4.9%

title: Percutaneous cholecystostomy in high-risk acute cholecystitis patients who cannot have surgery (PARTIAL completion of live #1667): symptoms resolve in about 9 of 10, but the one randomised trial found no mortality advantage over antibiotics and conservative care
question: Does percutaneous cholecystostomy improve outcomes in high-risk adults with acute cholecystitis who cannot have surgery?
balance: SPLIT (symptoms versus mortality) — for the non-surgical-candidate slice live shelf #1667 leaves open: CHOCOLATE compared drainage with surgery in high-risk patients who could still be randomised to an operation; this shelf asks what drainage achieves in patients who cannot have surgery at all. On symptoms, the series agree: drainage resolves the attack in 86–93% of patients (Hatzidakis 2002; Chung 2012), and in one grade-3 series 80% had no further attack after the drain was removed, with only 36% ever proceeding to cholecystectomy (Abdelsaid 2023) — drainage is often the definitive treatment, not just a bridge. On mortality, the one randomised trial is sobering: in 123 high-risk patients (APACHE II 12 or more), percutaneous cholecystostomy did NOT reduce 30-day mortality versus conservative treatment (17.5% versus 13%), and its authors suggest reserving drainage for patients not improving after 3 days of conservative care, ICU patients, or candidates for stone extraction (Hatzidakis 2002). Series mortality (90-day 9.3%, Aroori 2019; in-hospital 21% in acalculous disease, Chung 2012) tracks the underlying illness, not the drain. PROPOSED SPLIT: drainage reliably settles the gallbladder; it has never been shown to save lives compared with antibiotics and supportive care alone.
stamp: SPLIT (symptoms versus mortality) — percutaneous cholecystostomy resolves symptoms in 86–93% of high-risk patients who cannot have surgery and can be definitive treatment (80% had no further attack after drain removal in one grade-3 series), but the single randomised trial found no mortality benefit over conservative treatment (30-day mortality 17.5% versus 13%)

title: Continuing beta-blockers through major surgery in existing users (PARTIAL completion of live #352): withdrawal is associated with a three- to four-fold higher 30-day mortality in observational data; continuation is associated with lower mortality
question: In adults undergoing major surgery, should beta-blockers be continued perioperatively?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only, for the continuation slice live shelf #352 leaves open: that shelf's evidence is about STARTING beta-blockers around surgery (POISE: harm) and it carries the guideline rule to continue chronic therapy as a recommendation, without primary evidence on continuation itself. The continuation evidence is entirely observational, and it points one way: withdrawal is dangerous. In 38,779 operations under a perioperative cardiac risk protocol, patients whose beta-blocker was withdrawn had a 30-day mortality odds ratio of 3.93 relative to the comparison pattern, while continuous use was associated with lower 30-day (OR 0.68 relative) and 1-year mortality (Wallace 2010). In 711 vascular surgery patients, continuous use was associated with a 1-year mortality hazard ratio of 0.4 relative to non-use, and withdrawal with a hazard ratio of 2.7 relative (Hoeks 2007). A 136,745-patient VA cohort found perioperative beta-blocker exposure associated with lower 30-day mortality in propensity-matched analysis (relative risk 0.73), with benefit concentrated in patients with two or more cardiac risk factors (London 2013). No trial has randomised existing users to continue versus stop, so the stamp caps at POSSIBLE and is labelled observational — but the consistency of the withdrawal signal across cohorts is what the guideline rule rests on.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: in existing users undergoing major surgery, perioperative beta-blocker withdrawal was associated with markedly higher mortality (30-day odds ratio 3.93 relative in one cohort; 1-year hazard ratio 2.7 relative in vascular surgery), while continuous use was associated with lower mortality; no randomised trial has tested continuation versus withdrawal

title: Cascade screening for familial hypercholesterolemia — the treatment-uptake slice (PARTIAL completion of live #476): identified relatives start treatment (39% to 93% in the Dutch programme), but routine care still leaves most below target
question: Does cascade screening for familial hypercholesterolemia improve early treatment?
balance: POSSIBLE (observational) — this pack is a PARTIAL completion of live shelf #476, which already homes cascade identification (Wald child–parent screening; the CATCH randomised programme trial) and the absence of cardiovascular-outcome evidence. The slice built here is the middle link #476 leaves open: once relatives are identified, do they actually start treatment early? The Dutch national programme's first-five-years report is the anchor: among 2,039 relatives identified as heterozygotes, the share receiving lipid-lowering treatment rose from 39% at identification to 93% one year later (Umans-Eckenhausen 2001). A Turkish paediatric cascade series shows the same mechanism in miniature — screening children led to statins being started in 18 previously undiagnosed parents and 7 siblings (Kose 2020). The counterweight is a 2023 UK health-technology assessment: in linked primary–secondary care data, 70% of people coded with familial hypercholesterolemia did not achieve target treatment levels, so identification alone does not guarantee adequate treatment (Qureshi 2023). Every report here is observational or programme data — no trial has randomised relatives to cascade identification versus not and measured treatment — so the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE and labelled observational. Whether earlier treatment started this way prevents heart attacks remains the unproven inference fenced on #476.
stamp: POSSIBLE (observational) — cascade screening improves early treatment uptake: identified relatives in the Dutch national programme went from 39% on lipid-lowering treatment at identification to 93% one year later, and a paediatric cascade series started statins in 35.3% of parents; but UK routine-care data show 70% of identified patients still not at treatment targets, and no trial isolates the cascade step

title: Syphilis in pregnancy (PARTIAL completion of live #2192): penicillin prevents congenital syphilis in 98.2% of treated pregnancies, non-penicillin treatment carries threefold adjusted odds of congenital syphilis — and the comparison has never been randomised
question: For syphilis in pregnancy, does penicillin prevent congenital syphilis better than other antibiotics?
balance: POSSIBLE (observational) — this pack is a PARTIAL completion of live shelf #2192, which homes penicillin versus azithromycin for early syphilis in non-pregnant adults; the pregnancy question is different, because the outcome is the baby, and no randomised trial has ever compared antibiotics for syphilis in pregnancy (the Cochrane review found 26 studies and none with comparative groups). What exists is consistent observational evidence. Prospectively, CDC benzathine penicillin regimens prevented congenital syphilis in 334 of 340 treated pregnancies (98.2%), with failures concentrated in secondary syphilis (Alexander 1999). In the large Shenzhen programme cohort, non-penicillin treatment was independently associated with about threefold higher odds of congenital syphilis (adjusted OR 3.00) and about twofold higher odds of adverse pregnancy outcomes (adjusted OR 2.16) than penicillin treatment (Qin 2014). In Shanghai, congenital syphilis occurred in 12.5% of infants whose mothers completed treatment versus 50.8% with incomplete treatment (Zhu 2010). A 5-woman case series in which every infant developed congenital syphilis after maternal azithromycin exists (Zhou 2007) but is below this library's 10-person carding floor and is therefore described here, not carded. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (observational): penicillin prevents congenital syphilis better than the alternatives on all the comparative evidence available; the comparison has never been randomised.
stamp: POSSIBLE (observational) — penicillin prevents congenital syphilis better than other antibiotics on all available comparative evidence: 98.2% prevention with CDC penicillin regimens prospectively, threefold adjusted odds of congenital syphilis with non-penicillin treatment in the Shenzhen cohort, and no randomised comparison in pregnancy has ever been done

title: Argatroban versus the other non-heparin anticoagulants in HIT (PARTIAL completion of pack #2817): similar clinical outcomes to bivalirudin in retrospective comparisons, no randomised head-to-head anywhere
question: In adults with heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, is argatroban as effective as other non-heparin anticoagulants?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — this pack is a PARTIAL completion of pack #2817, which homes argatroban against historical controls (Lewis 2001); the slice built here is the head-to-head question #2817 does not answer: argatroban versus the other non-heparin anticoagulants actually used — bivalirudin, lepirudin, danaparoid and fondaparinux. No randomised trial compares any of them. The direct evidence is three retrospective comparisons. Against bivalirudin (138 patients), argatroban matched it on time to therapeutic anticoagulation and on thromboembolic and bleeding events, with more supratherapeutic aPTT values (Skrupky 2010). A small three-way comparison (48 patients) found argatroban slower to reach target aPTT than bivalirudin and with more clinically significant bleeding than bivalirudin but less than lepirudin (Bain 2015). A national registry (195 patients) found no HIT-specific complications in fondaparinux-treated patients versus 11.7% with the approved agents pooled (argatroban, danaparoid, lepirudin) — a contrast the registry's own design cannot separate from confounding by indication, since the sickest patients are channelled to argatroban (Schindewolf 2017). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): nothing shows argatroban inferior on thrombotic outcomes, but 'as effective as' rests entirely on small, confounded retrospective comparisons.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — argatroban appears as effective as other non-heparin anticoagulants for HIT on thrombotic and bleeding outcomes, but every head-to-head report is retrospective (largest: 138 patients vs bivalirudin) and no randomised comparison exists

title: Etonogestrel implant versus the standard 52 mg levonorgestrel IUD for long-term pregnancy prevention (PARTIAL completion of live #1337): both under 1 pregnancy per 100 woman-years for years, no demonstrated difference
question: How does the etonogestrel implant compare with the levonorgestrel IUD for long-term pregnancy prevention?
balance: POSSIBLE — this pack is a PARTIAL completion of live shelf #1337, which homes the etonogestrel implant against the low-dose 13.5 mg levonorgestrel intrauterine system on discontinuation and bleeding (Apter 2016). The slice built here is different: pregnancy prevention over years of use, against the standard 52 mg levonorgestrel IUD. No trial has randomised women to implant versus 52 mg IUD and counted pregnancies as the primary outcome, so the comparison is assembled from the one head-to-head cohort and each method's own long-term record. In the head-to-head extended-use cohort, implant users had no pregnancies in 444 woman-years of use beyond the approved duration, and 52 mg IUD users had failure rates of 0.25–0.43 per 100 woman-years in years 6–7 (McNicholas 2017). In the Contraceptive CHOICE cohort, intrauterine devices and implants pooled failed at 0.27 per 100 participant-years versus 4.55 for pills, patch or ring (Winner 2012). The 52 mg IUD's own 7-year randomised record gives a cumulative pregnancy rate of 0.5 per 100 women (Rowe 2016), and the implant's integrated trial analysis recorded no in-treatment pregnancies in 923 women over 24,100 cycles (Graesslin 2008). PROPOSED POSSIBLE: both methods prevent pregnancy at well under 1 per 100 woman-years for years; no difference between them has been demonstrated, and none could be detected without an enormous trial.
stamp: POSSIBLE — the etonogestrel implant and the standard 52 mg levonorgestrel IUD are comparably effective for long-term pregnancy prevention (every carded long-term rate is under 1 per 100 woman-years; no pregnancies in 444 implant woman-years of extended use versus 0.25–0.43 per 100 woman-years for the IUD in years 6–7), with no demonstrated difference and no head-to-head pregnancy trial

title: Multilayer compression versus no compression for venous leg ulcers (PARTIAL completion of live #1221): four-layer bandaging healed ulcers faster than usual care in both pragmatic trials, and all eight direct randomised comparisons favoured compression
question: For venous leg ulcers, does multilayer compression bandaging heal ulcers faster than no compression?
balance: LIKELY — this pack is a PARTIAL completion of live shelf #1221, which compares compression systems against each other (VenUS I, IV and 6); the slice built here is the prior question #1221 assumes: multilayer compression against no systematic compression at all. Two pragmatic randomised trials compared organised four-layer bandaging with the usual care of their era, in which compression was inconsistent or absent: healing was faster with four-layer bandaging in both (healing rate ratio 1.45 in Morrell 1998; 54% vs 34% healed at 3 months in O'Brien 2003). The Cochrane review of all compression trials found 8 randomised trials directly comparing compression with no compression, every one favouring compression on healing outcomes, and concluded compression increases ulcer healing rates compared with no compression (O'Meara 2012). PROPOSED LIKELY: multilayer compression heals venous leg ulcers faster than no compression — the remaining argument, homed on #1221, is only about which system delivers it best.
stamp: LIKELY — multilayer (four-layer) compression bandaging heals venous leg ulcers faster than no compression: two pragmatic randomised trials beat usual care (healing rate ratio 1.45; 54% vs 34% healed at 3 months) and all 8 direct compression-versus-no-compression trials in the Cochrane review favoured compression

title: Daily multivitamins for cardiovascular disease and cancer prevention (PARTIAL completion of live #349): a consistent cardiovascular null, and one modest total-cancer signal in PHS II that COSMOS did not reproduce
question: Does taking a daily multivitamin prevent cardiovascular disease or cancer in generally healthy adults?
balance: SPLIT (outcome) — this pack is a PARTIAL completion of live shelf #349, which homes the same trials' cognitive-ageing question; the slice built here is cardiovascular disease and cancer prevention. On cardiovascular disease the answer is uniform: no benefit in the Physicians' Health Study II over a median 11.2 years (major cardiovascular events HR 1.01) and none in COSMOS over 3.6 years (HR 0.98) — the treatment made no difference. On cancer the trials divide: PHS II found a modest, statistically significant 8% relative reduction in total cancer incidence (17.0 vs 18.3 per 1,000 person-years; HR 0.92, P = .04) with no significant effect on any site-specific cancer or on cancer mortality, while COSMOS found no reduction in total invasive cancer (HR 0.97). The older French SU.VI.MAX trial tested a single antioxidant capsule (not a broad multivitamin) and found a cancer benefit in men only (relative risk 0.69) with none in women (1.04). Product naming, per the supplement clarification rule: the PHS II and COSMOS records fetched describe the intervention only as a common daily multivitamin / daily multivitamin-multimineral and do not name the brand or manufacturer in the record; SU.VI.MAX's record gives the exact capsule contents, carded below. PROPOSED SPLIT (outcome): no cardiovascular prevention in any trial; a small total-cancer signal in one trial that the other large trial did not reproduce.
stamp: SPLIT (outcome) — a daily multivitamin does not prevent cardiovascular disease (HR 1.01 over 11.2 years in PHS II; HR 0.98 in COSMOS); for cancer, PHS II found a modest 8% relative reduction in total incidence (HR 0.92) with no site-specific or mortality effect, which COSMOS did not reproduce (HR 0.97)

title: BRCA testing in women with a strong family history (PARTIAL completion of live #478): testing triggers surveillance, surgery and early-stage detection — but the mortality link for testing itself has never been measured directly
question: Does genetic testing for BRCA1 and BRCA2 in women with a strong family history reduce cancer deaths through earlier intervention?
balance: POSSIBLE (observational) — this pack is a PARTIAL completion of live shelf #478, which homes risk-reducing surgery in women already known to carry BRCA mutations; the slice built here is the step before: the testing itself, offered to women because of a strong family history, and whether the chain it starts — identification, intensified surveillance, risk-reducing surgery — reaches cancer deaths. No trial has randomised women to genetic testing versus no testing and counted deaths; the USPSTF evidence review states the chain's benefit is inferred from intervention studies in identified carriers (Nelson 2014). The prospective testing-programme cohort is the closest direct evidence: after testing, surveillance intensified, 29 women chose risk-reducing mastectomy and 90 risk-reducing salpingo-oophorectomy, the cancers found were early-stage, and no stage III or IV cancer was detected after test results (Scheuer 2002). In European familial surveillance programmes, cancers arising in tested women were mostly detected early, with 5-year survival of 96% in BRCA2 carriers and 92% in mutation-negative women — but only 73% in BRCA1 carriers, whose tumour biology stays aggressive even when found early (Moller 2007). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (observational): testing plausibly reduces cancer deaths through earlier intervention, on cohort evidence for each link and none for the whole chain. Population-wide BRCA testing (a different strategy) is homed on live shelf #808 and is not re-carded here.
stamp: POSSIBLE (observational) — BRCA1/BRCA2 testing in women with a strong family history demonstrably triggers earlier intervention (intensified surveillance; 29 risk-reducing mastectomies and 90 salpingo-oophorectomies in the prospective testing cohort, with no stage III/IV cancers detected after results), but no trial has measured whether testing itself reduces cancer deaths, and BRCA1 carriers under surveillance still had only 73% 5-year survival

title: Implantable monitoring after cryptogenic stroke (PARTIAL completion of live #436): three randomised trials show several-fold more atrial fibrillation detected — a detection win, with stroke prevention untested
question: In adults with cryptogenic stroke, does prolonged monitoring with an implantable cardiac monitor detect atrial fibrillation more often than conventional follow-up?
balance: This pack is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #436 answers AF screening with wearable and implantable devices in people who feel well; this shelf asks the different, post-stroke question — after a cryptogenic or otherwise unexplained stroke, does prolonged implantable monitoring find atrial fibrillation that conventional follow-up misses? Three randomised trials agree, with large effects: CRYSTAL AF (cryptogenic stroke) found AF in 8.9% versus 1.4% by 6 months and 12.4% versus 2.0% by 12 months; STROKE AF (stroke attributed to large- or small-vessel disease) found 12.1% versus 1.8% at 12 months; PER DIEM (recent ischemic stroke, two-thirds of undetermined cause) found 15.3% with a 12-month implantable recorder versus 4.7% with a 30-day external recorder. Detection is therefore LIKELY proven. None of these trials was designed or powered to show that the extra detection prevents recurrent stroke — PER DIEM's recurrent-stroke numbers (3.3% versus 5.3%) were a non-significant secondary outcome — so this stamp covers detection yield only, not stroke prevention.
stamp: LIKELY — prolonged implantable monitoring detects substantially more atrial fibrillation after cryptogenic or otherwise unexplained stroke than conventional follow-up (three concordant randomised trials; detection yield only — none of these trials tested whether the extra detection prevents recurrent stroke)

title: Plozasiran specifically (PARTIAL completion of pack #5838): PALISADE's ~80% triglyceride fall and fewer pancreatitis episodes, with the SHASTA-2 trial left at its home
question: In adults with familial chylomicronemia syndrome or severe hypertriglyceridemia, does plozasiran reduce triglycerides and acute pancreatitis compared with placebo?
balance: This pack is a PARTIAL completion: pack #5838 answers the class-level question (treating severe hypertriglyceridemia to prevent pancreatitis) and homes the SHASTA-2 trial of plozasiran in severe hypertriglyceridemia, which is therefore not re-carded here; live shelf #1105 covers the neighbouring drug olezarsen, a different agent. This shelf carries the plozasiran-specific evidence that is not homed elsewhere. In PALISADE — the phase 3 trial in persistent chylomicronemia (75 patients, median triglycerides 2,044 mg/dL at baseline) — plozasiran lowered triglycerides by about 80% against 17% on placebo at 10 months, and acute pancreatitis was less frequent (odds ratio 0.17, a relative effect from a secondary outcome with few events). A pooled phase 2 lipoprotein-particle analysis and a two-year open-label extension of the SHASTA-2 and MUIR programmes support a large, sustained triglyceride effect, but neither is a placebo-controlled pancreatitis test. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): one pivotal trial for the pancreatitis claim, with concordant triglyceride data around it.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — plozasiran lowered triglycerides by about 80% versus 17% on placebo in the single phase 3 chylomicronemia trial (PALISADE, 75 patients) and pancreatitis was less frequent (odds ratio 0.17, relative), a secondary outcome with few events; supporting programme data are biomarker and open-label reports

title: Coronary artery calcium for prediction and statin allocation (GAP-E, observational): MESA shows strong prediction and two-way reclassification — with no trial of the scanning strategy itself
question: In intermediate-risk adults, does coronary artery calcium scoring predict events and guide statin allocation better than risk scores alone?
balance: This is a GAP-E prognosis and test-strategy shelf: the evidence is observational by design, and the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE and labelled observational. In the Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis (MESA), a calcium score above 300 carried roughly ten times the adjusted coronary risk of a score of zero, and adding calcium to standard risk factors improved prediction in all four racial and ethnic groups studied. Head-to-head in intermediate-risk adults, calcium beat five rival markers on discrimination and reclassification (net reclassification improvement 0.659, against 0.160 for the next best, family history). For statin allocation the score cuts both ways: 41% of guideline-recommended statin candidates in MESA had a calcium score of zero with a low observed event rate (5.2 per 1,000 person-years), while among adults below the guideline's 7.5% risk threshold a high calcium score identified a small subgroup whose observed event rate exceeded that threshold. No randomised trial has tested a calcium-guided statin strategy against score-guided care, so 'guides allocation better' rests on reclassification and observed event rates, not on outcomes of the strategy itself.
stamp: POSSIBLE (observational) — coronary artery calcium predicts coronary events beyond risk scores (adjusted risk about tenfold for scores above 300 versus zero) and reclassifies statin candidacy in both directions in large prospective cohorts; no randomised trial has tested a calcium-guided statin strategy against score-guided care

title: Clopidogrel plus aspirin after bypass surgery (PARTIAL completion of pack #3090): a SPLIT — blinded randomised null in CASCADE versus pooled, largely observational patency benefit off-pump
question: In adults after coronary artery bypass grafting, does dual antiplatelet therapy with aspirin plus clopidogrel improve vein graft patency compared with aspirin alone?
balance: This pack is a PARTIAL completion: pack #3090 answers the ticagrelor-plus-aspirin version of this question (DACAB) and homes that trial; this shelf asks the clopidogrel version. DACAB has no clopidogrel arm, so it contributes nothing here and is not carded. The evidence splits by design. The one double-blind randomised trial, CASCADE (113 patients), found no benefit from adding clopidogrel for a year: vein graft intimal area, overall patency (95.2% versus 95.5%) and vein graft patency (94.3% versus 93.2%) were all essentially identical (the treatment made no difference), and its 8-year follow-up still showed no patency or survival difference. Against that, a systematic review pooling 11 studies and 25,728 patients — six of them observational — found less early vein graft occlusion with dual therapy (relative risk 0.59), with the clearest benefit in off-pump surgery, alongside a trend to more major bleeding. PROPOSED SPLIT (design): pooled and off-pump data favour dual therapy for early patency; the only blinded randomised test, in mostly on-pump surgery, found none.
stamp: SPLIT (design) — the double-blind randomised CASCADE trial found no vein graft patency benefit from adding clopidogrel to aspirin (94.3% vs 93.2% at 1 year), while a pooled analysis of 11 mostly observational studies found less early graft occlusion (relative risk 0.59), concentrated in off-pump surgery, with a trend to more bleeding

title: Automated insulin delivery in insulin-treated type 2 diabetes outpatients (PARTIAL completion of live #955 and #561): HbA1c 0.6 points better than usual delivery with CGM in the one randomised trial
question: In adults with type 2 diabetes on multiple daily insulin injections, does automated insulin delivery improve glucose control compared with injections plus continuous glucose monitoring?
balance: PARTIAL completion: live shelf #955 already homes fully closed-loop delivery in type 2 diabetes in hospital inpatients and in one small outpatient crossover trial (Daly 2023, 28 randomised adults, not re-carded here), and live shelf #561 homes closed-loop therapy predominantly in type 1 diabetes. This shelf answers the uncovered slice — modern outpatient automated insulin delivery (AID) systems in insulin-treated type 2 diabetes, most participants previously on multiple daily injections, against continued usual insulin delivery with continuous glucose monitoring (CGM). The one randomised trial (Kudva 2025, 319 adults, 13 weeks) found HbA1c fell 0.6 percentage points more with AID than with continued pretrial insulin delivery plus CGM (adjusted difference −0.6, 95% CI −0.8 to −0.4), with time in range 14 percentage points higher. Two single-arm studies point the same way: in 305 adults (73% previously on multiple daily injections) HbA1c fell 0.8 points after switching to AID (Pasquel 2025), and in a 24-person feasibility study switching from injections HbA1c fell 1.3 points (Davis 2023). Hypoglycaemia stayed low in all three reports. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the randomised evidence is a single 13-week trial, and the supporting studies have no concurrent control group, so the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE despite the consistent direction.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — automated insulin delivery lowered HbA1c by 0.6 percentage points more than continued usual insulin delivery with CGM in the one randomised trial (13 weeks), with single-arm switch studies in the same direction and hypoglycaemia remaining low

title: Osteoporosis treatment sequence (precedent-b build; ARCH/FRAME homed on live #92, STRUCTURE on pack #1828): anabolic first, then antiresorptive — the reverse order blunts the gains
question: In postmenopausal women with osteoporosis, does an anabolic-first treatment sequence followed by an antiresorptive preserve bone density and prevent fractures better than starting with an antiresorptive first?
balance: FLAG — precedent (b) build: the slate's named anchors are already homed and are NOT re-carded here — ARCH and FRAME are carded on live shelf #92 and STRUCTURE is carded on pack #1828. This shelf is built only on the free sequence reports below, and the homed trials are cross-pointed, not re-used. What the free reports show: in DATA-Switch, women who went from teriparatide to denosumab kept gaining bone density (total hip +6.6% over 4 years), while women switched from denosumab to teriparatide gained less at the hip (+2.8%) and lost ground transiently at the radius — the antiresorptive-to-anabolic direction blunts or reverses gains at cortical sites. In ACTIVExtend, 18 months of the anabolic abaloparatide followed by alendronate produced far fewer vertebral fractures over 43 months than placebo followed by alendronate (0.9% vs 5.6%). And after a teriparatide course, following with denosumab preserved more spine density than following with a bisphosphonate (Niimi 2018). Together with the homed ARCH result on live #92 (romosozumab-then-alendronate beat alendronate alone on fractures), the direction is consistent: build first, then hold with an antiresorptive; starting with an antiresorptive attenuates the later anabolic response. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for the anabolic-first sequence: the fracture evidence for sequencing itself rests mainly on one extension study plus the homed ARCH trial, and the direct switch evidence is bone-density based.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — an anabolic-first sequence followed by an antiresorptive preserved and extended bone density and, in the one fracture-counting extension, cut vertebral fractures versus no anabolic first; the reverse order blunted the anabolic response (direct fracture head-to-head homed on live #92)

title: SGLT2 inhibitors and new-onset atrial fibrillation (GAP-E, secondary-analysis evidence): about a fifth fewer reported AF events across the outcome trials, no dedicated prevention trial
question: In adults with type 2 diabetes, do SGLT2 inhibitors reduce new-onset atrial fibrillation compared with placebo or other glucose-lowering drugs?
balance: GAP-E with care, as the slate directs: no trial has ever randomised patients to test atrial fibrillation (AF) prevention as its primary question. Everything carded here is secondary-analysis evidence — AF events collected as adverse-event reports inside cardiovascular outcome trials, plus meta-analyses pooling them. Within that limit the direction is consistent: the prespecified DECLARE-TIMI 58 analysis found dapagliflozin reduced first AF/atrial flutter events by 19% relative (hazard ratio 0.81) in 17,160 patients with type 2 diabetes, and two meta-analyses of the randomised trials found relative risks of 0.76 and an odds ratio of 0.82 for incident AF. Because AF was captured from adverse-event reporting rather than systematic rhythm monitoring, silent AF is undercounted in every source, and the finding is hypothesis-supporting rather than proof. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), labelled as secondary-analysis evidence: SGLT2 inhibitors are associated with fewer reported new AF events in trial populations with type 2 diabetes.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — secondary-analysis evidence only: SGLT2 inhibitors were associated with roughly a fifth fewer reported new atrial fibrillation events across the outcome-trial programme (DECLARE hazard ratio 0.81; pooled relative risk 0.76), with AF captured as adverse events, not a monitored endpoint

title: Dexamethasone suppression test accuracy in adrenal incidentaloma (GAP-E): sensitive at 50 nmol/L, specificity limited and threshold-dependent — positives need verification
question: In adults with an adrenal incidentaloma, how accurate is the 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test for autonomous cortisol secretion?
balance: GAP-E test-accuracy shelf. The honest headline is that accuracy here is threshold-dependent and partly circular: autonomous cortisol secretion (ACS) is itself defined by the post-dexamethasone cortisol value in the ESE/ENSAT guideline framework, so there is no independent gold standard against which the 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test (DST) can be validated — the carded studies instead measure what the test does at the standard 50 nmol/L (about 1.8 µg/dL) cortisol cutoff. At that cutoff the test is sensitive but poorly specific: in a 165-patient incidentaloma cohort the overnight test performed no better than longer suppression protocols and the companion tests (late-night salivary cortisol, urinary free cortisol, DHEAS) discriminated poorly (Ueland 2020). Measuring the dexamethasone level itself reclassified about a fifth of false positives and improved specificity (Ueland 2017), and a suppressed ACTH after the test helps verify true non-suppression (sensitivity 75–81%, specificity 78–85% for inadequate suppression; Puvaneswaralingam 2021). Live shelf #1758 covers adrenalectomy for this condition, not test accuracy, and is not re-carded. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (test-accuracy, observational evidence): the 1 mg overnight DST at 50 nmol/L is a reasonable rule-out screen whose positive results are frequently false or borderline and need confirmatory context — assay, dexamethasone level, ACTH and repeat testing — before ACS is diagnosed.
stamp: POSSIBLE (test-accuracy, observational evidence) — at the 50 nmol/L (about 1.8 µg/dL) cutoff the 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test is a sensitive screen for autonomous cortisol secretion but with limited, threshold- and assay-dependent specificity; positive results need verification (dexamethasone level, ACTH pattern, repeat testing)

title: rhTSH versus thyroid hormone withdrawal for radioiodine ablation (PARTIAL completion of pack #2901): ablation success equivalent, quality of life better with rhTSH
question: In adults with low-risk differentiated thyroid cancer after thyroidectomy, does preparation with recombinant human TSH work as well as thyroid hormone withdrawal for radioactive iodine ablation success?
balance: PARTIAL completion: pack #2901 already answers the neighbouring question — low-dose versus high-dose radioiodine, both prepared with thyrotropin alfa — and its HiLo card reports that trial's factorial preparation comparison as a secondary slice; the homed HiLo record is not re-carded here and no figures are taken from it. This shelf answers the uncovered slice head-on: the preparation-method comparison itself. Two randomised trials and a meta-analysis agree that ablation success is equivalent: in ESTIMABL (752 enrolled, 684 evaluable) ablation was complete in 92% overall and the rate was equivalent between recombinant human TSH (rhTSH) and thyroid hormone withdrawal; in the earlier international trial the strict ablation criterion was met by 100% of both groups (Pacini 2006); and pooling seven trials (1,325 patients) found no significant difference in ablation success (odds ratio 0.87, 95% CI 0.56 to 1.37), with better quality of life and fewer adverse events on rhTSH. PROPOSED LIKELY: rhTSH preparation works as well as withdrawal for ablation success in low-risk disease, while sparing patients the hypothyroid interval — concordant randomised evidence, with the equivalence shown in two independent large trials.
stamp: LIKELY — recombinant human TSH preparation achieved radioiodine ablation success equivalent to thyroid hormone withdrawal in low-risk differentiated thyroid cancer (ESTIMABL equivalence; pooled odds ratio 0.87 with confidence interval spanning 1), with better quality of life and fewer adverse events

title: Aldosterone-to-renin ratio accuracy (GAP-E): no single number — sensitivity 10–100% across verified studies, respectable only at locally derived, assay-specific cutoffs
question: In adults being screened for primary aldosteronism, how accurate is the aldosterone-to-renin ratio compared with confirmatory testing?
balance: GAP-E test-accuracy shelf, built around the slate's warning: the aldosterone-to-renin ratio (ARR) has no single accuracy. In the most rigorous meta-analysis — restricted to studies that applied confirmatory testing to everyone, whatever the ARR result, to limit verification bias — reported sensitivity ranged from 10% to 100% and specificity from 70% to 100% across ten studies (4,110 participants), three studies found sensitivity below 50%, and the authors could recommend no single threshold (Hung 2021). Performance is assay-dependent in direct comparisons too: in one 450-patient cohort the locally optimal cutoffs gave sensitivity 77% and specificity 93% for the activity-based ratio and sensitivity 80% and specificity 92% for the direct-renin ratio, with different numeric cutoffs for each assay method (Li 2019); pooling the direct-renin variant gave sensitivity 0.87 and specificity 0.85 (Gao 2022). The ratio is therefore a reasonable case-detection screen whose negative result can miss disease at some cutoffs and whose positive result always requires the confirmatory testing it is compared against here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (test-accuracy, observational evidence), accuracy labelled assay- and threshold-dependent on the face.
stamp: POSSIBLE (test-accuracy, observational evidence) — the aldosterone-to-renin ratio is a usable screen whose accuracy is assay- and threshold-dependent (sensitivity 10–100% across rigorously verified studies; about 77–87% sensitivity and 85–93% specificity at locally derived cutoffs), so positives need confirmatory testing and negatives can miss disease

title: Metformin in heart failure (GAP-E, observational only): associated with lower mortality across cohorts — confounding by indication faced, no randomised trial exists
question: In adults with heart failure and type 2 diabetes, is metformin use associated with better survival than other glucose-lowering therapy?
balance: GAP-E with care, as the slate directs: there is no randomised trial of metformin in heart failure — every carded source is observational, and the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE and labelled observational. The association is consistent: pooling nine cohort studies (about 34,000 patients), metformin users had lower mortality than controls, mostly sulfonylurea users (23% versus 37%; pooled adjusted estimate 0.80, 95% CI 0.74 to 0.87), with no excess lactic acidosis signal (Eurich 2013). The founding cohort found the same direction against sulfonylurea monotherapy (Eurich 2005), and a later meta-regression found the association in preserved as well as reduced ejection fraction (Halabi 2020). Confounding by indication must be faced squarely, and it is, on every card: metformin was long withheld from the sickest heart-failure patients, so users were plausibly healthier at baseline in ways adjustment cannot fully remove — the observed 'benefit' may partly be the fingerprint of who was allowed to receive the drug. The defensible reading is narrower than a survival claim: metformin use in heart failure is associated with lower mortality in observational data and shows no safety signal, which is why guidelines permit it — not proof that it prolongs life. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit, observational evidence only).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit, observational evidence only) — metformin use in heart failure with type 2 diabetes is associated with lower mortality than mostly sulfonylurea therapy (pooled adjusted estimate 0.80), with no randomised trial and confounding by indication unresolved

title: Home haemodialysis versus in-centre haemodialysis: lower mortality in every observational comparison (very low certainty), quality of life unproven — and the FHN trials test frequency, not location
question: In adults with kidney failure, does home hemodialysis improve survival and quality of life compared with in-center hemodialysis?
balance: POSSIBLE (observational) — with the location/frequency distinction on the face. This is a GAP-E shelf: there is no randomised trial of home versus in-centre haemodialysis on survival, so the survival claim rests on observational comparisons and is capped and labelled accordingly. The Cochrane review (1 small crossover trial plus 39 non-randomised studies) found all-cause death lower with home treatment in the pooled non-randomised studies (relative risk 0.80, 58,984 patients) at very low certainty; the ANZDATA registry analysis of 26,016 patients found adjusted mortality hazard ratios of 0.51 for conventional home and 0.53 for frequent/extended home haemodialysis against conventional facility treatment; and a matched cohort of intensive home treatment found a hazard ratio of 0.55 — but that home group also received far more dialysis hours, so it tests a package, not a postcode. Quality of life is not established: the dedicated meta-analysis found a marginal physical-score advantage (SMD 0.14), no mental-score difference, and was 95% peritoneal-dialysis studies. The FHN frequent-dialysis trials test frequency, not location (Daily was in-centre; Nocturnal was at home), and are homed on live shelf #293 — they are cross-pointed here, not re-carded. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (observational): home haemodialysis is associated with lower mortality than in-centre haemodialysis in every large observational comparison, with residual confounding by patient selection the standing alternative explanation, and no proven quality-of-life advantage.
stamp: POSSIBLE (observational) — home haemodialysis was associated with lower all-cause mortality than in-centre haemodialysis in pooled non-randomised studies (relative risk 0.80) and registry analyses (adjusted hazard ratios 0.51–0.55), at very low certainty with selection bias the main alternative explanation; quality of life was only marginally better physically (SMD 0.14, mostly peritoneal-dialysis studies) and no different mentally

title: The furosemide stress test in early AKI: under 200 mL in 2 hours predicts progression to stage 3 (AUC 0.87, derivation and validation) and later dialysis
question: In adults with acute kidney injury, does the furosemide stress test predict progression to severe AKI and need for kidney replacement therapy?
balance: POSSIBLE (observational, test-prognosis) — this is a GAP-E test/prognosis shelf, so the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE and labelled observational. The test is simple: one intravenous furosemide dose (1.0 mg/kg, or 1.5 mg/kg after prior exposure) and the urine produced in the next 2 hours. In the derivation cohorts (77 critically ill patients with early AKI), output under 200 mL over 2 hours predicted progression to AKIN stage III with an AUC of 0.87, sensitivity 87.1% and specificity 84.1%. An independent multicentre validation in 92 ICU patients with stage I–II AKI reproduced the AUC (0.87) and the cut-off, with sensitivity 73.9% and specificity 90.0%. Pooled across 11 studies and 1,366 patients, sensitivity/specificity were 0.81/0.88 for AKI progression and 0.84/0.77 for later kidney replacement therapy, with replacement-therapy prediction better in early (stage 1–2) than in stage 3 AKI. Live shelf #195 answers when to start replacement therapy; this shelf answers the different, earlier question of who is heading towards severe AKI. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (observational, test-prognosis): the furosemide stress test predicts progression to severe AKI and need for kidney replacement therapy with good discrimination, best when used early.
stamp: POSSIBLE (observational, test-prognosis) — urine output under 200 mL in the 2 hours after a furosemide stress test predicted progression to stage 3 AKI with an AUC of 0.87 in both derivation (sensitivity 87.1%, specificity 84.1%) and validation (73.9%, 90.0%), and pooled sensitivity/specificity of 0.84/0.77 for later kidney replacement therapy across 11 studies

title: Incremental peritoneal dialysis start: safe and no worse on survival or technique outcomes, but residual-function preservation unproven (one small randomised trial, null)
question: In adults starting peritoneal dialysis, does an incremental low-dose start preserve residual kidney function compared with a standard full-dose start?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — a PARTIAL completion of live shelf #1732, which covers the incremental twice-weekly haemodialysis start; this shelf is the peritoneal-dialysis slice only, and the randomised base is thin (flagged on the slate and confirmed at build: exactly one small randomised trial). That trial (Yan 2017, 139 incident CAPD patients, 3 vs 4 exchanges) found residual GFR, urine volume and anuria-free survival identical at 24 months (the treatment made no difference), and a post-hoc dose analysis of the balANZ cohort (154 patients; the balANZ solution question itself is homed on live #1738 and not re-carded) likewise found no difference in the slope of residual-function decline (P=0.78). Against those, one small retrospective cohort found higher GFR at 24 months on incremental prescriptions — in a group that started with roughly double the GFR, the textbook signature of confounding by indication — and the 2024 systematic review of 10 comparative studies found no survival, peritonitis or technique-survival differences and conflicting residual-function data. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): incremental starts look safe and no worse on hard outcomes, but the residual-function preservation they are usually sold on has not been demonstrated in the least confounded evidence.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — an incremental peritoneal dialysis start has not been shown to preserve residual kidney function: the one randomised trial (3 vs 4 exchanges, 139 patients) and the balANZ dose analysis both found no difference in residual-function decline, the one favourable cohort started with double the GFR, and a 10-study review found no survival or technique differences and conflicting residual-function data

title: Shifting potassium in acute hyperkalaemia: insulin-dextrose and salbutamol equal alone (about 0.65 mmol/L), additive together (1.21 mmol/L) — bicarbonate alone does nothing
question: In adults with acute hyperkalemia, how do insulin-dextrose, nebulized salbutamol and sodium bicarbonate compare at shifting potassium into cells?
balance: POSSIBLE — a PARTIAL completion of pack #2933, which compares insulin doses (5 vs 10 units); this shelf compares the shift agents themselves, head to head. Potassium is reported in mmol/L throughout; US laboratories report potassium in mEq/L, which is numerically identical, so no conversion is needed. Glucose values are given in mmol/L with their mg/dL equivalents. The head-to-head literature is old and small, and its ordering has never changed: insulin-glucose and nebulised salbutamol each lower potassium by about 0.65 mmol/L as single agents (0.65±0.09 vs 0.66±0.12 in the 1990 crossover) and by 1.21±0.19 mmol/L combined — their effects are additive; a second crossover found the same single-agent falls (−0.85 and −0.53 to −0.71 mmol/L). Sodium bicarbonate is the outlier: alone it lowered potassium by −0.03 mmol/L (the treatment made no difference), it did not potentiate insulin or albuterol, it ranked last as a single agent in a seven-arm randomised comparison (P<0.001), and a 101-study meta-analysis found no potassium effect for bicarbonate while putting the insulin/salbutamol/combination range at 0.7–1.2 mmol/L (very low to low certainty). Insulin's cost is hypoglycaemia, seen in a fifth to three-quarters of recipients across the small trials and blunted by co-given salbutamol. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: insulin-dextrose and salbutamol are equally effective single shift agents, best combined when the fall must be largest; bicarbonate should not be relied on to shift potassium.
stamp: POSSIBLE — insulin-dextrose and nebulised salbutamol each shift potassium by about 0.65–0.85 mmol/L and together by about 1.2 mmol/L (additive), while sodium bicarbonate alone made no difference (−0.03 mmol/L) and did not potentiate either agent; insulin's main cost is hypoglycaemia
