title: Cystatin C eGFR versus creatinine eGFR: better prediction of death and kidney failure in consortium cohorts (reclassification and discordance analyses)
question: In adults with chronic kidney disease, does cystatin C based estimated GFR predict kidney failure and death better than creatinine based estimated GFR?
balance: POSSIBLE (observational) — a GAP-E prognosis shelf: the evidence is cohort meta-analysis by design, so the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE and labelled observational. Three CKD Prognosis Consortium analyses agree. Reclassification (Shlipak 2013; 90,750 general-population and 2,960 CKD participants): cystatin C moved people to eGFR categories that matched their outcomes better than creatinine did, with a net reclassification improvement of 0.23 for death and 0.10 for end-stage kidney disease. Scale (Grams 2023; 720,736 people with creatinine–cystatin eGFR in 20 cohorts): the combined estimate was significantly associated with all 10 adverse outcomes, including kidney failure requiring replacement therapy and death. Discordance (Estrella 2025; 821,327 outpatients): the 11% whose cystatin eGFR was at least 30% below their creatinine eGFR had a mortality hazard ratio of 1.69 (28.4 vs 16.8 deaths per 1,000 person-years) and a kidney-failure hazard ratio of 1.29 — risk invisible to the creatinine estimate. Caveats on the face: the three analyses draw on overlapping consortium cohorts, cystatin C carries non-GFR influences (inflammation, adiposity), and no trial shows cystatin-guided care improves outcomes. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (observational): cystatin-based eGFR predicts kidney failure and death better than creatinine-based eGFR.
stamp: POSSIBLE (observational) — cystatin C-based eGFR predicts death and kidney failure better than creatinine-based eGFR: net reclassification improvement 0.23 for death and 0.10 for end-stage kidney disease, and a cystatin eGFR at least 30% below the creatinine eGFR carried a mortality hazard ratio of 1.69 and a kidney-failure hazard ratio of 1.29 (all relative measures, from cohort meta-analyses)

title: Febuxostat versus allopurinol for kidney protection in gout and CKD: positive indirect signals (FREED, small and biased direct comparisons), no rigorous head-to-head proof
question: In adults with gout and chronic kidney disease, does febuxostat protect kidney function compared with allopurinol?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — a PARTIAL completion of live shelf #168, which settled that urate lowering with allopurinol does not slow CKD progression and carded FEATHER (febuxostat vs placebo: no kidney protection) inside that answer; this shelf is the febuxostat-specific, head-to-head slice. It is thin where it matters. The largest positive signal, FREED (1,070 elderly patients), compared febuxostat with conventional therapy — not allopurinol — in asymptomatic hyperuricaemia rather than gout, and its renal finding is a soft impairment composite (16.2% vs 20.5%; hazard ratio 0.745 relative) plus a post-hoc macroalbuminuria result (HR 0.44 relative), with 40% eGFR decline null. Directly against allopurinol there is one 120-patient, 6-month, low-fixed-dose trial favouring febuxostat (its abstract does not print the primary outcome's numbers) and three retrospective studies all rated at serious risk of bias. The 5,002-patient CARES post-hoc ties slower eGFR decline to achieving urate under 6 mg/dL (adjusted odds ratio 0.66 relative), whichever drug achieved it. STOP Gout's gout-and-CKD subgroup, homed on pack #2571, is cross-pointed and not re-carded. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): febuxostat may protect kidney function better than allopurinol, but no direct, rigorous test has shown it.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — febuxostat may protect kidney function compared with allopurinol, but the supporting evidence is indirect: FREED compared febuxostat with conventional therapy (not allopurinol) in asymptomatic hyperuricaemia, the one direct randomised trial enrolled 120 patients for 6 months at low fixed doses, the retrospective comparisons are all at serious risk of bias, and the CARES post-hoc credits achieved urate under 6 mg/dL rather than the drug

title: Late belatacept conversion in established kidney transplant recipients: better graft function (two randomised trials), more early rejection, no graft-survival difference
question: In established kidney transplant recipients, does late conversion from a calcineurin inhibitor to belatacept improve graft function compared with continuing the calcineurin inhibitor?
balance: POSSIBLE — a PARTIAL completion of live shelf #2103 (everolimus-based calcineurin-inhibitor elimination in de novo recipients); this shelf is the belatacept conversion slice in established recipients, and it is distinct from live shelf #590 (de novo belatacept versus ciclosporin from the day of transplant). Two randomised trials randomised exactly this switch in stable recipients: the phase II trial (173 patients, 6–36 months post-transplant) found a better 12-month change in calculated GFR after switching, with 6 early rejections, all resolved; the phase 3b trial (446 patients, 6–60 months) quantified it — eGFR 55.5 versus 48.5 mL/min/1.73 m² at 24 months — with survival with a functioning graft unchanged (98% vs 97%), biopsy-proven rejection roughly doubled (8% vs 4%), and fewer de novo donor-specific antibodies (1% vs 7%). A 108-patient conversion cohort adds the boundary condition: eGFR slope improved after conversion in non-sensitised recipients (+0.28/year) but declined in HLA-sensitised recipients (−0.44/year). One correction to the slate: it named the anchor 'Rostaing 2015' — the verified randomised report is Rostaing 2011 (PMID: 21051752). PROPOSED POSSIBLE: late belatacept conversion improves graft function in stable established recipients, bought with more early rejection and no demonstrated graft-survival benefit.
stamp: POSSIBLE — late conversion from a calcineurin inhibitor to belatacept improved graft function in two randomised trials of stable established recipients (eGFR 55.5 vs 48.5 mL/min/1.73 m² at 24 months in the phase 3b trial), with survival with a functioning graft unchanged (98% vs 97%), biopsy-proven rejection roughly doubled (8% vs 4%), and fewer de novo donor-specific antibodies (1% vs 7%)

title: Neutral-pH, low-GDP PD solutions — peritonitis and technique failure: balANZ's benefit (homed on #1738) unreproduced across the trial programme and registry practice
question: In adults on peritoneal dialysis, do neutral-pH, low-glucose-degradation-product solutions reduce peritonitis and technique failure compared with conventional solutions?
balance: SPLIT (single trial vs programme) — a PARTIAL completion of live shelf #1738, built under the documented precedent for a homed anchor with a genuinely different slice: #1738 asks whether these solutions preserve residual kidney function (answer: no, on balANZ's primary outcome) and cards balANZ's two reports (PMIDs 22440906 and 22991015, both on the gate list and NOT re-carded here). This shelf asks the programme-wide peritonitis and technique-failure question, which #1738 touches only through balANZ's secondary peritonitis analysis. On the free reports, the answer splits: the Cochrane review of 29 neutral-pH low-GDP trials (1,971 participants) found peritonitis differences uncertain and technique failure or death little or no different (the treatment made no difference); a 50-patient randomised trial found no peritonitis difference; and the ANZDATA registry analysis found biocompatible-solution patients with a higher peritonitis rate (0.67 vs 0.47 episodes per patient-year; incidence rate ratio 1.49 relative). So balANZ's peritonitis advantage (0.30 vs 0.49 episodes per patient-year, on #1738) stands unreproduced across the wider programme, and no technique-failure benefit is shown anywhere carded. PROPOSED SPLIT (single trial vs programme): peritonitis reduction in one trial's secondary analysis; no confirmed peritonitis or technique-survival benefit programme-wide.
stamp: SPLIT (single trial vs programme) — balANZ (homed on live #1738) found fewer peritonitis episodes with neutral-pH, low-GDP solution, but the pooled trial programme (Cochrane, 29 trials) found peritonitis differences uncertain and technique failure or death little or no different, a small randomised trial found no peritonitis difference, and a national registry analysis found a higher peritonitis rate on biocompatible solutions (incidence rate ratio 1.49, relative)

title: What sets the glomerular filtration rate: glomerular pressure, arteriolar tone and Kf — the textbook equation confirmed by human protein-load and ANP studies
question: In healthy adults, what determines glomerular filtration rate — how do afferent and efferent arteriolar tone, glomerular pressure and filtration coefficient set GFR?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology and Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology). The textbooks state the governing relation: GFR equals the filtration coefficient (Kf — capillary surface area and permeability) multiplied by the net filtration pressure, which is set by glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure minus Bowman's capsule pressure and plasma oncotic pressure. Afferent arteriolar dilation (or efferent constriction) raises glomerular pressure and GFR; afferent constriction lowers both; efferent dilation lowers glomerular pressure. The carded human studies behave exactly as that framework predicts. A protein load recruits 'renal functional reserve' and drives GFR up by roughly a third within hours (Bosch 1983; Herrera 1988: inulin-clearance GFR 107 to 146 ml/min after a meat meal, with renal blood flow rising in parallel — a predominantly afferent-side vasodilator pattern). Atrial natriuretic peptide shows the pressure/filtration-fraction dissociation the textbooks describe: at low infusion doses in normal man, GFR itself did not change while renal plasma flow fell slightly and filtration fraction rose (Richards 1988) — a pattern consistent with a relatively greater efferent than afferent effect at those doses. Herrera's indomethacin arm is the caution: blocking prostaglandin synthesis by 73% did not blunt protein-induced hyperfiltration, so no single vasodilator mediator owns the afferent response. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED: in humans, GFR is set moment to moment by glomerular capillary pressure (afferent versus efferent tone), plasma flow and oncotic pressure acting through Kf, exactly as the textbook relation states.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — GFR is set by the filtration coefficient and net filtration pressure (Guyton & Hall; Boron & Boulpaep), and human clearance studies behave accordingly: protein loading raises GFR by about a third (107 to 146 ml/min by inulin clearance), while low-dose ANP raises filtration fraction without changing GFR

title: What moves potassium between cells and blood: insulin and beta-adrenergic uptake, quantified in human infusion studies; acid-base as the textbooks give it
question: In humans, how do insulin, beta-adrenergic stimulation and acid-base status determine the distribution of potassium between the intracellular and extracellular compartments?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology and Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology). Only about 2% of body potassium sits extracellularly, so plasma potassium is set less by intake or excretion minute-to-minute than by distribution: insulin and beta-2 adrenergic stimulation drive potassium into cells (via Na/K-ATPase), while acid-base status shifts it across the membrane in exchange for hydrogen ions. The carded human infusion studies quantify the hormonal legs directly. Epinephrine nearly abolished the rise from a standard potassium load (0.1 vs 0.6 mEq/L) and beta-blockade with propranolol exaggerated it (0.9 mEq/L) without any change in urinary excretion or aldosterone (Rosa 1980). Physiological insulin lowered serum potassium by about 0.3 mmol/L in healthy volunteers under clamp conditions (Gastaldelli 2000) and, in fasting dialysis patients, merely doubling plasma insulin within the physiological range completely prevented a 0.58 mmol/L fasting rise — and unmasked epinephrine's potassium-lowering effect (Allon 1993). During exercise, beta-blockade worsened the potassium rise by about 40% (Castellino 1987). The acid-base leg is presented as the textbooks give it — mineral (hyperchloraemic) acidosis shifts potassium out of cells and raises plasma potassium, alkalaemia does the reverse, with organic acidoses behaving less predictably — because no primary human acid-infusion record fetched this session reported the plasma potassium change with usable numbers; it is textbook account, not a carded result. Potassium units: US laboratories report mEq/L, which for potassium is numerically identical to mmol/L. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED for the insulin and beta-adrenergic determinants; the acid-base determinant is textbook-established and labelled as such.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — insulin and beta-adrenergic stimulation drive potassium into cells (epinephrine cut a load's rise from 0.6 to 0.1 mEq/L; physiological insulin lowered potassium ~0.3 mmol/L), beta-blockade does the reverse, and acid-base status shifts potassium as Ganong / Boron & Boulpaep describe (textbook-labelled leg)

title: The exercise cardiac-output rise, apportioned: early stroke-volume doubling, linear heart-rate rise, and stroke-volume rescue when rate is blocked
question: In healthy humans, what determines the rise in cardiac output during exercise — the relative contributions of heart rate, stroke volume and peripheral vasodilation?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology). The textbooks describe a roughly fourfold rise in cardiac output from rest to maximal exercise in untrained healthy adults, achieved by an early rise in stroke volume that plateaus at submaximal work, a heart-rate rise that continues linearly to maximum, and a large fall in total peripheral resistance from vasodilation in working muscle that lets output rise with only a modest rise in arterial pressure — venous return, driven by the muscle pump and sympathetic venoconstriction, keeping the heart filled so the Frank-Starling mechanism can operate. The carded human studies measure each leg. In 10 healthy men, output rose from 5.8 to 19.4 L/min while heart rate rose from 84 to 169 beats/min and stroke volume rose early (70 to 137 ml at 25% of VO2max) and then levelled off (116 ml at maximum) — and when beta-blockade capped heart rate near 90 beats/min, maximal output was fully maintained by a larger stroke volume (Bevilacqua 1989). At the top end, output and stroke volume plateau or fall beyond about 80% of peak power while heart rate keeps rising linearly (Mortensen 2005), and restoring heart rate by pacing under beta-blockade does not restore Doppler flow indices — stroke volume, not rate, is the adjustable reserve (Clifton 1990). PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED: heart rate carries the upper range of the output rise, stroke volume rises early then plateaus (and expands to compensate when rate is blocked), and peripheral vasodilation is what permits the rise without a proportional pressure rise.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — cardiac output rises ~3–4-fold in exercise: stroke volume roughly doubles early then plateaus (and expands to fully compensate when beta-blockade caps heart rate), heart rate rises linearly and carries the upper range, and muscle vasodilation permits the rise (Guyton & Hall)

title: The baroreflex as the fast pressure buffer: bidirectional human reflex testing, ganglion blockade, and the tilt-table division of labour
question: In humans, how does the arterial baroreflex determine short-term blood pressure variability and the response to standing?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology and Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology). The textbooks cast the arterial baroreflex as the fast buffer of blood pressure: carotid-sinus and aortic-arch stretch receptors fire in proportion to pressure, and the medullary response adjusts vagal outflow to the heart within a beat or two and sympathetic outflow to heart and vessels over seconds — which is why the reflex dominates short-term (seconds-to-minutes) pressure variability while contributing little to the long-term pressure level, and why standing, which pools blood and unloads the receptors, is answered by reflex tachycardia and vasoconstriction. The carded human studies test each element with the classic tools. Neck-chamber suction/pressure and phenylephrine/nitroglycerin boluses move heart rate and pressure in the predicted reciprocal directions in man (Ferrari 1981). Ganglionic blockade shows how much resting pressure the autonomic (baroreflex-driven) system is holding up: trimethaphan dropped systolic pressure below 125 mmHg in every normotensive subject but left it at 164 mmHg in pure autonomic failure, where pressure is maintained without the reflex arc (Diedrich 2003). And during head-up tilt, abolishing the vagal cardiac limb left baroreflex control of pressure itself intact — standing pressure is defended mainly by sympathetic vasomotor control, with the cardiac limb chiefly vagal (Ogoh 2006). PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — the arterial baroreflex buffers short-term pressure variability and answers standing mainly through sympathetic vasomotor control, with a fast vagal cardiac limb (neck-chamber, drug-bolus and ganglion-blockade evidence in humans; Ganong; Guyton & Hall)

title: What drives aldosterone: potassium's hair-trigger, angiotensin II's sodium-set gain, and ACTH's fading third place — human dose-response evidence
question: In humans, what determines aldosterone secretion — the relative potency of potassium, angiotensin II and ACTH?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology and Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology). The textbooks rank the regulators of aldosterone: potassium is the most sensitive direct stimulus — the zona glomerulosa responds to changes within the physiological range too small to matter for any other hormone; angiotensin II is the second major stimulus, with adrenal sensitivity itself set by sodium balance; ACTH stimulates aldosterone only transiently, its chronic effect being permissive at most. The carded human dose-response studies are unusually exact matches to that ranking. Graded potassium infusions raised aldosterone by 46% in response to a plasma potassium increment of only 0.2 mEq/L (5%), with renin and angiotensin II unchanged — a direct adrenal effect operating across the 0.1–0.5 mEq/L band (Himathongkam 1975). Graded angiotensin II infusions showed the aldosterone dose-response slope steepening on a low-sodium diet, an adrenal sensitisation that persisted when captopril normalised the circulating angiotensin level — sodium status sets the gain (Dawson-Hughes 1981). And ACTH behaved exactly as the textbooks say: continuous cosyntropin drove aldosterone back to pre-infusion levels by 72 hours despite sustained cortisol stimulation, while pulsatile ACTH maintained it (Seely 1989). PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED: potassium first (direct, exquisitely sensitive), angiotensin II second (gain set by sodium balance), ACTH third and transient.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — aldosterone answers potassium first (a 0.2 mEq/L rise raised it 46% with renin/angiotensin II unchanged), angiotensin II second with adrenal gain set by sodium balance, and ACTH only transiently (continuous ACTH back to baseline by 72 h) — Guyton & Hall; Boron & Boulpaep

title: Vasopressin as the urine-concentration dial: osmotic threshold and sensitivity, water-load excretion, and the graded desmopressin response in humans
question: In humans, how does vasopressin (ADH) determine urine concentration and free water clearance across states of water balance?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology and Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology). The textbooks describe a steep osmotic control system: plasma vasopressin is essentially off below an osmotic threshold near 280–287 mosmol/kg, rises linearly with osmolality above it (roughly 0.3–0.5 pmol/L per mosmol/kg in the human studies carded here), and at the kidney converts that signal into urine concentration — maximal dilution with free water excretion when vasopressin is absent, maximal concentration when it is high. The carded human studies measure the whole loop. A 20 ml/kg water load suppressed vasopressin to about 0.5 pmol/L and healthy men excreted 95% of the load within 4 hours; hypertonic saline gave a vasopressin sensitivity of 0.33 pmol/L per mosmol/kg with a threshold of 287 mosmol/kg (Faull 1991). Graded intravenous desmopressin in 72 overhydrated healthy men raised urine osmolality dose-dependently with plasma level, with a modelled pharmacodynamic delay of about 4 hours (Juul 2013). Water loading and hypertonic saline produced the expected reciprocal changes in vasopressin, urine osmolality and free water clearance across the menstrual cycle, with osmotic thresholds shifting 5 mosmol/kg lower in the luteal phase (Vokes 1988). PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED: vasopressin, set by plasma osmolality against a threshold, determines urine concentration and free water clearance across water balance states.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — vasopressin is switched off below an osmotic threshold of ~287 mosmol/kg and rises ~0.33 pmol/L per mosmol/kg above it, and its level sets urine concentration and free water clearance across water-balance states (Ganong; Boron & Boulpaep)

title: Terlipressin versus octreotide in acute variceal bleeding: equal control and survival in head-to-head trials — the difference is tolerability
question: In adults with acute variceal bleeding, is terlipressin as effective as octreotide for controlling bleeding and improving survival?
balance: LIKELY (equivalence) — the head-to-head evidence says the two drugs control acute variceal bleeding equally, with no survival difference, and the only consistent separation is tolerability. The largest direct test, a 780-patient multicentre randomised noninferiority trial (Seo 2014), found 5-day treatment success of 86.2% on terlipressin versus 83.8% on octreotide, with mortality 8.0% versus 8.8% — both comfortably inside the prespecified 0.1 noninferiority margin. The double-blind adjuvant-to-banding trial (Abid 2009, 324 patients) agreed: bleeding control 92.6% versus 95.6%, in-hospital deaths 5.5% versus 4.3%. Pooling all 21 randomised trials of the two drug families (Huaringa-Marcelo 2021) gives a mortality relative risk of 1.01 (95% CI 0.83–1.22) — no difference (the treatment made no difference) — but significantly more adverse events with terlipressin/vasopressin than with octreotide/somatostatin (relative risk 2.39, 95% CI 1.58–3.63). PROPOSED LIKELY: terlipressin is as effective as octreotide for controlling bleeding and for survival; choose on adverse-effect profile, availability and local practice, not on expected efficacy. No shelf previously answered this head-to-head question (the terlipressin shelf in the library concerns hepatorenal syndrome, a different question).
stamp: LIKELY — terlipressin is as effective as octreotide for controlling acute variceal bleeding and for survival (5-day success 86.2% vs 83.8%; pooled mortality relative risk 1.01), with more adverse events at drug-family level (relative risk 2.39)

title: After a variceal bleed, ligation plus a beta-blocker beats ligation alone for rebleeding — survival benefit still unproven
question: In adults with cirrhosis who survive a variceal bleed, does combined band ligation plus a nonselective beta-blocker prevent rebleeding better than band ligation alone?
balance: LIKELY (rebleeding) — adding a nonselective beta-blocker to band ligation prevents variceal rebleeding better than ligation alone; a survival benefit is suggested but not proven. The direct multicentre trial (de la Peña 2005) found variceal rebleeding in 14% with ligation plus nadolol versus 38% with ligation alone (P = 0.006) over a median 16 months, with mortality statistically indistinguishable (11.6% versus 10.8% — the addition made no difference to survival in that trial). Pooling all five randomised comparisons of ligation with and without drug therapy (476 patients; Puente 2014) gives a rebleeding relative risk of 0.44 (95% CI 0.28–0.69) — a relative measure, with absolute rates of 14% versus 38% in the largest direct trial — and a mortality relative risk of 0.58 (0.33–1.03), a trend that does not reach significance. The asymmetry matters: adding ligation to drug therapy did not reduce rebleeding in the García-Pagán trial (1-year recurrence 26% versus 33%, P = 0.3) and added adverse events — the proven direction is drugs added to ligation, which is the comparison this shelf answers. The only neighbouring shelf, live #1678, asks whether simvastatin adds anything on top of combined standard prophylaxis; it does not answer this question. PROPOSED LIKELY for rebleeding prevention; mortality benefit unproven.
stamp: LIKELY (rebleeding) — ligation plus a nonselective beta-blocker cut rebleeding versus ligation alone (14% vs 38%; pooled relative risk 0.44); mortality benefit unproven (relative risk 0.58, 95% CI 0.33–1.03)

title: Albumin in spontaneous bacterial peritonitis: pooled halving of renal failure and death, resting on a small Sort-dominated base (Sort itself homed on #167)
question: In adults with spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, does albumin plus antibiotics reduce kidney failure and death compared with antibiotics alone?
balance: POSSIBLE — three independent meta-analyses agree that albumin added to antibiotics in spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) roughly halves renal impairment and death, but the underlying randomised base is only four small trials (288 patients), and it is dominated by one trial — Sort 1999 — which is already homed, with its figures, on live shelf #167 ('When does infusing albumin actually help patients with cirrhosis?'). FLAG (precedent-b pattern): Sort's PMID is on the gate list and is NOT carded here and no figure from it is reproduced; this shelf answers the narrower SBP-specific question from the free pooled reports, each of which necessarily includes Sort among its trials — the reader should know the pooled estimates lean on that homed trial. Within those limits: Salerno 2013 pooled renal impairment of 8.3% with albumin versus 30.6% without (odds ratio 0.21 relative) and mortality of 16.0% versus 35.4% (odds ratio 0.34 relative); Leache 2023 found an SBP mortality relative risk of 0.49 (95% CI 0.32–0.75, low certainty); Bai 2022 found an SBP-subgroup mortality odds ratio of 0.36 (0.20–0.64). Direction and rough size are consistent everywhere, which is why the stamp is POSSIBLE rather than MAYBE (weak evidence) — but a base this small and this dependent on one 1999 trial caps it below LIKELY. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: albumin plus antibiotics probably reduces kidney failure and death in SBP compared with antibiotics alone; guideline practice already treats it as standard for high-risk patients.
stamp: POSSIBLE — albumin plus antibiotics reduced renal impairment (8.3% vs 30.6%) and mortality (16.0% vs 35.4%) across pooled SBP trials, but the base is four small trials (288 patients) dominated by one homed trial (Sort 1999, live #167, not re-carded here)

title: Carvedilol versus propranolol on portal pressure (PARTIAL of #3594): a greater mean HVPG fall in every direct trial, an inconsistent responder advantage, and a bigger pressure cost
question: In adults with cirrhosis, does carvedilol reduce portal pressure more than propranolol as measured by hepatic venous pressure gradient?
balance: PARTIAL completion — read with pack #3594, which already homes the clinical-outcome question ('For primary prophylaxis of variceal bleeding, is carvedilol as effective as propranolol or other non-selective beta blockers?') through a network meta-analysis of bleeding and mortality. FLAG (precedent b): that network meta-analysis is the homed anchor for the wider question; its PMID is deliberately kept out of every card source line on this shelf, and none of its figures are used here. This shelf answers only the uncovered slice #3594 does not measure directly: the head-to-head hepatic venous pressure gradient (HVPG) comparison in direct randomised trials. On the continuous measure the direction is unanimous: carvedilol lowers HVPG more — acutely −20.4% versus −12.7% (Bañares 1999), chronically −19% versus −12% (Bañares 2002), −19.3% versus −12.5% in the one trial where the difference was not significant (Hobolth 2012, P = 0.21), and a pooled mean advantage of −1.75 mmHg / −8.02 percentage points across six trials in the Cochrane analysis (Zacharias 2018). On the responder definition (≥20% fall or to ≤12 mmHg) the picture splits: Bañares found significantly more responders on carvedilol (64% vs 14% acute; 54% vs 23% chronic), but the largest trial (Kim 2016, 110 patients) found 49.1% versus 30.9% (P = 0.08, not significant) and the Cochrane responder pooling was likewise non-significant (relative risk 0.76 for failure to respond, 95% CI 0.57–1.02). The cost is systemic: carvedilol lowered mean arterial pressure more (−23.1% vs −11% acutely; −11% vs −5% chronically) and expanded plasma volume in the chronic trial. PROPOSED LIKELY for the question as asked — carvedilol reduces portal pressure more than propranolol on mean HVPG — with the responder-proportion inconsistency and the hypotension cost printed on the face.
stamp: LIKELY — carvedilol reduces HVPG more than propranolol on the mean (pooled −1.75 mmHg / −8.02 percentage points; every direct trial in the same direction), though the responder-proportion advantage was non-significant in the largest trial and Cochrane pooling, and carvedilol lowers arterial pressure more (PARTIAL of #3594: direct HVPG slice only)

title: Albumin in acute-on-chronic liver failure (PARTIAL completion of pack #2522): setting-specific signals — paracentesis cover and a bundle study positive, resuscitation-fluid trial null on survival
question: In adults with acute-on-chronic liver failure, does albumin infusion improve survival versus standard care?
balance: POSSIBLE — printed on the face, on ACLF-specific evidence only. This pack is a PARTIAL completion: pack #2522 already answers targeted albumin infusions in hospitalised decompensated cirrhosis broadly (the ATTIRE trial, homed there and NOT re-carded here — ATTIRE found no overall benefit in that broader population), and pack #2515 covers long-term outpatient albumin in decompensated cirrhosis with ascites. The uncovered slice is the ACLF population itself, and its direct evidence is thin and mixed. One small randomised trial in ACLF patients having a modest-volume paracentesis found albumin cover halved in-hospital mortality (27.5% vs 62.5%) alongside less circulatory dysfunction, kidney injury and encephalopathy. One prospective observational cohort of 230 ACLF patients found higher 28-day survival with a response-guided albumin-containing bundle (albumin–furosemide infusion ± a vasoconstrictor) than with standard medical therapy (75.7% vs 53.2%) — but the albumin cannot be separated from the bundle. The nearest randomised albumin-versus-other-fluid trial in critically ill cirrhosis (sepsis-induced hypotension, not enrolled by ACLF criteria) improved blood pressure faster with 20% albumin but made no difference to 28-day survival (58% vs 62%) and caused more pulmonary complications. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: albumin probably helps in specific ACLF settings (paracentesis cover; as part of volume/haemodynamic support), but a general survival benefit of albumin infusion in ACLF is not established, and the broad-population trial homed on #2522 was null.
stamp: POSSIBLE — in ACLF, albumin cover for paracentesis reduced circulatory dysfunction and in-hospital death in one small randomised trial, and an albumin-containing bundle was linked to better 28-day survival observationally, but albumin versus another fluid in critically ill cirrhosis improved blood pressure without improving survival; a general survival benefit in ACLF is unproven

title: Direct-acting antivirals in decompensated cirrhosis (PARTIAL completion of pack #2672): high cure rates even in Child-Pugh B/C, liver function improves after cure, survival benefit from programme comparisons
question: In adults with chronic hepatitis C and decompensated cirrhosis, do direct-acting antivirals improve liver function and survival?
balance: LIKELY — printed on the face. This pack is a PARTIAL completion: pack #2672 covers 8-week glecaprevir–pibrentasvir cure in patients without cirrhosis or with compensated cirrhosis, pack #5967 covers cure in compensated cirrhosis, and live #593 covers DAA cure rates generally. The uncovered slice is decompensated (Child-Pugh B/C) disease, and here the trials agree: sofosbuvir-based regimens cured roughly 83–94% of Child-Pugh B patients (ASTRAL-4) and 78–96% across the SOLAR-2 Child-Pugh B/C groups, with cure rates falling in Child-Pugh C (ALLY-1: 93% in Child-Pugh A/B vs 56% in class C). Cure was followed by better liver function: in the English expanded-access programme, MELD scores improved on treatment (−0.85) while they worsened in untreated patients (+0.75), and over 15 months serious decompensation events fell compared with untreated patients, though new liver cancers still occurred and some patients still died or needed transplant. No placebo-controlled survival trial exists or could now ethically be run, so the survival claim rests on these treated-versus-untreated programme comparisons. PROPOSED LIKELY: DAAs cure most patients with decompensated cirrhosis and improve liver function; a survival benefit is supported by cohort comparisons, not by a randomised survival trial.
stamp: LIKELY — sofosbuvir-based DAAs cured 83–94% of Child-Pugh B and most Child-Pugh C patients across ASTRAL-4, SOLAR-2 and ALLY-1, MELD scores improved after treatment while untreated patients worsened, and decompensation events fell; the survival benefit rests on treated-versus-untreated programme comparisons, not a randomised survival trial

title: Enzyme replacement after pancreatic surgery (PARTIAL completion of pack #3591): null as prescribed, positive as taken — the post-pancreatectomy slice
question: In adults with pancreatic exocrine insufficiency after pancreatic surgery, does enzyme replacement improve fat absorption and weight?
balance: POSSIBLE — printed on the face. This pack is a PARTIAL completion: pack #3591 covers enzyme replacement in chronic pancreatitis, and the mixed chronic-pancreatitis/pancreatic-surgery fat-absorption trial evidence is already carded elsewhere in the library and is not re-carded here. The uncovered slice is the post-pancreatectomy population on its own, and its dedicated evidence is thinner and mixed. The one large placebo-controlled trial after pancreatoduodenectomy (304 patients, named product Norzyme) found no weight benefit in the intention-to-treat analysis — the treatment made no difference — but among patients who actually completed the protocol, the enzyme group gained 1.09 kg while placebo lost 2.28 kg, and poor compliance predicted weight loss. A small randomised trial found high-dose pancrelipase did not significantly reduce post-pancreatectomy fatty liver versus conventional enzyme supplementation (21% vs 39%; the treatment made no difference). A retrospective cohort of 469 cancer pancreatoduodenectomy patients found enzyme use independently associated with better survival (hazard ratio 0.72), an association, not proof. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: enzyme replacement plausibly improves nutrition and weight after pancreatic surgery when actually taken at adequate dose — the trial record does not show a benefit for simply prescribing it.
stamp: POSSIBLE — after pancreatoduodenectomy the one large placebo-controlled trial was null on weight as prescribed (intention-to-treat) but positive as taken (per-protocol, +3.37 kg vs placebo), a small trial found no significant fatty-liver advantage over conventional enzymes, and a cohort linked enzyme use to better survival observationally

title: Combined oral and rectal mesalamine for ulcerative colitis induction: adding the enema raised remission from 43% to 64% in extensive disease
question: In adults with ulcerative colitis, is combined oral and rectal mesalamine more effective than oral mesalamine alone for inducing remission?
balance: LIKELY — printed on the face. The direct trial is PINCE (127 patients with extensive mild-to-moderate ulcerative colitis): adding a 1 g mesalamine enema nightly for the first 4 weeks to oral mesalamine 4 g/day raised remission at 8 weeks from 43% to 64% (p = 0.03), with improvement already separating at 4 weeks (89% vs 62%). Meta-analysis agrees: pooling the combined-versus-oral trials, combined therapy cut the risk of failing to achieve remission (relative risk 0.65, 95% CI 0.47–0.91; number needed to treat 5), and a 40-trial network meta-analysis ranked combined oral + topical therapy first or second for induction, and first in trials dominated by left-sided or extensive disease — the population in whom the rectal component can reach the worst-affected bowel. The benefit is clearest in extensive disease; for disease confined to the rectum, topical therapy alone ranked highest. PROPOSED LIKELY: combined oral and rectal mesalamine induces remission more often than oral mesalamine alone in mild-to-moderate ulcerative colitis, particularly extensive disease.
stamp: LIKELY — combined oral + rectal mesalamine beat oral mesalamine alone for inducing remission in the PINCE trial (64% vs 43% at 8 weeks) and in meta-analysis (relative risk of failing to achieve remission 0.65, number needed to treat 5), with the clearest benefit in extensive disease

title: Mesalamine dose in ulcerative colitis (ASCEND I–III): 4.8 g/day helps in moderate disease, not in mild — a severity split
question: In adults with mild to moderate ulcerative colitis, is high-dose mesalamine more effective than standard-dose mesalamine for inducing remission?
balance: SPLIT (severity) — printed on the face. The ASCEND programme asked the same question three times with the same answer pattern. In the whole mild-to-moderate population (ASCEND I, 301 patients), 4.8 g/day was not significantly better than 2.4 g/day (treatment success 56% vs 51%; the higher dose made no difference overall). In patients with moderate disease, the higher dose won each time: ASCEND I's prespecified moderate subgroup 72% vs 57% (p = 0.038), ASCEND II's moderate primary population 72% vs 59% (p = 0.036), and ASCEND III (772 patients, all moderate) met non-inferiority with a remission advantage for 4.8 g/day (43% vs 35%; p = 0.04), the advantage concentrated in patients previously treated with steroids or multiple ulcerative colitis medications. Tolerability was similar at both doses in all three trials. PROPOSED SPLIT (severity): high-dose mesalamine (4.8 g/day) is more effective than 2.4 g/day in moderately active ulcerative colitis; no advantage has been shown in mild disease.
stamp: SPLIT (severity) — 4.8 g/day beat 2.4 g/day in moderately active ulcerative colitis across the ASCEND trials (treatment success up to 72% vs 59%; remission 43% vs 35% in ASCEND III), but made no difference in the overall mild-to-moderate population of ASCEND I (56% vs 51%)

title: Once-daily versus twice-daily mesalamine for ulcerative colitis maintenance: equally effective in three trials and a meta-analysis
question: In adults with ulcerative colitis in remission, is once-daily mesalamine as effective as twice-daily mesalamine for maintaining remission?
balance: LIKELY — printed on the face, as an equivalence answer: once-daily mesalamine maintains remission as well as twice-daily dosing. The head-to-head trials agree. MMX mesalamine 2.4 g/day given once or in two divided doses held clinical and endoscopic remission at 12 months in 64.4% vs 68.5% of patients (no significant difference). Prolonged-release mesalamine granules 2 g once daily actually outperformed 1 g twice daily at 1 year (70.9% vs 58.9% in remission; p = 0.024), with better self-reported adherence. A 6-month endoscopic-remission trial (826 patients) met its non-inferiority objective for once-daily MMX. Pooling 7 trials (2,745 patients), relapse risk did not differ between once-daily and conventional schedules (relative risk 0.94, 95% CI 0.82–1.08), nor did adverse events. PROPOSED LIKELY: once-daily mesalamine is as effective as twice-daily mesalamine for maintaining remission — the point of the simpler schedule is adherence, and the trials show no efficacy price for it.
stamp: LIKELY — once-daily mesalamine maintained remission as well as twice-daily dosing in three head-to-head trials (64.4% vs 68.5% at 12 months for MMX; non-inferior endoscopic remission in 826 patients) and in a 7-trial meta-analysis (relapse relative risk 0.94, 95% CI 0.82–1.08)

title: Combined surgical closure plus anti-TNF for perianal fistulizing Crohn's (PISA programme): better MRI healing and fewer re-interventions, clinical closure not yet separated
question: In adults with perianal fistulizing Crohn's disease, does combined surgical drainage plus anti-TNF therapy heal fistulas better than anti-TNF therapy alone?
balance: POSSIBLE — printed on the face. Confirm-first check (done at build): at least three free reports with ≥10 patients exist — the two PISA trials and the comparative systematic review carded here. Read the question precisely: in the PISA programme every patient first received seton drainage; the tested strategy was then surgical closure under a short course of anti-TNF versus continuing anti-TNF alone for a year. On that comparison, PISA-II (94 patients) found radiological (MRI) healing at 18 months in 32% with closure plus anti-TNF versus 9% with anti-TNF alone (p = 0.005), and far fewer re-interventions (13% vs 43%), though clinical closure did not differ significantly (68% vs 52%). The earlier PISA randomised trial (44 patients, stopped early for futility) likewise found fewest re-interventions in the surgical-closure-after-anti-TNF arm (3/14) versus anti-TNF alone (6/15) and seton drainage alone (10/15). A systematic review of seton and anti-TNF studies found the cohort studies that directly compared strategies favoured combined treatment in two of four. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: adding a surgical step (closure after drainage) to anti-TNF probably improves deep (MRI) healing and reduces re-interventions; the clinical-closure advantage is not yet significant, and no trial isolates drainage-plus-anti-TNF against anti-TNF with no surgical contact at all.
stamp: POSSIBLE — adding surgical closure (after seton drainage) to anti-TNF tripled MRI healing at 18 months in PISA-II (32% vs 9%) and reduced re-interventions in both PISA trials, but clinical closure was not significantly better (68% vs 52%) and the randomised base is small and partly preference-based

title: Balloon dilation for Crohn's strictures (observational evidence only — shelve with care): usually postpones surgery, repeat dilation the rule, no randomised comparison with surgery
question: In adults with Crohn's disease and a symptomatic stricture, does endoscopic balloon dilation delay or avoid surgery compared with surgery alone?
balance: POSSIBLE (observational) — printed on the face, and this shelf should be shelved with care: there is NO randomised trial of balloon dilation against surgery for Crohn's strictures. Everything here is observational. What the series show: dilation usually works technically (89.1% of 3,213 procedures in a 1,463-patient pooled analysis) and relieves symptoms short-term (clinical efficacy 80.8%), with complications in 2.8% of procedures — but the benefit erodes: by 24 months, 73.5% of patients had been re-dilated and 42.9% had come to surgical resection, so dilation more often delays than permanently avoids surgery. Strictures of 5 cm or less fared best. The one direct comparison (79 patients, retrospective) found surgery more durable — re-intervention was more likely after dilation (odds ratio 5.62) — with similar major-complication rates (about 7.5% in both groups). A double-balloon dilation cohort kept 78.1% of patients surgery-free at 3 years, showing the delay can be long in selected patients. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (observational): dilation is a reasonable first move for short, accessible strictures to postpone surgery, accepting that repeat dilation is the rule and a large minority still reach surgery within two years.
stamp: POSSIBLE (observational) — no randomised trial exists: pooled series show dilation relieves symptoms in ~81% but 42.9% still reach surgery by 24 months, and the one direct comparison found re-intervention more likely after dilation than surgery (odds ratio 5.62); dilation delays surgery more reliably than it avoids it

title: Budesonide maintenance in microscopic colitis (PARTIAL completion of live #778): strong maintenance evidence — in collagenous colitis — with relapse after stopping
question: In adults with microscopic colitis, does low-dose budesonide maintain remission versus placebo after induction?
balance: LIKELY — printed on the face, with a population flag: every maintenance trial was in collagenous colitis, one of the two microscopic-colitis subtypes; maintenance in lymphocytic colitis has not been trialled in these reports. This pack is a PARTIAL completion: live #778 covers budesonide induction in microscopic colitis only. For maintenance after induction, two placebo-controlled trials agree strongly. Budesonide 6 mg/day for 24 weeks held remission in 76.5% versus 12% on placebo (Bonderup 2009). Low-dose budesonide (mean 4.5 mg/day) for 12 months held remission in 61.4% versus 16.7% (Münch 2016). A pooled analysis of the randomised programme found that not receiving maintenance therapy more than doubled relapse hazard (hazard ratio 2.71) and shortened median time to relapse from 207 to 56 days. The catch is what happens on stopping: relapse is the rule within weeks to months (82.1% relapsed during treatment-free follow-up in Münch), so maintenance works while it is taken rather than curing the tendency to relapse. PROPOSED LIKELY: low-dose budesonide maintains remission in collagenous colitis for as long as it is continued.
stamp: LIKELY — low-dose budesonide maintained remission far better than placebo after induction in collagenous colitis (76.5% vs 12% at 24 weeks on 6 mg/day; 61.4% vs 16.7% at 12 months on ~4.5 mg/day), with relapse the rule after stopping; maintenance in lymphocytic colitis is untrialled

title: Methylnaltrexone in chronic non-cancer pain (PARTIAL completion of live #1797): prompt laxation by injection or tablet in two phase 3 programmes
question: In adults with opioid-induced constipation, does methylnaltrexone improve bowel function versus placebo?
balance: LIKELY — printed on the face. This pack is a PARTIAL completion: live #1797 covers subcutaneous methylnaltrexone in advanced illness. The uncovered slice is chronic non-cancer pain, and it has its own two phase 3 placebo-controlled programmes. Subcutaneous methylnaltrexone 12 mg (daily or alternate-day) produced a rescue-free bowel movement within 4 hours of the first dose in 34.2% of patients versus 9.9% on placebo (number needed to treat about 4; Michna 2011, 460 patients). Oral methylnaltrexone (300–450 mg daily) beat placebo on the same kind of endpoint, with responders at 49.3–51.5% versus 38.3% (Rauck 2017, 803 patients). A crossover analysis of the subcutaneous programme confirmed the effect within the same patients (9.7% responding on placebo versus 45.9% after crossing to methylnaltrexone). Pain scores and opioid doses did not worsen and withdrawal was not seen in these programmes — the drug acts peripherally — while abdominal pain, nausea and diarrhoea were the common adverse effects. PROPOSED LIKELY: methylnaltrexone improves bowel function versus placebo in opioid-induced constipation in chronic non-cancer pain, by either route.
stamp: LIKELY — in chronic non-cancer pain, subcutaneous methylnaltrexone produced a rescue-free bowel movement within 4 hours in 34.2% vs 9.9% on placebo and oral methylnaltrexone raised responder rates to 49.3–51.5% vs 38.3%, in two phase 3 placebo-controlled programmes

title: Acute cholangitis: ERCP within 24 hours is associated with lower in-hospital mortality in observational timing studies — the only randomised trial tested drainage against surgery, not timing
question: In adults with acute cholangitis, does early ERCP drainage within 24 hours improve survival compared with delayed drainage?
balance: POSSIBLE (observational evidence for the timing comparison) — every timing study behind the Tokyo Guidelines' early-drainage recommendation is observational. Pooled across 14 observational studies (84,063 patients), ERCP within 24 hours was associated with lower in-hospital mortality than later drainage (odds ratio 0.81, 95% CI 0.73–0.90 — a relative measure; overall pooled in-hospital mortality was 1.9%), and a second meta-analysis of 7 non-randomised studies (88,562 patients) found the same direction for in-hospital mortality but no difference in 30-day mortality. The only randomised trial in the field (Lai 1992) did not test timing at all: it tested emergency endoscopic drainage against emergency surgery in severe cholangitis and found hospital mortality of 10% versus 32%. A large US inpatient cohort found mortality highest when ERCP was never performed or was delayed beyond 48 hours, with no mortality difference between ERCP within 24 hours and at 24–48 hours. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (observational): drainage within 24 hours is associated with lower in-hospital mortality, but the survival claim rests on observational timing data plus a randomised trial of drainage versus surgery — not on a randomised timing trial, which does not exist.
stamp: POSSIBLE (observational evidence for the timing comparison) — ERCP within 24 hours was associated with lower in-hospital mortality than later drainage in pooled observational studies (odds ratio 0.81, a relative measure), and emergency endoscopic drainage itself beat emergency surgery in the one randomised trial (10% versus 32% hospital mortality); no randomised trial has tested drainage timing directly

title: Urgent colonoscopy for acute lower gastrointestinal bleeding: finds the source sooner in one trial, improves no clinical outcome in any — elective timing is as good (LIKELY, the treatment made no difference)
question: In adults with acute lower gastrointestinal bleeding, does urgent colonoscopy within 24 hours improve outcomes compared with elective colonoscopy?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — three randomised trials and their meta-analysis agree. Urgent colonoscopy found a definite bleeding source more often in Green 2005 (odds ratio 2.6 for the difference — a relative measure), but in no trial did it reduce further bleeding, transfusion, length of stay, surgery or death: Laine & Shah 2010 found further bleeding in 22% on urgent versus 14% on elective colonoscopy; Niikura 2020, the largest trial, found stigmata of recent haemorrhage in 21.5% versus 21.3% and 30-day rebleeding in 15.3% versus 6.7% (not significant); the meta-analysis of the 4 randomised trials (463 patients) found no significant difference in stay, transfusion, additional intervention or mortality. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): in hospitalised acute lower gastrointestinal bleeding, colonoscopy within 24 hours does not improve clinical outcomes compared with elective colonoscopy — timing can be set by stability, bowel preparation and local logistics rather than by the clock.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — urgent colonoscopy within 24 hours did not reduce further bleeding, transfusion, length of stay, surgery or mortality versus elective colonoscopy in three randomised trials and their meta-analysis (463 randomised patients)

title: Capsule endoscopy after negative bidirectional endoscopy in iron deficiency anaemia: finds a lesion in about half and a likely source in ~40% — a yield question, not an outcomes question
question: In adults with iron deficiency anemia and negative bidirectional endoscopy, does small bowel capsule endoscopy find a bleeding source?
balance: POSSIBLE (observational evidence — this is a diagnostic-yield question, not a patient-outcome question) — capsule endoscopy finds something in about half of these patients. The 2012 systematic review (24 studies, 1,960 patients) pooled a diagnostic yield of 47% (95% CI 42%–52%), rising to 66.6% in studies enrolling only iron-deficiency-anaemia patients; the 2024 meta-analysis (12 studies, 1,703 patients without overt bleeding) found any small-bowel lesion in 61% but a lesion likely responsible for the anaemia in only 40%. In the one cohort matching this shelf's exact population — asymptomatic iron deficiency anaemia after negative bidirectional endoscopy (Kay 2025, 75 patients) — the yield was lower: 36% abnormal, only 8% actionable, angiodysplasia the commonest finding and no malignancies. Yield is not benefit: none of these studies shows that finding a source improves haemoglobin, transfusion or survival, and this shelf's stamp answers only the question asked — whether a source is found. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (observational, yield only): expect a lesion in roughly half, a plausibly responsible lesion in about 40%, and an actionable finding in under 1 in 10 of the asymptomatic exact-population patients.
stamp: POSSIBLE (observational evidence — diagnostic yield, not patient outcomes) — capsule endoscopy finds a small-bowel lesion in roughly half of adults with iron deficiency anaemia after negative bidirectional endoscopy (pooled yield 47–61% for any lesion, ~40% for a lesion likely responsible, 8% actionable in the exact-population cohort)

title: Healed erosive oesophagitis: daily maintenance PPI beats on-demand therapy for staying in remission (81% versus 58%) — the erosive slice left open by pack #5661
question: In adults with erosive esophagitis, does maintenance proton pump inhibitor therapy prevent relapse better than on-demand therapy after healing?
balance: PARTIAL completion of pack #5661, which answers on-demand versus daily proton pump inhibitor therapy in non-erosive reflux disease; this shelf covers the slice #5661 leaves open — patients whose erosive oesophagitis has healed. POSSIBLE — the one large head-to-head trial in exactly this population (Sjöstedt 2005, 477 patients randomised after healing) found 6-month remission in 81% on daily esomeprazole 20 mg versus 58% on on-demand treatment (P < 0.0001), with the gap wider in more severe baseline grades; overall symptomatic remission did not differ, though heartburn was more prevalent on demand. The systematic review of on-demand maintenance (Pace 2007, 17 studies, of which 2 enrolled erosive oesophagitis only) reached the matching conclusion: on-demand therapy is effective in non-erosive, mild and uninvestigated disease but not in (severe) erosive oesophagitis. In milder mixed disease (Bour 2005: non-erosive or grade 1–2 oesophagitis with frequent relapses), symptom relief at 6 months was 86.4% on continuous versus 74.6% on on-demand rabeprazole — not significant — at about a third of the drug use. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: after healing of erosive oesophagitis, daily maintenance prevents endoscopic relapse better than on-demand therapy; the advantage is endoscopic first, symptomatic second, and smallest in mild grades.
stamp: POSSIBLE — daily maintenance proton pump inhibitor therapy prevented relapse of healed erosive oesophagitis better than on-demand therapy (remission 81% versus 58% at 6 months in the one large head-to-head trial, concordant with the systematic review); symptom relief in mild disease was closer, and on-demand therapy used about a third as much drug

title: Bedtime H2 blocker added to twice-daily PPI: better nighttime acid control on night one, gone by week one — the slice left open by live #2654
question: In adults with reflux symptoms that do not respond to twice-daily proton pump inhibitors, does adding a bedtime H2 blocker improve nighttime acid control?
balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #2654, which covers H2 blockers for reflux generally; this shelf covers the uncovered slice — a bedtime H2 blocker added to twice-daily proton pump inhibitor therapy. SPLIT (duration) — the small pH studies agree that the add-on works on the first nights and disagree with its own continuation. Peghini 1998 (12 healthy volunteers on twice-daily omeprazole) found bedtime ranitidine cut the percentage of the night with intragastric pH <4 from 48% (bedtime placebo) to 5–6%. Xue 2001 (105 patients with reflux disease on twice-daily proton pump inhibitors) found nocturnal acid breakthrough in 82% without versus 40% with a bedtime H2 blocker, and median overnight time with pH >4 of 51% versus 96%. But Fackler 2002 — the only study that kept measuring (43 subjects) — found the advantage present on day 1 of the H2 blocker and gone by day 7 and day 28: tolerance. Orr 2003 (19 patients) adds a second caution: gastric acidity fell, but oesophageal reflux measures did not change. No carded study enrolled documented twice-daily-PPI non-responders as such, and none measured symptom relief as the primary outcome. PROPOSED SPLIT (duration): a bedtime H2 blocker improves nighttime gastric acid control acutely; sustained benefit beyond a week is not supported, and symptom benefit in true non-responders is untested.
stamp: SPLIT (duration) — a bedtime H2 blocker improves nocturnal gastric acid control on the first nights in small pH studies (breakthrough 82% without versus 40% with), but the only study that kept measuring found the advantage gone by one week (tolerance), and no study measured symptom relief in documented twice-daily-PPI non-responders

title: Grade II haemorrhoids: band ligation versus infrared coagulation — about equal efficacy, banding hurts more (the comparator live #1938 does not cover)
question: In adults with hemorrhoids, does rubber band ligation work better than infrared coagulation for grade II hemorrhoids?
balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #1938, which compares haemorrhoidal artery ligation with rubber band ligation; this shelf covers the infrared-coagulation comparator #1938 does not. SPLIT (outcome) — the head-to-head trials find the two office procedures close on efficacy and consistently apart on pain. In the trial restricted to grade II bleeding piles (Gupta 2003, 100 patients), band ligation controlled symptoms better but hurt more, and coagulation patients returned to work sooner (2 versus 4 days) yet recurred or failed more often (P = 0.03 for both comparisons). Templeton 1983 (137 patients, grades I–II) found satisfactory outcomes in 92% after banding versus 85% after coagulation, with significantly more discomfort after banding (P < 0.001). Poen 2000 (133 patients) found 97% versus 92% symptom-free or improved, pain scores of 5.5 versus 3.3 (P = 0.018), and relapse of 18% versus 20% at about 19 months. The 2023 meta-analysis of 9 randomised trials found no significant difference in efficacy, prolapse, recurrence or urinary retention, with more postoperative pain after banding and less postoperative bleeding. PROPOSED SPLIT (outcome): banding is not clearly better — efficacy is about equal with a small durability edge in some trials, bought with more pain; coagulation is the gentler, more repeatable procedure.
stamp: SPLIT (outcome) — rubber band ligation and infrared coagulation controlled grade II haemorrhoids about equally (satisfactory outcomes 92–97% versus 85–92%; no efficacy difference in the 2023 meta-analysis of 9 trials), with more recurrence or failure after coagulation in the grade II trial but consistently more pain after band ligation

title: Wilson disease maintenance: trientine non-inferior to penicillamine for copper control in CHELATE — the head-to-head live #2119 does not cover
question: In adults with Wilson disease, is trientine as effective as penicillamine for maintaining copper control?
balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #2119, which compares tetrathiomolybdate with trientine in newly presenting neurological Wilson disease; this shelf covers the maintenance head-to-head #2119 does not — trientine versus penicillamine in patients already stabilised. POSSIBLE — the one randomised head-to-head trial, CHELATE (2022), switched 53 patients who had been stable on penicillamine for at least a year to trientine tetrahydrochloride or kept them on penicillamine: non-caeruloplasmin-bound copper at 24 weeks differed by −9.1 μg/L (95% CI −24.2 to 6.1), inside the −50 μg/L non-inferiority margin, non-inferiority held at 48 weeks, and masked adjudication confirmed clinical stability in 100% of participants in both groups. The supporting cohorts are switch populations: 77 patients moved to trientine dihydrochloride after penicillamine withdrawal kept or improved hepatic symptoms in about 85% over a mean of 8 years with no progression to liver failure or transplant (Weiss 2022), and 51 patients maintained on trientine dihydrochloride prospectively were 98% responders at 12 months (Mohr 2025). PROPOSED POSSIBLE: yes — for maintaining copper control in stable patients, trientine performed as well as penicillamine in the single non-inferiority trial, with long-term cohort experience consistent; the trial does not address initial decoppering of newly diagnosed patients.
stamp: POSSIBLE — trientine was non-inferior to penicillamine for maintaining copper control in the one head-to-head randomised trial (CHELATE, 53 stable patients; non-caeruloplasmin-bound copper difference −9.1 μg/L, inside the −50 μg/L margin), with long-term switch cohorts consistent

title: Zinc for hepatic encephalopathy: psychometric scores improve in small trials (zinc acetate; polaprezinc) — recurrence and survival benefit unproven
question: In adults with cirrhosis and hepatic encephalopathy, does zinc supplementation improve encephalopathy versus standard therapy alone?
balance: POSSIBLE — zinc improves the psychometric tests by which mild encephalopathy is measured, in small trials, without a demonstrated effect on recurrence or survival. Reding 1984 randomised 22 patients with chronic encephalopathy to zinc acetate 600 mg/day or placebo for 7 days and found trail-making performance improved only in the supplemented group. Takuma 2010 randomised 79 patients to polaprezinc 225 mg/day added to standard therapy (protein-restricted diet including branched-chain amino acids, plus lactulose) or standard therapy alone for 6 months: encephalopathy grade, ammonia, Child-Pugh score and neuropsychological tests all improved significantly more with zinc, and physical quality of life improved while mental quality of life did not. Two meta-analyses pool the same small trial base: Chavez-Tapia 2013 (4 trials, 233 patients) found better number-connection-test performance (standardised mean difference −0.62) but no significant reduction in encephalopathy recurrence (relative risk 0.64, 95% CI 0.26–1.59) and no mortality data; Shen 2019 (4 trials, 247 patients) found the number-connection benefit for zinc added to lactulose (standardised mean difference −0.97, moderate certainty) but no significant difference in digit-symbol performance or ammonia. A further preliminary placebo-controlled trial (Katayama 2014; 18 enrolled, 12 analysed, cirrhosis with hyperammonaemia and low zinc) found ammonia fell on zinc acetate 150 mg/day — described here in prose, not carded, because of its size and its hyperammonaemia (rather than overt encephalopathy) population. On preparations (the clarification exception for supplements): the publications name zinc acetate (Reding; Katayama) and polaprezinc, a zinc–carnosine compound (Takuma); the meta-analyses pooled 'any oral zinc supplementation' without a single tested product, so no one preparation carries the pooled claim, and currently sold zinc products may differ from those tested. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: zinc supplementation improves psychometric encephalopathy measures versus standard therapy alone; benefit on recurrence, hospitalisation or death is unproven.
stamp: POSSIBLE — zinc supplementation improved psychometric encephalopathy tests versus standard therapy alone in small trials and their meta-analyses (number-connection standardised mean difference −0.62 to −0.97), but did not significantly reduce encephalopathy recurrence (relative risk 0.64, 95% CI 0.26–1.59) and no trial reported mortality; tested preparations were zinc acetate and polaprezinc

title: Uncomplicated diverticulitis needing antibiotics: oral therapy matched intravenous therapy in three small randomised trials — the route question live #178 and DINAMO do not ask
question: In adults with uncomplicated diverticulitis who need antibiotics, is oral therapy as effective as intravenous therapy?
balance: POSSIBLE — three small randomised trials, all concordant, none large or blinded. This shelf asks the route question in patients who are receiving antibiotics; it is distinct from live shelf #178 and pack #3621 (DINAMO), which ask whether antibiotics can be omitted altogether, and neither of those is re-carded here. McClintock 2024 randomised 118 patients with CT-proven uncomplicated diverticulitis (modified Hinchey 0–1a) to oral or intravenous antibiotics — both delivered as outpatients through a Hospital-in-the-Home service — and found no significant difference in 30-day unplanned admissions, inflammatory markers, pain resolution or return to normal nutrition and bowel function, meeting its non-inferiority design. Ridgway 2009 randomised 79 patients with clinically diagnosed uncomplicated diverticulitis to oral or intravenous ciprofloxacin plus metronidazole: no oral patient needed conversion to intravenous therapy, symptoms resolved completely in both groups, and day-3 tenderness was equivalent. Ribas 2010 tested the step-down version — a short intravenous course of amoxicillin-clavulanic acid followed by oral therapy and early discharge versus 7 days of intravenous therapy in 50 patients — with no significant difference in treatment failure and a saving of €1,244 per patient. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: in uncomplicated diverticulitis selected for antibiotic treatment, oral therapy performs as well as intravenous therapy; the trials are small, mostly unblinded, and enrolled patients well enough that route was genuinely in equipoise.
stamp: POSSIBLE — oral antibiotics performed as well as intravenous therapy in three small randomised trials of uncomplicated diverticulitis (79, 50 and 118 patients; one a step-down design, one with both routes given to outpatients), with no conversions, failures or readmission signals favouring the intravenous route

title: Standard-dose ursodeoxycholic acid in primary sclerosing cholangitis (PARTIAL completion of pack #2782): liver tests improve, transplant-free survival does not
question: In adults with primary sclerosing cholangitis, does standard-dose ursodeoxycholic acid improve transplant-free survival versus no treatment?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — printed on the face. This pack is a PARTIAL completion: pack #2782 already answers the high-dose question (high-dose ursodeoxycholic acid improved biochemistry but caused harm); this shelf asks the separate standard-dose efficacy question #2782 leaves open, and no high-dose PMID is re-carded here. The one standard-dose placebo trial (Lindor 1997, 13–15 mg/kg/day, 105 patients) found no difference in time to treatment failure (relative risk 1.01) and no difference in time to liver transplantation, despite clear improvement in alkaline phosphatase, transaminases, bilirubin and albumin. Two meta-analyses of the randomised trials (Shi 2009, 465 patients; Triantos 2011, 567 patients across standard- and high-dose trials) agree: no significant effect on death, liver transplantation, or death and/or transplantation combined. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): standard-dose ursodeoxycholic acid improves liver blood tests in primary sclerosing cholangitis but has not been shown to improve transplant-free survival.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — standard-dose ursodeoxycholic acid improved liver blood tests but did not improve transplant-free survival in the one standard-dose placebo trial or in either meta-analysis of the randomised trials

title: Endoscopic surveillance in gastric intestinal metaplasia (observational only): the cancer risk is real and quantified, but no study shows surveillance prevents gastric cancer death
question: In adults with gastric intestinal metaplasia, does endoscopic surveillance reduce gastric cancer death versus no surveillance?
balance: POSSIBLE (observational) — printed on the face, because this is a GAP-E question and the evidence is observational by design: there is no randomised comparison of surveillance versus no surveillance in gastric intestinal metaplasia, and no carded study compares gastric cancer death between surveyed and unsurveilled patients. What the cohorts do establish is the risk surveillance would have to act on: in the Dutch nationwide cohort (de Vries 2008), intestinal metaplasia carried an annual gastric cancer incidence of 0.25% within 5 years of diagnosis, yet only 28% of intestinal-metaplasia patients received any re-evaluation — surveillance practice was inconsistent with the risk. The Swedish population cohort (Song 2015) puts the annual incidence at 129 per 100,000 (standardised incidence ratio 3.4 versus the general population) and estimates about 1 in 39 people with intestinal metaplasia develops gastric cancer within 20 years. The only carded study that compares surveillance strategies (Zhang 2018, China) found that in extensive atrophic gastritis/intestinal metaplasia a 2–3-year surveillance interval was associated with earlier detection of gastric cancer — earlier detection, not shown lower mortality. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (observational): surveillance detects cancers in a genuinely at-risk group and may shift stage at detection, but a reduction in gastric cancer death versus no surveillance has never been demonstrated.
stamp: POSSIBLE (observational) — no randomised trial and no direct surveillance-versus-none mortality comparison exists; cohorts put the annual gastric cancer incidence in intestinal metaplasia at about 0.25% and one cohort links a 2–3-year surveillance interval in extensive disease to earlier cancer detection, so a death benefit is plausible but unproven

title: Pregabalin for chronic pancreatitis pain: one small positive placebo trial, a combination trial that cannot isolate the drug, and a mechanistic substudy of the same patients
question: In adults with chronic pancreatitis, does pregabalin reduce pain versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE — printed on the face, because the direct evidence is a single small short trial. Olesen 2011 randomised 64 patients with painful chronic pancreatitis to escalating pregabalin or placebo for 3 weeks as adjuvant therapy: pain relief was greater with pregabalin (36% vs 24%; mean difference 12%) and more pregabalin patients rated themselves much or very much improved (44% vs 21%). A mechanistic substudy of the same trial's patients (Bouwense 2015) found pregabalin responders — unlike placebo responders — showed anti-hyperalgesic changes and increased conditioned pain modulation, which supports a real central effect but adds no new patients. The only other randomised report (Sureshkumar 2021, 90 patients) tested pregabalin combined with antioxidants against placebo, so its positive result cannot be attributed to pregabalin alone. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: pregabalin probably reduces chronic pancreatitis pain modestly in the short term; there is no long-term or pregabalin-alone replication trial.
stamp: POSSIBLE — pregabalin reduced pain more than placebo in one small 3-week trial (64 patients; pain relief 36% vs 24%), with supportive mechanistic data from the same trial's patients and a positive combination-therapy trial that cannot separate pregabalin's own effect

title: Itopride for functional dyspepsia: a positive phase II trial, two null phase III trials, and a modestly positive mixed-comparator meta-analysis — a split record
question: In adults with functional dyspepsia, does itopride improve symptoms versus placebo?
balance: SPLIT — printed on the face. The dyspepsia shelves elsewhere in the library cover tricyclics, buspirone and STW 5; itopride itself had no home, and its record genuinely divides. Holtmann 2006 (the phase IIb trial, 554 patients) found itopride 50–200 mg three times daily clearly beat placebo: 57%, 59% and 64% of patients were symptom-free or markedly improved versus 41% on placebo. The two phase III trials that followed (Talley 2008, about 1,170 patients) found global responder rates essentially identical to placebo in both trials (45.2% vs 45.6% and 37.8% vs 35.4% — the treatment made no difference on the co-primary global assessment), with only one of the two showing a Leeds Dyspepsia Questionnaire responder advantage. A 2012 meta-analysis of 9 trials (2,620 patients) pooling placebo, domperidone and mosapride controls found a modest itopride advantage (global assessment relative risk 1.11). PROPOSED SPLIT: itopride's benefit over placebo is unproven at phase III standard despite a positive early trial and a positive mixed-comparator meta-analysis.
stamp: SPLIT — the phase IIb trial found clear benefit over placebo (57–64% vs 41% responders), but two larger phase III trials found no difference in global symptom response (the treatment made no difference on their co-primary global assessment), while a meta-analysis pooling placebo and active comparators found a modest advantage (relative risk 1.11 for global assessment)

title: Direct-acting antivirals in people who inject drugs (PARTIAL completion of live #593): cure rates of 87–94% — close to general-population rates, with no randomised comparison against non-users
question: In adults with hepatitis C who inject drugs, do direct-acting antivirals achieve cure rates as high as in non-users?
balance: POSSIBLE (single-arm and observational evidence) — printed on the face. This pack is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #593 answers direct-acting antiviral (DAA) cure rates generally (90–99% sustained virological response, SVR, in the registration trials); this shelf asks only about the people-who-inject-drugs population that #593 does not break out, and no #593 PMID is re-carded here. (The compensated- and decompensated-cirrhosis slices are homed elsewhere — wave-15 #5967 and wave-17 #6085 — and are not this population.) No trial randomises people who inject drugs against non-users, so the comparison is cross-study: SIMPLIFY (sofosbuvir-velpatasvir, 103 people with injection in the past 6 months) achieved 94% SVR12 with no virological failures; D3FEAT (a genotype-1 regimen, 87 people) achieved 91%; and the Hajarizadeh meta-analysis (38 studies, 3,634 participants) pooled SVR at 87.4% in people with recent injecting, 87.7% with recent drug use and 90.7% on opioid substitution therapy — a few points below registration-trial rates, with losses to follow-up, not virological failure, accounting for most of the gap. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (single-arm and observational evidence): cure rates in people who inject drugs are high and close to those in non-users, and ongoing drug use did not reduce cure in either prospective study.
stamp: POSSIBLE (single-arm and observational evidence) — in prospective treatment studies of people with recent injection drug use, direct-acting antivirals cured 91–94% (SIMPLIFY, D3FEAT), and a meta-analysis pooling 670 people with recent injecting found an 87.4% cure rate — near, but not proven equal to, the 90–99% rates in the general-population trials homed on live #593

title: Endoscopic combination therapy for bleeding peptic ulcer: adding a second method to epinephrine injection cuts rebleeding from about 19% to 10% and halves mortality
question: In adults with acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding from peptic ulcer, does endoscopic combination therapy reduce rebleeding compared with epinephrine injection alone?
balance: LIKELY — printed on the face. The index already homes second-look endoscopy (pack #3589) and endoscopy timing for ulcer bleeding; the combination-therapy question — whether epinephrine injection alone is enough — was not shelved. It is one of the most concordant answers in ulcer bleeding: the Cochrane review (Vergara 2007; 17 trials, 1,763 patients) found adding a second endoscopic method after epinephrine reduced further bleeding from 18.8% to 10.4% (Peto odds ratio 0.51), emergency surgery from 10.8% to 7.1% and mortality from 5% to 2.5%. The earlier Calvet meta-analysis (16 trials, 1,673 patients) found near-identical absolute rates (rebleeding 18.4% to 10.6%; mortality 5.1% to 2.6%). The largest single trial carded (Chung 1997, adrenaline plus heat probe in actively bleeding ulcers) was neutral overall but showed the benefit concentrated where the meta-analyses predict it — spurting haemorrhage, where operative intervention fell from 29.6% to 6.5%. PROPOSED LIKELY: epinephrine injection should not be used alone for high-risk bleeding ulcers; a second method (thermal, clip or other injection) reduces rebleeding, surgery and death.
stamp: LIKELY — adding a second endoscopic method after epinephrine injection reduced further bleeding from 18.8% to 10.4%, emergency surgery from 10.8% to 7.1% and mortality from 5% to 2.5% in the Cochrane pooling of 17 trials, with concordant results in the earlier meta-analysis and the individual trials
