title: Proton pump inhibitor before endoscopy for upper gastrointestinal bleeding: fewer bleeding stigmata and less endoscopic therapy — but no difference in death, rebleeding or surgery
question: In adults with nonvariceal upper gastrointestinal bleeding, does an intravenous proton pump inhibitor before endoscopy change outcomes versus after endoscopy?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference to patient outcomes) — printed on the face. No pre-endoscopy proton pump inhibitor (PPI) home existed in the index. A precision first: the trials compare PPI started before endoscopy against placebo, an H2 blocker or no treatment before endoscopy — all patients could receive standard care, including PPI, after endoscopy — so they answer 'start before versus not before', which is the practical form of this shelf's question. The largest trial (Lau 2007, 638 patients, high-dose intravenous omeprazole) reduced the need for endoscopic therapy (19.1% vs 28.4%) and shortened stay, with no difference in transfusion, recurrent bleeding, emergency surgery or 30-day death. Both Cochrane versions (2010 and the 2022 update, the same 6 trials and 2,223 participants) agree: mortality odds ratio 1.12–1.14, rebleeding and surgery not significantly different, while the need for endoscopic haemostatic treatment fell (odds ratio 0.68). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference to patient outcomes): pre-endoscopy PPI changes what the endoscopist finds and does, not whether the patient dies, rebleeds or needs surgery.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference to patient outcomes) — pre-endoscopy proton pump inhibitor reduced the need for endoscopic therapy (8.6% vs 11.7% pooled; 19.1% vs 28.4% in the largest trial) and down-staged bleeding stigmata, but made no difference to mortality, rebleeding or surgery in any pooling

title: Empagliflozin and liver fat in steatotic liver disease: MRI trials show a modest fall, elastography trials show none — an imaging-surrogate split
question: In adults with metabolic steatotic liver disease, does empagliflozin reduce liver fat on imaging versus placebo?
balance: SPLIT (measure; imaging surrogate) — printed on the face, with the surrogate warning the question requires: every carded outcome is an imaging number, not liver histology, fibrosis progression or a clinical event. The library's other liver-fat shelves cover other agents (efinopegdutide on live #2115; dapagliflozin on pack #3623); empagliflozin itself had no home. The split runs along the measuring instrument. On MRI proton-density fat fraction (MRI-PDFF), empagliflozin won twice: E-LIFT (Kuchay 2018, 50 patients with type 2 diabetes, empagliflozin added to standard care versus standard care alone — not a placebo comparison) found a −4.0% between-group difference, and Cheung 2024 (98 patients without diabetes, genuinely placebo-controlled for 52 weeks) found a greater median reduction (−2.49% vs −1.43%). On transient-elastography controlled attenuation parameter (CAP), Taheri 2020 found no difference versus placebo, and the Tang 2022 meta-analysis of 3 trials (212 patients) found no improvement in CAP, steatosis or stiffness. PROPOSED SPLIT (measure; imaging surrogate): empagliflozin probably lowers MRI-measured liver fat modestly; the elastography literature does not confirm it, and no carded study shows a histological or clinical benefit.
stamp: SPLIT (measure; imaging surrogate) — empagliflozin reduced liver fat on MRI proton-density fat fraction in two small trials (between-group difference −4.0% in E-LIFT; median change −2.49% vs −1.43% against placebo over 52 weeks), but elastography-based measurement showed no advantage (controlled attenuation parameter unchanged versus placebo, and a 3-trial meta-analysis found no improvement); liver fat is an imaging surrogate, with no histology or clinical-outcome evidence carded

title: Anamorelin in cancer cachexia: lean body mass rises in every trial — handgrip strength and walking do not (built on the non-ROMANA reports; the ROMANA programme is homed on live #12)
question: In adults with cancer cachexia, does anamorelin increase lean body mass versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE — printed on the face, with two flags stated plainly. FLAG 1 (one-home / precedent call): the flagship ROMANA 1 and ROMANA 2 phase 3 trials (Temel 2016) are already carded with their figures on live shelf #12, the library's cancer-cachexia deposit shelf, so under the one-home rule their PMID is NOT carded here and none of their numbers are re-used on this shelf's cards. This dedicated anamorelin shelf is built instead on the three independent, gate-free trial reports — the pooled phase 2 analysis (Garcia 2015), the Japanese phase 2 trial (Takayama 2016) and the Japanese phase 3 trial ONO-7643-04 (Katakami 2018) — which answer the same question in the same direction. FLAG 2 (population): every carded trial is in non-small-cell lung cancer cachexia, so the shelf's evidence is narrower than its question's wording. The pattern is unusually consistent: lean body mass rose by about 1.4–2.1 kg relative to placebo over 12 weeks in all three reports, appetite and weight improved, and the functional co-endpoints — handgrip strength in all three, 6-minute walk in Katakami — did not improve in any (function made no difference). That mass-without-function pattern is also what live #12's ROMANA card shows. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: anamorelin increases lean body mass in cancer (NSCLC) cachexia; whether added mass that does not strengthen grip or walking helps patients is unproven.
stamp: POSSIBLE — anamorelin increased lean body mass versus placebo in three independent trial reports outside the ROMANA programme (pooled phase 2 difference 2.09 kg; Japanese phase 2 and phase 3 trials concordant), but handgrip strength and walking did not improve in any of them (function made no difference)

title: Recombinant thrombomodulin in sepsis-associated coagulopathy: the SCARLET placebo trial was null (26.8% vs 29.4% mortality), and the pooled estimate remains nonsignificant
question: In adults with sepsis and disseminated intravascular coagulation, does recombinant thrombomodulin improve survival versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference in the placebo trial) — printed on the face. A population precision first: SCARLET enrolled sepsis-associated coagulopathy (raised INR with thrombocytopenia, plus organ failure) rather than overt disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) by score, and it is the only large placebo-controlled test; the earlier Japanese phase 3 trial (Saito 2007) enrolled DIC from infection or haematological malignancy but compared thrombomodulin with heparin, not placebo, and its endpoint was DIC resolution, not survival. SCARLET (800 patients analysed) found 28-day mortality 26.8% versus 29.4% (absolute difference 2.55%, 95% CI −3.68 to 8.77; P = .32) — not significant — with serious major bleeding numerically more frequent on thrombomodulin (5.8% vs 4.0%). The updated meta-analysis including SCARLET (Yamakawa 2019; 5 trials, 1,762 patients) gives a relative mortality risk of 0.87 (95% CI 0.74–1.03, P = 0.10) — a possible ~13% relative reduction that remains nonsignificant, with trial sequential analysis showing only 42% of the required information size. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference in the placebo trial): a survival benefit from recombinant thrombomodulin in sepsis with coagulopathy/DIC is unproven.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference in the placebo trial) — SCARLET, the only large placebo-controlled trial, found 28-day mortality of 26.8% on thrombomodulin versus 29.4% on placebo (P = .32, not significant), and the updated meta-analysis estimate (relative risk 0.87, 95% CI 0.74–1.03) remains nonsignificant with only 42% of the required information size accrued

title: Gluten-free diet and mucosal healing in adult celiac disease: recovery in about two-thirds by 5 years, complete normalisation rare early — symptoms do not prove healing (observational cohorts)
question: In adults with celiac disease, does a gluten-free diet heal the small intestinal mucosa in adults diagnosed by biopsy?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit, observational evidence) — printed on the face: this shelf rests on follow-up-biopsy cohorts, not randomised trials, so the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE and labelled observational. The cohorts agree on the shape of the answer: a gluten-free diet heals the mucosa in many adults, slowly, and far from universally. In the Mayo Clinic cohort (Rubio-Tapia 2010, 241 adults with diagnostic and follow-up biopsies), confirmed mucosal recovery was 34% at 2 years and 66% at 5 years, even though 82% had a clinical response — symptoms were not a reliable marker of healing. In the largest adult series (Lanzini 2009, 465 adults), complete histological normalisation after a median 16 months on the diet was only 8%, with a further 65% in 'remission' with persistent intraepithelial lymphocytosis. In the Finnish cohort (Pekki 2015, 263 adults), incomplete recovery at 1 year was common and was predicted by more severe damage at diagnosis, while dietary adherence was excellent in both groups (97% vs 87%). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit, observational): mucosal healing on a gluten-free diet is real but slow and incomplete in a substantial share of adults; a feeling of improvement does not prove the mucosa has healed.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit, observational evidence) — a gluten-free diet heals the mucosa in many adults but slowly and often incompletely: recovery 34% at 2 years and 66% at 5 years in the Mayo cohort, complete normalisation only 8% at a median 16 months in the largest adult series

title: Intravenous iron and quality of life in IBD anaemia (PARTIAL completion of pack #3231): quality of life improves on intravenous iron; the proven edge over oral iron is haemoglobin response, not a measured quality-of-life difference
question: In adults with iron deficiency anemia, does intravenous iron improve quality of life versus oral iron in inflammatory bowel disease?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — printed on the face, and narrowed on the face: quality of life clearly improves when intravenous iron corrects iron-deficiency anaemia in inflammatory bowel disease, but a quality-of-life advantage over oral iron specifically has not been directly demonstrated in the fetched records — the head-to-head evidence is about haemoglobin response. This pack is a PARTIAL completion: pack #3231 homes oral ferric maltol and haemoglobin in IBD anaemia and is not re-carded here; this shelf takes the intravenous-iron quality-of-life slice. In the one direct route comparison trial (Kulnigg 2008, 200 patients), intravenous ferric carboxymaltose was non-inferior to oral ferrous sulfate for haemoglobin rise (median 8.7 to 12.3 g/dL vs 9.1 to 12.1 g/dL) with faster early response. The Cochrane review (11 studies, 1,670 participants) pooled all intravenous versus all oral preparations and found more haemoglobin responders on intravenous iron (368/554 vs 205/373; relative risk 1.17, a relative measure; number needed to treat 11, low certainty), with fewer withdrawals for adverse events on intravenous iron. On quality of life itself: in FERGIcor (485 patients) both intravenous regimens improved quality-of-life scores by week 12, and in the PHOSPHARE-IBD analysis (97 patients) utility and SF-36 scores improved significantly after intravenous iron, driven by vitality — an improvement blunted when phosphate fell. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): intravenous iron improves quality of life as it corrects anaemia in IBD; the proven edge over oral iron is haemoglobin response and tolerability, not a measured quality-of-life difference.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — intravenous iron improves quality-of-life scores as it corrects IBD iron-deficiency anaemia (FERGIcor; PHOSPHARE-IBD), and beats oral iron on haemoglobin response pooled (relative risk 1.17; 368/554 vs 205/373), but a quality-of-life advantage over oral iron specifically is not directly demonstrated

title: Intravenous selenium in critical illness: pooled overall mortality lower in relative terms (relative risk 0.82–0.86), 28-day mortality not significantly reduced — low-certainty evidence, largest trial null on its primary analysis
question: In critically ill adults, does intravenous selenium supplementation reduce mortality versus standard care?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit, low-certainty evidence) — printed on the face. Selenium is a supplement; where a preparation is named it is named here for clarification: the trials used intravenous sodium selenite, typically a 1,000 microgram bolus followed by 1,000 micrograms daily in the largest trial. The pooled estimates point to a modest relative mortality reduction, but every synthesis rates the evidence low or very low quality, the 28-day endpoint is null, and the largest single trial was null on its intention-to-treat primary analysis. The Cochrane review (16 trials, 2,084 participants) found intravenous sodium selenite reduced overall mortality (relative risk 0.82, 95% CI 0.72–0.93, 1,391 participants, very low quality), driven mainly by high-risk-of-bias trials, with no significant difference at 28 days (relative risk 0.84, 95% CI 0.69–1.02) or 90 days. Two later meta-analyses land in the same place: total mortality relative risk 0.86 (Zhao 2019, 19 trials, 3,341 patients) and 28-day mortality relative risk 0.84 of borderline significance (Landucci 2014, 9 trials). The largest single trial, SIC (Angstwurm 2007, 249 patients with severe sepsis), found 28-day mortality of 39.7% on high-dose sodium selenite vs 50.0% on placebo in intention-to-treat analysis (P=.109 — not significant). Note the SIGNET trial, which tested selenium within parenteral nutrition, is homed on pack #6023 and is not re-carded here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit, low-certainty): intravenous selenium may reduce overall mortality modestly in relative terms, but the evidence is too weak and too bias-prone for a stronger stamp.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit, low-certainty evidence) — intravenous selenium (sodium selenite in the trials) pooled at relative risk 0.82–0.86 for overall mortality, but 28-day mortality was not significantly reduced and the largest trial's intention-to-treat primary analysis was null

title: Prophylactic gastrostomy vs reactive feeding in head and neck radiotherapy: short-term weight and quality of life favour prophylaxis in trial and pooled evidence; the largest matched cohort favours reactive feeding — split
question: In adults with head and neck cancer receiving radiotherapy, does prophylactic gastrostomy feeding preserve weight better than reactive nasogastric feeding?
balance: SPLIT (time horizon and study design) — printed on the face. The randomised and pooled evidence favours prophylactic gastrostomy for short-term weight and quality of life: Silander 2012 (134 patients randomised to prophylactic PEG or clinical practice) found significantly less weight loss and better quality of life at 6 months with prophylactic PEG, and a systematic review of 5 studies (298 patients) found prophylactic PEG associated with less short-term critical weight loss (>10%) and better short-term quality of life, with no effect on other outcomes. Against that, the largest comparison — a propensity-matched analysis of 526 patients with oral cavity cancer receiving adjuvant radiotherapy (Ghosh Laskar 2023) — found median weight loss at 6 weeks was greater in the prophylactic cohort (5 kg vs 3 kg, P=0.002) and lower in the reactive cohort at every later timepoint to 1 year, and its authors recommend the reactive approach. The only direct PEG-versus-nasogastric randomised trial in the Cochrane review enrolled just 33 patients before stopping early. PROPOSED SPLIT: prophylactic gastrostomy preserves weight and quality of life better in the first months in the trial and pooled evidence, but the largest matched cohort found the reactive strategy equal or better — the question is not settled.
stamp: SPLIT — prophylactic gastrostomy gave less weight loss and better quality of life at 6 months in the randomised trial and less short-term critical weight loss in the pooled review, but the largest propensity-matched cohort (526 patients) found greater weight loss with prophylaxis (median 5 kg vs 3 kg at 6 weeks) and less with the reactive approach to 1 year

title: Early oral feeding after esophagectomy: no complication penalty and faster bowel recovery in three randomised trials, but the largest trial found no faster functional recovery (7 vs 8 days)
question: In adults after esophagectomy, does early oral feeding improve recovery compared with tube feeding?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit, narrow) — printed on the face, with the largest trial's null primary outcome printed beside it. In NUTRIENT II (Berkelmans 2020, 132 patients after minimally invasive esophagectomy), starting oral feeding directly did not speed functional recovery — 7 days vs 8 days (P=0.436; the treatment made no difference) — and did not increase anastomotic leakage (18.5% vs 16.4%) or pneumonia (24.6% vs 34.3%). The larger Chinese non-inferiority trial (Sun 2018, 280 patients) found oral feeding on day 1 non-inferior for cardiorespiratory and gastrointestinal complications (30.0% vs 32.9%), with faster return of flatus (median 2 vs 3 days) and bowel movement (3 vs 4 days) and better quality of life at 2 weeks. A small randomised trial (Liao 2020, 41 patients) found shorter hospital stay and lower C-reactive protein with early oral feeding, with no difference in complications or mortality. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit, narrow): early oral feeding after esophagectomy appears safe — no increase in leak or pneumonia in any carded trial — and speeds bowel recovery and short-term quality of life, but the best trial found no faster overall functional recovery, so 'improves recovery' is supported only in that narrower sense.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit, narrow) — early oral feeding did not increase leakage or pneumonia in any carded trial and sped bowel recovery and 2-week quality of life, but NUTRIENT II found no faster functional recovery (7 vs 8 days; the treatment made no difference)

title: Glutamine-supplemented parenteral nutrition after major surgery (PARTIAL completion of live #1049 and pack #6023): infections reduced in relative terms in two surgical meta-analyses, no mortality benefit
question: In adults receiving parenteral nutrition after major surgery, does glutamine-supplemented parenteral nutrition reduce infections versus standard parenteral nutrition?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — printed on the face. This pack is a PARTIAL completion with two homes cross-pointed and not re-carded: live shelf #1049 homes enteral glutamine in severe burns only (RE-ENERGIZE), and pack #6023 homes glutamine in general critical illness with mortality as the outcome (including the REDOXS trial, homed on live #79). Neither answers this slice — parenteral glutamine in patients receiving parenteral nutrition after major surgery, with infections as the outcome. On that slice, two meta-analyses of surgical randomised trials agree: perioperative glutamine-supplemented parenteral nutrition in abdominal surgery reduced infectious complications (relative risk 0.48, 95% CI 0.32–0.72; 16 trials, 773 patients; Yue 2013 — a relative measure; the record does not report pooled absolute infection rates), and parenteral glutamine in critically ill surgical patients reduced infections (relative risk 0.60, 95% CI 0.45–0.80; 7 trials; Pimentel 2020), with hospital stay about 4 days shorter and no significant mortality difference in either synthesis (Yue mortality relative risk 1.52 with a very wide interval; Pimentel 0.76, not significant). The one double-blind surgical-ICU trial carded (Estívariz 2008, 59 patients) found fewer infections with glutamine dipeptide only in the non-pancreatic-surgery subgroup and no difference after pancreatic necrosis surgery. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): glutamine-supplemented parenteral nutrition probably reduces postoperative infections in relative terms in surgical patients on parenteral nutrition, with no demonstrated mortality benefit — POSSIBLE rather than LIKELY because the underlying trials are small and the one carded trial's benefit is subgroup-only.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — glutamine-supplemented parenteral nutrition reduced postoperative infections in relative terms in two surgical meta-analyses (relative risk 0.48 and 0.60), with no significant mortality difference in either

title: G-CSF primary prophylaxis at intermediate febrile-neutropenia risk (PARTIAL completion of live #370): untreated risk about 9% per course, observational benefit modest and concentrated in patients with added risk factors
question: In adults receiving chemotherapy at intermediate risk of febrile neutropenia, does primary G-CSF prophylaxis reduce febrile neutropenia compared with no prophylaxis?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit, observational evidence) — printed on the face: there is no randomised trial confined to the intermediate-risk (10–20%) band, so this slice rests on cohorts and claims data and is capped at POSSIBLE and labelled observational. This pack is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #370 homes primary G-CSF prophylaxis inside the ≥20%-risk fence, where meta-analyses show febrile neutropenia roughly halved in relative terms (relative risk about 0.51–0.54); that relative effect is not re-carded here. What the intermediate-risk evidence adds is the baseline: without prophylaxis, 9% of intermediate-risk patients developed at least one febrile-neutropenia episode over a course of chemotherapy in the prospective MASCC cohort (364 patients), concentrated in cycle 1 — so even a halving in relative terms buys only a few percentage points absolutely. In US claims data (13,937 intermediate-risk patients), 98% had at least one clinical risk factor yet only 35% received primary prophylaxis, and febrile-neutropenia risk rose with the number of risk factors; in a longitudinal claims cohort (142,730 patients on intermediate/high-risk regimens), first-cycle febrile neutropenia ran slightly lower with prophylaxis (2.6% across quarters) than without (2.7–3.7%). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit, observational): primary G-CSF prophylaxis probably reduces febrile neutropenia at intermediate risk too, but the absolute gain is small on average and concentrated in patients with added risk factors — which is why guidelines recommend it selectively in this band rather than routinely.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit, observational evidence) — no randomised trial in the intermediate-risk band; untreated febrile neutropenia was 9% per course prospectively, and prophylaxis was associated with modestly lower first-cycle rates in claims cohorts (2.6% vs 2.7–3.7%), with risk concentrated in patients with added risk factors

title: Same-day vs next-day pegfilgrastim: same-day administration is associated with more febrile neutropenia in every carded cohort — not as effective (observational evidence)
question: In adults receiving chemotherapy, is pegfilgrastim given on the same day as chemotherapy as effective as next-day pegfilgrastim for preventing febrile neutropenia?
balance: POSSIBLE (harm signal, observational evidence) — printed on the face: the evidence is entirely observational, so the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE and labelled observational — and it points one way: same-day pegfilgrastim is associated with MORE febrile neutropenia, not equal protection. In the largest study (Weycker 2018, Medicare claims; 65,003 patients, 261,184 cycles), cycle-1 febrile neutropenia was 11.4% in same-day cycles vs 8.4% in day 1–3 cycles (adjusted odds ratio 1.4 — a relative measure, printed beside the absolute rates), and 7.7% vs 6.0% across all cycles (adjusted odds ratio 1.3). In breast-cancer patients on dose-dense doxorubicin–cyclophosphamide (Hobbs 2023, 360 patients), febrile neutropenia occurred in 24.6% with same-day vs 11.7% with next-day administration (P=0.002), with more grade ≥3 neutropenia (38.4% vs 13.6%), dose reductions and antibiotic use. In lymphoma patients on CHOP with or without rituximab (Cheng 2014, 141 patients, 655 cycles), febrile neutropenia was 9.4% in same-day cycles vs 5.1% in next-day cycles (P=0.03). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (same-day administration is less effective, observational): on all carded evidence, pegfilgrastim given on the day of chemotherapy prevents febrile neutropenia less well than next-day administration — the convenience of a single visit is bought with a higher febrile-neutropenia rate.
stamp: POSSIBLE (same-day pegfilgrastim is less effective, observational evidence) — febrile neutropenia was higher with same-day administration in all three cohorts: 11.4% vs 8.4% in cycle 1 (Medicare), 24.6% vs 11.7% on dose-dense AC, and 9.4% vs 5.1% of CHOP cycles

title: Adding an NK1 antagonist in moderately emetogenic chemotherapy (PARTIAL completion of pack #3420): complete response improved, benefit concentrated in carboplatin-based regimens
question: In adults receiving moderately emetogenic chemotherapy, does adding an NK1 antagonist to a 5-HT3 antagonist and dexamethasone improve vomiting control?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — printed on the face, with the population split printed beside it: the benefit is clearest in carboplatin-based chemotherapy and not demonstrated for oxaliplatin-based regimens. This pack is a PARTIAL completion: pack #3420 homes NK1-antagonist addition in cisplatin (highly emetogenic) chemotherapy and is not re-carded here; this shelf takes the moderately emetogenic slice. In the carboplatin subgroup of the rolapitant phase 3 programme (Hesketh 2016, 401 patients), complete response over 0–120 hours was 80.2% with rolapitant added to granisetron and dexamethasone vs 64.6% on the two-drug control (P<.001). In the fosaprepitant phase 3 trial in non-AC moderately emetogenic chemotherapy (PN031, 1,000 patients; exploratory analysis by Weinstein 2018), complete response with fosaprepitant ran 76–80% in the delayed and overall phases in both carboplatin and non-carboplatin subgroups, with a larger treatment effect in carboplatin-based therapy in the delayed phase (14.1 vs 6.5 percentage points). The meta-analysis of 10 moderately-emetogenic trials (Zhang 2018, 2,928 patients) found the NK1 triple regimen improved complete response overall (relative risk 1.14, 95% CI 1.05–1.24 — a relative measure) and in the delayed phase (relative risk 1.13), with the subgroup benefit significant for carboplatin-based but not oxaliplatin-based chemotherapy. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): adding an NK1 antagonist to a 5-HT3 antagonist plus dexamethasone improves vomiting control in moderately emetogenic chemotherapy, driven by carboplatin-based regimens — roughly one extra complete response in every six to seven carboplatin patients in the rolapitant subgroup.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — adding an NK1 antagonist improved complete response in moderately emetogenic chemotherapy (80.2% vs 64.6% in the carboplatin phase 3 subgroup; pooled relative risk 1.14), with the benefit significant for carboplatin-based but not oxaliplatin-based regimens

title: Olanzapine 5 mg vs 10 mg in highly emetogenic chemotherapy (PARTIAL completion of live #769): similar complete response in the one direct trial and pooled dose literature, less sedation at the lower dose
question: In adults receiving highly emetogenic chemotherapy, is olanzapine 5 mg as effective as 10 mg for preventing nausea with less sedation?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit — 5 mg appears as effective, with less sedation) — printed on the face. This pack is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #769 homes adding olanzapine to triple prophylaxis (10 mg in Navari 2016; 5 mg in J-FORCE) and those placebo-controlled trials are not re-carded here; this shelf takes only the 5 mg vs 10 mg head-to-head slice. The one direct randomised comparison (Sukauichai 2022, 140 patients on high-dose cisplatin or doxorubicin–cyclophosphamide, without an NK1 antagonist in the backbone) found overall complete response of 58.6% on 5 mg vs 62.9% on 10 mg, meeting its (wide, −25%) non-inferiority margin, with no difference in adverse events including somnolence. A systematic review and meta-analysis of the dose literature (Wang 2021) concluded 5 mg may be as effective as 10 mg in highly and moderately emetogenic chemotherapy, with a sedative effect statistically and clinically lower at 5 mg than 10 mg, while cautioning that fewer 5 mg studies make the data uncertain. Supportive but indirect: a phase 3 non-inferiority trial of an even lower dose (Bajpai 2024, 267 patients analysed) found olanzapine 2.5 mg non-inferior to 10 mg for complete control (45% vs 44%) with far less daytime somnolence (any grade 65% vs 90%; severe on day 1, 5% vs 40%). PROPOSED POSSIBLE: 5 mg appears as effective as 10 mg for nausea and vomiting control, with less sedation — POSSIBLE rather than LIKELY because the single direct 5-vs-10 trial is small with a wide non-inferiority margin, and the sedation advantage at exactly 5 mg rests substantially on pooled and indirect evidence.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — olanzapine 5 mg appears as effective as 10 mg for nausea and vomiting control (complete response 58.6% vs 62.9% in the one direct trial, within a wide −25% non-inferiority margin) with less sedation in the pooled dose literature; the direct evidence is a single small trial

title: Empiric vancomycin in febrile neutropenia: no survival benefit in the EORTC trial or two meta-analyses — nephrotoxicity roughly doubled
question: In adults with febrile neutropenia, does adding empiric vancomycin improve outcomes in patients without resistant gram-positive infection?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — printed on the face. The EORTC/NCIC trial (747 febrile granulocytopenic patients) found adding vancomycin to ceftazidime plus amikacin improved response in gram-positive bacteraemia (72% vs 43%) but made no difference to fever course, and no gram-positive bacteraemia patient died in the first 3 days of empirical therapy; nephrotoxicity rose (6% vs 2%). Two 2005 meta-analyses of substantially the same trials agree: mortality did not differ (Paul relative risk 0.86, 95% CI 0.58–1.26; Vardakas odds ratio 0.67, 95% CI 0.42–1.05), while nephrotoxicity roughly doubled and adverse effects rose. The only consistent gain is fewer regimen modifications — a process outcome. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): routine empirical vancomycin in patients without resistant gram-positive infection does not improve survival and adds kidney harm; it can be deferred until a resistant gram-positive infection is documented.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — adding empirical vancomycin/glycopeptide in febrile neutropenia without resistant gram-positive infection did not reduce mortality in two meta-analyses (relative risk 0.86; odds ratio 0.67, both crossing 1) and roughly doubled nephrotoxicity

title: Aspirin vs enoxaparin in myeloma on immunomodulatory drugs: no significant difference in two trials — 6.4% vs 5.0% and 2.27% vs 1.20%
question: In adults with multiple myeloma receiving immunomodulatory drugs, is aspirin prophylaxis as effective as low-molecular-weight heparin for preventing venous thromboembolism?
balance: POSSIBLE — printed on the face. Two open-label randomised trials compare aspirin 100 mg/day with enoxaparin 40 mg/day head-to-head in myeloma on immunomodulatory drugs. Palumbo 2011 (thalidomide regimens, 659 analysed): the composite of serious thromboembolic events, acute cardiovascular events or sudden death was 6.4% on aspirin vs 5.0% on enoxaparin (absolute difference +1.3%, 95% CI −3.0 to 5.7). Larocca 2012 (lenalidomide regimens, 342 patients): venous thromboembolism 2.27% vs 1.20% (absolute difference 1.07%, 95% CI −1.69 to 3.83), with pulmonary embolism only on aspirin (1.70% vs 0%, three events). Neither difference is significant and both intervals are wide; a 51-trial pooling (9,069 patients) shows venous thromboembolism still occurs in 6.2% despite prophylaxis. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: aspirin appears as effective as low-molecular-weight heparin in the lower-risk patients enrolled — not an equivalence proof, and not evidence for high-risk patients.
stamp: POSSIBLE — aspirin vs enoxaparin in myeloma on immunomodulatory drugs: no significant difference in two randomised trials (composite 6.4% vs 5.0%; VTE 2.27% vs 1.20%), with wide confidence intervals and few events

title: Catheter thrombosis prophylaxis in cancer: venography trials positive, the symptomatic-event trial and pooling null — a split
question: In adults with cancer and a central venous catheter, does prophylactic low-dose anticoagulation prevent catheter-related thrombosis versus no prophylaxis?
balance: SPLIT (endpoint/era) — printed on the face. This shelf covers systemic prophylaxis only; catheter site choice (pack #3159, 3SITES) and lock solutions (pack #3219) are different questions and are not re-carded here. Two small early trials using routine venography were strongly positive: Bern 1990 (warfarin 1 mg; thrombosis 4/42 vs 15/40 among completers) and Monreal 1996 (dalteparin 2,500 IU; 1/16 vs 8/13, stopped early at 29 patients). The largest trial, Couban 2005 (255 patients, placebo-controlled, symptomatic endpoint), found warfarin 1 mg made no difference (4.6% vs 4.0%), and a meta-analysis of 8 trials (1,428 patients) found no significant pooled benefit (relative risk 0.59, 95% CI 0.31–1.13) and no bleeding penalty. PROPOSED SPLIT: venographic thrombosis falls in small early trials; symptomatic benefit is unproven — routine systemic prophylaxis is not supported by the symptomatic-outcome evidence.
stamp: SPLIT (endpoint/era) — small early venography trials found large reductions in catheter thrombosis with low-dose warfarin/dalteparin, but the largest placebo-controlled trial (symptomatic thrombosis 4.6% vs 4.0%) and an 8-trial meta-analysis (relative risk 0.59, CI crossing 1) found no benefit

title: Avatrombopag before procedures in chronic liver disease (PARTIAL of pack #2819): transfusion avoided in up to 88% vs 38% on placebo
question: In adults with chronic liver disease and thrombocytopenia, does avatrombopag raise platelet counts and reduce platelet transfusion before a procedure versus placebo?
balance: LIKELY — printed on the face. PARTIAL completion of pack #2819 (avatrombopag in chemotherapy-induced thrombocytopenia, a null trial — a different population, not re-carded here). In chronic liver disease before a scheduled procedure, ADAPT-1 (n = 231) and ADAPT-2 (n = 204) both found avatrombopag roughly doubled-to-tripled avoidance of platelet transfusion or rescue procedures (65.6% and 88.1% vs 22.9% and 38.2% by cohort in ADAPT-1; 68.6% and 87.9% vs 34.9% and 33.3% in ADAPT-2; all P < .001), an earlier phase 2 trial (130 patients) showed platelet responses in about 48–49% vs 6–10% on placebo, and an integrated analysis of the 435 ADAPT patients confirmed consistency across subgroups. PROPOSED LIKELY: avatrombopag raises platelet counts and reduces platelet transfusion/rescue before procedures in chronic liver disease — a transfusion-avoidance benefit, not a demonstrated bleeding reduction.
stamp: LIKELY — avatrombopag avoided platelet transfusion or rescue in 65.6–88.1% vs 22.9–38.2% across the two ADAPT phase 3 trials in chronic liver disease, with a concordant phase 2 trial

title: Romiplostim in chemotherapy-induced thrombocytopenia (PARTIAL of pack #2819): counts corrected 93% vs 12.5%; resumption data observational
question: In adults with chemotherapy-induced thrombocytopenia, does romiplostim allow chemotherapy to continue on schedule versus dose delay or reduction?
balance: POSSIBLE (observational evidence labelled) — printed on the face. PARTIAL completion of pack #2819 (the avatrombopag chemotherapy-induced-thrombocytopenia trial); the romiplostim agent slice is built here, with no #2819 study re-carded. Soff 2019's phase 2 trial randomised only 23 patients (platelet correction 93% vs 12.5%, P < .001); its resumption data (44 patients resuming, 6.8% recurrent delay/reduction) are from an uncontrolled extension. The schedule evidence beyond that is observational: a 173-patient retrospective multicentre cohort (79% avoided dose reduction/delay; 89% avoided platelet transfusion) and a 20-patient retrospective series (14 of 15 resuming patients completing at least two on-schedule cycles). title: Fluconazole prophylaxis vs placebo after stem cell transplant (PARTIAL of live #2180): systemic fungal infection 2.8% vs 15.8% and 7% vs 18%
question: In adults undergoing stem cell transplantation, does fluconazole prophylaxis reduce invasive fungal infection and death versus placebo?
balance: LIKELY — printed on the face. PARTIAL completion of live #2180 (micafungin vs fluconazole after stem cell transplant); the fluconazole-vs-placebo slice is built here and the #2180 trial is not re-carded. Goodman 1992 (356 patients): systemic fungal infection 2.8% on fluconazole 400 mg vs 15.8% on placebo (P < .001), fungal deaths 1/179 vs 10/177, overall mortality not significantly different. Slavin 1995 (300 patients): systemic infection 7% vs 18% (P = .004) and better survival to day 110 (31 vs 52 deaths, P = .004). A 64-trial meta-analysis found allogeneic transplant prophylaxis reduced all-cause mortality (relative risk 0.62, 95% CI 0.45–0.85). PROPOSED LIKELY: fluconazole prophylaxis reduces invasive candida infection after stem cell transplantation, with a probable survival benefit; it has no mould cover.
stamp: LIKELY — fluconazole prophylaxis reduced systemic fungal infection vs placebo in two randomised trials (2.8% vs 15.8% and 7% vs 18%), with better survival in one trial (31 vs 52 deaths) and in transplant-subgroup pooling (relative risk 0.62)

title: Corticosteroids for appetite and well-being in advanced cancer: short-term benefit in old placebo-controlled trials — POSSIBLE
question: In adults with advanced cancer, do corticosteroids improve appetite and well-being in the short term versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE — printed on the face. GAP verified: the appetite homes cover megestrol (live #1790) and mirtazapine, not corticosteroids as the tested drug; the modern dexamethasone datasets are carded on live #1790 (2021 anorexia trial, dexamethasone arm) and live #1999 (2013 fatigue trial) and are not re-carded here. The free placebo-controlled evidence is old and modest: Bruera 1985 (40-patient crossover; appetite increased in 24/31 on methylprednisolone 32 mg, preferred over placebo by 74%) and Della Cuna 1989 (403 patients; quality-of-life scores improved, P < .05–.001, with an unexplained higher mortality in treated women, 40.0% vs 27.7%). A 55-trial systematic review counts corticosteroids among only two classes with supporting evidence for cancer anorexia, with mixed results and no settled dose or duration. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: short-term appetite and well-being improve — short horizon only, no weight or survival claim.
stamp: POSSIBLE — corticosteroids improved appetite (77% of evaluable patients in a 40-patient crossover) and quality-of-life scores (403-patient trial) vs placebo in advanced cancer, on old short-term evidence with mixed review findings

title: Dexamethasone dose in malignant spinal cord compression: higher dose unproven for walking — MAYBE (weak evidence)
question: In adults with malignant spinal cord compression, does a higher dexamethasone dose improve walking outcomes versus a moderate dose?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — printed on the face. GAP verified: the cord-compression home (pack #2725) covers surgery plus radiotherapy vs radiotherapy alone, not steroid dose, and is cross-pointed here. The direct dose evidence is tiny and null: Vecht 1989 randomised 37 patients to a 100 mg vs 10 mg dexamethasone bolus (both then 16 mg/day) and found no difference in pain, ambulation or bladder function; Graham 2006 (Superdex pilot) randomised only 20 patients to 96 vs 16 mg/day, reported no by-arm ambulation result, and judged a full trial unfeasible. Sorensen 1994 (57 patients) compared 96 mg with NO steroid (walking 81% vs 63%) — it does not compare doses. A 2017 systematic review associates the moderate regimen (10 mg bolus, then 16 mg/day) with fewer complications. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): higher dose has not been shown to improve walking versus moderate dose.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — a higher dexamethasone dose has not been shown to improve walking in malignant spinal cord compression: the one bolus comparison (37 patients) found no difference, and the one dose pilot (20 patients) never completed

title: Ondansetron for radiotherapy-induced vomiting: complete emesis control 67% versus 45% on placebo in fractionated abdominal radiotherapy — one direct trial, bounded by a sceptical systematic review
question: In adults receiving abdominal radiotherapy, does ondansetron prevent vomiting versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE — ondansetron prevents vomiting during abdominal radiotherapy, on one direct placebo-controlled trial plus concordant active-comparator trials. The chemotherapy antiemetic shelves do not answer this question: the library's ondansetron homes are chemotherapy, postoperative and gastroenteritis settings, verified this session. In the one direct test in the exact population, Franzén 1996 randomised 111 patients starting fractionated abdominal radiotherapy to ondansetron or placebo and found complete control of emesis in 67% versus 45%. The quantitative systematic review (Tramèr 1998) is the caution printed alongside: of 40 trials and 1,404 patients, only five trials (197 patients) yielded valid data, and in the worst-day trials ondansetron's antivomiting effect versus placebo corresponded to a number needed to treat of 4.4, with no demonstrated benefit beyond 24 hours and no clear antinausea effect. Two older multicentre trials in the same abdominal-radiotherapy population found ondansetron clearly superior to the standard antiemetics of the day — metoclopramide (complete control on day 1 in all but one ondansetron patient versus 46%) and prochlorperazine (complete response 61% versus 35%) — which supports a real preventive effect without substituting for placebo evidence. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: a real antivomiting effect during abdominal radiotherapy, resting mainly on a single moderate placebo-controlled trial, with nausea benefit and any benefit beyond the treatment day unproven.
stamp: POSSIBLE — ondansetron prevented vomiting during abdominal radiotherapy in the one direct placebo-controlled trial (complete emesis control 67% vs 45%) and beat metoclopramide and prochlorperazine in the same population, but the systematic review found most published data invalid, no benefit beyond 24 hours, and an inconsistent nausea effect

title: Candidemia step-down to fluconazole after about 5 days: safe in responders across a prospective programme and two cohorts — observational evidence only (initial echinocandin choice is live #507)
question: In adults with candidemia that responds to an echinocandin, can therapy be safely stepped down to fluconazole after 5 days?
balance: POSSIBLE (observational evidence) — stepping down to an oral azole after about 5 days, in patients who are already responding, appears safe in the cohorts that studied it; there is no randomised trial of the step-down decision itself. Live shelf #507 answers the different, earlier question — which drug to start (an echinocandin first) — and is cross-pointed, not re-carded here. The prospective step-down programme (Vazquez 2014) treated 250 evaluable patients with intravenous anidulafungin and allowed step-down to oral fluconazole or voriconazole after 5 days when prespecified criteria were met: global response at end of treatment was 83.7%, and the early-switch subgroup did as well as the whole population. The multicentre retrospective candidemia cohort (Husni 2021) found step-down happened at an average of day 5, that stepped-down patients survived more often (78% versus 56%) — a comparison openly exposed to confounding, because clinicians step down patients who are already improving — and that stepping down at 1–4 days carried the same mortality as stepping down after more than 5 days (20% versus 24%). In Candida glabrata candidemia specifically (Droney 2025), 30-day clinical failure was 9% in the fluconazole step-down group versus 15% in patients kept on an echinocandin, not a significant difference. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (observational): in responding, non-neutropenic-leaning candidemia populations, step-down to fluconazole at about day 5 has repeatedly been used without a safety signal; the evidence cannot prove the step-down itself is what made outcomes good.
stamp: POSSIBLE (observational evidence) — stepping down from an echinocandin to fluconazole at about day 5 in candidemia patients who are already responding was associated with outcomes as good as continued intravenous therapy in one prospective programme and two retrospective cohorts, with no randomised trial of the step-down decision

title: Cellulitis route: oral therapy matched intravenous therapy for uncomplicated mild-to-moderate disease — one blinded trial, one route analysis, one Cochrane comparison (duration is live #506)
question: In adults with uncomplicated cellulitis, is oral antibiotic therapy as effective as intravenous therapy?
balance: POSSIBLE — for uncomplicated, mild-to-moderate cellulitis, oral therapy performed as well as intravenous therapy in the small route literature; severe cellulitis is not answered here. Live shelf #506 answers the neighbouring duration question (how many days), not route, and is cross-pointed, not re-carded. The one double-blind route trial (Dalen 2018) randomised 206 emergency-department patients with uncomplicated mild-to-moderate skin and soft-tissue infection to oral cephalexin or intravenous cefazolin plus oral probenecid: failure at 72 hours was 4.2% versus 6.1% and clinical cure at 7 days 100% versus 97.7%. A route analysis extracted from a multicentre cellulitis trial (Williams & Brindle 2020, 323 patients) found route was chosen by severity in practice, yet patients given only oral therapy were more likely to have improved by day 5 and were as likely to be back to normal activities at days 10 and 30. The older Cochrane review of cellulitis interventions (Kilburn 2010, 25 studies, 2,488 participants) found, in the two studies comparing an oral macrolide with intravenous penicillin, that oral therapy could be more effective than intravenous therapy (relative risk 0.85 for the symptom outcome). PROPOSED POSSIBLE: oral is a reasonable route for uncomplicated cellulitis that is mild to moderate and improving; the evidence base is one modest blinded trial in mixed skin infections, one non-randomised route analysis, and an old heterogeneous review — hence the cap.
stamp: POSSIBLE — oral antibiotic therapy was as effective as intravenous therapy for uncomplicated mild-to-moderate cellulitis in one double-blind non-inferiority trial (failure 4.2% vs 6.1%), one non-randomised route analysis, and a Cochrane subgroup comparison; severe cellulitis is untested

title: Aminoglycosides in native valve staphylococcal endocarditis: no outcome benefit in pooled trials, and a consistent kidney price — gentamicin fall in creatinine clearance 22% versus 8%
question: In adults with infective endocarditis, does adding an aminoglycoside improve outcomes in native valve staphylococcal infection?
balance: POSSIBLE (harm, observational and small-trial evidence) — adding an aminoglycoside to a beta-lactam for native valve staphylococcal endocarditis has not been shown to improve any outcome, and it does damage kidneys. This is a different organism and setting from the enterococcal combination-therapy pack #5445 (ampicillin plus ceftriaxone versus ampicillin plus gentamicin in Enterococcus faecalis), which is cross-pointed, not re-carded. The meta-analysis of the comparative trials (Falagas 2006; five trials, 261 patients with native valve endocarditis due to Staphylococcus aureus or viridans streptococci) found no significant difference in mortality (odds ratio 0.59, 95% CI 0.21–1.66), treatment success, success without surgery, or relapse — and significantly less nephrotoxicity without the aminoglycoside (odds ratio 0.38, 95% CI 0.16–0.88). The largest safety analysis (Cosgrove 2009), drawn from a randomised trial's cohort of 236 patients with S. aureus bacteremia and native valve endocarditis, found a clinically significant fall in creatinine clearance in 22% of patients who received any initial low-dose gentamicin versus 8% of those who did not, with gentamicin receipt an independent predictor. The one randomised with/without trial in staphylococcal disease (Ribera 1996, right-sided MSSA endocarditis in people who inject drugs) found success in 89% on cloxacillin alone versus 86% with gentamicin added. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm): no demonstrated benefit, a consistent kidney price — the combination should not be routine in native valve staphylococcal endocarditis.
stamp: POSSIBLE (harm, observational and small-trial evidence) — adding an aminoglycoside to a beta-lactam in native valve staphylococcal endocarditis showed no mortality, success or relapse benefit in pooled trials (261 patients) and increased kidney injury (significant fall in creatinine clearance 22% vs 8% with initial low-dose gentamicin)

title: Adjunctive corticosteroid in herpes simplex encephalitis: DexEnceph published null — verbal memory 71 versus 69 — with a null pooled estimate and a null 3,933-patient cohort
question: In adults with herpes simplex encephalitis, does adjunctive corticosteroid improve outcomes versus acyclovir alone?
balance: POSSIBLE — adjunctive corticosteroid made no difference to the outcomes measured, in the one completed phase 3 trial and in the pooled and nationwide evidence around it. Publication status was verified this session before carding: the DexEnceph randomised trial has now published its results (Lancet Neurology, 2026). DexEnceph randomised 94 adults with herpes simplex virus encephalitis in 53 UK hospitals to dexamethasone plus acyclovir or acyclovir alone; the primary outcome, verbal memory score at 26 weeks, was 71 versus 69 (adjusted difference 1.77, 95% CI −9.57 to 13.12; P = 0.76) — the treatment made no difference — with similar adverse-event rates and no treatment-related deaths. The 2026 meta-analysis of all comparative studies (four studies, 209 patients) found the randomised pooled estimates likewise centred on no effect: unfavourable outcome relative risk 1.00 (95% CI 0.68–1.47) and mortality relative risk 0.92 (95% CI 0.35–2.40), while the retrospective estimates conflicted and were seriously confounded. The largest single dataset, a Japanese nationwide retrospective cohort of 3,933 patients, found adjusted in-hospital mortality of 4.2% with early corticosteroid versus 3.2% without (difference 1.0%, 95% CI −0.6% to 2.1%), no difference in consciousness or functional independence at discharge, and a longer hospital stay in the steroid group. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: routine adjunctive corticosteroid is not supported — the trial was small and dexamethasone began a median 7 days after admission, so an earlier-treatment benefit is not excluded, only undemonstrated.
stamp: POSSIBLE — adjunctive corticosteroid made no difference in herpes simplex encephalitis: DexEnceph found verbal memory 71 vs 69 at 26 weeks (adjusted difference 1.77, 95% CI −9.57 to 13.12), the pooled randomised relative risk for unfavourable outcome was 1.00, and a 3,933-patient cohort found no mortality or functional benefit

title: Changing the catheter before antibiotics for catheter-associated urinary infection: SPLIT — one small trial favours exchange, the bundled second trial favours retention on recurrence
question: In adults with an indwelling urinary catheter and urinary infection, does changing the catheter before starting antibiotics improve cure versus leaving it in place?
balance: SPLIT — the two randomised studies point in opposite directions, and the 2024 systematic review of the whole literature says so explicitly. Raz 2000, the small trial guidelines rest on, randomised 54 elderly nursing-home residents with a chronic indwelling catheter and symptomatic urinary infection to catheter replacement before antibiotics or no replacement: clinical status at 72 hours had improved in 25 versus 11 patients (P < 0.001) and symptomatic relapse 28 days after therapy was lower with replacement (3 versus 11, P = 0.015). Darouiche 2014 randomised 61 patients with spinal cord injury and catheter-associated urinary infection to a 5-day antibiotic course after catheter exchange or a 10-day course with the catheter retained: clinical cure was 100% in both groups, but recurrence was higher in the exchange group — a comparison in which the exchange arm also got the shorter antibiotic course, so route and duration are bundled. The systematic review (Westgeest 2024) found only four relevant studies in total (two randomised, two observational): one randomised trial favoured replacement, the other favoured retention on recurrence, and the observational studies were inconclusive; a retrospective VRE urinary-infection cohort (Shah 2018) found cure of 90.5% with catheter exchange or removal versus 87.5% with retention in its catheter subgroup. PROPOSED SPLIT: replacement before antibiotics improved early response and relapse in the one small direct trial, but the only other randomised comparison — confounded by antibiotic duration — favoured retention on recurrence, and the total evidence base is four studies.
stamp: SPLIT — replacing the catheter before antibiotics improved early clinical status (25 vs 11 patients) and relapse (3 vs 11) in the one small direct randomised trial (Raz, 54 patients), but the only other randomised comparison, which bundled exchange with a shorter antibiotic course, found 100% cure both ways with higher recurrence after exchange; a 2024 review of all four existing studies calls the evidence conflicting

title: FLAG precedent (b): prosthetic joint infection oral step-down on PJI-specific cohorts only — failure 9.2% versus 15.6% in the largest — with OVIVA kept at its home on live #312
question: In adults with prosthetic joint infection, is oral step-down antibiotic therapy as effective as continued intravenous therapy?
balance: FLAG — PRECEDENT (b) BUILD: the anchor trial for this question, OVIVA (2019), is already carded as an evidence card on live shelf #312 (the general adult oral-versus-intravenous bone and joint infection question), so OVIVA is NOT re-carded here and its PMID is kept out of every card's source line, exactly as precedent (b) requires. This pack is built only on prosthetic-joint-infection-specific reports that are free of the library, and its evidence is entirely observational — hence the POSSIBLE (observational) cap. In the largest PJI-specific cohort (Roger 2024; 172 patients, 13 institutions), management failure over 24 months was 9.2% (7 of 76) in patients treated with oral therapy (exclusively oral or at most 3 days parenteral) versus 15.6% (15 of 96) in patients treated with prolonged parenteral therapy. In Staphylococcus aureus prosthetic bone and joint infection (Boclé 2021; 140 patients), 85% were switched to oral therapy within 5 days of intravenous treatment, the overall failure rate was 8.5%, and intravenous duration (5 days or less versus more than 5 days) was not associated with failure. In two-stage exchange PJI (Ascione 2017; 122 patients), administration of oral therapy was associated with a favourable outcome in both univariate and multivariate analysis. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (observational evidence): in selected PJI patients after appropriate surgery, oral step-down has repeatedly achieved failure rates no worse than prolonged intravenous therapy in cohorts — consistent with, but independent of, the randomised answer homed on live #312. The PJI duration question (6 versus 12 weeks) is a different question, homed on live #2223 (DATIPO).
stamp: POSSIBLE (observational evidence) — in prosthetic joint infection, oral step-down achieved failure rates no worse than prolonged intravenous therapy in three PJI-specific retrospective cohorts (failure 9.2% vs 15.6% in the largest, 172 patients); the randomised OVIVA anchor is homed on live #312 and is not re-carded here (precedent (b))

title: Linezolid vs vancomycin for MRSA complicated skin infection (PARTIAL completion of live #504): equivalent overall, superior in proven MRSA
question: In adults with complicated skin infection due to MRSA, is linezolid more effective than vancomycin for clinical cure?
balance: PARTIAL completion: live shelf #504 already answers linezolid versus vancomycin in MRSA pneumonia; this shelf answers the skin-infection population only, and no pneumonia study is re-carded here. In complicated skin and soft-tissue infection, the two randomised trials point the same way: linezolid is at least as effective as vancomycin overall, and in the patients with proven MRSA in the largest trial it was clearly more effective (clinical cure 88.6% vs 66.9% at test of cure). The second, MRSA-proven trial found similar per-protocol success, with linezolid ahead in the modified intention-to-treat population and on microbiological success at end of treatment, plus shorter hospital stay and intravenous therapy. The pooled analysis of three trials (1,056 patients) found the same pattern — comparable success in diabetic patients, higher success with linezolid in non-diabetic patients, and shorter stay. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: linezolid is at least as effective as vancomycin for clinical cure of MRSA complicated skin infection, with superiority shown in the proven-MRSA population of the largest trial — held at POSSIBLE because the dedicated MRSA trial's per-protocol analysis was not significant and the clearest superiority figure comes from a pathogen-confirmed subset.
stamp: POSSIBLE — linezolid is at least as effective as vancomycin for clinical cure of MRSA complicated skin infection, and was more effective in the proven-MRSA population of the largest trial (cure 88.6% vs 66.9%); the dedicated MRSA trial's per-protocol analysis was similar between the drugs

title: Doxycycline vs benzathine penicillin for early syphilis (PARTIAL completion of live #2192): no randomised trial — three retrospective series show no significant serological difference
question: In adults with early syphilis, is doxycycline as effective as benzathine penicillin for cure?
balance: PARTIAL completion: live shelf #2192 already answers single-dose azithromycin versus benzathine penicillin for early syphilis; this shelf answers the doxycycline slice only, and no azithromycin study is re-carded here. FLAG — premise correction: the slate described the Ghanem 2006 anchor as a 'pilot randomised study'; the fetched PubMed record shows it is a retrospective comparative study (Publication Type: Comparative Study; MeSH: Retrospective Studies), and every other cardable report found is also retrospective. There is no randomised trial of doxycycline versus benzathine penicillin for early syphilis in the fetched records. What the observational evidence shows is consistent: serological failure/response rates on doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 14 days are statistically indistinguishable from single-dose benzathine penicillin G in Baltimore clinic patients (failure 0% vs 5.5%), in a 601-case Chinese clinic series (12-month response 92.4% vs 96.2%), and in HIV-infected patients treated during a penicillin shortage (response 72% vs 70%). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (observational): the retrospective evidence is compatible with doxycycline being as effective as benzathine penicillin for serological cure of early syphilis, but confounding by indication — doxycycline is usually given when penicillin cannot be — caps the stamp at POSSIBLE and the finding is labelled observational throughout.
stamp: POSSIBLE (observational) — retrospective series totalling 873 patients found serological cure on doxycycline statistically indistinguishable from benzathine penicillin (failure 0% vs 5.5%; 12-month response 92.4% vs 96.2%); no randomised trial exists in the fetched records

title: Screening and treating latent TB before anti-TNF therapy (GAP-E, observational): registry cases cluster where screening or prophylaxis was incomplete
question: In adults about to start anti-TNF therapy, does screening and treating latent tuberculosis prevent tuberculosis reactivation?
balance: GAP-E, observational throughout — there is no randomised trial of tuberculosis screening before anti-TNF therapy, and the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE with the observational label on the face. The three national registries behind the guideline recommendations tell one coherent story. In Spain's BIOBADASER, after screening recommendations were disseminated, active tuberculosis still occurred at 172 per 100,000 patient-years, but the probability of developing it was 7 times higher when the recommendations were not followed (incidence rate ratio 7.09) — and the commonest failure was the two-step tuberculin skin test for latent infection. In France's RATIO registry, all 69 tuberculosis cases occurred in patients who had not received correct chemoprophylactic treatment, at a standardised incidence ratio of 12.2 against the background population. In the British BSRBR, all 40 tuberculosis cases occurred in the anti-TNF cohort and none in 3,232 DMARD-treated comparators. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (observational): screening for and treating latent tuberculosis before anti-TNF therapy prevents most reactivation — the cases that still occur cluster where screening or prophylaxis was incomplete — but the size of the preventive effect has never been randomised.
stamp: POSSIBLE (observational) — registry evidence: tuberculosis on anti-TNF therapy was 7 times more likely when latent-TB screening recommendations were not followed (BIOBADASER), and none of RATIO's 69 cases had received correct chemoprophylaxis; no randomised trial exists

title: Hepcidin: how the liver turns iron absorption down when stores rise — the textbook hormone confirmed in human iron-loading, dosing and transfusion studies
question: In adults, how does the liver regulate iron absorption through hepcidin when body iron stores rise?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology and Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology). The textbooks describe hepcidin as the liver's iron-regulatory hormone: when body iron stores rise, hepatocytes make more hepcidin; hepcidin binds ferroportin — the only iron exporter — on duodenal enterocytes (and macrophages), internalising and degrading it, so dietary iron taken into the enterocyte cannot reach the plasma and is shed with the cell, and stored iron stays locked in macrophages. The carded human studies show each limb of that account in people. Urinary hepcidin excretion was greatly increased in patients with iron overload and tracked serum ferritin (Nemeth 2003). A single oral iron dose of 60 mg or more raised serum hepcidin within 24 hours and cut fractional absorption of the next day's dose by 35% to 45% (Moretti 2015) — the stores signal acting on absorption in real time. And when transfusion raised haemoglobin and iron loading in thalassaemia major, hepcidin rose with ferritin and fell as erythropoiesis reasserted itself (Pasricha 2013), showing the stores signal competing with the erythropoietic signal exactly as the textbooks describe. The adjacent dosing shelf, live #1041, homes the alternate-day dosing consequence of this physiology and is not re-carded here. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — rising iron stores raise hepatic hepcidin (urinary hepcidin greatly increased in iron overload, tracking ferritin), hepcidin degrades ferroportin, and absorption falls measurably within 24 hours (next-dose fractional absorption down 35–45% after a ≥60 mg dose) (Guyton & Hall; Ganong)

title: Ammonia traffic in cirrhosis: made in the gut, missed by the shunted liver, cleared by muscle — human interorgan catheter studies
question: In adults, how is ammonia produced in the gut and cleared by the liver and muscle in cirrhosis?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: standard physiology texts — Guyton & Hall and Ganong — for the urea cycle and glutamine handling; the interorgan measurements are the Olde Damink/Jalan human catheterisation programme). The textbook account: ammonia is produced mainly in the gut — small-intestinal glutaminase splitting glutamine, and colonic bacteria splitting urea and amino acids — travels in portal blood to the liver, and is cleared there by the urea cycle (with a periportal glutamine-scavenging back-up); skeletal muscle is the main extrahepatic sink, fixing ammonia into glutamine. In cirrhosis the liver's clearance fails and portosystemic shunting lets gut ammonia bypass it, so muscle and kidney handling decide the blood level. The carded human studies measured exactly this: across catheterised organs in 24 patients with cirrhosis and a TIPSS, the portal-drained viscera produced the most ammonia, skeletal muscle removed more ammonia than the cirrhotic liver did, and the kidneys produced as much ammonia as the whole hepatosplanchnic area (Olde Damink 2002). After a simulated gut bleed, renal ammonia production rose 6-fold while gut production did not change, and muscle was again the major removal site (Olde Damink 2003). PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — gut (portal-drained viscera) is the largest ammonia source, the cirrhotic and shunted liver clears little, skeletal muscle removes more ammonia than the liver (fixing it as glutamine), and the kidney becomes a major producer after a gut bleed (production up 6-fold) (Guyton & Hall; Ganong)

title: The enterohepatic circulation: a gram-sized bile acid pool recycled many times a day, topped up by a few hundred milligrams of synthesis
question: In adults, how does the enterohepatic circulation recycle bile acids and how many times a day does the bile acid pool circulate?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology and Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology). The textbook account: the liver makes primary bile acids from cholesterol, conjugates them, and secretes them into bile; the gallbladder stores and concentrates bile between meals; after a meal the bile acids do their detergent work in the small intestine and are then actively reabsorbed in the terminal ileum (about 95% per pass), return in portal blood, and are re-secreted — the enterohepatic circulation. The textbooks put the pool at roughly 2–3 g, cycling about 4–12 times a day (the figure varies by source and by how cycling is counted), with the small faecal loss replaced by new synthesis of a few hundred milligrams a day. The carded human isotope studies measured the components of that account: cholic and chenodeoxycholic acid pools of 0.84 g and 0.64 g with fractional turnover rates of 0.28 and 0.17 per day and matching synthesis rates (Everson 1987); a cholic acid fractional turnover of 0.46 per day by a microscale stable-isotope method whose human values agreed with the classic literature (Hulzebos 2001); and the feedback limb — feeding one bile acid suppressed synthesis of the others by 38–67% and shrank their pools by about half (Tauber 1996), which is how the returning pool tells the liver to stop making more. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — the bile acid pool (measured primary-acid pools ~0.8 g cholic + ~0.6 g chenodeoxycholic; textbook total ~2–3 g) is secreted, reabsorbed in the terminal ileum and re-secreted about 4–12 times a day (textbook figure), while synthesis replaces only the small daily loss and is feedback-suppressed up to 65% by returning bile acids (Boron & Boulpaep; Guyton & Hall)

title: Why B12 needs intrinsic factor and a terminal ileum: the carrier-and-door physiology shown in human absorption studies
question: In adults, why does vitamin B12 absorption require intrinsic factor and an intact terminal ileum?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology and Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology). The textbook account is a relay: food B12 is freed by acid and pepsin, rides first on R-protein, is handed to intrinsic factor — secreted by gastric parietal cells — when pancreatic enzymes digest the R-protein in the duodenum, and the intrinsic-factor–B12 complex is then taken up by specific receptors (the cubilin–amnionless complex) that exist only in the terminal ileum. Both requirements are therefore anatomical: no intrinsic factor, no protected carrier through the small bowel; no terminal ileum, no receptor to land on. The carded human studies show each requirement operating in people. Whole-body counting after a 5 µg dose of intrinsic-factor-bound labelled B12 put normal absorption at 20.4% and showed the ileum's absorptive capacity adapting upward when proximal bowel was lost (Mackinnon 1975). Patients with diseased or resected ileums had low B12 (and low B12 analogues, which share the ileal route), while pernicious-anaemia patients — whose defect is intrinsic factor, not ileum — had normal analogue levels (Shaw 1989). And Schilling testing after continent ileostomy showed absorption preserved where functioning ileal mucosa remained in circuit (Jagenburg 1975). PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — dietary B12 reaches the blood only as the intrinsic-factor complex taken up by terminal-ileal receptors: normal absorption of an IF-bound test dose was 20.4%, ileal disease or resection lowers B12, and absorption adapts upward when ileum survives proximal resection (Ganong; Boron & Boulpaep)

title: Bilirubin's path from haem to bile — and why reduced conjugation raises the unconjugated form: human kinetics and the Gilbert natural experiment
question: In adults, how is bilirubin made, conjugated in the liver, and excreted into bile, and why does the unconjugated form rise when conjugation is reduced?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology). The textbook account: bilirubin is the end-product of haem breakdown — senescent red cells are dismantled in macrophages, haem oxygenase opens the haem ring to biliverdin (releasing iron and carbon monoxide), and biliverdin reductase yields unconjugated bilirubin, which is water-insoluble, travels to the liver bound to albumin, is taken up by hepatocytes, and is conjugated by UDP-glucuronyl transferase to mono- and diglucuronides; the water-soluble conjugates are secreted into bile and leave in the stool. Because plasma bilirubin is almost all unconjugated and its level is set by production against hepatic clearance, anything that cuts conjugation — Gilbert syndrome's reduced transferase activity is the human model — backs up the unconjugated form specifically. The carded human studies measured each step: production of 3.8 mg/kg/day and hepatic clearance of 47 ml/min in healthy adults (Berk 1969); bile from Gilbert patients carrying far less diglucuronide (68% vs 88%) and more monoglucuronide (23% vs 7%), localising the defect to adding the second glucuronic acid (Goresky 1978); and caloric restriction raising unconjugated bilirubin precisely in people with reduced transferase activity, not in haemolysis with normal enzyme (Felsher 1975). PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — bilirubin is produced from haem at 3.8 mg/kg/day, cleared by the liver at 47 ml/min, conjugated to mono- and diglucuronides and secreted into bile; when conjugation is reduced (Gilbert model: bile diglucuronide 68% vs 88%), the unconjugated substrate is what accumulates in plasma (Guyton & Hall)

title: From meal fat to blood: why long-chain fat takes the lymph in chylomicrons and medium-chain fat takes the portal vein
question: In adults, what happens to dietary fat between ingestion and absorption, and why do medium-chain triglycerides reach the liver directly through the portal vein?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology). The textbook account: dietary triglyceride is emulsified, hydrolysed by pancreatic lipase to 2-monoglycerides and free fatty acids, solubilised in bile-salt micelles, taken up by enterocytes, re-esterified, and exported in chylomicrons into lymph — reaching the blood via the thoracic duct and the liver only later, as remnants. Medium-chain triglycerides break every step of that chain: their fatty acids (C8–C10) are hydrolysed faster, are water-soluble enough to leave the enterocyte without re-esterification or chylomicron packaging, bind albumin, and drain straight into the portal vein to the liver. The carded human studies show the route difference in people. A single MCT dose produced a much smaller serum and chylomicron triglyceride response than the same dose of long-chain fat in healthy men (Kasai 2003) — the signature of fat that mostly bypassed chylomicrons. Position-labelled decanoic acid confirmed the main route is portal while showing a minority does enter chylomicron triglyceride (Yli-Jokipii 2004). And in patients with fat malabsorption, an MCT formula measurably increased fat absorption where a long-chain formula did not (Craig 1997) — the clinical consequence of a route that needs less lipolysis, no micellar packaging and no lymph. The index's MCT weight-loss shelf (pack #5280) asks a different question and is not re-carded here. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — long-chain fat is hydrolysed, micellar-solubilised, re-esterified and exported in chylomicrons via lymph, while medium-chain fatty acids are absorbed mainly into the portal vein (blunted chylomicron response in healthy men; absorption rescued in malabsorption), reaching the liver directly (Boron & Boulpaep)

title: Secretin and CCK after a meal: the alkaline river and the enzymes it carries — human infusion and blockade studies
question: In adults, how do secretin and cholecystokinin coordinate pancreatic enzyme and bicarbonate secretion after a meal?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology). The textbook division of labour: acid entering the duodenum releases secretin from S cells, and secretin drives the duct cells to secrete a large volume of bicarbonate-rich fluid that neutralises the acid; fat and protein products release cholecystokinin (CCK) from I cells, and CCK drives the acinar cells to secrete enzymes (and contracts the gallbladder), with the vagus nerve setting the gain on both — secretin's fluid also flushes CCK's enzymes down the duct. The carded human infusion studies show the coordination directly. On a background secretin infusion holding plasma secretin at postprandial levels (~5 pM), a physiological CCK-8 infusion (~9 pM, the postprandial range) stimulated trypsin, amylase and bicarbonate output, and blocking the CCK receptor cut those responses by about three quarters and virtually abolished gallbladder contraction (Cantor 1991). Meal-stimulated enzyme secretion was almost completely blocked by atropine and 60% blocked by a CCK antagonist (Adler 1991) — CCK is the hormonal driver, cholinergic tone the permissive amplifier. And combined secretin–CCK testing in healthy volunteers produced peak duodenal bicarbonate of 108 mmol/L, the neutralising fluid in action (Law 2012). PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — secretin (postprandial ~5 pM) drives bicarbonate-rich ductal fluid (peak 108 mmol/L in healthy volunteers) while CCK (postprandial ~9 pM) drives acinar enzyme output and gallbladder contraction, with CCK blockade cutting responses 74–98% and cholinergic tone setting the gain (Guyton & Hall)

title: What sets gastric emptying: meal form sets the pace (liquid half-time 44 minutes vs solid 162), and duodenal fat and acid apply the brake — pyloric pressure, cholecystokinin and tonic duodenal occlusion in human studies
question: In adults, what sets the rate of gastric emptying of a meal, and how do fat and acid in the duodenum slow it?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED, framed by Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology (named here as framing, not as an evidence card): the stomach empties at a rate set by meal volume, physical state and caloric/osmotic content, gated by duodenal feedback — the enterogastric brake. The human record fetched for this shelf shows each element directly. Meal form sets the baseline rate: in 73 healthy volunteers given a standard scintigraphic test meal, the liquid component emptied with a median half-time of 44 minutes and the solid component with a median half-time of 162 minutes (Parker 2017). Duodenal contents, not gastric contents, carry the brake: emptying was fastest when duodenal contents were isotonic, and non-isotonic duodenal contents slowed it, while non-isotonic solutions in stomach or jejunum did not slow emptying so long as the duodenum stayed isotonic (Meeroff 1975). Fat is a brake signal: intraduodenal fat inhibited gastric emptying in humans (Valenzuela 1981, whose title also names secretin and the cholecystokinin octapeptide), and intraduodenal lipid at 2 kcal/min stimulated isolated pyloric pressure waves and basal pyloric pressure, suppressed antral and duodenal pressure waves, and raised plasma cholecystokinin versus saline in 8 healthy men (Vozzo 2002). Acid is a brake signal with a mechanical face: in 8 volunteers studied by synchronised videofluoroscopy and manometry, duodenal HCl induced frequent large-amplitude contractions and prolonged tonic occlusion of the duodenum within 15–30 seconds, whereas oleate or bile increased duodenal diameter and reduced contractility — the duodenum restricting outflow either by tonic resistance or by delaying clearance (Rao 1996). Several of these classic studies are small (n = 8) or report no number in the fetched record (printed as N not documented on the card face); the physiology is established because the findings converge, not because any one study is large.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — gastric emptying is set by meal volume, form and caloric/osmotic content and gated by duodenal feedback: liquids empty far faster than solids (median half-times 44 vs 162 minutes), and duodenal fat (via cholecystokinin and pyloric pressure) and duodenal acid (via tonic duodenal occlusion) both slow outflow
