title: Fremanezumab for episodic and chronic migraine (drug-specific slice; HALO primaries homed on live #336): sustained migraine-day reductions over 52 weeks and pooled disability benefit versus placebo, built on free long-term and pooled reports
question: Does fremanezumab reduce monthly migraine days in episodic and chronic migraine versus placebo?
balance: FLAG — PRECEDENT (b), documented prominently: the two primary HALO trials (HALO EM, Dodick 2018; HALO CM, Silberstein 2017) are already carded with their figures on live shelf #336, the CGRP-class shelf, so under the one-home rule their PMIDs are NOT re-carded here and do not appear in any card source line on this shelf. This fremanezumab-specific shelf is built instead on three or more free, distinct reports of the same programme, as the genuinely different drug-specific slice. On those reports: over 52 weeks in a randomised long-term study of 1,890 patients, fremanezumab reduced monthly migraine days from baseline by 7.2 days (chronic, quarterly) and 8.0 days (chronic, monthly) and by 5.2 and 5.1 days in episodic migraine, with injection-site reactions the commonest adverse events (induration 33%, pain 31%, erythema 26%) — a within-treatment long-term study, not a placebo comparison (Goadsby 2020). The placebo-controlled benefit is carried by the pooled phase 3 analyses: clinically meaningful disability improvement (≥5-point HIT-6 reduction) in 53% (quarterly) and 55% (monthly) versus 39% on placebo, with MIDAS responder proportions also significantly higher (McAllister 2022, pooling HALO EM, HALO CM and FOCUS, 2,842 patients in the companion safety pooling); overall adverse events occurred in 58–65% and serious adverse events in under 1–2% across fremanezumab and placebo groups, with cardio- and cerebrovascular events infrequent at 2–6% regardless of vascular history (Diener 2022). Among patients who responded in the HALO trials, ≥50% reductions in monthly migraine days were achieved by 59.8–63.7% of episodic responders and 52.8–59.0% of chronic responders (Silberstein 2021, post hoc). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a single drug programme whose primary trials are homed on the class shelf — the drug-specific evidence is consistent and placebo-controlled in its pooled form, but this shelf's own cards are a long-term study, pooled analyses and a post hoc responder analysis, so the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE rather than upgraded on the homed primaries.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — fremanezumab reduced monthly migraine days over 52 weeks (episodic −5.1 to −5.2 days; chronic −7.2 to −8.0 days from baseline) and beat placebo on pooled disability outcomes (53–55% vs 39%); FLAG: the primary HALO trials are homed on live #336 and are not re-carded here — this shelf is built on free long-term, pooled and post hoc reports under precedent (b)

title: Diroximel versus dimethyl fumarate in relapsing-remitting MS: fewer gastrointestinal events in the head-to-head trial (34.8% vs 49.0%), with equal efficacy inferred from bioequivalent active-metabolite exposure — not from a relapse trial
question: Is diroximel fumarate as effective as dimethyl fumarate in relapsing-remitting MS with fewer gastrointestinal adverse events?
balance: The dimethyl fumarate home, pack #2359, answers dimethyl fumarate versus placebo (DEFINE/CONFIRM) and does not answer this head-to-head question — verified against that pack. The two fumarates deliver the same active metabolite: diroximel fumarate 462 mg and dimethyl fumarate 240 mg produce bioequivalent exposure of monomethyl fumarate and are therefore expected to have similar efficacy (Naismith 2020, EVOLVE-MS-2 record). That expectation is the efficacy leg — there is no head-to-head relapse trial — and it is supported only indirectly by diroximel's own open-label programme: in EVOLVE-MS-1, 1,057 patients treated for up to 96 weeks had an adjusted annualized relapse rate of 0.13 (95% CI 0.11–0.15) and a 72.7% reduction in gadolinium-enhancing lesions from baseline, exploratory endpoints without a comparator (Singer 2023). The tolerability leg is directly randomised: in the 5-week head-to-head EVOLVE-MS-2 trial, diroximel patients had a 46% relative reduction in days with a gastrointestinal symptom intensity score ≥2 (rate ratio 0.54, 95% CI 0.39–0.75), gastrointestinal adverse events in 34.8% versus 49.0%, and gastrointestinal discontinuations in 0.8% versus 4.8% (Naismith 2020); the companion quality-of-life analysis found gastrointestinal symptoms interfered 'quite a bit' or 'extremely' with daily activities in 9.5% on diroximel versus 28.9% on dimethyl fumarate (Wundes 2021). Early open-label data had already shown gastrointestinal events in 30.9% of 696 patients, under 1% discontinuing for them (Palte 2019, described in the synthesis). PROPOSED SPLIT (evidence type): fewer gastrointestinal adverse events than dimethyl fumarate is randomised-trial proven; equal effectiveness is inferred from bioequivalent active-metabolite exposure plus uncontrolled relapse data, not from a head-to-head efficacy trial.
stamp: SPLIT (evidence type) — diroximel fumarate caused fewer gastrointestinal adverse events than dimethyl fumarate in a randomised head-to-head trial (34.8% vs 49.0%; GI discontinuations 0.8% vs 4.8%), but equal effectiveness is inferred from bioequivalent monomethyl fumarate exposure and uncontrolled programme data, not trialled head-to-head

title: Natalizumab every 6 weeks versus every 4 weeks in stable relapsing MS (PARTIAL slice of #2360): clinical outcomes maintained in NOVA with a numerical MRI excess, and lower PML risk only in observational TOUCH data
question: In relapsing MS stable on natalizumab, does extended-interval dosing (every 6 weeks) preserve efficacy versus standard every-4-week dosing, and does it lower PML risk?
balance: PARTIAL completion of pack #2360 (natalizumab versus placebo, AFFIRM/SENTINEL): that home answers whether natalizumab works at all; this shelf answers only the uncovered slice — the dosing-interval strategy and PML risk by interval — and re-cards no PMID from #2360. The two sub-questions rest on different evidence types and are stamped separately, so the randomised leg cannot upgrade the observational leg. Efficacy (randomised): in NOVA, 499 patients stable on every-4-week natalizumab for at least 12 months were randomised to switch to every 6 weeks or continue every 4 weeks; at week 72 the adjusted mean numbers of new or newly enlarging T2 lesions were 0.20 versus 0.05 (mean lesion ratio 4.24, 95% CI 0.86–20.85; p = 0.076 on the primary estimand; ratio 4.93, p = 0.044 on the secondary estimand), with most excess lesions contributed by two patients with ≥25 lesions — a numerical difference in a trial where control-arm activity was lower than expected, not a clean preservation proof (Foley 2022). Exploratory clinical and patient-reported outcomes showed no significant differences between intervals (EDSS improvement 11.7% vs 10.8%; Ryerson 2023). PML risk (observational): in the TOUCH programme's 35,521 anti-JC-virus-antibody-positive patients, extended-interval dosing was associated with hazard ratios for PML of 0.06 (primary analysis) and 0.12 (secondary) versus standard dosing — relative risk reductions of 94% and 88% — in retrospective analyses, Class III evidence (Ryerson 2019). NOVA itself was not powered for PML and recorded one asymptomatic PML case in the 6-week arm. PROPOSED SPLIT (evidence type): clinical outcomes were maintained in the randomised trial with a small numerical MRI excess on extended dosing, while the lower PML risk rests on observational data only and is labelled observational.
stamp: SPLIT (evidence type) — randomised NOVA: clinical outcomes maintained on every-6-week dosing with numerically more new T2 lesions (0.20 vs 0.05); observational TOUCH: extended-interval dosing associated with 94% and 88% relative lower PML risk (labelled observational; the randomised leg does not upgrade the observational leg)

title: Simvastatin 80 mg in secondary progressive MS: the phase 2 brain-atrophy signal (43% relative reduction) failed in phase 3 — MS-STAT2 showed no difference in disability progression (40% vs 36%)
question: Does simvastatin 80 mg slow disability progression in secondary progressive MS versus placebo?
balance: The phase 2 signal did not survive phase 3, and this shelf's stamp follows the full evidence, not the phase 2 result. In MS-STAT (phase 2, 140 patients), simvastatin 80 mg reduced the annualised rate of whole-brain atrophy by 43% relative versus placebo (0.288% vs 0.584% per year; adjusted difference −0.254% per year, 95% CI −0.422 to −0.087; p = 0.003) — a surrogate imaging endpoint (Chataway 2014). Its cognitive secondary analysis found a 1.2-point better frontal assessment battery score and a 2.5-point better physical quality-of-life component at 24 months, with no effect on other cognitive, neuropsychiatric or quality-of-life measures (Chan 2017). In MS-STAT2 (phase 3, 964 patients, up to 4.5 years), the primary outcome went the other way numerically: 6-month confirmed disability progression occurred in 40% (192/482) on simvastatin versus 36% (173/482) on placebo (adjusted hazard ratio 1.13, 95% CI 0.91–1.39; p = 0.26) — the treatment made no difference, and the authors concluded simvastatin in MS should be confined to existing vascular indications (Chataway 2025). No emergent safety issues were seen in phase 3 apart from one serious adverse reaction of rhabdomyolysis in the simvastatin group. PROPOSED stamp: no benefit on disability progression — the large phase 3 trial is the answer to the question as asked, and the brain-atrophy finding is presented as the unconfirmed surrogate signal that prompted it.
stamp: NO BENEFIT — simvastatin 80 mg made no difference to disability progression in secondary progressive MS in the phase 3 MS-STAT2 trial (progression 40% vs 36%; adjusted HR 1.13; the treatment made no difference); the phase 2 brain-atrophy signal did not translate

title: Foslevodopa–foscarbidopa infusion in advanced Parkinson's: 1.75 extra hours of ON time without troublesome dyskinesia versus oral levodopa–carbidopa in the phase 3 trial (active-controlled, not placebo-infusion — premise corrected; BouNDless is a different product)
question: In advanced Parkinson's disease, does continuous subcutaneous foslevodopa–foscarbidopa infusion increase ON time without troublesome dyskinesia versus placebo infusion?
balance: PREMISE CORRECTION, verified from the fetched records: the foslevodopa–foscarbidopa phase 3 trial was NOT a placebo-infusion trial. It was a double-blind, double-dummy, active-controlled trial in which the control group received oral immediate-release levodopa–carbidopa plus a continuous subcutaneous placebo-solution infusion, and the treatment group received foslevodopa–foscarbidopa infusion plus oral placebo (Soileau 2022). So the question's 'versus placebo infusion' is answered in the only form the evidence allows: infusion versus oral therapy, with placebo infusion present in the control arm. (The placebo-infusion phase 3 named BouNDless tests a different product, ND0612 levodopa–carbidopa infusion, and is not carded here — a different intervention.) On the corrected comparison: foslevodopa–foscarbidopa increased ON time without troublesome dyskinesia by 2.72 hours versus 0.97 hours on oral levodopa–carbidopa at 12 weeks (difference 1.75 hours, 95% CI 0.46–3.05; p = 0.0083) and reduced OFF time more (−2.75 vs −0.96 hours; difference −1.79 hours; p = 0.0054), at the cost of infusion-site adverse events (erythema 27%, pain 26%, cellulitis 19%) and a 22% versus 1% premature discontinuation rate for adverse events (Soileau 2022). A separate 52-week single-arm open-label study of 244 patients found ON time without troublesome dyskinesia improved by 3.8 hours and OFF time by −3.5 hours from baseline, with 107 of 244 discontinuing (Aldred 2023 — uncontrolled, labelled as such). A phase 1 study in 28 patients showed the infusion holds levodopa exposure steady with minimal fluctuation over 72 hours (Rosebraugh 2021). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): one randomised active-controlled trial — a single programme caps at POSSIBLE — showing about 1.75 extra hours of good ON time versus oral levodopa–carbidopa, with a substantial infusion-site burden.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — continuous foslevodopa–foscarbidopa infusion increased ON time without troublesome dyskinesia by 1.75 hours versus oral levodopa–carbidopa in one active-controlled phase 3 trial (PREMISE CORRECTED: the trial's control arm received placebo infusion plus oral levodopa–carbidopa, not placebo infusion alone), with infusion-site events and 22% adverse-event discontinuation

title: Probiotics for constipation in Parkinson's disease: bowel frequency improved in three small placebo-controlled trials (+1.3 to +2.97 movements per week) — differing multi-strain products, strains named only where the publication names them
question: In Parkinson's disease with chronic constipation, do probiotics improve bowel-movement frequency and constipation scores versus placebo?
balance: Four small randomised trials and their meta-analysis point the same way on bowel frequency, over 4–8 weeks, with different multi-strain products — so the benefit is a class-of-products signal in small trials, not proof for any one formulation. The largest trial (Tan 2021, 72 patients, 4 weeks) used a multistrain probiotic capsule — the fetched record does not name the strains or a brand/company, and this shelf says so plainly rather than guessing — and found spontaneous bowel movements increased by 1.0 per week on probiotics versus a decrease of 0.3 on placebo (mean difference 1.3, 95% CI 0.8–1.8; p < 0.001), with stool consistency and constipation-related quality of life also improved and satisfaction 65.6% versus 21.6%. A 2025 trial (Zareie, 72 patients, 6 weeks) names its product's strains exactly — Lactobacillus acidophilus, Lactobacillus casei, Lactobacillus rhamnosus, Bifidobacterium lactis, Bifidobacterium longum and Bifidobacterium breve, 1 × 10⁹ CFU each, total 12 × 10⁹ CFU/day — and found a larger difference (spontaneous bowel movements +3.41 vs +0.44; between-group difference 2.97, 95% CI 2.46–3.53; p < 0.001) with constipation quality of life improved. A third small trial (Ghalandari 2023, 27 analysed patients, 8 weeks, multi-strain product whose strains are not named in the fetched record) found bowel-movement frequency 4 versus 2 per week favouring probiotics (p = 0.02). Pooling the three randomised trials available in 2023 gave a standardised mean difference of 0.92 (95% CI 0.65–1.19) for bowel-movement frequency (Ghalandari meta-analysis 2023). No trial showed a motor benefit. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): consistent direction across several small short trials of differing products, capped at POSSIBLE by size, duration and product heterogeneity.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — probiotics improved bowel-movement frequency versus placebo in several small short randomised trials in Parkinson's constipation (mean difference +1.3 to +2.97 movements per week; pooled SMD 0.92), with differing multi-strain products and only one record naming its strains

title: Depression in Parkinson's disease: pramipexole beat placebo in one large trial (80% of effect direct), paroxetine beat placebo in a smaller trial, but the pooled SSRI estimate was null — a drug-by-drug split
question: In Parkinson's disease with depression, does pramipexole improve depressive symptoms versus placebo, and how do SSRIs compare?
balance: Pramipexole has the single largest placebo-controlled trial in this question, and its benefit was mostly a direct antidepressant effect rather than a by-product of motor improvement. In Barone 2010 (287 patients analysed, 12 weeks), Beck Depression Inventory scores fell by an adjusted mean 5.9 points on pramipexole versus 4.0 on placebo (difference 1.9, 95% CI 0.5–3.4; p = 0.01), and a prespecified path analysis attributed 80% of the total treatment effect to a direct effect on depressive symptoms. In the earlier head-to-head trial, recovery (Hamilton Depression Rating Scale ≤8) occurred in 60.6% on pramipexole versus 27.3% on sertraline 50 mg in 67 patients without motor fluctuations (p = 0.006) — an open-label comparison, so it cannot carry the same weight (Barone 2006). For SSRIs proper, the best single trial is Richard 2012: paroxetine improved Hamilton scores by 6.2 points more than placebo (97.5% CI 2.2–10.3; p = 0.0007) and the SNRI venlafaxine XR by 4.2 points more (97.5% CI 0.1–8.4; p = 0.02) in 115 patients, with no effect on motor function. But the pooled SSRI record is weaker than that one trial: a 2010 meta-analysis of six SSRI-versus-placebo randomised trials found a combined risk ratio of 1.08 (95% CI 0.77–1.55; p = 0.67) — insufficient evidence to reject no difference — and warned a false negative could not be excluded given small samples (Skapinakis 2010). PROPOSED SPLIT (drug): pramipexole improves depressive symptoms versus placebo in one large trial (POSSIBLE, single-trial cap); SSRI evidence is mixed — one positive paroxetine trial against a null pooled SSRI estimate — so the SSRI leg is MAYBE (weak evidence) at class level.
stamp: SPLIT (drug) — pramipexole improved depressive symptoms versus placebo in one large trial (Beck difference 1.9 points; POSSIBLE, single-trial cap); SSRIs compare mixed — paroxetine beat placebo in one trial (+6.2 Hamilton points) but the pooled SSRI estimate was null (RR 1.08), so the SSRI leg is MAYBE (weak evidence)

title: Memantine for migraine prevention: one small positive placebo-controlled trial (n = 60) and two uncontrolled reports — a thin base that stays at MAYBE (weak evidence)
question: Does memantine prevent episodic migraine versus placebo?
balance: THIN BASE, confirmed at build: the ≥3-report gate is met only by counting one small placebo-controlled trial plus two uncontrolled reports — there is exactly one randomised placebo-controlled trial of memantine for migraine prevention in the fetched record. In that trial (Noruzzadeh 2016, 60 patients with migraine without aura, 12 weeks), memantine 10 mg/day reduced monthly attack frequency by a mean 3.4 attacks versus 1.0 on placebo (mean difference 2.3, 95% CI 1.1–3.5; p < 0.001), with migraine days also reduced more on memantine. The supporting reports have no placebo arm: in Bigal 2008, 28 patients with refractory migraine (episodic with 8–14 headache days per month or transformed migraine, having failed at least two preventives) fell from 21.8 to 16.1 headache days per month over 3 months on memantine 10–20 mg/day (p < 0.01, within-group); in Charles 2007, 36 of 54 patients treated for at least 2 months in a retrospective clinic series of 60 reported a significant reduction in estimated headache frequency. A 2014 review of the primary-headache literature reached the same shape of conclusion — data from several retrospective reports and two prospective trials suggested memantine may be useful, mostly in refractory chronic migraine (Huang 2014, described in the synthesis, not carded as a fourth evidence card to avoid double-counting the same reports). Because uncontrolled before–after falls in migraine frequency are exactly what placebo arms and regression also produce, the uncontrolled reports cannot corroborate the trial. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): one small positive trial, no replication, supporting evidence uncontrolled.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — memantine reduced monthly attack frequency versus placebo in one small trial (n = 60; mean difference 2.3 attacks), with only uncontrolled pilot and retrospective reports (n = 28; 54 analysed) behind it; total evidence base 148 participants, no replication

title: Lisinopril for migraine prevention: 21% relative fewer migraine days versus placebo in one small 2001 crossover trial — no replication, class pooling inconclusive, MAYBE (weak evidence)
question: Does lisinopril prevent migraine attacks versus placebo in frequent episodic migraine?
balance: THIN BASE, confirmed at build: lisinopril itself rests on exactly one placebo-controlled trial — the ≥3-report gate for this shelf is met by that trial plus two pooled analyses of the wider blood-pressure-drug class, and the stamp does not pretend otherwise. The candesartan home, pack #3686, is a different drug and does not answer this question — verified against that pack's question. In Schrader 2001, a double-blind placebo-controlled crossover trial in 60 patients with two to six migraine episodes a month, lisinopril 20 mg daily (after one week at 10 mg) reduced hours with headache by 20% (95% CI 5% to 36%), days with headache by 17% (5% to 30%), days with migraine by 21% (9% to 34%) and headache severity index by 20% (3% to 37%) versus placebo in the 47 participants with complete data, with intention-to-treat analysis of 55 patients supporting the differences; days with migraine fell by at least 50% in 14 participants on active treatment versus placebo. The class-level pooling is broader but shallower for lisinopril specifically: a 2023 meta-analysis of 50 blood-pressure-medication trials found ACE inhibitors as a class reduced monthly headache days by a standardised estimate of −1.3 (95% CI −2.9 to 0.2) versus placebo — a class estimate whose confidence interval crosses zero, with the separately significant specific drugs listed not including lisinopril (Carcel 2023). A 2019 systematic review of ACE inhibitors and ARBs in migraine found 18 reports, noted the lisinopril evidence was open-label in the reports it counted at 5 mg, and concluded these drugs are not recommended as first-line prophylactics on the limited trials and small samples, though they may be useful where hypertension coexists (Dorosch 2019). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): one small crossover trial from 2001, never followed by a second lisinopril trial in the fetched record.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — lisinopril reduced days with migraine by 21% relative versus placebo in one small 2001 crossover trial (60 patients, 47 with complete data), with no second lisinopril trial and a class-level ACE-inhibitor pooled estimate whose interval crosses zero

title: Acupuncture for migraine prevention: a small real advantage over sham (response 50% vs 41%), and short-term effects at least matching prophylactic drugs
question: Does acupuncture reduce migraine frequency versus sham acupuncture and versus prophylactic drug treatment?
balance: Acupuncture reduced migraine frequency a small amount more than sham acupuncture and at least as much as prophylactic drug treatment in the short term. The updated Cochrane review (Linde 2016; 22 trials, 4,985 participants) found a small but significant advantage over sham after treatment (standardised mean difference -0.18; response — headache frequency at least halved — in 50% on true acupuncture vs 41% on sham, relative risk 1.23) and a larger short-term advantage over prophylactic drugs (SMD -0.25 after treatment; response 57% vs 46%, relative risk 1.24) that was not maintained at follow-up, with fewer adverse-effect dropouts than drugs. Two later randomised trials point the same way against sham: Zhao 2017 (true acupuncture cut attack frequency by 3.2 vs 2.1 attacks on sham at week 16) and Xu 2020 (manual acupuncture cut migraine days more than non-penetrating sham at weeks 17–20). No single named acupuncture programme was tested across these studies: the records describe session-based manual acupuncture at true points (20 sessions in both Zhao and Xu), with point selection varying between trials, and no branded or single named protocol is given in the publications carded. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit, small over sham): a real but small advantage over sham, and short-term effects at least similar to prophylactic drugs, on moderate-quality evidence.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit, small over sham) — acupuncture reduced migraine frequency slightly more than sham (Cochrane response 50% vs 41%, relative risk 1.23) and at least as much as prophylactic drugs short-term (57% vs 46%), with fewer adverse effects than drugs

title: Vestibular migraine prevention: the only placebo-controlled trial (metoprolol) was null, and the positive evidence is small trials without placebo controls
question: In vestibular migraine, do preventive treatments used for migraine (e.g., beta-blockers, tricyclics, triptan-based strategies) reduce vertigo attack frequency versus placebo?
balance: The vestibular-migraine prevention evidence is thin and mostly not placebo-controlled. The only placebo-controlled trial carded, PROVEMIG, randomised 130 patients to metoprolol or placebo, was stopped early for poor accrual (266 planned), and found no difference in vertiginous attacks (incidence rate ratio 0.983, 95% CI 0.902 to 1.071) — the treatment made no difference. Small active-comparator trials report large within-group falls in attacks on propranolol and on venlafaxine (Salviz 2016, 64 patients, no placebo group) and a vertigo-frequency advantage for adding flunarizine to betahistine-based episodic treatment (Lepcha 2014, 48 patients). A 2023 network meta-analysis of the whole randomised base — 5 trials, 334 patients — found valproate superior to placebo or abortive treatment alone for vertigo frequency (mean difference -4.12 attacks) and handicap gains for flunarizine, valproate and venlafaxine, while grading the certainty low and metoprolol worst for efficacy. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): some migraine preventives may reduce vertigo attacks in vestibular migraine, but the one adequately blinded placebo test was null and the positive signals come from small trials without placebo controls.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — preventive migraine treatments may reduce vertigo attacks in vestibular migraine (thin comparative evidence: the only placebo-controlled trial, of metoprolol, was null; positive signals come from small trials without placebo controls and a 5-trial, 334-patient network meta-analysis at low certainty)

title: Soticlestat for Dravet and Lennox–Gastaut syndromes: phase 2 Dravet signal, phase 3 primary missed in Dravet and flatly null in Lennox–Gastaut (SKYLINE/SKYWAY, published 2026)
question: In Dravet syndrome and Lennox–Gastaut syndrome, does soticlestat reduce convulsive/drop seizure frequency versus placebo as adjunctive therapy?
balance: FLAG — phase 3 publication status verified from the fetched records this session: SKYLINE (Dravet) and SKYWAY (Lennox–Gastaut) have both now published in Epilepsia (2026), so the cardable base is three randomised reports, not ELEKTRA alone. The phase 2 ELEKTRA trial (141 children) met its combined primary endpoint (placebo-adjusted median seizure-frequency reduction 30.21%, P = .0008), driven by Dravet convulsive seizures (50.00%, P = .0002); its Lennox–Gastaut drop-seizure result was not significant (17.08%, P = .1160). The phase 3 trials did not confirm those signals on their primaries: SKYLINE (144 participants with Dravet) narrowly missed (median convulsive-seizure change -22.16% on soticlestat vs -8.64% on placebo; difference -15.64%, P = .061), although 27.4% vs 9.9% achieved a 50% response (nominal P = .008); SKYWAY (270 participants with Lennox–Gastaut) was flatly null on major motor drop seizures (difference -1.17%, P = .785 — the treatment made no difference). PROPOSED SPLIT (syndrome and phase): a phase 2 Dravet signal that phase 3 did not confirm on its primary endpoint, and no demonstrated benefit in Lennox–Gastaut syndrome in either phase.
stamp: SPLIT (syndrome and phase) — phase 2 ELEKTRA favoured soticlestat in Dravet syndrome (placebo-adjusted 50.00%) but phase 3 SKYLINE missed its primary endpoint (P = .061), and Lennox–Gastaut syndrome was null in both ELEKTRA's subgroup and phase 3 SKYWAY (P = .785, the treatment made no difference)

title: Plasma p-tau217 for Alzheimer's pathology in people with cognitive symptoms: about 90% accuracy at predefined cutoffs — with each figure tied to its named assay and setting
question: How accurately does a plasma phosphorylated-tau (p-tau217) blood test identify Alzheimer's disease pathology in people presenting with cognitive symptoms?
balance: In people with cognitive symptoms, plasma p-tau217 identified Alzheimer's disease pathology with high accuracy in every carded cohort — but the numbers are assay- and setting-dependent, and each card names the assay or method its figures belong to. Palmqvist 2020 (1,402 participants across an Arizona neuropathology cohort, BioFINDER-2, and a Colombian autosomal-dominant kindred) found an area under the curve of 0.96 for clinical Alzheimer's dementia versus other neurodegenerative diseases and 0.93 for abnormal tau-PET. Palmqvist 2024 tested a mass-spectrometry method (percentage p-tau217, alone and combined with the amyloid-beta 42/40 ratio as the APS2 score) prospectively in 1,213 Swedish patients with cognitive symptoms: diagnostic accuracy was 88–92% in primary and secondary care at predefined cutoffs, against 61% for primary care physicians and 73% for dementia specialists using clinical workup alone. Ashton 2024 validated the commercially available ALZpath pTau217 immunoassay in 786 participants (TRIAD, WRAP and SPIN cohorts): AUC 0.92–0.96 for amyloid pathology and 0.93–0.97 for tau pathology. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (test-accuracy, cohort evidence): accuracy around 90% at predefined cutoffs in symptomatic populations is consistently reported, but cutoffs and performance do not transfer automatically between assays, platforms or care settings.
stamp: POSSIBLE (test-accuracy, cohort evidence) — plasma p-tau217 identified Alzheimer's pathology with AUC 0.89–0.97 across cohorts and about 90% diagnostic accuracy at predefined cutoffs in primary and secondary care; performance is assay- and setting-dependent

title: Post-stroke dysphagia: thickened fluids and chin-down posture are unproven for preventing pneumonia or death in stroke — and protocolised free water showed no pneumonia penalty in selected patients
question: After stroke with dysphagia, do thickened fluids and chin-down posture prevent aspiration pneumonia and death versus thin fluids with free-water access?
balance: No stroke trial carded here shows that thickened fluids or chin-down posture prevent aspiration pneumonia or death. The direct head-to-head trial of chin-down posture versus nectar- and honey-thick liquids enrolled people with dementia or Parkinson disease, not stroke, so it is not carded on this shelf and no figures are taken from it. In stroke specifically, the randomised evidence tests the other side of the question — whether allowing thin water is harmful — and in carefully selected patients it did not show harm: a free-water trial in acute stroke and trauma patients (104 participants) found no significant outcome differences and too few pneumonias to compare, and a post-stroke water-protocol trial found no pneumonia in either group (with only 14 participants analysed). A systematic review of free-water protocols (8 studies, 245 patients with dysphagia, mostly in rehabilitation) found low-quality evidence of no increased lung complications. The Cochrane review of all swallowing therapy after stroke (41 trials, 2,660 participants) found no effect on death or dependency (OR 1.05) or case fatality (OR 1.00) — the treatment made no difference — although chest infection or pneumonia may have been reduced across a heterogeneous mix of interventions (OR 0.36, very low-quality evidence) that was not a test of thickened fluids or chin-down posture specifically. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): the preventive claim for thickened fluids and chin-down posture is unproven in stroke, and free-water access for selected patients has not been shown to increase pneumonia.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — no stroke trial shows thickened fluids or chin-down posture prevent aspiration pneumonia or death; free-water access in carefully selected patients did not increase pneumonia in small trials and a systematic review (low-quality evidence)

title: Vagus nerve stimulation for treatment-resistant depression: primary outcomes null versus sham in both blinded trials — secondary measures and a 5-year registry favour it
question: In treatment-resistant depression, does adjunctive vagus nerve stimulation improve response and remission versus sham or treatment as usual over 12 months?
balance: The sham-controlled evidence splits by outcome measure. RECOVER (493 adults with marked treatment-resistant depression, 12 months of active versus no-stimulation sham vagus nerve stimulation, both plus treatment as usual) missed its primary outcome — percent time in Montgomery–Åsberg response did not distinguish the groups — while clinician global impression, self-report and clinician-rated secondary measures showed significantly more time in response and partial response on active stimulation, and a companion report found quality-of-life and function advantages. The earlier acute sham trial (Rush 2005, D-02; 235 patients, 10 weeks) likewise missed its primary outcome (Hamilton response 15.2% vs 10.0%, P = .251 — the treatment made no difference on that measure) with one secondary self-report measure favouring active treatment. The long-term support comes from a non-randomised registry (Aaronson 2017; 795 patients, 5 years): cumulative response 67.6% with adjunctive vagus nerve stimulation plus usual care versus 40.9% on usual care alone, and first-time remission 43.3% versus 25.7% — observational evidence, with the vagus group more severely depressed at baseline. PROPOSED SPLIT (outcome measure and design): blinded primaries are null in both sham trials; secondary blinded measures and unblinded long-term observational data favour vagus nerve stimulation.
stamp: SPLIT (outcome measure and design) — adjunctive vagus nerve stimulation missed its primary symptom outcome versus sham in both the 10-week and the 12-month (RECOVER) trials, while secondary clinician/patient-rated measures favoured it and a 5-year observational registry found higher cumulative response (67.6% vs 40.9%) and remission (43.3% vs 25.7%) versus treatment as usual alone

title: Desvenlafaxine 50 mg vs 100 mg for major depression: both doses beat placebo in the pooled programme — and 100 mg has never been shown to beat 50 mg
question: Does desvenlafaxine (50 mg vs 100 mg) improve major depression versus placebo, and is the higher dose more effective?
balance: Both desvenlafaxine 50 mg and 100 mg beat placebo on the primary depression scale in the pooled phase 3 programme, but individual trials were inconsistent and no report carded here shows 100 mg outperforming 50 mg. Boyer 2008 (483 patients) found both doses effective (Hamilton change -13.2 on 50 mg and -13.7 on 100 mg vs -10.7 on placebo). Liebowitz 2008 (447 patients) found 50 mg significant (-11.5 vs -9.5, P = 0.018) while 100 mg missed on the primary scale (-11.0, P = 0.065) though it won on several secondary measures. Tourian 2009 (615 patients in the trial) failed its primary global test; pairwise, 100 mg was significant unadjusted (P = 0.028) and 50 mg was not — but that trial's own post hoc pooling with the two earlier 50/100 mg trials (1,388 patients) found both doses effective (-11.5 and -11.8 vs -9.6, both P < 0.001). A symptom-level pooling of 9 studies (Kornstein 2009) states symptom relief was similar at all doses examined, including 50 mg. All carded reports come from the single sponsor phase 3 programme, which caps the stamp. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit versus placebo; single programme): desvenlafaxine improves major depression versus placebo at both doses, with no demonstrated advantage for 100 mg over 50 mg.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit versus placebo; single programme) — desvenlafaxine 50 mg and 100 mg both improved major depression versus placebo in the pooled phase 3 programme (Hamilton -11.5 and -11.8 vs -9.6), with inconsistent individual trials and no demonstrated advantage of 100 mg over 50 mg

title: Chronic PTSD: venlafaxine extended-release beat placebo in two large trials — CAPS and remission both favoured the drug
question: In chronic PTSD, does venlafaxine extended-release improve core PTSD symptoms versus placebo?
balance: Two large placebo-controlled trials agree. In the 12-week trial (538 outpatients), venlafaxine extended-release (ER) lowered the Clinician-Administered PTSD Scale (CAPS-SX17) score by 41.8 points versus 33.9 on placebo, with remission in 30.2% versus 19.6%. In the 24-week trial (329 outpatients), the CAPS fall was 51.7 versus 43.9 points (P=.006), with remission in 50.9% versus 37.5%. A 2015 systematic review and meta-analysis of PTSD pharmacotherapy (51 studies) likewise found venlafaxine among the few individual agents with statistically significant efficacy over placebo in two or more trials, while noting effect sizes across the drug literature were small. The SSRI trials for this condition are homed separately on shelf-2410 and are not re-carded here; the 12-week trial's sertraline arm, which did not separate significantly from placebo on the primary score in that study, sits inside the venlafaxine trial report itself. PROPOSED LIKELY: venlafaxine ER improves core PTSD symptoms versus placebo over 12–24 weeks, with absolute remission gains of roughly 11–13 percentage points.
stamp: LIKELY — venlafaxine extended-release improved core PTSD symptoms versus placebo in two large trials (CAPS falls −41.8 vs −33.9 at 12 weeks and −51.7 vs −43.9 at 24 weeks), with remission 30.2% vs 19.6% and 50.9% vs 37.5%

title: Bipolar I depression: the olanzapine–fluoxetine combination beat olanzapine alone and placebo — remission 48.8% vs 32.8% vs 24.5%, at a metabolic cost
question: In bipolar I depression, does the olanzapine–fluoxetine combination improve depressive symptoms versus olanzapine alone and versus placebo?
balance: The pivotal 8-week trial (833 patients with bipolar I depression) found the olanzapine–fluoxetine combination (OFC) lowered MADRS scores by 18.5 points, against 15.0 on olanzapine alone and 11.9 on placebo; remission was 48.8% on OFC, 32.8% on olanzapine and 24.5% on placebo, with no excess of treatment-emergent mania (6.4% vs 5.7% vs 6.7%). A 2013 systematic review and meta-analysis of four randomised trials (1,330 patients) found OFC improved response versus olanzapine (relative risk 1.58) and versus placebo (relative risk 1.99) — relative measures; the record reports no absolute rates for those pooled comparisons, and the trial card above carries the absolute figures. Against lamotrigine, a separate 410-patient trial found OFC modestly more effective on depression scores but with more somnolence, weight gain and cholesterol elevation. The cost side is metabolic: weight gain and lipid rises are the combination's recurring price. PROPOSED LIKELY: OFC improves bipolar I depressive symptoms more than olanzapine alone and more than placebo over 8 weeks, at a metabolic tolerability cost.
stamp: LIKELY — the olanzapine–fluoxetine combination improved bipolar I depression more than olanzapine alone and more than placebo (MADRS falls 18.5 vs 15.0 vs 11.9 points; remission 48.8% vs 32.8% vs 24.5%), with more weight gain and lipid elevation

title: Generalised anxiety disorder: quetiapine XR beat placebo in three trials (evidence question, not a recommendation) — SSRI comparison rests on one paroxetine arm
question: In generalised anxiety disorder, does quetiapine extended-release reduce anxiety symptoms versus placebo, and how does it compare with SSRIs?
balance: This is an evidence question, not a recommendation: quetiapine extended-release (XR) is not a guideline-endorsed first-line treatment for generalised anxiety disorder (GAD), and this shelf presents the trial evidence plainly. Three placebo-controlled trials agree that it works over 8–9 weeks. Bandelow 2010 (873 patients, with a paroxetine active-control arm) found both quetiapine XR doses and paroxetine beat placebo on the Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale (HAM-A), with quetiapine separating from placebo by day 4 and remission at 42.6% for the 150 mg dose versus 27.2% on placebo and 38.8% on paroxetine — the trial was not powered as a formal head-to-head against the SSRI, so 'compares with SSRIs' rests on this single active-control arm showing effects in the same range. Khan 2011 (951 patients) found the 50 mg and 150 mg doses beat placebo (−13.31 and −13.54 vs −11.10 HAM-A points) but the 300 mg dose did not (−11.87; P=0.240). In older patients (Mezhebovsky 2013, 450 patients aged 66+), flexible-dose quetiapine XR beat placebo clearly (−14.97 vs −7.21; P<0.001). The recurring adverse events are somnolence, dry mouth, sedation, dizziness and fatigue. PROPOSED LIKELY (versus placebo): quetiapine XR reduces GAD symptoms over 8–9 weeks at 50–150 mg/day, with effects in the same range as the one SSRI comparator tested, and a sedative adverse-event profile.
stamp: LIKELY (versus placebo; evidence question, not a recommendation) — quetiapine XR 50–150 mg/day reduced HAM-A scores versus placebo in three trials over 8–9 weeks, with remission 42.6% vs 27.2% in the paroxetine-controlled trial; the 300 mg dose did not separate from placebo

title: OCD: clomipramine beats placebo clearly, but its claimed edge over SSRIs dissolves head-to-head — and tolerability favours the SSRIs
question: In obsessive-compulsive disorder, is clomipramine more effective than SSRIs, and at what tolerability cost?
balance: The answer divides by method. Clomipramine itself clearly works: the 1991 Clomipramine Collaborative Study (520 patients, two studies) found Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale (Y-BOCS) scores fell 38% and 44% on clomipramine versus 3% and 5% on placebo over 10 weeks. Whether it beats SSRIs is where the split sits. Older meta-analyses that compared effect sizes across separate placebo-controlled trials favoured clomipramine — but Pigott 1999's review notes 5 of 6 direct head-to-head comparisons against fluoxetine or fluvoxamine found similar efficacy with fewer side effects on the SSRI, and a multicentre paroxetine-versus-clomipramine trial found paroxetine as effective with significantly fewer adverse-effect dropouts. The 2016 Lancet Psychiatry network meta-analysis (54 trials, 6,652 participants) settled the direct-plus-indirect comparison: clomipramine's effect versus placebo (−4.72 Y-BOCS points) was numerically larger than the SSRI class effect (−3.49), but clomipramine was not better than SSRIs (difference −1.23, 95% credible interval −3.41 to 0.94 — the interval crosses no difference). The tolerability cost is the tricyclic profile: anticholinergic effects dominate, with seizures and raised aminotransferases as the uncommon serious risks named in the 1991 report. PROPOSED SPLIT (by method): indirect cross-trial comparisons favoured clomipramine; head-to-head trials and the network meta-analysis find no confirmed advantage over SSRIs, with worse tolerability.
stamp: SPLIT (by method) — clomipramine clearly beats placebo (Y-BOCS falls 38–44% vs 3–5%), but head-to-head trials and the 2016 network meta-analysis found it was not better than SSRIs (−1.23 points, credible interval crossing no difference), with a heavier tricyclic adverse-effect burden

title: Intravenous scopolamine for major depression: rapid effects in small single-centre crossover trials (N=19–52) — replicated internally, not yet at scale
question: Does intravenous scopolamine produce rapid antidepressant effects in major depression versus placebo infusion?
balance: FLAG — small, single-centre evidence base: every carded trial comes from one research group (the US National Institute of Mental Health intramural programme), samples are tiny (N=19, N=23 and N=52 across the three reports, and the N=52 report may overlap the earlier cohorts), and no large independent replication exists. Within those limits the results are striking and internally replicated: in the first crossover trial (19 randomised, 18 completing; recurrent major depressive or bipolar depression), three intravenous scopolamine infusions (4 µg/kg) reduced depression and anxiety scores versus placebo blocks (P<.001), with effects evident within days. The independent-sample replication restricted to major depressive disorder (23 patients, 22 analysed) found a 32% MADRS reduction after scopolamine versus 6.5% under placebo in the first block (P=.009 for the contrast), significant at the first post-infusion evaluation. The group's 2013 review reports placebo-adjusted remission rates of 56% and 45% for the initial and replication studies, with improvement persisting more than 2 weeks after the final infusion. A 2023 systematic review of all randomised scopolamine trials (PMID: 37893010, described here in prose, not carded) is more cautious: four trials, routes and combinations varied, and not all confirmed a significant reduction versus placebo. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: intravenous scopolamine produces rapid antidepressant effects versus placebo infusion in small crossover trials from a single centre; the finding awaits large independent confirmation.
stamp: POSSIBLE — intravenous scopolamine produced rapid antidepressant effects versus placebo infusion in small crossover trials from a single centre (N=19, N=23 and N=52 across reports; 32% vs 6.5% MADRS reduction in the major-depression replication), awaiting large independent confirmation

title: Wake therapy alone (PARTIAL of combined-chronotherapy shelf-2426): a next-day response in about half of patients, gone after recovery sleep
question: Does wake therapy (therapeutic sleep deprivation) alone, without combined light/phase-shift chronotherapy, speed antidepressant response in major depression?
balance: PARTIAL completion: shelf-2426 homes the combined chronotherapy package (wake therapy plus bright light plus sleep-phase stabilisation, added to duloxetine); this shelf asks only about wake therapy on its own, and no card here re-uses that trial. Alone, one night of total or partial sleep deprivation produces a response in roughly half of patients by the next day — the 2017 meta-analysis of 66 studies (which excluded studies that seamlessly combined sleep deprivation with other therapies) found response rates of 45% among studies with a randomised control group and 50% among those without. The effect is fast but fragile: in the tryptophan-depletion experiment, 22 of 30 drug-free inpatients responded to one night of total sleep deprivation, and the field's central problem is relapse after the next night of recovery sleep. A randomised crossover comparison (39 inpatients) found total sleep deprivation slightly more effective than late partial sleep deprivation, with day-after response rates of 0–53% depending on the rating scale used — a warning that the headline response rate is measurement-sensitive. Almost none of this literature is placebo-controlled in the drug-trial sense, so the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: wake therapy alone speeds antidepressant response within 24 hours in about half of patients, with relapse after recovery sleep the rule unless something sustains the gain.
stamp: POSSIBLE — wake therapy alone produced a next-day antidepressant response in 45% of patients in controlled studies (50% in uncontrolled studies) across a 66-study meta-analysis, with relapse after recovery sleep the rule; evidence is largely uncontrolled (PARTIAL of shelf-2426, standalone slice only)

title: Fibromyalgia CBT (PARTIAL of live #391): small, consistent gains in pain, mood, fatigue and function — about 5 extra large pain responses per 100 treated
question: In fibromyalgia, does cognitive-behavioural therapy (including CBT for insomnia) improve pain, fatigue and function versus education or usual care?
balance: PARTIAL completion: the live fibromyalgia family shelf (#391) homes the licensed drugs and exercise; this shelf asks only about structured psychological therapy as the tested intervention. Two Bernardy syntheses agree on a small, real benefit. The 2013 Cochrane review (23 studies, 2,031 patients, evidence graded low quality) found cognitive behavioural therapies (CBTs) reduced pain by 0.5 points on a 0–10 scale at end of treatment (standardised mean difference −0.29) and 0.6 points at long-term follow-up, with parallel small gains in negative mood and disability and no excess dropout (risk ratio 0.94). The 2018 updated systematic review (29 randomised trials, 2,509 patients) found CBTs gave at least 50% pain relief to 5 more patients per 100 than controls (risk difference 0.05, high-quality evidence), at least 20% quality-of-life improvement to 13 more per 100 (risk difference 0.13, moderate-quality), and small reductions in negative mood, disability and fatigue (standardised mean differences −0.43, −0.30 and −0.27). The specific programmes tested include CBT for insomnia (Edinger 2005: 57% of CBT patients met strict sleep-improvement criteria versus 17% on sleep-hygiene education and 0% on usual care, in a 47-patient trial) and an internet-delivered Web-Enhanced Behavioral Self-Management programme grounded in cognitive-behavioural pain principles (Williams 2010, 118 patients), which improved pain, physical functioning and global impression over standard care. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: CBT improves pain, fatigue, mood and function in fibromyalgia by small average amounts versus education or usual care — a benefit closer to the drugs' 'one patient in ten' scale than to a cure.
stamp: POSSIBLE — CBT improved fibromyalgia pain by about 0.5 points on a 0–10 scale and gave ≥50% pain relief to 5 more patients per 100 than controls, with small gains in mood, fatigue and disability (PARTIAL of live fibromyalgia family shelf #391, psychological-therapy slice only)

title: Chronic low back pain: transdermal and buccal buprenorphine beat placebo-switch in enriched-withdrawal trials — effects of 0.6–1.0 points in preselected responders
question: In chronic low back pain, do transdermal or buccal buprenorphine formulations reduce pain versus placebo in opioid-naïve and opioid-experienced patients?
balance: All three pivotal trials used enriched-enrolment randomised-withdrawal designs: patients first had to tolerate and respond to the drug in an open-label titration, and only those responders were randomised to continue it or switch to placebo — so every effect below is an effect in preselected responders, and the designs measure loss of benefit on withdrawal as much as benefit itself. The tested products are named because the formulation is the intervention: the buprenorphine transdermal system (Butrans, 7-day patch) and buccal buprenorphine film (Belbuca). In opioid-naïve patients, the transdermal trial (541 randomised) found week-12 pain scores lower on continued patch than placebo (treatment difference −0.58 on a 0–10 scale; P=.010), and the buccal trial in opioid-naïve patients (461 randomised) found pain rose less after randomisation on continued film than placebo (difference −0.67; P=.0012), with at least 30% pain reduction in 63% versus 47%. In opioid-experienced patients, the buccal trial (511 randomised) found the largest separation (difference −0.98; P<.001), with significantly more patients achieving 30% and 50% pain reductions on continued film. Nausea, constipation and vomiting were the common adverse events. Buprenorphine's opioid-use-disorder uses are homed on other shelves and are not this question. PROPOSED LIKELY (in enriched-withdrawal responders): continuing transdermal or buccal buprenorphine keeps chronic low back pain lower than switching to placebo, in both opioid-naïve and opioid-experienced patients — with average separations under one point on a 0–10 scale.
stamp: LIKELY (enriched-withdrawal designs) — continuing transdermal (Butrans) or buccal (Belbuca) buprenorphine kept chronic low back pain 0.58–0.98 points lower than switching to placebo at 12 weeks, in opioid-naïve and opioid-experienced preselected responders

title: Botulinum toxin A for peripheral neuropathic pain: pain fell more than on placebo in the trials and in the pooled analysis — small trials, moderate-quality evidence
question: In peripheral neuropathic pain, do botulinum toxin A injections reduce pain versus placebo injections?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the randomised evidence points the same way but is small. The largest trial (BOTNEP, 68 patients, two subcutaneous administrations up to 300 units, 12 weeks apart) found botulinum toxin A reduced mean weekly pain intensity over 24 weeks versus placebo (adjusted effect estimate −0.77, 95% CI −0.95 to −0.59). The earlier single-injection trial (29 patients with focal painful neuropathies and allodynia) found spontaneous-pain relief from week 2 to week 14. Pooling 10 randomised trials (505 patients), a 2022 meta-analysis found pain scores lower on botulinum toxin A by a mean difference of −1.87 points at 1 month and −1.38 at 3 months, with the largest effect in diabetic polyneuropathy, no demonstrated quality-of-life benefit, and no difference in adverse effects; the reviewers rated the evidence moderate quality. Neither trial record names a branded botulinum toxin A product or manufacturer, so no specific commercial product can be endorsed from this evidence — products differ by maker and current products may differ in safety and effectiveness. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a real analgesic signal, carried by small trials, which is why neuropathic-pain guidance positions botulinum toxin A as a later-line, specialist option rather than a first-line drug.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — botulinum toxin A reduced peripheral neuropathic pain more than placebo across two small randomised trials and a 10-trial meta-analysis (505 patients), with moderate-quality evidence and no excess of adverse effects beyond injection pain

title: Perioperative pregabalin (PARTIAL completion of #1249, which homes gabapentin): small pooled reductions in pain and opioid use, more sedation, dizziness and visual disturbance — and the largest synthesis calls the pain effect clinically unimportant
question: Does perioperative pregabalin reduce postoperative pain and opioid consumption versus placebo?
balance: SPLIT (clinical significance) — this pack is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #1249 already answers the perioperative question for gabapentin; this shelf asks it for pregabalin specifically, including its harms. The pregabalin-specific syntheses agree on direction and size: across 55 studies (Mishriky 2015), pregabalin lowered 24-hour pain at rest (mean difference −0.38) and on movement (−0.47) and opioid consumption by 8.27 mg morphine equivalents, with less nausea/vomiting and pruritus but more sedation (relative risk 1.46), dizziness (relative risk 1.33) and visual disturbance (relative risk 3.52); a second pregabalin-specific synthesis (Eipe 2015, 43 studies) found a 16% relative reduction in analgesic consumption, concentrated in surgeries with pronociceptive pain mechanisms. The split is over meaning, not arithmetic: the largest synthesis (Verret 2020, 281 gabapentinoid trials, 24,682 participants) found pain reductions of 3–10 points on a 100-point scale — at or below the 10-point minimally important difference at every time point, consistent for pregabalin and gabapentin alike — no effect on subacute or chronic pain, and more dizziness and visual disturbance, and concluded routine perioperative use is not supported. The earliest synthesis (Tiippana 2007) pooled gabapentin and pregabalin together and is not carded here because its effects cannot be separated by drug. PROPOSED SPLIT (clinical significance): statistically real, clinically small average benefit, bought with consistently more sedation-type harms.
stamp: SPLIT (clinical significance) — pregabalin-specific pooled analyses find small statistically significant reductions in 24-hour pain scores and opioid consumption versus placebo, but the largest synthesis of gabapentinoid trials judges the pain effect below the minimally important difference; sedation, dizziness and visual disturbance are consistently increased

title: Transmucosal fentanyl for cancer breakthrough pain: faster, stronger relief than placebo and than oral morphine in enriched titration trials of opioid-tolerant patients
question: In cancer breakthrough pain, do transmucosal fentanyl formulations relieve pain faster than oral morphine or placebo?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — three double-blind randomised trials, using the era's standard enriched design (dose titration first; only patients who found an effective dose were randomised to sequences of active and placebo units), point the same way. Oral transmucosal fentanyl citrate (OTFC lozenge) beat placebo on pain intensity and pain relief at every time point from 15 minutes (Farrar 1998; rescue medication needed for 15% of OTFC episodes vs 34% of placebo episodes). Head-to-head, OTFC — the record names the product as Actiq — beat oral morphine sulfate immediate release on pain intensity, pain-intensity difference and pain relief at all time points, including the 15-minute primary measure (Coluzzi 2001). The fentanyl buccal tablet likewise beat placebo, with a summed pain-intensity difference at 30 minutes of 3.0 versus 1.8 (Portenoy 2006); the buccal-tablet record does not give a brand name. All three trials enrolled opioid-tolerant patients on around-the-clock opioids, and roughly a third of patients never found a successful dose in titration and so never entered the randomised phase — the benefit is proven in titration responders, which is also how these products are prescribed. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): faster and greater relief than placebo and than oral morphine, in the population and design in which these formulations are actually used.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — transmucosal fentanyl (lozenge and buccal tablet) relieved breakthrough cancer pain significantly more than placebo at every measured time point from 15 minutes, and oral transmucosal fentanyl citrate outperformed oral immediate-release morphine, in three double-blind randomised trials in opioid-tolerant patients

title: Vitamin D for knee osteoarthritis progression: no slowing of cartilage loss and no pain benefit in two dedicated trials or in the VITAL knee-pain analysis
question: Does vitamin D supplementation slow cartilage loss or reduce knee pain progression in knee osteoarthritis versus placebo?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — the trials asked the question directly, raised blood vitamin D levels as intended, and found nothing. In the Tasmanian/Victorian trial (Jin 2016; the VIDEO programme), 413 patients with symptomatic knee osteoarthritis and low vitamin D (25-hydroxyvitamin D 12.5–60 nmol/L, ≈5–24 ng/mL) took monthly oral vitamin D3 50,000 IU or placebo for 2 years: blood levels rose by 40.6 nmol/L (≈16 ng/mL) more than on placebo, yet annual change in tibial cartilage volume and WOMAC pain did not differ, nor did cartilage defects or bone marrow lesions. The Boston trial (McAlindon 2013) titrated daily cholecalciferol 2,000 IU upward to push levels above 36 ng/mL in 146 patients for 2 years: knee pain fell similarly in both groups and cartilage volume fell by the same ~4.3% in both groups. The VITAL ancillary analysis (MacFarlane 2020) followed 1,398 US adults with chronic knee pain for a mean 5.3 years and found no difference in WOMAC pain, function or stiffness at any time point. The tested preparations were oral cholecalciferol (vitamin D3) — monthly 50,000 IU in Jin, daily 2,000 IU with dose escalation in McAlindon; the VITAL record does not state its dose, and no record names a branded product. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): supplementation corrects the blood level without changing the joint outcome.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — vitamin D supplementation did not slow tibial cartilage loss or reduce knee pain versus placebo in two dedicated 2-year randomised trials (monthly 50,000 IU or daily dosing titrated to blood level) or in the 1,398-person VITAL knee-pain analysis over ~5 years

title: Canakinumab and osteoarthritis: an exploratory CANTOS signal for fewer hip/knee replacements (hazard ratio 0.58) that dedicated knee-OA trials of IL-1 inhibition did not confirm for pain — hypothesis-generating only
question: In knee osteoarthritis, was the interleukin-1β inhibition signal (canakinumab) for fewer joint replacements and less OA pain real?
balance: SPLIT (outcome), and hypothesis-generating throughout — this is an evidence question about whether a signal was real, and the honest answer is: not established. The signal comes from an exploratory analysis of CANTOS (Schieker 2020), a cardiovascular trial of canakinumab in 10,061 people after myocardial infarction — not an osteoarthritis trial and not a knee-OA population: pooled canakinumab doses were associated with fewer incident total hip or knee replacements (0.31 vs 0.54 events per 100 person-years; hazard ratio 0.58, 95% CI 0.42–0.80) and fewer osteoarthritis-related adverse events (hazard ratio 0.73). But CANTOS collected no structural joint outcomes and measured no OA pain endpoint, and the analysis was exploratory. Against it: randomised trials that actually enrolled knee-OA patients and targeted the IL-1 pathway read out negatively (Brom 2025 review of the programme), and a network meta-analysis of anti-inflammatory biologics in OA (Li 2022; 15 studies, 1,566 patients) found no biologic — canakinumab among them — superior to placebo for function or stiffness, with only etanercept and infliximab superior for knee pain in the conventional analysis. The slate's premise of a published canakinumab knee-OA phase 2 trial could not be verified as a journal report on PubMed this session; the dedicated-trial record reaches this shelf through the programme review and the network meta-analysis, which is itself a reason the stamp is capped. PROPOSED SPLIT (outcome): POSSIBLE (benefit), hypothesis-generating only, for the joint-replacement signal; no demonstrated pain benefit in the population that actually has knee osteoarthritis.
stamp: SPLIT (outcome) — POSSIBLE (benefit), hypothesis-generating, for fewer incident hip or knee replacements in the exploratory CANTOS analysis (pooled hazard ratio 0.58); dedicated randomised trials of interleukin-1 inhibition in knee osteoarthritis read out negatively for pain (the treatment made no difference to OA pain in the dedicated trials)

title: Lorecivivint for knee osteoarthritis: the phase 2a trial and both phase 3 trials (OA-10, OA-11) missed their primary pain endpoints — subgroup signals only
question: In knee osteoarthritis, does lorecivivint improve pain and function versus placebo injection?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — the programme was given three fair tests and missed all three primary endpoints. In the phase 2a dose-ranging trial (Yazici 2020; 455 patients, single 2 mL intra-articular injection of 0.03, 0.07 or 0.23 mg versus placebo), no dose beat placebo on week-13 WOMAC pain (changes −23.3, −23.5 and −21.3 versus −22.1 on placebo, on a 0–100 scale; every group, placebo included, improved by a clinically meaningful ≥20 points). The phase 3 programme — reported in the journal records as OA-10 and OA-11 — used the selected 0.07 mg dose: OA-10 (498 patients, 28 weeks) failed its week-12 Pain NRS primary endpoint and showed no significant differences on other efficacy endpoints; OA-11 (513 patients, 56 weeks) found week-12 pain change of −2.24 on lorecivivint versus −2.49 on placebo (p = 0.185) — numerically favouring placebo — with no discernible effects on other endpoints and no meaningful joint-space-width loss in either group. Positive findings exist only in subgroups: week-52 benefits in the phase 2a prespecified unilateral-symptom subgroup (and a post-hoc no-widespread-pain subgroup), and a post-hoc week-4 signal in OA-10's Kellgren–Lawrence grade 2 subgroup. The drug was well tolerated throughout. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) on the question as asked — pain and function versus placebo injection in knee osteoarthritis overall.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — a single intra-articular lorecivivint injection did not improve pain versus vehicle placebo on the primary endpoint in the phase 2a trial (455 patients) or in either phase 3 trial (OA-10, 498 patients; OA-11, 513 patients); reported benefits are confined to prespecified or post-hoc subgroups

title: Memantine in Lewy body dementias: a small global-impression benefit concentrated in dementia with Lewy bodies — cognition scores, behaviour scores and daily function did not improve
question: In dementia with Lewy bodies and Parkinson's disease dementia, does memantine improve cognition and global function versus placebo?
balance: SPLIT (population and outcome) — the two randomised trials and their meta-analysis agree on a narrow pattern. On global clinical impression, memantine looked better: Aarsland 2009 (72 patients with Parkinson's disease dementia [PDD] or dementia with Lewy bodies [DLB]) found a 0.7-point better clinical global impression of change score at 24 weeks (p = 0.03), and the pooled meta-analysis (Matsunaga 2015) found the same outcome significant across both trials (standardised mean difference −0.26). But the larger trial (Emre 2010, 199 patients) found no significant global benefit in its total population (p = 0.120) — the significant result sat in the DLB subgroup (−0.6, p = 0.023), with PDD null (−0.1, p = 0.576) — and on everything else the evidence is flat: no significant differences in cognition test scores (including the Mini-Mental State Exam in the meta-analysis), neuropsychiatric inventory scores overall, activities of daily living, motor function, or caregiver burden. Memantine 20 mg/day was well tolerated in both trials, with adverse-event withdrawals similar to placebo. The neighbouring Lewy-body shelves home the cholinesterase inhibitors — donepezil on #3650 and rivastigmine on #2850 — and neither cards these memantine trials. PROPOSED SPLIT (population and outcome): a modest global-impression signal in DLB that does not extend to measured cognition or function, and no shown benefit in PDD.
stamp: SPLIT (population and outcome) — POSSIBLE (benefit) on global clinical impression, concentrated in dementia with Lewy bodies; no demonstrated improvement in cognition test scores, neuropsychiatric scores, or activities of daily living, and no significant benefit in Parkinson's disease dementia in the larger trial

title: Memantine in frontotemporal dementia: no benefit on behaviour or global impression in either randomised trial (81 and 49 patients) — a well-conducted negative evidence base
question: In frontotemporal dementia, does memantine improve behaviour or cognition versus placebo?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — this shelf is the clean negative the trials support. Memantine was widely used off-label in frontotemporal dementia (FTD) after an open-label study suggested transient benefit; the two randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials then tested it properly and both were negative. Boxer 2013 (81 patients with behavioural-variant FTD or semantic dementia, memantine 20 mg/day for 26 weeks) found no effect on the neuropsychiatric inventory (mean difference 2.2, 95% CI −3.9 to 8.3; p = 0.47) or on clinical global impression of change (mean difference 0.0; p = 0.90), and patients on memantine had more frequent cognitive adverse events (6 patients versus 1). Vercelletto 2011 (49 patients with behavioural-variant FTD, 10 mg twice daily for a full year) found no significant difference on the primary global endpoint (p = 0.4458) or on MMSE, dementia rating, neuropsychiatric, disability or caregiver-burden scores; the single positive secondary result (frontal behavioural inventory, p = 0.0417) sits among many null comparisons. Pooling both trials (130 patients), the Kishi 2015 meta-analysis found no significant differences on Mini-Mental State Exam, neuropsychiatric inventory, caregiver burden or discontinuation, with only a marginal, non-significant trend on global impression (standardised mean difference −0.34; p = 0.06). PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): the data do not support memantine use in FTD, in the words of the largest trial itself.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — memantine 20 mg/day did not improve neuropsychiatric symptoms, global impression, or cognition versus placebo in two randomised double-blind trials in frontotemporal dementia (81 and 49 patients), and the meta-analysis of both found no significant benefit on any efficacy outcome

title: SSRIs and trazodone in frontotemporal dementia: trazodone improved behaviour scores in one 26-patient crossover trial; paroxetine did not in a 10-patient blinded trial and impaired some cognitive measures — a thin, split evidence base
question: In frontotemporal dementia, do SSRIs or trazodone improve behavioural symptoms versus placebo or usual care?
balance: SPLIT (drug) — on a thin base that this shelf prints on its face: the entire double-blind primary evidence is two small crossover trials totalling 36 patients. For trazodone, Lebert 2004 (randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover; 26 evaluable patients) found a significant decrease in neuropsychiatric inventory (NPI) total score on trazodone (p = 0.028), with more than 50% NPI improvement in 10 patients, driven by irritability, agitation, depressive symptoms and eating disorders, and no change in MMSE. For paroxetine, the rigorous test was negative: Deakin 2004 (double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover; N = 10 patients) found no significant differences on the NPI or the Cambridge Behavioral Inventory, and paroxetine decreased accuracy on paired-associates learning, reversal learning and delayed pattern recognition. An open randomised study (Moretti 2003) reported behavioural improvement and reduced caregiver stress on paroxetine over 14 months, but with only 8 patients per arm (paroxetine versus piracetam) and no blinding it is described here in prose only and is not carded. The systematic review of the field (Nardell & Tampi 2014; 9 double-blind randomised trials across all FTD drug classes) concludes SSRIs and trazodone may reduce some behavioural symptoms, that none of the medications improved cognition, and that all were well tolerated. PROPOSED SPLIT (drug): a possible trazodone benefit for behaviour, an unproven and possibly cognitively costly paroxetine — neither established, both resting on very small trials.
stamp: SPLIT (drug) — POSSIBLE (benefit) for trazodone on behavioural symptoms from one small double-blind crossover trial (26 evaluable patients); paroxetine made no difference to behaviour in the one double-blind trial (10 patients) and impaired performance on several cognitive tasks (the treatment made no difference for paroxetine)

title: Mediterranean diet and cognition: in the one trial programme (PREDIMED), older adults at high vascular risk scored better on cognitive tests after 4–6.5 years than controls on a low-fat diet — a single-programme signal
question: Does a Mediterranean diet slow cognitive decline in older adults versus a control diet?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), single programme — every carded report comes from PREDIMED (ISRCTN35739639), one Spanish trial programme in older adults at high cardiovascular risk, so the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE however consistent the substudies look. In the Barcelona cognition substudy (Valls-Pedret 2015; 447 enrolled, 334 retested after a median 4.1 years), the control group declined on all composites (global cognition change −0.38 z) while the Mediterranean-diet-plus-olive-oil group held steady (+0.05; p = 0.005 versus controls) and the nuts group scored better on the memory composite (+0.09 versus −0.17; p = 0.04 versus controls). In the Navarra centre (Martínez-Lapiscina 2013; 522 assessed after 6.5 years), both Mediterranean groups scored higher than control on the Mini-Mental State Examination (adjusted differences +0.62 points for olive oil, p = 0.005, and +0.57 for nuts, p = 0.015) and the Clock Drawing Test. A smaller Navarra subsample (285 participants) found lower odds of mild cognitive impairment with the olive-oil diet (OR 0.34, 95% CI 0.12 to 0.97) but no significant difference for the nuts group on most domains. This shelf does not duplicate the MIND-diet home (shelf-2468): the MIND diet is a different dietary pattern tested in a different trial whose primary result was null, and no PREDIMED cognition report is carded there. The honest summary: within one trial programme, assignment to a supplemented Mediterranean diet was followed by less cognitive decline than advice to reduce dietary fat; there is no second programme and no dementia-incidence endpoint in the carded reports.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a Mediterranean diet supplemented with extra-virgin olive oil or nuts was associated with better cognitive scores than a low-fat control diet in three substudy reports of a single trial programme (PREDIMED); a single programme caps the stamp at POSSIBLE

title: Hearing intervention and falls: the ACHIEVE randomised trial's secondary analysis found 27% relatively fewer falls over 3 years with hearing aids and counselling; the wider hearing-loss-and-falls literature is observational
question: Do hearing aids reduce falls in older adults with hearing loss?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). The only randomised evidence on the aids themselves is a secondary analysis of ACHIEVE (Goman 2025; 977 adults aged 70–84 with untreated hearing loss): over 3 years the hearing-intervention group (audiological counselling plus hearing aids) averaged 1.45 falls versus 1.98 in the health-education control group — a mean difference of −0.54 falls and a 27% relative reduction in the mean number of falls. Falls were a prespecified exploratory outcome, self-reported for the past 12 months at annual visits, in an unmasked trial, which is why the stamp stays at POSSIBLE. The background risk link is observational and is labelled observational on its cards: in the Health, Aging and Body Composition cohort (Kamil 2016; 2,000 adults aged 70–79, observational), moderate-or-greater hearing impairment carried a 63% higher hazard of incident frailty and a faster annual rise in the odds of falling; in a large propensity-matched claims cohort (Deal 2019, observational), incident untreated hearing loss was followed by an excess of 3.57 falls per 100 persons attributable at 10 years. Those cohorts show hearing loss marks fall risk; they do not show that aids remove it. ACHIEVE's primary cognition outcome is homed on the live ACHIEVE shelf (see also pack 6015 for quality of life and cognition) and is not re-carded here; this shelf asks only the falls question.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one randomised trial's prespecified exploratory secondary analysis found fewer falls with a hearing intervention (hearing aids plus audiological counselling) versus health-education control; supporting cohort evidence is observational and labelled as such

title: Monthly high-dose vitamin D: no fewer falls or fractures than placebo in two large trials (ViDA, D-Health), and more falls than a lower monthly dose in prior fallers — the monthly regimen is its own slice, between the daily-dose and annual-bolus shelves
question: In older adults, does monthly high-dose vitamin D (e.g., 60,000 IU) increase or decrease falls and fractures versus daily standard dosing or placebo?
balance: SPLIT, by comparator — verified against the home shelves before building: the daily-dose falls shelf (pack 1491) cards daily 700–1,000 IU and fences the large daily trials in prose, the annual-bolus harm is live shelf #30 (Sanders, single 500,000 IU dose), pack 5987 covers daily high-dose versus standard-dose, and pack 6026 cards the D-Health fracture result (HR 0.94) under its non-deficiency fracture question. None of them asks the monthly intermediate-dose question, which is the slice carded here. Versus placebo, monthly dosing did nothing: in ViDA (Khaw 2017; 5,108 adults aged 50–84; 200,000 IU loading then 100,000 IU monthly for a mean 3.4 years), falls occurred in 52% on vitamin D versus 53% on placebo (adjusted HR 0.99, 95% CI 0.92 to 1.07) and non-vertebral fractures in 6% versus 5% (adjusted HR 1.19, 0.94 to 1.50; p = 0.15). In D-Health (Waterhouse 2021; 60,000 IU monthly for up to 5 years; falls analysis in 15,416 survey participants), vitamin D had no effect on falling in the past month (OR 1.02, 0.95 to 1.10), with a body-mass-index interaction: risk was increased in participants with BMI under 25 (OR 1.25, 1.09 to 1.43) and unchanged at BMI 25 or over (OR 0.95). Versus a lower monthly dose the direction flips to harm: in 200 prior fallers aged 70 or over (Bischoff-Ferrari 2016), 66.9% fell on 60,000 IU monthly versus 47.9% on 24,000 IU monthly over 12 months, with no benefit on lower-extremity function. PROPOSED SPLIT: monthly high-dose vitamin D neither prevents falls or fractures against placebo nor is it benign against a standard monthly dose in people who have already fallen.
stamp: SPLIT — versus placebo: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for falls and fractures in two large monthly-dose trials; versus a lower monthly dose: POSSIBLE (harm) — more falls at 60,000 IU monthly than at 24,000 IU monthly in one small trial of prior fallers
