title: GLP-1 weight loss and lean mass — an evidence question: about one quarter of the weight lost is lean mass in the DXA substudy and the pooled trial analyses; no carded trial measured frailty or function outcomes in older adults
question: In older adults treated with GLP-1 receptor agonists, how much of the weight lost is lean mass, and does it worsen frailty or function?
balance: EVIDENCE QUESTION — this shelf reports what is measured, it does not stamp a benefit or harm claim. What is measured: in the SURMOUNT-1 DXA substudy (Look 2025; 160 participants with baseline and week-72 scans), tirzepatide reduced body weight by 21.3%, fat mass by 33.9% and lean mass by 10.9% (placebo: 5.3%, 8.2% and 2.6%; p < 0.001 for all), and of the weight lost approximately 75% was fat mass and 25% was lean mass in both the tirzepatide and placebo groups, consistently across sex, age (including 65 years and over) and weight-loss tertiles. Across 22 randomised trials (2,258 participants), the network meta-analysis (Karakasis 2025) found GLP-1-based agents reduced weight by a mean 3.55 kg, fat mass by 2.95 kg and lean mass by 0.86 kg versus comparators — again with lean mass loss comprising approximately 25% of total weight loss, while relative lean mass (percentage of body weight) was unaffected; tirzepatide 15 mg weekly and semaglutide 2.4 mg weekly lost the most weight and were among the least lean-preserving. The frailty half of the question has no direct trial answer in the fetched records: the Metabolism review (Stefanakis 2024) states that over 25% of weight lost from pharmacotherapy or surgery typically comes from fat-free mass, and that muscle and bone loss can compromise physical function especially in older adults — a mechanistic and clinical concern, with candidate selection (advanced age, prefrailty) flagged as a judgement call, not a measured trial outcome. Premise correction: the STEP 1 body-composition substudy exists as a conference-abstract report, not a full journal article in the fetched PubMed records, so semaglutide's composition numbers are carried here by the pooled network analysis rather than by a carded STEP 1 substudy paper. PROPOSED: an evidence-question shelf — the lean-mass fraction is quantified and concordant (about one quarter); the frailty/function consequence in older adults is unmeasured, and the stamp says so.
stamp: EVIDENCE QUESTION — lean mass is consistently about 25% of the weight lost with potent GLP-1-based therapy in the carded body-composition data; whether that worsens frailty or physical function in older adults is not answered by any carded trial (no frailty or function endpoint in the fetched records)

title: Bimekizumab in axial spondyloarthritis: ASAS40 at week 16 was 47.7% versus 21.4% in non-radiographic disease and 44.8% versus 22.5% in radiographic disease (BE MOBILE 1 and 2), sustained to 2 years
question: In axial spondyloarthritis, does bimekizumab improve disease activity versus placebo in both radiographic and non-radiographic disease?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), single programme. BE MOBILE 1 (non-radiographic axial spondyloarthritis; 254 randomised) and BE MOBILE 2 (radiographic disease; 332 randomised) were parallel 52-week phase 3 trials of bimekizumab 160 mg every 4 weeks versus placebo, with all patients on bimekizumab from week 16. At week 16 the primary ASAS40 endpoint was met in both: 47.7% on bimekizumab versus 21.4% on placebo in non-radiographic disease, and 44.8% versus 22.5% in radiographic disease (p < 0.001 for both), with all ranked secondary endpoints met, responses in both TNF-inhibitor-naive and inadequate-responder patients, and improvements in ASDAS states, high-sensitivity CRP and MRI inflammation (van der Heijde 2023). Week-52 results (Baraliakos 2024) show the week-16 gains sustained in bimekizumab-randomised patients, with placebo-switchers catching up; treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 75.0% (non-radiographic) and 75.5% (radiographic) of patients over 52 weeks, oral candidiasis was the most frequent fungal infection (7.4% and 6.1%), and uveitis and inflammatory bowel disease were uncommon. At 2 years in the open-label extension (Baraliakos 2025), over 50% of randomised patients held an ASAS40 response and about 60% reached ASDAS low disease activity, with no new safety signals. The axial sequencing question (IL-17 versus a second TNF inhibitor after TNF failure) is homed on pack 5455 and is not re-opened here; bimekizumab's psoriasis homes do not ask the axial question.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two parallel phase 3 trials of a single programme (BE MOBILE 1 and 2) both met their primary endpoint against placebo; a single programme caps the stamp at POSSIBLE

title: Bimekizumab in psoriatic arthritis: ACR50 at week 16 was 44% versus 10% in biologic-naive patients (BE OPTIMAL) and 43% versus 7% after TNF-inhibitor failure (BE COMPLETE), with strong skin clearance in both
question: In psoriatic arthritis, does bimekizumab improve joint and skin responses versus placebo, including after TNF-inhibitor failure?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), single programme. In BE OPTIMAL (McInnes 2023; 852 randomised patients with active psoriatic arthritis naive to biologic DMARDs), ACR50 at week 16 was reached by 189 (44%) of 431 on bimekizumab 160 mg every 4 weeks versus 28 (10%) of 281 on placebo (OR 7.1, 95% CI 4.6 to 10.9; p < 0.0001), similar to the adalimumab reference arm (46%), with all secondary hierarchical endpoints met and treatment-emergent adverse events in 60% versus 49% to week 16. In BE COMPLETE (Merola 2023; 400 randomised patients with prior inadequate response or intolerance to one or two TNF inhibitors), ACR50 was reached by 116 (43%) of 267 on bimekizumab versus 9 (7%) of 133 on placebo (adjusted OR 11.1, 5.4 to 23.0; p < 0.0001), and among patients with psoriasis over at least 3% body surface area, 121 (69%) of 176 on bimekizumab reached PASI 90. A 52-week post-hoc analysis across both trials (McInnes 2024) found ACR50 held at 54.4–54.7% (BE OPTIMAL) and 48.0–56.3% (BE COMPLETE) with or without methotrexate, with complete skin clearance (PASI 100) achieved in similar proportions regardless of methotrexate. So the TNF-failure half of the question is answered by its own trial, not extrapolated from the naive population. Bimekizumab's plaque-psoriasis homes (for example pack 4353) do not ask the psoriatic-arthritis question.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two phase 3 trials of a single programme (BE OPTIMAL and BE COMPLETE) both met their primary endpoint against placebo, in biologic-naive and in TNF-inhibitor-experienced patients; a single programme caps the stamp at POSSIBLE

title: Cerebral autoregulation and ageing (physiology): dynamic autoregulation is preserved in healthy ageing while carbon-dioxide reactivity falls; after acute stroke dynamic autoregulation is impaired in both hemispheres — the physiological case for caution with abrupt blood-pressure lowering
question: How do cerebral autoregulation and cerebrovascular reactivity change with normal ageing in healthy humans, and what does that imply for blood-pressure lowering after stroke?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing (Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology; Boron and Boulpaep Medical Physiology): cerebral blood flow is held near-constant across a range of arterial pressures by autoregulation, and flow is exquisitely sensitive to arterial carbon dioxide — this is the textbook's account, and the carded human studies test what ageing and stroke do to it. The human data are concordant. Dynamic autoregulation does NOT decline with healthy ageing: Carey 2000 (27 young versus 27 older adults, matched for sex and systolic pressure) found identical autoregulatory indices (4.9 versus 5.0 across all stimuli) even though cardiac baroreceptor sensitivity was halved in the older group (8.6 versus 16.9 ms/mm Hg); Dineen 2011 (30 volunteers of mean age 25 versus 30 of mean age 64, studied through hypercapnia and hypocapnia) likewise found no age difference in the autoregulatory index, though flow velocity and its change with respiratory manoeuvres were greater in the young. Cerebrovascular reactivity DOES fall: Lipsitz 2000 (10 young, 10 healthy elderly, 10 treated hypertensive elderly) found carbon-dioxide reactivity of 0.19 in the young versus 0.14 in normotensive elderly and 0.11 in hypertensive elderly (p < 0.05), while the flow-velocity fall on standing was actually smaller in the older groups — autoregulation retained, vasodilator reserve reduced. After acute ischaemic stroke the picture reverses: Dawson 2000 (61 patients within 96 hours versus 54 matched controls) found dynamic autoregulation significantly impaired in BOTH hemispheres (indices 4.1 affected, 4.8 unaffected, 6.2 in controls) while static autoregulation was preserved. Implication, stated as physiology rather than a treatment verdict: a healthy older brain still defends its flow against pressure swings, which is why chronic blood-pressure lowering is generally tolerated; an acutely infarcted brain has lost dynamic defence in both hemispheres, which is the physiological reason acute post-stroke blood-pressure management is cautious about abrupt drops. Treatment thresholds themselves belong to the stroke-treatment shelves, not to this physiology shelf.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED

title: Central sensitisation and descending pain modulation (physiology): fibromyalgia patients show exaggerated wind-up and after-sensations, knee osteoarthritis patients show facilitated temporal summation, and conditioned pain modulation is impaired across chronic pain (pooled effect size 0.78)
question: What human experimental evidence supports central sensitisation and impaired descending pain modulation (conditioned pain modulation) in chronic pain states such as fibromyalgia and osteoarthritis?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing (Ganong Review of Medical Physiology; Boron and Boulpaep Medical Physiology): nociceptive input is amplified or damped centrally — repeated C-fibre input progressively increases dorsal-horn responses (wind-up, the laboratory signature of central sensitisation), and a second, distant painful stimulus normally suppresses pain elsewhere through descending inhibitory pathways (the basis of conditioned pain modulation, CPM). The carded human experimental studies show both systems behaving abnormally in chronic pain. In fibromyalgia, Staud 2001 found wind-up was evoked in patients and controls but was greater in patients at every level: the first stimulus in a series already felt stronger, temporal summation within the series was larger (patients reached painful levels at interstimulus intervals of 2–5 seconds at which controls rarely reported pain), and after-sensations were greater, longer and more often painful. Staud 2014 (38 fibromyalgia patients, 33 controls) integrated three heat-pulse trains into a wind-up response function whose slope — the measure of central pain sensitivity — was significantly steeper in patients (p < 0.003), and whose after-sensations predicted clinical pain intensity (r = 0.4). For descending modulation, the Lewis 2012 systematic review and meta-analysis (30 studies; 778 patients, 664 controls) found a large pooled effect size of 0.78 for reduced CPM in chronic pain populations versus healthy controls. In knee osteoarthritis specifically, Petersen 2017 (133 severe knee osteoarthritis patients, 50 matched controls) found widespread pressure hyperalgesia and facilitated temporal summation (p < 0.02) with a trend to impaired CPM (p = 0.06). No animal studies are carded; animal mechanism appears only as the textbook framing above.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED

title: Sleep gets lighter and more broken with adult ageing: slow-wave and REM shares fall, stage 1/2 and wake after sleep onset rise — and the spindles and REM that remain track next-morning cognition
question: How does human sleep architecture (slow-wave and REM proportions, sleep continuity) change across adult ageing, and how do those changes relate to next-day cognition?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology; Kryger-era sleep-medicine texts). The textbooks describe adult sleep as organised in nonREM–REM cycles in which slow-wave sleep predominates early and REM later, and describe ageing sleep as lighter and more fragmented. The carded human polysomnography data confirm that account quantitatively in direction: the Ohayon 2004 meta-analysis of 65 studies (3,577 subjects) found that in adults total sleep time, sleep efficiency, slow-wave %, REM % and REM latency decreased with age while sleep latency, stage 1 %, stage 2 % and wake after sleep onset increased, with only sleep efficiency continuing to decrease after 60. Primary studies agree (Landolt 1996: less slow-wave sleep, more stage 1 and wake after sleep onset in middle-aged versus young men). For cognition, the evidence is observational only and is labelled as such: spindle density and REM duration predicted next-morning performance in 58 older adults (Lafortune 2014), and short NREM/REM cycles predicted 4-year cognitive decline in 235 older adults (Suh 2019, 14 events). No intervention evidence is carded. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED for the architecture changes, with the cognition relation stated as association.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — across adult ageing, slow-wave sleep % and REM % fall, stage 1 % and stage 2 % rise, and sleep latency and wake after sleep onset rise, while total sleep time and sleep efficiency fall (only efficiency kept falling after 60 in the Ohayon meta-analysis); the cognition link (spindle density, REM duration, cycle length) is observational association, labelled as such

title: Glymphatic clearance in human sleep: consistent proxy evidence (CSF waves, tracer clearance, amyloid-beta shifts) but no direct human demonstration — an emerging physiology
question: In humans, does slow-wave sleep enhance glymphatic clearance of interstitial solutes including amyloid-beta, and what direct human evidence exists?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING (textbook framing: Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology for CSF physiology; the glymphatic pathway was defined in animal experiments and is presented in textbooks as the proposed route — animal mechanism is context here, never a card). Graded honestly: the direct human evidence is thin. What exists in humans is four proxy legs, each concordant and each indirect. Fultz 2019 imaged waves of CSF flow coupled to neural slow waves and haemodynamics in human nonREM sleep, but measured no solute. Eide 2021 gave humans an intrathecal MRI tracer and found one night of total sleep deprivation impaired its clearance from most brain regions, unrecovered the next night — the closest human analogue of a clearance experiment, with a deprivation arm of only n = 7. Ju 2017 disrupted slow-wave activity experimentally and saw next-morning CSF amyloid-beta40 rise (N = 17), an effect the authors attribute at least partly to neuronal activity rather than clearance alone. Shokri-Kojori 2018 found PET amyloid burden higher after one deprived night in 20 controls — a net-balance signal that cannot separate production from clearance. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING: the hypothesis is supported by consistent human proxies; it is not established human physiology.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING — direct human evidence is thin: CSF flow couples to slow waves (Fultz 2019), tracer clearance is impaired after one night of sleep deprivation (Eide 2021), and CSF/PET amyloid-beta rises when slow-wave sleep is disrupted or lost (Ju 2017; Shokri-Kojori 2018) — but no human study directly demonstrates slow-wave sleep clearing amyloid-beta via the glymphatic pathway

title: Sarcopenia is both: motor units and fibres are lost (and sarcopenic muscle fails to reinnervate), while the surviving muscle is anabolically resistant to amino acids and exercise
question: What drives human sarcopenia at the muscle level — motor-unit loss, anabolic resistance to dietary protein, or both — and what do human biopsy and tracer studies show?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology — motor-unit organisation, muscle fibre types and protein turnover). The question poses an either/or; the human biopsy, autopsy and tracer evidence answers both. On the denervation side: Lexell 1988 counted fibres in whole vastus lateralis from 43 men and found ageing atrophy from about age 25, accelerating, caused mainly by fibre loss with no fibre type spared; Piasecki 2018 measured motor units directly and found numbers reduced in all older men, with non-sarcopenic and pre-sarcopenic men compensating by enlarging surviving units through reinnervation — and sarcopenic men (n = 29) failing to do so. On the anabolic side: Cuthbertson 2005 (44 men, tracer/biopsy, insulin clamped) found basal synthesis normal in old muscle but the response to essential amino acids blunted, with reduced mTOR-pathway signalling; Kumar 2009 (25 young, 25 old) found the same blunting for resistance exercise at every intensity. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED: motor-unit loss removes fibres; anabolic resistance stops the remainder being maintained.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — both mechanisms are demonstrated in human tissue: fibre/motor-unit loss from about age 25 (Lexell 1988; Piasecki 2018, with failed motor-unit expansion distinguishing sarcopenic men) and anabolic resistance — blunted muscle protein synthesis responses to essential amino acids (Cuthbertson 2005) and to resistance exercise (Kumar 2009) despite normal basal synthesis

title: Benralizumab and steroid tapering in severe asthma: 75% median dose reduction versus 25% on placebo (ZONDA), and 63% eliminated steroids under a monitored taper (PONENTE)
question: In adults with severe asthma who depend on daily oral corticosteroids, does benralizumab allow the steroid dose to be tapered or stopped versus placebo?
balance: Premise verified: steroid-sparing is homed for dupilumab on live shelf #1031 (VENTURE) — a different drug; no benralizumab steroid-sparing home exists (live #813 covers benralizumab exacerbations in SIROCCO, not tapering), so this is the uncovered question. The placebo-controlled leg is ZONDA 2017: median oral glucocorticoid dose down 75% on benralizumab versus 25% on placebo (P<0.001), odds of reduction more than 4-fold, exacerbation rates relatively 55–70% lower with absolute rates printed on the card, and no FEV1 effect. PONENTE 2021/2022 is the practical leg — open-label and single-arm, labelled as such: a personalised rapid taper with adrenal monitoring eliminated oral corticosteroids in 376/598 (62.9%) and got 81.9% to elimination or 5 mg/day or less, with reductions largely maintained for 6 further months; adrenal insufficiency was found in 60% at first assessment, which is why the algorithm monitors it. A 2024 network meta-analysis of 7 RCTs (1,052 patients) places benralizumab's steroid-sparing odds (OR about 4.1 for both regimens) alongside dupilumab and mepolizumab, at low-to-moderate confidence. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single drug programme (one RCT plus its single-arm taper study) caps the stamp despite the large randomised effect.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single programme: benralizumab reduced the median oral glucocorticoid dose by 75% versus 25% on placebo in ZONDA (220 randomised), and 62.9% of 598 patients eliminated oral corticosteroids under PONENTE's monitored taper algorithm (single-arm, labelled)

title: Dupilumab in 6–11-year-olds (VOYAGE): exacerbations 0.31 versus 0.75 per year on placebo, with better lung function, control and quality of life
question: In children aged 6–11 years with moderate-to-severe asthma, does dupilumab reduce exacerbations versus placebo?
balance: Premise verified against the files themselves: live #1031 (QUEST/VENTURE) and pack #5903 (adults with severe eosinophilic asthma) are adult/adolescent only — the 6–11 population was uncovered. The evidence is one programme. VOYAGE 2021 randomised 408 children aged 6–11 with uncontrolled moderate-to-severe asthma to weight-banded dupilumab or placebo every 2 weeks for 52 weeks on background therapy: in the type 2 phenotype, annualised severe exacerbations were 0.31 versus 0.75 — a 59.3% relative risk reduction with the absolute rates printed beside it — predicted FEV1 improved 5.2 percentage points more, and asthma control was significantly better. A VOYAGE analysis (Fiocchi 2023, same children, not an independent trial) adds control and quality-of-life detail: 70% versus 46% well-controlled at week 52, with child and caregiver quality of life improved. EXCURSION (365 children, open-label, labelled) extends tolerability to 2 years with a profile consistent with the parent trial. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — the single-programme cap applies.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single trial programme: in VOYAGE (408 children aged 6–11, 52 weeks), dupilumab reduced the annualised severe exacerbation rate to 0.31 versus 0.75 on placebo in type 2 asthma (59.3% relative risk reduction, absolute rates on the card), with better FEV1, control and quality of life; EXCURSION supports longer-term tolerability (open-label, labelled)

title: Varenicline plus a nicotine patch: one positive trial, one null trial, and a fragile pooled benefit — a split, and not a COPD-specific evidence base
question: In adults who smoke, does adding a nicotine patch to varenicline improve quit rates versus varenicline alone? (Assigned as a COPD question — see the premise correction: the trials did not require COPD.)
balance: PREMISE CORRECTION (prominent): this question was assigned as 'in adults with COPD'. The fetched records do not support that framing — Koegelenberg 2014 enrolled 'generally healthy smokers' and Ramon 2014 enrolled clinic smokers of 20 or more cigarettes a day; neither required COPD, and no COPD-specific varenicline-plus-patch trial was found this session. The shelf is therefore built for adults who smoke, with the COPD application stated as extrapolation. Premise verified against neighbouring homes: combination NRT (pack #2608) and varenicline plus bupropion (pack #2800) are different questions. The evidence splits. Koegelenberg (446 randomised, patch pre-loaded 2 weeks before quit day): continuous abstinence 55.4% versus 40.9% at 12 weeks and 49.0% versus 32.6% at 24 weeks. Ramon (341 heavy smokers): 39.1% versus 31.8% at 12 weeks, not significant — the treatment made no difference overall, with only a post hoc heavier-smoker subgroup signal. Zhou 2026 (7 trials, 2,631 participants): relative abstinence 1.33 (1.04–1.69) versus varenicline alone, rated low-certainty, and not significant (1.26, 0.94–1.68) after excluding the high-risk-of-bias trial; skin reactions are increased (relative rate 1.67 for patch combinations). PROPOSED SPLIT.
stamp: SPLIT — Koegelenberg 2014 found higher abstinence with patch plus varenicline (55.4% vs 40.9% at 12 weeks) but Ramon 2014 found no overall difference (39.1% vs 31.8%; the treatment made no difference); the 7-trial meta-analysis is positive (relative rate 1.33) but low-certainty and loses significance without its high-bias-risk trial. PREMISE CORRECTION: no carded trial required COPD

title: Depemokimab every 6 months (SWIFT-1/-2): exacerbations roughly halved versus placebo in two replicate trials, with no significant quality-of-life difference
question: In adults with severe asthma, does depemokimab given every 6 months reduce exacerbations versus placebo? (Trials enrolled from age 12 — see cards.)
balance: Premise verified: live #813 homes mepolizumab (MENSA) and benralizumab (SIROCCO) exacerbations only — depemokimab was uncovered. title: Auto-titrating versus fixed CPAP: clinically interchangeable — 11 minutes more use and half an Epworth point for APAP, 1.3% minimum saturation for fixed, and no blood-pressure difference
question: In adults with obstructive sleep apnoea, is auto-titrating CPAP as effective as fixed-pressure CPAP for sleepiness, apnoea control and blood pressure?
balance: Desk-check: no APAP-versus-fixed home exists; CPAP shelves in the library cover other comparators. The answer to 'as effective?' is yes, clinically — and the wording follows the house null convention because the comparison, not either treatment, is what shows no difference (both modes work versus no treatment: Patil 2019 found PAP itself reduces disease severity, sleepiness and blood pressure). Ip 2012 pooled 24 RCTs: similar AHI, sleep measures and quality of life; APAP ahead by 11 minutes of use per night and 0.5 Epworth points, fixed CPAP ahead by 1.3% on minimum oxygen saturation — statistically real, clinically marginal, and in opposing directions. Patil 2019 (336 studies) concluded auto-adjusting PAP produced no clinically significant difference in patient outcomes versus standard CPAP. The Hukins 2004 crossover shows the same pattern at trial level (compliance 5.05 vs 4.86 h/night, Epworth 7.9 vs 8.4; N not documented in the record), with APAP's real advantages being lower pressures, fewer leaks and fewer side effects (15 vs 28 reports). PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — for the modality comparison, on two independent syntheses.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — across a 24-RCT meta-analysis and the AASM systematic review, auto-titrating and fixed CPAP did not differ clinically significantly on apnoea control, sleepiness or blood pressure; the statistical differences (11 min/night adherence and 0.5 Epworth points favouring APAP; 1.3% minimum oxygen saturation favouring fixed) are below clinical importance

title: CBT-I in pregnancy: four randomised programmes agree — insomnia severity, sleep quality and sleep duration improve, in person and digitally
question: In pregnant women with insomnia, does cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia improve sleep versus usual care or sleep education?
balance: Premise verified: CBT-I is homed for cancer (pack #5060), menopause and general digital delivery (live #437) — pregnancy was the uncovered population. Four independent randomised programmes, against four different comparators, agree. Manber 2019 (in-person, versus an active imagery control): ISI fell 15.4 to 8.0 versus 15.9 to 11.2 (P<.001, d = 0.5), remission 64% versus 52%, median time to remission 31 versus 48 days — though objective wake time did not differ. Felder 2020 (digital, versus unrestricted standard care): significantly greater insomnia improvement (d = −1.03) with secondary outcomes except sleep duration also improved, holding at follow-up. Kalmbach 2020 (digital, versus sleep education — the exact comparator named in the question): ISI −4.91 and PSQI −2.98 points, sleep 32 minutes longer, and 40 minutes longer after childbirth. Bei 2023 (scalable one-session-plus-emails programme versus attention-matched control): significant pregnancy-endpoint benefits, strongest in those with elevated baseline symptoms, with sleep benefits still present at 2 years. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) — multiple independent concordant programmes clear the single-programme cap; depression is not claimed (effects small in one trial, absent in two).
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — four independent randomised programmes (in-person, digital and scalable CBT-I; 641 participants) concordantly improved insomnia severity versus an active imagery control, standard care, sleep education and an attention-matched control, with better sleep quality and longer sleep; depression effects were small or absent

title: GLP-1 receptor agonists in PCOS infertility: exenatide beat metformin on pregnancy rate in one open-label trial and one meta-analysis, and liraglutide improved menstrual regularity versus placebo — but live-birth evidence is still sparse
question: In women with polycystic ovary syndrome and infertility, does a GLP-1 receptor agonist improve ovulation and pregnancy outcomes versus placebo or metformin?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), stamped honestly for a thin reproductive base. The pregnancy signal comes from exenatide: in Liu 2017 (176 overweight/obese women with PCOS, open-label), 12 weeks of exenatide before a 12-week metformin-only phase gave a natural pregnancy rate of 43.6% versus 18.7% after metformin alone, with more weight loss (4.29 kg vs 2.28 kg) and a higher menstrual frequency ratio (0.62 vs 0.37); the 2023 meta-analysis of 9 exenatide-versus-metformin trials (785 patients) points the same way (pregnancy relative risk 1.93, 95% CI 1.28 to 2.92; ovulation relative risk 1.41, 95% CI 1.11 to 1.80), though its authors call the evidence inconclusive. For liraglutide, the Frøssing programme's placebo-controlled trial (72 women, 26 weeks) improved bleeding ratio and androgen markers but reported no pregnancy outcomes. Live-birth data are sparse throughout: no carded trial uses live birth as its outcome, so this shelf answers ovulation, menstrual regularity and pregnancy rate — not live birth. Two neighbouring homes are cross-pointed, not re-carded: live shelf #245 covers letrozole, clomiphene and metformin for PCOS ovulation induction, and live shelf #2074 homes the 28-woman Salamun pilot of liraglutide added to metformin before IVF (PMID 29703793, carded there and kept out of this pack's cards under the one-home rule — this pack's question is the broader GLP-1 class question across placebo and metformin comparators, built on three free reports). Semaglutide: no randomised PCOS report with reproductive outcomes was found in this session's fetched records — only reviews and cohort reports — so no semaglutide claim is carded. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a real but preliminary reproductive advantage over metformin, resting on small, mostly open-label trials.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — exenatide beat metformin on natural pregnancy rate in one open-label trial (43.6% vs 18.7%) and across a 9-trial meta-analysis (pregnancy relative risk 1.93; ovulation relative risk 1.41, both relative measures); liraglutide improved bleeding regularity versus placebo in one 72-woman trial; no carded trial is powered for live birth

title: Elagolix with add-back therapy for fibroid bleeding: response in 68.5% and 76.5% of women versus 8.7% and 10% on placebo in the replicate Elaris UF-1 and UF-2 trials, sustained to 12 months
question: In women with heavy menstrual bleeding due to fibroids, does elagolix with add-back therapy reduce blood loss versus placebo?
balance: LIKELY (benefit). The Elaris UF-1 and UF-2 trials are identical replicate double-blind phase 3 trials (790 women randomised in total) and they agree closely: elagolix 300 mg twice daily with estradiol/norethindrone acetate add-back met the primary bleeding endpoint (final-month menstrual blood loss under 80 ml and at least 50% down from baseline) in 68.5% and 76.5% of women versus 8.7% and 10% on placebo. Elagolix alone responded slightly more often (84.1% in UF-1) but at a hypoestrogenic cost the add-back exists to blunt: bone mineral density loss was attenuated with add-back, in the trials and again in UF-EXTEND, where response held at 87.9% at 12 months. Hot flushes and (in UF-1) metrorrhagia were more common on elagolix plus add-back than placebo. The adenomyosis pooled analysis shows the bleeding benefit is not limited to women without adenomyosis (77.1% vs 12.2%). This shelf is the fibroid question only: elagolix for endometriosis pain is live shelf #246, and the other fibroid GnRH-antagonist shelves are relugolix (live #247) and linzagolix (live #1136). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): a large, replicated, placebo-controlled effect on measured blood loss, with bone and vasomotor costs printed on the cards.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — two replicate 6-month phase 3 trials agree: the bleeding-response definition was met by 68.5% (UF-1) and 76.5% (UF-2) of women on elagolix plus add-back versus 8.7% and 10% on placebo (P < 0.001 in both), and response was sustained at 87.9% through 12 months in the extension study

title: Dexamethasone versus betamethasone before preterm birth: death or neurosensory disability at 2 years in 33% versus 32% in the 1,346-woman ASTEROID trial — no difference found, either drug is a reasonable choice
question: In women at risk of preterm birth, is antenatal dexamethasone as effective as betamethasone for newborn outcomes?
balance: POSSIBLE (no difference found). This is the drug-choice question, not whether antenatal steroids work — steroid-versus-placebo is answered at live shelf #1352 (betamethasone, ALPS) and live shelf #1132 (dexamethasone, WHO ACTION-I/II). Head-to-head, the one large double-blind trial, ASTEROID (1,346 women, 1,509 fetuses, Australia and New Zealand), found the primary outcome — death or neurosensory disability at 2 years — in 33% on dexamethasone and 32% on betamethasone (adjusted relative risk 0.97, 95% CI 0.83 to 1.13, p = 0.66); the trial was not designed as a formal noninferiority study, but its interval excludes a large advantage for either drug. The Cochrane synthesis (Williams 2022; 9 dexamethasone-versus-betamethasone trials, 2,096 women and 2,319 infants) agrees: no conclusive difference in death (relative risk 1.03, 95% CI 0.66 to 1.63), little or no difference in respiratory distress syndrome (relative risk 1.06, high-certainty) or in neurodevelopmental disability at follow-up (relative risk 1.02), with a low-certainty cerebral palsy estimate (relative risk 2.50, 95% CI 0.97 to 6.39) that is compatible with both harm and no difference and keeps the stamp at POSSIBLE rather than a flat equivalence claim. ASTEROID's repeat-dose secondary analysis likewise found no difference (odds ratio 0.89). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (no difference found): on current evidence either drug can be given; availability and local practice, not efficacy, should drive the choice.
stamp: POSSIBLE (no difference found) — ASTEROID found death or neurosensory disability at 2 years in 33% on dexamethasone versus 32% on betamethasone (adjusted relative risk 0.97, 95% CI 0.83 to 1.13; the choice of drug made no difference to the primary outcome), and the Cochrane synthesis of 9 head-to-head trials found no conclusive difference in death, respiratory distress syndrome or neurodevelopmental disability

title: Risankizumab for plaque psoriasis: PASI 90 in 77% versus 40% on ustekinumab in the phase 2 head-to-head, superiority over adalimumab (IMMvent) and secukinumab (IMMerge) in phase 3 — the UltIMMa trials versus ustekinumab and placebo are carded at live shelf #377
question: In adults with plaque psoriasis, does risankizumab clear skin better than ustekinumab or placebo?
balance: LIKELY (benefit). FLAG — precedent (b) build, stated prominently: the anchor UltIMMa-1/UltIMMa-2 report (Gordon 2018, PMID 30097359) is already carded as Card 1 of live shelf #377, the class-efficacy shelf for plaque-psoriasis biologics, whose question is class-wide (how completely modern biologics clear skin, and at what safety cost). This pack's question is the narrower drug-specific head-to-head — does risankizumab beat ustekinumab or placebo — and at least three free (ungated) reports answer it, so the pack is built on those free reports with the UltIMMa home cross-pointed and PMID 30097359 kept out of every card source line; no UltIMMa figures are re-printed here. On the free reports: the direct ustekinumab comparison is Papp 2017 (phase 2, 166 patients): PASI 90 at week 12 in 77% on pooled 90/180 mg risankizumab versus 40% on ustekinumab, and complete clearance (PASI 100) in 45% versus 18%. Two further phase 3 head-to-heads against other proven biologics point the same way: IMMvent versus adalimumab (PASI 90 72% vs 47% at week 16; switching adalimumab intermediate responders to risankizumab beat continuing adalimumab at week 44, 66% vs 21%) and IMMerge versus secukinumab (PASI 90 noninferior at week 16 and superior at week 52, 86.6% vs 57.1%). Adverse-event frequencies were similar across arms in each trial. Risankizumab's other homes are different diseases and are not this question: Crohn's disease (live #771 and pack #5885), ulcerative colitis (pack #3576) and psoriatic arthritis (pack #5450). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): consistent superiority over active comparators across three randomised head-to-head programmes, with the placebo contrast housed at live #377.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — risankizumab cleared skin (PASI 90) more often than ustekinumab in the randomised head-to-head (77% vs 40% at week 12), more often than adalimumab in IMMvent (72% vs 47% at week 16) and more often than secukinumab at week 52 in IMMerge (86.6% vs 57.1%); the replicate UltIMMa phase 3 trials versus ustekinumab and placebo are carded at live shelf #377 and are cross-pointed here, not re-carded

title: Tranexamic acid in noncardiac surgery: composite bleeding 9.1% versus 11.7% on placebo in POISE-3 (9,535 patients) — bleeding benefit clear; formal cardiovascular noninferiority was not established in POISE-3 itself
question: In adults undergoing noncardiac surgery, does tranexamic acid reduce major bleeding without increasing thrombosis versus placebo?
balance: LIKELY (benefit for bleeding), with the safety wording kept exact. POISE-3 (9,535 patients at cardiovascular risk undergoing noncardiac surgery; tranexamic acid 1 g at the start and end of surgery) reduced the composite of life-threatening, major or critical-organ bleeding from 11.7% to 9.1% (hazard ratio 0.76, 95% CI 0.67 to 0.87; absolute difference −2.6 percentage points). On safety, the composite cardiovascular outcome was 14.2% versus 13.9% (hazard ratio 1.02, 95% CI 0.92 to 1.14) — a small difference, but the trial's own noninferiority test failed: the upper confidence bound (1.14) crossed the prespecified 1.125 margin, so noninferiority was not established, and this shelf does not claim it was. The wider randomised base is reassuring on thrombosis: Tsan 2023 pooled 191 trials (40,621 patients) and found thromboembolic events in 4.5% on tranexamic acid versus 4.9% on control (relative risk 1.02, 95% CI 0.94 to 1.11) with transfusion roughly halved (9.9% vs 19.4%), while noting trial sequential analysis reached only 64.6% of the required information size; Houston 2020 (69 trials in high-transfusion-risk noncardiac surgery, excluding hip/knee arthroplasty) likewise found fewer transfusions (relative risk 0.59, low-certainty) and no differences in thrombotic outcomes. This is the noncardiac-surgery question only: tranexamic acid in coronary surgery is live shelf #1246 (ATACAS), and its other indication homes (live #138 family, #1601, #1619) are separate questions. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit for bleeding): fewer major bleeds, no thrombotic increase demonstrated across the pooled trials, one formal noninferiority miss in the largest trial printed on the face.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit for bleeding) — POISE-3 cut the composite bleeding outcome (9.1% vs 11.7%; hazard ratio 0.76, a relative measure; absolute difference −2.6 percentage points), and across 191 randomised trials (40,621 patients) tranexamic acid showed no increase in thromboembolic events (4.5% vs 4.9%; relative risk 1.02) — although POISE-3 itself did not formally establish cardiovascular noninferiority (hazard ratio 1.02; upper confidence bound 1.14 against the 1.125 margin)

title: ERAS pathways in gynaecologic surgery: median stay 2 days shorter in both randomised trials (7 vs 9 days in PROFAST; 2 vs 4 days in the Italian trial) — the pooled complication benefit rests mainly on cohort data
question: In adults undergoing gynaecologic surgery, does an ERAS pathway shorten hospital stay and reduce complications versus conventional care?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), graded exactly as the assignment requires: the randomised legs support shorter stay; the complication leg is largely observational and is labelled as such. PROFAST (99 women having cytoreductive surgery for advanced ovarian cancer, ERAS protocol compliance 92%) found median stay 7 versus 9 days (p = 0.0099) and fewer readmissions (6% vs 20%) with no difference in complications or mortality. The Italian randomised trial (168 women, benign and malignant disease, protocol adherence 84.8%) found median stay 2 versus 4 days (P < .001) and a lower complication rate. The Bisch 2021 meta-analysis (31 studies, 6,703 patients — only 5 randomised, 26 cohorts) pooled a 1.6-day shorter stay and relatively fewer complications (odds ratio 0.68) and readmissions (odds ratio 0.80) with no mortality difference; because that base is mostly cohort data, its complication figure is observational evidence and cannot lift the stamp. Programme naming: no branded or single proprietary programme was tested — each publication describes an ERAS pathway built from the ERAS Society gynaecologic/gynaecologic-oncology perioperative elements (preoperative education and carbohydrate loading, opioid-sparing analgesia, early feeding and mobilisation, as itemised in the trials), and this pack names it that way rather than inventing a brand. ERAS in colorectal surgery is a different shelf (live #869); liver ERAS is pack #6221. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): stay is shorter on randomised evidence; fewer complications are suggested, mainly by cohorts.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit; observational legs labelled) — two randomised trials found median hospital stay 2 days shorter with an ERAS pathway (7 vs 9 days in PROFAST; 2 vs 4 days in the Italian trial) with no increase in complications or readmission; the pooled complication reduction (odds ratio 0.68, a relative measure) comes from a meta-analysis in which 26 of 31 studies were cohorts, so that leg is observational and capped at POSSIBLE here

title: ERAS pathways in liver surgery: discharge 3 days sooner in the one early randomised trial (4 vs 7 days) and fewer medical complications (7% vs 27%); pooled stay 2.2 days shorter across mostly cohort studies
question: In adults undergoing liver surgery, does an ERAS pathway shorten hospital stay and reduce complications versus conventional care?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), with the non-randomised weight of the base printed on the face. The randomised anchor is Jones 2013 (91 patients, open liver resection): the enhanced recovery programme — preoperative education and carbohydrate loading, goal-directed fluid therapy, early mobilisation and physiotherapy, as published in the trial — cut time to medically fit for discharge (3 vs 6 days) and actual stay (4 vs 7 days), and reduced medical complications (7% vs 27%) without changing surgical complications, readmissions or mortality. The syntheses agree on stay but rest mostly on cohorts: Noba 2020 pooled 6 randomised trials and 21 cohort studies (3,739 patients) — stay 2.22 days shorter, complications relatively fewer (relative risk 0.71), costs lower, no mortality or readmission increase — and Ahmed 2016 pooled 3 trials and 5 cohorts (810 patients) with the same direction. Premise correction, stated plainly: the slate named a 'Melloul programme' for this row — in the fetched records, Melloul's liver contribution is authorship of the ERAS Society liver-surgery guideline (2016), not a trial; no Melloul randomised trial of liver ERAS was found, so the pack is built on Jones and the syntheses instead. Programme naming: the tested intervention is the enhanced recovery programme as itemised in each publication (ERAS Society liver elements); no branded programme is named in the publications carded. Colorectal ERAS is live shelf #869 and gynaecologic ERAS is pack #6220 — different operations, different shelves. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a consistent stay advantage with a plausible complication advantage, on one small trial plus largely observational pooling.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit; partly non-randomised evidence, labelled) — the randomised trial (91 patients) found stay of 4 versus 7 days and fewer medical complications (7% vs 27%); meta-analyses pooling mainly cohort studies found stay about 2.2 days shorter and relatively fewer complications (relative risk 0.71), with no increase in mortality or readmission

title: Stopping alcohol before surgery: one month of abstinence cut complications from 74% to 31% in one 42-patient trial — but the whole randomised base is only about 210 patients, and a later trial found no complication difference
question: In adults who drink heavily and are having surgery, does stopping alcohol for about 4 weeks before surgery reduce postoperative complications?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), on a small and mixed base that this shelf prints on its face. The direct answer to the 'about 4 weeks before surgery' question is a single trial: Tønnesen 1999 randomised 42 asymptomatic heavy drinkers (at least 60 g ethanol/day) having colorectal surgery to one month of preoperative abstinence — supported and verified with disulfiram, the programme as published — or continued drinking; complications requiring treatment occurred in 31% versus 74% (P = 0.02), with less postoperative myocardial ischaemia (23% vs 85%) and fewer arrhythmias and hypoxaemic episodes. The Egholm Cochrane synthesis (2018 update; 3 randomised trials, 140 participants drinking 3–40 units/day, all testing intensive programmes with pharmacological withdrawal support, education and relapse prophylaxis) pooled complications at 20 of 61 on intervention versus 33 of 61 on control (relative risk 0.62, 95% CI 0.40 to 0.96; moderate-quality evidence), with more successful quitters (41 of 70 vs 5 of 70) and no demonstrated mortality or length-of-stay difference. Against that, the newest trial — Egholm 2022, 70 ankle-fracture patients on the manual-based Gold Standard Program (GSP-A) started on the day of surgery — achieved far more complete abstinence (18 of 35 vs 5 of 35) yet found complications, quality of life and costs similar between groups: the treatment made no difference to complications there. Premise notes: the slate cited an 'Egholm synthesis 2016' — the fetched synthesis is Egholm's Cochrane review in its 2018 update (first published 2012); and no separate Tønnesen 2002 abstinence trial record was found — the 1999 trial is the Tønnesen anchor inside the Cochrane pool. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): biologically coherent and positive in the one trial that tested the exact preoperative month, but far too small a base for LIKELY, and timing may matter — the null trial started at surgery, not a month before.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — intensive cessation programmes were associated with fewer postoperative complications in the Cochrane synthesis of 3 small trials (20 of 61 vs 33 of 61; relative risk 0.62, a relative measure), driven by one 42-patient trial of a full month's preoperative abstinence (31% vs 74%); a later 70-patient trial of a programme started on the day of (fracture) surgery produced more quitters but no difference in complications (the treatment made no difference to complications in that trial)

title: TAF/emtricitabine versus TDF/emtricitabine PrEP (DISCOVER): HIV incidence 0.16 versus 0.34 per 100 person-years at the primary analysis — non-inferior, with better bone and renal biomarkers; a single trial programme
question: In people at high risk of HIV, is tenofovir alafenamide/emtricitabine PrEP as effective as tenofovir disoproxil/emtricitabine PrEP?
balance: POSSIBLE (as effective; single programme). DISCOVER is the only head-to-head trial of the two tenofovir prodrug formulations as PrEP, and all three carded reports are reports of that one programme — the stamp cap for a single programme therefore applies despite the trial's size (5,387 participants who received study drug). At the primary analysis (Mayer 2020), HIV incidence was 0.16 per 100 person-years on tenofovir alafenamide/emtricitabine (7 infections) versus 0.34 on tenofovir disoproxil/emtricitabine (15 infections) over 8,756 person-years; the incidence rate ratio of 0.47 (95% CI 0.19 to 1.15) met the prespecified noninferiority margin of 1.62. At week 96 (Ogbuagu 2021) noninferiority was maintained (8 vs 15 infections; 0.16 vs 0.30 per 100 person-years; rate ratio 0.54, 95% CI 0.23 to 1.26), and in the week-144 open-label extension (Wohl 2024) incidence in those originally assigned to the alafenamide regimen was 0.13 per 100 person-years, with the 3 extension-phase infections all in non-adherent participants and no drug resistance. The alafenamide regimen was superior on all six prespecified bone mineral density and renal biomarker endpoints at the primary analysis, and both regimens were well tolerated (discontinuation for adverse events 1% vs 2%). Population limits are printed on the cards: DISCOVER enrolled cisgender men and transgender women who have sex with men in Europe and North America — it does not answer this question for receptive vaginal exposure. The neighbouring PrEP homes are different questions: daily tenofovir in people who inject drugs (live #2143) and on-demand tenofovir disoproxil/emtricitabine (live #2141). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (as effective; single programme): noninferiority is established within DISCOVER; independent replication does not exist.
stamp: POSSIBLE (as effective; single programme) — in the single DISCOVER trial programme, tenofovir alafenamide/emtricitabine was non-inferior to tenofovir disoproxil/emtricitabine for HIV prevention (primary incidence rate ratio 0.47, 95% CI 0.19 to 1.15, against a prespecified 1.62 margin; week 96 incidence 0.16 vs 0.30 per 100 person-years), so the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE because one programme, however large, is one programme

title: Optilume paclitaxel-coated balloon for BPH: IPSS fell 11.5 points at 1 year in the sham-controlled PINNACLE trial and peak flow more than doubled — one randomised programme plus a single-arm feasibility study
question: In men with benign prostatic hyperplasia, does the Optilume drug-coated balloon improve urinary symptoms and flow versus sham?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — this shelf answers the device-specific question for the Optilume BPH Catheter System, a paclitaxel drug-coated balloon catheter (a named device, named exactly as published; the trial records do not name the manufacturer). Neighbouring BPH devices are homed separately — prostatic urethral lift (UroLift) on pack #4260, Rezūm water-vapour therapy on pack #4262 and Aquablation on pack #3042 — and are not re-carded here. The sham-controlled evidence is one trial: PINNACLE randomised 148 men (100 Optilume, 48 sham); at the blinded comparison, symptom scores (IPSS) fell 11.5 points at 1 year on Optilume against an 8.0-point fall at 3 months on sham, and peak flow rose 10.3 mL/s (+125% relative, printed beside the absolute change) at 1 year, with erectile and ejaculatory function preserved. Two-year follow-up of the treated arm (blinding ended at 1 year) showed 67.5% remained responders (≥30% IPSS improvement without retreatment), with IPSS 11.0 and peak flow 19.0 mL/s. The earlier EVEREST-I feasibility study (80 men, single-arm, no comparator) showed the same direction — IPSS 22.3 to 8.2 and peak flow 10.9 to 17.2 mL/s at 2 years — but without a control group it cannot separate device effect from placebo and regression effects, which the large sham response in PINNACLE (8.0 IPSS points) shows are substantial in this condition. Premise note: the slate named the 'ROBUST programme' as supporting evidence; the ROBUST reports concern the same manufacturer's balloon used for anterior urethral strictures, a different indication, and were not carded — the BPH programme is PINNACLE plus EVEREST-I. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a real sham-controlled advantage at 1 year from one programme, durability open-label thereafter.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in the single sham-controlled trial (PINNACLE, 148 men), the Optilume BPH Catheter System improved symptom scores and peak flow more than sham, with gains held at 2 years; the supporting EVEREST-I study was single-arm, so the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE for a single programme

title: Daridorexant and next-day functioning: daytime scores (IDSIQ) improved at 50 mg across the phase 3 programme's secondary analyses — but by less than the questionnaire's own meaningful-change threshold, and 25 mg was inconsistent
question: In adults with insomnia, does daridorexant improve next-day functioning (not just sleep onset and maintenance) versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE — this pack is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #572 already answers the sleep onset and maintenance question for daridorexant and lemborexant versus placebo and a Z-drug, and its primary phase 3 report (Mignot 2022) is homed there and is not re-carded here. What #572 does not do is answer the daytime question in its own right; its balance notes only that daytime gains were clearest at 50 mg. The dedicated daytime reports — all secondary, post-hoc or extension analyses of that same programme (Studies 1 and 2, NCT03545191 and NCT03575104) — agree on a dose pattern: daridorexant 50 mg improved Insomnia Daytime Symptoms and Impacts Questionnaire (IDSIQ) total and domain scores versus placebo from the first weeks, in older and younger adults alike, and the improvement was maintained through a 40-week extension (least-squares mean advantage −9.3 to −9.5 IDSIQ points at weeks 12–36); pooled dose–response analysis found a significant linear dose–response for IDSIQ total score with no dose–response for adverse events. Two cautions cap the stamp. First, the programme's own anchor-based analysis puts the within-patient change patients consider meaningful at 17 IDSIQ total points — larger than the average between-group advantage observed. Second, 25 mg was inconsistent (daytime benefit only in younger adults in the age analysis) and morning-sleepiness visual-analogue gains in the quarter-of-night analysis were numerical rankings rather than tested differences. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: a real, dose-dependent daytime signal at 50 mg, of modest average size, resting entirely on secondary analyses of a single programme.
stamp: POSSIBLE — daridorexant 50 mg improved patient-reported daytime functioning (IDSIQ total and domain scores) versus placebo across secondary and extension analyses of the one phase 3 programme, with a significant dose–response; the average advantage (~9 IDSIQ points in the extension) is smaller than the 17-point within-patient change patients rate as meaningful, and 25 mg helped only in some analyses, so the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE

title: Attempting external cephalic version at term: pooled caesarean risk ratio 0.57 in two syntheses — but the Cochrane evidence is graded low to very low and the largest single trial was null
question: For breech presentation at term, does attempting external cephalic version itself (versus no attempt) increase cephalic birth and reduce caesarean delivery?
balance: POSSIBLE — this pack is a PARTIAL completion. Pack #3783 answers which tocolytic helps version succeed (beta-mimetics help; nifedipine and atosiban do not), and live shelf #664 answers planned caesarean versus planned vaginal breech birth and the timing of version before term; neither asks whether attempting version at term beats not attempting it. On that question, the Cochrane review (Hofmeyr 2015; 8 trials, 1,308 women) found attempted version at or near term reduced non-cephalic presentation at birth (average relative risk 0.42, 95% CI 0.29 to 0.61 — a relative figure), failure to achieve a vaginal cephalic birth (relative risk 0.46) and caesarean section (relative risk 0.57, 95% CI 0.40 to 0.82), with no significant difference in perinatal death (relative risk 0.39, 95% CI 0.09 to 1.64) — but graded the evidence low or very low, with no blinding and suboptimal allocation in several trials. A 2020 systematic review including non-randomised studies (184,704 breech pregnancies, high-resource settings) found near-identical relative effects (caesarean relative risk 0.57; non-cephalic presentation 0.45) but also a small increase in Apgar score below 7 at 5 minutes (relative risk 1.29, 95% CI 1.10 to 1.52). Against both syntheses stands the largest single trial (Kasule 1985, 640 women): no significant difference in vaginal breech delivery, caesarean rate or perinatal mortality, three perinatal deaths attributed to the procedure, and the authors' conclusion that version had no place before 36 weeks — its attempts began after 30 weeks, earlier than the at-term practice the syntheses describe. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: the direction is consistent across syntheses, but low-grade trials, one large null trial and a small neonatal signal forbid a stronger stamp.
stamp: POSSIBLE — attempting external cephalic version at or near term reduced non-cephalic presentation at birth (relative risk 0.42) and caesarean delivery (relative risk 0.57) in the Cochrane pooling of 8 small trials and in a larger review including non-randomised studies (relative risk 0.57 for caesarean), but the Cochrane authors graded the evidence low to very low, the largest single randomised trial found no difference, and one synthesis found slightly more low 5-minute Apgar scores after attempted version (relative risk 1.29)

title: Five versus ten days for otitis media beyond the under-twos: older and mixed-age trials look close, but the pooled failure rate still favours longer courses and no dedicated trial in children 2 and older exists
question: In children aged 2 years and older with acute otitis media, is a 5-day antibiotic course as effective as a 10-day course?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — this pack is a PARTIAL completion: pack #2948 homes the under-2s question, where the strict Hoberman trial found 5 days clearly worse (clinical failure 34% versus 16%); its two records are not re-carded here. The uncovered slice is children aged 2 and older — and the honest finding is that no trial has ever randomised only that age group to 5 versus 10 days. What exists is the wider-childhood literature in which older children predominate numerically: the Cochrane short-course review (49 trials, 12,045 children aged 1 month to 18 years) found treatment failure at one month modestly higher on courses under 7 days (21% versus 18% absolute; odds ratio 1.34, 95% CI 1.15 to 1.55 — the odds ratio is a relative measure, printed beside the absolute rates), with fewer gastrointestinal adverse events on short courses of short-acting antibiotics. The largest direct 5-versus-10-day comparison in this older-skewing literature (Gooch 1996; 719 children aged 3 months to 12 years, cefuroxime) found satisfactory outcomes of 69% on 5 days versus 70% on 10 days of the same drug. The oldest trial (Hendrickse 1988; 175 children) found no advantage to 10 days when the eardrum was intact (failure 10% versus 6% plus one relapse, not significant) — but a stark exception: with spontaneous perforation, failure was 53% on 5 days versus 8% on 10 days (p = 0.016). Two under-2 trials by Cohen (1998, 2000; mean ages 13–14 months) were deliberately NOT carded: their populations belong to the #2948 slice, and borrowing them here would mislabel the age evidence. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): for a child of 2 or older with an intact eardrum, 5 days looks close to 10 in the trials that include such children, but equivalence is inferred, not demonstrated, and perforation is a clear exception.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — in trials enrolling mainly older and mixed-age children, 5-day courses performed close to 10-day courses (satisfactory outcomes 69% versus 70% in the largest head-to-head), but the Cochrane pooling across childhood still found more treatment failure on short courses (odds ratio 1.34; 21% versus 18% absolute), the trials were not restricted to children aged 2 and older, and children with a perforated eardrum did clearly worse on 5 days (failure 53% versus 8%)

title: Atomoxetine versus stimulants in children: non-inferiority was met in two analyses, but the blinded head-to-head trials favoured methylphenidate on response rates — close, not equal
question: In children and adolescents with ADHD, is atomoxetine as effective as stimulant medication for core symptoms?
balance: SPLIT — this pack is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #1390 homes atomoxetine versus placebo in children (one trial), and live shelf #707 homes the medication-class comparison in adults only; the child head-to-head against stimulants is the uncovered slice, and neither home's records are re-carded here. The child comparisons split by design. Where non-inferiority was the test, atomoxetine passed: Wang 2007 (double-blind, 330 outpatients aged 6–16) found response rates of 77.4% on atomoxetine versus 81.5% on methylphenidate, meeting the non-inferiority criterion, though with more anorexia, nausea, somnolence, dizziness and vomiting and slightly more weight loss (−1.2 kg versus −0.4 kg); and the Hazell 2011 direct-comparison meta-analysis (7 studies, 1,368 children and adolescents) found 6-week response rates of 53.6% versus 54.4% (difference −0.9%, 95% CI −9.2 to 7.5), within its −15% non-inferiority margin. Where superiority was the test, the stimulant won: Newcorn 2008 (516 children aged 6–16, double-blind, placebo-controlled) found response in 56% on osmotic-release methylphenidate versus 45% on atomoxetine versus 24% on placebo, the stimulant significantly superior — while also showing about 42–43% of non-responders to one drug responded to the other. Kemner 2005 (open-label, community-based, 1,323 children aged 6–12) likewise favoured OROS methylphenidate on symptom-score change (20.24 versus 16.0 points at 3 weeks), a design whose lack of blinding flatters the familiar drug. PROPOSED SPLIT: on average atomoxetine is somewhat less effective than methylphenidate for core symptoms over 3–8 weeks, close enough to meet generous non-inferiority margins, and a genuine alternative for the substantial minority who do not respond to, or do not tolerate, a stimulant.
stamp: SPLIT — atomoxetine met formal non-inferiority against methylphenidate in a double-blind trial (response 77.4% versus 81.5%) and in a direct-comparison meta-analysis (response 53.6% versus 54.4%), but in the largest double-blind placebo-controlled comparison the stimulant's response rate was higher (56% versus 45%) and an open-label community study also favoured the stimulant — atomoxetine is a close alternative, not a demonstrated equal

title: Mepolizumab in younger children: the one placebo-controlled trial (ages 6–17) cut exacerbations by a relative 27% (0.96 versus 1.30 per year); the 6–11 study itself was a 36-child dosing study with no placebo arm
question: In children aged 6–11 years with severe eosinophilic asthma, does mepolizumab reduce exacerbations versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — this pack is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #813 homes mepolizumab and benralizumab in adult severe eosinophilic asthma (MENSA, SIROCCO) and is not re-carded here; the uncovered slice is the 6–11 age band. The placebo-controlled evidence touching that band is one trial: MUPPITS-2 randomised 290 urban US children and adolescents aged 6–17 with exacerbation-prone eosinophilic asthma (blood eosinophils ≥150 cells/µL) to mepolizumab (40 mg at ages 6–11; 100 mg at 12–17) or placebo for 52 weeks, and exacerbations averaged 0.96 versus 1.30 (rate ratio 0.73, 95% CI 0.56 to 0.96 — a 27% relative reduction, printed beside the absolute rates); treatment-emergent adverse events were reported in 29% on mepolizumab versus 11% on placebo, with no deaths attributed to the drug. The record prints no separate result for the 6–11 subgroup, so the trial supports the band only as part of its wider age range. The one study confined to ages 6–11 (Gupta 2019; 36 children) was open-label and non-randomised, designed for pharmacokinetics: weight-banded dosing (40 mg under 40 kg; 100 mg at or above) produced exposures within twofold of the adult target and cut blood eosinophils by 83–89% at 12 weeks, with no new safety signals — it establishes that the dose reaches children, not that it prevents attacks. The Cochrane anti-IL-5 review (17 studies, about 7,600 participants) found exacerbation rates roughly halved across the class in severe eosinophilic asthma (mepolizumab subcutaneous rate ratio 0.45), but only one of its studies was in children and its pooled estimate is adult-driven context, not child evidence. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): direction and biology align from trial, dosing study and class review, but a dedicated placebo-controlled efficacy result for ages 6–11 alone does not exist in these records.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — mepolizumab reduced exacerbations versus placebo in the one randomised trial enrolling this age band (rate ratio 0.73, a 27% relative reduction, with absolute rates of 0.96 versus 1.30 exacerbations over 52 weeks), but that trial spanned ages 6–17 with no separate 6–11 result printed, and the only study confined to ages 6–11 was an open-label 36-child pharmacokinetic study not designed to test efficacy — a single-programme cap applies

title: Intrarenal stones: ureteroscopy probably clears more stones than shock-wave lithotripsy — clearest at 1–2 cm and in the lower pole — on thin randomised proof
question: In adults with stones inside the kidney (not the ureter), does ureteroscopy achieve higher stone-free rates than shock-wave lithotripsy?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). Three sources, one direction, uneven strength. The Lower Pole Study Group randomised trial (Pearle 2005; stones ≤1 cm, lower pole) found stone-free rates of 50% on ureteroscopy versus 35% on shock-wave lithotripsy at 3 months — not statistically significant in 78 randomised patients. The Cochrane review (Srisubat 2014) found its only randomised ureteroscopy (RIRS) comparison — 58 patients — likewise non-significant (relative risk 0.91, 95% CI 0.64 to 1.30). The larger meta-analysis (Mi 2016; 2,348 patients, 6 randomised + 8 retrospective studies) found significantly higher stone-free rates with flexible ureteroscopy for stones under 2 cm, driven by the 1–2 cm stratum and the lower pole, with fewer auxiliary procedures and retreatments. Shock-wave lithotripsy remains quicker, avoids access failure and perforation, and scored better on patient-reported convalescence in the trial. This shelf covers stones inside the kidney only; ureteric stones are home shelf #913 (TISU).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — ureteroscopy probably achieves higher stone-free rates than shock-wave lithotripsy for stones inside the kidney, most clearly for 1–2 cm and lower-pole stones; the randomised-only comparisons are individually non-significant, so the advantage is probable, not proven

title: Dexamethasone implant versus anti-VEGF in diabetic macular oedema: no vision advantage — similar gains, far fewer injections, more cataract and raised pressure
question: In adults with diabetic macular oedema, does a dexamethasone implant improve vision compared with anti-VEGF therapy (rather than sham)?
balance: POSSIBLE. The head-to-head answer is no vision advantage. BEVORDEX (Gillies 2014; 88 eyes) found 10-or-more-letter gains in 41% of implant eyes versus 40% of bevacizumab eyes (P = 0.83), with 11% of implant eyes losing 10 or more letters (mostly cataract) versus none on bevacizumab; the implant thinned the macula more (−187 vs −122 µm) with a third of the injections (2.7 vs 8.6). DRCR Protocol U (Maturi 2018) found adding the implant to ranibizumab in persistent oedema made no difference to vision at 24 weeks (the treatment made no difference; −0.5 letters) despite greater thinning, with pressure rises in 29% versus 0%. Cochrane (Rittiphairoj 2020; 2 trials, 451 eyes) found slightly less acuity improvement with the implant than anti-VEGF therapy and more than 4-fold relative increases in cataract progression and pressure-lowering treatment. Implant and company are named exactly as published (Ozurdex; Allergan, Inc.) under the clarification exception. Implant versus sham is home pack #4021; this shelf is the anti-VEGF comparison it does not cover.
stamp: POSSIBLE — the dexamethasone implant (Ozurdex; Allergan, Inc.) does not improve vision more than anti-VEGF therapy: 10-letter gains were 41% versus 40% against bevacizumab in the one head-to-head trial, adding the implant to ranibizumab made no difference to vision (the treatment made no difference), and the pooled estimate slightly favours anti-VEGF — against fewer injections but more cataract and raised intraocular pressure

title: Tezepelumab for nasal polyps (WAYPOINT): polyp score down 2.07 points and congestion down 1.03 versus placebo at 52 weeks — one strongly positive phase 3 trial
question: In adults with chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps, does tezepelumab improve polyp size and nasal symptoms versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single programme. WAYPOINT (Lipworth 2025; 408 adults with severe, uncontrolled chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps) found tezepelumab 210 mg every 4 weeks beat placebo on both coprimary endpoints at 52 weeks: total nasal-polyp score −2.07 (95% CI −2.39 to −1.74) and nasal-congestion score −1.03 (95% CI −1.20 to −0.86), with significant gains in smell, SNOT-22 (−27.26), Lund-Mackay score (−5.72) and total symptom score, and far fewer indications for polyp surgery (0.5% vs 22.1%) or systemic glucocorticoids (5.2% vs 18.3%). The NAVIGATOR asthma trial's polyp subgroup (Laidlaw 2023) showed concordant SNOT-22 improvement (−10.58 at week 52). A 2025 review confirms WAYPOINT is the only dedicated trial and the drug was not yet approved for this indication. Home live shelf #375 is the biologics class shelf (dupilumab largest, omalizumab named); tezepelumab is not in its question and WAYPOINT postdates it.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — tezepelumab improved polyp size and nasal symptoms versus placebo in one phase 3 trial (polyp score −2.07, congestion −1.03 at 52 weeks); a single programme caps the stamp at POSSIBLE

title: HoLEP versus simple prostatectomy for very large prostates: identical symptom relief and flow at 5 years, with less blood loss, 1 versus 6 catheter days and 2 versus 10 hospital days
question: In men with very large prostates (over about 80 mL), how does holmium laser enucleation compare with simple prostatectomy?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one randomised programme plus concordant syntheses. The Kuntz trial randomised 120 men with prostates over 100 g to HoLEP or open transvesical prostatectomy: functional improvement was equivalent at every interval to 18 months and remained identical at 5 years (symptom score 3.0 in both groups; Qmax 24.4 mL/s in both; reoperations 5% vs 6.7%), while HoLEP halved blood loss, eliminated transfusions (0 vs 8), and cut catheter time (median 1 vs 6 days) and hospital stay (2 vs 10 days) at the cost of a longer operation (136 vs 91 minutes). The Jones 2016 systematic review of HoLEP versus simple prostatectomy for large prostates found the same pattern — equivalent efficacy, perioperative advantage to HoLEP. Home pack #3043 asks HoLEP versus TURP in benign prostatic hyperplasia generally; the very-large-gland population and simple-prostatectomy comparator are the slice it does not cover.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in prostates over 100 g, holmium laser enucleation matched open prostatectomy on symptom relief and flow through 5 years while losing less blood and shortening catheter time (1 vs 6 days) and hospital stay (2 vs 10 days); the randomised base is one programme, capping the stamp at POSSIBLE

title: Reflux treatment in IPF: SPLIT — an early cohort linked reflux medication to longer survival, but the largest pooled analysis and the one small surgical trial found no benefit
question: In adults with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, does treating gastro-oesophageal reflux (antacid therapy or fundoplication) slow progression or improve survival?
balance: SPLIT — grade with care: the evidence is observational plus one small surgical trial. Lee 2011 (retrospective cohort, 204 patients) found reported reflux-medication use was an independent predictor of longer survival with a lower fibrosis score. Kreuter 2016 (post-hoc pooled analysis of 624 placebo-arm patients from the three pirfenidone trials) found the opposite pattern: disease progression 39% versus 42%, mortality 7% versus 7% — antacid therapy made no difference (the treatment made no difference) — with more infections in advanced disease. WRAP-IPF (Raghu 2018; 58 randomised patients with IPF and proven abnormal acid reflux) found laparoscopic anti-reflux surgery did not significantly change 48-week FVC decline (−0.05 L vs −0.13 L; P = .28). The IPF family homes (live #810 antifibrotics; packs #2783, #2801) do not cover reflux treatment.
stamp: SPLIT (observational) — an early cohort associated reflux-medication use with longer survival, but the largest pooled analysis found antacid therapy made no difference to progression or mortality (the treatment made no difference) and the one small randomised fundoplication trial was non-significant; no benefit is demonstrated

title: Fluticasone versus budesonide inhalers in COPD (observational only): pneumonia rates consistently higher on fluticasone — 11.0 versus 6.4 per 100 patient-years in PATHOS
question: In adults with COPD, do fluticasone-containing inhalers carry a higher pneumonia risk than budesonide-containing inhalers?
balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — observational only, graded with care. PATHOS (Janson 2013; 2,734 propensity-matched patients per cohort) found pneumonia at 11.0 versus 6.4 events per 100 patient-years on fluticasone/salmeterol versus budesonide/formoterol (rate ratio 1.73, a relative figure), with higher pneumonia mortality (hazard ratio 1.76, a relative figure; 97 vs 52 deaths) but no difference in all-cause mortality. Suissa 2013 (163,514-patient Quebec cohort) found serious-pneumonia rate ratios versus non-use of 2.01 for fluticasone (dose-related) versus 1.17 for budesonide (relative figures). Choi 2021 (Korean nationwide matched cohort, 14,518 per group) found pneumonia in 14.22% versus 10.66% (hazard ratio 1.34, a relative figure), rising with cumulative dose. No randomised molecule head-to-head exists; severity confounding in records data is the standing caveat, printed on the face.
stamp: POSSIBLE (harm) — observational only: fluticasone-containing inhalers are associated with a higher pneumonia risk than budesonide-containing inhalers in COPD (PATHOS rate ratio 1.73, a relative figure; 11.0 vs 6.4 events per 100 patient-years), consistently across three large observational programmes; observational evidence is capped at POSSIBLE

title: Drospirenone versus levonorgestrel pills and venous thromboembolism (observational, SPLIT): registries find a relative rate ratio of 1.64 for drospirenone; the EURAS cohort found 1.0
question: In women, does a drospirenone-containing combined pill carry a higher venous thromboembolism risk than a levonorgestrel-containing pill?
balance: SPLIT — observational only, graded with care. Lidegaard 2009 (Danish national cohort, 10.4 million woman-years) found a venous thromboembolism rate ratio of 1.64 for drospirenone versus levonorgestrel at the same oestrogen dose and duration (a relative figure; absolute risk 6.29 per 10,000 woman-years in current users versus 3.01 in non-users). Vinogradova 2015 (UK nested case-control, 10,562 cases) found adjusted odds ratios versus non-use of 4.12 for drospirenone versus 2.38 for levonorgestrel (relative figures). EURAS (Dinger 2007; 58,674 women, prospective) found hazard ratio 1.0 — no difference. Larivée 2017 (17 studies) found relative risks spanning 1.0–3.3, with the three highest-quality studies at 1.0–1.57. FLAG (precedent b): Lidegaard 2011 is already carded on pack #5800 (combined versus progestin-only pill — a different question) and is kept out of this shelf's cards; this shelf rests on the free reports above. Pack #5800's question is different; the progestogen-to-progestogen comparison is this shelf's slice.
stamp: SPLIT (observational) — large registry studies associate drospirenone pills with a higher venous thromboembolism risk than levonorgestrel pills (rate ratio 1.64, a relative figure), while the prospective EURAS cohort found no difference (hazard ratio 1.0); the highest-quality studies span 1.0 to 1.57 — observational evidence, capped at POSSIBLE in either direction

title: IUD use, pelvic inflammatory disease and infertility (observational only): PID risk is confined to the first 20 days after insertion, and copper IUD use showed no association with tubal infertility in nulligravid women
question: In adolescents and nulliparous women, does IUD use increase pelvic inflammatory disease or later infertility versus non-use?
balance: POSSIBLE (no harm shown) — observational only, graded with care. Farley 1992 (WHO pooled data: 22,908 insertions, 51,399 woman-years) found pelvic inflammatory disease at 1.6 per 1,000 woman-years overall, more than six times higher in the first 20 days after insertion (9.7 vs 1.4 per 1,000 woman-years) and low and constant for up to 8 years — a pattern tied to insertion and background sexually transmitted infection risk. Hubacher 2001 (case-control, 1,895 women) found previous copper IUD use was not associated with tubal occlusion in nulligravid women (odds ratio 1.0 versus infertile controls; 0.9 versus pregnant controls), while chlamydia antibodies were associated with infertility. Hubacher 2014's review reads the wider literature the same way. Adolescent-specific data are thin in the carded set; that indirectness is stated on the face.
stamp: POSSIBLE (no harm shown) — observational only: IUD use is not associated with later tubal infertility in nulligravid women (odds ratio 1.0), and pelvic inflammatory disease risk is concentrated in the first 20 days after insertion (9.7 versus 1.4 per 1,000 woman-years thereafter); observational evidence is capped at POSSIBLE

title: Levonorgestrel 52 mg IUD to 8 years: efficacy persists in years 6–8 — Pearl Index 0.28 over years 6–8 in the Mirena Extension Trial and a 1.32% cumulative 8-year pregnancy rate for Liletta
question: In women, does keeping a levonorgestrel 52 mg IUD for up to 8 years remain effective contraception (versus the originally licensed 5 years)?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — framed as an evidence question, not a randomised comparison: the data are single-arm efficacy cohorts. The Mirena Extension Trial (Jensen 2022; 362 women starting year 6 with the Mirena 52-mg system, named as published) found 2 pregnancies in years 6–8, a 3-year Pearl Index of 0.28 and a cumulative failure rate of 0.68%. ACCESS IUS (Creinin 2022; Liletta 52-mg system, named as published) found a cumulative pregnancy rate of 1.32% through 8 years, with 2 pregnancies in year 7 and none in year 8. A Brazilian chart review of 776 women keeping the same Mirena device beyond 60 months (Bahamondes 2018; Mirena; Bayer Oy, Turku, Finland, as published) found zero pregnancies over 967 woman-years to year 7. Products and company are named exactly as published under the clarification exception.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single-arm cohort evidence: the levonorgestrel 52 mg system remains highly effective through 8 years (Pearl Index 0.28 for years 6–8 in the Mirena Extension Trial; cumulative pregnancy rate 1.32% through 8 years in the Liletta ACCESS IUS cohort); not a randomised comparison, so the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE
