title: Hepatitis B screening linked to treatment: recommended by the USPSTF (grade B), but the liver-outcome evidence is indirect — no screening trial exists and treatment-outcome data are inconsistent
question: In adults at increased risk, does hepatitis B screening linked to antiviral treatment improve liver outcomes (the USPSTF test-and-treat strategy)?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — grade with care; the indirectness is the finding. USPSTF 2020 (Krist) recommends screening adolescents and adults at increased risk (B recommendation; moderate certainty of moderate net benefit), noting up to 60% of infected people are unaware of their infection. Its evidence report (Chou 2020; 30 trials, 20 cohorts, 94,168 participants) states plainly that no study directly evaluated screening versus no screening on mortality, hepatocellular carcinoma or cirrhosis; antiviral therapy improved intermediate outcomes (numbers needed to treat 2.6 to 17) and might improve clinical outcomes on sparse, imprecise data. An independent review of the treatment link (Thiele 2013) found randomised trials showed no effect of antiviral therapy on hepatocellular carcinoma or mortality, with observational designs disagreeing in opposite directions. Antiviral shelves for diagnosed chronic hepatitis B are different questions; this shelf is the screening-strategy question.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the USPSTF recommends screening at-risk adults (grade B, moderate certainty), but no study directly tests screening against liver outcomes and the treatment link is inconsistent across designs; the benefit is an inference from an indirect chain, stated on the face

title: Repeat selective laser trabeculoplasty after the first treatment wears off: pressure falls again in cohort studies — observational evidence only, no randomised trial
question: In adults with open-angle glaucoma whose first selective laser trabeculoplasty worked and then wore off, does repeating the laser lower pressure again?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), observational evidence only. Four retrospective cohorts agree that repeating 360-degree selective laser trabeculoplasty (SLT) after a first successful treatment has worn off lowers intraocular pressure again: Hong 2009 (44 eyes) found a smaller reduction than the first treatment at 1–3 months (−2.9 vs −5.0 mm Hg) but no significant difference at other time points or in success rates; Avery 2013 (42 eyes) found no significant difference in reduction or success and significantly longer benefit from the repeat; Khouri 2014 found significant reductions sustained to 24 months (29% of eyes over 20% at 2 years). No randomised trial exists, retreatment was chosen clinically in every cohort, and concurrent drops were not controlled — so the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE and the evidence is labelled observational on every card. title: How fast PaCO2 rises during apnoea: a fast first minute, then about 3–6 mm Hg per minute depending on state — the Frumin and Stock measurements
question: In healthy humans, how fast does arterial carbon dioxide rise during apnoea, and what determines the rate?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Framed by Guyton & Hall and Ganong (textbook framing, not evidence). The human measurements are concordant: PaCO2 rise in apnoea is logarithmic — fast at first as arterial blood equilibrates toward mixed venous PCO2 (Stock 1988, awake: 7 mm Hg in the first 10 seconds; Stock 1989, anaesthetised and obstructed: 12 mm Hg in the first minute), then roughly linear at about 6 mm Hg/minute awake (Stock 1988, 20 volunteers) and 3.4 mm Hg/minute anaesthetised (Stock 1989, 14 adults). Frumin 1959 established that apnoeic oxygenation keeps oxygen flowing while CO2 accumulates; Stock 1989 showed the oxygen flow does not meaningfully eliminate CO2, so the steady rate is set by CO2 production and body stores. Classic small studies; Ns are printed on the card faces.

title: The ventilatory response to CO2: measured by rebreathing as a threshold and a slope — Read's method and the Duffin programme's human values
question: In healthy humans, how large is the ventilatory response to inhaled carbon dioxide, and how is it normally measured and distributed?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Framed by Ganong and Boron & Boulpaep (textbook framing, not evidence). The measurement is Read's 1967 rebreathing method and its modern Duffin modification: ventilation is plotted against rising PCO2 and the response is a threshold plus a slope. Duffin's 22-subject programme formalised the shape (basal ventilation below threshold, linear rise above, tidal volume dominant). The carded Duffin-programme measurement of central sensitivity is 1.87 ± 0.66 L/min per mm Hg under control conditions (Vovk 2000, N=7, printed on the face); textbook values for the overall response (roughly 2–3 L/min per mm Hg, widely distributed) are given as the textbook's account in the Synthesis. title: Ventilatory acclimatisation to altitude: CO2 falls about 10 Torr and the hypoxic response roughly doubles over the first 1–2 weeks — the Severinghaus and Birmingham programme measurements
question: In healthy humans, how do ventilation and arterial gases change over the first days of ascent to high altitude (ventilatory acclimatisation)?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Framed by Boron & Boulpaep and Guyton & Hall (textbook framing, not evidence). The Severinghaus programme's chamber studies at 3,810 m (N=6, printed on the faces) show the time course directly: hypoxic ventilatory response unchanged in the first day or so, then rising — 0.91 to 1.46 L/min per % fall in SaO2 by about day 5 (+60%, confirmed independently in the parallel cerebral blood-flow study) and still rising at day 12 — while resting end-tidal CO2 falls from 42.3 to 30.8 Torr and early hypoxic ventilatory depression (set point +9.2 Torr on day 2) recedes (+4.5 Torr by day 12). The Birmingham expedition cohort (Milledge 1988, N=32) adds that the rate of acclimatisation, not the sea-level response size, is what tracks symptoms.

title: What limits VO2max: mostly convective oxygen delivery (cardiac output and oxygen content), with extraction near its ceiling — Ekblom, Saltin and the Buick reinfusion experiment

balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Framed by Boron & Boulpaep (textbook framing, not evidence). title: The glucose-threshold hierarchy: hormones at 66–69 mg/dL, symptoms at 53 mg/dL, cognition below that — the Schwartz, Cryer and Fanelli clamp measurements
question: In humans, at what falling blood-glucose levels do counter-regulatory hormones switch on, symptoms appear, and cognition fail (the glucose-threshold hierarchy)?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Framed by Ganong and Boron & Boulpaep (textbook framing, not evidence). Schwartz & Cryer 1987 (N=10) measured the ladder in a single stepped clamp: epinephrine 69 ± 2 mg/dL, glucagon 68 ± 2, growth hormone 66 ± 2, cortisol 58 ± 3, symptoms 53 ± 2 mg/dL. The Fanelli programme placed cognitive failure below the symptom threshold (deterioration across the descent to 40 mg/dL) and showed the thresholds are plastic — antecedent hypoglycemia shifts hormone and symptom responses down (Heller & Cryer 1991), and in type 1 diabetes shifts the cognitive threshold too (Fanelli 1998). title: Standing up: leg volume up 2.5% in 10 minutes, a brief 25% pressure dip, then a baroreflex resistance defence — the normal orthostatic response quantified
question: In healthy humans, how much blood pools in the legs on standing, and how do baroreflex responses defend arterial pressure over the first minutes upright?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Framed by Guyton & Hall (textbook framing, not evidence). title: Renal functional reserve: a protein meal or amino-acid load raises GFR by roughly a quarter to a third in healthy kidneys — peaking at about 2.5 hours — and the reserve shrinks as nephrons are lost
question: In healthy humans, how much does glomerular filtration rate rise after a protein meal or amino-acid load (renal functional reserve), and for how long?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Healthy kidneys do not filter at maximum at rest: an oral protein load or intravenous amino-acid infusion raises glomerular filtration rate (GFR) by roughly 20–35% — Bosch's protein-loading test put mean filtration capacity at 157 mL/min against a reserve of 34 mL/min, Castellino's gluconeogenic amino-acid infusion raised GFR 16% within a 3-hour infusion, and Barai's amino-acid-stimulated clearance study measured a mean reserve of 23.4% in healthy volunteers. Bosch's original 1983 description (cited here in prose; its record is already carded elsewhere in the library and is not re-carded) found GFR maximal about 2.5 hours after the load. The reserve is a property of remaining nephrons: it falls steadily with chronic kidney disease stage and is blunted or absent when nephron number is reduced. Framing follows Boron & Boulpaep and Guyton & Hall (afferent arteriolar dilatation, raised glomerular pressure and renal plasma flow), named as textbook framing, not as evidence. Live shelf #1979 asks a different question — whether protein RESTRICTION slows GFR decline in chronic kidney disease (the MDRD question) — and is cross-pointed, not duplicated.

title: Fever costs energy: metabolic rate rises by roughly a tenth to an eighth for each 1 °C of fever — about 250 kcal/day per °C in ICU regression data, with sepsis adding a further rise of its own
question: In humans, by how much does metabolic rate rise for each 1 °C rise in body temperature during fever?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Every human calorimetry dataset agrees on direction and approximate size: resting energy expenditure climbs as body temperature climbs. Frankenfield's trauma/sepsis regression put the temperature term at +250 kcal/day for each 1 °C — roughly a tenth to an eighth of a typical resting expenditure, matching the classic textbook account (Guyton & Hall present the Du Bois-era fever calorimetry as about a 13% rise in metabolic rate per 1 °C, presented here as the textbook's account: the original Du Bois reports predate abstract-indexed records and no cardable record with per-degree numbers was fetched this session, so no Du Bois card is claimed). Two cautions run through the modern data: sepsis raises expenditure independently of temperature (Bruder), and in already-hypermetabolic patients the fever increment rides on top of an elevated baseline (Gore's burned children). Shivering, sedation and paralysis move the number as much as temperature does, which is why the per-degree figure is an average slope, not a constant of nature.

title: Calcium absorption: about a third of a typical 300–500 mg dose is absorbed — the fraction falls from ~64% at tiny loads to ~29% at 500 mg, rises about two-thirds when vitamin D status improves within the normal range, and is a stable personal trait
question: In healthy humans, what fraction of an oral calcium dose is absorbed, and how do dose size and vitamin D status change that fraction?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. The Heaney programme measured true fractional calcium absorption in healthy adults by isotopic-tracer methods over several decades, and its three determinants are consistent across reports: (1) the fraction absorbed at an ordinary load is roughly one third — 0.321 from milk and 0.409 from kale at a ~300 mg load; (2) the fraction is strongly load-dependent, falling from an average 64.0% at the smallest loads to 28.6% at 500 mg, inversely with the logarithm of load, so absorbed calcium rises with dose even as efficiency falls; and (3) vitamin D status matters well inside the laboratory reference range — absorption was 65% higher (relative) at a mean 25-hydroxyvitamin D of 86.5 nmol/L (34.6 ng/mL) than at 50.2 nmol/L (20.1 ng/mL) on identical 500 mg loads. A fourth finding frames all three: absorption is a consistent personal trait, correlated within individuals across loads, substances and years. Framing follows Ganong (vitamin-D-dependent active transport plus passive paracellular uptake), named as textbook framing. The library's calcium shelves ask supplementation outcomes (fractures, bone density); absorption physiology itself was uncovered.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED

title: The first three days of fasting: glucose and insulin fall steadily, counter-regulatory hormones and free fatty acids rise, ketones climb, and urinary nitrogen loss continues — the whole-body fuel switch, distinct from the liver's glucose-production fractions
question: In humans fasted for 24–72 hours, how do glucose, insulin, ketones and nitrogen loss change over time?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — for a deliberately narrow slice. Live shelf #34 already homes hepatic glucose production and its gluconeogenesis/recycling fractions during fasting (the Katz & Tayek tracer programme); this shelf does not re-card any of that work and asks the uncovered whole-body question: what happens to circulating glucose, insulin, ketones and nitrogen loss across 24–72 hours. The carded human studies agree: glucose, insulin, C-peptide and proinsulin all fall progressively through a 72-hour fast in 33 healthy subjects (Højlund 2001, the reference-interval study); counter-regulatory hormones and free fatty acids rise; and in non-obese subjects fasted 3–7 days, blood ketones rose progressively, glucose and alanine fell, insulin and triiodothyronine fell, urea nitrogen excretion fell while total urinary nitrogen did not change significantly (Garty 1985). Sherwin's ketone-infusion experiments supply the mechanism the time course implies: raising blood ketones itself lowers alanine and urinary nitrogen, part of how the fast becomes protein-sparing as ketones climb. The fuller Cahill/Owen account — respiratory quotient falling toward fat oxidation and nitrogen loss declining over weeks — is presented in the Synthesis as the Guyton & Hall textbook framing where the 24–72-hour carded records do not themselves print those numbers.

title: Normal pregnancy expands plasma volume by ~45–48% and filtration rate by ~45–50% — both rise from the first weeks, plasma volume peaking late in the third trimester, filtration peaking earlier and then easing
question: In pregnant women, how much do plasma volume and glomerular filtration rate normally rise, and at what gestation do they peak?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Two longitudinal human measurements, repeated decades apart, give the same magnitudes. Plasma volume rises ~6% in the first trimester and ~45–48% above the non-pregnant state by the late third trimester, peaking at 35–38 weeks (two meta-analyses of longitudinal studies: Aguree 2019, 10 studies, 347 pregnancies; de Haas 2017, 30 studies, pooled maximum +1.13 L, +45.6%). Glomerular filtration rate rises earlier and further in relative terms: 24-hour creatinine clearance is already up ~45% by the ninth week of gestation (Davison & Noble 1981, 11 women), and inulin clearance shows renal plasma flow and GFR rising by 6 weeks of gestation (Chapman 1998, 13 women). The two curves diverge late: filtration rate peaks around mid-pregnancy and then eases in the last month, while renal plasma flow falls more sharply in the third trimester even as inulin GFR is maintained (Ezimokhai/Davison 1981, 17 women). Framing follows Guyton & Hall and Ganong (systemic vasodilatation, renin-angiotensin activation, a higher cardiac output driving both changes), named as textbook framing, not as evidence.

title: About 20 g of high-quality protein per meal maximises muscle protein synthesis in young adults (~0.24 g/kg) — older adults need about 0.40 g/kg to reach the same plateau, and spreading 20 g doses every 3 hours beats bolus or pulse feeding
question: In healthy humans, what protein dose per meal maximises muscle protein synthesis, and is the dose–response blunted in older adults?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED, for the post-exercise per-meal dose question in men. The dose–response is concordant across three tracer programmes: muscle protein synthesis rises with ingested protein to a plateau at 20 g of egg protein (Moore 2009, 6 young men) and 20 g of whey (Witard 2014, 48 men — +49% above the 0 g condition at 20 g, +56% at 40 g, i.e. no meaningful further gain), and a 20 g dose every 3 hours outperforms the same 80 g given as 8 × 10 g or 2 × 40 g over 12 hours of recovery (Areta 2013, 24 men). The age question is answered by Moore's 2015 retrospective dose–response analysis: older men (~71 years) need 0.40 ± 0.19 g/kg per meal to reach the plateau versus 0.24 ± 0.06 g/kg in younger men (~22 years) — a blunted, right-shifted response, not an absent one; basal synthesis rates did not differ. Two limits run through all four cards: every carded dose–response cohort is male, and the 'maximal' dose depends on the muscle mass exercised (whole-body exercise shifted the plateau toward 40 g in one study). Framing follows Boron & Boulpaep (leucine-driven mTORC1 signalling), named as textbook framing. The protein shelves live #935 and pack #5126 ask supplementation outcomes in frail and sarcopenic-older populations — different questions, verified from their files.

title: Physiological dead space: an anatomic part that scales with height (~150 mL in adults) plus an alveolar part set by ventilation–perfusion matching — the fraction of each breath wasted falls from roughly a third at rest toward a tenth as tidal volume rises in exercise
question: In healthy humans, what determines physiological dead space, and how does the dead-space fraction of each breath change from rest to exercise?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Physiological dead space is the sum of anatomic dead space (the conducting airways, measured by Fowler's single-breath nitrogen method and scaling with height — Hart 1963, 73 normal subjects) and alveolar dead space (ventilated but under-perfused alveoli, the ventilation–perfusion matching term). What changes from rest to exercise is chiefly the denominator and the matching: tidal volume rises severalfold while anatomic volume changes little, and perfusion of the upper lung improves, so the dead-space fraction (VD/VT, by the Bohr equation in its Enghoff form) falls from roughly 0.3 at rest toward 0.1–0.15 in healthy exercise — the Sun 2002 Wasserman-group reference study of 474 healthy adults formalises VD/VT as the determinant, with arterial CO₂, of ventilatory efficiency; Balmain's healthy controls show the alveolar component staying near zero at rest and low workloads; and Weisman's healthy recruits measured 0.11–0.12 at steady-state strenuous exercise. Framing follows Boron & Boulpaep and Guyton & Hall, named as textbook framing. Where a carded record does not print a resting healthy VD/VT, the resting figure is carried as the textbook's account and labelled as such in the Synthesis.

title: Diffusing capacity rises ~26% from sitting to supine and rises linearly with pulmonary blood flow in exercise without reaching a plateau — capillary recruitment and distension, not the membrane, do the work
question: In healthy humans, how does lung diffusing capacity (DLCO) change with posture and exercise, and what drives the change?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Three human studies, three complementary legs. Posture: DLCO measured during exhalation was 26.3% higher supine than sitting in 8 healthy subjects, and the two postures converged at maximal exercise (Stokes 1981). Exercise: in 44 healthy non-smokers aged 17–68 from the Johnson programme's laboratory tradition (Hsia 1995), DLCO, membrane diffusing capacity and capillary blood volume all rose linearly with pulmonary blood flow from rest to 80% of maximal workload with no plateau — pulmonary blood flow was the dominant determinant of recruitment. Mechanism: the Roughton-Forster partition shows both components rising with flow, and the post-exercise study (Johns 2004, 9 women) shows the components moving in opposite directions when flow falls — capillary blood volume down 21.2% while membrane capacity rose 14.7% — proving the flow/volume term, not membrane injury, drives short-term DLCO change. Framing follows Boron & Boulpaep (recruitment and distension of pulmonary capillaries raising surface area and capillary blood volume), named as textbook framing.

title: Cerebral autoregulation in healthy humans (physiology): flow stays roughly constant across a mean arterial pressure of about 60–150 mm Hg on the Lassen plot, with the lower limit near 60 mm Hg — a textbook range the modern human studies defend dynamically, though the exact limits vary between individuals
question: In healthy humans, over what arterial-pressure range does cerebral blood flow stay roughly constant (cerebral autoregulation), and where is the lower limit?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing (Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology; Boron and Boulpaep Medical Physiology): cerebral blood flow is autoregulated — held roughly constant while mean arterial pressure (MAP) varies over a wide range, conventionally about 60–150 mm Hg, and falls once pressure drops below the lower limit near 60 mm Hg. That range and lower limit are the textbook's account of Lassen's 1959 synthesis (carded here; its PubMed record carries no abstract, so the figures are presented as the Lassen/textbook account, not as numbers from a fetched abstract). The carded primary human studies defend the plateau dynamically rather than re-measuring the static curve: flow velocity was fully restored within seconds of a ~20 mm Hg pressure step in 10 awake volunteers (Aaslid 1989); the cerebrovasculature corrected falling pressure more effectively than rising pressure in 26 volunteers (gain 0.57 versus 0.31 cm/s per mm Hg; Tzeng 2010, Willie/Ainslie programme); and flow stayed unchanged when posture raised mean pressure by 22 mm Hg in 21 young adults (Geinas 2012). Two honest limits. First, the exact lower limit is individual, not a fixed 60 mm Hg for everyone — modern revalidation of Lassen's plot against post-2000 data confirms the plateau in awake humans with normal brains while stressing variation between populations. Second, premise correction: the slate named 'Numminen lower-limit reports', but no PubMed record under that author name was found in this session's searches, so no Numminen report is carded and the lower limit rests on the Lassen/textbook account plus the dynamic studies. How autoregulation changes with ageing and after stroke is a different question, homed at pack #6202, which is cross-pointed here and none of whose reports are re-carded. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (the plateau concept and approximate range are textbook-settled and concordant; the precise limits in any one person are not).

title: Excreting a water load (physiology): a standard 20 mL/kg drink is essentially fully excreted by about 2 hours in young healthy adults, with peak free-water clearance around 8–10 mL/min — slower and lower-peaked in healthy elderly men
question: In healthy humans, how quickly is a standard water load excreted, and what does the free-water clearance time course look like?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing (Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology; Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology): drinking water lowers plasma osmolality, switches vasopressin off, and the kidney answers with a water diuresis — urine flow rises within tens of minutes, peaks, and the load is cleared over a few hours, the textbooks' account, which the carded human studies quantify. In young healthy adults a standard 20 mL/kg oral load was 100.7% excreted by 2 hours, with peak free-water clearance of 8.4 mL/min in water-replete and 9.5 mL/min in water-deprived young men (Crowe 1987). During established water diuresis, urine flow ran at about 12–14 mL/min with free-water clearance of 9.7 mL/min and urine osmolality of 71 mosmol/kg — and even a vasopressin infusion of 1 pg/min/kg, too small to raise plasma levels measurably, cut free-water clearance in half, showing how steeply the time course is gated by vasopressin (Andersen 1990). A 4-hour load-and-replace protocol in 6 men gives the outer time frame, and its indomethacin arm shows prostaglandin inhibition can blunt the diuresis (Vierhapper 1984). Healthy elderly men excreted only 41% by 2 hours with a delayed, lower peak (free-water clearance 5.7 mL/min), a difference that disappeared after adjustment for creatinine clearance (Crowe 1987). FLAG (precedent b): the vasopressin-threshold side of this same physiology — including a 20 mL/kg load study reporting 95% excretion within 4 hours and menstrual-cycle water-loading data — is homed at pack #6079; those reports are gated, are cross-pointed here in prose only, and appear in no card source line. This pack's narrower question is the excretion time course itself, built on three free reports. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

title: Growth hormone and slow-wave sleep (physiology): the night's largest GH pulse rides the first slow-wave episode, smaller pulses follow later slow-wave phases, and the coupling tracks sleep — not the clock — across the night
question: In healthy humans, how are growth-hormone pulses coupled to slow-wave sleep across the night?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing (Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology; Boron and Boulpaep Medical Physiology): most daily growth-hormone (GH) secretion in healthy adults is sleep-related, released in pulses entrained to slow-wave sleep (SWS) — the textbooks' account, and the carded human studies agree in detail. Takahashi 1968 found a major GH peak (13–72 mµg/mL, lasting 1.5–3.5 hours) appearing with the onset of deep sleep in 7 of 8 young adults, smaller peaks (6–14 mµg/mL) with later deep-sleep phases, the peak delayed when sleep onset was delayed, and a fresh peak (14–46 mµg/mL) when subjects returned to sleep after 2–3 hours awake. Sassin 1969 showed the release reverses when the sleep–wake cycle is reversed by 12 hours — coupling to sleep, not circadian time. The Van Cauter programme quantified it: about 70% of sleep GH pulses coincide with SWS and pulse size correlates with concurrent SWS (Van Cauter and Plat 1996), across 149 healthy men GH secretion fell by 372 µg per decade from early adulthood to midlife in parallel with SWS falling from 18.9% to 3.4% of sleep, with GH amount associated with SWS independently of age (Van Cauter 2000). Under chronic partial sleep loss the pattern adapts rather than simply shrinking — a presleep pulse appears alongside the postsleep-onset pulse (Spiegel 2000). Live shelf #47 asks a different question — what tracks GH pulses after weight loss (insulin versus leptin) — and is cross-pointed, not re-carded. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

title: Sweating and skin blood-flow thresholds (physiology): both switch on as core temperature climbs through its regulated zone, the two thresholds move together — about 0.6 °C lower at night, about 0.2 °C higher when hyperosmolar — and heat acclimation lowers the thresholds and the resting core temperature itself
question: In healthy humans, at what core temperatures do sweating and cutaneous vasodilation switch on, and how does heat acclimatisation shift those thresholds and sweat rates?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing (Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology): sweating and cutaneous vasodilation are threshold effectors — off below a core-temperature threshold in the regulated zone around 37 °C and rising steeply above it — the textbook's account of the set-point system. The carded primary studies (Nadel/Wenger programme) quantify how that threshold moves rather than printing one absolute onset temperature: thresholds for sweating and forearm vasodilation shifted together by about 0.57 °C and 0.63 °C between day and night (Wenger 1976), and were 0.57 °C (sweating) and 0.65 °C (vasodilation) higher at 16:00 than at 04:00 in a full circadian protocol (Stephenson 1984). Hyperosmolality raised both thresholds by 0.22 °C and cut the slope and maximum of the blood-flow response (Fortney 1984). Heat acclimation moves the system the other way: after a 9-day active acclimation protocol, baseline rectal and mean body temperature were significantly lower throughout heat stress and the mean-body-temperature thresholds for onset of both sweating and skin vasodilation were lower (Armstrong and Kenney 1993 — the Armstrong heat-acclimation programme's controlled-threshold study; the record's abstract is truncated at 250 words and gives the direction, not a numeric shift, so none is printed). Because no carded record prints a single absolute onset temperature, the absolute threshold is presented as the textbook's account (onset as core temperature rises through ~37 °C, varying with skin temperature, time of day and hydration), and every number on the cards is a measured shift or slope from a fetched record. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

title: The oestradiol trigger for the LH surge (physiology): a preovulatory oestradiol rise sustained for roughly 60 hours switches feedback from negative to positive — pituitary responsiveness is absent at 36 hours and augmented by 60–84 hours at oestradiol levels around 130–190 pg/mL
question: In healthy women, what oestradiol concentration, sustained for how long, triggers the mid-cycle LH surge?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing (Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology; Boron and Boulpaep Medical Physiology): oestradiol feeds back negatively for most of the follicular phase, then — when its rise is high enough and sustained long enough — switches to positive feedback and triggers the mid-cycle LH surge; the textbooks' commonly quoted form of the rule (oestradiol above ~200 pg/mL sustained for ~50 hours) is the textbook's account, and the carded 1970s–80s human experiments are what the rule rests on. Liu and Yen 1983 gave the duration directly: incremental oestradiol sustained over 96 hours produced reproducible LH and FSH surges after latencies of 58 ± 6.9 hours (midfollicular women) and 68.2 ± 2.6 hours (hypogonadal women) — 'incremental E2 sustained for about 60 h constitutes the ovarian signal'. Keye and Jaffe 1975 isolated duration from concentration: at similar oestradiol levels (about 128–186 pg/mL), gonadotropin responses to GnRH were absent at 36 hours but augmented and prolonged at 60–132 hours. Young and Jaffe 1976 mapped the concentration axis, achieving mean oestradiol levels of 43–305 pg/mL across a sixfold dose range over 6 days. March 1979 showed an oestradiol rise mimicking the preovulatory peak was sufficient to trigger an LH surge (with progesterone timing deciding whether an FSH peak accompanied it), and Hoff and Yen 1983 timed the natural event: the surge follows about 50 hours of rising oestradiol and lasts 48 hours. The honest summary: concentration and duration are jointly the trigger — levels in the preovulatory range (roughly 150–300 pg/mL in these experiments) must be sustained for roughly 50–60 hours. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

title: Diet-induced thermogenesis by macronutrient (physiology): protein burns off roughly a fifth to a third of its energy as heat, carbohydrate roughly a twentieth to a tenth, and fat almost none — the ranking protein > carbohydrate > fat is consistent across calorimetry studies
question: In healthy humans, how much extra energy is burned as diet-induced thermogenesis after protein, carbohydrate and fat meals?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing (Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology): digesting, absorbing and storing a meal costs energy — diet-induced thermogenesis (DIT) — and the cost differs sharply by macronutrient. The exact percentages most often quoted (protein 20–30% of its energy, carbohydrate 5–10%, fat 0–3%) are the textbook/synthesis account, stated here as such; the carded records confirm the ranking and anchor the protein end directly. Westerterp's 2004 synthesis puts a mixed diet's DIT at 5–15% of daily energy expenditure with the oxidation hierarchy alcohol > protein > carbohydrate > fat reflected in thermogenesis. Tappy's programme measured infused amino acids at 21.1% of infused energy in lean subjects by indirect calorimetry. Johnston 2002 found postprandial thermogenesis about twofold higher (a relative comparison) on a high-protein than a high-carbohydrate low-fat diet day in 10 young women. Aita 2022 measured all three single-macronutrient-rich meals head-to-head over 2 hours: DIT was 6.44% of ingested energy after the protein meal, 3.49% after carbohydrate and 2.32% after fat — a truncated 2-hour window, so these are lower bounds on the full postprandial totals, with the ranking intact. The ICU-feeding calorimetry shelves ask different questions (energy targets in critical illness) and are not duplicated. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (ranking and approximate magnitudes concordant; exact percentages vary with dose, window and method).
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED

title: Altitude erythropoietin and haemoglobin mass (physiology): erythropoietin rises within about 1.5–2 hours of hypoxia and keeps climbing over the first days, while total haemoglobin mass follows slowly — up about 5% by 3–4 weeks, on a sigmoidal course that plateaus after about 3 weeks
question: In healthy humans, how do erythropoietin and total haemoglobin mass change over the first weeks at altitude?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing (Boron and Boulpaep Medical Physiology): hypoxia is sensed within hours, erythropoietin (EPO) rises first, reticulocytes follow, and total haemoglobin mass expands over weeks — a fast hormone signal driving a slow red-cell response, the textbook's account, which the carded human studies time precisely. Eckardt 1989 put volunteers in a decompression chamber: serum EPO was significantly elevated after 114 minutes at a simulated 3,000 m and 84 minutes at 4,000 m, rising continuously thereafter (16.0 to 22.5 mU/mL and 16.7 to 28.0 mU/mL over 5.5 hours), corresponding to 1.8-fold and 3.0-fold increases in calculated EPO production rate (relative increases); after hypoxia ended, EPO kept rising for about 1.5 hours then fell with a half-life of 5.2 hours. At real altitude the mass response is far slower: in 9 lowlanders spending 28 days at 3,454 m, haemoglobin mass (CO rebreathing, Lundby programme) rose 5.26% (a relative increase; range 2.5–11.1%), with individual increases delayed by up to 12 days, a maximal rate of 4.04 g/day reached at about day 15, and a plateau after about 3 weeks; on return to sea level it decayed at −2.46 g/day to baseline within 2 weeks (Siebenmann 2015). Klein 2021 independently found total haemoglobin up 4.7% after a 19-day sojourn at 3,450 m, back to baseline within 11 days of descent, with EPO and reticulocytes falling rapidly after descent and no evidence of neocytolysis. Early haemoconcentration at altitude is plasma-volume contraction, not new red cells — the two must not be confused, and this shelf is about the hormone and the mass, not ventilatory acclimatisation. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — based on a very small N = 27

title: Mazdutide (Innovent, China only) for obesity and type 2 diabetes: phase 3 trials show 10-17% weight loss and HbA1c falls up to 2.15% - a single Chinese programme, capped at POSSIBLE
question: In adults with obesity (with or without type 2 diabetes), does the dual glucagon/GLP-1 receptor agonist mazdutide, compared with placebo or standard care, produce clinically important weight loss and glycaemic improvement?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), single-programme cap. Mazdutide is a once-weekly dual glucagon receptor / GLP-1 receptor agonist developed by Innovent Biologics (the tested product is named here under the clarification exception: it is not FDA-approved and was approved only in China as of 2025). PREMISE CORRECTION: the slate question called mazdutide a 'dual GIP/GLP-1 agonist'; every fetched record describes a glucagon/GLP-1 dual agonist, and the pack question is worded accordingly. In obesity without diabetes (GLORY-1, 610 adults), weight fell 10.09% on 4 mg and 12.55% on 6 mg at week 32 against +0.45% on placebo; in more severe obesity (GLORY-2, 9 mg), weight fell 16.65% against 1.50% at week 60. In type 2 diabetes, mazdutide monotherapy lowered HbA1c by 1.57-2.15% against 0.14% on placebo (DREAMS-1), and beat dulaglutide 1.5 mg on both HbA1c (differences -0.24% and -0.30%) and weight (differences -3.78% and -5.76%) (DREAMS-2). Gastrointestinal adverse events are frequent (vomiting in 53.1% on the 9 mg dose in GLORY-2) but mostly mild to moderate, with low discontinuation rates. All four trials are Innovent's Chinese phase 3 programme: the effects are large and internally consistent, but generalisability beyond Chinese populations and long-term cardiovascular safety are untested, which is why the stamp stops at POSSIBLE.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) - single development programme (Innovent Biologics), every trial conducted in Chinese populations; four concordant phase 3 trials with large weight and HbA1c effects, capped at POSSIBLE because the programme is single-sponsor and single-country, the product was approved only in China as of 2025, and no cardiovascular-outcome trial exists

title: Macimorelin stimulation test for adult GH deficiency (test accuracy): sensitivity 87% and specificity 96% at the 2.8 ng/mL cut-off against the insulin tolerance test; 92% and 96% at 5.1 ng/mL
question: In adults being evaluated for growth hormone deficiency, how accurately does the oral macimorelin stimulation test, compared with the insulin tolerance test, diagnose adult GH deficiency?
balance: Test-accuracy question - stamped as such. The phase 3 crossover validation trial (Garcia 2018; NCT02558829) compared single-dose oral macimorelin with the insulin tolerance test (ITT) in people at high, intermediate and low likelihood of adult GH deficiency plus matched controls. At the prespecified cut-offs (2.8 ng/mL for macimorelin, 5.1 ng/mL for ITT), sensitivity was 87% and specificity 96%, with negative agreement 95.38% and positive agreement 74.32%; 99% of macimorelin tests were evaluable against 82% of ITTs, test-retest reproducibility was 97%, and no serious adverse events occurred. Post hoc analyses in the same trial, confirmed by the 2021 reanalysis, found that a 5.1 ng/mL macimorelin cut-off raises sensitivity to 92% while holding specificity at 96%. The earlier 2013 validation study (against arginine+GHRH, not the ITT) found sensitivity 82% and specificity 92% at a 2.7 ng/mL cut point. The evidence is one development programme with spectrum-enriched samples (known likelihood strata plus healthy controls), which tends to flatter accuracy; that is why the accuracy verdict is POSSIBLE rather than stronger.
stamp: POSSIBLE (diagnostic accuracy) - a test-accuracy verdict, not a treatment verdict: against the insulin tolerance test, macimorelin showed sensitivity 87% and specificity 96% at the approved 2.8 ng/mL cut-off, and sensitivity 92% with specificity 96% at a 5.1 ng/mL cut-off in post hoc analyses; evidence rests on one phase 3 validation programme, so accuracy is graded POSSIBLE

title: Prolactinoma: surgery-first versus dopamine-agonist-first (observational only, no RCT exists) - pooled cohorts find long-term remission off treatment of 67-88% after surgery against 34-52% after drug withdrawal
question: In patients with prolactinoma, does first-line transsphenoidal surgery, compared with first-line cabergoline (dopamine-agonist therapy), achieve comparable remission with better long-term treatment freedom?
balance: Observational evidence only - no randomised trial of surgery-first versus drug-first exists, and the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE and labelled observational. Three meta-analyses pooling non-randomised cohorts point the same way on the question that matters for this shelf - durable remission after treatment stops. The JCEM 2020 analysis (55 medical studies, 3,564 patients; 25 surgical studies, 1,836 patients) found long-term remission of 34% after dopamine-agonist withdrawal against 67% after surgery (microprolactinoma: 36% against 83%), while on-treatment biochemical control with dopamine agonists was 81% with side effects in 26%; surgery carried 0% mortality, 2% permanent diabetes insipidus and 3% cerebrospinal fluid leak. The microprolactinoma analysis (2021) adds the key nuance: while treatment continues, dopamine agonists remit more (96% vs 86% at 12 months or more), but after withdrawal surgery remits more (78% vs 44%). The 2018 analysis found long-term remission of 88% (surgery) against 52% (drugs). Selection bias runs through all of this - surgical series take smaller, non-invasive tumours - so the honest reading is: for suitably selected (especially micro-) prolactinomas, surgery-first offers comparable control and a genuinely better chance of long-term treatment freedom, unproven by randomisation.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) - observational evidence only (no randomised trial exists, and none of the carded reports is randomised): pooled cohort comparisons find higher long-term remission off treatment after first-line surgery than after dopamine-agonist withdrawal, capped at POSSIBLE and labelled observational

title: Thyroid hormone replacement in nonthyroidal illness: no survival benefit in the small old trials, and a 2024 septic-shock pilot split in opposite directions by subgroup - weak, mixed evidence
question: In critically ill patients with nonthyroidal illness, does thyroid hormone replacement (T4 or T3), compared with no replacement, improve survival or organ outcomes?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) - the base is small, old and scattered, and it is presented as weak/mixed, not settled. The only trial in the exact population (Brent & Hershman 1986) randomised just 23 intensive-care patients with severe nonthyroidal illness and low T4: mortality was 73% on T4 against 75% on control (the treatment made no difference), and T4 suppressed TSH and delayed the spontaneous T3 rise of recovery. Klemperer 1995 (142 high-risk bypass patients - an adjacent population whose preoperative T3 was normal) found T3 raised cardiac index (2.97 vs 2.67 L/min/m2) and lowered vascular resistance but changed neither drug requirements nor mortality/morbidity. The 2024 Kovacevic pilots in septic shock with euthyroid sick syndrome split in opposite directions: in the low-T3 subgroup, 28-day mortality was higher on T3 (75% vs 33.3%; P=0.004), while in the low-T3/low-T4 subgroup ICU mortality was lower on T3 (25% vs 52.1%; P=0.039). Two small subgroups pointing opposite ways, on top of null older trials, support no routine replacement - and counsel caution rather than enthusiasm.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) - small, old, scattered trials: T4 did not change mortality in the one direct ICU trial (73% vs 75%), T3 improved haemodynamics but not outcomes after bypass surgery, and the 2024 septic-shock pilots gave opposite mortality signals in their two subgroups; no survival benefit is established

title: Amiloride as the fourth drug for resistant hypertension: noninferior to spironolactone in the SPARE randomised trial (home SBP -13.6 vs -14.7 mm Hg) and equal in the PATHWAY-2 runout (-20.4 vs -18.3 mm Hg clinic SBP)
question: In adults with resistant hypertension still uncontrolled on a thiazide-like diuretic, ACE inhibitor/ARB and calcium-channel blocker, is amiloride an effective fourth-line agent, and how does it compare with spironolactone?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). PREMISE VERIFIED this session: the home shelves #278 (the fourth drug for resistant hypertension) and #1559 (ReHOT) were read in full in the live ask-index - the word 'amiloride' appears in neither, so this slice is genuinely uncovered; the only other amiloride pack in the tree (#5636) concerns lithium-induced diabetes insipidus, a different question. The evidence: in the PATHWAY-2 mechanisms substudies, amiloride 10 mg in the optional open-label runout (146 patients) lowered clinic systolic pressure by 20.4 mm Hg against 18.3 mm Hg for spironolactone 25 mg. The SPARE trial (JAMA 2025; 118 Korean patients on fixed-dose triple therapy) is the first randomised head-to-head: home systolic pressure fell 13.6 mm Hg on amiloride against 14.7 mm Hg on spironolactone (difference -0.68 mm Hg, 90% CI -3.50 to 2.14), meeting the prespecified noninferiority margin, with one hyperkalaemia discontinuation on amiloride and no gynaecomastia in either arm. A 2025 review of the whole amiloride record reaches the same conclusion and notes amiloride's effect was consistent across renin and aldosterone levels, unlike spironolactone's. Amiloride is therefore a credible fourth-line alternative when spironolactone is not tolerated - on blood-pressure evidence only; neither trial measures clinical outcomes.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) - amiloride lowered blood pressure as much as spironolactone in the one head-to-head randomised trial (SPARE, noninferiority met) and in the PATHWAY-2 open-label runout; capped at POSSIBLE because the direct randomised comparison is a single 118-patient trial and the PATHWAY-2 amiloride data are open-label

title: Anakinra for acute myocarditis (ARAMIS): one small randomised trial (120 planned) - safe, but it did not reduce early complications; the results record prints no figures, flagged on the face
question: In adults with acute myocarditis, does anakinra, compared with standard care, reduce early complications?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) - single small trial, with an explicit reporting flag. PREMISE VERIFIED: home pack #3062 (immunosuppression in myocarditis - TIMIC/Mason/IMAC) was read in full; neither 'anakinra' nor 'ARAMIS' (myocarditis) appears in it, and the ARAMIS name-hits elsewhere in the tree are unrelated trials (a prostate-cancer ARAMIS and a stroke ARAMIS). ARAMIS randomised patients with cardiac-MRI-proven acute myocarditis to anakinra 100 mg daily during hospitalisation or placebo, on top of standard care; its primary endpoint was days alive free of myocarditis complications to 28 days after discharge. The trial's results report (European Heart Journal - Acute Cardiovascular Care 2023) is a two-page in-perspective piece whose PubMed record carries NO abstract and NO figures - so no per-arm numbers can be carded from the record, and this shelf does not invent any. The 2026 cardioimmunology review of the IL-1 pathway characterises ARAMIS plainly: it 'did not improve outcomes in a largely low-risk cohort', while suggesting any future role lies in fulminant or hyperinflammatory presentations supported only by case reports and small series (not carded here). On the evidence that can be verified from the records, anakinra in unselected acute myocarditis is safe and without demonstrated benefit.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) - single-trial cap: the one randomised trial (ARAMIS, 120 patients planned) found anakinra safe but without benefit on early complications, as characterised by its results report and a 2026 review; total evidence base is this single small trial, and the results record carries no abstract or figures (flagged)

title: PCSK9 inhibition started immediately after acute MI: PACMAN-AMI and HUYGENS show greater plaque regression and fibrous-cap thickening in non-culprit arteries at one year (imaging surrogates; GLAGOV stable-disease comparator agrees)
question: In patients started on a PCSK9 inhibitor immediately after acute myocardial infarction, does early intensive LDL lowering, compared with statin alone, regress and stabilise non-culprit plaque on intracoronary imaging?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) on imaging surrogates. PREMISE NOTE: the slate named home #45 for this slice; the live #45 in the ask-index is a type 2 diabetes plaque/icosapent-ethyl shelf, not a PCSK9 imaging shelf - but the substantive check holds either way: 'PACMAN-AMI', 'HUYGENS' and 'GLAGOV' return zero hits across the live index and the built packs, so the early post-MI PCSK9 imaging slice is genuinely uncovered. HUYGENS (161 treated NSTEMI patients; evolocumab monthly) found minimum fibrous cap thickness rose 42.7 against 21.5 micrometres, with greater lipid-arc reduction and percent atheroma volume regression (-2.29% vs -0.61%). GLAGOV, the stable-disease comparator (968 patients, evolocumab), found the same direction on percent atheroma volume (-0.95% vs +0.05%). title: Alirocumab in children and adolescents with heterozygous FH: LDL fell 43.3% (every-2-weeks) and 33.8% (every-4-weeks) more than placebo at 24 weeks in the phase 3 trial - a single programme, capped at POSSIBLE
question: In children and adolescents with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia, does alirocumab, compared with placebo on background statin, lower LDL cholesterol safely?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), single-programme cap. PREMISE VERIFIED: home #1415 is the evolocumab HAUSER-RCT shelf in paediatric heterozygous FH - a different antibody; the tree's other alirocumab packs concern adults (limb events, FH event extrapolation). The alirocumab paediatric programme: ODYSSEY KIDS (phase 2, 42 children aged 8-17) found the higher-dose cohorts lowered LDL cholesterol by 45-46% at week 8. The phase 3 trial (Santos 2024; 153 children aged 8-17 with LDL at least 130 mg/dL on statins or other lipid therapy) found least-squares mean LDL differences against placebo of -43.3% (every-2-weeks dosing) and -33.8% (every-4-weeks dosing) at week 24 (both P<.001), with no significant difference in adverse-event incidence and two discontinuations for adverse events on alirocumab. A 2024 meta-analysis pooling the paediatric PCSK9 trials (320 children in 3 RCTs, evolocumab and alirocumab together) found a weighted mean LDL difference of -37.92% and general tolerability. LDL is a surrogate - appropriately so in FH, where lifetime exposure is the disease mechanism - but long-term paediatric safety beyond the trial horizons is unproven, hence POSSIBLE.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) - single development programme for alirocumab in paediatric heterozygous FH (one phase 2 dose-finding study and one phase 3 trial, with a pooled meta-analysis in support): large LDL reductions against placebo on background statin and no short-term safety signal, capped at POSSIBLE because the programme is single-sponsor and follow-up is short

title: Apixaban versus warfarin in AF on haemodialysis (RENAL-AF): the one randomised trial stopped early at 154 patients - bleeding 32% vs 26% at one year (HR 1.20, wide interval), stroke 3.0% vs 3.3%; underpowered, so the verdict is MAYBE (weak evidence)
question: In patients with atrial fibrillation on maintenance haemodialysis, does apixaban, compared with warfarin, reduce bleeding without increasing thromboembolism?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence). PREMISE VERIFIED with a precedent-(a) call: home #1743 is AXADIA-AFNET 8 (apixaban vs phenprocoumon, a different vitamin K antagonist, in German dialysis practice). The #1743 pack mentions RENAL-AF only as fenced, uncarded context - its own text says no primary journal report of RENAL-AF 'could be pinned in this build, so it is fenced here by name without figures'. Fenced context is not carding (precedent a), and the RENAL-AF primary report (Circulation 2022; NCT02942407) is free in the gate file, so this shelf cards it directly. RENAL-AF randomised 154 patients and stopped early for enrolment failure: one-year major or clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding was 32% on apixaban against 26% on warfarin (HR 1.20, 95% CI 0.63 to 2.30 - a relative measure whose interval spans halving to doubling), stroke or systemic embolism 3.0% against 3.3%, and death - the commonest major event - 26% against 18%. Warfarin time in therapeutic range was only 44%. The large USRDS observational study (25,523 patients) found no difference in stroke/systemic embolism (HR 0.88) but less major bleeding with apixaban (HR 0.72) - hypothesis-consistent, not decisive. A 2024 review of all six studies (both trials plus four observational) likewise settles nothing. Neither 'apixaban reduces bleeding' nor 'it is equivalent' is earned by this base.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) - the one randomised trial (RENAL-AF, n=154) stopped early and was underpowered, with a bleeding hazard ratio of 1.20 (95% CI 0.63 to 2.30, relative) that excludes neither benefit nor harm; large observational data suggest less major bleeding with apixaban (HR 0.72, relative) but cannot settle a comparison the trial left open

title: Adding aliskiren to ACE inhibitor/ARB therapy: ALTITUDE (8,561 patients) found no outcome benefit and more hyperkalaemia and hypotension - surrogate trials (AVOID, ALOFT) improved markers only
question: In patients with type 2 diabetes and albuminuric kidney disease (or heart failure), does adding aliskiren to ACE inhibitor/ARB therapy, compared with ACE inhibitor/ARB alone, improve cardiovascular or renal outcomes or cause net harm?
balance: LIKELY (no benefit, with harm). The programme tells one coherent story in three acts. AVOID (2008; 599 patients with diabetic nephropathy) showed the surrogate promise: adding aliskiren to losartan reduced the urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio by a further 20% (a relative reduction) at 6 months. ALOFT (2008; 302 heart-failure patients) showed the same pattern on natriuretic peptides: NT-proBNP fell on aliskiren while rising on placebo (P=0.0106), with no clinically important blood-pressure or biochemistry differences. Then ALTITUDE (2012; 8,561 patients with type 2 diabetes and kidney disease, cardiovascular disease, or both) tested outcomes - and was stopped early: the primary cardiorenal composite occurred in 18.3% on aliskiren against 17.1% on placebo (HR 1.08, 95% CI 0.98 to 1.20; P=0.12 - the treatment made no difference), while hyperkalaemia (potassium at least 6 mmol/L, i.e. 6 mEq/L) affected 11.2% against 7.2% and reported hypotension 12.1% against 8.3% (both P<0.001). The trial's own conclusion: adding aliskiren to renin-angiotensin blockade in high-risk diabetes 'is not supported by these data and may even be harmful'. Surrogate gains did not survive contact with outcomes; the stamp is LIKELY because the outcomes trial is large, definitive in direction, and concordant with the harm pattern.
stamp: LIKELY (no benefit, with harm) - the large ALTITUDE outcomes trial found the treatment made no difference to cardiovascular or renal outcomes (primary endpoint 18.3% vs 17.1%; HR 1.08, 95% CI 0.98 to 1.20 - a relative measure) and significantly more hyperkalaemia and hypotension; the smaller AVOID and ALOFT trials improved surrogate markers only, so the overall verdict is no outcome benefit with net harm signals

title: Mipomersen in homozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia: LDL down by about a quarter, with injection-site reactions in 76% and a hepatic cost
question: In patients with homozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia on maximal lipid-lowering therapy, does mipomersen, compared with placebo, lower LDL cholesterol, and at what hepatic/injection-site cost?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single programme, one small HoFH trial. Raal 2010 randomised 51 HoFH patients on maximal therapy: LDL cholesterol −24.7% on mipomersen versus −3.3% on placebo at 26 weeks, with injection-site reactions in 76% versus 24% and ALT ≥3× the upper limit of normal in 12% versus none. The programme's severe-hypercholesterolaemia trial (McGowan 2012) and HeFH trial (Stein 2012, which measured a median +4.9% hepatic fat on MRI) are concordant on both efficacy and hepatic cost, and are flagged on their faces as neighbouring populations. No cardiovascular-outcome data exist. HoFH homes for lomitapide (#1568) and evinacumab (#1106) do not cover mipomersen — desk-checked this session.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — randomised phase 3 evidence in HoFH from a single programme (one 51-patient trial), with concordant LDL lowering in the programme's severe-hypercholesterolaemia and HeFH trials; the cost is injection-site reactions in about three quarters of patients, flu-like symptoms, transaminase rises and increased hepatic fat

title: Asfotase alfa in hypophosphatasia: survival 95% versus 42% at 1 year against historical controls — single-arm evidence in very small cohorts
question: In people with hypophosphatasia, does asfotase alfa, compared with supportive care/historical natural history, improve survival, respiratory function and skeletal mineralisation?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — an evidence question resting on single-arm studies against historical natural history, with small-N labelling throughout. Survival in perinatal/infantile disease was 95% versus 42% at 1 year and 84% versus 27% at 5 years against historical controls (Whyte 2016), rickets healed in 9 of the first 11 treated infants (Whyte 2012, where the product is published as ENB-0040), and older children gained sustained function over 5 years (JCI Insight 2016). The one randomised study (19 adolescents/adults) is a dose comparison with a biochemical co-primary endpoint. Effect sizes are large, but every comparison is historical or within-cohort.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single-arm evidence against historical controls, small N (11 infants in the founding study; 37 treated in the survival comparison; 12 children aged 6–12; one 19-patient randomised dose study in adolescents/adults); no placebo-controlled trial exists in the severe paediatric disease

title: Sodium thiosulfate for calciphylaxis: lesions often improve in uncontrolled series, but the comparative meta-analysis found no difference in healing or survival
question: In patients with calciphylaxis, does intravenous sodium thiosulfate, compared with standard wound/dialysis care, improve lesion healing or survival?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — observational only, capped and labelled. Uncontrolled series (Noureddine 2011, n=14; Nigwekar 2013, n=172 treated) report pain and lesion improvement in roughly 70% of patients, with one-year mortality still 35%. The only comparative evidence — a 2023 meta-analysis of 19 retrospective cohorts (422 patients) — found no difference in lesion improvement (risk ratio 1.23, 95% CI 0.85–1.78) or death (risk ratio 0.88, 0.70–1.10) with intravenous thiosulfate, and the apparent benefit shrank in more recent studies. Peritoneal-dialysis evidence is 30 case-literature patients. No RCT exists.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — observational evidence only: uncontrolled series report lesion improvement in most treated patients, but the comparative cohort meta-analysis found no difference in lesion improvement or survival (the treatment made no difference in the comparative data); no randomised trial exists

title: Adjuvant mitotane after resection of low-to-intermediate-risk adrenocortical carcinoma: ADIUVO found no significant benefit (79% vs 75% recurrence-free at 5 years)
question: In patients with resected adrenocortical carcinoma at low-to-intermediate recurrence risk, does adjuvant mitotane, compared with surveillance alone, prolong recurrence-free survival?
balance: SPLIT. The direct randomised evidence (ADIUVO, n=91, stopped early for slow recruitment) found 5-year recurrence-free survival of 79% on adjuvant mitotane versus 75% on surveillance (HR 0.74, 95% CI 0.30–1.85), with adverse events in all treated patients and 19% discontinuing. The retrospective literature behind the practice splits: Terzolo 2007 (n=177, broader risk) found median recurrence-free survival of 42 versus 10/25 months favouring mitotane, while the US 13-institution series (n=207) found no independent association after adjustment. ADIUVO's wide interval means benefit is not excluded — it is undemonstrated in this risk group.
stamp: SPLIT — in the low-to-intermediate-risk group itself, the one randomised trial (ADIUVO, 91 patients, stopped early) found no significant recurrence-free-survival difference (the treatment made no difference: 79% vs 75% at 5 years, HR 0.74, 95% CI 0.30–1.85); the older retrospective series in broader-risk patients conflict — one found much longer recurrence-free survival with mitotane, one found no independent association after adjustment

title: Pioglitazone versus sulfonylureas on metformin (TOSCA.IT): cardiovascular events identical at 1.5 per 100 person-years (HR 0.96) — less hypoglycaemia, no event benefit
question: In patients with type 2 diabetes and established cardiovascular disease or high risk, does pioglitazone, compared with sulfonylureas added to metformin, reduce cardiovascular events?
balance: POSSIBLE (no difference found). TOSCA.IT randomised 3,028 people with type 2 diabetes on metformin to add-on pioglitazone or a sulfonylurea (mostly glimepiride/gliclazide) and was stopped early for futility: the primary cardiovascular composite occurred at 1.5 per 100 person-years in both groups (HR 0.96, 95% CI 0.74–1.26). Pioglitazone caused far less hypoglycaemia (10% vs 34%) and no significant excess of heart failure, bladder cancer or fractures in the trial. Two smaller head-to-head imaging trials (PERISCOPE, CHICAGO) favoured pioglitazone on plaque progression — surrogates that did not convert into events. PREMISE NOTE: TOSCA.IT enrolled metformin-treated patients of whom only 11% had prior cardiovascular events, so it is a high-risk primary/secondary-prevention mix rather than a pure established-CVD cohort.
stamp: POSSIBLE (no difference found) — TOSCA.IT (3,028 patients, stopped early for futility) found cardiovascular events in 1.5 per 100 person-years on both pioglitazone and sulfonylureas (HR 0.96; the treatment made no difference to cardiovascular events), although pioglitazone slowed atherosclerosis progression in two smaller imaging trials and caused far less hypoglycaemia (10% vs 34%)

title: Natriuretic-peptide screening to prevent heart failure: STOP-HF cut LV dysfunction/HF to 5.3% vs 8.7%, and PONTIAC cut cardiac events in NT-proBNP-selected diabetes
question: In asymptomatic adults at risk of heart failure (including diabetes), does natriuretic-peptide-guided screening with collaborative care/treatment intensification, compared with usual care, prevent LV dysfunction and incident HF?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a screening-strategy shelf, stamped as such. STOP-HF (n=1,374): BNP screening plus collaborative care reduced LV dysfunction with or without heart failure to 5.3% versus 8.7% (OR 0.55) and emergency cardiovascular hospitalisation rates (rate ratio 0.60), though heart failure alone (1.0% vs 2.1%) was not significant. PONTIAC (n=300, diabetes, NT-proBNP >125 pg/mL): intensified RAS-antagonist/beta-blocker up-titration reduced cardiac hospitalisation/death (HR 0.351). PARABLE is carded, flagged as a downstream-treatment trial rather than screening evidence. Each strategy has been tested once — hence POSSIBLE, not LIKELY.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — screening-strategy question: two randomised strategy trials (STOP-HF, 1,374 at-risk adults; PONTIAC, 300 people with diabetes selected by NT-proBNP) both reduced prevention endpoints, but each is a single programme, the interventions bundle the test with intensified care, and the heart-failure component of STOP-HF alone was not significant

title: Fructosamine and glycated albumin when HbA1c is unreliable: they predict complications like HbA1c (ARIC), but in severe CKD they tracked glucose no better than HbA1c
question: In patients in whom HbA1c is unreliable (haemoglobin variants, anaemia, pregnancy, advanced CKD), do fructosamine or glycated albumin accurately reflect glycaemic control and predict complications compared with HbA1c and glucose measures?
balance: POSSIBLE — an evidence (test-accuracy/prognosis) shelf built on the three free ARIC reports. Prognosis: fructosamine and glycated albumin predict incident diabetes, retinopathy, CKD, cardiovascular events and death with strength comparable to HbA1c (Selvin 2014, 2015). Accuracy where it matters most: in severe/very severe CKD, correlations with fasting glucose were 0.39–0.41 for the alternative markers versus 0.48–0.52 for HbA1c (Jung 2018) — no advantage. FLAG: the dialysis slice is already homed at built shelf #2896; its PMIDs are kept out of this pack's card source lines and the free dialysis cohort was not carded, per the one-home rule (see Synthesis). No carded evidence covers haemoglobin variants or pregnancy.
stamp: POSSIBLE — test-accuracy/prognosis question (observational cohorts): fructosamine and glycated albumin predict diabetes complications about as strongly as HbA1c in ARIC, but in severe CKD neither marker tracked fasting glucose better than HbA1c, so the 'use when HbA1c is unreliable' premise is only partly supported; the dialysis prognosis slice is homed at shelf #2896 and is cross-pointed, not re-carded

title: The 10 g monofilament and future foot ulcers: insensitivity roughly doubles ulcer risk (RR 1.8–2.2; pooled OR 3.18) — a moderate-risk marker, not an interval-setter
question: In people with diabetes, does loss of protective sensation on the 10 g monofilament test predict future foot ulceration and amputation well enough to guide screening intervals?
balance: POSSIBLE — a prognosis/evidence shelf, observational throughout. Prospective cohorts agree: monofilament insensitivity predicts new ulceration with relative risks of 1.80 (Abbott 2002, 9,710 community patients) and 2.2 (Boyko 1999, 749 veterans), and the PODUS individual-patient meta-analysis (>16,000 people) gives a pooled OR of 3.184. The same evidence ranks it a moderate-risk marker below ulcer history (OR 6.589), and no carded study tests screening intervals. PREMISE CORRECTION: the slate's Perkins 2001 anchor is diagnostic accuracy against nerve conduction, not ulcer prognosis — fetched, checked, and not carded (see Synthesis).
stamp: POSSIBLE — prognosis question (observational cohorts): inability to feel the 10 g monofilament consistently predicts future foot ulceration (relative risks 1.80–2.2 in prospective cohorts; pooled individual-patient OR 3.18, a relative measure), placing patients in a moderate-risk stratum — but previous ulceration predicts far more strongly, amputation prediction is thinner, and no study has tested screening intervals

title: Hydrochlorothiazide and skin cancer: cumulative dose tracks squamous-cell carcinoma in Danish registries (OR 3.98 at ≥50,000 mg; 7.38 at ≥200,000 mg) — not seen in Taiwan
question: In people taking hydrochlorothiazide, is cumulative thiazide exposure associated with increased risk of cutaneous squamous-cell carcinoma and other skin cancers?
balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — observational, capped and labelled. The Danish nationwide programme (Pedersen 2018; Pottegård 2017; Pedersen 2019) shows a specific, monotone cumulative-dose association: SCC odds ratio 3.98 at ≥50,000 mg and 7.38 at ≥200,000 mg, lip SCC 7.7 at ≥100,000 mg, with no signal for other antihypertensives. The counterweight is a nationwide Taiwanese study with no association for any skin cancer at high cumulative use — one evidence stream, one population, no sun-exposure adjustment anywhere. All measures are relative; absolute SCC risk remains low.
stamp: POSSIBLE (harm) — observational evidence only: Danish nationwide case-control studies show a strong cumulative-dose relationship for cutaneous squamous-cell carcinoma (OR 3.98 at ≥50,000 mg and 7.38 at ≥200,000 mg — relative measures), but a nationwide Taiwanese study found no association, so the signal may depend on population and sun exposure; absolute excess is small

title: Atypical femoral fracture on bisphosphonates: 1.78 per 100,000/year early, 113.1 per 100,000/year at 8–10 years, falling rapidly after stopping
question: In long-term bisphosphonate users, what is the absolute risk of atypical femoral fracture, how does it change with treatment duration, and how quickly does it fall after stopping?
balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — a risk-quantification shelf, observational throughout, with absolutes on the face as commissioned. Incidence by duration (Dell 2012, Kaiser): 1.78 per 100,000/year at 0.1–1.9 years of use, rising to 113.1 per 100,000/year at 8–9.9 years. Black 2020 (196,129 women, 277 events) gives adjusted hazards of 8.86 (3–<5 years) and 43.51 (8+ years) versus <3 months and a rapid fall after discontinuation. The independent Danish case-cohort (Bauer 2024) concurs: HR 7.29 for 5–7 years versus <1 year, quick fall after stopping, 5-year NNH 1,424 against NNT 56 to prevent one hip fracture.
stamp: POSSIBLE (harm) — observational evidence only, but large and concordant on absolutes: atypical femoral fracture incidence rises from about 1.8 per 100,000/year with under 2 years of bisphosphonate use to about 113 per 100,000/year at 8–10 years (Dell 2012), and risk falls rapidly after stopping (Black 2020; Danish case-cohort 2024, 5-year NNH 1,424 vs NNT 56 for hip-fracture prevention)

title: Liraglutide in advanced HFrEF: no improvement in clinical stability in FIGHT (n=300) and no LV-function benefit with more serious cardiac events in LIVE (n=241) — two concordant cautionary trials
question: In patients with advanced heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, does GLP-1 receptor agonist therapy (liraglutide), compared with placebo, improve clinical stability or cause harm?
balance: POSSIBLE (harm) / no benefit, from the only two dedicated randomised trials of a GLP-1 receptor agonist in reduced-ejection-fraction heart failure. FIGHT (Margulies 2016; n=300 recently hospitalised patients, median LVEF 25%) found no effect of liraglutide on its primary global-rank endpoint of clinical stability (mean rank 146 vs 156, P=0.31), with numerically more deaths (19 [12%] vs 16 [11%]; HR 1.10, 95% CI 0.57 to 2.14) and heart-failure rehospitalisations (63 [41%] vs 50 [34%]; HR 1.30, 0.89 to 1.88) — neither excess significant, both pointing the wrong way. LIVE (Jorsal 2017; n=241 stable patients, LVEF ≤45%) found no difference in LVEF change (mean difference −0.8%, P=0.24), a 7 b.p.m. heart-rate increase, and significantly more serious cardiac events on liraglutide (12 [10%] vs 3 [3%], P=0.04). Against these, one 32-patient three-arm pilot (Arturi 2017) reported an ejection-fraction rise on liraglutide; at that size it cannot outweigh 541 patients in the two placebo-controlled trials, and it is carded so the shelf shows the whole base. This shelf is distinct from the library's GLP-1 shelves in obesity-phenotype HFpEF, where the population and the results differ. Desk-check: home corpus mentions of liraglutide in heart failure are incidental outcome-trial subgroups; FIGHT and LIVE had no shelf.
stamp: POSSIBLE (harm) — liraglutide made no difference to post-hospitalisation clinical stability in FIGHT (the treatment made no difference on the primary global-rank endpoint, P=0.31) with numerically more deaths (12% vs 11%) and heart-failure rehospitalisations (41% vs 34%), and did not improve ejection fraction in LIVE (the treatment made no difference, P=0.24) while serious cardiac events were more frequent (10% vs 3%, P=0.04); neither difference in hard events was itself statistically conclusive, so the honest reading is no benefit with a possible harm signal

title: Vericiguat in HFpEF: no improvement in quality of life or walking distance in VITALITY-HFpEF (n=789) — the treatment made no difference
question: In patients with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, does vericiguat, compared with placebo, improve quality of life or exercise capacity?
balance: No benefit demonstrated. VITALITY-HFpEF (Armstrong 2020; n=789 with recent decompensation) was built exactly on this shelf's question — its primary endpoint was the Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire physical limitation score — and vericiguat at both 15 mg/day and 10 mg/day made no difference to that score or to 6-minute walking distance at 24 weeks (all differences near zero, numerically favouring placebo). The phase 2b SOCRATES-PRESERVED dose-finding trial (Pieske 2017; n=477) was also neutral on its primary endpoints (NT-proBNP and left atrial volume at 12 weeks); an exploratory quality-of-life signal in its 10 mg arm was the stated rationale for VITALITY's higher doses, and VITALITY did not confirm it. A VITALITY frailty analysis (Butler 2023) adds that vericiguat did not alter frailty status. Symptomatic hypotension was somewhat more frequent on vericiguat (6.4% at 15 mg vs 3.4% on placebo). Desk-check: home #970 covers vericiguat in HFrEF (VICTORIA and VICTOR) and was read — VITALITY-HFpEF is not carded there; the HFpEF slice was genuinely uncovered. Nothing here contradicts #970: the drug's modest post-worsening HFrEF signal does not extend to quality of life or exercise capacity in HFpEF.
stamp: NO BENEFIT (the treatment made no difference) — in VITALITY-HFpEF (n=789), vericiguat 15 mg and 10 mg did not improve the KCCQ physical limitation score versus placebo (least-squares mean differences −1.5 and −0.5 points) or 6-minute walking distance (−5.5 m and −1.8 m) at 24 weeks; the earlier dose-finding SOCRATES-PRESERVED trial was likewise neutral on NT-proBNP and left atrial volume

title: AlloMap gene-expression profiling after heart transplant: IMAGE showed a non-inferior composite outcome with biopsies cut from 3.0 to 0.5 per person-year
question: In heart-transplant recipients, does gene-expression profiling (AlloMap) surveillance, compared with routine endomyocardial biopsy, safely reduce biopsies without increasing rejection or graft loss?
balance: LIKELY for the strategy as tested — in selected recipients more than 6 months post-transplant at low rejection risk. The named test, per the clarification exception, is the AlloMap peripheral-blood gene-expression profiling test as published in the IMAGE trial (Pham 2010, NEJM; n=602 randomised): the 2-year composite outcome was 14.5% on profiling-guided surveillance vs 15.3% on routine biopsy (HR 1.04, 95% CI 0.67 to 1.68; non-inferior), deaths were similar (6.3% vs 5.5%), and biopsies fell six-fold (0.5 vs 3.0 per person-year, P<0.001). The Outcomes AlloMap Registry (Khush 2019; n=1,504 prospective, multicentre) found the strategy performing concordantly outside the trial — moderate-to-severe cellular rejection prevalence ~2%, 5-year survival 94%, low composite event rates. An IMAGE cohort analysis (Kobashigawa 2014) adds prognostic texture: within-patient variability of profiling scores predicted future events (HR 1.76 per unit of variability) even though single scores did not. Limits printed on the face: IMAGE enrolled patients 6 months to 5 years post-transplant judged low-risk — the result does not cover the early high-risk period or antibody-mediated rejection surveillance.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit, for the surveillance strategy in selected low-risk recipients) — in the IMAGE randomised trial (n=602), gene-expression profiling surveillance was non-inferior to routine biopsy for the composite of rejection with haemodynamic compromise, graft dysfunction, death or retransplantation (2-year rates 14.5% vs 15.3%; HR 1.04, 95% CI 0.67 to 1.68) while biopsies fell from 3.0 to 0.5 per person-year (P<0.001); a 1,504-patient prospective registry found concordantly low rejection and event rates in real-world use

title: Teriparatide in men with osteoporosis: spine BMD rose 5.9% (20 µg) and 9.0% (40 µg) in 437 men; vertebral fractures fell by about half in follow-up, with moderate/severe fractures down 83%
question: In men with osteoporosis at high fracture risk, does teriparatide, compared with placebo, increase bone mineral density and reduce vertebral fractures?
balance: BMD benefit is consistent across both men's trials; the fracture evidence is one follow-up analysis and is graded POSSIBLE accordingly. Orwoll 2003 randomised 437 men with spine or hip BMD more than 2 SD below the young-adult male mean to placebo, teriparatide 20 µg or 40 µg daily; the trial was stopped at a median 11 months because of osteosarcomas in rat toxicology studies, yet spine BMD had already risen 5.9% and 9.0% (P<0.001 vs placebo for both) and femoral-neck BMD 1.5% and 2.9%. Kaufman 2005 followed 355 of those men for 30 months post-treatment (42 months total): incident vertebral fractures in the radiographed subset were 11.7% (placebo) vs 5.4% (20 µg) and 6.0% (40 µg) — a 51% relative risk reduction for combined teriparatide that did not reach significance (P=0.07), while moderate/severe fractures were significantly reduced by 83% (P=0.01, relative). The smaller independent Kurland 2000 trial (23 men with idiopathic osteoporosis, PTH(1-34) 400 IU/day as published) found a 13.5% lumbar-spine BMD gain vs no change on placebo (P<0.001), directionally concordant. Desk-check: the library's teriparatide shelves rest on the postmenopausal-women trials; the men question was unhomed (male-osteoporosis shelves cover other agents).
stamp: LIKELY (benefit, for BMD) / POSSIBLE (benefit, for vertebral fractures) — in the 437-man placebo-controlled trial, teriparatide raised spine BMD by 5.9% (20 µg) and 9.0% (40 µg) over a median 11 months (P<0.001 vs placebo for both); in the 42-month treatment-plus-follow-up report, incident vertebral fractures were 5.4–6.0% on teriparatide vs 11.7% on placebo (combined relative risk reduction 51%, P=0.07 — a relative measure) with moderate/severe fractures reduced by 83% (P=0.01)
