title: Semaglutide and NAION: a contested observational signal — relative risks of ~2–8 in referral and registry cohorts, but absolute excesses of only ~0.02–0.05 percentage points per year in population data
question: In people prescribed semaglutide (and other GLP-1 receptor agonists), is there an increased risk of nonarteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy (NAION), and how large is the absolute excess?
balance: POSSIBLE (harm), observational only, with the absolute framing leading. The signal began with Hathaway 2024 (JAMA Ophthalmology): in a single academic centre's neuro-ophthalmology referral registry, 36-month cumulative NAION incidence was 8.9% on semaglutide vs 1.8% on non-GLP-1 drugs in type 2 diabetes (HR 4.28, 95% CI 1.62 to 11.29) and 6.7% vs 0.8% in overweight/obesity (HR 7.64, 2.21 to 26.36) — percentages that reflect a referral population already enriched for optic-nerve disease, not ordinary prescribing. Two much larger active-comparator studies found smaller relative effects and tiny absolutes: a three-database claims target-trial emulation (~482,912 matched pairs, GLP-1 RA vs SGLT2 inhibitor initiators) found HR 1.85 (1.51 to 2.27) with a rate difference of 0.29 per 1,000 person-years; the Swedish nationwide cohort found AION risks of 0.04% vs 0.02% at 1 year (RD 0.02%) and 0.12% vs 0.07% at 5 years (RD 0.05%), attenuating to RR ~1.2–1.4 and RD ~0.01–0.02% when restricted to metformin users — the authors themselves raise residual confounding by diabetes severity. Per the slate, regulators have weighed in (EMA PRAC, June 2025, classing NAION as very rare; an FDA class review in November 2026) — those reviews are context for this shelf, not carded evidence; the carded base is the three observational studies above. Causality is not established; diabetes itself is a NAION risk factor and no randomised trial can realistically be powered for an event this rare.
stamp: POSSIBLE (harm, observational) — three observational designs point the same relative direction (HR 4.28 and 7.64 in a single-centre neuro-ophthalmology referral cohort; HR 1.85 vs SGLT2 inhibitors in a ~966,000-patient claims target-trial emulation; RR 1.93 at 1 year in a Swedish nationwide cohort), but absolute risks are very small in population data (risk difference 0.02% at 1 year and 0.05% at 5 years in Sweden; rate difference 0.29 per 1,000 person-years in the claims study) and the Swedish signal attenuated substantially when restricted to metformin users, leaving residual confounding a live alternative explanation; no randomised evidence exists

title: Low ankle-brachial index in asymptomatic adults: about double the 10-year event rates within every Framingham category in 48,294 people — but later reviews judge the added reclassification small
question: In asymptomatic adults, does a low ankle-brachial index predict cardiovascular events and mortality independently of traditional risk scores, and does adding it reclassify risk usefully?
balance: Two different claims, two different grades. The prognostic claim is strong: the Ankle Brachial Index Collaboration (Fowkes 2008) pooled individual data from 16 population cohorts (24,955 men, 23,339 women; 480,325 person-years) and found 10-year cardiovascular mortality of 18.7% in men with ABI ≤0.90 vs 4.4% with normal ABI (HR 4.2), and 12.6% vs 4.1% in women (HR 3.5), remaining ~2.9–3.0 after Framingham adjustment; a low ABI approximately doubled event rates within every Framingham risk category. The reclassification claim is weaker in later, bias-aware hands: the collaboration reported that adding ABI would change the risk category and treatment recommendations of ~19% of men and ~36% of women, but the USPSTF reviews (Lin 2013; Guirguis-Blake 2018) found the corrected net reclassification improvement was probably small, the largest discrimination gains were for ABI in women (C-statistic change 0.112, NRI 0.096 across 10 studies), and no adequately powered trial has tested whether ABI-guided management improves health outcomes — the one large treatment trial in screen-detected low ABI (aspirin, n=3,350) showed no event prevention and possible bleeding harm. This shelf is about ABI as a prognostic test in asymptomatic adults; it is distinct from coronary artery calcium scoring (pack #6049) and from the symptomatic peripheral-artery-disease treatment shelves.
stamp: LIKELY (prognostic association) / POSSIBLE (useful reclassification) — in the ABI Collaboration individual-participant meta-analysis (16 cohorts, 48,294 people), a low ABI (≤0.90) carried adjusted hazard ratios of ~2.9–3.0 for cardiovascular mortality after Framingham adjustment and roughly doubled 10-year total mortality, cardiovascular mortality and major coronary event rates within each Framingham category, reclassifying 19% of men and 36% of women; however, the USPSTF evidence reviews (2013, 2018) found the net reclassification improvement beyond Framingham was probably small and no trial shows that ABI-guided treatment improves outcomes

title: EBBINGHAUS: formal CANTAB testing in 1,204 FOURIER patients showed evolocumab was non-inferior to placebo on cognition — and 5 more years of follow-up stayed reassuring
question: In patients with cardiovascular disease treated with evolocumab, does profound LDL lowering impair cognition on formal neurocognitive testing?
balance: LIKELY no impairment, on the strongest design available for this question: a prespecified, prospective, formally tested substudy rather than adverse-event counts. EBBINGHAUS (Giugliano 2017, NEJM) embedded the Cambridge Neuropsychological Test Automated Battery (CANTAB) in FOURIER: 1,204 patients tested at baseline, week 24, yearly and end of trial (median 19 months) met non-inferiority on the spatial-working-memory strategy index and showed no between-group differences on any secondary domain, and exploratory analyses found no association between achieved LDL level and cognitive change. Two extensions widen the reassurance: patient-reported Everyday Cognition scores in the full FOURIER population (22,655 respondents; Gencer 2020) showed identical decline rates (3.7% evolocumab vs 3.6% placebo), including in the 2,338 patients who achieved LDL <20 mg/dL; and the EBBINGHAUS open-label extension (Zoungas 2025; 473 patients, median 5.1 additional years, median LDL 35 mg/dL) found no executive-function change in either original arm. Desk-check: home #191 mentions neurocognitive events only inside a FOURIER source line (adverse-event counts); no shelf posed the formal-testing question, which is this shelf's whole subject.
stamp: LIKELY (no impairment — formal testing) — in EBBINGHAUS (n=1,204 randomised FOURIER patients tested prospectively with the CANTAB battery), evolocumab was non-inferior to placebo on the primary executive-function endpoint (P<0.001 for non-inferiority; P=0.85 for superiority) with no differences in working memory, episodic memory or psychomotor speed over a median 19 months; patient-reported cognition in all 22,655 FOURIER patients and formal testing through a median 5.1 further years of very low LDL (median 35 mg/dL) were likewise unremarkable

title: PCSK9 antibodies in confirmed statin intolerance: LDL fell 53–56% (GAUSS-2), 54.5% (GAUSS-3) and 45.0% (ODYSSEY ALTERNATIVE) vs 15–17% on ezetimibe — with fewer muscle events than atorvastatin re-challenge
question: In patients with confirmed statin intolerance, do PCSK9 monoclonal antibodies (evolocumab, alirocumab), compared with placebo or ezetimibe, lower LDL cholesterol and improve statin re-challenge tolerance?
balance: LIKELY for LDL lowering; the tolerance half of the question is answered more narrowly (see below). GAUSS-2 (Stroes 2014; n=307, intolerance by history) found evolocumab cut LDL by 53–56% vs ezetimibe's ~15–17% implied by the 37–39-point treatment differences, with muscle events in 12% on evolocumab vs 23% on ezetimibe. GAUSS-3 (Nissen 2016) is the design centrepiece: in phase A, 491 patients with reported intolerance to ≥2 statins underwent a blinded atorvastatin/placebo crossover and only 209 (42.6%) had symptoms on atorvastatin but not placebo — 'confirmed' intolerance is a minority of reported intolerance; in phase B (n=218), evolocumab lowered LDL by 54.5% (absolute −106.8 mg/dL) vs 16.7% (−31.0 mg/dL) on ezetimibe (P<0.001). ODYSSEY ALTERNATIVE (Moriarty 2015; n=361) randomised alirocumab vs ezetimibe vs atorvastatin 20 mg re-challenge: LDL fell 45.0% vs 14.6% (difference 30.4 points; P<0.0001), and skeletal-muscle events were less frequent on alirocumab than on atorvastatin re-challenge (HR 0.61, 0.38 to 0.99; P=0.042). On 'improved re-challenge tolerance' strictly: the trials show a PCSK9 antibody is better tolerated than re-challenged statin and lowers LDL far more than ezetimibe — they do not show PCSK9 therapy makes patients subsequently tolerate statins. Desk-check: homes #191 and #262 (PCSK9 outcomes) and #268/#5622 (statin-intolerance treatments: bempedoic acid, intermittent dosing) were checked — none cards the PCSK9-in-intolerance trials; the slice was unhomed. Cardiovascular outcomes in this population are untested by these LDL-endpoint trials.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit, for LDL lowering in confirmed statin intolerance) — three randomised trials in intolerance populations show concordant large LDL reductions on PCSK9 antibodies vs ezetimibe (between-group differences of ~30–39 percentage points); on tolerance, ODYSSEY ALTERNATIVE found fewer skeletal-muscle events on alirocumab than on atorvastatin re-challenge (HR 0.61, 95% CI 0.38 to 0.99), and GAUSS-3's blinded crossover confirmed true statin-attributable muscle symptoms in only 42.6% of self-reported intolerant patients

title: Ferric derisomaltose vs ferric carboxymaltose: hypophosphataemia in 7.9–8.1% vs 73.7–75.0% in the PHOSPHARE trials, and 8.3% vs 51.0% in IBD — an FGF23-mediated formulation effect
question: In patients with iron-deficiency anaemia needing intravenous iron, does ferric derisomaltose (iron isomaltoside), compared with ferric carboxymaltose, cause less hypophosphataemia and fewer downstream mineral/bone effects?
balance: LIKELY for the biochemical outcome; the long-term bone consequences are less completely mapped and are stated as such. Formulations are named exactly as published, per the clarification exception: ferric derisomaltose (published in the PHOSPHARE trials as iron isomaltoside, now known as ferric derisomaltose) vs ferric carboxymaltose. Wolf 2020 (JAMA) reports the two PHOSPHARE trials (NCT03238911, NCT03237065; 245 patients with iron-deficiency anaemia intolerant of or unresponsive to oral iron): hypophosphataemia by day 35 in 7.9%/8.1% on iron isomaltoside vs 75.0%/73.7% on ferric carboxymaltose, with parallel differences in FGF23, parathyroid hormone and vitamin D biomarkers. PHOSPHARE-IBD (Zoller 2023, Gut; n=97, double-blind, identical haemoglobin/weight-based dosing) replicated the direction in inflammatory bowel disease: 8.3% vs 51.0% (adjusted risk difference −42.8%), with fatigue improving more slowly on ferric carboxymaltose in proportion to the phosphate fall — a patient-felt downstream correlate. ExplorIRON-CKD (Kassianides 2024; n=26, non-dialysis CKD) supplies the mechanism in miniature: intact FGF23 rose 146.1% and 235.1% after successive ferric carboxymaltose doses vs 3.0% and 3.2% after ferric derisomaltose (P<0.001 and P=0.001), with greater falls in phosphate and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D. Desk-check: home #122 covers IV iron efficacy in heart failure (FAIR-HF lineage) and was read — it does not compare formulations on phosphate safety; pack #6115 mentions hypophosphataemia only as attenuating vitality gains in IBD. The formulation-safety comparison was unhomed.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit, for phosphate safety) — two identically designed PHOSPHARE randomised trials (n=245) found hypophosphataemia (phosphate <2.0 mg/dL) in 7.9% and 8.1% on ferric derisomaltose (iron isomaltoside) vs 75.0% and 73.7% on ferric carboxymaltose (adjusted differences ~−66 percentage points), PHOSPHARE-IBD (n=97) found 8.3% vs 51.0%, and a CKD mechanistic trial confirmed the pathway: intact FGF23 rose ~146–235% after ferric carboxymaltose vs ~3% after ferric derisomaltose

title: Pressure natriuresis and salt sensitivity: Guyton's renal–body-fluid feedback sets long-term pressure — and humans whose pressure rises on salt loading carry a mortality risk like hypertension itself
question: How does pressure natriuresis — the renal–body-fluid feedback of Guyton — set long-term arterial pressure, and what human evidence links its impairment to salt-sensitive hypertension?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED, framed by Guyton & Hall's renal–body-fluid feedback (Textbook of Medical Physiology, Guyton & Hall): the renal-function curve relates arterial pressure to sodium excretion (pressure natriuresis); at equilibrium, intake must equal output, so long-term arterial pressure settles at the pressure where the curve crosses intake — a steeper/higher-pressure curve (impaired natriuresis) means any given salt intake is excreted only at a higher pressure, which is the textbook account of salt-sensitive hypertension. Those quantitative curve claims are presented as the textbook's account (framing, not an evidence card). The human evidence carded here is concordant with the framework: (1) Weinberger 2002 followed 708 people phenotyped by salt loading/depletion — salt sensitivity, even in normotensive people, carried survival no better than hypertension over up to 28 years; (2) Overlack 1995 showed the phenotype is real and graded under controlled double-blind conditions (46 hypertensive patients cycled between 20 and 300 mmol sodium/day: 23.9% salt-sensitive, 58.7% salt-resistant, 17.4% counter-regulators), with salt-sensitive patients showing lower creatinine clearance and suppressed renin — the human signature of a right-shifted renal-function curve; (3) Weinberger 1988 documents that the blood-pressure response to salt is heritable and continuously distributed, with salt sensitivity more frequent in Black than White Americans — a trait of the feedback system, not a binary disease. Animal mechanism (e.g., Dahl salt-sensitive rats) is mentioned only as labelled textbook background in prose; no animal study is carded.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED

title: Pulse pressure (physiology): stroke volume is ejected into an elastic reservoir — as the aorta stiffens, the forward wave grows, systolic pressure rises and diastolic falls, and isolated systolic hypertension is the haemodynamic signature of arterial ageing
question: What determines pulse pressure — stroke volume, arterial compliance (the Windkessel function) and wave reflection — and why does isolated systolic hypertension emerge with arterial stiffening?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Boron & Boulpaep, Medical Physiology, arterial-system chapters). In the textbook's Windkessel account, the elastic aorta and large arteries store roughly half the stroke volume during systole and discharge it during diastole, so pulse pressure is set by three things: the stroke volume ejected, the compliance of the arterial reservoir that receives it, and the reflected pressure wave returning from peripheral reflection sites — if it returns in diastole it supports diastolic pressure, but as pulse wave velocity rises with stiffening it returns ever earlier, augmenting systole instead. The carded human studies measure each limb of that account. Wave-reflection timing is real and movable: in paced patients the augmentation index fell by about 4% for every 10 beats/min rise in heart rate, purely because systole shortened and the reflected wave arrived relatively later (Wilkinson 2000). In healthy humans, worse endothelial function tracked higher aortic pulse wave velocity (r = −0.69), higher augmentation index (r = −0.59) and higher central pulse pressure (r = −0.34) — stiffness and reflection are biologically regulated, not fixed plumbing (McEniery 2006). And the longitudinal Framingham haemodynamic data settle the ageing question: pulse pressure widened markedly after midlife, faster in women, and the widening tracked the forward wave — proximal aortic stiffening raising characteristic impedance — far more strongly than it tracked wave reflection, whose coefficient actually fell as impedance rose (Mitchell 2023). That is why isolated systolic hypertension emerges: a stiff aorta converts the same stroke volume into a larger forward pressure wave, systolic pressure climbs, the diastolic cushion is lost, and diastolic pressure stagnates or falls. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

title: Adaptive thermogenesis (physiology): after a 10% weight loss, total energy expenditure falls by roughly 6–8 kcal per kg of fat-free mass per day beyond the change in mass — leptin repletion reverses the adaptation, and in the extreme Biggest Loser phenotype a ~500 kcal/day adaptation was still present 6 years later
question: After weight loss, how large is adaptive thermogenesis (the fall in energy expenditure beyond that predicted by lost mass), how long does it persist, and what hormonal signals (leptin) drive it?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology and Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology, energy-balance and hypothalamic-regulation chapters). The textbooks describe body weight as defended: lose weight and energy expenditure falls by more than the lost tissue explains, while hunger and neuroendocrine signals shift to restore the former weight — with leptin, the adipocyte signal of fat stores, as the central messenger. The carded human studies quantify that defence. In controlled inpatient weight perturbation, maintaining a weight 10% or more below usual was associated with total energy expenditure lower by 6 ± 3 kcal/kg fat-free mass/day in never-obese and 8 ± 5 kcal/kg fat-free mass/day in obese subjects, with resting and non-resting expenditure each contributing (Leibel 1995) — and the adaptation was bidirectional, expenditure rising symmetrically after 10% weight gain. The signal is leptin: in weight-reduced subjects, replacing leptin to pre-loss concentrations returned energy expenditure, skeletal muscle work efficiency, sympathetic tone and thyroid hormones to pre-weight-loss levels (Rosenbaum 2005) — the reduced state behaves as relative leptin insufficiency. Persistence is measured in years, not weeks: six years after the Biggest Loser competition, resting metabolic rate remained 704 ± 427 kcal/day below baseline and metabolic adaptation was −499 ± 207 kcal/day despite substantial regain (Fothergill 2016) — an extreme phenotype (58 kg lost in 30 weeks), but it proves the adaptation does not simply expire. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

title: Triglyceride clearance (physiology): lipoprotein lipase at the capillary wall hydrolyses chylomicron and VLDL triglyceride — switched on by apoC-II, braked by apoC-III and the ANGPTL proteins — and human loss-of-function genetics prove the brakes: APOC3 carriers run triglycerides ~40% lower, ANGPTL4 inactivation ~13% lower
question: How is triglyceride cleared from chylomicrons and VLDL by lipoprotein lipase, and how do apoC-II (activation), apoC-III and ANGPTL proteins (inhibition) regulate that clearance in humans?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Boron & Boulpaep, Medical Physiology, and Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology, lipid-transport sections). In the textbook account, lipoprotein lipase (LPL) sits on capillary endothelium in muscle and adipose tissue and hydrolyses the triglyceride core of chylomicrons and VLDL, releasing fatty acids for uptake; apoC-II, acquired from HDL, is the essential LPL activator — its inherited absence produces severe hypertriglyceridaemia because clearance fails — while apoC-III and the angiopoietin-like proteins ANGPTL3 and ANGPTL4 inhibit LPL and slow clearance. Human genetics supplies the proof in both directions, and it is the carded evidence here. Lifelong partial loss of the apoC-III brake lowers triglycerides by 39–44% (relative) in two independent 2014 NEJM datasets (Crosby; Jørgensen). Inactivating ANGPTL3 lowers triglycerides, LDL and HDL together, with coronary odds reduced (odds ratio 0.59; Dewey 2017), and pharmacologic inactivation in human volunteers reproduced the physiology, with fasting triglycerides falling up to 76% (a relative reduction). Inactivating ANGPTL4 (E40K) lowers triglycerides by 13% (relative) with higher HDL (Dewey 2016). No animal studies are carded; animal data appear only inside two records' supporting experiments and are flagged as such on the cards. Related drug shelves (evinacumab, apoC-III and ANGPTL3 antisense/antibody therapies) ask treatment questions; this shelf is the physiology those drugs exploit. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

title: Myocardial substrate switching (physiology): the Randle cycle in the human heart — fatty acids and glucose compete, insulin and fatty-acid supply move the switch, and in human diabetes the heart is locked toward fat (94% of fatty acids taken up oxidised, glucose use halved) while human heart failure shows no single uniform shift
question: How does the heart switch between fatty-acid and glucose oxidation (the Randle glucose–fatty-acid cycle), and how is substrate selection altered in diabetes and heart failure in humans?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING (textbook framing: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology and Boron & Boulpaep, Medical Physiology, metabolic-integration chapters). The Randle glucose–fatty-acid cycle, as the textbooks present it, is reciprocal competition: fatty-acid oxidation raises acetyl-CoA and citrate, inhibiting pyruvate dehydrogenase and glycolysis, while insulin and glucose availability suppress fatty-acid use — so the heart burns whichever fuel the circulation delivers, minute by minute. Human PET studies confirm the switch operates in people and quantify its diabetic distortion. In type 1 diabetes, myocardial fatty-acid utilisation and oxidation were roughly four-fold higher than in controls, 94% of fatty acids taken up were oxidised, and glucose utilisation was halved (Herrero 2006); yet the switch was not broken — raising insulin and lowering free fatty acids still moved diabetic myocardium back toward glucose (Peterson 2008). In uncomplicated type 2 diabetes the same pattern held — glucose uptake down, fatty-acid uptake and oxidation up — alongside impaired diastolic function (Rijzewijk 2009). Heart failure is where the human data refuse the tidy animal story: in non-ischaemic human heart failure, women had higher fatty-acid uptake and metabolism than men and no uniform fall in fat oxidation was shown (Kadkhodayan 2017). The diabetes limb is concordant human physiology; the heart-failure limb is not settled in humans — hence EMERGING rather than ESTABLISHED. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING.

title: RANK/RANKL/osteoprotegerin (physiology): osteoblast-lineage cells set the resorption rate through one ratio — RANKL drives osteoclasts via RANK, osteoprotegerin is the decoy that soaks it up — and human genetics proves the set-point at both extremes: no osteoprotegerin means runaway turnover, activated RANK means focal osteolysis
question: How does the RANK/RANKL/osteoprotegerin system couple osteoclast and osteoblast activity in bone remodelling, and what human genetic/physiological evidence establishes the set-point?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology, bone-remodelling sections). The historical anchor is Lacey and colleagues' 1998 discovery (Cell; PMID 9568710, verified by title search this session and not carded, because it is a molecular discovery paper rather than a human study) of osteoprotegerin ligand — the molecule now called RANKL — as the osteoblast-lineage cytokine that drives osteoclast differentiation and activation, with osteoprotegerin (OPG) as its decoy receptor. In the textbook account, remodelling is coupled through this single axis: osteoblast-lineage cells express RANKL, RANKL engages RANK on osteoclast precursors, osteoclasts form and resorb; OPG, secreted by the same lineage, binds RANKL and sets how much signal gets through — the RANKL/OPG ratio is the set-point. The carded human evidence tests every limb. Delete OPG entirely (homozygous TNFRSF11B deletion) and the result is juvenile Paget's disease — rapidly remodelling woven bone with undetectable OPG and markedly increased soluble RANKL (Whyte 2002) — and replacing OPG pharmacologically in two affected siblings suppressed resorption and rebuilt radial bone mass (Cundy 2005). Activate RANK itself by signal-peptide mutations and focal osteolysis follows (Hughes 2000). In ordinary physiology, oestrogen deficiency raises RANKL expression two- to three-fold on human marrow cells, tracking resorption markers (Eghbali-Fatourechi 2003). Denosumab, the anti-RANKL antibody, is the drug-shelf exploitation of this axis; this shelf is the physiology. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

title: Deiodinases (physiology): T4 is a prohormone — D1 and D2 strip one iodine to make active T3, D3 inactivates both hormones — so serum tests report the pool while tissues set their own T3; the common DIO2 Thr92Ala variant measurably lowers D2 conversion in humans, but what that means for combination therapy is still unsettled
question: How do the deiodinases (D1, D2, D3) control local and circulating T3 by converting T4, and what does that imply for interpreting thyroid tests and combination therapy in humans?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING (textbook framing: Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology, thyroid chapter; deiodinase physiology as synthesised by Bianco and colleagues). The textbook account: the thyroid secretes mostly T4, a prohormone. Type 1 deiodinase (D1, liver, kidney, thyroid) contributes much of the circulating T3 and clears reverse T3; type 2 deiodinase (D2, pituitary, brain, brown fat, skeletal muscle) generates T3 locally, inside the cell that will use it — so pituitary TSH feedback and brain T3 depend on D2 conversion, not just on serum levels; type 3 deiodinase (D3) inactivates T4 and T3. It follows that a normal TSH and free T4 do not guarantee identical tissue T3 in every person. The carded human genetic studies test that implication. Common D1 variation shifts serum hormone ratios measurably but explains under 2% of their variation (van der Deure 2009, 1,192 twins). The D2 Thr92Ala variant reduces D2-mediated T4-to-T3 conversion, and athyreotic patients carrying it ran lower free T3 after thyroidectomy at the same TSH on levothyroxine (Castagna 2017). In the WATTS cohort, the same variant's CC genotype was associated with worse baseline well-being on T4 alone and greater improvement when T3 was added — without any difference in circulating hormone levels (Panicker 2009). That last finding is unreplicated and contested, which is why the stamp is EMERGING: the enzymology is settled, the clinical meaning for combination therapy is not. The combination-therapy treatment question itself is homed on drug shelf #513; this shelf is the physiology underneath it. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING.

title: FGF23 and klotho (physiology): bone talks to kidney through one hormone — FGF23, acting only where klotho is present, orders phosphate excretion and switches off vitamin D activation — and humans break in both directions: too much FGF23 action wastes phosphate into rickets, too little calcifies soft tissue
question: How do FGF23 and klotho regulate phosphate excretion and vitamin D activation, and what happens to phosphate balance when this axis is disrupted in humans?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Boron & Boulpaep, Medical Physiology, phosphate-handling sections). In the textbook account, FGF23 is a hormone secreted by osteocytes that acts on the kidney only where its co-receptor klotho is expressed with an FGF receptor: it reduces proximal-tubule phosphate reabsorption (phosphaturia) and suppresses 1α-hydroxylase, lowering 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D and hence gut phosphate absorption — a bone-to-kidney negative-feedback loop for phosphate. Humans provide experiments of nature at every joint of that loop, and they are the carded evidence. FGF23 was identified as the ADHR gene: missense mutations at its proteolytic cleavage motif make it cleavage-resistant and overactive, wasting phosphate (ADHR Consortium 2000). The same molecule was cloned from a human tumour causing tumour-induced osteomalacia, a syndrome whose defining feature is that removing the tumour normalises phosphate metabolism (Shimada 2001). And when the co-receptor fails — a homozygous klotho mutation in a 13-year-old girl — FGF23 cannot signal, and the phenotype inverts: severe hyperphosphataemia with tumoral calcinosis despite elevated FGF23 (Ichikawa 2007). Excess action wastes phosphate; absent action retains it. The ferric carboxymaltose hypophosphataemia question built from slate row S4-1-29 is this axis operating iatrogenically, and burosumab treatment shelves (#1194 family) exploit it therapeutically; this shelf is the physiology. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

title: Coronary autoregulation (physiology): flow stays constant while pressure falls — until the plateau breaks — and in humans the break point shifts upward with hypertension and hypertrophy (flow fell 26% once pressure reached 90–80 mm Hg), with adenosine and K-ATP-channel metabolic coupling doing the day-to-day work
question: How does coronary autoregulation hold myocardial blood flow constant across perfusion pressures, which mediators (adenosine, metabolic coupling) dominate, and where does the autoregulatory range break in humans?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, coronary-circulation chapter). In the textbook account, coronary flow is autoregulated: across a wide range of perfusion pressures, arteriolar resistance adjusts so flow matches myocardial oxygen demand — metabolic coupling — with adenosine, released as ATP is consumed, as the classic mediator, alongside other local signals including ATP-sensitive potassium (K-ATP) channels. Below the lower limit of the range, vessels are maximally dilated and flow becomes pressure-dependent. The carded human studies measure the plateau, its break point, and its mediators in people. Lowering coronary perfusion pressure stepwise in patients with normal epicardial arteries left great-cardiac-vein flow unchanged down to the 60–70 mm Hg endpoints in controls and in hypertensives without hypertrophy — but in hypertensive patients with left ventricular hypertrophy, flow began to fall at 90–80 mm Hg and was down 26% at the endpoint: the lower limit shifts upward when baseline flow is high and arteriolar dilation is impaired (Polese 1991). For mediators: blocking adenosine receptors with theophylline cut human coronary flow by 23% across rest, hypoxia and exercise (Edlund 1995), and blocking K-ATP channels with intracoronary glibenclamide blunted pacing-induced metabolic vasodilation (Farouque 2004); exogenous adenosine itself reproduces near-maximal human coronary vasodilation (Wilson 1990). SCOPE: this shelf covers the autoregulatory plateau and its mediators only — the magnitude of coronary flow reserve is a separate question, deliberately not built here. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

title: Renin release (physiology): three inputs converge on the juxtaglomerular cell — the renal baroreceptor reads perfusion pressure, the macula densa reads distal NaCl, and sympathetic β1 drive reads the circulation at large — and human studies show them integrating within minutes of standing and over days of sodium restriction
question: What controls renin release at the juxtaglomerular apparatus — renal baroreceptor, macula densa NaCl sensing, and sympathetic β1 input — and how do these integrate in human volume/pressure homeostasis?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, renin–angiotensin chapter; macula densa signalling as in Vander's Renal Physiology). The textbook's three inputs to the juxtaglomerular (JG) cell: (1) the renal baroreceptor — JG cells themselves sense afferent arteriolar stretch, releasing more renin as perfusion pressure falls; (2) macula densa NaCl sensing — less NaCl delivered to the distal tubule (sensed via Na-K-2Cl cotransport) signals volume depletion and stimulates renin, more NaCl suppresses it; (3) sympathetic β1 input — renal sympathetic nerves and circulating catecholamines stimulate renin directly, the route by which posture and central volume sensing reach the kidney. The carded human studies show the integrated output. Posture: plasma renin activity rose significantly within 5 minutes of standing and was three-fold higher after 2 hours upright (Sassard 1976) — baroreceptor unloading plus sympathetic activation, before any sodium change. Sodium balance: dropping intake from 200 to 10 mEq/day raised renin activity roughly three-fold, diuretic volume depletion abolished the nocturnal fall, and renin was judged the dominant controller of the downstream aldosterone response (Williams 1972). Sympathetic/pressure interplay: sodium depletion stimulated total renin release, while propranolol lowered active renin in every patient and clonidine mimicked it — yet when β-blockade lowered blood pressure, baroreceptor-mediated release pushed back, the three inputs visibly negotiating (Atlas 1977). Downstream of renin sits aldosterone, whose own regulators are homed on pack #6078; this shelf stops at renin release. The later tubuloglomerular-feedback question (slate row 90) shares the macula densa but asks a different, glomerular question. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

title: Calcium-sensing receptor (physiology): the parathyroid does not measure a fixed calcium target, it obeys a receptor — inactivating CaSR mutations reset the set-point upward (familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia), activating mutations reset it downward (autosomal dominant hypocalcaemia), proving the receptor is the thermostat
question: How does the calcium-sensing receptor set the PTH–calcium set-point, and how do human activating/inactivating CaSR disorders demonstrate the physiology?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology, calcium-regulation chapter). The historical anchor is Brown and colleagues' 1993 cloning of the extracellular calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR) from parathyroid tissue (Nature 1993; the cloned receptor was bovine, so it is cited here as framing, not carded — no animal evidence is carded on this shelf). In the textbook account, the CaSR on parathyroid chief cells senses ionised calcium directly: rising calcium activates the receptor and suppresses PTH secretion along a sigmoidal curve whose midpoint — the set-point — is a property of the receptor's sensitivity. The same receptor in the kidney adjusts urinary calcium excretion. Human genetics then performed the decisive experiment in both directions, and it is the carded evidence. Inactivating mutations cause familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia (FHH) and, in homozygotes, neonatal severe hyperparathyroidism: the gland behaves as if calcium were lower than it is, so PTH is not suppressed until calcium is abnormally high — the set-point reset upward (Pollak 1993; Chou 1995). An activating mutation does the exact opposite: the receptor over-signals at low calcium, PTH is suppressed inappropriately, and patients are hypocalcaemic (Pollak 1994). A thermostat proven by breaking it both ways. The calcilytic encaleret, which pharmacologically re-resets the receptor in autosomal dominant hypocalcaemia, is homed on drug shelf #5537; this shelf is the physiology it exploits. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

title: Ketogenesis regulation: fat supply is the throttle, the insulin-to-glucagon ratio is the gate — and residual insulin is the ceiling that keeps a fast out of ketoacidosis
question: How do the insulin-to-glucagon ratio and substrate supply regulate hepatic ketogenesis during fasting, and what sets the ceiling that normally prevents ketoacidosis?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. This pack is the regulation mechanism behind the fasting time course built as pack #6255 (24–72 hours: glucose and insulin fall, fatty acids and ketones rise) — #6255 is cross-pointed, and none of its PMIDs is re-carded here. The carded human experiments agree on the architecture Guyton & Hall present from the McGarry & Foster and Cahill programmes: free-fatty-acid supply is a major determinant of ketone production even with insulin and glucagon held basal (Miles 1983, fivefold rise in production for a fivefold rise in fatty acids); glucagon augments ketogenesis only in insulin deficiency (Miles) and its suppression lowers production without changing fatty acids in insulin-deficient patients (Keller 1983); catecholamines add a direct ketogenic push (Schade & Eaton 1977). The ceiling that separates fasting ketosis from ketoacidosis is therefore not a ketone sensor but the fasting state itself: insulin falls but never vanishes, restraining lipolysis and the hepatic switch, while the brain's adaptation to ketones (Owen 1967) cuts demand. Classic small studies are carded with their Ns on the face (N = 3–6 on two cards; one record prints no N).

title: Biphasic insulin secretion: a small ready pool fires in minutes, a reserve sustains the second phase — and the first phase is already failing before glucose rises
question: What produces the biphasic (first- and second-phase) pattern of insulin secretion, why is first-phase secretion lost early in type 2 diabetes, and how is it measured in humans?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. The carded human studies carry the whole arc: Porte & Pupo's 1969 pulse experiments in man established the two-pool behaviour (a 3–5-minute acute response that a short glucose infusion depletes by 58% and a long one restores); Brunzell 1976 placed the acute response's disappearance at a fasting glucose of about 115 mg/dL across 66 subjects; Ward 1985 found relative first-phase responses already under a third of controls' in normoglycaemic women with prior gestational diabetes; and the IRAS frequently-sampled-IVGTT data (Festa 2008, n = 1,380) quantify the loss directly — about 40% in impaired glucose tolerance and up to 80% in new diabetes, far more than fasting surrogates suggest. Boron & Boulpaep / Guyton & Hall framing supplies the granule-pool mechanism (with Curry's rat-pancreas experiments named as animal framing, not carded). Small classic groups are labelled on the face (N = 8 per group on one card; one record prints no N).

title: Nerandomilast in IPF and progressive pulmonary fibrosis: two phase 3 trials slow FVC decline by about 45–80 mL over 52 weeks, with diarrhoea in a third or more
question: In adults with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis or progressive pulmonary fibrosis, does the oral PDE4B inhibitor nerandomilast slow the decline in forced vital capacity compared with placebo?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — for the forced-vital-capacity claim. Two independent phase 3, double-blind trials (FIBRONEER-IPF, n = 1,177; FIBRONEER-ILD, n = 1,176) each found both doses of the oral preferential PDE4B inhibitor nerandomilast slowed 52-week FVC decline versus placebo (adjusted differences 44.9–81.1 mL), building on a 12-week phase 2 stabilisation signal, and the FIBRONEER-ILD whole-follow-up report is directionally concordant on exacerbation, respiratory hospitalisation or death. The claim is a lung-function slope, not a proven symptom or survival benefit in the primary reports; diarrhoea (roughly 30–41% on drug vs 16–25% on placebo) is the consistent cost. The carded records present nerandomilast as an investigational agent; no regulatory status beyond what the records state is claimed.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: STOP2: 10 days of IV antibiotics was non-inferior to 14 in early responders with a CF exacerbation — and 21 days beat 14 in nobody
question: In adults with cystic fibrosis having a pulmonary exacerbation with early treatment improvement, is 10 days of intravenous antibiotics non-inferior to 14 days for recovery of lung function?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single randomised programme caps the stamp. STOP2 (982 adults with cystic fibrosis) randomised by early treatment response: in the 277 early responders, 10 days of intravenous antibiotics was non-inferior to 14 days for percent predicted FEV1 recovery (difference −0.65 points, 95% CI −3.3 to 2.0, excluding the non-inferiority margin); in the 705 non-early responders, extending to 21 days made no difference versus 14 days (difference −0.10 points). Two STOP2 secondary analyses are carded as labelled context (home-only treatment recovered less; 39.5% of exacerbations were virus-positive). title: MAC lung disease, first treatment: thrice-weekly triple therapy converts sputum as often as daily therapy in noncavitary disease — and patients stay on it more easily
question: In adults with newly diagnosed Mycobacterium avium complex lung disease, is intermittent (thrice-weekly) triple therapy as effective as daily triple therapy for sputum culture conversion and relapse?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). In treatment-naive noncavitary nodular bronchiectatic MAC lung disease, intermittent three-times-weekly macrolide–rifampin–ethambutol therapy achieved sputum culture conversion statistically indistinguishable from daily therapy in both a 217-patient retrospective cohort (adjusted 73.6% vs 71.3%; Jeong 2015 — a cohort, not an RCT, a premise correction to the slate) and the 2025 iREC randomised trial (70.3% vs 80.0%, P = 0.53; Nakagawa), with better tolerability on intermittent dosing in both. The trial's wide intervals and the cohort's retrospective design cap the stamp at POSSIBLE. Cavitary disease is excluded from every card — daily therapy remains its standard — and refractory MAC add-on therapy is home on #2673, not here.

title: Fibrotic hypersensitivity pneumonitis treatment: an observational, near-null base — steroids made no difference in fibrotic disease, mycophenolate moves DLCO only, avoidance unproven
question: In adults with fibrotic hypersensitivity pneumonitis, do antigen avoidance, corticosteroids or mycophenolate slow lung-function decline and improve survival?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — observational evidence only, labelled as such, with no dedicated randomised trial in existence. In the largest fibrotic-phenotype cohort (De Sadeleer 2018; 109 fibrotic patients), corticosteroids made no difference to survival or lung function and antigen avoidance showed only a non-significant trend (P = 0.15). Mycophenolate/azathioprine initiation was followed by a DLCO improvement (+4.2% at 1 year) but no significant FVC change (Morisset 2017), and registry immunosuppression in 344 fibrotic patients changed neither lung function nor symptoms, with worse survival in the unknown-antigen subgroup (Mullin 2024). Nothing carded shows a treatment slowing decline in fibrotic HP; the guideline-era practice rests on non-fibrotic disease and mechanism, not on fibrotic-phenotype outcomes.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence)

title: PREDMETH: first-line methotrexate was non-inferior to prednisone for FVC change at 24 weeks in new pulmonary sarcoidosis — with a different, not smaller, side-effect burden
question: In adults with newly diagnosed pulmonary sarcoidosis requiring treatment, is first-line methotrexate non-inferior to prednisone for lung-function change, with fewer glucocorticoid side effects?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single trial caps the stamp. Two second-line methotrexate cohorts are carded as labelled context only. title: ABPA: medium-dose prednisolone matched high-dose, and adding itraconazole has not been shown to prevent relapse
question: In adults with allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, what glucocorticoid regimen (dose and duration, with or without an azole) best achieves remission without relapse?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — three randomised trials from one specialist programme, capped at POSSIBLE for that single-programme base. On dose: medium-dose prednisolone matched high-dose on exacerbations at 1 year (50% vs 40.9%) and glucocorticoid dependence at 2 years (14.6% vs 11.4%), with a significantly lower cumulative dose and fewer side effects — so more steroid bought no protection against relapse. On drug choice: prednisolone alone produced a composite response in 100% vs 88% on itraconazole alone at 6 weeks, with similar IgE falls, exacerbations and time to first exacerbation, but significantly more side effects. Adding itraconazole to prednisolone showed only a trend to fewer 1-year exacerbations (20.6% vs 33%, P=.054). The regimen the record supports is a medium-dose glucocorticoid course, with an azole as an alternative or adjunct rather than a proven relapse-sparer. Itraconazole added to steroids in glucocorticoid-dependent ABPA is a different question, homed on Shelf #4255, and its trials are not re-carded here.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Mesenchymal stromal cells in ARDS: safe in three small phase 2 trials, efficacy unproven — no phase 3 evidence
question: In adults with moderate-to-severe ARDS, do mesenchymal stromal cells improve ventilator-free days or mortality compared with placebo? (Phase 2 evidence only.)
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — PHASE 2 EVIDENCE ONLY, flagged on the face of this shelf: there is no phase 3 trial of mesenchymal or multipotent stromal cells in ARDS. Three small randomised phase 1/2–2a trials point in different directions. START (60 patients) found one dose of mesenchymal stromal cells safe but 28-day mortality numerically higher on cells (30% vs 15%; adjusted HR 1.43, 95% CI 0.40–5.12), in a cell arm that was sicker at baseline. MUST-ARDS (30 patients in its randomised cohort) found mortality and ventilator-free days numerically favouring multipotent adult progenitor cells (28-day mortality 25% vs 45%; median ventilator-free days 18.5 vs 6.5), with the same baseline-imbalance problem in reverse. REALIST-COVID (59 analysed, COVID-19 ARDS only) found no difference in oxygenation or mortality at any point to 2 years (the treatment made no difference). Safety is consistent; efficacy is unproven.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence)

title: CENTERSTONE: treating the index patient with baloxavir reduced household influenza transmission (9.5% vs 13.4%)
question: In households with an influenza index case, does treating the index patient with single-dose baloxavir reduce laboratory-confirmed transmission to household contacts compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single randomised trial programme caps the stamp. In CENTERSTONE (1,457 index patients aged 5–64 treated within 48 hours of symptom onset), single-dose baloxavir given to the index patient reduced laboratory-confirmed transmission to household contacts by day 5: adjusted incidence 9.5% vs 13.4% on placebo (adjusted odds ratio 0.68; adjusted relative risk reduction 29% relative, beside the absolute incidences printed here). Transmission that produced symptoms was not significantly reduced (5.8% vs 7.6%; P=.16). A whole-genome-sequencing re-analysis confirmed the result was not an artefact of community-acquired infections misread as household spread (adjusted OR 0.69 after the most stringent pairing cutoff), and a large Japanese claims study found less household transmission from baloxavir-treated index patients than from oseltamivir-treated ones (observational). The counterweight: drug-resistant viruses emerged in 7.2% of baloxavir-treated index patients. This shelf is about treating the index case to protect contacts — post-exposure prophylaxis of contacts themselves is homed on Shelf #1630 (BLOCKSTONE) and treatment efficacy on Shelf #727, and neither is re-carded here.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Ribavirin for chronic hepatitis E in transplant recipients: sustained clearance in about 4 of 5 — observational evidence only
question: In immunosuppressed or transplant recipients with chronic hepatitis E, does ribavirin achieve sustained viral clearance, and what predicts relapse? (Observational evidence.)
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — OBSERVATIONAL EVIDENCE ONLY, labelled as such on every card: no randomised trial of ribavirin for chronic hepatitis E exists. Two retrospective multicentre cohorts from the same research network agree closely: in 59 solid-organ transplant recipients, a median 3-month course of ribavirin (median 600 mg/day) cleared the virus in 95% by end of therapy and produced a sustained virologic response in 78%, with recurrence in 10 patients after stopping; in the larger European cohort of 255 recipients, sustained response was 81.2% after one course and 89.8% after a second course in some patients. The relapse predictors are consistent across both: a higher lymphocyte count at treatment start predicts sustained response, while anaemia severe enough to force dose reduction (28–29%) or transfusion is associated with more relapse. Viral-kinetic data add an early marker: a flat-partial plasma response pattern was associated with treatment failure, and every patient whose plasma HEV fell by more than 15% by day 7 achieved sustained response in that 41-patient cohort. Anaemia is the main harm throughout.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational evidence only

title: Early oseltamivir in hospitalised influenza: observational data link starting within 2 days to about half the mortality odds — no randomised trial exists
question: In hospitalised adults with influenza, is early oseltamivir associated with lower mortality than late or no oseltamivir? (Observational evidence only.)
balance: All of the evidence on this shelf is observational — there is no randomised trial of oseltamivir timing in hospitalised influenza — so the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE and the observational label is carried on the stamp line. The direction is consistent across three different designs and eras: the PRIDE individual-patient-data meta-analysis of 29,234 hospitalised patients with 2009 pandemic H1N1 (early treatment within 2 days of symptom onset versus later treatment: adjusted odds ratio for death 0.48, 95% CI 0.41–0.56; each day of delay up to day 5 raised the mortality hazard, adjusted HR 1.23 per day); a Spanish ICU cohort in ventilated pandemic patients (ICU mortality 21.5% with early versus 34.3% with late treatment); and a 2022–23 US sentinel cohort of 840 hospitalised adults (treatment on the admission day versus late or none: adjusted OR for in-hospital death 0.36, 95% CI 0.18–0.72). These are adjusted associations, not proven effects: patients treated early differ from patients treated late, and confounding by indication and immortal-time bias can manufacture exactly this pattern. The neighbouring questions are homed elsewhere: oseltamivir for outpatient illness is live shelf #583, combination baloxavir–oseltamivir in hospital is pack #4799, and avian influenza is pack #5312.
stamp: POSSIBLE (observational) — early oseltamivir (within 2 days of symptom onset, or on the admission day) is associated with lower mortality than late or no treatment in hospitalised influenza (PRIDE adjusted OR 0.48 for early vs late; US cohort adjusted OR 0.36 for death), but all evidence is observational and confounding cannot be excluded

title: Non-HIV Pneumocystis pneumonia: steroid evidence splits by severity — possible benefit only in respiratory failure, possible harm when given unselectively; no study ranks the TMP-SMX alternatives
question: In non-HIV immunocompromised adults with Pneumocystis pneumonia, do adjunctive corticosteroids improve survival in hypoxaemic disease, and which alternative to trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole is best when it cannot be used? (Observational evidence.)
balance: This is an observational-evidence shelf (the HIV Pneumocystis questions are homed separately on packs #2965 and #2966) and the steroid evidence genuinely splits by severity. Two meta-analyses of overlapping retrospective studies disagree in emphasis: Fujikura 2017 (7 studies) found no mortality benefit overall (OR 1.26, 95% CI 0.60–2.67) and none in severe hypoxaemia (OR 0.90, 0.44–1.83); Ding 2020 (16 studies, 2,518 cases) found steroids associated with higher mortality in unselected patients (OR 1.37, 1.07–1.75) but lower mortality in the respiratory-failure subgroup (OR 0.63, 0.41–0.95). The one primary cohort (Pareja 1998, n=30, all with PO2 <65 mm Hg) found faster recovery with high-dose steroids but no mortality difference (44% vs 36%; the treatment made no difference to survival). On the second half of the question the record is thin: no carded study compares atovaquone, pentamidine or clindamycin–primaquine head-to-head in non-HIV disease, so no 'best alternative' can be named; the one comparative treatment study found (Nagai 2024) addresses trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole dose, not alternatives — low dose performed similarly to conventional dose with fewer adverse events. PROPOSED SPLIT for steroids; the alternatives question is an evidence gap, stated as such.
stamp: SPLIT (observational) — adjunctive corticosteroids in non-HIV Pneumocystis pneumonia: associated with higher mortality when given unselectively (OR 1.37) but with lower mortality in respiratory failure (OR 0.63) in one meta-analysis, and with no benefit in another (OR 1.26 overall; 0.90 in severe hypoxaemia); no comparative evidence ranks the trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole alternatives

title: Azole-resistant Aspergillus fumigatus: about 1 in 5 culture-positive invasive cases in Dutch–Belgian cohorts (6.1% of patients in Danish surveillance), TR34/L98H the commonest mechanism — and resistant infection carries roughly 20–25 points higher mortality
question: In adults with invasive aspergillosis caused by azole-resistant Aspergillus fumigatus, what is the prevalence of environmental TR34/L98H resistance and which treatment improves survival? (Observational evidence.)
balance: All evidence here is observational, so the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE and labelled. Prevalence depends on the denominator: among culture-positive invasive aspergillosis cases in Dutch and Dutch–Belgian haematology cohorts, voriconazole resistance was 19% (37/196, Lestrade 2019) and 20.2% (26/129, Resendiz-Sharpe 2019); in Danish national surveillance counting patients rather than invasive cases, azole resistance was 6.1% (66/1,083) and TR34/L98H specifically 3.6% (39/1,083), accounting for 59.1% of all resistance. In the haematology cohort almost every resistant isolate carried an environmental cyp51A mechanism — TR34/L98H (13 cases) or TR46/Y121F/T289A (12 cases). Mortality is consistently higher with resistance: day-42 mortality 49% versus 28% and day-90 mortality 62% versus 37% (Lestrade); 12-week mortality 57.7% versus 36.9% (Resendiz-Sharpe). On treatment, no randomised trial exists; the actionable observational finding is that receiving initially appropriate (non-azole) therapy mattered — mortality 24% with appropriate initial therapy versus 47% with inappropriate initial voriconazole, even though therapy was switched after a median of 10 days — which is the evidence behind guideline advice to use liposomal amphotericin B, alone or in combination, where resistance is suspected or proven. Susceptible-disease drug comparisons are homed elsewhere (posaconazole pack #4189; isavuconazole versus voriconazole, SECURE, live shelf #508) and are not re-carded here.
stamp: POSSIBLE (observational) — azole resistance is common where it is looked for (19–20% of culture-positive invasive cases in Dutch–Belgian cohorts; TR34/L98H the dominant mechanism) and resistant infection is associated with about 21–25 percentage points higher mortality; initially appropriate non-azole therapy (liposomal amphotericin B-based) is associated with lower mortality than starting voriconazole and switching late (24% vs 47%)

title: GALAD score for early HCC detection: better accuracy than AFP alone (phase 3 AUC 0.78 vs 0.66; sensitivity 62% vs 41% at matched specificity) — but never tested head-to-head against ultrasound surveillance in a randomised design
question: In adults with cirrhosis under hepatocellular carcinoma surveillance, does the GALAD score (gender, age, AFP-L3, AFP, DCP) detect early HCC better than ultrasound with or without AFP? (Test-accuracy question.)
balance: ACCURACY VERDICT (this is a test-accuracy shelf, stamped as such). The strongest design is the phase 3 biomarker validation (Marsh 2025): in 1,558 patients with cirrhosis followed prospectively, GALAD measured within 12 months before HCC diagnosis had an AUC of 0.78 versus 0.66 for AFP alone (p<.001), and at a matched 82% specificity its sensitivity was 62% versus 41% for AFP (p=.001). Pooled across 10 diagnostic studies (Lu 2024), GALAD's sensitivity and specificity were 0.86 and 0.90 for all-stage HCC (AUC 0.94) and 0.83 and 0.81 for early-stage HCC (AUC 0.90) — but most pooled studies are case-control designs, which flatter accuracy. The original model (Johnson 2014) reported AUC values above 0.88 across stages in case-control data. The honest limit: no carded study randomises patients to GALAD-based versus ultrasound-based surveillance or compares GALAD directly against ultrasound ± AFP in the same prospective cohort — the phase 3 comparator was AFP alone, with ultrasound remaining the surveillance backbone in that study. So GALAD is a better blood test than AFP; whether it detects more early HCC than, or adds enough to, ultrasound surveillance is not established by the carded record.
stamp: POSSIBLE (accuracy verdict) — GALAD detects HCC more accurately than AFP alone (phase 3 validation: AUC 0.78 vs 0.66; sensitivity 62% vs 41% at 82% specificity within 12 months of diagnosis), but a direct prospective comparison against ultrasound ± AFP surveillance has not been done, so superiority over imaging-based surveillance is unproven

title: EMERALD-1: adding durvalumab plus bevacizumab to TACE lengthened progression-free survival (median 15.0 vs 8.2 months; HR 0.77) — one trial, survival data immature, so POSSIBLE
question: In adults with unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma amenable to embolisation, does adding durvalumab plus bevacizumab to transarterial chemoembolisation (TACE) prolong progression-free survival compared with TACE alone? (EMERALD-1.)
balance: A single phase 3 trial answers this exact question, so the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE (single programme). In EMERALD-1 (616 patients randomised 1:1:1), TACE plus durvalumab plus bevacizumab gave a median progression-free survival of 15.0 months versus 8.2 months with TACE plus placebo (HR 0.77, 95% CI 0.61–0.98; p=0.032) — a relative measure, with an absolute median gain of about 6.8 months. Durvalumab without bevacizumab did not significantly improve progression-free survival (10.0 months; HR 0.94, 0.75–1.19) — the bevacizumab component appears necessary. Overall survival was immature at the report and is not claimed on this shelf. The parallel phase 3 trial of a different combination, LEAP-012 (lenvatinib plus pembrolizumab plus TACE, 480 patients), points the same way (median PFS 14.6 vs 10.0 months; HR 0.66), which supports the strategy class but is a different regimen and cannot substitute for replication of EMERALD-1 itself. A 17-study meta-analysis of TACE plus tyrosine-kinase inhibitor plus checkpoint inhibitor versus TACE plus TKI (mostly non-randomised) is carded only as low-grade supportive context. First-line systemic therapy for unresectable HCC is homed on live shelf #850 and adjuvant therapy on pack #1889; TACE versus no TACE is pack #6335.
stamp: POSSIBLE — a single phase 3 trial (EMERALD-1, n=616) found durvalumab plus bevacizumab added to TACE prolonged progression-free survival versus TACE alone (median 15.0 vs 8.2 months; HR 0.77, 95% CI 0.61–0.98); overall survival was immature, and single-trial evidence caps the stamp at POSSIBLE

title: TACE versus supportive care in unresectable HCC: two 2002 randomised trials and their meta-analysis agree — chemoembolisation improves survival in stringently selected patients (2-year survival about 63% and 31% versus 27% and 11%)
question: In adults with intermediate-stage hepatocellular carcinoma, does transarterial chemoembolisation (TACE) improve survival compared with best supportive care or systemic therapy?
balance: Two randomised trials from 2002, in different populations with different regimens, point the same way, and the systematic review of the era confirms the pooled result. Llovet 2002 (112 stringently selected patients, Child-Pugh A or B, Okuda I–II) was stopped early because chemoembolisation (gelatin sponge plus doxorubicin) beat conservative treatment (hazard ratio of death 0.47, 95% CI 0.25–0.91; 2-year survival 63% versus 27%); the embolisation-alone arm sat between (50% at 2 years). Lo 2002 (80 Asian patients, cisplatin in lipiodol) found actuarial survival of 57%, 31% and 26% at 1, 2 and 3 years versus 32%, 11% and 3% with symptomatic treatment (p=.002; adjusted relative risk of death 0.49, 0.29–0.81). Llovet & Bruix 2003 pooled 7 arterial-embolisation trials (545 patients): embolisation improved 2-year survival (odds ratio 0.53, 0.32–0.89), with the benefit carried by chemoembolisation with cisplatin or doxorubicin (OR 0.42) and not by embolisation alone (OR 0.59, not significant). The caveats are selection (both trials enrolled preserved-liver-function patients; Llovet screened 903 to randomise 112) and era (the comparator was symptomatic care, not modern systemic therapy — no trial compares TACE head-to-head with contemporary systemic regimens in intermediate-stage disease). Adding systemic/immune therapy to TACE is pack #6334; first-line systemic therapy is live shelf #850.
stamp: LIKELY — chemoembolisation improves survival versus supportive care in selected patients with unresectable/intermediate-stage HCC (two concordant randomised trials: HR of death 0.47 and adjusted relative risk 0.49; pooled OR for 2-year mortality 0.53), with the benefit specific to chemoembolisation rather than embolisation alone and no randomised comparison against modern systemic therapy

title: Acute gastric variceal bleeding: cyanoacrylate does not beat BRTO — a randomised trial and a cohort both show less rebleeding with BRTO and no mortality difference; the TIPS comparison is indirect only
question: In adults with acute gastric variceal bleeding, does endoscopic cyanoacrylate injection reduce rebleeding and mortality compared with transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS) or balloon-occluded retrograde transvenous obliteration (BRTO)?
balance: The premise of the question — that cyanoacrylate might be the better treatment — is not supported for rebleeding: the comparative evidence runs the other way, and mortality does not differ. In the one randomised head-to-head trial (Luo 2021, 64 patients after primary haemostasis), freedom from all-cause rebleeding at 1 and 2 years was 77% and 65.2% with cyanoacrylate versus 96.3% and 92.6% with BRTO (p=0.004), with similar survival and complications. A retrospective cohort with extended follow-up (Stein 2019, 161 patients treated for bleeding cardiofundal varices) found the same pattern: 1-year rebleeding 22.0% with cyanoacrylate versus 3.5% with BRTO (Cox HR 0.25 for BRTO), 6-week mortality 14.4% versus 13.1% and no long-term mortality difference (HR 0.89). A network meta-analysis of 9 secondary-prophylaxis RCTs (647 patients; Osman 2022) ranked BRTO best for rebleeding (versus cyanoacrylate: relative rate 0.18, 95% CI 0.04–0.77; low certainty) and found no intervention with a proven mortality advantage; its TIPS comparisons are indirect. No carded randomised trial compares cyanoacrylate directly with TIPS for gastric varices — that half of the question is unanswered by direct evidence, and this shelf says so rather than borrowing oesophageal-varix TIPS data. Cyanoacrylate versus band ligation for acute control is a different comparison and is not the question here.
stamp: POSSIBLE — cyanoacrylate is associated with more rebleeding than BRTO (randomised 2-year freedom from rebleeding 65.2% vs 92.6%; cohort 1-year rebleeding 22.0% vs 3.5%) with no mortality difference in either study; for TIPS there is no direct randomised comparison, so no verdict against TIPS can be given

title: Anticoagulation for portal vein thrombosis in cirrhosis: recanalisation up, bleeding not up — on observational evidence, plus one prevention trial
question: In adults with cirrhosis and portal vein thrombosis, does anticoagulation improve recanalisation and survival without increasing bleeding compared with no anticoagulation?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the treatment evidence is observational and is labelled as such. Two meta-analyses of mostly observational studies agree that anticoagulation roughly doubles recanalisation in relative terms (relative risk 2.61 in the 33-study analysis) and lowers thrombus progression, with no excess overall bleeding (11% in both groups in the 2017 analysis); the 2021 analysis also found a small relative survival advantage (relative risk 1.11). A large single-centre cohort found the same pattern (recanalisation in 56.8% treated vs 25.7% untreated; bleeding 19.7% vs 21.8%). Separately, the one randomised trial is a prevention trial: in 70 patients with advanced cirrhosis and patent portal veins, enoxaparin prevented portal vein thrombosis entirely (0% vs 16.6% at 48 weeks) with no haemorrhagic events reported. No randomised trial has tested anticoagulation as treatment for established portal vein thrombosis, so the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: High-volume plasma exchange in acute liver failure: transplant-free survival up in the one randomised trial (Larsen 2016 — no 'FULMAR' acronym in the record)
question: In adults with acute liver failure, does high-volume plasma exchange improve transplant-free survival compared with standard medical therapy?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single randomised trial caps the stamp. In the Larsen 2016 open multicentre randomised trial (182 adults with acute liver failure), high-volume plasma exchange plus standard medical therapy raised overall hospital survival to 58.7% vs 47.8% on standard therapy alone (relative hazard ratio 0.56, stratified for liver transplantation), on a primary endpoint of transplant-free survival; severe adverse events were similar. A 2024 meta-analysis of 8 studies (2 randomised, 6 cohorts) found the same direction for plasma exchange overall (mortality relative risk 0.64 at ≤60 days). The newest aetiology-specific cohort (amatoxin poisoning, retrospective) found no overall difference on its primary outcome, with benefit only in a sicker subgroup. Premise correction: the slate called this trial 'FULMAR' — the published record carries no such acronym; it is an open randomised controlled trial, reported simply as Larsen et al., J Hepatol 2016, NCT00950508.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Felzartamab in transplant antibody-mediated rejection (phase 2 only): biopsy resolution 82% vs 20% in 22 patients — and rejection returned when treatment stopped
question: In kidney transplant recipients with antibody-mediated rejection, does the anti-CD38 antibody felzartamab resolve rejection activity on biopsy compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — based on a very small N = 22. PHASE 2 EVIDENCE ONLY: the whole verdict rests on one phase 2 randomised programme in 22 kidney transplant recipients with late antibody-mediated rejection. At week 24, morphologic rejection had resolved in 9 of 11 patients on felzartamab (82%) vs 2 of 10 on placebo (20%) — a difference of 62 percentage points — but rejection recurred in 3 of the 9 responders by week 52, molecular recurrence was nearly universal after treatment stopped in the biopsy substudy, and an open-label extension retreated 11 patients with recurrent or persistent rejection. No graft-survival or kidney-function outcome has been tested. The N (22) is printed in the stamp line because the total evidence base is under 30 humans.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — based on a very small N = 22

title: SGLT2 inhibitors after kidney transplant: one small randomised trial (n=49) shows a modest HbA1c fall and weight loss with no eGFR or drug-level change; observational cohorts and a pooled synthesis agree on glycaemia and stable graft function, with urinary infection the main cost — graft-survival benefit is association only
question: In kidney transplant recipients with diabetes or post-transplant diabetes, do SGLT2 inhibitors improve glycaemic control and graft outcomes without increasing infection?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — evidence mix labelled on the face: one small randomised trial plus observational cohorts and a synthesis of mostly observational studies; observational evidence caps this shelf at POSSIBLE. The randomised trial (Halden 2019, n=49 randomised, 44 completing) found empagliflozin lowered HbA1c modestly against placebo (median change −0.2% vs +0.1%, P=0.025) and cut weight (−2.5 kg vs +1.0 kg), with no significant difference in adverse events, immunosuppressive drug levels or eGFR over 24 weeks. The pooled synthesis (Bellos 2024; SGLT2 inhibitor given to 1,003 recipients across 17 observational studies and the one trial) found HbA1c lower by a mean difference of −0.40% and weight by −2.21 kg, no difference in eGFR, and a urinary-tract-infection odds ratio of 0.84 (95% CI 0.43–1.64) versus control — no infection excess in the pooled estimate, though single-centre cohorts report urinary infection as the commonest adverse event (10 of 39 patients in Lemke 2022 had an adverse event, urinary infection most common; 43% had stopped the drug, mostly for cost or kidney-function decline). The largest single-centre pre/post cohort (Angjeli 2024, n=125) found eGFR essentially unchanged (64.6 before vs 64.3 mL/min/1.73 m² after), no difference in mean HbA1c, urinary infection 13.6% before vs 12% after (the treatment made no difference), and new genital mycotic infection in 4%. Graft outcomes: no carded study is powered for graft survival; the synthesis's reported association with less graft loss and mortality is preliminary observational data and is presented as such, not as a proven graft benefit. PROPOSED STAMP: POSSIBLE (benefit).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: BK nephropathy: immunosuppression reduction is the accepted backbone — pooled graft loss 8 per 100 patient-years — but adding cidofovir or leflunomide showed no graft-survival benefit in the pooled observational record, and the one randomised adjunct test (levofloxacin prophylaxis) was null with more resistance
question: In kidney transplant recipients with BK polyomavirus nephropathy, does reducing immunosuppression (with or without adjuncts such as leflunomide, cidofovir or a fluoroquinolone) improve graft survival compared with standard immunosuppression?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational evidence, labelled: apart from one randomised prophylaxis trial, every treatment datum on this shelf is observational, which caps the stamp at POSSIBLE. The systematic review of all published treatment (Johnston 2010; 40 studies) found death-censored graft loss of 8 per 100 patient-years with immunosuppression reduction alone, 8 per 100 patient-years when cidofovir was added, and 13 per 100 patient-years when leflunomide was added — no graft-survival benefit from either adjunct, on a poor evidence base the authors themselves flag. The long-term clinicopathological cohort managed with immunosuppression reduction (Drachenberg 2017; 71 patients, mean follow-up 3.09 years after reduction) recorded graft loss of 15.4%, complete viral clearance in 76% (mean 28 weeks), and rejection in 38% of patients overall — reduction works virologically but the rejection it invites is the main predictor of graft loss. A 2024 comparative cohort (Cho; 175 patients with BK viraemia) found tacrolimus dose reduction cleared virus at least as well as converting to an mTOR inhibitor, with less biopsy-proven rejection at lower viral loads and no difference in 12-month renal function. The one randomised adjunct test is null: levofloxacin prophylaxis did not prevent BK viruria (Knoll 2014; hazard ratio 0.91) and increased resistant infections (the prophylaxis made no difference to BK outcomes). PROPOSED STAMP: POSSIBLE (benefit) for immunosuppression reduction as the backbone; adjuncts unproven.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: The alveolar gas equation and the A–a gradient: alveolar PO2 is set by inspired oxygen, barometric pressure and the PaCO2/respiratory-quotient term; the gradient across to arterial blood is small at rest in health, widens with age and at high exercise intensity, and widens early in lung disease through V/Q mismatch
question: How does the alveolar gas equation determine alveolar oxygen tension, and what determines the size of the alveolar–arterial oxygen gradient in health and disease?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology and Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology, gas-exchange chapters). The textbook account: alveolar oxygen tension is given by the alveolar gas equation — PAO2 = FiO2 × (barometric pressure − water-vapour pressure) − PaCO2/R, where R is the respiratory exchange ratio — so alveolar PO2 rises with inspired oxygen and falls as PaCO2 rises. Arterial PO2 sits below alveolar PO2 by the alveolar–arterial (A–a) gradient, whose textbook determinants are ventilation–perfusion (V/Q) inequality (the dominant term even in health), anatomical shunt/venous admixture, and, at high cardiac outputs or in disease, alveolar–capillary diffusion limitation; mixed venous oxygen content modulates the effect of any given mismatch. The carded human studies fit that frame. In 78 healthy elderly subjects the A–a difference stayed within a maximum of 20.2 Torr while PaO2 fell only slowly with age (regression slope −0.126 Torr per year) (Yamasawa 1992). During incremental exercise in 6 healthy men the gradient barely moved at low work rates and then rose rapidly past a threshold at high metabolic rates (Powers 1991; N=6, labelled). In mild COPD — FEV1 still 94% predicted — the gradient was already elevated at rest and throughout exercise, alongside higher dead-space fraction (Elbehairy 2015). Note: the classic Mellemgaard 1966 components study was located by title search this session but its PubMed record carries no abstract, so no numbers could be sourced from a fetched record and it is NOT carded, per the standing rule. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED

title: Shunt and venous admixture: the shunt equation divides the flow that bypasses ventilated alveoli by total flow using oxygen contents; 100% oxygen can fully oxygenate blood passing even poorly ventilated units, but blood that never sees an alveolus stays venous — so shunt hypoxaemia is oxygen-refractory, and inert-gas studies show healthy lungs have essentially no shunt on air
question: What is intrapulmonary shunt and venous admixture, how is the shunt fraction calculated, and why does breathing 100% oxygen correct hypoxaemia from ventilation–perfusion mismatch but not from true shunt?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology and Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology, pulmonary circulation/gas-exchange chapters). The textbook account: venous admixture is the amount of mixed venous blood that must be added to fully oxygenated end-capillary blood to produce the observed arterial oxygen content, and the shunt fraction follows the shunt equation — Qs/Qt = (Cc′O2 − CaO2)/(Cc′O2 − CvO2), using end-capillary, arterial and mixed venous oxygen contents. True shunt is blood traversing unventilated units (V/Q = 0); low-V/Q units are not shunt, because raising inspired oxygen raises their alveolar PO2 until their end-capillary blood is fully saturated — which is why 100% oxygen corrects V/Q hypoxaemia but cannot correct the shunted fraction, whose blood never contacts alveolar gas. The carded human studies anchor each limb. In 12 normal subjects the inert-gas method found no intrapulmonary shunt breathing air at any age; on 100% oxygen a small shunt appeared (mean 0.5% of cardiac output in the young, 3.2% in older subjects) — absorption collapse of low-V/Q units, exactly as the textbook predicts (Wagner 1974). In 20 patients with acute respiratory failure, venous admixture was 12–63% and fell from 29% to 24% when FiO2 was raised to 1.0 while the inert-gas (true) shunt was unchanged (Lemaire 1985). And the shunt equation works in reverse at the bedside: assuming constant venous admixture, PaO2 at lower FiO2 was predicted from 100%-oxygen data with a regression coefficient of 0.97 in 19 ventilated patients (Ogawa 1989). PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

title: West's zones plus hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction: gravity stacks alveolar, arterial and venous pressures into flow zones from apex to base, imaging confirms posture redistributes flow — but lung structure outweighs gravity — and alveolar hypoxia constricts the feeding vessels within minutes, a response reversed by inhaled nitric oxide and blunted by volatile anaesthetics
question: How do West's zones of the lung and hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction together determine pulmonary vascular pressures and blood-flow distribution, and what inhibits hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology and Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology, pulmonary circulation chapters). The textbook account of West's zones: in the upright lung, alveolar pressure is roughly uniform while pulmonary arterial and venous pressures rise down the lung under gravity, so flow is set zone by zone — zone 1 (alveolar pressure exceeds arterial: no flow, normally absent), zone 2 (arterial exceeds alveolar exceeds venous: flow set by the arterial–alveolar difference), zone 3 (venous exceeds alveolar: flow set by the arterial–venous difference), with a zone 4 at the base from interstitial pressure. Superimposed on gravity, hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction (the Euler–Liljestrand mechanism) constricts vessels feeding hypoxic alveoli and diverts blood to ventilated units. The carded human studies support both layers — and qualify the first: perfusion per unit volume rose from upper to lower regions in upright and most other postures in 14 normal volunteers (Amis 1984), and flipping volunteers from upright to head-down clearly redistributed flow from base to apex, yet the authors concluded lung structure is the main determinant and gravity secondary (Ax 2017; N=8, labelled). HPV is directly demonstrable in humans: breathing 12% oxygen raised mean pulmonary artery pressure from 14.7 to 19.8 mmHg in 9 healthy adults, and inhaled nitric oxide (40 ppm) reversed it selectively, with no systemic effect (Frostell 1993; N=9, labelled). What inhibits HPV in practice: volatile anaesthetics — during one-lung ventilation, shunt fraction fell significantly when patients were switched from isoflurane or sevoflurane to propofol, which does not share the inhibition (Abe 1998). The MIGET anchors folded into this row (Wagner's inert-gas distributions) are carded on shelf #6350 for the shunt measurement and are the same dataset that mapped these V/Q distributions. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED
