title: CO2 transport: most CO2 travels as bicarbonate made inside the red cell by carbonic anhydrase, with chloride shifting in as bicarbonate leaves (the chloride shift); deoxygenated haemoglobin carries more CO2 and buffers the protons (the Haldane effect — 78% of the PaCO2 rise when hypoxic patients breathe oxygen), while CO2 and protons lower oxygen affinity in the tissues (the Bohr effect)
question: How is carbon dioxide transported in blood — as bicarbonate, carbamino compounds and dissolved gas — and how do the chloride shift, the Bohr effect and the Haldane effect link oxygen and carbon dioxide carriage?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology and Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology, respiratory chapters). The textbook account: CO2 leaves the tissues in three forms — dissolved, as carbamino compounds with haemoglobin and plasma proteins, and, for the bulk of the load, as bicarbonate: inside the red cell, carbonic anhydrase hydrates CO2 to carbonic acid, the proton is buffered by haemoglobin, bicarbonate exits to plasma on the band-3 exchanger, and chloride enters in its place (the chloride shift, or Hamburger phenomenon), reversing in the lungs. Two linkages couple the gases: the Bohr effect — CO2 and protons reduce haemoglobin's oxygen affinity, unloading oxygen where CO2 is produced — and its reciprocal, the Haldane effect — deoxygenated haemoglobin binds more CO2 and more protons, so oxygen unloading in the tissues promotes CO2 loading, and oxygenation in the lungs promotes CO2 release. The carded human studies quantify the linkages in people. In 20 severely hypoxic, hypercapnic patients, the Haldane shift accounted for 78% of the PaCO2 rise seen when they breathed 100% oxygen (Luft 1981). A regression built from 247 patient measurements expresses the Haldane contribution to venous PCO2 as a function of the arteriovenous HbO2 difference and haematocrit with r²=0.99 (Giovannini 1999). In human whole blood exposed to CO2-rich gas, plasma bicarbonate rose as plasma chloride fell — the chloride shift measured directly (Hirakawa 1993; human component n=9, labelled). And blocking the enzyme that starts the bicarbonate limb has the predicted in-vivo consequence: acetazolamide in 10 ventilated patients retained CO2 and shifted the oxygen dissociation curve rightward by the Bohr mechanism, as the authors describe (Berthelsen 1987). The textbook's percentage split between the three carriage forms is presented as the textbook's account; no carded record in this session prints that split, so it is not claimed as a carded number. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

title: Oxygen delivery, the Fick principle and DO2crit: above a critical delivery, consumption is set by metabolic demand and extraction rises as delivery falls; below it, consumption falls with delivery and lactate rises — the biphasic relation is demonstrated in humans, with the threshold near 330 mL/min/m² in anaesthetised surgical patients but only 3.8–4.5 mL/min/kg in dying critically ill patients, and sepsis did not move it
question: What are oxygen delivery and oxygen consumption, what determines critical oxygen delivery (DO2crit), and when does oxygen consumption become supply-dependent?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology and Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology, circulation/tissue-oxygen chapters). The textbook account: oxygen delivery (DO2) is cardiac output multiplied by arterial oxygen content, and oxygen consumption (VO2) follows from the Fick principle — VO2 = cardiac output × (arterial − mixed venous oxygen content). As delivery falls, tissues first compensate by extracting a larger fraction of the delivered oxygen, so consumption stays constant (supply independence); below a critical delivery (DO2crit), extraction can rise no further, consumption falls in proportion to delivery (supply dependence), and anaerobic metabolism with lactate production begins. The carded human studies demonstrate the biphasic curve directly and show the threshold is context-dependent, not a universal constant. In 58 anaesthetised surgical patients the critical value was 330 mL/min/m² (8.2 mL/min/kg), with consumption plateauing at 109 ± 16 mL/min/m² above it (Shibutani 1983). In 18 critically ill patients studied as life support was withdrawn, the biphasic relation appeared in every individual, with DO2crit of 3.8 ± 1.5 (septic) vs 4.5 ± 1.3 mL/min/kg (nonseptic) — no significant difference, and considerably lower than older pooled-group estimates (Ronco 1993). And supply dependence is a state, not a trait: the same 10 septic patients showed VO2 tracking DO2 during shock (extraction fixed) but not after recovery, when extraction adjusted and VO2 stayed constant (Friedman 1998). Any single textbook DO2crit number is therefore the textbook's simplification; the carded human values are the two measured settings above. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

title: Surfactant, Laplace's law and interdependence: Laplace's law says a smaller alveolus needs a higher collapsing pressure unless surface tension falls as it shrinks — surfactant does exactly that, and human material proves the point in reverse: lungs low in lecithin could not lower surface tension and developed hyaline membranes, and lavage surfactant from diseased human lungs bottoms out at 15–20 mN/m instead of near zero
question: How does surfactant lower alveolar surface tension (Laplace's law), stabilise alveoli of different sizes, and what is alveolar interdependence?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology and Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology, respiratory mechanics chapters). The textbook account: the pressure tending to collapse a spherical alveolus follows Laplace's law, P = 2T/r — at equal surface tension a smaller alveolus would need the higher pressure and would empty into its larger neighbour. Surfactant breaks that instability because its surface tension is area-dependent: as an alveolus shrinks, the surfactant film compresses and tension falls steeply, so small alveoli are not squeezed out; as it expands, tension rises, checking overdistension. Alveolar interdependence is the mechanical complement — alveoli share walls, so surrounding parenchyma tethers any unit that starts to collapse and pulls it back open. The carded human studies are the deficiency and dysfunction experiments nature and disease provide. In 95 stillbirths and neonatal deaths, lung lecithin content was negatively correlated with the minimum surface tension of lung extract, and lungs with hyaline membranes sat in the low-lecithin range (Boughton 1970). Healthy human lavage surfactant reaches a minimum surface tension of about 0–3.4 mN/m on a pulsating bubble surfactometer; after lung transplantation it could only reach 15.8 ± 1.1 mN/m (Hohlfeld 1998), and in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis about 15–20 mN/m versus ~0 in controls (Günther 1999) — when the film cannot lower tension, the Laplace instability the textbook describes is what the lung lives with. Note: the founding Avery & Mead 1959 study was located by title search this session, but its PubMed record carries no abstract, so no numbers could be sourced from a fetched record and it is NOT carded, per the standing rule; Boughton 1970 supplies the carded human lecithin–tension relation. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

title: Diaphragm fatigue and the tension–time index: TTdi multiplies the pressure load (mean Pdi as a fraction of maximum) by the duty cycle (Ti/Ttot); above a critical TTdi of about 0.15–0.18 the human diaphragm cannot sustain the pattern — endurance falls below an hour and the EMG fatigue signature appears — while resting breathing, even in COPD, normally sits well below the threshold
question: What is diaphragm fatigue, how is it quantified by the tension–time index of the diaphragm, and at what threshold does the diaphragm fatigue?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology and Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology, respiratory-muscle chapters; the tension–time framework is Bellemare & Grassino's). The textbook account: a rhythmically contracting muscle fatigues when the product of its relative force and its duty cycle exceeds what its blood supply can service. For the diaphragm that product is the tension–time index, TTdi = (mean transdiaphragmatic pressure / maximal transdiaphragmatic pressure) × (inspiratory time / total breath time). The carded human studies fix the threshold. Bellemare & Grassino's programme found the fatigue threshold in normal subjects at a TTdi of about 15% of maximum: in their COPD study, resting TTdi ran 1–12% (mean 5%), but when 5 patients raised their TTdi to an imposed 17%, the diaphragm's EMG developed the fatigue pattern seen in normals at similar levels (Bellemare 1983). The companion EMG study in 5 normal subjects showed the high/low-frequency power ratio decaying at a rate monotonically (hyperbolically) related to Pdi × Ti/Ttot, with the decay rate predicting how long the pattern could be sustained (Bellemare 1982; N=5, labelled). Zocchi 1993 independently reproduced the diaphragm figure — above a critical TTdi of 0.15–0.18, endurance is under an hour and falls as TTdi rises — and showed the rib-cage muscles have their own, higher critical index (0.30) when they are the predominantly recruited group (N=4, labelled). PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

title: Tubuloglomerular feedback: the macula densa reads distal NaCl and, through adenosine-mediated afferent constriction, trims single-nephron GFR — but in humans the loop has never been measured at the nephron; the human evidence is three indirect drug-perturbation studies, so this shelf is stamped EMERGING and says so plainly
question: How does tubuloglomerular feedback work — what does the macula densa sense, and how does it adjust afferent arteriolar tone and renin release?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING — thin-human-evidence flag, stated plainly as the slate required: tubuloglomerular feedback (TGF) as a mechanism rests on animal micropuncture; in humans it has never been measured at the single nephron, and every human datum on this shelf is an indirect inference from a drug perturbation. The textbook account (Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology; Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology): the macula densa cells of the juxtaglomerular apparatus sense NaCl concentration in the tubular fluid leaving the loop of Henle (via Na-K-2Cl cotransport); rising NaCl delivery signals that filtration is more than sufficient, and — through adenosine acting on the afferent arteriole — constricts it, lowering single-nephron GFR, while falling NaCl delivery dilates the arteriole and releases renin. The human studies are consistent with that loop but cannot isolate it. Blocking proximal sodium-glucose reabsorption with empagliflozin increased distal delivery and attenuated hyperfiltration by 33 mL/min/1.73 m² in type 1 diabetes, an effect the authors attribute to TGF mechanisms, accompanied by a rise in renal vascular resistance (Cherney 2014). Blocking proximal salt reabsorption with acetazolamide in obese hyperfiltering men cut GFR by 21% while equipotent furosemide — which blocks the macula densa's own cotransporter — did not, the cleanest human pharmacological dissociation available (Zingerman 2015; N=12). Blocking the proposed mediator tells a weaker story: the adenosine antagonist theophylline did not preserve GFR beyond hydration in contrast studies, though it blunted a tubular-injury marker (Erley 1999) — a null glomerular result, printed as such. Renin-release control at the same apparatus — the baroreceptor, sympathetic and macula-densa inputs to the juxtaglomerular cell — is homed on pack #6305 and cross-pointed, not re-carded here; this shelf is only the feedback's glomerular arm. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING, because the human base is indirect inference, however concordant.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING

title: Countercurrent multiplication: the loop of Henle builds the medullary gradient, urea recycling sustains it, medullary blood flow can wash it out — and the human ceiling is about 1,000 mOsm/kg, falling with age
question: How does countercurrent multiplication build the medullary osmotic gradient, what washes it out (medullary blood flow, urea recycling), and what is the concentrating ceiling — the maximum urine osmolality a healthy human kidney can reach?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. The textbook account (Guyton & Hall; Boron & Boulpaep) is the framing: countercurrent multiplication in the loop of Henle — NaCl extruded in the water-impermeable thick ascending limb, diluted tubular fluid leaving the loop, and single effects stacked along the corticomedullary axis — builds a medullary interstitial gradient that the vasa recta preserve by countercurrent exchange; urea recycling from the inner medullary collecting duct contributes roughly half the inner medullary osmolality in the textbook's account, and vasopressin-regulated water reabsorption lets final urine approach medullary osmolality. The textbook ceiling of about 1,200 mOsm/kg is the textbook's account: no record fetched this session confirms it directly, and the largest human series carded here measured a mean ceiling near 982 mOsm/kg in 20-year-olds after desmopressin, falling to 823 mOsm/kg by age 80. The human studies carded confirm the three load-bearing pieces in people: the ceiling and its age decline (Tryding, n=212), washout — concentrating capacity fell when medullary blood flow rose in acute pyelonephritis and recovered as flow normalised (Berg, n=14 children) — and the protein/urea dependence of concentrating activity (Hadj-Aïssa, n=10: free-water reabsorption rose 70% after a protein meal under low hydration and tracked urine urea). Animal micropuncture mechanism is textbook prose only, never a card, on this shelf.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED

title: Renal acid excretion: titratable acid is capped by phosphate supply, ammonium is the adaptable limb — and in CKD each surviving nephron makes more ammonia even as total ammonium excretion falls
question: How does the kidney excrete acid — titratable acid versus ammonium — and how does ammonium excretion adapt as chronic kidney disease progresses?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. The textbook account (Guyton & Hall; Boron & Boulpaep) is the framing: net acid excretion equals titratable acid plus ammonium minus bicarbonate; titratable acid is limited by the supply of urinary buffers, chiefly phosphate, and cannot rise much, whereas ammonium — made from glutamine in the proximal tubule — is the adaptable limb that rises severalfold under a sustained acid load. The carded human studies show both limbs and the CKD twist. In healthy people, glutamine delivery is rate-limiting for ammonium excretion, including after acid-loading adaptation (Welbourne 1972); in renal disease it is not — surviving mass and enzyme activity limit instead. In advanced chronic renal failure, total ammonium excretion was roughly a third of normal (11 vs 32 mEq/day) and titratable acid also fell (18 vs 28 mEq/day), yet expressed per 100 mL of GFR both were markedly increased (Ray 1990): per-nephron adaptation is real but cannot offset nephron loss, which is why acidosis supervenes as CKD advances. The CRIC analysis (Khairallah 2017, n=980) shows the titratable-acid limb being pushed in CKD — higher net acid excretion tracked higher urinary phosphate excretion, the adaptation that supplies more buffer. Healthy acid-load adaptation as a standalone question is a separate later slate row; this pack stays on mechanism plus CKD progression.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED

title: Hepatic extraction ratio: high-extraction drugs are flow-limited and lost to first pass, low-extraction drugs are capacity-limited — shown in humans by what a portacaval shunt does to each kind
question: What is the hepatic extraction ratio, how does it determine the first-pass effect and the difference between high- and low-extraction drugs, and how do liver blood flow versus intrinsic clearance each limit hepatic clearance?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. The textbook account (Guyton & Hall; Boron & Boulpaep) is the framing: the extraction ratio E is the fraction of drug removed in one pass through the liver; hepatic clearance equals liver blood flow times E; oral bioavailability falls toward 1 − E, which is the first-pass effect. For a high-extraction drug E approaches 1, clearance tracks blood flow, and most of an oral dose never reaches the systemic circulation; for a low-extraction drug clearance tracks intrinsic clearance — enzyme capacity and unbound fraction — and barely notices flow. The carded human studies demonstrate each pole in people. A surgical portacaval shunt that cut hepatic blood flow by 65% halved the systemic clearance of high-extraction indocyanine green and lidocaine in milder cirrhosis while leaving intrinsic clearance unchanged and driving oral bioavailability to 1, and left the low-extraction aminopyrine breath test untouched in both severity groups (Pomier-Layrargues 1986, n=35). In 99 healthy volunteers, apparent oral clearance of the CYP3A probes midazolam and alfentanil ran roughly 4-fold and 2.5-fold above their systemic clearances — first pass measured, not theorised (Kharasch 2007). And the classic paediatric disposition study found the same high-extraction, large-first-pass behaviour for propranolol in children, with wide individual variability (Wilson 1976).
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED

title: Thrombectomy for medium-vessel occlusion stroke: no functional benefit in DISTAL or ESCAPE-MeVO (the treatment made no difference) — with more symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage
question: In patients with acute ischaemic stroke from a medium-vessel occlusion, does endovascular thrombectomy improve functional outcome compared with best medical care?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — two large randomised trials and a study-level meta-analysis of all three completed trials agree. DISTAL (n=543) found no difference in 90-day disability between endovascular treatment plus best medical treatment and best medical treatment alone (common odds ratio for improvement 0.90, 95% CI 0.67 to 1.22), and ESCAPE-MeVO (n=530) found excellent outcome (modified Rankin scale 0–1) in 41.6% with thrombectomy versus 43.1% with usual care (adjusted rate ratio 0.95, 95% CI 0.79 to 1.15). Both trials showed numerically more symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage with intervention (5.9% vs 2.6%; 5.4% vs 2.2%), and ESCAPE-MeVO showed higher 90-day mortality with thrombectomy (13.3% vs 8.4%; adjusted hazard ratio 1.82, 95% CI 1.06 to 3.12). The meta-analysis pooling DISTAL, ESCAPE-MeVO and DISCOUNT found no functional benefit (relative risk 0.92) and more than double the odds of symptomatic haemorrhage (odds ratio 2.38, 95% CI 1.35 to 4.20). The large-vessel thrombectomy benefit does not extend to medium-vessel occlusion on this record.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference)

title: Restarting antiplatelet therapy after intracerebral haemorrhage: RESTART found no increase in recurrent haemorrhage — recurrence was numerically lower on antiplatelets (4% vs 9%)
question: In survivors of intracerebral haemorrhage who need antiplatelet therapy, does restarting it increase recurrent intracerebral haemorrhage compared with avoiding antiplatelet therapy?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — a single trial programme caps the stamp. RESTART randomised 537 intracerebral haemorrhage survivors who had been on antithrombotic therapy to start or avoid antiplatelet therapy; over a median 2.0 years, recurrent symptomatic intracerebral haemorrhage occurred in 12 of 268 (4%) allocated to antiplatelets versus 23 of 268 (9%) allocated to avoid (adjusted hazard ratio 0.51, 95% CI 0.25 to 1.03; P = 0.060) — restarting did not increase recurrence, and the point estimate leant the other way. Major haemorrhagic events (7% vs 9%) and major occlusive vascular events (15% vs 14%) were likewise similar. Extended follow-up to a median 3.0 years kept the same shape (recurrent haemorrhage 8.2% vs 9.3%; adjusted hazard ratio 0.87, 95% CI 0.49 to 1.55). The 2023 Cochrane review of antithrombotic treatment after intracerebral haemorrhage (9 randomised trials, 1,491 participants) is carded as context: RESTART remains the substantive long-term antiplatelet trial inside it. Restarting anticoagulation is a different drug class and question, answered elsewhere; this shelf is antiplatelets only.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference)

title: Entacapine as a levodopa adjunct in Parkinson's wearing-off: off-time fell by about 1 to 1.5 hours a day across NOMECOMT, SEESAW and Celomen — bought with more dyskinesia and diarrhoea
question: In people with Parkinson's disease and wearing-off on levodopa, does adding entacapine reduce daily off-time compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — three concordant placebo-controlled trials of the same programme plus a Cochrane synthesis, held at POSSIBLE because the trials are 24-week, diary-based and industry-era, and the benefit is modest. NOMECOMT (n=171, 6 months) cut off-time from 5.3 to 4.2 hours a day on entacapine 200 mg with each levodopa dose while on-time rose from 9.3 to 10.7 hours. The Parkinson Study Group trial (SEESAW; n=205, 24 weeks) raised the percentage of waking on-time by 5.0 percentage points. Celomen (n=301, 24 weeks) increased on-time 1.7 hours and decreased off-time 1.5 hours on entacapine versus 0.5 and 0.6 hours on placebo. The Cochrane review of COMT inhibitors (14 trials, 2,566 patients; 8 entacapine trials, 1,560 patients) concluded entacapine reduced off-time and levodopa dose and modestly improved motor impairment, at the cost of more dyskinesia, nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea. Benefit was lost on withdrawal in both trials that tested it — entacapine extends each levodopa dose; it does not modify the disease. (The drug is entacapine, a catechol-O-methyltransferase inhibitor — the slate's 'entacapone' was a misspelling.)
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Virtual reality for post-stroke upper-limb rehabilitation: no advantage over recreational activity in the one large matched-dose trial (EVREST); pooled effects are small and clearest when VR simply adds therapy time
question: In stroke survivors, does virtual-reality-based therapy improve upper-limb function compared with conventional therapy of the same intensity?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence). At matched therapy intensity — the comparison this question asks for — the one large trial was null: in EVREST (n=141), non-immersive virtual-reality Wii training added to conventional rehabilitation was not superior to simple recreational activities (cards, bingo, ball games) on the Wolf Motor Function Test (adjusted difference 4.1 s, 95% CI −14.4 to 22.6), with equal conventional-therapy time in both arms. The 2025 Cochrane update (190 trials, 7,188 participants) found a small pooled advantage over alternative therapy for upper-limb function (SMD 0.20, 95% CI 0.12 to 0.28; low-certainty evidence), and a larger effect when virtual reality was added on top of usual care (SMD 0.42, 0.26 to 0.58; moderate certainty) — a comparison in which the virtual-reality group simply received more therapy, so the gain may be a dose effect rather than an effect of the medium. Most trials are small (only 19% enrolled more than 50 participants; the largest enrolled 152), and one small 2026 trial reporting very large effects (PMID 42581516) is carded with that caution on its face. Virtual reality is a reasonable, safe way to deliver engaging practice; the evidence that the technology itself beats equal-intensity conventional therapy is weak.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence)

title: Hemiplegic shoulder pain after stroke: strapping delays pain onset by about 2 weeks but does not reduce it; electrical stimulation does not change pain; injection evidence rests on small trials and a network meta-analysis
question: In stroke survivors with hemiplegic shoulder pain or at risk of it, do strapping/taping, electrical stimulation, or corticosteroid injection prevent or reduce shoulder pain compared with usual care?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — every modality here rests on a small base, and the totals are printed on the face as the row requires: electrical stimulation, 4 trials and 170 patients (Cochrane); strapping and supportive devices, 4 trials and 142 participants (Cochrane); injection therapies, 17 studies and 595 participants in a network meta-analysis that includes non-randomised studies, plus one 60-patient randomised trial of injection technique. Electrical stimulation did not change pain incidence (OR 0.64, 95% CI 0.19 to 2.14) or pain intensity (SMD 0.13, −1.0 to 1.25), though it improved pain-free passive lateral rotation and reduced subluxation severity. Strapping delayed the onset of pain by about 14 days (WMD 14 days, 9.7 to 17.8) but did not reduce pain severity, improve function or prevent contracture; a hemisling was associated with more pain (Peto OR 8.7, 1.1 to 67.1). For injections, the network analysis ranked suprascapular nerve block best at 4 weeks and intramuscular botulinum toxin best between weeks 4 and 24 against placebo, while the one steroid-injection trial compared two injection targets against each other (dual-target better than single-target), not steroid against usual care. No modality has a large, definitive trial; positioning, handling and analgesia remain the untested usual-care backdrop.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence)

title: Stroke telerehabilitation: outcomes match in-person therapy in the trials done so far (Cochrane: no difference in daily-living ability; the one dose-matched trial met non-inferiority) — comparable, not better
question: In stroke survivors, is telerehabilitation as effective as in-person rehabilitation (or better than usual care) for activities of daily living and motor recovery?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the benefit claimed here is equivalence, not superiority, and the stamp is held at POSSIBLE because the pooled comparisons are thin. The Cochrane review (22 trials, 1,937 participants) found no difference in activities of daily living between post-discharge telerehabilitation and usual care (SMD −0.00, 95% CI −0.15 to 0.15; moderate-quality evidence, 661 participants) or between telerehabilitation and in-person physical therapy (SMD 0.03, −0.43 to 0.48; low-quality, 75 participants), and no difference in upper-limb function versus in-person therapy. The largest single head-to-head trial (Cramer 2019, n=124) delivered dose-matched arm therapy at home by telerehabilitation versus in clinic and met its non-inferiority criterion (adjusted Fugl-Meyer change difference 0.06 points, −2.14 to 2.26, against a 2.47-point margin), with higher adherence at home (98.3% vs 93.3% of sessions). A 2023 meta-analysis found a small Barthel Index advantage for telerehabilitation (MD 4.18 points, 1.79 to 6.57). Nothing here shows telerehabilitation beating good in-person care; the case for it is access — comparable outcomes for patients who cannot reach a clinic. No trial in the Cochrane review evaluated cost-effectiveness.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Family-led rehabilitation after stroke: the one large trial (ATTEND, n=1,250) was neutral — death or dependency 47% in both groups; smaller caregiver-mediated exercise studies point the other way on daily-living scores
question: In stroke survivors discharged home, does a family-led, caregiver-delivered rehabilitation programme improve death or dependency compared with usual care?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — this shelf rests principally on a single large trial, and it is labelled as such: ATTEND (n=1,250, 14 hospitals in India) trained family caregivers to deliver rehabilitation started in hospital and continued at home, and found death or dependency at 6 months in 47% of both groups (OR 0.98, 95% CI 0.78 to 1.23, p=0.87), with no difference in mortality, rehospitalisation or non-fatal events. A single-trial null caps the stamp at POSSIBLE. The surrounding evidence is genuinely two-sided: a small Dutch trial of caregiver-mediated exercises with telerehabilitation (41 dyads) was also null on its primary mobility outcome, while a meta-analysis of 11 caregiver-mediated exercise trials (2,120 participants) found a statistically significant benefit for basic activities of daily living — a softer outcome than ATTEND's death-or-dependency endpoint, in programmes where exercise was the major component. The fair summary: the ATTEND model, as delivered, did not reduce death or dependency; whether more intensive or better-supported caregiver exercise programmes improve daily-living scores remains open.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference)

title: Ibudilast in progressive MS (SPRINT-MS): brain atrophy progressed more slowly on ibudilast (about 2.5 mL less tissue loss over 96 weeks) — a phase 2 imaging result with no proven clinical benefit yet
question: In people with primary or secondary progressive multiple sclerosis, does ibudilast slow brain atrophy progression compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single phase 2 programme, so the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE. In SPRINT-MS (n=255, primary and secondary progressive MS, 96 weeks), ibudilast up to 100 mg daily slowed the rate of brain atrophy versus placebo: the brain parenchymal fraction changed by −0.0010 per year versus −0.0019 per year (difference 0.0009, 95% CI 0.00004 to 0.0017; P=0.04), which the investigators equate to roughly 2.5 mL less brain-tissue loss over 96 weeks. A secondary MRI analysis found 35% less gray-matter atrophy (a relative measure; p=0.038) but no reduction in new or enlarging T2 lesions (37.2% vs 29.0%; p=0.82) or new T1 lesions — a neurodegeneration-marker effect without an anti-inflammatory lesion effect. The earlier relapsing-MS phase 2 trial (n=297) likewise found no effect on new active lesions or relapses, with a smaller percent brain volume change at the 60 mg dose (0.8% vs 1.2%; p=0.04). No trial has shown ibudilast slows disability progression on a clinical primary endpoint, and adverse events included gastrointestinal symptoms, headache and depression. An imaging signal in search of a phase 3 clinical confirmation.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Opicinumab (anti-LINGO-1) in relapsing MS: a negative programme — SYNERGY, RENEW and AFFINITY all missed their primary endpoints (the treatment made no difference)
question: In people with relapsing multiple sclerosis, does opicinumab added to interferon beta improve disability recovery compared with interferon beta alone?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — three randomised trials of the anti-LINGO-1 remyelination programme, and every primary endpoint missed. SYNERGY (n=419, opicinumab added to intramuscular interferon beta-1a in relapsing MS) found confirmed disability improvement in 49% on placebo versus 47–65% across opicinumab doses with no linear dose–response (trend p=0.89) — a non-monotonic pattern the authors did not claim as efficacy. RENEW (n=82, acute optic neuritis) missed its remyelination primary endpoint in the intention-to-treat population (visual evoked potential latency difference −3.5 ms, 95% CI −10.6 to 3.7; p=0.33), with a nominally positive per-protocol analysis (p=0.050) that cannot carry the claim. AFFINITY Part 1 (n=263, opicinumab added to disease-modifying therapies) found an Overall Disability Response Score difference of 0.15 (−0.05 to 0.35; p=0.148), not significant. The shelf's question names the interferon-beta comparison (SYNERGY's design); RENEW and AFFINITY are carded as the rest of the same programme, and their designs are stated on their faces. A well-conducted negative programme: remyelination by LINGO-1 blockade, at these doses and timings, did not translate into measurable recovery.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference)

title: Citicoline in acute ischaemic stroke: SPLIT — an early pooled analysis was positive (recovery 25.2% vs 20.2%), but the definitive ICTUS trial (n=2,298) and the Cochrane review found no benefit
question: In patients with acute ischaemic stroke, does citicoline improve functional outcome compared with placebo?
balance: SPLIT — the evidence genuinely divides by era and size, and the split is named here rather than averaged away. The early trials, pooled patient-by-patient in 2002 (4 trials; 1,372 patients analysed), found complete recovery at 3 months in 25.2% on citicoline versus 20.2% on placebo (OR 1.33, 95% CI 1.10 to 1.62) — the result that kept citicoline licensed for stroke in some countries. The definitive test then disagreed: ICTUS (n=2,298, moderate-to-severe stroke) was stopped for futility, with global recovery odds ratio 1.03 (0.86 to 1.25; p=0.364) — the treatment made no difference. The 2020 Cochrane review (10 trials, 4,281 participants, all at high risk of bias) found little or no difference in mortality (17.3% vs 18.5%; RR 0.94, 0.83 to 1.07), disability or dependence (RR 1.11, 0.97 to 1.26) or Barthel-defined recovery (RR 1.03, 0.94 to 1.13), and its trial sequential analysis suggested no more trials are needed for the primary outcomes. Weight of evidence sits with ICTUS and Cochrane; the shelf is stamped SPLIT because the positive pooled analysis is real, published evidence that a reader will meet, not because the two sides are evenly matched. (Citicoline for traumatic brain injury — COBRIT — is a different question, homed on shelf #1267.)
stamp: SPLIT

title: Prehospital magnesium in acute stroke (FAST-MAG): treatment started a median 45 minutes after onset still did not improve 90-day disability — mean Rankin score 2.7 in both groups (the treatment made no difference)
question: In patients with suspected acute stroke, does intravenous magnesium sulphate started by paramedics in the field improve 90-day functional outcome compared with placebo?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference). FAST-MAG removed the usual excuse for neuroprotection failures — delay: paramedics started intravenous magnesium a median of 45 minutes after symptom onset, within 2 hours in all 1,700 enrolled patients with suspected stroke, yet 90-day disability was identical (mean modified Rankin score 2.7 in both groups, P=1.00; shift analysis P=0.28) and mortality was 15.4% versus 15.5%. The earlier in-hospital trial agreed: IMAGES (n=2,589, treatment within 12 hours) found a primary-outcome odds ratio of 0.95 (95% CI 0.80 to 1.13, p=0.59), with mortality if anything higher on magnesium (hazard ratio 1.18, 0.97 to 1.42). A 2019 meta-analysis of seven trials (4,347 patients) found no improvement in global outcome (SMD −0.01, −0.12 to 0.10), functional outcome or mortality (OR 1.10, 0.94 to 1.29); its one positive subgroup signal (ischaemic stroke only) is flagged by its own authors as needing extreme caution. Prehospital magnesium is feasible and safe — and ineffective for stroke outcome.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference)

title: Subdural drain after burr-hole evacuation of chronic subdural haematoma: recurrence fell from 24% to 9.3% in the Santarius trial, and two syntheses agree — drains roughly halve recurrence
question: In patients undergoing burr-hole evacuation of chronic subdural haematoma, does leaving a subdural drain reduce recurrence compared with no drain?
balance: LIKELY (benefit). The anchor trial was stopped early because the benefit was already clear: in Santarius 2009 (215 patients randomised after burr-hole evacuation), recurrence needing re-drainage occurred in 9.3% with a subdural drain versus 24% without (p=0.003) — an absolute reduction of about 15 percentage points — and 6-month mortality was also lower (8.6% vs 18.1%, p=0.042), with similar complication rates. Both syntheses agree on recurrence: the Cochrane review (9 trials, 968 participants) found a relative risk of recurrence of 0.45 (95% CI 0.32 to 0.61) with external drains — a 55% relative risk reduction, labelled relative — with no strong evidence of more complications (RR 1.15, 0.77 to 1.72) and an uncertain mortality effect (RR 0.78, 0.45 to 1.33); the 2023 meta-analysis (10 studies, 1,961 patients) found recurrence odds ratio 0.39 (0.28 to 0.55) and mortality odds ratio 0.65 (0.43 to 0.97). Recurrence is the outcome every source agrees on; the mortality benefit rests mainly on the single stopped-early trial and one meta-analysis, so it is stated more cautiously than the recurrence claim. (Dexamethasone for chronic subdural haematoma is a different, medical question, homed on shelf #2391; middle meningeal artery embolisation is homed on live shelf #339.)
stamp: LIKELY (benefit)

title: NITE-AD sleep programme in Alzheimer's dementia: fewer night awakenings at 2 months in two small trials — POSSIBLE
question: In people with Alzheimer's dementia and sleep disturbance, does the NITE-AD multicomponent programme (sleep hygiene, daily walking, light exposure) improve sleep compared with education control?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). The NITE-AD programme — caregiver-delivered sleep-hygiene education, daily walking and increased light exposure — was tested in two randomised trials from one research programme. In the first (McCurry 2005, n=36 — N printed on the face per the build flag), patients on NITE-AD showed significantly greater posttest reductions in number of nighttime awakenings, total time awake at night and depression, and more weekly exercise days, than education controls, with gains maintained at 6 months. In the larger four-arm trial (McCurry 2011, n=132), walking, light and the combination each improved actigraphic total wake time versus contact control at posttest (effect sizes 0.51–0.63), but no group differences remained at 6 months and caregiver-rated sleep quality did not significantly improve. A 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of non-pharmacological sleep interventions in Alzheimer's disease (14 randomised trials, 937 participants) found a modest improvement in subjective sleep quality (PSQI standardised mean difference −0.46, 95% CI −0.70 to −0.21), noted that caregiver-delivered programmes such as NITE-AD modestly reduced nocturnal awakenings, and found no significant effects on objective actigraphic outcomes. One programme, small first trial, fading durability: POSSIBLE.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — NITE-AD reduced nighttime awakenings and time awake at night at posttest in two randomised trials of one programme (n=36 and n=132; total programme N=168, printed on the face per the build flag), with gains not sustained at 6 months in the larger trial; a single programme caps at POSSIBLE

title: tDCS after stroke: the Cochrane pool and the largest trial find no arm-function benefit; two smaller trials are positive — SPLIT
question: In stroke survivors, does transcranial direct-current stimulation added to rehabilitation improve upper-limb motor recovery compared with sham stimulation?
balance: SPLIT. The biggest and most rigorous evidence is null for the arm itself: the Cochrane review (Elsner 2020; 67 studies, 1,729 participants in total) found no effect of tDCS on upper-extremity function at the end of intervention (34 trials, 985 participants; absolute-value analysis standardised mean difference 0.17, 95% CI −0.05 to 0.38) or at follow-up, and no effect on muscle strength or leg function; a small activities-of-daily-living signal (SMD 0.28) did not persist in the sensitivity analysis restricted to trials with proper allocation concealment. The largest single multicentre trial carded here (Hesse 2011, n=96, tDCS plus bilateral robot-assisted arm training in severe subacute paresis) found no between-group difference at 6 weeks or 3 months. Against that, two smaller trials were positive: Khedr 2013 (n=40; combined anodal/cathodal tDCS beat sham on functional scales at 3 months) and Garrido 2023 (n=70; bihemispheric tDCS with modified constraint-induced movement therapy beat sham on Fugl-Meyer and Wolf Motor Function Test, between-group Fugl-Meyer difference 4.9 points). Many small trials, heterogeneous montages and doses, and a null synthesis: the split is named on the stamp.
stamp: SPLIT — the Cochrane synthesis (67 studies, 1,729 participants in total; 34 trials, 985 participants for upper-extremity function) found no effect on arm function, and the largest multicentre trial (n=96) was negative, while two smaller trials (n=40 and n=70) reported significant gains; total N printed on the face

title: Brexpiprazole + sertraline for PTSD: two flexible-dose trials positive, the fixed-dose trial negative — SPLIT
question: In adults with PTSD, does brexpiprazole combined with sertraline reduce PTSD symptom severity compared with sertraline plus placebo?
balance: SPLIT — the programme genuinely divides by trial design. The full-factorial trial (Hobart 2025, n=321, flexible dose) found brexpiprazole + sertraline beat sertraline + placebo on CAPS-5 change at week 10 (−5.08 points, P=.011), while neither drug alone differed from placebo. Trial 071 (Davis 2025, JAMA Psychiatry, n=416, flexible-dose brexpiprazole 2–3 mg + sertraline 150 mg) was likewise positive: CAPS-5 least-squares mean difference −5.59 (95% CI −8.79 to −2.38; P<.001), with all key secondary endpoints met. Trial 072 (Davis 2025, J Clin Psychopharmacol, n=553, fixed-dose brexpiprazole 2 or 3 mg + sertraline) was negative at both doses (differences +1.03, P=0.52, and −0.71, P=0.66). A 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of the programme (4 randomised trials) found a significant pooled CAPS-5 advantage (mean difference −3.77, 95% CI −6.79 to −0.75) but no significant difference on CGI-S, with more weight gain (mean difference 1.47 kg) and somnolence (risk ratio 2.39, relative) on the combination. Two positives, one adequately sized negative, and a split meta-analysis: SPLIT.
stamp: SPLIT — two flexible-dose trials found significantly greater CAPS-5 improvement with brexpiprazole + sertraline (−5.59 and −5.08 points versus sertraline + placebo), while the fixed-dose phase 3 trial (n=553) met no endpoint at either dose; the 2026 meta-analysis is positive on CAPS-5 but null on global severity

title: Cariprazine for predominant negative symptoms: one large head-to-head trial beat risperidone by 1.46 PANSS-FSNS points — POSSIBLE
question: In adults with schizophrenia and predominant negative symptoms, does cariprazine improve negative symptoms compared with risperidone?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). This shelf is the dedicated negative-symptom slice: shelf #1430 cards cariprazine for acute exacerbation of schizophrenia (Durgam 2015, Kane 2015) and is cross-pointed, not re-carded — its PMIDs do not appear in this shelf's card source lines. In the dedicated trial (Németh 2017; 461 randomised adults with long-term stable schizophrenia and predominant negative symptoms, 26 weeks), cariprazine (target 4.5 mg/day) improved the PANSS factor score for negative symptoms more than risperidone (target 4 mg/day): least-squares mean change −8.90 versus −7.44 points, difference −1.46 (95% CI −2.39 to −0.53; P=0.0022; effect size 0.31). A post-hoc trajectory analysis of the same trial (Leucht 2023) found a single trajectory best described response — rapid, steady improvement rather than distinct responder subgroups. The systematic review of antipsychotics for predominant or prominent negative symptoms (Krause 2018; 21 trials, 3,451 participants) likewise records cariprazine outperforming risperidone in that one large, well-controlled trial (standardised mean difference −0.29, 95% CI −0.48 to −0.11), while noting it was manufacturer-sponsored and that amisulpride is the only agent to have beaten placebo in this population. One trial, modest margin over an active comparator: POSSIBLE.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single large randomised head-to-head trial (n=461) found cariprazine superior to risperidone on negative symptoms (difference −1.46 points, effect size 0.31), corroborated in direction by a systematic review, but one trial from the manufacturer's programme caps at POSSIBLE; the acute-schizophrenia question is homed on #1430 and is not re-carded here

title: Once-nightly sodium oxybate (FT218) in narcolepsy: one phase 3 trial positive on all three co-primary endpoints — POSSIBLE
question: In people with narcolepsy, does once-nightly sodium oxybate (FT218) improve excessive daytime sleepiness and cataplexy compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). The tested product is named as published, per the clarification exception: once-nightly sodium oxybate (FT218; marketed as LUMRYZ™), an extended-release formulation taken once at bedtime — distinct from the twice-nightly sodium oxybate programme homed on shelf #921, whose PMIDs are not re-carded here. In REST-ON (Kushida 2022; 222 randomised patients with narcolepsy type 1 or 2), all three doses (6, 7.5 and 9 g) beat placebo on all three co-primary endpoints (all P<0.001): at 9 g, Maintenance of Wakefulness Test sleep latency rose 10.8 versus 4.7 minutes (difference 6.13, 95% CI 3.52 to 8.75), 72.0% versus 31.6% were rated much/very much improved (odds ratio 5.56, relative), weekly cataplexy attacks fell −11.5 versus −4.9 (difference −6.65), and Epworth Sleepiness Scale fell −6.5 versus −2.7. Post-hoc analyses were concordant: sensitivity analyses accounting for missing data stayed significant with numbers needed to treat of 3 and effect sizes 0.7–0.9 (Roth 2025); sleepiness and sleep-quality gains were already detectable in weeks 1–2 (Krahn 2025); and about half of narcolepsy-type-1 participants on the higher doses halved their cataplexy attacks, ~10% eliminating them (Thorpy 2024). Common adverse reactions were nausea, vomiting, headache, dizziness and enuresis. One trial programme: POSSIBLE.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single phase 3 trial (REST-ON, n=222) of the tested product, once-nightly sodium oxybate (FT218), was positive on all three co-primary endpoints at all doses, with concordant post-hoc analyses; a single trial programme caps at POSSIBLE. The twice-nightly oxybate programme is homed on #921 and is not re-carded here

title: Galcanezumab for migraine prevention: EVOLVE-2, REGAIN and CONQUER all positive — POSSIBLE on this shelf, with EVOLVE-1 homed on live #336
question: In adults with episodic or chronic migraine, does galcanezumab reduce monthly migraine days compared with placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), with the #6155 precedent flag on the face: EVOLVE-1 (Stauffer 2018) is already carded with its figures on live shelf #336, the CGRP-class shelf (62.3% versus 38.6% achieving ≥50% response), so under the one-home rule its PMID does not appear in any card source line on this shelf; fremanezumab received the analogous drug-specific slice as pack #6155 under the same discipline. On the free reports carded here, galcanezumab is consistently positive: EVOLVE-2 (915 patients with episodic migraine) reduced monthly migraine headache days by 4.3 (120 mg) and 4.2 (240 mg) versus 2.3 on placebo (differences −2.0 and −1.9 days); REGAIN (1,113 patients with chronic migraine) reduced them by 4.8 and 4.6 versus 2.7 on placebo; CONQUER (462 patients who had failed preventive medications from two to four categories) reduced them by 4.1 versus 1.0 days (difference −3.1, effect size 0.72); and a 12-month open-label study (270 patients) sustained reductions of 5.6–6.5 days with injection-site pain the commonest adverse event. Injection-site reactions are the consistent harm across the programme.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — FLAG, precedent of pack #6155 (fremanezumab): EVOLVE-1, the first of galcanezumab's three primary phase 3 trials, is already carded with its figures on live shelf #336 (the CGRP-class shelf), so its PMID is not re-carded here; this drug-specific shelf is built on the remaining free primary reports (EVOLVE-2, REGAIN, CONQUER) plus the long-term safety study, all concordant, and is capped at POSSIBLE under that precedent

title: Parkinson's psychosis: clozapine beat placebo in both its trials; quetiapine failed in all three of its trials — SPLIT
question: In people with Parkinson's disease psychosis, do low-dose clozapine or quetiapine improve psychosis without worsening motor function compared with placebo?
balance: SPLIT — the two drugs have opposite trial records, and shelf #1112 (pimavanserin, cross-pointed here) does not cover either. Clozapine: the Parkinson Study Group trial (1999, n=60, mean dose 24.7 mg/day) improved all three psychosis measures versus placebo (Clinical Global Impression +1.6 versus +0.5 points, P<0.001; Brief Psychiatric Rating Scale +9.3 versus +2.6, P=0.002) with no deleterious effect on parkinsonism — tremor actually improved — at the price of weekly blood monitoring and one discontinuation for leukopenia. The French trial (Pollak 2004, n=60, mean dose 35.8 mg/day) replicated it (CGI +1.8 versus +0.6, P=0.001), and 19 of the patients who recovered relapsed within a month of stopping. Quetiapine: three double-blind trials (Ondo 2005, n=31; Rabey 2007, n=58; Shotbolt 2009, n=24) all failed to show significant benefit over placebo on any psychosis measure, though none showed motor worsening either. Total carded N=233, all pre-registration-era trials with no registry ID in their records. Clozapine works in trials but carries the blood-monitoring burden; quetiapine's trial record is negative despite its wide clinical use.
stamp: SPLIT — low-dose clozapine improved psychosis versus placebo in two randomised trials (n=60 each) without worsening parkinsonism, while quetiapine failed to beat placebo in all three of its randomised trials (n=31, 58, 24); total carded N=233. Pimavanserin is homed on #1112 and is not re-carded here

title: Shunting itself for iNPH: gait improved versus a closed valve in PENS and versus postponed surgery in SINPHONI-2 — POSSIBLE
question: In patients with idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus, does shunt surgery improve gait compared with conservative management or a placebo (closed-valve) shunt setting?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). Shelf #3655 cards which valve settings and designs to use once shunting is decided; this shelf asks the prior question — whether shunting itself beats no effective shunt — and #3655's PMIDs are not re-carded here. PENS (Luciano 2025, NEJM; n=99) is the first double-blind test: all participants received a shunt and were randomised to an open valve setting or a placebo (effectively closed, >400 mm water) setting; at 3 months gait velocity had risen 0.23 m/s on the open setting versus 0.03 m/s on placebo (treatment difference 0.21 m/s, 95% CI 0.12 to 0.31; P<0.001), with better Tinetti scores but no significant cognitive or bladder advantage, and more subdural bleeding (12% versus 2%) and positional headaches (59% versus 28%) on the open setting, against more falls on placebo (46% versus 24%). SINPHONI-2 (Kazui 2015; n=93, open-label) found favourable outcome (≥1-point modified Rankin improvement) at 3 months in 65% with immediate lumboperitoneal shunting versus 5% with surgery postponed 3 months (difference 61%). The SINPHONI-1 prospective cohort (Hashimoto 2010; n=100, observational) found 69% favourable outcome at 1 year after ventriculoperitoneal shunting. Both trials have real limits — PENS enrolled only patients who had already responded to temporary CSF drainage, and SINPHONI-2 was unblinded — hence POSSIBLE rather than LIKELY.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two randomised trials agree that an effective shunt improves gait/function (PENS 2025, blinded closed-valve control, n=99, in pre-selected CSF-drainage responders; SINPHONI-2, open-label postponed-surgery control, n=93), supported by a prospective cohort (n=100, observational, labelled); design limits in both trials cap the stamp at POSSIBLE. Valve settings/designs are homed on #3655 and are not re-carded here

title: Winter SAD itself: light and CBT-SAD are equal acutely; CBT-SAD halves second-winter recurrence (27.3% vs 45.6%) — SPLIT by time horizon
question: In adults with winter seasonal affective disorder, does bright light therapy or CBT-SAD reduce depressive symptoms acutely, and which better prevents recurrence the following winter?
balance: SPLIT by time horizon. Shelf #497 cards bright light for conditions other than seasonal depression (its Golden 2005 card addresses nonseasonal depression); the seasonal disorder itself — this shelf's question — was uncovered there, and the Rohan trials below are not carded on #497. Acutely, the large head-to-head trial (Rohan 2015; 177 adults with recurrent seasonal major depression; 6 weeks of group CBT-SAD versus 10,000-lux morning light) found the treatments indistinguishable: depression scores improved significantly and comparably, with remission 47.6% versus 47.2% on the SIGH-SAD and 56.0% versus 63.6% on the BDI-II. The earlier four-arm trial (Rohan 2007; n=61) found CBT, light and their combination each beat a wait-list control, with the combination's remission rate (73%) significantly above control (20%). The treatments separate only with time: in the follow-up of the 177-patient cohort (Rohan 2016), the first winter did not differ, but at the second winter recurrence was 27.3% after CBT-SAD versus 45.6% after light therapy, with remission (BDI-II ≤8) in 68.3% versus 44.5% — a durability advantage for the psychological treatment once the light box is put away.
stamp: SPLIT — split by time horizon: acutely the two treatments are indistinguishable (remission 47.6% CBT-SAD vs 47.2% light on the SIGH-SAD in the n=177 trial), but at the second winter after treatment CBT-SAD was superior (recurrence 27.3% vs 45.6%; remission 68.3% vs 44.5%). title: Intravenous lidocaine for chronic neuropathic pain: a small short-lived benefit over placebo in the 2005 meta-analyses, but the 2022 review found the trials too weak and varied to recommend it
question: In patients with chronic neuropathic pain, does intravenous lidocaine infusion reduce pain compared with placebo or active comparators?
balance: SPLIT. Two 2005 syntheses of the same trial generation (the Cochrane review by Challapalli and the Anesthesia & Analgesia meta-analysis by Tremont-Lukats, sharing authors) found systemic lidocaine and its oral analogues beat placebo by about 11 points on a 0–100 pain scale and matched carbamazepine, gabapentin, amitriptyline, amantadine and morphine — a real but modest, short-horizon effect, with drowsiness, fatigue, nausea and dizziness the common costs and no major toxicity in trials. The 2022 Clinical Journal of Pain review of 27 studies reached the opposite practical conclusion: only one class I and two class II studies, wide heterogeneity of dose, aetiology and design, and evidence insufficient to recommend infusion for spinal cord injury pain, peripheral nerve injury, diabetic neuropathy, postherpetic neuralgia or complex regional pain syndrome type II. This shelf covers chronic systemic infusion only; perioperative intravenous lidocaine is a different question, homed on shelf #1244, and topical lidocaine plaster questions are homed separately (#3571, #1457).
stamp: SPLIT — the 2005 meta-analyses found a small benefit over placebo; the 2022 systematic review found the evidence insufficient to recommend

title: Factor XIa inhibition after non-cardioembolic stroke: asundexian's phase 3 trial cut recurrent ischaemic stroke by 26% relative (6.2% vs 8.4%) with no excess major bleeding — after both phase 2 programmes had been neutral
question: In patients with acute non-cardioembolic ischaemic stroke or high-risk TIA, does adding a factor XIa inhibitor to antiplatelet therapy reduce recurrent ischaemic stroke without increasing major bleeding, compared with antiplatelet therapy alone?
balance: SPLIT, by development stage. The phase 3 OCEANIC-STROKE trial (n=12,327) found adding asundexian 50 mg daily to antiplatelet therapy lowered recurrent ischaemic stroke from 8.4% to 6.2% — a 26% relative reduction (hazard ratio 0.74) and a 2.2-percentage-point absolute reduction — with major bleeding essentially unchanged (1.9% vs 1.7%). Both earlier phase 2 dose-finding trials were neutral on their primary composites, which combined symptomatic stroke with MRI-detected covert infarcts: PACIFIC-Stroke (asundexian, n=1,808) showed no dose response, and AXIOMATIC-SSP (milvexian, n=2,366) likewise, neither with a meaningful major-bleeding signal. The split is therefore not drug-versus-drug contradiction so much as endpoint and power: the covert-infarct composites did not move, while the large symptomatic-event trial did. This shelf is the post-stroke antiplatelet add-on question; asundexian versus apixaban in atrial fibrillation (OCEANIC-AF) is a different population and comparator, homed on shelf #3108. Note: the slate for this row asserted a 2026 regulatory approval for asundexian; no fetched record in this session states any approval, so this pack makes no approval claim.
stamp: SPLIT — one large phase 3 trial (asundexian) is positive; both phase 2 programmes (asundexian and milvexian) were neutral on their composite outcomes

title: MONEAD: children exposed in utero to newer antiseizure medications scored the same on verbal ability at ages 3 and 6 as unexposed children — but higher drug concentrations tracked with worse scores on some secondary measures
question: In children exposed in utero to antiseizure medications, how do neurodevelopmental outcomes at ages 3 and 6 compare across medications (and with unexposed children), and how do maternal seizure control and breastfeeding on medication factor in?
balance: POSSIBLE, observational by design and labelled as such. MONEAD is a prospective multicentre cohort, not a trial: 456 pregnant women (351 with epilepsy, 105 without) enrolled at 20 US specialty centres and their children followed with blinded testing. Its primary comparisons are reassuring nulls — Verbal Index scores at age 3 (102.7 vs 102.3) and age 6 (difference −0.6; 95% CI −3.2 to 1.9) did not differ between children of women with epilepsy, mostly taking lamotrigine or levetiracetam, and children of healthy women (the exposures made no difference to the primary outcome). The caution lives in the secondary analyses: exposure-dependent effects appeared on several measures and varied by medication, including executive-function scores tracking third-trimester concentrations at age 4.5 years — the cohort's own reading is to dose high enough to protect mother and fetus from seizures but no higher. Early-pregnancy folate was positively associated with cognition and behaviour with no high-dose risk signal, and breastfeeding on contemporary regimens for at least 6 months was associated with better adaptive behaviour, not harm. Structural malformations after exposure are a separate question, homed on shelf #2676; periconception folic acid is homed on #5727/#6025.
stamp: POSSIBLE — observational cohort evidence only (prospective, non-randomised; no randomised comparison exists)

title: SUDEP and the night: nocturnal supervision was associated with lower SUDEP risk in case-control studies (odds ratios 0.4 and below), but the Cochrane review grades the evidence very low certainty — and no study has tested whether seizure-detection devices prevent SUDEP
question: In people with epilepsy at risk of sudden unexpected death in epilepsy (SUDEP), are nocturnal supervision or listening/seizure-detection devices associated with lower SUDEP risk?
balance: POSSIBLE, and observational throughout — there are no randomised trials of SUDEP prevention and there cannot readily be, given an incidence of roughly 1–2 per 1,000 patient-years. The strongest signal is for human supervision at night: in the UK case-control study (154 autopsy-confirmed SUDEP cases, 616 matched controls), sharing a bedroom or using special precautions such as a listening device was associated with lower odds of SUDEP (odds ratio 0.4 for supervision; 0.1 for the listening-device/special-precautions subgroup), while recent generalised tonic-clonic seizures carried an odds ratio of 13.8. A second analysis of the same case series found SUDEP was mainly sleep-related (58%) and unwitnessed (86%), and that nocturnal seizures independently raised risk — the mechanistic opening supervision is meant to close. The Cochrane review, however, found only one cohort and three case-control studies, all at serious to critical risk of bias, with results too heterogeneous to pool, and graded the supervision evidence 'limited, very low-certainty'. For seizure-detection devices specifically, no study has measured a SUDEP outcome at all — the device studies Cochrane found measured detection sensitivity only. Supervision is a reasonable, low-harm precaution to discuss; it is not a proven preventive.
stamp: POSSIBLE — observational evidence only (case-control and cohort studies at serious to critical risk of bias; Cochrane certainty very low)

title: Anti-NMDAR encephalitis: when first-line immunotherapy fails, second-line rituximab or cyclophosphamide was associated with better outcomes (OR 2.69 for good outcome) — in observational cohorts only; no randomised trial exists
question: In patients with anti-NMDAR autoimmune encephalitis who do not respond to first-line immunotherapy (steroids, IVIG, plasma exchange), does second-line therapy (rituximab and/or cyclophosphamide) improve functional outcome?
balance: POSSIBLE, observational throughout and labelled as such. The defining dataset is the 577-patient international cohort (Titulaer 2013): 94% received first-line immunotherapy (steroids, intravenous immunoglobulin, plasma exchange) or tumour removal, and 53% of those improved within 4 weeks. Among the 221 who did not improve, the 125 who went on to second-line therapy (rituximab and/or cyclophosphamide) reached a good outcome (modified Rankin Scale 0–2) more often than those who did not (odds ratio 2.69; 95% CI 1.24 to 5.80) — an association from non-randomised treatment choices, open to confounding in both directions (sicker patients may be escalated, or may be deemed too sick to escalate). Later observational work points the same way for relapse prevention: rituximab exposure was associated with a 71% relative lower hazard of first relapse in a US cohort (hazard ratio 0.29; Class IV evidence), and in an Italian paediatric cohort, receiving three or more different immune therapies at the first event was associated with a lower relapse hazard (HR 0.208). Recovery is slow — outcomes kept improving for up to 18 months — so 'failure' of first-line therapy should not be declared in days. No completed randomised trial of second-line therapy was found in the fetched records; treatment remains cohort-guided.
stamp: POSSIBLE — observational cohort evidence only (no completed randomised trials)

title: Driving in dementia: dementia severity (Clinical Dementia Rating) and a caregiver's rating of 'marginal or unsafe' are the useful signals; the patient's own rating is not, and no office cognitive test has a validated cut-off
question: In people with dementia who wish to keep driving, which clinical characteristics and tests (CDR stage, caregiver rating, cognitive tests, on-road assessment) best predict unsafe driving?
balance: POSSIBLE as an evidence synthesis — this is a prediction question, so the currency is what the American Academy of Neurology's evidence-graded parameter and three systematic reviews agree on. Useful for identifying increased risk: Clinical Dementia Rating stage (AAN Level A — the strongest single item), a caregiver rating the patient's driving as marginal or unsafe (Level B), a history of crashes or citations, reduced mileage or situational avoidance, MMSE scores of 24 or less, and aggressive or impulsive traits (all Level C). Not useful: the patient's own rating of their driving (Level A evidence against), and neuropsychological testing beyond dementia severity (Level U — insufficient evidence). The meta-analytic data quantify the gradient: on-road failure in 13.6% at CDR 0.5 and 33.3% at CDR 1 versus 1.6% in healthy controls, with executive function, attention, visuospatial function and global cognition each moderately predictive (effect sizes ~0.5–0.6) and the Maze test and Trail Making tests the best single cognitive predictors. The uncomfortable gap, shown by two reviews: the office tests guidelines recommend have no validated cut-off scores — fifteen of sixteen studies in one review reported none — so no test score by itself licenses or bans a driver; the on-road assessment remains the reference standard the office measures only approximate.
stamp: POSSIBLE — based on systematic-review and practice-parameter evidence (prediction question; no randomised evidence exists)

title: Naloxone co-prescription in primary care: patients given naloxone had 47% relatively fewer opioid-related ED visits at 6 months and 63% relatively fewer at 1 year — in one non-randomised study; the wider take-home naloxone literature is observational too
question: In primary-care patients receiving long-term opioid therapy for chronic pain, does co-prescribing naloxone reduce opioid-related emergency department visits and overdose events?
balance: POSSIBLE, with the non-randomised label on its face. Exactly one study in the fetched records tests the actual question: Coffin 2016, a 2-year non-randomised intervention study in six San Francisco safety-net primary care clinics, where 38.2% of 1,985 patients on long-term opioid therapy for pain received a naloxone prescription. Those prescribed naloxone had 47% relatively fewer opioid-related emergency department visits per month at 6 months (incidence rate ratio 0.53) and 63% relatively fewer at 1 year (IRR 0.37) than those not prescribed it — relative reductions from an observational comparison in which clinicians preferentially prescribed to higher-dose patients and those with a recent opioid-related ED visit, so confounding could run in either direction; opioid dose itself did not change. The supporting literature is one step removed: systematic reviews of take-home naloxone programmes for people who use drugs found those programmes met all nine Bradford Hill criteria for reducing overdose mortality and that roughly 9 of every 100 kits distributed are used for a peer rescue within three months — evidence that kits in hands get used and track with fewer deaths, not evidence about primary-care co-prescription itself. Nothing here is randomised; the honest claim is feasibility plus a consistent observational signal.
stamp: POSSIBLE — observational (non-randomised) evidence only

title: CSF production in adult humans: about 500–650 mL per day, swinging two- to three-fold across the day with a peak near 02:00 — the whole ~150 mL volume turning over roughly three to four times daily
question: At what rate is cerebrospinal fluid produced in adult humans, what fraction comes from the choroid plexus, and how many times per day does the CSF volume turn over?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED for the production rate and its circadian swing; the choroid-plexus fraction is presented as the textbook's account, because no fetched human record quantifies it. Textbook framing (Guyton & Hall; Ganong's Review; Boron & Boulpaep — named here as framing, not as evidence cards): CSF is formed at roughly 500 mL/day, the total CSF volume is about 150 mL, so the volume turns over about three to four times a day, and the choroid plexuses are credited with the majority of production, the remainder arising from extrachoroidal sources. The primary human records fetched this session confirm the rate's order and refine it: MRI aqueduct-flow measurement put 24-hour production near 650 mL with a strong circadian rhythm (from ~12 mL/h in the early evening to ~42 mL/h near 02:00 — i.e. roughly 0.2 to 0.7 mL/min across the day, averaging ~0.4 mL/min), and the nocturnal peak was blunted by a beta-1 blocker, pointing to sympathetic/choroid-plexus regulation. The 2018 mechanistic work states the adult human rate as 500 mL/day and identifies the choroid-plexus cotransporter NKCC1 as contributing approximately half of production — demonstrated in mice in vivo and ex vivo plexus preparations, so the 'half' is a mechanism finding, not a human fraction measurement. One further human datum: production was significantly lower in healthy elderly volunteers than in young ones (May 1990; the record reports the direction, not numeric rates). Two classic anchors were refused this session and are not carded: Cutler 1968 (formation and absorption in man) has an empty abstract in the fetched record, and the Ekstedt 1978 hydrodynamic record's abstract reports no numeric formation rate — neither could carry a verified number.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED

title: Placebo analgesia is opioid physiology: naloxone reverses it (in placebo responders only), placebo expectation activates μ-opioid neurotransmission on PET, and naloxone abolishes the brainstem coupling that carries the effect
question: Is placebo analgesia in humans mediated by endogenous opioid release — specifically, is it reversed by naloxone and accompanied by μ-opioid system activation in descending pain-control circuits?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Three independent human experimental approaches, three decades apart, converge on the same mechanism. Levine, Gordon & Fields (1978) showed pharmacological reversibility: after dental surgery, naloxone increased reported pain only in patients who had responded to a placebo — the naloxone effect was entirely accounted for by the placebo responders, exactly what an endogenous-opioid mechanism predicts. Zubieta (2005) showed the molecular event directly: during sustained pain, a placebo presented as an analgesic activated μ-opioid receptor-mediated neurotransmission in rostral anterior cingulate, dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, insula and nucleus accumbens, in parallel with lower pain ratings. Eippert (2009) closed the circuit: with fMRI, naloxone reduced behavioural and neural placebo effects and abolished the placebo-induced coupling between rostral anterior cingulate cortex and periaqueductal gray that predicted the analgesia — the descending pain-control system is opioidergically gated. Textbook framing (Guyton & Hall; Ganong's Review; Boron & Boulpaep — framing, not evidence cards): the descending analgesia system, periaqueductal gray and endogenous opioid peptides are the standard account into which these experiments fit. Honest limits: these are small laboratory studies (the fetched records do not print their sample sizes, so none are claimed), in experimental or postoperative pain, in selected volunteers — and 'mediated by endogenous opioids' applies to the expectation-driven placebo paradigm studied, not to every placebo response in every condition.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED

title: Blunted thirst in older adults: after 24 hours without water, older men were less thirsty and drank less despite higher plasma osmolality — while their vasopressin response was fully preserved (N = 7 per group in each classic study)
question: After 24 hours of water deprivation, do healthy older adults report less thirst and drink less than young adults despite equal or greater rises in plasma osmolality — and is vasopressin release preserved while thirst is blunted?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED as a directional finding, on a frankly small base: three classic human experiments, each with 7 older and 7 young men (total N = 42, printed here and on the stamp line per the small-N labelling rule). The answer to both halves of the question is yes. Phillips 1984: after 24 hours of water deprivation, older men (67–75 years) had greater rises in plasma osmolality, sodium and vasopressin than young men (20–31 years) at matched weight loss — yet they were less thirsty, drank less when water returned, and did not dilute their plasma and urine back to pre-deprivation levels; vasopressin osmoreceptor responsiveness was maintained or even increased, and the older men's lower urinary osmolality reflected the known renal concentrating deficit, not lack of hormone. Phillips 1991 isolated the osmotic limb: with hypertonic saline infusion (no volume depletion), older men were less thirsty and drank about a third as much (3.9 vs 11.1 mL/kg), mainly through lower thirst sensitivity to hypertonicity, while plasma vasopressin rises were the same as the young group's. McAloon Dyke 1997 confirmed the functional consequence: with free access to water during a hypertonic challenge, older volunteers' serum osmolality still climbed 17 mosmol/kg (vs 7 in the young) because they drank about half as much. Textbook framing (Guyton & Hall; Ganong's Review; Boron & Boulpaep — framing, not evidence cards): thirst and vasopressin are normally driven by the same osmoreceptor input; the ageing dissociation — hormone arm preserved, thirst arm blunted — is the physiological point, and it is why older patients cannot be relied on to drink their way out of hypertonicity.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — based on a very small total N = 42 (7 per group in each of the three studies)

title: Thermoregulation in ageing: cutaneous vasodilation is attenuated in older adults — a smaller nitric-oxide contribution, a blunted axon-reflex peak, reduced active vasodilator sensitivity, and less sweat output per gland
question: During heat stress, how much are reflex cutaneous vasodilation and sweating attenuated in healthy older adults compared with young adults, and what mechanisms (nitric oxide, axon reflex, active vasodilator sensitivity) account for the attenuation?
balance: Guyton & Hall, Ganong, and Boron & Boulpaep frame the textbook account: skin blood flow and sweating are the two heat-loss effectors driven by core temperature, and both are attenuated with healthy ageing. The fetched primary human studies agree on direction and mechanism. With local heating, the older plateau of cutaneous vascular conductance is lower and nitric oxide contributes less to it, and the axon-reflex initial peak is blunted (Minson 2002; N = 10 young vs 10 older, printed on the card). During exercise heat stress the conductance rise is shifted to a higher core temperature and forearm conductance runs 40–50% lower in older men, and blocking noradrenergic vasoconstriction does not explain the gap — the deficit is reduced active vasodilator sensitivity, not excess vasoconstriction (Kenney 1997; N = 15 vs 15). Sweat glands themselves respond less: methylcholine-stimulated sweat output per gland runs young > fit older > normally fit older men, with no difference in activated gland density — a per-gland, cholinergic-sensitivity deficit (Inoue 1999; N = 14 in total). These are classic small studies and their Ns are printed on each card's face. The neighbouring shelf #6263 asks when sweating and vasodilation switch on and how acclimation shifts those thresholds; this shelf asks the different, ageing-comparison question and cards none of #6263's references.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED

title: The human phase-response curve to bright light: delays before the temperature minimum, advances after it, a 5.02-hour peak-to-trough amplitude for a 6.7-hour pulse — and about 40% of that from a single 1-hour pulse
question: How does the direction and size of circadian phase shift from a single bright-light exposure depend on its timing relative to the core body temperature minimum — delays before, advances after — and what is the peak-to-trough amplitude?
balance: Guyton & Hall, Ganong, and Boron & Boulpaep frame the textbook account: light is the dominant time cue for the circadian pacemaker, and its resetting effect reverses sign around the core body temperature minimum. The fetched primary human studies quantify that curve under constant-routine conditions. A single 6.7-hour bright-light pulse gives a type 1 phase-response curve with a peak-to-trough amplitude of 5.02 hours — delays when the pulse is centred before the temperature minimum, advances after it, and no shift at the minimum itself (Khalsa 2003, N = 21). Duration matters non-linearly: a single 1-hour pulse still achieves a 2.20-hour amplitude, about 40% of the long pulse's effect from 15% of its duration (St Hilaire 2012, N = 36), and a 6.5-hour pulse of short-wavelength (480 nm) light achieves about 75% of the white-light response, with fitted maxima of −2.6 hours (delay) and +1.3 hours (advance) (Rüger 2013, N = 18). Sensitivity is high at low light levels too: about half the maximal phase-delaying and melatonin-suppressing effect of ~9,000 lux is already obtained at ~100 lux of ordinary room light (Zeitzer 2000, N = 23). The neighbouring treatment shelf #5917 (melatonin for delayed sleep-wake phase disorder) applies circadian timing clinically; this shelf states the underlying response curve itself.

title: Post-exercise hypotension: pressure falls for hours after one bout of dynamic exercise — roughly 8–10/3–5 mmHg in normotensive and 18–20/7–9 mmHg in hypertensive people — driven by sustained vasodilation, not by a fall in cardiac output
question: After a single bout of moderate-intensity dynamic exercise, how large and how prolonged is the fall in arterial pressure in normotensive versus hypertensive humans, and is it driven by a sustained fall in vascular resistance?
balance: Guyton & Hall, Ganong, and Boron & Boulpaep frame the textbook account: after dynamic exercise, arterial pressure settles below pre-exercise levels for hours because systemic vascular resistance stays reduced while cardiac output recovers. The fetched records support each element. In the primary laboratory study carded, 60 minutes of cycling at 60% of peak oxygen consumption left mean arterial pressure 5 mmHg lower and total peripheral resistance about 30% lower, while cardiac output was higher, not lower — and baroreflex heart-rate gain was augmented, restraining rather than causing the fall (Halliwill 1996, N = 12). The magnitude synthesis (Kenney & Seals 1993) puts maximal falls at 8–10 mmHg systolic and 3–5 diastolic in normotensive people versus 18–20 and 7–9 in hypertensive people, persisting 2–4 hours under laboratory conditions, with one free-living report of up to 13 hours. The mechanism review (Halliwill 2001) attributes the phenomenon to persistent reductions in vascular resistance mediated by the autonomic nervous system and vasodilator substances, more pronounced and longer in hypertension. Two of the three cards are expert syntheses rather than primary trials — labelled as such on their faces — because the primary literature is many small laboratory studies; the one primary study carded carries the haemodynamic mechanism directly.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED
