title: Longitudinal VO2max decline with ageing: not linear — it accelerates from 3–6% per decade in the 20s–30s to over 20% per decade in the 70s, in active and sedentary people alike (Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging)
question: How fast does peak oxygen consumption decline longitudinally with age in healthy adults — is the decline linear, or does it accelerate with each decade, and does habitual physical activity change the rate?
balance: Guyton & Hall, Ganong, and Boron & Boulpaep frame the textbook account of maximal oxygen consumption falling with age. The decisive fetched record is longitudinal: in the Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging, 810 healthy adults measured serially over a median 7.9 years lost peak VO2 at a rate that accelerated with every decade — 3–6% per decade in the 20s–30s rising to over 20% per decade in the 70s and beyond — and the same acceleration appeared in every quartile of self-reported leisure-time activity (Fleg 2005). The cross-sectional syntheses explain the apparent paradox that trained people lose more in absolute terms: endurance-trained women and men start higher and lose more millilitres per decade (−6.2 and −5.4 ml/kg/min per decade) than sedentary peers (−3.5 and −3.9), while the relative rate is essentially the same, about 10–11% per decade (Fitzgerald 1997, 4,884 women; Pimentel 2003, 153 men, in whom the trained decline steepened after ~50 alongside falling training volume). So habitual activity sets the level, not the relative slope — and cross-sectional estimates understate the true late-life loss. The neighbouring pack #6248 asks what limits VO2max; this shelf asks the different question of how fast it falls, and cards none of #6248's references.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED

title: Capivasertib plus fulvestrant in AKT-pathway-altered advanced breast cancer: progression-free survival roughly doubled in the phase 3 trial (7.3 vs 3.1 months in altered tumours, HR 0.50) — overall survival not yet reported in the fetched records
question: In adults with PIK3CA/AKT1/PTEN-altered hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative advanced breast cancer after endocrine therapy, does capivasertib plus fulvestrant improve progression-free and overall survival versus fulvestrant alone?
balance: One drug programme, two concordant randomised trials. The phase 3 CAPItello-291 trial (708 patients whose disease had progressed on an aromatase inhibitor, 69.1% after a CDK4/6 inhibitor) doubled median progression-free survival overall (7.2 vs 3.6 months; HR 0.60) and in the AKT-pathway-altered population the question asks about (7.3 vs 3.1 months; HR 0.50, a 50% relative reduction, with the absolute medians printed beside it). The earlier phase 2 FAKTION trial pointed the same way (10.3 vs 4.8 months; HR 0.58) in an unselected aromatase-inhibitor-resistant population, and a prespecified Chinese-cohort report of CAPItello-291 reproduced the benefit (altered tumours: HR 0.41). The harms are real and characteristic: grade 3 or higher rash 12.1% vs 0.3% and diarrhoea 9.3% vs 0.3% in the phase 3 trial, with 13.0% vs 2.3% discontinuing for adverse events. No overall-survival result appears in any fetched record, so the shelf claims progression-free survival only. A single programme, however concordant, caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.
stamp: POSSIBLE — single trial programme (phase 2 and phase 3 concordant); overall survival not yet reported

title: INAVO120: adding inavolisib to palbociclib–fulvestrant more than doubled progression-free survival (15.0 vs 7.3 months, HR 0.43) and extended overall survival (34.0 vs 27.0 months, HR 0.67) in endocrine-resistant PIK3CA-mutated disease
question: In adults with PIK3CA-mutated hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative advanced breast cancer, does first-line inavolisib plus palbociclib and fulvestrant improve progression-free and overall survival versus palbociclib and fulvestrant alone?
balance: A single phase 3 trial, but a complete one: INAVO120 randomised 325 patients with PIK3CA-mutated, hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative advanced breast cancer who had relapsed during or within 12 months of completing adjuvant endocrine therapy — the endocrine-resistant first-line population. Adding inavolisib to palbociclib–fulvestrant more than doubled median progression-free survival (15.0 vs 7.3 months; HR 0.43, a 57% relative reduction with the absolute medians beside it) and, at the final survival analysis, extended median overall survival by 7 months (34.0 vs 27.0 months; HR 0.67; P = 0.02). Responses more than doubled (62.7% vs 28.0% at the final analysis). The added toxicity is the PI3K-class ledger — hyperglycaemia, stomatitis, diarrhoea and ocular effects on top of palbociclib's neutropenia (grade 3–4 neutropenia ~80% in both arms) — and the dedicated safety analysis shows it was managed mainly with dose interruption and supportive medicines, with only 6.8% discontinuing inavolisib. One trial caps the stamp at POSSIBLE however clean its results.
stamp: POSSIBLE — single trial (one phase 3 programme); progression-free and overall survival both positive in that trial

title: TROPION-Breast01: datopotamab deruxtecan improved progression-free survival versus chemotherapy (HR 0.63) with fewer severe treatment-related events — but final overall survival was neutral (HR 1.01; the treatment made no difference to survival)
question: In adults with previously treated hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative advanced breast cancer, does datopotamab deruxtecan improve progression-free survival and response versus investigator's-choice chemotherapy?
balance: One large phase 3 trial with a split answer, and the shelf keeps both halves. TROPION-Breast01 randomised 732 patients with endocrine-pretreated HR-positive/HER2-negative advanced breast cancer after 1–2 lines of chemotherapy: datopotamab deruxtecan significantly reduced the risk of progression or death versus investigator's-choice chemotherapy (HR 0.63, a 37% relative reduction; the primary record does not print the median progression-free survivals, so none are carded) and caused fewer grade 3 or higher treatment-related adverse events (20.8% vs 44.7%). But at the final analysis, overall survival was neutral — HR 1.01 (the treatment made no difference to survival) — with a caveat the authors themselves raise: subsequent antibody-drug conjugate therapy was imbalanced (12.3% of the datopotamab arm vs 24.0% of the chemotherapy arm received one later), which may have diluted a survival difference. The detailed safety and patient-reported-outcome report adds the drug's signature costs — stomatitis in 57.2% and ocular surface events in 43.9%, mostly low grade, with rare interstitial lung disease including one grade 5 event — alongside delayed deterioration in quality of life, pain and physical functioning versus chemotherapy. A progression-free-survival win with a neutral survival result and a tolerability advantage: POSSIBLE, with the null printed in the title line where it belongs.
stamp: POSSIBLE — single trial; progression-free survival improved, overall survival neutral (the treatment made no difference to survival)

title: ExteNET: 1 year of extended adjuvant neratinib reduced invasive recurrence (2-year iDFS HR 0.67; 5-year HR 0.73) — at the cost of grade 3 diarrhoea in 40% without prophylaxis; benefit largest in hormone receptor-positive disease started within a year of trastuzumab
question: In adults with HER2-positive early breast cancer after locoregional treatment and neoadjuvant/adjuvant trastuzumab-based therapy, does 1 year of extended adjuvant neratinib reduce invasive recurrence versus placebo?
balance: One large trial followed for a decade, and its answer has stayed consistent while narrowing. ExteNET randomised 2,840 women with HER2-positive early breast cancer after trastuzumab-based therapy to 1 year of neratinib or placebo: invasive disease-free survival was better at 2 years (93.9% vs 91.6%; HR 0.67, a 33% relative reduction with the absolute rates beside it) and at 5 years (90.2% vs 87.7%; HR 0.73). The prespecified hormone receptor-positive analysis shows where the benefit concentrates: in women who started neratinib within a year of finishing trastuzumab, the 5-year absolute invasive disease-free survival benefit was 5.1% (HR 0.58), with an 8-year overall-survival difference that was numerical only (absolute 2.1%; HR 0.79; confidence interval crossing 1) — no fetched record shows a significant overall-survival benefit in the whole population. The cost is front-loaded and gastrointestinal: without diarrhoea prophylaxis, grade 3 diarrhoea affected 40% on neratinib vs 2% on placebo in both the 2- and 5-year reports. A real recurrence benefit in one trial, an unproven survival benefit, and a substantial tolerability price: POSSIBLE.
stamp: POSSIBLE — single trial; invasive disease-free survival improved, overall survival not significantly improved in any fetched record

title: Quizartinib added to intensive chemotherapy in newly diagnosed FLT3-ITD AML (QuANTUM-First): median survival 31.9 versus 15.1 months in the one phase 3 trial
question: In adults with newly diagnosed FLT3-ITD-positive acute myeloid leukaemia fit for intensive chemotherapy, does adding quizartinib to induction and consolidation chemotherapy and as continuation therapy improve overall survival versus chemotherapy alone?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one strong trial, honestly capped. In QuANTUM-First (Erba 2023, PMID: 37116523), 539 adults aged 18–75 with newly diagnosed FLT3-ITD-positive AML were randomised to quizartinib or placebo added to standard induction and consolidation (with or without allogeneic transplant) and continued as single-agent therapy for up to 3 years. Median overall survival was 31.9 months on quizartinib versus 15.1 months on placebo (HR 0.78, 95% CI 0.62 to 0.98; p=0.032 — a relative measure, with the absolute medians beside it). Post-hoc analyses of the same trial point the same way: the quizartinib association persisted when transplant in first remission was modelled as a time-dependent variable (Schlenk 2025, PMID: 40079105), and quizartinib produced deeper FLT3-ITD MRD-negative remissions, with end-of-induction MRD tracking relapse and survival (Levis 2026, PMID: 41052406). Grade 3 or higher adverse events were near-universal in both arms (92% versus 90%). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a single trial programme caps the stamp, and the confidence interval (to 0.98) leaves the true effect compatible with modest.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in the single phase 3 trial (QuANTUM-First, 539 patients), adding quizartinib to intensive chemotherapy and as continuation gave median overall survival of 31.9 versus 15.1 months (HR 0.78, 95% CI 0.62 to 0.98; p=0.032, a relative measure); a single trial programme caps the stamp at POSSIBLE

title: Gilteritinib versus salvage chemotherapy in relapsed/refractory FLT3-mutated AML (ADMIRAL): median survival 9.3 versus 5.6 months in the one phase 3 trial
question: In adults with relapsed or refractory FLT3-mutated acute myeloid leukaemia, does gilteritinib monotherapy improve overall survival versus salvage chemotherapy?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one decisive trial, honestly capped. In ADMIRAL (Perl 2019, PMID: 31665578), 371 adults with relapsed or refractory FLT3-mutated AML were randomised 2:1 to gilteritinib 120 mg daily or salvage chemotherapy: median overall survival 9.3 versus 5.6 months (HR 0.64, 95% CI 0.49 to 0.83; P<0.001 — a relative measure, absolute medians beside it), and complete remission with full or partial haematologic recovery in 34.0% versus 15.3%. The 2-year follow-up held the line — survival 20.6% versus 14.2%, HR 0.665 (Perl 2022, PMID: 35081255) — and the transplant analysis shows the mechanism of durability: gilteritinib got more patients to transplant (26% versus 15%), and the relapse-free long-term survivors were concentrated there (Perl 2023, PMID: 36526260). Absolute survival remains short in both arms. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a single trial programme caps the stamp.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in the single phase 3 trial (ADMIRAL, 371 patients), gilteritinib gave median overall survival of 9.3 versus 5.6 months against salvage chemotherapy (HR 0.64, 95% CI 0.49 to 0.83; P<0.001, a relative measure) and double the remission rate; a single trial programme caps the stamp at POSSIBLE

title: Ivosidenib plus azacitidine in unfit IDH1-mutated AML (AGILE): median survival 24.0 versus 7.9 months, confirmed at long-term follow-up
question: In older or unfit adults with newly diagnosed IDH1-mutated acute myeloid leukaemia, does ivosidenib plus azacitidine improve event-free and overall survival versus azacitidine alone?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one small but decisive trial, honestly capped. In AGILE (Montesinos 2022, PMID: 35443108), 146 patients with newly diagnosed IDH1-mutated AML ineligible for intensive chemotherapy were randomised to ivosidenib plus azacitidine or placebo plus azacitidine: event-free survival HR 0.33 (95% CI 0.16 to 0.69) and median overall survival 24.0 versus 7.9 months (HR 0.44, 95% CI 0.27 to 0.73 — relative measures, absolute medians beside them). The long-term report at 28.6 months' median follow-up held the result (median survival 29.3 versus 7.9 months, HR 0.42; transfusion independence 53.8% versus 17.1%) (Montesinos 2025, PMID: 40706052). The combination began in a 23-patient phase 1b study with a 60.9% complete remission rate (DiNardo 2021, PMID: 33119479). Infections were less frequent on the combination; neutropenia and bleeding more frequent. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a single trial programme caps the stamp.

title: Inotuzumab ozogamicin in relapsed/refractory B-ALL (INO-VATE): remissions 73.8% versus 30.9% and more transplants, with a modest survival gain and a 13–14% sinusoidal obstruction risk
question: In adults with relapsed or refractory B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, does inotuzumab ozogamicin improve remission and overall survival versus standard chemotherapy?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a large remission effect, a modest survival effect, one trial. In INO-VATE (Kantarjian 2016, PMID: 27292104), inotuzumab ozogamicin produced complete remission in 80.7% versus 29.4% in the primary first-218 analysis, with MRD negativity in 78.4% versus 28.1% of remitters; the survival hazard ratio at that point (0.77, 97.5% CI 0.58 to 1.03) crossed 1.0. The final report (Kantarjian 2019, PMID: 30920645) put full-population remission at 73.8% versus 30.9%, median survival at 7.7 versus 6.2 months and 2-year survival at 22.8% versus 10.0% (HR 0.75, 97.5% CI 0.57 to 0.99), with direct bridging to transplant in 39.6% versus 10.5%. The price is hepatic: sinusoidal obstruction syndrome in about 13–14% on inotuzumab versus about 1–2% on standard care (Kantarjian 2017, PMID: 28687420). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a single trial programme caps the stamp.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in the single phase 3 trial (INO-VATE, 326 patients), inotuzumab nearly tripled remission (73.8% versus 30.9%) and quadrupled direct bridging to transplant, with median survival 7.7 versus 6.2 months and 2-year survival 22.8% versus 10.0% (HR 0.75, a relative measure), at a 13–14% sinusoidal obstruction syndrome risk; a single trial programme caps the stamp at POSSIBLE

title: Ciltacabtagene autoleucel in lenalidomide-refractory myeloma (CARTITUDE-4): progression-free HR 0.26, overall-survival HR 0.55 at the update
question: In adults with lenalidomide-refractory multiple myeloma after 1–3 prior lines, does a single ciltacabtagene autoleucel infusion improve progression-free and overall survival versus standard regimens?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one trial with unusually large effects, honestly capped. In CARTITUDE-4 (San-Miguel 2023, PMID: 37272512), 419 patients with lenalidomide-refractory myeloma after 1–3 prior lines were randomised to a single ciltacabtagene autoleucel infusion or physician's-choice standard care: progression-free survival HR 0.26 (95% CI 0.18 to 0.38), complete response or better in 73.1% versus 21.8%, and MRD absence in 60.6% versus 15.6%. Overall survival had not separated at the primary analysis (HR 0.78, interval crossing 1.0) but did at the prespecified update — HR 0.55 (95% CI 0.39 to 0.79; p=0.0009) at 33.6 months (Einsele 2026, PMID: 41519141) — and patient-reported outcomes favoured cilta-cel (Mina 2025, PMID: 39756844). Cytokine release syndrome occurred in 76.1% of infused patients but was grade 3 or 4 in only 1.1%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a single trial programme caps the stamp.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in the single phase 3 trial (CARTITUDE-4, 419 patients), one cilta-cel infusion gave progression-free survival HR 0.26 and, at the updated analysis, overall-survival HR 0.55 (95% CI 0.39 to 0.79, relative measures) versus standard regimens; a single trial programme caps the stamp at POSSIBLE

title: Teclistamab in triple-class-exposed myeloma (MajesTEC-1, single-arm): responses in 63% lasting a median 18.4 months — infections in 76.4% in the trial, 44.8% of them grade 3 or 4
question: In adults with triple-class-exposed relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma, does teclistamab produce durable responses, and at what infection cost?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — durable single-arm responses, a heavy infection cost, no comparator. In MajesTEC-1 (Moreau 2022, PMID: 35661166), weekly teclistamab produced responses in 63.0% of 165 triple-class-exposed patients (median five prior lines), complete response or better in 39.4%, with a median response duration of 18.4 months — and infections in 76.4%, grade 3 or 4 in 44.8%. The pattern repeats: 52.5% response and 70.0% infection incidence (10% grade 5) in the 40-patient post-BCMA cohort (Touzeau 2024, PMID: 39172760); 62% response in a 110-patient real-world cohort, where intravenous immunoglobulin prophylaxis was associated with lower infection risk (Mohan 2024, PMID: 38443345); and a pooled infection incidence of 56.5% any grade and 27.6% grade 3 or higher across 714 patients (Huang 2026, PMID: 42148087). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): single-arm pivotal evidence, labelled as such, caps the stamp — response durability is shown, comparative benefit is not.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single-arm and observational evidence, labelled as such: teclistamab produced responses in 63.0% of 165 triple-class-exposed patients (complete response or better 39.4%; median response duration 18.4 months) in MajesTEC-1, with infections in 76.4% (grade 3 or 4 in 44.8%); no randomised comparator exists in the evidence carded, so the stamp caps at POSSIBLE

title: CD20×CD3 bispecifics in DLBCL after at least two lines (single-arm pivotal evidence): complete responses in about 4 in 10 with both glofitamab and epcoritamab, durable for years in responders
question: In adults with relapsed or refractory diffuse large B-cell lymphoma after at least two prior lines, do CD20×CD3 bispecific antibodies (glofitamab, given for a fixed duration, and epcoritamab, given until progression) produce durable complete responses?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — durable complete responses in a minority, from single-arm evidence only. Glofitamab (Dickinson 2022, PMID: 36507690) produced complete responses in 39% of 155 patients after at least two lines, 78% of them still ongoing at 12 months, on a fixed 12-cycle course. Epcoritamab (Thieblemont 2023, PMID: 36548927) produced complete responses in 38.9% of 157 patients, given until progression; at the 3-year update the complete-response rate was 41% with a median complete-response duration of 36.1 months — but median progression-free survival for all patients was only 4.2 months (Karimi 2026, PMID: 41634395). In 245 real-world patients treated with either drug, response rates were similar (51% and 53%) and survival lower than in the trials (Brooks 2025, PMID: 40663785). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): single-arm pivotal evidence, labelled as such, caps the stamp; nothing carded ranks the two drugs against each other.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single-arm pivotal evidence, labelled as such: glofitamab produced complete responses in 39% and epcoritamab in 38.9–41% of patients after at least two prior lines, with complete responses lasting a median 36.1 months for epcoritamab at 3 years, while median progression-free survival for all patients remained short; no randomised comparator exists in the evidence carded, so the stamp caps at POSSIBLE

title: Rusfertide in polycythaemia vera (VERIFY phase 3; REVIVE phase 2): clinical response 77% versus 33% and mean phlebotomies 0.5 versus 1.8 versus placebo
question: In adults with polycythaemia vera needing cytoreduction or frequent phlebotomy, does rusfertide reduce phlebotomy dependence and control haematocrit versus placebo on top of standard care?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two concordant randomised trials on control endpoints, no hard-outcome data yet. In VERIFY (Kuykendall 2026, PMID: 42868322), 293 phlebotomy-dependent patients were randomised to rusfertide or placebo on top of standard care: clinical response in 77% versus 33% (P<0.0001), mean phlebotomies 0.5 versus 1.8, and haematocrit below 45% maintained in 63% versus 14%, with better fatigue and symptom scores and no deaths reported. REVIVE's randomised-withdrawal period points the same way — response 60% on continued rusfertide versus 17% after switching to placebo (Kremyanskaya 2024, PMID: 38381675) — and a 20-patient open-label study shows haematocrit falling below 45% within about 5 weeks (PMID: 41175501). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the endpoints are haematocrit control and phlebotomy avoidance over weeks; neither trial shows fewer thromboses.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in the phase 3 VERIFY trial (293 patients), rusfertide on top of standard care gave clinical response (no phlebotomy eligibility) in 77% versus 33% on placebo and cut mean phlebotomies to 0.5 versus 1.8 over 32 weeks, concordant with the REVIVE randomised-withdrawal trial (60% versus 17%); the outcomes are haematocrit and phlebotomy endpoints with no thrombosis outcome shown, so the stamp stays at POSSIBLE

title: Sildenafil in severe early-onset fetal growth restriction (STRIDER UK, Netherlands, NZAus): no growth or survival benefit, with a Dutch neonatal pulmonary-hypertension signal
question: In women with severe early-onset fetal growth restriction, does sildenafil improve fetal growth or perinatal survival versus placebo?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — with a neonatal harm signal in one trial. Three placebo-controlled STRIDER trials agree that sildenafil does not improve growth or survival in severe early-onset fetal growth restriction: the UK trial (Sharp 2018, PMID: 30169244) found no prolongation of pregnancy (median 17 vs 18 days to delivery) and no difference in livebirth or birthweight; the New Zealand/Australia trial (Groom 2019, PMID: 30779295) found no increase in fetal growth velocity (52.5% vs 68.4% on placebo); and the Dutch trial (Pels 2020, PMID: 32585017) was stopped early for safety — its primary outcome of perinatal death or major morbidity was 60.2% on sildenafil vs 54.2% on placebo, and neonatal pulmonary hypertension occurred in 18.8% vs 5.1% (relative risk 3.67). Sildenafil should not be used for this indication outside research.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — three randomised STRIDER trials (473 women) show no improvement in fetal growth, pregnancy prolongation or perinatal survival from sildenafil, and the Dutch trial, stopped early, found neonatal pulmonary hypertension in 18.8% on sildenafil vs 5.1% on placebo (relative risk 3.67)

title: Apical prolapse: sacrocolpopexy vs vaginal native-tissue suspension — more durable repair (repeat surgery about 14% vs 6% favouring sacrocolpopexy), with mesh erosion reaching 10.5% by 7 years
question: In women with symptomatic apical pelvic organ prolapse, does abdominal sacrocolpopexy give more durable repair than vaginal native-tissue suspension, and at what mesh-complication cost?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — sacrocolpopexy looks more durable, paid for in mesh complications and a bigger operation; much of the long-term base is cohort data, so the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE and the observational parts are labelled. Randomised evidence pooled by Cochrane (Maher 2023, PMID: 37493538; 59 trials, 6,705 women) finds women having vaginal apical procedures more often aware of prolapse (relative risk 2.31; 8% after sacral colpopexy vs about 18% after vaginal procedures), more often needing repeat prolapse surgery (RR 2.33; 6% vs about 14%) and more often recurrent on examination (RR 1.87) than women having sacral colpopexy. The CARE cohort's 7-year extension (Nygaard 2013, PMID: 23677313) shows sacrocolpopexy failure probabilities still rising by year 7 and a mesh-erosion probability of 10.5%. A 2026 meta-analysis dominated by cohort studies (PMID: 42690266) likewise found lower retreatment after minimally invasive sacrocolpopexy with hysterectomy than after vaginal hysterectomy with native-tissue repair (1.59% vs 10.23%).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — pooled randomised data favour sacral colpopexy over vaginal apical procedures (repeat prolapse surgery about 14% vs 6%; awareness of prolapse about 18% vs 8%), and cohort syntheses agree on lower retreatment (1.59% vs 10.23%), but the head-to-head trials are small and short and much of the base is observational; sacrocolpopexy's mesh-erosion probability reaches 10.5% by 7 years (extended CARE)

title: Transperineal vs transrectal prostate biopsy (TRANSLATE, PREVENT, ProBE-PC): detection at least as good, antibiotics often unnecessary, infection advantage still a trend
question: In men being investigated for suspected prostate cancer, does a transperineal biopsy approach detect as much significant cancer as transrectal biopsy, with fewer infections?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — transperineal biopsy detects at least as much significant cancer and can be done without antibiotic prophylaxis, with infection rates no higher and a trend lower; it is somewhat more painful at the time. In TRANSLATE (Bryant 2025, PMID: 40139210; 1,126 men), Gleason Grade Group 2 or higher cancer was found in 60% on transperineal vs 54% on transrectal biopsy (odds ratio 1.32, p=0.031), and infection requiring hospital admission occurred in under 1% vs 2%. In PREVENT (Hu 2024, PMID: 38212178), transperineal biopsy without any antibiotic prophylaxis caused zero infections vs 1.4% with transrectal biopsy under targeted prophylaxis (p=0.059), with similar significant-cancer detection (53% vs 50%). ProBE-PC (Mian 2024, PMID: 37976319) found no infection difference (2.7% vs 2.6%), and a meta-analysis of the three prospective trials (PMID: 39095298) found no significant difference in detection or infection — so the benefit claim is equivalence-plus-stewardship, not proven superiority on infection.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — transperineal biopsy detected more Gleason Grade Group ≥2 cancer than transrectal in TRANSLATE (60% vs 54%, odds ratio 1.32) and produced zero infections without any antibiotic prophylaxis in PREVENT (vs 1.4%, p=0.059), while ProBE-PC found no complication difference (2.7% vs 2.6%); the randomised infection advantage is a consistent trend, not yet a significant endpoint

title: Cabazitaxel vs switching androgen-receptor inhibitor in mCRPC (CARD): survival 13.6 vs 11.0 months and imaging progression-free survival 8.0 vs 3.7 months
question: In men with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer progressing on an androgen-receptor inhibitor, does cabazitaxel improve survival versus switching to the alternative androgen-receptor inhibitor?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single strong randomised trial, so the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE. In CARD (de Wit 2019, PMID: 31566937; 255 men with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer previously treated with docetaxel and progressing within 12 months on abiraterone or enzalutamide), cabazitaxel doubled median imaging-based progression-free survival (8.0 vs 3.7 months; hazard ratio 0.54) and lengthened median overall survival (13.6 vs 11.0 months; HR for death 0.64, p=0.008) versus switching to the alternative androgen-receptor inhibitor, with grade 3 or higher adverse events in 56.3% vs 52.4%. CARD's quality-of-life analysis (Fizazi 2020, PMID: 32926841 — same patients) found pain response in 46% vs 19%. A Japanese real-world CARD-like analysis (Matsuyama 2023, PMID: 37308888 — observational, labelled) points the same way on time to treatment failure.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in the single CARD randomised trial (255 men, post-docetaxel, progressing within 12 months on an androgen-receptor inhibitor), cabazitaxel lengthened median overall survival to 13.6 vs 11.0 months (hazard ratio for death 0.64) and imaging progression-free survival to 8.0 vs 3.7 months versus switching inhibitor; a single trial programme caps the stamp at POSSIBLE

title: Prophylactic mesh at permanent end colostomy (Jänes, Serra-Aracil, STOMAMESH): SPLIT — early small trials positive, largest blinded trial and long-term follow-up null
question: In patients having a permanent end colostomy, does prophylactic mesh at stoma formation reduce later parastomal hernia versus no mesh?
balance: SPLIT — the early small trials and the pooled estimate favour mesh; the largest double-blind trial and the late follow-up do not. Jänes (PMID: 19011935) found parastomal hernia at 5 years in 2 of 15 surviving mesh patients vs 17 of 21 controls, and Serra-Aracil (PMID: 19300232) found clinical hernia in 14.8% with mesh vs 40.7% without (p=0.03). But STOMAMESH (Odensten 2019, PMID: 29064900; 232 patients, double-blind) found no difference at 1 year, and pooled long-term follow-up of three trials (López-Cano 2023, PMID: 36966221) found no significant difference in time to hernia. The updated meta-analysis of 12 RCTs (McKechnie 2022, PMID: 34671916) still pools to an odds ratio of 0.60 favouring mesh, but with high heterogeneity (I²=74%) and no significant effect among trials from the last 5 years. The split is named on the stamp: small early open trials positive, large blinded and long-term data null.
stamp: SPLIT — prophylactic mesh at end-colostomy formation reduced parastomal hernia in the early small randomised trials (Serra-Aracil: 14.8% vs 40.7%; Jänes at 5 years: 2/15 vs 17/21) and in the all-trials pooled estimate (odds ratio 0.60), but the largest double-blind trial, STOMAMESH (232 patients), found no difference at 1 year and pooled long-term follow-up of three trials found none either; the split is small/early/short vs large/blinded/long-term

title: Apnoeic oxygenation at intubation (THRIVE, ENDAO): SPLIT — safe apnoea time clearly prolonged, emergency desaturation benefit shown in pooled data but not in the largest ED trial
question: In adults having emergency intubation, does apnoeic oxygenation by high-flow nasal oxygen (THRIVE-style) or standard nasal cannula prolong safe apnoea time and reduce desaturation versus standard preoxygenation alone?
balance: SPLIT — apnoeic oxygenation clearly prolongs safe apnoea time in controlled/elective settings, but the largest emergency-department randomised trial found no desaturation benefit. THRIVE (Patel 2015, PMID: 25388828 — uncontrolled physiological series, labelled) kept 25 difficult-airway patients apnoeic for a median 14 minutes with no desaturation below 90%. In obese patients having elective surgery, nasal-cannula apnoeic oxygenation lengthened safe apnoeic duration by a median 103 seconds (Moon 2019, PMID: 31317460). A meta-analysis of emergency intubation (Pavlov 2017, PMID: 28647137; 8 studies, 1,953 patients) found hypoxaemia in 19.1% with apnoeic oxygenation vs 27.6% with usual care — a 30% relative risk reduction. But the ENDAO randomised trial (Caputo 2017, PMID: 28791755; 200 patients) found lowest mean saturation 92% with apnoeic oxygenation vs 93% with usual care (p=0.11). The split is named on the stamp: physiology and pooled data favour it; the biggest single emergency RCT does not. Cross-point: preoxygenation before the apnoeic period (PREOXI/FELLOW) is homed on Shelf #758 — this shelf is only about oxygen during apnoea itself.
stamp: SPLIT — apnoeic oxygenation prolongs safe apnoea time in controlled settings (THRIVE: median 14 min without desaturation below 90% in 25 difficult-airway patients; +103 s in an obese-patient RCT) and pooled emergency data show less hypoxaemia (19.1% vs 27.6%, a 30% relative risk reduction), but the largest emergency-department RCT, ENDAO (200 patients), found no difference in lowest saturation (92% vs 93%, p=0.11); the split is controlled physiology/pooled data vs the biggest single emergency trial

title: Intrathecal morphine after caesarean delivery (Palmer dose-response; Sultan and Yang meta-analyses; PROSPECT): 45.7 mg less PCA morphine at 0.075 mg versus none, benefit plateauing at 50-100 µg, pruritus rising with dose
question: In women after caesarean delivery, does intrathecal morphine improve pain and reduce systemic opioid need versus no intrathecal opioid, and what pruritus, nausea and respiratory monitoring does it cost?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) on pain and systemic opioid sparing, at a real cost in pruritus and nausea/vomiting. The dose-response randomised trial (Palmer 1999, PMID: 9952150) found patient-controlled morphine use over 24 hours was 45.7 mg lower with intrathecal morphine 0.075 mg than with no intrathecal morphine, with no further sparing above that dose, while pruritus rose in direct proportion to dose. The dose meta-analysis (Sultan 2016, PMID: 27089000) found higher doses (>100-250 µg) prolonged time to first analgesic request by a mean 4.49 hours versus low doses (50-100 µg) but with more nausea/vomiting and pruritus, and no difference in 24-hour morphine consumption. Against transversus abdominis plane block, intrathecal morphine used less systemic morphine but caused more pruritus and postoperative nausea and vomiting (Yang 2021, PMID: 34157985). The PROSPECT procedure-specific synthesis recommends intrathecal morphine 50-100 µg as part of the standard elective-caesarean regimen (Roofthooft 2021, PMID: 33370462). None of these fetched records quantifies respiratory-depression rates, so the monitoring cost is real but unquantified here: the low recommended dose is precisely the trade the evidence supports. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): multiple concordant randomised datasets and syntheses, with dose-dependent harms stated on the face.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — concordant randomised evidence (dose-response trial, two meta-analyses and the PROSPECT synthesis of 145 RCTs) that low-dose intrathecal morphine (50-100 µg) reduces pain and systemic opioid need after caesarean delivery, with dose-dependent pruritus and nausea/vomiting as the routine costs; respiratory-depression rates are not quantified in this evidence base

title: Early clear-lens extraction versus laser peripheral iridotomy in primary angle-closure disease (EAGLE): pressure 1.18 mm Hg lower, drop-free control 66% versus 18%, ICER £14,284 per QALY
question: In adults with primary angle-closure disease, is early clear-lens extraction more effective and safer than laser peripheral iridotomy for intraocular pressure and glaucoma progression? (EAGLE.)
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single large randomised programme (EAGLE). In EAGLE (Azuara-Blanco 2016, PMID: 27707497), 419 patients aged 50 or older with newly diagnosed primary angle closure (intraocular pressure 30 mm Hg or greater) or primary angle-closure glaucoma were randomised to clear-lens extraction or standard care (laser peripheral iridotomy plus topical treatment): at 36 months health status was 0.052 higher and mean intraocular pressure 1.18 mm Hg lower with lens extraction, and the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio was £14,284 per quality-adjusted life-year. The secondary analysis found 90% versus 67% met a good-response criterion and 66% versus 18% were drop-free with good control after lens extraction versus iridotomy (Mitchell 2023, PMID: 35387778), and the within-trial economic evaluation found lens extraction might become cost saving by 10 years (Javanbakht 2017, PMID: 28087548). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): one trial programme caps the stamp, however clean its result; the comparison is against iridotomy plus medical therapy, not iridotomy alone forever, and lens extraction is irreversible intraocular surgery.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single randomised programme (EAGLE, 419 patients): clear-lens extraction gave 1.18 mm Hg lower intraocular pressure, 66% versus 18% drop-free good control and an ICER of £14,284 per QALY versus iridotomy-based standard care at 36 months; single-programme evidence caps the stamp at POSSIBLE

title: XEN gel stent versus trabeculectomy in open-angle glaucoma: trabeculectomy lowers pressure ~2 mm Hg further with higher success; XEN needs more needling but fewer visits and less vision loss; hypotony not clearly different
question: In adults with open-angle glaucoma, does a subconjunctival gel stent (XEN) lower intraocular pressure as durably as trabeculectomy, with fewer hypotony complications?
balance: SPLIT — the two operations trade places by outcome, on an observational base (labelled). Trabeculectomy lowers intraocular pressure further and succeeds more often: across 11 comparative studies (1,260 eyes) the pooled pressure reduction favoured trabeculectomy by a mean 2.16 mm Hg, with higher qualified and complete success (Bhatti 2026, PMID: 42539846), and the 24-month cohort found final pressure 12.5 versus 14.6 mm Hg (Wanichwecharungruang 2021, PMID: 34411152). The XEN 45 gel stent (XEN Gel Stent, Allergan/AbbVie, as named in the publications) gave the gentler course: fewer early postoperative visits, less vision loss and less surgically induced astigmatism, at the price of more bleb needling/transconjunctival needle revision (Schlenker 2018, PMID: 32672652). On the question's hypotony point, the pooled analysis found no statistically significant difference in hypotony rates (with substantial heterogeneity, I²=76%), and the 24-month cohort reported a lower rate of numerical hypotony with XEN. PROPOSED SPLIT: trabeculectomy wins on pressure and success; XEN wins on postoperative burden; hypotony is not clearly different. All comparative evidence here is observational, which caps confidence.
stamp: SPLIT — trabeculectomy achieves greater intraocular pressure reduction (pooled mean difference 2.16 mm Hg) and higher success, while the XEN gel stent gives fewer postoperative visits and less vision loss at the price of more bleb needling; hypotony rates do not differ clearly. Observational evidence base (two retrospective cohorts and a meta-analysis of mostly non-randomised studies), which caps confidence at POSSIBLE-level certainty for either direction

title: DMEK versus DSAEK/DSEK for corneal endothelial failure (DETECT): 1.8 lines better acuity at 6 months and 1.4 lines at 12 months, with more rebubbling as the trade
question: In adults with corneal endothelial failure, does Descemet membrane endothelial keratoplasty (DMEK) give faster and better visual recovery than Descemet stripping automated endothelial keratoplasty (DSAEK/DSEK)? (DETECT.)
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one small randomised trial plus concordant observational syntheses. The DETECT randomised trial (Chamberlain 2019, PMID: 29945801) found Descemet membrane endothelial keratoplasty (DMEK) gave 1.5 lines better best spectacle-corrected visual acuity at 3 months, 1.8 lines at 6 months and 1.4 lines at 12 months than ultrathin Descemet stripping automated endothelial keratoplasty (UT-DSAEK), with similar complication rates and endothelial cell counts. The meta-analysis of retrospective comparisons found the same direction — 12-month acuity 0.16 versus 0.30 logMAR, fewer rejections with DMEK but more rebubbling (Marques 2019, PMID: 29661044) — and the Cochrane review, written before DETECT, found low-certainty evidence of better acuity with DMEK at the cost of more graft dislocations (Stuart 2018, PMID: 29940078). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): DETECT randomised only 38 patients, and the supporting base is retrospective, so the stamp stays at POSSIBLE despite concordance.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one small randomised trial (DETECT, 38 patients) plus concordant observational syntheses: DMEK gave 1.5-1.8 lines better acuity than ultrathin DSAEK over the first year with similar complications, at the cost of more rebubbling; the small randomised base caps the stamp at POSSIBLE

title: Vismodegib in locally advanced basal cell carcinoma unsuitable for surgery/radiotherapy (ERIVANCE; STEVIE — single-arm): response 43% by independent review, median response duration 26.2 months at final update, 36% stopping for adverse events
question: In adults with locally advanced basal cell carcinoma unsuitable for surgery or radiotherapy, does vismodegib produce durable tumour responses? (ERIVANCE, STEVIE — single-arm; label as such.)
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single-arm evidence throughout, labelled as such; there is no randomised or untreated comparator in this programme. In the pivotal ERIVANCE study, independently assessed response was 43% in locally advanced basal cell carcinoma (21% complete) and 30% in metastatic disease, with a median duration of response of 7.6 months at the primary analysis (Sekulic 2012, PMID: 22670903); the final update put investigator-assessed response at 60.3% in locally advanced disease with a median duration of response of 26.2 months (Sekulic 2017, PMID: 28511673). The STEVIE practice-setting study found investigator-assessed response in 66.7% of locally advanced patients, with treatment stopped for adverse events in 36% (Basset-Seguin 2015, PMID: 25981813). Muscle spasms, hair loss, taste disturbance, weight loss and fatigue are the standing costs. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): responses are real and sometimes durable, but single-arm data cannot separate drug effect from selection, and tolerability limits how long many patients stay on treatment.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single-arm evidence only (labelled): ERIVANCE response 43% by independent review in locally advanced BCC with median duration of response maturing to 26.2 months, and STEVIE response 66.7% by investigator assessment, against 36% discontinuation for adverse events; no comparator exists, so the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE

title: PARTIAL (home #625 for established field therapies): tirbanibulin 1% ointment 5-day for actinic keratosis — complete clearance 44% and 54% versus 5% and 13% on vehicle, 47% recurrence at 1 year, no head-to-head versus established therapies
question: In adults with actinic keratosis, does tirbanibulin 1% ointment (5-day course) clear lesions versus vehicle, and how does its clearance compare with the established field therapies?
balance: PARTIAL SHELF — flagged prominently: the established field therapies for actinic keratosis (5-fluorouracil, imiquimod, methyl aminolevulinate photodynamic therapy, ingenol mebutate) are already homed at Shelf #625, whose head-to-head trial found 5-fluorouracil the most durable of those four at 12 months. This shelf covers only the slice #625 does not: tirbanibulin 1% ointment (Klisyri, Athenex — the tested product as published), the newest field agent, which has never been randomised head-to-head against any of the #625 therapies. Against vehicle, the two identically designed phase 3 trials (Blauvelt 2021, PMID: 33567191) found complete clearance at day 57 in 44% and 54% on tirbanibulin versus 5% and 13% on vehicle, with recurrence in an estimated 47% of complete responders by 1 year. Phase 2 data set the 5-day course (Kempers 2020, PMID: 33196758), and a single-arm phase 3 study supports tolerability over a 100 cm² field (Bhatia 2024, PMID: 39268198). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): clear superiority over vehicle on a 5-day course, but no comparative claim against fluorouracil or the other established therapies can be made from this evidence, and 1-year recurrence is substantial. Cross-point: see Shelf #625 for the established-therapy comparison.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — PARTIAL shelf (the established field therapies are homed at Shelf #625): two phase 3 trials (702 patients) show tirbanibulin 1% ointment for 5 days clears lesions versus vehicle (complete clearance 44% and 54% versus 5% and 13% at day 57), but there is no head-to-head trial against any established field therapy and 47% of complete responders recurred by 1 year, capping the stamp at POSSIBLE

title: Efanesoctocog alfa weekly prophylaxis in severe haemophilia A without inhibitors (XTEND-1; XTEND-Kids — single-arm, intra-patient comparator): annualised bleeding rate 2.96 to 0.69 versus prestudy prophylaxis, factor VIII >40 IU/dL most of the week
question: In people with severe haemophilia A without inhibitors, does once-weekly efanesoctocog alfa prophylaxis maintain higher factor VIII levels and lower bleeding than standard prophylaxis? (XTEND-1 — single-arm, intra-patient comparator; label as such.)
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single-arm evidence with an intra-patient comparator, labelled as such; there is no randomised parallel control in this programme. In XTEND-1 (von Drygalski 2023, PMID: 36720133), once-weekly efanesoctocog alfa 50 IU/kg in 133 patients aged 12 or older gave an estimated mean annualised bleeding rate of 0.71, and the intra-patient comparison showed the mean rate falling from 2.96 on prestudy factor VIII prophylaxis to 0.69 on efanesoctocog alfa (P<0.001), with factor VIII activity above 40 IU/dL for most of the week and 15 IU/dL at day 7; no inhibitors were detected. XTEND-Kids found the same pattern in 74 children, with no inhibitors (Malec 2024, PMID: 39018533). Matching-adjusted indirect comparisons against standard and extended half-life products also favour efanesoctocog alfa, but they are indirect and industry-modelled (Klamroth 2025, PMID: 39576433). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the intra-patient design is stronger than a bare single-arm series, but without randomisation the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single-arm evidence with intra-patient comparator (labelled): XTEND-1 mean annualised bleeding rate fell from 2.96 on prestudy prophylaxis to 0.69 on once-weekly efanesoctocog alfa, with concordant XTEND-Kids results and no inhibitors in 233 patients; no randomised comparator exists, capping the stamp at POSSIBLE

title: Concizumab prophylaxis in haemophilia A/B (with or without inhibitors): treated bleeding rates fell by about four-fifths or more versus no prophylaxis in the explorer7 and explorer8 phase 3 trials (annualised rate 1.7 versus 11.8 episodes with inhibitors)
question: In people with haemophilia A or B, with or without inhibitors, does concizumab prophylaxis reduce treated bleeding episodes versus no prophylaxis?
balance: Concizumab is a monoclonal antibody against tissue factor pathway inhibitor, given as a once-daily subcutaneous prophylaxis and designed to restore thrombin generation in all haemophilia types. Two randomised phase 3 trials from the single explorer programme ask the same question against no prophylaxis (on-demand factor treatment). In explorer7 (haemophilia A or B WITH inhibitors; Matsushita 2023), the estimated mean annualised bleeding rate for treated spontaneous and traumatic episodes was 1.7 episodes on concizumab versus 11.8 episodes with no prophylaxis — a rate ratio of 0.14, an 86% relative reduction, with the absolute rates printed beside it. In explorer8 (haemophilia A or B WITHOUT inhibitors; Chowdary 2024), the annualised bleeding rate ratios were 0.14 for haemophilia A (an 86% relative reduction) and 0.21 for haemophilia B (a 79% relative reduction); the fetched record reports the ratios and does not print the two absolute annualised rates, so none are printed here. Both trials were paused after non-fatal thromboembolic events in three patients across the programme and restarted with a loading dose of 1.0 mg/kg followed by 0.2 mg/kg daily, adjustable by week-4 plasma concentration; no thromboembolic events were reported after restart in either trial, and explorer8 recorded one fatal intra-abdominal haemorrhage judged possibly treatment-related. The evidence is one sponsor programme with open-label designs and short randomised comparisons (at least 24 weeks without prophylaxis), so the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE. title: The incretin effect (physiology): oral glucose evokes roughly two to three times the insulin response of matched intravenous glucose — incretin factors contribute about 73% of the insulin response in health and about 36% in type 2 diabetes
question: In healthy humans, how much larger is the insulin response to oral glucose than to an isoglycaemic intravenous infusion (the incretin effect), and how much of it is lost in type 2 diabetes?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing (Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology; Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology): glucose taken by mouth evokes a far larger insulin response than the same glycaemic excursion produced intravenously, because gut-derived incretin hormones (GIP and GLP-1) amplify glucose-stimulated insulin secretion — the incretin effect. The carded primary human studies quantify it three ways. Perley and Kipnis (1967) found the plasma insulin response to intravenous glucose was only 30–40% of the response to oral glucose. Nauck's isoglycaemic-infusion programme (1986) put the incretin contribution to calculated insulin secretion rates at 19.2–61.0% depending on the oral load (25–100 g), with peripheral-insulin estimates running higher because hepatic insulin extraction falls after oral glucose. The direct health-versus-diabetes comparison (Nauck 1986, Diabetologia) measured the incretin contribution to the total insulin response at 72.8% in control subjects and 36.0% in type 2 diabetic patients — about half lost — and on C-peptide responses 58.4% versus 7.6%. The mechanism split (Nauck 1993) is that GIP's insulinotropic effect is blunted in type 2 diabetes (maximum effect 54% lower) while GLP-1 [7-36 amide] retains most of its activity. The classic 1964 McIntyre intrajejunal study that first framed the effect was checked this session: its PubMed record carries an empty abstract, so it is refused as an evidence card and named here only as the historical anchor. Every number on the cards is from a fetched record. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

title: Oxygen–haemoglobin curve shifts (physiology): normal P50 is about 26–27 mmHg; rising CO2 and falling pH shift the curve right (the Bohr effect), cold shifts it left, and 2,3-BPG rises within 24 hours at altitude to shift it right again
question: In healthy humans, how do carbon dioxide, pH, temperature and 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate shift the oxygen–haemoglobin dissociation curve (the Bohr effect and P50), and by how much?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing (Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology; Boron and Boulpaep Medical Physiology): the oxygen–haemoglobin dissociation curve is not fixed — acidity and carbon dioxide shift it right (the Bohr effect, promoting oxygen release in metabolising tissues), temperature shifts it right when warm and left when cold, and 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate (2,3-BPG) binds deoxyhaemoglobin and shifts it right, with the standard P50 (the PO2 at 50% saturation, at pH 7.4, 37 °C, PCO2 40 mmHg) given in the textbooks as about 26–27 mmHg and the Bohr coefficient (Δlog P50 per ΔpH unit, about −0.48) and temperature coefficient presented as the textbook's account — the carded records confirm the directions and the baseline but do not print those two coefficients, so they are not claimed as measured values here. The carded primary human studies quantify what can be quantified from fetched records: a modern factorial in-vitro study of blood from 30 healthy subjects measured mean P50 of 27.1 ± 2.6 mmHg at baseline (37 °C, PCO2 40 mmHg) with significant CO2-Bohr and temperature coefficients across PCO2 20–80 mmHg and 13.7–42 °C (Woyke 2021); the classic normal P50 of 26 mmHg (3.46 kPa) was the reference value in the Fournier 1984 study of 20 subjects, which also showed a reversible 8 mmHg left shift under nitrous oxide that could not be explained by pH, PCO2, temperature or 2,3-DPG; and Lenfant's 1968 altitude study showed haemoglobin affinity changing within 24 hours of moving between low and high altitude, in parallel with red-cell organic phosphate (2,3-DPG) — the rapid adaptive limb of the 2,3-BPG mechanism, including the altitude 2,3-BPG adaptation this row folds in. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

title: Spermatogenesis kinetics (physiology): one cycle of the seminiferous epithelium lasts about 16 days and the full process about 64 days (perhaps 6 days longer); daily production is about 4.25 million sperm per gram of testis — roughly 45 to 207 million per day in most men
question: In healthy men, how long does one full wave of spermatogenesis take, and how is daily sperm production quantified?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing (Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology; Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology): spermatogenesis proceeds in repeating cellular associations (the cycle of the seminiferous epithelium), and several cycles must elapse before a spermatogonium becomes a spermatozoon. The carded primary human studies supply the numbers. Heller and Clermont's 1963 tritiated-thymidine labelling study — biopsies taken at intervals after intratesticular injection — timed the labelled cohort's advance (preleptotene spermatocytes at 1 hour, midpachytene at 16 days, immature spermatids at 32 days), giving a cycle length of 16 days and a total duration of spermatogenesis estimated at approximately 64 days. Amann's 2008 re-examination warns that this accepted value might be in error by approximately 6 days and that the 1960s database is neither robust nor precise — a caveat printed on the face of this shelf rather than smoothed over. Daily sperm production is quantified not from ejaculates but from testicular sperm reserves: Amann and Howards (1980) measured 4.25 × 10^6 sperm per gram of testis per day (range 1.4–6.3 × 10^6), so that 67% of men aged 20–50 probably produce between 45 × 10^6 and 207 × 10^6 spermatozoa per day; production per gram tends to decline with age, and substantial potential sperm are lost by degeneration of spermatocytes. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (with the duration caveat carried on the cards).

title: Gastric acid secretion by phase (physiology): thinking about food alone reaches about two-thirds of the sham-feeding (cephalic) response, a meal secretes about 24 mmol/h of acid, and pentagastrin or histamine drive a peak of about 29 mmol/h
question: In healthy humans, how is gastric acid secretion divided among the cephalic, gastric and intestinal phases, and what is maximal acid output after pentagastrin or histamine stimulation?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing (Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology; Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology): acid secretion is conventionally divided into a cephalic phase (sight, smell, taste and thought of food, vagally mediated), a gastric phase (distension and peptides/amino acids in the stomach, largely gastrin-driven) and an intestinal phase — with the textbook's account assigning roughly 30% of the meal response to the cephalic phase, about 60% to the gastric phase and about 10% to the intestinal phase; those phase percentages are presented here explicitly as the textbook's account, because the carded primary studies measure the phases by stimulation and blockade rather than printing that exact split. What the carded human studies do quantify: thinking about food for 30 minutes raised acid output from 4 to 13 mmol/h, averaging 66% of the full modified-sham-feeding (cephalic) response, while sight and smell alone reached only 23–46% of sham feeding (Feldman & Richardson 1986); a simulated meal with sham feeding secreted 24.2 mmol/h, of which circulating gastrin could account for 89% on average — but anywhere from 51% to 162% in individuals (Blair 1987); sham feeding in the Konturek programme reached about 50% of the pentagastrin maximum; basal output in healthy volunteers was about 3.6–4.3 mmol/h against a pentagastrin-stimulated peak of 28.69 mmol/h (Klein 1989); and histamine and pentagastrin elicit equal maximal outputs of acid and pepsin, pentagastrin being the more potent and faster (Aubrey & Forrest 1970). PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

title: Aqueous humour dynamics (physiology): fluorophotometry measures formation at about 2.75 µL/min by day, falling to about half during sleep, and normal intraocular pressure varies by no more than about 5 mmHg across 24 hours
question: In healthy humans, at what rate is aqueous humour formed and drained, and how large is the normal diurnal swing in intraocular pressure?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing (Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology; Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology): aqueous humour is secreted by the ciliary processes into the posterior chamber, flows through the pupil, and drains through the trabecular meshwork and Schlemm's canal, with intraocular pressure set by the balance of formation and outflow resistance. The carded primary human studies quantify that system by fluorophotometry, the Brubaker programme's method: aqueous flow in normal subjects averages 2.75 ± 0.63 µL/min during office hours (95% range 1.8 to 4.3 µL/min), follows a circadian rhythm — highest in the morning, slightly lower in the afternoon, and about half the morning rate during sleep — and declines about 3.2% per decade after age 10 (Brubaker 1991, the Friedenwald Lecture synthesising the programme's clinical experiments). The companion fluorophotometry studies print the method's working values in untreated normal eyes (for example 2.4 µL/min in placebo-treated fellow eyes in the clonidine study, Lee 1984, where a 21% flow reduction accompanied a 2 mmHg pressure fall). For the pressure side, the carded 24-hour study of 25 normal subjects found that normal individuals did not show diurnal intraocular-pressure variation greater than 5 mmHg across six measurements in 24 hours — in contrast to pseudoexfoliation patients, over half of whom exceeded 5 mmHg (Altintaş 2004). Drainage rate equals formation rate at steady state by definition; no carded record prints a separate directly-measured drainage number, so none is claimed. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

title: Energy expenditure and NEAT (physiology): doubly labelled water puts free-living total expenditure at roughly 7–12 MJ/day depending on body size and activity, and when volunteers were overfed by 1,000 kcal/day, two-thirds of the rise in expenditure came from NEAT — whose activation predicted who resisted fat gain
question: In healthy humans, what is total daily energy expenditure measured by doubly labelled water, and how much does non-exercise activity thermogenesis (NEAT) change with overfeeding?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing (Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology; Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology): total daily energy expenditure is the sum of basal metabolic rate, the thermic effect of food, and activity thermogenesis — the last split into exercise and non-exercise activity thermogenesis (NEAT: posture, fidgeting, and the activities of daily life). Doubly labelled water is the reference method for measuring the total in free-living people: the carded validation study found expenditure by doubly labelled water averaged within 3 ± 6% of intake-balance during parenteral nutrition (Schoeller 1986, the Schoeller programme's validation work). Free-living totals from the carded population studies run from 7.1 MJ/day (about 1,700 kcal/day) in chronically energy-deficient urban men to 11.2 and 12.2 MJ/day (about 2,680 and 2,920 kcal/day) in urban-control and rural men, with physical activity levels (TEE/BMR) of 1.54 to 1.90 (Borgonha 2000), and 9.35 ± 2.00 MJ/day (about 2,235 kcal/day) in a 21-day study of healthy men (Kurpad 1997). The NEAT experiment (Levine 1999): 16 non-obese volunteers overfed by 1,000 kcal/day for 8 weeks increased total expenditure mainly through NEAT — two-thirds of the increase in total daily energy expenditure was due to increased NEAT — and changes in NEAT accounted for the 10-fold differences in fat storage and directly predicted resistance to fat gain (r = 0.77, p < 0.001); the companion report showed leptin rose with fat mass but did not mediate the NEAT activation. The fetched Levine abstract does not print the absolute kcal/day range of NEAT change, so none is claimed here. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

title: Mucociliary clearance in health: tracheal mucus at 7–19 mm/min, wide variation between people, no fall with age, no posture effect — and a beta-agonist reserve of about a fifth
question: In healthy humans, how fast is mucus transported up the airways (tracheobronchial mucociliary clearance), and how do age, posture and inhaled agents change it?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology and Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology — the textbooks describe the mucociliary escalator as a continuous cephalad transport of the mucus blanket by coordinated ciliary beating, the lung's first-line defence; the carded human studies supply the numbers). Direct tracheal measurement in volunteers gives mucus velocities of 7.4–19.4 mm/min (Friedman 1977, N = 7). Radioaerosol whole-lung clearance varies much more between people than within them (between-person COV 31%, within-person 11%; van Hengstum 1989), which is why the 62-person reference study matters: across ages 18–84 there was no influence of age on clearance and no convincing sex association, while central (versus peripheral) aerosol deposition and ex-smoking did matter (Mortensen 1994). Posture did not: erect and supine velocities did not differ consistently (Friedman 1977). Inhaled agents move the system in both directions in the wider literature; carded here, an inhaled secretagogue mediator, bradykinin, accelerated tracheobronchial clearance (median retention AUC 126%/h placebo to 87%/h; Polosa 1992), a beta-2 agonist raised lung clearance by a mean reserve of 21.3% (Mortensen 1994), and topical salmeterol shortened nasal saccharin transit by 21% (Tay 1997). PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED: clearance is fast, individually variable, age- and posture-stable, and pharmacologically accelerable.

title: Gut transit in health: colon about 35 hours (men faster than women by roughly 11 hours), small bowel about 5 hours, and wide normal variation
question: In healthy humans, what are normal whole-gut and colonic transit times, and how much do they vary between people and by sex?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Guyton & Hall and Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology — the textbooks present colonic transit as the slow, variable limb of gut transit, measured clinically by radio-opaque markers; the carded human studies supply the values). Total colonic transit averaged 35.0 ± 2.1 hours in 73 healthy people, split almost evenly — right colon 11.3, left colon 11.4, rectosigmoid 12.4 hours — and was significantly shorter in men than women (Metcalf 1987). The larger Swiss reference series (N = 128) puts the sex gap at 30 ± 2 hours in men versus 41 ± 3 hours in women, with no age effect and upper reference limits up to 70 hours in women (Meir 1992). Repeat scintigraphic testing confirms the sex difference and shows group means are stable while individual single measurements can vary considerably — intrinsic variation large enough that any menstrual-cycle effect must be small (Degen & Phillips 1996). The small bowel is fast by comparison: orocaecal transit ~295–301 minutes with no sex difference (Bennink 1999), so whole-gut transit time is essentially colonic transit plus about 5 hours. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED: quote colonic transit as ~35 hours with a wide normal range, expect women to run slower than men, and treat a single measurement in one person cautiously.

title: Colonic short-chain fatty acids: a concentrated fermentation product, absorbed almost completely, with butyrate feeding the colonocyte, propionate the liver, and acetate reaching the blood
question: In healthy humans, how much short-chain fatty acid does colonic fermentation produce each day, what fraction is absorbed, and what share of energy needs can it supply?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED, with the production and energy figures explicitly on a different footing from the carded measurements (textbook framing: Guyton & Hall; Boron & Boulpaep). The textbook/review account — Cummings' contemporary review of the primary literature, fetched this session — is that the colonic flora ferment 30 g or more of carbohydrate daily with production of at least 300 mmol of short-chain fatty acids, and the standard review estimate (Nordgaard & Mortensen 1995, fetched this session) puts the energy salvaged at about 5–10% of energy requirements in people with a normal-length gut; those two figures are presented here as the textbook/review account because no carded primary study measures 24-hour production or energy share directly. What the primary human studies do measure is consistent with near-complete absorption: colonic contents hold 131 mmol/kg SCFA in the caecum falling distally, while portal blood (375 µmol/L) carries several-fold the peripheral level (79 µmol/L) and molar ratios shift in a pattern showing butyrate taken up by the colonic epithelium and propionate by the liver (Cummings 1987). Colonic perfusion shows absorption is concentration-dependent, ~60% by nonionic diffusion, and coupled to sodium and water absorption (Ruppin 1980); a caecal lactulose load raises portal SCFA within 15–45 minutes while peripheral blood shows essentially acetate alone (Peters 1992); and whole-body acetate turnover is ~7.5 µmol/kg/min (Simoneau 1994). Very little SCFA appears in normal stool relative to these fluxes — the absorbed fraction is therefore conventionally put at well over 90% (textbook account). PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED for production, routing and near-complete absorption; the precise daily mmol and energy-share figures are textbook-account values.

title: Cutaneous vitamin D synthesis: one minimal erythemal dose raises serum vitamin D3 to ~26 ng/mL — abolished by sunscreen, more than halved by ageing, and needing ~6× the dose in heavily pigmented skin
question: In healthy humans, how much vitamin D does whole-body sun exposure synthesise in skin, and how do ageing, pigmentation and sunscreen change that yield?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Guyton & Hall; Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology — UV-B photolyses epidermal 7-dehydrocholesterol to previtamin D3, which thermally isomerises to vitamin D3; continued exposure photodegrades previtamin D3 to inert isomers, so synthesis self-limits and sun alone does not cause vitamin D toxicity). The textbook account commonly equates one whole-body minimal erythemal dose with a large oral dose (on the order of 10,000–25,000 IU) — that equivalence is a textbook account, not a value measured in the carded studies; the carded measurements are serum responses to defined doses. One minimal erythema dose raised mean serum vitamin D3 from 1.5 to 25.6 ng/mL in unprotected subjects, while through an SPF-8 sunscreen there was no rise at all (Matsuoka 1987, N = 8). Ageing attacks the substrate: epidermal 7-dehydrocholesterol falls with age and skin from 77–82-year-olds made less than half the previtamin D3 of skin from 8–18-year-olds under the same UV (MacLaughlin & Holick 1985). Pigmentation gates the photons: 1 minimal erythemal dose raised serum vitamin D up to 60-fold in lightly pigmented volunteers but not significantly in heavily pigmented volunteers, one of whom needed a sixfold dose to reach the same level (Clemens 1982, N = 5). PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED: the skin is a high-capacity vitamin D source whose yield is set by UV-B reaching epidermal 7-dehydrocholesterol — sunscreen, age and melanin each cut it, by the amounts carded.

title: Sleep restriction and glucose: a few nights at 4–5 hours cut insulin sensitivity by about a fifth and blunt glucose tolerance — with the defect demonstrable inside fat cells
question: In healthy humans, how much does restricting sleep to about 4 hours a night for several nights impair glucose tolerance and insulin sensitivity?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology and Guyton & Hall — sleep is presented as a metabolic state, not merely rest; the Van Cauter programme carded here is the primary human evidence that curtailing it moves glucose regulation within days). The anchor study restricted 11 young men to 4 hours in bed for 6 nights against a 12-hour recovery condition: glucose tolerance was significantly lower in sleep debt (P < 0.02), with raised evening cortisol and sympathetic activity (Spiegel 1999). The clamp study gives the size: after 7 nights at 5 hours, insulin sensitivity fell 20 ± 24% by IVGTT and 11 ± 5.5% by euglycaemic clamp, with no compensatory rise in insulin secretion and a reduced disposition index (Buxton 2010). The defect is peripheral and molecular, not just hormonal: after 4 nights at 4.5 hours, adipocytes from 7 volunteers needed nearly three times the insulin for half-maximal Akt signalling (Broussard 2012), and after only 2 nights at ~4 hours, breakfast glucose peaked at 6.8 mmol/L (≈122 mg/dL) versus 6.1 mmol/L (≈110 mg/dL) rested, with insulin peaks ~40% higher and no change in cortisol or IL-6 (Schmid 2011). Adjacent shelf: weekend catch-up sleep and metabolic recovery is asked separately (live Shelf #494) and is not re-carded here. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED: several nights of ~4-hour sleep produce a measurable, roughly one-fifth loss of insulin sensitivity in healthy young adults.

title: Renal adaptation to an acid load: ammonium excretion climbs over days to ~200 mmol/day (ceiling 200–300), and net acid excretion rises to match the load
question: In healthy humans, how does the kidney adapt to a sustained acid load over days — how much do ammonium excretion and net acid excretion rise, and over what time course?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Guyton & Hall; Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology). The textbook account of the time course: titratable acid can rise only modestly because it is capped by urinary phosphate, so the adaptable limb is ammonium — made from glutamine in the proximal tubule — which climbs over roughly 3–5 days of sustained loading as ammoniagenic enzymes are induced, from a baseline of a few tens of mmol/day to a plateau at which net acid excretion (titratable acid + ammonium − bicarbonate) equals the daily acid load and plasma bicarbonate stabilises at a new, lower steady state; that shape and the baseline figure are the textbook account. The carded human studies quantify the adapted state the textbook describes: under NH4Cl at 4.2 mmol/kg/day for 7 days, healthy subjects excreted 202 ± 17 mmol/day of ammonium (Jehle 2000); in chronic metabolic acidosis urinary ammonia excretion was 186% higher and total ammonia production 110% higher than in non-acidemic controls, with 82% (versus 65%) of produced ammonia partitioned into urine (Garibotto 2004); and the quantified ceiling is an ammonium excretion of 200–300 mmol/day, with loaded fasted controls excreting 176 ± 26 mmol/day of net acid (Kamel 1990). The acute phase is separately testable within hours by a single 50 mEq NH4Cl load (Bobulescu 2013). Refused anchor, reported plainly: the Pitts programme's 1949 balance studies (e.g. PMID 18127528) carry no abstract in their PubMed records, so no numbers could be verified from the record and they are not carded. Adjacency: renal acid excretion in CKD — per-nephron adaptation as total ammonium falls — is Pack #6358; its references (PMIDs 4555786, 2128531, 28645705) are deliberately not re-carded here. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

title: The acute hypoxic ventilatory response: flat until PO2 ~50–60 mmHg then steeply rising, ~0.68 L/min per % SaO2 awake — and a stable, partly hereditary trait that varies widely between people
question: In healthy humans, how large is the acute hypoxic ventilatory response to a step fall in oxygen saturation, and how much does it vary between individuals?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Guyton & Hall; Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology — the peripheral chemoreflex: carotid-body sensing of arterial PO2 drives ventilation, with an effective threshold in the 50–60 mmHg range and powerful multiplicative interaction with CO2; the Weil programme carded here built the human measurement). Weil's continuous-curve method showed the response is complete within 18–23 seconds and hyperbolic — ventilation barely moves until alveolar PO2 falls to 50–60 mmHg, then climbs steeply — quantified by the shape parameter A = 180.2 ± 14.5 in 10 normal men at resting CO2, swinging to 453 with +5 mmHg CO2 and 30 with −5 mmHg (Weil 1970). In saturation-slope units, the awake progressive-isocapnic response is 0.68 ± 0.07 L/min per % SaO2, roughly halving in sleep (Berthon-Jones & Sullivan 1982). The variation the question asks about is real and structured: pooled raw data from 60 datasets show positively skewed distributions with low responders common in healthy sea-level people, and isocapnic protocols yielding higher values than poikilocapnic (Oeung 2023); identical twins resemble each other in HVR while non-identical twins do not (Collins 1978); and an individual's response tracks himself over 8–10 years (r = 0.63) even as the group mean drifts down (Nishimura 1991). Adjacent shelves ask the different questions of the hypercapnic response and of ventilatory acclimatisation over days at altitude (Pack #6247) — neither is re-carded here. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

title: Starling forces in humans (physiology): interstitial pressure is slightly negative, plasma colloid osmotic pressure ~24–26 mmHg and interstitial COP roughly 6–13 mmHg, so net filtration is small — and when filtration rises, falling interstitial COP (washdown) is the measured buffer; Guyton's ~17 mmHg total safety-factor budget is the textbook's account
question: In healthy humans, what are the Starling forces across capillaries — interstitial fluid pressure and colloid osmotic pressures — and how large are the safety factors against oedema?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing (Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology): capillary exchange is set by four forces — capillary pressure pushing out, interstitial pressure (slightly negative, ~−3 mmHg in the textbook's account) pushing in, plasma colloid osmotic pressure (~28 mmHg in the textbook) pulling in, and interstitial colloid osmotic pressure pulling out — leaving a small net filtration that lymph returns; against oedema the textbook budgets ~17 mmHg of safety factors (negative interstitial pressure ~3 mmHg, increased lymph flow ~7 mmHg, interstitial protein washdown ~7 mmHg). The carded human wick studies measure the same system at slightly lower absolute values: interstitial pressure −0.8 mmHg in healthy ankle tissue (Stranden & Myhre 1983), plasma COP 23.2 mmHg in early pregnancy and 25.6 mmHg in healthy children (Øian 1985; Guthe 2015), interstitial COP 9.2 mmHg at the ankle and up to 13.1 mmHg on the thorax. The washdown factor is not just textbook arithmetic — in pregnancy interstitial COP fell further than plasma COP as filtration rose (Øian), and when bypass dilution reversed the COP gradient, interstitial pressure rose measurably until the gradient recovered (Rein 1988). The lymph-flow limb of the safety budget and the ~17 mmHg total are presented as the textbook's account: no carded record here measures human lymph flow or prints that budget.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED

title: Brain fuel in prolonged fasting (physiology) — PARTIAL slice: cerebral ketone uptake is proportional to blood ketone concentration and displaces glucose at unchanged oxygen use; after 5–6 weeks of starvation ketones are the brain's predominant fuel (Owen 1967, carded on pack #6307) — roughly two-thirds of brain energy by the textbook account
question: In humans fasted for weeks, what fraction of the brain's energy comes from ketone bodies, and how was cerebral glucose-versus-ketone uptake measured?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — PARTIAL slice, flagged prominently. Homes first: live shelf #34 already homes hepatic glucose production and its recycling fractions in fasting; pack #6255 homes the 24–72-hour whole-body fasting time course; and Owen 1967 — the anchor study for this row — is already carded on pack #6307 (hepatic ketogenesis regulation), where its cerebral finding is stated. Under the one-home rule Owen is NOT re-carded here; this shelf builds only on four free reports and cross-points the homes in prose. What the free reports establish is the measurement story the row asks for: cerebral ketone uptake rises in proportion to arterial ketone concentration and is limited by transport into the brain (Blomqvist 2002, ¹¹C-ketone PET; Mikkelsen 2015, arterio-jugular balance), and ketones displace glucose at unchanged cerebral oxygen consumption (Hasselbalch 1996, Kety–Schmidt: ketone uptake 1.11→5.60 µmol/100 g/min, glucose metabolism 25.8→17.2 µmol/100 g/min at β-hydroxybutyrate 2.16 mmol/L, ≈22 mg/dL; Svart 2018: glucose utilisation −14% at 5.5 mmol/L, ≈57 mg/dL). Owen's endpoint — after 5–6 weeks of starvation, ketones had replaced glucose as the brain's predominant fuel — and the textbook figure of roughly two-thirds (~60%) of brain energy from ketones in prolonged fasting are presented as the Guyton & Hall / Cahill account of the homed Owen study, not as numbers from this shelf's cards. Cahill's 1968 'Starvation and survival' record carries no abstract in PubMed and is therefore not carded, per the standing honesty pattern; it is carried here as programme framing only.
