title: Lipolysis and fatty-acid turnover by tracers (physiology): resting glycerol appearance ~2.0 µmol/kg/min in healthy adults; fasting raises lipolysis (partly via falling glucose/insulin, with a sensitised epinephrine response); in exercise lipolysis is maximally stimulated at low intensity while plasma fatty-acid release falls as intensity rises
question: In healthy humans, what are the rates of lipolysis and free-fatty-acid turnover at rest, in fasting and during exercise, measured by tracers?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing (Guyton & Hall): hormone-sensitive lipase hydrolyses adipose triglyceride to glycerol and free fatty acids; insulin restrains it, catecholamines and fasting release it, and fatty acids not oxidised are re-esterified. The tracer literature (Wolfe and Jensen programmes) turns that account into rates: glycerol appearance — one glycerol per triglyceride split, and adipose cannot re-use glycerol — measures whole-body lipolysis, and palmitate appearance measures fatty-acid flux. At rest after an overnight fast, healthy glycerol appearance is 2.00 ± 0.16 µmol/kg/min (Klein & Wolfe 1990). Fasting to 84 hours raises lipolytic rates; restoring glucose/insulin normalises them, yet lipolysis still rises when glucose is held constant, and the epinephrine response is sensitised (Klein, Holland & Wolfe 1990). Exercise inverts the intensity intuition: peripheral lipolysis is maximally stimulated at 25% of VO₂max while plasma fatty-acid release falls at higher intensities and muscle triglyceride takes over (Romijn 1993). The Jensen ultralow-dose [U-¹³C]palmitate method reproduces radiotracer flux with a coefficient of variation of ~8–13% (Guo 1997), which is what makes these small classic numbers trustworthy as physiology.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED

title: EPO and haemoglobin recovery after blood loss (physiology): erythropoietin rises within 6 hours and peaks at days 7–14 after a 400 mL phlebotomy, haemoglobin nadirs at days 3–7 and haemoglobin mass is rebuilt in a mean of 36 days after a standard donation — while ferritin is still ~55% of baseline at day 56
question: In healthy humans, how quickly do erythropoietin and reticulocytes respond after acute blood loss or phlebotomy, and how long does haemoglobin take to recover?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing (Guyton & Hall): erythropoietin, made mainly by the kidney in response to reduced oxygen delivery, drives reticulocyte production over days and red-cell mass over weeks. The phlebotomy/donation studies give that account a human clock — a different stimulus and time course from altitude hypoxia (pack #6266, cross-pointed; none of its studies re-carded). After 400 mL, erythropoietin is up within 6 hours (~20 mU/mL) but peaks only at days 7–14 (~26–29 mU/mL), haemoglobin nadirs at days 3–7, and haemoglobin concentration has not fully recovered by day 56 (Maeda 1992, N = 14). Measured properly as haemoglobin mass (CO rebreathing), a standard ~550 mL donation's 75 g loss is rebuilt in a mean of 36 ± 11 days, range 20–59 (Pottgiesser 2008, N = 29). The slowest limb is iron: ferritin is still ~55% of baseline at day 56 in repeat donors, with hepcidin shifting from day 1 (Lotfi 2015, N = 27). Reticulocyte values were sampled in these programmes but are not printed in the fetched abstracts, so the reticulocyte limb is carried as the textbook's account in the Synthesis, not as carded numbers.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED

title: Vestibulo-ocular reflex gain and adaptation (physiology): dark gain is ~0.7–0.75 and vision brings it to ~1.0; magnifying spectacles drive gain up within minutes (7–46% in 15 min), reversing prisms reshape it over days with retention for weeks, and two context-specific gains can coexist
question: In healthy humans, what is the gain of the vestibulo-ocular reflex, and how does it adapt when vision is magnified, minified or reversed?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing (Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology): the vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR) rotates the eyes opposite the head to hold the image still, ideally at a gain (eye velocity ÷ head velocity) of 1.0, and retinal image slip is its teaching signal. The human measurements refine the textbook number: in darkness the reflex alone runs at ~0.74 ± 0.10 (Demer 1987, N = 7) and ~0.7 at 0.1 Hz (Demer 1989); ordinary vision tops it up to 1.07. Adaptation is fast, specific and storable: 15 minutes in ×2.2–×6 telescopic spectacles raised dark gain 7–46% in about half to two-thirds of subjects and improved dynamic visual acuity 30–100% (Demer 1987, 1989); up to 27 days in reversing dove prisms reshaped the response across frequencies, with a retained gain attenuation lasting 2–3 weeks after removal (Melvill Jones & Gonshor 1982); and two gains can be held simultaneously and selected by gaze context (Shelhamer 1992, N = 3). The minifying-spectacle limb (gain driven down) rests on the same slip mechanism and is presented as the textbook's account; the carded records test magnification, reversal and context directly.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED

title: Sweat electrolytes and acclimatisation (physiology) — PARTIAL slice: whole-body sweat sodium centres near 41 mmol/L (potassium ~3.6 mmol/L) with wide individual spread, and heat acclimation dilutes sweat — sodium/chloride fall to ~60% of day-1 values over 10 days — even as sweat volume rises
question: In healthy humans, what is the sodium concentration and total electrolyte loss in sweat, and how does heat acclimatisation change sweat composition?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — PARTIAL slice, flagged prominently. Home first: pack #6263 already homes sweating and vasodilation thresholds and sweat rates (and their acclimation shifts); none of its studies is re-carded here, and this shelf asks only the composition question #6263 does not: what is in the sweat, and how does acclimatisation change that? Textbook framing (Guyton & Hall): the eccrine gland secretes a plasma-like fluid and the duct reabsorbs sodium, so composition depends on flow rate and on ductal reabsorptive capacity. The human data: by the reference whole-body washdown method, sweat sodium is 41 ± 19 mmol/L and potassium 3.6 ± 0.7 mmol/L during exercise in the heat, with regional patches overestimating sodium by ~44% (Baker 2009, N = 20). Acclimation dilutes sweat even as volume rises — sodium and chloride fall to ~60% of day-1 concentrations by day 10 of controlled hyperthermia, beginning by day 3, potassium unchanged (Klous 2020, N = 8); expressed against sweat rate, acclimation lowers sweat sodium by 15 mmol/L at any given rate, attributed to increased ductal reabsorption (Buono 2007, N = 8). One classic field study found no composition change with acclimatisation (Collins 1971, N = 6, at sea) and is carded as the counterweight.

title: Coronary flow reserve in healthy humans (physiology): flow can rise about fourfold above rest — 4.6 ± 0.9 by adenosine PET and 4.0–4.5 by transthoracic Doppler velocity reserve — measured non-invasively with PET tracers or bedside LAD Doppler during vasodilator infusion
question: In healthy humans, how much can coronary blood flow rise above rest (coronary flow reserve), and how is it measured non-invasively?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing (Guyton & Hall): resting coronary flow is tightly autoregulated, and the circulation holds a large vasodilator reserve in hand. Adjacency, stated plainly: pack #6304 already homes coronary autoregulation — the pressure range over which flow is held constant and its adenosine/K-ATP mediators — and deliberately excluded reserve magnitude; none of its PMIDs is re-carded here, and this shelf asks only how large the reserve is in healthy humans and how it is measured without a catheter. The measurements converge across methods: by ¹³N-ammonia PET during adenosine, healthy young adults show a flow reserve of 4.6 ± 0.9 (hyperaemic flow 340 ± 57 mL/100 g/min; Muzik 1996, N = 10), and dipyridamole PET gives healthy hyperaemic flow of 3.71 ± 0.86 mL/min/g (Parodi 1992, N = 13). By transthoracic Doppler of the LAD during ATP infusion — fully non-invasive — healthy velocity reserve is 4.02 ± 0.70 (Yamashita 2005, N = 11) and 4.5 ± 0.9 (Hirata 2004, N = 10). The honest summary is a range, ~4- to 4.6-fold, not a single canonical number.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED

title: GLOBAL LEADERS strategy in all-comer PCI: 1 month of DAPT then ticagrelor alone was not superior to 12 months of conventional DAPT — the primary endpoint was not met (3.81% vs 4.37%; p=0.073) and major bleeding did not fall (2.04% vs 2.12%)
question: In adults undergoing PCI (all-comers, not only complex PCI), does a strategy of 1 month of dual antiplatelet therapy followed by ticagrelor monotherapy, compared with 12 months of conventional dual therapy, reduce bleeding without increasing ischaemic events?
balance: PARTIAL build: pack #5821 already covers short DAPT followed by P2Y12-inhibitor monotherapy after complex PCI specifically; this pack builds only the uncovered all-comers slice — the GLOBAL LEADERS strategy trial itself — and cross-points to #5821 for the complex-PCI subgroup evidence. In GLOBAL LEADERS (15,968 all-comer PCI patients), 1 month of aspirin plus ticagrelor followed by 23 months of ticagrelor alone was not superior to 12 months of conventional DAPT followed by aspirin: the primary endpoint (death or new Q-wave myocardial infarction at 2 years) occurred in 3.81% versus 4.37% (rate ratio 0.87, 95% CI 0.75-1.01; p=0.073), and grade 3 or 5 bleeding was essentially identical (2.04% vs 2.12%; rate ratio 0.97). The prespecified GLASSY adjudication substudy (7,585 patients) found the strategy non-inferior for the ischaemic composite (7.14% vs 8.41%) but not superior, with BARC 3 or 5 bleeding unchanged (rate ratio 1.00). By presentation, bleeding fell in acute coronary syndrome patients (1.95% vs 2.68%) but not in stable disease (2.13% vs 1.62%; interaction p=0.007). So the honest answer to the question as posed is no: in all-comers this strategy did not reduce major bleeding, and its ischaemic safety rests on non-inferiority in an adjudicated substudy rather than on the parent trial's met primary endpoint. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for the all-comer strategy as tested.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — in the single large all-comer programme (15,968 patients), the 1-month-DAPT then ticagrelor-monotherapy strategy did not meet its primary endpoint and did not reduce grade 3 or 5 bleeding versus 12 months of conventional DAPT; the adjudicated GLASSY substudy showed ischaemic non-inferiority but not superiority and no major-bleeding reduction

title: Post-PCI FFR optimisation: optimisation raised final FFR modestly (median 0.81 to 0.86 in pooled patient data) but neither randomised trial showed fewer patients reaching FFR ≥0.90 as its primary result or a significant fall in target-vessel failure (FFR-REACT TVF 4.2% vs 4.8%)
question: In patients with a suboptimal fractional flow reserve (<0.90) after angiographically successful PCI, does physiology- or IVUS-guided post-PCI optimisation, compared with standard care, improve final FFR and reduce target-vessel failure?
balance: Both randomised trials of post-PCI optimisation missed their primary endpoints. TARGET-FFR (260 patients) found a physiology-guided incremental optimisation strategy did not significantly increase the proportion reaching a final FFR ≥0.90 (difference 10%, 95% CI -1.84 to 21.91; p=0.099), though it reduced the proportion left with FFR ≤0.80 (-11.2%, p=0.045); over two-thirds of patients had a suboptimal FFR after angiography-guided PCI. FFR-REACT (291 patients, all with post-PCI FFR <0.90) found IVUS-guided optimisation raised FFR in treated vessels (0.82 to 0.85) and got 20% of vessels to ≥0.90, but 1-year target-vessel failure was unchanged (4.2% vs 4.8%; p=0.79). An individual-patient-data meta-analysis of 314 patients confirms optimisation raises FFR (median 0.81 to 0.86, p<0.001) — a surrogate gain. No outcomes-powered trial exists, so whether chasing the number prevents events is unproven. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — two small single-centre randomised trials show optimisation improves the FFR number modestly but neither met its primary endpoint nor significantly reduced target-vessel failure; an individual-patient-data meta-analysis (314 patients) confirms the FFR gain (median 0.81 to 0.86) without establishing an outcomes benefit

title: PATHWAY-1: starting with losartan + hydrochlorothiazide lowered home systolic pressure faster than starting with monotherapy (4.9 mm Hg more fall over 32 weeks), but the monotherapy arm caught up once both groups were on combination therapy
question: In untreated adults with hypertension (systolic ≥150 or diastolic ≥95 mm Hg), does starting with a two-drug combination (losartan + hydrochlorothiazide), compared with starting with sequential monotherapy, achieve faster and better blood-pressure control?
balance: PATHWAY-1 (605 untreated patients with BP ≥150/95 mm Hg) is the direct strategy trial: initial combination (losartan + hydrochlorothiazide) lowered home systolic BP 4.9 mm Hg more than initial monotherapy averaged over 32 weeks (p<0.001), with a uniform response across renin tertiles, whereas monotherapy response varied substantially by renin. But once the monotherapy group crossed to combination therapy, pressures converged (difference 1.2 mm Hg at 32 weeks, p=0.13) — the advantage is speed and early control, not a different final pressure. Wider evidence agrees on the surrogate: a meta-analysis of 33 trials (13,095 participants) found initial dual therapy lowered systolic pressure by 2.8-7.5 mm Hg more than standard-dose monotherapy depending on dose, with better control rates and no excess withdrawals. The Cochrane review, restricted to trials reporting clinical outcomes, found the event evidence very uncertain (only 568 participants in its main comparison). No difference in withdrawals for adverse events in PATHWAY-1. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — faster, more predictable control; event benefit unproven.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single randomised strategy trial (PATHWAY-1, 605 patients) shows faster blood-pressure lowering with initial combination therapy, concordant with meta-analytic evidence that initial dual therapy lowers pressure more and controls more patients, while outcome (event) data for the strategy remain very uncertain in the Cochrane review; single-trial programme caps the stamp at POSSIBLE

title: PATHWAY-3: amiloride + hydrochlorothiazide prevented the thiazide rise in 2-hour glucose (-0.42 mmol/L [about -7.6 mg/dL] vs hydrochlorothiazide alone) and lowered home systolic pressure more, at equipotent starting doses
question: In adults with hypertension, does amiloride combined with hydrochlorothiazide, compared with hydrochlorothiazide alone, lower blood pressure as well while preventing thiazide-induced glucose intolerance?
balance: PATHWAY-3 (441 patients with hypertension and at least one metabolic-syndrome component, diabetes excluded) randomised amiloride alone, hydrochlorothiazide alone, or the half-dose combination for 24 weeks. Two-hour oral-glucose-tolerance glucose, averaged over 12 and 24 weeks, was lower on the combination than on hydrochlorothiazide alone (mean difference -0.42 mmol/L [about -7.6 mg/dL], 95% CI -0.84 to -0.004; p=0.048) and lower still on amiloride alone (-0.55 mmol/L [about -9.9 mg/dL]; p=0.0093), while the combination lowered home systolic pressure significantly more than hydrochlorothiazide alone (p=0.0068) — so the pairing answers both halves of the question in one trial: as good or better on pressure, better on glucose. Older randomised evidence is consistent in direction: in the MRC elderly trial's metabolic analysis (4,396 patients), hydrochlorothiazide plus amiloride produced no glucose difference versus placebo over 2 years. A 2026 factorial trial found amiloride 5 mg and 10 mg had similar, at-best-weak independent pressure effects alongside a thiazide-type diuretic, framing amiloride's role as metabolic protection rather than extra pressure lowering. Hyperkalaemia occurred in 4.8% on amiloride alone and 2.3% on the combination in PATHWAY-3. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single randomised trial (PATHWAY-3, 441 patients) shows the combination delays glucose intolerance and improves pressure control versus hydrochlorothiazide alone, supported by older randomised metabolic data for the same pairing; single-trial programme caps the stamp at POSSIBLE

title: TRANSCEND: telmisartan did not significantly reduce the primary cardiovascular composite versus placebo in ACE-inhibitor-intolerant patients (15.7% vs 17.0%; hazard ratio 0.92; p=0.216), with a modest signal on the death/MI/stroke composite (13.0% vs 14.8%)
question: In high-risk vascular patients who cannot tolerate an ACE inhibitor, does telmisartan, compared with placebo, reduce cardiovascular events?
balance: PARTIAL build: live shelf #105 cards ONTARGET (telmisartan versus ramipril, and dual-blockade harm) inside a diabetic-kidney question; it does not card the placebo-controlled TRANSCEND trial, which is built here and cross-points back to #105. In TRANSCEND (5,926 ACE-inhibitor-intolerant patients with cardiovascular disease or diabetes with end-organ damage, median follow-up 56 months), telmisartan 80 mg did not significantly reduce the primary composite of cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, stroke or heart-failure hospitalisation (15.7% vs 17.0%; hazard ratio 0.92, 95% CI 0.81-1.05; p=0.216), despite a 4.0/2.2 mm Hg lower mean pressure. The secondary composite without heart-failure hospitalisation was modestly lower (13.0% vs 14.8%; hazard ratio 0.87, 95% CI 0.76-1.00; p=0.048 unadjusted, p=0.068 after adjustment). The trial's own renal report found no benefit on the composite renal outcome (hazard ratio 1.29) — albuminuria rose less but estimated GFR fell more — and a prespecified analysis found no prevention of new diabetes (21.8% vs 22.4%). Telmisartan was well tolerated, with more hypotensive symptoms (0.98% vs 0.54% discontinuations). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): a well-tolerated drug with, at most, a modest unconfirmed event signal in this population.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the single placebo-controlled trial (TRANSCEND, 5,926 patients) missed its primary endpoint (the treatment made no difference on the primary composite: hazard ratio 0.92, p=0.216); a secondary composite of cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction or stroke was modestly lower (hazard ratio 0.87) but lost significance after adjustment, and renal outcomes were not improved

title: Zerlasiran lowers Lp(a) by more than 80% in phase 2 (time-averaged -81.3% to -85.6% vs placebo at 36 weeks) — PHASE 2 ONLY, surrogate endpoint, no cardiovascular outcomes trial has reported
question: In adults with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease and elevated lipoprotein(a), does the siRNA zerlasiran, compared with placebo, lower lipoprotein(a) — and is any outcome benefit yet shown?
balance: ⚠ PHASE-2 ONLY, SURROGATE ENDPOINT — flagged on the face: every zerlasiran result is a lipoprotein(a) concentration change; no outcomes trial has reported, so no event benefit can be claimed. In the phase 2 ALPACAR-360 trial (178 patients with stable ASCVD and Lp(a) ≥125 nmol/L), zerlasiran lowered time-averaged Lp(a) from baseline to week 36 by 81.3-85.6% more than placebo across the three dosing regimens, with median falls at week 36 of 90.0-96.4%; injection-site reactions were the commonest treatment-related effect and no serious adverse event was judged drug-related. The phase 1 single-ascending-dose study (32 participants without known cardiovascular disease) showed the same biology: maximal median Lp(a) falls of 46-98% by dose, persisting at least 150 days. A 2026 network meta-analysis of 25 Lp(a)-lowering trials (7,715 participants) placed zerlasiran's mean Lp(a) reduction at -80.6%, among the largest of the class. Whether an 80-90% Lp(a) fall converts into fewer events is exactly what this evidence cannot say. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit, surrogate only), capped for phase-2-only evidence.

title: MONITOR-HF: pulmonary-artery-pressure-guided care improved quality of life at 12 months (KCCQ difference 7.13 points; p=0.013) in 348 Dutch patients with NYHA class III heart failure, with consistent effects across ejection-fraction subgroups
question: In adults with heart failure across the ejection-fraction range in a European health system, does pulmonary-artery-pressure-guided management (CardioMEMS), compared with usual care, improve quality of life and reduce heart-failure hospitalisations?
balance: PARTIAL build: live shelf #976 cards CHAMPION and GUIDE-HF (US trials framed on hospitalisation and death); the uncovered slice built here is MONITOR-HF — the European, quality-of-life-primary trial — cross-pointed to #976 for the rest of the CardioMEMS evidence. In MONITOR-HF (348 Dutch patients, NYHA class III with a previous heart-failure hospitalisation, median ejection fraction 30% but eligible irrespective of ejection fraction, on contemporary guideline therapy), CardioMEMS-guided management improved the primary endpoint: the mean change in KCCQ overall summary score at 12 months differed by 7.13 points in favour of monitoring (95% CI 1.51-12.75; p=0.013), with more responders (odds ratio 1.69 for ≥5-point improvement) and fewer deteriorations (odds ratio 0.45). The trial report states heart-failure hospitalisations were also reduced, though the fetched record does not print the event counts, so this pack does not quote a hospitalisation figure. A prespecified subgroup analysis (Eur Heart J 2024) found the quality-of-life, clinical and pressure effects consistent across age, sex, atrial fibrillation, diabetes, ejection fraction, aetiology and device subgroups after multiplicity adjustment. A Dutch cost-effectiveness analysis based on the trial estimated €20,753 per quality-adjusted life year gained, below the Dutch €50,000 threshold. The trial was open-label, which matters for a patient-reported primary endpoint. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single open-label randomised trial (MONITOR-HF, 348 patients) showed a quality-of-life benefit (KCCQ overall summary difference 7.13 points) with consistent subgroup effects and a favourable Dutch cost-effectiveness estimate; single-trial evidence caps the stamp at POSSIBLE, and the hospitalisation claim rests on the trial's report rather than event counts in the fetched record

title: ⚠ DUPLEX-flagged PARTIAL: the adult phase 3 DUPLEX trial is already carded inside pack #1742 and is gated out here — on the free DUET programme evidence, sparsentan reduced proteinuria more than irbesartan at 8 weeks (45% vs 19%) with sustained falls in open-label follow-up, but no randomised eGFR-slope benefit is shown in the evidence carded here
question: In adults with primary FSGS, does sparsentan, compared with irbesartan, slow eGFR decline and reduce proteinuria?
balance: ⚠ PARTIAL — READ FIRST: the adult DUPLEX phase 3 trial (Rheault et al., N Engl J Med 2023, PMID: 37921461) is already carded inside pack #1742 (the paediatric-subgroup shelf, where the parent trial is its first card) and that PMID is on the gated carded list, so DUPLEX is NOT re-carded here; #1742 is the home to consult for DUPLEX, whose own result — proteinuria lower on sparsentan but the eGFR-slope primary endpoint not met — bounds everything below. This pack builds only the uncovered remainder of the adult question from ≥3 free reports, all from the earlier DUET programme. In DUET's 8-week double-blind phase (109 randomised, 96 analysed; ages 8-75, so a mixed adult-paediatric phase 2 population), sparsentan reduced urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio by 45% versus 19% on irbesartan (p=0.006), with the FSGS partial remission endpoint reached by 28% versus 9% (p=0.04). In the open-label extension (108 patients receiving sparsentan, follow-up to 4.6 years, no comparator), proteinuria reductions were sustained, 52.8% achieved partial remission within 9 months, and achieving remission was associated with slower eGFR decline (-2.70 vs -6.56 mL/min per 1.73 m² per year; p=0.03) — an association inside uncontrolled follow-up, not a randomised effect. A DUET post-hoc analysis likewise linked complete proteinuria remission (43% at least once over a median 47 months) with slower eGFR decline. Hypotension and oedema were the characteristic adverse effects. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit, proteinuria only) — the eGFR half of the question is not answered affirmatively by any evidence carded here, and DUPLEX (in #1742) answered it negatively on its primary endpoint.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit, proteinuria only) — ⚠ PARTIAL with the phase 3 DUPLEX trial homed in pack #1742 and excluded here: the free DUET programme (phase 2, 109 patients) shows greater proteinuria reduction than irbesartan and sustained open-label falls, with remission associated with slower eGFR decline in uncontrolled follow-up; no randomised eGFR benefit is carded on this shelf

title: Desmopressin in uraemia: bleeding time shortened in every patient in the 1983 crossover trial — a 28-patient evidence base built on a surrogate
question: In patients with kidney failure and uraemic platelet dysfunction, does desmopressin, compared with placebo or no treatment, shorten the bleeding time and reduce bleeding?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — based on a very small N = 28 randomised patients, and on a surrogate outcome. In the anchor randomised double-blind crossover trial (Mannucci et al., PMID: 6401193), all 12 uraemic patients with haemorrhagic tendencies and prolonged bleeding times had a shortened bleeding time after desmopressin infusion, lasting at least four hours in most, with rises in factor VIII coagulant activity and larger von Willebrand-factor multimers; a second double-blind crossover study (Malyszko et al., PMID: 1697836) found bleeding time fell from 21.3 ± 8 to 11.5 ± 6 minutes (p < 0.001) in 16 uraemic haemodialysis patients, with no change on placebo. What has never been shown in a randomised trial is fewer clinical bleeding events: the only systematic review of desmopressin before kidney biopsy (Lim et al., PMID: 32040251; 2 studies, 738 biopsies) rated the evidence low quality and insufficient to support routine use. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for temporary correction of the bleeding time; clinical bleeding prevention is unproven.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — based on a very small N = 28

title: Pre-dialysis midodrine for intradialytic hypotension: nadir systolic pressure up roughly 10–18 mm Hg in four small crossover-era studies — no placebo-controlled trial of size
question: In patients on haemodialysis with intradialytic hypotension, does pre-dialysis midodrine, compared with placebo or no treatment, reduce hypotensive episodes and improve dialysis tolerance?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — every study is small, old and from the crossover era, but they point the same way on blood pressure. In the first prospective series (Cruz et al., PMID: 9398120), 10 haemodialysis patients with persistent intradialytic hypotension had a lowest intradialytic systolic pressure of 114.7 mm Hg on pre-dialysis midodrine versus 96.6 mm Hg off it (P < 0.001), with uniform subjective improvement in cramps, fatigue, dizziness and weakness. A crossover comparison (Cruz et al., PMID: 10213650; 11 patients) found the lowest intradialytic systolic pressure was 103.9 mm Hg with midodrine and 102.6 mm Hg with cool dialysate versus 90.6 mm Hg in the control phase, with fewer nursing interventions and less saline infused; the one double-blind placebo-controlled crossover (Cotera et al., PMID: 12434648; 10 patients) found smaller falls in systolic pressure on midodrine (19.3 ± 28 mm Hg) than on placebo (23.4 ± 28 mm Hg), without statistical testing of the difference in the record. No trial was powered for symptoms, hospitalisation or death, and the only systematic review of this literature is already carded elsewhere in the library and so is not re-carded here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): midodrine raises the intradialytic pressure nadir; how much that helps patients feel or fare better is untested at scale.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Fosinopril in haemodialysis (FOSIDIAL): the primary endpoint was not met — relative risk 0.93 in 397 patients, and the class meta-analysis agrees
question: In haemodialysis patients with cardiovascular disease, does the ACE inhibitor fosinopril, compared with placebo, reduce cardiovascular events?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference). In FOSIDIAL (Zannad et al., PMID: 16871247), 397 haemodialysis patients with left ventricular hypertrophy were randomised to fosinopril 5 mg titrated to 20 mg daily (n = 196) or placebo (n = 201) for 24 months; the intention-to-treat analysis found no significant benefit on the composite of fatal and nonfatal major cardiovascular events (adjusted relative risk 0.93, 95% CI 0.68–1.26, P = 0.35). A per-protocol secondary analysis (n = 380) showed only a trend (adjusted relative risk 0.79, 95% CI 0.59–1.1, P = 0.099). The wider randomised record agrees: a meta-analysis of five ACE-inhibitor/ARB trials in 1,582 dialysis patients (Georgianos et al., PMID: 36069890) found no significant reduction in cardiovascular events (relative risk 0.79, 95% CI 0.57–1.11), cardiovascular mortality or all-cause mortality. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): the confidence intervals still admit a moderate benefit, so this is 'not shown to work' rather than proof of no effect.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference)

title: Carvedilol in dialysis cardiomyopathy (Cice): two-year mortality 51.7% vs 73.2% in one 114-patient single-centre trial — capped at POSSIBLE
question: In haemodialysis patients with dilated cardiomyopathy or reduced ejection fraction, does carvedilol, compared with placebo, improve survival and ventricular function?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single small trial, so the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE however large the effect looks. In the Cice trial (PMID: 12742278), 114 dialysis patients with dilated cardiomyopathy were randomised to carvedilol or placebo on top of standard therapy: at two years 51.7% of the carvedilol group had died versus 73.2% on placebo (p < 0.01) — a 21.5-percentage-point absolute difference — with fewer cardiovascular deaths (29.3% vs 67.9%) and hospital admissions (34.5% vs 58.9%). The one-year report (PMID: 11216954) showed ejection fraction rising from 26.3% to 34.8% on carvedilol with reduced ventricular volumes. A meta-analysis of beta-blockers in dialysis (Jin et al., PMID: 31039562) found the randomised pool — only 363 patients across 3 trials, this trial dominant — gave a relative risk of 0.73 (95% CI 0.54–0.97) for all-cause mortality, while its observational pool showed no significant cardiovascular mortality difference. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the direction is consistent and the mechanism plausible, but one single-centre trial of 114 patients from 2003 has never been replicated in this population.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Early erythropoietin to prevent AKI: EARLYARF was null, and the 2024 Cochrane review of 5,348 patients agrees — the treatment made no difference
question: In patients at risk of acute kidney injury after cardiac surgery or in critical illness, does early erythropoietin, compared with placebo, prevent AKI or reduce dialysis or death?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference). The anchor trial, EARLYARF (Endre et al., PMID: 20164823), randomised 162 biomarker-positive intensive-care patients (of 529 screened) to two doses of erythropoietin or placebo within hours of a urinary biomarker rise: there was no difference in the primary outcome (relative average plasma creatinine increase over 4–7 days) or in erythropoietin-specific adverse events. Note the population honestly: EARLYARF enrolled general ICU patients triaged by urinary gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase × alkaline phosphatase, not cardiac-surgery patients specifically. The cardiac-surgery slice agrees: a meta-analysis of 5 RCTs in 423 patients (Tie et al., PMID: 25312524) found no significant reduction in cardiac-surgery AKI overall (relative risk 0.64, 95% CI 0.35–1.16). The definitive synthesis is the 2024 Cochrane review (Nishiwaki et al., PMID: 39301879): 20 studies, 5,348 participants — erythropoiesis-stimulating agents probably make little or no difference to AKI (relative risk 0.97, 95% CI 0.85–1.10; moderate-certainty) or death (relative risk 0.92, 95% CI 0.80–1.06), and may make little or no difference to starting dialysis (relative risk 1.16, 95% CI 0.90–1.51). One smaller meta-analysis (Shin et al., PMID: 35244046) reports a benefit confined to pre-operative dosing — a subgroup signal the Cochrane analysis, testing timing and dose explicitly, did not confirm. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference).
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference)

title: Parathyroidectomy vs medical therapy in dialysis secondary hyperparathyroidism: every comparison is observational — surgery carries a 3.1% 30-day mortality, then lower long-term mortality in matched cohorts
question: In dialysis patients with severe secondary hyperparathyroidism, does parathyroidectomy, compared with medical therapy (calcimimetics or vitamin D analogues), improve survival, fractures and symptoms?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — OBSERVATIONAL EVIDENCE ONLY: no randomised trial of parathyroidectomy versus medical therapy in dialysis secondary hyperparathyroidism exists, and every number on this shelf comes from cohorts in which sicker or more refractory patients are selected for surgery. The largest matched cohort (Kestenbaum et al., PMID: 15496173; 4,558 parathyroidectomy patients matched to 4,558 USRDS controls) found a 3.1% 30-day postoperative mortality, survival curves that crossed at 587 days, and long-term relative risks of death 10–15% lower after surgery (median survival 53.4 vs 46.8 months). Against cinacalcet specifically, a Japanese propensity-matched cohort (Komaba et al., PMID: 35277957; 894 surgery vs 2,682 cinacalcet) found a mortality hazard ratio of 0.78 (95% CI 0.67–0.91), and a USRDS matched analysis (Alvarado et al., PMID: 35022799) found hazard ratio 0.77 (95% CI 0.70–0.85) but a higher rate of pathologic fractures after surgery (27.8% vs 24.9%). A meta-analysis of 23 cohort studies (Song et al., PMID: 38583772; 24,398 patients) pooled an all-cause mortality hazard ratio of 0.47 (95% CI 0.35–0.61) — yet in its subgroup where the medical group all received cinacalcet, the difference vanished (hazard ratio 1.02, 95% CI 0.49–2.11). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), labelled observational: surgery plausibly helps the most severe, refractory cases live longer, at a real upfront operative risk, and confounding by indication could manufacture much of the apparent benefit.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational evidence only

title: NephroCheck ([TIMP-2]·[IGFBP7]) accuracy for AKI: at the 0.3 cut-off it catches ~9 of 10 imminent stage 2–3 injuries but half of positives are false alarms; at 2.0 it rarely cries wolf
question: In hospitalised and perioperative patients, how accurately does urinary [TIMP-2]·[IGFBP7] (the NephroCheck test) predict moderate-to-severe AKI within 12 hours, and what changes between the 0.3 and 2.0 cut-offs?
balance: POSSIBLE (test accuracy) — this shelf answers the accuracy question only. The test's use as the triage tool for the biomarker-guided KDIGO care bundle is homed at live shelf #2083 (PrevAKI) and is not re-carded here; the homed trial records are deliberately left out of this pack's card sources. On accuracy: in the Sapphire validation cohort (Kashani et al., PMID: 23388612; 728 critically ill patients, 14% developing KDIGO stage 2–3 AKI within 12 hours), urinary [TIMP-2]·[IGFBP7] achieved an AUC of 0.80, superior to all previously described AKI markers (none above 0.72). The cut-off study (Hoste et al., PMID: 25237065) replicated across Sapphire and the Opal cohort (154 patients): at 0.3, sensitivity was 89% in both studies with specificity only 50–53%; at 2.0, sensitivity fell to 42–44% while specificity rose to 90–95%. The Topaz validation with blinded expert adjudication (Bihorac et al., PMID: 24559465; 420 patients) found sensitivity 92% at 0.3, a negative likelihood ratio of 0.18, and sevenfold risk above the cut-off. A cut-off meta-analysis (Zhang et al., PMID: 31261582; 1,619 patients) pooled sensitivity 0.89 / specificity 0.48 at 0.3 and sensitivity 0.45 / specificity 0.93 at 2.0. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (test accuracy): a rule-out test at 0.3 and a rule-in test at 2.0, with a wide grey zone between — not a stand-alone diagnosis.
stamp: POSSIBLE (test accuracy) — strong rule-out at 0.3, strong rule-in only at 2.0; overall discrimination moderate (AUC ~0.80)

title: dd-cfDNA for kidney transplant rejection: a good antibody-mediated-rejection test (AUC ~0.87–0.89), a moderate any-rejection test — and one small RCT that guided biopsies found rejection ~12 months sooner
question: In kidney transplant recipients, how accurately does donor-derived cell-free DNA (dd-cfDNA) detect active rejection compared with biopsy, and does dd-cfDNA-guided monitoring change management or outcomes?
balance: POSSIBLE (test accuracy). In the DART validation (Bloom et al., PMID: 28280140; 102 recipients, 107 biopsies), dd-cfDNA discriminated any rejection from no rejection with an AUC of 0.74 (95% CI 0.61–0.86) and antibody-mediated rejection (ABMR) with an AUC of 0.87 (95% CI 0.75–0.97); at a 1.0% cut-off, positive and negative predictive values were 61% and 84% for active rejection and 44% and 96% for ABMR. The diagnostic meta-analysis (Xiao et al., PMID: 32890130; 9 studies) pooled sensitivity 0.70 / specificity 0.78 / AUC 0.81 for main rejection episodes and sensitivity 0.84 / specificity 0.80 / AUC 0.89 for ABMR. The largest validation (Aubert et al., PMID: 38824959; 2,882 recipients enrolled, 1,134 in the primary analysis) found dd-cfDNA independently associated with rejection (odds ratio 2.275, 95% CI 1.902–2.739) and improved a standard-of-care model's AUC from 0.777 to 0.821. For the management limb, the only randomised test (Akifova et al., PMID: 39673311; 40 recipients with de novo donor-specific antibodies) found dd-cfDNA-guided biopsy diagnosed ABMR at a median 2.8 months versus 14.5 months with clinician-guided biopsy (P = 0.003), with 77% positive and 85% negative predictive value for ABMR. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (test accuracy): a useful adjunct that is strongest against ABMR and weakest for low-grade T-cell-mediated rejection; it does not replace biopsy, and outcome benefit from monitoring is unproven beyond earlier diagnosis in one 40-patient trial.
stamp: POSSIBLE (test accuracy) — good for antibody-mediated rejection, moderate for any rejection; monitoring benefit shown in one small trial

title: Kidney Failure Risk Equation: discrimination holds worldwide (C 0.88–0.90 in 721,357 patients) but calibration drifts outside North America — and a 30% fall in albuminuria carries its own prognostic information
question: In adults with CKD, how accurately does the Kidney Failure Risk Equation (Tangri) predict 2- and 5-year kidney failure, does adding more variables improve on the 4-variable version, and does change in albuminuria add prognostic information?
balance: LIKELY (prognostic accuracy) for discrimination, with a calibration caveat. In the original development and validation (Tangri et al., PMID: 21482743; development cohort 3,449 patients with 386 kidney-failure events, validation cohort 4,942 with 1,177), the full 8-variable model reached a C statistic of 0.917 in development and 0.841 in validation — and, importantly for the 'added value' limb, it beat the simpler 4-variable model (age, sex, eGFR, albuminuria) only modestly: integrated discrimination improvement 3.2% (95% CI 2.4%–4.2%), with better calibration and small net reclassification gains. The multinational meta-validation (Tangri et al., PMID: 26757465; 31 cohorts, 721,357 participants, 23,829 kidney-failure cases) found the original equations discriminated excellently everywhere (overall C statistic 0.90, 95% CI 0.89–0.92, at 2 years; 0.88, 95% CI 0.86–0.90, at 5 years) and pooled equations did not improve on them — but calibration was adequate in North American cohorts while risk was overestimated in some non-North American cohorts, fixed in most by a calibration factor lowering baseline risk by 32.9% at 2 years and 16.5% at 5 years. For albuminuria change (Coresh et al., PMID: 30635225; 675,904 individuals, 7,461 end-stage kidney disease events — observational consortium data), a 30% decrease in albumin-to-creatinine ratio over a 2-year baseline period carried an adjusted hazard ratio of 0.83 (95% CI 0.74–0.94) for subsequent end-stage kidney disease, 0.78 (0.66–0.92) after regression-dilution adjustment. PROPOSED LIKELY (prognostic accuracy): quote the risk with the regional calibration caveat, prefer the 4-variable equation for simplicity unless the extra variables are already in hand, and treat a sustained albuminuria fall as genuinely better prognosis — an association, not proof that lowering albuminuria causes the benefit.
stamp: LIKELY (prognostic accuracy) — discrimination excellent and internationally consistent; calibration needs a regional factor outside North America; albuminuria change adds information (observational)

title: Antiproliferative somatostatin analogues in GEP-NETs: lanreotide and octreotide LAR both delayed progression versus placebo (hazard ratios 0.47 and 0.34, relative) with no overall-survival difference shown
question: In patients with well-differentiated gastroenteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumours, do somatostatin analogues (lanreotide, octreotide LAR), compared with placebo, delay tumour progression (antiproliferative effect, separate from symptom control)?
balance: ⚠ PARTIAL row — flagged prominently: the stated home, live shelf #742, was verified against its own ask-index entry before building: #742 cards peptide-receptor radionuclide therapy (NETTER-1) and everolimus (RADIANT-4) only, and none of its PMIDs is re-carded here. This pack homes only the uncovered slice — the placebo-controlled antiproliferative somatostatin-analogue trials. Two double-blind placebo-controlled trials agree: CLARINET (lanreotide, N = 204) found median progression-free survival not reached versus 18.0 months on placebo, hazard ratio 0.47 (95% CI 0.30 to 0.73) — a relative measure, with absolute 24-month progression-free survival of 65.1% versus 33.0%; PROMID (octreotide LAR, N = 85) found median time to progression 14.3 versus 6.0 months, hazard ratio 0.34 (0.20 to 0.59), also relative. A meta-analysis of exactly these two trials (289 patients) gives a pooled hazard ratio of 0.41 (0.29 to 0.58). Neither trial showed an overall-survival difference, and CLARINET showed no quality-of-life difference — the benefit is delayed progression, not longer life. The tested lanreotide product is named in the record as lanreotide Autogel (Depot in the United States), Ipsen.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — for progression-free survival / time to progression; no overall-survival benefit shown

title: Telotristat ethyl for carcinoid syndrome diarrhoea: about 0.7–0.8 fewer bowel movements per day than placebo in TELESTAR, with responders 42–44% versus 20%, and large urinary 5-HIAA falls in TELECAST
question: In patients with carcinoid syndrome diarrhoea inadequately controlled on somatostatin analogues, does telotristat ethyl, compared with placebo, reduce bowel-movement frequency and urinary 5-HIAA?
balance: One development programme, two companion placebo-controlled phase 3 trials. In TELESTAR (N = 135, patients with ≥4 bowel movements/day despite stable somatostatin-analogue therapy), telotristat ethyl 250 mg and 500 mg three times daily reduced bowel-movement frequency by an estimated 0.81 and 0.69 movements/day more than placebo averaged over 12 weeks; durable responders (≥30% reduction for at least half the period) were 44% and 42% versus 20% on placebo, and urinary 5-HIAA fell significantly versus placebo at week 12. In TELECAST (N = 76, a broader carcinoid-syndrome population with <4 bowel movements/day on analogues), the primary biochemical endpoint fell sharply: median urinary 5-HIAA treatment differences from placebo of −54.0% (250 mg) and −89.7% (500 mg) at week 12. A prespecified pooled analysis found sustained ≥30% bowel-movement improvement in 69% of telotristat patients, reached significantly faster than on placebo in both trials. Long-term open-label follow-up (TELEPATH, N = 124) found no new safety signals. The bowel-movement gain is real but modest in absolute terms — under one movement per day on average — which, with the single-programme base, caps the stamp at POSSIBLE. Syndrome symptom control only; antitumour therapy for NETs is homed elsewhere (live shelf #742).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two companion phase 3 trials from a single development programme

title: FIRM-ACT: EDP-mitotane beat streptozocin-mitotane on response (23.2% versus 9.2%) and progression-free survival (5.0 versus 2.1 months), but overall survival was 14.8 versus 12.0 months — no significant difference
question: In advanced adrenocortical carcinoma, does first-line etoposide + doxorubicin + cisplatin with mitotane (EDP-M), compared with streptozocin + mitotane, improve progression-free and overall survival?
balance: A single randomised trial answers this question, supported by two earlier single-arm phase 2 studies of the winning regimen. In FIRM-ACT (N = 304), first-line EDP-mitotane gave a response rate of 23.2% versus 9.2% on streptozocin-mitotane and median progression-free survival of 5.0 versus 2.1 months (hazard ratio 0.55, 95% CI 0.43 to 0.69 — a relative measure, printed with its absolute medians). Overall survival was 14.8 versus 12.0 months (hazard ratio 0.79, 0.61 to 1.02; P=0.07) — not significantly different: on survival, the treatment made no difference that this trial could establish, and crossover to the alternative regimen at progression (185 patients) blurs any survival contrast. Serious adverse-event rates did not differ significantly. The phase 2 studies that led to FIRM-ACT reported higher response rates for EDP-mitotane (48.6% in 72 patients, 2005; 53.5% in 28 patients, 1998) than the randomised trial itself found — a familiar pattern when a regimen meets a control arm. One trial, in a rare cancer, caps the stamp at POSSIBLE. Adjuvant mitotane after resection is a different question, homed on pack #6280.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for response rate and progression-free survival only; overall survival: the treatment made no difference

title: Paltusotine in acromegaly: IGF-1 control maintained in 83.3% versus 3.6% on placebo after switching from injections (PATHFNDR-1), and IGF-1 normalised in 55.6% versus 5.3% in uncontrolled patients (PATHFNDR-2) — the tested product is paltusotine, once-daily oral
question: In adults with acromegaly, does once-daily oral paltusotine maintain or achieve biochemical control (IGF-1) compared with placebo / prior injectable somatostatin-receptor ligands?
balance: The tested product is named as published: paltusotine, a once-daily oral nonpeptide selective somatostatin receptor 2 agonist (the fetched records name the drug and its class; they do not name a brand or manufacturer). Two placebo-controlled phase 3 trials from one programme point the same way. PATHFNDR-1 (N = 58), in patients already controlled (IGF-I ≤1.0× ULN) on injected octreotide or lanreotide, found that switching to paltusotine maintained IGF-I ≤1.0× ULN in 83.3% versus 3.6% on placebo over 36 weeks. PATHFNDR-2 (N = 111), in biochemically uncontrolled, medically untreated or washed-out patients, found IGF-I normalisation in 55.6% versus 5.3% on placebo at 24 weeks. The earlier phase 2 ACROBAT Edge switch study (47 enrolled; primary group N = 25) found no significant IGF-I change 13 weeks after switching from injections, with IGF-I rising significantly during a 4-week washout — consistent with the tablet holding control. Adverse events in the trials were mainly acromegaly symptoms and the gastrointestinal effects typical of somatostatin-receptor ligands. A single programme with placebo comparators and no head-to-head trial against continued injections caps the stamp at POSSIBLE. Other acromegaly medical therapies are homed elsewhere (pasireotide/pegvisomant pack #5851 and live shelf #745; oral octreotide live shelf #957).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two placebo-controlled trials from a single development programme, plus a phase 2 switch study

title: Once-weekly growth hormone in children with GHD: all three products were non-inferior to daily somatropin for height velocity — lonapegsomatropin 11.2 versus 10.3 cm/year, somapacitan 11.2 versus 11.7 cm/year, somatrogon 10.10 versus 9.78 cm/year
question: In children with growth hormone deficiency, do once-weekly growth-hormone preparations (lonapegsomatropin, somapacitan, somatrogon), compared with daily somatropin, achieve non-inferior height velocity with acceptable IGF-1 exposure?
balance: Three separate phase 3 trials, one per product, each randomised against daily somatropin for 52 weeks in treatment-naive prepubertal children with growth hormone deficiency, and all three met non-inferiority for annualised height velocity. The products are named as published: lonapegsomatropin (described in its record as TransCon hGH, a once-weekly prodrug), somapacitan (a reversible albumin-binding GH derivative), and somatrogon (a long-acting recombinant human GH). Height velocity at 52 weeks: lonapegsomatropin 11.2 versus 10.3 cm/year (non-inferior and statistically superior, P=0.009); somapacitan 11.2 versus 11.7 cm/year (non-inferiority confirmed); somatrogon 10.10 versus 9.78 cm/year (difference 0.33, 95% CI −0.24 to 0.89, against a −1.8 cm/year non-inferiority margin). IGF-1 exposure was acceptable in the trial that reports it in detail (REAL4: mean IGF-I SDS similar between groups and within the −2 to +2 range at week 52), and safety profiles matched daily GH in all three. Each product still rests on its own single pivotal trial, and adult-height outcomes are not yet in these records — the LIKELY stamp is for one-year height velocity only. Weekly somapacitan in adults is a different question, homed on pack #4794.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit — non-inferior height velocity to daily somatropin) — three concordant phase 3 trials, one per product

title: Tocilizumab in corticosteroid-resistant Graves' orbitopathy: one small randomised trial (N = 32) found CAS improvement in 93.3% versus 58.8% on placebo, with uncontrolled cohorts and a single-arm meta-analysis in support
question: In moderate-to-severe corticosteroid-resistant Graves' orbitopathy, does tocilizumab, compared with placebo, improve clinical activity score and inactivate disease?
balance: The randomised evidence is a single small trial: Pérez-Moreiras 2018 randomised 32 adults with moderate-to-severe corticosteroid-resistant Graves' orbitopathy to intravenous tocilizumab 8 mg/kg or placebo, and the primary outcome — a fall of at least 2 points in the clinical activity score (CAS) at week 16 — was met by 93.3% versus 58.8% (P=.04), with CAS <3 (inactive disease) in 86.7% versus 35.2%. Everything else is uncontrolled: a 9-year single-centre series (54 treated patients meeting inclusion) found CAS 0–1 in 74% after the fourth dose, and a 2024 observational study (79 patients, including 15 paediatric) found CAS falls of ≥2 points in 71.4% of adults with active disease at follow-up. A 2025 single-arm meta-analysis of 12 studies and 219 patients pools a CAS response proportion of 0.98 and a mean CAS reduction of 4.60 points — but single-arm pooling cannot separate drug effect from natural history and steroid carry-over, and it overlaps the cohorts carded here. One small RCT (N = 32, printed) plus uncontrolled support caps the stamp at POSSIBLE. Other Graves' orbitopathy therapies are homed elsewhere (rituximab pack #4108; selenium live shelf #1752; teprotumumab/glucocorticoids live shelf #514).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — based on a single small RCT (N = 32) plus uncontrolled cohorts; N printed

title: Bisphosphonates in children with osteogenesis imperfecta: bone density rises consistently (risedronate +16.3% versus +7.6% lumbar spine BMD), but fracture reduction is inconsistent across the small trials — Ns printed (30, 147, 34; Cochrane 819 in 14 trials)
question: In children with osteogenesis imperfecta, do bisphosphonates (pamidronate, oral agents), compared with placebo/no treatment, increase bone density and reduce fractures?
balance: The base is old and small, and its two halves disagree in strength. Bone density: every strand rises — cyclic intravenous pamidronate in Glorieux 1998 (uncontrolled, N = 30) gave a mean annualised lumbar-spine BMD increase of 41.9% with z-score improving from −5.3 to −3.4; the largest randomised trial, Bishop 2013 (risedronate, N = 147), found lumbar-spine areal BMD up 16.3% versus 7.6% on placebo at 1 year (difference 8.7 percentage points). Fractures: Bishop found fewer first-year clinical fractures on risedronate (31% versus 49%, P=0.0446) and Sakkers 2004 (olpadronate, N = 34) found a long-bone fracture hazard ratio of 0.69 — a 31% relative reduction — but the Cochrane review (Dwan 2016; 14 trials, 819 participants) could not aggregate the oral trials, found fracture benefit in only two of five reporting trials, and found no significant fracture difference for intravenous bisphosphonates pooled (risk ratio 0.56, 95% CI 0.30 to 1.06 — a relative measure whose interval crosses 1). Growth, pain and function data are incomplete and inconsistent in the review. Density benefit is consistent; fracture benefit is plausible but unproven at this base size — POSSIBLE, with every N printed.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — bone mineral density increases consistently; fracture reduction is inconsistent across the small trials

title: PRISM and PRISM-EZ: intensive bisphosphonate treatment normalising alkaline phosphatase made no difference to fractures (7.0% versus 7.4%), surgery, pain or quality of life versus symptom-driven care — the treatment made no difference
question: In established Paget's disease of bone, does an intensive bisphosphonate strategy targeting normal alkaline phosphatase, compared with symptom-driven treatment, reduce fractures, orthopaedic procedures, pain and quality-of-life loss?
balance: Two randomised reports of the same strategy question agree, and both are null on every clinical endpoint. PRISM (N = 1,324, median follow-up 3 years) achieved its biochemical aim — alkaline phosphatase was significantly lower on intensive treatment from 4 months onward — yet clinical fractures occurred in 7.0% versus 7.4%, orthopaedic surgery in 7.3% versus 8.3%, and there was no difference in quality of life, overall or pagetic bone pain, or hearing thresholds: on clinical outcomes, the intensive strategy made no difference. The PRISM-EZ extension (N = 502, zoledronic acid as first-choice intensive agent) again found no quality-of-life or pain benefit, with nonsignificant point estimates running against intensive treatment (fracture hazard ratio 1.90, 95% CI 0.91 to 3.98 — a relative measure whose interval includes no difference). The Cochrane review of bisphosphonates in Paget's disease (20 trials, 3,168 participants) supplies the context that keeps this from reading as 'bisphosphonates do not work': against placebo they tripled the proportion whose bone pain disappeared (31% versus 9%) — the drugs relieve symptoms when given for symptoms; what adds nothing is treating repeatedly to normalise a number. Which bisphosphonate to use when treating is a different question, homed on live shelf #1822.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — intensive ALP-normalising strategy versus symptom-driven care, in two concordant randomised reports

title: Stimulated copeptin for polyuria–polydipsia: hypertonic saline testing is 95.6–96.5% accurate and beats the water deprivation test (76.6%) — arginine stimulation is easier but fell to 74.4% head-to-head
question: In adults with polyuria–polydipsia syndrome, how accurately does stimulated copeptin (hypertonic-saline-stimulated, or arginine-stimulated) distinguish AVP deficiency (central diabetes insipidus) from primary polydipsia, compared with the water deprivation test?
balance: Three prospective diagnostic studies from one Swiss-led programme answer this directly, and the head-to-head trial settles the ranking. Hypertonic saline-stimulated copeptin (cutoff >4.9 pmol/L once plasma sodium reaches at least 150 mmol/L) made the correct diagnosis in 96.5% of 141 analysed patients in Fenske 2018, against 76.6% for the indirect water deprivation test. Arginine-stimulated copeptin looked nearly as good in its own development/validation study (pooled accuracy 93% at 3.8 pmol/L at 60 minutes; Winzeler 2019), but when both tests were done in the same 158 patients (Refardt 2023), arginine's accuracy fell to 74.4% while hypertonic saline held at 95.6% — a 21.2-percentage-point gap. So: hypertonic saline-stimulated copeptin is the accurate test and has displaced the water deprivation test; arginine stimulation is simpler, safer-feeling and preferred by 72% of patients, but at the prespecified cutoff it misclassifies about one patient in four, and only extreme arginine values (3.0 pmol/L or less, or over 5.2 pmol/L) carry roughly 91% specificity. All three studies come from overlapping investigator groups and tertiary centres, which is the main reason the stamp is LIKELY rather than stronger.
stamp: LIKELY (test accuracy) — hypertonic saline-stimulated copeptin distinguishes AVP deficiency from primary polydipsia with 95.6–96.5% accuracy, well above the water deprivation test (76.6%); arginine-stimulated copeptin is simpler but materially less accurate head-to-head (74.4%)

title: Late-night salivary cortisol for Cushing's: pooled sensitivity 95.8% and specificity 93.4% across 14,140 participants — as accurate as the dexamethasone test and urinary free cortisol, provided the assay's own cutoff is used
question: In adults being evaluated for Cushing's syndrome, how accurate is late-night salivary cortisol for diagnosis, and how does it compare with urinary free cortisol and the 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test?
balance: Two meta-analyses fourteen years apart agree that late-night salivary cortisol (LNSC) is as accurate as the other first-line Cushing's tests. Elamin 2008 pooled 27 studies (8,631 patients): positive likelihood ratios were 8.8 for midnight salivary cortisol, 10.6 for urinary free cortisol (UFC) and 16.4 for the 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test (DST), with negative likelihood ratios of 0.07, 0.16 and 0.06 respectively — all highly accurate in referral populations. Galm 2020, pooling 139 studies and 14,140 participants with hierarchical models, put LNSC sensitivity at 95.8% and specificity at 93.4%, essentially level with the DST (98.6%/90.6%) and UFC (94.0%/93.0%). Primary studies add the practical caveats: in Bäcklund 2023 every assay method reached an ROC area of at least 0.96, but upper reference limits for the same 23:00 sample ranged from 3.4–3.9 nmol/L by mass spectrometry to 21.6 nmol/L for one immunoassay — the number is only interpretable against the local assay's own range. In a Chinese cohort (Lin 2019), midnight salivary cortisol at a 1.7 ng/mL cutoff gave 98% sensitivity and 100% specificity and outperformed UFC (AUC 0.99 versus 0.89). Verdict: LNSC is a first-line test of accuracy comparable to DST and UFC; its weaknesses are assay-dependent cutoffs, false positives with disturbed sleep–wake cycles or sample contamination, and false negatives in mild or intermittent disease.
stamp: LIKELY (test accuracy) — late-night salivary cortisol diagnoses Cushing's syndrome with pooled sensitivity ~96% and specificity ~93%, accuracy comparable to the 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test and urinary free cortisol; cutoffs are assay-specific

title: Low-dose versus standard-dose ACTH stimulation: two meta-analyses find the 1 µg and 250 µg tests equally accurate — both rule in secondary adrenal insufficiency, neither rules it out
question: In adults being evaluated for adrenal insufficiency, how accurate is the low-dose (1 µg) ACTH (cosyntropin) stimulation test compared with the standard-dose (250 µg) test, against reference standards (insulin tolerance / metyrapone testing)?
balance: Two diagnostic meta-analyses, thirteen years apart, reach the same answer: the 1 µg and 250 µg cosyntropin tests perform alike. Dorin 2003 found summary ROC areas that did not differ significantly for secondary adrenal insufficiency, with sensitivities at 95% specificity of 57% (250 µg) and 61% (1 µg). Ospina 2016 pooled 30 studies (1,209 adults, 228 children) for secondary adrenal insufficiency and likewise found similar accuracy for both doses — both tests rule in reasonably (adult LR+ 9.1 high-dose, 5.9 low-dose) but neither rules out (adult LR− 0.39 high-dose, 0.19 low-dose). For primary adrenal insufficiency the high-dose test's sensitivity was 92% (5 studies, 100 patients). Primary studies show what this means at the bedside: against the insulin tolerance test, the low-dose test at a 30-minute cortisol cutoff of 550 nmol/L (about 20 µg/dL) was 97% sensitive but only 78% specific (Choi 2002, 72 patients), and in 129 pituitary patients peak cortisol on the low-dose test ran higher than on the insulin tolerance test (Simsek 2015) — cutoffs are test-specific. The practical verdict: dose choice matters far less than the cutoff and assay; a positive result on either test supports adrenal insufficiency, and a negative result on either test does not exclude secondary disease when suspicion is high — an integrated test (insulin tolerance or metyrapone) is then needed. The low-dose test also requires diluting a 250 µg ampoule, a real source of error.
stamp: LIKELY (test accuracy) — the low-dose (1 µg) and standard-dose (250 µg) ACTH stimulation tests have similar diagnostic accuracy in two concordant meta-analyses; either can rule in adrenal insufficiency, but neither rules out secondary adrenal insufficiency

title: Thyroid ultrasound risk systems compared: ACR TI-RADS is the most specific and spares the most unnecessary biopsies across 18,750 pooled nodules — every system trades sensitivity for specificity at its size thresholds
question: In adults with a thyroid nodule, how accurately do ultrasound risk-stratification systems (ACR TI-RADS and comparators) classify malignancy risk, and what are the biopsy-yield and missed-cancer consequences of their size thresholds?
balance: The systems compared here — the points-based ACR TI-RADS (Tessler et al., J Am Coll Radiol 2017 white paper), the pattern-based ATA guidelines, Kwak TI-RADS, K-TIRADS and EU-TIRADS — all stratify malignancy risk reasonably, and they differ mainly in where they set the sensitivity–specificity trade. The head-to-head meta-analysis (Castellana 2020; 12 studies, 18,750 nodules) found diagnostic odds ratios of 2.2 to 4.9 across the five systems, with ACR TI-RADS performing best at selecting nodules for biopsy — a higher relative diagnostic odds ratio than ATA (P = .002) and K-TIRADS (P = .002), driven by stronger positive likelihood ratios. The largest single head-to-head cohort (Zhang 2020; 1,271 nodules) shows the mechanism: ACR TI-RADS had higher specificity and lower sensitivity than ATA, Kwak and KTA/KSThR systems in every size subgroup, and the lowest unnecessary-biopsy rates, including in the 10–19 mm subgroup where threshold choices bite hardest. A prospective routine-practice cohort (Grimmichova 2022) confirms ACR TI-RADS category is a significant independent predictor of malignancy alongside cytology and molecular results. The honest summary: ACR TI-RADS' larger size thresholds buy fewer unnecessary biopsies at the price of lower sensitivity; no system eliminates missed cancers, and the choice of system matters less than applying one consistently.
stamp: LIKELY (test accuracy) — ultrasound risk systems stratify thyroid nodule malignancy risk with diagnostic odds ratios of 2.2–4.9; ACR TI-RADS gives the highest specificity and fewest unnecessary biopsies, at lower sensitivity than ATA/Kwak/Korean systems

title: Deintensifying diabetes treatment in older adults: only about a quarter of tightly controlled patients are ever deintensified, but observational data show it succeeds in 62–75% with small HbA1c rises — and no trial has tested the hypoglycaemia benefit
question: In older adults with type 2 diabetes and tight glycaemic control or hypoglycaemia risk, does deintensification/deprescribing of glucose-lowering therapy, compared with continuation, reduce hypoglycaemia and harm without worsening control?
balance: This shelf is observational throughout — no completed randomised trial has tested whether deintensifying glucose-lowering therapy reduces hypoglycaemia. What the cohorts show consistently is, first, how rarely it happens: in 179,991 actively treated older veterans, only 27.0% of those with a very low HbA1c (under 6.0%) had treatment deintensified within six months, and under 0.8% of the rest later showed an elevated HbA1c (Sussman 2015). Second, the pattern repeats after harm and in frailty: even after a hypoglycaemia hospital episode or in frail inpatients, deintensification is the exception (19.1% in Melson 2024's 665 frail inpatients, where being overtreated — HbA1c under 7.0% [53 mmol/mol] on glucose-lowering medication — was itself associated with adverse inpatient outcomes). Third, when deintensification is done, the scoping-review evidence (Oktora 2021; 14 studies) finds it succeeds in 62–75% of attempts with only small HbA1c rises, and reminder systems that flag hypoglycaemia produced less overtreatment and fewer hypoglycaemic events. The neighbouring shelves #5629 (sulfonylurea deprescribing at limited life expectancy) and #5983 (structured deprescribing reviews) card different studies and questions; this shelf's studies are not carded there. Bottom line: deintensification is uncommon, feasible, and glycaemically safe in observational data — but the claim that it prevents hypoglycaemia rests on association, not experiment.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — observational only: deintensification of glucose-lowering therapy in tightly controlled older adults is uncommon (19–27% of eligible patients) but feasible, succeeding in 62–75% of attempts with small HbA1c rises; no randomised evidence shows it reduces hypoglycaemia

title: apoB versus LDL-C: risk follows apoB when the two disagree — 7.3% versus 4.0% ten-year event rates at the same LDL-C of 130 mg/dL — while in the concordant majority the markers are interchangeable
question: In adults at cardiovascular risk, does apolipoprotein B (apoB) predict events better than LDL cholesterol — particularly when the two are discordant — and should it change treatment thresholds?
balance: This is a prognosis question and the evidence is observational plus genetic. The consistent finding across designs is that when apoB and LDL-C disagree, risk follows apoB — because apoB counts atherogenic particles while LDL-C measures the cholesterol they happen to carry. INTERHEART (15,152 cases, 14,820 controls, 52 countries) found the apoB/apoA1 ratio was the strongest lipid marker of myocardial infarction (odds ratio 3.25 for the top versus lowest quintile; population attributable risk 49.2%). In UK Biobank discordance analysis (Sniderman 2024; 293,876 adults, 19,982 events over a median 11 years), apoB varied widely at any given LDL-C — at an LDL-C of 130 mg/dL the central 95% of apoB values spanned 85.8–108.8 mg/dL — 10-year event rates were 7.3% versus 4.0% for apoB one SD above versus below the mean at that LDL-C, and residual apoB stayed predictive after LDL-C, non-HDL-C and triglycerides were accounted for, while no cholesterol residual survived adjustment for apoB. Mendelian randomisation (Ference 2017) points the same causal way: genetic scores with naturally discordant LDL-C and apoB showed coronary risk tracking the change in apoB, not LDL-C. The counterweight is real and is carded: in a separate UK Biobank analysis (Welsh 2019; 346,686 participants), apoB, LDL-C and non-HDL-C had near-identical hazard ratios per SD (1.23, 1.20, 1.21) and adding apoB to a standard model did not improve discrimination — in unselected populations the markers are highly correlated (r over 0.90), so apoB's advantage is concentrated in the discordant minority, who are common enough (and include many people with diabetes, high triglycerides or metabolic syndrome) to matter clinically.
stamp: LIKELY (prognosis) — when apoB and LDL-C are discordant, cardiovascular risk follows apoB in cohort discordance analyses and Mendelian randomisation; in concordant (most) patients the markers predict equivalently and apoB adds no population-level discrimination

title: The adiponectin paradox: in heart failure and CKD, higher adiponectin predicts higher mortality (HR 3.23 in chronic heart failure) — a wasting and natriuretic-peptide marker signal, not a toxic effect, and it adds little beyond natriuretic peptides
question: In adults with heart failure or CKD, why do higher adiponectin levels predict higher mortality (the adiponectin paradox), and does adiponectin add prognostic information beyond natriuretic peptides?
balance: The paradox is consistent across cohorts: adiponectin, an insulin-sensitising, anti-inflammatory adipokine whose low levels mark metabolic risk in healthy people, predicts higher mortality once heart failure or CKD is established. In Kistorp 2005's 195 chronic heart failure patients, the upper two adiponectin tertiles carried a hazard ratio for death of 3.23 versus the lowest tertile, independent of NT-proBNP and clinical severity — and adiponectin tracked NT-proBNP (beta 0.47) and low BMI, leading the authors to read it as a marker of wasting. In the Cardiovascular Health Study (Karas 2014; 3,228 older adults), adiponectin above the median predicted new-onset heart failure (HR 1.25 per SD). In CKD, the KNOW-CKD cohort (1,303 patients) ties high adiponectin to protein-energy wasting (top-quartile OR 10.54 for wasting), the likely mechanistic bridge: natriuretic peptides stimulate adiponectin release, failing kidneys clear less of it, and weight loss/wasting raises it — so high adiponectin flags advanced disease rather than causing it. The natriuretic-peptide entanglement is decisive in Lindberg 2015 (680 STEMI patients): adiponectin predicted death (HR 1.31 per SD) until proANP entered the model, when the association vanished. Mendelian randomisation analyses (for example in Liu 2016's diabetes cohort) have likewise found the causal direction, if anything, opposite to the observational one. Answer to the shelf question: higher adiponectin is a robust prognostic marker in HF/CKD, best explained as a compensatory, natriuretic-peptide-driven signal of wasting and disease severity — a marker, not a mediator — and it adds little once natriuretic peptides are known.
stamp: LIKELY (prognosis) — in heart failure and CKD, higher adiponectin consistently predicts higher mortality across cohorts; the weight of evidence reads it as a marker of wasting, natriuretic-peptide drive and disease severity rather than a mediator, adding little beyond natriuretic peptides

title: The renal glucose threshold: a splayed titration curve — diabetes raises its ceiling, pregnancy halves it, SGLT2 blockade collapses it
question: In humans, what determines the renal threshold for glucose — how much filtered glucose do SGLT2 and SGLT1 reabsorb, where does glycosuria begin on the glucose titration curve, and how does this change in diabetes and pregnancy?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. The human titration-curve evidence is direct: stepped hyperglycaemic clamps (plasma glucose raised stepwise, e.g. 5.5–30.5 mmol/L, about 99–549 mg/dL) let investigators draw each person's glucose titration curve and read off its three features — the threshold at which glucose first spills, the splay (the rounded shoulder, reflecting nephron-to-nephron variation), and the tubular maximum for glucose (TmG). In type 2 diabetes all three are shifted up (DeFronzo 2013, n = 12 + 12; Al-Jobori 2017: baseline TmG 459 ± 53 vs 337 ± 25 mg/min in diabetes vs controls), which is one reason hyperglycaemia sustains itself; SGLT2 blockade cuts TmG by roughly half within 48 hours and drags the threshold below 40 mg/dL. The genetic and pregnancy experiments of nature point the same way: familial renal glycosuria pedigrees separate a low-TmG form (type A) from a pure increased-splay form (type B), and pregnancy roughly halves TmG. Boron & Boulpaep / Guyton & Hall framing assigns most reabsorption to SGLT2 in the early proximal tubule with SGLT1 completing uptake downstream — presented here as the textbook's account; the carded human studies measure the whole-kidney curve, not the transporter split directly. Classic small groups are labelled on the face (titration studies of 8–15 per group).
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED

title: First-pass hepatic insulin extraction: about half of secreted insulin is removed before it reaches the periphery — and clearance itself is regulated
question: In humans, how much of secreted insulin is extracted by the liver on first pass, how is peripheral insulin clearance regulated (insulin resistance, secretory pattern), and how is clearance measured by C-peptide deconvolution?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Human catheter and deconvolution studies agree on the shape of the answer: the splanchnic bed removed 42 ± 2% of insulin influx in the basal state and about 60% across physiological concentrations in Ferrannini's 32 catheterised subjects, falling to 29 ± 1% only at supraphysiological levels (>500 µU/mL) — extraction is large, first-pass, and saturable only far above physiology. Meier's hepatic-vein sampling in 5 healthy subjects (N = 5, printed on the face) showed the pulse pattern itself sets extraction: the liver preferentially extracts insulin pulses, so pulsatile secretion dictates systemic delivery. Clearance is regulated, not fixed: in insulin-resistant nondiabetic women the integrated insulin response was 90% higher while secretion was only 37% higher — the gap is reduced clearance (Jones 1997). Measurement rests on C-peptide: secreted equimolarly, negligibly extracted by liver, and recoverable by deconvolution — Van Cauter & Polonsky showed standard two-compartment kinetic parameters (adjusted for body surface area, sex, age) estimate secretion rates within 10–12% of individually measured ones across 200 decay curves. Guyton & Hall / Boron & Boulpaep framing (portal delivery, hepatic first pass, renal contribution to peripheral clearance) is named as textbook framing. One classic group is very small (N = 5) and is labelled on the face.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED

title: Glucose effectiveness: glucose disposes of itself at basal insulin — preserved in obesity, roughly halved in diabetes
question: In humans, what is glucose effectiveness (SG — insulin-independent glucose disposal), how is it measured with the minimal model, and how much of glucose disposal does it account for in health and type 2 diabetes?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Glucose effectiveness (SG) — glucose's ability, at basal insulin, to promote its own disposal and suppress its own production — is measured in humans by fitting Bergman's minimal model to a frequently sampled intravenous glucose tolerance test (FSIGTT). Bergman's 1989 Lilly Lecture reports the core contrast: insulin sensitivity (SI) varied widely across nondiabetic groups but SG was normal in all of them, whereas in non-insulin-dependent diabetes SI was reduced 90% below normal (0.61 ± 0.16 × 10⁻⁴ min⁻¹ per µU/mL) AND SG alone fell with it (from 0.026 ± 0.008 to 0.014 ± 0.002 min⁻¹) — the two defects are synergistic in causing intolerance. The measurement is usable but noisy: Steil 1994 found interday coefficients of variation of ~20% for SI and ~25% for SG in 11 men studied three times. A modified minimal model extends the method to insulin-dependent diabetes (Ward 1991: SG 1.6 ± 0.5 vs 2.6 ± 0.2 × 10⁻² min⁻¹ in IDDM vs controls), and SG is itself regulated — norepinephrine raised it in NIDDM (Walters 1997). Guyton & Hall / Boron & Boulpaep framing (mass-action glucose uptake and hepatic glucose output suppression) is named as textbook framing. Small physiological groups (8–11) are labelled on the face.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED

title: Human brown adipose tissue: present in adults, recruited by cold in nearly everyone, switchable by a β3-agonist — with a measurable but not yet isolated energy cost
question: In adult humans, how much functional brown adipose tissue is there, how is it activated (cold, β3-agonism), and how much energy can it expend?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Three 2009 PET-CT studies established that adult humans carry functional brown adipose tissue (BAT): cold activated it in 23 of 24 healthy men (van Marken Lichtenbelt), biopsy-confirmed UCP1-positive depots from neck to thorax appeared in 7.5% of women and 3.1% of men across 1,972 clinical scans (Cypess — the lower clinical-scan prevalence reflects scanning without deliberate cold stimulation), and cold raised glucose uptake 15-fold in paracervical fat in Virtanen's volunteers. On energy: Ouellet's tracer-PET study in 6 men showed cold-activated BAT oxidative metabolism rises with total energy expenditure and inversely with shivering — BAT is a genuine nonshivering-thermogenesis effector, though the record does not print a single kcal figure for BAT alone. Pharmacological activation works too: a single 200 mg dose of the β3-agonist mirabegron raised BAT activity in all 12 men studied and raised resting metabolic rate by 203 ± 40 kcal/day (+13%) (Cypess 2015). Boron & Boulpaep / Guyton & Hall framing (UCP1 uncoupling, sympathetic activation) is named as textbook framing. Small PET groups (5–24) are labelled on the face; absolute BAT mass/energy figures beyond the fetched records are presented as the textbook's account, not as carded data.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED
