title: Stunning and hibernation in humans: function fails after flow returns, and underperfused muscle stays alive by contracting less
question: In humans, what are myocardial stunning and hibernation — how long does contractile dysfunction persist after brief ischaemia and reperfusion, and how does chronically underperfused myocardium down-regulate function while staying viable?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. The human evidence is thinner than the animal literature and this shelf says so on its face. Stunning in humans is demonstrated most cleanly after exercise-induced ischaemia: Ambrosio 1996 found regional function still impaired 30–60 minutes after exercise ended, with perfusion already normal — dysfunction outlasting ischaemia with restored flow is the definition. A careful radionuclide study of briefer episodes (rest angina, effort angina, balloon angioplasty inflations) found NO persistent dysfunction in recovery (Marzullo 1993, n = 52) — the honest null that bounds the claim: episode duration and depth decide whether stunning is detectable. Hibernation rests on PET: Tillisch 1986 showed preserved glucose uptake in akinetic segments predicted recovery after bypass with 85–92% predictive accuracy, far above Q-wave ECG (43%); Uren & Camici 1992 frame the flow–metabolism mismatch as the detection standard. Guyton & Hall / Boron & Boulpaep framing is minimal here; the concepts are Rahimtoola's and Bolli's, presented through the carded human studies, with the animal stunning experiments (Heyndrickx; Bolli) named only as textbook/translational framing, never carded.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED

title: Endothelium-dependent vasodilatation in humans: NO holds vessels open — proven with L-NMMA, acetylcholine and the FMD test
question: In humans, how does endothelium-dependent vasodilatation work — how is nitric-oxide-mediated tone demonstrated and quantified in vivo (intra-arterial acetylcholine/L-NMMA forearm studies; flow-mediated dilatation of the brachial artery)?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. The human demonstration chain is complete and quantitative. Vallance, Collier & Moncada (Lancet 1989) infused the nitric-oxide-synthesis inhibitor L-NMMA into the brachial artery of healthy volunteers: basal forearm flow fell ~50% and the acetylcholine response was blunted while glyceryl trinitrate's was not — basal and stimulated tone in man is partly NO-maintained. In coronary arteries, acetylcholine dilates normal vessels but paradoxically constricts atherosclerotic ones (Ludmer 1986: diameter 1.05 → 0.32 mm at the highest dose in advanced stenoses) — the in-vivo signature of a lost endothelial dilator mechanism. In essential hypertension the forearm acetylcholine response is selectively impaired (maximal flow 9.1 ± 5 vs 20.0 ± 8 mL/min/100 mL; Panza 1990) while direct smooth-muscle dilators still work. The non-invasive limb — the folded-in flow-mediated dilatation row — is Celermajer 1992: reactive-hyperaemia FMD of ~10 ± 2% in control arteries ≤6.0 mm, much reduced or absent in smokers, children with familial hypercholesterolaemia and adults with coronary disease, with GTN responses preserved in all groups. Guyton & Hall / Ganong framing (endothelium-derived relaxing factor identified as NO) is named as textbook framing; Furchgott's and Ignarro's animal/aortic-ring work is framing only, never carded.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED

title: Cortisol pulsatility: the hourly rhythm is real and changes brain responses at the same dose — the patient benefit is not yet proven
question: In humans, how is cortisol secreted in ultradian pulses across the circadian cycle, and does the pattern (pulsatile vs continuous) of glucocorticoid exposure change tissue responses at the same total dose?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING. That cortisol is secreted in hourly ultradian pulses riding on the circadian wave is established human physiology (textbook framing: Guyton & Hall / Ganong; dynamics reviewed in the Lightman programme). Whether the pattern itself matters at equal total dose now has direct human experimental evidence — but from one research programme and small samples, hence EMERGING. In healthy men whose endogenous cortisol was suppressed and replaced at the same dose in different patterns, pulsatile vs non-pulsatile delivery changed emotional processing, recognition accuracy and attentional bias, sleep quality and working memory (Kalafatakis 2018). A 15-volunteer three-way crossover trial confirmed pattern effects on morning vigour/fatigue/concentration, diurnal mood and resting-state brain networks (Kalafatakis 2021). A validated subcutaneous pulsatile pump reproduces the physiological rhythm in volunteers (Russell 2014), and in adrenal insufficiency the 6-week PULSES crossover trial (21 analysed) found no change in its primary facial-recognition outcome but subjective fatigue/mood improvements and differential amygdala/insula processing — a null primary endpoint, printed as such. Refusal reported: the slate's named Henley et al. 2009 pulsatile-infusion anchor could not be verified as a fetched PubMed record this session and is therefore NOT carded; the shelf rests on the four fetched records below.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING

title: Albumin synthesis regulation in humans: ~7% of the pool replaced daily — doubled by protein loss, raised by feeding, suppressed by inflammation
question: In humans, how is the albumin synthesis rate regulated — what do tracer studies show about the effects of oncotic pressure, inflammation, nutrition and nephrotic-range protein loss on hepatic albumin synthesis?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — for synthesis-rate regulation as measured by human tracer studies (this shelf is deliberately NOT about low albumin as a prognostic marker). The measurement exists and is reproducible: Ballmer 1990's flooding-dose [¹³C]leucine method gave a fractional synthesis rate of 7.2 ± 1.3%/day and absolute synthesis of 157 ± 39 mg/kg/day in healthy postabsorptive men. Regulation, from the carded human studies: (1) protein loss — in nephrotic adults, absolute albumin synthesis more than doubled (160 ± 19 vs 71 ± 4 mg/kg/day) in proportion with fibrinogen synthesis, without raised CRP or serum amyloid A (de Sain-van der Velden/Kaysen 1998, N = 7 + 8) — a coordinated hepatic response to loss, not an acute-phase artefact; (2) nutrition — raising dietary protein in nephrotic patients raised synthesis from 12.61 ± 1.20 to 17.60 ± 1.25 g/1.73 m²/day (Kaysen 1987, n = 13), though serum albumin and lipids barely moved because losses rose too; (3) inflammation — in 79 HEMO haemodialysis patients followed with repeat kinetic measurements, a fall in albumin synthesis accompanied a stable >0.3 g/dL decline in serum albumin and tracked rising α1-acid glycoprotein (Kaysen 2004). Oncotic pressure: the classic hypothesis that falling plasma oncotic pressure directly signals hepatic albumin synthesis is presented as the textbook's account (Boron & Boulpaep / Guyton & Hall framing) — the fetched human records demonstrate the loss/nutrition/inflammation limbs directly and do not isolate an oncotic-pressure signal, and the shelf says so rather than dressing the hypothesis as measured fact. Small tracer groups are labelled on the face.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED

title: Seralutinib in pulmonary arterial hypertension (TORREY): a phase-2 PVR win, phase 3 still to come
question: In adults with pulmonary arterial hypertension on background therapy, does inhaled seralutinib (a PDGFR/CSF1R/c-KIT inhibitor) improve pulmonary vascular resistance and exercise capacity versus placebo?
balance: PHASE 2 ONLY — flagged on the face; a single phase 2 programme caps the stamp at POSSIBLE. TORREY (n = 86 randomised) met its primary endpoint: the least-squares mean difference in 24-week change in pulmonary vascular resistance was −96.1 dyne·s/cm⁵ (95% CI −183.5 to −8.8; P = 0.03) for inhaled seralutinib vs placebo on background therapy. The open-label extension (74 patients) reports durability descriptively — median PVR change from TORREY baseline to week 72 of −143 dyne·s/cm⁵ in those continued on seralutinib — but without a control group it cannot confirm benefit, and cough led 12.2% to discontinue. Phase 1 drug-interaction studies in healthy volunteers (n = 24 and 19) found all adverse events mild or moderate, with seralutinib a moderate CYP3A inhibitor (midazolam AUC 3.03-fold). No phase 3 result is published; the phase 3 PROSERA study is underway per the extension record. Nothing here shows a mortality or hospitalisation benefit.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — phase 2 only: the single TORREY phase 2 trial (86 patients) met its PVR endpoint and no phase 3 result is published, so a single programme caps the stamp at POSSIBLE

title: Imatinib in pulmonary arterial hypertension (IMPRES): walk and PVR gains bought with subdural haematomas — the programme's own verdict was no
question: In adults with pulmonary arterial hypertension, does oral imatinib added to background therapy improve exercise capacity and haemodynamics — and at what harm cost (subdural haematoma signal)?
balance: Imatinib in PAH is the classic efficacy–harm split, and the stamp stays at POSSIBLE with the harm on the face. IMPRES (n = 202, PVR ≥800 dyne·s·cm⁻⁵ on ≥2 background therapies) improved 6-minute walk distance by a placebo-corrected 32 m (95% CI 12–52; P = 0.002) and PVR by −379 dyne·s·cm⁻⁵ (P < 0.001) at 24 weeks — but functional class, time to clinical worsening and mortality did not differ (the treatment made no difference on those endpoints), serious adverse events were more frequent (44% vs 30%), discontinuations higher (33% vs 18%), and subdural haematoma occurred in 8 patients. The earlier pilot RCT (n = 59) was null on its walk endpoint in the intention-to-treat population (+22 ± 63 vs −1.0 ± 53 m; the treatment made no difference) despite PVR improvement. The open-label extension then largely collapsed: 93.8% discontinued (adverse events 31.3%), with 6 further subdural haematomas and 17 deaths during or within 30 days of study end; the extension authors conclude the risks outweigh any possible benefit. A single programme with a serious, mechanism-relevant harm signal caps at POSSIBLE — and the balance a reader needs is that the developer-side extension verdict was effectively negative.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single programme (IMPRES) with a serious harm signal: walk and PVR endpoints were met, but subdural haematoma, higher serious adverse events and a 93.8% extension discontinuation rate led the extension authors to conclude risks outweigh any possible benefit

title: Mepolizumab for nasal polyps (SYNAPSE): polyp score and obstruction improved, and fewer patients went on to sinus surgery
question: In adults with chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps inadequately controlled on intranasal steroids, does mepolizumab reduce polyp size, nasal obstruction and need for surgery versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE — one phase 3 programme only, so the stamp is capped. In SYNAPSE (407 adults with recurrent, refractory severe bilateral polyps, all previously operated and eligible for repeat surgery), mepolizumab 100 mg every 4 weeks for 52 weeks improved the total endoscopic polyp score by an adjusted median difference of -0.73 and nasal obstruction by -3.14 points versus placebo, and a prespecified surgery analysis found fewer patients were put on a waiting list for sinus surgery (13.9% vs 28.5% by week 52). This shelf is the mepolizumab slice only: the class home, live shelf #375, cards dupilumab and omalizumab and does not card SYNAPSE. Effects are real but modest next to the dupilumab gradient on #375 — a cross-trial reading, not a head-to-head trial.

title: Intravenous reslizumab in severe eosinophilic asthma: exacerbations roughly halved in two duplicate phase 3 trials
question: In adults with severe eosinophilic asthma uncontrolled on high-dose inhaled therapy, does intravenous reslizumab reduce exacerbations and improve lung function versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE — the trials agree, but they are one sponsor programme, so the stamp is capped. In two duplicate 52-week phase 3 trials (953 patients with eosinophils 400 cells per microlitre or higher and at least one prior exacerbation), intravenous reslizumab 3.0 mg/kg every 4 weeks cut the annual exacerbation rate to a rate ratio of 0.50 and 0.41 versus placebo — roughly a 50-59% relative reduction. A separate 16-week phase 3 trial showed the lung-function side: FEV1 improved by 160 mL more than placebo at the 3.0 mg/kg dose. The anti-IL-5 family home (live #813) covers mepolizumab and benralizumab only; reslizumab is the intravenous member of the family and is carded here on its own trials.

title: Vanzacaftor triple in cystic fibrosis (SKYLINE): non-inferior to the elexacaftor triple on lung function, once daily instead of twice
question: In people with cystic fibrosis aged 6 years and older with at least one F508del allele, does once-daily vanzacaftor-tezacaftor-deutivacaftor improve lung function and sweat chloride versus placebo — and how does it compare with elexacaftor-tezacaftor-ivacaftor?
balance: LIKELY — with the comparison stated plainly: the SKYLINE trials were active-controlled, not placebo-controlled. After a 4-week run-in on elexacaftor-tezacaftor-ivacaftor, 971 people aged 12 years and older were randomised to switch to once-daily vanzacaftor-tezacaftor-deutivacaftor or stay on the elexacaftor triple; lung function (FEV1 percent predicted) was non-inferior in both trials (treatment difference +0.2 percentage points in each). So the honest claim is 'as good as the current standard on lung function, with once-daily dosing', not 'better'. The paediatric card (RIDGELINE, ages 6-11) is single-arm and safety-led. These SKYLINE trials are the cystic fibrosis programme — not the unrelated soticlestat epilepsy programme of the same name (pack #6166). Live #811 homes the older modulators only.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — two concordant phase 3 non-inferiority trials against the active standard

title: Pamrevlumab in IPF (ZEPHYRUS-1): FVC fell in both groups and the treatment made no difference
question: In adults with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, does pamrevlumab (anti-CTGF antibody) slow forced vital capacity decline versus placebo?
balance: UNLIKELY — the phase 2 trial (PRAISE, 103 patients) reported slower FVC decline on pamrevlumab, but ZEPHYRUS-1, the phase 3 test of that promise, was negative: FVC fell by 260 mL on pamrevlumab and 330 mL on placebo over 48 weeks, a between-group difference of 70 mL that was not significant (P=.29), and no secondary or patient-reported outcome separated either (the treatment made no difference). title: Zinpentraxin alfa in IPF: a positive phase 2 was not confirmed — phase 3 STARSCAPE stopped for futility and showed no benefit
question: In adults with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, does zinpentraxin alfa (recombinant pentraxin-2) slow lung-function decline versus placebo?
balance: UNLIKELY — and the programme's history is the lesson. The phase 2 trial (117 patients) reported slower FVC decline on recombinant human pentraxin 2; the phase 3 STARSCAPE trial (664 patients) was terminated early after a prespecified futility analysis showed no treatment benefit, and its final analysis found FVC change essentially identical between groups (the treatment made no difference). A post hoc analysis traced the phase 2 signal to extreme FVC decline in two placebo patients. The programme is finished; both published reports are carded so the reversal is visible on the shelf.
stamp: UNLIKELY (benefit) — the phase 3 trial was terminated for futility and showed no benefit (the treatment made no difference)

title: Co-trimoxazole in IPF: two randomised trials, both negative — no gain in survival, hospitalisation, lung function or quality of life
question: In adults with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, does co-trimoxazole improve quality of life, lung function or survival versus placebo/usual care?
balance: UNLIKELY — three randomised trials asked the question and none found benefit on its primary analysis. The earliest (Shulgina 2013, 181 patients) found no intention-to-treat effect on lung function, with quality-of-life and mortality signals only in a per-protocol subgroup. EME-TIPAC (342 patients, double-blind, placebo-controlled) found co-trimoxazole did not reduce death, transplant or hospital admission (hazard ratio 1.2, P=.32), with no difference in lung function or patient-reported outcomes. CleanUP-IPF (513 patients, pragmatic) tested co-trimoxazole or doxycycline added to usual care and was itself stopped for futility: no improvement in respiratory hospitalisation or death (adjusted HR 1.04, P=.83), and no interaction favouring co-trimoxazole over doxycycline. Gastrointestinal and skin adverse events were commoner on co-trimoxazole across the trials.
stamp: UNLIKELY (benefit) — three randomised trials found no benefit on their primary analyses (the treatment made no difference)

title: Nebulised tranexamic acid for non-massive haemoptysis: one small trial — bleeding resolved within 5 days in 96% versus 50%
question: In adults with non-massive haemoptysis, does nebulised tranexamic acid shorten bleeding duration and hospital stay versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE, with the size printed in the stamp: the entire randomised evidence is one double-blind trial of 47 patients (Wand 2018). Nebulised tranexamic acid 500 mg three times daily resolved haemoptysis within 5 days in 96% versus 50% on saline placebo, shortened hospital stay by about 2 days, and no patient on tranexamic acid needed an invasive procedure to control bleeding versus 18.2% on placebo. The direction is encouraging and the drug was well tolerated, but a single 47-patient, single-centre trial cannot carry more than POSSIBLE. Massive haemoptysis was excluded — nothing here applies to it.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — based on a very small randomised base (anchor trial N = 47)

title: Ketamine as a bronchodilator in acute severe asthma: the small randomised trials found no added benefit
question: In adults with acute severe asthma not responding to standard bronchodilators, does ketamine improve airflow and avert intubation versus standard care?
balance: UNLIKELY — ketamine's bronchodilator reputation rests on physiology and case series; the randomised trials do not confirm it. The adult emergency-department trial (Howton 1996, 44 analysed patients) found both groups improved on standard therapy with no detectable difference from adding ketamine, and no difference in admission. A 2020 trial in ventilated adults with severe bronchospasm found ketamine no better than fentanyl on airway resistance at 3 or 24 hours. The one paediatric randomised trial (Allen 2005) is carded and labelled as paediatric — it too was negative. A 2022 systematic review of the prospective studies concluded the data do not support ketamine for refractory severe asthma exacerbations.
stamp: UNLIKELY (benefit) — small randomised trials found no added bronchodilator benefit (the treatment made no difference)

title: Inhaled treprostinil in IPF without pulmonary hypertension (TETON-1 and TETON-2): FVC decline roughly halved in two phase 3 trials
question: In adults with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (without pulmonary hypertension), does inhaled treprostinil slow FVC decline versus placebo?
balance: LIKELY — this shelf is built on the two peer-reviewed phase 3 reports (New England Journal of Medicine, 2026), not on the earlier topline press announcements. TETON-2 (593 patients): median FVC change at 52 weeks was -49.9 mL on inhaled treprostinil versus -136.4 mL on placebo (difference 95.6 mL, P<0.001). TETON-1 (598 patients) found the same pattern (difference 130.1 mL, P<0.001), and clinical worsening was less frequent in both trials (hazard ratios 0.71 and 0.67). Three quarters of patients were already on background antifibrotic therapy, so this is largely add-on evidence. Cough was the commonest adverse event (about half of treprostinil patients) and discontinuation was higher on treprostinil. This is a different population from live #1109, which homes inhaled treprostinil for pulmonary hypertension with interstitial lung disease (INCREASE).
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — two concordant phase 3 trials (TETON-1 and TETON-2), both published in full

title: Clofazimine in refractory MAC lung disease: observational cohorts only — about half convert, relapse is common, no randomised trial exists
question: In adults with refractory Mycobacterium avium complex lung disease, does adding clofazimine to a multidrug regimen improve culture conversion and survival?
balance: POSSIBLE, observational only — every card on this shelf is a cohort or case series; there is no randomised trial of clofazimine in MAC lung disease, so the stamp is capped and the design is labelled on each card. The largest MAC-specific cohort (Jarand 2016, 107 patients) found 95% eventually converted to negative cultures on clofazimine- or rifampin-based regimens, with conversion commoner on clofazimine (100% versus 71%) — but half relapsed microbiologically. A severe-disease cohort (170 patients) found 45.3% converted within 6 months, and a refractory-NTM series found 50% of pulmonary patients converted within 12 months. No carded study isolates a survival effect of clofazimine itself. Adjacent homes: pack #2673 (liposomal amikacin, CONVERT) and pack #6313 (first-line MAC regimens) ask different questions.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational evidence only (no randomised trials); capped at POSSIBLE and labelled observational

title: MENDS2: dexmedetomidine versus propofol in ventilated sepsis — delirium/coma-free days 10.7 vs 10.8 and 90-day death 38% vs 39% (the treatment made no difference)
question: In adults with sepsis requiring mechanical ventilation, does dexmedetomidine versus propofol increase days alive without delirium or coma?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, because 90-day mortality is co-reported throughout): In MENDS2 (Hughes CG et al., PMID: 33528922), 422 mechanically ventilated adults with sepsis randomised to dexmedetomidine or propofol under a light-sedation protocol had identical days alive without delirium or coma (adjusted median 10.7 vs 10.8 days; odds ratio 0.96, 95% CI 0.74 to 1.26), identical ventilator-free days (23.7 vs 24.0), and 90-day death of 38% versus 39% (hazard ratio 1.06 relative, 95% CI 0.74 to 1.52). The sepsis-specific pooled literature agrees on survival: a meta-analysis of 15 studies (Huang P et al., PMID: 34721015) found 28-day mortality risk ratio 0.97 (95% CI 0.83 to 1.13; P=0.70). A broader 41-trial meta-analysis (Heybati K et al., PMID: 35961815) likewise found no ICU length-of-stay difference in any patient subtype; its delirium and ventilation-duration advantages for dexmedetomidine were confined to cardiac-surgical patients, not sepsis, and bradycardia was more common with dexmedetomidine. The earlier MENDS trial's dexmedetomidine advantage was against lorazepam, a benzodiazepine comparator — it is homed elsewhere in this library and is not re-carded here; against propofol, the modern non-benzodiazepine comparator, there is no difference to find. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): in ventilated sepsis, choose between dexmedetomidine and propofol on haemodynamics, cost and nursing practicality, not on delirium, coma or survival.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — in mechanically ventilated adults with sepsis, dexmedetomidine and propofol gave identical delirium/coma-free days, ventilator-free days and 90-day mortality in MENDS2, and the pooled sepsis literature agrees

title: Prolonged methylprednisolone in ARDS: early courses improved lung injury and ICU mortality in two small Meduri trials — LaSRS found late rescue did not reduce mortality (29.2% vs 28.6%) and harmed patients started after 14 days
question: In adults with ARDS, does a prolonged low-dose methylprednisolone course (started early, or late for unresolving ARDS) improve mortality and ventilator-free days versus placebo?
balance: SPLIT by timing — POSSIBLE (benefit) for an early prolonged course; POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference), with a harm signal when started late, for rescue in persistent ARDS (Tier C, mortality co-reported): This shelf is the methylprednisolone slice only; dexamethasone in ARDS (DEXA-ARDS) is homed at pack #3002, which was read in full before building — it cards dexamethasone only, with no Meduri or methylprednisolone content. Early: Meduri's randomised trials of prolonged low-dose methylprednisolone found faster lung-injury resolution and shorter ventilation — in early severe ARDS (Meduri GU et al., PMID: 17426195; 91 patients), a 1-point lung injury score reduction by day 7 in 69.8% versus 35.7% and ICU mortality 20.6% versus 42.9%; in unresolving ARDS (PMID: 9669790; 24 patients), ICU mortality 0% versus 62%. Both trials are small and single-programme. Late: the ARDSNet LaSRS trial (Steinberg KP et al., PMID: 16625008; 180 patients with ARDS of at least 7 days) found 60-day hospital mortality of 29.2% on methylprednisolone versus 28.6% on placebo (P=1.0), more ventilator-free days and better physiology, more neuromuscular weakness, and significantly increased mortality when treatment was started at least 14 days after ARDS onset. The pre-LaSRS-era meta-analysis (Tang BM et al., PMID: 19325471) pooled a mortality relative risk of 0.51 in its four randomised trials (95% CI 0.24 to 1.09; P=0.08) — a trend built from the small Meduri-programme trials. PROPOSED: an early prolonged course is POSSIBLE (benefit) on small-trial evidence; routine late rescue is not supported, and starting at or beyond 14 days may kill.
stamp: SPLIT — POSSIBLE (benefit) for early prolonged low-dose methylprednisolone in ARDS (small single-programme trials); POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for late rescue in persistent ARDS, with increased mortality when started at or after 14 days (LaSRS)

title: CytoSorb in septic shock: the cartridge removes IL-6 (5–18% per pass) but plasma levels, organ failure and mortality did not improve in randomised trials — survival benefit unproven
question: In adults with septic shock, does cytokine haemoadsorption (CytoSorb) reduce vasopressor requirements, organ failure or mortality versus standard care?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the device removes cytokines from blood passing through it, and no randomised trial has shown that this improves organ function, vasopressor requirements or survival; a mortality benefit is unproven and must not be claimed (Tier C, mortality co-reported): The tested product is CytoSorb (CytoSorbents Corporation), a haemoadsorption cartridge — named here under the tested-product clarification exception because adsorption devices differ by maker. In septic patients with respiratory failure (Schädler D et al., PMID: 29084247; 97 analysed), CytoSorb removed interleukin-6 at 5–18% per blood pass yet systemic plasma IL-6 did not fall versus control (P=0.15), organ dysfunction, ventilation time and oxygenation did not differ, and unadjusted 60-day mortality was higher on treatment (44.7% vs 26.0%; P=0.039), a difference the authors attribute to baseline imbalance after adjustment (P=0.19). In the REMOVE trial (Diab M et al., PMID: 35213213; 288 patients having cardiac surgery for infective endocarditis), adding CytoSorb to the bypass circuit lowered some cytokines but changed neither the primary organ-dysfunction outcome (ΔSOFA 1.79 vs 1.93; P=0.68) nor 30-day mortality (21% vs 22%). The systematic review of sepsis use (Saldaña-Gastulo JJC et al., PMID: 37712812; 6 studies, 413 patients) found no mortality effect at 28–30 days and graded the certainty very low. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): cytokine clearance is a laboratory fact; patient benefit is not demonstrated.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — CytoSorb haemoadsorption removes cytokines per blood pass, but randomised trials show no fall in systemic IL-6, no organ-function benefit and no mortality benefit; a survival benefit is unproven

title: Inhaled epoprostenol versus inhaled nitric oxide in ARDS: near-identical oxygenation gains in small crossover trials (PaO2/FiO2 +21 vs +29 mmHg) — no mortality data exist for the comparison
question: In adults with ARDS and refractory hypoxaemia, does inhaled epoprostenol improve oxygenation as effectively as inhaled nitric oxide — and does either change mortality?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — on acute oxygenation the two inhaled vasodilators look equivalent in tiny crossover physiology trials; on mortality and every patient-important outcome there are no comparative data at all (Tier C): In the direct randomised crossover comparison (Walmrath D et al., PMID: 8630585; 16 patients with ARDS), individually titrated inhaled nitric oxide (mean 17.8 ppm) raised PaO2/FiO2 from 115 to 144 mmHg and aerosolised prostacyclin (epoprostenol; mean 7.5 ng/kg/min) from 114 to 135 mmHg, with shunt falling by about 7 points on each and near-identical efficacy profiles. A dose-response crossover study (Zwissler B et al., PMID: 8970353) found the same pattern — both agents selectively lowered pulmonary artery pressure and raised PaO2/FiO2 — in a record that does not report its patient number. A later three-way crossover pilot (Albert M et al., PMID: 28224110; 15 patients) found median PaO2 rises of 8.8 mmHg on nitric oxide and 6.0 mmHg on epoprostenol, with only nitric oxide reaching significance in that small sample. Each drug's effect against control is homed separately — inhaled nitric oxide at live #1323 (oxygenation improves briefly, outcomes do not) and inhaled prostacyclin at pack #3172 (a negative multicentre trial against placebo) — and neither home is re-carded here. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): epoprostenol is a physiologically credible, cheaper substitute for nitric oxide for short-term oxygenation rescue; equivalence on survival is unknown, not established.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — based on small crossover physiology trials (31 patients with documented N, plus one trial whose record does not report N): inhaled epoprostenol and inhaled nitric oxide improve oxygenation to a similar degree, and neither has mortality data in head-to-head comparison

title: Enteral omega-3 (EPA/GLA) in ARDS: early trials pooled a mortality odds ratio of 0.40 — then OMEGA was stopped for futility with fewer ventilator-free days (14.0 vs 17.2) and mortality trending the wrong way
question: In adults with ARDS, does enteral omega-3 fatty-acid supplementation (EPA/GLA/antioxidants) improve ventilator-free days or mortality versus standard enteral feeding?
balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — the early small trials promised benefit; the one large rigorous trial found the supplement cost ventilator-free days and trended toward more deaths, and was stopped for futility (Tier C, mortality co-reported): The conflict is structural. A 2008 meta-analysis of the three early trials (Pontes-Arruda A et al., PMID: 18974237; 411 patients) pooled a mortality odds ratio of 0.40 (95% CI 0.24 to 0.68) for enteral eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) plus gamma-linolenic acid (GLA) plus antioxidants, and a single-centre Brazilian trial in severe sepsis (PMID: 16850002; 165 patients) reported a 19.4-point absolute mortality reduction. Then the ARDSNet OMEGA trial (Rice TW et al., PMID: 21976613; 272 patients with acute lung injury) gave twice-daily EPA/GLA/antioxidant supplement separately from the feed and found fewer ventilator-free days (14.0 vs 17.2; P=.02), fewer ICU-free and organ-failure-free days, more diarrhoea (29% vs 21%), and 60-day hospital mortality of 26.6% versus 16.3% (P=.054; adjusted 25.1% vs 17.6%, P=.11) before stopping early for futility — despite an 8-fold rise in plasma EPA proving delivery. The earliest ARDS trial of the formula family (Gadek 1999) is homed at live #16 in this library and is not re-carded here; its positive results are inside the 2008 pooled estimate carded below. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm): as tested in OMEGA, enteral omega-3/GLA/antioxidant supplementation in ARDS should not be given expecting benefit, and may harm.
stamp: POSSIBLE (harm) — enteral omega-3 (EPA/GLA) plus antioxidant supplementation in ARDS: small early trials claimed large benefits, but the large ARDSNet OMEGA trial was stopped for futility with fewer ventilator-free days and a non-significant mortality excess

title: Driving pressure in ARDS: tidal volume per unit of remaining lung — a 1-SD rise (~7 cm H2O) carried a relative mortality risk of 1.41 in 3,562 trial patients; as a titration target it is still untested
question: In ventilated adults with ARDS, what is driving pressure (plateau pressure minus PEEP), how does it relate to survival compared with tidal volume and PEEP individually, and what human data support targeting it?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING (textbook framing: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology and Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology, which present transpulmonary stress as pressure applied per unit of aerated lung — the 'baby lung' concept in textbook form): Driving pressure (ΔP) is plateau pressure minus PEEP, equivalently tidal volume divided by respiratory-system compliance, so it expresses the tidal volume in units of the size of lung actually available to receive it. The human evidence that it tracks survival better than its components is consistent but entirely observational or re-analytic. In the anchor mediation analysis of individual data from 3,562 ARDS patients in nine randomised trials (Amato MBP et al., PMID: 25693014), ΔP was the ventilation variable most strongly associated with survival: a 1-standard-deviation increment (about 7 cm H2O) carried a relative risk of death of 1.41 (95% CI 1.31 to 1.51), and changes in tidal volume or PEEP were associated with survival only insofar as they changed ΔP (mediation P=0.004 and P=0.001). Prospective-style cohort data agree in direction: during assisted ventilation, higher ΔP independently predicted ICU death (odds ratio 1.34 per cm H2O; Bellani G et al., PMID: 31335543), and a derivation-validation analysis found risk rising above a ΔP of about 19 cm H2O — while also finding plateau pressure a slightly better predictor than ΔP (Villar J et al., PMID: 28252536), a genuine counterweight. No randomised trial has tested a driving-pressure-targeted strategy, so the association cannot yet be read as a treatment target. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING: the definition and the risk gradient are settled human physiology; the claim that titrating ventilation to ΔP improves survival is unproven.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING — driving pressure (plateau pressure minus PEEP) is the ventilator variable most consistently tied to ARDS survival in human mediation and cohort data, but no randomised trial has tested targeting it

title: Mechanical power: the ventilator's energy per minute — associated with death in 8,207 ICU patients (odds ratio ~1.06–1.10 per 5 J/min), yet no better a predictor than driving pressure plus rate in ARDS
question: In ventilated patients, what is mechanical power (the energy per minute delivered by the ventilator), and how does it relate to ventilator-induced lung injury and mortality in human data?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING (textbook framing: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology and Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology, which ground lung injury in the stress and strain energy applied to lung tissue each breath): Mechanical power is the energy the ventilator delivers to the respiratory system per minute — the per-breath energy (a function of tidal volume, driving pressure, flow and PEEP) multiplied by respiratory rate — proposed by Gattinoni's group as the single variable unifying the ventilator settings that cause ventilator-induced lung injury (VILI). The formulation paper (Gattinoni L et al., PMID: 27620287) showed the power computed from the equation of motion matched power measured from pressure-volume loops in 30 patients with normal lungs and 50 with ARDS (slopes 0.96–1.12, R²>0.96), and that power rises exponentially with tidal volume, driving pressure and flow and linearly with PEEP. The mortality association is human and consistent but observational: in 8,207 patients ventilated for at least 48 hours across two large databases (Serpa Neto A et al., PMID: 30291378), each 5 J/min increment in mechanical power carried an odds ratio for hospital death of 1.06–1.10, with risk rising consistently above about 17 J/min. The strongest counterweight is also carded: in 4,549 ARDS patients pooled from six trials and a cohort (Costa ELV et al., PMID: 33784486), mechanical power predicted mortality, but a simpler model using only driving pressure and respiratory rate was equivalent — power added no predictive information beyond its two dominant components. The animal threshold experiments behind the concept (piglets developing VILI above roughly 12 J/min) are animal data and are described here as labelled background only, not carded. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING: the quantity is real, measurable and associated with death in humans; that reducing power, as such, prevents VILI or death is unproven, and its information may be carried almost entirely by driving pressure and rate.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING — mechanical power (ventilator energy delivered per minute) is computable at the bedside and is associated with mortality in large human cohorts, but it has not been shown to add predictive value beyond driving pressure and respiratory rate, and no trial has tested targeting it

title: Pendelluft and patient self-inflicted lung injury: gas shifts to dependent lung when effort is strong — shown on tomography in human ARDS and scaled to effort in 20 patients, but human injury evidence rests on a single-patient observation and animal mechanics
question: In spontaneously breathing patients with injured lungs, what is pendelluft, how strong is the human evidence that vigorous inspiratory effort worsens lung injury (patient self-inflicted lung injury), and how is effort measured at the bedside?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING (textbook framing: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology and Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology, on pleural-pressure transmission and regional lung stress): Pendelluft is gas moving inside the lung from non-dependent to dependent regions at the start of inspiration — without any change in tidal volume at the airway — when a strong diaphragmatic contraction drops pleural pressure locally, in dependent lung, instead of uniformly. The concept entered human medicine through a single-patient electrical impedance tomography observation during mechanical ventilation, after which the same group demonstrated the mechanism experimentally in injured pig lungs (Yoshida T et al., PMID: 24199628): the human component of that paper is one patient (N = 1, printed on the face), and its quantitative mechanics are animal data, labelled as such on the card and not treated as human evidence. Human cohort data now confirm the phenomenon is real and effort-dependent: in 20 ventilated ARDS patients, pendelluft during patient-triggered breaths grew with oesophageal pressure swing, with distinct high- and low-pendelluft response patterns (Lin WC et al., PMID: 38092775). What remains unproven in humans is the injury claim itself — patient self-inflicted lung injury (P-SILI): no human study carded here shows pendelluft or effort causing worse lung injury or death. Effort, at least, can be measured at the bedside: a brief airway occlusion swing (ΔPocc) detected muscle pressure above 10 cm H2O with AUROC 0.92 and transpulmonary driving pressure above 15 cm H2O with AUROC 0.93 in 16 patients, validated in 12 more (Bertoni M et al., PMID: 31694692), and ventilator-displayed occlusion pressure (P0.1) tracks drive and flags potentially injurious effort (Telias I et al., PMID: 32097569). PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING: pendelluft exists in human ARDS and scales with effort; effort is measurable non-invasively; that vigorous effort worsens human lung injury is a coherent, experimentally grounded hypothesis without direct human outcome evidence.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING — pendelluft occurs in human ARDS and scales with inspiratory effort, and effort can be measured non-invasively (ΔPocc, P0.1); direct human evidence that vigorous effort worsens lung injury (P-SILI) is limited to a one-patient observation plus animal mechanics

title: Alveolar fluid clearance in human ALI/ARDS: mean 6%/hour and impaired in 56% of patients (Ware & Matthay) — maximal clearance predicts survival, and the human epithelium answers beta-adrenergic stimulation
question: In human acute lung injury, how fast is alveolar fluid clearance, how often is it impaired, and does its rate predict mortality and response to beta-adrenergic stimulation?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology and Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, which present alveolar oedema resolution as active epithelial sodium transport driving water reabsorption, upregulated by beta-adrenergic/cAMP signalling): In human acute lung injury the alveolar epithelium's ability to clear its own oedema fluid is measurable at the bedside from serial oedema-fluid protein concentrations, and the carded human studies agree quantitatively across two decades. In 79 patients with ALI/ARDS (Ware LB & Matthay MA, PMID: 11371404), mean net alveolar fluid clearance was 6%/hour; 56% had impaired clearance (<3%/hour), 32% submaximal and only 13% maximal (≥14%/hour) — and patients with maximal clearance had significantly lower mortality and shorter ventilation. The uninjured-lung comparator shows what intact epithelium does: in 65 patients with hydrostatic oedema (Verghese GM et al., PMID: 10517756), 75% had intact clearance and 38% maximal clearance at a mean of 25%/hour, and intact clearance tracked with better oxygenation and an 18% lower hospital mortality. Clearance fails further exactly where the textbook mechanism predicts — with epithelial/endothelial injury from shock and bacteraemia (Zeyed YF et al., PMID: 22821995; 116 patients). Beta-adrenergic stimulation increases clearance in the ex vivo human lung (salmeterol effective at 10⁻⁶ M; human basal clearance 11 ± 2% over 4 hours — Sakuma T et al., PMID: 9032186, ex vivo human lungs, with the paper's parallel rat experiments not carded), and the in-vivo proof of principle exists: intravenous salbutamol lowered extravascular lung water by day 7 in a 40-patient randomised trial (Perkins GD et al., PMID: 16254268) — a physiological effect that later large outcome trials of beta-agonists in ARDS, homed elsewhere, did not convert into survival benefit. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED for the clearance rates, their impairment in ALI/ARDS and their prognostic meaning in humans; the beta-adrenergic responsiveness is established ex vivo and as an in-vivo physiological effect, not as a treatment.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — alveolar fluid clearance in humans is rapid when the epithelium is intact, impaired in the majority of ALI/ARDS patients (mean 6%/hour; 56% impaired), predicts mortality and ventilation duration, and is upregulated by beta-adrenergic stimulation in human lung tissue and in vivo

title: Endothelial glycocalyx shedding in human sepsis: syndecan-1 and heparan sulfate are markedly raised and track organ failure and death (observational)
question: In human sepsis, what evidence shows endothelial glycocalyx shedding (circulating syndecan-1, heparan sulfate), and how do shedding markers relate to organ failure, fluid responsiveness and death?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED for the phenomenon, with the evidence graded honestly: every carded study is observational. In human sepsis the endothelial glycocalyx is shed — circulating syndecan-1, heparan sulfate and glycosaminoglycans are consistently and markedly elevated (Nelson 2008: syndecan-1 246 vs 26 ng/mL in controls, in only 18 patients; Steppan 2011: shedding in sepsis comparable to that after major abdominal surgery). Shedding markers track the cardiovascular SOFA score, respiratory failure, renal replacement, subsequent fluid volumes and death; the largest dataset, the 574-patient CLOVERS substudy, found 90-day mortality of 9.9%, 20.4% and 44.2% across baseline heparan sulfate tertiles (adjusted HR 3.12 per interquartile-range increase). Textbook framing (Guyton & Hall): the glycocalyx is the endothelial surface layer that helps govern capillary permeability — these fragments are its debris in plasma. What is NOT established: that shedding causes organ failure rather than marking it, that it is sepsis-specific (surgery sheds it too), or that any glycocalyx-directed therapy improves outcomes — the randomised fluid comparison inside CLOVERS changed neither shedding nor outcome by shedding level.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED

title: Alveolar dead space in ARDS: about 0.58 of each breath is wasted early on, and the fraction independently predicts death
question: In ARDS, what fraction of tidal volume is wasted as alveolar dead space, why does it rise, and how strongly does the dead-space fraction predict mortality in humans?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. In ARDS the alveolar dead-space fraction is roughly double the healthy resting value: Nuckton 2002 measured a mean of 0.58 ± 0.09 within hours of onset in 179 patients — about three-fifths of every tidal volume ventilating alveoli too poorly perfused to exchange gas. The fraction independently predicted death (odds ratio 1.45 per 0.05 increase, 95% CI 1.15–1.83), while hypoxaemia severity did not. Three further human cohorts agree: a sustained 0.63–0.66 trajectory in nonsurvivors over 6 days (n = 59), significant survivor separation by days 1–2 in trial-enrolled patients (n = 126), and the strongest adjusted mortality association in 685 patients measured by volumetric capnography (+22% per 0.05 rise; not discriminatory in mild ARDS). Textbook framing (Guyton & Hall; Bohr–Enghoff): dead space is ventilation that does not exchange — in health mostly anatomic, in ARDS mostly alveolar, from microvascular injury and thrombosis in ventilated units. All evidence is observational: the fraction is an established prognostic marker of lung injury severity, not a proven treatment target.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED

title: Aztreonam–avibactam (Emblaveo) for carbapenem-resistant Gram-negative infection: descriptive phase 3 support, MBL trial of only 15 patients
question: In adults with complicated urinary tract infection, intra-abdominal infection or hospital-acquired pneumonia caused by metallo-beta-lactamase-producing or otherwise carbapenem-resistant Gram-negative bacteria, is aztreonam–avibactam effective versus best available therapy?
balance: EVIDENCE-STRUCTURE CAVEAT, stated plainly: aztreonam–avibactam (Emblaveo — product named under the clarification exception) was approved (FDA, February 2025) substantially on a pooled descriptive programme plus prior aztreonam data, not on a large superiority trial in metallo-β-lactamase producers. REVISIT (n = 422, cIAI and HAP-VAP) was descriptive with no formal hypothesis testing: cure 68.4% vs 65.7% on meropenem, 28-day mortality 4% vs 7% — but only 19 of 80 tested isolates were carbapenemase-positive. ASSEMBLE, the one trial in confirmed MBL producers, randomised just 15 patients (cure 5/12 vs 0/3 on best available therapy; mortality 1/12 vs 1/3). REJUVENATE (n = 34) set the dose and showed aztreonam-like tolerability (hepatic enzyme rises 26.5%). The pharmacological logic — aztreonam survives MBLs, avibactam covers co-produced serine enzymes — is sound and the small data point the right way, but the MBL-specific randomised evidence is 15 patients, and the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — descriptive programme only: no formal hypothesis testing in any carded trial, and the MBL-specific randomised evidence is 15 patients (ASSEMBLE)

title: ADAPT-Sepsis: procalcitonin guidance saved about a day of antibiotics in ICU sepsis; CRP guidance saved none
question: In critically ill adults with sepsis, does daily procalcitonin-guided (or CRP-guided) antibiotic discontinuation shorten treatment duration without increasing mortality versus usual care?
balance: A single very large trial answers this, and its two biomarker arms split. ADAPT-Sepsis (2,760 ICU patients with suspected sepsis, 41 UK units) found daily procalcitonin-guided discontinuation shortened antibiotic duration by a mean of 0.88 days (9.8 vs 10.7 days; P = .01), with 28-day mortality noninferior only against a wide 5.4-percentage-point margin (20.9% vs 19.4%). Daily CRP-guided discontinuation made no difference to duration (difference 0.09 days; P = .79) and its mortality comparison was inconclusive — CRP guidance is not supported. The trial's own economic evaluation found PCT guidance cost €427 more per patient with a tiny QALY loss within the trial (dominated), becoming cost-effective only when pooled with older trials; the process evaluation shows clinicians often overruled early PCT stop advice, blunting the effect. The broader procalcitonin-guidance question is homed on live Shelf 314; this pack covers the ADAPT-Sepsis ICU sepsis-discontinuation slice. One trial, however large, caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single trial: PCT guidance saved 0.88 antibiotic days in ADAPT-Sepsis; CRP guidance made no difference

title: Olorofim in invasive mould disease: 28.7% strict response in a single-arm phase 2b study — no comparator, and no Mucorales activity
question: In patients with invasive mould disease (including azole-resistant Aspergillus and Mucorales) with limited options, what response and survival does olorofim achieve?
balance: SINGLE-ARM EVIDENCE ONLY — printed on the face of every card; no randomised comparator exists. In the phase 2b study of 202 patients with invasive fungal disease and few or no options, olorofim's strict global response rate was 28.7% at day 42 (75.2% if stable disease is counted as success — both definitions are carded, and must travel together), with all-cause mortality of 11.9% at day 42 and 16.3% at day 84. A French compassionate-use cohort (n = 17) found success in 5 of 15 evaluable patients. PREMISE CORRECTION: the question as posed included Mucorales, but olorofim has no Mucorales activity and no Mucorales patients were studied — its spectrum covers Aspergillus (including azole-resistant strains), Lomentospora, Scedosporium and Coccidioides. Liver enzyme elevations occurred in about 10%. With no comparator, benefit magnitude is unknowable from these data; the stamp is POSSIBLE, never LIKELY.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single-arm evidence only (phase 2b, n = 202, plus a 17-patient cohort); no randomised comparator exists

title: Oral sulopenem (Orlynvah) for uncomplicated UTI: superior in ciprofloxacin-resistant infection, noninferior overall — not for complicated UTI
question: In women with uncomplicated urinary tract infection, is oral sulopenem etzadroxil plus probenecid non-inferior to nitrofurantoin (or ciprofloxacin in susceptible infection) for composite clinical/microbiological response?
balance: Oral sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid (Orlynvah — product named under the clarification exception; FDA approval October 2024, for uncomplicated UTI in adult women with limited or no alternative oral options) rests on two phase 3 trials with a split pattern. SURE-1 (n = 1,671, vs ciprofloxacin): superior where the pathogen was ciprofloxacin-resistant (overall success 62.6% vs 36.0%), but it FAILED noninferiority where the pathogen was susceptible (66.8% vs 78.6%), driven by asymptomatic bacteriuria. REASSURE (n = 2,222, vs amoxicillin–clavulanate): noninferior overall (60.9% vs 55.6%). The programme's complicated-UTI trial failed noninferiority (67.8% vs 73.9% vs ertapenem step-down) — the licence is uncomplicated UTI only. PREMISE NOTE: no published nitrofurantoin-comparator trial exists in PubMed; the tested comparators are ciprofloxacin and amoxicillin–clavulanate. Diarrhoea 8–12% is the main cost. Single programme, mixed subgroup verdicts: POSSIBLE.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single programme: noninferior overall and superior in ciprofloxacin-resistant uUTI, but failed noninferiority in susceptible uUTI and in complicated UTI

title: Cefepime–enmetazobactam (Exblifep) in complicated UTI: 79.1% vs 58.9% composite success vs piperacillin–tazobactam in one phase 3 trial
question: In adults with complicated urinary tract infection (including acute pyelonephritis), is cefepime–enmetazobactam non-inferior to piperacillin–tazobactam for composite cure?
balance: One phase 3 trial carries this question, and it is a strong one: ALCHEMIST (1,041 adults with complicated UTI or acute pyelonephritis, double-blind) found overall treatment success — clinical cure combined with microbiological eradication — in 79.1% on cefepime–enmetazobactam (Exblifep; product named under the clarification exception) vs 58.9% on piperacillin–tazobactam (difference 21.2 percentage points, 95% CI 14.3–27.9), meeting both its −10% noninferiority margin and its prespecified superiority test on that composite. Adverse events were somewhat commoner on the new drug (50.0% vs 44.0%). Support beyond the trial is indirect: a 28-trial network meta-analysis ranks it ahead of carbapenems on composite/eradication endpoints, and a 20-volunteer study shows lung penetration (pharmacology, not efficacy). The record does not split the composite, so the 21-point gap must not be read as a clinical-cure gap. Single trial: POSSIBLE.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single phase 3 trial (ALCHEMIST): noninferior and composite-superior to piperacillin–tazobactam; one trial caps the stamp

title: Intravenous peramivir: futility-stopped and unproven in hospitalised influenza — licensed on outpatient data
question: In patients with influenza who cannot take oral/oseltamivir therapy, does intravenous peramivir improve time to clinical stability versus placebo or oseltamivir?
balance: The honest answer is split by setting, and this pack keeps the halves separate. In HOSPITALISED influenza — the setting IV therapy exists for — peramivir is unproven: the pivotal placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (de Jong 2014) was terminated for futility after its interim analysis (median time to clinical resolution 42.5 vs 49.5 hours, P = .97 — the treatment made no difference), and the other hospitalised study (234 patients, 2009 pandemic) compared two doses with no control arm. In OUTPATIENT uncomplicated influenza, a single IV dose beat placebo on time to symptom alleviation (Kohno 2010, n = 300) and was noninferior to 5 days of oral oseltamivir (Kohno 2011, n = 1,091) — that outpatient evidence is what the licence rests on. For a hospitalised patient who cannot take oral/oseltamivir therapy, peramivir is a route choice extrapolated from outpatients, not a proven hospital treatment: MAYBE (weak evidence).
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — unproven in hospitalised patients: the pivotal hospitalised trial was stopped for futility (the treatment made no difference); benefit is shown only in outpatients

title: Cell-based influenza vaccine (Flucelvax) vs egg-based: a possible small relative edge in observational data — hospitalisation benefit unproven
question: In adults, does cell-culture-based quadrivalent influenza vaccine (Flucelvax) prevent more laboratory-confirmed influenza and influenza hospitalisations than egg-based vaccines?
balance: OBSERVATIONAL ONLY — test-negative designs throughout, no randomised head-to-head trial exists; capped at POSSIBLE and labelled. The cell-culture quadrivalent vaccine (Flucelvax — product named because the question is product-specific) avoids egg-adaptation of the seed virus, and one large 3-season EHR/claims analysis (Stein 2024) found a consistent RELATIVE advantage over egg-based quadrivalent vaccine against test-confirmed outpatient influenza: rVE 14.8%, 12.5% and 10.0% across 2017–2020 (relative measures — not percentage-point gains). But the CDC US Flu VE Network's product-specific analysis (2014–2019) found relative VE not statistically significant, with absolute VE of 30% for each product, and the single hospitalisation study (Kaiser, 2017–2018) found non-significant relative estimates (43% under 65; 6% at 65+, CI −46 to 39). A modest relative edge in some datasets is possible; a hospitalisation advantage is unproven.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only (test-negative): relative advantage of 10–15% in one 3-season analysis, not significant in the CDC network; hospitalisation benefit unproven

title: Nivolumab plus ipilimumab in first-line unresectable HCC (CheckMate 9DW): median survival 23.7 versus 20.6 months, with early curve crossing
question: In adults with unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma and no prior systemic therapy, does nivolumab plus ipilimumab improve overall survival versus lenvatinib or sorafenib?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one first-line randomised trial caps the stamp. In CheckMate 9DW (Yau 2025, PMID: 40349714), 668 patients with previously untreated unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma were randomised to nivolumab plus ipilimumab or investigator's choice of lenvatinib or sorafenib: median overall survival 23.7 versus 20.6 months (HR 0.79, 95% CI 0.65 to 0.96; p=0.018 — a relative measure, absolute medians beside it), with 36-month survival 38% versus 24%. The curves crossed early — more deaths in the first 6 months on the combination (HR 1.65) before a sustained later separation (HR 0.61) — and treatment-related deaths were 12 versus 3. The same combination in sorafenib-pretreated patients (CheckMate 040) gave durable responses (objective response 32% in the regimen arm later used first-line; 5-year survival 29% in that arm), supporting the drug pair's activity but in a different, second-line population. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a single first-line trial programme caps the stamp.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in the single first-line phase 3 trial (CheckMate 9DW, 668 patients), nivolumab plus ipilimumab gave median overall survival of 23.7 versus 20.6 months against lenvatinib or sorafenib (HR 0.79, 95% CI 0.65 to 0.96; p=0.018, a relative measure), with more deaths in the first 6 months (HR 1.65); a single trial programme caps the stamp at POSSIBLE

title: Ivosidenib in IDH1-mutant cholangiocarcinoma (ClarIDHy): progression-free survival HR 0.37; survival benefit only after crossover adjustment
question: In adults with previously treated IDH1-mutant cholangiocarcinoma, does ivosidenib improve progression-free and overall survival versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one randomised trial programme caps the stamp. title: Lonafarnib in chronic hepatitis D: HDV RNA suppression in phase 2 studies only — D-LIVR phase 3 has no published primary report
question: In adults with chronic hepatitis D, does lonafarnib boosted with ritonavir (with or without peginterferon) achieve HDV RNA suppression and ALT normalisation versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — phase 2 evidence only, and the publication-status check is part of this shelf's face: as of this build, no published primary report of the D-LIVR phase 3 trial was found in PubMed — the exact search for 'D-LIVR' returned only review articles, not a trial report — so this shelf rests entirely on the published phase 2 programme and states the D-LIVR status plainly. In the proof-of-concept randomised phase 2A trial (Koh 2015, PMID: 26189433), 28 days of lonafarnib lowered HDV RNA by 0.73 log IU/mL (100 mg twice daily) and 1.54 log IU/mL (200 mg twice daily) versus placebo. LOWR HDV-1 (Yurdaydin 2018, PMID: 29152762; 15 patients) found ritonavir boosting or peginterferon alfa addition improved responses over higher-dose monotherapy with fewer gastrointestinal effects. LOWR HDV-2 (Yurdaydin 2022, PMID: 34860418; 55 patients) reached the primary endpoint (≥2 log decline or below quantification) in 46% on all-oral lonafarnib 50 mg plus ritonavir and 89% on the regimen adding peginterferon alfa. Premise correction: the published LOWR combinations use peginterferon alfa, not lambda — peginterferon lambda belongs to the unpublished D-LIVR design, so no lambda claim is carded. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): small phase 2 studies with virological endpoints cap the stamp.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — PHASE 2 BASIS ONLY: lonafarnib lowered HDV RNA versus placebo in a 14-patient randomised proof-of-concept trial and reached virological endpoints in 46–89% in the 55-patient LOWR HDV-2 dose-finding study; no published primary report of the D-LIVR phase 3 trial was found, and that status is stated on the face of this shelf

title: Antibiotic prophylaxis in acute variceal bleeding: fewer infections and lower mortality; ceftriaxone beat norfloxacin in advanced cirrhosis
question: In adults with cirrhosis and acute variceal bleeding, does antibiotic prophylaxis (intravenous ceftriaxone versus oral norfloxacin) reduce bacterial infections, rebleeding and mortality?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) for prophylaxis versus none, on concordant meta-analyses of randomised trials: Bernard 1999 (PMID: 10347104; 5 trials, 534 patients) found prophylaxis raised the mean survival rate by 9.1 percentage points and the infection-free rate by 32 points; the updated Cochrane review (Chavez-Tapia 2011, PMID: 21707680; 12 trials, 1,241 patients) found mortality relative risk 0.79 (95% CI 0.63 to 0.98), bacterial infections relative risk 0.35 and rebleeding relative risk 0.53 — relative measures, with the trial counts beside them. For the choice of agent, one randomised trial (Fernández 2006, PMID: 17030175; 111 patients with advanced cirrhosis and haemorrhage) found intravenous ceftriaxone beat oral norfloxacin on proved or possible infections (11% versus 33%) — that head-to-head slice is a single trial and is capped at POSSIBLE within this balance. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) for giving prophylaxis; POSSIBLE for ceftriaxone over norfloxacin specifically.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — meta-analyses of randomised trials (12 trials, 1,241 patients) show antibiotic prophylaxis in cirrhosis with acute variceal bleeding reduces mortality (relative risk 0.79, 95% CI 0.63 to 0.98, a relative measure), infections and rebleeding; in the one head-to-head trial in advanced cirrhosis, intravenous ceftriaxone beat oral norfloxacin on infections (11% versus 33%)

title: Midodrine plus octreotide plus albumin in type 1 hepatorenal syndrome: reverses some cases, but lost to terlipressin 28.6% versus 70.4%
question: In adults with cirrhosis and type 1 hepatorenal syndrome where terlipressin is unavailable, does midodrine plus octreotide plus albumin reverse renal failure versus albumin-based care — and how does it compare with terlipressin?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) versus albumin-based care without a vasoconstrictor — and clearly inferior to terlipressin where terlipressin is available; one small randomised trial plus retrospective cohorts cap the stamp. In the only head-to-head randomised trial (Cavallin 2016, PMID: 25644760; 49 patients with hepatorenal syndrome), recovery of renal function occurred in 28.6% on midodrine plus octreotide plus albumin versus 70.4% on terlipressin plus albumin (P=0.01). The largest cohort (Skagen 2009, PMID: 19238094; 75 treated versus 87 historical controls) found longer transplant-free survival and better renal function at 1 month with the triple regimen than in untreated historical controls — a comparison wide open to era and selection bias, including a higher transplant rate in the treated group. The Esrailian report named in mining is a single-patient case report and falls below the reference floor, so it is not carded. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) as a fallback where terlipressin is unavailable; it is not terlipressin's equal.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — midodrine plus octreotide plus albumin reversed renal failure in 28.6% versus 70.4% for terlipressin plus albumin in the one small head-to-head randomised trial (49 patients), with cohort evidence of benefit over no vasoconstrictor; one small RCT plus cohorts cap the stamp at POSSIBLE

title: G-CSF in acute-on-chronic liver failure: SPLIT — one positive single-centre trial versus one negative multicentre trial (GRAFT)
question: In adults with acute-on-chronic liver failure, does granulocyte colony-stimulating factor improve transplant-free survival versus standard care?
balance: SPLIT — the split is named on the face: the single-centre trial is positive and the multicentre trial is negative. Garg 2012 (PMID: 22119930; single centre, India, 47 patients) found 60-day survival of about 66–69.6% with G-CSF versus 26–29% on placebo (P=.001). The multicentre GRAFT trial (Engelmann 2021, PMID: 34364917; 176 patients, Europe) — the negative multicentre trial the slate calls REALISTIC — found 90-day transplant-free survival of 34.1% with G-CSF versus 37.5% on standard therapy (HR 1.05; p=0.805; the treatment made no difference) and was stopped early for futility. A meta-analysis of 4 randomised trials (310 patients; Martin-Mateos 2023, PMID: 36174797) pooled to a non-significant mortality relative risk of 0.64 (95% CI 0.39 to 1.07) with high heterogeneity (I²=74%), the benefit confined to Asian studies. PROPOSED SPLIT: POSSIBLE (benefit) on the single-centre evidence; POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) on the multicentre evidence — do not average them into a single verdict.
stamp: SPLIT — POSSIBLE (benefit) in the positive single-centre Garg 2012 trial (47 patients; 60-day survival 66% versus 26%) versus POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) in the negative multicentre GRAFT trial (176 patients; HR 1.05, stopped for futility): the split is single-centre/Asian versus multicentre/European evidence

title: Albumin dialysis (MARS) and Prometheus in ACLF: no survival difference in RELIEF or HELIOS despite biochemical clearance
question: In adults with acute-on-chronic liver failure, does extracorporeal albumin dialysis (MARS) — or fractionated plasma separation (Prometheus) — improve survival versus standard medical therapy?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) to survival at the doses tested, in two concordant randomised trials. RELIEF (Bañares 2013, PMID: 23213075; 189 patients with ACLF) found 28-day survival of 60.7% on MARS albumin dialysis versus 58.9% on standard therapy, with an adjusted odds ratio of 0.87 (95% CI 0.44 to 1.72). HELIOS (Kribben 2012, PMID: 22248661; 145 patients) found 28-day survival of 66% on Prometheus fractionated plasma separation and adsorption versus 63% on standard therapy (P=.70) and 90-day survival of 47% versus 38% (P=.35). Both devices cleared bilirubin and creatinine and MARS improved encephalopathy more often, without a survival gain. An individual-patient meta-analysis (Bañares 2019, PMID: 31632458) found no survival benefit overall, with a benefit only in the subgroup receiving more than 4 MARS sessions — a subgroup hypothesis, not a trial result. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for survival as tested.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — extracorporeal albumin dialysis (MARS, RELIEF: 28-day survival 60.7% versus 58.9%) and Prometheus fractionated plasma separation (HELIOS: 66% versus 63%) each made no difference to survival versus standard therapy in their randomised trials in acute-on-chronic liver failure

title: POINTER: postponed drainage in infected necrotising pancreatitis — no difference in complications or death, but fewer interventions
question: In adults with infected necrotising pancreatitis, does postponing catheter drainage until collections are walled off reduce complications and interventions versus immediate drainage?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) to complications and death — with a real reduction in interventions, which is the reason to postpone. In POINTER (Boxhoorn 2021, PMID: 34614330; 104 patients with infected necrotising pancreatitis), the Comprehensive Complication Index over 6 months was 57 with immediate drainage versus 58 with postponed drainage (mean difference −1, 95% CI −12 to 10; P=0.90), and mortality was 13% versus 10% (relative risk 1.25, 95% CI 0.42 to 3.68) — postponing made no difference to complications or death. But the postponed group needed fewer interventions (mean 2.6 versus 4.4), and 39% of postponed patients were treated with antibiotics alone and never needed drainage. Long-term follow-up (Van Veldhuisen 2024, PMID: 37450701; 88 patients re-evaluated at a median 51 months) confirmed no difference in death or major complications after 6 months and fewer total interventions with postponement (median 1 versus 4). A meta-analysis of 7 mostly non-randomised timing studies (742 patients; Gao 2022, PMID: 35488104) pointed the same way: early intervention brought more gastrointestinal fistula or perforation and longer hospital stay, with a non-significant mortality odds ratio of 1.65. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) on the complication question — a single trial caps the stamp — with fewer interventions as the practical gain.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — postponing catheter drainage until collections were walled off made no difference to complications (Complication Index 58 versus 57) or mortality (10% versus 13%) in the single POINTER trial (104 patients), but reduced interventions (mean 2.6 versus 4.4) and 39% of postponed patients never needed drainage; a single trial caps the stamp at POSSIBLE

title: Prophylactic antibiotics in predicted severe acute pancreatitis: infected necrosis 12% vs 9% and mortality 5% vs 7% in the double-blind trial — no benefit
question: In adults with predicted severe or necrotising acute pancreatitis, do prophylactic antibiotics prevent infected necrosis or death versus placebo?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — the only double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (Isenmann 2004, n=114) found infected pancreatic necrosis in 12% on ciprofloxacin–metronidazole versus 9% on placebo and mortality of 5% versus 7% (the treatment made no difference). Meta-analyses agree on the endpoints that matter: Ding 2020 (11 RCTs, 747 participants) found no significant difference in infected pancreatic necrosis (OR 0.74, 95% CI 0.50–1.09) or mortality (OR 0.71, 95% CI 0.44–1.15), and trial sequential analysis (Poropat 2022, 21 trials, 1,383 patients) likewise showed no significant reduction in infected necrosis (RR 0.81, 95% CI 0.63–1.04) or mortality (RR 0.85, 95% CI 0.66–1.10), although extra-pancreatic infections were fewer. The one positive trial (Pederzoli 1993, imipenem) was open-label against no treatment and predates modern care; the large meropenem trial (Dellinger 2007) is homed elsewhere in the library and is not carded here. This is why AGA/ACG guidance recommends against prophylactic antibiotics in severe or necrotising pancreatitis: antibiotics are for documented or strongly suspected infection, not prevention.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — double-blind RCT and meta-analyses: no reduction in infected pancreatic necrosis or mortality from prophylactic antibiotics

title: Over-the-scope clip vs standard endoscopic therapy in high-risk upper GI bleeding: further bleeding 15.2% vs 57.6% in recurrent ulcer bleeding (STING), but an intention-to-treat null in large ulcers
question: In adults with high-risk non-variceal upper gastrointestinal bleeding, is an over-the-scope clip more effective than standard endoscopic therapy (clips/thermal) as first-line treatment for initial haemostasis and rebleeding?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the randomised record is positive but split by setting. In STING (Schmidt 2018), which enrolled recurrent peptic ulcer bleeding after initially successful haemostasis — not first presentation — further bleeding occurred in 15.2% with the over-the-scope clip (OTSC; the tested Ovesco OTSC system may be named under the product-clarification exception) versus 57.6% with standard therapy (absolute difference 42.4 percentage points). In first-line high-risk bleeding, STING-2 (Meier 2022) found clinical success in 91.7% versus 73.1%. But in large ulcers (≥1.5 cm), Chan 2023 found no intention-to-treat difference in 30-day rebleeding (10% vs 18%; p=0.23). A 2025 meta-analysis (14 studies, 7,211 patients, only five randomised) reports 30-day rebleeding RR 0.44 in relative terms. One consistent, unselected first-line trial is still missing, so the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — OTSC beat standard therapy in recurrent bleeding (STING) and in one first-line high-risk trial (STING-2), but a large-ulcer trial was null on intention-to-treat

title: Retatrutide and liver fat (phase 2 substudy, n=98): liver fat fell 82.4% in relative terms on 12 mg vs +0.3% on placebo at 24 weeks — a surrogate, phase-2 result
question: In adults with obesity (the MASH-risk population), does retatrutide reduce liver fat content versus placebo, and how does the reduction track with weight loss?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — capped, because the entire liver-fat evidence base is one phase 2 MRI-PDFF substudy (Sanyal 2024, n=98) of the phase 2 obesity trial, and liver fat content is a surrogate outcome: no MASH-resolution, fibrosis or clinical liver outcome has been reported for retatrutide. Within that substudy the effect is large and dose-ordered: mean relative change in liver fat at 24 weeks was −42.9% (1 mg), −57.0% (4 mg), −81.4% (8 mg) and −82.4% (12 mg) versus +0.3% on placebo (all P<0.001), and liver fat normalised (<5%) in up to 86% on 12 mg versus 0% on placebo. Reductions tracked weight and abdominal-fat loss. The parent trial's weight and glycaemia results are homed on live shelf #1090 and are not re-carded here; this shelf covers only the liver-fat slice. Phase 3 and histology data will decide whether the surrogate converts into liver benefit.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single phase 2 MRI-PDFF substudy (n=98), surrogate outcome only: relative liver-fat reduction up to 82.4% vs +0.3% on placebo at 24 weeks; no histology or clinical liver outcomes yet

title: Linerixibat for cholestatic pruritus in PBC: phase 3 GLISTEN itch difference −0.72 points vs placebo, with diarrhoea in 61% vs 18%
question: In adults with primary biliary cholangitis and cholestatic pruritus, does linerixibat (an IBAT inhibitor) reduce itch severity versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — GLISTEN, the phase 3 trial, IS now published in full (Lancet Gastroenterology & Hepatology; 238 patients): linerixibat 40 mg twice daily improved worst-itch scores by −2.86 points versus −2.15 on placebo over 24 weeks (adjusted difference −0.72 points, 95% CI −1.15 to −0.28; p=0.0013) — statistically solid but a modest average gain on a 0–10 scale, bought with diarrhoea in 61% versus 18% and gastrointestinal discontinuations in 7% versus under 1%. The phase 2b GLIMMER trial missed its primary intention-to-treat endpoint (dose groups showed ≥2-point mean itch reductions but differences from placebo were not significant; significance appeared only in post-hoc monthly-itch and per-protocol analyses), and a modelling study links the itch gain to bile-acid lowering (correlation r=0.52). One positive phase 3 with a modest effect size and a missed phase 2 primary caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one published phase 3 RCT (GLISTEN, n=238): itch difference −0.72 points vs placebo at 24 weeks, diarrhoea 61% vs 18%; phase 2b primary endpoint was missed

title: Vibrating capsule (Vibrant) in chronic constipation: ≥1 extra complete spontaneous bowel movement per week in 39.3% vs 22.1% on sham in the phase 3 trial
question: In adults with chronic idiopathic constipation refractory to laxatives, does a vibrating capsule increase complete spontaneous bowel movements versus a sham capsule?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one phase 3 trial of the tested product (the Vibrant vibrating capsule, named under the product-clarification exception) met both primary endpoints: in Rao 2023 (n=312), responders gaining at least 1 complete spontaneous bowel movement (CSBM) per week numbered 39.3% versus 22.1% on placebo capsule (P=0.001), and those gaining at least 2 numbered 22.7% versus 11.4% (P=0.008), over 8 weeks. A second randomised trial (VICONS, n=107) used a different, smartphone-controlled vibrating capsule in functional constipation and also favoured the device (responder rate 64.2% vs 35.8%). But the pooled meta-analysis is more equivocal — across four trials (705 patients) the CSBM change did not reach significance (mean difference 0.153, 95% CI −0.218 to 0.523) while spontaneous bowel movements did — and the phase 3 population was chronic constipation broadly, not a strictly laxative-refractory cohort. Single-product phase 3 plus mixed pooling caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one phase 3 RCT of the Vibrant capsule (n=312): CSBM responder 39.3% vs 22.1%; pooled CSBM effect across devices not significant

title: PHASE 2 ONLY — tulisokibart (anti-TL1A) in ulcerative colitis (ARTEMIS-UC): clinical remission 26% vs 1% on placebo at week 12
question: In adults with moderately to severely active ulcerative colitis, does tulisokibart (anti-TL1A antibody) induce clinical remission versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — PHASE 2 ONLY, and the stamp is capped for that reason: the whole case is one 12-week phase 2 trial (ARTEMIS-UC, Sands 2024). In cohort 1 (135 patients, enrolled regardless of biomarker status), clinical remission at week 12 occurred in 26% on intravenous tulisokibart versus 1% on placebo (difference 25 percentage points, 95% CI 14–37; P<0.001). Among patients positive on the trial's genetic likelihood-of-response test (75 patients across both cohorts), remission was 32% versus 11% (difference 21 points, 95% CI 2–38; P=0.02). Adverse events were similar between groups and mostly mild to moderate. There is no phase 3, no maintenance data and no endoscopic-outcome confirmation at scale yet; a class meta-analysis pools the same early trials and adds no independent patients. Phase 3 will decide whether this becomes a treatment or another phase 2 promise.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — PHASE 2 ONLY: single 12-week phase 2 trial (ARTEMIS-UC, n=135 primary cohort): remission 26% vs 1% at week 12; no phase 3 yet
