title: Faecal microbiota transplantation in severe alcohol-associated hepatitis: pilot and retrospective series only — 3-month survival 75% with FMT vs 38% on steroids in one small comparative series
question: In adults with severe alcohol-associated hepatitis not responding to or ineligible for steroids, does faecal microbiota transplantation improve 90-day survival versus standard care/pentoxifylline?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — everything here is pilot-scale and non-randomised: there is no completed randomised trial of faecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) in severe alcohol-associated hepatitis in the published record fetched for this shelf. The Philips group's comparative series (2018) reported 3-month survival of 75% in 16 FMT patients versus 38% on corticosteroids, 29% on nutritional support and 30% on pentoxifylline — groups of 8–17 patients, not randomised. Their later single-centre retrospective series (2022) found 6-month survival of 83.0% in 47 FMT patients versus 56.0% in 25 matched pentoxifylline patients (P=0.012), with fewer infections, ascites and encephalopathy. A 2025 meta-analysis (8 studies, 444 patients) found higher 28- and 90-day survival with FMT in relative terms (RR 2.30 and 2.53 — relative measures) but no significant benefit at 6 or 12 months, and the benefit was restricted to the retrospective studies on subgroup analysis. The signal is consistent and the biology plausible, but confounding by patient selection is exactly what these designs cannot exclude — hence MAYBE, with the small numbers printed on the stamp.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — pilot and retrospective data only, no randomised trial: FMT recipients in the two carded Philips series total N = 63; short-term survival signals not confirmed at 6–12 months in pooled analysis

title: SPLIT — tenofovir vs entecavir and liver cancer risk in chronic hepatitis B: Korean nationwide cohort says tenofovir lower (HR 0.61); US veterans and an international consortium say no difference
question: In adults with chronic hepatitis B on long-term therapy, is tenofovir disoproxil fumarate associated with a lower risk of hepatocellular carcinoma than entecavir?
balance: SPLIT (observational only) — the cohorts directly conflict, and there is no randomised comparison, so no winner can be declared. Choi 2019 (Korean nationwide cohort, 24,156 patients) found hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) incidence of 0.64 per 100 person-years on tenofovir disoproxil versus 1.06 on entecavir (adjusted HR 0.61, 95% CI 0.54–0.70), with the same direction in matched and hospital-cohort analyses. Against that: Su 2021 (US Veterans Affairs, 3,287 patients) found no difference at all (adjusted HR 1.00, 95% CI 0.76–1.32), and Hsu 2020 (international consortium, 5,537 patients) found the crude tenofovir advantage (SHR 0.45) disappeared after adjustment (SHR 0.81, 95% CI 0.42–1.56) and in propensity matching (adjusted SHR 0.89, 95% CI 0.41–1.92). All hazard ratios are relative measures from retrospective data, where who gets which drug is not random. Both drugs remain guideline first-line therapy; this shelf records the disagreement rather than resolving it, and the stamp can never be LIKELY on this evidence type.
stamp: SPLIT (observational only) — retrospective cohorts conflict directly: HR 0.61 favouring tenofovir (Korea) vs adjusted HR 1.00 (US veterans) and 0.81–0.89 non-significant (international consortium); no randomised data

title: Odevixibat in Alagille syndrome (ASSERT phase 3, n=52): scratching score fell 0.9 points more than placebo and bile acids by 113 µmol/L more — diarrhoea 29% vs 6%
question: In children and adults with Alagille syndrome and cholestatic pruritus, does odevixibat reduce itch and serum bile acids versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one phase 3 trial in a rare disease (ASSERT, Ovchinsky 2024; 52 patients, median age 5.5 years): odevixibat 120 µg/kg daily improved caregiver-reported scratching by a least-squares mean of −1.7 points versus −0.8 on placebo over 24 weeks (difference −0.9, 95% CI −1.4 to −0.3; p=0.0024) and lowered serum bile acids by 90 µmol/L against a 22 µmol/L rise on placebo (difference −113 µmol/L, 95% CI −179 to −47; p=0.0012). Diarrhoea occurred in 29% versus 6%; no patient discontinued and there were no deaths. A 2026 systematic review of IBAT inhibitors confirms that for odevixibat in Alagille syndrome only this single dose (120 µg/kg/day) has reported outcomes, so there is no dose-ranging or replication. Note the acronym: this ASSERT is the Alagille odevixibat trial, verified by content (NCT04674761) — the same acronym is used by unrelated trials. The neighbouring maralixibat shelf (pack #3604) covers a different drug in a different disease (PFIC). A single small trial caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.

title: Tirofiban in acute ischaemic stroke without thrombectomy-eligible occlusion (RESCUE BT2, n=1,177): excellent outcome 29.1% vs 22.2% on aspirin — symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage 1.0% vs 0%
question: In adults with acute ischaemic stroke who are not eligible for (or are beyond) thrombolysis/thrombectomy, does intravenous tirofiban improve 90-day functional outcome versus aspirin/standard antiplatelet care?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one large trial carries the claim, and its harm sits beside its benefit. In RESCUE BT2 (Zi 2023; 1,177 patients in China with stroke and no large or medium-sized vessel occlusion), an excellent 90-day outcome (modified Rankin scale 0–1) occurred in 29.1% on intravenous tirofiban versus 22.2% on aspirin (adjusted risk ratio 1.26, 95% CI 1.04–1.53 — a relative measure; the absolute gain is 6.9 percentage points), while symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage occurred in 1.0% versus 0% and mortality was similar. The TREND trial (Zhao 2024; n=425) supports the mechanism on an earlier endpoint — early neurological deterioration in 4.2% versus 13.2% (adjusted relative risk 0.32, 95% CI 0.16–0.65), with no symptomatic haemorrhage — but did not show a significant 90-day functional difference. A 2026 meta-analysis of nine studies (3,225 patients) pools an odds ratio of 1.66 for excellent outcome in relative terms, driven by these same trials. All the randomised evidence is from China and the populations are heterogeneous (four different presentations in RESCUE BT2), so a single-programme cap applies: POSSIBLE.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one large RCT (RESCUE BT2, n=1,177): excellent outcome 29.1% vs 22.2% (absolute +6.9 points), symptomatic ICH 1.0% vs 0%; supporting TREND trial positive only on early deterioration; all trials from China

title: Intra-arterial alteplase after successful thrombectomy: excellent outcome rises in three randomised trials — but 90-day mortality rose in the largest one (CHOICE-2)
question: In adults with large-vessel-occlusion stroke and successful endovascular reperfusion, does adjunctive intra-arterial alteplase improve 90-day functional outcome versus thrombectomy alone?
balance: Three randomised trials of the same manoeuvre — a single intra-arterial alteplase dose (0.225 mg/kg) given after successful thrombectomy — point the same way on function and split on survival. CHOICE (Spain, n=121, stopped early) found excellent outcome (mRS 0–1 at 90 days) in 59.0% vs 40.4%. PEARL (China, n=324) found 44.8% vs 30.2%. CHOICE-2 (Spain, n=440), the largest and most recent, found 57.5% vs 42.5% (adjusted risk difference 15.0%) — and, in the same trial, 90-day mortality of 12.1% on alteplase vs 6.4% without it (adjusted risk difference 5.9%, P=.03), a signal PEARL echoed non-significantly (17.1% vs 11.3%) while the small CHOICE trial ran the other way (8% vs 15%). Symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage was not significantly increased in any trial. A treatment that frees more patients from disability while possibly killing more of them cannot be stamped above POSSIBLE until the mortality signal is explained or refuted.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — three randomised trials agree on more excellent outcomes, but the largest trial found significantly higher 90-day mortality on alteplase, so the net benefit is not settled

title: Intravenous prourokinase vs alteplase within 4.5 hours: non-inferior for excellent outcome in two Chinese phase 3 trials, with less systemic bleeding — a single-country (China) programme
question: In adults with acute ischaemic stroke within 4.5 hours who are ineligible for or refuse thrombectomy, is intravenous recombinant human prourokinase non-inferior to alteplase for excellent functional outcome, and with what bleeding cost?
balance: Every trial in this programme was run in China — that is printed here, not in fine print. In PROST-2 (n=1,552), intravenous recombinant human prourokinase (15 mg bolus + 20 mg infusion) was non-inferior to alteplase for excellent outcome at 90 days (mRS 0–1: 72.0% vs 68.7%), with less symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage (0.3% vs 1.3%) and less major bleeding. The earlier phase 3 trial (Song 2023, n=663 in the modified intention-to-treat population) found the same non-inferiority (65.2% vs 64.3%) with similar symptomatic haemorrhage and less systemic bleeding (25.8% vs 42.2%). A small phase 2a dose study in the later 4.5–6-hour window (n=80, no alteplase comparator) is carded for completeness and carries no comparative weight. Non-inferiority in one country's programme supports prourokinase as an alternative thrombolytic where alteplase supply is short — the use the PROST-2 authors themselves propose — and caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — non-inferiority shown twice, but the entire programme is single-country (China) and non-inferiority to alteplase is not superiority

title: Argatroban or eptifibatide added to intravenous thrombolysis: no functional benefit in either phase 3 programme — MOST was stopped for futility with higher mortality, and ARAIS was neutral (the treatment made no difference)
question: In adults receiving intravenous thrombolysis for acute ischaemic stroke, does adding argatroban or eptifibatide improve functional outcome versus thrombolysis alone?
balance: This shelf corrects a common misreading of the record. The two phase 3 programmes do not split positive-versus-negative on functional outcome: both are negative. MOST (United States, n=514), an adaptive three-arm trial of argatroban or eptifibatide added to intravenous thrombolysis, was stopped for futility — utility-weighted 90-day Rankin scores were lower on both adjuncts than on placebo, and 90-day mortality was higher (argatroban 24%, eptifibatide 12%, placebo 8%). ARAIS (China, n=817), testing argatroban added to alteplase, was neutral on its primary endpoint: excellent outcome 63.8% vs 64.9% (P=.78) — the treatment made no difference — with similar bleeding. The only positive signal in the programme's history is a 65-patient open-label pilot (2012) in which the combination looked safe and recanalisation was frequent; recanalisation is a surrogate, and the pilot had no control arm. Post-hoc ARAIS subgroup analyses do not overturn a neutral primary endpoint. On the phase 3 record, adding either drug to thrombolysis should not be expected to help, and in MOST it was associated with harm.
stamp: UNLIKELY (benefit) — neither phase 3 programme improved functional outcome (the treatment made no difference), and mortality was higher on both adjuncts in MOST

title: Edaravone dexborneol in acute ischaemic stroke: better than edaravone alone in TASTE, borderline against placebo before thrombectomy in TASTE-2 — a single-country (China) programme, and TASTE has no placebo arm
question: In adults with acute ischaemic stroke, does edaravone dexborneol improve 90-day functional outcome versus edaravone alone (TASTE) or versus placebo given before thrombectomy (TASTE-2)?
balance: The whole programme is single-country (China) — stated here on the face. Two design facts decide how this shelf may be quoted. First, TASTE (n=1,165) had no placebo arm: edaravone dexborneol beat edaravone alone on excellent outcome (67.2% vs 59.0%), which shows the dexborneol component adds something over edaravone, but cannot show either drug beats no treatment. Second, the placebo-controlled test, TASTE-2 (n=1,360 analysed), given before thrombectomy, landed exactly on the borderline: functional independence 55.0% vs 49.6% (risk ratio 1.11; 95% CI 1.00–1.23; P=0.05), with the effect concentrated in a prespecified mismatch subgroup, and a small phase 2 placebo-controlled trial after successful reperfusion (n=200) found no significant difference (58.7% vs 52.1%; P=0.29). Serious adverse events were similar to placebo in TASTE-2. That is a POSSIBLE: a real but fragile signal, untested outside China.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one active-comparator win and one borderline placebo-controlled result, all from a single-country (China) programme

title: Aducanumab in early Alzheimer's disease: two identical phase 3 trials disagreed — EMERGE met its endpoint at high dose, ENGAGE did not — and the programme was terminated and the drug withdrawn
question: In patients with early Alzheimer's disease, did aducanumab slow clinical decline versus placebo — and why did its two identical phase 3 trials disagree?
balance: This shelf cards only the aducanumab slice. The neighbouring live shelf #333 covers lecanemab and donanemab and mentions aducanumab only as a cautionary arc; the EMERGE and ENGAGE results themselves are carded here, from their joint report, and none of #333's references is carded on this shelf. The record is genuinely split. EMERGE (n=1,638) met its primary endpoint at the high dose: CDR-SB difference −0.39 versus placebo (95% CI −0.69 to −0.09; P=.012), described in the report as a 22% relative slowing. ENGAGE (n=1,647), an identically designed twin trial, did not: difference +0.03 (95% CI −0.26 to 0.33; P=.833). Both trials were halted early on a futility analysis of pooled data from roughly the first half of participants, then analysed on the larger dataset accumulated by the halt — the procedural fact at the centre of every later dispute about this programme. Both trials showed dose-dependent amyloid and biomarker reduction, and the commonest adverse event was amyloid-related imaging abnormality with oedema (ARIA-E). Aducanumab received accelerated US approval in 2021 on the amyloid surrogate, and the programme was subsequently terminated with the drug withdrawn in 2024, as the #333 shelf records. A split phase 3 pair, stopped early, followed by withdrawal is not a basis for expecting clinical benefit: the stamp is SPLIT because the trials themselves split.
stamp: SPLIT — the two phase 3 trials disagree on the primary endpoint (EMERGE positive at high dose, ENGAGE negative), and the programme was terminated with the drug withdrawn in 2024

title: Gantenerumab in early Alzheimer's disease: GRADUATE I and II both missed their primary endpoint (the treatment made no difference) despite lowering amyloid — a well-conducted negative programme
question: In patients with early Alzheimer's disease, does gantenerumab slow clinical decline versus placebo?
balance: This is a clean negative programme, and the shelf's job is to hold that answer plainly. In GRADUATE I (n=985) the CDR-SB difference at week 116 was −0.31 (95% CI −0.66 to 0.05; P=0.10); in GRADUATE II (n=980) it was −0.19 (95% CI −0.55 to 0.17; P=0.30) — neither significant, both small. The drug did what it was designed to do biologically: amyloid on PET fell by about 56–66 centiloids more than on placebo, and roughly 27–28% of treated participants reached amyloid-negative status. It also carried the class harm: ARIA-E in 24.9% of treated participants, symptomatic in 5.0%. The earlier SCarlet RoAD trial in prodromal disease (n=797, lower monthly doses) had already been halted for futility with no clinical differences, and its exploratory dose signal is what justified GRADUATE's higher, more frequent dosing — which then also failed on the clinical endpoint. Amyloid lowering without clinical slowing, twice at phase 3 scale, is the answer. The neighbouring live shelf #333 covers the two antibodies in this class that did slow decline (lecanemab, donanemab); gantenerumab is not among them.
stamp: UNLIKELY (benefit) — both GRADUATE trials missed the primary endpoint (the treatment made no difference to clinical decline), as did the earlier prodromal trial

title: Evobrutinib in relapsing multiple sclerosis: not superior to teriflunomide in evolutionRMS1 and 2 (relapse rates identical) — with a liver-enzyme cost (elevations ≥5× the upper limit of normal in 5.0% vs <1%)
question: In people with relapsing multiple sclerosis, is the BTK inhibitor evobrutinib superior to teriflunomide for relapse rate, and what is its liver cost?
balance: The phase 3 answer is unusually plain, because the trialists state it themselves: the efficacy of evobrutinib was not superior to that of teriflunomide, and together the efficacy and liver findings do not support its use in relapsing multiple sclerosis. In evolutionRMS1 (n=1,124 in the full analysis set) the annualised relapse rate was 0.15 on evobrutinib vs 0.14 on teriflunomide (adjusted rate ratio 1.02; p=0.55); in evolutionRMS2 (n=1,166) it was 0.11 vs 0.11 (rate ratio 1.00; p=0.51). The liver cost was asymmetric: alanine aminotransferase elevations of at least 5 times the upper limit of normal occurred in 5.0% on evobrutinib vs fewer than 1% on teriflunomide, concentrated in the first 12 weeks, and three evobrutinib patients (vs one on teriflunomide) met the biochemical definition of Hy's law, all resolving after discontinuation. The earlier phase 2 trial (n=267) had shown fewer gadolinium-enhancing MRI lesions at the 75 mg once-daily dose — a real imaging signal that did not convert into fewer relapses than an established oral comparator at phase 3. This shelf's verdict is about evobrutinib versus teriflunomide in relapsing MS; it is not a verdict on the BTK-inhibitor class in other MS phenotypes.
stamp: UNLIKELY (benefit over teriflunomide) — annualised relapse rates were identical in both phase 3 trials (the treatment made no difference to relapses), and liver-enzyme elevations were more frequent on evobrutinib

title: Tavapadon (tested product: tavapadon, AbbVie) in Parkinson's disease: motor scores improved in early disease (TEMPO-1 and TEMPO-2) and good on-time rose by 1.1 hours as a levodopa adjunct (TEMPO-3)
question: In people with Parkinson's disease, does the selective D1/D5 partial agonist tavapadon improve motor scores as monotherapy in early disease (TEMPO-1/2) and increase good on-time as levodopa adjunct in fluctuating disease (TEMPO-3), versus placebo?
balance: The tested product is named per the clarification exception: tavapadon (AbbVie), an oral once-daily selective D1/D5 dopamine-receptor partial agonist. Its three phase 3 trials are concordant. In early Parkinson's disease, TEMPO-1 (n=529) found MDS-UPDRS Parts II+III improvements of −11.5 points (5 mg) and −12.1 points (15 mg) versus placebo at week 26, and TEMPO-2 (n=304, flexible dose) found −9.1 points. In fluctuating disease on levodopa, TEMPO-3 (n=507) increased daily good on-time by 1.10 hours versus placebo and reduced off-time by 0.94 hours. The cost is tolerability, not a safety catastrophe: nausea in roughly a quarter to a third of treated patients, headache and dizziness commonly, and in TEMPO-2 discontinuation in 38% on tavapadon vs 15% on placebo, most often for adverse events. Trials ran 26–27 weeks, so long-term tolerability and any comparison against existing agonists or levodopa strategies are untested — a single programme with short follow-up caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — three concordant phase 3 trials from a single programme (tavapadon, AbbVie), with follow-up of only 26–27 weeks and a nausea/dizziness and discontinuation cost

title: Efgartigimod in CIDP (ADHERE): relapse risk cut in an enriched randomised-withdrawal trial — the denominator is open-label run-in responders (214 of 322 improved), not all CIDP; relapses 27.9% vs 53.6% on withdrawal to placebo
question: In adults with CIDP, does weekly subcutaneous efgartigimod PH20 reduce relapse risk versus placebo in patients who first respond in an open-label run-in?
balance: The design is the headline, and it is printed on the face: ADHERE is an enriched randomised-withdrawal trial. Of 322 adults with CIDP who entered the open-label run-in (stage A) on weekly subcutaneous efgartigimod PH20 1000 mg, 214 (66%) achieved confirmed clinical improvement; it was those responders — 221 participants entered the randomised stage B per the report — who were randomised to continue efgartigimod or switch to placebo for up to 48 weeks. In stage B, continuing efgartigimod reduced relapse risk with a hazard ratio of 0.39 (95% CI 0.25–0.61) — a 61% relative reduction in relapse risk — with absolute relapse rates of 27.9% (31/111) on efgartigimod vs 53.6% (59/110) on placebo. That is strong evidence that responders who stop, relapse — and no evidence at all about the third of patients who never responded in stage A, who are outside the randomised denominator. Adverse events were similar between stage B groups (treatment-emergent events 64% vs 56%; serious events 5% in each). A single trial with an enriched design caps the stamp at POSSIBLE, and any quotation of the hazard ratio without the run-in denominator misstates the trial. Efgartigimod's separate generalised myasthenia gravis evidence is a different disease and shelf (live #1116) and lends this one no support.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single enriched randomised-withdrawal trial: 61% relative reduction in relapse risk among run-in responders (hazard ratio 0.39), with absolute relapses of 27.9% vs 53.6%

title: Nipocalimab in generalised myasthenia gravis (Vivacity-MG3): MG-ADL improved by −4.70 vs −3.25 points on placebo over 24 weeks in antibody-positive adults, with adverse-event rates equal to placebo
question: In antibody-positive adults with generalised myasthenia gravis and insufficient response to standard care, does the FcRn blocker nipocalimab improve MG-ADL sustained over 24 weeks versus placebo?
balance: Vivacity-MG3 (199 enrolled; 196 treated) randomised antibody-positive adults with generalised myasthenia gravis inadequately controlled on standard care to nipocalimab (30 mg/kg loading, then 15 mg/kg every 2 weeks) or placebo, each added to standard care, for 24 weeks. The primary endpoint — least-squares mean MG-ADL change averaged over weeks 22–24 in the 153 antibody-positive patients — favoured nipocalimab: −4.70 vs −3.25 points (difference −1.45; 95% CI −2.38 to −0.52; p=0.0024). The population was the broadest in the FcRn class: anti-AChR, anti-MuSK and anti-LRP4 positive patients were all eligible. Tolerability matched placebo on the headline counts — any adverse event in 84% of both groups, infections in 43% of both — while serious adverse events were reported in 9% on nipocalimab vs 14% on placebo, with one fatal myasthenic crisis in the nipocalimab group among three fatal serious events in the trial. A prespecified quality-of-life analysis moved the same direction (MG-QoL15r difference −1.45; fatigue scores better from week 2). One 24-week trial, however consistent internally, caps the stamp at POSSIBLE; durability rests on the ongoing open-label extension. The FcRn neighbours — efgartigimod, rozanolixizumab and zilucoplan in generalised myasthenia gravis — are separate agents on separate shelves and are not interchangeable evidence.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single phase 3 trial (Vivacity-MG3) with a modest, sustained MG-ADL advantage and placebo-like adverse-event rates; longer-term data sit in an ongoing open-label extension

title: Risdiplam in spinal muscular atrophy: a randomised motor benefit in type 2/3 disease (SUNFISH) and single-arm milestone gains against natural history in type 1 infants (FIREFISH)
question: In infants with type 1 SMA (FIREFISH) and in children/young adults with type 2/3 SMA (SUNFISH), does daily oral risdiplam improve motor function versus placebo or natural-history controls?
balance: Risdiplam rests on two very different kinds of evidence, and this shelf keeps them separate. In type 2 and non-ambulant type 3 SMA, SUNFISH part 2 is a proper randomised placebo-controlled trial (n=180, ages 2–25): motor function improved by 1.55 points more on risdiplam than placebo at 12 months (95% CI 0.30 to 2.81) — real, but modest. In type 1 infants, FIREFISH was single-arm and open-label by design (the design is labelled on the face): 29% of 41 infants sat without support at 12 months and 85% survived without permanent ventilation, against natural-history boundaries in which sitting does not occur. RAINBOWFISH extends the single-arm picture to presymptomatic infants (81% sitting at 12 months). Because the infant evidence has no concurrent control, the programme as a whole is capped at POSSIBLE (benefit), with the randomised SUNFISH result the firmest part.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one randomised trial (SUNFISH, n=180) plus single-arm infant studies judged against natural history (FIREFISH, RAINBOWFISH); the single-arm design is printed on the face

title: Onasemnogene abeparvovec in SMA type 1 (single-arm evidence only; START n=15 + STR1VE n=22, total N=37): survival and sitting far beyond natural history, with hepatotoxicity on the harm side
question: In infants with SMA type 1, does a single intravenous dose of onasemnogene abeparvovec (AAV9 gene therapy) improve survival without permanent ventilation and motor milestones versus natural history?
balance: There is no randomised trial of onasemnogene abeparvovec in SMA type 1 — every efficacy claim rests on single-arm studies compared with natural history, and this shelf says so on its face. In START (n=15) all infants were alive and event-free at 20 months against 8% historical survival; in STR1VE (n=22) 59% sat independently versus 0 of 23 untreated infants; STR1VE-EU (n=32) found 44% sitting. The two trials named in the question total N = 37 treated infants, printed here and in the stamp line as the small-N rule requires. The harm side is dominated by hepatotoxicity — liver-enzyme elevations in most patients in a 325-patient pooled analysis, two cases of serious acute liver injury (both resolved), and prednisolone courses often lasting 2–4 months — plus a post-marketing warning for thrombotic microangiopathy. Dramatic single-arm effects in a disease whose natural history is uniform and lethal support POSSIBLE (benefit), and no higher stamp, on this evidence.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — based on a small N = 37 in the two named trials (START n=15 + STR1VE n=22), single-arm evidence only, compared with natural history; never randomised

title: Antisense therapy for transthyretin amyloid polyneuropathy: inotersen slowed neuropathy in a randomised trial (with glomerulonephritis and thrombocytopenia signals); eplontersen matched the effect only against an external, borrowed placebo
question: In adults with hereditary transthyretin amyloidosis with polyneuropathy, do the antisense oligonucleotides inotersen (weekly) or eplontersen (monthly) slow neuropathy progression versus placebo (inotersen) or an external placebo group (eplontersen)?
balance: The two antisense drugs on this shelf carry different strengths of evidence, and the shelf keeps them distinct. Inotersen was tested in a randomised, placebo-controlled trial (NEURO-TTR, n=172): neuropathy progression was 19.7 points less and quality of life 11.7 points better than placebo over 15 months — but glomerulonephritis and thrombocytopenia each occurred in about 3%, one thrombocytopenia death occurred, and five deaths versus none were recorded on inotersen. Eplontersen (NEURO-TTRansform) was never randomised against a concurrent placebo: its comparator is an external placebo group borrowed from NEURO-TTR, against which neuropathy was essentially halted (+0.3 vs +25.1 points). That design is stated honestly on the face: the effect size looks the same as inotersen’s, but a borrowed comparator cannot carry the same certainty, so the class shelf is POSSIBLE (benefit).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — inotersen: one positive randomised trial (n=172) with renal and platelet harms; eplontersen: open-label trial against an external/borrowed placebo only

title: Tominersen in Huntington’s disease: mutant huntingtin lowered by up to 42% in phase 1/2, but the phase 3 trial (GENERATION HD1) was halted early and has no full journal report — no clinical benefit demonstrated
question: In adults with early manifest Huntington’s disease, does intrathecal tominersen lower mutant huntingtin and slow clinical progression versus placebo?
balance: This shelf rests on a thin published base and says so plainly. The only full journal report of a tominersen trial is the phase 1/2 study (Tabrizi 2019, n=46): intrathecal tominersen lowered CSF mutant huntingtin dose-dependently, by up to 42%, with only grade 1–2 adverse events — but the trial made no efficacy claim, and a secondary EEG analysis of the same 46 patients adds a biomarker signal, not independent evidence. The phase 3 trial, GENERATION HD1, was halted early in 2021 on an unfavourable benefit–risk balance at higher exposure and has NO full journal report as of this build; its record here is labelled by source type (registry/sponsor record and journal correspondence). A lower-dose successor, GENERATION HD2, was checked at build and has no publication yet. Target engagement without demonstrated clinical benefit, plus a halted phase 3, supports UNLIKELY (benefit) for slowing progression.
stamp: UNLIKELY (benefit) — the phase 3 trial was halted early on an unfavourable benefit–risk balance and no clinical benefit has been demonstrated (the treatment made no difference on any clinical outcome reported to date); phase 1/2 showed biomarker lowering only

title: Exenatide for idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH:Pressure, phase 2, N=15): intracranial pressure fell about 6 cmCSF within hours and at 12 weeks in one very small randomised trial
question: In women with active idiopathic intracranial hypertension, does subcutaneous exenatide lower telemetrically measured intracranial pressure versus placebo, acutely and at 12 weeks?
balance: PARTIAL shelf — the GLP-1 slice only. The IIH family already homes acetazolamide at pack #2383 and bariatric surgery at pack #2384; both were read before building, neither cards a GLP-1 drug, and their references are not re-carded here. The randomised evidence for exenatide is a single phase 2 trial, IIH:Pressure: 15 women completed, with telemetric pressure monitors. Exenatide lowered pressure by 5.7 cmCSF at 2.5 hours, 6.4 at 24 hours and 5.6 at 12 weeks versus placebo — the 2.5-hour effect, long before weight change, is the mechanistically interesting result. A cognition substudy in the same 15 women found no cognitive harm. A large propensity-matched record cohort associates the GLP-1 class (not exenatide specifically) with fewer headaches and less medication use, but it is observational. With a randomised N of 15, the N is printed on the face and in the stamp line and the verdict is capped at POSSIBLE (benefit).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — based on a very small N = 15 (single phase 2 randomised trial, IIH:Pressure); larger observational class data are supportive only

title: Ulotaront in acute schizophrenia: a positive 4-week phase 2 trial (−7.5 PANSS points) followed by two phase 3 trials (DIAMOND 1 & 2) that missed their primary endpoints — announced only, with no journal report
question: In adults with an acute exacerbation of schizophrenia, does ulotaront (SEP-363856), a TAAR1/5-HT1A agonist with no D2 blockade, reduce PANSS total score versus placebo?
balance: HONESTY FLAG, carried on the face: ulotaront’s published record and its phase 3 record are different kinds of evidence. The published phase 2 trial (Koblan 2020, n=245) was positive — PANSS fell 7.5 points more than placebo at 4 weeks, without the extrapyramidal or metabolic signature of D2 blockade — and a 26-week open-label extension (n=157) found no extrapyramidal signal and minimal weight change, though it had no control group. But the two phase 3 trials, DIAMOND 1 and DIAMOND 2, both missed their primary endpoints, and at a publication-status re-check during this build they exist only as a July 2023 sponsor topline announcement and registry records — no full journal report was found. They are carded here labelled by source type, never as a journal report. One positive small trial followed by two larger announced failures is MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit).
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — one positive 4-week phase 2 trial (n=245); both phase 3 trials announced as missing their primary endpoints, with no journal report published

title: Pramipexole augmentation in treatment-resistant unipolar depression (PAX-D, n=151): symptoms fell 3.91 points more than placebo at 12 weeks — with discontinuation for adverse events in 20% vs 5%
question: In adults with treatment-resistant unipolar major depression, does pramipexole titrated to 2.5 mg/day added to ongoing antidepressant treatment reduce depressive symptoms versus placebo at 12 weeks?
balance: PAX-D is a clean, positive trial in exactly the population this shelf asks about: 151 adults with treatment-resistant unipolar depression, pramipexole titrated toward 2.5 mg/day added to their antidepressant, with QIDS-SR16 scores falling 3.91 points more than placebo at 12 weeks (P<0.0001). The price is printed on the face beside the benefit: 20% stopped pramipexole for adverse events versus 5% on placebo — nausea, headache and sleep disturbance or somnolence. The supporting record is thinner: a 2019 meta-analysis of small mixed unipolar and bipolar studies (response relative risk 1.77, a relative measure) and an 85-patient trial in anhedonia-selected mood disorders. Note the boundary: the bipolar sibling trial PAX-BD is homed at pack #3658 — a different population with a missed primary — and is not the home of this question. One positive trial caps the stamp at POSSIBLE (benefit).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one positive randomised trial (PAX-D, n=151) in treatment-resistant unipolar depression; discontinuation for adverse events 20% vs 5%

title: Viloxazine extended-release in adult ADHD (adult slice only): AISRS fell 3.8 points more than placebo at 6 weeks in the single adult phase 3 trial (n=374)

balance: PARTIAL shelf — the adult slice only. title: MM120 (lysergide) for generalised anxiety disorder — PHASE 2 ONLY: a single phase 2b trial (n=198) found 100 µg and 200 µg beat placebo by 5–6 HAM-A points at 4 weeks, while lower doses did not separate
question: In adults with moderate-to-severe generalised anxiety disorder, does a single supervised dose of MM120 (lysergide D-tartrate; name the tested product — MindMed MM120) reduce HAM-A score at 4 weeks versus placebo, and is there a dose–response?
balance: PHASE 2 ONLY — the flag is carried here, in the title and in the stamp, as this row required. The entire MM120 evidence base is one phase 2b dose-ranging trial (Robison 2025, n=198): a single supervised dose reduced HAM-A scores at 4 weeks by 5.0 points more than placebo at 100 µg and 6.0 points at 200 µg, while the 25 µg (−1.2) and 50 µg (−1.8) doses did not separate — the dose–response is on the face. The tested product is named under the clarification exception: MindMed MM120 (lysergide D-tartrate). Two small older trials of LSD-assisted therapy in anxiety associated with life-threatening illness (n=42; n=12) point the same way for the molecule but are different populations with psychotherapy, and are labelled as such. Near-universal visual perceptual changes at the effective doses (92.5–100% vs 10.3% on placebo) make functional unblinding the key caveat. A single phase 2 trial caps the verdict at POSSIBLE (benefit).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — PHASE 2 ONLY: a single phase 2b trial (n=198); no phase 3 evidence; lower doses (25–50 µg) did not separate from placebo

title: Ketamine-assisted therapy for alcohol use disorder (KARE, 2×2 factorial, n=96): days abstinent rose 10.1 points versus saline at 6 months, but relapse did not differ significantly
question: In adults with moderate-to-severe alcohol use disorder, do three weekly ketamine infusions with psychological therapy increase percentage of days abstinent over 6 months versus saline with therapy (or ketamine/therapy alone)?
balance: KARE is a 2×2 factorial trial and this shelf presents its cells honestly: 96 patients with severe alcohol use disorder received ketamine or saline infusions, crossed with relapse-prevention therapy or alcohol education. Pooling the drug contrast, ketamine groups had 10.1 percentage points more days abstinent than saline groups at 6 months (95% CI 1.1 to 19.0); the largest contrast, ketamine-plus-therapy versus saline-plus-education (15.9 points), is a diagonal comparison that mixes the drug and therapy effects and is labelled as such. Just as important, relapse did not differ significantly between ketamine and saline — the relapse outcome is less clear than the abstinence percentage. A 40-patient midazolam-controlled pilot (single infusion) supports the abstinence signal over 21 days; a 44-patient open-label inpatient pilot found no significant readmission benefit. Small phase 2 evidence with a split outcome pattern: POSSIBLE (benefit).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — small phase 2 evidence (KARE n=96 factorial plus two pilots): abstinence days improved, relapse did not differ significantly

title: SAINT accelerated iTBS for treatment-resistant depression (PARTIAL — the accelerated slice live #574 does not cover): remission 19 of 21 open-label; sham-controlled remission 50.0% vs 20.8% in the 2026 replication (randomised N=48); first RCT randomised N=29
question: In adults with treatment-resistant depression, does SAINT (accelerated, high-dose, fMRI-targeted intermittent theta-burst stimulation over 5 days) produce remission versus sham stimulation?
balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #574, which cards conventional once-daily rTMS versus sham only; sibling pack #5946 asks rTMS versus ECT. This shelf cards only the accelerated, fMRI-targeted SAINT/SNT slice, and no PMID homed on #574 or #5946 is re-carded. The record is promising but small: an open-label report (Cole 2020; 21 completers) with 90.5% remission; a first double-blind sham-controlled trial stopped at a planned interim analysis with only 29 randomised participants (Cole 2022), in which mean MADRS scores fell 52.5% on active treatment versus 11.1% on sham at 4 weeks; and a 2026 sham-controlled replication (Kratter 2026; 48 randomised) with remission 50.0% versus 20.8% and response 54.2% versus 25.0% at 1 month. A 2026 dose-response meta-analysis of accelerated iTBS generally (15 trials, 704 patients) also favours active treatment (response relative risk 1.99, remission relative risk 1.77 — relative measures). Two small concordant sham-controlled trials from one programme, with wide uncertainty around the true remission gain, cap the stamp at POSSIBLE; the randomised Ns (29 and 48) are printed on the face and in the stamp line, and the open-label report is labelled open-label wherever it appears.

title: Centanafadine for ADHD (tested product: Otsuka centanafadine SR/ER): two positive adult phase 3 trials (AISRS −2.7 to −4.5 points vs placebo); adolescent high dose positive, low dose missed; children rest on a pooled secondary analysis
question: In people aged 6 years and over with ADHD, does centanafadine (a norepinephrine–dopamine–serotonin reuptake inhibitor; tested product — Otsuka centanafadine SR/ER) reduce ADHD rating-scale scores versus placebo?
balance: The tested product throughout is Otsuka centanafadine SR/ER (sustained-/extended-release), named here under the tested-product clarification exception. In adults, two phase 3 trials (886 randomised across both) agree: both the 200 mg/day and 400 mg/day doses beat placebo on the Adult ADHD Investigator Symptom Rating Scale at day 42, by least-squares mean differences of −2.74 to −4.47 points, with small effect sizes (−0.24 to −0.40). In adolescents (459 randomised), the higher dose (328.8 mg) met its primary endpoint (ADHD-RS-5 −18.50 vs −14.15; p=0.0006) and the lower dose (164.4 mg) did not (the treatment made no difference at that dose on the prespecified primary analysis). For children aged 6–12, the carded record in this session is a pooled secondary analysis of the children and adolescent phase 3 trials (Conners 3 scales and clinically-meaningful-change), which favours the high dose; the children's primary report was not retrievable from PubMed in this session and is flagged in the build summary. Treatment-emergent events rose with dose (adolescents: 31.4% low dose, 50.3% high dose, 23.8% placebo), most commonly decreased appetite, nausea, headache and rash. Concordant randomised evidence with modest effect sizes and a failed low dose caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two adult phase 3 trials positive at 200 and 400 mg/day (AISRS differences −2.7 to −4.5 points, small effect sizes); adolescent high dose positive and low dose missed its primary; children's evidence carded here is a pooled secondary analysis

title: Oliceridine for acute postoperative pain (APOLLO-1/2): responders 50–76% vs 15–46% on placebo and equi-analgesic to morphine at mid/high doses — but respiratory safety burden was NOT significantly lower than morphine's
question: In adults with moderate-to-severe acute postoperative pain (bunionectomy, abdominoplasty), does intravenous oliceridine, a G-protein-biased μ-opioid agonist, provide analgesia versus placebo and versus morphine, with fewer respiratory and gastrointestinal adverse events?
balance: Two phase 3 trials agree that intravenous oliceridine works as an analgesic: responder rates were 50–66% across demand-dose regimens versus 15.2% on placebo after bunionectomy (APOLLO-1) and 61–76% versus 45.7% after abdominoplasty (APOLLO-2), and the 0.35 mg and 0.5 mg regimens were non-inferior/equi-analgesic to morphine in both. The safety claims need grading against what the trials actually showed: the composite respiratory safety burden rose dose-dependently on oliceridine and was NOT statistically different from morphine in APOLLO-1 (morphine 1.1 hours) nor significantly different from placebo in APOLLO-2, where morphine's burden (1.72 hours) did differ from placebo — so a respiratory advantage over morphine is suggested by point estimates, not demonstrated. Gastrointestinal events were frankly dose-dependent on oliceridine (up to 70.9% and 78.8% at the 0.5 mg regimen, close to morphine's 72.4% and 79.3%), though nausea/vomiting rates and rescue-antiemetic use favoured the equi-analgesic oliceridine regimens over morphine. The open-label ATHENA study (768 patients) found nausea 31%, constipation 11% and vomiting 10%, with no deaths or significant cardiorespiratory events reported. Analgesia: established. A proven respiratory-sparing advantage: not established. POSSIBLE (benefit).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two phase 3 trials: analgesia vs placebo established and equi-analgesic to morphine at 0.35/0.5 mg demand doses; respiratory safety burden not significantly different from morphine, and GI events dose-dependent up to morphine-like rates

title: Sublingual cyclobenzaprine TNX-102 SL for fibromyalgia (PARTIAL — the modern sublingual programme pack #2698 does not cover): pain −1.9 vs −1.5 in RELIEF (n=503) and −1.8 vs −1.2 in RESILIENT, with oral numbness in 17–23%
question: In adults with fibromyalgia, does bedtime sublingual cyclobenzaprine (tested product — Tonix TNX-102 SL) reduce daily pain versus placebo over 14 weeks?
balance: PARTIAL completion of pack #2698, which cards the older ORAL cyclobenzaprine literature in fibromyalgia (a meta-analysis of oral trials and a very-low-dose bedtime study); no PMID homed there is re-carded here. The tested product is Tonix TNX-102 SL, a bedtime sublingual formulation, named under the tested-product clarification exception. Two phase 3 trials of the same regimen (2.8 mg for 2 weeks, then 5.6 mg nightly for 12 weeks) agree on the primary endpoint: RELIEF (503 patients) found a week-14 pain reduction of −1.9 versus −1.5 on placebo (p=0.01), and RESILIENT (456 randomised; journal home verified at build as Pain Medicine, NCT05273749) found −1.8 versus −1.2 (p<0.001) with all six secondary endpoints also significant (p≤0.001) — sleep, fatigue, global impression and function. The honest margins are modest (0.4–0.6 points on a 0–10 pain scale beyond placebo), Patient Global Impression of Change was not significant in RELIEF, and the signature harms are local: oral hypoesthesia in 17.3% (RELIEF) and 23.4% (RESILIENT), with abnormal taste and oral paraesthesia, transient and self-limited; systemic events were close to placebo. Two concordant phase 3 trials carry LIKELY (benefit) for a modest pain effect.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — two phase 3 trials concordant on the primary pain endpoint (RELIEF n=503: −1.9 vs −1.5, p=0.01; RESILIENT: −1.8 vs −1.2, p<0.001, all six secondaries significant); margins modest (0.4–0.6 points) and oral hypoesthesia in 17–23%

question: In adults with knee or hip osteoarthritis pain inadequately controlled by standard analgesics, does fasinumab reduce pain and improve function versus placebo — and what is the rate of rapidly progressive osteoarthritis and joint replacement?
balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #1483, which cards tanezumab only; this shelf builds only the fasinumab slice, cross-points to #1483 for the class sibling, and re-cards no PMID homed there. Fasinumab, the second anti-NGF antibody programme, shows the class pattern in sharper relief: consistent, statistically robust but small analgesia — WOMAC pain least-squares differences versus placebo of −0.78 to −1.40 across doses in the phase IIb/III dose-ranging trial (421 randomised), −0.58 for pain at the licensed-candidate 1 mg every-4-weeks dose in the large naproxen-controlled phase III (3,307 randomised; −2.90 vs −2.32 raw changes), and −0.63 in the NSAID-controlled phase III (1,650 randomised) — against a dose-dependent joint-safety problem: arthropathies in 7% of fasinumab-treated patients versus 1% on placebo in the dose-ranging trial (dose-dependent, mostly found on scheduled imaging), adjudicated arthropathies in 7.2–9.7% on 1 mg regimens versus 1.1% on placebo and 2.6% on naproxen in the large phase III, of which 75.5–95.0% were rapid-progressive osteoarthritis type 1, and joint replacements in 5.6–6.4% versus 3.4% on placebo in that trial (3.4% vs 3.6% in the NSAID-controlled trial — no difference there). A 52-week safety study (5,331 randomised) confirms the dose relationship and that higher doses were discontinued for safety. Real analgesia, small margins, and a joint harm that ended the class's regulatory path: POSSIBLE (benefit), with the harm on the face.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — three phase 3 trials: WOMAC pain advantages ~0.6–1.4 points vs placebo, against adjudicated arthropathies 5.6–9.7% (mostly rapid-progressive OA) and joint replacements up to 6.4%; see tanezumab shelf #1483 for the class sibling

title: Vixotrigine for trigeminal neuralgia (PARTIAL — pack #5940 covers standard drugs; PHASE 2a ONLY): the prespecified primary endpoint was NOT met — treatment failure 33% vs 64%, p=0.097, in 29 randomised responders
question: In adults with trigeminal neuralgia, does vixotrigine (a state-dependent sodium-channel blocker, formerly raxatrigine) reduce paroxysmal pain versus placebo?
balance: PARTIAL completion of pack #5940, which asks the standard-drug guideline question (carbamazepine first, on the AAN–EFNS parameter); no PMID homed there is re-carded here — vixotrigine appears on #5940 only as a passing 'under development' mention inside a review card. PHASE-2-ONLY FLAG: the entire randomised efficacy record for vixotrigine (BIIB074) in trigeminal neuralgia is one phase 2a randomised-withdrawal trial (Zakrzewska 2017). Of 67 patients entering open-label treatment, 29 responders were randomised; the prespecified primary endpoint — treatment failure in the double-blind phase — occurred in 5 of 15 (33%) on vixotrigine versus 9 of 14 (64%) on placebo, p=0.0974: NOT met on the prespecified analysis (the difference was not statistically significant). Pain signals in secondary measures are reported in the trial's full text and are labelled secondary wherever this shelf refers to them; the abstract record carded here prints no secondary pain numbers, so none are quoted. Tolerability was good (headache 19% in the open-label phase; double-blind adverse events similar to placebo; no severe or serious events on drug in the double-blind phase). Two phase 3 enriched-withdrawal trials were designed (Kotecha 2020) but no phase 3 results report was found in this session's PubMed search. A missed primary in 29 randomised patients cannot carry a benefit stamp: UNLIKELY (benefit) on current evidence, with the favourable point estimate printed in full so the reader can judge the near-miss for themselves.
stamp: UNLIKELY (benefit) on current evidence — PHASE 2a ONLY: the single randomised-withdrawal trial (29 randomised of 67 enrolled) missed its prespecified primary endpoint (treatment failure 33% vs 64%, p=0.097 — not significant); no phase 3 results published

title: Prolonged-release oxycodone–naloxone for severe refractory restless legs syndrome: IRLS severity fell 8.15 points more than placebo over 12 weeks (n=306) — with treatment-related adverse events in 73% and constipation among the serious harms
question: In adults with severe restless legs syndrome refractory to first-line (dopaminergic/gabapentinoid) therapy, does prolonged-release oxycodone–naloxone improve IRLS severity versus placebo over 12 weeks?
balance: One large, well-conducted trial answers this question, supported by its own secondary-endpoint analysis and by current guideline positioning. In Trenkwalder 2013 (306 randomised; severe restless legs syndrome, mean IRLS score 31.6, inadequately controlled on mainly dopaminergic therapy), prolonged-release oxycodone–naloxone titrated from 5/2.5 mg twice daily to a maximum of 40/20 mg twice daily reduced IRLS severity by −16.5 points versus −9.4 on placebo at 12 weeks (between-group difference 8.15 points, 95% CI 5.46–10.85; p<0.0001), and the benefit persisted through a 40-week open-label extension (mean score 9.7). The secondary analysis (Oertel 2016) found sleep disturbance, sleep adequacy, sleep quantity (+0.77 hours) and quality of life all significantly better on drug. The harm side is substantial and belongs on the face: treatment-related adverse events in 73% on drug versus 43% on placebo during the blinded phase, and five serious treatment-related events on drug, including constipation, subileus and ileus — constipation is this combination's dominant clinical problem despite the naloxone component. The 2025 American Academy of Sleep Medicine guideline suggests extended-release oxycodone and other opioids over no opioids in adults with RLS (conditional recommendation, moderate certainty) — a second-line, refractory-disease position, not a first-line one. A single randomised programme caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single randomised programme (n=306): IRLS difference 8.15 points vs placebo at 12 weeks with sleep and quality-of-life gains, against treatment-related adverse events in 73% vs 43% and constipation/subileus/ileus among the serious harms; AASM 2025 conditional support for refractory disease

title: Oveporexton (tested product: Takeda TAK-861) for narcolepsy type 1: wakefulness latency up 14.3–19.8 minutes vs ~0 on placebo across two phase 3 trials (n=273), cataplexy down 79–89% median — with urinary frequency and insomnia in a majority
question: In adolescents and adults with narcolepsy type 1, does twice-daily oveporexton (tested product — Takeda TAK-861) improve wakefulness (MWT), daytime sleepiness (ESS) and weekly cataplexy rate versus placebo over 12 weeks?
balance: The tested product is Takeda's oveporexton (TAK-861), an oral orexin receptor 2-selective agonist, named under the tested-product clarification exception. The evidence is unusually concordant: a phase 2 trial (112 randomised) and two phase 3 trials (FirstLight, 168 enrolled; RadiantLight, 105 enrolled — 273 in total) all show large, dose-related gains on every core measure. In the phase 3 pair, Maintenance of Wakefulness Test latency rose by 14.3–19.8 minutes on oveporexton versus −0.4 to −0.8 minutes on placebo (all adjusted p<0.001), Epworth scores fell by 9.7–11.8 points versus 1.5–1.7, and median weekly cataplexy reductions were 79.0–88.8% versus 27.7–39.1%. A secondary analysis found attention, memory and executive-function measures also improved. The harms are frequent and belong on the face: adverse events in 86–89% on drug versus 43–54% on placebo, with increased urinary frequency and transient insomnia each occurring in a majority of oveporexton participants in the phase 3 trials (phase 2: insomnia 48%, urinary urgency 33%, urinary frequency 32%, with no hepatotoxicity — the class's earlier compound, TAK-994, was stopped for liver injury, and a 2026 class meta-analysis keeps that history visible). Twelve weeks is the longest blinded frame; durability and long-term safety are unproven. Two concordant phase 3 trials on top of a concordant phase 2 carry LIKELY (benefit) for the 12-week outcomes. The mechanism this drug replaces — cerebrospinal-fluid hypocretin-1 deficiency — is shelved as the hypocretin physiology pack #6599, built in this same wave.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — two phase 3 trials (n=273) plus a concordant phase 2: MWT latency +14.3 to +19.8 min vs ~0 on placebo, ESS −9.7 to −11.8 vs −1.5 to −1.7, median cataplexy reductions 79–89% vs 28–39% at 12 weeks; urinary frequency and transient insomnia each in a majority on drug

title: Lower-sodium (mixed-salt) oxybate in narcolepsy (PARTIAL — the slice live #921 sodium oxybate and live #922 idiopathic hypersomnia do not cover): under randomised withdrawal, placebo patients' cataplexy rose (median +2.35 attacks/week) while continuers held at 0.00; 92% less sodium than sodium oxybate
question: In people with narcolepsy, does lower-sodium oxybate (calcium/magnesium/potassium/sodium oxybates; tested product — Jazz lower-sodium oxybate, LXB/JZP-258) maintain control of cataplexy and daytime sleepiness under randomised withdrawal, and how does its sodium load compare with sodium oxybate?
balance: PARTIAL completion of two verified homes: live #921 cards the twice-nightly SODIUM oxybate programme in narcolepsy, and live #922 cards lower-sodium oxybate only in IDIOPATHIC HYPERSOMNIA. This shelf builds only the mixed-salt formulation IN NARCOLEPSY, and re-cards no PMID homed on either. The tested product is Jazz's lower-sodium oxybate (LXB; JZP-258) — a calcium/magnesium/potassium/sodium oxybate mixture with the same active moiety as sodium oxybate and, per the trial record's pharmacology reporting, 92% less sodium (labelled here as a formulation/pharmacology fact, not a clinical-outcome finding: no trial shows the sodium reduction itself improves cardiovascular outcomes). The single phase 3 trial (Bogan 2021) used randomised withdrawal: 201 adults with narcolepsy with cataplexy enrolled and entered open-label titration/transition; 134 were randomised to continue LXB or switch to placebo for 2 weeks — the denominator for every efficacy number is those 134 withdrawal-randomised patients, not all-comers with narcolepsy. Placebo patients worsened significantly (median weekly cataplexy change +2.35 attacks versus 0.00 on continued LXB, p<0.0001; Epworth median change +2.0 versus 0.0, p<0.0001), and a companion analysis (Dauvilliers 2022) documents the transition course, including a transient cataplexy rise while other anticataplectics were tapered. Commonest events on LXB were headache (20.4%), nausea (12.9%) and dizziness (10.4%). A withdrawal design in stabilised patients caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single randomised-withdrawal trial (201 enrolled, 134 randomised): switching to placebo worsened cataplexy (median +2.35 attacks/week vs 0.00) and Epworth (+2.0 vs 0.0) within 2 weeks; the 92%-less-sodium figure is a formulation fact, not an outcomes result

title: Ibutamoren (MK-677) in healthy older adults: fat-free mass +1.1 kg vs −0.5 kg on placebo over a year — with NO improvement in strength or function, and a glucose cost (fasting glucose +0.3 mmol/L [+5 mg/dL], insulin sensitivity down)
question: In healthy older adults, does two years of daily ibutamoren, an oral growth-hormone secretagogue, increase fat-free mass and strength and improve function versus placebo — and what does it cost in glucose tolerance and other adverse effects?
balance: SPLIT answer, and the split is the point of this shelf. On body composition, ibutamoren (MK-677) does what its mechanism promises: in Nass 2008 (65 healthy adults aged 60–81, 2-year double-blind trial with the primary endpoints at 1 year), growth hormone and IGF-I rose to young-adult levels and fat-free mass increased by +1.1 kg on drug while falling −0.5 kg on placebo (p<0.001) — a 1.6 kg between-group difference — with body weight up 2.7 kg versus 0.8 kg. On the outcomes that matter, it did not deliver: increased fat-free mass did not result in changes in strength or function, in Nass or in the second randomised trial (Bach 2004; 161 older hip-fracture patients, 6 months of MK-0677), where IGF-I rose 84% versus 17% on placebo yet functional performance measures and overall Sickness Impact Profile scores showed no significant differences (the treatment made no difference to function in either trial). The metabolic price is on the face: fasting blood glucose rose by an average of 0.3 mmol/L (5 mg/dL) on MK-677 in Nass (p=0.015) and insulin sensitivity decreased; cortisol rose by 47 nmol/L (1.7 µg/dL). (The fetched abstract record does not print an HbA1c figure, so none is quoted; the glucose and insulin-sensitivity findings are the record's own.) Other frequent effects were increased appetite (subsiding over months) and transient mild lower-extremity oedema and muscle pain; LDL cholesterol fell slightly (−0.14 mmol/L [−5.4 mg/dL]). Mass without function, with a metabolic price.
stamp: SPLIT — POSSIBLE (benefit) for fat-free mass (+1.1 kg vs −0.5 kg at 1 year, Nass 2008, n=65); LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for strength and function — null in both Nass 2008 and the 161-patient hip-fracture trial; fasting glucose +0.3 mmol/L (+5 mg/dL) and reduced insulin sensitivity on drug

title: Urolithin A in older adults (tested product: Mitopure in the randomised trials): leg and hand muscle endurance improved in a 66-person trial, but the 6-minute walk and maximal ATP production did not significantly separate from placebo
question: In older adults, does urolithin A (a mitophagy-activating metabolite; name the tested product in each trial) improve muscle endurance/strength and walk distance versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — small, short, industry-linked trials with mixed functional outcomes. The first-in-human study (Andreux 2019; n=60 sedentary elderly people) showed safety and a muscle mitochondrial gene-expression signature over 4 weeks, with no functional endpoint. In the older-adult randomised trial (Liu 2022; n=66, ages 65–90, tested product Mitopure 1000 mg/day for 4 months), muscle endurance in hand and leg muscles improved versus placebo at 2 months, but the two primary endpoints did not significantly separate: 6-minute walk distance rose 60.8 m on urolithin A versus 42.5 m on placebo (a non-significant difference), and maximal ATP production was essentially unchanged. In middle-aged adults (Singh 2022; n=88, Mitopure), muscle strength rose about 12% in relative terms and aerobic endurance measures improved, but the primary endpoint — peak power output — did not significantly improve. Plasma acylcarnitines and C-reactive protein fell in both randomised trials. No trial is large or long enough to answer falls, disability or independence, so the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE and the Ns are printed: 60, 66 and 88.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — small trials only (n=60 first-in-human with no functional endpoint; n=66 older adults: endurance improved, walk distance and ATP production not significant; n=88 middle-aged: strength up, primary peak-power endpoint missed); industry sponsorship; no long-term functional outcomes

title: Nicotinamide riboside in older adults (total N=182 across three trials; the two older-adult trials are n=30 and n=12): NAD+ rises reliably, but blood pressure, arterial stiffness and physical function are unproven — the only blood-pressure signal is a post-hoc subgroup
question: In healthy middle-aged and older adults, does nicotinamide riboside raise NAD+ and improve systolic blood pressure, aortic stiffness or physical performance versus placebo?
balance: MAYBE (benefit) — a biomarker answer, not a treatment answer, from very small trials: N=30, N=12 and N=140 (total 182). Nicotinamide riboside (tested product NIAGEN, nicotinamide riboside chloride, in the largest trial) reliably raises NAD+: by about 60% in blood cells over 6 weeks (Martens 2018; n=30 crossover, 24 completers in the blood-pressure analyses) and dose-dependently by 22%, 51% and 142% at 100, 300 and 1000 mg/day over 8 weeks (Conze 2019; n=140 overweight adults). It also raised the muscle NAD+ metabolome in 12 older men over 21 days (Elhassan 2019), without changing muscle mitochondrial bioenergetics. The clinical claims do not hold up at this size: overall systolic blood pressure and aortic pulse-wave velocity changes in Martens 2018 were not statistically significant after correction for multiple comparisons; the often-quoted 9 mmHg lower systolic pressure appeared only in a post-hoc subgroup of 13 participants whose baseline pressure was already elevated (subgroup-only signal, labelled as such), with no change in the normal-pressure subgroup. This shelf answers an evidence question about a heavily marketed supplement; it is not a treatment recommendation.
stamp: MAYBE (benefit) — based on a very small total N in older adults (n=30 crossover and n=12; plus n=140 overweight adults for NAD+/safety): NAD+ rises, but blood-pressure and stiffness effects are non-significant overall and the 9 mmHg figure is a post-hoc subgroup of 13 people

title: Senolytics (dasatinib + quercetin) — first human pilots only, total N=23 in the two single-arm reports (IPF n=14; diabetic kidney disease n=9), plus a 12-person randomised pilot in which function did not differ meaningfully: no efficacy claim beyond pilot size is supportable
question: In older adults with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis or diabetic kidney disease, does intermittent dasatinib + quercetin reduce senescent-cell burden markers and improve physical function versus baseline/controls?
balance: MAYBE (benefit) at most — and only as a statement about pilot feasibility and biology, with the small N printed: the two first-in-human reports total N=23, both single-arm and open-label. In idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (Justice 2019; n=14), three weeks of intermittent dasatinib + quercetin was feasible, retention was 100%, and 6-minute walk distance, gait speed and chair-stand time improved versus baseline — with no control group, so placebo, learning and regression effects cannot be separated from drug effect; pulmonary function and frailty measures did not change. In diabetic kidney disease (Hickson 2019; n=9), three days of dosing reduced senescent-cell burden in fat and skin biopsies and lowered circulating SASP factors within 11 days — a biological proof of mechanism in 9 people, with no clinical outcome. The one randomised pilot (Nambiar 2023; n=12, placebo-controlled) found more non-serious adverse events on dasatinib + quercetin and stated that frailty, pulmonary and physical-function measures did not appear to differ meaningfully between groups. No efficacy claim beyond these pilots is supportable.
stamp: MAYBE (benefit) — pilot evidence only, based on a very small total N=23 in the two single-arm first-in-human reports (n=14 and n=9, N printed), plus a randomised pilot of n=12 with no meaningful functional difference; efficacy is unproven

title: Spermidine (tested product: spermidine-rich wheat-germ extract) and memory: a 30-person pilot suggested benefit, but the larger 12-month phase 2b smartAGE trial (n=100) was NEGATIVE on its primary memory endpoint — the pair is the complete answer
question: In older adults with subjective cognitive decline, does daily spermidine supplementation (name the tested product — wheat-germ extract in the trials) improve memory performance versus placebo?
balance: UNLIKELY (benefit) at the tested dose — the complete record is a small positive pilot followed by a larger negative trial, and the larger trial governs. In the phase 2a pilot (Wirth 2018; n=30, 3 months), the tested product — a spermidine-rich wheat-germ plant extract — was associated with moderately better memory performance than placebo, reported as effect sizes (Cohen's d about 0.77) with confidence intervals that reached zero on the main contrast. In the 12-month phase 2b smartAGE trial (Schwarz 2022; n=100 randomised, 89 completers, 0.9 mg spermidine/day from wheat-germ extract), the primary endpoint — change in mnemonic discrimination performance — did not differ between groups (between-group difference -0.03, 95% CI -0.11 to 0.05; p=0.47; the treatment made no difference), and secondary outcomes were likewise unchanged; exploratory signals on verbal memory and inflammation were hypothesis-generating only. Adverse events were balanced. A benefit at higher doses remains untested, not established.
stamp: UNLIKELY (benefit) — pilot n=30 positive on effect sizes, but the larger phase 2b trial (n=100, 12 months, 0.9 mg/day wheat-germ extract) was negative on its primary memory endpoint (difference -0.03, p=0.47; the treatment made no difference)

title: mTOR inhibition and immune ageing: phase 2 trials improved influenza-vaccine responses by about 20% in relative terms and cut reported infections, but the phase 3 RTB101 trial (n=1,024) FAILED — symptomatic respiratory illness 26% versus 25% on placebo (the treatment made no difference)
question: In older adults, does low-dose mTOR inhibition (everolimus, or the TORC1-selective RTB101, alone or combined) improve vaccine response and reduce reported respiratory infections versus placebo?
balance: UNLIKELY (benefit) for preventing respiratory illness — the phase 2 positives and the phase 3 failure must be read together. Phase 2a (Mannick 2014; n=218 elderly volunteers): the mTOR inhibitor everolimus (RAD001) enhanced the antibody response to influenza vaccination by about 20% — a relative measure — at relatively well-tolerated doses, and reduced PD-1 expression on T cells. Phase 2a (Mannick 2018; n=264): six weeks of a low-dose TORC1-inhibitor combination (the catalytic inhibitor RTB101, then called BEZ235, plus everolimus) was associated with a significant decrease in infections reported over the following year (p=0.001) and better vaccine responses. But when RTB101 alone was tested at phase 3 scale (Mannick 2021; phase 3 n=1,024), it did not reduce clinically symptomatic respiratory illness: 26% on RTB101 versus 25% on placebo (odds ratio 1.07, 90% CI 0.80–1.42; p=0.65; the treatment made no difference), even though interferon-induced antiviral genes were upregulated. The phase 2b part of the same report was itself split: the prespecified part-2 primary analysis missed significance, and a pooled analysis found fewer laboratory-confirmed infections on RTB101 10 mg once daily (19% versus 28%). Vaccine-response gains remain a phase 2 biomarker finding; infection prevention failed its definitive test.
stamp: UNLIKELY (benefit) — phase 2 vaccine-response gains (about 20% relative) and an infection signal did not survive phase 3: RTB101 respiratory illness 26% vs 25% on placebo (p=0.65; the treatment made no difference)

title: Segesterone acetate/ethinyl estradiol one-year vaginal ring (tested product: the Population Council/TherapeuticsMD segesterone ring, Annovera) — SINGLE-ARM phase 3 programme in 2,265 women: Pearl Index 2.98 per 100 woman-years in women aged 35 and under; venous thromboembolism in 4 of 2,308 users of the final ring (0.2%)
question: In women seeking contraception, does the segesterone acetate + ethinyl estradiol vaginal ring used in 21/7 cycles for up to 13 cycles (name the tested product — Population Council/TherapeuticsMD segesterone ring) prevent pregnancy as effectively as benchmark combined hormonal contraception, and what are its discontinuation and VTE profiles?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — effective contraception on a single-arm programme, with the design printed: both phase 3 trials of the tested product (the Population Council/TherapeuticsMD segesterone acetate/ethinyl estradiol vaginal system, Annovera, releasing an average of 0.15 mg segesterone acetate and 0.013 mg ethinyl estradiol daily, used 21 days in / 7 days out for up to 13 cycles with the same ring) were open-label and single-arm, so efficacy is judged against regulatory benchmarks, not against a concurrent comparator. In 2,265 women in the efficacy analysis, the Pearl Index in the primary group (women aged 35 years and younger) was 2.98 per 100 woman-years (95% CI 2.13–4.06), and Kaplan–Meier analysis estimated the ring 97.5% effective over 13 cycles; 57.5% of participants completed 13 cycles. In the integrated safety analysis (2,308 women using the final manufactured ring), headache (26%), nausea (18%) and vaginal discharge/mycotic infection (10%) were most common, few women (under 1.5%) discontinued for these, and four women (0.2%) had venous thromboembolism — three of whom had risk factors (a Factor V Leiden mutation, or body mass index above 29 kg/m2). Satisfaction among prior pill/ring users was high (at least 90%). A single programme with no randomised comparator caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single-arm phase 3 programme only (design printed): Pearl Index 2.98 per 100 woman-years (age ≤35 subgroup), 97.5% Kaplan–Meier effectiveness; VTE 0.2% in the safety population; no randomised comparison

title: Phexxi vaginal gel for on-demand contraception (tested product: Evofem Phexxi) — SINGLE-ARM phase 3 with no concurrent control (design printed): typical-use pregnancy 13.7% over 7 cycles, so efficacy rests on comparison with the expected pregnancy rate without contraception
question: In women seeking hormone-free, on-demand contraception, does lactic acid/citric acid/potassium bitartrate vaginal gel (name the tested product — Evofem Phexxi) used before intercourse prevent pregnancy versus no contraception (historical/expected pregnancy rate), and what local adverse effects does it cause?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — with the design printed on the face: AMPOWER, the phase 3 trial of the tested product (Evofem Phexxi, a lactic acid/citric acid/potassium bitartrate vaginal pH modulator gel used within an hour before each act of intercourse), was SINGLE-ARM and open-label in 1,384 women, with no concurrent control group. Its efficacy estimate therefore rests on comparison with the pregnancy rate expected without contraception, judged against a prespecified regulatory bound — not on a randomised difference. The 7-cycle cumulative pregnancy percentage with typical use was 13.7% (95% CI 10.0%–17.5%), meeting the prespecified endpoint that the upper confidence bound be no more than 21%; expressed the other way, the gel was 86.3% effective over 7 cycles in this population — well below long-acting and hormonal methods, in the range of other user-dependent, coital methods. A review of the programme reports a Pearl Index of 27.5 and cumulative 6–7-cycle pregnancy rates of 4.1%–13.65% across the two phase 3 trials (the lower figure reflecting more perfect use). Local effects dominate the harm side: vulvovaginal burning and itching were the most common adverse events, fewer than 2% of users discontinued for any adverse event and fewer than 1% for genitourinary symptoms, and over 80% of women were satisfied. A single-arm programme caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — SINGLE-ARM phase 3, no concurrent control (design printed): typical-use pregnancy 13.7% over 7 cycles versus an expected-rate benchmark; efficacy is a benchmark judgement, not a randomised effect

title: PlGF-based testing for suspected preterm pre-eclampsia: an sFlt-1/PlGF ratio of 38 or lower rules out pre-eclampsia within a week with 99.3% negative predictive value; revealing the result halved time to diagnosis (1.9 vs 4.1 days), but REPEAT testing (PARROT-2) made no difference to perinatal outcomes
question: In women presenting with suspected preterm pre-eclampsia, does revealing a PlGF-based test result (PlGF alone or sFlt-1/PlGF ratio) to clinicians shorten time to diagnosis and improve maternal/perinatal outcomes versus concealed testing/usual care — and how accurately does the test rule out pre-eclampsia within 1–2 weeks?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) for a single revealed test as a diagnostic strategy; repeat testing is a null. Accuracy first (accuracy figures stated as accuracy): in PROGNOSIS (Zeisler 2016; 500-woman development cohort plus 550-woman validation cohort), an sFlt-1/PlGF ratio of 38 or lower had a negative predictive value of 99.3% (95% CI 97.9–99.9) for absence of pre-eclampsia within 1 week, with 80.0% sensitivity and 78.3% specificity; a ratio above 38 had a positive predictive value of only 36.7% for pre-eclampsia within 4 weeks — the test rules out far better than it rules in. Strategy next (strategy outcomes stated as outcomes): in PARROT (Duhig 2019; stepped-wedge cluster trial, 1,023 women), revealing the PlGF result with a management algorithm cut median time to diagnosis from 4.1 to 1.9 days (time ratio 0.36, 95% CI 0.15–0.87) and severe maternal adverse outcomes were less frequent (4% versus 5%; adjusted odds ratio 0.32, 95% CI 0.11–0.96), with no difference in perinatal adverse outcomes (15% versus 14%) or gestation at delivery. In PARROT-2 (Duhig/Hurrell 2024; 1,252 women), REVEALED REPEAT testing made no difference: the perinatal composite (stillbirth, early neonatal death or neonatal-unit admission) occurred in 31.2% versus 27.8% (p=0.18; the treatment made no difference), and routine repeat testing was not recommended. One positive strategy trial plus one null repeat-testing trial caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single revealed PlGF test: NPV 99.3% at ratio ≤38 (accuracy) and faster diagnosis with fewer severe maternal outcomes in one cluster trial (outcomes); repeat testing NULL in PARROT-2 (31.2% vs 27.8%, p=0.18; the treatment made no difference)

title: Drospirenone-only pill 4 mg 24/4 (tested product: Exeltis drospirenone-only pill, Slynd) — SINGLE-ARM phase 3 trials: Pearl Index 0.51 in Europe (n=713) and 4.0 in the US trial (n=953 in the primary analysis; 2.9 for confirmed pregnancies at clean sites); no venous thromboembolism in either trial
question: In women seeking progestin-only contraception, does drospirenone 4 mg in a 24/4 regimen (name the tested product — Exeltis drospirenone-only pill) prevent pregnancy versus benchmark progestin-only pills, with what bleeding pattern and VTE signal?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a distinct product from the combined drospirenone pills carded elsewhere in the library: this is the oestrogen-free drospirenone 4 mg pill taken 24 days on and 4 days off (tested product: the Exeltis drospirenone-only pill, marketed as Slynd). Both phase 3 trials were single-arm and non-comparative, so efficacy is benchmark-judged. In Europe (Archer 2015; 713 women, 7,638 cycles), the overall Pearl Index was 0.51 (95% CI 0.11–1.49); pooled with its sister European study (Palacios 2019; 1,571 women, 14,329 cycles), the overall Pearl Index was 0.73 (95% CI 0.31–1.43). In the US trial (Kimble 2020; 1,006 women dosed, only 35.0% completing), the Pearl Index in non-breastfeeding women aged 35 and under was 4.0 (95% CI 2.3–6.4) counting all 17 pregnancies, and 2.9 (95% CI 1.5–5.1) for confirmed pregnancies at sites without protocol violations — a reminder that the US figure was dragged by unconfirmed pregnancies and two excluded sites. Bleeding improved over time: in Europe, any bleeding fell from 72.7% of women in cycle 1 to 32.1% by cycle 13, and unscheduled bleeding from 49.1% to 22.8%. No venous thromboembolism was reported in either programme and hyperkalemia was rare (0.5% in the US trial; one case in the pooled European studies). Single-arm evidence caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single-arm phase 3 programme only: Pearl Index 0.51 (Europe) and 4.0 (US; 2.9 confirmed/clean-site); no VTE observed; bleeding settles over cycles; no randomised comparison with other progestin-only pills

title: Estetrol/drospirenone combined pill (tested product: Mithra/Gedeon Richter estetrol pill, Nextstellis) — SINGLE-ARM phase 3 programme: Pearl Index 0.47 in Europe/Russia and 2.65 in North America (pooled 1.52); one treatment-related venous thromboembolism in the European trial, none in North America
question: In women seeking combined oral contraception, does estetrol 15 mg + drospirenone 3 mg (name the tested product — Mithra/Gedeon Richter estetrol pill) prevent pregnancy versus benchmark combined pills, and what are its bleeding, metabolic and VTE profiles?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the first combined pill built on estetrol (E4), a native oestrogen, paired with drospirenone 3 mg in a 24/4 regimen (tested product: the Mithra/Gedeon Richter estetrol pill, marketed as Nextstellis). Both E4 FREEDOM phase 3 trials were open-label and single-arm, so Pearl Indices are benchmark judgements, printed per trial as reported: 0.47 per 100 woman-years (95% CI 0.15–1.11) in Europe/Russia (Gemzell-Danielsson 2022; 1,553 women treated, primary group aged 18–35) and 2.65 (95% CI 1.73–3.88) in North America (Creinin 2021; 1,864 enrolled, 1,674 aged 16–35), with a pooled Pearl Index of 1.52 (95% CI 1.04–2.16) and a 13-cycle life-table pregnancy rate of 1.28% across 3,027 participants (Jensen 2022). Bleeding was predictable: scheduled bleeding in about 83–94% of cycles depending on trial and cycle, with unscheduled bleeding/spotting falling over time. In the pooled safety analysis (Chen 2022; 3,417 users), 28.7% had a treatment-related adverse event — bleeding complaints (9.5%), breast pain (4.0%), acne (3.3%) and mood disturbance (3.2%) the most frequent — 8.0% discontinued for treatment-related events, and three treatment-related serious events included one venous thromboembolism; the European trial reported one treatment-related lower-extremity venous thromboembolism and the North American trial none. No clinically relevant changes in weight, blood pressure or laboratory parameters (including lipids, glucose and potassium) were found. Whether E4's hoped-for lower thrombosis risk is real is unproven — the trials were not powered for it and the authors call for large phase 4 studies — so a single single-arm programme caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single-arm phase 3 programme only: Pearl Indices 0.47 (Europe/Russia) and 2.65 (North America) as reported per trial, pooled 1.52; one treatment-related VTE in 3,417 pooled users; any lower-thrombosis advantage over ethinylestradiol pills is unproven
