title: Duloxetine 40 mg twice daily for stress urinary incontinence in women: median episode frequency fell ~50–54% in relative terms versus 29–41% on placebo across three trials — but 17–22% stopped for adverse events, mostly nausea; licensed for this indication in Europe, not the US
question: In women with stress urinary incontinence, does duloxetine 40 mg twice daily reduce incontinence-episode frequency versus placebo, and at what nausea/discontinuation cost?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — three concordant double-blind placebo-controlled trials (1,505 women carded) agree. Duloxetine 40 mg twice daily reduced incontinence-episode frequency by a median of 50% (van Kerrebroeck 2004, Europe/Canada, n=494) and 54% (Millard 2004, four continents, n=458) in relative terms, versus 29% and 40% respectively on placebo; the earlier dose-ranging trial (Norton 2002, n=553) showed a dose-dependent relative decrease of 54–64% across 20–80 mg/day versus 41% on placebo. These are relative (percentage) reductions in diary episode counts — entry frequencies were ≥7 episodes/week and mean baseline was 18.4/week in Millard — not absolute episode counts or dryness rates. The cost sits beside the benefit: discontinuation for adverse events was 22% versus 5% (van Kerrebroeck) and 17.2% versus 1.7% (Millard), with nausea the commonest reason; in Norton it rose dose-dependently to 15% at 80 mg/day versus 5%. Quality of life improved in parallel in most analyses, though van Kerrebroeck's prespecified I-QOL co-primary analysis was formally negative because of early discontinuers' carried-forward scores. Duloxetine is licensed for this indication in Europe, not in the US — say so plainly, because a US reader cannot be prescribed it for incontinence.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — three concordant RCTs (n=1,505 carded): median episode frequency fell ~50–54% relative on duloxetine 40 mg twice daily vs 29–41% on placebo; discontinuation for adverse events 17–22% vs 2–5%, mostly nausea; licensed for stress incontinence in Europe, not the US

title: Lasofoxifene 0.5 mg/day for postmenopausal osteoporosis (PEARL, n=8,556): vertebral fractures down 42% relative (13.1 vs 22.4 per 1,000 person-years) and non-vertebral down 24% relative — venous thromboembolism roughly doubled in relative terms (2.9 vs 1.4 per 1,000 person-years)
question: In postmenopausal women with osteoporosis, does lasofoxifene 0.5 mg/day reduce vertebral and non-vertebral fractures versus placebo over 5 years, and what are its VTE and endometrial profiles?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one large trial programme (PEARL, 8,556 women, 5 years) is the entire evidence base, which caps the stamp at POSSIBLE. Lasofoxifene 0.5 mg/day reduced vertebral fractures by 42% in relative terms (hazard ratio 0.58; absolute rates 13.1 versus 22.4 per 1,000 person-years) and non-vertebral fractures by 24% in relative terms (HR 0.76; 18.7 versus 24.5 per 1,000 person-years) — it is the one SERM whose pivotal trial showed a non-vertebral fracture reduction. The VTE cost must be read both ways: roughly doubled in relative terms (HR 2.06 at 0.5 mg; HR 2.67 at 0.25 mg), which in absolute terms is 2.9 versus 1.4 events per 1,000 person-years. Breast cancer fell in relative terms in a 49-event analysis (total breast cancer HR 0.21), and 5-year gynaecological follow-up found endometrial cancer in 2 women on 0.5 mg versus 3 on placebo, with more polyps, bleeding and endometrial thickening on the drug. Premise note: the slate attributed PEARL's fracture report to a 2009 Gennari paper; no such primary record was found on PubMed this session — the definitive fracture report is Cummings et al., N Engl J Med 2010, and that is what is carded.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single trial programme (PEARL, n=8,556): vertebral fractures −42% relative (13.1 vs 22.4 per 1,000 person-years), non-vertebral −24% relative (18.7 vs 24.5); VTE roughly doubled relative (HR 2.06; 2.9 vs 1.4 per 1,000 person-years)

title: Fitusiran prophylaxis in haemophilia A or B: annualised bleeding rates cut from 18.1 to 1.7 (with inhibitors) and 31.0 to 3.1 (without) versus on-demand therapy — with thromboembolic events in 3–5% and a 2020 voluntary dosing pause that replaced fixed dosing with an antithrombin-target (15–35%) regimen
question: In people aged 12+ with haemophilia A or B, does monthly subcutaneous fitusiran (an antithrombin-lowering siRNA) prophylaxis reduce treated bleeding episodes versus on-demand treatment or prior factor prophylaxis?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — two concordant open-label randomised phase 3 trials show large bleeding reductions, and the thrombotic safety history is stated here on the face, not in fine print. In ATLAS-INH (n=57, with inhibitors) mean annualised bleeding rate was 1.7 on monthly fitusiran versus 18.1 on on-demand bypassing agents (a 90.8% relative reduction); in ATLAS-A/B (n=120, without inhibitors) it was 3.1 versus 31.0 on on-demand factor concentrates (rate ratio 0.101). ATLAS-PPX showed further reductions after switching from prior prophylaxis. THE SAFETY HISTORY: suspected or confirmed thromboembolic events occurred in 2 participants (5%) in ATLAS-INH and 2 (3.0%) in ATLAS-PPX; alanine aminotransferase rose in 23–32% on fitusiran; the programme's original fixed-dose regimen was placed on a voluntary dosing pause in 2020 and replaced by an antithrombin-based regimen targeting antithrombin activity of 15–35%, after which the phase 2 extension (n=34, median 4.1 years) reported no thrombotic events and fewer transaminase and biliary events, with bleeding control maintained (median ABR 0.87). The carded trials used the superseded fixed 80 mg regimen — that caveat travels with every number above.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — two randomised phase 3 trials: mean annualised bleeding rate 1.7 vs 18.1 (with inhibitors) and 3.1 vs 31.0 (without) vs on-demand therapy; thromboembolic events 3–5%, ALT rise 23–32%, and a 2020 voluntary dosing pause that replaced fixed dosing with antithrombin-targeted (15–35%) dosing

title: Osocimab for VTE prevention after knee arthroplasty (FOXTROT, phase 2): venographic VTE 15.7–17.9% on postoperative osocimab versus 26.3% on enoxaparin (non-inferior) — PHASE 2 trial with a venographic surrogate endpoint
question: In adults undergoing total knee arthroplasty, does a single pre- or post-operative dose of osocimab prevent venous thromboembolism versus enoxaparin, and versus apixaban, with what bleeding cost?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — PHASE 2, VENOGRAPHIC SURROGATE: both labels belong on the face. FOXTROT (813 randomised; 600 in the primary per-protocol analysis) is the only efficacy trial: a single postoperative intravenous osocimab dose of 0.6, 1.2 or 1.8 mg/kg met non-inferiority versus enoxaparin for venous thromboembolism at days 10–13 (15.7–17.9% versus 26.3%), and a preoperative 1.8 mg/kg dose (11.3%) met superiority criteria versus enoxaparin — but the endpoint was assessed by mandatory bilateral venography, so most events were asymptomatic clots found by screening, not symptomatic VTE. Apixaban's rate was 14.5% with no formal comparison. Major or clinically relevant non-major bleeding was up to 4.7% on osocimab versus 5.9% on enoxaparin and 2% on apixaban. Phase 1 studies confirm long dose-dependent aPTT prolongation from a single dose, and a 4-trial class meta-analysis favours factor XI inhibitors over low-molecular-weight heparin on the same surrogate (VTE odds ratio 0.50, a relative measure). Class pair: pack #6596 (milvexian) asks the same arthroplasty question for an oral factor XIa inhibitor.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — PHASE 2, venographic surrogate endpoint: single postoperative osocimab 0.6–1.8 mg/kg non-inferior to enoxaparin (VTE 15.7–17.9% vs 26.3%); preoperative 1.8 mg/kg superior on the surrogate; bleeding up to 4.7% vs 5.9% on enoxaparin

title: Milvexian for VTE prevention after knee arthroplasty (AXIOMATIC-TKR, phase 2, n=1,242): VTE fell dose-dependently on twice-daily dosing — 21% at 25 mg to 8% at 200 mg — versus 21% on enoxaparin; major/clinically relevant non-major bleeding 1% versus 2%
question: In adults undergoing total knee arthroplasty, does twice-daily oral milvexian prevent venous thromboembolism versus enoxaparin, dose-dependently and with what bleeding cost?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single phase 2 trial (AXIOMATIC-TKR, n=1,242) with a venographic-predominant endpoint, labelled as such. Twice-daily milvexian showed a significant dose–response as reported: VTE in 21% at 25 mg, 11% at 50 mg, 9% at 100 mg and 8% at 200 mg twice daily, versus 21% on enoxaparin; once-daily dosing was mostly no better than enoxaparin (24–25% at 25–50 mg; 7% at 200 mg). The trial's formal comparison was against a prespecified 30% benchmark (pooled twice-daily incidence 12%, P<0.001), not a powered head-to-head. Bleeding of any severity was 4% in both groups; major or clinically relevant non-major bleeding was 1% on milvexian versus 2% on enoxaparin. First-in-human and Japanese multiple-dose studies (n=104 and n=32) confirm the pharmacology behind twice-daily dosing — half-life ~8–14 hours and exposure-related aPTT prolongation — with no clinically significant bleeding in healthy volunteers. Class pair: pack #6595 (osocimab, FOXTROT); the orthopaedic factor XI class meta-analysis is carded there and cross-pointed from here.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single phase 2 trial (AXIOMATIC-TKR, n=1,242), venographic endpoint: VTE 21%→8% across twice-daily milvexian doses vs 21% on enoxaparin (significant dose–response); major/clinically relevant non-major bleeding 1% vs 2%

title: Mitapivat in sickle cell disease (RISE UP, n=207): haemoglobin response 41% versus 3% (co-primary met) but annualised pain crises 2.6 versus 3.1, p=0.12 (co-primary NOT met) — a split result
question: In people aged 16+ with sickle cell disease and recurrent pain crises, does mitapivat 100 mg twice daily raise haemoglobin and reduce annualised pain crises versus placebo over 52 weeks?
balance: SPLIT — the co-primary result is split, and this shelf presents it as a split. In RISE UP phase 3 (n=207, 52 weeks), mitapivat 100 mg twice daily produced a haemoglobin response in 41% versus 3% on placebo (adjusted difference 38 percentage points; p<0.0001) — that co-primary was met — but the annualised rate of sickle cell pain crises was 2.6 versus 3.1 (p=0.12), so the pain-crisis co-primary was NOT met: on that outcome the treatment made no significant difference. The phase 2 portion (n=79) showed the same haemoglobin effect (46–50% versus 4%), and a 10-patient open-label study (9 at 1 year) reported haemoglobin and crisis signals against historic baseline that randomised testing did not confirm. Serious adverse events were 20% on mitapivat versus 29% on placebo in phase 3. PARTIAL build: mitapivat's verified homes are live shelf #1803 (pyruvate kinase deficiency) and pack #4882 (thalassaemia) — their records are homed there, are not carded here, and are cross-pointed in the synthesis prose only; this pack builds only the sickle cell slice. The fetched RISE UP record reports no transfusion-burden result, so none is claimed.
stamp: SPLIT — RISE UP phase 3 (n=207): haemoglobin response 41% vs 3% (co-primary met, p<0.0001); annualised pain crises 2.6 vs 3.1 (co-primary NOT met, p=0.12)

title: PHYSIOLOGY — CSF hypocretin-1 deficiency as the mechanism of narcolepsy type 1: undetectable in 7 of 9 patients in the founding report, <100 pg/mL in 32 of 38 cases versus all controls measurable, hypocretin neurons reduced 85–95% at autopsy, and ≤110 pg/mL validated as diagnostic in 570 subjects
question: In human narcolepsy type 1, is cerebrospinal-fluid hypocretin-1 absent or very low, are hypocretin-producing neurons lost at autopsy, and how specific is the deficiency for the cataplexy phenotype?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing (Kryger's Principles and Practice of Sleep Medicine): narcolepsy type 1 is the human hypocretin (orexin) deficiency syndrome — loss of the hypothalamic hypocretin neurons that stabilise wakefulness. The carded primary human data are concordant across three methods. Cerebrospinal fluid: hypocretin was undetectable in 7 of 9 narcolepsy patients in the founding report (Nishino 2000; N=9 printed plainly); in the larger series, hypocretin-1 was <100 pg/mL in 32 of 38 narcolepsy–cataplexy cases while all 34 controls were measurable at 169–376 pg/mL (Nishino 2001). Anatomy: post-mortem hypocretin neuron numbers were reduced by 85–95%, with intermixed melanin-concentrating hormone neurons preserved and gliosis in the region (Thannickal 2000; N not documented in the record). Accuracy: in 274 patients and 296 controls, cerebrospinal fluid hypocretin-1 below 110 pg/mL was diagnostic for narcolepsy, values above 200 pg/mL were normal, and low levels clustered in HLA-DQB1*0602-positive cataplexy (Mignot 2002). No animal studies are carded. This is the mechanism shelf for the orexin-agonist treatment shelf, pack #6579 (oveporexton), built this wave.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED

title: PHYSIOLOGY — KNDy neurons and neurokinin B in the menopausal hot flush: post-mortem NKB neurons hypertrophied (194% of premenopausal size, 15-fold more numerous), neurokinin B infusion provoked flushes in 8 of 10 women versus 0 on vehicle, and the thermoneutral zone was ~0.0 °C in symptomatic women versus 0.4 °C in symptom-free women
question: In postmenopausal women, does hypertrophy of hypothalamic KNDy (kisspeptin/neurokinin B/dynorphin) neurons and increased neurokinin B signalling narrow the thermoneutral zone so that small core-temperature rises trigger hot flushes — and does neurokinin B infusion provoke flush-like episodes in young women?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing (Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology; Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology): hypothalamic KNDy neurons — co-expressing kisspeptin, neurokinin B (NKB) and dynorphin — link estrogen feedback to thermoregulatory circuitry, and NKB signalling is the pathway blocked by the NK3-antagonist treatment shelves this pack partners. The carded primary human data form a complete chain. Post-mortem: infundibular neurons containing NKB mRNA hypertrophied after menopause (cross-sectional area 194% of premenopausal values; NKB-labelled neurons 15-fold more numerous; increased gene expression — Rance & Young 1991, n=3 versus n=3, printed plainly), and stereology shows the nucleus loses no neurons with age while soma volume rises 40% (Abel & Rance 2000) — hypertrophy, not degeneration. Provocation: intravenous NKB induced flushes in 8 of 10 healthy women versus 0 of 10 on vehicle, with flush-typical heart-rate and skin-temperature rises (Jayasena 2015). Downstream: symptomatic postmenopausal women had a thermoneutral zone of ~0.0 °C versus 0.4 °C in symptom-free women, so small core-temperature rises trigger a flush (Freedman & Krell 1999, n=20). No animal studies are carded; animal mechanism appears only as textbook framing.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED

title: PHYSIOLOGY — Offset analgesia in humans: a 1–3 °C decrease from tonic noxious heat produced pain relief as large as a 15 °C drop to innocuous levels, mediated by periaqueductal-grey/rostral-ventromedial-medulla activation — and attenuated in chronic-pain patients
question: In healthy humans, does a small decrease in a tonic noxious heat stimulus produce a disproportionately large drop in perceived pain (offset analgesia), how large is the effect, and is it attenuated in chronic-pain patients?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing (Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology; Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology): descending pathways from the periaqueductal grey (PAG) and rostral ventromedial medulla continuously modulate pain transmission, and offset analgesia is that system engaging at stimulus offset. The defining human psychophysics (Grill & Coghill 2002) show small 1–3 °C decreases from tonic noxious heat (47–50 °C) evoking pain reductions up to 271% greater than equal-magnitude increases — as large as those from a 15 °C drop to innocuous levels, and greater than adaptation to constant stimuli (N not documented in the record). fMRI in 12 healthy controls shows PAG/RVM activation during offset with pain-neuromatrix inhibition (Derbyshire & Osborn 2009). The response is attenuated in chronic pain in two independent cohorts: significantly smaller ΔOA in 12 patients versus 12 controls with an offset-analgesia index AUC of 0.897 (Kobinata 2017), and smaller OA magnitude in 23 patients versus 17 controls (P=0.047; Li 2022). No animal studies are carded. Distinct from pack #6203 (central sensitisation / conditioned pain modulation — facilitation and inhibition by a second distant stimulus), which was read and does not home this question.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED

title: PHYSIOLOGY — Closed-loop acoustic stimulation, slow-wave sleep and memory: in-phase stimulation enhances slow oscillations in anchor studies of N=11–13 and improved word retention in both, but a double-blind replication enhanced oscillations with no memory benefit, and the pooled memory effect is small and non-significant (g=0.25, p=0.07)
question: In humans, does phase-locked acoustic stimulation delivered during slow-wave sleep enhance slow-wave activity and improve overnight declarative-memory retention versus sham stimulation?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING. Textbook framing (Kryger's Principles and Practice of Sleep Medicine): the <1 Hz slow oscillation of non-REM sleep and its coupled spindles are the textbook substrate of declarative-memory consolidation, so entraining them is physiologically plausible. The human record splits by outcome type. Oscillations: in-phase closed-loop acoustic stimulation enhanced slow oscillations and spindle coupling in young adults (Ngo 2013; N=11, printed plainly) and increased slow-wave activity during stimulation intervals in older adults (Papalambros 2017; N=13), though whole-night slow-wave activity was unchanged in the latter. Memory: retention improved in both founding studies, but a double-blind replication that enhanced the same oscillations found no memory benefit in either of two experiments (Henin 2019; n=12 and n=19 — the treatment made no difference to behaviour), and the meta-analysis of 10 studies / 177 participants pools a small, non-significant effect (Hedges g=0.25, p=0.07), significant only in the phase-locked subgroup (g=0.36, p=0.047). No animal studies are carded. EMERGING, not ESTABLISHED, because the behavioural half of the claim remains unreplicated at anchor samples of n=11–13.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING

title: Delayed sodium thiosulfate to prevent cisplatin hearing loss in children and adolescents
question: In children and adolescents receiving cisplatin for solid tumours, does delayed intravenous sodium thiosulfate (given 6 hours after each cisplatin dose) reduce cisplatin-induced hearing loss versus cisplatin alone, without compromising tumour control?
balance: LIKELY — for hearing protection; the tumour-control caveat is on the face of this shelf, not buried. Two independent randomised phase 3 trials point the same way on hearing: in SIOPEL 6 (standard-risk hepatoblastoma, n=109), grade 1 or worse hearing loss occurred in 33% with delayed sodium thiosulfate versus 63% with cisplatin alone (relative risk 0.52, 95% CI 0.33 to 0.81 — a 48% relative reduction, 30 percentage points absolute); in ACCL0431 (mixed solid tumours, n=125 randomised, 104 assessable), hearing loss occurred in 28.6% versus 56.4% (adjusted odds ratio 0.31, 95% CI 0.13 to 0.73 — 27.8 percentage points absolute). On tumour control the trials differ in what they can say: SIOPEL 6, in localised hepatoblastoma only, showed no survival detriment (3-year overall survival 98% versus 92%; event-free survival 82% versus 79%). ACCL0431 was not powered for survival, and a post-hoc analysis reported in the Freyer 2019 review found significantly worse overall survival with sodium thiosulfate among patients with disseminated disease, but not among those with localised disease. The hearing benefit is LIKELY; use in disseminated disease carries an unresolved tumour-protection concern that families and oncologists must weigh explicitly. Product naming: both trials published the intervention simply as sodium thiosulfate and named no brand or manufacturer; the paediatric formulation later approved for this use is marketed as Pedmark (Fennec Pharmaceuticals) — that brand name does not appear in the trial records carded here, and current marketed product may differ from the trial material.
stamp: LIKELY

title: PICC versus implantable port for chemotherapy access
question: In adults with cancer needing long-term central venous access for chemotherapy, does a peripherally inserted central catheter (PICC) cause more catheter-related complications (thrombosis, infection, occlusion, unplanned removal) than a totally implantable port, and at what cost and quality-of-life difference?
balance: LIKELY — an implantable port causes fewer complications than a PICC for chemotherapy access. The PICCPORT randomised trial (399 patients with mainly breast and colorectal cancer) found catheter-related deep venous thrombosis in 8% with a PICC versus 1% with a port (hazard ratio 10.2, 95% CI 2.3 to 44.6) and more composite adverse events overall (hazard ratio 2.7, 95% CI 1.6 to 4.6). The RCT-based meta-analysis (6 reports, 1,127 patients) and the network meta-analysis of 11 randomised trials (2,585 patients) point the same way: ports had lower odds of overall complications (odds ratio 0.54, 95% CI 0.43 to 0.69), thrombotic and mechanical complications, and removal for complications. Ports cost more per device inserted but less per catheter day in the PICCPORT health-economic analysis (3.01 versus 6.58 EUR/day), driven by the cost of managing PICC adverse events; quality of life was similar, with a smaller post-implantation decline in global health status in the port group of the RCT meta-analysis. A PICC remains quicker to place and avoids a surgical pocket — the stamp is about complications, cost per day and durability, not about which device fits an individual patient's veins, treatment length or preference.
stamp: LIKELY

title: Pre-emptive versus reactive skin-toxicity management for EGFR inhibitors
question: In adults receiving an EGFR inhibitor (panitumumab or cetuximab), does a pre-emptive skin-toxicity regimen (moisturiser, sunscreen, topical steroid and oral tetracycline-class antibiotic started with treatment) reduce grade 2 or worse skin toxicity versus reactive treatment started after the rash appears?
balance: POSSIBLE — one randomised trial supports the full pre-emptive bundle; a second randomised trial of its antibiotic component alone was null on its primary endpoint. In STEPP (95 patients on panitumumab), protocol-specified grade 2 or worse skin toxicities during the 6-week treatment period occurred in 29% with pre-emptive treatment (moisturisers, sunscreen, topical steroid and doxycycline started with therapy) versus 62% with reactive treatment — an absolute reduction of 33 percentage points — and quality-of-life impairment was smaller (mean Dermatology Life Quality Index change 1.3 versus 4.2 points at week 3). But the only other randomised card, the placebo-controlled N03CB trial of prophylactic tetracycline alone (61 patients on various EGFR inhibitors), found rash incidence did not differ (the treatment made no difference: 70% versus 76%, P=.61), with only a severity signal at week 4 (grade 2 rash 17% versus 55%, P=.04) amid high dropout. A systematic review of anti-EGFR dermatologic toxicity likewise reports several studies finding pre-emptive treatment more effective than reactive treatment, without a pooled randomised estimate. A single positive phase 2 trial of the bundle caps this shelf at POSSIBLE.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Dexamethasone sparing after day 1 in moderately emetogenic chemotherapy
question: In adults receiving moderately emetogenic chemotherapy on a palonosetron- or NK1-antagonist-based antiemetic backbone, can dexamethasone be safely spared after day 1 (single-day versus multi-day dexamethasone) without losing complete-response rates — and does the answer differ by regimen?
balance: LIKELY — for the palonosetron doublet regimens actually tested; the NK1-triplet carboplatin regimen is carded separately and is less settled, so this shelf does not pool them into one claim. Regimen 1 — palonosetron plus dexamethasone with anthracycline/cyclophosphamide or other moderately emetogenic chemotherapy: an individual-patient meta-analysis of two phase 3 trials (405 women) found overall complete response of about 55% on the 1-day regimen versus about 51–59% on the 3-day regimen with no significant loss, and the five-trial individual-patient meta-analysis (1,194 patients) found the 1-day regimen non-inferior (pooled risk difference in complete response −1.5%, 95% CI −7.1 to 4.0, against a −8% margin). Regimen 2 — palonosetron plus dexamethasone with carboplatin/paclitaxel in gynaecological cancer: two small phase 2 trials were less reassuring (delayed complete response 69.8% versus 76.9% in one; overall complete response 60.7% versus 67.9% in the other, neither significant, one warning that reduced efficacy in women could not be refuted). Regimen 3 — NK1-antagonist triplet with carboplatin: a network meta-analysis estimated delayed complete response of 73.5% with 1-day versus 82.5% with 3-day dexamethasone (absolute difference 9.0%, 95% CI −2.3 to 21.1, not significant) and advised care with sparing in carboplatin triplet prophylaxis. Sparing after day 1 is LIKELY safe on a palonosetron doublet; on a carboplatin NK1 triplet the honest position is POSSIBLE, pending a direct trial.
stamp: LIKELY

title: Prophylactic swallowing exercises in head-and-neck chemoradiotherapy
question: In adults receiving chemoradiotherapy for head and neck cancer, do prophylactic swallowing exercises (started before or during treatment) preserve swallowing function and reduce long-term feeding-tube dependence versus usual care with exercises only after dysfunction appears?
balance: POSSIBLE — the randomised trials are small, use different exercise programmes and comparators, and show preserved muscle structure and some functional measures rather than a proven reduction in feeding-tube dependence. In Pharyngocise (58 patients), the swallowing musculature deteriorated less and functional swallowing, mouth opening, chemosensory acuity and salivation deteriorated less with active exercises than with usual care or sham. In the Dutch Preventief trial (49 patients), both preventive programmes (standard exercises and a TheraBite device programme) were feasible with satisfactory compliance, and fewer patients remained tube-dependent than in the institute's historical comparisons — but the trial's own randomised contrast was between two active programmes, not against no exercises, and at 2 years (29 patients) the programmes did not differ except for weight gain. The PRESTO adherence trial (148 patients) shows the binding constraint: adherence falls during radiotherapy in every delivery mode and is highest with therapist support. No carded trial demonstrates a statistically significant reduction in long-term feeding-tube dependence against a no-exercise control — POSSIBLE, with benefit most plausible for muscle preservation and function when patients actually do the exercises.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Tunnelled indwelling peritoneal catheter versus repeated paracentesis in recurrent malignant ascites
question: In adults with recurrent malignant ascites needing repeated drainage, does a tunnelled indwelling peritoneal catheter improve symptom control, days out of hospital and quality of life versus repeated large-volume paracentesis? (Observational evidence only.)
balance: POSSIBLE — observational evidence only, labelled as such. Comparative floor, verified before building: exactly one genuine head-to-head comparative report in malignant ascites was found — a retrospective single-institution cohort with cost-effectiveness modelling in gynaecological malignancy (Wu 2022), which found no significant difference in ascites-related hospital days (P=0.21) or emergency department visits (P=0.69) between tunnelled catheter and repeated paracentesis, with the catheter the more cost-effective strategy on lower cost and essentially equal modelled quality-adjusted survival. The rest of the base is single-arm: a systematic overview of 221 published patients plus a 19-patient chart review (Fleming 2009) found peritonitis in a median 5.9% of published cases and judged indwelling catheters a safe, effective palliative strategy without overwhelming infection rates; a small prospective observational study (Riedel 2018) included 14 patients with malignant ascites treated with a PleurX catheter alongside paracentesis-treated controls and found no significant differences in adverse events or mortality comparisons it was far too small to settle. No randomised trial in malignant ascites was found. Premise correction: the two Macken reports a title search suggests (a feasibility-trial protocol and a systematic review) concern refractory ascites in end-stage liver disease, not malignancy, and were therefore NOT carded here. POSSIBLE, observational — symptom and hospital-use benefit is plausible and unproven.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Endovascular stenting versus radiotherapy for malignant superior vena cava obstruction
question: In adults with malignant superior vena cava obstruction, does endovascular stenting relieve symptoms faster and more durably than radiotherapy (with chemotherapy where appropriate)? (Observational evidence only; symptom-relief speed is the honest endpoint.)
balance: POSSIBLE — observational evidence only, labelled as such; there is no randomised trial of stenting versus radiotherapy for malignant superior vena cava obstruction, and the honest endpoint is speed and completeness of symptom relief, not survival. The Rowell & Gleeson systematic review (44 non-randomised studies meeting inclusion) found chemotherapy and/or radiotherapy relieved obstruction in 77% of small-cell and 60% of non-small-cell lung cancer patients, with recurrence in 17–19%, while stent insertion relieved obstruction in 95%, with further obstruction in 11% but recanalisation possible in most, giving long-term patency of 92% — and the reviewers note stenting may provide relief in a higher proportion and more rapidly. A later pooled review of retrospective stenting series found clinical effectiveness of 90.5%, primary patency 86.2% and secondary patency 94.1%, with fatal complications in 1.46%. A 54-patient retrospective stent cohort reported 94.4% procedural success and 25% overall survival at 10 months, a reminder that prognosis is set by the cancer, not the stent. POSSIBLE: stenting probably relieves symptoms in more patients and faster than radiotherapy, on non-randomised comparisons vulnerable to selection bias; it does not treat the tumour, and radiotherapy or chemotherapy remains the disease-directed treatment where appropriate.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Intrathecal drug-delivery system for refractory cancer pain (single randomised trial)
question: In adults with refractory cancer pain despite systemic opioids, does an implantable intrathecal drug-delivery system improve pain control and reduce drug toxicity versus comprehensive medical management alone? (Single-trial shelf: one randomised trial carries this question.)
balance: POSSIBLE — a single-trial shelf, labelled as such: one randomised trial (Smith 2002, 202 patients enrolled) carries this question, and a single trial caps the stamp at POSSIBLE however positive its result. In that trial, clinical success (at least 20% pain reduction, or equal pain with at least 20% less toxicity) at 4 weeks was achieved by 84.5% of intrathecal drug-delivery patients versus 70.8% on comprehensive medical management alone (P=.05); success on both pain and toxicity together was 57.7% versus 37.5% (P=.02). Toxicity scores fell 50% with the device versus 17% without (P=.004), driven by fatigue and depressed consciousness, and 6-month survival was 53.9% versus 37.2% (P=.06) — a non-significant difference in a trial not powered for survival, reported here as the authors reported it, not as a survival claim. A planned crossover analysis (30 patients whose medical management had failed) found pain down 27% and toxicity down 51% after implant, consistent with the randomised result but uncontrolled. No second randomised trial exists in this evidence base; device harms, cost and the need for surgical implantation and refills sit outside the trial's 4-week primary endpoint.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: YOCAS yoga programme for sleep in cancer survivors
question: In cancer survivors with sleep disturbance after treatment, does the structured Yoga for Cancer Survivors (YOCAS) programme improve sleep quality versus standard care? (Programme named as published, per the non-drug-programme naming rule.)
balance: POSSIBLE — one large randomised trial of one named programme carries this question, and a single programme trial caps the stamp at POSSIBLE. The tested programme is the Yoga for Cancer Survivors (YOCAS) programme, named as published: pranayama breathing exercises, 16 gentle Hatha and restorative yoga postures, and meditation, in two 75-minute sessions per week for 4 weeks. In the Mustian 2013 multicentre trial (410 survivors with moderate or greater sleep disruption, 96% female, 75% breast cancer), YOCAS produced greater improvements than standard care in global sleep quality and, secondarily, in subjective sleep quality, daytime dysfunction, wake after sleep onset, sleep efficiency and sleep-medication use (all P≤.05, Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index and actigraphy). A mediation analysis of the same trial found improvements in sleep quality and daytime dysfunction accounted for 22% and 37% respectively of the programme's fatigue benefit — supportive of a real sleep effect, but the same trial, not independent confirmation. A separate randomised trial of a different, online yoga programme in breast cancer (173 patients) also improved PSQI sleep quality, which supports yoga generally but does not replicate YOCAS itself.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Barrier film and gel for radiation dermatitis in breast radiotherapy (physical-barrier slice)
question: In women receiving breast radiotherapy, does a physical barrier — a polyurethane film dressing (Mepitel Film) or a film-forming barrier gel (StrataXRT) — prevent moderate-to-severe radiation dermatitis versus standard skin care or sorbolene? (The barrier slice only; the topical-steroid slice is homed separately — see balance.)
balance: LIKELY — for Mepitel Film in breast radiotherapy, on one large phase 3 trial supported by meta-analysis; the gel evidence is thinner and is stated separately. Scope: this shelf is only the physical-barrier slice of the radiation-dermatitis question — prophylactic mometasone cream is a different intervention with its own home at live shelf #1792, which is cross-pointed here in prose and not re-carded. Mepitel Film (named as published; a silicone polyurethane film): in the Behroozian phase 3 trial (376 patients at higher dermatitis risk), grade 2–3 dermatitis occurred in 15.5% with the film versus 45.6% with standard care (odds ratio 0.20 — an 80% relative reduction in odds, 30.1 percentage points absolute), grade 3 dermatitis in 2.8% versus 13.6% (odds ratio 0.19) and moist desquamation in 8.0% versus 19.2% (odds ratio 0.36); three patients removed the film for rash or itching. StrataXRT (named as published; a silicone-based film-forming gel): the breast evidence is a 56-patient pilot (lower erythema and melanin indices) and a meta-analysis of three small randomised trials (189 patients) with a strong grade 3 signal (odds ratio 0.05, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.22) but no significant difference for grade 2–3 combined (odds ratio 0.32, 95% CI 0.03 to 3.18 — the treatment's effect on that combined endpoint is unproven); its largest randomised trial (197 patients) is in head-and-neck radiotherapy, carded here as supportive evidence from a different site. LIKELY for the film in breast radiotherapy; POSSIBLE for the gel in breast radiotherapy.
stamp: LIKELY

title: Pentoxifylline + tocopherol (PENTO/PENTOCLO) for osteoradionecrosis of the jaw: complete healing in the Delanian phase II cohorts — but no completed randomised trial exists
question: In patients with osteoradionecrosis of the jaw after head-and-neck radiotherapy, does pentoxifylline plus tocopherol (with or without clodronate — the PENTO/PENTOCLO regimens) heal or stabilise lesions versus conservative care or placebo?
balance: GAP-E evidence, capped at POSSIBLE. The Delanian programme reports remarkable results without a control group: in the 2005 phase II cohort, 16 of 18 patients with refractory mandibular osteoradionecrosis achieved complete recovery on pentoxifylline 800 mg + tocopherol 1000 IU daily (the worst 8 also received clodronate); in the 2011 PENTOCLO phase II cohort, all 54 eligible patients recovered completely, median 9 months, on the five-drug rotating regimen. A meta-analysis of 7 studies (211 patients) found 126 recovered fully or improved significantly, with progression in 15; an 11-study review found complete mucosal coverage ranging from 16.6% to 100%. PREMISE CORRECTION to the slate row: no completed randomised trial of PENTO/PENTOCLO for jaw osteoradionecrosis was found in this session's PubMed fetch — the Delanian reports are phase II single-arm trials, and the RAPTOR protocol (Shaw et al., PMID: 40708048, ISRCTN34217298; protocol only, not carded) itself describes RAPTOR as the first randomised controlled trial of PENTOCLO in this setting, still recruiting. The one completed Delanian placebo-controlled randomised trial of the same drug combination (PMID: 31987975, not carded) treated radiation-induced plexopathy, a different condition, and was negative. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the uncontrolled healing rates justify the ongoing trial, not a settled claim.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — GAP-E evidence: uncontrolled phase II cohorts and reviews only; no completed randomised trial in jaw osteoradionecrosis, so this is not a settled benefit

title: Liposomal bupivacaine (Exparel) versus plain bupivacaine: the Cochrane synthesis found no difference, and the pooled advantage is 0.37 pain points — 'small but not clinically relevant'
question: In adults having surgery, does liposomal bupivacaine (wound infiltration or perineural) reduce postoperative pain and opioid use versus plain bupivacaine or placebo?
balance: Graded against the Cochrane synthesis, as commissioned, not the most favourable single trial. For infiltration (Hamilton 2017, 9 studies, 1,377 participants), liposomal bupivacaine beat placebo on cumulative 72-hour pain in one study (very low quality) and showed no difference versus plain bupivacaine hydrochloride in two studies (very low quality). For peripheral nerve block (Hamilton 2016), three of seven trials never published results and the four reported studies (299 participants) did not report pain scores at set time points. The largest pooled comparison (Dinges 2021, 23 RCTs, 1,867 patients) found pain 0.37 points lower at 24 hours and a morphine-equivalent ratio of 0.85 versus plain bupivacaine — statistically significant but, in the authors' own words, small and not clinically relevant. A 100-patient placebo trial of the named product — Exparel (Pacira Pharmaceuticals Inc, Parsippany, NJ, as published) — found no difference at any time point. PROPOSED UNLIKELY (benefit beyond plain bupivacaine). Current marketed versions may differ from the tested product.
stamp: UNLIKELY (benefit) — versus plain bupivacaine the treatment made no difference in the Cochrane synthesis, and the pooled advantage is small and not clinically relevant

title: Targeted muscle reinnervation for amputation pain: one small randomised trial (N = 28) and concordant cohorts favour TMR — the at-amputation evidence is a cohort, not the trial
question: In adults undergoing major limb amputation, does targeted muscle reinnervation performed at the time of amputation reduce neuroma pain and phantom limb pain versus standard traction neurectomy?
balance: One small randomised trial plus cohorts — capped at POSSIBLE, with N printed on the face. The Dumanian RCT (N = 28, NCT02205385) randomised amputees with chronic postamputation pain to TMR or standard neuroma excision and burying: phantom pain change at 1 year was 3.2 versus −0.2 points (intention-to-treat adjusted P = 0.06; longitudinal model P = 0.03) and residual limb pain change 2.9 versus 0.9 (P = 0.15). PREMISE NUANCE: that trial treated established pain (secondary TMR); the evidence for TMR performed at the time of amputation is the Valerio multi-institutional cohort — 51 immediate-TMR patients versus 438 unselected amputee controls, median worst pain 1/10 versus 5/10 (phantom) and 4/10 (residual) — large gaps from a non-randomised comparison. A prospective 33-patient series and a 5-study, 127-patient meta-analysis point the same way, and the meta-analysis authors call the evidence 'limited… of good quality' in TMR's favour. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — based on one small randomised trial (N = 28) plus prospective cohorts; the at-amputation comparison is observational

title: Pasireotide after pancreaticoduodenectomy: SPLIT — the NEJM trial halved severe fistula, leak or abscess, but later prospective series and the meta-analysis found no fistula reduction
question: In adults undergoing pancreaticoduodenectomy, does perioperative pasireotide reduce clinically relevant postoperative pancreatic fistula versus placebo?
balance: SPLIT — determined after reading the follow-up literature first, as commissioned. The Allen NEJM trial (300 patients, single centre, Novartis-funded, NCT00994110) found grade ≥3 fistula, leak or abscess in 9% on pasireotide versus 21% on placebo (relative risk 0.44; pancreaticoduodenectomy subgroup 10% vs 21%, relative risk 0.49). The later reports conflict: Elliott's prospective series (111 treated vs 168 historical controls) found fistula in 17.1% versus 15.5% with 38% dose-limiting nausea; the Washington University prospective evaluation (459 pancreaticoduodenectomies, 112 propensity-matched pairs) found identical severe fistula rates of 7.1% versus 7.1%; and the Liu meta-analysis (4 studies, 919 patients) pooled an OR of 0.78 (95% CI 0.49 to 1.24) for clinically relevant fistula — no reduction. PROPOSED SPLIT: one positive single-centre RCT has not been reproduced, and no multicentre randomised trial has yet settled it.
stamp: SPLIT — the single-centre NEJM trial found fewer severe fistulas, but two later prospective series and a meta-analysis found no fistula reduction

title: Drains after pancreaticoduodenectomy: SPLIT — PANDRA found omission safe and fistula-reducing, the Van Buren trial was stopped early for higher mortality without drains; early removal in low-risk patients is the agreed part
question: In adults undergoing pancreaticoduodenectomy, does omitting a prophylactic intra-abdominal drain (or removing it very early) increase or decrease complications versus routine drainage?
balance: SPLIT on omission, concordant on early removal. PANDRA (Witzigmann 2016, 395 analysed, ISRCTN04937707) found drain omission noninferior for reintervention (16.6% no-drain vs 21.3% drain) with less clinically relevant fistula (5.7% vs 11.9%) and identical mortality (3.1% vs 3.0%). The Van Buren multicentre trial (137 patients, NCT01441492) reached the opposite conclusion and was stopped early by its DSMB because mortality rose from 3% to 12% without drains, with more and more severe complications. Early removal is the settled half: Bassi's RCT in low-risk patients (day-1 drain amylase ≤5000 U/L) found fewer fistulas and complications with day-3 removal, and the 2025 meta-analysis of 13 RCTs (2,796 patients) supports a selective early-removal policy in pancreaticoduodenectomy — while its no-drain verdict applies to left pancreatectomy, not the Whipple. PROPOSED SPLIT.
stamp: SPLIT — drain omission after pancreaticoduodenectomy is contested between two randomised trials; selective early removal in low-risk patients is supported

title: Epidural blood patch for post-dural-puncture headache: headache at day 7 in 16% versus 86% on conservative care in the one RCT; 75% complete relief in a 504-patient series, with early patching and large-bore needles predicting failure
question: In adults with post-dural-puncture headache that has failed conservative treatment, does an epidural blood patch relieve headache versus continued conservative care, and does timing or volume change success?
balance: The randomised evidence is one small observer-blind trial (van Kooten 2008, 40 analysed): headache persisted at 24 hours in 58% after blood patch versus 90% on conservative treatment (relative risk 0.64), and at day 7 in 16% versus 86% (relative risk 0.18), with remaining headaches mild after patching. The large prospective Safa-Tisseront series (504 patients with incapacitating headache) found 75% complete relief, 18% incomplete relief and 7% failure; failure was independently predicted by large-bore needle puncture (OR 5.96) and by patching less than 4 days after puncture (OR 2.63). On volume, the Paech randomised trial in 121 obstetric patients found complete relief in 10%, 32% and 26% with 15, 20 and 30 mL, supporting an attempt at 20 mL. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — a large and consistent effect, capped because the versus-conservative randomised base is a single small trial. The Cochrane blood-patch review was not carded: its update record is marked WITHDRAWN in PubMed.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a large effect in one small randomised trial (40 analysed) plus a 504-patient prospective series; timing and volume modify success

title: PECS I/II blocks for breast surgery (PARTIAL — the PECS slice only): less pain than no block on moderate-quality evidence, uncertain versus sham, and no better than paravertebral block in the pooled data
question: In women having mastectomy or breast-conserving surgery, does a pectoral nerve (PECS I/II) block reduce postoperative pain and opioid use versus placebo, no block, or paravertebral block?
balance: PARTIAL shelf — the PECS slice only, verified against its homes before building: pack #3011 asks the erector spinae plane block question for the same operation and pack #1240 asks paravertebral-versus-general anaesthesia for cancer recurrence; neither homes PECS, and no study carded on those packs is re-carded here. On the PECS evidence itself: Bashandy & Abbas (120 women) found lower pain scores and less morphine in the first 12 hours adding PECS I + II to general anaesthesia versus general anaesthesia alone; Kulhari (40 women) found PECS II gave longer analgesia (294.5 vs 197.5 minutes) and less 24-hour morphine (3.90 vs 5.30 mg) than a single-level paravertebral block. The Meißner meta-analysis (24 RCTs, 1,565 patients) tempers both: resting pain is reduced versus no treatment (mean difference −1.14, moderate quality), but the effect is uncertain versus sham block (−0.83, 95% CI −1.80 to 0.14, very low quality) and versus paravertebral block (−0.18, very low quality). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — PECS blocks reduce pain versus no block on moderate-quality evidence; the benefit versus sham is uncertain and they are no better than paravertebral block in pooled data

title: Flap fixation with quilting sutures after mastectomy: seroma roughly halved or better in every design — 22.5% versus 80.5% in the founding study, a pooled relative risk of 0.37 across 11 RCTs, and a better textbook outcome in the QUILT stepped-wedge RCT
question: In women having mastectomy (with or without immediate reconstruction), does flap fixation with quilting sutures reduce seroma formation and aspirations versus standard closure with drains?
balance: Concordant at every level of evidence. The founding ten Wolde study (2014) was a retrospective comparison of consecutive groups (176 patients) — PREMISE CORRECTION to the slate row, which described it as a randomised trial — finding seroma in 22.5% quilted versus 80.5% conventional, with fewer aspirations and fewer infections (11.2% vs 31.0%). The randomised evidence arrived later: the QUILT stepped-wedge cluster RCT (251 patients, 12 Dutch hospitals, NCT05272904) found textbook outcome in 65.7% versus 41.3% and wound complications including clinically significant seroma in 24.0% versus 55.6%, and the Eliav meta-analysis of 11 RCTs (2,009 patients) pooled a seroma relative risk of 0.367 (95% CI 0.25 to 0.539) — a 63% relative risk reduction, with the absolute rates from the comparative studies printed on the cards. No pain, shoulder-function or satisfaction penalty was found. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit).
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — concordant randomised and comparative evidence that quilting sutures reduce seroma after mastectomy

title: Endophthalmitis Vitrectomy Study (single trial, 1995): immediate vitrectomy benefited only eyes with light-perception-only vision (20/40 or better in 33% vs 11%) — no benefit at hand-motions or better, and none from intravenous antibiotics
question: In adults with acute postoperative endophthalmitis after cataract surgery, does immediate pars plana vitrectomy improve final vision versus vitreous tap/biopsy with intravitreal antibiotics — and does the answer depend on presenting vision (light perception only versus hand motions or better)?
balance: SINGLE-TRIAL SHELF, labelled as such on its face. The Endophthalmitis Vitrectomy Study (420 patients, reported 1995) is old and pre-dates modern small-gauge vitrectomy; a 2022 Cochrane review searched to May 2022 and found it is still the only randomised trial of early vitrectomy versus tap and inject, grading the evidence very low to low certainty. Its conclusion is driven by one subgroup: with light perception-only vision at presentation, immediate vitrectomy gave 20/40 or better acuity in 33% versus 11% and severe visual loss in 20% versus 47% versus tap/biopsy; with hand-motions vision or better there was no difference, and intravenous antibiotics made no difference to acuity or media clarity in any group. Modern retrospective series (Far 2021, 1,355 eyes) find tap and inject noninferior overall (relative risk 1.04 for ≥2-line improvement), but they are confounded by indication and do not test the light-perception subgroup. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — for the light-perception-only presentation only.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single-trial shelf: one randomised trial (EVS, 420 patients, 1995, pre-dating modern small-gauge vitrectomy); benefit only in the light-perception-only subgroup

title: Face-down posturing after macular-hole vitrectomy: SPLIT by hole size — small holes close either way; for holes ≥400 μm a closure advantage is suggested but unproven (95.5% vs 85.6%, P = .08 in the largest trial), with better acuity face-down
question: In adults having vitrectomy for full-thickness macular hole, does strict face-down posturing improve hole closure and vision versus face-forward or no positioning, and does hole size change the answer?
balance: SPLIT, with hole size as the effect modifier. For holes under 400 μm every source agrees positioning does not matter: closure was 100 versus 96 per 100 eyes in the Cochrane subgroup analysis, and Guillaubey's post hoc analysis found no positional influence. For holes of 400 μm or more the sources divide: Guillaubey (150 eyes) found overall closure of 97.4% face-down versus 87.5% seated (P = .027) and recommended face-down for large holes; the PIMS trial (Pasu 2020, 185 patients, all holes ≥400 μm) found closure of 95.5% versus 85.6% face-forward — not significant (P = .08) — but significantly better acuity improvement face-down (about 3 versus 1 Snellen lines, P = .01); Alberti & la Cour's noninferiority trial found closure identical at 97.1% in both arms, including large holes; and the Cochrane review (Cundy 2023, 8 RCTs, 709 eyes, low certainty) pooled a closure relative risk of 1.05 (95% CI 0.99 to 1.12) overall and 1.08 (0.93 to 1.26) in large holes. PROPOSED SPLIT (by hole size).
stamp: SPLIT (by hole size) — face-down posturing makes no difference for holes under 400 μm; for larger holes a closure benefit is suggested but not proven, with a possible visual-acuity advantage

title: Repeated low-level red-light therapy for progressing childhood myopia: axial elongation 0.13 mm versus 0.38 mm at 1 year in the pivotal Chinese randomised trial — but the base is short-term, from one country's programmes, and a retinal-damage case report has appeared
question: In children with progressing myopia, does repeated low-level red-light therapy slow axial elongation and refractive progression versus single-vision spectacles, and what retinal safety signals have appeared?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — with an open retinal-safety question. In the pivotal multicentre randomised trial (Jiang Y et al., PMID: 34863776), 264 Chinese children aged 8–13 were randomised to repeated low-level red-light (RLRL) therapy plus single-vision spectacles versus spectacles alone for 12 months: adjusted axial elongation was 0.13 mm versus 0.38 mm and refractive progression −0.20 D versus −0.79 D (between-group differences 0.26 mm and −0.59 D), with no severe adverse events, no functional visual loss and no structural damage on OCT in the trial. A meta-analysis of 7 randomised trials with 1,031 children (Wang F et al., PMID: 37565498) found the same direction (axial length mean difference −0.25 mm; spherical equivalent +0.60 D). In the 2-year post-trial follow-up (Xiong R et al., PMID: 36054314; 114 children analysed), children who continued RLRL had the least 2-year elongation (0.16 mm) and stopping treatment produced a modest rebound. Against this, a published case report (Liu H et al., PMID: 37227712) describes retinal damage after RLRL exposure in a 12-year-old girl — a single case, but in a therapy given to healthy children's eyes. The fetched trial records describe the device only by specification — a home-use desktop device emitting 650-nm red light, 3 minutes twice daily, 5 days per week — and do not name a brand or maker in the record; current marketed devices may differ. The randomised base is short-term and concentrated in Chinese trial programmes. The atropine slice is homed on live Shelf #614 and the multifocal-lens slice on live Shelf #618; neither is re-carded here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): RLRL slows axial elongation and refractive progression over 1 year in the trials done so far, but long-term and independent replication are lacking and retinal-safety case reports mean the harm side is not closed.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — 1-year axial elongation 0.13 mm versus 0.38 mm and a concordant 7-trial meta-analysis (1,031 children), but the base is short-term, concentrated in one country's programmes, and a retinal-damage case report has appeared

title: Intense pulsed light for evaporative dry eye from meibomian gland dysfunction: tear-film measures and symptoms improve versus sham in small masked trials, and a 15-trial meta-analysis agrees — but the trials are small and short
question: In adults with evaporative dry eye from meibomian gland dysfunction, does intense pulsed light therapy improve symptoms and tear-film measures versus sham light treatment?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — three concordant sources, all small or pooled from small trials. In a double-masked paired-eye placebo-controlled trial (Craig JP et al., PMID: 25678687), 28 participants had one eye treated with intense pulsed light (IPL) and the partner eye sham-treated: lipid layer grade and non-invasive tear break-up time improved only in treated eyes (break-up time 14.1 versus 8.6 seconds at day 45), and 86% reported fewer symptoms in the treated eye. In a parallel-group double-masked placebo-controlled trial of 87 participants (Xue AL et al., PMID: 32007523) using the E-Eye Intense Regulated Pulsed Light device (E-Swin, France) — the device class named as published in that trial — symptom scores (OSDI, SPEED, SANDE), lipid layer thickness and gland capping improved, with the five-flash regimen separating earlier and more fully than four flashes. A meta-analysis of 15 randomised trials with 1,142 patients (Miao S et al., PMID: 36044829) found IPL better than sham on symptom scores and tear break-up time, and IPL plus gland expression better than expression alone on several measures. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): IPL improves tear-film quality and symptoms in MGD over weeks to a few months; durability beyond a treatment course, optimal regimens, and any effect on gland structure long-term are not settled by this base.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — masked sham/placebo-controlled trials (28 paired-eye; 87 parallel-group) and a 15-trial meta-analysis (1,142 patients) agree on symptom and tear-film improvement; trials are small and short

title: Tonsillectomy for PFAPA syndrome: complete resolution in 63% versus 5% (Garavello) and all operated children symptom-free at 6 months versus half unoperated (Renko) — two small concordant randomised trials, 67 children in total
question: In children with PFAPA syndrome (periodic fever, aphthous stomatitis, pharyngitis, adenitis), does tonsillectomy resolve or markedly reduce fever episodes versus watchful waiting or medical management?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — on a small base that must be printed: two randomised trials, 67 children randomised in total (65 analysed in the Cochrane synthesis). In Renko M et al. (PMID: 17719940), 26 children were randomised to tonsillectomy or follow-up alone; at 6 months all 14 operated children and 6 of 12 control children (50%) were symptom-free (difference 50%, 95% CI 23% to 75%, P<.001) — half the control group resolved spontaneously. In Garavello W et al. (PMID: 19464029), 39 children were randomised to adenotonsillectomy or expectant management for 18 months: complete resolution in 63% versus 5% (P<.001), and mean episodes 0.7 versus 8.1 (P<.001). The Cochrane review (Burton MJ et al., PMID: 31886897) judged both trials at low risk of bias and concluded children with PFAPA likely experience less fever and less severe episodes after surgery (moderate-certainty evidence; resolution risk ratio 4.38, 95% CI 0.64 to 30.11 — a wide interval). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): surgery resolves or markedly reduces attacks in most operated children, with the honest caveats that the total randomised base is 67 children, PFAPA often remits on its own (half of Renko's controls by 6 months), and surgery carries its own risks, which these small trials were not sized to measure.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — two concordant randomised trials (67 children total): resolution 63% versus 5% at 18 months and 100% versus 50% symptom-free at 6 months; Cochrane moderate-certainty, with spontaneous remission common in controls

title: Posterior nasal nerve ablation for chronic rhinitis: responders 73% versus 37% on sham (cryoablation) and 68% versus 41% on sham (radiofrequency) at 3 months — real effects over a substantial sham response, in industry device trials; durability data are post-crossover extensions
question: In adults with chronic rhinitis inadequately controlled by medical therapy, does posterior nasal nerve ablation — cryoablation or temperature-controlled radiofrequency — improve nasal symptom scores versus a sham procedure?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two sham-controlled device trials agree, and both carry a large sham response that must stay on the face. Cryoablation of the posterior nasal nerve (the ClariFix device programme; Del Signore AG et al., PMID: 34355872): in 133 enrolled adults (127 analysed), responders at 90 days (≥30% fall in reflective Total Nasal Symptom Score) were 73.4% on active treatment versus 36.5% on sham (P<0.001). Temperature-controlled radiofrequency neurolysis (the RhinAer device programme; Stolovitzky JP et al., PMID: 34527852): in 116 randomised adults, responders at 3 months were 67.5% versus 41.0% on sham (P=.009), with mean symptom-score falls of −3.6 versus −2.2 (P=.013). Both pivotal trials are industry device trials; roughly 4 in 10 sham patients met the responder definition, so the procedure-specific gain is the roughly 27–37 percentage-point difference, not the headline responder rate. Longer-term figures come from extensions after the sham arm crossed over to active treatment (12-month responder rate 80.6% in the radiofrequency programme, PMID: 35714267; 2-year responder rate 87.3% in the combined treated group, PMID: 38266636) — those are uncontrolled follow-ups, labelled as such, not randomised durability evidence. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): both ablation modalities beat sham at 3 months by a similar margin; how much is device, how much is procedure ritual, and how long benefit lasts without a control group, remain open.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two sham-controlled trials: responders 73.4% versus 36.5% (cryoablation) and 67.5% versus 41.0% (radiofrequency) at 3 months; substantial sham response in both, and long-term data are post-crossover extensions without controls

title: House-dust-mite SLIT tablet for allergic rhinitis: symptom-and-medication scores about 17–22% lower (relative) than placebo across three large trials of two different tablets — benefit maintained a year after a 1-year course stopped (Bergmann)
question: In children and adults with house-dust-mite allergic rhinitis, does a house-dust-mite sublingual immunotherapy tablet reduce symptom-and-medication scores versus placebo, including after treatment stops?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — three large double-blind placebo-controlled trials, two different products, consistent relative gains of about a fifth. Bergmann KC et al. (PMID: 24388010) randomised 509 adults to the Stallergenes house-dust-mite sublingual tablet at 500 IR or 300 IR or placebo for 1 year: Average Adjusted Symptom Scores were reduced by 20.2% and 17.9% relative to placebo (P=.0066 and P=.0150), and efficacy was maintained through a subsequent treatment-free year — the after-stopping evidence in this base. Nolte H et al. (PMID: 27521719) randomised 1,482 North American adolescents and adults to the SQ HDM SLIT-tablet (MK-8237; Merck & Co, Kenilworth, NJ / ALK-Abelló, Hørsholm, Denmark, as named in the record) at 12 SQ-HDM or placebo for about 52 weeks: the total combined rhinitis score improved by 17% relative to placebo (95% CI 10% to 25%). Schuster A et al. (PMID: 39678704) randomised 1,460 children aged 5–11 to the same SQ tablet or placebo for about a year: total combined rhinitis score was 1.0 point lower in absolute terms, a 22.0% relative reduction (95% CI 12.0 to 31.1, P<.0001). Adverse events were mainly application-site reactions; no anaphylaxis was reported in Bergmann, and one non-serious systemic allergic reaction treated with epinephrine occurred at first supervised administration in Nolte. All percentage gains here are relative reductions, stated as such. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a real but modest relative improvement in symptom-and-medication scores, with one trial showing carry-over a year after stopping. The grass-pollen SLIT tablet is homed on pack #4283 and dust-mite avoidance for asthma on pack #4148; neither is re-carded here, and the gated Demoly and Virchow records already homed elsewhere are not used.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — three large placebo-controlled trials of two HDM SLIT tablets: relative symptom-score reductions of 17.9–20.2% (adults, Stallergenes tablet), 17% (adolescents/adults, SQ tablet) and 22.0% (children 5–11, SQ tablet); benefit maintained in the treatment-free year in the one trial that measured it

title: Intralesional therapy for keloid scars: combined triamcinolone + 5-fluorouracil beats either drug alone in the syntheses (odds ratios 3.45 and 4.17 for a good response) — but the trials underneath are small, heterogeneous and often unblinded; total randomised evidence is thin
question: In patients with established keloid scars, do intralesional therapies — corticosteroid alone, 5-fluorouracil alone, or the combination (with or without excision) — flatten scars and prevent recurrence better than each other or no injection treatment?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — the syntheses point one way and say plainly how weak the ground is. The most direct synthesis (Mavilakandy AK et al., PMID: 37337341) pooled 13 studies (12 randomised) of keloids and hypertrophic scars: combined intralesional triamcinolone acetonide (TAC) + 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) gave superior objective treatment efficacy versus TAC alone (odds ratio 3.45, 95% CI 2.22 to 5.35) and versus 5-FU alone (odds ratio 4.17, 2.21 to 7.87), with less telangiectasia than TAC alone (odds ratio 0.24, 0.11 to 0.52). The earlier 5-FU systematic review (Bijlard E et al., PMID: 25805099) covered 18 papers and 482 patients: 5-FU was reported effective in 45–96% of patients, only the TAC:5-FU combination may perform better than TAC alone, and the reviewers state the level of evidence is poor. A network meta-analysis (Sun P et al., PMID: 31853608; 23 studies, 1,513 patients with pathological scars) ranked combination injections highest and found corticosteroid + 5-FU better than corticosteroid alone or verapamil alone, with no significant difference from 5-FU alone. The one double-blind head-to-head trial carded directly (Darougheh A et al., PMID: 19018794; 40 patients) found good-to-excellent improvement in 55% on TAC + 5-FU versus 20% on TAC alone by patient report (P=.02). Total evidence base: the syntheses overlap and cannot simply be added; the unique-patient total across the reviews is in the low thousands at most, built from many small heterogeneous trials with variable recurrence windows. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): the combination is probably the better injection, on evidence that would not support a stronger word. Silicone gel/sheeting is homed on pack #4049 and is not re-carded here.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — combination TAC + 5-FU beats monotherapy in syntheses (OR 3.45 vs TAC; OR 4.17 vs 5-FU), but the base is many small, heterogeneous, often unblinded trials (482 patients in the 5-FU review; 13 studies in the combination meta-analysis)

title: Beremagene geperpavec (Vyjuvek, Krystal Biotech) for dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa: complete wound healing 67% versus 22% on placebo at 6 months in the GEM-3 intra-patient trial — total randomised N=31 patients, printed on the face by rare-disease necessity
question: In people with dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa, does topical beremagene geperpavec close wounds versus placebo gel applied to matched wounds in the same patient?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a positive phase 3 trial whose total randomised base is 31 patients, printed here and in the stamp line as required. In GEM-3 (Guide SV et al., PMID: 36516090), 31 patients aged 6 months or older with genetically confirmed dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa each contributed a matched primary wound pair; one wound received weekly beremagene geperpavec (B-VEC) and the other placebo for 26 weeks. Complete wound healing at 6 months occurred in 67% of B-VEC wounds versus 22% of placebo wounds (difference 46 percentage points, 95% CI 24 to 68; P=0.002), and at 3 months in 71% versus 20% (difference 51 points, 29 to 73; P<0.001). Pain on dressing change improved slightly more with B-VEC (adjusted difference −0.61 on a 0–10 scale at week 22); adverse events included pruritus and chills. The earlier GEM-1/2 randomised phase 1/2 trial (Gurevich I et al., PMID: 35347281) treated matched wounds in 9 patients (N printed plainly — below the usual 10-person floor, carded because it is the programme's first-in-human randomised evidence in a rare disease) and met its C7-expression, anchoring-fibril and wound-area objectives with no grade 2 or above treatment-related adverse events. The open-label extension (Marinkovich MP et al., PMID: 40220208) followed 47 subjects for up to 112 weeks with no new safety signals and maintained closure in rollover wounds (61.1–89.5%). The product is beremagene geperpavec (Vyjuvek), the HSV-1-based COL7A1 gene-therapy gel of Krystal Biotech, named exactly as published. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the intra-patient design makes 31 patients more informative than 31 patients in a parallel trial, but a single small phase 3 programme caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — based on a very small total randomised N = 31 patients (GEM-3 intra-patient trial: complete healing 67% versus 22% at 6 months), supported by a 9-patient phase 1/2 trial and a 47-subject open-label extension

title: PHYSIOLOGY — the Frank–Starling relationship in intact humans: stroke volume tracks end-diastolic volume (not filling pressure) when preload is changed directly — curves built from wedge-pressure surrogates, steep in the young, flattened and shifted by a stiff, ageing ventricle
question: In intact humans, what does the Frank–Starling relationship look like when preload is changed directly (volume infusion, lower-body negative pressure, postural change) — how much does stroke volume rise per unit rise in filling pressure, and how do contractility and pericardial constraint shift or flatten the curve?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING. Textbook framing (Guyton & Hall; Ganong; Boron & Boulpaep): the Frank–Starling relationship — stroke volume rises with end-diastolic volume along a curve whose slope and position are set by contractility and by pericardial/diastolic constraint — is presented in textbooks as settled physiology, and its direction in intact humans is not in doubt. What the primary human evidence actually consists of is thinner and older than the textbook confidence suggests, which is why this pack is graded EMERGING rather than ESTABLISHED. In healthy volunteers given 3 litres of saline over 3 hours (Kumar A et al., PMID: 15090949; 12 catheterised and 32 echocardiography volunteers), end-diastolic volume indexes and their changes tracked stroke volume index well, while pulmonary artery occlusion pressure and central venous pressure — the bedside 'preload' numbers — did not correlate with volumes or with the response to infusion at all: in intact humans the curve relates volume to output, and pressure is an unreliable stand-in for volume. Frank–Starling curves constructed from wedge pressure during lower-body negative pressure and saline infusion in 23 healthy young adults (Fu Q et al., PMID: 14527942) had maximal slopes of 12.5 ± 2.0 mL/mmHg in women versus 7.1 ± 1.5 mL/mmHg in men (stroke-index slopes 6.31 versus 4.29 mL·m⁻²·mmHg⁻¹) — a quantified human slope, from a pressure surrogate. When preload was manipulated by lower-body negative pressure and rapid saline infusion during right-heart catheterisation in 102 healthy seniors stratified by lifelong exercise dose (Bhella PS et al., PMID: 25236519), sedentary ageing was associated with a stiffer, less distensible ventricle (stiffness constant 0.062 ± 0.039) than lifelong competitive training (0.035 ± 0.033), with committed exercisers in between — the curve's diastolic substrate flattens with sedentary ageing and is preserved by training. There is no direct human pressure–volume-loop gold standard in healthy volunteers: every human 'curve' here is built from wedge-pressure or imaging surrogates across loading manoeuvres, and the classic catheterisation-era ventricular-function-curve programme (Ross & Braunwald era) survives in records whose abstracts could not be fetched and verified this session (one candidate, Mangano 1980, PMID: 7398014, carries no abstract in its PubMed record and was therefore refused as a card — see summary). Cross-point: pack #6076 (exercise cardiac output) invokes the Frank–Starling mechanism during exercise; this pack measures the preload–stroke-volume relation itself and does not re-card #6076's studies.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING — in intact humans stroke volume tracks end-diastolic volume under direct preload change (saline, lower-body negative pressure), with quantified wedge-pressure slopes of ~7–13 mL/mmHg in young adults, but every human curve rests on pressure/imaging surrogates — no direct pressure–volume gold standard exists in health, and filling pressures themselves fail to predict volume or response

title: PHYSIOLOGY — the Guyton venous-return curve in humans: what is measured at the bedside is a model-derived mean-systemic-filling-pressure ANALOGUE (about 15–21 mmHg by method) in postoperative and ICU patients — not a directly measured Guyton curve, and not in healthy volunteers
question: In humans, can the Guyton venous-return curve be measured — what is the analogue of mean systemic filling pressure at zero flow (the Pmsf analogue), how close does it sit to right atrial pressure at rest, and how do volume loading and vasopressors move it?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING. Textbook framing (Guyton & Hall): venous return is driven by the gradient between mean systemic filling pressure (Pmsf) — the equilibrated pressure in the systemic circulation at zero flow — and right atrial pressure, and the venous-return curve plots flow against right atrial pressure with its zero-flow intercept at Pmsf. In humans that intercept cannot be measured directly in an intact circulation; what the human literature measures is an ANALOGUE, and this pack says so plainly, as required. Parkin & Wright (PMID: 1919281) proposed deriving a mean systemic filling pressure analogue from cardiac output, right atrial pressure and arterial pressure by modelling a notional regional circulation at stop-flow — a model-derived estimate from the start, offered as a quantitative link between volume state and therapy. Maas JJ et al. (PMID: 22584797), in 11 mechanically ventilated postoperative cardiac-surgery patients, compared three estimates across supine, head-up tilt and 500 mL colloid loading: inspiratory-hold Pmsf averaged 20.9 ± 5.6 mmHg, arm equilibrium pressure 19.8 ± 5.7 mmHg, and the model analogue (Pmsa) 14.9 ± 4.0 mmHg — the analogue ran about 6 mmHg below the hold estimate (bias −6.0 ± 3.1 mmHg), while changes with tilt and loading were directionally concordant across methods. In a companion study (PMID: 22763909; 15 postoperative patients), systemic vascular compliance was linear at 64.3 ± 32.7 mL/mmHg and stressed volume was estimated at 1,265 ± 541 mL (28.5% of predicted blood volume) by extrapolating the Pmsf–volume curve to zero pressure. Guérin L, Teboul JL, Persichini R et al. (PMID: 26597901), in 30 patients with acute circulatory failure, built venous-return curves from cardiac index–central venous pressure pairs during ventilatory occlusions: in fluid responders, passive leg raising raised Psm from 25 ± 13 to 31 ± 13 mmHg and widened the Psm–CVP gradient by 20 ± 30%, while resistance to venous return did not change — volume recruitment moves the intercept, not the slope resistance, in that manoeuvre. Every measurement here is in postoperative or ICU PATIENTS, not healthy volunteers, and every 'Pmsf' value is method-dependent (hold, arm stop-flow, or model analogue disagree by several mmHg in the same patients). The honest statement is: the Guyton framework organises these bedside estimates coherently, but no study in this pack measured a Guyton venous-return curve directly in a healthy human.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING — the human Pmsf is a model-derived analogue, not a direct measurement: inspiratory-hold ~20.9 mmHg, arm equilibrium ~19.8 mmHg and model analogue ~14.9 mmHg in the same postoperative patients (methods disagree by ~6 mmHg); all human data are from postoperative/ICU patients, none from healthy volunteers

title: The exercise pressor reflex: muscle metabolites switch sympathetic outflow on — coupled to muscle-cell pH, isolated by post-exercise occlusion, and engaged in leg exercise only at fatigue
question: In healthy humans, how does the exercise pressor reflex work — how much do muscle metaboreflex and mechanoreflex activation raise muscle sympathetic nerve activity and arterial pressure during static exercise, and how is the metaboreflex isolated by post-exercise circulatory occlusion?
balance: Guyton & Hall, Ganong, and Boron & Boulpaep frame the textbook account: during exercise, central command sets the basic cardiovascular pattern while muscle chemoreflexes (the metaboreflex, from metabolite-sensitive group III/IV afferents) and mechanoreflexes modulate it, and the metaboreflex can be isolated by keeping the exercised limb occluded after exercise ends (post-exercise circulatory occlusion), which traps metabolites and holds sympathetic outflow up while central command and mechanoreflex input have stopped. The fetched human records support each element. Sympathetic activation is coupled to muscle-cell acidification: with simultaneous 31P-NMR and microneurography, the onset of muscle sympathetic nerve activity (MSNA) coincided with cellular acidification and MSNA tracked intracellular pH, not phosphocreatine, inorganic phosphate or ADP (Victor 1988). When the metaboreflex was engaged by ischemic static exercise, MSNA rose in parallel in exercising and resting muscle — from 29 ± 2 to 38 ± 2 bursts/min and from 30 ± 3 to 40 ± 2 bursts/min in the second minute — and stayed up during post-exercise ischemia (Hansen 1994, N = 7). In large-muscle exercise the reflex needs fatigue: non-fatiguing isometric knee extension did not durably raise MSNA, but exercise to fatigue raised total MSNA 96–107% above control in the final 30 seconds and kept it 83% above control during post-exercise muscle ischemia (Ray & Mark 1993, N = 7–8). The Rowell & O'Leary synthesis supplies the framework — chemoreflex raising sympathetic activity and pressure mainly in isometric exercise, mechanoreflex and baroreflex resetting alongside central command. This shelf covers the reflex during exercise itself; the fall in pressure during the recovery hours afterwards is a different question, homed at pack #6399 (post-exercise hypotension), which is cross-pointed here and not duplicated. The assembly-dropped slate row on the metaboreflex alone (S5-1-46) is folded into this pack, which covers the metaboreflex together with the mechanoreflex and central command as one pressor-reflex question.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — the exercise pressor reflex is metaboreflex-driven once muscle acidifies: MSNA tracks intracellular pH, rises ~9–10 bursts/min in ischemic small-muscle exercise and ~doubles with fatiguing leg exercise, and post-exercise occlusion isolates it (Guyton & Hall; Ganong; Boron & Boulpaep)
