title: Splenic contraction in exercise and breath-hold diving: up to half the spleen empties at maximal exercise, a fifth per apnoea series — worth a few percent more circulating red cells
question: In healthy humans, how much does the spleen contract during exercise and during breath-hold diving, how much does that raise circulating haemoglobin concentration, and how does splenic volume recover afterwards?
balance: Guyton & Hall, Ganong, and Boron & Boulpaep frame the textbook account: the human spleen is a small red-cell reservoir compared with athletic mammals — it sequesters roughly 200–250 mL of densely packed red cells — but it contracts under sympathetic/catecholamine drive during exercise and apnoea, expelling part of that store and transiently raising circulating haemoglobin and haematocrit. The fetched human records quantify it. In exercising men, spleen volume fell 28–36% during submaximal cycling and 56% on an incremental ride to exhaustion, recovering to baseline within 20 minutes, with plasma catecholamines inversely related to spleen volume (Stewart 2003, N = 9). In breath-hold apnoea with face immersion, spleen volume fell rapidly by about 20%, mainly within the first of five repeated apnoeas, with splenic arterial and venous flows unchanged — evidence of active contraction rather than passive collapse — and recovery was slow, still incomplete 60 minutes after the last apnoea (Baković 2003). Three maximal apnoeas contracted the spleen by a mean of 49 mL (18%) in all ten subjects while haematocrit rose 2.2% and haemoglobin 2.4%, with full splenic recovery only at 8–9 minutes (Schagatay 2005, N = 10). The cell-count study adds that repeated apnoeas raised circulating red-cell volume by 4.9% in trained divers and 1.7% in untrained intact subjects, with no change in splenectomised subjects — the control that pins the effect on the spleen (Baković 2005). Magnitudes differ by stimulus: maximal exercise contracts the spleen most; apnoea contracts it quickly but modestly, and its slow recovery lets repeated dives stack the effect.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — the human spleen contracts actively in exercise (to −56% at exhaustion) and apnoea (−18–20%, stacking across dives), raising circulating red-cell volume ~2–5% with slow recovery (Guyton & Hall; Ganong; Boron & Boulpaep)

title: The Valsalva manoeuvre: four phases, an age-dependent ratio — flattened by autonomic failure, squared off by heart failure
question: In healthy humans, what are the four phases of the Valsalva manoeuvre in arterial pressure and heart rate, what are the normal Valsalva-ratio ranges, and how do autonomic failure and heart failure deform the response?
balance: Guyton & Hall, Ganong, and Boron & Boulpaep frame the textbook account of the standardised manoeuvre (strain at ~40 mmHg for 15 seconds): phase I, a brief pressure rise as intrathoracic pressure squeezes the aorta; phase II, falling venous return drops pressure (early II) until reflex vasoconstriction and tachycardia recover it (late II); phase III, a brief further drop on release; and phase IV, an overshoot above baseline with reflex bradycardia as the restored venous return meets a still-constricted vasculature. The Valsalva ratio — longest R–R interval after release over shortest during strain — is conventionally about 1.21 or higher in healthy adults and falls with age; that numeric range is the textbook/testing-laboratory account, and the fetched normative record confirms the behaviour it rests on: in 557 normal subjects aged 10–83 the Valsalva ratio varied with both age and gender, and no autonomic test regressed to zero even past 80, so age-matched ranges are required (Low 1997). Technique matters as much as physiology: intra-strain tachycardia, post-strain bradycardia, Valsalva ratio and baroreflex sensitivity all shrink as lung volume rises and strain pressure falls, and at fully expanded lungs with low strain pressure many subjects show intra-strain bradycardia instead of tachycardia (Looga 2005, critical review). In autonomic (adrenergic) failure the late-II recovery and phase-IV overshoot are lost and pressure keeps falling through the strain; the blood-pressure recovery time after release lengthens in direct proportion to adrenergic failure grade and stays measurable after phase II is lost (Vogel 2005). In heart failure with raised filling pressures the response deforms the other way — pressure fails to fall normally during strain (the 'square-wave' pattern of the textbook account) — and the fetched review confirms the response correlates significantly with invasively measured ventricular filling pressures (Felker 2006). Beat-to-beat finger-cuff recording has replaced intra-arterial cannulation for the test, and the post-release pattern identifies sympathetic neurocirculatory failure while the interbeat-interval/systolic-pressure slope identifies baroreflex-cardiovagal failure (Goldstein & Cheshire 2017).
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — the four Valsalva phases and ratio are age/sex-dependent and technique-sensitive; autonomic failure abolishes late-II recovery and the IV overshoot and prolongs pressure recovery, while high filling pressures flatten the phase-II fall (Guyton & Hall; Ganong; Boron & Boulpaep)

title: Nephron urate handling: filtered, almost all reabsorbed, secreted, then mostly reabsorbed again — the four-component model the drug-probe tests actually proved
question: In healthy humans, how is urate handled along the nephron — the classic four-component model of filtration, reabsorption, secretion and post-secretory reabsorption — and what did the probenecid and pyrazinamide suppression tests actually show?
balance: Guyton & Hall, Ganong, and Boron & Boulpaep frame the textbook account — the classic four-component model built by Gutman & Yü and by Steele & Rieselbach from drug-probe studies in humans: urate is freely filtered at the glomerulus; most of the filtered load is reabsorbed before the secretory site (presecretory reabsorption); urate is then secreted into the tubule; and a large share of that secreted urate is reabsorbed again downstream (post-secretory reabsorption), leaving fractional excretion of roughly a tenth of the filtered load. The fetched probe records show what the tests actually demonstrated. Pyrazinamide, used to suppress secretion, cut urate excretion during probenecid-induced uricosuria from 463 to 135 µg/min, and from 2,528 to 574 µg/min at a larger probenecid dose — decrements two- to fourfold larger than total control-period excretion, proving secretion greatly exceeds final excretion and that much secreted urate is reabsorbed post-secretorily; the pyrazinamide test therefore underestimates secretion (Diamond & Paolino 1973). Combining pyrazinamide with probenecid pretreatment (blocking post-secretory reabsorption) unmasked abnormal tests that pyrazinamide alone called normal in tubular urate wasting — the non-suppressible fraction was 19.6 ± 12.7% of filtered urate in urate-wasting patients versus 3.4 ± 3.4% in controls (Colussi 1987; 8 controls, 9 low-excretory hyperuricaemics, 7 urate-wasting patients). Solving the four-component equations from benzbromarone and pyrazinamide states in 4 healthy volunteers put presecretory reabsorption at 93–98%, secretion at 30–44% and post-secretory reabsorption at 79–92% (Moriwaki 1990, N = 4 — printed on the face). Steele & Rieselbach's own 1975 summary states the model with its gaps honestly: extensive reabsorption after filtration, then secretion, then reabsorption of an unknown amount of secreted urate, with regulation most likely via secretion, post-secretory reabsorption, or both. The named classic anchors whose records carry no abstract (Gutman & Yü's programme papers; Steele's 1973 pyrazinamide paper) were refused as cards — see the build summary — and the model is presented as the textbook account anchored by the probe studies that do carry verifiable records.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — the classic four-component model (filtration; 93–98% presecretory reabsorption; 30–44% secretion; 79–92% post-secretory reabsorption) as solved from human probenecid/pyrazinamide probe studies, small Ns printed (Guyton & Hall; Ganong; Boron & Boulpaep)

title: Distal potassium secretion: delivery and voltage proven by human drug probes, adaptation by balance studies — the segment mechanism itself is animal work, and this shelf says so
question: In humans, what controls distal potassium secretion — how do distal sodium delivery/flow, aldosterone and plasma potassium itself each change urinary potassium excretion, and how does the kidney adapt excretion after potassium loading or depletion?
balance: THIN-HUMAN-EVIDENCE FLAG, stated plainly: the segment-level account in the textbooks (Guyton & Hall; Ganong; Boron & Boulpaep) — principal-cell sodium entry through ENaC making the lumen negative and driving potassium out through ROMK channels, flow washing secreted potassium away and sustaining the gradient — rests largely on animal micropuncture and isolated-tubule work, extrapolated to humans. What humans have directly is whole-kidney balance and drug-probe evidence, and this shelf grades itself EMERGING for that reason: each control is supported by a human probe, but no human study observes the segment itself. The human probes do converge. Raising distal sodium delivery with furosemide increased potassium excretion in 10 normal subjects, and amiloride — which blocks distal sodium reabsorption and collapses the lumen-negative voltage — obliterated that increase (Batlle 1986): the delivery/voltage limb, in humans. Adapting to a 300 mEq/day potassium diet for 18 days raised urinary potassium excretion from 50 ± 12 to 233 ± 45 mEq/day with only modest rises in serum potassium and aldosterone and no change in the distal tubule's handling of an acetazolamide delivery challenge or its sensitivity to infused aldosterone — the authors locate adaptation in a shift of sodium reabsorption toward the aldosterone-sensitive distal nephron rather than in a rebuilt tubule (Hené 1986, N = 6). Plasma potassium itself is not the whole story: oral potassium citrate produced a kaliuresis peaking 60–80 minutes after intake with no change in plasma potassium and no preceding aldosterone rise, pointing to a feedforward gut/portal signal (Calò 1995). And dietary sodium intake across 3–15 g/day of salt did not change 24-hour potassium excretion in 16 healthy men, while thiazide increased and amiloride decreased kaliuresis similarly on every diet (Pechère-Bertschi 2022) — distal delivery manipulations move potassium; background salt intake, within this range, did not. Neighbouring questions are homed elsewhere and not duplicated: potassium distribution between cells and blood is pack #6075, and what drives aldosterone secretion is pack #6078; this shelf asks only how the nephron secretes potassium. The build-or-fold determination: BUILD (not fold into #6078) — because furosemide/amiloride, thiazide/amiloride and loading-balance probes in humans test distal secretion directly at whole-kidney level; the fold would only be required if no direct human probe existed. Sebastian's human potassium-depletion balance paper was refused as a card because its PubMed record carries no abstract (see summary).
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING — distal K secretion's controls are verified by human whole-kidney probes (delivery/voltage, loading adaptation, feedforward kaliuresis), but the segment-level mechanism on the textbook page is extrapolated from animal micropuncture and is labelled as such (Guyton & Hall; Ganong; Boron & Boulpaep)

title: Transient sphincter relaxations: the stomach-distension reflex that carries four of five healthy reflux episodes — and fires no more often in reflux disease
question: In healthy humans, what are transient lower-oesophageal sphincter relaxations — how often do they occur after a meal, what triggers them (gastric distension), and what fraction of physiological and reflux-disease acid reflux episodes do they account for on manometry/pH-impedance?
balance: PARTIAL slice, verified against its home: pack #2657 asks whether adding baclofen helps PPI-refractory reflux and cards transient lower-oesophageal sphincter relaxation (TLESR) counts only as that drug trial's outcome. This shelf asks the physiology itself — frequency, trigger, and share of reflux episodes — and none of #2657's carded studies is used here (its PMIDs are kept out of this pack's source lines; the home is cross-pointed in this prose only). Guyton & Hall, Ganong, and Boron & Boulpaep frame the textbook account: TLESRs are vagally mediated, swallow-independent relaxations of the sphincter (with crural-diaphragm inhibition), triggered mainly by gastric distension, occurring chiefly after meals, and forming the main route by which gastric contents reflux in health. The fetched human records quantify it. In ambulant healthy subjects recorded for 24 hours, 66% of reflux episodes fell in the 3 hours after food, transient LES relaxation was the mechanism in 82% of episodes regardless of activity or position, swallow-related relaxation accounted for 13%, and straining for only 20% (Schoeman 1995, N = 10). Postprandially, TLESR frequency was 3.5 ± 0.5 per 30 minutes in normal subjects in the atropine study's control period, with TLESR the major mechanism even when basal sphincter pressure was pharmacologically lowered (Mittal, Holloway & Dent 1995, N = 13). The trigger experiment: insufflating the stomach with 300–900 mL of CO2 produced intermittent TLESR episodes, and pharyngeal micro-stimulation produced graded sphincter relaxation — gastric distension is a sufficient trigger in humans (Mittal 1997, N = 8–10 per limb). Frequency in disease is not higher: after a standard meal, TLESR rate was 5.0/hour in reflux disease versus 4.5/hour in matched controls, and what differed was how often refluxate reached the proximal oesophagus during a TLESR (48.1% vs 10.9% at 7 cm above the sphincter), not the relaxations themselves (Iwakiri 2005, N = 10 + 10).
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — TLESRs are gastric-distension-triggered, cluster postprandially (~3.5/30 min; ~4.5/hr in controls), carry 82% of healthy reflux episodes, and are not more frequent in reflux disease (Guyton & Hall; Ganong; Boron & Boulpaep)

title: Colonic motor patterns: a quiet fasting colon, ~60 gentle propagated waves a day, and a handful of 110 mmHg mass-movement contractions after waking and meals
question: In healthy humans, what are the colon's motor patterns — the migrating motor complex in the fasting state and high-amplitude propagated contractions around waking and meals — how often do they occur, and how do they relate to mass movement and defecation?
balance: Guyton & Hall, Ganong, and Boron & Boulpaep frame the textbook account, with one correction this shelf states plainly: the human colon does not show the small bowel's orderly fasting migrating motor complex as its dominant pattern. The fetched 24-hour human manometry records instead show long quiescent stretches — activity low before meals and minimal during sleep — punctuated by two propagated patterns: rare, forceful high-amplitude propagated contractions (HAPCs), the manometric equivalent of mass movements, clustered after morning awakening and meals; and frequent low-amplitude propagated waves that do most of the everyday propulsion. In 14 healthy volunteers recorded for 24 hours, most activity was low-amplitude contractions in no recognisable pattern, while isolated high-amplitude contractions (up to 200 mmHg) propagating at ~1 cm/s occurred at a mean of 4.4 per subject per 24 h, mostly after awakening and in the late postprandial period, often felt as an urge to defecate or preceding defecation (Narducci 1987). The dedicated HAPC study put the rate at 6.1 ± 0.9 per 24 h with mean amplitude 110 mmHg, duration 14 s and velocity 1.11 cm/s, maximal after meals and awakening and minimal in the late afternoon and at night (Bassotti & Gaburri 1988, N = 20). Low-amplitude propagated waves (<50 mmHg, mean ~20 mmHg) were constant in all 16 volunteers at about 61 events per subject per day, over 80% by day, rising after meals and awakening (Bassotti 2001). Pancolonic spatiotemporal mapping in 8 healthy women confirmed propagating sequences as the organising pattern across the whole colon, with normal nocturnal suppression — the baseline against which severe constipation showed mid-colon paucity and disorganisation (Dinning 2010). So the fasting colon is mostly quiet rather than cycling through a migrating complex; waking and eating are the great organisers, and defecation is typically preceded by the high-amplitude pattern.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — the human colon is quiet fasting and in sleep (no dominant migrating complex), with ~61 low-amplitude propagated waves/day for everyday propulsion and 4–6 high-amplitude propagated contractions/day (~110 mmHg) after waking and meals as the mass-movement/defecation pattern (Guyton & Hall; Ganong; Boron & Boulpaep)

title: Anorectal continence: tonic sphincter pressure, a sampling reflex with a guard contraction, and a sensation ladder from first filling to urge
question: In healthy humans, how is continence maintained and defecation controlled — resting anal sphincter pressure, squeeze pressure, the rectoanal inhibitory reflex and rectal sampling, and rectal sensation thresholds measured by manometry and balloon distension?
balance: Guyton & Hall, Ganong, and Boron & Boulpaep frame the textbook account: continence rests on the internal anal sphincter's tonic resting pressure (the larger share), voluntary external-sphincter squeeze, the rectoanal inhibitory reflex (RAIR) — rectal distension transiently relaxing the internal sphincter so the sensitive anal canal can 'sample' rectal contents and discriminate gas from stool — and rectal sensation thresholds that trigger protective external-sphincter contraction and, at higher volumes, the urge to defecate. The fetched human records supply the numbers. High-resolution manometry in 62 asymptomatic women gave mean resting pressure of 88 mmHg under age 50 and 63 mmHg at 50 and over (age association r = −0.47), with squeeze pressure not age-related (Noelting & Bharucha 2012). The expanded normative set (163 asymptomatic participants; 96 women and 47 men with normal balloon expulsion used for reference values) confirms age lowers resting pressure in both sexes, squeeze increment and duration are higher in men, and fewer than 15% of asymptomatic people have a balloon expulsion time over 60 seconds (Oblizajek & Bharucha 2019). Sensation is rate-dependent physiology, not a fixed volume: in 12 normal men, first perception arrived with the initial steep pressure rise on rectal distension, the sensation of wind during the plateau, and desire to defecate at the final rapid pressure ascent — at lower volumes when filling was slow, implicating slowly adapting mechanoreceptors in parallel with the rectal wall (Sun & Read 1990). Anal relaxation (the RAIR) was always evoked by rapid intermittent distension and almost always accompanied by rectal sensation and a rise in external-sphincter activity — sampling with its guard reflex attached (Sun & Read 1990); RAIR parameters (latencies, inhibition amplitude and slope, recovery time and area under the inhibitory curve) are quantifiable at each sphincter level in healthy volunteers, with recovery proceeding from distal to proximal sphincter (Zbar 1998). Duthie-era sphincter studies anchor the classic account historically; their PubMed records were not carded where abstracts are absent, and the values above come from the fetched normative records.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — continence rests on internal-sphincter resting tone (~88 mmHg <50 y, ~63 mmHg ≥50 y in women, falling with age), voluntary squeeze, the sampling rectoanal inhibitory reflex with its guard contraction, and a rate-dependent sensation ladder (Guyton & Hall; Ganong; Boron & Boulpaep)

title: Gallbladder emptying and refilling: a biphasic, meal-paced contraction with immediate tracer-level refilling — and a 38% ejection-fraction floor for the standard CCK infusion
question: In healthy humans, how completely and how fast does the gallbladder empty after a fatty meal or cholecystokinin infusion (ejection fraction by serial ultrasound), and how does it refill between meals?
balance: Guyton & Hall, Ganong, and Boron & Boulpaep frame the textbook account: fat and protein products in the duodenum release cholecystokinin (CCK), the gallbladder contracts and empties into the duodenum while the sphincter of Oddi relaxes, and between meals the gallbladder refills and concentrates hepatic bile. The fetched human records quantify the cycle. After a standard breakfast (40% fat), gallbladder emptying by serial ultrasound was biphasic — initially 0.015 ± 0.003/min, later 0.005 ± 0.001/min — the slower tonic contraction lasting while the stomach was still emptying solids; the gallbladder stayed small until refilling began at 249 ± 67 minutes, and refilling was 70% complete by 335 ± 57 minutes (Lawson & Everson 1983, N = 12). Refilling is not only a late event: with simultaneous scintigraphy and ultrasound, refilling begins immediately postprandially, and in healthy controls the gallbladder handles up to six times its basal volume within 90 minutes of a meal — emptying and refilling overlap as turnover, not sequence (Jazrawi 1995, 11 controls). The fatty-meal ultrasound study adds the resting side: healthy controls had smaller fasting volumes and greater fractional emptying than gallstone patients, whose abnormalities stemmed from a high resting volume (Kishk & Dodds 1987). For the CCK-infusion version, the multicentre normal-values study (60 healthy volunteers) fixed the standard: with sincalide 0.02 µg/kg infused over 60 minutes, the gallbladder ejection fraction at 60 minutes has the least variability (coefficient of variation 19%) and a lower limit of normal of 38% (Ziessman 2010). Meal ejection fractions by ultrasound vary with meal and method — which is why this shelf reports the meal studies as rates and timing, and reserves a single threshold number for the standardised infusion protocol that was designed to produce one.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — fatty-meal emptying is biphasic and paced by gastric emptying, refilling overlaps it as turnover (up to 6× basal volume in 90 min), and the standard 60-minute sincalide ejection fraction's lower limit of normal is 38% (Guyton & Hall; Ganong; Boron & Boulpaep)

title: Urea-synthesis capacity: the liver's nitrogen clearance, halved by cirrhosis, turned up by glucagon and down by glucose — insulin leaves it alone
question: In humans, what is the liver's urea-synthesis capacity — how is the functional hepatic nitrogen clearance measured (amino-acid infusion with urea-N synthesis rate), how does it fall in cirrhosis, and how do protein intake and glucagon regulate it?
balance: PARTIAL slice, verified against its home: pack #6148 asks how ammonia is produced in the gut and cleared by liver and muscle in cirrhosis, and mentions urea synthesis once as an exit route. This shelf asks the capacity-and-regulation question — how urea synthesis is quantified, how much of it cirrhosis removes, and what turns it up or down — and none of #6148's carded studies is used here (its PMIDs are kept out of this pack's source lines; the home is cross-pointed in this prose only). Guyton & Hall, Ganong, and Boron & Boulpaep frame the textbook account: urea synthesis is the liver's irreversible disposal route for amino-acid nitrogen, with a large reserve capacity, regulated by substrate supply and by glucagon (up) and glucose (down). The measurement is the Vilstrup programme's functional hepatic nitrogen clearance (FHNC): during a constant amino-acid (alanine) infusion, the urea-nitrogen synthesis rate rises linearly with blood alpha-amino-nitrogen concentration, and the slope of that line — in litres per hour — is the clearance, a measure of functioning liver cell mass. In cirrhosis the slope was roughly halved: 18.4 ± 6.7 L/h versus 37.5 ± 7.0 L/h in controls, tracking Child-Pugh status and galactose elimination capacity (r = 0.869) (Bianchi & Vilstrup 1991; 9 + 9). Regulation in healthy volunteers: glucagon infusion raised urea synthesis by 35 ± 11 mmol/h and raised hepatic nitrogen clearance from 23 ± 4 to 42 ± 13 L/h (Vilstrup 1990, N = 7). Glucose halved FHNC (32.5 ± 1.9 to 18.4 ± 0.9 L/h), partly by suppressing the glucagon response to alanine and partly directly; high-dose glucagon overruled glucose, raising FHNC 35% to 44.1 ± 1.5 L/h despite hyperglycaemia (Hamberg & Vilstrup 1994, N = 7). Insulin, by contrast, did not regulate the conversion itself: under somatostatin hormone control, hyperinsulinaemia left FHNC unchanged (13.2 ± 2.8 vs 12.2 ± 3.4 L/h) while hyperglycaemia (8.4 ± 0.5 mmol/L ≈ 151 mg/dL) cut it a further 40% to 7.4 ± 1.3 L/h — insulin's effect on urea production runs through amino-acid supply, glucose's through the liver itself (Hamberg & Vilstrup 1994, N = 6). Protein intake regulates capacity in the same direction as glucagon in the programme's wider work (dietary protein up-regulates, carbohydrate down-regulates), presented here as the textbook/programme account anchored by the infusion studies carded.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — urea-synthesis capacity (functional hepatic nitrogen clearance ~33–38 L/h in health) is halved in cirrhosis, raised by glucagon, lowered by glucose, and not directly regulated by insulin (Guyton & Hall; Ganong; Boron & Boulpaep)

title: Ghrelin around meals: plasma ghrelin rises nearly twofold before a meal and falls within an hour of eating, and intravenous ghrelin increases hunger and buffet energy intake by roughly a quarter in lean volunteers and more in obese subjects
question: In healthy humans, how does ghrelin behave around meals — how high is the preprandial rise and postprandial fall, and how much does infused ghrelin increase hunger and food intake at a buffet meal?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology and Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology). The textbook account: ghrelin, secreted mainly by the stomach, is a hunger signal — levels rise during fasting and before meals, fall after eating, and the hormone stimulates appetite and food intake, acting reciprocally to insulin and in the opposite direction to leptin's satiety signal. The carded human studies fit that frame quantitatively: a nearly twofold preprandial rise with a fall to trough within 1 hour in 10 subjects sampled 38 times over 24 hours (Cummings 2001); a 28% rise in buffet energy intake on intravenous ghrelin in 9 volunteers, in every individual (Wren 2001); dose-dependent increases in lean and obese subjects (Druce 2005); and lower fasting levels in obesity (Tschöp 2001). PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

title: GnRH pulse-frequency decoding: at a fixed GnRH dose, slower pulses raise FSH while LH holds and faster pulses erode per-pulse responsiveness (FSH most) — shown in GnRH-deficient men and women given exogenous pulses at varied frequency, across the same range the menstrual cycle uses
question: In humans, how does GnRH pulse frequency decode at the pituitary — why do faster pulses favour LH and slower pulses favour FSH secretion, and what did the GnRH-deficient 'pituitary clamp' experiments (fixed exogenous GnRH pulses at varied frequency) show?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology and Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology). The textbook account: GnRH must arrive in pulses; the gonadotroph decodes pulse frequency, faster frequencies favouring LH and slower frequencies favouring FSH, which is how one releasing hormone differentially controls two gonadotropins across the cycle. The human evidence is the 'pituitary clamp': in GnRH-deficient people the experimenter sets the pulse train. Slowing a constant daily dose raised FSH with LH unchanged (Gross 1987); accelerating pulses reduced per-pulse responsiveness, FSH more than LH (Spratt 1987); in women, 120-minute pulses blunted the LH surge and lowered ovulation versus 60-minute pulses, without raising FSH (Filicori 1989) — a nuance against the simplest form of the slogan, printed on that card. The endogenous LH pulse interval spans ~71 to ~216 minutes across the cycle (Filicori 1986). Note on the foundation: Belchetz et al. 1978 (PMID 100883, verified by title search this session) established pulsatile-versus-continuous decoding in rhesus monkeys — animal work, so under this library's physiology rules it is NOT carded; it is named here as labelled textbook prose only. title: The breath-hold breaking point: involuntary inspiratory contractions build through the hold and drive its dyspnoea; larger starting lung volume delays them, CO₂ accumulation sets the main timetable, and manoeuvres that slow the CO₂ rise lengthen the hold at an unchanged breakpoint CO₂ tension
question: In healthy humans, what sets the breath-hold breaking point — how much do starting lung volume, arterial CO₂ and O₂ each contribute, and how much can involuntary breathing movements be tolerated before the hold breaks?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology and Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology). The textbook account: a breath hold ends not at a fixed blood-gas value but when the involuntary respiratory drive — driven mainly by rising CO₂, amplified by falling O₂, and expressed as involuntary inspiratory contractions and air hunger — overcomes voluntary suppression; starting lung volume, metabolic rate and CO₂ storage all move the timing. The carded human studies support each limb: contractions in almost all of 52 subjects, growing to the breakpoint (Whitelaw 1981); larger lung volume delaying them (Whitelaw 1987); fasting slowing CO₂ production, lengthening the hold and lowering the breakpoint oxygen level (Lindholm 2007); immersion enlarging CO₂ storage and lengthening the hold at unchanged breakpoint CO₂ (Chang 1996). Parkes' 2006 review (PMID 16272264, fetched this session) is the standing caution: no single mechanism yet encompasses all the breakpoint's properties — that limit is printed in the Synthesis. Refusals: Fowler 1954 (PMID 13152037), Godfrey & Campbell 1968 (PMID 5684100) and 1969 (PMID 5193728) and Hill 1973 (PMID 4763084) were all verified by title search but their PubMed records carry empty abstracts, so under the standing rule they are NOT carded and no numbers are attributed to them. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

title: Lactate turnover during exercise: tracer appearance and disposal rise from ~15 µmol/kg/min at rest to many times that in exercise and stay matched until heavy loads; most disposed lactate is oxidised directly (75–90%), a minority is recycled to glucose, and blood lactate rises only when appearance outruns disposal
question: In healthy humans exercising, how fast is lactate turned over — what are resting and exercise lactate appearance/disposal rates by isotope tracer, how much lactate is oxidised versus recycled to glucose (the Cori cycle share), and where does the 'lactate threshold' sit relative to turnover?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology and Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology; the lactate-shuttle account associated with Brooks' programme). The textbook account: lactate is continuously produced and removed even at rest; during exercise both appearance and disposal rise steeply, most lactate is oxidised in muscle and heart, a minority returns to the liver for gluconeogenesis (the Cori cycle), and blood lactate concentration — the balance of the two fluxes — rises appreciably only when appearance outstrips disposal at heavy intensities. The carded tracer studies quantify each limb: Stanley 1985 (rest ~14–15 µmol/kg/min, matched to ~600 kg·m·min⁻¹, diverging at 900–1,200); Miller 2002 (lactate clamp: oxidation up, glucose oxidation and production down); Emhoff 2013 (direct oxidation 75% untrained / 90% trained; gluconeogenesis 1.7 → 4.4 mg/kg/min with clamped lactate). PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

title: Central versus peripheral fatigue: comparing voluntary force with electrically evoked force partitions the loss — in sustained maximal contractions a central (drive) component is demonstrable in most subjects, voluntary activation can fall to ~91%, and TMS put the central share at one-quarter of the force fall in fatigued elbow flexors
question: In healthy humans, how is fatiguing voluntary muscle contraction divided between peripheral failure (the muscle itself) and central failure (falling voluntary activation), and how is each measured — twitch interpolation, superimposed electrical stimulation and post-exercise potentiated twitches?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology and Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology). The textbook account: fatigue of a voluntary contraction has two sites — peripheral, failure of the muscle's own force-generating machinery (shown by a fall in force evoked by electrical stimulation), and central, a fall in voluntary activation (shown when stimulation superimposed on a maximal effort adds force the subject could not produce voluntarily). The carded human studies built and quantified that partition: voluntary versus 50 Hz tetanic force in quadriceps (Bigland-Ritchie 1978); cortical stimulation localising part of the central failure above the motor cortex (Gandevia 1996); train-versus-twitch sensitivity of the central activation ratio (Kent-Braun 1996); and TMS-based activation accounting for one-quarter of the force fall (Todd 2003). Refusal: Merton 1954 (PMID 13152698), the twitch-interpolation foundation, was verified by title search but its PubMed record carries an empty abstract, so it is NOT carded and no numbers are attributed to it. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

title: Dark adaptation: threshold falls in two steps — a fast cone step, then a slow rod step whose time course is rhodopsin regeneration (first-order, ~400-second time constant in the classic densitometry), reaching a final rod threshold that is reached progressively later with age
question: In healthy humans, what is the time course of dark adaptation — the rod–cone break, the rate of rhodopsin regeneration after a bleach, and the final rod threshold — measured by psychophysics and fundus reflectometry?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology and Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology). The textbook account: after a bleach, sensitivity recovers in two limbs — cones first (fast, limited range), then rods (slow, several log units) with the rod–cone break between them — and the rod limb's time course is the regeneration of rhodopsin from its bleached state, ending at the final rod threshold. The carded human studies supply each piece from primary measurement: the two-step psychophysical curve (Hecht 1935); densitometric regeneration kinetics and the shared ~400-second threshold/regeneration time constant (Alpern 1971, using Rushton's reflectometry method); fast cone pigment–threshold tracking (Hollins & Alpern 1973); and the quantified slowing with age in 94 adults (Jackson 1999). Lamb & Pugh's 2004 synthesis (PMID 15177205, fetched this session) frames the modern mechanism — recovery rate-limited by 11-cis retinal delivery — and is cited as framing, not carded as primary evidence. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

title: Closing capacity with age: closing volume and closing capacity rise steadily with age in every population regression, while FRC does not — so dependent airways close during tidal breathing (supine first, then upright), and when lung volume falls below closing capacity, shunt rises roughly fivefold
question: In healthy humans, how does closing capacity change with age — at about what age does closing capacity exceed functional residual capacity upright and supine, and what does that imply for dependent airway closure and the age-related widening of the alveolar–arterial gradient?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology and Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology). The textbook account: small dependent airways close at low lung volumes because local pleural pressure exceeds airway pressure; the lung volume at which this begins (closing volume, and closing capacity = closing volume + residual volume) rises with age as elastic recoil is lost, while functional residual capacity changes little — so closing capacity comes to exceed FRC first supine (textbook account: roughly the mid-40s) and then upright (roughly the mid-60s), producing dependent closure during tidal breathing, V/Q mismatch and the age-related widening of the A–a gradient. Those crossing ages are labelled here as the textbook's account: no record fetched this session prints them. The carded human evidence carries the age rise itself, three independent ways (Buist 1979 three-city regressions; Teculescu 1996, N=158; Sixt 1984, N=178), and the gas-exchange consequence of the crossed state (Dueck 1988: shunt 11.4% when FRC < closing capacity vs 2.4% when above). Refusals: Leblanc, Ruff & Milic-Emili 1970 (PMID 5437433), Buist & Ross 1973 (PMID 4695626) and McCarthy et al. 1972 (PMID 5030172) were verified by title search but their PubMed records carry empty abstracts, so they are NOT carded and no numbers are attributed to them. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

title: Evolocumab before any first event (VESALIUS-CV): in high-risk patients with atherosclerosis or diabetes but no prior myocardial infarction or stroke, evolocumab cut first major cardiovascular events (3-point MACE hazard ratio 0.75)
question: In adults with established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease or high-risk diabetes but NO prior myocardial infarction or stroke, does evolocumab, compared with placebo on background statin therapy, reduce major cardiovascular events?
balance: One large outcomes trial, reported four ways, gives a consistent answer. In VESALIUS-CV (12,257 patients with atherosclerosis or high-risk diabetes, LDL cholesterol at least 90 mg/dL, and no previous myocardial infarction or stroke), evolocumab 140 mg every 2 weeks reduced 3-point MACE (coronary heart disease death, myocardial infarction, or ischaemic stroke) with a hazard ratio of 0.75 (95% CI 0.65 to 0.86) — a 25% relative reduction; the 5-year Kaplan-Meier rates were 6.2% on evolocumab versus 8.0% on placebo, an absolute difference of 1.8 percentage points. The 4-point composite including ischaemia-driven revascularisation also fell (hazard ratio 0.81; 13.4% vs 16.2%). Prespecified reports of the same trial point the same way: total (first plus subsequent) events were reduced (total 4-point events incidence rate ratio 0.80), the prior-PCI subgroup showed a 30% relative reduction in 3-point MACE (hazard ratio 0.70; 7.0% vs 9.5%), and patients with diabetes but no known significant atherosclerosis showed a 31% relative reduction (hazard ratio 0.69; 5.0% vs 7.1%). The cap on the stamp is structural, not a doubt about the trial: this is a single trial programme, and the FOURIER-lineage evidence in patients WITH prior events is a different question, homed elsewhere. No safety difference was seen in the main report. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (Tier C: one large, internally concordant outcomes trial).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single outcomes trial (VESALIUS-CV, n=12,257; median follow-up 4.6 years): 3-point MACE hazard ratio 0.75, a 25% relative reduction (5-year rates 6.2% vs 8.0%); prespecified subgroup and total-event reports of the same trial are concordant

title: Obicetrapib plus ezetimibe fixed-dose combination (TANDEM): the single pill lowered LDL cholesterol 48.6% more than placebo and 16.8% more than obicetrapib alone at day 84 — a surrogate-endpoint slice of the obicetrapib programme (monotherapy homed at shelf #1569)
question: In patients with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia or ASCVD whose LDL remains raised on maximally tolerated therapy, does the fixed-dose combination of obicetrapib plus ezetimibe, compared with its components/placebo, lower LDL cholesterol more than obicetrapib alone?
balance: This shelf is the fixed-dose-combination slice only: obicetrapib MONOTHERAPY is homed at live shelf #1569 (BROADWAY and BROOKLYN), and the pooled events analysis and the PREVAIL outcomes trial fenced there stay fenced here. On the combination question, TANDEM (407 patients with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia or pre-existing/high-risk ASCVD, LDL at least 1.8 mmol/L (70 mg/dL) on maximally tolerated therapy) found the obicetrapib 10 mg plus ezetimibe 10 mg single pill beat every comparator at day 84: LDL cholesterol fell 48.6% more than placebo, 27.9% more than ezetimibe alone and 16.8% more than obicetrapib alone (all relative percent differences; obicetrapib alone fell 31.9% versus placebo). The phase 2 ROSE2 trial, on high-intensity statin, points the same way (combination −63.4% LDL from baseline versus −43.5% on obicetrapib alone and −6.35% on placebo at week 12). The third card is the phase 2 ROSE monotherapy trial, carded as programme support for the 'alone' side of the comparison — it is not carded at shelf #1569. Everything here is an 84-day to 12-week LDL surrogate: whether the combination prevents events is unanswered, and adverse-event rates on the combination (51%) sat between obicetrapib alone (54%) and placebo (37%) in TANDEM. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (Tier C: one phase 3 trial plus phase 2 programme support, surrogate endpoint only).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for LDL lowering only, on a surrogate endpoint: one phase 3 fixed-dose-combination trial (TANDEM, n=407) supported by the phase 2 combination trial ROSE2; no cardiovascular-outcomes data for the combination

title: Lerodalcibep (LIB Therapeutics), a monthly PCSK9-binding adnectin fusion protein: LDL cholesterol fell by about 56-65% versus placebo in high-risk and heterozygous FH phase 3 trials; in homozygous FH the response was small, variable, and non-inferiority to evolocumab was not shown
question: In adults with hypercholesterolaemia (including heterozygous FH) on background therapy, does monthly lerodalcibep (a PCSK9-binding adnectin fusion protein), compared with placebo, lower LDL cholesterol?
balance: Lerodalcibep is a single-source investigational product (LIB Therapeutics) — a small PCSK9-binding adnectin fused to albumin, given as a monthly 300 mg (1.2 mL) subcutaneous injection; it is named here under the clarification exception. In the two populations the question asks about, the phase 3 evidence is strong and concordant on the LDL surrogate: LIBerate-HR (922 patients with cardiovascular disease or at high/very high risk on maximally tolerated statins) found a placebo-adjusted LDL reduction of 56.2% at week 52 (62.7% for the mean of weeks 50 and 52), with 90% of lerodalcibep patients achieving both a reduction of at least 50% and guideline targets; LIBerate-HeFH (478 patients with heterozygous FH) found placebo-adjusted reductions of 58.6% at week 24 and 65.0% for the mean of weeks 22 and 24 — an absolute difference of 2.08 mmol/L (about 80 mg/dL) at week 24. Homozygous FH is different: in LIBerate-HoFH (66 patients, crossover against evolocumab), LDL fell only 4.9% on lerodalcibep versus 10.3% on evolocumab and non-inferiority was NOT shown (difference 5.4%, 95% CI −0.2 to 11.1, against a 6% margin), with wide individual variability. Safety was placebo-like except injection-site reactions (6.9% vs 0.3% in LIBerate-HR). There is no cardiovascular-outcomes trial: the claim is LDL lowering only. PROPOSED LIKELY for LDL lowering (Tier C: concordant phase 3 trials, surrogate endpoint, HoFH exception stated on the face).
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — for LDL lowering only, on a surrogate endpoint: two concordant phase 3 placebo-controlled trials (LIBerate-HR n=922; LIBerate-HeFH n=478) with placebo-adjusted LDL reductions of about 56-65%; the homozygous FH trial is the exception (small, variable response; non-inferiority to evolocumab not shown) and there is no outcomes trial

title: Solbinsiran (Eli Lilly), an ANGPTL3 siRNA, in mixed dyslipidaemia: phase 2 only — the 400 mg dose lowered apolipoprotein B by 14.3% versus placebo at day 180, but the 100 mg and 800 mg doses did not (a non-monotonic dose response on surrogate endpoints)
question: In adults with mixed dyslipidaemia, does the ANGPTL3 siRNA solbinsiran, compared with placebo, lower apolipoprotein B and triglycerides?
balance: Solbinsiran is a single-source investigational product (Eli Lilly) — a GalNAc-conjugated siRNA against hepatic ANGPTL3 (development code LY3561774), named under the clarification exception. The whole human record is early-phase. In the phase 2 PROLONG-ANG3 trial (205 adults with mixed dyslipidaemia on moderate- or high-intensity statins, given two injections 90 days apart), the placebo-adjusted change in apolipoprotein B at day 180 was −14.3% (relative) for the 400 mg dose (P=0.0085) but −2.8% (P=0.69) for 100 mg and −8.3% (P=0.14) for 800 mg — the middle dose worked and the highest dose did not reach significance, a non-monotonic pattern that weakens causal confidence. The phase 1 study (third and fourth cards — the single-ascending-dose and repeat-dose parts of one publication, NCT04644809) showed dose-dependent ANGPTL3 suppression of up to 86-89% with triglyceride falls of up to about 70-73%, so the pharmacology is real; what is unproven is a reliable dose, a durable lipid effect at phase 3 scale, and any effect on cardiovascular events. Treatment-emergent adverse events in PROLONG-ANG3 were no more frequent on solbinsiran (44-60% across doses) than placebo (65%). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (Tier C: phase 2 only, surrogate endpoints, non-monotonic dose response).
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — phase 2 only, surrogate endpoints only: in PROLONG-ANG3 (n=205) only the middle (400 mg) dose met the apolipoprotein B endpoint versus placebo (−14.3% relative; P=0.0085), while 100 mg (−2.8%; P=0.69) and 800 mg (−8.3%; P=0.14) did not — a non-monotonic dose response; no outcomes trial exists

title: GMRx2 (Widaplik, George Medicines) — a low-dose triple single pill of telmisartan/amlodipine/indapamide: it beat each of its dual combinations and beat placebo, lowering home systolic pressure by a further 2.5-5.4 mm Hg over duals at 12 weeks
question: In adults with hypertension, does the low-dose triple single-pill combination GMRx2 (telmisartan/amlodipine/indapamide), compared with dual combinations or placebo, lower blood pressure?
balance: The tested product must be named: GMRx2 (marketed as Widaplik), developed by George Medicines — a single pill combining low doses of telmisartan, amlodipine and indapamide (quarter dose 10/1.25/0.625 mg; half dose 20/2.5/1.25 mg; standard dose 40/5/2.5 mg). Two phase 3 trials answer the two halves of the question. Against its own dual components (1,385 patients), continued GMRx2 half dose, doubled at week 6, left home systolic pressure at week 12 lower than every dual pairing: by 2.5 mm Hg versus telmisartan-indapamide, 5.4 mm Hg versus telmisartan-amlodipine and 4.4 mm Hg versus amlodipine-indapamide, with clinic control below 140/90 mm Hg in 74% versus 53-61%. Against placebo (295 patients with mild-to-moderate elevation, initial treatment), home systolic pressure fell by a placebo-corrected 7.3 mm Hg (quarter dose) and 8.2 mm Hg (half dose) at week 4, with clinic control of 65-70% versus 37%. Withdrawal for adverse events did not differ significantly in either trial, and a 50-patient open-label extension of the placebo trial (third card) kept home control at 60% at one year. All endpoints are blood pressure — a validated surrogate for this drug class, but no trial here measures strokes or events. PROPOSED LIKELY for blood-pressure lowering (Tier C: two concordant phase 3 trials of one programme, surrogate endpoint).
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — two concordant phase 3 randomised trials of the tested product GMRx2/Widaplik (George Medicines): superior to each dual combination (n=1,385) and to placebo (n=295) on blood-pressure lowering, with similar withdrawal rates; no outcomes (event) data

title: Intravenous vernakalant for acute atrial fibrillation in the emergency department (RAFF4): conversion 62.4% versus 48.3% on procainamide, in about half the time (21.8 vs 44.7 minutes) — concordant with the older ACT placebo trials and AVRO versus amiodarone; available in Europe and Canada, not the US
question: In adults presenting to the emergency department with acute atrial fibrillation suitable for pharmacological cardioversion, does intravenous vernakalant, compared with procainamide (or amiodarone/placebo), convert to sinus rhythm faster and more often?
balance: Four randomised reports, three comparators, one direction. In the emergency-department head-to-head that matches this question (RAFF4, 350 patients in 12 Canadian EDs, open-label), vernakalant converted 62.4% of patients within 30 minutes of infusion versus 48.3% on procainamide (adjusted absolute difference 15.0 percentage points), roughly twice as fast (21.8 vs 44.7 minutes), with fewer patients needing electrical cardioversion (33.7% vs 44.2%) and similar, mostly mild adverse events. The older programme agrees: against amiodarone (AVRO, 254 patients, double-blind), conversion within 90 minutes was 51.7% versus 5.2%; against placebo in the ACT trials (Roy 2008, 336 patients; Pratt 2010 pooled ACT report, 265 treated), short-duration atrial fibrillation converted in about 51% versus about 4%. The honest limits: vernakalant works on recent-onset atrial fibrillation (hours to a few days) and much less well on longer-duration episodes or atrial flutter; serious events were uncommon but real (hypotension, and one death in a patient with severe aortic stenosis in the pooled ACT report); and the drug is marketed in Europe and Canada but is NOT available in the United States. PROPOSED LIKELY for rapid conversion of recent-onset atrial fibrillation (Tier C: concordant randomised trials; RAFF4 open-label).
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — concordant randomised evidence across three programmes for rapid conversion of recent-onset atrial fibrillation: RAFF4 versus procainamide (62.4% vs 48.3%), AVRO versus amiodarone (51.7% vs 5.2% at 90 minutes) and the ACT placebo trials (about 51% vs about 4% in short-duration atrial fibrillation); vernakalant is available in Europe and Canada, not in the US

title: Semaglutide 7.2 mg weekly (STEP UP): the higher dose beat both placebo and the standard 2.4 mg dose — weight change −18.7% versus −15.6% (2.4 mg) and −3.9% (placebo) without diabetes, and −13.2% versus −3.9% on placebo in type 2 diabetes — at the cost of more gastrointestinal effects and much more dysaesthesia
question: In adults with obesity, with or without type 2 diabetes, does semaglutide 7.2 mg weekly, compared with the standard 2.4 mg dose or placebo, produce greater weight loss?
balance: The within-drug dose question now has two phase 3b answers that agree. In STEP UP (1,407 adults with obesity without diabetes, 72 weeks), semaglutide 7.2 mg weekly produced a mean weight change of −18.7%, versus −15.6% on the standard 2.4 mg dose (estimated difference −3.1 percentage points; P<0.0001) and −3.9% on placebo (−14.8 points; P<0.0001), with higher proportions reaching 20% and 25% weight loss than on 2.4 mg. In STEP UP T2D (512 adults with obesity and type 2 diabetes), 7.2 mg gave −13.2% versus −3.9% on placebo (−9.3 points; P<0.0001) and lowered HbA1c by a further 1.5 percentage points versus placebo. The price of the higher dose is tolerability: gastrointestinal events were more frequent (70.8% vs 61.2% on 2.4 mg and 42.8% on placebo in STEP UP; 53.1% in T2D), and dysaesthesia — an abnormal skin sensation signal specific to the high dose — occurred in 22.9% (STEP UP) and 18.9% (T2D) on 7.2 mg versus 6.0% and 4.9% on 2.4 mg and almost none on placebo. Serious adverse events were not more frequent on 7.2 mg. A small MRI substudy of STEP UP (third card, n=55 scanned) found adipose and muscle-fat losses with preserved sit-to-stand function, but is far too small to settle body-composition safety. The standard 2.4 mg record and the tirzepatide comparison are homed elsewhere (live shelf #952); this shelf claims only the dose increment. PROPOSED LIKELY for greater weight loss (Tier C: two concordant phase 3b trials).
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — two concordant phase 3b randomised trials (STEP UP n=1,407 without diabetes; STEP UP T2D n=512 with type 2 diabetes): semaglutide 7.2 mg produced greater weight loss than placebo in both, and greater than 2.4 mg where compared (−18.7% vs −15.6%), with more gastrointestinal adverse events and a clear excess of dysaesthesia (about 19-23% vs about 5-6% on 2.4 mg)

title: Amycretin (now zenagamtide), a GLP-1/amylin co-agonist: large early weight losses, phase 2 diabetes data — no phase 3 yet
question: In adults with obesity (and, in phase 2, type 2 diabetes), does the unimolecular GLP-1/amylin co-agonist amycretin, compared with placebo, reduce body weight?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). Amycretin — renamed zenagamtide in the 2026 phase 2 reports — is a single-source investigational product of Novo Nordisk, named here under the clarification exception. Every randomised report so far favours the drug: in the subcutaneous phase 1b/2a study, weight fell 24.3% on the 60 mg maintenance dose versus 1.1% on placebo at 36 weeks, with 22.0%, 16.2% and 9.7% losses at 20 mg, 5 mg and 1.25 mg; in the two phase 2 type 2 diabetes trials (same registration, subcutaneous and oral formulations), HbA1c fell 0.9–1.7% across doses, with estimated differences versus placebo of −0.77 to −1.56 percentage points subcutaneously and −0.5 to −1.09 points orally. The cautions are structural, not directional: this is one sponsor's early-phase programme (phase 1–2 only, no phase 3), the first-in-human and phase 1b/2a cohorts are small, gastrointestinal events dominate, and the phase 1b/2a paper records a large number of withdrawals, many for reasons unrelated to adverse events — so the largest weight figures come from the cohorts most exposed to attrition. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): promising and consistent, but early-phase only.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — early-phase evidence only (phase 1–2, one sponsor programme): weight and HbA1c effects are large and concordant, but there is no phase 3 trial

title: Ecnoglutide, a cAMP-biased GLP-1 agonist from China: −13.2% weight in phase 3 obesity, HbA1c non-inferior to dulaglutide
question: In adults with obesity or type 2 diabetes, does the cAMP-biased GLP-1 receptor agonist ecnoglutide, compared with placebo, reduce body weight and HbA1c?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). Ecnoglutide is a single-source product of Sciwind Biosciences (Hangzhou Sciwind Biosciences), named under the clarification exception, and the entire evidence base is single-country: every trial was conducted in China. Within that limit the results are strong and concordant. In the phase 3 SLIMMER obesity trial, weight fell 9.1%, 10.9% and 13.2% at 1.2, 1.8 and 2.4 mg versus 0.1% on placebo at 40 weeks, with 77–87% achieving at least 5% loss versus 16% on placebo. In type 2 diabetes, a phase 2 placebo-controlled trial showed HbA1c reductions of 1.81–2.39% versus 0.55% on placebo, and the phase 3 EECOH-2 trial found ecnoglutide non-inferior to dulaglutide 1.5 mg (HbA1c −1.91% and −1.89% vs −1.65%); the 1.2 mg dose was statistically superior by 0.24 percentage points, a difference the trialists themselves state was not considered clinically relevant. Gastrointestinal events dominate the adverse-event profile. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): real phase 3 evidence, but one programme, one country, no outcomes data.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two phase 3 trials plus a phase 2, but a single sponsor programme conducted entirely in China; a single programme caps at POSSIBLE

title: Eloralintide, a selective amylin agonist: −20% bodyweight at 48 weeks in its single phase 2 trial — phase-2 only
question: In adults with obesity, does the selective amylin analogue eloralintide, compared with placebo, reduce body weight over 48 weeks?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — phase-2 only, stated plainly. Eloralintide is a single-source investigational product of Eli Lilly, named under the clarification exception. In its one phase 2 trial (n=263, 48 weeks), weight fell 9% at 1 mg and up to 20% at 9 mg and the 6–9 mg escalation, versus 0.4% on placebo — a clear dose response. Two phase 1 reports point the same way: 2.6–11.3% weight reduction over 12 weeks in a multiple-ascending-dose study (n=100), and −2.5%/−4.4% four weeks after single 4 mg/12 mg doses in a first-in-human study (human n=48). Nausea is the dominant adverse event at higher doses (up to 64% at 6 mg in phase 2), with fatigue also common; gastrointestinal events were notably infrequent in the phase 1 multiple-dose study, which used no dose escalation. There is no phase 3 trial, no diabetes population in the phase 2 (type 2 diabetes was excluded), and no outcomes data. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) on phase 2 evidence alone.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — phase-2 only: one randomised phase 2 trial with concordant phase 1 weight data; no phase 3 has been published

title: Pemvidutide in MASH: MASH resolution met at 24 weeks (58%/52% vs 20%), fibrosis improvement not met — phase 2b only
question: In adults with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) and fibrosis, does the GLP-1/glucagon co-agonist pemvidutide, compared with placebo, resolve MASH or improve fibrosis?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — phase-2b only. In the IMPACT phase 2b trial (n=212, biopsy-confirmed MASH with F2–F3 fibrosis), MASH resolution without worsening of fibrosis occurred in 58% on pemvidutide 1.2 mg and 52% on 1.8 mg versus 20% on placebo at 24 weeks — that primary endpoint was met. The other primary endpoint was not: fibrosis improvement without worsening of MASH occurred in 33% and 36% versus 28% on placebo, differences of 5 and 8 percentage points that were not significant (P=0.59 and P=0.27) — at 24 weeks, on fibrosis, the treatment made no demonstrated difference. Supporting programme data in MASLD (steatosis without the IMPACT histology population) show large liver-fat reductions (relative reductions up to 68.5% at 12 weeks and 75.2% at 24 weeks versus 4.4% and 14.0% on placebo), which support the mechanism but are not MASH histology evidence. Fenced and not carded: pemvidutide's obesity limb (MOMENTUM) exists only as press-release material with no journal publication. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), on one phase 2b trial whose two primary endpoints split.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — phase-2b only: the MASH-resolution endpoint was met at 24 weeks but the fibrosis endpoint was not; the obesity limb (MOMENTUM) is press-only and is not carded

title: Cotadutide in diabetic kidney disease: albuminuria down ~44–50% vs placebo in one phase 2b trial — surrogate endpoint, programme not advanced
question: In adults with type 2 diabetes and CKD with albuminuria, does the GLP-1/glucagon co-agonist cotadutide, compared with placebo, reduce albuminuria?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — phase-2b only, surrogate endpoint, programme not advanced: all three qualifiers belong on the face of this shelf. In the single kidney trial (n=248, type 2 diabetes with CKD and UACR >50 mg/g), cotadutide reduced UACR dose-dependently at week 14 — by 43.9% at 300 µg and 49.9% at 600 µg versus placebo (relative reductions as reported), with effects sustained at week 26 and serious adverse events balanced across arms; a companion pharmacokinetic-pharmacodynamic modelling report of the same trial (n=247 analysed) predicted a 45.6% relative UACR reduction versus placebo at 26 weeks for the 600 µg dose. Albuminuria is a surrogate: no eGFR-slope, kidney-failure or mortality outcome has been shown, and the programme was not advanced to a phase 3 kidney trial. The third card is glycaemic programme support from an earlier phase 2a diabetes trial, included to show the molecule's metabolic activity — it is not kidney evidence. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) on albuminuria alone.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — phase-2b only, single trial on the kidney question, surrogate (albuminuria) endpoint, and the programme was not advanced to phase 3

title: Saroglitazar (Lipaglyn, India only): triglycerides −45% vs placebo and vs pioglitazone; glycaemic control comparable to pioglitazone, not better
question: In adults with type 2 diabetes and hypertriglyceridaemia/diabetic dyslipidaemia, does the dual PPAR-α/γ agonist saroglitazar, compared with placebo or pioglitazone, improve triglycerides and glycaemic control?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). The tested product is named per the clarification exception for products not approved or well regulated in the US: saroglitazar (Lipaglyn), Zydus — approved in India since 2013, not FDA- or EMA-approved, and every trial was conducted in India (single-country evidence, stated on the face). On triglycerides the evidence is consistent: PRESS VI showed −45.5% and −46.7% on 2 mg and 4 mg versus placebo at 12 weeks in patients uncontrolled on atorvastatin (relative changes as reported), and PRESS V showed −45% on 4 mg versus −15.5% on pioglitazone 45 mg at 24 weeks. On glycaemia the honest reading is equivalence, not superiority: in PRESS XII (n=1,155, 56 weeks), HbA1c fell 1.38% and 1.47% within the saroglitazar groups versus 1.41% on pioglitazone — the record reports within-group reductions, not a between-group advantage. No cardiovascular outcomes trial exists. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for triglyceride lowering in diabetic dyslipidaemia, on Indian evidence only.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — consistent triglyceride lowering across three randomised trials, but a single-country (India) programme for a product not approved by the FDA or EMA; glycaemic effect matches pioglitazone rather than exceeding it

title: Telitacicept in IgA nephropathy: proteinuria −58.9% vs −8.8% on placebo in the phase 3 interim (NEJM 2026) — China programme, interim data
question: In adults with IgA nephropathy, does the dual BAFF/APRIL inhibitor telitacicept, compared with placebo on supportive care, reduce proteinuria?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). Telitacicept is a single-source product (RemeGen; ex-China rights Vor Biopharma), named under the clarification exception. Publication status, re-verified at build from the fetched record: the phase 3 primary report IS published — a prespecified interim analysis in the New England Journal of Medicine (2026), not merely a supplement or sponsor statement. In that trial (TELIGAN, n=318), the 24-hour urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio fell 58.9% on telitacicept 240 mg weekly versus 8.8% on placebo at 39 weeks — a relative difference of −55.0% in favour of the drug — while eGFR changed −1.0% versus −7.7%. The earlier phase 2 (n=44) agrees in direction (proteinuria −49% at 240 mg vs placebo, P=0.013). A small real-world observational study (n=38) is concordant on eGFR but its proteinuria difference was not significant (P=0.081) — it is labelled observational and adds no weight beyond consistency. Cautions: the phase 3 is an interim analysis, the programme is single-country (China), adverse events were commoner on drug (89.3% vs 78.6%) though serious events were fewer (2.5% vs 8.2%), and the 2-year results are conference-only and are fenced, not carded. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a positive phase 3 interim analysis plus a concordant phase 2, but a single sponsor programme with a single-country (China) phase 3 and interim (not final) data; a single programme caps at POSSIBLE

title: Povetacicept in IgA nephropathy: UPCR −52.0% vs −4.3% on placebo in the RAINIER phase 3 interim (NEJM 2026); earlier single-arm data in IgAN and membranous nephropathy
question: In adults with IgA nephropathy, does the dual BAFF/APRIL TACI-Fc povetacicept, compared with placebo, reduce proteinuria — and what did the earlier single-arm study show in IgA nephropathy and primary membranous nephropathy?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). Premise correction, flagged for the coordinator: at slate stage this row was framed on single-arm evidence alone because the randomised trial was still ongoing — the RAINIER phase 3 prespecified interim analysis has since been published (New England Journal of Medicine 2026), so the question and the balance are built on it. In RAINIER's interim efficacy set (the first 199 randomised participants), 24-hour UPCR fell 52.0% on povetacicept 80 mg every 4 weeks versus 4.3% on placebo at week 36 (adjusted difference −49.8 percentage points), galactose-deficient IgA1 fell 77.4% versus a 9.1% rise, and haematuria resolved in 85% versus 23% of those with baseline haematuria; adverse and serious adverse events were similar between groups (75% vs 78%; 3% vs 4%). The earlier RUBY-3 single-arm study (IgAN n=54, primary membranous nephropathy n=10 — Ns printed on the face) showed a 64% mean UPCR fall in the IgAN 80 mg cohort and 82% in pMN at week 48 against baseline only, with no comparator. Povetacicept is a single-source product of Vertex Pharmaceuticals, named under the clarification exception. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): strong interim randomised data, one programme, trial ongoing.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one phase 3 interim analysis within a single sponsor programme, supported by small single-arm data; a single programme caps at POSSIBLE

title: Isatuximab desensitisation in highly sensitised kidney-transplant candidates (single-arm, N = 23): composite response 83%/82% by cohort, but only 39% reached the cPRA target
question: In highly sensitised adults awaiting kidney transplantation (cPRA ≥80%), does isatuximab monotherapy, compared with baseline (single-arm), reduce anti-HLA antibodies enough to reach desensitisation targets?
balance: One open-label, single-arm phase 1/2 trial (N = 23; NCT04294459) is the whole efficacy evidence base, carded here as its two enrolled cohorts plus a mechanistic second report of the same trial. The predefined composite desensitisation response was 83.3% in the cPRA ≥99.90% cohort and 81.8% in the cPRA 80.00% to <99.90% cohort — but cPRA values were minimally affected overall, and only 9 of 23 patients (39%) reached the cPRA target, which is printed as plainly as the composite figure. Anti-HLA antibody decreases were maintained for 26 weeks after the last dose in most responders; by a median follow-up of 68 weeks, six patients had received transplant offers and four had accepted. Isatuximab was well tolerated, with exposure similar to multiple-myeloma trials. A mechanistic report on 16 of the trial's patients found that pretreatment memory B-cell phenotypes predicted serologic response (AUC 0.958), validated in a separate 10-patient daratumumab cohort — a different CD38 antibody, printed as such. There is no randomised or comparative evidence, and no standardised desensitisation regimen exists to compare against. The imlifidase desensitisation question is homed on pack #3199 and is not re-carded here.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — based on a very small N = 23: single-arm, no comparator, and only 39% reached the cPRA target

title: Urinary CCL14 for persistent severe AKI (observational): AUC 0.83 in RUBY and 0.81 on external validation, but 0.70 in the adjudicated Diamond validation — cut-offs 1.3 and 13 ng/mL
question: In critically ill adults with stage 2–3 acute kidney injury, how accurately does urinary CCL14 predict persistent severe AKI (stage 3 lasting ≥72 h, or death/dialysis), and at which cut-offs?
balance: This is a prognosis/test-accuracy question and the evidence is observational by design, so the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE and labelled observational. In the RUBY discovery cohort (331 patients analysed), urinary C-C motif chemokine ligand 14 (CCL14) predicted persistent severe AKI with an AUC of 0.83, better than urinary KIM-1, plasma cystatin C or urinary NGAL (none above 0.75). The standardised clinical assay — named in the publications as the NEPHROCLEAR uCCL14 Test on the Astute 140 Meter (Astute Medical) — uses two cut-offs: 1.3 ng/mL (sensitivity 91%, negative predictive value 92%) and 13 ng/mL (specificity 93%, positive predictive value 72%). External validation in SAPPHIRE gave an AUC of 0.81, and serial measurements added information (a falling category: odds ratio 0.20; a rising category: 4.04 — relative measures). The largest, clinically adjudicated validation (Diamond, 476 patients) was weaker: AUC 0.70, and at 1.3 ng/mL sensitivity 78.1% with specificity only 49.8%, though values above 13 ng/mL still carried a hazard ratio of 5.70 for kidney replacement therapy. CCL14 stratifies risk; it does not by itself direct a proven treatment. The neighbouring [TIMP-2]·[IGFBP7] imminent-AKI question is a different question, homed elsewhere, and is not re-carded here.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit — observational prognostic accuracy): discrimination was good in RUBY/SAPPHIRE (AUC 0.83/0.81) but weaker in the adjudicated Diamond validation (AUC 0.70)

title: Proactive desmopressin clamp in severe hyponatraemia (SPLIT): the large cohort found less overcorrection (6.8% vs 27.1%), the one small randomised trial found no significant difference
question: In adults with severe hyponatraemia (sodium ≤120–125 mmol/L) treated with hypertonic saline, does a proactive desmopressin “clamp” strategy, compared with reactive/rescue desmopressin or none, reduce overcorrection without causing harm?
balance: PARTIAL row, verified before building: live shelf #126 covers bolus-versus-infusion delivery and correction ceilings, and pack #5655 covers correction RATE versus osmotic demyelination risk; neither poses the proactive-clamp STRATEGY question, and no PMID from either home is re-carded here. The strategy evidence splits. The largest cohort (184 admissions, sodium ≤120 mEq/L, four hospitals) found overcorrection by >8 mEq/L in 24 hours in 6.8% with proactive desmopressin versus 27.1% without, despite the proactive group starting lower (110.2 vs 115.2 mEq/L) — but sodium was also checked more often in the proactive group, and the design is retrospective. The only randomised trial (n = 49, sodium <125 mmol/L ≈ <125 mEq/L) found overcorrection in 16.7% proactive versus 28% reactive (P = 0.54) — no significant difference (the treatment made no difference to the primary outcome in this small trial). An earlier ICU cohort likewise found no significant difference in goal correction or overcorrection, with longer hypertonic-saline duration when desmopressin was used. No osmotic demyelination cases occurred in the large cohort, and mortality did not differ in any carded report. Sodium values are given in mmol/L, numerically equal to mEq/L as used in US practice.
stamp: SPLIT — observational-dominant: a multicentre cohort associates the proactive clamp with less overcorrection, but the only randomised trial (n = 49) and an ICU cohort found no significant difference

title: Evocalcet and upacicalcet in dialysis secondary hyperparathyroidism: evocalcet non-inferior to cinacalcet with fewer gut effects; upacicalcet beat placebo in three placebo-controlled programmes — iPTH surrogates only
question: In patients on haemodialysis with secondary hyperparathyroidism, do the newer calcimimetics evocalcet (oral) and upacicalcet (intravenous), compared with cinacalcet or placebo, achieve parathyroid-hormone targets with fewer gastrointestinal effects?
balance: PARTIAL row, verified before building: home live #1197 cards etelcalcetide only, and no evocalcet or upacicalcet record appears there; none of its PMIDs is re-carded here. Evocalcet (oral): in the Japanese phase 3 head-to-head (n = 634), 72.7% on evocalcet versus 76.7% on cinacalcet reached the intact PTH target of 60–240 pg/mL (difference −4.0 percentage points, within the −15% non-inferiority margin), with gastrointestinal adverse events in 18.6% versus 32.8%; a 52-week East Asian trial (n = 403) confirmed non-inferiority (mean iPTH change −34.7% vs −30.2%) with fewer gastrointestinal events (33.5% vs 50.5%). Upacicalcet (intravenous, given after each dialysis session): in the Japanese phase 3 (n = 153), 67% versus 8% on placebo reached the iPTH target; in the twin PATH-1/PATH-2 phase 3 trials (n = 768), a ≥30% iPTH reduction occurred in 42.1%/43.5% versus 16.8%/17.4% on placebo, with gastrointestinal rates similar to placebo but more asymptomatic hypocalcaemia (corrected calcium <7.5 mg/dL in 31%/45% vs 12%/19%) and more dose interruptions; symptomatic hypocalcaemia was infrequent (0.8% and 2%). Regulatory status, stated on the face: the evocalcet evidence is Japan-only (the second trial is East Asian), and upacicalcet is approved in Japan and investigational in the US. Every end point here is a biochemical surrogate (iPTH) — no carded trial measured fractures, cardiovascular events or death.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit — for intact PTH control, a biochemical surrogate; no outcome benefit shown)

question: In ADULTS with growth hormone deficiency, does once-weekly lonapegsomatropin, compared with placebo (and daily somatropin), improve body composition (trunk fat, lean mass)?
balance: PARTIAL row, verified before building: home pack #6477 is the PAEDIATRIC once-weekly growth-hormone question (heiGHt/REAL4 generation) and cards no adult lonapegsomatropin report; none of its PMIDs is re-carded here. title: Cabozantinib in previously treated advanced NETs (CABINET): median PFS 8.4 vs 3.9 months in extra-pancreatic NET (HR 0.38, relative) and 13.8 vs 4.4 months in pancreatic NET (HR 0.23, relative)
question: In adults with previously treated, progressive advanced pancreatic or extra-pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours, does cabozantinib, compared with placebo, prolong progression-free survival?
balance: One phase 3 trial (CABINET, Alliance A021602; NCT03375320) with two independently randomised cohorts is the evidence base, carded here as its two cohorts plus a grade 3 subgroup report. In extra-pancreatic NET (n = 203), median progression-free survival was 8.4 months on cabozantinib 60 mg daily versus 3.9 months on placebo (stratified hazard ratio 0.38 — a relative measure, printed with its absolute medians); in pancreatic NET (n = 95), 13.8 versus 4.4 months (hazard ratio 0.23, relative). Confirmed objective response was 5% (extra-pancreatic) and 19% (pancreatic) versus 0% on placebo in both cohorts. The grade 3 subgroup (24 patients pooled across cohorts) showed the same direction (median PFS 7.9 vs 3.0 months; hazard ratio 0.15, relative) but rests on very small numbers. Grade 3 or higher adverse events occurred in 62–65% on cabozantinib versus 23–27% on placebo, most commonly hypertension, fatigue, diarrhoea and thromboembolic events. The end point is progression-free survival; overall survival was a secondary end point and is immature/not reported as a benefit in these records — no survival claim is made. US approval for this indication followed in March 2025, per the slate record.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit — for progression-free survival; overall survival immature): one phase 3 trial with two independent cohorts caps at POSSIBLE

title: Leptin physiology: the adiposity signal — what congenital deficiency, fasting and replacement experiments in humans show leptin does
question: In humans, what does leptin do — as shown by congenital leptin deficiency and its reversal, leptin replacement during fasting, and leptin replacement in hypothalamic amenorrhoea?
balance: Framing (textbook account, Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology and Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology): leptin is secreted by adipocytes in proportion to fat mass and signals energy-store adequacy to the hypothalamus; when leptin falls, the brain reads starvation and adapts. The human experiments of nature and replacement agree with that account. In congenital leptin deficiency, replacement reversed hyperphagia, fat mass, hyperinsulinaemia and immune defects in 3 children treated for up to 4 years (PMID 12393845), and in the only 3 leptin-deficient adults identified at the time, physiological-dose replacement for 18 months took mean BMI from 51.2 to 26.9 kg/m2 and resolved type 2 diabetes and hypogonadism (PMID 15070752). During a 72-hour fast in healthy men, holding leptin at fed-state levels prevented the starvation-induced changes in the gonadal axis and partly in the thyroid axis — the fall in leptin is a necessary signal for that adaptation, while the adrenal, renin-aldosterone and growth-hormone axes changed independently of leptin in humans (PMID 12727933). In women with hypothalamic amenorrhoea, replacement restored LH pulsatility and produced ovulatory cycles in 3 of 8 women (PMID 15342807). Fenced neighbours, not re-carded here: metreleptin treatment in lipodystrophy (pack #2884), leptin as a probe in adaptive thermogenesis after weight loss (pack #6298), leptin vs insulin tracking of GH pulses (live #47) and setmelanotide in LEPR-deficiency obesity (live #1093). PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED: the primary human studies are tiny by design (experiments of nature, N printed on every card) but concordant with each other and with the textbook account.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — based on a very small N = 26–28

title: Contraction-mediated glucose uptake: exercising muscle takes up glucose without needing insulin — a 13- to 18-fold rise in leg uptake, GLUT4 moved to the surface, AMPK alpha2 switched on
question: In humans, how does exercising skeletal muscle take up glucose independently of insulin (contraction-mediated glucose uptake), and how large is the effect?
balance: Framing (textbook account, Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology and Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology): contracting muscle disposes of glucose through a pathway that does not require insulin — which is why exercise lowers glucose even when insulin is absent or its signalling is defective. The primary human studies measure each step. Arteriovenous balance across the leg: glucose uptake by the exercising leg rose 13- to 18-fold in healthy controls and in insulin-dependent diabetic patients studied 24 hours after insulin withdrawal alike, supplying 25–28% of the leg's oxygen consumption (PMID 1133176) — uptake preserved with essentially no insulin on board. The transporter step: a single bout of cycling moved GLUT4 to the muscle plasma membrane, +71% in controls and +74% in type 2 diabetes (PMID 10331428) — the contraction pathway is intact where the insulin pathway is not. The signalling step: the alpha2 isoform of AMP-activated protein kinase was activated 3- to 4-fold by high-intensity exercise and not by low-intensity exercise, while alpha1 was not activated at either intensity (PMID 11018120). PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED: three independent human methods (balance, biopsy fractionation, kinase assay) converge on the textbook account. Adjacent but different questions are homed elsewhere and not re-carded: glucose effectiveness at rest (pack #6494) and the exercise cardiac-output and metaboreflex physiology shelves.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED
