title: A DUE: one Opsynvi tablet (macitentan + tadalafil) cut pulmonary vascular resistance 29% relative vs macitentan and 28% relative vs tadalafil at 16 weeks — a haemodynamic surrogate endpoint
question: In adults with pulmonary arterial hypertension on background therapy, does a single-tablet combination of macitentan 10 mg + tadalafil 40 mg, compared with either agent alone, improve pulmonary vascular resistance and clinical outcomes?
balance: The tested product is the single tablet Opsynvi (macitentan/tadalafil, Janssen/Johnson & Johnson), named per the clarification exception because the question is about this fixed combination. In the single phase 3 programme (A DUE, n=187), the single tablet reduced pulmonary vascular resistance at week 16 by 29% relative versus macitentan alone (geometric mean ratio 0.71) and 28% relative versus tadalafil alone (geometric mean ratio 0.72) (PMID 38267108). FLAG: the primary endpoint is a haemodynamic surrogate (PVR) — the trial was not powered for, and does not report, a clinical-worsening or mortality benefit. In the open-label extension, 91% of patients who started on the single tablet were alive at end of study and walk distance and NT-proBNP gains were sustained to week 120, uncontrolled (PMID 41820779, a second report of the same A DUE programme). A Chinese subgroup (n=23) showed larger relative PVR reductions (PMID 41250682) — a subgroup, not independent confirmation. Anaemia, hypotension and oedema were more frequent on the combination. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): one programme, surrogate primary endpoint — the stamp cannot be LIKELY on this base.

title: IMPALA-2: inhaled molgramostim improved DLCO by 6.0 percentage points over placebo in autoimmune pulmonary alveolar proteinosis (n=164) — a physiological surrogate; whole-lung lavage remains the practical standard
question: In adults with autoimmune pulmonary alveolar proteinosis, does inhaled molgramostim, compared with placebo, improve gas exchange?
balance: Two randomised trials of one programme (Savara) point the same way. IMPALA (n=138): continuous daily inhaled molgramostim improved the alveolar-arterial oxygen difference by 6.2 mm Hg more than placebo at 24 weeks (PMID 32897035). IMPALA-2 (n=164 — large for this rare disease but small in absolute terms; N printed on the face): DLCO rose 9.8 vs 3.8 percentage points at week 24 (difference 6.0 points, P<0.001) and the gap persisted at week 48 (PMID 40834301). A 2026 meta-analysis of 4 inhaled GM-CSF RCTs (402 patients) found the same direction (DLCO mean difference 5.09 points) (PMID 42045620). FLAGS: DLCO and A-aDo2 are physiological surrogates, not lavage avoided, hospitalisation or survival; whole-lung lavage is the practical standard of care and was NOT the trial comparator — the trials compare molgramostim with placebo. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): concordant randomised evidence from a single sponsor programme, on surrogate endpoints.

title: HI-PEITHO and PRAGUE-26: catheter-directed fibrinolysis cut the 7-day composite in intermediate-high-risk pulmonary embolism (4.0% vs 10.3%; 0.7% vs 6.8%) — driven by decompensation, not mortality
question: In adults with intermediate-high-risk acute pulmonary embolism, does ultrasound-facilitated catheter-directed fibrinolysis plus anticoagulation, compared with anticoagulation alone, reduce early death, decompensation and major bleeding?
balance: Standalone pack cross-pointed to live shelf #237 (thrombolysis and catheter treatment for intermediate-risk PE), which cards PEITHO, MOPETT, TOPCOAT, ULTIMA and PEERLESS; neither 2026 trial is carded there and none of #237's PMIDs is re-used here. Two 2026 randomised trials of catheter-directed fibrinolysis versus anticoagulation alone now agree on the composite: HI-PEITHO (n=544, ultrasound-facilitated catheter-directed alteplase, funded by Boston Scientific) 4.0% vs 10.3% at 7 days (relative risk 0.39, relative) (PMID 41910345); PRAGUE-26 (n=558, catheter-directed alteplase) 0.7% vs 6.8% (relative risk 0.10, relative) (PMID 42678032). STATED PLAINLY, as the slate requires: both composites are driven by decompensation/collapse and rescue events, not by mortality — deaths were few and not significantly different in either trial. An RCT-only meta-analysis (6 trials, 886 patients) found the same pattern on earlier, smaller trials: less early deterioration (relative risk 0.36, relative), no mortality difference (PMID 42844669). Major bleeding was not significantly increased in either 2026 trial, though PRAGUE-26 recorded 2 intracranial haemorrhages on lysis vs none on anticoagulation. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): concordant randomised evidence for preventing early decompensation; a mortality benefit is not shown.

title: Anaesthesia-induced atelectasis: within 5 minutes of induction, dependent lung collapses in nearly everyone — and the size of the collapse tracks the shunt (r = 0.93–0.99)
question: In patients under general anaesthesia, what is the physiological basis, extent and time course of anaesthesia-induced atelectasis and the resulting shunt?
balance: Framing (textbook account, Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology and Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology — respiratory mechanics and ventilation-perfusion matching, cited as framing, not as evidence cards): induction of general anaesthesia drops functional residual capacity, the dependent lung is compressed, and collapsed but perfused alveoli create shunt. The Uppsala human CT programme measured every element of that account. The densities appear within 5 minutes of induction in all 20 patients studied, occupy about 4.8% of the transverse lung area in the most caudal slice, and do not grow over the next 20 minutes (PMID 3885791). Their extent correlates with shunt at r=0.93 and with impaired arterial oxygenation at r=0.99 (PMID 3085429); shunt after 15 minutes of anaesthesia ranged from 1% to 17% of cardiac output (PMID 3813078). Pooled CT data in 243 subjects found atelectasis in 90% of anaesthetised patients, larger with 100% inspired oxygen than with 30–50% (12.8 vs 8.1 cm2) (PMID 31918847). PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED: a single research group's classic programme, replicated internally across four decades of human studies and concordant with the textbook account; no animal study is carded (animal work appears nowhere in this pack's evidence).
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED

title: SESAR: sevoflurane sedation in ARDS backfired — fewer ventilator-free days and 90-day survival 47.1% vs 55.7% on propofol
question: In adults with ARDS, does inhaled sevoflurane sedation, compared with intravenous propofol sedation, improve oxygenation and survival?
balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — one large trial found harm, against a small earlier pilot's oxygenation signal. In SESAR (PMID 40098564), 687 adults with early moderate-to-severe ARDS in 37 French ICUs randomised to inhaled sevoflurane versus intravenous propofol for up to 7 days had fewer ventilator-free days at day 28 (median difference −2.1 days, 95% CI −3.6 to −0.7) and lower 90-day survival (47.1% vs 55.7%; hazard ratio 1.31, 95% CI 1.05 to 1.62, a relative measure), with higher 7-day mortality (19.4% vs 13.5%; relative risk 1.44, 95% CI 1.02 to 2.03). The earlier 50-patient pilot (PMID 27611637) had found better day-2 oxygenation with sevoflurane versus midazolam — a surrogate, in a different comparator, that the large trial's patient-important outcomes reversed. A retrospective COVID-19 ARDS study (PMID 36614813, n=196, observational) found no ventilator-free-day difference. This shelf is cross-pointed to pack #2999, which homes the separate SAVE-ICU question of inhaled isoflurane in hypoxaemic respiratory failure; SESAR's sevoflurane harm signal in ARDS is a different agent and a different lesson and is not folded into that shelf. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm): in moderate-to-severe ARDS, sevoflurane sedation should not be assumed equivalent to propofol — the one large trial found fewer ventilator-free days and lower survival with sevoflurane.
stamp: POSSIBLE (harm) — inhaled sevoflurane sedation in moderate-to-severe ARDS gave fewer ventilator-free days and lower 90-day survival than propofol in the SESAR trial

title: VExUS ultrasound: severe congestion grades tracked kidney injury in cohorts of 145, 30 and 75 patients — observational only, no management trial
question: In critically ill adults with suspected venous congestion, does VExUS (venous excess ultrasound) grading identify clinically important congestion and predict kidney injury or guide decongestion, compared with conventional assessment?
balance: POSSIBLE (observational) — VExUS grading identifies venous congestion associated with subsequent acute kidney injury, but every carded study is observational and no randomised trial of VExUS-guided management exists, so this shelf answers a diagnostic/prognostic question, not a treatment claim. In the derivation cohort of 145 post-cardiac-surgery patients, severe congestion (dilated IVC ≥2 cm plus severe flow abnormalities in multiple Doppler patterns) carried a hazard ratio of 3.69 (95% CI 1.65 to 8.24) for subsequent AKI and a positive likelihood ratio of 6.37 at ICU admission, outperforming central venous pressure (PMID 32270297). A 30-patient cardiorenal cohort found AKI resolution tracked improvement in VExUS grade (PMID 33132560), and a 75-patient septic-shock pilot found severe congestion in 19% on day 1 with a non-significant association with renal replacement therapy (hazard ratio 3.35, 95% CI 0.94 to 11.88; P=0.06) (PMID 38548949). Cohort sizes are printed on every card: the total carded base is 395 patients, dominated by one 145-patient surgical cohort reported twice. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (observational): VExUS can flag clinically important congestion linked to AKI; whether acting on it improves outcomes is untested.
stamp: POSSIBLE (observational) — VExUS grading identifies venous congestion associated with acute kidney injury in small observational cohorts; no trial of VExUS-guided management exists

title: Ventilator-induced diaphragm dysfunction: human fibres shrank by over half within 18–69 hours of inactivity, and the diaphragm is weak in most patients by the first breathing trial
question: In mechanically ventilated patients, what is ventilator-induced diaphragm dysfunction — its mechanism, time course and contribution to weaning failure?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. The human physiology, as framed in standard texts (Boron & Boulpaep's Medical Physiology and Guyton and Hall's Textbook of Medical Physiology describe the diaphragm as a continuously active skeletal muscle exquisitely dependent on its own activity, and skeletal-muscle disuse proteolysis via the ubiquitin–proteasome system generally), is that complete diaphragmatic inactivity under controlled ventilation triggers rapid proteolysis and fibre atrophy — measurable within 18 to 69 hours in humans (Levine et al., PMID 18367735: slow- and fast-twitch fibre cross-sectional areas 57% and 53% smaller than controls, with atrogin-1 and MuRF-1 expression up 200% and 590%). By the time of the first spontaneous breathing trial, diaphragm dysfunction is commoner than limb weakness (63% vs 34% in 76 patients, PMID 27310484) and independently tracks weaning failure and mortality, and it is present in 80% of patients with ICU-acquired weakness (PMID 26572511). Cross-point: pack #3131 asks whether diaphragm ultrasound predicts weaning success — a test question; this shelf is the underlying physiology it rests on. Textbook framing is context, not an evidence card; every quantitative claim here is tied to a carded human study.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED

title: What lactate actually is: in stable sepsis a raised level mainly means failed clearance, not overproduction — and some production is adrenergic, not hypoxic
question: In sepsis and critical illness, what does the blood lactate concentration actually represent — production, clearance, adrenergic aerobic glycolysis vs tissue hypoxia?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (core), with one EMERGING element flagged as such. A blood lactate concentration is a balance — production minus clearance — not a direct readout of tissue hypoxia; that core is established human physiology, framed in standard texts (Guyton and Hall's Textbook of Medical Physiology; Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology) and demonstrated directly in septic patients: in Levraut 1998 (PMID 9563714), mildly hyperlactataemic stable septic patients produced lactate at the same rate as normolactataemic patients but cleared it at less than half the rate (473 vs 1,002 mL/kg/h), and across patients lactate tracked the reciprocal of clearance (r²=0.73), not production (r²=0.03). Clearance also carries prognosis even when the level is near-normal (PMID 12626973). The EMERGING element — worded here as the current best interpretation, not settled fact — is how much of septic lactate production is adrenergic aerobic glycolysis (catecholamine-driven Na+/K+-ATPase activity in well-oxygenated muscle) rather than anaerobic production from hypoperfusion; the human endotoxin experiment carded here (PMID 12446281, N = 8, labelled plainly) supports that mechanism but is very small. Cross-point: pack #3152 asks the different, strategic question of lactate-clearance-guided resuscitation; this shelf explains what lactate is. Values no carded record confirms are not asserted.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED

title: Pivmecillinam (Pivya): a 40-year-old Scandinavian UTI drug whose re-scored historical trials beat placebo and ibuprofen and matched cephalexin
question: In adult women with uncomplicated urinary tract infection, does pivmecillinam, compared with placebo, cephalexin or ibuprofen-based symptomatic treatment, achieve clinical and microbiological cure?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the efficacy base is largely reanalysed historical (predominantly Scandinavian) trials plus modern supportive analyses, and that vintage is stated plainly here rather than hidden. The US product is Pivya (pivmecillinam, Utility Therapeutics), approved by the FDA in April 2024 for uncomplicated UTI in women ≥18 years. The 2025 reanalysis (PMID 40567143) applied current FDA criteria to the three historical randomised trials with usable subject-level data (185 mg three times daily for 3–7 days) and found overall (composite clinical + microbiological) success of 62.0%–71.7%, clearly above placebo (95% CI for the difference 41.2 to 62.0) and ibuprofen (31.2 to 56.5) and similar to cephalexin (−15.6 to 7.4). A 24-trial meta-analysis (PMID 28341436) could not identify an optimal dose/duration and rated the underlying trials at high risk of bias. A susceptibility caveat runs through the whole base: mecillinam testing is method-sensitive — S. saprophyticus is conventionally reported non-susceptible yet responded clinically in 72% of 74 women (PMID 31067667), and a 2025 laboratory study found no commercial susceptibility test met ISO standards on carbapenemase-producing isolates (disc-diffusion categorical agreement 77.0%–84.5%) — so a 'resistant' report and a clinical failure are not the same thing, and breakpoints deserve the correspondence they have attracted. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): pivmecillinam cures uncomplicated UTI more often than placebo or ibuprofen and about as often as cephalexin, on a historical-trial base re-scored by modern criteria.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — pivmecillinam (Pivya) cures uncomplicated UTI more often than placebo or ibuprofen and similarly to cephalexin, on a largely historical reanalysed trial base

title: Cefepime–taniborbactam (CERTAIN-1): beat meropenem 70.6% vs 58.0% in complicated UTI — but Venatorx's drug is not yet FDA-approved
question: In adults with complicated urinary tract infection including acute pyelonephritis, does cefepime–taniborbactam, compared with meropenem, achieve composite clinical/microbiological success, including against resistant Gram-negative pathogens?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single phase 3 programme. In CERTAIN-1 (PMID 38354140), 661 hospitalised adults with complicated UTI or acute pyelonephritis were randomised 2:1 to cefepime–taniborbactam 2.5 g or meropenem 1 g every 8 hours; in the microbiological intention-to-treat population (436 patients), composite clinical + microbiological success at days 19–23 was 70.6% vs 58.0% (treatment difference 12.6 percentage points, 95% CI 3.1 to 22.2; P=0.009) — superiority after non-inferiority was confirmed, with adverse events in 35.5% vs 29.0%. A prespecified resistance-subset report of the same trial (PMID 38780262) found success preserved against cefepime-, multidrug- and carbapenem-resistant pathogens, in very small subsets. Regulatory status, stated honestly: the sponsor is Venatorx Pharmaceuticals, and the FDA issued a complete response letter on manufacturing grounds — cefepime–taniborbactam was NOT yet FDA-approved at the time this evidence was mined, so this shelf describes an investigational therapy with a positive trial, not an available treatment. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), capped by the single-programme rule.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — cefepime–taniborbactam beat meropenem in the single CERTAIN-1 trial; investigational only, not yet FDA-approved (complete response letter, manufacturing grounds)

title: Simnotrelvir: symptoms resolved ~36 hours sooner in a 1,208-patient Chinese trial — a symptom endpoint only, single-country evidence
question: In adults with mild-to-moderate COVID-19 at risk of progression, does oral simnotrelvir (with ritonavir), compared with placebo, shorten time to symptom resolution?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one randomised programme, single-country, on a symptom endpoint. In the phase 2/3 trial (PMID 38231624), 1,208 adults with mild-to-moderate COVID-19 at 35 sites in China — flagged on the face: all sites were in China — randomised within 3 days of symptom onset to simnotrelvir 750 mg plus ritonavir 100 mg or placebo twice daily for 5 days had a shorter time to sustained resolution of 11 COVID-19 symptoms (180.1 vs 216.0 hours; median difference −35.8 hours, 95% CI −60.1 to −12.4; P=0.006) and a greater day-5 viral-load fall (mean difference −1.51 log10 copies/mL). The endpoint is symptom resolution, not hospitalisation or mortality — no such benefit is shown. Adverse events were commoner on simnotrelvir (29.0% vs 21.6%), mostly mild or moderate. A Chinese retrospective cohort (PMID 40597719, observational) found no difference from nirmatrelvir–ritonavir in disease progression, death or respiratory support. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): simnotrelvir–ritonavir shortens symptoms by about a day and a half when started within 3 days, in the population and variant era studied.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — simnotrelvir–ritonavir shortened time to symptom resolution by about 36 hours in a single-country (China) trial; no hospitalisation or mortality benefit shown

title: Sipavibart (SUPERNOVA): 34.9% relative protection for immunocompromised people — and none shown against the Phe456Leu variants that came to dominate
question: In immunocompromised people, does monoclonal-antibody pre-exposure prophylaxis with sipavibart, compared with placebo or comparator antibody, prevent symptomatic COVID-19?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit, variant-dependent and time-limited) — the variant caveat is the headline, not a footnote. In SUPERNOVA (PMID 40015292), 3,349 immunocompromised participants aged ≥12 years in 18 countries received intramuscular sipavibart 300 mg or a comparator (tixagevimab–cilgavimab or placebo): symptomatic COVID-19 from any variant within 181 days occurred in 7.4% vs 10.9% (relative risk reduction 34.9%, 97.5% CI 15.0 to 50.1 — a relative measure; absolute difference 3.5 percentage points). Against non-Phe456Leu variants the relative reduction was 42.9%, but against Phe456Leu-containing variants (e.g. KP.2/KP.3 lineages, dominant by November 2024) the trial showed NO efficacy (2.9% vs 3.9%; relative reduction 30.4%, 95% CI −1.8 to 52.5, spanning no effect; the authors' own conclusion states no efficacy was shown against resistant variants). Protection is therefore only as good as the match to currently circulating variants, and wanes with the 181-day dosing interval studied. The second programme, pemivibart (CANOPY, PMID 40410927), showed a large relative reduction in a randomised cohort without immunocompromise (composite COVID-19 1.9% vs 11.9% through month 6; standardised relative risk reduction 84.1%) with an anaphylaxis risk (4 of 623 recipients, 0.6%). Products are named exactly as the publications name them: sipavibart and pemivibart. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) with the variant caveat carried in the stamp itself.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit, variant-dependent) — sipavibart reduced symptomatic COVID-19 by 34.9% relative in immunocompromised people, with no efficacy shown against Phe456Leu variants

title: Oral vancomycin prophylaxis during systemic antibiotics: observational data favour secondary prevention after a prior C. difficile episode, primary prevention was not significant, and the two small randomised trials (N=81 and N=21) did not reach significance
question: In hospitalised adults receiving high-risk systemic antibiotics, does oral vancomycin prophylaxis, compared with no prophylaxis, prevent Clostridioides difficile infection?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — and the primary/secondary split is the whole story. This is an OBSERVATIONAL-ONLY evidence base for the main signal, with confounding by indication as the dominant bias: clinicians give prophylaxis to the patients they judge highest-risk, so cohort comparisons can flatter or sink the drug for reasons unrelated to it. For SECONDARY prevention (prophylaxis during new systemic antibiotics in patients with a prior CDI episode), the Tariq 2021 meta-analysis of observational studies found future CDI in 13.3% on prophylaxis vs 21.9% without (OR 0.34, 95% CI 0.20-0.59; 10 studies, 9,258 patients). For PRIMARY prevention the same meta-analysis found NO significant effect (7.4% vs 10.4%; OR 0.18, 95% CI 0.03-1.03; p=0.06; 4 studies, 1,352 patients; heterogeneity I2=76%). A 2025 Bayesian meta-analysis of primary prophylaxis in stem-cell transplant (6 studies, 1,236 patients) found OR 0.31 before adjustment but OR 0.88 and non-significant after accounting for strong publication bias. The two randomised trials are small and both non-significant: Keating 2025 (N=81) recurrence 43.6% vs 57.1% on placebo (absolute difference -13.5 percentage points, 95% CI -35.1 to 8.0), with vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus carriage doubled (50.0% vs 24.0%, P=.048); PREVAN 2026 (N=21) recurrence 14.3% vs 42.9% (P=0.30), explicitly underpowered. Stamp wording must not imply proven prevention: no adequately powered randomised trial exists.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — observational data suggest oral vancomycin prophylaxis lowers recurrence when given during systemic antibiotics after a prior C. difficile episode, but primary prevention was not significant and the only randomised trials were small (N=81 and N=21) and non-significant, with a VRE-carriage harm signal

title: Rapid multiplex PCR for hospital-acquired and ventilator-associated pneumonia (INHALE WP3): stewardship clearly improved (76.5% vs 55.9% on appropriate therapy at 24 h) — but clinical cure was numerically worse and non-inferiority was not demonstrated (56.7% vs 64.5%)
question: In critically ill adults with suspected hospital-acquired or ventilator-associated pneumonia, does rapid syndromic multiplex PCR testing of respiratory samples, compared with standard culture-based microbiology, improve antimicrobial stewardship and clinical cure?
balance: SPLIT — the stewardship half and the clinical half of this question point in different directions, and both halves are on the face of this shelf. The panel carried into the INHALE WP3 randomised trial was the FilmArray Pneumonia Panel (BioFire/bioMérieux), named here per the clarification exception because the evidence is panel-specific. In INHALE WP3 (n=554, 14 UK ICUs), the stewardship co-primary endpoint was met clearly: 76.5% vs 55.9% of patients were on antibacterially appropriate and proportionate antibiotics at 24 hours (estimated difference 21 percentage points, 95% CI 13-28). But the clinical-cure co-primary endpoint FAILED its non-inferiority test: cure at 14 days was 56.7% on PCR-guided care vs 64.5% on standard care (estimated difference -6 points, 95% CI -15 to 2; the pre-set non-inferiority margin was -13%), and secondary mortality and SOFA outcomes narrowly favoured the control arm without clear statistical significance. Two smaller randomised trials rhyme: a French HAP trial (n=109 analysed, stopped early) improved day-0 appropriateness (47% vs 24%) but did not reduce broad-spectrum exposure; a VAP/vHAP trial (n=146 analysed) found targeted therapy at 24 hours in 35.1% vs 23.6% (p=0.13, not significant overall). The INHALE economic analysis found PCR-guided care cheaper overall (-£7,802 per patient, CI crossing zero) and dominant on the stewardship outcome, but could not show cost-effectiveness on clinical cure. Faster, better-targeted antibiotics: shown. Patients doing better: not shown, and the largest trial's cure point estimate favours standard care.
stamp: SPLIT — rapid multiplex PCR (FilmArray Pneumonia Panel) improves antimicrobial stewardship in HAP/VAP (INHALE WP3: 76.5% vs 55.9% on appropriate therapy at 24 h), but clinical cure was not shown to be non-inferior and was numerically worse (56.7% vs 64.5%); clinical benefit is unproven

title: PCV20 and PCV21 in adults: licensed on antibody bridging, not disease endpoints — immunogenicity was non-inferior to older vaccines, and ACIP now recommends a single conjugate dose for all adults aged 50 and over
question: In adults, do the higher-valency pneumococcal conjugate vaccines PCV20 and PCV21, compared with earlier PCV15/PCV13 and PPSV23 strategies, provide immunogenic and clinically meaningful protection against pneumococcal disease?
balance: IMMUNOGENICITY-ONLY evidence — this shelf is a recommendations-and-evidence-quality answer, and it says so plainly. No clinical-endpoint efficacy randomised trial exists for PCV20 or PCV21 in adults: licensure rests on opsonophagocytic antibody (OPA) bridging against vaccines whose disease protection was established in earlier eras. PCV20's pivotal phase 3 trial met its primary immunogenicity objectives — responses non-inferior to PCV13 for the 13 matched serotypes and to PPSV23 for 6 of 7 additional serotypes (serotype 8 missed the statistical criterion). PCV21 (V116, an adult-specific 21-valent vaccine) was non-inferior to PCV20 for the 10 shared serotypes in STRIDE-3 (2,663 randomised) and superior for 10 of its 11 unique serotypes (15C excepted), and it was immunogenic in 717 vaccine-experienced adults regardless of which vaccine they had received before. Serotype-coverage percentages must never be quoted as effectiveness: a vaccine covering serotypes that cause a given share of disease has not been shown to prevent that share of disease. What clinicians actually use is the recommendation layer: since October 2024, ACIP recommends a single dose of a conjugate vaccine (PCV20, PCV21, or PCV15 followed by PPSV23) for all PCV-naive adults aged 50 years and over, extending the previous age-65 threshold, with risk-based recommendations unchanged at 19-49 years. Products are named exactly as the ACIP report names them: PCV20 is Prevnar 20 (Wyeth Pharmaceuticals); PCV21 is CAPVAXIVE (Merck Sharp & Dohme); PCV15 is VAXNEUVANCE (Merck Sharp & Dohme).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit, immunogenicity only) — PCV20 and PCV21 met antibody non-inferiority/bridging criteria against older vaccines in phase 3 trials, but no adult disease-endpoint efficacy trial exists for either; recommendations (ACIP: one conjugate dose from age 50) rest on immunobridging, not measured disease prevention

title: Single-dose moxidectin vs ivermectin for uncomplicated strongyloidiasis: cure 93.6% vs 95.7% in a 726-person trial — non-inferior only against a wide -10-point margin, in endemic community settings
question: In adults with uncomplicated strongyloidiasis, does single-dose moxidectin, compared with ivermectin, achieve parasitological cure?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a genuine non-inferiority result, read at the width of its margin. In the phase 2b/3 trial (Sprecher 2024; 726 adults in communities in Laos and Cambodia), single-dose moxidectin 8 mg cured 93.6% vs 95.7% on single-dose ivermectin 200 micrograms/kg — a difference of -2.1 percentage points (95% CI -5.5 to 1.3). Non-inferiority was declared because the CI's lower limit stayed above the pre-set margin of -10 PERCENTAGE POINTS, printed here on the face as required: that margin would have accepted a cure rate up to 10 points worse than ivermectin, so 'non-inferior' means 'not shown to be more than 10 points worse', not 'equal'. The earlier exploratory trial (Barda 2017; n=127) could NOT demonstrate non-inferiority against its tighter 7-point margin (difference -1.5 points, 95% CI -9.6 to 6.5), and the phase 2a dose-ranging trial (Hofmann 2021; n=223 randomised) is what fixed the 8 mg dose (predicted cure 87%, plateauing across 4-12 mg). Safety was similar throughout (abdominal pain about 9% in both arms of the large trial; no serious adverse events in the dose-ranging trial). APPLICABILITY CAVEAT: all three trials enrolled adults in endemic community settings in Laos/Cambodia; the patients in whom strongyloidiasis is most dangerous — immunocompromised people at risk of hyperinfection — were not the tested population, and nothing on this shelf speaks to hyperinfection or disseminated disease.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single-dose moxidectin was non-inferior to ivermectin for parasitological cure in one phase 2b/3 trial (93.6% vs 95.7%; difference -2.1 points) against a wide -10-point non-inferiority margin, in endemic community settings; the immunocompromised hyperinfection-risk group is untested

title: Zanidatamab (Ziihera) in previously treated HER2-positive biliary tract cancer: a 41.3% response rate in a single-arm trial (HERIZON-BTC-01) — accelerated approval, confirmatory trial still owed
question: In adults with previously treated HER2-positive (IHC 3+) unresectable or metastatic biliary tract cancer, does zanidatamab, compared with historical or standard second-line outcomes, produce durable tumour responses?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — SINGLE-ARM evidence, capped at POSSIBLE by rule, and the regulatory status must be read with it. HERIZON-BTC-01 (87 patients with HER2-amplified, previously treated biliary tract cancer) found confirmed responses by independent review in 33 of 80 patients in the HER2-positive cohort 1 — an objective response rate of 41.3% (95% CI 30.4-52.8) — with grade 3 treatment-related adverse events in 18% (diarrhoea 5% and decreased ejection fraction 3% the most common) and no grade 4 treatment-related events or treatment-related deaths. There is no randomised comparator: 41.3% is a rate in a selected, centrally tested population, not an effect against chemotherapy. The drug is zanidatamab, marketed as Ziihera (Jazz Pharmaceuticals) — named per the clarification exception, exactly as the approval record gives it. Its November 2024 FDA approval was ACCELERATED and is contingent on the ongoing confirmatory first-line trial (HERIZON-BTC-302); if that trial fails, the approval can be withdrawn, and this stamp must be revisited. Supporting context: the first-in-human phase 1 programme included a 22-patient biliary tract cancer expansion cohort at the 20 mg/kg every-2-weeks dose, and a 2025 systematic review of anti-HER2 agents in biliary tract cancer (368 patients, eight publications, several different agents) pooled a 34% response rate — class-level support, not zanidatamab-specific proof. Final results of HERIZON-BTC-01 were published in JAMA Oncology in 2026; the PubMed record carries no abstract, so no numbers beyond the primary report are carded from it.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single-arm evidence only: zanidatamab produced a 41.3% confirmed response rate in previously treated HER2-positive biliary tract cancer (HERIZON-BTC-01, cohort 1 n=80); approval is accelerated and contingent on the confirmatory HERIZON-BTC-302 trial

title: Zolbetuximab plus chemotherapy in CLDN18.2-positive, HER2-negative advanced gastric/GEJ cancer: two phase 3 trials agree (PFS HR 0.75 and 0.69; OS HR 0.75 and 0.77) — with a heavy nausea and vomiting burden and an absolute dependence on the CLDN18.2 test
question: In adults with untreated CLDN18.2-positive, HER2-negative advanced gastric or gastro-oesophageal junction adenocarcinoma, does zolbetuximab plus chemotherapy, compared with chemotherapy alone, improve survival?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — two large, concordant, double-blind phase 3 trials, the standard this library requires for LIKELY. SPOTLIGHT (zolbetuximab + mFOLFOX6; n=565): median progression-free survival 10.61 vs 8.67 months (HR 0.75, 95% CI 0.60-0.94 — a relative measure) and overall survival HR 0.75 (0.60-0.94). GLOW (zolbetuximab + CAPOX; n=507): median PFS 8.21 vs 6.80 months (HR 0.687, 0.544-0.866) and median OS 14.39 vs 12.16 months (HR 0.771, 0.615-0.965). Three qualifications belong on the face. First, the benefit is concentrated in HIGH CLDN18.2 expression: both phase 3 trials required at least 75% of tumour cells to show moderate-to-strong membranous CLDN18 staining, and the earlier phase 2 FAST trial (which enrolled at a 40% threshold) found its clearest benefit in the 70%-and-over subgroup (PFS HR 0.38) — so the tested population is the high-expression population, defined by a COMPANION DIAGNOSTIC: no test, or a lower-expression tumour, means no evidence. Second, the gastrointestinal burden is substantial: in SPOTLIGHT the most common grade 3-or-worse adverse events were nausea, vomiting and decreased appetite, with grade 3-or-worse events overall in 87% vs 78%; in GLOW grade 3-or-worse treatment-emergent events were 72.8% vs 69.9%. Third, the absolute gains are modest — about 2 months of median PFS and, in GLOW, 2.2 months of median OS — against hazard ratios that sound larger; both are printed so the relative and absolute stories can be read together. The SPOTLIGHT and GLOW citations were not re-verified at slate mining; both were verified from fetched PubMed records at build (PMIDs 37068504 and 37524953).
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — zolbetuximab plus chemotherapy improved progression-free and overall survival in two concordant phase 3 trials (PFS HR 0.75 and 0.69; OS HR 0.75 and 0.77, relative measures) in CLDN18.2-high (≥75% of tumour cells), HER2-negative disease, at the cost of substantial nausea and vomiting

title: Perioperative durvalumab plus FLOT in resectable gastric/GEJ cancer (MATTERHORN): 2-year event-free survival 67.4% vs 58.5% (HR 0.71), and the final analysis confirms an overall-survival benefit (HR 0.78)
question: In adults with resectable gastric or gastro-oesophageal junction adenocarcinoma, does perioperative durvalumab added to FLOT chemotherapy, compared with FLOT alone, improve event-free and overall survival?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single large trial, capped at POSSIBLE by the single-programme rule, but a complete one: MATTERHORN (n=948, double-blind, placebo-controlled) met its primary endpoint and its key secondary endpoint in two separate journal reports of the same trial, each labelled as such on this shelf. Event-free survival: 2-year EFS 67.4% with perioperative durvalumab plus FLOT vs 58.5% with FLOT alone (HR 0.71, 95% CI 0.58-0.86 — a relative measure; absolute difference 8.9 percentage points at 2 years). Overall survival: the interim analysis at the primary report had NOT met its stringent significance threshold (P=0.03 against a threshold of P<0.0001), but the final OS analysis — presented at ESMO 2025 when the slate was mined and now verified from its journal report (Lancet 2026) — shows HR 0.78 (95% CI 0.63-0.96; p=0.021, against a threshold of p<0.0499). Pathological complete response was 19.2% vs 7.2% (relative risk 2.69): pCR is a SURROGATE, and it is not the basis of the survival claim — the claim rests on the EFS and OS analyses above. Grade 3-4 adverse events were near-identical (71.6% vs 71.2%), and surgery was not materially delayed (10.1% vs 10.8%). A 2025 meta-analysis of phase 3 perioperative checkpoint trials supports the FLOT-plus-immunotherapy strategy at class level (EFS HR 0.732 vs FLOT alone) while noting discordance across agents and backbones. NAME-COLLISION NOTE: this MATTERHORN is the gastric-cancer trial (NCT04592913); pack #4169 homes an unrelated mitral-valve trial of the same name — the two share nothing but the acronym and must not be cross-contaminated.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in the single MATTERHORN phase 3 trial (n=948), perioperative durvalumab plus FLOT improved event-free survival (2-year EFS 67.4% vs 58.5%; HR 0.71, relative) and, in the final analysis, overall survival (HR 0.78, relative); a single trial caps at POSSIBLE

title: Avapritinib in PDGFRA D842V-mutant GIST (NAVIGATOR, single-arm): 88–91% of 56 patients responded, median response 27.6 months — but cognitive effects in 57%, and no randomised evidence in this genotype
question: In adults with PDGFRA D842V-mutant gastrointestinal stromal tumour, does avapritinib produce tumour responses compared with historical outcomes on other tyrosine-kinase inhibitors?
balance: Single-arm evidence only — there is no randomised trial of avapritinib in PDGFRA D842V-mutant GIST, and none is likely: the mutation (5–10% of GISTs) is intrinsically resistant to imatinib and every previously approved tyrosine-kinase inhibitor, so historical response rates on standard TKIs are near zero. Against that background the NAVIGATOR phase 1 programme is striking: in the D842V population (n=56), 88% responded at first report (Heinrich 2020, PMID 32615108) and 91% at the long-term update of the SAME trial (Jones 2021, PMID 33465704 — two labelled reports of one trial, not two trials), with median duration of response 27.6 months and median progression-free survival 34.0 months. The harm side is real and belongs on the face: cognitive effects occurred in 57% of the D842V population in the long-term report, treatment-related grade 3–4 events in 57% of the safety population at first report, and memory impairment appeared among the dose-limiting toxicities at 600 mg. The randomised VOYAGER trial (PMID 34343033) is the discipline check: in molecularly UNSELECTED late-line GIST, avapritinib did not beat regorafenib — the benefit is specific to the D842V (and KIT-mutant) biology, not a class effect in all GIST. PROPOSED: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single-arm, single-programme base caps the stamp at POSSIBLE however large the response rate.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — avapritinib produced responses in 88–91% of 56 patients with PDGFRA D842V-mutant GIST in the single-arm NAVIGATOR programme (median response duration 27.6 months), a genotype resistant to all standard TKIs; cognitive effects occurred in 57%

title: Daraxonrasib in previously treated RAS-mutant pancreatic cancer: published evidence is single-arm phase 1–2 only (35% response in a 26-patient subgroup) — phase 3 RASolute 302 is ⚠ congress-reported, not yet a journal report
question: In adults with previously treated RAS-mutant metastatic pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, does daraxonrasib (RMC-6236) improve survival compared with standard chemotherapy?
balance: The published evidence is a single-arm phase 1–2 programme — nothing randomised is in a journal yet. In the NEJM report (Wolpin 2026, PMID 42090791), 168 previously treated patients with RAS-mutated pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma received daraxonrasib at 300 mg or less; the headline 35% objective response rate rests on a 26-patient subgroup (second-line, 300 mg, RAS G12 mutations), with median progression-free survival 8.5 months and overall survival 13.1 months in that subgroup — print that N whenever the 35% is quoted. Treatment-related grade 3-or-worse events occurred in 30%. Supporting syntheses are consistent but not independent: a daraxonrasib systematic review (PMID 42882807) found only the same phase 1–2 study plus the phase 3 trial as its evidence base, and a KRAS-targeted-therapy meta-analysis (PMID 42956271) pooled a pan-RAS(ON) response rate of 26.6% across early-phase cohorts. ⚠ CONGRESS/PRESS-REPORTED ONLY: the phase 3 RASolute 302 trial is reported in reviews and secondary sources as showing median overall survival 13.2 vs 6.7 months (HR 0.40, a relative measure) versus chemotherapy — as of this build (November 2026) NO full primary journal report of RASolute 302 was found on PubMed; only reviews citing it. Those phase 3 numbers are therefore NOT carded as published evidence and must not be quoted as established until the primary report appears. PROPOSED: POSSIBLE (benefit) on the published single-arm base.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — daraxonrasib showed antitumour activity in a single-arm phase 1–2 programme (35% relative response measure in a 26-patient second-line subgroup; grade ≥3 treatment-related events 30%); the phase 3 RASolute 302 result is ⚠ congress/press-reported only, with no primary journal report at build

title: PREOPANC-2: neoadjuvant FOLFIRINOX vs gemcitabine chemoradiotherapy in resectable pancreatic cancer — no survival difference shown (HR 0.88, p=0.32); sibling of pack #4824
question: In adults with resectable or borderline-resectable pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, does neoadjuvant FOLFIRINOX improve overall survival compared with neoadjuvant gemcitabine-based chemoradiotherapy?
balance: No survival difference was shown. PREOPANC-2 (Janssen 2025, PMID 40945523) randomised 375 patients with resectable or borderline-resectable pancreatic cancer to neoadjuvant FOLFIRINOX or neoadjuvant gemcitabine-based chemoradiotherapy (followed by adjuvant gemcitabine): median overall survival 21.9 vs 21.3 months (HR 0.88, 95% CI 0.69–1.13 — a relative measure; p=0.32). This is a null head-to-head between two active strategies, not evidence that either beats upfront surgery — that separate question, and the PREOPANC-1 and NORPACT-1 trials, are homed on pack #4824 and are not re-carded here. The choice between the two regimens therefore turns on toxicity and logistics: grade 3–4 diarrhoea was 23% with FOLFIRINOX vs 1% with chemoradiotherapy, neutropenia was similar (25% vs 22%), and serious adverse events were 49% vs 43%. Two prespecified/secondary analyses of the same trial add practical detail: staging laparoscopy at surgery cut non-therapeutic laparotomy (4.5% vs 17.1%; NNT 8), and venous thromboembolism occurred in 9% within a year and was associated with worse survival. PROPOSED: no difference shown between the regimens (the treatment made no difference to overall survival). The unpublished Alliance A021806 trial is not used as an anchor anywhere on this shelf.
stamp: NO DIFFERENCE shown — neoadjuvant FOLFIRINOX made no difference to overall survival versus neoadjuvant gemcitabine-based chemoradiotherapy (median 21.9 vs 21.3 months; HR 0.88, p=0.32) (the treatment made no difference)

title: EUS-guided vs percutaneous gallbladder drainage in high-risk acute cholecystitis (DRAC 1): equal clinical success (~92%), but far fewer 1-year adverse events and reinterventions with the endoscopic route
question: In adults with acute cholecystitis at high surgical risk, does endoscopic-ultrasound-guided gallbladder drainage reduce adverse events and reintervention compared with percutaneous gallbladder drainage?
balance: One small randomised trial plus concordant meta-analyses. DRAC 1 (Teoh 2021, PMID 32165407) randomised 80 very-high-surgical-risk patients with acute calculous cholecystitis to EUS-guided gallbladder drainage (EUS-GBD) with a lumen-apposing metal stent or percutaneous cholecystostomy (PT-GBD): 1-year adverse events were 25.6% vs 77.5%, reinterventions after 30 days 2.6% vs 30%, and recurrent cholecystitis 2.6% vs 20% — while technical success (97.4% vs 100%), clinical success (92.3% vs 92.5%) and 30-day mortality (7.7% vs 10%) did not differ. Two meta-analyses point the same way: fewer delayed and overall adverse events with EUS-GBD using lumen-apposing metal stents (overall adverse events OR 0.43, a relative measure; PMID 37871846) and fewer adverse events (OR 0.35) and reinterventions (OR 0.18) across 11 mostly observational studies (PMID 36832143), with no difference in clinical success. The advantage is in downstream burden — readmissions, reinterventions, recurrence — not in surviving the acute episode. PROPOSED: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single 80-patient randomised trial caps the stamp, and the procedure needs expertise that is not everywhere available (the DRAC 1 authors make the same condition). Product naming: the fetched DRAC 1 record does not name the specific lumen-apposing stent product, and this shelf does not guess it.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — EUS-guided gallbladder drainage reduced 1-year adverse events (25.6% vs 77.5%) and reintervention (2.6% vs 30%) versus percutaneous drainage in the single 80-patient DRAC 1 trial, with concordant meta-analyses and no mortality difference

title: Pre-endoscopy erythromycin in upper GI bleeding: a clearer stomach (82% vs 33% in the largest trial) and fewer second-look endoscopies — a visualisation benefit from small trials, with no mortality evidence
question: In adults with acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding going to endoscopy, does pre-endoscopy intravenous erythromycin improve gastric visualisation and reduce repeat endoscopy compared with placebo or no prokinetic?
balance: A small-trial base that agrees on a process outcome — not on survival. The largest single trial (Frossard 2002, PMID 12105828; n=105) found a clear stomach at endoscopy in 82% after intravenous erythromycin vs 33% after placebo, and halved second-look endoscopy (6 vs 17 cases). Two meta-analyses of the same small trials point the same way: adequate gastric visualisation OR 4.89 across 4 studies totalling 269 patients (PMID 21561232) and OR 3.43 across 6 studies totalling 558 patients, with second endoscopy OR 0.47 (PMID 24045593) — odds ratios are relative measures, and the absolute gains depend on how bloody the stomach would otherwise be. No trial or pool shows a mortality benefit, and none was powered to: the honest claim is a cleaner, shorter first endoscopy and fewer repeat procedures. PROPOSED: POSSIBLE (benefit) — consistent direction across small trials and their meta-analyses, resting on visualisation and repeat-endoscopy outcomes only.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — pre-endoscopy intravenous erythromycin improved gastric visualisation (OR 3.43–4.89, relative) and reduced repeat endoscopy (OR 0.42–0.47) across small trials totalling 558 patients in the largest meta-analysis; no mortality benefit shown

title: Haemostatic powder TC-325 (Hemospray, Cook Medical) for non-variceal upper GI bleeding: SPLIT by indication — strong immediate haemostasis in tumour oozing, no rebleeding or mortality benefit anywhere, and not definitive therapy for peptic ulcers
question: In adults with non-variceal upper gastrointestinal bleeding, does haemostatic powder TC-325 (Hemospray, Cook Medical) achieve haemostasis and prevent rebleeding compared with standard endoscopic therapy?
balance: SPLIT by indication — the powder is good at stopping bleeding now and unproven at changing what happens next, and the mix differs by bleeding type. The tested product is Hemospray (TC-325, Cook Medical) — named throughout because haemostatic powders are not interchangeable. In non-variceal bleeding overall, a meta-analysis of 5 randomised trials (362 patients; 48% peptic ulcer, 35% malignancy) found no significant difference in primary haemostasis versus standard endoscopic therapy (RR 1.09, relative) but fewer haemostasis failures with TC-325 (RR 0.30) and no difference in rebleeding (RR 1.13) (PMID 36968978). In tumour bleeding specifically, immediate haemostasis is the powder's strength: a 19-study meta-analysis found much higher immediate haemostasis than standard therapy (OR 17.14, relative) with comparable rebleeding (PMID 39012642), yet the one randomised trial in malignant bleeding (n=59) achieved haemostasis in all TC-325 cases without reducing 30-day mortality (28.6% vs 19.4%, not significant) or rebleeding (PMID 36262517). In peptic-ulcer-predominant bleeding, the pilot randomised comparison against clipping (n=39) found equal primary haemostasis (100% vs 90%) but more additional procedures needed at second look in the powder arm (PMID 30927124). PROPOSED SPLIT: a useful immediate-haemostasis and rescue tool — most defensible in diffuse tumour oozing — with no demonstrated rebleeding or mortality advantage in any indication.
stamp: SPLIT (by indication) — Hemospray (TC-325, Cook Medical) is an effective immediate/temporising haemostatic, most defensible in diffuse tumour bleeding, but no carded comparison shows a rebleeding or mortality benefit, and in peptic ulcer bleeding it does not replace definitive clip/thermal therapy

title: Intermittent vs continuous-infusion high-dose PPI after endoscopic haemostasis for bleeding peptic ulcer: non-inferior within a prespecified 3% margin in the randomised meta-analysis — not proven equivalent
question: In adults with bleeding peptic ulcer successfully treated endoscopically, does intermittent high-dose proton-pump inhibitor therapy prevent rebleeding compared with continuous-infusion high-dose PPI?
balance: The randomised evidence, pooled, meets a prespecified non-inferiority standard — it does not prove the two regimens identical. Sachar's meta-analysis (PMID 25201154) tested intermittent PPI against the guideline regimen (80 mg bolus then 8 mg/hour for 72 hours) in endoscopically treated high-risk bleeding ulcers, with a non-inferiority margin set in advance at a 3% absolute risk difference for 7-day rebleeding: the observed absolute difference was −2.64% (favouring intermittent), and the upper boundary of its one-sided 95% CI (−0.28%) sat well inside the margin. The relative risk of 7-day rebleeding was 0.72 (a relative measure), and no secondary outcome (30-day or 3-day rebleeding, mortality, urgent intervention, transfusion, stay) showed increased risk with intermittent dosing. Two later retrospective cohorts (n=446, PMID 35135340; n=335, PMID 34889253) found no adjusted disadvantage for intermittent dosing — but both are observational, and in both the continuous-infusion patients were sicker, which is exactly the confounding that makes their unadjusted numbers untrustworthy. PROPOSED: POSSIBLE — intermittent high-dose PPI is a reasonable substitute within the meta-analysis's 3% non-inferiority margin; 'equivalent' would overstate what a non-inferiority pool of small trials establishes.
stamp: POSSIBLE — intermittent high-dose PPI met a prespecified 3% absolute non-inferiority margin versus bolus-plus-continuous-infusion for 7-day rebleeding in the randomised meta-analysis (absolute difference −2.64%); non-inferiority within the margin, not proven equivalence

title: Obefazimod in ulcerative colitis: published phase 2b only — all doses beat placebo on Mayo-score change at week 8 (n=254), durability open-label; ⚠ phase 3 ABTECT is congress/press-reported, not yet a journal report
question: In adults with moderately-to-severely active ulcerative colitis, does obefazimod induce and maintain clinical remission compared with placebo?
balance: Built on the published phase 2b programme only. In the randomised induction trial (Vermeire 2023, PMID 36075249; 254 patients), all three obefazimod doses (25, 50, 100 mg once daily) improved the modified Mayo score at week 8 significantly more than placebo (least-squares mean change −3.1 to −3.2 vs −1.9); headache was the commonest adverse event and was dose-related (42% at 100 mg vs 8% on placebo). In the 96-week open-label maintenance extension (PMID 40417999; 217 patients, no control group), clinical remission was 52.5% and endoscopic improvement 59.0% at week 96 by non-responder imputation — durability data, not comparative efficacy. ⚠ PHASE 3 STATUS: the ABTECT phase 3 induction/maintenance programme has been reported at congresses and in sponsor releases, but as of this build (November 2026) no full journal report of ABTECT was found on PubMed, so NO phase 3 numbers are carded or quoted on this shelf; any phase 3 figure circulating from congress/press reporting must be treated as unverified until a journal report exists. PROPOSED: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single phase 2 programme caps the stamp.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — obefazimod beat placebo on disease-activity change at week 8 in one phase 2b trial (254 patients) with 96-week open-label durability data; ⚠ the phase 3 ABTECT programme is congress/press-reported only, with no journal report at build

title: Duvakitug (anti-TL1A) in ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease (RELIEVE UCCD, phase 2b): 900 mg roughly doubled placebo remission/response at week 14 — ⚠ phase-2 only, with a Bayesian primary analysis
question: In adults with moderately-to-severely active ulcerative colitis or Crohn's disease, does duvakitug (anti-TL1A) induce clinical remission or response compared with placebo?
balance: Phase-2 evidence only, analysed Bayesianly — both facts are on the face. RELIEVE UCCD randomised separate ulcerative colitis (137 patients) and Crohn's disease (138 in the modified intention-to-treat set) cohorts to duvakitug 450 mg or 900 mg every 2 weeks (after a 2250 mg loading dose) or placebo for 14 weeks. In ulcerative colitis, clinical remission was 36% (450 mg) and 48% (900 mg) vs 20% on placebo (Reinisch 2026, PMID 42462750). In Crohn's disease, endoscopic response was 26% and 48% vs 13% on placebo (Jairath 2026, PMID 42462749). ⚠ ANALYSIS METHOD: both trials' primary analyses were Bayesian — a dose was declared successful if the posterior probability that its response rate exceeded placebo reached a prespecified threshold (0.90 or greater; the papers report posterior probabilities of 0.94 to >0.99 and differences in posterior mean rates with credible intervals, not conventional p-values or confidence intervals). The 450 mg Crohn's result (posterior probability 0.94, credible interval for the difference including −3%) is correspondingly softer than the 900 mg results. A class-level systematic review of anti-TL1A phase 2 trials (PMID 42726749) is directionally consistent (duvakitug dose-response in UC; Crohn's endoscopic response RR 3.67 at 900 mg, a relative measure). Adverse events were similar to placebo in both trials. PROPOSED: POSSIBLE (benefit) — phase 2 only, one programme, Bayesian primary analysis.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — duvakitug beat placebo in the phase 2b RELIEVE UCCD programme (UC remission 48% at 900 mg vs 20%; Crohn's endoscopic response 48% vs 13% at week 14); ⚠ phase-2 only, and the primary analyses were Bayesian (posterior-probability rule), not conventional frequentist tests

title: Vedolizumab for chronic pouchitis after ileal pouch–anal anastomosis (EARNEST)
question: In adults with chronic pouchitis after ileal pouch–anal anastomosis (IPAA) for ulcerative colitis, does vedolizumab, compared with placebo, induce remission?
balance: One randomised trial only — a single programme caps the stamp at POSSIBLE. EARNEST (n = 102 randomised) is the first placebo-controlled trial in chronic pouchitis: modified Pouchitis Disease Activity Index (mPDAI)-defined remission at week 14 was 31% on vedolizumab vs 10% on placebo (difference 21 percentage points), with the advantage persisting in direction at week 34 and supported by a second report showing endoscopic improvement and mucosal healing. The population is small and rare (chronic pouchitis after IPAA for ulcerative colitis), every patient also received 4 weeks of ciprofloxacin, and there is no comparison against antibiotics alone as chronic therapy, other biologics, or surgery. Nothing here addresses patients whose pouchitis is not chronic, or pouch failure as an outcome.

title: EUS-guided gastroenterostomy for malignant gastric outlet obstruction (ENDURO and DRA-GOO)
question: In adults with malignant gastric outlet obstruction in a palliative setting, does endoscopic ultrasound-guided gastroenterostomy (EUS-GE), compared with surgical gastrojejunostomy or enteral stenting, speed resumption of oral intake and reduce reintervention?
balance: Two randomised trials point the same way against two different comparators. ENDURO (n = 98, 12 Dutch academic and teaching hospitals) found EUS-GE superior to surgical gastrojejunostomy for time to resumption of solid oral intake (median 1 vs 3 days) and non-inferior for reintervention. DRA-GOO (n = 97, seven international sites) found EUS-GE markedly reduced 6-month reintervention vs uncovered duodenal stenting (4% vs 29%; risk ratio 0.15, a relative measure). Both are expertise-dependent procedures: ENDURO centres had to show experience in at least 20 LAMS placements and at least ten endoscopic gastroenterostomies before treating trial patients independently, so results may not transfer to low-volume settings. Neither trial showed a survival difference, and 30-day mortality in DRA-GOO was numerically higher with EUS-GE (21% vs 12%, not significant). Citation discipline: the original DRA-GOO report was retracted and republished; this shelf cites ONLY the republished version (PMID 40347959).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two concordant multicentre RCTs against two different comparators, but an expertise-dependent procedure tested in selected centres; a two-trial procedural base caps the stamp at POSSIBLE

title: Lumen-apposing metal stents vs plastic stents for pancreatic walled-off necrosis
question: In adults with pancreatic walled-off necrosis undergoing endoscopic drainage, do lumen-apposing metal stents (LAMS), compared with double-pigtail plastic stents, improve treatment success and reduce adverse events?
balance: The randomised record is split, and the honest summary is 'no consistent advantage'. Bang et al. (n = 60) found non-superiority of LAMS with MORE stent-related adverse events (32.3% vs 6.9%); PROMETHEUS (n = 64) found similar clinical success and similar stent adverse events; a 2024 multicentre trial in infected walled-off necrosis (n = 46) found no difference in necrosectomy number but higher 8-week clinical success with a novel electrocautery-enhanced LAMS; and a 2025 meta-analysis of seven RCTs found no difference in treatment success, bleeding, necrosectomy, reintervention, hospitalisation or mortality — only shorter procedure time with metal stents. The safety story is protocol-dependent, and it changed practice mid-programme: in Bang's trial, significant LAMS adverse events (including bleeding) clustered at ≥3 weeks, an interim audit changed the protocol to CT imaging at 3 weeks with LAMS removal if the collection had resolved, and after that amendment the adverse-event difference disappeared. A LAMS result quoted without its removal protocol is not the intervention that was finally tested. Where publications name the stent it is named on the card (clarification exception); several reports describe the device class without a brand the abstract records, and those cards say so.
stamp: SPLIT — randomised trials disagree and the pooled result shows no advantage in treatment success: LAMS shorten procedures, and their early safety disadvantage disappeared after protocols changed to 3-week imaging and early removal

title: Efimosfermin alfa (FGF21 analogue) for MASH with fibrosis
question: In adults with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) and fibrosis, does efimosfermin alfa (a long-acting FGF21 analogue), compared with placebo, improve liver histology?
balance: PHASE-2 + SMALL-N flags, printed on the stamp line as required: the histology claim rests on 65 evaluable paired biopsies from the 84 patients randomised in the biopsy trial. PREMISE CORRECTION to the slate: the 24-week histology trial was expected as a Gastroenterology 2025 paper; the verified full journal report is in The Lancet (PMID 41655584), and its published primary endpoint was safety and tolerability — the fetched record does not report histology response percentages, so none are printed here and the biopsy cohort (65 of 84) is stated instead of invented response rates. The earlier phase 2a trial (n = 102, phenotypic MASH without biopsy entry criteria) showed a large hepatic-fat signal (≥30% fat reduction in 89% of evaluable efimosfermin patients vs 7% on placebo at 12 weeks). Monthly subcutaneous dosing is part of the intervention's appeal. There are no clinical-outcome data (no decompensation, transplant or mortality endpoints) and no basis for extrapolating histology to outcomes. An open-label extension report exists (PMID 41660650) but its abstract was not captured from the record this session, so no numbers are taken from it.

title: Fazirsiran for alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency liver disease (PiZZ)
question: In adults with alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency liver disease (PiZZ), does fazirsiran (RNA interference against Z-AAT), compared with placebo or no treatment, reduce hepatic Z-AAT accumulation and improve liver histology?
balance: The published human base is very small and is printed on the stamp line: 16 patients in the open-label NEJM report (the base the slate flagged as N = 16) plus 40 randomised patients in SEQUOIA — 56 patients in total, all phase 2. PREMISE UPDATE: SEQUOIA's journal status was unverified at slate time; at build it is verified as a full journal report (Gastroenterology 2024, PMID 38964420) and is carded. The biology is coherent and the effect on the target is large and dose-dependent (serum Z-AAT down 61–94% by dose; median liver Z-AAT down 93% on biopsy vs a 26% increase on placebo), with globule-burden reduction in every fazirsiran-treated SEQUOIA patient. But every endpoint is a biomarker or a histology score — no trial shows prevention of decompensation, transplant or death — fibrosis regression in the open-label report (7 of 15) comes from 15 biopsied patients without a control group, and pulmonary function was stable over these short horizons in a disease whose other organ manifestation is emphysema. A single small programme caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — phase 2 only and a very small published base: N = 16 in the first open-label report, with the randomised SEQUOIA trial adding 40 (total published base 56 patients); biomarker and histology endpoints only, no clinical outcomes

title: Larsucosterol for severe alcohol-associated hepatitis (AHFIRM)
question: In adults with severe alcohol-associated hepatitis, does larsucosterol, compared with placebo, reduce 90-day mortality or liver transplantation?
balance: NEGATIVE PRIMARY ENDPOINT — the honest shelf leads with the null. AHFIRM (n = 307 enrolled, 301 dosed) did not meet its primary endpoint: the difference in 90-day mortality or liver transplantation between either larsucosterol dose (30 mg or 90 mg) and placebo did not reach statistical significance. Ninety-day mortality counts were 15 of 102 (30 mg), 17 of 102 (90 mg) and 25 of 103 (placebo). Sponsor communications have quoted '41% / 35% mortality reductions' from these counts: those figures are RELATIVE reductions computed from the same counts, they are NON-SIGNIFICANT, and they come from a trial that missed its primary endpoint — they are printed on the cards only with those three labels attached. The prespecified US analysis and the subgroup treated within 10 days of hospitalisation show larger numerical gaps, but both are slices of a negative trial and cannot rescue the primary result. The earlier phase 2a study (n = 19, open-label, uncontrolled) reported no deaths at 28 days, which is encouraging safety background and nothing more. The trial authors' own conclusion is that equipoise exists for a further trial — not that benefit is shown.
stamp: NO BENEFIT DEMONSTRATED (the treatment made no difference) — AHFIRM (n = 307) missed its primary endpoint of 90-day mortality or liver transplantation; lower mortality counts on larsucosterol were non-significant

title: DIALIVE albumin dialysis for acute-on-chronic liver failure
question: In adults with acute-on-chronic liver failure, does DIALIVE albumin dialysis, compared with standard care, improve organ failure resolution and survival?
balance: One small first-in-human randomised trial is the entire published base — the randomised N (32) is printed on the stamp line, and all three evidence cards are explicitly labelled aspects of that single report (PMID 37268222); there is no second trial to card. The citation and N the slate left unverified were verified at build from the fetched record: Journal of Hepatology 2023, 32 patients with alcohol-related ACLF, NCT03065699. DIALIVE is a specific device (DIALIVE, Yaqrit) that exchanges dysfunctional albumin and removes damage- and pathogen-associated molecular patterns — it is not interchangeable with other extracorporeal liver-support systems (the MARS/Prometheus question is homed separately in pack #6540 and is not merged here). The trial's primary aim was safety, and safety was acceptable; 28-day mortality did not differ. The positive findings are day-10 prognostic scores (CLIF-C organ failure and CLIF-C ACLF), faster ACLF resolution and a coherent set of inflammatory biomarkers — surrogate and score outcomes in 30 patients with at least three treatment sessions, from a trial far too small to test survival. A larger trial of an updated device (DIALIVE 2.0) exists only as a published protocol (PMID 42994933), which is mentioned here as a protocol and is not evidence.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single first-in-human randomised trial, N = 32 randomised; the safety primary aim was met and prognostic scores improved, but no mortality difference was shown

title: Hepatic venous pressure gradient and portal pressure physiology (PHYSIOLOGY)
question: In chronic liver disease, what does the hepatic venous pressure gradient (HVPG) measure, how is portal pressure physiologically determined, and which HVPG thresholds carry prognostic meaning?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY entry — no intervention stamp. What HVPG is: a catheter in a hepatic vein measures wedged (occluded) hepatic venous pressure and free hepatic venous pressure; their difference, the HVPG, estimates the portal pressure gradient across the liver in sinusoidal portal hypertension. Textbook framing (Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology; Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology — named here as framing, not as evidence cards): portal pressure is determined by portal venous inflow multiplied by the resistance to that flow, and in cirrhosis the dominant change is increased intrahepatic resistance (fixed architectural distortion plus a dynamic, vasoactive component), later compounded by increased splanchnic inflow — values or mechanisms stated in this paragraph that no carded cohort confirms are the textbooks' account. The threshold ladder is NOT free-floating: each rung on the cards is tied to its source cohort — below 10 mmHg, compensated patients in the Ripoll cohort (n = 213) had a 90% probability of remaining free of decompensation over a median 4 years, and 10 mmHg is the conventional boundary of clinically significant portal hypertension; a post-TIPS portosystemic gradient below 12 mmHg was the threshold associated with protection from rebleeding in a 2,100-patient retrospective series (the 12 mmHg rung comes from the bleeding-protection literature, not from a natural-history cohort); 16 mmHg or above predicted further decompensation after oesophageal variceal bleeding in a 145-patient prospective cohort; and in acute variceal bleeding, an HVPG of 20 mmHg or above measured within about a day of admission marked failure to control bleeding and far worse 1-year survival (Moitinho, n = 65). Drug effects on HVPG are a treatment question homed elsewhere — see packs #3594 and #6083, cross-pointed here in prose only; none of their PMIDs are carded in this pack.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED

title: Prasinezumab in early Parkinson's disease (PASADENA and PADOVA)
question: In adults with early-stage Parkinson's disease, does the anti-α-synuclein antibody prasinezumab, compared with placebo, slow clinical progression on the MDS-UPDRS?
balance: Two randomised programmes, two missed primary endpoints — the shelf leads with that. PASADENA (phase 2, n = 316, largely treatment-naive or MAO-B-inhibitor patients) missed its primary endpoint (change in MDS-UPDRS parts I+II+III at week 52) at both doses. PADOVA (phase 2b, n = 586, patients on stable symptomatic medication) missed its primary endpoint too (time to confirmed motor progression: HR 0.84; p = 0.066). PREMISE CORRECTION to the slate: PADOVA existed only as sponsor/congress material at mining time, but at build it is a full journal report in The Lancet (PMID 42208564, verified from the fetched record) and is therefore carded as published evidence, not fenced as congress-reported — the developer may wish to note the change. What remains positive is exploratory: smaller Part III motor-score increases during PASADENA's double-blind year, and an open-label extension analysis against an external observational comparator (PMI/PPMI cohort) suggesting sustained separation — a non-randomised comparison that cannot confirm efficacy. Infusion reactions were common in PASADENA (19% and 34% by dose). Class lesson: prasinezumab's sister anti-α-synuclein antibody cinpanemab also missed definitively in its phase 2 programme (SPARK) — that shelf is being built this wave as #6729 and is cross-pointed here in prose; two antibodies against the same target have now missed their primaries, which is the honest state of the anti-synuclein antibody hypothesis in early Parkinson's disease. A phase 3 trial (PARAISO) is ongoing per the PADOVA report.
stamp: NO BENEFIT DEMONSTRATED (the treatment made no difference) — both randomised programmes missed their primary endpoints (PASADENA phase 2, PADOVA phase 2b); only exploratory motor signals remain

title: SPARK: cinpanemab made no difference in early Parkinson's disease — every dose matched placebo on the MDS-UPDRS and DaT-SPECT, and development was discontinued
question: In adults with early Parkinson's disease, does the anti-alpha-synuclein antibody cinpanemab, versus placebo, slow progression on the MDS-UPDRS or DaT-SPECT?
balance: SPARK (Lang et al., PMID 35921450) randomised 357 people with early Parkinson's disease to placebo or cinpanemab 250/1250/3500 mg every 4 weeks: MDS-UPDRS total score worsened 10.8 points on placebo vs 10.5, 11.3 and 10.9 points on the three doses at week 52 (all differences non-significant), DaT-SPECT showed no separation, and the trial was stopped after the week-72 interim analysis for lack of efficacy, after which development was discontinued. The biomarker companion report (PMID 38315945) found no treatment effect on any CSF, plasma or imaging measure. A phase 1 CSF analysis (PMID 39892989) shows the antibody did engage alpha-synuclein in the central compartment, dose-dependently — so this is target engagement without clinical benefit, the same pattern as the second anti-alpha-synuclein antibody programme, prasinezumab, homed on Shelf #6728 (built this wave): two antibodies, two missed programmes, and a mechanism-concordant meta-analysis of both (PMID 42992461; n=673) pooling to a mean difference of -0.047 (95% CI -0.202 to 0.108). PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference).
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — cinpanemab did not slow progression in early Parkinson's disease in the phase 2 SPARK trial

title: evoke and evoke+: oral semaglutide made no difference in early Alzheimer's disease — both phase 3 trials negative in 3,808 participants
question: In adults with early symptomatic Alzheimer's disease, does oral semaglutide 14 mg daily, versus placebo, slow decline on the CDR-SB over about 2 years?
balance: The evoke and evoke+ phase 3 trials (Cummings et al., PMID 41865758 — the PMID re-verified against its PubMed record at build time) randomised 3,808 people with amyloid-confirmed early Alzheimer's disease to oral semaglutide 14 mg daily or placebo: CDR-SB difference at week 104 was -0.08 (p=0.57) in evoke and +0.10 (p=0.46) in evoke+, and both trials were discontinued for the negative outcome. Adverse events were more frequent on semaglutide (91.2% vs 84.8%), gastrointestinal events dominate the older-adult safety profile (PMID 40337158), and weight loss — a liability in this population — was consistent. A 2026 meta-analysis of all seven GLP-1-agonist RCTs in Alzheimer's disease and MCI (PMID 42890838; 4,132 participants) is concordant: no cognitive or CDR-SB benefit. The shelf's value is closing the GLP-1-in-Alzheimer's question at phase 3 scale. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference).
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — oral semaglutide did not slow clinical progression in early Alzheimer's disease in the evoke and evoke+ phase 3 trials

title: ELAD: liraglutide did not preserve cerebral glucose metabolism in Alzheimer's disease — the phase 2b primary outcome was negative, with only exploratory secondary signals
question: In adults with mild Alzheimer's disease, does liraglutide, versus placebo, preserve cerebral glucose metabolism, cognition or brain volume over 52 weeks?
balance: ELAD (Edison et al., PMID 41326666; the slate's 'Femminella' attribution is corrected by the PubMed record) randomised 204 people with mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease without diabetes to daily liraglutide or placebo for 52 weeks and missed its primary outcome: cerebral glucose metabolic rate difference -0.17 (95% CI -0.39 to 0.06; p=0.14). The ADAS-Exec secondary favoured liraglutide (0.15; unadjusted p=0.01) but was unadjusted for multiplicity, and ADCS-ADL and CDR-Sum of Boxes were null. The earlier supporting trial (Gejl et al., PMIDs 27252647 and 29235507 — two reports of one 38-patient trial) found placebo-group metabolic decline that liraglutide appeared to prevent, and a rise in blood-brain glucose transfer capacity, but no cognitive change and no amyloid effect. Phase-2-only evidence; the small-trial surrogate story has not been confirmed at ELAD's scale. PROPOSED SPLIT, leaning negative on the primary outcome.

title: SNIFF: intranasal insulin made no difference in MCI and Alzheimer's dementia over 12 months — and the 5-trial meta-analysis agrees
question: In adults with amnestic MCI or Alzheimer's dementia, does daily intranasal insulin, versus placebo, improve cognition or function over 12 months?
balance: SNIFF (Craft et al., PMID 32568367) randomised 289 adults with amnestic MCI or Alzheimer's dementia to intranasal insulin 40 IU daily (Humulin R U-100, Lilly, as named in the record) or placebo for 12 months and found an ADAS-Cog12 difference of 0.03 points (p=0.98) in its primary cohort, with all clinical and CSF secondaries null. The delivery device is part of the intervention: the first device proved unreliable in the first 49 participants and was replaced; neither SNIFF device is named in the record, while the earlier positive pilot (PMID 21911655; n=104) used a device named in its record as Kurve Technology (Bothell, Washington). A secondary white-matter imaging analysis (PMID 34101779) and the pilot's memory signal were not borne out clinically, and a 2026 meta-analysis of five RCTs (PMID 41436338; 540 participants) found no benefit on any cognitive, functional or biomarker outcome. Presented as a settled negative at trial scale. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference).
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — intranasal insulin did not improve cognition or function in MCI or Alzheimer's dementia in the SNIFF trial or the pooled RCT evidence

title: GEMINI 1 & 2: tolebrutinib was no better than teriflunomide for relapses in relapsing MS — a disability signal outside the testing hierarchy, and a liver-injury risk that needs weekly monitoring
question: In adults with relapsing MS, is the BTK inhibitor tolebrutinib superior to teriflunomide on relapses or disability worsening?
balance: Premise verified at build: Shelf #2849 holds tolebrutinib only for non-relapsing secondary progressive MS (HERCULES), and its trial (PMID 40202696) is not carded here. In relapsing MS, GEMINI 1 and GEMINI 2 (Oh et al., PMID 40202623; 1,873 participants) compared tolebrutinib 60 mg daily with teriflunomide 14 mg daily and missed their primary endpoint in both trials: annualised relapse rate ratios 1.06 and 1.00. The pooled 6-month confirmed disability worsening result (8.3% vs 11.3%; hazard ratio 0.71 relative) was a secondary outcome that received no formal hypothesis testing because the hierarchy stopped at the failed primary — a genuine signal, honestly labelled, not a demonstrated benefit. Phase 2b MRI data (PMID 34418400) show real anti-inflammatory activity that did not convert into relapse superiority. The safety price is hepatic: across 2,958 exposed participants programme-wide (PMID 42546561), ALT rose >3x ULN in 4.7%, six participants met Hy's-law criteria, and one died after liver transplantation; weekly liver testing for the first 12 weeks mitigates but does not remove the risk. PROPOSED SPLIT.
stamp: SPLIT — not superior to teriflunomide for relapses (primary endpoint missed in both GEMINI trials) / POSSIBLE disability-worsening benefit (secondary outcome, outside the formal testing hierarchy), with a drug-induced liver injury risk

title: MINT: inebilizumab improved MG-ADL by 1.9 points more than placebo at week 26 in generalised myasthenia gravis, on a protocolised steroid taper
question: In adults with generalised MG (AChR- or MuSK-positive), does inebilizumab, versus placebo, improve MG-ADL with protocolised steroid taper?
balance: Premise verified at build: inebilizumab's existing homes are NMOSD (live Shelf #1118, N-MOmentum) and IgG4-related disease (live Shelf #1818, MITIGATE) — neither touches myasthenia gravis, and MINT is a distinct trial answering a distinct question. MINT (Nowak et al., PMID 40202593) randomised 238 adults with AChR- or MuSK-positive generalised MG to inebilizumab or placebo with a protocolised glucocorticoid taper in both arms: MG-ADL change at week 26 was -4.2 vs -2.2 (difference -1.9; p<0.001) and QMG -4.8 vs -2.3 (difference -2.5). A prespecified analysis (PMID 42573995) found fewer exacerbations on inebilizumab (hazard ratio 0.41 relative at week 26), with the MuSK-positive subgroup small (48 participants) and its estimate imprecise. Serious adverse events were not more frequent on inebilizumab. An indirect network meta-analysis (PMID 42495790) ranks another class member first on most endpoints, so MINT establishes that inebilizumab works in generalised MG, not that it leads the class. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single trial caps the stamp.
