title: EPIDYS: givinostat (Duvyzat, Italfarmaco) slowed four-stair-climb decline in Duchenne muscular dystrophy — a slowing, not an improvement
question: In ambulant boys >=6 years with Duchenne MD on stable corticosteroids, does the HDAC inhibitor givinostat, versus placebo, slow functional decline on the four-stair climb?
balance: Product naming, per the clarification exception: the tested drug is givinostat, marketed as Duvyzat (Italfarmaco); the publications use the generic name. EPIDYS (Mercuri et al., PMID 38508835) randomised 179 ambulant boys with Duchenne muscular dystrophy on stable corticosteroids to givinostat or placebo for 72 weeks: in the primary population (group A, n=120), four-stair climb worsened in both groups but significantly less on givinostat (geometric least-squares ratio 1.27 vs 1.48; ratio 0.86; p=0.035). The effect is a slowing of decline, not an improvement, and the commonest costs were diarrhoea (36% vs 18%) and vomiting (29% vs 13%), with a mid-trial dose reduction after an interim safety analysis. Supporting evidence is uncontrolled: a 20-boy phase 2 biopsy study (PMID 27566866) showed histological improvement without functional gain, and an open-label extension (PMID 40830818) offers post hoc natural-history comparisons only. FDA approval followed in March 2024. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single phase 3 trial (EPIDYS) showed significantly slower functional decline on givinostat; a single programme caps the stamp at POSSIBLE

title: Masitinib in ALS (AB10015): a 3.4-point ALSFRS-R advantage only in the 'normal progressor' population, a post-hoc enriched survival cohort (69 vs 44 months) — and no regulatory approval; the confirmatory trial has never reported
question: In adults with ALS, does masitinib added to riluzole, versus riluzole alone, slow ALSFRS-R decline or prolong survival?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence), and the contest is the story of this shelf. AB10015 (394 patients, masitinib plus riluzole versus riluzole alone) met its primary endpoint only inside its prospectively declared 'Normal Progressor' primary population (progression from onset to baseline under 1.1 ALSFRS-R points/month): a 3.4-point advantage at 48 weeks on the 4.5 mg/kg/day dose, a 27% relative slowing of decline. In the broader 'Normal and Fast Progressor' population the same dose showed no significant effect, and the 3.0 mg/kg/day dose showed none anywhere. The survival headline — median 69 versus 44 months, hazard ratio 0.53 — comes from a long-term follow-up analysis in an enriched cohort defined after the fact (107 of the trial's patients), built to resemble the population of the planned confirmatory trial; it is a post-hoc subgroup result, not a trial-level survival finding. Against the benefit: adverse events were more frequent on masitinib (88% versus 79% on placebo at 4.5 mg/kg/day; serious adverse events 31% versus 18%), and a safety meta-analysis across the masitinib neurodegenerative programme found adverse events, severe events and discontinuations all significantly more common on the drug. Regulators in Europe and the US have refused approval on this evidence base. Confirmatory status at build (November 2026, checked against sponsor and registry reporting): the original confirmatory trial AB19001 was suspended in 2021 after a potential ischaemic heart disease signal and has never reported results; a replacement confirmatory study (AB23005) has been authorised but has published nothing. Until a confirmatory trial reports, masitinib in ALS is an unproven, subgroup-dependent claim — presented here in full because patients ask about it, not because the evidence is settled.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the favourable results rest on a progression-rate-restricted primary population and a post-hoc enriched survival cohort; the broader-population analysis was not significant, regulators have refused approval, and no confirmatory trial has reported

title: CNM-Au8 in ALS (HEALEY Platform, Regimen C): no benefit on the clinical primary endpoint (disease rate ratio 0.97) — the case for the drug rests on exploratory survival and biomarker signals from a 45-patient phase 2 trial
question: In adults with ALS, does CNM-Au8 (gold nanocrystal suspension), versus placebo, slow disease progression over 24 weeks?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence). CNM-Au8 is a suspension of catalytically active gold nanocrystals made by Clene Nanomedicine — an unapproved, single-source product, named here under the library's clarification exception because its identity and maker are the point. The randomised clinical evidence is negative where it was designed to be read: in the HEALEY ALS Platform Trial's Regimen C (161 participants), the primary endpoint — a Bayesian model of function and survival — gave a disease rate ratio of 0.97 (95% credible interval 0.783 to 1.175), and all three secondary endpoints likewise suggested no benefit or harm. In the smaller RESCUE-ALS phase 2 trial (45 participants), the primary neurophysiological endpoint (motor unit number index) and forced vital capacity did not differ significantly at 36 weeks. What keeps the programme alive is exploratory: in RESCUE-ALS's long-term follow-up, originally active-treated patients had lower all-cause mortality (hazard ratio 0.408, with a confidence interval reaching 1.001) and slower progression-event accrual in the open-label extension — analyses the trialists themselves label exploratory and hypothesis-supporting rather than confirmatory. Tolerability was acceptable in both trials (diarrhoea and nausea the commonest excess events in HEALEY). The honest summary: a well-tolerated, biologically interesting product with two negative randomised primaries and an unconfirmed survival signal that only a further adequately powered trial can settle.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — both randomised trials missed their primary endpoints; the survival signal is exploratory, from a 45-patient trial's extension phase, and no clinical benefit has been demonstrated

title: Ultra-high-dose methylcobalamin in early ALS (JETALS): ALSFRS-R decline slowed by 1.97 points over 16 weeks (a ~43% relative slowing) in selected early, moderate-progressor patients — a single-country (Japan) programme
question: In adults within 1 year of ALS onset with moderate progression rate, does methylcobalamin 50 mg intramuscularly twice weekly, versus placebo, slow ALSFRS-R decline?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), tightly fenced. JETALS is a properly positive phase 3 trial: in 130 Japanese patients within a year of ALS onset who were still progressing at a moderate rate after a 12-week observation run-in, methylcobalamin 50 mg intramuscularly twice weekly slowed ALSFRS-R decline over 16 weeks by 1.97 points versus placebo — a ~43% relative slowing of decline over that short window. The earlier, larger phase 2/3 programme (373 patients, all disease durations up to 36 months) missed both its primary endpoints outright; its supportive early-treatment signal is post-hoc, in patients entered within 12 months of onset — the observation JETALS was then designed to test prospectively, which is the right order of operations and raises the signal above pure data-dredging. The fences: every randomised patient in this programme is Japanese; JETALS's randomised period is only 16 weeks, so nothing here speaks to survival or to benefit beyond four months; the population is selected twice over (early disease, moderate progression, preserved respiratory function, ambulatory); and the very first study in the line (1998, n=24) measured a nerve-electrophysiology surrogate, not function. Methylcobalamin at this dose is approved for ALS in Japan and is not licensed for ALS in the US or Europe. Adverse events in JETALS were similar between groups (the trial reports no excess on drug).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one positive phase 3 trial in a narrowly selected early-ALS population, supported by a post-hoc signal in the earlier phase 2/3 programme; single country, 16-week randomised period, single programme

title: Azetukalner (XEN1101) in focal epilepsy: median seizure-frequency reduction 53.2% at 25 mg vs 10.4% on placebo in phase 3 (X-TOLE2), replicating phase 2b — an unapproved Kv7 opener from a single development programme
question: In adults with focal-onset seizures on stable antiseizure medication, does the Kv7 potassium-channel opener XEN1101 (azetukalner), versus placebo, reduce monthly seizure frequency?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). The drug developed as XEN1101 is now named azetukalner (Xenon Pharmaceuticals) — both names are carried on this shelf, as the publications themselves use both. The randomised evidence is unusually consistent for an epilepsy programme: in phase 2b (X-TOLE, 325 patients) median monthly focal-seizure frequency fell 52.8% on 25 mg versus 18.2% on placebo, with a clean dose-response (46.4% at 20 mg, 33.2% at 10 mg); in phase 3 (X-TOLE2, 374 patients with highly drug-resistant epilepsy — a median of five previously failed antiseizure medications) the 25 mg dose again gave a 53.2% median reduction versus 10.4% on placebo, and the 15 mg dose 34.5%. The open-label extension suggests the effect is sustained over two years in patients who stay on the drug, though extension data have no comparator and shed non-responders. The limits are structural: this is one company's programme with no independent replication; the randomised periods are 8–12 weeks; the commonest adverse events are dizziness and somnolence (with memory impairment reported in 10.9% in the extension); and the Kv7-opener class carries a cautionary history — the earlier Kv7 opener retigabine was withdrawn from the market — so long-term, large-population safety is not yet characterised. Azetukalner was not an approved drug at the time this shelf was built; a US new drug application was submitted in 2026 (sponsor-reported).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two concordant randomised trials (phase 2b and phase 3) from one sponsor programme, with sustained open-label extension data; the drug is not yet approved and there is no independent programme

title: Intravenous glibenclamide in large hemispheric infarction (CHARM): no improvement in 90-day functional outcome (common OR 1.17; p=0.42) in a phase 3 trial stopped early by its sponsor — benefit not shown, and not definitively excluded
question: In adults 18–70 with large hemispheric infarction, does intravenous glibenclamide (glyburide), versus placebo, improve 90-day functional outcome by limiting cerebral oedema?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — with the underpowered caveat printed, not buried. The phase 3 CHARM trial (431 patients in its primary analysis population) found no favourable shift in 90-day modified Rankin Scale scores with intravenous glibenclamide (the drug called glyburide in the US) versus placebo (common odds ratio 1.17; 95% CI 0.80 to 1.71; p=0.42), and mortality was numerically higher on drug (32% vs 29%). But CHARM was stopped early by its sponsor for strategic and operational reasons — slow COVID-era enrolment — before unblinding, so it is underpowered for the modest effect it sought: the honest answer is 'not shown to work', not 'disproven'. The phase 2 GAMES-RP trial was likewise neutral on its composite primary outcome (41% vs 39%), though it and its exploratory follow-ups showed less midline shift and lower MMP-9 on drug, and an exploratory survival advantage in patients aged 70 or under — the signal that shaped CHARM's design. A post-hoc CHARM analysis restricted to infarct cores under 125 mL found a favourable shift (adjusted common OR 2.11), strongest in thrombectomy-treated patients; that is a hypothesis for a future trial, not a result to act on. Hypoglycaemia is the drug's predictable harm (6% vs 2% in CHARM). This shelf is the companion answer to the oedema question in large hemispheric infarction: a biologically coherent idea, tested at phase 3 scale, that has not demonstrated a functional benefit.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the phase 3 primary analysis was negative, but the trial was stopped early and underpowered; phase 2 was neutral on its primary outcome, and the favourable subgroup findings are post-hoc and exploratory

title: Colchicine started acutely after stroke or TIA (CHANCE-3): new stroke in 6.3% vs 6.5% over 90 days (HR 0.98) — no benefit from starting colchicine within 24 hours in hs-CRP-selected patients
question: In adults with acute minor ischaemic stroke or high-risk TIA and hs-CRP ≥2 mg/L, does colchicine 0.5 mg started within 24 hours for 90 days, versus placebo, prevent new stroke?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference). This shelf answers the acute question — start colchicine within 24 hours of a minor stroke or high-risk TIA, in patients selected for inflammation (hs-CRP at least 2 mg/L), and treat for 90 days — and the answer from CHANCE-3 (8,343 patients, 244 hospitals in China) is no: new stroke occurred in 6.3% on colchicine versus 6.5% on placebo (hazard ratio 0.98), with serious adverse events balanced (2.2% vs 2.1%). Unlike many negative trials, this one was large enough for its null to mean something. Two further cautions sit on the face. First, the trial's prespecified intracranial-stenosis analysis found the point estimate reversed in patients with symptomatic intracranial atherosclerotic stenosis (10.5% vs 8.5% recurrent stroke on colchicine; adjusted HR 1.30), with a significant treatment-by-subgroup interaction — hypothesis-grade, but a harm signal, not a benefit signal. Second, a 2026 meta-analysis of five randomised trials (18,336 participants, including the long-term trials) found no significant reduction in recurrent stroke (relative risk 0.86; 95% CI 0.65 to 1.12). This is the companion shelf to live shelf #1613, which holds the separate long-term colchicine question (CONVINCE); the acute-initiation slice is not carded there, and CONVINCE's own card stays in its home — it appears here only as one pooled component of the meta-analysis card. Flags: CHANCE-3 is a single-country (China) trial in a biomarker-selected population; its result does not answer colchicine questions in other populations or at other timings.
stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — a large, well-powered acute-initiation trial was cleanly negative, a prespecified subgroup analysis pointed toward harm in intracranial stenosis, and a 2025 meta-analysis of five trials is concordantly null

title: Butylphthalide as an adjunct to reperfusion in acute ischaemic stroke (BAST): favourable 90-day outcome in 56.7% vs 44.0% (OR 1.70) — a positive trial from a single-country (China) programme; the drug is not licensed in the US or Europe
question: In adults with acute ischaemic stroke receiving intravenous thrombolysis and/or endovascular treatment, does dl-3-n-butylphthalide for 90 days, versus placebo, improve 90-day functional outcome?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), with the geography on the face: every randomised patient in this evidence base was treated in China, where dl-3-n-butylphthalide (NBP; Shijiazhuang Pharmaceutical Group) is an approved stroke drug; it is not licensed in the United States or Europe, and the product is named here under the library's clarification exception because preparations and regulatory status differ by market. The pivotal result is genuinely positive: in BAST (1,216 patients, 59 Chinese centres, all receiving intravenous thrombolysis and/or endovascular treatment), a favourable 90-day outcome occurred in 56.7% on butylphthalide versus 44.0% on placebo (odds ratio 1.70; 95% CI 1.35 to 2.14), with serious adverse events no higher on drug (10.1% vs 12.0%). Two qualifications define the claim. First, BAST's primary outcome used a baseline-severity-stratified definition of 'favourable' — modified Rankin Scale thresholds of 0 to 2 points depending on baseline NIHSS — rather than a single cut-off, so the 56.7% figure is not interchangeable with a plain mRS 0–2 rate. Second, the supporting evidence is thinner than the headline: a post-hoc BAST analysis tying benefit to favourable immune-inflammation trajectories is exploratory, and the one other placebo-controlled trial on this shelf (EBCAS, 99 patients) measured cerebral autoregulation, a physiological surrogate, not clinical outcome. A 2026 Chinese timing trial (204 patients, all receiving butylphthalide; early start within 3 hours versus 3–6 hours) found no significant difference on its primary outcome (relative risk 1.16; 95% CI 0.94 to 1.44; PMID: 43021208) — it had no placebo arm and does not test efficacy. Independent replication outside China is the missing piece.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one positive multicentre randomised trial (BAST) with supportive smaller placebo-controlled data, all from China, where the drug is licensed; no non-Chinese randomised evidence exists

title: Lumateperone as adjunctive therapy in major depression: MADRS advantage of −4.5 and −4.9 points at 6 weeks in two phase 3 trials, with a small independent Iranian replication — benefit with a discontinuation cost (adverse-event dropouts up to 12.4% vs 0.8%)
question: In adults with major depressive disorder and inadequate response to 1–2 antidepressants, does adjunctive lumateperone 42 mg, versus adjunctive placebo, improve MADRS at 6 weeks?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). This is lumateperone's third indication home in the library — schizophrenia is live shelf #1433 and bipolar depression is pack #2404; the adjunctive major-depression question is answered here on its own trials, and those trials' cards are not duplicated in the other homes. Two phase 3 trials from the development programme (Studies 501 and 502; pooled n=964) agree: adjunctive lumateperone 42 mg beat adjunctive placebo on MADRS change at day 43 by −4.5 points (American Journal of Psychiatry report) and −4.9 points (Journal of Clinical Psychiatry report, NCT04985942), with matching advantages on clinician severity and self-reported symptoms. A small independent Iranian trial (n=58, added to sertraline, HDRS outcome) points the same way, though its response rates (100% vs 82.1% at week 8) are implausibly high and it found no remission advantage. The cost side is consistent and should not be softened: treatment-emergent adverse events in the pooled programme occurred in 68.1% on lumateperone versus 45.1% on placebo, and discontinuation because of adverse events was 8.7% versus 0.8% pooled — 12.4% versus 0.8% in the American Journal of Psychiatry trial — driven by dizziness, somnolence, dry mouth, nausea, fatigue, diarrhoea and tremor. In the drug's favour, weight gain and cardiometabolic changes were minimal and similar to placebo, and extrapyramidal effects were uncommon. Record note: the two primary reports do not map onto their registry numbers the way secondary sources describe — the Journal of Clinical Psychiatry report carries NCT04985942 in its own record, while the American Journal of Psychiatry report carries no registry ID in its record; the pooled analysis identifies the pair as NCT04985942 and NCT05061706, and the cards follow each record exactly. The US FDA approved the adjunctive-MDD indication in 2025.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two concordant sponsor phase 3 trials plus one small independent randomised replication; effect size is the class-typical ~5 MADRS points, bought with substantially higher adverse-event discontinuation than placebo

title: Serdexmethylphenidate/dexmethylphenidate (Azstarys) in ADHD: one laboratory-classroom trial showed SKAMP benefit across the school day, a small China phase 3 agreed, and a 1-year open-label study found stimulant-typical harms
question: In children 6–12 with ADHD, does once-daily serdexmethylphenidate/dexmethylphenidate, versus placebo, improve classroom behaviour (SKAMP) across the school day?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). The tested product is the specific prodrug co-formulation serdexmethylphenidate/dexmethylphenidate (Azstarys, named in the pivotal report); results do not transfer to other methylphenidate products, and the fetched records do not name the manufacturer. One pivotal dose-optimised laboratory-classroom trial (149 children completing) found a least-squares SKAMP-Combined advantage of −5.41 points versus placebo averaged over the classroom day (p<0.001), significant from 1 to 10 hours post-dose on the prespecified analysis; the often-quoted 0.5-to-13-hour duration comes from a post hoc analysis and is labelled as such on the card. A small China phase 3 bridging trial (n=55) pointed the same way on ADHD-RS-5 (−5.8 points at week 3, p=0.0292). A 12-month open-label safety study (282 enrolled) found the stimulant-typical profile — decreased appetite 18.5%, decreased weight 7.6%, irritability 6.7% — with 60.1% reporting at least one treatment-emergent adverse event and no unexpected cardiac signal. Adult evidence is open-label only and is not carded; this shelf answers the paediatric question only. Record note: the pivotal report's PubMed record carries no registry ID, so none is printed on its card.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single development programme: one pivotal laboratory-classroom trial plus one small bridging phase 3, with open-label safety follow-up only

title: Deep TMS (H-coil) for OCD: Y-BOCS fell 6.0 vs 3.3 points vs sham in the pivotal trial, with response 38.1% vs 11.1% — one programme, one pivotal trial
question: In adults with OCD inadequately responsive to pharmacotherapy/psychotherapy, does high-frequency deep TMS over medial prefrontal/anterior cingulate cortex after symptom provocation, versus sham, reduce Y-BOCS?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). The intervention as tested is high-frequency (20 Hz) deep transcranial magnetic stimulation over the medial prefrontal cortex and anterior cingulate cortex, delivered daily for 6 weeks immediately after individualised symptom provocation; the fetched records do not name the device manufacturer or coil model, so none is printed here. In the pivotal multicentre sham-controlled trial (n=99), Y-BOCS fell 6.0 points on active treatment versus 3.3 on sham, with response (≥30% reduction) in 38.1% versus 11.1%, widening slightly at 1-month follow-up (45.2% versus 17.8%). An earlier small randomised feasibility trial from the same group pointed the same way, and a secondary analysis of the pivotal trial reports benefit even in patients who had failed multiple medications and CBT — though its abstract prints no subgroup figures, and the card says so. Deep TMS appears as a card inside other OCD shelves in this library; this is its question home. The sham response (3.3 Y-BOCS points, 11.1% response) is a reminder that provocation plus daily clinic ritual is itself an intervention.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single programme resting on one pivotal multicentre trial, preceded by a small feasibility randomised trial

title: VER-01 full-spectrum cannabis extract in chronic low back pain: pain fell 0.6 NRS points more than placebo in phase A, the randomised-withdrawal phase D missed its endpoint, and a head-to-head trial favoured VER-01 over opioids on constipation and pain
question: In adults with chronic low back pain, does the standardised full-spectrum cannabis extract VER-01, versus placebo, reduce pain intensity?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). The tested product is VER-01, a standardised full-spectrum extract from Cannabis sativa DKJ127; the fetched records do not name its manufacturer, so none is printed, and these results must not be generalised to other cannabis preparations, which differ in composition. In the placebo-controlled phase 3 (n=820), 12-week pain fell 1.9 NRS points on VER-01 versus a mean difference of −0.6 points against placebo (p<0.001) — statistically clear, small on average — but the randomised-withdrawal phase D missed its primary endpoint (HR 0.75, p=0.288), so durability after stopping is not established by the design built to test it. Adverse events were commoner on VER-01 (83.3% vs 67.3%), mostly mild to moderate, with no signs of dependence or withdrawal reported. A second phase 3 (n=384) found VER-01 superior to a range of opioids on its primary gastrointestinal endpoint and modestly superior on pain over 6 months, though week-27 secondary endpoints alone were not significant. A 2026 systematic review of cannabinoids for low back pain found no class-wide effect and rested its chronic-low-back-pain conclusion substantially on this same VER-01 trial — corroboration of interpretation, not independent replication.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single programme: one placebo-controlled phase 3 whose withdrawal phase missed, plus one opioid-comparator phase 3; no independent replication

title: ReActiv8 restorative neurostimulation for mechanical chronic low back pain: the sham-controlled primary endpoint was inconclusive (57.1% vs 46.6%, p=0.138), while an open-label trial vs medical management and 5-year follow-up favoured the device
question: In adults with refractory mechanical chronic low back pain and multifidus dysfunction who are not surgical candidates, does implanted restorative neurostimulation of the L2 medial branch (ReActiv8), versus sham or optimal medical management, improve pain and disability?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), with the central caveat on the face: in ReActiv8-B, the only sham-controlled trial (n=204), the primary responder endpoint at 120 days was inconclusive for superiority (57.1% vs 46.6%; difference 10.4%, 95% CI −3.3 to 24.1; p=0.138) — the blinded comparison did not prove the device beats sham. Prespecified secondary analyses favoured treatment, gains accrued after the sham group crossed over, and at 5 years the (by then uncontrolled) cohort showed large maintained improvements. The open-label RESTORE trial (n=203) found a large disability advantage over optimal medical management (ODI −19.7 vs −2.9 at 1 year), a design that cannot exclude expectancy and attention effects for an implanted device. The tested system is the ReActiv8 Restorative Neurostimulation system; the fetched records do not name its manufacturer, so none is printed. The population is narrow — refractory mechanical pain with a positive prone instability test indicating multifidus dysfunction and no surgical indication — and nothing here answers back pain generally. Serious procedure- or device-related adverse events were 3.9% in ReActiv8-B. Note: a two-year RESTORE report cited elsewhere was not found on PubMed this session; the carded RESTORE report is the 1-year publication.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — sham-controlled primary endpoint inconclusive; benefit rests on secondary analyses, an open-label comparator trial and uncontrolled long-term follow-up in a narrowly selected population

title: Pain reprocessing therapy for primary chronic back pain: 66% were pain-free or nearly so after 4 weeks vs 20% on placebo and 10% on usual care in the single pivotal trial — not yet independently replicated at scale
question: In adults with primary (nociplastic) chronic back pain, does pain reprocessing therapy, versus placebo injection or usual care, reduce pain intensity?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). The tested intervention is the specific Pain Reprocessing Therapy protocol (Gordon/Ashar) — one physician telehealth session plus eight psychological sessions over 4 weeks teaching patients to reattribute pain to nondangerous brain processes — not generic pain psychology. In the Boulder Back Pain Study (n=151), 66% of the PRT group were pain-free or nearly pain-free (0–1 of 10) post-treatment versus 20% on open-label placebo injection and 10% on usual care, with mean pain 1.18 vs 2.84 vs 3.13, maintained at 1 year. Three qualifications belong on the face: the population was selected primary back pain with low-to-moderate baseline pain (mean 4.10 of 10) and disability, treated by experienced therapists in a university setting; the trial is single and not yet independently replicated at scale — the only independent randomised report is a 53-person feasibility pilot in chronic widespread pain, a different condition; and the 5-year follow-up report's PubMed record carries no abstract figures this session, so no 5-year numbers are printed. A secondary analysis supports the proposed mechanism: increases in mind-brain attribution mediated the treatment effect.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one pivotal randomised trial with large effects, plus its own secondary and 5-year follow-up reports and one small independent feasibility pilot in a different pain condition

title: GlyNAC in older adults: one 24-person trial reported broad improvements, the independent 114-person trial missed its primary glutathione endpoint, and an 8-person open-label pilot is the rest of the base
question: In older adults, does high-dose GlyNAC (glycine + N-acetylcysteine), versus placebo, correct glutathione deficiency and improve oxidative stress, physical function and ageing-hallmark measures?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence). Two randomised trials answer this question and they disagree at the primary endpoint. The Baylor (Sekhar-group) trial — 24 older adults randomised for 16 weeks, with 12 young adults as a reference group — reported that GlyNAC improved or corrected glutathione deficiency, oxidative stress, mitochondrial function, inflammation, insulin resistance, gait speed and strength, but its abstract prints no effect sizes, so none are quoted here. The independent trial (114 healthy older adults, 2 weeks at 2.4–7.2 g/day) missed its primary endpoint: glutathione redox status did not improve in the full cohort (p=0.739 for the high dose), with a signal only in a post-hoc high-oxidative-stress/low-glutathione subgroup. An earlier open-label pilot from the same Baylor group treated just 8 older adults. Single-research-group dominance and the failed independent primary are both on the face of this shelf. Doses in these trials are gram-level and far above typical retail supplement doses, the fetched records do not name a commercial product, and current retail GlyNAC products may differ from what was tested. Surrogate and biomarker outcomes dominate; no trial here measured clinical endpoints such as falls, hospitalisation or mortality.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — total randomised older-adult evidence N=138 across two trials with discordant primary results, plus an 8-person open-label pilot

title: Nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) in older adults: it raises blood NAD+, one small clamp study found better muscle insulin sensitivity, and pooled trials show no significant benefit on glucose, HbA1c, lipids, muscle mass or strength
question: In middle-aged and older adults, does oral NMN, versus placebo, improve insulin sensitivity, muscle function, walking or metabolic measures?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence). NMN does the biochemical thing it promises — blood NAD+ rose significantly in every randomised trial carded here — and almost nothing clinical follows in the pooled data: the 2026 meta-analysis of 15 trials found no significant effects on body weight, BMI, fasting glucose, HbA1c, lipid profiles or systolic blood pressure, and no increase in adverse events. The one positive metabolic result is Yoshino 2021's clamp study in postmenopausal women with prediabetes, where muscle insulin sensitivity and insulin signalling increased on NMN but not placebo; its fetched abstract states neither the sample size nor the dose, so none is printed, and a published Comment in the same journal (PMID 34326206) challenged the trial's baseline comparability (hepatic lipid content 6.3% in the NMN group vs 14.8% on placebo, p=0.003, as printed in that Comment's record). Walking results split by trial: Yi 2023 found longer 6-minute walk distances at all doses with no HOMA-IR change; Pencina 2023 (MIB-626, a named microcrystalline β-NMN formulation from Metro International Biotech, as printed in its record) found no change in muscle strength, fatigability, aerobic capacity or insulin sensitivity, alongside reductions in weight, diastolic pressure and LDL cholesterol. Tested products differ by maker — the Yoshino record does not name its product's supplier — and current retail NMN products may differ in content and purity from trial material. Regulatory status has swung in recent years (FDA supplement exclusion in 2022, reversed in 2025, per the commissioning slate); this shelf rules on evidence, not legal status.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — NMN raises NAD+ reliably, but clinical and metabolic benefits are unproven: one small positive clamp study against pooled null results across 15 trials

title: Low-dose paroxetine mesylate 7.5 mg for menopausal hot flushes: two phase 3 trials met their frequency endpoints, severity separation was partial, and pooled analyses showed fewer night-time awakenings with no weight or sexual-function cost
question: In postmenopausal women with moderate-to-severe vasomotor symptoms, does paroxetine mesylate 7.5 mg at bedtime, versus placebo, reduce hot-flush frequency and severity?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). This shelf answers the specific product question — paroxetine mesylate 7.5 mg once daily at bedtime (the Noven Pharmaceuticals programme, per a fetched review record, PMID 24601805; the brand name does not appear in the fetched trial records) — and is not interchangeable with antidepressant-dose paroxetine hydrochloride or with the controlled-release paroxetine 12.5–25 mg carded, with escitalopram, on live shelf #667, which this shelf cross-points and does not duplicate: the Stearns 2003 trial homed there is deliberately not re-carded here. The two phase 3 trials (1,184 women randomised) both significantly reduced weekly vasomotor-symptom frequency at weeks 4 and 12; severity separation was complete in the 24-week study but partial in the 12-week study (the week-12 severity endpoint was the one primary endpoint missed), and the trials' abstract reports p-values rather than absolute flush counts, so the size of the benefit cannot be stated from these records — the class context from #667 is a modest absolute gain over a large placebo response. Pooled analyses of the same two trials found fewer night-time awakenings attributed to flushes (39% vs 28% reduction at week 4, percentages as reported) and about 15 extra minutes of sleep, with no weight gain or sexual-function deterioration versus placebo. Paroxetine mesylate 7.5 mg remains the only FDA-approved non-hormonal drug for vasomotor symptoms (per the fetched records); SSRI-class cautions apply, including the CYP2D6 interaction that makes paroxetine a poor choice alongside tamoxifen — a caution from class pharmacology, flagged here because the trial populations were not breast-cancer populations. Neighbouring homes: fezolinetant live #250, elinzanetant live #949, gabapentin pack #1343, oxybutynin pack #2802.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one phase 3 programme of two concordant trials from a single sponsor programme; effect modest, severity benefit inconsistent in the shorter trial

title: Fractional CO2 laser for genitourinary syndrome of menopause: sham-controlled trials show no benefit over sham (the treatment made no difference)
question: In postmenopausal women with vaginal symptoms of genitourinary syndrome of menopause, does fractional CO2 laser therapy, versus sham laser, improve symptom severity at 12 months?
balance: This is a heavily marketed, usually cash-pay intervention, and the sham-controlled evidence is the crux: it is null. In the LIGHT trial in breast-cancer survivors on aromatase inhibitors, sexual function improved in both arms with no difference between laser and sham at 6 months, and the trial's 12-month report was likewise null on every outcome. A small US sham-controlled trial found 64% improved on laser vs 67% on sham. A pilot in gynaecologic cancer survivors found no difference in vaginal symptoms, with a preliminary sexual-function signal in 18 women that the larger trials do not confirm. The largest sham-controlled trial of this question (Sydney, 85 women, 12 months) is already carded elsewhere in this library and was also null on symptom severity; it is cross-pointed here in prose and is not re-carded. The US FDA issued a safety communication in 2018 warning against energy-based devices marketed for 'vaginal rejuvenation' outside cleared indications. Product naming: the abstracts of the carded trials do not name a specific commercial laser system, so no system can be named on this shelf's face; results should not be assumed to transfer between systems, and no system-specific claim is made. Uncontrolled case series reporting large improvements exist, but they cannot separate laser effect from the contextual improvement the sham arms demonstrate.
stamp: NO BENEFIT DEMONSTRATED (the treatment made no difference) — in every sham-controlled trial carded here, fractional CO2 laser did not beat sham on symptom or sexual-function outcomes; both arms improved, which is the placebo/contextual effect the sham design exists to expose

title: Marstacimab (Hympavzi, Pfizer) prophylaxis in haemophilia A/B: treated bleeding fell sharply versus prior on-demand or prophylaxis care in the phase 3 BASIS trial — with and without inhibitors
question: In adolescents and adults with severe haemophilia A or moderate-to-severe haemophilia B, with or without inhibitors, does once-weekly subcutaneous marstacimab (anti-TFPI), versus on-demand or prior routine prophylaxis, reduce treated bleeding?
balance: Marstacimab (Hympavzi, Pfizer) is a monoclonal antibody against tissue factor pathway inhibitor, given as a 300 mg loading dose then 150 mg subcutaneously once weekly. In BASIS, participants were observed for 6 months on their prior on-demand or routine prophylaxis care, then treated for 12 months; the headline comparisons are therefore within-patient (run-in vs on-treatment), a design labelled observational in structure on the face of each card — regression to the mean and period effects cannot be excluded the way a randomised parallel arm would exclude them. The effects are nonetheless large: in the non-inhibitor cohort, mean annualised bleeding rate (ABR) for treated bleeds fell from 39.86 to 3.20 against prior on-demand care, and from 7.90 to 5.09 against prior routine prophylaxis; in the inhibitor cohort (n=51 treated), from 19.78 to 1.39 against prior on-demand bypassing-agent care. No deaths or thromboembolic events occurred in either cohort — the class harm that matters most for rebalancing agents — but a single programme with 167 treated phase 3 participants cannot exclude uncommon thrombosis. One home per agent is this library's rule for the rebalancing class: concizumab (pack #6431), fitusiran (pack #6594) and efanesoctocog alfa (pack #6430) each have their own shelf; marstacimab's is this one, and there is no head-to-head trial between these agents.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single phase 3 programme (BASIS, one trial reported in two cohort papers) caps the stamp at POSSIBLE; the comparisons are within-patient against a 6-month observational run-in, not a randomised parallel control

title: Denecimig (Mim8; Frehemgo, Novo Nordisk) prophylaxis in haemophilia A: treated bleeding cut by 96–99% relative versus on-demand care in FRONTIER2 — no head-to-head trial against emicizumab
question: In adults and adolescents ≥12 years with haemophilia A, with or without inhibitors, does denecimig (FVIIIa-mimetic bispecific antibody) once weekly or once monthly, versus on-demand treatment or prior factor prophylaxis, reduce treated bleeding?
balance: Denecimig (Mim8; Frehemgo, Novo Nordisk) is a bispecific antibody that mimics activated factor VIII, given subcutaneously once weekly or once monthly at weight-tiered doses. In FRONTIER2, against on-demand treatment the annualised treated-bleed rate fell by 96.4% relative (weekly) and 98.7% relative (monthly) — absolute rates 0.57 and 0.20 bleeds/year against 15.76 on on-demand care. Against patients' own prior factor prophylaxis (within-patient run-in comparison), the relative decreases were 54.0% and 42.8% (absolute 2.25 vs 4.90 and 1.78 vs 3.12 bleeds/year). Injection-site reactions occurred in 2.6% of injections; no thromboembolic events and no neutralising antibodies were reported in the carded reports. The neighbouring home is emicizumab (live shelf #1414, the HAVEN programme) — cross-pointed here in prose; its PMIDs are not carded on this shelf, and there is NO head-to-head trial of denecimig against emicizumab, so no comparative claim between the two mimetics can be made. FRONTIER2 was open-label. Paediatric (FRONTIER3) and every-2-week extension (FRONTIER4) reports support the programme's safety picture but are single-arm.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one phase 3 programme (FRONTIER) caps the stamp at POSSIBLE; FRONTIER2 was open-label, and there is no head-to-head trial against emicizumab

title: Efgartigimod in primary immune thrombocytopenia: the intravenous form worked in ADVANCE IV (22% vs 5% sustained response); the subcutaneous form failed in ADVANCE SC (13.7% vs 16.2%) — a split record by formulation
question: In adults with chronic primary immune thrombocytopenia, does efgartigimod, versus placebo, produce a sustained platelet response?
balance: The record splits by formulation, and this shelf keeps the two apart. Intravenous efgartigimod (10 mg/kg) in ADVANCE IV produced a sustained platelet response in 22% of chronic-ITP patients vs 5% on placebo (adjusted difference 16 percentage points) — a real but modest absolute yield in a heavily pretreated population (mean 10.6 years since diagnosis; 67% had received at least three prior ITP therapies). The subcutaneous PH20 formulation in ADVANCE SC did not beat placebo at all (13.7% vs 16.2%, p=0.51), with the report noting platelet rises higher than expected on placebo and lower than expected on efgartigimod. Regulatory status therefore differs by formulation, and the IV result must not be used to carry the SC product. An earlier phase 2 trial of the IV form (n=38) pointed the same way as ADVANCE IV. Efgartigimod's other homes in this library are different diseases and questions — generalised myasthenia gravis (live #1116, ADAPT) and CIDP (pack #6560, ADHERE); their PMIDs are not carded here and lend this shelf no support. Other ITP homes: fostamatinib (pack #1800) and rilzabrutinib (pack #4873).
stamp: SPLIT — intravenous efgartigimod beat placebo in one phase 3 trial (ADVANCE IV: sustained response 22% vs 5%), while the subcutaneous PH20 formulation missed its primary endpoint in a second phase 3 trial (ADVANCE SC: 13.7% vs 16.2%); the two formulations' results must not be merged

title: Recombinant ADAMTS13 (Adzynma, Takeda) in congenital TTP: no acute events on prophylaxis in the phase 3 crossover trial (n=48 — the recruitable population of an ultra-rare disease), with activity restored to ~101% of normal
question: In patients with congenital thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, does recombinant ADAMTS13 prophylaxis, versus standard (plasma-based) therapy, prevent acute TTP events and maintain ADAMTS13 activity?
balance: Recombinant ADAMTS13 (Adzynma, Takeda) replaces the missing enzyme in congenital TTP. The phase 3 trial was an open-label crossover — every patient received both recombinant ADAMTS13 (40 IU/kg IV) and standard plasma-based therapy in randomised order — because a placebo arm was not ethical in this disease; that design is stated, not apologised for. No acute TTP event occurred during recombinant prophylaxis, versus one event (annualised rate 0.05) on standard therapy, and mean maximum ADAMTS13 activity was 101% of normal vs 19%. Thrombocytopenia manifestations were less frequent on recombinant therapy (annualised rate 0.74 vs 1.73), drug-related adverse events were less frequent (9% vs 48%), and no patient interrupted recombinant treatment for adverse events (vs 8 on standard therapy); no neutralising antibodies developed. The N of 48 is small because congenital TTP is ultra-rare — it is close to the recruitable trial population, and the stamp line carries it for that reason. Supporting evidence is a 15-patient first-in-human pharmacokinetic study and a 14-patient Japanese real-world switch series (observational, labelled as such), which included 5 patients with end-stage renal disease whom the phase 3 trial excluded. This shelf is about congenital TTP only; caplacizumab in acquired (immune) TTP is a different disease and question, homed at live #846.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — based on the phase 3 crossover trial's N = 48 (the recruitable population of an ultra-rare disease, printed here per the small-N rule), supported by a 15-patient phase 1 study and a 14-patient real-world switch series; a single programme caps the stamp at POSSIBLE

title: Lusutrombopag for thrombocytopenia of chronic liver disease before procedures: two phase 3 trials — 79.2% vs 12.5% (L-PLUS 1) and 64.8% vs 29.0% (L-PLUS 2) avoided pre-procedure platelet transfusion
question: In adults with chronic liver disease and severe thrombocytopenia scheduled for an invasive procedure, does lusutrombopag, versus placebo, avoid the need for platelet transfusion?
balance: Lusutrombopag is an oral thrombopoietin-receptor agonist given as 3 mg daily for up to 7 days before a planned invasive procedure. Both phase 3 trials met their primary endpoints: in L-PLUS 1 (Japan), 79.2% vs 12.5% avoided pre-procedure platelet transfusion; in L-PLUS 2 (global), 64.8% vs 29.0% met the composite of avoiding pre-procedure transfusion and rescue therapy for bleeding (difference 36.7 percentage points [95% CI 24.9–48.5]). An integrated analysis of the two trials (a labelled pooled report of the same trials, not independent evidence) found the same pattern in patients with and without hepatocellular carcinoma (68.0% vs 8.9% and 77.0% vs 21.6%). Platelet counts stayed ≥50 × 10⁹/L for a median 19.2 days in L-PLUS 2. Thrombotic events were uncommon and similar to placebo in the carded reports (one per group in L-PLUS 1), but portal-vein thrombosis is the class harm to watch with thrombopoietin agonists in liver disease. The neighbouring home is avatrombopag in the same indication (packs #2819/#6129) — a distinct drug and programme, cross-pointed here; the two are not merged and there is no carded head-to-head comparison. Per-trial results are printed from the primary papers, not from the pooled NICE figure (transfusion-avoidance relative risk 3.42, a relative measure) cited in the slate.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — two concordant phase 3 placebo-controlled trials (L-PLUS 1, n=96; L-PLUS 2, n=215) both met the transfusion-avoidance endpoint with similar safety to placebo; the endpoint is transfusion avoidance, a procedure-enabling outcome, not a bleeding or survival outcome

title: Danazol in telomere diseases: one small single-arm trial showed telomere elongation and blood-count responses — but an independent cohort found no difference in attrition, and a second trial found it poorly tolerated in pulmonary fibrosis
question: In patients with telomere maintenance/repair defects (telomere biology disorders), does danazol 800 mg/day slow telomere attrition and improve blood counts?
balance: Danazol 800 mg/day is a high, prolonged androgen dose, and the evidence tier here is the best available for an ultra-rare disease — which is not the same as proof. The anchor is Townsley 2016: a prospective single-arm phase 1–2 study, halted early because the primary endpoint was met in every evaluable patient; but only 12 of 27 enrolled patients were evaluable for that endpoint (intention-to-treat 44%), and there was no control group, so natural history and selection are unmeasured. Its long-term follow-up report (a second, explicitly labelled report of the same trial) found responses were usually lost a median 1.6 years after stopping, that lower-dose re-treatment re-induced responses in 6 of 7 evaluable patients, and no signal that danazol expanded premalignant clones. Against this, an independent NIH-cohort observational study found telomere attrition rates statistically indistinguishable between androgen-treated and untreated dyskeratosis congenita patients (−62 vs −76 base pairs/year, p=.71; adjusted p=.24) — a direct tension the stamp names as SPLIT. ANDROTELO, a second single-arm phase 2 trial at the same daily dose in telomere-related-gene carriers, found danazol poorly tolerated in pulmonary fibrosis (only 10 of 24 completed 12 months; 9 stopped for side effects), though all 5 marrow-failure patients completed treatment with at least a partial response. Androgen class effects at this dose need full weight: grade ≤2 liver-enzyme elevation in 41% and muscle cramps in 33% in Townsley, plus the class's virilising, hepatic and lipid effects with prolonged use.
stamp: SPLIT — the single-arm phase 1–2 trial (anchor cohort N = 27, printed per the small-N rule) met its attrition endpoint in all 12 evaluable patients with haematologic responses in 79%, but an independent observational comparison found no significant difference in telomere attrition between androgen-treated and untreated patients, and the ANDROTELO trial found danazol poorly tolerated in telomere-related pulmonary fibrosis; no randomised trial exists

title: PHYSIOLOGY — Homeostatic sleep pressure (Process S): NREM slow-wave activity rises with prior wakefulness, rebounds after deprivation, and declines exponentially across sleep
question: In healthy humans, does NREM EEG slow-wave activity behave as a homeostatic marker of sleep need — rising with duration of prior wakefulness, rebounding after sleep deprivation, and declining exponentially across sleep?
balance: Framing (textbook account, named as such): the two-process model — presented in Kryger's Principles and Practice of Sleep Medicine and in the standard physiology texts (Guyton & Hall; Ganong; Boron & Boulpaep) as framing, not as an evidence card — holds that sleep timing and depth are governed by a homeostatic Process S, which builds during wakefulness and dissipates during sleep, interacting with a circadian Process C. What the human studies carded here directly show is the EEG behaviour: slow-wave activity (SWA; spectral power 0.75–4.5 Hz in NREM sleep) is enhanced after prolonged wakefulness, increases by roughly 20% after partial sleep restriction and falls immediately after recovery sleep, declines monotonically and exponentially across successive NREM–REM cycles, and can be quantitatively simulated from prior wake/sleep history alone (Achermann's model fit). Forced desynchrony separates the two processes: SWA's circadian modulation is low-amplitude and does not parallel the circadian rhythm of sleep propensity, which is dominated by Process C — the circadian half of the model is homed separately at pack #6250, and closed-loop acoustic stimulation exploiting SWA physiology is pack #6601; both are cross-pointed, neither is carded here. What human data do NOT establish is what S is made of: adenosine is the best-characterised candidate substrate signal (caffeine's antagonism of adenosine receptors is the everyday pharmacological probe), but equating Process S with adenosine outright goes beyond the human evidence, and this entry does not do so.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — in human EEG studies, slow-wave activity (0.75–4.5 Hz) tracks prior wakefulness, rebounds after deprivation, and declines exponentially across sleep, quantitatively fit by the two-process model; the classic studies are small (N = 8–16, printed on each card's face), and the molecular identity of 'S' remains unsettled

title: PHYSIOLOGY — Cortical spreading depolarisation: the human physiology of migraine aura, and of secondary injury after stroke, subarachnoid haemorrhage and traumatic brain injury
question: In humans, does a slowly propagating wave of cortical depolarisation (≈2–9 mm/min) account for the migraine aura, and do the same events, recorded directly from injured human cortex, worsen outcome after stroke, subarachnoid haemorrhage and traumatic brain injury?
balance: Framing (textbook account, named as such): Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology and Boron & Boulpaep's Medical Physiology present cortical spreading depolarisation (spreading depression) as a slowly propagating wave (≈2–9 mm/min, the range in this entry's question) of near-complete neuronal and glial depolarisation with silencing of electrical activity, followed by recovery in healthy tissue. What human studies directly show, carded here: during spontaneous migraine visual aura, fMRI BOLD changes propagate across occipital cortex at 3.5 ± 1.1 mm/min, retinotopically matched to the patient's percept, with at least eight features of spreading depolarisation (Hadjikhani, n=3 — printed on the card; the claim rests on convergence, not that n alone); direct electrocorticography in neurocritical-care patients records spreading depolarisations abundantly after subarachnoid haemorrhage, stroke and traumatic brain injury, with clusters time-locked to delayed ischaemic deficits (Dreier 2006: 298 events in 13 of 18 patients) and an independent association with unfavourable outcome after TBI (Hartings 2011: 1,328 events in 56% of 103 analysed patients; isoelectric spreading depolarisation common odds ratio 7.58 for unfavourable outcome). Direct electrophysiological evidence that spreading-depolarisation-induced spreading depression is the aura's correlate is reviewed by Major/Dreier 2020. The ESTABLISHED/EMERGING split, explained: that spreading depolarisation IS the aura mechanism and DOES occur in injured human brain is established by convergent human imaging plus direct recordings. That these events CAUSE lesion growth in injured brain — rather than marking severely injured tissue — is supported by their timing, their association with delayed infarcts in the recording area, and animal experiments (animal mechanism appears in this entry only as this labelled sentence), but no human trial of suppressing them has proven an outcome benefit; that causal clause is therefore graded EMERGING within the entry.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED for the migraine-aura mechanism and for the occurrence of spreading depolarisations in injured human brain (convergent human imaging and direct electrocorticography); the causal contribution of spreading depolarisations to lesion growth in injured brain is graded EMERGING within this entry — strongly supported by observational human data, not trial-proven (choice explained in the balance and synthesis)

title: Amifostine cytoprotection: grade ≥2 acute xerostomia 51% versus 78% without it in head-and-neck radiotherapy, and less cisplatin kidney and nerve toxicity in ovarian cancer — with no sign of tumour protection
question: In adults receiving radiotherapy (head-and-neck, thoracic) or cisplatin-based chemotherapy, does amifostine reduce moderate-to-severe xerostomia, mucositis, nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity versus no cytoprotection, without protecting the tumour?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) for xerostomia and for cisplatin cumulative toxicity, with the mucositis claim split. In the phase III head-and-neck trial (Brizel 2000; 303 patients in the 2-year report), daily intravenous amifostine before each fraction cut grade ≥2 acute xerostomia from 78% to 51% and grade ≥2 chronic xerostomia from 57% to 34%, with median saliva production 0.26 g versus 0.10 g — but it did NOT reduce mucositis in that trial. In ovarian cancer (Kemp 1996, 242 patients), amifostine before cyclophosphamide/cisplatin reduced protracted creatinine elevations, ≥40% falls in creatinine clearance, neurologic toxicity severity and febrile-neutropenia hospital care, with pathologic response 37% versus 28% and median survival 31 months in both arms. A 17-trial meta-analysis found relative reductions in grade 3–4 mucositis, acute and late xerostomia and dysphagia with radiotherapy alone, but NO significant benefit in the concomitant-chemoradiotherapy subgroup. The tumour-protection fear is answered by an individual-patient-data meta-analysis of 12 trials (1,119 patients): hazard ratio for death 0.98 (95% CI 0.84–1.14). The fetched records name the drug only as amifostine (generic); no brand or company is named in these records. Costs on the face: nausea/vomiting in 53% of patients (5% of doses), transient hypotension and allergic reactions.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — amifostine reduced acute and chronic xerostomia in head-and-neck radiotherapy and cumulative cisplatin kidney/nerve toxicity in ovarian cancer, with no survival or response penalty in 1,119-patient individual-data meta-analysis; the mucositis benefit is split (absent in the largest trial and in chemoradiotherapy subgroups)

title: Dexrazoxane for anthracycline extravasation: surgery was avoided in 53 of 54 patients in the two prospective single-arm licensing studies — no randomised or comparative study exists
question: In patients with anthracycline extravasation from a central or peripheral line, does intravenous dexrazoxane (the extravasation formulation tested in the licensing programme) prevent tissue necrosis and the need for surgery versus conservative management?
balance: POSSIBLE — single-arm evidence only, and the shelf says so on its face: NO randomised or comparative study of dexrazoxane for anthracycline extravasation exists. The entire prospective base is two open-label, single-arm, multicentre licensing studies reported together (Mouridsen 2007): in 54 assessable patients with biopsy-verified extravasation treated within 6 hours with the 3-day dexrazoxane schedule, 53 (98.2%) avoided surgery-requiring necrosis and one (1.8%) needed debridement; 71% continued scheduled chemotherapy without postponement. A Belgian clinical-practice survey (Fontaine 2012, retrospective; 41 patients) points the same way: debridement avoided in 95% (39/41). The product is named in the licensing record as Savene (EU) / Totect (US); no manufacturer is named in the fetched record. Because there is no untreated comparator, the 98% figure cannot be read as a treatment effect — some extravasations resolve with conservative care alone, and this shelf cannot say how many. The liposomal-anthracycline slice is weaker still (17 published cases, dexrazoxane in only 3).
stamp: POSSIBLE — single-arm evidence only (no randomised or comparative study exists): surgery avoided in 53 of 54 patients in the two prospective licensing studies and 39 of 41 in a retrospective practice survey, with no untreated comparator to size the true effect

title: Magnesium for cisplatin kidney protection: the large observational base points one way (adjusted odds ratio 0.80 in 13,719 patients; pooled odds ratio 0.24 in observational meta-analysis) — the randomised trials are small and mixed
question: In adults receiving high-dose cisplatin, does supplemental magnesium (intravenous or oral, added to standard saline hydration) reduce cisplatin-induced kidney injury (creatinine rise / KDIGO stage) versus hydration alone?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a mixed randomised/retrospective base, with designs labelled card by card and never pooled into one claim. The largest report is observational: a 5-centre US cohort of 13,719 patients (Gupta 2025) found cisplatin-associated AKI or death in 2.7% with first-day intravenous magnesium versus 5.3% without (adjusted odds ratio 0.80, 95% CI 0.66–0.97). A systematic review (Hamroun 2019) could meta-analyse only the 15 observational magnesium studies (1,841 patients) and found a pooled odds ratio of 0.24 (95% CI 0.19–0.32) — a much larger apparent effect than the best-adjusted cohort, which is itself a warning about confounding. The randomised evidence is two small trials pointing in different strengths: a double-blind phase II trial in ovarian cancer (Bodnar 2008, 40 eligible) showed significantly less GFR decline with magnesium on all three measures, while the pilot PRAGMATIC trial (30 patients, weekly low-dose cisplatin) found similar acute AKI (4.6% versus 1.3% of cycles) but less acute kidney disease over the course (6.7% versus 46.7%). The retrospective Kidera cohort (401 patients) found magnesium associated with a risk ratio of 0.175 for nephrotoxicity. Observational designs cap this shelf at POSSIBLE.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit, largely observational) — magnesium supplementation was associated with less cisplatin kidney injury in large cohorts and a small double-blind trial, but the randomised base is two small trials and the observational effect sizes disagree with each other

title: Radiation-induced nausea and vomiting beyond the abdomen: one small total-body-irradiation trial (6 of 10 completed without rescue on ondansetron versus 0 of 10 on placebo) and field-based guideline stratification — the direct evidence outside the abdomen is thin
question: In adults receiving radiotherapy outside the abdomen — pelvic, thoracic, head-and-neck or total-body irradiation — does prophylactic 5-HT3-antagonist therapy (ondansetron, granisetron or palonosetron) prevent radiation-induced nausea and vomiting versus placebo or rescue-only treatment, and how does risk vary by irradiated field?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) for the beyond-abdomen slice specifically. This pack is the PARTIAL companion to Shelf #6134, which homes the abdominal-radiotherapy question (Franzén placebo trial and the Priestman active-comparator trials — none of those reports is re-carded here). Outside the abdomen, the direct placebo evidence found is a single 20-patient total-body-irradiation trial (Spitzer 1994): oral ondansetron produced significantly fewer emetic episodes (P=.005), and 6 of 10 ondansetron patients completed 4 days of TBI without rescue versus 0 of 10 on placebo. A multicentre trial of ondansetron orally-disintegrating tablets for ESTABLISHED emesis during fractionated radiotherapy to thorax-to-pelvis sites (LeBourgeois 1999; N not documented in the record) found the active drug superior to placebo over 12 hours — treatment evidence, not prophylaxis. The only pelvic-field prophylaxis report carded is single-arm: palonosetron plus prednisolone during cervical chemoradiotherapy left a 57% probability of completing five cycles without emesis (Ruhlmann 2013, 48 patients). The MASCC/ESMO guidelines (2016, reaffirmed 2023) stratify prophylaxis by field — upper abdomen highest risk, with 5-HT3 antagonists the cornerstone for high and moderate emetic-risk radiotherapy — but state plainly that no new randomised prophylaxis data supported changed recommendations, i.e. the field recommendations rest largely on the abdominal evidence homed at #6134 plus expert consensus.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — beyond the abdomen, prophylaxis rests on one 20-patient total-body-irradiation placebo trial, one treatment (not prophylaxis) trial with N not documented, and one single-arm pelvic chemoradiotherapy study; guideline field stratification is extrapolated mainly from the abdominal data homed on Shelf #6134

title: Lymphoedema surgery (lymphovenous anastomosis / vascularised lymph-node transfer): limb volume fell about 6–10% relative at 1 year versus a 3.2% rise on decongestive therapy alone in the one controlled prospective cohort — no completed randomised trial; the rest is prospective-cohort meta-analysis
question: In adults with established secondary lymphoedema (chiefly breast-cancer-related arm lymphoedema) despite complete decongestive therapy, do microsurgical procedures — lymphovenous anastomosis or vascularised lymph-node transfer — reduce limb volume, cellulitis episodes and compression dependence versus continued conservative therapy?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — prospective/observational evidence only; no completed randomised trial of these operations versus conservative therapy was found (the international LYMPH randomised trial exists as a 2025 protocol, not results). This is the surgical PARTIAL companion to the conservative homes: weight lifting (Shelf #1786), bioimpedance surveillance (Shelf #3427) and decongestive therapy (Shelf #5421) — none of their reports is re-carded here. The one controlled prospective report (Zeltzer 2026, 92 patients) compared surgery plus decongestive therapy against decongestive therapy alone: relative interlimb volume difference changed by −6.21% (LVA), −9.61% (VLNT) and −7.00% (combined) versus +3.23% on conservative therapy alone at 1 year (all P<0.0001) — a non-randomised comparison. Meta-analyses of prospective series agree in direction: lymphovenous bypass gave a mean 14.26% limb-volume reduction at 1 year across 431 patients, with 46.3% reducing or stopping compression; and across 648 limbs followed >2 years, annual cellulitis events fell by about 1.1–1.3 episodes after LVA and 1.4–2.4 after VLNT. Without randomisation, selection (earlier-stage, motivated patients get surgery) can account for part of every one of these numbers.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit, observational) — lymphovenous anastomosis and vascularised lymph-node transfer reduced limb volume and cellulitis in prospective cohorts and their meta-analyses, but no completed randomised trial versus conservative therapy exists, so selection bias cannot be excluded

title: Paediatric antiemetics: adding aprepitant doubled delayed-phase complete response (51% versus 26%) in the phase 3 trial; palonosetron was non-inferior to ondansetron acutely, with a delayed-phase edge in one large trial and none in another
question: In children and adolescents receiving moderately or highly emetogenic chemotherapy, does adding aprepitant (or fosaprepitant) to a 5-HT3 antagonist ± dexamethasone improve complete response versus the backbone alone, and is palonosetron superior to ondansetron in this age group?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — each half of the question rests on essentially one programme. Aprepitant add-on: in the single phase 3 trial (Kang 2015, 302 analysed children aged 6 months–17 years), adding aprepitant to ondansetron ± dexamethasone raised delayed-phase (25–120 h) complete response from 26% to 51% (p<0.0001), with similar grade 3–4 adverse events (febrile neutropenia 15% versus 15% as the commonest serious event). A single trial caps the stamp at POSSIBLE however clean the result. Palonosetron versus ondansetron is a SPLIT within the second half: the international phase 3 non-inferiority trial (Kovács 2016, 493 analysed) showed acute-phase complete response of 59% on palonosetron 20 µg/kg versus 59% on ondansetron — non-inferior, not superior — while a large Chinese randomised trial (Tan 2018, 555 analysed, all with dexamethasone) found acute-phase rates similar (69.7% versus 64.6%) but delayed-phase superiority for palonosetron 10 µg/kg (53.5% versus 32.8%), and a smaller Indian trial (200 children) found no significant differences in any phase. So: aprepitant add-on works in the delayed phase; palonosetron is at least as good as ondansetron acutely, with delayed-phase superiority shown in one of two head-to-head trials.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — aprepitant added to ondansetron ± dexamethasone improved delayed-phase complete response in the one paediatric phase 3 trial (51% vs 26%); palonosetron was non-inferior to ondansetron for acute control, with delayed-phase superiority in one of two further trials (a split on that comparison)

title: Honey for radiation-induced oral mucositis: grade 3/4 mucositis 20% versus 75% (Biswal) and 15% versus 65% grade 3+ (Rashad) in two small unblinded trials — meta-analyses agree, but preparations differ by trial and none names a product
question: In adults with radiation-induced oral mucositis, does honey (topical/oral, the preparations tested in the trials) reduce moderate-to-severe mucositis, pain and weight loss versus standard oral care or placebo gel?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — consistent direction, weak architecture. Two small randomised trials of 'pure natural honey' (no brand, maker or standardised preparation named in either record — current commercial products may differ in safety and effectiveness) found large reductions in severe mucositis: Biswal 2003 (40 patients, radiotherapy alone) grade 3/4 mucositis 20% versus 75% (p=0.00058), with 55% versus 25% maintaining or gaining weight (p=0.053); Rashad 2009 (40 patients, chemoradiotherapy) grade 3 mucositis 15% and no grade 4, versus 65% grade 3/4 in controls, with candida colonisation 15% versus 60%. Two meta-analyses of the wider trial literature (11 trials/715 patients; 19 trials/1,276 patients) pool the same direction — odds ratio 0.24 for grade 3 and 0.17 for grade 4 mucositis in one; relative risk 0.18 for intolerable mucositis in the prophylactic phase in the other — but the trials are small, heterogeneous in preparation and schedule, and largely unblinded (honey is hard to blind), and the MASCC/ESMO mucositis guideline assessment of this literature is 'suggestive but inconsistent', which is how this shelf presents it. Pain and weight effects are inconsistent across the pooled analyses.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — honey reduced moderate-to-severe radiation mucositis in small, largely unblinded trials and their meta-analyses, but preparations differ by trial, no trial names a standardised product, and the guideline verdict on this literature is suggestive-but-inconsistent

title: Hormone therapy after breast cancer — a SPLIT: HABITS was stopped early for more recurrences on hormones (hazard ratio 2.4 at extended follow-up), the Stockholm trial found no excess recurrence (relative hazard 0.82), and the two trials differed significantly from each other
question: In breast-cancer survivors, is systemic hormone therapy after treatment safe — what did the randomised HABITS and Stockholm trials show about recurrence, and why did they disagree?
balance: SPLIT — two randomised trials, two answers, and a statistically significant difference between the trials themselves (heterogeneity P=.02), so the disagreement is unlikely to be chance alone. HABITS (434 randomised; extended follow-up 447 assigned, 442 followed): hormone therapy increased new breast-cancer events — 26 versus 7 at the 2.1-year safety analysis that stopped the trial in December 2003, and at extended follow-up (median 4 years) 39 of 221 versus 17 of 221 (hazard ratio 2.4, 95% CI 1.3–4.2; 5-year cumulative incidence 22.2% versus 8.0%). Stockholm (378 randomised; designed to minimise progestogen exposure): at median 4.1 years the recurrence relative hazard was 0.82 (95% CI 0.35–1.9), and at 10.8 years new breast-cancer events were 60 versus 48 (hazard ratio 1.3, 95% CI 0.9–1.9) — no significant difference overall, though contralateral breast cancers were more frequent on hormones (14 versus 4; hazard ratio 3.6, 95% CI 1.2–10.9). Neither trial found increased mortality. The leading explanation offered by the trialists is regimen: HABITS used more continuous progestogen (estradiol with norethisterone), while Stockholm deliberately minimised progestogen. Both trials closed early, so neither answer is definitive; current guidelines typically consider systemic hormone therapy contraindicated after breast cancer, which is the practice context, not a carded result.
stamp: SPLIT — HABITS: hormone therapy increased recurrence (HR 2.4, trial stopped early) · Stockholm: no significant excess recurrence (RH 0.82; HR 1.3 at 10.8 years) but more contralateral cancers (HR 3.6); the trials differed significantly from each other (P=.02), plausibly by progestogen exposure

title: Low-dose intravenous amisulpride for PONV: complete response 57.7% versus 46.6% added to standard prophylaxis in high-risk patients, and 41.7% versus 28.5% as rescue at the 10 mg dose after failed prophylaxis
question: In adults at risk of postoperative nausea and vomiting, does low-dose intravenous amisulpride prevent PONV — and rescue established PONV after failed prophylaxis — versus placebo or ondansetron?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — a concordant multi-trial randomised programme, all placebo-controlled (no head-to-head ondansetron trial was carded; the comparisons are amisulpride added to, or after, standard antiemetics). The formulation was developed as APD421 (named in the dose-finding record); the fetched records name no manufacturer. Dose-finding (Kranke 2013, 215 patients) identified 5 mg as the effective dose: PONV incidence 40% on 5 mg versus 69% on placebo. Two concurrent phase 3 prophylaxis trials of 5 mg alone (Gan 2017, 689 randomised) were individually mixed — complete response 46.9% versus 33.8% (P=0.026) in the US study and 57.4% versus 46.6% (P=0.070) in the European study. The largest prophylaxis trial (Kranke 2018, 1,147 high-risk patients, amisulpride 5 mg ADDED to a standard non-dopaminergic antiemetic) was clearly positive: complete response 57.7% versus 46.6% (difference 11.1 points, 95% CI 5.3–16.8; P<0.001), with less emesis, nausea and rescue use. Rescue after failed prophylaxis (Habib 2019) worked at 10 mg (complete response 41.7% versus 28.5%; P=0.006) but not significantly at 5 mg (33.8%). Safety across trials showed no excess QT prolongation, extrapyramidal effects or sedation versus placebo.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — low-dose IV amisulpride improved complete response in the large add-on prophylaxis trial and as 10 mg rescue after failed prophylaxis, with concordant dose-finding and one of two single-agent phase 3 trials positive; all comparisons are against placebo, not ondansetron

title: Lung-protective ventilation bundle in major abdominal surgery: major complications 10.5% versus 27.5% in IMPROVE (relative risk 0.40) — the bundle, not the PEEP level, is the slice the PEEP shelf does not cover
question: In adults having major abdominal surgery, does a lung-protective ventilation strategy (low tidal volume with PEEP and recruitment manoeuvres, as a bundle) reduce postoperative pulmonary complications versus conventional ventilation?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the bundle claim rests mainly on one large trial, which caps the stamp. This pack is the PARTIAL companion to live Shelf #1959, which homes the PEEP-LEVEL question (PROVHILO and iPROVE: high or individualised PEEP versus low PEEP, both null) — neither of those reports is re-carded here, and their null result is part of this shelf's logic: within low-tidal-volume ventilation, pushing PEEP higher added nothing, so the benefit below is attributed to the bundle as tested, not to PEEP escalation. In IMPROVE (Futier 2013, 400 patients at intermediate-to-high risk), the full bundle — low tidal volume with PEEP and recruitment manoeuvres — versus nonprotective ventilation (high tidal volume, no PEEP) cut the composite of major pulmonary and extrapulmonary complications at 7 days from 27.5% to 10.5% (relative risk 0.40, 95% CI 0.24–0.68), noninvasive ventilation or intubation for respiratory failure from 17.0% to 5.0%, and hospital stay by 2.45 days. A small single-centre trial (Severgnini 2013, 56 patients) found better pulmonary function and infection scores with a protective bundle but was not powered on clinical complications. The individual-patient meta-analysis (Serpa Neto 2014, 3,365 patients) found protective ventilation reduced postoperative lung injury but did NOT improve mortality (adjusted hazard ratio for death with lung injury 0.71, 95% CI 0.41–1.22, independent of strategy). Because IMPROVE changed tidal volume, PEEP and recruitment together against a now-dated control, which component carries the benefit cannot be separated from these cards.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the lung-protective bundle reduced major complications in the one large bundle trial (IMPROVE: 10.5% vs 27.5%, relative risk 0.40) with supportive small-trial and meta-analytic data, but no mortality benefit was shown and the bundle's active component cannot be isolated (PEEP escalation alone was null on Shelf #1959)

title: Quantitative neuromuscular monitoring: residual paralysis in recovery falls sharply when a number guides reversal — but the largest observational study found no fewer postoperative pulmonary complications in monitored patients
question: In adults having major surgery under general anaesthesia with neuromuscular blockade, does quantitative (objective) neuromuscular monitoring, with reversal guided by it, reduce residual paralysis and postoperative pulmonary complications versus qualitative (peripheral-nerve-stimulator / clinical) assessment?
balance: SPLIT by outcome. For residual paralysis itself the evidence is concordant and favourable: in the one randomised trial (Murphy 2008, 185 patients), residual blockade on arrival in recovery (train-of-four ratio ≤0.9) occurred in 4.5% with intraoperative acceleromyography versus 30.0% with qualitative monitoring (P<0.0001), with fewer hypoxaemic and airway-obstruction events in transit; a 2024 prospective cohort (Thilen, 200 patients) using a quantitative-monitoring-guided reversal protocol recorded 0% residual paralysis at extubation. But for the harder outcome — postoperative pulmonary complications — the largest dataset points the other way: POPULAR (22,803 patients, prospective observational) found neuromuscular monitoring was NOT associated with fewer pulmonary complications (adjusted odds ratio 1.31, 95% CI 1.15-1.49, an association in the direction of more complications, most plausibly confounding by indication), and neither reversal nor extubation at a train-of-four ratio ≥0.9 was associated with better pulmonary outcomes. Residual paralysis is clearly measurable and clearly linked to critical respiratory events in recovery (Murphy case-control: mean train-of-four ratio 0.62 in patients with critical respiratory events versus 0.98 in matched controls); whether monitoring-driven care reduces lung complications at population level is unproven. PROPOSED SPLIT (residual paralysis reduced; pulmonary-complication benefit unproven).
stamp: SPLIT — quantitative monitoring sharply reduces residual paralysis in recovery (4.5% vs 30.0% in the one randomised trial), but the large POPULAR observational study found no reduction in postoperative pulmonary complications with monitoring
