title: Extended thromboprophylaxis after cancer surgery: four weeks of low-molecular-weight heparin roughly halves venographic clots versus one week (12.0% to 4.8% in ENOXACAN II; 16.3% to 7.3% in FAME), with no increase in bleeding
question: In adults undergoing major abdominal or pelvic cancer surgery, does extended pharmacological thromboprophylaxis (low-molecular-weight heparin for ~4 weeks) reduce symptomatic venous thromboembolism versus in-hospital-only prophylaxis, at what bleeding cost?
balance: LIKELY (benefit). Two randomised trials from two programmes point the same way. ENOXACAN II (Bergqvist 2002, double-blind, 332 patients in the intention-to-treat efficacy analysis after abdominal or pelvic cancer surgery): venographic venous thromboembolism at days 25-31 was 12.0% on one week of enoxaparin followed by placebo versus 4.8% on four weeks of enoxaparin (P=0.02), a difference that persisted at three months (13.8% versus 5.5%, P=0.01), with no significant difference in bleeding. FAME (Rasmussen 2006, open-label assessor-blinded, 427 randomised after major abdominal surgery, 343 evaluable): cumulative venous thromboembolism fell from 16.3% with 7 days of dalteparin to 7.3% with 28 days — a 55% relative risk reduction (95% CI 15-76; P=0.012), number needed to treat 12 — again with no increase in bleeding. The Cochrane synthesis of four trials found objectively confirmed venous thromboembolism in 14.3% of controls versus 6.1% with prolonged prophylaxis (Peto odds ratio 0.41, 95% CI 0.26-0.63), symptomatic venous thromboembolism 1.7% versus 0.2% (odds ratio 0.22, 95% CI 0.06-0.80), and bleeding 3.7% versus 4.1% (not significant). The honest caveat: most events prevented are venogram-detected, largely asymptomatic clots; the symptomatic benefit is real in the pooled data but rests on small absolute numbers (1.7% to 0.2%). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit).
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — two randomised trials and a Cochrane synthesis agree: ~4 weeks of low-molecular-weight heparin after major abdominal/pelvic cancer surgery roughly halves objectively confirmed venous thromboembolism (symptomatic events 1.7% to 0.2% pooled), with no significant increase in bleeding

title: Intercostal cryoanalgesia: SPLIT — after Nuss repair it halves the stay (3 vs 5 days) and cuts opioids, but after thoracotomy two randomised trials found more neuropathic-type pain weeks to months later
question: In children and adults undergoing Nuss repair of pectus excavatum or thoracotomy, does intercostal cryoanalgesia (cryoablation of intercostal nerves at surgery) reduce postoperative pain, opioid use and length of stay versus epidural or systemic analgesia?
balance: SPLIT — by operation and by time horizon. For the Nuss procedure, the single randomised trial (Graves 2019; 20 patients — a very small trial, N printed here and on the cards) found intercostal cryoablation beat thoracic epidural on the outcomes that drive Nuss recovery: median stay 3 versus 5 days (P=0.0001) and a mean 416 mg less oral morphine equivalent per patient (52-82% less on postoperative days 1-3), with equal pain scores and no neuropathic pain signal at up to one year — at the cost of 46.5 minutes longer operating time. For thoracotomy, acute results are favourable or neutral (Sepsas 2013, 50 patients: significantly better pain scores and less morphine with cryoanalgesia added to intravenous patient-controlled analgesia; Ju 2008, 107 patients: acute pain scores equal to epidural), but the chronic-pain data point the other way: Ju found allodynia-like pain significantly more frequent after cryoanalgesia at 6 and 12 months, with more moderate-to-severe chronic pain interfering with daily life, and Mustola 2011 (42 patients) found more neuropathic-type pain at 8 weeks when cryoanalgesia was added to epidural. PROPOSED SPLIT (acute benefit, chiefly Nuss; chronic neuropathic-pain concern after thoracotomy).
stamp: SPLIT — cryoanalgesia shortens stay and opioid use after Nuss repair (one small randomised trial, N = 20) and eases acute thoracotomy pain, but randomised thoracotomy trials found more neuropathic-type chronic pain after cryoanalgesia

title: Perioperative probiotics and synbiotics in GI surgery: postoperative infections roughly halved in the trial literature (relative risk 0.56 across 34 trials) — but every trial used a different preparation, so no single product carries the claim
question: In adults having elective gastrointestinal surgery, do perioperative probiotics or synbiotics reduce postoperative infectious complications (surgical-site infection, pneumonia, anastomotic leak sepsis) versus placebo or standard care?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) for the class question, with a binding product caveat. The largest synthesis (Chowdhury 2020; 34 randomised trials, 2,723 participants in elective abdominal surgery) found perioperative probiotics or synbiotics reduced postoperative infectious complications with a relative risk of 0.56 (95% CI 0.46-0.69), with synbiotics stronger (relative risk 0.46, 95% CI 0.33-0.66) than probiotics alone (relative risk 0.65, 95% CI 0.53-0.80), no mortality difference (relative risk 0.98) and no significant adverse events. The individual trials agree in direction: Rayes 2005 (66 liver-transplant recipients) found bacterial infections in 3% with a four-strain lactic-acid-bacteria plus four-fibre synbiotic versus 48% with fibres alone; Kanazawa 2005 (44 completing patients, biliary-cancer hepatectomy) found infectious complications in 19% versus 52%; Sugawara 2006 (81 completing patients) found adding preoperative synbiotics cut infections from 30.0% to 12.1% versus postoperative-only synbiotics. The caveat is structural: preparations differ by maker and strain in every trial, several records name organisms but no brand, and where a trial names no product this shelf says so — current commercial products may differ in safety and effectiveness from what was tested. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit), class-level only.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — perioperative probiotics/synbiotics reduce postoperative infections after elective abdominal surgery (relative risk 0.56 across 34 randomised trials; synbiotics 0.46), with no mortality effect; preparations differ by trial and maker, so the claim is class-level, not product-level

title: Inverted ILM flap for large macular holes: closure 98% versus 88% in the originating randomised trial, with flat-open holes almost abolished (2% vs 19%) and better 12-month vision; a four-trial meta-analysis gives odds ratio 4.89 for anatomic success
question: In adults with large full-thickness macular holes (>400 µm), does vitrectomy with an inverted internal-limiting-membrane flap improve hole closure and vision versus conventional ILM peeling?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) for closure of large holes. This pack is the PARTIAL slice the library lacked: pack #4614 asks about ocriplasmin injection and pack #6621 asks about face-down posturing after macular-hole vitrectomy — neither asks the flap-versus-peel technique question, and no homed report is carded here. The originating randomised trial (Michalewska 2010; 101 eyes with holes >400 µm) found closure in 98% with the inverted flap versus 88% with standard peeling, flat-open holes (closed but with bare pigment epithelium and poor vision) in 2% versus 19%, and better mean 12-month acuity (0.28 versus 0.17; P=0.001). A second randomised trial in still larger holes (Kannan 2018; 60 patients, holes 600-1500 µm) found anatomical success 90.0% versus 70.0% — the same direction, not statistically significant on its own (P=0.125). The meta-analysis of the four randomised trials (Chen 2020; 276 eyes) pooled an odds ratio of 4.89 (95% CI 2.09-11.47) for anatomic success and 5.23 (95% CI 2.83-9.66) for type 1 closure in favour of the flap, with better postoperative acuity. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) for anatomical closure; the visual advantage is smaller and less certain than the closure advantage.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — for large macular holes (>400 µm) the inverted ILM flap closes more holes than conventional peeling (98% vs 88% in the originating trial; pooled odds ratio 4.89 across four randomised trials) and nearly abolishes the flat-open outcome, with a smaller visual-acuity advantage

title: Voretigene neparvovec (Luxturna, Spark Therapeutics) for RPE65 retinal dystrophy: functional vision improved in the phase 3 trial (mobility-test change 1.8 vs 0.2 light levels; 65% passed at the lowest light level vs none) — a single programme with a pivotal N of 31
question: In people with biallelic RPE65 mutation-associated inherited retinal dystrophy, does subretinal voretigene neparvovec (the AAV2 gene therapy tested in the licensing programme — name the product and maker as published) improve functional vision (multi-luminance mobility testing) and visual fields versus no gene therapy?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single development programme, capped at POSSIBLE, with a small pivotal N stated plainly. A premise correction to the build brief: the pivotal evidence is NOT single-arm or externally controlled. The phase 3 trial (Russell 2017) was randomised and controlled — 31 participants assigned 2:1 to bilateral subretinal voretigene neparvovec (1.5×10^11 vector genomes per eye) or to a concurrent no-treatment control group, with outcome graders masked; controls crossed over to treatment after the one-year primary endpoint, so controlled comparison exists only for year 1. At one year the mean bilateral multi-luminance mobility test change was 1.8 (SD 1.1) light levels in the intervention group versus 0.2 (1.0) in controls (difference 1.6, 95% CI 0.72-2.41; P=0.0013), and 65% of treated participants passed the mobility course at the lowest luminance tested (1 lux) versus no controls. The product is voretigene neparvovec (Luxturna), developed by Spark Therapeutics, named as published in the trial record. Durability comes only from within-programme follow-on reports: the phase 1 contralateral-eye study (Bennett 2016; 11 participants) and the combined phase 1/3 durability report (Maguire 2019; 40 treated subjects) found mobility and light-sensitivity gains maintained to 4 years in the phase 1 cohort and 2 years in phase 3, with a safety profile consistent with vitrectomy and subretinal injection and no product-related serious adverse events or deleterious immune responses in phase 3. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — single programme; pivotal trial N = 31.

title: Tube shunt versus trabeculectomy as the FIRST glaucoma operation (PTVT): failure rates did not differ significantly at 3 or 5 years (33% vs 28%; 42% vs 35%) — trabeculectomy gave lower pressure on fewer drops, tube surgery fewer serious early complications
question: In adults with open-angle glaucoma and no prior incisional surgery, is a tube shunt non-inferior to trabeculectomy with mitomycin as the first operation for pressure control, failure and complications?
balance: POSSIBLE (no difference) — a single trial programme, so the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE, and all four cards below are explicitly labelled reports of the one Primary Tube Versus Trabeculectomy (PTVT) Study (242 patients, no prior incisional surgery, 350-mm² Baerveldt implant versus trabeculectomy with mitomycin C). This is the PARTIAL slice the library lacked: live shelf #617 asks the tube-versus-trabeculectomy question only in eyes with prior surgery or high failure risk (the TVT population), and none of its reports is carded here. In PTVT, trabeculectomy was ahead at 1 year (failure 7.9% versus 17.3%; P=0.01), but the gap closed: failure at 3 years was 28% versus 33% (P=0.17) and at 5 years 35% versus 42% (P=0.21) — no significant difference at either later point. Pressure told a steadier story in trabeculectomy's favour early (12.1 versus 14.0 mmHg at 3 years) and converged by 5 years (13.0 versus 13.4 mmHg; P=0.52), while medication burden stayed lower after trabeculectomy throughout (1.3 versus 2.2 drops at 5 years; P<0.001). Serious complications requiring reoperation or costing ≥2 lines of vision were fewer with the tube at 1 year (1% versus 7%; P=0.03) and similar by 3 years (2% versus 8%; P=0.11). Visual fields declined at statistically indistinguishable rates (-0.47 versus -0.32 dB/year; P=0.23). On the trial's own primary outcome at its longest follow-up, the treatment made no significant difference — but PTVT was a superiority trial, not a formal noninferiority trial, so 'non-inferior' is a description of the result, not a tested claim. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (no difference).
stamp: POSSIBLE (no difference) — single trial programme (PTVT, 242 patients): as a first operation, tube shunt and trabeculectomy with mitomycin did not differ significantly in failure at 3 or 5 years (the treatment made no difference on the primary outcome); trabeculectomy needed fewer drops, the tube had fewer serious early complications

title: Submacular haemorrhage in wet AMD: no randomised trial has tested pneumatic displacement against anti-VEGF alone — the one randomised trial (STAR, 90 patients) found surgery no better than pneumatic displacement (+16.8 vs +16.4 letters), and the comparative cohorts are size-dependent and confounded
question: In adults with submacular haemorrhage secondary to neovascular age-related macular degeneration, does pneumatic displacement with subretinal or intravitreal tissue plasminogen activator (± anti-VEGF) improve vision versus anti-VEGF therapy alone?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — graded GAP-E, and the evidence map matters more than any single number. No randomised trial has compared pneumatic displacement (± tissue plasminogen activator) against anti-VEGF therapy alone, which is the question as asked. The one randomised trial in the field, STAR (Gabrielle 2023; 90 patients, haemorrhage within 14 days, over 2 disc areas), compared the two active displacement strategies against each other — vitrectomy with subretinal tPA and gas versus pneumatic displacement with intravitreal tPA and gas, both with ranibizumab — and found no superiority for surgery: acuity change at 3 months was +16.8 letters with surgery versus +16.4 letters with pneumatic displacement (adjusted difference 1.9 letters, 95% CI -11.0 to 14.9; P=0.767), with similar outcomes at 6 months and no unexpected safety concerns; the authors note the trial cannot establish equivalence either. The only direct evidence on displacement versus anti-VEGF alone is a retrospective three-way comparison (Jeong 2020; 77 eyes, treatment chosen by the surgeon): for medium-sized haemorrhages, displacement rates were 67% (pneumatic displacement) and 83% (surgery) versus 33% with anti-VEGF alone, with better acuity in the displacement groups; for large haemorrhages surgery displaced more than pneumatic displacement (86% versus 25%); for small haemorrhages all three strategies improved acuity similarly. A 2026 network meta-analysis (150 studies reviewed, 38 in the network, 2,125 eyes) found non-vitrectomy therapies had better acuity outcomes and fewer complications than vitrectomy-based treatment, but concluded there is no consensus standard and large randomised trials are still needed. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) for displacement over anti-VEGF alone in medium-to-large haemorrhages — cohort-grade only.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — pneumatic displacement ± tPA may beat anti-VEGF alone for medium-to-large submacular haemorrhage, but that contrast rests on one retrospective cohort; the only randomised trial (STAR) compared surgery with pneumatic displacement and found no difference (+16.8 vs +16.4 letters, P=0.767)

title: Dropless cataract surgery: injected antibiotic–steroid regimens match drops on inflammation — the depot needed rescue drops in over half, and no trial was powered for endophthalmitis
question: In adults having routine cataract surgery, does a "dropless" regimen (intracameral or transzonular antibiotic–steroid, as tested in the programmes) prevent endophthalmitis and postoperative inflammation as well as conventional topical drops, and does it reduce drop-burden problems?
balance: The randomised evidence says dropless regimens control postoperative inflammation and macular thickening about as well as drops — with one sharp exception: in the Danish five-arm trial the sub-Tenon dexamethasone depot arm needed additional anti-inflammatory treatment in 56.6% of patients, and early aqueous flare was higher with the depot than with combination drops. The intracameral dexamethasone suspension IBI-10090 (named Dexycu in the record; the publication record names no company) cleared anterior-chamber cells at the same rate as prednisolone drops by day 8. The antibiotic-containing regimens (transzonular triamcinolone–moxifloxacin; intravitreal triamcinolone–moxifloxacin–vancomycin) rest on a single-arm series and a retrospective comparison, not randomisation. On endophthalmitis — the outcome patients most fear — no carded study reports a powered comparison: the infection claim for dropless surgery is cohort-grade at best, exactly as the slate flagged. Patient preference, where measured, strongly favours not using drops.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — dropless regimens matched topical drops on inflammation and vision in the randomised reports, but the sub-Tenon depot needed rescue drops in 56.6% of its arm and no carded study was powered for endophthalmitis

title: Oral tranexamic acid for melasma: pigmentation falls by about half in small placebo-controlled trials — off-label, with thrombosis screening part of the deal
question: In adults with moderate-to-severe melasma, does oral tranexamic acid improve pigmentation (MASI) versus placebo or topical therapy alone, and at what thrombotic-safety cost in screened patients?
balance: This shelf is the oral-tranexamic-acid slice the library was missing: pack #4222 homes the topical triple-combination cream question and does not card oral tranexamic acid. Four small randomised trials point the same way — modified MASI falls by about half on oral tranexamic acid 250 mg twice daily over 3 months, against ~11–19% on placebo or hydroquinone alone, and much of the gain persists 3 months after stopping. The safety side must be read honestly: these were screened patients, the samples are far too small to detect a rare thrombotic event, and 'no serious adverse events' in ~230 trial patients is not proof of thrombotic safety. Cross-point: pack #4222 (topical triple-combination cream versus hydroquinone).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — four small randomised trials agree that oral tranexamic acid roughly halves melasma severity scores versus placebo or topical therapy alone, but every trial is small and single-centre and the use is off-label

title: Low-dose oral minoxidil for androgenetic alopecia: head-to-head trials find it about equal to topical minoxidil — with more unwanted hair growth
question: In adults with androgenetic alopecia, does low-dose oral minoxidil improve hair density versus placebo — and how does it compare with topical minoxidil — at what cost in hypertrichosis, oedema and cardiovascular effects?
balance: The library's homes ask the neighbouring questions — pack #6008 (oral finasteride versus topical minoxidil) and pack #6009 (topical minoxidil in women) — and neither cards the oral route; this shelf builds only on the oral-minoxidil reports those homes do not contain. Three randomised head-to-head trials, carded per dose as the slate required and never pooled, converge on equivalence rather than superiority: oral 2.5 mg (men) / 1.25 mg (women) matched topical on photographic improvement (67% versus 73%); oral 1 mg matched 5% topical on hair diameter; and a three-arm trial found one-grade improvement in 25% on oral versus 10% on topical, a non-significant difference. The cost side is consistent: hypertrichosis in 30% versus 9% in the double-dummy trial, plus headache (20%), dizziness (15%) and pedal oedema (5%) in the three-arm trial's oral group. No placebo-controlled oral-minoxidil trial is carded here, so the stamp caps at POSSIBLE; the use is off-label at every dose carded.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in three randomised head-to-head trials oral minoxidil performed about the same as topical minoxidil, with significantly more hypertrichosis; no placebo-controlled trial is carded on this shelf and the use is off-label

title: Sofpironium gel for axillary hyperhidrosis: two phase 3 programmes beat vehicle on severity and sweat weight
question: In adults with primary axillary hyperhidrosis, does sofpironium bromide gel (the topical anticholinergic tested in the CARDIGAN programme) reduce sweat production and severity scores versus vehicle?
balance: Pack #2476 homes botulinum toxin injections and the glycopyrronium tosylate cloth for this condition; sofpironium gel — a different product and formulation — appears nowhere in it, and this shelf cards only the sofpironium reports. The evidence is unusually tidy for a dermatology shelf: the pooled CARDIGAN I and II phase 3 trials of sofpironium topical gel 12.45% (701 patients) met both co-primary endpoints against vehicle; the Japanese phase 3 trial of the 5% gel (BBI-4000; 281 patients) met its combined severity-plus-sweat-weight endpoint 53.9% versus 36.4%; a phase 2 dose-ranging trial found all three concentrations superior to vehicle on severity scores; and a 52-week open-label extension held the response at ~58%. Harms are the expected local and anticholinergic ones — application-site dermatitis and erythema, with adverse-drug-reaction rates of 16.3% versus 5.0% in the Japanese trial — and no serious treatment-related events were reported. Where a publication record names no manufacturer, the card says so plainly, per the product-naming rule.

title: The diving response: face immersion plus apnoea cuts heart rate by a third in trained divers and slows oxygen use — the integrated cardiovascular picture
question: In healthy humans, what is the integrated diving response — how much do heart rate and cardiac output fall and peripheral vascular resistance rise with face immersion in cold water plus apnoea, how is blood redistributed to heart and brain, and how do trained divers differ from untrained people?
balance: Textbook framing (Guyton & Hall, nervous regulation of the circulation; Boron & Boulpaep): the diving response is a trigeminally triggered, vagally mediated bradycardia with sympathetically mediated peripheral vasoconstriction that redistributes the reduced cardiac output toward heart and brain — that redistribution account is the textbook's, and the cards below measure its human signatures (heart rate, blood pressure, pulmonary oxygen uptake), not cardiac output or regional flow directly. This shelf builds only the slice pack #6633 does not home: #6633 cards the spleen-contraction and haemoglobin side of apnoea (its PMIDs are not reused here), and pack #6644 homes the breath-hold breaking point. What the primary human studies add: face immersion augments the apnoea response at rest and in exercise, trained divers show the deepest bradycardia, and the response measurably conserves the lung oxygen store. Classic studies are small; every N is printed on its card.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — apnoea with cold-water face immersion reproducibly deepens bradycardia (heart-rate fall 33% in trained divers during exercise), raises blood pressure and slows pulmonary oxygen uptake in every carded human study (Guyton & Hall; Boron & Boulpaep)

title: Accommodation across the lifespan: objective amplitude is far below the push-up numbers, holds to about age 20, then collapses to zero by the 50s — while the ciliary muscle keeps contracting
question: In healthy humans, how does the amplitude of eye accommodation decline across the lifespan — what did the classic subjective (push-up, minus-lens) and objective (dynamic retinoscopy / open-field autorefraction) measurements show, and how much of presbyopia is lenticular stiffening versus ciliary/zonular failure on human lens-stretching and imaging studies?
balance: Textbook framing (Guyton & Hall; Ganong, optics and accommodation): the Helmholtz mechanism — ciliary contraction releases zonular tension and the elastic lens rounds up. The human measurement literature separates the two candidate failures cleanly. Objective autorefraction (Anderson programme) shows true amplitude is far below the classic subjective push-up figures — which overestimate, especially in young children — plateaus until about age 20, then declines sigmoidally to zero beyond 50. Human MRI (Strenk programme) shows the ciliary muscle contracting in every subject into the ninth decade, with an accommodative diameter change undiminished by age: the muscle works; the ageing, thickening lens stops answering. The lens-stiffening side of the mechanism rests partly on ex vivo human donor-lens work (the Fisher spinning-lens lineage and later donor-lens stretching studies) — that is labelled here as ex vivo/textbook prose, not carded as in-vivo human evidence, and primate lens-stretching data are not carded at all.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — objective autorefraction shows amplitude plateauing to about age 20, falling steeply between 20 and 50 and reaching ~0 beyond 50, while human MRI shows the ciliary muscle still contracting in old age — presbyopia is chiefly a lens failure (Guyton & Hall; Ganong)

title: The post-illumination pupil response: the pupil stays constricted ~1.5 mm after bright blue light is switched off — a melanopsin signal that shrinks in glaucoma and retinitis pigmentosa
question: In healthy humans, what is the post-illumination pupil response — how long does the pupil stay constricted after a bright (especially short-wavelength) light is switched off, how is the response isolated as melanopsin/ipRGC-driven, and how does it fail in outer-retinal disease while the afferent light reflex survives?
balance: Textbook framing (Ganong; Boron & Boulpaep, retinal phototransduction): a small population of intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs) containing melanopsin signals irradiance directly, with slow, sustained kinetics unlike the transient rod/cone response. The human pupillometry literature isolates that signal by colour and timing: the constriction that persists after a bright short-wavelength stimulus is switched off — the post-illumination pupil response (PIPR) — matches melanopsin's spectral tuning, is present in all healthy subjects, and survives as a measurable inner-retinal signal even when outer-retinal disease has degraded the rod/cone-driven components. The disease cards (glaucoma, retinitis pigmentosa) are carded as physiology-in-disease contrasts, the standard way this response is characterised, not as treatment evidence.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — a sustained post-offset constriction driven by intrinsically photosensitive (melanopsin) ganglion cells is present in every healthy subject tested, is ~1.4 mm net for blue over red light, and is reduced in glaucoma and retinitis pigmentosa (Ganong; Boron & Boulpaep)

title: Postprandial splanchnic hyperaemia: superior mesenteric flow rises two- to threefold after a meal, peaking at 30–60 minutes — water alone does nothing
question: In healthy humans, how much does splanchnic (superior mesenteric and portal) blood flow rise after a meal — what is the time course and peak of postprandial hyperaemia by Doppler ultrasound and hepatic-vein catheterisation, which meal components drive it, and how is flow redistributed away again in exercise?
balance: Textbook framing (Guyton & Hall, splanchnic circulation and gastrointestinal blood-flow regulation): meal ingestion is the gut's dominant hyperaemic stimulus, driven by absorbed nutrients, gastrointestinal hormones and local metabolites, with cardiac output rising in parallel. The primary human base is the Doppler ultrasound literature — small, careful volunteer studies, every N printed on its card as this stream requires. Its findings are consistent: superior mesenteric flow rises two- to threefold, peaks at 30–60 minutes and stays up for about two hours; carbohydrate, protein and fat meals all do it and water does not; the coeliac and femoral beds do not share the response, marking it as a true splanchnic redistribution; and a pressor challenge (sustained handgrip) shows the fed splanchnic bed defending its flow differently from the fasting bed. title: Functional sympatholysis: contracting muscle blunts sympathetic vasoconstriction by more than half — a protection that ageing and oestrogen loss erode
question: In healthy humans exercising, how is muscle blood flow protected from sympathetic vasoconstriction — how large is functional sympatholysis (the blunting of sympathetically mediated vasoconstriction in exercising versus resting muscle), and how is it demonstrated with intra-arterial agonist infusions, tyramine and lower-body negative pressure during exercise?
balance: Textbook framing (Guyton & Hall, local control of blood flow and sympathetic control during exercise): metabolites in contracting muscle override sympathetic vasoconstrictor signals locally, so the sympathetic outflow that constricts resting muscle and viscera during exercise spares the working muscle. The human demonstration is pharmacological and elegant: infuse tyramine (which releases endogenous noradrenaline) or α-agonists into the brachial artery and compare the vasoconstriction they produce in a resting forearm against the same forearm doing rhythmic handgrip — conductance falls by roughly half or less in the contracting muscle. The carded studies add the time course (blunting within 10–20 seconds of onset), the mechanism probe (nitric-oxide blockade does not restore the constriction, so NO alone is not the obligatory mediator), and the human limits (the protection is impaired in older men and in postmenopausal women, and restored by oestrogen in the latter). Adjacent shelves: pack #6632 (the exercise pressor reflex that raises pressure) and pack #6076 (what sets cardiac output in exercise) — different questions, cross-pointed only.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — intra-arterial agonist and tyramine responses in contracting human forearm are blunted by roughly half or more versus the resting state, the blunting appears within seconds of exercise onset, and it is impaired in older men and postmenopausal women (Guyton & Hall)

title: Respiratory sinus arrhythmia: the heart speeds with each breath in and slows out — a vagally gated rhythm set mainly by breathing rate
question: In healthy humans, what is respiratory sinus arrhythmia — how much does heart rate speed in inspiration and slow in expiration, how much of it is vagal efferent traffic versus central irradiation and the Bainbridge/baroreflex loops, and how do breathing rate and tidal volume scale it in the classic blockade and pacing studies?
balance: Guyton & Hall and Ganong frame respiratory sinus arrhythmia (RSA) as the visible signature of phasic vagal efferent traffic to the sinus node: vagal motoneuron firing is gated by the respiratory cycle (suppressed in inspiration, released in expiration), so heart period shortens as a breath begins and lengthens as it ends. The fetched human records support that framing quantitatively. In 17 seated volunteers breathing at controlled rates and volumes, RSA was large and stable below 6 breaths/min — a low-frequency intercept of 20 ± 5 beats/min of peak-to-trough heart-rate swing — and rolled off above a corner frequency of 7.2 ± 1.5 cycles/min, with RSA scaling linearly with tidal volume (Hirsch & Bishop 1981). Eckberg's controlled-breathing study in 6 healthy young adults showed the complementary asymmetry: a 50% increase in tidal volume raised the peak-valley P-P interval by only about 15%, while lengthening the breathing interval widened RSA asymptotically — breathing rate matters more than depth (Eckberg 1983). The mechanism is central gating of vagal outflow interacting with the baroreflex, not a purely reflex loop: in 6 volunteers, carotid baroreceptor stimuli (neck suction) delivered in inspiration produced blunted sinus-node responses at moderate intensity, while intense stimuli broke through the gate (Eckberg & Orshan 1977); and in 22 healthy young adults, low-dose atropine paradoxically increased RSA and baroreflex responses while high-dose atropine abolished them exponentially, with resting RSA correlating with baroreflex responsiveness at r = 0.78 (Raczkowska, Eckberg & Ebert 1983). The Bainbridge reflex and central irradiation from the respiratory centre are named in the textbooks as contributing loops; no carded record here isolates the Bainbridge contribution, so that part stands as the textbook's account rather than a measured share. Net: RSA in health is a vagally mediated, respiration-gated rhythm whose size is set mainly by breathing interval, modestly by tidal volume, and which fades as breathing quickens past roughly 7 breaths/min.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — respiratory sinus arrhythmia is vagal gating made visible: a 20 ± 5 beats/min swing at slow breathing rates, rolling off above ~7 breaths/min, scaled mainly by breathing interval and modestly by tidal volume, and abolished by full muscarinic blockade (Guyton & Hall; Ganong)

title: Heart-rate recovery after exercise: a vagal first half-minute, then a sympathetic tail that tracks noradrenaline washout
question: In healthy humans, how fast does heart rate fall in the first 1–2 minutes after stopping maximal exercise (heart-rate recovery), what autonomic sequence produces the fast and slow phases on blockade studies, and how do fitness and age change the time constant?
balance: Guyton & Hall frames post-exercise recovery as the mirror of the exercise response: the fast early fall in heart rate is vagal reactivation, and the slower tail is sympathetic withdrawal as muscle metaboreflex input and circulating catecholamines clear. The fetched blockade and time-course records support that two-phase account with numbers. In 6 men recovering from peak treadmill exercise, heart rate fell exponentially under every condition — no drugs, atropine, propranolol, or both — with the exponential coefficients differing most between parasympathetic and sympathetic blockade (Savin 1982). Imai's protocol separated the phases directly: in 8 normal volunteers, the time constants of heart-rate decay over the first 30 s (T30) and first 120 s (T120) after exercise were both markedly prolonged by atropine, but T30 was almost independent of exercise intensity and of sympathetic blockade, marking it as primarily vagal reactivation, while T120 also tracked sympathetic activity and workload; recovery was accelerated in trained cross-country skiers and blunted in heart-failure patients (Imai 1994). Perini's catecholamine study in 6 sedentary young men put times on the slow phase: heart rate fell mono-exponentially with tau values of 13.6, 32.7 and 55.8 s after exercise at 21%, 43% and 65% of VO2max, dropped about 35 beats/min in the first minute regardless of intensity (prompt vagal restoration), and thereafter tracked the exponential decay of venous noradrenaline (tau ~87–101 s) (Perini 1989). Pierpont's modelling study adds the measurement caution: a single-exponential time constant is a reasonable index after submaximal exercise but fits maximal-exercise recovery poorly (Pierpont 2000). So in health the first half-minute is a vagal event, the next minutes are sympathetic washout, and both fitness and intensity move the constants in predictable directions.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — heart-rate recovery is two-phase: a vagal first ~30 seconds (atropine-sensitive, intensity-independent, faster in the trained) over a sympathetic tail that tracks noradrenaline washout, with tau lengthening from ~14 s to ~56 s as prior intensity rises (Guyton & Hall)

title: Oxygen-uptake kinetics at exercise onset: a 15-second cardiodynamic phase, then an exponential rise with a ~30-second time constant
question: In healthy humans, how fast do oxygen-uptake kinetics respond at exercise onset — what is the phase II time constant for pulmonary VO2 in moderate exercise, how much does it slow in heavy/severe domains and with ageing or deconditioning, and what does the oxygen deficit represent?
balance: Guyton & Hall and Boron & Boulpaep frame the exercise on-transient in phases: an immediate cardiodynamic phase (phase I, the first ~10–15 s, driven by the rise in pulmonary blood flow before venous blood from the exercising muscle reaches the lungs), then phase II, in which pulmonary VO2 rises mono-exponentially toward the steady state with a time constant (tau) that mirrors muscle VO2 consumption, leaving an oxygen deficit that is repaid by the aerobic system catching up. The fetched human records measure each piece. Grassi's group measured leg VO2 directly by thermodilution leg blood flow plus arteriovenous O2 difference in 6 trained subjects and found phase I confined to the first 10–15 s, then mono-exponential phase II responses whose half-times were statistically indistinguishable between alveolar VO2 (25.5 ± 2.6 s) and leg VO2 (27.9 ± 5.7 s) — pulmonary kinetics faithfully track muscle kinetics after phase I (Grassi 1996). DeLorey's near-infrared programme timed the muscle side: in 11 young adults the phase II pulmonary tau was 30 ± 8 s while muscle deoxygenation, after a 13 ± 2 s delay, rose faster (tau 10 ± 3 s) (DeLorey 2003). Ageing slows phase II substantially — tau 26 ± 7 s in young adults versus 42 ± 9 s in older adults at the same relative moderate intensity (DeLorey 2004) — and a heavy-intensity warm-up ('priming') speeds the older tau from 38 ± 5 s to 30 ± 7 s while leaving young adults unchanged (DeLorey 2004). In heavy and severe domains the textbooks describe an additional delayed slow component that prolongs or prevents the steady state; that feature is carried here as the textbook's account (Whipp's slow-component synthesis is a review, not a primary record, and is not carded — see the Synthesis card).
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — VO2 at exercise onset shows a 10–15 s cardiodynamic phase I, then a mono-exponential phase II (tau ~30 s in young adults, ~42 s in older adults, re-speeded toward 30 s by priming in the old) — the oxygen deficit is the gap that exponential leaves (Guyton & Hall; Boron & Boulpaep)

title: Small-intestine motor patterns: a migrating motor complex every ~97 minutes that slows, fades distally, and vanishes the moment a meal arrives
question: In healthy humans, what are the small intestine's motor patterns — the fasting migrating motor complex (phase I–III cycle length and propagation), the immediate fed-pattern replacement after a meal, and how do the patterns differ between jejunum and ileum on prolonged ambulatory manometry?
balance: Guyton & Hall describes the fasting small intestine as cycling through the migrating motor complex (MMC): quiescence (phase I), irregular activity (phase II), then a propagating burst of maximal-frequency contractions (phase III, the 'activity front' or housekeeper) that sweeps residual debris aborally, with a meal abolishing the cycle and substituting the irregular fed pattern. The fetched human manometry records give the cycle its real, wide numbers. In 11 healthy subjects recorded from jejunum to terminal ileum, 96 MMCs occurred at a grand-mean interval of 97 minutes — but individual intervals ranged from 15 to 195 minutes — with the activity front slowing as it travelled (4.7 cm/min in jejunum, 0.9 cm/min in terminal ileum) and its contraction rate falling distally (about 12.5–10.5/min jejunal to 10.0–8.6/min terminal ileal); a 600-kcal liquid meal interrupted fasting cycling for 2.75 to more than 10 hours (Kerlin & Phillips 1982). Kellow's stomach-to-colon recordings in 16 volunteers add the attrition: fewer than half of MMCs were recognisable beyond the midpoint of the small bowel and less than 10% reached the distal ileum, the complex was more prominent at night, and small meals of 345–395 kcal interrupted fasting patterns for 90–240 minutes (Kellow 1986). Prolonged ambulatory recording in 30 volunteers found at least one phase III in every subject over 6 hours of fasting or sleep, at 0.52 ± 0.04 per hour fasting and 0.59 ± 0.04 per hour asleep, with postprandial contraction frequency and motility index maximal in the first 2 hours after the meal and no substantive duodenum-versus-jejunum or sex differences (Soffer 1998). The largest normative series — 51 volunteers, 419 phase III episodes — confirms wide normal ranges and large within-subject variability (Scott 2006). This shelf is the small-bowel companion to shelf #6638, which homes the colon's quite different patterns (a quiet fasting colon with no dominant migrating complex); the two share no carded studies.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — the fasting small bowel cycles through the migrating motor complex (mean ~97 min between fronts, true range 15–195 min), the front slowing from 4.7 to 0.9 cm/min and usually fading before the distal ileum, persisting in sleep and abolished at once by a meal (Guyton & Hall)

title: Jejunal sugar absorption: glucose on a saturable sodium-coupled carrier, fructose on a small separate one that easily overflows
question: In healthy humans, how are glucose and fructose absorbed across the jejunum — what did the classic triple-lumen perfusion studies show about sodium-coupled glucose uptake, solvent drag and maximal absorptive capacity, and why is fructose absorption capacity-limited and malabsorbed in a fraction of healthy people on breath-hydrogen testing?
balance: Boron & Boulpaep and Guyton & Hall frame intestinal sugar absorption as two different machines: glucose (and galactose) cross the brush border on the sodium-coupled SGLT1 transporter — saturable, sodium-dependent, and dragging water and sodium with it — while fructose crosses on the facilitative, sodium-independent GLUT5 carrier, whose capacity is limited and varies widely between people, so unabsorbed fructose reaches colonic bacteria and is fermented to hydrogen. The fetched perfusion and breath-test records measure both machines in living humans. Jejunal perfusion with an occluding-balloon technique showed glucose absorption is a saturable function of load — a single maximum velocity and half-saturating load fitted all flow rates and starting concentrations — and that glucose stimulated water and sodium movement progressively as its concentration rose from 14 to 133 mmol/L (≈252 to ≈2,394 mg/dL) (Modigliani & Bernier 1971). The Fordtran group's ileal perfusion study then complicated the simple sodium story: replacing luminal sodium with mannitol cut active glucose absorption by only 23% in vivo (magnesium substitution, 45%), raising the apparent Km without changing Vmax, while fructose absorption was entirely unaffected by sodium removal — direct human evidence for fructose's separate carrier (Bieberdorf, Morawski & Fordtran 1975). Rumessen & Gudmand-Høyer's breath-hydrogen studies quantified the fructose ceiling: absorption capacity for fructose alone ranged from under 5 g to over 50 g across 10 healthy adults, with malabsorption in 8 of 10 at a 50 g dose, while the same fructose given as sucrose, or with equimolar glucose, was absorbed completely — glucose rescues fructose uptake dose-dependently (Rumessen & Gudmand-Høyer 1986) — and sorbitol does the opposite, provoking malabsorption of a fructose-sorbitol mixture in 7 of 10 even at individually tolerated doses (Rumessen & Gudmand-Høyer 1987).
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — glucose absorption is saturable and sodium-coupled (dragging water and sodium with it), while fructose uses a separate sodium-independent carrier with a capacity of <5 g to >50 g in health — rescued by glucose, sabotaged by sorbitol (Boron & Boulpaep; Guyton & Hall)

title: Saliva production: a circadian, sex-patterned resting flow — with stimulated gland capacity that survives healthy ageing
question: In healthy humans, how much saliva is produced — unstimulated and stimulated whole-saliva flow rates, the glands' relative contributions at rest versus stimulation, and the circadian rhythm of flow and composition?
balance: Guyton & Hall and Ganong give the textbook account of salivary secretion: roughly 1,000–1,500 ml of saliva a day, produced at a low unstimulated whole-saliva flow of a few tenths of a ml/min at rest — dominated by the submandibular glands — and rising severalfold on stimulation, when the parotid glands' share grows; those specific figures are the textbooks' account, since the fetched primary records below mostly report rhythms and comparisons rather than printing the canonical rates. What the primary human records do establish is the rhythm and the modifiers. Dawes showed that unstimulated whole-saliva flow and its sodium and chloride concentrations follow a significant circadian rhythm, as does the composition of parotid saliva stimulated at a clamped flow of 1.0 ml/min (Dawes 1972, N = 8), and that unstimulated submandibular flow likewise cycles across the day (Dawes 1975, N = 9) — so a 'normal' flow value is meaningless without its clock time. The large cross-sectional records fix the person-level modifiers: in 629 adults, resting and stimulated whole-saliva secretion rates were significantly lower in women than men, and women's resting rate fell with age (Heintze 1983); in 116 unmedicated healthy people, unstimulated whole-saliva flow fell significantly with age (P < 0.001) while stimulated parotid flow did not differ across age groups from 20 to over 80 years (Percival 1994); and gland-specific measurement found no diminution at all in submandibular output, resting or stimulated, across ages 26–93 (Tylenda 1988, N = 90). The reconciled picture: resting whole-mouth flow ebbs with age and time of day, but the glands' stimulated secretory capacity is largely preserved in healthy ageing — the dry mouth of old age is more often medication and disease than gland failure, a conclusion Dawes' framework anticipates in noting that the sensation of dry mouth appears when unstimulated flow falls by roughly 40–50%.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — salivary flow follows a circadian rhythm, runs lower in women, and ebbs at rest with age while stimulated gland capacity is preserved into the tenth decade; the canonical ~1,000–1,500 ml/day and resting/stimulated rates are the textbook's account (Guyton & Hall; Ganong)

title: Exocrine pancreatic response: a brisk, saturable secretin response and a gland that only a mixed meal switches from cycling to feeding
question: In healthy humans, how does the exocrine pancreas respond to a meal and to secretin/CCK stimulation — what are enzyme and bicarbonate outputs in the classic duodenal-aspiration and secretin-test studies, and how is the cephalic versus intestinal phase divided?
balance: Guyton & Hall and Boron & Boulpaep divide pancreatic secretion into a small cephalic phase (vagal, anticipatory), a gastric phase, and the dominant intestinal phase, in which acid-driven secretin releases a bicarbonate-rich fluid from the duct cells while fat- and protein-driven cholecystokinin (CCK) releases enzyme-rich secretion from the acini; between meals the gland cycles with the interdigestive migrating motor complex instead of secreting steadily. The fetched human aspiration and cannulation records measure those responses directly. Pure pancreatic juice collected by endoscopic duct cannulation from 20 normal subjects responded briskly even to small secretin doses (1 and 4 clinical units), with peak bicarbonate concentration after the 4-unit stimulus and the greatest volumes and bicarbonate and protein outputs after 70 units; protein and amylase concentrations were highest in the first specimens and fell after stimulation, and all indices plateaued 10–20 minutes into combined secretin–pancreozymin infusion (Denyer & Cotton 1979). An extended function test adding a second secretin–pancreozymin bolus showed the standard test already exhausts the discriminatory signal — repeat bolus stimulation cannot wring more diagnostic separation from the gland (Gilinsky 1983). The Lundh test meal gives the endogenous version: volume secretion rises immediately and identically in health and pancreatic insufficiency, while enzyme secretion is what fails in disease, with lipase and trypsin outputs tracking the secretin–cerulein test (Bozkurt 1990). And the phase logic was proven by duodenal perfusion in 6 healthy men: only a mixed meal converted the cyclical interdigestive secretory pattern into the sustained fed pattern — glucose, fat or protein alone, each releasing less or no CCK, left the cycle intact (Katschinski 1992). A modern endoscopic secretin test in 16 healthy volunteers confirms the textbook kinetics with contemporary methods: juice flow peaks early, bicarbonate concentration peaks late, and chloride and bicarbonate vary reciprocally at constant sodium and potassium (Conwell 2005).
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — the pancreas answers small secretin doses briskly (bicarbonate concentration peaking at low dose, outputs maximal at high dose, plateau at 10–20 min), secretes cyclically between meals, and converts to the fed pattern only under a mixed meal via CCK (Guyton & Hall; Boron & Boulpaep)

title: Phosphate handling in health: the TmP/GFR threshold, its fall with rising PTH, and adaptation to a phosphate load
question: In healthy humans, how is phosphate handled — what is the tubular maximum for phosphate corrected for GFR (TmP/GFR), how do PTH and dietary phosphate loading change fractional excretion within hours to days, and what did the classic phosphate-infusion and deprivation studies show about adaptation?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Framed by Guyton & Hall and Boron & Boulpaep (textbook framing, not evidence). The kidney defends plasma phosphate at a tubular threshold, TmP/GFR: Walton & Bijvoet's method (PMID 923101) made that threshold measurable from single paired samples. In health the threshold is not fixed — it falls as PTH rises with ageing (Endres, PMID 2821053) and the system adapts to a sustained load by excreting it, with an early FGF23 rise that normalises by 8 weeks and no change in fasting plasma phosphate (Trautvetter, PMID 26786148). The textbook's normative TmP/GFR range (about 0.80–1.35 mmol/L, about 2.5–4.2 mg/dL) is the textbook's account: no carded record prints it. Adjacent pack #6306 covers the calcium-sensing set-point — a different question; this pack does not duplicate its calcium content.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED

title: The daily melatonin rhythm as a circadian phase marker: DLMO timing, reliability, and suppression by evening light
question: In healthy humans, what does the daily melatonin rhythm look like as a circadian phase marker — dim-light melatonin onset timing relative to sleep, peak amplitude, and suppression by evening light — measured under controlled dim-light protocols?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Framed by Ganong and Boron & Boulpaep (textbook framing, not evidence). Home pack #6250 measures the clock's endogenous period (24.18 h) under forced desynchrony — verified by reading its file: it cards Czeisler 1999, Dijk & Duffy 1999, Wright 2005 and Scheer 2007 (PMIDs 10381883, 10087357, 15834113, 17684566), none of which is carded here, and it does not card DLMO timing, reliability or light-suppression figures. This pack cards that uncovered slice: melatonin is light-suppressible in humans (Lewy, PMID 7434030, N = 6); its phase markers are more stable than the temperature nadir and track sleep offset best (Benloucif, PMID 15834114, N = 42); the calculated DLMO moves ~22–24 minutes with threshold choice (Molina & Burgess, PMID 21823817, N = 122); and ordinary room light before bedtime delays onset in 99% and shortens duration by ~90 minutes (Gooley, PMID 21193540, N = 116).

title: Muscle glycogen resynthesis after depleting exercise: fast early rates, a dose plateau near 0.7–1.5 g/kg, and a timing penalty for delayed feeding
question: In healthy humans, how fast is muscle glycogen resynthesised after depleting exercise — what are the biopsy-measured resynthesis rates with and without carbohydrate feeding in the first hours, how much carbohydrate maximises them, and how long does full restoration take?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Framed by Guyton & Hall and Ganong (textbook framing, not evidence). Four biopsy programmes agree: resynthesis is fastest in the first 2 hours when carbohydrate is fed immediately (7.7 µmol/g/h, Ivy timing study, PMID 3132449, N = 12) and is cut to 2.5 by a 2-hour delay; the rate plateaus with dose — no gain doubling 1.5 to 3.0 g/kg (Ivy, PMID 3145274, N = 8) and none between 0.70 and 1.40 g/kg per feed (Blom, PMID 3316904); fructose alone is slow (3.2 versus 5.8–6.2 mmol/kg/h for glucose/sucrose); and oral versus intravenous glucose at matched glycaemia gives the same 3-hour gain (Blom, PMID 2689169, N = 5). Unfed storage is ~0.5 µmol/g/h. Full restoration over ~24 hours with adequate carbohydrate is the textbook's account — the carded records measure the first 3–6 hours.

title: Red-cell lifespan in health: ~106–120 days by every labelling method — once each label's own leak is corrected
question: In healthy humans, how long do red cells live — what did the classic chromium-51, DF32P and biotin-labelling studies measure as mean red-cell lifespan (~120 days), how is senescent-cell removal signalled, and how much do lifespan estimates differ between labelling methods?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Framed by Guyton & Hall and Ganong (textbook framing, not evidence). Methods disagree until their label artefacts are handled, then converge: biotin enumeration matches 51Cr once the early loss of ~half the biotin label is recognised (Mock, PMID 10037125) and works in healthy volunteers (Cordle & Mock, PMID 10532599, N = 20); corrected 51Cr and DF32P agree fairly well, with 51Cr elution ≤2.3%/day (Uchida, PMID 996847); and an independent stable-isotope cohort label measures lifespan 106 ± 21 days (2 SD) in 9 normal people (Khera, PMID 25293624). Refusals: Ashby's differential-agglutination studies — the original human lifespan measurements — predate PubMed indexing and no verifiable record could be fetched, so they are not carded; the ICSH 51Cr panel document (PMID 7426443) has an empty abstract in its record and likewise could not be verified, so it is not carded either. Both refusals are stated on the Synthesis card.

title: Platelet survival and production in health: ~8.4–9.3 days, near-linear disappearance, and a third of the pool resting in the spleen
question: In healthy humans, how long do platelets circulate and how fast are they produced — what did radiolabelled-platelet survival studies measure (~9–10 days, linear versus exponential disappearance), and what fraction of production replaces the circulating pool daily, including splenic pooling of the labelled cohort?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Framed by Guyton & Hall and Ganong (textbook framing, not evidence). title: Neutrophil turnover: marrow transit is settled (~6.6 days, ~0.9 × 10⁹/kg/day) — blood lifespan is not (hours by DF32P versus 5.4 days by deuterium)
question: In healthy humans, how fast do neutrophils turn over — what is the circulating half-life measured by in-vivo labelling (DF32P and modern deuterium studies), how large is the marginated pool relative to the circulating pool on epinephrine/exercise mobilisation, and how long is marrow transit from mitosis to release?

title: Cough-reflex calibration (physiology): capsaicin and citric-acid thresholds (C2/C5) are reproducible within a person but vary widely between people — women need 3–5-fold less capsaicin than men, and an ACE inhibitor can shift the threshold within a week
question: In humans, how is the cough reflex calibrated — what are capsaicin and citric-acid cough thresholds (C2/C5) in healthy volunteers, how reproducible are they, and how do sex, smoking and ACE inhibition shift sensitivity in the challenge studies?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing (Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology; Boron & Boulpaep, Medical Physiology — respiratory-reflex sections): cough is a vagal airway reflex whose afferent limb runs through capsaicin-sensitive (TRPV1-bearing) sensory nerves, and inhaled tussigen challenge is how its sensitivity is calibrated in humans. The carded primary studies quantify that calibration. Thresholds are defined by the concentration provoking 2 (C2) or 5 (C5) coughs. Between people they span orders of magnitude (C5 from 0.95 to 1000 µM capsaicin in one volunteer series), but within a person the single-breath capsaicin method is reproducible over repeated tests, with a first-test effect that can overestimate sensitivity (Hoffmeyer 2013; N = 16). Sex is the largest ordinary determinant: women had 3–5-fold lower capsaicin thresholds than men at both young and middle age (Fujimura 1996; N = 160), confirmed across three ethnic groups with no ethnic difference once sex was accounted for (Dicpinigaitis 2001; N = 182). Citric-acid thresholds by a portable hand-held method correlate tightly with the hospital dosimeter method (r = 0.95) but read 2–3 times higher — thresholds are method-specific and must be carded per method (Barber 2005; N = 25). One week of the ACE inhibitor ramipril measurably increased cough sensitivity to both capsaicin and citric acid in healthy volunteers, while zofenopril did not on the C2 endpoint (Lavorini 2014; N = 40) — the challenge-study demonstration behind ACE-inhibitor cough. Smoking effects named in the row question were not carded: the fetched smoking literature was preclinical or paediatric, so no smoking number is printed. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

title: Transepidermal water loss (physiology): healthy skin leaks 2–44 g/m²/h depending on the body site — lowest on the breast, highest in the axilla and palm — and after tape-stripping the barrier recovers ~20% by 6 hours and ~55% by 48 hours in light skin, faster in dark skin
question: In healthy humans, how leaky is the skin barrier at rest — what are normal transepidermal water-loss rates by body site, how fast does the barrier recover after tape-stripping disruption, and how do age and humidity change both?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing here is thinner than for other physiology rows — Boron & Boulpaep and Ganong treat the skin as a barrier organ only briefly — and this shelf rests chiefly on the primary measurement literature, as the row itself directs. Measurement was standardised by the European Society of Contact Dermatitis group (Pinnagoda 1990, cited in prose as the methods anchor, not carded as an evidence study). The pooled reference literature (212 studies, 86 skin areas) puts healthy adult TEWL between 2.3 g/m²/h on breast skin and 44.0 g/m²/h in the axilla — site dominates every other variable (Akdeniz 2018). A modern four-site primary study agrees in pattern: forearm lowest at 11 g/m²/h, palm highest at 41 g/m²/h (John 2023; N = 15). A 500-volunteer normative cohort found the forehead the highest-TEWL facial/trunk site tested and lower TEWL in middle and older age groups (Mehta 2018) — consistent with the pooled finding that TEWL in elderly skin is similar to or lower than in younger adults, which corrects the intuitive 'older skin leaks more' assumption: basal leak does not rise with age, even though aged barrier recovery is slower (the recovery-age literature is partly murine and is not carded). Recovery after tape-stripping is quantified in humans: light skin types recovered ~20% by 6 hours and ~55% by 48 hours, dark skin types ~43% and ~72% (Reed 1995), and psychological stress delayed recovery by 10% at 2 hours in a randomised laboratory study (Robles 2007; N = 85). Humidity effects named in the row question are handled by the standardisation literature (measurements are made under controlled temperature/humidity) rather than by a carded dose-response study, and no humidity number is printed. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

title: Skeletal turnover (physiology): calcium-tracer kinetics put whole-skeleton remodelling at ~0.34 g of calcium turned over per day before the menopause, rising after it — and tetracycline-labelled iliac biopsies give a mineral apposition rate of 0.53 µm/day, formation rates of ~15%/year in younger women, and remodelling periods from 0.28 to 4.5 years
question: In healthy humans, how fast does the skeleton turn over — what do calcium-tracer kinetics and transiliac bone-biopsy histomorphometry measure as activation frequency and bone-remodelling period, and what fraction of the skeleton is replaced per year in young adults versus after menopause?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing (Guyton & Hall; Boron & Boulpaep — bone-physiology sections): the adult skeleton is continuously remodelled by coupled resorption and formation, and the textbook's account is that a measurable fraction of bone is replaced each year, faster in trabecular than cortical bone. This shelf's numbers come from the two classic human measurement traditions, which cross-check each other. Calcium-tracer kinetics under metabolic-balance conditions (Heaney 1978; 151 perimenopausal women) put premenopausal mineral accretion at 0.337 g/day and resorption at 0.358 g/day — near-balanced turnover of roughly a third of a gram of calcium a day — rising after the menopause in untreated women to 0.387 and 0.425 g/day, with a more negative computed skeletal balance (−0.038 vs −0.021 g/day); oestrogen-treated postmenopausal women matched the premenopausal values. Tetracycline-labelled transiliac biopsy histomorphometry (Recker 1988; 34 normal postmenopausal women recruited to define normal values) gives the tissue-level clock: mineral apposition rate 0.53 ± 0.08 µm/day, volume-based bone formation rate ranging 0.7–28%/year, and a remodelling period of 0.28–4.5 years. A head-to-head study (Eastell 1988; 12 younger vs 11 older normal women) found histomorphometric bone formation rate higher in the older group (31.1 ± 4.9 vs 15.1 ± 2.7%/year) while calcium-kinetic accretion did not differ (5.9 ± 1.0 vs 7.5 ± 1.2 in the record's units) — the methods disagree about the age direction, and the card prints that disagreement rather than smoothing it. This shelf is the quantitative-rate companion to pack #6301 (the RANK/RANKL/OPG molecular coupling set-point) and pack #6254 (calcium absorption); it cards none of their references and answers none of their questions. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

title: Lactation (physiology): mothers feed ~11 times a day and a feed transfers ~76 g of milk; suckling releases oxytocin in discrete pulses (about 2 per 20 minutes, fewer under stress) that eject milk, while prolactin rises with suckling early on and its basal level falls across established lactation — and milk secretion is insulated from short-term glucose and insulin swings
question: In lactating humans, how much milk is produced and how is ejection controlled — 24-hour milk production volumes by test-weighing/isotope methods, the frequency and amplitude of oxytocin pulses with suckling on frequent-sampling studies, and prolactin's permissive time course across established lactation?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing (Guyton & Hall; Ganong — lactation sections): milk secretion is prolactin-permitted and supply follows removal, while milk ejection is a neuroendocrine reflex — suckling triggers pulsatile oxytocin release, oxytocin contracts myoepithelial cells, milk is ejected. The carded human studies quantify each limb. Production: in 71 exclusively breastfeeding mothers test-weighing every feed for 24–26 hours, infants fed 11 ± 3 times a day and took 76.0 ± 12.6 g per feed, about two-thirds of the milk available in the breast — and feed frequency did not predict 24-hour production (Kent 2006). Ejection: suckling-induced oxytocin release is pulsatile with discrete short pulses — 2.25 ± 0.71 pulses per 20 minutes of nursing at rest, falling to ~1.1–1.3 under mental-arithmetic or noise stress, with no change in prolactin rise or milk yield in that session (Ueda 1994; N = 22). Hormone time course: basal oxytocin and prolactin were higher on day 4 than at 3–4 months, both rose with suckling throughout, basal prolactin fell within 24 hours of weaning, and prolactin at 3–4 months — not oxytocin — correlated with how much longer breastfeeding continued; milk yield correlated with neither hormone's level (Uvnäs-Moberg 1990; N = 55). Secretion is metabolically insulated: 20 hours of fasting and 4 hours of clamped hyperinsulinaemia did not change milk volume or lactose secretion, and doubling plasma glucose raised milk glucose threefold without raising lactose synthesis (Neville 1993) — consistent with local, removal-driven control (the autocrine limb the textbooks describe; the Wilde programme's primary work is in ruminants and is presented here only as that textbook framing, never as a card). PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

title: Thermoregulation under anaesthesia (physiology): the interthreshold range widens from ~0.5 °C awake to 2.3 °C at 0.5 MAC and 4.6 °C at 0.8 MAC desflurane — volatile agents and propofol push the vasoconstriction and shivering thresholds down by degrees while barely moving the sweating threshold, which is why surgical patients cool
question: In healthy humans under general anaesthesia, how wide does the thermoregulatory interthreshold range become — by how much do volatile anaesthetics and propofol lower the vasoconstriction and shivering thresholds while barely moving the sweating threshold, in the volunteer threshold studies?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — graded, per this row's flag, as physiology measured under a drug intervention in volunteers, not resting physiology: the subjects were healthy volunteers given anaesthetics, a patient-adjacent preparation, and every card says so. Textbook framing (Guyton & Hall, body-temperature regulation, as extended by the anaesthesia-physiology literature): awake, sweating, vasoconstriction and shivering switch on within a narrow interthreshold range of core temperatures. The volunteer threshold programme (Sessler and colleagues) measures how anaesthetics tear that range open from the cold side. Desflurane raised the sweating threshold linearly (37.1 → 37.6 → 38.1 °C at 0, 0.5 and 0.8 MAC) but cut the vasoconstriction threshold by ~3 °C at 0.8 MAC, widening the interthreshold range from 0.5 ± 0.3 °C to 2.3 ± 0.7 and 4.6 ± 2.0 °C (Annadata 1995; N = 9). Propofol did the same intravenously: vasoconstriction threshold fell linearly with concentration (slope −0.6 ± 0.1 °C per µg/ml) and shivering similarly (−0.7 ± 0.1), while sweating moved only slightly (+0.1 ± 0.1) (Matsukawa 1995; N = 5). An independent propofol study using an epidural-based model found the interthreshold range was 0.51 ± 0.46 °C on epidural alone and grew by 0.49 ± 0.31 °C per µg/ml of propofol (Leslie 1994; N = 6). The vasoconstriction-to-shivering gap stays ~1–1.5 °C, so patients rarely shiver under anaesthesia simply because vasoconstriction alone usually cannot hold core temperature above the shivering threshold once the range has widened — they cool passively through the dead zone first. The awake counterpart — thresholds, circadian and acclimation shifts without drugs — is pack #6263, cross-pointed here and not duplicated. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (physiology measured under a drug intervention, per the row's grading note).
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — based on a very small N = 20

title: Lenadogene nolparvovec for Leber hereditary optic neuropathy: all three phase 3 trials missed their primary endpoints — treated and sham/placebo eyes improved together, and the bilateral-benefit claim rests on post hoc interpretation, not on any randomised contrast
question: In patients with Leber hereditary optic neuropathy (chiefly m.11778G>A) treated within a year of vision loss, does intravitreal lenadogene nolparvovec improve visual acuity versus sham injection?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — a missed-primary programme, presented as published. Lenadogene nolparvovec (the rAAV2/2-ND4 allotopic gene therapy, designated GS010 in the REVERSE report; the fetched records name the vector and the GS010 designation but do not name a company, so none is printed) was tested in three phase 3 sham- or placebo-controlled trials in m.11778G>A LHON, each using the fellow eye as the control. RESCUE (treated ≤6 months from onset; 38 subjects in the efficacy analysis): the week-48 primary endpoint — difference in BCVA change between treated and sham eyes — was −0.01 logMAR (P = 0.89) against a −0.3 logMAR target; not met. REVERSE (treated 6–12 months from onset; 37 subjects): the same primary contrast was not met (P = 0.894), because sham eyes improved almost as much as treated eyes by week 96 (+13 vs +15 ETDRS letters) — the unexpected bilateral improvement the programme attributes, post hoc and with nonhuman-primate vector-transfer data, to contralateral spread. REFLECT (bilateral versus unilateral treatment; 98 patients): the primary endpoint in second-affected/not-yet-affected eyes was again not statistically different between lenadogene and placebo at 1.5 years, though within-group improvements from baseline were reported and intraocular inflammation occurred in 70.7% of treated versus 10.2% of placebo eyes. Three trials, three missed primaries, and improvement in control eyes in all of them: the randomised evidence does not separate the product from sham on any prespecified primary contrast, and claims of benefit rest on within-group change, comparison with natural history, and a post hoc bilateral-effect mechanism. The product is not approved in the US/EU (per the row's flag). The other LHON treatment shelf is pack #4253 (idebenone) — a different intervention, cross-pointed here; none of its references is carded on this shelf. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence), with the null primary contrasts printed on the face.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — all three phase 3 trials missed their primary endpoints (the treatment made no difference between treated and sham/placebo eyes on the primary contrast); improvement in sham/placebo eyes too makes the bilateral-benefit claim post hoc

title: Recaticimab (long-acting PCSK9 antibody, dosing up to every 12 weeks) for hypercholesterolaemia
question: In adults with hypercholesterolaemia, including heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia, does recaticimab — a long-acting PCSK9 monoclonal antibody engineered for dosing intervals up to 12 weeks — compared with placebo on background therapy, lower LDL cholesterol?
balance: Three phase 3 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials from one programme in China agree: recaticimab lowered LDL cholesterol by roughly 45–62% relative to placebo across regimens given every 4, 8 or 12 weeks — as monotherapy in nonfamilial hypercholesterolaemia (REMAIN-1, n=703), as add-on to statins (REMAIN-2, n=689, effect maintained to week 48), and in heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia (REMAIN-3, n=143). An earlier phase 1b/2 study (n=110) showed the same pattern. SINGLE-REGION flag: every trial was conducted in China, where recaticimab (Jiangsu Hengrui) is approved; generalisability beyond that population is untested in print. SURROGATE flag: LDL cholesterol is the only efficacy outcome — there is no cardiovascular-event trial, so no event claim is made. Safety was comparable to placebo apart from more injection-site reactions. The extended dosing interval (up to every 12 weeks, versus every 2–4 weeks for the established PCSK9 antibodies) is the intervention's distinguishing feature and held up at the 450 mg every-12-weeks regimen in all three trials.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — three concordant phase 3 randomised trials show large LDL-cholesterol reductions at dosing intervals up to every 12 weeks; surrogate endpoint only, no cardiovascular-outcome data, and the entire evidence base is from China

title: Balcinrenone added to dapagliflozin in heart failure and chronic kidney disease (MIRACLE) and in CKD with albuminuria (MIRO-CKD)
question: In adults with heart failure (EF <60%) and chronic kidney disease (eGFR 30–60) already taking dapagliflozin, does adding the selective mineralocorticoid-receptor modulator balcinrenone, compared with dapagliflozin alone, reduce albuminuria — and at what potassium and eGFR cost?
balance: The two phase 2b trials of the same combination answer differently in different populations, and the shelf is that split. In the population this question asks about — symptomatic heart failure with ejection fraction <60% and eGFR 30–60 — MIRACLE (n=133) did NOT meet its primary endpoint: relative reductions in urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR) at 12 weeks were not significantly different between balcinrenone plus dapagliflozin and dapagliflozin plus placebo (the treatment made no difference), with no clear dose-response; MIRACLE was also under-enrolled (133 randomised of about 500 planned; enrolment stopped early for slow recruitment), so the null is an underpowered null. In CKD with albuminuria without a heart-failure entry requirement, MIRO-CKD (n=324) was positive: UACR differences versus dapagliflozin alone of −22.8% and −32.8% relative at 15 mg and 40 mg. The cost side: in MIRACLE there were possible dose-dependent increases in serum potassium, a reduced eGFR in the highest-dose group, and two hyperkalaemia discontinuations on the combination versus none on dapagliflozin alone; in MIRO-CKD investigator-reported hyperkalaemia was 6–7% on the combination versus 5% on dapagliflozin alone. An earlier phase 1b study (n=68) found balcinrenone's potassium rise over 28 days was similar to spironolactone's. UACR is a surrogate endpoint in both trials; there are no heart-failure hospitalisation, kidney-progression or mortality data. The DapaBalci-Leap mechanistic study is conference-abstract only and is not carded.
stamp: SPLIT — in CKD with albuminuria (MIRO-CKD, n = 324) adding balcinrenone lowered albuminuria more than dapagliflozin alone, but in heart failure with CKD (MIRACLE, n = 133, enrolment stopped early) the primary albuminuria endpoint was not met (the treatment made no difference); potassium rose and eGFR fell in a dose-dependent pattern in MIRACLE

title: Cagrilintide monotherapy for weight management in obesity
question: In adults with obesity, does cagrilintide monotherapy, compared with placebo (and liraglutide in phase 2), reduce body weight?
balance: This shelf asks only about cagrilintide ALONE. The combination question (cagrilintide plus semaglutide, CagriSema) is homed on live shelf #1092, which cards REDEFINE 1 and REDEFINE 2; the cagrilintide-alone arm inside REDEFINE 1 belongs to that homed report and is not re-carded here (one-home rule). PREMISE NOTE: the slate proposed that REDEFINE 1 arm as an anchor, but its PMID is already carded at #1092, so this pack is built from the remaining free monotherapy reports. On monotherapy itself: the phase 2 dose-finding trial (Lau 2021, n=706, no diabetes) found weight reductions of 6.0–10.8% across cagrilintide doses versus 3.0% on placebo at 26 weeks, with the 4.5 mg dose also beating liraglutide 3.0 mg (10.8% vs 9.0%). In type 2 diabetes, the cagrilintide-alone arm of the Frias 2023 phase 2 trial (n=30 of 92) lost 8.1% of body weight at 32 weeks, with an HbA1c fall of 0.9 percentage points — less than the combination arm in the same trial, which is #1092's subject. A 2026 pharmacokinetic report confirms single-dose cagrilintide exposure is not materially changed by renal or hepatic impairment. Gastrointestinal adverse events are the main cost (41–63% across doses versus 32% on placebo in phase 2). The dedicated phase 3 monotherapy programme (RENEW) had not reported at building, so there is no phase 3 monotherapy evidence on this shelf.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one phase 2 dose-finding trial (n = 706) plus the small cagrilintide-alone arm of a phase 2 diabetes trial (n = 30 on monotherapy) both show weight loss versus placebo; the phase 3 monotherapy programme (RENEW) is unreported and the phase 3 monotherapy arm inside REDEFINE 1 is homed on the combination shelf, so it is not carded here

title: Danuglipron (oral GLP-1 receptor agonist) in type 2 diabetes and obesity — a discontinued programme
question: In adults with type 2 diabetes or obesity, does the oral small-molecule GLP-1 receptor agonist danuglipron, compared with placebo, improve HbA1c and reduce body weight — and why was the programme stopped?
balance: PROGRAMME DISCONTINUED — printed on the face, as the question requires: Pfizer stopped development of danuglipron in April 2025 after a potential drug-induced liver injury case in an asymptomatic participant, and the drug will not be marketed. What the phase 2 evidence showed before that: in type 2 diabetes (n=411), twice-daily danuglipron lowered HbA1c by up to 1.16 percentage points versus placebo at 16 weeks and reduced weight at the higher doses; in obesity without diabetes (n=626 treated), weight fell 5.0–12.9% relative to placebo over 26–32 weeks. The tolerability price was high throughout the programme: in the obesity trial only 39.3% of participants completed treatment and about 38% discontinued because of adverse events (nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea predominating), and the earlier phase 2a study saw discontinuation of 27.3–72.7% across danuglipron groups versus 16.7–18.8% on placebo. So the honest balance is: genuine glycaemic and weight efficacy at phase 2, a gastrointestinal tolerability problem that dose escalation never solved, and a liver-safety signal that ended the programme. No phase 3 trial was ever run, and no cardiovascular or other outcome data exist.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — phase 2 trials show real HbA1c and weight effects, but tolerability was poor (about 38% stopped for adverse events in the obesity trial) and Pfizer discontinued the programme in April 2025 after a potential drug-induced liver injury case; this is a historical, cautionary shelf for a drug that will not be marketed
