title: Cenicriviroc (CCR2/CCR5 antagonist) for MASH (NASH) with fibrosis — a failed programme
question: In adults with MASH (NASH) and fibrosis, does the CCR2/CCR5 antagonist cenicriviroc, compared with placebo, improve fibrosis without worsening steatohepatitis?
balance: This is a failed programme, and the shelf's value is the negative answer. Phase 2b CENTAUR (n=289) missed its primary endpoint (≥2-point NAS improvement: 16% on cenicriviroc versus 19% on placebo — the treatment made no difference) but met a secondary fibrosis endpoint at year 1 (≥1-stage fibrosis improvement without worsening steatohepatitis: 20% versus 10%), and its year-2 final analysis showed that most year-1 fibrosis responders on cenicriviroc maintained their response. The phase 3 AURORA trial (n=1,778 randomised; part 1 n=1,293) then tested exactly that fibrosis claim and did not confirm it: 22.3% on cenicriviroc versus 25.5% on placebo achieved ≥1-stage fibrosis improvement without worsening steatohepatitis at month 12 (the treatment made no difference), and steatohepatitis resolution was likewise no better than placebo. Safety and tolerability were comparable to placebo throughout — the drug failed on efficacy, not on safety. There are no clinical-outcome data (decompensation, transplant, death) for cenicriviroc in MASH, and development for this indication did not proceed after AURORA.
stamp: UNLIKELY (benefit) — the phase 2b fibrosis signal (CENTAUR) was not confirmed by the phase 3 AURORA trial, in which the treatment made no difference on the primary histology endpoint (22.3% vs 25.5% on placebo)

title: Firsocostat-based combinations (with cilofexor, and with semaglutide) for MASH with advanced fibrosis
question: In adults with MASH (NASH) and advanced fibrosis (F3–F4), do firsocostat-based combinations (with the FXR agonist cilofexor, and with semaglutide), compared with placebo or semaglutide alone, improve fibrosis or steatohepatitis activity?
balance: Phase-2-only evidence, and it must lead with the negative: in ATLAS (n=392, bridging fibrosis or compensated cirrhosis, F3–F4), the primary endpoint — ≥1-stage fibrosis improvement without worsening of NASH at 48 weeks — was not met by any regimen (the treatment made no difference on the primary endpoint): cilofexor/firsocostat 21% versus 11% on placebo, P = 0.17, and the other combinations and monotherapies were further from significance. What ATLAS did show for cilofexor/firsocostat was significant improvement on exploratory measures — a machine-learning fibrosis score, ≥2-point NAS reduction, steatosis, inflammation and ballooning components, liver enzymes and non-invasive fibrosis markers — plus pruritus in 20–29% on cilofexor-containing regimens versus 15% on placebo. The semaglutide-combination trial (n=108, F2–F3) was open-label with a safety primary endpoint: combinations with cilofexor and/or firsocostat improved liver fat (MRI-PDFF) and biochemistry more than semaglutide alone on exploratory analyses, despite similar weight loss. The monotherapy card explains the combination rationale: firsocostat (GS-0976) alone reduced hepatic fat (≥30% MRI-PDFF response in 48% on 20 mg versus 15% on placebo) but raised serum triglycerides (median relative increases of 11–13%) — the liability the FXR-agonist pairing was meant to offset. No trial shows a confirmed histological fibrosis benefit, and there are no clinical-outcome data.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — phase 2 only: the ATLAS primary fibrosis endpoint was not met by any regimen (the treatment made no difference on the primary endpoint), the semaglutide-combination trial was small and open-label with exploratory efficacy, and firsocostat monotherapy improved liver fat but raised triglycerides

title: Dotinurad (selective URAT1 inhibitor) for gout and hyperuricaemia
question: In adults with gout and hyperuricaemia, does the selective URAT1 inhibitor dotinurad, compared with febuxostat or placebo, lower serum urate to target?
balance: The urate-lowering answer is consistent across the whole Japanese and Chinese programme. In the China phase 3 trial in gout (n=451), dotinurad 4 mg/day was superior to febuxostat 40 mg/day on the primary endpoint: 73.6% versus 38.1% reached serum urate ≤6.0 mg/dL at week 24. In Japan, phase 3 trials showed dotinurad titrated to 2 mg/day was non-inferior to febuxostat 40 mg/day (urate fall 41.82% versus 44.00%; n=203) and non-inferior to benzbromarone 50 mg/day (45.9% versus 43.8%; n=201), and the phase 2 dose-finding study (n=80) showed a clear dose-response against placebo (urate falls of 37.03%, 50.91% and 64.37% at 1, 2 and 4 mg versus 0.85% on placebo). SINGLE-REGION flag: all trials are from Japan (where dotinurad has been approved since 2020) and China; there is no trial programme outside East Asia. SURROGATE flag: every endpoint is serum urate — no trial measures gout flares, tophus resolution, kidney outcomes or cardiovascular events, so urate lowering is not equated here with flare prevention. Adverse-event profiles were similar to the comparators in each trial, with no noteworthy safety concerns raised in the phase 3 reports.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — three phase 3 trials and a phase 2 dose-finding study agree that dotinurad lowers serum urate to target at least as well as febuxostat or benzbromarone and far beyond placebo; surrogate endpoint only (serum urate), single-region evidence (Japan and China), and no gout-flare or outcome trial

title: Lutetium-177 edotreotide versus everolimus in GEP neuroendocrine tumours (COMPETE): progression-free survival 23.9 vs 14.1 months in the first head-to-head phase 3 — with a single-arm phase 2 and a heterogeneous meta-analysis behind it
question: In adults with grade 1–2 gastroenteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumours progressing on somatostatin analogues, does lutetium-177 edotreotide, compared with everolimus, prolong progression-free survival?
balance: POSSIBLE — the randomised evidence is one trial. In COMPETE (309 patients with advanced, somatostatin-receptor-positive grade 1–2 GEP NETs), lutetium-177 edotreotide (the DOTATOC peptide, from ITM — named here under the clarification exception as the specific tested radiopharmaceutical) prolonged median progression-free survival versus everolimus: 23.9 vs 14.1 months, stratified hazard ratio 0.67 (95% CI 0.48–0.95; p=0.022) — a relative measure; overall survival was immature in the record. Treatment-related grade 3–4 adverse events were less frequent with edotreotide (18% vs 40%). Behind the trial sit only uncontrolled data: a 56-patient retrospective phase 2 series of lutetium-177 DOTATOC (median PFS 17.4 months, objective response 33.9%) and a 2026 systematic review/meta-analysis of eight uncontrolled studies (GEP-NET objective response 34%, median PFS 24.9 months, with heterogeneity I² >70% throughout) — consistent with COMPETE but unable to confirm it. The slate noted an FDA complete response letter in August 2026 on non-clinical grounds; that is a regulatory fact, not an efficacy signal, and is not verified in the fetched records, so it is flagged rather than asserted. One positive head-to-head trial with supportive uncontrolled data: POSSIBLE, not LIKELY.
stamp: POSSIBLE — one positive phase 3 head-to-head trial (COMPETE) supported by single-arm phase 2 and pooled uncontrolled data; a single randomised trial caps the stamp at POSSIBLE

title: Surufatinib in advanced neuroendocrine tumours (SANET-p and SANET-ep): progression-free survival roughly tripled versus placebo in two Chinese phase 3 trials — final overall survival not significantly different, with 69% crossover
question: In adults with advanced pancreatic or extrapancreatic neuroendocrine tumours, does surufatinib, compared with placebo, prolong progression-free survival?
balance: LIKELY for delaying progression; not shown to extend life. Two double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trials conducted in China were both stopped early for efficacy at interim analysis: SANET-p (pancreatic NETs, n=172) median PFS 10.9 vs 3.7 months, hazard ratio 0.49; SANET-ep (extrapancreatic NETs, n=198) median PFS 9.2 vs 3.8 months, hazard ratio 0.33 — hazard ratios are relative measures, printed beside the absolute medians. The pooled final overall-survival analysis (398 patients) found median OS 50.1 vs 46.8 months, hazard ratio 0.935 (95% CI 0.684–1.278; p=0.67) — not significant — after 69% of the placebo group crossed over to surufatinib; crossover-corrected estimates ranged from 0.558 to 0.825 and are model-dependent. Quality of life was preserved overall except diarrhoea, which worsened. The main grade 3+ harms were hypertension (36–38%) and proteinuria (~10%). Surufatinib (marketed as Sulanda by HUTCHMED — named under the clarification exception) is a single-country evidence base: both trials enrolled only in China, and the slate records an FDA complete response letter in 2022 requiring a multi-regional trial. LIKELY on progression, with the null survival result and the single-region base printed on the face.
stamp: LIKELY — two concordant double-blind phase 3 trials with large progression-free-survival effects; the survival endpoint itself was null after heavy crossover, and the evidence base is single-country (China)

title: Capecitabine plus temozolomide (CAPTEM) versus temozolomide alone in pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours (E2211): progression-free survival 22.7 vs 14.4 months in a randomised phase 2 — overall survival not significantly different
question: In adults with advanced pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours, does capecitabine plus temozolomide (CAPTEM), compared with temozolomide alone, prolong progression-free survival?
balance: POSSIBLE. The only randomised comparison is ECOG-ACRIN E2211 (144 patients with advanced low- or intermediate-grade pancreatic NETs progressing within the previous 12 months): median progression-free survival 22.7 months on capecitabine plus temozolomide vs 14.4 months on temozolomide alone (hazard ratio 0.58, a relative measure; stratified log-rank p=0.022), while median overall survival was 58.7 vs 53.8 months (hazard ratio 0.82; p=0.42) — not significantly different. MGMT deficiency was associated with response. The supporting evidence is retrospective: the original 30-patient first-line series (objective response 70%, median PFS 18 months, grade 3–4 events in 12%) and a 462-patient single-centre cohort (response 46%, median PFS 18 months, median OS 51 months; grade 4 thrombocytopenia 7% and neutropenia 3%, both significantly more frequent in women; the only myelodysplastic-syndrome cases had prior peptide receptor radionuclide therapy). Retrospective response rates of 46–70% come from selected, uncontrolled cohorts and should not be read as randomised effects. Generic agents; no product-naming issue. One randomised phase 2, null on survival: POSSIBLE.
stamp: POSSIBLE — a single randomised phase 2 trial with a significant progression-free-survival benefit but a non-significant survival result, supported by retrospective series; a single randomised trial caps the stamp at POSSIBLE

title: Sunitinib in metastatic phaeochromocytoma and paraganglioma (FIRSTMAPPP): the first randomised trial in this disease — 12-month progression-free survival 36% vs 19% on placebo, in 78 patients recruited over seven years
question: In adults with metastatic phaeochromocytoma or paraganglioma, does sunitinib, compared with placebo, prolong progression-free survival?
balance: POSSIBLE, on a very small base — the stamp carries the N. FIRSTMAPPP is the first randomised trial ever done in metastatic phaeochromocytoma/paraganglioma: 78 patients recruited across 14 centres in four European countries between 2011 and 2019 (a decade-scale recruitment effort for a rare disease). Its primary endpoint was met: 12-month progression-free survival was 36% (14/39) on sunitinib 37.5 mg daily vs 19% (7/39) on placebo, against a design hypothesis of 40% vs 20%. Grade 3–4 asthenia (18% vs 3%) and hypertension (13% vs 10%) were the most frequent severe events; three deaths occurred on sunitinib, one (rectal bleeding) judged drug-related. The single-arm SUTNET phase 2 (50 patients, sunitinib 50 mg 4-weeks-on/2-weeks-off) found a 1-year PFS rate of 53.4%, median PFS 14.1 months and objective response 15.6%, with grade ≥3 treatment-related events in 34%. A 2026 meta-analysis of the sunitinib arms of three prospective trials (114 patients) pooled an objective response rate of 21.2% and 12-month PFS of 48.2%, rating its own evidence low to very low certainty. No overall-survival benefit has been shown in a randomised comparison. The neighbouring systemic-therapy questions are different interventions; no sunitinib card from any other shelf is duplicated here.
stamp: POSSIBLE — based on a very small total evidence base (N = 78 randomised; 192 patients across all carded reports): one small randomised phase 2 meeting its primary endpoint, one single-arm phase 2, and a low-certainty prospective meta-analysis

title: Astegolimab in COPD (ALIENTO and ARNASA): a split result — each dose regimen missed significance in one of the two trials; the prespecified pooled analysis shows a 15% relative reduction with every-2-week dosing
question: In adults with COPD and a history of exacerbations despite inhaled maintenance therapy, does astegolimab (anti-ST2 monoclonal antibody) versus placebo reduce the rate of moderate-to-severe exacerbations?
balance: SPLIT — the split is between the two trials and the two dose regimens, and it is printed here rather than pooled away. ALIENTO (phase 2b, n=1,301) and ARNASA (phase 3, n=1,375) randomised current or former smokers with COPD and frequent exacerbations, irrespective of blood eosinophil count, to astegolimab 476 mg every 2 weeks, every 4 weeks, or placebo for 52 weeks on top of optimised inhaled therapy. In ALIENTO, the adjusted exacerbation rate ratio vs placebo was 0.85 (95% CI 0.72–1.00; p=0.049) for every-2-week dosing but 0.93 (0.79–1.10; p=0.38) for every-4-week dosing. In ARNASA the pattern reversed: 0.85 (0.72–1.01; p=0.068) every 2 weeks and 0.82 (0.70–0.98; p=0.024) every 4 weeks. Rate ratios are relative measures. The prespecified pooled analysis (2,682 participants) was significant for both regimens — a 15% relative reduction in the annualised rate of moderate/severe exacerbations with every-2-week dosing (rate ratio 0.85; 95% CI 0.76–0.96; p=0.0077) and 12% relative with every-4-week dosing (0.88; 0.78–0.99; p=0.0265) — and a nominally significant reduction in severe exacerbations with every-2-week dosing (rate ratio 0.68). Adverse events and deaths (3.1–3.2%) were balanced. Phase 1 studies (152 participants) established tolerability and pharmacokinetics but contain no COPD efficacy data. SPLIT: a real pooled signal whose individual trials do not each confirm it.
stamp: SPLIT — the two pivotal trials are discordant by dose regimen (each regimen significant in one trial and not the other); the prespecified pooled analysis is significant for both regimens

title: Tozorakimab in COPD (OBERON and TITANIA): exacerbation rates about 30% relatively lower than placebo in two replicate phase 3 trials — the primary endpoint was defined in former smokers
question: In adults with COPD (current or former smokers) with exacerbations despite standard inhaled therapy, does tozorakimab (anti-IL-33 monoclonal antibody) 300 mg every 4 weeks versus placebo reduce moderate-to-severe exacerbations?
balance: LIKELY. Two replicate phase 3 trials — OBERON (877 patients) and TITANIA (873 patients) — randomised adults with COPD who were current or former smokers, with exacerbations in the previous year despite stable standard inhaled therapy and no eosinophil-count eligibility criterion, to tozorakimab 300 mg or placebo every 4 weeks for 52 weeks. The primary endpoint was defined in former smokers: annualised moderate/severe exacerbation rates were 1.34 vs 1.90 events (rate ratio 0.71; 95% CI 0.57–0.88; p=0.002) in OBERON and 1.37 vs 2.07 (rate ratio 0.66; 0.55–0.80; p<0.001) in TITANIA. In the overall population the rate ratios were 0.70 and 0.71 (both p<0.001) — all rate ratios are relative measures, printed beside the absolute rates. Because the primary population was former smokers, benefit in current smokers is established within the combined population rather than independently — as the slate flagged. The phase 2a FRONTIER-4 trial (135 patients, 600 mg dose) missed its primary lung-function endpoint (pre-bronchodilator FEV1 difference 24 mL, p=0.216) while showing exacerbation signals in patients with ≥2 prior exacerbations. The pooled FRONTIER phase 2 safety analysis (1,076 patients across four diseases) found tolerability similar to placebo apart from more injection-site reactions. The slate noted a long-term extension (PROSPERO) that missed its primary endpoint exists only as congress data — it is fenced here, not carded. LIKELY on the two concordant phase 3 trials.
stamp: LIKELY — two replicate phase 3 trials concordant on the primary (former-smoker) and overall-population endpoints, with a phase 2a that missed its lung-function primary but pointed the same way on exacerbations

title: Fevipiprant in asthma: a failed programme — the phase 2 sputum-eosinophil signal did not replicate; LUSTER-1/2 missed on exacerbations after multiplicity adjustment and ZEAL-1/2 were null on lung function (the treatment made no difference)
question: In adolescents and adults with uncontrolled asthma, does fevipiprant (oral CRTh2/DP2 antagonist) versus placebo improve lung function and reduce exacerbations?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the honest answer is that the phase 3 programme failed. Fevipiprant (QAW039, Novartis) reduced sputum eosinophils in a 61-patient single-centre phase 2 trial (sputum eosinophil percentage fell 4.5-fold vs 1.3-fold on placebo; between-group difference 3.5-fold, p=0.0014), but that biomarker signal did not convert: in LUSTER-1 and LUSTER-2 (1,771 patients with severe asthma), neither trial showed a statistically significant reduction in moderate-to-severe exacerbations after adjusting for multiple testing — high-eosinophil rate ratios ranged from 1.04 (150 mg, LUSTER-1) to 0.69 (150 mg, LUSTER-2), with only modest, inconsistent reductions at 450 mg. In ZEAL-1 and ZEAL-2 (1,347 patients completing treatment), the primary lung-function endpoint was null in both — FEV1 differences of +41 mL (p=0.088) and −31 mL (p=0.214); the ZEAL authors conclude DP2 inhibition with fevipiprant is not effective in the studied population (the treatment made no difference). The SPIRIT long-term safety study (2,538 randomised) found a placebo-like safety profile, with exploratory, multiplicity-unadjusted efficacy signals the authors say should be interpreted with caution; SPIRIT was terminated early by the sponsor. Per the slate, Novartis stopped development after the phase 3 results. This shelf is kept for completeness of a guideline-era question: a real phase 2 biomarker effect, no demonstrated clinical benefit at phase 3.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — for any benefit: four phase 3 trials failed to show a significant effect on their primary endpoints; the development programme was stopped

title: Depemokimab in chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps (ANCHOR-1 and ANCHOR-2): twice-yearly dosing improved polyp score by 0.7 and 0.6 points vs placebo — a real but modest effect, the smallest in its class in indirect comparison
question: In adults with severe chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps inadequately controlled on intranasal corticosteroids, does depemokimab (ultra-long-acting anti-IL-5) versus placebo improve nasal polyp score and nasal obstruction?
balance: POSSIBLE. This shelf asks the depemokimab-specific question that live shelf #375 (biologics in CRSwNP) does not: #375 cards dupilumab (SINUS-24/52) and omalizumab (POLYP 1/2) only, and is cross-pointed here rather than duplicated — none of its references is carded on this shelf. Depemokimab in asthma is a separate, already-homed question (pack #6210). ANCHOR-1 and ANCHOR-2 are two replicate phase 3 trials reported in ONE Lancet publication; under the library convention (the PROMIS precedent) that publication counts as one report, with both trials explicitly labelled on its card. Together they randomised 540 patients with inadequately controlled CRSwNP (polyp score ≥5, prior surgery or systemic corticosteroids) to depemokimab 100 mg or placebo every 26 weeks: polyp-score differences vs placebo were −0.7 (ANCHOR-1; p<0.001) and −0.6 (ANCHOR-2; p=0.004), and nasal-obstruction differences −0.23 (p=0.047) and −0.25 (p=0.025) on a 0–3 scale — statistically significant but modest absolute effects. A pooled safety analysis of SWIFT-1/-2 and ANCHOR-1/-2 (1,290 patients) found adverse events in 73% on depemokimab vs 78% on placebo and serious adverse events in 5% vs 10%, with no fatal or treatment-related serious events. A 2026 network meta-analysis of 15 CRSwNP biologic trials (3,642 patients) placed depemokimab behind dupilumab (and, at later time-points, tezepelumab) on polyp and congestion scores — an indirect comparison, labelled as such. The twice-yearly dosing is the practical distinction; the effect size is the smallest in its class in that indirect ranking. The slate records FDA approval for CRSwNP on Dec 16, 2025.
stamp: POSSIBLE — one publication reporting two concordant replicate phase 3 trials (counted as one report under the library convention), supported by a pooled safety analysis and a network meta-analysis that places the effect below dupilumab's

title: Sputum-eosinophil-guided asthma management: titrating treatment to the sputum eosinophil count cut severe exacerbations in two small randomised trials (35 vs 109 events in the first), and a Cochrane synthesis favoured the strategy — but the trials are old, small and single-programme, and sputum induction exists in few clinics
question: In adults with moderate-to-severe asthma, does treatment titrated to sputum eosinophil counts versus guideline/symptom-based management reduce severe exacerbations?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). Two randomised trials asked whether titrating asthma treatment to normalise the induced sputum eosinophil count beats symptom/guideline-based care. Green et al. (Lancet 2002, n=74) found far fewer severe exacerbations with sputum management (35 vs 109 events; p=0.01) and fewer hospital admissions (1 vs 6 patients), at no higher corticosteroid dose. Jayaram et al. (Eur Respir J 2006, n=117, 2 years) found the same direction: fewer exacerbations needing prednisone (5 vs 15) and a 49% relative reduction in the risk of a first exacerbation, driven by fewer eosinophilic exacerbations — the sputum strategy did not change the frequency of non-eosinophilic exacerbations, which were the majority. The Cochrane synthesis (Petsky 2017; six studies, 374 participants randomised) pooled an odds ratio of 0.57 (0.38–0.86) for having any exacerbation — a relative measure; the absolute risks printed in the review were 82% (control) vs 62% (sputum) for one or more exacerbations over 16 months, NNTB 6. The honest limits: the trials are small, old and from specialist centres with sputum laboratories; sputum induction is not available in most clinics, so this shelf supports the strategy where the assay exists, not as a general practice recommendation. This is a different biomarker question from FeNO-guided management (live #1728, pack #5904), which is not duplicated here.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two small randomised trials and a Cochrane synthesis agree that sputum-guided titration reduces exacerbations, but the trials are old, small and from few centres, and the strategy needs a sputum-induction service most clinics do not have

title: Rituximab added to mycophenolate in NSIP-pattern ILD: EVER-ILD improved FVC by 3.60% predicted versus mycophenolate alone — one positive trial, supported by an SSc-ILD meta-analysis and a small rescue cohort; the rituximab-versus-cyclophosphamide head-to-head lives on pack #3950 and is not re-carded here
question: In adults with connective-tissue-disease-associated ILD or idiopathic interstitial pneumonia with an NSIP pattern, does adding rituximab to mycophenolate mofetil slow FVC decline compared with mycophenolate alone?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), for the add-on question only. PREMISE CORRECTION recorded at build: the slate row's lead anchor, RECITAL (rituximab vs intravenous cyclophosphamide in CTD-ILD), is already carded as the whole question of pack #3950, and its PMID is on this wave's gate list — it is therefore NOT carded here; pack #3950 is the home for rituximab versus cyclophosphamide, and this shelf cross-points to it rather than duplicating it. What remains genuinely unasked is the add-on question. EVER-ILD (double-blind, n=122, NSIP-pattern ILD on background mycophenolate) found rituximab improved percent-predicted FVC by a between-group 3.60% (95% CI 0.41–6.80; p=0.0273) at 6 months, with better progression-free survival (crude HR 0.47 — a relative measure) and similar serious adverse event rates (41% vs 39%), at the cost of more infections (9 vs 4 reports, including viral). A 2025 meta-analysis in systemic-sclerosis ILD (six studies, two randomised) found rituximab reduced FVC decline versus conventional treatment (SMD 0.65, 0.08–1.22). A small retrospective rescue cohort (18 transplant-listing-grade patients) is carded as labelled observational support only. The two comparisons in the original slate question (versus cyclophosphamide; as add-on to mycophenolate) are not merged into one claim: the first lives on #3950, the second is answered here, capped at POSSIBLE because it rests on a single trial.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one double-blind trial showed adding rituximab to mycophenolate improved FVC in NSIP-pattern ILD, with supportive but weaker synthesis and cohort evidence; the cyclophosphamide head-to-head question is homed separately on pack #3950

title: Transbronchial lung cryobiopsy versus surgical lung biopsy for ILD diagnosis: agreement was 70.8% histopathologically and 76.9% at multidisciplinary discussion (COLDICE), and a cryobiopsy-first step-up strategy matched surgical yield (89% vs 88%) with far fewer serious adverse events (4% vs 50%) — agreement is not identity, and low-confidence cryobiopsy diagnoses still need surgery
question: In adults with undiagnosed interstitial lung disease needing tissue, does transbronchial lung cryobiopsy (including a cryobiopsy-first step-up strategy) versus surgical lung biopsy achieve comparable diagnostic yield at multidisciplinary discussion with fewer serious adverse events?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), as a test-strategy shelf. COLDICE (n=65, both biopsies under one anaesthetic) found histopathological agreement between cryobiopsy and surgical biopsy of 70.8% (weighted κ 0.70) and multidisciplinary-discussion (MDD) agreement of 76.9% (κ 0.62) — good, not identical; where the cryobiopsy MDD diagnosis was high-confidence (60% of cases) it matched surgery in 95%, but in the 40% with low-confidence or unclassifiable cryobiopsy diagnoses, surgery reclassified 23% to a definite alternative. The randomised COLD study (n=55) tested the strategy rather than the sample: cryobiopsy-first with surgery only if inconclusive reached an MDD diagnostic yield of 89% vs 88% for immediate surgery, with serious adverse events in 1 of 28 (4%) vs 12 of 24 (50%) and a hospital stay of 1 vs 5 days. Earlier prospective series are less tidy — Casoni 2014 (n=69) reported a 76% high-confidence pattern yield but pneumothorax in 28%, and a technique study (n=46) found yield depended on sampling two segments (69% for one sampling vs 96% with two-segment sampling) — the disagreement across cohorts on yield and complications is printed on the cards, not smoothed over. These are diagnostic-agreement and yield outcomes, not patient-outcome endpoints.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a cryobiopsy-first strategy achieves near-surgical diagnostic yield with substantially fewer serious adverse events and shorter stay; framed as a diagnostic-strategy (GAP-E) shelf, since agreement and yield — not patient outcomes — are the endpoints

title: Talc poudrage versus talc slurry for malignant pleural effusion: the randomised trials found no overall difference (TAPPS failure 22% vs 24%; Dresler success 78% vs 71%) — a lung-or-breast-primary subgroup favoured poudrage in the older trial, and the one positive comparative study allocated its sickest patients to slurry
question: In adults with malignant pleural effusion undergoing pleurodesis, does talc poudrage (thoracoscopic) versus talc slurry (bedside) differ in pleurodesis failure?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) for a poudrage advantage; the overall randomised answer is no difference. This is a PARTIAL shelf: live #816 asks indwelling pleural catheter versus talc pleurodesis (TIME2/AMPLE) and pack #3958 covers IPC-PLUS — the delivery-route comparison (poudrage vs slurry) is not asked in either, and none of #816's references is carded here. TAPPS (JAMA 2020, n=330, open-label) found 90-day pleurodesis failure in 22% with thoracoscopic poudrage vs 24% with bedside slurry (adjusted OR 0.91, 95% CI 0.54–1.55 — a relative measure; absolute difference −1.8%), with no significant difference in any of 24 prespecified secondary outcomes; the authors note the trial may have been underpowered for small differences. The older intergroup phase 3 trial (Dresler 2005, n=501 registered) likewise found no overall difference in 30-day success (78% vs 71%), but in the prespecified subgroup with lung or breast primaries success was 82% vs 67% favouring poudrage, while respiratory complications were more common after poudrage (14% vs 6%). The one clearly positive comparative study (Stefani 2006, n=109) was not randomised: patients at high anaesthetic risk or with short life expectancy were given slurry by design, so its poudrage advantage (life-long symphysis 81.9% vs 62.2%) is confounded by allocation and is carded as such.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) for any poudrage advantage — the two randomised trials found (the treatment made no difference) in overall pleurodesis failure or success; the only positive signals are a subgroup of one older trial and a non-randomised study whose allocation favoured poudrage

title: The cuff-leak test predicts post-extubation stridor with high specificity but only moderate sensitivity: pooled specificity 0.87–0.88 and sensitivity 0.62–0.66 across 28 studies (4,493 extubations) — a low leak flags risk, but a normal leak does not clear a patient, and early single-centre cut-offs (110–130 mL) performed better than the pooled test
question: In mechanically ventilated adults being considered for extubation, does the cuff-leak test (cuff-leak volume/percentage) predict post-extubation stridor and reintubation accurately enough to guide extubation decisions?
balance: POSSIBLE, framed as diagnostic accuracy (GAP-E), not as a treatment effect. The three classic prospective cohorts agree that patients who develop post-extubation stridor have much smaller cuff leaks: Miller & Cole 1996 (100 intubations; stridor in 6%; mean leak 180 vs 360 mL; a leak <110 mL had positive predictive value 0.80 and specificity 0.99), Jaber 2003 (112 extubations; stridor incidence 12%; at thresholds of 130 mL and 12% of tidal volume, sensitivity 85% and specificity 95%), and Sandhu 2000 (110 trauma patients; stridor/reintubation groups had leaks of about 8–9% of tidal volume; a leak <10% had 96% specificity). The 2020 meta-analysis (28 studies, 4,493 extubations) tempers the early numbers: pooled sensitivity 0.62 and specificity 0.87 for post-extubation airway obstruction, and sensitivity 0.66 / specificity 0.88 for reintubation, with substantial heterogeneity. The clinical reading the source literature supports: use a low leak to trigger preparation (steroids, anaesthesia presence, delayed extubation in selected patients) — but do not treat a reassuring leak as clearance, and do not let a single low leak postpone extubation indefinitely, since most low-leak patients still extubate without stridor. Extubation-strategy shelves (packs #1309/#3133–#3135) and the SBT shelf (live #1321) ask different questions and are not duplicated.
stamp: POSSIBLE — as a diagnostic-accuracy (GAP-E) shelf: the cuff-leak test is a specific but only moderately sensitive screen; a positive (low-leak) result usefully flags risk, a negative result does not exclude stridor, and a low leak alone should not postpone extubation indefinitely

title: Xuebijing injection in sepsis: EXIT-SEP (n=1,817, 45 Chinese ICUs) cut 28-day mortality to 18.8% vs 26.1% with placebo, and a severe-pneumonia trial found the same direction — large, double-blind and concordant, but the entire randomised base is single-country, and the product is a specific non-FDA-approved herbal preparation
question: In adults with sepsis, does Xuebijing injection added to standard care versus standard care alone reduce 28-day mortality?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). Product naming under the clarification exception: Xuebijing injection is a specific herbal-based intravenous preparation, not a generic class; it is not FDA-approved, and preparations of this kind may differ by maker. The fetched PubMed records for the trials carded here do not name the manufacturer, so no manufacturer is printed on this shelf. EXIT-SEP (JAMA Intern Med 2023; 1,817 randomised patients with sepsis at 45 ICUs in China; Xuebijing 100 mL every 12 h for 5 days vs volume-matched saline placebo) found 28-day mortality of 18.8% vs 26.1% — an absolute difference of 7.3 percentage points (95% CI 3.4–11.2); adverse events were similar (22.9% vs 25.3%). The earlier severe community-acquired pneumonia trial (Song 2019; 710 critically ill patients, 33 Chinese hospitals) found the same direction on its secondary mortality outcome (28-day mortality 15.87% vs 24.63%; absolute difference 8.8 percentage points) alongside its positive primary pneumonia-severity endpoint. A 2022 network meta-analysis of integrative medicines in sepsis rated the Xuebijing mortality estimate (OR 0.71 — a relative measure) as very-low-level evidence, which is the honest counterweight: the two big trials are modern and well-conducted, but every randomised patient was enrolled in China, by overlapping investigator networks, for one manufacturer's preparation — independent replication outside that system does not exist, and that is why the stamp caps at POSSIBLE despite the trial sizes.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two large double-blind placebo-controlled trials from one country agree on a mortality reduction; capped at POSSIBLE because the evidence is a single-country programme for a specific non-FDA-approved preparation with no independent replication elsewhere

title: Infectious-diseases consultation in Staphylococcus aureus bacteraemia: every strand of evidence is observational — consultation is associated with roughly halved mortality in meta-analysis (30-day RR 0.53; absolute mortality 12.39% vs 26.07%) and with better adherence to quality measures, but no randomised trial exists and confounding by indication is the central caveat
question: In adults with Staphylococcus aureus bacteraemia, is infectious-diseases consultation (versus no consultation) associated with lower mortality and better adherence to quality-of-care measures?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational evidence only, capped and labelled per the standing rule; this is a GAP-E (evidence/strategy) shelf, not a proven intervention effect. Lahey 2009 (retrospective cohort, 240 patients) found hospital mortality of 13.9% with infectious-diseases consultation vs 23.7% without (adjusted hazard ratio 0.46 — a relative measure), alongside closer blood-culture follow-up, better antibiotic selection and more frequent removal of pus or prosthetic material; notably, consulted patients were sicker (more endocarditis, CNS involvement and osteomyelitis), which biases against consultation, yet they still fared better. The Vogel 2016 meta-analysis (18 studies, 5,337 patients) pooled 30-day mortality of 12.39% vs 26.07% (relative risk 0.53, a relative measure), with better appropriateness of antistaphylococcal agent and duration and more follow-up cultures and echocardiography. The largest recent cohort (Papadimitriou-Olivgeris 2023; 839 episodes) found consultation within 48 h independently associated with better survival in a multivariable model, as was early source control. The central caveat stays on the face: none of this is randomised — consultation may be a marker for better-resourced care or for surviving long enough to be consulted, and the meta-analysis authors themselves call for cluster-randomised trials. SAB treatment questions (oral switch, live #502; dalbavancin, live #1636) are separate homes and are not duplicated.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational evidence only, capped at POSSIBLE and labelled as such: consultation is consistently associated with lower mortality and better process adherence, but no randomised trial exists and confounding by indication cannot be excluded

title: PHYSIOLOGY — Dynamic heart–lung indices of fluid responsiveness: pulse pressure variation above ~13% identifies fluid responders (sensitivity 94%, specificity 96% in the founding study), stroke volume variation behaves similarly, and a 15-second end-expiratory occlusion that raises cardiac index ≥5% predicts responsiveness — all of it valid only under controlled ventilation, adequate tidal volume, sinus rhythm and no spontaneous effort
question: In mechanically ventilated adults, how do respiratory variations in pulse pressure and stroke volume, and the end-expiratory occlusion test, predict fluid responsiveness — what are the thresholds, and under what conditions (tidal volume, rhythm, spontaneous effort, lung compliance) do they fail?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. The textbook framing (Guyton & Hall's account of heart–lung interaction: positive-pressure inspiration cyclically raises intrathoracic pressure, impedes venous return and left-ventricular preload, and so makes arterial pulse pressure swing with the breath — the swing is large only when the ventricles sit on the steep part of the Frank–Starling curve, which is precisely the fluid-responsive state) is borne out by concordant primary human data. Michard 2000 (40 septic, ventilated patients): a pre-infusion pulse pressure variation of 13% separated responders from non-responders with sensitivity 94% and specificity 96%, and the variation correlated tightly with the cardiac-index response (r²=0.85). Berkenstadt 2001 (15 neurosurgical patients, 140 graded volume loads): stroke volume variation ≥9.5% predicted a stroke-volume rise with sensitivity 79% and specificity 93%, far outperforming central venous pressure (AUC 0.870 vs 0.493). Monnet 2009 (34 ventilated patients with shock): a 15-second end-expiratory occlusion — which removes the cyclic inspiratory impediment and acts as a reversible internal fluid challenge — predicted responsiveness when cardiac index rose ≥5% (sensitivity 91%, specificity 100%). The meta-analytic average (Yang 2014: 22 studies, 807 patients, pooled AUC 0.94) was earned only in patients ventilated with tidal volume >8 mL/kg, without spontaneous breathing and without arrhythmia — those validity conditions are part of the physiology, printed on the cards, not fine print: with low tidal volumes, spontaneous efforts, irregular rhythm or poor lung compliance the indices lose discrimination. Passive leg raising is a separate, already-homed test (pack #3151), cross-pointed and not duplicated.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED

title: PHYSIOLOGY — Volume kinetics of infused crystalloid: Ringer's expands a ~5.9 L central space in volunteers and is eliminated with a half-life of 24 minutes in women and 38 minutes in men; elimination slows in proportion to falling arterial pressure, and under general anaesthesia distribution doubles in speed while the half-life stretches from 1.8 to 16.6 hours
question: In healthy humans, how is an infused crystalloid distributed between plasma and interstitium and eliminated over time — what are the volumes of distribution and elimination half-lives, and how do sex, arterial pressure and general anaesthesia change them?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING. The textbook framing (Guyton & Hall's body-fluid compartments: infused isotonic crystalloid distributes across the extracellular space, plasma plus interstitium, and is cleared by the kidneys) is given quantitative, time-resolved form by the volume-kinetic literature: serial haemoglobin dilution is fitted to a two-volume model (a central space, Vc, approximating plasma volume, exchanging with a peripheral interstitial space) to yield distribution and elimination rate constants. The stamp is EMERGING rather than ESTABLISHED for a reason printed here, not hidden: this evidence base is dominated by one research group (Hahn and co-workers), the quantities are model-derived rather than directly measured, and the framework is not yet textbook-settled in Guyton & Hall or Ganong. Within that frame the human data are concordant: the founding volunteer study (Svensén & Hahn 1997; N=8, labelled on its card as a sub-10 physiology classic) estimated the space expanded by Ringer's at 5.9 L with an elimination rate constant of 94 mL/min, far faster than dextran 70 (12 mL/min). Population analyses then quantified the modifiers: elimination half-life 24 min in female vs 38 min in male volunteers (111 infusions); elimination rate falling in proportion to mean arterial pressure (78 subjects); and, in 262 infusions, distribution twice as fast under general anaesthesia with the elimination half-life stretching from 1.8 to 16.6 hours and 88% more fluid residing extravascularly in the first hour. Values no fetched record confirms are presented as the model's account, not as measurements.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING

title: PHYSIOLOGY — Work of breathing and its oxygen cost: respiratory muscles take only a few percent of total oxygen consumption at rest in health, but the share rises steeply under load — ~16% of total VO2 at rest in morbid obesity (from the record's absolute values), an oxygen cost per litre of ventilation 3.5-fold higher in malnourished COPD, and an oxygen cost of breathing that predicted weaning failure better than the rapid-shallow-breathing index
question: In healthy humans and in patients with lung disease or critical illness, what fraction of total oxygen consumption do the respiratory muscles use at rest and under load, how is that cost measured, and how high does it rise in obstructive disease, obesity and failed weaning?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. The textbook framing (West's Respiratory Physiology and Nunn's Applied Respiratory Physiology: at rest the respiratory muscles consume only a small fraction — of the order of a few percent — of total oxygen uptake, because the work of quiet breathing is small; the cost rises disproportionately when ventilation must increase or when the respiratory system becomes inefficient, until breathing itself becomes a major claimant on oxygen delivery) is supported by concordant primary human studies using the standard measurement: the fall in total oxygen consumption when the respiratory muscles are rested by mechanical ventilation, or the rise in oxygen consumption per litre of added ventilation. Kress 1999 showed that in morbid obesity the cost is already high at rest: total VO2 fell from 354.6 to 297.2 mL/min when obese patients were ventilated and paralysed (a 57.4 mL/min respiratory share, about 16% of total VO2 by the record's absolute values), while non-obese controls showed no significant fall (221.4 to 219.8 mL/min). Donahoe 1989 measured the oxygen cost of augmenting ventilation directly: 1.23 mL O2 per litre in controls, 2.61 in normally nourished COPD and 4.28 in malnourished COPD. Shikora 1994 found the oxygen cost of breathing predicted weaning outcome better than the respiratory-rate/tidal-volume ratio (sensitivity 100%, specificity 87% in 28 patients), and Shikora 1992 (N=8 patients, labelled sub-10 classic) showed pressure support titrated the cost down from 22% to 8% of VO2. Two slate anchors could not be carded and their refusal is reported on the Synthesis card: the fetched records for the 1957/1961 classics carried no abstract this session, so no numbers from them are printed anywhere on this shelf.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED

title: Sublingual microcirculation in sepsis: perfused-vessel density and flow fall, dissociate from systemic pressures, and persistent loss predicts organ failure and death
question: In humans with sepsis and septic shock, what happens to sublingual microvascular flow and perfused-vessel density, how do these changes relate to systemic haemodynamics, and do persistent alterations predict organ failure and death?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (descriptive physiology). Framed by the textbook account of capillary exchange and distributive shock (Guyton & Hall; Ganong; Boron & Boulpaep — framing, not evidence), the primary human OPS/SDF imaging studies agree: in severe sepsis the proportion of perfused small sublingual vessels falls from about 90% (healthy volunteers) to 48% (De Backer 2002, PMID: 12091178) and vessel density falls from 5.4 to 4.5/mm, while mean arterial pressure and cardiac index may be near-normal — a dissociation between the systemic circulation and the microcirculation. In septic shock (Sakr 2004, PMID: 15343008), perfusion recovered in survivors and stayed low (57.4% versus 79.3%) in patients dying with multiple organ failure. In the pooled 252-patient analysis (De Backer 2013, PMID: 23318492), perfused small-vessel proportion was the strongest outcome predictor (AUC 0.818), independent of systemic variables. This is prognostic physiology: no trial shows that treating the microcirculation improves outcome.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — sublingual perfused small-vessel proportion and density fall in sepsis (about 48-65% perfused versus 90% in health), dissociate from systemic haemodynamics, and persistent alterations predict organ failure and death (observational human imaging studies)

title: Ridinilazole for C. difficile infection: sustained response not superior to vancomycin at phase 3 (73.0% versus 70.7%), but recurrence lower (8.1% versus 17.3%)
question: In adults with C. difficile infection, does ridinilazole versus vancomycin achieve sustained clinical response and reduce recurrence?
balance: SPLIT. Ridinilazole is a narrow-spectrum antibiotic designed to treat C. difficile infection while sparing the gut microbiota. The phase 2 CoDIFy trial (PMID: 28461207) found sustained clinical response in 66.7% versus 42.4% on vancomycin, but the efficacy population was only 69 patients. The phase 3 Ri-CoDIFy 1 and 2 programme (PMID: 38305378) did NOT meet superiority on that same primary endpoint: 73.0% versus 70.7% (difference 2.2%, 95% CI -4.2% to 8.6%). Recurrence, a secondary endpoint, was lower: 8.1% versus 17.3% — a 53% relative reduction, 9.2 percentage points absolute (p=0.0002) — and a nested microbiota cohort (PMID: 30071046) showed far less disruption of gut flora with ridinilazole, the plausible mechanism. Ridinilazole is not FDA-approved.
stamp: SPLIT — ridinilazole versus vancomycin in C. difficile infection: sustained clinical response not superior at phase 3 (73.0% vs 70.7%, primary endpoint missed), but recurrence lower (8.1% vs 17.3%; 53% relative reduction) in the Ri-CoDIFy programme

title: Y-90 radioembolisation (SIRT) versus sorafenib in unresectable HCC: no survival difference in SARAH or SIRveNIB (8.0 vs 9.9 and 8.8 vs 10.0 months); fewer severe adverse events with SIRT
question: In adults with locally advanced/unresectable HCC, does selective internal radiation therapy with yttrium-90 resin microspheres versus sorafenib improve overall survival and tolerability?
balance: No survival benefit in either head-to-head trial. In SARAH (PMID: 29107679), median overall survival was 8.0 months on SIRT with yttrium-90 resin microspheres (SIR-Spheres, Sirtex — the tested device, named under the clarification exception) versus 9.9 months on sorafenib (HR 1.15, p=0.18); in SIRveNIB (PMID: 29498924) it was 8.8 versus 10.0 months (HR 1.1, p=0.36) — in both, (the treatment made no difference) to survival. Tolerability favoured SIRT in both trials (grade 3 or worse adverse events 27.7% versus 50.6% in SIRveNIB). SORAMIC (PMID: 31421157) is carded with its premise stated plainly: it tested SIRT ADDED TO sorafenib, not SIRT instead of it, and was also null (12.1 versus 11.4 months, HR 1.01). The honest answer: choose on tolerability and liver-directed considerations, not on survival.
stamp: NO SURVIVAL BENEFIT — SIRT versus sorafenib in unresectable HCC made no difference to overall survival in SARAH and SIRveNIB (HR 1.15 and 1.1, both NS); SIRT caused fewer grade ≥3 adverse events

title: SIRT added to first-line FOLFOX in colorectal liver metastases: liver progression delayed (20.5 vs 12.6 months) but overall survival unchanged (22.6 vs 23.3 months, HR 1.04)
question: In adults with liver-dominant metastatic colorectal cancer, does adding Y-90 radioembolisation to first-line FOLFOX chemotherapy versus chemotherapy alone improve liver progression-free survival or overall survival?
balance: SPLIT by endpoint. Adding SIRT (yttrium-90 resin microspheres, SIR-Spheres, Sirtex — tested device) to first-line FOLFOX delayed progression in the liver in SIRFLOX (PMID: 26903575): median liver progression-free survival 20.5 versus 12.6 months (HR 0.69). But overall progression-free survival did not improve (HR 0.93), and the prespecified combined analysis of FOXFIRE, SIRFLOX and FOXFIRE-Global (1,103 patients, PMID: 28781171) found overall survival of 22.6 versus 23.3 months (HR 1.04, p=0.61) — (the treatment made no difference) to survival. A secondary analysis (PMID: 30033117) found a survival signal confined to right-sided primaries (HR 0.641, n=179), unconfirmed. Keep the liver result and the survival result separate: this is a liver-control intervention, not a life-prolonging one, on current evidence.
stamp: SPLIT — SIRT + FOLFOX versus FOLFOX in colorectal liver metastases: liver PFS improved (20.5 vs 12.6 months, HR 0.69) but overall survival made no difference (22.6 vs 23.3 months, HR 1.04, NS)

title: Hepatic arterial infusion chemotherapy in advanced HCC: FOLFOX-HAIC strongly positive in two Chinese trials (HR 0.41 and 0.35); cisplatin-based HAIC null in SILIUS (HR 1.009)
question: In adults with advanced HCC (including portal-vein invasion), does hepatic arterial infusion chemotherapy (FOLFOX-HAIC, alone or added to sorafenib) versus sorafenib alone improve overall survival?
balance: SPLIT — by regimen and region. Two Chinese randomised trials of oxaliplatin-based (FOLFOX) hepatic arterial infusion were strongly positive against sorafenib: FOHAIC-1 (PMID: 34905388), HAIC instead of sorafenib, median survival 13.9 versus 8.2 months (HR 0.41); and He 2019 (PMID: 31070690), HAIC added to sorafenib in portal-vein invasion, 13.37 versus 7.13 months (HR 0.35). The Japanese SILIUS trial (PMID: 29631810) of a different, low-dose cisplatin/fluorouracil infusion was null: 11.8 versus 11.5 months (HR 1.009) — (the treatment made no difference). All evidence is single-region (China/Japan, predominantly hepatitis B) against a sorafenib comparator that is no longer first-line standard in many regions; the regimens must not be pooled.
stamp: SPLIT — hepatic arterial infusion in advanced HCC: FOLFOX-HAIC improved survival versus sorafenib in two Chinese trials (HR 0.41; HR 0.35), while cisplatin-based HAIC made no difference in SILIUS (HR 1.009, NS)

title: Camrelizumab plus rivoceranib first-line in unresectable HCC (CARES-310): final median survival 23.8 versus 15.2 months on sorafenib (HR 0.64) — one trial, three reports
question: In adults with unresectable HCC and no prior systemic therapy, does camrelizumab plus rivoceranib (apatinib) versus sorafenib improve overall and progression-free survival?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single large trial, reported three times, and the shelf says so. CARES-310 randomised 543 patients with untreated unresectable HCC to camrelizumab plus rivoceranib or sorafenib. The primary analysis (PMID: 37499670) showed progression-free survival of 5.6 versus 3.7 months (HR 0.52) and interim survival of 22.1 versus 15.2 months (HR 0.62). The final analysis (PMID: 41308676) confirmed median overall survival of 23.8 versus 15.2 months (HR 0.64) — an 8.6-month absolute median gain — with grade 3-4 hypertension in 38% versus 15%. A post-hoc patient-reported-outcomes analysis by age (PMID: 41972014) is the third cardable report and favoured the combination in both age groups. No second trial exists; enrolment was 83% Asian, and the combination is not FDA-approved in the US.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single phase 3 trial (CARES-310, 543 patients): camrelizumab plus rivoceranib improved median survival from 15.2 to 23.8 months versus sorafenib (HR 0.64)

title: Retifanlimab plus carboplatin-paclitaxel in advanced anal cancer (POD1UM-303): progression-free survival 9.3 versus 7.4 months (HR 0.63); final overall survival 32.8 versus 22.2 months (HR 0.75)
question: In adults with inoperable locally recurrent or metastatic squamous-cell anal carcinoma, does retifanlimab added to carboplatin/paclitaxel versus chemotherapy alone improve progression-free and overall survival?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one randomised programme. In POD1UM-303/InterAACT-2 (308 patients, no prior systemic therapy), adding retifanlimab to carboplatin-paclitaxel lengthened median progression-free survival from 7.4 to 9.3 months (HR 0.63, PMID: 40517007), and the final survival analysis (PMID: 42097353) found median overall survival of 32.8 versus 22.2 months (HR 0.75) despite 77 placebo patients crossing over to retifanlimab. Grade 3 or worse adverse events were more frequent with retifanlimab (83.1% versus 75.0%). The single-arm POD1UM-202 study (PMID: 35816951) is carded as supporting evidence only: response 13.8% after platinum failure, showing drug activity but no comparative estimate. Single programme, so the stamp caps at POSSIBLE.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single phase 3 trial (POD1UM-303, 308 patients): retifanlimab plus carboplatin-paclitaxel improved progression-free survival (9.3 vs 7.4 months, HR 0.63) and overall survival (32.8 vs 22.2 months, HR 0.75) in advanced anal cancer

title: Trastuzumab deruxtecan in HER2-positive gastric/GEJ cancer: second-line survival 14.7 versus 11.4 months versus ramucirumab plus paclitaxel (HR 0.70, DESTINY-Gastric04); interstitial lung disease in 13.9%
question: In adults with HER2-positive advanced gastric or gastro-oesophageal-junction cancer, does trastuzumab deruxtecan versus standard therapy improve survival, in second-line and later settings?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). The randomised anchor is DESTINY-Gastric04 (PMID: 40454632): in second line, after progression on trastuzumab-based therapy with HER2 re-confirmed on biopsy, trastuzumab deruxtecan gave median overall survival of 14.7 versus 11.4 months against ramucirumab plus paclitaxel (HR 0.70) and response of 44.3% versus 29.1%. Single-arm support is consistent: DESTINY-Gastric02 in the USA/Europe (PMID: 37329891) response 42%, and the phase 1 gastric cohort (PMID: 31047804) response 43.2%. The harm to keep on the face is interstitial lung disease/pneumonitis: 13.9% adjudicated drug-related cases in the randomised trial and two treatment-associated deaths in Gastric02. PREMISE NOTE: the DESTINY-Gastric01 primary report is already carded elsewhere in the library, so under the one-home rule it is cross-pointed here, not re-carded; this shelf leads with the second-line randomised question.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — trastuzumab deruxtecan in HER2-positive gastric/GEJ cancer: randomised second-line survival benefit (14.7 vs 11.4 months, HR 0.70, DESTINY-Gastric04) with interstitial lung disease in 13.9%

title: BREAKWATER first-line BRAF V600E colorectal cancer: encorafenib + cetuximab + mFOLFOX6 — PFS 12.8 versus 7.1 months (HR 0.53), interim overall survival 30.3 versus 15.1 months (HR 0.49)
question: In adults with previously untreated BRAF V600E-mutant metastatic colorectal cancer, does encorafenib + cetuximab + mFOLFOX6 versus standard chemotherapy improve progression-free and overall survival?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one first-line trial programme. BREAKWATER randomised patients with untreated BRAF V600E-mutant metastatic colorectal cancer to encorafenib plus cetuximab plus mFOLFOX6 or standard care. Response was 60.9% versus 40.0% (PMID: 39863775), progression-free survival 12.8 versus 7.1 months (HR 0.53) and interim overall survival 30.3 versus 15.1 months (HR 0.49) (PMID: 40444708); Cohort 3, using a FOLFIRI backbone, was concordant (PMID: 42219860). PARTIAL-shelf note: this is the first-line, chemotherapy-combination question only. The previously treated question — BEACON, encorafenib plus cetuximab after prior therapy — is homed at pack #5165, which was read in full before building; no BEACON PMID is carded here. Serious adverse events were 46.1% versus 38.9%. Single programme with interim survival, so the stamp caps at POSSIBLE.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single phase 3 programme (BREAKWATER): first-line encorafenib + cetuximab + mFOLFOX6 improved PFS (12.8 vs 7.1 months, HR 0.53) and interim overall survival (30.3 vs 15.1 months, HR 0.49) in BRAF V600E colorectal cancer

title: Sotorasib plus panitumumab in KRAS G12C colorectal cancer (CodeBreaK 300): PFS 5.6 versus 2.2 months (HR 0.49), response 30.2% versus 1.9%; overall survival not significant (HR 0.70, p=0.20)
question: In adults with previously treated KRAS G12C-mutant metastatic colorectal cancer, does sotorasib + panitumumab versus investigator's-choice therapy improve progression-free survival?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — on progression-free survival and response, not on proven survival. CodeBreaK 300 randomised 160 patients with chemorefractory KRAS G12C-mutated metastatic colorectal cancer to sotorasib (960 mg or 240 mg) plus panitumumab or investigator's choice (trifluridine-tipiracil or regorafenib). At the approved 960-mg dose, median progression-free survival was 5.6 versus 2.2 months (HR 0.49, PMID: 37870968) and updated response was 30.2% versus 1.9%. The phase 1b CodeBreaK 101 cohort (PMID: 38177853, response 30.0%) is carded as supporting evidence. KRAS G12C is present in only about 3-4% of metastatic colorectal cancers.

title: Aspirin after resected colorectal cancer in an unselected population (ASCOLT)
question: In adults with resected non-metastatic colorectal cancer who have completed standard adjuvant therapy, does daily aspirin versus placebo improve disease-free survival, irrespective of tumour PI3K status?
balance: In an unselected population the answer is no on the trial's own terms. ASCOLT randomised 1,550 patients (modified intention-to-treat) with resected Dukes' C or high-risk Dukes' B colon cancer or Dukes' B/C rectal cancer, after completion of standard adjuvant therapy, to aspirin 200 mg daily or placebo for 3 years: 5-year disease-free survival was 77.0% versus 74.8% (HR 0.91, 95% CI 0.73–1.13; p=0.38 — the treatment made no difference), and serious adverse events were 12% versus 14%. ASCOLT's own preplanned translational analysis found no significant benefit in PIK3CA-mutated or COX-2-overexpressing subgroups either (all subgroup confidence intervals wide and crossing 1), although its pooled meta-analysis of the three published trials in PIK3CA exon 9/20-mutated tumours gave HR 0.61 (95% CI 0.39–0.96) — a biomarker-selected signal that belongs with Shelf #1849 (ALASCCA, aspirin restricted to PI3K-pathway-altered tumours), not with this unselected question. A 2026 systematic review pooling observational studies and RCTs likewise found no survival or disease-free-survival benefit (observational OS OR 0.92, DFS OR 0.90 — relative measures, both non-significant). The Add-Aspirin trial's colorectal cohort (950 registered) has reported feasibility only — tolerability and adherence, no colorectal efficacy result — so it is not carded as efficacy evidence here. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) for any unselected benefit.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the large unselected-population trial was null (the treatment made no difference on disease-free survival); any biomarker-selected benefit is a different question, homed at Shelf #1849

title: Darvadstrocel for complex perianal fistulas in Crohn's disease (ADMIRE-CD programme) — SPLIT
question: In adults with Crohn's disease and complex perianal fistulas refractory to conventional or biologic therapy, does a single local injection of darvadstrocel (expanded allogeneic adipose-derived stem cells) versus placebo achieve combined clinical and radiological remission?
balance: SPLIT, and the split is the story. In ADMIRE-CD (212 patients, Europe and Israel), a single intralesional injection of 120 million darvadstrocel cells (the manufactured cell product Alofisel, Takeda — named under the clarification exception for manufactured cell products) beat saline placebo on combined remission at week 24 (50% versus 34% in the intention-to-treat population; difference 15.2 percentage points) and at week 52 (56.3% versus 38.6%). The much larger replication, ADMIRE-CD II (568 patients, Europe, Israel and North America), found combined remission of 48.8% versus 46.3% (difference 2.4 percentage points; p=0.571) — the treatment made no difference — with a notably higher placebo remission rate than in the first trial. A retrospective chart review of ADMIRE-CD participants (INSPECT, 89 patients) found remission was often sustained to 156 weeks in both arms, with no significant between-group difference in relapse. Safety was similar between arms in both trials. No regulatory status is asserted on this shelf: the record set carded here does not establish the product's current approval status in any jurisdiction, and that must be verified separately before any clinical use is contemplated. PROPOSED SPLIT.
stamp: SPLIT — the first phase 3 trial (ADMIRE-CD) was positive at 24 and 52 weeks, but the larger replication trial (ADMIRE-CD II) was null (the treatment made no difference on its primary endpoint)

title: Etrolizumab in ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease — a split, stopped programme
question: In adults with moderately-to-severely active ulcerative colitis or Crohn's disease, does etrolizumab (anti-β7 integrin monoclonal antibody) versus placebo induce and maintain remission?
balance: SPLIT, trial by trial — this programme must not be averaged into a single verdict. Ulcerative colitis induction: HIBISCUS I met its endpoint (remission at week 10, 19.4% versus 6.9% on placebo; p=0.017) and its identical twin HIBISCUS II missed (18.2% versus 11.1%; p=0.17); etrolizumab was not superior to adalimumab in the pooled head-to-head analyses. In anti-TNF-experienced UC (HICKORY), induction was met (18.5% versus 6.3% at week 14; p=0.0033) but maintenance was missed (24.1% versus 20.2% at week 66; p=0.50 — the treatment made no difference). UC maintenance in LAUREL was also missed (29.6% versus 20.6% at week 62; p=0.19). Crohn's disease (BERGAMOT) inverted the pattern: induction missed on both co-primary endpoints, but maintenance was met (clinical remission 35% versus 24% and endoscopic improvement 24% versus 12% at week 66). Safety was unremarkable throughout, with adverse-event rates close to placebo. Development was stopped by the sponsor after this programme; etrolizumab is not an available therapy. This is a completeness shelf for a guideline-era question whose honest answer is: inconsistent induction, mostly failed maintenance, one positive Crohn's maintenance limb. PROPOSED SPLIT.
stamp: SPLIT — induction was met in HIBISCUS I and HICKORY but missed in HIBISCUS II and in BERGAMOT (Crohn's) induction; maintenance was missed in HICKORY and LAUREL but met in BERGAMOT maintenance; the programme was stopped

title: Cendakimab in eosinophilic oesophagitis
question: In adolescents and adults with eosinophilic oesophagitis, does cendakimab (anti-interleukin-13 monoclonal antibody) versus placebo improve dysphagia days and histological response?
balance: One programme, internally consistent. The phase 3 trial (430 patients aged 12–75) met both co-primary endpoints at week 24: dysphagia days fell more on weekly cendakimab than placebo (least-squares mean change −6.1 versus −4.2 days; p<0.001) and histological response (peak oesophageal eosinophil count ≤6 per high-power field) was achieved by 28.6% versus 2.2% (p<0.001), with endoscopic severity also improved and efficacy maintained at week 48. The earlier phase 2 HEROES trial of the same antibody (then called RPC4046; 99 adults) showed large reductions in oesophageal eosinophil counts and endoscopic and histological scores at week 16, though its dysphagia-diary difference was only numerical (p=0.0733). A gene-expression substudy of HEROES showed cendakimab normalised the oesophageal transcript profile in line with the histological changes. Symptom and tissue endpoints are kept separate on this shelf: the histological separation is dramatic, the symptom separation (about 2 extra dysphagia-free days) is modest. Adverse events were more frequent on cendakimab in phase 3 (about 84% versus 73% through week 48) but were not dose-limiting. No long-term-extension report was found in PubMed this session, so none is carded. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — a single programme, however concordant, caps at POSSIBLE.
stamp: POSSIBLE — one phase 3 trial met both co-primary endpoints, supported by one phase 2 trial of the same antibody; a single programme caps at POSSIBLE

title: Carotegrast methyl (AJM300) in ulcerative colitis
question: In adults with moderately active ulcerative colitis, does oral carotegrast methyl (α4-integrin antagonist) versus placebo induce clinical response?
balance: Two randomised trials from one country, both positive on induction. The phase 3 trial (203 patients in Japan with moderately active UC and an inadequate response or intolerance to mesalazine) found clinical response at week 8 in 45% on carotegrast methyl 960 mg three times daily versus 21% on placebo (odds ratio 3.30, 95% CI 1.73–6.29 — a relative measure, printed beside the absolute rates). The earlier phase 2 trial (102 patients) found response in 62.7% versus 25.5% (OR 5.35 — relative), remission in 23.5% versus 3.9%, and mucosal healing in 58.8% versus 29.4%. Adverse events were similar to placebo in both trials (about 38–39% in phase 3), with nasopharyngitis most common and no progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy observed — though trials of 8 weeks and a few hundred patients cannot exclude a rare class risk of α4-integrin blockade. A retrospective re-analysis of the phase 3 population (ASPECT) found lower baseline disease activity and lower anti-integrin αvβ6 antibody titres predicted remission, with symptom improvement detectable from week 2. Product naming (clarification exception): carotegrast methyl is marketed in Japan as CAROGRA tablets (EA Pharma / Kissei Pharmaceutical), approved in Japan in March 2022 per the approval report carded in the literature; it is not FDA-approved, and all evidence is Japanese. PROPOSED POSSIBLE.
stamp: POSSIBLE — two Japanese randomised trials (phase 2 and phase 3) met their response endpoints; single-country evidence, induction only

title: Appendicectomy for ulcerative colitis (ACCURE and COSTA)
question: In adults with ulcerative colitis, does appendicectomy added to standard therapy (versus standard therapy alone, or versus switching advanced therapy) reduce relapse and maintain remission?
balance: Two studies at two different disease moments, pointing the same way, with different evidentiary weight. ACCURE, the randomised trial, enrolled 201 patients with UC in remission but treated for a relapse within the previous 12 months: laparoscopic appendicectomy plus continued maintenance therapy cut the 1-year relapse rate to 36% versus 56% on medical therapy alone (relative risk 0.65, 95% CI 0.47–0.89 — a relative measure, beside the absolute rates; p=0.005). COSTA asked the harder question — active UC after biologic failure — but as a patient-preference cohort, not a randomised trial: patients who chose appendicectomy (continuing their existing advanced therapy) reached clinical remission without therapy failure at 12 months more often than patients who chose to switch to a JAK inhibitor (32.8% versus 12.2%; adjusted difference 22.9 percentage points), while therapy-failure and colectomy rates were similar. A histopathology report from ACCURE's Dutch appendicectomy arm found active appendiceal inflammation in 55.4% of specimens from patients whose colitis was quiescent — a plausible substrate, not proof of mechanism. Surgery's harms were modest in both studies (ACCURE serious adverse events 2% versus 0%; two incidental low-grade appendiceal mucinous neoplasms were found in resected specimens). PROPOSED POSSIBLE: one open-label randomised trial plus one preference cohort does not make a surgical standard.
stamp: POSSIBLE — one randomised trial showed fewer relapses with appendicectomy; the second study was a patient-preference cohort (observational comparison, labelled as such), not randomised

title: Neostigmine for acute colonic pseudo-obstruction (Ogilvie syndrome)
question: In adults with acute colonic pseudo-obstruction without mechanical obstruction or perforation, does intravenous neostigmine versus placebo or conservative care achieve prompt colonic decompression?
balance: The effect is dramatic and the evidence base is tiny — both facts belong on the face. In the landmark Ponec trial (21 patients with acute colonic pseudo-obstruction, caecal diameter at least 10 cm, unresponsive to at least 24 hours of conservative treatment), a single 2.0 mg intravenous dose of neostigmine produced prompt decompression in 10 of 11 patients versus 0 of 10 on saline (p<0.001), with a median time to response of 4 minutes. A second small randomised infusion study reported the same immediate pattern (10 of 11 versus 0 of 10) with less complete sustained response at 3 hours. The meta-analysis of all four randomised trials (127 patients in total) found single-dose resolution in 89.2% versus 14.65% (p<0.001). Harms are cholinergic and predictable: crampy abdominal pain, salivation and vomiting are common, and symptomatic bradycardia requiring atropine occurred in two patients in each of the small trials — cardiac monitoring and atropine at hand are part of the treatment, not an afterthought. Patients with bradycardia, hypotension, bronchospasm, perforation or mechanical obstruction were excluded from these trials. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — based on a very small N = 127: the stamp carries the N because four small trials, however lopsided, are still four small trials.
stamp: POSSIBLE — based on a very small N = 127 (total randomised patients across all trials in the meta-analysis; effects are large but rest on very small trials)

title: Treatment of autoimmune pancreatitis: steroid induction, maintenance, and relapse therapy
question: In adults with autoimmune pancreatitis, do corticosteroid induction with long-term maintenance (versus cessation after remission), and immunomodulator or rituximab strategies for relapse, reduce relapse rates?
balance: Framed as an evidence (GAP-E) shelf, because almost everything here is observational. Induction is not in serious doubt: in the Japanese standard-treatment survey (563 patients), remission was 98% with steroids versus 74% without, and in the international cohort (1,064 patients) 99% of treated type 1 and 92% of type 2 patients remitted on steroids. Relapse is the real problem — 31% in type 1 disease internationally, and 56% of relapses arrive within a year in the Japanese data. On maintenance, the single randomised trial (Masamune, 49 patients) found relapse over 3 years in 23.3% with continued low-dose prednisolone versus 57.9% after cessation at 26 weeks (p=0.011); the Japanese survey points the same way observationally (relapse 23% on maintenance versus 34% after stopping; p=0.048). For established relapse, the Mayo experience (116 type 1 patients) found relapse-free survival was similar whether relapse was treated with steroids alone or steroids plus an immunomodulator, nearly half of immunomodulator-treated patients failed or could not tolerate the drug, and rituximab produced complete remission in 10 of 12 steroid- or immunomodulator-resistant or intolerant patients. Relapse definitions vary across these cohorts and are not pooled on this shelf. Cross-point: inebilizumab in IgG4-related disease as a whole (MITIGATE) is Shelf #1818 — a disease-wide flare question, not this pancreas-specific treatment question. PROPOSED POSSIBLE, with the observational basis stated on the face.
stamp: POSSIBLE — observational evidence labelled as such throughout; the one randomised trial is a small maintenance trial (N = 49)

title: Treatment of chronic radiation proctopathy: hyperbaric oxygen helps refractory proctitis in one trial but not broader bowel dysfunction; sucralfate enemas rest on small trials
question: In adults with chronic radiation proctopathy (rectal bleeding after pelvic radiotherapy), how do hyperbaric oxygen therapy, sucralfate enemas, formalin application and argon plasma coagulation compare for bleeding control?
balance: SPLIT, and the split is by population and intervention, not noise. For endoscopy-defined refractory radiation proctitis, the Clarke double-blind crossover RCT (150 entered, 120 evaluable) found responders in 88.9% on hyperbaric oxygen vs 62.5% on sham air — an absolute risk reduction of 32%, NNT 3. For the broader HOT2 population (chronic bowel dysfunction after pelvic radiotherapy, 84 randomised), hyperbaric oxygen made no difference (the treatment made no difference) to bowel scores (p=0.50) or rectal bleeding scores (p=0.092). Sucralfate enemas were clinically superior to oral sulfasalazine plus rectal prednisolone in a 37-patient double-blind RCT, with durable responses in a 26-patient uncontrolled series (92.3% good response by 16 weeks, labelled observational). Formalin application and argon plasma coagulation are widely used but no randomised report for them is carded here, so this shelf makes no comparative claim for them. RICH-ART, sometimes cited in this area, is a radiation cystitis trial and is not evidence for proctopathy. PROPOSED SPLIT.
stamp: SPLIT — hyperbaric oxygen improved refractory proctitis in the Clarke crossover RCT (absolute risk reduction 32%, NNT 3) but made no difference in HOT2's broader bowel-dysfunction population; sucralfate enemas beat a steroid combination in one 37-patient RCT; no randomised formalin or argon plasma coagulation evidence is carded

title: Treatment of bile acid diarrhoea: colesevelam beats placebo short-term, liraglutide beat colesevelam in one small head-to-head trial, and colestyramine intolerance drives sequestrant failure
question: In adults with bile acid diarrhoea, do bile-acid sequestrants (colesevelam, cholestyramine) or liraglutide versus placebo or each other reduce stool frequency?
balance: This shelf asks the TREATMENT question only. The diagnostic question — whether to test for bile acid diarrhoea before rifaximin in IBS-D — is homed on Shelf #5678, which is cross-pointed here in prose; none of its references are carded here. On treatment: the SINBAD phase 4 trial (Borup 2023) randomised 168 patients and, in its C4-diagnosed primary population, colesevelam induced remission in 64% vs 16% on placebo over 12 days (adjusted odds ratio 9.1, a relative measure, with a very wide confidence interval). Kårhus 2022 (n=52) found liraglutide superior to colesevelam, the standard sequestrant, on a ≥25% stool-frequency reduction (77% vs 50% at 6 weeks) in a trial designed for non-inferiority. Practice data (Orekoya 2015, observational, labelled) show ~63% respond to a first sequestrant, colestyramine failure is often intolerance (45% of failures), and colesevelam rescues about half of colestyramine failures. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): consistent direction, small and short trials.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — colesevelam induced remission in 64% vs 16% on placebo over 12 days and liraglutide achieved ≥25% stool-frequency reduction in 77% vs 50% against colesevelam over 6 weeks, but both randomised trials are small and short

title: ESD versus EMR for early GI neoplasia: ESD wins en-bloc and R0 resection and recurrence at every site, and loses on perforation and time — on mostly non-randomised evidence
question: In adults with early gastrointestinal neoplasia (Barrett's, gastric, colorectal), does endoscopic submucosal dissection versus endoscopic mucosal resection achieve higher en-bloc and R0 resection and lower recurrence, at what cost in perforation and procedure time?
balance: Framed as an evidence (GAP-E) shelf: the comparative base is predominantly non-randomised, and the site strata are kept separate rather than pooled. Gastric (Tao 2019, 18 studies, 6,723 patients): en-bloc odds ratio 9.00 and recurrence odds ratio 0.18 favouring ESD, perforation odds ratio 2.55 against it — all relative measures from mostly retrospective data. Colorectal laterally spreading tumours (Zhao 2020, 3,062 lesions): en-bloc 95% vs 42.8%, recurrence 0.5% vs 15.9%, perforation 2.4% vs 1.8%. Barrett's (Terheggen 2017, the only RCT, n=40): R0 10/17 vs 2/17 for ESD, yet complete remission at 3 months was 15/16 vs 16/17 — the resection-quality win did not change the clinical outcome at this lesion size. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), observational basis stated on the face.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational evidence labelled as such: ESD achieves higher en-bloc/R0 resection and lower recurrence than EMR across Barrett's, gastric and colorectal strata, with more perforation and longer procedures; the single small RCT found the R0 advantage changed no clinical outcome
