title: EUS-guided biliary drainage versus ERCP first-line for malignant distal biliary obstruction: equal drainage success, less pancreatitis and stent dysfunction with the EUS route
question: In adults with malignant distal biliary obstruction, does first-line EUS-guided biliary drainage versus ERCP achieve comparable technical and clinical success with less post-procedure pancreatitis and stent dysfunction?
balance: The randomised base is FIRST-LINE drainage (the slate row was reframed on verification): three carded RCTs (Paik 2018, n=125; DRA-MBO/Teoh 2023, n=155; Bang 2018, n=67) and their meta-analysis (Miller 2019). Success is a tie everywhere: technical 93.8% vs 90.2% (Paik), 96.2% vs 76.3% (DRA-MBO, against an unusually low ERCP rate), 90.9% vs 94.1% (Bang); clinical success 90–97% in all arms. The differences are in harms and durability: pancreatitis 0% vs 14.8% in Paik and pooled risk ratio 0.12 (a relative measure) against ERCP; stent dysfunction requiring reintervention pooled RR 0.41; reintervention 15.6% vs 42.6% in Paik — though DRA-MBO found equal 1-year patency (91.1% vs 88.1%) and Bang found no significant difference in anything. The after-failed-ERCP comparison (EUS-guided vs percutaneous drainage) is a thinner limb, labelled as such on the meta-analysis card and not part of this shelf's claim. Device note (clarification exception): DRA-MBO used a lumen-apposing metal stent for choledochoduodenostomy. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit), expert-centre caveat on the face.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — first-line EUS-guided drainage matches ERCP on technical and clinical success across randomised trials, with less post-procedure pancreatitis (0% vs 14.8% in Paik; pooled RR 0.12) and less stent dysfunction/reintervention (pooled RR 0.41) — in expert centres

title: Endoscopic treatment of Zenker's diverticulum: Z-POEM, flexible and rigid septotomy all succeed in about 9 of 10 patients — no randomised trials, and the techniques separate on adverse events, not success
question: In adults with symptomatic Zenker's diverticulum, how do Z-POEM, flexible endoscopic septotomy and rigid septotomy compare on clinical success, adverse events and recurrence?
balance: Framed as an evidence (GAP-E) shelf: there are no randomised trials of Zenker's diverticulum treatment — every card is retrospective, and that is stated on the face. The largest comparison (Al Ghamdi 2022, 245 patients, 12 centres) found clinical success statistically indistinguishable (Z-POEM 92.7%, rigid 89.2%, flexible 86.7%; p=0.26) and recurrence similar, but adverse events clearly graded (rigid 30.0%, Z-POEM 16.8%, flexible 2.3%). A meta-analysis of seven non-randomised studies (Singh 2025, 580 patients) gives Z-POEM a clinical-success edge over flexible septotomy (risk ratio 1.11, a relative measure) with equal technical success, recurrence and adverse events — a point estimate the largest cohort does not confirm, so it is not upgraded here. Sarkis 2025 (60 patients) likewise found equal success with more and worse adverse events after needle-knife septotomy. PROPOSED POSSIBLE, observational basis stated.
stamp: POSSIBLE — observational evidence only (labelled): clinical success is 87–93% for Z-POEM, rigid and flexible septotomy alike with no proven efficacy winner; adverse events run highest with rigid septotomy (30.0%) and lowest with flexible septotomy (2.3%) in the largest cohort; no randomised trial exists

title: SIREC: metal stent versus single-dose brachytherapy for malignant dysphagia — stent relieves faster, brachytherapy relieves longer with fewer complications, at equal survival and cost (one randomised programme)
question: In adults with inoperable oesophageal cancer and dysphagia, does a self-expanding metal stent versus single-dose intraluminal brachytherapy differ in speed and durability of dysphagia relief, complications and quality of life?
balance: Single-trial-programme structure, stated plainly: SIREC (Homs 2004, nine Dutch hospitals, 209 patients) is the only randomised trial, and the quality-of-life (PMID: 15288288) and prognostic-model (PMID: 16111947) cards are further reports of it — their PMIDs appear here in the balance prose only as companion reports of the same programme, and the cards themselves carry their own records. The clinical answer is a timing trade-off: stent placement improved dysphagia more rapidly; brachytherapy gave better long-term relief, fewer complications (33% vs 21%, p=0.02; late haemorrhage 13% vs 5%) and better generic quality of life, with no difference in survival, recurrent dysphagia or total medical costs. The prognostic report supports stent when expected survival is short and brachytherapy when it is longer. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — a single programme caps the stamp at POSSIBLE however clean the trial.
stamp: POSSIBLE — single randomised programme (SIREC, 209 patients): stent relieves dysphagia faster, brachytherapy relieves it better long-term with fewer complications (33% vs 21%) and better quality of life; survival and costs did not differ

title: Alfapump for refractory ascites: paracentesis falls to near zero in every report including one small RCT — at the cost of serious adverse events, reinterventions and explants
question: In adults with cirrhosis and refractory ascites, does an implanted alfapump (automated low-flow ascites pump) versus standard serial large-volume paracentesis reduce paracentesis requirements, and at what cost in adverse events?
balance: PREMISE CORRECTION: the slate row stated all alfapump evidence is single-arm; verification this session found a multicentre randomised trial (Bureau 2017, n=60, NCT01528410) — it is carded first, and the GAP-E framing is retained because the randomised base remains one small trial. Device naming (clarification exception): alfapump® (Sequana Medical). The pattern is unusually consistent: paracentesis falls from ~2–3.4 to ~0.2 sessions per month in the RCT, the POSEIDON pivotal cohort (n=40; 77% with ≥50% reduction) and both European cohorts; quality of life improves; survival does not change. The harms are equally consistent: serious adverse events 85.2% vs 45.2% in the RCT, early acute kidney injury, catheter blockage, reinterventions in about a third, explants 15% by 6 months (POSEIDON) and 48% over longer follow-up in a TIPS-ineligible cohort. The EASL 2026 recompensation post-hoc analysis is congress/press only and is fenced, not carded. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the alfapump cut paracentesis from about 3 to about 0.2 sessions per month in every report including one small RCT (time to first paracentesis HR 0.13, a relative measure), with better quality of life but significantly more serious adverse events (85.2% vs 45.2% in the RCT) and a substantial explant/reintervention burden

title: L-carnitine and acetyl-L-carnitine for hepatic encephalopathy: ammonia and psychometric scores improve in every small trial — surrogates only, dominated by one research group, no clinical-outcome endpoint
question: In adults with hepatic encephalopathy, does L-carnitine or acetyl-L-carnitine versus placebo improve ammonia levels, psychometric performance and encephalopathy grade?
balance: The evidence base is dominated by a single research group (Malaguarnera and colleagues, Catania) — printed here as the slate requires. Their two double-blind RCTs (n=150 in 2005; n=120 in 2003, grades 1–2) found significant ammonia reductions and psychometric gains on L-carnitine 2 g twice daily; a third, smaller open-control trial (Cecere 2002, 27 completers, 6 g/day) found ammonia normalised in 14 of 16 treated patients. The Cochrane review of the sister compound acetyl-L-carnitine (five RCTs, 398 participants) found all trials single-team, high risk of bias and underpowered, with none reporting mortality, serious adverse events or hospitalisation. Outcomes throughout are surrogates (ammonia, psychometric tests); no mortality endpoint exists. Supplement note (clarification exception): preparations differ by maker and no commercial brand is named in the publications. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), with those limits on the face.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — L-carnitine lowered ammonia and improved psychometric tests in three small RCTs (n=150, 120, 31), but every outcome is a surrogate, the base is dominated by a single research group, and no trial reports mortality, encephalopathy episodes or hospitalisation

title: Baveno non-invasive criteria to spare screening endoscopy: the VI rule safely spares about a third of endoscopies (pooled missed varices-needing-treatment 0.3%); the expanded rule spares 40% at a 1.6% missed rate
question: In adults with compensated advanced chronic liver disease, do the Baveno VI/VII non-invasive criteria (platelet count plus liver stiffness measurement) safely identify patients who can avoid screening endoscopy without missing varices needing treatment?
balance: PARTIAL build, synthesis-only per the miner: Shelf #6727 is the HVPG PHYSIOLOGY home (what the gradient measures; the 10/12/16/20 mmHg ladder) — Baveno appears there only in aliases, and the validation question is not asked there. title: Semorinemab in early Alzheimer's disease: no slowing of functional or global decline in two phase 2 trials — one cognitive coprimary met in Lauriet, everything else null
question: In adults with prodromal-to-moderate Alzheimer's disease, does the anti-tau antibody semorinemab, versus placebo, slow decline on the CDR-SB or ADAS-Cog?
balance: Phase-2-only, split record — presented exactly that way. Tauriel (prodromal-to-mild, n=422 analysed) was flatly negative: CDR-SB worsening 2.19 on placebo vs 2.36–2.41 across three semorinemab doses over 73 weeks. Lauriet (mild-to-moderate, n=238 analysed) split its coprimaries: ADAS-Cog11 met (42.2% relative slowing, −2.89 points, p=0.0008 — relative measure labelled) while ADCS-ADL missed (−0.83 points, p=0.52) and MMSE and CDR-SB were also null, making the trial negative on its prespecified endpoints and Class I evidence against a functional benefit. The joint biomarker report shows pathway engagement (plasma pTau181 and CSF YKL-40 rose; GFAP stabilised in Lauriet only) without clinical benefit. Cross-point: the other anti-tau antibodies, gosuranemab and tilavonemab, are homed at pack #5405 in progressive supranuclear palsy — a different disease and question. PROPOSED SPLIT.
stamp: SPLIT — Tauriel was negative at all doses (CDR-SB 2.36–2.41 vs 2.19 on placebo); Lauriet met its ADAS-Cog11 coprimary (42.2% relative slowing) but missed its ADCS-ADL coprimary and all functional/global secondaries, so it was negative on its prespecified endpoints; semorinemab (the treatment made no difference) to functional or global decline at either stage

title: Hydromethylthionine (LMTM) in Alzheimer's disease: negative randomised primaries, positive only in revised and delayed-start analyses
question: In adults with MCI or mild-to-moderate dementia due to Alzheimer's disease, does oral hydromethylthionine mesylate, versus low-dose methylthioninium control, slow cognitive and functional decline?
balance: The randomised record is negative and the positive record is not randomised — that asymmetry is the whole story of this shelf. Two prespecified phase 3 primary analyses (Gauthier 2016, n = 891, mild-to-moderate disease; LUCIDITY's 52-week co-primaries, n = 598) found no separation from control. The programme's explanation — that the low-dose methylthioninium 'control', included to mask urine discolouration, is itself symptomatically active — is stated on the face of the LUCIDITY report, and it cuts both ways: it may have masked a real effect, and it also means no trial in the programme ever tested the drug against a truly inert placebo on a clinical endpoint. The supportive evidence is a pre-unblinding-revised, non-randomised monotherapy cohort analysis of the mild-Alzheimer's phase 3 (Wilcock 2018; monotherapy subgroups of only 79 and 76 patients) and LUCIDITY's delayed-start MCI findings at 78–104 weeks with biomarker support (neurofilament light chain, grey-matter atrophy). Those are reasons to run a clean trial, not evidence that the drug works. Harms are modest (headache, diarrhoea, gastrointestinal/urinary effects, haemoglobin reductions at high doses). The tau-antibody shelves elsewhere in this library ask a different question about a different mechanism and are not evidence for or against this small molecule.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — hydromethylthionine made no difference on the prespecified co-primary endpoints in its phase 3 trials (the treatment made no difference); the positive signals come only from a non-randomised monotherapy cohort analysis and delayed-start MCI analyses

title: Sodium oligomannate (GV-971) in Alzheimer's disease: one positive Chinese phase 3, a negative phase 2 primary, no confirmation elsewhere
question: In adults with mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's disease, does sodium oligomannate 900 mg daily, versus placebo, improve cognition over 36 weeks?
balance: One positive pivotal trial, one negative phase 2 primary, and nothing confirmatory outside China. The phase 3 result (−2.15 ADAS-Cog12 points at 36 weeks, n = 818) is a real randomised finding and is printed in full; so is the phase 2 trial's failure on the same scale at the same dose, and the small third trial's scattered significant time points. The product — sodium oligomannate (Shanghai Green Valley Pharmaceuticals), named under the clarification exception — was conditionally approved in China in 2019 and its development outside China was halted after the international phase 3 was terminated without results (slate desk-check). Its gut-microbiota mechanism rests principally on animal work, which this shelf does not card as evidence. A clinician reading this shelf should take away: possible cognitive benefit in the population and setting tested, unproven anywhere else, with a placebo-like adverse-event profile in the trials.
stamp: POSSIBLE — sodium oligomannate (GV-971, Shanghai Green Valley Pharmaceuticals) improved cognition in one Chinese phase 3 trial, but its phase 2 primary endpoint was negative and no confirmatory trial outside China exists

title: Delandistrogene moxeparvovec (EMBARK) in Duchenne muscular dystrophy: missed randomised primary, favourable external-control follow-up
question: In ambulant boys aged 4 to <8 years with Duchenne muscular dystrophy, does one intravenous dose of delandistrogene moxeparvovec, versus placebo or external controls, improve motor function (NSAA) over 1–3 years?
balance: EMBARK is two different kinds of evidence wearing one name. Year 1 is a proper randomised trial and it missed: NSAA difference 0.65 points, p = 0.2441, despite clear micro-dystrophin expression (34.29%) and an exploratory MRI substudy showing slower fat-fraction progression. Years 2–3, after crossover destroyed the internal control, compare treated boys with propensity-matched external controls and look progressively better (+4.39 NSAA points at 3 years, nominal p values). Both halves are printed here at full strength, with the design of each stated in its headline, because quoting either half alone misleads. Safety in-trial was manageable (11.1% treatment-related serious adverse events in year 1; no treatment-related deaths to year 3), but hepatic risk is a labelled concern for this product (Elevidys, Sarepta Therapeutics — named under the clarification exception) and is not quantified in the carded abstracts. Cross-point: the exon-skipping phosphorodiamidate morpholino shelf in this library covers the other dystrophin-raising drug class in Duchenne muscular dystrophy, with a similarly surrogate-led record.
stamp: POSSIBLE — delandistrogene moxeparvovec made no difference on EMBARK's randomised primary endpoint at 1 year, but 2- and 3-year comparisons against external (non-randomised) controls favoured treatment

title: Exon-skipping PMOs in Duchenne muscular dystrophy: dystrophin up, functional benefit unproven in randomised trials
question: In boys with DMD amenable to exon 51, 53 or 45 skipping, do the PMO antisense drugs (eteplirsen, golodirsen, casimersen, viltolarsen), versus placebo or natural history, improve motor function — or only dystrophin production?
balance: This shelf's value is stating plainly what the published record does and does not show. All four phosphorodiamidate morpholinos (eteplirsen, golodirsen, casimersen, viltolarsen — generic names; these are regulated pharmaceutical products, so no clarification-exception naming applies) hold FDA accelerated approval on increased dystrophin production, a surrogate. The carded journal reports demonstrate that surrogate — dystrophin rising to roughly 1% of normal with golodirsen and roughly 6% with viltolarsen — in cohorts of 12 to 79 boys, and show generally mild tolerability. What they do not contain is a randomised placebo-controlled functional benefit; functional claims are open-label or external-control comparisons. The confirmatory randomised trials that were meant to settle function (ESSENCE for golodirsen/casimersen, RACER53 for viltolarsen) were recorded at slate stage as having missed their primary functional endpoints, but no journal publications of them were found in this session's PubMed search, so they are fenced in prose on the synthesis card rather than carded. Cross-point: the delandistrogene moxeparvovec (EMBARK) shelf in this library covers the gene-therapy approach to the same dystrophin problem, with its own missed randomised primary.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the exon-skipping PMOs raise dystrophin (a surrogate) in small cohorts, but no carded randomised trial shows improved motor function

title: Remibrutinib in relapsing multiple sclerosis (REMODEL-1/2): fewer relapses than teriflunomide in two concordant phase 3 trials
question: In adults with relapsing MS, does the oral BTK inhibitor remibrutinib 100 mg twice daily, versus teriflunomide, reduce relapses and MRI lesion activity?
balance: Two large, identical, double-blind phase 3 trials, both positive on the same primary endpoint against an active comparator — that is a better randomised record than most new multiple-sclerosis drugs arrive with, and it is printed here at full strength: rate ratios 0.648 and 0.688 for annualised relapse rate, labelled relative with the small absolute differences (about 0.04 relapses per patient-year) beside them. The limits are equally plain: a single sponsor programme reported in a single publication (hence the POSSIBLE cap), teriflunomide rather than a high-efficacy monoclonal as comparator, follow-up to 30 months, and no MRI or disability-progression numbers in the carded abstract record — so this shelf claims relapse reduction only. On safety, the absence of a liver signal is the class-relevant finding, contrasting with the hepatic problems of the tolebrutinib programme covered elsewhere in this library; remibrutinib's other library home is its chronic spontaneous urticaria shelf, a separate question.
stamp: POSSIBLE — remibrutinib beat teriflunomide on relapse rate in two concordant phase 3 trials (REMODEL-1 and REMODEL-2), but the record is a single programme in one publication and reports no disability outcome on this shelf

title: Venous sinus stenting in refractory idiopathic intracranial hypertension: consistent observational improvement, no randomised trial
question: In adults with IIH and a transverse-sinus stenosis with a significant pressure gradient who have failed or not tolerated medical therapy, does venous sinus stenting improve papilloedema, headache and visual outcomes?
balance: There is no randomised trial of venous sinus stenting in idiopathic intracranial hypertension — everything on this shelf is observational, and it is labelled that way on every card. What the observational record shows consistently is that carefully selected patients (transverse-sinus stenosis, usually a measured pressure gradient, failure or intolerance of medical therapy) usually improve after stenting: papilloedema improvement around 89%–94% and headache improvement around 79% in the pooled series, against treatment failure around 8%, symptom recurrence around 10%, major complications around 2%–5%, later shunting in 6.2% of one large series, and a re-stenting burden for restenosis. Two cautions are built into the cards: the two meta-analyses pool overlapping series, so they are one evidence base, not two; and the low-gradient series suggests the manometry thresholds used to select patients may not predict who improves. Dual antiplatelet therapy after stenting is a real cost. The competing strategies — weight-loss surgery and acetazolamide-class medical therapy — have their own shelves in this library.
stamp: POSSIBLE (observational evidence only) — venous sinus stenting is followed by improvement in most selected patients with refractory IIH, but no randomised trial exists and about 1 in 12 treatments fail

title: Adjunctive risperidone in chronic PTSD: small positive trials, one large negative trial, guideline answer no
question: In adults with chronic PTSD whose symptoms persist despite antidepressant treatment, does adjunctive risperidone, versus placebo, reduce PTSD symptom severity (CAPS)?
balance: The split on this shelf is real but not symmetrical. Three small trials from 2003–2005 (n = 21–65) found benefits on some scales, each in a narrow setting — a residential veterans' programme, veterans with comorbid psychotic features (where the PTSD scale itself was null), and 21 women with childhood-abuse PTSD. The VA Cooperative Study (Krystal 2011, n = 296 randomised) then tested the exact clinical question — adjunctive risperidone for chronic PTSD persisting despite antidepressants — and found no benefit on symptoms or quality of life, with more weight gain, fatigue and somnolence. That is why VA/DoD guidance recommends against antipsychotic augmentation in PTSD, and why this shelf's practical answer is negative despite its SPLIT stamp: the split is between small early positives and one large definitive null. Other PTSD pharmacotherapy questions in this library (prazosin, venlafaxine, topiramate, ketamine) are separate shelves and are not evidence here.
stamp: SPLIT — small early trials were positive on some scales, but the largest trial (VA Cooperative Study, N = 296) found adjunctive risperidone made no difference in chronic PTSD (the treatment made no difference), with more weight gain and sedation

title: Agomelatine in generalised anxiety disorder: positive sponsor-run programme, no independent replication
question: In adults with generalised anxiety disorder, does agomelatine 25–50 mg, versus placebo (and versus escitalopram), reduce anxiety (HAM-A) over 12 weeks and prevent relapse?
balance: Within its own programme, agomelatine's record is consistent: two positive short-term placebo-controlled trials, a positive relapse-prevention trial, and a pooled response advantage of 67.1% versus 32.5%. The qualifications are structural and are printed on the face: every pivotal trial was sponsor-run by Servier (the maker of agomelatine, Valdoxan — named under the clarification exception), two headline p values are 0.040 and 0.046, the relapse trial studies only prior responders, and no independent group has replicated any of it. The drug is not FDA-approved for generalised anxiety disorder, and its labelled liver-enzyme monitoring requirement is a real-world cost the short, selected trial populations do not capture. Agomelatine for major depression is homed on a separate shelf in this library and is not evidence for this question.
stamp: POSSIBLE — agomelatine reduced anxiety versus placebo and prevented relapse in its trials, but the entire pivotal programme was sponsor-run (Servier) with no independent replication, and it is not FDA-approved for GAD

title: Cannabidiol for anxiety disorders: small single-dose laboratory positives, a null largest trial, consumer products untested
question: In people with anxiety disorders (chiefly social anxiety disorder), does pharmaceutical cannabidiol, versus placebo, reduce anxiety — acutely and with daily dosing?
balance: The pattern on this shelf is the classic early-signal pattern, and it is printed without rounding up. Single large doses of pharmaceutical cannabidiol calmed a laboratory speaking test in two small studies — with an inverted-U dose curve (300 mg worked in healthy volunteers; 150 mg and 600 mg did not) — and 4 weeks of 300 mg daily helped 37 adolescents with social anxiety disorder in a single-author trial. The largest, most clinically realistic trial — 300 mg added to exposure therapy in 80 patients — found nothing. Several positives come from one Brazilian research group. The product point is central and is made under the clarification exception: the tested preparations were pharmaceutical-grade cannabidiol at 300–600 mg (Masataka's published as cannabis oil containing 300 mg cannabidiol; no carded record names a brand or manufacturer), roughly 30–60 times typical consumer doses. Consumer CBD products are not what was tested and may differ in content and effect. Cannabidiol for epilepsy, tuberous sclerosis and schizophrenia are separate shelves in this library and are not evidence for anxiety.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — pharmaceutical cannabidiol calmed single-dose laboratory anxiety tests in small studies, but the largest trial (adjunct to exposure therapy, N = 80) found it made no difference, and consumer CBD products were not tested

title: Deep brain stimulation in severe treatment-refractory OCD: a real blinded effect on a very small randomised base
question: In adults with severe, treatment-refractory OCD, does deep brain stimulation (ventral capsule/ventral striatum, nucleus accumbens/ALIC, or subthalamic targets), versus sham stimulation, reduce Y-BOCS severity, and do benefits persist long-term?
balance: The blinded evidence points one way: across all 9 sham-controlled trials (91 patients in total), active DBS lowered Y-BOCS by 5.1 points more than sham (95% CI 2.0 to 8.1), and the two landmark crossover trials found 8-9 point active-versus-sham differences at the subthalamic nucleus (Mallet 2008, n=16) and nucleus accumbens (Denys 2010, n=16). A 30-patient Cologne cohort followed for 3-21 years found 73.3% responders at final follow-up, with response, once achieved, usually retained — but that cohort is retrospective and uncontrolled. The counterweights are structural: the entire randomised base is 91 patients, GRADE quality is low, targets differ between trials, and the surgery is not benign (in Mallet, 15 serious adverse events including 1 intracerebral haemorrhage and 2 infections in 16 patients; hypomania and cognitive problems are the commonest stimulation-related events in the pooled record). PROPOSED POSSIBLE: a real effect in carefully selected, severely refractory patients, at a specialist centre, with the small randomised base and surgical harms printed on the face.
stamp: POSSIBLE — consistent blinded benefit, but the entire randomised evidence base is only 91 patients across 9 small crossover trials, and GRADE quality is low

title: Varenicline in alcohol use disorder: drinking falls, heavy-drinking days split
question: In adults with alcohol use disorder, does varenicline, versus placebo, reduce heavy drinking and increase abstinent days?
balance: SPLIT is the honest stamp. On the amount consumed, the record is fairly consistent: Litten 2013 (n=200) met its primary outcome, the 2025 Swedish factorial trial (n=384) showed varenicline alone and with bupropion reducing both an objective biomarker (blood phosphatidylethanol) and percent heavy drinking days versus placebo, and the 2019 meta-analysis of 9 trials (N=585) found significantly reduced consumption. On heavy drinking days — the endpoint patients and guidelines care most about — the record divides: the same meta-analysis found no significant superiority over placebo, and O'Malley 2018 (n=131, AUD with comorbid smoking) was null on its primary outcome overall, with benefit confined to men in a sex interaction (no heavy drinking days 29% versus 6% in men; the small female subgroup ran the other way). The price is nausea: 51% on varenicline alone versus 11% on placebo in the factorial trial, lasting a median 45 days. PROPOSED SPLIT, naming the split: consumption down, heavy-drinking-day benefit inconsistent, male subgroup signal unconfirmed.
stamp: SPLIT — alcohol consumption falls consistently, but heavy-drinking-day benefit is inconsistent (one large trial null overall; pooled heavy-drinking-day effect not significant)

title: Ondansetron in early-onset / genotype-selected alcohol use disorder: a subgroup claim, fenced as such
question: In adults with alcohol use disorder of early onset (or with serotonergic genotypes predicting response), does low-dose ondansetron, versus placebo, reduce drinking?
balance: Every positive result on this shelf lives inside a subgroup, and the shelf is built to keep it there. Johnson 2000 (JAMA, n=271 randomised) found benefit only in early-onset alcoholism (drinks per day 1.56-1.89 across microgram doses versus 3.30 on placebo). Johnson 2011 (n=283) moved the fence from onset age to genotype: serotonin-transporter LL carriers on ondansetron drank less and had more abstinent days than LL carriers on placebo. The AD04 phase 3 (n=303, genotype-selected, 6 months) then showed its benefit in the prespecified heavy-drinker endophenotype (-8.5 percentage points on monthly heavy drinking days at month 6, p=0.03) while very heavy drinkers did not respond the same way, and a companion report found 6-month liver safety indistinguishable from placebo. The tested intervention is the genotype-paired low-dose programme AD04 (Adial Pharmaceuticals) — not ordinary antiemetic ondansetron. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: concordant randomised evidence, one dominant investigative programme, no approval, no independent replication, and no basis for use in unselected AUD.
stamp: POSSIBLE — benefit shown only within onset-age and genotype-defined subgroups, from a single dominant programme; not approved and not generalisable to unselected alcohol use disorder

title: Cannabinoids for fibromyalgia pain and sleep: small trials, split by outcome
question: In adults with fibromyalgia, do cannabinoids (nabilone, dronabinol/THC), versus placebo or amitriptyline, reduce pain and improve sleep?
balance: The controlled evidence is three small trials that do not tell one story. For pain: Skrabek 2008 (n=40) found pharmaceutical nabilone improved pain and function scores at 4 weeks, with all benefit lost after washout; Ware 2010 (n=29) found no pain effect at all; van de Donk 2019 (n=20, single inhalations of defined pharmaceutical-grade varieties) found no variety beat placebo on spontaneous pain overall. For sleep: Ware 2010 found nabilone superior to low-dose amitriptyline (Insomnia Severity Index difference 3.2) over 2 weeks. The largest dataset, a 367-patient observational cohort, reports pain falling from a median 9.0 to 5.0 over 6 months with mostly mild adverse effects — but it has no control group and cannot estimate efficacy. Clarification exception applied in full: the tested products were pharmaceutical nabilone and named Bedrocan varieties of exactly known THC/CBD content; dispensary cannabis is not interchangeable with them. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — three controlled trials of 20-40 patients disagree by outcome, and the only large dataset is uncontrolled

title: Sodium oxybate in paediatric narcolepsy: the child slice of the oxybate programme
question: In children and adolescents aged 7-16 with narcolepsy and cataplexy, does sodium oxybate, versus placebo (randomised withdrawal), maintain control of cataplexy and sleepiness?
balance: This is the paediatric slice of the oxybate question; the adult programme is homed at Shelf #921 (read alongside this shelf) and is not re-carded here. Within its own programme, the evidence is one trial in three reports: Plazzi 2018 randomised 63 stabilised children to continue oxybate or switch to placebo, and withdrawal cost a median 12.7 extra cataplexy attacks per week within 2 weeks (versus 0.3 on continued treatment, p<0.0001) — a maintenance effect in responders, shown by a withdrawal design, not an initiation effect. The open-label extension (95 entered) maintained control for up to a year, and a BMI report found percentiles falling over the first year before plateauing — in growing children, a monitoring signal as much as a benefit. The burden is real: enuresis in 21% of oxybate-naive children, nausea in 22%, twice-nightly dosing of a controlled substance. PROPOSED POSSIBLE, capped by the single-programme rule on the same precedent as Shelf #921 itself.
stamp: POSSIBLE — single trial programme (63 randomised in the blinded phase); randomised-withdrawal evidence shows maintenance of control, not initiation benefit

title: Dronabinol in obstructive sleep apnoea (PACE): an AHI signal the specialty academy advises against acting on
question: In adults with moderate-to-severe OSA, does dronabinol at bedtime, versus placebo, reduce the apnoea-hypopnoea index?
balance: The signal is real and the shelf still lands low. PACE (n=73, the only randomised trial) found dronabinol lowered the apnoea-hypopnoea index by 10.7 events/hour at 2.5 mg and 12.9 at 10 mg versus placebo over 6 weeks, with self-reported sleepiness improved at the higher dose — but overnight oxygenation and objectively measured wakefulness did not change, and AHI is a surrogate for the outcomes that matter. The only other human data are a 17-patient uncontrolled pilot from the same group. Against that base, the American Academy of Sleep Medicine's 2018 position statement — carded on the face, as it must be — advises that medical cannabis and its synthetic extracts should not be used to treat OSA. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): one small trial, one surrogate endpoint, one programme, and the specialty academy formally against.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — one 73-patient trial on the surrogate AHI endpoint, a 17-patient pilot, and the AASM formally advises against use for OSA

title: Dipyridamole in restless legs syndrome: a blinded positive from a single small programme
question: In adults with idiopathic RLS, does dipyridamole, versus placebo, reduce RLS severity (IRLS) and periodic limb movements?
balance: One Madrid group has built the whole record, and it is coherent but small. An open-label study (n=15) showed IRLS falling from 23.4 to 10.7 over 8 weeks; the double-blind crossover trial that followed (n=28, 2-week limbs) confirmed a real short-term effect under blinding — IRLS 11.1 on dipyridamole versus 18.7 on placebo (p<0.001), with periodic leg movements also sharply lower (index 8.2 versus 28.1). A 2025 post-hoc analysis of the same patients adds the key fence: those previously treated with dopaminergic drugs responded significantly worse, so the headline effect belongs mainly to untreated RLS. The adenosine hypothesis framing is the investigators' own and is labelled as such. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — total evidence base 43 patients, one centre, no long-term or comparative data.
stamp: POSSIBLE — one blinded positive crossover trial, but a single-centre, single-group programme with a total evidence base of 43 patients and 2-week treatment limbs

title: Rapamycin for healthy ageing: celebrated in mice, null on human primary endpoints so far
question: In healthy older adults, does intermittent low-dose rapamycin, versus placebo, improve measures of ageing (body composition, immune function, physical performance)?
balance: The animal longevity data behind rapamycin's reputation have not yet translated. PEARL, the largest and longest human trial (48 weeks of weekly compounded rapamycin in healthy adults, run by AgelessRx, which sells the intervention), was null on its primary endpoint — visceral adiposity did not change (p=0.942) — with positive signals only in secondary subgroups of women. RAPA-EX-01 (n=40, rapamycin with exercise) was likewise null on its primary analysis, and its prespecified sensitivity analyses significantly favoured placebo, with a higher adverse-event burden on the drug (99 versus 63 events, including one possibly related pneumonia). The earlier 25-person pilot found feasibility and red-cell index falls, and no cognitive, physical or metabolic benefit. Clarification exception in full: PEARL tested compounded rapamycin at roughly one-third the bioavailability of commercial sirolimus — nothing here reads across to pharmacy sirolimus or grey-market supply. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence), with the nulls worded plainly on the face.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — both larger randomised trials were null on their primary endpoints; positive signals are confined to small secondary subgroups

title: US POINTER: structured multidomain lifestyle intervention versus self-guided — a small win for intensity
question: In older adults at risk of cognitive decline, does a structured, intensive multidomain lifestyle intervention, versus a self-guided version of the same intervention, preserve global cognition?
balance: This pack is the US POINTER slice of the multidomain-lifestyle question whose home is Shelf #332 (the FINGER family — read the two together; nothing carded here duplicates that shelf's cards). POINTER asks a narrower question than FINGER did: not intervention versus advice, but structured, coached, accountable delivery versus a self-guided version of the same programme, in 2,111 at-risk US adults. Structured delivery won by 0.029 SD per year on global cognition (p=0.008) and by 0.014 on a frailty index (p<0.0001) — small, statistically firm differences. The fences matter as much as the result: there is no untreated control arm, so POINTER cannot show either version beats nothing; both arms improved, as practice effects predict; the imaging ancillary found no difference in amyloid, tau or hippocampal trajectories; and dementia incidence was not measured. PROPOSED POSSIBLE, capped by the single-trial rule.
stamp: POSSIBLE — a single large trial; structured delivery beat self-guided delivery by a small margin, with no untreated control arm

title: Radiofrequency ablation for uterine fibroids (Sonata / Acessa): symptom relief on a single-arm base
question: In premenopausal women with symptomatic uterine fibroids who wish to avoid hysterectomy, does ultrasound-guided radiofrequency ablation (transcervical or laparoscopic), versus myomectomy, hysterectomy or expectant care, reduce fibroid volume and symptom severity, and at what reintervention rate?
balance: Radiofrequency ablation shrinks fibroids and relieves symptoms in every series that reports it — the AAGL Practice Committee's 2025 review (30 studies) pools fibroid-volume reductions of 46.0% at 3 months and 65.4% at 12 months, with bleeding and quality-of-life scores improved throughout. The two pivotal programmes agree: SONATA (transcervical Sonata system, Gynesonics; n=147) halved symptom severity (55 to 24 at 2 years, 22 at 3) with reintervention of 5.5% at 2 years and 9.2% at 3; HALT (laparoscopic Acessa; n=135) showed the same pattern with 11% repeat intervention at 36 months. The discipline is in the design column: 26 of the 30 reviewed studies are single-group, the few RCTs are unblinded, and post-RFA hysterectomy across the literature ranges from 1.0% to 24.1% as follow-up lengthens. The devices are named separately (clarification exception) because the routes differ — transcervical and incisionless (Sonata) versus laparoscopic (Acessa ProVu, Hologic). Fertility data are insufficient, per the AAGL committee itself. PROPOSED POSSIBLE.
stamp: POSSIBLE — consistent symptom benefit and low 2-3 year reintervention, but the base is almost entirely single-arm and unblinded, with scarce fertility data

title: Sovleplenib for chronic immune thrombocytopenia (ESLIM-01)
question: In adults with chronic immune thrombocytopenia who have failed prior therapy, does the SYK inhibitor sovleplenib, versus placebo, produce durable platelet responses?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single-country (China), single-programme record. The phase 3 ESLIM-01 trial (188 patients, all Asian, median 4 previous lines of therapy) found a durable platelet response in 48% on sovleplenib versus 0% on placebo, and the earlier phase 1b/2 trial pointed the same way at the 300 mg dose; a 2026 network meta-analysis of the kinase-inhibitor trials in ITP is consistent. That caps the stamp at POSSIBLE: there is no trial outside China, no head-to-head against another SYK inhibitor, and no bleeding or mortality endpoint. The same-target drug fostamatinib is homed on its own shelf (#1800) and the thrombopoietin receptor agonists for ITP are homed separately (live shelf #672) — those records are not carded here. Harms in ESLIM-01 were mostly mild or moderate; grade 3 or higher neutrophil-count decrease and hypertension each occurred in 3% on sovleplenib versus 0% on placebo, and serious treatment-emergent events were 21% versus 18%.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — durable platelet response 48% versus 0% on placebo in the single phase 3 trial (ESLIM-01, 188 patients, China only), supported by its phase 1b/2 trial; single-country, single-programme evidence with a platelet-count endpoint caps the stamp at POSSIBLE

title: Rituximab for immune thrombocytopenia (RITP)
question: In adults with primary immune thrombocytopenia unresponsive to corticosteroids, does rituximab, versus placebo, reduce long-term treatment failure (splenectomy or meeting splenectomy criteria) and produce durable responses?
balance: SPLIT — the record splits by time horizon. Short-term platelet responses are common on rituximab (81% overall response in RITP versus 73% on placebo, not significant; about 65% at 3 months in the low-dose randomised comparison), and responders who do respond stay in response longer on rituximab (median 8.2 versus 1.8 months in the RITP extended follow-up). But the only placebo-controlled trial powered on the outcome that matters — long-term treatment failure (splenectomy or meeting splenectomy criteria) — was negative: 58% versus 69% failure, hazard ratio 0.89 (95% CI 0.55–1.45, p=0.65), and by 5 years only about one in five patients in the low-dose trial remained in sustained response on either regimen. Harms to weigh: in RITP, infections occurred in 40% on rituximab versus 24% on placebo (p=0.09), and rituximab carries the class risks of infusion reactions, prolonged B-cell depletion and hypogammaglobulinaemia with repeated courses. Rituximab's records in vasculitis, Sjögren syndrome, myositis and lupus nephritis are homed on their own shelves and are not carded here — this shelf is the ITP question only.
stamp: SPLIT — short-term platelet responses are frequent (81% in RITP) and last longer than on placebo, but the placebo-controlled RITP trial found no reduction in long-term treatment failure (HR 0.89, p=0.65), and only about 1 in 5 patients remained in response at 5 years in the low-dose trial

title: Avatrombopag for immune thrombocytopenia
question: In adults and in children with chronic immune thrombocytopenia and an insufficient response to prior therapy, does avatrombopag, versus placebo, produce durable platelet responses?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — three concordant trials, but the adult pivotal trial randomised only 49 patients, which keeps the stamp at POSSIBLE. Avatrombopag beat placebo on platelet response in adults (median 12.4 versus 0.0 cumulative weeks of response; day-8 response 65.6% versus 0%) and in children and adolescents (durable response 28% versus 0%), and a small open-label Japanese phase 3 study (19 patients, labelled as such) was consistent. This shelf is the avatrombopag slice only: the thrombopoietin receptor agonist class question for ITP is homed at live shelf #672, which cards romiplostim and eltrombopag — those studies are not carded here — and avatrombopag's other indications are homed separately (chemotherapy-induced thrombocytopenia at pack #2819; pre-procedure use in chronic liver disease at pack #6129). The endpoint throughout is platelet response, a surrogate; no carded trial was powered for bleeding or mortality. Class cautions for thrombopoietin receptor agonists (thrombosis at high platelet counts, dose holds above 250 × 10⁹/L in the paediatric programme) belong in counselling.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — platelet responses beat placebo in both the adult phase 3 trial (49 patients) and the paediatric phase 3b trial (75 patients), with a consistent small open-label Japanese study; the small adult pivotal trial and surrogate endpoints cap the stamp at POSSIBLE

title: Afamelanotide for erythropoietic protoporphyria
question: In adults with erythropoietic protoporphyria, does the afamelanotide 16 mg implant every 60 days, versus placebo, increase pain-free sunlight exposure and reduce phototoxic reactions?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — two placebo-controlled phase 3 trials (combined 168 patients) both found more pain-free sunlight exposure and fewer phototoxic reactions on afamelanotide (Scenesse, Clinuvel Pharmaceuticals — the specific tested product, named under the clarification exception), and large observational cohorts since approval point the same way. Two cautions belong on the face. First, partial unblinding is intrinsic: the drug visibly darkens skin, so patients could often tell their allocation, and the endpoints are patient-reported exposure and pain — the randomised differences (median pain-free sunlight 69.4 vs 40.8 hours in the US trial; 6.0 vs 0.8 hours in the EU trial) should be read with that bias in mind; the far lower EU figures reflect different exposure recording and climate, not a different drug effect. Second, afamelanotide does not lower protoporphyrin: the US cohort found no improvement in protoporphyrin levels or liver biochemistries, so it treats light tolerance, not the underlying disease or its liver risk. The oral challenger for the same disease, bitopertin, is a separate question (see the bitopertin shelf).
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — two placebo-controlled phase 3 trials (168 patients) both showed more pain-free sunlight exposure and fewer phototoxic reactions, corroborated by observational cohorts; partial unblinding (the drug darkens skin) and the absence of any protoporphyrin or liver benefit are stated on the face

title: Avapritinib for indolent systemic mastocytosis (PIONEER)
question: In adults with indolent systemic mastocytosis and moderate-to-severe symptoms despite supportive care, does avapritinib 25 mg daily, versus placebo, improve total symptom score?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single programme (one randomised trial, PIONEER, reported three ways) caps the stamp at POSSIBLE. In the placebo-controlled part, avapritinib 25 mg daily reduced the total symptom score by 15.6 points versus 9.2 points on placebo at 24 weeks — note the large placebo response: the drug's advantage over placebo is the 6.4-point difference, not the full 15.6. Objective markers moved far more decisively (54% versus 0% achieved at least a 50% reduction in serum tryptase), cutaneous outcomes improved in the trial's skin report, and symptom improvement was sustained at about 3 years in the open-label extension (mean change −19.39 points among those still assessed). The primary endpoint is patient-reported and subjective, which is why concordant objective markers matter. Harms at the 25 mg dose were dominated by oedema, with few discontinuations. This shelf is the mastocytosis question only: avapritinib in PDGFRA D842V-mutant gastrointestinal stromal tumour is a different question, homed at pack #6709, and none of that record is carded here.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in the single PIONEER trial, avapritinib beat placebo on total symptom score (−15.6 vs −9.2 points at 24 weeks) with a 54% versus 0% rate of at least 50% tryptase reduction, sustained in open-label follow-up; a single programme with a subjective primary endpoint caps the stamp at POSSIBLE

title: Pirtobrutinib after covalent BTK-inhibitor failure in CLL (BRUIN / BRUIN CLL-321)
question: In adults with relapsed or refractory chronic lymphocytic leukaemia or small lymphocytic lymphoma previously treated with a covalent BTK inhibitor, does the non-covalent BTK inhibitor pirtobrutinib improve response and progression-free survival versus investigator's-choice therapy?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — pirtobrutinib (Jaypirca, Eli Lilly — the specific marketed product, named under the clarification exception) works after covalent BTK-inhibitor failure, on the evidence of one single-arm phase 1/2 cohort and one open-label phase 3 trial. In BRUIN, 73.3% of 247 covalent-BTKi-pretreated patients responded; in BRUIN CLL-321, pirtobrutinib lengthened progression-free survival versus investigator's-choice idelalisib/rituximab or bendamustine/rituximab (median 14.0 vs 8.7 months; HR 0.54, 95% CI 0.39–0.75 — a relative measure; the absolute median gain was 5.3 months) and delayed next treatment (median 24.0 vs 10.9 months). Overall survival was NOT improved (HR 1.09) — that null sits beside the PFS result on purpose: the trial allowed crossover, which contaminates survival, but no survival benefit has been shown. Tolerability favoured pirtobrutinib (grade 3 or higher events 57.7% vs 73.4%). Resistance is already documented: in the BRUIN genomic analysis, 68% of patients progressing had acquired at least one mutation, including new BTK gatekeeper (T474) and kinase-impaired (L528W) mutations that pirtobrutinib itself selects for — this is a further line of therapy, not a permanent answer.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one randomised phase 3 trial showed longer progression-free survival than investigator's-choice therapy (HR 0.54; median 14.0 vs 8.7 months) with no overall-survival benefit (HR 1.09), supported by a 73.3% response rate in the single-arm BRUIN cohort; a single programme caps the stamp at POSSIBLE

title: Zanubrutinib versus ibrutinib in relapsed CLL (ALPINE)
question: In adults with relapsed or refractory chronic lymphocytic leukaemia or small lymphocytic lymphoma, does zanubrutinib, versus ibrutinib, improve progression-free survival with fewer cardiac events?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one large, definitive head-to-head trial (ALPINE, 652 patients) caps the stamp at POSSIBLE under the single-trial rule, however clean its result. Zanubrutinib was superior to ibrutinib on progression-free survival (HR 0.65, 95% CI 0.49–0.86 — a relative measure; 24-month PFS 78.4% vs 65.9%, an absolute difference of 12.5 percentage points), with higher response rates (85.6% vs 75.4% at the final analysis) and a sustained benefit at 42.5 months (PFS HR 0.68). The cardiac advantage is consistent across every report: atrial fibrillation/flutter was lower on zanubrutinib (7.1% vs 17.0% at the final analysis), cardiac events overall were fewer (25.9% vs 35.5%), and there were no cardiac deaths on zanubrutinib versus six on ibrutinib. Overall survival has not been shown to differ (HR 0.77, 95% CI 0.55–1.06, medians not reached). The balance must also carry the published debate that the ibrutinib arm may have underperformed historical ibrutinib results, which would flatter the comparison — the within-trial randomisation still stands, but the size of the advantage should be read with that caveat. Zanubrutinib's other programmes ask different questions — SEQUOIA (treatment-naïve CLL, versus bendamustine–rituximab) and ASPEN (Waldenström macroglobulinaemia, versus ibrutinib) — and are cross-pointed here in prose only, not carded on this shelf. The other second-generation head-to-head, acalabrutinib versus ibrutinib (which showed non-inferiority, not superiority), is homed at pack #3445.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the single ALPINE trial (652 patients) showed superior progression-free survival for zanubrutinib over ibrutinib (HR 0.65, sustained at HR 0.68 at 42.5 months) with fewer cardiac events and no overall-survival benefit shown; a single trial caps the stamp at POSSIBLE

title: Revumenib in relapsed or refractory acute leukaemia: about one in four patients reached complete remission in single-arm trials
question: In patients with relapsed/refractory acute leukaemia with KMT2A rearrangement (or NPM1-mutated AML), does the menin inhibitor revumenib produce complete remissions?
balance: Single-arm evidence throughout — there is no randomised comparator, so remission rates cannot be turned into a survival claim. In AUGMENT-101 phase 2, revumenib (Revuforj, Syndax Pharmaceuticals) produced complete remission or remission with partial haematological recovery (CR+CRh) in 22.8% of efficacy-evaluable patients with KMT2A-rearranged leukaemia (57 patients) and 23.4% in NPM1-mutated AML (64 efficacy-evaluable adults), with overall response rates of 63.2% and 46.9% respectively; the earlier phase 1 study reported a 30% CR/CRh rate. Class harms are defining: differentiation syndrome occurred in 16.0% (grade ≥3 events listed) and QTc prolongation in 13.8% in the KMT2A cohort, alongside febrile neutropenia in 37.2%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): roughly one in four heavily pretreated patients reaches CR/CRh, and some responders proceed to transplant — promising targeted activity, unproven against any alternative.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single-arm phase 2 cohorts only; remission rates have no comparator, so no survival or comparative claim is made

title: Normal pregnancy raises cardiac output by about half: the serial echocardiography record
question: In healthy pregnant women, how much do cardiac output, stroke volume, systemic vascular resistance and plasma volume change across gestation, when do they peak, and how fast do they normalise postpartum?
balance: Framed by the standard maternal-physiology account in Cunningham's obstetrics and the Guyton & Hall / Ganong tradition: cardiac output rises early and substantially, systemic vascular resistance falls in the first half of pregnancy, and plasma volume expands by roughly 40–50% against a smaller rise in red-cell mass (the physiological 'anaemia of pregnancy') — the plasma-volume and red-cell figures are presented here as the textbook's account, because no record fetched this session measured them directly. The primary human record fetched agrees on the cardiac side: in 13 women measured from before conception, cardiac output rose from 4.88 L/min to a maximum of 7.21 L/min at 32 weeks (about a 48% rise), significant by 5 weeks after the last menstrual period, with total peripheral resistance falling over the first 20 weeks. Labour adds large transient surges, and values return to prelabour levels within 24 hours of delivery in the labour study. Pre-eclampsia haemodynamics are a different, pathological question and are not covered here.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED

title: The luteal phase resets the thermostat upward: sweating and vasodilation thresholds rise by about half a degree
question: In healthy women, how do resting core temperature and the thresholds for sweating and cutaneous vasodilation shift between the follicular and luteal phases, and by how much (~0.3–0.5 °C)?
balance: Framed by Ganong and Boron & Boulpaep on progesterone's thermogenic effect: after ovulation the regulated core temperature sits higher, and the thresholds at which sweating, cutaneous vasodilation and shivering begin all shift upward together — a resetting of the set point, not a failure of the effectors, whose slopes above threshold are essentially unchanged. The primary record fetched is concordant: resting oesophageal temperature averaged 0.3 °C higher in the luteal phase in Stephenson & Kolka's exercise study (4 women), and 0.59 °C higher at night in Hessemer & Brück's 10 women, whose shivering, sweating and vasodilation thresholds were all raised by an average of 0.47 °C in the luteal phase. Effect sizes are small and method-sensitive — threshold values depend on the temperature site and the mean-body-temperature weighting used — so this shelf gives the range (~0.3–0.6 °C), not a single point value.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED

title: Hot flushes are triggered by small core-temperature rises: the sweating threshold is lowered in symptomatic women
question: In postmenopausal women, is the hot flush triggered by small elevations of core temperature acting on a narrowed thermoneutral zone — and how wide is that zone in symptomatic versus asymptomatic women?
balance: Framed by Ganong / Boron & Boulpaep on the thermoneutral (interthreshold) zone, and by the Freedman laboratory programme this shelf is built from: in symptomatic postmenopausal women the sweating threshold is lowered, so small elevations of core temperature — of the size produced by ordinary activity, a warm room or the circadian rise — trigger the full heat-loss response experienced as a flush. The classic laboratory comparison that measured the zone's width directly (symptomatic women's zone near 0.0 °C by rectal temperature versus about 0.4 °C in asymptomatic women) is homed elsewhere in this library and is cross-pointed here in prose, not carded: its finding is stated as that programme's account. The free primary record fetched this session supports the mechanism at every step it measures: most flushes were preceded by core-temperature elevations on 24-hour ambulatory monitoring, and symptomatic women had significantly lower sweating thresholds and higher maximum sweat rates than asymptomatic and cycling women in the controlled-laboratory comparison. The further claim that central sympathetic (noradrenergic) activation narrows the zone is thinner — supported indirectly, including an association of flush bother with higher baseline plasma noradrenaline in a stress-protocol cohort — and is labelled accordingly. This mechanism is the frame the neurokinin-antagonist treatment shelves in the library presuppose.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED

title: One bout of exercise blunts pain sensitivity: hypoalgesia is largest at the exercised part and scales with intensity
question: In healthy humans, how much does a single bout of aerobic or isometric exercise reduce experimental pain sensitivity, how long does the effect last, and how do intensity and muscle group (local vs remote) scale it?
balance: Framed by Guyton & Hall / Ganong on endogenous pain modulation: a single bout of exercise produces exercise-induced hypoalgesia (EIH) — a generalised reduction in pain sensitivity during and for some time after exercise — distinct from conditioned pain modulation (a second noxious stimulus) and from offset analgesia, both of which have their own shelves in this library and are not duplicated here. The primary record fetched is concordant on the scaling rules: in 80 healthy adults, pressure pain thresholds rose at local and remote sites after all exercise conditions except low-intensity cycling, the response was larger in the exercising body part than in non-exercising parts for every condition, and high-intensity exercise produced greater responses than low-intensity exercise; isometric-exercise studies in 58 young adults showed raised pressure pain thresholds and reduced pain ratings after just 3 minutes of submaximal contraction, with an endocannabinoid (not opioid, by naltrexone blockade) mechanism signal. EIH in healthy humans is PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED; its attenuation in chronic-pain populations is the emerging clinical corollary, presented as such and not merged into the main claim.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED

title: Trilaciclib before chemotherapy shortens severe neutropenia in small-cell lung cancer — a supportive-care benefit, with no survival benefit shown
question: In adults receiving myelosuppressive chemotherapy for extensive-stage small-cell lung cancer, does trilaciclib given before chemotherapy reduce the duration and occurrence of severe neutropenia and other myelosuppression outcomes versus chemotherapy alone?
balance: The benefit is on myelosuppression and supportive-care endpoints — no survival benefit has been shown, and none may be implied: across the trials, overall survival was essentially unchanged (10.9 vs 10.6 months, HR 0.87, P=0.61 in the first-line etoposide/carboplatin trial; 12.0 vs 8.8 months, HR 0.69 with a confidence interval crossing 1, in TRACES). What trilaciclib (Cosela, as published) does consistently is protect marrow: duration of severe neutropenia in cycle 1 fell from 7 to 2 days before topotecan and from 2 days to a mean of 0 days in TRACES, severe neutropenia occurrence fell, grade ≥3 adverse events were fewer (50% vs 83.8% in the first-line trial, driven by haematological toxicity), and supportive-care interventions and dose reductions fell in the pooled analyses. title: Glucarpidase cuts plasma methotrexate by about 99% within minutes — on single-arm evidence, with no randomised trial
question: In patients with delayed methotrexate clearance and methotrexate-induced kidney injury after high-dose methotrexate, does glucarpidase (carboxypeptidase G2) lower plasma methotrexate fast enough to change dialysis need and recovery versus supportive care with leucovorin?
balance: No randomised trial exists — the entire base is single-arm cohorts and compassionate-use programmes, graded accordingly, with small-N labelling applied per the slate flag (the pooled programme treated 476 patients, of whom 169 were efficacy-evaluable for the level fall). Glucarpidase (Voraxaze, as published — carboxypeptidase G2) does the pharmacokinetic thing dramatically and consistently: a median 99% reduction in plasma methotrexate from the first post-dose measurement (median 15 minutes) sustained to the last (median 40 hours) in the pooled analysis, and an immediate >97% reduction in the adult cohort. The clinical-outcome claims are cohort-grade only: 64% of patients with grade ≥2 renal impairment recovered to grade 0–1 at a median of 12.5 days in the pooled analysis, and 93% of the adult cohort had normalisation or improvement of creatinine — but with no comparator, how much of that recovery the enzyme caused, versus leucovorin and supportive care, cannot be known. The methotrexate-level fall is a pharmacokinetic surrogate. Timing matters: the consensus guideline states administration should optimally occur within 48–60 hours of the start of the methotrexate infusion.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — based on single-arm cohorts (476 patients treated in the pooled compassionate-use programme; no randomised trial exists)

title: Compression works about as well as cooling against taxane neuropathy: the POLAR trial's within-patient result
question: In patients receiving taxane chemotherapy, does limb compression — alone or combined with cooling as cryocompression — prevent grade ≥2 chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy versus no intervention or cooling alone?
balance: This shelf asks the compression question that the library's existing cryotherapy shelf (the frozen gloves and socks shelf for paclitaxel neuropathy) does not: that shelf covers cooling alone, and compression — tight surgical gloves, alone or combined with cooling as cryocompression — is the unasked slice cross-pointed here. The POLAR randomised trial is the anchor: within each patient, the treated dominant hand was compared with the untreated other hand, and both cooling (grade ≥2 sensory neuropathy 29% vs 50%) and compression (24% vs 38%) significantly reduced high-grade neuropathy on the treated hand, with no randomised difference established between cooling and compression themselves. The earlier surgical-glove compression programme points the same way (grade ≥2 sensory neuropathy 21.4% on protected hands vs 76.1% on control hands in the within-patient phase II study; 13.8% in the single-arm confirmatory study), and a conventionally randomised compression trial (80 patients, gloves and elastic socks) found significantly lower neuropathy incidence after the fourth and sixth cycles. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): compression is a cheap, tolerable alternative where freezing is impractical — the evidence is promising, not settled.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one randomised within-patient trial (POLAR) plus concordant smaller compression studies; no blinded conventional trial

title: Acupuncture for established painful CIPN: symptoms improve versus usual care, but real and sham acupuncture have not separated
question: In patients with established painful chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy, does acupuncture (manual or electroacupuncture, as tested) reduce neuropathic pain and symptom scores versus sham acupuncture or usual care?
balance: The record splits on the comparator, and the stamp names that split. Against usual care, acupuncture improves CIPN-related quality of life and symptom scores (the Bao trial's FACT/GOG-Ntx scores rose significantly versus usual care at week 8, P=.001). Against sham acupuncture, real acupuncture has not separated: in the same trial, sham improved alongside real on quality of life (P=.01 versus usual care), there was no statistically significant difference between real and sham, and the trial's quantitative-sensory-testing report likewise found real and sham both better than usual care with no difference between them — expectancy and non-specific effects are doing measurable work here. A separate electroacupuncture programme (160 women with paclitaxel-induced neuropathy) found higher overall effective rates for 2 Hz (79.5%) and 2/100 Hz (81.1%) electroacupuncture than for oral mecobalamin (47.4%), with greater symptom-score reductions — a drug comparator, not a sham. Prevention claims are a different question and are not folded in. PROPOSED SPLIT, as above.
stamp: SPLIT — acupuncture improves symptoms versus usual care, but real versus sham acupuncture did not separate in the sham-controlled trial; electroacupuncture beat a drug comparator in one trial

title: Submandibular gland transfer prevented radiation dry mouth better than pilocarpine — in a pre-IMRT-era trial programme
question: In patients with head-and-neck cancer about to receive radiotherapy, does submandibular gland transfer to the submental space (with shielding of the transferred gland) prevent radiation-induced xerostomia versus pilocarpine or no gland-sparing surgery?
balance: A pre-IMRT-era technique, and the caveat belongs on the face: the randomised comparison is transfer versus oral pilocarpine, and the phase II programme explicitly did not allow intensity-modulated radiotherapy — so the modern-comparator question (transfer versus IMRT parotid/submandibular sparing) has never been randomised, and this shelf does not pretend otherwise. Within its era, the record is consistent: the phase III interim analysis (120 patients) found stimulated salivary flow of 0.18 mL/min with transfer versus 0.05 mL/min with pilocarpine (P=.003) and better quality-of-life saliva scores, leading to premature closure; the functional-outcomes report (69 patients) found better swallowing and quality-of-life outcomes with transfer at every time point; and the multicentre phase II RTOG 0244 study found the technique reproducible (per protocol or acceptable variation in 77.3%) with 74% of patients prevented from acute grade ≥2 xerostomia — in a programme that also barred amifostine and pilocarpine. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for the pilocarpine-era comparison only.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — randomised against pilocarpine (not against modern IMRT gland sparing, which has never been randomised against transfer)

title: Droperidol at low antiemetic doses prevents postoperative nausea and vomiting as well as ondansetron — with a boxed warning written for higher doses
question: In adults at risk of postoperative nausea and vomiting, does droperidol — alone and within combination prophylaxis — prevent PONV versus placebo or ondansetron, and what is the QT/sedation cost at antiemetic doses?
balance: The boxed-warning context belongs on the face, stated plainly: droperidol carries an FDA boxed warning about QT prolongation and torsades de pointes, issued in an era of much larger (including antipsychotic) doses, and it sharply reduced antiemetic use. The low-dose evidence is a separate question and is stated separately: at 0.625–1.25 mg, droperidol prevented PONV as well as ondansetron in adults (Fortney's 2,061-patient programme and the Domino meta-analysis), did not prolong QTc beyond saline in a placebo-controlled study, produced only a transient QTc rise at 1.25 mg in a second randomised QT study, and had no attributed torsades or death in a 20,122-patient retrospective cohort (observational evidence, labelled as such). This shelf asks the droperidol-as-antiemetic question only: the live shelf on combination prophylaxis and aprepitant for PONV already covers droperidol as one component of the IMPACT factorial trial, and droperidol's emergency-department sedation use is a different shelf — neither is duplicated here. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) at low antiemetic doses.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — at low antiemetic doses (0.625–1.25 mg); the FDA boxed-warning context is on the face, with the low-dose QT evidence stated separately

title: Preoperative botulinum toxin for large ventral hernia: series report closure in over 90%, matched comparisons show no added benefit
question: In adults with large incisional/ventral hernias with loss of domain, does preoperative botulinum toxin A injection of the lateral abdominal wall muscles (± progressive pneumoperitoneum) increase fascial-closure rates and reduce component-separation need and recurrence versus repair without chemical component separation?
balance: No randomised trial was found for this question — the whole base is observational and is labelled as such on every card. The split is real: consecutive programmes (Bueno-Lledó's 100 loss-of-domain cases with toxin plus pneumoperitoneum, Deerenberg's 108 reconstructions) report fascial closure in 91–97%, and a prospective comparison achieved closure in all toxin patients; but the 2025 propensity-matched meta-analysis (851 patients) found the treatment made no difference to closure, recurrence or component-separation need, and its trial sequential analysis says the matched evidence is still too small to settle the question. Product and protocol discipline: doses and timing vary widely (an average 243 units in one programme; toxin given ~38 days ahead combined with pneumoperitoneum in another), and the botulinum toxin product/brand is not named in the carded records — so no single pooled closure-rate claim is made. PROPOSED SPLIT (observational).
stamp: SPLIT — observational evidence only: uncontrolled series report high closure rates, but the propensity-matched meta-analysis found no significant added benefit

title: Nerve monitoring in thyroid surgery: transient palsy fell in some analyses, permanent palsy in none
question: In adults undergoing thyroid (or parathyroid) surgery, does intraoperative nerve monitoring of the recurrent laryngeal nerve — intermittent or continuous — reduce permanent (and transient) vocal-cord palsy versus visual nerve identification alone?
balance: Permanent vocal-cord palsy is the outcome patients fear, and it is the outcome this evidence cannot settle: permanent event rates are around half a percent, so every carded analysis is underpowered for it, and none shows a significant reduction. What splits is the transient-palsy and overall-injury evidence — the largest randomised trial (Barczyński, 1,000 patients) and the high-risk meta-analysis favour monitoring, while the Cochrane review (very low certainty) and the RCT-only meta-analysis find no significant difference. The two monitoring modes (intermittent and continuous) are not separated by the carded analyses. PROPOSED SPLIT.
stamp: SPLIT — transient palsy was reduced in the largest RCT and in high-risk meta-analysis, but RCT-only meta-analyses found no significant reduction overall and no analysis showed a permanent-palsy reduction

title: Elective neck dissection in early oral cancer improved survival over watch-and-wait in two randomised trials
question: In adults with early (T1–T2, clinically node-negative) oral cavity squamous-cell carcinoma, does elective neck dissection at the time of primary surgery improve overall and disease-free survival versus watch-and-wait with therapeutic dissection on nodal relapse?
balance: Two randomised trials from different eras and health systems point the same way, and the trials are carded separately rather than pooled: in the Indian trial, 3-year overall survival was 80.0% with elective dissection versus 67.5% with watch-and-wait (hazard ratio for death 0.64 — a relative measure, printed beside the absolute rates); in the UK SEND trial the survival hazard ratio was 0.71 but not significant alone, with disease-free survival significantly favouring elective dissection. The seven-trial randomised meta-analysis (HR 0.67 for death) supports the same conclusion. The cost, per the UK trial, is more facial/neck nerve damage and neck surgery in the majority whose nodes prove negative (occult disease was found in 19.1% of T1 and 34.7% of T2 necks). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit).
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — elective dissection improved overall and disease-free survival across two randomised trials and their pooled evidence

title: Extracapsular dissection for benign parotid tumours: less temporary facial weakness and Frey syndrome, no recurrence penalty — in selected tumours
question: In adults with benign parotid tumours, does extracapsular dissection reduce facial-nerve injury, Frey syndrome and recurrence versus superficial (or partial superficial) parotidectomy?
balance: The unresolved build-time floor check for this row is resolved on the face: at least three comparative reports were required and four verify (a 9-study meta-analysis of 1,882 patients, and comparative cohorts of 182, 89 and 55 patients), so the shelf is built — but the base is entirely observational, which caps the stamp at POSSIBLE and is labelled on every card. The central bias is stated plainly, per the slate flag: extracapsular series select smaller, mobile tumours (explicitly so in the smallest cohort), so part of the lower complication rate is case selection. Within that fence, the findings are consistent: less transient facial paresis and Frey syndrome, no difference in permanent paralysis, and no recurrence difference even at a mean 13 years of follow-up. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), observational.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational evidence only (no randomised trials), in the smaller, mobile tumours selected for the technique

title: Intravenous paracetamol relieves postoperative pain versus placebo — but randomised trials found no advantage over the oral form
question: In adults having major surgery, does intravenous paracetamol (acetaminophen) reduce postoperative pain and opioid consumption versus placebo — and does it add anything over oral paracetamol or NSAIDs where those can be given?
balance: The two halves of this question have different answers, and both are on the face. Versus placebo, intravenous paracetamol works modestly: 37% versus 16% achieve at least 50% pain relief over 4 hours after a single dose (NNT 4.0), opioid use falls by 30% relative over 4 hours (labelled relative; it did not reduce opioid adverse events), and repeated 1 g doses beat placebo over 24 hours in orthopaedic surgery. Versus active comparators in the Cochrane review, differences were neither statistically nor clinically significant — and against the oral form specifically, a 486-patient equivalence trial and a 120-patient trial both found the intravenous route made no difference to pain or opioid use beyond, in one trial, the first 4 hours. So the intravenous form's real indication is the patient who cannot take oral medication. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) versus placebo, qualified as in the stamp.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) versus placebo — but no added benefit over oral paracetamol where the oral route can be used (two randomised trials)

title: Perioperative intravenous magnesium: opioid sparing of about 6–8 mg and small pain-score gains, on highly heterogeneous trials
question: In adults having surgery under general or regional anaesthesia, does perioperative intravenous magnesium sulfate reduce postoperative pain, opioid use and shivering versus placebo?
balance: Two meta-analyses, thirteen years apart, point the same way — 24-hour morphine down by 7.6 mg (24.4% relative, labelled as such) in the 2013 pooling and by 6.28 mg morphine equivalents in the 2026 pooling, with pain scores lower by roughly half to one point on a 0–10 scale — but heterogeneity is very high (I² up to 96%) and certainty low-to-moderate, which caps the stamp at POSSIBLE. Dosing and timing vary across trials (the carded individual trials used 50 mg/kg loading then 15 mg/kg/hour). The slate question also asked about shivering: none of the carded reports measured shivering, so this shelf makes no shivering claim rather than borrowing one. This is the analgesia question only — it is explicitly distinct from the magnesium-for-cisplatin-nephroprotection question in an earlier slate. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — meta-analyses agree on modest opioid sparing and small pain-score reductions, but heterogeneity is substantial and certainty low-to-moderate; no shivering claim is carded

title: Wound-edge protectors: meta-analyses claim a third fewer infections, the large ROSSINI trial found none
question: In adults having open or laparoscopic abdominal (and other clean-contaminated) surgery, does a wound-edge protector reduce surgical-site infection versus no protector, and do dual-ring devices outperform single-ring devices?
balance: This is the natural SPLIT the slate predicted. Three syntheses of mostly small, older trials — all at considerable risk of bias in one review's assessment — pool to relative risk ratios of 0.55–0.65 for surgical-site infection, with dual-ring devices looking better than single-ring in subgroup analyses (0.29–0.31 vs 0.71–0.83), a contrast one synthesis explicitly warns may reflect poorer double-ring data. The ROSSINI trial, the large multicentre randomised trial with blinded outcome assessment, found 24.7% versus 25.4% — the treatment made no difference. Devices are named by design only: the carded records do not give brands. PROPOSED SPLIT.
stamp: SPLIT — meta-analyses of small trials favour protectors (relative risk ~0.6), but the large ROSSINI randomised trial found no difference (24.7% vs 25.4%)
