title: Coblation tonsillectomy: a little less pain for the first days, no difference by day 7, and a possible increase in secondary bleeding
question: In children and adults having tonsillectomy (± adenoidectomy), does coblation reduce postoperative pain, haemorrhage and time to normal diet versus cold-steel dissection with bipolar haemostasis?
balance: The trial and synthesis data split exactly as the slate flag predicted, and both sides are presented. For pain: within-patient randomised trials found the coblation side significantly less painful for the first 1–3 days and no differently thereafter, and the Cochrane review (29 trials, 2,561 participants) found the same shape — a day-1 advantage shrinking to nothing by day 7 — on very low to low quality evidence. For bleeding: primary haemorrhage was similar, but secondary haemorrhage was higher with coblation in the Cochrane absolute risks (5% vs 3.6%) and in the largest single trial (1,004 patients), which otherwise favoured coblation on time, blood loss and recovery. The tested coblation system is not named by brand in the carded records, so no brand claim is made. PROPOSED SPLIT.
stamp: SPLIT — small early-pain benefit (days 1–3, none by day 7) against a possible increase in secondary haemorrhage, on low/very-low quality evidence

title: Ahmed valve versus Baerveldt implant: Baerveldt controlled pressure better in both randomised trials, with more hypotony-type failures
question: In adults with advanced glaucoma inadequately controlled on drops or after failed trabeculectomy, how do the two valved/non-valved tube shunts compare — Ahmed valve versus Baerveldt implant — on pressure control, failure, hypotony and reoperation (the ABC and AVB randomised trials)?
balance: Two independent randomised trials of exactly the devices named in the question — the tested products are named as published, per the clarification exception: the Ahmed FP7 Glaucoma Valve (New World Medical) versus the Baerveldt 101-350 / Baerveldt-350 Glaucoma Implant (Abbott Medical Optics). Both trials agree on direction: Baerveldt eyes ran about 2–3 mmHg lower, failure was significantly lower with Baerveldt in the AVB trial at 1 and 5 years and non-significantly lower in the ABC trial, and the failure modes flipped — Ahmed failures were mostly uncontrolled pressure, Baerveldt failures disproportionately hypotony, explantation or lost light perception, with more early postoperative complications in ABC's Baerveldt arm. The trials' failure definitions differ (21 vs 18 mmHg ceilings), so rates are compared within trials only. This shelf is device-versus-device only — it does not duplicate the tube-versus-trabeculectomy comparison shelved elsewhere. PROPOSED LIKELY.
stamp: LIKELY — Baerveldt (non-valved) gave lower pressure and lower or equal failure than Ahmed (valved) in both randomised trials, at the cost of more hypotony-type failures

title: Trifocal and extended-depth-of-focus intraocular lenses versus monofocal lenses in bilateral cataract surgery: better intermediate/near vision and spectacle independence, at a cost in contrast sensitivity and halos
question: In adults having cataract surgery in both eyes, do trifocal or extended-depth-of-focus intraocular lenses improve spectacle independence and intermediate/near vision versus monofocal lenses, at what cost in dysphotopsia and contrast sensitivity?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — randomised EDOF trials and a non-randomised trifocal comparison agree that presbyopia-correcting lenses improve intermediate and near vision and spectacle independence over monofocal lenses, with distance vision preserved; the costs are reduced contrast sensitivity and more halos. Industry sponsorship is near-universal in this base, and the trifocal limb rests on a non-randomised comparison, so the stamp stays at POSSIBLE. Tested lenses are named exactly as published, per the clarification exception: TECNIS Symfony ZXR00 and AT LARA 829MP (EDOF), CT ASPHINA 409MP and TECNIS 1-piece ZCB00 (monofocal controls); the trifocal report does not name a single branded lens in its record.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — EDOF lenses beat monofocal lenses on intermediate/near acuity and spectacle independence in two randomised trials (211 and 299 patients) and in meta-analysis, and a non-randomised trifocal comparison (91 patients) points the same way; contrast sensitivity is lower and halos more frequent

title: Descemet stripping only (DSO) for Fuchs dystrophy without stromal scarring: corneas clear in most selected patients in cohort reports, but no completed randomised comparison with DMEK exists yet
question: In adults with Fuchs endothelial dystrophy and no stromal scarring, does Descemet stripping only (DSO/DWEK, with or without topical rho-kinase inhibitor) clear the cornea and restore vision versus Descemet membrane endothelial keratoplasty (DMEK)?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the DSO limb rests entirely on observational reports: a prospective 23-eye series with adjunctive ripasudil (clearance in 22 of 23 eyes), a retrospective long-term series (12 of 13 eyes cleared; 10 of 13 maintained clearance at 5 years) and an individual-patient meta-analysis of 68 cases (85% clearance). No completed randomised DSO-versus-DMEK result exists: the DETECT II randomised trial (DMEK versus DSO with ripasudil, 60 patients planned, NCT05275972) has published a protocol only. The DMEK comparator evidence is homed on shelf #6427 (the DETECT trial of DMEK versus ultrathin DSAEK) and is not re-carded here. Patient selection is the whole question: every DSO report required central-only guttae with a healthy peripheral endothelial reserve. Build-time floor check (item U2): the free DSO base is exactly three cardable reports at or above the 10-human floor — a fourth 5-patient series falls below the floor and was not carded.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — DSO cleared the cornea in 85% of 68 pooled cases and in 22 of 23 eyes in the largest prospective series, but all evidence is observational, highly selected, and no randomised comparison with DMEK has reported

title: Varenicline nasal spray for dry eye disease: tear production and symptoms improve across severity, menopausal and fellow-eye analyses of the ONSET programme
question: In adults with dry eye disease, does varenicline nasal spray improve tear production (Schirmer) and dry-eye symptoms versus vehicle spray?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single randomised programme (the ONSET-1 and ONSET-2 vehicle-controlled trials) supports varenicline solution nasal spray 0.03 mg: the integrated analyses carded here show Schirmer gains of about 5.5-6.7 mm over vehicle and roughly 2.3-3.4 times the odds (relative measure) of a 10-mm Schirmer improvement, consistent across disease severity, menopausal status and study/fellow eyes. The primary ONSET-1 and ONSET-2 trial reports are carded on another shelf in this library and are not re-carded here; this shelf cards the programme's integrated and post-hoc analyses, which is why the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE. The tested product as published is OC-01 (varenicline solution) nasal spray. Sneezing is the signature adverse effect (82-84% in the autoimmune subgroup report, graded mild by 98%). The Schirmer endpoint is a sign, not a symptom — symptom (eye dryness score) differences were smaller and not significant in every subgroup.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one vehicle-controlled programme: integrated analyses (602 and 891 randomised patients) show Schirmer improvement of about 5-6 mm over vehicle with consistent effects across subgroups; primary trial reports are homed on another shelf, capping this slice at POSSIBLE

title: Fluticasone by exhalation delivery system (EDS-FLU, XHANCE) for chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps: polyp grade, congestion and quality of life improve in two replicate randomised trials
question: In adults with chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps, does fluticasone delivered by an exhalation delivery system (EDS-FLU) reduce polyp grade, congestion and exacerbations versus placebo delivery system — including in patients who would otherwise be surgical candidates?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — two replicate 323-patient randomised trials (NAVIGATE I and II) of the exhalation delivery system with fluticasone (EDS-FLU; XHANCE, OptiNose — named exactly as published, per the clarification exception) beat the placebo delivery system on both co-primary endpoints (congestion and polyp grade, P<.05 to P<.001), improved Sino-Nasal Outcome Test scores by about 10 points more than placebo, eliminated polyps on at least one side in about 25% versus 8.7%, and cut the number of patients meeting surgical-indication criteria by 62-67% in NAVIGATE II. The later ReOpen trials extend the finding to chronic rhinosinusitis with or without polyps and show 56-66% fewer exacerbations (relative measure) — carded here as a third limb with its broader population stated. This shelf does not answer device-versus-conventional-spray: every comparator was the same device delivering placebo.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — two replicate randomised trials (323 patients each) concordant on congestion, polyp grade and quality of life, with a third programme (ReOpen, 555 patients) showing fewer exacerbations; comparator throughout was the placebo delivery system, not a conventional spray

title: Steroid-eluting sinus implants after sinus surgery: fewer postoperative interventions and less polyposis in intrapatient randomised trials; in-office implants also help recurrent polyposis
question: In adults having endoscopic sinus surgery for chronic rhinosinusitis, does a steroid-eluting sinus implant placed at surgery reduce postoperative interventions, oral-steroid need and polyp recurrence versus no implant (or a non-eluting spacer)?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — three randomised programmes of mometasone-furoate-eluting bioabsorbable implants (the PROPEL family, Intersect ENT — named as published, per the clarification exception) point the same way: ADVANCE II (105 patients, intrapatient control) found a 29.0% relative reduction in postoperative interventions and a 44.9% relative reduction in frank polyposis on drug-eluting versus non-eluting sides; the frontal-ostia trial (80 patients, intrapatient control) found postoperative intervention needed in 11.5% versus 32.8% of sides at day 30 (absolute difference -21.3%); and RESOLVE (100 patients, in-office placement for recurrent polyposis — a different population, carded as its own limb) improved obstruction scores and polyp grade versus sham at 6 months. The stamp stays at POSSIBLE: two of three trials use within-patient side comparisons with short horizons, and the base is one manufacturer's programme.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — steroid-eluting implants reduced postoperative interventions (29.0% relative reduction in ADVANCE II; 11.5% versus 32.8% of frontal ostia needing intervention) and polyposis across three randomised trials totalling 285 patients, on short-horizon, largely intrapatient evidence

title: Botulinum toxin for adductor spasmodic dysphonia: voice improves for weeks in two small double-blind trials, with breathiness in up to three-quarters and benefit fading across each injection cycle
question: In adults with adductor spasmodic dysphonia, do botulinum toxin injections into the thyroarytenoid muscles improve voice quality and fluency versus sham or no injection, how long does benefit last, and what is the breathiness cost?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the randomised limb verifies (so this shelf is built as a treatment shelf, not demoted): a 13-patient double-blind placebo-controlled study found marked acoustic improvement and patient-rated benefit, and a 24-patient multicentre double-blind trial found aberrant phoneme counts fell by 7.0 versus 0.2 at 4 weeks (p=0.0148), with benefit persisting 12 weeks. The cost is breathiness: breathy hoarseness in 77.3% and aspiration when drinking in 40.9% in the multicentre trial, resolving within about 4 weeks. A prospective 22-patient cycle study shows the lived pattern: quality-of-life scores peak at 30% of each ~26-week cycle and exceed 75/100 for only 14% of the cycle. The tested product in the multicentre trial is named as published (Botox); dosing is individualised in practice. Outcomes are perceptual/acoustic scales, presented as such.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two small double-blind randomised trials (13 and 24 patients) show improved voice measures for about 12 weeks, but breathy hoarseness affects up to 77% and benefit occupies only part of each injection cycle

title: Platelet-rich plasma for androgenetic alopecia: hair density rises versus placebo in pooled randomised trials, but diameter gains are inconsistent and publication bias is documented — a SPLIT base
question: In adults with androgenetic alopecia, does platelet-rich plasma injection improve hair density and diameter versus saline placebo — and how does it compare with topical minoxidil?
balance: SPLIT — the density limb favours platelet-rich plasma (PRP): the 2024 meta-analysis of 14 randomised trials (431 patients) found +27.55 hairs/cm² versus placebo, and the two carded primary trials are positive. But the split is real: hair diameter did not significantly beat placebo in the 2023 pooling (and the 2024 diameter estimate's confidence interval crosses zero), heterogeneity is extreme (I² about 96%), the 2024 reviewers document evident publication bias and grade the evidence low quality, and one carded trial's clinical limb is a half-head design whose record mixes human efficacy with a mouse mechanistic experiment. Preparation protocols (activation, centrifugation, session spacing) are heterogeneous and not interchangeable — protocols are stated per report as published, per the clarification exception. The neighbouring questions are homed elsewhere and not re-carded here: shelf #6008 asks oral finasteride versus topical minoxidil head-to-head, and shelf #6009 asks topical minoxidil versus placebo in women; no carded trial here compares PRP directly with minoxidil, so that half of the question remains unanswered by direct evidence.
stamp: SPLIT — hair density favours PRP versus placebo (+27.55 hairs/cm² pooled; two positive small trials), but hair diameter does not consistently beat placebo, heterogeneity is about 96% and publication bias is documented in the largest synthesis

title: Cysteamine 5% and thiamidol for melasma: both lighten pigmentation about as much as hydroquinone 4% in small randomised trials, with more early irritation from cysteamine
question: In adults with moderate-to-severe melasma, do cysteamine 5% cream or thiamidol-containing regimens improve pigmentation (MASI) versus hydroquinone or vehicle, and how do irritation and relapse compare?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit, as hydroquinone alternatives) — both limbs verify with at least three reports each in total across the shelf: cysteamine 5% cream lightened melasma in two randomised comparisons with hydroquinone 4% (mMASI reductions 21-38% on cysteamine versus 32-53% on hydroquinone — hydroquinone numerically ahead on the index, differences significant in the larger trial), and thiamidol 0.2% matched hydroquinone in one randomised trial (mMASI -43% versus -33%, no significant difference) and beat vehicle over 24 weeks in another, with pigmentation regressing toward baseline after stopping. Tested products as published, per the clarification exception: cysteamine 5% cream (the records do not name a brand or maker); thiamidol (isobutylamido thiazolyl resorcinol) 0.2% in the hydroquinone comparison, and a thiamidol Dual Serum/Day Care SPF30/Night Care regimen in the vehicle trial (maker not named in either record). This shelf is a PARTIAL completion: shelf #4222 asks the triple-combination cream versus hydroquinone question and is not re-carded here; the oral tranexamic acid slice is a separate shelf again. Irritation: cysteamine caused more early local effects (erythema, burning) than hydroquinone; thiamidol's effects were mild, with allergic contact dermatitis in 2 of about 25 hydroquinone users in the comparison trial record as published.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit as alternatives to hydroquinone) — cysteamine 5% (two trials, 20 and 40 women) and thiamidol (two trials, 50 women and 48 women) each lightened melasma comparably to hydroquinone 4% or better than vehicle, in small short trials with relapse after stopping

title: Daylight versus conventional photodynamic therapy for actinic keratoses: clearance is similar for thin lesions and lower when thick lesions are included — with far less pain
question: In adults with facial actinic keratoses, is daylight photodynamic therapy as effective as conventional (lamp) photodynamic therapy for lesion clearance, with less pain?
balance: SPLIT — the split is by lesion grade. Pooled across six randomised trials (369 patients, 5,556 lesions, methyl aminolevulinate with red light as the conventional arm), complete response did not differ significantly overall (relative risk 0.93, p=0.07); daylight therapy was non-inferior where trials included only grade I-II lesions (relative risk 0.97) but less effective where grade III (thick) lesions were included (relative risk 0.87, p<0.001). The pain limb is not split: daylight therapy's maximal pain score was 4.51 points lower (pooled mean difference) and adverse events fewer (relative risk 0.70), and the founding split-face trial found lesion reductions of 79% (daylight) versus 71% (lamp). Tested photosensitiser as published: methyl aminolevulinate (MAL) cream in the pooled and founding trials; the Chinese trial used photodynamic therapy as practised locally (record names aminolevulinic-acid class agents). Daylight dose depends on latitude and season — the founding trials are Danish, the confirmatory trial is from Shanghai, China.
stamp: SPLIT — daylight PDT matches conventional PDT for grade I-II actinic keratoses (complete-response relative risk 0.97) but is less effective when grade III lesions are included (relative risk 0.87); pain is consistently and substantially lower with daylight (pooled difference -4.51 points)

title: Autologous skin cell suspension (RECELL) for burns: healing matches conventional grafting with about a third less donor skin in the pivotal trial, and re-epithelialisation is about 1.7 days faster in pooled trials
question: In patients with deep partial- or full-thickness burns, does autologous skin cell suspension sprayed over widely meshed autograft (the RECELL programme) reduce donor-skin requirements and match healing/graft take versus conventional autografting?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the tested system is named exactly as published, per the clarification exception: the RECELL System / RECELL Autologous Cell Harvesting Device (AVITA Medical, as published). In the pivotal within-subject randomised trial (30 patients, mixed-depth burns), cell suspension over widely meshed graft healed 92% versus 85% of control areas at 8 weeks (non-inferiority met) while using 32% less donor skin (relative measure, P<.001). In the deep partial-thickness trial, healing at 4 weeks was 98% versus 100% for conventional grafting, while donor areas were about 40 times smaller and donor sites healed faster with less pain — that record does not state its patient number, so it is printed as N not documented. The 2025 meta-analysis of 9 randomised trials (358 patients) found re-epithelialisation 1.71 days faster, but (the treatment made no difference) to complete healing by week 4, pain, scar scores, infection or further-intervention rates. Donor-site and healing endpoints are reported separately throughout, not composited.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — healing is non-inferior to conventional grafting in the pivotal 30-patient trial with 32% less donor skin used, and pooled trials show 1.71 days faster re-epithelialisation but no difference in complete healing, pain or scarring

title: Microwave thermolysis for armpit sweating: beats sham at 30 days, and about 7 in 10 treated patients were still responders at 12 months
question: In adults with primary axillary hyperhidrosis, does microwave thermolysis of the sweat glands reduce sweat production and severity durably (12 months or more) versus sham treatment?
balance: One randomised, sham-controlled, blinded trial anchors this slice. In Glaser 2012, 89% (72/81) of microwave-treated adults were responders (Hyperhidrosis Disease Severity Scale score 1 or 2) at 30 days versus 54% (21/39) on sham, and the active group's responder rate was 69% when follow-up ended at 12 months. Later reports are smaller and uncontrolled or within-patient: an energy-level comparison in 20 adults found high energy slightly better than medium at 3 months; a telephone survey (18 of 24 patients, mean follow-up 38 months) found a mean HDSS fall of 1.6 points and self-reported sweat reduction of 61-70%; and a 103-patient clinic cohort with 45 survey responders at 3 years found median HDSS improved from 3 to 2. Adverse events were generally mild and transient (swelling, bruising, pain, numbness, nodules), all resolved in the survey cohort within 12 weeks. The tested device is the miraDry microwave system (Miramar Labs) programme device; the sham trial's record describes it as a proprietary microwave energy device. This shelf is the microwave slice of the hyperhidrosis family: the home shelf #2476 covers botulinum toxin injections and the glycopyrronium cloth, and a separate slice covers sofpironium gel - neither is duplicated here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a single sham-controlled trial with a large early margin, with durability beyond the trial resting on small cohorts and surveys.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Fractional laser for hypertrophic burn scars: split - one within-scar trial clearly positive, one mixed, one donor-site trial found no difference
question: In patients with hypertrophic burn scars, does fractional laser treatment (ablative carbon dioxide or non-ablative, as tested) improve scar pliability, thickness and symptoms versus untreated or conventionally treated control scars?
balance: The randomised base is small and it points in different directions - a genuine split. A paediatric split-scar trial (23 enrolled, 20 completed) found total Patient and Observer Scar Assessment Scale (POSAS) scores of 44.95 on low-energy fractional carbon dioxide laser sites versus 64.85 on untreated control sites at 6 months. The ELIPSE trial (15 adults, each patient their own control, three ablative fractional CO2 treatments) found no significant difference in Vancouver Scar Scale (VSS), erythema or pigmentation, although patient POSAS thickness and texture improved and blinded photo raters scored treated scars better. A donor-site scar trial (20 patients) found laser-treated and standard-care-only sites were not different on any measure over time (the treatment made no difference). A three-arm trial of pulsed dye laser, ablative fractional CO2, or both found improvement in all arms with the largest (non-significant) gains for combination treatment, mainly in immature scars; its record does not state the patient number. Laser-assisted drug delivery is a separate question and is not carded here. PROPOSED SPLIT: benefit is shown against untreated within-scar controls in one small trial, mixed in a second, and absent in a third - scar type (early burn scar versus donor-site scar) and control choice appear to decide the result.
stamp: SPLIT

title: Picosecond versus nanosecond lasers for tattoo removal: split - faster clearance in three head-to-head studies, no clearance advantage in two
question: In adults seeking tattoo removal, do picosecond-domain lasers clear pigment faster (fewer sessions to 75% or greater clearance) than nanosecond Q-switched lasers, by ink colour, and at what cost in blistering and dyspigmentation?
balance: Five head-to-head comparisons, and they split. The 1998 intratattoo trial (16 patients, black tattoos, all parameters held constant except pulse duration) found picosecond pulses lightened significantly more than nanosecond pulses in 12 of 16 tattoos. The largest randomised split-tattoo study (49 patients) reached 75% or greater clearance in 33% of picosecond halves versus 14% of nanosecond halves (P = 0.008), driven by black/blue tattoos (34% versus 9%); only 1 of 5 polychromic tattoos cleared that well on either laser. The newest randomised split-tattoo trial (30 subjects, 755-nm alexandrite both arms) found higher clearance scores and satisfactory clearance in 73.3% versus 23.3%. Against that, a randomised split-study of 1064-nm Nd:YAG (21 patients, 30 black tattoos, two sessions) found no difference in clearance at all (P = 1.00), though picosecond hurt less (pain 3.8 versus 7.9 of 10), and a retrospective eyeliner-tattoo comparison (40 versus 32 patients) found no difference after one session. Harms: blistering and crusting were less frequent with picosecond in the alexandrite trial, but hyperpigmentation was more frequent (21.33% versus 12%). Several programmes are industry-supported and device-specific; tested devices are named per card as published, and where the record names no commercial device that is stated. PROPOSED SPLIT: picosecond clears black/blue ink faster in most comparisons, but the advantage disappears in the 1064-nm two-session trial and in eyeliner tattoos, and it does not extend to polychromic ink.
stamp: SPLIT

title: Quantitative sensory testing profiles (physiology): thresholds are site- and age-dependent, pain thresholds are lower in women, and detection thresholds mostly do not differ by sex
question: In healthy humans, what are normal quantitative sensory testing profiles - cold and warm detection and pain thresholds, mechanical detection and pain thresholds, vibration and pressure-pain thresholds - by body site, sex and decade of age, on the standardised DFNS protocol?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY - ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing (Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology; Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology): somatosensory receptors transduce thermal and mechanical stimuli whose detection and pain thresholds can be profiled psychophysically. The German Research Network on Neuropathic Pain (DFNS) standardised a 30-minute battery giving a complete profile for one region, and its normative programme is the anchor: 180 healthy subjects assessed bilaterally over face, hand and foot (Rolke 2006), extended to the trunk in 162 healthy subjects (Pfau 2014). The consistent findings across the carded cohorts: QST parameters are region-specific and age-dependent; pain thresholds are significantly lower in women than men while detection thresholds are generally independent of gender; the trunk is less sensitive than the hand on the upper back and more sensitive than the foot on the lower back; and side-to-side (relative) comparisons are 1.1 to 2.5 times more sensitive than absolute reference values. Independent cohorts agree in direction: 124 pain-free African American adults showed lower-body sites less sensitive than upper-body sites across thermal modalities, and 84 Italian adults tested with the Q-sense device showed all thermal measures affected by age, sex and site, with worse discrimination and higher heat-pain thresholds on the foot after age 40. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY - ESTABLISHED.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED

title: Sebum excretion rates (physiology): low in childhood, rising at puberty, steady in men to age 80, and falling gradually in women after the menopause
question: In healthy humans, how fast is sebum excreted - sebum excretion rates and casual levels by site, sex and age (the post-pubertal peak and the post-menopausal fall), measured by absorbent-tape and solvent-extraction methods?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY - ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing here is thin (Boron & Boulpaep; Ganong cover skin appendages briefly), and this shelf rests chiefly on the primary measurement literature, as stated plainly. Two quantities are measured: the casual level (surface lipid on unprepared skin) and the sebum excretion rate (SER, surface lipid flow from a previously cleaned area, by absorbent-paper gravimetry in the Strauss-Pochi tradition and by photometric tape/sebumeter methods since). The age pattern is concordant: Pochi, Strauss and Downing (1979) found secretion low in children, rising from mid-to-late childhood under androgen influence into the late teens, then essentially unchanged in men until age 80, while in women secretion falls gradually after the menopause with no further change after the seventh decade - attributed to falling endogenous androgen production, with glands paradoxically enlarging as cellular turnover slows. Modern measurement cohorts add scale and variability: casual level and SER run 1.6-2.1 times higher in self-described oily than dry skin (62 Thai women), forehead SER measured twice 7 days apart in 40 healthy adults varied with sleep timing, free testosterone and 5-alpha-reductase type 1 expression in women, and parallel trials in 100 Japanese and 30 Caucasian volunteers formalised the SER-versus-casual-level distinction across populations. This is gland output, a different quantity from transepidermal water loss (barrier leak), which is shelved separately. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY - ESTABLISHED.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED

title: Epidermal turnover time (physiology): about 39-48 days for the whole epidermis by autoradiographic kinetics, about 19 days across the stratum corneum by dansyl chloride
question: In healthy humans, how long does the epidermis take to renew - stratum-corneum transit time and total epidermal turnover time measured by dansyl-chloride fluorescence decay, autoradiography and modern fluorescence methods, and how do age and body site change them?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY - ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing (Boron & Boulpaep, epithelial renewal): the epidermis renews continuously, with keratinocytes born in the basal layer transiting the viable layers and the stratum corneum before shedding. The carded human measurements agree on a weeks-scale total but differ by method, and that method-dependence is core content. Weinstein's tritiated-thymidine autoradiography programme (1984) built the compartment model - proliferative, viable differentiated and stratum corneum compartments turning over at very similar rates (1246, 1417 and 1490 cells/day/mm2) - and put the mean total epidermal turnover time at 39 days, with a germinative cell cycle of 311 hours. Iizuka's 1994 re-computation from Weinstein's own compartment data put the total at 47-48 days instead of 39, and Bergstresser and Taylor's desquamation-based model (1977) independently derived 45 days for volar forearm. For the stratum corneum alone, dansyl-chloride staining in 18 healthy women gave a turnover time of 19.3 days on untreated skin, roughly halving to 10.9 days under subclinical irritant exposure - a stimulus limb, labelled as such. The classic dansyl-chloride transit report by Baker and Kligman (1967) was checked this session: its PubMed record carries an empty abstract, so it is refused as an evidence card and named here only as the historical anchor of the method. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY - ESTABLISHED (total turnover in the 39-48 day range, method-dependent; stratum-corneum transit about 19 days at rest).
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED

title: Nail growth rates (physiology): fingernails about 0.10 mm a day, slowing by about half across the lifespan; the classic record is one man's 35-year thumbnail
question: In healthy humans, how fast do nails grow - fingernail versus toenail linear growth rates, the digit gradient, and the slowing with age - measured by marked-nail and photographic methods?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY - ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing for skin appendages is thin (Ganong; Boron & Boulpaep), and this shelf rests on the primary measurement literature, stated plainly. The classic anchor is Bean's single-subject longitudinal record (N = 1, labelled on its face): his left thumbnail grew 0.123 mm/day at age 32 and 0.095 mm/day at age 67, over 35 years of self-measurement. Orentreich's ageing programme generalised the pattern - linear nail growth falls by about 50% over the lifespan, with circadian and roughly 7-year rhythms superimposed. The modern normative cohort (50 young adults, all 500 fingernails measured) puts average fingernail growth at 0.103 mm/day, with a digit gradient (left index fastest at 0.13 mm/day in that cohort, little fingers slowest) and no sex or hand-dominance correlation; a thumb-measurement study found 0.09 mm/day in controls and 0.10 mm/day in pregnancy (no significant difference). On toenails: the carded records quantify fingernails and the thumbnail; the slower toenail rate given in textbooks (Ganong; Boron & Boulpaep) is presented here as the textbook's account, because no carded record in this session confirms a toenail value. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY - ESTABLISHED.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED

title: Saccadic eye movements (physiology): the main sequence - peak velocity rises with amplitude (about 213 degrees/s at 5 degrees to 455 degrees/s at 30 degrees horizontally) at every age
question: In healthy humans, how fast do saccadic eye movements run - the main-sequence relationship between saccade amplitude, peak velocity and duration, latency distributions, and how fatigue and age change them, measured by infrared oculography?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY - ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing (Ganong; Boron & Boulpaep, oculomotor control): saccades are the rapid conjugate eye movements that refixate the visual target, and their amplitude, peak velocity and duration are so tightly coupled - the 'main sequence' - that a saccade's size predicts its speed. The carded normative cohorts quantify it with infrared/video oculography. Hopf 2018 (100 healthy participants aged 6-76) gives the cleanest main sequence: mean horizontal peak velocity 213 degrees/s for 5-degree, 352 for 15-degree and 455 for 30-degree target steps (vertical values lower: 208, 303 and 391 degrees/s), with the velocity-amplitude association present at every age and no relevant age effect on peak velocity, gain or latency in adults - latency shortens through childhood and adolescence and trends slightly up in the elderly. Two larger cohorts put more weight on ageing: Seferlis 2015 (250 subjects in five age bands of 50) found significant age differences in saccade latency, velocity and accuracy, with elderly subjects deteriorating on all parameters, and Bonnet 2013 (145 subjects aged 19-82) found latency of pro- and antisaccades increased with age and upward prosaccade velocity fell. The classic Bahill main-sequence characterisations were checked this session: their fetched records carry empty abstracts or describe computer simulation rather than human measurement, so they are refused as evidence cards and named here only as the historical anchor of the term. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY - ESTABLISHED (main sequence concordant in all cohorts; the size of the ageing effect on velocity is the one point of disagreement, stated on the face).
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED

title: Taste thresholds (physiology): salt and bitter detection thresholds rise modestly with age, sweet and sour do not - and the method decides the answer
question: In healthy humans, what are taste thresholds - detection and recognition thresholds for sweet, salt, sour, bitter and umami by whole-mouth and regional (filter-paper and electrogustometry) methods, and how much do they rise with age and smoking?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY - ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing (Ganong; Boron & Boulpaep, chemical senses): taste buds transduce sweet, salt, sour, bitter and umami, and thresholds are measured either chemically (whole-mouth solutions, filter-paper discs, taste strips) or electrically (electrogustometry). The methods are not interchangeable, so this shelf cards per method. The classic whole-mouth ageing cohort (Weiffenbach 1982, 81 adults aged 23-88) found quality-specific change: sodium chloride detection thresholds rose a small but significant amount with age, quinine (bitter) thresholds rose more weakly, and sucrose and citric acid thresholds were not significantly related to age. Electrogustometry in a normal population (Grant 1987) likewise found detection thresholds significantly elevated with age - and with smoking - with no sex difference. Regional chemical testing in 203 healthy participants (Cavazzana 2019) found front-of-tongue thresholds lower than back-of-tongue for quinine, PTC and PROP taste strips, and confirmed that genetic non-tasting is common for PTC/PROP but rare for quinine. The PROP programme (Lucchina 1998) formalised the inherited bitter phenotype - nontasters, medium tasters and supertasters - which dominates bitter thresholds more than age does. No carded record quantifies umami thresholds, and none is claimed. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY - ESTABLISHED.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED

title: Smell thresholds across the lifespan (physiology): identification peaks in the third to fifth decades, falls markedly after the seventh, and women outperform men at every age
question: In healthy humans, how do smell detection thresholds and odour identification scores change across the lifespan - at what age does decline accelerate, how large is the sex difference, and what fraction of older adults are functionally anosmic on standardised testing (UPSIT and Sniffin' Sticks)?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY - ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing (Ganong; Boron & Boulpaep, olfaction): olfactory receptor neurons project to the olfactory bulb, and function is tested by detection thresholds (weakest perceived odour) and by suprathreshold identification and discrimination - related but distinct measures, carded as such. The lifespan curve is concordant across the two great normative programmes. Doty's University of Pennsylvania Smell Identification Test (UPSIT) programme (1984; 1,955 persons aged 5-99) found women outperforming men at all ages, nonsmokers outperforming smokers, peak performance in the third through fifth decades, and decline markedly after the seventh: more than half of 65-80-year-olds and more than three-quarters of those over 80 evidenced major olfactory impairment. The Sniffin' Sticks programme agrees and adds thresholds: in 3,282 subjects (Hummel 2007) the composite TDI score's 10th percentile fell from 30.3 at ages 16-35 to 19.6 over age 55, with odor thresholds declining most dramatically of the three subtests; the extended norms (9,139 subjects, Oleszkiewicz 2019) found the steepest score fall between ages 60 and 71 and hyposmia defined at TDI under 30.75. The population check (Beaver Dam Offspring Study, 2,838 adults) found measured olfactory impairment in 3.8% overall, rising from 0.6% under 35 to 13.9% at 65 or older, more common in men. Identification tests are culture- and language-loaded, and each programme's norms describe its own population - stated on the face, per this row's flag. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY - ESTABLISHED.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED

title: Pure-tone hearing thresholds with age: the ISO 7029 curves climb fastest at high frequencies and faster in men — and longitudinal decline starts earlier than cross-sectional curves suggest
question: In healthy humans, what do pure-tone hearing thresholds do with age — the ISO 7029 median threshold-versus-age curves by frequency and sex, and what did the longitudinal (Baltimore) measurements show about within-person decline rates versus cross-sectional estimates?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — for the age course of pure-tone thresholds as standardised in ISO 7029 and measured in the carded human cohorts, framed by Ganong / Boron & Boulpaep (audition). Three concordant limbs: (1) the cross-sectional shape — thresholds rise with age, steepest at high frequencies, men poorer than women (Framingham, N = 1,662; the Robinson unscreened-population companion analysis, which found the 'pathological overlay' of an unscreened population equivalent to accelerated ageing); (2) the longitudinal correction — in the Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging (681 men, 416 women, screened), within-person decline was detectable in men by age 30 and ran more than twice as fast in men as in women, while learning effects bias cross-sectional and short-term estimates, so cross-sectional curves and true within-person decline are different quantities; (3) the standard's own limits — a Norwegian validation (232 sampled, 60 otologically normal) found the ISO female low-frequency coefficient may be set too low and the otologically-normal screen inconsistent after age 60. Exact decibel cells of the ISO 7029 tables are the standard's account, not re-derived from the fetched records, and the shelf says so on its Synthesis card. This shelf is about normative thresholds; the hearing treatment and device shelves ask different questions.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED

title: The scalp hair cycle: years-long anagen that ageing and balding shorten, a distinct shedding (exogen) phase — measured by following the same hairs for over a decade
question: In healthy humans, what is the hair cycle at the scalp — anagen duration and fraction, daily shedding counts, and linear hair growth rate — measured by phototrichogram and unit-area trichogram, and how do site, sex and age change them?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING — the phase sequence (anagen → catagen → telogen → exogen) is textbook-settled (Boron & Boulpaep framing on skin appendages is thin here, and this shelf rests chiefly on the primary measurement literature, as its slate row directs), but the quantitative human base is small and the classic anchor unverifiable: Kligman's 1959 characterisation was refused as a card because its record fetched this session has no abstract (refusal reported on the Synthesis card). What the carded human studies do show, concordantly: phototrichogram follow-up of the same scalps for 8–15 years (two series of 10 men, ~10,000 cycles counted) finds ageing and balding shorten anagen in a growing share of follicles, thin the shaft and lengthen the empty latency before regrowth; contrast-enhanced phototrichogram is validated against biopsy for staging every phase; linear growth rate tracks shaft thickness and is slower in pattern loss than in equally thick control hair (13 healthy controls); and shedding is a distinct exogen phase, normally under 7 hairs/cm² at sampling. The familiar absolute figures (anagen ~2–6 years, ~85–90% in anagen, growth ~0.3–0.4 mm/day, shedding ~50–100/day) are carried explicitly as the textbook's account, not as values a carded record measured. The alopecia treatment shelves (finasteride/minoxidil, PRP) ask different questions.

title: The tear film in health: basal turnover ~15%/min by fluorophotometry, break-up at ~11–12 seconds, osmolarity just under 300 mOsm/L
question: In healthy humans, what does the tear film do — tear turnover rate by fluorophotometry, break-up time distributions, tear osmolarity ranges, and basal versus reflex secretion rates?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — for the healthy tear film's measured behaviour, framed by Ganong / Boron & Boulpaep (lacrimal apparatus — thin framing; this shelf rests chiefly on the primary measurement literature, as its slate row directs). Turnover is the concordant limb: basal tear turnover by fluorophotometry was 15.6 ± 5.4%/min in 41 healthy controls (Kuppens & van Best) and 13.1–17.5%/min across three European centres under one standardised protocol — roughly a sixth of the film per minute. Break-up time in health centres at ~11 s by automated non-invasive measurement (N = 237) and ~12 s by fluorescein (N = 30), carded per method, never pooled. title: Pharyngeal critical closing pressure (Pcrit) in sleep: −13 cmH₂O in normal sleepers, climbing through zero into apnea — with loop gain and arousal threshold as the other dials
question: In healthy humans, how collapsible is the upper airway during sleep — what is the pharyngeal critical closing pressure (Pcrit) in normal sleepers versus snorers and patients with sleep apnoea, and how large are ventilatory loop gain and arousal threshold in health?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — for Pcrit as the measured index of upper-airway collapsibility, framed by Boron & Boulpaep / Ganong and Kryger (sleep physiology). The gradient is concordant across independent preparations: in natural NREM sleep, Pcrit was −13.3 ± 3.2 cmH₂O in 7 normal subjects (Schwartz), rising to −6.5 ± 2.7 in snorers, −1.6 ± 1.4 in obstructive hypopnea and +2.5 ± 1.5 in obstructive apnea (Gleadhill) — the airway becomes self-closing as Pcrit crosses zero. In the anaesthetised, paralysed passive pharynx (Isono), velopharyngeal closing pressure showed the same ordering at higher absolute values (−3.77 ± 3.44 normal vs +0.90 and +2.78 in sleep-disordered breathing), because that preparation removes neuromuscular compensation — values are carded per protocol and never merged. The phenotyping limb (Eckert/Wellman, 75 studied) qualifies the anatomy story: OSA Pcrit averaged +0.3 vs −6.2 cmH₂O in controls, but 36% of patients had high loop gain, 37% a low arousal threshold, and 19% obstructed with a near-normal Pcrit. The OSA treatment shelves ask different questions.

title: Noradrenaline spillover in humans: ~0.33 µg/m²/min reaches plasma at rest — a clearance-filtered, organ-specific index of sympathetic firing, not the plasma level itself
question: In healthy humans, how much noradrenaline spills over into plasma — total-body and regional (cardiac, renal) noradrenaline spillover rates by isotope-dilution, how do they rise with exercise, standing and age, and how little of synaptic release does plasma clearance-based spillover capture?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — for isotope-dilution noradrenaline kinetics in humans, framed by Guyton & Hall / Ganong (sympathetic transmitter kinetics). The method-defining record (Esler, 34 normal subjects) gives resting total spillover of 0.33 µg/m²/min (range 0.17–0.61) with clearance 1.32 ± 0.28 L/m²/min, and shows plasma concentration alone misleads wherever clearance changes. The carded limbs are concordant: ageing raises plasma noradrenaline chiefly by reducing clearance (total spillover unchanged; hepatomesenteric spillover 50% higher in old men at rest — a relative difference); exercise raises limb spillover with active muscle mass, steeply above ~70% VO₂max, without matching vasoconstriction (N = 6); cardiac spillover is higher in older than younger healthy subjects (20.1 vs 14.3 ng/min) and roughly tripled in cardiac failure (59 vs 18 ng/min); and regional regulation is organ-specific (renal spillover +49%/+26% relative after enalaprilat in healthy subjects, cardiac and total unchanged). How little of synaptic release spillover captures is presented as the textbook's account on the Synthesis card — no carded record measures total synaptic release. Cross-point: pack #6632 (exercise pressor reflex) measures nerve traffic, not transmitter kinetics.

title: Albumin transcapillary escape rate: ~5% of the intravascular mass leaves per hour in health — roughly doubled by arterial or portal pressure, acute inflammation and major surgery
question: In humans, how fast does albumin escape the circulation — what is the transcapillary escape rate of labelled albumin in health (per cent of intravascular mass per hour), and how does it rise in inflammation, burns and sepsis?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — for the transcapillary escape rate (TER) of labelled albumin in humans, framed by Guyton & Hall (capillary exchange; albumin distribution). PARTIAL slice, built after reading its home pack #6499 in full: that pack asks only how the albumin synthesis rate is regulated — 'escape' and 'transcapillary' appear nowhere in it — so distribution kinetics are the genuinely unasked half, cross-pointed in prose here and not duplicated. The healthy reference is concordant across laboratories: ~5.2–5.4%/h (Parving normals, N = 28 in the cirrhosis record) and 4.3 ± 2.6%/h (Ballmer normals). Rises, each beside its own record's normals: severe hypertension 7.8 ± 0.9%/h (N = 7), cirrhosis with portal hypertension 10.2%/h (N = 9, elevated in every patient), acute infectious inflammation 8.6 ± 3.4%/h (N = 8), and major surgery (escape elevated intra-operatively; 24 ± 17 g shifted by mass balance). Two qualifications are carried on the face: chronic malignancy barely raised TER (6.6%/h), and one modern acute-inflammation cohort had a normal TER despite marked hypoalbuminemia while synthesis rose ~50% (relative) — a low plasma albumin proves neither leak nor failed synthesis. The classic burns/sepsis permeability report already has a home elsewhere in the library and is cross-pointed in prose only, per the one-home rule; ≥3 free primary reports verified this session, so the slice is built as a full pack, not synthesis-only.

title: The low-dose endotoxin challenge model in humans: a brief TNF pulse at 90–180 minutes drives fever, cytokine release, leukocyte trafficking and cortisol — dose-, preparation- and sex-dependent
question: In healthy humans, what happens in the standardised low-dose endotoxin challenge model — the dose–response and time course of fever, cytokine release (TNF, IL-6), leukocyte trafficking, heart-rate/blood-pressure change and cortisol activation after intravenous reference endotoxin?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — for the human experimental endotoxemia model as a standardised, reproducible inflammatory stimulus (physiology under a controlled stimulus, not resting physiology), framed by Guyton & Hall / Ganong (fever and innate immunity). The classic characterisation (Michie, 4 ng/kg E. coli endotoxin, 13 healthy men) fixes the clock: a brief TNF pulse peaking at 90–180 minutes (240 ± 70 vs 35 ± 5 pg/mL after saline), IL-1β unchanged, symptoms, white-cell change and ACTH tracking the TNF peak, and ibuprofen attenuating the responses without blocking TNF; infusing TNF to similar peaks reproduced the package. Later programmes fill in the dials: at 2 ng/kg the response is sex-modulated (TNF-α 965 ± 193 in women vs 411 ± 35 pg/mL in men; 15 + 15); in a placebo-controlled 4 ng/kg trial the LPS-alone limb moved vital signs, white cells, cytokines, cortisol and echocardiographic haemodynamics together; and dose–response has a floor (systemic activation at 0.4 ng/kg, a downstream pain-sensitivity effect only at 0.8 ng/kg, at 3 hours). Every value is carded with its dose and preparation — they are never pooled. The repeat-challenge tolerance limb is explicitly not carded: no systemic human tolerance primary met the carding standard this session (stated on the Synthesis card).

title: Excess post-exercise oxygen consumption (EPOC): ~15% of the exercise oxygen cost after prolonged aerobic work, exponential in intensity, and still detectable 38 hours after heavy resistance exercise
question: In healthy humans, how large and how long is excess post-exercise oxygen consumption after aerobic and resistance exercise — what fraction is the fast (phosphagen/lactate) versus slow component, and how do intensity and duration scale the total?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — for EPOC's magnitude and time course in humans, framed by Guyton & Hall / Boron & Boulpaep (exercise metabolism and recovery). The two anchor programmes named for this row that are reviews (Gaesser & Brooks; Børsheim & Bahr) are not carded as evidence — the carded primaries carry the numbers: duration scales EPOC linearly at 70% VO₂max (12-hour EPOC 14.4% / 6.8% / 5.1% of exercise cost after 80 / 40 / 20 minutes; ~15.2% on average; N = 6); intensity scales it exponentially (1.3 L at 29%, 5.7 L at 50%, 30.1 L at 75% VO₂max for 80 minutes, lasting 0.3, 3.3 and 10.5 hours; the prolonged component requires sustained work above ~40–50% VO₂max); heavy resistance exercise leaves oxygen consumption elevated at 38 hours (N = 7); and circuit-training EPOC in the first hour is rest-interval-sensitive (10.3 vs 7.4 L) while total exercise-plus-recovery cost runs the other way. The fast-versus-slow component split is carried as the textbook's account on the Synthesis card — the primaries measure totals and time courses, not component fractions. Cross-points (prose only): the VO₂ on-kinetics and heart-rate-recovery shelves — different quantities, not duplicated.

title: Measured GFR in humans: iohexol and ⁵¹Cr-EDTA plasma clearances agree with inulin within a few mL/min — but iohexol and iothalamate differ from each other by ~15%, and PAH plasma flow is an approximation
question: In healthy humans, how well do measured-GFR methods agree — inulin, iohexol, iothalamate and 51Cr-EDTA clearances against each other — and what are normal effective renal plasma flow (PAH clearance) and filtration fraction?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — for measured-GFR method agreement and PAH plasma flow, framed by Guyton & Hall / Boron & Boulpaep. Agreement with the inulin reference is close and quantified: iohexol plasma clearance correlates highly across GFR 6–169 with four calculation formulas equivalent (best median bias −0.5 mL/min/1.73 m² at high GFR, N = 144), and two-sample ⁵¹Cr-EDTA plasma clearance biases ~2.8 mL/min against inulin (N = 44 + 22). The discordance limb is equally firm: iohexol urinary clearance runs at 0.85 (relative) of iothalamate across the range (N = 150) — surrogates that each agree with inulin are not interchangeable with each other. Flow: in healthy men, PAH clearance fell 52 mL/min/decade after age 50 against iohexol's 12, so filtration fraction rises with age, and a total-versus-renal PAH discrepancy shows renal PAH metabolism — extraction is incomplete even in health (the row's caveat, on the face). REFUSAL: the 1969 Bröchner-Mortensen-era inulin-versus-EDTA anchor was refused as a card — its fetched record has no abstract (reported on the Synthesis card). Textbook normal values are carried as the textbook's account. The companion pack #6959 covers creatinine secretion — the endogenous-marker error, a different quantity.

title: Tubular creatinine secretion: creatinine clearance overestimates GFR by a share that grows as GFR falls — and cimetidine blockade brings the ratio to 1.01–1.02 against inulin
question: In healthy humans, how much creatinine is secreted — by how much does creatinine clearance overestimate true GFR, and what do cimetidine-blocked creatinine-clearance studies show about the secreted fraction across GFR levels?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — for tubular creatinine secretion as measured against true filtration markers, framed by Boron & Boulpaep / Guyton & Hall (tubular secretion). The size of the error: creatinine's fractional clearance against inulin averaged 1.64 ± 0.05 in 171 glomerulopathic patients (Shemesh) — an average ~64% relative overestimation — with individual baseline creatinine/inulin ratios of 1.14–2.27 in the van Acker cohort, and the secreted fraction varying inversely with GFR, so the overestimation grows as filtration falls and blunts creatinine-based monitoring. The blockade proof is concordant across three studies: after adequate oral cimetidine (which does not change true GFR), creatinine clearance matched ⁵¹Cr-EDTA (ratio 1.02 ± 0.13) and inulin (1.01 ± 0.13) across renal-function ranges (Hilbrands, 10 healthy men + 29 patients), reached unity in lupus nephritis under double-blind conditions (DTPA ratio 1.33 on placebo → 1.07 on cimetidine, N = 13), and failed at 1.33 in half of one cohort until the cimetidine dose was raised — dose adequacy is part of the method. The healthy-GFR overestimation figure (~10–20% relative) is carried as the textbook's account on the Synthesis card. Cross-point (prose only): pack #6958, exogenous-marker agreement — a different quantity, not duplicated.

title: Quantitative liver-clearance tests: ICG disappearance runs ~23%/min in health and galactose elimination capacity falls with age and liver failure
question: In healthy humans, what do the quantitative liver-clearance tests measure — indocyanine green disappearance rate and galactose elimination capacity in health, how do they fall with age and liver blood flow, and how were their normal ranges established?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — for what these two tests measure and their healthy ranges, framed by Guyton & Hall / Boron & Boulpaep on hepatic clearance: indocyanine green (ICG) is removed almost exclusively by the liver, so its plasma disappearance is a flow-and-uptake-limited clearance signal, while galactose elimination capacity (GEC) at saturating dose is a capacity-limited measure of functional hepatocyte mass. The carded human data: in 41 adults without liver disease, noninvasive ICG plasma disappearance rate averaged 23.1 ± 7.9%/min but ranged 9.7–43.2%/min — wide enough that the commonly cited 18%/min 'liver failure' cutoff sits inside the healthy range (Reekers 2010). Ageing shrinks the signal: in 65 healthy subjects aged 24–91, liver volume, ICG-derived apparent liver blood flow and flow per unit liver volume all fell significantly with age (Wynne 1989). For galactose, GEC per kg is highest in young children and falls to the adult level by about age 16, and is lower in chronic liver disease at every age (Lange 2011, 10 healthy + 30 diseased children); in 781 newly diagnosed cirrhosis patients the normal-range threshold was ≥1.75 mmol/min, and below it each 0.5 mmol/min higher GEC carried a relative hazard of death of 0.64 after adjustment (Jepsen 2009). REFUSAL: the classic Caesar-era ICG anchor (Caesar et al., Clin Sci 1961) was refused — its PubMed record carries no abstract, so nothing from it is carded or quoted; the same applies to Tygstrup's original galactose-elimination reports, which no fetched record verifies. This shelf is about clearance-test physiology, not about the urea-synthesis (functional hepatic nitrogen clearance) question shelved elsewhere in the library.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED

title: Small-intestinal permeability in health: lactulose leaks through at ~0.3% of dose against ~30% for mannitol — and NSAIDs open the barrier within months
question: In healthy humans, how permeable is the small intestine on sugar-probe testing — urinary lactulose/mannitol (and lactulose/rhamnose) recovery ratios in health, how do NSAIDs and coeliac disease move them, and how reproducible are the ratios within a person?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — for the sugar-probe measurement and its healthy behaviour, framed by Boron & Boulpaep on the intestinal barrier and paracellular transport. The principle, from the carded human studies: a disaccharide (lactulose) crosses mainly paracellularly and barely at all in health, while a monosaccharide (mannitol or rhamnose) crosses freely, so the urinary recovery ratio corrects for transit, dilution and renal handling. In the modern standardised measurement in 60 healthy adults, median 24-hour urinary recovery was ~30% of dose for 13C-mannitol and ~15% for rhamnose against only 0.32% for lactulose (Khoshbin 2021) — a roughly hundredfold separation — but between-person variation is large (median interindividual coefficient of variation 76.5%). Timing is not a detail: in 12 healthy volunteers the lactulose/mannitol ratio in 0–2 h urine was 0.08 against 0.32 in 8–24 h urine, because liquid reaches the colon within 2 hours in most people, so early urine mixes small-bowel and colonic signals (Camilleri 2010). The barrier is drug-sensitive: permeability was normal in untreated rheumatoid arthritis but almost invariably abnormal on NSAIDs (Bjarnason 1984), and in long-term NSAID users small-intestinal inflammation was present in 54–72% across conventional NSAIDs, developing in 9 of 13 followed patients by 6 months (Sigthorsson 1998). In coeliac disease the lactulose/rhamnose ratio and 51Cr-EDTA both rise while polyethylene glycol permeation falls — markers travel by different routes and are not interchangeable (Bjarnason 1994). This is the paracellular-leak question; the library's transcellular sugar-absorption shelf asks a different quantity and is cross-pointed, not duplicated.

title: Thyroid-hormone kinetics: most T3 is made outside the thyroid — conversion of T4 supplies ~22 µg/day by the classic tracer count and ~80% of production by compartmental analysis
question: In healthy humans, what are thyroid-hormone kinetics — daily thyroxine production rate, the fraction of T4 converted peripherally to T3 versus reverse T3, and T3 production from conversion versus direct secretion — measured by radiolabelled-hormone tracer studies?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — for the architecture of thyroid-hormone production, framed by Guyton & Hall / Ganong: the thyroid secretes mainly thyroxine (T4), and most of the active hormone T3 is generated in peripheral tissues by monodeiodination, with inner-ring deiodination yielding inactive reverse T3 (rT3) instead. The carded tracer record: conversion exists and is obligatory — athyreotic patients maintained on T4 alone have circulating T3 far above what contamination of the dose explains (Braverman 1970, N = 13). The classic quantification in 8 normal subjects put extrathyroidal conversion at 4% of the T4 pool per day — 33% of total T4 production — generating 22 µg of T3 daily, counted as 41% of daily T3 production (Pittman 1971). The later multicompartmental analysis, which added the plasma appearance curve of labelled T3 generated from T4, revised the partition: of total T3 production of 16.0 µg/day/m², the thyroid contributed 3.3 and the periphery 12.7 µg/day/m² — roughly 80% from conversion (Pilo 1990, 14 studies in normal subjects). The two figures are both on the face: the discrepancy is methodological (disappearance-only analysis misassigns conversion to slowly exchanging pools), and the shelf presents the modern compartmental partition as the better measurement while keeping the classic number visible. For rT3, the double-tracer study bounded production at 1.12–2.15 µg/h, with 65–90% degraded in rapidly exchanging peripheral tissues and all degradation yielding iodide (Pilo 1993). The daily T4 production rate itself (~80–100 µg/day in the textbooks' account) is presented as the textbook's account: the fetched records quantify conversion as fractions of T4 production rather than printing a single verified production figure, and the shelf says so rather than dressing the textbook number as measured fact.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED

title: Cortisol production rate: stable-isotope re-measurement cut the classic figure roughly in half — ~5.7 mg/m²/day (9.9 mg/day), not the accepted 12–15 mg/m²/day
question: In healthy humans, what is the cortisol production rate — what did the classic isotope-dilution studies measure, why did modern LC-MS/MS-era re-measurement revise the figure downward, and how does production vary with body size, sex and time of day?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — for the modern (stable-isotope) production figure and for the direction of the classic error, framed by Guyton & Hall / Ganong on adrenocortical secretion. This shelf's question is the discrepancy itself. The classic radioisotope era's production estimates were high enough that replacement practice settled at 33–41 µmol/day/m² (12–15 mg/m²/day) — the figure Esteban 1991 cites as 'currently accepted' — and patients on it developed Cushingoid features and growth retardation, which prompted re-measurement. With continuous [2H3]cortisol infusion and LC-MS, 12 normal volunteers produced 27.3 ± 7.5 µmol/day — 9.9 ± 2.7 mg/day, i.e. 15.7 µmol/day/m² or 5.7 mg/m²/day: roughly half the accepted figure (Esteban 1991). Independent stable-isotope work agrees in scale: healthy children produced 4.8 ± 0.6 (boys) and 4.4 ± 0.5 (girls) mg/m²/24 h by GC-MS, with the record stating plainly that these values 'are lower than those derived by radio tracer methods, but are in agreement with previous isotopic dilution studies' (Brandon 1999). Sex matters at the modern figure: afternoon-window production estimates were 0.94 ± 0.15 mg/h in men against 0.38 ± 0.14 mg/h in women, and the difference survives body-surface correction (0.48 vs 0.22 mg/m²/h, P < 0.001; Vierhapper 1998, N = 7 + 7). Time of day matters too: Esteban found a previously unreported circadian variation in the production rate itself, with plasma cortisol tracking secretion rather than metabolism. REFUSALS: the classic series anchor — Kenny et al., 'Cortisol production rate. II. Normal infants, children, and adults' (Pediatrics 1966) — was refused because its PubMed record carries no abstract, as was the 1973 diurnal-clearance paper; no classic number is quoted from either. The classic-era figure on this shelf (12–15 mg/m²/day) is the one the Esteban record itself prints as the accepted replacement dose of its day. Cross-point: the library's cortisol-pulsatility shelf asks the secretion-pattern question — dynamics, not this daily quantity.

title: Aldosterone secretion rate: the classic isotope-dilution values are unverifiable in the fetched record — what survives is the method, the metabolite index, and the sodium/age/posture behaviour
question: In healthy humans, what is the aldosterone secretion rate, and how do posture, sodium intake and potassium loading move it — the classic isotope-dilution secretion-rate measurements and their modern successors?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING — and the stamp itself is the honest headline of this shelf: the regulation story is textbook-settled (Guyton & Hall / Ganong: secretion rises with sodium restriction, upright posture and potassium, driven mainly through renin–angiotensin), but the classic isotope-dilution secretion-rate measurements that originally quantified it could not be verified from any record fetched this session — the two classic method anchors carry no abstracts and were refused (see Synthesis). What the verifiable record does establish: (1) method — a radioimmunoassay-based secretion-rate method agreed 'in perfect agreement' with the double-isotope dilution derivative assay it was checked against (de Man 1977); (2) an index — in cirrhosis, urinary aldosterone 18-glucuronide excretion tracked the directly measured secretion rate closely enough to serve as its index in 50 further patients, in whom the index related to plasma renin activity and plasma sodium but NOT to plasma potassium (Wilkinson 1981); (3) sodium and posture in health-adjacent data — urinary aldosterone excretion was lower in subjects over 50 than under 30 before and after sodium depletion, and upright (not recumbent) plasma aldosterone showed the same age fall, with metabolic clearance unchanged (Hegstad 1983); (4) the secretion pattern — in 9 normal men, aldosterone is released in bursts (≥60% of secretion, 80–85 min interpulse interval), and sodium restriction raises output by enlarging bursts and basal secretion (Vieweg 1992 — a plasma-concentration deconvolution study, NOT an isotope-dilution secretion rate, and labelled so wherever it appears, per this shelf's rule that the two literatures must not be conflated). The textbooks' account of the normal rate — on the order of a hundred micrograms per day on usual sodium intakes, rising severalfold when sodium is restricted — is presented as the textbook's account only; no fetched record verifies a healthy-volunteer secretion-rate value, and this shelf does not pretend otherwise. That verification gap, not disagreement, is why the stamp is EMERGING.

title: Calibrated thrombin generation in health: peak thrombin and ETP rise with age and on oral contraceptives — but every number is platform-specific
question: In healthy humans, what does calibrated thrombin generation measure — lag time, peak thrombin and endogenous thrombin potential distributions in health, and how do age, sex and oral contraception shift them?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING — because the measurement is real and reproducible within a platform, but assay standardisation between laboratories and platforms is incomplete, so there is no single healthy distribution to quote — exactly the flag this row carries. The textbook framing (Guyton & Hall / Ganong on haemostasis) is thin for this assay, and the shelf says so: it rests on the primary measurement literature. What calibrated thrombin generation measures, from the carded records: plasma is triggered with tissue factor and the thrombin formed over time is read against a calibrator, yielding lag time, peak thrombin, time to peak and the area under the curve — endogenous thrombin potential (ETP). The healthy distributions are condition-specific: in 120 healthy Chinese subjects the CAT ranges (as printed, mean ± 2SD) were lag time 3.648 ± 2.465 min, peak 367.39 ± 151.93 nmol/L, ETP 2277 ± 1030 nmol/L·min (Wu 2014); on the automated ST Genesia platform, mean peak height in 117 healthy donors was 164–167 nM with one reagent and 335–351 nM with another in the same donors (Ninivaggi 2021) — the same blood, a twofold different 'normal' peak, which is the standardisation problem in one line. Age and sex move the curve: thrombin generation increased with age and was higher in women than men in 140 healthy people, with lag time set mainly by free TFPI, free protein S, factor VII, FIX and fibrinogen, and ETP/peak by fibrinogen, factor XII, free TFPI and antithrombin at low tissue factor (Dielis 2008). Oral contraception shifts it further: users had the shortest lag and time-to-peak and the highest peak and ETP with and without added activated protein C, and on ST Genesia their mean peak ran ~263–473 nM across reagents against ~164–351 nM in non-users, with thrombomodulin suppressing ETP by only 25% in users versus 47–54% in non-users (Tchaikovski 2007; Ninivaggi 2021).
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING

title: Cerebral metabolic rate for oxygen: ~3.0–3.3 mL/100 g/min at resting wakefulness — the classic Kety–Schmidt 3.5 was an overestimate — falling ~21% in sleep and ~26–38% under volatile anaesthesia
question: In healthy humans, what is the cerebral metabolic rate for oxygen — CMRO2 and cerebral blood flow values by the Kety–Schmidt nitrous-oxide method and their modern PET/MRI successors, and how do CMRO2 and flow change with sleep, anaesthesia depth surrogates and ageing in health?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — for the resting value and its state-dependence, framed by Guyton & Hall / Boron & Boulpaep on cerebral metabolism. The classic Kety–Schmidt nitrous-oxide values — CBF 54 mL/100 g/min and CMRO2 3.5 mL/100 g/min — enter this shelf only as quoted by the fetched critical appraisal, because the 1948 originals' records carry no abstracts and were refused (see Synthesis). The appraisal (Madsen 1993), from 57 Kety–Schmidt measurements in young normal adults at EEG-verified wakeful rest, shows the classic figures overestimate: incomplete tracer equilibration inflates them, and the corrected equilibrium values are ~46 mL/100 g/min and ~3.0 mL/100 g/min, with interindividual CMRO2 variation of 11% (coefficient of variation). The modern PET database lands beside the corrected figure: in 70 healthy volunteers across 11 Japanese centres, cortical CMRO2 was 3.3 ± 0.5 mL/100 mL/min with CBF 44.4 ± 6.5 and oxygen extraction fraction 0.44 ± 0.06 (Ito 2004). A modern Kety–Schmidt repeatability study in 29 healthy men found the method robust in its best (discontinuous desaturation) form — CBF 64 (95% CI 59–71) mL/100 g/min and CMRO2 1.8 (1.7–2.0) µmol/g/min — values on the higher side, kept on the face as the method's own spread (Taudorf 2009). State changes: CMRO2 falls in sleep — by a relative 21% (range 14–32%) from a waking 118 ± 12 µmol/min/100 g to a nadir of 98 ± 16 on OxFlow MRI in 12 healthy subjects (Caporale 2021) — and under volatile anaesthesia, where sevoflurane and isoflurane at 1.5 MAC lowered CMRO2 by a relative 26% and 38% while raising CBF by a relative 17% and 25% (Oshima 2003, N = 20, Kety–Schmidt with 15% N2O; the record prints relative changes, not the absolute pair, and the card says so). Ageing lowers CMRO2 regionally — significantly lower mean CMRO2 over 51 than under 50 in 32 healthy volunteers, with flow comparatively preserved (Takada 1992). Cross-points, not duplicated: the library's cerebral autoregulation and CO2-reactivity shelves ask how flow is regulated; this shelf asks the metabolic rate itself.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED

title: Ianalumab in Sjögren's disease: phase 3 ESSDAI differences of about one point, no symptom benefit — a marginal systemic effect from the first programme to reach phase 3
question: In adults with primary Sjögren's disease with moderate-to-severe systemic activity, does the anti-BAFF-receptor antibody ianalumab, compared with placebo plus standard care, improve systemic disease activity (ESSDAI response)?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit): Ianalumab 300 mg monthly produced a statistically significant but small extra fall in ESSDAI versus placebo in two phase 3 trials (−1.3 points, P=0.0496, NEPTUNUS-1, n=275; −1.0 points, P=0.04, NEPTUNUS-2, n=504), with no significant difference in ESSDAI response or in patient-reported symptom scores (SSSD/ESSPRI). The phase 2 programme points the same way (dose–response in the 190-patient dose-finding trial; sustained effect to 52 weeks; B-cell depletion with favourable trends in a 27-patient single-dose trial). A single manufacturer's programme caps the stamp at POSSIBLE, and the effect size — about 1 point on a 123-point index, without symptom benefit — is the central caveat. Hydroxychloroquine alone and rituximab in Sjögren's are homed on shelf #2716; symptomatic pilocarpine is shelf #1796 — neither is carded here.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit)

title: Abatacept in early Sjögren's syndrome (ASAP-III): no difference from placebo on ESSDAI or gland histology — open-label gains only
question: In adults with early active primary Sjögren's syndrome, does abatacept, compared with placebo, improve systemic disease activity and glandular function (ASAP-III programme)?
balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): In the single randomised trial (ASAP-III, 80 patients with early active primary Sjögren's syndrome), abatacept did not improve the primary ESSDAI endpoint versus placebo at week 24 (adjusted difference −1.3 points, 95% CI −4.1 to 1.6), and a biopsy substudy found virtually no effect on salivary gland inflammation. The 48-week open-label extension showed improvement (median ESSDAI 14.0 to 4.0; 73% CRESS responders), but with no control group it cannot establish benefit. A single small trial caps the stamp at POSSIBLE. Hydroxychloroquine and rituximab in Sjögren's are homed on shelf #2716 and are not carded here.

title: Leflunomide plus hydroxychloroquine in Sjögren's disease: two small trials, the same ~4-point ESSDAI gain — a replicated pilot signal
question: In adults with primary Sjögren's syndrome, does the combination of leflunomide plus hydroxychloroquine, compared with placebo, improve systemic disease activity (ESSDAI)?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit): Leflunomide 20 mg plus hydroxychloroquine 400 mg daily beat placebo on ESSDAI by −4.35 points (P=0.0078) in RepurpSS-I (29 patients) and by −4.135 points (P=0.0012) in the replication trial RepurpSS-II (46 patients) — two concordant positive trials, but both small and from the same single centre, which caps the stamp at POSSIBLE. A pooled transcriptomic analysis suggests the benefit concentrates in one endotype. This shelf asks the combination question only: hydroxychloroquine alone (which failed in JOQUER) and rituximab are homed on shelf #2716 and are not carded here. Harms were mainly gastrointestinal discomfort and transient liver-enzyme rises.

title: Secukinumab in giant cell arteritis: phase 2 promised, phase 3 missed its primary endpoint — a split record
question: In adults with giant cell arteritis, does secukinumab, compared with placebo plus a glucocorticoid taper, sustain remission?
balance: SPLIT: The evidence disagrees with itself. The phase 2 TitAIN trial (52 patients) found a large advantage (median sustained remission 70% vs 20% to week 28, Bayesian analysis), but the phase 3 GCAptAIN trial (353 patients) missed its primary endpoint (the treatment made no difference at conventional significance): sustained remission 25.6% on secukinumab 300 mg with a 26-week glucocorticoid taper versus 16.9% on placebo with a 52-week taper (difference 8.7 points, 95% CI −1.3 to 18.8; P=0.09). An Italian observational cohort (36 patients, labelled observational) reports high remission and steroid-sparing without a comparator. Interleukin-6 blockade in giant cell arteritis is homed on live shelf #385 and upadacitinib on live shelf #1812 — not carded here.
stamp: SPLIT

title: Tocilizumab in Takayasu arteritis: hazard ratio 0.41 for relapse, primary endpoint narrowly missed — suggestive evidence in a rare disease
question: In adults with refractory Takayasu arteritis, does tocilizumab, compared with placebo (and in long-term follow-up, continued therapy), reduce relapse?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence): The only randomised trial, TAKT (36 Japanese patients with refractory Takayasu arteritis), favoured tocilizumab on time to relapse (hazard ratio 0.41) but missed its primary endpoint (95.41% CI 0.15 to 1.10; P=0.0596). Its 96-week open-label extension showed glucocorticoid doses roughly halving with mostly stable imaging, and a retrospective series (11 patients, labelled observational) plus a 211-patient literature pool (73% remission) point the same way. That is a consistent direction on very thin, largely uncontrolled evidence — 47 distinct patients in primary data — hence MAYBE (weak evidence). No Takayasu question is homed elsewhere in the library.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence)

title: Mepolizumab in hypereosinophilic syndrome: flares 28% versus 56% in one phase 3 trial — fewer flares, some steroid-sparing
question: In adults with hypereosinophilic syndrome, does mepolizumab, compared with placebo plus standard care, reduce disease flares and spare glucocorticoids?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit): In the single phase 3 trial (108 patients with FIP1L1-PDGFRA-negative hypereosinophilic syndrome and recent flares), mepolizumab 300 mg every 4 weeks halved the proportion with one or more flares over 32 weeks (28% vs 56%; odds ratio 0.28, 95% CI 0.12 to 0.64). The effect was consistent across baseline eosinophil subgroups, and the open-label extension showed continued flare control with at least 50% oral corticosteroid dose reductions in 28% of steroid-treated patients. A single trial programme caps the stamp at POSSIBLE. Mepolizumab in EGPA is a different question, homed on pack #1653, and is not carded here.

title: Dazukibart in dermatomyositis: skin activity down ~16 points versus placebo in phase 2 — large, rapid, and not yet phase 3
question: In adults with dermatomyositis, does the interferon-beta-specific monoclonal antibody dazukibart, compared with placebo, improve skin disease activity (CDASI) and muscle outcomes?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit): In the single phase 2 programme (75 patients), dazukibart produced a large reduction in skin disease activity — pooled CDASI-A change −19.2 on 600 mg versus a placebo-adjusted difference of −16.3 points at week 12 (P<0.0001) — with significant improvement already by week 4 and persistence to week 76 in a small open-label extension. Muscle outcomes were secondary and rest on an 18-patient cohort, so the programme is skin-primary. Phase-2-only, single-programme evidence caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.
