title: Rituximab in systemic sclerosis (DESIRES): skin score −8.44 points versus placebo — the strongest skin signal in the disease, from one small trial
question: In adults with systemic sclerosis, does rituximab, compared with placebo, improve skin thickening (modified Rodnan skin score) and lung function (DESIRES programme)?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit): In the DESIRES trial (56 Japanese patients with systemic sclerosis and mRSS ≥10), rituximab improved skin thickening versus placebo at week 24 (mRSS change −6.30 vs +2.14; difference −8.44, 95% CI −11.00 to −5.88; P<0.0001), with further improvement after a second course in the open-label extension and sustained skin and lung gains in long-term follow-up. title: Olokizumab in rheumatoid arthritis (CREDO): three positive phase 3 trials, noninferior to adalimumab — effective, unapproved, long-term safety unknown
question: In adults with active rheumatoid arthritis with inadequate response to conventional or biologic DMARDs, does the anti-IL-6 monoclonal antibody olokizumab, compared with placebo or adalimumab, improve disease activity (CREDO programme)?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit): Three phase 3 CREDO trials (2,444 patients) consistently show olokizumab 64 mg (every 2 or 4 weeks) plus methotrexate beating placebo on ACR20 at week 12 — CREDO-1: 63.6%/70.4% vs 25.9%; CREDO-2: 70.3%/71.4% vs 44.4%, with noninferiority to adalimumab; CREDO-3 (TNF-inadequate responders): 60.9%/59.6% vs 40.6%. The stamp stays at POSSIBLE because the programme is a single sponsor's, predominantly Russia/Eastern Europe in origin, limited to 24-week trials, and the drug is not FDA-approved, so long-term interleukin-6-class safety is uncharacterised. The interleukin-6 receptor blockers tocilizumab and sarilumab in rheumatoid arthritis are homed on pack #5446 and are not carded here.

title: High-dose antithrombin III in severe sepsis: KyberSept was null overall (28-day mortality 38.9% vs 38.7%) — signals only in non-randomised no-heparin subgroups
question: In adults with severe sepsis, does high-dose antithrombin III versus placebo reduce 28-day mortality — and does concomitant heparin change the answer?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence): KyberSept (n=2,314) — the only large trial — found high-dose antithrombin III made no difference to 28-day mortality in severe sepsis (38.9% versus 38.7%, P=.94). Favourable signals appear only in the non-randomised subgroup that received no concomitant heparin (90-day mortality 44.9% versus 52.5%) and, within it, in patients with DIC (absolute 28-day mortality reduction 14.6%) — subgroup findings inside a null trial, graded as such and never as the headline. Antithrombin plus heparin increased bleeding (23.8% versus 13.5%). A historical programme: the drug was never adopted for sepsis.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence)

title: Interleukin-1 receptor antagonist in sepsis: SPLIT — phase 3 trials null overall; a post-hoc macrophage-activation subgroup (n=43) is the only signal
question: In adults with sepsis/severe sepsis, does recombinant human interleukin-1 receptor antagonist versus placebo reduce mortality?
balance: SPLIT: for unselected sepsis, interleukin-1 receptor antagonist (anakinra) failed — the phase 2 dose gradient (n=99) was not confirmed: the first phase 3 trial's pre-specified analyses were null (n=893) and the confirmatory phase 3 was stopped for futility (28-day mortality 33.1% versus 36.4%, P=.36; n=696). The split is a post-hoc 2016 reanalysis: in the 43 patients (5.6%) with macrophage-activation-syndrome features (hepatobiliary dysfunction plus DIC), 28-day survival was 65.4% versus 35.3% (hazard ratio for death 0.28) — hypothesis-generating only, awaiting the prospective trial its authors call for.

title: Filgrastim in pneumonia and severe sepsis: neutrophils rose, outcomes did not — three trials, no survival benefit (the treatment made no difference)
question: In non-neutropenic adults hospitalised with pneumonia (including multilobar pneumonia and pneumonia with severe sepsis), does adjunctive filgrastim versus placebo improve survival and shorten illness?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence): three randomised trials (1998–2003) in non-neutropenic hospitalised pneumonia — community-acquired, multilobar (n=480) and pneumonia with severe sepsis — agree: filgrastim raised neutrophil counts as designed and the treatment made no difference to mortality, resolution of morbidity, organ dysfunction, ICU or ventilator days. It was safe and well tolerated throughout. A closed question, settled against routine adjunctive use; the only favourable notes are unvalidated secondary/subgroup observations.

title: Intravenous immunoglobulin in sepsis: SPLIT — small old trials positive, the large SBITS trial (n=653) null
question: In adults with sepsis or septic shock, does adjunctive polyclonal intravenous immunoglobulin versus placebo or albumin reduce mortality?
balance: SPLIT: the evidence divides by rigour. Three small randomised trials from 1991–2005 (n=62, 55 and 56) report large mortality benefits for polyclonal IVIG in sepsis, while SBITS — the one large, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (n=653) — found 28-day mortality of 39.3% versus 37.3% (the treatment made no difference), and the Cochrane review's low-risk-of-bias sensitivity analysis likewise shows no benefit (relative risk 0.97). ⚠ Several older trials are small and at high risk of bias. Preparations differ (IgG versus IgM-enriched), so the positive limb is not a single consistent intervention.

title: Obeldesivir in COVID-19: viral load fell in both phase 3 trials, but hospitalisation (0 vs 1 event) and symptom time (5.9 vs 6.0 days) did not significantly improve
question: In non-hospitalised adults with COVID-19 (high-risk and low-risk populations), does oral obeldesivir versus placebo reduce hospitalisation or death and speed symptom resolution?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence): a two-trial programme (BIRCH, high-risk, n=465; OAKTREE, low-risk, n=1,955) reported four ways. Obeldesivir reduced viral RNA and infectious titre and showed a high barrier to resistance, but neither clinical endpoint was met: BIRCH had one hospitalisation/death event in total (0 versus 1; the authors state the trial was underpowered), and OAKTREE's time to symptom alleviation was 5.9 versus 6.0 days (P=0.068, not significant). No mortality claim is made. Safety was comparable to placebo in both trials.

title: Cefazolin for MSSA bacteraemia: non-inferior to flucloxacillin/cloxacillin in SNAP (90-day mortality 15.0% vs 17.0%) with less kidney injury
question: In adults with MSSA bacteraemia, is cefazolin non-inferior to flucloxacillin/cloxacillin (antistaphylococcal penicillins) for 90-day mortality, with fewer adverse events?
balance: POSSIBLE: the randomised evidence is one platform domain (SNAP, 1,287 evaluable patients): cefazolin was non-inferior to flucloxacillin/cloxacillin for 90-day mortality (15.0% versus 17.0%; probability of non-inferiority 99.2%) with less acute kidney injury (13.9% versus 19.6%). The pre-2026 observational literature (30 studies, 15,513 patients) pointed the same way but is confounded by indication and graded separately. A single randomised programme caps this shelf at POSSIBLE; superiority for survival is not claimed.

title: Tigecycline in complicated intra-abdominal infection: non-inferior for clinical cure in three randomised comparisons — under an FDA boxed warning on all-cause mortality
question: In hospitalised adults with complicated intra-abdominal infection, is tigecycline non-inferior to imipenem/cilastatin (or ceftriaxone plus metronidazole) for clinical cure?
balance: LIKELY: across three randomised comparisons (2005–2010), tigecycline was non-inferior to imipenem/cilastatin and to ceftriaxone plus metronidazole for clinical cure of complicated intra-abdominal infection (evaluable-population cure ~81–86% versus ~82–86% against imipenem/cilastatin), with consistently more nausea and vomiting. title: Vimkunya (chikungunya VLP vaccine): 97.8% seroresponse at day 22 in ages 12–64 and 87% over 65 — an antibody surrogate, with no disease-efficacy trial
question: In adolescents, adults and older adults, does the chikungunya virus-like-particle vaccine (Vimkunya, PXVX0317) versus placebo produce seroprotective neutralising antibody responses with acceptable safety?
balance: POSSIBLE: Vimkunya (chikungunya virus-like-particle vaccine, PXVX0317, Bavarian Nordic — named under the clarification exception) produced neutralising-antibody seroresponse in 97.8% of ages 12–64 at day 22 (versus 1.2% on placebo) and 87% of adults 65 and older (76% at day 183), with a mostly grade 1–2 safety profile across two phase 3 trials (n=3,258 and n=413). title: Selonsertib in MASH: a failed programme — STELLAR-3 and STELLAR-4 both missed their primary endpoint (fibrosis improvement 10–14% vs 13% on placebo)
question: In adults with MASH (NASH) and bridging fibrosis (F3) or compensated cirrhosis (F4), does selonsertib (ASK1 inhibitor) versus placebo improve liver fibrosis without worsening steatohepatitis?

title: Emricasan in MASH cirrhosis: a failed programme — portal pressure, decompensation and fibrosis endpoints all null across four trials
question: In adults with MASH (NASH) cirrhosis — including decompensated cirrhosis and cirrhosis with severe portal hypertension — does emricasan (pan-caspase inhibitor) versus placebo reduce portal pressure, prevent decompensation, or improve fibrosis?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence): a failed programme, with the failure on the face. Emricasan (pan-caspase inhibitor) missed every primary endpoint in four randomised trials: portal pressure did not fall in NASH cirrhosis with severe portal hypertension (ENCORE-PH, n=263), death/new decompensation was not prevented in decompensated cirrhosis (n=217; hazard ratios 1.02 and 1.28), fibrosis improvement in F1–F3 NASH was numerically below placebo (11–12% versus 19%; ENCORE-NF, n=318), and post-transplant fibrosis was unchanged (n=64). Target engagement without clinical effect, consistently.

title: Oral vancomycin in primary sclerosing cholangitis: the 2026 placebo-controlled trial found no liver benefit — the claimed benefit is bowel, and observational only
question: In adults (and, in the earlier literature, children) with primary sclerosing cholangitis, with or without inflammatory bowel disease, does oral vancomycin versus placebo or metronidazole improve liver biochemistry and liver-related endpoints?
balance: SPLIT — the randomised and observational limbs point different ways, and the randomised limb governs the liver question. The 2026 Mayo phase 3 placebo-controlled trial (82 randomised adults, 18 months) found alkaline phosphatase normalisation in 5% on placebo vs 6.7% on oral vancomycin (the treatment made no difference), with no difference in Mayo PSC risk score or liver stiffness, although the fall in alkaline phosphatase was larger on vancomycin (-21.9% vs +1.2%). The small 2013 pilot randomised trial (35 patients, 12 weeks) had found alkaline phosphatase falls of about 40-43% on vancomycin, reaching its primary endpoint — a short, small, surrogate-only signal the larger trial did not confirm on liver-related endpoints. The observational limb answers a different question: in a 90-patient retrospective PSC-IBD cohort, vancomycin was associated with bowel improvement (clinical improvement 50%, endoscopic inactivity rising from 18.8% to 60.3%) while the median alkaline phosphatase change was not significant (-48.5 U/L, P=0.57). So: no demonstrated liver benefit in the only large randomised trial; a possible bowel benefit in PSC-IBD that rests on uncontrolled data. The Italian VanC-IT trial is protocol-only and is not carded.
stamp: SPLIT

title: Fenofibrate add-on in primary biliary cholangitis with incomplete UDCA response: liver tests improve in randomised and cohort data — clinical outcomes unproven
question: In adults with primary biliary cholangitis and an incomplete response to ursodeoxycholic acid, does adding fenofibrate versus continued UDCA alone improve alkaline phosphatase and biochemical response?
balance: POSSIBLE — concordant biochemical benefit across two randomised trials and comparative cohorts, but the evidence is surrogate-led and the hard-outcome signal is observational. Premise resolved on the face: the slate's PICO asks about UDCA incomplete responders, and that population does have its own randomised trial (48 patients: complete normalisation of alkaline phosphatase, gamma-GT and bilirubin in 20.8% on fenofibrate add-on vs 0% on UDCA alone; normal alkaline phosphatase 54.2% vs 4.2%) — the 2023 trial the miner verified (117 patients, biochemical response 81.4% vs 64.3% by the Barcelona criterion) was in treatment-naive patients and is carded as that separate, earlier-treatment slice, not as evidence about incomplete responders. Cohorts in incomplete responders, including a cirrhotic cohort (alkaline phosphatase normalisation 37% vs 11%), point the same way, and one propensity-adjusted cohort associated fenofibrate with better transplant-free survival — observational and labelled as such. Harms: early creatinine and transaminase rises that settled in the trial; about 22% discontinued for adverse events in one cohort, and bilirubin rose faster in cirrhotic patients in that cohort, so cirrhosis needs monitoring. Bezafibrate evidence (a different fibrate, with its own home in the PPAR family) is not imported here. Stamp is POSSIBLE, not LIKELY: no randomised trial is powered on clinical outcomes.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Liver abscess: catheter drainage beats needle aspiration on success and speed of recovery, with no added complications — aspiration remains the fallback for small, liquefied abscesses
question: In adults with liver abscess (pyogenic or amoebic) large enough to drain, does percutaneous catheter drainage versus percutaneous needle aspiration achieve higher success rates with fewer repeat interventions?
balance: LIKELY — percutaneous catheter drainage (PCD) beats percutaneous needle aspiration (PNA) on treatment success across multiple independent randomised trials and three successive meta-analyses, with no complication penalty. The largest single randomised comparison on this shelf (543 patients) and two smaller ones (190 and 60 patients) all found faster clinical improvement and faster halving of the cavity with a catheter; pooled across 15 randomised trials (1,626 patients) the success-rate risk ratio was 1.21 favouring PCD with less recurrence at 6 months (relative risk 0.41), and the 2026 synthesis of 12 trials (1,425 patients) found higher success (odds ratio 4.12) with complication rates the same (odds ratio 1.02, the treatment made no difference to complications). Stratification the shelf must keep: the catheter advantage is clearest in larger, partially liquefied or thick-pus abscesses; aspiration remains a reasonable, simpler option for smaller, fully liquefied abscesses and where catheter care is unavailable, accepting more repeat procedures. Amoebic and pyogenic abscesses are pooled in most trials — a limitation printed on the cards. The trials are small, single-centre and mostly South Asian, which is why the stamp rests on concordance across trials and syntheses rather than on any one study.
stamp: LIKELY

title: Rebyota (fecal microbiota, live-jslm) for recurrent C. difficile: randomised subgroups favour it over placebo; the large open-label cohort succeeded in 73.8% at 8 weeks
question: In adults with recurrent Clostridioides difficile infection after standard antibiotic therapy, does a single rectally administered live microbiota suspension (RBX2660) versus placebo reduce recurrence at 8 weeks?
balance: POSSIBLE — a single programme (one randomised phase 3 trial, reported through subgroup and post-hoc analyses, plus a large single-arm phase 3 cohort) for one named product. Clarification exception applied: the tested product is fecal microbiota, live-jslm (Rebyota, Ferring Pharmaceuticals) — a single rectally administered dose given after standard-of-care antibiotics — and it is named, with its manufacturer, because the product is the intervention. The randomised limb: subgroup and post-hoc analyses of the PUNCH CD3 placebo-controlled trial (with its phase 2 predecessor) show treatment differences favouring the product over placebo at 8 weeks that were consistent across risk-factor subgroups, with the largest relative reductions in patients with a 3-day antibiotic washout and with four or more previous episodes; older adults with comorbidities likewise stayed recurrence-free more often than on placebo in all but two subgroups. The open-label limb: in PUNCH CD3-OLS, 697 treated participants had a 73.8% treatment success rate at 8 weeks and, among successes, a 91.0% sustained response at 6 months — single-arm, so those percentages have no comparator and are graded weaker. Safety across five prospective trials (1,192 recipients): treatment-emergent adverse events in 70.9%, mostly mild-to-moderate and gastrointestinal; serious events mostly reflected pre-existing conditions or the infection itself. This shelf's home neighbour, live shelf #983, asks the microbiome question for donor-faeces infusion and the defined oral spore product SER-109; the rectal live suspension is the unasked slice carded here, and the PUNCH CD3 primary report itself is not re-carded (one home per study). Single programme, so POSSIBLE caps the stamp.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: The diaphragmatic tension-time index: above a critical zone of about 0.15-0.20 the human diaphragm fatigues — measured in small classic loaded-breathing experiments
question: In healthy humans, how does the tension-time index of the diaphragm (mean transdiaphragmatic pressure per breath as a fraction of maximum, multiplied by the inspiratory duty cycle) determine whether the diaphragm fatigues — what is the critical threshold above which fatigue is inevitable, and how was it measured?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — for the existence and approximate location of a diaphragmatic fatigue threshold, framed by Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology and Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology on respiratory-muscle energetics and blood-flow limitation. The tension-time index of the diaphragm (TTdi) is the mean transdiaphragmatic pressure per breath as a fraction of maximum, multiplied by the inspiratory duty cycle (TI/Ttot). In the founding experiment (4 normal subjects), the pattern that could be sustained beyond 45 minutes had a TTdi of about 0.15 — the critical TTdi — and above it, endurance time fell steeply as TTdi rose, consistent with diaphragmatic blood-flow limitation; textbook accounts (Guyton & Hall / Boron & Boulpaep framing) commonly quote the critical zone as about 0.15-0.18, and the upper part of that range is the textbook's account, not a value the carded records separately confirm. An independent 1983 study (4 male subjects) using relaxation-rate and electromyographic fatigue markers found those markers changed only at TTdi above 0.20 and not below it — bracketing the threshold from the other side. A 1985 exercise study (5 normal young men) adds the necessary caution: with rib-cage restriction, diaphragmatic fatigue occurred during heavy exercise at a TTdi of only 0.06 ± 0.02, which the authors attributed to the higher inspiratory flow rate and breathing frequency — the threshold is a property of the breathing task, not a universal constant. A 1986 critique further showed TTdi values run about 15% higher when the duty cycle is computed from the duration of diaphragmatic tension rather than from inspiratory airflow time. All founding studies are small classics, carded with their Ns on the face under the physiology labelling rule. One classic COPD report was refused as a card because its PubMed record carries no abstract and its claims could not be verified this session (see Synthesis).
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED

title: Belumosudil in chronic graft-versus-host disease after at least two prior lines: responses in about three quarters of patients, in single-arm studies only
question: In patients with chronic GVHD after two or more prior systemic lines, does the ROCK2 inhibitor belumosudil 200 mg daily (or twice daily), versus no concurrent control, produce overall responses, and how durable are they?
balance: POSSIBLE — a single programme of dose-randomised but not placebo-controlled studies: response rates are single-arm readings against response criteria and must be framed that way. ROCKstar (132 patients, 2-5 prior lines) found best overall response rates of 74% on belumosudil (Rezurock, Kadmon/Sanofi) 200 mg daily and 77% on 200 mg twice daily, with a median response duration of 54 weeks and symptom improvement in about six in ten patients; 12% discontinued for possibly drug-related adverse events. The earlier KD025-208 study (54 patients) found response rates of 62-69% across doses, corticosteroid discontinuation in 19%, and 2-year overall survival of 82% (no comparator). The pooled long-term analysis (208 patients, median follow-up 31.4 months) held the response rate at 72% with median response duration 62.3 weeks. A 20-patient tissue companion study is mechanistic support, not efficacy evidence. No randomised comparison against another treatment exists, so POSSIBLE — not LIKELY — is the ceiling.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Axatilimab in recurrent or refractory chronic graft-versus-host disease: 74% response at the lowest dose — less drug worked better, in a single uncontrolled programme
question: In patients with recurrent or refractory chronic GVHD after ≥2 prior lines, does the CSF-1R antibody axatilimab (0.3, 1.0 or 3.0 mg/kg), versus no concurrent control, produce overall responses?
balance: POSSIBLE — a single programme (one pivotal dose-randomised phase 2 trial, one earlier phase 1/2 study, and an exposure-response analysis of the same patients) for the CSF-1R antibody axatilimab (Niktimvo, Incyte/Syndax), with no placebo or active comparator. AGAVE-201 (241 patients) met its primary endpoint at every dose, but with an inverted dose-response: overall response was 74% at 0.3 mg/kg every 2 weeks, 67% at 1 mg/kg every 2 weeks and 50% at 3 mg/kg every 4 weeks, while discontinuations for adverse events rose with dose (6%, 22% and 18%). The exposure-response analysis explains the inversion — lower exposure raised the odds of response while higher exposure raised the odds of adverse events on 10 of 11 safety endpoints — and the earlier phase 1/2 study (40 patients) had already shown an 82% response rate in the first six cycles at the doses carried forward. The common adverse events are dose-dependent transient laboratory abnormalities of CSF1R blockade. One programme, however consistent, caps at POSSIBLE. A reduced-frequency dosing report in the slate row was not carded: its PubMed record carries no abstract, so its claims could not be verified from its own record this session.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Fedratinib in myelofibrosis: spleen responses of 47% vs 1% before ruxolitinib and 36% vs 6% after it — with a thiamine/Wernicke warning that is part of the treatment
question: In adults with intermediate-2/high-risk myelofibrosis, JAK-inhibitor-naïve or previously treated with ruxolitinib, does fedratinib 400 mg daily, versus placebo or best available therapy, shrink spleen volume and improve symptoms?
balance: POSSIBLE — strong randomised spleen and symptom effects in two distinct populations, but from one drug programme, which caps the stamp. In JAK-inhibitor-naive patients (JAKARTA, placebo-controlled), fedratinib 400 mg daily produced a spleen volume response in 47% vs 1% on placebo and a symptom response in 40% vs 9% at week 24. After ruxolitinib failure, FREEDOM2 (201 patients, randomised against best available therapy) found spleen volume reduction of at least 35% in 36% vs 6%. The smaller FREEDOM study (38 enrolled, cut short by COVID-19) showed the same direction with protocol gastrointestinal mitigation and thiamine supplementation, and a low-platelet analysis (platelets 50 to under 100) found spleen responses similar to higher-platelet patients (36% vs 49% in JAKARTA; 36% vs 28% in JAKARTA2). The defining harm line is mandatory: fedratinib carries a boxed warning for Wernicke encephalopathy — thiamine must be checked and supplemented; no case occurred at the 400 mg dose in JAKARTA's updated analysis or in FREEDOM, but gastrointestinal adverse events (diarrhoea, nausea, vomiting), anaemia and thrombocytopenia are common, and grade 3 or worse treatment-related events occurred in 40% vs 12% in FREEDOM2's first six cycles.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Ponatinib in resistant chronic-phase CML: deep responses including T315I, with response-based dose reduction cutting serious arterial events from 18% to 4%
question: In patients with chronic-phase CML resistant or intolerant to ≥2 tyrosine kinase inhibitors (or with T315I), does response-based dose-optimised ponatinib, versus fixed-dose ponatinib or historical expectations, produce molecular responses at an acceptable vascular cost?
balance: POSSIBLE — one programme, two trials, and a dosing lesson bought with vascular harm. PACE (449 heavily pretreated patients with CML or Ph+ ALL, fixed 45 mg daily) produced major cytogenetic responses in 56% of chronic-phase patients — 70% in those with the T315I mutation — but arterial occlusive events emerged as the programme's defining toxicity. OPTIC prospectively tested response-based dosing (283 chronic-phase patients randomised to start at 45, 30 or 15 mg, dropping to 15 mg on reaching BCR::ABL1 at or below 1%): response at 12 months was 44.1%, 29.0% and 23.1% by starting dose, and the 45-to-15 mg strategy gave the best benefit-risk balance. Five-year OPTIC follow-up kept 5-year overall survival above 80% in every cohort, with exposure-adjusted arterial occlusive event rates of 4.1, 3.8 and 2.0 per 100 patient-years by starting dose. A pooled PACE/OPTIC comparison in post-second-generation-TKI patients quantified the trade: serious arterial occlusive events in 18% under PACE's fixed dosing vs 4% under OPTIC's response-based dosing, at similar or better responses. The frontline Ph+ ALL comparison (ponatinib vs imatinib, PhALLCON) is an adjacent slice, cross-pointed here and not carded into this resistance question. Single programme: POSSIBLE.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Midostaurin plus chemotherapy in newly diagnosed FLT3-mutated AML: RATIFY showed a survival benefit (hazard ratio 0.78) — one randomised trial, consistently supported
question: In younger adults with newly diagnosed FLT3-mutated AML, does adding midostaurin to intensive induction/consolidation (and as maintenance), versus chemotherapy alone, improve overall survival?
balance: POSSIBLE — the survival claim rests on one randomised trial (RATIFY), which caps the stamp, supported by a single-arm phase 3b, a historically controlled phase 2 and a large real-world registry analysis. RATIFY (717 patients aged 18-59 with newly diagnosed FLT3-mutated AML) found overall survival longer with midostaurin added to standard induction, consolidation and maintenance than with placebo (hazard ratio for death 0.78; event-free survival hazard ratio also 0.78), with benefit consistent across FLT3 subtypes and in the transplant-censored analysis — and, as the slate required on the face, the trial's advance was survival, reported without a remission-rate difference in its record. Two fences: the maintenance phase was not separately randomised, so no card here attributes the benefit to maintenance; and transplantation was allowed and common, so the estimate is for a midostaurin-containing strategy, not for the drug in isolation. The phase 3b study (301 patients, including patients over 60) reported complete remission or remission with incomplete recovery in 80.7% with a similar adverse-event pattern across age groups; the AMLSG phase 2 (440 patients) beat its historical controls (event-free survival hazard ratio 0.55). The real-world PETHRATIFY analysis (1,658 registry patients) found median survival 47.2 vs 19.3 months favouring midostaurin, attenuated in propensity-matched pairs (overall survival hazard ratio 0.77, P=0.06 — not significant), and is labelled observational.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: CPX-351 beats 7+3 on survival in older secondary AML in one randomised trial with a durable 5-year benefit — but it has never been randomised against venetoclax-based therapy, which matched it retrospectively
question: In older adults with newly diagnosed therapy-related AML or AML with myelodysplasia-related changes, does CPX-351 (liposomal cytarabine–daunorubicin), versus conventional 7+3 cytarabine–daunorubicin, improve overall survival and remission?
balance: POSSIBLE — a single randomised phase 3 programme supports CPX-351 (Vyxeos, Jazz Pharmaceuticals — the fixed 5:1 molar-ratio liposomal cytarabine–daunorubicin product, named under the clarification exception because the ratio formulation is the intervention, not generic 7+3) over conventional 7+3 in older adults with therapy-related AML or AML with myelodysplasia-related changes: median survival 9.56 vs 5.95 months (hazard ratio 0.69, relative), remission 47.7% vs 33.3%, and the advantage persisted at 5 years (survival 18% vs 8%). Real-world registry data (283 patients, observational) show a similar 54% remission rate. What the evidence does not show: any randomised advantage over venetoclax plus a hypomethylating agent — the one large retrospective comparison (600 patients) found similar remission and survival with more infections on CPX-351, despite CPX-351 patients being younger. Costs of the drug: prolonged cytopenias and slower neutrophil/platelet recovery than 7+3, in a population fit enough for intensive chemotherapy. Single-programme randomised evidence caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Oral azacitidine maintenance nearly doubled median survival after first AML remission in the QUAZAR trial — one strong trial, not yet replicated, and the oral drug is not interchangeable with injectable azacitidine
question: In adults with AML in first remission after intensive chemotherapy who are not proceeding to transplant, does oral azacitidine (CC-486) maintenance, versus placebo, prolong overall and relapse-free survival?
balance: POSSIBLE — oral azacitidine maintenance after first remission is supported by one large placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (QUAZAR AML-001, 472 patients): median overall survival 24.7 vs 14.8 months and relapse-free survival 10.2 vs 4.8 months, with benefit independent of baseline MRD status, a higher MRD conversion rate (37% vs 19%), and no evidence that maintenance compromised later salvage therapy. The stamp is capped at POSSIBLE because this is a single-programme evidence base — one trial and its analyses, per the standing single-programme precedent. Two identity points belong on the face: oral azacitidine (CC-486) is NOT bioequivalent to injectable azacitidine and must not be substituted for it, and the population was patients in first remission after intensive chemotherapy who were not proceeding to transplant. Main harms: gastrointestinal symptoms (mostly grade 1–2) and grade 3–4 neutropenia (41% vs 24%).
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Oral decitabine–cedazuridine matches intravenous decitabine's drug exposure (98.93% of AUC in ASCERTAIN) — an equivalence result, with clinical outcomes reported only descriptively
question: In adults with MDS or CMML, does oral decitabine 35 mg plus cedazuridine 100 mg, versus intravenous decitabine, deliver equivalent decitabine exposure and comparable clinical outcomes?
balance: POSSIBLE — and the claim must be stated exactly: this programme's pivotal evidence is a pharmacokinetic-equivalence design, not an outcomes trial. In ASCERTAIN (phase 3 randomised crossover, 133 treated patients with MDS/CMML), oral decitabine 35 mg plus cedazuridine 100 mg (Inqovi) delivered 98.93% of the 5-day decitabine AUC of intravenous decitabine, meeting the equivalence endpoint, with a similar safety profile; the phase 2 crossover study (80 patients) found the same (AUC ratio 93.5–97.6%, demethylation within 1%). Clinical-outcome data — response rates of 60–76% and a 35.7-month median survival in the small CMML subset — are secondary and uncontrolled, because after the crossover cycles every patient received the oral drug. The face of this shelf claims equivalent exposure with oral convenience, and nothing more.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Glasdegib plus low-dose cytarabine doubled median survival in one small randomised phase 2 trial of unfit AML patients — a single-programme result (n=132), unconfirmed in the intensive-chemotherapy setting
question: In adults with newly diagnosed AML ineligible for intensive induction, does glasdegib plus low-dose cytarabine, versus low-dose cytarabine alone, improve overall survival?
balance: POSSIBLE — glasdegib plus low-dose cytarabine rests on a single small randomised phase 2 programme (BRIGHT AML 1003, n=132 with AML or high-risk MDS): median survival 8.8 vs 4.9 months (hazard ratio 0.51, relative) and complete remission 17.0% vs 2.3%, with the advantage maintained on long-term analysis (hazard ratio 0.495) and strongest in secondary AML. All four cards here are that one trial and its analyses — the single-programme precedent caps the stamp at POSSIBLE, and the small N is printed on the face. Fenced, not carded: the phase 3 BRIGHT AML 1019 trials of glasdegib with intensive chemotherapy in fitter patients did not confirm benefit — a different slice that warns against extrapolation. The shelf also cannot answer the modern comparison against venetoclax-based regimens, which were not the control here.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Fractionated gemtuzumab ozogamicin improves survival in favourable- and intermediate-risk AML across five randomised trials — with no benefit in adverse cytogenetics and veno-occlusive disease as the price to watch
question: In patients with de novo CD33-positive AML, does adding fractionated gemtuzumab ozogamicin to standard induction chemotherapy, versus chemotherapy alone, improve event-free and overall survival?
balance: LIKELY — adding fractionated-dose gemtuzumab ozogamicin (3 mg/m² on days 1, 4, 7) to standard induction improves outcomes in de novo CD33-positive AML: ALFA-0701 showed 2-year event-free survival of 40.8% vs 17.1% (hazard ratio 0.58, relative), and the individual-patient-data meta-analysis of five randomised trials (3,325 patients) found improved 5-year survival driven by fewer relapses, not more remissions. The benefit is cytogenetically graded and that gradient is the shelf: absolute survival benefit 20.7% in favourable-risk, 5.7% in intermediate-risk, and none (odds ratio 0.99) in adverse-risk disease. History on the face: the drug was withdrawn in 2010 after single-bolus dosing failed (SWOG S0106) and returned on fractionated dosing; 3 mg/m² caused fewer early deaths than 6 mg/m² at equal efficacy. Defining harms: veno-occlusive disease/sinusoidal obstruction syndrome and prolonged thrombocytopenia; a transplant-subset analysis found no excess post-transplant veno-occlusive disease or mortality. LIKELY is earned by multiple independent randomised trials with a concordant individual-patient synthesis.
stamp: LIKELY

title: Enasidenib: remissions yes, survival unproven — a 40% response rate in IDH2-mutated relapsed AML, but the randomised IDHENTIFY trial missed its overall-survival endpoint
question: In patients with relapsed or refractory IDH2-mutated AML, does enasidenib, versus no concurrent control (or conventional care in the phase 3 trial), produce remissions and improve survival?
balance: SPLIT — the evidence divides cleanly by endpoint. On responses, enasidenib works: 40.3% overall response and 19.3% complete remission in the single-arm pivotal study, and in the randomised IDHENTIFY trial (319 older patients with late-stage IDH2-mutated relapsed/refractory AML) a 40.5% vs 9.9% response rate, better event-free survival, haematologic improvement (42.4% vs 11.2%) and red-cell transfusion independence (31.7% vs 9.3%). On survival, the only randomised test was null: median overall survival 6.5 vs 6.2 months (hazard ratio 0.86, P=0.23; the treatment made no difference to the primary endpoint), with the caveat that 12% of the control arm never received randomised treatment and many patients in both arms received later AML therapies. An observational real-world comparison favouring enasidenib on survival is carded but labelled and discounted — it does not outrank the randomised null. Class harms: differentiation syndrome and indirect hyperbilirubinaemia. The MDS subgroup (17 patients, 53% response) is programme context only.
stamp: SPLIT

title: Olutasidenib puts about a third of relapsed/refractory IDH1-mutated AML patients into durable complete remission — single-arm pivotal evidence only, with differentiation syndrome as the defining harm
question: In patients with relapsed or refractory IDH1-mutated AML, does olutasidenib 150 mg twice daily, versus no concurrent control, produce complete remissions?
balance: POSSIBLE — olutasidenib (Rezlidhia, Rigel Pharmaceuticals) rests entirely on single-arm evidence from one phase 1/2 programme: in the pivotal cohort of 153 heavily pretreated patients with relapsed/refractory IDH1-mutated AML, complete remission/CRh was 35% and overall response 48%, with a median CR/CRh duration of about 25 months and median survival of 11.5 months, confirmed at the final 5-year analysis. There is no randomised or controlled comparison, so single-arm framing applies throughout and the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE. Response varied by mutation subtype (R132C 42% vs R132H 17%) and fell with more prior regimens. Defining harms: differentiation syndrome (14% in the pivotal cohort, including one fatal case) and cytopenias; hepatotoxicity is a labelled class concern. The programme's MDS cohort (22 patients, mostly combination therapy) and its maintenance-after-response report — whose record carries no extractable results and so was not carded — are context, not support.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Ziftomenib alone induces complete remissions in about a fifth of relapsed/refractory NPM1-mutated AML patients — a three-report single-arm base (one of them a pharmacokinetic analysis), with differentiation syndrome the key harm
question: In adults with relapsed or refractory NPM1-mutated AML, does ziftomenib monotherapy, versus no concurrent control, produce complete remissions?
balance: POSSIBLE — ziftomenib (Komzifti, Kura Oncology) monotherapy in relapsed/refractory NPM1-mutated AML rests on exactly three on-question monotherapy reports, all from the single KOMET-001 programme: the phase 2 pivotal cohort (92 patients; CR/CRh 22%, overall response 33%, 61% of responders MRD-negative), the phase 1 study (83 patients; 35% complete remission in the 20-patient NPM1 subgroup at the 600 mg recommended dose), and a population-pharmacokinetic/exposure–response analysis in the same monotherapy population showing flat exposure–response and supporting the fixed 600 mg dose. That third report is a modelling analysis, not an independent efficacy trial — the floor is met, but the base is thin, single-programme and entirely single-arm, which caps the stamp at POSSIBLE. Median response duration was 4.6 months and median survival 6.6 months in phase 2. Differentiation syndrome is the defining harm (25% any grade in phase 2; one treatment-related death in phase 1). The combination report (ziftomenib with venetoclax and azacitidine, same population) is a different question and is cross-pointed in prose only, never carded here.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Liso-cel beats salvage chemotherapy/transplant pathways on event-free survival in a randomised second-line trial, and produces durable complete responses in later lines on single-arm evidence
question: In adults with relapsed or refractory large B-cell lymphoma after at least 1–2 prior lines, does lisocabtagene maraleucel (CD19 CAR T), versus salvage chemotherapy/autologous transplant pathways, produce durable complete responses and improve event-free survival?
balance: POSSIBLE — for the shelf's combined question, with the two limbs stated separately. Second line: the randomised TRANSFORM trial (184 transplant-eligible patients with primary refractory or early-relapsed large B-cell lymphoma) showed large, durable event-free and progression-free survival advantages for lisocabtagene maraleucel over salvage chemotherapy plus autologous transplant (event-free survival hazard ratio 0.375, progression-free survival hazard ratio 0.422 — relative measures; 36-month progression-free survival 51% vs 26.5%), while overall survival was not significantly different (hazard ratio 0.757) in a trial where 66% of controls crossed over to liso-cel. Third line or later: the evidence is the single-arm TRANSCEND study (73% objective response, 53% complete response; 5-year survival 38% in efficacy-evaluable patients, 33% of everyone leukapheresed) plus a concordant real-world analysis in older, comorbid patients — single-arm evidence caps that limb, and so the shelf, at POSSIBLE. Liso-cel is a defined-composition product (separate CD4 and CD8 CAR T components at equal target doses) and is named exactly for that reason. Grade 3-or-worse cytokine release syndrome was 2–3% and neurotoxicity about 10% across reports; there is no head-to-head trial against any other CAR T product, and cross-product comparisons are not made here.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Brexu-cel induces complete remissions in two-thirds of post-BTK-inhibitor mantle cell lymphoma patients, durable to 5 years — single-arm evidence with a heavy toxicity burden
question: In adults with relapsed or refractory mantle cell lymphoma after a BTK inhibitor, does brexucabtagene autoleucel (CD19 CAR T), versus no concurrent control, produce durable complete responses?
balance: POSSIBLE — brexucabtagene autoleucel in relapsed/refractory mantle cell lymphoma rests entirely on the single-arm ZUMA-2 programme: in the licensed post-BTK-inhibitor population, objective response was 93% and complete response 67% at primary analysis, holding at 91%/68% at 3 years, with median duration of response 36.5 months and median overall survival 46.5 months at 5 years. Cohort 3 extends similar responses (91% objective, 73% complete) to BTK-inhibitor-naïve patients — a different slice, labelled as such and not merged into the licensed-population claim. Single-arm evidence throughout caps the stamp at POSSIBLE: there is no randomised comparison against any alternative. The harm burden is heavy and belongs on the face: grade 3-or-worse cytopenias 94%, infections 32%, grade 3-or-worse neurological events 31%, and 22% non-relapse mortality among responders by 5 years. ZUMA-3 in B-cell ALL is a different disease — cross-pointed in prose only.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Obecabtagene autoleucel in relapsed/refractory adult B-ALL (FELIX): 77% remission, low severe immunotoxicity — single-arm evidence
question: In adults with relapsed or refractory B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, does obecabtagene autoleucel, versus no concurrent control, produce complete remissions with lower severe immunotoxicity than earlier CD19 CAR T products?
balance: Single-programme, single-arm evidence: every card comes from the one FELIX phase 1b/2 study (no randomised or concurrent control exists). In the morphologic-disease cohort, overall remission was 77% and median overall survival in infused patients was 15.6 months, with grade ≥3 cytokine release syndrome in only 2.4% and grade ≥3 neurotoxicity in 7.1% — the low severe-immunotoxicity claim rests on the product's intermediate-affinity CAR and its tumour-burden-guided split dosing, and the burden analysis (grade ≥3 CRS 2% vs 3%, ICANS 4% vs 9% in low- vs high-burden groups) is consistent with that design rather than proof of it. The external-control comparison favours obe-cel over historical non-CAR therapy but is a propensity-matched, non-randomised comparison and is labelled as such. Cross-product claims of lower toxicity than earlier CD19 CAR T products are cross-trial impressions only; no head-to-head trial exists. Product naming (clarification exception): obecabtagene autoleucel (Aucatzyl, Autolus) — the tested product as published.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Mosunetuzumab in relapsed/refractory follicular lymphoma: complete responses ~60%, fixed duration — single-arm evidence
question: In adults with relapsed or refractory follicular lymphoma after ≥2 prior lines, does fixed-duration mosunetuzumab (CD20×CD3 bispecific), versus no concurrent control, produce durable complete responses?
balance: Single-arm evidence throughout: no randomised or concurrent control exists for mosunetuzumab in follicular lymphoma. The intravenous pivotal phase 2 (n=90, ≥2 prior lines) found a complete response rate of 60.0% against a 14% historical-control benchmark, with cytokine release syndrome in 44% — predominantly grade 1–2 and confined to cycle 1 under step-up dosing. The subcutaneous pivotal analysis (n=94) showed non-inferior exposure to the intravenous form with complete responses in 61.7%, median progression-free survival 23.7 months, and a numerically lower cytokine release syndrome rate (29.8% vs 44.4% in the within-study intravenous cohort) — a formulation comparison, not a randomised one. An older-patient subgroup found responses at least as high at age ≥65 (complete response 70.0% in the pivotal follicular cohort) with no excess serious adverse events. Fixed duration (complete responders stop after cycle 8) is part of the tested intervention. Cross-point: the library's DLBCL bispecific shelf asks a different question in a different disease with different molecules and is not duplicated here.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Loncastuximab tesirine in relapsed/refractory DLBCL (LOTIS-2): ~48% responses in trials, less in real-world use — single-arm evidence
question: In adults with relapsed or refractory DLBCL after ≥2 prior lines, does loncastuximab tesirine (CD19 antibody–drug conjugate), versus no concurrent control, produce durable responses?
balance: Single-arm pivotal evidence with a sobering real-world limb. LOTIS-2 (n=145, ≥2 prior lines) found an overall response rate of 48.3% with complete responses in 24.1%, and the long-term report shows the complete responders drive the benefit (24-month survival 68.2% in complete responders; median overall survival 9.5 months overall). A Chinese phase 2 (n=64) reproduced the response rate (51.6%). But the largest real-world series (n=187, 21 US centres, more heavily pretreated and higher-risk than LOTIS-2) found responses of only 32% and median overall survival of 4.6 months — labelled observational. The pyrrolobenzodiazepine-dimer payload's signature harms belong on the face: oedema and effusions, photosensitivity, and gamma-glutamyltransferase elevation (grade ≥3 in 17% in LOTIS-2), alongside neutropenia (26%) and thrombocytopenia (18%). Responses cannot be separated into antibody vs payload effects. Product naming (clarification exception): loncastuximab tesirine (Zynlonta, ADC Therapeutics) — the tested product as published.

title: Tafasitamab plus lenalidomide in transplant-ineligible relapsed/refractory DLBCL (L-MIND): durable responses, single-arm base
question: In adults with relapsed or refractory DLBCL ineligible for autologous transplant, does tafasitamab plus lenalidomide, versus no concurrent control, produce durable responses?
balance: Single-arm pivotal evidence, tempered by real-world data. L-MIND (n=80, transplant-ineligible, 1–3 prior lines) found objective responses in 60% at the primary analysis and 57.5% at the final 5-year analysis, with complete responses in ~41–43% and median overall survival of 33.5 months — durable for the responders. But there is no randomised comparison: the matched Re-MIND analysis sometimes cited alongside is observational, and the two real-world limbs carded here are explicitly observational — a US multicentre retrospective study whose record reports substantially lower progression-free and overall survival than L-MIND (its abstract reports no patient number, printed as N not documented), and the Spanish GELTAMO series (n=99; response 51% in the intention-to-treat cohort, median overall survival 12.2 months). Responses also cannot be attributed to tafasitamab alone: lenalidomide is an active partner drug, and GELTAMO found lenalidomide dose intensity itself predicted response and survival. The honest face: a well-tolerated, chemotherapy-free option with durable complete responses in a minority-to-half of trial patients, unproven against any comparator.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Belantamab mafodotin combinations in relapsed/refractory myeloma (DREAMM-7/8): two positive phase 3 trials after the DREAMM-3 monotherapy failure
question: In patients with relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma after ≥1 prior line, does belantamab mafodotin plus bortezomib–dexamethasone (vs daratumumab–bortezomib–dexamethasone) or plus pomalidomide–dexamethasone (vs bortezomib–pomalidomide–dexamethasone) improve progression-free and overall survival?
balance: A three-act story, and all three acts are on the face. Act one: belantamab mafodotin won accelerated approval as monotherapy, then the phase 3 DREAMM-3 trial of the single agent vs pomalidomide–dexamethasone missed its primary endpoint (progression-free survival hazard ratio 1.03; the treatment made no difference) and the drug was withdrawn in the US. Act two: two randomised phase 3 combination trials were clearly positive — DREAMM-7 (BVd vs DVd, n=494): median progression-free survival 36.6 vs 13.4 months (hazard ratio 0.41, a relative measure), with an overall-survival benefit at the updated analysis (hazard ratio 0.58); DREAMM-8 (BPd vs PVd, n=302, lenalidomide-exposed): hazard ratio 0.52 for progression or death, 12-month progression-free survival 71% vs 51%. Act three: re-approval as combination therapy. The defining harm is ocular: ocular events in 79% on BVd vs 29% on DVd in DREAMM-7 (mostly managed with dose modification, visual-acuity events mostly resolving), and blurred vision reported as severe or very severe by 43% of BPd patients in the DREAMM-8 patient-reported outcomes — the reason for the monitoring burden that accompanies this drug. The LIKELY stamp applies to the combinations only; the monotherapy limb is null and carded as such.
stamp: LIKELY

title: Elranatamab in relapsed/refractory myeloma (MagnetisMM-3): 61% responses, single-arm — infection burden is the defining harm
question: In patients with triple-class-exposed relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma, does elranatamab (BCMA×CD3 bispecific), versus no concurrent control, produce durable responses?
balance: Single-arm evidence: MagnetisMM-3 cohort A (n=123, no prior BCMA-directed therapy) is the whole trial base — objective responses in 61.0%, with 35.0% complete response or better, and medians for duration of response, progression-free and overall survival not yet reached at 14.7 months. The US subgroup (n=47 of the same cohort, longer follow-up) is consistent (response 66.0%; median overall survival 43.6 months) but is a subset of the same patients, not independent evidence. The real-world ALTITUDE claims cohorts (n=183 and n=391, observational) show the drug is dosed less intensively in practice than on label, with 60.7–70.0% of patients estimated alive at 18 months. The mandatory harm line for the BCMA-bispecific class is infection: infections in 69.9% (grade 3–4 in 39.8%) in the trial, alongside cytokine release syndrome in 57.7% (no grade 3–4 events) and neutropenia (grade 3–4 in 48.8%). Cross-point: the library's teclistamab shelf asks the same class question for a different molecule and is not duplicated here.

title: Talquetamab in relapsed/refractory myeloma (MonumenTAL-1): responses ~67–74% at 3 years — GPRC5D taste/skin/nail toxicity defines the harm line
question: In patients with relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma after ≥3 prior lines, does talquetamab (GPRC5D×CD3 bispecific), versus no concurrent control, produce responses, including after prior T-cell-redirection therapy?
balance: Single-arm evidence throughout, from the one MonumenTAL-1 programme. The phase 1 primary report established the two recommended subcutaneous doses (0.4 mg/kg weekly, 0.8 mg/kg every other week) with responses in 70% and 64% of heavily pretreated patients (median six prior lines). The 3-year follow-up (n=143 weekly, n=154 every-other-week, plus a 78-patient prior-T-cell-redirection cohort) shows overall responses of 67–74% across cohorts — including after prior T-cell-redirection therapy — with median overall survival of 34.0 months (weekly) and not reached (every-other-week). The defining harm line is unique to the GPRC5D target: on-target off-tumour effects on taste, skin, nails and weight — taste changes in 72–76% and dysgeusia in ~57–63% at the recommended doses in the primary report, skin events in ~67–70% — characterised in detail by the China cohort card (n=41), where they were predominantly grade 1–2, mostly resolved, and rarely forced dose change. Cytokine release syndrome was common (73–79%) but almost entirely low-grade, and the programme reports lower high-grade infection rates than BCMA bispecifics — a cross-trial impression, fenced as such.

title: Linvoseltamab in relapsed/refractory myeloma (LINKER-MM1): 71% responses on a response-adapted schedule — single-programme evidence
question: In patients with triple-class-exposed relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma, does linvoseltamab (BCMA×CD3 bispecific, response-adapted dosing), versus no concurrent control or real-world standard care, produce durable responses?
balance: Single-programme, single-arm evidence (the standing single-programme precedent applies — it is stated on the face): LINKER-MM1's 200 mg cohort (n=117, triple-class exposed) produced an objective response rate of 71% with 50–52% complete response or better and a median duration of response of 29.4 months, under the programme's defining response-adapted schedule — weekly to week 14, then every 2 weeks, then every 4 weeks in patients reaching at least a very good partial response by week 24. That de-escalating schedule is part of the tested intervention's identity and is named as such. The comparative limb is an external-control analysis (LINKER-MM1 phase 2 cohort n=105 vs 149 real-world standard-care patients, inverse-probability weighted; response odds ratio 3.8, survival hazard ratio 0.41) — observational, labelled as such, and supportive only. Patient-reported outcomes improved in responders and worsened numerically in non-responders, tracking response rather than adding an independent benefit claim. Harms mirror the BCMA class: infections in ~74–75% (grade ≥3 in ~48% in the follow-up report), cytokine release syndrome 46% (grade 3 in 1% in follow-up), neutropenia 44%.

title: First-line steroids in newly diagnosed ITP: SPLIT — dexamethasone faster early, no proven durability advantage over prednisone
question: In adults with newly diagnosed primary ITP, does high-dose dexamethasone (40 mg × 4 days, one or more cycles), versus standard-dose prednisone tapered over weeks, produce faster and more durable platelet responses?
balance: SPLIT — and the split is the answer to the commonest first-line ITP question. On speed and early response, high-dose dexamethasone wins: Wei 2016 (n=192 randomised; 95 dexamethasone, 97 prednisone) found initial overall response 82.1% vs 67.4% and complete response 50.5% vs 26.8%, with shorter time to response; the meta-analysis of nine randomised trials (n=1,138) likewise found higher response at 14 days (79% vs 59%; relative risk 1.22). On durability, the advantage disappears: Wei's sustained response was 40.0% vs 41.2% (the treatment made no difference), the meta-analysis found no difference in overall response at 6 months (54% vs 43%; relative risk 1.16, 95% CI 0.79–1.71), and the second randomised trial (n=113) found persistent responses at 12 months actually favouring prednisone (80.65% vs 55.56%). Regimens differ between trials (one or two 4-day dexamethasone courses in Wei; three courses every 14 days in Mazzucconi), which is part of why the durability limb is inconsistent. Harm burden differs by shape rather than clearly by total: short intense dexamethasone pulses (generally tolerated better in Wei; fewer reported toxicities in the meta-analysis) vs weeks of tapered prednisone exposure. Practical read: choose dexamethasone when a rapid rise matters (severe bleeding risk), without expecting more durable remission.
stamp: SPLIT

title: Arimoclomol in Niemann-Pick disease type C: slowed progression in one 50-patient randomised trial, strongest with miglustat
question: In patients with Niemann-Pick disease type C, does arimoclomol (with or without miglustat), versus placebo, slow progression on the NPC clinical severity scale?
balance: One small randomised trial is the whole controlled base: NPC-002 randomised 50 patients aged 2–18 years (34 arimoclomol, 16 placebo) for 12 months and found slower progression on the 5-domain NPC Clinical Severity Scale (mean change 0.76 vs 2.15; treatment difference −1.40, 95% CI −2.76 to −0.03; P=.046) — a borderline-significant result in 50 patients, with the effect larger in the prespecified miglustat stratum (difference −2.06; P=.006), where arimoclomol essentially stabilised scores. Most patients received miglustat as routine care, so this is substantially an add-on question — and the US approval (September 2024) is explicitly in combination with miglustat. The rescored 4-domain analysis is a post-hoc re-scoring of the same trial (difference −1.70; P=.0155), supportive but not independent. The 48-month open-label extension (41 entered, 29 completed) has no control group: switchers from placebo slowed after starting arimoclomol, consistent with — not proof of — a sustained effect. Tolerability was good (serious adverse events 14.7% on arimoclomol vs 31.3% on placebo in the trial; two treatment-related serious events, urticaria and angioedema). Product naming (clarification exception, as directed for this shelf): arimoclomol (Miplyffa, Zevra Therapeutics) — the tested product as published. The stamp carries the small base: N = 50 randomised patients underpin every efficacy claim.
stamp: POSSIBLE — based on a small N = 50

title: Levacetylleucine in Niemann-Pick disease type C: a 1.28-point SARA advantage over placebo in a 60-patient crossover trial
question: In patients with Niemann-Pick disease type C, does levacetylleucine (N-acetyl-L-leucine), versus placebo in a crossover design, improve ataxia and neurological function on the SARA and related scales?
balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED: one small randomised programme from a single sponsor. The phase 3 crossover trial (60 patients) found a least-squares mean SARA difference of -1.28 points favouring levacetylleucine over 12 weeks (95% CI -1.91 to -0.65; P<0.001), and the earlier open-label rater-blinded phase 2 (33 patients) met its blinded-rater primary endpoint, with the effect lost after washout — the pattern of a symptomatic treatment. The 2025 open-label extension compares 53 patients against a historical natural-history trajectory and its authors frame the result as disease-modifying and neuroprotective; that framing is the investigators' interpretation of a Class IV, historically controlled comparison, not a randomised finding, and is labelled as such here. A separate phase 3 trial in ataxia-telangiectasia asks a different disease question and is cross-pointed in prose only, not carded here. title: Selumetinib in NF1 plexiform neurofibromas (SPRINT): confirmed partial responses in 70% of 50 children, single-arm against natural history
question: In children with neurofibromatosis type 1 and symptomatic, inoperable plexiform neurofibromas, does selumetinib, versus natural history with no concurrent control, shrink tumour volume and improve pain and function?
balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED: single-arm evidence throughout, framed as such. In the SPRINT phase 2 study, 35 of 50 children (70%) had a confirmed partial response (≥20% volumetric shrinkage), most durable ≥1 year, with a mean 2-point fall in child-reported tumour pain at 1 year; the preceding phase 1 study saw confirmed partial responses in 17 of 24 children (71%). There is no randomised or concurrent control — the comparison is with the known natural history of plexiform neurofibromas, which rarely shrink spontaneously, which is why volumetric response carries weight despite the design; the stamp still caps at POSSIBLE for a single programme without a control arm. Harms are dominated by gastrointestinal effects, acneiform rash, paronychia and asymptomatic creatine kinase rises; 5 of 50 children stopped for possibly related toxicity, and ocular and cardiac monitoring is part of the treatment burden. A different MEK inhibitor programme in a broader (adult-inclusive) population asks a separate question and is cross-pointed in prose only. Product naming (clarification exception): selumetinib (Koselugo, AstraZeneca) as published.

title: Thymic involution: the epithelial space shrinks from the first year of life, TREC output falls with age, and the adult naive T-cell pool is kept up mainly by peripheral division
question: In healthy humans, how fast does thymic epithelial volume and thymic output (signal-joint T-cell receptor excision circles, recent thymic emigrants) fall from childhood to old age, how much of the naive T-cell pool in older adults is maintained by peripheral division rather than new thymic production, and what happens to repertoire diversity?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED for the involution and output decline, framed by the standard textbook account (Guyton & Hall / Ganong tradition): the thymus is largest relative to body size in childhood and its T-cell-producing epithelial tissue is progressively replaced by fat and connective tissue with age. The primary human record fetched agrees and quantifies it: morphometry of 204 thymuses (ages 1 month to 107 years) shows total organ size roughly constant (median 19.5 cm3) while the epithelial space involutes continuously from the first year of life on a negative-logarithmic course, independent of puberty (Steinmann 1985). Function follows structure: T-cell receptor excision circle (TREC) measurements show thymic output declining with age yet remaining substantial into late adulthood (Douek 1998). Two cautions are EMERGING-grade within this shelf: TREC content is diluted by peripheral division, so it is only an indirect gauge of output (Hazenberg 2000), and deuterium-labelling work concludes the adult human naive pool is maintained almost exclusively by peripheral division rather than new thymic production (den Braber 2012) — the exact quantitative split between production and peripheral maintenance in the elderly is model-dependent. Repertoire diversity figures that no fetched record measured are not stated here.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED

title: The normal endometrial cycle: ~12 mm thick at ovulation on ultrasound, histologic dating far less precise than the classic criteria claimed, and measured loss over 80 mL in only a third of women complaining of heavy periods
question: In healthy ovulatory women, how does the endometrium change across the cycle (thickness, glandular and stromal histology by cycle day), what mechanism triggers shedding (progesterone withdrawal, spiral-artery vasoconstriction, tissue breakdown), and how much blood is actually lost in a normal cycle when measured objectively?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED for the cycle pattern and the progesterone-withdrawal mechanism, framed by the standard reproductive-physiology textbook account (Cunningham's / Ganong tradition): oestrogen drives proliferative growth, ovulation switches the gland to progesterone-driven secretion, and progesterone withdrawal at the end of an infertile cycle triggers spiral-artery vasoconstriction, ischaemia and tissue breakdown — the shedding mechanism is presented here as the textbook's account, because the classic experimental observations behind it could not be carded from verifiable records this session (see the Synthesis card's refusals). What the fetched primary record does quantify: on serial transvaginal ultrasound in 23 healthy volunteers the endometrium reaches a mean 12 mm (both layers) at ovulation and then plateaus (Bakos 1993); MRI in 6 women shows endometrial area rising linearly through the follicular phase with the rate dropping after ovulation (Haynor 1986; N = 6, printed plainly). The classic histologic dating criteria are much less precise than originally claimed — in 130 fertile women they could not reliably distinguish any specific cycle day (Murray 2004). For measured loss, the distribution is method-bound (alkaline haematin): among 226 women referred complaining of heavy periods, only 34% actually measured over 80 mL (Warner 2004) — the >80 mL line is a statistical tail definition, and the population mean of roughly 30-40 mL often quoted from the classic Swedish population study is the textbook's account, since that study's record could not be verified this session.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED

title: Rolapitant for chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting: delayed-phase complete response 71% versus 60-62% across three phase 3 trials
question: In adults receiving moderately or highly emetogenic chemotherapy, does rolapitant (single-dose oral NK1 antagonist, as tested) added to a 5-HT3 antagonist plus dexamethasone improve complete response in the delayed phase versus the same backbone without an NK1 antagonist?
balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED: three phase 3 trials, carded as trials not papers (the HEC paper reports two trials, HEC-1 and HEC-2, and they are carded as one programme card with both results printed, not as two independent trials). Delayed-phase complete response favoured rolapitant in every trial: HEC-1 73% versus 58%, HEC-2 70% versus 62%, pooled HEC 71% versus 60%, and the moderately emetogenic/anthracycline-cyclophosphamide trial 71% versus 62% (odds ratio 1.6, 95% CI 1.2-2.0). The meta-analysis of five randomised trials (n=2984) agrees (delayed complete response odds ratio 1.68, 95% CI 1.44-1.96 — a relative measure; the absolute gains are the 8-15 percentage points printed on the cards). Adverse events were similar to control, with fatigue, constipation and headache the commonest treatment-related events and no treatment-related deaths. Product naming (clarification exception): rolapitant (Varubi, TESARO) as published, a single 180 mg oral dose before chemotherapy.

title: Granisetron transdermal patch for CINV: non-inferior to oral, intravenous and ondansetron comparators in most trials — with a day-1 weakness in the Chinese phase 3
question: In adults receiving multi-day or moderately/highly emetogenic chemotherapy, does the granisetron transdermal system (patch, as tested) prevent chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting as effectively as oral/intravenous 5-HT3 antagonists (including palonosetron comparators), particularly in the long-delayed phase?
balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED: the claim tested is equivalence, not superiority, and comparators differ by trial, so the cards are kept per-comparator and never pooled into one efficacy number. The patch met its prespecified 15% non-inferiority margin against daily oral granisetron in multi-day chemotherapy (complete control 60% versus 65%), against intravenous/oral granisetron in moderately emetogenic chemotherapy (complete response 75.0% versus 74.6%), against palonosetron in the acute phase of a crossover study (75.2% versus 79.8% of cycles), and against ondansetron in highly emetogenic chemotherapy (86.84% versus 90.36%). The exception is the Chinese phase 3 trial: complete control was numerically lower with the patch (47.52% versus 59.29%; p=0.0559), driven by a significantly worse day 1 (70.13% versus 91.03%) — the patch's slow onset is its real weakness, and the stamp stays at POSSIBLE because of it. Constipation was the commonest adverse event throughout. Product naming (clarification exception): the granisetron transdermal system (Sancuso patch, as published), one patch delivering granisetron continuously for up to 7 days.

title: Octreotide for chemotherapy-induced diarrhoea: treatment trials positive (19 of 21 resolved versus 3 of 20 on loperamide), prophylaxis negative in RTOG 0315 — SPLIT
question: In adults with chemotherapy-induced diarrhoea (fluoropyrimidine- or cisplatin-based) that persists despite standard loperamide, does octreotide control diarrhoea (stool frequency / grade) versus placebo or versus continued loperamide — and does prophylactic long-acting octreotide prevent chemoradiation-induced diarrhoea in anorectal cancer?
balance: SPLIT — the split is treatment versus prevention, and the two limbs must not be merged. Treatment limb: in two small 1990s randomised trials, octreotide controlled established chemotherapy diarrhoea — resolution in 19 of 21 patients versus 3 of 20 on loperamide in fluorouracil-induced diarrhoea (n=41), and diarrhoea in 5% versus 75% against placebo after cisplatin (n=43); Ns are printed on the face because these trials are small by modern standards. Prevention limb: the large modern trial went the other way — in RTOG 0315 (n=215), prophylactic long-acting octreotide did not reduce grade 2-4 acute diarrhoea during chemoradiation for anorectal cancer (44% versus 49% on placebo; P=.21) (the treatment made no difference), with no benefit in bowel function or quality of life. So: plausible rescue treatment on thin old evidence; prophylaxis tested and negative.
stamp: SPLIT

title: Probiotics for chemotherapy/radiotherapy diarrhoea: large positive trials for two named preparations, a null trial for a third — preparations are not interchangeable (SPLIT)
question: In adults receiving chemotherapy and/or pelvic radiotherapy, do orally administered probiotics (the named strains/preparations as tested) prevent or reduce grade 2 or worse treatment-induced diarrhoea versus placebo?
balance: SPLIT — the split is by preparation and setting, because probiotic preparations are NOT interchangeable: each card names the exact tested product/strains as published (clarification exception), and where a publication does not identify its product beyond genus composition, the card says so plainly; current commercial products may differ from what was tested in safety and effectiveness. Positive limb: the high-potency preparation VSL#3 (as named in the trial) cut radiation-induced diarrhoea from 51.8% to 31.6% in 482 analysed patients, and live Lactobacillus acidophilus plus Bifidobacterium bifidum cut grade 2-3 diarrhoea during cervical-cancer radiotherapy from 45% to 9% in 63 patients; a 100-patient colorectal trial of an unnamed-composition combination also reported significantly less diarrhoea. Null/mixed limb: a 28-patient 2025 trial of a named five-strain mixture found no significant benefit, and a 52-patient six-strain trial's clear effects were on inflammatory cytokines, not a demonstrated diarrhoea reduction. The chemotherapy-diarrhoea meta-analysis (13 trials, 1024 patients) pools these unlike preparations into a relative risk of 0.47 for total diarrhoea — a relative measure across heterogeneous products, printed here as the synthesis it is, not as a claim about any one product. Per the coordinator's note, an earlier VSL#3 radiation-diarrhoea report whose PubMed record has an empty abstract was excluded and is not carded; this shelf stands on the anchors below. Probiotic content for perioperative GI-surgery infections is homed on a separate shelf and cross-pointed in prose only.

title: Caphosol (supersaturated calcium phosphate rinse) for mucositis: adult transplant trials positive, the paediatric trial negative — SPLIT
question: In patients undergoing haematopoietic stem-cell transplantation (or other mucositis-intensive chemotherapy), does a supersaturated calcium phosphate oral rinse (the tested Caphosol programme) reduce incidence, severity or duration of oral mucositis versus saline / standard oral care?
balance: SPLIT — the split is adult versus paediatric programmes, carded as separate limbs as the slate directs. Adult limb: two randomised trials favoured the rinse — in 95 HSCT patients, Caphosol plus fluoride versus fluoride rinse alone cut days of mucositis (3.72 versus 7.22; P=0.001) and morphine dose (34.54 mg versus 122.78 mg); in 40 allogeneic HSCT patients, a supersaturated calcium phosphate rinse versus customary topical solutions lowered WHO oral toxicity (0.9 versus 1.8; P=0.02) and peak mouth pain. Paediatric limb: the largest and most rigorous trial went the other way — in 220 children and adolescents undergoing myeloablative HCT, Caphosol versus placebo saline did not reduce severe mucositis duration at all (4.5 ± 5.0 versus 4.5 ± 4.8 days; P=0.99) (the treatment made no difference). Product naming (clarification exception): Caphosol, a neutral supersaturated Ca2+/PO43- oral rinse, as published; the 2012 trial tested the same class of rinse (SCPR) against a non-saline customary-care control, which is part of why the adult limb is graded cautiously.
stamp: SPLIT

title: Zinc sulfate for radiation-induced taste change: the largest trial (NCCTG, 169 patients) was negative, two small trials positive, one chemoradiation trial negative — SPLIT, set by the largest trial
question: In patients with head-and-neck cancer receiving radiotherapy or chemoradiotherapy, does zinc sulfate supplementation prevent or lessen treatment-induced taste alteration (dysgeusia) versus placebo?
balance: SPLIT — and per the slate flag, the balance is set by the largest trial, not the smaller positive ones. The NCCTG phase 3 double-blind trial (169 evaluable patients) found zinc sulfate 45 mg three times daily did not prevent taste alterations during oral/pharyngeal radiotherapy (73% versus 84% reported taste alterations in the first 2 months; p=0.16) and did not speed taste recovery. Against that stand two small positive trials: Ripamonti 1998 (n=18) found less worsening and faster recovery of measured taste thresholds on the same 45 mg three-times-daily dose started when taste change appeared, and Najafizade 2013 (n=35 completers) found thresholds rose significantly on placebo but barely on zinc 50 mg three times daily. A fourth trial in oral-cancer chemoradiation (Khan 2019, n=70) found no benefit for most tastes. Total evidence base is about 292 patients across four trials pointing both ways — SPLIT, weighted sceptical.
stamp: SPLIT

title: Methadone as the first strong opioid for cancer pain: analgesia equal to morphine in three small comparative trials — paid for in drop-outs, dose instability and monitoring
question: In adults with cancer pain requiring a first-line strong opioid, does methadone provide analgesia equivalent to morphine, at what cost in adverse effects, dose instability and QT/monitoring burden?
balance: Methadone gave analgesia equivalent to morphine as a first-line strong opioid — never superior — across the three comparative trials carded here (229 patients in total, so this shelf carries small-base labelling). In the double-blind multicentre trial (Bruera 2004), the proportion with at least 20% pain improvement at 4 weeks was 0.49 on methadone versus 0.56 on morphine, but opioid-related drop-outs were 22% (11 of 49) on methadone versus 6% (3 of 54) on morphine (P = .019). In the three-way randomised comparison (Mercadante 2008), pain, symptoms and adverse effects did not differ between methadone, sustained-release morphine and transdermal fentanyl, the opioid escalation index was significantly lower with methadone, yet methadone needed more up-and-down dose changes — the dose-instability cost named in the question. The small pharmacokinetic comparison (Gourlay 1986, N = 18) explains why: methadone's terminal half-life was 30.4 hours with wide between-patient variation (SD 16.3 hours) against 2.7 hours for morphine, so dosing intervals need individual adjustment and accumulation is a real risk without close monitoring. This shelf is the first-line slice only: methadone for refractory neuropathic cancer pain under specialist supervision is a different question, homed on the library's existing methadone shelf (#5754), whose Cochrane synthesis is not re-carded here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: methadone is a usable first-line alternative with equivalent analgesia, bought with more drop-outs, harder titration and a monitoring burden morphine does not carry.
stamp: POSSIBLE — based on a small base of 229 patients in three comparative trials: methadone gave analgesia equivalent to morphine as a first-line strong opioid for cancer pain, with more opioid-related drop-outs (22% vs 6% in the double-blind trial), more up-and-down dose changes, and a long, highly variable half-life requiring close monitoring; no trial showed superiority

title: Dexamethasone for breathlessness in advanced cancer: the definitive trial found no difference from placebo — and more harm
question: In adults with advanced cancer and dyspnoea, does systemic dexamethasone (the doses tested) reduce breathlessness intensity versus placebo, and what is the cost in hyperglycaemia, insomnia and other steroid effects over days-to-weeks horizons?
balance: The largest and best trial is null, and it was stopped for futility: in the ABCD trial (128 randomised), high-dose dexamethasone and placebo both improved dyspnoea by 1.6 points at day 7, with a between-group difference of 0 (95% CI -0.8 to 0.7; P = 0.48) — dexamethasone made no difference (the treatment made no difference) — while infections, insomnia and serious adverse events were all more frequent on dexamethasone. The earlier pilot RCT (Hui 2016, N = 41) found faster within-group improvement on dexamethasone but no statistically significant between-arm difference. The symptom-cluster secondary analysis (Yennurajalingam 2016, N = 114) found no significant change in the pain/dyspnoea cluster. The Cochrane review (Haywood 2019) pooled the only two trials then available (157 participants enrolled, 114 analysed) to a mean difference of -0.85 points (95% CI -1.73 to 0.03) at one week on very low-quality evidence — a confidence interval that includes no effect, and a pool the later ABCD trial outweighs. Hyperglycaemia is a recognised steroid cost in this population but was not quantified in the carded records, so this shelf does not put a number on it. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): routine dexamethasone for unselected cancer dyspnoea is not supported; any benefit is unproven and the harm signal is consistent.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — dexamethasone made no difference to dyspnoea versus placebo in the largest trial (ABCD, N = 128, stopped for futility; the treatment made no difference), smaller reports are inconclusive, and infections, insomnia and serious adverse events were more frequent on dexamethasone
