title: Jaw-stretching devices for trismus: they widen an already stiff jaw, they do not prevent the stiffness — and patients find them hard to keep using
question: In patients with head-and-neck cancer at risk of, or with established, radiation/surgery-related trismus, do jaw-exercise programmes and stretching devices (as tested) preserve or improve maximal interincisal opening versus no exercise / usual care?
balance: SPLIT, and the split is treatment versus prevention. For established trismus, the meta-analysis of 13 randomised trials (733 patients) found exercise therapy with a jaw-mobilising device significantly improved maximal interincisal opening; for prevention, the same analysis found no significant difference in trismus incidence versus usual care (risk ratio 1.20, 95% CI 0.61 to 2.34). The head-to-head device trial (van der Geer 2020, N = 27) found no significant difference between the two named devices — mouth opening rose 3.0 mm with the TheraBite programme and 1.5 mm with the Dynasplint programme — and exercising was hard: pain, fitting problems and deterioration stopped many patients. The prevention feasibility trial (Zatarain 2018, N = 40) found adding the Jaw Dynasplint to conventional stretching lowered compliance (only 25% used it as prescribed) and trismus was diagnosed in 4 Dynasplint patients versus 2 controls. Device names are given as published, per the clarification exception: the TheraBite Jaw Motion Rehabilitation System and the Dynasplint Trismus System (the Jaw Dynasplint System in the prevention trial). PROPOSED SPLIT: jaw exercise with a device probably helps established trismus; it does not prevent trismus, and adherence is the binding constraint either way.
stamp: SPLIT — exercise with a jaw-mobilising device improves mouth opening in established trismus (meta-analysis of 13 RCTs), but does not prevent trismus during radiotherapy (risk ratio 1.20, 95% CI 0.61 to 2.34), the two named devices did not differ, and adherence to device regimens was poor

title: Pentoxifylline plus vitamin E for superficial radiation fibrosis: one small randomised trial and the founding centre's cohorts show slow regression — over years, not months
question: In patients with established superficial radiation-induced fibrosis (non-jaw sites), does combined pentoxifylline plus tocopherol (vitamin E) regress fibrosis area/volume and improve function versus placebo or no treatment?
balance: GAP-E framing, labelled observational: the direct randomised base for superficial (non-jaw) radiation fibrosis is one small double-blind trial from the founding centre, and everything else carded here is that centre's uncontrolled cohort programme. In the randomised trial (Delanian 2003; 24 women, 29 fibrosis areas), combined pentoxifylline 800 mg/day plus tocopherol (vitamin E) 1,000 units/day for 6 months regressed fibrosis surface by 60% ± 10% versus 43% ± 17% on double placebo (P = .038), and each drug alone was ineffective — the combination is the intervention. The founding centre's earlier cohort (Delanian 1999; 43 patients, 50 areas) reported continuous regression on the same combination (surface area -53% at 6 months, -66% at 12 months), and its kinetics report (Delanian 2005; 44 patients) estimated a maximum effect of 68% surface regression reached after a mean of 24 months, with a rebound after stopping short treatment (+40% surface area at 1 year in the short-treatment group versus +8.5% after long treatment). The adjacent randomised limb in the same programme — pentoxifylline-tocopherol-clodronate for radiation plexopathy — was negative, a reminder that this programme's uncontrolled successes have not always survived randomisation. The jaw osteoradionecrosis question is a different shelf in this library and none of its cards is borrowed here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational cohorts plus one small randomised trial: combined pentoxifylline-tocopherol probably regresses superficial radiation fibrosis, slowly, over years of treatment.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational cohorts plus one small randomised trial (24 women): combined pentoxifylline + tocopherol regressed superficial radiation fibrosis more than placebo (60% vs 43% surface regression at 6 months), with cohort evidence of slow further regression over 2-3 years and rebound after early stopping; no independent-centre replication

title: Preventing acute radiation proctitis: prophylactic sucralfate does not work by either route — and mesalazine made things worse
question: In adults receiving pelvic radiotherapy (chiefly prostate), do prophylactic rectal/oral sucralfate regimens (or the other tested prophylactic agents in the same trial programmes) prevent acute radiation proctitis versus placebo?
balance: Prophylaxis does not work, and the trials are consistent about it. Rectal sucralfate enemas made no difference to acute proctitis in the phase III double-blind trial (some degree of proctitis in 88% on sucralfate versus 95% on placebo; grade 2 in 61% versus 71%, all differences non-significant), and its 5-year follow-on found no significant difference in late toxicity either (late grade 2 probability 5% versus 12%, P = 0.26; late rectal bleeding 54% versus 59%). Oral sucralfate in the largest trial (338 patients) made no difference to any bowel symptom and was associated with more rectal bleeding (64% versus 47%, P = 0.001). In the three-arm trial, hydrocortisone foam was not superior to sucralfate (hazard ratio 0.7, 95% CI 0.5 to 1.2) and mesalazine gel was significantly worse (hazard ratio 2.5, 95% CI 1.1 to 5.7) — its arm was stopped early. This shelf asks the prevention question only: treatment of established chronic radiation proctopathy (hyperbaric oxygen, sucralfate enemas as treatment, formalin, argon plasma) is a different question, homed on the library's existing chronic radiation proctopathy shelf (#6870), and its treatment evidence must not be read across to prevention. PROPOSED LIKELY (no benefit): prophylactic sucralfate, rectal or oral, does not prevent acute radiation proctitis.
stamp: LIKELY (no benefit) — prophylactic sucralfate, rectal or oral, made no difference to acute radiation proctitis across three randomised trials (the treatment made no difference), oral sucralfate was associated with more rectal bleeding, hydrocortisone was not superior, and mesalazine appeared harmful

title: Frozen gloves and socks against taxane nail damage: striking protection in within-patient studies, no effect in the randomised trial — and the cold drives patients out
question: In patients receiving taxane chemotherapy, does local cryotherapy (frozen glove/sock, as tested) prevent taxane-induced nail toxicity (onycholysis, subungual haemorrhage, nail loss) versus the untreated contralateral hand/foot?
balance: SPLIT, and the split is by study design. The within-patient frozen glove and sock studies from the French programme (Scotté 2005, 45 patients; Scotté 2008, 50 patients) found much less nail toxicity on the protected side — onycholysis grade 1-2 in 11% of protected hands versus 51% of control hands, and grade 1-2 nail toxicity in 0% of protected feet versus 21% of control feet — using the Elasto-Gel frozen glove and sock as published. But the only conventionally randomised trial (McCarthy 2014) found no significant differences between gloved and ungloved hands, with a 60% withdrawal rate for discomfort and only 21 of 53 enrolled patients evaluable; and a 200-patient comparative study (Can 2012) also found no significant difference with frozen gloves and socks. The meta-analysis (Huang 2019; 3 RCTs and 6 prospective studies, 708 patients) pools to a lower total nail toxicity with cryotherapy (risk ratio 0.49, 95% CI 0.30 to 0.79 — a relative measure), driven largely by the within-patient studies. This shelf asks the nail question only: cryotherapy for chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy is homed on the library's existing paclitaxel cryotherapy shelf and its compression/cryocompression companion shelf, and none of their neuropathy endpoints is re-carded here. PROPOSED SPLIT: cooling probably reduces docetaxel nail toxicity in patients who can tolerate it, but the randomised evidence is null and tolerability is the weak point.
stamp: SPLIT — within-patient frozen glove/sock studies found much less nail toxicity on the cooled side (onycholysis grade 1-2: 11% vs 51%), but the randomised trial and a 200-patient comparison found no significant difference, and 60% of randomised-trial patients withdrew because of cold discomfort

title: Training the breathing muscles before bypass surgery: pulmonary complications halved in high-risk patients — in one centre's trial programme
question: In adults at high risk of postoperative pulmonary complications undergoing coronary-artery bypass (or other major cardiac) surgery, does preoperative inspiratory muscle training reduce postoperative pulmonary complications and length of stay versus sham / usual preoperative care?
balance: One programme dominates this evidence, and it is positive. In the Hulzebos randomised trial (279 high-risk CABG patients), preoperative inspiratory muscle training cut postoperative pulmonary complications from 35.0% to 18.0% (odds ratio 0.52, 95% CI 0.30 to 0.92) and pneumonia from 16.1% to 6.5% (odds ratio 0.40, 95% CI 0.19 to 0.84), and shortened median postoperative stay from 8 to 7 days (P = .02). The same programme's pilot (26 patients) found significantly less atelectasis and good feasibility, and its secondary quality-of-life analysis (235 patients) confirmed the pneumonia and stay benefits while finding no quality-of-life improvement. The Cochrane review of preoperative physical therapy for elective cardiac surgery (8 trials, 856 patients) points the same way — atelectasis relative risk 0.52 (95% CI 0.32 to 0.87) and pneumonia relative risk 0.45 (95% CI 0.24 to 0.83), both relative measures — but it pools mixed physical-therapy programmes, not inspiratory muscle training alone. This is the preoperative prehabilitation question only: inspiratory muscle training for COPD and for weaning from prolonged ventilation are different questions, homed on their own shelves in this library, and none of their evidence is re-carded here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): preoperative inspiratory muscle training probably prevents pulmonary complications in high-risk CABG patients — resting largely on one centre's trial programme.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — preoperative inspiratory muscle training reduced postoperative pulmonary complications (18.0% vs 35.0%) and pneumonia (6.5% vs 16.1%) in one high-risk CABG trial programme, with a concordant Cochrane review; quality of life did not improve and independent replication is lacking

title: Showering with chlorhexidine before surgery: the skin gets cleaner, the wound-infection rate does not clearly fall
question: In adults undergoing elective surgery, does preoperative whole-body bathing/showering with chlorhexidine (wash or impregnated cloths, as tested) at home before admission reduce surgical-site infection versus plain soap / no antiseptic bathing?
balance: SPLIT, and the split is comparator and era. Against placebo detergent, the largest trial (Lynch/Byrne 1992, 3,482 patients) found wound infection rates essentially identical (inpatient 5.79% versus 5.75%; outpatient 8.54% versus 9.38%) and chlorhexidine not cost-effective, and the Cochrane review (Webster & Osborne 2015; 7 trials, 10,157 participants) pooled chlorhexidine versus placebo to a relative risk of 0.91 (95% CI 0.80 to 1.04) — no clear benefit — and versus bar soap to 1.02 (95% CI 0.57 to 1.84). Against weaker comparators the older trials look better: Hayek 1987 (1,989 patients) found overall infection of 9.0% on chlorhexidine versus 12.8% on bar soap and 11.7% on placebo, and Wihlborg 1987 (1,530 operations) reported a significant reduction with chlorhexidine showering versus local washing or no washing. Chlorhexidine unquestionably reduces skin bacterial counts (Garibaldi 1988) — the gap between cleaner skin and fewer infections is the story of this literature. The Cochrane verdict is presented here as it stands: equivocal, with no clear evidence of benefit over other wash products. This shelf asks the at-home, whole-population preoperative bathing question only: universal ICU decolonisation and intraoperative skin preparation are different questions, homed on their own shelves in this library (live shelves #587 and #656), and none of their trials is re-carded here. PROPOSED SPLIT: bathing with chlorhexidine before surgery has not been shown to beat placebo or soap in the largest trials, whatever it does to skin flora.
stamp: SPLIT — chlorhexidine bathing reduced wound infection versus soap or no washing in older trials, but versus placebo the largest trial (N = 3,482) found identical infection rates and the Cochrane pool (10,157 participants) shows no clear benefit (relative risk 0.91, 95% CI 0.80 to 1.04)

title: TAR versus anterior component separation for large incisional hernias: less wound trouble in the cohort evidence, no proven recurrence gain — and almost no randomised data
question: In adults with complex/large incisional hernias, does posterior component separation with transversus abdominis release (TAR) reduce recurrence and wound morbidity versus anterior component separation (with or without mesh), and how do open and robotic TAR compare?
balance: Evidence-question (GAP-E) framing: this comparison rests overwhelmingly on cohort studies pooled in systematic reviews, not on randomised trials — one small randomised study (43 patients) verified at build is the exception, and it is carded and labelled as such. The cohort syntheses agree that posterior component separation with transversus abdominis release (TAR) carries less wound morbidity than anterior component separation: overall wound complications odds ratio 2.58 favouring TAR (Mohamedahmed 2025; 8 studies, 2,293 patients), surgical site infection odds ratio 1.32, seroma odds ratio 1.93 and haematoma odds ratio 1.81 in the earlier synthesis (Oprea 2023; 19 studies, 3,412 patients) — odds ratios comparing anterior with posterior separation, printed as relative measures. Recurrence does not clearly favour TAR: 4.27% after anterior separation versus 6.11% after posterior separation in Oprea 2023, and no significant recurrence difference in Mohamedahmed 2025. Open TAR alone, pooled across 22 cohort studies (4,910 patients), shows 6% recurrence but 34% overall morbidity. The small randomised study (Demetrashvili 2025) found surgical site occurrences in 19% on TAR versus 50% on anterior separation (P = 0.033), with no significant differences in infection, recurrence or quality of life. Hybrid robotic TAR versus open TAR (propensity-matched cohorts) shortened stay (3 versus 5 days) with fewer surgical site occurrences (5% versus 15%). Pooled cohort rates must not be read as randomised effects. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational evidence, labelled: TAR probably reduces wound morbidity compared with anterior separation, with no proven recurrence advantage.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational evidence, labelled: posterior component separation with transversus abdominis release was associated with less wound morbidity than anterior component separation in cohort syntheses and in one small randomised study (N = 43), with no proven difference in recurrence; no large randomised trial exists

title: Biological mesh after extralevator APR (BIOPEX): no better wound healing — but far fewer perineal hernias at five years, in the only trial there is
question: In patients undergoing extralevator abdominoperineal resection for rectal cancer, does biological mesh closure of the pelvic floor reduce perineal wound complications and later perineal hernia versus primary perineal wound closure?
balance: Single-programme flag, stated plainly: every card on this shelf is one trial — BIOPEX, a Dutch multicentre randomised trial of 104 patients — reported at three horizons (the protocol paper, the primary results and the 5-year results). The reports are not three independent trials. On its primary endpoint the trial was negative: uncomplicated perineal wound healing at 30 days was 66% (33 of 50) after primary closure versus 63% (30 of 48) after biological mesh closure (relative risk 1.056, 95% CI 0.7854 to 1.4197; P = 0.7177) — the mesh made no difference to wound healing (the treatment made no difference). The hernia signal is the interesting half: freedom from perineal hernia at 1 year was 73% after primary closure versus 87% after mesh closure (P = 0.0316), and at 5 years the actuarial symptomatic perineal hernia rate was 7% (95% CI 0 to 30) after mesh versus 30% (95% CI 10 to 49) after primary closure (P = 0.006), with hernia repair in 2% versus 13% (P = 0.062). Quality of life, functional outcomes, recurrence and survival did not differ at 5 years. The mesh tested was a non-cross-linked porcine acellular dermal mesh; the trial record does not give a brand name, so none is claimed here. PROPOSED SPLIT: no wound-healing benefit, a real-looking late hernia benefit — from a single trial programme of 104 patients, which caps confidence.
stamp: SPLIT — single trial programme (BIOPEX, N = 104): biological mesh closure made no difference to perineal wound healing at 30 days (the treatment made no difference), but symptomatic perineal hernia at 5 years was lower after mesh (7% vs 30%); no other trial exists

title: Robotic versus laparoscopic hernia repair
question: In adults undergoing minimally invasive inguinal or ventral hernia repair, does robotic repair improve pain, recovery, recurrence or complications versus laparoscopic repair, and at what cost in operating time and resource use?
balance: SPLIT — the two limbs answer differently over time. Inguinal: the RIVAL randomised programme (102 patients, follow-on to 2 years) found no difference in pain, quality of life, wound events or recurrence (1 recurrence per arm at 2 years), while robotic repair took a median 75.5 versus 40.5 minutes and cost a median $3258 versus $1421. Ventral: the Houston blinded randomised trial (124 patients) found no difference in its primary outcome — days in hospital within 90 days (relative rate 0.90, 95% CI 0.37 to 2.19) — or in early complications, again with longer operating time (141 vs 77 minutes) and higher cost (adjusted difference $2767); its 2-year follow-on reported recurrence 4% robotic versus 13% laparoscopic (relative risk 0.3, 95% CI 0.06 to 1.39; not significant) and reoperation 0% versus 11% (P=0.019), which the authors themselves label hypothesis-generating. So: early outcomes and costs consistently favour laparoscopy or neutrality; a possible late durability advantage for robotic ventral repair is unconfirmed. A robotic-versus-open protocol exists with no results yet, so the open comparison is unanswered.
stamp: SPLIT

title: Balloon sinuplasty versus functional endoscopic sinus surgery
question: In adults with chronic rhinosinusitis (without polyps, or with limited disease) who are candidates for sinus surgery, does standalone balloon catheter dilation of the sinus ostia achieve symptom relief and patency comparable to functional endoscopic sinus surgery, with what recovery and revision-surgery trade-offs?
balance: POSSIBLE — one randomised programme plus one small independent trial point the same way, which caps the stamp. In REMODEL, standalone balloon dilation was noninferior to FESS for symptom improvement at 6 months (SNOT-20 improvement 1.67 vs 1.60) and at 1 year (−1.64 vs −1.65), with ostial patency 96.7% versus 98.7%, revision surgery 2% in each arm, and clear recovery advantages (debridements 0.1 vs 1.2 per patient; shorter pain-medication use and recovery time). The full-cohort/meta-analysis report (135 randomised patients; 358 pooled dilation patients) found comparability out to 24 months. An independent Finnish randomised trial against uncinectomy in isolated maxillary disease also found equal symptom improvement and less synechia with balloon treatment. The population fence is strict: uncomplicated maxillary, with or without anterior ethmoid, disease in patients who already met criteria for surgery. The tested dilation system is not named in the REMODEL record's abstract, so no brand claim is made here.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Inferior turbinate reduction techniques for nasal obstruction
question: In adults with chronic rhinitis / inferior turbinate hypertrophy and nasal obstruction despite medical therapy, does inferior turbinate reduction (radiofrequency ablation or the tested surgical techniques) improve nasal obstruction versus sham, medical therapy or alternative techniques?
balance: POSSIBLE — the sham-controlled limb rests on a single trial, which caps the stamp. In that trial (98 patients), radiofrequency ablation, diode laser and microdebrider-assisted turbinoplasty each reduced nasal-obstruction scores significantly more than a placebo procedure at 3 months (P=.03, .02 and .04 respectively) — while the placebo procedure itself also improved symptoms significantly, so the increment over sham is real but modest. Technique-comparison evidence is separate: temperature-controlled versus bipolar radiofrequency were equivalent on symptoms and objective measures to 1 year (84 patients; bipolar much faster to perform), and a split-side study (60 patients) ranked ultrasound reduction above radiofrequency above submucosal cauterisation. No record names a device brand or maker, so techniques are named generically here, exactly as published.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Punctal plugs for dry eye disease
question: In adults with dry eye disease, does punctal occlusion (punctal plugs, the types tested) improve symptoms, tear-film measures and corneal staining versus no occlusion / sham, and how do plug types compare on retention and complications (epiphora, canaliculitis, extrusion)?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the pooled evidence does not establish a symptom benefit. The Cochrane review (18 trials, 711 participants) found little or no improvement in symptom scores with punctal plugs versus no plugs (very low-certainty evidence), with only small favourable differences in fluorescein staining (mean difference −1.50 points in one trial) and tear-film stability (+1.93 seconds in one trial), and fewer artificial-tear applications in one trial. Small individual trials report within-group improvements in symptoms, break-up time and staining (SmartPlug vs silicone, 36 eyes; post-LASIK plugs vs no plugs, 18 patients — the one direct comparison favouring plugs on signs and symptoms), but most lack an untreated control. Where plug types were compared head-to-head, efficacy was similar and retention was the real difference: Parasol plugs (Odyssey Medical / Beaver Visitec, as published) were retained in 68% versus 32% for Super Flex plugs (Eagle Vision / Oasis Medical, as published) at 6 months, and one trial lost 33% of silicone plugs spontaneously. Harms are mostly epiphora, itching and displacement, with inflammatory complications such as dacryocystitis less common. Symptoms and signs are kept separate throughout, as they frequently disagree in this literature.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence)

title: Autologous serum eye drops for dry eye disease
question: In adults with moderate-to-severe dry eye disease (including Sjögren-related and post-LASIK), do autologous serum eye drops improve symptoms, corneal staining and tear-film measures versus artificial tears / conventional lubricant therapy?
balance: POSSIBLE — several small randomised trials agree on tear-film signs, while symptom effects are less consistent, which caps the stamp. Against artificial tears, 20% autologous serum (the commonest concentration where a record states one) prolonged tear break-up time in the severe-dry-eye crossover (20 patients; OSDI fell 55.18% on serum versus 19.50% on artificial tears, P<0.001, with no staining difference), improved nearly all clinical parameters in a 144-patient Hansen's-disease trial, and prolonged break-up time with lower rose Bengal staining after LASIK (27 patients) without a symptom difference. A pilot crossover found allogeneic serum comparable to autologous, with neither significantly improving OSDI. Preparation protocols vary between trials and one record does not state its concentration; where a publication does not document a standardised product, current preparations may differ in composition and effect. Sjögren-specific randomised evidence was not separately verified, so the shelf makes no Sjögren-specific claim.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Thermal pulsation (LipiFlow) for meibomian gland dysfunction
question: In adults with meibomian gland dysfunction and evaporative dry eye, does a single vectored thermal pulsation treatment (the tested LipiFlow programme) improve gland function, tear break-up and symptoms versus warm-compress / sham / alternative thermal pulsation systems, and how long does benefit last?
balance: SPLIT — the gland-function and symptom-superiority questions answer differently. Named as published, per the clarification exception: the tested system is LipiFlow® (vectored thermal pulsation). A single 12-minute treatment improved gland secretion number, secretion score and lipid layer thickness for at least 3 months versus warm compress with lid massage (50 subjects), and a second system, SYSTANE iLux, was noninferior to LipiFlow on gland score, break-up time and symptom bother at every visit out to 12 months (236 subjects). A 10-trial meta-analysis (761 patients) found LipiFlow superior to lid hygiene on OSDI (mean difference −7.4) and SPEED scores — but the Cochrane review (13 trials, 1155 participants) found conflicting symptom evidence versus warm compresses, no difference in gland expression or break-up time in that comparison, and low/very low certainty throughout, with thermostatic devices actually ahead on OSDI at 4 weeks in pooled data. Industry sponsorship is common in this base. No vision-threatening adverse events were reported in any carded trial.
stamp: SPLIT

title: Systemic antibiotics for chronic rhinosinusitis: doxycycline in polyps and long-term macrolides
question: In adults with chronic rhinosinusitis, do systemic antibiotics — oral doxycycline in CRSwNP, and long-term low-dose macrolide in CRS (chiefly without polyps) — improve symptoms, endoscopy and polyp size versus placebo?
balance: SPLIT — each limb is internally mixed, and the limbs are never pooled. Doxycycline in CRSwNP (3 randomised reports, 196 patients): polyp size fell significantly versus placebo with an effect present at 12 weeks in a 47-patient three-arm trial, and SNOT-22 and smell improved versus placebo in a 100-patient trial (P=.037 and P=.048) — but adding doxycycline to a 20-day oral steroid course made no difference in a 49-patient trial that lost ~53% of participants. Long-term low-dose macrolide in CRS (3 randomised reports, 190 patients): roxithromycin 150 mg daily for 3 months improved SNOT-20, endoscopy and saccharine transit time versus placebo (64 patients, benefit correlating with low IgE), and postoperative azithromycin improved SNOT-22 statistically without proven clinical significance (66 patients) — but the MACS trial of weekly azithromycin in recalcitrant disease (60 patients) found no benefit on any symptom, endoscopic, flow, smell or microbiology outcome (the treatment made no difference). Antimicrobial resistance and, for macrolides, QT prolongation are the standing harms of long courses and are not measured by these small trials.
stamp: SPLIT

title: Normal carotid–femoral pulse wave velocity by age and blood pressure
question: In healthy humans, what is normal carotid–femoral pulse wave velocity by age and blood-pressure category — the Reference Values for Arterial Stiffness Collaboration distributions — and how much of the age rise is pressure-dependent versus intrinsic wall stiffening?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Framed by Guyton & Hall's account of arterial distensibility — a stiffer aorta transmits the pulse wave faster — the human reference data are consistent across three large primary studies. The Reference Values for Arterial Stiffness Collaboration (11,092 reference individuals; 1455 with optimal/normal pressure as the 'normal' subset) established cfPWV reference tables by age decade and blood-pressure category, finding the age rise steepens at higher pressures and the pressure effect grows with age. In strictly healthy ELSA-Brasil adults (2158), cfPWV was higher in men (8.74 ± 1.15 vs 8.31 ± 1.13 m/s) and higher whenever mean arterial pressure reached 85 mmHg; major risk factors doubled the age-related slope of rise (about 0.09 vs 0.05 m/s per year in men), so much of the population age rise is pressure/risk-factor-dependent, with a residual rise in healthy normotensive people that reflects intrinsic wall stiffening. The Spanish EVA study (501 randomly sampled adults) found a mean cfPWV of 6.53 ± 2.03 m/s at ages 35–75, with age, sex and mean pressure explaining 49% of variance. Cross-points: endothelial vasodilatation/flow-mediated dilatation is a different quantity, covered elsewhere in the library.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED

title: Normative heart rate variability values by age and sex
question: In healthy humans, what are normal short-term heart rate variability values (SDNN, RMSSD, LF/HF power) by age and sex, and how steeply do time- and frequency-domain indices fall across adult life?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Framed by Guyton & Hall's and Ganong's accounts of autonomic control of the heart — beat-to-beat variation as the visible signature of vagal and sympathetic modulation of the sinoatrial node — four primary human datasets agree on the shape of normality. A 44-study collation (21,438 healthy participants) found published short-term HRV values lower than the 1996 Task Force norms, with enormous inter-individual variation in spectral measures (up to 260,000%). The Danish DanFunD population study (6891 adults) provides age- and sex-stratified time- and frequency-domain reference values, with parasympathetic predominance commoner in women and younger adults. A Korean cohort (1828) shows conventional time- and frequency-domain indices falling more steeply with age than entropy measures, and Framingham (2722) shows age and heart rate are the dominant determinants of every measure (partial R² 0.125–0.389), ahead of blood pressure, diabetes, smoking, caffeine and common drugs. Exact percentile values live in these studies' tables, matched by age, sex and recording method; where a fetched record does not print a number, this shelf presents it as that study's published table rather than re-deriving it. Cross-point: respiratory sinus arrhythmia — the underlying vagal mechanism — is shelved separately.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED

title: Maximal inspiratory and expiratory mouth pressures: men exceed women, expiratory exceeds inspiratory, values fall with age — weakness begins below 62/83 cmH2O (inspiratory) and 81/109 cmH2O (expiratory)
question: In healthy humans, what are maximal inspiratory and expiratory mouth pressures (MIP/MEP) by age, sex and height — the population reference equations — and where are the lower limits that define respiratory muscle weakness?
balance: Textbook framing (Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology; Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology): maximal inspiratory pressure (MIP, measured near residual volume) and maximal expiratory pressure (MEP, near total lung capacity) are the standard volitional tests of respiratory muscle strength, and a value is only interpretable against a reference equation for the person's age, sex and size. The fetched human data are concordant on the pattern and give the numbers. In the population sample of Bruschi 1992 (N = 625), MEP exceeded MIP at matched lung volumes, men's pressures exceeded women's, body surface area was the strongest size correlate, and age added a smaller downward effect; the authors' own conclusion was that pressures are most useful for following change within a patient, with equations as the interpretive frame. Neder 1999 (N = 100, randomly selected) built sex-specific equations in which age and anthropometry explained up to 56% of the variability — and found earlier reference studies systematically underestimated the MIP values actually observed, a warning that equations do not travel unchanged between populations. The Polish cohort of Adamiak-Kardas (N = 166) prints the scale directly: mean PImax/PEmax 60/87.5 cmH2O in women and 73.2/115.9 cmH2O in men. The largest uniform-methodology dataset, Lista-Paz 2023 (N = 610, 14 centres), supplies the weakness cut-offs this shelf exists to state: PImax below 62 cmH2O (women) or 83 cmH2O (men), and PEmax below 81 cmH2O (women) or 109 cmH2O (men), defined as 2.5 SD below the young-adult peak mean. The systematic review (Sclauser Pessoa 2014; meta-analysis n = 840) agrees on direction — MIP higher in men, falling from the 40- to 60-year range onward — while stressing that technique and participant characteristics move the values, which is why this shelf cards equations and cut-offs per study rather than one pooled norm. Inspiratory muscle TRAINING is an intervention question housed on its own shelves; this shelf is the normative measurement underneath it. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED

title: Lung clearance index: ~6.2 in healthy children (upper limit 7.0-7.9 by method), flat through school age, then rising with adult age to a mean of 8.8 by age 90 — repeatable within about 5%
question: In healthy humans, what is the lung clearance index (and related multiple-breath washout indices) by age — the Global Lung Function Initiative reference values for nitrogen and SF6 washout — and how repeatable is LCI within a person?
balance: Textbook framing (Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology; Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology): even in healthy lungs, ventilation is not perfectly uniform, and the multiple-breath washout quantifies that heterogeneity — the lung clearance index (LCI) is the number of functional residual capacity (FRC) turnovers needed to wash an inert tracer gas (resident nitrogen, or inhaled sulfur hexafluoride, SF6) down to 1/40 of its starting concentration, so a higher LCI means more uneven ventilation. The fetched human data give the scale. In healthy children the index sits near 6: Fuchs 2009 measured mean LCI 6.2 (SD 0.4) with an upper limit of normal of 7.0 on the EasyOne Pro ultrasonic system, with within-test repeatability of 5.1% and short- and long-term reproducibility of 4.2-5.1% — the test is stable within a person. The school-age nitrogen-washout norms (Anagnostopoulou 2020, Exhalyzer D) set a fixed upper limit of 7.91 for LCI at the 2.5% endpoint, because the age rise across 6-18 years was negligible (0.04 units per year). In adults the picture changes: with SF6, Trinkmann 2021 found age explained 47% of LCI variance, mean LCI rising from 6.3 (upper limit 7.4) at age 20 to 8.8 (upper limit 9.9) at age 90. The Global Lung Function Initiative equations (Ramsey 2024; 1,579 unique healthy observations, ages 2-81) pool the field: LCI prediction needs age alone, FRC needs height, age and sex, and — at the level of the prediction equations — equipment type, tracer gas and dead space did not significantly change the equations. The device-specific upper limits on the cards below (7.0 vs 7.91 vs age-dependent SF6 limits) are therefore not a contradiction of the GLI pooling but its practical boundary: interpret a patient's LCI against the reference set for their method and age. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

title: Body water compartments by dilution: total water ~0.61 L/kg in men and 0.54 L/kg in women, split about 39% extracellular / 61% intracellular in young men
question: In healthy humans, how large are the body water compartments — total body water by deuterium dilution, extracellular water by bromide dilution, and the derived intracellular volume — as fractions of body weight by sex, age and adiposity?
balance: Textbook framing (Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, body-fluid compartments chapter; Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology): in a healthy young man total body water is about 60% of body weight, split roughly one-third extracellular and two-thirds intracellular, with the extracellular share falling as adiposity rises because fat tissue is water-poor. The dilution measurements fetched this session land on that account. In 13 healthy young men (mean body mass 80.6 kg), deuterium dilution gave total body water 51.00 L — about 63% of body mass — and bromide dilution gave extracellular water 19.88 L, leaving intracellular water (by subtraction) 31.12 L: about 39% extracellular and 61% intracellular (Armstrong 1997). Measured per kilogram by deuterium dilution, Norberg 2001 found 0.61 L/kg in men and 0.54 L/kg in women (44.1 vs 37.4 L) — the sex difference the textbook attributes to women's higher average fat fraction. Janssen 1997 used the same deuterium/bromide pair in 28 healthy controls as the comparator for growth-hormone-deficient patients, who had lower total and extracellular water and a lower extracellular-to-total ratio. Silva 2013 (N = 30 healthy young men; NCT01477294) confirms the derived intracellular volume is a subtraction (total minus extracellular), not a direct measurement. A standing caution runs through these records and is stated on the cards: impedance estimates are NOT dilution measurements — multifrequency impedance overestimated both compartments in Janssen 1997 and differed significantly from dilution for extracellular and intracellular volumes in Armstrong 1997, so impedance numbers must never be quoted as dilution values. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED

title: Vestibulo-ocular reflex testing in health: vHIT gain ~1.02-1.06, catch-up saccades in up to half of healthy ears, little change with age until after 70 — and every number belongs to its device
question: In healthy humans, what are normal vestibulo-ocular reflex measures — video head impulse test gain by canal and device, refixation-saccade prevalence, and caloric response magnitudes — and how do they change with age?
balance: Textbook framing (Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology; Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology): the vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR) holds gaze steady by rotating the eyes at the same speed as the head, so its gain (eye velocity / head velocity) should be 1.0 — the companion physiology shelf on VOR gain and adaptation (pack #6449) covers the reflex in darkness and its recalibration by magnifying or reversing spectacles. This shelf covers the CLINICAL normative measurements: the video head impulse test (vHIT), which impulses the head in each semicircular canal's plane, and the caloric test. The fetched healthy-subject data converge on gain at or just above 1.0 for the lateral canal — 1.06 (SD 0.07) in 212 healthy subjects (Matiño-Soler 2015) and 1.02 (SD 0.07) in 50 subjects tested decade by decade (Yang 2016) — with gain falling as head-impulse velocity rises, and refixation (catch-up) saccades appearing in a substantial minority of entirely healthy people: 52 of 212 subjects in one series, and in 49% of ears (22.6% of trials) in the other, so a saccade alone is not disease. Age effects are small and late: gain held steady until about age 70 for fast impulses and 90 for slow ones (Matiño-Soler), was largely unaffected by age into the 80s across all six canals (McGarvie 2015), and showed no effect up to age 78 on any of three devices (Janky 2017). The caloric/rotational battery (Maes 2010, N = 80) found only subtle age change — caloric slow-component velocity actually increased with age, rotational gains were essentially flat — with the large age trends confined to vestibular-evoked myogenic potentials. The one systematic distortion is the instrument: gains differ significantly between commercial devices and between gain-calculation methods (Janky 2017; Lee 2018), so each device needs its own normal values — devices are named on the cards as published. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

title: Diurnal testosterone rhythm: peak at 07:00-07:30, at least a 43% peak-to-nadir fall over 24 hours and a relative 15% by early afternoon in young men — blunting with age is real in pooled data, contested in fit older men
question: In healthy men, how large is the diurnal rhythm of serum testosterone (morning peak to afternoon/evening nadir, as a percentage), and how much does ageing blunt its amplitude?
balance: Textbook framing (Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology; Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology): serum testosterone in men is secreted with a circadian rhythm — highest in the early morning, lowest in the late evening — superimposed on ultradian pulses, which is why diagnostic sampling is standardised to the morning. The fetched human records size the rhythm and disagree instructively about ageing. With 30-minute sampling over 24 hours, Diver 2003 found BOTH young (N = 10) and middle-aged (N = 8) men had a significant rhythm with a minimum fall of 43% from peak to nadir in every subject, acrophase at 07:00-07:30, and no significant difference in total-testosterone amplitude between the groups (P = 0.061) — the rhythm, in fit healthy men, is maintained into the seventh decade, though bioavailable-testosterone amplitude did differ (P = 0.031). Population modelling of hourly literature data (Gupta 2000) tells the other half: the elderly deviation from the daily mean to the maximum was 7%, less than half the young men's 16%, with modelled healthy-young peak 577 ng/dL at 06:00 and nadir 420 ng/dL at 21:42. Morning-to-afternoon sampling gives the clinic-scale number: in young men with normal testosterone (N = 11 of 21 volunteers), levels fell a relative 15% from 8 a.m. to 2 p.m. (423 to 358 ng/dL; Shlykova 2020), while men with low testosterone showed no rhythm (a relative 4% fall, not significant). In 506 older men with symptoms of testosterone deficiency (median age 65 — a symptomatic cohort, labelled as such, NOT healthy men), Novaes 2024 found no significant morning-afternoon mean difference at all, with the largest variations in men under 30 and a weak negative correlation between age and the morning-afternoon difference. The review framework (Pastuszak 2022) summarises the field as blunting with age and a flat profile in testosterone deficiency. This shelf therefore presents the rhythm itself as established and the size of age-blunting as genuinely unsettled between intensive-sampling studies in fit men and larger clinical cohorts. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED for the rhythm and its morning-peak timing; the age-blunting limb is presented as mixed on the face of the cards.

title: Urinary flow–volume nomograms: Qmax and average flow rise with voided volume and fall with age
question: In healthy humans, how do maximum urinary flow rate (Qmax) and average flow vary with voided volume, age and sex — the flow–volume nomograms (Liverpool and successors) — and how repeatable is uroflowmetry within a person?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Framed by Guyton & Hall's and Boron & Boulpaep's accounts of micturition — detrusor contraction against urethral resistance, so flow is a joint product of bladder pressure and outlet calibre and cannot be read off a single number without the volume voided — three primary human datasets agree on the shape of normality. In 308 healthy women a single clinic void gave mean Qmax 23.06 ml/s and average flow 13.08 ml/s at a mean voided volume of about 290 ml, with flow–volume and corrected flow–age nomograms built from the data. In 101 healthy Japanese men recording repeated home voids, the flow–volume relationship was best fit by a saturating (quadratic/exponential) curve and Qmax at volumes over 150 ml was about 24 ml/s in men under 50 but 21.8 ml/s in men aged 50–59. In 58 randomly selected symptom-free men contributing 1,286 home voidings, maximum flow again rose with voided volume on nomograms, while a single measurement carried wide uncertainty — the true median Qmax could sit about 5 ml/s below or 6 ml/s above one reading. The settled teaching: quote flow only against volume and age, and treat one void as a sample, not a trait. Cross-point: invasive pressure–flow values in asymptomatic volunteers are shelved separately (urodynamics in healthy volunteers).
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED

title: Invasive urodynamics in healthy volunteers: normal pressure–flow values, and how poorly they repeat
question: In healthy asymptomatic volunteers, what do invasive urodynamic studies show — detrusor pressure at maximum flow, bladder capacity and compliance, and pressure–flow parameters — and how reproducible are they on repeat study?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Framed by Guyton & Hall's and Boron & Boulpaep's accounts of bladder filling and voiding — a compliant reservoir that fills at low pressure, then a coordinated detrusor contraction against a relaxing outlet — four primary human studies in asymptomatic volunteers agree on two settled points. First, normal voiding pressures are substantial: ambulatory studies in young men found maximum detrusor pressures around 59–70 cmH2O depending on fluid intake, and a mean detrusor pressure at maximum flow of 53 cmH2O at a mean Qmax of 24 ml/s, with a urethral resistance (URA) of 21 cmH2O proposed as the upper border of normal outflow. Second, 'normal' overlaps 'abnormal' and repeats poorly: among asymptomatic men aged 47–80, 13% met criteria for unequivocal obstruction and 63% showed unstable contractions, and in healthy women repeated urodynamics — immediate and at 1–5 months — had high coefficients of repeatability, i.e. poor reproducibility. The teaching is therefore double: these are the reference values, and a single invasive study in an individual must be read against their known scatter. Cross-point: non-invasive flow–volume nomograms are shelved separately.

title: Follicular waves: two or three waves of follicle development in every natural cycle
question: In healthy women, what does serial ultrasound show about ovarian follicular development across a natural menstrual cycle — how many follicular waves occur per cycle, when is the dominant follicle selected, and how fast does it grow to ovulation?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Framed by Guyton & Hall's and Ganong's accounts of the ovarian cycle — FSH-driven antral recruitment, selection of a dominant follicle, and the LH surge — the serial-ultrasound literature has replaced the textbook's single-cohort picture with a wave model, and the primary human data are concordant. In 50 healthy women scanned daily for one interovulatory interval, 68% showed two waves of follicle development and 32% showed three; no woman showed a single wave. A 39-woman cohort from the same programme confirmed the two/three-wave split and linked three-wave cycles to higher systemic inflammation (C-reactive protein). A 56-woman comparison then characterised the ovulatory follicle itself against luteinised unruptured follicles: selection (deviation) timing, growth rates and final diameters differ measurably between follicles that rupture and those that luteinise unruptured, with matching endocrine differences. All three cohorts come from one research programme (Baerwald, Pierson and colleagues), which is stated plainly; within that programme the wave model is consistent and is now the textbook framing. Exact day-by-day growth rates in mm/day live in the studies' tables; where a fetched record does not print a number, this shelf does not invent one.

title: Whole-body protein turnover: feeding balances protein chiefly by suppressing breakdown
question: In healthy humans, what are whole-body protein synthesis, breakdown and net balance rates in the fasted and fed states, measured by leucine/nitrogen tracer kinetics — and how do feeding and age change the balance chiefly through synthesis or breakdown?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Framed by Guyton & Hall's and Ganong's accounts of protein metabolism — a body protein pool in continuous turnover, with insulin and amino-acid supply shifting the balance between synthesis and proteolysis — the tracer literature is concordant on the central mechanism. In a classic leucine-infusion study (N = 6, printed plainly), feeding achieved positive leucine balance by cutting degradation from 89.5 to 31.7 µmol/kg/h with no apparent change in synthesis in the short-infusion protocol. In 12 elderly women, meal feeding likewise increased flux and oxidation and decreased breakdown, with no effect of feeding on synthesis. The largest dataset (91 young and 66 older adults, phenylalanine/tyrosine tracers) found basal turnover higher, not lower, with age — older adults had greater synthesis and breakdown and a less negative net balance — and women had higher turnover than men at every age. The settled teaching: in the acute fed/fasted transition the lever is breakdown suppression; protocol duration and tracer recycling can manufacture apparent synthesis effects, which is why the classic paper's own methodological warning belongs on the face. Cross-point: the per-meal muscle protein synthesis dose–response is a different, muscle-level quantity, shelved separately.

title: Insulin sensitivity by the euglycaemic clamp: the M-value, and how obesity and family history shift it
question: In healthy humans, what is insulin sensitivity measured by the euglycaemic–hyperinsulinaemic clamp (glucose disposal / M-value) — its distribution in non-obese non-diabetic people, and how much do obesity, sex and family history shift it?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED, with the assembly caveat on the face: there is no single GLI-style normative clamp cohort, so the distribution is assembled here from the technique's defining paper, one large standardised database and two same-protocol comparison programmes — and M-values are protocol-bound (insulin dose and normalisation differ), never interchangeable across protocols. The defining paper (DeFronzo 1979) sets the method: insulin held at about 100 µU/ml with glucose clamped at basal, so the glucose infusion rate equals whole-body tissue glucose uptake. The EGIR database (1,146 people with normal glucose tolerance, one standardised 1 mU/min/kg clamp at 20 centres) found M fell only 0.9 µmol/min/kg per decade of age, an effect abolished by adjusting for BMI — age per se is not a significant cause of insulin resistance. At a lower insulin dose (20 µU/min/m²), non-diabetic women without a family history disposed of about 5.9–6.6 mg/min/kg fat-free mass, while a positive family history cut total disposal to 3.55; and obese non-diabetic people were as insulin resistant as type 2 diabetic patients, with hypertension adding nothing further. Framing follows Guyton & Hall's and Ganong's accounts of insulin action on muscle, adipose tissue and liver, as textbook context.

title: True maximal heart rate: 208 − 0.7×age beats 220 − age on average, and no equation predicts an individual
question: In healthy humans, what is true maximal heart rate by age — how accurate are the 220−age (Fox) and 208−0.7×age (Tanaka) equations against measured maxima, and what is the between-person scatter around any age prediction?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Framed by Guyton & Hall's and Ganong's accounts of sinoatrial-node ageing and maximal sympathetic drive — maximal heart rate falls roughly linearly with age whatever the training state — the measurement literature is concordant on both the better equation and its limits. The Tanaka meta-analysis (351 studies, 492 groups, 18,712 subjects) derived HRmax = 208 − 0.7×age (r = −0.90), cross-validated almost identically (209 − 0.7×age) in 514 laboratory-tested healthy adults, independent of sex and habitual activity; 220 − age systematically underestimates true maxima in older adults. But group accuracy is not individual accuracy: in 99 graded treadmill tests every one of nine equations showed poor Bland–Altman agreement with measured maxima, and in 320 soccer players the fitted equation still carried a standard error of the estimate of 8.6 beats/min, with Fox overestimating by a mean of 2.8 beats/min and Tanaka underestimating by 3.3 beats/min in that sample. The settled teaching: use 208 − 0.7×age for group-level prescription, and expect any individual's true maximum to sit roughly ±10 beats/min or more from any prediction — measure it when the number matters. Cross-point: VO2peak reference standards are shelved separately.

title: FRIEND reference standards for peak oxygen uptake: treadmill medians fall from 48.0 (men) and 37.6 (women) mL/kg/min in the twenties to 24.4 and 18.3 in the seventies, with cycle values systematically lower
question: In healthy humans, what are reference percentile values for peak oxygen uptake (VO2peak) by age, sex and exercise mode — the FRIEND registry standards for treadmill and cycle ergometry — and how fast does VO2peak fall per decade in each sex?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Framed by Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology (textbook framing, not evidence). This shelf answers the measurement question — population percentile standards for peak oxygen uptake — which is a different question from the determinants question homed on the existing VO2max-limits shelf (what limits maximal oxygen uptake: cardiac output versus peripheral extraction); that shelf is cross-pointed here in prose only, and none of its studies is re-carded. The carded base is one registry programme (FRIEND) in three reports: treadmill standards (N=7,783), cycle-ergometry standards (N=4,494) and the updated combined standards (N=22,379). The pattern is concordant across all three: values are higher in men than women at every age, higher on the treadmill than the cycle, and fall with age at roughly 10% per decade in relative terms in the original reports (13.5–16.4% per decade in the updated report, printed beside the absolute falls of 4.0–4.3 mL/kg/min per decade). Registry volunteers are self-selected people referred for or volunteering for maximal exercise testing, not a random population sample — the standards describe tested, apparently healthy adults without cardiovascular disease, and the updated treadmill standards came in 1.5–4.6 mL/kg/min lower than the 2015 standards as the sample broadened.

title: Grip-strength centiles across the life course: median grip peaks at 51 kg in men and 31 kg in women, holds to midlife, then declines — with developing-region norms about 0.85 SD below British centiles
question: In healthy humans, what are grip-strength centiles across the life course by sex (peak, plateau and decline), harmonised across dynamometer studies — and how much do values vary between world regions?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Framed by Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology (skeletal-muscle physiology; textbook framing, not evidence). The carded base meets the row's condition of at least one primary normative cohort alongside the syntheses: a pooled primary-data analysis of twelve British general-population studies (49,964 participants), a primary population-based household-survey cohort from Brazil (N=3,050, Jamar dynamometer), and a global systematic review/meta-analysis of normative data (63 samples, 96,537 observations). All three agree on the life-course shape — rise to a peak in early adult life, maintenance through midlife, decline from midlife onwards, men stronger than women from adolescence — and on the size of the sex gap at peak (median 51 kg men versus 31 kg women in the British centiles). The honest regional caveat is quantified, not hand-waved: developed-region norms sit essentially on the British centiles (+0.12 SD), while developing-region norms sit clearly lower (−0.85 SD), so British cut-points travel across developed regions but not worldwide. Dynamometer type and test position were examined in sensitivity analyses in the British pooled analysis and did not change the findings; the primary Brazilian cohort used a single named device and protocol and is carded as such.

title: Normal nerve conduction: velocity and amplitude fall with age (motor velocity correlations r −0.37 to −0.46), sensory amplitudes fall earliest, and height — not temperature within the studied range — drives late-response latencies
question: In healthy humans, what are normal nerve conduction velocities and amplitudes (median, ulnar, sural) by age, height and skin temperature — how much does conduction slow per decade and per degree of cooling?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Framed by Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology (nerve conduction and its temperature dependence; textbook framing, not evidence). Three primary healthy-subject studies are carded: a four-limb study of 68 healthy Chinese adults correlating conduction with age, sex, height and skin temperature; a prospectively standardised upper-limb study of 155 carefully screened healthy elderly people with temperature controlled; and a 150-person study stratified into three age bands (18–30, 31–45, 46–60) for median and common peroneal conduction and late responses. They agree: ageing brings longer latencies, smaller amplitudes and slower velocities, with sensory amplitudes and late responses changing most; height lengthens late-response latencies (longer axons); and within the warm, controlled ranges actually studied, skin temperature showed no significant correlation — the familiar per-degree slowing is the textbook's account of the wider temperature range, stated as such on the Synthesis card, not as a carded measurement. No carded study reports a per-decade m/s slope, so none is printed as data.

title: The nasal cycle: present in every subject on 48-hour rhinometry, mostly as a mixed pattern when awake and a classic reciprocal pattern in sleep, with a mean phase of about 3–4 hours that lengthens during sleep
question: In healthy humans, what is the nasal cycle — the spontaneous alternating congestion/decongestion of the two nasal passages: its period, the fraction of people who show a classic reciprocal pattern on long-term rhinometry, and how do posture and sleep stage affect it?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing for the nasal cycle is thin — Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology and Boron & Boulpaep treat nasal vasculature briefly (textbook framing, not evidence) — so, as the slate row directs, this shelf rests chiefly on the primary measurement literature and says so. Four primary human studies are carded: the posture experiments of Cole & Haight 1986; a 6-person, 7-hour rhinomanometry study (Preece & Eccles 1994, N printed on its face per the labelling rule); a 20-person 24-hour rhinoflowmetry study with simultaneous polysomnography (Kimura 2013); and the first continuous 48-hour long-term rhinoflowmetry study (Lindemann 2024, N=30). Together they settle the existence and rough period of the cycle (mean phase about 3–4 hours, with very wide between- and within-person variation), and they correct the single-measurement picture: on continuous recording every subject shows a cycle, but the textbook 'classic' reciprocal pattern is only one component — awake recordings are dominated by a mixed pattern, while sleep recordings are dominated by the classic pattern. Posture modulates amplitude without abolishing the cycle, and phase reversals cluster in REM sleep and with postural change, never in slow-wave sleep.

title: Normal voice acoustics are population- and protocol-bound: fundamental frequency near 110–155 Hz in men and 215–260 Hz in women across Hindi, Turkish and Persian cohorts, with jitter near 0.2% and shimmer near 1.2% where reported — no universal norm exists
question: In healthy humans, what are normal voice acoustics — speaking fundamental frequency by sex and age, jitter, shimmer and harmonics-to-noise ratio on standardised sustained-vowel and reading tasks — and how do they change with ageing?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING. Framed by Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology (phonation; textbook framing, not evidence). The stamp is EMERGING, not ESTABLISHED, for a specific reason the carded data themselves demonstrate: the sex difference in fundamental frequency is large and consistent everywhere, but the absolute values differ by language community, vowel, task and analysis software, and no harmonised cross-population reference standard exists — each carded cohort explicitly presents its values as norms for its own population and system. Three primary healthy-speaker cohorts are carded: 62 North Indian Hindi speakers (ages 18–40), 83 young Turkish speakers (ages 18–32, Computerized Speech Lab) and 90 Iranian Persian speakers (ages 20–50, Dr. Speech software). Male fundamental frequency spans roughly 113–156 Hz and female roughly 215–262 Hz across cohorts and vowels; jitter (about 0.22–0.23%) and shimmer (about 1.21–1.22%) are quantified in the Iranian cohort and were statistically indistinguishable between the sexes there. None of the carded cohorts covers ages over 50, so the ageing limb of the question is answered honestly: within 20–50 years values were relatively stable, and older-age norms are not established by this base.

title: The cortisol awakening response: free cortisol rises by about 50% within 30 minutes of awakening in roughly three-quarters of healthy adults, is moderately heritable and stable within a person, and is valid only under strict awakening-referenced sampling
question: In healthy humans, what is the cortisol awakening response — the rise in cortisol over the first 30–45 minutes after awakening: its typical size, its dependence on awakening time, light and sleep, and its day-to-day within-person variability under the expert-consensus measurement protocol?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Framed by Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology and Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology (HPA-axis circadian regulation; textbook framing, not evidence), with the measurement protocol framed by the Stalder expert-consensus guidelines for cortisol awakening response assessment (2016, updated 2022) — named here and on the Synthesis card as protocol framing, not as evidence cards, per this stream's rule. Three primary healthy-cohort studies are carded: the four-study normative dataset of Wüst and colleagues (N=509 combined), their twin study (52 monozygotic and 52 dizygotic pairs sampled on two days), and the Federenko awakening-time experiment (24 shift-working nurses and 31 students, N=55). They agree the response is real and sizable — a mean free-cortisol increase of about 50% (a relative rise) within the first 30 minutes, present in about 75% of healthy adults — and moderately stable within a person (correlations up to r=0.63). One honest tension is kept on the face: the normative dataset found no considerable effect of awakening time across ordinary morning ranges, while the experiment spanning shifts and evening naps found awakening time matters and that waking per se is insufficient — the consensus position, reflected here, is that sampling must be strictly referenced to the moment of awakening, with objective verification, because timing non-adherence is the dominant threat to validity.

title: LH pulsatility in healthy men: ~19.5 pulses per 24 h (every ~74 min) at intensive sampling, amplitudes 1–28 mIU/mL — basal secretion preserved with ageing, stimulated bioactive reserve attenuated
question: In healthy men, what is the pulsatile pattern of luteinising hormone secretion — pulse frequency and amplitude over 24 hours, the sleep-related changes of puberty/young adulthood, and how pulse frequency, amplitude and bioactivity change with ageing?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — for pulse frequency and amplitude in healthy young men and for the ageing pattern, framed by Ganong / Guyton & Hall on pulsatile gonadotropin secretion as textbook framing, not as an evidence card. Intensive 5-minute sampling over 24 hours gives a stable estimate in men of about 19.5 pulses per 24 hours — a periodicity near 74 minutes — with very wide normal ranges: interpulse intervals from 10 to 330 minutes (median 60) and pulse amplitudes from 1 to 28 mIU/mL (median 4.1) (Veldhuis 1986, N = 8 men). Two mathematically independent peak-detection methods (Cluster and Detect) agree on that frequency in the same sampling series, so the number is not an artefact of one algorithm (Veldhuis 1988) — but that second report reanalyses the same eight men's series and is carded as methods cross-validation, not as an independent cohort. Ageing: basal bioactive LH concentrations and spontaneous pulse properties are preserved in healthy older men, yet the pituitary reserve is attenuated — responses to exogenous GnRH pulses and to antiestrogen (tamoxifen) release are reduced or absent (Urban 1988). The textbooks describe sleep-entrained augmentation of LH pulses at puberty; the fetched records on this shelf sampled across 24 hours but do not report a sleep-stage breakdown in their abstracts, so that sleep/puberty detail is presented here as the textbook's account, not as carded data. Cross-points, not duplicated: the library's GnRH pulse-frequency decoding shelf asks how the pituitary responds to imposed pulses, and the testosterone diurnal-rhythm shelf asks about the downstream circadian signal; this shelf asks the endogenous pulse statistics themselves.

title: Semen characteristics in fertile men: WHO 5th-centile limits (concentration 15–16 million/mL, normal forms 4%) are fertile-population percentiles, not infertility cut-offs — and within-man variability is wide
question: In men of proven fertility, what is the distribution of semen characteristics (volume, concentration, motility, morphology) — the WHO reference values and their lower 5th-percentile reference limits — and how large is within-man variability between samples?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — for the fertile-population distributions, framed by Guyton & Hall / Ganong on semen production and composition as textbook framing, not as an evidence card. The core teaching point, on the face: these are one-sided lower 5th-percentile reference limits from men whose partners conceived within 12 months — descriptions of a fertile population, NOT diagnostic cut-offs separating fertile from infertile men. The WHO 2010 distribution (over 4,500 men, 14 countries) gives 5th centiles of volume 1.5 mL, concentration 15 million/mL, total number 39 million, progressive motility 32% and normal forms 4.0% (Cooper 2010). The updated collation behind the WHO 6th edition (over 3,500 men, 12 countries, five continents) lands almost identically — concentration 16 million/mL, progressive motility 30% (total 42%), normal forms 4% (Campbell 2021) — which is why the stamp is ESTABLISHED: two global collations a decade apart agree. Within-man variability is large: repeated samples from 25 fathers varied widely within and between men for essentially every parameter except pH (Cooper 1991), so a single sample characterises a man poorly. Morphology percentages are criteria-dependent — the 1991 fathers study's 42% lower limit for normal forms used the scoring of its era and is not comparable with the 4% strict-criteria figure; the cards keep them separate rather than averaging them.

title: Diaphragm ultrasound in health: end-expiratory thickness lower limits 1.3 mm (men) / 1.1 mm (women) seated, thickening-fraction lower limits ~39–48%, deep-breathing excursion ~5 cm supine
question: In healthy humans, what are diaphragm thickness, thickening fraction and excursion on ultrasound at rest and during deep breathing, by sex and posture — the reference values and limits of normality?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — for thickness and thickening in healthy adults, framed by Guyton & Hall / Boron & Boulpaep on the diaphragm and respiratory mechanics as textbook framing, not as an evidence card. Two large healthy cohorts measured in different postures converge on the same muscle: seated, end-expiratory thickness has a lower limit of normality of 1.3 mm in men and 1.1 mm in women, with thickening-fraction lower limits around 39–48% by side and sex (Boussuges 2021, N = 200); supine, mean end-expiratory thickness is 0.14 ± 0.05 cm (1.4 mm) rising to 0.29 ± 0.10 cm at end-inspiration, with quiet-breathing excursion 1.68 ± 0.37 cm and deep-breathing excursion 5.06 ± 1.40 cm (Zhang 2024, N = 212). Women have thinner diaphragms than men in both cohorts, while thickening fraction does not differ by sex — the pattern is consistent across posture and centre. A smaller study (N = 64) ties the ultrasound measures to function: deep-breathing mobility, total-lung-capacity thickness and thickening fraction correlate with lung function and inspiratory strength, including inspiratory gastric pressure in a 40-person subgroup (Cardenas 2018). Posture and breathing manoeuvre move the numbers, so each card names its own; the values are not pooled across postures. title: Contrast sensitivity and ageing: loss concentrated at high spatial frequencies and in dim light — Pelli–Robson falls 0.20 log photopic vs 0.33 log mesopic, low frequencies spared
question: In healthy humans, how does contrast sensitivity (spatial contrast sensitivity function and letter contrast sensitivity, e.g. Pelli–Robson) change with age under photopic and mesopic conditions — at which spatial frequencies is the loss greatest, and how much is optical versus neural?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — for the direction and frequency-selectivity of the age change, framed by Ganong / Boron & Boulpaep on visual processing as textbook framing, not as an evidence card. Letter contrast sensitivity (Pelli–Robson) in 292 adults falls late and modestly under bright (photopic) conditions — decline from the 61–70 group onward, 0.20 log units between youngest and oldest — and earlier and further in dim (mesopic) conditions — decline from 51–60 onward, 0.33 log units (Puell 2004). The spatial-frequency studies explain the shape: with forced-choice methods the age loss is concentrated at high spatial frequencies, with low frequencies spared, centrally and at 10 degrees in the periphery alike (Higgins 1988; Crassini 1988). On the optical-versus-neural question the fetched records support a neural component: the high-frequency decline persists with pupil size controlled and is, in Higgins and colleagues' judgement, too large to be explained by lens-density change alone — presented as those authors' inference from their data, not as a settled partition of optical versus neural shares, which no carded record quantifies. Method matters and is part of the physiology: the method of adjustment exaggerates the age decline at all frequencies and its authors advise against it for ageing studies. Small classic cohorts (8 young versus 8 older observers in Crassini) carry their Ns on the face.

title: Resting metabolic rate: prediction equations fit groups but miss individuals by ±300–450 kcal/day — Mifflin–St Jeor and Oxford lead on individual accuracy, indirect calorimetry is the reference
question: In healthy humans, what is resting metabolic rate measured by indirect calorimetry by age, sex and body composition — and how accurate are the standard prediction equations (Mifflin–St Jeor, Harris–Benedict, Schofield) against measured values in non-obese and obese adults?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — for the verdict on equation accuracy, framed by Guyton & Hall / Ganong on metabolic rate and energy balance as textbook framing, not as an evidence card. The settled finding is about the equations, and it is consistent across a systematic review and two primary validation studies using different calorimetry rigs: no standard equation is accurate at the individual level. The systematic review found Mifflin–St Jeor the most reliable of the four common equations, predicting resting metabolic rate within 10% of the indirect-calorimetry measurement in more nonobese and obese individuals than Harris–Benedict, Owen or WHO/FAO/UNU, with the narrowest error range — while noting older adults and US ethnic minorities were underrepresented in both development and validation (Frankenfield 2005). Against a gas-exchange-corrected reference measurement, all 13 equations correlated well yet overpredicted on average by 89–312 kcal/day; the Mifflin, Oxford and Müller equations were within 200 kcal/day for over 60% of individuals, and only the Oxford equations performed better in both sexes separately (Galgani 2018, N = 69). In a smaller cross-validation the ranking flipped at group level — Harris–Benedict and WHO had the lowest mean bias (−14 and −25 kcal/day) — yet every equation's individual limits of agreement were moderate to large (about ±314 to ±445 kcal/day), and equations underestimated progressively as fat-free mass rose (Flack 2016, N = 30). That disagreement on which equation 'wins' at group level, alongside unanimity that individual error stays large, is exactly what the cards show: group means can look right while the person in front of you is off by several hundred kilocalories. Cross-points, not duplicated: the doubly-labelled-water shelf asks total daily expenditure, and the diet-induced thermogenesis shelf asks the post-meal rise — this shelf asks the resting rate and its estimation.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED

title: Wideband middle-ear measures: absorbance curves shift with age, sex and pressure — older ears lower at 1587–3175 Hz, negative pressure cuts absorbance near 1 kHz; norms still system-specific (EMERGING)
question: In healthy adults, what are normal wideband acoustic absorbance / tympanometry measures of middle-ear function across frequency — and how do age, sex and middle-ear pressure shift them?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING — the measurement family is established but its normative distributions are still accumulating and are device- and pressure-condition-dependent, so this shelf is graded EMERGING rather than ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing is thin — Ganong / Boron & Boulpaep cover middle-ear impedance matching in principle, named here as framing, not as an evidence card; the shelf rests chiefly on the primary measurement literature, as its slate row directs. What the primary studies show: in 95 adults with normal middle-ear function measured on an Interacoustics Titan system (226–8000 Hz), energy absorbance at tympanometric peak pressure differs by age in a frequency-specific pattern — older adults higher at 500–794 Hz and 5040–6350 Hz, lower at 1587–3175 Hz than young adults — with resonance frequency lower in older adults, and a consistent sex pattern (men higher absorbance at low frequencies, lower at high frequencies) in every age group (Kavruk 2024). Middle-ear pressure itself moves the measurement: induced negative pressure in 8 normal ears reduced power absorbance most strongly at 0.8–1.9 kHz, consistent with increased stiffness at the tympanic membrane (Robinson 2016; N = 8 on the face). Wideband reflex thresholds run lower than clinical 226 Hz thresholds in 39 normal-hearing adults, and differ between peak-pressure and ambient-pressure measurement (Schairer 2022). Because absorbance depends on the test system, the pressure condition and the frequency band, no single universal normal curve is claimed — values are carded per system and condition. Cross-point, not duplicated: the pure-tone hearing-threshold shelf measures cochlear sensitivity; this shelf measures the middle-ear mechanics in front of the cochlea.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING

title: Ozoralizumab in rheumatoid arthritis: ACR20 about 76–80% versus 37% on placebo plus methotrexate in the Japanese OHZORA trial; NATSUZORA tested it without methotrexate
question: In adults with active rheumatoid arthritis despite methotrexate, does the anti-TNF multivalent NANOBODY compound ozoralizumab, compared with placebo plus methotrexate (and, in a second trial, without methotrexate), improve disease activity (OHZORA / NATSUZORA programme)?
balance: POSSIBLE. In OHZORA (381 patients with active rheumatoid arthritis despite methotrexate), ozoralizumab 30 mg and 80 mg every 4 weeks plus methotrexate produced ACR20 responses at week 16 of 79.6% and 75.3% versus 37.3% on placebo plus methotrexate (P<0.001), with significantly more structural nonprogression at week 24. In NATSUZORA (140 patients), ozoralizumab without methotrexate was tested in an open-label randomised dose comparison — responses were high at week 24 and maintained to 52 weeks, but there was no placebo arm, and antidrug antibodies appeared in about 40% of patients. The integrated long-term analysis of both trials and their HOSHIZORA extension (521 enrolled; mean treatment duration 200 weeks) found no new safety concerns and maintained responses. The limits are printed on the face: this is a single-country (Japan) programme, the drug is approved there and not FDA-approved, only one trial is placebo-controlled, and no trial compares ozoralizumab with an established anti-TNF agent. Ozoralizumab is a single-source product of Taisho (named for clarification, as a product not approved or regulated outside Japan).
stamp: POSSIBLE — one Japanese programme: a single placebo-controlled trial (OHZORA) with a large ACR20 win, an open-label no-methotrexate trial (NATSUZORA), and an integrated long-term extension analysis; a single programme caps at POSSIBLE

title: Mavrilimumab in rheumatoid arthritis: phase 2 DAS28-CRP response 55.7% versus 34.7% on placebo; long-term extension followed the pulmonary signal for 899 patient-years
question: In adults with active rheumatoid arthritis, does the anti-GM-CSF-receptor-α antibody mavrilimumab, compared with placebo (on background methotrexate), improve disease activity — and what did its long-term extension show about the pulmonary safety signal that defines this class?
balance: POSSIBLE. Mavrilimumab, a human monoclonal antibody against the GM-CSF receptor α subunit, showed rapid, dose-related efficacy in phase 2: the primary DAS28-CRP response at week 12 was 55.7% on mavrilimumab versus 34.7% on placebo (p=0.003), reaching 66.7% at 100 mg, and a 51-patient Japanese phase IIa population report pointed the same way (75.0% at 30 mg and 100 mg versus 23.5% on placebo). The long-term report of two phase IIb studies and their open-label extension (442 patients, 899 patient-years, median 2.5 years) found sustained efficacy (DAS28-CRP <2.6 in 40.6% at week 122) and addressed the class-defining pulmonary watch: reductions in FEV1 or FVC occurred in roughly 3–6% of patients at weeks 74–104, were mostly transient, and were only infrequently associated with adverse events. The programme was discontinued after phase 2 and mavrilimumab was never marketed — this shelf records a positive but unfinished programme, in the precedent of other discontinued-programme shelves.
stamp: POSSIBLE — a discontinued phase 2 programme only: concordant dose-related efficacy in short randomised trials and sustained extension responses, with no phase 3 trial; a phase 2 programme caps at POSSIBLE
