title: Iguratimod in rheumatoid arthritis: ACR20 53.8% versus 17.2% on placebo, 69.5% versus 30.7% added to methotrexate, and non-inferior to methotrexate alone in the 911-patient SMILE trial
question: In adults with active rheumatoid arthritis, does the oral immunomodulator iguratimod, compared with placebo or salazosulfapyridine, and added to methotrexate in methotrexate inadequate responders, improve disease activity?
balance: POSSIBLE. Iguratimod, an oral immunomodulator approved as a DMARD in Japan and China (not FDA/EMA-approved — flagged on the face), has three concordant randomised trials. Against placebo and salazosulfapyridine in 376 patients, ACR20 was 53.8% versus 17.2% on placebo (P<0.001) and non-inferior to salazosulfapyridine. Added to methotrexate in 253 inadequate responders, ACR20 at week 24 was 69.5% versus 30.7% (P<0.001). In SMILE (911 methotrexate-naïve patients with early RA), iguratimod monotherapy and iguratimod plus methotrexate both achieved higher ACR20 at week 52 than methotrexate alone (77.4% and 77.1% versus 65.9%), with non-inferiority on radiographic progression for monotherapy but no radiographic superiority. No trial compares iguratimod with a biologic or targeted synthetic DMARD, and all evidence is single-region — that is what holds the stamp at POSSIBLE.
stamp: POSSIBLE — three concordant randomised trials (placebo-controlled, methotrexate add-on, and a 911-patient early-RA non-inferiority trial), but all from Japan/China where the drug is approved and not FDA/EMA-approved; a single-region programme caps at POSSIBLE

title: Denosumab for rheumatoid arthritis erosions: erosion progression slowed on methotrexate in phase 2 and pooled phase 3 data — but no effect on joint-space narrowing or disease activity
question: In adults with rheumatoid arthritis on methotrexate, does adding the anti-RANKL antibody denosumab, compared with placebo, slow bone erosion and joint-space narrowing — without improving synovitis or disease activity?
balance: POSSIBLE — for structural protection only. Adding denosumab to methotrexate slowed bone erosion in every randomised report: in the phase 2 MRI trial (218 patients), MRI erosion score rose by 0.06 on denosumab 180 mg versus 1.75 on placebo at 6 months (P=0.007); in DRIVE (350 Japanese patients), modified Sharp erosion change at 12 months was 0.09–0.27 across dosing intervals versus 0.99 on placebo; and in the pooled DRIVE + DESIRABLE analysis (909 patients), total Sharp progression was 0.66–0.88 versus 1.50 on placebo, driven entirely by the erosion component. The honest balance is the dissociation itself, printed on the face: no report found an effect on joint-space narrowing, synovitis, or measures of RA disease activity (the treatment made no difference to disease activity), which is why denosumab was never approved for RA. Its osteoporosis questions are homed elsewhere in the library and are not re-carded here.
stamp: POSSIBLE — concordant radiographic erosion benefit across phase 2 trials and a pooled phase 2/3 analysis, but structural surrogate endpoints only, with no effect on joint-space narrowing or disease activity in any report

title: Deucravacitinib in systemic lupus erythematosus: PAISLEY phase 2 — SRI-4 in 58% versus 34% on placebo at the 3 mg twice-daily dose (one trial, reported three ways)
question: In adults with active systemic lupus erythematosus, does the oral TYK2 inhibitor deucravacitinib, compared with placebo plus standard therapy, improve disease activity (SRI-4 / BICLA response; PAISLEY programme)?
balance: POSSIBLE. The SLE evidence for deucravacitinib is one trial, printed on the face: PAISLEY (363 adults with active SLE) found SRI-4 response at week 32 of 58% on 3 mg twice daily (odds ratio 2.8; P<0.001) and 50% on 6 mg twice daily (P=0.02) versus 34% on placebo, with the 12 mg once-daily dose at 45% (nominal P=0.08); BICLA, CLASI-50, low-disease-activity and joint-count responses also favoured deucravacitinib. The trial's own patient-reported-outcomes report found larger pain and fatigue improvements on deucravacitinib at week 48, and its pharmacodynamic analysis showed rapid, sustained suppression of interferon-pathway markers — supportive, but the same 363 patients, not independent confirmation. Infections and cutaneous events were commoner on deucravacitinib; serious adverse events were comparable. Phase 3 (POETYK SLE) was designed but unreported at the time of these reports, so no phase 3 claim is made. Deucravacitinib in plaque psoriasis is homed on live shelf #1155 and in psoriatic arthritis on pack #6989; this shelf asks only the unasked SLE slice and re-cards none of their evidence.
stamp: POSSIBLE — a single phase 2 trial (PAISLEY, 363 patients) with a significant SRI-4 win at two of three doses, supported by its own patient-reported-outcome and pharmacodynamic reports; one trial caps at POSSIBLE and phase 3 is unreported

title: Enpatoran in lupus (WILLOW): skin cohort met its dose-response endpoint (CLASI-A, p=0.0002) while the systemic SLE cohort missed its primary dose-response objective (p=0.14) — SPLIT
question: In adults with systemic lupus erythematosus or cutaneous lupus erythematosus with active skin disease, does the oral TLR7/8 inhibitor enpatoran, compared with placebo plus standard care, improve systemic disease activity and skin activity (WILLOW programme)?
balance: SPLIT. WILLOW is one phase 2 basket trial reported by cohort, and the cohorts answer different questions in different populations — they are not merged on this shelf. In Cohort A (102 participants with cutaneous lupus or SLE with active skin disease), enpatoran produced a significant, dose-dependent improvement in skin activity at week 16 (CLASI-A change −64 to −72 percentage points across doses versus −44 on placebo; p=0.0002 for dose-response). In Cohort B (354 participants with moderate-to-severe SLE), BICLA response at week 24 was numerically higher at every dose (49–58% versus 39% on placebo) but the trial did not meet its primary objective of a statistically significant dose-response relationship (p=0.14). A 25-patient phase Ib study adds clean tolerability and dose-dependent interferon-gene-signature suppression, as programme support only. Enpatoran is an oral TLR7/8 inhibitor from a single source (Merck KGaA, named for clarification); the evidence is phase 2 only.
stamp: SPLIT (by cohort) — Cohort A (skin-predominant CLE/SLE) met a significant dose-dependent CLASI-A benefit, while Cohort B (moderate-to-severe SLE) missed its primary dose-response objective on BICLA (p=0.14) despite numerically higher response rates

title: Bimagrumab in inclusion body myositis (RESILIENT): no difference in 6-minute walk distance at any dose, deterioration in all groups over 2 years — muscle mass rose, function did not
question: In adults with sporadic inclusion body myositis, does the activin-receptor-IIB antibody bimagrumab, compared with placebo, improve walking performance and slow functional decline (RESILIENT programme)?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference). RESILIENT (251 adults with sporadic inclusion body myositis) found no difference in 6-minute walk distance at week 52 at any bimagrumab dose versus placebo (+17.6 m, p=0.22; +18.6 m, p=0.19; −1.3 m, p=0.93). Its long-term extension (211 participants) showed progressive deterioration in all groups over 2 years and was terminated early because the core trial had missed its endpoint. A 10-patient long-term safety cohort showed the programme's characteristic dissociation: lean body mass rose 6.9% while walk distance declined. This is a failed programme, presented in the failed-programme precedent: the drug did what it was built to do to muscle mass and made no difference to walking or strength. Bimagrumab in type 2 diabetes with obesity is homed on live shelf #1095 and is not re-carded here.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — the large RESILIENT randomised trial missed its primary walking endpoint at all three doses, its 2-year extension showed deterioration in all groups, and long-term follow-up showed lean-mass gains without functional benefit

title: Netakimab in axial spondyloarthritis: ASAS20 up to 90.9% versus 42.9% on placebo in phase 2, ASTERA phase 3 subgroup-consistent, and 85.5% two-year real-world retention (observational) — all Russian evidence
question: In adults with active radiographic axial spondyloarthritis (ankylosing spondylitis), does the anti-IL-17A antibody netakimab, compared with placebo, improve disease activity (ASTERA programme) — and what does Russian real-world use show on retention and safety?
balance: POSSIBLE. Netakimab, a humanised anti-IL-17A antibody approved in Russia (single-source Biocad product, named for clarification), beat placebo in its phase 2 dose-finding trial (89 patients): ASAS20 at week 16 was 72.7%, 81.8% and 90.9% across doses versus 42.9% on placebo, with superiority confirmed at 80 and 120 mg. The ASTERA phase 3 programme (228 randomised) is represented in PubMed-indexed journals by a post-hoc analysis showing effectiveness regardless of baseline CRP or MRI sacroiliac inflammation — a title search this session located no primary ASTERA publication in a PubMed-indexed journal, and that gap is printed on the face. The real-world limb is observational and labelled as such: the LIBRA cohort (137 patients) showed 90.4% retention at 1 year and 85.5% at 2 years, with sustained BASDAI/ASDAS-CRP reductions and treatment-related adverse events in about 5–6%. All evidence is single-country (Russia), and the real-world reports sit in a low-visibility translated journal.
stamp: POSSIBLE — positive phase 2 randomised trial and ASTERA phase 3 post-hoc analysis, with an observational real-world limb (labelled; observational evidence caps at POSSIBLE); single-country evidence and no PubMed-indexed ASTERA primary report located

title: Pentosan polysulfate in knee osteoarthritis: synovial biomarker changes in a phase 2 injectable trial, a positive 2005 intramuscular pilot (n=114), and an uncontrolled oral pilot — MAYBE (weak evidence)
question: In adults with painful knee osteoarthritis, does pentosan polysulfate sodium (oral or subcutaneous), compared with placebo, reduce knee pain and improve function?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence). The knee-osteoarthritis evidence for pentosan polysulfate is three small reports, each in a different route, and they are not merged on this shelf. The modern phase 2 trial (61 participants) tested subcutaneous injectable pentosan (iPPS; no brand or manufacturer named in the publication) against placebo with synovial-fluid biomarkers as the primary endpoint: the cartilage-degradation marker ARGS fell significantly versus placebo at day 56 and day 168, while pain outcomes were secondary. The only placebo-controlled pain evidence is a 2005 randomised pilot (114 patients, verified from the record) of four weekly intramuscular injections, positive on stiffness duration, pain at rest and patient global assessment but on only 3 of 7 direct assessments. The oral evidence is a single-arm, open-label pilot in 38 patients taking the named product Elmiron®, in which pain fell without any comparator — labelled single-arm on its card. Pentosan in bladder pain syndrome is homed on live shelf #917 and is not re-carded here.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — three small reports in three different routes/formulations: a biomarker-primary phase 2 trial, one positive 2005 randomised pilot, and one single-arm open-label pilot (labelled); no formulation has confirmatory evidence

title: Lobeglitazone in type 2 diabetes: HbA1c down about 0.6–1.0 points — non-inferior to pioglitazone and sitagliptin on metformin, and better than placebo added to dual therapy (single-region TZD evidence)
question: In adults with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled on metformin (with or without additional oral agents), does the thiazolidinedione lobeglitazone, compared with placebo, sitagliptin or pioglitazone, improve glycaemic control?
balance: POSSIBLE. Lobeglitazone, a thiazolidinedione approved in South Korea and India and not FDA/EMA-approved (flagged on the face; a single-source Chong Kun Dang product, named for clarification), lowers HbA1c consistently across designs: non-inferior to pioglitazone 15 mg in SENSITIZE INDIA (328 patients; HbA1c −1.01 points) and to sitagliptin as a metformin add-on (247 patients; −0.79% versus −0.86%), and superior to placebo when added to metformin + sitagliptin (231 patients; −1.00% versus +0.02%) and to empagliflozin + metformin in two replicate trials reported in one publication (−0.71% and −0.62% versus placebo). Both cautions are printed on the face: HbA1c is a surrogate endpoint throughout and no cardiovascular-outcomes trial exists, and the thiazolidinedione class safety history (fluid retention, weight gain, fracture) is cross-pointed in the synthesis rather than re-carded — the short trials here showed broadly comparable adverse events, which does not settle class risks.
stamp: POSSIBLE — multiple concordant randomised trials (two placebo-controlled add-on programmes and two active-comparator non-inferiority trials), but single-region (South Korea/India) evidence, a surrogate endpoint throughout, and no cardiovascular-outcomes trial

title: Abaloparatide in men with osteoporosis (ATOM): lumbar spine BMD rose 8.48% versus 1.17% on placebo over 12 months in the single men's trial
question: In men with osteoporosis, does abaloparatide, compared with placebo, increase bone mineral density (ATOM programme)?
balance: POSSIBLE — this shelf asks only the men's question. The companion shelf for postmenopausal women (the ACTIVE trial) is a separate home (pack #1820) and is not re-carded here; this shelf rests entirely on ATOM, the single randomised trial in men, reported in several publications that are distinct reports of ONE trial of 228 men — the trial base is single and the face says so. In ATOM, 12 months of daily abaloparatide 80 micrograms raised lumbar spine BMD by 8.48% versus 1.17% on placebo, with smaller gains at total hip (2.14% versus 0.01%) and femoral neck (2.98% versus 0.15%), all P<0.0001. A prespecified response-rates report found a >3% BMD gain at all three sites in 31.9% of abaloparatide men versus 1.5% on placebo at month 12, and a bone-turnover-marker report found early PINP rises correlated with the 12-month spine BMD gain (r=0.614 at 3 months). BMD is a surrogate endpoint: ATOM was not powered for fractures and reports no fracture outcome, so no fracture claim is made for men on this shelf. The stamp caps at POSSIBLE because the evidence is one trial and a surrogate endpoint.
stamp: POSSIBLE — single trial (ATOM, 228 men); BMD is a surrogate endpoint and the trial was not powered for fractures

title: Rademikibart in moderate-to-severe uncontrolled asthma: one phase 2b trial (322 patients) — FEV1 rose 140–189 mL over placebo at week 12; all three reports are of that single trial
question: In adults with moderate-to-severe persistent uncontrolled asthma, does rademikibart (anti-IL-4R-alpha monoclonal antibody, 150 mg or 300 mg every other week after a loading dose) versus placebo improve lung function and asthma control over 24 weeks?
balance: POSSIBLE — SINGLE-TRIAL FLAG, printed plainly: every card on this shelf is a report of ONE phase 2b randomised trial of 322 adults with moderate-to-severe uncontrolled asthma (rademikibart 150 mg or 300 mg every other week after a 600 mg loading dose, versus placebo, for 24 weeks). There is no second trial and no phase 3 report; a single trial caps the stamp at POSSIBLE. In that trial, trough FEV1 at week 12 improved over placebo by 140 mL (150 mg) and 189 mL (300 mg), gains appeared in week 1 and held to week 24, and asthma control scores improved. The proportion with one or more exacerbations through week 24 was 7.5% (150 mg) and 9.3% (300 mg) versus 16.7% on placebo — absolute differences of about 9 and 7 percentage points, i.e. roughly 55% and 44% relative reductions — but a 24-week phase 2b trial is not powered to settle exacerbation benefit, and the shelf does not claim it. Exploratory subgroup reports found the largest gains where type 2 biomarkers were high (baseline eosinophils at least 300 cells/microlitre and FeNO at least 25 ppb), and a dedicated eosinophil analysis found counts fell slightly rather than rising, unlike the hypereosinophilia seen with some IL-4R-alpha blockade — an exploratory safety observation, not a settled class distinction. Rademikibart is a single-source investigational product (developed as CBP-201); it is not an approved asthma treatment.
stamp: POSSIBLE — SINGLE-TRIAL FLAG: three reports of one phase 2b trial (322 patients); a single trial caps the stamp at POSSIBLE

title: CPAP versus non-invasive ventilation in obesity hypoventilation syndrome (Pickwick): the two treatments matched on symptoms and long-term heart changes; NIV edged ahead on blood gases, lung function and early heart measures, and neither beat lifestyle advice on hospital days without severe sleep apnoea
question: In adults with obesity hypoventilation syndrome (with and without severe obstructive sleep apnoea), is long-term non-invasive ventilation superior to CPAP — or to lifestyle modification alone — for gas exchange, cardiovascular outcomes and survival?
balance: SPLIT — and the split runs exactly where the Pickwick programme itself split it: by whether severe obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA) is present, and by endpoint. All four cards come from the one Spanish Pickwick programme (a single registry entry covering its trials and their secondary reports); the reports share populations and must not be counted as independent trials. In patients WITH severe OSA (221 randomised), 2 months of non-invasive ventilation (NIV) and CPAP both beat lifestyle modification on symptoms and sleep measures; NIV improved daytime PaCO2 and bicarbonate most, with a significant difference against lifestyle but not against CPAP, while spirometry, 6-minute walk and some quality-of-life measures improved more with NIV. At 2 months only NIV lowered systolic pulmonary artery pressure (-3.4 mm Hg versus control) and left ventricular mass index; over 3 years, however, pulmonary pressure and diastolic function improved to the same degree on both treatments. In patients WITHOUT severe OSA (98 randomised, median follow-up about 5 years), NIV versus lifestyle modification made no difference to hospital days per year (2.71 versus 2.60; adjusted rate ratio 1.07, 95% CI 0.44 to 2.59) — the treatment made no difference on the primary endpoint — though blood gases, quality of life and sleepiness improved more on NIV. No card here shows a mortality advantage for either device. Practical reading: CPAP is a reasonable first treatment when severe OSA dominates; NIV earns its place on gas-exchange and functional grounds, not on hospitalisation or survival.
stamp: SPLIT — with severe OSA, NIV and CPAP improve symptoms similarly while NIV improves respiratory function and early echocardiographic measures more; without severe OSA, long-term NIV did not reduce hospital days versus lifestyle modification (the treatment made no difference on that endpoint)

title: Pulmonary artery catheter-guided management in general intensive care, shock and ARDS: two randomised trials found no survival benefit (PAC-Man hospital mortality 68% versus 66%; Richard 28-day mortality 59.4% versus 61.0%)
question: In critically ill adults with shock, ARDS or general ICU admission (not acute heart failure specifically), does management guided by a pulmonary artery catheter versus clinical assessment without a catheter improve survival?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — this shelf asks the general intensive care, shock and ARDS question only. The heart-failure slice of this question is homed separately at pack #3306, where the ESCAPE trial of catheter-guided therapy in severe heart failure sits; ESCAPE stays in that home under the one-home rule and is cross-pointed here in prose only, not re-carded. On the general-ICU question, two randomised trials agree: PAC-Man (1041 patients in 65 UK intensive care units) found hospital mortality of 68% with a pulmonary artery catheter versus 66% without (adjusted hazard ratio 1.09, 95% CI 0.94 to 1.27), and the French trial of early catheter use in shock and ARDS (676 patients) found 28-day mortality of 59.4% versus 61.0% (relative risk 0.97, 95% CI 0.86 to 1.10), with no difference at 14 or 90 days or in organ-support-free days. The older observational SUPPORT analysis (5735 patients) had associated catheterisation with higher 30-day mortality (odds ratio 1.24, 95% CI 1.03 to 1.49) and higher cost — it is carded as the hypothesis-generating limb that prompted the trials, graded below them: it is confounded by indication, and the randomised trials that followed found neither the harm it suggested nor any benefit. Insertion complications occurred in 46 of 486 PAC-Man patients in whom a catheter was placed, none fatal. This is a closed historical question: routine catheter-guided management was abandoned on this evidence, and the shelf presents it as such, not as a live option.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — two randomised trials concordant on no survival benefit; the older observational harm signal was not confirmed as benefit or harm at randomisation

title: Solithromycin for community-acquired bacterial pneumonia: non-inferior to moxifloxacin in both phase 3 trials (early response 78.2% versus 77.9% oral; 79.3% versus 79.7% intravenous-to-oral) — and never approved, over liver-safety concerns
question: In adults with community-acquired bacterial pneumonia, is solithromycin (oral, or intravenous-to-oral) non-inferior to moxifloxacin for early clinical response and clinical success?
balance: POSSIBLE on the narrow non-inferiority question — with the failure printed on the face: solithromycin is a FAILED programme. It met non-inferiority against moxifloxacin in both of its phase 3 pneumonia trials, yet it was never approved — regulators refused it over hepatotoxicity concerns — and it is not an available treatment. This shelf is a completeness record, not a treatment option. In SOLITAIRE-ORAL (860 adults), early clinical response was 78.2% on oral solithromycin versus 77.9% on oral moxifloxacin (difference 0.29 percentage points, 95% CI -5.5 to 6.1; 10% non-inferiority margin). In SOLITAIRE-IV (863 adults), intravenous-to-oral solithromycin gave early response in 79.3% versus 79.7% (difference -0.46, 95% CI -6.1 to 5.2), with investigator-assessed clinical success at short-term follow-up of 84.6% versus 88.6%. A meta-analysis of three randomised trials (1855 patients) found no significant difference in early response (odds ratio 1.00, 95% CI 0.80 to 1.24) or adverse-event outcomes. Within the trials, short-course safety looked similar to moxifloxacin — but the trials were short and sized for efficacy, and the liver-safety record that stopped the programme sits outside them: infusion-site events were commoner with intravenous solithromycin, a paediatric trial run by the sponsor was stopped early by the sponsor before completion, and the regulatory refusal over liver concerns is the defining fact of this drug's history. Non-inferiority to moxifloxacin also deserves its plain meaning: as good as an existing drug within a 10% margin, not better.
stamp: POSSIBLE — non-inferiority shown in two phase 3 trials, but this is a failed programme: the drug was never approved (regulatory refusal over hepatotoxicity concerns) and is not available

title: Glepaglutide in short bowel syndrome with intestinal failure: twice-weekly dosing cut parenteral-support volume by 5.13 versus 2.85 L/week on placebo in the phase 3 trial; once-weekly dosing did not beat placebo
question: In adults with short bowel syndrome and intestinal failure dependent on parenteral support, does glepaglutide (long-acting GLP-2 analogue, twice-weekly or once-weekly) versus placebo reduce parenteral-support volume over 24 weeks?
balance: POSSIBLE — a single programme from a single sponsor (Zealand Pharma, named here for clarification because glepaglutide is its specific long-acting GLP-2 analogue product), and the shelf says so. The established GLP-2 home in this library is teduglutide, a different drug with daily dosing, cross-pointed here and not re-carded. In the phase 3 EASE-1 trial (106 patients with short bowel syndrome and intestinal failure on parenteral support at least 3 days a week), glepaglutide 10 mg twice weekly reduced weekly parenteral-support volume by 5.13 L/week versus 2.85 L/week on placebo at 24 weeks (P=.0039); clinical response (at least 20% reduction) was 65.7% versus 38.9%, at least one day per week off parenteral support was gained by 51.4% versus 19.4%, and 5 patients (14%) on twice-weekly dosing weaned off parenteral support completely versus none on placebo. Once-weekly dosing did NOT differ significantly from placebo on the primary or key secondary endpoints — the dose schedule is part of the answer. The supporting reports are thinner than the report count suggests: the phase 2 trial (18 patients) and its morphology companion come from one small single-centre Copenhagen cohort family, and the phase 3b absorption study enrolled exactly 10 patients (N=10, printed on its card). Parenteral-support volume is a clinical-use endpoint, not a mortality endpoint: no survival or intestinal-transplant claim is made anywhere in this evidence.
stamp: POSSIBLE — one sponsor programme; the phase 3 result is positive for twice-weekly dosing only, and the supporting reports come from small, partly overlapping Copenhagen cohorts

title: Aramchol in MASH (NASH): the one placebo-controlled MASH trial (ARREST, 247 patients) missed its primary liver-fat endpoint (P=0.066); the supporting reports are a small NAFLD trial and an uncontrolled open-label biopsy cohort of 51 patients
question: In adults with MASH (NASH) and fibrosis, does aramchol (fatty-acid–bile-acid conjugate, SCD1 modulator) versus placebo reduce liver fat and improve fibrosis?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — read the structure before the signals. The floor for this shelf is met by REPORT count, not by three independent controlled populations, and the face says so: (1) a 60-patient phase 2 trial in fatty liver disease (only 6 of its 60 patients had steatohepatitis) showed a dose-dependent fall in liver fat at the 300 mg dose; (2) ARREST, the one placebo-controlled trial in MASH (247 patients), MISSED its primary endpoint — the placebo-corrected fall in liver triglycerides on 600 mg was -3.1 (95% CI -6.4 to 0.2; P=0.066), which precluded further formal statistical testing, leaving the histology numbers (steatohepatitis resolution 16.7% versus 5%; fibrosis improvement 29.5% versus 17.5%, both with wide confidence intervals crossing no-effect) as unconfirmed signals; (3) the third report is NOT a controlled trial at all: it is an open-label, single-arm cohort of 51 patients from the ARMOR study given aramchol 300 mg twice daily, whose paired biopsies improved by 31% on conventional staging and more often on a continuous digital-pathology score — with no placebo group, some or all of that improvement may be natural history, regression to the mean, or biopsy sampling. The phase 3 ARMOR randomised trial has no published report; no phase 3 evidence exists and none is implied. Liver fat and biopsy fibrosis are surrogate endpoints throughout. Aramchol (the tested product was made by Trima Israel Pharmaceutical Products Ltd, named in the phase 2 record — named here for clarification) remains investigational.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the floor is met by report count (three reports of at least 10 patients), not by three independent controlled populations: ARREST missed its primary endpoint and the third report is open-label and uncontrolled

title: Pegbelfermin in MASH with bridging fibrosis or compensated cirrhosis: a failed programme — FALCON 1 missed its biopsy primary endpoint (24–31% versus 14%, P=.134) and FALCON 2 responses ran below placebo (24–28% versus 31%, P=.361)
question: In adults with MASH (NASH) and stage 3 (bridging) fibrosis or compensated cirrhosis, does pegbelfermin (pegylated FGF21 analogue) versus placebo improve fibrosis by at least one stage without worsening steatohepatitis?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — present the failure on the face: pegbelfermin is a FAILED programme. Both of its phase 2b trials missed their primary biopsy endpoints, and the shelf reports the two fibrosis stages as two separate limbs, never pooled. In FALCON 1 (stage 3 bridging fibrosis, 197 patients), the week-24 primary endpoint — at least a 1-point fibrosis improvement without steatohepatitis worsening, or steatohepatitis improvement without fibrosis worsening — was met by 14% on placebo versus 24–31% across the pegbelfermin dose arms, but the prespecified dose-response test was not significant (P=.134), so the endpoint was not met: the treatment made no difference that the trial could confirm. In FALCON 2 (compensated cirrhosis, stage 4; 155 patients), week-48 fibrosis improvement without worsening was 24–28% on pegbelfermin versus 31% on placebo (P=.361) — numerically favouring placebo. What did move were surrogates around the biopsy: liver fat fraction, elastography stiffness, collagen propeptide and liver enzymes improved on pegbelfermin in FALCON 1, and a biomarker report from that trial found significant improvements in composite fibrosis scores (ELF, FIB-4, APRI), fibrogenesis markers and all four blood protein signatures — while its own concordance analysis showed biomarker 'responses' exceeding and sometimes disagreeing with biopsy responses. Biopsy endpoints are themselves surrogates for clinical outcomes; here even the surrogates disagreed with each other. The FGF21-class homes for other drugs in earlier fibrosis stages are separate shelves and are not evidence for this drug in F3/F4 disease.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — failed programme: both FALCON trials missed their primary biopsy endpoints (the treatment made no difference on those endpoints); biomarker and liver-fat measures moved without a histology win

title: Natalizumab in Crohn's disease: induction results split (ENACT-1 missed, ENCORE met in patients with raised CRP), maintenance in responders was clearly positive (sustained response 61% versus 28%) — and the indication was abandoned over progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy
question: In adults with moderately to severely active Crohn's disease, does natalizumab (anti-alpha4-integrin monoclonal antibody) versus placebo induce response/remission and maintain remission?
balance: SPLIT — and the safety fact comes first on this shelf: natalizumab's Crohn's disease use was abandoned because of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML), the JC-virus brain infection that killed a patient in this programme's open-label extension. This is a historical/completeness shelf for a withdrawn indication, not a live treatment option; the gut-selective integrin drug vedolizumab is a different agent with its own homes in this library and is not evidence here. The efficacy record itself splits. Induction: the large ENACT-1 trial (905 patients) missed its primary contrasts — response 56% versus 49% (P=0.05) and remission 37% versus 30% (P=0.12) at week 10, small and nonsignificant — while ENCORE (509 patients selected for raised C-reactive protein) met its primary endpoint clearly (sustained response 48% versus 32%, P<.001; sustained remission 26% versus 16%, P=.002), and the earlier dose-ranging trial (248 patients) missed its week-6 remission primary at the 6 mg/kg dose while showing higher response rates. Maintenance is the strong limb, with a design caveat printed on its card: ENACT-2 re-randomised only the 339 patients who had already responded to natalizumab, and in that responder-enriched population continuing the drug beat switching to placebo decisively (sustained response 61% versus 28%, P<.001; remission 44% versus 26%, P=0.003). Serious adverse events were similar between arms in the controlled trials (about 7–10%); the PML death occurred in open-label extension use, which is where rare catastrophic harm characteristically appears.
stamp: SPLIT — induction split between ENACT-1 (primary response/remission not significant) and ENCORE (met, in CRP-elevated patients); maintenance in induction responders was positive; the Crohn's indication was abandoned over PML risk, so this is a historical shelf, not a live option

title: Filgotinib in Crohn's disease: a failed phase 3 — FITZROY phase 2 remission was 47% versus 23%, but DIVERSITY missed its week-10 co-primary endpoints in both induction studies (endoscopic response difference 5.5% and 0.1%, both not significant)
question: In adults with moderately to severely active Crohn's disease, does filgotinib (JAK1 inhibitor) versus placebo induce and maintain clinical remission and endoscopic response?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — present the failure on the face: filgotinib in Crohn's disease is a FAILED phase 3 programme. The floor rests on two trials plus a post hoc report of one of them, and the shelf says so. FITZROY, the phase 2 trial (174 patients), was positive: clinical remission at week 10 in 47% on filgotinib 200 mg versus 23% on placebo (difference 24 percentage points, 95% CI 9 to 39; P=0.0077). Its 2025 post hoc analysis asked whether ileal disease responds differently from colonic disease and, after adjusting for baseline activity and within-patient clustering, found no significant difference — a methods report of the same trial, adding no patients. DIVERSITY, the phase 3 programme (induction studies A and B, 707 and 665 patients; maintenance 481), then missed its week-10 co-primary endpoints: PRO2 clinical remission on 200 mg reached significance in study B (29.7% versus 17.9%; P=0.0039) but not study A (32.9% versus 25.7%; P=0.0963), and endoscopic response was not significant in either (differences 5.5 and 0.1 percentage points); the 100 mg dose met no co-primary endpoint anywhere. At week 58, among patients re-randomised after responding during induction, filgotinib 200 mg did meet both co-primary endpoints versus withdrawal to placebo (PRO2 remission 43.8% versus 26.4%; endoscopic response 30.4% versus 9.4%) — a responder-enriched maintenance result that does not rescue the failed induction. Filgotinib's ulcerative colitis and rheumatoid arthritis questions are homed on separate shelves; nothing here transfers to them.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — failed phase 3: DIVERSITY missed its induction co-primary endpoints; the positive limbs are a single phase 2 trial and a responder-re-randomised maintenance analysis

title: Mepolizumab in eosinophilic oesophagitis: oesophageal eosinophils fall sharply, but dysphagia does not improve more than with placebo — a histology–symptom split
question: In children, adolescents and adults with eosinophilic oesophagitis, does mepolizumab (anti-IL-5) versus placebo reduce oesophageal eosinophilia and improve dysphagia symptoms?
balance: SPLIT — the split is between tissue and symptoms, and it is the recurring anti-IL-5 pattern in eosinophilic oesophagitis (the same lesson as the benralizumab MESSINA shelf, pack #3613). On histology, mepolizumab works in every report: in the largest randomised trial (Dellon 2023, n=66) peak eosinophil counts fell from 113 to 36 per high-power field against a rise on placebo, with histologic responses (<15 eos/hpf) in 42% versus 3%; the paediatric dose-ranging trial (Assa'ad 2011, n=59, no placebo arm) and the small adult pilot (Straumann 2010, N = 11, printed on the face) point the same way. On symptoms, the largest trial missed its primary endpoint: dysphagia scores improved no more than with placebo at 3 months (p=0.14 — the treatment made no difference to dysphagia), and longer treatment to 6 months added nothing. A shelf that converted the histology win into a symptom claim would misstate this evidence. The paediatric programme's post-hoc analysis (Wong 2023) is a report of the Assa'ad trial, not an independent population, and is labelled as such. A 2006 four-patient report is sub-floor and is not carded. Stamp: SPLIT, naming the split.
stamp: SPLIT — histologic response improves; dysphagia symptoms do not

title: Octreotide for angiodysplasia bleeding: the OCEAN randomised trial cut transfusion needs by about 10 units a year versus standard care, concordant with the earlier pooled patient-level data
question: In adults with recurrent or transfusion-dependent bleeding from gastrointestinal angiodysplasias, does octreotide (long-acting release) versus standard care reduce transfusion requirements and rebleeding?
balance: LIKELY — two randomised-era limbs and one large pooled analysis agree on direction and rough size. The OCEAN trial (2024, n=62, open-label against standard care that included endoscopic therapy) found about 10 fewer transfusion units over a year with octreotide long-acting release (11.0 vs 21.2 units). The individual-patient-data meta-analysis of the pre-OCEAN literature (212 patients; one randomised trial and ten cohort studies, the cohort limb graded low-certainty and kept visibly separate here) found transfusions falling from a mean 12.8 units at baseline to 2.3 on treatment, with 83% good responders. The oldest limb (Junquera 2007) compared an octreotide cohort with an external placebo control group from a concurrent trial — an external-control design, labelled as such, not a within-study randomisation. Transfusion need and rebleeding are the outcomes; no mortality claim is made. For the overlapping population treated with a different drug, see the sibling shelf on thalidomide for recurrent small-intestinal angiodysplasia bleeding (#7113) — a distinct evidence base, cross-pointed here in prose and not re-carded.
stamp: LIKELY

title: Thalidomide for recurrent small-intestinal angiodysplasia bleeding: a 150-patient placebo-controlled trial found effective responses in 68.6% (100 mg) and 51.0% (50 mg) versus 16.0% on placebo
question: In adults with recurrent bleeding from small-intestinal angiodysplasia, does thalidomide (100 mg or 50 mg daily for four months) versus placebo reduce bleeding episodes over the following year?
balance: LIKELY — one large, well-conducted placebo-controlled trial dominates and the syntheses agree with it. In the Chen 2023 multicentre trial (n=150; four months of treatment, at least a year of follow-up), an effective response — at least a 50% reduction in bleeding episodes in the year after treatment versus the year before — occurred in 68.6% on thalidomide 100 mg and 51.0% on 50 mg versus 16.0% on placebo. A meta-analysis with trial-sequential analysis of the three randomised trials (279 patients, 87.1% small-intestinal) found the cumulative evidence already exceeded the required information size, and a 2026 systematic review of six studies (265 patients) reports the same direction, including the earlier iron-controlled randomised trial (response 71.4% vs 3.7%). The harm face is mandatory: thalidomide is teratogenic — pregnancy prevention is an absolute condition of use — and the trial's common adverse events were constipation, somnolence, limb numbness, peripheral oedema, dizziness and raised liver enzymes, with peripheral neuropathy the standing long-term concern. Cross-point in prose: octreotide (somatostatin analogues) for gastrointestinal angiodysplasia bleeding is the sibling drug question, homed at shelf #7112 with a distinct evidence base; neither shelf re-cards the other's trials.
stamp: LIKELY

title: Endoscopic versus surgical drainage of pancreatic pseudocyst: success is equivalent in the small randomised trials — endoscopy wins on hospital stay (2 vs 6 days) and cost, not on cure
question: In adults with a symptomatic pancreatic pseudocyst suitable for either approach, does endoscopic (including EUS-guided) cystogastrostomy/drainage versus surgical cystogastrostomy achieve equivalent success with shorter stay and lower cost?
balance: POSSIBLE — a procedure-strategy (GAP-E) shelf, confined to pseudocyst (no or minimal solid debris); walled-off necrosis is a different collection with its own step-up shelves and is not re-carded here. The randomised trials are small and single-centre, so equivalence claims are necessarily soft: in the one head-to-head trial of endoscopic versus open surgical cystogastrostomy (Varadarajulu 2013, n=40), recurrence, success, complications and re-interventions did not differ (the treatment made no difference on those outcomes), while stay (median 2 vs 6 days) and cost ($7,011 vs $15,052) favoured endoscopy. The endoscopic-versus-laparoscopic trial (Garg 2020, n=60) mixed pseudocyst with walled-off necrosis and is carded as a mixed-population limb, not pure pseudocyst evidence. A third randomised trial answers the within-endoscopy question (EUS-guided versus conventional transmural drainage, Park 2009), and a systematic review of ten comparative studies — most of them cohort comparisons, labelled observational — reaches the same shape of conclusion. Technique has moved since the earliest trial (lumen-apposing metal stents postdate much of this record), so the evidence is dated on its face. Observational and small-trial structure caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Dordaviprone in recurrent H3 K27M-mutant diffuse midline glioma: single-arm pooled response rate 20% by RANO-HGG with median response duration 11.2 months — no controlled evidence yet
question: In patients with recurrent H3 K27M-mutant diffuse midline glioma, does single-agent dordaviprone (ONC201), versus no concurrent control, produce objective responses and clinical benefit?
balance: POSSIBLE, capped by design: every carded report is single-arm or uncontrolled, so response rates have no comparator and are framed as such throughout (GAP-E). The pooled integrated analysis of four trials plus an expanded-access protocol (n=50) found an objective response rate of 20.0% by RANO-HGG (30.0% by combined RANO criteria) with a median response duration of 11.2 months in a disease with no established therapy beyond radiation — the signal that supported FDA accelerated approval in August 2025 for recurrent H3 K27M-mutant diffuse midline glioma. The large international compassionate-use cohort (n=174) is sobering real-world context: median survival after starting the drug was 4.7 months. The two paediatric phase 1 reports are dose/safety limbs of the same early programme (one, NCT03416530, also feeds the pooled analysis — the overlap is labelled, not hidden). Product naming, clarification exception: dordaviprone (Modeyso, Chimerix/Jazz Pharmaceuticals). Cross-points in prose only: the phase 3 ACTION trial in newly diagnosed disease is a different slice with no results published, and the non-midline H3 K27M cohort is an adjacent slice — neither is carded here.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Tovorafenib in relapsed/refractory BRAF-altered paediatric low-grade glioma: FIREFLY-1 response rate 67% by RANO-HGG (51% by RAPNO), vision preserved in 80% of the optic-pathway subgroup — single-arm, single programme
question: In children with relapsed or refractory BRAF-altered paediatric low-grade glioma, does once-weekly tovorafenib, versus no concurrent control, produce objective responses and preserve vision in optic-pathway disease?
balance: POSSIBLE, capped by structure: this is a single-arm, single-programme shelf — all three carded reports describe the same FIREFLY-1 (PNOC026) trial and are labelled as one programme throughout, on the established single-programme precedent. Within that limit the signal is strong and consistent across assessment criteria: response rate 67% by RANO-HGG and 51% by RAPNO (including minor responses) in arm 1 (n=77), median response duration 16.6 and 13.8 months respectively, and in the optic-pathway subgroup vision was preserved in 80% of patients and improved in 31%. The FDA granted accelerated approval in April 2024 for relapsed/refractory BRAF-altered paediatric low-grade glioma from 6 months of age, with the frontline FIREFLY-2 trial required as the postmarketing study (a design for a different, frontline question — cross-pointed in prose, not carded). Product naming, clarification exception: tovorafenib (Ojemda, Day One Biopharmaceuticals). The harm face: hair colour changes (76%), raised creatine phosphokinase (56%) and anaemia (49%) are the commonest treatment-related events, grade ≥3 treatment-related events occurred in 42%, and 7% discontinued for toxicity. title: Siltuximab in idiopathic multicentric Castleman disease: the one randomised trial found durable responses in 34% versus 0% on placebo, with real-world cohorts concordant
question: In patients with HIV-negative, HHV-8-negative idiopathic multicentric Castleman disease, does the anti-IL-6 antibody siltuximab, versus placebo (both with best supportive care), produce durable tumour and symptomatic responses and prolong progression-free survival?
balance: POSSIBLE — one randomised trial anchors this shelf and everything else is its supporting limb, labelled as such. The pivotal double-blind trial (van Rhee 2014, n=79, HIV-negative/HHV-8-negative symptomatic disease) found durable tumour and symptomatic responses in 34% on siltuximab plus best supportive care versus 0% on placebo plus best supportive care, with similar grade ≥3 adverse-event rates despite much longer exposure on the drug. A post-hoc analysis of the same trial (same programme, labelled) shows progression-free survival significantly prolonged (median not reached versus 14.5 months). The independent real-world limbs — a 48-patient Greek/Romanian retrospective cohort with a 71.1% overall response rate among the 38 assessed, and a 9-patient Italian named-patient series (N = 9, sub-floor, printed on its face and not counted toward this shelf's evidence floor) — are observational and graded accordingly. A single randomised trial caps the stamp at POSSIBLE even with concordant cohorts.

title: Emapalumab in primary HLH: single-arm pivotal response 63% in previously treated children, about 70% bridged to transplant — real-world and pre-transplant cohorts concordant
question: In children with primary haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis that is refractory, recurrent, progressive or intolerant of conventional therapy, does the anti-interferon-γ antibody emapalumab, versus no concurrent control, produce responses and bridge patients to transplantation?
balance: POSSIBLE, capped by design: the pivotal evidence is a single-arm phase 2/3 study (GAP-E), so response and transplant-bridging rates are framed without any comparator claim. In that study (Locatelli 2020, n=34), 63% of previously treated children responded — significantly above the prespecified 40% null — about 70% proceeded to transplantation, and about three-quarters were alive at last observation. Two observational limbs, labelled as such, point the same way: the 46-patient US real-world primary-HLH cohort (REAL-HLH) reproduced the pivotal trial's pattern, and a 50-patient single-centre retrospective comparison found children who received emapalumab shortly before reduced-intensity transplant had markedly less mixed chimerism (48% vs 77%) and better intervention-free survival (73% vs 43%), though overall survival did not differ significantly. Product naming, clarification exception: emapalumab (Gamifant, Sobi). Cross-point in prose only: the malignancy-associated (secondary) HLH real-world population is a different question and is not carded here. The defining harm is infection: severe infections developed in 10 of 34 pivotal-trial patients during treatment, in a disease whose immune suppression is itself profound.

title: Tagraxofusp in BPDCN: single-arm complete-response rate 72% in untreated patients at the 12 µg/kg dose, about half bridged to transplant — capillary leak syndrome is the defining harm
question: In patients with blastic plasmacytoid dendritic cell neoplasm, does the CD123-directed cytotoxin tagraxofusp, versus no concurrent control, produce complete responses, and can responders be bridged to stem-cell transplantation?
balance: POSSIBLE, capped by design: all carded evidence is single-arm (GAP-E), so response rates are framed without a comparator. In the pivotal multicohort trial (Pemmaraju 2019), untreated patients at the 12 µg/kg dose achieved the primary outcome (complete response plus clinical complete response) in 72%, with an overall response rate of 90% and 45% bridged to stem-cell transplantation; the long-term report of the same programme (labelled one programme) puts the treatment-naive complete-response rate at 57% in the larger 12 µg/kg population with a median response duration of 24.9 months. The 2026 real-world frontline cohort (n=32, Letter-format, observational) found similar response rates (overall 82.1%, complete 60.7%) — but its propensity-matched comparison against a pre-tagraxofusp historical cohort showed no survival advantage (2-year survival 59.4% vs 60.8%), an honesty anchor this shelf keeps on its face. Capillary leak syndrome is the defining, potentially fatal harm: 19–21% in the trial reports and 53.1% in the real-world cohort, managed per the product label with albumin monitoring, weight/fluid checks and dose holds. Product naming, clarification exception: tagraxofusp (Elzonris, Stemline/Menarini). Cross-point in prose only: the tagraxofusp-plus-azacitidine-plus-venetoclax combination programme is a different question and is not carded here.

title: Moxetumomab pasudotox in relapsed/refractory hairy cell leukaemia: single-arm durable complete response 36% at long-term follow-up, with most complete responders MRD-negative — a withdrawn product whose remissions outlast it
question: In adults with relapsed or refractory hairy cell leukaemia after purine-analogue therapy, does the CD22 immunotoxin moxetumomab pasudotox, versus no concurrent control, produce durable complete remissions with minimal-residual-disease clearance?
balance: POSSIBLE, capped by design: all carded evidence is single-arm (GAP-E), framed without a comparator throughout. The pivotal trial (n=80, at least two prior systemic therapies including a purine analogue) produced complete responses in 41% and — at long-term follow-up of the same programme, labelled as such — a durable complete-response rate of 36%, with 82% of complete responders MRD-negative and a median progression-free survival without loss of haematologic remission of 71.7 months. The earlier phase 1 programme (two overlapping reports of the same dose-escalation study and its extension cohort, labelled as one programme) found the same pattern: complete remissions in about half to two-thirds, lasting longer when MRD-negative (median 42.1 vs 13.5 months). The defining harms are capillary leak syndrome and haemolytic uraemic syndrome, each in up to about 10% and generally reversible. Market history belongs on the face: the product was withdrawn from the US market in 2023 for commercial reasons and later from the EU — this shelf's value is the durable MRD-negative remissions it demonstrated in a no-option population, and the frontline purine-analogue question lives in its own home (pack #5300) and is not re-carded here.

title: Nelarabine added to frontline therapy in newly diagnosed T-ALL: disease-free survival 88.2% vs 82.1% in the one large randomised trial, with neurotoxicity the defining harm
question: In children, adolescents and young adults with newly diagnosed T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, does adding nelarabine to intensive multi-agent chemotherapy, versus the same chemotherapy without nelarabine, improve disease-free and overall survival?
balance: POSSIBLE — one large randomised trial carries the claim, supported by two non-randomised programme reports. In COG AALL0434 (1,562 evaluable patients; 323 randomised to nelarabine vs 336 to no nelarabine in the relevant comparison), 5-year disease-free survival was 88.2% with nelarabine vs 82.1% without (P = .029), and isolated/combined CNS relapse was much less frequent (1.3% vs 6.9%, P = .0001); there was no interaction with the methotrexate randomisation (P = .41), and the best arm was escalating-dose methotrexate plus nelarabine (5-year disease-free survival 91%, n = 147). The Japanese ALL-T11 programme (349 patients) gave nelarabine to high- and very-high-risk patients without randomising it and reported 3-year event-free survival of 86.4% overall. The adult JALSG T-ALL213-O study was small (24 analysed, only 14 actually received nelarabine) and found grade 3 peripheral neuropathy and/or gait disturbance in 7 of 14 treated patients (50%) — far above the 3% grade 3 peripheral motor neuropathy rate in ALL-T11 and the acceptable, arm-similar toxicity in AALL0434. Neurotoxicity (central and peripheral) is the defining harm and the reason for the boxed warning. The relapsed-disease nelarabine combination experience (NECTAR) is a different, relapsed slice and is cross-pointed here only, not carded.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Pelabresib plus ruxolitinib in JAK-inhibitor-naive myelofibrosis (MANIFEST-2): spleen response 65.9% vs 35.2%, but the symptom advantage was not significant
question: In adults with JAK-inhibitor-naive myelofibrosis, does adding the BET inhibitor pelabresib to ruxolitinib, versus ruxolitinib alone, improve spleen-volume response, symptoms and anaemia?
balance: POSSIBLE — one phase 3 randomised trial (MANIFEST-2, 430 patients) anchors the shelf, which caps the stamp, supported by the earlier single-arm MANIFEST programme. The spleen claim is strong: spleen-volume reduction of at least 35% at week 24 in 65.9% on pelabresib plus ruxolitinib vs 35.2% on ruxolitinib alone (absolute difference 30.4 percentage points). The symptom claim is weaker and must stay subordinate: absolute total-symptom-score change differed by -1.94 points (P = 0.0545, not significant) and the symptom-response rates were 52.3% vs 46.3% (confidence interval crossing zero) — on symptoms, the combination made no proven difference. The anaemia claim is secondary and mixed: anaemia as an adverse event was actually less frequent on the combination (44.8% vs 55.1%), and the phase 2 programme reported haemoglobin improvement in 36%, but no randomised anaemia endpoint is carded. Added harms of the combination are thrombocytopenia (52.8% vs 37.4%; grade 3 or worse 13.2% vs 6.1%) and gastrointestinal effects from the wider programme. Nearby homes ask different questions: ruxolitinib alone, momelotinib, pacritinib and fedratinib each have their own shelves.

title: Mogamulizumab in previously treated cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (MAVORIC): progression-free survival 7.7 vs 3.1 months, with responses concentrated in blood and Sezary disease
question: In patients with previously treated mycosis fungoides or Sezary syndrome, does the anti-CCR4 antibody mogamulizumab, versus vorinostat, improve progression-free survival and produce responses, particularly in blood-involved disease?
balance: POSSIBLE — one phase 3 randomised trial (MAVORIC, 372 patients) anchors the shelf, with a post hoc analysis, a small French real-world cohort and a 2026 systematic review as support. MAVORIC found median progression-free survival of 7.7 months on mogamulizumab vs 3.1 months on vorinostat (hazard ratio 0.53, a relative measure; the absolute medians are printed on the card). The compartment split is the shelf's clinical point: in the pooled systematic review, response rates were 52.5% in Sezary syndrome vs 31.1% in mycosis fungoides, and 82.6% in the blood compartment vs 43.7% in skin. Benefit did not depend on how many or which prior therapies patients had received (post hoc MAVORIC analysis). Two harms are mandatory on the face: mogamulizumab-associated rash, which can mimic progression and lead to wrong treatment decisions, and the warning that giving mogamulizumab before allogeneic transplantation increases the risk of severe graft-versus-host disease. Grade 3-4 adverse events in MAVORIC were 41% in both arms; in the French cohort (21 patients), 10 of 21 had grade III-IV events.

title: Omacetaxine in TKI-resistant or intolerant CML: major cytogenetic responses in about one in five chronic-phase patients, single-arm evidence throughout, myelosuppression the dominant harm
question: In adults with chronic- or accelerated-phase chronic myeloid leukaemia resistant or intolerant to two or more tyrosine kinase inhibitors (including T315I disease), does omacetaxine mepesuccinate, versus no concurrent control, produce haematologic and cytogenetic responses?
balance: POSSIBLE — single-arm evidence throughout (GAP-E): every card is an uncontrolled phase 2 report from one development programme, so response rates have no comparator and the stamp is capped. In chronic phase, major cytogenetic response occurred in 23% of 62 T315I patients (complete haematologic response 77%) and in 22% of 46 patients resistant/intolerant to at least two TKIs; the programme's final pooled analysis put chronic-phase major cytogenetic response at 18% with a median duration of 12.5 months and median overall survival of 40.3 months. Accelerated-phase results are weaker: major haematologic response 37% in one report but only 14% achieved or maintained in the pooled final analysis, with no major cytogenetic response and median survival of 14.3 months. Myelosuppression is the dominant harm — grade 3 or worse haematologic toxicity in 79% (chronic phase) and 73% (accelerated phase) in the pooled analysis, with grade 3/4 thrombocytopenia in 54-76% across reports; about 10% of chronic-phase patients stopped for toxicity. Product naming (clarification): omacetaxine mepesuccinate is marketed as Synribo; the carded records do not name a company. The higher-risk MDS phase 2 experience is a different disease and is cross-pointed only.

title: Olverembatinib in TKI-resistant CML including T315I: high cumulative cytogenetic and molecular response rates in Chinese single-arm and cohort evidence, no randomised trial
question: In adults with chronic- or accelerated-phase chronic myeloid leukaemia resistant to prior tyrosine kinase inhibitors, including BCR::ABL1 T315I-mutated disease, does olverembatinib, versus no concurrent control, produce cytogenetic and molecular responses?
balance: POSSIBLE — single-arm evidence throughout (GAP-E), generated almost entirely in China, where olverembatinib was first approved (2021); no randomised trial exists in the carded record. The phase 1/2 programme (165 patients, over 80% after at least two TKIs) reported 3-year cumulative major cytogenetic response of 79.0% in chronic phase (complete cytogenetic response 69.0%, major molecular response 56.0%) and 47.4% in accelerated phase, with the highest rates in single-T315I disease. A retrospective dose comparison (216 patients starting at 40 mg every other day vs 66 at 30 mg) found no significant difference in responses or outcomes between doses — on efficacy the lower dose made no difference — but significantly fewer dose reductions or discontinuations for adverse events (21% vs 41%). A 130-patient accelerated-phase cohort reported 6-year cumulative major cytogenetic response of 59% and survival of 71%. Common treatment-related events in the programme were skin hyperpigmentation, hypertriglyceridaemia, proteinuria and severe thrombocytopenia. Arterial occlusive events are a class concern with third-generation BCR::ABL1 inhibitors, but no rates from this drug's carded records are printed here and ponatinib's rates must not be imported into this shelf.

title: Hetrombopag in immune thrombocytopenia: platelet response 58.9-64.3% vs 5.9% on placebo in adults and 61.4% vs 9.7% in children — China-generated evidence, not FDA/EMA-approved
question: In adults, and in children and adolescents, with persistent or chronic primary immune thrombocytopenia, does the thrombopoietin-receptor agonist hetrombopag, versus placebo, produce durable platelet responses and reduce bleeding?
balance: POSSIBLE — two placebo-controlled phase 3 trials (adults; children and adolescents) from one Chinese development programme agree on a large platelet-response benefit, which is strong, but a single programme in a single country caps the stamp; the drug is approved in China and is not FDA/EMA-approved, and that is stated plainly. Adults: response at week 8 in 58.9% (2.5 mg) and 64.3% (5 mg) vs 5.9% on placebo (odds ratios 25.97 and 32.81 — relative measures; the absolute rates are printed on the card). Children aged 6-17: response at week 10 in 61.4% vs 9.7% (absolute difference 52.7 percentage points), with sustained response 43.9% vs 0%. The extension study supplies the durability warning: when hetrombopag was tapered to withdrawal, 88.1% relapsed, at a median of just 15 days — this is a maintenance treatment, not a cure. Harms are mainly infections (upper respiratory tract infection in 42-58% across reports) and liver-enzyme elevations (treatment-related hepatotoxicity events in 17.5% over 24 weeks in the paediatric trial, all grade 1-2). The chemotherapy-induced-thrombocytopenia reports are a different question — cross-point only.

title: Dapsone in primary ITP: SPLIT — older series and a pooled analysis suggest about half respond, but the one randomised trial found no significant benefit and most patients stopped the drug
question: In adults with primary immune thrombocytopenia needing a low-cost second-line option, does dapsone, versus no concurrent control or standard care, produce platelet responses, and at what haemolytic cost?
balance: SPLIT — the split is between designs. On one side, the observational record: a 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis (4 studies, over 270 patients) pooled an overall response rate of 47% and a complete response rate of 28%, and two paediatric series report responses in about two thirds of children. On the other side, the only randomised trial (93 adults, prednisone plus dapsone vs prednisone alone, reported together with a 46-patient real-world cohort in the same 2025 publication) found a week-52 response of 21.7% vs 8.5% (P = .17) — on its primary endpoint the added dapsone made no significant difference — while 78.3% of the dapsone arm discontinued the drug after a median of 4.6 weeks, mostly for adverse events; the trial authors concluded the risk-benefit ratio is unfavourable and preferred standard second-line options where available. The haemolytic cost is real: the meta-analysis found a mean haemoglobin fall of 1.74 g/dL and adverse effects in 18% (haemolytic anaemia and methaemoglobinaemia commonest). Haemolysis (especially in G6PD deficiency — G6PD testing belongs before use), methaemoglobinaemia and dapsone hypersensitivity syndrome are the defining harms. The dapsone gel shelf for acne is a different formulation and question.
stamp: SPLIT

title: Helicobacter pylori eradication in H. pylori-positive ITP: SPLIT by biogeography — about half respond in Japanese, Italian and Korean cohorts, far fewer in US and northern-European and paediatric data
question: In adults with immune thrombocytopenia who test positive for Helicobacter pylori, does eradication therapy, versus no eradication, raise platelet counts and produce durable responses?
balance: SPLIT — the split is biogeography and age, and it is the shelf. In the large systematic review (25 studies, 1,555 patients), overall response after eradication was 50.3% and complete response 42.7%, with response rates tending to be higher in countries with high background H. pylori prevalence (the Japanese and Italian cohorts) and lower in US and northern-European data; patients starting below 30 x 10^9/L responded less (overall response 35.2%). The randomised evidence is small but real: the first RCT found a platelet response in 46.2% of the eradication group vs 0% without eradication, and a Korean phase 3 trial in moderate thrombocytopenia found a significant response difference (P = 0.017) after sequential eradication. Against that, the meta-analysis restricted to randomised trials (6 trials, 241 patients) found only a borderline overall-response advantage (odds ratio 1.93, 95% CI 1.01 to 3.71 — a relative measure) and, in children, the eradication group made no significant difference (odds ratio 1.80, confidence interval crossing 1). The underlying randomised trials are small — the largest carded enrolled 28 H. pylori-positive patients — so testing for and eradicating H. pylori is a reasonable, cheap step in H. pylori-positive ITP, with response expectations set by region: roughly one in two in high-prevalence settings, substantially fewer elsewhere. Eradication regimens varied by era and region (standard triple therapy in the early trials; 10-day sequential therapy in the Korean phase 3).
stamp: SPLIT

title: Ruxolitinib in steroid-refractory or dependent chronic GVHD (REACH3): overall response 49.7% vs 25.6% and median failure-free survival 38.4 vs 5.7 months at 3 years
question: In patients aged 12 years and older with glucocorticoid-refractory or glucocorticoid-dependent chronic graft-versus-host disease after allogeneic transplantation, does ruxolitinib, versus investigator's-choice best available therapy, improve overall response and failure-free survival?
balance: POSSIBLE — a single randomised programme (REACH3) carries the shelf, which caps the stamp, however large its effects. In 329 patients aged 12 years and older, overall response at week 24 was 49.7% on ruxolitinib vs 25.6% on investigator's-choice best available therapy (odds ratio 2.99, a relative measure; absolute rates printed on the card), symptom response was 24.2% vs 11.0%, and at the 3-year final analysis median failure-free survival was 38.4 vs 5.7 months (hazard ratio 0.36, a relative measure). The Japanese subgroup (37 patients) pointed the same way. Two structural cautions: the trial was open-label against a heterogeneous comparator list, and best-available-therapy patients could cross over to ruxolitinib (70 did, responding at rates consistent with the main trial), which limits any survival reading — median overall survival was not reached and no survival advantage is claimed here. Added harms against best available therapy are cytopenias (grade 3 or worse thrombocytopenia 15.2% vs 10.1% and anaemia 12.7% vs 7.6% to week 24) and infection vigilance; cytomegalovirus infection/reactivation rates were similar. Ruxolitinib was FDA-approved for this indication in September 2021. The acute-GVHD ruxolitinib shelf is a different question and its evidence is not used here; belumosudil and axatilimab shelves cover later-line chronic GVHD.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Post-transplant cyclophosphamide prophylaxis (BMT CTN 1703): GVHD-free, relapse-free survival 52.7% vs 34.9% at 1 year in reduced-intensity matched-donor transplantation
question: In adults undergoing reduced-intensity or non-myeloablative matched-donor allogeneic transplantation, does post-transplant cyclophosphamide plus tacrolimus plus mycophenolate prophylaxis, versus tacrolimus plus methotrexate, improve GVHD-free, relapse-free survival?
balance: POSSIBLE — a single trial programme (BMT CTN 1703) carries the shelf, which caps the stamp, with three reports of that one trial carded and labelled as one programme. In 431 adults receiving reduced-intensity conditioning and HLA-matched related or matched/7-of-8-mismatched unrelated donor grafts, GVHD-free, relapse-free survival at 1 year was 52.7% with post-transplant cyclophosphamide plus tacrolimus plus mycophenolate vs 34.9% with tacrolimus plus methotrexate (hazard ratio 0.64 for the composite event — a relative measure; absolute rates printed on the card), and the advantage held at 2 years (42.4% vs 28.8%). Patients on the cyclophosphamide regimen also reported lower chronic-GVHD symptom burden in the first year. Overall survival, disease-free survival, relapse, transplant-related death and engraftment did not differ substantially between the groups — on those endpoints the regimens made no clear difference; the gain is in GVHD control and time free of immunosuppression. The population fence is part of the tested intervention's identity: reduced-intensity conditioning, matched donors, peripheral-blood grafts predominating. Nothing here generalises to myeloablative conditioning or haploidentical transplantation, which have their own literatures and shelves.
stamp: POSSIBLE

title: Abatacept added to standard prophylaxis for acute GVHD prevention (ABA2)
question: In patients undergoing unrelated-donor allogeneic transplantation, does adding abatacept to calcineurin-inhibitor-based prophylaxis, versus prophylaxis alone, reduce severe acute GVHD without increasing relapse or infection?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single programme (the ABA2 trial, reported three ways, plus one small single-arm paediatric cohort) caps the stamp at POSSIBLE. In ABA2's randomised 8/8-matched stratum, grade 3–4 acute GVHD by day +100 was 6.8% on abatacept versus 14.8% on placebo (P = .13 — not conventionally significant on the primary endpoint, in a phase 2 trial designed with a higher type-1 error), while severe-GVHD-free survival favoured abatacept (93.2% vs 82%, P = .05). The 7/8-mismatched stratum was single-arm: grade 3–4 acute GVHD of 2.3% against 30.2% in a non-randomised registry comparator — a comparison that cannot carry the same weight. The exposure–response report adds a dose lesson, not new patients: patients whose first-dose trough reached at least 39 µg/mL had a lower grade 2–4 GVHD risk (hazard ratio 0.35, a relative measure), while those below that trough looked indistinguishable from placebo. The paediatric bone-marrow-failure cohort (10 children) showed tolerability and no severe acute or chronic GVHD, but it is a single-arm phase 1 experience. EBV reactivation and post-transplant lymphoproliferative disease are the monitoring burden that comes with co-stimulation blockade: one probable PTLD case occurred in the small paediatric cohort, and the exposure analysis found no association between higher exposure and CMV or EBV viraemia. The licensed slice (FDA approval December 2021, with a calcineurin inhibitor and methotrexate, for patients aged 2 years and over receiving matched or 1-allele-mismatched unrelated-donor grafts) is the population this shelf covers.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single programme (ABA2): in the randomised 8/8-matched stratum severe acute GVHD was 6.8% versus 14.8% (P = .13) with severe-GVHD-free survival 93.2% versus 82%; the 7/8 stratum was single-arm against registry controls, so a single programme with a non-significant randomised primary endpoint caps the stamp at POSSIBLE

title: Romiplostim for refractory aplastic anaemia
question: In patients with aplastic anaemia refractory to immunosuppressive therapy, does romiplostim, versus no concurrent control, produce haematologic responses, including trilineage responses?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — all of the evidence is single-arm, which caps the stamp at POSSIBLE: there is no randomised or concurrent-control comparison anywhere on this shelf, so response rates have no counterfactual. In the phase 2/3 study, 84% of 31 patients refractory to immunosuppressive therapy achieved some haematological response by week 27, with trilineage response in 39% at week 53 — striking in a refractory population, but a proportion, not a treatment effect. The nationwide Japanese post-marketing surveillance (470 patients) found similar response proportions in routine practice (78.6% at 27 weeks among those assessed) and gives the best harm picture: adverse drug reactions in 18.1%, with thromboembolism in 1.49% and haematopoietic tumour in 1.28% recorded as reactions of special interest. The eltrombopag-refractory series is small (10 patients, 7 responding) and supports switching within the class, no more. Clonal evolution is the standing worry with thrombopoietin-receptor agonists in aplastic anaemia: 2 of 31 patients in the phase 2/3 study developed cytogenetic abnormalities (one later returned to a normal karyotype), and marrow and cytogenetic monitoring is part of the treatment's follow-up burden, not an optional extra. Romiplostim for immune thrombocytopenia and for chemotherapy-induced thrombocytopenia are different questions, homed elsewhere, and none of that record is carded here.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — entirely single-arm evidence: 84% haematological response at week 27 in the 31-patient phase 2/3 study and 78.6% in 470-patient nationwide surveillance, with no randomised comparator anywhere, so observational/single-arm structure caps the stamp at POSSIBLE

title: Avapritinib for advanced systemic mastocytosis (EXPLORER / PATHFINDER)
question: In adults with advanced systemic mastocytosis (aggressive systemic mastocytosis, systemic mastocytosis with an associated haematological neoplasm, or mast cell leukaemia), does avapritinib, versus no concurrent control or best available therapy, produce overall responses and improve survival?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the pivotal evidence is single-arm (EXPLORER phase 1 and PATHFINDER phase 2, one programme), which caps the stamp at POSSIBLE; the only comparative report is a retrospective external comparison against best available therapy, which is observational and labelled as such. Response rates were consistent: overall response 75% in both the phase 1 response-evaluable set (53 patients) and the PATHFINDER interim set (32 response-evaluable of 62 enrolled), and 71% in the pooled previously-treated analysis (31 response-evaluable patients). Mast-cell burden fell deeply (at least 50% reductions in tryptase in 89–99% and in marrow mast cells in 88–92% across reports). The external comparison found better survival on avapritinib than on best available therapy (adjusted hazard ratio 0.48 — a relative measure, from a non-randomised comparison, so confounding by era and selection is expected). The defining harms are intracranial haemorrhage — 13% overall in EXPLORER but only 1% in patients without severe thrombocytopenia, which is why platelet-count gating is part of the tested intervention — and cognitive effects, alongside periorbital oedema and cytopenias (grade 3 or worse neutropenia 24%, thrombocytopenia 16%, anaemia 16% in PATHFINDER). This shelf is the advanced-disease question only: avapritinib in indolent systemic mastocytosis is homed at pack #6906 and in PDGFRA D842V gastrointestinal stromal tumour at pack #6709, and none of that record is carded here.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single-arm pivotal evidence (EXPLORER/PATHFINDER): overall response rates of 75% in both trials' response-evaluable sets, with the only comparison a retrospective one against best available therapy, so single-arm/observational structure caps the stamp at POSSIBLE

title: Anselamimab (CAEL-101) added to anti-plasma-cell therapy in AL amyloidosis (CARES)
question: In patients with newly diagnosed Mayo stage IIIa/IIIb AL amyloidosis, does adding anselamimab to standard anti-plasma-cell therapy (CyBorD, with or without daratumumab), versus standard therapy alone, improve the hierarchical composite of all-cause mortality and cardiovascular hospitalisations?
balance: SPLIT — and the headline is the null: in the CARES phase 3 programme (two randomised trials, stage IIIa and IIIb, 406 patients), adding the antifibril antibody anselamimab (CAEL-101; Caelum/AstraZeneca) to standard anti-plasma-cell therapy made no difference on the primary endpoint in the overall population (the treatment made no difference: hierarchical composite win ratio 1.11, 95% CI 0.83–1.50, P = .332; all-cause mortality hazard ratio 0.80, P = .290). A published erratum to the CARES report (J Clin Oncol 2026;44(26):2563) is linked to the paper in the record and is incorporated on the CARES card; the figures carded here are those of the record as fetched this session. The split is by light-chain isotype: in the small kappa subgroup (n = 72) the composite favoured anselamimab, with a 62% relative reduction in all-cause mortality (hazard ratio 0.38; nominal P = .012) and a 71% relative reduction in cardiovascular hospitalisations (incidence rate ratio 0.29; nominal P = .028) — nominal, subgroup, small-N findings that are a hypothesis for a kappa-restricted trial, NOT population benefit, and the lambda population showed no clinical benefit. The earlier record explains why the drug was plausible: in the phase 1a/b study 15 of 24 patients (63%) with organ involvement had a therapeutic response, and a phase 2 study (25 patients) found the antibody tolerable alongside CyBorD with or without daratumumab — but tolerability and early organ responses did not translate into a positive phase 3 primary endpoint. The anti-plasma-cell question in AL amyloidosis (daratumumab plus CyBorD) is a different question, homed at pack #2648; this shelf is only about amyloid removal by an antifibril antibody.
stamp: SPLIT — overall population versus kappa subgroup: CARES (406 patients) did NOT meet its primary endpoint in the overall population (win ratio 1.11, P = .332 — the treatment made no difference), while the kappa-isotype subgroup (n = 72) showed nominally significant relative reductions in mortality and cardiovascular hospitalisations and the lambda population showed no benefit; the subgroup signal is not upgraded to population benefit

title: Motixafortide plus G-CSF for stem-cell mobilisation in multiple myeloma (GENESIS)
question: In patients with multiple myeloma undergoing autologous transplantation, does one dose of motixafortide plus G-CSF, versus placebo plus G-CSF (with plerixafor rescue available), mobilise enough CD34+ cells for collection in ≤2 apheresis days?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one clean phase 3 randomised trial (GENESIS) anchors the shelf, and a single trial caps the stamp at POSSIBLE. Against placebo plus G-CSF, one dose of motixafortide (Aphexda, BioLineRx) plus G-CSF was dramatically better at the collection goal: 92.5% versus 26.2% collected at least 6 × 10⁶ CD34+ cells/kg within two apheresis procedures, and 88.8% versus 9.5% did so in a single apheresis. The honest complication is the comparator that matters in many centres: in the single-centre real-world comparison (30 patients per group), motixafortide plus G-CSF was feasible but NOT superior to plerixafor plus G-CSF — yields and procedure times were similar, 27 patients per group reached targets in one day, and motixafortide caused substantially more injection-site and systemic reactions requiring intervention, with extra premedication and monitoring workload; that centre kept plerixafor as its default. The third carded report is a companion, not myeloma evidence: in allogeneic donors, one motixafortide injection (without the GENESIS regimen) collected the target in most donors within two leukaphereses (25 donor–recipient pairs enrolled, 24 evaluable), which supports the drug's mobilisation pharmacology in a different setting. Harms on the GENESIS regimen were mainly transient grade 1/2 injection-site reactions (pain 50%, erythema 27.5%, pruritus 21.3%).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single phase 3 trial (GENESIS): 92.5% versus 26.2% met the ≤2-apheresis collection goal against placebo plus G-CSF; a single trial caps the stamp at POSSIBLE, and the one real-world comparison against plerixafor found no superiority
