title: Tazemetostat for relapsed/refractory follicular lymphoma
question: In adults with relapsed or refractory follicular lymphoma after at least two prior lines, does tazemetostat, versus no concurrent control, produce objective responses in EZH2-mutant and wild-type disease?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — every cohort is single-arm, which caps the stamp at POSSIBLE: response rates have no comparator, and follicular lymphoma can behave indolently, so duration figures need particular care. The pattern across three independent cohorts is consistent and graded by EZH2 status: objective response in about two-thirds of EZH2-mutant disease (69% in the pivotal phase 2, 63.6% in the Chinese bridging study, 76.5% in the small Japanese phase 2) versus about one-third in wild-type disease (35% in both the pivotal and Chinese studies, the latter investigator-assessed). The propensity-matched re-analysis of the pivotal trial is a companion, not a cohort: after matching, wild-type response rose to 50% and progression-free survival looked similar between groups, which warns that part of the mutant-versus-wild-type gap may be baseline differences rather than biology. Harms were modest in the pivotal trial (treatment-related grade 3 or worse events in single digits per type; no treatment-related deaths), though all patients in the Chinese study had treatment-related events and 13.6% had grade 3 or worse. Product naming (clarification exception): tazemetostat (Tazverik, Epizyme/Ipsen). The epithelioid-sarcoma programme is a different, solid-tumour question and is not carded here.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — entirely single-arm evidence across three independent cohorts: objective response 69% (pivotal), 63.6% (Chinese) and 76.5% (Japanese) in EZH2-mutant disease versus about 35% in wild-type, with no comparator anywhere, so single-arm structure caps the stamp at POSSIBLE

title: Ecopipam for Tourette syndrome
question: In children, adolescents and adults with Tourette syndrome, does the selective dopamine D1-receptor antagonist ecopipam, versus placebo, reduce tic severity (YGTSS) without the metabolic and movement harms of D2-blocking antipsychotics?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — three randomised trials from one development programme point the same way, but samples are small-to-moderate and the acute effect is modest (about 3 points on the Yale Global Tic Severity Scale total tic score), which keeps the stamp at POSSIBLE. The acute claim rests on the phase 2b trial (153 children and adolescents; least-squares mean difference −3.44 versus placebo at 12 weeks) and the small crossover trial (40 children; difference −3.2 at 30 days). The phase 3 trial is a randomised-withdrawal study in prior responders — it shows maintenance (relapse risk roughly halved in paediatric participants, hazard ratio 0.47, a relative measure) and must not be read as an acute-effect estimate; its adult stratum was tiny (14 randomised) and not significant. The shelf's clinical point is the harm contrast with D2-blocking antipsychotics: across the programme there was no clinically meaningful weight or metabolic signal and no drug-induced movement disorders were observed — but that is absence of signal in small, short samples, not proof of long-term safety. The commonest adverse events were central (somnolence, anxiety, headache, insomnia, fatigue). The 12-month open-label extension (121 patients, a follow-on from the phase 2b trial) supports tolerability over a year; being open-label it cannot re-prove efficacy.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — concordant randomised trials from one programme: acute tic-score advantage of about 3 points versus placebo in two trials and halved relapse risk on continued treatment in responders, but small samples and a modest effect size keep the stamp at POSSIBLE

title: Glabellar botulinum toxin A injection for major depressive disorder
question: In adults with major depressive disorder, does a single session of botulinum toxin A injected into the glabellar (frown) musculature, versus placebo injection, reduce depressive symptoms over the following 6–24 weeks?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the direction is consistent across three small randomised trials, a pooled analysis of them and an updated meta-analysis, but every primary trial is small and the intervention visibly paralyses the frown, so functional unblinding is this shelf's central bias problem: a participant who cannot frown knows they were treated, and mood ratings are subjective. The pooled individual-patient analysis of the three early trials (134 patients) found response in 54.2% on botulinum toxin A versus 10.7% on placebo at 6 weeks; the updated meta-analysis (8 randomised trials, 636 participants) found a standardised mean difference of −0.81 versus control, with a null result in the high-dose pan-facial subgroup — the effect, if real, belongs to the standard glabellar protocol, not to more toxin in more places. Product naming (clarification exception): the early trials tested onabotulinumtoxinA preparations, named on each card as the trials report them (29 units for women and about 39–40 units for men in two of the trials); the meta-analysis reports facial botulinum toxin A across trials without a single tested product. The facial-feedback mechanism — that paralysing frown muscles feeds back to lift mood — is a hypothesis, not an established mechanism, and is labelled as such wherever it appears here. Harms in the meta-analysis were no more frequent overall than in controls, with transient local reactions the typical cost.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — small randomised trials agree (pooled response 54.2% versus 10.7% at 6 weeks; meta-analysis of 8 trials, 636 participants, standardised mean difference −0.81) but every trial is small and the treatment visibly paralyses the frown, so functional unblinding caps the stamp at POSSIBLE

title: Sodium benzoate as adjunctive treatment in schizophrenia
question: In people with schizophrenia on stable antipsychotics — including clozapine-treated and early-psychosis populations — does adjunctive sodium benzoate, versus placebo, improve positive, negative and overall symptoms?
balance: SPLIT — by population, and averaging the split away would misstate the record. In chronic schizophrenia on stable antipsychotics, a 52-patient Taiwanese trial found a 21% improvement in PANSS total score with large effect sizes; in clozapine-resistant schizophrenia, a 60-patient trial found both 1 g/day and 2 g/day beat placebo on negative symptoms, with the 2 g dose also better on PANSS total and positive scores. Against that, the largest and most rigorous trial — 100 participants with early psychosis in Australia — found no benefit at all (the treatment made no difference: PANSS difference −1.2 points, P = .63, with no differences on any secondary measure), and a 68-patient early-schizophrenia feasibility trial of benzoate (with N-acetylcysteine, factorial) was not powered for effect and found no main effects on most outcomes. The meta-analysis lands between: across four trials, add-on benzoate improved positive symptoms (mean difference −1.87 PANSS points) but made no difference to negative symptoms, total PANSS, cognition, functioning or quality of life, and extrapyramidal symptoms were significantly higher on benzoate. So the honest claim is narrow: possible benefit for positive (and, in the clozapine trial, negative) symptoms in chronic/clozapine-resistant disease, no demonstrated benefit in early psychosis, and no established cognitive or functional benefit. All trials are small and short (6–12 weeks); print the Ns.
stamp: SPLIT — chronic/clozapine-resistant versus early psychosis: small trials in chronic (n = 52) and clozapine-resistant (n = 60) schizophrenia were positive, the largest trial in early psychosis (n = 100) was null (the treatment made no difference), and the meta-analysis supports an effect on positive symptoms only

title: Home-based, fully remote tDCS for major depressive disorder
question: In adults with major depressive disorder, does self-administered home-based transcranial direct-current stimulation (prefrontal, typically 2 mA, multi-week courses), versus sham, improve depressive symptoms — and does a longer active course beat a shorter one?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the sham-controlled evidence for the home-based, fully remote delivery model rests mainly on one well-run phase 2 trial (Woodham 2025, 174 participants: Hamilton score improvement 9.41 points on active versus 7.14 on sham at 10 weeks, P = .012; response 58.3% versus 37.8% in the follow-up report), supported by a meta-analysis of five small home-based trials (415 patients) finding modest advantages over sham. That is a single-trial-plus-synthesis base, so the stamp is POSSIBLE. The duration question has a clean answer from the second randomised trial (197 participants): 3 weeks of active stimulation followed by 3 weeks of sham did just as well as 6 weeks of active stimulation (the treatment made no difference between the longer and shorter courses; both groups improved, but with no sham-only arm those within-group improvements are comparative, not causal). Six-month follow-up of the Woodham trial showed high sustained response (76% at 6 months among the UK follow-up attenders), but by then everyone had been offered open-label active treatment, so durability is uncontrolled. Blinding integrity is the standing caveat for home devices: active stimulation tingles, and sham protocols mimic it only briefly. Tested product (clarification exception): the Woodham trial used the Flow Neuroscience headset, named as reported. This shelf is only the home-based, fully remote, self-administered slice: the clinic-based stimulation question (theta-burst/rTMS non-inferiority and clinic tDCS against escitalopram) is homed at live shelf #993, and none of that record is carded here.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one fully remote sham-controlled trial (n = 174; Hamilton improvement 9.41 versus 7.14 points) plus a meta-analysis of five small trials, so a single-trial-led base caps the stamp at POSSIBLE; a separate randomised trial found a 3-week active course did as much as 6 weeks

title: Crisugabalin in diabetic peripheral neuropathic pain: beat placebo from week 1 in a 596-patient phase 2/3 trial and pregabalin in a small inadequate-responder trial; dizziness in 27% over a year
question: In adults with diabetic peripheral neuropathic pain, does the alpha-2-delta ligand crisugabalin (HSK16149), versus placebo or pregabalin, reduce average daily pain scores, and how durable and tolerable is it over a year?
balance: POSSIBLE. In the phase 2/3 adaptive trial (596 patients with diabetic peripheral neuropathic pain), crisugabalin 40 and 80 mg/day reduced average daily pain scores versus placebo from week 1 through week 13, while pregabalin 300 mg/day separated only from week 6 (the report gives significance, not absolute point differences). In a separate small phase 2 trial (93 patients whose pain was inadequately controlled on pregabalin), crisugabalin 40 mg/day beat pregabalin 300 mg/day on Short-Form McGill pain change at 4 weeks (least-squares mean difference −7.2). Over a 52-week single-arm extension of the phase 2/3 trial (301 patients, no comparator), treatment-related adverse events occurred in 38.9% — dizziness 27.2%, somnolence 8.3%, peripheral oedema 3.0%. The whole programme is China-generated: crisugabalin (HSK16149) is approved in China and is not FDA- or EMA-approved. A separate phase 3 trial of crisugabalin in postherpetic neuralgia (JAMA Dermatology 2024) asks a different diagnosis question and is cross-pointed here only — it is not evidence for the diabetic-pain question.
stamp: POSSIBLE — one China-generated programme: a positive placebo-controlled phase 2/3 trial (n=596) and a small pregabalin-controlled trial in pregabalin inadequate responders (n=93), with single-arm 52-week tolerability data; no evidence outside China and no FDA/EMA approval

title: Radical surgery in resectable mesothelioma: MARS 2 — surgery shortened survival (19.3 vs 24.8 months) and doubled serious harm; MARS — no benefit from extrapleural pneumonectomy
question: In adults with resectable malignant pleural mesothelioma, does radical surgery — extrapleural pneumonectomy (MARS feasibility programme) or (extended) pleurectomy decortication added to chemotherapy (MARS 2) — improve survival and quality of life versus chemotherapy / non-surgical management alone, and at what cost in perioperative mortality and morbidity?
balance: LIKELY harm, on a two-trial base. Only two randomised trials of radical surgery in resectable malignant pleural mesothelioma exist, and both point against surgery. MARS (feasibility, 50 randomised): extrapleural pneumonectomy within trimodal therapy gave median survival 14.4 versus 19.5 months without it, adjusted hazard ratio 2.75 favouring no surgery, with 10 versus 2 serious adverse events. MARS 2 (phase 3, 335 randomised): (extended) pleurectomy decortication plus chemotherapy SHORTENED median survival versus chemotherapy alone (19.3 vs 24.8 months; restricted mean survival difference at 2 years −1.9 months, P=0.019) and produced 318 versus 169 grade 3-or-worse serious adverse events. The two operations are different limbs — pneumonectomy versus pleurectomy decortication — and are carded separately. Two clearly-labelled programme reports of the MARS 2 programme (patient experience, n=15; the embedded recruitment intervention) complete the record; they are not independent trials, and no cohort series have been used to pad the base.
stamp: LIKELY (harm) — on the only two randomised trials that exist: MARS 2 showed (extended) pleurectomy decortication plus chemotherapy shortened survival versus chemotherapy alone (19.3 vs 24.8 months) with far more serious adverse events, and the MARS feasibility trial showed no benefit and a harm signal for extrapleural pneumonectomy; programme reports are labelled as programme reports, not independent trials

title: Prophylactic tract irradiation in mesothelioma: no significant reduction in tract metastases in SMART (9% vs 16%), PIT (3.2% vs 5.3%) or the 2007 trial
question: In adults with malignant pleural mesothelioma who have undergone large-bore pleural interventions or chest-wall procedures, does prophylactic irradiation of the procedure tracts prevent procedure-tract metastases versus no prophylactic irradiation?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference). Three randomised trials asked whether irradiating mesothelioma procedure tracts prevents tract metastases, and none found a significant reduction: SMART (203 patients, immediate vs deferred radiotherapy) 9% versus 16% tract metastases (odds ratio 0.51; P=0.14); PIT (375 patients, prophylaxis vs none) 3.2% versus 5.3% at 6 months (odds ratio 0.60; P=.44); and the earlier two-centre trial (61 patients) found no difference (P=0.748). SMART and PIT differ — SMART's control was deferred irradiation at metastasis, PIT's was no irradiation, and the procedures covered differ — so they are carded per-trial, not pooled. The consistent cost of prophylaxis was skin toxicity (grade 1 dermatitis in roughly half of treated patients). Low event rates mean a small preventive effect is not excluded; routine prophylaxis is nevertheless unsupported.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — three randomised trials (SMART, PIT, and the 2007 drain-site trial) each found no significant reduction in procedure-tract metastases from prophylactic irradiation

title: Preoperative hair removal: razor shaving raises surgical-site infection risk versus clipping (relative risk 1.64) and versus no removal (1.82); clip on the day of surgery instead
question: In adults undergoing elective surgery, does preoperative hair removal method matter for surgical-site infection — clipping or depilatory cream versus shaving with a razor, and any removal versus no removal — and does timing (day before vs day of surgery) change the risk?
balance: LIKELY. The randomised record — three primary trials carded here (1,013, 253 and 200 patients) inside a Cochrane review of 25 trials and 8,919 participants — says the razor is the harmful method: shaving probably increases surgical-site infection versus clipping (relative risk 1.64, a relative measure; 7 studies, 3,723 participants) and versus no removal at all (relative risk 1.82; about 17 more infections per 1,000 patients in absolute terms), and razors also caused more skin injury (relative risk 1.74). Clipping versus no removal showed little difference (relative risk 0.95), and depilatory cream was statistically indistinguishable from shaving in its 253-patient head-to-head trial and from no removal in the review. Timing mattered in the largest primary trial: clipping on the morning of surgery had the fewest infections. The classic trials predate modern surgical-site infection surveillance definitions — stated here as the row directs — so their absolute rates, not their direction, are the dated part.
stamp: LIKELY — razor shaving probably raises surgical-site infection risk versus clipping (relative risk 1.64, a relative measure) and versus no removal (relative risk 1.82; ~17 more infections per 1,000); clipping and depilatory cream are the lower-risk methods, and clipping is no worse than no removal

title: Surgical hand antisepsis: alcohol rubbing equalled scrubbing on infections (2.44% vs 2.48% in 4,387 patients); the rest of the evidence is hand bacterial counts, a surrogate
question: In surgical teams, does alcohol-based hand rubbing achieve surgical-site infection rates and hand bacterial counts equivalent to traditional aqueous antiseptic hand scrubbing for surgical hand antisepsis?
balance: POSSIBLE. On the patient outcome, the base is essentially one trial: Parienti 2002 (4,387 patients) found 30-day surgical-site infection of 2.44% with alcohol hand-rubbing versus 2.48% with traditional antiseptic scrubbing (difference 0.04%, 95% CI −0.88% to 0.96%) — (the treatment made no difference) — with better antisepsis-duration compliance (44% vs 28%) and less skin dryness/irritation with rubbing. The Cochrane review (14 trials) found no clear infection difference in any comparison and graded the evidence low to very low quality. Everything else measures hand bacterial counts — a surrogate, labelled as such on its cards: alcohol-based protocols matched or beat aqueous scrubs on counts (240-staff and 23-nurse trials). Colony-count equivalence is NOT surgical-site infection equivalence, and this shelf does not present it as such.
stamp: POSSIBLE — alcohol-based hand rubbing matched traditional scrubbing on surgical-site infection in the one large equivalence trial (2.44% vs 2.48%; the treatment made no difference), with better compliance and skin tolerance; the supporting trials measure hand bacterial counts only (surrogate endpoint, labelled)

title: Heparin vs saline port locking: split — saline met non-inferiority in the 802-patient trial but not on the smaller trial's margin; no significant occlusion difference in either
question: In adults with cancer and a totally implanted venous access port (or other long-term central venous catheter), does locking/flushing with normal saline alone maintain patency as safely as heparin locking — occlusion, catheter-related thrombosis and infection?
balance: SPLIT — on the formal non-inferiority question. The larger port trial (Goossens 2013, 802 patients with cancer and non-valved implanted ports) met non-inferiority for saline versus heparin lock (300 units/3 mL): the dysfunction outcome occurred in 3.70% versus 3.92% of accesses (relative risk 0.94; upper confidence limit below the 1.4 margin), with catheter-related bloodstream infection of 0.03 versus 0.10 per 1,000 catheter days. The smaller Italian trial (Dal Molin 2015, 430 recruited) FAILED to demonstrate non-inferiority on its own 4-percentage-point margin (occlusions 14 saline vs 10 heparin), although it too found no significant difference. The Cochrane review across all central venous catheters (6 trials, 1,433 participants) found no conclusive efficacy or safety difference. Protocols differ per trial and are named on the cards; heparin-induced thrombocytopenia is the harm the saline limb avoids by design.
stamp: SPLIT — saline met non-inferiority for port dysfunction in the larger trial (relative risk 0.94) but the smaller trial failed to demonstrate non-inferiority on its own margin; neither found a significant difference, and the Cochrane synthesis is inconclusive

title: Chalazion: injection vs surgery — split: trials show near-equal resolution and less pain with injection; pooled data favour one surgery over one injection; depigmentation risk in pigmented skin
question: In patients with chalazion, does intralesional triamcinolone injection resolve the lesion as effectively as incision and curettage, and how do the two compare on recurrence, skin depigmentation and other harms — by lesion size?
balance: SPLIT. The two largest head-to-head trials found intralesional triamcinolone and incision and curettage resolve primary chalazia at near-equal rates — 81% versus 79% (94 patients) and 84% versus 87% at 3 weeks (136 patients, with hot compresses alone at 46%) — with less pain and inconvenience from injection. The meta-analysis of 8 randomised trials (552 patients) instead favours surgery for a single attempt (aggregate success 78.0% vs 60.4%; relative risk 0.77 for injection, a relative measure), narrowing after up to two attempts (86.7% vs 72.5%). Size and type modify the comparison: in the size-stratified trial (118 patients) the methods were equal overall except in large suppurating granulomas, where surgery was superior. In pigmented skin (141 patients), first-attempt success favoured surgery (79% vs 62%) and the authors report skin depigmentation was relatively common after injection — the defining harm of the injection limb, carded on the face.
stamp: SPLIT — individual trials: injection ≈ surgery on resolution (81% vs 79%; 84% vs 87%) with less pain from injection; pooled older trials: one surgery beats one injection (78.0% vs 60.4%); surgery favoured for large suppurating granulomas, and injection carries depigmentation risk in pigmented skin

title: Recurrent corneal erosion: weak evidence — diamond-burr polishing cut recurrence in one 48-patient trial; lens and lubrication resolved equally (lens faster); delamination equalled laser
question: In patients with recurrent corneal erosion syndrome, which treatment best prevents recurrence and relieves pain — long-term ocular lubrication, bandage contact lens, anterior stromal puncture, diamond-burr polishing, or phototherapeutic keratectomy?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence). Every comparison rests on one small trial. Diamond-burr polishing after epithelial debridement reduced recurrences versus debridement alone in 48 patients (relative risk 0.07 in the Cochrane summary, a relative measure from a small trial). Bandage contact lens and ocular lubrication resolved episodes at the same rate in 29 patients (71% vs 73% complete resolution — (the treatments made no difference)) — though symptoms settled faster with the lens (5 vs 9 weeks). Alcohol delamination and phototherapeutic keratectomy were indistinguishable in 33 patients (resolution 65% vs 63%). The Cochrane review (10 trials, 505 participants) judges the whole base too small and poorly reported for firm guidance, and the older anterior-stromal-puncture comparisons inside it were inconclusive — so no procedure is pooled into a class claim here, and any limb resting on case series alone has been left uncarded, as the row directs.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — three small single trials (n=29–48): diamond-burr polishing reduced recurrence versus debridement alone; bandage lens equalled lubrication on resolution but was faster; alcohol delamination equalled phototherapeutic keratectomy; the Cochrane base (505 participants) is judged insufficient for firm guidance

title: Bilateral cochlear implants in children: cohorts favour two implants for speech in noise, localisation and vocabulary; each year of delay between implants cost localisation accuracy
question: In children with bilateral severe-to-profound sensorineural hearing loss, does bilateral cochlear implantation — simultaneous or sequential — improve speech perception in noise, sound localisation and language outcomes versus unilateral implantation, and does the inter-implant interval matter?
balance: POSSIBLE — observational throughout, labelled as such (GAP-E, per the assembly adjudication). No randomised trial of bilateral versus unilateral cochlear implantation in children exists. The comparative cohorts and their syntheses consistently favour two implants for the functions that need two ears: the 2026 meta-analysis (50 studies) found bilateral implantation better on speech perception in noise (standardised mean difference +0.70), sound localisation (+0.74) and receptive vocabulary (+0.65); a matched longitudinal cohort (24 bilateral vs 26 unilateral) found significantly higher speech recognition and vocabulary 5–6 years after sequential implantation; and a 127-child cohort found each year of inter-implant delay cost 1.7 degrees of localisation accuracy (P<0.001), favouring simultaneous or promptly sequential implantation. The exception that proves the framing: against bimodal fitting (implant plus hearing aid, 49 vs 44 children), bilateral implantation showed no significant language or noise advantage — a different comparison. Confounding by family and centre selection runs through all of it, which is why the stamp caps at POSSIBLE.
stamp: POSSIBLE (observational, labelled) — no RCT exists; cohorts and syntheses consistently favour bilateral implantation for speech in noise, localisation and vocabulary, with shorter inter-implant intervals doing better; confounding by family/centre selection is unremoved

title: GLI-2012 spirometry: continuous FEV1, FVC and FEV1/FVC equations for ages 3–95 from 97,759 healthy nonsmokers — FEV1/FVC is virtually ancestry-independent, and the race-neutral GLI Global (2022) equations fit about as well with wider limits of normal
question: In healthy humans, what are the reference values for forced spirometry (FEV1, FVC, FEV1/FVC) across the 3–95-year age range — the Global Lung Function Initiative 2012 multi-ethnic equations — including the lower limit of normal and how predicted values differ by ancestry group and by the newer race-neutral (GLI Global) equations?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Framing follows Boron & Boulpaep's respiratory-mechanics account and Guyton & Hall ch. 37 (spirometric volumes as the measurable expression of lung and chest-wall mechanics), named as textbook framing; the numbers below are the primary measurement literature. The GLI-2012 programme (Quanjer 2012) pooled 97,759 records of healthy nonsmokers and derived continuous LMS equations for ages 3–95 in four ancestry groups, with age-dependent lower limits of normal; FEV1 and FVC differed proportionally between groups while FEV1/FVC remained virtually independent of ancestry — so the ratio is the most portable index and the volumes are the equation-sensitive ones. The race-neutral re-analysis (Bowerman 2023) built GLI Global (2022) equations from 74,185 GLI records: fit was similar to the GLI-2012 'other' equations but limits of normal were wider, and sitting height did not explain between-group differences in NHANES III. An independent primary dataset (Madanhire 2020, 712 Zimbabwean children — a population GLI-2012 did not sample) found the African-American equations fit well (all z-score means within ±0.5). Equation choice changes who is labelled abnormal: that dependence is the core teaching content of this shelf.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED

title: Static lung volumes: GLI-2021 equations from 7,190 Europeans aged 5–80 — plethysmography reads higher than dilution in the elderly, and borrowed middle-aged equations misclassify up to 62.5% of healthy older women as below the TLC lower limit
question: In healthy humans, what are normal static lung volumes — total lung capacity, functional residual capacity, residual volume and RV/TLC — by body plethysmography and gas dilution, per the Global Lung Function Initiative 2021 reference values?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Framing follows Boron & Boulpaep's lung-volumes account and Guyton & Hall ch. 37, named as textbook framing. The GLI-2021 technical standard (Hall 2021) derived sex-specific equations for TLC, FRC, RV, inspiratory capacity, vital capacity, expiratory reserve volume and RV/TLC from 7,190 observations in people of European ancestry aged 5–80, combining plethysmography and dilution FRC after finding physiologically insignificant differences between techniques in the pooled data. The independent cohorts qualify that pooling: in 321 healthy never-smokers aged 65–85 (Garcia-Rio 2009), plethysmography gave higher values than helium dilution for all volumes with wide limits of agreement, and extrapolated middle-aged equations branded 17.9–62.5% of healthy women and 12.5–42.2% of healthy men as below the TLC lower limit of normal. In 5,371 healthy Austrians (Mraz 2024), the GLI equations themselves fit poorly (mean z-scores above +0.5 for RV, RV/TLC and TLC in both sexes), prompting population-derived equations. Method and population both move the 'normal' line — values are carded per-method and per-population.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED

title: DLCO reference values: GLI-2017 equations from 12,660 measurements (ages 5–85, Caucasians) — haemoglobin-uncorrected at derivation, and older national equations read up to 111% of predicted against them
question: In healthy humans, what are the reference values for lung diffusing capacity (DLCO / transfer factor) and transfer coefficient (KCO) by age, sex, height and haemoglobin — the GLI-2017 equations — and what lower limit of normal do they define?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Framing follows Boron & Boulpaep's gas-transfer account and Guyton & Hall ch. 40, named as textbook framing. This shelf is the measurement slice only: how DLCO changes with posture and exercise, and what drives that change, is a different question, already homed in the diffusing-capacity posture-and-exercise shelf (pack #6259) — it is cross-pointed here in prose and none of its studies is re-carded. The GLI-2017 standard (Stanojevic 2017) pooled 12,660 transfer-factor measurements from 19 centres and derived Caucasian reference values for ages 5–85 for TLCO, KCO and alveolar volume — with all data uncorrected for haemoglobin at derivation, so haemoglobin handling belongs on the face of any clinical use. Independent population datasets show why equation vintage matters: in 282 healthy Danes the combined DLCO/DLNO method produced its own equations with haemoglobin built into the CO conductance term (Munkholm 2018), and in 631 healthy Finns the 1982 national values under-predicted so far that mean measured DLCO ran at 111.0% of predicted in men and 104.4% in women (Kainu 2017). Altitude and haemoglobin corrections are part of the measurement, not afterthoughts.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED

title: Respiratory impedance by oscillometry: height drives the adult equations, women run higher resistance than men, and the 1994 equations still in laboratory use misread healthy older adults by −34% to +76%
question: In healthy humans, what are normal respiratory impedance values by impulse oscillometry / forced oscillation (resistance at 5 and 20 Hz, reactance, area of reactance) by age, height and sex — and how do values differ between devices and populations?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing for oscillometry specifically is thin in Boron & Boulpaep's respiratory-mechanics chapters — this shelf rests chiefly on the primary measurement literature and says so. Three primary cohorts from three populations agree on the structure: in 567 healthy Chinese adults from 19 hospitals (Liang 2021), height — not age — was the dominant predictor, and both the equations and the manufacturer's ranges in routine use mis-stated the normal limits; in 397 never-smoking lung-healthy adults aged 45–91 from the population-based KORA cohorts (Schulz 2013), women had higher resistance and lower low-frequency reactance than men, R5−R20, reactance area and resonant frequency rose with age, and the Vogel & Smidt 1994 equations in widespread use erred by −34% to +76% where the new equations erred by −1% to +5% (relative differences); in 75 asymptomatic Norwegians over 70 (Aarli 2013), within-breath impedance (the inspiratory–expiratory reactance difference at 5 Hz) gained its first elderly reference values, with higher resistance than earlier studies reported. Values are carded per-device and per-population: IOS and FOT generations and their signal processing are not interchangeable.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED

title: FeNO in healthy people: upper limits run 24–54 ppb by age and height in never-smokers, the prediction equations explain only ~10% of the variation, and atopy and male sex push values up while current smoking breaks the equations
question: In healthy humans, what is the distribution of fractional exhaled nitric oxide (FeNO at 50 mL/s) — its geometric mean and upper reference limit in lifelong never-smokers, and how much do atopy, height, age, sex and current smoking shift it?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing for FeNO is thin in Boron & Boulpaep (airway nitric-oxide signalling) — this shelf rests chiefly on the primary measurement literature and says so. This shelf is the measurement slice only: whether FeNO should guide asthma treatment is a different, management question, already homed in the live adolescent shelf (#1728) and the adult FeNO-guided-treatment pack (#5904) — cross-pointed here in prose, with none of their studies re-carded. In healthy lifelong never-smokers (Olin 2007, n=1,131), FeNO at 50 mL/s is predicted from height and age, but the equations explain only 9–11% of the variation and the upper limit spans 24.0–54.0 parts per billion across age and height. The larger general-population study (Torén 2017, n=3,378 after exclusions) found never- and former smokers similar enough to merge, built sex-specific equations with atopy included — and found current smokers' values so unstable to model that fixed cut-off limits are proposed instead. In 166 healthy Korean adults (Kim 2010), male sex and atopy independently raised FeNO, with group means from 24.1 ppb (nonatopic women) to 37.3 ppb (atopic men). Analyser type matters: the Swedish cohorts used chemiluminescence (NIOX) analysers, and values from electrochemical devices are not assumed interchangeable.

title: SNIP norms: healthy adults sniff harder than they can suck — mean 76.8 cm H₂O in Japanese men and 60.0 in women (lower limits 32.9 and 28.8), children aged 6–17 already reach adult-range values, and SNIP complements rather than replaces mouth pressure
question: In healthy humans, what is sniff nasal inspiratory pressure (SNIP) — its mean and lower limit of normal by age and sex — and how does it compare with maximal inspiratory mouth pressure as a measure of inspiratory muscle strength?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Framing follows Guyton & Hall ch. 37 and Boron & Boulpaep's mechanics of breathing, named as textbook framing. This shelf is the nose-measured manoeuvre only; mouth-pressure (MIP/MEP) reference values are a neighbouring question (Slate 8's S8-4-27) and are not duplicated here. Three cohorts from three age bands agree: in 160 healthy adults aged 20–80 (Uldry & Fitting 1995), maximal SNIP fell with age, was the same sitting and supine, and equalled or exceeded maximal inspiratory mouth pressure in 107 of 160 subjects (mean SNIP/PImax ratio 1.08 in men, 1.17 in women) — with agreement low enough that the authors call the two tests complementary, not interchangeable. In 223 healthy Japanese adults (Kamide 2009), mean SNIP was 76.8 ± 28.9 cm H₂O in men and 60.0 ± 20.0 in women, with lower limits of normal of 32.9 and 28.8 cm H₂O. In 180 healthy children aged 6–17 (Stefanutti & Fitting 1999), SNIP was already 104 ± 26 cm H₂O in boys and 93 ± 23 in girls — adult-range values, higher than mouth pressure at the same lung volume.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED

title: Cough flows rest on a thin base: three small healthy-volunteer studies (N = 52, 30 and 40) — peak cough flow agrees between pneumotachograph and portable meter above 270 L/min, the meter over-reads below it, and no GLI-style normative programme exists
question: In healthy humans, what are voluntary cough flows and cough aerodynamics — peak cough flow by sex and age, glottic compression-phase behaviour and expulsive-phase flow — and how reproducible is peak cough flow measurement between pneumotachograph and portable peak-flow meter?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING — stamped emerging, not established, because the base is genuinely thin and this shelf says so on its face: there is NO GLI-style normative programme for cough flow. Framing follows Guyton & Hall ch. 37 (the cough reflex and airway mechanics) and Boron & Boulpaep's respiratory mechanics, named as textbook framing. The entire healthy-human distribution is assembled from three small volunteer studies, their Ns printed here and on every card: cough aerodynamics in 52 healthy adults (Feinstein 2017 — peak airflow rose with height, peak pressure was greater in men, expiratory rise time was longer in women); a device-agreement study with 30 healthy subjects alongside 32 neuromuscular patients (Sancho 2004 — pneumotachograph and portable meter agreed closely overall, r = 0.95, but the meter overestimated flows below 270 L/min); and airflow features of cough versus throat clearing in 40 healthy participants (Mootassim-Billah 2025 — throat clearing is aerodynamically a weaker manoeuvre than cough, P < 0.001). The widely used clinical peak-cough-flow thresholds in neuromuscular care rest on this thin base — that thinness is the teaching content of this shelf, and nothing here inflates it.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING

title: Ventilatory efficiency: the VE/VCO2 slope rises ~0.12–0.13 units per year of age and runs higher in women — about 24–26 in healthy 20-somethings, with the ventilatory-equivalent nadir at 24.2 (men) to 27.0 (women)
question: In healthy humans, what is ventilatory efficiency during exercise — the VE/VCO2 slope and the ventilatory equivalent nadir — by age and sex, and how much does the slope rise with normal ageing?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Framing follows Boron & Boulpaep's control-of-breathing and exercise account and Guyton & Hall ch. 84, named as textbook framing. The slope-distribution question is this shelf's own: the mathematical coupling between ventilatory efficiency and the dead-space fraction is analysed in the physiological dead-space shelf (pack #6258), which homes the Sun and colleagues 2002 ventilatory-efficiency analysis — cross-pointed here in prose only; that analysis is not re-carded and no number from it is used. The distribution itself rests on three free-standing cohorts. In 101 healthy volunteers (Habedank 1998), the exercise VE vs VCO2 slope rose linearly with age — slope = 0.13 × age + 19.9 in men and 0.12 × age + 24.4 in women — and resting ventilatory equivalent was higher in women (57.6 vs 50.5). In 529 healthy Japanese adults (Ashikaga 2021), the slope in the 20s was 24.4 ± 3.2 (men) and 25.7 ± 3.2 (women) and the minimum VE/VCO2 (the nadir) was 24.2 ± 2.3 and 27.0 ± 2.8, both rising with age. The FRIEND registry analysis (Nevill 2021) supplies sex-by-age centile curves for ages 20–80 from treadmill testing, so an individual slope can be placed on a population centile rather than against a single cut-off.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED

title: Six-minute walk distance: median 576 m in healthy men and 494 m in women aged 40–80 (Enright), mean 571 ± 90 m across seven countries with real geographic variation, and 631 ± 93 m in healthy 50–85-year-olds on a 50-m corridor
question: In healthy adults, what distance is walked in six minutes — the reference equations (Enright) and the seven-country reference standards for the 6-minute walk test — by age, sex, height and weight, and how large is the learning effect between a first and second test?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing for the walk test is general (Guyton & Hall ch. 84; Boron & Boulpaep exercise physiology) — this shelf rests chiefly on the primary measurement literature and says so. Three primary cohorts built the normative base. Enright & Sherrill (1998) tested 290 healthy adults aged 40–80 on the standardised protocol: median distance 576 m in men and 494 m in women, with sex-specific equations in height, age and weight explaining about 40% of the variance (relative share of variance, printed as reported). The seven-country study (Casanova 2011) tested 444 adults at 10 centres: mean 571 ± 90 m, men walking 30 m more than women, strong age decline — but centre-to-centre variability wide enough (adjusted r² 0.09–0.73 across centres) that the authors do not recommend routine use of a single pooled equation, offering age-specific standard curves instead. In healthy 50–85-year-olds on a 50-m corridor (Troosters 1999), distance averaged 631 ± 93 m, 84 m greater in men, with age, height, sex and weight explaining 66% of variability. Corridor length and encouragement protocol change distances, so values are carded per-protocol. On the learning effect: none of the three carded records quantifies a first-to-second-test gain in its abstract — the shelf states that gap plainly rather than borrowing a number from elsewhere.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED

title: Usual gait speed: pooled mean 0.92 m/s at mean age 73.5 across 34,485 older adults in nine cohorts — each 0.1 m/s faster carries a pooled hazard ratio of 0.88 for death, and decade means run from 1.43 m/s (men in their 40s) down to 0.94 m/s (women in their 80s)
question: In community-dwelling older adults, what is usual gait speed by age and sex — the pooled nine-cohort distributions — and what speeds mark the transitions to disability and survival risk?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing is thin (Guyton & Hall ch. 84 and the motor-control chapters) — this shelf rests chiefly on the primary cohort literature and says so. The pooled analysis (Studenski 2011) combined individual data from nine cohorts: 34,485 community-dwelling adults aged 65+, mean age 73.5, mean gait speed 0.92 (SD 0.27) m/s; gait speed predicted survival across the whole range, with a pooled hazard ratio of 0.88 per 0.1 m/s faster (a relative measure, labelled as such wherever used here) — at age 75, predicted 10-year survival spanned 19–87% in men and 35–91% in women across the speed range. The descriptive meta-analysis (Bohannon & Williams Andrews 2011) pooled 23,111 healthy adults from 41 articles: decade means from 143.4 cm/s (1.43 m/s) in men aged 40–49 down to 94.3 cm/s (0.94 m/s) in women aged 80–99. The population-representative NHANES analysis (Bohannon 2008, n=1,923 aged 50+) found slower, more representative speeds — 3.26 ft/s (≈0.99 m/s) over 8 feet and 3.29 ft/s (≈1.00 m/s) over 20 feet — with the two course lengths effectively interchangeable (r = 0.933). Course length and protocol are carded per-study: a short-course standing-start speed is not a long-course usual-pace speed.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED

title: Timed Up and Go reference values by decade in healthy older adults
question: In healthy older adults, what are reference values for the Timed Up and Go test by decade (60s–90s) — the descriptive meta-analysis norms — and how wide is the normal range before a time counts as slow?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing is thin for this test: Guyton & Hall's exercise and motor-control chapters frame mobility generally, and this shelf rests chiefly on the primary measurement literature, as its slate row directs). The carded record is concordant. Bohannon's descriptive meta-analysis of 21 studies gives mean Timed Up and Go (TUG) times of 8.1 seconds in the 60s, 9.2 seconds in the 70s and 11.3 seconds from 80 to 99 years, with a time above the upper 95% confidence limit counting as worse than average. The primary cohorts behave the same way: Steffen's 96 community-dwelling elders showed the same age-related slowing with very high test–retest reliability (ICC 0.95–0.97), Vereeck's 318 asymptomatic adults found TUG times rising with age yet still at or under 10 seconds even in older subjects, and a dedicated oldest-old cohort (mean age 90.3 years) averaged 12.6 seconds. So the normal range widens with age — roughly 8 seconds in the 60s to roughly 11–13 seconds in the 80s and 90s — and a single young-adult cut-off mislabels healthy old people as slow. Chair height and exact course protocol were not stated in the fetched records and are a standing source of between-study spread, which the wide confidence interval at 80–99 years (10.0–12.7 seconds) reflects.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — Timed Up and Go decade means of 8.1 s (60s), 9.2 s (70s) and 11.3 s (80–99) from a 21-study meta-analysis, confirmed in direction and reliability by three primary cohorts including an oldest-old mean of 12.6 s at mean age 90.3 years

title: Five-times sit-to-stand and 30-second chair-stand reference values by age and sex
question: In healthy adults, what are reference values for the five-times sit-to-stand test (and the 30-second chair-stand count) by age and sex — the pooled 14-country analysis and national cohort norms?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing thin, as the slate row directs: Guyton & Hall's exercise/motor chapters frame mobility generally; the row rests on the primary measurement literature). Three large normative datasets agree on the shape of five-times sit-to-stand (FTSST) performance: fastest in the 50s (median about 9–10 seconds), slowing steadily to a median of about 15 seconds by the late 80s and 90s, with women slower than men at every age and a very wide spread in old age (in the English cohort, the 5th-to-95th performance span at 85+ runs from about 26 seconds down to about 10 seconds in women). A younger adult cohort (Chile, 18–80 years) extends the curve downward: medians of about 7–8 seconds in the 20s rising to 11–13 seconds at 70–80. The companion 30-second chair-stand count rests on a much thinner base — its founding validation study (76 older adults) established reliability and validity against leg-press strength but the fetched record does not print decade mean counts, so this shelf gives the 30-second test's measurement credentials, not invented counts. Note the percentile convention in the two GeroScience reports: their 5th percentile is the SLOWEST time and their 95th the fastest, the reverse of the usual direction, and the cards print them exactly as reported.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — five-times sit-to-stand medians of about 9–10 s in the 50s rising to about 15 s at 85+, concordant across 45,470 SHARE participants, 7,658 ELSA participants and a 463-person healthy Chilean cohort; the 30-second chair-stand limb is validated (ICC 0.84–0.92) but normatively thinner

title: Heart-rate recovery after exercise: normal distribution, the ≤12-beat threshold and reproducibility
question: In healthy adults, how fast does heart rate fall after maximal exercise — the normal heart-rate-recovery distribution at 1 and 2 minutes by age, sex and fitness, its within-person reproducibility, and where the abnormal threshold (≤12 beats at 1 minute) came from?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, exercise and autonomic chapters; Boron & Boulpaep, cardiovascular control — recovery of heart rate after exercise is a function of vagal reactivation, as the Cole record itself states). Three different questions are often confused, and the carded record separates them. (1) Where the abnormal line came from: Cole's 1999 referred-patient cohort (2,428 adults having diagnostic exercise testing — NOT healthy volunteers, and labelled so on its card) defined an abnormal 1-minute recovery as a fall of 12 beats/min or less and showed it predicted death (relative risk 4.0 unadjusted, 2.0 adjusted). (2) The normal distribution: a 2025 cycle-ergometry study of 9,917 tested subjects derived normal values from its 2,242 apparently healthy members, defining blunted recovery as below the 5th percentile for age — all indices were age-dependent — and blunted HRR1/HRR2 remained the strongest mortality predictors (hazard ratios 1.70 and 1.57). (3) Reproducibility: in UK Biobank repeat testing about 3 years apart, heart-rate dynamics during exercise and 1-minute recovery were highly reproducible within a person (intra-individual correlations 0.70–0.81 for the dynamics indices), with abnormal values consistent about 60–70% of the time. The mechanism of the fall itself — a vagal first phase and a sympathetic tail — is a separate shelf (pack #6800) and is cross-pointed here, not re-carded. Recovery protocol matters: Cole used a symptom-limited treadmill protocol and the 2025 study cycle ergometry, and active versus passive recovery changes the numbers, so values are carded per-protocol.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — heart-rate recovery is age-dependent with blunted values below the age-specific 5th percentile (9,917 cycle tests; healthy subset 2,242), the ≤12 beats/min 1-minute line derives from Cole's 2,428 referred patients (adjusted relative risk of death 2.0), and recovery dynamics repeat within a person over ~3 years (ρ 0.70–0.81)

title: Left-ventricular global longitudinal strain: normal values by speckle-tracking echocardiography
question: In healthy adults, what are normal left-ventricular global longitudinal strain values by speckle-tracking echocardiography — the meta-analytic normal range, the EACVI NORRE reference ranges, and how much do vendor, sex and age shift them?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED for the central range, with vendor dependence as a core caveat (textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, cardiac muscle / ventricular function; strain imaging itself is textbook-thin, as the slate row directs, and the shelf rests on the primary measurement literature). Two meta-analyses and one large multicentre reference study converge on the same centre: mean left-ventricular global longitudinal strain (GLS) in healthy adults is about −19% to −20% (2D meta-analysis: −19.7%, with study means spanning −15.9% to −22.1%; 3D meta-analysis: −19.05%, study means −15.8% to −23.4%). The EACVI NORRE study (549 healthy volunteers, vendor-independent analysis software) puts the lowest expected value at −16.7% in men and −17.8% in women — that is, a healthy GLS is generally more negative than about −17%. What is NOT settled is a single universal cut-off: between-study heterogeneity is very high (I² ≈ 99% in the 3D analysis), analysis software was consistently associated with the reported values, and systolic blood pressure — not age, sex, frame rate or equipment — tracked GLS variation in the 2D meta-regression. So the honest summary is a centre (about −19.5%), a lower reference boundary (about −17% by NORRE), and a standing instruction to interpret a value beside its vendor/software and the patient's blood pressure, never against one universal number.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — healthy global longitudinal strain centres at about −19.7% (2D meta-analysis, 2,597 subjects) and −19.05% (3D meta-analysis, 2,346 subjects), with NORRE lower reference limits of −16.7% (men) and −17.8% (women); software and blood pressure are established modifiers, so no platform-free cut-off is claimed

title: QT interval distribution: QTc by age, sex and correction formula
question: In healthy humans, what is the distribution of the QT interval — how QTc varies by age, sex and heart-rate correction formula (Bazett vs Fridericia vs Framingham linear), and what fraction of a general population exceeds the conventional 450/470 ms thresholds under each formula?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, ECG chapters — the QT interval lengthens as heart rate falls, so every quoted QT is a corrected QT and the correction formula is part of the measurement). The carded record makes one point four ways: the formula reclassifies the same ECG. Bazett's square-root formula (1920) was derived from only 39 young subjects; in the Framingham baseline ECGs (5,018 adults) it overcorrected at fast heart rates and undercorrected at slow ones, while a simple linear correction (QTLC = QT + 0.154 × (1 − RR)) fitted better. In 31,558 young active people, Bazett again performed least favourably at removing the heart-rate effect and Fridericia best, and Bazett-based cut points captured less than half of those in the top percentiles of uncorrected QT — the authors propose Fridericia thresholds of 460 ms (men) and 470 ms (women), with 485 ms marking prolongation. In a general population of 20,261 adults, corrected QT averaged about 413–419 ms in men and 419–422 ms in women across iron-store strata — women run longer than men, as every record here agrees. The multiparameter healthy-subject study adds that QT dispersion and related indices correlate with age and that simultaneous ECG parameters are reproducible. Practical reading: always print the formula beside the value; a QTc of 460 ms by Bazett at a fast heart rate and 460 ms by Fridericia are not the same finding.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — the QT interval's rate correction is formula-dependent in every large fetched record: Bazett overcorrects at fast rates (Framingham, 5,018 adults) and performed worst in 31,558 young people, where Fridericia thresholds of 460 ms (men) and 470 ms (women) were proposed; general-population corrected QT averages about 413–419 ms in men and 419–422 ms in women (20,261 adults)

title: Resting pulmonary artery pressures in healthy humans: catheter and echocardiographic reference values
question: In healthy humans, what are resting pulmonary artery pressures — mean pulmonary artery pressure and systolic pressure by invasive catheterisation and by echocardiographic tricuspid-regurgitant velocity — and how much do they rise with age, body-mass index and exercise?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, pulmonary circulation; Boron & Boulpaep, pulmonary haemodynamics). The invasive and echocardiographic records tell one consistent story. By right-heart catheterisation (systematic review: 1,187 healthy individuals, 47 studies), resting mean pulmonary artery pressure is 14.0 ± 3.3 mmHg, essentially independent of sex and ethnicity, slightly higher after age 50 (14.7 ± 4.0) than under 30 (12.8 ± 3.1), and it rarely exceeds 20 mmHg at rest — while exercise values are a different matter, frequently exceeding 30 mmHg in people over 50 even at mild exercise (29.4 ± 8.4 mmHg). By echocardiography, pulmonary artery systolic pressure in 3,790 echocardiographically normal subjects averaged 28.3 ± 4.9 mmHg, with an upper 95% limit of 37.2 mmHg in lower-risk subjects and values over 40 mmHg in 6% of those over 50 and 5% of those with BMI over 30 — age and BMI move the echo number. The tricuspid-regurgitant velocity that feeds the echo estimate averages about 2.0 m/s in healthy adults (prospective cohort 2.01 ± 0.29 m/s; pooled 1.96 m/s), with a 95% quantile of 2.55 m/s. Reading: a resting mean pressure near 14 mmHg and a TR velocity under about 2.5 m/s are the healthy centre and edge; echo systolic estimates up to about 40 mmHg occur in healthy older or heavier people and are not, alone, pulmonary hypertension.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — resting mean pulmonary artery pressure 14.0 ± 3.3 mmHg by catheterisation in 1,187 healthy people (rarely over 20 mmHg), echo systolic pressure 28.3 ± 4.9 mmHg in 3,790 normal subjects with an upper 95% limit of 37.2 mmHg, and tricuspid velocity centred at about 2.0 m/s with a 95% quantile of 2.55 m/s

title: Total blood volume, haemoglobin mass and plasma volume in healthy humans
question: In healthy humans, how large are total blood volume, red-cell (haemoglobin) mass and plasma volume — measured by carbon-monoxide rebreathing and by indicator dilution — per kilogram and by sex, training state and body composition, and how well do the classic prediction formulas (Nadler) match measured values?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, body-fluid compartments; Boron & Boulpaep, blood-volume regulation — the haemoglobin concentration that laboratories report is the ratio of total haemoglobin mass to plasma volume, so concentration alone cannot say whether the mass, the volume or both have changed). The carded record gives the measured quantities three ways. First, method precision: the optimised CO-rebreathing method repeats to a typical error of about 2% (and to within 0.8% for a repeated 1.0 mL/kg bolus), can be repeated within 3 hours if oxygen is used to clear carbon monoxide, and a 30-second single-breath variant matches the established method in healthy volunteers. Second, absolute values: in small healthy samples total haemoglobin mass was about 776–849 g (Plumb 808 ± 190 g in 24 subjects; Turner 785–791 g in 12; Krehl 843 ± 293 g in 11), so the healthy absolute range in these samples is broad and tracks body size. Third, the per-kilogram and training comparison: elite runners carry about 14.0–14.2 g/kg of haemoglobin mass and about 100–102 mL/kg of blood volume, and endurance-trained people carry roughly 30% more haemoglobin mass than untrained controls. The classic Nadler prediction formulas are named here only as the textbook-era prediction approach: none of the fetched records tests them head-to-head against measured volumes, so no accuracy figure is printed for them. Cross-points: haemoglobin mass after altitude exposure is homed at pack #6266 and after blood loss at pack #6448 — this shelf is the at-rest baseline, not a change-over-time question.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — total haemoglobin mass about 780–850 g in small healthy samples (≈14 g/kg and blood volume ≈100 mL/kg in elite runners), about 30% higher with endurance training, measured by optimised CO rebreathing to about 2% typical error; the Nadler formulas are not validated by any fetched record and carry no accuracy figure here

title: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate by age and sex: the healthy population distribution
question: In healthy adults, what is the erythrocyte sedimentation rate by age and sex — the population distribution in subjectively healthy adults and the empirical upper-limit rules (age/2 for men, (age+10)/2 for women) — and how do haemoglobin, fibrinogen and the test method (Westergren vs automated) shift it?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing is brief: Guyton & Hall, blood cells, inflammation and ESR — as the slate row directs, the shelf rests chiefly on the primary population literature). Three healthy-population datasets, spanning 1990 to 2025 and totalling more than 9,000 people, agree on the shape: ESR rises with age, is higher in women than in men at every age, and most healthy people have low values — in the 1996 Norwegian population study about 76% of all recordings were under 9 mm/h. The Norwegian 95% upper reference limits were, at ages 20, 55 and 90: men 12, 14 and 19 mm/h; women 18, 21 and 23 mm/h. A 2025 Italian study using the Westergren method and two automated analysers found almost identical reference intervals (women ≥18 years: 1–22 mm/h; men under 70: 1–14 mm/h; men 70+: 1–22 mm/h), with the automated analysers averaging within 1 mm/h of the gold standard. The classic age/2 (men) and (age+10)/2 (women) rules are the textbook account of the upper limit — and the fetched population limits sit well below them (at age 55 the rules would allow about 28 mm/h for men and 33 mm/h for women, against measured 95% limits of 14 and 21 mm/h), so the rules are generous, not tight. Method matters: Westergren and automated values are close but not identical — the CUBE 30 Touch read up to 29 mm/h in the upper limit for men over 70 against 22 mm/h by Westergren — so a value should be read beside its method. One classic was refused: Böttiger & Svedberg 1967 (a paper titled 'Normal erythrocyte sedimentation rate and age') has an EMPTY abstract in PubMed, so its numbers could not be verified from the record and it is not carded; the refusal is recorded on the Synthesis card.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — erythrocyte sedimentation rate in health is low (about 76% under 9 mm/h), rises with age and runs higher in women, with 95% upper limits of 12–19 mm/h (men) and 18–23 mm/h (women) in 3,910 Norwegians, corroborated by 4,202 Danish donors and 989 Italians across Westergren and automated methods; one classic (Böttiger & Svedberg 1967) was refused for an empty abstract

title: Bioelectrical impedance phase angle at 50 kHz: reference values by age, sex and ethnicity
question: In healthy humans, what is the bioelectrical impedance phase angle at 50 kHz by age, sex and ethnicity — its population reference values and percentile curves — and how tightly does it track body cell mass and nutritional state?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING (textbook framing is thin for impedance specifically: Boron & Boulpaep's body-composition chapters frame the water compartments, and this shelf rests on the primary measurement literature, as the slate row directs). Two very large 2026 reference studies and one determinants study draw a consistent SHAPE but population-specific VALUES. In 13,256 Chinese adults measured at 50 kHz, phase angle peaked at 30–39 years in Han and Korean men and 40–49 years in Yao men and in all women, fell steeply after 50 in men, and was always higher in men; the 5th–95th percentile ranges were 5.33–7.16° (Han men), 4.62–6.34° (Han women), 5.53–7.65° (Korean men), 5.04–6.79° (Korean women), 5.15–6.94° (Yao men) and 4.49–6.12° (Yao women). In 5,049 healthy Colombians the same arc appeared — rising through adolescence and early adulthood, peaking at 40–49, declining thereafter, men above women at every age. The determinants study (1,442 people with dilution-measured body composition) explains why no universal number can exist yet: phase angle tracks fat-free mass (positive) and the extracellular-to-intracellular water ratio (negative), and even with age, height, race and composition in the model only 42–54% of its variance is explained. Impedance-derived indices are not dilution measurements and must not be presented as such. Until devices and populations are harmonised, a phase angle is interpretable only against its own population's age- and sex-specific percentiles.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING — phase angle at 50 kHz follows a concordant life-course arc (midlife peak, men above women, decline after 50) across 13,256 Chinese and 5,049 Colombian adults, but values are population-specific (5th–95th ranges from 4.49–6.12° in Yao women to 5.53–7.65° in Korean men) and its determinants explain only 42–54% of variance, so no universal range exists yet

title: Bone turnover marker reference intervals: serum P1NP and CTX (IOF/IFCC analytes)
question: In healthy adults, what are the reference intervals for the bone turnover markers used as the IOF/IFCC reference analytes — serum P1NP (formation) and serum CTX (resorption) — by sex, menopausal status and age, and how large are their circadian and fasting-related swings?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING (textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, parathyroid hormone, calcitonin and bone physiology; Ganong, endocrine control of bone). The IOF/IFCC reference analytes — serum P1NP for formation and serum CTX for resorption — have solid reference intervals, but they are assay- and population-specific, and that specificity is the shelf's core content. The largest intervals come from the Study of Health in Pomerania (1,939 people, IDS-iSYS platform): in men the intervals narrow with age (P1NP 31.1–95.9 ng/mL at 25–29 years falling to 15.7–68.1 ng/mL at 75–79; CTX 0.12–0.83 falling to 0.05–0.58 ng/mL), in premenopausal women (30–54) P1NP was 19.3–76.3 ng/mL and CTX 0.05–0.67 ng/mL, and in postmenopausal women (50–79) both ran higher (P1NP 18.2–102.3; CTX 0.09–1.05 ng/mL). The young-premenopausal reference study (637 women aged 30–39 across four countries) found significant country differences — P1NP and serum β-CTX higher in France — that largely disappeared once smoking, contraceptive-pill use, exercise, cycle timing and vitamin D were allowed for: behaviour and sampling conditions move these markers. The Danish assay comparison (2,308 fasting samples) is the caution: the two automated platforms (IDS-iSYS and Roche Cobas) disagreed significantly for both markers (P1NP mean difference −3 µg/L with limits of agreement −19 to +14; CTX mean difference 13 ng/L, limits −187 to +214, with a systematic concentration-dependent bias), so intervals and monitoring must stay on one assay. CTX sampling in the carded record was fasting; the size of CTX's circadian and food-related swings is part of the textbook account of sampling discipline, but no fetched record here quantifies those swings, so no swing number is printed.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING — P1NP and CTX reference intervals are robust within their assay and population (Pomeranian IDS-iSYS intervals: men P1NP 31.1–95.9 ng/mL at 25–29 years narrowing with age; postmenopausal women CTX 0.09–1.05 ng/mL), but the two automated platforms disagree significantly and concentration-dependently (Danish comparison, 2,308 samples), so no platform-free universal interval exists yet

title: Anti-Müllerian hormone by age in healthy women: peak at ~24.5 years, then a non-linear fall to menopause
question: In healthy women, how does serum anti-Müllerian hormone fall with age from adolescence to menopause — the population centile curves and validated decline models — and how much do assay generation and ethnicity shift the values?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — framed by Ganong (female reproductive endocrinology) and Guyton & Hall ch. 83, and resting on concordant population data: in 1,015 naturally fertile women AMH fell non-linearly with age; a validated model built on a combined n = 3,260 peaks at age 24.5 years and then declines to menopause, with age alone explaining 34% of the variation; and external validation in 15,834 US women confirmed the quadratic decline model (earlier models overestimated AMH by about 11% relative to the nomogram — a relative difference, printed beside the model it describes). The shape — rise to a mid-20s peak, then a long fall — is settled; the exact centile a woman sits on is assay- and population-dependent, so values are carded per cohort and no single number is presented as universal. Cross-point: the follicular-wave imaging dynamics shelf (Slate 8 row S8-4-35's build) describes the ovarian process AMH indexes — a different measurement, not carded here.

title: IGF-I reference intervals by age and sex: adolescent peak, steady adult fall — and intervals that belong to their assay
question: In healthy adults, what are serum IGF-I reference intervals by age and sex — the standardised centile curves — and how much do the six common immunoassays disagree on the same samples?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — framed by Guyton & Hall ch. 75 (growth hormone / somatomedins) and Ganong, and resting on large standardised reference programmes: 1,685 healthy Japanese subjects give LMS centile curves peaking in mid-adolescence (median 310 ng/mL in boys at 14 years, 349 ng/mL in girls at 13) and falling to about 124/103 ng/mL by age 70; 14,970 healthy subjects across 11 cohorts anchor the IDS iSYS intervals across the lifespan; and the six-assay comparison in 911 French adults shows why the assay must be named beside every interval — lower reference limits were similar across kits but upper limits varied markedly, with pairwise concordance only moderate to good (weighted kappa 0.38–0.70). title: CGM profiles without diabetes: mean ~100 mg/dL (5.6 mmol/L), 96% of time at 70–140 mg/dL (3.9–7.8 mmol/L), and excursions are normal
question: In healthy humans without diabetes, what do continuous glucose monitoring profiles look like — mean glucose, time above 140 mg/dL (7.8 mmol/L), glycaemic variability and the 'glucotype' patterns — by age, BMI and time of day?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — framed by Guyton & Hall ch. 79 (insulin, glucagon and glucose regulation), and resting on concordant current-generation sensor data: in 153 healthy non-diabetic people aged 7–80, mean glucose was 98–99 mg/dL (5.4–5.5 mmol/L), rising to 104 mg/dL (5.8 mmol/L) over age 60, with a median 96% of time between 70 and 140 mg/dL (3.9–7.8 mmol/L) and a within-person coefficient of variation of 17 ± 3%; 39 healthy children aged 1–6 read almost identically (mean 103 mg/dL (5.7 mmol/L), median 96% in range). Two qualifications are part of the physiology, not footnotes: people normoglycaemic by standard measures still spend time in prediabetic and diabetic sensor ranges (the glucotype finding), and in the 12-week ADAG monitoring 93% of non-diabetic participants exceeded 7.8 mmol/L (140 mg/dL) at some point. All CGM homes in diabetes ask a different (management) question; this shelf is the non-diabetic norm only.

title: DHEA-S across adult life: peak in the early 20s, then a steady fall to about a fifth of peak after 70
question: In healthy adults, what are serum dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate (DHEA-S) concentrations across adult life — the peak in the third decade and the rate of decline ('adrenopause') by sex — in cross-sectional population samples?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — framed by Guyton & Hall ch. 78 (adrenocortical hormones) and Ganong on adrenal androgens, and resting on the classic cross-sectional programme: in 981 men and 481 women aged 11–89, DHEA-S peaked at age 20–24 years in men (log mean 3,470 ng/mL) and 15–19 years in women (log mean 2,470 ng/mL), then declined steadily to log means of 670 ng/mL (men) and 450 ng/mL (women) after age 70 — the 'adrenopause' pattern — with a second healthy cohort (n = 216) and the population-based Massachusetts Male Aging Study (1,709 men enrolled) both confirming a significant decline with age, the MMAS longitudinally within the same men. This is a measurement shelf only: it carries no supplementation claim of any kind (DHEA replacement in adrenal insufficiency is a separate treatment shelf, live #1750, and none of its record is carded here).

title: CSF opening pressure at lumbar puncture: 95% interval 10–25 cm CSF, falling with age, higher in men and with higher BMI — upper limit unsettled
question: In adults having lumbar puncture in the lateral decubitus position, what is the cerebrospinal fluid opening pressure — its reference interval, the 90th/95th percentiles, and how much do body-mass index, age and position move it?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING — framed by Guyton & Hall ch. 62 (cerebrospinal fluid system) and Boron & Boulpaep on CSF formation and pressure, and resting on three human lumbar-puncture datasets that agree on the shape but not on the upper limit — which is the point. The prospective reference-interval study (242 adults) gives a 95% reference interval of 10–25 cm CSF; the 339-patient outpatient study gives a mean of 17.5 cm H2O (range 4.0–30.0) and proposes higher, factor-adjusted cut-offs (men <30 cm H2O, <25 if over 70; women <25, 27.5 if BMI over 30); and the 12,118-patient Mayo record review shows pressure in mmHg falling steadily after age 50 (mean 11.5 ± 2.8 mmHg at 20–49 years, 8.4 ± 2.4 mmHg at 90–95). Age (lower), male sex (higher) and BMI (higher) move pressure in every dataset. The 'upper limit of normal' — 20 versus 25 versus factor-adjusted 30 cm H2O — is genuinely unsettled, so the stamp is EMERGING, not a settled interval.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING

title: Multiple Sleep Latency Test in health: wide spread, protocol-dependent, and the 8-minute line is a convention not a percentile
question: In healthy adults, what is normal daytime sleep propensity on the Multiple Sleep Latency Test — mean sleep latency by age and sex, the spread around the mean, and how protocol choices (nap number, prior sleep, the 8-minute convention) move the result?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING — framed by Kryger's Principles and Practice of Sleep Medicine (the named framing source for this row) with Guyton & Hall ch. 60 as secondary framing, and resting on primary healthy-cohort MSLT data plus the AASM practice parameters: in 100 healthy adults (MSLT-30, five 30-minute naps) mean latency to sleep was 13.9 ± 6.9 minutes with a quadratic age pattern, shortest in middle age; in 176 healthy adults (four naps) latency ranged from 2 to 20 minutes within each age group and young adults were sleepier; and in 55 normal young adults sleepiness was better captured by sleep-onset frequency, peaking around 14:00. The evidence base is thin, protocol-sensitive and old — and the 8-minute 'pathological sleepiness' line is a convention, not a percentile of any of these distributions, so the stamp is EMERGING. Cross-point: overnight sleep architecture and ageing (pack #6204) is a different measurement — overnight structure, not daytime propensity.

title: AHI in unselected adults: common, higher in men, and the scoring rule halves or doubles who counts
question: In unselected general-population adults, how common are raised apnoea–hypopnoea index values on polysomnography — the AHI distribution by age and sex in the HypnoLaus and Wisconsin cohorts — and how much does the hypopnoea scoring rule (3% desaturation/arousal vs 4% desaturation) change who counts as having sleep apnoea?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — framed by Kryger's Principles and Practice of Sleep Medicine (epidemiology/scoring chapters) with Guyton & Hall ch. 60 as secondary framing, and resting on two large population cohorts plus a scoring-rule analysis of the same HypnoLaus data: in the HypnoLaus general population (2,121 with polysomnography), median AHI was 6.9 events/h in women and 14.9 in men, and moderate-to-severe sleep-disordered breathing (AHI ≥15) was present in 23.4% of women and 49.7% of men; the Wisconsin cohort's US estimates are lower but the same order of magnitude (AHI ≥15 in 10–17% of men and 3–9% of women by age band) and rose by a relative 14–55% over two decades with obesity. The scoring rule is the core content: in HypnoLaus, median AHI was 10.9, 4.4 or 10.1 events/h under the AASM 1999, 2007 and 2012 hypopnoea definitions respectively, and AHI ≥15 prevalence was 39.3%, 18.8% or 36.6% — the rule more than doubles who counts. This is a measurement/prevalence shelf: it carries no CPAP or device content (those homes are live #635/#923 and the OSA treatment family), and no treatment claim is carded here.

title: Corneal sensitivity: falls with age on the filament, instrument-defined thresholds, and a discordant air-pulse finding in women
question: In healthy humans, how sensitive is the cornea — corneal sensitivity thresholds by Cochet–Bonnet and non-contact air-pulse esthesiometry across the cornea and conjunctiva — and how much does sensitivity fall with age, contact-lens wear and time of day?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — framed by Ganong (somatosensory / special senses chapters; thin framing for corneal esthesiometry specifically — this shelf rests chiefly on the primary measurement literature, as its slate row directs), and resting on three human studies whose core finding is concordant for the filament method: corneal touch threshold rises with age — the 1977 classic (205 healthy people) found thresholds increasing gradually throughout life, more significantly after the fifth decade, and a 2025 Cochet–Bonnet cohort (324 volunteers) found central sensitivity falling with age with correlations of about −0.78 across all quadrants, accelerating in the 50s and 60s. title: Spontaneous blink rate: ~17/min at rest, 4.5/min reading, 26/min in conversation — the task sets the rate
question: In healthy humans, what is the spontaneous eye blink rate at rest, during reading and during conversation — its mean and wide between-person spread — and how do gaze position, lighting and age change it?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — framed by Ganong and Guyton & Hall on eyelid and lacrimal physiology (thin framing — this shelf rests chiefly on the primary measurement literature, as its slate row directs), and resting on three human video studies that agree on the shape and the scale: at rest, spontaneous blink rate is roughly 12–17 blinks/min; reading collapses it to about 4.5/min (a 55.08% relative fall from rest in the 150-person study, with the absolute values 17 → 4.5/min printed beside it); conversation raises it to about 26/min (a 99.70% relative rise from rest, 17 → 26/min); and the spread between healthy people is wide and skewed, with a distinct 'frequent blinker' cluster above 20/min. title: Peripapillary RNFL thickness on SD-OCT: ~87–105 μm by cohort and device, thinning 0.38 μm/year
question: In healthy eyes, what is peripapillary retinal nerve fibre layer thickness on spectral-domain OCT — its mean and 1st/5th-percentile limits by age, sex, ethnicity and optic-disc size — and how fast does it thin with normal ageing?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — framed by Ganong on vision / retinal structure (thin framing for OCT biometry — this shelf rests chiefly on the primary measurement literature, as its slate row directs), and resting on three primary SD-OCT records plus a 617-subject interocular-symmetry cohort: across the European Eye Epidemiology consortium's eight cohorts (16,084 adults), mean peripapillary RNFL thickness ranged from 86.8 ± 21.4 μm (Rotterdam Study I) to 104.7 ± 12.5 μm (Rotterdam Study III), thinning with age at −0.38 μm per year; the Cirrus-versus-Stratus comparison (97 healthy subjects) shows device values are not interchangeable (proportional bias, and Cirrus intervisit reproducibility 4.31–22.01 μm); and in 103 healthy myopic participants the RNFL bundle pattern itself shifts with axial length, changing how maps must be read.
