title: Macular thickness in health is a device number: Spectralis central subfield ~270 µm (ceiling 315 µm), swept-source ~228 µm in the same population, Cirrus ~241 µm in children — conversion equations exist because raw values differ
question: In healthy eyes, what is macular thickness on spectral-domain OCT — central subfield and ETDRS-sector means by age, sex and ethnicity — and how reproducible are the measurements?
balance: Textbook framing (Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology, vision/retinal structure) is thin for OCT biometry, as the slate row states — the primary measurement literature carries this shelf. Healthy macular thickness is a device-relative quantity. On Spectralis spectral-domain OCT, 50 healthy adults gave a central subfield (CSF) mean of 270.2 µm (SD 22.5) and central point thickness of 227.3 µm, with a proposed normal CSF ceiling of 315 µm and no significant age or sex effect (Grover 2009). The same retinas measure differently on other platforms: in 290 normal Chinese eyes, swept-source OCT read CSF at 227.8 µm where spectral-domain read 260.0 µm (Xiong 2021), and an 11-site international cohort of 546 healthy controls derived explicit Spectralis-to-Cirrus conversion equations for retinal layer thicknesses, with layer thinning after age 40 of 2.4 µm per decade (peripapillary RNFL) and 1.4 µm per decade (macular GCIPL) (Kenney 2022). Cirrus norms in healthy children give CSF 240.6 µm (Raffa 2023). The companion peripapillary RNFL thickness question is homed on the sibling shelf (slate row S9-4-38) and is cross-pointed here in prose only. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

title: Normal cornea ~535 µm on average (SD ~31 µm): population means run 511 µm (South India) to 556 µm (Tehran), thinning a few µm per decade, and shifting applanation IOP ~2 mmHg per 100 µm
question: In healthy adults, what is central corneal thickness — its population mean and spread by ethnicity, age and sex — and by how much does a thick or thin cornea bias applanation intraocular-pressure readings?
balance: Textbook framing (Ganong, vision/aqueous dynamics) is brief; the population measurement literature carries this shelf, and the related pressure-dynamics physiology lives on the aqueous humour/diurnal IOP shelf (pack #6436). The pooled literature normal for central corneal thickness (CCT) is 0.534-0.536 mm with a standard deviation of about 0.031 mm (Doughty & Zaman 2000, labelled meta-analysis of ~600 datasets). Primary population studies bracket that pooled value: Tehran 555.6 µm (SD 39.9; N = 410, Orbscan), healthy Italians 532.2 µm (N = 400), and South India 511.4 µm (SD 33.5; N = 6,754, ultrasound) — a spread to which both ancestry and pachymetry method contribute. Age thins the cornea by roughly 2.4-4.3 µm per decade in the Chennai data; sex differences are small and inconsistent. The clinical stake is applanation tonometry: about 2.0-2.5 mmHg of measured IOP per 100 µm of CCT in Chennai, versus ~1.1 mmHg per 10% CCT difference in healthy eyes in the meta-analysis. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

title: The normal pupil: ~5.4 mm in darkness, ~2.8 mm at 250 lux, shrinking 0.015-0.043 mm per year of age depending on light — with anisocoria growing 0.03 mm per decade
question: In healthy humans, how large is the pupil — light-adapted and dark-adapted pupil diameter by age and luminance — and how much anisocoria is normal?
balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, ch. 51 (pupillary reflexes/autonomic control of the eye); Ganong (vision). The healthy pupil is a moving quantity set by luminance and age. In 245 normal subjects, mean diameter ran from 5.39 mm (SD 1.04) in darkness (0 lux) to 2.84 mm (SD 0.50) at 250 lux, and normal anisocoria grew by 0.03 mm per decade, larger in scotopic/mesopic light (Rickmann 2017). Age shrinks the pupil at every illuminance: light-adapted diameter fell linearly by 0.043 mm/year at low illuminance and 0.015 mm/year at high illuminance in 91 healthy subjects, independent of sex, refractive error and iris colour (Winn 1994); an independent normative sample found resting diameter correlating r = -0.63 with age (Tekin 2018), and a young-vs-old comparison (N = 12 + 14) confirmed smaller resting diameters and blunted darkness reflexes in the elderly (Bitsios 1996). This shelf covers resting pupil SIZE; the melanopsin post-illumination response is homed separately (pack #6796). PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

title: Colour discrimination peaks at 20-29 years, then 100-hue errors climb steadily — gathering on the blue-yellow axis, with lens yellowing carrying part of the rise
question: In healthy humans, how does colour discrimination change with age — Farnsworth–Munsell 100-hue total error scores by decade and the emergence of blue–yellow (tritan-like) errors — in people with no eye disease?
balance: Textbook framing: Ganong (colour vision); Guyton & Hall, ch. 50 (retinal colour mechanisms). In disease-free eyes, Farnsworth-Munsell 100-hue performance follows a shallow U across life, replicated on three continents: total error scores are lowest at 20-29 years (Huang 1993, N = 120), discrimination is best between 20 and 50 years (Roy 1991, N = 115, North America — norms comparable with Verriest's European data), and total scores as published rise from ~7.4-7.6 in youth to ~10.1-10.2 in the 60s, correlating significantly with age in both eyes (Mantyjarvi 2001, N = 160, Macbeth lamp at 1000 lux). The added errors concentrate on the blue-yellow (tritan) axis (Huang), and lens changes are significantly associated with higher scores alongside age (Roy) — so part of 'ageing' colour loss is lenticular. Sex and eye side do not matter. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

title: Normal field sensitivity is flat to age 40, then falls — 5.5 dB peripherally by age 75 — while a healthy person's first-ever field runs ~4 dB low from learning alone
question: In healthy humans, how does automated static perimetry sensitivity fall with age — differential light sensitivity by eccentricity and decade (Octopus/Humphrey normative studies) — and how large is the learning effect between a first and second visual field?
balance: Textbook framing: Ganong (vision/visual pathways); Guyton & Hall, ch. 51. Automated static perimetry sensitivity is age-shaped and platform-bound. The Octopus 101 normative model (81 healthy subjects, 10-79 years) shows differential luminance sensitivity nearly constant from 10-40 years, then declining ever more steeply, the loss growing with eccentricity — 5.5 dB at 25° superiorly between ages 10 and 75 — with total random SD 1.75 dB (Hermann 2008). Across six field tests in 100 normal subjects, standard automated perimetry had the least ageing effect, practice effect and variability, and short-wavelength perimetry the most (Gardiner 2006); SWAP variability is 2.7× white-on-white and shrinks toward 1.9× after correcting for lens media absorption, which also flattens its age slope by ~25% (Wild 1998). The learning effect is large: naive healthy adults improved mean deviation from -7.40 to -3.29 dB over three FDT sessions, with 50-64% of first fields falsely classifying as abnormal (Pierre-Filho 2010). PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

title: VEMP holds to ~50, then amplitudes and response rates fall and thresholds rise: galvanic norms are p1 7.8 ms, n1 22.1 ms, ~67 µV, ~16% asymmetry — always read age- and protocol-matched
question: In healthy humans, what are vestibular-evoked myogenic potential norms — cervical VEMP p13–n23 latency, amplitude and threshold, and galvanic/ocular VEMP values, by age — and how steeply do amplitudes fall and response rates drop after age 60?
balance: Textbook framing: Ganong (hearing and equilibrium — vestibular apparatus); Guyton & Hall, ch. 49 (vestibular sensations). PARTIAL slice, per assembly adjudication: the vestibular-test battery shelf (pack #7071) reports VEMP age-trend directions inside a test-battery card and holds no normative values; this shelf builds only the quantitative-norms slice and cross-points #7071 in prose. The dedicated datasets converge on a post-50 inflection: in 280 healthy volunteers aged 10-85, cervical VEMP response rate and amplitude declined beyond the fifth decade while p13/n23 latencies prolonged and thresholds worsened (Singh 2014); an age-group study with manometer-controlled sternocleidomastoid contraction likewise found amplitude falling and thresholds rising in older adults, with latencies and asymmetry ratios unchanged in that protocol (Tourtillott 2010). Absolute values come from galvanic VEMP in 100 healthy adults: P1 latency 7.82 ms (SD 3.29), N1 22.06 ms (SD 3.95), P1-N1 amplitude 66.64 µV (SD 24.5), asymmetry 16.29% (SD 11.99), with significant age-group differences (Avci 2022). Stimulus (air/bone-conducted vs galvanic) and EMG normalisation dominate comparability — values are carded per protocol. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED

title: Normal ears need only about -3 to -4 dB SNR with noise ahead and -11 dB with noise at the side — HINT norms that each language version must earn from its own listeners
question: In normal-hearing adults, what are speech reception thresholds in noise — Hearing in Noise Test (HINT) sentence thresholds in quiet and in noise — and how do they vary across language versions and noise direction?
balance: Textbook framing: Ganong (hearing) — speech-audiometry framing is brief, as the slate row states; the primary test-norming literature carries this shelf. In normal-hearing adults, the English Hearing in Noise Test gives a sentence reception threshold of 23.91 dB(A) in quiet and -2.92 dB signal-to-noise ratio in 72 dB(A) noise, with 95% measurement confidence intervals of about ±2.4-3.0 dB (Nilsson 1994). The Mandarin HINT (226 normal-hearing subjects across two dialect versions) gives quiet thresholds of 14.7 and 19.4 dB(A), noise-front thresholds of -4.3/-4.0 dB SNR and noise-side thresholds near -11 dB SNR (Wong 2007); the Cantonese HINT (142 subjects) gives 19.4 dB(A) in quiet, -3.9 dB front and about -10.5 dB at the side (Wong & Soli 2005). The consistent physiology: a ~7 dB spatial release from masking when noise moves to the side, and speech-in-noise thresholds that are a separate measurement from pure-tone thresholds (whose physiology shelf is homed separately). Norms are language-, dialect- and materials-specific. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED

title: Normal bowel habit is wide and mostly irregular: once daily is a minority pattern in Bristol, near-universal in Nigeria, and a quarter of Dutch adults meet constipation criteria while calling their habit good
question: In healthy general-population adults, what is normal bowel habit — defecation frequency per week, usual timing and stool form — and how wide is the range (the 'three times a day to three times a week' rule) by sex and population?
balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, ch. 63-64 (GI motility/defecation reflexes); Boron & Boulpaep (GI motility); colonic transit — the mechanism under the habit — is homed on pack #6439. The prospective East Bristol study (838 men, 1,059 women) found the textbook picture wrong in detail: once daily was a minority habit, a regular 24-hour cycle appeared in only 40% of men and 33% of women, a third of women defecated less often than daily and 1% once a week or less, and symptom-free stool types were only 56-61% of all stools (Heaton 1992). A south-western Nigerian community sample (N = 506) sits at the frequent end: 97.2% defecate at least daily (Jemilohun 2021). Symptom criteria cut across frequency: 24.5% of Dutch adults (N = 1,259) meet Rome III constipation criteria and 7.9% faecal-incontinence criteria, while about half of each group call their own habit good (Meinds 2017). The 'three a day to three a week' rule is the envelope of these distributions, not their centre. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED

title: The normal voiding diary: ~6-8.5 voids and ~1.7 L per 24 hours, ~0.5-1.6 nocturnal voids rising with age, and voided volumes shrinking from ~313 to ~209 mL in men
question: In asymptomatic adults reporting no voiding complaints, what does a 24-hour frequency–volume chart show — voids per day, nocturnal voids, mean and maximum voided volume and 24-hour urine production — by age and sex?
balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, ch. 26 (micturition); Boron & Boulpaep (bladder function). In 1,152 adults reporting no voiding complaints, the 24-hour frequency-volume chart shows: voiding frequency rising with age in men from 6.0 (third decade) to 8.5 (past 70) and in women from 6.9 to a peak of 8.2 in the sixth decade then 7.8; nocturia rising from 0.5 to 1.6 in men and 0.7 to 1.4 in women; mean voided volume falling from 313 to 209 mL in men and 274 to 240 mL in women; and mean 24-hour urine production of 1,718 mL (men) and 1,762 mL (women) (van Haarst 2004). The classic women's studies establish the instrument: the 48-hour chart is reliable, with mean voided volume its most reproducible parameter (Larsson & Victor 1988, N = 151), and a 12-parameter normal pattern was defined in 33 healthy women (Kassis & Schick 1993, small-N labelled). This diary slice is the third leg of bladder measurement beside uroflowmetry and urodynamics, and supplies the normal thresholds that nocturia treatment shelves presuppose. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED

title: Handheld peak flow has its own equations (Nunn & Gregg 15-85; NHATS past 65), published formulae disagree by up to 229 L/min, and a healthy day's swing is only ~6-7%
question: In healthy humans, what is peak expiratory flow — the reference equations for adults (Nunn & Gregg) and for older US adults — how do the many published prediction formulas disagree, and how large is diurnal PEF variability in people without asthma?
balance: Textbook framing: Boron & Boulpaep (respiratory mechanics/forced expiration); Guyton & Hall, ch. 37. Distinct from laboratory spirometry (pack #7150): this is handheld-meter PEF, the asthma self-management measurement, with its own devices and scales (Wright vs EU/EN13826 values differ). The adult reference standard is Nunn & Gregg's 1989 age-and-height regression equations for ages 15-85, derived from strictly normal lifelong non-smokers with an added older cohort (23 men, 29 women). For older US adults, NHATS handheld-meter equations from 1,740 healthy adults aged 65+ validate in a later cohort, whereas spirometry-based NHANES equations overestimate handheld PEF by ~29.3 L/min in men and ~10.1 L/min in women (Donahue 2024). Formula choice is not academic: across published formulae, one young man's 100% predicted spans 501-730 L/min (Radeos & Camargo 2004). Healthy diurnal variability is small — amplitude 7.23% of the mean in 152 young adults (Aggarwal 2000) and 6.26% of the daily mean by cosinor in healthy men (Casale & Pasqualetti 1997) — with a morning nadir and afternoon peak. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED

title: Peficitinib in rheumatoid arthritis: ACR20 56–64% vs 22–24% on placebo across two Asian phase 3 trials, with less joint damage in RAJ4 — a Japan-approved, single-region JAK programme
question: In adults with active rheumatoid arthritis (including methotrexate inadequate responders), does the oral pan-JAK inhibitor peficitinib (ASP015K), compared with placebo on background therapy, improve disease activity (RAJ programme)?
balance: Peficitinib 100 mg and 150 mg once daily beat placebo consistently across the RAJ programme: ACR20 responses of 58.6% and 64.4% versus 21.8% in RAJ4 (methotrexate inadequate responders, with methotrexate), 56.6% and 56.3% versus 24.2% in the 2024 Asian phase 3 trial, and a dose-related ACR20 advantage as monotherapy in the phase IIb trial, with less radiographic progression in RAJ4 (modified total Sharp score change 1.62 and 1.03 versus 3.37 on placebo). Patient- and physician-reported outcomes from RAJ3 and RAJ4 moved the same way. The whole programme is single-region (Japan/Asia; peficitinib is approved in Japan and is not FDA- or EMA-approved), and the harms are the JAK-class harms seen in the trials themselves — serious infections and herpes zoster were more frequent on peficitinib. The wider JAK-class cardiovascular and malignancy warnings (from ORAL Surveillance) are homed on the library's JAK-inhibitor shelves and are cross-pointed here, not re-carded. Proposed stamp: LIKELY (benefit).
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — two phase 3 placebo-controlled trials (RAJ4 and the 2024 Asian phase 3) plus a dose-finding phase IIb trial concordantly show peficitinib 100/150 mg superior to placebo on ACR20 (about 56–64% vs 22–24%) with less radiographic progression in RAJ4; the base is single-region (Japan/Asia, approved in Japan only) and carries JAK-class harms (serious infections, herpes zoster)

title: Diacerein in knee osteoarthritis: no better than placebo in the 2026 trial, non-inferior to celecoxib in DISSCO — with diarrhoea in up to 39% and a retracted older trial fenced out
question: In adults with painful knee osteoarthritis, does the oral IL-1α/β inhibitor (SYSADOA) diacerein, compared with placebo or celecoxib, reduce knee pain and improve function?
balance: The evidence splits by comparator. Against placebo, the best and newest test is negative: the 2026 multicentre randomised trial in patients selected for an inflammatory phenotype (effusion-synovitis on MRI) found no greater improvement in knee pain with diacerein than placebo over 24 weeks (between-group difference −1.3 mm on a 0–100 mm scale). Against an active comparator, the large DISSCO trial found diacerein non-inferior to celecoxib for pain and function over 6 months — a result compatible with a modest symptom effect, with a small effect shared with placebo response, or with celecoxib itself being modest in that population. The remaining reports (generic versus branded diacerein; a small diacerein + celecoxib combination study) have no placebo arm and cannot settle efficacy. Diarrhoea is the consistent harm (38.6% vs 22.3% on placebo in the 2026 trial; 10.2% vs 3.7% versus celecoxib in DISSCO), and diacerein is not marketed in the US. RETRACTION FENCE: the Pavelka et al. 2007 diacerein knee-OA trial (PMID 18050202) is a Retracted Publication and is deliberately NOT carded here; older meta-analyses that pool it should be read with that stated. Proposed stamp: SPLIT.
stamp: SPLIT — versus placebo, the 2026 randomised trial in inflammatory-phenotype knee OA found no pain benefit (−1.3 mm on 0–100 mm); versus celecoxib, the DISSCO trial found diacerein non-inferior on pain and function; diarrhoea is the consistent harm, and the retracted Pavelka 2007 trial (PMID 18050202) is fenced out, not carded

title: Oral salmon calcitonin in knee osteoarthritis: a failed programme — two phase 3 trials (2,206 patients) showed no structural benefit and no claimable symptom benefit
question: In adults with symptomatic knee osteoarthritis, does oral salmon calcitonin, compared with placebo, improve pain/function and slow structural progression?
balance: A failed development programme. The two phase 3 trials (1,176 and 1,030 patients, reported together) missed their structural endpoint in both studies — no significant treatment effect on joint space narrowing at 24 months — and the symptom (WOMAC) effect seen in one trial could not be claimed significant under the hierarchical testing procedure, so oral salmon calcitonin never gained an OA indication. The earlier phase 2 trial (53 randomised, 41 completing) showed a functional-score and biomarker signal at 1 mg, and a 2021 post-hoc endotype analysis found no overall treatment effect on progression, with a hypothesis-generating subgroup pattern only. Nasal salmon calcitonin for postmenopausal osteoporosis (live #1829) is a different formulation and question, cross-pointed here and not re-carded. Proposed stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference).
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — a failed programme: both phase 3 trials (1,176 and 1,030 patients) missed the structural endpoint with no claimable symptom benefit, and the post-hoc endotype analysis found no significant overall treatment effect; only a small 84-day phase 2 trial (n=53) pointed the other way

title: Strontium ranelate in knee osteoarthritis: SEKOIA (one trial) slowed joint space narrowing by 0.10–0.14 mm over 3 years — a single-trial shelf for a drug later withdrawn in Europe
question: In adults with knee osteoarthritis, does strontium ranelate, compared with placebo, slow structural progression (joint-space narrowing) and improve symptoms (SEKOIA programme)?
balance: ONE trial, several reports — printed here on the face, as the row directs. SEKOIA (1,683 randomised; 1,371 in the intention-to-treat population) found strontium ranelate slowed joint space narrowing over 3 years versus placebo by 0.14 mm (1 g/day) and 0.10 mm (2 g/day) — statistically significant but absolutely small differences — with fewer radiological progressors, and a symptom responder advantage at 2 g/day only (≥20% WOMAC pain improvement 58% vs 47%). The MRI, responder and meniscal-extrusion reports are all analyses of this same SEKOIA population, not independent trials. Strontium ranelate was restricted and then withdrawn in Europe over cardiovascular safety and was never FDA-approved; its osteoporosis question (SOTI/TROPOS) is homed at live #1823, cross-pointed here and not re-carded. Proposed stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit), single-trial.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — SINGLE-TRIAL FLAG: one phase 3 trial (SEKOIA) reported in several publications showed a small slowing of joint space narrowing (0.10–0.14 mm over 3 years) and a symptom responder advantage at 2 g/day only; the drug was restricted and withdrawn in Europe over cardiovascular safety and never FDA-approved

title: Colchicine in Behçet's syndrome: two placebo trials favour it for ulcers, erythema nodosum and arthritis — benefit concentrated in women in the 2-year trial, and no long-term sparing of immunosuppressives
question: In people with Behçet's syndrome, does colchicine, compared with placebo, reduce mucocutaneous (oral/genital ulcer, erythema nodosum) and articular manifestations?
balance: An old, small trial base that points modestly in colchicine's favour for mucocutaneous and articular disease. The 2-year double-blind trial (116 randomised) found benefit concentrated in women — fewer genital ulcers, erythema nodosum lesions and arthritic joints — with an arthritis benefit in men but no genital-ulcer or erythema nodosum benefit in men. The larger crossover trial (169 patients) found the overall disease activity index improved on colchicine and worsened on placebo, with no significant sex difference. The long-term survey of the 2001 trial cohort found early colchicine did not reduce later immunosuppressive use. One further anchor, the Aktulga et al. 1980 double-blind study (PMID 6778795), was REFUSED at build because its PubMed record carries an empty abstract, and is recorded as refused on the Synthesis card, not carded. Eye and major-organ Behçet disease are outside this question — they are immunosuppression territory — and adverse effects in the 2001 trial were similar between groups. Proposed stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two placebo-controlled trials (n=116 over 2 years; n=169 crossover) favour colchicine for mucocutaneous and articular manifestations, but the base is old, the 2001 benefit was concentrated in women, the long-term follow-up found no reduction in immunosuppressive use, and one 1980 anchor was refused at build for an empty PubMed abstract

title: Benzbromarone in gout: beats low-dose febuxostat and probenecid on urate target attainment in three randomised trials — a withdrawn-in-several-markets drug with a hepatotoxicity history
question: In adults with gout, does the uricosuric benzbromarone, compared with febuxostat or probenecid, lower serum urate to target — and at what hepatic cost?
balance: On the surrogate that decides these trials — reaching serum urate target — benzbromarone performs at least as well as its comparators at the doses tested: clearly better than low-dose febuxostat 20 mg in men with renal uric-acid underexcretion (61% vs 32% reaching <6 mg/dL at 12 weeks), essentially equal to low-dose febuxostat in a second Chinese trial (35.7% vs 39.5% reaching <360 μmol/L, ≈6.0 mg/dL), and better than probenecid after allopurinol failure (92% vs 65% reaching ≤0.30 mmol/L, ≈5.0 mg/dL). The comparators are low, non-titrated doses, so these are comparisons against weak versions of the alternatives, and urate target is a surrogate, not flares or tophi. The harm side leads with history: benzbromarone was withdrawn in several markets over hepatotoxicity and is unavailable in the US; within these short trials, transaminase elevation was actually more frequent on febuxostat in the 2022 trial (15% vs 4%), but 12-week trials cannot exclude the rare severe liver injury that drove the withdrawals. Use is single-region (Japan/China/Europe legacy). The dotinurad shelf's benzbromarone-comparator trial is homed elsewhere (pack #6829) and is not re-carded here. Proposed stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — three randomised head-to-head trials show benzbromarone reaching urate target at least as often as low-dose febuxostat (61% vs 32% in one; 35.7% vs 39.5% in another) and more often than probenecid after allopurinol failure (92% vs 65%), but the endpoint is a surrogate, comparators were fixed low doses, trials were short, and the drug was withdrawn in several markets over hepatotoxicity and is unavailable in the US

title: Molidustat in CKD anaemia: noninferior to darbepoetin on haemoglobin in three Japanese phase 3 trials (differences −0.38 to +0.13 g/dL) — a single-region HIF-PHI programme
question: In adults with anaemia of chronic kidney disease (dialysis and non-dialysis), does the HIF prolyl-hydroxylase inhibitor molidustat, compared with placebo or an erythropoiesis-stimulating agent, control haemoglobin (MIYABI / DIALOGUE programme)?
balance: Across the Japanese MIYABI phase 3 programme, oral molidustat was noninferior to darbepoetin alfa for haemoglobin control in every population tested: ESA-naive non-dialysis patients (evaluation-period mean Hb 11.28 vs 11.70 g/dL; difference −0.38 g/dL against a 1.0 g/dL margin), ESA-treated non-dialysis patients (11.67 vs 11.53 g/dL; difference +0.13 g/dL), and haemodialysis patients (10.63 vs 10.77 g/dL; difference −0.13 g/dL), with the DIALOGUE long-term extensions showing similar Hb maintenance and adverse-event proportions for up to 36 months against darbepoetin or epoetin. Haemoglobin is a surrogate endpoint throughout, and treatment-emergent adverse events were near-universal in both arms (~93–96%) in these sick populations, with small numbers of deaths in both arms of the phase 3 trials. This is a single-region programme (Japan; approved there, not FDA- or EMA-approved). The HIF-PHI class question, including cardiovascular-safety experience across the class, is homed at live #731 and pack #5753 and is cross-pointed here, not re-carded. Proposed stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — noninferiority to darbepoetin on haemoglobin shown in three Japanese phase 3 trials (ESA-naive non-dialysis, ESA-treated non-dialysis, and haemodialysis; differences −0.38 to +0.13 g/dL) with up-to-36-month extension support, but haemoglobin is a surrogate throughout, the programme is single-region (Japan; not FDA/EMA-approved), and cardiovascular-safety experience is shorter than for ESAs

title: Enarodustat in CKD anaemia: noninferior to darbepoetin and to erythropoietin on haemoglobin, +1.60 g/dL versus placebo in non-dialysis CKD — a Japan/China HIF-PHI programme
question: In adults with anaemia of chronic kidney disease (haemodialysis, peritoneal dialysis and non-dialysis), does the HIF prolyl-hydroxylase inhibitor enarodustat, compared with placebo, recombinant human erythropoietin or standard ESA therapy, control haemoglobin (SYMPHONY / ENARODIAL programme)?
balance: Enarodustat controlled haemoglobin wherever it was tested in this programme: a dose-related Hb rise versus placebo over 6 weeks in the phase 2b haemodialysis trial; noninferiority to darbepoetin alfa in SYMPHONY HD (mean Hb 10.73 vs 10.85 g/dL; difference −0.12 g/dL); noninferiority to recombinant human erythropoietin in ENARODIAL (mean Hb 106.81 g/L [10.68 g/dL] vs 99.68 g/L [9.97 g/dL] over weeks 20–24); a clear placebo-controlled Hb rise in Chinese non-dialysis patients (+15.99 g/L [+1.60 g/dL] vs −0.14 g/L over weeks 7–9); and target-range maintenance in the small single-arm peritoneal dialysis study ENAROPERA (mean Hb 110.50 g/L [11.05 g/dL], n=37). Haemoglobin is a surrogate endpoint throughout, several records do not report their randomised N in the abstract, and this is a single-region programme (Japan/China; approved in Japan, not FDA- or EMA-approved). The HIF-PHI class question is homed at live #731 and pack #5753, cross-pointed here and not re-carded. Proposed stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — haemoglobin control shown across the programme: noninferiority to darbepoetin (SYMPHONY HD) and to erythropoietin (ENARODIAL), a clear placebo-controlled Hb rise in non-dialysis CKD (+1.60 g/dL), phase 2b dose response, and single-arm target maintenance in peritoneal dialysis (n=37); haemoglobin is a surrogate throughout and the programme is single-region (Japan/China; approved in Japan, not FDA/EMA-approved)

title: Desidustat in CKD anaemia: noninferior to epoetin alfa and to darbepoetin on haemoglobin in the Indian DREAM-D and DREAM-ND phase 3 trials, with more responders
question: In adults with anaemia of chronic kidney disease (dialysis-dependent and non-dialysis-dependent), does the HIF prolyl-hydroxylase inhibitor desidustat, compared with epoetin alfa, control haemoglobin (DREAM programme)?
balance: In the Indian DREAM programme, oral desidustat (thrice weekly) was noninferior to injectable ESAs on haemoglobin in both settings: versus epoetin alfa in dialysis-dependent CKD (Hb change to weeks 16–24 of 0.95 vs 0.80 g/dL; difference 0.14 g/dL, inside the prespecified margin, with more haemoglobin responders on desidustat, 59.22% vs 48.37%) and versus darbepoetin in non-dialysis CKD (Hb change 1.95 vs 1.83 g/dL; difference 0.11 g/dL against a −0.75 g/dL margin, responders 77.78% vs 68.48%). The phase 2 dose-ranging trial showed the expected dose-related Hb rise versus placebo over 6 weeks (1.57, 2.22 and 2.92 g/dL at 100, 150 and 200 mg). Haemoglobin is a surrogate endpoint throughout, both phase 3 trials were open-label and 24 weeks, and this is a single-region programme (India; approved there, not FDA- or EMA-approved). The HIF-PHI class question is homed at live #731 and pack #5753, cross-pointed here and not re-carded. Proposed stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — noninferiority to epoetin alfa (DREAM-D, n=392) and to darbepoetin (DREAM-ND, n=588) on haemoglobin, with more Hb responders on desidustat in both and a dose-related phase 2 signal; haemoglobin is a surrogate throughout, both phase 3 trials were open-label and 24 weeks, and the programme is single-region (India; not FDA/EMA-approved)

title: Leflunomide in lupus nephritis: comparable to azathioprine for maintenance and to cyclophosphamide for induction in Chinese trials — never superior, with teratogenicity and hepatotoxicity leading the harm side
question: In adults with lupus nephritis, does leflunomide, compared with cyclophosphamide for induction or azathioprine for maintenance (each with glucocorticoids), achieve and sustain renal remission?
balance: The randomised evidence, all from China and all with glucocorticoids in both arms, shows leflunomide performing comparably to the standard it was tested against — not better. As maintenance after cyclophosphamide induction, kidney flares occurred in 15.7% on leflunomide versus 17.8% on azathioprine over 36 months (time to flare 16 vs 14 months, p=0.676), with similar adverse-event incidence (56.5% vs 58.9%). As induction in proliferative lupus nephritis, complete remission at 24 weeks was 23% on leflunomide versus 27% on cyclophosphamide and partial remission 56% versus 42% — neither difference significant. A small prospective study in refractory disease (n=20, no comparator) and a 2005 multicentre controlled trial (n=51) point the same general way without adding comparative weight. The harm side must lead with leflunomide's class warnings — teratogenicity and hepatotoxicity — which these trials are too small and short to quantify. The CIST combined-immunosuppression trial (PMID 30488367) is NOT counted here: its oral agent was mycophenolate, azathioprine or leflunomide at clinician choice, so it is not a leflunomide report. Lupus nephritis homes for other agents (obinutuzumab live #1819, anifrolumab pack #6975) are cross-pointed, not re-carded. Proposed stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — randomised trials from a single region (China) show leflunomide comparable to azathioprine for maintenance (kidney flares 15.7% vs 17.8%) and to cyclophosphamide for induction (complete remission 23% vs 27%), never superior; supporting reports are a single-arm refractory study (N=20, labelled, not load-bearing) and a 2005 controlled trial (n=51); teratogenicity and hepatotoxicity warnings lead the harm side

title: Mizoribine in lupus nephritis: one phase 3 trial (n=250) found it noninferior to IV cyclophosphamide (remission 66.1% vs 76.8%); older Japanese reports are small and uncontrolled
question: In adults with lupus nephritis, does the oral purine-synthesis inhibitor mizoribine, compared with intravenous cyclophosphamide (and in earlier Japanese reports, as pulse or long-term therapy), induce and maintain renal remission?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), as a noninferior alternative to intravenous cyclophosphamide — not as a superior treatment. The entire comparative base is one modern open-label phase 3 randomised trial from China (n=250 randomised): at 52 weeks total remission was 66.1% on oral mizoribine versus 76.8% on intravenous cyclophosphamide (relative risk ratio 0.861, 95% CI 0.729 to 1.016), which met the prespecified noninferiority margin of 0.726, with similar rates of treatment-related adverse events (80.5% vs 78.7%). The supporting Japanese reports are small and uncontrolled: weekly pulse therapy in refractory disease (n=17), long-term maintenance (n=10, exactly at the reference floor), and one sub-floor pilot (N=6, printed on its card and never load-bearing). Single-region programme (China/Japan; mizoribine is not FDA/EMA-approved for lupus nephritis) — flagged on the face. The mizoribine/tacrolimus multitarget cohort is a combination study and is not carded here.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one open-label phase 3 randomised trial (n=250) found oral mizoribine noninferior, not superior, to intravenous cyclophosphamide for lupus nephritis induction (total remission 66.1% vs 76.8%); the remaining base is small uncontrolled Japanese reports (n=17, n=10 and a labelled sub-floor N=6), and the programme is single-region (China/Japan)

title: Chiglitazar in type 2 diabetes: three phase 3 trials lowered HbA1c (placebo-adjusted −0.87% to −1.05%; noninferior to sitagliptin; added benefit on metformin) — surrogate endpoint, China only
question: In adults with type 2 diabetes, does the PPAR pan-agonist (α/γ/δ) chiglitazar, compared with placebo, sitagliptin, or added to metformin, improve glycaemic control (CMAP / CMAS / RECAM programme)?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) for glycaemic control, on three consistent phase 3 trials — with two limits printed on the face: HbA1c is a surrogate endpoint throughout, and the evidence is single-region (China; chiglitazar is approved there and not FDA/EMA-approved), with no cardiovascular-outcomes trial. CMAP (n=535): placebo-adjusted HbA1c reductions of −0.87% (32 mg) and −1.05% (48 mg) at 24 weeks. CMAS (n=739): chiglitazar was noninferior to sitagliptin 100 mg (HbA1c −1.40% and −1.47% vs −1.39%). RECAM (n=533): added to metformin, HbA1c fell −0.91% and −1.14% versus −0.49% on placebo. The recurring harms are the glitazar-pattern ones seen in the trials: slight weight gain and mild oedema. Chiglitazar is a single-source product (Chipscreen) — named here under the clarification exception. The wider glitazone/glitazar class history is cross-pointed, not re-carded.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — three phase 3 randomised trials (n=535, 739, 533) consistently showed chiglitazar lowered HbA1c versus placebo, was noninferior to sitagliptin, and added benefit on metformin, with slight weight gain and mild oedema; the stamp is for glycaemic control only — HbA1c is a surrogate, the evidence is single-region (China), and no cardiovascular-outcomes trial exists

title: Avexitide for post-bariatric hypoglycaemia: small phase 2 reports only (n=18, 16 completers, n=19) — glucose nadir rose a relative 21–26% vs placebo in PREVENT; no phase 3 evidence
question: In adults with post-bariatric (post-surgical) hypoglycaemia, does the GLP-1-receptor antagonist avexitide (exendin 9-39), compared with placebo, raise glucose nadir and reduce hypoglycaemic events?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — based on a very small total evidence base (n=18, 16 completers and n=19 across three short phase 2 reports; every N is printed on the face). Avexitide, a GLP-1-receptor antagonist, consistently raised glucose nadir and reduced hypoglycaemic events over treatment periods of 3 to 28 days: in the placebo-controlled crossover PREVENT trial (n=18 women) the glucose nadir rose by a relative 21% (30 mg twice daily) and 26% (60 mg once daily) versus placebo; in the phase 2b study (16 completers, broader post-surgical population) diurnal Level 2 events fell by a relative 47.7% and 59.0% versus a baseline run-in — not versus placebo. Two of the three reports enrolled women only. There is no approved therapy for post-bariatric hypoglycaemia and no phase 3 results are carded — all phase 3 claims are fenced. Avexitide is a single-source investigational product, named under the clarification exception.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — based on a very small evidence base (n=18, 16 completers and n=19; three short phase 2 reports, treatment 3–28 days): avexitide consistently raised glucose nadir and reduced hypoglycaemic events, including against placebo in the n=18 PREVENT crossover, but there is no phase 3 or long-term evidence and two reports enrolled women only

title: Eldecalcitol in osteoporosis: ONE phase 3 trial (n=1,054) in three reports — vertebral fractures 13.4% vs 17.5% versus alfacalcidol, an active comparator (no placebo trial)
question: In adults with osteoporosis, does the active vitamin D3 analogue eldecalcitol, compared with alfacalcidol, reduce vertebral and non-vertebral fractures?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) versus an active comparator — on a ONE-TRIAL programme, printed on the face: all three carded reports are publications of a single Japanese phase 3 trial of 1,054 patients (the primary report plus two post-hoc analyses), so the trial base is one, however many reports it generated. In that trial, eldecalcitol 0.75 μg daily reduced incident vertebral fractures versus alfacalcidol 1.0 μg daily over 3 years (13.4% vs 17.5%; hazard ratio 0.74, a relative measure). The post-hoc reports add WHO-defined fragility fractures (18.6% vs 25.2%; hazard ratio 0.70, relative) and severe vertebral fractures (3.8% vs 6.7%). The comparator is another active vitamin D analogue, not placebo, so this is a within-class comparison. Increases in serum and urinary calcium were more frequent on eldecalcitol — hypercalcaemia monitoring is the class harm. Single-region evidence (Japan; approved there).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single phase 3 trial (n=1,054, Japan) reported in three publications (primary plus two post-hoc analyses, labelled as one programme) found eldecalcitol reduced vertebral fractures versus the active comparator alfacalcidol (13.4% vs 17.5%; hazard ratio 0.74, relative), with more frequent increases in serum and urinary calcium; there is no placebo comparison and no second trial

title: Benralizumab in hypereosinophilic syndrome: NATRON phase 3 (n=133) cut first-flare hazard (HR 0.35, relative); phase 2 programme (n=20) with follow-up to 10.1 years — two programmes
question: In patients with FIP1L1::PDGFRA-negative hypereosinophilic syndrome, does benralizumab (anti-IL-5 receptor α, 30 mg every 4 weeks) versus placebo, added to background therapy, reduce disease flares and allow background-therapy tapering?
balance: LIKELY (benefit), on a base of TWO programmes, labelled as such (per the assembly adjudication): Programme 1 — NATRON, the phase 3 randomised trial (n=133), in which benralizumab 30 mg every 4 weeks added to background therapy reduced the hazard of a first HES flare versus placebo (hazard ratio 0.35, 95% CI 0.18 to 0.69 — a relative effect) over 24 weeks, with similar adverse-event rates (64.2% vs 66.7%). Programme 2 — the small phase 2 randomised trial (n=20) in which 90% versus 30% achieved at least a 50% eosinophil-count reduction at week 12, plus its long-term report: 14 of the 20 followed on open-label extension, with eosinophil suppression sustained and 10 participants treated for at least 8 years (maximum exposure 10.1 years). Mepolizumab in HES is a different drug with its own home (pack #6982) — cross-pointed, not re-carded. The NATRON erratum is not carded.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — the NATRON phase 3 trial (n=133) showed benralizumab added to background therapy reduced the hazard of a first HES flare versus placebo (hazard ratio 0.35, relative) with similar adverse-event rates, supported by a separate small phase 2 programme (n=20) and its long-term extension (14 followed, exposure up to 10.1 years); the base is two programmes, not three trials

title: Beraprost in pulmonary arterial hypertension: SPLIT — walk benefit at 12 weeks in one trial (n=130), but the 12-month trial's (n=116) benefit attenuated and was gone by 9–12 months
question: In adults with pulmonary arterial hypertension (WHO/NYHA functional class II–III), does oral beraprost sodium versus placebo improve exercise capacity and delay disease progression?
balance: SPLIT. The two randomised trials disagree in time-frame and durability. The European 12-week trial (n=130) found beraprost improved exercise capacity versus placebo (difference in mean change in 6-minute walk distance 25.1 m, 95% CI 1.8 to 48.3). The US 12-month trial (n=116) found less disease progression at 6 months and better walk distance at 3 and 6 months, but the effect attenuated and was not evident at 9 or 12 months. The third card is a network meta-analysis of the prostacyclin-analogue class (epoprostenol, treprostinil, iloprost and beraprost pooled) — it is a class synthesis, NOT a third beraprost trial, and within it beraprost's own signal was a higher withdrawal probability versus iloprost. A second prostacyclin network meta-analysis that has been withdrawn is deliberately NOT carded (fenced). Beraprost is licensed for PAH in Japan and parts of Asia, not in the US/EU — printed on the face. Other prostacyclin-pathway drugs (selexipag, treprostinil, ralinepag) have their own homes and are cross-pointed, not re-carded.
stamp: SPLIT — the European 12-week trial (n=130) showed a walk-distance benefit for beraprost versus placebo, but the US 12-month trial (n=116) found benefits only at 3–6 months, not at 9–12 months; the network meta-analysis carded here is a prostacyclin-class pool, not a third beraprost trial, and the withdrawn prostacyclin network meta-analysis is fenced and not carded

title: Inhaled levofloxacin in cystic fibrosis: SPLIT — FEV1 and Pseudomonas density improved and noninferior to tobramycin, but the placebo phase 3 trial (n=330) missed its exacerbation endpoint
question: In people with cystic fibrosis (≥12 years in the phase 3 trials) and chronic Pseudomonas aeruginosa airway infection, does levofloxacin inhalation solution (240 mg twice daily, 28-day cycles) versus placebo — or versus tobramycin inhalation solution — improve lung function and delay exacerbation?
balance: SPLIT. Levofloxacin inhalation solution (the tested product — development names MP-376 / APT-1026, marketed in the EU as Quinsair; named under the clarification exception) reduced sputum Pseudomonas density and improved FEV1 in the phase 2 trial (n=151), and was noninferior to tobramycin inhalation solution on FEV1 in a phase 3 trial (n=282), with an open-label extension (n=88) showing continued tolerability. But the placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (n=330) MISSED its primary endpoint — there was no statistically significant difference in time to exacerbation versus placebo — although FEV1 % predicted improved (mean difference 1.31%). Dysgeusia (taste distortion) was the most frequent adverse event in both phase 3 trials. The shelf therefore supports a lung-function / bacterial-density effect and comparability with inhaled tobramycin, not an exacerbation-prevention claim. Tobramycin and dornase alfa in CF have their own homes and are cross-pointed, not re-carded.
stamp: SPLIT — levofloxacin inhalation solution improved FEV1 and sputum Pseudomonas density (phase 2, n=151) and was noninferior to tobramycin inhalation solution (phase 3, n=282), but the placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (n=330) missed its primary endpoint of time to exacerbation; dysgeusia was the most frequent adverse event

title: Laninamivir for influenza treatment: single inhaled dose noninferior to 5-day oseltamivir in three Japanese trials (73.0 vs 73.6 hours in adults) — treatment only, Japan only
question: In children and adults with influenza, is a single inhaled dose of laninamivir octanoate non-inferior to a 5-day course of oseltamivir for time to illness alleviation?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) versus oseltamivir — that is what these noninferiority trials were designed to show, and they showed it: a single inhaled dose of laninamivir octanoate gave times to illness alleviation similar to a 5-day course of oral oseltamivir in adults (median 73.0 hours on laninamivir 40 mg vs 73.6 hours on oseltamivir, n=996 analysed) and in patients with chronic respiratory diseases (64.7 vs 59.7 hours, n=201 analysed). The paediatric trial (184 children analysed) found an advantage only against oseltamivir-resistant A(H1N1)2009 virus (a 2009-era context, printed on the card), with no significant differences for A(H3N2) or B. This shelf is confined to TREATMENT: the laninamivir post-exposure-prophylaxis programme is a separate question and is deliberately NOT folded in. Laninamivir is licensed in Japan only, and all three trials are Japanese, oseltamivir-controlled noninferiority designs. Other influenza antivirals (baloxavir, peramivir, oseltamivir itself) have their own homes and are cross-pointed, not re-carded.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — three Japanese noninferiority trials (996, 184 and 201 patients analysed) found a single inhaled dose of laninamivir gave times to illness alleviation similar to a 5-day oseltamivir course in adults, children and patients with chronic respiratory disease; treatment question only, the prophylaxis programme is deliberately not folded in, and laninamivir is licensed in Japan only

title: High-dose rifampicin in pulmonary TB: SPLIT — faster culture conversion (35 mg/kg HR 1.78, relative) but 50 mg/kg intolerable and 4-month high-dose regimens failed noninferiority in RIFASHORT
question: In adults with newly diagnosed rifampicin-susceptible pulmonary tuberculosis, does rifampicin at doses above the standard 10 mg/kg (20–35 mg/kg, or fixed 1200–1800 mg/day in shortened regimens) versus standard dosing improve culture conversion and treatment success without unacceptable toxicity?
balance: SPLIT, with the three design limbs kept separate. (1) Dose-ranging / bactericidal-activity limb: in PanACEA HIGHRIF1's final cohorts, early bactericidal activity rose with dose, but 50 mg/kg was not tolerated (all 17 patients had adverse events; 11 withdrew or stopped) while 40 mg/kg (n=15) was selected for further study — small cohorts, Ns printed on the card, and a surrogate endpoint. (2) Regimen-selection limb: in the PanACEA multi-arm multi-stage trial (n=365), 35 mg/kg rifampicin speeded liquid-media culture conversion versus standard dosing (median 48 vs 62 days; adjusted hazard ratio 1.78, a relative measure), with no difference on solid media. (3) Treatment-shortening limb — the outcome that matters: RIFASHORT (672 enrolled) found 4-month regimens with rifampicin 1200 mg or 1800 mg/day FAILED to meet noninferiority against the 6-month standard (favourable responses 93% control vs 90% and 87%), though grade 3–4 adverse events were similar (about 4% in each group). The meta-analysis card (8 RCTs, 1,897 subjects) is a synthesis card, not a primary trial: week-8 culture conversion was higher with high doses (83.7% vs 80.6%; relative risk 1.06, relative) with no significant difference in treatment failure. Faster culture conversion has not translated into a proven shorter or more successful regimen. Intensified rifampicin in tuberculous meningitis is a different population and question (pack #1707) — cross-pointed, not re-carded.
stamp: SPLIT — high-dose rifampicin speeds sputum culture conversion (PanACEA 35 mg/kg hazard ratio 1.78, relative; meta-analysis of 8 RCTs: week-8 conversion relative risk 1.06, relative) and 40 mg/kg was tolerable in small cohorts, but 50 mg/kg was not tolerated (n=17) and RIFASHORT's 4-month high-dose regimens failed noninferiority versus 6-month standard treatment, so no shorter or more effective regimen is proven

title: Certolizumab pegol in Crohn's disease (PRECISE): modest response gain, no remission difference in PRECISE 1; maintained response 63% vs 36% in responders in PRECISE 2
question: In adults with moderate-to-severe Crohn's disease, does certolizumab pegol (400 mg subcutaneous) versus placebo induce response and maintain response/remission, including after prior loss of response to infliximab?
balance: POSSIBLE benefit — modest in unselected patients, clearer in responders. PRECISE 1 (662 randomised): response 35% vs 27% at week 6 and 23% vs 16% at weeks 6 and 26, with NO significant remission difference. PRECISE 2 (428 of 668 induction patients who responded, re-randomised — responder-enriched): maintained response 63% vs 36% and remission 48% vs 29% through week 26. WELCOME (infliximab-experienced; dose-interval comparison, no placebo) showed quality-of-life gains, and PRECISE 4 showed uncontrolled recapture after relapse. title: Mongersen in Crohn's disease: a failed programme — phase 2 remission 55-65% vs 10% was not reproduced in phase 3 (22.8% vs 25% on placebo); batch controversy on the face
question: In adults with active Crohn's disease, does mongersen (GED-0301, oral SMAD7 antisense oligonucleotide) versus placebo induce clinical remission?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — a failed programme, presented as failed. The phase 2 trial reported striking day-15 remission after only 2 weeks of treatment (55% at 40 mg, 65% at 160 mg, versus 10% on placebo), but the phase 3 trial (701 randomised, terminated for futility) found week-12 remission of 22.8% on mongersen versus 25% on placebo, with placebo ahead on endoscopic response. title: Budesonide MMX in mild-to-moderate ulcerative colitis: remission 17.9% and 17.4% vs 7.4% and 4.5% on placebo — a real benefit, but absolute remission under 18%
question: In adults with active mild-to-moderate ulcerative colitis, does once-daily budesonide MMX 9 mg versus placebo induce combined clinical and endoscopic remission at 8 weeks?
balance: LIKELY benefit, but small in absolute terms — stated plainly. CORE I: week-8 remission 17.9% on budesonide MMX 9 mg versus 7.4% on placebo. stamp: LIKELY (benefit, small absolute gain) — budesonide MMX 9 mg induced remission in 17.9% (CORE I) and 17.4% (CORE II) versus 7.4% and 4.5% on placebo: absolute remission under 18%, gains of about 10-13 percentage points; 6 mg ineffective

title: Omega-3 for Crohn's maintenance: positive in the small 1996 trial (relapse 28% vs 69%), negative in the large EPIC trials — the split that decides the shelf
question: In patients with Crohn's disease in remission at high risk of relapse, does enteric-coated omega-3 free fatty acid / fish-oil supplementation versus placebo prolong remission?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) on the large trials, with a visible era split. title: Latiglutenase in coeliac disease: challenge trials suggest mucosal protection, but the 494-patient symptomatic trial was negative — a split record
question: In adults with coeliac disease on a gluten-free diet, does latiglutenase (ALV003 / IMGX003, oral mixture of two recombinant gluten-specific proteases) versus placebo protect against gluten-induced mucosal injury and symptoms — during controlled gluten challenge, and in symptomatic patients on a gluten-free diet?
balance: SPLIT. The two gluten-challenge trials (n=41 and n=50; 2 g/day gluten, 6 weeks) show mucosal-protection signals on the surrogate villus-height/crypt-depth endpoint — clear in 2014, with the 2022 trial's primary endpoint at P=.057. The one large real-world trial — 494 symptomatic patients on a gluten-free diet — was NEGATIVE on its primary histology endpoint, with no symptom advantage either. The seropositive-subgroup symptom report is a post-hoc analysis of that negative trial and is labelled as such. ALV003 and IMGX003 are the same enzyme mixture under successive names.
stamp: SPLIT — small gluten-challenge trials show mucosal protection on a surrogate endpoint (2014 positive; 2022 primary endpoint P=.057), but the large symptomatic-patient trial (n=494) was negative on its primary endpoint, and the seropositive symptom signal is post-hoc

title: Growth hormone in short bowel syndrome: small trials (n=41, 12, 10) show short-term PN and absorption gains — Cochrane calls the evidence inconclusive
question: In adults with short bowel syndrome dependent on parenteral nutrition, does recombinant human growth hormone — alone, or combined with glutamine and a high-carbohydrate/low-fat diet — versus placebo increase intestinal absorption and reduce parenteral-nutrition requirements?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence). Small trials throughout — every N printed on the face: Byrne 2005 (n=41) found GH-containing regimens reduced PN volume more than glutamine + diet at 4 weeks, with only GH + glutamine + diet holding the gain at 3 months, and its design cannot separate GH from glutamine/diet in the combination arm; Séguy 2003 (n=12, crossover) found absorption gains; Ellegård 1997 (n=10, at the floor exactly) found body-composition gains but null absorption endpoints; a sub-floor n=8 crossover is carded as a labelled limb only, never load-bearing. The Cochrane review calls the evidence inconclusive, with effects short-lived after treatment stops. Endpoints are short-term (3-8 weeks); no long-term PN-independence or survival claim.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — small trials only (n=41; crossover n=12; crossover n=10 at the floor; one labelled sub-floor n=8 limb): short-term PN/absorption gains, Cochrane verdict inconclusive, effects short-lived after stopping

title: Sphincterotomy for sphincter of Oddi dysfunction: benefit only in manometry-verified stenosis in small older trials; EPISOD found sham better in unselected patients
question: In adults with biliary-type pain after cholecystectomy attributed to sphincter of Oddi dysfunction, does endoscopic sphincterotomy versus sham sphincterotomy reduce pain and pain-related disability — and does sphincter manometry predict who benefits?
balance: SPLIT — by era and population, and that split is the answer. The 1989 and 2000 trials randomised manometry-characterised patients and found benefit only with elevated basal pressure / manometric stenosis (small subgroups: 10/11 vs 3/12; 11/13 vs 5/13), and none at normal pressure. EPISOD (2014, n=214) randomised unselected suspected type III dysfunction irrespective of manometry and found sphincterotomy WORSE than sham (success 23% vs 37%) with no predictive value for manometry. The 2024 Cochrane review (4 trials, 433 participants) rates all outcomes very low certainty. ERCP/sphincterotomy carries a real pancreatitis risk (11-15% in EPISOD, both arms).
stamp: SPLIT — sphincterotomy benefited only manometry-verified stenosis in two small older trials (n=47, n=81), while EPISOD (n=214, unselected suspected dysfunction) found it worse than sham (23% vs 37% success) and manometry non-predictive; Cochrane certainty very low

title: Ramosetron in IBS-D: stool consistency 50.3% vs 19.6% in men (5 µg), global improvement 50.7% vs 32.0% in women (2.5 µg) — sex-specific dosing, PARTIAL to pack #2772
question: In adults with diarrhoea-predominant irritable bowel syndrome, does ramosetron (5 µg daily in men; 2.5 µg daily in women) versus placebo improve stool consistency and global IBS symptoms?
balance: LIKELY benefit in the populations tested — PARTIAL shelf (home for the class question: pack #2772). Men's phase 3 (n=296, 5 µg): improved stool consistency 50.3% vs 19.6% on placebo (relative risk 2.57, labelled relative). Women's phase 3 (n=576, 2.5 µg): global improvement 50.7% vs 32.0% (relative risk 1.58). The women's dose-finding trial (n=409) is why dosing is sex-specific: 2.5 µg, not 5 µg, was effective and least harmful in women. A ramosetron-specific meta-analysis (4 RCTs, 1,623 participants) pools relative risks of 1.41-1.72 across outcomes. Pack #2772 (ondansetron in IBS-D) cards a class-level 5-HT3 meta-analysis with ramosetron as a pooled limb — cross-pointed here, NOT re-carded. All primary trials are Japanese, 12-week, Rome III; constipation is the main harm, and the alosetron class history (ischaemic colitis) is context, not ramosetron evidence.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — ramosetron at sex-specific doses (5 µg men, 2.5 µg women) beat placebo in three Japanese phase 2/3 trials (stool consistency 50.3% vs 19.6% in men; global improvement 50.7% vs 32.0% in women) and a ramosetron-specific meta-analysis (relative risks 1.41-1.72); PARTIAL to pack #2772's class question, whose meta-analysis is not re-carded

title: Apraglutide in short bowel syndrome-intestinal failure (STARS, n=163): parenteral-support volume -25.5% vs -12.5% relative change — FLOOR-RISK, all supporting reports n≤9
question: In adults with short bowel syndrome and intestinal failure dependent on parenteral support, does once-weekly apraglutide (long-acting GLP-2 analogue) versus placebo reduce parenteral-support volume?
balance: POSSIBLE benefit — FLOOR-RISK, on the binding condition in the commissioning row. Only ONE report meets the floor: STARS phase 3 (n=163), where once-weekly apraglutide gave a mean relative change in weekly parenteral-support volume of -25.5% versus -12.5% on placebo at week 24 (P=.001), with the stoma subgroup at -25.6% versus -7.8% and ≥1 day/week off PS in 43.0% versus 27.5%; week-48 colon-in-continuity secondary endpoints were not significant. Every supporting report is sub-floor — n=8 (randomised crossover), n=8 (metabolic-balance), n=9 (colon-in-continuity cohort) — with those Ns printed on the face of each card and in the stamp. Built on the report-count rule (≥3 cardable reports, sub-floor labelled); if the developer requires ≥3 at-floor reports, this shelf demotes to Audit B. Parenteral-support volume is the endpoint; no mortality or enteral-autonomy claim beyond STARS' (non-significant) secondary results.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one phase 3 trial (n=163); all supporting reports n≤9 (n=8, n=8, n=9, printed on the face): STARS gave a mean relative parenteral-support volume change of -25.5% versus -12.5% at week 24; FLOOR-RISK — demotes to Audit B if the developer requires ≥3 at-floor reports

title: Navitoclax + ruxolitinib in myelofibrosis: spleen response 63.2% vs 31.5% in TRANSFORM-1 — but symptom score did not differ (P=.2852), with more cytopenia
question: In adults with myelofibrosis — JAK-inhibitor-naive, or with progression/suboptimal response on ruxolitinib — does adding the BCL-XL/BCL-2 inhibitor navitoclax to ruxolitinib, versus ruxolitinib alone (or versus continuing ruxolitinib), increase spleen-volume response, and does it improve symptoms?
balance: SPLIT, on one randomised trial plus single-arm phase 2. TRANSFORM-1 (252 randomised, JAK-inhibitor-naive): spleen response at week 24 was 63.2% versus 31.5% — a clear benefit — but mean total-symptom-score change did not differ significantly (-10.2 vs -11.6, P=.2852), and grade 3/4 thrombocytopenia (54.0% vs 19.2%) and neutropenia (40.3% vs 8.8%) were much more common with navitoclax. The symptom null is printed beside the spleen result, as the evidence requires. In patients progressing or responding suboptimally on ruxolitinib, the evidence is single-arm REFINE phase 2 only (n=34; SVR35 26.5% at week 24, reversible thrombocytopenia 88%, platelet-gated escalation); the combined REFINE + TRANSFORM-2 report was refused for an effectively empty PubMed abstract, so no randomised post-ruxolitinib comparison is carded. The naive and post-ruxolitinib slices are labelled and their response rates are not pooled.
stamp: SPLIT (benefit) for spleen-volume response / (no difference) for symptom score — TRANSFORM-1 randomised data show SVR35 63.2% vs 31.5% with a non-significant symptom-score difference (P=.2852) and more cytopenia; post-ruxolitinib evidence is single-arm phase 2 only

title: Zanubrutinib vs ibrutinib in Waldenstrom (ASPEN): primary endpoint non-significant — no complete responses, VGPR 28% vs 19% (P=.09); the difference is tolerability
question: In patients with symptomatic Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia, does the selective BTK inhibitor zanubrutinib, versus ibrutinib, deepen responses (complete + very good partial response) and improve tolerability?
balance: SPLIT, on a single programme (one trial, four reports). ASPEN's primary endpoint was non-significant: no complete responses in either arm and VGPR 28% versus 19% (P=.09) at the primary analysis, with major response rates 77% versus 78% — this shelf is not an efficacy win for either drug. The separation is tolerability over 44.4 months: atrial fibrillation/flutter 7.9% versus 23.5%, and less diarrhoea, hypertension and pneumonia with zanubrutinib, against more neutropenia (34.7% vs 20.4%). In MYD88 wild-type disease the evidence is a 26-patient single-arm zanubrutinib cohort (VGPR 27%, no complete responses). The CLL/SLL version of this comparison is homed separately at pack #6909.
stamp: SPLIT (no difference) on the primary efficacy endpoint / (benefit) on tolerability for zanubrutinib — ASPEN's primary endpoint was non-significant (VGPR 28% vs 19%, P=.09; no complete responses) while atrial fibrillation and several other adverse events were less common and neutropenia more common with zanubrutinib

title: Odronextamab in relapsed/refractory lymphoma: complete response 73.4% in follicular lymphoma, 31.5% in DLBCL — all single-arm (ELM-1/ELM-2)
question: In adults with relapsed or refractory follicular lymphoma or diffuse large B-cell lymphoma after at least 2 prior lines, does the CD20xCD3 bispecific antibody odronextamab, versus no concurrent control, produce objective and complete responses, including after CAR T-cell therapy?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), on an entirely single-arm base (GAP-E discipline: no concurrent control anywhere). ELM-2 follicular lymphoma (n=128): objective response 80.0%, complete response 73.4%, median progression-free survival 20.7 months. ELM-2 DLBCL (n=127): objective response 52.0%, complete response 31.5%. ELM-1 post-CAR-T DLBCL (n=60): objective response 48.3%, complete response 31.7%. Cytokine release syndrome affected roughly half of patients (almost always low grade with the 0.7/4/20 mg step-up) and infections were reported in 64.6% of the DLBCL cohort. stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single-arm, uncontrolled evidence only (ELM-1/ELM-2): complete response 73.4% in relapsed/refractory follicular lymphoma and 31.5% in DLBCL, with cytokine release syndrome in roughly half of patients; no randomised or comparative data exist

title: Lifileucel in advanced melanoma after checkpoint inhibition: response 31.4%, median response duration 36.5 months at 5 years — single-arm only
question: In patients with unresectable or metastatic melanoma progressed on anti-PD-1 therapy (and targeted therapy where appropriate), does one-time autologous tumour-infiltrating lymphocyte therapy with lifileucel, versus no concurrent control, produce objective responses, and how durable are they at 5 years?

title: Dostarlimab in dMMR rectal cancer: sustained complete response 68% at 12 months in AZUR-1 — organ preservation, single-arm evidence only
question: In patients with stage II-III mismatch-repair-deficient (dMMR) locally advanced rectal adenocarcinoma, does neoadjuvant single-agent dostarlimab for 6 months, versus standard chemoradiotherapy and surgery, produce sustained clinical complete responses that allow chemoradiation and surgery to be omitted?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), on single-arm evidence throughout (GAP-E discipline applied to this PARTIAL slice). In the expanded phase 2 rectal cohort, all 49 patients who completed 6 months of dostarlimab had a clinical complete response and 37 had a sustained response at 12 months; in the global AZUR-1 trial the sustained 12-month clinical complete response rate was 68% (76% counting pathological complete responses in operated patients), with no recurrences among complete responders at median follow-up 26.3 months. The claim is organ preservation in a biomarker-defined minority under protocol surveillance — response-guided omission of chemoradiotherapy and surgery — not proof that standard therapy is unnecessary. The endometrial-cancer dostarlimab question is homed at live #853.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single-arm, uncontrolled evidence only: sustained clinical complete response at 12 months in 37 of 49 completed rectal patients in the expanded phase 2 and 68% in AZUR-1, allowing omission of chemoradiation and surgery under surveillance; no randomised comparison exists

title: Camizestrant in ER-positive breast cancer: SERENA-6 switch at ESR1 emergence — progression-free survival 16.8 vs 9.2 months; SERENA-2 also positive

title: Imlunestrant in advanced breast cancer (EMBER-3): benefit only in ESR1-mutated disease as monotherapy; adding abemaciclib helps all comers at more toxicity
question: In patients with ER-positive, HER2-negative advanced breast cancer recurring or progressing on aromatase-inhibitor therapy (with or without a CDK4/6 inhibitor), does imlunestrant, versus standard endocrine monotherapy, prolong progression-free survival in ESR1-mutated and in all patients — and does adding abemaciclib beat imlunestrant alone?
balance: SPLIT, on a single programme (one trial, four reports). EMBER-3's monotherapy comparison is positive only where the biology predicts: ESR1-mutated disease (median progression-free survival 5.5 vs 3.8 months) and not in all patients (5.6 vs 5.5 months; hazard ratio 0.87, a relative measure; P=0.12). The combination comparison is positive in all comers (updated median progression-free survival 10.9 vs 5.5 months; hazard ratio 0.59, relative) but grade 3-or-higher events were 48.6% versus 17.1% for monotherapy. Interim overall survival in ESR1-mutated disease (34.5 vs 23.1 months; hazard ratio 0.60, relative) did not reach its significance boundary and is not claimed as a survival benefit. Product: imlunestrant (Inluriyo, Eli Lilly).
stamp: SPLIT (benefit) for imlunestrant in ESR1-mutated disease and for imlunestrant + abemaciclib in all patients / (no difference) for imlunestrant in the overall population — EMBER-3: monotherapy progression-free survival 5.5 vs 3.8 months in ESR1-mutated disease but hazard ratio 0.87 (P=0.12) overall; combination 10.9 vs 5.5 months with more grade 3+ toxicity

title: Niraparib + abiraterone in mCRPC (MAGNITUDE, prostate): progression delayed in BRCA/HRR-positive disease — final overall survival not different, futility without HRR alterations
question: In men with treatment-naive metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer and homologous-recombination-repair gene alterations (notably BRCA1/2), does niraparib plus abiraterone acetate + prednisone, versus placebo plus abiraterone + prednisone, prolong radiographic progression-free and overall survival?
balance: SPLIT, on a single programme (one trial, five reports). MAGNITUDE (prostate, NCT03748641 — not the nex-z ATTR trial of the same name) delayed radiographic progression in HRR-positive disease (16.5 vs 13.7 months; hazard ratio 0.73, a relative measure) and most in BRCA1/2 disease (16.6 vs 10.9 months; hazard ratio 0.53, relative), and delayed symptomatic progression and cytotoxic chemotherapy. But final overall survival did not differ (hazard ratio 0.931 in HRR-positive; 0.788 in BRCA1/2, nominal P=0.183), the HRR-negative cohort (n=247) was stopped for futility, and the FDA limited approval to BRCA-mutated disease, finding the broader HRR benefit was driven by that subgroup. Anaemia (including transfusion in 27%) and hypertension are the added harms. Benefit must not be generalised to unselected mCRPC.
stamp: SPLIT (benefit) on radiographic progression-free survival in BRCA/HRR-positive disease / (no difference) on final overall survival — MAGNITUDE: rPFS 16.6 vs 10.9 months in BRCA1/2 disease (hazard ratio 0.53, relative) but final OS hazard ratio 0.931 in HRR-positive disease, with futility in HRR-negative disease and approval limited to BRCA-mutated disease

title: TALAPRO-2: talazoparib + enzalutamide prolongs survival in first-line mCRPC — benefit concentrated in HRR-deficient disease (OS 45.1 vs 31.1 months), priced in anaemia
question: In men with asymptomatic or mildly symptomatic first-line metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer, does talazoparib plus enzalutamide, versus placebo plus enzalutamide, prolong radiographic progression-free and overall survival — in all comers and in HRR-deficient disease — and at what cost in anaemia and treatment burden?
balance: LIKELY (benefit), on a single-programme base — one phase 3 trial, TALAPRO-2, reported for two overlapping populations. In all comers (805 randomised), talazoparib + enzalutamide improved radiographic PFS (median not reached vs 21.9 months at primary analysis; hazard ratio 0.63, relative) and, at the final analysis, overall survival (median 45.8 vs 37.0 months; hazard ratio 0.80, relative). In HRR-deficient disease (399 randomised) the effects were larger: radiographic PFS hazard ratio 0.45 and final overall survival 45.1 vs 31.1 months (hazard ratio 0.62, relative), with BRCA1/2-altered patients showing 4-year survival of 53% vs 23%. In HRR-non-deficient/unknown disease the survival hazard ratio was 0.88 and not significant, and the US FDA limited approval to HRR gene-mutated disease — keep the all-comer and HRR-deficient claims separate. The price is anaemia: grade 3–4 in about 41–49% on the combination, transfusion in about 36–39%, dose reduction in about half. The MAGNITUDE question (niraparib + abiraterone) is the parallel PARP shelf — cross-point, do not merge.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — one phase 3 randomised trial (TALAPRO-2) showed talazoparib + enzalutamide improved radiographic PFS and final overall survival versus enzalutamide alone in first-line mCRPC, with the survival benefit concentrated in HRR-deficient (especially BRCA1/2) disease (HRR-deficient OS 45.1 vs 31.1 months, HR 0.62 relative; all-comer OS 45.8 vs 37.0 months, HR 0.80 relative), at the cost of grade 3–4 anaemia in about 41–49%; the US approval is limited to HRR gene-mutated disease, and the HRR-non-deficient survival effect was not significant

title: CROWN: first-line lorlatinib vs crizotinib — median PFS still not reached at 7 years (5-year PFS 60% vs 8%) with near-complete intracranial protection
question: In patients with previously untreated advanced ALK-positive non-small-cell lung cancer, does lorlatinib, versus crizotinib, prolong progression-free survival and prevent intracranial progression, and at what cost in chronic toxicity?
balance: LIKELY (benefit), on a single-programme base — one phase 3 trial, CROWN (296 randomised). Lorlatinib versus crizotinib gave 12-month progression-free survival of 78% vs 39%, and the advantage proved exceptionally durable: median PFS was still not reached at 7 years versus 9.1 months on crizotinib (hazard ratio 0.19, a relative measure), with 5-year PFS 60% vs 8% and 7-year PFS 55% vs 3%. Intracranial progression was nearly abolished (time-to-intracranial-progression hazard ratio 0.06, relative; 12-month CNS progression 7% vs 72% in patients with baseline brain metastases). No completed overall-survival comparison exists in the fetched records. Two caveats price the claim: the comparator is crizotinib, a first-generation agent no longer the benchmark where alectinib or brigatinib are available (no head-to-head trial among later-generation agents exists), and lorlatinib's harms are chronic — hyperlipidaemia, oedema, weight gain, peripheral neuropathy and CNS effects (mood/cognition/speech), with grade 3–4 events in about three quarters of patients over 5 years but permanent discontinuation in only 11%. Cross-point: alectinib first-line is live #1833; brigatinib first-line is the ALTA-1L shelf.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — the single phase 3 CROWN trial showed first-line lorlatinib gave far more durable progression-free and intracranial control than crizotinib (median PFS not reached at 7 years vs 9.1 months; 5-year PFS 60% vs 8%, absolute rates printed), with chronic hyperlipidaemia, oedema, weight gain and CNS effects as the main harms; no completed overall-survival comparison exists yet, and crizotinib is a superseded first-generation comparator

title: ALTA-1L: first-line brigatinib vs crizotinib — PFS 24.0 vs 11.1 months and delayed quality-of-life worsening; no overall-survival advantage shown
question: In patients with advanced ALK-positive non-small-cell lung cancer who have not received an ALK inhibitor, does brigatinib, versus crizotinib, prolong progression-free survival and improve intracranial response, and at what harm?
balance: LIKELY (benefit), on a single-programme base — one phase 3 trial, ALTA-1L (275 randomised). Brigatinib 180 mg daily (after a 7-day 90 mg lead-in) versus crizotinib roughly doubled progression-free survival: final median 24.0 vs 11.1 months (hazard ratio 0.48, a relative measure), 3-year PFS 43% vs 19%, with higher intracranial response (78% vs 29% in measurable lesions) and delayed worsening of global quality of life (median 26.7 vs 8.3 months to worsening). Overall survival was not significantly different (hazard ratio 0.81; medians not reached). The defining harm is early-onset pulmonary events — the dose lead-in exists because of them and is part of the tested intervention; the fetched abstract records do not quantify those events, so no rate is printed. Same caveat as CROWN: the comparator is crizotinib, a first-generation agent no longer the benchmark where alectinib or lorlatinib are available, and there is no head-to-head trial among the later-generation agents. Cross-points: lorlatinib first-line is the CROWN shelf; alectinib first-line is live #1833.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — the single phase 3 ALTA-1L trial showed first-line brigatinib (90 mg lead-in, then 180 mg) prolonged progression-free survival versus crizotinib (final median 24.0 vs 11.1 months; 3-year PFS 43% vs 19%) and delayed quality-of-life worsening, without a significant overall-survival difference; early-onset pulmonary events are the defining harm behind the lead-in, and crizotinib is a superseded first-generation comparator

title: MET exon 14 NSCLC: capmatinib and tepotinib each respond in roughly half of patients — two single-arm programmes, no randomised evidence
question: In patients with advanced non-small-cell lung cancer harbouring a MET exon 14 skipping mutation, do the selective MET inhibitors capmatinib or tepotinib, versus no concurrent control, produce objective responses, in treatment-naïve and previously treated disease?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — on an entirely uncontrolled base, stated plainly: this shelf rests on two single-arm phase 2 programmes with no concurrent comparator for either drug. Capmatinib (GEOMETRY mono-1) produced responses in 68% of treatment-naïve and 41–44% of previously treated patients with MET exon 14-skipping NSCLC (160 such patients at final analysis). Tepotinib (VISION) produced responses in 46% at its primary report and 51.4% overall at long-term follow-up in 313 patients (57.3% treatment-naïve, 45.0% previously treated), with median response durations up to 18.0 months. Response in a biomarker-selected, uncontrolled population supports possible benefit but cannot establish a survival effect or rank the two drugs against each other. Peripheral oedema is the class-defining harm (47–67% across the programmes; grade 3-or-worse in 11.2% on tepotinib at long-term follow-up). The MET-amplified cohorts of GEOMETRY mono-1 are a different biomarker question — cross-point only, not carded here.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — based entirely on single-arm, uncontrolled phase 2 programmes (GEOMETRY mono-1 for capmatinib, VISION for tepotinib) in MET exon 14-skipping NSCLC: response rates of 41–68% (capmatinib) and 45–57% (tepotinib) by treatment line, with no randomised comparator, no survival comparison, and no basis for ranking the two drugs; peripheral oedema is the class harm
