title: TRIDENT-1: repotrectinib responds in 79% of TKI-naïve and 38% of previously treated ROS1-positive NSCLC — single-arm evidence, dizziness the defining harm
question: In patients with advanced ROS1 fusion-positive non-small-cell lung cancer, TKI-naïve or previously treated (including with the ROS1 G2032R resistance mutation), does repotrectinib, versus no concurrent control, produce objective and intracranial responses?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — on a single-arm, single-programme base, stated plainly: TRIDENT-1 has no concurrent control. Repotrectinib (Augtyro, Bristol Myers Squibb) produced responses in 56 of 71 TKI-naïve patients (79%; median duration of response 34.1 months) and 21 of 56 patients after one prior ROS1 TKI (38%; median duration 14.8 months) with ROS1 fusion-positive NSCLC, including 10 of 17 patients with the G2032R resistance mutation and responses in CNS metastases — enough for traditional FDA approval in November 2023, but uncontrolled response data cannot establish a survival effect or superiority over any other ROS1 inhibitor. The defining harms are neurological: dizziness (58%), dysgeusia (50%), paraesthesia, ataxia and cognitive effects, with dose interruption in 39% and reduction in 38% but discontinuation in only about 3%. Taletrectinib (separate shelf) asks the same question of a different agent with no head-to-head trial. TRIDENT-1's NTRK cohort is homed by cross-reference to the TRK question — not carded here.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — based on a single-arm, uncontrolled registrational programme (TRIDENT-1) in ROS1 fusion-positive NSCLC: response in 79% of TKI-naïve and 38% of previously treated patients, including activity against G2032R, with dizziness/ataxia as the defining harm; no randomised comparator exists, so no survival or superiority claim can be made

title: TRUST-I/II: taletrectinib responds in 88.8% of TKI-naïve and 55.8% of pretreated ROS1-positive NSCLC — single-arm evidence, no head-to-head trial
question: In patients with advanced ROS1-positive non-small-cell lung cancer, TKI-naïve or previously treated, does taletrectinib, versus no concurrent control, produce objective and intracranial responses?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — on a single-arm base throughout, stated plainly: TRUST-I and TRUST-II are both uncontrolled phase 2 trials of one programme. Taletrectinib (Ibtrozi, Nuvation Bio) produced confirmed responses in 88.8% of 160 TKI-naïve and 55.8% of 113 TKI-pretreated patients in the pooled analysis (intracranial responses 76.5% and 65.6%; G2032R responses in 8 of 13), with median response durations of 44.2 and 16.6 months, sustained at TRUST-I long-term follow-up. Harms are mainly gastrointestinal events and transaminase rises, with unusually infrequent neurological events for this class (dizziness 21–23%, mostly grade 1) and discontinuation in 5–6.5%. Uncontrolled response data cannot establish a survival effect. This shelf and the repotrectinib shelf ask the same clinical question of two different agents with NO head-to-head trial — cross-programme response-rate comparisons are not evidence of superiority for either drug.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — based on single-arm, uncontrolled phase 2 evidence only (TRUST-I and TRUST-II, pooled n=273) in ROS1-positive NSCLC: confirmed response in 88.8% of TKI-naïve and 55.8% of pretreated patients with durable and intracranial responses and low neurological toxicity; no randomised comparator and no head-to-head trial against repotrectinib exists, so no survival or superiority claim can be made

title: NTRK fusion tumours: larotrectinib and entrectinib respond across histologies — pooled 75–79% and 57–61%, but only 30% in primary CNS tumours; single-arm evidence
question: In adults and children with advanced solid tumours harbouring NTRK1/2/3 gene fusions, do the TRK inhibitors larotrectinib or entrectinib, versus no concurrent control, produce objective responses across tumour types, including primary CNS tumours?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — on single-arm, tumour-agnostic evidence throughout, with the histology spread printed rather than a single headline rate. Larotrectinib responded in 75% of 55 patients (17 tumour types, ages 4 months to 76 years) at its primary analysis and 79% of 153 evaluable patients in the pooled analysis — but in only 30% of 33 patients with primary CNS tumours (24-week disease control 73%). Entrectinib responded in 57% of 54 adults (10 tumour types, 19 histologies) and 61.2% of 121 adults in the updated analysis (14 types, at least 30 histologies; intracranial response 63.6% in 11 patients). Children are inside both programmes. Responses were often durable and toxicity mostly low-grade with no treatment-related deaths, but uncontrolled pooled response rates cannot establish a survival effect, cannot be promised to any individual histology, and cannot rank the two drugs. Repotrectinib's NTRK cohort is a cross-point only — not re-carded here.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — based entirely on single-arm, tumour-agnostic pooled analyses (larotrectinib: 75–79% response across 17 tumour types but 30% in primary CNS tumours; entrectinib: 57–61% across 10–14 tumour types), in adults and children, with no randomised comparator, no survival comparison, and no basis for ranking the two drugs or promising the pooled rate to any single histology

title: Sunvozertinib in EGFR exon 20 NSCLC: first-line PFS 10.3 vs 7.5 months vs chemotherapy in a randomised trial; pretreated evidence is single-arm only (response 46–61%)
question: In patients with locally advanced or metastatic NSCLC with EGFR exon 20 insertion mutations — after platinum chemotherapy, and as first-line therapy — does sunvozertinib, versus no concurrent control (pretreated) or versus platinum chemotherapy (first-line), produce objective responses and prolong progression-free survival?
balance: SPLIT — the base is two different kinds of evidence for two different slices, and they must not be merged. Pretreated disease: single-arm only — confirmed response 61% in WU-KONG6 (97 evaluable; China-generated, stated plainly) and 45.9% at 200 mg / 47.2% at 300 mg in the dose-randomised WU-KONG1B, which randomised dose, not treatment; that slice supports POSSIBLE at best. First-line disease: one phase 3 randomised trial showed sunvozertinib beat carboplatin–pemetrexed on progression-free survival (median 10.3 vs 7.5 months; hazard ratio 0.65, a relative measure; response 58.9% vs 31.1%), with overall survival immature and more grade 3-or-higher toxicity (75.5% vs 56.7%) — that slice is LIKELY (benefit) against chemotherapy, not against amivantamab-based therapy (homed at pack #5184). Defining harms: diarrhoea and rash, creatine-kinase rises and interstitial lung disease (5% serious in WU-KONG6). Class context only: mobocertinib was withdrawn after a failed confirmatory trial — context for caution about the uncontrolled slice, not evidence about this drug.
stamp: SPLIT — first-line: LIKELY (benefit) versus platinum chemotherapy on one phase 3 randomised trial (median PFS 10.3 vs 7.5 months, HR 0.65 relative, OS immature); pretreated: POSSIBLE (benefit) at best on single-arm evidence only (response 61% in China-only WU-KONG6 and about 46–47% in WU-KONG1B, which randomised dose rather than treatment), with diarrhoea, rash, creatine-kinase rises and interstitial lung disease as the harms

title: Beamion LUNG-1: zongertinib responds in 71% of pretreated and 76% of first-line HER2-mutant NSCLC — single-arm evidence; EGFR-type harms frequent but rarely severe
question: In patients with advanced HER2 (ERBB2)-mutant non-small-cell lung cancer — previously treated, including after HER2-directed antibody–drug conjugates, and as first-line therapy — does the HER2-selective tyrosine kinase inhibitor zongertinib, versus no concurrent control, produce objective responses?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — on a single-arm, single-programme base, stated plainly: Beamion LUNG-1 has no concurrent control at any line. Zongertinib (Hernexeos, Boehringer Ingelheim) produced confirmed responses in 71% of 75 previously treated patients with tyrosine-kinase-domain HER2 mutations at 120 mg (median duration 14.1 months), 48% of 31 patients after a HER2 antibody–drug conjugate, 30% of 20 with non-TKD mutations, and 76% of 74 first-line patients (median duration 15.2 months), with intracranial responses in 47% of 30 patients with active brain metastases. The HER2-selectivity claim is printed and tested, not just asserted: in phase Ia, diarrhoea occurred in 50% and rash in 16% — EGFR-type effects are present — but grade 3-or-worse rates were only 1% and 2%, and no drug-related interstitial lung disease occurred in the pretreated cohorts. Uncontrolled response data cannot establish a survival effect or rank this drug against HER2-directed antibody–drug conjugates (homed elsewhere — cross-point only).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — based on a single-arm, uncontrolled single programme (Beamion LUNG-1) in HER2-mutant NSCLC: confirmed response in 71% of pretreated TKD-mutant and 76% of first-line patients, with EGFR-type harms frequent but rarely severe in the printed phase Ia rates (diarrhoea 50%, grade 3-or-worse 1%; rash 16%, 2%); no randomised comparator exists, so no survival or superiority claim can be made

title: MARIPOSA: amivantamab + lazertinib beats osimertinib first-line — PFS 23.7 vs 16.6 months and 3-year survival 60% vs 51%, with grade 3+ toxicity in 80% vs 52%
question: In patients with previously untreated EGFR-mutated (exon 19 deletion or L858R) advanced NSCLC, does amivantamab plus lazertinib, versus osimertinib, prolong progression-free and overall survival, and at what added toxicity?
balance: LIKELY (benefit), on a single-programme base — one phase 3 trial, MARIPOSA (1,074 randomised 2:2:1), for the first-line exon 19 deletion / L858R question only (PARTIAL scope: EGFR exon 20 insertion disease is homed at pack #5184 and is not asked here). Amivantamab + lazertinib beat osimertinib on progression-free survival (median 23.7 vs 16.6 months; hazard ratio 0.70, a relative measure) and, at the protocol-specified final analysis, on overall survival (hazard ratio 0.75, relative; 3-year survival 60% vs 51% — the final report, fetched at build, supersedes the interim and Asian-subgroup survival reads). The lazertinib-alone arm showed lazertinib performs like osimertinib alone (hazard ratio 0.98), so the gain belongs to the combination. The price: grade 3-or-higher adverse events in 80% vs 52% — particularly skin-related events, venous thromboembolism (with its prophylactic-anticoagulation burden) and infusion-related events — and discontinuation of all agents for toxicity in 10% vs 3%. FLAURA2 (osimertinib + chemotherapy, pack #5183) is the competing intensification question — cross-point only; there is no head-to-head trial between the two intensifications.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — the single phase 3 MARIPOSA trial showed first-line amivantamab + lazertinib improved progression-free survival (23.7 vs 16.6 months) and final overall survival (HR 0.75 relative; 3-year survival 60% vs 51%) versus osimertinib in exon 19 deletion/L858R EGFR-mutated NSCLC, with the lazertinib-alone arm comparable to osimertinib alone, at the cost of grade 3-or-higher toxicity in 80% vs 52% including venous thromboembolism and infusion-related events

title: Adjuvant alectinib after resection of ALK-positive NSCLC (ALINA): 2-year disease-free survival 93.8% vs 63.0% on chemotherapy; overall survival immature
question: In patients with completely resected stage IB (≥4 cm)–IIIA ALK-positive non-small-cell lung cancer, does 24 months of adjuvant alectinib, versus platinum-based chemotherapy, improve disease-free and CNS disease-free survival, and at what cost in harms and quality of life? (PARTIAL scope: alectinib in metastatic ALK-positive NSCLC is homed at live #1833.)
balance: LIKELY (benefit), on a single-programme base — one phase 3 trial, ALINA (257 randomised), for the adjuvant question only (PARTIAL scope: alectinib in metastatic ALK-positive NSCLC is homed at live #1833 and is not asked here). Adjuvant alectinib 600 mg twice daily for 24 months markedly improved disease-free survival versus four cycles of platinum-based chemotherapy: in stage II–IIIA disease, 93.8% versus 63.0% were alive and disease-free at 2 years (hazard ratio 0.24 — a relative measure; the absolute rates are printed beside it), with the same hazard ratio in the full intention-to-treat population and a CNS disease-free-survival hazard ratio of 0.22 (relative). Overall survival was immature at the primary report and remained unreported in the 2026 companion reports carded here, so the claim is a recurrence claim, not yet a survival claim. Companion reports show quality of life improved and was maintained over the 2 years of treatment, with fewer discontinuations for adverse events than chemotherapy (5% vs 13%) but a long treatment exposure and characteristic laboratory harms (grade 3–4 creatine phosphokinase increase 6%).
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — single-programme evidence (ALINA, n=257): adjuvant alectinib for 24 months improved 2-year disease-free survival versus platinum chemotherapy (93.8% vs 63.0% in stage II–IIIA; hazard ratio 0.24, relative) with a CNS disease-free-survival advantage; overall survival was immature, so this is a recurrence benefit, not yet a proven survival benefit

title: Osimertinib after chemoradiotherapy in stage III EGFR-mutated NSCLC (LAURA): progression-free survival 39.1 vs 5.6 months; CNS progression 9% vs 36% at 12 months
question: In patients with unresectable stage III EGFR-mutated non-small-cell lung cancer without progression after definitive chemoradiotherapy, does osimertinib, versus placebo, prolong progression-free survival and prevent CNS progression, and at what cost in pneumonitis and other harms? (PARTIAL scope: adjuvant osimertinib is homed at live #763, first-line metastatic osimertinib at live #1832, and osimertinib plus chemotherapy at pack #5183.)
balance: LIKELY (benefit), on a single-programme base — one phase 3 trial, LAURA (216 randomised), for the post-chemoradiotherapy consolidation question only (PARTIAL scope: adjuvant osimertinib after resection is homed at live #763, first-line metastatic osimertinib at live #1832, and osimertinib plus chemotherapy at pack #5183 — none is re-carded here). Osimertinib until progression gave median progression-free survival of 39.1 versus 5.6 months on placebo (hazard ratio 0.16 — a relative measure; 74% vs 22% were progression-free at 12 months), with CNS progression markedly reduced (cumulative incidence at 12 months 9% vs 36%). Overall survival was interim and immature (20% maturity; hazard ratio 0.81, not significant; 36-month survival 84% vs 74%), so the proven claim is progression delay, not yet longer life. The comparator was placebo, not durvalumab consolidation (the PACIFIC standard, which many LAURA patients had not received) — the trial does not answer osimertinib versus durvalumab. Harms: grade 3-or-worse adverse events 35% vs 12%, radiation pneumonitis 48% vs 38% (mostly grade 1–2), and treatment discontinuation 13% vs 5% over a median exposure of 24.0 versus 8.3 months; patient-reported quality of life was maintained, with no substantial difference in time to deterioration.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — single-programme evidence (LAURA, n=216): osimertinib after chemoradiotherapy prolonged progression-free survival versus placebo (median 39.1 vs 5.6 months; hazard ratio 0.16, relative) and reduced CNS progression (12-month incidence 9% vs 36%); overall survival was interim and not significant, and the comparator was placebo, not durvalumab consolidation

title: Adjunctive cariprazine in major depression: SPLIT — two of four RCTs positive at one dose each (in opposite directions), two negative; no dose has won twice
question: In adults with major depressive disorder and inadequate response to antidepressant monotherapy, does adjunctive cariprazine (1.5–4.5 mg/day), versus adjunctive placebo, improve depressive symptoms (MADRS), response and remission — and at which dose? (PARTIAL scope: cariprazine's schizophrenia, bipolar and negative-symptom questions are homed at live #1430 and packs #2403, #3678, #3705 and #6381.)
balance: SPLIT, on four distinct randomised trials (PARTIAL scope: cariprazine in schizophrenia is homed at live #1430, in bipolar I depression at pack #2403, in mania at pack #3678, in bipolar maintenance at pack #3705 and for negative symptoms at pack #6381 — none is re-carded here). The four adjunctive-MDD trials disagree, and they disagree by dose in opposite directions: Durgam 2016 (n=819) found the higher flexible dose (2–4.5 mg/day) effective (MADRS least-squares mean difference −2.2 vs placebo) but not 1–2 mg/day; Sachs 2023 (mITT n=751) found 1.5 mg/day effective (−14.1 vs −11.5 MADRS change) but not 3.0 mg/day; Riesenberg 2023 (mITT n=750), a near-identical phase 3 design, found NEITHER 1.5 nor 3 mg/day significantly different from placebo; and Fava 2018 (n=231, phase 2, low doses 0.1–2.0 mg/day) found no significant effect at either dose. No dose has separated from placebo in more than one trial. The 2024 meta-analysis of these four trials pools a small average benefit (standardised mean difference −1.79 as printed in its abstract, with a variable magnitude of effects; response relative risk 1.21, relative; remission relative risk 0.99 — no difference). Added harms over antidepressant alone are consistent across trials: akathisia (up to 22.3% at 2–4.5 mg/day), restlessness, insomnia and nausea.
stamp: SPLIT — four distinct adjunctive-MDD randomised trials disagree: Durgam 2016 was positive only at 2–4.5 mg/day and Sachs 2023 only at 1.5 mg/day (opposite dose directions, no dose positive twice), while Riesenberg 2023 and Fava 2018 were negative at every dose tested; the pooled response relative risk is 1.21 (relative) with no remission benefit, and akathisia is the consistent added harm

title: Intrathecal ziconotide for severe refractory pain: all three (old, short) RCTs positive on pain scores — 53.1% vs 18.1% fast-titrated, 14.7% vs 7.2% slow-titrated — with CNS harms scaling with dose speed
question: In adults with severe chronic pain (malignant and non-malignant) refractory to conventional therapy including intrathecal opioids, does intrathecal ziconotide, versus placebo infusion, reduce pain intensity, and at what neuropsychiatric cost — and how does titration speed change both?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) for short-term pain reduction, at a substantial neuropsychiatric price — and the entire randomised base is three small, old, short trials (enrolment era 1996–2004), with no modern trial in existence. All three placebo-controlled trials found significantly greater pain-intensity (VASPI) reduction on intrathecal ziconotide: Staats 2004 (cancer/AIDS pain, fast titration) 53.1% vs 18.1% mean improvement; Wallace 2006 (nonmalignant pain, fast titration later dose-reduced for adverse events) 31.2% vs 6.0%; Rauck 2006 (slow titration to a low maximum dose) 14.7% vs 7.2% — the smallest effect, and the best tolerated. Titration speed is the shelf's central fact: the fast-titration trials bought larger pain reductions with heavy burdens of dizziness, confusion, ataxia, abnormal gait, memory impairment, nausea, urinary retention and other CNS effects, while slow titration shrank both benefit and harm. Treatment courses in these trials were days to three weeks — nothing in the randomised base speaks to long-term efficacy or safety.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) for short-term pain reduction — all three randomised trials (n=111, 255, 220; 1996–2004 era) found significantly greater VASPI improvement on intrathecal ziconotide than placebo, but courses were days to 3 weeks and CNS harms (confusion, ataxia, memory impairment, dizziness) scale with the titration speed that also scales the benefit; no long-term randomised evidence exists

title: Vornorexant in insomnia (FLOOR-RISK — exactly 2 patient reports): 2-week RCT showed ~10 min subjective latency gain vs placebo; 52-week open-label tolerability, Japan only
question: In adults with insomnia disorder, does the dual orexin receptor antagonist vornorexant (5–10 mg nightly), versus placebo, improve subjective sleep onset and maintenance, and is it safe over 52 weeks? (FLOOR-RISK: the patient-population base is exactly two reports, both from Japan.)
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) on a FLOOR-RISK base, stated plainly: the entire patient-population evidence for vornorexant (Vorzzz, Taisho) in insomnia is exactly TWO reports, both Japanese — one 2-week placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (n=596) and one 52-week open-label dose-randomised study (n=371) with no placebo arm. The phase 3 trial showed statistically significant but modest subjective benefits at week 2: sleep latency improved by least-squares mean differences of −10.6 minutes (5 mg) and −10.1 minutes (10 mg) versus placebo, and subjective sleep efficiency by +3.41% and +2.94%. The long-term study observed sustained diary improvements to 52 weeks (subjective latency changes of −31.8 and −44.0 minutes) with nasopharyngitis and somnolence as the commonest adverse events and no withdrawal or rebound signal in a 1-week placebo run-out — but without a control arm those long-term changes cannot be separated from expectancy and natural history. Vornorexant is approved in Japan; it is not FDA- or EMA-approved. A driving-simulator trial in healthy volunteers (cross-point card) found no clinically meaningful next-morning impairment at 10–20 mg. No phase 2 dose-finding report in insomnia patients could be verified, so the base stays at two patient reports.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — FLOOR-RISK, based on exactly 2 patient reports: one 2-week placebo-controlled phase 3 trial in Japanese insomnia patients (n=596) showed modest subjective gains (sleep latency −10.6 and −10.1 min vs placebo at 5 and 10 mg), and one 52-week open-label study (n=371) showed tolerability without a control arm; the drug is approved in Japan only

title: Surgical antibiotic prophylaxis DURATION: a single preoperative dose matched multiple/prolonged doses at every tested site (gastric, bypass, colorectal, caesarean, orthopaedic)
question: In adults undergoing surgery, does a single preoperative dose of antibiotic prophylaxis prevent surgical-site infection as effectively as multiple-dose or prolonged postoperative prophylaxis — answered per surgical site (gastric, colorectal, coronary bypass, orthopaedic, caesarean) — and what is saved in adverse effects and resistance pressure? (DURATION only: prophylaxis TIMING is homed at pack #5749.)
balance: LIKELY (no difference) — carded PER SURGICAL SITE, never as one pooled claim, and cross-pointing the separate TIMING question (when the dose is given) to pack #5749, which is not re-carded here. At every site with a direct randomised comparison, a single preoperative dose prevented surgical-site infection as well as multiple or prolonged doses: gastric cancer surgery (SSI 9.5% single vs 8.6% multiple, n=486 analysed), coronary bypass (sternal infection 14% vs 13% and donor-site 38% vs 39% as reported in 1994, 844 evaluable), elective colorectal surgery (overall infection 16.7% vs 13.3%, small n=93 — its N is printed on its card), and caesarean section (wound infection 6.6% vs 7.4%, n=162; clinical endometritis was actually lower with the single dose, 0.0% vs 6.1%). The orthopaedic syntheses agree: 14 implant RCTs (9,691 procedures) gave infection 2% vs 2% (odds ratio 0.92, relative) and 7 closed-fracture trials (3,808 patients) a risk ratio of 1.24 with a wide interval — both rated low/very-low quality. The 1998 all-surgery systematic review likewise found no clear advantage either way (combined odds ratio ~1.05). Extra doses therefore buy antibiotic exposure, cost and resistance pressure without a demonstrated infection benefit at any tested site; the older trials predate modern SSI surveillance and resistance ecology, which is stated on the face.
stamp: LIKELY (no difference) — carded per surgical site: single preoperative-dose prophylaxis matched multiple/prolonged doses for surgical-site infection in gastric (9.5% vs 8.6%), coronary bypass (sternal 14% vs 13%), colorectal (small n=93) and caesarean (6.6% vs 7.4%) randomised trials and in the orthopaedic implant meta-analysis (2% vs 2%); no site showed a benefit from prolonging prophylaxis

title: Ponsegromab for cancer cachexia (single programme, floor-risk): phase 2 weight gain vs placebo 1.22–2.81 kg by dose at 12 weeks; phase Ib N=10 for tolerability
question: In adults with cancer cachexia and elevated serum GDF-15, does the anti-GDF-15 antibody ponsegromab improve body weight, appetite, physical activity and quality of life versus placebo, and is it safe? (FLOOR-RISK: a single programme — one randomised trial plus one open-label first-in-patient study with N=10.)
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), on a FLOOR-RISK single-programme base, labelled as such: the ponsegromab programme has exactly two RESULT reports — one phase 2 randomised trial (n=187) and one open-label phase Ib first-in-patient study at the reference floor (N=10, printed on its card) — plus a study-design paper carded as provenance only, not as evidence. In the phase 2 trial, patients with cancer cachexia and serum GDF-15 ≥1500 pg/mL gained more weight on ponsegromab than placebo over 12 weeks, with a dose gradient (median between-group differences of 1.22 kg at 100 mg, 1.92 kg at 200 mg and 2.81 kg at 400 mg), and the 400 mg group also improved on appetite/cachexia-symptom measures and digital physical-activity measures. Adverse events of any cause were reported in 70% on ponsegromab versus 80% on placebo. The phase Ib study (n=10) showed no treatment-related adverse events, complete suppression of unbound GDF-15, and a least-squares mean weight increase of 4.63 kg at week 12 — exploratory and uncontrolled, so efficacy rests on the phase 2 trial alone. Twelve weeks is short for a cachexia claim, and no survival or phase 3 result exists. A 2026 anti-GDF-15 combination paper (PMID 42126170) was NOT carded or counted: its fetched record describes mouse and cell-line experiments despite human-trial publication-type tags.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — FLOOR-RISK single-programme evidence: one phase 2 randomised trial (n=187) showed dose-ordered 12-week weight gain versus placebo in GDF-15-elevated cancer cachexia (median differences 1.22–2.81 kg by dose), supported only by an open-label phase Ib study at the floor (N=10) for tolerability and GDF-15 suppression; no phase 3 or survival data exist

title: Shortened preoperative fasting vs nil-by-mouth-from-midnight: no increase in gastric volume or acidity in 4 verified primary RCTs or the Cochrane review (surrogates); less thirst with drinking
question: In adults having elective surgery under general anaesthesia, does a shortened preoperative fast — clear fluids permitted up to about 2 hours before anaesthesia — cause more regurgitation/aspiration or larger, more acidic gastric contents than the traditional nil-by-mouth-from-midnight policy, and does it reduce thirst and preoperative discomfort? (Gastric volume and pH are surrogates for aspiration risk throughout.)
balance: SPLIT — (no difference) on the gastric-contents safety surrogate, (benefit) on preoperative comfort. Four primary randomised trials verified individually from their own records from inside the Cochrane review's programme (Brady 2003: 22 trials, 38 comparisons), plus the review itself, agree: permitting clear fluids 2–3 hours before anaesthesia did NOT increase residual gastric volume or lower gastric pH versus an overnight/standard fast — Hutchinson 1988 (n=300 inpatients: volumes 24.5, 23.7 and 23.2 mL across coffee, orange-juice and fasted groups; pH ~2.0 in all), Phillips 1993 (n=100: residual volume 22 vs 19 mL, pH 2.64 vs 2.26, for free clear fluids until premedication vs a 6-hour fast), McGrady 1988 (n=50: water 100 mL 2 hours preoperatively — gastric residue non-significantly lower, pH identical) and Maltby 1986 (n=140: 150 mL water 2.5 hours preoperatively gave LOWER gastric volume than a sip-only regimen, 17.6 vs 26.7 mL, in the placebo-tablet groups). Gastric volume and pH are SURROGATES, labelled as such on every card: aspiration itself is too rare for any of these trials to power, and the Cochrane review found few trials reporting aspiration/regurgitation at all and almost none in high-risk patients. On comfort, Phillips found less preoperative thirst with drinking, and the review concluded a shortened fluid fast carries no evidence of increased aspiration risk. This shelf is about fasting-DURATION policy for ordinary fluids and food — the proprietary carbohydrate-drink question is homed at live #1956 and is not re-carded here.
stamp: SPLIT (no difference) on the gastric-contents safety surrogate / (benefit) on preoperative comfort — four individually verified primary RCTs inside the Cochrane programme (n=300, 100, 50, 140) and the review itself found a shortened clear-fluid fast did not increase gastric volume or acidity versus standard fasting, and drinking reduced thirst; aspiration itself was too rare for any trial to measure and high-risk patients were barely studied

title: Posturography norms are per-platform: balance improves to ~45 then reverses (N = 914 percentiles), RombergLab equilibrium score 0.72 ± 0.22 (N = 350), and sway velocity is the most informative parameter
question: In healthy humans, what are force-plate posturography norms — centre-of-pressure sway path, velocity, area and frequency-domain measures, eyes open and closed, firm and foam surfaces — by age and sex, and how much does sway increase with normal ageing?
balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, vestibular sensations / motor control; Ganong, hearing and equilibrium. That framing is general — this shelf rests chiefly on the primary measurement literature, and says so. The fragmentation objection that once sank this question is answered by carding PER PLATFORM AND PER PARAMETER SET, never pooling one 'normal sway' number across systems: a 914-person European plantar-pressure percentile cohort (balance improves to ~45 years, then reverses), a 350-participant multicentre RombergLab global equilibrium score (0.72 ± 0.22, falling with age and height), virtual-surround dynamic posturography in 50 adults (matching published norms except SOT condition 4 and adaptation), pressure-platform sway in 106 young women (9.50 mm frontal, 13.00 mm sagittal), frequency-domain spectra in 30 elderly vs 30 young adults, and a >850-experiment parameter comparison naming mean displacement velocity the most informative measure. Cross-points in prose only: the built VEMP and vHIT/caloric shelves are vestibular-reflex measures, and the timed unipedal-stance shelf (#7252) is the bedside companion — neither is re-carded here. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

title: DPOAE norms by device: ILO92 database (101 ears), emission thresholds within ±13 dB at f2/f1 = 1.21, and Titan vs Eclipse agreeing on amplitude but not on SNR
question: In normal-hearing adults, what are distortion-product otoacoustic emission (DPOAE) levels and signal-to-noise ratios by frequency (the 2f1-f2 DP-gram) — their means, lower reference limits and test-retest behaviour — and how do device, primary-tone levels, sex and age shift them?
balance: Textbook framing: Ganong, hearing (cochlear mechanics) — the framing is brief, and this shelf rests chiefly on the primary test-norming literature, and says so. Three adult normative datasets span three device generations, carded PER DEVICE / PROTOCOL as the measurement demands: the 1996 ILO92 database (101 normal ears), a 2007 research protocol deriving an emission-threshold reference standard in 20 excellent-hearing young adults (optimal at f2/f1 = 1.21, 1-6 kHz, 95% within ±13 dB), and a 2024 head-to-head of Titan vs Eclipse in 63 normal-hearing adults (amplitudes agree; noise and SNR differ; both pass ≥6 dB SNR across frequencies, with unreliable responses at the edge frequencies). DPOAE dissociates from the pure-tone audiogram — that dissociation, against the built pure-tone threshold shelf, is core content; the TEOAE companion is shelf #7250. The stamp is graded down because the total adult base is small and every number is device-bound. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING.

title: TEOAE norms in young adults: larger in women and in Chinese ears, absent in 5 of 186 otologically normal ears, and linear protocols give better SNR than non-linear
question: In normal-hearing young adults, what are transient-evoked otoacoustic emission (TEOAE) amplitudes, whole-response reproducibility and signal-to-noise ratios — by sex, ear and ethnic group — and in what fraction of otologically normal ears is no response recordable despite normal hearing?
balance: Textbook framing: Ganong, hearing (cochlear mechanics) — thin framing, and this shelf rests chiefly on the primary test-norming literature, and says so. Three adult datasets: a representative population sample aged 18-25 (345 adults; norms from 186 otologically normal ears, including the distributional fact that 5 normal ears had no recordable response despite thresholds better than 20 dB), a sex-and-ethnic-group comparison (81 Caucasian + 81 Chinese young adults; amplitude higher in women and in Chinese ears at equal hearing sensitivity), and a protocol study (42 adults; post-processed linear recordings superior on noise, SNR and reproducibility, with tolerance-interval scoring criteria). TEOAE is kept separate from DPOAE (shelf #7249): a click-evoked whole-cochlea response is not a frequency-specific DP-gram. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

title: ABR norms are a protocol, not a number: latencies adult by age 3, wave V shifts ~350 µs with electrode site and lengthens with click rate, BIC peaks at 6.06 ms (click) vs 9.47 ms (tone burst)
question: In normal-hearing humans, what are auditory brainstem response (ABR) norms — absolute latencies of waves I, III and V and the I-III, III-V and I-V interpeak intervals by age and sex, at standard click rates — and how do stimulus rate, intensity and binaural interaction change them?
balance: Textbook framing: Ganong, hearing / auditory pathways; Guyton & Hall, hearing chapters — brief framing for evoked-potential norming; this shelf rests chiefly on the primary literature, and says so. title: Unipedal stance norms: time falls significantly with age in both eye conditions across 549 adults, a 1,000-person lifespan dataset and 240 Iranian adults — with no overall sex effect
question: In healthy adults, how long can a single-leg (unipedal) stance be held, eyes open and eyes closed — mean and best-of-three times by decade and sex — and at what age does the eyes-closed time collapse?
balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, motor control / vestibular chapters — thin framing; this shelf rests chiefly on the primary measurement literature, and says so. Three primary normative datasets: 549 healthy adults in six age groups with mean and best-of-3 eyes-open and eyes-closed times (significant age decline, no gender effect, ICC 0.994/0.998 for best-of-3); a 1,000-person lifespan reference dataset (ages 3-101) carrying single-leg stance eyes closed among 12 functional measures; and 240 healthy Iranian adults in six age bands confirming age-specific declines. title: ISWT reference values: distance falls steeply with age in Indian (N = 862), Japanese (N = 590) and Singaporean (N = 199) adults — and each population needs its own equation
question: In healthy adults, what distance is walked on the incremental shuttle walk test — reference values and prediction equations by age, sex, height and weight — and how large is the learning effect between the first and second test?
balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, ch. 84 (sports physiology); Boron & Boulpaep, exercise physiology — general framing; this shelf rests chiefly on the primary measurement literature, and says so. Three large primary datasets (862 Indian adults aged 17-75; 590 Japanese adults; 199 Singaporean adults aged 21-80) agree that ISWT distance falls steeply with age and is higher in men, each publishing its own reference equation (R² 0.50-0.74) — and the Singapore study demonstrates that foreign equations mispredict its population, so equations are carded per population, never pooled. All three used the standard two-trial protocol; no fetched record quantifies the learning effect numerically, and none is claimed. Distinct from the built 6-minute walk shelf (self-paced, submaximal): cross-point in prose only. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

title: Ferritin reference intervals are unsettled: laboratory lower limits (median 8 µg/L women, 25 µg/L men) sit below the 30 µg/L iron-deficiency threshold, and primary intervals span 11 to 88 µg/L at the lower limit
question: In healthy adults, what is the reference interval for serum ferritin — and why do laboratory lower limits sit below the ~30 µg/L threshold that best detects iron deficiency — by sex, age and menopausal status, and how much do inflammation and assay choice move the limits?
balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, blood / iron metabolism; Boron & Boulpaep, haematology sections — brief framing; this shelf rests chiefly on the primary reference-interval literature, and says so. The row's core teaching is a gap, carded head-on: a systematic review of 61 studies (21,882 women, 23,650 men) finds laboratory lower limits a median 8 µg/L (women) and 25 µg/L (men) — below the ~30 µg/L threshold that best detects iron deficiency — on source data at high risk of bias. Four primary datasets show the spread that produces it: geriatric Shanghai intervals (24.44-627.09 µg/L men; 48.18-554.88 women, Roche), a Kenyan IFCC cohort with CRP measured (only the 15 µg/L cut-off anchored to anaemia), 1,223 Chinese Han men (88.2-771.7 µg/L), and a two-assay study with iron deficiency and inflammation explicitly excluded (men 12-399 / 14-415 µg/L; menopausal split in women). Ferritin is an acute-phase reactant: every interval is printed beside its cohort's inflammation handling. Units µg/L (= ng/mL) throughout. The ESR shelf is the prose cross-point. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING.

title: Without diabetes, HbA1c centres near 5.0% and skews right with age — a small black–white gradient (~0.2%) survives adjustment for glucose itself
question: In people without diabetes, what does the HbA1c distribution look like — mean, spread and the fraction above 5.7% and 6.5% — by age, sex and race/ethnicity in population surveys, and how much of the between-group difference survives adjustment for glucose itself?
balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, ch. 79 (insulin, glucagon and glucose regulation). HbA1c is a single-analyte distribution question — the companion to the continuous-glucose profiles shelf — and the population surveys agree on its shape: unimodal and right-skewed, centred near 5.0% in young people, shifting higher and more skewed with age (Menke 2014, NHANES A1C N = 16,209, a whole-population sample that includes people with diabetes — flagged on its card). In people not treated for diabetes, US youth mean HbA1c was 4.99% (SD 0.50), with a small but persistent race/ethnicity gradient that survives adjustment (non-Hispanic black 5.17% vs white 4.93% unadjusted; Saaddine 2002, N = 7,968). Brazilian cohorts without diabetes show the same skin-colour gradient at ages 18 and 30 (Buffarini 2016), and Korean nationwide data give dual-unit means — 5.42% (35.7 mmol/mol) at ages 10–19 and 5.32% (34.7 mmol/mol) at 20–29 (Seo 2018, N = 6,418). This is a measurement shelf only: it carries no diagnostic-threshold recommendations, which live on the diabetes shelves, and anaemia and haemoglobin-variant distortion of HbA1c belongs on the face. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

title: Axial length centres at 23.3–23.5 mm in older populations on two continents — men ~0.5 mm longer, with deeper chambers and flatter corneas
question: In healthy adults, what are ocular axial length, anterior chamber depth and corneal curvature — population means, spreads and percentiles by age, sex and ethnicity — and how do the distributions differ between European and East Asian population eye studies?
balance: Textbook framing: Ganong, vision / ocular anatomy — thin framing for biometry; this shelf rests chiefly on the primary population literature, and says so. Three population eye studies on two continents put mean axial length within a third of a millimetre of each other: 23.25 ± 1.14 mm in older Beijing adults (optical low-coherence reflectometry; Yin 2012, 3,159 measured), 23.44 mm in older white Australians (IOL Master; Fotedar 2010, 1,335 right phakic eyes), and 23.48 mm in aged South China adults (IOL Master; Chen 2016, 1,015 right eyes). Men run longer, deeper and flatter than women in every study that reports sex splits. Device is named per study and right-eye conventions are carded as published. Myopia prevalence differences between populations are the context, not the content: this shelf reports distributions, not myopia-control treatment (homed at live #614). title: OCTA norms are protocol-bound: superficial density ~44% at 6×6 mm vs ~53% at 3×3 mm, falling with age after 50 — and FAZ has no agreed abnormal cut-off
question: In healthy eyes, what are OCT-angiography vessel density (superficial and deep capillary plexuses, radial peripapillary capillaries) and foveal avascular zone area — normative values by age, sex and ethnicity — and how fast does vessel density fall with normal ageing?
balance: Textbook framing: Ganong, vision / retinal circulation — thin framing for OCT-angiography; this shelf rests chiefly on the primary measurement literature, and says so. The normative values are real but protocol-bound: a large Chinese elderly cohort on 6×6-mm scans reports superficial plexus density 43.9% and deep plexus 44.3% (Xu 2024, N = 1,461), while a 3×3-mm study reports 52.58% and 57.87% for the same plexuses (Coscas 2016, 135 eyes) — scan size, segmentation slab and device move the numbers systematically, so values are carded per-protocol and never pooled. Foveal avascular zone area has a wide normal spread and no agreed abnormal cut-off, stated plainly on the face. Ageing lowers vessel density in every dataset that tests it, most prominently after 50. Because the base is device-bound and the between-study spread is wide, the stamp is graded down. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING.

title: Stapedial reflex thresholds depend on component, probe tone and stimulus — absent in 4% of normal values at 226 Hz — and 1,565 older adults support no separate older range (PARTIAL slice of #7090)
question: In healthy adults, what are acoustic (stapedial) reflex thresholds — by stimulus frequency, probe tone and age — and what fraction of normal ears have absent reflexes at the highest stimulus levels?
balance: Textbook framing: Ganong, hearing — middle-ear reflex framing brief; this shelf rests chiefly on the primary measurement literature, and says so. PARTIAL slice, carved from home pack #7090: #7090 asks normal wideband absorbance / tympanometry across frequency (and includes one wideband reflex-estimation methods study); it does not ask the conventional acoustic stapedial reflex threshold distribution — by stimulus frequency, probe tone and age, with the fraction of normal ears whose reflexes are absent — which is this shelf's question alone. The conventional data: thresholds depend on the immittance component read, the probe tone and the stimulus (lowest for admittance at a 226-Hz probe with a 1,000-Hz stimulus), with 4% missing values at 226 Hz in 100 healthy adults (Ferekidou 2008); the wideband ipsilateral broadband-noise threshold runs 12 dB below the clinical threshold in 33 normal-hearing adults (Feeney 2017); and in 1,565 older adults the age effect on reflex thresholds is inconsistent and not clinically significant once hearing loss is allowed for (Golding 2007). Because the age question is unsettled and thresholds are component- and probe-specific, the stamp is graded down. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING

title: Gastric-emptying 'normal' is per-meal: solid half-time median 68.7 min on a rice meal, liquid 10–60 min — women slower for solids, slowest in the luteal phase (PARTIAL slice of #6154)
question: In healthy adults, what are the reference values for gastric-emptying scintigraphy — percentage retention at 1, 2 and 4 hours and half-emptying time for standard solid and liquid test meals — by sex and meal type, and how much do camera view and analysis method move them?
balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, ch. 63–64 (gastrointestinal motility); Boron & Boulpaep, GI motility. PARTIAL slice, carved from home pack #6154: #6154 asks what SETS the rate of gastric emptying and how fat and acid slow it — a regulation/mechanism question; it does not give scintigraphic reference values, which are this shelf's question alone. One normative dataset (the Nottingham test-meal reference intervals) is already carded inside #6154 and is NOT re-carded here. The free normative programme: a multicentre rice-meal study (189 completers) gives median half-time 68.7 minutes with 4-hour retention 1.1% (Vasavid 2014); a vegetarian-meal study (N = 36) gives a half-time reference range of 23–109 minutes (Saifi 2022); a liquid-meal study (N = 35) gives a half-time range of 10–60 minutes (Dhukia 2024); and a compartmental study (20 women, 31 men) shows solid emptying far slower in women (half-time 86.2 vs 52.2 minutes) with no liquid sex difference (Bennink 1998). Meal composition is destiny in this measurement — values are carded per-meal, never pooled — and the small Ns on three anchors are printed on their faces. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING.

question: In adults free of clinical cardiovascular disease, what is the distribution of the ankle–brachial index — mean, spread, the fraction below 0.9 and the fraction at or above 1.4 (incompressible arteries) — by age, sex and deprivation, in a general population?

title: Fostamatinib in rheumatoid arthritis (OSKIRA): modest ACR20 benefit, no radiographic benefit, a negative biologic-failure trial — programme discontinued after phase III
question: In adults with active rheumatoid arthritis (including methotrexate and TNF-inhibitor inadequate responders), does the oral spleen tyrosine kinase (Syk) inhibitor fostamatinib, compared with placebo (on background therapy, or as monotherapy), improve disease activity (OSKIRA programme)?
balance: SPLIT — a discontinued programme with a genuinely divided record. On the benefit side, fostamatinib on background methotrexate beat placebo on ACR20 in phase III (OSKIRA-1: 49.0% and 44.4% vs 34.2%; OSKIRA-3, TNF inadequate responders: 36.2% vs 21.1% for the 100 mg twice-daily regimen only) and as short-term monotherapy (OSKIRA-4, week 6). On the other side: OSKIRA-1's radiographic co-primary endpoint was negative (no slowing of joint damage), the phase II trial in biologic inadequate responders was negative on its primary endpoint (ACR20 38% vs 37%), every monotherapy regimen was inferior to adalimumab at week 24, and the authors of OSKIRA-1 themselves called the benefit statistically but not clinically significant. Harms were consistent — hypertension (24-hour ambulatory systolic +2.9 mm Hg vs placebo; blood pressure ≥140/90 mm Hg at ≥1 visit in ~42–52% vs ~19–27%), diarrhoea and neutropenia. The sponsors stopped developing fostamatinib in RA after phase III; it was never marketed for RA (it is marketed only for chronic immune thrombocytopenia).
stamp: SPLIT — fostamatinib beat placebo on ACR20 in methotrexate and TNF inadequate responders in phase III, but failed its radiographic endpoint, failed outright in biologic inadequate responders, was inferior to adalimumab as monotherapy, and carries consistent hypertension/diarrhoea/neutropenia harm; the RA programme was discontinued after phase III and the drug was never marketed for RA

title: Iguratimod in primary Sjögren syndrome: small Chinese RCT base — ESSPRI benefit vs placebo; primary endpoint missed vs hydroxychloroquine (REBUILD)
question: In adults with primary Sjögren syndrome (Sjögren disease), does the oral immunomodulator iguratimod, compared with placebo (or hydroxychloroquine), improve patient-reported dryness/fatigue (ESSPRI), disease activity (ESSDAI) and glandular measures?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — small, single-region evidence. One small placebo-controlled RCT (66 patients) found iguratimod improved the patient-reported ESSPRI and several activity measures more than placebo over 24 weeks. Against hydroxychloroquine, the multicentre RCT (78 patients) MISSED its primary endpoint (SSRI-30 57.9% vs 40.0%, P=0.114) but favoured iguratimod on secondary STAR and ESSDAI responder rates and on IgG reduction, with more frequent but mostly mild adverse events (60.6% vs 37.8%). An open-label pilot (N=27, labelled as such) and a mechanistic B-cell comparison complete the base. All trials are from China; iguratimod is approved there and in Japan as a DMARD and is not FDA/EMA-approved — printed on the face. A retracted iguratimod-combination report (PMID 34805398) is fenced and is not carded or counted here.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one small placebo-controlled RCT improved patient-reported ESSPRI versus placebo, and an active-comparator RCT missed its primary endpoint while favouring iguratimod on secondary activity measures; the whole base is small and single-region (China), and a retracted iguratimod report is fenced and not counted

title: Tripterygium wilfordii glycosides in rheumatoid arthritis (TRIFRA): not inferior to methotrexate in one open-label Chinese programme; herb-rule and toxicity limits on the face
question: In adults with active rheumatoid arthritis, do Tripterygium wilfordii Hook F (tripterygium glycosides) preparations — alone compared with methotrexate, or added to methotrexate or a TNF inhibitor — improve disease activity and slow radiographic progression (TRIFRA programme)?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — with the herb rule and single-region limits printed on the face. In the TRIFRA programme (China, open-label, assessor-blinded), Tripterygium wilfordii Hook F monotherapy was not inferior to methotrexate (ACR50 at week 24: 55.1% vs 46.4%) and the combination was better (76.8%), with comparable radiographic progression at 2 years. Combination evidence is mixed: TwHF + a TNF-receptor fusion protein beat methotrexate + the same agent at week 12 (ACR50 57.1% vs 41.3%), but adalimumab + TwHF was no better than adalimumab + methotrexate at week 24. HERB RULE: tripterygium glycoside preparations are not FDA-approved and differ by maker; none of the carded publications names a branded product or manufacturer in its record — the preparation is described only as Tripterygium wilfordii Hook F (20 mg three times daily in TRIFRA) — and current products may differ in safety and effectiveness. Reproductive toxicity (infertility/amenorrhoea; irregular menstruation was seen in TRIFRA), hepatotoxicity and gastrointestinal harm lead the harm side. All evidence is single-region (China).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — TRIFRA showed tripterygium glycoside monotherapy not inferior to methotrexate with comparable 2-year radiographic progression, but the pivotal trial was open-label, all evidence is from China, combination results are mixed, and no carded publication names a branded product or maker (herb rule: current products may differ in safety and effectiveness)

title: Prasterone (DHEA) in women with SLE: one positive trial, one subgroup-only steroid-sparing result — androgenic harms; never approved for lupus
question: In women with systemic lupus erythematosus, does oral prasterone (dehydroepiandrosterone, DHEA), compared with placebo plus standard therapy, improve disease activity and reduce corticosteroid requirements?
balance: SPLIT — a women-only programme (1995–2004, never approved for SLE) with one positive, one subgroup-only and one small pilot result. Petri 2004 (381 women) found prasterone 200 mg/day improved or stabilised disease without deterioration in 58.5% versus 44.5% on placebo among women with active disease (P=0.017, ≈14 percentage points, on a composite counting stabilisation as response). Petri 2002's corticosteroid-sparing endpoint MISSED overall (55% vs 41%, P=0.110) and was significant only in the active-disease subgroup (51% vs 29%, P=0.031). The first trial was small (N=28). Harms are androgenic — acne (33% vs 14%), hirsutism (16% vs 2%) — with HDL cholesterol lowering. The sex restriction is printed on the face: there is no trial evidence in men.
stamp: SPLIT — prasterone 200 mg/day was positive on a stabilisation composite in women with active SLE (58.5% vs 44.5%) but its corticosteroid-sparing trial missed overall significance (P=0.110) and was positive only in the active-disease subgroup; women-only 1995–2004 base, never approved for SLE, with androgenic harms and HDL lowering

title: Ipriflavone in postmenopausal osteoporosis: JAMA 2001 found no bone-loss or fracture benefit — and lymphocytopenia in 13.2%
question: In postmenopausal women with osteoporosis, does the isoflavone ipriflavone, compared with placebo (with calcium), prevent bone loss and reduce vertebral fractures?
balance: LIKELY (no difference) on efficacy, with a harm signal — a negative-result shelf. The large JAMA 2001 trial (474 postmenopausal women, 3 years) found ipriflavone did NOT prevent bone loss at any site (lumbar spine annual change 0.1% vs 0.8% on placebo, P=0.14), did not change bone-resorption markers, and produced identical or near-identical new vertebral fracture counts — while 13.2% of treated women developed subclinical lymphocytopenia. The older, smaller Italian reports (Agnusdei 1997, two trials, 149 enrolled; Maugeri 1994, 100 enrolled) reported forearm/radial BMD gains, but they are peripheral-site, largely within-group analyses that the JAMA trial supersedes. Ipriflavone is a synthetic isoflavone marketed as a drug in some countries and as a supplement in others; no carded record names a branded tested product.
stamp: LIKELY (no difference) — the large JAMA 2001 randomised trial found ipriflavone did not prevent bone loss or fractures in postmenopausal osteoporosis and caused subclinical lymphocytopenia in 13.2%; the older smaller positive reports are peripheral-site and within-group and do not outweigh it

title: Bazedoxifene monotherapy for osteoporotic fractures: vertebral benefit (42% relative at 3 years) from ONE phase III programme; no overall nonvertebral benefit (PARTIAL vs #1341)
question: In postmenopausal women with osteoporosis, does bazedoxifene 20 mg daily (monotherapy), compared with placebo (and raloxifene as active control), reduce new vertebral and nonvertebral fractures? (The bazedoxifene + conjugated estrogens combination question is homed separately at live shelf #1341 and is not asked here.)
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for vertebral fractures, from a SINGLE phase III programme (printed on the face). Bazedoxifene 20 mg/day reduced new vertebral fractures versus placebo at 3 years (2.3% vs 4.1% — a 42% relative risk reduction, ≈1.8 percentage points absolute), sustained in the programme's 5-year (4.5% vs 6.8%; 35% relative) and 7-year (7.6% vs 9.9%; 30.4% relative) extensions. Nonvertebral fractures were NOT significantly reduced in the primary population at any time point; the nonvertebral signal appears only in higher-risk subgroups in post-hoc/FRAX-stratified analyses (significant at ≥20% baseline 10-year fracture probability). SERM-class harms (venous thromboembolism, hot flushes/vasodilatation, leg cramps) were more frequent than on placebo. PARTIAL slice: live shelf #1341 covers only the bazedoxifene + conjugated estrogens tissue-selective estrogen complex for menopausal hot flushes and endometrial protection — this shelf asks the monotherapy osteoporosis question that #1341 does not, and the combination evidence is not re-carded here.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — bazedoxifene 20 mg monotherapy reduced vertebral fractures versus placebo (42% relative risk reduction at 3 years, sustained to 7 years) in a single phase III programme and its extensions; no overall nonvertebral fracture benefit (higher-risk subgroup/post-hoc only), with SERM-class harms including venous thromboembolism

title: Palovarotene in FOP: negative small RCT; open-label MOVE vs natural history (post-hoc benefit, futility at 12 months) — growth-plate closure in ~1 in 3 children
question: In adults and children with fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva (FOP), does oral palovarotene, compared with placebo (phase 2) or with natural-history comparators (phase 3 MOVE), reduce new heterotopic ossification?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the design asymmetry is printed on the face. The only randomised placebo-controlled trial (phase 2, 40 patients) was NOT significant on its primary endpoint (responders 100%/88.9% on palovarotene vs 88.9% on placebo, P=0.17) or on CT heterotopic-ossification volume. The efficacy case rests on the phase 3 MOVE trial — OPEN-LABEL and SINGLE-ARM, analysed against an external natural-history cohort (97 vs 101): post-hoc 18-month analyses suggested 54–60% relative reductions in annualised new HO volume, but the prespecified 12-month analysis met futility criteria and the month-48 comparison was not significant (46.4% relative, nominal P=0.0585). Retinoid harms lead the harm side: ≥1 retinoid-associated adverse event in 97.0%, and premature physeal (growth-plate) closure in 36.8% of children under 14 (30.0% of under-18s by month 48), with computational signals of vertebral bone weakening. Single-source product: palovarotene (Ipsen, Sohonos), named per the clarification exception.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the sole placebo-controlled trial was small and non-significant, and the phase 3 MOVE evidence is open-label and single-arm versus natural history with post-hoc analyses and an earlier futility stop; retinoid harms include premature growth-plate closure in about a third of treated children

title: Garetosmab in FOP: OPTIMA phase 3 — 19 new lesions on placebo vs 1–2 on garetosmab; LUMINA-1 missed its primary endpoint but suppressed new lesions
question: In adults with fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva (FOP), does the activin-A-blocking antibody garetosmab, compared with placebo, reduce new heterotopic ossification lesions and flare-ups (LUMINA-1 / OPTIMA programme)?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two genuine randomised trials in an ultra-rare disease (total randomised N=107, printed on the face). OPTIMA phase 3 (63 adults) found 19 new heterotopic bone lesions on placebo versus 1 on garetosmab 3 mg/kg and 2 on 10 mg/kg at week 56 (rate ratios 0.06 and 0.10, both significant; no deaths). LUMINA-1 phase 2 (44 adults) MISSED its primary PET-CT lesion-activity endpoint (P=0.0741) but suppressed new lesions, with no new lesions after placebo patients crossed over (0% vs 40.9%, P=0.0027); all patients had treatment-emergent adverse events (epistaxis, madarosis, skin abscesses) and 5 deaths (11.4%) occurred in its open-label period — considered unlikely related, causality not excludable. The flare-up analysis is post-hoc and labelled as such. Adults only; single-source product (Regeneron), named per the clarification exception.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — OPTIMA phase 3 showed a large significant reduction in new heterotopic bone lesions versus placebo (19 vs 1–2 lesions; rate ratios 0.06–0.10) and LUMINA-1 phase 2 suppressed new lesions despite missing its primary imaging endpoint; total randomised base is 107 adults with FOP (ultra-rare disease), and LUMINA-1's open-label period included 5 deaths with causality not excludable

title: Setrusumab in osteogenesis imperfecta: ASTEROID missed its primary BMD endpoint (strength estimates up ~3%, no fracture difference) — phase 3 fenced (press-only)
question: In adults with osteogenesis imperfecta, does the sclerostin-neutralising antibody setrusumab (BPS804), compared with placebo or baseline, increase bone mineral density and bone formation (ASTEROID programme)?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — ONE development programme (BPS804/setrusumab) reported across phase 2 publications and imaging/biopsy substudies, with SURROGATE endpoints only (printed on the face). ASTEROID phase 2b (110 adults) MISSED its primary endpoint (no change in radial trabecular volumetric BMD at 12 months); modelled bone-strength estimates rose ~3% at 8–20 mg/kg, and annualised fracture rates did NOT differ between doses. The phase 2a study was open-label with N=14. The timelapse and bone-matrix reports are ASTEROID substudies, labelled as such. PHASE 3 FENCE: the phase 3 programme's fracture endpoints were reported missed in a December 2025 topline press release with no journal publication — it is fenced, never carded or counted on this shelf, and no fracture benefit is claimed.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — a single phase 2 programme (ASTEROID and a 14-patient phase 2a) with surrogate endpoints only: primary volumetric-BMD endpoint missed, modelled bone strength up ~3%, no fracture-rate difference; the phase 3 programme is press-release only (fracture endpoints reported missed) and is fenced, not carded or counted

title: Teriparatide in adults with osteogenesis imperfecta: BMD up (alone, mainly type I) but TOPaZ combination did not reduce fractures (HR 0.97)
question: In adults with osteogenesis imperfecta, does teriparatide (in the TOPaZ trial, combined with zoledronic acid, compared with standard care; and in an earlier trial, compared with placebo) increase bone mineral density and reduce fractures?
balance: SPLIT — BMD and fractures point in different directions, across two trials asking different questions (printed on the face). Teriparatide ALONE (Orwoll 2014, 79 adults, placebo-controlled) raised lumbar spine BMD (+6.1% vs +2.8%) and hip BMD (+2.6% vs −2.4%) over 18 months, with the response essentially confined to type I OI and NO difference in self-reported fractures. Teriparatide PLUS zoledronic acid (TOPaZ, JAMA 2026, 349 adults, vs standard care) did NOT reduce adjudicated incident fractures (36.9% vs 36.4%; HR 0.97) despite significantly greater BMD gains — a combination result that must never be worded as a teriparatide-alone effect. Fracture outcomes are secondary/surrogate-limited in the alone trial (BMD primary) and null-primary in TOPaZ. The third card is a biomarker report of the 2014 trial's lineage (verified before carding, per the row's stop-condition), not an independent trial.
stamp: SPLIT — teriparatide alone increased BMD versus placebo in adults with OI (mainly type I; no fracture difference, fractures self-reported), while teriparatide plus zoledronic acid in TOPaZ did not reduce adjudicated fractures versus standard care (HR 0.97) despite greater BMD gains; no report shows a fracture reduction

title: Bixalomer for hyperphosphataemia in CKD: lowered phosphate versus placebo (−0.98 mg/dL in predialysis CKD) and non-inferior to sevelamer on dialysis — Japan-only programme, surrogate endpoint, no outcomes trial
question: In patients with hyperphosphataemia due to chronic kidney disease (on haemodialysis, and not on dialysis), does the non-calcium, non-metal phosphate binder bixalomer, compared with placebo or sevelamer hydrochloride, control serum phosphate?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) on the surrogate only. Bixalomer lowered serum phosphate dose-dependently versus placebo over 4 weeks in haemodialysis patients (−1.80 mg/dL at 4.5 g/day versus +0.24 mg/dL), was non-inferior to sevelamer hydrochloride at 12 weeks (5.87 versus 5.55 mg/dL; difference 0.31 mg/dL, upper 95% CI below the 1.0 mg/dL margin), and beat placebo in CKD patients not on dialysis (mean difference −0.98 mg/dL, P<0.001). Two open-label 48-week programme reports support durability, with constipation the commonest drug reaction (21.0% in the haemodialysis report). Two limits lead the balance: this is a single-region programme (Japan; bixalomer — Astellas, Kiklin — is approved there and is not FDA/EMA-approved), and serum phosphate is a surrogate endpoint throughout the binder class — no bixalomer trial exists for mortality, cardiovascular events or fractures.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit, surrogate endpoint only) — bixalomer lowered serum phosphate versus placebo in two randomised trials (dose-finding in haemodialysis; phase 3 in CKD not on dialysis, mean difference −0.98 mg/dL) and was non-inferior to sevelamer hydrochloride in haemodialysis patients; single-region (Japan) programme, single-source product (Astellas, Kiklin), not FDA/EMA-approved, and no trial tests mortality, cardiovascular or fracture outcomes

title: Peginesatide in CKD anaemia — WITHDRAWN 2013 after fatal anaphylaxis: non-inferior for haemoglobin in EMERALD and PEARL, with a cardiovascular-safety signal in non-dialysis patients (HR 1.32)
question: In adults with anaemia of chronic kidney disease (undergoing haemodialysis, not receiving dialysis, or on peritoneal dialysis), does the erythropoiesis-stimulating agent peginesatide, compared with epoetin/darbepoetin or placebo, control haemoglobin (EMERALD / PEARL programme)?
balance: SPLIT, and the product is WITHDRAWN. Peginesatide (Omontys) was withdrawn from the market in 2013 after fatal anaphylaxis reactions, including first-dose reactions in the post-marketing setting — that history leads this shelf; the drug cannot be prescribed. On the trials: once-monthly peginesatide was non-inferior to epoetin for haemoglobin in haemodialysis patients (EMERALD 1 and 2 — two trials in one paper) and non-inferior to darbepoetin in CKD patients not on dialysis (PEARL 1 and 2 — two trials in one paper). The split is safety by population: pooled composite cardiovascular hazard ratio 1.06 (95% CI 0.89 to 1.26), but 1.32 (95% CI 0.97 to 1.81) in PEARL, with more deaths, unstable angina and arrhythmia in non-dialysis patients. A 59-patient open-label peritoneal-dialysis conversion report is programme support only. Haemoglobin is a surrogate endpoint; ESA-class cardiovascular-safety evidence is cross-pointed to the ESA class shelves, not re-carded here.
stamp: SPLIT — WITHDRAWN product (peginesatide, Omontys, withdrawn 2013 after fatal anaphylaxis including first-dose post-marketing reactions): non-inferior haemoglobin control versus epoetin (EMERALD 1/2, haemodialysis) and versus darbepoetin (PEARL 1/2, not on dialysis), but a cardiovascular-safety signal in the non-dialysis programme (hazard ratio 1.32, 95% CI 0.97 to 1.81, with more deaths, unstable angina and arrhythmia); each NEJM paper reports two trials and is labelled as such

title: Ongericimab in hypercholesterolaemia: LDL cholesterol down by about two-thirds versus placebo in three Chinese phase 3 trials — surrogate endpoint, no outcomes trial
question: In adults with hypercholesterolaemia (primary hypercholesterolaemia/mixed dyslipidaemia, heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia, and statin-intolerant patients), does the PCSK9 monoclonal antibody ongericimab, compared with placebo on background therapy, lower LDL cholesterol?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) on the surrogate only. Three Chinese phase 3 trials consistently show ongericimab lowering LDL cholesterol by about two-thirds versus placebo on background therapy: least-squares mean differences of −67.7% (150 mg every 2 weeks) in primary hypercholesterolaemia/mixed dyslipidaemia, −66.2% in statin-intolerant patients, and −69.4% to −80.6% in heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia, with adverse-event rates similar to placebo; a device study (programme support) shows syringe and autoinjector delivery perform alike. These percentages are changes in LDL cholesterol, a surrogate endpoint — no cardiovascular-outcomes trial of ongericimab exists (class outcomes evidence is cross-pointed to the evolocumab/alirocumab shelves). The evidence is single-region (China; ongericimab is a single-source Junshi Biosciences product approved there).
stamp: LIKELY (benefit, surrogate endpoint only) — ongericimab lowered LDL cholesterol by least-squares mean differences of about −61% to −81% versus placebo across three phase 3 trials (primary hypercholesterolaemia/mixed dyslipidaemia, statin-intolerant patients, heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia); single-region (China) evidence for a single-source product (Junshi Biosciences), with no cardiovascular-outcomes trial

title: Lorcaserin for obesity — WITHDRAWN 2020 over a cancer imbalance in CAMELLIA-TIMI 61: it did produce weight loss (BLOOM/BLOSSOM) and passed cardiovascular non-inferiority, with no cardiovascular benefit
question: In adults with overweight or obesity (with or without type 2 diabetes), does the serotonin 2C agonist lorcaserin, compared with placebo plus lifestyle intervention, produce weight loss — and what was its cardiovascular-safety profile (BLOOM / BLOSSOM / CAMELLIA-TIMI 61 programme)?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) on weight loss — for a WITHDRAWN product. Lorcaserin (Belviq) was withdrawn from the US market in 2020 after CAMELLIA-TIMI 61 showed a numerical excess of cancers; that history leads this shelf, the cancer data are presented as the trial programme reported them (an imbalance in a safety trial not powered for cancer), and the drug cannot be prescribed. On efficacy the record is consistent: BLOOM and BLOSSOM showed about 47% versus 20–25% of patients losing at least 5% of body weight at 1 year (absolute differences about 22–27 percentage points), with mean losses around 5.8 kg / 5.8% versus 2.2 kg / 2.8% on placebo plus lifestyle intervention. CAMELLIA-TIMI 61 (12,000 high-risk patients) met cardiovascular non-inferiority (major cardiovascular events 2.0% versus 2.1% per year; hazard ratio 0.99) but no cardiovascular superiority (hazard ratio 0.97) — cardiovascular outcomes were a safety question, not an efficacy benefit, and relative measures above are labelled relative with the absolute rates beside them.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit on weight loss) — WITHDRAWN product (lorcaserin, Belviq, withdrawn from the US market in 2020 after a numerical excess of cancers in CAMELLIA-TIMI 61): BLOOM and BLOSSOM showed consistent modest weight loss versus placebo plus lifestyle intervention (about 47% vs 20–25% achieving ≥5% loss at 1 year), and CAMELLIA-TIMI 61 met cardiovascular non-inferiority (HR 0.99) with no cardiovascular benefit (HR 0.97 for the extended outcome)

title: Rimonabant for obesity — WITHDRAWN 2008 over psychiatric harm, never FDA-approved: the RIO trials showed consistent weight loss (−5.3 to −6.7 kg vs −1.4 to −1.8 kg) on surrogate endpoints only
question: In adults with overweight or obesity (including patients with dyslipidaemia, type 2 diabetes, or metabolic risk factors), does the cannabinoid-1 receptor blocker rimonabant, compared with placebo plus diet, reduce weight and improve cardiometabolic risk factors (RIO programme)?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) on weight and surrogate risk factors — for a WITHDRAWN product. title: Orbital radiotherapy in Graves' orbitopathy: SPLIT — one sham-controlled trial positive on motility only (60% vs 31%), the other negative on all outcomes; equal to prednisone, better tolerated
question: In adults with active Graves' orbitopathy (thyroid eye disease), does orbital (retrobulbar) radiotherapy, compared with sham irradiation or oral prednisone, improve eye outcomes (motility, diplopia, soft-tissue signs)?
balance: SPLIT — the sham-controlled trials disagreed with each other, and that disagreement is the balance. Mourits (2000) found radiotherapy successful in 18 of 30 (60%) versus 9 of 29 (31%) on sham (relative risk 1.9; absolute difference 29 percentage points), driven by diplopia/motility only, with no effect on proptosis or eyelid swelling. Gorman (42 patients, internally controlled) found no clinically or statistically significant difference on any main outcome at 6 months. Against oral prednisone, radiotherapy was equally successful (13 of 28 versus 14 of 28; Prummel 1993) and better tolerated. Harms lead the other side: retinopathy risk, especially with diabetes, and a theoretical secondary-malignancy risk. The trial base is old (1993–2001) and small.
stamp: SPLIT — orbital radiotherapy in active Graves' orbitopathy: the two sham-controlled trials disagreed (Mourits 2000 positive on motility/diplopia only, 60% vs 31% success; Gorman negative on every main outcome), while the prednisone comparison (Prummel 1993) showed equal success (13/28 vs 14/28) with better tolerability for radiotherapy; retinopathy risk (especially with diabetes) and theoretical secondary-malignancy risk on the harm side

title: Aclidinium bromide in COPD: better lung function (+124 to +128 mL trough FEV1), cardiovascularly non-inferior and fewer exacerbations in ASCENT-COPD (rate ratio 0.78)
question: In adults with moderate-to-severe COPD, does twice-daily inhaled aclidinium bromide (400 μg) versus placebo improve lung function and reduce exacerbations — and is it cardiovascularly safe in patients at increased cardiovascular risk?
balance: LIKELY (benefit). Two short placebo-controlled trials showed aclidinium 400 μg twice daily improving trough FEV1 by 124 mL at 12 weeks (ACCORD COPD I) and 128 mL at 24 weeks (ATTAIN), with better symptom and health-status scores. The large ASCENT-COPD trial (3630 patients at increased cardiovascular risk, up to 3 years) showed cardiovascular non-inferiority (major events 3.9% versus 4.2%; hazard ratio 0.89, against a wide 1.8 margin) and fewer first-year moderate-to-severe exacerbations (0.44 versus 0.57 per year; rate ratio 0.78 — a 22% relative reduction, absolute difference 0.13 per year). The efficacy trials are 12–24 weeks with lung-function primary endpoints — the exacerbation and cardiovascular claims rest on ASCENT alone, and this shelf says so.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — aclidinium bromide 400 μg twice daily improved trough FEV1 versus placebo in ACCORD COPD I (+124 mL, 12 weeks) and ATTAIN (+128 mL, 24 weeks), and in ASCENT-COPD was non-inferior for major cardiovascular events (3.9% vs 4.2%; HR 0.89) with fewer moderate-to-severe exacerbations (rate ratio 0.78, a 22% relative reduction; absolute rates 0.44 vs 0.57/year) — exacerbation and cardiovascular claims rest on ASCENT alone

title: Nebulised revefenacin in COPD: trough FEV1 up 146–147 mL versus placebo at 12 weeks — a single programme (two replicate trials plus one 52-week safety trial), labelled on the face
question: In adults with moderate-to-very-severe COPD, does once-daily nebulised revefenacin (175 μg) versus placebo improve lung function over 12 weeks and maintain benefit and safety over 52 weeks?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), on a SINGLE PROGRAMME, labelled as such. Revefenacin (nebulised solution, marketed as Yupelri — the nebulised delivery is the point of the question) rests on one development programme: two replicate 12-week placebo-controlled trials (Studies 0126/0127, reported together) showing day-85 trough FEV1 advantages of 146–147 mL for the 175 μg once-daily dose, and one 52-week safety trial (1055 patients, versus open-label tiotropium) showing comparable tolerability and maintained exploratory lung-function gains. Endpoints are lung function and health status; there is no exacerbation-outcome trial.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single programme, labelled: nebulised revefenacin 175 μg once daily improved trough FEV1 versus placebo by 146–147 mL at day 85 in the programme's two replicate 12-week phase 3 trials (reported together), and was tolerated over 52 weeks in one safety trial versus open-label tiotropium; all other carded papers are programme reports of those same trials, and no exacerbation-outcome trial exists

title: Zileuton in asthma: better lung function and fewer steroid-requiring exacerbations in 1990s trials (6.1% vs 15.6%) — short trials, no outcomes trial, liver monitoring required
question: In patients with mild-to-moderate chronic asthma, does zileuton versus placebo — or versus theophylline — improve lung function and asthma control?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). Four 1990s trials in mild-to-moderate asthma show zileuton improving lung function versus placebo (FEV1 +0.32 L versus +0.05 L over 4 weeks at 2.4 g/day) and, in the largest (401 patients, 13 weeks), fewer corticosteroid-requiring exacerbations (6.1% versus 15.6% — absolute difference 9.5 percentage points); against theophylline it appeared comparable, and responders maintained control on reduced dosing frequency. All trials are short (≤3 months of randomised treatment, one 6-month responder study), with lung-function and symptom endpoints — no exacerbation-outcome trial exists. Hepatotoxicity monitoring is part of the drug's real-world use and is on this shelf's face: liver-enzyme elevations over three times normal occurred on zileuton 600 mg four times daily in the largest trial and reversed on withdrawal. Original dosing was four times daily (later extended-release), stated as the publications give it.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — zileuton improved lung function versus placebo in 1990s trials of mild-to-moderate asthma and reduced corticosteroid-requiring exacerbations in the largest (6.1% vs 15.6% over 13 weeks), and matched theophylline head-to-head; all trials short with surrogate endpoints, no exacerbation-outcome trial, and a reversible liver-enzyme signal requiring monitoring

title: Zafirlukast in asthma: better symptoms and lung function versus placebo over 13 weeks (symptom-free days 7.0 vs 3.7/month) — 1990s programme, and low-dose fluticasone beat it on bronchial hyper-responsiveness
question: In patients with mild-to-moderate asthma, does zafirlukast 20 mg twice daily versus placebo improve symptoms and lung function, and how does it compare with low-dose inhaled corticosteroid?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). Two 13-week placebo-controlled trials in mild-to-moderate asthma showed zafirlukast 20 mg twice daily improving symptoms and lung function: in the 762-patient trial, daytime symptom scores fell 26.5% and FEV1 rose 6.3% versus placebo; in the 146-patient trial, symptom-free days were 7.0 versus 3.7 per month in absolute terms (an 89% relative increase) with 55% fewer health-care contacts in relative terms (18.5 versus 40.7 per 100 per month).
