title: Montelukast in chronic asthma (adolescents/adults): better than placebo (FEV1 +7.4% vs +0.7%), less than inhaled beclomethasone (+13.1%); largest effect in aspirin-intolerant asthma
question: In adolescents and adults with chronic asthma, does once-daily oral montelukast versus placebo — alone, versus inhaled beclomethasone, or added to inhaled corticosteroid — improve lung function and asthma control, including in aspirin-intolerant asthma?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). In adolescents and adults with chronic asthma, once-daily oral montelukast 10 mg was better than placebo on lung function and symptoms in a 895-patient phase 3 trial (FEV1 +7.4% vs +0.7% over 12 weeks), but inhaled beclomethasone was better still (+13.1%, P<0.01 versus montelukast). Added to inhaled beclomethasone in 642 incompletely controlled patients, montelukast gave significant additional benefit on FEV1, daytime symptoms and nocturnal awakenings. In aspirin-intolerant asthma (80 patients, most already on moderate-to-high-dose glucocorticosteroids) the effect was large: a 10.2% between-group FEV1 difference and 54% fewer exacerbations as reported. Limits printed on the cards: the pivotal trials are from 1999, before modern ICS/LABA standard care, and current US labelling for montelukast carries a boxed warning about serious neuropsychiatric events, which belongs in any prescribing decision. This shelf is confined to chronic asthma in adolescents and adults — preschool episodic wheeze (pack #1426) and allergic rhinitis (pack #2666) stay in their own homes, and acute-exacerbation montelukast is a different question, not folded in.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — montelukast beat placebo in a 895-patient phase 3 trial and added significant benefit to inhaled beclomethasone in 642 patients, but was inferior to inhaled beclomethasone head-to-head and the trials predate modern ICS/LABA care; the largest effect is confined to aspirin-intolerant asthma (80 patients)

title: Levalbuterol vs racemic albuterol in asthma: SPLIT — modest chronic bronchodilator edge, no advantage in acute asthma (meta-analysis of 1,625) and one acute trial favouring racemic albuterol
question: In children and adults with asthma — chronic use and acute exacerbations — does levalbuterol (the (R)-enantiomer) versus racemic albuterol improve bronchodilation and reduce hospitalisation or adverse effects?
balance: SPLIT. The limbs point different ways and are kept separate. Chronic nebulised dosing (Nelson 1998, 362 patients): levalbuterol gave a larger first-dose peak FEV1 response than racemic albuterol (combined groups 0.92 vs 0.82 L, P=0.03), with the week-4 difference similar but not significant, and levalbuterol 0.63 mg matching racemic albuterol 2.5 mg with fewer beta-adrenergic side effects. Paediatric MDI (173 children): levalbuterol significantly beat placebo on peak FEV1 change (25.6% vs 16.8%) while racemic albuterol's 21.8% did not reach significance versus placebo — not a demonstrated head-to-head superiority. Acute asthma is the opposite limb: a continuous-nebulisation ED trial (99 children) found racemic albuterol SUPERIOR on FEV1 and asthma score, and a meta-analysis of 7 acute-asthma trials (1,625 participants) found no significant efficacy or safety difference and concluded levalbuterol should not be used over albuterol for acute asthma. No hospitalisation claim is pooled across these limbs — the carded records do not support one. Product naming under the clarification exception: levalbuterol is the single-(R)-enantiomer product (marketed as Xopenex), named as the publications name it.
stamp: SPLIT — chronic-dosing trials show a modest bronchodilator edge for levalbuterol (first-dose peak FEV1 0.92 vs 0.82 L; paediatric MDI significant versus placebo where racemic albuterol was not), while acute-asthma evidence shows no advantage: one continuous-nebulisation trial favoured racemic albuterol and a 7-trial meta-analysis (1,625 participants) found no significant difference

title: Zanamivir for influenza treatment: symptoms relieved a median 1.5 days earlier (MIST, 455 patients) and 2.5 days earlier in high-risk patients — pre-2000 trial base
question: In adolescents and adults with influenza A or B, does inhaled zanamivir (10 mg twice daily for 5 days) versus placebo shorten illness and reduce complications, including in high-risk patients?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). Two pre-2000 placebo-controlled trials in largely healthy adolescents and adults found inhaled zanamivir 10 mg twice daily for 5 days shortened influenza illness by about 1 to 1.5 days: GG167 (417 randomised, 262 with confirmed influenza) — median time to alleviation of all major symptoms 4 versus 5 days, and 4 versus 7 days in patients febrile at entry or treated within 30 hours; MIST (455 patients) — symptoms relieved a median 1.5 days earlier (intention-to-treat), 2 days earlier if febrile at entry, and 2.5 days earlier in the high-risk subgroup, with fewer complications in high-risk patients (P=0.004). The high-risk evidence beyond that subgroup is a retrospective pooled analysis (2,751 recruited across the programme, 321 high-risk, 154 on zanamivir): 2.5 days' benefit, return to normal activities 3.0 days earlier, and a 43% relative reduction in complications requiring antibiotics (absolute incidences are not printed in that record). Cross-point: the Cochrane neuraminidase-inhibitor review (PMID 24718923) is already carded inside live shelf #583 (the oseltamivir shelf) and is deliberately NOT re-carded here. This shelf is treatment only; zanamivir prophylaxis is a separate question and is not folded in.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two placebo-controlled trials showed inhaled zanamivir shortened influenza by a median 1–1.5 days (2.5 days in high-risk patients), with the complication evidence resting on a small high-risk subgroup and a retrospective pooled analysis rather than a dedicated high-risk trial

title: Favipiravir for uncomplicated influenza: SPLIT — one phase 3 trial cut illness by 14.4 hours, the other did not; antiviral effect consistent, symptom benefit inconsistent
question: In adults with uncomplicated influenza, does oral favipiravir versus placebo — or versus standard neuraminidase/baloxavir therapy — shorten time to symptom alleviation?
balance: SPLIT. The two phase 3 placebo-controlled trials, reported in ONE publication, disagree on the clinical endpoint: US316 found a significant 14.4-hour reduction in time to illness alleviation (median 84.2 vs 98.6 hours, P=0.004), while US317 found no significant reduction (77.8 vs 83.9 hours); both showed clear antiviral effects (reduced viral titres, RNA load and time to virus detection, P<0.001). A post-hoc exposure analysis of those same trials found 41–43% of favipiravir recipients never reached the target average minimum concentration of 20 µg/mL, and those who did had larger antiviral effects. The AD ASTRA platform trial (944 randomised; favipiravir arm 223) is open-label and virological: favipiravir accelerated viral clearance by 66% relative to no study drug but was 10% slower than baloxavir with non-inferiority not shown, and time to resolution of all symptoms did not differ significantly. On the STRATOS convention the two phase 3 trials count as one publication, so the floor here is three reports covering four trials — stated on the face. Favipiravir is not licensed for influenza in the US or EU (licensed in Japan under restricted conditions), and its embryotoxicity warning is part of the real-world answer.
stamp: SPLIT — the two phase 3 trials (one publication) disagree on time to illness alleviation (+14.4 hours significant in US316, not significant in US317) despite consistent antiviral effects, and the open-label AD ASTRA platform trial was positive on viral clearance but not on symptom resolution

title: Laninamivir for post-exposure prophylaxis: single 40 mg dose cut household influenza to 4.5% vs 12.1% on placebo; 11% vs 19% in children — Japan-only programme
question: In household contacts of an influenza patient (adults and children), does a single inhaled dose — or two daily doses — of laninamivir octanoate versus placebo prevent influenza illness?
balance: LIKELY (benefit), on three Japanese household-contact trials from a single development programme — the single-programme structure is stated on the face. Clinical influenza over 10 days: 3.9% (20 mg for 2 days) and 3.7% (20 mg for 3 days) versus 16.9% on placebo in 1,451 analysed contacts — relative risk reductions of 77.0% and 78.1% relative; a single 40 mg dose gave 4.5% versus 12.1% on placebo (relative risk reduction 62.8% relative) in 801 analysed contacts; and in children under 10, a single 20 mg dose gave 11% versus 19% (relative risk reduction 45.8% relative). Adverse events were similar to placebo in all three trials. All effect measures are relative risks of influenza illness and are labelled relative, with the absolute rates beside them on every card. Laninamivir is licensed in Japan only. Cross-point: laninamivir TREATMENT is a different question, homed at pack #7208 — its studies are not re-carded here, and the two shelves are not merged.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — three randomised household-contact trials from one Japanese programme consistently reduced clinical influenza (4.5% vs 12.1% for a single 40 mg dose; 11% vs 19% in children), with relative risk reductions of 45.8–78.1% relative and absolutes printed on every card; laninamivir is licensed in Japan only

title: Sivelestat in ALI/ARDS: SPLIT — STRIVE negative (no mortality or ventilator-free-day benefit, 180-day mortality signal) versus Japanese physiological benefit; meta-analysis null
question: In adults with acute lung injury or ARDS associated with systemic inflammatory response syndrome, does intravenous sivelestat versus placebo improve mortality, ventilator-free days or oxygenation?
balance: SPLIT — by region and era, and the split is the answer. The international STRIVE trial (492 mechanically ventilated patients with acute lung injury) was negative: no effect on ventilator-free days (11.4 vs 11.9, P=0.536) or 28-day mortality (64 deaths in each group), the trial was stopped early on a negative long-term mortality trend, and 180-day all-cause mortality was significantly higher on sivelestat (P=0.006 in the curve comparison reported). The earlier Japanese phase 3 programme (230 patients, ALI with systemic inflammatory response syndrome) reported the opposite direction on physiological endpoints: improved pulmonary-function rating, reduced duration of mechanical ventilation and shortened ICU stay, with no significant effect on survival. A 2017 meta-analysis of 6 randomised trials (804 patients) sits with STRIVE on clinical endpoints: no significant difference in 28–30-day mortality (relative risk 0.94, 95% CI 0.71 to 1.23), ventilation days or ICU stay, with a possible oxygenation signal only in sensitivity analysis. Sivelestat is licensed only in Japan (and a small number of other Asian markets) — that regulatory status is part of the face of this shelf.
stamp: SPLIT — the international STRIVE trial (492 patients) found no effect on mortality or ventilator-free days with a higher 180-day mortality signal, while the earlier Japanese phase 3 programme (230 patients) reported improved pulmonary-function ratings and shorter ventilation without a survival benefit; the 2017 meta-analysis (6 RCTs, 804 patients) was null on mortality (relative risk 0.94)

title: Sargramostim in Crohn's disease: a failed programme — NEJM phase 2 missed its primary endpoint (54% vs 44%, P=0.28) and the Cochrane pool (537 patients) was not significant for remission
question: In adults with moderately-to-severely active Crohn's disease, does daily subcutaneous sargramostim (6 µg/kg for 56 days) versus placebo induce clinical response or remission?
balance: A FAILED PROGRAMME, stated plainly. The phase 2 NEJM trial (124 patients, sargramostim 6 µg/kg/day for 56 days) MISSED its primary endpoint: clinical response (at least a 70-point CDAI decrease at day 57) was 54% versus 44% on placebo (P=0.28). Its secondary endpoints were positive — 100-point response 48% versus 26% (P=0.01) and remission 40% versus 19% (P=0.01) — but the Cochrane review pooling the randomised base (3 studies, 537 patients, one in abstract form only) found no significant difference for remission (25.3% vs 17.5%; relative risk 1.67, 95% CI 0.80 to 3.50) or 100-point response (relative risk 1.71, 95% CI 0.98 to 2.97), and graded the evidence low quality. The small Japanese phase 1–2 study (11 patients total, open-label) is carded as a programme limb and is never load-bearing. No phase 3 programme confirmed the phase 2 signal and development stopped. Endpoints throughout are clinical (CDAI-based); no endoscopic-outcome trial exists.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — a failed programme: the phase 2 NEJM trial missed its primary endpoint (70-point response 54% vs 44%, P=0.28), the Cochrane pool of 3 studies (537 patients) found no significant remission benefit (relative risk 1.67, 95% CI 0.80 to 3.50) on low-quality evidence, and no phase 3 confirmation ever followed

title: Satavaptan for ascites in cirrhosis: a failed programme — 1,200-patient long-term programme failed every primary endpoint despite short-term weight and sodium effects; never marketed
question: In patients with cirrhosis and ascites — with or without hyponatraemia, and after large-volume paracentesis — does satavaptan added to diuretic therapy improve ascites control and delay recurrence versus placebo?
balance: A FAILED PROGRAMME, stated plainly. Short-term phase 2 trials showed real pharmacology: in hyponatraemic patients (110) satavaptan reduced body weight dose-dependently and raised serum sodium, and in patients without hyponatraemia (148) it reduced weight by about 2.1–2.5 kg versus 0.36 kg on placebo over 14 days; after large-volume paracentesis (151 patients) it reduced paracentesis frequency. But the definitive long-term programme — three randomised trials, 1,200 patients across the spectrum of ascites severity — failed every primary endpoint (worsening of ascites; cumulative large-volume paracenteses over 12 weeks), showed only slight secondary-endpoint advantages, did not reduce hepatic encephalopathy (395 episodes pooled), and in one trial mortality was higher on satavaptan (hazard ratio 1.47, 95% CI 1.01 to 2.15). Satavaptan was never marketed for ascites and development was abandoned: this shelf is the record of a complete randomised evidence base for a drug patients cannot be prescribed. Ascites endpoints are weight, volume and recurrence measures, not survival. Cross-point: tolvaptan in cirrhotic ascites (pack #7291) is the same class with a different drug and a different evidence fate — the shelves are not merged.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — a failed programme: the three-trial long-term programme (1,200 patients) failed every primary ascites endpoint, did not reduce hepatic encephalopathy, and showed higher mortality on satavaptan in one trial (hazard ratio 1.47); short-term weight and sodium effects never converted into long-term ascites control, and the drug was never marketed

title: Tolvaptan for diuretic-resistant cirrhotic ascites: short-term weight and ascites-volume reductions in a Japanese 7-day programme (3.21 vs 1.75 kg vs added furosemide, 56 patients); hard outcomes untested
question: In patients with liver cirrhosis and ascites/hepatic oedema responding insufficiently to conventional diuretics, does adding tolvaptan (3.75–7.5 mg daily) versus placebo or diuretic adjustment improve body weight, ascites volume and oedema?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for short-term weight and oedema only. The entire programme is Japanese and short (7 days of randomised treatment in both double-blind reports): a dose-finding trial found tolvaptan 7.5–30 mg/day reduced body weight and abdominal circumference versus placebo, with 7.5 mg/day giving the maximum change with preferable tolerability; a phase 3 pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic study found dose-dependent decreases in body weight and ascites volume and increased urine output at 3.75 and 7.5 mg/day. Neither double-blind record prints its participant count or numeric effect sizes — both cards say so on their faces ('N not documented' in the record). The one fully quantified randomised comparison is small and open-label (56 patients): adding tolvaptan 7.5 mg lost 3.21 kg versus 1.75 kg with added furosemide over 7 days (P=0.0412 between groups). No trial tests decompensation, transplant or survival, and none should be implied. Tolvaptan's hepatic-oedema licence is Japan-specific; in the US the drug carries a liver-injury warning from the ADPKD programme — that tension is part of the face. Cross-points: satavaptan in ascites (pack #7290, same class, failed programme) and the refractory-ascites shelves are different questions.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a Japanese short-term programme: dose-dependent reductions in body weight and ascites volume over 7 days in two double-blind studies (participant counts and numeric effects not documented in their records) and a greater 7-day weight loss than added furosemide in one small open-label randomised study (56 patients; −3.21 vs −1.75 kg); no decompensation, transplant or survival outcomes tested

title: Flumazenil in overt hepatic encephalopathy: brief improvement in a subset (17.5% vs 3.8% neurological improvement in grade III, 527-patient crossover trial), no mortality effect — a probe, not a treatment strategy
question: In patients with cirrhosis and grade III–IV hepatic encephalopathy, does intravenous flumazenil versus placebo produce short-term clinical improvement in encephalopathy grade or consciousness?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for TRANSIENT improvement only, with the Ns printed. One large trial carries the base: the Italian multicentre crossover study (527 cirrhotic patients with grade III–IVa encephalopathy) found neurological-score improvement in 17.5% of grade III and 14.7% of grade IVa patients on flumazenil versus 3.8% and 2.7% on placebo, with EEG improvement in 27.8% and 21.5% versus 5% and 3.3%. Everything else is small and old: the pragmatic trial behind it is 14 patients contributing 18 episodes. The Cochrane review (14 trials, 867 participants; analyses on 842) found a beneficial effect on hepatic encephalopathy (relative risk 0.75, 95% CI 0.71 to 0.80, as reported) but NO effect on all-cause mortality (7.4% vs 9.3%; relative risk 0.75, 95% CI 0.48 to 1.16), on low-quality evidence with most trials at high risk of bias and follow-up under one day in the majority. Flumazenil is therefore framed as a short-acting diagnostic/therapeutic probe that can briefly lighten encephalopathy in a subset of patients — not a treatment strategy, and not episode prevention. The duplicate 2017 Cochrane record (the same review under a second record) is deliberately not carded; one review, one card.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for transient improvement only: the one large crossover trial (527 patients) found neurological improvement in 17.5%/14.7% versus 3.8%/2.7% on placebo, the rest of the base is small and old (the next carded trial is 14 patients, 18 episodes), and the Cochrane review (867 participants) found an encephalopathy benefit but no mortality effect, on low-quality evidence

title: Lexipafant in predicted severe acute pancreatitis: a failed programme — small trials improved organ-failure scores, but the phase 3 trial (n=290) found no prevention of organ failure (57% vs 58%) and no mortality benefit
question: In patients with predicted severe acute pancreatitis, does lexipafant (a platelet-activating-factor antagonist) versus placebo prevent organ failure and reduce mortality?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — a failed programme, stated plainly. Two small early trials (n=83 and n=50) reported reduced organ-failure scores with the platelet-activating-factor antagonist lexipafant, but the adequately powered phase 3 trial (n=290) found no effect on new organ failure (organ failure in 57% on lexipafant versus 58% on placebo) and no significant mortality difference, and the Cochrane review of pharmacological interventions found no evidence that any drug, lexipafant included, reduces short-term mortality in acute pancreatitis. Lexipafant was never licensed. Severity prediction used 1990s criteria (APACHE II / Glasgow), which dates the context.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — failed programme: the phase 3 trial (n=290) found no effect on new organ failure (57% vs 58% developed organ failure) and no significant mortality difference, superseding two small early trials (n=83, n=50) that improved organ-failure scores only; lexipafant was never licensed

title: Susoctocog alfa in acquired haemophilia A (REBUILD): bleeds resolved in most patients in three single-arm reports (n=28 trial; n=53 and n=50 cohorts) — inhibitors to porcine factor VIII are the defining harm
question: In adults with acquired haemophilia A and a serious bleeding episode, does susoctocog alfa (recombinant porcine-sequence factor VIII, dosed and titrated against measured factor VIII activity), versus no concurrent control, control bleeding at 24 hours, and with what immunogenicity and thrombotic cost?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single-arm evidence throughout, with no concurrent control in any report, so response proportions cannot be read as comparative efficacy. The pivotal prospective phase 2/3 trial (n=28) found a positive response at 24 hours in all 28 subjects and ultimate bleed control in 24 of 28, with no related serious adverse events or thrombotic events. Two post-authorisation cohorts (US n=53; EU n=50) found 80.3% of treated bleeds and 37 of 50 initial bleeding events resolved, respectively. The defining harm is immunogenicity against the porcine sequence: treatment-related serious adverse events in 12.0% in the US study, most commonly inhibitors to porcine factor VIII (8.0%), and 4 of 5 probably-related serious events in the EU study were anti-porcine-FVIII inhibitor events. A Japanese phase II/III report enrolled only 5 patients — below the library floor — and is excluded from this shelf, as the commissioning row directs; it is not carded and carries no weight here. Product naming under the clarification exception: susoctocog alfa (Obizur, Takeda), a recombinant porcine-sequence factor VIII whose dose can be titrated against measured factor VIII activity, unlike bypassing agents — that monitoring contrast is context, not comparative evidence.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single-arm, uncontrolled base stated: pivotal trial n=28 (response at 24 h in 28/28; bleed control 24/28) plus US (n=53) and EU (n=50) post-authorisation cohorts with 80.3% and 37/50 bleeds resolved; the defining harm is anti-porcine-FVIII inhibitors (8.0% in the US cohort). REBUILD: the at-floor cohort base slate 10 missed. The Japanese n=5 report is excluded, below floor

title: Bomedemstat in myelofibrosis and essential thrombocythemia (FLOOR-RISK — exactly 2 single-arm reports): spleen reduction in 66% with data (MF) and platelet response in 77% evaluable (ET)
question: In patients with myelofibrosis refractory/resistant to, inadequately controlled by, or intolerant of approved therapy, or with essential thrombocythemia requiring cytoreduction after inadequate response/intolerance to at least 1 standard therapy, does the irreversible LSD1 inhibitor bomedemstat (dose-titrated to a target platelet count), versus no concurrent control, reduce spleen volume (myelofibrosis) or durably control platelet count (essential thrombocythemia), and does it reduce driver-mutation variant allele frequency?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — FLOOR-RISK: this shelf rests on exactly 2 reports, one in myelofibrosis (phase 1/2, n=89) and one in essential thrombocythemia (phase 2, n=73), both single-arm with no concurrent control, and the two disease slices are labelled separately and never pooled. In myelofibrosis, 23 of 35 patients with week-24 spleen-volume data (66%) had a spleen-volume reduction and 9 (26%) a reduction of 20% or more, against thrombocytopenia in 48% and grade 3–5 adverse events in 69%. In essential thrombocythemia, response (platelets 400 ×10⁹/L or below without new thromboembolism) occurred in 49 of 64 evaluable patients (77%) at week 24, with haemorrhagic events in 15 of 73 (21%). There is no polycythaemia-vera report and no third report at floor. The dose is titrated to a target platelet count, so the titration is part of the tested intervention.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — FLOOR-RISK, exactly 2 reports, both single-arm with the uncontrolled base stated: myelofibrosis phase 1/2 (n=89; spleen-volume reduction in 23/35 with week-24 data) and essential thrombocythemia phase 2 (n=73; platelet response 49/64 evaluable, 77%); slices labelled separately and never pooled; no third report exists

title: Divarasib in KRAS G12C NSCLC: phase 3 beat sotorasib/adagrasib — PFS 9.8 vs 5.7 months and OS 17.7 vs 12.0 months, response 58.4% vs 32.3%

title: Trastuzumab deruxtecan in HER2-mutant NSCLC: response ~50% at the licensed 5.4 mg/kg dose, with ILD in 14.9% — versus 56% response and 32.0% ILD at 6.4 mg/kg
question: In patients with previously treated metastatic HER2 (ERBB2)-mutant non-small-cell lung cancer, does trastuzumab deruxtecan (5.4 or 6.4 mg/kg), versus no concurrent control, produce objective responses, and what is the interstitial lung disease cost at each dose?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single-arm evidence throughout (DESTINY-Lung02 randomised dose, not treatment), so response rates have no concurrent comparator. The dose story is the shelf: at 5.4 mg/kg, confirmed response was 50.0% in DESTINY-Lung02's final analysis with adjudicated drug-related interstitial lung disease (ILD) in 14.9%; at 6.4 mg/kg, response was 56.0% with ILD in 32.0% — and in the earlier DESTINY-Lung01 at 6.4 mg/kg, response was 55% with ILD in 26% including 2 deaths. The licensed 5.4 mg/kg dose follows from that balance. ILD is the class-defining harm for every deruxtecan shelf and is not softened here. The DESTINY-Lung01 HER2-overexpressing cohort is a different biomarker question and is cross-pointed in prose only, not carded. The Lung02 final analysis carded here supersedes the primary report to which two errata (against that earlier report) were issued.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single-arm base stated (Lung02 randomised dose, not treatment): confirmed response 50.0% at the licensed 5.4 mg/kg dose vs 56.0% at 6.4 mg/kg, while adjudicated drug-related ILD was 14.9% vs 32.0% (Lung02 final analysis) and 26% with 2 deaths at 6.4 mg/kg in Lung01 — the lower dose carries roughly half the ILD for a similar response rate

title: Datopotamab deruxtecan in NSCLC: SPLIT — PFS gain vs docetaxel (HR 0.75) with null OS and a squamous reversal; single-arm response 35.8% in genomically selected disease
question: In patients with previously treated advanced or metastatic NSCLC — unselected by histology, and with actionable genomic alterations after targeted therapy and platinum chemotherapy — does the TROP2-directed antibody–drug conjugate datopotamab deruxtecan, versus docetaxel (or no concurrent control), prolong progression-free survival and produce responses?
balance: SPLIT — by histology and by slice. In the randomised TROPION-Lung01 (n=604), datopotamab deruxtecan improved progression-free survival versus docetaxel (median 4.4 vs 3.7 months; hazard ratio 0.75, a relative measure) but overall survival was not significantly different (12.9 vs 11.8 months; HR 0.94, relative). The PFS effect was driven by nonsquamous histology (HR 0.63, relative), while the squamous subgroup numerically favoured docetaxel (PFS HR 1.41, OS HR 1.32 — relative, neither significant). The single-arm TROPION-Lung05 in genomically selected disease found a 35.8% response rate (43.6% in EGFR-mutated disease). The two slices are labelled and never pooled as one verdict. Stomatitis (any grade 56.2% in Lung05) and interstitial lung disease (8.8% adjudicated drug-related in Lung01 versus 4.1% on docetaxel) are the harms on the face. The breast-cancer datopotamab question is homed separately (pack #6405) and is not folded in.
stamp: SPLIT — randomised TROPION-Lung01 (n=604): PFS improved vs docetaxel (4.4 vs 3.7 months; HR 0.75, relative) but OS was null (HR 0.94, not significant), the benefit was driven by nonsquamous histology (HR 0.63, relative) and squamous disease numerically favoured docetaxel (HR 1.41, relative); single-arm TROPION-Lung05 response was 35.8% in genomically selected disease. Stomatitis and ILD are the priced harms

title: Ivonescimab in NSCLC (HARMONi programme): PFS wins in three randomised slices — vs pembrolizumab 11.1 vs 5.8 months; squamous 11.1 vs 6.9; post-TKI survival 16.8 vs 14.1 months in China, non-significant globally
question: In patients with advanced NSCLC — first-line PD-L1-positive disease, first-line squamous disease, or EGFR-mutated nonsquamous disease after EGFR-TKI progression — does ivonescimab, alone versus pembrolizumab or added to chemotherapy versus chemotherapy (or versus tislelizumab plus chemotherapy), prolong progression-free and overall survival?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — across three distinct randomised questions, labelled as separate slices and never pooled: (1) first-line PD-L1-positive disease (HARMONi-2, China, n=398): ivonescimab beat pembrolizumab on PFS (11.1 vs 5.8 months; HR 0.51, a relative measure) with overall survival immature; (2) first-line squamous disease (HARMONi-6, China, n=532 randomised): ivonescimab plus chemotherapy beat tislelizumab plus chemotherapy on PFS (11.1 vs 6.9 months; HR 0.60, relative); (3) EGFR-mutated disease after EGFR-TKI progression: HARMONi-A (China, n=322) showed an overall-survival benefit for ivonescimab plus chemotherapy (16.8 vs 14.1 months; HR 0.74, relative; 30-month survival 29.1% vs 18.4%, absolute rates), while the global HARMONi trial (n=438) showed a PFS benefit (6.8 vs 4.4 months; HR 0.52, relative) with an overall-survival estimate that was not significant (HR 0.79, 95% CI 0.62 to 1.01). Every trial except the global HARMONi was run in China. VEGF-class and immune harms price the gain: grade 3 or higher treatment-related events were 29% versus 16% against pembrolizumab in HARMONi-2 and 64% versus 54% against tislelizumab-chemotherapy in HARMONi-6. Product naming: ivonescimab (Akeso/Summit), a PD-1×VEGF bispecific antibody.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — three distinct randomised slices, never pooled: HARMONi-2 PFS 11.1 vs 5.8 months vs pembrolizumab (HR 0.51, relative; OS immature); HARMONi-6 PFS 11.1 vs 6.9 months vs tislelizumab + chemotherapy (HR 0.60, relative); post-TKI HARMONi-A OS 16.8 vs 14.1 months (HR 0.74, relative) with the global HARMONi showing PFS benefit (HR 0.52, relative) but non-significant OS (HR 0.79). All but the global trial were run in China; grade ≥3 toxicity is consistently higher on ivonescimab

title: Amivantamab + chemotherapy after osimertinib (MARIPOSA-2, PARTIAL): PFS 6.3 months (8.3 with lazertinib) vs 4.2 on chemotherapy alone; response 64% vs 36%
question: In patients with EGFR-mutated (exon 19 deletion or L858R) locally advanced or metastatic NSCLC progressed on osimertinib, does amivantamab plus carboplatin–pemetrexed, with or without lazertinib, versus chemotherapy alone, prolong progression-free survival, and at what added toxicity?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single-programme evidence: one phase 3 trial (MARIPOSA-2, n=657) reported across a primary report, a patient-relevant-outcomes report and an Asian-subgroup analysis, which are reports of one trial, not three trials. title: Furmonertinib vs gefitinib first-line in EGFR NSCLC (FURLONG, one China trial): PFS 20.8 vs 11.1 months; CNS PFS 20.8 vs 9.8 months — no osimertinib comparison exists

title: Aumolertinib vs gefitinib first-line in EGFR NSCLC (AENEAS, one China trial): PFS 19.3 vs 9.9 months, CNS PFS 29.0 vs 8.3 months — the gain is durability, not response rate
question: In Chinese patients with previously untreated locally advanced or metastatic EGFR-mutated (exon 19 deletion or L858R) NSCLC, does the third-generation EGFR inhibitor aumolertinib (110 mg/day), versus gefitinib, prolong progression-free survival, including in the central nervous system?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single-programme comparative evidence: one phase 3 trial (AENEAS, n=429, China) reported across a primary report and a CNS efficacy report — reports of one trial, not two trials. Aumolertinib beat gefitinib on progression-free survival (median 19.3 vs 9.9 months; hazard ratio 0.46, a relative measure) through durability rather than response (objective response 73.8% vs 72.1%, absolute rates; median duration of response 18.1 vs 8.3 months), with a strong CNS slice (CNS PFS 29.0 vs 8.3 months; HR 0.31, relative) and less rash (23.4% vs 41.4%) and diarrhoea (16.4% vs 35.8%) at similar grade 3 or higher event rates (36.4% vs 35.8%). A third carded report is a small single-arm real-world study (n=33) — it is NOT an AENEAS report (the commissioning row described it as one; the fetched record shows a real-world cohort), and it carries no comparative weight. The comparator is gefitinib, a first-generation agent: the shelf answers 'aumolertinib versus gefitinib in China', not 'aumolertinib versus osimertinib'. Aumolertinib (formerly almonertinib, HS-10296) is approved in China only and is not FDA/EMA-approved. There is no head-to-head against furmonertinib (shelf #7301) — cross-trial PFS comparisons are not evidence of superiority. The separate stage III programme (ADVANCE) is a different setting, cross-pointed in prose only and not carded.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single-programme (one trial, AENEAS n=429, two reports; plus a small n=33 real-world cohort carded as context only, not an AENEAS report): aumolertinib vs gefitinib median PFS 19.3 vs 9.9 months (HR 0.46, relative), response 73.8% vs 72.1% with duration 18.1 vs 8.3 months, CNS PFS 29.0 vs 8.3 months (HR 0.31, relative). Comparator is first-generation gefitinib, not osimertinib; aumolertinib is approved in China only, not FDA/EMA-approved

title: Sacituzumab govitecan in pretreated HR+/HER2− metastatic breast cancer (TROPiCS-02): PFS 5.5 vs 4.0 months and overall survival 14.4 vs 11.2 months versus physician's-choice chemotherapy
question: In patients with endocrine-resistant, chemotherapy-pretreated hormone-receptor-positive, HER2-negative metastatic breast cancer, does the TROP2-directed antibody–drug conjugate sacituzumab govitecan, versus treatment of physician's choice chemotherapy, prolong progression-free and overall survival?
balance: LIKELY benefit, on a single phase 3 programme. TROPiCS-02 (543 randomised, heavily pretreated: 99% prior CDK4/6 inhibitor, median three prior chemotherapy lines) found sacituzumab govitecan improved median progression-free survival versus treatment of physician's choice chemotherapy (5.5 vs 4.0 months; hazard ratio 0.66 — a relative measure) and, in the final analysis, median overall survival (14.4 vs 11.2 months; HR 0.79, relative). title: Asciminib first-line in newly diagnosed chronic-phase CML (ASC4FIRST): week-48 major molecular response 67.7% vs 49.0% vs investigator-selected TKIs — clear vs imatinib, not significant vs second-generation TKIs
question: In patients with newly diagnosed chronic myeloid leukaemia in chronic phase, does asciminib (the STAMP inhibitor targeting the ABL myristoyl pocket, 80 mg once daily), versus investigator-selected ATP-competitive tyrosine kinase inhibitors (imatinib or a second-generation TKI), increase major molecular response at week 48, and with what tolerability advantage? (The previously-treated question is asked at pack #4481.)
balance: LIKELY benefit on a molecular endpoint, on a single phase 3 trial. ASC4FIRST (405 randomised, newly diagnosed chronic-phase CML) found major molecular response at week 48 in 67.7% on asciminib versus 49.0% on investigator-selected TKIs — but the comparator is a stratified mix: the advantage was large against imatinib (69.3% vs 40.2%) and small and not significant against second-generation TKIs (66.0% vs 57.8%). Asciminib had fewer grade ≥3 adverse events (38.0% vs 44.4% on imatinib and 54.9% on second-generation TKIs) and fewer discontinuations (4.5% vs 11.1% and 9.8%). Major molecular response is a surrogate; no survival advantage is shown in these reports. This shelf asks only the FIRST-LINE question; asciminib after ≥2 prior TKIs (ASCEMBL) is homed at pack #4481 and is not re-carded here.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — on a single phase 3 trial (ASC4FIRST, 405 randomised): asciminib gave a higher week-48 major molecular response than investigator-selected TKIs overall (67.7% vs 49.0%, absolute rates), driven by the imatinib stratum (69.3% vs 40.2%); against second-generation TKIs the difference was smaller and not significant (66.0% vs 57.8%), and grade ≥3 events and discontinuations were fewer on asciminib — a molecular-surrogate benefit, with no survival advantage shown

title: Isatuximab plus VRd in transplant-ineligible newly diagnosed myeloma (IMROZ): 60-month PFS 63.2% vs 45.2% (HR 0.60, relative), with deeper MRD-negative responses
question: In patients aged 18–80 with newly diagnosed multiple myeloma ineligible for transplantation, does adding the anti-CD38 antibody isatuximab to bortezomib–lenalidomide–dexamethasone (followed by isatuximab–Rd), versus VRd (followed by Rd), prolong progression-free survival and deepen responses, including in frail patients?
balance: LIKELY benefit, on a single phase 3 trial. IMROZ (446 randomised, transplant-ineligible newly diagnosed myeloma, age 18–80) found estimated 60-month progression-free survival of 63.2% with isatuximab-VRd (followed by isatuximab-Rd) versus 45.2% with VRd (followed by Rd) — hazard ratio 0.60, a relative measure, printed beside those absolute rates — with deeper responses (complete response or better 74.7% vs 64.1%; MRD-negative complete response 55.5% vs 40.9%). A frailty subgroup analysis found the PFS benefit held in frail and non-frail patients, and an MRD-dynamics report found deeper and more durable MRD negativity. Serious adverse events and discontinuations were similar between arms in the primary report. Transplant-ELIGIBLE isatuximab-VRd is a different question and is not carded here.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — on a single phase 3 trial (IMROZ, 446 randomised): adding isatuximab to VRd in transplant-ineligible newly diagnosed myeloma gave estimated 60-month PFS of 63.2% vs 45.2% (HR 0.60, a relative measure) with deeper responses (MRD-negative complete response 55.5% vs 40.9%) and similar serious-event and discontinuation rates, the benefit holding in frail and non-frail subgroups; no overall-survival result is reported in the carded records

title: Daratumumab vs active monitoring in high-risk smouldering myeloma (AQUILA; FLOOR-RISK — one trial): progression delayed (5-year PFS 63.1% vs 40.8%), while ~59% of monitored patients had not progressed at 5 years
question: In patients with high-risk smouldering multiple myeloma, does subcutaneous daratumumab monotherapy for up to 36 months, versus active monitoring, delay progression to active multiple myeloma and prolong survival?
balance: FLOOR-RISK — the base is stated plainly: ONE phase 3 trial (AQUILA, 390 randomised) with one regional subgroup report and one review; there is no second trial. AQUILA found subcutaneous daratumumab monotherapy for up to 36 months delayed progression to active myeloma or death versus active monitoring (HR 0.49 — a 51% relative reduction; 5-year PFS 63.1% vs 40.8%, absolute rates) and 5-year overall survival was 93.0% versus 86.9% (deaths 15 vs 26; OS HR 0.52, relative). The counterweight belongs on the face: about 59% of monitored patients had NOT progressed at 5 years, so monitoring remains a strategy in which most patients in this trial avoided treatment for years, while daratumumab commits everyone treated to up to 3 years of therapy for a precursor condition. This is a delay-of-progression result under a treat-versus-monitor strategy — it is not prevention of myeloma. The commonest grade 3–4 event was hypertension (5.7% vs 4.6%).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — FLOOR-RISK, on a single phase 3 trial (AQUILA, 390 randomised) with one small subgroup report: daratumumab monotherapy delayed progression to active myeloma or death versus active monitoring (HR 0.49, a relative measure; 5-year PFS 63.1% vs 40.8%, absolute) with 5-year survival 93.0% vs 86.9%, but about 59% of monitored patients had not progressed at 5 years, so the stamp stays at POSSIBLE until a second report exists; the benefit is delayed progression, not prevention

title: ¹⁷⁷Lu-PSMA-617 in taxane-naïve mCRPC (PSMAfore): rPFS 11.60 vs 5.59 months, but ITT overall survival null (24.48 vs 23.13 months; HR 0.91) with 60.3% crossover
question: In men with PSMA-positive metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer who have progressed on one androgen-receptor pathway inhibitor and have not received a taxane, does [¹⁷⁷Lu]Lu-PSMA-617, versus a change of ARPI (abiraterone or enzalutamide), prolong radiographic progression-free survival, and what happens to overall survival when crossover is allowed? (The post-taxane question is asked at live #1862.)
balance: SPLIT on its own endpoints, on a single phase 3 trial. title: Darolutamide + ADT without docetaxel in mHSPC (ARANOTE): radiological PFS HR 0.54 (relative); overall survival HR 0.81, not significant at the primary cutoff
question: In men with metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer, does darolutamide plus androgen-deprivation therapy — without docetaxel — versus placebo plus ADT, prolong radiological progression-free survival, and is overall survival improved? (The triplet question with docetaxel is asked at live #1868.)
balance: LIKELY benefit on radiological progression, on a single phase 3 trial — with overall survival not significant at the primary cutoff. ARANOTE (669 randomised) found darolutamide plus ADT — WITHOUT docetaxel — improved radiological progression-free survival versus placebo plus ADT (HR 0.54, a 46% relative reduction in risk of radiological progression or death), with overall survival HR 0.81 (95% CI 0.59 to 1.12 — not significant). Time to castration-resistant disease (HR 0.40, relative) and to pain progression (HR 0.72, relative) also favoured darolutamide, the benefit was consistent across disease-volume and risk subgroups, and fatigue was less frequent on darolutamide (5.6% vs 8.1%). This shelf is only the doublet-without-chemotherapy slice: the triplet question (darolutamide added to ADT plus docetaxel, ARASENS) is homed at live #1868, and ARASENS's survival result must not be borrowed for the doublet.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — on a single phase 3 trial (ARANOTE, 669 randomised): darolutamide plus ADT without docetaxel improved radiological progression-free survival versus ADT alone (HR 0.54, a relative measure), consistently across disease-volume and risk subgroups, with delayed pain progression and less fatigue than placebo; overall survival was not significant at the primary cutoff (HR 0.81; 95% CI 0.59 to 1.12) and no survival claim is made

title: Voice therapy for functional dysphonia: small RCTs favour named programmes (semi-occluded tract, stretch-and-flow) over vocal hygiene alone; biofeedback adds no voice benefit over placebo
question: In adults with functional (muscle-tension / behavioural) dysphonia, does structured voice therapy — semi-occluded vocal-tract exercises, stretch-and-flow, vocal function exercises, with or without electromyographic biofeedback — improve voice handicap, acoustic measures and laryngeal appearance versus vocal hygiene alone, sham or waitlist, and do the protocols differ?
balance: POSSIBLE benefit, protocol by protocol — never pooled. The randomised base is four small trials, each testing a NAMED programme against a weak comparator: a semi-occluded vocal-tract exercise programme plus vocal hygiene beat vocal hygiene alone (n=34); stretch-and-flow beat vocal hygiene alone (N not documented in the record) with large effect sizes in a preliminary trial; semi-occluded-tract therapy with EMG biofeedback equalled the same therapy with placebo biofeedback for voice, with added muscle-activity effects (n=22 women); and flow-resistant-tube therapy was noninferior to Vocal Function Exercises (n=20). A 2008 systematic review of six treatment RCTs found combined direct-plus-indirect therapy improved self-reported, observer-rated and instrumental functioning versus no intervention, while warning the real effects are probably smaller (publication bias). Samples are small (Ns printed on each card's face), blinding of a behavioural therapy is inherently partial, and no trial compares these programmes against each other adequately — the shelf answers each protocol family separately.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — on four small randomised trials, each of a named programme: semi-occluded vocal-tract therapy plus vocal hygiene beat vocal hygiene alone (n=34), stretch-and-flow beat vocal hygiene alone (N not documented in the record), EMG biofeedback added muscle-activity but not voice benefit over placebo biofeedback (n=22), and flow-resistant-tube therapy was noninferior to Vocal Function Exercises (n=20); a 2008 systematic review supports combined therapy versus no intervention but warns true effects are probably smaller — weak comparators and small samples throughout

title: Donor-site dressings for split-thickness skin grafts: SPLIT by class — hydrogel unsupported, povidone-iodine foam fastest in one RCT, polyurethane vs alginate a comfort/workload trade-off
question: In patients with split-thickness skin-graft donor sites, which dressing class — hydrogel, hydrocellular foam, polyurethane film, calcium alginate, petrolatum / povidone-iodine gauze — heals the donor site fastest with least pain, infection and dressing-change burden, and does the answer differ in burns versus elective grafting?
balance: SPLIT by dressing class and endpoint — there is no single winner. A Cochrane review found only two hydrogel trials (162 participants) and insufficient evidence for hydrogel, with amorphous hydrogel possibly SLOWER to heal than alginate or acetate gauze (low certainty). A 3-arm RCT (67 adults, 73 donor sites) found the hydrocolloid Aquacel and the film Mediskin I re-epithelialised faster than the foam Allevyn, with less pain on dressing change for Aquacel. A small burns-unit RCT (n=36) found no healing or pain difference between polyurethane (Allevyn) and calcium alginate (Kaltostat) but more dressing changes and cost with polyurethane, while a meta-analysis of the same comparison (4 RCTs, 127 subjects) found no pain difference and better patient comfort with polyurethane. A Korean phase 4 RCT (n=106) found povidone-iodine foam (Betafoam) epithelialised fastest (12.74 days vs 16.61 hydrocellular foam vs 15.06 petrolatum gauze) with no infections in any arm. Healing-time definitions differ by trial and are carded as published, never pooled. Tested products and companies are named on each card where the publication gives them.
stamp: SPLIT — by dressing class and endpoint: hydrogel is unsupported by a Cochrane review (2 trials, 162 participants; possibly slower healing than alginate/gauze, low certainty); povidone-iodine foam epithelialised fastest in one 106-patient RCT and a hydrocolloid and a film beat a foam in a 73-site RCT, while polyurethane versus calcium alginate shows no healing or pain difference (comfort favours polyurethane, dressing-change burden favours alginate); no class differed on infection

title: Thalidomide for delayed-phase CINV: SPLIT by backbone — benefit on older 5-HT3 backbones (delayed response 70.6% vs 50.4%), null when added to a modern four-drug regimen after its failure
question: In patients receiving highly emetogenic chemotherapy, does adding thalidomide to standard antiemetic prophylaxis (5-HT3 antagonist / NK1 antagonist / dexamethasone, with or without olanzapine) improve complete response and nausea control in the acute and especially the delayed phase, and at what cost in sedation, constipation and neuropathy?
balance: SPLIT by backbone regimen and by trial generation. Two meta-analyses dominated by older, largely Chinese RCTs of thalidomide added to a 5-HT3 antagonist ± dexamethasone found higher complete-response and no-nausea rates, with the largest gains in the DELAYED phase (delayed complete response 70.6% vs 50.4%, RR 1.53 — a relative measure; delayed no-nausea RR 1.69, relative). The earliest primary trial (crossover, n=50 assessable, on a ramosetron + dexamethasone backbone with modified FOLFOX7) agrees for delayed nausea and emesis, at the cost of much more sedation/dizziness (42% vs 9.6%). But the one modern trial — thalidomide added to a FOUR-drug backbone (ondansetron, aprepitant, dexamethasone, olanzapine) in patients who had already failed that backbone — was NULL for its primary endpoint (no nausea 0–120 h: 16% vs 21% on placebo), though severe delayed nausea was less frequent and mild constipation more frequent. So the synthesis benefit belongs to weaker backbones; on a modern four-drug backbone, no added nausea control is shown. Thalidomide is teratogenic and requires strict pregnancy-prevention handling, and sedation, constipation and drowsiness/dizziness are its recurring harms — all on the face, not in a footnote. The olanzapine CINV shelves (live #769, #1789) ask a different agent's question.
stamp: SPLIT — by backbone regimen: thalidomide improved delayed-phase complete response and no-nausea rates when added to older 5-HT3-antagonist ± dexamethasone backbones (two overlapping meta-analyses, delayed complete response 70.6% vs 50.4%, RR 1.53, a relative measure; one crossover RCT agreeing), but the single modern trial adding it to a four-drug olanzapine-containing backbone after failure of that backbone was null on its primary endpoint (no nausea 16% vs 21%); sedation, constipation and teratogenicity handling price any use

title: Prophylactic incisional NPWT beyond fracture & caesarean (PARTIAL of live #651): groin RCTs support it (SSI OR 0.35, relative); laparotomy unsettled — RCT-only synthesis null (RR 0.56, CI crosses 1)
question: In adults with primarily closed surgical incisions other than lower-limb fracture and caesarean incisions — closed laparotomy (general / colorectal), vascular groin incisions, orthopaedic and breast incisions — does prophylactic incisional negative-pressure wound therapy reduce surgical-site infection and wound complications versus a standard dressing? (The fracture and caesarean question is asked at live #651.)
balance: SPLIT by incision site and by study design — carded per site, never as one pooled closed-incision claim. This shelf is the PARTIAL slice beyond live #651, which asks only the lower-limb fracture and caesarean question. GROIN (arterial surgery): a meta-analysis of 7 RCTs (1,049 incisions) found SSI reduced (OR 0.35, relative), and two primary RCTs carded here agree in direction, one significant (major wound complications 8.5% vs 25% in high-risk patients) and one not (30-day SSI 11% vs 19%, underpowered). LAPAROTOMY: syntheses disagree — a JAMA Surgery meta-analysis including non-randomised studies found SSI lower (OR 0.25, relative), while the RCT-only meta-analysis found no significant difference (RR 0.56; 95% CI 0.30 to 1.03), and the one primary laparotomy RCT carded here (n=50) was significant only on a one-sided test. ALL CLOSED INCISIONS (2016): infection RR 0.54 (relative), moderate-quality evidence with heterogeneity. Three retracted syntheses in this literature were fenced and NOT carded (see the synthesis card).
stamp: SPLIT — by incision site and study design: for closed groin incisions in arterial surgery, RCT evidence supports incisional NPWT (7 RCTs, SSI OR 0.35, a relative measure; primary trials split — one significant, one null and underpowered); for closed laparotomy incisions the evidence is unsettled (a mixed-design meta-analysis found OR 0.25, relative, but the RCT-only meta-analysis found RR 0.56, 95% CI 0.30 to 1.03, not significant); three retracted syntheses in this literature were fenced and not carded

title: Barbed vs conventional sutures: closure 4–16 minutes faster and cheaper in arthroplasty and spine syntheses, complications split by layer — full-layer barbed closure raised complications to 19.7%
question: In adults having wound closure with sutures — total knee and hip arthroplasty, spine surgery and other fields as tested — do knotless barbed sutures shorten closure and operating time versus conventional sutures, and do they differ in wound complications, dehiscence and cost?
balance: SPLIT. The time benefit is consistent everywhere it was randomised: the TKA synthesis (6 RCTs, 826 knees) found closure 4.41 minutes faster with barbed suture, the hip/knee synthesis (4 level-I trials, 588 patients) found 6.3 minutes faster, and the spine synthesis (7 studies, 8,645 patients) found closure 16.36 minutes and operating time 20.13 minutes shorter. Cost follows time in most reports (synthesis cost difference −282.61 in the units reported; $298 per case in the hip/knee synthesis; $324 vs $419 in the largest TKA RCT). Wound complications are where the record splits: the syntheses find no significant difference, and two TKA RCTs found fewer complications with barbed suture, but a 582-patient three-arm TKA RCT found full-layer barbed closure RAISED incision complications to 19.7% versus 7.2% for capsule-only barbed and 9.3% for traditional capsule closure, and an early TJA RCT reported more frequent and severe wound complications with barbed suture. The defensible reading is layer-specific: barbed suture for the capsule/deep layer saves time without a complication penalty in the randomised record; full-layer (including skin) barbed closure is the limb with a harm signal. Stop-condition check: at least three primary RCTs from inside the syntheses are carded per field for arthroplasty (Gililland 2014, Chan 2017, Sah 2015, Feng 2020) and one primary spine RCT from inside the spine synthesis (Shi 2022) — the spine primary base is one RCT, stated on the face. The retracted TKA synthesis PMID 37519132 is NOT carded, per the row fence. Tested products are named where the publication gives them (Stratafix in Chan 2017); where the record names no brand, the card says so.
stamp: SPLIT — closure time and cost consistently favour barbed suture in every synthesis and primary RCT carded, and pooled wound complications do not differ, but primary RCTs split on complications by layer: full-layer barbed closure raised incision complications to 19.7% in a 582-patient three-arm trial while capsule-only barbed closure (7.2%) matched traditional closure, and one TKA RCT found fewer complications with barbed suture (2 vs 11)

title: Early postoperative showering (FLOOR-RISK): no infection increase in any randomised report — Cochrane's only trial 8.5% vs 8.8% (RR 0.96, CI 0.62–1.48), 7-RCT meta-analysis null — but the base is thin
question: After surgery, does early bathing or showering (within about 48 hours, wound uncovered or as tested) increase wound infection or dehiscence versus keeping the wound dry and covered until suture removal or a later time point — and how do pain, comfort and satisfaction compare?
balance: FLOOR-RISK, stated on the face: this shelf rests on a thin primary base — the Cochrane review found exactly ONE eligible randomised trial (857 patients having minor skin excision), and the primary randomised reports carded here total four (857; 444; 32; 51 patients) plus a 2020 meta-analysis pooling 7 RCTs (1,881 patients for infection). Within that base, no report finds early showering increases infection: the Cochrane trial found surgical site infection in 8.5% with bathing from 12 hours versus 8.8% with bathing delayed at least 48 hours (risk ratio 0.96, 95% CI 0.62 to 1.48 — wide, so a clinically important effect either way is not excluded); the 2020 meta-analysis of showering on or before postoperative day 2 versus later found no difference in infection or complications; the largest primary RCT (444 patients, showering from 48 hours) found 1.8% versus 2.7% infection; and the small sternotomy RCT (51 patients) found FEWER sternal infections with showering at 48–72 hours (7.7% vs 32.0%) alongside less pain and higher comfort and satisfaction (patient-reported outcomes). Comfort and satisfaction favour early showering wherever measured. PROPOSED STAMP: MAYBE (weak evidence) — no infection increase is shown, but the base is too thin and the confidence intervals too wide to call the question settled.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — FLOOR-RISK base stated on the face: the Cochrane review found only one eligible RCT (857 minor-excision patients; infection 8.5% vs 8.8%, RR 0.96, 95% CI 0.62 to 1.48) and the carded primary RCTs total 444, 51 and 32 patients, with a 7-RCT meta-analysis (1,881 patients) finding no infection difference for showering on or before day 2; no increase in infection is shown anywhere, comfort and satisfaction favour early showering, but the intervals are too wide to settle the question

title: 2-minute walk test norms: healthy Chinese mean 199.1 m (973 adults), NIH Toolbox personalised percentiles in 1,385 US adults, obesity limb mean 176 m — equations explain only ~a third of variance
question: In healthy adults, what distance is walked in two minutes — reference equations and percentile values for the 2-minute walk test by age, sex and height — and how do the equations from different populations compare?
balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, ch. 84 (sports physiology) and Boron & Boulpaep, exercise physiology — the framing is general, and this shelf rests chiefly on the primary measurement literature, and says so. Two large healthy-adult datasets anchor the row: 973 healthy Chinese adults aged 18–85 (mean 2-minute walk distance 199.1 ± 25.81 m; age and height the independent predictors, explaining only about a third of the variance) and 1,385 healthy community-dwelling US adults from the NIH Toolbox study, whose personalised (age, sex, height neighbours-based) reference values were slightly more precise than smooth age-based values (average interquartile range 149 ft (≈45 m) vs 158 ft (≈48 m); agreement ICC 0.96). A third dataset (295 middle-aged and elderly Chinese adults WITH OBESITY, mean 176 ± 20 m) is carded as an obesity limb only, never merged into the healthy norms, per the commissioning row. The stamp is graded down because the equations are population-specific, the predictors explain only ~28–35% of the variance, and corridor/encouragement protocol moves distances — there is no single universal 2-minute distance. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING. Cross-points: the 6-minute walk reference shelf and the incremental shuttle walk shelf (#7253) are different tests with different reference sets, not re-carded here.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING

title: 1-minute sit-to-stand norms (PARTIAL to #7161): sea-level medians 38 reps in the 20s falling to 23–24 in the 70s (Chile, n=499; Portugal, n=546), high-altitude equations kept as a separate limb (n=400)
question: In healthy adults, how many repetitions of the one-minute sit-to-stand test are performed — reference values by age and sex at sea level and at high altitude — and how do they relate to the five-times and 30-second variants?
balance: Textbook framing: as for the companion walk-test shelf, Guyton & Hall's exercise/motor chapters frame mobility generally — the framing is thin, and this shelf rests on the primary measurement literature, and says so. PARTIAL home: pack #7161 asks the FIVE-TIMES sit-to-stand time and the 30-SECOND chair-stand count; the 1-minute repetition-count protocol — the variant used in respiratory and cardiac clinics — is not its question, and only that unasked slice is carded here, with #7161 cross-pointed. Stop-condition check: the row required a third primary healthy reference dataset beyond the two verified at mining (Chilean sea-level, n=499; high-altitude, n=400); a third was verified this session from its fetched record — Vilarinho 2024, 546 Portuguese adults without disabilities — so the condition is MET. The three datasets agree on shape: medians/counts fall steadily with age (Chilean medians 38 repetitions at 18–29 years falling to 23–24 at 70–80 years, lower limits of normality 15–17 in the oldest group), the Portuguese equation subtracts 0.34 repetitions per year of age, and the high-altitude equations are carded as a SEPARATE limb — altitude and sea-level norms are never merged. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING: all three datasets are from 2024–2025, each is population-bound, and none has been replicated across protocols. The Short Physical Performance Battery shelf (which embeds the five-times variant only) is a further cross-point, not re-carded here.

title: Cystatin C reference intervals: 0.61–1.01 mg/L on ERM-DA471/IFCC-traceable methods (n=304) vs 0.54–1.21 mg/L pre-standardisation (n=270); age moves the upper limit, sex barely does
question: In healthy adults, what is the reference interval for serum / plasma cystatin C — the 2.5th–97.5th percentile range by age and sex — and how much do assay calibration (ERM-DA471/IFCC traceability), population and age move the limits that feed cystatin-C eGFR?
balance: Textbook framing: Boron & Boulpaep, renal physiology / glomerular filtration, and Guyton & Hall, kidney chapters — framing only; the row rests chiefly on the primary reference-interval literature, and says so. Four datasets, three of them healthy blood-donor series from the same Danish group across two calibrator generations, tell one coherent story with a calibration lesson at its centre: pre-standardisation (1998, DAKO PET kit) the common adult interval was 0.54–1.21 mg/L; with the Gentian method traceable to the international calibrator ERM-DA471/IFCC (2018) the common interval narrowed and fell to 0.61–1.01 mg/L. The independent UK donor series (2000) gave 0.51–0.98 mg/L overall, with the upper limit rising after age 50 (0.53–0.92 mg/L under 50; 0.58–1.02 mg/L over 50). The large Chinese health-examination cohort (10,640 healthy adults) centres lower (median 0.73 mg/L; men 0.79, women 0.67) and confirms age, male sex and BMI push values up. Sex differences for cystatin C are small or absent in the donor series — unlike creatinine, whose intervals are sex-split on every card. Pre- and post-standardisation values are NOT interchangeable, and the assay generation is printed beside every interval. This shelf reports the analyte interval only; cystatin-C eGFR prediction is homed at pack #6070 and the CKD shelves. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED

title: Prolactin reference intervals are per-platform: Elecsys monomeric 3.4–18.5 ng/mL (women) / 2.7–13.1 (men), VITROS total 94–500 mIU/L in women, and macroprolactin explained 22.9% of raised totals
question: In healthy adults, what are the reference intervals for total and for monomeric (post-PEG-precipitation) prolactin — by sex and assay platform — and in what fraction of apparently raised prolactin results is macroprolactin the explanation?
balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, pituitary hormone chapters, and Ganong, endocrine physiology — the framing is brief, and this shelf rests chiefly on the primary reference-interval literature, and says so. Three platform-bound datasets: a six-platform study (healthy donors: 96 women, 127 men) that derived parametric total and monomeric (post-PEG) sex-specific intervals for six immunoassays and validated them against gel filtration chromatography — its fetched record does not print the numeric intervals, and this shelf claims none from it, but it establishes that PEG-precipitation macroprolactin screening is required on current automated assays and that misclassification counts differ by platform (Cobas fewest, Architect/Kryptor most among the macroprolactinaemic sera tested); a Chinese Elecsys study that DOES print monomeric intervals (women 3.4–18.5 ng/mL; men 2.7–13.1 ng/mL, from 120 healthy donors of each sex) and found macroprolactinaemia in 261 of 1,140 (22.9%) patients with raised total prolactin; and a Russian VITROS ECi 3600 study (879 healthy subjects) printing total prolactin intervals of 66–436 mIU/L in men and 94–500 mIU/L in women, systematically above the manufacturer's expected values. The fraction of raised results due to macroprolactin is therefore assay- and population-dependent — about a quarter in the one large screened series carded. Pregnancy intervals are NOT this row. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING: the intervals are platform-specific by the evidence's own showing, and only one carded dataset prints monomeric numeric limits. Hyperprolactinaemia treatment is homed at live shelves #2070/#2071, cross-pointed, not re-carded.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING

title: hs-troponin 99th-percentile limits are assay- and rule-bound: NHANES URLs 19 (T) / 13 / 5 / 37 ng/L (I assays) vs manufacturers up to 46.5; outlier removal alone moved Siemens URLs from ~60 to ~13.5 ng/L
question: In healthy adults, what is the 99th-percentile upper reference limit for high-sensitivity cardiac troponin I (and T) — by assay, sex and age — how large is the male–female gap, and how much do reference-population selection rules (imaging / biomarker screening vs questionnaire only) and outlier handling move the limit that defines myocardial injury?
balance: Textbook framing: Boron & Boulpaep, cardiac muscle / excitation — the framing is brief for a measurement row, and this shelf rests chiefly on the primary reference-limit literature, and says so. This is a measurement row only: it carries no ACS diagnostic-pathway recommendations, which live on the chest-pain shelves. The evidence's central fact is that the 99th-percentile upper reference limit (URL) is a property of assay × sex × age × selection rules, not a universal troponin number: in strictly healthy NHANES adults (n=2,746) the hs-cTnT URL matched the manufacturer (19 ng/L) while the three hs-cTnI URLs came out well below manufacturers' (Abbott 13 vs 28 ng/L; Ortho 5 vs 11 ng/L; Siemens 37 vs 46.5 ng/L); in 2,183 healthy Chinese adults the VITROS hs-cTnI URL was 11.1 ng/L overall (men 12.5, women 9.6), higher at age ≥55; in a strictly selected Korean population the two Siemens hs-cTnI URLs were about 60 ng/L BEFORE outlier elimination and about 13.5 ng/L AFTER removing ~8% of samples as outliers — a more than fourfold swing from a statistical rule alone; and the 2024 systematic review (19 studies, 11 hs-cTnI and 9 hs-cTnT assays) found female 99th percentiles below male and overall values in over 90% of hs-cTnI studies and 8 of 9 hs-cTnT studies. URLs were significantly lower under age 40 than at 60+ for all four NHANES assays, and did not differ by race/ethnicity there. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING: the sex gap and assay dependence are consistent, but the limit itself moves severalfold with reference-population selection and outlier handling, so no settled single threshold exists to state.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING

title: NT-proBNP reference intervals (pg/mL = ng/L): 97.5th percentile 225 (men) / 292 (women) at 50–59 years, women up to +150% in their 20s, and 37.4% of healthy over-65s above the 125 cut-off
question: In healthy people, what are the reference intervals for NT-proBNP — the median and 97.5th percentile by age decade and sex — how steeply do values rise with age and differ by sex and ethnicity, and what fraction of healthy people fall below the proposed "natriuretic peptide deficiency" range?
balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, cardiac failure / natriuretic peptide chapters, and Boron & Boulpaep, cardiovascular control — framing only; the row rests chiefly on the primary reference-interval literature, and says so. Values are in pg/mL, which is the same number as ng/L (1 pg/mL = 1 ng/L) — the equivalence is stated on every card. Age dominates this analyte: a single adult interval is misleading, so values are carded per age band. In healthy NHANES adults (1,949 with values in the interval study) the 97.5th percentile at 50–59 years was 225 ng/L in men and 292 ng/L in women; women run higher than men from late adolescence to middle age (in the companion NHANES normative analysis the female–male difference peaked at 150.5% at age 20–30 years), and non-Hispanic Black participants ran lower than White participants (up to 40.2% lower at 30–40 years). In strictly screened community-dwelling older adults (reference sample 441 of 2,459), 37.4% of healthy people over 65 had NT-proBNP above the 125 ng/L heart-failure cut-off, with 97.5th percentiles from 264 to 2,641 ng/L across age/sex strata — the fixed cut-off and the healthy distribution collide in old age. The 'natriuretic peptide deficiency' limb is a distribution fact, not a treatment claim: deficiency was defined as below the cohort's 2.5th percentile and an estimated 9.1 million US individuals fell in that range. A US–Vietnam comparison (1,157 healthy people) found medians of 28 vs 16 ng/L — real but small beside the age effect. The troponin reference shelf is the companion cross-point. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (the age/sex pattern and its size are concordant across four independent populations; the exact 97.5th percentile in the oldest strata remains imprecise, as the older-adult card states).
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED

title: Full blood count intervals must be partitioned: red cells by sex, neutrophils by ancestry — Duffy-null ANC 820–6,370/µL (Namibia) to 1,210–5,390/µL (US), with 21.7–50.9% misclassified as neutropenic by standard ranges
question: In healthy adults, what are the reference intervals for the full blood count — haemoglobin, white cell count and differential (including absolute neutrophil count), and platelet count — by sex, age and ancestry, and how much lower are neutrophil counts in healthy Duffy-null individuals?
balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, blood / white-cell chapters, and Boron & Boulpaep, haematology sections — the framing is brief, and this shelf rests chiefly on the primary reference-interval literature, and says so. Ancestry-specific intervals are the content of this shelf, not a caveat. Three multicentre interval studies (4,642 healthy Han Chinese adults; 750 healthy Japanese adults at seven centres, white-cell parameters; a healthy urban South African population reported by ancestry group under the international C-RIDL protocol) establish sex-specific red-cell intervals and confirm lower white-cell and neutrophil counts in African-ancestry participants — the fetched records of these three report their intervals in full tables and describe their structure and comparisons rather than printing every limit in the abstract, so this shelf cards their design, their comparisons and the numbers their records DO print, and invents none. The numeric centre of the shelf is the Duffy-null study (8,018 healthy Duffy-null adults across four continents): absolute neutrophil count reference intervals of 820–6,370/µL (Namibia), 1,140–5,290/µL (Saudi Arabia), 1,185–5,462/µL (UK) and 1,210–5,390/µL (US), against which institutional intervals misclassified 21.7–50.9% of healthy Duffy-null people as neutropenic. The haemoglobin limb (absorbed into this row under the one-home rule) is the multinational anaemia cut-off evaluation: pooled healthy fifth percentiles of 10.81 g/dL in women (and 9.65 g/dL in children) sat BELOW current WHO cut-offs, with sTfR inflection points at 11.01 g/dL in women. Haemoglobin is in g/dL throughout (g/L = g/dL × 10). PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED for the structure (sex-split red cells; ancestry-split neutrophils; Duffy-null limits), with the per-analyte numeric tables of the three regional studies residing in their full reports, as each card states.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED

title: Steroid panel by LC-MS/MS: intervals are sex-, age- and time-of-day-banded (2,458 healthy subjects); immunoassays agreed with mass spectrometry only patchily — cortisol on Elecsys E170 the exception
question: In healthy humans, what are the reference intervals for serum cortisol and the wider steroid panel when measured by LC-MS/MS — by sex, age and time of day — and how do mass-spectrometry intervals differ from the immunoassay intervals laboratories have historically printed?
balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, adrenocortical hormone chapters, and Ganong, adrenal physiology. Cross-points: pack #6498 (cortisol pulsatility / circadian pattern — a secretion-pattern question) and pack #7084 (cortisol awakening response — a dynamic-response question); neither gives laboratory reference intervals for a timed serum sample, which is this shelf's slice, and neither is re-carded. Three mass-spectrometry datasets: a lifespan LC-MS/MS panel study (2,458 healthy subjects aged 0–77 years, 16 steroid metabolites, cortisol and cortisone quantifiable in at least 90% of samples, with sex- and age-specific intervals modelled across minipuberty, puberty, adulthood and the menopausal transition); an isotope-dilution LC-MS/MS adult study (416 healthy adults) that established adult intervals and showed only the Elecsys E170 cortisol immunoassay agreed with mass spectrometry among the four immunoassays compared, with the other comparisons (testosterone in females, low progesterone, androstenedione, DHEA, 17-hydroxyprogesterone) in poor agreement; and a diurnal study (120 healthy women, 62 healthy men, paired AM/PM samples) showing cortisone, cortisol, corticosterone, 11-deoxycortisol, androstenedione, 17-hydroxyprogesterone and DHEA all differ significantly by time of day in both sexes. Sampling time is therefore part of the interval — a morning and an afternoon cortisol are different measurements, carded per time band — and immunoassay cross-reactivity is the reason this row exists. The fetched records establish and model the intervals but do not print the numeric cortisol limits in their abstracts, so this shelf prints no invented µg/dL or nmol/L limits (the US-units pairing — µg/dL with nmol/L, ×27.59 — is stated for when local MS intervals are read). Pregnancy and oral-contraceptive limbs are separate limbs, not this row. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING: the method conclusion (mass spectrometry over immunoassay; time-banded intervals) is consistent across all three datasets, but the numeric limits themselves are not yet in the fetched record to state as settled.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING

title: 25(OH)D distribution, VDSP-standardised: 13.0% of 55,844 Europeans below 30 nmol/L (12 ng/mL), 40.4% below 50 nmol/L (20 ng/mL); standardisation itself moved Canada's below-50 fraction from 29.0% to 36.8%
question: In general populations, what does the serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D distribution look like — median, spread and the fractions below the deficiency / inadequacy thresholds — by age, sex, ancestry, latitude and season, once values are standardised to the reference measurement procedure (VDSP)?
balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, calcium / vitamin D chapters (framing brief — this shelf rests chiefly on the primary population-survey literature, and says so). This is a DISTRIBUTION shelf, not a supplementation or threshold-recommendation shelf. Four VDSP-era population reports agree on the central lesson: standardisation to the reference measurement procedure moves the whole distribution and reclassifies deficiency — in Canada the fraction below 50 nmol/L (20 ng/mL) rose from 29.0% to 36.8% after standardisation, and in Europe 13.0% of 55,844 people sat below 30 nmol/L (12 ng/mL) on standardised values (40.4% below 50 nmol/L, 20 ng/mL), with a clear winter excess and far higher deficiency in dark-skinned subgroups. Unstandardised historical values are not comparable with VDSP-standardised ones, and that non-comparability is core content. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED

title: SPPB distribution: mean 11.4 (SD 1.3) in 7,474 Norwegians ≥40 with ceiling in every age group, 11.5–11.6 in Singapore, and 8.73 (2.0) in 4,211 Colombians ≥60 — read the distribution, per protocol
question: In community-dwelling adults, what is the distribution of the Short Physical Performance Battery — the 0–12 composite score and its gait-speed, chair-stand and balance subtest scores — by age and sex, and what fraction of healthy older adults score below the conventional ≤9 / ≤10 disability-risk cut-points?
balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, motor control chapters (thin framing — this shelf rests chiefly on the primary normative literature, and says so). Three large community cohorts give the composite 0–12 Short Physical Performance Battery distribution: Tromsø (7,474 Norwegians aged ≥40; mean 11.4, SD 1.3, with a hard ceiling in every age group), Yishun, Singapore (538 adults aged 21–90; means 11.6 in men and 11.5 in women, most adults scoring the maximum) and SABE, Colombia (4,211 adults aged ≥60; mean 8.73, SD 2.0 — a genuinely older, lower-scoring population, not a contradiction). The score is ordinal with a ceiling: the distribution, not the mean alone, is the content, and protocol variants (4-m vs 8-ft gait course) are carded per study. The battery's components are homed separately (gait speed, five-times sit-to-stand pack #7161, single-leg stance) and are cross-pointed, not re-carded. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

title: Normal temperature is not 98.6 °F (37.0 °C): oral mean 98.2 °F (36.8 °C) in 148 volunteers, upper limit 99.9 °F (37.7 °C), diurnal swing 0.9 °F (0.5 °C); review ranges by site put axillary at 95.0–98.5 °F (35.01–36.93 °C)
question: In healthy adults, what is normal body temperature — the mean and the 2.5th–97.5th percentile range by measurement site (oral, axillary, tympanic, core), time of day, age and sex — and how far below 98.6 °F (37.0 °C) does the modern population mean sit?
balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, chapter on body temperature and its regulation, and Boron & Boulpaep, thermoregulation — the classic Wunderlich axioms this shelf re-examines are textbook content. The modern record agrees that 98.6 °F (37.0 °C) is not the population mean: Mackowiak's 148 volunteers gave a mean oral temperature of 98.2 °F (36.8 °C) with an overall upper limit of 99.9 °F (37.7 °C) and a diurnal swing of 0.9 °F (0.5 °C); a systematic review of 7,636 subjects gives site-specific ranges that never merge — oral 96.3–99.3 °F (35.73–37.41 °C), axillary distinctly lower at 95.0–98.5 °F (35.01–36.93 °C) — and older adults run about 0.4 °F (0.23 °C) lower. Site and time of day are part of the measurement. Cross-point pack #6263 (sweating / vasodilation thresholds — thermoregulatory responses, not resting values). PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
