title: MVV (PARTIAL of #7067): means 150.6 L/min in Brazilian men and 103.4 in women; the FEV1 × 35–40 shortcut fails in Chinese adults (fitted multiplier ~45) and at 2,240 m, where ×35 underestimates by ~26% in men
question: In healthy adults, what is maximal voluntary ventilation — measured MVV in litres per minute and its prediction equations by age, sex and height — how well does the FEV1 × 35–40 shortcut approximate measured MVV, and how do values differ at altitude?
balance: PARTIAL — home pack #7067. Pack #7067, read in full, asks maximal inspiratory / expiratory mouth pressures (MIP/MEP) and their weakness cut-offs; maximal voluntary ventilation is not its question, and this shelf cards only the MVV slice. One MVV dataset is already carded inside #7067 — Neder 1999 (PMID 10412550) — it is GATED for this shelf and is NOT re-carded here. Textbook framing: Boron & Boulpaep, respiratory mechanics / ventilatory capacity; Guyton & Hall, ch. 37. Four free datasets (Brazil 243; China 95; Mexico City at 2,240 m, 381; Madras 256) agree that MVV is strongly sex- and age-dependent and that the FEV1 × 35–40 shortcut fails outside its home population: in healthy Chinese adults the fitted multiplier was about 45, and at 2,240 m altitude MVV approached FEV1 × 45, with ×35 underestimating by about 26% in men. Manoeuvre duration (12 s extrapolated to a minute, where stated) is carded per study. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING.

title: Echo reference ranges are population-bound: NORRE limits higher in men and age-dependent, septal e′ <8 cm/s in 55% of healthy ≥60s, INDEA indexed volumes much smaller than Western guidelines, MESA guidelines labelling 81.6% of healthy older adults abnormal
question: In healthy adults, what are echocardiographic chamber-size and Doppler reference ranges — left and right ventricular dimensions and volumes, atrial volumes, wall thickness and the standard diastolic Doppler indices — by age, sex, body size and ethnicity?
balance: Textbook framing: Boron & Boulpaep, cardiac mechanics (framing general — this shelf rests chiefly on the primary normative imaging literature, and says so). Four normative programmes: the EACVI NORRE chamber study (734 healthy volunteers; limits higher in men, age-dependent, mostly persisting after body-surface-area normalisation), the NORRE Doppler study (449 volunteers; septal e′ below 8 cm/s in 55% of healthy people aged ≥60 — a 'disease' cut-off sitting inside normality), INDEA (880 healthy Indians; indexed LV volumes much smaller than the ASE/EACVI 2015 guideline values — ethnicity-specific ranges are content, not caveat) and MESA (608 healthy older adults; current guidelines labelled 81.6% of them abnormal). Indexing changes who counts as dilated, and each card states indexed and unindexed findings as published. The INDEA paper's strain limb is NOT carded here — strain is homed at Slate 9's S9-4-22 shelf; only its chamber data are used. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED

title: DXA T-score reference: the primary NHANES III dataset itself (14,646 adults) carded; Irish BMD matches it, Swedish 25-year-olds sit +0.54 SD above manufacturer reference, and reference choice once swung femoral-neck osteoporosis from 2.3% to 27.6% of patients
question: In healthy adults, what are DXA bone-mineral-density reference values — the young-adult mean and SD at the femoral neck and lumbar spine from which T-scores are calculated, and the BMD distribution by age, sex and ancestry in population samples — and how much does the choice of reference population (NHANES III vs manufacturer vs country-specific) reclassify who has osteoporosis?
balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, bone / calcium metabolism chapters (framing brief — this shelf rests chiefly on the primary densitometry-reference literature, and says so). STOP-CONDITION MET, as printed on the face: the primary NHANES III young-adult proximal-femur reference dataset itself is carded (Looker 1998 — 14,646 US adults from both NHANES III phases, whose non-Hispanic white total-femur data were selected as the reference database for femur standardisation), alongside three further reports (total 4). Around it: Irish proximal-femur BMD proved broadly similar to the NHANES III Caucasian reference (DXA-HIP, 6,729 adults); Swedish 25-year-old women sat ABOVE manufacturer and NHANES III references (Peak-25, n=1,061), arguing for country-specific young-adult data; and in over 2,000 patients the choice of standardisation plus reference set swung femoral-neck osteoporosis classification from 2.3% to 27.6%. This shelf reports reference data and reclassification only — treatment thresholds live on the osteoporosis shelves. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

title: Retinal calibre: MESA means 144.1 ± 14.4 µm arteriolar and 214.0 ± 22.2 µm venular in 5,979 adults; in healthy Asians arterioles run 158.94 µm (Indian), 138.31 µm (Malay), 131.20 µm (Chinese) — ethnicity moves the mean by ~28 µm
question: In general-population adults, what are retinal arteriolar and venular calibres — central retinal arteriolar and venular equivalents (CRAE / CRVE) and the arteriole-to-venule ratio — their means, spreads and percentiles by age, sex, ethnicity and blood pressure, measured from standardised fundus photography?
balance: Textbook framing: Ganong, vision / retinal circulation (thin framing for a population-measurement row — this shelf rests chiefly on the primary population literature, and says so). These are general-population samples, not disease-free cohorts (except the Asian study, which is disease-free by design) — each card states its sampling frame. MESA (5,979 people aged 45–84, four ethnic groups) sets the scale: mean arteriolar calibre 144.1 ± 14.4 µm and venular 214.0 ± 22.2 µm, narrower arterioles with higher blood pressure, and larger calibres in Black and Hispanic participants than in White and Chinese participants. The disease-free Asian study sharpens the ethnic gradient (arterioles: Indians 158.94 µm, Malays 138.31 µm, Chinese 131.20 µm). Grading software and photograph field change values — values are carded per protocol population, and blood-pressure associations are context, not treatment claims. Distinct from the OCT structural shelves and the OCT-angiography pack #7258: calibre is a fundus-photograph measurement in micrometres. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

question: In healthy adults, what is brachial-artery flow-mediated dilatation — the percentage dilatation after cuff-release hyperaemia: its mean, spread and sex-specific percentiles by age — how steeply does it fall with normal ageing, and how do cuff position, occlusion time and baseline diameter move it?
balance: Textbook framing: Boron & Boulpaep, endothelial physiology / vascular control; Guyton & Hall, local control of blood flow. PARTIAL logic, stated on the face: pack #6497, read at question level, asks how NO-mediated endothelium-dependent dilatation is DEMONSTRATED and quantified (forearm acetylcholine / L-NMMA studies and FMD as a method) — a mechanism question giving no normative distribution; this shelf is the distribution slice only and does not re-card #6497's studies. The dedicated reference study (Königstein 2021; 457 healthy non-smokers aged 20–91, sex-specific percentiles) shows FMD falling steeply with age — relative declines of 63.6% in women and 47.1% in men across 20–91 years — and its 6.4% FMD value is a cardiovascular-risk discrimination cut-off in that cohort, NOT a universal normal limit, and is never presented as one here. Supporting limbs are small and print their Ns (four age/sex groups of 16–19; a 30-person fibrinogen study with a short abstract, supporting only). FMD is notoriously protocol-sensitive: values are carded per protocol population and never merged. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING.

title: Clevudine in chronic hepatitis B: potent 12–24-week suppression in three placebo trials (59–92% undetectable, ALT normalisation 68–75%) — and myopathy in 3.9% on longer exposure, the cost that halted development outside South Korea
question: In adults with chronic hepatitis B (HBeAg-positive and HBeAg-negative), does the nucleoside analogue clevudine, compared with placebo or adefovir, suppress HBV DNA and normalise ALT — and what is its myopathy cost?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) for short-term viral suppression — on three Korean placebo-controlled randomised trials (n = 243, 98 and 86) in which 12–24 weeks of clevudine 30 mg daily cut median HBV DNA by about 4.3–5.1 log10 copies/mL against about 0.2–0.5 on placebo, normalised ALT in 68–75% versus 18–33%, and left durable off-therapy suppression. THE MYOPATHY COST STAYS ON THE FACE: clevudine is a single-region programme (developed and marketed in South Korea as Levovir; never FDA-approved), its development elsewhere was halted over myopathy on longer exposure, and in a 102-patient Korean series on treatment beyond 6 months, myopathy developed in 3.9% (reversible on stopping) and resistance reached 11% by 60 weeks. The trials carded here ran only 12–24 weeks — too short to show that harm. The emtricitabine-plus-clevudine combination trial is a different question and is not counted or carded here.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — for short-term (12–24 week) HBV DNA suppression and ALT normalisation in three Korean placebo-controlled trials (median reductions about 4.3–5.1 vs 0.2–0.5 log10 copies/mL); single-region programme (Levovir, South Korea; never FDA-approved) whose development elsewhere was halted over myopathy — 3.9% on longer exposure, reversible — with resistance in 11% by 60 weeks

title: Entecavir + adefovir rescue in lamivudine-resistant HBV: 29% vs 4% below 60 IU/mL at 52 weeks vs continuing lamivudine + adefovir, rising to 42% by 104 weeks — a historical-era answer on one randomised programme
question: In adults with lamivudine-resistant chronic hepatitis B (including suboptimal responders to lamivudine plus adefovir and multiple-drug-refractory infection), does entecavir plus adefovir combination rescue therapy, compared with lamivudine plus adefovir or adefovir-based strategies, achieve virological response?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a historical-era question, printed on the face: lamivudine resistance is now uncommon where entecavir / tenofovir are first-line, and this shelf answers the rescue question as it stood in that era, in small single-region trials (Korea / China lineage). One randomised programme (Lim: 90 patients who had suboptimal response to lamivudine plus adefovir) found entecavir plus adefovir clearly superior to continuing lamivudine plus adefovir at 52 weeks — virological response 29% vs 4%, mean HBV DNA reduction −2.2 vs −0.6 log10 IU/mL, new resistance mutations 0% vs 15% — and its 104-week extension (the same trial, labelled as such, not a second trial) showed progressive response once both arms received the combination. A three-way comparison (91 patients) points the same way. One commissioned anchor was REFUSED: the Heo 2014 randomised trial (PMID 25587617) has an empty abstract in its PubMed record, so no numbers could be verified from the record this session and it is not carded — the refusal is stated on the Synthesis card. The ACE study (add adefovir vs switch to entecavir, PMID 23295056) asks a different strategy question and is cross-pointed, not carded.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — entecavir plus adefovir beat continuing lamivudine plus adefovir in one randomised rescue programme (virological response 29% vs 4% at 52 weeks; extension to 104 weeks and a concordant three-way comparison), on a small single-region base answering a historical-era question; one commissioned anchor (PMID 25587617) refused for an empty abstract record

title: Lorundrostat phase 3 programme in uncontrolled hypertension (PARTIAL vs live #743): Launch-HTN — office systolic pressure fell a placebo-adjusted 9.1 mm Hg; Advance-HTN — 24-hour systolic pressure fell 7.9 mm Hg at the stable 50 mg dose; a two-trial, surrogate-endpoint base
question: In adults with uncontrolled or treatment-resistant hypertension, does the aldosterone synthase inhibitor lorundrostat, compared with placebo on background therapy, lower blood pressure in its phase 3 programme (Launch-HTN; Advance-HTN)? (PARTIAL — the phase 3 slice of live shelf #743, which cards lorundrostat's phase 2 Target-HTN trial and the class question.)
balance: PARTIAL shelf — LIKELY (benefit) for blood-pressure lowering, on a FLOOR-RISK base of exactly 2 reports from 2 distinct trials, stated here on the face. This shelf cards ONLY lorundrostat's phase 3 programme; lorundrostat's phase 2 Target-HTN trial is carded at live shelf #743 (the aldosterone-synthase class question, with baxdrostat) and is NOT re-carded here (one-home rule) — #743 is cross-pointed, and this shelf is the phase 3 slice #743 fenced rather than carded. Launch-HTN (phase 3, 1,083 randomised): pooled lorundrostat 50 mg lowered automated office systolic pressure by a least-squares mean difference of −9.1 mm Hg versus placebo at week 6. Advance-HTN (285 randomised; its PubMed record types it Clinical Trial, Phase II — that designation is printed on its card, not silently upgraded): placebo-adjusted 24-hour systolic reductions of −7.9 mm Hg (stable 50 mg dose) and −6.5 mm Hg (dose-adjustment group) at week 12. Harms were the class harms: hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and reduced kidney function occurred more often on lorundrostat, with small numbers of discontinuations for each. Blood pressure is a surrogate endpoint; no cardiovascular-outcomes trial exists for lorundrostat or its class — printed here, as at #743.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — lorundrostat's phase 3 programme (carded here as a PARTIAL slice of live shelf #743, which holds the phase 2 and class evidence) lowered systolic pressure beyond placebo in two distinct randomised trials: Launch-HTN (phase 3, n=1,083) by a placebo-adjusted 9.1 mm Hg in office pressure at week 6, and Advance-HTN (n=285; typed phase II in its PubMed record) by 7.9 mm Hg (stable dose) and 6.5 mm Hg (dose-adjustment) in 24-hour pressure at week 12; benefit is on the blood-pressure surrogate only — no outcomes trial exists — and hyperkalaemia, hyponatraemia and reduced kidney function were more frequent on lorundrostat. FLOOR-RISK base: exactly 2 reports / 2 trials, stated on the face

title: Lamivudine as treatment for chronic hepatitis B — a superseded first-line agent (YMDD resistance): NEJM trials showed HBV DNA suppression (44% vs 16% sustained), ALT normalisation and histologic improvement over placebo
question: In patients with chronic hepatitis B (HBeAg-positive initial treatment; advanced liver disease; and children), does lamivudine, compared with placebo or interferon-era controls, suppress HBV DNA, normalise ALT and slow liver-disease progression — and at what resistance cost?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) in its era, on three placebo-controlled NEJM trials — and a historical-foundation shelf: lamivudine is a SUPERSEDED first-line agent because viral resistance (YMDD) emerges on continued therapy, and that history leads this face. Dienstag 1995 (preliminary, 32 patients): 100 mg and 300 mg doses made HBV DNA undetectable in 100% of patients during 12 weeks, but DNA reappeared in most after stopping. Dienstag 1999 (US initial treatment, 143 randomised, 52 weeks): histologic response 52% vs 23% on placebo, sustained HBV DNA suppression 44% vs 16%, ALT normalisation 41% vs 7%. Jonas 2002 (children, 288 randomised): virologic response 23% vs 13%. The fetched trial reports do not print a resistance rate, so none is printed here; the resistance cost is stated qualitatively, as the commissioning row records it. The advanced-liver-disease NEJM trial of lamivudine is carded in the live library and is cross-pointed in the synthesis only — it is NOT carded on this shelf (gate discipline). Lamivudine's HIV and chemotherapy-prophylaxis questions live on other shelves and are not re-carded here.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — three placebo-controlled NEJM trials (a 32-patient preliminary dose-ranging trial, a 143-patient US initial-treatment trial and a 288-child trial) consistently showed lamivudine suppresses HBV DNA, normalises ALT and improves histology in chronic hepatitis B; the stamp is historical — lamivudine is a superseded first-line agent because YMDD resistance accumulates on continued therapy (the carded reports print no resistance rate, so none is claimed), and the advanced-liver-disease trial is carded in the live library and cross-pointed, not re-carded here

title: Adefovir dipivoxil in chronic hepatitis B — a superseded agent: histologic improvement 53–64% vs 25–33% on placebo and HBV DNA suppression in both NEJM trials; stopping lost the benefit, resistance reached 5.9% by 144 weeks
question: In adults with chronic hepatitis B (HBeAg-positive and HBeAg-negative), does adefovir dipivoxil, compared with placebo, suppress HBV DNA and improve liver histology?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) in its era, on two NEJM placebo-controlled trials plus the HBeAg-negative programme's long-term extension report (labelled as extension lineage on its card) — and a historical shelf: adefovir is a SUPERSEDED agent (nephrotoxicity at higher doses; resistance emerging on long therapy), printed here on the face. Marcellin 2003 (HBeAg-positive, 515 randomised): histologic improvement 53% on adefovir 10 mg vs 25% on placebo, with HBV DNA undetectable in 21% vs 0%. Hadziyannis 2003 (HBeAg-negative, 185 randomised): histologic improvement 64% vs 33%, HBV DNA below 400 copies/mL in 51% vs 0%, ALT normalisation 72% vs 29%. The 2005 long-term report (the same HBeAg-negative programme, continued): benefit was maintained to 144 weeks on continued therapy (HBV DNA <1,000 copies/mL in 79%) and lost in most patients switched to placebo; resistance mutations (rtN236T, rtA181V) had emerged in 5.9% by 144 weeks. At the licensed 10 mg dose the 48-week safety profile resembled placebo; the 30 mg dose produced more adverse events and renal laboratory abnormalities. Tenofovir-versus-adefovir is a tenofovir question, cross-pointed in the synthesis, not carded here.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — two independent NEJM placebo-controlled trials (HBeAg-positive, n=515; HBeAg-negative, n=185) showed adefovir dipivoxil 10 mg improves liver histology (53% and 64% vs 25% and 33%), suppresses HBV DNA and normalises ALT at 48 weeks, and the HBeAg-negative programme's extension report (labelled lineage, not a third trial) showed benefit maintained to 144 weeks on continued therapy and lost on stopping; the stamp is historical — adefovir is superseded, with renal laboratory abnormalities at the 30 mg dose and resistance mutations in 5.9% by 144 weeks

title: Telbivudine vs lamivudine in chronic hepatitis B — ONE PROGRAMME ONLY (GLOBE): superior therapeutic response and DNA suppression at 1 and 2 years, more creatine-kinase elevation; withdrawn from the US market in 2016
question: In adults with chronic hepatitis B, does telbivudine, compared with lamivudine, achieve greater HBV DNA suppression and therapeutic response (GLOBE programme) — and at what cost in creatine-kinase elevation, myopathy and peripheral neuropathy?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) versus lamivudine — ONE-PROGRAMME flag, printed on the face: every report carded here comes from the single GLOBE trial programme (its 1-year primary, its 2-year report, and a programme renal-function secondary analysis, labelled as such), so there is no independent replication. Within GLOBE, telbivudine was superior to lamivudine: therapeutic response at 1 year in HBeAg-positive patients 75.3% vs 67.0%, and at 2 years 63% vs 48% (HBeAg-positive) and 78% vs 66% (HBeAg-negative), with deeper HBV DNA suppression and less viral resistance (2-year resistance 25.1% vs 39.5% in HBeAg-positive patients). The cost was muscle: grade 3/4 creatine-kinase elevations were more common on telbivudine (12.9% vs 4.1% at 2 years). Telbivudine was withdrawn from the US market in 2016 (commercial withdrawal) and carries a boxed-warning history for myopathy and peripheral neuropathy, especially with interferon — printed here as the commissioning row records it. The renal report's eGFR improvement is a secondary analysis of programme data, not an independent renal trial.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — telbivudine was superior to lamivudine on therapeutic response, HBV DNA suppression and resistance at 1 and 2 years, but the entire base is ONE programme (the single GLOBE trial and its reports, flagged on the face), the comparator is itself a superseded agent, grade 3/4 creatine-kinase elevations were more frequent on telbivudine (12.9% vs 4.1%), and telbivudine was withdrawn from the US market in 2016 with a myopathy/peripheral-neuropathy warning history; the renal report is a labelled secondary analysis and carries no independent weight

title: WITHDRAWN — Sibutramine for obesity: dose-related weight loss and better maintenance (STORM), but SCOUT showed more nonfatal myocardial infarction and stroke in high-risk patients (11.4% vs 10.0%) and it was withdrawn in 2010
question: In adults with overweight or obesity (including patients at high cardiovascular risk), does the serotonin–noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor sibutramine, compared with placebo plus lifestyle intervention, produce and maintain weight loss — and what was its cardiovascular-outcomes profile (SCOUT)?
balance: WITHDRAWN — that status leads this shelf. Sibutramine (Meridia/Reductil) was withdrawn in 2010 after SCOUT, and LIKELY (harm) is the governing stamp for the high-risk population SCOUT studied. The efficacy side is real: Bray 1999 (1,047 randomised, 24 weeks) showed dose-related weight loss (completers: 6.1% of body weight at 10 mg, 7.4% at 15 mg, vs 1.2% on placebo), and STORM showed sibutramine maintained weight loss better than placebo after an initial loss (43% vs 16% of completers kept at least 80% of the loss at 2 years). The outcomes side overrides it in high-risk patients: SCOUT (9,804 randomised, age ≥55 with cardiovascular disease and/or type 2 diabetes, mean treatment 3.4 years) found the primary cardiovascular outcome in 11.4% on sibutramine vs 10.0% on placebo (hazard ratio 1.16 — a relative measure; the absolute difference was 1.4 percentage points), driven by nonfatal myocardial infarction (4.1% vs 3.2%; HR 1.28, relative) and nonfatal stroke (2.6% vs 1.9%; HR 1.36, relative), with no increase in cardiovascular or all-cause death. Populations differ and are printed exactly: the weight-loss trials were in lower-risk obesity; SCOUT's harm was in high-risk patients and must not be generalised beyond that population without saying so. A labelled SCOUT secondary analysis (weight loss itself associated with lower subsequent risk) is carded as programme support, not as an independent trial.
stamp: WITHDRAWN (2010) — LIKELY (harm): sibutramine (Meridia/Reductil) was withdrawn after SCOUT (9,804 randomised high-risk patients) showed a higher primary cardiovascular outcome rate on sibutramine than placebo (11.4% vs 10.0%; hazard ratio 1.16, a relative measure), driven by nonfatal myocardial infarction (4.1% vs 3.2%) and nonfatal stroke (2.6% vs 1.9%) with no increase in death; its weight-loss efficacy (dose-related in Bray 1999; maintenance in STORM) is real but does not offset that harm, and SCOUT's harm figure belongs to its high-risk population, as printed on the face

title: WITHDRAWN 1997 — Fenfluramine and dexfenfluramine for obesity: modest short-term weight loss (ISIS n=822; 3–7 kg in comparator trials), withdrawn worldwide for valvular heart disease and pulmonary hypertension
question: In adults with obesity, do the serotonergic appetite suppressants fenfluramine and dexfenfluramine, compared with placebo (or active comparators), produce weight loss?
balance: WITHDRAWN 1997 — that status leads this shelf. Fenfluramine and dexfenfluramine were withdrawn worldwide in 1997 after the valvular-heart-disease and pulmonary-hypertension signals; nothing in the modest efficacy record below rehabilitates them as obesity treatment. The efficacy base is old (1989–1998) and short: ISIS (822 patients, dexfenfluramine 15 mg twice daily — 30 mg/day — plus diet vs placebo; the report carded is the 6-month interim of a planned 1-year trial, published in a French-language journal and carded here from its English abstract, as printed on its card) found about twice as many dexfenfluramine patients achieved an important weight loss, with greater cumulative loss, but its abstract prints no kilogram figure and none is claimed here. The active-comparator trials quantify the size of effect: dexfenfluramine lost 3.2 kg in 12 weeks against sibutramine's 4.5 kg (Hanotin 1998), and 6.9 kg in 15 weeks against an ephedrine/caffeine combination's 8.3 kg (Breum 1994); a small combination trial (n=33, printed on its card) found adding dexfenfluramine to fluoxetine lost more than fluoxetine alone. These obesity doses (15 mg twice daily) were far higher than the low-dose fenfluramine used for Dravet and Lennox–Gastaut syndromes at live shelf #992 — a different population and question, cross-pointed in the synthesis and never merged or re-carded here.
stamp: WITHDRAWN (1997) — POSSIBLE (benefit) for short-term weight loss only: fenfluramine and dexfenfluramine were withdrawn worldwide in 1997 after valvular-heart-disease and pulmonary-hypertension signals, and that withdrawal leads this stamp; the carded 1989–1998 evidence shows only modest short-term weight loss at obesity doses (dexfenfluramine 15 mg twice daily: 3.2 kg in 12 weeks and 6.9 kg in 15 weeks in active-comparator trials; the placebo-controlled ISIS interim report gives proportions, no kilogram figure), on an old, short-duration base. The low-dose epilepsy use at live shelf #992 is a different question and is not covered by this stamp

title: WITHDRAWN 2000 — Troglitazone in type 2 diabetes: real insulin-sensitising, glucose-lowering efficacy (approximately 20% lower glucose at 400–600 mg), withdrawn for hepatocellular injury including liver-failure deaths
question: In adults with type 2 diabetes, does the thiazolidinedione troglitazone, compared with placebo (alone or added to sulfonylurea therapy), improve glycaemic control?
balance: WITHDRAWN — that status leads this shelf. Troglitazone (Rezulin) was withdrawn in 2000 for idiosyncratic hepatocellular injury, including liver-failure deaths; the glycaemic efficacy below is historical and does not rehabilitate the drug. Maggs 1998 (randomised placebo-controlled monotherapy, 93 patients, 6 months): troglitazone 400 mg and 600 mg lowered fasting and postprandial glucose by approximately 20% (as reported) and increased insulin-stimulated glucose disposal by approximately 45%, in clamp studies. Ghazzi 1997 (Troglitazone Study Group, 154 patients, 48 weeks vs glyburide): no increase in left ventricular mass, with long-term HbA1c and C-peptide improvement (its abstract prints no HbA1c figures, so none are claimed here). Fonseca 2000 — OPEN-LABEL extension studies, labelled as such: at a fixed 600 mg dose, HbA1c changes from baseline were −0.4% (monotherapy), −1.8% (with sulfonylurea) and −1.0% (with insulin), in patients who had completed the parent double-blind studies (758 completed the extensions). FENCE, printed here so it cannot be missed: the Diabetes Prevention Program troglitazone report is a diabetes-ONSET question in prediabetes; it is NOT carded on this treatment shelf, and any diabetes-onset wording for it says 'delay', never 'prevent'.
stamp: WITHDRAWN (2000) — POSSIBLE (benefit) for glycaemic control: troglitazone (Rezulin) was withdrawn in 2000 for idiosyncratic hepatocellular injury including liver-failure deaths, and that withdrawal leads this stamp; the carded record shows real glycaemic efficacy (approximately 20% lower fasting and postprandial glucose at 400–600 mg in a 6-month placebo-controlled metabolic trial; HbA1c −0.4% to −1.8% at 600 mg in labelled open-label extensions, completers only), which is historical and does not rehabilitate the drug. The Diabetes Prevention Program onset report is fenced — not carded here — and any onset wording says 'delay', never 'prevent'

title: Aleglitazar in type 2 diabetes — DISCONTINUED programme: SYNCHRONY lowered HbA1c dose-dependently, but AleCardio showed no cardiovascular benefit (HR 0.96) with more renal dysfunction and GI haemorrhage, and was terminated early
question: In adults with type 2 diabetes (including patients stabilised after an acute coronary syndrome), does the dual PPAR-α/γ agonist aleglitazar, compared with placebo on standard therapy, improve glycaemic control and reduce cardiovascular events (SYNCHRONY / AleCardio programme)?
balance: SPLIT, on a discontinued programme — that history leads this face. This is a programme-level shelf holding two questions, as the commissioning row directs: glycaemia (SYNCHRONY) and post-ACS cardiovascular outcomes (AleCardio). Glycaemia: SYNCHRONY (phase II, 332 randomised, 16 weeks) showed dose-dependent HbA1c lowering versus placebo, from −0.36% at 50 µg to −1.35% at 600 µg, with dose-dependent oedema, haemodilution and weight gain. Outcomes: AleCardio (phase 3, 7,226 patients with type 2 diabetes after an acute coronary syndrome) was TERMINATED EARLY for futility plus safety signals, and showed no cardiovascular benefit — primary endpoint 9.5% on aleglitazar vs 10.0% on placebo (hazard ratio 0.96, a relative measure; 95% CI 0.83 to 1.11; P=.57) — with more renal dysfunction (7.4% vs 2.7%), more gastrointestinal haemorrhage (2.4% vs 1.7%) and numerically more heart failure (3.4% vs 2.8%). Programme support carded and labelled: a renal study at the supratherapeutic 600 µg dose (measured GFR fell 16.9%, reversible on stopping) and an AleCardio exposure–response secondary analysis (not an independent trial). Distinct-trial count is 3 (SYNCHRONY, AleCardio, the renal study) with 4 cardable reports; the two AleCardio reports are one trial reported twice and are labelled as such. Aleglitazar was never marketed.
stamp: SPLIT — aleglitazar lowered HbA1c dose-dependently in the SYNCHRONY phase II study (−0.36% at 50 µg to −1.35% at 600 µg vs placebo), but in AleCardio (7,226 post-ACS patients) it showed no difference in cardiovascular outcomes (9.5% vs 10.0%; hazard ratio 0.96, a relative measure) with more renal dysfunction (7.4% vs 2.7%) and gastrointestinal haemorrhage (2.4% vs 1.7%); AleCardio was terminated early for futility and safety and the programme was discontinued, never marketed. The renal and exposure–response cards are labelled programme reports, not independent trials

title: Evogliptin in type 2 diabetes (single-region evidence — South Korea/India, not FDA/EMA-approved): non-inferior to sitagliptin and linagliptin on HbA1c, and superior to placebo added to dapagliflozin plus metformin; no outcomes trial
question: In adults with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled on metformin (or on metformin-based combinations), does the DPP-4 inhibitor evogliptin, compared with sitagliptin or placebo, improve glycaemic control?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) for glycaemic control, on four randomised trials — with two framings printed on the face: this is SINGLE-REGION evidence (South Korea and India; evogliptin is approved there, not FDA/EMA-approved), and HbA1c is a surrogate endpoint with no cardiovascular-outcomes trial for this agent (class outcomes evidence lives on the sitagliptin/linagliptin shelves and is not re-carded here). Three trials are active-comparator non-inferiority studies: EVERGREEN (207 patients, vs linagliptin — the comparator is linagliptin, printed exactly) found HbA1c −0.85% vs −0.75% (difference −0.10%, 95% CI −0.32 to 0.11, within the 0.4% margin); Hong 2017 (222 patients, added to metformin, vs sitagliptin) found −0.59% vs −0.65% (difference 0.06%, 95% CI −0.10 to 0.22, within the 0.35% margin); EVOLUTION INDIA (184 patients, added to metformin, vs sitagliptin) likewise met non-inferiority at 12 weeks. The fourth is placebo-controlled superiority: added to dapagliflozin plus metformin (283 patients), evogliptin beat placebo by a least-squares mean HbA1c difference of −0.65% at week 24 and −0.55% at week 52. Adverse events and hypoglycaemia were comparable to comparators across the trials.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — evogliptin 5 mg improved glycaemic control across four randomised trials: non-inferior to sitagliptin added to metformin (difference 0.06%, 95% CI −0.10 to 0.22; and −0.022% in EVOLUTION INDIA) and to linagliptin (−0.10%, 95% CI −0.32 to 0.11), and superior to placebo when added to dapagliflozin plus metformin (−0.65% at week 24, −0.55% at week 52); the benefit is on the HbA1c surrogate only, the evidence is single-region (South Korea/India; not FDA/EMA-approved), and no cardiovascular-outcomes trial exists for this agent

title: Gemigliptin in type 2 diabetes (renal impairment included): HbA1c −0.66 points vs placebo on dapagliflozin + metformin; no difference vs linagliptin in renal impairment; BALANCE is a combination read
question: In adults with type 2 diabetes (including patients with renal impairment and patients on metformin-based combinations), does the DPP-4 inhibitor gemigliptin, compared with sitagliptin, linagliptin or placebo, improve glycaemic control?
balance: POSSIBLE benefit, on a single-region (South Korea) base with a surrogate endpoint. Gemigliptin is a DPP-4 inhibitor approved in South Korea and some other markets, not FDA/EMA-approved; HbA1c is a surrogate and no cardiovascular-outcomes trial exists for this agent. The one clean placebo-controlled read is SOLUTION: added to dapagliflozin plus metformin, gemigliptin lowered HbA1c by 0.66 points more than placebo at 24 weeks (315 randomised). In renal impairment, the GUARD extension found no significant difference between continued gemigliptin and a switch to linagliptin at 52 weeks (HbA1c reductions 1.00 vs 0.65 points from baseline; between-group P=0.148). BALANCE is carded third and is labelled throughout as a fixed-dose COMBINATION read (gemigliptin/rosuvastatin) — it is not gemigliptin-alone evidence. Adverse-event rates were similar across arms in all three reports.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — gemigliptin lowered HbA1c versus placebo as add-on to dapagliflozin + metformin (SOLUTION, −0.66 points at 24 weeks) and matched linagliptin in renal impairment (GUARD extension), but the base is single-region (South Korea), HbA1c is a surrogate, no outcomes trial exists, and the BALANCE report is a fixed-dose combination read labelled as such

title: Teneligliptin in type 2 diabetes: HbA1c 0.71–0.94 points lower than placebo across four East Asian phase 3 trials, alone and added to metformin
question: In adults with type 2 diabetes (drug-naïve, on metformin, or on metformin-based combinations), does the DPP-4 inhibitor teneligliptin, compared with placebo, improve glycaemic control?
balance: LIKELY benefit for glycaemic control only, on a single-region (East Asian) base with a surrogate endpoint. Teneligliptin is a DPP-4 inhibitor approved in Japan, India, Korea and China, not FDA/EMA-approved; HbA1c is a surrogate and no cardiovascular-outcomes trial exists for this agent. Four randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 3 trials agree: teneligliptin 20 mg lowered HbA1c by 0.71 to 0.94 points more than placebo over 16–24 weeks, as monotherapy in Chinese and Korean patients and added to metformin in Chinese and Korean patients. Fasting glucose fell in parallel, and adverse-event and hypoglycaemia rates were similar to placebo in every report.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit, glycaemic control only) — four randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 3 trials in China and Korea consistently show teneligliptin 20 mg lowers HbA1c by 0.71–0.94 points more than placebo over 16–24 weeks, alone or added to metformin, with placebo-like safety; HbA1c is a surrogate, the base is single-region (East Asia), and no outcomes trial exists

title: Anagliptin in type 2 diabetes: HbA1c −0.80 points vs placebo on metformin + empagliflozin; REASON is open-label with an LDL endpoint (−4.5 mg/dL vs sitagliptin)
question: In adults with type 2 diabetes, does the DPP-4 inhibitor anagliptin, compared with sitagliptin or placebo (alone, with metformin, or added to metformin plus an SGLT2 inhibitor), improve glycaemic control and glycaemic variability?
balance: POSSIBLE benefit, on a single-region (Japan/Korea) base with surrogate endpoints. Anagliptin is a DPP-4 inhibitor approved in Japan, not FDA/EMA-approved; HbA1c is a surrogate and no cardiovascular-outcomes trial exists for this agent. The REASON trial is OPEN-LABEL with an LDL-cholesterol primary endpoint — labelled as such on its card and here: anagliptin lowered LDL cholesterol by 4.5 mg/dL more than sitagliptin over 52 weeks, with HbA1c non-inferior (a secondary endpoint). A small double-blind trial found the twice-daily anagliptin regimen improved glycaemic variability (MAGE, post-dinner time in range) more than once-daily sitagliptin, with no HbA1c difference. The strongest glycaemic read is the 2026 phase 3 trial: added to metformin plus empagliflozin, anagliptin lowered HbA1c by 0.80 points more than placebo at 24 weeks.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — anagliptin lowered HbA1c by 0.80 points versus placebo added to metformin + empagliflozin in one phase 3 trial, and twice-daily dosing improved glycaemic variability versus once-daily sitagliptin, but REASON — its longest trial — is open-label with an LDL-cholesterol primary endpoint and only a −4.5 mg/dL absolute difference; single-region (Japan/Korea) evidence, surrogate endpoints, no outcomes trial

title: Piclidenoson (CF101) in plaque psoriasis: COMFORT-1 PASI 75 was 9.7% vs 2.6% on placebo, and the phase II/III trial missed its primary endpoint — modest effects, placebo-like safety
question: In adults with moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis, does the oral A3 adenosine-receptor agonist piclidenoson (CF101), compared with placebo (or apremilast in the phase 2/3 lineage), improve psoriasis severity (PASI response)?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence). Piclidenoson (CF101, Can-Fite — the specific tested product, named under the clarification exception because the agent is not FDA/EMA-approved for psoriasis) is an oral A3 adenosine-receptor agonist developed over a long, slow programme (2012–2024). The responses are modest throughout: the exploratory phase 2 trial's best dose (2 mg) achieved PASI 50 in 35.3%; the phase II/III trial MISSED its primary endpoint (PASI 75 at week 12: 8.5% vs 6.9% on placebo, P=0.621); and the phase 3 COMFORT-1 trial met its primary endpoint only at the 3 mg dose with a PASI 75 rate of 9.7% versus 2.6% on placebo (P=0.037) — far below the response rates of the biologic-era psoriasis treatments homed on their own shelves (cross-pointed in prose, not re-carded). Safety was consistently placebo-like and is the programme's strongest feature.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — piclidenoson (CF101) met COMFORT-1's primary endpoint only at 3 mg with a modest PASI 75 rate of 9.7% versus 2.6% on placebo, its phase II/III trial missed the same endpoint (8.5% vs 6.9%), and the phase 2 signal rests on 75 patients; safety is consistently placebo-like, but the efficacy base is weak and the agent is not FDA/EMA-approved for psoriasis

title: Glycopyrronium monotherapy in COPD (GLOW programme): trough FEV1 ~100 mL above placebo, dyspnoea and health status improved, exacerbations down 31–34% in relative terms
question: In adults with moderate-to-severe COPD, does once-daily inhaled glycopyrronium bromide (50 µg, NVA237) versus placebo — or versus tiotropium — improve lung function, dyspnoea and exacerbations?
balance: LIKELY benefit, from a single programme (GLOW) — two trials reported directly plus their pooled analysis, which is a programme report and not a third trial. Once-daily glycopyrronium bromide 50 µg (NVA237) improved trough FEV1 versus placebo by 108 mL at week 12 in GLOW1 (822 randomised) and by 97 mL in GLOW2 (1,066 randomised), with improved dyspnoea and health status and a 31% relative reduction in the risk of a first moderate/severe exacerbation in GLOW1 and 34% relative reduction in moderate-to-severe exacerbations in GLOW2 (both secondary endpoints; absolute exacerbation rates are not given in the fetched records). In GLOW2 glycopyrronium was comparable to open-label tiotropium on all outcomes. Primary endpoints are lung function at 12 weeks; the indacaterol–glycopyrronium combination and triple-therapy questions stay homed on their own shelves (live #1644, #1033) and are not re-carded here.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — in the single GLOW programme, glycopyrronium 50 µg once daily improved trough FEV1 by ~100 mL versus placebo in two trials (822 and 1,066 randomised), improved dyspnoea and health status, reduced moderate/severe exacerbations by 31–34% in relative terms on secondary endpoints, and matched open-label tiotropium; the pooled analysis is a programme report, not a third trial

title: Olodaterol monotherapy in COPD: FEV1 improved vs placebo in two replicate 48-week trials (one publication); one-year pooled safety comparable to placebo; licensed dose 5 µg
question: In adults with GOLD 2–4 COPD, does once-daily olodaterol (5 or 10 µg via Respimat) versus placebo improve lung function over 48 weeks, and how does it compare with its fixed-dose partner tiotropium as a mono-component?
balance: LIKELY benefit for lung function, from a single programme. The floor of this shelf is three reports: two replicate 48-week trials published as ONE publication, a mono-component comparison from the tiotropium/olodaterol combination programme (TONADO), and a pre-specified pooled one-year safety analysis — stated plainly so the replicate trials are never double-counted. Olodaterol 5 µg and 10 µg once daily via Respimat significantly improved FEV1 AUC0–3 and trough FEV1 versus placebo at week 12 in both replicate trials (624 and 642 patients evaluated), on top of usual-care background therapy. The licensed dose is 5 µg; the 10 µg arm is a trial dose and is labelled as such wherever it appears. In TONADO, the fixed-dose combination beat its mono-components — that comparison is carded for what it shows about the olodaterol component, not as combination evidence. Pooled safety over 48 weeks (3,104 patients) was comparable to placebo and formoterol.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit, lung function) — two replicate 48-week placebo-controlled trials (one publication; 624 and 642 patients evaluated) show olodaterol 5 µg and 10 µg significantly improve FEV1 responses, pooled one-year safety in 3,104 patients is comparable to placebo and formoterol, and TONADO shows the fixed-dose combination beats the olodaterol mono-component; the licensed dose is 5 µg and the 10 µg arm is a trial dose

title: Indacaterol monotherapy in COPD: trough FEV1 170–180 mL above placebo across three trials, ahead of salmeterol and formoterol; no exacerbation-outcome trial exists
question: In adults with moderate-to-severe COPD, does once-daily indacaterol (150 or 300 µg) versus placebo — or versus tiotropium, salmeterol or formoterol — improve lung function and symptoms?
balance: LIKELY benefit for lung function and symptoms, from a 2010–2011 programme with lung-function and symptom endpoints — no exacerbation-outcome or mortality trial of indacaterol monotherapy exists, and that absence is stated on the face. Once-daily indacaterol raised trough FEV1 versus placebo by 180 mL at week 12 in INHANCE (1,683 randomised; both 150 and 300 µg), by 170 mL versus placebo and 60 mL versus twice-daily salmeterol in INLIGHT-2 (1,002 randomised), and by 170 mL versus placebo and 100 mL versus twice-daily formoterol in the one-year Dahl trial (1,732 randomised), with dyspnoea and health-status improvements. The tiotropium arm of INHANCE was open-label — stated on its card. This is one of three separate once-daily bronchodilator monotherapy shelves (with glycopyrronium, #7347, and olodaterol, #7348); the indacaterol–glycopyrronium combination and triple-therapy questions stay homed elsewhere (live #1644, #1033).
stamp: LIKELY (benefit, lung function and symptoms) — three randomised trials (1,683, 1,002 and 1,732 patients) consistently show once-daily indacaterol raises trough FEV1 by 170–180 mL versus placebo and by 60–100 mL versus twice-daily salmeterol/formoterol, with dyspnoea and health-status improvements; a 2010–2011 programme with no exacerbation-outcome or mortality trial, and INHANCE's tiotropium arm was open-label

title: Arformoterol (nebulised) in COPD: trough FEV1 beat placebo across four 12-week trials in three reports; one open-label year shows no tolerance, more tremor than salmeterol
question: In adults with moderate-to-severe COPD, does twice-daily nebulised arformoterol (the (R,R)-enantiomer of formoterol) versus placebo — or versus salmeterol/formoterol — improve airway function, and is long-term use safe?
balance: LIKELY benefit for airway function, with one-year safety data. Arformoterol is the (R,R)-enantiomer of formoterol given as a nebulised solution (marketed as Brovana — the specific tested product, named under the clarification exception because the nebulised delivery is the point of the question). The floor is three reports covering at least four trials: two 12-week trials pooled in one publication (1,456 subjects), a separate 12-week placebo- and active-controlled trial (717 patients), and a one-year open-label safety comparison against salmeterol (793 treated) — the two-trials-one-publication report counts as one publication, stated on the face. Nebulised arformoterol improved trough FEV1 versus placebo by 10.9–15.4 percentage points across doses over 12 weeks, improved dyspnoea versus placebo where salmeterol did not reach significance, and over one year showed no increase in exacerbation frequency and no clinically meaningful tolerance; tremor was more frequent than with salmeterol (13.4% vs 1.1%). Endpoints are airway function and safety/tolerance, not exacerbations or mortality.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit, airway function) — nebulised arformoterol beat placebo on trough FEV1 across at least four 12-week trials in three reports (1,456 pooled subjects and 717 patients), improved dyspnoea versus placebo, and showed stable one-year safety in an open-label comparison with salmeterol, with more tremor (13.4% vs 1.1%); endpoints are airway function and safety, not exacerbations or mortality, and the two-trials-one-publication report counts once

title: Nedocromil sodium in chronic asthma: modest symptom and peak-flow benefits in four small 1988–1996 trials; the steroid-resistant trial had N=12 completers and is never load-bearing
question: In adults with chronic asthma — including asthma dependent on inhaled corticosteroids and steroid-resistant asthma — does inhaled nedocromil sodium versus placebo improve symptoms and lung function and spare corticosteroids?
balance: POSSIBLE benefit — modest, on small, old evidence, and the era is printed on the face: every trial is from 1988–1996, short (4 weeks to 3 months), with symptom and lung-function endpoints and no exacerbation-outcome trial. Inhaled nedocromil sodium 4 mg four times daily (twice daily in one trial) added to existing therapy gave small but significant advantages over placebo in inhaled-corticosteroid-dependent asthma (89 and 188 patients), in a 30-patient bronchodilator-maintained trial, and in steroid-resistant asthma — that last trial is very small (26 randomised; N=12 nedocromil patients completed treatment) and is never load-bearing on this shelf. Nedocromil was withdrawn from several markets for commercial (not safety) reasons. Sodium cromoglicate does not join this shelf — its adult base did not verify at floor, as the commissioning row records.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — four small placebo-controlled trials from 1988–1996 (89, 188, 30 and 26 randomised) consistently show modest symptom and peak-flow benefits from adding inhaled nedocromil in chronic and steroid-dependent asthma; the steroid-resistant trial (N=12 nedocromil completers, printed on its card) is never load-bearing, there is no exacerbation-outcome trial, and the drug was withdrawn from several markets for commercial reasons

title: Intrapleural streptokinase for pleural infection (MIST1): the large trial was negative (31% vs 27% death or surgery); pooled small-trial benefits vanish in low-bias sensitivity analysis
question: In adults with parapneumonic effusion or empyema, does intrapleural streptokinase (or another fibrinolytic alone) versus placebo or conservative management reduce death, surgical referral and hospital stay?
balance: SPLIT — a large negative trial against a tail of small positive older trials, presented plainly and not pooled away. MIST1, the definitive trial of intrapleural streptokinase ALONE (454 randomised), found no difference in death or surgical drainage at 3 months (31% vs 27%; relative risk 1.14, 95% CI 0.85 to 1.54) and no benefit for mortality, surgery rate, radiographic outcome or hospital stay. The Cochrane syntheses, which pool MIST1 with the older small streptokinase/urokinase trials, find fewer surgical interventions with fibrinolysis (2019: odds ratio 0.37, 95% CI 0.21 to 0.68, low certainty) but no mortality difference — and in the 2019 sensitivity analysis confined to low/unclear risk-of-bias trials, the surgery and treatment-failure benefits disappeared. This shelf is fibrinolytic ALONE only: the tPA-plus-DNase combination question (MIST2) is homed at live #816, is cross-pointed here in prose, and none of its studies are re-carded on this shelf.
stamp: SPLIT — MIST1, the large definitive trial of intrapleural streptokinase alone (454 randomised), found no benefit on death or surgical drainage (31% vs 27%; relative risk 1.14), while the Cochrane syntheses pooling MIST1 with smaller older trials report fewer surgical interventions (2019 odds ratio 0.37, low certainty) that disappear when restricted to low/unclear risk-of-bias trials; no mortality benefit in any analysis; the tPA + DNase (MIST2) question stays at live #816 and is not re-carded here

title: Levosulpiride in functional dyspepsia: two small placebo trials positive on symptoms and gastric emptying; at least as effective as cisapride in a 140-patient pilot — old, short evidence, D2-antagonist harms, not licensed in the US/UK
question: In adults with functional dyspepsia (dysmotility-like / postprandial distress, with or without delayed gastric emptying), does levosulpiride versus placebo — or versus cisapride — improve dyspeptic symptoms and gastric emptying?
balance: POSSIBLE benefit, on a small, old base. Two small double-blind placebo trials (42 patients with delayed gastric emptying, 1998; 30 patients, 1994) found levosulpiride improved dyspeptic symptoms more than placebo and accelerated gastric (and gall-bladder) emptying. A larger exploratory pilot trial (140 patients, 2004) found levosulpiride at least as effective as the active comparator cisapride (total symptom score fell 79.9% versus 71.3%; P=0.07), with medication-related adverse effects in 18.8% versus 11.3%. There is no modern Rome-IV-era trial. Levosulpiride is a dopamine D2 antagonist — hyperprolactinaemia and extrapyramidal effects are part of the real-world answer — and it is not licensed in the US/UK.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two small double-blind placebo trials (n=42 with delayed gastric emptying; n=30) found levosulpiride improved dyspeptic symptoms and accelerated gastric emptying versus placebo, and a 140-patient pilot found it at least as effective as cisapride; the base is small, old and short, the drug is a dopamine D2 antagonist (hyperprolactinaemia and extrapyramidal effects) and it is not licensed in the US/UK

title: Mosapride in functional dyspepsia: largest placebo trial and overall meta-analysis negative (the treatment made no difference vs placebo); later trials match nortriptyline and acotiamide but have no placebo arm
question: In adults with functional dyspepsia, does mosapride (including controlled-release) versus placebo — or versus acotiamide or nortriptyline strategies — improve postprandial distress and global dyspeptic symptoms?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence). The placebo-controlled record is negative overall: the largest dose-finding trial (566 patients evaluated, 2002) found mosapride made no difference versus placebo at any dose, and a 2015 meta-analysis of 13 randomised trials (1,091 mosapride-treated and 1,129 control patients) found an overall relative risk of 0.999 for global efficacy, with a positive signal only in a high-quality-trials sensitivity analysis and none in Rome III studies. Two later trials compare mosapride with active treatments — nortriptyline (2024) and acotiamide (2021) — and found similar improvement in both arms, but with no placebo arm they cannot separate drug effect from placebo response and natural course. The acotiamide question itself is homed elsewhere (pack #2767); this shelf cards that trial only as a mosapride comparator limb.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the largest placebo-controlled trial (566 patients evaluated) and the overall meta-analysis of 13 trials (relative risk 0.999) found mosapride made no difference versus placebo; positive signals appear only in sensitivity subsets, and the 2021 and 2024 active-comparator trials have no placebo arm, so a small benefit cannot be excluded but is not demonstrated

title: Gabexate mesilate in acute pancreatitis: large German trial negative on mortality and complications; meta-analysis — no mortality effect but fewer complications; small severe-disease trial claimed a survival benefit
question: In patients with acute pancreatitis (including severe pancreatitis with organ dysfunction), does intravenous gabexate mesilate versus placebo/no treatment — or versus aprotinin — reduce mortality and complications?
balance: SPLIT. The large German Pancreatitis Study Group trial (223 patients with moderate/severe pancreatitis, 1993) found gabexate made no difference to mortality or complications versus placebo. A 1995 meta-analysis of five randomised trials agreed on mortality (no effect at 90 days, P=0.27) but found fewer complications overall (odds ratio 0.69 — a relative measure) and fewer complications requiring surgery (odds ratio 0.61 — relative). Against that, a small severe-disease trial (52 patients, 26 treated, 2000) reported significantly reduced 7- and 90-day mortality, and the GA.ME.P.A. trial found gabexate more efficacious than aprotinin on early complications of necrotising pancreatitis. This is the treatment question only: gabexate for post-ERCP prophylaxis is a separate question, homed elsewhere, and the 2017 Cochrane pharmacological-interventions review is not carded here (it is a limb of the lexipafant shelf).
stamp: SPLIT — the large German placebo trial (n=223) found gabexate made no difference to mortality or complications and the 1995 meta-analysis of five trials found no mortality effect, but the same meta-analysis found fewer complications (relative odds ratio 0.69) and a small 52-patient severe-disease trial and an aprotinin-comparator trial read positively; an old programme split by severity, era and endpoint

title: Ulinastatin in acute pancreatitis: two placebo trials suggest less death and organ dysfunction in severe disease; 2025 meta-analysis agrees — small single-region (Asia-only licensing) base, and one named anchor refused as a protocol with no results
question: In patients with acute pancreatitis (mild or severe), does intravenous ulinastatin added to standard supportive care versus placebo/standard care reduce complications, organ failure and mortality?
balance: POSSIBLE benefit in severe disease, on a small single-region base — with the builder position stated plainly: this shelf rests on two placebo-controlled randomised trials (India, n=135 randomised; China, n=181) plus a 2025 meta-analysis of seven studies. The third anchor named at mining, Yao & Li 2019 (PMID 31651883), was checked at build and is a systematic-review PROTOCOL (PROSPERO CRD42019149566) with no results — it is refused and not carded as evidence. The 2025 meta-analysis pools ulinastatin given alone or in combination with other agents, so it must not be read as ulinastatin-alone evidence; the surrounding combination literature (ulinastatin plus somatostatin/octreotide) is likewise not presented here as ulinastatin-alone evidence. Ulinastatin is licensed in parts of Asia only. The post-ERCP prophylaxis question is separate and not folded in.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two placebo-controlled randomised trials (n=135 randomised in India; n=181 single-centre in China) and a 2025 meta-analysis of seven studies suggest ulinastatin reduces death and new organ dysfunction in severe acute pancreatitis; the base is small and single-region, one trial's abstract gives no mortality counts, the meta-analysis mixes ulinastatin-alone and combination use, and a third named anchor (Yao & Li 2019) was refused at build as a results-free review protocol

title: Metadoxine in severe alcohol-associated hepatitis: two open-label RCTs from one Mexican programme (n=70, n=135) found large survival gains, echoed by a 2026 synthesis limb — unreplicated elsewhere
question: In patients with severe alcohol-associated hepatitis, does adding metadoxine to standard care (with or without corticosteroids) improve short- and medium-term survival versus standard care alone?
balance: POSSIBLE benefit, with the base stated on the face: this shelf rests on TWO randomised trials from a single Mexican programme (n=70 in 2014; n=135 in 2015), both open-label, plus the metadoxine limb of a 2026 systematic review — that limb was verified at build and is extractable (28-day mortality relative risk 0.47 for metadoxine plus corticosteroids versus corticosteroids alone). Both trials found large survival differences (90-day survival 68.6% versus 20.0% in 2014; 3-month survival 68.6% versus 20% for prednisone plus metadoxine versus prednisone in 2015), and the 2015 trial also found patients on metadoxine maintained abstinence more often (74.5% versus 59.4%) — itself a survival factor, and a confounder of the drug claim. There is no replication outside this one programme, and nothing here extends to non-severe disease.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — base stated on the face: two open-label randomised trials from a single Mexican programme (n=70 and n=135) found large survival gains when metadoxine was added to prednisone or pentoxifylline in severe alcohol-associated hepatitis, and the verified metadoxine limb of a 2026 systematic review agrees (28-day mortality relative risk 0.47 versus corticosteroids alone); there is no replication outside that programme, and better abstinence on metadoxine confounds the drug claim

title: Propylthiouracil in alcohol-associated liver disease: long-term trial halved mortality in compliant patients (0.13 vs 0.25), but severe-hepatitis trial negative and Cochrane pooling of 710 patients found no benefit — a historical, unconfirmed programme
question: In patients with alcoholic liver disease / alcoholic hepatitis, does propylthiouracil versus placebo improve short-term and long-term mortality?
balance: SPLIT — a historical programme with an unconfirmed signal. The programme's long-term trial (Orrego 1987, 310 compliant patients, up to two years) found cumulative mortality of 0.13 on propylthiouracil versus 0.25 on placebo, with a hazards ratio of 0.38 (a relative measure). But the short-term severe-hepatitis trial (Hallé 1982, n=67) found the treatment made no difference (deaths 7 of 31 versus 7 of 36), the 1979 short-term trial improved a composite clinical-laboratory index without assessing mortality, and the Cochrane review (2005 version carded here — ONE version only, per the flumazenil precedent) pooling six trials and 710 patients found no significant effect on all-cause mortality (relative risk 0.93), liver-related mortality, complications or histology. No modern trial has confirmed the long-term signal, and current alcohol-hepatitis reviews largely omit this programme. The tension belongs on the face: propylthiouracil carries a severe-hepatotoxicity warning from its thyroid use, yet was tested as a liver treatment.
stamp: SPLIT — the Orrego programme's long-term trial (310 compliant patients) found cumulative mortality 0.13 versus 0.25 with a relative hazards ratio of 0.38, but the severe-hepatitis trial (n=67) found the treatment made no difference and the Cochrane review (2005 version, the one version carded) pooling six trials and 710 patients found no significant effect on mortality, complications or histology; a historical programme with an unconfirmed signal, for a drug that itself carries a severe-hepatotoxicity warning

title: Nicotine in active ulcerative colitis: patches beat placebo for induction (remission 19/71 vs 9/70) but not standard therapy, with heavy side effects; enemas negative — a programme abandoned in practice
question: In adults with active ulcerative colitis, does transdermal nicotine — or nicotine enemas — added to standard therapy versus placebo/standard therapy induce clinical improvement or remission?
balance: SPLIT — by route and by comparator. Transdermal nicotine beat placebo for induction in the pooled placebo trials carded by the 2004 Cochrane review (remission 19 of 71 versus 9 of 70; odds ratio 2.56 — a relative measure), and the founding NEJM trial (Pullan 1994, n=72) found complete remission in 17 of 35 on nicotine versus 9 of 37 on placebo — but with far more side effects (23 versus 11 patients). Against standard therapy (prednisone or mesalamine) the same Cochrane review found no advantage for nicotine, and across all five studies the pooled result was not significant. Nicotine enemas (Ingram 2005, n=104) made no difference versus placebo enemas (remission 27% versus 33%). This is an induction-only, 1990s programme that was never adopted in practice — nicotine-naïve patients had substantial nausea, light-headedness, headache and sleep disturbance, and adverse-event withdrawals were much commoner on nicotine. The trials, not the smoking epidemiology, are this shelf.
stamp: SPLIT — transdermal nicotine was superior to placebo for induction of remission in the small pooled placebo trials (19 of 71 versus 9 of 70; relative odds ratio 2.56) but showed no advantage over standard therapy and caused far more adverse-event withdrawals (relative odds ratio 5.82), while nicotine enemas made no difference versus placebo (remission 27% versus 33%); an induction-only programme abandoned in practice

title: Olsalazine in ulcerative colitis: modest benefit in small 1980s trials (Ns printed — 60+40, 105, 66), clearest in sulfasalazine-intolerant patients; dose-limiting secretory diarrhoea
question: In adults with mild-to-moderate ulcerative colitis — including patients intolerant of sulfasalazine — does olsalazine versus placebo induce and maintain remission?
balance: POSSIBLE benefit, on small, old evidence — the Ns are printed on the face of every card: 60 randomised to enemas plus a separate 40-patient oral trial in one 1985 paper; 105 patients in the 1989 Gut trial; 66 sulfasalazine-intolerant patients in the 1987 dose-ranging trial. The consistent findings are modest: significant endoscopic improvement in the rectum in 1989 (with most symptom measures not significantly different), significant clinical and sigmoidoscopic improvement for oral olsalazine in the small 1985 oral trial, and a dose-response pattern in sulfasalazine-intolerant patients (improvement in 16% on placebo rising to 50% at 3 g/day). Olsalazine's dose-limiting secretory diarrhoea is the clinically decisive harm — it caused premature termination in the 1989 trial and a withdrawal in 1987. Olsalazine is a distinct azo-bonded 5-ASA dimer with its own trial base; the mesalamine dose/route shelves (packs #6087–#6089) and the balsalazide shelf (#7361) are separate questions, and no one of them is a class verdict.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — small 1980s trials with Ns printed on the face (60 randomised to enemas plus a 40-patient oral trial; 105 patients; 66 sulfasalazine-intolerant patients) show modest benefit, strongest on rectal endoscopy and in sulfasalazine-intolerant patients (improvement 35% versus 16% on placebo, rising to 50% at 3 g/day); olsalazine's dose-limiting secretory diarrhoea is the clinically decisive harm

title: Balsalazide in ulcerative colitis: dose-response and faster onset than mesalamine — but all comparators are low-dose mesalamine (1.2–2.4 g/day), no placebo arm, and 12-month remission was equal (58% both)
question: In adults with mild-to-moderate ulcerative colitis, does balsalazide versus mesalazine/mesalamine induce remission faster, and does it maintain remission as well or better?
balance: POSSIBLE benefit — with the comparator warning on the face: every comparison here is against LOW-DOSE mesalamine by modern standards (2.4 g/day in the induction trial; 1.5 g/day and 1.2 g/day in the maintenance trials), there is no placebo arm anywhere, and these results must not be read as superiority over modern-dose mesalamine. Within those limits: the dose-response trial (n=154) found balsalazide 6.75 g/day significantly better than balsalazide 2.25 g/day on bleeding, stool frequency, sigmoidoscopy and global assessment, and faster in onset than mesalamine 2.4 g/day; the maintenance trial (n=133) found high-dose balsalazide (3 g twice daily) superior to low-dose balsalazide and to mesalazine 1.5 g/day in maintaining remission (77.5% versus 43.8% and 56.8%); and ABACUS (n=99) found equal 12-month remission (58% both) with fewer early relapses and better nocturnal symptom control on balsalazide 3 g/day versus mesalazine 1.2 g/day. The olsalazine question (#7360) and the mesalamine dose/route questions (packs #6087–#6089) are separate shelves.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — balsalazide shows a dose-response (6.75 g/day significantly better than 2.25 g/day for induction; 3 g twice daily maintained remission in 77.5% versus 43.8% on low-dose balsalazide) and faster onset than mesalamine, BUT every mesalamine comparator is low-dose by modern standards (1.2–2.4 g/day, flagged on the face), there is no placebo arm, and 12-month remission in ABACUS was equal (58% both) — nothing here shows superiority over modern-dose mesalamine

title: Aldafermin (FGF19 analogue) in MASH — FAILED programme: ALPINE 2/3 missed its primary fibrosis endpoint and development was discontinued; liver fat fell in phase 2, and a later cirrhosis trial improved a biomarker score only
question: In adults with MASH and stage 2–3 fibrosis — or compensated cirrhosis — does aldafermin versus placebo improve liver fat, fibrosis or MASH resolution?
balance: FAILED PROGRAMME — stated plainly. Aldafermin, an engineered FGF19 analogue, reduced liver fat in its phase 2 trial (78 patients) but did NOT significantly improve fibrosis or resolve MASH there (38% versus 18% fibrosis improvement, P=0.10; 24% versus 9% MASH resolution, P=0.20). The phase 2b ALPINE 2/3 trial (171 randomised) MISSED its primary endpoint — no significant dose response for fibrosis improvement of at least one stage with no worsening of MASH (placebo 19%; aldafermin 0.3 mg 31%, 1.0 mg 15%, 3.0 mg 30%; dose-response P=0.55) — and development of aldafermin for MASH was discontinued. A later, separate trial in compensated cirrhosis (160 patients, 48 weeks) found a significant reduction in the Enhanced Liver Fibrosis score at 3 mg (least-squares mean difference −0.5) with fibrosis improvement in 23% versus 15% — a biomarker-led result in a different population, which must not be pooled with the F2–F3 question as if confirmatory. LDL-cholesterol elevation is the FGF19 class effect and belongs on the face (it was managed with statins in the trials; the fetched abstracts give no LDL numbers). This shelf is the FGF19 limb only — efruxifermin (live #1710) and pegbelfermin (pack #7108) are FGF21 analogues and different questions.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — failed programme, stamped plainly: ALPINE 2/3 (171 randomised) missed its primary fibrosis endpoint with no dose response (P=0.55) and aldafermin's development for MASH was discontinued; the phase 2 trial (n=78) significantly reduced liver fat but not fibrosis or MASH resolution, and the later compensated-cirrhosis trial (n=160) improved a fibrosis biomarker score (ELF −0.5 at 3 mg) in a separate population, which does not rescue the failed F2–F3 programme; LDL-cholesterol elevation is the FGF19 class effect

title: Besifovir in chronic hepatitis B (all evidence South Korean): noninferior HBV suppression to entecavir and tenofovir, with preserved bone and kidney measures — and carnitine depletion
question: In adults with chronic hepatitis B, does besifovir dipivoxil maleate, compared with entecavir or tenofovir disoproxil fumarate, suppress HBV DNA with less kidney and bone toxicity? (All trial evidence is from South Korea, where besifovir is approved; it is not FDA- or EMA-approved.)
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), on a single-region (South Korea) programme. Besifovir dipivoxil maleate suppressed HBV DNA to the same degree as entecavir over 96 weeks in a phase 2 trial (undetectable HBV DNA in about 80% on each drug) and was noninferior to tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) in the phase 3 programme: virological response was 87.7% versus 92.1% at 144 weeks and 92.5% versus 93.1% at 192 weeks for continuing besifovir versus switching from TDF, with no drug-resistant mutations detected. A separate randomised switch trial (n=153) found 100.0% versus 98.5% maintained HBV DNA <20 IU/mL after switching from long-term TDF to besifovir versus staying on TDF. The distinguishing claim is safety: bone mineral density and renal function were preserved on besifovir and improved after switching from TDF. The offsetting harm is carnitine depletion — carnitine supplements were prescribed to 83.9% (90 mg) and 100% (150 mg) of besifovir patients with a low carnitine level in the phase 2 trial. All trials were conducted in South Korea, where besifovir is approved; it is not FDA- or EMA-approved. The phase 3 efficacy reads after week 48 come from open-label extensions, not continued blinded comparison.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — besifovir was noninferior to entecavir and to tenofovir for HBV DNA suppression in every comparative report, with consistently better-preserved bone mineral density and renal function and no detected resistance, but the whole programme is single-region (South Korea), the long-term phase 3 reads are open-label extensions, and carnitine depletion is a real offsetting harm; POSSIBLE rather than LIKELY because no non-Korean or independently replicated evidence exists

title: Granulocyte/monocyte apheresis (Adacolumn) in ulcerative colitis: a sham-negative programme — 17% vs 11% remission against sham, with positive reads only from open-label trials
question: In adults with active moderate-to-severe ulcerative colitis, does granulocyte/monocyte adsorptive apheresis (the Adacolumn Apheresis System) versus sham apheresis induce remission or response — and can it maintain remission?
balance: LIKELY (no difference) on the blinded evidence — a sham-negative programme. The only large sham-controlled induction trial (Sands 2008, pivotal n=168) found clinical remission in 17% on granulocyte/monocyte apheresis (the Adacolumn Apheresis System) versus 11% on sham (P=.361), with response 44% versus 39% (P=.620); the companion study and pooled data were the same. A small double-blind sham-controlled maintenance trial (n=33) also found no significant difference overall. The more positive reads come from designs without a sham control: the open-label maintenance trial (n=164) missed its primary endpoint (cumulative clinical remission 46.6% versus 36.4%, P=0.1621) though endoscopic remission was higher (42.5% versus 25.9%, P=0.0480), and adding apheresis to prednisone in steroid-dependent disease did not increase steroid-free remission (13% versus 7%, P=0.11). The 2010 systematic review states the split plainly: remission rates looked higher against medical therapy but NOT against sham. That blinded-negative versus open-positive design split is this shelf's central fact and is not pooled away.
stamp: LIKELY (no difference) — the only large sham-controlled trial found no efficacy for induction (remission 17% vs 11% on sham), the small sham-controlled maintenance trial was also non-significant, the 2010 systematic review found no significant benefit against sham across 10 RCTs, and the open-label trials' positive signals are secondary endpoints after missed primaries; the blinded evidence governs the stamp

title: Tradipitant in gastroparesis — 2 randomised reports only: phase 2 reduced nausea, but the phase 3 trial missed its primary endpoint (P=.741); programme presented as failed at phase 3
question: In adults with diabetic or idiopathic gastroparesis, does tradipitant (a neurokinin-1 receptor antagonist) versus placebo reduce nausea and overall gastroparesis symptoms? (Evidence base: exactly 2 randomised reports — phase 2, n=152; phase 3, n=201.)
balance: SPLIT, on exactly 2 randomised reports (phase 2, n=152; phase 3, n=201) — the base is printed here because it is the whole evidence. The phase 2 trial (4 weeks) was positive: nausea score fell by 1.2 on tradipitant versus 0.7 on placebo (P=.0099), with more nausea-free days (28.8% versus 15.0% increase; P=.0160). The larger, longer phase 3 trial (12 weeks) FAILED its prespecified primary endpoint in the intention-to-treat population (difference in nausea severity change, P=.741) and its prespecified secondary endpoints; its supportive findings are post hoc (patients with high tradipitant blood levels, and sensitivity analyses adjusting for rescue medication and baseline severity inflation). Per the commissioning row's builder condition, the programme is therefore presented as failed at phase 3 on the face of this shelf: a positive small phase 2 that the definitive trial did not confirm. A healthy-volunteer mechanistic study (n=24) is carded, clearly labelled, only to record that tradipitant did not retard gastric emptying; it is not efficacy evidence and does not count toward the base.
stamp: SPLIT — on exactly 2 randomised reports (phase 2, n=152; phase 3, n=201): the phase 2 trial significantly reduced nausea versus placebo at 4 weeks, but the phase 3 trial missed its prespecified primary endpoint (P=.741) and secondary endpoints, with positive findings only post hoc; per the row's builder condition the programme is presented as failed at phase 3 on the face, so no benefit stamp is proposed

title: Momelotinib vs ruxolitinib / best available therapy in myelofibrosis (SIMPLIFY-1/-2): a split result — spleen noninferiority, symptom noninferiority missed, no post-ruxolitinib superiority, transfusion benefit throughout (MOMENTUM homed at #4865)
question: In patients with myelofibrosis — Janus kinase inhibitor-naive (SIMPLIFY-1) or previously treated with ruxolitinib with suboptimal response or haematologic toxicity (SIMPLIFY-2) — does momelotinib 200 mg once daily, versus ruxolitinib or best available therapy, achieve spleen-volume and symptom responses, and does it improve transfusion outcomes and survival? (PARTIAL shelf: momelotinib versus danazol, MOMENTUM, is homed at pack #4865 and is not re-carded here.)
balance: SPLIT — a PARTIAL shelf: momelotinib versus danazol in anaemic myelofibrosis (the MOMENTUM trial) is homed at pack #4865 and is cross-pointed here in prose only, never re-carded; this shelf cards only the unasked SIMPLIFY head-to-head slice, and fedratinib is homed separately at pack #7014. The result is genuinely split. In JAK-inhibitor-naive patients (SIMPLIFY-1, n=432), momelotinib was noninferior to ruxolitinib for spleen-volume response (26.5% vs 29%; noninferior, P=.011) but noninferiority was NOT met for symptom response (28.4% vs 42.2%; P=.98), while transfusion rate, independence and dependence all favoured momelotinib (nominal P at most .019). In ruxolitinib-pretreated patients (SIMPLIFY-2, n=156), momelotinib was NOT superior to best available therapy for spleen response (7% vs 6%; P=.90) — and the control was effectively continued ruxolitinib in 89% of patients. Survival was similar in both trials (overall-survival hazard ratios 1.02 and 0.98, both relative measures, both non-significant). Peripheral neuropathy is momelotinib's recurring harm (10–11% versus 0–5%).
stamp: SPLIT — in JAK-inhibitor-naive myelofibrosis momelotinib met spleen-response noninferiority versus ruxolitinib but missed symptom-response noninferiority (28.4% vs 42.2%) while improving transfusion outcomes, and in ruxolitinib-pretreated disease it was not superior to best available therapy (89% continued ruxolitinib) for spleen response, with similar survival in both trials (PARTIAL shelf: MOMENTUM versus danazol stays homed at pack #4865, cross-pointed only)

title: Ponatinib vs imatinib in frontline Ph+ ALL (PhALLCON, one trial): MRD-negative remission doubled (34.4% vs 16.7%) — a remission-depth benefit; survival not yet established
question: In adults with newly diagnosed Philadelphia chromosome-positive acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, does frontline ponatinib (30 mg/day, reduced to 15 mg on MRD-negative complete remission), versus imatinib (600 mg/day), each with reduced-intensity chemotherapy, increase MRD-negative complete remission and event-free survival, and with what arterial-occlusive cost? (Single programme: the PhALLCON trial.)
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), on a single programme — one trial (PhALLCON), three reports. Ponatinib (30 mg/day, reduced to 15 mg on achieving MRD-negative complete remission) with reduced-intensity chemotherapy doubled the primary endpoint versus imatinib (600 mg/day): MRD-negative complete remission at the end of cycle 3 in 34.4% (53/154) versus 16.7% (13/78) (risk difference 0.18; P=.002). The primary endpoint is a molecular-depth endpoint, not a survival endpoint: event-free survival was immature at the interim cutoff (median not reached versus 29 months; the prespecified event count had not been met), and in the quality-adjusted analysis restricted mean overall survival was itself similar between arms (1082.2 versus 1024.8 days; P=.373). The two companion reports (patient-reported outcomes; Q-TWiST, with mean time without symptoms or toxicity 214.5 days longer on ponatinib) are supportive analyses of the same patients and must not upgrade this into a survival claim. Arterial occlusive events — the reason for ponatinib's dose-reduction-on-response design — were infrequent and comparable (2.5% versus 1.2%) at this cutoff.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single-programme evidence (one trial, three reports): ponatinib significantly increased the molecular primary endpoint, MRD-negative complete remission (34.4% vs 16.7%), with comparable early safety, but event-free survival was immature and overall survival did not differ in the companion analysis, so the stamp rests on remission depth, not on a proven survival benefit
