title: Blinatumomab vs chemotherapy in relapsed/refractory adult B-ALL (TOWER, one trial): survival 7.7 vs 4.0 months, deeper remissions, better quality of life
question: In adults with heavily pretreated, Philadelphia chromosome-negative relapsed or refractory B-cell precursor acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, does the CD19xCD3 bispecific T-cell engager blinatumomab, versus standard-of-care chemotherapy, prolong overall survival and deepen remission, and with what quality-of-life effect? (Single programme: the TOWER trial.)
balance: LIKELY (benefit), on a single programme — one trial (TOWER), three reports. In heavily pretreated, Philadelphia chromosome-negative relapsed or refractory B-cell precursor ALL, blinatumomab prolonged overall survival versus standard chemotherapy: median 7.7 versus 4.0 months (hazard ratio for death 0.71 — a relative measure; the absolute frame, a 3.7-month median gain in a population with very short expected survival, is the honest headline). Remission was deeper (complete remission with full haematologic recovery 34% vs 16%; with full, partial or incomplete recovery 44% vs 25%) and 6-month event-free survival was 31% versus 12%. Grade 3-or-worse adverse events were similarly frequent (87% vs 92%), and the exposure-adjusted analysis found lower event rates per patient-year on blinatumomab for most categories except cytokine-release syndrome. Health-related quality of life favoured blinatumomab across subscales. This is strictly the relapsed/refractory setting: blinatumomab consolidation in MRD-negative frontline disease is a separate question (pack #7369, E1910), and blinatumomab in children is homed at pack #5008 — both cross-pointed in prose only.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — a single phase 3 trial (TOWER) showed significantly longer overall survival with blinatumomab than chemotherapy in relapsed/refractory adult B-ALL (median 7.7 vs 4.0 months; hazard ratio 0.71, relative) with deeper remissions and better quality of life in companion reports of the same trial; LIKELY rather than stronger because the entire base is one trial and absolute survival remains short

title: Blinatumomab added to consolidation in MRD-negative adult B-ALL (E1910, one trial): 3-year survival 85% vs 68% — with more neuropsychiatric events
question: In adults aged 30–70 with BCR::ABL1-negative B-cell precursor ALL in measurable-residual-disease-negative complete remission after induction and intensification chemotherapy, does adding four cycles of blinatumomab to consolidation chemotherapy, versus consolidation chemotherapy alone, prolong overall and relapse-free survival? (Single programme: the E1910 trial.)
balance: LIKELY (benefit), on a single programme — one trial (E1910), with an FDA approval summary and a small single-centre integration series as companions. In adults aged 30–70 with BCR::ABL1-negative B-cell precursor ALL already in MRD-negative complete remission after induction and intensification, adding four cycles of blinatumomab to consolidation chemotherapy improved survival: 3-year overall survival 85% versus 68% (hazard ratio for death 0.41 — a relative measure, printed with the absolute rates) and 3-year relapse-free survival 80% versus 64% (hazard ratio 0.53, relative), at a median follow-up of 43 months. Only 224 of 488 enrolled patients reached the MRD-negative randomisation — the benefit applies to that selected, deep-remission population, and the population boundary is the question: this shelf must not borrow the relapsed/refractory TOWER result (pack #7368) or the MRD-positive literature. The cost on the face: a higher incidence of neuropsychiatric events with blinatumomab. The FDA summary records the same trial (hazard ratio 0.42 in the FDA analysis population) and notes that one paediatric consolidation trial in the approval package (AALL1331) did not meet its primary objectives — context, not adult evidence.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — a single phase 3 trial (E1910) showed significantly better overall survival when blinatumomab was added to consolidation in MRD-negative adult B-ALL (3-year survival 85% vs 68%; hazard ratio 0.41, relative), corroborated as the approval basis in the FDA summary; LIKELY rather than stronger because the base is one trial reported at an interim analysis in a selected deep-remission population, with more neuropsychiatric events on blinatumomab

title: Brexucabtagene autoleucel in relapsed/refractory adult B-ALL (ZUMA-3, single-arm): remission 71–73%, median survival 25.6 months at 3 years — uncontrolled, with grade 3+ CRS/neurotoxicity in ~25–31%
question: In adults with relapsed or refractory B-cell precursor acute lymphoblastic leukaemia with more than 5% marrow blasts, does a single infusion of the CD19 CAR T-cell therapy brexucabtagene autoleucel (1 x 10^6 CAR T cells/kg), versus no concurrent control, produce complete remissions and prolong survival, and with what cytokine-release and neurotoxicity cost? (Single-arm trial evidence plus one real-world cohort; no randomised comparator exists.)
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the ceiling for a single-arm base, with the uncontrolled base stated: no randomised comparator exists for brexucabtagene autoleucel (Tecartus, Kite/Gilead) in relapsed or refractory adult B-cell ALL. In the single-arm phase 2 ZUMA-3 trial, complete remission or remission with incomplete recovery occurred in 39 of 55 infused patients (71%; complete remission 56%), with median overall survival 18.2 months at the primary analysis; the 3-year analysis of the pooled treated population (N=78) found remission in 73% (complete remission 60%) and median overall survival 25.6 months (38.9 months in responders). A US real-world cohort (189 infused) found 151 complete remissions, 79% of them MRD-negative, and median progression-free survival 9.5 months — but 42% were treated in morphologic remission and would have been ZUMA-3-ineligible, so the trial and cohort populations differ and their rates are not pooled. The toxicity cost is substantial: grade 3-or-worse cytokine-release syndrome in 24% and grade 3-or-worse neurological events in 25% in the trial; grade 3–4 cytokine-release syndrome 11% and grade 3–4 neurotoxicity (ICANS) 31% in the real-world cohort. Brexucabtagene in mantle cell lymphoma (ZUMA-2) is homed at pack #7026 and obecabtagene in R/R B-ALL at pack #7027 — different questions/products, cross-pointed in prose only.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single-arm bases cap at POSSIBLE with the uncontrolled base stated: the single-arm ZUMA-3 trial produced complete remission or better in 71–73% of infused adults with relapsed/refractory B-ALL and median overall survival of 25.6 months at 3 years, echoed by a 189-patient real-world cohort, but no randomised comparator exists and grade 3-or-worse cytokine-release syndrome and neurotoxicity affected roughly a quarter to a third of patients

title: Nivolumab-AVD vs brentuximab vedotin-AVD in advanced classic Hodgkin lymphoma (S1826, one trial): 2-year PFS 92% vs 83%, with the largest gains and least harm in older patients
question: In patients aged 12 years and older with newly diagnosed stage III–IV classic Hodgkin lymphoma, does nivolumab plus doxorubicin–vinblastine–dacarbazine (N-AVD), versus brentuximab vedotin plus AVD (BV-AVD), prolong progression-free survival, and with what comparative toxicity — including in older patients and adolescents? (Single programme: the SWOG S1826 trial.)
balance: LIKELY (benefit), on a single programme — one trial (S1826), three reports. In patients 12 years and older with newly diagnosed stage III–IV classic Hodgkin lymphoma, nivolumab plus AVD beat brentuximab vedotin plus AVD — an active modern standard, not ABVD — on progression-free survival: 2-year progression-free survival 92% versus 83% (hazard ratio for progression or death 0.45 — a relative measure, printed with the absolute rates). The tolerability split carries as much weight as the efficacy split: brentuximab vedotin was associated with more treatment discontinuation, and in patients 60 and older (n=99) the differences were stark — 2-year progression-free survival 89% versus 64% (hazard ratio 0.24, relative), 2-year overall survival 96% versus 85% (hazard ratio 0.16, relative), non-relapse mortality 16% versus 6%, and six cycles delivered without dose reduction in 69% versus 26%. In adolescents (n=240), 3-year progression-free survival was 93% versus 82% (hazard ratio 0.37, relative), with grade 2-or-worse sensory neuropathy 7% versus 14% and thyroid dysfunction in 7% on nivolumab-AVD. Overall survival for the whole population was immature at the primary report — survival claims on this shelf are confined to the older-patient subset. Brentuximab vedotin plus AVD versus ABVD (ECHELON-1) is homed at pack #3444 and is not re-carded here.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — a single phase 3 trial (S1826) showed significantly better progression-free survival with nivolumab-AVD than with the active standard brentuximab vedotin-AVD (2-year 92% vs 83%; hazard ratio 0.45, relative), with consistent subset reports in older patients (where overall survival and non-relapse mortality also favoured nivolumab-AVD) and adolescents, and a better tolerability profile; whole-population overall survival was immature, which is stated on the face

title: Enzalutamide + radium-223 in first-line mCRPC (PEACE-3, one trial): final survival 38.2 vs 32.6 months — benefit conditional on mandatory bone-protecting agents
question: In men with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer and bone metastases receiving first-line therapy, does adding six cycles of radium-223 to enzalutamide, versus enzalutamide alone, prolong radiographic progression-free and overall survival — and what bone-protecting-agent co-treatment does the combination require? (Single programme: the PEACE-3 / EORTC 1333 trial; bone-protecting-agent co-administration was mandated from March 2018 and is part of the tested intervention.)
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — with a mandatory condition printed on the face: co-administration of a bone-protecting agent (zoledronic acid or denosumab), mandated mid-trial from March 2018 after the ERA-223 fracture signal, is part of the tested intervention as finally delivered, and this combination must not be presented without it. On a single programme (one trial, PEACE-3 / EORTC 1333, three reports), adding six cycles of radium-223 to first-line enzalutamide in metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer with bone metastases improved radiographic progression-free survival (median 19.4 vs 16.4 months; hazard ratio 0.69 — a relative measure) and, in the final analysis superseding the interim read, overall survival (median 38.2 vs 32.6 months; hazard ratio 0.76, relative; P=.0096, meeting the predefined significance level; 317 deaths at median follow-up 58 months). The cost: grade 3-or-worse treatment-emergent events in 69.3% versus 57.6% at the final analysis, and fractures in 24.3% versus 13.4% across the trial's pre- and post-mandate eras — with a bone-protecting agent, 1-year fracture rates fell from 15.6% to 2.6% in the enzalutamide-alone arm (the combination-arm read is taken from the safety report as carded). Radium-223 versus placebo in symptomatic bone-metastatic disease (ALSYMPCA) is homed at live #1869 — cross-pointed in prose only.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — a single phase 3 trial (PEACE-3) showed improved radiographic progression-free survival (hazard ratio 0.69, relative) and, at the final analysis, improved overall survival (median 38.2 vs 32.6 months; hazard ratio 0.76, relative; P=.0096) for enzalutamide plus radium-223 versus enzalutamide alone in first-line bone-metastatic mCRPC, conditional on the mandatory bone-protecting-agent co-treatment that is part of the tested intervention and is printed on the face, with more grade 3-or-worse toxicity and fractures as the costs

title: Capivasertib + abiraterone in PTEN-deficient mHSPC (CAPItello-281): PFS 33.2 vs 25.7 months on exactly 2 reports — survival not confirmed, diarrhoea in half
question: In men with PTEN-deficient (≥90% of viable malignant cells without cytoplasmic PTEN staining) metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer, does adding the AKT inhibitor capivasertib to abiraterone (with prednisone/prednisolone and androgen deprivation therapy), versus placebo plus abiraterone, prolong radiographic progression-free and overall survival, and at what toxicity cost?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — FLOOR-RISK, on exactly 2 reports of one trial. CAPItello-281 (1,012 randomised with PTEN-deficient tumours; only 25.3% of 6,003 validly tested tumours qualified) found radiographic progression-free survival of 33.2 versus 25.7 months with capivasertib plus abiraterone versus placebo plus abiraterone (hazard ratio 0.81, relative, P=0.034). Overall survival was NOT significant at the primary, confirmatory read (hazard ratio 0.90, relative, P=0.401, at 26.4% maturity); a later ad hoc descriptive update at 42% maturity gave hazard ratio 0.82 (relative, nominal P=0.044; medians 57.4 vs 46.5 months) — supportive only, not prespecified. Harms are common: diarrhoea 51.9% vs 8.0%, hyperglycaemia 38.0% vs 12.9%, rash 35.4% vs 7.0%, adverse-event-associated deaths 7.2% vs 5.2%.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — FLOOR-RISK, exactly 2 reports of one trial (CAPItello-281): the primary report showed a significant radiographic-PFS benefit for capivasertib plus abiraterone in PTEN-deficient mHSPC (33.2 vs 25.7 months; relative hazard ratio 0.81) but overall survival was not significant at that confirmatory read (relative hazard ratio 0.90); the second report is an ad hoc descriptive update only (relative hazard ratio 0.82, nominal), and toxicity is frequent (diarrhoea 51.9%, hyperglycaemia 38.0%, rash 35.4%)

title: Durvalumab ± olaparib maintenance in endometrial cancer (DUO-E, PARTIAL): PFS hazard ratios 0.71 and 0.55 — olaparib's increment is mainly in pMMR disease

balance: LIKELY (benefit, progression-free survival) — PARTIAL shelf, one trial (DUO-E, 718 randomised) in three reports. title: Encorafenib + binimetinib in BRAF V600 melanoma (COLUMBUS): PFS 14.9 vs 7.3 months vs vemurafenib, durable to 7 years — no head-to-head vs dabrafenib + trametinib
question: In patients with locally advanced unresectable or metastatic BRAF V600E/K-mutant melanoma, treatment-naïve or progressed after first-line immunotherapy, does encorafenib 450 mg daily plus binimetinib 45 mg twice daily, versus vemurafenib (or encorafenib alone), prolong progression-free and overall survival?

title: Zanidatamab ± tislelizumab in HER2+ gastroesophageal cancer (HERIZON-GEA-01, exactly 2 reports): PFS win for both arms, survival win only with tislelizumab so far
question: In patients with previously untreated, centrally confirmed HER2-positive advanced gastroesophageal adenocarcinoma, does the HER2×HER2 bispecific antibody zanidatamab plus chemotherapy — with or without the PD-1 inhibitor tislelizumab — versus trastuzumab plus chemotherapy, prolong progression-free and overall survival?

title: Subcutaneous vs IV amivantamab (PALOMA-3, PARTIAL, exactly 2 reports): noninferior exposure, reactions 13% vs 66%, 4.8 minutes vs 5 hours — survival difference exploratory only
question: In patients with EGFR-mutated advanced NSCLC progressed after osimertinib and platinum-based chemotherapy, does subcutaneous amivantamab, versus intravenous amivantamab (both with lazertinib), achieve noninferior pharmacokinetics and response, and what does it change in infusion reactions, venous thromboembolism, administration time and patient experience?
balance: LIKELY (benefit, route and tolerability) — PARTIAL + FLOOR-RISK, exactly 2 reports of one trial (PALOMA-3, 418 randomised). Subcutaneous amivantamab (with lazertinib) met pharmacokinetic noninferiority versus the intravenous route (trough ratio 1.15, cycle-2 AUC ratio 1.03 — relative ratios) with similar response (30% vs 33%) and median PFS 6.1 vs 4.3 months. Its advantages are practical: infusion-related reactions 13% vs 66%, venous thromboembolism 9% vs 14%, first administration 4.8 minutes vs 5 hours, cycle-1 time in chair 0.4 vs 6.5 hours, and better patient experience. The overall-survival difference (hazard ratio 0.62, relative, nominal P=0.02) was a predefined exploratory endpoint, not powered or alpha-controlled — a route change is not a plausible sole cause of such a gap, and no survival claim is made. Amivantamab's efficacy itself is homed at pack #7239 / the MARIPOSA-2 row, cross-pointed only.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit, route and tolerability) — PARTIAL + FLOOR-RISK, exactly 2 reports of one trial (PALOMA-3): subcutaneous amivantamab + lazertinib was pharmacokinetically noninferior to the intravenous route with similar response (30% vs 33%), far fewer infusion-related reactions (13% vs 66%) and far shorter administration (4.8 minutes vs 5 hours first dose); the overall-survival difference was exploratory only and is explicitly not claimed

title: Telisotuzumab vedotin in c-Met NSCLC (LUMINOSITY, exactly 2 reports, single-arm): response 29% — about 35% c-Met-high, 23–24% intermediate; neuropathy in a third
question: In patients with previously treated (≤2 prior lines, ≤1 chemotherapy) locally advanced or metastatic c-Met protein-overexpressing, EGFR-wildtype nonsquamous NSCLC, does the c-Met-directed antibody–drug conjugate telisotuzumab vedotin 1.9 mg/kg every 2 weeks, versus no concurrent control, produce objective responses, and with what neuropathy cost?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — FLOOR-RISK, exactly 2 reports of one single-arm phase 2 trial (LUMINOSITY; 172 treated, 168 efficacy-evaluable), and single-arm throughout, so the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE. Telisotuzumab vedotin 1.9 mg/kg every 2 weeks produced responses in 28.6% (primary report) and 29.2% (updated analysis) of patients with previously treated c-Met-overexpressing (≥25% of tumour cells 3+, SP44 assay), EGFR-wildtype nonsquamous NSCLC — 34.6%/34.5% in c-Met-high and 22.9%/23.8% in c-Met-intermediate disease — with median duration of response 8.3 then 7.2 months. There is no comparator: no survival or comparative claim can be made. Peripheral sensory neuropathy is the price (30–31% any grade, 7% grade ≥3). Product: telisotuzumab vedotin (Emrelis, AbbVie), US-approved on the accelerated pathway on this evidence.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — FLOOR-RISK, exactly 2 reports of one single-arm phase 2 trial (LUMINOSITY): responses in 28.6–29.2% of biomarker-selected patients (about 35% c-Met-high, about 23–24% c-Met-intermediate) with median duration about 7–8 months and neuropathy in about a third; a single-arm base has no comparator and can support no more than POSSIBLE, with the base stated

title: Tislelizumab vs sorafenib in HCC (RATIONALE-301, exactly 2 reports): noninferiority met, superiority NOT met — better responses and QoL, worse median PFS
question: In systemic-therapy-naïve adults with unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma (Barcelona Clinic Liver Cancer stage B or C, Child-Pugh A), does tislelizumab 200 mg every 3 weeks, versus sorafenib, prolong overall survival (noninferiority, then superiority), and with what response durability and quality-of-life effect?
balance: SPLIT — FLOOR-RISK, exactly 2 reports of one trial (RATIONALE-301, 674 randomised), and the headline is printed exactly as the row directs: overall-survival NONINFERIORITY was met (median 15.9 vs 14.1 months; hazard ratio 0.85, relative, interval crossing 1) and SUPERIORITY was NOT met. Tislelizumab gave a higher response rate (14.3% vs 5.4%, absolute) with far more durable responses (median 36.1 vs 11.0 months), fewer grade ≥3 treatment-related events (22.2% vs 53.4%) and better quality of life (no difference for pain) — but median progression-free survival was numerically worse (2.1 vs 3.4 months; hazard ratio 1.11, relative, favouring sorafenib). All three reads stay on the face together; this is not stamped as a superiority win.
stamp: SPLIT — FLOOR-RISK, exactly 2 reports of one trial (RATIONALE-301): tislelizumab met overall-survival noninferiority versus sorafenib (15.9 vs 14.1 months; relative hazard ratio 0.85) but did NOT meet superiority, while response (14.3% vs 5.4%), response durability (36.1 vs 11.0 months), tolerability (grade ≥3 treatment-related events 22.2% vs 53.4%) and quality of life favoured tislelizumab and median progression-free survival numerically favoured sorafenib (2.1 vs 3.4 months)

title: Antimicrobial dressings on closed incisions: silver RR 0.78 (22% relative reduction) and DACC RR 0.49 pooled — primary trials mixed, mupirocin null
question: In patients with primarily closed surgical incisions, do antimicrobial dressings — silver, dialkylcarbamoyl chloride (DACC), PHMB, chlorhexidine or mupirocin-impregnated — reduce surgical-site infection versus a standard inert dressing, and does the answer differ by antimicrobial class and by surgical field?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — synthesis-anchored, carded per class and never as one pooled claim. The 2026 synthesis of 35 RCTs (8,718 participants) found silver dressings at relative risk 0.78 — a 22% RELATIVE reduction, moderate-certainty — and DACC dressings at relative risk 0.49 (a 51% relative reduction, 3 studies, moderate-certainty), while mupirocin dressings were not associated with benefit. The primary trials carded from inside the synthesis keep the claim at POSSIBLE: for silver, one large positive trial (gastrointestinal, 6.8% vs 11.4%) against three non-significant trials (caesarean 4.6% vs 4.2%; colorectal 15.5% vs 20.4%; breast 6.6% vs 12.9%); for DACC, two sequential single-centre caesarean trials (1.8% vs 5.2% significant; pilot 2.8% vs 9.8% not) plus their costing — below the ≥3-independent-trial threshold for a DACC class claim, stated on the face.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — per class, from a 35-RCT synthesis with its primary trials carded: silver relative risk 0.78 (a 22% relative reduction, moderate certainty) with mixed primary trials (one significant, three not), DACC relative risk 0.49 on a thin, single-centre caesarean base that does not meet a ≥3-independent-trial class claim, and mupirocin not associated with benefit; no pooled 'antimicrobial dressings work' claim is made

title: Postoperative coffee/caffeine for bowel recovery: SPLIT — coffee works in gynaecological trials, null as coffee in colorectal, caffeine capsules positive on one endpoint only
question: After abdominal or pelvic surgery (colorectal, gynaecological and other abdominal fields as tested), does postoperative coffee or caffeine speed recovery of bowel function — time to first flatus, first bowel motion and tolerance of diet — and shorten ileus and hospital stay versus water, tea or no drink?
balance: SPLIT — by surgical field and by agent, with coffee and isolated-caffeine arms kept separate throughout, as the row directs. In gynaecological surgery, coffee sped bowel recovery in both trials (flatus 19 vs 25 hours laparoscopic and 30.2 vs 40.2 hours after open staging surgery; ileus 2.0% vs 14.9% in the laparoscopic trial). In colorectal surgery, the one three-arm trial found NO effect of caffeinated coffee, decaffeinated coffee or warm water on time to first bowel movement (2.86 / 2.58 / 2.94 days, P=0.53), while isolated caffeine capsules shortened time to first stool by 18 hours on one endpoint only (flatus, diet tolerance and stay not significant), a direction the colorectal synthesis supports for bowel movement and food intake but not flatus or stay. No carded trial showed a shorter hospital stay. Whether caffeine is the active agent is unresolved — the trials disagree, and that disagreement is the balance.
stamp: SPLIT — coffee sped bowel recovery in both gynaecological trials (flatus, defecation and food tolerance all significantly sooner; ileus 2.0% vs 14.9% laparoscopic) but caffeinated and decaffeinated coffee were both null in the one three-arm colorectal trial, while isolated caffeine capsules shortened time to first stool by 18 hours on a single endpoint in one small trial; no trial showed a shorter hospital stay, and whether caffeine is the active agent remains unresolved

title: Small bites fascial closure (STITCH): hernia 13% vs 21% at 1 year and 34% vs 49% at 13 years; 7-trial pooled relative risk 0.46
question: In adults having elective midline laparotomy, does fascial closure with the small-bites technique (5 mm x 5 mm bites of slowly absorbable continuous suture, suture-length-to-wound-length ratio at least 4:1) reduce incisional hernia, burst abdomen and wound infection versus conventional large-bites closure?
balance: LIKELY benefit. Four distinct randomised trials plus a 7-trial synthesis point the same way on hernia, with one small null factorial trial in high-risk patients as the exception. STITCH (560 randomised, elective midline laparotomy): incisional hernia at 1 year 13% with small bites versus 21% with large bites (adjusted odds ratio 0.52), and its 13-year follow-up report found cumulative hernia incidence 34% versus 49% (hazard ratio 0.61). Millbourn (691 randomised) found infection and herniation less common with small stitches, without printing event percentages in its record. ESTOIH's 5-year report (362 in the analysis) found hernia 9.14% versus 13.90%, not significant. The 2025 synthesis of 7 RCTs / 2,299 patients gives a relative risk of 0.46 for incisional hernia — a 54% relative risk reduction — and 0.73 for surgical-site infection (a 27% relative risk reduction). Coelho's 107-patient 2x2 factorial trial in overweight/obese high-risk patients found no difference in 1-year major complications (18% vs 19%). Follow-up length and hernia ascertainment differ by trial and are carded as published, never pooled. PROPOSED STAMP: LIKELY (benefit).
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — small bites fascial closure reduces incisional hernia after elective midline laparotomy: STITCH showed 13% vs 21% hernia at 1 year with a 13-year cumulative incidence of 34% vs 49%, Millbourn and ESTOIH point the same way, and the 7-trial synthesis gives a relative risk of 0.46; the one null trial was a small factorial study in high-risk patients using a composite outcome

title: Oral glutamine for oral mucositis: SPLIT — small chemo/BMT trials favoured it (morphine days 5.0 vs 10.3 in autologous BMT); radiotherapy trial and pooled incidence (relative risk 0.91) are null
question: In patients receiving chemotherapy, radiotherapy or chemoradiation (including bone-marrow transplantation), does oral glutamine (swish-and-swallow or dissolved oral dosing, as tested) reduce the incidence, duration and severity of oral mucositis / stomatitis versus placebo or standard oral care?
balance: SPLIT — by treatment setting, and the split is the shelf. In chemotherapy and autologous bone-marrow transplantation, three small early randomised reports favoured oral glutamine: a 14-patient pilot (mucositis days 2.7 vs 9.9 across successive courses), a 24-patient randomised crossover trial (mouth pain 4.5 days shorter than placebo) and a 193-patient BMT trial in which autologous recipients used morphine for 5.0 versus 10.3 days — while allogeneic recipients showed no benefit and longer opiate use. In head-and-neck radiotherapy, the one modern phase 3 trial (71 randomised) found no significant effect on mucositis severity, and the 2020 synthesis of randomised trials found the same risk of oral mucositis with glutamine as control (relative risk 0.91, 95% CI 0.78 to 1.05; n=314; low-confidence evidence). The early trials are small and their Ns are printed on their faces. PROPOSED STAMP: SPLIT.
stamp: SPLIT — oral glutamine reduced mucositis pain and duration in small chemotherapy and autologous bone-marrow-transplant trials, but the head-and-neck radiotherapy phase 3 trial was null and the pooled randomised estimate for mucositis incidence is a relative risk of 0.91 (95% CI 0.78 to 1.05); the answer differs by treatment setting

title: Glove and instrument change before abdominal closure (ChEETAh, single programme): SSI 16.0% vs 18.9% in 13,301 LMIC patients (adjusted risk ratio 0.87)
question: In patients having abdominal surgery in low- and middle-income settings, does a routine change of sterile gloves and separate sterile instruments immediately before abdominal wound closure reduce surgical-site infection versus continuing with the gloves and instruments used for the operation?
balance: FLOOR-RISK, single programme — stated on the face: the entire randomised base is ONE trial programme (ChEETAh), and the three reports carded here are reports OF that programme (the trial, its protocol and its cost-effectiveness analysis), labelled as such, exactly as single-programme shelves are labelled elsewhere in this library. In that one pragmatic cluster-randomised trial (81 hospitals, seven low- and middle-income countries, 13,301 patients), routine glove and instrument change before abdominal closure reduced 30-day surgical-site infection from 18.9% to 16.0% (adjusted risk ratio 0.87, 95% CI 0.79 to 0.95 — a 13% relative risk reduction, an absolute reduction of 2.9 percentage points), and the model-based cost-effectiveness analysis found similar costs ($259.92 vs $261.10 per patient). The setting — LMIC abdominal surgery with a high baseline SSI rate — is part of the claim and is not generalised to high-income settings on this shelf. PROPOSED STAMP: POSSIBLE (benefit), single-programme.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single-programme (FLOOR-RISK): the only randomised evidence is the ChEETAh cluster trial (13,301 patients, seven LMICs), which reduced 30-day SSI from 18.9% to 16.0% (adjusted risk ratio 0.87) with essentially unchanged cost; the protocol and cost-effectiveness reports are labelled reports of that same programme, and the claim is confined to LMIC abdominal surgery

title: Carotid IMT reference intervals by method and population: UK 97.5th percentile 0.60 mm at 35-39 rising to 0.81 mm at 60+; Chinese IMT rises 5.5-5.8 micrometres/year
question: In healthy adults, what is common carotid intima-media thickness — its mean, spread and age-, sex- and ethnicity-specific reference intervals / percentiles measured by B-mode ultrasound (manual, semiautomated and echotracking methods) — and how much do measurement method and population move the values that define 'increased' cIMT?
balance: Textbook framing: Boron & Boulpaep, vascular physiology / arterial wall mechanics — the framing is general, and this shelf rests chiefly on the primary normative imaging literature, and says so. Four primary datasets, carded PER METHOD and PER POPULATION as the measurement demands: echotracking in 24,871 pooled individuals (healthy sub-population 4,234) generating age- and sex-specific percentile equations; B-mode ultrasound in 1,448 Andean-Hispanic adults (healthy reference sample 472) with age- and sex-dependent 95th percentiles; semiautomated border detection in 137 strictly healthy UK adults, whose 97.5th-percentile common carotid limits rise from 0.60 mm at age 35-39 to 0.81 mm at age 60+ (bifurcation limits are higher, to 1.05 mm); and radiofrequency-signal ultrasound in 3,053 healthy Han Chinese adults, with IMT rising 5.5 micrometres/year in women and 5.8 in men. Near-wall vs far-wall and mean vs maximum IMT are different numbers, and ethnicity-specific intervals are content, not caveat. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — carotid IMT reference intervals are established in four primary datasets across three ultrasound methods (echotracking percentiles in 4,234 healthy people; B-mode norms in Andean-Hispanic and UK populations; RF-ultrasound values in 3,053 Han Chinese adults), with age-, sex-, segment- and population-specific limits printed per dataset

title: Blood-pressure response to exercise: treadmill maxima plateau after the sixth decade; bicycle SBP/watt slope 0.52 (women) vs 0.41 (men) mmHg/watt; athlete ceilings 220/200 mmHg
question: In healthy adults, what is the blood-pressure response to maximal and submaximal exercise — peak systolic pressure percentiles and upper limits of normal by age, sex, exercise mode (treadmill vs bicycle) and workload (including workload-indexed systolic pressure, mmHg per MET or per watt) — and what counts as an exaggerated response?
balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, ch. 84 (sports physiology), and Boron & Boulpaep, exercise physiology — the framing is brief, and this shelf rests chiefly on the primary exercise-testing literature, and says so. Four datasets, carded PER MODE as the measurement demands (treadmill and bicycle values are not interchangeable): maximal treadmill testing in 2,917 apparently healthy US adults (FRIEND), where peak systolic pressure rises with age to the sixth decade then plateaus; submaximal treadmill norms in 2,544 multiethnic NHANES participants aged 12-49, with exaggerated responses defined at the 90th percentile; workload-indexed bicycle values in 3,839 healthy Swedes drawn from 12,976 tests (peak systolic 188 +/- 24 mmHg in women vs 202 +/- 22 in men, but workload-indexed slopes higher in women: 0.52 vs 0.41 mmHg/watt); and maximal bicycle values in 1,876 Olympic athletes (upper reference 220 mmHg systolic in men, 200 in women) — a separate athlete limb, never merged into general-population norms. Unindexed peak pressure rises with achieved workload, so the workload-indexed limb is core content. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — blood-pressure responses to maximal treadmill (FRIEND, 2,917 adults), submaximal treadmill (NHANES, 2,544 multiethnic participants), workload-indexed bicycle ergometry (3,839 healthy subjects with reference equations) and maximal bicycle exercise in athletes (1,876) are established per mode, with upper limits and percentiles printed per dataset

title: DXA body-composition references in four populations: NHANES, LEAD (10,894 adults), Mexican (9,518) and Singapore (537) — lean mass read against fat mass, per device
question: In healthy adults, what are DXA whole-body body-composition reference values — fat-mass index, lean-mass index, appendicular lean-mass index, percentage fat and android/gynoid distribution — by age, sex and ancestry, and how much does the reference population move the values used to define low lean mass and sarcopenia?
balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, energy balance / body-composition sections — the framing is brief, and this shelf rests chiefly on the primary densitometry-reference literature, and says so. Four adult population datasets, carded PER DEVICE as the measurement demands (scanner generation and software move soft-tissue values): NHANES 1999-2004 fan-beam whole-body data (ages 8-85, partitioned by sex and ethnicity) providing percentage fat, fat-mass index, lean-mass index and appendicular lean-mass index references; the Austrian LEAD cohort (10,894 adults aged 18-81, GE-Lunar Prodigy) with visceral adipose tissue mass; 9,518 healthy Mexican adults with total and appendicular lean-mass references; and 537 Singaporean adults (Hologic Discovery Wi) with Lambda-Mu-Sigma percentiles, in whom lean-mass indices fell with age in men (r -0.45 to -0.54) but barely in women. Ancestry-specific centiles are the content. This shelf cards DXA soft-tissue data only — DXA bone density / T-score references are a different shelf, and bioelectrical-impedance phase angle is a different method. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — DXA whole-body body-composition reference values are established in four adult population datasets (NHANES 1999-2004; LEAD 10,894 adults; Mexican cohort 9,518 subjects; Singapore Yishun 537 adults), carded per device with age-, sex- and ancestry-specific fat-mass, lean-mass and appendicular lean-mass indices

title: Central BP and augmentation-index references per device: indexes not equivalent across site or technique; Omani SphygmoCor mean AIx 13 +/- 11%, aortic PWV 6.7 +/- 1.6 m/s
question: In healthy adults, what are central (aortic) systolic pressure, central pulse pressure and augmentation index — their means, spreads and age-, sex- and height-specific reference values by applanation tonometry and oscillometric devices — how far does central pressure sit below brachial pressure (pressure amplification), and how do device and recording site move the values?
balance: Textbook framing: Boron & Boulpaep, arterial pulse / wave reflection, and Guyton & Hall, arterial system chapters (framing). Four primary datasets, carded PER DEVICE as the measurement demands — transfer-function-derived aortic pressures are device-specific and no device's central values are presented here as universal: carotid/radial tonometry plus brachial oscillometry profiles in 1,688 healthy subjects aged 2-84 (indexes were NOT equivalent across recording site or technique, so reference intervals were defined per site and technique); Mobil-O-Graph office references in 867 rigorously healthy adults (with a 5,632-person risk-factor comparison group); Arteriograph values in 1,009 Mexican adults, whose central pressures ran higher than previously reported populations, especially in women, older and obese subjects; and SphygmoCor values in just 120 healthy Omani Arabs (mean central augmentation index 13 +/- 11%; aortic PWV 6.7 +/- 1.6 m/s). Augmentation index is heart-rate-dependent and AIx and AIx@75 are stated separately as published. The stamp is graded down because every value is device-bound, one dataset is very small (N=120), and the healthy denominators are modest. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING. Cross-points: pack #6297 (pulse-pressure mechanism) and pack #7065 (carotid-femoral PWV) — neither gives central-pressure reference values, and neither is re-carded here.

title: 24-h ABPM normal values vs outcome thresholds: normotensive 95th percentiles 129/80 (24-h), 137/88 (day), 121/72 (night); IDACO hypertension thresholds 130/80, 140/85, 120/70
question: In adults without hypertension, what are normal 24-hour ambulatory blood-pressure values — daytime, night-time and 24-hour means and upper reference limits (95th percentiles) — how large is the normal night-time dip, and how do statistically derived reference limits compare with outcome-driven ambulatory thresholds?
balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, long-term blood-pressure control chapters — the framing is brief, and this shelf rests chiefly on the primary population-monitoring literature, and says so. Two KINDS of number are carded and never presented as interchangeable: (1) statistical reference limits from normotensive population samples — the Belgian Population Study (1,057 people; normotensive 95th percentiles 129/80 mmHg over 24 hours, 137/88 daytime, 121/72 night-time) and a normal British sample (282 people; awake mean 115/72, asleep mean 97/58, with 2-standard-deviation upper limits of 136/86 awake and 121/73 asleep — a normal night-time dip of about 18/14 mmHg between the printed means); and (2) outcome-driven thresholds from IDACO (5,682 participants), whose rounded ambulatory-hypertension thresholds (130/80 for 24 hours, 140/85 daytime, 120/70 night-time) sit close to, but are derived differently from, the statistical limits. A companion subject-level analysis (5,018 untreated participants) found home/conventional thresholds did not need to differ by sex or age. The row's third-dataset stop condition is MET: alongside PAMELA and IDACO, the Belgian Population Study was verified from its fetched record this session as a third primary reference dataset (the British sample is a fourth). The PAMELA card is transparent that its fetched record is the study's design report and prints no values. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — normal 24-hour ambulatory values are established by population reference datasets (Belgian 95th percentiles 129/80 mmHg 24-hour, 137/88 daytime, 121/72 night-time; British means 115/72 awake and 97/58 asleep) and outcome-driven thresholds by IDACO (ambulatory hypertension 130/80, 140/85 and 120/70 mmHg), with the two kinds of number distinguished on the face and the row's third-dataset condition met by the verified Belgian dataset

title: Brachial-ankle PWV reference ranges: healthy mean 13.90 m/s; decade upper limits rise to 17.98 m/s (men) and 19.15 m/s (women) by the sixties — not a cfPWV scale
question: In healthy adults, what is brachial-ankle pulse wave velocity — its distribution and age- and sex-specific reference ranges — and how do its values relate to (without being interchangeable with) carotid-femoral PWV?
balance: Textbook framing: Boron & Boulpaep, arterial mechanics (framing). Three primary datasets, all East-Asian and all using volume-plethysmographic baPWV devices, carded per dataset: 21,094 Chinese subjects whose healthy subgroup (no cardiovascular disease or risk factors) averaged 1,389.9 +/- 288.4 cm/s (13.90 m/s), with discrimination cut-offs of 1,450-1,566 cm/s; 12,517 Japanese subjects without medication or cardiovascular history, from whom 7,881 healthy subjects showed baPWV lower in women than men until age 60 and converging thereafter, rising on a quadratic curve with age; and — the third dataset whose verification the row made a build condition, VERIFIED from its fetched record this session — 974 healthy Northern Chinese subjects with decade upper limits rising from 1,394/1,264 cm/s (men/women, twenties) to 1,798/1,915 cm/s (sixties). baPWV includes a long peripheral muscular-artery path and runs systematically higher than carotid-femoral PWV (the aortic measure, pack #7065): the two scales must never be interchanged, and that contrast is this shelf's core teaching point. The stamp is graded down because every dataset is East-Asian and one device family — reference ranges outside those populations are not established by this base. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING — brachial-ankle PWV reference ranges are established in three large East-Asian datasets (21,094 Chinese subjects; 7,881 healthy Japanese subjects; 974 healthy Northern Chinese subjects with decade upper limits), graded down because all datasets are East-Asian and single-device-family, so ranges beyond those populations are not established; the row's third-dataset condition was met at build

title: Liver-panel reference intervals: sex/age partitioning required; metabolically verified ALT upper limits 34 U/L (men) and 22 U/L (women) sit below historically printed limits
question: In healthy adults, what are the reference intervals for the liver panel — alanine and aspartate aminotransferases, alkaline phosphatase, gamma-glutamyltransferase and bilirubin — by sex, age and ancestry, and how far do metabolically defined 'healthy' upper limits for ALT sit below the limits laboratories have historically printed?
balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, liver / gastrointestinal physiology chapters — the framing is brief, and this shelf rests chiefly on the primary reference-interval literature, and says so. Three primary datasets: a Chinese multicentre study (3,210 healthy adults aged 20-79 across six regions, seven analytes on three analytical systems, validated in 21 hospitals) which found the intervals then in use were no longer applicable — under the old intervals, 15.2% of results for total bilirubin fell outside on one side against a nominal 2.5%; a metabolically and histologically verified Korean living-liver-donor analysis (5,455 screened; 1,553 with no steatosis who met Prati metabolic criteria) setting the ALT upper reference limit at 34 U/L for men and 22 U/L for women — well below historically printed laboratory limits; and CARDIA (over 5,000 young US adults), in which values for six liver-associated tests differed significantly by race and sex and at least one test was out of range in 38% of men and 19% of women using common intervals. The contested number is the ALT upper limit, and the population-definition rule (which metabolic exclusions were applied) moves it more than the assay does — that rule is printed beside the interval on its card. Values are in U/L; no fetched record on this shelf prints bilirubin in mmol/L, and where bilirubin appears it is handled in mg/dL terms only as the records allow (none prints a numeric bilirubin interval, and none is claimed). The stamp is graded down: only three datasets, from three different population-definition traditions, and the ALT limit is definition-dependent. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING — liver-panel reference intervals are supported by three primary datasets (Chinese multicentre intervals in 3,210 adults; CARDIA distributions in over 5,000 young US adults; metabolically verified ALT limits of 34 U/L in men and 22 U/L in women in 1,553 screened donors), graded down because the base is three datasets from different population-definition traditions and the ALT upper limit is definition-dependent

title: Coagulation screening intervals: a common adult interval fits PT/INR, thrombin time and fibrinogen — minor age/sex variation in 1.78M data-mined samples — but aPTT is reagent- and analyser-specific
question: In healthy non-pregnant adults, what are the reference intervals for the coagulation screening tests — prothrombin time / INR, activated partial thromboplastin time, thrombin time and fibrinogen — by age (including older adults), sex, analyser and reagent, and how much do data-mined (indirect) intervals agree with directly recruited healthy-volunteer intervals?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, haemostasis chapters, and Boron & Boulpaep, blood sections (framing brief — this shelf rests chiefly on the primary reference-interval literature, and says so). Four datasets converge on the same practical picture: directly and indirectly derived intervals for PT/INR, aPTT, thrombin time and fibrinogen show only minor age and sex variation, supporting a common adult interval (Zierk 2019: 1,778,738 samples from 116,754 patients, data-mined; Wu 2025: 630,946 records, cross-platform), BUT aPTT intervals are batch-, reagent- and analyser-specific to a degree unusual among routine tests, so no universal aPTT range is printed here. In healthy people over 60 a proportion of aPTT and TEG results fell outside adult intervals while derived fibrinogen stayed inside them (Donkin 2020, n=60), and in 121 healthy young female athletes the fibrinogen interval ran higher (1.9–4.4 g/L (190–440 mg/dL)) than the national non-athlete interval (1.8–3.5 g/L (180–350 mg/dL)) while PT and aPTT-ratio intervals were confirmed (HemSter 2021). Pregnancy-specific intervals are a separate literature and are NOT this shelf.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — four primary datasets (two very large indirect derivations, an over-60 verification study and an athlete verification study) agree the screening panel needs no sex partitioning and only minor age adjustment, while aPTT remains reagent/analyser-specific and no universal aPTT range is claimed

title: Trabecular bone score norms: peak ≈1.42 in young adults, falling 0.27%/year in women vs 0.11%/year in men (Thai data), with Japanese women below Caucasian women at every age
question: In healthy adults, what is the trabecular bone score (TBS) of the lumbar spine — its mean, spread and age-related decline by sex and ancestry — and how much does the choice of reference population move the values against which an individual's bone microarchitecture is judged?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, bone / calcium metabolism chapters (framing brief — rests chiefly on the primary densitometry-reference literature, and says so). Four population datasets on three continents tell one story: lumbar trabecular bone score peaks in young adulthood (peak mean ≈1.42 in both Thai and Iranian data) and declines with age — slowly in men (≈0.11%/year in Thai data) and faster in women (≈0.27%/year; a 16.0% linear fall from age 45 to 90 in US white women), with absolute levels differing by ancestry (Japanese women lower than Caucasian women at every age, the gap widening to age 65). TBS is a texture index from the spine DXA image, NOT bone mineral density — the DXA BMD / T-score reference shelf is the cross-point, not re-carded here. Every curve is software-version-bound (TBS iNsight, Med-Imaps) and the version is carded beside the data.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — four population datasets (Japanese, Thai, Iranian, US white) agree on a young-adult peak near 1.42 and an age decline that is faster in women, while absolute levels and cut-points are population- and software-specific, as printed on each card

title: Plasma homocysteine distributions: post-fortification US means ≈8–9 µmol/L, Hordaland 95% ranges 5.1–16.5 (women) and 6.2–18.7 µmol/L (men) — shaped by folate, smoking and coffee
question: In general populations, what is the distribution of plasma total homocysteine — median, spread and upper percentiles by age, sex, folate status and MTHFR genotype — and how far did population folic-acid fortification shift the whole distribution?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall / Ganong, one-carbon and B-vitamin metabolism sections (framing brief — rests chiefly on the primary population-survey literature, and says so). All values are in µmol/L (the unit used in both US and metric practice for this analyte; it is not reported in mmol/L). Four population datasets agree on the shape: homocysteine is higher in men than women, rises with age, and is driven strongly by folate status, smoking and coffee. Post-fortification US adults (NHANES 1999–2002, n=9,196) had age-adjusted means of 8.39 µmol/L (non-Hispanic white), 8.92 (non-Hispanic black) and 8.12 (Mexican American/Hispanic). Pre-fortification Norway (Hordaland, n=11,941) gives the widest 95% ranges — 5.1–16.5 µmol/L in women and 6.2–18.7 in men aged 40–42 — narrowing to 4.8–12.8 and 6.2–14.7 in the favourable-lifestyle subgroup. Pre- and post-fortification distributions are nutritionally different populations and are never merged here. This is a distribution shelf, not a treatment shelf: homocysteine-lowering B-vitamin trials live on their own shelves (cross-point live #203), not re-carded here.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — four population datasets (NHANES post-fortification n=9,196; Hordaland n=11,941; Canary Islands n=557; Turkish N=159 labelled small) agree on the sex/age gradient and on folate, smoking and coffee as the dominant acquired determinants; fortification-stratified, never merged

title: Vitamin B12 and methylmalonic acid: US mean B12 518 pg/mL (382 pmol/L) with ≈3% below 200 pg/mL (148 pmol/L) — and MMA rises with age, needing age-specific intervals
question: In healthy people, what are the distributions and reference intervals for serum vitamin B12 and its functional marker methylmalonic acid — by age, sex and ancestry — how common are low and borderline B12 values in apparently healthy populations, and why does methylmalonic acid need age-specific ranges?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING. Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, gastrointestinal absorption / haematology sections (framing brief — rests chiefly on the primary population and reference-interval literature, and says so). The B12 distribution itself is well described: NHANES III (n=11,851 with serum B12) centres the US mean at 518 pg/mL (382 pmol/L), with only ≈3% below 200 pg/mL (148 pmol/L). The emerging limb is the functional marker: in NHANES 2011–2014, serum methylmalonic acid rose across its whole distribution in vitamin-B12-replete older adults with normal renal function — especially at ≥70 years — so MMA needs AGE-SPECIFIC reference intervals, and its intervals in a B12-replete, normal-renal-function subpopulation were considerably narrower than in the overall population (Mineva 2019). B12 assays are notoriously non-harmonised: a directly established Chinese interval on a second-generation Roche ECLIA was 250.8–957.1 pg/mL (185–706 pmol/L) in 391 healthy adults (Jiang 2020), carded with its assay generation, not as a universal range. Cross-points: pack #6150 (B12 absorption MECHANISM — no intervals) and pack #2039 (metformin-associated B12 deficiency — a monitoring question) are not re-carded here. The folate limb of the NHANES III report is carded inside this shelf (one home); no separate folate-distribution shelf is spawned from the same dataset.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING — the B12 population distribution is settled (NHANES III, n=11,851) and a modern-assay interval is directly established (250.8–957.1 pg/mL (185–706 pmol/L)), but methylmalonic acid's need for age-specific intervals (NHANES 2011–2014) is a stated need not yet standard practice, and B12 intervals remain assay-generation-bound

title: Harmonised testosterone interval: 264–916 ng/dL (9.2–31.8 nmol/L) in non-obese men 19–39 — the interval slice pack #7072 (diurnal rhythm) does not give
question: In healthy men, what is the reference interval for serum total testosterone measured by harmonised / standardised assays — the 2.5th–97.5th percentile range in non-obese young men and its decline across adult age bands — and how much do assay calibration and population (obesity exclusion, ancestry) move the lower limit used to define hypogonadism?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED for the harmonised interval. PARTIAL shelf: pack #7072 homes the DIURNAL RHYTHM of testosterone (morning peak to afternoon nadir) — a rhythm is not an interval, and #7072 gives no 2.5th–97.5th percentile reference range. This shelf cards ONLY the reference-interval slice and cross-points #7072 in prose for sampling time; the rhythm is not re-carded. Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, male reproductive hormone chapters, and Ganong, gonadal physiology (framing brief — rests chiefly on the primary reference-range literature). The harmonised range: in healthy non-obese men aged 19–39, cross-calibrated to the CDC reference method across four US/European cohorts (9,054 men), the 2.5th–97.5th percentiles are 264–916 ng/dL (9.2–31.8 nmol/L), median 531 ng/dL (18.4 nmol/L) (Travison 2017). Age moves the whole distribution down: 27,687 Korean men aged ≥40 averaged 4.8 ± 1.8 ng/mL (480 ng/dL (16.7 nmol/L)), declining ≈0.021 ng/mL per year (2.1 ng/dL/year (0.07 nmol/L/year)), with biochemical hypogonadism (<2.5 ng/mL = 250 ng/dL (8.7 nmol/L)) rising from 5.5% at 40–49 to 11.6% at ≥70 (Kim 2026). Symptom-anchored thresholds in Han Chinese men cluster higher than the harmonised lower limit (≈12.55–14.35 nmol/L (362–414 ng/dL) for individual sexual symptoms; Liu 2016) — a threshold-for-symptoms is a different kind of number from a population percentile, and the two are never merged here. Morning sampling underlies the harmonised range; for the size of the morning-to-evening fall see pack #7072.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — PARTIAL slice vs pack #7072 (diurnal rhythm home): the harmonised 2.5th–97.5th percentile interval of 264–916 ng/dL (9.2–31.8 nmol/L) in non-obese men 19–39 (Travison 2017, 9,054 men, CDC-harmonised assays) is the settled reference range; age decline and symptom thresholds are carded as distinct kinds of number

title: Peak nasal inspiratory flow norms: bilateral charts by age, height and sex, unilateral charts by height alone (pilot), and a Turkish control mean of 137.8 L/min — a flow, not the SNIP pressure of pack #7155
question: In healthy adults, what is peak nasal inspiratory flow — bilateral and unilateral normal ranges in litres per minute by age, sex and height — and how reproducible is the measurement for serial and home use?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING. Textbook framing: Boron & Boulpaep, respiratory mechanics / nasal airflow sections, and Guyton & Hall, respiration chapters (framing brief — rests chiefly on the primary measurement literature, and says so). PNIF is a FLOW (L/min) reflecting nasal patency — distinct from sniff nasal inspiratory PRESSURE (SNIP, cmH2O, diaphragm strength), homed at pack #7155 and not re-carded here; the nasal cycle (pack territory S8-4-42) is a pattern question, not a flow range. The normative base is three datasets: bilateral PNIF charts against age, height and sex from 137 fulfilling volunteers (Ottaviano 2006 — the fetched record prints the chart construction, not numeric L/min values, and this shelf claims none from it); unilateral PNIF charts against height alone, the only correlating variable, in 97 fulfilling volunteers, explicitly a pilot (Ottaviano 2012); and a Turkish dataset giving the one printed mean — 137.8 L/min in 219 healthy controls (Ozkul 2013). Considerable between-person variability was unexplained by age, height or sex in the largest charting study. The stamp is EMERGING because two of three datasets print no numeric range in their records and the unilateral data are a pilot.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING — three normative datasets (bilateral charts n=137 fulfilling; unilateral pilot n=97 fulfilling; Turkish controls n=219, mean 137.8 L/min) establish PNIF's normative structure, but two print no numeric range in their records, values are technique-bound, and serial/home reproducibility is unquantified in the fetched records

title: Trelagliptin (once-weekly DPP-4 inhibitor, Japan): non-inferior to daily alogliptin, and HbA1c −0.72% vs placebo in severe renal impairment and −0.63% added to insulin — surrogate endpoints only
question: In adults with type 2 diabetes (including patients with severe renal impairment or end-stage renal disease, and patients inadequately controlled on insulin), does the once-weekly DPP-4 inhibitor trelagliptin, compared with daily alogliptin or placebo, improve glycaemic control?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). Single-region evidence — every trial is Japanese, and trelagliptin is approved in Japan as a once-weekly agent, not FDA/EMA-approved; that flag leads this shelf. On the surrogate endpoint HbA1c, three randomised trials are consistent: trelagliptin 100 mg weekly was non-inferior to alogliptin 25 mg daily over 24 weeks (HbA1c change −0.33% vs −0.45%; difference 0.11%, 95% CI −0.054 to 0.281, against a 0.4% margin; Inagaki 2015); trelagliptin 25 mg beat placebo in severe renal impairment / end-stage renal disease (−0.71% vs +0.01%; difference −0.72%, P < 0.0001; Kaku 2020); and trelagliptin 100 mg added to insulin beat placebo (least-squares mean difference −0.63%, P < 0.0001) with no severe hypoglycaemia (Kaku 2018). HbA1c is a surrogate endpoint and NO cardiovascular-outcomes trial exists for this agent — both facts are printed here, not buried. The stamp is POSSIBLE, not higher, because the base is one region, one development programme and surrogate outcomes only.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — three Japanese randomised trials show consistent HbA1c efficacy (non-inferior to daily alogliptin; superior to placebo in severe renal impairment/ESRD and as insulin add-on, differences −0.72% and −0.63%), but HbA1c is a surrogate, the evidence is single-region, and no cardiovascular-outcomes trial exists

title: Mitiglinide in type 2 diabetes: matched nateglinide in two trials and lowered HbA1c −0.45%/−0.67% added to pioglitazone — Japan/China evidence, surrogate endpoints only
question: In adults with type 2 diabetes, does the rapid-acting insulin secretagogue mitiglinide, compared with nateglinide or added to pioglitazone, improve glycaemic control (fasting and postprandial glucose, HbA1c)?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). Single-region evidence (Japan/China; mitiglinide is not FDA/EMA-approved) — that flag leads this shelf. The meglitinide class home is pack #2886, whose question names repaglinide and nateglinide only; mitiglinide is not carded there and this agent question is unasked there — #2886 is cross-pointed in prose, its studies are not re-carded here. Three randomised trials: mitiglinide 10–20 mg three times daily was non-inferior in effect to nateglinide 120 mg three times daily over 20 weeks (HbA1c −0.77% vs −0.71%; Gao 2009, n=291); in newly diagnosed patients the HbA1c fall was numerically larger on mitiglinide (−1.11% vs −0.76%) but not statistically significant (P = 0.06), with hypoglycaemic episodes in 2.8% on nateglinide and none on mitiglinide (Li 2012, n=225); and added to pioglitazone, mitiglinide 5 mg and 10 mg lowered HbA1c −0.45% and −0.67% vs −0.02% on pioglitazone alone (both P < 0.001; Kaku 2009, n=381). HbA1c is a surrogate endpoint; no outcomes trial exists — printed here. Mitiglinide/voglibose fixed-dose-combination reports are a combination question and are NOT carded on this shelf.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — mitiglinide matched nateglinide in two randomised trials (n=291, n=225; the one numerical advantage was non-significant, P = 0.06) and beat pioglitazone alone as add-on (−0.45%/−0.67% vs −0.02%), but the evidence is single-region (Japan/China), HbA1c is a surrogate, and no outcomes trial exists

title: Efpeglenatide glycaemic programme (AMPLITUDE-M/-D/-L/-S): HbA1c −0.5% to −1.0% vs placebo and non-inferior to dulaglutide — trials stopped early for funding, drug never marketed; outcomes live at #72
question: In adults with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled on diet and exercise alone, on oral agents, or on basal insulin, does once-weekly efpeglenatide, compared with placebo or dulaglutide, improve glycaemic control and body weight (the AMPLITUDE glycaemic programme)?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). PARTIAL shelf: live #72 asks the class-level cardiovascular-benefit question and homes efpeglenatide's outcomes trial, AMPLITUDE-O — AMPLITUDE-O is gated at #72, is NOT re-carded here, and is cross-pointed only; the outcomes evidence lives there. This shelf cards only the glycaemic programme: exactly 2 publications reporting 4 distinct phase 3 trials (AMPLITUDE-M, -D, -L, -S) — the report count is stated exactly, per the row's flag. AMPLITUDE-M (monotherapy vs placebo): least-squares mean HbA1c reductions superior to placebo at every dose at week 30 (−0.5%, −0.8%, −1.0% at 2, 4, 6 mg). AMPLITUDE-D: non-inferior to dulaglutide 1.5 mg (treatment differences −0.03% at 4 mg, −0.08% at 6 mg). AMPLITUDE-L and -S: numerically greater HbA1c and weight reductions than placebo at all doses. Two facts lead the face alongside the efficacy: all three trials in the 2023 report were TERMINATED EARLY BY THE SPONSOR FOR FUNDING REASONS, not safety or efficacy; and efpeglenatide was NEVER MARKETED (development discontinued). HbA1c is a surrogate endpoint; hypoglycaemia level 2 (<54 mg/dL (<3.0 mmol/L)) was reported in few participants; gastrointestinal events were the most frequent adverse events, consistent with the GLP-1 class.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — PARTIAL vs live #72 (AMPLITUDE-O gated there, cross-point only): the glycaemic programme (2 publications, 4 phase 3 trials) shows superiority to placebo as monotherapy and non-inferiority to dulaglutide, but three trials were terminated early for sponsor funding, the drug was never marketed, and HbA1c is a surrogate endpoint

title: Probucol: SPLIT record — events trend not significant in PROSPECTIVE (n=876), femoral imaging null in PQRST, carotid IMT −13.9% and events 2.4% vs 13.6% in FAST; HDL falls ≈24% relative
question: In patients with hypercholesterolaemia or established coronary heart disease, does the antioxidant lipid-lowering agent probucol, compared with placebo, control therapy or a statin, slow atherosclerosis progression and reduce cardiovascular events — and at what cost to HDL cholesterol?
balance: SPLIT. Withdrawn / restricted product history leads this shelf: probucol was withdrawn from the US market (1995) and remains in use chiefly in Japan — the regulatory history as stated in the commissioning row, printed here on the face. The three anchor trials answer three DIFFERENT endpoint levels and are never merged into one 'works' claim. Events: PROSPECTIVE (876 Japanese patients with coronary heart disease) found the primary cerebrovascular/cardiovascular composite incidence showed a trend to be lower with probucol 500 mg/day added to conventional therapy — a trend, NOT statistically significant, despite reduced HDL cholesterol and without serious adverse events. Femoral imaging: PQRST (303 randomised, 274 analysed, all on diet plus cholestyramine) was NULL on its primary — no significant difference in femoral-artery lumen-volume change — while probucol lowered total cholesterol 17%, LDL cholesterol 12% and HDL cholesterol 24% relative to control; that HDL lowering is the drug's paradox and is printed, not buried. Carotid imaging: FAST (246 patients) found carotid IMT fell 13.9% on probucol and 13.9% on pravastatin while the diet-only control thickened 23.2%, with cardiac events 2.4% on probucol vs 13.6% on control (P = 0.0136) — absolute rates as printed. One positive small imaging trial with an events signal, one null imaging trial, one large events trial with a non-significant trend: that is a SPLIT record.
stamp: SPLIT — PROSPECTIVE (n=876) showed only a non-significant trend to fewer events, PQRST (n=274 analysed) was null on femoral imaging, and FAST (n=246) was positive on carotid IMT with fewer cardiac events (2.4% vs 13.6% absolute); probucol lowers HDL cholesterol (≈24% relative) and was withdrawn from the US market in 1995, remaining in use chiefly in Japan

title: Mazindol in obesity: a split 1970s base — significant 1 lb/week loss in the four-centre trial, no advantage over placebo in the therapist-comparison trial
question: In adults with obesity, does the non-amphetaminic anorectic mazindol, compared with placebo (with or without behavioural modification), produce weight loss?
balance: SPLIT — a 1970s trial base that splits. The four-centre six-week trial (245 assigned) found mazindol without behavioural modification and behavioural modification alone each produced a statistically significant mean weight loss of 1 lb/patient/week, with the combination greater still; a crossover/long-term evaluation found weight loss greater on mazindol than in controls and maintained for longer. Against that, the double-blind therapist-comparison trial (60 patients) found weight loss averaged 1.1 lb/week overall with NO advantage of either mazindol preparation over placebo — a null drug result inside the base, printed as such. Two further typed-RCT reports (PMIDs 322112 and 1097046) have empty PubMed abstracts and were refused as anchors this session. Mazindol's marketing status differs by country and it is not FDA-approved for obesity in the US.
stamp: SPLIT — the three abstracted 1970s reports split: Walker 1977 found a statistically significant mean weight loss of 1 lb/patient/week on mazindol and Enzi 1976 found greater, longer-maintained loss than controls, but Atkinson 1977 found no advantage of either mazindol preparation over placebo; two empty-abstract typed-RCT reports were refused as anchors

title: Diethylpropion (amfepramone) in obesity: about 10% body-weight loss vs about 3% on placebo at 6 months, sustained in three placebo-controlled trials
question: In adults with obesity, does the sympathomimetic anorectic diethylpropion (amfepramone), compared with placebo plus diet, produce and maintain weight loss over six to twelve months?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) on weight loss, on three placebo-controlled trials of the same drug under its two names (diethylpropion = amfepramone — one drug, one home). At 6 months: −9.8% of initial body weight vs −3.2% on placebo (69 adults, P < 0.0001) and −7.7 kg vs −1.1 kg (156 Mexican patients); at 52 weeks in the five-drug comparative trial: −10.0 kg vs −3.1 kg on placebo (P < 0.001), with at least 5% weight loss in 71.4% vs 33.3%. No differences in blood pressure, pulse, ECG or psychiatric evaluation in the long-term trial; dry mouth and insomnia were the most frequent adverse events, with constipation, anxiety and irritability signals in the comparative trial. Diethylpropion is a sympathomimetic anorectic with short-term-use regulatory status. One further long-term report (PMID 4589633) has an empty PubMed abstract and was refused as an anchor this session.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — three placebo-controlled trials of diethylpropion/amfepramone (the same drug under two names) agree on weight loss at 6–12 months (−9.8% vs −3.2% of body weight; −7.7 vs −1.1 kg; −10.0 vs −3.1 kg), with dry mouth and insomnia the most frequent harms and no cardiovascular or psychiatric signal in the trial that measured them; the empty-abstract 1973 report was refused as an anchor

title: Conivaptan in euvolaemic/hypervolaemic hyponatraemia: sodium rose about 6–9 mEq/L vs about 1–3 mEq/L on placebo in three programme trials — a biochemical benefit, no outcomes trial
question: In hospitalised adults with euvolaemic or hypervolaemic hyponatraemia, does the vasopressin V1A/V2-receptor antagonist conivaptan (intravenous or oral), compared with placebo, raise serum sodium?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) on the biochemical endpoint — serum sodium — on three randomised placebo-controlled trials from one development programme (two oral, one intravenous). Least-squares mean sodium change from baseline to end of treatment: 6.4 and 8.2 mEq/L at oral 40 and 80 mg/day vs 3.4 mEq/L on placebo (74 patients); 6.3 and 9.4 mEq/L on intravenous 40 and 80 mg/day vs 0.8 mEq/L on placebo (84 patients); and 6.8 and 8.8 mEq/L on oral 40 and 80 mg/day vs 1.2 mEq/L on placebo (83 patients). Serum sodium is a biochemical endpoint: no trial here measured mortality, falls or cognition. The oral formulation was investigational; the intravenous product (Vaprisol) was FDA-approved in 2005. Overly rapid correction is the class harm; infusion-site reactions led to withdrawal in 3% and 15% at the two intravenous doses. The tolvaptan question is homed separately (live #744) and is cross-pointed only.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — on the biochemical endpoint only: three randomised programme trials (n=74, 84, 83) each found conivaptan raised serum sodium by about 6–9 mEq/L vs about 1–3 mEq/L on placebo over 4–5 days; no trial measured mortality, falls or cognition, the oral formulation was investigational, and infusion-site reactions caused withdrawal in up to 15% at the higher intravenous dose

title: Molsidomine in stable angina: exercise capacity improved and anginal attacks and nitrate use fell vs placebo in three crossover trials (largest n=533) — symptoms only, no outcomes trial
question: In adults with stable angina pectoris, does the nitric-oxide donor molsidomine, compared with placebo, improve exercise capacity and reduce anginal attacks and sublingual nitrate use?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) on exercise capacity and anginal symptoms, on three randomised double-blind crossover placebo-controlled trials (90, 533 and 50 patients): total work performance and exercise duration improved significantly vs placebo for up to 8–12 hours after dosing, effects were maintained after 2–6 weeks with no attenuation, and anginal-attack frequency and sublingual nitrate consumption fell significantly. This is an exercise-capacity/symptom trial base — no outcomes trial exists. Molsidomine is a European-market agent, not FDA-approved; the tested formulations are named exactly on the cards. Hypotension was significantly more frequent on the 16 mg once-daily formulation than placebo; headache is the other harm-side item. A further single-dose add-on-to-atenolol trial (n=12) is carded as programme support only, not as an anchor.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — on exercise capacity and anginal symptoms only: three randomised crossover placebo-controlled trials (n=90, 533, 50) consistently improved work performance and exercise duration and reduced anginal attacks and sublingual nitrate use, maintained over 2–6 weeks; no outcomes trial exists, the agent is not FDA-approved, and hypotension was significantly more frequent on the 16 mg once-daily formulation

title: Oral fasudil in stable angina (FLOOR-RISK — exactly 2 publications / 3 trials): time to ST depression prolonged vs placebo, exercise duration not significantly — surrogate endpoints only
question: In adults with stable (effort) angina, does the oral Rho-kinase inhibitor fasudil, compared with placebo, improve exercise time and time to ischaemic ST-segment depression?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), on a FLOOR-RISK base stated on the face: exactly 2 publications reporting 3 component trials (the phase IIa dose-escalation studies, the phase IIb double-blind dose-ranging trial, and the US double-blind placebo-controlled phase 2 trial). Time to at least 1 mm ST-segment depression increased by 172.1 seconds on fasudil vs 44.0 seconds on placebo at peak (P = 0.001) in the US trial, whose exercise duration was numerically, not significantly, greater and which found no significant differences in angina frequency or nitroglycerin use; the Japanese programme prolonged maximum exercise time and time to ST depression with a significant dose–response for the exercise tolerance index (P = 0.006). These are surrogate exercise endpoints only. The intracoronary fasudil studies in vasospastic and microvascular angina are a different route and different questions — they are NOT counted or merged here. Fasudil is approved in Japan for cerebral vasospasm, not for angina anywhere.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — FLOOR-RISK base of exactly 2 publications / 3 component trials, stated on the face: the placebo-controlled phase 2 trial prolonged time to ST depression (172.1 vs 44.0 s at peak, P = 0.001) but not exercise duration significantly and not angina frequency, and the Japanese programme showed a significant dose–response on exercise measures; surrogate endpoints only, and intracoronary vasospastic/microvascular reports were not merged

title: Omapatrilat vs enalapril (DISCONTINUED programme): better blood-pressure lowering and non-inferior heart-failure outcomes, at angioedema 2.17% vs 0.68% — never marketed
question: In adults with hypertension or chronic heart failure, does the vasopeptidase (ACE + neutral-endopeptidase) inhibitor omapatrilat, compared with enalapril, lower blood pressure and reduce death or heart-failure hospitalisation — and what is its angioedema cost?
balance: SPLIT — a discontinued, never-marketed programme whose efficacy and harm are both real. OVERTURE (5,770 heart-failure patients): the primary composite of death or heart-failure hospitalisation occurred in 914 patients on omapatrilat vs 973 on enalapril (hazard ratio 0.94, 95% CI 0.86 to 1.03, P = 0.187) — prespecified non-inferiority met, superiority not met. OCTAVE (25,302 hypertension patients): omapatrilat lowered systolic blood pressure 3.6 mm Hg more than enalapril at week 8, with less adjunctive therapy by week 24 (19% vs 27%) — but angioedema occurred in 2.17% on omapatrilat vs 0.68% on enalapril, the risk that ended the programme. A single-dose haemodynamic study is carded as mechanism support only. Omapatrilat was never marketed; its development was abandoned over the angioedema risk OCTAVE quantifies, and that history leads this shelf.
stamp: SPLIT — DISCONTINUED, never-marketed programme: omapatrilat lowered blood pressure more than enalapril (OCTAVE, n=25,302) and was non-inferior, not superior, on heart-failure outcomes (OVERTURE, n=5,770; hazard ratio 0.94), but angioedema occurred in 2.17% vs 0.68% — the risk that ended the programme; the single-dose haemodynamic report is mechanism support only

title: Quinagolide vs bromocriptine in hyperprolactinaemia: prolactin normalised at least as often and tolerability was better in a small 1990–1991 base (total N under 90; one n=7 phase sub-floor, not counted)
question: In women with hyperprolactinaemia, does the non-ergot dopamine agonist quinagolide (CV 205-502), compared with bromocriptine, normalise prolactin, restore menstrual bleeding and relieve galactorrhoea — and is it better tolerated?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), on a small, old (1990–1991) trial base whose total randomised N across the three anchors is under 90. Prolactin normalised in 8 of 11 women on quinagolide vs 2 of 9 on bromocriptine by 8 weeks in the first trial (P < 0.002), and in 81% vs 70% in the second (47 patients); the third found the two drugs equally effective over six months. Tolerability favoured quinagolide in two trials — adverse reactions milder and less persistent, with four bromocriptine patients but no quinagolide patients discontinuing for adverse reactions in the first trial — and did not differ in the third. The third anchor's acute crossover phase (n=7) is below the ~10-human floor, is labelled sub-floor on its card, and is never load-bearing; only its randomised long-term phase (n=12) is counted. Prolactin normalisation is a biochemical endpoint; tumour-shrinkage outcomes are not in this base. Quinagolide was never FDA-approved — a European-market agent whose licences have since been withdrawn or discontinued in several markets. The cabergoline-vs-bromocriptine home is cross-pointed only.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a small, old base (total randomised N under 90): prolactin normalised more often on quinagolide in two trials (8/11 vs 2/9 at 8 weeks, P < 0.002; 81% vs 70%) with milder, less persistent adverse reactions, while the third trial's counted long-term phase (n=12) found equivalence; its n=7 acute phase is sub-floor, labelled, and never load-bearing; quinagolide was never FDA-approved

title: Doxercalciferol in dialysis secondary hyperparathyroidism: PTH fell 55% and target was reached in 83% in the one efficacy trial (withdrawal design); conversion factor 0.57 vs paricalcitol; paediatric anchor printed as paediatric
question: In patients on dialysis with secondary hyperparathyroidism, does the vitamin D analogue doxercalciferol (1α-hydroxyvitamin D2), compared with placebo, paricalcitol or calcitriol, suppress parathyroid hormone — and at what cost in calcium and phosphate?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) on the surrogate endpoint of parathyroid hormone suppression, resting on one efficacy trial: in 138 haemodialysis patients, intact PTH fell 55% by week 16 of open-label doxercalciferol, reached the 150–300 pg/mL target in 83% of patients, and in the randomised double-blind withdrawal phase PTH returned to baseline on placebo while remaining suppressed on doxercalciferol — at the cost of more hypercalcaemia measurements above 11.2 mg/dL (3.26% vs 0.46% of measurements, P < 0.01). The second anchor (n=27) answers a dose-conversion question, not efficacy: doxercalciferol at about 0.57 of the paricalcitol dose gave equivalent suppression. The third anchor is a PAEDIATRIC peritoneal-dialysis population (60 children), printed as such and not presented as adult evidence: PTH fell 35% in all groups and bone formation rates fell into the normal range in 72%, with FGF-23 rising over fourfold on both vitamin D agents. PTH is a surrogate endpoint; no outcomes trial exists for this agent.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — on the surrogate endpoint of PTH suppression: one efficacy trial (n=138 haemodialysis) showed a 55% fall, target reached in 83%, and maintenance on drug vs return to baseline on placebo in a randomised withdrawal phase, with more hypercalcaemia on drug; the n=27 report is a dose-conversion study and the n=60 report is in children on peritoneal dialysis — neither is adult efficacy evidence, and no outcomes trial exists
