title: Maxacalcitol in haemodialysis secondary hyperparathyroidism: no significant PTH difference vs calcitriol or paricalcitol in three Japanese trials (dose ratio 5.5:1 vs calcitriol) — single-region, surrogate endpoint
question: In patients on haemodialysis with secondary hyperparathyroidism, does the vitamin D analogue maxacalcitol (22-oxacalcitriol), compared with calcitriol or paricalcitol, suppress parathyroid hormone with comparable calcium control?
balance: LIKELY (no difference) — single-region evidence (Japan; an intravenous agent, not FDA/EMA-approved), flagged on the face. Against calcitriol over 12 months (91 patients) there were no significant differences in intact PTH, phosphate, calcium–phosphate product or bone alkaline phosphatase, with serum calcium significantly higher on maxacalcitol during early treatment only; in the crossover dose-equivalence study (31 patients) intact PTH was 267 pg/mL on maxacalcitol vs 343 pg/mL on calcitriol (P = 0.11) at a dose ratio of 5.5:1. Against paricalcitol in the phase 3 trial (255 Japanese haemodialysis patients), target intact PTH without hypercalcaemia was achieved by 30.5% on maxacalcitol vs 27.7% on paricalcitol; that trial's primary non-inferiority test concerned paricalcitol against maxacalcitol and was not met, and both agents reduced intact PTH with similar safety. Parathyroid hormone is a surrogate endpoint; no outcomes trial exists for this agent. This shelf and the doxercalciferol shelf are different agents in the same condition — their anchors are never pooled.
stamp: LIKELY (no difference) — single-region (Japan) base: maxacalcitol did not differ significantly from calcitriol on intact PTH over 12 months (n=91) or in crossover (267 vs 343 pg/mL, P = 0.11; dose ratio 5.5:1; n=31), and target achievement vs paricalcitol was 30.5% vs 27.7% (n=255); serum calcium was higher on maxacalcitol during early treatment only, PTH is a surrogate, and no outcomes trial exists

title: Colestipol in hypercholesterolaemia: relative LDL reductions of 16.3–27.2% by dose vs 2.7% on placebo (n=152) — pre-statin-era, surrogate endpoints only; n=27 single-blind report labelled, not load-bearing
question: In adults with moderate-to-severe primary hypercholesterolaemia, does the bile-acid sequestrant colestipol, compared with placebo or clofibrate, lower total and LDL cholesterol?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) on the surrogate lipid endpoint, on an old, pre-statin-era trial base (1981–1992) with no outcomes trial. The load-bearing trial is the double-blind dose-ranging study (152 randomised, 141 completing): relative LDL cholesterol reductions of 16.3%, 22.8% and 27.2% at 5, 10 and 15 g/day vs 2.7% on placebo (P < 0.001). The 65-patient comparison found mean total cholesterol falling from 333 to 266 mg/dL on colestipol at 6 months (P < 0.01), with more responders to colestipol than to clofibrate. The 1981 Metabolism comparison (n=27, single-blind) is labelled on its card and is never load-bearing; in it, colestipol lowered total cholesterol 25% relative and LDL cholesterol 31% relative while VLDL triglyceride rose — the triglyceride rise and gastrointestinal tolerability are the harm side of this class. All percentage reductions on this shelf drawn from relative measures are labelled relative, with absolute changes printed beside them where the reports give them.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — on the surrogate lipid endpoint in a pre-statin-era base: the load-bearing dose-ranging trial (n=152) found relative LDL reductions of 16.3%, 22.8% and 27.2% at 5, 10 and 15 g/day vs 2.7% on placebo (P < 0.001), supported by the n=65 comparison (total cholesterol 333 to 266 mg/dL); the n=27 single-blind report is labelled and never load-bearing, no outcomes trial exists, and triglyceride rise is the harm-side signal

title: Istaroxime in acute heart failure: wedge pressure, E/e' and blood pressure all improved over 6-24 hours in three small trials (HORIZON-HF, SEISMiC) — no outcomes trial exists and the drug is unapproved
question: In patients hospitalised with acute heart failure — including heart-failure-related pre-cardiogenic shock, SCAI stage B — does the intravenous inotrope/lusitrope istaroxime, compared with placebo, improve haemodynamics, diastolic function and blood pressure?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — on short-term haemodynamics only. Three distinct randomised placebo-controlled trials, in three different acute-heart-failure populations that must not be pooled, all show the same 6- to 24-hour pattern: pulmonary capillary wedge pressure fell (-3.2, -3.3 and -4.7 mm Hg at 0.5, 1.0 and 1.5 µg/kg/min vs 0.0 mm Hg on placebo in HORIZON-HF, n=120), the diastolic E/e' ratio improved at 24 hours (-4.55 vs -1.55 and -3.16 vs -1.08 in acute heart failure with LVEF ≤40%, n=120), and in SCAI stage B pre-cardiogenic shock systolic blood pressure rose more than on placebo (adjusted 6-hour AUC 53.1 vs 30.9 mm Hg·hour, P=0.017; SEISMiC, n=60) — with heart rate falling rather than rising, the opposite pattern to conventional inotropes. NO OUTCOMES TRIAL EXISTS: every endpoint is a haemodynamic or echocardiographic surrogate, and dyspnoea and NT-proBNP did not separate from placebo where measured. Istaroxime is investigational and unapproved. A 2025 prolonged-infusion (up to 60-hour) report from the same pre-shock programme is carded as programme support only and is not counted in the three-trial base.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — three randomised placebo-controlled trials (n=120, n=120, n=60) in distinct acute-heart-failure populations consistently improved haemodynamic and echocardiographic surrogates over 6-24 hours (wedge pressure, E/e', systolic blood pressure), but no trial tested mortality, hospitalisation or symptoms, dyspnoea and NT-proBNP did not separate from placebo, and istaroxime is investigational and unapproved; the 2025 prolonged-infusion report is programme support, not a fourth trial

title: Ciclesonide in chronic asthma: better lung function and control than placebo, and prednisone dose cut 47-63% in severe asthma — over 8-12 weeks only, with no exacerbation trial
question: In adults (and adolescents) with persistent asthma — including severe oral-steroid-dependent asthma — does once-daily inhaled ciclesonide versus placebo improve lung function and asthma control, and can it replace oral corticosteroids?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — for lung function, asthma control and oral-steroid sparing over 8-12 weeks. The Cochrane review (18 trials, 6,343 participants) found ciclesonide improved lung function, symptoms and rescue inhaler use versus placebo at 100-400 µg/day in mild-to-moderate asthma, with no dose-response. Two adult switch-off-steroid trials (n=329 and n=311) showed morning peak flow maintained on ciclesonide while it fell on placebo, and in severe prednisone-dependent asthma (n=141) ciclesonide 640 and 1,280 µg/day cut prednisone dose by 47% and 63% versus a 4% rise on placebo. The limits are printed on the face: all horizons are 8-12 weeks, there is NO exacerbation-outcome or mortality trial, and the Cochrane review could not assess the safety profile from the reported adverse-event data.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — a Cochrane pool of 18 trials (6,343 participants) plus three adult primaries show ciclesonide improves lung function and control versus placebo over 8-12 weeks and reduces prednisone dose by 47-63% in severe steroid-dependent asthma; no exacerbation, mortality or long-term safety evidence exists

title: Pranlukast in asthma: better than placebo and a useful beclomethasone add-on in tiny old trials, but switching off inhaled steroid to pranlukast left fewer patients controlled (72.2% vs 90%)
question: In patients with mild-to-severe asthma, does oral pranlukast (a cysteinyl-leukotriene receptor antagonist) versus placebo — or added to inhaled beclomethasone, or substituted for low-dose inhaled corticosteroid at step-down — improve lung function and symptoms?
balance: SPLIT — benefit in the placebo and add-on limbs, against the switch in the step-down limb, on a small, old, short base that must be printed with its Ns. Versus placebo over 4 weeks (1997, N not documented in the record) pranlukast improved morning peak flow and trough FEV1 by 210-340 mL. Added to inhaled beclomethasone in two protocols of only 41 and 39 patients, pranlukast 450 mg/day performed like doubling the beclomethasone dose in moderate asthma and helped severe asthma not on oral steroids, but not severe asthma already on prednisolone. In the only step-down trial (n=40), switching well-controlled patients off low-dose inhaled steroid to pranlukast left 72.2% controlled at 6 months versus 90% on reduced-dose inhaled steroid, with FeNO significantly increased. Pranlukast is licensed in Japan and a few other markets, not in the US/UK. No exacerbation or mortality evidence exists.
stamp: SPLIT — pranlukast improved peak flow and FEV1 versus placebo (4 weeks, 1997) and matched a doubled beclomethasone dose as an add-on in two protocols of 41 and 39 patients, but in the only step-down trial (n=40) switching from low-dose inhaled steroid to pranlukast left fewer patients controlled (72.2% vs 90%) with FeNO rising; small, old, short evidence throughout, and the drug is not licensed in the US/UK

title: Bambuterol in asthma: a full 24 hours of bronchodilation versus placebo in a 487-patient trial — a 1990s oral beta-agonist, never US-licensed, with no outcome evidence
question: In adults with asthma — including nocturnal asthma and elderly patients — does once-daily oral bambuterol versus placebo improve 24-hour lung function and reduce rescue bronchodilator use?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — for 24-hour lung function only, in a 1990s pre-LABA-era programme that must not read as a modern treatment option. The one large trial (n=487, 4 weeks) found bambuterol 10 mg once daily raised mean daily morning and evening peak flow by 11 L/min versus placebo throughout the study, and 20 mg improved FEV1 as well. A 29-patient crossover showed 24-hour mean FEV1 of 3.2-3.4 L on bambuterol versus 2.9 L on placebo, with evening dosing best for lung function on awakening. A one-week dose-finding crossover in elderly patients (N not documented in the record) showed dose-related peak-flow improvement and reduced night-time rescue use, with tremor and palpitations mild and dose-related — the systemic beta-agonist harms of an oral drug. No exacerbation, hospitalisation or mortality evidence exists, and bambuterol was never licensed in the US.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — for 24-hour bronchodilation only: a 487-patient placebo-controlled trial showed significant peak-flow (10 and 20 mg) and FEV1 (20 mg) benefit over 4 weeks, supported by a 29-patient dosing-time crossover and an elderly dose-finding study; a pre-LABA-era oral beta-agonist with dose-related tremor and palpitations, never licensed in the US, and no exacerbation or outcome evidence

title: High-dose inhaled flunisolide in acute asthma: helped airflow in the ED, matched steroids in a tiny inpatient trial, and did nothing after discharge — a split record
question: In adults presenting with acute severe asthma, does high-dose inhaled flunisolide — added to salbutamol in the emergency department, substituted for systemic corticosteroids after initial intravenous treatment, or continued after ED discharge — improve airflow and outcomes versus placebo or systemic corticosteroids?
balance: SPLIT — three acute settings, three different answers, never pooled. Added to salbutamol in the emergency department (n=94), high cumulative-dose inhaled flunisolide separated from placebo on FEV1 and peak flow at 90-180 minutes, mainly in patients whose attack had lasted 24 hours or more. Substituted for systemic corticosteroids after 48 hours of intravenous steroids in hospital (n=40), it performed comparably over 7 days — a trial far too small to establish equivalence. Continued after ED discharge on top of 5 days of prednisone (n=104 randomised, 28% lost to follow-up), it gave no benefit at 24 days and more nocturnal wheezing (48% vs 18%). This is the acute question only; the chronic-asthma flunisolide base is not folded in, and flunisolide inhaler availability is now limited.
stamp: SPLIT — inhaled flunisolide added to salbutamol in the ED improved airflow at 90-180 minutes (n=94), was indistinguishable from continued systemic steroids after IV treatment in a 40-patient inpatient trial too small to prove equivalence, and gave no benefit with more nocturnal wheezing after ED discharge (n=104, 28% lost to follow-up)

title: IV aminophylline in acute asthma (adults): no added bronchodilation or fewer admissions in the Cochrane pool of 17 trials — and more vomiting and arrhythmias
question: In adults with acute asthma treated in the emergency department or hospital, does adding intravenous aminophylline to inhaled beta-2 agonists (with systemic corticosteroids) improve lung function, admission and outcomes versus placebo?
balance: LIKELY (no difference) — with more harm. The Cochrane 2012 update (17 trials) found adding intravenous aminophylline to inhaled beta-2 agonists produced no statistically significant additional bronchodilation at any time point and no significant reduction in hospital admission (OR 0.58, 95% CI 0.30 to 1.12; 6 studies, n=315), and no subgroup — by baseline airflow limitation or corticosteroid use — in which it worked better. It did produce more vomiting (OR 4.21, 95% CI 2.20 to 8.07) and palpitations/arrhythmias (OR 3.02, 95% CI 1.15 to 7.90): about 20 extra patients vomiting and 15 extra with arrhythmias or palpitations per 100 treated. The named primaries are small and old, with their Ns on the face — one positive inpatient trial of 21 adults and one negative trial of 59 — and they do not outweigh the pool. Aminophylline's narrow therapeutic index belongs on the face. Adults only.
stamp: LIKELY (no difference) — the Cochrane 2012 pool of 17 trials found no significant added bronchodilation or reduction in admission when IV aminophylline was added to inhaled beta-2 agonists, with significantly more vomiting and palpitations/arrhythmias; the two named primaries are small old trials (n=21 positive, n=59 negative) that do not outweigh the pool

title: Octreotide in acute pancreatitis: no benefit in the 302-patient double-blind trial or the 720-patient meta-analysis — the small positive reports are design-flagged
question: In patients with moderate-to-severe or severe acute pancreatitis, does octreotide versus placebo or conservative care reduce mortality, complications and hospital stay?
balance: LIKELY (no difference) — the two reports that can carry weight agree. The large randomised double-blind multicentre trial (n=302, 32 hospitals) found no significant difference in mortality (16% placebo vs 15% and 12% on octreotide 100 and 200 µg three times daily), complications, pain duration, surgery or hospital stay. The agent-specific meta-analysis (11 randomised trials, 720 participants) found mortality relative risk 0.88 (95% CI 0.53 to 1.45) and complications relative risk 1.08 (95% CI 0.94 to 1.26) — relative measures, neither significant. Against that stand two small positive reports with their design flags on the face: a severe-pancreatitis study analysing 50 of 60 entered patients whose record describes its design inconsistently (case-control indexing over a prospective randomised description), and a 43-patient sequentially allocated (quasi-randomised) high-dose study with 48-hour biochemical endpoints and one death in each group. The 2017 Cochrane pharmacological-interventions review (PMID 28431202) is fenced to the lexipafant build at pack #7293 and is not carded here.
stamp: LIKELY (no difference) — a 302-patient double-blind multicentre trial found no benefit on mortality, complications, pain, surgery or stay, and the agent-specific meta-analysis (11 trials, 720 participants) found non-significant relative risks for mortality (0.88) and complications (1.08); the two small positive reports carry design flags (inconsistent design wording with 50 of 60 analysed; sequential allocation, n=43) and do not outweigh them

title: Mesalamine in Crohn's disease: no induction benefit (CDAI -18 points, not remission) but fewer symptomatic recurrences after surgery (31% vs 41%) — two limbs, never pooled
question: In adults with mildly-to-moderately active Crohn's disease, does oral mesalamine versus placebo induce remission or response — and, in the separate postoperative limb, after surgical resection does it prevent recurrence?
balance: SPLIT — two limbs, labelled, never pooled. INDUCTION limb: mesalamine does not induce remission in mildly-to-moderately active Crohn's disease — the Cochrane review (20 studies, 2,367 patients) found high-dose controlled-release mesalamine 4 g/day not superior to placebo (CDAI mean difference -19.8 points, 95% CI -46.2 to 6.7) and low-dose mesalamine not superior either, while the meta-analysis of the three Pentasa 4 g/day trials (304 vs 311 patients) found a net CDAI difference of -18 points (P=0.04) whose clinical significance its own authors call unclear. POSTOPERATIVE limb: mesalamine 3 g/day after resection reduced symptomatic recurrence versus placebo in one trial (31% vs 41%; relative risk 0.628, 90% CI 0.40 to 0.97; n=163), and in a two-year three-arm trial (n=131) clinical recurrence was 58% on mesalamine versus 77% on placebo and 50% on 6-mercaptopurine — mesalamine the middle arm — while endoscopic recurrence was 63% on mesalamine versus 64% on placebo. Pre-biologic-era evidence throughout.
stamp: SPLIT — induction limb: mesalamine does not induce remission in active Crohn's disease (Cochrane, 20 studies: 4 g/day not superior to placebo; the Pentasa meta-analysis's net CDAI gain is -18 points, of unclear clinical significance); postoperative limb: symptomatic recurrence reduced in one trial (31% vs 41%, n=163) and clinical recurrence intermediate in another (58% vs 77% on placebo, n=131) with endoscopic recurrence identical to placebo — the two limbs are labelled and never pooled

title: Rifaximin in Crohn's disease: 800 mg twice daily induced remission (62% vs 43%) in the large trial — but the maintenance report's 100% remission rate is implausibly complete and is flagged
question: In adults with mild-to-moderately active Crohn's disease, does rifaximin versus placebo induce remission — and, in the separate maintenance limb, after steroid-induced remission does it maintain remission?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for induction at 800 mg twice daily, on two multicentre placebo-controlled trials: remission 52% versus 33% on placebo in 83 patients (not statistically significant overall; significant in the elevated-CRP subgroup, with treatment failures 4% vs 33%, P=0.010), and 62% (61/98) versus 43% (43/101) (P=0.005) in 402 patients with the extended-intestinal-release formulation, maintained through follow-up (45% vs 29%). There is no dose-response — the 400 mg and 1,200 mg doses and once-daily dosing all failed against placebo. The MAINTENANCE limb is flagged on the face and does not carry this shelf: the single 2014 report (n=168) reports 100% (83/83) remission at 12 weeks on rifaximin and 78% versus 41% maintained at 24 weeks, an implausibly complete result for this disease from a small single-programme report.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — induction only, at 800 mg twice daily: two multicentre placebo-controlled trials (n=83, remission 52% vs 33%, not significant overall; n=402 for the extended-intestinal-release formulation, 62% vs 43%, P=0.005), with no dose-response; the 2014 maintenance report's implausibly complete result (100% remission at 12 weeks) is flagged on the face and does not carry the shelf

title: Tacrolimus for steroid-refractory ulcerative colitis: response 50% vs 13% and mucosal healing 44% vs 13% at 2 weeks — small Japanese trials, low-certainty Cochrane support, remission unproven
question: In patients with corticosteroid-refractory ulcerative colitis, does oral tacrolimus versus placebo induce clinical response, mucosal healing and remission?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for short-term clinical response and mucosal healing, at low certainty. The Cochrane review (5 RCTs, 347 participants) found tacrolimus may be superior to placebo for clinical remission (14/87 vs 1/61; risk ratio 3.76, 95% CI 1.03 to 13.73 — a relative measure; absolute rates 16% vs 2%) and clinical improvement (45/87 vs 7/61; risk ratio 4.47, 95% CI 2.15 to 9.29), both rated LOW certainty, and its authors state no clinical practice conclusions can be made. The two primaries are small, Japanese and short: a trough-target dose-finding trial (n=63) with DAI improvement in 68.4% at a 10-15 ng/mL trough versus 10.0% on placebo at 2 weeks, and a hospitalised steroid-refractory trial (n=62) with response 50.0% versus 13.3% and mucosal healing 43.8% versus 13.3% at 2 weeks, but remission 9.4% versus 0.0% and not significant. Tacrolimus nephrotoxicity, tremor and glucose effects, and the need for trough monitoring, belong on the face.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two small Japanese placebo-controlled trials (n=63, n=62) show more clinical response and mucosal healing on oral tacrolimus at 2 weeks, and the Cochrane pool (5 RCTs, 347 participants) agrees at low certainty for remission and improvement; remission in the hospitalised trial was 9.4% vs 0.0% and not significant, horizons are 2 weeks, and trough monitoring plus nephrotoxicity, tremor and glucose effects are part of the intervention

title: Cisapride in functional dyspepsia (WITHDRAWN drug): no significant benefit over placebo in three trials — therapeutic gain 0.1% in the largest — and withdrawn for QT/torsades risk
question: In adults with functional (non-organic) dyspepsia, does cisapride versus placebo improve dyspeptic symptoms?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) for any benefit — and the drug was withdrawn. Cisapride was withdrawn/restricted because of QT prolongation and torsades risk, and this shelf is the historical record of its functional-dyspepsia programme, not a treatment option. Of the three placebo-controlled trials carded, two found no significant advantage over placebo on global symptom outcomes (overall response 63% vs 44%, not significant, in general practice; therapeutic gain 0.1% [95% CI −14% to 14%] in the 330-patient primary-care trial), and the third found total symptom scores fell similarly on cisapride and placebo. Cisapride's gastroparesis trials are NOT folded in here — they are limbs of the prokinetic network home at shelf #3601. The Cochrane prokinetics-for-functional-dyspepsia class review is a cross-point only and is not carded.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — no placebo-controlled trial carded showed a significant benefit of cisapride on global dyspepsia outcomes (therapeutic gain 0.1% in the largest trial), and the drug was withdrawn/restricted for QT prolongation and torsades risk; this shelf records a negative-to-mixed programme, not a treatment option

title: Dexlansoprazole in erosive oesophagitis: healing non-inferior to lansoprazole (92–95% vs 86–92%); maintenance 75–87% vs 26–27% on placebo (3 publications, 4 trials)
question: In adults with erosive oesophagitis, does dexlansoprazole MR (dual delayed-release) heal oesophagitis versus lansoprazole, and does it maintain healing and heartburn relief versus placebo?
balance: LIKELY (benefit), on three publications covering four trials. On the STRATOS convention stated on the face of this shelf, the two identical healing trials count as ONE publication: the floor rests on three reports covering four trials. Healing: in two identical randomised trials reported together (4,092 patients), dexlansoprazole MR 60/90 mg healed 92–95% by week 8 by life-table versus 86–92% on lansoprazole 30 mg — non-inferior, with the life-table differences not statistically significant (crude-rate analyses favoured the 90 mg dose). Maintenance: in two separate trials in already-healed patients, 6-month maintenance of healing was 87%/82% (60/90 mg) and 75%/83% (30/60 mg) versus 26% and 27% on placebo by life-table — a large, consistent placebo-controlled benefit. Healing comparisons are against an active comparator (lansoprazole), maintenance comparisons against placebo; the non-erosive reflux disease reports are a separate slice and are not folded in.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — maintenance of healing was clearly superior to placebo in two randomised trials (87%/82% and 75%/83% vs 26% and 27% at 6 months by life-table) and healing was non-inferior to lansoprazole across two trials in one publication (92–95% vs 86–92% at week 8); three publications covering four trials, counted on the STRATOS convention stated on the face

title: Colchicine in primary biliary cholangitis: biochemistry improved, survival and histology did not — Cochrane pool of 11 trials (716 patients) found no mortality benefit, and UDCA beat it head-to-head
question: In patients with primary biliary cirrhosis/cholangitis, does colchicine versus placebo (or added to ursodeoxycholic acid) improve liver biochemistry, histology and survival?
balance: SPLIT — the classic older-programme pattern. Colchicine consistently improved liver biochemistry (albumin, bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, cholesterol and aminotransferases in the 1986 NEJM trial; alkaline phosphatase fell from 281 to 112 IU/L over 4 years in the 1988 trial), but no trial showed a symptom or histology benefit, the 1995 head-to-head trial found colchicine only modest while ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) improved liver tests significantly, and the Cochrane pool of 11 trials (716 patients) found no significant difference in deaths (relative risk 1.21, 95% CI 0.71 to 2.06) or death/transplantation — with a worst-best-case sensitivity analysis suggesting possible detriment. These trials predate modern UDCA-standard care (the 1995 trial is the transition point). This is one of three separate pre-UDCA-era PBC drug questions — see also methotrexate (shelf #7426) and D-penicillamine (shelf #7427); they are not merged into a class verdict. Colchicine's gastrointestinal and neuromuscular toxicity in liver disease belongs on the face alongside the diarrhoea reported in the trials.
stamp: SPLIT — liver biochemistry consistently improved (alkaline phosphatase 281→112 IU/L over 4 years in one trial) but the Cochrane pool of 11 trials (716 patients) found no significant effect on deaths (relative risk 1.21) or death/transplantation, no trial showed a histology benefit, and UDCA was superior head-to-head; a pre-UDCA-era programme

title: Methotrexate in primary biliary cholangitis: the mortality concern leads — PUMPS (n=265) stopped for futility, long-term trial showed a 2.9-fold higher death/transplant rate, no benefit shown
question: In patients with primary biliary cirrhosis/cholangitis, does methotrexate — alone versus placebo, or added to ursodeoxycholic acid — improve disease course, and what is its mortality signal?
balance: The pooled mortality concern leads. Methotrexate improved some biochemistry in PBC trials, but the long-term placebo-controlled trial found a 2.9-fold (95% CI 0.85 to 10.25) higher rate of death or liver transplantation on methotrexate alongside rising bilirubin and Mayo score with time, the Cochrane record carries the 2005 version's finding that methotrexate seemed to significantly increase mortality (the 2010 update's pooled estimate is relative risk 1.32, 95% CI 0.66 to 2.64, not significant), and the large PUMPS trial (265 patients, median 7.6 years) found adding methotrexate to UDCA had no effect on the course of PBC and was stopped early for futility. Methotrexate is not presented here as a PBC treatment option. Its hepatotoxicity and pulmonary toxicity on a liver-disease shelf belong on the face. Cross-points: colchicine in PBC (shelf #7425) and D-penicillamine in PBC (shelf #7427) are separate drug questions from the same pre-UDCA era.
stamp: POSSIBLE (harm) — no benefit was shown (PUMPS, 265 patients over a median 7.6 years, was stopped for futility), while the mortality record points the wrong way: a 2.9-fold higher death/transplant rate in the long-term placebo-controlled trial (95% CI 0.85 to 10.25), a significant mortality increase in the 2005 Cochrane version, and a pooled relative risk of 1.32 (not significant) in the 2010 update; the mortality concern leads

title: D-penicillamine in primary biliary cholangitis: two negative NEJM trials, no efficacy, major side effects in 22–31% — a failed copper-chelation programme
question: In patients with primary biliary cirrhosis/cholangitis, does D-penicillamine versus placebo improve survival, symptoms, biochemistry and histology?
balance: A negative, toxic programme — the failure is on the face. Two NEJM randomised trials found no benefit: in advanced disease (227 patients) penicillamine did not improve survival, symptoms, laboratory values or histology, and major side effects forced permanent discontinuation in 22% of patients on the drug; in the earlier prospective trial (52 patients) there was no improvement in survival or symptoms after 28 months, with major side effects in 31% and less serious side effects in a further 46%. The Cochrane pool of seven trials (706 patients) found D-penicillamine tended to increase mortality (relative risk 1.34, 95% CI 1.09 to 1.64 by fixed-effect; 1.46, 95% CI 0.85 to 2.50 by random-effects, with substantial heterogeneity) and significantly increased adverse events (RR 3.11, 95% CI 2.33 to 4.16, fixed-effect), and its authors do not support its use. This shelf is the historical record of the copper-chelation era of PBC care, not a treatment option. Cross-points: colchicine (shelf #7425) and methotrexate (shelf #7426) in PBC are separate drug questions from the same era.
stamp: LIKELY (harm) — two NEJM randomised trials showed no survival, symptom or histology benefit, major side effects forced permanent discontinuation in 22% of patients in one and occurred in 31% in the other, and the Cochrane pool (7 trials, 706 patients) found adverse events significantly increased (relative risk 3.11) with mortality tending to increase; a failed, toxic programme, not a treatment option

title: Foscarnet vs ganciclovir in CMV retinitis in AIDS (SOCA, pre-HAART): survival favoured foscarnet (deaths 34% vs 51%), eye control equal, tolerability worse — 2 trials, 4 reports, one programme
question: In patients with AIDS and cytomegalovirus retinitis, does foscarnet versus ganciclovir — and, for relapsed retinitis, combination therapy versus monotherapy — differ in mortality, retinitis progression, vision and toxicity?
balance: SPLIT — and era-bound. This shelf is a single research programme (the Studies of Ocular Complications of AIDS, SOCA, in collaboration with the AIDS Clinical Trials Group): TWO trials and FOUR reports — the Foscarnet-Ganciclovir CMV Retinitis Trial (FGCRT) contributes three of the four reports (mortality, visual outcomes, morbidity/toxicity) and must not be read as three trials. In the FGCRT (234 patients), foscarnet was associated with longer survival (deaths 34% vs 51%; relative risk 1.79 for ganciclovir vs foscarnet; median survival 12.6 vs 8.5 months; the treatment protocol was suspended early on this signal), while retinitis control and vision were equivalent (relative risk of progression 0.97; progression in 85% of each group by 120 days). Tolerability pointed the other way: neutropenia was more common on ganciclovir (34% vs 14%), infusion-related symptoms on foscarnet (58% vs 24%), and 46% of foscarnet patients switched treatment, mostly for toxicity. In the second trial (Cytomegalovirus Retreatment Trial, 279 patients with relapsed retinitis), combination reinduction/maintenance controlled retinitis longest (median time to progression 4.3 vs 2.0 and 1.3 months) with no mortality difference and the greatest quality-of-life cost. ERA FLAG (load-bearing): this is pre-HAART AIDS care, against zidovudine-era antiretroviral therapy — foscarnet's anti-HIV activity and the ganciclovir–zidovudine neutropenia interaction are part of the record, and the foscarnet survival advantage must not be carried into modern practice. Both trials were unblinded.
stamp: SPLIT — in the single SOCA programme (2 trials, 4 reports, labelled as such), foscarnet was associated with longer survival than ganciclovir in the pre-HAART FGCRT (deaths 34% vs 51%; relative risk 1.79) while retinitis control and vision were equivalent and tolerability favoured ganciclovir (46% of foscarnet patients switched, mostly for toxicity); for relapsed retinitis, combination therapy controlled retinitis longest with no mortality difference. The pre-HAART era flag is load-bearing: this record must not be carried into modern practice

title: Brivudine in herpes zoster: equivalent to famciclovir (PHN 11.3% vs 9.6%, n=2,027); PHN advantage over aciclovir is a survey-design result — and the fluoropyrimidine interaction can be lethal
question: In immunocompetent adults with herpes zoster, does once-daily oral brivudine versus aciclovir — or versus famciclovir — improve acute disease outcomes and reduce postherpetic neuralgia?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), with two load-bearing cautions printed on the face. First, design: the favourable postherpetic neuralgia (PHN) result against aciclovir (PHN incidence 32.7% vs 43.5%, P=0.006) comes from a SURVEY follow-up of two randomised trials — former participants aged ≥50 interviewed 8–17 months later — not from a primary-endpoint RCT analysis, and the abstract itself notes the design's methodological disadvantages. Against famciclovir, in a true double-blind randomised trial of 2,027 patients, brivudine was only equivalent (PHN prevalence at 3 months 11.3% vs 9.6%). A 2024 meta-analysis of seven RCTs (2,095 brivudine, 2,076 control patients) found brivudine superior on efficacy and PHN incidence with no significant difference in adverse reactions, while concluding the safety evidence is insufficient. Second, safety: brivudine's interaction with fluoropyrimidines (5-fluorouracil and its prodrugs) is potentially lethal and belongs on the face of any brivudine record. Brivudine is licensed in parts of Europe, not in the US — regulatory status on the face.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — brivudine was equivalent to famciclovir in the 2,027-patient double-blind trial and favoured for postherpetic neuralgia in a seven-trial meta-analysis, but its headline PHN advantage over aciclovir (32.7% vs 43.5%) comes from a survey follow-up of two trials, labelled as such, and its potentially lethal interaction with fluoropyrimidines (5-fluorouracil and prodrugs) is flagged on the face; licensed in parts of Europe, not in the US

title: Carfilzomib in relapsed/refractory myeloma: ASPIRE — PFS 26.3 vs 17.6 months, OS 48.3 vs 40.4; ENDEAVOR — PFS 18.7 vs 9.4 months vs bortezomib; cardiac, hypertension and renal harm is the price
question: In patients with relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma after 1–3 prior lines, does the irreversible proteasome inhibitor carfilzomib — added to lenalidomide–dexamethasone (ASPIRE), or as carfilzomib–dexamethasone against bortezomib–dexamethasone (ENDEAVOR) — prolong progression-free and overall survival, and with what cardiac, renal and hypertension cost?
balance: LIKELY (benefit), on two large phase 3 trials testing two different comparisons — labelled as separate limbs and never pooled. Add-on limb (ASPIRE, 792 patients): carfilzomib added to lenalidomide–dexamethasone (KRd, carfilzomib in the 27 mg/m²-era regimen) prolonged progression-free survival (median 26.3 vs 17.6 months; hazard ratio 0.69, relative) and overall survival at final analysis (median 48.3 vs 40.4 months; HR 0.79, relative), with overall response 87.1% vs 66.7%. Head-to-head limb (ENDEAVOR, 929 patients): carfilzomib 56 mg/m²–dexamethasone beat bortezomib–dexamethasone on progression-free survival (median 18.7 vs 9.4 months; HR 0.53, relative) and on interim overall survival (median 47.6 vs 40.0 months; HR 0.791, relative). The pricing harms are cardiac failure (grade ≥3: 4.3% vs 2.1% in ASPIRE), hypertension (6.4% vs 2.3% in ASPIRE; grade ≥3 15% vs 3% at ENDEAVOR's survival analysis) and acute renal failure (3.8% vs 3.3%), with more serious adverse events on carfilzomib in ENDEAVOR (48% vs 36% at the primary report). CANDOR (carfilzomib–dexamethasone ± daratumumab) is NOT carded here — it belongs to the daratumumab question at shelf #7431 and is cross-pointed in prose only.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — two large phase 3 trials in two labelled limbs both showed progression-free and overall survival benefits: ASPIRE (KRd vs Rd: median PFS 26.3 vs 17.6 months, HR 0.69 relative; median OS 48.3 vs 40.4 months, HR 0.79 relative) and ENDEAVOR (Kd vs Vd: median PFS 18.7 vs 9.4 months, HR 0.53 relative; interim median OS 47.6 vs 40.0 months, HR 0.791 relative), priced in cardiac failure, hypertension and renal harm

title: Daratumumab in relapsed/refractory myeloma (PARTIAL beside first-line #844): POLLUX, CASTOR, CANDOR and APOLLO all prolonged progression-free survival; POLLUX final OS 67.6 vs 51.8 months
question: In patients with relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma after ≥1 prior line, does adding the anti-CD38 antibody daratumumab to a standard backbone — lenalidomide–dexamethasone (POLLUX), bortezomib–dexamethasone (CASTOR), carfilzomib–dexamethasone (CANDOR) or pomalidomide–dexamethasone (APOLLO) — prolong progression-free survival, and with what infusion-reaction and cytopenia cost?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) for progression-free survival in the relapsed/refractory slice — this shelf is PARTIAL beside live shelf #844, which asks daratumumab FIRST-LINE in transplant-ineligible newly diagnosed myeloma (MAIA/ALCYONE) only; only the relapsed/refractory slice is carded here, and #844 is cross-pointed, not re-carded. Four phase 3 trials, four backbones, each slice labelled and never pooled: POLLUX (daratumumab + lenalidomide–dexamethasone, 569 patients) — progression or death 18.5% vs 41.0% at interim (hazard ratio 0.37, relative), and at final analysis median overall survival 67.6 vs 51.8 months (HR 0.73, relative); CASTOR (daratumumab + bortezomib–dexamethasone, 498 patients) — median PFS not reached vs 7.2 months (HR 0.39, relative); CANDOR (daratumumab + carfilzomib–dexamethasone, 466 patients) — median PFS not reached vs 15.8 months (HR 0.63, relative); APOLLO (daratumumab + pomalidomide–dexamethasone, 304 patients) — median PFS 12.4 vs 6.9 months (HR 0.63, relative). The class costs are infusion-related reactions (47.7% in POLLUX and 45.3% in CASTOR, mostly grade 1/2 and mostly at the first infusion; APOLLO used subcutaneous daratumumab 1800 mg as an alternative to intravenous dosing) and neutropenia (grade 3/4: 51.9% vs 37.0% in POLLUX; 68% vs 51% in APOLLO). One-home assignments: CANDOR is carded HERE (its question is adding daratumumab) and only cross-pointed at the carfilzomib shelf #7430; APOLLO is carded HERE and only cross-pointed at the pomalidomide shelf #7432.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — for progression-free survival in relapsed or refractory myeloma (PARTIAL beside first-line live shelf #844; only the relapsed/refractory slice is carded here): four phase 3 trials across four backbones all favoured adding daratumumab (hazard ratios 0.37, 0.39, 0.63 and 0.63, relative measures printed with absolutes), and POLLUX's final analysis showed an overall-survival benefit (median 67.6 vs 51.8 months; HR 0.73, relative); priced in infusion-related reactions and neutropenia

title: Pomalidomide in relapsed/refractory myeloma: PFS improved in MM-003 and OPTIMISMM, but OPTIMISMM final overall survival was null unadjusted (35.6 vs 31.6 months; HR 0.94, P=.571) — a split result
question: In patients with relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma previously treated with lenalidomide (and, in MM-003, bortezomib) — does pomalidomide plus dexamethasone, alone against high-dose dexamethasone (MM-003) or added to bortezomib–dexamethasone (OPTIMISMM), prolong progression-free survival, and does the progression benefit convert to survival?
balance: SPLIT — a large relative progression-free-survival benefit in both trials, but the mature survival read is null unadjusted, and that null is flagged on the face. MM-003 (455 patients refractory to both bortezomib and lenalidomide): pomalidomide plus low-dose dexamethasone versus high-dose dexamethasone alone gave median progression-free survival of 4.0 vs 1.9 months (hazard ratio 0.48, relative), with grade 3/4 neutropenia in 48% vs 16% and pneumonia in 13% vs 8%. OPTIMISMM (559 lenalidomide-pretreated patients): adding pomalidomide to bortezomib–dexamethasone gave median PFS of 11.20 vs 7.10 months (HR 0.61, relative), but the final survival analysis at 70% maturity found median overall survival of 35.6 vs 31.6 months (HR 0.94, relative, NOT significant, P=.571). The subsequent-therapy-adjusted analysis (HR 0.76) is a sensitivity analysis and is labelled as such wherever it appears — it is never the headline. MM-003's comparator (high-dose dexamethasone alone) is a last-resort control in a doubly refractory population; that population is printed exactly. APOLLO (daratumumab + pomalidomide–dexamethasone) belongs to shelf #7431 and OCEAN (melflufen vs pomalidomide–dexamethasone) to the melflufen row — both are cross-pointed in prose only and are not re-carded here.
stamp: SPLIT — progression-free survival improved in both trials (MM-003: median 4.0 vs 1.9 months, HR 0.48 relative, against high-dose dexamethasone alone in doubly refractory disease; OPTIMISMM: median 11.20 vs 7.10 months, HR 0.61 relative) but OPTIMISMM's final overall survival was null unadjusted (median 35.6 vs 31.6 months; HR 0.94, not significant, P=.571), flagged on the face, with the adjusted HR 0.76 labelled a sensitivity analysis only; priced in neutropenia and infection

title: Ixazomib + lenalidomide–dexamethasone in relapsed myeloma (TOURMALINE-MM1): PFS win (20.6 vs 14.7 months), no significant overall-survival benefit at 85 months
question: In patients with relapsed, refractory, or relapsed-and-refractory multiple myeloma after 1–3 prior therapies, does adding the oral proteasome inhibitor ixazomib to lenalidomide–dexamethasone, versus placebo plus lenalidomide–dexamethasone, prolong progression-free and overall survival?
balance: SPLIT — progression-free survival benefit without a significant overall-survival benefit, on a single-trial base (TOURMALINE-MM1, three reports of one trial). Adding oral ixazomib to lenalidomide–dexamethasone prolonged median progression-free survival (20.6 vs 14.7 months; hazard ratio 0.74, a relative measure) and raised overall response (78% vs 72%). At the final analysis, with median follow-up of 85 months, median overall survival was 53.6 vs 51.6 months (hazard ratio 0.939, relative, not significant, P=.495) — the PFS win did not convert to a significant survival win on intention-to-treat analysis, and a subsequent-therapy-adjusted modelling analysis is carded only as a labelled sensitivity analysis, never as the survival headline. Serious adverse events were similar (47% vs 49%); grade 3–4 thrombocytopenia and rash were more frequent with ixazomib. Cross-point: ixazomib maintenance in newly diagnosed myeloma is a different setting and question (shelf #7434).
stamp: SPLIT — ixazomib plus lenalidomide–dexamethasone significantly prolonged progression-free survival in TOURMALINE-MM1 (hazard ratio 0.74, relative) but did NOT significantly prolong overall survival at the final 85-month analysis (53.6 vs 51.6 months; hazard ratio 0.939, P=.495); single-trial base, three reports of one trial

title: Ixazomib maintenance in newly diagnosed myeloma (TOURMALINE-MM3/MM4): PFS benefit in both trials, no overall-survival benefit in either
question: In patients with newly diagnosed multiple myeloma who responded to induction — after autologous stem-cell transplantation (TOURMALINE-MM3) or without transplantation (TOURMALINE-MM4) — does fixed-duration single-agent ixazomib maintenance, versus placebo, prolong progression-free survival, and does it prolong overall survival?
balance: SPLIT — consistent relative progression-free survival benefit in both trials, no overall-survival benefit in either at final analysis. Post-transplant (TOURMALINE-MM3): median PFS 26.5 vs 21.3 months (hazard ratio 0.72, relative). Without transplant (TOURMALINE-MM4): median PFS from randomisation 17.4 vs 9.4 months (hazard ratio 0.659, relative). At final survival analysis (~8 years in MM3, ~5 years in MM4), median overall survival was not reached in either MM3 arm (hazard ratio 1.025, relative, not significant) and was 64.8 vs 69.5 months in MM4 (hazard ratio 1.090, relative, not significant) — both halves belong on the face. The two populations are labelled separately and never pooled. Maintenance was fixed-duration (up to 26 cycles / 24 months). Cross-points in prose only: lenalidomide maintenance after transplant (live #675) is the established comparator strategy, and ixazomib in relapsed disease is shelf #7433.
stamp: SPLIT — ixazomib maintenance significantly prolonged progression-free survival in both TOURMALINE-MM3 (hazard ratio 0.72, relative) and TOURMALINE-MM4 (hazard ratio 0.659, relative), but final overall-survival analyses showed NO benefit in either trial (hazard ratios 1.025 and 1.090, both not significant)

title: Elotuzumab + IMiD in relapsed myeloma (ELOQUENT-2/3): PFS and overall-survival benefit with both backbones; frontline ELOQUENT-1 was negative (cross-pointed)
question: In patients with relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma, does adding the SLAMF7 antibody elotuzumab to lenalidomide–dexamethasone (ELOQUENT-2) or to pomalidomide–dexamethasone in lenalidomide- and proteasome-inhibitor-exposed disease (ELOQUENT-3) prolong progression-free and overall survival?
balance: LIKELY benefit, on two randomised trials with two different immunomodulatory backbones, labelled separately and never pooled. With lenalidomide–dexamethasone (ELOQUENT-2, phase 3, n=646): median progression-free survival 19.4 vs 14.9 months (hazard ratio 0.70, relative) and, at final analysis, median overall survival 48.3 vs 39.6 months (hazard ratio 0.82, relative; P=.0408). With pomalidomide–dexamethasone in lenalidomide- and proteasome-inhibitor-exposed disease (ELOQUENT-3, randomised phase 2, n=117): median progression-free survival 10.3 vs 4.7 months (hazard ratio 0.54, relative) and median overall survival 29.8 vs 17.4 months (hazard ratio 0.59, relative; P=.0217). Infusion reactions were uncommon and mostly low-grade (10% in ELOQUENT-2; 5% in ELOQUENT-3). Cross-point, never silent: the programme's frontline trial ELOQUENT-1 (elotuzumab + lenalidomide–dexamethasone in newly diagnosed, transplant-ineligible myeloma, PMID 35550060) was NEGATIVE for progression-free survival (31.4 vs 29.5 months; hazard ratio 0.93; P=.44) — a different setting, not carded into this relapsed shelf's balance, and not evidence for the relapsed question either way.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — elotuzumab plus an immunomodulatory backbone prolonged progression-free and overall survival in both randomised trials in relapsed/refractory myeloma: ELOQUENT-2 phase 3 (OS hazard ratio 0.82, relative) and ELOQUENT-3 randomised phase 2, n=117 (OS hazard ratio 0.59, relative); the negative frontline ELOQUENT-1 trial is cross-pointed in the balance, not carded here

title: Panobinostat + bortezomib–dexamethasone in relapsed myeloma (PANORAMA-1/2): PFS win, no survival win, heavy diarrhoea and thrombocytopenia
question: In patients with relapsed or relapsed-and-refractory multiple myeloma after 1–3 prior regimens, does adding the pan-deacetylase inhibitor panobinostat to bortezomib–dexamethasone, versus placebo plus bortezomib–dexamethasone, prolong progression-free and overall survival — and in bortezomib-refractory disease, what response does the combination produce (PANORAMA-2) — at what gastrointestinal and haematologic cost?
balance: SPLIT — a progression-free survival win with no overall-survival win, at a heavy gastrointestinal and haematologic cost. PANORAMA-1 (phase 3, n=768): median progression-free survival 11.99 vs 8.08 months (hazard ratio 0.63, relative), but final median overall survival was 40.3 vs 35.8 months (hazard ratio 0.94, relative, not significant, P=.54). Grade 3–4 thrombocytopenia occurred in 67% vs 31%, diarrhoea in 26% vs 8% and fatigue/asthenia in 24% vs 12%; serious adverse events in 60% vs 42%. PANORAMA-2 (phase 2, n=55) is single-arm support in bortezomib-refractory disease (response 34.5%, uncontrolled) and is never presented as comparative. Product naming (clarification exception): panobinostat (Farydak, Novartis/Secura Bio lineage as published) — a product whose boxed-warning history and restricted uptake followed its diarrhoea and fatigue burden.
stamp: SPLIT — panobinostat plus bortezomib–dexamethasone significantly prolonged progression-free survival in PANORAMA-1 (hazard ratio 0.63, relative) but did NOT significantly prolong overall survival (hazard ratio 0.94, P=.54), with substantially more grade 3–4 thrombocytopenia and diarrhoea; PANORAMA-2 is single-arm support only

title: Melflufen + dexamethasone in relapsed myeloma (HORIZON/OCEAN): WITHDRAWN product — PFS win over pomalidomide, survival favoured pomalidomide
question: In patients with relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma — heavily pretreated, including triple-class-refractory disease (HORIZON) — does the peptide–drug conjugate melphalan flufenamide plus dexamethasone produce responses, and against pomalidomide–dexamethasone in lenalidomide-refractory disease (OCEAN) does it prolong progression-free survival without an overall-survival cost?
balance: WITHDRAWN PRODUCT — this history leads the shelf: melphalan flufenamide (melflufen; Pepaxto/Pepaxti, Oncopeptides) was withdrawn from the US market in 2021 after the OCEAN survival signal, and the EU authorisation was later revoked. The evidence is SPLIT: in OCEAN (phase 3, n=495), melflufen plus dexamethasone beat pomalidomide plus dexamethasone on progression-free survival (median 6.8 vs 4.9 months; hazard ratio 0.79, relative) but overall survival numerically favoured the comparator (median 19.8 vs 25.0 months; hazard ratio 1.10, relative, not significant), with grade 3–4 thrombocytopenia in 63% vs 11%. HORIZON (phase 2, n=157) is single-arm support in heavily pretreated, largely triple-class-refractory disease (response 29%, uncontrolled). A longer-follow-up benefit–risk analysis exploring post-transplant-timing subgroups is carded as a labelled subgroup analysis, not a rescue of the survival read. OCEAN belongs to this shelf; the pomalidomide shelf cross-points it in prose only.
stamp: SPLIT — WITHDRAWN product (US withdrawal 2021 after the OCEAN survival signal; EU authorisation later revoked): melflufen + dexamethasone beat pomalidomide + dexamethasone on progression-free survival in OCEAN (hazard ratio 0.79, relative) but overall survival numerically favoured pomalidomide (19.8 vs 25.0 months; hazard ratio 1.10, not significant), with grade 3–4 thrombocytopenia 63% vs 11%; HORIZON is single-arm support only

title: Bosutinib in chronic-phase CML (BFORE/BELA/BYOND): BFORE positive at 400 mg, BELA missed its primary endpoint at 500 mg, BYOND single-arm in pretreated disease
question: In adults with Philadelphia chromosome-positive chronic-phase CML — newly diagnosed, against imatinib (BFORE at 400 mg; BELA at 500 mg) — does the dual SRC/ABL inhibitor bosutinib produce faster and deeper molecular and cytogenetic responses than imatinib, and in patients resistant or intolerant to prior tyrosine kinase inhibitors (BYOND) what response does it produce, at what gastrointestinal and hepatic cost?
balance: SPLIT across the first-line programme — one positive and one negative trial at two different doses, never averaged into a win. BFORE (bosutinib 400 mg, n=536): major molecular response at 12 months 47.2% vs 36.9% on imatinib (P=.02) and complete cytogenetic response by 12 months 77.2% vs 66.4% (P=.0075). BELA (bosutinib 500 mg, n=502): the primary endpoint was NOT met — complete cytogenetic response at 12 months 70% vs 68% (P=.601) — although major molecular response was higher (41% vs 27%; P<.001). BYOND (phase 4, n=163) is single-arm support in pretreated disease (confirmed major cytogenetic response by 1 year 75.8% after 1–2 prior TKIs, 62.2% after 3; diarrhoea in 87.7% — uncontrolled). Gastrointestinal and hepatic events price the drug: grade 3-or-worse diarrhoea 7.8% vs 0.8% and ALT increase 19.0% vs 1.5% in BFORE. Cross-points in prose only: asciminib packs #4481 and #7304 and ponatinib pack #7015 ask different questions.
stamp: SPLIT — first-line bosutinib beat imatinib on 12-month molecular response in BFORE at 400 mg (47.2% vs 36.9%) but BELA at 500 mg MISSED its primary cytogenetic endpoint (70% vs 68%, P=.601); BYOND is single-arm support in pretreated disease; diarrhoea and transaminase elevation are the pricing harms

title: Hypomethylating agents in higher-risk MDS (AZA-001/CALGB 9221/decitabine): azacitidine survival win (24.5 vs 15.0 months); decitabine response without a survival win
question: In patients with higher-risk myelodysplastic syndromes, do hypomethylating agents — azacitidine against conventional care regimens (AZA-001) or supportive care (CALGB 9221), and decitabine against best supportive care — prolong overall survival, delay leukaemic transformation and improve response, compared with the pre-hypomethylating standard?
balance: SPLIT across the class — the shelf must not be read as a uniform survival claim. Azacitidine carries the survival evidence: AZA-001 (phase 3, n=358) showed median overall survival 24.5 vs 15.0 months against conventional care (hazard ratio 0.58, relative; P=.0001), and CALGB 9221 (n=191) showed responses in 60% vs 5% against supportive care with delayed leukaemic transformation, in a trial whose crossover design qualifies its survival read. Decitabine (phase 3, n=170, tested on a 3-day inpatient schedule) improved response (17% vs 0%) and time to AML progression or death in the intermediate-2/high-risk slice (12.0 vs 6.8 months; P=.03) but the all-patient read was a non-significant trend (P=.16) with no overall-survival win shown. Cross-points in prose only: lower-risk MDS (live #674), oral decitabine–cedazuridine bioequivalence (pack #7019) and oral azacitidine maintenance in AML remission (pack #7018) are different questions.
stamp: SPLIT (across the class) — azacitidine significantly prolonged overall survival in higher-risk MDS in AZA-001 (24.5 vs 15.0 months; hazard ratio 0.58, relative) with supportive response/transformation evidence from CALGB 9221, while decitabine improved response (17% vs 0%) without a demonstrated overall-survival benefit; the class must not be upgraded to a uniform survival claim

title: Relugolix vs leuprolide in advanced prostate cancer (HERO): superior sustained castration (96.7% vs 88.8%) and far faster testosterone recovery; cardiovascular difference unpowered
question: In men with advanced prostate cancer requiring androgen deprivation, does oral relugolix 120 mg daily, versus leuprolide injections every 3 months for 48 weeks, achieve sustained testosterone suppression to castrate levels faster and more completely, what happens to testosterone recovery after stopping, and with what cardiovascular-event profile?
balance: LIKELY benefit on the trial's pharmacodynamic endpoint, on a single-trial base (HERO, three reports of one trial) — stated plainly: the primary endpoint is sustained testosterone suppression to castrate levels, a pharmacodynamic endpoint, not a cancer-outcome endpoint. Relugolix 120 mg orally daily (Orgovyx, Myovant/Pfizer lineage as published) achieved sustained castration through 48 weeks in 96.7% vs 88.8% on 3-monthly leuprolide (difference 7.9 percentage points; noninferiority and superiority both met), with castrate testosterone on day 4 in 56.0% vs 0% — the no-surge, rapid-onset profile. Testosterone recovery after stopping was far faster (recovery to >280 ng/dL at 90 days in 54% vs 3.2% in the 184-man subset). Major adverse cardiovascular events occurred in 2.9% vs 6.2% (hazard ratio 0.46, relative) — a secondary/safety analysis in a trial not powered for cardiovascular outcomes; it is printed labelled and must NOT be read as a proven cardiovascular benefit. Health-related quality of life did not differ significantly during treatment. Cross-point in prose only: degarelix, the injectable GnRH antagonist, is shelf #7441.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit, on a pharmacodynamic endpoint) — in the single HERO trial, oral relugolix was superior to leuprolide for sustained castration through 48 weeks (96.7% vs 88.8%) with far faster onset and testosterone recovery; the cardiovascular-event difference (hazard ratio 0.46, relative) is an unpowered secondary analysis, not a proven cardiovascular benefit, and no cancer-outcome endpoint was tested

title: Degarelix vs LHRH agonists in prostate cancer (CS21): noninferior suppression, castrate by day 3 vs none, injection-site reactions 40% vs <1%; no established survival benefit
question: In men with prostate cancer requiring androgen deprivation therapy, does the GnRH antagonist degarelix (240 mg loading, 80 or 160 mg monthly), versus leuprolide (or goserelin in the pooled programme), achieve and maintain testosterone suppression without an initial surge, and what do the long-term extension and pooled disease-control data show?
balance: POSSIBLE benefit, on a pharmacodynamic-endpoint base — stated plainly: the primary endpoint throughout is testosterone suppression, not cancer survival. In CS21 (phase 3, n=610), degarelix (240 mg loading, then 80 or 160 mg monthly) was noninferior to monthly leuprolide at maintaining testosterone at or below 0.5 ng/mL from day 28 to day 364 (97.2%, 98.3% and 96.4% respectively), with castrate levels by day 3 in about 96% on degarelix vs none on leuprolide — the no-surge, rapid-onset profile. The maintenance dose that survived is 80 mg monthly; the 240/160 arm was not the marketed regimen. Injection-site reactions are the pricing harm (40% vs <1% in CS21). Extension and 5-year reports show maintained suppression after continuing or crossing over from leuprolide. The pooled five-trial analysis (n=1,925) reports PSA progression-free survival favouring degarelix overall (hazard ratio 0.71, relative) but NOT significant in the baseline-PSA >20 ng/mL slice (hazard ratio 0.74; P=.052 — printed exactly), and an overall-survival read confined to a baseline-testosterone subgroup of that pooled analysis (hazard ratio 0.36, relative) — secondary and subgroup reads that must not present degarelix as improving survival. Cross-point in prose only: relugolix, the oral antagonist, is shelf #7440.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit, on a pharmacodynamic endpoint) — degarelix was noninferior to leuprolide for sustained testosterone suppression in CS21 with far faster onset (castrate by day 3 in ~96% vs none) and maintained suppression in extensions, at the cost of injection-site reactions in 40% vs <1%; pooled PSA and survival reads are secondary/subgroup and do not establish improved survival

title: Pyrotinib in HER2-positive metastatic breast cancer (PHOEBE/PERMEATE/PHILA): large PFS wins in two China phase 3 trials; single-arm brain-metastases activity; diarrhoea the price
question: In patients with HER2-positive metastatic breast cancer, does the irreversible pan-HER tyrosine kinase inhibitor pyrotinib — plus capecitabine after trastuzumab and taxanes, against lapatinib plus capecitabine (PHOEBE); plus capecitabine for brain metastases (PERMEATE); or added to trastuzumab–docetaxel first-line, against placebo (PHILA) — prolong progression-free survival and produce intracranial responses, at what diarrhoea cost?
balance: LIKELY benefit for progression-free survival, on single-region evidence — flagged on the face: all three trials were conducted in China, where pyrotinib is approved; it is not FDA/EMA-approved. Three settings, labelled separately and never pooled. After trastuzumab and taxanes (PHOEBE, phase 3, n=267): pyrotinib plus capecitabine prolonged median progression-free survival vs lapatinib plus capecitabine (12.5 vs 6.8 months; hazard ratio 0.39, relative). First-line (PHILA, phase 3, n=590): adding pyrotinib to trastuzumab–docetaxel prolonged median progression-free survival (24.3 vs 10.4 months; hazard ratio 0.41, relative). For brain metastases (PERMEATE, phase 2, n=78): intracranial response 74.6% in the radiotherapy-naive cohort and 42.1% after radiotherapy progression — single-arm, uncontrolled. Diarrhoea prices the whole programme: grade 3-or-worse diarrhoea in 31% vs 8% in PHOEBE and about a quarter of PERMEATE patients; grade 3-or-worse treatment-related events in 90% vs 76% in PHILA. Cross-points in prose only: neratinib extended adjuvant (pack #6406) and the tucatinib HER2CLIMB neighbourhood are different settings.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit for progression-free survival; single-region evidence, China only — not FDA/EMA-approved) — pyrotinib significantly prolonged progression-free survival in two phase 3 trials (PHOEBE hazard ratio 0.39, relative; PHILA hazard ratio 0.41, relative), with single-arm intracranial activity in PERMEATE and grade ≥3 diarrhoea in roughly a quarter to a third of patients; no overall-survival benefit yet established

title: Alpelisib plus fulvestrant in PIK3CA-mutated breast cancer (SOLAR-1): progression-free survival 11.0 vs 5.7 months, overall survival not significant — one trial, with grade 3/4 hyperglycaemia in 36.6%
question: In patients with hormone-receptor-positive, HER2-negative advanced breast cancer progressing after endocrine therapy whose tumours carry a PIK3CA mutation, does adding the PI3Kα inhibitor alpelisib to fulvestrant, versus placebo plus fulvestrant, prolong progression-free and overall survival, and with what hyperglycaemia, rash and diarrhoea cost?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), on a single-trial base (SOLAR-1, three reports). In the PIK3CA-mutated cohort (n=341), alpelisib plus fulvestrant prolonged median progression-free survival versus placebo plus fulvestrant (11.0 vs 5.7 months; hazard ratio 0.65, a relative measure). Final overall survival was numerically longer but NOT significant (39.3 vs 31.4 months; hazard ratio 0.86, relative; P=0.15, and the analysis did not cross its prespecified boundary). No progression-free-survival benefit was established in the cohort without PIK3CA mutations (hazard ratio 0.85, relative) — the benefit is biomarker-restricted. The price is substantial: grade 3/4 hyperglycaemia in 36.6% versus 0.7%, grade 3/4 rash 9.9% versus 0.3%, grade 3 diarrhoea 6.7% versus 0.3%, and discontinuation for adverse events in 25.0% versus 4.2%. Quality of life was maintained overall, with symptom subscales favouring placebo. BYLieve, the post-CDK4/6-inhibitor cohort study, is NOT carded as evidence on this shelf: it carries a published Expression of Concern (PMID 38142701) and is barred as load-bearing; this shelf rests on SOLAR-1 alone. Cross-points (prose only): capivasertib (pack #6403) and inavolisib (pack #6404) answer different biomarker questions.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — SOLAR-1 (one trial, three reports) showed a significant progression-free-survival benefit for alpelisib plus fulvestrant in PIK3CA-mutated disease (11.0 vs 5.7 months; hazard ratio 0.65, relative) but final overall survival was not significant (hazard ratio 0.86, relative; P=0.15), the benefit is restricted to the mutated population, and grade 3/4 hyperglycaemia (36.6%) and a 25% discontinuation rate price the gain; BYLieve is excluded under its Expression of Concern

title: Eribulin in pretreated metastatic breast cancer: SPLIT — EMBRACE survival win vs physician's choice (13.1 vs 10.6 months); Study 301 not superior to capecitabine
question: In women with locally recurrent or metastatic breast cancer previously treated with an anthracycline and a taxane, does the microtubule inhibitor eribulin, versus treatment of physician's choice in heavily pretreated disease (EMBRACE) or versus capecitabine in earlier-line advanced disease (Study 301), prolong overall survival?
balance: SPLIT across the programme's two trials. EMBRACE (heavily pretreated disease, 2–5 prior regimens): eribulin significantly prolonged median overall survival versus treatment of physician's choice (13.1 vs 10.6 months; hazard ratio 0.81, a relative measure; P=.041). Study 301 (earlier-line disease, first- to third-line): eribulin was NOT superior to capecitabine for overall survival (15.9 vs 14.5 months; hazard ratio 0.88, relative; P=.056, not significant) or progression-free survival (4.1 vs 4.2 months). Quality of life in Study 301 was similar overall, with worse systemic-therapy side-effects on eribulin and worse nausea/vomiting and diarrhoea on capecitabine. The harms that price eribulin are neutropenia (52% vs 30% all grades in EMBRACE) and peripheral neuropathy, the commonest reason for eribulin discontinuation (5%). The two trials test different lines of therapy against different comparators and are carded as separate slices, never pooled. Cross-point (prose only): eribulin in liposarcoma/leiomyosarcoma is live #1925, a different disease.
stamp: SPLIT — EMBRACE showed a significant overall-survival benefit for eribulin in heavily pretreated metastatic breast cancer versus treatment of physician's choice (13.1 vs 10.6 months; hazard ratio 0.81, relative), while Study 301 showed no superiority over capecitabine in earlier-line disease (hazard ratio 0.88, relative; not significant); the verdict differs by line of therapy and comparator

title: Dalpiciclib in HR-positive/HER2-negative advanced breast cancer (DAWNA-1/2): FLOOR-RISK two-trial base — progression-free survival hazard ratios 0.42 and 0.51 (relative), survival immature, single-region (China)
question: In patients with hormone-receptor-positive, HER2-negative advanced breast cancer — progressing after endocrine therapy, with fulvestrant (DAWNA-1), or untreated in the advanced setting, with letrozole or anastrozole (DAWNA-2) — does adding the CDK4/6 inhibitor dalpiciclib, versus placebo, prolong progression-free survival?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) on a FLOOR-RISK base — stated on the face: the randomised evidence is exactly TWO phase 3 trials (DAWNA-1 and DAWNA-2), both conducted in China (dalpiciclib is approved there, not by the FDA or EMA), plus one labelled phase Ib dose-finding programme report that carries no comparative efficacy weight. Both phase 3 trials showed large relative progression-free-survival benefits: DAWNA-1, after endocrine therapy, with fulvestrant — median 15.7 vs 7.2 months (hazard ratio 0.42, a relative measure); DAWNA-2, first-line, with letrozole or anastrozole — median 30.6 vs 18.2 months (hazard ratio 0.51, relative). Overall survival was immature in both primary reports, so this shelf makes NO survival claim. The price is very frequent high-grade cytopenia: grade 3/4 neutropenia 84.2% (DAWNA-1) and 86% (DAWNA-2), grade 3/4 leukopenia 62.1% and 67%; grade 3/4 events overall in 90% versus 12% in DAWNA-2, with two treatment-related deaths in the dalpiciclib arm. No CDK4/6 classmate's data are borrowed: palbociclib, ribociclib and abemaciclib answer their own questions (live #365 neighbourhood, cross-pointed in prose only).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — FLOOR-RISK base of exactly two phase 3 trials, stated on the face: DAWNA-1 (hazard ratio 0.42, relative, for progression-free survival with fulvestrant after endocrine therapy) and DAWNA-2 (hazard ratio 0.51, relative, first-line with an aromatase inhibitor), both single-region (China), both with immature overall survival and grade 3/4 neutropenia in ~85%; the phase Ib card is a labelled programme report carrying no comparative weight

title: Sintilimab plus chemotherapy first-line in advanced NSCLC (ORIENT-11/12): progression-free survival hazard ratios 0.48 and 0.54 (relative); survival benefit shown in nonsquamous disease — single-region (China)
question: In patients with previously untreated locally advanced or metastatic NSCLC without sensitising EGFR/ALK alterations, does adding the PD-1 inhibitor sintilimab to platinum chemotherapy — pemetrexed–platinum in nonsquamous disease (ORIENT-11) or gemcitabine–platinum in squamous disease (ORIENT-12) — versus placebo plus the same chemotherapy, prolong progression-free and overall survival?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), on two phase 3 trials in two histologies, both single-region (China; sintilimab is approved there, not by the FDA or EMA) — the slices are labelled and never pooled. Nonsquamous (ORIENT-11): sintilimab plus pemetrexed-platinum prolonged progression-free survival (median 8.9 vs 5.0 months; hazard ratio 0.482, a relative measure) and, at final analysis, overall survival (median 24.2 vs 16.8 months; hazard ratio 0.65, relative), despite 47% of the placebo arm crossing over to sintilimab. Squamous (ORIENT-12): sintilimab plus gemcitabine-platinum prolonged progression-free survival (hazard ratio 0.536, relative); the carded primary report does not report a mature overall-survival read, so no survival claim is made for the squamous slice. Grade ≥3 adverse events were similar between arms in both trials (61.7% vs 58.8% in ORIENT-11; 86.6% vs 83.1% in ORIENT-12) — the chemotherapy backbone drives most high-grade toxicity. Cross-point (prose only): tislelizumab in NSCLC (pack #7299) is a separate agent's programme.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two single-region (China) phase 3 trials showed consistent relative progression-free-survival benefits for sintilimab plus chemotherapy (hazard ratios 0.482 nonsquamous, 0.536 squamous), with a final overall-survival benefit in the nonsquamous trial (hazard ratio 0.65, relative) but no carded mature survival read for the squamous trial; not FDA/EMA-approved

title: Anlotinib third-line or later in advanced NSCLC (ALTER0303 — one trial, three reports): survival 9.6 vs 6.3 months vs placebo, in a pre-chemo-immunotherapy-era population (China)
question: In patients with advanced NSCLC progressing after at least two lines of systemic therapy, does the multitarget antiangiogenic tyrosine kinase inhibitor anlotinib 12 mg daily, versus placebo, prolong overall and progression-free survival, and with what hypertension cost?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), on a single-trial base — stated on the face: ONE trial (ALTER0303) with three reports (primary, quality-of-life, histology subgroup), conducted in China (anlotinib is approved there, not by the FDA or EMA). Anlotinib 12 mg daily prolonged median overall survival versus placebo (9.6 vs 6.3 months; hazard ratio 0.68, a relative measure; P=.002) and median progression-free survival (5.4 vs 1.4 months; hazard ratio 0.25, relative). Quality of life favoured anlotinib on most scales. The era is part of the claim: the control was placebo in a post-second-line population enrolled in 2015–16, before chemo-immunotherapy became first-line standard, so this shelf is not evidence against modern later-line options. The commonest grade ≥3 events on anlotinib were hypertension and hyponatraemia. In the histology subgroup report, the survival benefit was significant in adenocarcinoma (9.6 vs 6.9 months; P=.0051) but not in squamous disease (10.7 vs 6.5 months; P=.2570, not significant) — a subgroup read, labelled as such.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single-trial base labelled as such (ALTER0303, three reports, China): anlotinib prolonged overall survival versus placebo in third-line-or-later NSCLC (9.6 vs 6.3 months; hazard ratio 0.68, relative) with better quality of life, but the placebo comparator and 2015–16 pre-chemo-immunotherapy era limit what the result can be read against today

title: Zonisamide adjunctive in Parkinson's wearing-off: 'off' time −0.72 vs −0.01 hours at 50 mg (n=389), no extra dyskinesia — modest benefit, Japanese trial base; retracted meta-analysis excluded
question: In patients with Parkinson's disease on levodopa with insufficient response or wearing-off, does adjunctive zonisamide (25–50 mg daily), versus placebo, improve motor scores (UPDRS Part III) and reduce daily 'off' time, without increasing dyskinesia?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) of modest size. Three randomised placebo-controlled trials support adjunctive zonisamide in Parkinson's disease on levodopa: a Japanese dose-ranging trial (2007; the PubMed record does not state the total randomised N — printed as N not documented in the record) found significant UPDRS Part III improvement at 25 mg and 50 mg and reduced 'off' time at 50 mg and 100 mg, with adverse-event incidence higher at 100 mg; a Japanese confirmatory wearing-off trial (2015, n=389 randomised) found 'off' time reduced by 0.719 hours with zonisamide 50 mg versus 0.011 hours with placebo (P=.005) — an absolute benefit of about 0.7 hours a day; and a 2024 randomised crossover trial (n=69 assessed at 1 month) found MDS-UPDRS III 'on' scores significantly improved with zonisamide 25 mg versus placebo (P=.009). Dyskinesia was NOT increased in any trial. Somnolence was the recurring excess harm (6.3% at 50 mg vs 2.3% on placebo in the 2015 trial). The two large trials are Japanese, and zonisamide is approved for Parkinson's disease in Japan, not for this indication by the FDA or EMA — that single-region weight is stated on the face. A 2022 zonisamide-in-Parkinson's meta-analysis (PMID 36132085) is a RETRACTED publication and is deliberately NOT carded anywhere on this shelf. Cross-points (prose only): opicapone (pack #2369), istradefylline (pack #2370), safinamide (live #1445), and zonisamide in epilepsy (pack #2825) answer different questions.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — three randomised placebo-controlled trials show adjunctive zonisamide improves motor scores and reduces 'off' time (0.719 vs 0.011 hours at 50 mg in the 389-patient confirmatory trial) without increasing dyskinesia, but the absolute effect is modest, the two large trials are single-region (Japan, the only Parkinson's approval), and the retracted 2022 meta-analysis (PMID 36132085) is excluded

title: Early vs later postoperative catheter removal: fewer infections and shorter stays with early removal, but retention noninferiority unproven in the rectal synthesis — a field-by-field split
question: After surgery, does early removal of the indwelling urinary catheter (immediately, on the day of surgery, or on postoperative day 1, as tested by field) versus standard later removal change urinary retention and re-catheterisation, urinary tract infection and length of stay — and does the answer differ between rectal / pelvic colorectal surgery, gynaecological and pelvic-floor surgery, and upper gastrointestinal surgery?
balance: SPLIT — the retention–infection trade-off stays unresolved on the face, exactly where the trials leave it. Earlier removal consistently reduces urinary infection and shortens stay where measured: after pelvic colorectal surgery, day-1 removal (with an oral α-antagonist, part of that trial's intervention) was noninferior for retention (8.5% vs 9.9%) with infection 0% vs 11.3% and a day shorter in hospital; after radical gastrectomy, immediate removal was noninferior to early removal for retention (4.4% vs 3.4%; difference 1.0 percentage point, 95% CI −4.6 to 6.6, within the 10% margin) with better comfort. But the rectal-surgery synthesis (4 trials, 409 patients) could NOT establish noninferiority for retention (risk difference +9 percentage points, 90% CI −1 to +19) even while confirming the infection advantage (risk difference −11 percentage points). The gynaecological/pelvic-floor trials are small (57 women in the day-of-surgery voiding-trial study) and mixed on their primary reads. The answer differs by surgical field, so the cards are kept per field and never pooled into one 'remove early' claim.
stamp: SPLIT — earlier catheter removal reliably reduces urinary infection and shortens stay, and individual trials in gastrectomy, pelvic colorectal (with α-blockade) and prolapse surgery found retention noninferior, but the rectal-surgery meta-analysis could not establish noninferiority for urinary retention (risk difference +9 percentage points, 90% CI −1 to +19); the retention–infection trade-off is unresolved at programme level

title: BIS-guided protocols for preventing intraoperative awareness: SPLIT by comparator — beats routine care (B-Aware, 2 vs 11 cases), no better than end-tidal-agent alerts (B-Unaware, BAG-RECALL)
question: In adults at high risk of intraoperative awareness having general anaesthesia, does a bispectral-index (BIS)-guided protocol — BIS-guided care versus routine care, or a BIS-alert protocol versus an end-tidal anaesthetic concentration (ETAC)-alert protocol — reduce confirmed awareness with explicit recall versus the comparator?
balance: SPLIT — the answer turns entirely on the comparator, and the cards are kept per comparator, never pooled. Against ROUTINE CARE, BIS guidance worked: B-Aware (2,463 high-risk patients) found confirmed awareness in 2 patients on BIS-guided care versus 11 on routine care (P=0.022) — an 82% relative risk reduction (95% CI 17 to 98), with absolute rates of roughly 0.16% versus 0.89% and a number needed to treat of 138. Against an active END-TIDAL anaesthetic concentration (ETAC) alert protocol, BIS guidance did not work: B-Unaware (2,000 patients) found definite awareness in 2 patients in each group, and BAG-RECALL (6,041 patients) found definite awareness in 7 of 2,861 (0.24%) on BIS-alert versus 2 of 2,852 (0.07%) on ETAC-alert — superiority of BIS not demonstrated, with numerically MORE awareness on BIS. The Cochrane synthesis matches the split exactly: BIS beats clinical signs (Peto odds ratio 0.36, relative; low-certainty) but does not differ from ETAC (Peto odds ratio 1.13, relative; low-certainty). Awareness is rare, so absolute event counts are printed beside every relative measure on this shelf. This shelf is distinct from live #1123 (anaesthetic DEPTH targets — BIS 50 vs 35 — for mortality, and EEG guidance for delirium; BALANCED and ENGAGES are homed there and are not re-carded here); cross-point in prose only.
stamp: SPLIT — BIS guidance reduced awareness versus routine care in B-Aware (2 vs 11 cases; 82% relative risk reduction) and versus clinical signs in the Cochrane synthesis, but showed no superiority over end-tidal-agent alert protocols in B-Unaware or BAG-RECALL (definite awareness numerically higher on BIS, 0.24% vs 0.07%); the verdict is determined by the comparator
