title: Active warming/prewarming vs unwarmed care: wound infection 19%→6% (colorectal) and 14%→5% (clean surgery) — the unwarmed-comparator slice presupposed by PROTECT (live #1125)
question: In adults having surgery, does active perioperative warming — maintaining intraoperative normothermia, or preoperative warming (prewarming) before induction — versus unwarmed / routine thermal care permitting mild hypothermia reduce surgical-site infection and wound complications, and how much inadvertent perioperative hypothermia does each warming strategy prevent?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) for the unwarmed-comparator question, with the era boundary printed on the face. Against care that permitted mild hypothermia, warming clearly reduced wound infection: intraoperative normothermia in colorectal surgery (final core temperature 36.6 °C vs 34.7 °C) cut wound infection from 19% (18/96) to 6% (6/104) and shortened hospitalisation by 2.6 days (Kurz 1996), and preoperative warming before clean surgery cut wound infection from 14% (19/139) to 5% (13/277) (Melling 2001). The Cochrane synthesis of active body-surface warming versus control found surgical-site infection reduced (risk ratio 0.36, a relative measure; 3 trials, 589 participants, low-quality evidence). Prewarming also reduces intraoperative hypothermia exposure even when everyone is warmed during surgery (Lau 2018), and resistive-fabric warming matched forced-air warming on temperature in elderly hemiarthroplasty (Kümin 2021). The boundary: Kurz and Melling are pre-modern-ERAS trials whose control arms reached temperatures no current routine permits, and the modern PROTECT trial (live #1125) found no cardiac-composite benefit from aggressive warming to ≥37 °C over routine management targeting 35.5 °C — both arms warmed. This shelf is the warming-versus-unwarmed / infection slice that live #1125 presupposes; it does not re-ask PROTECT's question. Where a publication names a warming product it is named on its card (BairPaws forced-air system, 3M, in Lau 2018), per the product-naming rule.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — active warming/prewarming versus unwarmed care reduced surgical-site infection in the classic trials (19% to 6% colorectal, 14% to 5% clean surgery) and in the Cochrane synthesis (risk ratio 0.36, relative, low-quality evidence), but the control arms are pre-modern-era and permitted hypothermia depths current routine warmed care avoids, and PROTECT (live #1125) bounds the claim for modern practice

title: Multimodal prehabilitation in non-colorectal major surgery: fewer complications in high-risk abdominal (relative risk 0.5), lung-resection (34% vs 55%) and sarcopenic hepatectomy (13.3% vs 50%) trials — the slice outside live #936
question: In adults having major surgery OTHER than colorectal resection — elective major abdominal surgery in high-risk patients, lung resection, and major hepatectomy in patients with sarcopenia — does multimodal prehabilitation (structured exercise, nutrition, respiratory-muscle training and psychosocial components, as tested) reduce postoperative complications and shorten hospital stay versus usual care or postoperative rehabilitation?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), carded per surgical field and per programme — never as a general 'prehabilitation works' claim, because every trial selected its population differently. High-risk elective major abdominal surgery (Barberan-Garcia 2018; analysed 125): personalised prehabilitation roughly halved the proportion of patients with postoperative complications (relative risk 0.5, a relative measure). Lung resection in physiologically high-risk patients (Brat 2025; 122 completed): multimodal prehabilitation with high-intensity respiratory-muscle training reduced postoperative pulmonary complications (34% vs 55%) and shortened stay (7 vs 9 days). Major hepatectomy in sarcopenia (PREHEP, Berardi 2025; 60 analysed): 6-week exercise-and-nutrition prehabilitation reduced overall morbidity (13.3% vs 50%; absolute risk reduction 36.7 percentage points, number needed to treat 3), with all major complications in the control group. The BMJ network/component meta-analysis (186 trials, 15,684 participants) supports exercise and nutrition as the active components, but at mostly very-low certainty — component-level claims rest on that synthesis, not on any single trial. This shelf is the non-colorectal slice: frail patients awaiting colorectal resection are homed at live #936 (whose PREHAB colorectal trial is not re-carded here), and prehabilitation before hip/knee arthroplasty is homed at pack #3746; both are cross-pointed in prose only.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — three randomised trials in three distinct non-colorectal fields (high-risk major abdominal surgery, lung resection in CPET-defined high-risk patients, major hepatectomy in sarcopenia) each reduced postoperative complications with multimodal prehabilitation, and the BMJ component network analysis credits exercise and nutrition, but each trial is small and differently selected and the synthesis certainty is low to very low; the colorectal/frail question stays homed at live #936

title: DASI before major non-cardiac surgery (METS programme reports): subjective assessment had 19.2% sensitivity for inability to reach 4 METs; DASI — threshold 34 — was the only bedside measure predicting 30-day death or MI
question: Before major non-cardiac surgery, how well do bedside measures of functional capacity — the Duke Activity Status Index (DASI) questionnaire and clinicians' subjective assessment in metabolic equivalents — predict 30-day death, myocardial infarction / myocardial injury and complications, and how do they compare with cardiopulmonary exercise testing (peak oxygen consumption) and NT-proBNP?
balance: POSSIBLE — the DASI questionnaire carries prognostic information, clinicians' subjective assessment does not. All three reports are reports OF one programme, labelled as such on the face: the METS international cohort (1,401 patients; 30-day death or myocardial infarction in 28, 2%), its nested DASI analysis (1,546 participants), and a pooled analysis of METS with the FIT After Surgery cohort (3,485 patients). In METS, subjective assessment had only 19.2% sensitivity (95% CI 14.2 to 25) for identifying inability to attain 4 METs on cardiopulmonary exercise testing, and only DASI scores were associated with 30-day death or myocardial infarction (adjusted odds ratio 0.96, 95% CI 0.83 to 0.99, per DASI point). The nested analysis located a threshold at a DASI score of 34. The pooled analysis found DASI added prognostic information beyond age, the Revised Cardiac Risk Index and natriuretic peptide (likelihood ratio test p=0.009 for the primary outcome), but final-model discrimination stayed modest (c-index 0.70-0.71) with limited net clinical benefit. This is a prognostic-accuracy shelf, not a treatment shelf: no report shows that raising a DASI score changes outcomes. PROPOSED STAMP: POSSIBLE.
stamp: POSSIBLE — DASI, a structured self-report questionnaire, was the only bedside functional-capacity measure associated with 30-day death or myocardial infarction in the METS cohort and added modest incremental prognostic information in pooled data, while clinicians' subjective assessment performed poorly (19.2% sensitivity); all reports are labelled programme reports of the METS programme (the pooled report adds FIT After Surgery), and the evidence is prognostic, not therapeutic

title: Population IOP distribution (PARTIAL beside pack #6436): means of 14.2-14.5 mmHg in Tehran, Yazd and Karachi — and 3.5-3.7% of healthy Pakistanis above the conventional 21 mmHg limit
question: In healthy general populations, what is the distribution of intraocular pressure measured by applanation tonometry — mean, spread and upper percentiles by age, sex and ethnicity — and how far do population means sit from the conventional 21 mmHg upper limit?
balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall and Ganong, ocular physiology sections — the framing is brief, and this shelf rests chiefly on the primary population eye-study literature, and says so. This is the between-person DISTRIBUTION slice only: pack #6436 homes aqueous-humour formation/drainage rates and the within-person DIURNAL SWING of intraocular pressure, a different question, cross-pointed here and not re-carded. Three independent population studies (Tehran, n=3,834 glaucoma-free participants aged 10 and over; Yazd, 2,098 healthy participants aged 40-80; Karachi, 7,201 healthy subjects) agree closely on the centre of the distribution — mean IOP 14.5, 14.2 and about 14.3-14.8 mmHg by applanation tonometry — while the conventional 21 mmHg upper limit sits in the tail: in Karachi 3.5% of men and 3.7% of women exceeded 21 mmHg despite being healthy. Ancestry breadth is limited — two of the three datasets are Iranian and the third is Pakistani — and that limit is on the face, not generalised past. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — three independent population studies totalling over 13,000 screened-healthy people agree on a mean IOP of about 14-15 mmHg by applanation tonometry, with the full frequency distribution printed in the largest; the ancestry limit (Iranian and Pakistani populations) is stated on the face

title: Arterial blood-gas reference intervals (PARTIAL beside pack #6349): PaO2 falls about 2.2 mmHg per decade, healthy over-70s centre PaCO2 at 36.9 mmHg, and altitude values need barometric-pressure equations
question: In healthy adults, what are the reference intervals for arterial blood gases and acid–base status — pH, PaCO2, PaO2, bicarbonate and the alveolar–arterial oxygen difference — by age (including older adults) and sex, at sea level and at moderate altitude, and how much do analyser and sampling conditions move them?
balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, respiration and acid–base chapters, and Boron & Boulpaep, respiratory physiology. This is the reference-INTERVALS slice only: pack #6349 homes the alveolar gas EQUATION and what determines the A–a gradient (a mechanism question, which cards one elderly-Japanese ABG dataset as a supporting card) — cross-pointed here, its dataset not re-carded, and no intervals are derived there. Three independent free datasets are carded: reference equations from 96 healthy lifetime nonsmokers at sea level and 243 at 1,400 m (Crapo 1999); non-parametric intervals from 182 medical students plus health professionals aged 21-76 on a named Radiometer ABL analyser (Klaestrup 2011), in which PaO2 fell by 0.29 kPa (about 2.2 mmHg) per decade; and an elderly cohort aged over 70 (Epshtein 2025) whose HEALTHY subgroup — subgroup N not printed in the fetched record — had mean PaCO2 36.9 ± 4.2 mmHg, inside the conventional range. The stamp is graded down: the largest dataset publishes equations rather than printed intervals, the elderly healthy subgroup N is not printed, and altitude rests on a single dataset. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING — three independent datasets agree that PaO2 falls with age and that PaCO2 centres in the high 30s mmHg into old age, but the largest publishes reference equations rather than printed interval limits, the healthy-elderly subgroup N is not printed in its record, and the altitude limb rests on a single dataset

title: CMR chamber reference ranges: LV end-diastolic volume 160 ± 29 mL in men vs 135 ± 26 mL in women (SSFP), UK Biobank LV ejection fraction 61% women vs 58% men — ranges must be normalised to sex, body size and age
question: In healthy adults, what are the cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) reference ranges for cardiac chamber structure and function — left- and right-ventricular volumes, mass and ejection fraction, and atrial dimensions, indexed to body surface area — by age and sex, and how much do cohort, contouring convention and indexing move the limits of normal?
balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, cardiac muscle and circulation chapters — the framing is brief, and this shelf rests chiefly on the primary CMR reference literature, and says so. Three independent steady-state free-precession (SSFP) cohorts: 108 healthy volunteers with manually analysed LV, RV and left-atrial dimensions (Hudsmith 2005 — LV end-diastolic volume 160 ± 29 mL in men vs 135 ± 26 mL in women); a normalised-range modelling study whose fetched abstract prints no cohort N and no numeric ranges, carded for its normalisation principle only (Maceira 2006); and the UK Biobank cohort (Petersen 2017 — 5,065 scanned at 1.5 T, 804 in the healthy Caucasian reference cohort aged 45-74, LV ejection fraction 61 ± 5% in women vs 58 ± 5% in men, indexed LV mass 42 ± 7 vs 53 ± 9 g/m2). Contouring convention (papillary muscles and trabeculations) and indexing move the limits materially and are stated per card; SSFP CMR values are not interchangeable with echocardiographic volumes — the speckle-tracking strain shelf #7163 is the echo cross-point, a different modality and measure. The stamp is graded down: one of three records prints no numbers in its abstract, and the largest cohort is Caucasian and aged 45-74 only. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING — three independent SSFP CMR cohorts agree on the sex, age and indexing structure of normal chamber values, but contouring conventions move the limits materially, one record prints no numeric ranges in its abstract, and the largest cohort is Caucasian and aged 45-74 only

title: Impedance–pH normal values are population-specific: median total reflux episodes 20.5 in Argentina, 40 in China, 49 in rural South Africa — 95th percentiles from 50 to 97
question: In healthy asymptomatic adults, what are the normal values for 24-hour ambulatory oesophageal multichannel intraluminal impedance–pH monitoring — total, acid, weakly acid and weakly alkaline reflux episode counts (median and 95th percentile), bolus exposure and acid exposure time — and how much do population and diet move the upper limits used to define abnormal reflux?
balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, gastrointestinal physiology chapters — the framing is brief, and this shelf rests chiefly on the primary normative monitoring literature, and says so. Four independent healthy-volunteer populations give four different 'normal' pictures, and that spread is the finding: multicentre 2004 (60 volunteers — reflux common upright, median 27 episodes, rare recumbent, median 1); Chinese 2009 (70 volunteers — median total 40 episodes, 95th percentile 75); rural South African 2016 (median total 49, 95th percentile 97 — roughly double the Chinese 95th percentile); Argentine 2022 (median total 20.5, 95th percentile 50 — the lowest reported). No single normal episode count may be printed without its population. The Lyon-consensus thresholds are clinical decision limits derived partly from these data, not a fifth dataset, and are not carded as one. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING, because the upper limits are population-bound and no universal limit survives the four datasets.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING — four independent healthy-population datasets exist, but their median total reflux episodes (20.5 to 49) and 95th percentiles (50 to 97) differ roughly two-fold by population, so the normal values are established only per population, not as a universal limit

title: HR-pQCT normative centiles: lifespan curves from 1,072 Hong Kong and 863 mainland Chinese adults (XtremeCT II) — trabecular parameters peak near 20, cortical loss after 50; young-adult references from Franco-Swiss and Canadian cohorts
question: In healthy adults and young adults, what are the normative values and centile curves for high-resolution peripheral quantitative computed tomography (HR-pQCT) at the distal radius and tibia — volumetric bone mineral density, cortical and trabecular microarchitecture and finite-element bone-strength estimates — by age, sex, skeletal site and population, and how much do scanner generation and population move them?
balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, bone and calcium-metabolism chapters — the framing is brief, and this shelf rests chiefly on the primary HR-pQCT reference literature, and says so. Four independent cohorts: Hong Kong lifespan centile curves in 1,072 adults aged 20-79 (Zhu 2018); mainland Chinese lifespan centiles in 863 adults aged 20-80 on the second-generation XtremeCT II scanner (Yu 2020 — the two Chinese populations are counted separately as published: different sampling frames and scanner generations); a Franco-Swiss young-women reference subset of 43 women aged 22-27 derived by discriminant analysis from 339 women (Koy 2022); and a Canadian youth reference cohort of 251 young adults aged 16-29 (Burt 2014). The shared pattern: trabecular and strength parameters peak around age 20 and decline steadily, while cortical loss comes mainly after 50 and is faster in women around menopause. First- and second-generation scanner values are NOT interchangeable and the generation is carded per dataset. DXA areal BMD / T-score reference data and trabecular bone score are different measurements, homed in their own rows and not re-carded. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED for the lifespan centile structure, with the scanner-generation and young-cohort limits on the face.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — two independent lifespan centile programmes (1,072 Hong Kong and 863 mainland Chinese adults) agree on the age, sex and site structure of HR-pQCT norms, with two young-adult peak-bone-mass cohorts in other populations; scanner generation is stated per dataset and values are not interchangeable across generations

title: Serum urate population distributions: median 5.16 mg/dL (about 307 µmol/L) in 3,099 healthy Mexico City adults, 95% interval to 7.98 mg/dL (about 475 µmol/L); Hangzhou indirect intervals shift by season; 13.2% hyperuricaemia in Brazil
question: In healthy adults, what is the population distribution of serum urate — mean, spread, reference interval and the fraction above the conventional hyperuricaemia thresholds (6.8 mg/dL, and sex-specific thresholds as published) — by sex, age and population, and how do directly recruited healthy cohorts compare with big-data (indirect) laboratory intervals?
balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, renal and purine-metabolism sections — the framing is brief, and this shelf rests chiefly on the primary population literature, and says so. This is a DISTRIBUTION row, not a treat-to-target row; renal urate HANDLING (fractional excretion physiology) is a different, mechanism question homed in its own row and not re-carded. Three independent populations plus one historical supporting limb: Mexico City Tlalpan 2020 (3,099 directly recruited healthy adults — median urate 5.16 mg/dL (about 307 µmol/L), central 95% interval 3.05 to 7.98 mg/dL (about 181 to 475 µmol/L), hyperuricaemia prevalence 16.5%); Hangzhou big-data indirect intervals (749,739 adult results — intervals shift by season, sex and age, e.g. winter/spring men 18-44: 262-539 µmol/L, i.e. about 4.4-9.1 mg/dL); a Brazilian population study (1,346 individuals — hyperuricaemia prevalence 13.2% at thresholds of 6.8 mg/dL (about 404 µmol/L) in men and 5.4 mg/dL (about 321 µmol/L) in women, as published); and the 1984 Reykjavik cohort of middle-aged men as a historical supporting limb whose fetched abstract prints no urate centile values, so none are claimed from it. Direct (healthy-cohort) and indirect (big-data laboratory) intervals are different kinds of number and are never merged on this shelf. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — three independent populations (a 3,099-person direct healthy cohort, 749,739 indirect laboratory results, and a 1,346-person population study) plus a historical limb agree on a sex-split urate distribution centred near 5.2 mg/dL (about 307 µmol/L), with direct and indirect intervals kept separate on the face

title: IOPI tongue strength and endurance norms: anterior maximum 55.95 ± 14.13 kPa and posterior 53.23 ± 12.24 kPa in Taiwan adults; Korean strength falls from 46.7 kPa (young men) to 35.2 kPa over 60; Belgian strength lower after 70
question: In healthy adults, what are maximum tongue strength and endurance — anterior and posterior, measured with the Iowa Oral Performance Instrument (IOPI) — by age and sex, and how much do bulb position, visual feedback and testing order move the values used to judge lingual weakness in dysphagia assessment?
balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall and Boron & Boulpaep, gastrointestinal and swallowing sections — the framing is brief, and this shelf rests chiefly on the primary measurement literature, and says so. Three independent populations, ONE instrument (the Iowa Oral Performance Instrument, IOPI) — the values are instrument-specific and must not be generalised to other tongue-pressure devices. Belgian lifespan data (420 healthy adults): strength falls after age 70, endurance stays stable through most of life, anterior tongue exceeds posterior on both. Taiwan data (150 healthy adults) print the numbers: anterior maximum isometric pressure 55.95 ± 14.13 kPa, posterior 53.23 ± 12.24 kPa, anterior endurance 13.86 ± 7.08 s, posterior 10.06 ± 5.40 s, with 33 kPa proposed in that study as a demarcation of weak tongue strength. Korean data (120 healthy adults, 40 per age band): young men averaged 46.7 ± 10.2 kPa maximal tongue strength vs 32.1 ± 7.9 kPa in young women, falling to 35.2 ± 9.0 and 34.5 ± 6.9 kPa in the over-60s. Strength and endurance are different measures and are carded separately. The stamp is graded down: one dataset's record prints no numeric pressures, and the Korean age-band Ns are modest (120 total across six age-by-sex cells). PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING — three independent IOPI datasets (420 Belgian, 150 Taiwan, 120 Korean adults) agree on the anterior-over-posterior and age patterns, but one record prints no numeric pressures, the Korean age-by-sex cells are modest, and every value is specific to the IOPI instrument

title: Bexagliflozin in type 2 diabetes (6 randomised reports): HbA1c -0.37% in stage 3a/3b CKD, -0.79% placebo-adjusted as monotherapy, non-inferior to sitagliptin, glimepiride and dapagliflozin — no outcomes trial, never marketed at scale
question: In adults with type 2 diabetes (as monotherapy, added to metformin, or with stage 3a/3b chronic kidney disease), does the SGLT2 inhibitor bexagliflozin 20 mg, compared with placebo, sitagliptin, glimepiride or dapagliflozin, improve glycaemic control?
balance: LIKELY benefit for glycaemic control, on exactly 6 randomised reports, printed as the row directs. Against placebo: HbA1c lowered by 0.37% in stage 3a/3b CKD (312 analysed), placebo-adjusted change -0.79% at week 24 in the 96-week monotherapy trial (288 randomised), and a difference of -0.53% added to metformin (317 randomised). Against active comparators, bexagliflozin was non-inferior each time: versus sitagliptin on metformin (HbA1c -0.74% vs -0.82%; 386 participants), versus glimepiride on metformin at week 60 (426 randomised; odds ratio 0.12 for severe or documented symptomatic hypoglycaemia — a relative measure, with fewer events on bexagliflozin), and versus dapagliflozin on metformin in Chinese patients (-1.08% vs -1.10%, difference 0.03% against a 0.4% margin; 406 randomised). Status flags, on the face: bexagliflozin is FDA-approved in the US (2023) but was never marketed at scale, and there is NO cardiovascular- or renal-outcomes trial — the CKD report's endpoint is glycaemic (HbA1c in stage 3a/3b CKD), not kidney progression. HbA1c is a surrogate endpoint throughout. PROPOSED STAMP: LIKELY (benefit — glycaemic control only).
stamp: LIKELY (benefit — glycaemic control only) — six randomised reports consistently show bexagliflozin 20 mg lowering HbA1c against placebo (0.37% to 0.79%) and non-inferior to sitagliptin, glimepiride and dapagliflozin; the stamp is limited to the surrogate HbA1c endpoint because no cardiovascular- or renal-outcomes trial exists, and the agent, though FDA-approved in 2023, was never marketed at scale

title: Henagliflozin in type 2 diabetes — SINGLE-REGION (China) evidence: placebo-adjusted HbA1c -0.91%/-0.94% as monotherapy and -0.76%/-0.80% on metformin in two phase 3 trials; 7-day open-label CSII trial raised time in range to 79.85% vs 74.06%
question: In adults with type 2 diabetes, does the SGLT2 inhibitor henagliflozin, compared with placebo (as monotherapy or added to metformin) or added to continuous subcutaneous insulin infusion in severe hyperglycaemia, improve glycaemic control?
balance: LIKELY benefit for glycaemic control — SINGLE-REGION EVIDENCE (China; approved there, not FDA/EMA-approved), flagged here and on the title as the row directs. The chronic-efficacy claim rests on two phase 3 placebo-controlled trials: monotherapy (468 randomised — placebo-adjusted HbA1c -0.91% at 5 mg and -0.94% at 10 mg, both P<0.001) and add-on to metformin (483 randomised — least-squares mean differences versus placebo -0.76% at 5 mg and -0.80% at 10 mg, all P<0.0001). The retagliptin + henagliflozin combination trial is a combination question, not counted here and cross-pointed only. HbA1c and time-in-range are surrogate endpoints; no outcomes trial exists — both printed. PROPOSED STAMP: LIKELY (benefit — glycaemic control, single-region China evidence).
stamp: LIKELY (benefit — glycaemic control, single-region China evidence) — two phase 3 placebo-controlled trials show placebo-adjusted HbA1c reductions of 0.76% to 0.94% at 5-10 mg as monotherapy and added to metformin, with a supporting 7-day open-label CSII report in severe hyperglycaemia; the stamp is limited to the surrogate glycaemic endpoint, the evidence is single-region (China; not FDA/EMA-approved), and no outcomes trial exists

title: Enavogliflozin in type 2 diabetes (3 Korean phase 3 trials): HbA1c −0.99% vs placebo as monotherapy, non-inferior to dapagliflozin on metformin — single-region (Korea) evidence, no outcomes trial
question: In Korean adults with type 2 diabetes, does the SGLT2 inhibitor enavogliflozin 0.3 mg, compared with placebo or dapagliflozin (as monotherapy or added to metformin, with or without gemigliptin), improve glycaemic control?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) for glycaemic control only, on single-region (Korea) evidence. Three Korean phase 3 randomised trials of enavogliflozin 0.3 mg: as monotherapy it lowered HbA1c by 0.99% more than placebo at 24 weeks, with 71% versus 24% reaching HbA1c <7.0%; added to metformin it was non-inferior to dapagliflozin (HbA1c change −0.80% vs −0.75%, difference −0.04% against a 0.35% margin); and added to metformin plus gemigliptin it matched dapagliflozin (−0.92% vs −0.86%). SINGLE-REGION FLAG: all evidence is Korean; enavogliflozin is approved in Korea and is not FDA/EMA-approved. HbA1c is a surrogate endpoint and no cardiovascular- or renal-outcomes trial exists for this agent. The placebo-controlled efficacy claim rests on the monotherapy trial; the other two anchors are active-comparator non-inferiority trials.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit — glycaemic control only, single-region Korea evidence) — one phase 3 placebo-controlled trial showed a placebo-adjusted HbA1c reduction of 0.99% at 24 weeks, and two further phase 3 trials showed non-inferiority/equivalence to dapagliflozin added to metformin (with or without gemigliptin); HbA1c is a surrogate, all evidence is Korean, and no outcomes trial exists

title: Remogliflozin etabonate in type 2 diabetes: non-inferior to dapagliflozin at 24 weeks (−0.72%/−0.77% vs −0.58% HbA1c), with 12-week dose-ranging placebo data — limited-region programme, no outcomes trial
question: In adults with type 2 diabetes, does the SGLT2 inhibitor remogliflozin etabonate, compared with placebo, pioglitazone or dapagliflozin, improve glycaemic control?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) for glycaemic control only, on a single-/limited-region programme. In the 24-week Indian phase 3 trial, remogliflozin etabonate 100 mg and 250 mg twice daily were non-inferior to dapagliflozin on metformin (HbA1c change −0.72% and −0.77% vs −0.58%). Two earlier 12-week dose-ranging trials in drug-naïve / treatment-naïve patients showed significant dose-response HbA1c effects versus placebo (reductions versus placebo of 0.64% to 1.07% across twice-daily doses in one). HbA1c is a surrogate endpoint and no outcomes trial exists.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit — glycaemic control only, single-/limited-region evidence) — one 24-week phase 3 trial showed non-inferiority to dapagliflozin on metformin and two 12-week dose-ranging trials showed significant placebo-controlled HbA1c effects, but the durable base is a single non-inferiority trial; HbA1c is a surrogate and no outcomes trial exists

question: In Japanese adults with type 2 diabetes, does the SGLT2 inhibitor tofogliflozin, compared with placebo (as monotherapy, dose-ranging, or added to insulin), improve glycaemic control and body weight?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) for glycaemic control only, on single-region (Japan) evidence. title: Ertugliflozin glycaemic programme (VERTIS MET / SITA2 / SU): HbA1c −0.7% to −0.9% vs placebo, non-inferior to glimepiride — glycaemic slice only; VERTIS CV outcomes trial homed at #7512
question: In adults with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled on metformin (alone, or with sitagliptin), does the SGLT2 inhibitor ertugliflozin, compared with placebo, sitagliptin or glimepiride, improve glycaemic control (the VERTIS glycaemic programme)?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) for glycaemic control only — the glycaemic slice of the VERTIS programme. VERTIS MET: placebo-adjusted HbA1c changes of −0.7% (5 mg) and −0.9% (15 mg) at 26 weeks on metformin (both P<0.001). VERTIS SITA2: −0.7% and −0.8% added to metformin plus sitagliptin (both P<0.001), maintained to 52 weeks. VERTIS SU: ertugliflozin 15 mg was non-inferior to glimepiride on metformin at 52 weeks (HbA1c change −0.6% vs −0.7%), with less symptomatic hypoglycaemia and more genital mycotic infections than glimepiride. Ertugliflozin is a globally approved agent (FDA/EMA) — NOT single-region. This shelf asks the glycaemic question only: the VERTIS CV cardiovascular-outcomes trial builds separately at shelf #7512 and is cross-pointed here, never carded on this shelf. HbA1c is a surrogate endpoint in all three anchors.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit — glycaemic control only) — two placebo-controlled VERTIS trials showed HbA1c reductions of 0.7% to 0.9% versus placebo and a third showed non-inferiority to glimepiride at 52 weeks; this stamp covers the glycaemic slice only — the VERTIS CV outcomes trial is homed separately at shelf #7512 — and HbA1c is a surrogate endpoint

title: Esaxerenone in essential hypertension (PARTIAL — hypertension slice only; albuminuria slice at #3204): non-inferior to eplerenone and to trichlormethiazide, dose-response vs placebo — single-region (Japan) evidence, potassium the harm
question: In adults with essential hypertension, does the non-steroidal mineralocorticoid-receptor blocker esaxerenone, compared with placebo, eplerenone or trichlormethiazide, lower blood pressure?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) for blood-pressure lowering only, on single-region (Japan) evidence. ESAX-HTN (phase 3, 1,001 patients): esaxerenone 2.5 mg/day was non-inferior to eplerenone 50 mg/day for sitting and 24-hour blood-pressure reduction, the 5 mg/day dose reduced blood pressure significantly more than 2.5 mg/day, and target sitting blood pressure was reached by 31.5%, 41.2% and 27.5% respectively. The phase 2 placebo-controlled study showed a dose-response (sitting change −20.6/−10.4 mm Hg at 5 mg vs −7.0/−3.8 mm Hg on placebo and −17.4/−8.5 mm Hg on eplerenone). EXCITE-HT: esaxerenone was non-inferior to trichlormethiazide as second-line therapy for morning home blood pressure. PARTIAL: pack #3204 already homes esaxerenone for albuminuria in diabetic kidney disease (the ESAX-DN programme) — this shelf cards only the essential-hypertension slice and cross-points #3204; none of #3204's studies is re-carded. SINGLE-REGION FLAG: all evidence is Japanese; esaxerenone is approved in Japan for hypertension and is not FDA/EMA-approved. Blood pressure is a surrogate endpoint and no outcomes trial exists for this agent. Hyperkalaemia is the class harm and leads the harm side: serum potassium elevations were more frequent on esaxerenone in EXCITE-HT and rose dose-proportionally in phase 2.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit — blood-pressure lowering only, single-region Japan evidence) — a phase 2 placebo-controlled dose-response, phase 3 non-inferiority to eplerenone (ESAX-HTN) and non-inferiority to trichlormethiazide as second-line therapy (EXCITE-HT); blood pressure is a surrogate, no outcomes trial exists, and serum potassium elevation is the standing harm; the diabetic-albuminuria slice is homed at pack #3204

title: Topiroxostat in hyperuricaemia ± gout (3 Japanese trials): urate −36.3% vs −34.3% on allopurinol (non-inferior), dose-response vs placebo — biochemical endpoint only, no flare-outcome trial, single-region (Japan)
question: In Japanese adults with hyperuricaemia with or without gout, does the selective xanthine-oxidoreductase inhibitor topiroxostat, compared with placebo or allopurinol, lower serum urate?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) for serum urate lowering only, on single-region (Japan) evidence. In the phase 3 double-blind trial, topiroxostat 120 mg/day reduced serum urate by −36.3% versus −34.3% on allopurinol 200 mg/day over 16 weeks (percent change from baseline), and non-inferiority was proved. The phase 2b study confirmed a dose-response, with a −44.8% reduction at 160 mg/day; the phase 2a study showed a dose-dependent reduction from 40 to 120 mg/day, with a mean percent change of −30.8% at 120 mg/day versus +1.6% on placebo over 8 weeks. SINGLE-REGION FLAG: all evidence is Japanese; topiroxostat is approved in Japan and is not FDA/EMA-approved. Serum urate is a biochemical endpoint — NO flare-outcome trial is in this base, so nothing here shows topiroxostat prevents gout attacks. Percent changes are printed as the abstracts print them (percent change from baseline).
stamp: LIKELY (benefit — serum urate lowering only, single-region Japan evidence; no flare-outcome trial) — phase 3 non-inferiority to allopurinol (−36.3% vs −34.3% percent change in serum urate) with concordant dose-response in two phase 2 studies; serum urate is a biochemical endpoint and no trial in this base measured gout flares or other clinical outcomes

title: Suplatast tosilate in asthma (Japanese programme): Lancet trial — deterioration on steroid halving significantly worse on placebo; small mechanistic limbs (n=28/25/20) show eosinophilic inflammation falling
question: In adults with asthma — steroid-dependent asthma undergoing inhaled-steroid reduction, mild-to-moderate asthma, and cough-variant asthma — does oral suplatast tosilate versus placebo improve lung function and symptoms, permit inhaled-corticosteroid reduction, and reduce eosinophilic airway inflammation?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), on a Japanese programme whose load-bearing report is one Lancet trial. In steroid-dependent asthma (85 randomised, 77 analysed), suplatast tosilate 100 mg three times daily improved pulmonary function and symptoms during a 4-week add-on phase and, when inhaled beclomethasone was halved over the next 4 weeks, pulmonary function, symptoms and beta-agonist use deteriorated significantly more on placebo than on suplatast. Three smaller randomised reports (n=28, n=25, n=20 — printed on their cards) support an anti-eosinophilic mechanism: blood and sputum eosinophils, exhaled nitric oxide and airway responsiveness fell; bronchial-biopsy goblet-cell metaplasia measures fell; and in cough-variant asthma the capsaicin cough threshold rose from 2.72 to 39.7 μM with sputum eosinophil cationic protein falling. JAPANESE PROGRAMME FLAG: suplatast is licensed in Japan and not in the US/UK. Endpoints are lung function, symptoms and inflammatory markers over 4 weeks to 3 months; there is no exacerbation-outcome or mortality trial. The paediatric suplatast reports are not folded into this adult shelf.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one double-blind Lancet trial in steroid-dependent asthma (85 randomised) showed suplatast allowed inhaled-steroid halving with significantly less deterioration than placebo, supported by three small mechanistic randomised reports (n=28, n=25, n=20) showing reduced eosinophilic inflammation; a Japanese programme, not licensed in the US/UK, with no exacerbation-outcome or mortality trial

title: Seratrodast (AA-2414 — one drug) in asthma (Japanese programme): symptoms and PEF variability improved in two small trials (n=45, n=31), FEV1 unchanged in one; phase II report is PK/PD only
question: In patients with mild-to-moderate asthma, does oral seratrodast (AA-2414, thromboxane A2 receptor antagonist) versus placebo improve symptoms, peak-flow variability and airway inflammation/hyperresponsiveness?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), on a mechanistic, short and dose-inconsistent Japanese programme — presented as such. Seratrodast is the thromboxane A2 receptor antagonist developed as AA-2414 — the two names are ONE drug, and this shelf states that identity so they are not read as two agents. In the multicentre placebo-controlled trial (45 patients with sputum-producing asthma, 40 mg/day for 6 weeks), diurnal peak-flow variation, daytime symptoms and rescue beta-agonist use fell significantly versus placebo and sputum amount and viscosity fell — but FEV1 and peak-flow changes did NOT differ between groups. In the bronchial-biopsy trial of AA-2414 (31 patients, 80 mg/day for 4 months), symptom score, peak flow, diurnal variation and bronchial responsiveness improved versus placebo with reduced submucosal eosinophils and chemokine-expressing cells. The phase II report (183 patients) is a population pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic analysis of its trial, not a conventional efficacy report, and is labelled as such. Seratrodast is licensed in Japan, not in the US/UK. Endpoints are symptoms, peak-flow variability and biopsy/sputum markers; no exacerbation-outcome trial exists.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two small double-blind placebo-controlled trials (n=45, n=31) showed improvements in symptoms, peak-flow variability and airway inflammation markers, one of them with no difference in FEV1/PEF change, supported by a phase II PK/PD programme report (n=183) that is not a conventional efficacy report; a mechanistic, short, dose-inconsistent Japanese programme, not licensed in the US/UK

title: Tegoprazan in erosive oesophagitis: healing matched esomeprazole (98.9% vs 98.9%) and maintenance matched lansoprazole (90.6% vs 89.5%) — the patient trials pack #5882 does not card
question: In adults with erosive oesophagitis, does tegoprazan heal oesophagitis versus esomeprazole or lansoprazole, and does it maintain healing versus lansoprazole?
balance: LIKELY (benefit, as a PPI-equivalent healer) — on four patient trials, none carded at pack #5882. Healing: tegoprazan matched esomeprazole at week 8 in Korea (98.9% vs 98.9%, n=302) and in China as LXI-15028 (91.1% vs 92.8%, n=261), and beat lansoprazole numerically to week 4 in a phase 4 trial (95.2% vs 86.2%, n=218; non-inferior, superior on that trial's own analysis, which its authors say needs confirmation in severe disease). Maintenance: 24-week remission 90.6% vs 89.5% on lansoprazole (n=351), in mostly mild (LA A/B) healed disease. PARTIAL against pack #5882, which cards tegoprazan only as healthy-volunteer pharmacodynamic limbs for the severe-disease/night-time question — those limbs are not re-carded here; cross-point #5882. Korean and Chinese programmes only.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — tegoprazan healed erosive oesophagitis non-inferiorly to esomeprazole in two phase 3 trials (98.9% vs 98.9%; 91.1% vs 92.8%) and to lansoprazole in a phase 4 trial, and maintained healing non-inferiorly to lansoprazole over 24 weeks (90.6% vs 89.5%); benefit is PPI-equivalence, not established superiority, and the programmes are Korean/Chinese

title: Fexuprazan in erosive oesophagitis: healing matched esomeprazole in two trials and did not depend on meal timing — one retracted phase III report fenced, never carded
question: In adults with erosive oesophagitis, does fexuprazan 40 mg heal oesophagitis versus esomeprazole 40 mg, and does healing differ by dosing timing relative to meals?
balance: LIKELY (benefit, as a PPI-equivalent healer) — fexuprazan 40 mg healed erosive oesophagitis non-inferiorly to esomeprazole 40 mg in two trials (week-8: 88.5% vs 89.0% full-analysis, 97.3% vs 97.9% per-protocol, n=332 in the full set; 99.1% vs 99.1% per-protocol, 263 randomised), and a third trial (n=175) found after-meal dosing non-inferior to before-meal dosing (100.00% vs 98.77% at week 4) — a timing limb with no PPI comparator, not a third healing trial. Cross-point #5882 and #7473 without merging agents into a class verdict.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — fexuprazan 40 mg healed erosive oesophagitis non-inferiorly to esomeprazole 40 mg in two randomised trials and healing was independent of meal timing in a third; benefit is PPI-equivalence in a Korean programme, and the retracted phase III report (PMID 38892973) is fenced and never carded

title: Ilaprazole: duodenal-ulcer healing matched other PPIs (relative risk 1.02; 89.7% vs 87.0%) and reflux-oesophagitis healing matched esomeprazole (83.54% vs 82.79%) — two limbs, never pooled
question: In adults with active duodenal ulcer, does ilaprazole heal ulcers versus omeprazole or rabeprazole — and in reflux oesophagitis, does it heal versus esomeprazole?
balance: LIKELY (benefit, as a PPI-equivalent healer) — in two limbs that are labelled and never pooled. Duodenal ulcer: week-4 healing 93.0% vs 90.8% on omeprazole (494 in efficacy analyses), 77.86%/83.72% on ilaprazole 5/10 mg vs 75.38% on rabeprazole (390 completed), and a meta-analysis of 5 articles (1,481 patients) giving a week-4 healing relative risk of 1.02 (95% CI 0.98–1.06) with absolute rates 89.7% vs 87.0%. Reflux oesophagitis: week-8 healing 83.54% vs 82.79% on esomeprazole (537 randomised) in the trial published under the spelling 'Ilaparazole'. All comparators are active PPIs — no placebo-controlled healing trial exists in either limb. Chinese/Korean programme.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — ilaprazole healed duodenal ulcers at rates matching omeprazole and rabeprazole (pooled relative risk 1.02, absolutes 89.7% vs 87.0%) and healed reflux oesophagitis at a rate matching esomeprazole (83.54% vs 82.79%), in two separately labelled limbs from a Chinese/Korean programme with active-PPI comparators only

title: Rebamipide in functional dyspepsia: both placebo-controlled primaries negative on overall symptoms — a meta-analytic signal on one metric only
question: In adults with functional dyspepsia, does rebamipide versus placebo improve dyspeptic symptoms and quality of life?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — and the negative primaries lead. Both named placebo-controlled primaries failed on their overall symptom outcomes: the two multicentre studies in one publication (272 randomised across the two studies) found rebamipide not superior to placebo on individual symptom scores at end of treatment, and the Japanese trial (81 recruited) found no significant difference in overall symptom change at 4 weeks, with three individual items favouring rebamipide. The meta-analysis (17 publications, 2,170 subjects) found a functional-dyspepsia signal on the standardised mean difference only (SMD −0.62, 95% CI −1.16 to −0.08) and none on the risk-ratio analysis (RR 1.01, 95% CI 0.71 to 1.45). Report-count convention: the 2001 publication contains two studies — three reports covering three trials plus the meta-analysis. Japanese programme predominance.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — both placebo-controlled primary trials of rebamipide in functional dyspepsia were negative on overall symptoms (272 randomised across two studies in one publication; 81 in the Japanese trial), and the meta-analytic signal is confined to the standardised mean difference (SMD −0.62) with a null risk-ratio analysis (RR 1.01)

title: Somatostatin in acute pancreatitis: signals on markers, CT evolution and surgery in three old small trials (one unblinded, n=50) — no mortality effect shown
question: In patients with acute pancreatitis (including severe disease), does intravenous somatostatin versus control/standard care reduce complications, need for surgery, hospital stay and mortality?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — on an old, small, mostly unblinded primary-trial programme, carded as the slice slate-13's octreotide row (S13-2-06) expressly did not fold in; cross-point that row, never a merged analogue verdict. Signals: day-2 laboratory markers and a trend to fewer local complications (n=71, 1989); CT evolution and hospital stay significantly favouring somatostatin (n=100, 1994); and, in severe disease, fewer surgical interventions (45.8% vs 86.4%, P=0.005) in a prospective randomised UNBLINDED trial of 50 patients (1998), with no difference in stay or ICU mortality. No trial was powered for mortality. The gated 2017 Cochrane review (PMID 28431202, pack #7293) is NOT carded — primaries only. Dosing differed (100 vs 250 micrograms/h after a 250 microgram bolus).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — three old, small primary trials (n=71, 100, 50; 1989–1998) show surrogate, imaging and surgical-intervention signals for intravenous somatostatin in acute pancreatitis, the largest from an unblinded severe-disease trial, with no mortality benefit shown and no trial powered for mortality

title: Glycyrrhizin in chronic hepatitis C: ALT fell (phase III ≥50% reduction 28.7–29.0% vs 7.0% on placebo) but viraemia did not — a biochemical, interferon-era benefit
question: In patients with chronic hepatitis C who were ineligible for, or non-responders to, interferon therapy, does intravenous glycyrrhizin versus placebo (or across dose frequencies) reduce ALT and improve liver histology — and does it affect viraemia?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit — biochemical only, ALT not viraemia) — across four randomised reports in interferon-ineligible/non-responder chronic hepatitis C: mean ALT fell 26% vs 6% on placebo at 4 weeks with no viral clearance and no significant HCV-RNA effect (n=57); mean ALT fell 26% (three-times-weekly) and 47% (six-times-weekly) vs no significant placebo change, disappearing after cessation (72 treatment courses); ALT response was maintained by dose frequency at 26 weeks (60%/24%/9%, P<0.001) with NO significant histological improvement (121 entered, 72 responders randomised); and the phase III trial (379 patients) found at least 50% ALT reduction in 28.7%/29.0% vs 7.0% on placebo at 12 weeks (P<0.0001), with necro-inflammation improvement in about 45–46% at 52 weeks in an uncontrolled open phase. Interferon-era evidence — not against the direct-acting-antiviral standard. Mineralocorticoid-type harms are homed at pack #3467; cross-point it.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit, biochemical only) — intravenous glycyrrhizin consistently reduced ALT in chronic hepatitis C across four randomised reports including a 379-patient phase III trial (≥50% ALT reduction 28.7–29.0% vs 7.0% on placebo), but HCV viraemia did not change in the trial that measured it, histology was negative at 26 weeks and positive only in an uncontrolled 52-week phase, and all evidence is from the interferon era

title: Nitazoxanide in childhood cryptosporidiosis: the HIV split is the answer — benefit in HIV-negative children (56% vs 23% resolution), none in HIV-positive children
question: In children with cryptosporidial diarrhoea — stratified by HIV status — does nitazoxanide versus placebo (or standard care) improve clinical and parasitological response and reduce mortality?
balance: SPLIT — the split is HIV status, and it is the answer. In HIV-seronegative Zambian children, a 3-day course resolved diarrhoea in 56% vs 23% on placebo and eradicated C. parvum in 52% vs 14%, with 0 vs 4 deaths by day 8 (100 recruited, 96 analysed). HIV-seropositive children did not benefit in that trial's stratum, and a dedicated high-dose prolonged-course trial in HIV-positive children was negative (clinical response 42% vs 35%; eradication 27% vs 35%; mortality 31% overall; 60 randomised). A 2025 Bangladeshi pilot in undernourished children (64 randomised; standard-care arm n=10) found no difference in infection duration or growth in any arm. Paediatric, low-income-setting programme throughout.
stamp: SPLIT (by HIV status) — nitazoxanide benefited HIV-seronegative children with cryptosporidiosis in the one stratified trial (diarrhoea resolution 56% vs 23% on placebo) but showed no benefit in HIV-positive children in that trial or in a dedicated high-dose prolonged trial (response 42% vs 35%), and a 2025 pilot in undernourished children was negative

title: IV cidofovir for CMV retinitis in AIDS (pre-HAART): progression delayed 120 vs 22 days in two trials of one programme — nephrotoxicity priced in probenecid and monitoring
question: In patients with AIDS and previously untreated peripheral cytomegalovirus retinitis, does immediate intravenous cidofovir versus deferred treatment delay retinitis progression, and what are its long-term outcomes and toxicities?
balance: LIKELY (benefit, in its pre-HAART setting) — two distinct randomised immediate-versus-deferred trials in one programme family: median time to progression 120 vs 22 days (P<0.001; n=48) and, in the HPMPC trial (n=64), 64 days on low-dose maintenance (P=0.052) and not reached on high-dose maintenance (P=0.009) vs about 21 days deferred. The HPMPC long-term follow-up (58 patients) is a report OF the second trial, not a third trial: median progression 2.5 months, discontinuation for intolerance at a median 6.6 months. Toxicity leads the safety face: nephrotoxicity managed with probenecid and hydration in every report (treatment-limiting in 24% in the first trial; proteinuria at least 2+ at 1.22 per person-year in follow-up; probenecid intolerance 0.35 and uveitis 0.20 per person-year). ERA FLAG: pre-HAART care; deferred comparators must not be carried into modern practice.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit, pre-HAART era only) — intravenous cidofovir delayed CMV retinitis progression versus deferred treatment in two randomised trials (median 120 vs 22 days; HPMPC high-dose maintenance not reached vs 21 days, P=0.009), at the cost of nephrotoxicity requiring probenecid, hydration and monitoring; the evidence is a single pre-HAART programme family and does not transfer to modern practice

title: CLEOPATRA: pertuzumab plus trastuzumab–docetaxel prolonged survival in HER2-positive metastatic breast cancer (median 56.5 vs 40.8 months) — one trial, three reports
question: In patients with HER2-positive metastatic breast cancer, does adding pertuzumab to trastuzumab plus docetaxel prolong progression-free and overall survival versus trastuzumab plus docetaxel alone?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — on one trial reported three times (CLEOPATRA, 808 randomised), labelled a single-programme shelf. Adding pertuzumab to trastuzumab plus docetaxel prolonged median progression-free survival from 12.4 to 18.5 months (hazard ratio 0.62, a relative measure) and median overall survival from 40.8 to 56.5 months at the final analysis (hazard ratio 0.68; 15.7-month absolute median difference), maintained at end of study (57.1 vs 40.8 months; 8-year survival 37% vs 23%). The survival analyses are unadjusted for crossover and therefore conservative. Added toxicity was grade 3 or above febrile neutropenia and diarrhoea, with no increase in left ventricular systolic dysfunction. The PUFFIN bridging trial is a separate regional programme — cross-point only, never pooled.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — in the single CLEOPATRA trial (808 randomised), pertuzumab added to trastuzumab–docetaxel prolonged median progression-free survival (18.5 vs 12.4 months; hazard ratio 0.62, relative) and median overall survival (56.5 vs 40.8 months; hazard ratio 0.68, relative), maintained beyond 8 years

title: APHINITY: adjuvant pertuzumab improved disease-free survival in node-positive HER2-positive early breast cancer — overall survival still not significant at 8.4 years (92.7% vs 92.0%)
question: In patients with node-positive or high-risk node-negative HER2-positive early breast cancer, does one year of adjuvant pertuzumab added to trastuzumab plus chemotherapy improve invasive disease-free and overall survival?
balance: SPLIT — the split is nodal status, and the survival null leads beside it. One trial reported three times (APHINITY, 4,805 randomised): invasive disease-free survival improved overall (3-year 94.1% vs 93.2%; hazard ratio 0.81, a relative measure), concentrated in node-positive disease (hazard ratio 0.77 primary; 8-year rates 86.1% vs 81.2%, hazard ratio 0.72), with no benefit seen in node-negative disease (primary hazard ratio 1.13). Overall survival has NOT reached significance at any analysis: hazard ratio 0.85 (P=.17) at 6 years and 0.83 (P=.078, above the 0.006 threshold) at 8.4 years, 8-year rates 92.7% vs 92.0%. Added harm was grade 3 or higher diarrhoea during chemotherapy (9.8% vs 3.7%); cardiac events were infrequent. Do not let the stamp outrun the survival null.
stamp: SPLIT (by nodal status; overall survival not significant) — adjuvant pertuzumab improved invasive disease-free survival in APHINITY, concentrated in node-positive disease (8-year 86.1% vs 81.2%; hazard ratio 0.72, relative) with no benefit in node-negative disease, while overall survival remained NOT significant at 8.4 years (92.7% vs 92.0%; hazard ratio 0.83; P=.078)

title: T-DM1 in pretreated HER2-positive metastatic breast cancer: EMILIA — survival 29.9 vs 25.9 months with less toxicity than lapatinib-capecitabine; TH3RESA — 22.7 vs 15.8 months vs physician's choice
question: In patients with HER2-positive metastatic breast cancer previously treated with trastuzumab and a taxane, does trastuzumab emtansine (T-DM1) prolong progression-free and overall survival versus lapatinib plus capecitabine (EMILIA) or versus treatment of physician's choice (TH3RESA), and with what toxicity trade?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — two independent phase 3 trials in pretreated HER2-positive metastatic breast cancer, each showing both a progression-free and an overall-survival advantage for T-DM1, with absolutes printed beside every relative measure. EMILIA (991 randomised, vs lapatinib plus capecitabine): PFS 9.6 vs 6.4 months (HR 0.65, relative); final median OS 29.9 vs 25.9 months (HR 0.75, relative); grade 3/4 adverse events 41% vs 57% at the primary analysis — the control was more toxic. TH3RESA (602 randomised, later line, vs physician's choice): PFS 6.2 vs 3.3 months (HR 0.528, relative); final median OS 22.7 vs 15.8 months (HR 0.68, relative). PARTIAL beside #1856 (KATHERINE, adjuvant residual disease) and #856 (DESTINY-Breast03, T-DXd vs T-DM1): only the pretreated-metastatic slice is carded here.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — two phase 3 randomised trials (EMILIA, n=991; TH3RESA, n=602) each showed T-DM1 prolonged both progression-free survival (HR 0.65 and 0.528, relative) and overall survival (final HR 0.75 and 0.68, relative) in pretreated HER2-positive metastatic breast cancer, with less grade 3-or-worse toxicity than the EMILIA control; PARTIAL beside KATHERINE #1856 and DESTINY-Breast03 #856, whose questions are not re-carded

title: Lapatinib in HER2-positive metastatic breast cancer: progression delayed with capecitabine (8.4 vs 4.4 months) but survival not significant; dual blockade with trastuzumab improved survival vs lapatinib alone
question: In patients with HER2-positive metastatic breast cancer progressing after trastuzumab, does lapatinib — added to capecitabine, or combined with trastuzumab chemotherapy-free — prolong time to progression and overall survival?
balance: SPLIT — progression and survival point in different strengths. Adding lapatinib to capecitabine after trastuzumab doubled time to progression (8.4 vs 4.4 months; HR 0.49 interim / 0.57 updated, relative) but overall survival was only a non-significant trend (HR 0.78; P=.177). Adding trastuzumab to lapatinib (EGF104900, chemotherapy-free) improved progression-free survival (HR 0.73, relative) and, at final analysis, overall survival (HR 0.74, relative; +4.5 months median) — but against lapatinib alone. A first-line paclitaxel trial was negative overall with a positive HER2-positive subset (n=86) — carded labelled, never load-bearing. CNS first progression 4 vs 13 is a small-count signal.
stamp: SPLIT — lapatinib combinations consistently delayed progression after trastuzumab (time-to-progression HR 0.57 updated, relative, with capecitabine; PFS HR 0.73, relative, with trastuzumab), but overall survival was not significant against capecitabine (HR 0.78, P=.177) and was significant only against lapatinib monotherapy in EGF104900 (HR 0.74, relative); the first-line HER2-positive subset (n=86) is labelled and not load-bearing

title: Everolimus plus exemestane in HR-positive advanced breast cancer (BOLERO-2): progression-free survival more than doubled, overall survival not significant (31.0 vs 26.6 months, P=.14)
question: In postmenopausal patients with hormone-receptor-positive, HER2-negative advanced breast cancer recurring after a non-steroidal aromatase inhibitor, does everolimus plus exemestane prolong progression-free survival versus exemestane alone, and does it prolong overall survival?
balance: SPLIT, on a single trial (BOLERO-2, 724 randomised). Progression-free survival: a large relative gain — final local assessment 7.8 vs 3.2 months (HR 0.45, relative), central 11.0 vs 4.1 months (HR 0.38, relative). Overall survival: NO significant benefit — median 31.0 vs 26.6 months (HR 0.89; P=.14), printed on the face as the row directs. Quality-of-life deterioration was delayed at a 5% threshold (HR 0.74) but not at a 10-point threshold (HR 0.80; P=.1017). Pricing harms: grade 3/4 stomatitis 8% vs 1%, pneumonitis 3% vs 0%, anaemia 6% vs <1%.
stamp: SPLIT — POSSIBLE (benefit: delays progression) on BOLERO-2's large relative progression-free-survival gain (final HR 0.45 local / 0.38 central, relative, absolutes printed) / no overall-survival benefit demonstrated (median 31.0 vs 26.6 months; HR 0.89, P=.14); a single-trial base, priced in grade 3/4 stomatitis 8% vs 1% and pneumonitis 3% vs 0%

title: Afatinib in EGFR-mutant NSCLC: progression-free survival 11.1 vs 6.9 and 11.0 vs 5.6 months vs platinum doublets; vs gefitinib HR 0.73 with medians 11.0 vs 10.9 months
question: In patients with EGFR-mutation-positive advanced non-small-cell lung cancer, does first-line afatinib prolong progression-free survival versus platinum doublet chemotherapy (LUX-Lung 3, LUX-Lung 6), and versus gefitinib (LUX-Lung 7)?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit, on progression-free survival only) — three randomised trials, two comparator classes, labelled separately. title: Ceritinib in ALK-positive NSCLC: progression-free survival 16.6 vs 8.1 months first-line and 5.4 vs 1.6 months after crizotinib — at the superseded 750 mg fasted dose
question: In patients with ALK-rearranged advanced non-small-cell lung cancer, does ceritinib prolong progression-free survival versus chemotherapy — first-line (ASCEND-4) and after crizotinib plus chemotherapy (ASCEND-5)?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit, on progression-free survival) — two phase 3 randomised trials versus chemotherapy: ASCEND-4 first-line (376 randomised) PFS 16.6 vs 8.1 months (HR 0.55, relative); ASCEND-5 after crizotinib and chemotherapy (231 randomised) PFS 5.4 vs 1.6 months (HR 0.49, relative). Pricing harms at the trial dose: diarrhoea 85%, grade 3–4 ALT elevation 21%. No overall-survival claim is carded.

title: Panitumumab plus FOLFOX in metastatic colorectal cancer (PRIME): benefit in RAS wild-type (survival 26.0 vs 20.2 months), harm in RAS-mutant tumours (PFS HR 1.29)
question: In patients with metastatic colorectal cancer, does adding panitumumab to FOLFOX4 improve progression-free and overall survival in RAS wild-type tumours — and does it harm patients whose tumours carry RAS mutations?
balance: SPLIT by biomarker — one trial (PRIME, 1,183 randomised), opposite answers by RAS status, and the harm half is on the face. RAS wild-type: progression-free survival 10.1 vs 7.9 months (HR 0.72, relative) and overall survival 26.0 vs 20.2 months (HR 0.78, relative) in the fully RAS wild-type group (n=512). KRAS wild-type final overall survival was HR 0.88 (P=.17, not significant) at the prespecified analysis and HR 0.83 (P=.03) in an exploratory update — both printed. RAS-mutant: progression-free survival significantly worse with panitumumab (HR 1.29, relative) in mutant KRAS, and other RAS mutations likewise predicted harm. Full RAS testing is therefore part of the intervention.
stamp: SPLIT (by RAS status) — in RAS wild-type metastatic colorectal cancer panitumumab plus FOLFOX4 improved progression-free survival (HR 0.72, relative) and overall survival (HR 0.78, relative; absolutes printed) in PRIME's extended RAS analysis, while in RAS-mutant tumours it caused harm (progression-free-survival HR 1.29, relative); the KRAS wild-type final survival analysis was not significant (HR 0.88, P=.17) with a significant exploratory update (HR 0.83, P=.03), both printed

title: Sunitinib in pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours: progression-free survival doubled (11.4 vs 5.5 months) in an early-stopped trial; final overall survival not significant (P=.094)

title: Docetaxel in metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer: TAX 327 — 3-weekly docetaxel prolonged survival (18.9 vs 16.5 months), weekly did not; SWOG 9916 — docetaxel plus estramustine 17.5 vs 15.6 months
question: In men with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer, does docetaxel-based chemotherapy prolong overall survival versus mitoxantrone-based treatment?
balance: LIKELY benefit, for the every-3-weeks schedule. Two randomised trials against mitoxantrone plus prednisone found a survival benefit for docetaxel-based chemotherapy in metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer: TAX 327 (3-weekly docetaxel plus prednisone, median survival 18.9 vs 16.5 months; hazard ratio 0.76, a relative measure; benefit confirmed on updated follow-up, 19.2 vs 16.3 months) and SWOG 9916 (docetaxel plus estramustine, 17.5 vs 15.6 months; HR 0.80, relative). title: Gemcitabine plus nab-paclitaxel in metastatic pancreatic cancer: MPACT — survival 8.5 vs 6.7 months, priced in neutropenia (38% vs 27%) and neuropathy (17% vs 1%)

title: Idelalisib in relapsed CLL: huge PFS gains (HR 0.15 and 0.27) — but 22 vs 6 treatment-related deaths with ofatumumab and cumulative colitis, pneumonitis and diarrhoea
question: In patients with relapsed chronic lymphocytic leukaemia, does idelalisib — added to rituximab (Study 116) or combined with ofatumumab — prolong progression-free survival, and what serious toxicity emerged with longer exposure?
balance: SPLIT — very large efficacy, very serious toxicity. Idelalisib plus rituximab in relapsed CLL (Study 116, stopped early for efficacy) gave a progression-free-survival hazard ratio of 0.15 (a relative measure), response 81% vs 13% and 12-month survival 92% vs 80%; idelalisib plus ofatumumab gave PFS 16.3 vs 8.0 months (HR 0.27, relative). title: Glatiramer acetate in relapsing-remitting MS: relapses cut by about a third in relative terms across three placebo-controlled trials (annualised rate 0.331 vs 0.505 in GALA), with injection reactions the main harm
question: In patients with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis, does glatiramer acetate 20 mg daily (or 40 mg three times weekly) reduce relapse rates and MRI lesion activity versus placebo?
balance: LIKELY benefit, modest in size. Three placebo-controlled trials in relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis agree: glatiramer acetate reduced relapses by about a third in relative terms — pivotal 20 mg daily trial (mean relapses over 2 years 1.19 vs 1.68, a 29% relative reduction), European/Canadian MRI trial (relapses reduced 33% relative; total enhancing lesions −10.8 vs placebo) and GALA (40 mg three times weekly; annualised relapse rate 0.331 vs 0.505, a 34% relative reduction). Harms are modest: injection-site reactions (35.5% vs 5.0% in GALA) and a transient systemic post-injection reaction (15.2% vs 3.2% in the pivotal trial). No long-term disability effect is claimed from these trials.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — glatiramer acetate reduced relapse rates versus placebo in three randomised trials in relapsing-remitting MS (29%, 33% and 34% relative reductions, each printed beside its absolute rates) and reduced MRI lesion activity, with injection-site and transient systemic reactions as the main harms and no immunosuppression

title: Interferon beta in relapsing-remitting MS: beta-1b cut annual exacerbations (0.84 vs 1.27) with no discernible disability effect; PRISMS beta-1a cut relapses by 27–33% relative and delayed disability progression

title: Divalproex for migraine prophylaxis: three placebo-controlled trials show a real but modest reduction (about 0.6–2.2 fewer attacks per 4 weeks); teratogenicity is the dominant harm frame
question: In patients with frequent migraine, does divalproex sodium (immediate- or extended-release) reduce migraine frequency versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE benefit — real but modest, on small short trials, with a heavy harm frame. Three placebo-controlled trials agree that divalproex sodium reduces migraine frequency: mean frequency 3.5 vs 5.7 attacks per 4 weeks (Mathew 1995, 107 randomised); mean reductions of 1.7–2.0 vs 0.5 attacks per 4 weeks across 500–1500 mg with no gain at the top dose (Klapper 1997, 176 randomised); and a reduction of 1.2 vs 0.6 attacks for the extended-release form (Freitag 2002; N not documented in its record). Absolute effects, not responder percentages alone, are printed. Teratogenicity is the dominant harm frame for valproate in a largely female, reproductive-age population, with weight gain and tremor; nausea and dizziness were also more frequent at higher doses.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — three small, short placebo-controlled trials (1995–2002) consistently showed divalproex reducing migraine frequency, but the absolute effect is modest (about 0.6 to 2.2 fewer attacks per 4 weeks versus placebo across the trials), the extended-release trial's N is not documented in its record, and valproate's teratogenicity dominates the harm frame in a reproductive-age population

title: Zolpidem in chronic insomnia: ER 12.5 mg 'helped me sleep' 92.3% vs 59.7% at 24 weeks (n=1,018); IR 10 mg worked over 35 nights in a small trial (n=75); ER 6.25 mg improved polysomnography in older adults
question: In adults with chronic primary insomnia, does zolpidem — immediate-release nightly, or extended-release taken 3–7 nights per week — improve sleep onset and maintenance versus placebo, and what happens on discontinuation?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) for sleep onset and maintenance over the periods tested, on three randomised trials carded separately by formulation. Immediate-release zolpidem 10 mg (n=75, 35 nights, sleep-laboratory) improved latency to persistent sleep and sleep efficiency from week 1 with no tolerance and no post-treatment difference from placebo; 15 mg added nothing and reduced REM sleep at weeks 3–4. Extended-release 12.5 mg taken 3–7 nights per week (n=1,018, 24 weeks) beat placebo on every subjective measure — the primary endpoint was the patient's global impression that the drug 'helped me sleep' (89.8% vs 51.4% at week 12; 92.3% vs 59.7% at week 24) — with no rebound over the first 3 discontinuation nights; commonest adverse events were headache, anxiety and somnolence. In older adults (n=205, mean age 70.2), zolpidem ER 6.25 mg improved polysomnographic wake after sleep onset, latency and total sleep time over 3 weeks, with some polysomnographic measures worsening for a single night after abrupt discontinuation and no next-morning residual effects detected. The 1994 trial is small (n=75) and labelled as such; the weight rests on the two ER trials. None of the carded trials reports falls, fractures or complex sleep behaviours as outcomes — those harms are not measured in this evidence base and are not claimed either way here.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — zolpidem improves sleep onset and maintenance versus placebo in all three randomised trials carded (immediate-release 10 mg over 35 nights, n=75; extended-release 12.5 mg taken 3–7 nights/week over 24 weeks, n=1,018; extended-release 6.25 mg by polysomnography in older adults, n=205), with no tolerance signal; the largest trial's primary endpoint is subjective and none of the trials measures falls, fractures or complex sleep behaviours

title: Incentive spirometry after abdominal surgery: Cochrane found no benefit vs no therapy or deep breathing (12 trials); small trials beat only other breathing therapies on lung function; the PRIME-AIR bundle including it was null
question: After upper abdominal or other major surgery, does incentive spirometry — volume- or flow-oriented, as tested — versus no therapy, deep-breathing exercises or other lung-expansion therapy reduce postoperative pulmonary complications, and does a structured perioperative lung-expansion bundle that includes it (PRIME-AIR) beat usual care?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the device itself is unproven against the comparators that matter. The Cochrane synthesis (12 trials, 1,834 participants; 1,160 in meta-analysis) found NO statistically significant difference between incentive spirometry and no respiratory treatment for clinical complications (relative risk 0.59, 95% CI 0.30 to 1.18), none versus deep-breathing exercises for respiratory failure, and none versus other chest physiotherapy — its conclusion is low-quality evidence of lack of effectiveness, and that uncertainty stays on the face of this shelf. The small head-to-head trials carded here compare one breathing therapy against another (volume spirometry vs diaphragmatic breathing, n=58; spirometry vs EzPAP, n=112, complications 3.6% vs 7.1%, not significant; flow vs volume spirometry, n=50) and show at most better spirometric recovery — they must not be pooled into a 'spirometry works' claim. The one large trial, PRIME-AIR (n=751 analysed), tested a perioperative lung-expansion BUNDLE that included supervised postoperative incentive spirometry and found no reduction in pulmonary-complication severity versus usual care (mean severity 1.60 vs 1.53, P=0.19); a bundle's result cannot be attributed to the spirometer, and it is carded as a bundle limb only.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — incentive spirometry has no demonstrated reduction in postoperative pulmonary complications versus no therapy, deep-breathing exercises or other physiotherapy in the Cochrane synthesis of 12 trials (relative risk 0.59, 95% CI 0.30 to 1.18 vs no treatment, low-quality evidence); small head-to-head trials show only better spirometric recovery versus other active breathing therapies, and the PRIME-AIR bundle that included supervised spirometry was null in 751 patients

title: Hypotension Prediction Index guidance: less time hypotensive in small trials, but no less AKI (6.1% vs 7.0% in the 917-patient multicentre trial), no fewer complications, no mortality benefit
question: In adults having surgery under general anaesthesia, does haemodynamic management guided by the Hypotension Prediction Index (HPI) — a machine-learning early-warning algorithm for impending hypotension — versus standard care or conventional goal-directed therapy reduce the depth and duration of intraoperative hypotension and postoperative acute kidney injury?
balance: SPLIT — the index moves the process measure and not the patient outcomes. In two small randomised trials, HPI-guided management (Hypotension Prediction Index, Edwards Lifesciences, USA — a named commercial product, named per card as published) reduced the burden of intraoperative hypotension: time-weighted average MAP below 65 mmHg 0.02 vs 0.37 in a 60-patient trial, and time-weighted area below threshold 0.19 vs 0.66 mmHg when HPI was added to conventional goal-directed therapy in 64 patients — the Sapporo design, which separates the index itself from simply doing more goal-directed therapy, though at the cost of more norepinephrine use. But the one large trial — 917 patients, 28 hospitals, moderate-to-severe AKI as the primary outcome — found no benefit: AKI 6.1% vs 7.0% (risk ratio 0.89, 95% CI 0.54 to 1.49), complications 31.9% vs 29.7%, mortality 1.1% vs 0.9%. The 2026 meta-analysis of 8 randomised trials (1,534 patients) agrees: no significant difference in AKI, complications, mortality, length of stay or fluid use, with the hypotension-metric reductions confined to post hoc analyses in unblinded trials at high risk of bias. The related intraoperative blood-pressure STRATEGY trials (INPRESS individualised targets; POISE-3 hypotension-avoidance) are cross-points only — they are carded elsewhere and are not evidence about this device.
stamp: SPLIT — HPI-guided management reduces the depth and duration of intraoperative hypotension in small randomised trials and in pooled process metrics, but the 917-patient multicentre trial found no reduction in moderate-to-severe AKI (6.1% vs 7.0%), complications or mortality, and the 8-trial meta-analysis (1,534 patients) found no significant patient-outcome benefit

title: Preoperative frailty predicts death or new disability: CFS and modified Fried perform alike (adjusted ORs 2.51 and 2.60 at 90 days), CFS is easier to use; cardiac cohort — hospital mortality 9.8% frail vs 1.0% nonfrail
question: Before major elective surgery in older adults, how well does a bedside frailty assessment — the Clinical Frailty Scale and the (modified) Fried phenotype, as tested — predict death or new disability after surgery, and how do the instruments compare?
balance: LIKELY (predictive) — this is a prognostic-accuracy shelf, not a treatment shelf, and no card on it implies that modifying a frailty score changes outcomes. In the prospective multicentre Canadian cohort of patients ≥65 having elective noncardiac surgery (702 enrolled, 645 with complete follow-up), frailty by either instrument predicted death or patient-reported new disability at 90 days with near-identical adjusted odds ratios (Clinical Frailty Scale 2.51, 95% CI 1.50 to 4.21; modified Fried Index 2.60, 95% CI 1.57 to 4.31), true- and false-positive rates did not differ significantly, frailty was the only significant predictor in the multivariable analysis, and the CFS was easier and quicker to use with less missing data — the head-to-head comparison is this shelf's core content. The prespecified 1-year follow-up of the SAME programme (labelled as such, not an independent cohort) found frailty associated with the disability trajectory over a year (P<0.0001), including an early increase in disability in more than a third of people with frailty before a net decrease by 365 days. The independent limb is a cardiac-surgery cohort (Alberta, n=529, CFS ≥5 in 9.6%): hospital mortality 9.8% in frail versus 1.0% in nonfrail patients (adjusted hazard ratio 3.84, 95% CI 0.90 to 16.34 — imprecise), with longer intensive-care and hospital stays. Cross-points: frailty as the population for colorectal prehabilitation (live #936) and the DASI/subjective functional-capacity question (Slate 13 row S13-4-05) are different questions and are not carded here.
stamp: LIKELY (predictive) — preoperative frailty by the Clinical Frailty Scale or the (modified) Fried phenotype predicts death or new disability after major elective surgery (adjusted odds ratios 2.51 and 2.60 at 90 days in 645 patients with complete follow-up, with the CFS easier to use), supported by an independent cardiac-surgery cohort; prognostic evidence only — no card shows that modifying frailty changes outcomes

title: Measured-GFR reference values: 103 ± 17 mL/min/1.73 m² (percentiles 76–137) in healthy adults by iohexol; ≈100 until age 35 in 2,974 donors, then declining 6.6–7.7 per decade; 67.7 ± 10.8 at ages 70–110
question: In healthy adults, what are the reference values for measured glomerular filtration rate (mGFR) — mean, spread and 2.5th–97.5th percentile range by age and sex, and the size of the decline after age 40 — measured by exogenous-marker clearance (iohexol, iothalamate), and how far do donor-cohort ranges sit from general-population ranges?
balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, renal physiology chapters; Boron & Boulpaep, glomerular filtration sections — framing only; this shelf rests on four primary measured-GFR datasets in healthy adults, carded per marker and per cohort. PARTIAL slice, stated plainly: home pack #6958 asks how measured-GFR METHODS AGREE (inulin vs iohexol vs iothalamate vs 51Cr-EDTA, plus renal plasma flow and filtration fraction) and cards none of these datasets; this shelf cards only the reference-VALUES slice — what the values are, by age and sex — and cross-points #6958 rather than re-carding it (its gated iohexol age-dependence dataset, PMID 2609107, stays solely at #6958 under the one-home rule). The values: a general healthy-adult West African cohort (n=237, iohexol) gives mean mGFR 103 ± 17 mL/min/1.73 m² with 2.5th–97.5th percentiles 76–137 and a decline after age 40, with no sex difference. Three of the four datasets are donor or donor-adjacent cohorts — screened, healthier than the general population — and that selection is stated on the face, never merged with the general-population dataset: 2,974 UK prospective living donors (mean ≈100 mL/min/1.73 m² until age 35, then a linear decline, faster in women, 7.7 vs 6.6 mL/min/1.73 m² per decade; 10.5% of donors over 60 had mGFR <60); 365 US potential donors by iothalamate (normalised mean 111 mL/min/1.73 m² at age 20, declining 4.9 per decade); and 52 healthy elderly people aged 70–110 by iohexol (mean 67.7 ± 10.8 mL/min/1.73 m²; decline ≈1.05 mL/min per year; the elderly dataset's N of 52 is printed on its card). PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED
