title: TCD normal velocities: MCA 58 ± 15.6 cm/s by conventional TCD (106 volunteers, falling with age); women-only MCA ≈68 cm/s falling to ≈60 after 50; angle-corrected duplex MCA range 37.7–112.5 cm/s
question: In healthy adults, what are the normal transcranial Doppler (TCD) blood-flow velocities — mean velocities in the middle cerebral, anterior and posterior cerebral, carotid siphon and basilar arteries — by age and sex, and how much do insonation-angle correction (transcranial colour-coded duplex) and age move them?
balance: Textbook framing: Boron & Boulpaep / Guyton & Hall, cerebral circulation sections — the framing is brief, and this shelf rests chiefly on the primary normative ultrasound literature, and says so. Three independent adult datasets, carded PER METHOD because conventional transcranial Doppler (uncorrected insonation angle) and transcranial colour-coded duplex (angle-corrected) velocities are not interchangeable: the 1990 conventional-TCD dataset of 106 normal volunteers (middle cerebral artery M1 mean 58 ± 15.6 cm/s, posterior cerebral 39 ± 9.9, carotid siphon 47 ± 13.8, basilar trunk 41 ± 10, with a marked decrease with age and low side-to-side differences); a women-only dataset of 100 healthy Italian women (middle cerebral mean ≈67–68 cm/s overall, falling from ≈81–83 cm/s under 20 years to ≈59–61 cm/s over 50 — labelled women-only on its card); and a 2020 colour-coded-duplex dataset (195 enrolled, 162 analysed) whose angle-corrected 2.5th–97.5th percentile ranges (middle cerebral 37.7–112.5 cm/s; anterior cerebral 25.6–71.2; posterior cerebral 29.2–80.8) differ widely from its own 0° values. The paediatric dataset and the normative-ranges book chapter named at mining are NOT carded — a secondary source and a different population, respectively. The stamp is graded down because the total base is three datasets, one is women-only, one predates colour-coded duplex, and the method split means there is no single method-free normal velocity. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING

title: Serum free light chain reference intervals: kappa 6.3–20.6 mg/L and ratio 0.46–1.23 (Freelite verification) vs kappa 7.20–20.0 and ratio 0.5–2.11 on Optilite; Saudi intervals run higher; renal impairment breaks the manufacturer's ratio interval
question: In healthy adults, what are the reference intervals for serum free light chains — kappa, lambda and the kappa/lambda ratio — by assay platform, age and renal function, and how far do locally derived intervals sit from the manufacturer's original interval?
balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall / Boron & Boulpaep, plasma-protein and renal-handling sections — framing brief; this shelf rests chiefly on the primary reference-interval literature, and says so. Four independent populations, carded PER ASSAY PLATFORM because the intervals are assay-specific and must never be printed platform-free. The locally derived intervals cluster near — but not on — the manufacturer's original interval: in 120 healthy South African adults (113 analysed after exclusions; Freelite) the 95% intervals were kappa 6.3–20.6 mg/L, lambda 8.7–25.9 mg/L and ratio 0.46–1.23, most values falling within the manufacturer's limits; in 246 healthy Spanish blood donors (Optilite analyser) kappa was 7.20–20.0 mg/L and lambda 6.72–20.23 mg/L, with a kappa/lambda diagnostic interval of 0.5–2.11 as published — and using the local versus manufacturer intervals reclassified 14.5% of MGUS and 16.3% of myeloma results in their collected data. In 180 healthy Saudi adults (Freelite reagents, IFCC harmonised protocol) the new intervals for free kappa and the ratio were shifted HIGHER than the manufacturer-adapted intervals (the record does not print the numeric limits, and this shelf claims none for that dataset). The renal-function limb is core content: renal impairment elevates the ratio and produces a high false-positive rate against the manufacturer's interval, and the 2023 Clinical Chemistry study (Freelite on a Roche Cobas c501) derived renally robust single intervals — ratio-based and principal-component-based — with significantly lower false-positive rates and equivalent sensitivity for monoclonal gammopathy. The immunoglobulin limb of the Saudi dataset is NOT carded here (one dataset, one home). PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED

title: Metanephrine reference intervals by LC-MS/MS: supine normetanephrine upper limit rises to 1.05 nmol/L over age 60 (age adjustment lifts specificity 88.3% to 96.0%); seated samples need seated limits (specificity 94.6% vs 83.5%)
question: In healthy adults, what are the reference intervals for plasma free metanephrines and normetanephrine (and urinary free metanephrines) measured by LC-MS/MS — by sampling posture (supine vs seated), age and sex — and how much do posture and the age adjustment for normetanephrine move the upper limits used to exclude phaeochromocytoma?
balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, adrenal medulla / catecholamine chapters — framing brief; this shelf rests chiefly on the primary reference-interval literature, and says so. Three independent reference populations, carded PER SAMPLING POSTURE because posture is part of the measurement and supine and seated intervals are different numbers, never merged. Supine (Eisenhofer 2013; 1,226 subjects sampled supine, including 575 normotensive and hypertensive adults and 535 patients in whom phaeochromocytoma was ruled out): the upper cut-off for plasma normetanephrine rises with age, from 0.47 nmol/L in children to 1.05 nmol/L in subjects over 60 — the age adjustment for normetanephrine is this shelf's core content — and an age-adjusted curvilinear model plus a higher metanephrine cut-off (0.45 vs 0.32 nmol/L) raised diagnostic specificity from 88.3% to 96.0% with minimal sensitivity loss (93.9% to 93.6%). Seated (Lin 2023; reference population 736 people aged 14–92 — the record includes adolescents from age 14 and the adult bands are the carded content): seated intervals applied to seated samples gave the same 100% sensitivity and better specificity (94.6% vs 83.5%) than applying published age-adjusted supine intervals, and halved-to-a-third the borderline band (5.3% vs 15.7% of suspected patients fell between the upper limit and twice it). Plasma and urine by LC-MS/MS (Eisenhofer 2019; 590 hypertensive and normotensive reference subjects, intervals optimised against 2,056 patients tested for phaeochromocytoma/paraganglioma): age is the dominant consideration for plasma normetanephrine and sex the most practical basis for urinary metabolite intervals. CKD-specific intervals are a patient-population limb and are not a dataset here. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED

title: TSH distribution and reference intervals: reference mean ≈1.40 mIU/L (NHANES III), but upper limits of 3.60 (South Germany), 7.06 (screened Koreans) and 8.86 mIU/L (Chinese ≥65, vs 6.57 under 65)
question: In healthy adults, what is the population distribution and reference interval for serum thyrotropin (TSH) — median, spread and 97.5th percentile by age, sex, ancestry and iodine status — how much does the upper limit rise in older adults, and how far do antibody-negative 'reference population' limits sit below whole-population limits?
balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, thyroid hormone chapters — framing brief; this shelf rests chiefly on the primary population-survey literature, and says so. This is a DISTRIBUTION row, not a treatment-threshold row: subclinical-hypothyroidism therapy lives on its own shelves. Four independent populations, carded with the reference-population DEFINITION beside every interval, because the definition (antibody-negative, ultrasound-screened, or disease-free by history) moves the upper limit more than the assay does — and iodine status differs by population (US / Korean / German / Chinese) as content, not caveat. NHANES III (17,353 US participants aged ≥12; antibody-negative reference population 13,344): geometric mean TSH 1.40 mIU/L in the reference population, rising with age, and lower in Black participants (1.18) than White (1.45) or Mexican American (1.37) participants. An ultrasonography- and antibody-screened Korean health-check population (19,465) produced a WIDER interval, 0.73–7.06 mIU/L — positive antibodies or abnormal ultrasound widened the central 95% interval, and smokers' values shifted lower. South German KORA F4 (3,080 examined; 710 thyroid-healthy after exclusions) gave 0.52–3.60 mIU/L with a median of 1.49 and no significant age or sex influence. A 10-city Chinese survey (15,008) shows the age effect the other datasets flatten: the older-adult (≥65) interval was 0.75–8.86 mIU/L (median 2.58) versus 0.76–6.57 (median 2.38) in younger adults, and applying the age-specific range cut the labelled prevalence of subclinical hypothyroidism in older adults from 19.87% to 3.3%. title: VERTIS CV (one trial, four reports): ertugliflozin NONINFERIOR for MACE (11.9% vs 11.9%), not superior — with prespecified heart-failure (HR 0.70 for first hospitalisation) and exploratory kidney signals in the same trial
question: In adults with type 2 diabetes and established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, does ertugliflozin, compared with placebo, reduce major adverse cardiovascular events, heart-failure hospitalisation and kidney progression (the VERTIS CV outcomes trial and its prespecified companion reports)?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit, confined to heart-failure and kidney signals) — and the headline must be read exactly as the trial printed it: VERTIS CV is a NONINFERIORITY result, not an outcomes win. Report count stated exactly: this shelf cards four reports of the SINGLE VERTIS CV trial (primary, prespecified heart-failure, prespecified kidney, prespecified eGFR-slope) plus one further secondary analysis in older adults, labelled programme support — one programme, not five trials. In 8,246 randomised patients with type 2 diabetes and established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease followed a mean of 3.5 years, major adverse cardiovascular events occurred in 11.9% on ertugliflozin and 11.9% on placebo (hazard ratio 0.97, 95.6% CI 0.85 to 1.11; P<0.001 for noninferiority against the 1.3 margin), and the first key secondary composite — cardiovascular death or heart-failure hospitalisation — did NOT reach superiority (8.1% vs 9.1%; hazard ratio 0.88, 95.8% CI 0.75 to 1.03; P=0.11). The favourable signals live in the prespecified companion reports and are printed as such: first heart-failure hospitalisation hazard ratio 0.70 (95% CI 0.54 to 0.90) with total heart-failure events rate ratio 0.70; the exploratory kidney composite (sustained 40% eGFR reduction, dialysis/transplant or renal death) at 6.0 vs 9.0 events per 1,000 person-years (hazard ratio 0.66, 95% CI 0.50 to 0.88), while the trial's own secondary kidney composite gave hazard ratio 0.81 (95.8% CI 0.63 to 1.04); and a placebo-adjusted chronic eGFR-slope difference of 1.19 mL/min/1.73 m² per year over weeks 6–156. Amputations were numerically more frequent on ertugliflozin (2.0% on 5 mg, 2.1% on 15 mg, vs 1.6% on placebo). The glycaemic question for this drug (the VERTIS MET / SITA2 / SU programme) is a different question, homed at pack #7468; it is cross-pointed here in prose and none of its studies is carded on this shelf (one-home rule).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit, confined to the heart-failure and kidney signals) — VERTIS CV, ONE trial reported four times plus labelled older-adult programme support, showed ertugliflozin NONINFERIOR to placebo for major adverse cardiovascular events (11.9% vs 11.9%; hazard ratio 0.97) without superiority on cardiovascular death or heart-failure hospitalisation (P=0.11), while prespecified analyses found fewer first heart-failure hospitalisations (hazard ratio 0.70) and a lower exploratory kidney-composite rate (6.0 vs 9.0 per 1,000 person-years)

title: Efsubaglutide alfa in type 2 diabetes (China-only programme): HbA1c −1.26%/−1.68% vs placebo in SUPER 1 and −1.06% in SUPER 2 at 24 weeks — no outcomes trial
question: In Chinese adults with type 2 diabetes (drug-naïve on lifestyle alone, or inadequately controlled on metformin), does the once-weekly GLP-1 receptor agonist efsubaglutide alfa, compared with placebo, improve glycaemic control?
balance: LIKELY (benefit — glycaemic control only), on single-region evidence: every trial was conducted in China and efsubaglutide alfa is not FDA/EMA-approved — that flag is on the face of this shelf. Two seamless phase IIb/III placebo-controlled programmes agree: SUPER 1 (drug-naïve, phase III stage 297 randomised) cut HbA1c by 1.73% on 1 mg and 2.15% on 3 mg at week 24 (estimated treatment differences versus placebo −1.26% and −1.68%), and SUPER 2 (added to metformin) cut HbA1c by 1.80% on 3 mg versus 0.74% on placebo (difference −1.06%, P<0.001). A third, small (59-patient), open-label, 12-week dosing-interval trial found 3 mg every two weeks comparable to 1 mg weekly — it has no placebo arm and is not load-bearing for efficacy. HbA1c is a surrogate endpoint; no cardiovascular-outcomes trial exists. Gastrointestinal adverse events (nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, decreased appetite) were the most common, mostly mild to moderate.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit — glycaemic control only; single-region China evidence, not FDA/EMA-approved; no outcomes trial) — SUPER 1 and SUPER 2, two seamless phase IIb/III placebo-controlled programmes, each showed significant HbA1c reductions versus placebo at 24 weeks (treatment differences −1.26%/−1.68% and −1.06%); the third card is a 59-patient open-label dosing-interval trial with no placebo arm and is not load-bearing

question: In Chinese adults with type 2 diabetes, does the once-weekly GLP-1 receptor agonist polyethylene glycol loxenatide (pegloxenatide, PEX168), compared with placebo (as monotherapy or added to metformin) or insulin glargine, improve glycaemic control?
balance: LIKELY (benefit — glycaemic control only), on single-region evidence: every trial was conducted in China, where pegloxenatide is approved; it is not FDA/EMA-approved — that flag is on the face of this shelf. Two phase 3 placebo-controlled trials agree: monotherapy (361 randomised) cut HbA1c by −1.02% on 100 µg and −1.34% on 200 µg versus −0.17% on placebo at week 24, and added to metformin the least-squares mean changes were −1.16% and −1.14% versus +0.35% on placebo. A third card — a 78-patient, open-label, single-centre CGM trial versus insulin glargine — found more time in range on pegloxenatide; it is not load-bearing for durable efficacy. HbA1c and time in range are surrogate endpoints, and the BALANCE-3 cardiovascular-outcomes trial is a protocol only: no outcomes trial has reported.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit — glycaemic control only; single-region China evidence, not FDA/EMA-approved; no outcomes trial has reported) — two phase 3 placebo-controlled trials (monotherapy, 361 randomised; add-on to metformin) each showed significant HbA1c reductions versus placebo at 24 weeks; the third card is a 78-patient open-label single-centre CGM trial versus insulin glargine and is not load-bearing

title: Taspoglutide in type 2 diabetes (DISCONTINUED, never marketed): HbA1c beat placebo, exenatide and sitagliptin in T-emerge — abandoned for nausea, injection-site and allergic reactions
question: In adults with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled on metformin-based therapy, does the once-weekly GLP-1 receptor agonist taspoglutide, compared with placebo, exenatide or sitagliptin, improve glycaemic control (the T-emerge programme)?
balance: DISCONTINUED AGENT — this flag leads. Taspoglutide's development was halted in 2010 and it was never marketed; this shelf is a historical programme record. The glycaemic efficacy was real: across the T-emerge programme, once-weekly taspoglutide lowered HbA1c more than placebo (T-emerge 3: −1.35%/−1.40% versus −0.45%), more than twice-daily exenatide (T-emerge 2: −1.24%/−1.31% versus −0.98%) and more than sitagliptin (T-emerge 4: −1.23%/−1.30% versus −0.89%). The tolerability was the failure: nausea in 35–59% across trials, vomiting in up to 37%, injection-site reactions in 24% versus 5% on placebo, systemic allergic reactions, anti-taspoglutide antibodies in 46–49%, and high discontinuation — the gastrointestinal intolerance and hypersensitivity that ended the programme are printed on every card. HbA1c is a surrogate endpoint; no outcomes trial exists.
stamp: DISCONTINUED (development halted 2010; never marketed) — POSSIBLE (benefit) for glycaemic control only: taspoglutide lowered HbA1c more than placebo, exenatide and sitagliptin across the T-emerge programme, but nausea in up to 59%, injection-site reactions, systemic allergic reactions and antibodies in 46–49% ended the programme; the discontinuation leads this stamp

title: Muraglitazar in type 2 diabetes (NEVER MARKETED): JAMA 2005 CV-safety relative risk 2.23 (1.47% vs 0.67%) ended the programme despite real HbA1c efficacy
question: In adults with type 2 diabetes, does the dual PPARα/γ agonist muraglitazar, compared with placebo, pioglitazone or glimepiride, improve glycaemic control and lipids — and what did the cardiovascular safety record show?
balance: NEVER-MARKETED AGENT — the harm record leads. Muraglitazar, a dual PPARα/γ agonist, was abandoned after the 2005 JAMA cardiovascular safety meta-analysis of its phase 2/3 programme (3,725 patients): death, nonfatal myocardial infarction or nonfatal stroke occurred in 35 of 2,374 (1.47%) on muraglitazar versus 9 of 1,351 (0.67%) on placebo/pioglitazone controls — relative risk 2.23 (95% CI 1.07 to 4.66; P=0.03), a relative measure with the absolute rates printed beside it; the wider composite including transient ischaemic attack and heart failure gave a relative risk of 2.62 (2.11% versus 0.81%). This was despite an 8:1 FDA advisory vote recommending approval. The glycaemic efficacy underneath was real (monotherapy HbA1c −1.05%/−1.23% versus −0.32% on placebo; better HbA1c and lipid changes than pioglitazone 30 mg added to metformin), and the trials themselves showed more oedema, weight gain and heart failure on muraglitazar. The meta-analysis rests on sponsor trial documents released for the advisory meeting, not on a dedicated outcomes trial. HbA1c and lipids are surrogate endpoints.
stamp: NEVER MARKETED — LIKELY (harm) on cardiovascular safety, and that harm leads: the JAMA 2005 meta-analysis of the phase 2/3 programme found death, nonfatal MI or stroke in 1.47% on muraglitazar versus 0.67% on controls (relative risk 2.23, labelled relative, absolutes beside it), and the agent was abandoned despite an 8:1 FDA advisory vote for approval; its glycaemic efficacy (HbA1c −1.23% vs −0.32% on placebo) is carded underneath, not above, that record

title: Tesaglitazar in type 2 diabetes (DISCONTINUED; GALLANT programme): HbA1c matched pioglitazone and beat placebo in four 24-week trials — dose-dependent creatinine rises ended development
question: In adults with type 2 diabetes (as add-on to sulfonylurea, metformin or insulin, or versus pioglitazone), does the dual PPARα/γ agonist tesaglitazar improve glycaemic control and lipids (the GALLANT programme)?
balance: DISCONTINUED AGENT — this flag leads. Tesaglitazar, a dual PPARα/γ agonist, was discontinued during development over a renal signal that runs through every carded report: dose-dependent increases in serum creatinine (and decreases in haemoglobin) that no comparator produced. The GALLANT programme's four 24-week trials — published as a single journal-issue programme set — show consistent surrogate efficacy: tesaglitazar 1 mg was non-inferior to pioglitazone 45 mg for HbA1c, and placebo-corrected HbA1c reductions were −0.93%/−1.3% added to sulfonylurea, significant versus placebo added to metformin, and −0.66% added to insulin, with triglyceride, HDL-C and non-HDL-C improvements throughout. All four reports are 24-week surrogate-endpoint trials (HbA1c, lipids); no outcomes trial exists, and the creatinine signal must stay on the face, not in a footnote.
stamp: DISCONTINUED (never marketed) — POSSIBLE (benefit — surrogate endpoints only): the four GALLANT trials show consistent HbA1c and lipid improvements (non-inferior to pioglitazone 45 mg head-to-head; placebo-corrected −0.93%/−1.3% on sulfonylurea; −0.66% on insulin), but dose-dependent serum creatinine rises run through every report and ended development; the discontinuation and the creatinine signal lead this stamp

title: Avosentan in diabetic nephropathy (FLOOR-RISK — 2 reports, 1 trial): ASCEND stopped early for cardiovascular harm; heart-failure HR 2.76; no progression benefit detected
question: In adults with type 2 diabetes and overt diabetic nephropathy on ACE-inhibitor / ARB therapy, does the endothelin-receptor antagonist avosentan, compared with placebo, slow kidney progression?
balance: LIKELY (harm) — FLOOR-RISK: for the kidney-progression question this shelf rests on exactly 2 reports, both from the single ASCEND trial, and that count is on the face. ASCEND (1,392 randomised) was terminated prematurely after a median follow-up of only 4 months because of an excess of cardiovascular events on avosentan; no difference in the primary composite of doubling of serum creatinine, ESRD or death was detected in that truncated follow-up. The albuminuria reduction (median albumin-to-creatinine-ratio reductions of 44.3% and 49.3% relative on 25 mg and 50 mg versus 9.7% on placebo — relative changes) never translated into a detectable progression benefit, and it must not be read as kidney protection. The post-hoc ASCEND analysis quantifies the harm: avosentan increased congestive heart failure risk versus placebo (hazard ratio 2.76, 95% CI 1.68 to 4.54), with fluid overload and heart failure dominating the excess discontinuations (19.6% and 18.2% versus 11.5%). A fourth card — the programme's earlier 12-week dose-ranging albuminuria trial (286 patients) — is labelled programme support only: it tested a surrogate over 12 weeks, is not a progression report, and is not counted in the 2-report progression base. Avosentan was never marketed.
stamp: LIKELY (harm) — FLOOR-RISK, exactly 2 reports / 1 trial for the progression question: ASCEND (1,392 randomised) was terminated early (median follow-up 4 months) for excess cardiovascular events, detected no progression benefit, and its post-hoc analysis gives a heart-failure hazard ratio of 2.76 (95% CI 1.68 to 4.54); the albuminuria reduction is a surrogate that never translated, and a labelled 12-week dose-ranging albuminuria trial is programme support only, not counted in the base

title: Beinaglutide for weight (FLOOR-RISK — exactly 2 randomised reports, China only): −6.0% vs −2.4% vs placebo at 16 weeks; thrice-daily dosing; no randomised diabetes anchor
question: In Chinese adults with overweight or obesity, with or without type 2 diabetes, does the thrice-daily GLP-1 receptor agonist beinaglutide, compared with placebo or metformin, reduce body weight?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — FLOOR-RISK: the randomised report count is exactly 2, and that count is on the face. Both randomised trials are short (16 and 12 weeks), both are from China (where beinaglutide is approved; it is not FDA/EMA-approved — single-region flag), and both enrolled NON-diabetic people with overweight or obesity: the phase 3 trial (427 randomised) found mean weight change of −6.0% on beinaglutide 0.2 mg thrice daily versus −2.4% on placebo (difference −3.6%), and the metformin comparison (78 randomised, 64 completed) found 9.5% versus 5.1% weight loss. The type 2 diabetes weight claim has NO randomised anchor in this base — the diabetes reports are single-arm, are carded here as one labelled programme-support card only, and are explicitly not counted. Thrice-daily dosing is itself part of the answer: every other GLP-1 shelf in this library concerns an agent dosed daily or less often. Nausea was frequent (49.3% versus 7.1% on placebo) and adverse-event discontinuation was 5.9% versus 0.7%.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — FLOOR-RISK, exactly 2 randomised reports (single-arm reports explicitly not counted), single-region China evidence: beinaglutide thrice daily beat placebo (−6.0% vs −2.4% at 16 weeks, 427 randomised) and metformin (9.5% vs 5.1% at 12 weeks, 78 randomised) for weight loss in non-diabetic overweight/obesity; no randomised anchor exists in type 2 diabetes, and nausea occurred in 49.3% versus 7.1%

title: Procaterol in asthma (bronchodilator programme, Japan/Asia licensing): matched albuterol over 12 weeks with longer action; matched nebulised salbutamol in acute asthma; cough benefit added to budesonide
question: In patients with asthma, does procaterol — oral, inhaled or nebulised — versus placebo or another short-acting beta-2 agonist improve lung function and symptoms, in chronic use, in moderate acute asthma, and as an adjunct in cough-variant asthma?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit — bronchodilation only): this is a bronchodilator programme, not an outcomes programme, and it is presented as such. The load-bearing reports are three: a 333-patient 12-week double-blind trial in which procaterol aerosol matched albuterol aerosol on FEV1 with a longer duration of action (effect maintained 4–7 hours versus 3–6 hours, and more patients controlled three times daily); a 140-patient emergency-department trial in moderate acute asthma in which nebulised procaterol matched nebulised salbutamol on peak flow and asthma score; and a 159-patient 8-week trial in cough-variant asthma in which procaterol added to inhaled budesonide improved cough scores more than budesonide plus placebo — a combination (adjunct) limb, labelled as such. The remaining three cards are small or short pharmacodynamic crossovers (n=20, n=20, and one whose fetched abstract states no N — printed as 'N not documented'), labelled and never load-bearing. Endpoints throughout are FEV1/PEF, symptom and cough scores over single doses to 12 weeks; there is no exacerbation, hospitalisation or mortality trial. Procaterol is licensed in Japan and parts of Asia, not in the US/UK.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit — bronchodilation and symptom scores only; no outcomes trial) — procaterol matched albuterol over 12 weeks (333 patients, longer duration of action), matched nebulised salbutamol in moderate acute asthma (140 patients), and improved cough scores as an adjunct to budesonide in cough-variant asthma (159 patients, combination limb); the three remaining reports are small/short pharmacodynamic studies (n=20, n=20, N not documented), labelled and never load-bearing

title: Aerosolised ribavirin in infant RSV (SPLIT, small old programme): positive in 1983/1991, negative in ventilated infants in 1994/1999; 2004 Cochrane non-significant — 2010 version withdrawn and fenced
question: In infants and young children hospitalised with RSV lower respiratory tract infection — spontaneously breathing and mechanically ventilated — does aerosolised ribavirin versus placebo improve illness severity, oxygenation, duration of ventilation, hospital stay and survival?
balance: SPLIT — the split leads, and this shelf must not be averaged into a benefit claim. The programme is small and old: every primary trial enrolled 28–41 infants. The two earliest trials were positive — spontaneously breathing infants improved faster on ribavirin (1983, n=33), and ventilated infants spent fewer days on ventilation (4.9 versus 9.9), oxygen and in hospital (1991, n=28). The two later ventilated-infant trials were NEGATIVE: no significant difference in ventilator, oxygen, ICU or hospital days in 1994 (n=41) or in 1999 (n=41 analysed). The cardable synthesis — the 2004 Cochrane version — found mortality of 5.8% on ribavirin versus 9.7% on placebo across 4 trials and 158 patients (odds ratio 0.58, 95% CI 0.18 to 1.85 — non-significant, wide intervals) and concluded the trials lack sufficient power. FENCE: the 2010 Cochrane update of this review (PMID 20464715) is typed WITHDRAWN and is fenced — it is named here only as fenced and is never carded. This is a pre-palivizumab/nirsevimab-era treatment question; aerosol administration carried occupational-exposure concerns and high cost in its era. It does not bear on the RSV prevention shelves.
stamp: SPLIT — the two earliest, smallest trials were positive (1983, n=33, spontaneously breathing; 1991, n=28, ventilated: 4.9 vs 9.9 ventilation days) and the two later ventilated-infant trials were negative (1994 and 1999, n=41 each, no significant difference); the 2004 Cochrane review's mortality estimate is non-significant (5.8% vs 9.7%; odds ratio 0.58, 95% CI 0.18 to 1.85, labelled relative) and its authors concluded the trials lack sufficient power. The 2010 Cochrane update is WITHDRAWN and fenced, named on the Synthesis card only

title: Teprenone for gastric mucosal protection (one drug, three names — teprenone = geranylgeranylacetone = tetraprenylacetone): less NSAID/aspirin mucosal injury and fewer recurrences as an adjunct; endoscopic endpoints only
question: In adults with gastric mucosal injury — NSAID- or low-dose-aspirin-associated injury, active gastric ulcer, gastritis with erosions, and healed ulcer at risk of recurrence — does teprenone, alone or added to acid suppression, versus control improve endoscopic injury, ulcer healing and recurrence?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit — endoscopic endpoints only), on an adjunct-and-prevention programme whose limbs are labelled and never pooled. IDENTITY, stated on the face: teprenone, geranylgeranylacetone (GGA) and tetraprenylacetone (TAP) are the SAME drug under three names in these publications — the five reports are not three drugs. No report tests teprenone as sole ulcer therapy against placebo. The prevention limbs: in long-term NSAID users (158 randomised), Lanza scores and dyspeptic symptom scores fell on teprenone and rose on control over 12 weeks; in low-dose-aspirin prevention (130 patients), gastric mucosal injury occurred in 13.38% on teprenone versus 40.0% on placebo — with NO ulcers in either arm, so that trial's endpoint is mucosal injury, not ulcer. The adjunct limbs: added to cimetidine, 4-week ulcer healing was 72.4% versus 52.1% (converging by 8 weeks); added to omeprazole, 12-week healing was similar but recurrence within 12 months was significantly less frequent; and as a sole-agent comparison in gastritis, geranylgeranylacetone beat cimetidine on endoscopic improvement (86.0% versus 64.8%). Endoscopic surrogate endpoints throughout; no bleeding or perforation outcome trial. An East Asian programme (China and Japan, with the aspirin trial from the same regional literature) — single-region flag on the face; the 1996 healing report is in a Chinese-language journal with an English abstract.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit — endoscopic endpoints only; adjunct-and-prevention limbs, never pooled) — teprenone (= geranylgeranylacetone = tetraprenylacetone, one drug) reduced NSAID and low-dose-aspirin mucosal injury (13.38% vs 40.0% on aspirin, with no ulcers in either arm), sped early healing and reduced recurrence as an adjunct to acid suppression, and beat cimetidine endoscopically in gastritis without a significant symptom advantage; no bleeding/perforation outcome trial and no sole-therapy placebo-controlled healing trial exists

title: Polaprezinc in gastric ulcer: spontaneous-ulcer trial NOT significant vs rebamipide (81.5% vs 74.3%); post-ESD, added to a PPI it cut ulcer-base protrusion (1.3% vs 20.7%) — two limbs, never pooled
question: In adults with gastric ulcer, does polaprezinc (zinc-L-carnosine) heal spontaneous ulcers versus rebamipide, and — added to a proton pump inhibitor after endoscopic submucosal dissection (ESD) — does it improve healing of the artificial ulcer versus PPI alone or versus rebamipide + PPI?
balance: SPLIT — the two limbs point differently and are never pooled. Spontaneous gastric ulcer: one double-blind trial (224 patients) found polaprezinc's 8-week endoscopic effective rate 81.48% versus 74.31% on rebamipide, NOT significant (P=0.1557). Post-ESD artificial ulcer: two trials — lansoprazole + polaprezinc cut ulcer-base protrusion versus lansoprazole alone (1.3% [1/77] vs 20.7% [16/77], P=0.0001, with better healing), and polaprezinc + pantoprazole was non-inferior to rebamipide + pantoprazole for 4-week healing (90.3% vs 91.4%). No placebo-controlled healing trial exists; the programme is Japanese/Chinese (single-region flag). Polaprezinc is the zinc-L-carnosine chelate as the publications name it.
stamp: SPLIT — spontaneous-ulcer limb non-significant versus rebamipide (81.48% vs 74.31%, P=0.1557, one trial); post-ESD limb positive on a healing-quality endpoint versus PPI alone (protrusion 1.3% vs 20.7%) and non-inferior versus rebamipide + PPI — limbs labelled, never pooled, no placebo-controlled healing trial

title: Thymosin alpha-1 in chronic hepatitis B: the phase III double-blind trial was NEGATIVE (14% vs 4%, P=0.084) — positive readings come only from an untreated-control trial and an uncontrolled dose comparison
question: In patients with chronic hepatitis B, does thymosin alpha-1 (thymalfasin) versus placebo, no treatment or a lower dose improve HBV-DNA and HBeAg clearance, ALT normalisation and histology?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — and the failure leads: the programme's one phase III double-blind placebo-controlled trial (97 patients) did NOT confirm efficacy (complete response 14% vs 4% on placebo, P=0.084; 25% vs 13% including delayed responses, P<0.11). The positive readings come from an untreated-control trial (98 patients; complete virological response 40.6% [26 weeks] and 26.5% [52 weeks] vs 9.4% at 18 months, separating only after treatment ended) and a 316-patient dose comparison with no untreated control arm. A 12-patient mixed-preparation pilot is labelled sub-floor and never load-bearing. Pre-nucleos(t)ide-era evidence (1991–2005) — not a comparison against entecavir/tenofovir.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the phase III double-blind placebo-controlled trial was negative (14% vs 4%, P=0.084); positive readings rest on an untreated-control trial and an uncontrolled dose comparison, with a sub-floor n=12 mixed-preparation pilot labelled never load-bearing; pre-nucleos(t)ide era

title: PCP primary prophylaxis in HIV (pre-HAART): regimens close on PCP, split on toxoplasmosis and toxicity — pentamidine protects the lung only, dapsone-pyrimethamine stopped for toxicity 42 vs 3
question: In HIV-infected patients with CD4 counts below 200–250/mm3 and no prior Pneumocystis pneumonia, do dapsone (± pyrimethamine) or aerosolised pentamidine, versus co-trimoxazole (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole) or each other, prevent first episodes of Pneumocystis pneumonia and toxoplasmosis, and at what cost in toxicity and discontinuation?
balance: SPLIT — a trade-off, not a ranking, in pre-HAART HIV care (1993–1995; era flag load-bearing). For PCP the regimens were close: per-year rates 3% on co-trimoxazole, 5.6% on aerosolised pentamidine and 8.3% on dapsone + pyrimethamine (not significant); PRIO found 10 PCP cases per group (adjusted relative risk 1.13); intermittent co-trimoxazole beat dapsone-pyrimethamine head-to-head (0 of 104 evaluable vs 6.3%). The deciding split is toxoplasmosis versus toxicity: aerosolised pentamidine protects the lung only (toxoplasmosis adjusted relative risk 1.81 vs dapsone-pyrimethamine), while dapsone-pyrimethamine had by far the most toxicity discontinuations (42 vs 3 in PRIO). Open-label designs throughout.
stamp: SPLIT — PCP prevention broadly similar across co-trimoxazole, dapsone-based regimens and aerosolised pentamidine, but pentamidine leaves toxoplasmosis uncovered (adjusted relative risk 1.81) and dapsone-pyrimethamine carries the heaviest toxicity discontinuations (42 vs 3); pre-HAART era flag on the face

title: Atovaquone for PCP in AIDS: treatment — less effective than co-trimoxazole (non-response 20% vs 7%; deaths 11 vs 1) but gentler; prophylaxis in sulfa-intolerant patients — similar to dapsone and pentamidine
question: In patients with AIDS and mild-to-moderate Pneumocystis pneumonia, does oral atovaquone versus co-trimoxazole or intravenous pentamidine achieve treatment success — and in HIV-infected patients intolerant of trimethoprim/sulfonamides, does atovaquone versus dapsone or aerosolised pentamidine prevent Pneumocystis pneumonia?
balance: SPLIT — two limbs, never pooled, pre-/early-HAART era. Treatment (mild-to-moderate PCP only; no severe-PCP evidence): atovaquone was less effective than co-trimoxazole — non-response 20% vs 7% (P=0.002) and 11 vs 1 deaths within four weeks of treatment (P=0.003), the death split printed on the face — but had fewer treatment-limiting adverse effects (7% vs 20%); versus intravenous pentamidine the small trial split (success 57% vs 40%, non-response 29% vs 17%, discontinuations 4% vs 36%). Prophylaxis in sulfa-intolerant patients: atovaquone similar to dapsone (15.7 vs 18.4 per 100 person-years; relative risk 0.85) and to aerosolised pentamidine, at the 1500-mg suspension dose.
stamp: SPLIT — treatment limb: less effective than co-trimoxazole (non-response 20% vs 7%; deaths 11 vs 1) but fewer treatment-limiting adverse effects, mild-to-moderate disease only; prophylaxis-in-intolerance limb: similar to dapsone and aerosolised pentamidine at 1500 mg; limbs never pooled, pre-HAART era

title: Intravitreal fomivirsen for CMV retinitis in AIDS (one programme, three reports): immediate treatment delayed progression 71 vs 13 days in a 28-patient trial; schedules did not differ; drug since withdrawn
question: In patients with AIDS and cytomegalovirus retinitis, does intravitreal fomivirsen versus deferred treatment delay retinitis progression in newly diagnosed peripheral disease, do dosing schedules differ in reactivated or persistently active disease, and what are its ocular toxicities?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one programme, labelled: three reports of a single development programme (Vitravene), not independent trials. Immediate fomivirsen delayed progression versus deferred treatment in newly diagnosed peripheral CMV retinitis (median 71 vs 13 days, P=.0001) but in only 28 patients; in reactivated/persistently active disease a more-intense schedule did not beat a less-intense one (106 vs 267 days, P=.2179). Pooled safety (150 patients): ocular adverse events dose- and schedule-dependent (4.06–8.35 events/patient-year), chiefly anterior-chamber inflammation and raised intraocular pressure. Era flag load-bearing: pre-/early-HAART AIDS care; fomivirsen has since been withdrawn from the market.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single programme, labelled: immediate fomivirsen delayed CMV retinitis progression vs deferral (71 vs 13 days) in a 28-patient trial; dose schedules did not differ; pooled safety report is a programme report, not independent evidence; pre-HAART era, drug since withdrawn

title: Adjuvant trastuzumab vs observation in HER2-positive early breast cancer (HERA / B-31+N9831): DFS and survival improved — the founding benefit; duration (6 vs 12 months) is shelf #760
question: In women with HER2-positive early breast cancer who have completed locoregional therapy and adjuvant chemotherapy, does adding one year of trastuzumab improve disease-free and overall survival versus observation alone?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — PARTIAL beside shelf #760: this shelf cards only trastuzumab versus OBSERVATION; duration (6 vs 12 months) lives on #760 and is cross-pointed, not re-carded. Two programmes, two designs, never pooled. HERA (sequential, after chemotherapy): DFS hazard ratio 0.54 (relative) with an absolute 2-year DFS benefit of 8.4 percentage points; death hazard ratio 0.66 at 2 years and 0.74 at 11 years (relative), 10-year DFS 69% vs 63%, despite 52% selective crossover from observation. NSABP B-31 / NCCTG N9831 joint analysis (concurrent with paclitaxel): a 39% relative reduction in the death rate. Pricing harm: cardiotoxicity (severe 0.5% in HERA's primary report; secondary cardiac endpoints 4.4% vs 0.9% at 11 years).
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — adjuvant trastuzumab vs observation improved disease-free survival in HERA (HR 0.54 relative; absolute 2-year benefit 8.4 points) and overall survival at 2 and 11 years (HR 0.66 and 0.74, relative), with a concordant 39% relative death-rate reduction in the B-31/N9831 joint analysis; cardiotoxicity on the face; PARTIAL beside the duration shelf #760, vs-observation slice only

title: Adjuvant aromatase inhibitor vs tamoxifen (ATAC / BIG 1-98 / IES): disease-free survival improved across upfront and switch strategies; no survival advantage shown; harm trade is the teaching content
question: In postmenopausal women with hormone-receptor-positive early breast cancer, does an aromatase inhibitor — anastrozole (ATAC) or letrozole (BIG 1-98) upfront, or a switch to exemestane after 2–3 years of tamoxifen (IES) — improve disease-free survival versus tamoxifen, and with what harm trade?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — for disease-free survival, across three trials and three labelled strategies (never pooled): upfront anastrozole (ATAC: DFS hazard ratio 0.83 at 3 years, 0.86 at 10 years in hormone-receptor-positive patients, both relative; absolute recurrence difference 4.3% at 10 years), upfront letrozole (BIG 1-98: 5-year DFS 84.0% vs 81.4%; hazard ratio 0.81, relative) and switching to exemestane after 2–3 years of tamoxifen (IES: hazard ratio 0.68, relative; absolute benefit 4.7 points at 3 years). No overall-survival advantage was shown (ATAC mortality HR 0.95; IES deaths 93 vs 106, not significant). ATAC's combination arm was null (HR 1.02) and is on the face. Harm trade: fractures and arthralgia on aromatase inhibitors against endometrial cancer and thromboembolism on tamoxifen.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — aromatase inhibitors improved disease-free survival versus tamoxifen in three trials across upfront and switch strategies (DFS hazard ratios 0.68–0.87, relative, with absolute benefits printed), with no demonstrated overall-survival advantage; harm trade (fractures/arthralgia vs endometrial cancer/thromboembolism) and the null ATAC combination arm on the face

title: Adjuvant FOLFOX vs FL in stage II–III colon cancer (MOSAIC — one trial, three reports): survival improved, driven by stage III; stage II null (HR 1.00); neuropathy is the price
question: In patients with resected stage II or III colon cancer, does adding oxaliplatin to fluorouracil–leucovorin (FOLFOX4) improve disease-free and overall survival versus fluorouracil–leucovorin alone, and does the benefit reach stage II disease?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — in stage III disease; ONE trial (MOSAIC, 2,246 patients) reported three times, labelled as a single programme. FOLFOX4 improved disease-free survival versus FL (3-year 78.2% vs 72.9%; recurrence hazard ratio 0.77, relative) and overall survival overall (10-year 71.7% vs 67.1%; hazard ratio 0.85, relative), driven by stage III (hazard ratio 0.80). title: Cetuximab + first-line chemotherapy in mCRC (CRYSTAL / OPUS): small overall PFS gain, survival null — the entire benefit lives in RAS wild-type tumours
question: In patients with metastatic colorectal cancer, does adding cetuximab to first-line FOLFIRI (CRYSTAL) or FOLFOX-4 (OPUS) improve progression-free survival and response — and is the benefit confined to RAS wild-type tumours?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit, confined to RAS wild-type tumours) — a biomarker-selection shelf. CRYSTAL (1,198 patients): cetuximab + FOLFIRI gave a small relative PFS gain overall (hazard ratio 0.85) and NO significant overall-survival benefit (hazard ratio 0.93) — both on the face. In KRAS wild-type tumours the PFS hazard ratio was 0.68 (relative); the extended-RAS reanalysis found benefit across all endpoints in fully RAS wild-type tumours and none in RAS-mutant tumours (14.7% of KRAS exon-2 wild-type tumours carried another RAS mutation). OPUS (phase 2) concurs in KRAS wild-type disease (PFS hazard ratio 0.567, relative). Price: grade 3 skin reactions 19.7% vs 0.2%, more diarrhoea.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit, confined to RAS wild-type tumours) — CRYSTAL's overall PFS effect was small (HR 0.85 relative) and overall survival null (HR 0.93); benefit across endpoints in fully RAS wild-type tumours and none in RAS-mutant tumours, with OPUS concordant; skin toxicity on the face

title: First-generation EGFR TKIs vs platinum chemotherapy in EGFR-mutant NSCLC (IPASS / NEJ002 / WJTOG3405 / OPTIMAL / EURTAC / ENSURE): PFS roughly doubled in all six trials; overall survival NOT improved; mutation-negative harm in IPASS
question: In patients with advanced EGFR-mutation-positive non-small-cell lung cancer, does first-line gefitinib or erlotinib prolong progression-free survival versus platinum-doublet chemotherapy — and does it prolong overall survival?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — for progression-free survival: six trials, two agents (gefitinib: IPASS, NEJ002, WJTOG3405; erlotinib: OPTIMAL, EURTAC, ENSURE), labelled by agent, never pooled, consistently showed large relative PFS gains versus platinum chemotherapy (hazard ratios 0.16–0.49 in mutation-confirmed populations; median PFS roughly doubled) with less grade 3/4 toxicity. NO overall-survival benefit was demonstrated (NEJ002 P=.31; ENSURE hazard ratio 0.91, not significant) in crossover-era trials. IPASS's mutation-negative harm signal (hazard ratio 2.85, relative) is on the face — it is why testing precedes treatment. Gefitinib interstitial-lung-disease deaths are printed on the relevant cards.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit, for progression-free survival; no overall-survival benefit demonstrated) — six trials of gefitinib or erlotinib vs platinum chemotherapy in EGFR-mutant NSCLC consistently doubled median PFS (HRs 0.16–0.49, relative) with less severe toxicity, while survival was not significantly improved (NEJ002 P=.31; ENSURE HR 0.91); IPASS mutation-negative harm (HR 2.85) on the face

title: Pemetrexed in advanced NSCLC: non-inferior first-line with a histology reversal (squamous disease favoured gemcitabine), and maintenance prolonged survival in JMEN and PARAMOUNT
question: In advanced non-small-cell lung cancer, is cisplatin–pemetrexed non-inferior to cisplatin–gemcitabine first-line with a histology-dependent advantage (JMDB) — and does pemetrexed maintenance after platinum induction prolong survival (JMEN, PARAMOUNT)?
balance: LIKELY (benefit), in two labelled limbs that are never pooled. First-line (JMDB, 1,725 randomised): cisplatin–pemetrexed was non-inferior to cisplatin–gemcitabine overall (median OS 10.3 vs 10.3 months, HR 0.94) with less haematologic toxicity — but histology reversed the direction: adenocarcinoma favoured pemetrexed (12.6 vs 10.9 months) while squamous histology favoured gemcitabine (10.8 vs 9.4 months). Maintenance (JMEN, 663 non-progressors after platinum induction; PARAMOUNT, 539 nonsquamous non-progressors after pemetrexed–cisplatin induction): pemetrexed prolonged overall survival in both trials (13.4 vs 10.6 months, HR 0.79; and 13.9 vs 11.0 months, HR 0.78 — both relative measures, absolute median gains 2.8 and 2.9 months), at the cost of more grade 3–4 fatigue, neutropenia and anaemia. The maintenance benefit applies only to patients whose disease did not progress on induction.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — cisplatin–pemetrexed is non-inferior first-line with a histology interaction favouring pemetrexed in nonsquamous and gemcitabine in squamous disease (JMDB), and pemetrexed maintenance after induction prolonged overall survival in two randomised trials (JMEN HR 0.79; PARAMOUNT HR 0.78, relative measures with ~3-month absolute median gains), in non-progressors only

title: Adjuvant cisplatin chemotherapy in resected NSCLC: survival benefit in stage II–III (IALT, ANITA, LACE) — none shown in stage IB, harm trend in stage IA
question: In patients with completely resected non-small-cell lung cancer, does adjuvant cisplatin-based chemotherapy improve overall survival versus observation, and in which stages (IALT / ANITA / LACE)?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) in stage II–III, not shown in stage I. IALT (1,867 randomised): 5-year survival 44.5% vs 40.4% with cisplatin-based adjuvant chemotherapy (death HR 0.86, relative; absolute gain 4.1 points). ANITA (840 randomised, vinorelbine–cisplatin): median survival 65.7 vs 43.7 months (adjusted HR 0.80, relative; 5-year advantage 8.6 points). The LACE pooled individual-patient analysis (4,584 patients, including IALT and ANITA — labelled, not independent) gave HR 0.89 and a 5.4-point absolute 5-year benefit, varying by stage: IA HR 1.40 (harm trend), IB 0.93, II 0.83, III 0.83. Toxic deaths were 0.8% in IALT and 2% in ANITA, with neutropenia in 92% of ANITA's treated patients.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) in stage II–III resected NSCLC — adjuvant cisplatin-based chemotherapy improved survival in IALT (5-year 44.5% vs 40.4%, HR 0.86) and ANITA (HR 0.80), with LACE's pooled HR 0.89 and 5.4-point absolute 5-year benefit; no benefit shown in stage IB and a harm trend in stage IA (HR 1.40), against ~1–2% toxic deaths (all hazard ratios are relative measures)

title: Lenalidomide-based first-line myeloma therapy: continuous Rd beat MPT (FIRST) and VRd beat Rd (SWOG S0777)
question: In patients with newly diagnosed multiple myeloma not planned for immediate autologous transplant, does continuous lenalidomide–dexamethasone beat melphalan–prednisone–thalidomide (FIRST) — and does adding bortezomib to lenalidomide–dexamethasone improve outcomes further (SWOG S0777)?
balance: LIKELY (benefit), as a two-rung ladder from two trials (four reports, each trial's follow-up labelled as the same trial). FIRST (1,623 transplant-ineligible patients): continuous lenalidomide–dexamethasone beat melphalan–prednisone–thalidomide — final-analysis median OS 59.1 vs 49.1 months (HR 0.78, relative), with fewer haematologic and neurologic events but more infections than MPT, and grade 3/4 events in 70% vs 78%. SWOG S0777 (525 patients without intent for immediate transplant): adding bortezomib (VRd) beat Rd — median PFS 43 vs 30 months (HR 0.712) and median OS 75 vs 64 months (HR 0.709), persisting at 84 months (HR 0.709; median OS not reached vs 69 months) — all hazard ratios are relative measures. The cost of VRd was more grade ≥3 events (82% vs 75%) and more discontinuations (23% vs 10%).
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — continuous lenalidomide–dexamethasone beat MPT in transplant-ineligible newly diagnosed myeloma (FIRST final median OS 59.1 vs 49.1 months, HR 0.78) and adding bortezomib to Rd improved survival further (SWOG S0777 HR 0.709), two trials with their follow-up reports labelled as the same trials (hazard ratios are relative measures)

title: Bortezomib plus melphalan–prednisone in transplant-ineligible myeloma (VISTA, one trial / three reports): longer progression-free and overall survival, neuropathy in 47% that mostly reversed
question: In patients with previously untreated multiple myeloma ineligible for high-dose therapy, does adding bortezomib to melphalan–prednisone prolong time to progression and overall survival, and at what neuropathy cost (VISTA)?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — on ONE trial (VISTA, 682 randomised) reported three times, each report labelled as the same trial. VMP beat melphalan–prednisone on time to progression (24.0 vs 16.6 months, HR 0.48) and, at updated follow-up (median 36.7 months), on survival: HR 0.653 — a 35% relative reduction in the risk of death — with 3-year OS 68.5% vs 54.0% (absolute rates) and median OS not reached vs 43 months. Complete responses were 30% vs 4%. The pricing harm is peripheral neuropathy: 47% on VMP (13% grade ≥3), dose-related with a plateau at ~45 mg/m² cumulative dose, but 79% of events improved within a median 1.9 months and 60% resolved completely within 5.7 months; grade 3 events overall were 53% vs 44% with no excess of grade 4 events or treatment-related deaths.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — one trial, three labelled reports: VISTA showed bortezomib plus melphalan–prednisone prolonged time to progression (HR 0.48) and survival (updated HR 0.653, a 35% relative reduction in the risk of death; 3-year OS 68.5% vs 54.0%) versus melphalan–prednisone in transplant-ineligible myeloma, with peripheral neuropathy in 47% that plateaued at ~45 mg/m² and mostly reversed (hazard ratios are relative measures)

title: Adjunctive levetiracetam in refractory partial seizures: responder rates roughly tripled versus placebo with a dose gradient, in three randomised trials
question: In patients with refractory partial seizures, does adjunctive levetiracetam (1,000–3,000 mg/day) reduce seizure frequency versus placebo, and can responders convert to levetiracetam monotherapy?
balance: LIKELY (benefit). Three randomised placebo-controlled trials of adjunctive levetiracetam in refractory partial seizures agree, with a dose gradient: ≥50% responder rates 22.8% (1,000 mg/day, European trial) and 33.0% (1,000 mg/day, Cereghino) rising to 31.6% (2,000 mg/day) and 39.8% (3,000 mg/day), versus 10.4–10.8% on placebo (absolute rates). In Cereghino, 11 levetiracetam patients became seizure-free and no placebo patient did. Harms are modest: asthenia, somnolence and dizziness, with overall adverse-event incidence no different from placebo in the European trial (73.2%). The third report (Ben-Menachem) is a labelled responder-selected design: its monotherapy conversion figures (59.2% responder rate, 18.4% seizure-free) describe only patients who had already responded to add-on levetiracetam, never unselected patients.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — adjunctive levetiracetam reduced refractory partial seizures in three randomised trials with a dose gradient (≥50% responder rates 22.8–33.0% at 1,000 mg/day and 31.6–39.8% at 2,000–3,000 mg/day vs 10.4–10.8% on placebo), with modest harms; the monotherapy-conversion report is labelled responder-selected

title: Adjunctive lamotrigine in refractory partial seizures: modest benefit, significant only at 500 mg/day in the one parallel-group trial, with two small labelled crossovers
question: In patients with partial seizures refractory to established antiseizure drugs, does adjunctive lamotrigine reduce seizure frequency versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). One parallel-group randomised trial carries the weight (Matsuo, n=216): adjunctive lamotrigine reduced median seizure frequency by 36% at 500 mg/day versus 8% on placebo, with one-third of the 500-mg group achieving ≥50% reduction — but the 300-mg dose was not significant. Two labelled crossover companions point the same way: Smith (n=81) found a 29.7% relative reduction in total seizures yet only 11 patients halved their seizures, and Schapel (n=41 — small, labelled) found 22% versus 0% achieving ≥50% reduction. Harms in the trials were mostly minor, with 9% withdrawing for adverse experiences in Matsuo; none of the carded records quantifies lamotrigine's serious-rash titration risk, which is a label matter outside this evidence base.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — adjunctive lamotrigine reduced refractory partial seizures in one parallel-group trial significant only at 500 mg/day (Matsuo, n=216), supported by two labelled crossover companions (Smith n=81; Schapel n=41, small and labelled); a real but modest effect at adequate dose

title: Gabapentin for neuropathic pain: modest benefit in postherpetic neuralgia (two trials) and painful diabetic neuropathy (one trial) — limbs labelled, never pooled
question: In adults with postherpetic neuralgia or painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy, does gabapentin (titrated to up to 3,600 mg/day) reduce daily pain versus placebo, and at what dizziness/somnolence cost?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — real but modest, in two labelled indication limbs that are never pooled. Postherpetic neuralgia (two trials, 229 and 334 randomised): gabapentin reduced daily pain 6.3→4.2 versus 6.5→6.0 on placebo (Rowbotham) and improved pain scores by −34.5%/−34.4% at 1,800/2,400 mg versus −15.7% on placebo, a difference of about 18.8 percentage points (Rice & Maton). Painful diabetic neuropathy (one trial, 165 randomised): end-point pain 3.9 versus 5.1 (Backonja). In absolute terms the advantage is about 1–2 points on an 11-point scale beyond placebo. The consistent price is dizziness and somnolence — 24% and 23% versus 4.9% and 6% in the diabetic-neuropathy trial — concentrated in titration and most consequential in the elderly PHN population.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — gabapentin reduced pain versus placebo in postherpetic neuralgia (two trials) and in painful diabetic neuropathy (one trial), labelled as separate limbs and never pooled; the absolute advantage is a modest ~1–2 points on an 11-point scale, bought with dizziness and somnolence in roughly a fifth to a quarter of patients

title: Modafinil for excessive daytime sleepiness in narcolepsy: wakefulness improved in three randomised reports, including a labelled withdrawal trial
question: In patients with narcolepsy, does modafinil (200–400 mg/day) improve objective and subjective daytime sleepiness versus placebo, and does the benefit persist under randomised withdrawal?
balance: LIKELY (benefit). Three randomised reports with three labelled designs agree. Broughton (75 patients, crossover): modafinil 200 and 400 mg increased Maintenance of Wakefulness Test sleep latency by 40% and 54% versus placebo (relative measures), reduced Epworth scores equally at both doses, and did not disturb nocturnal sleep; nausea and nervousness increased only at 400 mg. The U.S. multicentre trial (283 randomised, 9 weeks): modafinil significantly reduced every subjective and objective sleepiness measure and improved global impression, with few, dose-dependent, mostly mild-to-moderate adverse experiences. Moldofsky (labelled randomised withdrawal after 16 weeks open-label): continuing modafinil held MWT latency at 16.4 versus 9.7 minutes and Epworth at 13.2 versus 15.4 versus switching to placebo — evidence the benefit persists on treatment and is lost on stopping, not a fresh placebo contrast.

title: Sumatriptan for acute migraine: subcutaneous relief at 1 hour and oral relief at 2 hours, with no gain above 100 mg orally
question: In adults treating an acute migraine attack, does sumatriptan — 6 mg subcutaneously or 100 mg orally — relieve headache and associated symptoms versus placebo, and what does the dose–response look like?
balance: LIKELY (benefit), by both routes, carded as labelled limbs. Subcutaneous 6 mg (two trials, 1,104 randomised): at 1 hour, headache reduced to mild/none in 70% versus 22% and complete relief in 49% versus 9% (absolute rates), with tingling, dizziness, warm/hot sensations and injection-site reactions, and no statistical evidence that a second injection adds benefit. Oral (1,130 patients): 2-hour response 67% at 100 mg, 73% at 200 mg and 67% at 300 mg versus 27% on placebo, while adverse events rose with dose (36%, 47%, 53% vs 17%) — no efficacy gain above 100 mg. The labelled Ferrari meta-analysis (53 triptan trials, 24,089 patients) gives class context: sumatriptan 100 mg response 59%, pain-free 29%, sustained pain-free 20%, with placebo-subtracted chest adverse events of 1.9%.

title: NEWS/NEWS2 discrimination for 24-hour death, arrest or ICU admission: AUROCs 0.72–0.89, best or joint-best in 120 of 123 diagnostic groups, confirmed in an independent Finnish cohort
question: On general wards and in acute medical admissions, how well does the National Early Warning Score (NEWS, and its NEWS2 revision) discriminate patients who will die, suffer cardiac arrest or need unanticipated intensive-care admission within 24 hours, how does it compare with other early warning scores, and does its performance hold across diagnostic groups and in COVID-19?
balance: LIKELY (predictive) — a predictive-performance balance, not a treatment effect. NEWS discriminated patients who would die, arrest or need unanticipated ICU admission within 24 hours with AUROCs of 0.894 (death), 0.857 (ICU admission), 0.722 (cardiac arrest) and 0.873 (combined) in the original database study, above all 33 comparator scores; NEWS2 was best or joint-best in 120 of 123 diagnostic groups against 36 other scores; and the independent Finnish prospective ward cohort (18,889 patients) found AUROC 0.91 for 1-day mortality but only 0.75 for 30-day mortality, with respiratory rate the strongest single component. Performance held in COVID-19 (AUROC 0.882, within the 0.842–0.894 range of the control cohorts). Three of the four reports share the Smith group's Portsmouth database lineage and are labelled as one data programme; the Finnish cohort is the independent limb. No report here shows that using the score changes outcomes.
stamp: LIKELY (predictive) — NEWS/NEWS2 showed good discrimination for death, cardiac arrest or unanticipated ICU admission within 24 hours (AUROCs 0.72–0.89; 0.91 for 1-day mortality in the independent Finnish cohort), best or joint-best in 120 of 123 diagnostic groups and undiminished in COVID-19; this is predictive performance only — no evidence here that using the score improves outcomes — and three of four reports share the Smith-group database lineage, labelled

title: ARISCAT score: excellent at derivation (AUROC 0.88–0.90), good in emergency abdominal surgery (0.83), poor in lung resection (0.60) — accuracy is field-dependent
question: Before surgery, how well does the ARISCAT score (preoperative oxygen saturation, recent respiratory infection, age, preoperative anaemia, incision site, duration and emergency status) predict postoperative pulmonary complications, how does it calibrate and discriminate outside its derivation population — emergency abdominal, lung-resection and other fields — and how does it compare with the other published pulmonary-complication prediction models?
balance: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — field-dependent, and that dependence is the answer. At derivation in a broad surgical population (2,464 patients, 59 hospitals) the ARISCAT score discriminated excellently (AUROC 0.90 development, 0.88 validation). In prospective external validation in major emergency abdominal surgery it held up well (AUC 0.83, observed complications 36.1% vs 24.9% predicted — good discrimination with under-prediction of absolute risk). In lung resection it performed poorly (c-index 0.60), as did every comparator score in that field (LAS VEGAS 0.68, SPORC 0.63, CARDOT 0.64). Across 116 published pulmonary-complication models, the 2025 meta-analysis gives ARISCAT a summary c-statistic of 0.76 (95% CI 0.67 to 0.86). The derivation AUROC must never be printed as the score's accuracy in general. This is a prognostic-accuracy shelf: no card claims that computing ARISCAT changes outcomes.
stamp: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — field-dependent: ARISCAT discriminated excellently at derivation (AUROC 0.88–0.90), held up in emergency abdominal surgery (AUC 0.83, absolute risk under-predicted), performed poorly in lung resection (c-index 0.60, as did all comparators), and pools at a summary c-statistic of 0.76 across cohorts; a prognostic-accuracy stamp, not a treatment stamp

title: ROX index for HFNC failure: AUROC 0.68→0.76 over 12 h in pneumonia (≥4.88 = success), but only 0.57–0.61 at 2 h in COVID-19 validations
question: In adults with acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure treated with high-flow nasal cannula (HFNC), how well does the ROX index (oxygen saturation / inspired oxygen fraction divided by respiratory rate), measured at 2, 6 and 12 hours, predict HFNC failure (intubation) — what cut-offs separate success from failure at each time point, and does the index hold up in external validation, including in COVID-19 pneumonia and emergency-department cohorts?
balance: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — time-point- and population-dependent. In the pre-COVID pneumonia derivation/validation cohort, the ROX index (SpO2/FiO2 divided by respiratory rate) discriminated modestly and better with time: AUROC 0.679 at 2 hours, 0.703 at 6 hours and 0.759 at 12 hours, with ROX ≥4.88 at any of those points associated with a lower risk of intubation and failure cut-offs of <2.85, <3.47 and <3.85 respectively. The two COVID-19 validations are materially weaker early: in 300 Japanese patients ROX AUROC was 0.57 at 2 hours, rising to 0.75 only at 48 hours; and in 173 Thai emergency-department patients the plain SpO2/FiO2 ratio (AUROC 0.651) discriminated better than ROX (0.612) at 2 hours. Cut-offs are time-point-specific and are never a single number. This is a prognostic-accuracy shelf: no randomised ROX-guided strategy trial is carded, and no card claims that acting on a ROX threshold improves outcomes. Two of the three reports are COVID-19 cohorts; the pre-COVID pneumonia cohort is the generalisable limb.
stamp: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — modest and time-dependent: ROX AUROC rose from 0.679 (2 h) to 0.759 (12 h) at derivation in pneumonia with time-point-specific cut-offs (≥4.88 success; <2.85 / <3.47 / <3.85 failure), but COVID-19 validations found weak 2-hour discrimination (0.57 in Japan; 0.612 in Thai EDs, below the plain SpO2/FiO2 ratio's 0.651); a prognostic-accuracy stamp, not a treatment stamp

title: Normal liver stiffness by transient elastography: screened-healthy ranges 2.3–5.9 kPa (Hong Kong) and 3.9–5.3 kPa (Korean donors) vs 3.2–8.5 kPa in a free-living population
question: In healthy adults, what are the normal values for liver stiffness measured by transient elastography (FibroScan) — mean, spread and 5th–95th percentile range in kilopascals — by sex, body-mass index and metabolic status, and how far do screened-healthy reference ranges sit below general-population values that include people with the metabolic syndrome?
balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall / Boron & Boulpaep, gastrointestinal / hepatic sections — the framing is brief, and this shelf rests chiefly on the primary elastography reference literature, and says so. Four independent populations, and the reference-population definition moves the upper limit more than the device does. Screened-healthy ranges are tight: 2.3–5.9 kPa in 530 rigorously screened Hong Kong Chinese volunteers (mean 4.1 kPa) and a 5th–95th percentile range of 3.9–5.3 kPa in 69 healthy Korean living donors (mean 4.6 kPa). Less-screened general populations run higher and wider: mean 5.49 kPa in 429 French check-up attendees, with metabolic syndrome at 6.51 kPa after adjustment; and a 5th–95th percentile range of 3.2–8.5 kPa in 437 healthy Indian adults, in whom both lean and obese subjects were stiffer than normal-BMI subjects. The screened Hong Kong ceiling (5.9 kPa) and the unscreened Indian ceiling (8.5 kPa) are different kinds of 'normal' and are never merged on this shelf. All values are transient-elastography (FibroScan) values in kilopascals — not interchangeable with MR-elastography or shear-wave values — and measurement failure rises steeply with BMI (4.6% overall, 88% at BMI >40 in the French cohort). PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED

title: Normal optic nerve sheath diameter: healthy means span 3.68 mm to 6.3 mm by ultrasound (CT 5.28 mm; pooled 4.78 mm) — the disagreement is the finding
question: In healthy adults, what is the normal optic nerve sheath diameter (ONSD) — mean and upper range in millimetres, measured 3 mm behind the globe — by measurement method (transorbital ultrasound vs computed tomography), sex and eyeball size, and how wide is the disagreement between published "normal" values that the raised-intracranial-pressure thresholds are built on?
balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, cerebrospinal-fluid / intracranial-pressure sections — the framing is brief, and this shelf rests chiefly on the primary sonographic reference literature, and says so. The between-study spread IS the finding: published healthy mean optic nerve sheath diameters span 3.68 mm (ultrasound, 120 volunteers) to 6.3 mm (ultrasound, 100 South Iranian adults) — a 2.6 mm gap, wider than the distance between 'normal' and most raised-intracranial-pressure cut-offs in clinical use. A CT dataset (360 Chinese adults) sits between them at 5.28 mm measured 3 mm behind the globe and 4.34 mm at 10 mm, so measurement position is part of the number. The meta-analytic pooled transorbital-sonography mean across 39 studies and 2,927 volunteers is 4.78 mm (95% CI 4.63 to 4.94) with substantial heterogeneity (I² 50.6%), attributed by its authors in part to differing measurement methods. No single normal value may be printed without its method and population; ultrasound and CT values are carded per method and never merged. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING — the datasets are real and independent, but they do not converge on a transferable normal value, which is precisely the shelf's content.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING

title: Flow-cytometry subset reference intervals: CD3+ ~71–77%, CD4+ ~41–45%, CD8+ ~30%, CD19+ ~13–14% across four populations — panel- and population-bound, distinct from FBC pack #7321
question: In healthy adults, what are the reference intervals for peripheral-blood lymphocyte and leukocyte subsets measured by flow cytometry — CD3, CD4, CD8, CD19/CD20 B cells, CD16/CD56 natural-killer cells and regulatory T cells, as percentages and absolute counts — by age, sex and population, and how much do panel, platform and population move them? balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, immunity / white-cell chapters — the framing is brief, and this shelf rests chiefly on the primary immunophenotyping reference literature, and says so. PARTIAL-adjacent distinction, stated on the face: pack #7321 cards full-blood-count reference intervals (haemoglobin, total white-cell count, the automated differential and platelets) and reports no flow-cytometric subset percentages; this shelf is the immunophenotyping slice #7321 presupposes, and NONE of #7321's datasets is re-carded here. Four independent flow-cytometry populations: harmonised Human Immunophenotyping Consortium panels across six European centres (more than 300 healthy volunteers, absolute and relative frequencies of T, regulatory-T, B, NK and myeloid subpopulations); a population-based 10-colour study of 608 German adults aged 40–79 (men higher for monocytes and NK cells, women higher for B, helper-T and regulatory-T cells; cytotoxic-T counts falling about 8% per 5 years of age); 221 Iranian adults aged 20–40 with full numeric subset means (CD3+ 70.90%, CD4+ 41.04%, CD8+ 31.11%, CD19+ 12.77%, CD56+ 15.53%, CD4/CD8 ratio 1.39); and 50 Omani adults with median-based intervals (CD3+ 76.5%, CD4+ 45%, CD8+ 29.5%, CD19+ 14%, NK 7%) — the Omani N (50 total) is printed on its card. Intervals are panel- and platform-specific (harmonised HIPC vs 10-colour vs 4-colour) and percentages and absolute counts are carded as published, never converted silently. title: Orforglipron glycaemic control (ACHIEVE-1 + ACHIEVE-2 only): HbA1c −0.83 to −1.07 points vs placebo and −0.42 to −0.75 vs dapagliflozin — PARTIAL + FLOOR-RISK, 2 reports, #1091 fence on the face
question: In adults with type 2 diabetes (treated with diet and exercise alone, or inadequately controlled on metformin), does once-daily oral orforglipron, compared with placebo or dapagliflozin, improve glycaemic control — the uncarded ACHIEVE-1 and ACHIEVE-2 slice of the phase 3 diabetes programme, beside live shelf #1091?
balance: PARTIAL + FLOOR-RISK — exactly 2 reports, stated on the face. FENCE POSITION, printed deliberately: live shelf #1091 (orforglipron phase 2 and the ATTAIN-1 obesity trial) fences the ACHIEVE phase 3 diabetes programme in its synthesis BY NAME, naming ACHIEVE-3 (against oral semaglutide), ACHIEVE-5 (added to insulin glargine) and the cardiovascular-safety trial ACHIEVE-4 — those three trials are fenced and gated and are NEVER carded here. ACHIEVE-1 and ACHIEVE-2 were never named in that fence, never carded and are gate-free; the slate-16 assembly adjudication (adjudication 2, common-questions-slate16) rows this uncarded ACHIEVE-1/-2 slice deliberately as a PARTIAL + FLOOR-RISK pack, so the developer can pull it at verdict if he reads the fence more broadly. On that 2-report base: ACHIEVE-1 (559 randomised, diet-and-exercise only) — HbA1c change at week 40 of −1.24, −1.47 and −1.48 percentage points on orforglipron 3, 12 and 36 mg vs −0.41 on placebo (differences −0.83, −1.06, −1.07, all P < 0.001). ACHIEVE-2 (962 randomised on metformin) — HbA1c change −1.23%, −1.50% and −1.56% vs −0.81% on dapagliflozin (differences −0.42%, −0.70%, −0.75%, all P < 0.0001, meeting and exceeding the 0.3% non-inferiority margin), at a gastrointestinal price: GI events in 46–54% on orforglipron vs 12% on dapagliflozin and discontinuation in 15–20% vs 6%. HbA1c is a surrogate endpoint, and NO outcomes claim is made: the cardiovascular-safety trial (ACHIEVE-4) is fenced and gated and forms no part of this pack.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — PARTIAL + FLOOR-RISK, exactly 2 reports: ACHIEVE-1 (HbA1c −0.83 to −1.07 percentage points vs placebo) and ACHIEVE-2 (−0.42 to −0.75 vs dapagliflozin, non-inferiority exceeded) show glycaemic benefit at 40 weeks on a surrogate endpoint, with GI events in 46–54% and discontinuation in 15–20% in the active-comparator trial; the #1091 fence (ACHIEVE-3/-5/-4, gated, never carded) and the deliberate slate-16 adjudication rowing this slice are printed on the face; no outcomes claim

title: Albiglutide glycaemic control (HARMONY slice): beat placebo and sitagliptin, failed non-inferiority vs liraglutide — a withdrawn drug; its CV trial lives at live #72
question: In adults with type 2 diabetes, does once-weekly albiglutide, compared with placebo, liraglutide or sitagliptin, improve glycaemic control — the HARMONY phase 3 glycaemic programme, beside live shelf #72, which cards Harmony Outcomes (cardiovascular) only?
balance: PARTIAL — and the withdrawn-agent flag leads: albiglutide was withdrawn from the market (2018, a commercial decision), and live shelf #72 already prints 'a drug no longer sold' for its cardiovascular card. This pack cards the glycaemic HARMONY slice that #72 does not: #72 cards Harmony Outcomes (cardiovascular) only, cross-pointed here and never re-carded. The glycaemic record is mixed by comparator. Against placebo added to pioglitazone ± metformin (HARMONY 1, 310 randomised), albiglutide won clearly: HbA1c difference −0.8 percentage points at week 52, with hyperglycaemia rescue in 24.4% vs 47.7%. Against sitagliptin in renal impairment it won modestly (−0.83% vs −0.52% at week 26, P = 0.0003). But the head-to-head anchor FAILED its test: in HARMONY 7, albiglutide was NOT non-inferior to once-daily liraglutide (HbA1c −0.78% vs −0.99%; difference 0.21%, 95% CI 0.08 to 0.34; non-inferiority P = 0.0846 against the 0.3% margin) — HARMONY 7 must not be presented as equivalence. A 3-year pooled report of five HARMONY trials (3,132 randomised) supports durability, labelled as programme support. HbA1c is a surrogate endpoint; the cardiovascular-outcomes result lives at #72.
stamp: SPLIT — PARTIAL (glycaemic HARMONY slice beside live #72): albiglutide beat placebo (HbA1c −0.8 percentage points, HARMONY 1) and sitagliptin in renal impairment (−0.83% vs −0.52%), with 3-year durability in the pooled programme, but FAILED non-inferiority against liraglutide in HARMONY 7 (difference 0.21%, non-inferiority P = 0.0846) — and the agent was withdrawn from the market in 2018; the cardiovascular-outcomes result is homed at live #72

title: Omarigliptin: weekly DPP-4 inhibition matched daily sitagliptin (HbA1c −0.47% vs −0.43%); CV safety study neutral (HR 1.00) but terminated early — Japan-only, never US-marketed
question: In adults with type 2 diabetes, does the once-weekly DPP-4 inhibitor omarigliptin, compared with placebo, sitagliptin or usual therapy, improve glycaemic control — and what did its cardiovascular safety study show?
balance: Single-region approval on the face: omarigliptin, a once-weekly DPP-4 inhibitor, is approved in Japan and was NEVER marketed in the US — the fetched safety-study record states the sponsor made a business decision not to submit a US marketing application and terminated the cardiovascular safety study early; both facts are printed here, not footnoted. Glycaemically it behaved like its daily class sibling: non-inferior to sitagliptin 100 mg daily on metformin at week 24 (HbA1c −0.47% weekly vs −0.43% daily; difference −0.03%, 95% CI −0.15 to 0.08, meeting the 0.3% criterion; 642 randomised), and modestly better than placebo as monotherapy (−0.49% vs −0.10%; difference −0.39%, P < 0.001; 329 randomised). The cardiovascular safety study (4,202 randomised with established cardiovascular disease) found MACE in 5.45% on omarigliptin vs 5.43% on placebo (HR 1.00, 95% CI 0.77 to 1.29) over a median follow-up of about 96 weeks — but it was TERMINATED EARLY, so that neutral estimate rests on truncated follow-up and is printed with that caveat. HbA1c is a surrogate endpoint.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit, glycaemic) — omarigliptin was non-inferior to daily sitagliptin (HbA1c −0.47% vs −0.43%) and modestly beat placebo (−0.39 percentage points) on a surrogate endpoint, with a neutral cardiovascular estimate (MACE HR 1.00, 95% CI 0.77 to 1.29) from a safety study TERMINATED EARLY on truncated follow-up; approved in Japan only, never marketed in the US — both facts on the face

title: Odanacatib (LOFT): fractures halved (vertebral 3.7% vs 7.8%; hip 0.8% vs 1.6%) but stroke rose (HR 1.32) — development abandoned, never marketed
question: In postmenopausal women (and, in a separate trial, men) with osteoporosis, does the cathepsin K inhibitor odanacatib, compared with placebo, reduce fractures — and what cardiovascular harm ended its development (the LOFT programme)?
balance: Discontinued agent — the flag leads: odanacatib was NEVER marketed; its sponsor abandoned development on the benefit–risk balance printed in the LOFT report itself, and the stroke signal leads this balance rather than following the fracture win. LOFT (16,071 randomised postmenopausal women) succeeded on fractures: radiographic vertebral fractures 3.7% vs 7.8% (HR 0.46), hip fractures 0.8% vs 1.6% (HR 0.53) and non-vertebral fractures 5.1% vs 6.7% (HR 0.77), all P < 0.0001 — hazard ratios are relative measures, printed beside their absolute rates. Against that, stroke occurred in 1.7% vs 1.3% (HR 1.32, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.70; P = 0.034), and with the LOFT Extension data the cardiovascular composite (cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction or stroke) reached HR 1.17 (95% CI 1.02 to 1.36) with stroke at HR 1.37. The other two reports are bone-density (surrogate) trials only — a 2-year phase 2 dose-ranging study (lumbar spine BMD +5.5% and total-hip +3.2% on 50 mg weekly vs −0.2% and −0.9% on placebo) and a phase 3 trial in 292 men (lumbar spine BMD difference +5.6% at 24 months) — only LOFT answers the fracture question, and that distinction is printed on each card.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit on fractures, with development-ending harm) — LOFT showed odanacatib reduced vertebral (3.7% vs 7.8%, HR 0.46), hip (0.8% vs 1.6%, HR 0.53) and non-vertebral fractures, but increased stroke (1.7% vs 1.3%, HR 1.32; HR 1.37 with extension data), on which the sponsor abandoned development; the agent was never marketed, the stroke signal leads the balance, and the supporting trials are BMD (surrogate) trials only
