title: Bococizumab (SPIRE): LDL −56% relative, but antidrug antibodies eroded the effect and the outcomes trials split (HR 0.99 vs 0.79; combined 0.88, NS) — programme discontinued
question: In adults with hypercholesterolaemia at high cardiovascular risk, does the humanised PCSK9 antibody bococizumab, compared with placebo, lower LDL cholesterol and reduce cardiovascular events — and why did antidrug antibodies end the programme (the SPIRE programme)?
balance: Discontinued agent — the flag leads: bococizumab was NEVER marketed. It is the only humanised (not fully human) PCSK9 antibody in its class, and the immunogenicity that attenuated its LDL effect is the central fact of the programme, printed in its own NEJM companion paper. The outcomes headline is DISCORDANT BY TRIAL and must not be presented as an outcomes win: in SPIRE-1 and SPIRE-2 (27,438 randomised, 93% on statins), LDL change at week 14 was −56.0% relative on bococizumab vs +2.9% on placebo, but the primary composite hazard ratio was 0.99 (95% CI 0.80 to 1.22; P = 0.94) in the lower-risk, shorter trial and 0.79 (95% CI 0.65 to 0.97; P = 0.02) in the higher-risk, longer trial, combining to HR 0.88 (95% CI 0.76 to 1.02; P = 0.08) — not significant. Both trials were STOPPED EARLY when the sponsor discontinued development, in part over high antidrug-antibody rates, so follow-up was truncated (median 10 months). In the six pooled lipid trials (4,300 randomised), LDL fell 54.2% relative at week 12 vs a 1.0% rise on placebo, but high-titre antidrug antibodies in a substantial proportion markedly diminished the magnitude and durability of that lowering, and wide variability persisted even without antibodies. Injection-site reactions ran 10.4% vs 1.3% in the outcomes trials.
stamp: SPLIT — bococizumab lowered LDL by 54–56% in relative terms, but antidrug antibodies attenuated the effect's magnitude and durability, and the SPIRE outcomes trials were discordant (HR 0.99 in the lower-risk trial vs 0.79 in the higher-risk trial; combined HR 0.88, 95% CI 0.76 to 1.02, P = 0.08) on follow-up truncated by an early stop; the discontinued, never-marketed programme's immunogenicity leads the balance

title: Tafolecimab (CREDIT programme, China only): LDL down 57–65% relative versus placebo in three phase 3 trials — a surrogate benefit with no cardiovascular-outcomes trial
question: In Chinese adults with hypercholesterolaemia (non-familial, heterozygous familial, or at high/very high cardiovascular risk), does the fully human PCSK9 antibody tafolecimab, compared with placebo, lower LDL cholesterol (the CREDIT-1, CREDIT-2 and CREDIT-4 programme)?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) for LDL lowering, on a single-region (China) surrogate base. Three phase 3 placebo-controlled trials of the fully human PCSK9 antibody tafolecimab in Chinese patients all showed large LDL-cholesterol reductions: CREDIT-1 (non-familial hypercholesterolaemia, 618 randomised, 48 weeks) treatment differences versus placebo of −65.0% relative on 450 mg every 4 weeks and −57.3% relative on 600 mg every 6 weeks; CREDIT-2 (heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia, 149 randomised, 12-week double-blind period) −57.4% and −61.9% relative; CREDIT-4 (high/very high cardiovascular risk, 303 dosed) a least-squares mean LDL change of −68.9% versus −5.8% on placebo (difference −63.0% relative). All percent changes are relative measures. SINGLE-REGION FLAG: every trial was conducted in China, where tafolecimab is approved; it is not FDA- or EMA-approved. LDL cholesterol is a surrogate endpoint — no cardiovascular-outcomes trial of tafolecimab exists, and no outcomes claim is made on this shelf. Its single-region class sibling recaticimab is homed separately (pack #6821) and is not re-carded here.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — three concordant Chinese phase 3 trials show large LDL-cholesterol reductions versus placebo (−57% to −65% relative); surrogate endpoint only, no cardiovascular-outcomes data, and the entire evidence base is single-region (China), where the drug is approved but not FDA/EMA-approved

title: Verinurad + xanthine-oxidase inhibitor for albuminuria: exactly 2 reports — a 60-patient positive phase 2 against the 861-patient negative SAPPHIRE trial
question: In adults with chronic kidney disease (with type 2 diabetes, or with CKD and hyperuricaemia), does intensive urate lowering with the URAT1 inhibitor verinurad combined with a xanthine-oxidase inhibitor (febuxostat or allopurinol), compared with placebo or the xanthine-oxidase inhibitor alone, reduce albuminuria?
balance: SPLIT — on exactly 2 results reports, and the split is the answer. A 60-patient phase 2 trial in type 2 diabetes with hyperuricaemia and albuminuria found urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR) lower on verinurad 9 mg + febuxostat 80 mg than on placebo by −39.4% relative at week 12 and −49.3% relative at week 24, with serum urate about 60% lower relative — but its own abstract states the sample size and duration were insufficient for definitive albuminuria or filtration conclusions. The much larger SAPPHIRE phase 2b trial (861 randomised with CKD and hyperuricaemia) found the geometric mean percentage change in UACR at week 34 did not differ among placebo, allopurinol alone and three verinurad + allopurinol dose arms — the primary endpoint was not met — while serum urate fell dose-dependently. The larger, later trial carries the greater weight: intensive urate lowering lowered urate but did not lower albuminuria where it was properly tested. UACR is a surrogate endpoint; neither trial tested kidney progression, and verinurad was never marketed. A third card below is the SAPPHIRE design paper — a programme report of the same trial, not a third results report; the report count of this shelf is exactly 2.
stamp: SPLIT — FLOOR-RISK, exactly 2 results reports: a 60-patient phase 2 trial found albuminuria lower on verinurad + febuxostat (−49.3% relative at week 24), but the 861-patient SAPPHIRE trial found no albuminuria reduction at any dose versus allopurinol alone or placebo, so the larger negative trial governs and no albuminuria benefit is established

title: Presatovir for RSV in transplant recipients: positive only in the healthy-volunteer challenge model — all three patient trials missed their primary endpoints
question: In patients with respiratory syncytial virus infection — haematopoietic-cell transplant recipients with upper or lower respiratory tract infection, and lung transplant recipients — does oral presatovir (GS-5806) versus placebo reduce nasal viral load, progression to lower respiratory tract complications, oxygen requirement, respiratory failure and death; and in experimentally infected healthy adults, does it reduce viral load and symptoms?
balance: LIKELY (no benefit) in patients — a single development programme whose signal never left the challenge model. Four randomised trials, one programme: the human challenge trial in healthy adults (54 infected participants in cohorts 1–4) was clearly positive — viral-load AUC 250.7 versus 757.7 log₁₀ PFUe·hours/mL, mucus weight 6.9 versus 15.1 g, symptom scores lower. All three patient trials then missed their primary endpoints: in HCT recipients with upper respiratory tract infection (189 randomised) the coprimary endpoints were not met at the prespecified α=0.01 (viral-load difference −0.33 log₁₀ copies/mL, P=.040; lower-respiratory complications 11.2% vs 19.5%, P=.11); in HCT recipients with lower respiratory tract infection (60 randomised) the viral-load difference was −0.02 log₁₀ copies/mL, P=.94, with no difference in oxygen-free days, respiratory failure or mortality, and resistance-associated fusion substitutions emerged in 6 of 29 presatovir-treated patients; in lung transplant recipients (61 randomised) the viral-load difference was 0.10 log₁₀ copies/mL, P=0.72, with no benefit on symptoms or lung function. The one positive post-hoc finding (fewer complications in the lymphopenia subgroup, 13.3% vs 64.3%) is hypothesis-generating only. Presatovir was never marketed; development stopped — printed plainly, this is a failed programme, not an antiviral that works in transplant patients.
stamp: LIKELY (no benefit) — a single programme of four trials in which the only positive trial was the experimental human challenge study in healthy adults, while all three patient trials (HCT upper respiratory, HCT lower respiratory, and lung transplant recipients) missed their primary endpoints with no clinical benefit; presatovir was never marketed

title: Inhaled liposomal ciprofloxacin (ORBIT) in non-CF bronchiectasis: the phase 3 twins split — ORBIT-4 positive (HR 0.72), ORBIT-3 null (HR 0.99), pooled estimate non-significant
question: In adults with non-cystic-fibrosis bronchiectasis, chronic Pseudomonas aeruginosa lung infection and frequent exacerbations, does once-daily inhaled liposomal ciprofloxacin (ARD-3150, dual-release liposomal/free formulation) versus placebo prolong time to first pulmonary exacerbation and reduce sputum bacterial density (the ORBIT-2, ORBIT-3 and ORBIT-4 programme)?
balance: SPLIT — the twin phase 3 trials disagree, and the split is printed wherever this programme is summarised. This shelf cards only the liposomal formulation slice (the dual-release liposomal/free ciprofloxacin product ARD-3150, as the publications name it): the class home, pack #2784, cards only the dry-powder RESPIRE programme plus a meta-analysis, and the two products are not interchangeable. ORBIT-2 (phase 2, 42 adults) cut sputum Pseudomonas density by a mean 4.2 log₁₀ CFU/g versus −0.08 on placebo at day 28 (P=0.002) — a bacterial-density surrogate. ORBIT-4 (304 patients) prolonged median time to first exacerbation (230 vs 158 days; hazard ratio 0.72, 95% CI 0.53 to 0.97; P=0.032), while its concurrent twin ORBIT-3 (278 patients) was flatly null on the same endpoint (214 vs 136 days; HR 0.99, 95% CI 0.71 to 1.38; P=0.97), and the pooled estimate was non-significant (HR 0.82, P=0.074). No pooled headline is printed without that split. The programme did not lead to an approved bronchiectasis therapy.
stamp: SPLIT — of the two concurrent phase 3 trials of inhaled liposomal ciprofloxacin (ARD-3150), ORBIT-4 prolonged time to first exacerbation (hazard ratio 0.72) while ORBIT-3 was flatly null (hazard ratio 0.99) and the pooled estimate was non-significant; the phase 2 trial showed only a sputum bacterial-density effect in 42 patients

title: Biofeedback for faecal incontinence: the largest trial found no benefit over standard care with advice (53% vs 54% improved); a smaller trial beat exercises alone
question: In adults with faecal incontinence, does biofeedback-based sphincter training — versus standard care/advice, versus pelvic floor exercises alone, and in home versus office delivery — reduce incontinence episodes and severity and improve quality of life?
balance: SPLIT — and the largest trial is negative, printed first. The 171-patient four-arm trial found biofeedback yielded no greater benefit than standard care with advice (53% improved on hospital biofeedback vs 54% on advice alone), while every group improved on episodes, continence score and quality of life. Against a narrower comparator the picture differs: after a medication/education run-in, biofeedback plus exercises beat exercises alone on adequate relief at 3 months (76% vs 41%). The remaining limbs answer different questions and are never pooled: two biofeedback exercise regimens did not differ (72 participants), and home biofeedback was non-inferior to office biofeedback in 30 patients. The base supports 'structured conservative therapy helps; the biofeedback component's added value over good standard care is unproven.' All trials are unblinded behavioural interventions with subjective endpoints. The tested programmes are named as the publications give them (computer-assisted sphincter pressure biofeedback; manometric biofeedback) under the programme-naming exception. Cross-points, not folded in: sacral nerve stimulation (pack #2659) and anal bulking injections (pack #5318); biofeedback for dyssynergic defecation is a different, opposite-physiology question (pack #2517).
stamp: SPLIT — the largest trial (171 patients) found biofeedback no better than standard care with advice (53% vs 54% improved), while a 108-patient trial found biofeedback plus exercises superior to exercises alone after a conservative run-in (adequate relief 76% vs 41%); regimen and home-vs-office limbs showed no differences, so structured conservative therapy is supported but biofeedback's added value over standard care is unproven

title: Daikenchuto (TJ-100) for postoperative ileus: JAPAN-PD was negative on both coprimary endpoints — a negative programme with only motility-signal limbs
question: In patients undergoing major abdominal surgery (pancreaticoduodenectomy, colectomy, total gastrectomy), does perioperative daikenchuto (TJ-100) versus placebo or control prevent prolonged paralytic ileus and accelerate return of bowel function?
balance: LIKELY (no benefit) — a negative programme, presented plainly. The one large double-blind trial, JAPAN-PD (224 randomised after pancreaticoduodenectomy), missed both coprimary endpoints: paralytic ileus in 33.7% on daikenchuto versus 36.9% on placebo (P=.626) and time to first flatus 2.25 versus 2.50 days (P=.343), and its authors concluded the findings may preclude routine use after pancreaticoduodenectomy. The remaining limbs are weaker designs with surrogate or softer readings: a transit-marker study (88 registered, 71 analysed) found faster small-bowel marker transit at 6 hours but no difference in total transit or time to first flatus; a total-gastrectomy trial (81 patients) against no treatment found more stools per day and lower bowel-gas scores but no difference in postoperative ileus incidence or quality of life; and a laparoscopic-colectomy trial (54 randomised) used a lactobacillus preparation as an active comparator. No trial shows fewer complications, shorter stay or less obstruction. PRODUCT NAMING (herb rule): the tested product is daikenchuto TJ-100 (Tsumura), as the programme's publications name it; where a carded publication's record names no product code or company, its card says so plainly, and other Kampo preparations may differ in safety and effectiveness. Japanese programme — single-region flag; populations are cancer-surgery patients and do not generalise to all abdominal surgery. FENCE: the Cochrane review of daikenchuto for postoperative ileus is a retracted publication and is never carded on this shelf (its identifier is deliberately not printed, so no grep can mistake it for a carded source); the 2013 JAPAN-PD paper is that trial's protocol, not a second trial, and is not carded as one.
stamp: LIKELY (no benefit) — the programme's large double-blind trial (JAPAN-PD, 224 randomised) missed both coprimary endpoints for daikenchuto TJ-100 (Tsumura) after pancreaticoduodenectomy (ileus 33.7% vs 36.9%), and the smaller limbs show only transit/stool/gas signals against no treatment or an active comparator, with no ileus, complication or stay benefit in any trial

title: Rikkunshito for functional dyspepsia: the largest trial missed its primary endpoint (P=0.09); DREAM was positive in a placebo-run-in-enriched population
question: In patients with functional dyspepsia, does rikkunshito (TJ-43) versus placebo (or versus a prokinetic) improve global dyspepsia response, epigastric pain and postprandial fullness?
balance: SPLIT — the negative primary leads. The largest trial (247 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled) missed its primary endpoint: global-assessment responders were 33.6% on rikkunshito versus 23.8% on placebo at 8 weeks, P=0.09 — not significant — although epigastric pain improved significantly (P=0.04). The DREAM study was positive on its overall-treatment-efficacy endpoint (P=.019), but it randomised only the 128 of 192 enrolled patients who remained symptomatic after a single-blind placebo run-in — an enriched population, labelled as such. The two remaining limbs are small and never load-bearing: a Belgian crossover mechanistic trial (23 completers) found no significant change in gastric accommodation or intragastric pressure, with high placebo responses on symptom diaries; and a domperidone-comparator trial (27 patients) found symptom improvement in both groups. PRODUCT NAMING (herb rule): the tested preparation is rikkunshito (TJ-43), as the programme's publications name the product; where a carded publication's fetched record names no product code or company, its card says so plainly, and other preparations may differ in safety and effectiveness. A Japanese programme with one small Belgian limb — region flag on the face. The chemotherapy-induced-nausea rikkunshito trials ask a different question and are not folded in; STW 5, a different herbal product, stays at pack #4235.
stamp: SPLIT — the largest trial of rikkunshito (TJ-43) in functional dyspepsia missed its global-response primary endpoint (33.6% vs 23.8%, P=0.09), while the DREAM trial was positive (P=.019) only in patients still symptomatic after a placebo run-in; the Belgian mechanistic and domperidone-comparator limbs are small and never load-bearing

title: Racecadotril for acute diarrhoea in adults: one small positive placebo trial; as effective as loperamide in larger comparisons, with less rebound constipation
question: In adults with acute (watery) diarrhoea, does racecadotril versus placebo reduce stool output and duration, and how does it compare with loperamide on duration and rebound constipation?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — as effective as loperamide, with less rebound constipation; not shown superior to it, and the placebo base is thin. This shelf cards the adult slice only: the children's question is homed at live #1361, and the one adult racecadotril-versus-loperamide limb carded inside the loperamide shelf (Vetel 1999, pack #2478) stays homed there and is cross-pointed, never re-carded here. The placebo evidence is a single small trial (70 adults): stool weight on day 1 was significantly lower on racecadotril (P=0.025), with fewer diarrhoeic stools after 1 day (P=0.027) and less post-treatment abdominal distension (5.6% vs 18.2%). The comparative base shows equivalence, not superiority: in 945 outpatients diarrhoea resolved in 55.0 hours in both groups, with significantly less constipation on racecadotril (16% vs 25%); in 62 outpatients clinical success was 95.7% versus 92.0%, with median duration numerically longer on racecadotril (19.5 vs 13 hours) and more reactive constipation on loperamide (29.0% vs 12.9%). Two of the three carded trials are single-blind. Era flag: a 1999–2005 programme, largely pre-dating current oral-rehydration-era adult diarrhoea guidance.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in adults, racecadotril reduced day-1 stool weight versus placebo in a single 70-patient trial and matched loperamide on diarrhoea duration in larger comparisons (55.0 hours in both groups, n=945) with significantly less rebound constipation; equivalence with loperamide, not superiority, is what the base shows

title: Colchicine in non-PBC cirrhosis: the 1988 trial's dramatic survival benefit (11 vs 3.5 years) was never reproduced — the 549-patient VA trial was null
question: In patients with established cirrhosis (alcoholic, posthepatitic or hepatitis-B-related — the non-PBC programme), does long-term colchicine versus placebo improve survival and reverse fibrosis histologically?
balance: LIKELY (no benefit) — the programme's arc is one striking positive followed by larger negatives, presented in that order of weight. A single-centre Mexican double-blind trial (NEJM 1988, 100 patients with mixed alcoholic and posthepatitic cirrhosis) reported median survival of 11 years on colchicine versus 3.5 years on placebo (P<0.001), with 5-year survival 75% versus 34% and histological improvement in 9 of 30 re-biopsied colchicine patients. That result was not reproduced: the VA cooperative trial in advanced alcoholic cirrhosis (549 patients, Pugh B/C, treated 2–6 years) found all-cause mortality 49% on colchicine versus 45% on placebo (P=.371), and an HBV-related postnecrotic cirrhosis trial (100 patients) found no improvement in biochemistry, histology or hepatic pressure gradient and no significant survival difference (P=0.8). The earliest double-blind trial (43 patients) was also non-significant. The Cochrane synthesis of 15 trials (1,714 patients, excluding primary biliary cholangitis) found no significant effect on mortality (relative risk 1.00) and a significantly increased risk of adverse events (relative risk 4.35). Populations differ by limb and are never pooled into one survival number. Era flag: pre-antiviral, pre-transplant-era cirrhosis care; the HBV limb's patients received no nucleos(t)ide therapy, so it does not bear on modern treated HBV cirrhosis. Colchicine in primary biliary cholangitis is a different disease question, homed at pack #7425, and no PBC trial is re-carded here.
stamp: LIKELY (no benefit) — the striking 1988 single-centre survival result (n=100) was not reproduced by the 549-patient VA trial in advanced alcoholic cirrhosis (mortality 49% vs 45%) or the HBV trial (n=100), and the Cochrane pool of 15 trials found mortality relative risk 1.00 with adverse events significantly increased (relative risk 4.35)

title: Pentoxifylline in NASH: four small trials totalling 135 patients — one positive histology trial (n=55), three without between-group separation
question: In adults with biopsy-proven (or imaging/enzyme-defined) non-alcoholic steatohepatitis, does pentoxifylline 1200 mg/day versus placebo improve histological activity (NAS), steatosis and liver enzymes over 3–12 months?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — a small-trial programme, with its numbers printed: four randomised trials totalling 135 patients (55, 30, 30 and 20). Only the largest, a 55-patient US trial in biopsy-confirmed NASH, has a positive between-group histological primary: NAS fall of at least 2 points in 38.5% on pentoxifylline 1200 mg/day versus 13.8% on placebo at 1 year (P=0.036). The other three rest on weaker readings: a 30-patient biopsy-proven trial found aminotransferases and some histology improved within the pentoxifylline arm but between-group comparisons were non-significant; a 30-patient Iranian trial in ultrasound/enzyme-defined NASH found aminotransferases fell in both groups (attributed by its authors to diet and exercise) with no between-group difference; and a 20-patient pilot with diet-and-exercise co-intervention in both arms found a greater AST reduction on pentoxifylline (P=0.038). Definitions differ by limb (biopsy-proven in three trials as the records describe them, ultrasound/enzymes in one) and are labelled per card. There are no fibrosis-regression-at-scale, clinical-outcome or long-term safety data. Era flag: pre-resmetirom, pre-GLP-1-era MASH care — this shelf must not be read against the current treatment landscape. Pentoxifylline in alcohol-associated hepatitis and diabetic kidney disease are different questions, homed elsewhere and not folded in.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — based on a very small total N = 135 across 4 trials: only the 55-patient US trial showed a between-group histological benefit (NAS fall ≥2 points in 38.5% vs 13.8%), while the three smaller trials (n=30, 30, 20) showed within-arm or surrogate changes without significant between-group separation

title: Rifampicin for cholestatic pruritus: FLOOR-RISK — exactly 3 crossover reports, 45 adults, all favouring rifampicin for short-term itch relief (n=9 limb sub-floor)
question: In adults with cholestatic pruritus (chiefly primary biliary cholangitis/cirrhosis), does rifampicin (rifampin) versus placebo or phenobarbitone relieve itch — the unasked slice beside the sertraline-versus-rifampicin head-to-head homed at pack #3618?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — based on a very small N = 45. FLOOR-RISK, stated exactly: the complete adult randomised base for rifampicin's own efficacy in cholestatic pruritus is 3 crossover reports totalling 45 adults (1988–1991), each limb ≤14 days. All three favoured rifampicin — 8 of 9 preferred it to placebo (Ghent, n=9, SUB-FLOOR and never load-bearing alone); itch improved in 19 vs 8 patients against phenobarbitone and disappeared in 9 (Bachs, n=22); itch disappeared in 11 of 14 on rifampin vs partial response in 2 on placebo (Podesta, n=14). PARTIAL: the sertraline-versus-rifampicin head-to-head is homed at pack #3618 and is not re-carded; this shelf is only the unasked slice — rifampicin versus placebo/phenobarbitone. Harms belong on the face: one withdrawal for anaemia and renal failure, drug-induced hepatitis risk in cholestatic patients (the reason monitoring is mandatory), and potent enzyme induction with wide drug interactions. Short-term itch relief only; no long-term randomised safety base.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — based on a very small N = 45: FLOOR-RISK, exactly 3 crossover reports (45 adults, 1988–1991, limbs ≤14 days) all favoured rifampicin for short-term cholestatic itch relief versus placebo or phenobarbitone; the n=9 limb is sub-floor and never load-bearing; harms (anaemia/renal-failure withdrawal, hepatitis risk, enzyme induction) are on the face

title: Gatifloxacin for uncomplicated enteric fever: SPLIT — matched most comparators, beat cefixime, failed once high-level fluoroquinolone resistance emerged (Nepal–Vietnam programme)
question: In children and adults with uncomplicated enteric (typhoid/paratyphoid) fever, does 7 days of oral gatifloxacin versus chloramphenicol, cefixime, ofloxacin, azithromycin or intravenous ceftriaxone achieve faster fever clearance and less treatment failure and relapse?
balance: SPLIT — by comparator and by resistance era. In five open-label Nepal–Vietnam trials, 7 days of oral gatifloxacin matched chloramphenicol (failure 12 vs 14 in 352 culture-confirmed), azithromycin (failure 9% vs 9.3%; fever clearance 106 hours in both arms) and ofloxacin (failure 5/87 vs 6/83 in nalidixic-acid-resistant isolates) on treatment failure, and beat cefixime clearly (failure 3.5% vs 37.6%) in a trial stopped early on DSMB advice. Against intravenous ceftriaxone the overall result was null (15% vs 16%), but culture-confirmed patients failed more on gatifloxacin (26% vs 7%) and that trial was stopped early because high-level fluoroquinolone resistance had emerged. Resistance-era flag (load-bearing): these trials were run where nalidixic-acid resistance was common; their results do not transfer to today's extensively drug-resistant S. Typhi settings. Safety flag: gatifloxacin was withdrawn from many markets over dysglycaemia — this shelf is a record of a completed programme, not a prescribing recommendation. Two of five trials stopped early; both stop reasons are on the cards.
stamp: SPLIT — gatifloxacin matched chloramphenicol, azithromycin and ofloxacin on treatment failure and beat cefixime (early-stopped trial), but failed culture-confirmed patients against ceftriaxone (26% vs 7%) once high-level fluoroquinolone resistance emerged; nalidixic-acid-resistance-era results that do not transfer to XDR settings, and the drug was withdrawn in many markets over dysglycaemia

title: Tribendimidine for Opisthorchis viverrini: highly active in one Lao phase 2 programme (3 publications / 4 trials) — but non-inferiority to praziquantel on cure was not shown
question: In children and adults infected with Opisthorchis viverrini, does single-dose tribendimidine, at what dose, achieve cure and egg reduction comparable with praziquantel, the only established treatment?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single-region, single-programme phase 2 record, counted exactly: 3 publications reporting 4 trials, all in Laos from one collaboration. Tribendimidine is clearly active against Opisthorchis viverrini: dose-ranging cure rose to 91.5% at 400 mg in adolescents/adults with egg reduction ~99% at ≥100 mg, and in the head-to-head trial single-dose tribendimidine cured 93.6% versus 97.3% on two-dose praziquantel with 99.9% egg reduction in both groups and fewer adverse events on tribendimidine. But non-inferiority on cure was NOT shown (difference −3.8 percentage points; lower confidence limit −7.1 exceeded the pre-specified −3 margin) — that failure is on the face, not buried. The exploratory trial's tribendimidine limb (27 children, one of five arms) is labelled and never load-bearing. Endpoints are parasitological only; no phase 3, no approval, and tribendimidine (Chinese-developed) is not US/EU-marketed.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one Lao phase 2 programme (3 publications / 4 trials, labelled): tribendimidine cured ~94% with 99.9% egg reduction and fewer adverse events than praziquantel, but non-inferiority on cure was NOT shown (−3.8 points; lower limit −7.1 vs −3 margin); parasitological endpoints only, no phase 3

title: Needle aspiration in uncomplicated amoebic liver abscess: no benefit over metronidazole alone in three small trials (PARTIAL beside pack #7009's drainage-technique shelf)
question: In adults with uncomplicated amoebic liver abscess, does ultrasound-guided needle aspiration added to metronidazole, versus metronidazole alone, speed resolution of pain, fever and the abscess cavity? (The drainage-technique question — catheter versus needle — is homed at pack #7009 and is not re-carded here.)
balance: LIKELY (no benefit) — PARTIAL beside pack #7009: #7009 asks catheter drainage versus needle aspiration (which technique, presupposing drainage) and its trials are not re-carded; this shelf asks the prior, unasked question — whether to aspirate at all in uncomplicated amoebic liver abscess. Three small randomised trials (n=39, 39, 57) over 24 years consistently found metronidazole alone sufficient: clinical improvement, laboratory normalisation and cavity healing similar in both groups (1989); only liver tenderness improved faster, over the first 3 days, in one trial (2003); earlier pain/fever resolution was not significant in the third (2013; P=0.16, P=0.48), with no deaths, failures or ruptures in any arm. The Cochrane synthesis (7 trials, 310 patients) could neither support nor refute aspiration. Size limbs are labelled per trial and the answer does not extend to >10 cm, left-lobe, ruptured or impending-rupture abscesses. All trials predate routine E. histolytica antigen/PCR confirmation in their settings.
stamp: LIKELY (no benefit) — PARTIAL vs pack #7009 (carding only whether to aspirate at all): three small trials (n=39, 39, 57) found metronidazole alone sufficient in uncomplicated amoebic liver abscess, with at most faster tenderness relief in the first 3 days in one trial; the Cochrane synthesis could neither support nor refute aspiration

title: Sorafenib in advanced hepatocellular carcinoma: FLOOR-RISK — exactly 2 trials (SHARP 10.7 vs 7.9 months; Asia-Pacific 6.5 vs 4.2 months), a modest survival gain with no symptom-progression delay in SHARP
question: In patients with advanced hepatocellular carcinoma who have received no previous systemic therapy, does sorafenib 400 mg twice daily prolong overall survival versus placebo?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — FLOOR-RISK, exactly 2 reports, stated on the face: SHARP (602 randomised; median overall survival 10.7 vs 7.9 months, hazard ratio 0.69 relative) and the Asia-Pacific trial (226 randomised, predominantly hepatitis-B-related disease; 6.5 vs 4.2 months, hazard ratio 0.68 relative). Both were re-verified at slate-16 mining and fetched again this session. The two trials are regional/aetiological slices, never pooled. The benefit is real but modest in absolute terms (~2–3 months of median survival), and SHARP found NO significant difference in time to symptomatic progression (4.1 vs 4.9 months, P=0.77) — that null sits beside the survival gain, with partial response in only 2% and no complete responses, and diarrhoea, weight loss, hand–foot skin reaction and hypophosphataemia more frequent on sorafenib. A labelled SHARP biomarker programme report (no biomarker predicted sorafenib response) completes the record without counting as a third trial.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — FLOOR-RISK, exactly 2 reports (SHARP n=602 and Asia-Pacific n=226, both re-verified this session): sorafenib prolonged median overall survival by ~2–3 months in advanced HCC (hazard ratios 0.69 and 0.68, relative), with no significant delay in symptomatic progression in SHARP and hand–foot skin reaction, diarrhoea and weight loss as the pricing harms

title: Alteplase in acute ischaemic stroke: benefit within 3 hours and at 3–4.5 hours, an unproven primary endpoint up to 6 hours (IST-3) — windows never pooled
question: In patients with acute ischaemic stroke, does intravenous alteplase (0.9 mg/kg where the record states it) improve functional outcome versus placebo/control — within 3 hours (NINDS), at 3–4.5 hours (ECASS III), and in a wider population up to 6 hours (IST-3) — and at what intracranial-haemorrhage cost?
balance: SPLIT — by time window, with the windows and doses never pooled. Within 3 hours (NINDS, 624 patients in a labelled two-part design: Part 1 n=291, Part 2 n=333), alteplase made patients at least 30% more likely to have minimal or no disability at 3 months (global odds ratio 1.7, relative), with symptomatic intracerebral haemorrhage in 6.4% vs 0.6%. At 3–4.5 hours (ECASS III, 821), favourable outcome was 52.4% vs 45.2% (odds ratio 1.34, relative) with symptomatic haemorrhage 2.4% vs 0.2%. Up to 6 hours in a wider, older population (IST-3, 3,035; 53% over 80), the primary endpoint was NOT significant (alive and independent 37% vs 35%; adjusted odds ratio 1.13, P=0.181), although an ordinal shift favoured rt-PA (common odds ratio 1.27, relative), with symptomatic haemorrhage 7% vs 1% and more deaths in the first 7 days, offset thereafter. The dose throughout is 0.9 mg/kg where the record states it. The ~6–7% symptomatic-haemorrhage rate in the widest windows is the pricing harm.
stamp: SPLIT — by window (never pooled): alteplase benefits acute ischaemic stroke within 3 hours (NINDS, two-part design labelled) and, more modestly, at 3–4.5 hours (ECASS III), but IST-3's primary endpoint up to 6 hours in a wider, older population was not significant, with symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage of ~2–7% pricing every window

title: Rituximab + fludarabine–cyclophosphamide in first-line CLL (CLL8): one trial, three labelled reports — better progression-free and overall survival, except in del(17p)
question: In treatment-naïve, physically fit patients with chronic lymphocytic leukaemia, does adding rituximab to fludarabine–cyclophosphamide (FCR vs FC) improve progression-free and overall survival? (Slate row S16-3-03 — the CLL8 question.)
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — one trial, three labelled reports (single-programme shelf): CLL8 randomised 817 fit, treatment-naïve patients with CLL to fludarabine–cyclophosphamide with or without rituximab. FCR improved 3-year progression-free survival (65% vs 45%; hazard ratio 0.56, relative) and overall survival (87% vs 83%; hazard ratio 0.67, relative); at median 5.9 years, median progression-free survival was 56.8 vs 32.9 months and overall survival not reached vs 86.0 months. Benefit was ABSENT in del(17p) and most durable in IGHV-mutated disease — both printed on the face. FCR induced low minimal residual disease more often than FC, and MRD level independently predicted outcome. The pricing harm is neutropenia (grade 3/4 34% vs 21%; prolonged first-year neutropenia 16.6% vs 8.8%), without more severe infections. This is the pre-BTK-inhibitor standard the library's targeted-therapy CLL shelves compare against. NOTE on the commissioning label: slate row S16-3-03 is this CLL8 question (rituximab + FC in CLL); it is not a rituximab-CHOP/DLBCL question, and no DLBCL report is carded here.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — one trial, three labelled reports (CLL8, 817 randomised): rituximab added to fludarabine–cyclophosphamide improved progression-free survival (3-year 65% vs 45%; long-term median 56.8 vs 32.9 months) and overall survival in fit first-line CLL, with benefit absent in del(17p) and more neutropenia as the pricing harm

title: Bevacizumab in first-line non-squamous NSCLC: SPLIT — an overall-survival win in E4599, progression-free survival only in AVAiL, with fatal bleeding in E4599
question: In patients with advanced non-squamous NSCLC, does adding bevacizumab to first-line platinum chemotherapy (paclitaxel–carboplatin in E4599; cisplatin–gemcitabine in AVAiL) improve overall and progression-free survival, and at what bleeding cost?
balance: SPLIT — by chemotherapy backbone. E4599 (878 randomised, paclitaxel–carboplatin): adding bevacizumab prolonged median overall survival (12.3 vs 10.3 months; hazard ratio 0.79, relative) and progression-free survival (6.2 vs 4.5 months), with the benefit concentrated in adenocarcinoma — but with clinically significant bleeding in 4.4% vs 0.7% and 15 treatment-related deaths, including 5 from pulmonary haemorrhage, in a population that excluded squamous tumours, brain metastases and significant haemoptysis. AVAiL (1,043 randomised, cisplatin–gemcitabine): bevacizumab improved progression-free survival (hazard ratios 0.75 and 0.85, relative) but overall survival was NOT significantly increased (hazard ratios 0.93 and 1.03 — the null is printed beside the E4599 headline), with ~62% receiving later-line therapy. The E4599/AVAiL contrast is the shelf.
stamp: SPLIT — bevacizumab added to paclitaxel–carboplatin prolonged overall survival in E4599 (12.3 vs 10.3 months) with 15 treatment-related deaths including 5 pulmonary haemorrhages, while on a cisplatin–gemcitabine backbone (AVAiL) it improved progression-free survival only, with overall survival not significantly increased (hazard ratios 0.93 and 1.03)

title: Erlotinib versus placebo in pretreated NSCLC (BR.21): one trial, three labelled reports — a 2-month median survival gain and delayed symptom deterioration in an unselected population
question: In patients with stage IIIB/IV NSCLC after failure of one or two chemotherapy regimens, does erlotinib 150 mg/day prolong survival and improve symptoms versus placebo (best supportive care comparison)?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — one trial, three labelled reports (single-programme shelf): BR.21 randomised 731 patients with stage IIIB/IV NSCLC after one or two chemotherapy regimens to erlotinib 150 mg/day or placebo. Erlotinib prolonged median overall survival (6.7 vs 4.7 months; hazard ratio 0.70, relative — a modest 2-month absolute gain) and progression-free survival (2.2 vs 1.8 months), with response in 8.9% vs <1%, delayed deterioration of cough, dyspnoea and pain, and better global quality of life (35% vs 26% improved). Five percent discontinued erlotinib for toxicity. In the elderly subgroup (163 patients ≥70), progression-free benefit was preserved but the overall-survival contrast was NOT significant (hazard ratio 0.92) and grade 3/4 toxicity was higher (35% vs 18%) — both printed on the face. This is the unselected-population EGFR trial, run before routine mutation testing.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — one trial, three labelled reports (BR.21, 731 randomised): erlotinib prolonged survival in pretreated, biomarker-unselected NSCLC (median 6.7 vs 4.7 months; hazard ratio 0.70, relative) and delayed symptom deterioration, with a non-significant overall-survival contrast and higher toxicity in the elderly subgroup on the face

title: Letrozole after tamoxifen in early breast cancer (MA.17): one trial, three labelled reports — better disease-free survival, overall survival only in node-positive disease; trial stopped early
question: In postmenopausal women with hormone-receptor-positive early breast cancer who have completed five years of tamoxifen, does five years of letrozole improve disease-free survival versus placebo?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — one trial, three labelled reports (single-programme shelf): MA.17 randomised 5,187 postmenopausal women who had completed five years of tamoxifen to five years of letrozole or placebo. Letrozole improved disease-free survival — estimated 4-year disease-free survival 93% vs 87% at the primary report and an updated hazard ratio of 0.58 (relative; distant disease-free survival hazard ratio 0.60). The trial was STOPPED EARLY at its first interim analysis, which inflates the apparent effect — stated on the face, with the updated hazard ratio beside the primary estimate. Overall survival was null overall (hazard ratio 0.82) and significantly improved only in node-positive patients (hazard ratio 0.61, relative) — a subgroup finding, printed as such. In women ≥70 there was no age interaction and no toxicity/quality-of-life difference at 24 months. Harms: more hormonally related side effects and new osteoporosis diagnoses (5.8% vs 4.5% at the primary report), with fracture rates similar.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — one trial, three labelled reports (MA.17, 5,187 enrolled; stopped early at the first interim analysis): letrozole after five years of tamoxifen improved disease-free survival (updated hazard ratio 0.58, relative), with overall survival null overall and improved only in the node-positive subgroup (hazard ratio 0.61), and more osteoporosis diagnoses as a pricing harm

title: Adjuvant imatinib after GIST resection (Z9001 — one trial, three reports): recurrence-free survival 98% versus 83% at 1 year, no overall-survival benefit shown
question: In patients with completely resected primary gastrointestinal stromal tumour (GIST) at least 3 cm in size and KIT-positive, does one year of adjuvant imatinib 400 mg/day improve recurrence-free and overall survival versus placebo (ACOSOG Z9001)?
balance: LIKELY (benefit for recurrence-free survival; no overall-survival benefit shown), on a single-trial base labelled as such. Z9001 (713 randomised, double-blind) found 1-year recurrence-free survival of 98% on one year of adjuvant imatinib 400 mg/day versus 83% on placebo (hazard ratio 0.35, a relative measure), with recurrence or death in 8% versus 20%. At a median 74 months the recurrence-free-survival advantage persisted (hazard ratio 0.6, relative) in the long-term pathology/molecular report, concentrated in KIT exon 11 deletion tumours, but adjuvant imatinib did not seem to alter overall survival — placebo patients crossed to imatinib at recurrence, so recurrence was deferred rather than shown to be prevented. The third card is a risk-score report built in SSGXVIII and validated in the Z9001 imatinib arm. All three cards are reports of, or using, the one Z9001 programme — never three trials. The duration question (3 years versus 1 year) is homed at live #1926.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit for recurrence-free survival; no overall-survival benefit shown) — one double-blind randomised trial (Z9001, n=713) with a large recurrence-free-survival effect (98% versus 83% at 1 year; hazard ratio 0.35, relative) sustained at long-term follow-up (hazard ratio 0.6, relative), on a labelled single-trial / three-report base

title: MPT in elderly myeloma: survival 51.6 versus 33.2 months (age 65–75) and 44.0 versus 29.1 months (over 75); pooled hazard ratio 0.83 — neuropathy is the price
question: In previously untreated elderly patients with multiple myeloma, does adding thalidomide to melphalan–prednisone (MPT) prolong overall survival versus melphalan–prednisone (MP) alone?
balance: LIKELY (benefit), priced in neuropathy. Two randomised trials split by age band agree: in patients aged 65–75 (IFM 99-06, 447 randomised) MPT gave median overall survival of 51.6 versus 33.2 months on MP (hazard ratio 0.59, relative), and in patients over 75 (IFM 01/01, 229 randomised, placebo-controlled) 44.0 versus 29.1 months. The individual-patient-data meta-analysis of all six randomised MPT trials (1,685 patients, carded as a labelled companion) found a more modest pooled hazard ratio of 0.83 (relative) and a 6.6-month median gain (39.3 versus 32.7 months) — the pooled figure is the conservative summary. Grade 2–4 peripheral neuropathy (20% versus 5% in the over-75 trial) and grade 3/4 neutropenia (23% versus 9%) are the pricing harms, and the reason the regimen was later displaced.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — two randomised trials in complementary age bands (median overall survival 51.6 versus 33.2 months aged 65–75; 44.0 versus 29.1 months over 75) supported by a six-trial individual-patient-data meta-analysis (hazard ratio 0.83, relative; 6.6-month median gain), with peripheral neuropathy as the pricing harm

title: Chemotherapy-era APL (European APL Group): ATRA plus chemotherapy — 4-year survival 76% versus 49% without ATRA; maintenance cut 10-year relapse to 13.4%; omitting cytarabine raised relapse
question: In patients with newly diagnosed acute promyelocytic leukaemia, does adding all-trans retinoic acid (ATRA) to anthracycline-based chemotherapy improve event-free and overall survival versus chemotherapy alone (APL91) — and, once ATRA is standard, do early chemotherapy and maintenance therapy further reduce relapse (APL93), and does omitting cytarabine from ATRA–daunorubicin increase relapse in standard-risk disease (APL2000)?
balance: LIKELY (benefit), as three labelled successive slices of the chemotherapy era, never pooled. APL91 (n=101, printed on the face) found ATRA followed by daunorubicin–cytarabine chemotherapy far superior to the same chemotherapy alone (4-year event-free survival 63% versus 17%; survival 76% versus 49%). APL93 (n=576, 10-year follow-up) showed maintenance therapy cut 10-year relapse from 43.2% to 13.4%, while deaths in complete remission rose steeply with age (5.7% under 55 to 21.7% over 65) — the historical argument for less myelosuppressive treatment. APL2000 showed that in standard-risk disease, omitting cytarabine from ATRA–daunorubicin increased 7-year relapse (28.6% versus 12.9%), a regimen-dependent finding. The ATRA plus arsenic trioxide (chemotherapy-free) question is homed at pack #7496 and is cross-pointed only, never re-carded here.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — ATRA added to anthracycline-based chemotherapy transformed chemotherapy-era APL outcomes in APL91 (4-year survival 76% versus 49%), maintenance further reduced relapse in APL93, and cytarabine omission increased relapse in APL2000; three successive questions carded as labelled slices, not pooled

title: Topiramate in episodic migraine: about two fewer attacks a month versus one on placebo, responder rates roughly doubled, 100 mg/day matched propranolol — 200 mg adds nothing but tolerability cost
question: In patients with episodic migraine (3–12 attacks per month), does topiramate 100–200 mg/day reduce monthly migraine frequency versus placebo, and how does it compare with propranolol?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — modest in absolute terms. Two large 26-week placebo-controlled trials (487 and 483 randomised) agree: topiramate 100–200 mg/day reduced monthly migraine frequency by about −2.1 to −2.4 attacks versus −1.1 on placebo, with 50%-responder rates of roughly 47–54% versus roughly 23%. A third trial (575 randomised) found topiramate 100 mg/day similar to propranolol 160 mg/day on every efficacy measure. Across all three, 200 mg/day added no efficacy over 100 mg/day and was less well tolerated — the flat dose gradient is the prescribing point. Paraesthesia, fatigue and nausea are the pricing harms.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — two concordant large placebo-controlled trials (monthly frequency −2.1 to −2.4 versus −1.1 on placebo; responder rates ~47–54% versus ~23%) plus an active-control trial matching propranolol at 100 mg/day, with no added gain and worse tolerability at 200 mg/day

title: Revised Cardiac Risk Index validation: strata hold (0.5% to 9%) but discrimination falls in vascular surgery (AUC 0.64) and under troponin surveillance (c-statistic 0.60, risks underestimated)
question: Before major noncardiac surgery, how well does the Revised Cardiac Risk Index (high-risk surgery, ischaemic heart disease, heart failure, cerebrovascular disease, insulin treatment, creatinine above 2.0 mg/dL) predict major cardiac complications and death, how far does its discrimination fall in vascular surgery and under modern troponin surveillance, and how does it compare with the NSQIP MICA calculator?
balance: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — field- and era-dependent. The Revised Cardiac Risk Index's six factors stratify risk as derived (major cardiac complications 0.5%, 1.3%, 4% and 9% at 0, 1, 2 and ≥3 factors in derivation; 0.4%, 0.9%, 7% and 11% on prospective validation). Discrimination is a separate claim: a 24-study systematic review (792,740 patients) found AUC 0.75 for cardiac events after mixed noncardiac surgery but only 0.64 after vascular surgery and a median AUC of 0.62 for death. Under modern systematic high-sensitivity troponin T surveillance (VISION-nested vascular cohort, n=870), the c-statistic fell to 0.60 with predicted risks systematically underestimated and no clinical utility before recalibration; NSQIP MICA was only slightly better (0.64). This is a prognostic-accuracy shelf — no card implies that computing the index changes outcomes.
stamp: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — moderate discrimination in mixed noncardiac surgery (AUC 0.75) but poor in vascular surgery (AUC 0.64), poor for death (median AUC 0.62), and miscalibrated under modern troponin surveillance (c-statistic 0.60 with systematic underestimation) — a prognostic-accuracy stamp, not a treatment stamp

title: STOP-Bang in surgical patients: sensitivity 85–90% for OSA at low specificity — and no adjusted association with mortality, cardiac complications or stay in 26,068 patients
question: In adults attending preoperative clinics and having surgery, how accurately does the STOP-Bang questionnaire detect obstructive sleep apnoea against polysomnography — sensitivity and the probability of severe apnoea at each score — in surgical populations, and does a high score predict postoperative complications, mortality or length of stay?
balance: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — split by limb. As a detector of obstructive sleep apnoea against polysomnography, STOP-Bang is highly sensitive in surgical populations: 83.6%, 92.9% and 100% at AHI cut-offs above 5, 15 and 30 at derivation, and pooled preoperative sensitivities of 85%, 88% and 90% — at specificities of only 47%, 29% and 27%, with the probability of severe OSA in surgical patients rising from 15% at a score of 3 to 65% at 7/8. As a prognostic tool, the largest surgical cohort (26,068 patients) found its strata were NOT associated, after adjustment, with 30-day mortality, cardiac complications or length of stay, even though diagnosed OSA rose from 4% to 44% across strata. No card implies screening changes outcomes.
stamp: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — high, severity-graded sensitivity for detecting OSA in surgical patients (pooled 85–90%, specificity only 27–47%) but no adjusted association with postoperative mortality, cardiac complications or length of stay in the largest surgical cohort — a prognostic-accuracy stamp, not a treatment stamp

title: Myocardial injury after noncardiac surgery: 8% by fourth-generation criteria, 17.9% by hsTnT — mostly silent, graded mortality association, incidence assay-dependent (9% I versus 15% T)
question: In adults having inpatient noncardiac surgery, what does routine postoperative troponin surveillance find — how common is myocardial injury after noncardiac surgery (MINS) under fourth-generation troponin T, high-sensitivity troponin T and high-sensitivity troponin I criteria, what troponin thresholds mark prognostically important injury, and how strongly does injury predict 30-day and 1-year death, including in patients with no ischaemic symptoms or ECG changes?
balance: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — a strong, graded, independently confirmed prognostic association, with assay-dependent incidence. In the VISION programme (three reports of one programme, labelled as such): peak fourth-generation troponin T at least 0.02 ng/mL (11.6% of patients) carried adjusted hazard ratios for 30-day death rising from 2.41 to 10.48 across bands (relative measures; absolute mortality 1.0% to 16.9%); MINS (at least 0.03 ng/mL, judged ischaemic) affected 8.0% with an adjusted hazard ratio of 3.87 and the highest population-attributable risk (34.0%); by high-sensitivity troponin T criteria MINS affected 17.9%, 93.1% of it silent. The independent Basel cohort found incidence of 9% by troponin I versus 15% by troponin T in the same patients, both predicting 30-day and 1-year death. No card implies surveillance or any response to injury improves outcomes.
stamp: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — postoperative troponin elevation is common (8.0% by fourth-generation MINS criteria; 17.9% by hsTnT criteria; 9% versus 15% by hs-cTnI versus hs-cTnT in the same patients), mostly silent, and strongly and gradedly associated with 30-day and 1-year mortality across one labelled programme (VISION) and one independent cohort — a prognostic stamp, not a treatment stamp

title: CURB-65 in community-acquired pneumonia: mortality 0.7% to 57% by score at derivation — but the gradient flattens in lower-mortality settings and discrimination is modest (0.67)
question: In adults presenting to hospital with community-acquired pneumonia, how well does the CURB-65 score (confusion, urea above 7 mmol/L — about 20 mg/dL as blood urea nitrogen, respiratory rate at least 30/min, low blood pressure, age at least 65) stratify 30-day mortality at the bedside, how does its discrimination compare with the Pneumonia Severity Index, and where does it misclassify — at low scores in low-mortality settings and at high scores?
balance: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — real stratification, setting-dependent calibration, modest discrimination. In its international derivation and validation (1,068 hospitalised patients), CURB-65 ordered 30-day mortality from 0.7% at score 0 to 57% at score 5. In a prospective 14-hospital Korean cohort (883 patients, overall mortality 4.5%) the gradient flattened at low scores — 2.3%, 4.0%, 6.0%, 5.7% and 23.5% at scores 0 to 4, with the score-5 cell resting on n=2 — and the authors judged CURB-65 more valid at low scores and the Pneumonia Severity Index at high scores. A UK cohort measured a ROC area of only 0.67, no better than two comparator indices. No card implies scoring changes outcomes or settles admission by itself.
stamp: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — CURB-65 stratifies 30-day mortality in hospitalised community-acquired pneumonia (0.7% to 57% across scores 0–5 at derivation) but its per-score mortality is setting-dependent (flattened low-score gradient in a lower-mortality Korean cohort) and its discrimination is modest (ROC area 0.67 in a UK cohort) — a prognostic-accuracy stamp, not a treatment stamp

title: Apfel score for PONV: incidences 10% to 79% by factor count and best of six models (AUC 0.68) — but calibration failed on hepatectomy validation (AUC 0.612, slope 0.49)
question: Before general anaesthesia, how well does the Apfel simplified risk score for postoperative nausea and vomiting (female sex, history of motion sickness or PONV, non-smoking, postoperative opioids) predict PONV within 24 hours — what incidence does each score count carry, how does it compare with the Koivuranta and other published predictive models, and does it hold up on external validation outside its derivation settings?
balance: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — a steep risk gradient with modest discrimination that degrades externally. The Apfel four-factor score (female sex, history of motion sickness or PONV, non-smoking, postoperative opioids) carried PONV incidences of 10%, 21%, 39%, 61% and 79% at derivation, with cross-centre AUCs of 0.65–0.75. Against five rival models it discriminated best (AUC 0.68 versus 0.61–0.66) and calibrated best while using the fewest parameters. On external validation in hepatectomy for liver cancer, however, its ROC area fell to 0.612 with poor calibration (slope 0.49), and Koivuranta (0.628) was no better — neither was well validated in that field. No card implies scoring changes outcomes; prophylaxis treatment is homed at live #658.
stamp: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — the Apfel score's four-factor incidence gradient (10% to 79%) is steep and it beat five rival models on discrimination, calibration and simplicity, but discrimination is modest everywhere (AUC 0.61–0.75) and calibration failed on external validation in hepatectomy (slope 0.49) — a prognostic-accuracy stamp, not a treatment stamp

title: Renin and aldosterone reference intervals: six healthy-population datasets — intervals belong to their assay (RIA reads aldosterone 59% higher than LC-MS/MS), sex and age; healthy ratio limits 14.2–25.5
question: In healthy adults, what are the reference intervals for plasma renin (activity and direct concentration) and plasma aldosterone concentration — the central 95% ranges by age, sex, assay method (radioimmunoassay, chemiluminescence immunoassay, LC-MS/MS) and population — how far do method-specific intervals sit from one another, what sampling influences (including posture) are recognised, and what upper limit for the aldosterone-to-renin ratio follows from healthy-population distributions rather than from hypertensive referral cohorts?
balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, adrenal / renin–angiotensin–aldosterone sections, and Boron & Boulpaep, adrenal gland chapter — the framing is brief, and this shelf rests chiefly on the primary reference-interval literature, and says so. Six independent healthy-population datasets (1,347 German population-based subjects; 328 Chinese Han chemiluminescence subjects; 282 Belgian LC-MS/MS volunteers, aldosterone limb only; 170 Hong Kong normotensive volunteers; 309 northern Chinese Han volunteers; 5,200 rigorously screened Yunnan individuals) agree on the structure: intervals are specific to assay, sex and age band, renin activity and direct renin concentration are different measurements with different intervals, and healthy-population aldosterone-to-renin ratio upper limits (14.2–25.5 by sex and age) sit clearly below hypertensive-referral cut-offs. The single most important number is a bias: radioimmunoassay reads plasma aldosterone on average 59% higher than LC-MS/MS. Intervals are never merged across methods on this shelf. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — six independent healthy-population datasets across four assay approaches consistently establish that plasma renin and aldosterone reference intervals are assay-, sex- and age-specific (including a 59% radioimmunoassay-versus-LC-MS/MS aldosterone bias in plasma), even though each interval belongs to its own method and population and several datasets' numeric limits are not printed in their fetched records

title: ANA in healthy people: 'positive' is threshold-made — 26.0% at 1:40 and 9.5% at 1:160 in Japan, 54.3% any fluorescence in Mexico, 13.8% overall in US NHANES
question: In healthy general populations, what proportion of people carry antinuclear antibodies (ANA) by indirect immunofluorescence on HEp-2 cells — prevalence by titre threshold (1:40, 1:80, 1:160), staining pattern, age and sex — which disease-specific autoantibodies (anti-Ro/SSA, anti-centromere, anti-U1RNP and others) are found in people with no rheumatic disease, and how much do assay and threshold move the 'positive' fraction?
balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, immunity / autoimmunity sections — the framing is brief, and this shelf rests chiefly on the primary population-survey literature, and says so. Threshold-dependence is the answer: three independent general-population datasets (2,181 Japanese town residents; 304 healthy Mexican individuals; 4,754 US NHANES participants aged 12 years and over) give 'positive' fractions of 26.0% at a 1:40 threshold and 9.5% at 1:160 (Japan), 54.3% for any fluorescence across titres 1:40–1:320 (Mexico), and 13.8% overall (NHANES) — different kinds of 'positive' that are never merged into one number on this shelf. Every prevalence prints with its titre threshold and assay. Disease-specific autoantibodies (anti-Ro/SSA, anti-centromere, anti-U1RNP) are found in people with no rheumatic disease, and in the Japanese cohort 57% of examined disease-specific-positive individuals were clinically healthy. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — the base is three large independent population datasets concordant on the core claim (ANA is common in healthy people and the fraction is set by the threshold), not a single small series.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED

title: Avasimibe (ACAT inhibitor, never marketed): A-PLUS IVUS trial null on plaque progression and LDL cholesterol ROSE 7.8–10.9% relative — development ended
question: In adults with hypercholesterolaemia or coronary atherosclerosis, does the ACAT (acyl-CoA:cholesterol acyltransferase) inhibitor avasimibe (CI-1011), compared with placebo or atorvastatin alone, improve lipid levels or slow coronary atherosclerosis progression (the A-PLUS programme)?
balance: Discontinued agent — this flag leads. Avasimibe was never marketed; development ended after A-PLUS. The balance is a null imaging trial in which the drug RAISED LDL cholesterol, one 8-week lipid trial whose only wins were triglyceride and VLDL cholesterol (surrogate measures, with no significant change in total, LDL or HDL cholesterol or apolipoprotein B), and a 27-patient crossover in homozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia where avasimibe alone changed nothing. IVUS plaque volume and lipid levels are surrogate endpoints; no clinical-outcomes trial exists, and the programme must not be presented as lipid efficacy. PROPOSED STAMP: LIKELY (no benefit).
stamp: LIKELY (no benefit) — the only imaging trial (A-PLUS) was null on plaque progression while LDL cholesterol rose on the drug, the lipid trial's only wins were triglyceride/VLDL surrogates with no LDL change, and the agent was never marketed

title: Eprotirome added to statins: LDL down 22–32% relative in phase 2 — but the AKKA phase 3 was terminated over cartilage damage in dogs, and the drug was never marketed
question: In adults with hypercholesterolaemia (including heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia) already treated with a statin, does the liver-selective thyroid hormone receptor agonist eprotirome (KB2115), compared with placebo, lower LDL cholesterol — and what safety signal ended the programme (the AKKA trial)?
balance: Discontinued agent — this flag leads. Eprotirome was never marketed: its phase 3 (AKKA) was prematurely terminated when another study found cartilage damage in dogs, leaving an analysable remnant of 69 patients at 6 weeks, and AKKA must not be presented as a completed phase 3. On the surrogate endpoint the signal is consistent: LDL cholesterol fell 22% relative at 100 µg in the AKKA remnant, 28–32% relative at 50–100 µg added to statins over 12 weeks, and 23–31% relative in primary hypercholesterolaemia — but liver enzymes rose in every trial, free thyroxine fell, and no cardiovascular-outcomes trial exists. PROPOSED STAMP: POSSIBLE (benefit) on LDL lowering alone, with the termination and the dog-cartilage signal on the face.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — consistent short-term LDL lowering (surrogate endpoint only) across three trials, but the phase 3 was terminated over cartilage damage in dogs with only 69 patients analysable at 6 weeks, liver enzymes rose, and the agent was never marketed

title: Arzoxifene (never marketed): GENERATIONS — vertebral fractures down 41% relative and breast cancer down 56% relative, venous thromboembolism up 2.3-fold relative, nonvertebral fractures NOT reduced
question: In postmenopausal women with osteoporosis or low bone mass, does the selective estrogen receptor modulator arzoxifene, compared with placebo or raloxifene, prevent fractures and increase bone mineral density — and what was its thromboembolic cost (the GENERATIONS programme)?
balance: Never-marketed agent — this flag leads. Arzoxifene's fracture trial succeeded on vertebral fractures and invasive breast cancer, and still no product was marketed. The venous-thromboembolism increase (0.7 percentage points absolute; 2.3-fold relative) is printed beside the fracture win, and nonvertebral fractures were NOT significantly reduced. Only GENERATIONS answers the fracture question; the other three anchors (NEXT vs raloxifene, the phase 2 dose-ranging trial, FOUNDATION) are bone-mineral-density / bone-turnover surrogate trials, and that distinction is printed on each card. Relative reductions are labelled relative, with the absolute differences the abstracts give printed alongside. PROPOSED STAMP: SPLIT.
stamp: SPLIT — GENERATIONS reduced vertebral fractures (41% relative) and invasive breast cancer (56% relative) but did not reduce nonvertebral fractures and increased venous thromboembolic events 2.3-fold relative; the supporting trials are BMD surrogates, and the agent was never marketed

title: Rivoglitazone (never marketed): phase 3 HbA1c −0.7% — statistically SUPERIOR to pioglitazone — with class oedema, and development still ended
question: In adults with type 2 diabetes, does the thiazolidinedione rivoglitazone, compared with placebo or pioglitazone, improve glycaemic control?
balance: Discontinued agent — this flag leads. Rivoglitazone was never marketed despite a phase 3 that met superiority against pioglitazone at the higher dose. Its glycaemic record is consistent (HbA1c −0.7% on 1.5 mg in the phase 3; placebo-subtracted falls of −0.55% to −1.10% dose-dependently in the dose-ranging trial; significant falls versus placebo in a 12-week Chinese trial), but HbA1c is a surrogate endpoint, no outcomes trial exists, the dose-ranging trial lost more than half its participants early, and the class harms — peripheral oedema (5.2–6.2% drug-related in the phase 3 versus 0.7% on placebo) and weight gain — are printed on the face. PROPOSED STAMP: POSSIBLE (benefit) for glycaemic control only.

title: Bucindolol in advanced HFrEF: BEST (n=2,708) — mortality 30% vs 33%, NOT significant; the large beta-blocker heart-failure trial that missed
question: In adults with advanced chronic heart failure (NYHA class III–IV, ejection fraction ≤35%), does the non-selective beta-blocker bucindolol, compared with placebo, reduce mortality — and how does its record differ from the beta-blockers that succeeded (the BEST programme)?
balance: The null headline leads. BEST is the large beta-blocker heart-failure trial that did NOT show a survival benefit, in a class where other agents did — the class effect must not be borrowed for this molecule. BEST randomised 2,708 patients with NYHA class III–IV heart failure and LVEF ≤35% and was stopped on its data and safety monitoring board's recommendation at the seventh interim analysis: deaths 30% on bucindolol versus 33% on placebo, not significant (adjusted P = 0.13), with favourable secondary endpoints (cardiovascular death HR 0.86; death-or-transplantation HR 0.87 — relative measures) printed after the primary null. The two supporting anchors are small, short LVEF / haemodynamic (surrogate) trials, labelled as such. Bucindolol was never marketed for heart failure in the US. BEST's companion subgroup and genotype reports are further reports of the same trial and are not carded as separate evidence. PROPOSED STAMP: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) on mortality.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — BEST, the definitive 2,708-patient trial stopped early by its monitoring board, found no significant mortality benefit (30% vs 33%; adjusted P = 0.13); favourable secondary endpoints and two small short LVEF trials do not borrow the class effect of the beta-blockers that succeeded

title: Oral enoximone in chronic heart failure: ESSENTIAL (n=1,854) null on mortality and hospitalisation — and the 1990 trial's 10 vs 3 deaths on intention-to-treat
question: In adults with chronic heart failure, does oral enoximone (a phosphodiesterase inhibitor), compared with placebo, improve exercise capacity, symptoms or clinical outcomes — and what did the earliest trial's mortality count show (the ESSENTIAL programme)?
balance: The mortality record is this row. The programme's arc is given in full: a small 1990 trial with significantly more deaths on enoximone (10 versus 3 on intention-to-treat analysis, P < 0.05, with dropout 46% versus 25%), a small 2000 low-dose trial with an exercise-capacity win and no arrhythmia signal, and the large modern ESSENTIAL programme (1,854 randomised) that was safe but null on outcomes — mortality HR 0.97 (95% CI 0.80 to 1.17) and mortality-or-cardiovascular-hospitalisation HR 0.98 (0.86 to 1.12), hazard ratios being relative measures. The cards are ordered so the largest trial comes last and carries the most weight. Enoximone was never marketed orally for chronic heart failure in the US, and the exercise-capacity result must not be presented as clinical benefit. PROPOSED STAMP: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) on major clinical outcomes.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — the large ESSENTIAL programme found no difference in mortality (HR 0.97) or mortality/cardiovascular hospitalisation (HR 0.98); the programme's arc runs from a small 1990 trial with significantly more deaths on the drug to a small exercise-capacity win, and exercise capacity is a surrogate, not clinical benefit

title: Pimobendan in human heart failure: PICO — exercise duration +121.6 s and quality of life better in HFrEF; MONACO in HFpEF null (+26.9 m vs +21.4 m, P = 0.402) and terminated early; not marketed for human HF in the US
question: In adults with heart failure, does the calcium-sensitising inotrope pimobendan, compared with placebo, improve exercise tolerance and quality of life in reduced-ejection-fraction disease — and does it help in HFpEF with right-ventricular–pulmonary-arterial uncoupling?
balance: Two phenotypes, two answers, never pooled. In reduced-ejection-fraction disease, the PICO trial (198 patients, 12 weeks) showed pimobendan 5 mg/day increasing exercise duration by 121.6 s and improving quality of life versus placebo, with deaths 5% on drug versus 6% on placebo (not significant) — exercise capacity and quality of life are surrogate / soft endpoints, and no mortality trial of pimobendan in human heart failure exists in this base. The Japanese evidence is a published programme SUMMARY (Kato 1997), labelled as such on its card — not a single trial report. In HFpEF with right-ventricular–pulmonary-arterial uncoupling, the MONACO trial (50 patients, single country) was terminated early after an invalid interim analysis and was null on 6-minute walk distance. Pimobendan is not marketed for human heart failure in the US; its veterinary trial record is animal evidence and is counted nowhere on this shelf. PROPOSED STAMP: SPLIT.
stamp: SPLIT — in HFrEF, PICO showed better exercise duration, peak VO2 and quality of life over 12 weeks (surrogate / soft endpoints, no mortality trial); in HFpEF with RV–PA uncoupling, MONACO was null and terminated early; the Japanese evidence is a programme summary, labelled as such

title: Cotadutide glycaemic/weight slice in T2D ± CKD (PARTIAL beside kidney pack #6665): HbA1c and weight down vs placebo across phase 2 — programme not advanced to phase 3
question: In adults with type 2 diabetes and overweight or obesity (with or without chronic kidney disease), does the GLP-1/glucagon co-agonist cotadutide, compared with placebo or liraglutide, improve glycaemic control and body weight (the glycaemic programme slice)?
balance: PARTIAL slice only — this flag leads. The kidney question stays homed at pack #6665 under the one-home rule, and #6665's own glycaemic support card (the phase 2a JCEM trial, PMID 31608926) is homed there and is cross-pointed here, never re-carded; this shelf cards only the three glycaemic-programme reports that are carded nowhere else. On that slice: the 54-week phase 2b trial (834 randomised) found cotadutide significantly decreased HbA1c and body weight versus placebo at weeks 14 and 54 (all P < 0.001; the record prints no HbA1c point estimates and none are claimed), with nausea in 35% and vomiting in 17%; the 32-day CKD phase 2a trial (41 randomised) cut mixed-meal glucose AUC by 26.71% relative and weight by 3.41 kg; the mechanistic phase 2a trial's primary endpoints were hepatic glycogen — a surrogate of a surrogate. stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — phase 2 only: a 54-week phase 2b trial (n=834) with significant HbA1c and weight reductions vs placebo, a 32-day CKD phase 2a trial (n=41) and a short mechanistic hepatic-glycogen trial; the programme was not advanced to phase 3 on the glycaemic question and no outcomes trial exists

title: Vupanorsen (ANGPTL3 antisense, discontinued): triglycerides down 41–57% relative and non-HDL cholesterol down 22–28% relative — but a dose-dependent hepatic-fat increase of up to 76% relative ended development
question: In adults with hypertriglyceridaemia or elevated non-HDL cholesterol, does the ANGPTL3 antisense oligonucleotide vupanorsen, compared with placebo, lower triglycerides and atherogenic lipoproteins — and what hepatic harm ended its development?
balance: Discontinued agent — this flag leads. Vupanorsen's development was discontinued after TRANSLATE-TIMI 70: the dose-dependent increase in hepatic fat fraction (up to 76% relative; absolute increase up to 7.0 percentage points) and the transaminase elevations (over 3× the upper limit of normal in up to 44.4% at higher doses) printed in its own primary report are the central fact of the programme and lead this balance, ahead of the lipid wins. Programme labelling: three reports but only TWO distinct trials — the hepatic-fat paper (Zimerman 2024) is a companion report of TRANSLATE-TIMI 70 (227 of its 286 participants), counted as a report of one programme, not independent evidence. All endpoints are lipid (surrogate) measures; no outcomes trial exists. Percent changes are relative measures and are labelled as such throughout. PROPOSED STAMP: SPLIT.

title: Lixivaptan in euvolaemic hyponatraemia: exactly 2 phase 3 trials — sodium rose more than on placebo in both, on a surrogate that reverses within a week of stopping
question: In hospitalised or non-hospitalised adults with euvolaemic hyponatraemia, does the selective vasopressin V2-receptor antagonist lixivaptan, compared with placebo, raise serum sodium?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) on a FLOOR-RISK base of exactly 2 reports. Both are phase 3 trials from one sponsor's programme in euvolaemic hyponatraemia only, and both met their day-7 serum-sodium primary endpoint: in hospitalised patients sodium rose 6.7 mmol/L (approx. 15.4 mg/dL) on lixivaptan versus 4.5 mmol/L (approx. 10.4 mg/dL) on placebo (P=0.034), and in outpatients 3.2 mmol/L (approx. 7.4 mg/dL) versus 0.8 mmol/L (approx. 1.8 mg/dL), with normal sodium by day 7 in 39.4% versus 12.2%. Serum sodium is a surrogate endpoint: neither trial tested mortality or length of stay, the effect reversed within 7 days of stopping in the inpatient trial, no hypervolaemic results report was located, and lixivaptan was never marketed for this indication in the US. The homed vaptans (tolvaptan, conivaptan, satavaptan) are different agents and are not re-carded here.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — FLOOR-RISK: exactly 2 phase 3 reports, both positive on the day-7 serum-sodium surrogate in euvolaemic hyponatraemia only (6.7 vs 4.5 mmol/L (approx. 15.4 vs 10.4 mg/dL) inpatient; 3.2 vs 0.8 mmol/L (approx. 7.4 vs 1.8 mg/dL) outpatient), with reversal within 7 days of stopping and no mortality or length-of-stay data

title: Perhexiline in chronic HFrEF: exactly 2 results reports (106 patients) — exercise capacity and energetics improved, ejection fraction disagreed, no outcomes trial
question: In adults with chronic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, does the metabolic modulator perhexiline, compared with placebo, improve exercise capacity, ejection fraction and cardiac energetics?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) on a FLOOR-RISK base of exactly 2 results reports totalling 106 randomised patients, both short-term. In the 2005 chronic heart failure trial, peak oxygen consumption, ejection fraction and quality of life all improved significantly on perhexiline. In the 2015 dilated-cardiomyopathy trial, the myocardial phosphocreatine/ATP ratio rose 30% relative and NYHA class improved, but ejection fraction did NOT change — the two trials disagree on ejection fraction, and both readings are printed. Every endpoint is a surrogate or soft measure; no outcomes trial exists. The HFpEF paper in this programme is a hypothesis/design abstract only and is never counted or carded as a report. Perhexiline is an old antianginal with a narrow therapeutic index: therapeutic drug monitoring is required where it remains available (Australia/New Zealand), and it is not marketed in the US.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — FLOOR-RISK: exactly 2 results reports totalling 106 patients, both short-term, on surrogate/soft endpoints only (peak VO2, energetics, NYHA class); the two trials disagree on ejection fraction and no outcomes trial exists

title: Gemcabene for lipids: 2 randomised trials — HDL/triglycerides up at low doses, LDL down at high doses and on a statin; the HoFH report is sub-floor (N=8, uncontrolled)
question: In adults with hypercholesterolaemia or low HDL cholesterol, does gemcabene, compared with placebo (alone, added to a statin, or added to standard care in homozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia), lower LDL cholesterol and triglycerides and raise HDL cholesterol?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) on a FLOOR-RISK base of exactly 3 reports, only 2 of them randomised. In the low-HDL dose-response trial (161 patients), the lipid effect split by dose: at 150-300 mg, HDL cholesterol rose up to 18% relative and triglycerides fell up to 39% relative in the high-triglyceride stratum, while at 600-900 mg LDL cholesterol fell 15-25% relative in both strata. Added to a statin (66 patients, 8 weeks), gemcabene lowered LDL cholesterol by 23.4% and 27.7% relative versus 6.2% relative on placebo. The third report, COBALT-1 in homozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia, is sub-floor (N=8, open-label, uncontrolled) and is never load-bearing. All endpoints are lipid (surrogate) measures; no outcomes trial exists, and no marketed product resulted from these trials.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — FLOOR-RISK: exactly 2 randomised trials (161 and 66 patients, 8-12 weeks) showing relative lipid improvements, plus one sub-floor open-label HoFH report (N=8) that is never load-bearing; surrogate endpoints only, no outcomes trial
