title: Inhaled ciclesonide for COVID-19: six trials, no primary endpoint met anywhere — and one imaging-defined pneumonia-progression harm signal
question: In adolescents and adults with COVID-19 — non-hospitalised with symptoms, hospitalised with mild disease, or hospitalised on oxygen — does inhaled ciclesonide versus placebo, usual care or control shorten symptoms or oxygen therapy, and reduce worsening, emergency visits, admission and pneumonia progression?
balance: LIKELY (no difference) — a consistently negative programme: six randomised trials across three care settings (outpatients, hospitalised mild disease, hospitalised patients on oxygen), and no primary endpoint was met anywhere. The single positive reading is a secondary endpoint (fewer emergency visits or admissions, odds ratio 0.18) inside a primary-negative US trial. The Japanese RACCO trial is a harm limb: pneumonia progressed more often on ciclesonide (39.0% versus 18.8%; relative risk 2.08) on an imaging endpoint, without worse clinical symptoms. Settings and eras are not pooled: pre-vaccination 2020-21 outpatient trials, a hospitalised-on-oxygen trial, and a 2026 trial in a 96%-vaccinated Omicron population are separate limbs. Inhaled budesonide for COVID-19 is a different agent, homed at pack #2213, and is cross-pointed only — its trials are not re-carded here.
stamp: LIKELY (no difference) — six randomised trials across outpatient, mild inpatient and hospitalised-on-oxygen settings met no primary endpoint anywhere; the one positive reading is a secondary endpoint, and the RACCO trial showed an imaging-defined pneumonia-progression harm signal (relative risk 2.08)

title: Stretta radiofrequency for GERD: symptoms move, acid exposure doesn't — and the PPI-refractory heartburn trial was flatly negative
question: In adults with gastro-oesophageal reflux disease — including PPI-responsive disease and PPI-refractory heartburn — does endoluminal radiofrequency energy delivery (the Stretta procedure) to the gastro-oesophageal junction versus a sham procedure improve heartburn, reflux quality of life, acid exposure and medication use?
balance: SPLIT — symptoms move, reflux does not. In the early sham-controlled trials, heartburn and reflux quality-of-life scores improved more on active radiofrequency (Stretta) than on sham, while oesophageal acid exposure and medication use did not differ in the first trial and did not change in the mechanistic crossover trial. The three-arm dose trial's improvements are within-group readings against baseline, labelled as such. The programme's most rigorous trial — in PPI-refractory heartburn, the population most often offered the procedure — was flatly negative: its primary endpoint was reached by 3.4% on radiofrequency versus 15.1% on sham. Every trial is small (n=22-64) with subjective primary endpoints, so expectation effects are the standing alternative explanation. The tested procedure is the Stretta radiofrequency system as the publications name it (clarification exception); results do not transfer to other endoluminal devices.
stamp: SPLIT — symptom and quality-of-life scores improved versus sham in the early small trials while oesophageal acid exposure and medication use did not, and the one trial in PPI-refractory heartburn was flatly negative (primary endpoint 3.4% radiofrequency vs 15.1% sham)

title: Torasemide vs furosemide in cirrhotic ascites: 6 small reports (1988-1997, documented N=87 + one N not documented) — more natriuresis short-term, surrogates only
question: In patients with cirrhosis and ascites — including diuretic-resistant ascites — does torasemide versus furosemide (each on a background of an aldosterone antagonist) produce greater natriuresis, diuresis and weight loss?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) on a FLOOR-RISK base stated exactly: 6 randomised reports, all from 1988-1997, with documented N=87 plus one report whose abstract states no N (printed as N not documented). Every trial is small (n=7-28 where stated), short (single dose to 70 days), and powered only on surrogate endpoints — urine sodium, urine volume and weight over hours to days. Torasemide produced greater natriuresis or diuresis in most of the short trials, while the one long-term (70-day) trial found similar weight, urinary volume and sodium effects with less electrolyte excretion on torasemide. No trial measures ascites resolution, hospitalisation, renal failure or survival. All trials gave an aldosterone antagonist to both arms — this is loop-diuretic choice on top of spironolactone/canrenoate, not torasemide monotherapy — and the equipotency doses were set from healthy-volunteer data. One retrieved record (a xipamide trial with an open torasemide series appended) is fenced out of this count and is not carded.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — FLOOR-RISK: exactly 6 randomised reports from 1988-1997, documented N=87 plus one report with N not documented, all on surrogate endpoints (natriuresis, diuresis, weight over hours to days); greater short-term natriuresis on torasemide, no difference at 70 days, and no clinical-outcome data

title: Losartan for portal hypertension: a non-randomised ~45% HVPG fall never replicated — four small randomised trials (n=136) split, the largest negative with a renal harm limb
question: In patients with cirrhosis and portal hypertension, does losartan versus propranolol (or versus untreated control) reduce hepatic venous pressure gradient, and at what cost to arterial pressure and renal function?
balance: SPLIT — an unreplicated dramatic start, then small split trials. The programme's originating controlled study (1999, NOT randomised, labelled programme support) reported a ~45% relative fall in hepatic venous pressure gradient (HVPG) on losartan — a result no later trial approached. The four randomised trials (n=27-40, total 136) split: two report responder-rate or within-group HVPG advantages for losartan, while the largest and longest — in patients treated after variceal bleeding — found losartan did not reduce HVPG at all (-2% versus -10% on propranolol) and concluded losartan is not an alternative to propranolol. Every endpoint is the HVPG surrogate over 2-12 weeks; no trial measures variceal bleeding or death. The harm limb is on the face: arterial pressure fell in most reports, and glomerular filtration rate fell in Child-Pugh B patients in the 2001 trial. Populations differ (post-bleeding, compensated, decompensated) and are never pooled.
stamp: SPLIT — four small randomised trials (total n=136) split on the HVPG surrogate: responder/within-group advantages in two, equal responders in one, and no HVPG effect in the largest post-bleeding trial, which also showed a GFR fall in Child-Pugh B patients; the originating ~45% relative fall was non-randomised programme support and was never replicated

title: UDCA in NASH/MASH: histology negative at both doses (n=166 and n=185) — the positive trial measured ALT, not the disease
question: In adults with biopsy-proven non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH/MASH), does ursodeoxycholic acid — at conventional dose, at high dose, or combined with vitamin E — versus placebo improve liver histology and liver enzymes over 12-24 months?
balance: LIKELY (no difference) on histology — the disease answer is negative at both doses, and it is printed on the face. The two trials with histological primary endpoints (n=166 at conventional dose over 2 years; n=185 at high dose over 18 months) found no benefit over placebo in steatosis, necroinflammation, fibrosis or overall histology. The positive trial (n=126) had a biochemical primary endpoint: ALT fell 28.3% relative on high-dose UDCA versus 1.6% on placebo, and ALT normalised in 24.5% versus 4.8% — an enzyme answer, not a disease answer, in a programme where liver biochemistries also improved on placebo in the 2004 trial. The combination limb (UDCA plus vitamin E, n=48) improved enzymes and steatosis-driven activity but cannot attribute its signal to UDCA rather than vitamin E, and UDCA alone in that same trial did not separate histologically. Era flag: pre-resmetirom, pre-GLP-1-era MASH care in biopsy-defined NASH populations — a closed question, not a treatment option. Norursodeoxycholic acid is a different drug; its NAFLD trial is never counted here.
stamp: LIKELY (no difference) — both histology-primary trials were negative at conventional dose (n=166) and high dose (n=185); the one positive trial had an ALT (surrogate) primary endpoint, and the UDCA-plus-vitamin-E limb cannot attribute its signal to UDCA

title: Nitazoxanide in HCV genotype 4: one positive programme trial (SVR 79% vs 50%), then two larger independent negatives — an interferon-era record
question: In patients with chronic hepatitis C genotype 4, does nitazoxanide — as monotherapy, or added to peginterferon + ribavirin (with a nitazoxanide lead-in) — versus placebo or standard peginterferon + ribavirin increase rapid and sustained virological response?
balance: LIKELY (no difference) as an adjunct — and the interferon-era flag leads: every trial here is peginterferon-era, genotype 4, Egyptian, and the question is closed by the direct-acting-antiviral era; this shelf is a record of a tested-and-failed adjunct, never an option against current standard care. One positive programme trial (2009, from the developer-linked Egyptian programme) reported sustained virological response of 79% with nitazoxanide triple therapy versus 50% on standard care. Two larger independent trials then failed to reproduce it: SVR 50% versus 48% (n=100, open-label) and 58.2% versus 60.8% (n=195 evaluated, double-blind placebo-controlled) — differences of 2 and -2.6 percentage points. The earlier monotherapy signal (undetectable HCV RNA in 30.4% versus 0%) was confined to patients with low baseline viral load, a subgroup reading. Nitazoxanide is a licensed antiparasitic used off-label here, stated plainly.
stamp: LIKELY (no difference) — one positive developer-linked programme trial (SVR 79% vs 50%) was not reproduced by two larger independent trials (50% vs 48% and 58.2% vs 60.8%); all evidence is peginterferon-era genotype 4 and the question is closed by the direct-acting-antiviral era

title: Topical paromomycin for cutaneous leishmaniasis: ulcerative lesions respond (vs vehicle in two trials), non-ulcerative disease does not — and Panama had no vehicle arm
question: In patients with cutaneous leishmaniasis, does topical 15% paromomycin — alone, with gentamicin, or in an aquaphilic base — versus vehicle/placebo (or versus an intralesional active control) cure lesions, and does the answer differ between ulcerative and non-ulcerative disease?
balance: SPLIT — lesion type and species decide the answer, and the trials are never pooled. For ulcerative lesions, topical 15% paromomycin beat vehicle in Tunisia (cure 81-82% versus 58%) and in Bolivia (77.5% versus 10%) — note how much natural history varies by species and setting (vehicle cure 58% versus 10%), so the absolute benefit is setting-dependent and is printed per trial, not averaged. The Panama trial compared the two active creams with each other (79% versus 78%) and has NO vehicle arm, so its cure rates cannot by themselves establish efficacy over natural healing. The one trial in non-ulcerative disease was negative. The tested formulations differ (WR 279,396 paromomycin-gentamicin cream; paromomycin in aquaphilic base; paromomycin with urea in white paraffin) and are named as the publications give them, under the clarification exception; other preparations may differ in safety and effectiveness. No trial measures mucosal-leishmaniasis prevention or scarring — lesion cure only.
stamp: SPLIT — topical paromomycin beat vehicle in ulcerative disease in Tunisia (81-82% vs 58%) and Bolivia (77.5% vs 10%), the Panama trial compared two active creams with no vehicle arm (79% vs 78%), and the one non-ulcerative trial was negative; absolute benefit is species- and setting-dependent

title: HSV suppression to slow HIV progression in ART-naive dually infected people: acyclovir cut progression hazards by 16% and 25% in relative terms (HR 0.84 and 0.75, absolutes beside) — a pre-treat-all-era record
question: In people dually infected with HIV-1 and HSV-2 who are not taking antiretroviral therapy, does daily suppressive acyclovir (or valacyclovir) versus placebo delay HIV-1 disease progression (CD4 decline, ART initiation, death) and lower plasma HIV-1 RNA?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a real but modest and now-superseded effect. Two randomised progression trials in ART-naive people dually infected with HIV-1 and HSV-2 found daily acyclovir slowed a composite progression endpoint: hazard ratio 0.84 (284 vs 324 events, n=3,381) and adjusted hazard ratio 0.75 (95 vs 110 events, n=440) — both relative measures, labelled relative, with absolute event counts beside them. A postpartum valacyclovir trial (n=148) moved CD4 and viral-load markers only and is a labelled supportive limb, never load-bearing. The composites were driven mainly by CD4 thresholds and ART initiation, not mortality, and every participant was ART-naive by pre-treat-all standards — in the treat-all era this intervention has no place in routine care. The transmission question is homed at shelf #2196 and is not re-carded here.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — daily acyclovir modestly slowed HIV-1 disease progression in two randomised trials in ART-naive, HSV-2-dually infected people (hazard ratios 0.84 and 0.75, both relative measures with absolute event counts 284 vs 324 and 95 vs 110 printed beside them), supported on markers only by a postpartum valacyclovir limb that is never load-bearing; a pre-treat-all-era record, not a current treatment option

title: Camostat for COVID-19: four double-blind trials, all null — no benefit on improvement, viral clearance or symptoms, even at 4–8 times the clinical dose
question: In adults with COVID-19 — hospitalised, or non-hospitalised with mild-to-moderate disease — does oral camostat mesilate versus placebo speed clinical improvement or viral clearance and reduce hospitalisation and death?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — a uniformly negative programme, presented as one. Four double-blind placebo-controlled randomised trials of oral camostat mesilate in COVID-19 — two hospitalised (n=205; n=155) and two in mild-to-moderate / non-hospitalised disease (n=342; n=216) — met no primary endpoint anywhere: clinical improvement, viral clearance and symptom resolution were the same on camostat as on placebo, including at four to eight times the Japanese clinical dose in the CANDLE study, which closes the 'underdosed' objection. Camostat was not notably unsafe; it simply did not work. Endpoints, variants and vaccination eras differed per trial and are labelled, never pooled.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — failed programme: four double-blind placebo-controlled trials of camostat in COVID-19 (n=205, 155, 342 and 216) met no primary endpoint in hospitalised or outpatient disease, including at supratherapeutic dose in CANDLE; the in-vitro TMPRSS2 rationale did not translate

title: Thymosin alpha-1 in sepsis (FLOOR-RISK — exactly 2 trials): ETASS borderline positive (26.0% vs 35.0% mortality), TESTS phase 3 null (23.4% vs 24.1%)
question: In adults with severe sepsis / sepsis (Sepsis-3), does thymosin alpha-1 added to standard care versus placebo or standard care reduce 28-day all-cause mortality?
balance: SPLIT — FLOOR-RISK, exactly 2 trials. ETASS (n=361, single-blind, China) reported lower 28-day mortality on thymosin alpha-1 (26.0% vs 35.0%; relative risk 0.74, 95% CI 0.54–1.02 — a relative measure beside its absolute rates), but the result was borderline: P=0.062 unstratified and P=0.049 by log-rank, printed exactly as reported. TESTS (n=1,106, double-blind placebo-controlled phase 3, China) then found nothing: 23.4% vs 24.1% (hazard ratio 0.99, 95% CI 0.77–1.27; P=0.93) and no secondary-outcome benefit. That arc — not an averaged estimate — is the shelf's answer. Ulinastatin + thymosin combination trials are never counted here; the hepatitis B question is homed at pack #7524.
stamp: SPLIT — based on exactly 2 trials: ETASS (n=361, single-blind) was borderline positive on 28-day mortality (26.0% vs 35.0%; relative risk 0.74, 95% CI 0.54–1.02; P=0.062 unstratified / P=0.049 log-rank), while the TESTS phase 3 trial (n=1,106, double-blind) found no benefit (23.4% vs 24.1%; hazard ratio 0.99, 95% CI 0.77–1.27; P=0.93)

title: Isatuximab combinations in relapsed/refractory myeloma: PFS improved in both programmes (11.5 vs 6.5 and 35.7 vs 19.2 months); survival borderline in ICARIA-MM, null in IKEMA
question: In patients with relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma, does adding the anti-CD38 antibody isatuximab to pomalidomide–dexamethasone (ICARIA-MM, after ≥2 prior lines including lenalidomide and a proteasome inhibitor) or to carfilzomib–dexamethasone (IKEMA, after 1–3 prior lines) improve progression-free and overall survival?
balance: LIKELY (benefit, for progression-free survival) — the honest headline is a PFS drug. Both phase 3 programmes improved progression-free survival clearly: ICARIA-MM (isatuximab–pomalidomide–dexamethasone, after ≥2 prior lines) 11.5 vs 6.5 months (hazard ratio 0.596, relative) and IKEMA (isatuximab–carfilzomib–dexamethasone, after 1–3 prior lines) 35.7 vs 19.2 months on updated analysis (hazard ratio 0.58, relative), with deeper responses in IKEMA (MRD negativity 33.5% vs 15.4%). Overall survival is weaker: ICARIA-MM's final analysis is borderline (24.6 vs 17.7 months; hazard ratio 0.78, 95% CI 0.59–1.02, interval crossing 1, with daratumumab crossover in the control arm) and IKEMA's is null (hazard ratio 0.855, 95% CI 0.608–1.202). Two trials, six reports — labelled slices by backbone, never pooled.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit, for progression-free survival) — ICARIA-MM and IKEMA both improved PFS when isatuximab was added (hazard ratios 0.596 and 0.58 on updated analysis, relative measures with absolute medians beside them), while overall survival is borderline in ICARIA-MM (final hazard ratio 0.78, 95% CI 0.59–1.02) and not different in IKEMA (hazard ratio 0.855, 95% CI 0.608–1.202)

title: Pembrolizumab in relapsed/refractory Hodgkin lymphoma: responses 69–71% (single-arm KEYNOTE-087) and PFS 13.2 vs 8.3 months vs brentuximab (KEYNOTE-204); survival not analysed
question: In patients with relapsed or refractory classical Hodgkin lymphoma, does pembrolizumab produce durable responses after autologous transplant and/or brentuximab vedotin failure (KEYNOTE-087, single-arm) — and does it beat brentuximab vedotin head-to-head on progression-free survival (KEYNOTE-204)?
balance: LIKELY (benefit, for response and progression-free survival; no overall-survival comparison) — KEYNOTE-087 is single-arm and is stamped as such: pembrolizumab gave response rates of 69.0% (complete response 22.4%) after autologous transplant and/or brentuximab failure, and 71.4% at 5 years with a median duration of response of 16.6 months. The randomised evidence is KEYNOTE-204, where pembrolizumab beat brentuximab vedotin on progression-free survival (13.2 vs 8.3 months; hazard ratio 0.65 — a relative measure beside its absolute medians), with quality of life improving on pembrolizumab and worsening on brentuximab; overall survival was not analysed at the reported interim analysis, and no survival claim is made. Cross-point: the nivolumab programme in the same setting is shelf #7608, never pooled.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit, for response and progression-free survival) — single-arm KEYNOTE-087 response rates of 69.0–71.4% with durable responses, and randomised KEYNOTE-204 superiority over brentuximab vedotin on progression-free survival (13.2 vs 8.3 months; hazard ratio 0.65, relative); overall survival was not analysed at the reported interim analysis, so no survival claim is made

title: Nivolumab in R/R Hodgkin lymphoma after transplant failure (single programme, single-arm — labelled): CheckMate 205 responses 66–71%, median response duration up to 18.2 months
question: In patients with relapsed or refractory classical Hodgkin lymphoma whose disease has failed autologous haematopoietic cell transplantation, does nivolumab produce durable responses — in brentuximab-naïve patients and in those who received brentuximab before and/or after transplant (CheckMate 205)?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single programme, labelled: the entire shelf rests on one single-arm phase 2 programme, CheckMate 205 (243 patients after autologous transplant failure, in brentuximab-naïve and brentuximab-exposed cohorts). Objective response rates were 66.3% in the primary cohort B report, 69% at extended follow-up and 71.2% at 5 years, with median durations of response of 16.6–18.2 months and median progression-free survival of 15.1 months at 5 years. Five-year overall survival of 71.4% is a within-cohort description, not a treatment effect. Entirely single-arm evidence — response and durability claims only; no comparative claim is available. Cross-point: pembrolizumab in the same setting is shelf #7607, never pooled.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single programme, labelled: CheckMate 205 alone (single-arm, 243 patients after autologous transplant failure) showed nivolumab objective response rates of 66.3–71.2% across its three reports with median response durations of 16.6–18.2 months; there is no comparator, so no comparative or survival-effect claim is made

title: Eculizumab in PNH — the founding slice (PARTIAL beside #1804/#845): TRIUMPH 49% vs 0% haemoglobin stabilisation, 0 vs 10 median units; SHEPHERD and the pre/post TE analysis
question: In patients with paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria, does the terminal-complement (C5) inhibitor eculizumab reduce intravascular haemolysis, stabilise haemoglobin and cut transfusion requirements versus placebo (TRIUMPH) — and are the effects maintained in a broader, openly treated population (SHEPHERD), including on thromboembolism, the disease's leading cause of death?
balance: PARTIAL beside live #1804 and live #845 — only the founding slice is carded here: eculizumab versus placebo (TRIUMPH) and versus the pre-treatment course (SHEPHERD and the pooled analyses). LIKELY (benefit) on that slice: TRIUMPH, the one placebo RCT (n=87), found haemoglobin stabilisation without transfusion in 49% (21/43) vs 0% (0/44) and a median of 0 vs 10 transfused units, with the LDH area under the curve 85.8% lower (a relative measure beside its absolutes). SHEPHERD (n=97, single-arm) extended the effect to a broader population (LDH down 87% against baseline; 51% transfusion-independent for 52 weeks). The thromboembolism figure (1.07 vs 7.37 events per 100 patient-years; 85% relative, 6.3 absolute) is a pre/post contrast, not a randomised endpoint. Meningococcal infection risk on terminal-complement blockade is the pricing harm. Ravulizumab vs eculizumab is live #1804 and proximal inhibitors are live #845 — neither re-carded.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — PARTIAL, founding slice only, beside live #1804/#845: one small placebo RCT (TRIUMPH, n=87; haemoglobin stabilisation 49% vs 0%, median transfused units 0 vs 10) plus a single-arm companion (SHEPHERD, n=97) and pre/post analyses, including thromboembolism at 1.07 vs 7.37 events per 100 patient-years (85% relative reduction, 6.3 absolute, not a randomised contrast)

title: Cabazitaxel vs mitoxantrone after docetaxel in mCRPC (FLOOR-RISK — exactly 2 reports, TROPIC): survival 15.1 vs 12.7 months; pain palliation comparable, neutropenia 82% vs 58%
question: In men with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer progressing during or after docetaxel, does cabazitaxel 25 mg/m² plus prednisone prolong overall survival versus mitoxantrone plus prednisone?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — FLOOR-RISK, exactly 2 reports, both of one trial. TROPIC (n=755 men with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer progressing during or after docetaxel) found cabazitaxel 25 mg/m² plus prednisone prolonged median overall survival versus mitoxantrone plus prednisone (15.1 vs 12.7 months; hazard ratio 0.70, 95% CI 0.59–0.83 — a relative measure beside its absolute medians, a gain of about 2.4 months). The second report, the 2-year survival and pain analysis, found more patients alive at 2 years (odds ratio 2.11, relative) and pain palliation comparable — not superior — to mitoxantrone. The price was taxane toxicity: grade ≥3 neutropenia 82% vs 58%, febrile neutropenia 8% vs 1%. The CARD question at pack #6420 presupposes this founding benefit; cross-point only.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — FLOOR-RISK, based on exactly 2 reports of one trial (TROPIC, n=755): cabazitaxel plus prednisone prolonged median overall survival after docetaxel versus mitoxantrone plus prednisone (15.1 vs 12.7 months; hazard ratio 0.70, 95% CI 0.59–0.83, relative), with pain palliation comparable to mitoxantrone and grade ≥3 neutropenia in 82% vs 58%

title: Preoperative CPET prediction by surgical field: AT rules out risk (NPV 96–100%) far better than it rules it in (PPV 2.9–42.1%); thresholds are field-specific, never one cut-off
question: Before major noncardiac surgery, how well does cardiopulmonary exercise testing (CPET) predict postoperative death and cardiopulmonary complications — what anaerobic-threshold (AT) and ventilatory-efficiency (VE/VCO2) thresholds separate high from low risk, how do the thresholds move by surgical field (major abdominal, hepatic resection, pancreaticoduodenectomy, oesophagogastric resection), and how good is the test's classifier performance (sensitivity, specificity, predictive values) when it is audited as a test rather than as a cohort association?
balance: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — rule-out strong, rule-in weak, and field-specific. The founding cohorts separated risk sharply at an anaerobic threshold (AT) of 11 mL/min/kg (mortality 18% vs 0.8% in elderly surgery; no cardiopulmonary deaths among CPET-assigned ward patients in major abdominal surgery, whose assignment was not randomised). By field: hepatic resection — AT 9.9 mL/kg/min, 100% sensitive and 76% specific for in-hospital death, NPV 100% but PPV 19%, with VE/VCO2 at AT of 34.5 predicting complications; pancreaticoduodenectomy — AT and peak VO2 did not predict, VE/VCO2 at AT did (AUC 0.84, threshold 41); oesophagogastric resection — a complication gradient only (42% / 29% / 20% across AT bands), discrimination low. The 36-study classifier audit (Stubbs 2020) is the counterweight: AT sensitivities for mortality 20–100%, NPVs 96–100%, PPVs only 2.9–42.1%, and no CPET score externally validated. A prognostic-accuracy balance, not a treatment balance: nothing here shows CPET-guided triage improves outcomes.
stamp: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — CPET rules out postoperative risk far better than it rules it in: anaerobic-threshold negative predictive values of 96–100% against positive predictive values of only 2.9–42.1% in the 36-study classifier audit, with field-specific thresholds (AT 11 general, 9.9 hepatic; VE/VCO2 34.5 hepatic vs 41 pancreaticoduodenectomy) that are never merged, and no CPET score externally validated

title: POSSUM / P-POSSUM prediction: discrimination moderate (c 0.79–0.85) but the original equation overpredicts death >2× overall and 6–7× in low-risk patients; calibration fails externally without recalibration
question: In adults having general and specialist surgery, how accurately do POSSUM and its Portsmouth modification (P-POSSUM) — a 12-factor physiological score plus a 6-factor operative severity score — predict postoperative mortality and morbidity, where does the original POSSUM equation miscalibrate (and by how much in the lowest-risk patients, who are most surgical patients), and how do the scores perform on external validation in emergency laparotomy and in specialist fields against the NELA and ACS-NSQIP models?
balance: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — discrimination moderate, calibration the problem. POSSUM (a 12-factor physiological score plus a 6-factor operative severity score) and its Portsmouth modification rank patients moderately well — concordance statistics 0.79 for P-POSSUM to 0.85 for NELA in external emergency-laparotomy validation, and AUC 0.755 for in-hospital mortality (about 0.70 for morbidity) in elective hepatic resection. But the original POSSUM mortality equation miscalibrates badly: it overpredicted deaths more than twofold overall and sixfold (1996 evaluation) to more than sevenfold (1998, 10,000 episodes) in the lowest-risk group — most surgical patients — with a minimum predicted mortality of 1.08%. P-POSSUM fitted its derivation-era data closely, yet in external validation every model except surgeon-adjusted ACS-NSQIP was poorly calibrated, and hepatic-resection calibration slopes were below 1: the scores are usable only after local recalibration. The operative severity score is not fully knowable before surgery. A prognostic-accuracy balance, not a treatment balance.
stamp: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — POSSUM / P-POSSUM discriminate moderately (concordance 0.79–0.85 externally; AUC 0.755 for mortality in hepatic resection) but the original POSSUM equation overpredicts mortality more than twofold overall and six- to sevenfold in the lowest-risk patients, and external validations find poor calibration without local recalibration; a prognostic-accuracy stamp, not a treatment stamp

title: ASA physical status: a single subjective grade predicts mortality only moderately (sensitivity 0.74, specificity 0.67) — better in low-death-rate settings, and assigned unreliably
question: Before surgery, how much does the American Society of Anesthesiologists physical status (ASA-PS) classification — a single subjective grade from I (healthy) to V (moribund) — actually predict postoperative mortality and medical complications, how does its accuracy vary with the population's underlying death rate and surgical field (inpatient vs ambulatory), and how reliably do anaesthetists assign the same patient to the same class?
balance: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — moderate, setting-dependent, and unreliably assigned. A single subjective grade (ASA physical status I–V) discriminates postoperative mortality only moderately on pooled evidence (77 studies, 165,705 patients: sensitivity 0.74, specificity 0.67, summary ROC area 0.736), performing better where underlying death rates are lower. The gradient is real and steep — in 2,089,830 ambulatory cases ASA class associated stepwise with complications (c-statistic 0.70), mortality (0.74) and readmission (0.67), with an odds ratio of 89 for death in ASA IV versus healthy patients against 0.08% absolute mortality — and the grade tracks objective comorbidity (27 of 31 Elixhauser groups), yet an objective-measures model predicted 30-day mortality better than ASA alone. The reliability limb is weak: in a 601-anaesthetist fictitious-case survey agreement was low and accuracy fell with experience. Neither 'ASA works' nor 'ASA is useless' is the finding; a c-statistic near 0.74 for a one-item subjective grade, with low inter-rater agreement, is.
stamp: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — ASA physical status discriminates postoperative mortality moderately (pooled sensitivity 0.74, specificity 0.67, summary ROC 0.736 across 77 studies; mortality c-statistic 0.74 in 2,089,830 ambulatory cases), performs better in lower-death-rate settings, tracks objective comorbidity but is beaten by objective-measures models, and is assigned with low inter-observer agreement that falls with experience — a prognostic-accuracy finding, not evidence that assigning a class changes outcomes

title: Rapid shallow breathing index: founding sensitivity 0.97 settles to pooled sensitivity 0.83 and specificity 0.58 at <105 — a permissive test, not an extubation rule
question: In mechanically ventilated adults being assessed for liberation from the ventilator, how accurately does the rapid shallow breathing index (RSBI — respiratory frequency divided by tidal volume, f/VT) predict successful weaning and extubation, what does the classic threshold of 105 breaths/min/L actually deliver in sensitivity and specificity on modern pooled evidence, and how far does the threshold (105 vs 80 vs 65, and the measurement conditions) move the answer?
balance: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — a founding near-perfect result settling to moderate sensitivity and poor specificity. The rapid shallow breathing index (f/VT) began with sensitivity 0.97 and the largest ROC area (0.89) among weaning indexes in Yang & Tobin's 100-patient founding study. On modern pooled evidence — 48 studies, 10,946 patients — RSBI <105 breaths/min/L has sensitivity 0.83 (95% CI 0.78 to 0.87) and specificity only 0.58 (95% CI 0.49 to 0.66) for extubation success, with thresholds <80 and 80–105 performing similarly; the 2001 evidence review already showed the asymmetry (positive likelihood ratios ≤2.23; negative 0.09 to 0.23). The index is permissive / rule-out-flavoured, not a pass–fail extubation rule, and no card implies acting on it improves outcomes.
stamp: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — the rapid shallow breathing index (f/VT) at the classic <105 threshold has moderate pooled sensitivity (0.83) and poor pooled specificity (0.58) for extubation success across 48 studies and 10,946 patients, down from the founding study's sensitivity 0.97 in 100 patients; thresholds <80 and 80–105 perform similarly, so 105 is a permissive criterion, not a stand-alone pass–fail extubation rule

title: CAM-ICU for ICU delirium: specificity stays ~0.95 on pooling while sensitivity falls to 0.80–0.84 — better than ICDSC chiefly at ruling delirium out
question: In critically ill adults, including mechanically ventilated patients who cannot speak, how accurately does the Confusion Assessment Method for the Intensive Care Unit (CAM-ICU) detect delirium against a DSM reference standard — what are its pooled sensitivity and specificity, how do they compare with the Intensive Care Delirium Screening Checklist (ICDSC), and what moderates accuracy (hypoactive delirium, ventilation, ICU type)?
balance: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — very high specificity, moderate pooled sensitivity. CAM-ICU's founding validation was near-perfect (sensitivities 100% and 93%, specificities 98% and 100%, kappa 0.96 in 96 evaluable ventilated patients), but pooling costs sensitivity: 80.0% sensitivity with 95.9% specificity (9 studies, 969 patients; AUC 0.97) in 2012, and 0.84 / 0.95 across 29 studies in the 2021 bivariate meta-analysis. Against ICDSC (74% / 81.9%, then 0.83 / 0.87), CAM-ICU's advantage is chiefly specificity. Accuracy is moderated by hypoactive-delirium proportion, ICU type, ventilation and case mix — no single pooled pair is the test's performance in all ICUs, and no card implies screening improves outcomes.
stamp: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — CAM-ICU detects ICU delirium against a DSM reference standard with pooled sensitivity 0.80–0.84 and specificity 0.95–0.96 (founding validation 93–100% / 98–100%), outperforming ICDSC mainly on specificity (0.87–0.82 pooled), with accuracy moderated by hypoactive delirium, ICU type and ventilation — a diagnostic-accuracy finding, not evidence that screening improves outcomes

title: 4AT for delirium: pooled sensitivity 0.88 / specificity 0.88 on 2 anchors + 1 supporting validation — ROC 0.89 even with dementia, weaker in severe cognitive impairment
question: In hospitalised older adults on wards, in the emergency department and after surgery, how accurately does the 4AT (the 4 'A's Test — alertness, AMT-4, attention, acute change or fluctuating course) detect delirium against a reference standard, how does it perform in patients with dementia and after stroke, and how long does it take at the bedside?
balance: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — good pooled accuracy on a stated base of 2 anchors + 1 verified supporting validation (3 reports in total). The founding validation (236 patients aged ≥70) gave sensitivity 89.7%, specificity 84.1% and ROC area 0.93 — 0.89 in patients with dementia, the population where the test is hardest. The anchor meta-analysis (17 studies, 3,702 observations) pooled sensitivity 0.88 and specificity 0.88 at 24.2% prevalence (ex-stroke 0.86 / 0.89). The one supporting independent validation (Swedish, 200 patients) was weaker — sensitivity 0.70, specificity 0.92, AUROC 0.808, worst on the severe-cognitive-impairment ward. The test takes under 2 minutes. No card implies detection improves outcomes.

title: Braden scale: AUC 0.82 in general hospital studies, but specificity 0.28 in ICU and sensitivity 0.42 in surgical patients — one scale, three different tests
question: In hospitalised and critically ill adults, how well does the Braden scale (sensory perception, moisture, activity, mobility, nutrition, friction / shear) predict who will develop a pressure injury — what are its pooled sensitivity, specificity and discrimination at the usual cut-offs, what cut-off performs best, and how badly does its performance fall in surgical and intensive-care populations?
balance: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — moderate overall, and sharply setting-dependent. Across 60 general hospital studies (49,326 individuals) the Braden scale pools at sensitivity 0.78, specificity 0.72 and AUC 0.82, with 18 the optimal cut-off in that one analysis. The same scale in ICU (11 studies, 10,044 patients) over-flags — sensitivity 0.89, specificity 0.28, AUC 0.78 — and in surgical patients (3 studies, 609 patients) under-detects — sensitivity 0.42, specificity 0.84, AUC 0.69, with the authors concluding it cannot be used alone there. No pooled figure stands without its setting, and no card implies scoring or score-allocated prevention reduces injuries.
stamp: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — the Braden scale predicts pressure injury moderately in general hospital populations (pooled sensitivity 0.78, specificity 0.72, AUC 0.82; optimal cut-off 18 in that analysis) but performs very differently by setting: sensitivity 0.89 / specificity 0.28 in ICU and sensitivity 0.42 / specificity 0.84 (AUC 0.69, cannot be used alone) in surgical patients — a prognostic-accuracy finding, not evidence that scoring or score-allocated prevention reduces injuries

title: Soluble α-Klotho reference intervals: 4 datasets — levels fall with age (founding range 239–1,266 pg/mL), but two assays on the same samples do not correlate, so intervals are assay-specific
question: In healthy adults, what are the reference intervals for soluble α-Klotho in serum — the central range by age and sex — how steeply do levels fall with age, and how far apart are the intervals given by different immunoassays measuring nominally the same protein?
balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, mineral / ageing-related sections, and Boron & Boulpaep — the framing is brief, and this shelf rests chiefly on the primary reference-interval literature, and says so. Four independent adult datasets (N = 142, 120, 346 and 890) agree that soluble α-Klotho falls with age and shows no, or only a slight, sex difference (population medians 678 pg/mL in women vs 651 pg/mL in men). The defining problem is assay discordance: in the 120-adult head-to-head, two immunoassays did not correlate and neither recognised the other's standard (TRF medians 61 ng/mL in men / 99 ng/mL in women vs ELISA mean 472 pg/mL), so intervals are assay-specific to an unusual degree and units differ by three orders of magnitude as published, never converted silently. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (age gradient and assay-specificity consistent across 4 datasets; no universal interval exists).
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — four independent adult datasets (142, 120, 346 and 890 people) consistently show soluble α-Klotho falling with age with no or only a slight sex difference, and establish that reference intervals are assay-specific — two immunoassays on the same samples do not correlate — so each interval stands only with its named assay and units as published

title: CSF protein and glucose reference values: 5 protein + 3 glucose datasets — protein rises with age (upper limits to 93.4 mg/dL, not 45), and the glucose ratio falls as serum glucose rises; most datasets are indirect derivations
question: In adults, what are the reference intervals for cerebrospinal fluid total protein and for cerebrospinal fluid glucose (and the CSF:serum glucose ratio) — how steeply does total protein rise with age, how much higher is it in men, how far do modern age-partitioned upper limits sit above the traditional 45 mg/dL, and how must the normal glucose ratio be adjusted for the serum glucose?
balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, cerebrospinal fluid sections, and Boron & Boulpaep — brief, and this shelf rests chiefly on the primary reference-interval literature, and says so. Datasets: 5 for total protein and 3 for glucose / the CSF:serum ratio. Protein rises markedly with age and is higher in men in every dataset; modern age-partitioned upper limits sit far above the traditional ~45 mg/dL (Mayo 95% interval to 93.4 mg/dL; Huashan upper limit 900 mg/L (90 mg/dL) above 76 years). The glucose limb is a ratio limb — median CSF glucose ~60% of serum, with lower limits that fall as serum glucose rises. METHOD HONESTY IS THE SPINE: only 2 of the 8 datasets sampled people not undergoing diagnostic work-up; the rest are indirect derivations from screened patient / reference-like populations, the field's standard method, stated on every card. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED for the age / sex protein pattern and the serum-adjusted ratio; the exact limits remain method- and population-bound.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — five protein datasets and three glucose / ratio datasets consistently establish that CSF total protein rises with age and is higher in men (modern age-partitioned upper limits to ~93 mg/dL, above the traditional ~45 mg/dL) and that the CSF:serum glucose ratio must be adjusted for serum glucose (5th-percentile limits 0.5 / 0.4 / 0.3 by rising serum band); most datasets are indirect derivations from screened patient populations, stated on the face, which is the field's standard method

title: Serum NfL reference values: 4 datasets — levels rise 2.9% per year, so 'normal' exists only age-banded (upper limit 9.7 ng/L at 18–40 years, 53.8 ng/L over 65) or as Z scores
question: In healthy adults, what are the reference intervals for serum neurofilament light chain (NfL) — how steeply do levels rise with age (and body-mass index), what do age-banded upper limits look like on single-molecule-array (Simoa) measurement, and how are individual values expressed as age-corrected percentiles and Z scores against a large reference database?
balance: Guyton & Hall and Boron & Boulpaep have no NfL reference chapter — this shelf rests on the primary reference literature alone, with the textbooks framing axonal-injury biology only, and says so. Four datasets (one of them a pooled four-cohort reference database, labelled as such and counted as one): Benkert's 5,390-control database (exponential age rise, steeper after ~50, BMI-modulated, expressed as percentiles and Z scores); Scandinavian Simoa intervals in 342 subjects (+2.9% per year; upper limits 9.7 ng/L at 18–40 years rising to 53.8 ng/L over 65); a Thai range in 223 adults (median 5.8 pg/mL; 97.5th percentiles 8.7 pg/mL in the 20s to 18.2 in the 60s); and age-split values in 116 adults (<10 pg/mL below 45, <15 above; GFAP limb secondary, single-dataset). NfL is meaningless without age — no unbanded range is printed. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED for the age-banded structure across 4 datasets.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — four datasets (342, 223 and 116 subjects plus a labelled pooled four-cohort database of 5,390 controls) consistently establish that serum neurofilament light chain rises steeply with age (2.9% per year; upper limits rising roughly fivefold from young adults to over-65s) and is properly expressed only as age-banded reference intervals, age-corrected percentiles or Z scores, with BMI a secondary modifier

title: Creatine kinase population distribution: upper limits 2–5× the manufacturer's — 97.5th percentile 1,001 U/L in black men vs 382 U/L in white men, and 49% of healthy black participants misclassified
question: In healthy general populations, what is the distribution of serum creatine kinase (CK) activity — the upper reference limits (97.5th percentile) by sex and ancestry — how far do population-derived upper limits sit above assay manufacturers' limits, and what fraction of healthy people are misclassified as having 'hyperCKaemia' by manufacturer limits?
balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, muscle / enzyme sections — brief, and this shelf rests chiefly on the primary population-distribution literature, and says so. Datasets: 3 independent populations, plus one supporting dataset with its N not documented in its abstract (labelled, not counted). Population-derived upper limits sit 2–5 times above assay manufacturers' limits (random sample of 1,444 rested adults), so manufacturer limits misclassify 13% of white Europeans, 23% of South Asians and 49% of black participants as having 'hyperCKaemia'. NHANES (10,096 adults) gives 97.5th percentiles of 382 U/L (white men), 1,001 U/L (black men), 295 U/L (white women) and 487 U/L (black women); ancestry differences are not explained by body composition, though age differences largely are. Ancestry partitioning is the content, not a caveat. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — three independent population datasets (1,444 rested adults in a stratified random sample; 10,096 NHANES adults; 1,537 employee-population individuals), plus one labelled N-not-documented supporting dataset, consistently establish that serum creatine kinase is partitioned by sex and ancestry, that population upper limits sit 2–5 times above manufacturer limits (97.5th percentile 1,001 U/L in black men vs 382 U/L in white men), and that manufacturer limits misclassify up to 49% of healthy black participants

title: Fasiglifam (GPR40) for T2D: HbA1c fell −0.65% to −0.93% vs placebo — and liver injury (ALT ≥3× ULN 2.1% vs 0.5%) terminated the programme and its outcomes trial; never marketed
question: In adults with type 2 diabetes, does the GPR40 (free fatty acid receptor 1) agonist fasiglifam (TAK-875), compared with placebo or added to sitagliptin, improve glycaemic control — and what liver injury ended its development?
balance: LIKELY harm-led, discontinued agent — the termination leads. Fasiglifam (TAK-875), a GPR40 agonist, lowered HbA1c consistently (global phase 3: −0.65% and −0.93% vs −0.17% on placebo; Japanese phase 3: −0.57% and −0.83% vs +0.16%; added to sitagliptin: a further −0.45% to −0.61%) — and was never marketed, because its own trials documented drug-induced liver injury: ALT >3× ULN in 3.6% and 2.8% versus none on placebo in the global phase 3, and in the cardiovascular-outcomes trial — terminated at 3,207 of 5,000 planned participants for liver safety — ALT or AST ≥3× ULN in 2.1% versus 0.5% and ≥10× ULN in 0.31% versus 0.06%. That terminated trial's HR 1.05 rests on 40 events and is uninformative about cardiovascular safety. HbA1c is a surrogate endpoint throughout; one anchor is a single-region (Japan) trial, flagged on its card.
stamp: LIKELY (harm) — fasiglifam improved glycaemic control consistently across 4 reports (HbA1c −0.57% to −0.93% vs placebo; −0.45% to −0.61% added to sitagliptin, a surrogate endpoint) but was terminated for drug-induced liver injury documented in its own trials (ALT >3× ULN 3.6% / 2.8% vs 0% on placebo in phase 3; ALT or AST ≥3× ULN 2.1% vs 0.5% in the cardiovascular-outcomes trial, which was stopped at 3,207 of 5,000 planned and whose HR 1.05 on 40 events is uninformative); the agent was never marketed

title: Insulin peglispro (IMAGINE): HbA1c wins over glargine in type 1 and type 2 diabetes — against increased liver fat, triglycerides and liver enzymes; discontinued, never marketed
question: In adults with type 1 or type 2 diabetes, does the hepato-preferential basal insulin peglispro (LY2605541), compared with insulin glargine, improve glycaemic control — and what did it do to liver fat, triglycerides and liver enzymes (the IMAGINE programme)?
balance: SPLIT — a discontinued, never-marketed hepato-preferential basal insulin whose glycaemic wins came with a hepatic price, printed beside every win. Across the IMAGINE programme peglispro beat insulin glargine on HbA1c in type 2 diabetes (IMAGINE 2 difference −0.29%; IMAGINE 5 difference −0.52% at 26 weeks) and in type 1 diabetes (IMAGINE 1 difference −0.37%), with less nocturnal hypoglycaemia in relative terms in all three trials. Against that, triglycerides and aminotransferases were higher on peglispro in every trial, MRI liver fat content rose on peglispro versus glargine in IMAGINE 5 and failed to fall as it did on glargine in IMAGINE 2, injection-site reactions were more frequent, and in type 1 diabetes total hypoglycaemia was 29% higher in relative terms with more severe hypoglycaemia. Development stopped after phase 3; there is no outcomes trial. HbA1c is a surrogate endpoint.
stamp: SPLIT — peglispro beat glargine on HbA1c in all three IMAGINE trials carded (−0.29%, −0.52% and −0.37%) with less nocturnal hypoglycaemia in relative terms, but raised triglycerides, aminotransferases and MRI liver fat content, caused more injection-site reactions, and increased total and severe hypoglycaemia in type 1 diabetes; a discontinued, never-marketed agent with no outcomes trial

title: Tezosentan in acute heart failure (VERITAS/RITZ): haemodynamics improved, dyspnoea and outcomes did not — 26% vs 26% death or worsening heart failure at 7 days
question: In adults hospitalised with acute decompensated heart failure, does the intravenous dual endothelin-receptor antagonist tezosentan, compared with placebo, improve dyspnoea, haemodynamics or clinical outcomes (the RITZ / VERITAS programme)?
balance: LIKELY (no difference) — the null headline leads. Tezosentan, an intravenous dual endothelin-receptor antagonist, genuinely improved haemodynamics in a 292-patient invasive trial (cardiac index up, wedge pressure down 3.9 mm Hg more than placebo), but that physiology converted into nothing clinically: in VERITAS-1 and VERITAS-2 (1,448 randomised) dyspnoea did not improve more than placebo in either trial and death or worsening heart failure at 7 days was 26% in each group (odds ratio 0.99); in RITZ-4 (acute heart failure with acute coronary syndrome) the composite endpoint was numerically worse on tezosentan (28.9% vs 24.2%, not significant) with more symptomatic hypotension. title: Xamoterol in chronic heart failure: symptom benefit in mild disease — but 9.1% vs 3.7% mortality in severe heart failure; the harm leads
question: In adults with chronic heart failure, does the beta-1 partial agonist xamoterol, compared with placebo or digoxin, improve symptoms and exercise capacity — and what did it do to mortality in severe heart failure?
balance: SPLIT, severity-dependent — and the mortality harm leads. In the programme's largest trial, 516 patients with severe (NYHA class III–IV) heart failure, xamoterol improved breathlessness scores but not exercise duration, and significantly MORE patients died on xamoterol within 100 days: 32 (9.1%) vs 6 (3.7%) on placebo (P = 0.02) — an absolute excess of 5.4 percentage points. The mirror image comes from milder disease: a sponsor programme summary of randomised monotherapy studies in 425 patients with mild-to-moderate heart failure (labelled a programme report) found improved exercise capacity, signs, symptoms and quality of life, and a 19-patient crossover found xamoterol comparable to digoxin on exercise duration. The mild-disease symptom reports must not be pooled against the severe-disease mortality result. Xamoterol was withdrawn / never marketed for heart failure in the US. Exercise capacity and symptom scores are surrogate / soft endpoints.
stamp: SPLIT — severity-dependent: xamoterol eased symptoms in mild-to-moderate heart failure (programme-summary evidence, labelled) but significantly increased mortality in severe heart failure — 9.1% vs 3.7% dead within 100 days (P = 0.02) in the 516-patient trial, which carries the greatest weight; the mortality harm leads

title: Flosequinan in chronic heart failure: PROFILE — mortality increased (HR 1.39), trial stopped for harm; REFLECT/FACET exercise wins do not offset it
question: In adults with chronic heart failure, does the oral vasodilator / inotrope flosequinan, compared with placebo (added to digoxin, diuretics and an ACE inhibitor), improve exercise capacity and symptoms — and what did its mortality trial show (the PROFILE programme)?
balance: LIKELY (harm) — the mortality harm leads, printed first and heaviest. Flosequinan, an oral vasodilator with inotropic effects, won consistently on exercise and symptoms in two smaller trials (REFLECT: maximal exercise time +96 s vs +47 s on placebo; FACET: median exercise time +64 s vs +5 s at the once-daily dose, with a better quality-of-life score). But in PROFILE, the one trial large enough to measure survival (2,354 patients with NYHA class III–IV disease and ejection fraction ≤35%), flosequinan increased mortality: 255 deaths vs 192 on placebo over an average of 10 months, hazard ratio 1.39 (95% CI 1.15 to 1.67; P = 0.0006) — a 39% relative increase — and the trial was terminated early on the data and safety monitoring board's recommendation because of that harm. The exercise results must not be presented as benefit without the mortality record attached. Flosequinan was withdrawn and is not marketed. PROFILE's primary results were published only in 2017, 24 years after the trial.

title: Pramlintide in insulin-treated type 2 diabetes: modest HbA1c benefit with weight loss across two 52-week trials (the type 2 slice; type 1 homed at #1779)
question: In adults with type 2 diabetes treated with insulin, does adjunctive pramlintide (the amylin analogue), compared with placebo, improve glycaemic control and body weight (the type-2-diabetes slice)?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the type 2 diabetes slice only (the type 1 programme is homed at pack #1779 and is not re-carded). Four reports but only TWO distinct trials: two 52-week randomised trials in insulin-treated type 2 diabetes (656 and 538 randomised) plus two pooled post-hoc analyses of those same trials, carded and labelled as programme reports. Effects are modest and consistent: on the higher doses HbA1c fell about 0.6–0.7% from baseline at 52 weeks, significantly more than placebo (placebo-corrected ≈ −0.4 to −0.6% in the pooled analyses), with weight loss instead of insulin-associated gain (−1.4 kg vs +0.7 kg at week 52 in one trial; placebo-corrected −1.8 to −2.0 kg in the pooled analyses) and no overall increase in severe hypoglycaemia. Nausea is the signature harm. The trials predate modern background therapy (insulin ± sulfonylurea/metformin era, baseline HbA1c ≈ 9%). HbA1c is a surrogate endpoint; no outcomes trial exists.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two 52-week randomised trials in insulin-treated type 2 diabetes (656 and 538 randomised) show modest HbA1c benefit with weight loss instead of gain and no overall increase in severe hypoglycaemia, at the cost of frequent nausea; the two further reports are pooled analyses of the same trials, labelled as programme reports; type 2 slice only, beside the type 1 home at pack #1779

title: Fimasartan in hypertension (Korea-only programme): non-inferior to losartan, superior to valsartan on ambulatory pressure in FAST — 6–12-week blood-pressure trials, no outcomes data
question: In Korean adults with mild-to-moderate essential hypertension, does the angiotensin-receptor blocker fimasartan, compared with losartan, valsartan, placebo or its own monotherapy (when combined with amlodipine), lower blood pressure?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single-region (Korea) programme, and that flag leads: every anchor is a Korean trial of 6–12 weeks with blood pressure, a surrogate endpoint, as the outcome; there is no outcomes trial and fimasartan is not marketed in the US or Europe. Within that fence the results are consistent across four phase 3/4 reports: fimasartan was non-inferior to losartan on sitting diastolic pressure at 12 weeks (−11.26 mm Hg from baseline; between-group difference 2.70 mm Hg favouring fimasartan in a post-hoc comparison), low-dose fimasartan 30 mg beat placebo (−9.93 vs −2.08 mm Hg diastolic) and valsartan 80 mg, adding amlodipine to fimasartan lowered sitting systolic pressure far more than continuing fimasartan alone (−20.5 vs −7.8 mm Hg), and in the FAST forced-titration trial fimasartan 120 mg beat valsartan 160 mg on office systolic (−16.26 vs −12.81 mm Hg) and 24-hour ambulatory systolic pressure (−15.22 vs −9.45 mm Hg) at 6 weeks. Tolerability was comparable to the comparators throughout. Within-class comparisons are against first-generation ARBs at standard doses; the FAST result must not be generalised beyond its 6-week forced-titration design.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single-region (Korea) programme, flagged on the face: four phase 3/4 trials show fimasartan lowers blood pressure non-inferiorly or superiorly to losartan/valsartan comparators over 6–12 weeks, with comparable tolerability; blood pressure is a surrogate endpoint, there is no outcomes trial, and the agent is not marketed in the US or Europe

title: Manidipine in hypertension with type 2 diabetes: DEMAND's kidney primary outcome was null (GFR slope P = 0.87/0.53) — blood pressure matched enalapril; albuminuria beat amlodipine in one small trial
question: In adults with hypertension and type 2 diabetes (with or without microalbuminuria), does the dihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker manidipine, compared with enalapril, delapril-based therapy or amlodipine, lower blood pressure and albuminuria (the DEMAND programme)?
balance: SPLIT — and DEMAND's null primary outcome leads. The programme's only long-term trial, DEMAND (380 hypertensive patients with type 2 diabetes, 3 years), found NO difference in its primary outcome: median monthly GFR decline was 0.32 mL/min/1.73 m² on manidipine/delapril, 0.36 on delapril and 0.30 on placebo (P = 0.87 and P = 0.53), with albuminuria stable in all three groups. DEMAND's striking hazard ratio for major cardiovascular events on the combination vs placebo (0.17, 95% CI 0.04 to 0.78) rests on a secondary endpoint with a wide confidence interval in a 380-patient trial and is printed as such, never as an outcomes win. Around that null: manidipine lowered blood pressure as effectively as enalapril over 24 weeks in 111 patients (responders 66.7% vs 60.0%, not significant), and in one small 91-patient trial with 2:1 randomisation, adding manidipine to full-dose renin-angiotensin blockade reduced urinary albumin excretion far more than adding amlodipine at equal blood-pressure reduction (65.5% relative vs 20% relative at 6 months). Albuminuria and blood pressure are surrogate endpoints. Manidipine is marketed in parts of Europe and Asia, not the US.
stamp: SPLIT — DEMAND (380 patients, 3 years) found no GFR-slope or albuminuria benefit for manidipine/delapril over placebo on its primary outcome, which leads; manidipine matched enalapril on blood pressure and beat amlodipine on albuminuria in one small 91-patient add-on trial; DEMAND's cardiovascular HR 0.17 is a wide-interval secondary endpoint, not an outcomes win

title: Azilsartan medoxomil in hypertension: 80 mg beat valsartan 320 mg and olmesartan 40 mg on 24-hour pressure (−14.3 mm Hg placebo-adjusted); chlorthalidone combination strongly additive
question: In adults with essential hypertension, does the angiotensin-receptor blocker azilsartan medoxomil, compared with olmesartan, valsartan, telmisartan or (combined with chlorthalidone) its own components, lower clinic and ambulatory blood pressure?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — azilsartan medoxomil is a marketed agent (US/EU) whose absence from the library is a coverage gap, not a discontinued-programme story; it is presented plainly as the last unrowed ARB. Three reports, all 6–8-week blood-pressure (surrogate) trials, with no outcomes trial: in the 1,291-patient ambulatory head-to-head, azilsartan 80 mg lowered placebo-adjusted 24-hour systolic pressure −14.3 mm Hg, more than valsartan 320 mg (−10.0, P < 0.001) and olmesartan 40 mg (−11.7, P = 0.009), with azilsartan 40 mg non-inferior to olmesartan 40 mg; in the 1,714-patient factorial trial, azilsartan/chlorthalidone 40/25 and 80/25 mg combinations lowered trough ambulatory systolic pressure 28.9 mm Hg, exceeding either component alone by about 13–14 mm Hg, with dose-dependent discontinuations and creatinine elevations; and in a 303-patient Indian phase 3 trial (single-region, flagged), azilsartan 40 and 80 mg were non-inferior to telmisartan 40 mg on trough sitting systolic pressure (−27.2 and −28.2 vs −26.7 mm Hg). The within-class superiority claims rest on maximum-dose comparisons in a single sponsor programme.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — three short-term blood-pressure trials: azilsartan 80 mg beat maximal-dose valsartan and olmesartan on 24-hour ambulatory pressure, the azilsartan/chlorthalidone combination was strongly additive, and azilsartan was non-inferior to telmisartan in a single-region Indian trial (flagged); a marketed ARB with surrogate-endpoint evidence only and no outcomes trial

title: Velaglucerase alfa in type 1 Gaucher disease: small-N base on the face (N = 25 + N = 34 treated; extension N = 57) — haemoglobin +2.4 g/dL, non-inferior to imiglucerase
question: In children and adults with type 1 Gaucher disease, does enzyme replacement with velaglucerase alfa, compared with imiglucerase or between its own two doses, improve haemoglobin, platelet counts and spleen volume?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a small-N rare-disease base, and the counts lead: the entire randomised base for velaglucerase alfa (VPRIV, the tested product as published) in type 1 Gaucher disease is 59 patients across two trials (N = 25 and N = 34 treated), with no placebo-controlled trial. In the 25-patient dose-comparison trial (no untreated arm, so its within-group gains are uncontrolled), haemoglobin rose +2.43 and +2.44 g/dL on the 60 and 45 U/kg doses over 12 months, platelet counts rose about 66% relative, and spleen volume fell 50.4% and 39.9% relative. In the 34-treated-patient head-to-head, velaglucerase 60 U/kg was non-inferior to imiglucerase 60 U/kg on haemoglobin change at 9 months (difference +0.14 g/dL, non-inferiority margin −1.0 g/dL met), with antibodies in 0 of 17 velaglucerase patients vs 4 of 17 (23.5%) on imiglucerase. The third report is a long-term extension of the SAME patients (57 enrolled, 1.2–4.8 years), carded and labelled as a programme report: gains were maintained, with no drug-related serious adverse event. Percent changes are relative measures. Endpoints are haematological / organ-volume surrogates; no fracture, bone-crisis or mortality outcomes trial exists.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — based on a very small randomised base (59 patients across two trials, Ns on the face): velaglucerase alfa raised haemoglobin ≈ +2.4 g/dL and cut spleen volume up to 50.4% relative in a dose-comparison trial with no placebo arm, and was non-inferior to imiglucerase head-to-head; the third report is a long-term extension of the same patients, labelled as a programme report

title: Enlicitide in non-HeFH hypercholesterolaemia: LDL −57.1% relative vs +3.0% on placebo (CORALreef Lipids, n = 2,909); beat ezetimibe and bempedoic acid — outcomes pending (HeFH homed at #3106)
question: In adults with hypercholesterolaemia and atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease or cardiovascular risk (not restricted to heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia), does the oral PCSK9 inhibitor enlicitide (MK-0616), compared with placebo or oral non-statin therapies, lower LDL cholesterol (the non-HeFH slice of the CORALreef programme)?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the non-HeFH slice only (the heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia question is homed at pack #3106, cross-pointed and not re-carded). Enlicitide, the first oral PCSK9 inhibitor, lowers LDL cholesterol by injectable-class magnitudes in general hypercholesterolaemia: in the phase 2b trial (published under the development code MK-0616 only) placebo-adjusted LDL changes at 8 weeks were −41.2% to −60.9% relative across the 6–30 mg doses; in CORALreef Lipids (2,909 patients with a prior major atherosclerotic event or at risk of a first event, mean baseline LDL 96.1 mg/dL) mean LDL change at week 24 was −57.1% relative on enlicitide 20 mg vs +3.0% on placebo (adjusted difference −55.8 percentage points), sustained in direction at week 52; and in a 56-day active-comparator trial enlicitide (−64.6% relative) beat bempedoic acid (−6.3%), ezetimibe (−27.8%) and their combination (−36.5%). Adverse-event rates resembled placebo or comparators throughout. All endpoints are LDL cholesterol, a surrogate; the active-comparator trial ran only 56 days, and NO cardiovascular-outcomes trial of enlicitide exists — the injectable PCSK9 class's outcomes record must not be borrowed. Percent LDL changes are relative measures.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — enlicitide lowers LDL cholesterol by injectable-class magnitudes in non-HeFH hypercholesterolaemia (−55.8 percentage points vs placebo at week 24 in CORALreef Lipids, n = 2,909; superior to bempedoic acid, ezetimibe and their combination at 56 days), with placebo-like tolerability; LDL is a surrogate endpoint and no cardiovascular-outcomes trial exists; non-HeFH slice only, beside the HeFH home at pack #3106

title: Emodepside for intestinal nematodes: one programme, 4 trials — cure 96.6% vs 81.2% on albendazole for hookworm, 85% predicted vs 17% for whipworm, matching ivermectin for Strongyloides in a dose-finding design
question: In adolescents and adults infected with hookworm, Trichuris trichiura (whipworm) or Strongyloides stercoralis, does a single oral dose of emodepside (5-30 mg) versus albendazole, ivermectin or placebo achieve parasitological cure 14-21 days after treatment?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one development programme, 3 publications reporting 4 randomised trials, labelled as one programme with species limbs never pooled. Against whipworm (Trichuris), predicted cure at emodepside 5 mg was 85% versus 10% on placebo and an observed 17% on albendazole; against hookworm, cure rose dose-dependently from 32% at 5 mg to 95% at 30 mg in the phase 2a trials, and in the phase 2b superiority trial cure was 96.6% on emodepside 30 mg versus 81.2% on albendazole; against Strongyloides, predicted cure plateaued at 89.1% at 15 mg versus an observed 88.0% on ivermectin in a dose-ranging (not powered head-to-head) design and 0% on placebo. The endpoint throughout is parasitological cure at 14-21 days — no trial measures anaemia, growth, transmission or clinical outcomes. Harms belong on the face: transient visual blurring, headache, dizziness and somnolence in roughly a third of recipients at higher doses, predominantly mild, with no serious adverse events. Emodepside is a veterinary anthelmintic repurposed for human use and is not licensed for human use; veterinary preparations are not the tested product. There is no independent replication outside this programme.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one development programme only (3 publications, 4 randomised trials, no independent replication): single-dose emodepside produced high parasitological cure rates at 14-21 days against whipworm, hookworm and Strongyloides, superior to albendazole for hookworm (96.6% vs 81.2%), with transient visual blurring, headache, dizziness and somnolence in roughly a third at higher doses; not licensed for human use and no clinical-outcome data exist

title: Inhaled interferon beta-1a (SNG001) in hospitalised COVID-19: FLOOR-RISK, exactly 2 trials — phase 2 (n=101) positive, SPRINTER phase 3 (n=623) primary not met
question: In adults hospitalised with COVID-19, does nebulised interferon beta-1a (SNG001) added to standard care versus placebo improve clinical status, speed recovery and prevent progression to severe disease or death?
balance: SPLIT — FLOOR-RISK, exactly 2 efficacy reports, stated on the face. The phase 2 pilot (101 randomised, UK, spring 2020, pre-vaccination era) found greater odds of improvement on the WHO Ordinal Scale at day 15/16 (odds ratio 2.32, a relative measure) and faster recovery (hazard ratio 2.19, relative), with 3 deaths on placebo and 0 on SNG001. The SPRINTER phase 3 trial (623 randomised, hospitalised patients requiring oxygen, later era) met NOTHING: median time to discharge 7.0 versus 8.0 days (hazard ratio 1.06, p=0.51), time to recovery 25.0 days in both groups (hazard ratio 1.02), and progression to severe disease or death 10.7% versus 14.4% (odds ratio 0.71, p=0.161 — the abstract's '25.7% relative risk reduction' is a non-significant relative measure and is never printed without its confidence interval and p-value). Serious adverse events were 12.6% versus 18.2%. The arc — a small positive phase 2 followed by a phase 3 six times its size that met no endpoint — is the shelf's answer. Results apply to the tested nebulised SNG001 formulation and do not transfer to systemic interferon preparations.
stamp: SPLIT — FLOOR-RISK, exactly 2 trials (phase 2 n=101 positive on ordinal-scale and recovery measures; SPRINTER phase 3 n=623 with its primary objective not met and no significant secondary endpoint): the small-positive / large-negative arc is the answer, and no efficacy claim for nebulised SNG001 in hospitalised COVID-19 is supported on this base

title: Ulinastatin in sepsis: FLOOR-RISK, exactly 2 multicentre trials, split — Karnad's signal only in a modified-ITT subset; ADJUST (n=347) null with more adverse events on treatment
question: In adults with severe sepsis / sepsis (Sepsis-3), does intravenous ulinastatin (urinary trypsin inhibitor) added to standard care versus placebo or standard care reduce 28-day all-cause mortality?
balance: SPLIT — FLOOR-RISK, exactly 2 multicentre randomised reports, stated on the face, and they split the way small-positive / large-negative programmes split. Karnad 2014 (122 randomised, seven Indian hospitals): 28-day mortality 7.3% on ulinastatin versus 20.3% on placebo in the modified intention-to-treat analysis (p=0.045), but the intention-to-treat comparison did NOT reach significance (10.2% versus 20.6%, p=0.11) — both analyses are printed exactly as reported. ADJUST 2026 (347 randomised, multicentre, Sepsis-3): 28-day mortality 23.6% on ulinastatin versus 22.9% on placebo — an absolute difference of 0.7 percentage points in the wrong direction (p=0.98; hazard ratio 1.03, relative) — with adverse events MORE frequent on ulinastatin (56.8% versus 42.7%, p=0.009). Two small single-centre reports (post-traumatic sepsis, n=60, no mortality difference; a mechanistic lymphocyte-apoptosis study, n=40) are carded labelled and are never load-bearing. Both multicentre trials are single-country (India; China). The ulinastatin-plus-thymosin combination trials ask a different, combination question and are not counted.
stamp: SPLIT — FLOOR-RISK, exactly 2 multicentre trials (Karnad 2014, n=122: mortality signal only in the modified-ITT analysis, p=0.045, with the ITT analysis null at p=0.11; ADJUST 2026, n=347: 28-day mortality 23.6% vs 22.9%, p=0.98, with more adverse events on ulinastatin, 56.8% vs 42.7%); 2 small single-centre reports are labelled and never load-bearing

title: Enteral nutrition as induction in adult Crohn's disease: FLOOR-RISK, exactly 3 trials, N=150 — the multicentre trial found it inferior to steroids (53% vs 79% remission); two small trials read positive
question: In adults with active Crohn's disease, does enteral nutrition as sole therapy (elemental or oligopeptide diet) versus corticosteroid-based drug treatment induce clinical remission?
balance: SPLIT — FLOOR-RISK, exactly 3 randomised reports totalling 150 patients (1984-1997), stated on the face, with the largest and only multicentre trial negative. ECCS IV (107 randomised): remission within 6 weeks in 29 of 55 on enteral nutrition versus 41 of 52 on methylprednisolone plus sulfasalazine (p<0.01), with median time to remission 30.7 versus 8.2 days — enteral nutrition was less effective than drug treatment. The two small trials point the other way: O'Morain 1984 (21 patients) found an elemental diet improved patients as much as, and by some criteria more than, prednisolone over 4 weeks; the Italian trial (22 enrolled, 20 analysed, 2 weeks) found significant activity-index and nutritional improvements on an oral elemental diet and concluded short-term equivalence on activity with better nutritional recovery. The small positive readings cannot carry the balance against the multicentre result. Era flag, load-bearing: every comparator is a steroid-era regimen — no trial compares enteral induction with any modern therapy, so this shelf is a record of a closed question, not an induction option. The separate maintenance question (one trial) is not folded in. Tested feeds are named as the publications give them (Vivonex; Peptamen, Clintec), with the standing statement that current products may differ.
stamp: SPLIT — FLOOR-RISK, exactly 3 reports totalling 150 patients (1984-1997): the largest and only multicentre trial (n=107) found enteral induction inferior to methylprednisolone plus sulfasalazine (remission 53% vs 79%, and far slower), while two small trials (n=21; n=20 analysed over 2 weeks) read positive/equivalent — the small readings do not outweigh the multicentre result, and all comparators are steroid-era

title: Plasma exchange in acute-on-chronic liver failure: FLOOR-RISK, exactly 2 trials, both 2026 — short-term survival benefit (28-day mortality 44.3% vs 63.9%), no 90-day benefit in the larger trial, prior randomised pooling null
question: In adults with acute-on-chronic liver failure (ACLF), does therapeutic plasma exchange added to standard medical therapy versus standard medical therapy alone improve short-term (28-30-day) survival?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — FLOOR-RISK, exactly 2 modern randomised reports, both 2026, both single-centre and open-label, stated on the face. The Indian trial (194 randomised, EASL-CLIF grades 1-3b): 28-day mortality 44.3% on therapeutic plasma exchange plus standard therapy versus 63.9% on standard therapy alone (p=0.006; absolute reduction 19.6 percentage points) — but 90-day mortality did NOT differ, and only 57.7% of the exchange group completed all 5 planned sessions, haemodynamic instability the leading cause of discontinuation. The alcohol-related ACLF trial (100 randomised, up to 3 sessions): in-hospital mortality 24% versus 52% (p=0.007) and 30-day survival 72% versus 36% (p<0.001; adjusted hazard ratio for mortality 0.43, a relative measure). Against these stands the pre-2026 randomised record: the 2024 systematic review's randomised-trial subgroup analysis in ACLF found NO survival difference between plasma exchange and standard therapy. The shelf's answer is that tension, printed whole: two positive 2026 single-centre trials against a pooled randomised null, with the larger trial's benefit not persisting to 90 days. Population limbs are labelled and never pooled. Cross-point: albumin dialysis (MARS) and fractionated plasma separation (Prometheus) are a different modality, homed at pack #6540 — RELIEF and HELIOS are not re-carded here.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — FLOOR-RISK, exactly 2 randomised reports (both 2026, both single-centre and open-label: n=194, 28-day mortality 44.3% vs 63.9% but 90-day mortality not different; n=100 alcohol-related ACLF, 30-day survival 72% vs 36%), read against the 2024 systematic review's randomised-trial subgroup in ACLF, which found no survival difference

title: Sunitinib versus interferon alfa, first-line metastatic RCC: one trial, three reports — PFS 11 vs 5 months and response 47% vs 12%, with a borderline survival analysis (HR 0.82; p=0.051 / p=0.049)
question: In patients with previously untreated metastatic (predominantly clear-cell) renal-cell carcinoma, does sunitinib 50 mg daily (4 weeks on, 2 weeks off) improve progression-free and overall survival versus interferon alfa?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) on progression-free survival and response — one trial, three reports, labelled a single-programme shelf. In 750 randomised patients with previously untreated metastatic renal-cell carcinoma, sunitinib gave median progression-free survival of 11 versus 5 months (hazard ratio 0.42, relative) and an objective response rate of 31% versus 6% in the primary report (47% versus 12% with updated follow-up), with significantly better reported quality of life on sunitinib. The overall-survival analysis is borderline and crossover-contaminated, and both facts are on the face: median overall survival 26.4 versus 21.8 months, hazard ratio 0.821 with p=0.051 by the primary unstratified log-rank analysis and hazard ratio 0.818 with p=0.049 by the stratified test — and within the interferon group, 33% of patients later received sunitinib and 32% other VEGF-signalling inhibitors. The honest headline is a progression-free-survival and response drug with a borderline survival analysis, not a clean survival win. The third report is a programme report of the same trial: baseline quality of life predicted progression-free survival. Sunitinib's other library homes (comparator in later RCC trials, GIST, adjuvant RCC, pancreatic NET) are different questions and are not re-carded.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — one trial, three reports (750 randomised): sunitinib doubled median progression-free survival versus interferon alfa (11 vs 5 months; hazard ratio 0.42, relative) with far higher response (47% vs 12% updated), while overall survival was borderline (hazard ratio 0.821, p=0.051 unstratified; 0.818, p=0.049 stratified) and contaminated by post-progression VEGF therapy in the interferon arm
