title: Sorafenib versus placebo in pretreated clear-cell RCC (TARGET): FLOOR-RISK, exactly 2 reports — PFS 5.5 vs 2.8 months, final overall survival not significant on ITT (17.8 vs 15.2 months)
question: In patients with advanced clear-cell renal-cell carcinoma resistant to standard (cytokine-era) therapy, does sorafenib 400 mg twice daily improve progression-free and overall survival versus placebo?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit, progression-free survival only) — FLOOR-RISK, exactly 2 reports, stated on the face, both reports of the single TARGET trial (903 randomised). Sorafenib doubled median progression-free survival (5.5 versus 2.8 months; hazard ratio 0.44, relative) with partial responses in 10% versus 2%. Overall survival was NOT significantly different on the intention-to-treat final analysis (17.8 versus 15.2 months; hazard ratio 0.88, p=0.146); the first interim survival hazard ratio of 0.72 did not cross the prespecified O'Brien-Fleming threshold. A secondary analysis censoring placebo patients after they crossed over to sorafenib gave 17.8 versus 14.3 months (hazard ratio 0.78, p=0.029) — a sensitivity analysis shaped by the crossover the PFS result itself triggered, not the headline. Baseline VEGF was prognostic, and both high- and low-VEGF groups benefited on progression-free survival. Diarrhoea, rash, fatigue and hand-foot skin reactions were the commonest sorafenib adverse events. Cross-point: sorafenib in hepatocellular carcinoma (SHARP / Asia-Pacific) is a different question in a different disease, homed at pack #7567 — the two shelves cross-point and neither re-cards the other.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit, progression-free survival only) — FLOOR-RISK, exactly 2 reports of the TARGET trial (903 randomised): sorafenib doubled median PFS versus placebo (5.5 vs 2.8 months; hazard ratio 0.44, relative) but final overall survival was not significant on intention-to-treat (17.8 vs 15.2 months; hazard ratio 0.88, p=0.146) after crossover; the crossover-censored analysis (hazard ratio 0.78, p=0.029) is a sensitivity analysis, not the headline

title: Pazopanib versus sunitinib, first-line metastatic RCC (COMPARZ): one trial, three reports — noninferior PFS (HR 1.05), similar survival, better early tolerability and quality of life on pazopanib
question: In patients with treatment-naive clear-cell metastatic renal-cell carcinoma, is pazopanib 800 mg daily noninferior to sunitinib for progression-free survival, and how do overall survival, toxicity and quality of life compare?
balance: LIKELY (noninferior) — one trial, three reports, labelled a single-programme shelf. COMPARZ (1,110 randomised, treatment-naive clear-cell metastatic RCC) met its prespecified noninferiority margin for progression-free survival: hazard ratio 1.05 (95% CI 0.90-1.22), with the upper confidence bound below 1.25. Overall survival was similar (hazard ratio 0.91, 95% CI 0.76-1.08 — an interval spanning 1, so no survival claim is made). The clinical payload is tolerability: sunitinib caused more fatigue (63% versus 55%), hand-foot syndrome (50% versus 29%) and thrombocytopenia (78% versus 41%), pazopanib more alanine aminotransferase elevation (60% versus 43%), and 11 of 14 quality-of-life domains favoured pazopanib in the first 6 months. The Q-TWiST programme report qualifies its own finding: mean time with grade 3/4 toxicity was 31 days longer on sunitinib, but the quality-adjusted advantage for pazopanib was significant in fewer than half of the utility combinations examined — that qualifier is printed on the face. The Asian versus non-Asian programme report (363 Asian and 703 non-Asian patients in the safety population) found haematologic toxicity, transaminase elevation and hand-foot syndrome more prevalent in Asian patients on both drugs. 'Noninferior PFS plus better early quality of life' is never converted into a survival claim on this shelf.
stamp: LIKELY (noninferior) — one trial, three reports (COMPARZ, 1,110 randomised): pazopanib met the prespecified noninferiority margin for PFS versus sunitinib (hazard ratio 1.05, 95% CI 0.90-1.22, upper bound <1.25) with similar overall survival (hazard ratio 0.91, interval spanning 1); the demonstrated advantage is early tolerability and quality of life, not survival

title: Everolimus versus placebo after VEGF therapy in RCC (RECORD-1): PARTIAL beside #1877 — PFS 4.9 vs 1.9 months, overall survival null on ITT (14.8 vs 14.4 months) after 80% crossover
question: In patients with metastatic renal-cell carcinoma progressing on sunitinib, sorafenib, or both, does everolimus 10 mg daily improve progression-free survival versus placebo (both with best supportive care)?
balance: LIKELY (benefit, progression-free survival only) — PARTIAL beside live #1877, carding only the everolimus-versus-placebo slice named in the row. Live #1877 (second-line RCC after antiangiogenic therapy: nivolumab in CheckMate 025 and cabozantinib in METEOR, both versus everolimus) presupposes everolimus as its comparator background but cards no RECORD-1 report; this shelf cards that founding placebo-controlled question only, and does not re-card CheckMate 025 or METEOR. RECORD-1 is a PFS-only win, with all three caveats on the face: the trial was halted early at its second interim analysis; median progression-free survival was 4.0 versus 1.9 months at the primary analysis (hazard ratio 0.30, relative) and 4.9 versus 1.9 months in the final results (hazard ratio 0.33, relative); and overall survival was NULL on intention-to-treat — 14.8 versus 14.4 months (hazard ratio 0.87, p=0.162) — after 80% of the placebo arm crossed over to everolimus. The crossover-corrected rank-preserving structural failure-time estimate (1.9-fold longer survival, 95% CI 0.5-8.5) has an interval spanning no effect and is printed as such. Pricing harms are stomatitis (40% versus 8%), rash (25% versus 4%) and pneumonitis (8% any grade in the primary report; 27% in the small Japanese subgroup, all grade 1-2 and reversible, versus 14% overall in the final subgroup report). The Japanese subgroup (24 patients) is a programme report of the same trial, not independent evidence.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit, progression-free survival only) — PARTIAL beside live #1877, one trial, three reports (RECORD-1): everolimus prolonged median PFS versus placebo after VEGF therapy (4.9 vs 1.9 months final; hazard ratio 0.33, relative) in a trial halted early, while overall survival was null on ITT (14.8 vs 14.4 months; hazard ratio 0.87, p=0.162) after 80% placebo crossover, and the crossover-corrected estimate (95% CI 0.5-8.5) spans no effect

title: Temsirolimus in advanced RCC: SPLIT by line — ARCC first-line survival win in poor-prognosis disease (10.9 vs 7.3 months); INTORSECT second-line loss to sorafenib (OS 12.3 vs 16.6 months)
question: In patients with advanced renal-cell carcinoma, does the mTOR inhibitor temsirolimus improve survival — as first-line therapy versus interferon alfa in poor-prognosis metastatic disease (ARCC), and as second-line therapy after sunitinib versus sorafenib (INTORSECT)?
balance: SPLIT (by line of therapy) — two trials, three reports, with the two slices labelled and never pooled, pointing in opposite directions. First-line, poor-prognosis disease (ARCC, 626 randomised, previously untreated): temsirolimus alone improved overall survival versus interferon alfa (median 10.9 versus 7.3 months; hazard ratio 0.73, relative), with fewer serious adverse events on temsirolimus — but the temsirolimus-plus-interferon combination did NOT beat interferon (hazard ratio 0.96; median 8.4 months), and that null combination arm is on the face. The ARCC biomarker programme report is a negative predictive-biomarker result: baseline tumour PTEN and HIF-1alpha levels did not correlate with temsirolimus efficacy. Second-line after sunitinib (INTORSECT, 512 randomised): progression-free survival did NOT differ between temsirolimus and sorafenib (median 4.3 versus 3.9 months; hazard ratio 0.87, 95% CI 0.71-1.07), and overall survival favoured SORAFENIB (median 16.6 versus 12.3 months; hazard ratio 1.31 for temsirolimus versus sorafenib, relative). The shelf's value is exactly that contrast: an mTOR inhibitor won first-line in poor-prognosis disease and lost second-line to continued VEGF blockade.
stamp: SPLIT (by line of therapy) — two trials, three reports: first-line in poor-prognosis disease (ARCC, 626 randomised) temsirolimus improved overall survival versus interferon alfa (median 10.9 vs 7.3 months; hazard ratio 0.73, relative), while the combination arm did not (hazard ratio 0.96) and PTEN/HIF-1alpha did not predict benefit; second-line after sunitinib (INTORSECT, 512 randomised) temsirolimus showed no PFS advantage over sorafenib (hazard ratio 0.87) and worse overall survival (median 12.3 vs 16.6 months; hazard ratio 1.31, relative)

title: Ibrutinib + obinutuzumab vs chlorambucil + obinutuzumab in first-line CLL (iLLUMINATE): PFS not reached vs 19.0 months (HR 0.23), sustained at final analysis — exactly 2 reports (FLOOR-RISK)
question: In patients with previously untreated chronic lymphocytic leukaemia or small lymphocytic lymphoma who are aged 65 years or older or have coexisting conditions, does ibrutinib plus obinutuzumab improve progression-free survival versus chlorambucil plus obinutuzumab (iLLUMINATE)?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) for progression-free survival, on an exactly-two-report FLOOR-RISK base. Only two reports of the iLLUMINATE trial exist and both are carded: the primary report (229 randomised) found median progression-free survival not reached versus 19.0 months (hazard ratio 0.23, a relative measure; 30-month PFS 79% vs 31%), and the final analysis at 45 months found the same pattern (hazard ratio 0.25; median not reached vs 22 months; undetectable MRD 38% vs 25%). The price in the primary report was serious adverse events in 58% versus 35%. Neither report demonstrates an overall-survival benefit, and the shelf claims none. PARTIAL context: neighbouring first-line CLL shelves presuppose this comparison without carding it; this shelf cards only the iLLUMINATE question.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — ibrutinib + obinutuzumab prolongs progression-free survival versus chlorambucil + obinutuzumab in first-line CLL (HR 0.23 primary, 0.25 final analysis; relative measures), on an exactly-two-report FLOOR-RISK base (iLLUMINATE primary + final analysis only), with serious adverse events 58% vs 35% and no overall-survival benefit demonstrated

title: Ipilimumab in advanced melanoma: first survival win — 10.1 vs 6.4 months vs gp100 (MDX010-20) and 11.2 vs 9.1 months with dacarbazine — with 2.1% drug-related deaths (PARTIAL beside #764)
question: In patients with unresectable or metastatic melanoma, does ipilimumab improve overall survival — alone or with a gp100 peptide vaccine versus gp100 alone in previously treated disease (MDX010-20), and at 10 mg/kg with dacarbazine versus dacarbazine alone in previously untreated disease?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) for overall survival, with serious immune toxicity — a PARTIAL shelf beside live #764. Live #764 (first-line nivolumab–ipilimumab and nivolumab–relatlimab) presupposes ipilimumab's founding benefit but cards neither founding trial; this shelf cards only that slice. MDX010-20 (676 randomised, previously treated): median survival 10.1 months on ipilimumab alone and 10.0 months with gp100 versus 6.4 months on gp100 alone (hazard ratios 0.66 and 0.68, relative measures), with grade 3–4 immune-related adverse events in 10–15% and 14 drug-related deaths (2.1%). Ipilimumab 10 mg/kg + dacarbazine first-line (502 randomised): median 11.2 versus 9.1 months (hazard ratio 0.72, relative), grade 3–4 adverse events 56.3% versus 27.5%. The pooled analysis of 1,861 treated patients (median survival 11.4 months; plateau from year 3) is a within-treatment description, not a randomised contrast, and is labelled as such. The two randomised slices differ in dose and setting and are never pooled.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — ipilimumab improved overall survival in advanced melanoma in two phase 3 trials (vs gp100 after prior therapy, HR 0.66–0.68; with dacarbazine first-line at 10 mg/kg, HR 0.72; relative measures), at the cost of grade 3–4 immune toxicity and a 2.1% drug-related death rate in MDX010-20; the pooled plateau is a within-treatment description, not an effect (PARTIAL beside live #764)

title: Pembrolizumab in advanced melanoma: KEYNOTE-006 — survival beats ipilimumab (32.7 vs 15.9 months at 5 years); KEYNOTE-002 — PFS beats chemotherapy after ipilimumab (PARTIAL beside #764)
question: In patients with advanced melanoma, does pembrolizumab improve survival versus ipilimumab in ipilimumab-naïve disease (KEYNOTE-006) — and progression-free survival versus investigator-choice chemotherapy in ipilimumab-refractory disease (KEYNOTE-002)?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — a PARTIAL shelf beside live #764, carding only the pembrolizumab monotherapy founding slice that #764 presupposes. KEYNOTE-006 (834 randomised, ipilimumab-naïve; three reports carded): pembrolizumab 10 mg/kg beat ipilimumab on progression-free survival (hazard ratio 0.58, relative) and overall survival — hazard ratio 0.68 for both schedules at the final analysis (24-month survival 55% / 55% vs 43%), and at 5 years median survival 32.7 versus 15.9 months (hazard ratio 0.73, relative) — with less grade 3–5 toxicity than ipilimumab. KEYNOTE-002 (540 randomised, ipilimumab-refractory; separate slice): pembrolizumab improved progression-free survival versus chemotherapy (hazard ratios 0.57 and 0.50, relative) — a PFS claim, not a survival claim. KEYNOTE-006's dose (10 mg/kg) was above the later standard, and its comparator is the ipilimumab of shelf #7644.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — pembrolizumab improved overall survival versus ipilimumab in ipilimumab-naïve advanced melanoma (KEYNOTE-006: HR 0.68 final analysis, 0.73 at 5 years; relative measures; median 32.7 vs 15.9 months at 5 years) and progression-free survival versus chemotherapy in ipilimumab-refractory disease (KEYNOTE-002: HR 0.57 / 0.50, relative), with less high-grade toxicity than either comparator (PARTIAL beside live #764)

title: Nivolumab vs dacarbazine in untreated BRAF wild-type melanoma (CheckMate 066): survival 72.9% vs 42.1% at 1 year, 39% vs 17% at 5 years (PARTIAL beside #764)
question: In patients with previously untreated metastatic melanoma without a BRAF mutation, does nivolumab improve overall survival versus dacarbazine (CheckMate 066)?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — a PARTIAL, single-programme shelf beside live #764: one trial (CheckMate 066, 418 randomised), three reports, all carded. title: Vemurafenib in BRAF V600-mutant melanoma (BRIM-3 / BRIM-2): survival 13.6 vs 9.7 months, responses ~50%, cutaneous squamous-cell carcinoma in ~1 in 5 (PARTIAL beside #1902)
question: In patients with metastatic melanoma harbouring a BRAF V600 mutation, does vemurafenib improve overall and progression-free survival versus dacarbazine in previously untreated disease (BRIM-3) — and what responses does it produce after prior therapy (BRIM-2, single-arm)?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — a PARTIAL shelf beside live #1902. Live #1902 (combined BRAF + MEK inhibition versus BRAF inhibition alone, COMBI-d/v) presupposes the founding vemurafenib benefit but cards neither BRIM-3 nor BRIM-2; this shelf cards only that slice. title: Ramucirumab + docetaxel vs docetaxel, second-line stage IV NSCLC (REVEL): survival 10.5 vs 9.1 months (HR 0.86) — a 1.4-month median gain
question: In patients with stage IV non-small-cell lung cancer progressing during or after first-line platinum-based chemotherapy, does adding ramucirumab 10 mg/kg to docetaxel improve overall survival (REVEL)?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — small in absolute terms, on a single-programme base: one trial (REVEL, 1,253 randomised), three reports, all carded. Adding ramucirumab 10 mg/kg to docetaxel improved overall survival second-line in stage IV NSCLC (median 10.5 vs 9.1 months; hazard ratio 0.86, a relative measure — the absolute difference in medians is 1.4 months, printed as prominently as the hazard ratio) and progression-free survival (median 4.5 vs 3.0 months; hazard ratio 0.76, relative), at the cost of more grade 3-or-worse neutropenia (49% vs 40%), febrile neutropenia (16% vs 10%) and hypertension (6% vs 2%). The prespecified age analysis found the benefit clear under 65 (hazard ratio 0.74) and not evident at 65 or older after adjustment (0.96, CI spanning 1) while establishing no true age interaction; the exposure–response report is exploratory pharmacology and implies no dosing recommendation.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit, small absolute gain) — ramucirumab + docetaxel improved overall survival versus docetaxel alone as second-line treatment of stage IV NSCLC (REVEL: median 10.5 vs 9.1 months, an absolute median gain of 1.4 months; HR 0.86, relative), with more high-grade neutropenia, febrile neutropenia and hypertension; one trial, three reports (single-programme shelf)

title: qSOFA vs SIRS predicting death in suspected infection outside the ICU: pooled non-ICU sensitivity only 51.2% (specificity 79.6%) — the prompt misses about half who die (GAP-E)
question: In adults with suspected infection outside the intensive care unit — on wards, in the emergency department and before admission — how accurately does the quick Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (qSOFA: systolic blood pressure ≤100 mm Hg, respiratory rate ≥22/min, altered mentation; score ≥2) predict death, how do its sensitivity and specificity trade off against the systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS) criteria, and how far does its accuracy move between ICU and non-ICU populations?
balance: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — a specific but insensitive prompt outside the ICU (GAP-E). qSOFA (systolic BP ≤100 mm Hg, respiratory rate ≥22/min, altered mentation; ≥2 positive) was derived in the Sepsis-3 analysis of 1.3 million encounters, where outside the ICU it discriminated in-hospital mortality better than SOFA and SIRS (AUROC 0.81 vs 0.79 and 0.76) — but discrimination is not bedside sensitivity. Two independent meta-analyses put pooled non-ICU sensitivity at only 51.2% (38 studies, 385,333 patients; specificity 79.6%) and 0.48 (45 studies, 406,802 patients; specificity 0.83): the prompt misses roughly half of non-ICU patients who die. SIRS is the mirror image (sensitivity 88.1%, specificity 25.8%). In the ICU the pattern partly reverses (qSOFA sensitivity 87.2%, specificity 33.3%; SOFA AUROC 0.74 vs qSOFA 0.66). No carded evidence shows scoring itself improves outcomes.
stamp: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — qSOFA ≥2 predicts death in suspected infection with pooled non-ICU sensitivity of only 51.2% (specificity 79.6%; second meta-analysis 0.48 / 0.83), so it misses roughly half of non-ICU patients who die, while SIRS is far more sensitive (88.1%) and far less specific (25.8%); ICU accuracy differs (sensitivity 87.2%, specificity 33.3%) and is a separate claim (GAP-E)

title: Morse Fall Scale predicting inpatient falls: cut-off 45 in acute care, 40 in obstetrics / gynaecology — and retrospective design inflates its accuracy by 0.22 Youden points (GAP-E)
question: In hospitalised adults, how well does the Morse Fall Scale (fall history, secondary diagnosis, ambulatory aid, intravenous therapy, gait, mental status; usual high-risk cut-off ≥45) predict who will fall during the admission — what sensitivity, specificity and discrimination does it deliver at the standard and at locally re-derived cut-offs, how much does the ward type move the answer, and how much of the published accuracy is an artefact of retrospective study design?
balance: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — modest, local, and inflated by design (GAP-E). The Morse Fall Scale (fall history, secondary diagnosis, ambulatory aid, intravenous therapy, gait, mental status) was validated at its conventional ≥45 cut-off in a Korean acute-care sample (66 fallers, 100 non-fallers; the record prints qualitative accuracy descriptors only), while an obstetrics-and-gynaecology re-evaluation (136 fall, 120 no-fall) found the locally optimal cut-off was 40 (AUC 0.772; sensitivity 0.735, specificity 0.808). The core finding is methodological: across 51 tool evaluations, retrospective designs reported Youden indices 0.22 higher than prospective ones, and prospectively the Morse scale, STRATIFY and nursing clinical judgement had comparable accuracy; a cross-instrument meta-analysis likewise found STRATIFY ahead (diagnostic odds ratio 7.64) and in-stay reassessment reducing the Morse DOR (relative DOR 0.75). A psychogeriatric report (Morse sensitivity 50% on only 4 in-stay falls) is carded as a labelled caution, never as evidence. No sensitivity / specificity pair is printed without its design and ward type.
stamp: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — the Morse Fall Scale predicts inpatient falls modestly, with locally derived cut-offs (45 in acute care; 40 in obstetrics / gynaecology, AUC 0.772, sensitivity 0.735, specificity 0.808), and its published accuracy is inflated by retrospective design (Youden index +0.22 versus prospective evaluations, under which it matches nursing clinical judgement) (GAP-E)

title: Preoperative Mini-Cog predicting postoperative delirium: pooled odds ratio 3.79 (relative) but sensitivity only 0.50 — and one cohort's association vanishes on adjustment (GAP-E)
question: Before elective surgery in older adults, how well does a positive Mini-Cog screen (three-item recall plus clock draw; standard cut-off <3) predict postoperative delirium — what are its pooled sensitivity, specificity and odds ratio on modern meta-analysis, how far does the association survive adjustment for age, frailty and ASA grade in individual cohorts, and how stable is the score itself between the preoperative clinic and the day of surgery?
balance: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — a real association with coin-flip sensitivity (GAP-E). The first systematic review and meta-analysis of preoperative Mini-Cog for postoperative delirium (16 studies, 4,980 patients) found low scores associated with delirium at a pooled odds ratio of 3.79 — a relative measure, labelled as such — with pooled sensitivity of only 0.50 and specificity 0.80 (standardised-cut-off subgroup odds ratio 3.40). The tension prints in full: in a 319-patient high-risk colorectal cohort the delirium association (univariate odds ratio 3.04) lost significance after adjustment for age, frailty and ASA grade (0.49), while an association with 90-day mortality remained (4.65); and in an 80-patient prospective cohort the score itself was stable between the preoperative clinic and the day of surgery (kappa 0.78), with impairment on either occasion strongly associated with PACU delirium. No carded evidence shows screening prevents delirium.
stamp: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — preoperative Mini-Cog impairment is associated with postoperative delirium at a pooled odds ratio of 3.79 (relative measure; 3.40 in the standardised-cut-off subgroup) but with pooled sensitivity of only 0.50 (specificity 0.80), so the screen misses half of those who become delirious; one adjusted cohort found no independent delirium association (GAP-E)

title: Normal intrarenal resistive index in healthy adults: age-defined values 0.59 / 0.61 / 0.63 at ages 25 / 45 / 65 across 4 datasets — and a single reading exceeds 0.70 in health 6% of the time (PHYS)
question: In healthy adults, what are the normal values for the intrarenal (renal) resistive index on Doppler ultrasound — the central range at the renal, interlobar and cortical arteries — how steeply does the index rise with age (and does it differ by sex or by arterial level), and how much measurement variability sits inside a single reported value?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall and Boron & Boulpaep frame renal haemodynamics briefly, and this shelf rests chiefly on the primary normative literature, as stated on its face. Four independent healthy-adult datasets (78, 80, 58 and 90 subjects; 1996–2018) agree that the intrarenal resistive index (RI) is age-defined, not a single normal number: Kaiser 2007 gives 0.59 at age 25, 0.61 at 45 and 0.63 at 65 (RI = 0.565 + 0.001 × age), with no significant effect of sex, region or side; the Nigerian dataset (Ismail 2018) likewise found a significant RI–age correlation and no gender correlation; Keogan 1996 found region, territory and side without consistent effect but age significant — and quantified single-reading variability (a healthy 45-year-old's single reading exceeds 0.70 with probability 6%, falling to 3% averaged over three readings); Rivolta 2000 found interlobar and cortical RI rising selectively with age as renal blood flow fell, RI higher in women, and cortical RI lower than interlobar and renal RI. Levels are never merged, and the sex disagreement between datasets prints unresolved.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — normal intrarenal resistive index in healthy adults is age-defined (0.59 at 25 years, 0.61 at 45, 0.63 at 65; RI = 0.565 + 0.001 × age) across four independent datasets, differs by arterial level (cortical < interlobar / renal), and carries quantified single-reading variability (6% probability of exceeding 0.70 in a healthy 45-year-old, 3% when three readings are averaged)

title: Normal thyroid volume by ultrasound: German equations give upper limits of 38.7 mL (men) and 28.6 mL (women) vs conventional 25 / 18 mL — Spanish median 7.31 mL, Cuban mean 6.6 mL
question: In healthy adults, what is the normal thyroid volume on ultrasound — median, mean and upper reference limits by sex — how much do age, body size (weight, height, body surface area) and population iodine status move it, and how far do individualised reference equations move the enlargement threshold away from the conventional fixed limits (25 mL in men, 18 mL in women)?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED, on three independent population datasets (plus one supporting lobe-asymmetry report, not counted). Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, thyroid sections — brief framing only; this shelf rests chiefly on the primary population literature, and says so. The German SHIP/KORA equations (8,606 thyroid-healthy reference individuals) put the individualised upper limit at 38.7 mL (men) and 28.6 mL (women) — the conventional fixed limits (25 / 18 mL) would label 34% of that population enlarged, vs 7% by the equations, and both sets of limits print on the face. Central values in non-iodine-deficient populations are far lower (Spanish median 7.31 mL; Cuban mean 6.6 mL), men exceed women in every dataset, and body size (weight, height, body surface area) moves volume in every dataset that tested it. Iodine status is a population property, not a caveat: the German limits come from a previously iodine-deficient region and are never presented as universal, and datasets are carded per population, never merged.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — three independent population datasets (German SHIP/KORA equations, N = 8,606 reference; Spanish, N = 268; Cuban, N = 100) agree that thyroid volume is larger in men and rises with body size, while the numeric upper limits are population- and iodine-status-specific and are printed per population, never merged

title: Age-specific prostate volume in healthy men: Arab TRUS 8–22 mL at 40–49 to 10–33 mL at 70–79; Iranian 95th-percentile ranges to 18–73 mL; German MRI median 31.29 mL
question: In healthy men, what is the normal prostate volume by age — the age-specific ranges and upper limits on transrectal ultrasound and on MRI — how steeply does volume rise from the fifth to the eighth decade, and how far do population (ancestry / region) reference ranges sit from one another? (The datasets' paired serum PSA and PSA-density ranges are carded as co-analytes of the same reference studies.)
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED, on three independent population datasets. Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, reproductive sections — brief framing only; this shelf rests chiefly on the primary population literature, and says so. Prostate volume rises steeply with age in every dataset, but the ranges sit far apart by population and modality: healthy Arab men (transrectal ultrasound) 8–22 mL at 40–49 years to 10–33 mL at 70–79; healthy Iranian men (ultrasound, 95th-percentile ranges) 14–59 mL at 50–59 to 18–73 mL at 70–79; healthy German men (MRI) median 31.29 mL with a 95th percentile of 51.39 mL. The datasets' paired PSA and PSA-density ranges are carded as co-analytes of the same reference studies. Every dataset excluded men with urinary symptoms or known prostate disease — these are healthy-gland ranges, not screening thresholds, and no card presents an upper limit as a biopsy or referral trigger; that question belongs to live #212 (PSA screening), cross-pointed only.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — three independent populations (Arab N = 396, Iranian N = 913, German MRI 1,037 analysed) agree on a steep age gradient in prostate volume, with paired PSA / PSA-density co-analyte ranges; numeric ranges are population- and modality-specific and printed per dataset, never merged

title: Chromogranin A reference intervals are assay- and sample-type-bound: serum 21.0–108.0 vs plasma 31.0–153.0 ng/mL; second serum interval 30.3–94.4 ng/mL; 44% decay at 48 hours
question: In healthy adults, what are the reference intervals for chromogranin A — the central 95% range in serum and in EDTA plasma — how far apart are the intervals given by different assays measuring nominally the same protein, how large are within-person and between-person biological variation, and how fast does the measured value decay in a stored sample?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING, on three independent datasets. Guyton & Hall / Boron & Boulpaep have no chromogranin A reference chapter — this shelf rests on the primary reference literature alone, with the textbooks framing neuroendocrine secretion biology only. The intervals are assay- and sample-type-specific to an unusual degree, and that specificity is the content: in paired samples from 145 healthy male donors, EDTA plasma ran a median 26% higher than serum (reference ranges 31.0–153.0 vs 21.0–108.0 ng/mL, immunoradiometric assay); a second serum dataset (120 healthy individuals) gave 30.3–94.4 ng/mL, with within-person variation 11.9% vs between-person 50.2% and measured values decaying 44% by 48 hours at 4 °C; and an ELISA evaluation found a cross-assay slope of 9.05 against the reference-laboratory method. No interval is printed without its assay and sample type.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING — three independent datasets (145 male donors, paired serum/plasma; 120 healthy individuals; 60 + 60 healthy volunteers in an assay evaluation) establish intervals only within assay- and sample-type-specific cells, with a 9.05 cross-assay slope and 44% 48-hour storage decay documented on the face

title: Ruboxistaurin (never marketed): visual loss 5.5% vs 9.1% in PKC-DRS2, but PKC-DMES missed its macular-edema primary endpoint
question: In adults with diabetic retinopathy or diabetic macular edema, does the oral protein kinase C-β inhibitor ruboxistaurin, compared with placebo, reduce sustained moderate visual loss and delay progression to sight-threatening macular edema (the PKC-DRS / PKC-DMES programme)?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for sustained moderate visual loss only, on one never-marketed programme. Ruboxistaurin was never marketed: it was refused / left unapproved after regulatory review despite the visual-loss signal, and that flag leads. PKC-DRS2 (685 randomised) found sustained moderate visual loss in 5.5% on ruboxistaurin vs 9.1% on placebo (P = 0.034) — a 40% relative risk reduction but only 3.6 percentage points absolute. The one trial with a macular-edema primary endpoint, PKC-DMES (686 randomised), MISSED that primary endpoint (P = 0.14; adjusted HR 0.73, 95% CI 0.53 to 1.0). Two of the four reports are combined analyses overlapping the individual trials (6.1% vs 10.2%; 2.3% vs 4.4%, not significant) — the base is one programme, never four independent trials. All trials predate anti-VEGF therapy.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for sustained moderate visual loss in diabetic retinopathy (PKC-DRS2: 5.5% vs 9.1%, P = 0.034), on a single never-marketed programme in which the macular-edema trial PKC-DMES missed its primary endpoint and two of four reports are combined analyses, not independent trials

title: Benfluorex (withdrawn): valvular regurgitation 27% vs 11% in its own REGULATE trial (OR 2.97, relative) leads — HbA1c fell ~1% vs placebo
question: In adults with type 2 diabetes, does the anorectic/insulin-sensitising agent benfluorex (Mediator), compared with placebo, metformin, sulfonylurea alone or pioglitazone, improve glycaemic control — and what valvular harm did its own randomised echocardiography trial show?
balance: LIKELY (harm) — the withdrawal harm leads the balance. Benfluorex, a fenfluramine derivative marketed in France for decades, was withdrawn in 2009 over valvular heart disease, and its own randomised echocardiography trial (REGULATE, 846 randomised vs pioglitazone) documented emergent valvular regurgitation in 27% on benfluorex vs 11% on pioglitazone (OR 2.97, 95% CI 1.91 to 4.63 — a relative measure; absolutes 27% vs 11%), while glycaemic non-inferiority was not confirmed. The glycaemic effects were real but surrogate-only: HbA1c −1.01% vs placebo as sulfonylurea add-on and −0.86% endpoint difference vs placebo as monotherapy (+0.28% vs metformin). No card on this shelf presents the glycaemic wins without the valvular harm.
stamp: LIKELY (harm) — benfluorex's own randomised echocardiography trial (REGULATE) found emergent valvular regurgitation in 27% vs 11% on pioglitazone (OR 2.97, a relative measure), the harm that withdrew the drug in 2009; its HbA1c benefit (~−1% vs placebo) is a surrogate effect that does not offset that harm

title: IV clevidipine in cardiac surgery: target BP in ~5–6 minutes (failure ~8% vs ~80% on placebo); ECLIPSE outcomes null except mortality vs nitroprusside
question: In adults undergoing cardiac surgery who develop acute perioperative hypertension, does intravenous clevidipine, compared with placebo, nitroglycerin, sodium nitroprusside or nicardipine, control blood pressure — and how did the comparators differ on 30-day death, myocardial infarction, stroke and renal dysfunction (the ESCAPE / ECLIPSE programme)?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — for rapid perioperative blood-pressure control, a surrogate endpoint. In ESCAPE-1 and ESCAPE-2, intravenous clevidipine failed to reach target in only 7.5% (4/53) and 8.2% (5/61) of treated patients vs 82.7% (43/52) and 79.6% (39/49) on placebo infusion, with median times to target of 6.0 and 5.3 minutes — contrasts against placebo in pre-selected hypertensive patients, printed with their treated denominators. The clinically informative report is ECLIPSE (three open-label trials in one paper, 1,512 treated): 30-day myocardial infarction, stroke and renal dysfunction did not differ against nitroglycerin, nitroprusside or nicardipine, and mortality did not differ vs nitroglycerin or nicardipine but was higher on nitroprusside than on clevidipine (P = 0.04). No patient-important outcome benefit over modern comparators is shown.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — for rapid perioperative blood-pressure control in cardiac surgery (ESCAPE-1/-2 failure ~8% vs ~80% on placebo infusion, target in ~5–6 minutes; ECLIPSE: better range control than nitroglycerin / nitroprusside), with no patient-important outcome advantage shown except mortality vs nitroprusside in open-label ECLIPSE data

title: Rilmenidine: old small base — BP normalised 61% vs 23% on placebo at 4 weeks (N = 126); LVH regression no different from nifedipine (per-protocol N = 56)
question: In adults with mild-to-moderate essential hypertension, does the centrally acting imidazoline-receptor agonist rilmenidine, compared with placebo, nifedipine or lisinopril, lower blood pressure and regress left ventricular hypertrophy?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — old, small, surrogate-only, and those flags lead. Rilmenidine's randomised base is a 1988 programme paper (two 4-week double-blind placebo-controlled trials in one report, 126 patients; blood-pressure normalisation 61% vs 23%), a 1-year double-blind LVH trial vs nifedipine whose result is a per-protocol analysis of 56 patients with no between-group difference (LV mass index −22.1 vs −26.9 g/m², P = 0.5), and a 12-week open-label ambulatory trial vs lisinopril in 51 women with no significant between-group blood-pressure difference. There is no outcomes trial, the agent was never marketed in the US, and blood pressure and LV mass are surrogates. The three reports' effects are never pooled — different comparators answer different questions.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — rilmenidine lowers blood pressure vs placebo in two 4-week trials (N = 126, one report) and matches nifedipine on LVH regression (per-protocol N = 56) and lisinopril on ambulatory pressure (N = 51), but the base is old, small and surrogate-only with no outcomes trial

title: Cyclical etidronate: vertebral fractures 29.5 vs 62.9 per 1,000 patient-years (Watts) — but Cochrane 2024 finds little to no difference; no nonvertebral evidence
question: In postmenopausal women with established osteoporosis, does intermittent cyclical etidronate, compared with placebo or sodium fluoride, increase spinal bone density and reduce new vertebral fractures?
balance: SPLIT — the superseded first-generation drug leads. Etidronate was the first bisphosphonate used for osteoporosis and has been displaced by agents with nonvertebral and hip fracture data; it has NO nonvertebral fracture evidence. Two 1990 NEJM trials were positive on their own terms — Watts (429 women): spinal density +4.2% / +5.2% and vertebral fractures 29.5 vs 62.9 per 1,000 patient-years; Storm (only 66 women): vertebral mineral content +5.3% vs −2.7% — but the fluoride head-to-head (118 women, heavy dropout) gave etidronate less density gain and a higher vertebral fracture count (19 vs 6), and the current Cochrane synthesis (2024) finds little to no difference on clinical fractures. The withdrawn 2007 Cochrane version is fenced and cited nowhere on this shelf.
stamp: SPLIT — two 1990 NEJM trials found cyclical etidronate reduced vertebral fracture rates and raised spinal density (Watts N = 429; Storm N = 66), but the fluoride head-to-head favoured the comparator on fracture count and the current Cochrane synthesis (2024; withdrawn 2007 version fenced, uncited) finds little to no difference on clinical fractures; no nonvertebral evidence exists

title: Ibandronate: vertebral fractures 4.7% / 4.9% vs 9.6% on placebo (BONE) — vertebral-only evidence; monthly oral and IV dosing match daily on BMD
question: In postmenopausal women with osteoporosis, does oral or intravenous ibandronate, compared with placebo or its own daily oral regimen, reduce vertebral fractures and increase bone mineral density (the BONE / MOBILE / DIVA programme)?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — for vertebral fractures only, and that qualifier leads. BONE, the programme's only placebo-controlled fracture trial (2,946 randomised, 3 years), found new vertebral fractures in 4.7% (daily) and 4.9% (intermittent) on oral ibandronate vs 9.6% on placebo — 62% and 50% relative reductions, about 5 percentage points absolute — and NO nonvertebral fracture benefit in the overall population (9.1% / 8.9% vs 8.2%); the abstract reports none and this shelf implies none. MOBILE (monthly oral) and DIVA (quarterly IV) are BMD (surrogate) non-inferiority trials against the daily regimen: they establish that monthly oral and IV dosing match daily dosing on density, nothing more.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — for vertebral fractures in postmenopausal osteoporosis (BONE: 4.7% daily and 4.9% intermittent vs 9.6% on placebo over 3 years), with monthly oral (MOBILE) and IV (DIVA) regimens non-inferior to daily on BMD; no nonvertebral fracture benefit was shown in BONE's overall population

title: Taliglucerase alfa in type 1 Gaucher disease (one programme, small N): spleen volume −26.9% / −38.0% relative at 30 / 60 U/kg in 29 adults; switch patients stable
question: In children and adults with type 1 Gaucher disease, does enzyme replacement with taliglucerase alfa (plant cell-expressed glucocerebrosidase), compared between its own two doses or after switching from imiglucerase, improve haemoglobin, platelet counts and spleen volume?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — on a small-N rare-disease base, with the counts leading: one programme, three reports. The randomised base is a single dose-comparison trial in which 29 treatment-naïve adults completed the protocol — spleen volume fell −26.9% relative at 30 U/kg and −38.0% relative at 60 U/kg over 9 months, with gains in haemoglobin, liver volume and (at 60 U/kg) platelets — but there was NO placebo or active-comparator arm, so the gains are uncontrolled. A 31-patient open-label switch study (from imiglucerase) and a 15-child extension report show stability / within-group improvement only. Endpoints are haematological and organ-volume surrogates; no fracture, bone-crisis or mortality trial exists. The tested product is named as the publications give it — taliglucerase alfa (Protalix Biotherapeutics, Carmiel, Israel), plant cell-expressed — for clarification, not promotion.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — taliglucerase alfa improved spleen volume, haemoglobin and (at 60 U/kg) platelets in a single 29-completer dose-comparison trial with no placebo arm, with stability shown in a 31-patient switch study and a 15-child extension report; small-N rare-disease base, surrogate endpoints only

title: Cipaglucosidase alfa + miglustat in late-onset Pompe (PROPEL): the phase 3 primary endpoint was MISSED (+13.6 m, 95% CI −2.8 to 29.9); open-label reports show stability, not proven superiority
question: In adults with late-onset Pompe disease, does the two-component enzyme therapy cipaglucosidase alfa plus miglustat, compared with alglucosidase alfa, improve walking distance and respiratory function (the PROPEL programme: one randomised trial and its labelled extension and phase 1/2 reports)?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit), on one programme of three reports / two trials — labelled as such. PROPEL, the only randomised trial (125 randomised), MISSED its primary endpoint: 6-minute walk distance improved by 20.8 m on cipaglucosidase alfa plus miglustat versus 7.2 m on alglucosidase alfa plus placebo, a between-group difference of 13.6 m (95% CI −2.8 to 29.9), and the abstract's own conclusion is that the combination did not achieve statistical superiority. The two remaining reports are open-label and uncontrolled: the PROPEL extension (118 patients to 104 weeks) showed maintained or stable walk distance and forced vital capacity rather than decline, and the phase 1/2 ATB200-02 report (29 adults to 48 months) showed within-group gains with shrinking denominators (n = 9 remaining at 48 months in the pooled experienced ambulatory cohorts). Respiratory and subgroup signals in PROPEL are, in the abstract's own framing, hypothesis-generating. The missed primary endpoint leads this shelf; the combination is not presented as proven superior to alglucosidase alfa. Cross-point: avalglucosidase alfa versus alglucosidase alfa is a different agent and question, homed at pack #5194.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — PROPEL, the programme's only randomised trial (125 randomised), missed its primary endpoint (6-minute walk difference 13.6 m, 95% CI −2.8 to 29.9; superiority not achieved, in the abstract's own words); the affirmative content is open-label extension and phase 1/2 stability data, which cannot establish superiority over alglucosidase alfa

title: Diazoxide choline ER in Prader-Willi hyperphagia (DESTINY): phase 3 primary MISSED (P = 0.198); severe subgroup and withdrawal study in prior responders positive
question: In children and adults with Prader-Willi syndrome and hyperphagia, does diazoxide choline extended-release (DCCR), compared with placebo or with its own withdrawal, reduce hyperphagia (the DESTINY PWS programme: one phase 3 trial, its labelled open-label report, and a randomised withdrawal study)?
balance: SPLIT, on one programme of three reports — labelled as such. DESTINY PWS, the phase 3 placebo-controlled trial (127 randomised), MISSED its primary endpoint: Hyperphagia Questionnaire for Clinical Trials (HQ-CT) change was −5.94 on diazoxide choline extended-release (DCCR) versus −4.27 on placebo (P = 0.198). The affirmative evidence sits in narrower frames: a significant result in the severe-baseline-hyperphagia subgroup (−9.67 vs −4.26, P = 0.012), a pre-COVID sensitivity analysis that met the primary endpoint (P = 0.037), significant secondary endpoints (Clinical Global Impression of Improvement, P = 0.029; fat mass, P = 0.023), uncontrolled open-label improvement over up to 52 weeks (HQ-CT −9.9 within group), and a positive randomised-withdrawal study (77 prior responders/completers after 2.5–4.5 years of open-label treatment: HQ-CT worsened +2.6 on continued DCCR versus +7.6 on switched-to-placebo, P = 0.0022) — a design that enriches for patients already tolerating and apparently benefiting from the drug and does not re-establish the primary endpoint in an unselected population. The agent was approved in the US in 2025 on this totality; the approval and the missed primary are printed together here. Hyperglycaemia — an on-mechanism harm of a diazoxide product — is on the face of the open-label card. HQ-CT is a caregiver-reported questionnaire score, not a weight or survival outcome.
stamp: SPLIT — the phase 3 DESTINY PWS trial missed its primary endpoint in the unselected population (HQ-CT −5.94 vs −4.27, P = 0.198), while the severe-baseline subgroup (P = 0.012), the pre-COVID sensitivity analysis (P = 0.037) and a randomised-withdrawal study in prior responders (P = 0.0022) favoured DCCR; open-label improvement is uncontrolled

title: Sulodexide in diabetic kidney disease (PARTIAL vs live #1598): Di.N.A.S. positive on albuminuria (n = 223), but SUN-micro (n = 1,056) and SUN-MACRO (n = 1,248) both null
question: In adults with diabetic kidney disease, does oral sulodexide, compared with placebo on top of renin-angiotensin blockade, reduce albuminuria or slow kidney progression (the Di.N.A.S. / SUN programme)? PARTIAL beside live #1598, which homes sulodexide for recurrent venous thromboembolism — that question is not re-asked here.
balance: LIKELY (no difference) for kidney protection, on a PARTIAL slice beside live #1598. This shelf cards only the diabetic-kidney-disease question; the venous-thromboembolism question (SURVET) is homed at live #1598 and is not re-carded here. The programme arc runs small-and-positive to large-and-null twice, and the two SUN trials carry the weight: Di.N.A.S. (223 randomised, 4 months, albuminuria surrogate) found dose-linear relative reductions in albumin excretion versus placebo of 30%, 49% and 74% at 50/100/200 mg/day; SUN-microalbuminuria (1,056 randomised on maximal ACE-inhibitor/ARB therapy) then MISSED its own albuminuria primary endpoint (achieved in 16.5% on sulodexide vs 18.4% on placebo); and SUN-MACRO (1,248 enrolled of 2,240 planned, terminated early) found no difference on a hard kidney composite (doubling of creatinine, ESRD, or creatinine at least 6.0 mg/dL: 26 events on sulodexide vs 30 on placebo over 1,029 person-years). Albuminuria is a surrogate; the one trial that measured kidney outcomes found nothing, and the larger trial that measured the surrogate itself also found nothing.
stamp: LIKELY (no difference) — PARTIAL slice beside live #1598 (VTE): the two large SUN trials are both null — SUN-micro missed its albuminuria primary endpoint (16.5% vs 18.4%) and SUN-MACRO found no difference on hard kidney outcomes (26 vs 30 composite events, stopped early); only the small, short Di.N.A.S. surrogate trial (n = 223) was positive

title: IV fenoldopam vs nitroprusside in acute severe hypertension (PARTIAL vs pack #2911): equivalent blood-pressure control in three pre-modern trials — a surrogate only, no clinical outcomes
question: In adults with acute severe hypertension, does intravenous fenoldopam (a dopamine-1 agonist), compared with sodium nitroprusside, control blood pressure as effectively and safely? PARTIAL beside pack #2911, which homes fenoldopam in cardiac-surgery acute kidney injury — that question is not re-asked here.
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (no difference), on a PARTIAL slice beside pack #2911. This shelf cards only the acute-severe-hypertension comparison; fenoldopam in cardiac-surgery acute kidney injury is homed at pack #2911 and is not re-carded here. Three randomised comparisons from 1990–1995 — all open-label or single-blind, all against sodium nitroprusside, all with blood pressure (a surrogate) as the outcome — found the two agents equivalent in controlling and maintaining diastolic pressure: the Fenoldopam Study Group trial (183 enrolled; 15 patients per arm excluded from the efficacy analysis for protocol violations), a 33-patient single-blind trial, and an open-label crisis study whose abstract prints no N (none is claimed here). Equivalence here means equivalent pressure lowering over hours, in trials far too small to compare harms and from the pre-modern era; neither agent was compared with any modern alternative, and this slice's tidy equivalence is not a reason to prefer fenoldopam over modern agents. A renal-effects substudy (n = 11) is sub-floor — support only, never load-bearing, not counted and not carded.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (no difference) — PARTIAL slice beside pack #2911 (cardiac-surgery AKI): three 1990–1995 open-label or single-blind randomised comparisons found fenoldopam equivalent to nitroprusside on blood pressure, a surrogate, over hours; the base is pre-modern, small, and carries no clinical-outcome or modern-comparator evidence

title: Dasiglucagon in congenital hyperinsulinism (PARTIAL vs live #1777; FLOOR-RISK — exactly 2 trials, N = 44): larger trial's primary MISSED; CGM signal post-hoc; infant crossover cut IV glucose need
question: In infants and children with congenital hyperinsulinism and persistent hypoglycaemia, does continuous subcutaneous dasiglucagon, added to standard care or compared with placebo, reduce hypoglycaemia and intravenous glucose requirements? FLOOR-RISK — exactly 2 trials, N = 44 in total. PARTIAL beside live #1777, which homes dasiglucagon rescue use in type 1 diabetes — that question is not re-asked here.
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — FLOOR-RISK: exactly 2 trials, N = 44 children in total, printed on the face. PARTIAL beside live #1777, which homes dasiglucagon as severe-hypoglycaemia rescue in type 1 diabetes; only the congenital-hyperinsulinism (CHI) slice is carded here. The larger trial (32 randomised, open-label, dasiglucagon infusion plus standard care vs standard care alone for 4 weeks) MISSED its primary endpoint: self-monitored-glucose-detected hypoglycaemia event rate ratio 0.85 (95% CI 0.54 to 1.36, P = 0.5028). Its affirmative result — a 43% relative reduction in blinded continuous-glucose-monitoring-detected hypoglycaemia (event rate ratio 0.57, 95% CI 0.39 to 0.83, P = 0.0029) — is a POST-HOC analysis and is labelled post-hoc wherever it appears on this shelf. The smaller trial (12 infants, double-blind crossover) found intravenous glucose infusion rate over 48-hour periods was 4.3 mg/kg/min on dasiglucagon versus 9.5 mg/kg/min on placebo (P = 0.004) — a 48-hour surrogate in 12 infants. Skin and gastrointestinal events were more frequent on dasiglucagon in the larger trial. This row is kept at FLOOR-RISK because CHI is a rare disease with no competing randomised therapy base — not because the base is strong.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — FLOOR-RISK, exactly 2 trials, N = 44 total, PARTIAL beside live #1777 (rescue use): the larger trial (n = 32) missed its primary endpoint (rate ratio 0.85, P = 0.5028) and its CGM benefit is post-hoc; the smaller trial (n = 12) reduced IV glucose requirement over 48 hours (4.3 vs 9.5 mg/kg/min, P = 0.004)

title: Anakinra in type 2 diabetes (FLOOR-RISK — exactly 2 reports, 1 trial, N = 70): HbA1c −0.46 points at 13 weeks in the sole Larsen trial; secretion gain not maintained after withdrawal
question: In adults with type 2 diabetes, does interleukin-1 blockade with anakinra, compared with placebo, improve glycaemia and beta-cell function? FLOOR-RISK — exactly 2 reports, 1 trial, N = 70 (the Larsen trial and its withdrawal follow-up).
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — FLOOR-RISK: exactly 2 reports, 1 trial, N = 70, printed on the face. The entire base is the single Larsen trial: 70 patients randomised (34 anakinra 100 mg/day, 36 placebo) for 13 weeks, in which glycated haemoglobin was 0.46 percentage points lower on anakinra (P = 0.03), C-peptide secretion was enhanced (P = 0.05), the proinsulin-to-insulin ratio fell (P = 0.005), and interleukin-6 (P < 0.001) and C-reactive protein (P = 0.002) fell, with no difference in insulin resistance, body-mass index or adipokines and no drug-related serious adverse events. The second report is a follow-up OF THE SAME TRIAL, not an independent trial: 39 weeks after treatment withdrawal, the proinsulin-to-insulin ratio and the inflammatory-marker reductions were maintained, but stimulated C-peptide was NOT maintained except in a genetically defined low-baseline-IL-1Ra subgroup. A mechanistic muscle gene-expression substudy of the same trial is carded labelled as a programme report and is not counted. The HbA1c effect is modest, the trial predates modern background therapy, and no second trial of anakinra for glycaemia in type 2 diabetes has ever published. The canakinumab shelves (live #2020; pack #2021) are a different agent and question and are not re-carded.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — FLOOR-RISK, exactly 2 reports / 1 trial, N = 70: the single Larsen trial found HbA1c 0.46 percentage points lower on anakinra over 13 weeks (P = 0.03) with improved beta-cell and inflammatory measures; the follow-up report is the same trial after withdrawal (secretion gain not maintained) and no second trial exists

title: Albendazole–ivermectin vs albendazole alone for Trichuris/STH (PARTIAL vs pack #2172): large cure gains in Laos, Pemba, Uganda and the FDC trial — but a NULL in Côte d'Ivoire (limbs never pooled)
question: In children, adolescents and adults infected with soil-transmitted helminths — principally Trichuris trichiura (whipworm), also hookworm and Strongyloides stercoralis — does a single dose of albendazole 400 mg combined with ivermectin (co-administered, or as a fixed-dose combination tablet) versus albendazole 400 mg alone achieve parasitological cure 14–21 days after treatment? PARTIAL beside pack #2172, which homes the Pemba 2015 four-arm combination trial (no albendazole-alone arm) — that trial is not re-carded here.
balance: SPLIT by setting — the setting limbs are never pooled on this shelf. PARTIAL beside pack #2172, which homes the Pemba 2015 four-arm whipworm-combination trial (no albendazole-alone arm); only the combination-versus-albendazole-alone trials are carded here. In the three-country phase 3 trial (1,673 randomised), Trichuris cure on the combination versus albendazole alone was 66% vs 8% in Laos (difference 58 percentage points) and 49% vs 6% on Pemba Island (43 points) — but 14% vs 10% in Côte d'Ivoire (4 points, 95% CI −2 to 10, P = 0.24): the Côte d'Ivoire null is load-bearing and forbids any pooled headline. The fixed-dose coformulation trial (1,001 recruited, ages 5–18) found Trichuris cure of 82.9% (single-dose FDC) and 97.2% (3-day FDC) versus 35.9% on albendazole, with its Strongyloides efficacy sample size NOT met (unproven, printed as such); the Ugandan co-administration trial found 31.3% vs 12.3% cure (difference 18.9 points). Absolute cure rates vary widely by setting and product (12–36% on albendazole alone across trials), so no cross-trial pooled rate is printed. The endpoint throughout is parasitological cure / egg reduction at 14–21 days — no trial measures anaemia, growth, transmission or clinical outcomes. Product naming (clarification exception): the fixed-dose albendazole–ivermectin coformulation is the tested product as the publication names it — an investigational coformulation, not a marketed product at publication; co-administered separate tablets are the programme's other tested form, and current products may differ.
stamp: SPLIT (benefit, by setting) — PARTIAL beside pack #2172: albendazole–ivermectin beat albendazole alone on Trichuris cure in Laos (+58 points), on Pemba Island (+43 points), in Uganda (+18.9 points) and as a fixed-dose coformulation (+47 to +61 points), but showed no advantage in Côte d'Ivoire (+4 points, P = 0.24); the setting limbs are never pooled

title: Scorpion antivenom + prazosin for Mesobuthus tamulus envenomation: resolution within 10 hours in 91–92% vs 23–40% on prazosin alone (4 randomised reports, N = 301; Egyptian mirror trial's mortality difference non-significant)
question: In children and adults with grade 2–severe Mesobuthus tamulus envenomation and autonomic storm, does adding scorpion antivenom to prazosin — or, in the mirror comparison, adding prazosin to antivenom — versus either agent alone speed resolution of the autonomic syndrome and prevent deterioration? (4 randomised reports, N = 301; comparison and species limbs labelled.)
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), on 4 randomised reports (N = 301 in total) with the comparisons and species limbs labelled and never pooled. Three trials ask whether antivenom added to prazosin helps in Mesobuthus tamulus envenomation: the BMJ trial (70 patients, grade 2) found complete resolution of the clinical syndrome within 10 hours in 91.4% on antivenom plus prazosin versus 22.9% on prazosin alone, with mean recovery 8.0 vs 17.7 hours; the paediatric trial (50 children) found 92% vs 40% clear of autonomic symptoms within 10 hours and deterioration to grade 3–4 in 8% vs 44%; and the three-arm trial (81 patients, severe envenomation) found complete recovery in 4.14 hours on antivenom versus 19.28 hours on prazosin. The fourth trial asks the mirror question — prazosin added to antivenom, in Egypt, where the scorpion species is not M. tamulus (population limb labelled): hospital stay was identical (median 3 days), antivenom consumption was lower on the combination (median 6 vs 9 vials), and mortality was 8% vs 20% — NOT statistically significant, printed as such. All four trials are open-label; three are single-centre Indian studies from one research tradition. Endpoints are time to resolution of a clinical syndrome score — no trial is powered for mortality. Product naming (clarification exception): the tested antivenom is the Indian polyvalent scorpion antivenom as the publications describe it; antivenoms are species- and maker-specific, and these results do not transfer to other regions' antivenoms (the North American Centruroides product homed at live #1257 included). The 2007 Mahad comparison is non-randomised and is never counted here.

title: Posaconazole for chronic Chagas disease (FLOOR-RISK — exactly 2 RCTs): durable clearance failed in both — at placebo level in STOP-CHAGAS (13.3% vs 10%), far below benznidazole in CHAGASAZOL
question: In adults with chronic Trypanosoma cruzi infection, does oral posaconazole — alone or combined with benznidazole — versus benznidazole (or placebo) achieve sustained parasite clearance on real-time PCR after treatment? FLOOR-RISK — exactly 2 randomised trials.
balance: LIKELY (no difference) from placebo for durable parasite clearance — FLOOR-RISK: exactly 2 randomised trials, printed on the face. Both trials tell the same arc: posaconazole suppressed Trypanosoma cruzi on treatment and failed after it. In CHAGASAZOL (78 patients, intention-to-treat), during follow-up 92% on low-dose and 81% on high-dose posaconazole tested PCR-positive, versus 38% on benznidazole (P < 0.01). In STOP-CHAGAS (120 asymptomatic carriers), persistent negative PCR by day 180 was achieved by 13.3% on posaconazole and 10% on placebo, versus 80% on benznidazole plus posaconazole and 86.7% on benznidazole alone (P < 0.0001); at 360 days both benznidazole arms stood at 96% versus 16–17% on posaconazole/placebo, and adding posaconazole to benznidazole gave no advantage over benznidazole alone. The outcome in both trials is PCR parasite detection — a surrogate, not clinical cure, cardiomyopathy progression or mortality; neither trial measures a clinical endpoint. Populations were chronic carriers without advanced cardiomyopathy, so the results do not speak to established Chagas cardiomyopathy (benznidazole's clinical-outcome question is homed at pack #3309 and is not imported here).
stamp: LIKELY (no difference) — FLOOR-RISK, exactly 2 trials (n = 78 and n = 120): posaconazole's durable PCR clearance was at placebo level in STOP-CHAGAS (13.3% vs 10% by day 180; 16% vs 17% at 360 days) and far below benznidazole in both trials (follow-up PCR positivity 81–92% vs 38% in CHAGASAZOL), despite on-treatment suppression in both

title: Varespladib adjunctively for snakebite envenoming (FLOOR-RISK — exactly 2 phase 2 RCTs): BRAVO primary null with point estimate favouring placebo; 2026 post-antivenom trial missed both limb primaries
question: In patients with snakebite envenoming receiving standard care including antivenom, does varespladib (oral methyl prodrug, or intravenous-then-oral) versus placebo improve early severity scores and functional recovery? FLOOR-RISK — exactly 2 phase 2 randomised trials, both primary-null.
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (no difference) — FLOOR-RISK: exactly 2 phase 2 randomised trials, both primary-null, printed on the face. BRAVO (95 randomised in India and the USA) gave oral varespladib methyl twice daily for 1 week added to standard care including antivenom: Snakebite Severity Score improvement to the 6–9-hour average was 1.1 on varespladib versus 1.5 on placebo (difference −0.4, 95% CI −0.8 to 0.1, P = 0.13) — the point estimate favours placebo, printed as reported. Its prespecified subgroup treated within 5 hours of the bite (n = 37) showed clinically important differences, but that is a subgroup reading of a null trial, labelled hypothesis-generating only wherever it appears here, and the later trial does not test it. The 2026 adjunctive trial (140 randomised, 139 analysed) gave intravenous-then-oral varespladib started a mean 7.3 hours after the bite and 3.3 hours after antivenom: the elapid primary (time to recovery of 5-second head-lift) was 27.6 vs 36.2 hours (P = 0.6) and the viper primary (severity-score AUC to day 14) was 660 vs 629 (P = 0.7) — both primaries unmet, the limbs labelled and never pooled. Nothing in either trial supports varespladib instead of, or before, antivenom. The BRAVO protocol paper is carded labelled as a protocol — it is not a results report and is never counted.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (no difference) — FLOOR-RISK, exactly 2 phase 2 trials (n = 95 and n = 140), both primary-null: BRAVO's point estimate favoured placebo (difference −0.4, P = 0.13) and the 2026 adjunctive trial missed both limb primaries (P = 0.6 elapid; P = 0.7 viper); the BRAVO within-5-hours subgroup is hypothesis-generating only

title: Trichuris suis ova for IBD: a small positive UC index trial (n=54, null on remission), then two large null trials — Crohn's n=252 and UC PROCTO n=119 (remission 30% vs 34% on placebo)
question: In patients with active ulcerative colitis or Crohn's disease, do orally administered embryonated Trichuris suis ova (2,500–7,500 ova every 2 weeks) versus placebo improve disease activity or induce clinical remission?
balance: LIKELY (no benefit), on a four-report randomised base (461 randomised in total) whose limbs must never be pooled. ULCERATIVE COLITIS limb: the small 2005 Iowa trial (n=54) was positive on an improvement index (43.3% vs 16.7%) but NOT on remission, and the larger 2024 PROCTO trial (n=119) found clinical remission at or below placebo (30% vs 34%; risk ratio 0.89, a relative measure). CROHN'S DISEASE limb: the only efficacy trial (n=252, three doses) found no dose beating placebo on remission, response, inflammatory markers or mucosal healing; the remaining Crohn's report (n=36) is a single-dose SAFETY trial only. The arc is a tested-and-failed hypothesis: a small positive index trial followed by two adequately sized null trials. The tested preparation — embryonated Trichuris suis ova produced for clinical use — is an investigational biological product, not a supplement, and preparations differ by maker.
stamp: LIKELY (no benefit) — four randomised reports (461 randomised): the only positive reading is a 54-patient UC improvement index (its remission reading was null), and both adequately sized efficacy trials were null — Crohn's n=252 (no dose beat placebo) and UC PROCTO n=119 (remission 30% vs 34%); the n=36 Crohn's report is safety-only and the disease limbs are never pooled

title: Cannabis/CBD for active Crohn's disease: symptoms and quality of life improved in 2 of 3 tiny trials (total N=97), but no endoscopic or inflammatory change — and low-dose CBD was null
question: In adults with active Crohn's disease not responding to standard therapy, does a cannabis preparation (smoked THC-rich cannabis, oral cannabidiol, or CBD-rich cannabis oil) versus placebo induce remission or improve disease activity over 8 weeks?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit, symptoms only) — based on a very small randomised base of 3 trials totalling 97 patients. The symptom–inflammation split is the answer: every positive reading is a symptom or quality-of-life index (the Crohn's Disease Activity Index is symptom-weighted), while the one trial that scoped patients found NO endoscopic change and inflammatory markers never moved. The smoked-cannabis trial MISSED its primary remission endpoint (45% vs 10%, P=.43); the purified low-dose CBD trial was outright null; the CBD-rich oil trial improved CDAI and quality of life but not endoscopic scores (SES-CD), C-reactive protein or calprotectin. Nothing here is disease modification. The three tested preparations are DIFFERENT products — THC-rich smoked cannabis, purified low-dose oral CBD (10 mg twice daily), and a CBD-rich oil with THC (160/40 mg/mL) — named exactly as published; current commercial cannabis/CBD products may differ in composition, safety and effectiveness and were not what was tested. All three trials are from Israel and all lasted 8 weeks; smoked THC is effectively unblindable by subjective effect, and the symptom endpoints are the ones most exposed to that bias.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit, symptoms only) — based on a very small randomised base of 3 trials totalling 97 patients (n=21, 20, 56): CDAI and quality of life improved in two trials, but the smoked-cannabis trial missed its primary remission endpoint (P=.43), low-dose CBD was null, and the one endoscopic trial showed no mucosal or inflammatory-marker change — no disease modification

title: Low-dose naltrexone for Crohn's induction: FLOOR-RISK, exactly 2 trials (N=81) directly split — 2011 positive (n=40) vs 2026 futility-stopped, remission favouring placebo (n=41)
question: In adults with active Crohn's disease, does low-dose naltrexone 4.5 mg daily versus placebo induce clinical and endoscopic remission over 12 weeks?
balance: SPLIT — FLOOR-RISK: exactly 2 adult randomised trials exist, totalling 81 patients, and they split completely. The 2011 single-centre trial (n=40; entry by clinical activity, CDAI 220–450) reported striking benefit: ≥70-point CDAI decline in 88% vs 40% (P=0.009) and endoscopic response in 78% vs 28% (P=0.008). The 2026 Dutch multicentre trial (n=41; entry REQUIRED mucosal ulcers on endoscopy, SES-CD 3–15) was STOPPED EARLY FOR FUTILITY, with endoscopic remission 5.6% vs 18.8% (P=0.233) and clinical remission 22.2% vs 70.0% (P=0.037 — favouring placebo). The populations differ — clinically active versus endoscopically confirmed, milder disease — which is part of why the readings may differ, and both entry rules are stated rather than the trials being averaged. The 2026 trial's only positive reading was a fatigue score, a lone secondary outcome in a futility-stopped trial — never a headline. No serious adverse events occurred in either trial.
stamp: SPLIT — FLOOR-RISK, exactly 2 adult randomised trials totalling 81 patients (n=40 and n=41), directly split: the 2011 trial reported endoscopic response 78% vs 28% on placebo, while the 2026 multicentre trial was stopped early for futility with clinical remission 22.2% vs 70.0% favouring placebo; the only 2026 positive reading was a secondary fatigue score

title: Mesenchymal stem cells for decompensated cirrhosis: SPLIT — the only placebo-controlled trial (n=27) was negative; the largest open-label trial (n=219, umbilical-cord MSCs) reported higher survival; products differ by trial
question: In patients with decompensated cirrhosis, does mesenchymal stem cell therapy (autologous bone-marrow-derived, or allogeneic umbilical-cord-derived) added to standard care versus standard care or placebo improve liver function, fibrosis, or survival?
balance: SPLIT — the only placebo-controlled trial is negative and the largest trial is open-label and positive, and the four trials do not test the same treatment. Products, named exactly as published (clarification exception — these are investigational manufactured cell products and no marketed equivalent was tested): autologous bone-marrow MSCs by peripheral-vein infusion (Iran, n=27 — NEGATIVE: no difference in Child, MELD, albumin, INR, transaminases or liver volumes at 12 months, with 3 deaths in the MSC arm, all in patients with significantly higher baseline MELD); autologous bone-marrow MSC transplantation on entecavir (China, HBV cirrhosis, 56 enrolled / 39 completed — liver function improved further, framed mechanistically via Treg/Th17 shifts); autologous bone-marrow MSCs by hepatic-artery injection, one or two doses (Korea, abstinent alcoholic cirrhosis, n=72 — histological fibrosis fell WITHIN the treated groups, 25% and 37% relative reductions, a within-group before–after reading, and Child-Pugh improved; two injections were not superior to one); and allogeneic umbilical-cord MSCs, three infusions, plus conventional therapy (China, HBV decompensated cirrhosis, n=219 — overall survival significantly higher over follow-up to 75 months, HCC-free survival not different, liver-function indices improved over 48 weeks). Four countries (Iran, China, Korea, China), 2013–2021, standard care of their eras. Never an averaged 'stem cells improve cirrhosis' headline.
stamp: SPLIT — four randomised trials of three different cell products: the only placebo-controlled trial (n=27, autologous bone-marrow MSCs intravenously) found no benefit, while the largest trial (n=219, open-label, umbilical-cord MSCs) reported significantly higher overall survival, an HBV trial (56 enrolled / 39 completed) reported improved liver function, and the fibrosis claim rests on within-group histology in an open-label per-protocol analysis — heterogeneity is load-bearing and the limbs are never pooled

title: Founding thrombectomy trials: all five 2015 trials favoured thrombectomy in anterior-circulation LVO stroke (HERMES pool NNT 2.6); MR CLEAN independence 32.6% vs 19.1%
question: In patients with acute ischaemic stroke caused by a proximal intracranial occlusion of the anterior circulation, does endovascular (intra-arterial) thrombectomy plus usual care improve 90-day functional outcome versus usual care alone?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — the founding 2015 programme: five randomised trials of endovascular thrombectomy for proximal anterior-circulation occlusion, every one favouring thrombectomy on 90-day functional outcome, pooled by the HERMES individual-patient meta-analysis (1,287 patients; adjusted common odds ratio 2.49 for reduced disability — a relative measure — with a number needed to treat of 2.6 for one patient to improve by at least one Rankin level; mortality and symptomatic haemorrhage did not differ in the pool). The trials are labelled limbs, never a single pooled trial: MR CLEAN (n=500) is the generalisability anchor — broad eligibility, treatment within 6 hours, 89% pre-treated with intravenous alteplase, functional independence 32.6% vs 19.1%; ESCAPE (n=316), EXTEND-IA (n=70), REVASCAT (n=206) and SWIFT PRIME (n=196) used progressively tighter imaging selection (small infarct core, moderate-to-good collaterals, salvageable tissue) and several stopped early — ESCAPE, EXTEND-IA and SWIFT PRIME for efficacy, REVASCAT for loss of equipoise — which belongs on the face. This shelf cards the founding early-window question only; the library's later, different thrombectomy questions (large-core, basilar, post-thrombectomy blood pressure, nerinetide) are separate homes and are not folded in.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — the five founding 2015 trials (MR CLEAN, ESCAPE, EXTEND-IA, REVASCAT, SWIFT PRIME; 1,287 patients in the HERMES individual-patient pool) unanimously favoured thrombectomy for proximal anterior-circulation occlusion on 90-day functional outcome (pooled adjusted common odds ratio 2.49, relative; NNT 2.6), with no pooled mortality or symptomatic-haemorrhage excess; the imaging-selected trials stopped early, and MR CLEAN's broader population is the generalisability anchor

title: Pazopanib vs placebo in advanced RCC (VEG105192): PFS 9.2 vs 4.2 months (HR 0.46, relative), response 30% vs 3% — final overall survival not significant (22.9 vs 20.5 months)
question: In treatment-naïve or cytokine-pretreated patients with locally advanced or metastatic renal-cell carcinoma, does pazopanib 800 mg daily improve progression-free survival versus placebo?
balance: LIKELY (benefit, progression-free survival only) — one trial (VEG105192, 435 randomised 2:1), three reports, labelled a single-programme shelf. title: Founding Hodgkin chemotherapy: ABVD displaced MOPP on toxicity at equal efficacy; BEACOPP's first-progression edge over ABVD (85% vs 73%) faded after planned salvage (OS 89% vs 84%, NS) — eras never pooled
question: In patients with advanced Hodgkin lymphoma, how do the founding regimens compare — ABVD versus MOPP and MOPP/ABV-hybrid therapy (CALGB; Intergroup), and intensified BEACOPP versus COPP-ABVD and versus ABVD with planned high-dose salvage (HD9; Viviani)?
balance: SPLIT (by comparison and era) — four founding trials, four reports, labelled slices that are NEVER pooled, because the two eras teach opposite lessons. MOPP-ERA slice: ABVD displaced MOPP on toxicity at equal-or-better efficacy. CALGB (361 patients): complete responses 67% on MOPP vs 82% on ABVD vs 83% on MOPP alternating with ABVD (P=0.006), 5-year failure-free survival 50% vs 61% vs 65%, 5-year overall survival 66% vs 73% vs 75% (P=0.28 — not significant), with more severe marrow toxicity on MOPP. Intergroup (856 patients): ABVD versus the MOPP/ABV hybrid showed NO efficacy difference (complete remission 76% vs 80%; 5-year failure-free survival 63% vs 66%; 5-year OS 82% vs 81%) but more acute toxicity and significantly more MDS/leukaemia with the MOPP-containing hybrid (13 vs 2 in the attributable sequence; P=.011) — on which the report concludes ABVD should be the standard. BEACOPP-ERA slice: intensification bought first-progression control at higher toxicity, and its survival meaning depends on the comparator and on salvage. HD9 (1,195 evaluable): escalated BEACOPP beat COPP-ABVD on 5-year freedom from treatment failure (87% vs 69%) and 5-year OS (91% vs 83%; P=0.002). Viviani (331 patients, both arms with planned high-dose salvage): 7-year freedom from FIRST progression favoured BEACOPP (85% vs 73%; P=0.004), but after the full planned strategy including salvage, freedom from second progression (88% vs 82%; P=0.12) and overall survival (89% vs 84%; P=0.39) were NOT significantly different, with more severe adverse events on BEACOPP.
stamp: SPLIT (by comparison and era) — four founding trials, never pooled: in the MOPP era ABVD displaced MOPP-containing therapy on toxicity at equal efficacy (CALGB n=361; Intergroup n=856 — MDS/leukaemia significantly more frequent with the MOPP/ABV hybrid, P=.011, with no efficacy difference), while in the BEACOPP era escalated BEACOPP beat COPP-ABVD on tumour control and survival in HD9 (n=1,195; 5-year OS 91% vs 83%) but against ABVD with planned high-dose salvage (Viviani n=331) its advantage was confined to first progression (85% vs 73%), with overall survival not significantly different (89% vs 84%; P=0.39) and more severe adverse events

title: Bedside airway tests predict difficult intubation specifically but not sensitively: upper lip bite class 3 likelihood ratio 14, pooled sensitivities only 0.38–0.52
question: Before tracheal intubation in adults without obvious airway abnormality, how accurately do the bedside airway examination tests — the modified Mallampati classification, the upper lip bite test, thyromental and hyomental distance, retrognathia and multivariate scores such as Wilson and LEMON — predict difficult laryngoscopy, difficult intubation and difficult mask ventilation, and how far apart are the tests' sensitivities (all of them low) from their specificities (all of them high)?
balance: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — rule-in strong, rule-out weak, and that asymmetry is the whole content. Across four syntheses the bedside tests are consistently specific (0.83–0.98) and consistently insensitive (sensitivities 0.38–0.52 in the 2024 meta-analysis; Cochrane summary sensitivities as low as 0.17–0.24 for some test/outcome pairs): a positive upper lip bite test (class 3) is the strongest single finding (positive likelihood ratio 14, raising difficult-intubation probability from 10% to over 60% in the JAMA review), but no negative bedside test reliably excludes a difficult airway. The four difficulty descriptors — mask ventilation, laryngoscopy, intubation, failed intubation — are different reference standards and are never pooled here. This is a prognostic-accuracy shelf only: nothing carded shows that testing, or any preparation a positive test triggers, improves outcomes. PROPOSED STAMP: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — high specificity, low sensitivity (see proposedStamp).
stamp: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — bedside airway tests rule in far better than they rule out: specificities 0.83–0.98 across syntheses but sensitivities only 0.38–0.52 in the largest meta-analysis (upper lip bite class 3 the strongest single finding, positive likelihood ratio 14 in the JAMA review), so a positive test usefully raises difficult-intubation risk while no negative test excludes it; accuracy figures are per reference standard (laryngoscopy, intubation, mask ventilation, failed intubation) and are never pooled
