title: Hendrich II Fall Risk Model: AUC 0.765 and 78.7% sensitivity at ≥5 across nine hospitals, but AUC 0.57 and 29.5% sensitivity at the same cut-off in a single-centre re-validation
question: In hospitalised adults, how well does the Hendrich II Fall Risk Model (confusion / disorientation, depression, altered elimination, dizziness / vertigo, male sex, antiepileptics, benzodiazepines, and the Get-Up-and-Go rising item; standard high-risk cut-off ≥5) predict who will fall during the admission — what sensitivity, specificity and discrimination does it deliver at the standard cut-off and at locally lowered cut-offs, and how far does its accuracy swing between the large multisite validations and single-centre re-validations?
balance: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — moderate in the large multisite validation, poor at the same cut-off in a single-centre re-validation, and that transportability swing is the content. In 214,358 inpatients across nine hospitals the Hendrich II model at its standard cut-off ≥5 gave sensitivity 78.72%, specificity 64.07% and AUC 0.765; lowering the cut-off to ≥4 raised sensitivity to 90.56% and dropped specificity to 44.43%. In a single Taiwanese centre (303 fall events) the same ≥5 cut-off gave sensitivity of only 29.5% with specificity 86.3% and AUC 0.57, with acceptable discrimination (AUC 0.75) only at ≥2. A small prospective geriatric-unit validation found sensitivity 86% and specificity 43% at its optimal cut-off of 5 (AUC 0.72). The 2003 derivation report is the model originators' own and is labelled as such. No sensitivity/specificity pair on this shelf prints without its setting and cut-off, and nothing carded shows that scoring — or any bundle a high score triggers — prevents falls. PROPOSED STAMP: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — setting-dependent (see proposedStamp).
stamp: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — highly setting-dependent: moderate discrimination in the nine-hospital validation (AUC 0.765; sensitivity 78.72% and specificity 64.07% at the standard cut-off ≥5, sensitivity 90.56% at ≥4) but poor discrimination at the same ≥5 cut-off in a single-centre re-validation (AUC 0.57, sensitivity 29.5%), so no accuracy figure is valid without its setting and cut-off; the derivation report is the originators' own and is programme-labelled

title: Preoperative IVC collapsibility predicts post-induction hypotension moderately: pooled sensitivity 0.68 / specificity 0.78, best at a 40–45% threshold, on a definitionally heterogeneous literature
question: Before elective surgery under general anaesthesia, how accurately do preoperative inferior-vena-cava ultrasound measures — the collapsibility index and the maximum IVC diameter — predict hypotension after induction, what pooled sensitivity and specificity do they deliver, at what collapsibility thresholds does performance peak, and how much of the literature's spread is definitional (differing hypotension definitions, measurement methods and cut-offs) rather than biological?
balance: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — moderate for general-anaesthesia induction hypotension, on a definitionally heterogeneous literature. The 2024 meta-analysis of 14 prospective observational studies (1,166 patients) pooled IVC collapsibility-index sensitivity 0.68 and specificity 0.78 (HSROC-AUC 0.80), with performance peaking at a 40–45% collapsibility threshold (HSROC-AUC 0.86). The 2023 systematic review (21 studies, spinal and general anaesthesia carded as separate slices here) could not pool at all: post-spinal collapsibility-index sensitivity ranged 58.8–84.6% and specificity 23.5–93.1%, and the spread was driven by differing hypotension definitions, measurement methods and cut-offs. The single primary study carded (83 analysable patients, standardised propofol induction) shows the pattern in miniature at a ≥50% threshold: high specificity (90.0%) but sensitivity of only 45.5%. This is a prognostic-accuracy shelf only: nothing carded shows an IVC-guided fluid or vasopressor strategy prevents post-induction hypotension. PROPOSED STAMP: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — moderate, threshold- and definition-dependent (see proposedStamp).
stamp: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — moderate for post-induction hypotension under general anaesthesia: pooled IVC collapsibility-index sensitivity 0.68 and specificity 0.78 (HSROC-AUC 0.80) across 14 prospective studies, peaking at a 40–45% threshold, but the wider literature is too heterogeneous in hypotension definitions, measurement methods and cut-offs to pool (post-spinal specificity alone ranged 23.5–93.1%), and no carded study shows acting on the measurement prevents hypotension

title: Preoperative six-minute walk distance predicts postoperative complications: thresholds 325 m (mixed high-risk) vs 450–454 m (cancer resection), and performable when spirometry is contraindicated
question: Before elective surgery, how well does the preoperative six-minute walk test distance predict postoperative pulmonary complications and other postoperative complications — what thresholds have been derived in thoracic, oesophageal and mixed high-risk cohorts (325 m, 450 m, 454 m), how do their sensitivities and specificities compare, and how does the test perform in patients who cannot perform spirometry at all?
balance: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — a consistent direction on a small, mostly retrospective base, with thresholds that are cohort property, not constants. Four non-METS reports: a prospective mixed high-risk cohort (N = 78) derived a ≤325 m threshold with 77% sensitivity and 100% specificity for postoperative pulmonary complications, and showed the test could be completed by the 17.9% of patients who had contraindications to spirometry; an oesophageal-cancer cohort (N = 111) derived ≤454 m (sensitivity 71.0%, specificity 54.8%) for Clavien–Dindo grade ≥II complications; a lung-resection cohort (N = 321, the largest) derived ≤450 m for pneumonia (69.2% / 71.1%); and a small VATS lobectomy cohort (N = 66) found ≤450 m carried an odds ratio of 5.674 for 30-day pulmonary complications, labelled an odds ratio. Three of four cohorts are retrospective and none exceeds 321 patients, which prints on the face. A fifth report — a secondary analysis of the METS cohort (PMID 33442834) — was verified at mining but is deliberately NOT carded on this shelf, per the commissioning row. This is a prognostic-accuracy shelf only. PROPOSED STAMP: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — consistent, threshold-variable, small-base (see proposedStamp).
stamp: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — consistent direction, cohort-bound thresholds: preoperative walk distance ≤325 m predicted pulmonary complications at 77% sensitivity / 100% specificity in a prospective mixed high-risk cohort (N = 78), while cancer-resection cohorts derived 450–454 m thresholds with sensitivities 69–71% and specificities 55–71% (largest N = 321; three of four reports retrospective), and the test remained performable in patients with contraindications to spirometry; no universal cut-off exists and the METS-cohort report is deliberately not carded

title: Stair climbing before lung resection: poor performance carries a pooled relative risk of 2.34 for complications; <12 m vs >22 m strata differ 2-fold in complications and 13-fold in mortality (relative)
question: Before major lung resection, how well does performance on the symptom-limited stair-climbing test — height climbed, time, desaturation and heart-rate change — predict postoperative cardiopulmonary complications and death, what height thresholds separate risk (about 10–12 m vs more than 22 m), and when should a poor stair-climbing result trigger formal cardiopulmonary exercise testing instead of deciding the question itself?
balance: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — poor stair-climbing performance is consistently associated with more postoperative complications after lung resection, but the test is not standardised and its thresholds are strata from individual cohorts. The 2020 meta-analysis (13 articles, 2,038 patients; 6 pooled) found poor performance associated with complications at a pooled risk ratio of 2.34 (95% CI 1.59 to 3.43) — a relative measure, labelled as such — with the complication threshold estimated at a 10 m climb, across studies that used incompatible criteria (height, rise time, desaturation, heart-rate change). The founding prospective cohort (640 lobectomy / pneumonectomy patients) found patients climbing less than 12 m had 2-fold cardiopulmonary complications, 13-fold mortality and 2.5-fold costs compared with patients climbing more than 22 m — relative comparisons between extreme strata in one centre, printed with their strata; the fetched record does not print the strata's absolute rates, and none is claimed. A 2022 cohort in limited-pulmonary-function patients (424 tested) found height achieved and heart-rate change (ΔHR >30 bpm) independently predictive. Both the meta-analysis and the founding cohort position a poor result as a trigger for formal cardiopulmonary exercise testing, not as a decision in itself. PROPOSED STAMP: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — associated, non-standardised, extreme-strata (see proposedStamp).
stamp: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — poor stair-climbing performance is associated with postoperative cardiopulmonary complications after major lung resection (pooled risk ratio 2.34, a relative measure; <12 m vs >22 m strata at 2-fold complications and 13-fold mortality in the founding 640-patient cohort, relative comparisons without absolute stratum rates in the record), but the test is not standardised — height, time, desaturation and heart-rate criteria are never merged — and a poor result is a trigger for formal cardiopulmonary exercise testing, not a decision in itself

title: Preoperative spirometry does not establishedly predict pulmonary complications: 2002 review null, 2022 review inconclusive (65% for / 35% against), possible exception in upper abdominal surgery with COPD indicators
question: Before non-thoracic surgery, how well do preoperative pulmonary function tests — spirometry (FEV1, FVC), hypercarbia and blood-gas measures — predict postoperative pulmonary complications, why do the two systematic reviews reach null and inconclusive conclusions respectively, and in which subgroup (upper abdominal surgery, patients with COPD indicators) does the primary literature still argue for testing?
balance: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — NOT ESTABLISHED, and the null / inconclusive direction is this shelf's content. The 2002 systematic review of blinded studies (7 studies, 28 predictors) found neither hypercarbia nor reduced spirometry values independently associated with postoperative pulmonary complications after non-thoracic surgery; only anaesthesia duration and postoperative nasogastric tube placement were significant in more than one study. The 2022 systematic review (46 original studies, high risk of bias on QUADAS-2) could reach only a qualitative verdict — inconclusive, with 65% of prospective studies for and 35% against preoperative spirometry — and named one possible-benefit subgroup: upper abdominal surgery in the low-selection-bias studies (3 studies, 959 participants, for; 1 study, 60 participants, against), with spirometry to be considered in patients with COPD indicators scheduling for upper abdominal surgery. The single positive primary report carded (N = 78, FEV1 % predicted an independent predictor alongside walk distance) is small and is shared with the six-minute-walk shelf #7686, stated on both; it is not pooled with the syntheses into a positive summary. Outside that named subgroup, no card presents spirometry as an established preoperative risk tool. PROPOSED STAMP: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — NOT ESTABLISHED (null / inconclusive syntheses; see proposedStamp).
stamp: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — NOT ESTABLISHED: the 2002 blinded-study review found neither hypercarbia nor reduced spirometry values independently associated with postoperative pulmonary complications, and the 2022 review of 46 studies (high risk of bias) was inconclusive (65% of prospective studies for, 35% against), with a possible benefit confined to upper abdominal surgery in patients with COPD indicators; the one positive primary report is a single small cohort (N = 78) shared with the walk-test shelf and is not pooled into a positive summary

title: Testicular volume on ultrasound by population: ~17 mL in European fertile men (lower limits 12 / 11 mL), 13.64 mL in Vietnamese healthy fathers, ~10.4 mL in Somali men (95% intervals 5.7–18.0 / 5.2–17.0 mL)
question: In healthy adult men, what are the reference values for testicular volume on ultrasound — mean volume and lower and upper reference limits — how far do population reference intervals sit from one another (European fertile men vs Somali vs Vietnamese reference figures), and how well do ultrasound volumes agree with Prader-orchidometer volumes?
balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, reproductive sections — the framing is brief, and this shelf rests chiefly on the primary population literature, and says so. Three independent datasets, carded per population because the population gradient IS the content: a prospective European Academy of Andrology multicentre standardisation study of 248 healthy fertile men found mean ultrasound volume ~17 mL with lower reference limits of 12 mL (right) and 11 mL (left); a retrospective Vietnamese andrology-service dataset (24,440 attendees; the reference figure is its healthy-fathers subgroup, mean 13.64 ± 3.44 mL — the subgroup's own N is not documented in the record and the headline 24,440 is never printed as the reference N); and a retrospective Somali reference-interval study (212 sonographically normal men) found means of 10.61 / 10.19 mL with 95% intervals of 5.7–18.0 / 5.2–17.0 mL. No interval here may be printed as universal. The EAA overview paper (PMID 35930758) is the same cohort as the EAA dataset carded here and is counted once — it is not a fourth dataset and is not carded. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING (see proposedStamp).
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING — ultrasound testicular volume reference values exist for three populations (European fertile men: mean ~17 mL, lower limits 12 / 11 mL; Vietnamese healthy fathers: 13.64 ± 3.44 mL; Somali men: 95% intervals 5.7–18.0 / 5.2–17.0 mL), but only one dataset is a prospective standardisation study, two are retrospective clinic-based derivations, and the population gradient is larger than any single interval, so no value is universal

title: Serum ceruloplasmin reference values: upper limit ~25 mg/dL in men vs ~45 mg/dL in young women (1,706 donors); oral contraceptives raise the mean ~65% (181 vs 110 IU/ml, 1987)
question: In healthy adults, what are the reference values for serum ceruloplasmin — the central range by sex and age — how large is the sex difference, how strongly do oestrogen exposure (oral contraceptives, pregnancy, lactation) and population move the values, and why do the published datasets report in different units (mg/dL vs IU/ml) that cannot be merged?
balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall and Boron & Boulpaep have no ceruloplasmin reference chapter — this shelf rests on the primary reference literature alone, with the textbooks framing copper transport and acute-phase biology only, and says so. Four independent datasets, never pooled: the modern anchor (1,706 healthy Italian blood donors, 2024) derives quantile-regression reference curves in mg/dL — the upper reference value plateauing at about 25 mg/dL around age 25 in men, while in women it rose to about 45 mg/dL in young adults before falling below 30 mg/dL after the fifties. The oestrogen effect is large: in 200 healthy young women (1987), oral-contraceptive users averaged 181 ± 43.9 IU/ml against 110 ± 22.7 IU/ml in non-users — a ~65% higher mean, a relative comparison labelled as such. Units are assay-era property (IU/ml in 1987 vs mg/dL in 2024) and are never converted or merged. Three of the four datasets are women-only or women-predominant, so sex and hormonal status print on every card and no mixed 'adult range' is offered. The Zairean dataset's non-pregnant / non-lactating subgroup is small (N = 27) and prints as such; the Omani dataset's N is not documented in its record and prints as such. This shelf gives reference values only — Wilson-disease diagnostic accuracy is a different question and is not asked here. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING (see proposedStamp).
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING — serum ceruloplasmin reference values are established as sex-, age- and oestrogen-dependent across four datasets (modern curves in mg/dL: upper reference ~25 mg/dL in men vs ~45 mg/dL in young women; oral contraceptives raised the mean ~65% in IU/ml in 1987), but the datasets span incompatible assay eras and units that are never converted or pooled, three are women-only or women-predominant, and two print no numeric values in their records

title: Nasal nitric oxide reference values by technique: healthy controls 304.6 ± 118.8 nl/min (PCD cut-off 77 nl/min) vs 426.76 ± 143.27 ppb by tidal breathing — never pooled
question: In healthy adults, what are the reference values for nasal nitric oxide — the mean, spread and upper range by measurement technique (breath-hold / velum-closure sampling in nl/min vs tidal-breathing NIOX MINO measurement in ppb) — which subject factors (sex, age, body size, lung function, blood eosinophils) move the value, and how far below the healthy range does the primary-ciliary-dyskinesia cut-off (77 nl/min) sit?
balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall and Boron & Boulpaep have no nasal-nitric-oxide reference chapter — this shelf rests on the primary reference literature alone, and says so. Three independent datasets, carded per technique because technique is destiny in this literature: velum-closure aspiration values in nl/min and tidal-breathing NIOX MINO values in ppb are different quantities and are never converted or pooled. The dedicated reference study (Antosova 2017; 141 healthy adults, NIOX MINO per ATS/ERS recommendations) derived reference values and studied the affecting factors, but its fetched record prints no numeric nasal NO values, and none is claimed from it. The numeric anchor in nl/min comes from the healthy-control arm of the primary-ciliary-dyskinesia standardisation study (Leigh 2013; 78 healthy controls, mean 304.6 ± 118.8 nl/min, range 125.5–867.0) — a control group inside a diagnostic study, not a dedicated interval derivation, printed as such — against which the PCD cut-off of 77 nl/min (sensitivity 0.98, specificity >0.999) sits roughly fourfold below the healthy mean. The tidal-breathing dataset (Gelardi 2016; 32 healthy subjects) gives 426.76 ± 143.27 ppb with a wide interval, its small N and width printing beside any range claim. Fractional EXHALED nitric oxide (FeNO, the lower-airway measurement, pack #7154) is a cross-point only — the two are never merged. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING (see proposedStamp).
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING — nasal nitric oxide reference values rest on three independent datasets that agree healthy values sit far above the primary-ciliary-dyskinesia cut-off (healthy controls 304.6 ± 118.8 nl/min vs cut-off 77 nl/min), but the values are technique-bound — nl/min velum-closure aspiration and ppb tidal-breathing figures are different quantities, never converted or pooled — the one dedicated derivation prints no numeric values in its record, and the tidal-breathing dataset is small (N = 32) with a wide interval

title: Complement C3 / C4 reference intervals: C3 0.656–1.52 g/L (65.6–152 mg/dL) and C4 0.181–0.561 g/L (18.1–56.1 mg/dL) in 1,234 Chinese Han men, BMI-dependent; 1980s nephelometry datasets as comparators
question: In healthy adults, what are the reference intervals for serum complement C3 and C4 — the central 95% ranges by immunoturbidimetric / nephelometric assay — how strongly do body-mass index and age move them, and how far do the modern population-derived intervals sit from the rate-nephelometry intervals of the early 1980s?
balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, immunity / complement sections — the framing is brief, and this shelf rests chiefly on the primary reference literature, and says so. Three independent datasets, carded per assay era and never pooled: the modern anchor (Qin 2014; 1,234 healthy Chinese Han men aged 20–69, FAMHES, immunoturbidimetry) gives two-sided 95% reference intervals of 0.656–1.52 g/L for C3 (65.6–152 mg/dL) and 0.181–0.561 g/L for C4 (18.1–56.1 mg/dL), with BMI positively associated with both (r = 0.342 and 0.258) and BMI-specific intervals calculated — a men-only dataset, printed as such and never presented as adult-universal. The 1982 rate-nephelometry dataset (Jolliff; 750 well children and 120 healthy adults — the adult slice is the cardable one and prints with its N) established intervals by the then-new method, but its fetched record prints no numeric C3 / C4 intervals, and none is claimed. The 1981 dataset (Hapke; two geographically separate healthy populations; N not documented in the record and printed as such) is carded for its methods finding: mean ± 2 SD intervals are unsafe for these analytes and non-parametric 2.5th–97.5th percentile intervals should be used. The 1981–82 intervals are historical comparators for the 2014 immunoturbidimetric intervals, never pooled with them. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING (see proposedStamp).
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING — complement C3 and C4 reference intervals are numerically established in one large modern dataset (1,234 Chinese Han men: C3 0.656–1.52 g/L [65.6–152 mg/dL], C4 0.181–0.561 g/L [18.1–56.1 mg/dL], BMI-associated), but that dataset is men-only and single-population, and the two 1981–82 rate-nephelometry datasets print no numeric intervals in their records — one supplying instead the standing method warning that these analytes need percentile-based, not mean ± 2 SD, intervals

title: Haptoglobin reference interval: 0.08–1.97 g/L (8–197 mg/dL) in men and 0.08–2.19 g/L (8–219 mg/dL) in women in 2,923 healthy subjects — and the interval should be partitioned by the rs2000999 polymorphism
question: In healthy adults, what is the reference interval for plasma / serum haptoglobin — the central range by sex — how much of its variation is genetic (the HP phenotype and the rs2000999 polymorphism), and how far do pregnancy and population move the levels of this acute-phase protein in people without inflammation?
balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, blood / haemolysis sections (framing brief — this shelf rests chiefly on the primary reference literature, and says so). Three datasets: the STANISLAS Family Study derivation in 2,923 selected healthy subjects is the only dataset that prints a full sex-specific interval — plasma haptoglobin 0.08–1.97 g/L (8–197 mg/dL) in men and 0.08–2.19 g/L (8–219 mg/dL) in women — and its distinctive finding is genetic partitioning: sex, age, smoking, haemoglobin and the rs2000999 polymorphism were the strongest predictors, with levels falling with each minor allele, so an unpartitioned interval mixes genotypes with systematically different levels. The other two datasets are SHARED CROSS-ANALYTE anchors, stated on the face: the 1994 Zairean women's dataset (419 women by pregnancy / lactation status; haptoglobin means did not differ between groups) is shared with the ceruloplasmin shelf, and the 1981 nephelometry distributions paper (N not documented in its record) is shared with the complement C3/C4 shelf — the same papers measured several serum proteins, which is not double-counting one population for one analyte. Haptoglobin is an acute-phase protein, so every dataset's health screen is part of the interval's meaning. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING — only one of the three datasets prints a full numeric interval, and the other two print no haptoglobin range in their records, so the interval is established for the STANISLAS population rather than as a universal range.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING — the STANISLAS derivation in 2,923 selected healthy subjects establishes a sex-specific plasma interval (men 0.08–1.97 g/L (8–197 mg/dL); women 0.08–2.19 g/L (8–219 mg/dL)) and shows it should be partitioned by rs2000999, but the two supporting datasets (419 Zairean women; a 1981 two-population nephelometry study with N not documented in its record) print no haptoglobin interval of their own, and both are shared cross-analyte anchors stated on the face

title: Normal aortic dimensions by modality: echo root diameters in 1,687 healthy Hamburg subjects, CT diameters at seven landmarks in 902 screened Copenhagen subjects, and MRI ascending-aorta upper limits of 20–23 mm/m² (men) and 21–28 mm/m² (women) by age band in MESA
question: In healthy adults, what are the normal aortic dimensions — diameters at the annulus, sinuses of Valsalva, sinotubular junction, ascending, descending and abdominal aorta — by imaging modality (echocardiography, CT, MRI), age, sex and body surface area, and how large is the indexing reversal (men larger absolutely, women larger once indexed to body surface area)?
balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, vascular sections (framing brief — this shelf rests chiefly on the primary population literature, and says so). Three datasets, three modalities, carded per modality and never merged: echocardiography (Hamburg City Health Study, 1,687 healthy subjects, aortic root at four levels in systole and diastole), contrast CT (Copenhagen General Population Study, 902 rigorously screened healthy subjects, maximal diameters at seven landmarks from the sinuses of Valsalva to the infrarenal abdominal aorta) and MRI (MESA, 3,573 participants, ascending-aorta diameter with upper limits defined in a healthy subgroup). All three agree on the structure: men are larger absolutely at every level, diameters rise with age and body surface area — and in the Hamburg echo data the sex order REVERSES once diameters are indexed to body surface area (women larger at all levels), so indexed and absolute diameters answer different questions and no card gives one without naming which it is. The MESA dataset is a general population cohort with a defined healthy subgroup for its upper limits, not a screened-healthy sample like Copenhagen's, and that distinction prints. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — three independent population datasets across three modalities agree on the age, sex and indexing structure of normal aortic size, with numeric limits printed per modality.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — three independent population datasets, one per modality (echocardiography N = 1,687; contrast CT N = 902 rigorously screened; MRI N = 3,573 with a healthy subgroup), consistently establish that normal aortic diameters rise with age and body surface area, are larger in men absolutely at every level, and reverse by sex once indexed to body surface area; limits are printed per modality and per measurement level, never merged

title: Lacosamide for painful diabetic neuropathy: SPLIT — two of three phase 3 trials met their primary at 400 mg/day (responder 58% vs 46% in one), the third missed it, and 23–40% stopped the effective doses for adverse events
question: In adults with painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy, does oral lacosamide (200–600 mg/day), compared with placebo, reduce neuropathic pain?
balance: PARTIAL slice only — the home, pack #2351, was read in full: it is the adjunctive-epilepsy shelf (partial-onset seizures; Ben-Menachem 2007 and Chung 2010) and contains zero mention of diabetes or neuropathy, so the epilepsy question stays homed there under the one-home rule and only this diabetic-neuropathy slice is carded here. This is a failed programme with SPLIT primaries, and the split leads: of three 18-week phase 3 trials, the fixed-dose trial met its primary at 400 mg/day (responders with ≥2-point or 30% pain reduction 58% vs 46% on placebo — a 12-percentage-point contrast) and the flexible-titration trial met it at exactly P = 0.05, while the slow/standard-titration trial did NOT meet its primary (400 mg/day P = 0.12; 600 mg/day P = 0.18). The 200 mg/day dose never separated significantly, and 600 mg/day was significant only in observed cases in one trial. The dose that works is also the dose at which nearly a quarter of patients stopped for adverse events (23% at 400 mg/day and 40% at 600 mg/day vs 9% on placebo; dizziness, nausea, tremor). Pain scores are symptom surrogates. Lacosamide was never approved for diabetic neuropathic pain. The three trials are not pooled into a single clean win on this shelf. PROPOSED STAMP: SPLIT.
stamp: SPLIT — two of three phase 3 trials met their primary endpoint at lacosamide 400 mg/day (one at exactly P = 0.05; responder contrast 58% vs 46% in the fixed-dose trial) and the third trial missed its primary at both 400 and 600 mg/day (P = 0.12 and P = 0.18), with adverse-event discontinuation of 23% at the effective 400 mg/day dose vs 9% on placebo; never approved for diabetic neuropathic pain

title: Ranirestat for diabetic sensorimotor polyneuropathy: conduction-only benefit — sub-1 m/s nerve-conduction differences across 1,906 randomised patients, with clinical scores (mTCNS) and sensory testing null in every trial
question: In adults with diabetic sensorimotor polyneuropathy, does the aldose reductase inhibitor ranirestat (AS-3201), compared with placebo, slow nerve-conduction deterioration or improve symptoms and signs?
balance: Electrophysiology-only benefit — the flag leads. Across three placebo-controlled trials totalling 1,906 randomised patients, ranirestat's consistent finding is a sub-1 m/s nerve-conduction difference: the dose-ranging trial's summed SENSORY conduction primary did not differ significantly (change 2.0 m/s placebo vs 3.2–3.8 m/s ranirestat), with summed motor conduction improved at 20 mg/day; the global 24-month trial missed its own prespecified clinically-meaningful goal (peroneal motor NCV changes +0.49 placebo vs +0.95 and +0.90 m/s, not significant; the +0.44 m/s combined-dose figure is POST-HOC, labelled as such wherever used); and the Japanese phase 3 trial found a +0.52 m/s tibial motor difference (P = 0.021). Against that, the modified Toronto Clinical Neuropathy Score and quantitative sensory testing did NOT differ in any trial — no benefit on symptoms, signs or quality of life anywhere. Nerve conduction velocity is a surrogate endpoint. Ranirestat was never marketed. Every conduction number on this shelf prints beside the clinical-score nulls. PROPOSED STAMP: POSSIBLE — for nerve-conduction velocity only.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit, nerve conduction only) — three placebo-controlled trials (1,906 randomised) show small conduction differences favouring ranirestat (largest significant between-group difference +0.52 m/s), but the largest trial missed its prespecified ≥1.2 m/s goal, the sensory primary in the dose-ranging trial was not significant, and no trial showed any benefit on the modified Toronto Clinical Neuropathy Score, sensory testing or quality of life

title: Acetyl-L-carnitine for diabetic neuropathy: SPLIT — the two anchor papers DISAGREE on conduction (De Grandis 2002: significant gains, sural +7 vs +1.0 m/s; Sima 2005, 1,257 patients: conduction did NOT improve), with biopsy regeneration and vibration gains and pain better in one of two large trials
question: In adults with chronic diabetic neuropathy, does acetyl-L-carnitine (500–1,000 mg three times daily), compared with placebo, improve pain, nerve fibre regeneration and vibration perception?
balance: Three trials reported in two papers — labelled as such — and the anchor papers are DISCORDANT on conduction, which is printed on the face, not smoothed over. The 2002 De Grandis trial (333 enrolled; 294 with impaired electrophysiology at baseline) reports significant nerve conduction velocity and amplitude gains vs placebo over 1 year (sensory sural +7 vs +1.0 m/s) and a 39% within-group fall in visual-analogue pain vs 8% on placebo. The much larger 2005 Sima analysis of two 52-week trials (1,257 intention-to-treat patients) reports the opposite on electrophysiology — conduction velocities and amplitudes did NOT improve — with its positive findings on sural nerve fibre numbers and regenerating clusters (biopsy morphometry, a surrogate), vibration perception (improved in both studies) and pain (significant in one of the two studies, and in the combined 1,000 mg three-times-daily cohort). Per the standing naming rule: the trials tested pharmaceutical-grade acetyl-L-carnitine (levacecarnine) at 1.5–3 g/day; current supplement products may differ in content and effect. Cross-point: in chemotherapy-induced neuropathy this agent WORSENED neuropathy (pack #2809) — a different population, stated here so the diabetic result is not read as a general neuropathy claim. PROPOSED STAMP: SPLIT.
stamp: SPLIT — the two anchor papers disagree on the electrophysiology (De Grandis 2002 reports significant conduction gains; the larger Sima 2005 two-trial analysis, 1,257 patients, reports none), while agreeing that vibration perception improves; pain improved significantly in the smaller trial and in only one of the two larger trials (and its combined 1,000 mg cohort), and the regeneration evidence is biopsy morphometry, a surrogate

title: Benfotiamine for diabetic polyneuropathy: SPLIT by duration — a 40-patient 3-week pilot and a 6-week trial (primary significant only per-protocol) are positive-short, while the only 12-month trial (BOND, structural primary) is null across essentially every measure
question: In adults with diabetic polyneuropathy, does benfotiamine (a lipid-soluble thiamine prodrug), compared with placebo, improve neuropathy symptoms — and what did the 12-month trial with a structural primary endpoint find?
balance: The short-small-positive / long-rigorous-null arc leads. BEDIP is a 40-inpatient, 3-week pilot whose Katzenwadel neuropathy score improved significantly (P = 0.0287), driven by pain. BENDIP is a 6-week phase 3 trial (165 randomised; 133 intention-to-treat) whose primary Neuropathy Symptom Score was significant only in the PER-PROTOCOL population (P = 0.033) and just above significance intention-to-treat (P = 0.055), with the Total Symptom Score not differing. BOND — the only 12-month trial, with a structural primary endpoint (corneal nerve fibre length) — found NO difference on its primary and essentially no difference on any secondary morphometric, neurophysiological, clinical or quality-of-life measure, with only the Neuropathy Symptom Score tending to improve (P = 0.098), even though thiamine analyte levels rose as expected (all P ≤ 0.003). Symptom scores are subjective endpoints, and the positive trials last 3 and 6 weeks. A fourth located report (PMID 33069584) has an EMPTY abstract in its PubMed record and is refused as an anchor — support-only at most, stated on the Synthesis card. Benfotiamine is a supplement: no tested brand is named in any anchor abstract, stated plainly on this shelf, and current products may differ in safety and effectiveness. PROPOSED STAMP: SPLIT.
stamp: SPLIT — the short trials are positive (BEDIP, 40 inpatients over 3 weeks, P = 0.0287; BENDIP, 6 weeks, primary significant per-protocol at P = 0.033 but not intention-to-treat at P = 0.055) while the only long trial, BOND (57 randomised over 12 months, structural primary endpoint), is null on its primary and essentially all secondary measures; the fourth located report has an empty abstract and is not counted

title: Epalrestat for diabetic peripheral neuropathy: FLOOR-RISK — exactly 3 reports of ONE trial (ADCT, Japan, N = 603 randomised), open-label with NO placebo; epalrestat prevented the median motor conduction deterioration seen in untreated controls (between-group change difference 1.6 m/s)
question: In adults with diabetic peripheral neuropathy, does the aldose reductase inhibitor epalrestat (150 mg/day), compared with no treatment, prevent deterioration of nerve conduction and symptoms over 3 years (the ADCT trial)?
balance: FLOOR-RISK — the exact base is printed here and on every card: 3 reports, 1 trial, N = 603 randomised (594 analysed in the primary report), the ADCT trial at 112 Japanese facilities. THE DESIGN IS THE CAVEAT: ADCT was open-label and randomised patients to epalrestat 150 mg/day or to NO TREATMENT — there is no placebo and no blinding. Over 3 years epalrestat prevented the deterioration in median motor nerve conduction velocity, minimum F-wave latency and vibration perception threshold seen in controls (between-group difference in median motor NCV change 1.6 m/s, P < 0.001); numbness, sensory abnormality and cramping improved significantly, while cardiovascular autonomic measures did not reach significance. The stratified report's efficacy odds ratio was approximately 2:1 overall and approximately 4:1 in the HbA1c ≤7.0% subgroup — odds ratios are relative measures, labelled as such. The primary endpoint is a nerve-conduction surrogate, the symptom benefits are secondary and unblinded, and the effect is concentrated in well-controlled patients without advanced retinopathy. Epalrestat is marketed only in parts of Asia (Japan, India, China) — a single-region programme. Its class sibling ranirestat (shelf #7696) has the stronger, placebo-controlled base. PROPOSED STAMP: MAYBE (weak evidence).
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — FLOOR-RISK base of exactly 3 reports of 1 trial (ADCT, N = 603): a single open-label, placebo-free Japanese trial in which epalrestat prevented median motor conduction deterioration over 3 years (change difference 1.6 m/s, P < 0.001) with secondary symptom gains concentrated in well-controlled patients; no blinded or placebo-controlled evidence exists

title: Olipudase alfa for ASMD (ASCEND programme): adults — DLCO +22% vs +3.0%, spleen volume −39% vs +0.5% and liver volume −28% vs −1.5% at 52 weeks in the one randomised trial (36 adults); children — single-arm, spleen and liver volumes improved by over 40%
question: In children and adults with chronic acid sphingomyelinase deficiency (ASMD), does enzyme replacement with olipudase alfa, compared with placebo (adults) or within-patient change (children), improve lung diffusion capacity and spleen and liver volumes (the ASCEND programme)?
balance: One programme, three reports carded and labelled as such — the counts lead. The randomised base is a single 36-adult trial (ASCEND): at 52 weeks percent-predicted DLCO rose +22% vs +3.0% (P = 0.0004), spleen volume fell −39% vs +0.5% (P < 0.0001) and liver volume fell −28% vs −1.5% (P < 0.0001) — percent changes as published, with the placebo-arm changes beside them — while the splenomegaly-related score did not differ (P = 0.64). The paediatric evidence (ASCEND-Peds, 20 children) is open-label and single-arm: spleen and liver volumes improved by over 40% within patient, DLCO improved +32.9% in those able to perform it, and height Z-scores improved +0.56. The adult open-label extension (35 of 36 continuing) shows the former placebo group paralleling the original group after crossover and continued gains to year 2. Endpoints are organ volumes and DLCO — disease-pathology surrogates; no mortality or hospitalisation trial exists. Per the standing product-naming rule the tested product is named as published: olipudase alfa, recombinant human acid sphingomyelinase — clarification, not promotion. Its lysosomal sibling sebelipase alfa is homed at live #1408 (cross-point only). PROPOSED STAMP: LIKELY (benefit).
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — on a small-N rare-disease base stated on the face: one randomised trial of 36 adults showed large, significant gains in DLCO and spleen and liver volumes vs placebo at 52 weeks, a single-arm trial in 20 children showed concordant within-patient improvements, and the extension showed crossover replication; endpoints are organ-volume and DLCO surrogates, with no mortality or hospitalisation trial

title: Pegzilarginase for arginase 1 deficiency (PEACE programme): plasma arginine fell from 354.0 to 86.4 µmol/L and normalised in 90.5% vs 0% on placebo in the one randomised trial (32 patients), with mobility gains sustained in extensions on very small remaining denominators
question: In children and adults with arginase 1 deficiency, does pegzilarginase (recombinant human arginase 1 enzyme therapy), added to standard dietary management, lower plasma arginine and improve mobility (the PEACE programme)?
balance: One programme, three reports carded and labelled as such — the small-N rare-disease counts lead. The randomised base is one phase 3 trial of 32 patients (PEACE, 21 pegzilarginase vs 11 placebo, 24 weeks, on individualised disease management): geometric-mean plasma arginine fell from 354.0 to 86.4 µmol/L on pegzilarginase vs 464.7 to 426.6 µmol/L on placebo (P < 0.0001) and normalised in 90.5% vs 0%; the abstract reports clinically relevant functional mobility improvements on the key secondary endpoints (GMFM-E, 2-minute walk) without printing their magnitudes, and none are claimed here. The primary endpoint is biochemical (plasma arginine). The earlier phase 1/2 report (16 patients, open-label) showed a median arginine fall of 277 µmol/L after 20 cumulative doses with improvement in at least one mobility assessment in 79%. The long-term extensions (Study 102A, n = 14, up to 5 years; PEACE extension, n = 31, up to 3 years) show sustained arginine control and spasticity improvement in 21 of 25 (84%), but some walk-test cells rest on n = 6 and n = 2, printed on the face. No trial measures survival or developmental outcomes against control beyond 24 weeks. Per the standing product-naming rule the tested product is named as published — pegzilarginase, recombinant human arginase 1 — clarification, not promotion. PROPOSED STAMP: LIKELY (benefit).

title: Pabinafusp alfa for neuronopathic MPS II: NO placebo-controlled trial exists — one single-arm trial (28 patients, Japan) and one open-label dose-ranging trial (Brazil), 62 patients in total, with CSF heparan sulfate significantly reduced and positive neurocognitive changes in 21 of 28 in the Japanese trial
question: In children and adults with neuronopathic mucopolysaccharidosis II (Hunter syndrome), does pabinafusp alfa (iduronate-2-sulfatase fused to an anti-transferrin-receptor antibody, JR-141), compared with within-patient baseline, reduce cerebrospinal-fluid heparan sulfate and stabilise neurocognitive development?
balance: No controlled efficacy trial exists — the flag leads. The entire clinical base is one programme of 62 patients in total (Japan and Brazil): a single-arm open-label phase 2/3 trial in 28 Japanese patients (cerebrospinal-fluid heparan sulfate fell significantly from baseline, P < 0.001; neurocognitive evaluations showed positive changes in 21 of 28 patients — a within-patient judgement without a comparator in a variably progressive disease) and a 26-week open-label dose-randomised trial in Brazil (1.0 / 2.0 / 4.0 mg/kg/week; the 2.0 mg/kg group showed marked reductions in CSF, serum and urine substrate and was judged the best dose; the record prints no N for this trial and none is claimed on its card), summarised in an integrated analysis of the programme. The primary clinical evidence is a CSF substrate surrogate plus uncontrolled neurocognitive readings. The agent is approved in Japan and not in the US/EU — a single-region programme (Japan/Brazil). Per the standing product-naming rule the tested product and its development code are named as the publications give them — pabinafusp alfa, JR-141 — clarification, not promotion. The homed MPS II shelf is conventional idursulfase (live #1405), which does not cross the blood-brain barrier — a different agent and question, cross-point only. PROPOSED STAMP: MAYBE (weak evidence).
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — no placebo-controlled trial exists: the whole base is one programme of 62 patients (a single-arm 52-week trial, n = 28, and an open-label dose-ranging trial whose record prints no N), showing a significant within-patient fall in CSF heparan sulfate (a surrogate) and uncontrolled neurocognitive readings (positive changes in 21 of 28), with no comparator for any clinical outcome

title: Nitisinone for alkaptonuria: homogentisic acid fell 99.7% relative to control, but clinical benefit is modest — a slower severity-score rise over 4 years, and the NIH trial's primary clinical outcome missed
question: In adults with alkaptonuria, does nitisinone (10 mg daily), compared with no treatment, reduce homogentisic acid excretion and slow clinical disease progression (the SONIA programme and the NIH trial)?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — with the biochemical/clinical split on the face. Nitisinone's effect on homogentisic acid is near-total (SONIA 2: 99.7% relative reduction vs no treatment at 12 months; SONIA 1: clear dose-response to 0.15 mmol at 8 mg). The clinical benefit is much more modest: SONIA 2 found a significantly smaller increase in the cAKUSSI severity score over 48 months (adjusted difference −8.6 points, P=0.023), while the separate NIH randomised trial's selected primary outcome did not demonstrate significant clinical benefit and its supportive SF-36 / 6-minute-walk findings are a post-hoc per-protocol analysis. Neither SONIA trial had a placebo arm (no-treatment controls, effectively unblinded), and tyrosinaemia occurred at every dose.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — nitisinone almost abolishes homogentisic acid excretion (99.7% relative reduction in SONIA 2) and slowed the rise of a composite severity score over 4 years, but the NIH trial's primary clinical outcome missed and the clinical evidence rests on open-label, no-treatment-controlled trials plus post-hoc patient-reported outcomes

title: Lactitol vs lactulose for hepatic encephalopathy: never shown different in 3 trials totalling only 89 patients (one a 9-patient crossover) — equivalence by underpowering, with a tolerability signal from the smallest trial
question: In patients with cirrhosis and acute or chronic hepatic (portal-systemic) encephalopathy, does oral lactitol versus lactulose improve encephalopathy grade, psychometric performance and ammonia, and how do the two non-absorbable disaccharides compare on tolerability?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — based on a very small total N = 89. Three randomised trials (1987–1991) compared lactitol with lactulose in acute PSE (n=40), chronic HE (n=9 crossover, sub-floor, labelled and never load-bearing alone) and maintenance PSE (n=40). None showed a difference, none prespecified a non-inferiority margin, and the labelled meta-analysis gives a pooled odds ratio of 0.83 (95% CI 0.38 to 1.82). Lactitol was never shown different from lactulose in trials too small to show a difference; a tolerability signal favouring lactitol on flatulence/diarrhoea comes from the 9-patient crossover, while the 1991 study found crystalline lactulose better accepted.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — based on a very small total N = 89 across 3 trials: lactitol was never shown different from lactulose for hepatic encephalopathy, no trial prespecified non-inferiority, and the one sub-floor 9-patient crossover is labelled and never load-bearing alone

title: Ornithine phenylacetate for overt hepatic encephalopathy: exactly 2 trials (N=279) — the one adequately sized trial missed its primary endpoint (P=.129); the oral trial is a 5-day ammonia study its authors call hypothesis-generating
question: In patients with cirrhosis and overt hepatic encephalopathy (or a history of overt episodes), does ornithine phenylacetate — intravenous in hospitalised acute episodes, or oral in stable outpatients — versus placebo (or rifaximin) speed clinical improvement or lower ammonia?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — FLOOR-RISK: exactly 2 randomised trials, total N=279, one programme. STOP-HE (intravenous, n=231) missed its primary endpoint (P=.129); its median-21-hours-sooner reading is a central-laboratory subset analysis. stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — based on exactly 2 trials (total N = 279): the adequately sized intravenous trial missed its primary endpoint (P=.129) and the oral trial's endpoint is 5-day plasma ammonia, described by its own authors as hypothesis-generating

title: Cobitolimod for ulcerative colitis: COLLECT's primary endpoint missed (remission 44.4% vs 46.5% on placebo) and CONDUCT was positive in only 1 of 4 dose arms, on an 80% CI with a one-sided p-value
question: In patients with moderate-to-severe left-sided (COLLECT: refractory) ulcerative colitis, do rectally administered cobitolimod enemas (two to four doses over 3–4 weeks) versus placebo induce clinical or symptomatic remission?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence). title: Recombinant human interleukin-10 for Crohn's disease: a failed programme — no dose beat placebo on remission in the 329-patient trial (18–28% vs 18%), and postoperative prevention was null
question: In patients with active Crohn's disease — or immediately after ileal/ileocolonic resection — does daily subcutaneous recombinant human interleukin-10 versus placebo induce remission, improve disease activity, or prevent endoscopic recurrence?
balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference). Three randomised trials, three labelled limbs: in therapy-refractory disease (n=329) no dose of recombinant human IL-10 beat placebo on remission; in mild-to-moderate disease (n=95) a single mid-dose cell (5 µg/kg, 23.5% vs 0%) combined remission with endoscopic improvement in a safety-first dose-ranging trial and higher doses were less effective; after resection (n=65) endoscopic recurrence was 46% on Tenovil vs 52% on placebo. question: In patients with mild-to-moderate active left-sided / distal ulcerative colitis, does a nightly alicaforsen enema (120–240 mg, or 0.1–4 mg/mL dose cohorts) for 4–6 weeks versus placebo — or versus mesalazine enema — improve disease activity, and does any response last longer after treatment stops?

title: Pleconaril for picornavirus colds: a median 1-day shortening, only in virus-confirmed colds with susceptible isolates — 2 trials in 1 primary publication, plus 1 labelled secondary analysis; never marketed after CYP3A induction
question: In adults with a naturally acquired common cold, does oral pleconaril started early versus placebo shorten illness — and is any benefit confined to patients whose infecting picornavirus is drug-susceptible?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — narrowly. One programme: 2 trials reported in 1 primary publication found a median 1-day shorter illness (P<.001) among 1,363 picornavirus-infected participants, with no effect in participants without picornavirus infection; the labelled susceptibility analysis confines the benefit to infections with drug-susceptible isolates (median 1.9–3.9 days gained) and documents resistance emergence in 10.7% of treated patients. stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a median 1-day shortening confined to picornavirus-confirmed colds with susceptible isolates, from 2 trials in 1 primary publication plus 1 labelled secondary analysis; no effect in undifferentiated colds, and the drug was never marketed

title: Tisagenlecleucel in relapsed/refractory B-cell malignancies: single-arm remission 81% in B-ALL (ELIANA), response 52% in DLBCL (JULIET), complete response 69.1% in follicular lymphoma (ELARA) — but the randomised second-line trial (BELINDA) was null

balance: SPLIT. The single-arm pivotal cohorts report high remission/response rates in heavily pretreated patients (ELIANA 81% remission in B-ALL; JULIET 52% response in DLBCL; ELARA 69.1% complete response in follicular lymphoma), priced with substantial cytokine-release and neurologic toxicity — but none has a concurrent control. title: Pramipexole in early Parkinson's disease: starting the agonist instead of levodopa halved dyskinesias (relative HR 0.37) but gave no long-term disability advantage at 6 years; extended-release matched immediate-release against placebo in early and advanced disease
question: In early Parkinson's disease, does starting pramipexole rather than levodopa change the development of dopaminergic motor complications and long-term disability (CALM-PD)? And in early and advanced disease, does once-daily extended-release pramipexole improve UPDRS scores and off-time versus placebo?
balance: SPLIT — the CALM-PD trade-off is the face. Initial pramipexole reduced dyskinesias (24.5% vs 54%; relative hazard ratio 0.37) and wearing off (47% vs 62.7%; relative hazard ratio 0.68) vs initial levodopa, but initial levodopa reduced freezing, gave greater UPDRS improvement, and caused less somnolence and oedema — and at a mean of 6 years self-reported disability was similar (79.9 vs 82.5, P=.19), so the complication advantage did not convert into a disability advantage. Separately, labelled limbs: extended-release pramipexole beat placebo and matched immediate-release over 18 weeks in advanced disease (n=507) and early disease (n=259). Limbs are labelled per report and never pooled.
stamp: SPLIT — initial pramipexole vs levodopa trades fewer dyskinesias and wearing-off (relative HR 0.37 and 0.68) against more freezing, somnolence and oedema, with no long-term disability difference at 6 years; the ER-vs-placebo limbs are separately positive in early and advanced disease

title: Ropinirole prolonged release (and patch) as adjunct in advanced Parkinson's disease: off-time fell a net ~1.8 hours/day vs placebo in the pivotal trial, the dose-response study points to 8 mg as the likely lowest maximally effective dose, and the patch was non-inferior to the tablet
question: In patients with advanced Parkinson's disease and motor fluctuations on levodopa, does adjunctive ropinirole 24-hour prolonged release reduce daily off-time versus placebo — and is a once-daily ropinirole patch superior to placebo and non-inferior to the prolonged-release tablet?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — as an adjunct for motor fluctuations. Three distinct randomised trials: the 393-patient pivotal trial found ropinirole 24-hour prolonged release reduced daily off-time by 2.1 hours vs 0.3 hours on placebo (net ~1.8 hours/day) with levodopa dose reduction; the fixed-dose study significantly reduced awake off-time at 16 mg and reads 8 mg as the likely lowest maximally effective dose (against the pivotal trial's 18.8 mg mean dose); the patch trial showed superiority over placebo and non-inferiority to the prolonged-release tablet on UPDRS Part III. The price is dyskinesia and the dopamine-agonist class harms (nausea, dizziness, somnolence, hallucinations, orthostatic hypotension).
stamp: LIKELY (benefit — adjunctive off-time reduction in advanced Parkinson's disease) — prolonged-release ropinirole cut daily off-time by a net ~1.8 hours vs placebo in the pivotal trial, with the patch superior to placebo and non-inferior to the tablet in a separate trial

title: Adjunctive pramipexole in advanced Parkinson's disease: UPDRS parts II and III improved 26.7% and 34% vs 4.8% and 5.7% on placebo in the founding 247-patient trial, and the Cochrane synthesis of 4 trials (669 patients) found off-time cut by a weighted mean 1.8 hours — at the cost of more dyskinesia
question: In patients with advanced Parkinson's disease and levodopa-induced motor complications, does adjunctive pramipexole (immediate-release, and extended-release as its modern form) improve motor scores and reduce off-time versus placebo?
balance: LIKELY (benefit) — as an adjunct in advanced disease, on short- and medium-term trials only (up to 24 weeks' maintenance). The founding 247-patient trial (Guttman 1997) found UPDRS part II improved 26.7% on pramipexole (P = 0.0002) and part III 34% (P = 0.0006) against 4.8% and 5.7% on placebo, with more dyskinesia and nausea on active treatment. The Cochrane synthesis (Clarke 2000) pooled 4 randomised trials in 669 patients: off-time fell by a weighted mean difference of 1.8 hours (95% CI 1.2 to 2.3) versus placebo, levodopa dose fell by a weighted mean 115 mg, UPDRS ADL scores improved in all studies — and dyskinesia as an adverse event was reported more frequently with pramipexole, with significantly more hallucinations. A second founding trial (Lieberman 1997) reports the same direction qualitatively; its abstract prints no sample size and no numeric effects, so it is never load-bearing. The extended-release versus placebo trial in advanced disease (507 patients) is the modern form of this same contrast and lives on shelf #7711 as a cross-point — it is not double-carded here (one-home rule). Nothing here speaks to long-term disability: that strategy question is CALM-PD, on shelf #7711.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — adjunctive immediate-release pramipexole improved UPDRS scores versus placebo in the founding advanced-disease trials and cut off-time by a weighted mean 1.8 hours in the Cochrane synthesis of 4 trials (669 patients), at the cost of more dyskinesia reported as an adverse event; the modern extended-release form of the same contrast is carded on shelf #7711 and is cross-pointed, not re-carded here

title: STRATIFY falls tool: pooled sensitivity 67.2% and specificity 51.2% in geriatric rehabilitation — but sensitivity collapsed to 11.3% after stroke at the same ≥2 cut-off, so its accuracy is a property of the setting, not the tool
question: In hospitalised adults, how well does the STRATIFY falls risk-assessment tool (recent falls, agitation, visual impairment, frequent toileting, impaired transfer / mobility; standard high-risk cut-off ≥2) predict who will fall during the admission — what pooled sensitivity and specificity does it deliver in geriatric rehabilitation, and how far does its accuracy collapse in stroke rehabilitation, nursing-home and general acute-care validations?
balance: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — modest at best, and setting-bound. The pooled geriatric-rehabilitation figures (Oliver 2008: sensitivity 67.2%, specificity 51.2%, PPV 23.1%, NPV 86.5%) are the tool's best case, and even there three of four flagged patients do not fall. Transport is the story: after stroke, sensitivity was 11.3% in the first 28 days (Smith 2006) — the tool missed almost nine of ten fallers; in a nursing home, sensitivity was 50% with a relative risk of falling of 2.35 at ≥2 (Wijnia 2006, a relative measure); and in 93,347 general acute-care records, sensitivity was 0.672 and specificity 0.612 with an AUC of 0.69 (Cortés 2023). A single sensitivity/specificity pair for STRATIFY does not exist; every pair on this shelf prints with its setting and cut-off. This is a prognostic-accuracy shelf, not a treatment shelf: nothing here shows that scoring patients, or acting on a high score, prevents a fall. Distinct instruments, distinct shelves: Morse is #7650 and Hendrich II is a separate row — no anchor is shared.
stamp: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — STRATIFY at the standard ≥2 cut-off predicts falls only modestly where it performs best (pooled geriatric-rehabilitation sensitivity 67.2%, specificity 51.2%, positive predictive value 23.1%) and collapses in transport (stroke rehabilitation sensitivity 11.3%; nursing-home sensitivity 50%; 93,347-record acute-care validation sensitivity 0.672, specificity 0.612, AUC 0.69); no card implies that scoring, or any bundle a high score triggers, prevents falls (GAP-E)

title: Behavioural pain scales in patients who cannot self-report: BPS separates nociceptive from non-nociceptive procedures (4.9 vs 3.5), CPOT is 'a fair but not excellent tool' (diagnostic odds ratio 11.52 during procedures), and a BPAT score >3.5 classifies severe pain with sensitivity and specificity of only 61.8–75.1%
question: In critically ill adults who cannot self-report pain — sedated, mechanically ventilated, or brain-injured — how accurately and reliably do the behavioural pain scales (the Behavioral Pain Scale, BPS; the Critical-Care Pain Observation Tool, CPOT; and the 8-item Behavior Pain Assessment Tool, BPAT) detect pain, what scores separate nociceptive from non-nociceptive procedures and rest, and how far does accuracy fall outside the derivation settings?
balance: MEASUREMENT ACCURACY — reliable observation, fair classification. The BPS derivation (Payen 2001; the scale originators' own report, labelled as such) separated nociceptive from non-nociceptive procedures (4.9 vs 3.5) in 30 patients; an independent validation (Aïssaoui 2005) found inter-rater ICC 0.95 and rest-versus-procedure means of 3.9 vs 6.8, again in 30 patients — the patient N, not the 269–360 observation counts, is the evidence size. The CPOT synthesis (Zhai 2020; 25 articles, 1,920 subjects) gives diagnostic odds ratios of 11.52 during nociceptive procedures and 9.14 at rest or during non-nociceptive procedures (odds ratios, as published), with heterogeneity I² 57.2% and the authors' own verdict: 'a fair but not excellent tool.' The BPAT's international validation (Gélinas 2017; 3,851 patients) is the largest and the most sobering: a cut-point >3.5 classified severe pain (≥8/10) with sensitivity and specificity ranging from 61.8% to 75.1%, and scores correlated only moderately with self-reported intensity (r = 0.54). Three different item sets — never pooled into one accuracy figure. This shelf measures detection, not treatment: whether acting on these scores improves outcomes is a different, unrowed question.
stamp: MEASUREMENT ACCURACY — the behavioural scales detect procedure-related pain behaviour reliably (BPS inter-rater ICC 0.95 in independent validation) but classify pain only fairly: CPOT diagnostic odds ratio 11.52 during nociceptive procedures with the authors' verdict 'a fair but not excellent tool' at a threshold of two or three, and BPAT >3.5 classifies severe pain with sensitivity and specificity ranging only 61.8% to 75.1%; no card implies scale-guided analgesia improves outcomes (GAP-E)

title: 3D-CAM delirium interview: sensitivity 95% and specificity 94% at derivation in 201 inpatients aged ≥75 (96% / 86% in dementia), 94% / 97% for the Chinese version on general units — and 84.6–87.2% / 96.7–97.4% in surgical ICU, at a median 3 minutes
question: In hospitalised older adults on general wards and in surgical intensive care, how accurately does the 3D-CAM (the 3-minute diagnostic interview operationalising the Confusion Assessment Method) diagnose delirium against an expert / DSM reference standard — what sensitivity and specificity does it deliver in its derivation population, in patients with dementia, and in translated-version validations, and how long does it take at the bedside?
balance: DIAGNOSTIC ACCURACY — high, with a setting gradient and a translation caveat. At derivation (Marcantonio 2014; the instrument originators' own report, labelled as such), the 3D-CAM reached sensitivity 95% and specificity 94% against an expert-panel reference standard in 201 inpatients aged ≥75, and held up in dementia (96% / 86%). The Chinese version on general units matched it (Ji 2021: 94% / 97% in 204 patients). In surgical ICU the same translated instrument lost sensitivity (Mu 2020: 87.2% and 84.6% for two interviewers; specificity 96.7% and 97.4%; kappa 0.82) — roughly one in seven delirious patients missed. Median administration was about 3 minutes in both ward studies. Two of the three reports validate the Chinese version: independent cohorts and centres, but the derivation figures may not be presented as replicated in the original-language form outside the derivation centre. A diagnostic-accuracy shelf only — nothing here tests whether finding delirium with the 3D-CAM changes treatment or outcomes. Distinct instruments: CAM-ICU (for patients who cannot speak) and 4AT are separate shelves with no shared anchor.
stamp: DIAGNOSTIC ACCURACY — the 3D-CAM diagnoses CAM-defined delirium accurately in about 3 minutes (derivation sensitivity 95%, specificity 94%; Chinese general-unit version 94% / 97%), with sensitivity lower in surgical ICU (84.6–87.2% across two interviewers, specificity 96.7–97.4%); two of three reports validate the Chinese translation, stated on every card (GAP-E)

title: Preoperative Timed-Up-and-Go predicting complications: odds ratio 3.43 for major complications in onco-geriatric surgery (AUC 0.64) and adjusted odds ratio 4.97 at a ≥18.4 s cut-off in spine surgery — but no complication prediction at all in gynaecological laparoscopy at a >12 s frailty cut-off
question: Before elective surgery, how well does the preoperative Timed-Up-and-Go (TUG) time predict postoperative complications — what thresholds have been derived (about 12 s as a frailty cut-off, 18.4 s in spine surgery), what odds and discrimination does a slow TUG carry in onco-geriatric and spine cohorts, and in which surgical population (gynaecological laparoscopy) did it fail to predict complications at all?
balance: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — positive in two cohorts, null in a third, and never with a shared threshold. In onco-geriatric surgery (Huisman 2014; 280 patients), high TUG independently predicted major complications at an odds ratio of 3.43 (an odds ratio, as published), but discrimination was weak — AUC 0.64 for TUG against 0.59 for ASA class — even though absolute major-complication risk was 50.0% in the high-TUG group against 25.6% for ASA ≥3. In thoracolumbar spine surgery (Komodikis 2020; 103 patients), slow TUG (unable to perform, or ≥18.4 s) independently predicted high-grade complications at an adjusted odds ratio of 4.97, with a wide interval (95% CI 1.18 to 22.47). In gynaecological cancer surgery (Anastasio 2025; 174 patients, 70.6% laparoscopy), frailty at TUG >12 s predicted transfusion (19.2% vs 4.1%) but there were no differences in major or minor complication rates after laparoscopic surgery, and TUG predicted neither length of stay nor discharge disposition. The >12 s frailty cut-off and the ≥18.4 s spine cut-off are different operationalisations of the same test; no card prints a universal threshold. This is the prediction question — TUG reference values in healthy people are a different shelf (pack #7160).
stamp: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — a slow preoperative TUG predicted major complications in two small prospective cohorts (odds ratio 3.43, AUC 0.64 in onco-geriatric surgery; adjusted odds ratio 4.97 at ≥18.4 s in spine surgery) but did not predict complications after gynaecological laparoscopy at a >12 s cut-off; thresholds are cohort property (12 s vs 18.4 s), never a universal cut-off, and all cohorts are small (largest N = 280) (GAP-E)

title: Pulse oximetry across skin pigmentation: occult hypoxaemia is more common in Black patients (pooled prevalence ratio 1.67, a relative measure) and Hispanic patients (adjusted odds ratio 1.44 and 1.31 in one 151,070-reading cohort); with objectively measured skin tone, readings ran 0.6–1.5 points higher at the darkest tone — but one controlled laboratory study of a signal-extraction device found bias of only −0.20% vs −0.05%
question: At the bedside and in hospital, how accurate is pulse oximetry across skin pigmentation — how much more common is occult hypoxaemia (arterial saturation <88% while the oximeter reads >92%) in Black, Hispanic and other darker-skinned patients than in White patients, how large is the device bias when skin tone is measured objectively rather than by self-reported race, and what does the one controlled laboratory study of a modern signal-extraction device find against the clinical cohorts?
balance: MEASUREMENT ACCURACY — a consistent clinical-cohort signal and one discordant laboratory result, kept apart. The synthesis (Parr 2024; 15 studies, 732,505 paired measurements in 207,464 hospitalised patients) finds occult hypoxaemia more common in Black patients than White patients (pooled prevalence ratio 1.67 — a relative measure) and in patients identifying as Asian, Latinx, Indigenous, multiracial or other (1.39). The largest single cohort (Burnett 2022; 151,070 intraoperative paired readings) found occult hypoxaemia in 2.1% of Black, 1.8% of Hispanic and 1.1% of White paired readings, with adjusted odds ratios of 1.44 and 1.31 (odds ratios, as published) — small absolute rates, consistently ordered. The objective-measurement study (Martin 2026, BMJ; 903 ICU patients, skin tone by spectrophotometer) found SpO2 read 0.6–1.5 percentage points higher at the darkest than the lightest tone, with false-negative proportions 5.3–35.3 percentage points higher in darker tones (rate ratio 2.3–7.1, a relative measure). Against all of this, the laboratory study (Barker 2023; 75 healthy volunteers, controlled desaturation, one manufacturer's signal-extraction sensor) found bias of −0.20% in Black and −0.05% in White subjects and no occult hypoxaemia in Black subjects — under conditions its authors state do not reflect clinical care. Race/ethnicity in the clinical cohorts is self-reported; the BMJ study measured skin tone objectively; the two operationalisations are never merged. The field's founding report (Sjoding 2020) is NOT carded: its PubMed record carries an empty abstract and it is excluded under the standing fetch discipline, as recorded on the Synthesis card. No card implies any corrective action improves outcomes — that intervention question is unrowed.
stamp: MEASUREMENT ACCURACY — in clinical cohorts, occult hypoxaemia is consistently more frequent in darker-skinned patients (pooled prevalence ratio 1.67 for Black vs White patients, a relative measure; objective skin-tone study: SpO2 0.6–1.5 percentage points higher at the darkest tone, false-negative proportions 5.3–35.3 points higher, rate ratio 2.3–7.1, a relative measure), while the one controlled laboratory study of a single signal-extraction device in healthy volunteers found near-identical bias (−0.20% Black vs −0.05% White) — a discordant, device- and setting-specific counterpoint, never pooled with the clinical cohorts (GAP-E)

title: Serum anion gap reference interval: 3–11 mmol/L on ion-selective-electrode analysers, 5–10 / 9–14 / 8–13 mmol/L across three 1997 analysers, and 10–18 mmol/L in a contemporary screening population — the interval is analyser property, not a biological constant (5 datasets)
question: In healthy adults, what is the reference interval for the serum anion gap — the central range by analyser / method — how far apart do the published intervals sit (3–11 mmol/L on ion-selective-electrode analysers against 10–18 mmol/L in a contemporary screening population), how much of that spread is instrument and derivation method rather than biology, and how often does an outdated interval misclassify healthy people as having a high gap?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED, as an instrument property. Textbook framing (Guyton & Hall; Boron & Boulpaep, acid–base sections) is brief — this shelf rests chiefly on the primary reference literature, and says so. Five datasets: three direct healthy-volunteer derivations (Roberts 1997: 5–10, 9–14 and 8–13 mmol/L on three analysers in the same volunteers; Lolekha 2001: 3–11 mmol/L on four ion-selective-electrode analysers in 124 volunteers, against 8–16 or 9–18 mmol/L on the older continuous-flow methods; Chionh 2022: 10–18 mmol/L in 284 screening volunteers) and two indirect derivations from patient populations with healthy or normal-electrolyte subgroups (Ayala-Lopez 2020: 7–18 mmol/L, median 13, in a 17,137-patient derivation, with 5% of healthy adults misclassified as high by the previous 6–16 mmol/L interval; Pratumvinit 2020: all-patient intervals 9–19, 5–15 and 5–15 mmol/L across three hospitals, with albumin shifting the gap). The 3–11 and 10–18 mmol/L intervals may never be merged: the spread is method, not biology. Values print in mmol/L, numerically equal to mEq/L for this monovalent calculated quantity. The potassium-inclusive gap (AGK, 14.6–22.5 mmol/L) is a different calculated quantity and is carded separately on its own card line.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — five independent datasets consistently establish that the serum anion gap reference interval is analyser- and derivation-specific (3–11 mmol/L on ion-selective-electrode analysers; 10–18 mmol/L in a contemporary health-screening derivation; 7–18 mmol/L in a large indirect derivation), so no interval prints without its analyser and derivation, and the intervals are never merged into one normal range

title: Normal kidney size on ultrasound by population: European volunteer medians 11.2 cm (left) and 10.9 cm (right) against Jamaican means of 9.7 and 10.0 cm and a Saudi right-kidney mean of 9.79 cm — no length is a universal normal (5 populations)
question: In healthy adults, what are the normal kidney dimensions on ultrasound — renal length, width, thickness, cortical thickness and volume — by side, sex and body size, how much smaller are the Saudi, Kuwaiti and Jamaican population means than the classic European volunteer medians, and does renal length actually fall with age once body size is accounted for?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED, population by population. Textbook framing (Guyton & Hall, kidney sections) is brief — this shelf rests chiefly on the primary population literature, and says so. The population gradient is the content: the classic European random-sample medians (Emamian 1993; 665 volunteers: length 11.2 cm left, 10.9 cm right; volumes 146 cm³ left, 134 cm³ right) sit about 1.5 cm above the Jamaican means (Barton 2000; 49 adults: 9.7 ± 0.7 cm right, 10.0 ± 0.7 cm left) and the Saudi right-kidney mean (Alyami 2024; 95 adults: 9.79 cm right, 10.1 cm left), with Kuwaiti means between (El-Reshaid 2014; 252 adults: 10.68 ± 1.4 cm right, 10.71 ± 1.0 cm left; minimum cortical thickness 0.6 cm). Left exceeds right in every dataset. The age question is genuinely unsettled: size fell with age, almost entirely through parenchymal reduction, in the European sample, while the Kuwaiti dataset found no significant age variation in length or cortical thickness — printed as a disagreement, not a consensus. The Turkish cohort (Tiryaki 2024; 1,918 adults) is shared with the spleen shelf #7721 for its spleen limb and is carded here for its kidney limb only, with its abstract-level findings stated as such. Each card carries its population; no length prints as a universal normal.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — five independent populations consistently establish left-greater-than-right asymmetry and body-size correlation, and just as consistently refuse a universal length: European medians 11.2 / 10.9 cm, Kuwaiti means 10.71 / 10.68 cm, Saudi means 10.1 / 9.79 cm and Jamaican means 10.0 / 9.7 cm print per population, never merged; whether length falls with age is genuinely unsettled between the two largest direct datasets and prints as a disagreement

title: Normal spleen size: the conventional 12 cm sonographic upper limit was exceeded by 26% of healthy men (234 of 906) and 6% of women — length and volume are height- and sex-dependent, and CT volume in 4,732 Japanese adults is predicted from weight alone (3.08 + 1.96 × weight in kg)
question: In healthy adults, what are the normal spleen dimensions on imaging — sonographic length and volume, and CT volume — by sex and body height, how badly does the conventional 12 cm upper limit of sonographic length misclassify healthy men, and how stable is a spleen measurement on repeat scanning?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED, per modality. Textbook framing (Guyton & Hall, reticuloendothelial / spleen sections) is brief — this shelf rests chiefly on the primary population literature, and says so. The row's distinctive finding: in 1,230 healthy stem-cell-donor volunteers (Chow 2016), spleen length and volume were independently associated with sex, height and weight, and the previously reported 12 cm upper limit was exceeded by 26% of men (234 of 906) and 6% of women (20 of 324) — a fixed limit labels a quarter of healthy men enlarged; repeat measurement in 75 volunteers was stable (median length difference 0.10 cm). The Turkish cohort (Tiryaki 2024; 1,918 adults; shared with shelf #7720 for its kidney limb) found splenic length did not differ across BMI groups while splenic thickness did. On CT, in 4,732 healthy Japanese adults (Tamura 2025), the final reference model predicted spleen volume from weight alone (3.08 + 1.96 × weight in kg; mean absolute error 38.5 mL). The founding 1983 derivation (Niederau; 915 healthy subjects) set 95th-percentile upper limits prospectively for liver, spleen, pancreas and portal vein; its abstract reports the method and cohort, and spleen-specific figures are not printed in the fetched record — none are claimed from it here. Sonographic length, sonographic volume and CT volume are different quantities and are never merged. The donor cohort is a screened-healthy population, not a general-population sample, and prints as such. Cross-point: spleen contraction during exercise and diving (pack #6633) is a mechanism question, not a size norm.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — four independent populations across two modalities consistently establish that spleen size is sex-, height- and weight-dependent and that a fixed 12 cm sonographic limit misclassifies healthy men (26% above it); values print per modality (sonographic length / volume; CT volume) and per population, never merged, and 12 cm never prints as a stand-alone definition of splenomegaly
