title: Normal ovarian volume by age: decade means fall from 6.6 cm³ under 30 years to 1.8 cm³ at ≥70 (13,963 women, 58,673 observations), with upper limits of 20 cm³ premenopausal and 10 cm³ postmenopausal; by years since menopause, volume falls from 8.6 cm³ in the first year to 2.2 cm³ after 15 years
question: In healthy women, what is the normal ovarian volume by age and menopausal status — the decade means from the twenties to the seventies, the postmenopausal nomogram by years since menopause, and the upper limits of normal before and after menopause (20 cm³ and 10 cm³) — and how do ultrasound and MRI values compare?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED, per modality and per partition. Textbook framing (Guyton & Hall, reproductive sections) is brief — this shelf rests chiefly on the primary population literature, and says so. The lead dataset is one programme's cohort and is labelled as such wherever carded: the University of Kentucky Ovarian Cancer Screening Program (Pavlik 2000; 13,963 women aged 25–91, 58,673 transvaginal-sonography observations) gives decade means of 6.6 cm³ (<30 years), 6.1 (30–39), 4.8 (40–49), 2.6 (50–59), 2.1 (60–69) and 1.8 (≥70), premenopausal 4.9 vs postmenopausal 2.2 cm³, and upper limits of normal of 20 cm³ premenopausal and 10 cm³ postmenopausal. A self-selected screening population, not a general-population sample — stated on its card. The postmenopausal nomogram (Tepper 1995; 311 women) partitions by years since menopause instead: 8.6 ± 2.3 cm³ in the first menopausal year falling curvilinearly to 2.2 ± 1.4 cm³ more than 15 years after menopause. Its first-year mean (8.6) sits far above the screening cohort's 50–59 decade mean (2.6) because the partitions differ — the two series may not be spliced into one curve, and the partition prints on every card. On MRI (Hauth 2006; 100 women), mean volume rose with age to a peak at 31–40 years and fell thereafter, with no significant difference between menstrual-cycle phases. The 2022 systematic review (Mathis; 33 studies, 1970–2020) is carded as the synthesis of this same literature, not as a fourth dataset: normal ovarian-volume distributions are narrow, with small postmenopausal volumes. This shelf gives size norms only — ovarian-volume screening accuracy for cancer is a different question and is not rowed here.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — three independent populations plus a systematic review of the same literature consistently establish that ovarian volume falls steeply with age and menopause (decade means 6.6 cm³ under 30 to 1.8 cm³ at ≥70; upper limits 20 cm³ premenopausal and 10 cm³ postmenopausal), with values printed per modality (transvaginal ultrasound vs MRI) and per partition (age decade vs years since menopause), never spliced into one curve

title: Normal bile and pancreatic duct diameters: MRCP limits 8 mm (<65) / 11 mm (≥65) and 3 / 4 mm — ultrasound means ~2.5–2.8 mm, with the two ultrasound series disagreeing (7 mm vs 10 mm)
question: In healthy adults, what are the normal diameters of the common bile duct and the pancreatic duct — by imaging modality (ultrasound vs MRCP) and age — how steeply does duct diameter rise with age, and how many healthy people exceed the conventional upper limits (about 6–7 mm for the bile duct) that trigger further investigation?
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING, on three independent populations in two modalities, carded separately and never merged. Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall / Boron & Boulpaep, hepatobiliary sections — brief framing only; this shelf rests chiefly on the primary population literature, and says so. On MRCP (Pomerania, 938 / 774 healthy individuals) the age-dependent 95th-percentile upper limits are 8 mm (<65 years) and 11 mm (≥65 years) for the common bile duct and 3 mm and 4 mm for the pancreatic duct, and 10.9% / 18.2% of healthy people exceed the conventional limits. On ultrasound the means are far smaller (2.5 ± 1.1 mm at the porta hepatis, 2.8 ± 1.2 mm at the widest point in 830 donors, none above 7 mm), while a whole-duct-visualisation series reports up to 10 mm — the two ultrasound series disagree, and that disagreement is content, preserved on the face.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING — three independent populations (MRCP N = 938 / 774; ultrasound N = 830; ultrasound N = 256, 203 visualised) agree duct diameter rises with age, but the upper limits are modality-, site- and age-specific (MRCP bile duct 8 mm <65 years / 11 mm ≥65 years; ultrasound none above 7 mm in one series, up to 10 mm in another) and are printed per modality, never merged

title: Sorbinil for diabetic neuropathy: a largely negative founding programme — null in the 497-patient trial, positive only in the smallest (N = 15) trial
question: In adults with diabetic peripheral neuropathy, does the aldose reductase inhibitor sorbinil, compared with placebo, improve neuropathic pain, nerve conduction or clinical neuropathy measures?
balance: LIKELY (no benefit) — the nulls lead. This is the aldose reductase class's founding programme, and sorbinil was never marketed. The 497-patient trial found no evidence that early clinical signs and symptoms of diabetic neuropathy were altered; the 22-patient and 31-patient trials were null on nerve function and on every clinical and neurophysiological measure respectively. The only positive signals are in the smallest trial (N = 15, with a 4-patient idiosyncratic reaction) and in one peroneal-nerve velocity distribution — a surrogate — in the largest. A hypersensitivity reaction recurs across the programme.
stamp: LIKELY (no benefit) — four trials (N = 15, 22, 31 and 497 randomised) of a never-marketed drug: the two middle trials and the 497-patient trial's clinical measures are null, and the only positive signals are in the N = 15 trial and in one nerve-conduction distribution

title: Mexiletine for painful diabetic neuropathy: split old base — top-dose nighttime benefit in the largest trial, null global result in the second, underpowered null in the third
question: In adults with painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy, does oral mexiletine (a class IB antiarrhythmic / oral local-anaesthetic analogue), compared with placebo, reduce neuropathic pain?
balance: SPLIT — a split, small, old base, and the split leads. The largest trial (216 patients) is positive only at its top dose (675 mg/day) and only on nighttime pain and sleep; the second-largest (95 patients) is null on its global measure with positive exploratory subgroups; the third (29 patients) is frankly underpowered and null; only the 16-completer crossover is clearly positive on symptoms. All treatment periods are 3 weeks where stated. Mexiletine is a cardiac antiarrhythmic: one patient was hospitalised for palpitations, and the trial authors' own restriction — patients without heart disease, unresponsive or intolerant to standard therapy — prints on the face.
stamp: SPLIT — the largest trial (N = 216) positive only at 675 mg/day on nighttime pain and sleep, the N = 95 trial null on its global measure, the N = 29 trial underpowered and null, and the 16-completer crossover positive on symptoms only; all periods 3 weeks where stated

title: Sepiapterin in phenylketonuria: phenylalanine −63% vs +1% vs placebo and greater than sapropterin — in responder-enriched phase 3 trials, on a surrogate endpoint
question: In children and adults with phenylketonuria, does oral sepiapterin (a synthetic tetrahydrobiopterin precursor), compared with placebo or with sapropterin, lower blood phenylalanine?
balance: LIKELY (benefit, blood phenylalanine only) — a biochemical-surrogate base in enriched populations, and both flags lead. title: Cerliponase alfa in CLN2 disease: far slower decline than historical controls in a single-arm programme of 23 children — no concurrent control exists

title: Elosulfase alfa in Morquio A syndrome: one randomised trial — weekly dosing improved 6-minute walk by 22.5 m, stair climb null, extension uncontrolled
question: In patients aged 5 years and older with mucopolysaccharidosis IVA (Morquio A syndrome), does enzyme replacement with elosulfase alfa, compared with placebo, improve endurance and daily function (the MOR-004 / MOR-005 programme)?

title: Laronidase in mucopolysaccharidosis I: FVC and walk improved in a 45-patient trial — walk endpoint significant by one analysis, not the other
question: In children and adults with mucopolysaccharidosis I, does enzyme replacement with laronidase (recombinant human α-L-iduronidase), compared with placebo, improve respiratory function and walking capacity?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a small-N rare-disease base, and the counts lead. The placebo-controlled base is 45 patients over 26 weeks, one co-primary endpoint (6-minute walk) is significant by one analysis and not the other (P = .066 / .039 — both printed), and the long-term data are uncontrolled. title: Triheptanoin in long-chain fatty acid oxidation disorders: cardiac measures improved in a 32-patient trial — event-rate falls are uncontrolled before/after data
question: In children and adults with long-chain fatty acid oxidation disorders, does triheptanoin (an anaplerotic odd-chain triglyceride), compared with trioctanoin or with pre-treatment event rates, improve cardiac function and reduce major clinical events?

The single randomised trial is a 32-patient, 4-month, active-comparator study whose positive endpoints are echocardiographic measures, with its event outcome (rhabdomyolysis) null; the dramatic event-rate reductions come from uncontrolled pre/post comparisons in extension and compassionate-use cohorts, where regression to the mean and survivorship cannot be excluded. title: Miglustat in Niemann-Pick disease type C (one programme, three reports): the 29-patient randomised trial's surrogate primary — saccadic eye-movement velocity — was significant only after excluding benzodiazepine users (P = 0.028); extensions report stabilisation
question: In children and adults with Niemann-Pick disease type C, does miglustat monotherapy (substrate reduction), compared with standard care, slow neurological progression?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one programme, three reports, labelled as such. The single randomised trial (29 patients aged ≥12 years) found its primary endpoint — horizontal saccadic eye-movement velocity, a surrogate chosen for its correlation with progression — improved on miglustat vs standard care, reaching significance only when patients taking benzodiazepines were excluded (P = 0.028); swallowing improved, auditory acuity was stable and ambulatory deterioration was slower. The two other reports are open-label extensions of the same programme (adult/juvenile and paediatric), not independent confirmations. No trial measures survival. The control was standard care, not placebo.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit — slowing/stabilisation of neurological markers) — based on a very small N = 29 randomised patients in one programme (three reports, two of them extensions): the surrogate primary reached significance only when benzodiazepine users were excluded (P = 0.028), against standard care, not placebo

title: Doxofylline vs theophylline and placebo in asthma: 5 reports covering at least 4 and at most 5 distinct trials (the 2002 trial and DOROTHEO 1 may be the same trial reported twice) — theophylline-like lung-function effects with fewer adverse events and drop-outs
question: In patients with asthma (and, in the older literature, reversible chronic airways obstruction), does oral doxofylline versus placebo — or versus theophylline — improve lung function and asthma events, and does its safety profile differ from theophylline's?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit — a tolerability claim, not an efficacy-superiority claim). Counted as REPORTS, exactly as printed: 5 randomised reports in asthma / obstructive airways disease covering at least 4 and at most 5 distinct trials — the 2002 trial and DOROTHEO 1 may be the same trial reported twice (identical designs, no registry number for either), and they are never presented here as independent confirmations. Wherever doxofylline and theophylline were compared, lung-function effects were similar, with a consistently smaller adverse-event and drop-out burden on doxofylline. No trial was powered on exacerbations or hospitalisation; endpoints are spirometry, symptom/event diaries and rescue use over 28 days to 6 months, on 1989–2002-era background therapy. The DOROTHEO pooled publication is one publication covering two trials, never counted as two. Labelled limbs (COPD crossover; paediatric steroid-sparing pilot) are carded separately and never folded into the asthma count.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit — theophylline-like lung-function effects with fewer adverse events and drop-outs; a tolerability claim, not efficacy superiority) — 5 reports covering at least 4 and at most 5 distinct trials: the 2002 trial and DOROTHEO 1 may be the same trial reported twice, and the DOROTHEO pooled publication is one publication covering two trials

title: Somatostatin analogues for polycystic liver volume (3 randomised primaries, total N = 144): liver volume fell roughly 3–5% over 6–12 months on imaging — a surrogate endpoint only — and pasireotide caused new diabetes in 59% vs 7%
question: In patients with polycystic liver disease (autosomal-dominant polycystic kidney disease or autosomal-dominant polycystic liver disease, including severe liver involvement), does a somatostatin analogue versus placebo reduce total liver volume over 6–12 months, and at what metabolic cost?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit — on imaging liver volume only). Three randomised primaries, three different molecules, total N = 144: lanreotide −2.9% vs +1.6% on placebo (p < .01), octreotide −4.95% vs +0.92% (p = 0.048) and pasireotide −3% vs +6% (p < 0.001) in height-adjusted total liver volume over 6–12 months. SURROGATE-ENDPOINT FLAG: every primary is imaging volume; whether shrinking a polycystic liver by roughly 3–5% over a year helps patients is untested. HARM ASYMMETRY: the pasireotide limb's glycaemic harm — hyperglycaemia 79% vs 27%, and new diabetes in 59% vs 7% of patients without diabetes at baseline — is far larger than any harm signal in the other two limbs and is never averaged away in this balance.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit — imaging liver volume only, a surrogate endpoint; no symptom, complication or transplant benefit shown) — based on 3 trials, total N = 144; pasireotide's glycaemic harm (new diabetes 59% vs 7%) is stated on its card and never averaged away

title: Fontolizumab (anti-interferon-gamma antibody, never marketed) in moderate-to-severe Crohn's disease: 3 randomised reports, total N = 379 — both larger trials missed their primary endpoints while CRP and endoscopic measures moved
question: In patients with moderate-to-severe Crohn's disease (CDAI 250–450), does fontolizumab versus placebo induce clinical response or remission, and does any clinical effect track the drug's clear biological (C-reactive protein / endoscopic) activity?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — a tested-and-failed interferon-gamma hypothesis: the biology engaged without clinical benefit at the tested doses/schedules. Three randomised reports, total N = 379. Both adequately sized trials missed their primary clinical endpoints (day-29 response 31–38% across all groups including placebo in the 201-patient trial; the single-dose primary did not differ in the 133-patient trial), while C-reactive protein and endoscopic measures moved. Every positive clinical reading is a later-timepoint or two-dose-subgroup analysis after a null primary, stated on the face. Era: 2006–2010, CDAI-era endpoints. Fontolizumab is an investigational humanised antibody that was never marketed — stated plainly.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — biological activity without primary-endpoint clinical benefit: both adequately sized trials missed their primaries, and every positive clinical reading is a later-timepoint or subgroup analysis; fontolizumab was never marketed

title: Ontamalimab (anti-MAdCAM-1 antibody PF-00547659, never marketed) in IBD — SPLIT by disease: ulcerative colitis positive in phase 2 and phase 3, Crohn's phase 2 primary missed and phase 3 supplementary only; programme discontinued commercially in 2020
question: In patients with moderate-to-severe ulcerative colitis — or, as a labelled second limb, moderate-to-severe Crohn's disease — does ontamalimab versus placebo induce and maintain clinical remission?
balance: SPLIT — by disease, and the limbs are never pooled. Ulcerative colitis limb: positive across phase 2 (TURANDOT week-12 remission 11.3% / 16.7% / 15.5% / 5.7% across dose groups vs 2.7% on placebo, significant in three of four dose groups, with no benefit at the highest dose and one-sided multiplicity-adjusted p-values, printed as reported) and phase 3 (two induction studies and a re-randomised maintenance study; 75 mg week-12 remission 29.8% vs 15.8% and 29.5% vs 12.5%; week-52 maintenance remission 53.5% at 25 mg and 40.2% at 75 mg vs 8.2% and 12.8% on placebo). Crohn's limb: the phase 2 primary (CDAI-70 response at week 8 or 12) was missed, and the Crohn's phase 3 results exist only in the phase 3 publication's supplementary data. The programme was discontinued in 2020 for reasons unrelated to drug safety or efficacy, as its publication states — a commercial discontinuation, stated plainly. Ontamalimab (PF-00547659) is an investigational antibody that was never marketed.

title: Interleukin-17 blockade in Crohn's disease (FLOOR-RISK — exactly 2 trials, total N = 189; both harmful/null): secukinumab's analysis favoured placebo and brodalumab was stopped early for worsening disease
question: In patients with moderate-to-severe Crohn's disease, does blocking interleukin-17 signalling — secukinumab (anti-IL-17A) or brodalumab (anti-IL-17 receptor) — versus placebo improve disease activity, or does it worsen Crohn's disease?
balance: LIKELY (harm) — FLOOR-RISK, stated exactly: exactly 2 trials, 2 molecules, 1 pathway, 189 randomised patients, and the harm direction is the content. The secukinumab proof-of-concept trial's Bayesian primary analysis estimated a <0.1% probability that secukinumab reduces CDAI by ≥50 points more than placebo, and its secondary area-under-curve analysis differed in favour of placebo (mean ΔCDAI 49 [95% CI 2 to 96], p = 0.043), with 20 infections including four local fungal infections on secukinumab vs none on placebo. The brodalumab phase 2 trial was terminated early because of an imbalance in worsening Crohn's disease in the active groups, with no meaningful efficacy. This is a 'do not extrapolate the psoriasis result to Crohn's' shelf: its balance leads with worsening, not with the single 15% mid-dose remission cell (no dose-response; the 700 mg arm read 9% and the 210 mg arm 3%).
stamp: LIKELY (harm — worsening Crohn's disease) — FLOOR-RISK: exactly 2 trials, total N = 189; one trial's secondary analysis favoured placebo outright and the other was terminated early for worsening disease on treatment

title: Abrilumab (anti-α4β7 integrin antibody AMG 181, never marketed) in moderate-to-severe ulcerative colitis (FLOOR-RISK — exactly 2 trials, total N = 399): week-8 remission 13.3% and 12.7% vs 4.3% in the global trial, in 1–2-patient cells in the Japanese trial
question: In patients with moderate-to-severe ulcerative colitis despite conventional therapy, does subcutaneous abrilumab versus placebo induce clinical remission at week 8?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — FLOOR-RISK, stated exactly: exactly 2 trials totalling 399 patients, one programme, both phase 2, both 8-week induction reads; no maintenance trial was ever reported and the programme did not proceed. In the global phase 2b trial, week-8 remission was 13.3% on 70 mg and 12.7% on 210 mg vs 4.3% on placebo (p < .05 for both), with odds ratios 3.35 and 3.33 carrying 90% (not 95%) confidence intervals, printed as reported. In the Japanese phase 2 trial, week-8 remission was 12.9% across the abrilumab groups vs 0 of 13 on placebo, in per-dose cells of 1–2 patients. No progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy and no deaths in either trial. Abrilumab (development name AMG 181) is an investigational antibody that was never marketed — stated plainly. The base is ulcerative-colitis-only: no abrilumab Crohn's trial report exists.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit — week-8 induction of remission) — FLOOR-RISK: exactly 2 trials, total N = 399, both phase 2; the global trial's odds ratios carry 90% CIs as reported and the Japanese trial's cells are 1–2 patients; abrilumab was never marketed

title: Visilizumab (anti-CD3 antibody, never marketed) in severe corticosteroid-refractory ulcerative colitis (FLOOR-RISK — exactly 2 randomised reports, only one placebo-controlled): the controlled trial was null on every endpoint, with colectomy 18% vs 7%
question: In patients with severely active ulcerative colitis despite at least 5 days of intravenous corticosteroids, does visilizumab (two daily intravenous doses) versus placebo — or across dose levels — induce response or remission without unacceptable harm?
balance: LIKELY (no benefit — with a harm shadow). FLOOR-RISK, stated exactly: exactly 2 randomised reports, total treated N ≈ 231 across the two studies, and only one of them has a placebo arm. The placebo-controlled trial is null on every efficacy endpoint — day-45 response 55% vs 47% (p = 0.475), remission 8% vs 9%, mucosal healing 29% vs 26% — with numerically more colectomies on visilizumab (18% vs 7%, p = 0.130) and more cardiac and vascular disorders. The dose-escalation report's uncontrolled symptomatic response rates (50–71%) are never printed without that controlled null beside them. The honest summary: visilizumab did not work in the population that most needed rescue therapy, and carried a safety shadow. Era: 2010-era severe-UC rescue landscape, before modern rescue sequencing. Visilizumab is an investigational antibody that was never marketed — stated plainly.
stamp: LIKELY (no benefit — with a harm shadow: numerically more colectomies and more cardiac/vascular events) — FLOOR-RISK: exactly 2 randomised reports, total treated N ≈ 231, and only one of them placebo-controlled; visilizumab was never marketed

title: Nitazoxanide for rotavirus diarrhoea in children: 3 small single-centre randomised trials (total N = 175) all found diarrhoea roughly 24–44 hours shorter on a 3-day course, with a mixed-virus adult trial as labelled support
question: In children hospitalised with rotavirus diarrhoea, does a 3-day course of oral nitazoxanide versus placebo (or versus probiotics / rehydration alone) shorten the duration of diarrhoea and hospitalisation?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — three small single-centre paediatric trials, all pointing the same way on the same endpoint: diarrhoea duration roughly 24–44 hours shorter on a 3-day course of nitazoxanide (median time to resolution 31 h vs 75 h in the 2006 Lancet trial's analysis set of 38 of 50 enrolled children; median diarrhoea duration 54 h vs 79 h and hospitalisation 81 h vs 108 h in the Bolivian trial; 54 h vs 80 h and 68 h vs 90 h in the Indian trial), with no significant adverse events reported. The limits are size and setting: each trial is single-centre (Cairo, Bolivia, India) and under 80 patients, no trial followed children beyond the hospital stay, and the rotavirus epidemiology in these trials predates today's vaccine coverage in most settings. A mixed-virus adult/adolescent trial is carded as labelled support only, never counted as a paediatric rotavirus primary.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit — diarrhoea shortened by roughly 24–44 hours) — based on 3 small single-centre paediatric trials, total N = 175 randomised (the 2006 trial's analysis set was 38 of 50 enrolled), all from the pre-vaccine-coverage era

title: Peginterferon lambda for COVID-19 — SPLIT by limb: TOGETHER (outpatients) found hospitalisation or prolonged emergency care in 2.7% vs 5.6% (relative risk 0.49, relative), the small outpatient trials split, and the hospitalised trial was null and stopped early; all trials are pre-Omicron era
question: In outpatients with mild-to-moderate COVID-19, and in hospitalised patients with COVID-19, does peginterferon lambda versus placebo prevent clinical events (hospitalisation or prolonged emergency care), speed viral clearance, or shorten symptoms?
balance: SPLIT — the limb split is the answer, and this shelf is never readable as 'peginterferon lambda treats COVID-19' without it. Outpatient limb: the one large trial (TOGETHER, 1,951 assigned) is positive on clinical events — hospitalisation or emergency-department visit >6 h within 28 days in 2.7% vs 5.6% (relative risk 0.49, a relative measure beside its absolute rates) — while the two small outpatient trials are split (a viral-load signal with a non-significant unadjusted primary in Toronto; fully null on shedding and symptoms at Stanford). Hospitalised limb: null, in a trial stopped prematurely (WHO-severity global odds ratio 0.76 [95% CI 0.35–1.66], p = 0.49). ERA FLAG (load-bearing): all four trials ran in the pre-Omicron / early-vaccine era against variants that no longer circulate, in populations whose vaccination and prior-infection status differs from today's. Peginterferon lambda is investigational for this use; generic name only.
stamp: SPLIT (by limb — outpatient: one large trial positive on clinical events, 2.7% vs 5.6%, relative risk 0.49 relative, with the two small outpatient trials split; hospitalised: null, stopped early) — all four trials are from the pre-Omicron / early-vaccine era

title: Pimodivir for influenza A (one programme: 4 reports covering 5 trials): viral-load primaries consistently met, but the phase 3 hospital study was null and the outpatient phase 3 gain was 12.5 hours of symptom time
question: In patients with influenza A infection — challenged healthy volunteers, uncomplicated outpatients, hospitalised patients, and high-risk outpatients — does pimodivir (alone or with oseltamivir) versus placebo (with or without oseltamivir) reduce viral load, shorten symptoms, or prevent complications?
balance: One programme only — 4 publications covering 5 trials (challenge study, TOPAZ, OPAL, and two phase 3 studies in one publication) — stated in exactly those terms. The virologic arc is consistent: pimodivir significantly reduced viral shedding in the challenge model and viral-load AUC to day 8 in TOPAZ (combination −8.6 day·log10 copies/mL [95% CI −12.0 to −5.1]). The clinical arc is thin and split: OPAL's symptom and complication readings are secondary readings of a pharmacokinetic-primary trial; the phase 3 hospital study showed no clinical benefit on the day-6 Hospital Recovery Scale (common odds ratio 0.943 [95% CI 0.609–1.462], P = .397 — a relative measure), while the phase 3 outpatient study found median time to resolution of 7 symptoms 92.6 h vs 105.1 h (P = .0216) — a 12.5-hour difference. The programme was discontinued. Pimodivir (development code JNJ-63623872) is an investigational antiviral that was never marketed — stated plainly under the clarification exception. Every positive primary in this programme is a viral-load endpoint; symptom and complication readings are secondary or trend-only.
stamp: SPLIT — one programme (4 reports covering 5 trials): virologic primaries consistently positive, but the phase 3 hospital study was null on its clinical primary and the outpatient phase 3 gain was only 12.5 hours of symptom time; programme discontinued

title: Sitamaquine for visceral leishmaniasis (3 randomised phase II reports): day-180 cure 87% in India and 83% in Kenya in uncontrolled dose-ranging trials, 85% vs 95% on amphotericin B in the one comparative trial — and recurrent renal harm; programme abandoned
question: In patients with visceral leishmaniasis in India and Kenya, does oral sitamaquine (dose-ranging 1.5–3.0 mg/kg/day for 21–28 days) versus another dose, or versus intravenous amphotericin B, achieve clinical cure at 6 months, and what renal toxicity appears?
balance: Three randomised phase II reports, and the design limits lead: two of the three trials compare sitamaquine doses with each other, not with a standard treatment, so their day-180 cure rates (87% overall in India, 92 of 106 intention-to-treat; 83% overall in Kenya, 79 of 95) are uncontrolled absolutes with no dose-response in either trial. The only comparative readout is the 61-patient Bihar trial: final clinical cure at day 180 was 85% on sitamaquine vs 95% on intravenous amphotericin B (no p-value for the comparison printed in the abstract). The harm limb is load-bearing: nephrotic syndrome in 3% (3 of 120) and glomerulonephritis in 2% (2 of 120) in the Indian trial, and a severe renal adverse event at each of the two highest doses in the Kenyan trial — renal injury recurred across the programme and is a named reason it was abandoned. Sitamaquine is an investigational oral 8-aminoquinoline that was never marketed — stated plainly. Populations were Indian and Kenyan Leishmania donovani patients (mean ages 21 and 16 years in the two dose-ranging trials); no HIV-co-infected or relapsed-patient data.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit — day-180 cure rates of 83–87% in uncontrolled dose-ranging trials and 85% vs 95% on amphotericin B in the one small comparative trial, priced in recurrent renal harm; programme abandoned for that harm)

title: Ganaplacide (KAF156) plus lumefantrine solid dispersion formulation for uncomplicated falciparum malaria (one programme: 2 patient trials plus a labelled challenge study): day-29 PCR-corrected response 92–100% in dose-finding, and non-inferior to artemether–lumefantrine in children in KALUMI (99% vs 99%)
question: In patients with uncomplicated Plasmodium falciparum malaria, does the novel combination ganaplacide plus lumefantrine solid dispersion formulation versus artemether–lumefantrine achieve PCR-corrected adequate clinical and parasitological response at day 29, and is it non-inferior?
balance: One programme only — 2 patient trials plus a labelled controlled-human-infection (challenge) study — stated in exactly those terms. The phase 2 dose-finding trial (337 patients in part A, 175 in part B) found day-29 PCR-corrected response of 92–100% across the ganaplacide–lumefantrine regimens vs 100% on artemether–lumefantrine in the per-protocol set, with only the 3-day regimen meeting the prespecified endpoint in children in part B. KALUMI, the phase 2 non-inferiority trial in children, met non-inferiority in its main part (220 children enrolled, 110 per arm): day-29 PCR-corrected response 99% (97 of 98) on ganaplacide–lumefantrine vs 99% (98 of 99) on artemether–lumefantrine, treatment difference −0.0% (95% CI −2.9 to 2.8), the lower limit above the −10% margin. Design flags on the face: both patient trials are open-label; KALUMI is phase 2, not phase 3, and its main-part population is children under 12 in five African countries — efficacy in adults beyond the dose-finding trial and in Southeast Asian artemisinin-resistant settings is not established by this base. Ganaplacide (development code KAF156) plus lumefantrine solid dispersion formulation is an investigational combination that is not a marketed product — named as the publications give it under the clarification exception. Vomiting (29% vs 11%) and hypokalaemia (25% vs 15%) were more common on ganaplacide–lumefantrine in KALUMI.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit — non-inferior to artemether–lumefantrine in children in the KALUMI phase 2 trial, 99% vs 99% at day 29; one programme: 2 patient trials plus a labelled challenge study, both patient trials open-label)

title: Ferroquine combinations for uncomplicated falciparum malaria (one programme: 3 randomised reports): artesunate combinations cured 97–99% in dose-ranging, but the single-dose artefenomel–ferroquine programme missed its efficacy target (78.4–91.7% in African children; 20–40% in Vietnamese patients)
question: In patients with uncomplicated Plasmodium falciparum malaria in Africa and Asia, do ferroquine-containing combinations (with artesunate, or single-dose with artefenomel) versus amodiaquine–artesunate or other comparators achieve PCR-corrected cure at day 28/63?
balance: One programme only — 3 trials — stated in exactly those terms. The arc is the answer: ferroquine plus artesunate cleared parasites rapidly with no recurrence to day 28 in the small safety-focused phase 2a trial (72 adult men), and in the phase 2 dose-ranging trial the three artesunate combination doses met non-inferiority against a 90% reference cure rate (day-28 PCR-corrected cure 97%, 99% and 99%, vs 79% on ferroquine monotherapy). The programme's decisive test then failed: in the single-dose phase 2b trial of artefenomel 800 mg plus ferroquine, no treatment arm met the target efficacy criterion (lower 95% confidence limit >90% for PCR-adjusted response at day 28); response ranged from 78.4% to 91.7% across doses in African children ≤5 years and only 20–40% in Vietnamese patients. Safety flags from the early trials: grade-1 alanine-aminotransferase rises with a dose trend, and one QTcF prolongation >60 ms on the lowest ferroquine dose in phase 2a. Ferroquine (development code SSR97193) is an investigational drug that was never marketed — stated plainly under the clarification exception. Populations differ by trial and are labelled per card: adult men only in phase 2a; the phase 2b primary population is African children ≤5 years.
stamp: SPLIT — one programme (3 trials): ferroquine–artesunate met its dose-ranging non-inferiority readings (97–99% cure), but the single-dose artefenomel–ferroquine programme missed its efficacy target in its primary population and read 20–40% in Vietnamese patients; programme discontinued

title: Brentuximab vedotin plus CHP versus CHOP in untreated CD30-positive peripheral T-cell lymphoma (ECHELON-2 — one trial, 4 reports): median PFS 48.2 vs 20.8 months, and at 5 years PFS 51.4% vs 43.0% and overall survival 70.1% vs 61.0% — with peripheral neuropathy in 52% vs 55%
question: In adults with previously untreated CD30-positive peripheral T-cell lymphoma, does replacing vincristine with brentuximab vedotin (A+CHP) versus CHOP improve progression-free and overall survival — and does the benefit hold at 5 years, and does interim PET or consolidative stem-cell transplant modify it?
balance: One trial — ECHELON-2 (452 patients randomised 1:1) — reported in 4 publications, labelled as such and never pooled with any other trial. The primary report found median progression-free survival 48.2 vs 20.8 months (hazard ratio 0.71 [95% CI 0.54–0.93], P = 0.0110 — a relative measure). At 5 years (median follow-up 47.6 months), PFS was 51.4% vs 43.0% (hazard ratio 0.70 [95% CI 0.53–0.91] — relative) and overall survival 70.1% vs 61.0% (hazard ratio 0.72 [95% CI 0.53–0.99] — relative; the interval just inside significance, printed with its interval, not as a bare win). The pricing harm is on the face: peripheral neuropathy occurred in 52% on A+CHP vs 55% on CHOP — it did not fall when vincristine was removed — with febrile neutropenia 18% vs 15% and fatal adverse events 3% vs 4%; neuropathy had resolved or improved in 72% (A+CHP) and 78% (CHOP) of affected patients at 5 years. The two ancillary reports are exploratory and labelled: interim PET4-negative status was prognostic in BOTH arms (not a reason to choose one arm), and the stem-cell-transplant analysis is a non-randomised subgroup analysis in complete responders, never a randomised transplant comparison.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit — one trial, the ECHELON-2 programme: A+CHP improved progression-free survival and, at 5 years, overall survival 70.1% vs 61.0% [relative HR 0.72, 95% CI 0.53–0.99] over CHOP, priced in peripheral neuropathy that did not fall when vincristine was removed, 52% vs 55%)

title: Brentuximab vedotin versus physician's choice in previously treated CD30-positive cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (ALCANZA — one trial, 4 reports): durable response (ORR4) 56.3% vs 12.5%, median PFS 16.7 vs 3.5 months at final data, and a large skin-symptom gain — priced in peripheral neuropathy (67% any grade)
question: In adults with previously treated CD30-positive cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (mycosis fungoides or primary cutaneous anaplastic large-cell lymphoma), does brentuximab vedotin improve durable objective response and progression-free survival versus physician's choice (methotrexate or bexarotene) — and at what symptom and neuropathy cost?
balance: One trial — ALCANZA (131 patients randomised; 128 in the intention-to-treat population) — reported in 4 publications, labelled as such. The primary endpoint is a durable-response endpoint, not survival: objective global response lasting ≥4 months (ORR4) was 56.3% vs 12.5% at the primary analysis and 54.7% vs 12.5% in the final data, with median progression-free survival 16.7 vs 3.5 months — no overall-survival advantage is printed in these reports, and the shelf does not present PFS as a survival claim. The comparator (methotrexate or bexarotene) is weak by design, and the trial is open-label — the honest frame is a large durable-response and symptom gain in a rare, incurable disease: the Skindex-29 symptom score fell by a mean maximum of −27.96 vs −8.62 (difference −18.9 [95% CI −26.6 to −11.2]), exceeding the study-defined minimally important difference, while general quality-of-life measures (FACT-G, EQ-5D) were comparable between arms. The price is peripheral neuropathy: 67% any grade on brentuximab vedotin in the primary report (44 patients in the final data, of whom 86% had complete resolution or improvement to grade 1–2). Response was seen across CD30-expression levels and regardless of large-cell transformation in the exploratory sub-analysis.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit — one trial, the ALCANZA programme: durable response 54.7% vs 12.5% and median PFS 16.7 vs 3.5 months vs a weak physician's-choice comparator, with a large skin-symptom gain; no survival advantage printed, priced in peripheral neuropathy in 67%)

title: Lenalidomide plus rituximab (R²) versus rituximab–chemotherapy in untreated advanced follicular lymphoma (RELEVANCE — one trial, 4 reports): similar efficacy at 3, 6 and 10 years (10-year PFS 46.4% vs 46.6%; overall survival 82.4% vs 81.1%) — an equivalence result, with less neutropenia but more grade 3/4 skin reactions on R²
question: In adults with previously untreated advanced follicular lymphoma, is chemotherapy-free lenalidomide plus rituximab (R²) as effective as rituximab plus chemotherapy — and does the toxicity trade (less neutropenia, more skin reactions) change the choice?
balance: One trial — RELEVANCE (1,030 patients randomised: R² n = 513, R-chemotherapy n = 517, both followed by rituximab maintenance) — reported in 4 publications, labelled as such. The verdict is equivalence, not superiority: both co-primary endpoints were similar at every maturity. Complete response at 120 weeks was 48% vs 53% (P = 0.13, not significant) with interim 3-year progression-free survival 77% vs 78%; at 6 years, PFS was 60% vs 59% (hazard ratio 1.03 [95% CI 0.84–1.27] — a relative measure centred on no difference) and overall survival 89% in both groups; at 10 years, median PFS was 110.6 vs 102.8 months but the 10-year PFS rates were 46.4% vs 46.6% and overall survival 82.4% vs 81.1% — the median-PFS difference must not be read as a win. The toxicity trade belongs whole on the face: grade 3/4 neutropenia 32% on R² vs 50% on R-chemotherapy and febrile neutropenia 2% vs 7% favoured R², while grade 3/4 cutaneous reactions 7% vs 1% favoured R-chemotherapy — a different toxicity bill, not a smaller one. Secondary primary malignancies were 11% vs 13% at 6 years (P = .34). The molecular-response ancillary study is a labelled ancillary report of the same trial, in a French subset.
stamp: LIKELY (comparable efficacy — one trial, the RELEVANCE programme: R² is a chemotherapy-free alternative with efficacy similar to rituximab–chemotherapy at 3, 6 and 10 years, not superior, trading less neutropenia [32% vs 50% grade 3/4] for more grade 3/4 cutaneous reactions [7% vs 1%])

title: Rituximab in generalised myasthenia gravis — FLOOR-RISK, exactly 2 trials, total N = 99, directly split: RINOMAX positive in new-onset disease (minimal manifestations 71% vs 29%) and BeatMG futility in established steroid-dependent disease (steroid-sparing primary 60% vs 56%)
question: In generalised myasthenia gravis, does add-on rituximab improve disease control versus placebo — and does the answer depend on whether the disease is new-onset or long-established and steroid-dependent?
balance: FLOOR-RISK, stated exactly: the complete placebo-controlled base is exactly 2 trials totalling 99 randomised patients, and the two trials are directly split — the count and the split are printed on the face and carried in the stamp line. RINOMAX (47 randomised; new-onset generalised myasthenia gravis, onset ≤12 months, single 500 mg rituximab infusion): minimal disease manifestations at 16 weeks in 71% (17 of 24) vs 29% (6 of 21), P = .007, probability ratio 2.48 (95% CI 1.20–5.11 — a relative measure). BeatMG (52 randomised; established acetylcholine-receptor-antibody-positive disease on prednisone ≥15 mg/day, two-cycle regimen): the steroid-sparing primary was achieved in 60% vs 56%, and the study reached its prespecified futility endpoint (P = 0.03) — the predefined clinically meaningful improvement was unlikely in a larger trial. The populations must never be merged: new-onset, single-dose, QMG-based in one trial; established, steroid-dependent, steroid-sparing, futility-designed in the other. No replacement anchor exists — the rest of the rituximab–myasthenia literature is observational — so this shelf rests on these 99 patients alone, and no pooled verdict is offered.
stamp: SPLIT — based on exactly 2 trials, total N = 99: RINOMAX (n = 47, new-onset) positive on minimal disease manifestations (71% vs 29%), BeatMG (n = 52, established steroid-dependent) reached futility on its steroid-sparing primary (60% vs 56%); the two populations are never pooled

title: Richmond Agitation-Sedation Scale (RASS): inter-rater reliability was high at derivation (r = 0.956), in independent JAMA validation (weighted kappa 0.91, vs Glasgow Coma Scale 0.64) and in Swedish translation (kappa 0.86, N = 15)
question: In critically ill adults, how reliable and valid is the Richmond Agitation-Sedation Scale (RASS) as the bedside measure of sedation and agitation — what inter-rater reliability did its derivation study and the independent JAMA validation deliver, how does it compare with the Glasgow Coma Scale and the Ramsay scale head-to-head, and does reliability survive translation?
balance: MEASUREMENT PERFORMANCE — high inter-rater reliability in every setting tested, and that is all this shelf claims. The derivation study (the scale originators' own report, Richmond) found inter-rater r = 0.956 (kappa 0.73) across 192 encounters and, after implementation, r = 0.964 (kappa 0.80) between a nurse educator and 27 trained bedside nurses. The independent Vanderbilt validation in JAMA found RASS weighted kappa 0.91 — equal to the Ramsay scale's 0.94 and superior to the Glasgow Coma Scale's 0.64 — with criterion and construct validity in 411 paired observations. A Swedish translation kept weighted kappa 0.86, but in only 15 patients (40 paired assessments). This is a measurement shelf: no card claims that RASS-guided sedation protocols improve outcomes.
stamp: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — measurement reliability established: RASS inter-rater reliability was high at derivation (r = 0.956, kappa 0.73; originators' own report), in independent validation (weighted kappa 0.91, superior to the Glasgow Coma Scale's 0.64 and level with Ramsay's 0.94) and after Swedish translation (weighted kappa 0.86, N = 15 patients); a measurement stamp, not a treatment stamp — no card claims RASS-guided protocols improve outcomes

title: PAINAD in advanced dementia: reliable between raters (ICC 0.92–0.98 in acute hospitals) but validity unsettled — the blinded placebo-controlled test was null and the largest validation found weak concurrent validity (τ = 0.29)
question: In people with advanced dementia who cannot self-report pain, how well does the PAINAD scale (Pain Assessment in Advanced Dementia; five observed items, score 0–10) detect pain — what reliability and validity did its derivation study show, what happened when the German version was put to a double-blind placebo-controlled analgesic test of validity, and how does it perform in acute general-hospital inpatients?
balance: MEASUREMENT PERFORMANCE — genuinely split, and the split is the answer. The derivation study (the originators' own report; only 19 residents observed) found adequate inter-rater reliability and internal consistency, correlation with the Discomfort Scale, and scores that fell after pain medication. But the one double-blind placebo-controlled test of responsiveness — German PAINAD in advanced dementia — found that neither PAINAD-G nor any of three comparator observational tools separated oxycodone from placebo. And the largest validation, in 230 acute general-hospital inpatients, found excellent inter-rater reliability (ICC 0.92 at rest, 0.98 in movement) beside only modest test–retest reliability (ICC 0.54–0.66) and weak concurrent validity against self-rated pain (Kendall τ = 0.29), with its authors raising concerns about validity in acute hospitals. No card presents PAINAD as settled-valid. Settings print on every card: VA dementia unit, German trial, London acute wards.
stamp: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — split and NOT ESTABLISHED as settled-valid: derivation (originators' report, observed N = 19) and acute-hospital data show good inter-rater reliability (ICC 0.92–0.98), but the one double-blind placebo-controlled test found PAINAD-G did not separate oxycodone from placebo, and the largest validation (N = 230) found weak concurrent validity (τ = 0.29) and questioned validity in acute hospitals; a measurement stamp, not a treatment stamp

title: Nu-DESC delirium screening on wards: sensitivity 0.98 and NPV 1.00 in the largest validation but PPV only 0.43 at 9% prevalence, and the cut-off is unsettled (Italian optimum 3, not the derivation cut-off)
question: On hospital wards, how accurately does the Nu-DESC (Nursing Delirium Screening Scale; five nurse-observed items) detect delirium against CAM / DSM reference standards — what sensitivity and specificity did its derivation study deliver, and what do the general-medical-ward and translated-version validations find, including the cut-off disagreement?
balance: MEASUREMENT PERFORMANCE — high sensitivity in the ward validations, with two numbers that must travel with it: the positive predictive value and the unsettled cut-off. At derivation (the originators' own report, oncology inpatients, CAM reference) sensitivity was 85.7% and specificity 86.8%. On German general medical wards (698 patients aged ≥65, DSM-5 reference, delirium occurrence 9.0%) sensitivity was 0.98 and specificity 0.87 — but PPV was only 0.43 at that prevalence, so most positive screens were not delirium. The Italian validation (101 elderly inpatients, CAM reference) found its optimum at a cut-off of 3, not the derivation cut-off, with sensitivity 100% and specificity 76% and AUC 0.946. No card prints one cut-off as universal. This is a diagnostic-accuracy shelf: no card claims Nu-DESC screening improves outcomes.
stamp: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — high sensitivity on wards (0.98 in the largest validation, NPV 1.00) but PPV only 0.43 at 9% prevalence and the cut-off unsettled (derivation vs Italian optimum of 3, sensitivity 100% / specificity 76%); derivation sensitivity was 85.7% in oncology inpatients; a diagnostic-accuracy stamp, not a treatment stamp

title: Capillary refill time in adults: pooled prognostic accuracy is poor (AUC 0.66, sensitivity 54%), unaided visual assessment shows no agreement with image-derived CRT (κ = 0.00), and quantitative CRT crosses the 3-s threshold in both directions during one inflammatory episode
question: At the bedside, what is capillary refill time (CRT) worth as a perfusion measure in adults — how well does a prolonged CRT predict death or adverse events in acute circulatory failure (and how does it compare with lactate), how much of its unreliability is removed by a standardised timed technique, and what does a controlled human endotoxemia study show about the behaviour of quantitative CRT and its 3-second threshold during acute inflammation?
balance: MEASUREMENT / PROGNOSTIC PERFORMANCE — poor pooled accuracy is the headline, not a caveat. One synthesis is carded beside three primary reports, labelled as such: across 23 studies and 60,656 patients, prolonged CRT predicted death in acute circulatory failure with pooled AUC 0.66, sensitivity 54% and specificity 72% (pooled AUC 0.69 across all at-risk / confirmed-failure analyses), not significantly different from lactate, with accuracy greater when CRT measurement was high-quality. A single-centre septic-shock cohort found much higher AUCs (0.84 index finger, 0.90 knee at 6 hours) — never printed without the pooled figure beside them. Technique moves the value materially: unaided visual CRT showed no agreement with image-derived CRT (κ = 0.00), while a chronograph-standardised method correlated strongly (r = 0.64). And in a controlled human endotoxemia study, quantitative CRT crossed the 3-second threshold in both directions within one inflammatory episode. No card implies CRT-targeted resuscitation improves outcomes — the ANDROMEDA-SHOCK programme asks that different question and is deliberately not carded here.
stamp: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — NOT ESTABLISHED as a stand-alone prognostic test: pooled AUC 0.66 (sensitivity 54%, specificity 72%) for death in acute circulatory failure in the one labelled synthesis (23 studies, 60,656 patients), not significantly different from lactate; single-centre AUCs of 0.84–0.90 (N = 59) do not override the pooled figure, unaided visual CRT showed no agreement with image-derived CRT (κ = 0.00), and quantitative CRT crossed the 3-s threshold in both directions in a healthy-volunteer endotoxemia model; a measurement / prognostic stamp, not a treatment stamp

title: Portable bladder scanner vs catheterisation: accuracy is setting-dependent — systematic underestimation postpartum (median 42.7 mL, worse at BMI ≥30), fluid- and volume-dependent errors in critical care, prolapse-stage effects, and r = 0.89 for the named BladderScan BVI 9400 after hysterectomy
question: How accurate is a portable bladder scanner (and bedside bladder ultrasound) against catheterised volume — the reference standard — for measuring bladder / post-void residual volume in postpartum women, critically ill adults with low urine output, women with pelvic organ prolapse, and postoperative gynaecological patients, and in which settings (obesity, ascites / abdominal fluid, advanced prolapse, very low or very high volumes) does its error grow?
balance: MEASUREMENT PERFORMANCE — setting-dependent accuracy, with no pooled bias figure, because the direction of bias differs by population. Postpartum, the scanner systematically underestimated catheterised volume (median difference 42.7 mL; underestimation in 82.9% of 70 women) and was significantly less accurate at BMI ≥30. In 73 critically ill adults with low urine output, mean bias was near zero overall (−1.3 mL for 2D ultrasound, +3.3 mL for bladder scanning vs catheter), but abdominal fluid (present in 28%) degraded scanner decisions at low volumes while scanning outperformed horizontal ultrasound at catheter volumes ≥300 mL. In 70 women with stage ≥II prolapse, mean PVR differences were small and non-significant (5.94 mL initial, 1.37 mL final), but stage III/IV prolapse increased scanner error. Postoperatively after radical hysterectomy, the named tested device (BladderScan BVI 9400) correlated r = 0.89 with catheter volume and gave 90.0% overall accuracy for the re-catheterisation decision at the 100 mL cut-off. Patient N (70–73 per study) prints, not paired-measurement counts alone. This is a measurement-accuracy shelf: no card claims scanner-guided catheterisation policies improve outcomes.
stamp: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — measurement accuracy setting-dependent: the scanner systematically underestimated postpartum (median 42.7 mL; worse at BMI ≥30), showed near-zero mean bias in critical care with decision errors concentrated where abdominal fluid met low volumes, agreed closely on post-void residual in prolapse except at stage III/IV, and correlated r = 0.89 with catheter volume for the named BladderScan BVI 9400 postoperatively; no pooled bias figure — direction of bias differs by population; a measurement-accuracy stamp, not a treatment stamp

title: SARC-F sarcopenia screening (3 syntheses, overlapping primary sets): pooled sensitivity only 0.21–0.39 against most reference definitions beside specificity 86–91% — a negative SARC-F misses most sarcopenia; Ishii (79%) and MSRA (82%) were more sensitive
question: In older adults, how accurate is the SARC-F questionnaire (five self-reported items; score ≥4 screens positive) as a bedside / clinic screen for sarcopenia — what pooled sensitivity and specificity does it deliver against the EWGSOP, AWGS, IWGS and FNIH reference definitions, and how does it compare with the other screening instruments (Ishii score, MSRA) in head-to-head synthesis? (This shelf rests on 3 syntheses with overlapping primary-study sets, counted as 3 syntheses on its face.)
balance: SCREENING PERFORMANCE — the sensitivity failure is the headline, printed as 3 syntheses, never as independent-cohort support. This shelf rests on three meta-analyses / systematic reviews whose primary-study sets overlap; the count is 3 syntheses, not 3 independent cohorts. Against EWGSOP, pooled SARC-F sensitivity was 0.21 (specificity 0.90) in the 2018 synthesis of 7 studies / 12,800 subjects, and 32% in the 2021 diagnostic meta-analysis of 20 studies — which also showed how criterion-dependent the estimate is (EWGSOP2 77%, AWGS 27%, IWGS 39%, FNIH 35%, specificities 63–91%). The 2023 head-to-head synthesis of five screening tools (42 studies) found SARC-F specificity 87% but the Ishii score combining sensitivity 79% with the best negative likelihood ratio (relative, 0.25) and MSRA reaching sensitivity 82% — SARC-F was not the most sensitive instrument. A negative SARC-F misses most sarcopenia against most criteria and must never be presented as a rule-out test. Pooled figures are criterion-specific and are never merged into one accuracy pair. No grip-strength data is carded on this shelf. This is a screening-accuracy shelf: no card claims SARC-F-triggered pathways improve outcomes.
stamp: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — NOT ESTABLISHED as a rule-out screen (3 syntheses, overlapping primary sets, counted as syntheses only): pooled SARC-F sensitivity was 0.21 against EWGSOP and 27–39% against AWGS / IWGS / FNIH, beside specificities of 86–91%, and the Ishii score (79%) and MSRA (82%) were more sensitive in head-to-head synthesis; a screening-accuracy stamp, not a treatment stamp

title: Viscoelastic test reference ranges (TEG / ROTEM) in healthy adults: population-derived ranges sit far from manufacturers' ranges (up to 74% of healthy volunteers outside on at least one parameter), with sex, age and native-vs-citrated differences throughout
question: In healthy adults, what are the reference ranges for whole-blood viscoelastic clotting tests — thromboelastography (TEG) and rotational thromboelastometry (ROTEM) — how far do population-derived ranges sit from the manufacturers' ranges, how do the ranges differ by sex, age and population, and how much do native vs citrated-recalcified samples move the ROTEM values? (Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall / Boron & Boulpaep haemostasis sections — framing only; the shelf rests chiefly on the primary datasets carded.)
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — reference ranges for whole-blood viscoelastic tests rest on 6 independent populations (4 TEG, 2 ROTEM), counted per modality and never merged. Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall and Boron & Boulpaep, haemostasis sections — framing only; this shelf rests chiefly on the primary reference literature, and says so. Population-derived TEG ranges sit materially apart from the manufacturers' ranges: the manufacturer's ranges would have labelled 8.5% of 118 healthy Brazilian volunteers coagulopathic (specificity 81%), 74% of 200 North Indian volunteers had at least one value outside the manufacturer's range, and about 40% of a second Indian sample (120 volunteers, including 33 children) fell outside at least one manufacturer range — three different comparisons (diagnosis-level vs any-parameter), each printed with its own definition. Sex differences recur (women more hypercoagulable in the Brazilian and Beijing datasets). For ROTEM, native-blood (NATEM) clotting time, α-angle and maximum clot firmness correlated with age in 132 healthy adults; and recalcification itself moves the values — TRUE-NATEM clotting time 872–1595 s vs NATEM 757–1327 s in a dataset whose volunteer N is not documented in its abstract, labelled as such. Activator and sample handling (citrated kaolin vs native) print on every card.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — whole-blood viscoelastic reference ranges are established in 6 independent populations (4 TEG, 2 ROTEM, counted per modality and never merged), and are population-, sex- and sample-handling-specific: manufacturers' ranges misclassify healthy volunteers (8.5% diagnosis-level in Brazil; 74% any-parameter in North India), and recalcification alone shifts ROTEM values (TRUE-NATEM CT 872–1595 s vs NATEM 757–1327 s; that dataset's N is not documented)

title: Reticulocyte-profile reference intervals in healthy adults: intervals are platform-specific — reticulocyte haemoglobin content 22.84–29.70 pg on the Mindray BC-6200 vs 29.95–35.12 pg in Chengdu and 30.9–35.7 pg on the BC-6800, across 4 independent populations
question: In healthy adults, what are the reference intervals for the reticulocyte profile — absolute reticulocyte count, reticulocyte percentage, immature reticulocyte fraction, reticulocyte haemoglobin content / equivalent (CHr / Ret-He / RHE) and mean reticulocyte volume — how far apart do the intervals sit between analyser platforms (Beckman Coulter DxH, Sysmex, Mindray) and populations, and which parameters need sex partitioning? (Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, red-cell / erythropoiesis sections — framing only; the shelf rests chiefly on the primary datasets carded.)
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — reticulocyte-profile reference intervals rest on 4 independent populations, and platform is the content: no haemoglobin-content figure prints without its analyser. Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, red-cell / erythropoiesis sections — framing only; this shelf rests chiefly on the primary reference literature, and says so. The Madrid dataset (175 healthy adults, Beckman Coulter DxH 900) established intervals for 14 reticulocyte-profile parameters per CLSI EP28-A3c, with sex partitioning required for two derived parameters (low haemoglobin density, microcytic anaemia factor) but not the core reticulocyte measures; its abstract does not print the numeric intervals, and none are invented here. The Chengdu dataset (691 healthy Han adults) gives reticulocyte haemoglobin content 29.95–35.12 pg (men) and 29.77–34.52 pg (women), mean reticulocyte volume 99.76–115.97 fL (men) and 98.72–113.83 fL (women), and reticulocyte percentage 0.485–1.504%. The Mindray BC-6800 dataset (184 healthy adults) gives reticulocytes 23.2–93.2 ×10⁹/L and haemoglobin equivalent 30.9–35.7 pg, with the Sysmex XE-5000 comparison showing a different upper count limit (101.3 vs 93.2 ×10⁹/L). The Thai BC-6200 dataset — the smallest, N = 60, printed on the face — gives a haemoglobin-content interval of 22.84–29.70 pg, well below the Chengdu and BC-6800 intervals on other platforms. Counts print in ×10⁹/L as in the records.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — reticulocyte-profile reference intervals are established in 4 independent populations and are platform-specific: reticulocyte haemoglobin content runs 29.95–35.12 pg (Chengdu, men) and 30.9–35.7 pg (Mindray BC-6800) but only 22.84–29.70 pg on the Mindray BC-6200 (N = 60), and sex partitioning is needed only for selected derived parameters (DxH 900 dataset)

title: Tolrestat for diabetic neuropathy: a surrogate-led 1990s programme — conduction, reflex and vibration gains and a paraesthetic-symptom signal across five reports, inside a class whose Cochrane synthesis was null overall (SMD −0.25, 95% CI −0.56 to 0.05)
question: In adults with diabetic peripheral (sensorimotor and autonomic) neuropathy, does the aldose reductase inhibitor tolrestat (200 mg/day), compared with placebo, improve neuropathic symptoms, nerve conduction or autonomic function?
balance: A surrogate-heavy 1990s programme — the surrogates lead. Five reports of tolrestat 200 mg/day (analysis sets from 45 to 372 patients, plus a labelled single-centre report with no centre N in its abstract) show improvement or non-deterioration on nerve conduction velocities, cardiovascular reflex tests and vibration thresholds, a withdrawal trial in which stopping long-term tolrestat led to deterioration, and one symptom signal confined to paraesthetic symptoms — painful symptoms improved equally on placebo in the largest trial. The class-level Cochrane synthesis of 32 aldose reductase inhibitor trials found no overall significant difference in neurological function (standardised mean difference −0.25, 95% CI −0.56 to 0.05), with a tolrestat subgroup favouring treatment; that null class context is part of this shelf's balance, and the concordant-responder analysis (28% vs 5%) is not a patient-important outcome. The withdrawal trial randomised patients after a mean 4.2 years of open treatment, enriching for tolerators and responders.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit on nerve-function surrogates) — tolrestat 200 mg/day improved conduction, reflex and vibration measures and paraesthetic (not painful) symptoms across five 1990s reports, but the Cochrane class synthesis of 32 aldose reductase inhibitor trials was null overall (SMD −0.25, 95% CI −0.56 to 0.05)

title: Ponalrestat for diabetic neuropathy: a uniformly negative programme — four randomised trials totalling 423 patients found no significant benefit on symptoms, conduction or autonomic measures
question: In adults with chronic symptomatic diabetic peripheral neuropathy, does the aldose reductase inhibitor ponalrestat (600 mg/day), compared with placebo, improve symptoms, nerve conduction or autonomic function?
balance: A uniformly negative programme — the nulls lead, in full. Four randomised placebo-controlled reports of ponalrestat 600 mg/day totalling 423 patients (259 over 18 months; 50 and 60 over one year; 54 over 24 weeks at 300/600 mg) found no significant benefit on any prespecified symptom, conduction, vibration, thermal or autonomic measure. The single positive signal is one autonomic subgroup in the largest trial (patients with an abnormal 30:15 ratio on ponalrestat did not deteriorate on that test while placebo patients did; n = 84). Ponalrestat was never marketed. This shelf records the aldose reductase class's negative pole beside tolrestat (pack #7759) and sorbinil; no benefit is claimed.
stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — ponalrestat 600 mg/day showed no significant benefit on any prespecified symptom or electrophysiological measure in four randomised trials totalling 423 patients; the only positive signal is one autonomic subgroup in the largest trial

title: Oxcarbazepine for painful diabetic neuropathy: a split base — the small titrated trial was positive (pain −24.3 vs −14.7), while the two larger trials missed their primary endpoints at every dose
question: In adults with painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy, does oxcarbazepine (600–1,800 mg/day), compared with placebo, reduce neuropathic pain?
balance: A split base — the split leads. Three 16-week placebo-controlled trials totalling 634 patients disagree on their primary endpoints: the smallest (N = 146), which titrated oxcarbazepine 300→1,800 mg/day to effect, was positive (visual-analogue pain −24.3 vs −14.7, p = 0.01; >50% reduction 35.2% vs 18.4%); the fixed-dose 1,200 mg/day trial (N = 141) found no significant difference; and the dose-ranging trial (N = 347) found no difference at 600, 1,200 or 1,800 mg/day on its primary endpoint, with significant differences only in a secondary whole-phase analysis at the two higher doses. Any benefit appears dose-dependent at 1,200–1,800 mg/day, doses at which the carbamazepine family's tolerability burden matters; the fetched abstracts report adverse events as mostly mild-to-moderate and titration-phase, and nothing here supports a cleaner record than 16-week trials show.
stamp: SPLIT — the smallest, titrated-dose trial was positive on its primary endpoint (pain −24.3 vs −14.7, p = 0.01), but the two larger trials (fixed 1,200 mg/day, and dose-ranging 600–1,800 mg/day) both missed their primary endpoints, with positive findings only in a secondary whole-phase analysis at 1,200–1,800 mg/day

title: Lamotrigine for painful diabetic neuropathy: inconsistent at scale — a strongly positive 59-patient trial, then a 720-patient replicate programme positive in one study only at 400 mg
question: In adults with painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy, does lamotrigine (200–400 mg/day), compared with placebo or amitriptyline, reduce neuropathic pain?
balance: Inconsistent at scale — the inconsistency leads. The 59-patient placebo trial was strongly positive (pain 6.4→4.2 vs 6.5→5.3, p < 0.001), but the adequately powered replicate programme — two studies of 360 patients each in a single report — found a lamotrigine 400 mg effect on the week-19 primary endpoint in Study 2 only (−2.7 vs −1.6, p ≤ 0.05), not replicated in Study 1, with 200 and 300 mg null in both studies; the authors themselves conclude lamotrigine was inconsistently effective. A 53-patient crossover against amitriptyline found no significant difference between treatments. Rash recurs in both the replicate programme (adverse events 71–82% on lamotrigine vs 63–70% on placebo; headache and rash commonest) and the crossover (rash in 7%), and lamotrigine's slow titration requirement applies. The crossover's preferred dose (25 mg twice daily) is far below the placebo-tested doses and the two findings are not merged into a dose claim here.
stamp: SPLIT — a 59-patient trial was strongly positive, but the 720-patient replicate programme found a 400 mg effect in one study and not the other (200 and 300 mg null in both), and a crossover trial found no significant difference from amitriptyline; the authors call lamotrigine inconsistently effective

title: Tramadol for painful diabetic neuropathy: pain reduced over 42–66 days in two placebo-controlled trials (444 patients) — an opioid-class agent on short double-blind evidence, with only an open extension beyond that
question: In adults with painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy, does tramadol (alone or as the fixed tramadol/acetaminophen combination), compared with placebo, reduce neuropathic pain?
balance: An opioid-class agent on short double-blind evidence — the class flag leads. Two placebo-controlled trials totalling 444 patients show tramadol reduces diabetic neuropathic pain over 42 days (monotherapy, average 210 mg/day, p < 0.001 on mean pain intensity) and 66 days (tramadol/acetaminophen combination, pain −2.71 vs −1.83, p = 0.001); an open extension of the monotherapy trial's completers shows maintenance to 6 months without a control group. The combination trial had no tramadol-alone or acetaminophen-alone arm, so it cannot isolate tramadol's contribution. Tramadol's dependence, hyponatraemia and falls record is homed at pack #5874 and is cross-pointed here; 6-week efficacy is not a long-term benefit–harm balance.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit, short-term only) — tramadol beat placebo over 42 days as monotherapy (p < 0.001) and over 66 days as the tramadol/acetaminophen combination (−2.71 vs −1.83, p = 0.001, a combination result that cannot isolate tramadol); an opioid-class agent whose long-term benefit–harm balance this base does not establish (harm shelf: pack #5874)

title: Tapentadol ER for painful diabetic neuropathy: maintenance of relief in enriched responders in both phase 3 randomised-withdrawal trials (differences −1.3 and −0.95 points; pooled −1.14) — not an all-comer effect
question: In adults with chronic painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy, does tapentadol extended release (100–250 mg twice daily), compared with placebo in an enriched-enrollment randomised-withdrawal design, maintain pain relief?
balance: An enriched-enrollment randomised-withdrawal base — the design flag leads. The corrected base is three reports: both individual phase 3 trials (395 and 318 patients randomised after open-label titration) plus their pooled analysis of the same patients. In both trials, patients who had already responded to open-label tapentadol ER (100–250 mg twice daily) and were then randomised to continue it worsened less than patients withdrawn to placebo (least-squares mean differences −1.3 and −0.95 points; pooled −1.14, 95% CI −1.435 to −0.838). These are maintenance effects in responders, not all-comer treatment effects, and the placebo worsening is withdrawal in responders. Tapentadol is an opioid: nausea in 21.1% and vomiting in 12.7% during maintenance in trial 2, and treatment-emergent adverse events in 74.7% vs 56.0% in the pooled maintenance data; its other homed question (vs oxycodone in low back pain) is pack #5723.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit — maintenance in enriched responders only) — in both phase 3 randomised-withdrawal trials, patients who had already responded to open-label tapentadol ER worsened less on continued treatment than on withdrawal to placebo (differences −1.3 and −0.95 points; pooled −1.14); an opioid, with nausea 21.1% and vomiting 12.7% in maintenance

title: Methylcobalamin for diabetic neuropathy: exactly one placebo-controlled trial (N = 90, B12-low metformin users) — the rest of the base is dose, route and combination comparisons without placebo, with monotherapy the weakest arm head-to-head
question: In adults with diabetic peripheral neuropathy (largely with low vitamin B12 status), does oral methylcobalamin (vitamin B12), compared with placebo, a different B12 dose or route, or combination therapy, improve neuropathy symptoms, signs or nerve function?
balance: Exactly one placebo-controlled trial — the composition leads. The base is four reports plus a supporting synthesis, but the placebo contrast rests on a single 90-patient, 1-year trial in metformin-treated patients selected for B12 < 400 pmol/L, which was positive across neurophysiological, sudomotor, pain and quality-of-life measures. The other three reports have no placebo group: a dose comparison (1,000 vs 2,000 µg/day, both arms improved, no between-dose difference, likewise B12-low patients only), an open-label comparison in which methylcobalamin alone was by far the weakest arm (pain fall 0.58 vs ~4 points for the pregabalin and duloxetine combinations), and a route comparison on a corneal-microscopy surrogate (32 completers). The supporting meta-analysis found mecobalamin alone not effective on pain or symptom outcomes across a mostly high-risk-of-bias literature. Nothing in this base estimates an effect in B12-replete diabetic neuropathy, and no wording here generalises beyond B12-low populations.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — exactly one placebo-controlled trial (N = 90, B12-low metformin users, positive) supports methylcobalamin in diabetic neuropathy; the rest of the base is dose, route and combination comparisons without placebo, in which monotherapy was the weakest arm — never '≥3 placebo-controlled RCTs'

title: Fidarestat for diabetic neuropathy — FLOOR-RISK, exactly 1 report (N = 279): a single 52-week trial with two of eight conduction measures better than placebo and a uniformly significant symptom battery; carded as four labelled slices of that one report
question: In adults with diabetic peripheral neuropathy, does the aldose reductase inhibitor fidarestat (1 mg/day), compared with placebo, improve nerve conduction or subjective symptoms over 52 weeks?
balance: FLOOR-RISK: the entire clinical base is exactly 1 report — the count leads. One 52-week multicentre placebo-controlled trial (Hotta 2001, 279 patients, fidarestat 1 mg/day) found five of eight electrophysiological measures improved from baseline on fidarestat (two of eight significantly better than placebo at study end: median F-wave conduction velocity and minimal latency), a subjective-symptom battery uniformly significant vs placebo, and an adverse-event profile not differing significantly from placebo. This shelf cards that single report as four labelled slices (design, electrophysiology, symptoms, tolerability/context) to meet the format without inflating the count: the report count is 1. One unreplicated trial from a single-region programme, for a drug never marketed, rowed deliberately under slate 21's explicit invitation to complete the aldose reductase class shelf — it contracts back to the audit record if the developer declines.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — FLOOR-RISK: based on exactly 1 report, N = 279 (Hotta 2001): two of eight electrophysiological measures significantly better than placebo at 52 weeks and a uniformly significant symptom battery, from a single unreplicated trial of a never-marketed drug

title: Agalsidase alfa and beta in Fabry disease: a 123-patient placebo-controlled base across two products — pain and cardiac-mass signals for alfa, and a beta event trial whose primary analysis missed significance (HR 0.47, P = 0.06)
question: In children and adults with Fabry disease, does enzyme replacement therapy with agalsidase alfa or agalsidase beta, compared with placebo, improve neuropathic pain, kidney function, cardiac mass or clinical-event outcomes?
balance: A small, old, two-product base — the counts lead. The placebo-controlled evidence for agalsidase itself is 123 patients across three trials of two different products (alfa 0.2 mg/kg; beta 1 mg/kg) that have never been compared head-to-head in this base: alfa reduced neuropathic pain and improved biopsy/creatinine-clearance measures in 26 men (inulin clearance null), alfa reduced MRI left ventricular mass in 15 men (myocardial substrate change null), and beta's clinical-event trial — the only event-outcome trial — missed significance on its primary intention-to-treat analysis (hazard ratio 0.47, 95% CI 0.21 to 1.03, P = 0.06, a relative measure; absolute events 27% vs 42%), with the protocol-adherent analysis significant (HR 0.39, P = 0.034). Both analyses are printed on the face. Product names are given exactly as the publications give them — clarification, not promotion.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — agalsidase alfa improved pain (N = 26) and MRI left ventricular mass (N = 15) in small placebo-controlled trials, and agalsidase beta's event trial gave HR 0.47 (95% CI 0.21 to 1.03; P = 0.06, relative; events 27% vs 42%) on its primary intention-to-treat analysis — not significant — with a significant protocol-adherent analysis (HR 0.39); two products, 123 patients, never compared head-to-head in this base

title: Atidarsagene autotemcel for early-onset metachromatic leukodystrophy: one programme, three reports, no concurrent control — survival free from severe motor impairment 100% vs 0% at age 6 (pre-symptomatic late-infantile) against natural-history cohorts
question: In children with early-onset metachromatic leukodystrophy, does atidarsagene autotemcel (arsa-cel; autologous lentiviral haematopoietic stem-cell gene therapy), compared with untreated natural-history controls, preserve motor function and survival?
balance: One programme, three reports — and no randomised or concurrent control exists anywhere in the base; the flag leads. Atidarsagene autotemcel (arsa-cel; autologous lentiviral haematopoietic stem-cell gene therapy) was given to 39 children with early-onset metachromatic leukodystrophy across two open-label studies and expanded access (the 2022 report's 29 are inside that 39), compared throughout with non-concurrent untreated natural-history cohorts. Survival free from severe motor impairment was 100% vs 0% at age 6 in pre-symptomatic late-infantile disease, and 87.5% / 80.0% vs 11.2% at age 10 in early-juvenile disease — dramatic differences that carry the full bias risk of historical comparison in a disease whose ascertainment has changed, with very wide early-juvenile confidence intervals (38.7 to 98.1). Benefit is concentrated in children treated pre-symptomatically. Treatment requires busulfan conditioning, with febrile neutropenia the commonest severe adverse event; no insertional oncogenesis was observed. The product is named as the publications give it — clarification, not promotion.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit — one programme, no randomised or concurrent control) — in the programme's long-term report (39 treated vs 49 untreated natural-history patients), survival free from severe motor impairment was 100% vs 0% at age 6 in pre-symptomatic late-infantile disease and 87.5% / 80.0% vs 11.2% at age 10 in early-juvenile disease, with benefit concentrated in pre-symptomatic treatment and busulfan conditioning required
