title: Elivaldogene autotemcel (eli-cel) for early cerebral adrenoleukodystrophy: most boys remained free of major functional disability at 6 years in a single-group programme — and 7 of 67 developed haematologic cancer
question: In boys with early cerebral adrenoleukodystrophy, does elivaldogene autotemcel (eli-cel; autologous lentiviral haematopoietic stem-cell gene therapy), compared with the untreated course of disease, preserve neurologic function and survival — and at what haematologic-malignancy risk? (GAP-T: one programme, three reports — the ALD-102 interim and full reports are the same study, labelled; no randomised or concurrent control exists in this base; haematologic cancer in 7 of 67 treated patients is load-bearing on the face.)
balance: GAP-T — one programme, three reports, labelled: this shelf rests on one programme's reports (the ALD-102 interim report, the ALD-102 full report — the same study, never counted as two studies — and a haematologic-cancer safety report across ALD-102 and ALD-104). NO randomised or concurrent control exists anywhere in this base; every efficacy contrast is against the untreated course of disease, so the survival-without-disability figures carry the full bias risk of non-concurrent comparison. The harm report is load-bearing: haematologic cancer developed in 7 of 67 treated patients (myelodysplastic syndrome in 6, acute myeloid leukaemia in 1), with lentiviral vector insertions at MECOM-EVI1 in 5 of the 6 patients with data. The 2017 interim report's 'no treatment-related death' must never be quoted without the 2024 cancer report beside it. Per the standing product-naming rule the tested product is named for clarification, not promotion: elivaldogene autotemcel (eli-cel; autologous CD34+ cells transduced with the Lenti-D lentiviral vector). ALD-104 contributes patients to the safety denominator only; its efficacy is not separately reported and none is claimed.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit, with a load-bearing malignancy harm) — one programme with no concurrent control: 81% of 32 ALD-102 patients had no major functional disabilities at a median 6 years, while haematologic cancer developed in 7 of 67 treated patients across the programme

title: Cysteamine eye drops for corneal cystinosis: standard drops clear crystals and viscous 0.55% drops clear them faster — on small samples of 29, 16 and 31 patients
question: In patients with nephropathic cystinosis, do cysteamine eye drops, compared with placebo (fellow eye) or with a standard cysteamine formulation, clear corneal cystine crystals and reduce photophobia? (GAP-T: small-N formulation-comparison base — Ns 29 / 16 / 31 printed on the face; the only placebo-controlled evidence is the 1990 paired-eye trial.)
balance: GAP-T — small-N formulation-comparison base, labelled: the three reports enrol 29, 16 (efficacy study) and 31 patients, and the counts lead. The only placebo-controlled evidence is the 1990 paired-eye trial (10 clear responders of 29 entered); the other two reports compare formulations against each other, so this base shows standard cysteamine drops clear corneal crystals and a viscous formulation clears them faster — it does not contain a modern parallel-group placebo trial. Corneal crystal density is a surrogate for the visual outcomes patients care about; photophobia, improved in the viscous trial, is the only patient-felt endpoint in the base. Per the standing product-naming rule the tested formulations are named as the publications give them, for clarification not promotion: standard cysteamine hydrochloride 0.10% drops and viscous cysteamine hydrochloride 0.55% drops. title: Denufosol for cystic fibrosis lung disease: a borderline 24-week FEV1 positive followed by a fully null 48-week phase 3 in 466 patients

title: Enfortumab vedotin vs chemotherapy in previously treated advanced urothelial carcinoma (EV-301, one trial, N = 608): overall survival 12.88 vs 8.97 months (relative HR 0.70), maintained at 2 years — priced in skin reactions (47.3%) and neuropathy (48.0%)
question: In adults with locally advanced or metastatic urothelial carcinoma previously treated with platinum chemotherapy and a PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitor, does enfortumab vedotin monotherapy improve overall survival versus investigator-chosen chemotherapy — and does the benefit hold at 2 years, in the Japanese subgroup, and in patient-reported outcomes? (EV-301; four reports, ONE trial.)
balance: One phase 3 trial, four reports — labelled as such throughout, never pooled with the first-line combination question homed at live #859. EV-301 randomised 608 previously treated patients: enfortumab vedotin prolonged overall survival (median 12.88 vs 8.97 months; HR for death 0.70, a relative measure) and progression-free survival (5.55 vs 3.71 months; HR 0.62), and the benefit held at a median 23.75 months (HR 0.70, 0.58–0.85; 444 deaths). Quality of life was maintained, pain improved more and appetite loss worsened more than on chemotherapy, and the Japanese subgroup (N = 86, supportive only) was consistent. The trial was open-label and the comparator was single-agent docetaxel, paclitaxel or vinflunine — both facts print on the face. The pricing harms are skin reactions (treatment-related skin reactions in 47.3% vs 15.8%) and peripheral neuropathy (48.0% vs 31.6%), against cytopenias commoner on chemotherapy.
stamp: LIKELY (benefit) — one phase 3 trial (EV-301, N = 608; four reports, one trial): overall survival 12.88 vs 8.97 months (relative HR 0.70) maintained at ~2 years, against an open-label single-agent chemotherapy comparator, priced in skin reactions (47.3%) and peripheral neuropathy (48.0%)

title: Anti-GD2 immunotherapy in high-risk neuroblastoma: ANBL0032 — dinutuximab + cytokines vs isotretinoin alone improved 5-year survival (73.2% vs 56.6%); HR-NBL1/SIOPEN — adding interleukin-2 to dinutuximab beta gave no benefit (P = 0.76) and more toxicity (two programmes, never pooled)
question: In children with high-risk neuroblastoma who have responded to induction and myeloablative consolidation, does adding anti-GD2 immunotherapy to isotretinoin improve event-free and overall survival (ANBL0032) — and, within the European programme, does adding subcutaneous interleukin-2 to dinutuximab beta improve outcomes or only toxicity (HR-NBL1/SIOPEN)? (Three reports, TWO trials — limbs never pooled.)
balance: Two randomised programmes answering different questions, never pooled. ANBL0032 (N = 226, stopped early for efficacy at 61% of expected events): isotretinoin plus ch14.18 (dinutuximab, SP2/0) with alternating GM-CSF and interleukin-2 beat isotretinoin alone — 2-year event-free survival 66±5% vs 46±5% and, at the load-bearing 5-year follow-up, event-free survival 56.6% vs 46.1% and overall survival 73.2% vs 56.6% — at a severe price: grade 3–5 pain in 52%, capillary leak syndrome in 23% and hypersensitivity reactions in 25%. HR-NBL1/SIOPEN (N = 406): adding subcutaneous interleukin-2 to dinutuximab beta (ch14.18/CHO) gave no evidence of benefit (3-year event-free survival 60% vs 56%, P = 0.76) and plainly more toxicity, with only 62% vs 87% completing allocated treatment. The products are named exactly as the publications give them — US dinutuximab (SP2/0) versus European dinutuximab beta (CHO) — related but not identical, and never silently merged.

title: Gugging Swallowing Screen (GUSS) in acute stroke: sensitivity 96.5–100% at the 14-point cut-off but specificity only 50–69% — collapsing to 20% in severe stroke, with nasogastric feeding overestimated; GUSS-ICU adaptation AUC 0.923 after extubation (N = 45)
question: In acute stroke (and, in its ICU adaptation, in recently extubated patients), how accurately does the Gugging Swallowing Screen (GUSS — a graded bedside screen scoring saliva, semisolid, liquid and solid swallowing in sequence, 0–20 points, with diet recommendations by score band) detect aspiration and dysphagia against fiberoptic endoscopic evaluation of swallowing (FEES) — what sensitivity and specificity did its derivation study and its independent revalidation deliver at the 14-point cut-off, how do they collapse in severe stroke, and what pooled accuracy does the systematic review find?
balance: A screening-accuracy shelf, not a treatment shelf: no card implies GUSS-guided diet pathways improve pneumonia or mortality. The GUSS (graded saliva/semisolid/liquid/solid sequence, 0–20 points) was derived by its originators in 50 acute-stroke patients (samples of 20 and 30 — Ns on the face) with sensitivity 100% and specificity 50–69% at the 14-point cut-off against FEES, and independently revalidated in 100 patients at sensitivity 96.5% / specificity 55.8% — splitting by severity to 71.4% / 88.8% in NIHSS <5 and 100% / 20% in NIHSS ≥15, with diet recommendations more conservative than FEES and nasogastric feeding overestimated. The systematic review (8 studies, a synthesis overlapping the primaries) pools sensitivity at 0.97 and specificity at 0.67. The GUSS-ICU adaptation (45 post-extubation patients, a modified instrument, never pooled with the stroke figures) gave AUC 0.923. Specificity is the weak limb throughout, and its false-positive cost — over-restricted diets and excess tube feeding — prints beside the sensitivity headline.
stamp: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — sensitivity established, specificity weak (GAP-E): at the 14-point cut-off, sensitivity 96.5–100% across derivation, revalidation and pooled synthesis (0.97) beside specificity 50–69% (pooled 0.67) collapsing to 20% in NIHSS ≥15, where nasogastric feeding is overestimated; a screening-accuracy stamp, not a treatment stamp

title: Peripheral thermometry vs core temperature in adults: 3 overlapping syntheses (labelled as syntheses, never independent cohorts) — limits of agreement beyond the acceptable ±0.5 °C, fever-detection sensitivity only 64%, and only oesophageal measurement clinically acceptable in ICU
question: At the bedside, how accurately do peripheral thermometers (tympanic membrane, temporal artery, axillary and oral) estimate core body temperature in adults — what are their pooled limits of agreement against central thermometry (pulmonary artery, bladder, oesophageal, rectal), how poor is fever detection, and does any non-invasive method reach clinically acceptable accuracy in intensive care? (Base: 3 syntheses whose primary-study sets overlap — counted as syntheses, never as independent cohorts.)
balance: This shelf rests on 3 syntheses whose primary-study sets overlap — the count prints as 3 syntheses, not 3 independent cohorts, everywhere. The largest (75 studies, 8,682 patients) found pooled 95% limits of agreement outside the pre-defined clinically acceptable ±0.5 °C range — −1.44 °C to 1.46 °C in febrile adults and −2.07 °C to 1.90 °C in hypothermia — with fever-detection sensitivity of only 64% beside specificity of 96%. The adult-ICU synthesis (13 studies, 632 patients, 105,375 measurements) found axillary, tympanic infrared and zero-heat-flux thermometers all underestimated intravascular temperature, only oesophageal measurement was clinically acceptable, and heterogeneity was 99–100%. The oldest, smallest synthesis (3 febrile-ICU studies) is the most favourable — mean differences within ±0.2 °C for most tympanic combinations and the one oral study — and that disagreement between syntheses is content, not noise to be averaged away. No single 'peripheral thermometers are accurate / inaccurate' verdict prints without method, population and the limits-of-agreement framing; no card implies a thermometer-guided pathway improves outcomes.
stamp: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — NOT ESTABLISHED as clinically acceptable (GAP-E): 3 overlapping syntheses, counted as syntheses only — pooled limits of agreement outside ±0.5 °C (febrile adults −1.44 °C to 1.46 °C) and fever-detection sensitivity 64% in the largest synthesis, with only oesophageal measurement clinically acceptable in ICU; a measurement-accuracy stamp, not a treatment stamp

title: Nutrition-risk screening in hospitalised adults (NRS-2002 / MUST / MST / MNA-SF): pooled against SGA — MUST sensitivity 0.84 / specificity 0.85, NRS-2002 0.76 / 0.86 — and NRS-2002's own derivation is trial-level (128 trials sorted by treatment benefit), not patient-level accuracy
question: In hospitalised adults, how valid are the bedside nutrition-risk screening tools — NRS-2002 (Nutritional Risk Screening 2002: impaired nutrition, disease severity, age ≥70), MUST, MST and MNA-SF — against Subjective Global Assessment and ESPEN reference standards: what pooled sensitivity and specificity does each deliver, and what did NRS-2002's derivation (a retrospective analysis of 128 controlled trials) and its prospective hospital validation actually show?
balance: A screening-validity shelf, not a treatment shelf: no card implies screening-triggered nutritional support improves outcomes in screen-positive patients. NRS-2002's derivation (the ESPEN working group's own report, programme-labelled) is trial-level — across 128 controlled trials, support helped in 43 of 75 at-risk-classified trials vs 14 of 53 not-at-risk (P = 0.0006; likelihood ratio 1.7) — and that distinction prints on the face wherever the derivation is quoted. Patient-level validity, pooled in the 2024 synthesis (60 studies, 21 meta-analysed) against Subjective Global Assessment, is moderate: MUST sensitivity 0.84 / specificity 0.85, MST 0.81 / 0.79, NRS-2002 0.76 / 0.86 — MUST, not NRS-2002, had the strongest pooled profile, and this shelf is not an NRS-2002 vindication. Reference standards differ (SGA, ESPEN criteria, clinician assessment) and pooled figures are never merged across them; the single-centre Turkish validation (N = 271, geriatrician reference) found 88% / 92%, well above the pooled NRS-2002 sensitivity, and that gradient prints.
stamp: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — moderate, reference-standard-dependent validity (GAP-E): pooled against SGA, MUST sensitivity 0.84 / specificity 0.85, MST 0.81 / 0.79 and NRS-2002 0.76 / 0.86, with NRS-2002's derivation a trial-level validation only (likelihood ratio 1.7 across 128 trials); a screening-validity stamp, not a treatment stamp

title: MOBID / MOBID-2 pain scale in advanced dementia: total-score reliability good (test–retest ICC 0.81–0.85, smallest detectable change 2.3–3.1 points) and US validity moderate (rho 0.54–0.57 vs expert ratings) — but derivation N = 26 and individual behaviour items unreliable (kappa down to 0.05)
question: In people with advanced dementia who cannot self-report pain, how well does the MOBID / MOBID-2 pain scale (Mobilization-Observation-Behavior-Intensity-Dementia — pain behaviours observed during five standardised guided movements, inferred intensity 0–10) perform — what reliability and validity did its derivation study show, what are MOBID-2's test–retest reliability, measurement error and responsiveness in nursing-home residents, and does the scale hold up in English-speaking US nursing homes?
balance: A measurement shelf, not a treatment shelf. MOBID observes pain behaviour during five standardised guided movements and infers intensity 0–10 for people with advanced dementia who cannot self-report. Its derivation (the originators' own report, programme-labelled) studied only 26 nursing-home patients — N printed on the face — finding α 0.90 and inter-tester ICC 0.70–0.96 for inferred intensity, but kappa 0.05–0.84 across individual behaviour indicators, a weakness that prints beside the strong total-score figures. MOBID-2's test–retest reliability in 352 Norwegian nursing-home patients was ICC 0.81–0.85, with standard error of measurement 1.4–1.9 and smallest detectable change 2.3–3.1 points, and 5 of 6 responsiveness hypotheses confirmed inside that one trial programme's dataset (labelled as such). In 138 US residents, the overall score correlated moderately with expert clinician ratings (rho 0.54 current, 0.57 worst week; α 0.83) and was completable by trained non-clinical staff. The movement-provocation that makes the scale work is also its burden — guided mobilisation and trained raters are required.
stamp: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — measurement reliability established for the total score, validity moderate (GAP-E): MOBID-2 test–retest ICC 0.81–0.85 with smallest detectable change 2.3–3.1 points and US correlations rho 0.54–0.57 against expert ratings, beside a derivation N = 26 and individual-item kappas down to 0.05; a measurement stamp, not a treatment stamp

title: Glasgow Coma Scale reliability between raters: adequate only in good-quality studies (7 of 52 reviewed), 33.1% exact accuracy on standardised vignettes, and high agreement (kappa/ICC 0.85–0.96) only after 19 hours of training — motor is the least reliable component throughout
question: At the bedside, how reliable is the Glasgow Coma Scale (eye, verbal and motor components and their sum) between raters — what does the systematic review of 52 reliability studies find once study quality is accounted for, how accurate is scoring by mixed emergency providers against expert scoring of standardised cases, and what reliability is achievable after standardised training in a high-volume trauma centre?
balance: A measurement-reliability shelf, not a prognostic or treatment shelf: no card converts reliability data into claims about GCS-based triage or intubation thresholds. The three anchors genuinely disagree in register, and the training-dependence is the content. The systematic review of 52 studies found good methodological quality in only 7 (13%); in those, kappa was ≥0.6 in 85% and all ICCs indicated excellent reliability, while poor-quality studies showed lower estimates, and component reliability exceeded sum-score reliability. Mixed emergency providers scored standardised video vignettes with only 33.1% exact total-score accuracy (verbal most accurate at 69.2%, motor least at 59.8%, and 9.2% assigning scores that do not exist) — a vignette figure, printed as such. After a 19-hour standardised training programme, triage and resuscitation nurses reached weighted kappa and ICC 0.85–0.96 with 65.3% exact agreement — and agreement fell in traumatic brain injury and ISS ≥16, where the score matters most. The motor component is the least reliable in both primary studies.
stamp: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — reliability NOT ESTABLISHED as a property of the scale in ordinary practice (GAP-E): adequate in the 7 good-quality studies of 52 reviewed, 33.1% exact accuracy on vignettes, and high agreement only after 19 hours of standardised training, with motor the least consistent component; a measurement-reliability stamp, not a prognostic or treatment stamp

title: Shock index in adult trauma — FLOOR-RISK: exactly 2 syntheses, no third report (~905,000 patients inside them): moderate accuracy for massive transfusion (AUC 0.85) against near-chance mortality discrimination in the larger synthesis (AUC 0.553 vs 0.747 in the smaller)
question: In adult trauma patients at arrival, how accurately does the shock index (heart rate divided by systolic blood pressure) predict massive transfusion and death — what pooled sensitivity, specificity and AUC do the trauma syntheses deliver for each outcome, and how does it compare with the Revised Trauma Score and the (post-resuscitation, anatomical) Injury Severity Score as a mortality predictor? (FLOOR-RISK: basis is exactly 2 syntheses, no third report — printed on the face and carried in the stamp line.)
balance: FLOOR-RISK, per the coordinator's ruling: this shelf's basis is exactly 2 syntheses, no third report — printed here, in the title and in the stamp line. Inside them sit 35 studies / 670,728 patients and 12 studies / 234,129 patients (about 905,000 patients in total, with overlapping primary-study sets — a mass statement, not independent patients). The verdict splits by outcome. For massive transfusion (assessed in the larger synthesis only): pooled sensitivity 0.68, specificity 0.84, AUC 0.85, likelihood ratios 4.24 and 0.39. For mortality the syntheses disagree — AUC 0.553 (near chance; sensitivity 0.358, specificity 0.742) in the larger synthesis vs 0.747 in the smaller — and both sit below the Revised Trauma Score (AUC 0.852) and ISS (0.855) for mortality, with RTS and ISS not significantly different in paired studies (P = 0.91). No single shock-index AUC prints without its outcome and synthesis named; cut-offs vary across primary studies and no universal threshold is printed; no card implies shock-index-triggered transfusion pathways improve outcomes.
stamp: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — split by outcome, on a FLOOR-RISK base of exactly 2 syntheses, no third report (GAP-E): massive transfusion AUC 0.85 (sensitivity 0.68, specificity 0.84) in the larger synthesis, against mortality AUC 0.553 in that synthesis vs 0.747 in the smaller, below RTS (0.852) and ISS (0.855); a prognostic-accuracy stamp, not a treatment stamp

title: Yale Swallow Protocol (3-ounce water swallow challenge): 907 passers ate and drank without overt signs at 12–24 h in the 1,000-patient originators' series (no instrumental comparator), nurses administer it with 98.01% agreement with pathologists, and against videofluoroscopy in TBI (N = 50) sensitivity was 96.8% / specificity 78.9%
question: In hospitalised adults at risk of dysphagia, how well does the Yale Swallow Protocol (a brief cognitive screen and oral-mechanism examination followed by an uninterrupted 3-ounce / 90 cc water swallow challenge; pass = drink the full volume without coughing or wet voice) identify patients who can safely start an oral diet — what happened in the 1,000-patient implementation series, how accurately do trained nurses administer it against speech-language pathologists, and what is its diagnostic accuracy against videofluoroscopy in acute moderate-to-severe traumatic brain injury?
balance: A screening/implementation shelf, not a treatment shelf — and its three reports answer three different questions, never merged. The implementation series (1,000 consecutively referred patients at the originators' own centre, programme-labelled) found all 907 included passers eating and drinking thin liquids without overt signs of dysphagia 12–24 h later (median next-meal liquid volume 340 cc; diet recommendations followed with 100% accuracy) — but the design has no instrumental reference standard, so it cannot support an aspiration-accuracy claim, and that limitation prints on the face. Trained nurses administered the protocol with 98.01% agreement with speech-language pathologists (101 inpatients) — an agreement result, not accuracy against swallowing physiology. Accuracy rests on the TBI study alone (50 patients against videofluoroscopy: sensitivity 96.8%, specificity 78.9%, PPV 88.2%, NPV 93.8%), whose N prints wherever its figures do. Examiner training is part of the intervention in every report, and no figure extends to postoperative patients.
stamp: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — high sensitivity in its one instrumental test, implementation-supported (GAP-E): sensitivity 96.8% / specificity 78.9% against videofluoroscopy in acute moderate-to-severe TBI (N = 50), beside a 1,000-patient implementation series with no instrumental comparator and 98.01% nurse–pathologist administration agreement; a screening-accuracy stamp, not a treatment stamp

title: Urinary albumin excretion reference values in healthy adults (PHYS, 3 datasets, all 1988–1993 RIA/turbidimetric era — era on the face): excretion rate 0.6–10.6 µg/min (≈0.9–15 mg/day), daytime higher than overnight, high within-person variability; third dataset mixed ages 6–39, flagged
question: In healthy adults, what are the reference values for urinary albumin excretion — the distribution and upper reference range for overnight albumin excretion rate, the albumin/creatinine ratio and first-morning urine albumin concentration — how much higher is excretion in daytime ambulant than overnight recumbent samples, how large is within-person variability on repeat measurement, and how do the reference values shift across age and sex in the years around puberty? (Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, glomerular filtration / tubular handling sections — framing only; the shelf rests chiefly on the primary datasets carded. Datasets: 3 independent populations, all 1988–1993 radioimmunoassay / turbidimetric era — the era prints on the face.)
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — no intervention stamp applies. Three independent datasets, all 1988–1993 radioimmunoassay / turbidimetric era — the era prints on the face, because all three predate modern immunoturbidimetric/HPLC albumin assays and creatinine standardisation, and no figure may be printed as a current-assay reference interval without the assay era beside it. Watts 1988 (127 healthy normotensive adults) derived reference values for concentration, albumin/creatinine ratio (mg/mmol) and excretion rate (µg/min): distributions positively skewed, Gaussian after log transformation, excretion significantly higher in daytime ambulant than overnight recumbent samples (P < 0.001), and within-person variability on repeat measurement high and comparable across all three expressions. Giampietro 1988 (122 healthy subjects; the paper's 145 diabetic patients are not counted) gives the healthy excretion-rate range 0.6–10.6 µg/min (≈0.9–15 mg/day). Yokoyama 1993 (2,990 healthy individuals aged 6–39 — a mixed child–adult dataset, flagged on the face; only its 17–39 bands are adult data) gives first-morning concentration by age and sex: 1.3–2.2 mg/dL at ages 6–11, rising through puberty with significant sex differences at 12–14, then falling after 17 to 3.3 mg/dL (females) and 2.9 mg/dL (males); its one internally inconsistent abstract figure is omitted at build, per the row. The three expressions are never merged into one range. Textbook framing (Guyton & Hall) is framing only; the shelf rests on these datasets.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED for the adult overnight excretion-rate range (0.6–10.6 µg/min, ≈0.9–15 mg/day, 1988 radioimmunoassay) / EMERGING for any age-curve claim, which rests on one mixed-age (6–39 years) dataset — 3 datasets, all 1988–1993 RIA/turbidimetric era, expressions never merged

title: Venlafaxine for painful diabetic neuropathy — composition on the face: only 1 of 3 reports is a placebo-controlled DPN trial, and its benefit is confined to 150–225 mg/day
question: In adults with painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy, does venlafaxine (75–225 mg/day), compared with placebo, imipramine or pregabalin/carbamazepine, reduce neuropathic pain?
balance: Composition first: of the 3 reports carded, only ONE is a placebo-controlled trial in diabetic neuropathy — Rowbotham 2004 (N = 244, 6 weeks), where pain fell 50% on venlafaxine extended-release 150–225 mg/day vs 27% on placebo (P < 0.001; NNT 4.5 for 50% pain reduction), while 75 mg was near-placebo (32% vs 27%). The second DPN report (Razazian 2014, N = 257) has no placebo group and ranked venlafaxine last of three active drugs (pregabalin more efficacious; no significant superiority between carbamazepine and venlafaxine). The third report (Sindrup 2003) is a mixed-aetiology polyneuropathy crossover — not diabetes-specific — in which venlafaxine matched imipramine. Seven patients on venlafaxine in the placebo-controlled trial had clinically important ECG changes. Cross-points only: venlafaxine's hot-flush shelf (#1788) and the homed DPN agents (duloxetine pathway #3522, capsaicin 8% patch #2697, mirogabalin #2031) ask different questions and share no anchors with this shelf.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit at 150–225 mg/day only) — composition on the face: only 1 of 3 reports is a placebo-controlled DPN trial (N = 244, 6 weeks); the second DPN report has no placebo group and the third is a mixed-aetiology polyneuropathy crossover (29 completers)

title: Sodium valproate for painful diabetic neuropathy — one programme, three reports: pain scores improved in both placebo-controlled trials, nerve conduction never did, and there is no independent replication
question: In adults with painful diabetic neuropathy, does sodium valproate, compared with placebo (alone or in a factorial combination with glyceryl trinitrate spray), reduce neuropathic pain?
balance: Provenance first: all 3 reports come from one research group in one country, enrol 43–83 patients each and run 1–3 months — there is no independent replication anywhere in this base. Both placebo-controlled trials (Kochar 2002, 52 analysed, 1 month; Kochar 2004, 43 randomised, 3 months) found significant improvement on subjective pain scores (P < 0.05; p < 0.001) with electrophysiological changes not significant in either. The factorial trial (Agrawal 2009, 83 randomised) gave numbers needed to treat of 7 for valproate, 5 for glyceryl trinitrate spray and 4 for the combination. One patient in each of the first two trials stopped treatment for raised transaminases; valproate's teratogenicity and weight-gain record (homed in the epilepsy/pregnancy shelves) is cross-pointed on the face.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit on subjective pain scores) — one programme only: 3 reports from a single research group with no independent replication; electrophysiology null in both placebo-controlled trials

title: Desipramine for painful diabetic neuropathy — a very-small-N crossover base: 3 reports from 1990–92 totalling 96 assigned patients, none a parallel-group trial
question: In adults with painful diabetic neuropathy, does desipramine, compared with active placebo, clomipramine, amitriptyline or fluoxetine, reduce neuropathic pain?
balance: The counts lead: 3 reports, all 2–6-week crossovers from 1990–92, totalling 96 assigned patients (20 vs active placebo; 19 completers in a three-way crossover; 57 assigned across two studies, of whom 38 form the desipramine comparison) — no parallel-group trial exists in this base. The direction is consistent: 11 of 20 patients reported at least moderate relief on desipramine vs 2 on active placebo (Max 1991); both desipramine and clomipramine beat placebo in the three-way crossover, with three withdrawals for side effects on each drug (Sindrup 1990); and moderate-or-greater relief was 61% on desipramine vs 74% on amitriptyline, 48% on fluoxetine and 41% on placebo, with desipramine and amitriptyline both superior to placebo and not significantly different from each other (Max 1992). The row exists because desipramine is the least anticholinergic/sedating first-generation tricyclic and its founding trials were never agent-checked — not because the base is strong.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — based on a very small N = 96 assigned across 3 crossover reports from 1990–92 (largest desipramine arm 38); no parallel-group trial

title: Capsaicin 0.075% cream/lotion for painful diabetic neuropathy (PARTIAL slice beside the 8%-patch home #2697) — a split base: 1991–92 positives, a null 2019 placebo-controlled trial, and a 300-patient trial with no placebo group
question: In adults with painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy, does low-concentration capsaicin cream/lotion (0.075%), compared with vehicle/placebo or an active topical comparator, reduce neuropathic pain?
balance: PARTIAL slice, stated plainly: pack #2697 asks only the clinic-applied capsaicin 8% patch question in painful DPN (read in full at build); this shelf asks the self-applied 0.075% cream/lotion question, which #2697 does not ask, and borrows none of the patch's evidence. The base is 4 reports — PMID 1737537 is a same-subjects sensory companion of the 22-subject trial, never a fifth report. The split leads: the two positive vehicle-controlled reports are from 1991–92 (22 refractory subjects; and one whose abstract documents no N — N not documented), the only modern placebo-controlled report (2019 crossover, 42 enrolled) was null on every pain measure, and the largest report (300 patients, vs turpentine oil) had no placebo group and showed no between-group difference (p = 0.399).
stamp: SPLIT — two small 1991–92 vehicle-controlled positives (one N not documented) against a null 2019 placebo-controlled crossover and a 300-patient no-placebo comparison; the 8% patch's evidence (pack #2697) is not borrowed

title: Tralokinumab for severe, uncontrolled asthma — one programme, 4 publications covering 5 trials: every primary endpoint was null, and the one positive biomarker subgroup did not replicate
question: In patients with severe, uncontrolled asthma despite inhaled corticosteroids and a long-acting β2-agonist, does subcutaneous tralokinumab 300 mg every 2–4 weeks versus placebo reduce the annual asthma exacerbation rate over 52 weeks, improve lung function and asthma control, or spare oral corticosteroids in patients who require them?
balance: One programme, counted exactly: 4 publications covering 5 randomised trials. The arc is the answer — tralokinumab improved FEV1 modestly and repeatedly but never improved its primary endpoint in any population: asthma control was null in phase 2 (ACQ-6 p = 0.375), exacerbations were null in phase 2b (rate changes 6% and −2% vs placebo — relative measures) and in STRATOS 1 all-comers (7.0% relative reduction, rate ratio 0.93, p = 0.59), the FENO-high subgroup positive in STRATOS 1 (44.0% relative reduction, p = 0.028) did not replicate in STRATOS 2 (15.8%, p = 0.47), and oral-corticosteroid sparing was null in TROPOS (37.62% vs 29.85% dose reduction, p = 0.271). Tralokinumab was never marketed for asthma — the asthma programme was discontinued (it is marketed for atopic dermatitis, homed at pack #1650, cross-point only).
stamp: LIKELY (no benefit) — one programme, 4 publications covering 5 trials: no primary endpoint was met in any trial, and the single positive subgroup failed its prospective replication

title: Losmapimod for COPD — one programme, 3 randomised reports: a biomarker effect (fibrinogen −11%) with no clinical benefit on any endpoint, and an exacerbation trial stopped early for futility
question: In patients with moderate-to-severe COPD, does oral losmapimod versus placebo reduce systemic/airway inflammation (sputum neutrophils, plasma fibrinogen), improve exercise tolerance (6-minute walk distance), or reduce moderate/severe exacerbations?
balance: One programme, counted exactly: 3 publications covering 3 trials. The arc is the answer — losmapimod reduced plasma fibrinogen by 11% (ratio of effect 0.89 [95% CI 0.83–0.96], p = 0.002 — a relative ratio as reported) yet produced no clinical benefit on any endpoint in any trial: sputum neutrophils (its first primary) unchanged, 6-minute walk distance numerically worse than placebo at all three doses (−6.7, −4.7, −3.4 m), and exacerbations numerically more frequent (rate ratio 1.04) in a trial terminated early at a planned interim analysis for low probability of success, with only 24 of 184 randomised subjects completing. Losmapimod (GW856553) was never marketed.
stamp: LIKELY (no clinical benefit demonstrated) — one programme, 3 trials: biomarker effect only; walk distance and exacerbations numerically favoured placebo, and the exacerbation trial was stopped for futility

title: CDP571 for Crohn's disease — the founding anti-TNF programme (5 randomised reports, 1997–2006): short-term response signals, both steroid-sparing primaries missed at their prespecified timepoints
question: In patients with Crohn's disease — moderately active disease, or corticosteroid-dependent disease — does intravenous CDP571 versus placebo induce clinical response or remission, and can it spare corticosteroids without disease flare?
balance: The arc is the answer: CDP571, the engineered humanised anti-TNF antibody that preceded certolizumab pegol, produced a real short-term response signal (week-2 response 45% vs 27%, p = 0.023, in 169 patients; median CDAI 263→167 after a single infusion in 31 patients) that did not hold — the only long-term active-disease primary (week 28, 396 patients) was null (30.4% vs 23.5%, p = 0.102) outside a post-hoc CRP subgroup, and both steroid-sparing trials missed their prespecified primaries (week 36: 29.3% vs 36.7%, p = 0.24, numerically favouring placebo; week 10: p = 0.452, with a secondary week-16 reading). One steroid-sparing report's abstract prints mutually inconsistent Ns (71 treated; arms 39+42; a percentage implying n = 32) — printed unresolved on its card rather than resolved by choice. Era flag: 1997–2006, every endpoint CDAI-based. CDP571 was never marketed.
stamp: SPLIT — short-term (week-2) response signals in active disease, but the long-term primary and both prespecified steroid-sparing primaries were null; programme discontinued, never marketed

title: Saroglitazar for MASLD/MASH — FLOOR-RISK, exactly 2 abstract-verified reports (N = 281): ALT and imaging-fat improvements on surrogate endpoints only, over 16–24 weeks
question: In adults with NAFLD/MASH, does saroglitazar 4 mg daily versus placebo — or versus vitamin E or no treatment — improve alanine aminotransferase, liver fat (MRI-PDFF / controlled attenuation parameter) and liver stiffness over 16–24 weeks?
balance: FLOOR-RISK, stated exactly: exactly 2 abstract-verified randomised reports, total N = 281 — the phase 2 placebo-controlled trial (Gawrieh 2021, N = 106, 16 weeks: ALT −45.8% on 4 mg vs +3.4% on placebo, P < 0.001; MRI-PDFF liver fat −19.7% vs +4.1%) and the open four-arm SVIN trial (Mir 2024, N = 175, 24 weeks, no placebo arm: ALT and CAP improved vs untreated control; liver stiffness improved only in the combination arm). The summary-level proof-of-concept report and the pooled analysis are never counted. Surrogate flag (load-bearing): every endpoint is ALT, imaging fat or elastography stiffness — no verified report has a histologic primary with results in its abstract, and no clinical-outcome data exist. Both verified trials are Indian-population studies of a drug approved in India and not FDA-approved; the diabetes/hypertriglyceridaemia question is homed at pack #6666 (diagnosis-first, cross-point only).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit on surrogate endpoints) — FLOOR-RISK: exactly 2 abstract-verified reports, N = 281; no histologic or clinical-outcome data

title: Anakinra-based combinations vs corticosteroids for severe alcohol-associated hepatitis — FLOOR-RISK, exactly 2 trials (N = 251): the combinations differ and the readings conflict; the larger, later trial found its combination significantly worse than prednisone
question: In adults with severe alcohol-associated hepatitis (MELD >20), does a combination built on the interleukin-1 receptor antagonist anakinra — with zinc, or with pentoxifylline plus zinc — versus corticosteroids improve survival at 90–180 days?
balance: FLOOR-RISK, stated exactly: exactly 2 randomised trials, total 251 participants randomised as reported. Both readings are printed and they conflict: COMB (Szabo 2022, N = 104; anakinra + pentoxifylline + zinc vs methylprednisolone) gave a non-significant 180-day survival trend favouring the combination (67.9% vs 56%, HR 0.69, p = 0.3001), while DASH (Gawrieh 2024, N = 147; anakinra + zinc vs prednisone) was stopped early at a prespecified interim analysis because prednisone was superior — 90-day survival 90% vs 70% (HR for death 0.34 [0.14–0.83], p = 0.018) with more acute kidney injury on the combination (45% vs 22%, p = 0.001). The combinations differ and are never averaged into a class claim. Neighbouring severe-AH homes (G-CSF #6539, FMT #6548, larsucosterol #6724) ask different questions and share no anchors.
stamp: SPLIT — FLOOR-RISK: exactly 2 trials, N = 251, with conflicting readings (a non-significant trend favouring the triple combination in 2022; the larger 2024 trial stopped early with its combination significantly worse than prednisone)

title: Alisporivir for chronic hepatitis C — one programme, 3 randomised reports (N = 1,880): higher SVR than peginterferon/ribavirin in every trial, in a programme halted by a regulatory clinical hold and never resumed
question: In patients with chronic hepatitis C — genotype 1 treatment-naïve, genotype 1 prior non-responders/relapsers, or genotype 2/3 treatment-naïve — does alisporivir (400 mg twice daily or 600–1,000 mg daily) added to peginterferon-α/ribavirin, or given interferon-free with ribavirin, improve sustained virological response versus peginterferon/ribavirin alone?
balance: One programme, counted exactly: 3 publications covering 3 trials, N = 1,880. Alisporivir raised SVR over peginterferon/ribavirin in every population tested — SVR12 69% vs 53% in treatment-naïve genotype 1 (ESSENTIAL II, phase 3), superior early response and SVR12 in prior non-responders/relapsers (FUNDAMENTAL), and SVR24 80–85% vs 58% including interferon-free arms in genotype 2/3 (VITAL-1). Two load-bearing flags frame all of it: the era flag — every comparator is the obsolete peginterferon/ribavirin standard — and the hold flag — an FDA partial clinical hold over pancreatitis cases truncated dosing in both genotype 1 trials, the programme was never resumed, and alisporivir (DEB025) was never marketed. The 90% and 92% subset figures in this base are duration-/response-selected readings, never headline rates.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit vs peginterferon/ribavirin) — one programme, 3 trials, peginterferon-era only: dosing was truncated by a regulatory clinical hold in both genotype 1 trials and the drug was never marketed

title: Bemnifosbuvir for COVID-19 — one programme, 3 randomised reports (only 1 a full report; N not documented for the other two): every trial was discontinued early or missed its primary endpoint
question: In patients with COVID-19 — ambulatory adults with mild-to-moderate disease, or hospitalised adults with moderate disease — does oral bemnifosbuvir 550–1,100 mg twice daily for 5 days versus placebo reduce nasopharyngeal viral load, alleviate symptoms faster, or prevent hospitalisation and death?
balance: One programme, composition on the face: 3 randomised reports, of which only one (MOONSONG, phase 2, N = 100) is a full report; the other two survive only as short summary-level reports whose abstracts state no participant count — N not documented for both. The arc is the answer: no trial met its primary endpoint — MOONSONG's viral-load primary was null at both doses (−0.25 and −0.08 log10, p = 0.426 and 0.808), MORNINGSKY (phase 3) was discontinued prematurely and missed its symptom primary, and the hospital study ended early and missed its primary. The one positive clinical claim — fewer hospitalisations in MORNINGSKY — is a secondary reading from a discontinued trial, expressed as a 71% relative risk reduction (labelled relative) with no viral-load reduction. Bemnifosbuvir (AT-527) was never marketed for COVID-19.
stamp: LIKELY (no benefit demonstrated) — one programme, 3 reports (1 full, 2 summary-level with N not documented): every primary endpoint was missed and the phase 3 was discontinued prematurely

title: Naxitamab plus GM-CSF in high-risk neuroblastoma — two disease limbs, never pooled: responses in relapsed/refractory bone/bone-marrow disease (Limb A) and consolidation of complete remission (Limb B, post-protocol-therapy-confounded)
question: In children with high-risk neuroblastoma, does naxitamab (humanised anti-GD2 3F8) plus granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF) (A) produce objective responses in relapsed or primary-refractory disease confined to bone/bone marrow, and (B) consolidate first or later complete remission — and at what infusion-toxicity cost? (Four reports, three registered trials, ONE programme — labelled as such; the two limbs answer different questions and are never pooled.)
balance: Every report is single-arm; there is no randomised naxitamab trial and this shelf says so on its face. The two disease limbs are never pooled. LIMB A — active disease: the pivotal phase 2 trial (74 treated, efficacy population 52, relapsed/refractory disease in bone/bone marrow) found overall response 50% (95% CI 36–64), complete response 38%, with bone-compartment response 58% and bone-marrow response 74%, against naxitamab-related grade 3 hypotension in 58% and grade 3 pain in 54% — the harm bill belongs whole on the face. The MSK primary-refractory cohort (32 patients, stepped-up GM-CSF dosing — a different schedule from the pivotal trial's; schedules are printed as published and never merged) found complete response in 24 of 32 (75%). LIMB B — consolidation of complete remission (single-arm, confounded, labelled): in first complete remission (59 patients, naxitamab + stepped-up GM-CSF plus isotretinoin), 3-year event-free survival was 73% and overall survival 93% — BUT 50 of 59 patients received post-protocol treatment (vaccine and/or difluoromethylornithine), so those survival figures cannot be attributed to naxitamab alone; the load-bearing content of this limb is that the regimen was tolerable and outpatient-deliverable. The second-or-later-CR report (60 patients) carries the same attribution warning in its own conclusion, with post-protocol anti-neuroblastoma vaccine routine. Naxitamab is a humanised 3F8 antibody, FDA-approved for the Limb A setting (relapsed/refractory disease in bone/bone marrow, patients ≥1 year). Cross-point only to pack #7778 (dinutuximab programmes) — a different antibody, schedule and evidence shape; the two anti-GD2 shelves are never presented as a class comparison.
stamp: SPLIT — by disease limb, never pooled: Limb A (relapsed/refractory bone/bone-marrow disease) POSSIBLE (benefit — single-arm response data only: overall response 50%, complete response 38% in the pivotal trial; complete response 75% in the primary-refractory cohort); Limb B (consolidation of complete remission) MAYBE (weak evidence) — survival figures are descriptive and confounded by post-protocol vaccine and/or difluoromethylornithine in 50 of 59 first-CR patients, so they cannot be attributed to naxitamab alone. No randomised naxitamab trial exists. Grade 3 hypotension 58% and pain 54% in the pivotal trial

title: Dichlorphenamide for prevention of attacks in primary periodic paralysis — the only randomised evidence in the disease: Class I evidence in hypokalemic paralysis, an underpowered non-significant trial in hyperkalemic paralysis
question: In patients with primary (hereditary) periodic paralysis, does the carbonic-anhydrase inhibitor dichlorphenamide reduce the frequency and severity of paralytic attacks versus placebo — in hypokalemic periodic paralysis, in hyperkalemic / potassium-sensitive periodic paralysis, and over one year of continued treatment?
balance: The hypokalemic limb is the load-bearing evidence — two randomised programmes, concordant. In the 2000 Working Group crossovers (hypokalemic N = 42; potassium-sensitive N = 31), 11 of the 13 hypokalemic patients who showed an endpoint preference preferred dichlorphenamide, and dichlorphenamide significantly reduced attack rates in the potassium-sensitive trial and in the hypokalemic subjects. In the 2016 parallel trials (hypokalemic N = 44; hyperkalemic N = 21), the median attack rate in hypokalemic patients was 0.3 vs 2.4 attacks/week on placebo (P = 0.02), with a better SF-36 Physical Component Summary change (treatment effect 7.29 points, 95% CI 2.26–12.32, P = 0.006). The hyperkalemic limb must never be averaged into a class claim: the 2016 median attack rate was 0.9 vs 4.8 but NOT significant (P = 0.10), and the paper's own classification — Class I evidence for the hypokalemic limb, insufficient precision for the hyperkalemic limb — is carried exactly. The one-year open-label extension (63 completers of the double-blind phase; 47 completed 61 weeks) showed sustained median attack-rate falls (−1.00 continuous, P < 0.0001; −0.63 after switching from placebo, P = 0.01). The adolescent analysis rests on 7 adolescents and is supportive only. Attack frequency is a patient-counted outcome in all trials. Harms: paresthesia (47% vs 14%) and confusion (19% vs 7%); in the extension, paresthesia and cognition-related events typically appeared in the first month and dose reductions frequently resolved them. Dichlorphenamide is FDA-approved for primary periodic paralysis (2015, on the 2016 programme); the 2000 trials are of the older Daranide formulation era — doses as published. Acetazolamide has no randomised report in this base and is not a limb of this shelf.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for hypokalemic periodic paralysis, supported by two randomised programmes (2000 crossovers; 2016 parallel trials, median attack rate 0.3 vs 2.4 attacks/week, P = 0.02); the hyperkalemic limb is SPLIT within this shelf (significant in the 2000 potassium-sensitive crossover; NOT significant in the 2016 trial, P = 0.10, N = 21 — the paper's own classification is Class I evidence for hypokalemic, insufficient precision for hyperkalemic). Commonest harms: paresthesia 47% vs 14% and confusion 19% vs 7% on dichlorphenamide vs placebo

title: Mexiletine for nondystrophic myotonia, lamotrigine as the alternative sodium-channel blocker, and their head-to-head trial — both drugs beat placebo in small crossovers; lamotrigine's non-inferiority to mexiletine was NOT concluded
question: In patients with genetically confirmed nondystrophic myotonia (myotonia congenita, paramyotonia congenita; CLCN1/SCN4A), do the sodium-channel blockers mexiletine and lamotrigine reduce myotonia stiffness versus placebo — and is lamotrigine non-inferior to mexiletine head-to-head?
balance: Mexiletine's placebo-controlled base is three reports totalling 114 patients: the 2012 JAMA crossover (59 patients; stiffness improved, reported by period because of a treatment-by-period interaction), the 2018 aggregated N-of-1 series (30 enrolled, 27 completed; clinically meaningful effect in 24 of 27 completers, 100% posterior probability of a meaningful group effect), and MYOMEX (25 patients; stiffness VAS 71.0 → 16.0 on mexiletine vs 81.0 → 78.0 on placebo, P < 0.001). Lamotrigine's own crossover (26 included, 22 completed) improved the Myotonic Behaviour Scale by 1.3 points vs 0.2 on placebo (estimated effect 1.0, 95% CI 0.5–1.5; number needed to treat 2.6), with one withdrawal for allergic reaction — lamotrigine requires slow titration, printed here. The 2024 head-to-head phase 3 crossover (60 randomised, 53 in the primary analysis) found mean IVR stiffness 2.54 on mexiletine vs 2.77 on lamotrigine (difference −0.23, −0.63 to 0.17) and the trialists were UNABLE to conclude non-inferiority — printed exactly as they stated it; the shelf's balance is 'both drugs beat placebo in small crossovers; they have never been shown equivalent.' Mexiletine is a class IB antiarrhythmic: the cardiac caution (and the diabetic-neuropathy row's 'no heart disease' restriction) carries over onto this face, even though the myotonia trials report no serious cardiac signal at these Ns and durations — gastrointestinal effects were the commonest harm (9 vs 1 in 2012; 70% vs 3% in the N-of-1 series, with one serious allergic skin reaction). Cross-points to packs #4247 (ALS cramps), #5382 (long-QT) and #7725 (painful diabetic neuropathy) are prose only — different questions, no shared anchors.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — mexiletine and lamotrigine each reduced stiffness versus placebo in small randomised crossovers (total placebo-controlled mexiletine N = 114 across three reports, in a rare disease where these are the only randomised reports); the head-to-head trial did NOT conclude lamotrigine non-inferior to mexiletine (difference −0.23, 95% CI −0.63 to 0.17, against a 0.5 margin), although improvements from baseline were similar. Mexiletine is a class IB antiarrhythmic — the cardiac caution belongs on the face

title: Zaleplon versus placebo in insomnia (adults and older adults): sleep-latency efficacy over 2–4 weeks without the rebound seen with zolpidem in the same trials — four double-blind reports of ONE 1999–2000 programme, plus one open-label extension labelled as such
question: In adults — including older adults — with insomnia, does zaleplon (5–20 mg, a short-half-life pyrazolopyrimidine hypnotic) shorten sleep latency versus placebo over 2–4 weeks, does it maintain sleep, and what happens on discontinuation? (Four double-blind reports of ONE development programme, 1999–2000, plus one open-label extension labelled as such — counted as a programme, never as four independent confirmations.)
balance: One development programme (1999–2000), four double-blind reports, counted as a programme — never as four independent confirmations. The efficacy signal is sleep latency: in the adult pivotal (615 outpatients, 28 nights), median latency was significantly lower than placebo on zaleplon 10 and 20 mg in all 4 weeks (5 mg, weeks 1–3); the adult confirmatory (Fry et al. — sample size NOT documented in its abstract, labelled as such on its card) found latency shorter at week 1 on all doses, persisting to week 4 only at 20 mg. Maintenance is weak, exactly as the drug's ~1-hour half-life predicts: sleep duration increased only at 20 mg in adults and only in week 1 at 10 mg in the older-adult pivotal (549 patients ≥65, 14 nights). Discontinuation is the programme's distinguishing claim and is printed whole, including its internal contrast: no rebound insomnia or withdrawal after zaleplon in the adult pivotal, the adult confirmatory and the older-adult pivotal — whereas the zolpidem comparator arms in the same trials showed significantly more withdrawal symptoms and rebound indications — BUT the older-adult confirmatory reports a weak indication of rebound after the 10 mg dose, which qualifies the cleaner picture and prints beside it. Every efficacy outcome is subjective (morning questionnaires); no report rests on polysomnography — printed on the face. Treatment durations are 2–4 weeks; the only long-term data are the 1-year open-label extension in older patients, which itself states placebo-controlled trials are needed. These trials predate the modern class safety record for Z-drugs (complex sleep behaviours, next-day impairment warnings): no 1999–2000 adverse-event table on this shelf stands as a current safety statement.
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit — sleep latency only, over 2–4 weeks, on subjective questionnaire outcomes; one programme, 1999–2000, never four independent confirmations) — sleep-duration benefit was narrow (20 mg in adults; week 1 only at 10 mg in older adults); no rebound or withdrawal after zaleplon in three reports, against a weak rebound indication after the 10 mg dose in the fourth; the zolpidem arms of the same trials showed rebound/withdrawal. The 1999–2000 adverse-event tables predate the modern Z-drug class safety record and are not a current safety statement

title: Wells score for suspected deep-vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism (two related rules, figures never merged): derivation strata of 3% / 17% / 75% in DVT, high-stratum likelihood ratio 5.2 and low-stratum 0.25, and a 1.2% residual DVT probability for 'unlikely' plus negative D-dimer
question: In adults with suspected deep-vein thrombosis or suspected pulmonary embolism, how well does the Wells score (the two related clinical prediction rules — for DVT: prior VTE, active cancer, immobilisation/paralysis, localised tenderness, whole-leg and calf swelling, pitting oedema, collateral veins, and an alternative diagnosis at least as likely; for PE: the DVT items plus prior PE, tachycardia, haemoptysis and clinical signs of DVT, with PE judged the top diagnosis) stratify the probability of disease — what prevalence did the derivation cohort find in each stratum, what likelihood ratios do the meta-analyses give for the high and low strata in DVT, what happens to the residual probability when an 'unlikely' Wells score is combined with a negative D-dimer in the individual-patient-data meta-analyses of each condition, and how does the score's accuracy compare with the revised Geneva score in PE — including where the two-tier version underperforms the three-tier version?
balance: The two limbs are different rules sharing a name and an originator; every figure prints with its limb (DVT vs PE) and its version (two-tier vs three-tier) attached, and the limbs are never merged. DVT limb: the 1997 derivation/management cohort (593 outpatients; programme-labelled — the originators' own report) found DVT in 3% of low, 17% of moderate and 75% of high pretest-probability patients — 1997 Canadian outpatient figures, printed with their setting. The 2005 meta-analysis found individual features weak (best rule-in features malignancy, likelihood ratio 2.71, and previous DVT, 2.25 — labelled as likelihood ratios) while the Wells score stratified into high (LR 5.2) and low (LR 0.25) probability groups. The 2014 individual-patient-data meta-analysis (13 studies, 10,002 outpatients) found an unlikely Wells score (≤1) plus a negative D-dimer carried a DVT probability of 1.2% (95% CI 0.7–1.8), a combination occurring in 29% of patients — with the cancer penalty printed beside the headline: in patients with cancer the combination occurred in only 9% and carried a 2.2% probability, and the authors judge it neither safe nor efficient in cancer. The one randomised anchor (1,096 outpatients) tests a D-dimer STRATEGY built on the score, not the score itself: among patients ruled out initially, 3-month confirmed VTE was 0.4% (D-dimer strategy) vs 1.4% (ultrasound-alone control), and D-dimer testing cut ultrasound use from 1.34 to 0.78 tests per patient. PE limb: the 2016 meta-analysis gave Wells a weighted AUC of 0.778 vs revised Geneva 0.693; the 2016 IPD meta-analysis (7,268 patients) found imaging could be withheld in 28% (fixed D-dimer threshold) rising to 33% (age-adjusted), with failure rates below 3% in every subgroup; the 2025 comparative network meta-analysis (40 studies, 37,027 patients) found three-tier Wells and three-tier revised Geneva similar for ruling out PE (negative likelihood ratios 0.34 vs 0.39, labelled as such) while the two-tier Wells underperformed in every aspect (negative LR 0.56). No card on this shelf implies Wells-guided pathways improve outcomes — no anchor tests that.
stamp: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — established for probability stratification in both limbs (GAP-E): DVT derivation prevalences 3% (low) / 17% (moderate) / 75% (high); meta-analytic likelihood ratios 5.2 (high) and 0.25 (low), labelled as likelihood ratios; 'unlikely' Wells plus negative D-dimer leaves a 1.2% DVT probability (2.2% in cancer, where the combination is neither safe nor efficient). In PE, Wells' weighted AUC 0.778 exceeded revised Geneva's 0.693 in one meta-analysis, three-tier Wells and three-tier Geneva performed similarly for rule-out in the 2025 network meta-analysis, and the TWO-tier Wells underperformed in every aspect. This is a prediction-accuracy shelf, not a treatment shelf

title: Bedside swallow screening after surgery: a structured targeted screen reached 90% sensitivity / 83% specificity after liver transplantation, while the unstructured clinical examination missed silent aspiration in 27% of lung-transplant patients who looked normal at the bedside
question: After surgery, how well do bedside swallow screens and bedside clinical swallowing examinations detect postoperative dysphagia and aspiration against instrumental evaluation (fiberoptic endoscopic evaluation of swallowing or videofluoroscopy) — what sensitivity and specificity did a targeted bedside swallow screen achieve after liver transplantation, how discriminative is the patient-reported EAT-10 after anterior cervical spine surgery, and how much aspiration does the unstructured clinical bedside examination miss after lung transplantation, where silent aspiration predominates?
balance: This is a screening-accuracy shelf, not a treatment shelf: no card may imply screen-guided postoperative feeding pathways improve pneumonia or mortality outcomes — no anchor tests that. The headline is the instrument gradient. At the structured end, a targeted bedside swallow screen (mental status, laryngeal sensation/elevation, progressively larger water volumes — a screen previously validated by the same programme after cardiac surgery, programme-labelled) achieved 90% sensitivity and 83% specificity against FEES in 50 liver-transplant patients screened within 24 hours of extubation, with 40% failing the screen and 90% of failures confirmed dysphagic. In the middle, the patient-reported EAT-10 after anterior cervical spine surgery discriminated only moderately (AUC 0.68; at a cut score of ≥7, sensitivity 72.7%, specificity 64.3%, PPV 51.6%, NPV 81.8%) in a 64-patient prospective study where instrumentally confirmed dysphagia doubled from 15.6% to 34.4% after surgery. At the unstructured end, the clinical bedside examination demonstrably misses silent aspiration after lung transplantation: in 321 referred patients (297 completing evaluation), clinical signs were apparent in 54% but instrumental testing found deep penetration or aspiration in 67%, and 27% had an entirely normal clinical examination yet deep penetration or aspiration; in the earlier 263-recipient series, provocative evaluation was positive in 70.5% of those tested, aspiration occurred in 63.8% of positive evaluations, and 77.6% of aspirations were clinically silent. Both lung-transplant series are retrospective and subject to referral selection (patients referred for evaluation) — printed on their cards. The fifth report's reference standard is another questionnaire (the MD Anderson Dysphagia Inventory), not an instrumental standard: its AUCs (>0.9 for the HSS-Dysphagia subscale) are never printed beside the FEES-referenced figures without that distinction. The evidence comes from transplant and anterior cervical populations only; no verified screen-validation report in general, cardiac or abdominal surgical populations was carried through — no figure may be generalised across operations. Distinct from the GUSS (stroke/ICU) and Yale Swallow Protocol (general hospital/TBI) shelves: no anchor is shared.
stamp: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — split by instrument (GAP-E): a structured targeted bedside screen performed well in one 50-patient liver-transplant series (sensitivity 90%, specificity 83% against FEES); the patient-reported EAT-10 discriminated only moderately after anterior cervical spine surgery (AUC 0.68; at ≥7, sensitivity 72.7% / specificity 64.3%); the unstructured clinical bedside examination is NOT ESTABLISHED as sensitive enough — after lung transplantation, 27% of referred patients had an entirely normal clinical examination yet deep penetration or aspiration instrumentally, and 77.6% of aspirations were clinically silent. No figure generalises across operations

title: NIH Stroke Scale reliability between raters: a respectable total-score ICC of 0.85 beside a clinically material spread — total scores varied by four or more points in 64% of certification vignettes, and the ataxia item's kappa was 0.15
question: At the bedside, how reliable is the NIH Stroke Scale (NIHSS — 15 items: consciousness, gaze, visual fields, facial palsy, arm and leg motor, ataxia, sensory, language, dysarthria, extinction/inattention) between raters — what inter-rater agreement did its first reliability study find item by item, how wide is the spread of total scores when thousands of clinicians rate the same standardised patients for certification, and which items drive the disagreement?
balance: This is a measurement-reliability shelf, not a prognostic or treatment shelf: no card may convert reliability data into claims about thrombolysis or thrombectomy thresholds. The content is the split. On one side, the total score looks respectable: in the DVD certification validation among general users (8,214 raters), the intraclass correlation coefficient for the total score was 0.85 (95% CI 0.72–0.90), with 11 of 15 items showing moderate agreement and 2 excellent. On the other side, the spread is clinically material: in the large videotape certification analysis (7,405 unique raters, 38,148 item responses), total scores for 7 of 11 patients (64%) had a 5th-to-95th percentile spread of four or more points; the aphasia (kappa 0.60) and facial palsy (0.65) items contributed most to the variance; and taking the examination repeatedly did not improve agreement. Item-level weakness is specific: kappas ranged from 0.15 (ataxia — poor) to 0.81 (level-of-consciousness commands). The first reliability study (1989; 20 stroke patients, each rated by a pair of four clinical stroke fellows — its N prints on the face) found moderate-to-substantial agreement for 9 of 13 items; its abstract reports agreement qualitatively by item, and no pooled kappa may be printed from it. Two of the three anchors measure scoring of videotaped/DVD standardised patients, not live bedside examinations, and print as such — live-examination reliability could differ in either direction and is not what these numbers measure.
stamp: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — reliability split between the total score and its items (GAP-E): total-score intraclass correlation 0.85 (95% CI 0.72–0.90) in the DVD certification validation, BUT the 5th-to-95th percentile spread of total scores was four or more points for 7 of 11 videotaped patients (64%), item kappas ranged from 0.15 (ataxia) to 0.81 (level-of-consciousness commands), and repeat examination did not improve agreement. Two of the three anchors score videotaped/DVD standardised patients, not live bedside examinations; the derivation-era study rated 20 patients. No card may print the ICC without the spread

title: FOUR score versus Glasgow Coma Scale in impaired consciousness: excellent inter-rater reliability for both (weighted kappa 0.88 vs 0.86) and pooled prognostic parity in traumatic brain injury (AUC 0.91 vs 0.92 for mortality) — FOUR's advantage is content the GCS cannot express, not superior accuracy
question: In patients with impaired consciousness, how well does the FOUR score (Full Outline of UnResponsiveness — eye, motor, brainstem reflexes and respiration, each 0–4, replacing the Glasgow Coma Scale's verbal component) perform against the Glasgow Coma Scale — what inter-rater reliability did its emergency-department validation by non-neurology staff show, how does it behave in spontaneous subarachnoid haemorrhage, and what pooled accuracy do the two scores deliver for predicting death and unfavourable outcome after traumatic brain injury?
balance: This is a measurement/prognostic-accuracy shelf, not a treatment shelf. The pooled evidence shows parity, and no card may print a FOUR-superiority claim: in the traumatic-brain-injury meta-analysis (20 articles, 2,083 patients), AUC for in-hospital mortality was 0.91 (95% CI 0.88–0.93) for FOUR and 0.92 for GCS, and for unfavourable outcome 0.93 (0.91–0.95) vs 0.95 (0.93–0.97), with diagnostic odds ratios labelled as such in the source (45.16 vs 44.51 for mortality). One figure binds the build: the meta-analysis abstract prints the GCS mortality AUC confidence interval as 0.80–0.91, which does not contain its own point estimate (0.92) — that interval is omitted on this shelf, never printed as fetched. The broader systematic review (37 studies) found FOUR prognosticated in-hospital mortality well to excellently in most studies (AUC >0.80) and poor functional outcome at AUC 0.80–0.90, with some evidence its motor and eye components out-prognosticate its brainstem components. The primary validations are small and their Ns print: the emergency-department validation (69 patients, rated by ED physicians, residents and nurses) found excellent inter-rater reliability for both scores (weighted kappa 0.88 FOUR, 0.86 GCS) with both predicting outcome; the subarachnoid-haemorrhage study (72 ICU patients) reports significant correlations with Hunt–Hess and Fisher stage and 1-month recovery prediction, with reliability reported qualitatively in its abstract — no numeric kappa may be printed from it. FOUR's claimed advantage is content the GCS cannot express — brainstem reflexes, respiratory pattern, usability in intubated patients — not superior pooled accuracy, and the shelf is written that way. Distinct from the GCS-reliability shelf (pack #7784): that shelf asks how reliably the GCS itself is scored; here the GCS is the comparator and no anchor is shared.
stamp: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — prognostic accuracy established at parity with the GCS; superiority NOT ESTABLISHED (GAP-E): traumatic-brain-injury meta-analysis AUCs 0.91 (FOUR) vs 0.92 (GCS) for in-hospital mortality and 0.93 vs 0.95 for unfavourable outcome, with diagnostic odds ratios labelled as such; inter-rater reliability excellent for both in the ED validation (weighted kappa 0.88 vs 0.86, N = 69). The two primary validations are small (N = 69 and N = 72) and their Ns print; the subarachnoid study's reliability is qualitative in its abstract and no numeric kappa is printed from it

title: MoCA and MMSE at the bedside: MoCA's conventional cut-off of 26 buys sensitivity of 0.94 or more at specificity of 0.60 or less for dementia, MCI accuracy maximises at cut-offs 23–25, and a single MMSE does not identify which patients with MCI will convert to dementia
question: In older adults, how accurately do the two standard bedside cognitive screens — the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA, 30 points) and the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE, 30 points) — detect mild cognitive impairment and dementia against clinical diagnostic criteria: what pooled sensitivity and specificity does MoCA deliver for MCI at cut-offs below the conventional 26, what did the Cochrane review find for MoCA in dementia at that threshold, what pooled accuracy does MMSE achieve for dementia in community settings at cut-offs 24 and 25, and how poorly does a single MMSE predict which patients with MCI will convert to dementia?
balance: This shelf rests on 4 syntheses whose primary-study sets overlap — the count prints as 4 syntheses, not 4 independent cohorts. It is a diagnostic-accuracy shelf, not a treatment shelf: no card may imply screen-triggered pathways improve outcomes. The cut-off dependence is the content. For MCI, the 2023 meta-analysis (13 studies, 2,158 participants, 44% with MCI) found accuracy maximised below the conventional 26: at cut-off <25 sensitivity was 83.8% (95% CI 75.6–89.6) and specificity 70.8% (62.1–78.3); at <24, 79.5% / 83.7%; at <23, 73.5% / 91.3% — with risk of bias high or unclear in most domains, printed. For dementia, the Cochrane MoCA review (7 studies, 9,422 participants) could not meta-analyse because of methodological variation; in the four studies using the recommended threshold of 26, sensitivity was 0.94 or more but specificity 0.60 or less, and the reviewers judged the evidence insufficient to recommend on clinical utility. For dementia in community settings, the Cochrane MMSE review pooled sensitivity 0.85 (95% CI 0.74–0.92) / specificity 0.90 (0.82–0.95) at cut-off 24 and 0.87 (0.78–0.93) / 0.82 (0.65–0.92) at cut-off 25 — and education adjustment moved the estimates materially (in seven adjusted studies, sensitivity 0.97 / specificity 0.70), which prints where figures are given. For prognosis, the Cochrane conversion review (11 studies, 1,569 patients with MCI) found baseline MMSE accuracy for conversion ranging across studies from sensitivity 23% to 76% and specificity 40% to 94%, with no evidence supporting MMSE as a stand-alone single-administration test for identifying who will convert. No single sensitivity/specificity pair may be printed without its cut-off, target condition (MCI vs dementia) and setting attached. Distinct from the Mini-Cog postoperative-delirium shelf and the delirium-instrument shelves (CAM-ICU, 4AT, 3D-CAM, Nu-DESC), which detect an acute confusional state, not chronic cognitive impairment.
stamp: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — cut-off-dependent, on 4 overlapping syntheses counted as syntheses (GAP-E): MoCA for MCI maximises accuracy at cut-offs <23 to <25 (at <25, sensitivity 83.8% / specificity 70.8%); MoCA for dementia at the recommended threshold of 26 had sensitivity 0.94 or more but specificity 0.60 or less, with the Cochrane reviewers judging the evidence insufficient on clinical utility; MMSE for dementia in community settings pooled at sensitivity 0.85 / specificity 0.90 (cut-off 24) and 0.87 / 0.82 (cut-off 25); MMSE prediction of MCI conversion is NOT ESTABLISHED as a stand-alone single-administration test (sensitivity ranged 23–76%, specificity 40–94% across studies). No sensitivity/specificity pair prints without its cut-off, target condition and setting

title: Alvarado score for suspected appendicitis: a strong rule-out at a cut-off of 5 (sensitivity 99%) and a weak rule-in at 7 (specificity 81% overall, 57% in men) — well calibrated in men, over-predicting in women, and not the most accurate score in the 2025 adult meta-analysis
question: In patients with suspected acute appendicitis, how accurately does the Alvarado score (migration of pain, anorexia, nausea/vomiting, right-lower-quadrant tenderness, rebound, fever, leucocytosis and neutrophil shift; 10 points) separate appendicitis from other causes of abdominal pain — what sensitivity does the score achieve at the rule-out cut-off of 5, how poorly does it rule in at 7, what stratum-specific likelihood ratios does the prospective-studies review derive for adults, and how does the score compare with the RIPASA score in the 2025 adult meta-analysis?
balance: This shelf rests on 3 syntheses whose primary-study sets overlap — the count prints as 3 syntheses. It is a diagnostic-accuracy shelf, not a management shelf: no card may imply Alvarado-guided imaging or observation pathways improve outcomes. The asymmetry is the content. Rule-out: at cut-point 5, sensitivity was 99% overall (96% men, 99% women, 99% children) in the 42-study systematic review. Rule-in: at cut-point 7, specificity was only 81% overall — 57% in men, 73% in women, 76% in children. Calibration splits by sex: the score was well calibrated in men across all risk strata but over-predicted the probability of appendicitis in women across all strata (and in children in the intermediate and high groups) — printed beside the headline 99% wherever that figure appears. The prospective-studies review (26 cohort studies avoiding verification bias) gives adult stratum likelihood ratios, labelled as likelihood ratios: 0.03 at <4 points, 0.42 at 4–6 and 3.4 at ≥7; and 0.01 / 0.98 / 6.7 across the <5 / 5–8 / ≥9 bands — with pretest probability differing systematically between the child (~33%) and adult (~66%) study sets, printed with those ratios. The 2025 adult meta-analysis (40 studies) found the RIPASA score most accurate (sensitivity 0.93, specificity 0.81, AUC 0.913, diagnostic odds ratio labelled as such in the source), significantly exceeding the Alvarado and modified Alvarado scores: the Alvarado score is the most studied but not the most accurate, and the shelf says so.
stamp: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — rule-out established, rule-in weak (GAP-E): 3 overlapping syntheses counted as syntheses — at cut-point 5 the score ruled out appendicitis with sensitivity 99% overall (96% in men, 99% in women and in children); at cut-point 7, the recommended rule-in threshold, specificity was only 81% overall and 57% in men, 73% in women and 76% in children; adult stratum likelihood ratios (labelled as such) were 0.03 at <4 points and 3.4 at ≥7. The score is well calibrated in men but over-predicts in women across all risk strata, and in the 2025 adult meta-analysis RIPASA (sensitivity 0.93, specificity 0.81, AUC 0.913) significantly exceeded Alvarado — the most studied score is not the most accurate

title: Centor score for streptococcal pharyngitis in primary care: well calibrated, with a specificity of 0.82 at the antibiotic-consideration threshold of ≥3 — but in low-prevalence settings most score-positive patients do not have streptococcal pharyngitis (post-test probability 12–40% at 5–20% prevalence)
question: In adults presenting with sore throat in primary care, how accurately does the Centor score (fever, tonsillar exudate, tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy, absence of cough — with the McIsaac age adjustment) predict group A streptococcal pharyngitis against throat culture — what pooled specificity does the score achieve at the antibiotic-consideration threshold of ≥3, what probability of streptococcal infection did the 206,870-patient validation find at each score from 0 to 4, and how did the score perform in a low-prevalence Malaysian primary-care cohort?
balance: This is a diagnostic-accuracy shelf, not an antibiotic-prescribing shelf. The synthesis (21 studies, 4,839 adults) found individual signs and symptoms weak — positive likelihood ratios of only 1.45–2.33, labelled as likelihood ratios — while the Centor score as a decision rule at ≥3 achieved specificity 0.82 (95% CI 0.72–0.88) and was well calibrated (no significant difference between predicted and observed case counts across strata). The base-rate warning is part of every figure: at prior prevalences of 5–20%, a score of ≥3 yields a post-test probability of streptococcal pharyngitis of only 12–40% — in low-prevalence settings most score-positive patients do not have streptococcal pharyngitis. The large-scale validation (206,870 patients aged ≥3 at a US retail health chain; rapid-test/culture pathway — its setting prints with its figures) found, among patients ≥15, positivity rising by Centor score: 7% at 0, 12% at 1, 21% at 2, 38% at 3 and 57% at 4 (overall positivity 23% in that age group). The Malaysian primary-care cohort (215 adults, throat-swab culture) shows the low-prevalence extreme: only 6 isolates (2.4%) were group A streptococcus, so its sensitivities at scores 3 and 4 (each 50% — i.e. 3 of 6 cases; specificities 97.6% and 100%) rest on a very small positive count that prints on the face, and no card headlines them.
stamp: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — calibrated but base-rate-limited (GAP-E): pooled specificity 0.82 (95% CI 0.72–0.88) at a score of ≥3, with individual signs shifting probability only slightly (positive likelihood ratios 1.45–2.33, labelled as such); the 206,870-patient retail-clinic validation found group A streptococcus positivity rising from 7% at score 0 to 57% at score 4 (patients ≥15); the Malaysian cohort's estimate rests on only 6 group A isolates (2.4%) — its 50% sensitivity figures rest on 3 of 6 cases and print with that count on the face. This is a diagnostic-accuracy shelf, not an antibiotic-prescribing shelf
