title: HINTS examination for acute vestibular syndrome: 94.0% sensitive and 86.9% specific in the Cochrane pooling — but examiner-dependent, with specificity of 44% in the mixed emergency-physician cohort; the near-perfect figures come from neurologists and neuro-otology specialists
question: In emergency-department patients with acute vestibular syndrome (continuous vertigo with nystagmus, nausea and gait unsteadiness), how accurately does the HINTS examination (head impulse test, nystagmus direction, test of skew — with the hearing limb in HINTS-plus) identify a central cause, principally posterior-circulation stroke, against MRI-based diagnosis — what sensitivity and specificity does the Cochrane review pool for the clinical examination, how much worse is accuracy when the examination is performed by emergency physicians rather than neurologists in the earlier meta-analysis, and how did HINTS compare with the ABCD2 score and with early MRI in the specialist-examined derivation cohort?
balance: Examiner dependence is the headline of this shelf, not a caveat. The Cochrane review (16 studies, 2,024 participants) pooled the clinical HINTS examination at 94.0% sensitivity (95% CI 82.0–98.2) and 86.9% specificity (75.3–93.6) for a central cause, and HINTS-plus at 95.3% sensitive and 72.9% specific — all on LOW-certainty evidence, which prints. The examiner split comes from the 2020 meta-analysis (5 studies, 617 participants): performed by neurologists, HINTS sensitivity was 96.7% (95% CI 93.1–98.5) and specificity 94.8% (91–97.1%); in the mixed emergency-physician/neurologist cohort, sensitivity was 83% and specificity 44% — and the authors conclude HINTS used in isolation by emergency physicians has not been shown accurate enough to rule out stroke. The derivation cohort (190 high-risk acute-vestibular-syndrome patients examined by neuro-otology specialists, MRI in 97.4% — programme-labelled in effect: the derivation group's own centre and specialist examiners) found HINTS sensitivity for stroke 96.5% and specificity 84.4% (positive likelihood ratio 6.19, negative 0.04, labelled as such), far ahead of ABCD2 ≥4 (61.1% / 62.3%), and initial MRI was falsely negative in 14.3% of infarctions — specialist figures, printed with their examiners attached, never as frontline performance. title: DN4 for neuropathic pain: strong discrimination in diabetic polyneuropathy (AUC 0.94) against specificity ≤0.65 in a 729-patient referral cohort — accuracy is population-dependent
question: In patients with chronic pain, how accurately does the DN4 questionnaire (seven interview items and three bedside sensory-examination items; positive at ≥4 of 10) identify neuropathic pain against expert clinical diagnosis — what did its derivation study establish, what accuracy did it achieve in painful diabetic polyneuropathy, and how did it and its questionnaire competitors perform in a 729-patient polyneuropathy-referral cohort judged against NeuPSIG criteria?
balance: The population gradient is the content of this shelf. title: Respiratory-rate measurement accuracy — FLOOR-RISK: exactly 2 reports (a 49-study systematic review + one 130-patient GP study): five structural sources of inaccuracy, and tachypnoea sensitivity 86% when the rate is counted vs 43% when it is estimated
question: At the bedside, how accurate is the manually counted respiratory rate — the vital sign that feeds every early-warning score — what five sources of inaccuracy does the quantitative systematic review of 49 studies identify, and how accurate are general practitioners' respiratory-rate assessments in acutely ill patients when the rate is actually counted for a full period versus estimated? (FLOOR-RISK: basis is exactly 2 reports — 1 systematic review of 49 studies + 1 primary study, N = 130 — printed on the face and carried in the stamp line. A results-free device-agreement protocol, PMID 32706740, is excluded from the base.)
balance: FLOOR-RISK, per the coordinator's ruling: this shelf's basis is exactly 2 reports — one quantitative systematic review of 49 studies and one primary study — printed here, in the title and in the stamp line; the primary study is carded in two labelled slices, never counted twice. The review (Kallioinen 2021) identifies five sources of inaccuracy in manually measured adult respiratory rate: an awareness effect (being observed artefactually lowers the rate), systematic underscoring with shorter counting periods, substantial inter- and intra-observer variability in either direction, value bias (particular values over-represented, suggesting estimation rather than counting) and widespread recording omission, worse in inpatient than in triage contexts; no single pooled error figure is printed from it. The primary study (Loots 2022, 130 acutely ill adults, 14 Dutch out-of-hours GPs, reference measurement) found GPs counted the rate in only 33 patients (25%); when counted, mean difference 0.27 breaths/min (95% CI −5.7 to 6.3) with tachypnoea (≥22/min) sensitivity 86% (57% to 98%), but when estimated, sensitivity fell to 43% (22% to 66%). One apparent third report (PMID 32706740) is a protocol with recruitment not yet started and no results, and is excluded — the exclusion is stated on the face. This is a measurement shelf: no card implies any counting protocol improves patient outcomes.
stamp: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — FLOOR-RISK: exactly 2 reports (1 systematic review of 49 studies + 1 primary study, N = 130): counted respiratory rate accurate on average (mean difference 0.27 breaths/min) with tachypnoea sensitivity 86% (95% CI 57% to 98%) when counted vs 43% (22% to 66%) when estimated; a measurement-accuracy stamp, not a treatment stamp

title: Sedation-Agitation Scale (SAS) reliability and validity in critically ill adults: weighted kappa 0.92 at validation, 0.85–0.87 in inexperienced nurses' hands, psychometric score 19/20 — agitation limb under-validated
question: In critically ill adults, how reliable and valid is the Sedation-Agitation Scale (SAS / Riker scale — seven levels from 1, unarousable, through 4, calm and cooperative, to 7, dangerous agitation) as the bedside measure of sedation and agitation — what inter-rater reliability did its prospective validation show against the Ramsay and Harris scales, how reliably do ICU nurses with no prior experience of the scale score it against investigators, and where does the scale rank in the systematic psychometric analysis of eleven subjective sedation scales?
balance: A measurement shelf, not a sedation-strategy shelf: no card implies SAS-guided sedation improves outcomes. The Sedation-Agitation Scale (SAS / Riker scale — 1 unarousable, 4 calm and cooperative, 7 dangerous agitation) was prospectively validated by its originators (programme-labelled) in 45 ICU patients examined 69 times: inter-rater weighted kappa 0.92, correlations with the Ramsay (r² = 0.83) and Harris (r² = 0.86) scales, and three agitation categories where Ramsay used one. ICU nurses with no prior experience of the scale scored it against investigators at weighted kappa 0.85–0.87 (investigators 0.93 between themselves) in 60 medical-cardiac ICU patients, and SAS tracked the sedation visual-analogue scale (ρ = −0.77) — but agitation validity could not be determined in that study because few agitated patients were observed, and that under-validation prints on the face. The 2013 SCCM-guideline psychometric analysis of 11 subjective sedation scales scored SAS 19/20 ('very good'), second only to RASS (19.5), with Ramsay moderate at 13.2. All validity evidence here is construct validity against other subjective scales, not against a physiological standard.
stamp: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — reliability established (inter-rater weighted kappa 0.92 in the originators' validation; 0.85–0.87 for nurses with no prior experience of the scale), psychometric rank second of 11 scales (19/20, behind RASS 19.5); agitation validity under-determined in the nurse study — a measurement stamp, not a sedation-strategy stamp

title: Modified Early Warning Score (MEWS) prognostic accuracy: derivation odds ratios at ≥5, AUC 0.83 in a Chinese ED (cut-off 3.5), AUROC 0.76 vs NEWS 0.805 in a Zambian surgical cohort — cut-offs not portable
question: In acutely admitted hospital patients, how well does the Modified Early Warning Score (MEWS — systolic blood pressure, heart rate, respiratory rate, temperature and AVPU consciousness, each scored 0–3) identify patients who will die or need higher-level care — what odds of death and intensive-care admission did its derivation cohort show at a score of 5 or more, what discrimination and cut-off did a prospective Chinese emergency-department validation find, and how did MEWS compare with NEWS for 30-day mortality in a Zambian surgical cohort?
balance: A prognostic-accuracy shelf, not an intervention shelf: no card implies MEWS-triggered escalation pathways improve outcomes. The Modified Early Warning Score (systolic blood pressure, heart rate, respiratory rate, temperature and AVPU consciousness, each scored 0–3) was derived by its own development group (programme-labelled) in 709 medical emergency admissions: a score of 5 or more carried odds ratios (relative measures, unadjusted, from a single 2000 admissions unit) of 5.4 for death (95% CI 2.8–10.7), 10.9 for ICU admission (2.2–55.6) and 3.3 for HDU admission (1.2–9.2). A prospective Chinese emergency-department validation (383 patients, triage categories 1–3) found AUC 0.83 (0.786–0.881) for in-hospital mortality at a locally derived cut-off of 3.5 (sensitivity 87%, specificity 66%) — a different cut-off from derivation, printed with its cohort: cut-offs are not portable. In a Zambian surgical cohort (254 patients), MEWS AUROC for 30-day mortality was 0.76 (0.63–0.88) against NEWS 0.805 (0.688–0.92) in the same patients — a single small cohort whose difference is not a settled hierarchy. MEWS remains in use in many low-resource settings, which the Zambian cohort documents.
stamp: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — moderate discrimination across three cohorts: derivation odds ratios at ≥5 (death 5.4, ICU 10.9 — relative measures, wide intervals), AUC 0.83 in a Chinese ED at a locally derived 3.5 cut-off, AUROC 0.76 vs NEWS 0.805 in a Zambian surgical cohort; cut-offs not portable — a prognostic-accuracy stamp, not an intervention stamp

title: Antral follicle count age nomograms (PHYS, 4 datasets, all fertility-clinic populations): decline ≈0.4–0.8 follicles/year with published age centiles — not norms for unselected women
question: Across a woman's reproductive life, how does the antral follicle count (the number of 2–10 mm follicles visible on transvaginal ultrasound in the early follicular phase) decline with age in normally cycling and fertility-clinic populations — what annual rate of decline and what age-specific centiles (5th to 95th, or 3rd to 97th) do the four nomogram datasets report, and how does the decline differ between women attending fertility services and women with regular cycles? (PHYSIOLOGY: every dataset is a fertility-clinic or subfertile population — flagged on the face; textbook framing only, the shelf rests on these datasets.)
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — no intervention stamp applies. Four nomogram datasets, and every one is a fertility-clinic or subfertile population (the nearest to a general sample, La Marca 2011, mixes infertile women with oocyte donors) — no figure on this shelf may be presented as a norm for unselected women, and the population prints on every figure. The decline is consistent in direction and roughly linear: median −0.4 follicles/year in 362 regularly cycling women (5th–95th centiles per year of age, 24–50); a biphasic decline in 1,866 infertile McGill patients without polycystic ovaries (3rd–97th percentiles; the polycystic-ovary exclusion is this dataset's, unspecified in others); −0.6 to −0.8/year under 45 in 2,495 Arabian Peninsula fertility-centre women (median AFC 11 overall); and −0.79/year in 1,009 subfertile Singaporean Chinese women (LMS nomograms). Counting technique (2D vs 3D ultrasound, follicle diameter band) is not standardised across the four datasets and no centile is merged across them. Framing: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED for the age-decline rate and centile method in regularly cycling / clinic populations; PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING for transport to unselected populations.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED for the age-decline rate (≈0.4–0.8 follicles/year) and the centile method in regularly cycling / fertility-clinic populations / EMERGING for transport to unselected populations — 4 datasets, all clinic populations, centiles never merged

title: Total serum IgE distribution in healthy non-atopic adults (PHYS, 4 datasets, 1984–2001 PRIST/CAP era): geometric means 12.1–43.7 across populations, 95% range up to 3.2–602.5 kU/L — population- and assay-dependent, no single normal figure
question: What is the distribution of total serum IgE in healthy non-atopic adults — what geometric mean and upper reference limit do the population datasets report, and how wide is the spread between populations and between men and women? (PHYSIOLOGY: 1984–2001 PRIST/CAP assay era prints on the face; values are log-normally distributed, so geometric means print.)
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — no intervention stamp applies. Four population datasets, 1984–2001, spanning PRIST- and CAP-era methods — the assay era prints on the face, because absolute values are not interchangeable across assay generations and each dataset's value prints with its method era and population. The distribution is wide and log-normal (geometric means print, never arithmetic): a 1984 Canadian reference group (from 1,814 rural white adults; reference-group N not documented in the abstract) had mean IgE 12.1 U/mL with an upper normal limit of 87.3 U/mL; non-atopic Greek adults (1,187) had geometric means of 38 IU/mL (men) and 29.3 IU/mL (women); Italian 'normals' (558 of 1,905, a mixed-age dataset whose adult stratum is the limb used here) had adult geometric means of 29 kU/L (men) and 19 kU/L (women); and 542 non-atopic young Kuwaiti adults (CAP assay) had a geometric mean of 43.7 kU/L with a 95% range of 3.2–602.5 kU/L. The width of the distribution is the content: no single 'normal IgE' figure is printed. Atopy definitions differ across datasets (questionnaire/history, prick, skin-test based) and print. Framing: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (population- and assay-dependence of the distribution).
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (population- and assay-dependence of the total IgE distribution): geometric means 12.1–43.7 units/mL across four 1984–2001 PRIST/CAP-era datasets, one 95% range spanning 3.2–602.5 kU/L — no single 'normal IgE' figure

title: Platelet indices reference intervals in healthy adults (PHYS, 4 datasets): MPV intervals are analyser-bound — 7.2–11.7 fL (CELL-DYN) vs 9.6–13.1 and 9.20–13.30 fL (Sysmex) — never a single merged range
question: What are the reference intervals for the platelet indices — mean platelet volume (MPV), platelet distribution width and the immature platelet fraction — in healthy adults, and how much do the intervals move with the analyser used to derive them? (PHYSIOLOGY: each interval prints with its named analyser and population; no merged interval.)
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — no intervention stamp applies. Analyser dependence is the headline, not a caveat: the MPV lower reference limit moves from 7.2 fL (CELL-DYN 3700 SL, Turkish cohort — final healthy N = 326 after screening 2,298, printed as the final N) to 9.6 fL (Sysmex XE-5000, Danish GESUS, N = 1,674) and 9.20 fL (Sysmex XE-2100, Chinese Han, N = 4,642, with significant regional differences and the published interval excluding Chengdu), with ELSA-Brasil (N = 580; analyser not named in the abstract) at 8.9–11.8 fL. Each interval prints with its named analyser (specific tested platforms named per the standing product rule) and population, and no merged MPV interval is printed. The immature platelet fraction interval (1.3–9.0%) rests on the Danish dataset alone. EDTA dwell time artefactually raises MPV and is uncontrolled in several datasets, which prints. The platelet-count values inside these datasets are background to the built platelet-count physiology and are not re-presented as new. Framing: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED for the existence and analyser-dependence of the intervals; values never transport across platforms.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED for the existence and analyser-dependence of platelet-index intervals: MPV lower limit 7.2 fL (CELL-DYN) vs 9.2–9.6 fL (Sysmex) across 4 datasets — values never transport across platforms

title: Choroidal thickness in healthy eyes (PHYS, 4 Asian datasets): standardised subfoveal thickness 291.2 µm (N = 9,850), thinning ≈2.0 µm/year (N = 27,965), vascularity index far stabler than thickness — absolute values do not transport across populations
question: What is the thickness of the choroid (the vascular layer beneath the retina, measured by enhanced-depth-imaging OCT) in healthy eyes — what population-standardised subfoveal choroidal thickness do the large Asian cohorts report, how fast does it thin with age, and how much less variable is the choroidal vascularity index than thickness itself? (PHYSIOLOGY: platform, segmentation method and axial-length confounding print with each value.)
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — no intervention stamp applies. Four datasets, all Asian populations, with imaging platform and segmentation method printed beside each value (Nidek RS-3000 Advance EDI-OCT in Nagahama; Heidelberg Spectralis EDI in the Indian dataset — specific devices named where the publication gives them, per the standing product rule; the KNHANES and Beijing records' platforms are as published). The age- and sex-standardised subfoveal choroidal thickness in 9,850 Nagahama participants was 291.2 µm, with axial length, age and sex the dominant determinants — axial length is the dominant confounder (highly myopic eyes thin the choroid) and prints beside every population mean. In 27,965 KNHANES participants (a general health-survey sample, not an eye-screened healthy cohort — printed as such) thickness declined at β −2.00 µm/year (right eye), with sex differences at ages 30–49 diminishing later. The choroidal vascularity index in 345 healthy Beijing eyes averaged 65.61 ± 2.33% with a coefficient of variation of 3.55% against 40.30% for thickness itself. The Indian dataset is small (43 individuals, 73 eyes; mean thickness 331.6 ± 63.9 µm) and its N prints on the face. Ethnic composition differs across all four datasets and no value transports across them. Framing: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED for the age decline and the vascularity-index stability; EMERGING for any single population's absolute thickness as a cross-population norm.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED for the age decline (≈−2.0 µm/year) and the choroidal vascularity index's stability (CV 3.55% vs 40.30% for thickness) / EMERGING for any single population's absolute thickness as a cross-population norm — 4 Asian datasets, axial length the dominant confounder

title: Serum zinc and selenium population distributions (PHYS): zinc timing-bound (−15.3 µg/dL by evening in NHANES), selenium geography-bound (means 80.7–100.6 µg/L) with no universal reference value feasible — whole-blood dataset kept matrix-separate
question: What are the population distributions of serum zinc and serum selenium in adults — what means and below-cutoff proportions does the US national survey report (including the effect of time of day of the blood draw), what did the Northern Ireland population surveys find for zinc and copper, and why does the critical review of 36 selenium studies conclude that no universal reference value is feasible? (PHYSIOLOGY: matrix discipline binds — the Czech dataset is whole blood, flagged wherever it appears; µmol/L values carry µg/dL equivalents.)
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — no intervention stamp applies. Matrix discipline binds this shelf: the Czech dataset is whole blood and its values are never printed beside serum values without the matrix attached. Zinc — 3 datasets: NHANES 2011–2014 (4,347 participants aged ≥6 — a mixed child/adult survey whose adult-relevant strata print as such; means 84.9 µg/dL in males and 80.6 µg/dL in females, with afternoon and evening draws lower by 9.7 and 15.3 µg/dL in the adjusted model and 8.6% of males / 8.2% of females aged ≥10 below the suggested cutoffs); two Northern Ireland surveys (≈4,375 adults; 1983–84 zinc 12.1 µmol/L in men, ≈79 µg/dL, and 11.6 µmol/L in women, ≈76 µg/dL, with copper 17.2 / 19.0 µmol/L, ≈109 / ≈121 µg/dL — US-unit equivalents per the standing rule); and 1,216 Czech blood donors whose zinc (median 5,800 µg/L) and selenium (76 µg/L) are whole-blood values. Selenium — 4 datasets + 1 synthesis, counted separately on the face: Barcelona (150 adults; mean 80.7 ± 10 µg/L), Italian regions (4,201 adults; regional means 87–93 µg/L), Tehran (adult mean 100.6 ± 13 µg/L; adult N not separately documented in the abstract, labelled as such), and the whole-blood Czech observation (counted in neither serum set); the TRACY critical review of 36 suitable papers concludes geographical variability makes a single universal reference value infeasible — labelled a synthesis, not a dataset. Diurnal/fasting effects on zinc are large and print beside every mean; soil/dietary geography drives selenium (means 80.7–100.6 µg/L across the serum datasets, i.e. 8.07–10.06 µg/dL) and no universal interval is printed. Framing: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED for population- and matrix-dependence; EMERGING for any single cutoff.
stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED for population-, timing- and matrix-dependence of serum zinc and selenium / EMERGING for any single cutoff — zinc 3 datasets, selenium 4 datasets + 1 synthesis (counted separately), one whole-blood dataset never merged with serum

title: Serum osteocalcin reference values in healthy adults (PHYS, 3 datasets, 3 named assays): medians and intervals differ by platform and menopausal status — no merged interval
question: What are the reference intervals for serum osteocalcin (the osteoblast-derived bone-formation marker) in healthy adults — what medians does the German population study report for men, premenopausal and postmenopausal women on the IDS-iSYS N-Mid assay, what interval does the Chinese male cohort derive on the Elecsys assay, and what interval do healthy premenopausal ASEAN women show on the cobas assay? (PHYSIOLOGY: assay dependence is the headline; no merged interval.)
balance: PHYSIOLOGY — no intervention stamp applies. Assay dependence is the headline: three named assay platforms give three different distributions (medians vs intervals as published), and no merged osteocalcin interval is printed. On the IDS-iSYS N-Mid assay (Study of Health in Pomerania; 1,107 men, 545 premenopausal and 498 postmenopausal women) medians were 15.4 ng/mL in men, 14.4 in premenopausal women and 18.6 in postmenopausal women — menopausal status moves the distribution materially within one study and prints. On the Elecsys assay (COBAS 6000 E601), 2,018 healthy Han Chinese men gave an interval of 12.49–43.94 ng/mL. On the cobas assay, 746 healthy premenopausal ASEAN women gave 9.0–33.0 µg/L (= 9.0–33.0 ng/mL), falling to 3.5–27.0 µg/L when women in their 20s were excluded. The male-only and female-only datasets do not cross-validate each other's sex, which prints. Specific assays are named per the standing product rule. Framing: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED for assay- and menopause-dependence of the distribution.

title: Single-fibre EMG jitter reference values in healthy volunteers (PHYS, 3 small datasets, N = 57/32/19): suggested limits are muscle- and method-specific — 32/49 µs volitional orbicularis oculi, 26/34 µs stimulated tibialis anterior, 21/30 µs stimulated masseter
question: What are the reference values for single-fibre electromyography jitter (mean consecutive difference, MCD — the variability of neuromuscular transmission timing between muscle fibres of one motor unit) in healthy volunteers — what upper limits do the concentric-needle orbicularis oculi and frontalis datasets suggest, what mean jitter and suggested limits does stimulated single-fibre EMG give in the tibialis anterior, and what limits were derived for the stimulated masseter? title: Colestilan (colestimide; MCI-196) for hyperphosphataemia in CKD stage 5 on dialysis
question: In adults with chronic kidney disease stage 5 on dialysis and hyperphosphataemia, does colestilan (colestimide; MCI-196), compared with placebo or sevelamer, lower serum phosphorus?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit on serum phosphorus, a surrogate endpoint) — a phosphorus-surrogate base: every report's primary outcome is serum phosphorus (with LDL cholesterol as a genuine second action of the drug), and no report is powered for death, cardiovascular events or fractures; the binder-mortality question is homed separately at live #295 and is not borrowed here. Four reports: a 642-patient fixed-dose trial (significant phosphorus lowering only at 9 g/day and pooled 12/15 g/day), a 1-year placebo-withdrawal/sevelamer study whose abstract prints no total enrolment N (labelled N not documented for that figure), a 245-patient North American withdrawal trial (169 randomised), and a 120-patient 3-week dose trial. Two of the four reports are withdrawal designs in pre-stabilised populations. Gastrointestinal adverse events were the most common in every report. Colestilan, colestimide and MCI-196 are the same compound's European/North American, Japanese and development names, printed as the publications give them (clarification, not promotion).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit on serum phosphorus, a surrogate endpoint)

title: Ferric citrate as a phosphate binder in patients on dialysis (PARTIAL beside live #1747, which asks the non-dialysis iron question only)
question: In patients on dialysis with hyperphosphataemia, does ferric citrate, compared with placebo, active control or sevelamer, control serum phosphorus — and what does it do to iron indices and intravenous-iron / ESA use?
balance: POSSIBLE — PARTIAL beside live #1747: #1747 asks only whether ferric citrate improves haemoglobin and iron indices in NON-dialysis CKD with iron deficiency; this pack cards only the dialysis phosphate-binder slice (different population, different primary outcome) and pools nothing with #1747. The placebo contrast is a 4-week withdrawal tail: the large phase 3 trial's placebo comparison rests on its final 4-week placebo-control period in completers after a 52-week active-control period, not on a 52-week placebo arm. In that tail ferric citrate controlled phosphorus vs placebo (difference −2.2 ± 0.2 mg/dL, P < 0.001). A 28-day open-label dose-response trial and a 12-week head-to-head vs sevelamer (non-inferior) complete the base. The iron/ESA-sparing findings are prespecified secondaries of the same sponsor programme — real, but one programme's. JTT-751 is ferric citrate's development name as the publication gives it (clarification, not promotion).

title: Polystyrene-sulfonate binders (sodium/calcium polystyrene sulfonate) for hyperkalaemia in CKD
question: In adults with chronic kidney disease (non-dialysis or on haemodialysis) and hyperkalaemia, do the polystyrene-sulfonate binders (sodium polystyrene sulfonate, SPS; calcium polystyrene sulfonate, CPS), compared with placebo, no binder or a newer binder, lower serum potassium?
balance: POSSIBLE (lowers serum potassium) — the composition leads: the only placebo-controlled report in this base enrols 33 outpatients for 7 days in mild hyperkalaemia (between-group difference −1.04 mEq/L). The CPS dose trial (107 patients) has NO placebo or untreated arm; the CPS crossover (58 patients) compares against blank control; and the largest report (120 patients) is a head-to-head the old binder lost on speed (normokalaemia at 6 weeks on SPS vs 2 weeks on sodium zirconium cyclosilicate). Nothing here addresses acute severe hyperkalaemia, hard outcomes, or the historical intestinal-necrosis safety question — no report is powered for it. Dose misprint flagged: the CPS dose trial's abstract prints its doses as 15 or 30 mg/day in its methods line but 15 or 30 g/day in its conclusion; this pack prints g/day, the trial's actual doses. The newer binders' own questions stay homed at live #301 and live #1059 — cross-point only.
stamp: POSSIBLE (lowers serum potassium) — composition on the face: one small 33-patient placebo-controlled trial carries the placebo contrast

title: Androgens (nandrolone decanoate above all) for anaemia in patients on dialysis — a four-drug 1981 comparison and null ESA-era adjuvant trials
question: In patients receiving dialysis with anaemia, do androgens — nandrolone decanoate above all — raise haemoglobin/haematocrit, alone, compared with other androgens, or added to / compared with erythropoietin?
balance: SPLIT — an era-stratified base whose modern limb is null, and the eras lead. The positive reports are pre-ESA (the 1981 NEJM paper — a FOUR-DRUG sequential comparison of nandrolone decanoate, testosterone enanthate, oxymetholone and fluoxymesterone, labelled as such, never a nandrolone-only trial, with completers falling 77 → 56 → 35 across drug periods) or an EPO-comparator trial in men over 50 on CAPD (2002). Both ESA-era adjuvant trials (1992, n = 12; 2005, n = 32) found NO significant added benefit from nandrolone, and both record tolerability failures (acne withdrawals; four women stopping for hirsutism and hepatic dysfunction). No wording may present this as a live alternative to ESAs. The CAPD trial's nutritional findings are cross-pointed to pack #7836 (nandrolone for lean body mass) and are not counted there.
stamp: SPLIT (pre-ESA and EPO-comparator reports positive; both ESA-era adjuvant trials null)

title: Nandrolone decanoate for lean body mass and muscle function in kidney failure (dialysis and predialysis)
question: In patients with kidney failure (on dialysis, or predialysis with malnutrition), does nandrolone decanoate, compared with placebo or conventional treatment (alone or factorially with resistance exercise), increase lean body mass and muscle function?
balance: POSSIBLE (benefit on lean body mass, a surrogate) — a lean-mass surrogate base with one discordant nutritional signal, and the split leads. All three reports are small (29–79 patients, 12 weeks to 6 months) and their shared positive outcome is lean body mass; no report measures falls, hospitalisation or survival. The two dialysis reports are positive (+4.5 vs +1.9 kg vs placebo; +3.1 kg in the factorial trial, where exercise did not significantly increase lean mass). The one predialysis report (malnourished patients, GFR 5–30 mL/min — population labelled, not silently pooled with the dialysis reports) also raised lean mass BUT serum albumin FELL (P < 0.05) — printed on the face beside the dialysis positives, per the binding note. Androgen harms from the sister shelf #7835 (hirsutism, hepatic dysfunction, acne withdrawals) belong on this face too, cross-pointed. The CAPD trial carded at #7835 reported nutritional secondaries and is cross-pointed only, never counted twice (one-home rule).
stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit on lean body mass, a surrogate) — with the predialysis report's albumin fall printed on the face

title: Ataluren for nonsense-mutation cystic fibrosis — one programme, 4 publications covering 4 studies; both phase 3 primaries null
question: In patients aged ≥6 years with cystic fibrosis caused by a nonsense (premature stop-codon) CFTR mutation, does oral ataluren (10, 10 and 20 mg/kg/day in three divided doses) versus placebo over 48 weeks preserve percent-predicted FEV1 and reduce pulmonary exacerbations?
balance: LIKELY (no benefit) — one programme, stated in exactly those terms: 4 publications covering 4 studies, of which only the two phase 3 trials (238 + 279 patients) are clinical-efficacy reports; the two phase 2 reports measure nasal chloride transport, a pharmacodynamic surrogate. The arc is the answer, and it is unusually clean: phase 2 pharmacodynamic activity was real and reproducible, the first phase 3 missed its primary endpoint (difference 3.0%, p = 0.12), its rescue hypothesis was a POST-HOC subgroup of patients not using chronic inhaled tobramycin (5.7% difference, nominal p = 0.0082), and the sponsor then ran the correct experiment — a second phase 3 (ACT CF) restricted to that exact population — which was also null on every endpoint (difference 0.6, p = 0.54). The post-hoc 5.7% figure is never printed without the ACT CF result beside it. Ataluren was never approved for cystic fibrosis and the CF programme was discontinued after ACT CF (clarification, not promotion); its Duchenne muscular dystrophy question stays homed at pack #4316 — cross-point only, under diagnosis-first. A chest-CT secondary analysis of the first phase 3 trial exists in the programme and is never counted as a fifth report.
stamp: LIKELY (no benefit) — one programme, 4 publications covering 4 studies, of which only the two phase 3 trials are clinical-efficacy reports

title: Nemonoxacin versus levofloxacin for community-acquired pneumonia — non-inferiority met in 3 trials, exclusively East Asian base
question: In adults with community-acquired pneumonia, is nemonoxacin 500 mg once daily for 7–14 days — oral, or intravenous — non-inferior to levofloxacin 500 mg once daily for clinical cure at the test-of-cure visit?
balance: POSSIBLE (non-inferior to levofloxacin) — the non-inferiority framing is load-bearing: every trial in this base (3 randomised reports, 1,244 patients randomised as reported) is an active-comparator non-inferiority trial against levofloxacin; there is NO placebo-controlled evidence, and 'non-inferior to levofloxacin' must never be printed as 'effective' without the comparator and design beside it. Setting flag: all three trials were conducted in China/Taiwan populations, and local pneumococcal fluoroquinolone-resistance epidemiology is part of the result. Safety flag: in the intravenous trial, drug-related adverse events were more frequent on nemonoxacin (37.1% vs 22.2%), including QT prolongation and transaminase elevation, mostly mild. Nemonoxacin is a non-fluorinated quinolone, structurally distinct from the fluoroquinolones it was compared against — it must not be merged into a fluoroquinolone class shelf. It is approved in China and Taiwan and is NOT FDA-approved (named for clarification, not promotion). An integrated phase II/III safety summary pools these same trials and is never counted as a fourth report.
stamp: POSSIBLE (non-inferior to levofloxacin for clinical cure) — no placebo-controlled evidence; exclusively East Asian trial base

title: Asimadoline for irritable bowel syndrome pain — FLOOR-RISK: exactly 2 efficacy reports, N = 696, both ITT primaries null
question: In adults with irritable bowel syndrome, does oral asimadoline (0.15–1.0 mg twice daily for 12 weeks, or on-demand dosing for pain episodes) versus placebo increase adequate relief of IBS pain/discomfort or reduce episode pain severity?
balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — FLOOR-RISK, stated exactly: exactly 2 efficacy reports, total N = 696 (596 + 100), and BOTH missed their intention-to-treat primary endpoints. The adequately powered trial (n = 596) was null at every dose in the ITT population; its positive readings live in a diarrhoea-predominant subgroup with at least moderate baseline pain at a single dose (0.5 mg) and in the alternating-IBS subgroup — subgroup readings from a null trial. The on-demand trial (100 women only) was likewise null on its primary, with post-hoc, unadjusted readings pointing in OPPOSITE directions by subtype (mixed IBS p = .003; diarrhoea-predominant p = .065, towards worse). A colonic-distension mechanistic crossover study exists in the programme and is fenced off — a physiology experiment, never counted as an efficacy report; the functional-dyspepsia and healthy-volunteer satiation studies ask different questions and are not counted. No phase 3 programme followed for IBS. Asimadoline is an investigational drug that was never marketed for IBS (clarification, not promotion). The shelf presents a tested-and-failed visceral-analgesic strategy whose mechanistic premise was stronger than its clinical results. It must never be merged with fedotozine into a κ-opioid class row.
stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) — FLOOR-RISK: exactly 2 efficacy reports, N = 696, both intention-to-treat primaries null
